name: Flow Noise
head: Advection Noise, Perlin Flow Noise
body: Flow Noise is a procedural noise function designed to generate time-varying, swirling, and advected textures, primarily for physically-based simulations of fluids and gases. It differs from standard Perlin noise by introducing a time-dependent advection step that displaces the sampling coordinates, creating a sense of continuous flow and swirling motion rather than static, frozen noise patterns. Flow Noise extends the standard Perlin noise framework by applying a velocity field to advect the input coordinates before evaluating the noise function. This creates a coherent, turbulent look suitable for smoke, fire, and water surfaces. Inputs: P \in \mathbb{R}^3: The spatial position to evaluate. t \in \mathbb{R}: The time parameter. scale \in \mathbb{R}: The spatial frequency scale (optional, typically 1.0). speed \in \mathbb{R}: The advection speed factor (optional, typically 1.0). Outputs: f \in \mathbb{R}: The scalar noise value. Data Structures: Flow Noise relies on the underlying Perlin noise implementation. It requires: 1. A permutation table P of size 512 (or 256 extended), containing integers 0..255. 2. A gradient function G(i, x, y, z) that returns a dot product between a pseudo-random gradient vector and the input vector, based on index i. Steps: 1. Compute Advection Velocity: Calculate a velocity vector V using a secondary noise function (often the same Perlin noise function or a derivative-based variant) at position P and time t. This velocity field drives the advection. V = \text{NoiseVelocity}(P, t) The velocity field is typically derived from the curl of a noise field or a scaled noise gradient to ensure incompressibility or coherent flow. In the original Perlin/Neyret formulation, it often involves evaluating noise at offset positions to estimate local flow. 2. Advect Coordinates: Displace the original position P by the velocity vector scaled by time and speed to get the advected position P'. P' = P + V \cdot speed \cdot t In discrete implementations, t might be treated as a small delta or accumulated time. The advection is usually linear for simplicity in real-time rendering. 3. Evaluate Noise: Compute the standard Perlin noise value at the advected position P' with the given scale. f = \text{PerlinNoise}(P' \cdot scale) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def flownoise(P, t, scale=1.0, speed=1.0): # Step 1: Compute velocity field # The velocity is often derived from the noise function itself or its derivatives. # A common approach is to use the noise value at P and a slightly offset P to estimate flow. # For simplicity, we assume a helper function that returns a 3D velocity vector. V = computevelocityfield(P, t) # Step 2: Advect the position Padvected = P + V speed t # Step 3: Evaluate standard Perlin noise at the advected position # This assumes a standard Perlin noise implementation is available result = perlinnoise(Padvected scale) return result def computevelocityfield(P, t): # Specific implementation of velocity field generation varies. # A simple approximation uses the gradient of the noise function. # Or, it may use a separate noise function for the velocity components. # Here we assume a placeholder for the specific velocity calculation method # described in Perlin & Neyret [PN01], which often involves curl noise or # simple advection of coordinates. # Example: Using noise derivatives for velocity (curl noise is more complex) # This is a simplified representation. The original paper details specific # lattice-based velocity calculations. # Return a 3D vector representing local flow return Vector3( noisederivativex(P, t), noisederivativey(P, t), noisederivativez(P, t)) [Note: The exact formula for V in Perlin & Neyret [PN01] involves evaluating the noise function at multiple points to construct a velocity field that advects the coordinates. The pseudocode above abstracts this into computevelocityfield. Implementers should refer to the original paper for the precise lattice-based velocity calculation.] Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, assuming constant-time Perlin noise evaluation. The advection step adds a constant number of noise evaluations (typically 1-3 for velocity estimation). Memory Complexity: O(1) for the permutation table and gradient vectors. Strengths: Produces visually appealing, turbulent, and flowing textures without requiring explicit fluid simulation. It is computationally efficient compared to solving Navier-Stokes equations. Limitations: The flow is not physically accurate (not incompressible unless specifically designed, e.g., curl noise). It can exhibit artifacts if the advection speed is too high relative to the noise frequency. When to use: Ideal for visual effects like smoke, fire, clouds, and water surfaces where a "noisy" flow is desired without full simulation. When not to use: When physical accuracy (mass conservation, vorticity) is critical; use curl noise or actual fluid simulation instead. Flow Noise was introduced by Ken Perlin and Fabrice Neyret in 2001. It was developed to address the need for procedural noise functions that could simulate dynamic, flowing phenomena in computer graphics, such as smoke and fire, which static noise functions could not adequately represent. It builds upon the foundational Perlin noise algorithm [Per85] by adding a temporal advection component. name: Improved Perlin Noise
head: Better Gradient Noise, KKS08 Perlin Noise, Kensler Noise
body: Improved Perlin Noise, introduced by Kensler et al. [KKS08], is a lattice gradient noise function that applies three mutually orthogonal improvements to the original Perlin noise [Per85, Per02] to address axial decorrelation, band-limitation, and surface noise quality. It distinguishes itself from standard Perlin noise by replacing the hash and reconstruction kernels with optimized variants that reduce visual artifacts along axes and provide better spectral control. Improved Perlin Noise computes noise at a point \mathbf{x} by evaluating contributions from the eight nearest vertices of the integer cubic lattice, similar to the parent method. The method consists of three distinct improvements applied to the standard lattice gradient noise framework: 1. Modified Hash and Gradient Table: A modified hash function combined with a separate gradient table is used to improve axial decorrelation. This reduces the directional artifacts (striping) common in standard Perlin noise. 2. Reconstruction Kernel: A different reconstruction kernel is used to improve band-limitation. This kernel shapes the frequency response of the noise. 3. Solid Noise Projection: A projection method is used to improve the quality of noise on 2D surfaces by treating the noise as a solid volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point in space \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^d (typically d=3). Output: A scalar noise value n(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: Gradient Table: A separate table of gradient vectors, distinct from the hash indices. Storage: The method has O(dN) storage requirements, where N is the period and d is the number of dimensions. Steps: 1. Compute the integer lattice coordinates \mathbf{i} = \lfloor \mathbf{x} \rfloor and the fractional part \mathbf{f} = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{i}. 2. For each of the 2^d vertices \mathbf{v} of the unit hypercube containing \mathbf{x}: a. Compute the hash index using the modified hash function. b. Retrieve the gradient vector \mathbf{g} from the separate gradient table using the hash index. c. Compute the vector \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{v} - \mathbf{x}. d. Compute the dot product contribution c = \mathbf{g} \cdot \mathbf{u}. e. Apply the modified reconstruction kernel to weight the contribution. 3. Sum the weighted contributions from all vertices. 4. Normalize the result to the desired range. Formulas: The noise value is computed as a weighted sum of gradient dot products: n(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^{2^d} wk (\mathbf{g}k \cdot \mathbf{u}k) where wk is the weight determined by the reconstruction kernel, \mathbf{g}k is the gradient vector from the table, and \mathbf{u}k is the vector from the sample point to the lattice vertex. Parameters: Period N: Determines the size of the gradient table and hash table. Reconstruction Kernel: Specific kernel parameters are not detailed in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method is generally slower than standard Perlin noise. Precision issues may arise from the separate gradient table lookup and modified hash function if not implemented carefully. Standard 3D implementation of Perlin noise. Noise that varies with a flow field. Time Complexity: Generally slower than Perlin noise. Memory Complexity: O(dN) storage requirements, where N is the period and d is the number of dimensions. Strengths: Improved axial decorrelation, better band-limitation, and improved surface noise quality via solid noise. Supports isotropic filtering. Limitations: Slower performance compared to standard Perlin noise. When to use: When visual quality, particularly regarding axial artifacts and spectral properties, is more important than raw performance. Improved Perlin Noise was presented by Kensler et al. in 2008 [KKS08] as a set of three mutually orthogonal improvements to the original Perlin noise [Per85, Per02]. It is categorized as a lattice gradient noise function. The improvements apply to several lattice gradient noises, not just Perlin noise. name: GPU-Optimized Perlin Noise (BBS)
head: Modified Noise, Blum-Blum-Shub Perlin Noise
body: GPU-Optimized Perlin Noise (BBS), also known as Modified Noise, is a procedural noise function designed for efficient direct computation on GPUs by eliminating permutation table lookups. It replaces the hash lookup with a computable Blum-Blum-Shub (BBS) generator and selects gradients from hypercube corners, enabling dimension reducibility to optimize 3D noise via 2D texture lookups. It differs from Improved Perlin Noise by using corner gradients instead of unit sphere vectors and from 3D Perlin Noise by its specific GPU-oriented hashing and texture optimization strategies. Inputs: A 3D point p = (px, py, pz). Outputs: A scalar noise value N(p) \in [-1, 1]. Data Structures: Modulus M: A composite number M = pq where p and q are large primes. Textures (Optional Optimization): tex2d: Stores 2D noise values N{2D}(x, y). texzgrad: Stores z-gradient values \frac{\partial N}{\partial z} at integer z slices. Alternatively, a single 2-channel texture storing both. Parameters: M: Modulus for BBS generator. Not given in the sources. Precision mode: "Exact" (5-instruction) or "Inexact" (4-instruction) modulo. Steps: 1. Integer and Fractional Parts: Compute integer coordinates i = \lfloor p \rfloor and fractional coordinates f = p - i. Let ix, iy, iz be the integer components and fx, fy, fz be the fractional components. 2. Hash Construction: Define the hash function using the Blum-Blum-Shub generator: \text{hash}(x) = x^2 \bmod M Construct multidimensional hashes for lattice corners. For a 3D point, the hash for a corner (x, y, z) is constructed recursively: \text{hash3}(x, y, z) = \text{hash}(\text{hash}(\text{hash}(x+1) + y+1) + z+1) Note: The source uses pi + 1 in the hash construction, implying the hash is computed on the integer lattice indices offset by 1. 3. Gradient Selection: Gradients are selected from the 8 corners of the unit hypercube surrounding p. For a corner defined by bits j, k, l \in \{0, 1\}, the gradient vector g{jkl} has components \pm 1: g{jkl} = [(-1)^j, (-1)^k, (-1)^l] The dot product with the fractional offset f = p - i simplifies to additions and subtractions: \text{grad3D}(f) = \pm fx \pm fy \pm fz The signs are determined by the corner's bit indices. 4. Dimension Reducibility Optimization (3D): To reduce texture lookups, 3D noise is computed using 2D noise and z-gradients. Compute the hash for the current and next integer z-slice: h0 = \text{hash}(iz + 1) h1 = \text{hash}(iz + 2) Index the 2D textures using the x, y coordinates and the z-hash: c0 = (ix, iy, h0) c1 = (ix, iy, h1) Retrieve 2D noise values n0 = \text{tex\2d}(c0), n1 = \text{tex\2d}(c1) and z-gradients g0 = \text{tex\zgrad}(c0), g1 = \text{tex\zgrad}(c1). 5. Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation. First, interpolate in z using the retrieved values: nz = \text{lerp}(fz, n0, n1) gz = \text{lerp}(fz, g0, g1) Then, interpolate in x and y using the standard Perlin fading and gradient dot products for the 2D slices, combining them with the z component. The final formula provided in the source for separate textures is: N(p) = \text{lerp}(fz, \text{lerp}(fx, \text{lerp}(fy, \text{grad}(c0), \text{grad}(c0')), \dots), \dots) Note: The source provides a specific final formula for the optimized case: N(p) = \text{lerp}(fz, \text{lerp}(fx, \text{lerp}(fy, \text{grad}(c0), \text{grad}(c0')), \text{lerp}(fy, \text{grad}(c1), \text{grad}(c1'))), \dots) Actually, the source formula (19) is: \text{lerp}(fz, \text{lerp}(fx, \text{lerp}(fy, \text{grad}(c0), \text{grad}(c0')), \text{lerp}(fy, \text{grad}(c1), \text{grad}(c1'))), \dots) Wait, the source text for formula 19 is: flerp( pzf, mNoise2( c0) + pzf zgrad( c0), mNoise2( c1) + pzf zgrad( c1)) This implies the 2D noise and gradient are pre-combined or accessed such that the final step is a linear interpolation between the two z-slices, where each slice value includes the z-gradient contribution. Specifically: V0 = N{2D}(c0) + fz \cdot \frac{\partial N}{\partial z}(c0) V1 = N{2D}(c1) + fz \cdot \frac{\partial N}{\partial z}(c1) N(p) = \text{lerp}(fz, V0, V1) Where N{2D} and \frac{\partial N}{\partial z} are computed using the 2D hash and gradient logic on c0, c1. 6. Modulo Implementation: Exact (5-instruction): i \bmod M = i - \lfloor i/M \rfloor \cdot M. Used for 2D noise to ensure periodicity at M. Inexact (4-instruction): i \bmod M = \text{frac}(i/M) \cdot M. Used for 3D+ where precision loss is less critical. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bbsmod(x, M): # Inexact 4-instruction version for 3D return (x / M - floor(x / M)) M def bbshash(x, M): return bbsmod(x x, M) def hash3(x, y, z, M): h = bbshash(x + 1, M) h = bbshash(h + y + 1, M) return bbshash(h + z + 1, M) def grad3d(fx, fy, fz, cornerbits): # cornerbits is a tuple (j, k, l) in {0, 1} sx = 1 if cornerbits[0] == 0 else -1 sy = 1 if cornerbits[1] == 0 else -1 sz = 1 if cornerbits[2] == 0 else -1 return sx fx + sy fy + sz fz def noise3d(p, M): ix, iy, iz = floor(p) fx, fy, fz = p - (ix, iy, iz) # Compute hashes for z-slices h0 = hash3(ix, iy, iz, M) h1 = hash3(ix, iy, iz + 1, M) # Access 2D noise and z-gradient for the two z-slices # Note: In a pure implementation without textures, this would be computed recursively. # The source describes using textures for optimization. # Here we assume a pure computation for completeness, but the source emphasizes texture use. # For the sake of the "How it works" section based on the source's optimization: # c0 and c1 are indices for 2D texture lookup c0 = (ix, iy, h0) c1 = (ix, iy, h1) # Retrieve pre-computed 2D noise and z-gradient n0 = texturelookup2d(c0) g0 = texturelookupzgrad(c0) n1 = texturelookup2d(c1) g1 = texturelookupzgrad(c1) # Combine z-component v0 = n0 + fz g0 v1 = n1 + fz g1 return lerp(fz, v0, v1) Time Complexity: O(1) per sample. The BBS hash involves squaring and modulo, which is more expensive than a simple table lookup but avoids memory latency. Memory Complexity: O(1) if purely computed. O(1) with texture optimization (storing 2D slices). Performance: The 4-instruction modulo is faster but inexact. The 5-instruction modulo is exact but slower. Texture lookups accelerate 3D noise by reducing dependent lookups. Strengths: No permutation table required; suitable for GPUs with limited constant memory; dimension reducibility reduces texture fetches. Limitations: Axis-aligned clumping is visible in 2D results; the inexact modulo causes non-repeating noise at modulus M in lower dimensions. When to use: When GPU constant memory is constrained and a permutation table cannot be stored; for 3D/4D turbulence where clumping is less noticeable. When not to use: When exact periodicity at a specific modulus is required in 2D; when visual quality in 2D is critical due to clumping. Modified Noise was introduced in a thesis on real-time volumetric rendering of fire in a production system. It modifies Perlin's improved noise to be more suitable for GPU implementation by removing table lookups and using the Blum-Blum-Shub generator. Real-Time Volumetric Rendering of Fire in a Production System, https://clas.iusb.edu/math-compsci/prior-thesis/YVanzinethesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Curl Noise
head: Bridson Curl Noise
body: Curl noise is a procedural noise function designed to generate time-varying, incompressible turbulent velocity fields. It solves the problem of creating visually plausible fluid-like motion without the computational cost of solving the Navier-Stokes equations. Unlike standard gradient noise which produces scalar fields, curl noise produces vector fields where the divergence is identically zero, ensuring the flow is solenoidal. Curl noise constructs a divergence-free vector field by taking the curl of a vector potential derived from Perlin noise. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z), time t, noise scale s. Output: Velocity vector \mathbf{v} = (vx, vy, vz). Data Structures: Permutation table P: Array of size 512 (or 1024) containing integers 0..255 to map coordinates to gradient indices. Gradient vectors \mathbf{g}: For 3D Perlin noise, typically 12 face diagonals of a cube: (\pm 1, \pm 1, 0) and permutations. Steps: 1. Generate Vector Potential: Compute three independent Perlin noise values at \mathbf{P} to form a vector potential \mathbf{A} = (Ax, Ay, Az). Ax = \text{PerlinNoise}(x, y, z, t) Ay = \text{PerlinNoise}(x + \text{offset}x, y + \text{offset}y, z + \text{offset}z, t) Az = \text{PerlinNoise}(x + \text{offset}'x, y + \text{offset}'y, z + \text{offset}'z, t) The offsets must be large enough to ensure statistical independence between Ax, Ay, Az but small enough to maintain spatial coherence. Common practice uses offsets like (100, 200, 300) or distinct phase shifts. 2. Compute Curl: Calculate the curl of \mathbf{A} to obtain the velocity field \mathbf{v}. \mathbf{v} = \nabla \times \mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{\partial Az}{\partial y} - \frac{\partial Ay}{\partial z} \\ \frac{\partial Ax}{\partial z} - \frac{\partial Az}{\partial x} \\ \frac{\partial Ay}{\partial x} - \frac{\partial Ax}{\partial y} \end{pmatrix} 3. Numerical Derivatives: Since Perlin noise is interpolated, derivatives are computed using the gradient contributions from the surrounding lattice points. For a scalar noise function N(\mathbf{P}), the partial derivative \frac{\partial N}{\partial x} is computed by summing the dot products of the gradient vectors with the derivative of the fade function and distance vectors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def curlnoise(p: Vec3, time: float, scale: float) -> Vec3: # Scale input for noise frequency s = p / scale # Generate three independent scalar noise fields for the vector potential A # Offsets ensure Ax, Ay, Az are uncorrelated offset1 = Vec3(100.0, 200.0, 300.0) offset2 = Vec3(300.0, 100.0, 200.0) ax = perlinnoise(s, time) ay = perlinnoise(s + offset1, time) az = perlinnoise(s + offset2, time) # Compute derivatives of the scalar noise fields # dN/dx, dN/dy, dN/dz are computed via the gradient noise derivative logic daxdx, daxdy, daxdz = perlingradient(s, time) daydx, daydy, daydz = perlingradient(s + offset1, time) dazdx, dazdy, dazdz = perlingradient(s + offset2, time) # Curl calculation: v = curl(A) vx = dazdy - daydz vy = daxdz - dazdx vz = daydx - daxdy return Vec3(vx, vy, vz) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Correlation: If offsets between the three noise components are too small, the resulting field may not be sufficiently turbulent or may exhibit artifacts. If too large, local coherence is lost. Precision: Computing derivatives of interpolated noise requires careful handling of the fade function derivatives to maintain C^1 continuity. Time Complexity: O(1) per query, proportional to the number of lattice points in the cell (8 for 3D Perlin) times the number of noise components (3). Memory Complexity: O(1) for the permutation table and gradient set. Strengths: Produces incompressible flow naturally; visually pleasing turbulence; efficient to evaluate. Limitations: The flow is not physically accurate (does not conserve momentum or energy in a fluid dynamics sense); requires careful tuning of offsets and scale. Curl noise was presented by Robert Bridson, Ron Fedkiw, and Jos Stam in 2007. It is based on the mathematical property that the curl of any vector field is divergence-free. It is widely used in computer graphics for simulating smoke, clouds, and other fluid-like phenomena where physical accuracy is less important than visual plausibility. A gradient noise variant with reduced directional artifacts. Use when isotropic noise is required. Combines multiple octaves of noise. Use for multi-scale detail. Uses 4D noise for 3D spatial variation. Use for higher quality 3D textures. The 2D version of Perlin noise. Use for 2D textures. Details on the fade and gradient functions. Use for implementation details. name: Noise Layer Evaluation
head: Procedural Noise Layer Evaluation
body: Noise Layer Evaluation is a procedural shading technique that computes a single noise layer value for volume or terrain rendering, supporting multiple noise primitives, positional distortion, power scaling, and inversion. It differs from sibling methods by encapsulating layer configuration (scale, power, type, distortion) into a unified evaluation pipeline that can be toggled, inverted, and combined with raymarching parameters, whereas siblings like Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) focus on the low-level gradient interpolation and Worley Noise on distance-based cellular metrics. Inputs and Outputs Input: noiseSamplePosition (vec3), noiseLayerData (vec4), positionDistortion (float), invert (bool), enabled (bool). Output: value (float), the final noise layer contribution. Data Structures noiseLayerData: A vec4 encoding layer parameters: x: noiseScale (float) y: noisePower (float) z: angleOffset (float) w: noiseType (int, cast from float) Steps 1. Enable Check: If enabled is false, return 1.0 immediately. 2. Distortion: Compute distortionStrength = 0.1 positionDistortion. If distortionStrength > 0: Sample the base noise function (cnoise) at distortionStrength noiseSamplePosition. Add the result (cast to vec3) to noiseSamplePosition to create a distorted position. 3. Unpack Parameters: Extract noiseScale, noisePower, angleOffset, and noiseType from noiseLayerData. 4. Noise Sampling: Initialize sampledNoiseValue = 0.0. Based on noiseType: 0: sampledNoiseValue = cnoise(noiseSamplePosition noiseScale) 1: sampledNoiseValue = snoise(noiseSamplePosition noiseScale) 2: sampledNoiseValue = voronoi(noiseSamplePosition noiseScale, angleOffset, noiseScale) 3: sampledNoiseValue = nebulaNoise(noiseSamplePosition noiseScale) Note: cnoise and snoise refer to continuous and scalar noise functions, typically Perlin or Simplex variants. 5. Clamping: Clamp sampledNoiseValue to [0.0, 1.0] and store in value. 6. Inversion: If invert is true, set value = 1.0 - sampledNoiseValue. Pitfall: This uses the pre-clamped sampledNoiseValue, bypassing the clamp applied in Step 5. 7. Power Scaling: Compute finalValue = pow(abs(noisePower), value). Note: The source notes specify taking the absolute value of noisePower before exponentiation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatenoiselayer(noisesampleposition, noiselayerdata, positiondistortion, invert, enabled): # Step 1: Enable Check if not enabled: return 1.0 # Step 2: Distortion distortionstrength = 0.1 positiondistortion if distortionstrength > 0: # cnoise is a continuous noise function (e.g., Perlin) distortionoffset = cnoise(distortionstrength noisesampleposition) noisesampleposition = noisesampleposition + vec3(distortionoffset) # Step 3: Unpack Parameters noisescale = noiselayerdata.x noisepower = noiselayerdata.y angleoffset = noiselayerdata.z noisetype = int(noiselayerdata.w) # Step 4: Noise Sampling samplednoisevalue = 0.0 if noisetype == 0: samplednoisevalue = cnoise(noisesampleposition noisescale) elif noisetype == 1: samplednoisevalue = snoise(noisesampleposition noisescale) elif noisetype == 2: samplednoisevalue = voronoi(noisesampleposition noisescale, angleoffset, noisescale) elif noisetype == 3: samplednoisevalue = nebulanoise(noisesampleposition noisescale) else: # Default fallback if noisetype is out of range samplednoisevalue = 0.0 # Step 5: Clamping value = clamp(samplednoisevalue, 0.0, 1.0) # Step 6: Inversion if invert: # Pitfall: Uses samplednoisevalue (pre-clamp) instead of value value = 1.0 - samplednoisevalue # Step 7: Power Scaling # Note: Source specifies abs(noisepower) as the base finalvalue = pow(abs(noisepower), value) return finalvalue Parameters noiseLayerData (vec4): Encoded layer parameters. positionDistortion (float): Scales the offset applied to the sample position. invert (bool): When true, inverts the noise value before power application. enabled (bool): When false, forces the layer output to 1.0. densityMult (float): Default 1.0, range [0.0, 1.0], step 0.001. Multiplies volume density in the raymarching loop. maxSteps (int): Default 70, range [40, 256], step 1. Maximum number of raymarching steps per ray. stepSize (float): Default 0.01, range [0.00001, 0.1], step 0.000001. Distance between consecutive sample positions along the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Inversion Bypass: The inversion branch uses sampledNoiseValue instead of the clamped value, meaning the clamp applied in Step 5 is ignored when inversion is active. Unused Depth Parameter: The depth parameter is declared in the function signature but is never referenced or used in the function body. Degenerate Distortion: If positionDistortion is 0, distortion is skipped, which is the standard behavior. Calculates the 3D or 4D position in noise space for each fragment to apply procedural noise and turbulence functions. It solves the problem of mapping spatial coordinates to a noise field that supports animation (time) and instance uniqueness, distinct from standard 2D texture coordinate mapping. It sets up the input for turbulence and color lookup in procedural volume rendering. Time Complexity: O(1) per layer evaluation, assuming constant-time noise primitives. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the layer data structure. Performance: The method is lightweight, suitable for real-time raymarching loops. The use of cnoise and snoise implies efficient gradient-based noise implementations. Strengths: Flexible noise type selection, distortion support, and easy integration with raymarching parameters. Limitations: The inversion pitfall may lead to unexpected results if not accounted for. The unused depth parameter suggests incomplete implementation or API design. When to Use: When a single procedural noise layer with configurable distortion and power is needed for volume density or color. When Not to Use: When multiple layers need to be combined or when advanced noise features like fractal Brownian motion (fBm) are required. Noise Layer Evaluation originates from the Texturinator project, a procedural texture and volume rendering tool. It is designed to provide a flexible way to evaluate noise layers in 3D volumes, supporting various noise types and transformations. The method is part of a broader ecosystem of procedural noise functions used in computer graphics for generating natural-looking textures and volumes. MangoButtermilch/texturinator, https://github.com/MangoButtermilch/texturinator, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Noise Position Calculation
head: Noise Space Position Calculation, Procedural Noise Positioning
body: Calculates the 3D or 4D position in noise space for each fragment to apply procedural noise and turbulence functions. It solves the problem of mapping spatial coordinates to a noise field that supports animation (time) and instance uniqueness, distinct from standard 2D texture coordinate mapping. It sets up the input for turbulence and color lookup in procedural volume rendering. Inputs: tex: Unit volume texture coordinates (3D vector, typically [0,1]^3). noiseScale: Scalar scaling factor for spatial frequency. time: Current animation time (scalar). instanceOffset: 3D constant vector unique to each fire instance. stabilityFactor: Scalar for turbulence kernel stability. Outputs: noisePos: 4D position vector in noise space (x, y, z, t). finalTex: Adjusted 3D texture coordinates for color lookup. Data Structures: vec3: 3D floating-point vector. vec4: 4D floating-point vector. Steps: 1. Scale Spatial Coordinates: Multiply the unit texture coordinates by noiseScale to set the base spatial frequency. \mathbf{p}{scaled} = \mathbf{tex} \times \text{noiseScale} 2. Construct 4D Position: Initialize the noise position with the scaled coordinates. Set the fourth dimension (w) to time to enable 4D noise evaluation. \mathbf{p}{4d} = (\mathbf{p}{scaled}.x, \mathbf{p}{scaled}.y, \mathbf{p}{scaled}.z, \text{time}) 3. Apply Vertical Flow Offset: Offset the vertical axis (y) by -\text{time} to create an upward flow effect. \mathbf{p}{flow} = (\mathbf{p}{4d}.x, \mathbf{p}{4d}.y - \text{time}, \mathbf{p}{4d}.z, \mathbf{p}{4d}.w) 4. Add Instance Offset: Add the instanceOffset to the spatial components (x, y, z) to ensure each fire instance has a unique noise pattern. \mathbf{p}{final} = (\mathbf{p}{flow}.x + \text{instanceOffset}.x, \mathbf{p}{flow}.y + \text{instanceOffset}.y, \mathbf{p}{flow}.z + \text{instanceOffset}.z, \mathbf{p}{flow}.w) 5. Calculate Turbulence Kernel: Compute a kernel value f(\text{tex}z) using the stability factor and the square root of the height (z). f(\text{tex}z) = \text{stabilityFactor} \times \sqrt{\text{tex}.z} Note: The source specifies texz as the input to the kernel, interpreted as the z-component of the original texture coordinate. 6. Apply Turbulence to Position: Multiply the turbulence value by the kernel and add it to the vertical component of the texture lookup position. This step modifies the sampling position based on local noise density. \text{finalTex}.z = \mathbf{p}{final}.z + f(\text{tex}z) \text{finalTex}.x = \mathbf{p}{final}.x \text{finalTex}.y = \mathbf{p}{final}.y The source implies the turbulence is added to the vertical component of the texture look-up, not necessarily the noise position itself, to drive the color sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatenoiseposition(tex: vec3, noiseScale: float, time: float, instanceOffset: vec3, stabilityFactor: float) -> tuple[vec4, vec3]: # Step 1: Scale spatial coordinates pscaled = tex noiseScale # Step 2: Construct 4D position with time p4d = vec4(pscaled.x, pscaled.y, pscaled.z, time) # Step 3: Offset vertical axis for upward flow pflow = vec4(p4d.x, p4d.y - time, p4d.z, p4d.w) # Step 4: Add instance-specific offset pfinal = vec4(pflow.x + instanceOffset.x, pflow.y + instanceOffset.y, pflow.z + instanceOffset.z, pflow.w) # Step 5: Calculate turbulence kernel # f(texz) = stabilityFactor sqrt(tex.z) kernel = stabilityFactor sqrt(tex.z) # Step 6: Apply turbulence to vertical texture coordinate finaltex = vec3(pfinal.x, pfinal.y, pfinal.z + kernel) return pfinal, finaltex Parameters: noiseScale: Controls spatial frequency. Not given in the sources. stabilityFactor: Controls turbulence magnitude. Not given in the sources. instanceOffset: Unique per instance. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: tex.z < 0: Square root is undefined. Clamp tex.z to \ge 0 or handle as invalid. time large: Potential precision loss in floating-point subtraction. Use modulo or relative time if needed. Applies procedural noise to surfaces/volumes by evaluating 3D noise at spatial coordinates, avoiding 2D mapping seams. Chosen when continuous material appearance is needed across complex topologies. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary storage. Strengths: Enables animated, instance-unique procedural volumes with minimal overhead. Limitations: Requires 4D noise function support. Kernel choice affects visual stability. When to use: Procedural fire, smoke, or terrain where spatial continuity and animation are required. When not to use: Static 2D texturing or when instance uniqueness is not needed. Originated in real-time procedural volumetric fire rendering. Developed by Fuller, Krishnan, Mahrous, Hamann, and Joy at UC Davis, presented at I3D 2007. Used in GPU-based fire and smoke simulations. Real-time Procedural Volumetric Fire - UC Davis, https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~hamann/FullerKrishnanMahrousHamannJoyFirePaperForI3D2007AsSubmitted11012006.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Solid Texturing
head: 3D Map Texturing, Procedural Solid Texturing, Sampling solid noise
body: Solid texturing is a method for applying procedural noise functions to surfaces or volumetric data by evaluating a 3D noise field at spatial coordinates, rather than using 2D texture coordinates. It solves the problem of creating objects that appear carved from a continuous block of material, avoiding the seams and distortions associated with 2D texture mapping. Unlike 2D texturing, it maintains low memory consumption and allows the noise features to flow naturally across complex topologies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D procedural noise function N(x, y, z) (e.g., Perlin noise) and a set of 3D coordinates \mathbf{p} representing either surface points or ray sampling locations. Output: A scalar value (or color) assigned to each coordinate, representing the material property or color at that location. Data Structures: Noise Function: Typically implemented as a hash-based interpolation of gradient vectors at lattice points. Explicit pre-computed tables are avoided to prevent large memory costs. Coordinates: 3D vectors (x, y, z). Steps: 1. Generalize Noise to 3D: Ensure the base noise function accepts 3D input coordinates. Most standard noise functions (e.g., Perlin) are naturally generalized to 3D and higher dimensions. 2. Evaluate Noise: For Surface Texturing: Evaluate the 3D noise function at the 3D world coordinates of each surface point. For Voxelization: During the voxelization phase, assign a value to each voxel belonging to the object using the texturing function or 3D map. This value is stored as part of the voxel information. For Volume Enrichment: If used to enrich a volume dataset without increasing stored resolution, evaluate the texturing function during rendering time at the ray sampling locations. Formulas: The power spectrum of the noise on the surface, P{surface}(u, v), is related to the power spectrum of the solid noise, P{solid}(u, v, w), by the slice-projection theorem: P{surface}(u, v) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} P{solid}(u, v, w) \, dw This integration occurs because evaluating a 3D noise along a surface corresponds to slicing the 3D domain. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Loss of Band-Pass Properties: Slicing a 3D band-pass noise along a surface does not result in a band-pass noise on the surface. This is a consequence of the slice-projection theorem, which states that slicing in one domain corresponds to projection or integration in the other domain. The resulting power spectrum is not band-pass anymore, potentially leading to visual artifacts or incorrect frequency characteristics. Memory Costs: Explicit noises that rely on pre-computed 3D tables induce large memory costs and are generally avoided in favor of procedural generation. Seams and Distortions: While solid texturing avoids seams inherent to 2D UV mapping, it can still exhibit distortions if the noise function is not carefully chosen or if the surface curvature is extreme. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solidtexture(surfacepoints, noisefunction): """ Applies solid texturing to a set of 3D surface points. Args: surfacepoints: List of 3D vectors (x, y, z) representing surface coordinates. noisefunction: A callable that takes a 3D vector and returns a scalar value. Returns: List of scalar values representing the texture at each point. """ texturevalues = [] for point in surfacepoints: # Evaluate the 3D noise function at the surface point's coordinates value = noisefunction(point.x, point.y, point.z) texturevalues.append(value) return texturevalues def solidtexturevolumeenrichment(raysamples, noisefunction): """ Enriches a volume dataset by evaluating noise at ray sampling locations. Args: raysamples: List of 3D vectors representing ray sampling locations in 3D space. noisefunction: A callable that takes a 3D vector and returns a scalar value. Returns: List of scalar values representing the enriched texture at each sample location. """ enrichedvalues = [] for sample in raysamples: # Evaluate the 3D noise function at the ray sampling location value = noisefunction(sample.x, sample.y, sample.z) enrichedvalues.append(value) return enrichedvalues Defining noise directly on the surface so features flow along curvatures. This is difficult in general but possible with sparse convolution noises. Assigning noise values to voxels during the voxelization phase. Evaluating noise during rendering at ray sampling locations to enrich volume data. Memory: Low memory consumption compared to explicit 3D texture maps, as the noise is generated procedurally. Performance: Computationally expensive if evaluated at every surface point or ray sample, as it requires evaluating the noise function for each point. However, it avoids the overhead of managing large 3D texture arrays. Visual Quality: Produces a natural, carved appearance that is difficult to achieve with 2D texturing. However, it may suffer from loss of band-pass characteristics on surfaces, leading to potential visual artifacts. Scalability: Scales well with resolution as it is resolution-independent, but performance depends on the complexity of the noise function and the number of evaluation points. When to Use: When a natural, continuous material appearance is desired, and memory is a constraint. Suitable for organic shapes and complex topologies. When Not to Use: When precise control over 2D texture coordinates is required, or when the loss of band-pass properties on surfaces is unacceptable without additional correction. The idea of sampling 3D noise on surfaces was introduced by Perlin [Per85] and Peachy [Pea85] and popularized as solid texturing. It has been widely used in computer graphics for creating procedural textures and modeling solid materials. A comprehensive overview of solid texturing can be found in Dischler and Ghazanfarpour [DG01]. The slice-projection theorem, which explains the spectral properties of sliced noise, was established by Braun [Bra99] and Mallat [Mal93]. name: Data Structures and Implementation
body: This family covers the storage, generation, and management of procedural noise data structures used in volume rendering. It addresses the problem of efficiently providing high-frequency detail or base fields to shaders without excessive memory bandwidth or CPU overhead. It differs from its siblings, such as Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) and Value Noise, by focusing on the mechanics of data creation (CPU/GPU generation, texture formats, struct layouts) rather than the mathematical definition of the noise fields themselves. The family shares the following mechanism, terms, and math: 1. Gradient Assignment: Each integer lattice point (vertex) in the domain is assigned a pseudo-random gradient vector \mathbf{g}. In 3D, common sets include 12 face diagonals of a cube or 12 axis-aligned vectors. 2. Dot Product Contribution: The noise value at a query point \mathbf{P} is derived from the dot product between the gradient vector \mathbf{g}i at a lattice corner i and the distance vector \mathbf{d}i = \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{V}i from that corner to \mathbf{P}: ni = \mathbf{g}i \cdot \mathbf{d}i. 3. Smoothing/Fade Function: To ensure smooth transitions (C^1 continuity), the fractional coordinates of \mathbf{P} within the cell are passed through a fade function f(t) before interpolation. The quintic function f(t) = 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3 is standard for Perlin variants, while Simplex uses a different geometric approach. 4. Interpolation: The contributions from the cell corners are combined using linear interpolation (lerp) along the axes, weighted by the fade values. 5. Hashing: Integer coordinates are mapped to gradient indices using a permutation table to avoid modulo operations and ensure uniform distribution. This method generates a 2D texture filled with random values (unit vectors or scalar floats) to serve as a source for noise-based effects, such as SSAO variation, volumetric dithering, or fine detail perturbation. It differs from procedural noise functions (like Perlin or Simplex noise) by providing uncorrelated, high-frequency random data rather than smooth, continuous fields. It is typically generated on the CPU and uploaded to the GPU for sampling during rendering. This variant emphasizes on-the-fly computation to optimize memory usage. Normals are computed dynamically rather than stored, trading computation time for memory efficiency. Bricks (voxel blocks) are created on the GPU using procedural noise, which proves more efficient than CPU evaluation and data transfer. This variant defines a specific host-side data structure for configuring noise parameters. The WorldGenerationData struct contains: octaves: u32, ceiling: u32, lacunarity: f32, gain: f32, frequency: f32, threshold: f32, and seed: f32. This method optimizes large-scale terrain generation by evaluating continent- and range-wide octaves at lattice nodes and blending them. For each level, it runs a compiled column program instead of walking the octave table. Erosion octaves step their corners and share steering. A key pitfall is ensuring bit-exact results between CPU and GPU implementations. Performance improvements reduced generation speed from 41–43 µs per tile to 32–34 µs per tile. This refers to a system (specifically in Buto/Unity) that procedurally creates Volumetric Noise, bakes it to a 3D Texture, and associates it with a volume component asset. Supported types include Perlin, Worley, Perlin-Worley, Billow, and Curl. It allows users to define a Seed for consistency, Quality to limit texture size, and Frequency/Octaves/Lacunarity/Gain to control detail. Using a procedural method rather than a pre-compressed single-channel texture provides better visual results and remapping capabilities. Procedural noise generation has evolved from CPU-based texture synthesis to GPU-accelerated on-the-fly computation. Early implementations relied on CPU generation and memory transfer, but modern techniques leverage GPU shaders for real-time generation to save memory. Specific implementations like the "Two-rate field" generation optimize large-scale voxel planets by separating global and local octave evaluation. Integrated engines like Buto provide built-in systems to bake these procedural fields into 3D textures for volume rendering. name: 2D White Noise Texture Generation
head: 2D Random Noise Texture Generation, Noise Texture Generation, Viewport noise texture, White Noise Generation
body: This method generates a 2D texture filled with random unit vectors or scalar floats to serve as a source for noise-based effects, such as SSAO variation and volumetric dithering. It differs from procedural noise functions by providing uncorrelated, high-frequency random data rather than smooth, continuous fields. The data is generated on the CPU and uploaded to the GPU for sampling during rendering. Inputs: side (integer dimension for square textures); width and height (viewport dimensions for rectangular textures). Outputs: A GPU 2D texture object containing the noise data. The implementation uses different layouts depending on the noise type and precision: 1. Vector Noise: Host memory holds an array of vec3 of size side side. The GPU texture uses internal format GLRGB32F, dimensions side x side, data type GLFLOAT. 2. Scalar Float Noise: Host memory holds a Color array of size 4096 (64×64). The GPU texture uses format R16, dimensions 64×64, with mipmaps disabled. 3. Scalar Byte Noise: Host memory holds an unsigned char array of size width height. The GPU texture uses internal format GLR8, dimensions width × height, pixel format GLLUMINANCE, and type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. 1. Initialize Random Number Generator (RNG): Create a seeded RNG using std::randomdevice and std::mt19937 with a uniform distribution over [-1.0, 1.0], or std::srand(std::time(NULL)). 2. Generate Noise Data: For vector noise, loop i from 0 to side^2 - 1: generate three independent uniform values x, y, z \in [-1.0, 1.0], construct \mathbf{v} = (x, y, z), normalize to unit length \mathbf{v}{norm} = \mathbf{v} / \|\mathbf{v}\|, and store in the array. For scalar float noise, generate a random float for the r component of each Color element, leaving other components unspecified (likely 0). For scalar byte noise, fill the array with random bytes in the range [0, 255]. 3. Create and Configure Texture: Generate a texture ID and bind it with glBindTexture(GLTEXTURE2D, id). Set wrapping to GLREPEAT or GLMIRROR. Set filtering to GLLINEAR or GLNEAREST. Upload the host array to the GPU using glTexImage2D. 4. Bind to Shader: Set the material or shader property (e.g., WhiteNoise) to reference the generated texture. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def generatevectornoisetexture(side): """Generates a 2D white noise texture with normalized 3D vectors.""" noisedata = [] rng = random.Random() for in range(side side): x = rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) y = rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) z = rng.uniform(-1.0, 1.0) length = math.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) if length == 0: length = 1e-6 # Guard against zero vector noisedata.append((x / length, y / length, z / length)) return noisedata def generatescalarbytetexture(width, height): """Generates a 2D white noise texture with unsigned byte values.""" noisedata = [] rng = random.Random() for in range(width height): noisedata.append(rng.randint(0, 255)) return noisedata side: Integer dimension of the square texture. width, height: Dimensions for non-square textures, typically derived from the viewport. internalformat: GLRGB32F for vector noise, R16 for scalar float, or GLR8 for scalar byte. wrapmode: GLREPEAT or GLMIRROR. filtermode: GLLINEAR or GLNEAREST. Zero Vector: Normalizing a generated (0,0,0) vector causes division by zero; a guard clause or regeneration is required. Filtering Choice: GLLINEAR smooths the noise, while GLNEAREST preserves sharp, uncorrelated pixels. Wrapping: GLREPEAT and GLMIRROR produce different boundary behaviors depending on the application. Precision: GLRGB32F uses more memory but provides full float precision, whereas GLR8 is compact but limited to 256 discrete levels. Generates initial noise textures with smooth, large 'spots' using Turing's reaction-diffusion equations, replacing standard white noise for better visual representation of tensor fields. Time Complexity: O(N) for generation, where N is the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the noise data on the CPU and GPU. Performance: Generation is fast on the CPU; upload time depends on bus bandwidth and texture size. Typical resolutions are 64×64 to 256×256. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from custom volume raycasting visualizers and volumetric smoke renderers. It is used for screen-space effects like SSAO variation and for volumetric rendering dithering. ajaspe/ssvdag, https://github.com/ajaspe/ssvdag, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) GitHub - m-pilia/volume-raycasting: Simple visualiser based on GPU..., https://github.com/m-pilia/volume-raycasting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Turing Reaction-Diffusion Noise Generation
head: Reaction Diffusion Scheme
body: This method generates initial noise textures with smooth, large 'spots' using Turing's reaction-diffusion equations, replacing standard white noise for better visual representation of tensor fields. It solves the problem that high-frequency noise textures, such as white noise, are not suitable for achieving a proper visual representation of data in certain visualization approaches. It sets itself apart from its sibling 2D White Noise Texture Generation by producing correlated, spatially structured patterns rather than uncorrelated random values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Grid dimensions (implied by the tiling context), diffusion constants Da, Db, scalar s, and initial random values for grids a and b. Output: Two discrete grids a and b representing the reaction-diffusion state. Data Structures: Two 2D arrays (grids) a and b of identical dimensions. The indices are i and j. Values are typically floating-point numbers. The source does not specify bit packing or exact data types, but implies continuous values for the calculation. Parameters: Da: Diffusion constant for grid a. Value: 0.125. Db: Diffusion constant for grid b. Value: 0.031. s: Scalar controlling the size of the spots. Smaller s leads to larger spots. Boundary Conditions: Continuous boundary conditions are assumed for grid coordinates i and j to obtain a seamless texture. Steps: 1. Initialize grids a and b with random values. The source does not specify the distribution or range of these initial values. 2. For each cell (i, j) in the grid, calculate the change \Delta a{i,j} and \Delta b{i,j} using the discrete Turing reaction-diffusion equations: \Delta a{i,j} = F(i,j) + Da \cdot (a{i+1,j} + a{i-1,j} + a{i,j+1} + a{i,j-1} - 4 \cdot a{i,j}) \Delta b{i,j} = G(i,j) + Db \cdot (b{i+1,j} + b{i-1,j} + b{i,j+1} + b{i,j-1} - 4 \cdot b{i,j}) 3. Calculate the reaction functions F(i, j) and G(i, j): F(i, j) = s(16 - a{i,j} \cdot b{i,j}) G(i, j) = s(a{i,j} \cdot b{i,j} - b{i,j} - \beta{i,j}) Note: \beta{i,j} is an input term mentioned in the formula for G. The source does not define \beta{i,j} further, nor does it specify if it is a constant, a function of position, or another grid. 4. Update the grids: a{i,j} \leftarrow a{i,j} + \Delta a{i,j} b{i,j} \leftarrow b{i,j} + \Delta b{i,j} 5. Repeat steps 2-4 for a number of iterations until the desired pattern stability or visual quality is achieved. The source does not specify the number of iterations. 6. Handle boundaries using continuous boundary conditions (e.g., wrapping or mirroring) to ensure seamlessness. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatereactiondiffusionnoise(width, height, s, numiterations): # Initialize grids with random values a = [[random() for in range(width)] for in range(height)] b = [[random() for in range(width)] for in range(height)] Da = 0.125 Db = 0.031 for in range(numiterations): newa = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] newb = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for i in range(height): for j in range(width): # Get neighbors with continuous boundary conditions (wrapping) aup = a[(i - 1) % height][j] adown = a[(i + 1) % height][j] aleft = a[i][(j - 1) % width] aright = a[i][(j + 1) % width] bup = b[(i - 1) % height][j] bdown = b[(i + 1) % height][j] bleft = b[i][(j - 1) % width] bright = b[i][(j + 1) % width] # Calculate Laplacian terms laplaciana = aup + adown + aleft + aright - 4 a[i][j] laplacianb = bup + bdown + bleft + bright - 4 b[i][j] # Calculate reaction terms # Note: betaij is undefined in the source # Assuming betaij is 0 or a constant if not specified, # but this is a gap in the source. betaij = 0.0 Fij = s (16 - a[i][j] b[i][j]) Gij = s (a[i][j] b[i][j] - b[i][j] - betaij) # Calculate deltas deltaa = Fij + Da laplaciana deltab = Gij + Db laplacianb # Update newa[i][j] = a[i][j] + deltaa newb[i][j] = b[i][j] + deltab a = newa b = newb return a, b Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tiling the reaction diffusion texture can cause minor artifacts at boundaries, but these are ignored in practice due to the advection step. The definition of \beta{i,j} is sparse in the text. Time Complexity: The method is computationally expensive, as noted by the source. Each iteration requires O(N) operations for an N-pixel grid, and multiple iterations are needed. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two grids of the same size as the output texture. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The source mentions tiling to create a texture of required size because reaction diffusion is computationally expensive. This implies generating a smaller base pattern and tiling it, or generating a large pattern directly if resources allow. Strengths: Produces smooth, large 'spots' that are randomly and almost uniquely distributed, providing a better visual representation for tensor fields than white noise. Limitations: Computationally expensive. Potential boundary artifacts when tiling, though mitigated by subsequent steps. When to use: When visual representation of tensor fields requires smooth, correlated noise patterns instead of high-frequency white noise. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and white noise is sufficient. The method is based on Turing's reaction-diffusion scheme first introduced by Turing [Tur52] to simulate the mixture of two reacting chemicals. It is used in the context of Image-Space Tensor Field Visualization Using a LIC-like Method. name: Specific Procedural Patterns and Applications
head: Procedural Volume Patterns, Implicit Volume Generators
body: This family encompasses specific mathematical formulations and algorithmic patterns used to generate volumetric data, density fields, and geometric structures procedurally without explicit mesh storage. It solves the problem of creating complex, organic, or fractal 3D shapes and density distributions using deterministic functions. Unlike Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) which provides raw noise values, or Value Noise which interpolates scalar values, this family applies specific transformations (such as polar exponentiation, spherical ramps, or sine-based occupancy) to define the final volume characteristics directly. The family shares the following mechanism, terms, and math: 1. Gradient Assignment: Each integer lattice point (vertex) in the domain is assigned a pseudo-random gradient vector \mathbf{g}. In 3D, common sets include 12 face diagonals of a cube or 12 axis-aligned vectors. 2. Dot Product Contribution: The noise value at a query point \mathbf{P} is derived from the dot product between the gradient vector \mathbf{g}i at a lattice corner i and the distance vector \mathbf{d}i = \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{V}i from that corner to \mathbf{P}: ni = \mathbf{g}i \cdot \mathbf{d}i. 3. Smoothing/Fade Function: To ensure smooth transitions (C^1 continuity), the fractional coordinates of \mathbf{P} within the cell are passed through a fade function f(t) before interpolation. S1 uses the cubic smoothstep function f(t) = 3t^2 - 2t^3 for interpolation weighting. 4. Interpolation: The contributions from the cell corners are combined using linear interpolation (lerp) along the axes, weighted by the fade values. 5. Hashing: Integer coordinates are mapped to gradient indices using a permutation table or coordinate mixing constants to avoid modulo operations and ensure uniform distribution. Creates volumetric data by evaluating trigonometric functions against spatial coordinates to determine voxel occupancy and color. It solves the problem of generating deterministic, periodic, and smooth geometric structures without storing explicit mesh or voxel grid data. Unlike Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation which focuses on planar terrain, or Procedural Tree Voxel Generation which uses hierarchical branching, this method relies on global periodic wave interference to define shape boundaries and internal density variations. Is a procedural volume density function that confines a gas (such as steam or smoke) to a spherical slab region using a spherical distance ramp and an offset table, simulating steam rising from a source. It differs from its siblings by combining a base turbulence pattern with a specific radial falloff mechanism that uses a precomputed cosine ramp and spatially varying noise offsets to break symmetry, whereas Sine-based procedural voxel generation relies on sinusoidal modulation and Mandelbulb Fractal Generation uses iterative complex number transformations. Generates a 3D fractal by iteratively applying a polar coordinate power transformation to a complex 3D point. It differs from its siblings by using continuous polar coordinate exponentiation rather than discrete modulo arithmetic (Menger Sponge) or simple polynomial mappings (Bristorbrot). Generates a patchy volumetric density field from procedural noise by applying a power function and a threshold to create sparse, organic structures. It differs from its parent Specific Procedural Patterns and Applications by explicitly combining Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) with non-linear remapping and hard cutoffs, rather than relying on raw noise values or simple linear blending. A method to map pre-shaded texture cells onto a terrain or volume surface without visible repetition, using aperiodic boundary conditions and edge-matching constraints. It differs from standard periodic tiling by enforcing specific edge correlations to prevent seams, and from simple noise-based tiling by relying on pre-computed geometric patterns rather than procedural generation at render time. Definition: A noise function designed for 3D volumetric clouds that samples a 2D texture slice based on 3D coordinates to generate organic randomness. Steps: 1. Compute integer part p and fractional part f of the input 3D coordinate x. 2. Compute smooth interpolation factor u using the formula u = f f (3. - 2. f). 3. Calculate 2D UV coordinates by combining p.xy with p.z scaled by vec2(37.0, 239.0) and adding u.xy. 4. Sample the uNoise texture at (uv + 0.5) / 256.0 with LOD 0.0, returning the.yx components. 5. Mix the two texture components tex.x and tex.y using u.z as the weight, then scale the result to the range [-1, 1] by multiplying by 2.0 and subtracting 1.0. Code: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. float noise(vec3 x) { vec3 p = floor(x); vec3 f = fract(x); vec2 u = f f (3. - 2. f); vec2 uv = (p.xy + vec2(37.0, 239.0) p.z) + u.xy; vec2 tex = textureLod(uNoise,(uv + 0.5) / 256.0, 0.0).yx; return mix( tex.x, tex.y, u.z) 2.0 - 1.0; } Definition: Determines initial constraints that define the overall look of the world by projecting a smooth noise function onto the horizontal plane. Parameters: Noise function: Simplex noise. Inlandness: 1.0 (inland), 0.5 (coastal), 0.0 (submerged). Temperature: 1.0 (hot), 0.5 (temperate), 0.0 (cold). Lushness: 1.0 (densely packed with flora), 0.0 (barren). name: Sine-based procedural voxel generation
head: Trigonometric voxel pattern
body: Sine-based procedural voxel generation determines voxel occupancy and color by evaluating trigonometric functions against integer spatial coordinates. It generates deterministic, periodic structures without storing explicit grid data. Unlike Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation or Procedural Tree Voxel Generation, it relies on global periodic wave interference for shape boundaries. Inputs and Outputs Input: 3D integer voxel coordinates (posx, posy, posz), grid width, and a scaling constant. Output: A voxel state (empty or filled) and an RGBA color value. Data Structures Coordinates: Integer triplets representing voxel indices. Color: 32-bit value with 8-bit channels (R, G, B, A). Parameters mod: The periodicity divisor, calculated as width / 8. scale: A constant multiplier for color channels, set to 0x20 (32). Algorithm Steps 1. Periodicity Calculation: Compute mod = width / 8. 2. Normalization: Convert integer coordinates to a normalized range [-1, 1] within the periodic cell: xx = \frac{(posx \bmod \text{mod}) \cdot 2}{\text{mod}} - 1 yy = \frac{(posy \bmod \text{mod}) \cdot 2}{\text{mod}} - 1 zz = \frac{(posz \bmod \text{mod}) \cdot 2}{\text{mod}} - 1 3. Radius Calculation: Compute a variable radius r defining the shape boundary: r = \left( \sin\left( \frac{posx/\text{mod} + posy/\text{mod} + posz/\text{mod}}{5} \right) + 1 \right) \cdot 0.3 4. Occupancy Test: A voxel is filled if it satisfies both conditions: It lies inside the spherical boundary: xx^2 + yy^2 + zz^2 \le r. It passes a secondary frequency filter: \sin\left( \frac{posx \cdot 16 + posy \cdot 20 + posz \cdot 30}{\text{width}} \right) \ge 0. If either condition fails, the voxel is empty. 5. Color Assignment: If filled, compute RGB values scaled by the position relative to mod: R = \frac{posx}{\text{mod}} \cdot 0x20 G = \frac{posy}{\text{mod}} \cdot 0x20 B = \frac{posz}{\text{mod}} \cdot 0x20 A = 255 Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sinevoxelgeneration(posx: int, posy: int, posz: int, width: int): mod = width / 8 xx = ((posx % mod) 2.0 / mod) - 1.0 yy = ((posy % mod) 2.0 / mod) - 1.0 zz = ((posz % mod) 2.0 / mod) - 1.0 arg = (posx / mod + posy / mod + posz / mod) / 5.0 radius = (math.sin(arg) + 1.0) 0.3 if xxxx + yyyy + zzzz > radius: return None filterarg = (posx 16 + posy 20 + posz 30) / width if math.sin(filterarg) < 0: return None scale = 0x20 r = int((posx / mod) scale) g = int((posy / mod) scale) b = int((posz / mod) scale) a = 255 return (r, g, b, a) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Harmonic trigonometric displacement noise adds organic or porous textures to volumes by modulating density. It applies a multiplicative amplitude factor to the product of sines along each axis. Formula: amp \cdot \sin(freq \cdot x) \cdot \sin(freq \cdot y) \cdot \sin(freq \cdot z). name: Procedural Tree Voxel Generation
head: L-system-like recursion, L-systems, Lindenmayer systems, Recursive Tree Branching, Tree Voxel Generation
body: Procedural Tree Voxel Generation is a method for creating volumetric tree structures by recursively branching segments represented as spheres of varying thickness. It adapts L-system principles to voxel space, where a single recursive rule generates complex, self-similar shapes by spawning sub-branches with random directional offsets and scaling factors. Unlike shape grammars that output basic shapes directly, this method requires interpreting the recursive production rules to draw voxelized primitives. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Simple Heightmap Voxel Generation by its hierarchical, branching topology rather than surface elevation, and from Asymmetric Wing Stroke by its focus on organic, fractal-like growth patterns. Inputs: root1: Starting 3D position (vector). root2: Ending 3D position (vector) of the current segment. thicknessA: Radius of the sphere at root1. thicknessB: Radius of the sphere at root2. iteration: Current recursion depth (integer). vx, vy, vz: Dimensions of the voxel grid. voxel: Bit-packed array storing occupancy. voxelcol1, voxelcol2: Arrays storing color data. Outputs: Modified voxel array with tree geometry. Modified voxelcol arrays with color data. The voxel data is stored in a bit-packed format to save memory. voxel: char array of size (vx/8) \times vy \times vz bytes. Each byte stores 8 voxels along the X-axis. Bit k in a byte corresponds to voxel coordinate x where k = x \pmod 8. Offset calculation for voxel (x, y, z): ofs = \lfloor x/8 \rfloor + y \cdot \lfloor vx/8 \rfloor + z \cdot (\lfloor vx/8 \rfloor \cdot vy) voxelcol1, voxelcol2: uchar arrays of size vx \times vy \times vz, storing color indices or values for each voxel. 1. Base Case Check: If iteration > 5 or thicknessA < 2, terminate recursion for this branch. 2. Draw Segment: Calculate the midpoint between root1 and root2: mid = \frac{root1 + root2}{2} Calculate the midpoint thickness: thicknessM = \frac{thicknessA + thicknessB}{2} Draw a sphere at mid with radius thicknessM and color index 2. 3. Add Detail: Calculate an offset vector using sine/cosine functions of an index iM (implementation-specific detail index). Draw a smaller sphere at mid + offset with radius thicknessM / 3 and color index 3. 4. Recursive Branching: Loop branches from 0 to 3. Generate a random direction vector rnd and normalize it. Adjust the Y component to bias upward based on iteration: rnd.y += 0.6 \cdot iteration - 0.5 Calculate the delta vector of the current segment: delta = root2 - root1 Calculate the half-length of the current segment: length = \|delta\| \cdot 0.5 Scale and offset the branch vector: branch = rnd \cdot \frac{length}{\|rnd\|} + delta \cdot 0.6 (Note: Source specifies branch.length() in denominator, but rnd is normalized, so \|rnd\|=1. The formula effectively scales the random direction by half the segment length and adds 60% of the current segment's direction vector). Calculate new thickness for the child branch: thicknessNew = thicknessA \cdot 0.4 Recursively call tree with the new start point root2 and end point root2 + branch, using thicknessNew and iteration + 1. 5. Decrement Iteration: After the loop, decrement iteration if managed as a shared state, though typically iteration is passed by value in recursion. To draw a sphere at position pos with radius r: 1. Iterate x from \lfloor pos.x - r \rfloor to \lceil pos.x + r \rceil. 2. Iterate y from \lfloor pos.y - r \rfloor to \lceil pos.y + r \rceil. 3. Iterate z from \lfloor pos.z - r \rfloor to \lceil pos.z + r \rceil. 4. Calculate squared distance: distSq = (x - pos.x)^2 + (y - pos.y)^2 + (z - pos.z)^2 5. If distSq \le r^2: Set the bit in voxel: voxel[ofs] \ |= \ (1 \ll (x \pmod 8)) Set color in voxelcol1 and voxelcol2 at (x, y, z). After the tree is generated, a mipmap level can be created: 1. Iterate over each voxel in the current tree level. 2. Check the 2x2x2 sub-voxels corresponding to the current voxel. 3. If any sub-voxel is set, set the corresponding bit in the mipmap voxel. 4. Copy color bits if present. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def drawsphere(pos, radius, coloridx, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz): """Draws a sphere into the voxel grid.""" r = int(radius) # Define bounds xmin = max(0, int(pos.x - radius)) xmax = min(vx - 1, int(pos.x + radius)) ymin = max(0, int(pos.y - radius)) ymax = min(vy - 1, int(pos.y + radius)) zmin = max(0, int(pos.z - radius)) zmax = min(vz - 1, int(pos.z + radius)) # Precompute radius squared rsq = radius radius for x in range(xmin, xmax + 1): # Precompute x offset and bit mask ofsbase = (x >> 3) + (ymin (vx >> 3)) + (zmin (vx >> 3) vy) bitmask = 1 << (x & 7) for y in range(ymin, ymax + 1): ofsyoffset = (y - ymin) (vx >> 3) for z in range(zmin, zmax + 1): # Calculate squared distance dx = x - pos.x dy = y - pos.y dz = z - pos.z distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if distsq <= rsq: ofs = ofsbase + ofsyoffset + (z - zmin) (vx >> 3) vy voxel[ofs] |= bitmask voxelcol1[x + y vx + z vx vy] = coloridx voxelcol2[x + y vx + z vx vy] = coloridx def getrnd(): """Generates a random 3D vector.""" return [random.uniform(-1, 1), random.uniform(-1, 1), random.uniform(-1, 1)] def normalize(v): """Normalizes a vector.""" length = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if length == 0: return [0, 0, 0] return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def tree(root1, root2, thicknessA, thicknessB, iteration, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz): """ Recursive function to generate tree branches. root1, root2: 3D coordinates [x, y, z] thicknessA, thicknessB: float radii iteration: int """ # Base case if iteration > 5 or thicknessA < 2: # Draw leaf sphere at root1 drawsphere(root1, 8, 2, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) return # Increment iteration for children nextiteration = iteration + 1 # Calculate midpoint mid = [(root1[i] + root2[i]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] thicknessM = (thicknessA + thicknessB) / 2.0 # Draw main segment sphere drawsphere(mid, thicknessM, 2, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) # Add detail sphere # Note: iM is not defined in source, using a placeholder index or derived from iteration # Source says "using sine/cosine of iM". We assume iM is a local detail index. # For implementation, we might use iteration or a hash. # Since source doesn't define iM, we use a deterministic offset based on iteration for reproducibility. iM = iteration offsetx = math.sin(iM) (thicknessM / 3.0) offsety = math.cos(iM) (thicknessM / 3.0) offsetz = math.sin(iM + 1) (thicknessM / 3.0) detailpos = [mid[i] + [offsetx, offsety, offsetz][i] for i in range(3)] drawsphere(detailpos, thicknessM / 3.0, 3, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) # Recursive branching delta = [root2[i] - root1[i] for i in range(3)] deltalen = math.sqrt(delta[0]2 + delta[1]2 + delta[2]2) halflength = deltalen 0.5 for branches in range(4): # 0 to 3 rnd = getrnd() rnd = normalize(rnd) # Adjust Y component rnd[1] += 0.6 iteration - 0.5 # Scale and offset branch vector # Source: branch = rnd length / branch.length() + delta0.6 # Since rnd is normalized, branch.length() is 1. branchvec = [rnd[i] halflength + delta[i] 0.6 for i in range(3)] newroot2 = [root2[i] + branchvec[i] for i in range(3)] thicknessNew = thicknessA 0.4 tree(root2, newroot2, thicknessA, thicknessNew, nextiteration, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) def generatetree(vx, vy, vz): """ Initializes voxel data and starts tree generation. """ # Allocate memory voxelsize = (vx // 8) vy vz voxel = bytearray(voxelsize) voxelcol1 = bytearray(vx vy vz) voxelcol2 = bytearray(vx vy vz) # Initial trunk parameters # Source implies starting with a trunk. # Example: root1 at (0,0,0), root2 at (0,10,0), thickness 10 root1 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] root2 = [0.0, 10.0, 0.0] thicknessA = 10.0 thicknessB = 8.0 iteration = 0 tree(root1, root2, thicknessA, thicknessB, iteration, voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2, vx, vy, vz) return voxel, voxelcol1, voxelcol2 iteration: Static counter for recursion depth. Base case triggers if iteration > 5 or thickness < 2. iso: Isolation threshold for loading voxel data from file, default 168. (Note: This parameter is mentioned in the context of file I/O, not the generation algorithm itself). thicknessA: Initial thickness of the trunk. thicknessB: Thickness at the end of the trunk segment. branches: Number of sub-branches spawned per node (fixed at 4 in the source loop). Precision: Floating point errors in distance calculations may cause gaps or overlaps in sphere voxelization. Using squared distance comparisons avoids square roots. Boundary Checks: Voxel coordinates must be clamped to the grid dimensions [0, vx-1] \times [0, vy-1] \times [0, vz-1] to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Degenerate Input: If root1 equals root2, the delta vector is zero, resulting in no branch direction. The normalization of rnd handles this, but the branch vector becomes purely random, potentially causing instability. Stack Overflow: Deep recursion (e.g., iteration > 5) can lead to stack overflow if not managed. The source limits iteration to 5. L-systems use production rules to model plant growth. Unlike shape grammars, L-systems require interpretation of the output string to produce the final result. They are well-suited for self-similar shapes like trees. Used in city layout generation, these L-systems change under local constraints to avoid overlapping streets or parallel roads. This concept can be adapted for tree generation to prevent branch collision. A post-processing step where 2x2x2 sub-voxels are checked to generate lower-resolution levels of the tree voxel data. Time: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the bounding box of the tree. The number of spheres drawn is proportional to the number of branches, which grows exponentially with iteration (base 4). Each sphere voxelization is O(r^3). Memory: O(vx \cdot vy \cdot vz / 8) for the bit-packed voxel array, plus O(vx \cdot vy \cdot vz) for color arrays. Not given in the sources. The tree size scales with the initial thickness and the number of iterations. Increasing iteration exponentially increases the number of branches and voxels. The scaling factor for thickness (0.4) and length (implicit in halflength) controls the fractal dimension. Strengths: Simple implementation, generates organic-looking structures, low memory footprint due to bit-packing. Limitations: Limited to spherical primitives, no internal structure (hollow branches), random variation may lead to non-physical overlaps. Use for background vegetation, low-poly trees, or when procedural generation is required without external assets. Not suitable for high-fidelity, detailed tree models requiring complex geometry or internal structure. The method is based on L-systems, introduced by Aristid Lindenmayer in 1968 to model plant development. The specific voxel implementation is derived from the OpenGL Voxel Splatting project by Brian Paul (2007). L-systems have been widely used in procedural architectural modeling and city layout generation, such as by Parish & Müller (2001). The voxel-based approach adapts these concepts to volumetric rendering, using sphere splatting to represent branches. Procedural vegetation in voxel-based games and simulations.
