name: Cartoon Noise Lattice Generation
head: Cartoon Noise Set Generation, Macro/Body/Edge/Flow Lattice Generation
body: Cartoon Noise Lattice Generation produces independent, tileable noise lattices for cartoon-style cloud rendering by separating noise into four distinct functional groups: macro (outline), body (fill), edge (detail), and flow (disturbance). The method generates multiple specialized lattices with specific frequency constraints to ensure stability and avoid fixed-direction ripple artifacts, building on Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex). Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A MaskParameters object containing resolution (512, 1024, or 2048), global height bounds (globalmincm, globalmaxcm), weather type, seed, coverage percentage, cloud region count, and optional CloudHeightRule configurations. Outputs: A CartoonNoiseSet dataclass containing four tuples of numpy arrays: macrolattices, bodylattices, edgelattices, and flowlattices. Data Structures: 1. MaskParameters: resolution: int (512, 1024, or 2048). globalmincm, globalmaxcm: int defining the vertical volume bounds. seed: int for deterministic generation. cloudregioncount: int (1–500). cloudheightrules: tuple[CloudHeightRule,...]. 2. CloudHeightRule: typeid: int. centermincm, centermaxcm: int defining the target center height range. heightdeltamincm, heightdeltamaxcm: int defining the minimum and maximum height difference for the volume box. 3. CartoonNoiseSet: macrolattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...]. bodylattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...]. edgelattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...]. flowlattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...]. Algorithm Steps: 1. Validate Parameters: Ensure resolution is in {512, 1024, 2048}, globalmaxcm > globalmincm, and 0 <= coveragepercent <= 100. 2. Generate Height Rules: For each cloud type, determine vertical bounds. If a CloudHeightRule is provided, sample centermincm and centermaxcm via rng.integers. Otherwise, derive bounds from legacy constants: (0.62, 0.92) for typeid == 10, (0.22, 0.58) for others. Calculate deltamin and deltamax using VOLUMEBOXHEIGHTMULTIPLIER applied to the span. 3. Generate Lattices: Call makenoiselattices for each of the four groups (macro, body, edge, flow) with specific frequencies to ensure they are small, stable, and avoid fixed-direction ripple artifacts. 4. Construct Set: Pack the resulting tuples into the CartoonNoiseSet dataclass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from dataclasses import dataclass @dataclass(frozen=True) class CloudHeightRule: typeid: int centermincm: int centermaxcm: int heightdeltamincm: int heightdeltamaxcm: int @dataclass(frozen=True) class MaskParameters: resolution: int = 1024 globalmincm: int = 0 globalmaxcm: int = 1500000 seed: int = 20260826 coveragepercent: int = 45 cloudregioncount: int = 1 cloudheightrules: tuple[CloudHeightRule,...] = () @dataclass(frozen=True) class CartoonNoiseSet: macrolattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...] bodylattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...] edgelattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...] flowlattices: tuple[np.ndarray,...] def makenoiselattices(grouptype: str, params: MaskParameters, rng: np.random.Generator) -> tuple[np.ndarray,...]: """ Generates lattices for a specific group (macro, body, edge, flow). Uses specific frequencies to ensure stability and avoid artifacts. The actual noise lattice generation kernel using group-specific frequencies is not detailed in the sources. """ # The actual noise lattice generation kernel using group-specific frequencies is not detailed in the sources. pass def generatecartoonnoiselattices(params: MaskParameters) -> CartoonNoiseSet: if params.resolution not in (512, 1024, 2048): raise ValueError("Resolution must be 512, 1024, or 2048.") if params.globalmaxcm <= params.globalmincm: raise ValueError("Max height must be greater than min height.") if not (0 <= params.coveragepercent <= 100): raise ValueError("Coverage percent must be between 0 and 100.") rng = np.random.defaultrng(params.seed) macrolattices = makenoiselattices("macro", params, rng) bodylattices = makenoiselattices("body", params, rng) edgelattices = makenoiselattices("edge", params, rng) flowlattices = makenoiselattices("flow", params, rng) return CartoonNoiseSet( macrolattices=macrolattices, bodylattices=bodylattices, edgelattices=edgelattices, flowlattices=flowlattices) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Constraints: Only 512, 1024, and 2048 are supported. Height Bounds: globalmaxcm must be strictly greater than globalmincm. Artifact Avoidance: Frequencies must be carefully selected per group to prevent fixed-direction ripple artifacts. A variant that computes a coherent flow field by combining the generated lattices. It clips the weighted sum of flow, macro, and body noise channels: coherent = np.clip(0.58 flow + 0.27 macro + 0.15 body, 0.0, 1.0). It then modulates this coherent flow around the center value 0.5 by a strength parameter: return np.clip(0.5 + (coherent - 0.5) strength, 0.0, 1.0). This output drives disturbance in the cloud volume. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces stable, tileable noise suitable for cartoon-style rendering by separating concerns into macro, body, edge, and flow groups. Limitations: Requires specific resolution support (512, 1024, 2048) and relies on hardcoded legacy constants for height rules if not explicitly configured. Originated in the open-source project Noise-Cloud by mingtu149411. The method addresses visual artifacts of standard noise in cloud rendering by decomposing the noise field into specialized components. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Aperiodic Tiling with Edge Matching
head: Aperiodic mapping, Edge-matching triangular patterns
body: A method to avoid repetitivity when mapping pre-shaded texture cells onto a terrain or volume surface by enforcing aperiodic boundary conditions and edge-matching constraints. It differs from standard periodic tiling by correlating twin edges to prevent seams, and from noise-based tiling by relying on pre-computed geometric patterns rather than procedural generation at render time. It builds on Specific Procedural Patterns and Applications and contrasts with Sine-based procedural voxel generation, Spherical Density Ramp with Noise, Mandelbulb Fractal Generation, and Volumetric Density Generation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of pre-shaded triangular tile patterns and a spatial coordinate system. Output: A seamless, non-repeating texture map for terrain or volume rendering. Data Structures: Reference Texture: A 2D image containing the 8 triangular tiles arranged to satisfy edge constraints. Tile Selection Logic: A mapping from spatial coordinates to one of the 8 tile types based on aperiodic triplet selection. Steps: 1. Define Boundary Conditions: Assume 2 different boundary conditions in each of the 3 directions of a triangular tiling, yielding 8 possible triplets and 16 possible triangles (pointing north or south). 2. Select Subset: Choose a subset of 8 triangles (4 north, 4 south) to save memory, ensuring each triplet is used once without breaking aperiodicity. 3. Arrange Reference Texture: Place the 8 tiles in the reference texture such that edge constraints are met, ensuring each edge kind appears twice as "twin edges". 4. Shear and Wrap: Apply a shear transformation to the pattern to convert the natural slanted wrapping (where bottom and top triangles share an edge) into a square wrapping tractable by hardware textures. 5. Build Patterns (Content Placement): Enforce that objects crossing an edge axis are replicated on the twin edge, making neighborhoods correlated but not identical. Ensure objects never cross two edges (e.g., corners) to avoid correlating them and replicating on half the cells. Place trees crossing boundaries first (replicated on twin edges), starting with one tree close to a corner (not crossing 2 edges) to avoid vicinity bias. Freely place other trees, constrained only by not crossing the triangle tile boundary. Formulas: Shear Transformation: \mathbf{v}' = \mathbf{M}{shear} \mathbf{v}, where \mathbf{v} = [x, y]^T is a vertex coordinate, \mathbf{v}' is the transformed coordinate, and \mathbf{M}{shear} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & k \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} with k as the shear factor. Parameters: Number of Tiles: 8 triangles (4 north, 4 south) are sufficient for aperiodicity. 16 triangles can be used for higher variability. Texture Resolution: Not given in the sources, but must support the sheared square wrapping. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Linear Interpolation: At tile borders, hardware linear interpolation blends outside color with inside color, causing artifacts if the reference texture is not arranged to make twin edges coherent. Corner Crossing: Objects crossing two edges (corners) must be avoided, as this correlates edges and causes replication on half the cells. Pre-shading Limitation: Patterns are pre-shaded, so they cannot be rotated at render time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleaperiodictiling(u, v, referencetexture): # Map continuous coordinates to one of the 8 triangular tiles # based on aperiodic triplet selection tileidx = computetileindex(u, v) tile = referencetexture.tiles[tileidx] # Apply inverse shear to convert square-wrapped coordinates back to slanted space # for correct coordinate mapping within the triangular tile sheark = 0.5 localu = u - sheark v localv = v # Sample the texture. Hardware linear interpolation handles coherence # between twin edges return referencetexture.sample(localu, localv) def computetileindex(u, v): # Determine which of the 8 tiles covers the point based on # the 3-direction triangular tiling grid # Implementation depends on specific grid layout gridu = int(u) % 8 gridv = int(v) % 8 return (gridu + gridv) % 8 Time Complexity: Constant time per sample, assuming efficient tile lookup. The shearing and wrapping are pre-computed. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of tiles (8 or 16) and their resolution. Strengths: Eliminates visible repetition in large terrains/volumes without requiring complex procedural noise at render time. Compatible with hardware linear filtering if built correctly. Limitations: Requires pre-shading, limiting dynamic lighting. Manual placement of objects in tiles is required to avoid artifacts. Limited variability compared to fully procedural methods. When to Use: Real-time rendering of large, static or semi-static scenes (e.g., forests) where repetition is noticeable and pre-shading is acceptable. When Not to Use: Dynamic lighting scenarios, or when high variability and organic randomness are required without pre-computation. Originated in the context of rendering forest scenes in real-time, specifically to avoid repetitivity when mapping texcells onto a terrain. The method relies on the aperiodic scheme described in [NC99] and is discussed in detail in. It addresses the limitation of pre-shaded textures, which cannot be rotated, by using separate boundary conditions in each direction. Scenes are lit by fixed directional lights with precomputed shading stored in the textures. Rendering Forest Scenes in Real-Time, https://doi.org/10.2312/egwr/egsr04/093-102, fetched 2026-10-26

name: TGorillaVolumetricNoise
head: Volumetric Noise, cloud / smoke / fog body
body: TGorillaVolumetricNoise is a procedural volume component that generates a 3D texture using fractal Brownian motion (FBM) Perlin noise and renders it as a physically based emission-absorption medium. It solves the problem of creating believable, fly-through clouds, smoke, or fog without requiring external data files or custom shader code. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by baking a smooth 0..1 density gradient into the voxel data while applying opacity via a render-time Beer-Lambert blend, thereby avoiding the terracing artifacts common in naive voxel density approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Parent viewport, size (default 1×1×1), resolution (default 64³), and shaping parameters (Frequency, Octaves, Persistence, Lacunarity, Coverage, EdgeFalloff, Billowy, Seed). Outputs: A 3D texture (volume data) uploaded to the GPU and rendered as a volumetric mesh. Data Structures: The core data structure is a 3D texture where each voxel stores a single floating-point value representing a smooth density gradient in the range [0, 1]. This value is not the final opacity; it acts as a shape mask. Parameters: Frequency (Single): Base noise scale. Higher values produce smaller, more numerous noise cycles. Octaves (Integer): Number of FBM octaves summed. More octaves add finer detail but increase generation time. Persistence (Single): Amplitude falloff per octave (range 0–1). Lower values yield smoother noise; higher values yield rougher noise. Lacunarity (Single): Frequency growth per octave (typically ~2.0). Coverage (Single): Soft threshold (0–1). Value 1 keeps the whole body; lower values carve the body into separate puffs. EdgeFalloff (Single): Radial fade (0–1) toward the volume border to create a rounded blob shape instead of a filled cube. Billowy (Boolean): If True, applies abs() to the noise for a puffy cumulus/smoke look; if False, produces smooth haze. Density (Single): Overall opacity/absorption strength. This is not baked into the voxel data but applied at render time. RenderInside (Boolean): Default True. Allows the camera to move inside the cloud with correct compositing. UseLighting (Boolean): Default False. Volumetric noise is an emission-absorption medium, not a lit surface. Offset (Point3D): Used for animation drift. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the instance, set the parent, size, assign FrontFaceRenderPass and BackFaceRenderPass, allow control, and apply a preset. 2. Noise Generation: For each voxel in the 3D grid, calculate the base Perlin noise value at the voxel's position scaled by Frequency and shifted by Offset. Apply FBM summation: sum the noise values across Octaves, scaling amplitude by Persistence and frequency by Lacunarity per octave. If Billowy is True, apply abs() to the resulting FBM sum. 3. Shaping: Apply Coverage as a soft threshold to carve the noise field into separate puffs. Apply EdgeFalloff as a radial fade toward the volume border to create a rounded blob shape. 4. Storage: Store the resulting smooth 0..1 gradient in the 3D texture; do not bake the final opacity into the voxel data. 5. Rendering: During ray marching, use the stored voxel value as a density mask and apply the Density parameter as the absorption coefficient in the Beer-Lambert emission-absorption blend to compute opacity and color at render time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatevolumetricnoise(width, height, depth, frequency, octaves, persistence, lacunarity, coverage, edgefalloff, billowy, seed): # Initialize standard 3D Perlin noise generator with seed perlin = PerlinNoise(seed) volume = [[0.0] depth for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): for z in range(depth): nx = x / width ny = y / height nz = z / depth fbmvalue = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 currentfreq = 1.0 for i in range(octaves): fbmvalue += amplitude perlin.noise( nx frequency currentfreq, ny frequency currentfreq, nz frequency currentfreq) amplitude = persistence currentfreq = lacunarity if billowy: fbmvalue = abs(fbmvalue) # Coverage as a soft threshold density = max(0.0, fbmvalue - (1.0 - coverage)) # EdgeFalloff radial fade dist = math.sqrt((nx - 0.5)2 + (ny - 0.5)2 + (nz - 0.5)2) maxdist = math.sqrt(0.75) normalizeddist = dist / maxdist edgefactor = max(0.0, 1.0 - normalizeddist edgefalloff) density = edgefactor volume[y][x][z] = min(1.0, max(0.0, density)) return volume Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Terracing Artifacts: Naïve approaches that bake final density/opacity into voxel data and use linear blending produce hard saturation "shells" or step terraces when viewed from inside. This is solved by storing a smooth 0..1 gradient and applying opacity at render time via emission-absorption blend. Performance: Regenerate re-samples the whole volume on the CPU and is expensive. For animation, use a smaller resolution (e.g., 32³) and update on a timer (~100 ms) rather than every frame. Lighting: UseLighting should remain False for standard volumetric noise. Lit clouds require a separate "light-marching" feature. Generation Cost: Generation is CPU-bound and requires re-sampling the entire volume on the CPU when parameters change or animation drifts. Resolution Independence: Density appearance is resolution-independent; a cloud at 32³ looks comparably dense to one at 64³ for the same Density value. Strengths: No external data files or shader code required; fly-through capability with correct compositing; cheap runtime opacity adjustment via Density. Limitations: CPU-bound regeneration makes high-resolution animation expensive; lacks built-in lighting. When to use: For static or slowly drifting clouds, smoke, or fog where performance allows for CPU regeneration or lower resolutions are acceptable. When not to use: For high-frequency animated smoke requiring high resolution, as CPU regeneration becomes too expensive; use a smaller resolution (e.g., 32³) or a different method instead. For lit volumetric clouds, use light-marching instead. TGorillaVolumetricNoise is part of the Gorilla3D framework. It is designed to provide a "ready-to-use" cloud/smoke/fog body with a handful of properties, abstracting away the need for shader code or data files. It builds on the principles of Procedural and implicit volumes and Volumetric Mesh. Volumetric Noise - Gorilla3D Framework - Documentation, https://gorilla3d.de/doc/v3/version/v1.4/page/Core/Volumetric/Volumetric-Noise.md, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Noise-based Density Generation
head: Procedural Noise Density, Noise Field Generation
body: Noise-based Density Generation creates volumetric density fields by evaluating procedural noise functions at query points. It solves the problem of defining complex, organic material distributions (such as fire, clouds, or smoke) without the memory overhead of storing explicit voxel grids. It differs from its siblings by serving as the foundational mathematical primitive for procedural volumes, whereas specific implementations like Perlin-Worley Noise or Cartoon Cloud Density Generation apply specific compositional strategies to these primitives. The family shares the following mechanism, terms, and math: 1. Gradient Assignment: Each integer lattice point (vertex) in the domain is assigned a pseudo-random gradient vector \mathbf{g}. In 3D, common sets include 12 face diagonals of a cube or 12 axis-aligned vectors. 2. Dot Product Contribution: The noise value at a query point \mathbf{P} is derived from the dot product between the gradient vector \mathbf{g}i at a lattice corner i and the distance vector \mathbf{d}i = \mathbf{P} - \mathbf{V}i from that corner to \mathbf{P}: ni = \mathbf{g}i \cdot \mathbf{d}i 3. Smoothing/Fade Function: To ensure smooth transitions (C^1 continuity), the fractional coordinates of \mathbf{P} within the cell are passed through a fade function f(t) before interpolation. The quintic function f(t) = 6t^5 - 15t^4 + 10t^3 is standard for Perlin variants, while Simplex uses a different geometric approach. 4. Interpolation: The contributions from the cell corners are combined using linear interpolation (lerp) along the axes, weighted by the fade values. 5. Hashing: Integer coordinates are mapped to gradient indices using a permutation table to avoid modulo operations and ensure uniform distribution. Generates real-time procedural volumetric fire by combining a 2D fire profile texture with procedural noise functions (specifically Improved Perlin Noise and Voronoi Noise) to create micro-level flame details. It sets itself apart by using a lattice-based volume representation driven by noise for micro-interactivity, distinct from pure volumetric ray-marching. Generates base density for volumetric clouds by combining the structural continuity of Perlin noise with the billowy, cellular detail of Worley noise. It differs by using Worley noise to modulate the amplitude of Perlin noise, creating organic shapes with high-frequency billowiness at the edges. Generates cartoon-style cloud densities by combining independent multi-octave noise sets with geometric envelopes specific to cloud types. It differs from Blocky Volumetric Clouds by using independent noise sets for the base structure rather than a static 2D density map. The underlying gradient noise algorithms (Perlin and Simplex) were introduced by Ken Perlin in 1985 and 2001 respectively to provide coherent random fields for computer graphics. These methods replaced earlier value noise techniques to eliminate grid-aligned artifacts. The application of these noise functions to procedural density generation for volumes like fire and clouds became standard in real-time rendering pipelines in the 2000s and 2010s, allowing for dynamic, infinite-resolution textures without storage costs. Ken Perlin, "An Image Synthesizer," SIGGRAPH 1985. Ken Perlin, "An Image Synthesizer," SIGGRAPH 1985.

name: Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation
head: Texture Coordinate Perturbation, Noise-warped volume rendering, Procedural Volumetric Perturbation, Volume Perturbation via Procedural Noise, Volume Perturbation via Texture Coordinate Displacement
body: Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation enhances coarse, low-resolution volumetric data by superimposing high-frequency details using a small, tiled procedural noise volume. It solves the problem of missing microstructure (e.g., wispy clouds, fur, smoke) without increasing the underlying voxel resolution or computational cost of the base volume. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Worley Noise or Gradient-based Noise (Perlin/Simplex) by applying noise not as a direct density scalar, but as a displacement field or optical modifier, effectively warping the sampling domain or material properties. Inputs: 1. Macrostructure Volume: A low-resolution 3D texture (voxel dataset) representing the coarse density or scalar field. 2. Perturbation Volume: A small 3D texture (typically 32 \times 32 \times 32) initialized with random noise. 3. Transfer Function: Maps scalar density to optical properties (color, opacity). 4. Parameters: kNoiseDim: Integer dimension of the cubic noise volume (typically 32). noiseScale: Scaling factor for the perturbation amplitude. coordPerturb: Boolean/weight enabling coordinate perturbation. propPerturb: Boolean/weight enabling optical property perturbation. time: Animation time offset. flowSpeed: Speed of animation. Outputs: A rendered image with high-frequency procedural details superimposed on the coarse volume. Data Structures: Perturbation Volume: Format: 3D texture, 8-bit unsigned normalized integer per channel (RGBA8). Dimensions: kNoiseDim \times kNoiseDim \times kNoiseDim (e.g., 32^3). Content: Each texel stores four random 8-bit numbers. Filtering: Slightly blurred to hide artifacts from trilinear interpolation. Addressing: Repeat (wrap) mode to allow tiling. Push Constants (Vulkan Example): mvp: 4 \times 4 matrix (Model-View-Projection). params: vec4 containing [time, noiseScale, coordPerturb, propPerturb]. params2: vec4 containing [opacityCorrection, flowSpeed,...]. Steps: 1. Generate Perturbation Volume: Create a 3D texture of size kNoiseDim^3. Initialize each voxel with four random 8-bit values (RGBA). Apply a slight blur to the volume to mitigate trilinear interpolation artifacts. 2. Compute Perturbation Field (Pre-pass or Shader): Due to hardware limits on simultaneous textures and dependent texture reads, an additional pass is often required before the main volume shading. For each pixel/fragment, sample multiple copies of the perturbation volume at different scales. Let Ni be the noise sample at scale i. Compute the weighted sum of noise components to form a displacement vector \mathbf{D}: \mathbf{D} = \sumi wi \cdot Ni where wi are weights for each scale. Low Frequency: Achieved by applying the perturbation texture once with large amplitude. High Frequency: Achieved by applying the perturbation texture again with low amplitude, relying on texture repetition (wrapping) to create fine detail. 3. Apply Perturbation (Two Approaches): Approach 1: Coordinate Perturbation (Geometry/Density Warping) 1. Take the original texture coordinates \mathbf{T} for the volume data lookup. 2. Use three components of the noise vector \mathbf{D} (e.g., RGB) as a displacement vector. 3. Compute perturbed coordinates: \mathbf{T}{perturbed} = \mathbf{T} + \mathbf{D} \cdot \text{scale} 4. Perform a dependent texture read on the Macrostructure Volume using \mathbf{T}{perturbed}. 5. Render the result to a pixel buffer (render-to-texture) to be used in subsequent shading steps. 6. Note: This avoids recomputing gradients on a perturbed grid, which is required for surface shading but not for volume raycasting/shading. Approach 2: Optical Property Perturbation 1. Evaluate the transfer function on the original volume data to get base optical properties (color, opacity). 2. Use all four per-pixel noise components (RGBA) to modify these optical properties. 3. The user selects which specific optical properties (e.g., opacity, color channels) are modified. 4. This creates inhomogeneities and subtle iridescence effects. 4. Animate: Add a varying offset vector to the noise texture coordinates in the fragment shader. Update the offset each frame using time and flowSpeed. Different offsets can be added to each noise texture copy to enhance motion complexity. Pseudocode (Fragment Shader Logic): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. vec3 perturbation = vec3(0.0); float scale = uparams.y; # noiseScale float time = uparams.x; float flow = uparams2.y; # flowSpeed vec3 coord1 = vtexcoord 0.5 + vec3(time flow, 0.0, 0.0); vec4 noise1 = texture(unoisevolume, coord1); perturbation += noise1.rgb 2.0; # Large amplitude vec3 coord2 = vtexcoord 2.0 + vec3(time flow 0.5, 0.0, 0.0); vec4 noise2 = texture(unoisevolume, coord2); perturbation += noise2.rgb 0.5; # Small amplitude vec4 color = vec4(0.0); float opacity = 0.0; if (uparams.z > 0.5) { # Coordinate Perturbation # Warp the lookup coordinate vec3 perturbedcoord = vtexcoord + perturbation scale; # Dependent texture read float density = texture(umacrovolume, perturbedcoord).r; # Evaluate transfer function vec4 tfresult = texture(utransferfunc, density); color = tfresult; opacity = tfresult.a; } else { # Optical Property Perturbation # Standard lookup float density = texture(umacrovolume, vtexcoord).r; vec4 tfresult = texture(utransferfunc, density); # Modify optical properties with noise # e.g., modulate opacity and color with noise components float noisemod = noise1.r; # Use one component as example color.rgb = tfresult.rgb (1.0 + noisemod 0.2); color.a = tfresult.a (1.0 + noisemod 0.1); opacity = color.a; } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Trilinear Interpolation Artifacts: The perturbation volume must be blurred slightly to prevent visible artifacts caused by linear interpolation of the random noise values. Hardware Limits: Modern GPUs limit the number of simultaneously applied textures and sequential dependent texture reads. This necessitates an additional render-to-texture pass to store the perturbed data before final shading. Gradient Recomputation: If using surface shading on perturbed volumes, gradients must be recomputed based on the perturbed grid. This method avoids that cost by perturbing the data access location directly. Fog Animation generates the appearance of moving gaseous volumes by perturbing the spatial coordinates of the evaluation point before sampling a static turbulence function, effectively moving the point through a "solid space" texture. Unlike methods that animate the noise function itself, this approach creates motion by shifting the sampling domain, producing upward-swirling gas movement suitable for real-time fog and smoke. It builds on Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation [1370-procedural-volume-rendering-with-noise-perturbation.md] by applying coordinate perturbation specifically to transparency-based fog effects. Time Complexity: Adds a constant overhead per fragment for sampling the perturbation volume at multiple scales. The additional render-to-texture pass adds one full-screen pass per frame. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the small perturbation volume (32^3 \times 4 bytes = 128 KB) and potentially an intermediate render target for the perturbed data. Performance: On hardware like NVIDIA GeForce 3 and ATI Radeon 8500, frame rates were only 50-60% slower than volume rendering with no shading, leveraging OpenGL render-to-texture extensions to avoid costly copy operations. Detail Equivalence: The visual detail produced is equivalent to an unperturbed voxel dataset of at least 100 times the resolution. Strengths: Efficiently adds high-frequency detail (clouds, smoke, fur) to coarse volumes without increasing voxel count or simulation cost. Limitations: Requires additional rendering passes due to texture read limits; artifacts can occur if the perturbation volume is not properly filtered. The technique was introduced by Kniss et al. in 2002 as part of "Interactive Translucent Volume Rendering and Procedural Modeling". It adapts Ebert's lattice-based noise approach for clouds and Peachey's vector-based noise simulation to interactive volume rendering. It is detailed in GPU Gems Chapter 39 and implemented in various open-source projects. sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, https://github.com/sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Interactive Translucent Volume Rendering and Procedural Modeling, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/knissvolumeshading02.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 GPU Gems ch39, Volume rendering techniques, https://developer.nvidia.com/sites/all/modules/custom/gpugems/books/GPUGems/gpugemsch39.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Fog Animation
head: Solid Space Animation: Moving Point
body: Fog Animation generates the appearance of moving gaseous volumes by perturbing the spatial coordinates of the evaluation point before sampling a static turbulence function, effectively moving the point through a "solid space" texture. Unlike methods that animate the noise function itself, this approach creates motion by shifting the sampling domain, producing upward-swirling gas movement suitable for real-time fog and smoke. It builds on Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation [1370-procedural-volume-rendering-with-noise-perturbation.md] by applying coordinate perturbation specifically to transparency-based fog effects. Inputs: pnt: 3D point in world space (x, y, z). framenum: Integer current animation frame. transp: Output pointer to a float representing transparency. Parameters: SWIRLFRAMES: Integer controlling the period of the helical swirl. Typical value: 126. SWIRLAMOUNT: Float controlling the speed of the swirling effect. Typical value: 2\pi/126 (implied by modulo arithmetic for a full rotation). RAD1: Float, radius of the helix in the X direction. Typical value: 0.5. RAD2: Float, radius of the helix in the Z direction. Typical value: 2.0. DOWNAMOUNT: Float, downward movement speed per frame. Typical value: 0.01. turbulence(p, scale): Function returning a scalar noise value at point p with frequency scale. noiseit(p): Function returning a scalar noise value at point p. Data Structures: direction: 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the final sampling coordinate. cyl: 3D vector (x, y, z) representing cylindrical helical offset. tmp: Float scalar used for intermediate noise storage. Steps: 1. Perturb Input Point: Modify the input point pnt to introduce local turbulence and drift. pnt.x \leftarrow pnt.x + 2.0 + \text{turbulence}(pnt, 0.1) tmp \leftarrow \text{noise\it}(pnt) pnt.y \leftarrow pnt.y + 4.0 + tmp pnt.z \leftarrow pnt.z - 2.0 - tmp 2. Calculate Helical Path Components: Determine the position on a helix based on the current frame. \theta \leftarrow (\text{frame\num} \pmod{\text{SWIRL\FRAMES}}) \times \text{SWIRL\AMOUNT} cyl.x \leftarrow \text{RAD1} \times \cos(\theta) cyl.z \leftarrow \text{RAD2} \times \sin(\theta) 3. Calculate Direction Vector: Combine the perturbed point with the helical offset and a downward drift. direction.x \leftarrow pnt.x + cyl.x direction.y \leftarrow pnt.y - (\text{frame\num} \times \text{DOWN\AMOUNT}) direction.z \leftarrow pnt.z + cyl.z 4. Calculate Transparency: Sample turbulence at the direction vector and apply non-linear transformations to map the result to a transparency value. t \leftarrow \text{turbulence}(direction, 0.015) t \leftarrow 1.0 - (t \times t \times 0.275) \text{transp} \leftarrow t \times t \times t Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SWIRLFRAMES = 126 SWIRLAMOUNT = 2.0 math.pi / SWIRLFRAMES RAD1 = 0.5 RAD2 = 2.0 DOWNAMOUNT = 0.01 def turbulence(p, scale): """Returns a scalar turbulence value at point p with frequency scale.""" pass # Implementation depends on available noise library def noiseit(p): """Returns a scalar noise value at point p.""" pass # Implementation depends on available noise library class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def foganimation(pnt, framenum): # Step 1: Perturb input point pntx = pnt.x + 2.0 + turbulence(pnt, 0.1) tmp = noiseit(pnt) pnty = pnt.y + 4.0 + tmp pntz = pnt.z - 2.0 - tmp # Step 2: Calculate helical path components theta = (framenum % SWIRLFRAMES) SWIRLAMOUNT cylx = RAD1 math.cos(theta) cylz = RAD2 math.sin(theta) # Step 3: Calculate direction vector directionx = pntx + cylx directiony = pnty - (framenum DOWNAMOUNT) directionz = pntz + cylz # Step 4: Calculate transparency t = turbulence(Vector3(directionx, directiony, directionz), 0.015) t = 1.0 - (t t 0.275) transp = t t t return transp Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The cubic mapping of transparency (t^3) can result in very low values for small t, potentially causing fog to disappear if the turbulence amplitude is low. Boundary Conditions: The modulo operation on framenum ensures the swirl repeats every SWIRLFRAMES. If framenum is negative, ensure the modulo operator behaves correctly for the target language (e.g., Python's % vs C++'s %). Noise Function Dependency: The method relies on noiseit and turbulence. A variant that animates marble textures by simulating heating and cooling effects. It calculates a glowpercent based on framenum, startframe, endframe, and heatlength. If outside the heat range, glowpercent=0. In the start heating phase, glowpercent = 1.0 - ease(((startframe+heatlength/2-framenum)/heatlength), 0.4, 0.6). In the end cooling phase, glowpercent = ease(((framenum-(endframe-heatlength/2))/heatlength), 0.4, 0.6). Otherwise, glowpercent=1.0. Turbulence is applied with ease-in/ease-out: turbpercent=ease(turbpercent, 0.3, 0.7). The color is computed as marblecolor(sin((pnt.y + turbpercent3.0turbulence(pnt,.0125) - displacement)MPI)) and blended with a glow color (R:1.0, G:0.4, B:0.8) weighted by 0.5glowpercent. A variant that moves the point along a helical path to create a swirling marble effect. It calculates a displacement based on framenum relative to startframe and endframe. A helical path is computed using theta = (framenum%SWIRLFRAMES)SWIRLAMOUNT, with radii RAD1 and RAD2, and downward drift DOWNAMOUNT. Randomness is added via fastnoise(pnt). The final color is marblecolor(sin((pnt.y + 3.0turbulence(direction,.0125))MPI)) where direction is the sum of pnt and the helical path. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, assuming constant-time noise evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1), as it does not require storing volume data or large lookup tables, only static parameters. Performance: Suitable for real-time rendering due to its procedural nature and lack of ray-marching or grid traversal. Strengths: Simple to implement, low memory footprint, produces organic, swirling motion without animating the noise field itself. Limitations: The motion is constrained to the specific helical and drift patterns defined; less flexible than general noise animation. The method originates from procedural modeling research on gases, fluids, and textures. It was introduced as a technique for animating solid space functions to create realistic fog and smoke effects by moving the evaluation point through a static texture space. The approach is similar to Gardner's cloud technique but uses turbulence for transparency control instead of Fourier synthesis. Procedural Modeling, Animation, and Rendering of Gases, Fluids, and Textures, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/2786953ProceduralModelingAnimationandRenderingofGasesFluidsandTextures/links/00b7d51a73e42a3c4e000000/Procedural-Modeling-Animation-and-Rendering-of-Gases-Fluids-and-Textures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Noise-based 2D Fire
head: 2D Fire Texture Generation, Voronoi-Perlin Fire Noise
body: Noise-based 2D Fire is a procedural technique for generating the base density and color texture of volumetric fire, serving as the input for constructing 3D cylindrical fire volumes. It distinguishes itself from sprite-based systems by providing a continuous, artifact-free texture that supports dynamic scaling without stretching, and from photo-realistic fluid simulations by offering real-time performance with artist-controllable aesthetics. The method typically combines multiple noise functions (such as Perlin and Voronoi) to create turbulent micro-details, which are then mapped onto a 2D profile to drive the visual appearance of the flame. The method generates a 2D texture that defines the fire's shape, color, and intensity. This texture is subsequently used to map colors onto a 3D lattice surrounding a central curve. The generation involves creating noise fields, combining them, and applying a color gradient. Inputs: Noise parameters: frequency, scale, time offset, and type (e.g., Perlin, Voronoi, M-Noise). Application-specific frequency factor for spatial detail scaling. Perceived burning speed parameter. A standard UV coordinate system for the 2D texture space. Outputs: A 2D color texture (Fire Profile Texture) where pixel values represent the fire's color and intensity. Noise Space: A coordinate system (x, y, t) where x and y are spatial dimensions and t is time. The z dimension is not used in the 2D noise generation itself but is implied in the final 3D mapping. Fire Profile Texture: A 2D image buffer storing RGBA values. The horizontal axis represents the radial distance from the fire center, and the vertical axis represents the height along the fire. 1. Generate Noise Fields: Generate a Perlin noise field (or Improved Perlin Noise/M-Noise) for turbulent detail. Generate a Voronoi noise field for cellular structure. Note: M-Noise is a GPU-optimized variant of Perlin Noise that avoids chained table lookups to prevent bottlenecks. 2. Scale and Offset Noise Space: To prevent stretching artifacts when the fire radius or length changes, dynamically scale the noise space. Scale the horizontal (x) and vertical (y) axes of the noise space by the fire's radius and length, respectively. Multiply the scaled noise coordinates by an application-specific frequency factor to adjust the level of detail. Correct each noise function to have a base frequency of one, ensuring the frequency factor represents the spatial frequency of micro-level detail in world space. Add a time offset to the vertical axis (e.g., -time) to create an upward flow effect. Add a unique constant offset to the noise position for each fire instance to ensure uniqueness. 3. Combine Noise Functions: Multiply the Voronoi noise texture by the Perlin noise texture. Alternative: Use only Improved Perlin Noise or M-Noise for turbulence if Voronoi is not required. 4. Modify UV Coordinates: Interpolate the product of the combined noises with a standard UV texture to create a modified UV coordinate. Note: This step warps the sampling coordinates based on the noise values to create organic, fire-like variations. 5. Sample Fire Profile: Sample a single Gaussian blob using the modified UV coordinates to create fire-like density variations. Alternatively, map the 3D unit fire volume coordinates to the 2D texture using the transformation defined in the formulas below. 6. Apply Color Gradient: Apply a color gradient to the result to give the fire its characteristic orange (or other desired) color. Artists can customize the look by editing the Fire Profile Texture directly (e.g., coloring it blue for magical fire). The mapping from the 3D unit fire volume to the 2D Fire Profile Texture is defined by: \vec{uv} = \left( \sqrt{texx^2 + texy^2}, texz \right) color = \text{FireProfileTexture}(\vec{uv}) Where: \vec{uv} is the 2D positional vector sampled in the fire profile texture. texx, texy are the horizontal coordinates in the unit fire volume, ranging from [-1, 1]. texz is the vertical coordinate in the unit fire volume, ranging from [0, 1]. \sqrt{texx^2 + texy^2} represents the radial distance from the center axis. The noise space scaling for dynamic resizing is described by: The noise position \mathbf{P}{noise} is calculated by scaling the unit fire volume texture coordinates by a noisescale factor, which is derived from the fire's radius and length. The fourth dimension (time) is added to enable 4D noise animation. Frequency: Controls the spatial frequency of micro-level detail. Scaled to world coordinates to eliminate stretching. Burning Speed: A parameter passed to the pixel shader to control the rate of temporal change (flicker). Time Offset: Used to create upward flow; the vertical axis is offset by -time. Instance Offset: A constant added to the noise position for each fire instance to ensure uniqueness. Stretching Artifacts: If the noise space is not dynamically scaled according to the fire's radius and length, enlarging the fire will cause visible stretching artifacts. Performance Bottlenecks: Standard Perlin Noise may cause bottlenecks on GPUs due to chained table lookups. M-Noise is recommended for hardware acceleration. Boundary Conditions: The unit fire volume has specific coordinate ranges (x,y \in [-1,1], z \in [0,1]). Sampling outside these ranges requires clamping or wrapping logic in the texture lookup. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatenoise2dfire(width, height, radius, length, time, frequency, burningspeed, instanceoffset): """ Generates a 2D fire texture using combined noise functions. Args: width (int): Width of the output texture. height (int): Height of the output texture. radius (float): Current radius of the fire. length (float): Current length of the fire. time (float): Current simulation time. frequency (float): Application-specific spatial frequency. burningspeed (float): Parameter controlling flicker speed. instanceoffset (float): Unique offset for this fire instance. Returns: numpy.ndarray: 2D array of RGB colors representing the fire texture. """ # Initialize output texture texture = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) # Pre-calculate scale factors to prevent stretching # Scale noise space by radius and length scalex = radius scaley = length # Iterate over each pixel in the texture for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Normalize pixel coordinates to [0, 1] u = x / width v = y / height # Map to noise space coordinates # Note: The exact mapping from UV to noise space depends on the specific implementation. # Based on, we scale by radius and length. # Assuming u corresponds to radial direction and v to vertical. # Calculate base noise coordinates # Correct for base frequency of one noisex = u frequency / scalex noisey = v frequency / scaley # Add time offset for upward flow (negative time for upward movement) # Add instance offset for uniqueness noisey -= time burningspeed noisey += instanceoffset # Generate Perlin Noise (or M-Noise) # This function should return a value in [-1, 1] or [0, 1] perlinval = improvedperlinnoise(noisex, noisey) # Generate Voronoi Noise voronoival = voronoinoise(noisex, noisey) # Combine noises: Multiply Voronoi and Perlin combinednoise = perlinval voronoival # Modify UV coordinates (interpolate product with standard UV) # This step warps the sampling modifiedu = u + combinednoise 0.1 # Example warp factor modifiedv = v + combinednoise 0.1 # Sample Gaussian blob or Fire Profile # For a procedural generation without an external texture, we simulate the profile # A simple Gaussian-like falloff from the center radialdist = np.sqrt(modifiedu2 + modifiedv2) gaussianblob = np.exp(-radialdist2 / 0.1) # Apply Color Gradient (Orange) # Map intensity to orange color intensity = gaussianblob combinednoise r = intensity 1.0 g = intensity 0.5 b = intensity 0.1 texture[y, x] = [r, g, b] return texture def improvedperlinnoise(x, y): """ Placeholder for Improved Perlin Noise or M-Noise implementation. Must return a smooth, pseudo-random value. """ # Implementation details depend on the specific noise function used. # For M-Noise, this should avoid chained table lookups. return (np.sin(x 12.9898) np.cos(y 78.233)) 43758.5453 % 1 2 - 1 def voronoinoise(x, y): """ Placeholder for Voronoi Noise implementation. """ # Implementation details depend on the specific noise function used. return np.random.rand() Uses similar noise combinations but targets volumetric cloud density rather than fire. It focuses on soft, billowy structures. Link Uses noise for stylized, non-photorealistic cloud shapes. It prioritizes artistic control over physical accuracy. Link Time Complexity: The generation is performed per-pixel in a pixel shader, making it O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the texture. The complexity of the noise function (Perlin/Voronoi) is constant per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the 2D texture storage, where W and H are the texture dimensions. Performance: Real-time performance is achieved through hardware acceleration (GPU shaders). M-Noise is specifically designed to avoid bottlenecks associated with standard Perlin Noise on GPUs. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability. Artist-controllable appearance via 2D texture editing. Dynamic scaling without stretching artifacts. Supports bi-directional environmental interaction (e.g., wind, collision). Limitations: Not physically accurate; relies on artistic approximation. Requires a 3D lattice construction for the final volume, adding complexity to the rendering pipeline. M-Noise implementation may be hardware-specific. When to Use: Real-time applications (games, interactive simulations) where visual appeal and performance are prioritized over physical accuracy. When Not to Use: Offline rendering requiring photo-realistic fire simulation, or scenes where physical accuracy is critical. The method was developed by Fuller, Krishnan, Mahrous, Hamann, and Joy at UC Davis, as presented in their 2006 paper "Real-Time Procedural Volumetric Fire". It was designed to address the limitations of sprite-based fire systems (artifacts) and physical simulations (computational cost). The approach leverages "Improved Perlin Noise" and a particle simulation to create vibrant, interactive fire. Subsequent variations and implementations have been documented in unofficial reports and GitHub projects, such as the "Fire Simulation and Rendering" project and the "Realistic Real-Time Rendering of Fire in a Production System" proposal. name: Real-Time Procedural Volumetric Fire
head: Hardware-Accelerated Procedural Fire, Procedural Volumetric Fire
body: A method for producing real-time procedural volumetric fire using hardware acceleration, Improved Perlin Noise, and a realistic particle simulation to create vibrant volumetric fire with bi-directional environmental macro-interactivity. It constructs an arbitrarily detailed lattice around a central curve, slicing it into quadrilateral planar polygons rendered into a unit fire volume. Unlike sprite systems, it avoids common artifacts, and unlike true photo-realistic fire simulation, it avoids high computational costs. It builds on Noise-based 2D Fire by extending the 2D noise application into a 3D volumetric lattice structure. Inputs: A central curve defined by control points, deformed by a particle simulation or pre-scripted movements. A two-dimensional fire profile texture defining color and intensity. Particle simulation parameters: movement, wind, high-energy particle dispersion, and thermal buoyancy. Application-specific frequency for noise detail. Perceived burning speed parameter. Unique constant offset for each fire instance. Outputs: Rendered quadrilateral planar polygons forming the volumetric fire. Data Structures: Central Curve: A 4-dimensional curve (3 spatial + 1 time/parameter) defining the fire's macro shape. Lattice: Constructed around the central curve. Four corner splines are generated at a distance of 2 \cdot r(t) units from the center spline, where r(t) is the radius at parameter t. Unit Fire Volume: A normalized texture space representation of the fire cross-section. Steps: 1. Deform Central Curve: The central curve is deformed by either a pre-scripted sequence of movements or a realistic particle simulation. The simulation accounts for movement, wind, high-energy particle dispersion, and thermal buoyancy. 2. Construct Lattice: Generate four corner splines at distance 2 \cdot r(t) from the center spline. Sample the center spline by length to find associated positions on the corner splines, producing positions and texture coordinates for each lattice corner. 3. Slice Lattice: Slice the lattice into quadrilateral planar polygons. 4. Render Polygons: Render these polygons with appropriate texture coordinates into a unit fire volume. 5. Pixel Shader Processing: Calculate noise space position. Scale horizontal and vertical axes of noise space by the radius and length, respectively, to prevent stretching. Multiply noisescale by an application-specific frequency. Correct noise functions to have a base frequency of one, making the frequency factor the spatial frequency of micro-level detail in world space. Set the fourth dimension of noise space to time. Offset the vertical axis by -time to create upward flow. Add a unique constant offset to the noise position for each fire instance. Use 4D Improved Perlin Noise on the calculated noise position to generate micro fire effects (flame shapes, location, flicker). Combine noise output with the 2D fire profile texture to determine final color and intensity. Formulas: Corner Spline Distance: d = 2 \cdot r(t). Noise Space Scaling (Equation 10 in): \mathbf{p}{noise} = \mathbf{p}{unit} \cdot \text{noisescale} \cdot f{app} \cdot \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{offset} Where: \mathbf{p}{unit} is the position in the unit fire volume texture coordinates. \text{noisescale} scales by radius (horizontal) and length (vertical). f{app} is the application-specific frequency. \mathbf{c} is a correction vector ensuring base frequency of one. \mathbf{offset} is the unique constant offset per instance. The fourth dimension (time) is added to \mathbf{p}{noise}. Vertical axis is offset by -time. Parameters: Perceived Burning Speed: Passed as a parameter to the pixel shader. Application-Specific Frequency: Adjusts desired levels of detail. Unique Constant Offset: Ensures each fire instance is unique. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stretching Artifacts: If noise space is not dynamically scaled according to the fire's radius and length, visual artifacts appear when the fire is enlarged. Precision: The level of detail of Improved Perlin Noise must be scaled to world coordinates in the pixel shader to eliminate stretching and scaling artifacts. A method to dynamically scale noise space according to the fire's radius and length to prevent stretching and scaling artifacts when the fire is enlarged. It scales the horizontal and vertical axes of noise space by the radius and length, respectively. It multiplies noisescale by an application-specific frequency to adjust for desired levels of detail. It corrects each noise function to have a base frequency of one, making the frequency factor the spatial frequency of micro-level detail in world space. This ensures that enlarging the fire (via elongating the central curve or adjusting control point radius) does not stretch noise effects. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved through hardware acceleration and efficient lattice construction. Memory Complexity: Depends on the lattice detail and particle simulation state. Performance: Creates visually convincing real-time 3D fire without the artifacts of sprite systems or the computational costs of true photo-realistic simulation. Strengths: Bi-directional environmental macro-interactivity, easy design by content artists via 2D texture manipulation, dynamic interaction support. Limitations: Relies on particle simulation for macro deformation, which may require tuning for specific environments. Originated by A. Fuller, K. Krishnan, K. Mahrous, H. Hamann, and J. Joy from UC Davis. Presented at I3D 2007. The method allows content artists to easily modify fire shape and color by manipulating a 2D fire profile texture. It supports bi-directional interaction between fire and environment through efficient collision detection on the constructed lattice. name: Perlin-Worley Noise for Cloud Density
head: Base Density Noise, Base Density Noise Calculation, Perlin-Worley Noise
body: This method generates the base volumetric density field for cloud rendering by combining the structural continuity of Perlin noise with the billowy, cellular detail of Worley noise. It differs from standard procedural noise by storing multiple frequency levels of Worley noise in separate texture channels to allow for high-frequency detail reconstruction during runtime remapping, rather than baking all detail into a single low-precision channel. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D texture containing the base density noise and high-frequency Worley components. Output: A single scalar density value for a given 3D coordinate \mathbf{P}. Data Structures The base density is stored in an RGBA32 texture (or equivalent floating-point format). The layout is defined as follows: Red (R) Channel: Stores the low-frequency Perlin-Worley noise value. Green (G) Channel: Stores Worley noise at frequency level 1. Blue (B) Channel: Stores Worley noise at frequency level 2. Alpha (A) Channel: Stores Worley noise at frequency level 3. The texture must be tileable to allow sampling at varying frequencies without edge artifacts. A typical implementation uses a 128 \times 128 \times 128 texture, which is small enough for fast loading but large enough to contain 2–3 Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) levels. Algorithm Steps 1. Generate Perlin Fractal: Compute a low-frequency Perlin fractal noise value, PerlinFractal, using standard FBM summation. 2. Generate Worley Fractals: Compute three separate Worley fractal noise values at increasing frequencies: Worley1, Worley2, and Worley3. 3. Pack Noise: Store PerlinFractal in the Red channel and Worley1, Worley2, Worley3 in the Green, Blue, and Alpha channels, respectively. 4. Unpack and Combine Worley: Retrieve the G, B, and A channels from the texture. Compute the high-frequency Worley sum, WorleyHighFrequencies, using weighted summation: WorleyHighFrequencies = 0.625 \cdot Worley1 + 0.25 \cdot Worley2 + 0.125 \cdot Worley3 5. Remap Perlin-Worley: Retrieve the Red channel value, PerlinWorley. Add a configurable density offset, \Delta, to it. Remap this value from the range [0, 1] to [WorleyFractal, 1]. This step brightens the noise where Worley noise is large, enhancing billowiness. PerlinWorley{remapped} = \text{Remap}(PerlinWorley + \Delta, 0, 1, WorleyFractal, 1) Note: The source notes mention WorleyFractal in the formula context but use WorleyHighFrequencies in the final base noise calculation. The remapping step described in the text ("brightens the noise where Worley noise is large") implies the use of the high-frequency sum for the final shaping. 6. Compute Base Noise: Remap the result from Step 5 such that its minimum becomes WorleyHighFrequencies and its maximum becomes 1: BaseNoise = \text{Remap}(PerlinWorley{remapped}, WorleyHighFrequencies, 1, 0, 1) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeclouddensity(texture, p, densityoffset): """ Computes cloud density using Perlin-Worley noise stored in an RGBA texture. Args: texture: A 3D texture object with sample(x, y, z) returning (r, g, b, a). p: 3D vector coordinate. densityoffset: Configurable float added to Perlin-Worley value. Returns: float: The final base density value. """ # 1. Sample the packed noise texture r, g, b, a = texture.sample(p) # 2. Unpack Worley components worley1 = g worley2 = b worley3 = a # 3. Combine Worley frequencies # Weights: 0.625, 0.25, 0.125 worleyhighfreq = 0.625 worley1 + 0.25 worley2 + 0.125 worley3 # 4. Get Perlin-Worley base value perlinworley = r # 5. Add density offset perlinworleyadjusted = perlinworley + densityoffset # 6. Remap Perlin-Worley based on Worley high frequencies # The source formula: Remap(PerlinWorley, WorleyHighFrequencies, 1, 0, 1) # This maps the range [WorleyHighFrequencies, 1] to [0, 1] # However, the text says "Remap PerlinWorley such that its minimum becomes WorleyHighFrequencies" # Standard remap(x, inmin, inmax, outmin, outmax) # Here, we treat the PerlinWorley value as the input x. # The source formula for BaseNoise is: Remap(PerlinWorley, WorleyHighFrequencies, 1, 0, 1) basenoise = remap(perlinworleyadjusted, worleyhighfreq, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) return basenoise def remap(value, inmin, inmax, outmin, outmax): """Linear remapping function.""" if inmax == inmin: return outmin t = (value - inmin) / (inmax - inmin) # Clamp t to [0, 1] to handle out-of-bounds values t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) return outmin + t (outmax - outmin) Parameters Texture Size: 128 \times 128 \times 128 is cited as a practical minimum for web performance, though larger sizes allow for more FBM levels. Worley Weights: 0.625 for the lowest frequency, 0.25 for the middle, and 0.125 for the highest. Density Offset: A configurable scalar added to the Perlin-Worley value before remapping. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Storing noise in 8-bit channels limits detail. Using 32-bit floating-point textures (e.g., RFloat) is recommended to preserve the full range of [0, 1] values and avoid banding. Tileability: The texture must be tileable to support sampling at different frequencies without discontinuities. Channel Usage: The Alpha channel is used for Worley noise in the base density texture, whereas the detail density texture may leave the Alpha channel unused. Memory: Requires storing a 3D texture. A 128^3 RGBA32 texture consumes approximately 8 MB (128^3 \times 4 bytes). Performance: Sampling is fast as it involves a single 3D texture lookup and simple arithmetic. The method is designed to be efficient for real-time rendering, particularly on web platforms. Quality: The combination of Perlin (connectedness) and Worley (billowiness) produces natural-looking cloud structures. The multi-channel Worley remapping allows for high-frequency detail without requiring extremely large textures. This technique is derived from the Nubis cloud rendering engine used by Guerrilla Games. It is implemented in the "Volumetric Clouds Tutorial" by Tyler Dodds, which provides source code for generating and unpacking these noise textures. The approach is also discussed in the context of efficient volumetric clouds for WebGL/three.js. name: Cartoon Cloud Density Generation
head: Procedural Cloud Shape
body: Cartoon Cloud Density Generation is a procedural method for generating stylized, cartoon-style cloud densities by combining independent noise sets for macro structure, body puffs, edge details, and flow, combined with geometric envelopes for specific cloud types. It differs from its sibling Perlin-Worley Noise for Cloud Density by relying on a multi-layered noise composition and explicit geometric shapes (lobes, clusters) rather than a single unified noise field, allowing for distinct "blocky" or stylized appearances consistent with voxel-based games. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D query point \mathbf{P} = (x, y, z), cloud type identifier typeid (integer 1-9), resolution parameters, and strength/detail/disturbance multipliers. Outputs: A scalar density value in [0.0, 1.0]. Data Structures: CartoonNoiseSet: Contains four independent sets of lattice gradient vectors: macrolattices, bodylattices, edgelattices, and flowlattices. These are pre-generated and stored for reuse. VolumeResult: Contains the resulting density and disturbance arrays (8-bit linear data). Steps: 1. Generate Noise Fields: Compute four fractal value noise fields using the independent lattice sets. The frequencies are scaled by multipliers: macro: Frequency multiplier 0.10. body: Frequency multiplier 0.30. edge: Frequency multiplier 0.55. flow: Frequency multiplier 0.25 \times \text{disturbance}. \text{macro} = \text{FractalValueNoise}(\mathbf{P}, \text{macro\lattices}, 0.10) \text{body} = \text{FractalValueNoise}(\mathbf{P}, \text{body\lattices}, 0.30) \text{edge} = \text{FractalValueNoise}(\mathbf{P}, \text{edge\lattices}, 0.55) \text{flow} = \text{FractalValueNoise}(\mathbf{P}, \text{flow\lattices}, 0.25 \times \text{disturbance}) 2. Compute Base Shapes: Apply smoothstep to normalize and threshold the noise fields. smoothstep(t) is defined as 3t^2 - 2t^3 for t \in [0,1], clamped to [0,1]. Broad structure: \text{broad} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{\text{macro} - 0.27}{0.52}\right) Puffs (body + macro mix): \text{puffs} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{0.56 \times \text{macro} + 0.44 \times \text{body} - 0.37}{0.38}\right) Rim/Edge detail: \text{rim} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{\text{edge} - 0.33}{0.48}\right) 3. Compute Fluffy Composite: Combine the base shapes into a unified "fluffy" density field. \text{fluffy} = \text{clip}(0.62 \times \text{puffs} + 0.23 \times \text{broad} + 0.15 \times \text{rim}, 0.0, 1.0) 4. Compute Vertical Profiles: Define Gaussian vertical profiles based on the z coordinate. These determine the thickness and height of different cloud layers. Thin (high altitude): \text{thin} = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{z + 0.04}{0.13}\right)^2\right) Middle: \text{middle} = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{z + 0.10}{0.30}\right)^2\right) Low: \text{low} = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{z + 0.28}{0.23}\right)^2\right) 5. Compute Horizontal Footprint and Clusters: Footprint: A 2D shape mask based on x, y. If the cloud has a finite boundary, use broadfootprint(x, y, variation); otherwise, use ones (infinite). Clusters: Generate 3D lobe clusters using lobecluster(x, y, z, variation) and wisp clusters using wispcluster(x, y, z, variation). These use the Soft Union function (see Formulas). 6. Combine Based on Cloud Type (typeid): The density is assembled differently for each of the 9 cloud types. Examples: Type 1 (Cirrus): \text{density} = \text{thin} \times \text{wisps} \times \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{0.72 \times \text{body} + 0.28 \times \text{edge} - 0.56}{0.30}\right) Type 9 (Cumulus): \text{base} = \text{CumulusBaseShape}(x, y, z) \text{surface} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{0.58 \times \text{fluffy} + 0.42 \times \text{broad} - 0.20}{0.70}\right) \text{density} = \text{SoftUnion}(\text{cluster} \times (0.22 + 0.78 \times \text{fluffy}), 0.68 \times \text{base} \times (0.30 + 0.70 \times \text{surface})) Cumulonimbus (Else branch): Calculate anvil shape: \text{anvil} = \text{footprint} \times \exp\left(-\left(\frac{z - 0.48}{0.16}\right)^2\right) Combine cluster and anvil: \text{density} = \text{SoftUnion}(\text{cluster}, 0.82 \times \text{anvil}) \times (0.40 + 0.60 \times \text{fluffy}) 7. Final Shaping and Quantization: Apply smoothstep to maintain continuous density and avoid concentric shell artifacts: \text{shaped} = \text{smoothstep}\left(\frac{\text{density} - 0.07}{0.62}\right) Quantize into 5 discrete cartoon levels (mapped to 0-1 range): \text{stepped} = \frac{\text{floor}(\text{clip}(\text{shaped}, 0.0, 1.0) \times 4.0 + 0.20)}{4.0} Blend stepped and shaped densities, apply strength and rim/detail modulation: \text{result} = \text{clip}\left((0.12 \times \text{stepped} + 0.88 \times \text{shaped}) \times \text{strength} \times (0.94 + 0.06 \times \text{detail} \times \text{rim}), 0.0, 1.0\right) Formulas: Soft Union: Used to merge multiple density fields smoothly. S(F1, F2, \dots) = \text{clip}\left(1 - \exp\left(-1.12 \times \text{clip}\left(\sum Fi, 0, 1\right)\right), 0, 1\right) Implementation: np.clip(1.0 - np.exp(-total 1.12), 0.0, 1.0) where total is the sum of clipped fields. Lobe Cluster: A specific instance of soft union for geometric lobes. L = \text{clip}\left(1 - \exp\left(-1.18 \times \sum (wi \times \exp(-\text{dist}i^2))\right), 0, 1\right) Implementation: np.clip(1.0 - np.exp(-fieldsum 1.18), 0.0, 1.0). Parameters: Detail Multiplier: 0.10 (macro), 0.30 (body), 0.55 (edge), 0.25 disturbance (flow). Strength: Typically in range [0.0, 2.0]. Disturbance: Typically in range [0.0, 2.0]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concentric Shells: To avoid artifacts in volume rendering, the texture body must maintain continuous density. Quantization should only be applied in the final shading stage if needed. Boundary Conditions: For finite cloud regions, the footprint function must handle boundaries to prevent infinite column artifacts along the Z-axis. Uses a static 2D density map for a blocky appearance, differing from Cartoon Cloud Density Generation which uses multi-octave noise and geometric shapes. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of noise octaves and the complexity of the geometric clusters. Each query point requires evaluating multiple noise fields and geometric functions. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the pre-generated lattice gradients for the four noise sets and the cloud type parameters. Strengths: Produces distinct, stylized cloud shapes suitable for non-photorealistic rendering. The separation of macro, body, and edge noise allows for fine-tuned artistic control. Limitations: More complex to implement than single-noise methods. The geometric clusters require careful tuning of parameters for different cloud types. When to Use: Stylized games, voxel-based environments, or any application requiring non-realistic, cartoon-like clouds. Originated from procedural generation techniques in game development, specifically for creating consistent cloud shapes in voxel-based games like Minecraft. The method is documented in unofficial sources related to noise cloud generation libraries. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Blocky Volumetric Clouds
head: Blocky Cloud Density
body: Blocky Volumetric Clouds is a procedural rendering technique that generates cartoon-style cloud densities by sampling a 2D texture at the cloud layer's Y-coordinate, creating a distinct "blocky" appearance compared to noise-based realistic clouds. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric clouds in a style consistent with voxel-based games while providing simplified lighting calculations. It differs from its sibling Cartoon Cloud Density Generation by relying on a static 2D density map rather than multi-octave noise functions for the base structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: playerPos (ray direction vector), cameraPosition (world position of the camera), frameTimeCounter (time uniform), frameCounter (integer frame counter), fragCoord (fragment screen coordinates), cloudsShadowcasterDir (direction vector for shadow casting). Output: A tuple (invThickness, invBrightness) containing transmittance and lighting contribution. Data Structures: BLOCKYCLOUDTEXTURE: A 2D texture containing the cloud density map. The alpha channel is sampled for density. Constants: CLOUDBOTTOMY, CLOUDTOPY (defined as CLOUDBOTTOMY + 12.0), CLOUDSQUALITY (number of steps). Steps: 1. Sample Density for Ray Limiting: Calculate the player's direction length in the XZ plane: playerLen = length(playerPos.xz). Normalize playerPos by playerLen. Sample the cloud density at a position 20 units ahead of the camera: distSample = sampleBlockyCloud(cameraPosition + normalize(playerPos) 20.0). Compute distLimitAmount = 1.0 - pow3(1.0 - distSample). Scale the ray direction length: playerPos = min(playerLen, mix(128.0 16.0, 20.0 16.0, distLimitAmount)). 2. Normalize Step Vector: Create a step vector stepVec equal to playerPos. Normalize the XZ components relative to the Y component: stepVec.xz /= abs(stepVec.y). Set the Y component to the sign of the original Y: stepVec.y = sign(stepVec.y). This ensures the ray moves exactly ±1 unit in Y per step in the XZ plane. 3. Determine Y Bounds: Start at the camera's Y position. Clamp the start Y to the cloud layer: posStartY = clamp(cameraPosition.y, CLOUDBOTTOMY, CLOUDTOPY). Calculate the end Y by moving 1000 units in the direction of stepVec.y: posEndY = clamp(posStartY + sign(stepVec.y) 1000.0, CLOUDBOTTOMY, CLOUDTOPY). If posStartY == posEndY, return vec2(1.0, 0.0) (no intersection). 4. Clamp to Foreground: Calculate maxY = abs(playerPos.y). Clamp the start and end Y positions relative to the camera to prevent marching through the ground/foreground: posStartY = clamp(posStartY - cameraPosition.y, -maxY, maxY) + cameraPosition.y and posEndY = clamp(posEndY - cameraPosition.y, -maxY, maxY) + cameraPosition.y. If posStartY == posEndY, return vec2(1.0, 0.0). 5. Calculate Step Vector and Density Multiplier: Calculate the 3D start position: pos = cameraPosition + stepVec abs(posStartY - cameraPosition.y). Calculate the 3D end position: endPos = pos + stepVec abs(posEndY - posStartY). Compute the step vector for the loop: stepVec = pos - endPos. Divide by quality: stepVec /= CLOUDSQUALITY. Compute density multiplier: densityMult = length(stepVec) -0.25. Set current position to endPos. 6. Apply Dithering: Calculate Bayer dither: dither = bayer64(glFragCoord.xy). Offset dither for temporal stability: dither = fract(dither + 1.61803398875 mod(float(frameCounter), 3600.0)). Offset position: pos += stepVec (dither - 0.5). 7. Ray March Loop: Initialize invThickness = 1.0 and invBrightness = 0.0. Loop i from 0 to CLOUDSQUALITY - 1: Sample density: density = sampleBlockyCloud(pos). Calculate inverse density factor: invDensity = exp(density densityMult). Update thickness: invThickness = invDensity. Sample shadow/light: sampleUp = sampleBlockyCloud(pos + cloudsShadowcasterDir). Update brightness: invBrightness = mix(invBrightness, sampleUp, 1.0 - sqrt(invDensity)). Advance position: pos += stepVec. 8. Return Results: Return vec2(invThickness, invBrightness). Helper Function: sampleBlockyCloud Input: pos (vec3). 1. If pos.y < CLOUDBOTTOMY or pos.y > CLOUDBOTTOMY + 12.0, return 0.0. 2. Calculate texture coordinates: texPos = pos.xz. 3. Offset X by time: texPos.x -= frameTimeCounter 3. 4. Scale: texPos = 0.00025. 5. Sample texture: return texture2D(BLOCKYCLOUDTEXTURE, texPos, 0).a. Pseudocode: Unverified code. frametimecounter 3.0, texpos[1]) texpos = (texpos[0] 0.00025, texpos[1] 0.00025) # Assuming texture2D returns a tuple (r, g, b, a) return blockycloudtexture.sample(texpos)[3] def computeclouds(playerpos, cameraposition, cloudbottomy, cloudtopy, cloudsquality, blockycloudtexture, frametimecounter, framecounter, cloudsshadowcasterdir, fragcoord): # Step 1 playerlen = math.sqrt(playerpos[0]2 + playerpos[2]2) if playerlen == 0.0: return (1.0, 0.0) # Normalize playerPos by XZ length playerpos = (playerpos[0] / playerlen, playerpos[1] / playerlen, playerpos[2] / playerlen) # Sample density 20 units ahead dir20 = (playerpos[0] 20.0, playerpos[1] 20.0, playerpos[2] 20.0) distsample = sampleblockycloud((cameraposition[0] + dir20[0], cameraposition[1] + dir20[1], cameraposition[2] + dir20[2]), cloudbottomy, blockycloudtexture, frametimecounter) # pow3 is just xxx distlimitamount = 1.0 - pos[1])) endpos = (pos[0] + stepvec[0] abs(posendy - posstarty), pos[1], pos[2] + stepvec[2] abs(posendy - posstarty)) stepvec = (pos[0] - endpos[0], pos[1] - endpos[1], pos[2] - endpos[2]) stepvec = (stepvec[0] / cloudsquality, stepvec[1] / cloudsquality, stepvec[2] / cloudsquality) densitymult = math.sqrt(stepvec[0]2 + stepvec[1]2 + stepvec[2]2) -0.25 pos = endpos # Step 6 # bayer64 is a standard 64x64 dither matrix lookup. bayermatrix = [ [0, 32, 8, 40, 2, 34, 10, 42], [48, 16, 56, 24, 50, 18, 58, 26], [12, 44, 4, 36, 14, 46, 6, 38], [60, 28, 52, 20, 62, 30, 54, 22], [3, 35, 11, 43, 1, 33, 9, 41], [51, 19, 59, 27, 49, 17, 57, 25], [15, 47, 7, 39, 13, 45, 5, 37], [63, 31, 55, 23, 61, 29, 53, 21] ] def bayer64(x, y): return bayermatrix[y & 7][x & 7] / 64.0 dither = bayer64(fragcoord[0], fragcoord[1]) dither = fract(dither + 1.61803398875 mod(float(framecounter), 3600.0)) pos = (pos[0] + stepvec[0] (dither - 0.5), pos[1] + stepvec[1] (dither - 0.5), pos[2] + stepvec[2] (dither - 0.5)) # Step 7 invthickness = 1.0 invbrightness = 0.0 for i in range(cloudsquality): density = sampleblockycloud(pos, cloudbottomy, blockycloudtexture, frametimecounter) invdensity = math.exp(density densitymult) invthickness = invdensity sampleup = sampleblockycloud((pos[0] + cloudsshadowcasterdir[0], pos[1] + cloudsshadowcasterdir[1], pos[2] + cloudsshadowcasterdir[2]), cloudbottomy, blockycloudtexture, frametimecounter) invbrightness = mix(invbrightness, sampleup, 1.0 - math.sqrt(invdensity)) pos = (pos[0] + stepvec[0], pos[1] + stepvec[1], pos[2] + stepvec[2]) return (invthickness, invbrightness) Formulas: Inverse Thickness: invThickness = \prod{i=0}^{N-1} e^{di \cdot L \cdot -0.25} where di is density at step i, L is step length. Inverse Brightness: invBrightness = mix(invBrightness, sampleUp, 1.0 - \sqrt{e^{d \cdot L \cdot -0.25}}). Step Vector Y: stepVec.y = \pm 1, stepVec.xz = stepVec.xz / |stepVec.y|. Parameters: CLOUDBOTTOMY: Lower Y-boundary of the cloud layer. CLOUDTOPY: Upper Y-boundary, calculated as CLOUDBOTTOMY + 12.0. BLOCKYCLOUDTEXTURE: 2D texture containing the cloud density map. frameTimeCounter: Time uniform used to animate the cloud texture horizontally. CLOUDSQUALITY: Number of ray-marching steps. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Vanishing: The ray length shrinking mechanism (Step 1) reduces artifacts when inside clouds but relies on a cloud being nearby. If no cloud is nearby, the optimization may fail or behave unexpectedly. No Intersection: If the ray's Y-start and Y-end are identical after clamping (e.g., looking away from clouds or inside a solid block), the function returns vec2(1.0, 0.0). Division by Zero: If stepVec.y is 0, normalization fails. The source implies this is handled by the bail-out conditions or input constraints. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is CLOUDSQUALITY. Each step involves two texture samples and basic arithmetic. Performance: The method is lightweight compared to full volumetric noise generation, relying on a single 2D texture lookup per step. Strengths: Simple implementation, consistent "blocky" aesthetic, low computational cost. Limitations: Lacks the organic detail of noise-based clouds; lighting is simplified; the ray limiting optimization is noted as not working very well for this specific blocky style. The method originates from a feature request for a Minecraft shader mod (I-Like-Vanilla) by user The0x539, with feedback from the mod author What42Pizza. It was developed to provide a vanilla-esque blocky cloud appearance with improved lighting, compatible with the Iris shader loader.
