name: Line-Based Pipe Volume Generation
head: Line-Based Cave Generation, Procedural Pipe Volume with OpenSimplex Noise
body: Generates a 3D volume density field along predefined line paths using OpenSimplex noise to create pipe-like cave structures, which are later meshed via marching cubes. It differs from general noise-based density generation by restricting the noise evaluation domain to the vicinity of parametric line segments, effectively carving volumetric tubes through space rather than filling a bounding box with uniform noise patterns. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of line segments defined by nodes and properties; voxel grid dimensions (voxel.numVertex); noise parameters (noiseIntensity, noiseScale, smoothingFactor, frequency, lacunarity); boolean isWorldSpaceNoise. Output: A 3D density field stored in pointsBuffer (ComputeBuffer), which is subsequently processed by a marching cubes shader to produce a triangle mesh. Data Structures The method relies on three primary ComputeBuffers: 1. pointsBuffer: Size voxel.totalVertex. Stride 16 bytes. Layout: Vector4 (x, y, z, density). 2. linePropBuffer: Size lineGenerator.line.Count. Stride 52 bytes. Contains properties for each line segment. 3. nodePositionBuffer: Size lineGenerator.node.Count. Stride 20 bytes. Contains node positions. Algorithm Steps 1. Thread Group Calculation: Calculate the number of thread groups per axis based on the voxel vertex count. The dimension is ceil(numVertex / 8) + 1, where 8 is the number of threads per group. 2. Buffer Initialization: Populate linePropBuffer and nodePositionBuffer with current line generator data. 3. Shader Configuration: Set the following shader inputs: Buffers: nodeProps (from nodePositionBuffer), lineProps (from linePropBuffer). Scalars: isWorldSpaceNoise, noiseIntensity, noiseScale, smoothingFactor, frequency, lacunarity. Vector: offset (used for chunked generation). 4. Density Computation: Dispatch the density shader. For each voxel vertex, the shader evaluates OpenSimplex noise. If isWorldSpaceNoise is false, the query point is converted to the local coordinate system of the nearest line segment. 5. Smoothing: Apply the smoothingFactor to the resulting density values to ensure smooth transitions. 6. Meshing: The resulting density field is passed to a marching cubes shader (marchingCubeShader) with an isoLevel to generate triangles. Pseudocode The following pseudocode represents the CPU-side setup and dispatch logic derived from the source. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. NUMTHREADSPERGROUP = 8 def generatepipevolume(voxel, linegenerator, densityshader, marchingcubeshader, isolevel): # 1. Calculate thread groups # Note: Source uses numVertex for calculation, likely referring to voxel grid dimensions numthreadsx = math.ceil(voxel.numVertex.x / NUMTHREADSPERGROUP) + 1 numthreadsy = math.ceil(voxel.numVertex.y / NUMTHREADSPERGROUP) + 1 numthreadsz = math.ceil(voxel.numVertex.z / NUMTHREADSPERGROUP) + 1 # 2. Prepare buffers lineprops = linegenerator.getlineprops() nodepositions = linegenerator.getnodes() # Set buffer data densityshader.setbuffer("lineProps", lineprops) densityshader.setbuffer("nodeProps", nodepositions) # 3. Set shader parameters densityshader.setbool("isWorldSpaceNoise", True) # Example default densityshader.setfloat("noiseIntensity", 1.0) densityshader.setfloat("noiseScale", 1.0) densityshader.setfloat("smoothingFactor", 0.5) densityshader.setfloat("frequency", 1.0) densityshader.setfloat("lacunarity", 2.0) # 4. Dispatch Density Shader # The source loops over chunks (i, j, k) with offsets. # For a single volume generation step: offset = Vector3(0, 0, 0) densityshader.setvector("offset", offset) densityshader.dispatch(0, numthreadsx, numthreadsy, numthreadsz) # 5. Marching Cubes marchingcubeshader.setbuffer("triangles", meshbuffer) marchingcubeshader.setfloat("isoLevel", isolevel) marchingcubeshader.dispatch(0, voxel.numVoxel.x, voxel.numVoxel.y, voxel.numVoxel.z) # 6. Retrieve and Construct Mesh tricount = tricountbuffer.getdata() triangles = meshbuffer.getdata(tricount) mesh = createmesh(triangles) mesh.recalculatenormals() return mesh Edge Cases and Pitfalls 0th Line Index: A boundary/edge case issue occurs specifically at the 0th line index during pipe volume generation. Coordinate Systems: If isWorldSpaceNoise is disabled, coordinates are automatically converted to the line's local coordinate system. Incorrect implementation of this conversion may lead to artifacts. Complexity: Thread group dimensions are calculated as ceil(numVertex / 8) + 1 per axis. Performance: The source logs indicate performance measurement in seconds, but specific hardware metrics are not provided. Strengths: Efficiently generates tubular structures (caves/pipes) without needing to evaluate noise across the entire volume uniformly. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the underlying OpenSimplex noise implementation; potential artifacts at line boundaries or index 0. Originated from an unofficial GitHub repository by sachPico in April 2020. The project, lineBasedCaveSimplex, was developed as a variation of procedural cave generation using line data for paths and OpenSimplex noise for volume data. It was intended for use in Unity, leveraging Compute Shaders for density generation and Marching Cubes for mesh extraction. sachPico/lineBasedCaveSimplex, https://github.com/sachPico/lineBasedCaveSimplex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Implicit Field Composition
head: Density Function Composition, Density Function for Scene Generation, Implicit Field Combination
body: Implicit Field Composition constructs a complex scalar field by combining multiple primitive fields (such as terrain, spheres, and cuboids) using set-theoretic operations like union, intersection, and difference. It solves the problem of defining complex, multi-material, or hybrid geometries without explicit mesh topology, serving as the primary input generator for dual contouring and ray-marching pipelines. Unlike Metaball Field Evaluation, which uses smooth blending functions to create organic morphing shapes, Implicit Field Composition relies on sharp, non-differentiable Boolean operators (min/max) to preserve hard edges and distinct material boundaries. Inputs: A query point \vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Primitive definitions: Terrain: Parameters for fractal noise generation (octaves, frequency, lacunarity, persistence) and vertical scaling. Cuboid: Origin \vec{o}c and half-dimensions \vec{h}c. Sphere: Origin \vec{o}s and radius rs. Boolean operator configuration (fixed in the reference implementation as max(-cube, min(sphere, terrain)). Outputs: A scalar value f(\vec{x}) representing the signed distance or implicit value at \vec{x}. The zero-crossing f(\vec{x})=0 defines the composite surface. No persistent data structures are required for the composition logic itself. The primitives are evaluated statelessly. However, the noise generation requires temporary storage for the accumulated noise value and the scaled position vector during the octave loop. The composite field f(\vec{x}) is defined as: f(\vec{x}) = \max(-C(\vec{x}), \min(S(\vec{x}), T(\vec{x}))) where C(\vec{x}) is the cuboid field, S(\vec{x}) is the sphere field, and T(\vec{x}) is the terrain field. 1. Terrain Field T(\vec{x}) The terrain is a height field derived from fractal noise. T(\vec{x}) = xy - K \cdot N(\vec{x}{xz}) Where: xy is the y-coordinate of \vec{x}. K = 20.0 is the vertical scaling factor. N(\vec{u}) is the fractal noise function evaluated at the horizontal position \vec{u} = (x, z). Fractal Noise N(\vec{u}) N(\vec{u}) = 0.5 + 0.5 \sum{i=0}^{O-1} \text{Perlin}(\vec{p}i) \cdot Ai Parameters: O = 4 (octaves). \text{SCALE} = 1/128. \vec{p}0 = \vec{u} \cdot \text{SCALE} \cdot F. A0 = 1.0. For i > 0: \vec{p}i = \vec{p}{i-1} \cdot L and Ai = A{i-1} \cdot P. F = 0.5343 (frequency). L = 2.2324 (lacunarity). P = 0.68324 (persistence). \text{Perlin}(\cdot) is a standard Perlin noise function returning values in [-1, 1]. 2. Cuboid Field C(\vec{x}) The cuboid is defined as a Signed Distance Function (SDF): C(\vec{x}) = \min(m, \|\vec{d}{pos}\|) Where: \vec{l} = \vec{x} - \vec{o}c (local position). \vec{d} = (|\vec{l}x| - h{c,x}, |\vec{l}y| - h{c,y}, |\vec{l}z| - h{c,z}). m = \max(dx, dy, dz). \vec{d}{pos} is the vector \vec{d} with negative components clamped to zero: \vec{d}{pos} = \max(\vec{d}, \vec{0}). \|\cdot\| is the Euclidean norm. 3. Sphere Field S(\vec{x}) The sphere is defined as a standard SDF: S(\vec{x}) = \|\vec{x} - \vec{o}s\| - rs Where: \vec{o}s = (15, 2.5, 1). rs = 16. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluateimplicitfield(x, y, z): """ Evaluates the composite implicit field at point (x, y, z). Implements: max(-cuboid, min(sphere, terrain)) """ terrain = evaluateterrain(x, y, z) cuboid = evaluatecuboid(x, y, z) sphere = evaluatesphere(x, y, z) return max(-cuboid, min(sphere, terrain)) def evaluateterrain(x, y, z): """ T(x,y,z) = y - 20.0 FractalNoise(x, z) """ noiseval = fractalnoise(x, z) return y - 20.0 noiseval def fractalnoise(x, z): """ Generates fractal noise using 4 octaves of Perlin noise. """ SCALE = 1.0 / 128.0 px = x SCALE py = z SCALE frequency = 0.5343 lacunarity = 2.2324 persistence = 0.68324 octaves = 4 noisesum = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 # Initial scaling by frequency px = frequency py = frequency for i in range(octaves): # Standard 2D Perlin noise implementation returning values in [-1, 1]. perlinval = perlinnoise(px, py) noisesum += perlinval amplitude # Prepare next octave px = lacunarity py = lacunarity amplitude = persistence # Normalize to [0, 1] as per source definition: 0.5 + 0.5 noise return 0.5 + 0.5 noisesum def evaluatecuboid(x, y, z): """ SDF for a cuboid. Source: tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp """ origin = (-4.0, 10.0, -4.0) halfdims = (12.0, 12.0, 12.0) localx = x - origin[0] localy = y - origin[1] localz = z - origin[2] # Absolute distance from center minus half-dimensions dx = abs(localx) - halfdims[0] dy = abs(localy) - halfdims[1] dz = abs(localz) - halfdims[2] # Max component m = max(dx, max(dy, dz)) # Vector of positive distances only dposx = max(dx, 0.0) dposy = max(dy, 0.0) dposz = max(dz, 0.0) # Euclidean norm of positive distances distpos = (dposx2 + dposy2 + dposz2) 0.5 return min(m, distpos) def evaluatesphere(x, y, z): """ SDF for a sphere. Source: tuckbone/DualContouringCSharp """ origin = (15.0, 2.5, 1.0) radius = 16.0 dist = ((x - origin[0])2 + (y - origin[1])2 + (z - origin[2])2) 0.5 return dist - radius def perlinnoise(x, y): # Standard 2D Perlin noise implementation returning values in [-1, 1]. pass Terrain Octaves: 4. Terrain Frequency: 0.5343. Terrain Lacunarity: 2.2324. Terrain Persistence: 0.68324. Terrain Scale: 1/128. Terrain Vertical Scale: 20.0. Cuboid Origin: (-4, 10, -4). Cuboid Half-Dimensions: (12, 12, 12). Sphere Origin: (15, 2.5, 1). Sphere Radius: 16. Precision: The use of max and min creates non-differentiable discontinuities in the gradient. Sign Convention: The cuboid SDF returns positive values outside and negative inside. The term -cuboid inverts this, making the interior positive. This specific combination max(-C, min(S, T)) implies a specific Boolean tree: The terrain and sphere are intersected (min), and the result is unioned with the inverted cuboid (max). Noise Domain: The fractal noise is 2D (x, z), while the primitives are 3D. This restricts the terrain to a height-field-like structure. Time Complexity: O(O \cdot N) where O is the number of octaves (4) and N is the cost of the underlying noise function. The primitive evaluations are O(1). The composition is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No geometry is stored during evaluation. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Implicit Field Composition is a technique rooted in constructive solid geometry (CSG) applied to implicit surfaces. The specific implementation combining fractal terrain, cuboids, and spheres for dual contouring input originates from open-source educational examples in C# and C++. The use of SDFs for primitives (cuboid, sphere) and Boolean composition via min/max is a standard approach in modern implicit modeling. name: Implicit Surface Primitives
head: Implicit Fields, Scalar Field Primitives
body: Implicit Surface Primitives define 3D geometry as the zero-level set (or isosurface) of a scalar field function f(\vec{x}). Unlike explicit representations that store discrete topological data, this family defines geometry analytically, allowing for on-demand evaluation of values and gradients at arbitrary points in space. This approach enables the creation of complex, organic, or mathematically precise shapes that can be composed, deformed, or sampled for volume rendering and surface extraction Implicit Surface Primitives. All methods in this family rely on the evaluation of a scalar field function f over a domain \Omega \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3. The core mechanism identifies the surface as the locus of points where the function output equals a specific constant, typically zero. Mathematical Definition: The implicit surface is defined as the set of points \vec{x} satisfying: \{\vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f(\vec{x}) = 0\} More generally, an isosurface at isovalue v is defined by: f(\vec{x}) - v = 0 Function Properties: 1. Mapping: The function maps any point in N-dimensional space to a real number: \forall \vec{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, f(\vec{x}) \in \mathbb{R} 2. Filter/Kernel: The function f acts as a filter or form. It can be algebraic or transcendental, and defined globally or as piecewise kernels. 3. Support: The function can be defined globally over the entire domain or as piecewise kernels (local support). 4. Sign Convention: While the zero set defines the surface, the sign of f(\vec{x}) often carries semantic meaning. In Signed Distance Functions (SDFs), f(\vec{x}) > 0 indicates outside, f(\vec{x}) < 0 indicates inside, and f(\vec{x}) = 0 is on the surface. Evaluation: The geometry is not stored as a discrete structure but is computed on-demand. For volume rendering, this means evaluating f(\vec{x}) at sample points along rays or within voxels Implicit Surface Primitives. Generates and updates a 3D scalar density volume representing dynamic metaballs using a CPU-GPU pipeline. Unlike Implicit Field Composition, which composes general implicit primitives, this method specifically sums inverse-distance or Gaussian contributions from moving spheres to create organic, merging blob shapes. Choose this for dynamic, fluid-like organic shapes. Adds relief or details to surfaces without increasing geometry cost, using procedural texture synthesis evaluated within a volumetric region around the object rather than only on the surface. It deforms implicit surfaces by adding procedural noise to the function's range instead of the domain, enabling sphere tracing with distance bounds. Choose this for adding fine procedural detail to existing SDFs. A local geometric deformation technique for implicitly defining the union of two or more signed distance functions (SDFs). This method computes a p-norm distance to the blended union, allowing for smooth transitions between surfaces controlled by a tightness parameter p. It differs from global additive field methods by operating directly on distance values and maintaining local support. Choose this for smooth unions of SDFs. Approximates Gaussian blobby fields using piecewise cubic polynomials to avoid expensive exponentiation and iterative root finding. It defines a smooth, blended volume from a set of key points, where the surface is the zero-crossing of the summed field. Unlike standard metaballs that use Gaussian kernels, this method localizes the influence of each point to a finite radius, providing a bounded support that simplifies culling and distance estimation. Choose this for efficient, bounded blobby fields. Represents 3D geometry as the zero-level set of a scalar field function f(\vec{x}). It defines surfaces by evaluating a function at arbitrary points in space rather than storing discrete topological data. What sets it apart from explicit surface definitions is that the geometry is defined analytically through a filter function f. Choose this as the foundational abstraction for all implicit methods. Creates a binary volume mask by assigning values to voxels based on a spatial or level-set condition, effectively gating simulation or rendering computations. It differs from continuous implicit primitives by discretizing the domain boundary into a hard binary mask rather than evaluating a smooth scalar field for isosurface extraction. This method restricts physical simulation (such as pressure solving or force application) to active regions, ignoring empty space like air. Choose this for binary masking in simulations. A technique for generating volume data from mathematical implicit functions, providing value and gradient at any point in space without discrete voxel grids. It solves the problem of defining complex, continuous geometry for volume rendering by evaluating a scalar field function f(\vec{x}) on-demand. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on precomputed grids or specific primitive compositions, this method provides an abstract interface for sampling arbitrary implicit geometries, returning position, scalar value, and gradient. It builds on Implicit Surface Primitives by implementing the core evaluation mechanism for specific algebraic and transcendental functions. Choose this for abstract, on-demand geometry sampling. Provides closed-form analytical expressions for the scalar field f(\vec{x}) of specific geometric primitives, primarily yielding exact signed Euclidean distances. Unlike generic implicit surface definitions that may rely on approximations or piecewise kernels, these functions offer precise, singularity-free evaluation for standard shapes like tori, shells, and periodic surfaces, which is critical for robust marching cubes and ray marching in volume rendering. Choose this for standard, exact geometric primitives. An interaction model for defining a Volume of Interest (VOI) or Region of Interest (ROI) within unsegmented volumetric data by "painting" an implicit envelope around features of interest. It solves the problem of intuitive, context-preserving volume exploration by replacing complex transfer function tuning with a direct spatial marking metaphor. Unlike techniques using independent surface-bound brushes or fixed-depth peeling regions, this method uses a higher-level shape representation (Metaballs) to create organic, merging envelopes that allow for real-time previewing of the visualization effect before final deposition. Choose this for interactive volume selection. Definition: A kernel family used to define skeleton-based implicit surfaces, characterized by local support required for efficient field evaluation on large skeletons and efficient closed-form evaluation of the integral field equation for line segment primitives with linearly interpolated prescribed thickness. Formula: The support of an individual primitive is a sphere-cone defined by scaling the two primitive endpoints' radius by a factor \sigma. Parameters: Degree parameter i: A parameter defining the polynomial degree of the kernel. Scale parameter \sigma: A parameter scaling the primitive endpoints' radius to define the support of an individual primitive. Definition: Generates voxel coordinates defined by an implicit function. Parameters: f: function of form f(x, y, z) returning a numeric value. lower, upper: range of values considered inside the object. Default: [-\infty, 0]. Values \le 0 are inside, > 0 are outside. scale: extra scaling factor applied to coordinates before calling function. nx, ny, nz: dimensions of the volume within which the function will be evaluated. Default: nx=51, ny=nx, nz=nx. Layout: Returns a data.frame of coordinates. Implicit surfaces were introduced as a way to represent complex geometry using a single mathematical function, allowing for smooth blending and deformation. The concept has evolved from simple algebraic surfaces to complex procedural fields and skeleton-based integral surfaces. Modern implementations leverage GPU compute shaders for real-time evaluation of dense scalar fields, enabling dynamic effects like metaballs and procedural hypertexturing. The family includes specific kernels like Cauchy, Inverse, and Compact Polynomial for skeleton-based rendering, and tools for voxel generation from arbitrary functions. name: Metaball Field Evaluation
head: Dynamic Metaball Volume Update Pipeline, GPU Field Generation, GPU volume generation, Implicit Metaball Field, Metaball Density Function, Metaball Field Computation, Metaball density field update
body: Metaball Field Evaluation generates and updates a 3D scalar density volume representing dynamic metaballs using a CPU-GPU pipeline, typically via compute or fragment shaders. It solves the problem of converting discrete, moving atomic positions into a continuous volumetric representation suitable for surface extraction or raymarching. Unlike Implicit Field Composition, which composes general implicit primitives, this method specifically sums inverse-distance or Gaussian contributions from moving spheres to create organic, merging blob shapes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N metaballs, each defined by position \vec{p}i, radius ri, and strength si; a 3D grid domain of resolution W \times H \times D; and a time parameter t. Outputs: A 3D texture (volume) where each voxel stores the summed scalar field value (density) and optionally color/normal data. Data Structures: Ball Buffer (Constant Buffer): Stores ball parameters in a structured buffer or constant buffer CBBalls. fBalls[150]: Array of XMFLOAT4 (x,y,z = position, w = power/radius squared). fBallsCol[150]: Array of XMFLOAT4 (color). iNumBalls: Integer count of active balls. Max balls supported is typically 150. Volume Texture: ID3D11Texture3D with format DXGIFORMATR32G32B32A32FLOAT. Dimensions: (W, H, D), often derived from half-resolution bounds. Layout: XYZ channels store color/intensity, W channel stores density. Flag Volume (Optional): ID3D11Texture3D with format DXGIFORMATR8SINT. Dimensions: Downsampled by VOXELBRICKRATIO. Purpose: Marks empty space for skipping during raymarching. Steps: 1. Initialization (CPU): Create volume textures with fixed resolution (e.g., 384 \times 384 \times 384). Initialize ball parameters: Radius r: Randomized, e.g., r = (0.6 \cdot \text{rand}() + 0.7) \cdot \text{halfReso} \cdot \text{voxelSize} \cdot 0.1. Power w = r^2. Orbit Radius: Randomized within bounds, clamped so r + \text{orbitRadius} < 0.45 \cdot \text{fullReso}. Speed: Randomized, clamped to \pm 1.0, scaled by 1/w. Phase: Random angle 0, 2\pi). Upload initial ball data to GPU constant buffers. 2. Dynamic Update (CPU): For each frame, update ball positions based on time t: xi(t) = ri \cos(t \cdot \text{speed}i + \text{phase}i). yi(t) = ri \sin(t \cdot \text{speed}i + \text{phase}i). zi(t) = 0.3 \cdot ri \sin(2 \cdot t \cdot \text{speed}i + \text{phase}i). Update the CBBalls buffer on the GPU. 3. Field Evaluation (GPU): Dispatch a compute shader or fragment shader to evaluate the field for each voxel. [Voxel Coordinate Mapping: Map fragment/pixel coordinates to 3D grid indices (x, y, z). Normalize to [0, 1]: fx = x/(W-1), fy = y/(H-1), fz = z/(D-1). Field Calculation: Initialize field value V = 0.0. For each ball i (up to N): Calculate squared distance: di^2 = (fx - p{ix})^2 + (fy - p{iy})^2 + (fz - p{iz})^2. Calculate contribution: ci = \frac{si}{di^2 + \epsilon}. Apply threshold (optional): If ci - \text{threshold} > 0, add to V. Add background/floor contributions if defined (e.g., floor plane at y=0). Write Output: Store V (and color) in the volume texture. Formulas: The density D at point \vec{x} is the sum of contributions from N metaballs: D(\vec{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \frac{si}{\|\vec{x} - \vec{p}i\|^2 + \epsilon} where: si is the strength of ball i. \vec{p}i is the position of ball i. \epsilon is a small constant to prevent division by zero (e.g., 0.001 or 0.000001). \|\cdot\| denotes Euclidean distance. Some implementations subtract a threshold T before accumulation: V(\vec{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \max\left(0, \frac{si}{\|\vec{x} - \vec{p}i\|^2 + \epsilon} - T\right) where T is typically 12.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatemetaballfield(gridsize, balls, time, epsilon=0.001, threshold=0.0): volume = np.zeros((gridsize, gridsize, gridsize)) invsize = 1.0 / (gridsize - 1) for z in range(gridsize): for y in range(gridsize): for x in range(gridsize): fx = x invsize fy = y invsize fz = z invsize fieldval = 0.0 for ball in balls: dx = fx - ball.pos.x dy = fy - ball.pos.y dz = fz - ball.pos.z distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz contribution = ball.strength / (distsq + epsilon) if contribution - threshold > 0.0: fieldval += contribution - threshold volume[x, y, z] = fieldval return volume Parameters: \epsilon: Epsilon for stability. Values: 0.001, 0.000001. Threshold T: Isosurface cutoff. Value: 12.0. Grid Size: e.g., 384 \times 384 \times 384. Max Balls: 150. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Avoid converting large integer voxel indices to floats in shaders if latency is a concern; store resolutions as floats in constant buffers. Boundary Conditions: Discard fragments outside the valid grid bounds [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1] \times [0, D-1]. Clamping: Ensure ball orbits do not exceed the volume bounds to prevent artifacts. Generates a 3D scalar density field by summing normalized radial Gaussian functions centered at predefined atomic positions, then scaling and clamping the result to a [0,1] range. It solves the problem of converting discrete atomic coordinates into a continuous volumetric representation suitable for surface extraction. Unlike Metaball Field Evaluation, which evaluates a dynamic scalar field composed of moving metaballs, this method uses static, smooth Gaussian falloffs centered on fixed points. Blob Field Generation is a procedural method for constructing a 3D scalar field by summing inverse-squared Euclidean distance contributions from a set of source points (metaballs). It solves the problem of defining smooth, organic implicit surfaces for isosurface extraction algorithms like Marching Cubes. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific use of the inverse square falloff (1/r^2) rather than Gaussian decay or fuzzy hyper-parameter blending, resulting in sharper, more defined "blob" interactions. This family defines the five scalar hyper-parameters used to tune the algebraic intersection and alpha-mask generation stages of the Fuzzy Metaballs rendering method. It solves the problem of converting raw implicit field evaluations into differentiable depth and alpha masks suitable for gradient-based pose optimization. What sets this apart from sibling methods like Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation or Blob Field Generation is that these parameters are not intrinsic properties of the volume geometry itself, but rather optimization targets for the rendering pipeline's differentiability and silhouette accuracy, specifically tuned for algebraic surface approximation. Generates a diagonal weight matrix for point cloud processing based on Welland functions. Step: Initialize diagonal matrix W of size P \times P with zeros. For each point P(i), calculate distance r = \|P(i) - X\|. Set W(i,i) = w. Formula: w = \left(\left(\frac{4r}{h} + 1\right)\left(1 - \frac{r}{h}\right)\right)^4. Parameter: h is the height of the Welland function, used as a scaling factor for radius r. Generates a 3D density field by blending signed distances of multiple spheres using a smooth minimum function, optionally perturbed by noise. Step: Calculate bounding box. Initialize density field. Iterate voxels. Compute signed distance for each sphere. If blendfactor < 0.01, use simple minimum. Otherwise, iteratively blend distances using SmoothUnion(mindist, signeddist, blendfactor). Parameter: blendfactor controls smoothness; noiseamplitude controls perturbation. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot N), where V is the number of voxels and N is the number of metaballs. Each voxel evaluates contributions from all balls. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, plus O(N) for ball parameters. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPU via compute shaders. Performance scales with grid resolution and ball count. Using a flag volume for empty space skipping reduces raymarching costs but requires additional generation overhead. Strengths: Real-time dynamic updates; organic merging shapes; simple implementation. Limitations: O(N) per voxel is expensive for large N; fixed grid resolution limits detail; inverse-square falloff can cause high values near centers requiring careful thresholding. Originated in the context of GPU-accelerated volume rendering and implicit surface generation. Early implementations used CPU updates with GPU texture uploads. Modern approaches use compute shaders for direct GPU-side field generation. The method is widely used in real-time visualization of fluid-like dynamics and organic modeling. pengliu916/DynamicVolumeRayCasting, https://github.com/pengliu916/DynamicVolumeRayCasting, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nff747/marching-cubes-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/marching-cubes-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 3merillon/WebGL2-GPU-Marching-Cubes, https://github.com/3merillon/WebGL2-GPU-Marching-Cubes, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) mwrazam/marchingtets-reconstruction, https://github.com/mwrazam/marchingtets-reconstruction, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) lijiemark/floating-islands-generator, https://github.com/lijiemark/floating-islands-generator, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation
head: Caffeine Molecule Volume Generation, Sum of Radial Gaussians
body: Generates a 3D scalar density field for volume rendering by summing normalized radial Gaussian functions centered at predefined atomic positions, then scaling and clamping the result to a [0,1] range. It solves the problem of creating smooth, continuous volumetric representations of discrete particle systems (such as molecules) from implicit surface primitives. Unlike Blob Field Generation, which may use different falloff characteristics, this method specifically employs smooth Gaussian decay, and unlike Fuzzy Metaballs Hyper-parameters, it relies on fixed analytical Gaussian kernels rather than tunable fuzzy boundaries for the core density definition. Inputs: Volume dimensions: dimX, dimY, dimZ (integers). Set of atoms, where each atom has a center (cX, cY, cZ) and a variance parameter \sigma^2 (or scale). postDensityScale: Global multiplier (default 2.5). isoValue: Threshold for surface extraction, clamped to [0,1] (default 0.5). Outputs: A 3D volume array of type uint16t (or specified bit depth), storing density values scaled to [0, 65535]. Data Structures: The RadialGaussian class stores: cX, cY, cZ: Center coordinates (float). normalization: Precomputed constant 1.0 / \sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2} (float). falloff: Precomputed constant -0.5 / \sigma^2 (float). Steps: 1. Initialize volume dimensions (e.g., 128 \times 128 \times 128) and allocate memory for volume.data. Set volume.bitDepth (e.g., 16). 2. Compute inverse dimensions: invDimX = \frac{1.0}{dimX - 1}, \quad invDimY = \frac{1.0}{dimY - 1}, \quad invDimZ = \frac{1.0}{dimZ - 1} 3. Define atom centers and their associated variance-derived scales. For the caffeine molecule example, a global scale s = 0.1 and offsets oX=0.5, oY=0.5, oZ=0.5 are applied to atomic coordinates. 4. For each voxel (z, y, x): a. Compute normalized coordinates: nX = x \cdot invDimX, \quad nY = y \cdot invDimY, \quad nZ = z \cdot invDimZ b. Initialize density \rho = 0.0. c. For each atom i: i. Calculate squared distance from atom center to normalized voxel position: d^2 = (nX - cXi)^2 + (nY - cYi)^2 + (nZ - cZi)^2 (Inferred from Gaussian definition and usage of falloff) ii. Evaluate atom contribution: \rho \leftarrow \rho + normalizationi \cdot e^{falloffi \cdot d^2} (Derived from normalization and falloff fields and standard Gaussian form) d. Apply global scaling: \rho \leftarrow \rho \cdot postDensityScale e. Clamp \rho to [0.0, 1.0]. f. Convert to target bit depth: value = \rho \cdot 65535 (Assuming 16-bit uint16t max) g. Store value in volume.data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class RadialGaussian: def init(self, cx, cy, cz, variance): self.cx = cx self.cy = cy self.cz = cz self.normalization = 1.0 / math.sqrt(2.0 math.pi variance) self.falloff = -0.5 / variance def eval(self, nx, ny, nz): dx = nx - self.cx dy = ny - self.cy dz = nz - self.cz distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz return self.normalization math.exp(self.falloff distsq) def generateradialgaussianvolume(dimx, dimy, dimz, atoms, postdensityscale=2.5, bitdepth=16): # 1. Initialize dimensions and memory numvoxels = dimx dimy dimz volumedata = [0] numvoxels # 2. Compute inverse dimensions invdimx = 1.0 / (dimx - 1) invdimy = 1.0 / (dimy - 1) invdimz = 1.0 / (dimz - 1) # 3. Determine max value for bit depth conversion maxval = 65535 if bitdepth == 16 else 255 # 4. Iterate over voxels for z in range(dimz): for y in range(dimy): for x in range(dimx): # Normalize coordinates nx = x invdimx ny = y invdimy nz = z invdimz rho = 0.0 # Sum contributions from all atoms for atom in atoms: rho += atom.eval(nx, ny, nz) # Scale and clamp rho = postdensityscale if rho < 0.0: rho = 0.0 if rho > 1.0: rho = 1.0 # Convert to bit depth volumedata[z dimy dimx + y dimx + x] = int(rho maxval) return volumedata Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If dimX, dimY, or dimZ is 1, invDim becomes undefined (division by zero). The source assumes dimensions >1. Invalid isoValue (NaN or out of bounds) is clamped to 0.0. Precision issues may arise if variance is extremely small, leading to numerical overflow in the exponential term. Particle Density Field Computation generates a 3D scalar density field by evaluating a radial kernel function for every voxel in a 3D grid, summing contributions from a set of particles. Unlike Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation, which uses smooth Gaussian falloffs, this method employs a specific polynomial kernel with a sharp cutoff at a normalized squared distance of 0.5, resulting in a compact support that strictly excludes distant particles. Synthetic Active Region Generation creates a synthetic bipolar active region magnetogram by summing Gaussian flux concentrations, satellite flux, polarity inversion line (PIL) shear, diffuse background, and instrument noise. It solves the problem of generating realistic, volumetric magnetic field data for visualization by converting parametric tube geometry into a discrete set of 3D points with associated vector field values and intensity. It differs from direct field evaluation methods by explicitly tracing a path with a restoring force and random walk, rather than sampling a static analytical field at grid points. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot A), where V is the number of voxels and A is the number of atoms. Each voxel requires evaluating the Gaussian function for every atom. Memory Complexity: O(V) for storing the volume data. Performance: The example uses a 128^3 grid, resulting in 2,097,152 voxels. The performance depends heavily on the number of atoms and the efficiency of the exponential function evaluation. Strengths: Produces smooth, continuous density fields suitable for isosurface extraction (e.g., Dual Marching Cubes). The Gaussian kernel is infinitely differentiable, leading to smooth surfaces. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large numbers of atoms or high-resolution volumes due to the O(V \cdot A) complexity. The support is theoretically infinite, though contributions decay rapidly. When to use: Suitable for molecular visualization or any scenario requiring smooth, overlapping density fields from discrete sources. When not to use: When computational resources are limited and a compact support kernel (like the one in Particle Density Field Computation) is preferred for faster culling. Originated from the dualmc project by Dominik Wodniok, which demonstrates volume rendering and isosurface extraction using the Dual Marching Cubes algorithm. The specific "Caffeine Molecule" example serves as a canonical test case for generating implicit surfaces from atomic coordinates. The method is part of a broader family of procedural volume generation techniques used in scientific visualization and computer graphics. dominikwodniok/dualmc, https://github.com/dominikwodniok/dualmc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Particle Density Field Computation
head: Particle Power Summation, Particle-to-Grid Transfer
body: Particle Density Field Computation generates a 3D scalar density field by evaluating a radial kernel function for every voxel in a 3D grid, summing contributions from a set of particles. Unlike Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation, which uses smooth Gaussian falloffs, this method employs a specific polynomial kernel with a sharp cutoff at a normalized squared distance of 0.5, resulting in a compact support that strictly excludes distant particles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A structured buffer posBuffer containing N particles, where each particle is a float4 (x, y, z, r) representing position and radius. A 3D grid with dimensions GRIDDIMX, GRIDDIMY, GRIDDIMZ and voxel spacing textureSizeScale. Output: A structured buffer pixels of float4 values storing the computed scalar field as (density, density, density, 1.0). Data Structures: posBuffer: RWStructuredBuffer<float4> storing particle positions and radii as (x, y, z, radius). pixels: RWStructuredBuffer<float4> storing the output density field as (density, density, density, 1.0). gParams: float4 constant buffer where gParams.z holds textureSizeScale (voxel spacing) and gParams.y holds the grid dimension in Y. Algorithm Steps: 1. Dispatch: Launch a compute shader with thread groups of size 8 \times 8 \times 8, where each thread handles one voxel. 2. Voxel Position: Calculate the world position \mathbf{t} of the current voxel using the thread ID (id.x, id.y, id.z) and textureSizeScale: \mathbf{t} = (id.x \cdot \text{textureSizeScale}, \ id.y \cdot \text{textureSizeScale}, \ id.z \cdot \text{textureSizeScale}) 3. Accumulator Initialization: Initialize a scalar accumulator p to 0.0. 4. Particle Iteration: Iterate over all N particles in posBuffer. For each particle i with position \mathbf{p}i and radius ri: a. Compute the normalized squared distance m^2: m^2 = \frac{\|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{t}\|^2}{ri^2} b. Evaluate the kernel function f(m^2): f(m^2) = \begin{cases} 0.25 - m^2 + (m^2)^2 & \text{if } m^2 < 0.5 \\ 0.0 & \text{if } m^2 \ge 0.5 \end{cases} c. Add the result to the accumulator: p \leftarrow p + f(m^2). 5. Write Output: Store the accumulated density p into the output buffer at the linearized index corresponding to the voxel (id.x, id.y, id.z): \text{pixels}[idx] = (p, p, p, 1.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedensityfield(posBuffer, numParticles, gParams, pixels, GRIDDIMX, GRIDDIMY, GRIDDIMZ): textureSizeScale = gParams.z for idz in range(GRIDDIMZ): for idy in range(GRIDDIMY): for idx in range(GRIDDIMX): # 1. Calculate world position of the voxel testPos = (idx textureSizeScale, idy textureSizeScale, idz textureSizeScale) # 2. Initialize accumulator p = 0.0 # 3. Iterate over all particles for i in range(numParticles): particle = posBuffer[i] dx = particle.x - testPos[0] dy = particle.y - testPos[1] dz = particle.z - testPos[2] # 4. Compute normalized squared distance and kernel msqr = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz) / (particle.w particle.w) if msqr < 0.5: p += 0.25 - msqr + msqr msqr # 5. Linearize index for output buffer (standard row-major order) idx = (idz GRIDDIMY + idy) GRIDDIMX + idx # 6. Write result pixels[idx] = (p, p, p, 1.0) Parameters: textureSizeScale: The physical spacing between adjacent grid voxels. numParticles: The total count of particles in posBuffer. Kernel Cutoff: The normalized squared distance threshold is hardcoded to 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Cutoff: The kernel function returns exactly 0.0 for m^2 \ge 0.5, creating a strict boundary rather than a smooth falloff. A technique to prevent higher-order rounding error propagation during the recursive computation of polynomial coefficients used in particle-wise field approximation. It converts floating-point quantities to fixed-point integers to ensure exact arithmetic. Definition: Shifts numbers encoding contribution approximations into integer multiples of quantum values. Knots (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}) and localized coefficients a{kd} are quantized such that tk \approx \bar{t}k \tau and \hat{a}{kd} \approx \bar{\hat{a}}{kd} \zetad, a{kd} \approx \bar{a}{kd} \zetad for integers \bar{t}k, \bar{\hat{a}}{kd}, \bar{a}{kd}. Formula: The update rule becomes integer-only: \bar{a}{kd} = \bar{a}{kd} + \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} \bar{a}{(k-1)j} (\bar{t}k - \bar{t}{k-1})^{j-d} provided \zetad = \frac{\zeta}{\tau^d}. Parameters: \tau is the length quantum value (resolution of knot positions). \zeta is the field value quantum value (resolution of coefficients, where \zeta0 = \zeta). Pitfall: Direct application of the recursive coefficient update using floating-point numbers causes rounding errors to propagate at higher order from front to back along the viewing ray, leading to unstable results and 'sprinkling' artifacts. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of particles and V is the number of voxels in the grid, as each voxel iterates over all particles. Memory Complexity: O(N + V) for storing the particle buffer and the output density grid. Not given in the sources: measured performance on specific hardware, scaling behavior, or explicit usage recommendations. The method is implemented in the context of GPU-based marching cubes and particle rendering, specifically within the Unity engine ecosystem using HLSL compute shaders. The specific kernel function 0.25 - m^2 + (m^2)^2 with a cutoff at m^2=0.5 is designed to plot a curve that is 0.25 at r=0 and 0 at r = \sqrt{0.5} \cdot \text{power}, providing a "nice curve" for particle visualization. The quantization variant is discussed in the context of particle-wise higher-order SPH field approximation to avoid rounding errors in recursive coefficient updates. kristofe/UnityGPUMarchingCubes, https://github.com/kristofe/UnityGPUMarchingCubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation for DVR, https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.02896v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Synthetic Active Region Generation
head: Mode C, Synthetic Bipole
body: Synthetic Active Region Generation creates a synthetic bipolar active region magnetogram by summing Gaussian flux concentrations, satellite flux, polarity inversion line (PIL) shear, diffuse background, and instrument noise. It generates a 2D scalar field representing magnetic field strength on a grid, which serves as input for subsequent 3D volume rendering methods. Inputs: seed: Integer seed for the random number generator. GRIDSIZE (g): Integer resolution of the output grid. Outputs: bz: A 2D array of shape (g, g) with dtype=np.float32, representing the magnetic field strength. Data Structures: rng: A random number generator instance initialized with seed. XX, YY: 2D arrays of shape (g, g) created via np.meshgrid, containing the x and y coordinates of each grid cell ranging from -4.0 to 4.0. Steps: 1. Initialize RNG and Grid: Create the random number generator and coordinate grids. python rng = np.random.defaultrng(seed) g = GRIDSIZE x = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, g) y = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, g) XX, YY = np.meshgrid(x, y) 2. Initialize Bz Grid: Create a zero-filled grid for the magnetic field. python bz = np.zeros((g, g), dtype=np.float32) 3. Add Primary Positive Bipole: Sample parameters for the positive flux concentration and add a Gaussian. pospeak: Sampled from uniform distribution [1200, 1800]. possigma: Sampled from uniform distribution [0.60, 0.85]. poscx, poscy: Fixed centers at (-1.35, 0.10). Formula: bz \ += \ pos\peak \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(XX - pos\cx)^2 + (YY - pos\cy)^2}{2 \cdot pos\sigma^2}\right) 4. Add Primary Negative Bipole: Sample parameters for the negative flux concentration and add a Gaussian. negpeak: Sampled from uniform distribution [-1400, -900] (implemented as -rng.uniform(900, 1400)). negsigma: Sampled from uniform distribution [0.75, 1.00]. negcx, negcy: Fixed centers at (1.50, -0.05). Formula: bz \ += \ neg\peak \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(XX - neg\cx)^2 + (YY - neg\cy)^2}{2 \cdot neg\sigma^2}\right) 5. Add Satellite Flux: Generate 3 to 6 satellite flux concentrations (inclusive). nsatellites: Sampled from integers [3, 7). For each satellite: scx: Sampled from uniform distribution [-3.0, 3.0]. scy: Sampled from uniform distribution [-2.5, 2.5]. scpeak: Sampled as \pm \text{uniform}(80, 350), where the sign is chosen randomly from \{-1, 1\}. scsig: Sampled from uniform distribution [0.20, 0.50]. Formula: bz \ += \ sc\peak \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{(XX - sc\x)^2 + (YY - sc\y)^2}{2 \cdot sc\sig^2}\right) 6. Add PIL Shear: Add a shear component modulated by a Gaussian envelope. pilshear: Sampled from uniform distribution [0.08, 0.25]. pilwarp: Calculated as \tanh((XX + pil\shear \cdot YY) \cdot 1.5) \cdot \text{uniform}(30, 80). Formula: bz \ += \ pil\warp \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{XX^2 + YY^2}{8.0}\right) 7. Add Diffuse Background: Add a diffuse background noise term. bgval: Sampled from uniform distribution [-40, 40]. Formula: bz \ += \ bg\val \cdot \exp\left(-\frac{XX^2 + YY^2}{12.0}\right) 8. Add Instrument Noise: Add Gaussian noise to simulate instrument error. noise: Sampled from normal distribution \mathcal{N}(0, 15.0) with shape (g, g), cast to float32. Formula: bz \ += \ noise 9. Apply Boundary Apodisation: Smoothly fade the field to zero at the boundaries to prevent artifacts. r2: Calculated as (XX / 4.2)^2 + (YY / 4.2)^2. apod: Calculated as \sqrt{\max(0, 1.0 - r2)}. Formula: bz \ = \ apod Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def generateactiveregion(seed, GRIDSIZE): # 1. Initialize RNG and Grid rng = np.random.defaultrng(seed) g = GRIDSIZE x = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, g) y = np.linspace(-4.0, 4.0, g) XX, YY = np.meshgrid(x, y) # 2. Initialize Bz Grid bz = np.zeros((g, g), dtype=np.float32) # 3. Add Primary Positive Bipole pospeak = rng.uniform(1200, 1800) possigma = rng.uniform(0.60, 0.85) poscx, poscy = -1.35, 0.10 bz += pospeak np.exp(-((XX - poscx)2 + (YY - poscy)2) / (2 possigma2)) # 4. Add Primary Negative Bipole negpeak = -rng.uniform(900, 1400) negsigma = rng.uniform(0.75, 1.00) negcx, negcy = 1.50, -0.05 bz += negpeak np.exp(-((XX - negcx)2 + (YY - negcy)2) / (2 negsigma2)) # 5. Add Satellite Flux nsatellites = rng.integers(3, 7) for in range(nsatellites): scx = rng.uniform(-3.0, 3.0) scy = rng.uniform(-2.5, 2.5) scsign = rng.choice([-1, 1]) scpeak = scsign rng.uniform(80, 350) scsig = rng.uniform(0.20, 0.50) bz += scpeak np.exp(-((XX - scx)2 + (YY - scy)2) / (2 scsig2)) # 6. Add PIL Shear pilshear = rng.uniform(0.08, 0.25) pilwarp = np.tanh((XX + pilshear YY) 1.5) rng.uniform(30, 80) bz += pilwarp np.exp(-(XX2 + YY2) / 8.0) # 7. Add Diffuse Background bgval = rng.uniform(-40, 40) bz += bgval np.exp(-(XX2 + YY2) / 12.0) # 8. Add Instrument Noise noise = rng.normal(0, 15.0, (g, g)).astype(np.float32) bz += noise # 9. Apply Boundary Apodisation r2 = (XX / 4.2)2 + (YY / 4.2)2 apod = np.clip(1.0 - r2, 0, 1)0.5 bz = apod return bz Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The source specifies dtype=np.float32 for the grid and noise. Boundaries: The apodisation factor becomes zero when r2 \ge 1, effectively masking the field outside the radius of 4.2 units. Points exactly on the boundary are handled by np.clip. Degenerate Input: If GRIDSIZE is too small, the Gaussian peaks may not be resolved, leading to aliasing. The source does not specify a minimum resolution. Flux Tube Filament Generation is a procedural algorithm that traces sample points along magnetic field lines (filaments) within a synthetic flux tube volume, incorporating radial convergence and stochastic noise to simulate magnetic field line wandering. It solves the problem of generating structured, volumetric magnetic field data for visualization by converting a parametric tube geometry into a discrete set of 3D points with associated vector field values and intensity. It differs from direct field evaluation methods by explicitly tracing a path with a restoring force and random walk, rather than sampling a static analytical field at grid points. Time Complexity: O(g^2) per Gaussian addition, where g is the grid size. With a constant number of Gaussians (2 primary, 3-6 satellites, 1 shear, 1 background), the total time is linear in the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: O(g^2) for the bz grid and coordinate arrays. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast to generate; produces visually realistic bipolar structures with shear and noise. Limitations: The output is a 2D magnetogram, not a full 3D volume, though it serves as input for 3D generation methods. The parameters are hardcoded ranges, limiting fine control over specific physical properties. When to use: When a quick, realistic synthetic magnetogram is needed for testing or visualization pipelines. When not to use: When precise physical accuracy or 3D volumetric data is required directly from this step. Origin: The method is described in the repository. It is used in the context of astrophysical vector field visualization, specifically for generating synthetic data that mimics solar active regions. name: Flux Tube Filament Generation
head: Dataset Generation and Encoding, Saturn Polar Magnetic Flux Tube Generation, flux tube filament tracing
body: Flux Tube Filament Generation is a procedural algorithm that traces sample points along magnetic field lines (filaments) within a flux tube, incorporating radial convergence and stochastic noise. It generates, constrains, encodes, and saves the flux tube dataset as a discrete set of 3D points with associated vector field values and intensity. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Parameters defining the tube geometry (TUBERADIUS, TUBEHEIGHT), filament count (NSTRANDS), sampling density (POINTSPERSTRAND), noise magnitude (NOISESCALE), dipole tilt (DIPOLETILTDEG), dipole scaling (FIELDSTRENGTH), and a global point limit (MAXPOINTS). Outputs: A list of point records, each containing position (x, y, z), magnetic field vector (Bx, By, Bz), intensity, and a derived grayscale value, saved as a compact JSON dataset. Data Structures: Point Record: A dictionary with keys x, y, z (float, 5 decimal precision), Bx, By, Bz (float, 4 decimal precision), and intensity (float, 4 decimal precision). Dataset: A list of point records, serialized to JSON with compact separators (no spaces). Parameters: TUBEHEIGHT: 10.0 [scene units]. TUBERADIUS: 0.6 [scene units]. NSTRANDS: 8. POINTSPERSTRAND: 500. NOISESCALE: 0.08 [standard deviation per step]. DIPOLETILTDEG: 3.0 [degrees]. FIELDSTRENGTH: 20000.0 [arbitrary units]. MAXPOINTS: 5000 [absolute ceiling]. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list allpoints. 2. Loop filamentidx from 0 to NSTRANDS - 1: a. Initialize a deterministic random number generator rng with seed filamentidx 7919. b. Calculate initial angular position: \phi0 = \frac{2.0 \pi \cdot \text{filament\idx}}{\text{N\STRANDS}}. c. Calculate initial radial offset: r0 = \text{TUBE\RADIUS} \cdot \text{rng.uniform}(0.15, 0.85). d. Initialize position at the lower boundary: cx = r0 \cos(\phi0) cy = r0 \sin(\phi0) cz = -\frac{\text{TUBE\HEIGHT}}{2.0}. e. Calculate vertical step size: \text{step\z} = \frac{\text{TUBE\HEIGHT}}{\text{POINTS\PER\STRAND}}. f. Calculate tilt offset: \text{tilt\rad} = \text{radians}(\text{DIPOLE\TILT\DEG}), \text{tilt\x} = \sin(\text{tilt\rad}). g. Loop i from 0 to POINTSPERSTRAND - 1: i. Calculate normalized height: \text{frac} = \frac{i}{\text{POINTS\PER\STRAND}}. ii. Calculate radial convergence: r{\text{now}} = r0 (1.0 - 0.4 \cdot \text{frac}). iii. Calculate target position: \text{target\x} = r{\text{now}} \cos(\phi0) + \text{tilt\x} \cdot cz \cdot 0.1 \text{target\y} = r{\text{now}} \sin(\phi0). iv. Update position using Euler integration with restoring force and noise: cx \leftarrow cx + (\text{target\x} - cx) \cdot 0.08 + \mathcal{N}(0, \text{NOISE\SCALE}) cy \leftarrow cy + (\text{target\y} - cy) \cdot 0.08 + \mathcal{N}(0, \text{NOISE\SCALE}) cz \leftarrow cz + \text{step\z}. v. Evaluate a dipole field at (cx, cy, cz) to obtain (Bx, By, Bz). The exact dipole orientation and formula are not specified in the source. vi. Calculate magnitude: \text{mag} = \sqrt{Bx^2 + By^2 + Bz^2}. vii. Append point record with rounded coordinates and field values: x, y, z (5 decimals), Bx, By, Bz (4 decimals), intensity (4 decimals). 3. If len(allpoints) > MAXPOINTS, truncate allpoints to the first MAXPOINTS elements. 4. Extract intensities from all points to find i{\min} and i{\max}. 5. For each point, compute a grayscale value from its intensity using min-max normalization. The exact normalization function is not specified in the source. 6. Save dataset to magnetospheredata.json in compact JSON format. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random import json def generatefluxtubefilaments(): # Parameters TUBEHEIGHT = 10.0 TUBERADIUS = 0.6 NSTRANDS = 8 POINTSPERSTRAND = 500 NOISESCALE = 0.08 DIPOLETILTDEG = 3.0 FIELDSTRENGTH = 20000.0 MAXPOINTS = 5000 allpoints = [] for filamentidx in range(NSTRANDS): # Deterministic seeding per filament rng = random.Random(filamentidx 7919) # Initial conditions phi0 = (2.0 math.pi filamentidx) / NSTRANDS r0 = TUBERADIUS rng.uniform(0.15, 0.85) cx = r0 math.cos(phi0) cy = r0 math.sin(phi0) cz = -TUBEHEIGHT / 2.0 stepz = TUBEHEIGHT / POINTSPERSTRAND tiltrad = math.radians(DIPOLETILTDEG) tiltx = math.sin(tiltrad) for i in range(POINTSPERSTRAND): frac = i / POINTSPERSTRAND rnow = r0 (1.0 - 0.4 frac) targetx = rnow math.cos(phi0) + tiltx cz 0.1 targety = rnow math.sin(phi0) # Euler integration with restoring force and noise cx += (targetx - cx) 0.08 + rng.gauss(0, NOISESCALE) cy += (targety - cy) 0.08 + rng.gauss(0, NOISESCALE) cz += stepz # Evaluate dipole field [G: Standard dipole aligned with Z axis, scaled by FIELDSTRENGTH] rmag = math.sqrt(cx2 + cy2 + cz2) if rmag == 0: bx, by, bz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 else: bx = FIELDSTRENGTH (3 cz cx) / (rmag5) by = FIELDSTRENGTH (3 cz cy) / (rmag5) bz = FIELDSTRENGTH (3 cz2 - rmag2) / (rmag5) mag = math.sqrt(bx2 + by2 + bz2) # Create record record = { 'x': round(cx, 5), 'y': round(cy, 5), 'z': round(cz, 5), 'Bx': round(bx, 4), 'By': round(by, 4), 'Bz': round(bz, 4), 'intensity': round(mag, 4) } allpoints.append(record) # Truncate if exceeding hardware safety constraint if len(allpoints) > MAXPOINTS: allpoints = allpoints[:MAXPOINTS] # Normalize intensity to grayscale [G: Standard min-max normalization] if allpoints: intensities = [p['intensity'] for p in allpoints] imin = min(intensities) imax = max(intensities) for p in allpoints: if imax == imin: p['gray'] = 0.5 else: p['gray'] = (p['intensity'] - imin) / (imax - imin) # Save to JSON with open('magnetospheredata.json', 'w') as f: json.dump(allpoints, f, separators=(',', ':')) return allpoints Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Blob Field Generation
head: Inverse Distance Weighting for Isosurfaces, Inverse Square Blob Field, Metaball Scalar Field Construction, Procedural Blob Field
body: Blob Field Generation is a procedural method for constructing a 3D scalar field by summing inverse-square distance contributions from a set of source points (blobs), creating smooth, organic "metaball" shapes suitable for isosurface extraction via Marching Cubes. It differs from Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation by using 1/r^2 falloff instead of exponential decay, resulting in sharper, more compact isosurfaces with heavier tails, and from Fuzzy Metaballs Hyper-parameters by relying on explicit inverse-distance weighting rather than probabilistic or fuzzy logic blending. Inputs: A set of N source points (blob centers) Pi = (xi, yi, zi) for i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}. A set of weights wi for each blob. A query point Q = (x, y, z) in 3D space. Optional: Time parameter t for animated blob positions. Optional: Floor effect parameters if a ground plane is included. Outputs: A scalar field value f(x, y, z) representing the density at Q. Data Structures: sSourcePoint: An array of N structures, each containing three floating-point coordinates (fX, fY, fZ). weights: An array of N floating-point values wi. Steps: 1. Initialize Result: Set fResult = 0.0. 2. Iterate Blobs: For each blob i from 0 to N-1: a. Calculate the squared Euclidean distance between the query point Q and the blob center Pi: distSq = (x - xi)^2 + (y - yi)^2 + (z - zi)^2. b. Handle Singularity: Add a small epsilon \epsilon to the denominator to prevent division by zero if Q coincides with Pi. c. Compute Contribution: Add the weighted inverse square distance to the result: fResult \leftarrow fResult + \frac{wi}{distSq + \epsilon}. 3. Optional Floor Effect: If a floor is defined at height y{floor}: a. Calculate vertical distance dy = y - y{floor}. b. Compute floor contribution: floorVal = \frac{w{floor}}{dy^2 + \epsilon{floor}} - C{offset}. c. If floorVal > 0, add it to fResult. 4. Return: Return fResult. Formulas: Standard Euclidean Blob Field: f(x,y,z) = \sum{i} \frac{wi}{(x - xi)^2 + (y - yi)^2 + (z - zi)^2}. Distance Metrics for Non-Spherical Shapes: Euclidean: dist(p1, p2) = \sqrt{(p1.x - p2.x)^2 + (p1.y - p2.y)^2 + (p1.z - p2.z)^2}. Taxicab (Manhattan): dist1(p1, p2) = |p1.x - p2.x| + |p1.y - p2.y| + |p1.z - p2.z|. Max-Metric: distMax(p1, p2) = \max(|p1.x - p2.x|, |p1.y - p2.y|, |p1.z - p2.z|). Parameters: weights (wi): Control the influence of each blob. In the example, weights are 0.5, 1.0, 1.5. epsilon (\epsilon): Small constant to prevent division by zero. Value 0.000001 is used in, 0.0001 for floor in. time (t): Used to animate blob positions via sinusoidal functions. strength: In, a uniform strength is calculated as 1.2 / ((\sqrt{numBlobs} - 1) / 4 + 1). offset: A constant subtracted from the field value to control the isovalue threshold. Value -12.0 is used in. alpha: Constant for fading effect in cloud variants. Value 0.6 used in. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluateblobfield(x, y, z, sourcepoints, weights, epsilon=1e-6, usefloor=False, floory=0.0, floorweight=2.0, floorepsilon=1e-4, flooroffset=12.0): """ Evaluates the blob field at point (x, y, z). Args: x, y, z: Coordinates of the query point. sourcepoints: List of tuples (px, py, pz) representing blob centers. weights: List of floats representing blob weights. epsilon: Small constant to prevent division by zero. usefloor: Boolean to enable floor effect. floory: Y-coordinate of the floor plane. floorweight: Weight for the floor effect. floorepsilon: Epsilon for floor distance calculation. flooroffset: Constant subtracted from floor value. Returns: Scalar field value at (x, y, z). """ fresult = 0.0 # Iterate over all blobs for i in range(len(sourcepoints)): px, py, pz = sourcepoints[i] w = weights[i] # Calculate squared Euclidean distance dx = x - px dy = y - py dz = z - pz distsq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz # Add epsilon to prevent division by zero fresult += w / (distsq + epsilon) # Optional floor effect if usefloor: fy = y - floory floorval = floorweight / (fyfy + floorepsilon) - flooroffset if floorval > 0: fresult += floorval return fresult Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If the evaluation point coincides exactly with a source point, the distance term becomes zero, causing the value to approach infinity. A small epsilon must be added to the denominator. Metric Selection: Using standard Euclidean distance creates spherical metaballs. To create cubic or "Minecraft-like" isosurfaces, Taxicab or Max-metric distances should be used instead. Applies Blinn's metaball technique for organic n-dimensional objects to generate cumulus clouds. It differs from other methods by using optimized equations and pre-calculating the mean value on the CPU for high performance. The field is evaluated as f(x) = \sumi \frac{ri^2}{|x - ci|^2}, where ri is the sphere radius and ci is the center. A constant \alpha = 0.6 adjusts the fading effect at the cloud edges. Render quality is sufficient but lower than Algorithm 1, using only six spheres with randomized radii. Time Complexity: O(N) per query point, where N is the number of blobs. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store source points and weights. Performance: High performance, especially when mean values are pre-calculated on the CPU. Strengths: Simple to implement, produces smooth organic shapes, computationally efficient. Limitations: Sharp falloff can lead to aliasing if not sampled finely; singularities require handling. Use Cases: Isosurface generation for organic shapes, cloud rendering. When Not to Use: When exponential falloff (Gaussian) is preferred for softer edges, or when complex procedural noise is needed. Originated from Blinn's metaball technique for creating organic-looking n-dimensional objects. The inverse square distance method is commonly used in conjunction with the Marching Cubes algorithm for isosurface extraction. It has been applied in computer graphics for generating clouds, organic shapes, and fluid-like surfaces. 3merillon/WebGL2-GPU-Marching-Cubes, https://github.com/3merillon/WebGL2-GPU-Marching-Cubes, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) 2 Isovalue in Marching Cubes Algorithm, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/11177604/isovalue-in-marching-cubes-algorithm?rq=4, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Efficient Algorithms for Real-Time GPU Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Enhanced Geometry, https://doi.org/10.3390/sym10040125, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Fuzzy Metaballs Hyper-parameters
head: Fuzzy Metaballs Parameters, Metaball Field Hyper-parameters
body: This family defines the five scalar hyper-parameters used to tune the algebraic intersection and alpha-mask generation stages of the Fuzzy Metaballs rendering method. It solves the problem of converting raw implicit field evaluations into differentiable depth and alpha masks suitable for gradient-based pose optimization. What sets this apart from sibling methods like Radial Gaussian Density Field Generation or Blob Field Generation is that these parameters are not intrinsic properties of the volume geometry itself, but rather optimization targets for the rendering pipeline's differentiability and silhouette accuracy, specifically tuned for algebraic surface approximation. The Fuzzy Metaballs approach relies on a fully algebraic formulation of ray-surface intersection, allowing gradients to flow through the rendering process. The hyper-parameters are divided into two functional groups: those influencing the geometric intersection logic and those scaling the final output masks. 1. Intersection Weights (\beta1, \beta2, \beta3): These parameters weight different criteria during the computation of ray-surface intersections. 2. Alpha Mask Scaling (\beta4, \beta5): These parameters apply a linear transformation (scale and offset) to the raw intersection results to generate the final alpha masks. Empirical evidence shows that optimal values for these parameters are robust across varying resolutions, mixture component counts, and intersection polynomial degrees (linear, quadratic, cubic). Prioritizes hits that are geometrically close to the ray origin during intersection computation. Prioritizes hits that are closer to the camera viewpoint. Prioritizes hits that lie in front of the camera plane. The scale factor applied to the raw field value to generate the alpha mask. The offset factor applied to the raw field value to generate the alpha mask. The Fuzzy Metaballs hyper-parameters were introduced in the context of "Approximate Differentiable Rendering with Algebraic Surfaces". The method was developed to enable gradient-based pose optimization for 3D reconstruction using algebraic surface approximations. The authors noted that while the algebraic formulation naturally supports gradient descent into these hyper-parameters (via tools like JAX), they did not use this approach in practice. Instead, they optimized the five parameters using standard black-box optimization techniques on a small simulated dataset (the Stanford bunny) to maximize depth and alpha mask accuracy. This pre-optimization step was performed before running the main experiments. The robustness of these parameters was validated by finding similar optimal values across multiple tested resolutions, a wide range of mixture components, and different intersection computation methods (linear, quadratic, and cubic). name: Distance to Hypertextures
head: Fractal noise deformation, Hypertexture, Hypertexture noise
body: Distance to Hypertextures is a technique for adding relief or details to surfaces without increasing geometry cost, using procedural texture synthesis evaluated within a volumetric region around the object rather than only on the surface. It deforms implicit surfaces by adding procedural noise to the function's range instead of the domain, enabling sphere tracing with distance bounds. Unlike standard hypertexturing which may deform the domain, this variant affects the range, allowing the use of signed distance functions for efficient rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base signed distance function f(\vec{x}), a noise function noise(\vec{x}), and a spectral exponent \alpha. Output: A deformed implicit surface defined by f(\vec{x}) + noise\alpha(\vec{x}) = 0. Data Structures: \Gamma: An array of random values used for solid noise interpolation. Octaves: A finite integer n controlling the number of noise layers. Steps: 1. Define Base Noise: Construct band-limited solid noise using a piecewise cubic Gaussian approximation \phi and random values \Gamma: noise(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=-1}^{1} \sum{j=-1}^{1} \sum{k=-1}^{1} \Gamma(i,j,k) \cdot \phi(\mathbf{x} - (i,j,k)) where \phi is a scalar piecewise cubic approximation of a Gaussian distribution. 2. Compute Lipschitz Constant for Base Noise: The Lipschitz constant for the base noise is derived from the composition of \phi and \Gamma. Given Lip{\phi} = 3/2 and Lip{\Gamma} = 2, the composition results in Lip{noise} = 3. 3. Generate Fractal Noise: Sum scaled versions of the base noise over n octaves to create fractal noise with spectral exponent \alpha: noise\alpha(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{n} \frac{noise(2^i \mathbf{x})}{2^{i\alpha}} 4. Deform Surface: Evaluate the deformed implicit field F(\vec{x}) = f(\vec{x}) + noise\alpha(\vec{x}). 5. Sphere Tracing: Use the Lipschitz constant of the total function to determine safe step sizes for sphere tracing. Parameters: \alpha: Spectral exponent. \alpha=0 is white noise, \alpha=1 is 1/f noise, \alpha=2 is Brownian motion. n: Number of octaves. Must be finite to ensure the function remains Lipschitz. \Gamma: Array of random values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unbounded 1/f noise is not Lipschitz; it must be band-limited to a finite number of octaves n to remain Lipschitz for sphere tracing. For 1/f noise, the Lipschitz constant equals the sum of individual noise functions, Lip{1/f \ noise} = 3. For Brownian motion (\alpha=2), the Lipschitz constant is Lip{B} = 3(2^{1-n} - 1) \approx 6. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hypertexturedeformation(x, f, alpha, n, Gamma): """ Computes the deformed implicit surface value using Distance to Hypertextures. Args: x: 3D point (list of 3 floats) f: Base signed distance function (callable, returns float) alpha: Spectral exponent (float) n: Number of octaves (int) Gamma: 3x3x3 array of random scalars (list of lists of lists of floats) Returns: Deformed field value (float) """ noisevalue = 0.0 for i in range(n + 1): scaledx = [x[j] (2 i) for j in range(3)] currentnoise = 0.0 for di in range(-1, 2): for dj in range(-1, 2): for dk in range(-1, 2): vec = Gamma[di + 1][dj + 1][dk + 1] offset = [scaledx[0] - di, scaledx[1] - dj, scaledx[2] - dk] r = (offset[0]2 + offset[1]2 + offset[2]2)0.5 phival = cubicgaussianapprox(r) currentnoise += vec phival noisevalue += currentnoise / (2 (i alpha)) return f(x) + noisevalue def cubicgaussianapprox(r): """ Piecewise cubic approximation of Gaussian distribution. Based on Wyvill et al. """ if r < 1.0: return (2.0 / 3.0) - r2 + 0.5 r3 return 0.0 A method where a distance field is derived from the mesh on the fly on the GPU, and surface vicinity is used for hypertexture lookups. It uses 20 octaves of Perlin noise for shading and complex materials. Due to complex GPU computations, frame rate is around 20 FPS for a 1024^3 volume. The time complexity is high due to multiple noise evaluations and octaves, resulting in low frame rates such as 20 FPS for a 1024^3 volume. The memory complexity depends on the number of octaves and the size of the Gamma array, though streaming implementations can optimize usage with node pools and bricks. Strengths include adding high-frequency detail without increasing geometric complexity and enabling sphere tracing for efficient rendering. Limitations arise because unbounded 1/f noise is not Lipschitz and must be band-limited to a finite number of octaves to remain Lipschitz for stable sphere tracing. It should be used when high-quality procedural detail is needed on implicit surfaces and performance allows for complex GPU computations. Proposed by Perlin [PH89], hypertextures were inspired by the idea of evaluating procedural texture synthesis within a volumetric region around an object rather than only on the surface. This allows for the modeling of phenomena intermediate between surface and texture. The specific variant affecting the range to enable sphere tracing was detailed in subsequent work. name: Superelliptic Blends
head: Pseudonorm Blend, Ricci blend, Rockwood and Owen blend
body: Superelliptic blends (also known as pseudonorm blends) are a local geometric deformation technique for implicitly defining the union of two or more signed distance functions (SDFs). This method computes a p-norm distance to the blended union, allowing for smooth transitions between surfaces controlled by a tightness parameter p. It differs from global additive field methods by operating directly on distance values and maintaining local support. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Two signed distance functions f1(\mathbf{x}) and f2(\mathbf{x}), a blend parameter p > 0 (thumbweight), and support radii d1, d2 defining the local domain of influence for each function. Output: A new implicit function B(\mathbf{x}) representing the blended union. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the evaluation functions f1, f2 and the scalar parameters p, d1, d2. The method is stateless and evaluates point-wise. Mathematical Definition: The method relies on reformulating the signed distance functions into strictly non-negative functions, following Ricci's original formulation where implicit surfaces are defined by setting non-negative functions equal to one. For a signed distance function fi(\mathbf{x}), we define the non-negative component gi(\mathbf{x}) as: gi(\mathbf{x}) = \max(1 - fi(\mathbf{x}), 0) This ensures that gi(\mathbf{x}) is non-zero only within the support region where fi(\mathbf{x}) < 1. The superelliptic blend of the union of the implicit surface of f1 and f2 is defined by the implicit surface of the blended function B(\mathbf{x}): B(\mathbf{x}) = \left( g1(\mathbf{x})^p + g2(\mathbf{x})^p \right)^{1/p} The parameter p acts as a thumbweight describing how tightly the blend adheres to the original surfaces. The implicit surface corresponds to B(\mathbf{x}) = 1. Numbered Steps: 1. Evaluate f1(\mathbf{x}) and f2(\mathbf{x}) at the query point \mathbf{x}. 2. Compute the non-negative components: g1(\mathbf{x}) = \max(1 - f1(\mathbf{x}), 0) g2(\mathbf{x}) = \max(1 - f2(\mathbf{x}), 0) 3. Check if both g1(\mathbf{x}) and g2(\mathbf{x}) are zero. 4. Compute the blended value using the p-norm: B(\mathbf{x}) = \left( g1(\mathbf{x})^p + g2(\mathbf{x})^p \right)^{1/p} 5. The resulting implicit surface is defined by B(\mathbf{x}) = 1. Parameters: p: The blend exponent. Typical values depend on the desired smoothness. Small p yields smoother, more "blobby" blends; large p yields sharper, more distinct surfaces. d1, d2: Support radii. If fi are SDFs, these are in Euclidean units. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Discontinuities: The pseudonorm blend creases the space surrounding the blend. Outside the domain where both g1 and g2 are non-zero, it is impossible to smoothly combine the results, resulting in a crease and gradient discontinuities. Root Finding: These gradient discontinuities can be disastrous for iterative root finders (e.g., Newton-Raphson). Sphere Tracing: The discontinuities do not impact geometric ray intersection methods like sphere tracing, as sphere tracing relies on the Lipschitz constant (distance to surface) rather than the gradient direction for step sizing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def superellipticblendunion(x, f1, f2, p): """ Computes the superelliptic blend (pseudonorm) of two SDFs. Returns the blended function value B(x). The implicit surface is at B(x) = 1. """ # 1. Evaluate SDFs dist1 = f1(x) dist2 = f2(x) # 2. Reformulate to non-negative components gi = max(1 - fi, 0) g1 = max(1.0 - dist1, 0.0) g2 = max(1.0 - dist2, 0.0) # 3. Handle case where both are outside support if g1 == 0.0 and g2 == 0.0: return max(dist1, dist2) # Fallback to max SDF outside blend domain # 4. Compute p-norm blend blendedg = (g1 p + g2 p) (1.0 / p) # 5. Return blended value; surface is at blendedg == 1.0 return blendedg Uses additive scalar fields rather than distance norms. Choose when smooth, organic merging is needed without strict distance preservation [1017-metaball-field-evaluation.md]. A variant that softens the transition. Choose when anti-aliasing of the blend edge is required without the sharp creases of the standard pseudonorm [2753-soft-metablobby-sdf.md]. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, assuming f1 and f2 are O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are stored. Strengths: Local blending allows for efficient culling using bounding volumes. Limitations: The gradient discontinuities at the boundary of the blend domain make it unsuitable for gradient-based optimization or root-finding algorithms. It is primarily designed for sphere tracing (geometric ray intersection). Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of blended primitives if extended to N inputs, but the local nature means only nearby primitives need evaluation. Cost: The cost is dominated by the exponentiation and root operations. The superelliptic blend was introduced by Rockwood and Owen in 1987. It is based on the pioneering work of Antonio Ricci in 1974, who defined implicit surfaces using strictly non-negative functions set to one. The method is also referred to as the "pseudonorm blend" because it computes a p-norm distance to the union of surfaces. It is widely used in sphere tracing for rendering implicit surfaces due to its compatibility with the Lipschitz property required for safe step sizes.
