name: NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling
head: NeUDF sampling, ws(t)
body: NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling is a two-stage ray sampling strategy for Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) volume rendering that balances surface reconstruction accuracy with Eikonal loss regularization. Unlike Naive UDF Solution (NeuS-based) which relies on uniform or simple heuristic sampling, this method hierarchically refines point distribution by first establishing a baseline and then concentrating samples where the UDF value indicates proximity to the surface, ensuring well-balanced gradients on both sides of the implicit surface. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a UDF network f(\mathbf{x}); a transformation function \Psi; a monotonic density function \zetas; a position mapping p(t); and the number of initial samples N{init}=64 and importance samples N{imp}=64. Output: A set of 128 sample points \{ti\}{i=0}^{127} along the ray and their corresponding normalized sampling weights \{ws''(ti)\}. Data Structures: Sample Points: An array of 128 floating-point distances t along the ray. Weights: An array of 128 floating-point values representing the normalized importance weights. Steps: 1. Uniform Initialization: Sample N{init}=64 points uniformly along the ray within the bounding volume (typically the unit sphere or masked region). Let these points be t0, \dots, t{63}. 2. Density Calculation: For each sample point ti, compute the UDF value di = f(p(ti)). Apply the transformation \Psi to di to get \Psi(di). Then, compute the view-invariant sampling density \taus(ti) using the monotonically decreasing function \zetas: \taus(ti) = \zetas(\Psi(di)) The function \zetas must satisfy \zetas(d) > 0 and \zeta's(d) < 0 for all d > 0, ensuring higher density for smaller UDF values (closer to surface). 3. Base Weight Computation: Compute the unnormalized sampling weight ws(ti) for each point using the volume rendering accumulation formula: ws(ti) = \taus(ti) e^{-\int0^{ti} \taus(s) ds} In practice, the integral is approximated by the sum of densities of previous points multiplied by the step size. 4. Neighbor Maximization: Modify the weights to prevent local minima from suppressing valid samples. For each i, compute the modified weight w's(ti): w's(ti) = \max\{ws(t{i+k}) \mid k \in \{-1, 0, 1\}\} This takes the maximum of the current weight and its immediate neighbors. 5. Normalization: Normalize the modified weights so they sum to one: ws''(ti) = \frac{w's(ti)}{\sum{j=0}^{N{init}-1} w's(tj)} This yields the importance sampling distribution for the second stage. 6. Importance Sampling: Perform importance sampling using the distribution ws''(ti) to select N{imp}=64 new points. These points are added to the initial 64, resulting in a total of 128 points per ray. 7. Boundary Handling: If no masks are provided, randomly sample 32 additional points outside the unit sphere to represent the background scene, bringing the total to 160 points. These background points are handled using a NeRF++ representation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neudfhierarchicalsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, udfnet, psifunc, zetasfunc, numinit=64, numimp=64): # Step 1: Uniform sampling tuniform = sampleuniform(rayorigin, raydirection, numinit) # Step 2 & 3: Compute density and base weights densities = [] for t in tuniform: pos = rayorigin + t raydirection udfval = udfnet(pos) transformed = psifunc(udfval) tau = zetasfunc(transformed) densities.append(tau) # Compute unnormalized weights ws(t) # Approximating integral: exp(-sum(tauprev dt)) weightss = [] cumsum = 0.0 for i, tau in enumerate(densities): if i > 0: dt = tuniform[i] - tuniform[i-1] cumsum += tau dt ws = tau math.exp(-cumsum) weightss.append(ws) # Step 4: Neighbor maximization weightsprime = [] for i in range(numinit): maxw = weightss[i] if i > 0: maxw = max(maxw, weightss[i-1]) if i < numinit - 1: maxw = max(maxw, weightss[i+1]) weightsprime.append(maxw) # Step 5: Normalization sumweights = sum(weightsprime) weightsnorm = [w / sumweights for w in weightsprime] # Step 6: Importance sampling for additional points timp = sampleimportance(weightsnorm, tuniform, numimp) # Combine points allt = tuniform + timp # Step 7: Boundary handling (if no mask) if nomaskprovided: tbg = samplerandomoutsidesphere(32) allt = allt + tbg return allt Parameters: numinit: 64 (initial uniform samples). numimp: 64 (importance samples). zetas: Monotonically decreasing function with \zetas(d) > 0 and \zeta's(d) < 0. Psi: Transformation function applied to UDF values. Edge Cases: No Mask: Requires 32 extra random samples outside the unit sphere for background representation. Degenerate UDF: The condition \zeta's(d) < 0 ensures density remains positive and decreases with distance, preventing singularities at large distances. Provides the specific mathematical formulation for the sampling density \taus(t) used in the second stage of the hierarchy. It sets itself apart by distributing weights before intersection points to balance Eikonal loss gradients, unlike the parent method which focuses on the hierarchical refinement structure itself. Complexity: O(N) per ray where N=128 (or 160 with background). The importance sampling step requires sorting or cumulative sum computation, adding a constant factor overhead to the uniform sampling. Performance: The two-stage approach (64 + 64) provides a balance between computational cost and sampling quality. The neighbor maximization step is negligible in cost but crucial for stability. Strengths: Improves UDF quality by preventing unbalanced gradient magnitudes on either side of the surface, which is a common issue in UDF rendering. View-invariant density reduces sensitivity to camera position. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \zetas and \Psi. The background handling relies on NeRF++, adding complexity if background modeling is not needed. NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling was introduced in the NeUDF paper (2023) to address the challenges of training Unsigned Distance Fields with volume rendering. It builds on the NeuS weight function [3238-neus-weight-function.md] but adapts it for UDFs, where the distance is unsigned, requiring specific handling of the Eikonal loss regularization. name: Importance Points Sampling
head: sampling weight function
body: Importance Points Sampling is a specialized sampling weight function ws(t) designed to achieve well-balanced Eikonal loss regularization for Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) volume rendering. Unlike standard rendering weights that concentrate points near the surface, this function distributes more sampling weights before the intersection points to prevent unbalanced gradient magnitudes on the two sides of the surface, which would otherwise hamper UDF quality. It provides the specific mathematical formulation for the sampling density \taus(t) used in the second stage of NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes the ray parameter t, the UDF value \Psi(p(t)) at the ray point p(t), and hyperparameters s and b as inputs. It outputs the opaque density \taus(t) and the sampling weight ws(t). Data Structures: The method requires no complex data structures and relies entirely on scalar arithmetic operations on the ray parameter and UDF values. Formulas: The sampling weight is defined as ws(t) = \taus(t) e^{-\int0^t \taus(u) du}. The opaque density is derived from a transformation function \zetas as \taus(t) = \zetas(\Psi(p(t))). The transformation function is defined as \zetas(d) = s \frac{e^{-bd}}{(1 + e^{-bd})^2}. Constraints: The function \zetas(d) must satisfy \zetas(d) > 0 and \zeta's(d) < 0 for all d > 0. Parameters: The parameter s starts at 0.05 and changes every sampling step z with a rate of 2^{z-1}. The parameter b controls the intensity of the weight at d=0. Steps: 1. Evaluate the UDF value d = \Psi(p(t)) at the current ray point. 2. Compute \zetas(d) using the current values of s and b. 3. Set the opaque density \taus(t) = \zetas(d). 4. Compute the cumulative opacity integral A(t) = \int0^t \taus(u) du, which in discrete implementation is the accumulated sum of \taus along the ray. 5. Compute the sampling weight ws(t) = \taus(t) e^{-A(t)}. 6. Use ws(t) to guide the selection of sample points along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computesamplingdensity(t, udfvalue, s, b): """ Computes the opaque density taus(t) for importance sampling. Args: t: Current ray parameter (distance). udfvalue: The Unsigned Distance Function value d at p(t). s: Scaling parameter (dynamic). b: Intensity control parameter. Returns: taus: The opaque density for sampling. """ # Compute zetas(d) = s exp(-bd) / (1 + exp(-bd))^2 expbd = math.exp(-b udfvalue) denominator = (1 + expbd) 2 taus = s expbd / denominator # Note: The integral term exp(-int0^t taus(u) du) is handled by the # renderer's accumulation buffer or ray marching loop. # This function provides the local density taus(t) which is then # combined with the accumulated transmittance T(t) = exp(-int0^t taus(u) du). # The final weight used for sampling probability is taus(t) T(t). # The discrete accumulation of taus along the ray is performed externally. return taus Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the sampling function employs the same weights as the rendering function, the Eikonal loss regularization leads to highly unbalanced gradient magnitudes on the two sides of the surface, significantly hampering UDF quality. A technique to upsample points along a ray for UDF volume rendering, addressing sampling bias inherent in standard importance sampling. It introduces an auxiliary point sampling prior to refine sampling densities and a uniform upsampling strategy. Choose this when rendering efficiency and 3D perception quality are critical for UDFs. The method requires O(1) time per sample point for weight evaluation. It requires O(1) auxiliary memory. Its primary strength is achieving well-balanced regularization across all space, preventing the unbalanced gradient magnitudes that degrade UDF reconstruction quality. Its main limitation is the requirement for careful tuning of parameters s and b. It should be used when performing volume rendering with Neural Unsigned Distance Fields where Eikonal loss regularization is critical for surface accuracy. It should not be used when using Signed Distance Functions, as the specific bias correction for UDFs is not needed and standard rendering weights may suffice. The method was introduced in the paper "NeUDF: Leaning Neural Unsigned Distance Fields with Volume Rendering". It addresses the specific challenges of rendering UDFs, where the lack of a signed distinction causes standard importance sampling to fail in balancing the Eikonal loss. The approach is inspired by NeuS [53] but adapts the weight function specifically for the UDF domain to ensure unbiased rendering and stable gradient propagation. name: Hierarchical Volume Sampling for UDFs
head: UDF importance sampling, VRP-UDF hierarchical sampling
body: Hierarchical Volume Sampling for UDFs is a technique to upsample points along a ray for Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) volume rendering, addressing the sampling bias inherent in standard importance sampling methods when applied to UDFs. Unlike Signed Distance Functions (SDFs), UDFs lack an explicit zero-level set distinction, causing standard sampling weight functions to concentrate points erroneously before the actual ray-surface intersection due to cumulative multiplicative effects. This method mitigates that bias by introducing an auxiliary point sampling prior to refine sampling densities and a uniform upsampling strategy to ensure even point distribution within intervals, thereby improving 3D perception and rendering efficiency. Inputs: Original sampled points along a ray: \{qn\}{n=1}^{N1}. UDF values at these points: fu(qn). Interval lengths: \deltan = \|q{n+1} - qn\|. Fixed standard deviation parameter: s. Number of points to upsample: N2. Auxiliary point sampling prior network: f{wp} (optional, for bias mitigation). Outputs: Set of N2 upsampled points \{q'm\}{m=1}^{N2} distributed along the ray. Data Structures: Array of original points Q = [q1,..., q{N1}]. Array of sampling densities \tau = [\tau1,..., \tau{N1}]. Array of cumulative probabilities \Omega = [\Omega1,..., \Omega{N1}]. Array of uniform random numbers U = [u1,..., u{N2}] where ui \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 1]. Parameters: s: Fixed standard deviation for the sampling density function. Typical value not specified in sources. Steps: 1. Compute Sampling Densities (\taun): For each original point qn, calculate the sampling density \taun using the UDF value fu(qn) and the fixed standard deviation s: \taun = \frac{s \cdot e^{-s \cdot fu(qn)}}{(1 + e^{-s \cdot fu(qn)})^2} 2. Refine Densities with Auxiliary Prior (Optional but Recommended): If using the auxiliary point sampling prior f{wp} to mitigate bias: a. Input a window of UDF values around qn into f{wp} to obtain a mask value mn \in [0, 1], representing the probability that the window contains a ray-surface intersection. b. Update the sampling density: \taun \leftarrow \taun \times mn. Note: f{wp} is trained separately using mask images as optimizing objectives to produce binary-like outputs, avoiding circular dependency with the volume rendering prior training. 3. Compute Cumulative Probabilities (\Omegan): Calculate the cumulative probability \Omegan that a new point falls between qn and q{n+1}: \Omega(n) = (1 - e^{-\taun \deltan}) \times \prod{n'=1}^{n-1} e^{-\tau{n'} \delta{n'}} where \Omega(n) is the sampling weight for the interval [qn, q{n+1}]. Implementation Note: Compute the product term iteratively to avoid numerical underflow. Let P0 = 1. For n=1 to N1-1: Pn = P{n-1} \times e^{-\tau{n-1} \delta{n-1}}, then \Omega(n) = (1 - e^{-\taun \deltan}) \times Pn. 4. Inverse Transform Sampling: Generate N2 uniform random numbers um \sim \text{Uniform}[0, 1]. Determine the initial positions of the upsampled points by finding the interval index k for each um such that \sum{i=1}^{k-1} \Omega(i) < um \le \sum{i=1}^{k} \Omega(i), and then interpolating within that interval based on the inverse CDF F^{-1}{\Omega}. Note: The exact interpolation formula within the interval is not explicitly detailed in the sources, but standard inverse transform sampling for piecewise constant densities implies linear interpolation within the selected interval [qk, q{k+1}] based on the relative position of um within the cumulative probability mass of that interval. 5. Uniform Upsampling Strategy: To correct the non-smooth distribution caused by discrete inverse transform sampling: a. Group the upsampled points that fall within the same interval [qn, q{n+1}] into sets \{q'{n,1}, q'{n,2},..., q'{n,m}\}, where m is the number of points in that interval. b. Re-order these m points to be evenly distributed within the interval. The new positions are calculated such that the distance between consecutive points is \frac{\deltan}{m+1}. Specifically, for j=1 to m: q'{n,j} = qn + \frac{j}{m+1} \deltan Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Bias: Standard hierarchical sampling without the auxiliary prior concentrates points erroneously before the intersection due to the cumulative multiplicative effect of high sampling densities in non-intersection regions. Non-Uniform Distribution: Inverse transform sampling on discrete intervals results in a non-smooth step function for the inverse CDF, leading to highly uneven point distribution and perception degeneration. The uniform upsampling strategy addresses this. Circular Dependency: Cannot directly use the trained volume rendering prior for \taun because its training relies on hierarchical sampling, which itself suffers from bias. The auxiliary prior f{wp} is trained independently using mask images. An auxiliary neural network f{wp} that acts as a mask function for sampling densities. It takes a window of UDFs as input and outputs the probability that the window contains a ray-surface intersection. It is trained similarly to the volume rendering prior but uses mask images as optimizing objectives to produce binary outputs. The mask value is multiplied with the refined sampling densities \{\taun\} for subsequent hierarchical sampling. Unlike standard hierarchical sampling which concentrates points erroneously before intersection, this prior effectively concentrates upsampled points near the actual intersection. A post-processing step for inverse transform sampling results. It groups upsampled points falling within the same interval formed by original sampled points and re-orders them to evenly distribute them within the interval. This prevents perception degeneration caused by the non-smooth nature of the inverse CDF in discrete sampling. Time Complexity: The method involves computing densities, cumulative probabilities, and sorting/grouping points. The dominant cost is likely the evaluation of the UDF and the prior network f{wp} if used, and the sorting/grouping step for uniform upsampling. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing original points, densities, cumulative probabilities, and upsampled points. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method improves 3D perception and rendering efficiency by mitigating sampling bias and ensuring uniform point distribution. Specific numerical performance metrics (FPS, memory usage) are not provided in the sources. Strengths: Mitigates bias in non-intersection regions; ensures uniform distribution of upsampled points; improves 3D perception. Limitations: Requires training an auxiliary network f{wp}; relies on UDF values; standard hierarchical sampling without this method suffers from bias. When to use: When rendering with UDFs and needing to upsample points along rays while avoiding the bias of standard importance sampling. When not to use: When SDFs are available and standard SDF sampling methods are sufficient; when computational resources for training f{wp} are not available. Hierarchical volume sampling for UDFs was introduced in the VRP-UDF paper. It addresses the limitations of NeuS [1], which uses S-density functions with fixed standard deviations for importance sampling, a method that becomes complex and biased when applied to UDFs due to the lack of an explicit zero-level set. Recent solutions [2, 31] proposed tailored weight functions, but VRP-UDF identified significant bias in these approaches and introduced the auxiliary point sampling prior and uniform upsampling strategy to mitigate it. name: Naive UDF Solution (NeuS-based)
head: Naive UDF, Naive UDF solution based on SDF renderer, UDF extension of NeuS
body: The Naive UDF Solution is a direct extension of the NeuS weight function to Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF) for volume rendering. It solves the problem of integrating UDF values into the standard volume rendering integral but suffers from inherent bias in color rendering, leading to geometric errors such as redundant surfaces and floating noise. It differs from its sibling NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling by using a fixed, non-adaptive weight formulation derived directly from NeuS, whereas NeUDF employs hierarchical sampling to mitigate sampling bias. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin o, view direction v, UDF field \Psi(x), learnable parameter s. Output: Rendered color C(o, v). Data Structures: \Psi(x): Unsigned Distance Field value at position x. s: Scalar learnable parameter controlling the Sigmoid steepness. Formulas: The rendered color is calculated by integrating the product of a weight term wn(t) and the color c(p(t), v) along the ray from t=0 to +\infty: C(o, v) = \int0^{+\infty} wn(t) c(p(t), v) dt \quad (11) where p(t) is the point on the ray at distance t. The rendering weight wn(t) is defined as: wn(t) = \rhos(t) e^{-\int0^t \rhos(u) du} \quad (12) The opaque density \rhos(t) is derived from the UDF \Psi using a Sigmoid function \Phis and an operator \Phi{op} (typically identity or simple scaling depending on implementation context, but formally defined via the derivative in the source): \rhos(t) = \max\left\{-\frac{\partial(\Phis \circ \Phi{op})}{\partial t}(t), 0\right\} \quad (13) Where: \Phis(d) is the Sigmoid function: \Phis(d) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-s \cdot d}}. \Psi(x) is the UDF value at position x. s is a learnable parameter expected to increase to infinity during training to approximate a step function. Steps: 1. For a given ray (o, v), sample points p(t) along the ray. 2. Evaluate the UDF value \Psi(p(t)) at each sample point. 3. Compute the density \rhos(t) by taking the negative derivative of the Sigmoid-transformed UDF with respect to t, clamped to non-negative values. 4. Compute the accumulated transmittance T(t) = e^{-\int0^t \rhos(u) du}. 5. Compute the weight wn(t) = \rhos(t) T(t). 6. Integrate wn(t) c(p(t), v) over t \in [0, +\infty). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def naiveudfrender(o, v, udffield, s, numsamples): """ Renders color using the naive UDF extension of NeuS. Args: o: Ray origin (3D vector) v: Ray direction (3D vector) udffield: Function returning UDF value at a 3D point s: Learnable Sigmoid steepness parameter numsamples: Number of discrete samples along the ray Returns: C: Rendered color (3D vector) """ # Initialize accumulated transmittance and color T = 1.0 C = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Ray marching parameters tmin = 0.0 tmax = 10.0 # Not given in the sources. Placeholder for ray length. dt = (tmax - tmin) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = tmin + i dt p = o + t v # Get UDF value d = udffield(p) # Compute Sigmoid value # Phis(d) = 1 / (1 + exp(-s d)) sigmoidval = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-s d)) # Compute density rhos(t) # rhos(t) = max(-d/dt(Phis(d(t))), 0) # Using finite difference for derivative approximation # Sample a small epsilon step eps = 1e-5 deps = udffield(o + (t + eps) v) sigmoidvaleps = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-s deps)) # Derivative of Sigmoid w.r.t t: d(Sigmoid)/d(d) d(d)/dt # d(Sigmoid)/d(d) = -s Sigmoid (1 - Sigmoid) # d(d)/dt is approximated by (deps - d) / eps dsigmoiddd = -s sigmoidval (1.0 - sigmoidval) dddt = (deps - d) / eps density = max(-dsigmoiddd dddt, 0.0) # Accumulate transmittance # T(t) = T(t-dt) exp(-density dt) # Note: The integral in the exponent is approximated by sum # We update T for the next step based on current density Tnext = T math.exp(-density dt) # Weight wn(t) = density T(t) (using T before update for current segment) # Actually, standard volume rendering uses T(t) as transmittance AT t. # w(t) = rho(t) T(t) # Here T is transmittance from 0 to t. # Get color at p c = getcolor(p, v) # Placeholder for color evaluation # Add contribution # C += wn(t) c(t) dt ? # The integral is continuous. Discrete approximation: # C += wn(t) c(t) dt # However, wn(t) in Eq 12 includes the exponential term. # Let's stick to the standard discrete volume rendering equation: # C = sum( T(ti) rho(ti) c(ti) dt) # Using the definition wn(t) = rhos(t) exp(-int0^t rhos(u) du) # The term exp(-int0^t rhos(u) du) is exactly T(t). contribution = T density c C = [C[k] + contribution[k] dt for k in range(3)] # Update T for next step T = Tnext return C Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias: The method suffers from inherent bias in color rendering, leading to geometric errors such as redundant surfaces and floating noise. Parameter s: The parameter s is expected to increase to infinity during training. If s is too small, the surface will be blurry; if too large, numerical instability may occur. Derivative Calculation: The density relies on the derivative of the Sigmoid-transformed UDF. Numerical instability can arise if the UDF is not smooth or if the step size for derivative approximation is inappropriate. This variant adapts the learned volume rendering prior to transform signed distance fields (SDF) into rendering weights for alpha blending, replacing the handcrafted differentiable renderer used in methods like NeuS. It differs from the naive UDF solution by using SDF inputs instead of UDF inputs and learning a weight function f{ws} rather than relying on the fixed NeuS weight formulation. It is chosen when superior numerical Chamfer Distance results are required and reconstruction artifacts such as holes and uneven surfaces need to be corrected. Definition: Adapts the learned volume rendering prior to transform signed distance fields into rendering weights for alpha blending, replacing the handcrafted differentiable renderer used in methods like NeuS. Steps: 1. Sample ground truth signed distances f{s{gt}}^h from ground truth meshes \{Sh\}{h=1}^H. 2. Replace the UDF input f{u{gt}}^h in the training equation with the SDF input f{s{gt}}^h. 3. Train the weight function f{ws} with all other settings identical to UDF training. 4. During inference, use the learned f{ws} to estimate signed distance fields fs instead of the differentiable renderer of NeuS. Parameters: f{ws}: Learned weight function that maps signed distance values to rendering weights for alpha blending. Comparison: Differs from NeuS [1] by replacing its handcrafted differentiable renderer with the learned f{ws}, which yields superior numerical Chamfer Distance results and corrects reconstruction artifacts such as holes and uneven surfaces. Strengths: Simple to implement as a direct extension of NeuS. Limitations: Suffers from inherent bias in color rendering, leading to geometric errors such as redundant surfaces and floating noise. When to use: When a baseline UDF-based volume rendering method is needed for comparison or as a starting point. When not to use: When high-quality geometry without floating noise or redundant surfaces is required; consider NeUDF Hierarchical Importance Sampling or SDF Inference with Volume Rendering Prior instead. name: U-density Function
head: NeUDF rendering weight function, NeUDF weight, U-density, cumulative distribution function of U-density
body: The U-density function is a rendering weight function designed for Unsigned Distance Fields (UDF) to ensure globally unbiased volume rendering. It solves the volume-surface gap inherent in naive extensions of Signed Distance Field (SDF) techniques to UDFs, specifically preventing redundant floating faces and irregular noises caused by improper weight distribution. Unlike the NeuS weight function, which violates the unbiased property for UDFs by allowing weight leakage to invisible surfaces, the U-density function concentrates rendering weight near the first surface intersection, ensuring the final color is derived solely from the visible surface geometry. Input: A ray defined by origin o and direction v, sampled at discrete points ti along the ray. At each point, a UDF network \Psi outputs a distance value d = \Psi(p(t)) where p(t) = o + tv. Output: A rendering weight wr(t) for each sample point, used in alpha-compositing to compute the final pixel color. Ray Samples: A list of distances t along the ray. UDF Values: A list of scalar distances di = \Psi(p(ti)) retrieved from the neural network. Transformation Function: \varsigmar(d), a parametric function mapping distance to cumulative probability. The rendering weight wr(t) is defined as: wr(t) = \taur(t) e^{-\int0^t \taur(u) du} where \taur(t) is the density derived from the UDF. The density \taur(t) is calculated using the derivative of a transformed UDF: \taur(t) = \left| \frac{\frac{\partial(\varsigmar \circ \Psi \circ p)}{\partial t}(t)}{\varsigmar \circ \Psi \circ p(t)} \right| Here, \circ denotes function composition, \Psi is the UDF network, p(t) is the ray position, and \varsigmar is the transformation function. The transformation function \varsigmar(d) must satisfy the following constraints for all d > 0: 1. \varsigmar(0) = 0 2. \lim{d \rightarrow +\infty} \varsigmar(d) = 1 3. \varsigma'r(d) > 0 (strictly increasing) 4. \varsigma''r(d) < 0 (concave) The specific form of \varsigmar(d) used in the source is: \varsigmar(d) = \frac{r d}{1 + r d} where r is a learnable parameter. r: A learnable parameter controlling the distribution of the density. Initial Value: 0.05. 1. Sample Ray: Discretize the ray into N points t1, \dots, tN. 2. Query UDF: For each point ti, compute the unsigned distance di = \Psi(p(ti)). 3. Transform Distance: Compute the transformed value si = \varsigmar(di) = \frac{r di}{1 + r di}. 4. Compute Density: Calculate the density \taur(ti) using the chain rule: \taur(ti) = \left| \frac{\varsigma'r(di) \cdot \frac{\partial di}{\partial ti}}{\varsigmar(di)} \right|. The term \frac{\partial di}{\partial ti} is the gradient of the UDF along the ray direction, computed via automatic differentiation of \Psi with respect to p(ti) projected onto v. 5. Compute Weight: Calculate the weight wr(ti) using the exponential integral approximation. 6. Composite: Accumulate colors using standard alpha compositing with the computed weights. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmar(d, r): """Transformation function: s = rd / (1 + rd)""" return (r d) / (1 + r d) def sigmarprime(d, r): """Derivative: s' = r / (1 + rd)^2""" denom = 1 + r d return r / (denom denom) def computetau(d, gradalongray, r): """Compute density taur(t) = | (d/dt sigma(d)) / sigma(d) |""" s = sigmar(d, r) sprime = sigmarprime(d, r) numerator = abs(sprime gradalongray) # Guard against division by zero at d=0 if s < 1e-8: return 1e6 return numerator / s def udensityrender(rayso, raysv, udfnetwork, r, numsamples, near, far): """ Discretized volume rendering using U-density weight function. Implements alpha compositing: wr(t) = tau(t) exp(-integral0^t tau(u) du). """ results = [] for o, v in zip(rayso, raysv): T = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = 0.0 deltat = (far - near) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = near + (far - near) (i + 0.5) / numsamples p = o + t v d = udfnetwork(p) gradd = udfnetwork.gradient(p) @ v tau = computetau(d, abs(gradd), r) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-tau deltat) c = udfnetwork.color(p) accumulatedcolor += alpha T c T = (1.0 - alpha) results.append(accumulatedcolor) return results Division by Zero: \varsigmar(0) = 0. If a sample point lies exactly on the surface (d=0), the denominator in \taur(t) becomes 0, causing the density to concentrate sharply near the surface. Naive Sigmoid Extension: Using a standard Sigmoid function (as in NeuS) violates \varsigmar(0)=0 because \text{Sigmoid}(0) = 0.5, which leads to bias in rendering weights and results in redundant floating faces and irregular noises. Negative Distances: UDFs are non-negative. The constraints apply for d > 0. Time Complexity: Dominated by the neural network inference for \Psi and its gradient computation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray sample. Strengths: Guarantees global unbiased rendering for UDFs and prevents color mixing from invisible surfaces (cm, cn). Limitations: Requires gradient computation of the UDF network, which can be computationally expensive. When to Use: When rendering with Unsigned Distance Fields and unbiased surface reconstruction is required. When Not to Use: When using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) where other methods may be more appropriate. The U-density function was introduced in the paper "NeUDF: Learning Neural Unsigned Distance Fields with Volume Rendering". It was developed to address the limitations of applying SDF-based neural rendering techniques directly to UDFs. The authors observed that naive extensions violate the unbiased property due to the different value domains of SDFs and UDFs. The method builds on the concept of volume rendering but adapts the weight function to the specific properties of UDFs, ensuring that the rendering process converges to the correct surface geometry without artifacts. name: SDF-based Voxel Rendering
head: SDF Voxelization, Implicit Voxel Rendering
body: SDF-based Voxel Rendering determines voxel visibility by evaluating a Signed Distance Function (SDF) at each voxel center; a voxel is drawn if the SDF value is less than or equal to zero. It differs from ray-marching volume rendering by using a discrete grid traversal with a binary occupancy test based on the implicit field, rather than continuous integration of density along rays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Signed Distance Function SDF(\mathbf{p}) defining a shape, a voxel grid defined by bounds and step sizes, and a frame buffer. Output: A rendered image where voxels satisfying the condition are colored. Data Structures: point3d: A structure or tuple containing three floating-point fields: x, y, z. voxieframet: The rendering context/frame buffer object. voxiedrawvox: A function signature void voxiedrawvox(voxieframet vf, float x, float y, float z, uint32t color). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the voxel grid bounds (e.g., -vw.aspx to vw.aspx) and compute voxel step sizes based on resolution and field of view. 2. Iterate through the 3D grid using nested loops for x, y, and z axes: \text{for } p.x \text{ from } -vw.aspx \text{ to } vw.aspx \text{ step } \Delta x \text{for } p.y \text{ from } -vw.aspy \text{ to } vw.aspy \text{ step } \Delta y \text{for } p.z \text{ from } -vw.aspz \text{ to } vw.aspz \text{ step } \Delta z 3. Evaluate the SDF for the current point \mathbf{p} = (p.x, p.y, p.z). 4. Apply the emission condition: SDF(\mathbf{p}) \le 0 5. If the condition is true, call the drawing function with the point coordinates and a specified color (e.g., 0x00ff00 or 0xffffff). Formulas: Sphere SDF: SDF(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}\| - r. Torus SDF: Let \mathbf{t} = (R, r) be major and minor radii. Let \mathbf{q} = (\|\mathbf{p}{xz}\| - R, py). Then SDF(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{q}\| - r. Box SDF: Let \mathbf{b} be half-extents. Let \mathbf{q} = \max(\|\mathbf{p}\| - \mathbf{b}, \mathbf{0}). Then SDF(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{q}\| + \max(\min(\|\mathbf{p}\| - \mathbf{b}), 0). Parameters: Voxel size: Computed dynamically based on view volume dimensions and resolution (e.g., voxelsize.x = (2.0f vw.aspx) / vw.xdim 5.0f). Color: Hardcoded constants like 0x00ff00 (green) or 0xffffff (white). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point comparisons (SDF \le 0) may suffer from precision errors at the surface boundary. Boundaries: The loop bounds must strictly cover the volume of interest; otherwise, voxels may be missed or drawn outside the intended view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersdfvoxels(viewbounds, resolution, sdffunc, color): # Compute voxel step sizes stepx = (2.0 viewbounds.maxx) / resolution.x stepy = (2.0 viewbounds.maxy) / resolution.y stepz = (2.0 viewbounds.maxz) / resolution.z # Iterate through grid for x in range(-viewbounds.maxx, viewbounds.maxx, stepx): for y in range(-viewbounds.maxy, viewbounds.maxy, stepy): for z in range(-viewbounds.maxz, viewbounds.maxz, stepz): p = Point3D(x, y, z) # Evaluate SDF dist = sdffunc(p) # Check visibility condition if dist <= 0.0: drawvoxel(p.x, p.y, p.z, color) A technique to jointly evaluate local and contextual radiance consistency for more reliable color predictions by rendering colors of a patch of size k x k instead of a single pixel. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the grid, as each voxel is visited once. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if rendering directly to the frame buffer, or O(N) if storing a voxel grid. Strengths: Simple implementation; efficient for solid objects; no need for ray marching or density integration. Limitations: Aliasing at surfaces; no transparency or subsurface scattering; resolution-dependent quality. When to use: Real-time visualization of solid implicit shapes; voxel-based collision detection. When not to use: Volumetric data with varying density; soft shadows; translucent materials. Originating from early voxel rendering techniques in the "voxie" library ecosystem, this method leverages the mathematical properties of Signed Distance Functions to determine occupancy in a discrete grid. It is commonly used in procedural fractal rendering and holographic displays where solid implicit shapes are rendered efficiently. jtomori/holographicfractals, https://github.com/jtomori/holographicfractals, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Patch-based Color Blending
head: Patch-based Volume Rendering, Homography-based Patch Blending
body:
Patch-based Color Blending is a technique for jointly evaluating local and contextual radiance consistency to produce more reliable color predictions than single-pixel blending. It renders colors for a local patch of size k 	imes k instead of a single pixel, leveraging the local surface assumption and homography transformation to efficiently derive colors from multiple input views. This method is chosen when regions have weak texture or changing intensity, as it produces more informative and consistent shape context by incorporating neighboring geometric information. Inputs: A query ray r and a set of sampled points q along the ray. A signed distance function (SDF) network s(\cdot) to estimate normals. N input views \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} with known poses and intrinsic matrices. Blending weights wi for each input view (computed via a separate weight prediction module, assumed available). Patch dimension k (odd integer, e.g., 3, 5). Outputs: Final predicted patch colors for the ray, aggregated via volume rendering. Data Structures: Local Plane Points: A set of 3D points \mathcal{P}q centered at q on the tangent plane defined by normal nq. For a k 	imes k patch, this contains k^2 points. Homography Matrix H: A 3 	imes 3 matrix mapping points from the rendered view Ir to input view Ii. Steps: 1. Estimate Normal: For a sampled point q on the query ray, compute the spatial gradient of the SDF network to estimate the surface normal direction nq: nq = 
abla s(q) 2. Define Local Plane Points: Select a set of points \mathcal{P}q on the local plane defined by (q, nq). These points represent the k 	imes k patch centered at q. The points are typically generated by offsetting q along the tangent basis vectors of the plane. 3. Compute Homography: For each input view Ii (where i 
eq r), compute the homography matrix H between the rendered view Ir and Ii, induced by the local plane (q, nq): H = K \left( Ri +  rac{ti nq^T Rr^T}{nq^T (q + Rr^T tr)} ight) K^{-1} where: K is the camera intrinsic matrix. Ri is the 3 	imes 3 rotation matrix of Ii relative to Ir. ti is the 3D translation vector of Ii relative to Ir. (Rr, tr) is the pose of the rendered view Ir in the world coordinate system. nq is the normal vector at q. 4. Project and Interpolate Colors: Apply the homography H to the set of points \mathcal{P}q to obtain their projected pixel locations in view Ii. For each point in \mathcal{P}q, obtain its color by interpolation on the input image Ii. Specifically, for the center point q, the projected pixel location Hq is obtained by the matrix product of H and q (in homogeneous coordinates), and its color is interpolated. 5. Assign Blending Weights: Assign the same blending weights wi to all points on the local plane \mathcal{P}q. This requires only one query of the blending weights for the entire patch, assuming the weight prediction is based on the central point q. 6. Blend Patch Colors: Blend the patch colors interpolated from each of the N-1 input views \{Ii\}{i=0}^{N-1} using the blending weights wi to obtain the final patch colors for point q. Let Ci(p) be the color of point p \in \mathcal{P}q in view Ii. The blended color for point p is: C{patch}(p) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} wi Ci(p) 7. Volume Rendering Aggregation: Use SDF-based volume rendering to aggregate the interpolated patch colors of all points sampled in the query ray r to generate the final predicted patch colors of the ray. This follows the standard volume rendering integral, but using the patch colors C{patch} instead of single-pixel colors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def patchbasedcolorblending(q, nq, K, poses, images, weights, k): """ q: 3D point on the ray nq: Normal vector at q K: Intrinsic matrix (3x3) poses: List of (Ri, ti) for each input view i images: List of input images Ii weights: Blending weights wi for each view k: Patch dimension (k x k) """ # Step 2: Generate local plane points # Generate k x k grid of points on the tangent plane at q with normal nq # This requires constructing a local basis from nq and offsetting by patch size patchpoints = generatelocalplanepoints(q, nq, k) blendedpatchcolors = [] # Step 3-6: For each input view for i, (Ri, ti) in enumerate(poses): # Step 3: Compute Homography H # Rr, tr are the pose of the rendered view (assumed known or identity if local) # Note: The formula uses Rr and tr. In the context of the paper, # these refer to the target view's pose relative to world. # Assuming Rr, tr are available from the rendering context. H = computehomography(K, Ri, ti, Rr, tr, nq, q) # Step 4: Project points and interpolate colors # Project all points in patchpoints to view i using H projectedpoints = applyhomography(H, patchpoints) # Interpolate colors from image Ii for each projected point # Handle boundary checks and invalid projections colorsi = interpolatecolors(images[i], projectedpoints) # Step 5: Assign weights (same for all points in patch) wi = weights[i] # Step 6: Blend colors from this view # Cpatch(p) = sum(wi Ci(p)) across views # We accumulate this contribution blendedpatchcolors.append(wi colorsi) # Sum contributions from all views finalpatchcolors = sum(blendedpatchcolors) return finalpatchcolors def computehomography(K, Ri, ti, Rr, tr, nq, q): """ Computes H = K (Ri + (ti nq^T Rr^T) / (nq^T (q + Rr^T tr))) K^-1 """ # Calculate denominator: nq^T (q + Rr^T tr) # Note: q and tr are column vectors. nq is column vector. # The term (q + Rr^T tr) is a 3x1 vector. # nq^T is 1x3. Result is scalar. denom = np.dot(nq.T, q + Rr.T @ tr) # Calculate numerator term: ti nq^T Rr^T # ti is 3x1, nq^T is 1x3, Rr^T is 3x3. # Result is 3x3 matrix. numterm = ti @ (nq.T @ Rr.T) # Calculate inner matrix: Ri + numterm / denom innermatrix = Ri + numterm / denom # Final H = K innermatrix K^-1 H = K @ innermatrix @ np.linalg.inv(K) return H Parameters: Patch size k 	imes k: The dimension of the patch used for blending. Typical values are small odd integers (e.g., 3, 5) to capture local context without excessive computational cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Estimation: If the SDF gradient 
abla s(q) is zero or noisy, the normal nq will be inaccurate, leading to incorrect homography and misaligned patches. Homography Singularity: If the denominator nq^T (q + Rr^T tr) is close to zero, the homography becomes unstable. This occurs when the local plane is parallel to the ray direction or the camera center lies on the local plane. Boundary Conditions: Points in the patch may project outside the image boundaries of input views. Interpolation should handle these cases (e.g., by ignoring or padding). Weight Consistency: The assumption that all points in the patch share the same blending weights may not hold if the patch spans regions with significantly different visibility or texture quality. Time Complexity: Higher than pixel-based blending due to the need to process k^2 points per sample and compute homographies for each view. However, the homography allows efficient batched interpolation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the patch points and intermediate projected coordinates. Strengths: Produces more reliable color predictions in regions with weak texture or changing intensity by leveraging contextual information. Enforces better geometric consistency. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than pixel-based blending. Sensitive to normal estimation errors. When to Use: When high-quality color synthesis is needed in textureless or low-texture regions, and computational resources allow for the additional cost. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and texture is rich and stable, pixel-based blending may suffice. Patch-based Color Blending was introduced in the SparseNeuS paper by Xiaoxiao Long, Cheng Lin, Peng Wang, Taku Komura, and Wenping Wang in 2022. It is part of the SparseNeuS framework for fast generalizable neural surface reconstruction from sparse views. The method builds on SDF-based voxel rendering and aims to improve color prediction reliability by considering local context. SparseNeuS: Fast Generalizable Neural Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-313, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Surfaceness Finetuning
head: DtoOModel
body: Adaptive Surfaceness Finetuning refines density representation in Signed Distance Function (SDF) volume rendering by making the sharpness parameter \beta spatially adaptive. It solves the degradation of rendering quality near fine-grained or transparent structures caused by a uniform \beta by using the Eikonal loss as an indicator to increase surfaceness only where the SDF constraint is violated, preventing arbitrary density predictions. Unlike methods that optimize \beta directly or use fixed functions, this approach relies on accumulated per-sample triplets to update a 512^3 voxel grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained SDF field f(\mathbf{x}), a coarse occupancy grid, and training rays. Output: An adaptive \beta grid (surfaceness grid) and refined density estimates \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha \beta(\mathbf{x}) \exp(-\beta(\mathbf{x}) |f(\mathbf{x})|). Data Structures: 1. Coarse Occupancy Grid: Binary grid initialized with AABB scale 1.0 and resolution 32. 2. Fine Occupancy Grid: Generated during finetuning. Voxel size is 2.0 / 32. Contains fine offset cube coordinates. 3. Surfaceness Grid (\beta): A 512^3 voxel grid storing \betav for each voxel v. 4. Sample Triplets: Accumulated data (\mathbf{x}, \eta, w), where \mathbf{x} is the sample position, \eta is the SDF value, and w is the weight. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the coarse occupancy grid with AABB scale 1.0 and resolution 32. 2. Sampler Setup: Configure samplers: PDFSampler for importance sampling, UniformSampler for uniform sampling, NeuSSampler for NeuS-style sampling, and ErrorBoundedSampler for VolSDF sampling. 3. Accumulation: Collect per-sample triplets (\mathbf{x}, \eta, w) rendered during the finetuning process. Accumulate these triplets over multiple training iterations (specifically 5,000 steps). 4. Grid Generation (Conditional): During training, if stepcounter > 5000 and stepcounter % 5000 == 1, generate a fine occupancy grid. Calculate voxel size as 2.0 / 32. Generate fine offset cube coordinates. 5. Partitioning: Partition the accumulated triplets across the voxels of the surfaceness grid. Let \Lambdav be the subset of triplets associated with voxel v. 6. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF at fine voxel positions using occupancyfield.forwardgeonetwork. Reshape SDF results to match the coarse voxel structure. 7. Ray Marching (Fine Grid): If the fine grid exists, perform ray marching using the fine binary grid with a smaller threshold (10^{-3}). Update ray near/far bounds by subtracting/adding 0.03 to the hit positions. 8. Sampling (VolSDF Mode): If the method is 'volsdf', sample points using ErrorBoundedSampler with densityfn set to occupancyfield.laplacedensity and sdffn set to occupancyfield.getsdf. 9. Merging: Merge samples from the uniform sampler (voxelsamples) and the importance sampler (occupancysamples) using UniSurfSampler.mergeraysamplesineculidean. 10. Weight Computation: For VolSDF method, query field outputs from occupancyfield. Compute weights and transmittance using occupancysamples.getweightsandtransmitance from the DENSITY field head. 11. Surfaceness Update: For each voxel v, calculate the weighted average Eikonal loss. If the loss is below threshold \bar{\gamma}, increase \betav by a fixed increment. Formulas: The density is computed using the Laplace distribution approximation: \sigma(\mathbf{x}) = \alpha \beta(\mathbf{x}) \exp(-\beta(\mathbf{x}) |f(\mathbf{x})|) The condition for increasing \betav is: \frac{\sum{(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\eta}, w) \in \Lambda{v}} w \eta (\|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\| - 1)^2}{\sum{(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\eta}, w) \in \Lambda{v}} w} < \bar{\gamma} Where: \Lambdav: Subset of triplets in voxel v. w: Weight of the sample. \eta: SDF value (used as a multiplier in the numerator). \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|: Norm of the gradient of the SDF. \bar{\gamma}: Predefined threshold for increasing surfaceness. Parameters: \bar{\gamma} = 0.25: Threshold for increasing surfaceness. Increment for \betav = 100: Fixed value added to \betav when the condition is met. smoothlossmulti: 0.005. Smoothness loss multiplier applied to surface points in the UniSurf context. s3imlossmult: 0.0. Multiplier for the S3IM perceptual loss. s3imkernelsize: 4. Kernel size for the S3IM loss calculation. s3imstride: 4. Stride for the S3IM loss calculation. s3imrepeattime: 10. Number of times the S3IM patch is repeated. s3impatchheight: 32. Virtual patch height for S3IM. annealend: 20000. The training step at which the cosine annealing for NeuS is completed. name: Distance-Adjusted Eikonal Loss
head: Distance-weighted Eikonal Regularization, SDF Radiance Field Parameterization, VolSDF density parameterization, Weighted Eikonal Loss
body:
Distance-Adjusted Eikonal Loss is a regularization technique used in Signed Distance Function (SDF) based neural rendering to enforce the geometric validity of the SDF while preventing the regularization from degrading background reconstruction quality. It modifies the standard Eikonal loss by applying per-sample weights inversely proportional to the square of the sample's distance from the camera, thereby downweighting the constraint in far-field regions. This approach allows the model to maintain well-defined surfaces in the foreground while behaving like a standard volume renderer in the background, avoiding the artifacts associated with uniform Eikonal regularization. The method operates on a neural network that outputs a signed distance value d(x) for any 3D query point x. The core mechanism is the application of a weighted Eikonal loss during training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D query points \{xi\} sampled along camera rays, where each xi has an associated metric distance di from the camera origin along the ray. Output: A scalar loss value L{Eikonal} used for backpropagation. Data Structures: Query Points: A list or tensor of 3D coordinates xi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Distances: A list or tensor of scalar distances di \in \mathbb{R}^+ corresponding to each xi. SDF Values: The network output d(xi) \in \mathbb{R}. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampling: Efficiently approximate the expectation of the loss by performing stratified sampling across the bounding volume of the scene. 2. Distance Calculation: For each sampled point xi, calculate its metric distance di from the camera origin along the viewing ray. 3. Weight Calculation: Compute the per-sample weight \etai using the inverse square of the distance: \etai = di^{-2} 4. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient of the SDF output with respect to the input query point xi, denoted as 
ablax d(xi). This requires double differentiation with respect to the input query points. 5. Loss Calculation: Compute the Eikonal loss for each sample as the squared difference between the norm of the gradient and 1, scaled by the weight \etai: L{Eikonal} = \sumi \etai \left( \|
ablax d(xi)\| - 1 ight)^2 Note: The source defines the expectation form L{Eikonal} = Ex [ (\|
ablax d(x)\| - 1)^2 ], which is approximated by the summation over samples. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distanceadjustedeikonalloss(sdfnetwork, querypoints, cameraorigin): """ Computes the distance-adjusted Eikonal loss. Args: sdfnetwork: Neural network returning SDF value d(x) for input x. querypoints: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D query points xi. cameraorigin: Tensor of shape (3,) containing the camera position. Returns: loss: Scalar tensor representing the weighted Eikonal loss. """ # 1. Compute SDF values and their gradients # Requires double differentiation support in the network implementation querypoints.requiresgrad(True) # Forward pass to get SDF values sdfvalues = sdfnetwork(querypoints) # Compute gradient of SDF w.r.t. input points # This requires computing the gradient of the sum of sdfvalues # w.r.t. querypoints to enable backpropagation through the network gradsdf = torch.autograd.grad( sdfvalues.sum(), querypoints, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] # 2. Compute the norm of the gradient gradnorm = torch.norm(gradsdf, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Shape: (N, 1) # 3. Compute metric distances from camera origin # di is the distance along the ray, which is the Euclidean distance # from the camera origin to the query point raydirections = querypoints - cameraorigin distances = torch.norm(raydirections, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Shape: (N, 1) # 4. Compute weights: etai = di^-2 # Guard against division by zero if a point is at the camera origin # Add a small epsilon to distances to prevent numerical instability epsilon = 1e-8 weights = 1.0 / (distances + epsilon)2 # 5. Compute the Eikonal loss term: (||grad|| - 1)^2 eikonalterm = (gradnorm - 1.0)2 # 6. Apply distance-adjusted weights weightedloss = weights eikonalterm # 7. Sum over all samples (approximating the expectation) loss = weightedloss.sum() return loss Parameters: Weight Exponent: The exponent in the distance weight is fixed at 2 (i.e., di^{-2}). Initialization: The SDF is initialized to a unit sphere via pre-training to provide a valid starting geometry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double Differentiation: The method requires computing the gradient of the SDF with respect to the input coordinates, which in turn requires the gradient of the network's output with respect to its input. This necessitates a custom bilinear sampling implementation or a network architecture that supports double differentiation with respect to input query points. Background Artifacts: Using standard uniform Eikonal weights (\etai=1) negatively affects background reconstruction. Applying Eikonal loss in contracted space affects the foreground. Omitting the loss entirely causes the model to revert to standard NeRF behavior, resulting in poor foreground surface reconstruction. Precision: Care must be taken with numerical precision when computing gradients, especially for points far from the camera where distances are large and weights are small. Time Complexity: The method adds a computational overhead proportional to the number of samples N due to the gradient computation. The gradient calculation requires an additional backward pass through the SDF network, effectively doubling the forward/backward cost for the Eikonal term. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the gradients of the SDF with respect to the input points, which scales with the number of samples N and the dimensionality of the input (3). Strengths: Improves background reconstruction quality without degrading foreground surface quality. It allows a single model to handle both foreground (SDF) and background (volume) effectively. Limitations: Requires careful implementation of gradient computation (double differentiation). The choice of weight exponent (d^{-2}) is specific to the method and may not be optimal for all scenes. When to use: When using SDF-based neural rendering and experiencing background artifacts or poor surface definition due to uniform Eikonal regularization. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the overhead of double differentiation is prohibitive, or when the scene does not have a clear foreground/background distinction requiring different regularization strengths. The Distance-Adjusted Eikonal Loss was introduced in the context of neural rendering methods that use Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) to represent surfaces. It was proposed to address the limitations of standard Eikonal regularization, which tends to negatively impact background reconstruction. The method builds upon the VolSDF approach, which parameterizes the object surface as an SDF to facilitate surface extraction and provide analytical normals. The specific distance-adjusted weighting scheme was detailed in HybridNeRF, while the broader context of SDF representation and Eikonal loss in radiance field inversion was presented in. name: Constrained Jacobi Smoothing for SDFs
head: Constrained Jacobi Smoothing for Signed Distance Functions, constrained smoothing, energy minimization via Jacobi iteration [S1, unofficial]
body: Constrained Jacobi Smoothing converts a binary volume into a smooth signed distance function (SDF) by minimizing an energy functional through Jacobi iteration, subject to constraints that preserve the binary topology. It differs from sibling methods like Gaussian smoothing by guaranteeing the preservation of the exact binary topology (sign of the level set) and producing a valid SDF, whereas Gaussian smoothing may alter topology and does not guarantee an SDF. Inputs and Outputs Input: A binary volume array V{\text{binary}} of dimension D \in \{2, 3\}. Output: A signed distance function array V{\text{sdf}} of the same dimensions and resolution. Data Structures Stencil (J): A convolution kernel. For 3D, J is a 5 \times 5 \times 5 float64 array. Center element (2,2,2): -4. Neighbors at distance 1 along axes: -4. Neighbors at distance 1 along two axes (face diagonals): 1. All other elements: 0. For 2D, a corresponding 2D stencil (JACOBI\R\2D) is used. Parameters: jacobid: Scaling factor. 1/12 for 2D, 1/18 for 3D. jacobiweight: Relaxation weight. Default 0.5. maxiters: Maximum iterations. Default 500. Algorithm Steps 1. Initial SDF Construction: Convert the binary input V{\text{binary}} into an initial signed distance field V{\text{init}}. Set positive values to 1.0 and others to 0.0. Compute the Euclidean Distance Transform (EDT) for positive regions, subtract 0.5. Negate the EDT for negative regions, add 0.5. 2. Bound Initialization: For each voxel v, determine constraints L[v] (lower bound) and U[v] (upper bound) based on V{\text{init}}[v]. If V{\text{init}}[v] < 0: U[v] = V{\text{init}}[v], L[v] = -\infty. If V{\text{init}}[v] \ge 0: L[v] = V{\text{init}}[v], U[v] = \infty. 3. Bound Clamping: Refine bounds near the zero-level set. If |U[v]| < 1, set U[v] = 0. If |L[v]| < 1, set L[v] = 0. 4. Jacobi Iteration: Repeat up to maxiters times: Compute residual R by convolving the current array with the stencil J using nearest-neighbor padding. Compute update \Delta V = -\text{jacobi\d} \times R. Update array: V{\text{new}} = \text{jacobi\weight} \times \Delta V + (1 - \text{jacobi\weight}) \times V{\text{curr}}. Apply constraints: clamp V{\text{new}} to be at least L and at most U. Set V{\text{curr}} = V{\text{new}}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from scipy.ndimage import convolve, distancetransformedt def constrainedjacobismoothing(binaryvolume: np.ndarray, maxiters: int = 500) -> np.ndarray: if binaryvolume.ndim not in (2, 3): raise ValueError("Input must be 2D or 3D array") # 1. Initial SDF Construction norm = np.where(binaryvolume > 0, 1.0, 0.0) edtpos = distancetransformedt(norm == 1.0) edtneg = distancetransformedt(norm == 0.0) sdf = np.zeroslike(norm, dtype=np.float64) sdf[norm == 1.0] = edtpos[norm == 1.0] - 0.5 sdf[norm == 0.0] = -edtneg[norm == 0.0] + 0.5 # 2. Bound Initialization lowerbound = np.fulllike(sdf, -np.inf) upperbound = np.fulllike(sdf, np.inf) negmask = sdf < 0 posmask = ~negmask upperbound[negmask] = sdf[negmask] lowerbound[posmask] = sdf[posmask] # 3. Bound Clamping upperclose = np.abs(upperbound) < 1.0 lowerclose = np.abs(lowerbound) < 1.0 upperbound[upperclose] = 0.0 lowerbound[lowerclose] = 0.0 # 4. Jacobi Iteration jacobiweight = 0.5 jacobid = 1.0 / 18.0 if binaryvolume.ndim == 3 else 1.0 / 12.0 if binaryvolume.ndim == 3: stencil = np.zeros((5, 5, 5), dtype=np.float64) stencil[2, 2, 2] = -4.0 for axis in range(3): for offset in [-1, 1]: idx = [2, 2, 2] idx[axis] += offset stencil[tuple(idx)] = -4.0 for i in range(3): for j in range(i + 1, 3): for si in [-1, 1]: for sj in [-1, 1]: idx = [2, 2, 2] idx[i] += si idx[j] += sj stencil[tuple(idx)] = 1.0 else: # 2D stencil layout not provided in sources stencil = np.zeros((3, 3), dtype=np.float64) stencil[1, 1] = -4.0 stencil[0, 1] = -1.0 stencil[2, 1] = -1.0 stencil[1, 0] = -1.0 stencil[1, 2] = -1.0 currentsdf = sdf.copy() for in range(maxiters): residual = convolve(currentsdf, stencil, mode='nearest') update = -jacobid residual newsdf = jacobiweight update + (1.0 - jacobiweight) currentsdf currentsdf = np.clip(newsdf, lowerbound, upperbound) return currentsdf Edge Cases and Pitfalls Dimensionality: The method requires 2D or 3D input arrays. 1D or 4D+ arrays raise a ValueError. Precision: The stencil and intermediate calculations use float64 to maintain precision during the iterative process. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Guarantees topological preservation of the binary input and produces a valid SDF. Limitations: Computationally expensive compared to single-pass methods, requires an initial EDT which can be costly, and maxiters affects the accuracy/speed trade-off. When to use: When topological correctness is critical and the input is a binary volume. When not to use: When real-time performance is required or when the input is already a smooth SDF. The technique preprocesses binary volumes for surface extraction, ensuring that the resulting representation preserves the original topology. Implementation details, including the stencil values and iteration logic, are derived from the source code of the PyMCubes library. pmneila/PyMCubes, https://github.com/pmneila/PyMCubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: SDF Volume Generation & Ping-Pong Buffering
head: SDFGen, SDFMutate, double-buffered SDF update
body: This method generates and maintains a 3D Signed Distance Field (SDF) volume on the GPU using a double-buffered ping-pong architecture, supporting both initial generation and interactive volumetric mutation. It differs from static SDF generation by integrating immediate brush-based modifications with iterative Eikonal propagation to restore distance field validity, and from simple voxel carving by ensuring the resulting scalar field satisfies the Eikonal equation locally. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D SDF volume stored in a ping-pong buffer of two textures, mouse/brush parameters (origin, direction, radius, height, mode), and the current active buffer index. Output: An updated 3D SDF volume written to the opposite buffer in the ping-pong pair. Data Structures: The SDF volume is stored in a ping-pong array of two 3D RenderTextures (sdfVolumeTexture[2]). Each texture is configured with: TextureDimension: Tex3D colorFormat: RFloat (single-channel 32-bit float) enableRandomWrite: true msaaSamples: 1 mipCount: 0 Dimensions: width = SDFResolution.x, height = SDFResolution.y, volumeDepth = SDFResolution.z. Parameters: SDFResolution (Vector3Int): Dimensions of the 3D SDF volume in voxels. Typically set as DebugWindow.Instance.SdfResolution 8. SDFRadius (float): Radius of the SDF brush/kernel used for mutation and Eikonal propagation. Passed to shaders as sdfRadius. SDFMaxDist (float): Maximum distance value to compute or store in the volume. Passed to shaders as sdfMaxDist. BrushSize (float): Radius of the interactive brush. BrushHeight (float): Height parameter for the brush interaction. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create two RFloat 3D render textures with the target resolution defined by SDFResolution. Dispatch the SDFGen compute kernel to populate the initial SDF (e.g., a sphere) into the first buffer. Calculate thread group counts as numKernels = SDFResolution / kernelSize, where kernelSize is 8 (from [numthreads(8,8,8)]). 2. Buffer Selection: Determine the output buffer index using bitwise operation: outSdfTex = (activeSdfTex + 1) & 2. Note: The source uses & 2 which implies a specific indexing scheme or potential typo for & 1 given two buffers, but the source explicitly states & 2. Update activeSdfTex = outSdfTex after dispatch. 3. Mutation Dispatch: Bind the input texture sdfVolumeTexture[inSdfTex] and output texture sdfVolumeTexture[outSdfTex] to the SDFMutate kernel. Dispatch the kernel with numKernels. 4. Eikonal Passes (if needed): If the left mouse button is pressed and mode is subtract (or add), calculate the required number of Eikonal propagation passes to fill the cut radius: eikonelPasses = (int)(BrushSize / (SDFRadius 2.0 / SDFResolution.x)) 2. Dispatch the SDFMutate kernel with doEikonel = true for this many iterations. Pseudocode (Compute Shader Kernel SDFMutate): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kernelToUV(id): # Converts thread ID to UV coordinates in [0, 1] # Assuming id is uint3 and sdfTexSizeX is width return float3(id.x / sdfTexSizeX, id.y / sdfTexSizeY, id.z / sdfTexSizeZ) def uvToWorld(uv): # Converts UV to world space coordinates # Implementation details not provided in source, assumed to be a standard transform return uv 2.0 - 1.0 # Placeholder for actual world transform def sdSphere(worldPos, center, radius): return length(worldPos - center) - radius def raySphereIntersect(origin, direction, center, radius): # Returns distance to intersection, or large value if no hit oc = origin - center b = dot(oc, direction) c = dot(oc, oc) - radius radius disc = b b - c if disc < 0: return 1e10 t = -b - sqrt(disc) return max(t, 0.0) def opSmoothUnion(d1, d2, k): h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 (d2 - d1) / k, 0.0, 1.0) return mix(d2, d1, h) - k h (1.0 - h) def opSmoothSubtraction(d1, d2, k): # Smooth subtraction is typically smooth union of d1 and -d2 return opSmoothUnion(d1, -d2, k) def neighborMin(kernel, delta): # Accesses neighbor SDF values and returns min absolute value # sdfUV is assumed to read from sdfTexIn a = abs(sdfUV(kernelToUV(kernel + delta))) b = abs(sdfUV(kernelToUV(kernel - delta))) return min(a, b) def eikonal1d(h, v, g): return min(h, v) + g def eikonal2d(h, v, g): if abs(h - v) >= g: return eikonal1d(h, v, g) hv = h + v d = hv hv - 2.0 (h h + v v - g g) return 0.5 (hv + sqrt(d)) def eikonal3d(u, g): xyz = u.x + u.y + u.z n = 3.0 d = (xyz xyz) - n ((u.x u.x + u.y u.y + u.z u.z) - (g g)) if d < 0.0: return False, 0.0 e = (1.0 / n) (xyz + sqrt(d)) return True, e def eikonal(u, g): valid, e = eikonal3d(u, g) if valid: return e e1 = eikonal2d(u.x, u.y, g) e2 = eikonal2d(u.x, u.z, g) e3 = eikonal2d(u.y, u.z, g) return min(min(e1, e2), e3) def pack(value): # Placeholder for packing logic if not direct float assignment return value [numthreads(8, 8, 8)] def SDFMutate(id: uint3): uv = kernelToUV(id) world = uvToWorld(uv) # Initial SDF value (e.g., sphere) current = sdSphere(world, float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), sphereRadius) # Mouse Interaction if mouseAdd or mouseSubtract: toSdf = raySphereIntersect(mouseOrigin.xyz, mouseDir.xyz, float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), sphereRadius + brushHeight) ro = mouseOrigin.xyz + mouseDir.xyz toSdf d = sdSphere(world, ro, brushSize (1.25 if mouseSubtract else 1.0)) if mouseAdd: current = opSmoothUnion(d, current, 0.025) elif mouseSubtract: current = opSmoothSubtraction(d, current, 0.025) # Eikonal Propagation if doEikonel: u = float3( neighborMin(id, uint3(1, 0, 0)), neighborMin(id, uint3(0, 1, 0)), neighborMin(id, uint3(0, 0, 1))) g = sdfRadius 2.0 / sdfTexSizeX e = eikonal(u, g) if current > g: current = e sdfTexOut[id.xyz] = pack(current) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of RFloat (32-bit float) may lead to precision issues for very large volumes or fine details. Boundary Conditions: The neighborMin function accesses neighbors. At volume boundaries, these accesses may read uninitialized or zero values, potentially causing artifacts. Bitwise Operation: The source uses outSdfTex = (activeSdfTex + 1) & 2. For a two-buffer system, this should likely be & 1. If & 2 is intentional, it implies a different indexing scheme or a bug. Eikonal Passes Calculation: The formula eikonelPasses = (int)(BrushSize / (SDFRadius 2.0 / SDFResolution.x)) 2 assumes a specific relationship between brush size, SDF radius, and resolution. Incorrect parameters may lead to insufficient propagation. SDF Mutation & Eikonal Propagation is a GPU-based method for interactively modifying Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) using volumetric brushes. It solves the problem of maintaining geometrically correct distance values after local modifications (addition or subtraction) by combining immediate ray-casting-based brush application with iterative Eikonal equation propagation. It differs from static SDF generation by supporting real-time user input and from simple voxel carving by ensuring the resulting field remains a valid distance function through distance propagation. Time Complexity: O(N) per voxel per pass, where N is the number of voxels in the volume. Eikonal propagation requires multiple passes, scaling with the brush radius and resolution. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the two ping-pong buffers. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades with increased resolution and brush size due to more Eikonal passes. Strengths: Real-time interactive modification, GPU-accelerated, maintains distance field validity. Limitations: Limited to GPU execution, potential precision issues, boundary artifacts. When to use: Interactive SDF editing, real-time volume modification. When not to use: Static SDF generation, CPU-only environments, high-precision requirements. This method originates from the Unity-based implementation by samuelbigos, as documented in the GitHub repository samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity. It is designed for interactive SDF manipulation within the Unity engine, leveraging compute shaders for parallel processing. samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity, https://github.com/samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
