name: Procedural Cirrus Cloud Rendering
body: Procedural Cirrus Cloud Rendering is a technique for generating the appearance of high-altitude ice-crystal clouds using layered fractal Brownian motion (fbm) noise on a 2D plane projected from the view ray, modulated by wind direction and time to create strands, hooks, and fibres. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: View ray direction (rayDir), sun direction (sunDir), sun height (sunHeight), time (time), sky radiance scale (SKY\RADIANCE\SCALE), cloud plane scale (CIRRUS\SCALE), and cloud brightness (CIRRUS\BRIGHTNESS). Outputs: Final linear radiance color (outColor) and cloud density. Data Structures No persistent data structures are required; the method is stateless and computed per ray. Parameters CIRRUS\HEIGHT = 0.15. CIRRUS\WIND = (0.94, 0.34). CIRRUS\DRIFT = 0.02. CIRRUS\COVERAGE = 0.45. CIRRUS\MAX\OPACITY = 0.85. CIRRUS\SCALE and CIRRUS\BRIGHTNESS are not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Projection: Project the view ray direction onto the cloud plane using plane = rayDir.xz \times \frac{CIRRUS\HEIGHT}{\max(rayDir.y, 0.02)} \times CIRRUS\SCALE. 2. Wind Frame: Compute wind-aligned coordinates: across = (-CIRRUS\WIND.y, CIRRUS\WIND.x), wind\frame.x = dot(plane, CIRRUS\WIND), wind\frame.y = dot(plane, across). 3. Animation: Drift the wind frame: wind\frame.x += time \times CIRRUS\DRIFT. 4. Aliasing Control: Calculate pixel width across the wind: pixel\across = fwidth(wind\frame.y). 5. Visibility: Return zero density if rayDir.y < 0.02. 6. Patches: Generate base coverage: patches = fbm(wind\frame \times (0.25, 0.5), 4). 7. Patch Smoothing: patches = smoothstep(0.55 - CIRRUS\COVERAGE \times 0.3, 0.75 - CIRRUS\COVERAGE \times 0.3, patches). 8. Hooks: hooks = fbm(wind\frame \times (0.6, 1.2) + (31.7, 5.3), 3). 9. Strand Frame: strand\frame = wind\frame + (0.0, hooks \times 0.8). 10. Strands: strands = fbm(strand\frame \times (0.8, 7.0) + (-12.1, 47.9), 4). 11. Strand Smoothing: strands = smoothstep(0.3, 0.85, strands). 12. Fibres: fibres = fbm(strand\frame \times (1.5, 28.0) + (7.3, -21.4), 3). 13. Fibre Smoothing: fibres = smoothstep(0.25, 0.75, fibres). 14. Fibre Horizon Fade: fibres = mix(fibres, 0.5, smoothstep(0.15, 0.4, pixel\across \times 28.0)). 15. Density: density = patches \times strands \times mix(0.35, 1.0, fibres). 16. Fray: fray = fbm(strand\frame \times (3.0, 16.0) + (-3.9, 13.1), 2). 17. Fray Horizon Fade: fray = mix(fray, 0.6, smoothstep(0.15, 0.4, pixel\across \times 16.0)). 18. Fray Application: density = mix(fray \times fray \times 1.6, 1.0, smoothstep(0.1, 0.5, density)). 19. Density Horizon Fade: density = smoothstep(0.03, 0.22, rayDir.y). 20. Final Density: return density \times CIRRUS\MAX\OPACITY. 21. Radiance Base: colour = vec3(1.0) \times CIRRUS\BRIGHTNESS. 22. Sun Scattering: colour += vec3(1.0, 0.97, 0.9) \times pow(sunDot, 8.0) \times 1.5 \times sunHeight. 23. Sunset Factor: sunsetFactor = smoothstep(0.0, 0.2, sunHeight) \times (1.0 - smoothstep(0.2, 0.5, sunHeight)). 24. Sunset Tint: colour = mix(colour, colour \times vec3(1.0, 0.75, 0.5), sunsetFactor \times 0.4). 25. Sky Scaling: return colour \times SKY\RADIANCE\SCALE. 26. Integration: In the main shader, compute rayDir from fragment clip position, sunDir and time from push constants, base sky color from aerial and sun disc radiance, mix cloud radiance by density, and output linear radiance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def proceduralcirruscloudrendering(rayDir, sunDir, sunHeight, time, SKYRADIANCESCALE, CIRRUSSCALE, CIRRUSBRIGHTNESS): # Constants CIRRUSHEIGHT = 0.15 CIRRUSWIND = vec2(0.94, 0.34) CIRRUSDRIFT = 0.02 CIRRUSCOVERAGE = 0.45 CIRRUSMAXOPACITY = 0.85 # 1. Project ray onto cloud plane plane = vec2(rayDir.x, rayDir.z) (CIRRUSHEIGHT / max(rayDir.y, 0.02)) CIRRUSSCALE # 2. Compute wind-aligned coordinates across = vec2(-CIRRUSWIND.y, CIRRUSWIND.x) windframe = vec2(dot(plane, CIRRUSWIND), dot(plane, across)) # 3. Animate wind frame windframe.x += time CIRRUSDRIFT # 4. Calculate pixel width across wind pixelacross = fwidth(windframe.y) # 5. Visibility check if rayDir.y < 0.02: return 0.0, vec3(0.0) # 6. Generate patches patches = fbm(windframe vec2(0.25, 0.5), 4) # 7. Smoothstep patches patches = smoothstep(0.55 - CIRRUSCOVERAGE 0.3, 0.75 - CIRRUSCOVERAGE 0.3, patches) # 8. Generate hooks hooks = fbm(windframe vec2(0.6, 1.2) + vec2(31.7, 5.3), 3) # 9. Offset strand frame strandframe = windframe + vec2(0.0, hooks 0.8) # 10. Generate strands strands = fbm(strandframe vec2(0.8, 7.0) + vec2(-12.1, 47.9), 4) # 11. Smoothstep strands strands = smoothstep(0.3, 0.85, strands) # 12. Generate fibres fibres = fbm(strandframe vec2(1.5, 28.0) + vec2(7.3, -21.4), 3) # 13. Smoothstep fibres fibres = smoothstep(0.25, 0.75, fibres) # 14. Fade fibres near horizon fibres = mix(fibres, 0.5, smoothstep(0.15, 0.4, pixelacross 28.0)) # 15. Combine density density = patches strands mix(0.35, 1.0, fibres) # 16. Generate fray noise fray = fbm(strandframe vec2(3.0, 16.0) + vec2(-3.9, 13.1), 2) # 17. Fade fray near horizon fray = mix(fray, 0.6, smoothstep(0.15, 0.4, pixelacross 16.0)) # 18. Apply fray to density density = mix(fray fray 1.6, 1.0, smoothstep(0.1, 0.5, density)) # 19. Fade density near horizon density = smoothstep(0.03, 0.22, rayDir.y) # 20. Return final density finaldensity = density CIRRUSMAXOPACITY # 21. Compute radiance colour = vec3(1.0) CIRRUSBRIGHTNESS # 22. Add sun scattering sunDot = dot(normalize(rayDir), normalize(sunDir)) colour += vec3(1.0, 0.97, 0.9) pow(sunDot, 8.0) 1.5 sunHeight # 23. Compute sunset factor sunsetFactor = smoothstep(0.0, 0.2, sunHeight) (1.0 - smoothstep(0.2, 0.5, sunHeight)) # 24. Apply sunset warm tint colour = mix(colour, colour vec3(1.0, 0.75, 0.5), sunsetFactor 0.4) # 25. Scale by sky radiance cloudradiance = colour SKYRADIANCESCALE return finaldensity, cloudradiance def fbm(p, octaves): value = 0.0 amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 1.0 for in range(octaves): value += amplitude noise(p frequency) amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 2.0 return value def fwidth(val): # In a CPU implementation, derivatives must be computed from neighboring pixels # or passed as inputs. This placeholder assumes dx and dy are available. return abs(dx(val)) + abs(dy(val)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Downward Rays: Rays with y < 0.02 are treated as having zero density. Horizon Aliasing: The pixelacross calculation controls aliasing near the horizon where the cloud plane is viewed at a grazing angle. Undefined Parameters: CIRRUS\SCALE and CIRRUS\BRIGHTNESS are used in formulas but no values are provided in the sources. Derivatives: The use of fwidth requires access to screen-space derivatives, which are typically available in fragment shaders but not in CPU-based ray tracers without additional logic. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it involves a fixed number of noise evaluations and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), as no volume data structures are stored. Strengths: Extremely fast rendering; no memory bandwidth issues; easy to integrate into existing ray tracers; visually plausible for high-altitude clouds. Limitations: No volumetric scattering (no self-shadowing, no subsurface scattering); limited to a single plane; aliasing can occur if not handled by the horizon fade; requires manual tuning of parameters for different scenes. When to Use: Real-time rendering of high-altitude cirrus clouds; background sky elements; when performance is critical and volumetric accuracy is not required. When Not to Use: Low-altitude clouds requiring volumetric effects; scenes with complex lighting interactions within the cloud; when physical accuracy is required. The method is implemented in the VoxelPhase project using Rust and GLSL. It is designed for real-time graphics and integrates with a sky rendering pipeline that includes aerial radiance and sun disc radiance. migaelstrydom/VoxelPhase, https://github.com/migaelstrydom/VoxelPhase, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: IsimCloudTexture density evaluation
head: Cloud texture generation, IsimCloudTexture, Procedural Cloud Density Generation
body: IsimCloudTexture density evaluation computes the volumetric density of a cloud at a given point in space by combining geometric primitives (text segments or implicit cloud bodies), fractal Brownian motion (FBM) noise, and depth-based fading. It differs from general procedural gas modeling by focusing on specific cloud structures (text-based or layered bodies) and from simple cloud density sampling by generating the density field procedurally via CUDA kernels rather than sampling pre-baked data. The method outputs a grayscale density value (replicated to RGB) suitable for volume rendering. The method exists in two primary variants: a text-segment-based approach (Variant A) and a CUDA-generated implicit body approach (Variant B). Both variants evaluate density at a point p or grid index (x,y,z). Inputs: Point p = (p.x, p.y, p.z) in world or local space. Grid indices (x, y, z) and dimensions (width, height, depth) for Variant B. Volume bounds box{min}, box{max}. Text segments defining letter shapes (Variant A). Noise generator instance with FBM capability. Parameters: cloud\scale, letter\radius, smooth\width, segments (Variant A); thread block size, grid size (Variant B). Outputs: Density value d \in [0, 1]. RGB vector (d, d, d). Written to a 3D CUDA surface object (Variant B). Point3/Vector3: 3D vector with components x, y, z. Segment: Defined by endpoints, used for distance calculation. CUDA Surface: 3D texture surface object written to via surf3Dwrite. 1. Boundary Check: If p is outside box{min} and box{max}, return (0, 0, 0). 2. Text Density Calculation: Initialize text\density = 0.0. For each segment in segments: Compute squared distance d{sq} from p to the segment. If d{sq} < (letter\radius + smooth\width)^2: Compute d = \sqrt{d{sq}}. Update text\density = \max(text\density, \text{smoothstep}(letter\radius + smooth\width, letter\radius, d)). If text\density < 0.001, return (0, 0, 0). 3. Noise Evaluation: Compute n = \text{noise\}.fbm(p \times cloud\scale, 5). Compute cloud\noise = \text{clamp}((n - 0.3) \times 3.0, 0.0, 1.0). 4. Combine: final\density = text\density \times cloud\noise. 5. Depth Fading: Compute center\z = (box{min}.z + box{max}.z) \times 0.5. Compute depth\fade = \text{smoothstep}(1.5, 0.5, |p.z - center\z|). final\density = final\density \times depth\fade. 6. Return: (final\density, final\density, final\density). 1. Coordinate Normalization: Calculate normalized device coordinates px, py, pz \in [-1, 1] from thread indices (x, y, z) and dimensions (width, height, depth): px = 2.0 \times \frac{x}{width - 1} - 1.0 py = 2.0 \times \frac{y}{height - 1} - 1.0 pz = 2.0 \times \frac{z}{depth - 1} - 1.0 2. Upper Cloud Body: Calculate warped coordinates: upperX = px - 0.18 \times \sin(4.0 \times py) upperZ = pz - 0.12 \times \cos(5.0 \times py) Compute upper cloud density: upperCloud = \exp(-8.0 \times (upperX^2 + upperZ^2) - 3.5 \times (py - 0.35)^2) 3. Lower Cloud Body: Compute lower cloud density: lowerCloud = \exp(-4.5 \times (px^2 + pz^2) - 2.2 \times (py + 0.25)^2) 4. Detail Noise: Compute detail factor: detail = 0.68 + 0.20 \times \sin(11.0 \times px + 7.0 \times py) \times \sin(9.0 \times pz - 5.0 \times py) + 0.12 \times \sin(23.0 \times (px + pz)) 5. Boundary Fade: Compute boundary fade factor: boundaryFade = \text{saturate}((1.0 - \max(|px|, |py|, |pz|)) \times 8.0) where \text{saturate}(v) = \min(\max(v, 0.0), 1.0). 6. Final Density: Combine components: density = \text{saturate}((0.85 \times lowerCloud + 0.75 \times upperCloud - 0.18) \times detail \times boundaryFade) 7. Write Output: Write density to the 3D surface at (x, y, z) using surf3Dwrite with pitch x \times \text{sizeof(float)}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): """Standard smoothstep function.""" t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def clamp(v, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(v, maxval)) def saturate(v): return max(0.0, min(v, 1.0)) def distancepointtosegment(p, segstart, segend): """Euclidean distance from point p to line segment.""" segvec = segend - segstart pvec = p - segstart seglensq = segvec.dot(segvec) if seglensq == 0: return pvec.norm() t = clamp(pvec.dot(segvec) / seglensq, 0.0, 1.0) projection = segstart + segvec t return (p - projection).norm() def fbmnoise(p, scale, octaves): """ Placeholder for FBM noise evaluation. In source, this is noise.fbm(p cloudscale, 5). Implementation details of the noise generator are not provided in the sources. """ # Generic FBM implementation assumed for completeness value = 0.0 amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 1.0 for i in range(octaves): value += amplitude noisefunction(p frequency scale) amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 2.0 return value def noisefunction(p): """Placeholder for base noise function (e.g., Perlin, Simplex).""" # Not specified in sources return 0.0 def evaluateisimcloudvarianta(p, boxmin, boxmax, segments, letterradius, smoothwidth, cloudscale): """ Variant A: Text Segment Based Density Evaluation. """ # 1. Boundary Check if not (boxmin.x <= p.x <= boxmax.x and boxmin.y <= p.y <= boxmax.y and boxmin.z <= p.z <= boxmax.z): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 2. Text Density textdensity = 0.0 for seg in segments: d = distancepointtosegment(p, seg.start, seg.end) if d < (letterradius + smoothwidth): densityval = smoothstep(letterradius + smoothwidth, letterradius, d) if densityval > textdensity: textdensity = densityval if textdensity < 0.001: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 3. Noise n = fbmnoise(p, cloudscale, 5) cloudnoise = clamp((n - 0.3) 3.0, 0.0, 1.0) # 4. Combine finaldensity = textdensity cloudnoise # 5. Depth Fade centerz = (boxmin.z + boxmax.z) 0.5 depthfade = smoothstep(1.5, 0.5, abs(p.z - centerz)) finaldensity = depthfade # 6. Return return (finaldensity, finaldensity, finaldensity) def evaluateisimcloudvariantb(x, y, z, width, height, depth): """ Variant B: CUDA Implicit Body Density Evaluation. """ # 1. Normalized Coordinates px = 2.0 x / (width - 1) - 1.0 py = 2.0 y / (height - 1) - 1.0 pz = 2.0 z / (depth - 1) - 1.0 # 2. Upper Cloud upperX = px - 0.18 sin(4.0 py) upperZ = pz - 0.12 cos(5.0 py) upperCloud = exp(-8.0 (upperX2 + upperZ2) - 3.5 (py - 0.35)2) # 3. Lower Cloud lowerCloud = exp(-4.5 (px2 + pz2) - 2.2 (py + 0.25)2) # 4. Detail Noise detail = 0.68 + 0.20 sin(11.0 px + 7.0 py) sin(9.0 pz - 5.0 py) + 0.12 sin(23.0 (px + pz)) # 5. Boundary Fade maxabs = max(abs(px), abs(py), abs(pz)) boundaryFade = saturate((1.0 - maxabs) 8.0) # 6. Final Density density = saturate((0.85 lowerCloud + 0.75 upperCloud - 0.18) detail boundaryFade) return density cloudscale: Scales input position for noise evaluation. letterradius: Radius for text segment influence, typically 0.25. smoothwidth: Smoothness width for text segments, typically 0.2. segments: Vector of line segments defining letter shapes. boxmin, boxmax: Volume bounds. Thread block size: 8x8x8 threads (dim3 threads{8, 8, 8}). Grid size: \lceil width/8 \rceil \times \lceil height/8 \rceil \times \lceil depth/8 \rceil blocks. Division by Zero: In smoothstep, if edge0 == edge1, division by zero occurs. The sources assume valid ranges where edge0 < edge1. Null Vector: Normalization operations throw if the vector norm is zero. Boundary Conditions: Points outside the bounding box return zero density immediately. Precision: CUDA implementation uses float (32-bit) while C++ implementation uses double (64-bit) for intermediate calculations. Time Complexity: O(N \times S) for Variant A, where N is the number of points and S is the number of segments. O(1) per voxel for Variant B. Memory Complexity: O(S) for Variant A (storing segments). O(1) auxiliary memory for Variant B, plus output texture storage. Performance: Variant B is optimized for GPU execution via CUDA, utilizing 3D surface writes. Variant A is a general-purpose CPU implementation. Strengths: Procedural generation allows infinite resolution and easy parameter tweaking. Limitations: Variant A requires explicit segment definitions. Variant B is hardcoded to specific implicit shapes. The method originates from two unofficial GitHub repositories: "Volumetric-Path-Tracing" by TakTikFR and "HZL-fluidEffectsStudio" by pvasbob. It is used in procedural volume cloud modeling to generate density fields for visualization. TakTikFR/Volumetric-Path-Tracing, https://github.com/TakTikFR/Volumetric-Path-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, https://github.com/pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Procedural Gas Modeling via Turbulence
head: basic_gas procedural gas modeling, turbulence-based gas density function
body: Procedural Gas Modeling via Turbulence generates volumetric gas density by evaluating a turbulence function and mapping the result through a precomputed power table. It solves the problem of efficiently computing realistic gas density fields for volume rendering by replacing expensive per-sample power function calls with a lookup table. Inputs and Outputs: Input: pnt (point in solid/world space), parms (parameter array), POWTABLESIZE (table size constant). Output: density (float, gas density value). Data Structures: powtable: A static array of floats of size POWTABLESIZE. parms: An array of floats. parms[1] is the maximum density value (range 0.0 to 1.0). parms[2] is the exponent for the power function. Steps: 1. Precompute Lookup Table: Calculate powtable once per image. For i from POWTABLESIZE-1 down to 0: \text{pow\table}[i] = \left( \frac{i}{\text{POW\TABLE\SIZE}-1} \times \text{parms}[1] \times 2.0 \right)^{\text{parms}[2]} 2. Evaluate Turbulence: Compute turb = fastturbulence(pnt). 3. Index Calculation: Compute the integer index: \text{idx} = \text{int}\left( \text{turb} \times 0.5 \times (\text{POW\TABLE\SIZE}-1) \right) 4. Output Density: Set density = powtable[idx]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fastturbulence(pnt): # Standard 3D turbulence evaluation returning a value in [0, 1] # Implements layered noise (fractal Brownian motion) x, y, z = pnt val = 0.0 amp = 1.0 freq = 1.0 for in range(4): val += amp (math.sin(x freq) + math.sin(y freq) + math.sin(z freq)) / 3.0 amp = 0.5 freq = 2.0 return (val + 1.0) / 2.0 def basicgas(pnt, parms, powtablesize): powtable = [0.0] powtablesize calcd = True if calcd: calcd = False for i in range(powtablesize - 1, -1, -1): val = (i / (powtablesize - 1)) parms[1] 2.0 powtable[i] = math.pow(val, parms[2]) turb = fastturbulence(pnt) idx = int(turb 0.5 (powtablesize - 1)) density = powtable[idx] return density Parameters: parms[1]: Maximum density value. Range: 0.0 to 1.0. parms[2]: Exponent for the power function. Typical value for steam: 6.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The turbulence function must return values in the range [0, 1] to map correctly to the table indices. Values outside this range cause out-of-bounds array access or incorrect density. Precision issues may arise if turb is exactly at the boundary; the source uses a truncating cast (int), which maps turb=1.0 to the last valid index. A procedural shaping technique that applies a sine function to turbulence output to create vein-like structures in the gas density. Unlike the power function which increases contrast and separates plumes, the sine function creates continuous vein-like patterns similar to marble texturing. Code: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. turb = (1.0 + math.sin(fastturbulence(pnt) math.pi 5)) 0.5 Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Uses a precomputed table of size 10,000 (for POWTABLESIZE=10000). Time: Replaces per-sample pow() calls with a table lookup. For a 640x480 image with 100 volume samples per pixel, this saves approximately 30,710,000 pow() function calls. Strengths and Limitations: Strength: High performance due to table lookup optimization. Limitation: Limited to simple shaping functions (power, sine) unless extended. The method uses a visual simulation of turbulent flow similar to Ken Perlin’s approach. It is part of a broader framework for procedural volume cloud modeling. Procedural Modeling, Animation, and Rendering of Gases, Fluids, and Textures, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/2786953ProceduralModelingAnimationandRenderingofGasesFluidsandTextures/links/00b7d51a73e42a3c4e000000/Procedural-Modeling-Animation-and-Rendering-of-Gases-Fluids-and-Textures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Cloud Density Sampling
head: Base Cloud Density Generation, Low-Frequency Cloud Density, SampleCloudDensity, Schneider's Cloud Noise
body: Cloud Density Sampling generates the base volumetric density of clouds by combining low-frequency 3D noise textures using a weighted sum (Fractal Brownian Motion, FBM) and remapping the result to control cloud shape and coverage. It differs from sibling methods like Procedural 3D Worley-Perlin Fractal Noise Density by relying on pre-baked multi-channel 3D textures rather than procedural noise functions, allowing for distinct control over vertical stratification and global distribution via texture channels. It serves as the foundational density evaluation step in procedural volume cloud modeling, building on Procedural Volume Cloud Modeling. Inputs: samplepoint: vec3, world or texture space coordinate for density evaluation. weatherdata: vec4, containing cloud coverage in the red channel (weatherdata.r) and potentially other atmospheric parameters. relativeHeight: float, normalized height of the sample point within the atmosphere. winddirection: vec3, default (1.0, 0.0, 0.0). cloudspeed: float, default 10.0. cloudtopoffset: float, default 5.0. Time: float, global time variable. iscCheap: bool, if true, skips high-frequency sampling. lowFrequencyTexture: sampler3D, precomputed noise texture. highFrequencyTexture: sampler3D, precomputed high-frequency noise texture (used if !iscCheap). curlNoiseTexture: sampler2D, 2D curl noise texture (used if !iscCheap). Outputs: finalcloud: float, the computed cloud density at samplepoint in the range [0.0, 1.0]. Data Structures: lowFrequencyTexture: A 3D texture where channels store specific noise components: R: Base noise values. G: Component weighted by 0.625 in FBM. B: Component weighted by 0.250 in FBM. A: Component weighted by 0.125 in FBM. highFrequencyTexture: A 3D texture with similar channel packing for high-frequency details: R: Component weighted by 0.625. G: Component weighted by 0.250. B: Component weighted by 0.125. Formulas: The core remapping function is defined as: \text{Remap}(v, v{min}, v{max}, u{min}, u{max}) = u{min} + \frac{v - v{min}}{v{max} - v{min}}(u{max} - u{min}) Low-frequency FBM is computed from the RGBA sample N of the low-frequency texture: F{low} = 0.625 Ng + 0.250 Nb + 0.125 Na D{base} = \text{Remap}(Nr, -(1.0 - F{low}), 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) High-frequency FBM (if used) is computed from the RGBA sample H of the high-frequency texture: F{high} = 0.625 Hr + 0.250 Hg + 0.125 Hb M{high} = \text{mix}(F{high}, 1.0 - F{high}, \text{clamp}(relativeHeight \times 10.0, 0.0, 1.0)) Steps: 1. Wind Skew: Adjust the sample point based on wind and height: \mathbf{p}{skewed} = \mathbf{p} + relativeHeight \times \mathbf{wind\direction} \times cloud\top\offset \times 0.005 2. Time Movement: Apply time-based drift: \mathbf{p}{final} = \mathbf{p}{skewed} + (\mathbf{wind\direction} + (0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) \times Time \times cloud\speed \times 0.001 3. Low-Frequency Sampling: Sample the low-frequency texture at \mathbf{p}{final}: N = \text{SampleLowFrequencyTexture}(\mathbf{p}{final}) 4. Low-Frequency FBM: Compute the weighted sum: F{low} = Ng \times 0.625 + Nb \times 0.250 + Na \times 0.125 5. Base Cloud Remap: Remap the red channel to create the base cloud shape: base\cloud = \text{Remap}(Nr, -(1.0 - F{low}), 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) 6. Height Gradient: Compute the vertical attenuation factor: gh = \text{GetDensityHeightGradientForPoint}(\mathbf{p}, \text{weather\data}, relativeHeight) 7. Apply Height Gradient: base\cloud \leftarrow base\cloud \times gh 8. Coverage Mask: Retrieve cloud coverage from weather data: C = \text{weather\data}.r 9. Apply Coverage: Remap the base cloud against the coverage mask: base\cloud\with\coverage = \text{Remap}(base\cloud, C, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) 10. Clamp: Ensure density is within bounds: base\cloud\with\coverage = \text{clamp}(base\cloud\with\coverage, 0.0, 1.0) 11. Aesthetic Enhancement: Boost density based on coverage: base\cloud\with\coverage \leftarrow base\cloud\with\coverage \times C \times 4.0 12. High-Frequency Details (if !iscCheap and basecloudwithcoverage > 0.0): a. Sample curl noise: C{noise} = \text{SampleCurlNoiseTexture}(\mathbf{p}{final}.xy). b. Displace UVs: \mathbf{p}{final}.xy \leftarrow \mathbf{p}{final}.xy + C{noise}.xy \times (1.0 - relativeHeight). c. Sample high-frequency texture: H = \text{SampleHighFrequencyTexture}(\mathbf{p}{final} \times 0.1). d. Compute high-frequency modifier: F{high} = Hr \times 0.625 + Hg \times 0.250 + Hb \times 0.125 M{high} = \text{mix}(F{high}, 1.0 - F{high}, \text{clamp}(relativeHeight \times 10.0, 0.0, 1.0)) e. Erode by remapping: final\cloud = \text{Remap}(base\cloud\with\coverage, 0.2 \times M{high}, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) f. Clamp against modifier: final\cloud = \text{clamp}(final\cloud, 0.2 \times M{high}, 1.0) 13. Return: If iscCheap or step 12 was skipped, return base\cloud\with\coverage. Otherwise, return final\cloud. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def SampleCloudDensity(samplepoint, weatherdata, relativeHeight, winddirection, cloudspeed, cloudtopoffset, Time, isCheap, lowFrequencyTexture, highFrequencyTexture, curlNoiseTexture): # 1. Wind Skew p = samplepoint + relativeHeight winddirection cloudtopoffset 0.005 # 2. Time Movement p = p + (winddirection + vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) Time cloudspeed 0.001 # 3. Low-Frequency Sampling N = lowFrequencyTexture.sample(p) # Returns vec4 (RGBA) # 4. Low-Frequency FBM Flow = N.g 0.625 + N.b 0.250 + N.a 0.125 # 5. Base Cloud Remap # Remap(N.r, -(1.0 - Flow), 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) vmin = -(1.0 - Flow) vmax = 1.0 umin = 0.0 umax = 1.0 basecloud = umin + (N.r - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) (umax - umin) # 6. Height Gradient # GetDensityHeightGradientForPoint is a helper defined in parent or weather system gh = GetDensityHeightGradientForPoint(samplepoint, weatherdata, relativeHeight) # 7. Apply Height Gradient basecloud = gh # 8. Coverage Mask C = weatherdata.r # 9. Apply Coverage # Remap(basecloud, C, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) vmin = C vmax = 1.0 basecloudwithcoverage = umin + (basecloud - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) (umax - umin) # 10. Clamp basecloudwithcoverage = clamp(basecloudwithcoverage, 0.0, 1.0) # 11. Aesthetic Enhancement basecloudwithcoverage = C 4.0 # 12. High-Frequency Details if not isCheap and basecloudwithcoverage > 0.0: # 12a. Sample Curl Noise curlnoise = curlNoiseTexture.sample(vec2(p.x, p.z)) # Assuming XY mapping from source logic # 12b. Displace UVs pxy = vec2(p.x, p.z) # Assuming 2D UVs for curl noise pxy += curlnoise.xy (1.0 - relativeHeight) # 12c. Sample High-Frequency Texture # Source says samplepoint 0.1, but we displaced UVs. # Assuming the displacement affects the UVs passed to the high-freq texture. # The source code snippet: highfrequencynoises = SampleHighFrequencyTexture(samplepoint 0.1) # But step 12b displaces samplepoint.xy. We must use the displaced point. # Note: Source code snippet uses 'samplepoint' directly in the function call, # but the step description says 'Displace UVs: samplepoint.xy +=...'. # We assume the displaced UVs are used for the high-freq sample. H = highFrequencyTexture.sample(pxy 0.1) # vec3 to vec2 conversion implied or pxy is vec2 # 12d. Compute High-Frequency Modifier Fhigh = H.r 0.625 + H.g 0.250 + H.b 0.125 mixfactor = clamp(relativeHeight 10.0, 0.0, 1.0) Mhigh = mix(Fhigh, 1.0 - Fhigh, mixfactor) # 12e. Erode by Remapping # Remap(basecloudwithcoverage, 0.2 Mhigh, 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) vmin = 0.2 Mhigh vmax = 1.0 finalcloud = umin + (basecloudwithcoverage - vmin) / (vmax - vmin) (umax - umin) # 12f. Clamp against modifier finalcloud = clamp(finalcloud, 0.2 Mhigh, 1.0) return finalcloud else: return basecloudwithcoverage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The remapping formula involves division by (v{max} - v{min}). If v{max} \approx v{min}, precision loss or division by zero may occur. In step 5, if F{low} \approx 1.0, v{min} \approx 0.0, which is safe. In step 9, if C \approx 1.0, v{min} \approx 1.0, which is safe. In step 12e, if M{high} \approx 0.5, v{min} \approx 0.1, which is safe. Boundaries: The clamp operations ensure density stays within [0.0, 1.0]. Degenerate Input: If weatherdata.r (coverage) is 0, the base cloud is remapped to 0, and the aesthetic enhancement results in 0. High-frequency details are skipped if basecloudwithcoverage is 0. Generates billowy cloud shapes by synthesizing cloud density \rho(\mathbf{x}) procedurally using inverted Worley fractal Brownian motion (FBM), vertical gradient attenuation, and coverage thresholding. It differs from standard Perlin-based cloud noise by using the distance-to-nearest-cell metric of Worley noise, inverted to create bright, puffy "billowy" structures characteristic of cumulus clouds, rather than the smooth, turbulent gradients of Perlin noise. Choose this when procedural generation without pre-baked textures is required and billowy shapes are desired. The Full Cloud Density Function is a procedural method for computing the volumetric density of clouds by combining a vertical atmospheric profile with horizontal noise-based structures and a global coverage mask. It differs from sibling methods like Procedural 3D Worley-Perlin Fractal Noise Density by explicitly separating the vertical stratification (via a texture) from the horizontal structural modulation (via noise and a cubemap). This separation allows for distinct control over cloud layering and global distribution. Choose this when explicit control over vertical and horizontal cloud structures is needed. Samples cloud density along a cone by iterating through a pre-generated noise kernel, transforming positions to weather map coordinates, and summing densities. It differs from standard point sampling by accumulating density along a cone path, which can improve visual quality at the cost of multiple texture samples. Choose this when cone tracing is used for anti-aliasing or volumetric integration in cloud rendering. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point for low-frequency sampling. O(1) for high-frequency sampling if enabled. Cone tracing variant is O(k) where k is the number of cone samples (e.g., 5). Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the pre-baked 3D textures (lowFrequencyTexture, highFrequencyTexture, curlNoiseTexture). Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of sample points. High-frequency sampling doubles the texture lookups. Strengths: Pre-baked textures allow for complex noise patterns without runtime computation of noise functions. Separation of low and high frequencies allows for LOD control. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of textures. Less flexible than purely procedural methods. When to Use: When high-quality, pre-defined cloud shapes are needed and texture memory is available. When Not to Use: When procedural generation without pre-baked assets is required, or when memory is constrained. Originated in the context of real-time volumetric cloud rendering, specifically in the work associated with "realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes". The method is attributed to Schneider's Cloud Noise, suggesting a connection to earlier work by Schneider on cloud rendering. The use of multi-channel textures for FBM is a technique to accelerate noise evaluation by baking the fractal sum into texture channels. erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, https://github.com/erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Procedural 3D Worley-Perlin Fractal Noise Density
head: Billowy fractal cumulus noise, Inverted Worley FBM Cloud Density, Multi-Octave Inverted Worley FBM
body: Generates billowy cloud shapes by synthesizing cloud density \rho(\mathbf{x}) procedurally using inverted Worley fractal Brownian motion (FBM), vertical gradient attenuation, and coverage thresholding. It differs from standard Perlin-based cloud noise by using the distance-to-nearest-cell metric of Worley noise, inverted to create bright, puffy "billowy" structures characteristic of cumulus clouds, rather than the smooth, turbulent gradients of Perlin noise. Inputs: World position \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z). Cloud volume bounds: cloudBottom and cloudTop (Y-coordinates). Cloud coverage parameter coverage (float, typically 0.52). Extinction coefficient \sigmat (float, typically 0.035). FBM parameters: octaves (default 3), scale (default 0.0008). Outputs: Cloud density \rho(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required; the method is stateless and procedural. Steps: 1. Initialize FBM accumulators: sum = 0.0, freq = 1.0, amp = 1.0, totalAmp = 0.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to octaves (default 3): compute inverted Worley value w = 1.0 - \text{worley3D}(x \cdot \text{freq}, y \cdot \text{freq}, z \cdot \text{freq}), add to sum sum += w amp, accumulate amplitude totalAmp += amp, update frequency freq = 2.0, update amplitude amp = 0.5. 3. Return normalized FBM sum: sum / totalAmp. 4. Check height bounds: if world Y coordinate y is outside [cloudBottom, cloudTop], return density 0.0. 5. Scale coordinates: scale = 0.0008, compute baseNoise = worleyFBM(x scale, y scale, z scale, octaves). 6. Compute height normalization: h = \frac{y - \text{cloudBottom}}{\text{cloudTop} - \text{cloudBottom}}. 7. Compute height gradient: heightGrad = sin(π h). 8. Compute raw density: rawDensity = (baseNoise heightGrad) - (1.0 - coverage). 9. Return clamped and normalized density: max(0.0, rawDensity / (coverage + 1e-4)) σt. Formulas: The normalized height h is defined as: h = \frac{y - \text{cloudBottom}}{\text{cloudTop} - \text{cloudBottom}} The final density \rho(\mathbf{x}) is: \rho(\mathbf{x}) = \max\left(0, \frac{\text{FBM}(\mathbf{x}) \cdot \sin(\pi h) - (1 - \text{coverage})}{\text{coverage}}\right) \cdot \sigmat Where \text{FBM}(\mathbf{x}) is the multi-octave inverted Worley noise value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hash3d(x: int, y: int, z: int) -> float: """Deterministic integer hash mapped to [0, 1). Standard implementation detail.""" h = (x 374761393 + y 668265263 + z 1274126177) & 0xFFFFFFFF h = (h ^ (h >> 13)) 1274126177 h = h ^ (h >> 16) return abs(h) / 4294967296.0 def worley3D(x: float, y: float, z: float) -> float: """Distance to the nearest cell center in a 3x3x3 grid.""" ix, iy, iz = math.floor(x), math.floor(y), math.floor(z) mindistsq = float('inf') for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dz in range(-1, 2): rx = hash3d(ix + dx, iy + dy, iz + dz) ry = hash3d(iy + dy, iz + dz, ix + dx) rz = hash3d(iz + dz, ix + dx, iy + dy) distsq = (x - rx)2 + (y - ry)2 + (z - rz)2 if distsq < mindistsq: mindistsq = distsq return math.sqrt(mindistsq) def worleyFBM(x: float, y: float, z: float, octaves: int = 3) -> float: """Multi-octave inverted Worley FBM.""" sumval = 0.0 freq = 1.0 amp = 1.0 totalamp = 0.0 for in range(octaves): w = 1.0 - worley3D(x freq, y freq, z freq) sumval += w amp totalamp += amp freq = 2.0 amp = 0.5 return sumval / totalamp if totalamp != 0 else 0.0 def computeclouddensity(x: float, y: float, z: float, cloudbottom: float, cloudtop: float, coverage: float, sigmat: float, scale: float = 0.0008, octaves: int = 3) -> float: """Procedural 3D Worley-Perlin Fractal Noise Density.""" if y < cloudbottom or y > cloudtop: return 0.0 basenoise = worleyFBM(x scale, y scale, z scale, octaves) hnorm = (y - cloudbottom) / (cloudtop - cloudbottom) heightgrad = math.sin(math.pi hnorm) rawdensity = (basenoise heightgrad) - (1.0 - coverage) epsilon = 1e-4 normalizeddensity = max(0.0, rawdensity / (coverage + epsilon)) return normalizeddensity sigmat Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Height Culling: Check if the world Y-coordinate y is within [cloudBottom, cloudTop]. Division by Zero: The normalization step divides by coverage. If coverage is 0, the result is undefined. A small epsilon (10^{-4}) is added to the denominator to prevent division by zero. Height Normalization: If cloudBottom equals cloudTop, the height normalization h is undefined. A cell-based noise function that uses the distance to the nearest seed point. It produces cellular, puffy structures ideal for clouds. A technique of summing multiple octaves of noise at different frequencies and amplitudes to create detailed, self-similar structures. Subtracting the Worley distance from 1.0 transforms the dark "cells" into bright "puffs," matching the visual appearance of cumulus clouds. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Produces realistic, billowy cloud shapes; fully procedural and resolution-independent; no texture memory required. Limitations: Computationally intensive; lacks the fine-scale turbulence of Perlin noise; requires careful tuning of coverage and height parameters. When to Use: Real-time volumetric cloud rendering where procedural generation is preferred over texture-based approaches. The method is derived from the "volumetric-clouds-wgsl" repository by nff747, which implements a real-time volumetric cloud renderer using WebGPU. The use of inverted Worley noise for cloud density is a known technique in computer graphics, popularized by its ability to generate "billowy" structures. The specific combination of Worley FBM, height gradient, and coverage thresholding is presented in this repository as a practical implementation for real-time rendering. nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Full Cloud Density Function
body: The Full Cloud Density Function is a procedural method for computing volumetric cloud density by combining a vertical atmospheric profile with horizontal noise-based structures and a global coverage mask. It differs from sibling methods like Procedural 3D Worley-Perlin Fractal Noise Density by explicitly separating vertical stratification from horizontal structural modulation. Inputs: point: A 3D vector representing the sample position in world space. lod: A float parameter controlling the level of detail for high-frequency noise. radius: A float defining the radius of the cloud volume. cloudscale: A float scaling factor for low-frequency cloud shapes. detailscale: A float scaling factor for high-frequency noise detail. gradient, multiplier, threshold, cap: Tuning parameters for density modulation and clamping. powderdecay: A float parameter for the powder sugar scattering effect. cover: A samplerCube texture representing global cloud cover. cloudprofile: A function or texture lookup returning the vertical atmospheric profile value at point. Outputs: density: A float value representing the cloud density at point, clamped between 0.0 and cap. Data Structures: cover: A 3D cubemap texture representing global cloud cover. In the reference implementation, this is a 6x512x512 cubemap. cloudprofile: A vertical profile texture containing 10 values. Formulas: 1. Remap: \text{remap}(v, \text{orig\min}, \text{orig\max}, \text{new\min}, \text{new\max}) = \text{new\min} + \frac{v - \text{orig\min}}{\text{orig\max} - \text{orig\min}} \times (\text{new\max} - \text{new\min}) 2. Powder Effect: \text{powder}(d) = 1.0 - e^{-\text{powder\decay} \times d} Steps: 1. Compute low-frequency cloud shape using Perlin octaves: \text{clouds} = \text{perlin\octaves}\left(\frac{\text{normalize}(\text{point}) \times \text{radius}}{\text{cloud\scale}}\right) 2. Retrieve the vertical atmospheric profile: \text{profile} = \text{cloud\profile}(\text{point}) 3. Sample the global coverage mask and modulate it: \text{cover\sample} = \text{texture}(\text{cover}, \text{point}).r \times \text{gradient} + \text{clouds} \times \text{multiplier} - \text{threshold} Note: The original source removed the clamping operation for this step in an update. 4. Combine coverage and vertical profile: \text{base} = \text{cover\sample} \times \text{profile} 5. Compute high-frequency noise detail: \text{noise} = \text{cloud\octaves}\left(\frac{\text{point}}{\text{detail\scale}}, \text{lod}\right) In the reference implementation, this uses 5 octaves of 64x64x64 Worley noise. 6. Map the noise to the density range based on the base: \text{density} = \text{clamp}\left(\text{remap}(\text{noise}, 1.0 - \text{base}, 1.0, 0.0, \text{cap}), 0.0, \text{cap}\right) 7. Return density. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clouddensity(point: vec3, lod: float, radius: float, cloudscale: float, detailscale: float, gradient: float, multiplier: float, threshold: float, cap: float, powderdecay: float, cover: Cubemap, cloudprofilefunc: callable) -> float: # Step 1: Low-frequency cloud shape (3 octaves of Perlin-Worley noise) normalizedpoint = normalize(point) clouds = perlinoctaves((normalizedpoint radius) / cloudscale) # Step 2: Vertical profile profile = cloudprofilefunc(point) # Step 3: Coverage mask modulation coversample = texture(cover, point).r gradient + clouds multiplier - threshold # Note: Clamping removed per source update # Step 4: Combine base base = coversample profile # Step 5: High-frequency noise (5 octaves of Worley noise) noise = cloudoctaves(point / detailscale, lod) # Step 6: Remap and clamp density # Guard against division by zero when base is 0 if abs(base) < 1e-6: base = 1e-6 remapped = 0.0 + ((noise - (1.0 - base)) / base) (cap - 0.0) density = clamp(remapped, 0.0, cap) return density def perlinoctaves(p: vec3) -> float: # Standard octave noise accumulation value = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 for in range(3): # 3 octaves as per source value += amplitude noiseperlin(p frequency) amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 2.0 return value def cloudoctaves(p: vec3, lod: float) -> float: # Standard octave noise accumulation value = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 for in range(5): # 5 octaves as per source value += amplitude noiseworley(p frequency) amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 2.0 return value def remap(value: float, originalmin: float, originalmax: float, newmin: float, newmax: float) -> float: return newmin + ((value - originalmin) / (originalmax - originalmin)) (newmax - newmin) def powder(d: float, powderdecay: float) -> float: return 1.0 - exp(-powderdecay d) Parameters: cloudscale: Not given in the sources. detailscale: Not given in the sources. gradient, multiplier, threshold, cap: Not given in the sources. powderdecay: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Division by zero in remap if originalmax == originalmin. In this implementation, originalmax is 1.0 and originalmin is 1.0 - base. If base is 0, originalmin is 1.0, causing division by zero. This occurs when coversample or profile is zero. A guard checks if base is near zero and substitutes a small epsilon before division. Negative density values before clamping. The remap function can produce values outside [0.0, cap] if noise is outside [1.0-base, 1.0]. The final clamp handles this. Computes cloud density by combining vertical atmospheric profiles with horizontal footprints and noise-based structural variations. It generates visually distinct cloud layers for specific types (Cirrus through Cumulonimbus) within a unified procedural framework. Choose this when type-specific vertical stratification is required. Models particle density as a continuous function with density-dependent emission. Choose this when simulating light scattering effects where brightness is modulated by local density, rather than just geometric density. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Rendered at 28.5 frames per second on an AMD Ryzen 7 4700U (PassMark 2034) at 640x480 resolution. The render used 3 deep opacity maps with one 512x512 offset layer and a 7x512x512 transmittance array per frame. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Explicit separation of vertical and horizontal cloud features allows for detailed control over cloud types and global coverage. Limitations: Performance depends on the complexity of noise functions and texture sampling. The reference implementation uses multiple large textures (512x512 layers, 64x64x64 noise volumes) which may be memory-intensive. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The implementation uses 3 octaves of 64x64x64 Perlin-Worley noise for horizontal shapes and 5 octaves of 64x64x64 Worley noise for high-frequency detail. A 6x512x512 cubemap is used for global cloud cover, and a vertical profile texture with 10 values defines the atmospheric stratification. The author also introduced a "powder sugar" effect for scattered light, defined as 1.0 - e^{-\text{powder\decay} \times d}. name: Sabella's Density Emitter
head: Sabella's Method
body: Sabella's Density Emitter is a volume rendering technique that models the density of particles as a continuous function rather than discrete entities, allowing for varying light intensity along a ray. It distinguishes itself from Blinn’s fixed-intensity method by introducing a density-dependent emission term, where the brightness contribution of each sample is modulated by the local density value. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A parameterized density field \rho(x, y, z), ray start t1, ray end t2, and attenuation parameter \beta. Output: The calculated brightness (intensity) reaching the eye. Data Structures: The method operates on a continuous density field \rho. In implementation, this is typically sampled at discrete intervals along a ray. Key statistics accumulated during ray traversal include: M: The maximum (peak) density value encountered along the ray. D: The distance (parameter t) at which the peak value M is encountered. C: The center of gravity of the density distribution along the ray. R: The total attenuation integral along the ray, defined as R = \int{t1}^{t2} \rho(\tau) d\tau. Formulas: The brightness B is calculated by integrating the emission along the ray path: B = \int{t1}^{t2} \frac{R}{\rho(t)} e^{-\int{t1}^{t} \rho(\tau) d\tau} dt Where: \rho(t) is the parameterized density field \rho(x(t), y(t), z(t)). R is the total attenuation integral \int{t1}^{t2} \rho(\tau) d\tau. \beta is a parameter value to adjust the rate of attenuation. Steps: 1. Define the ray path from t1 to t2. 2. Sample the density field \rho(t) along the ray. 3. Compute the total attenuation R over the full ray segment [t1, t2]. 4. Compute the partial attenuation integral \int{t1}^{t} \rho(\tau) d\tau for each point t along the ray. 5. Evaluate the integrand \frac{R}{\rho(t)} e^{-\int{t1}^{t} \rho(\tau) d\tau} at each sample point. 6. Integrate the result over t from t1 to t2 to obtain Brightness. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def pointatt(t, raystart, rayend): """Returns the 3D position at parameter t along the ray from raystart to rayend.""" return raystart + t (rayend - raystart) def sabelladensityemitter(raystart, rayend, densityfield, numsamples): """ Calculates brightness using Sabella's Density Emitter method. Args: raystart: 3D start point of the ray. rayend: 3D end point of the ray. densityfield: Function rho(x,y,z) returning density at a 3D point. numsamples: Number of discrete samples along the ray. Returns: brightness: The calculated intensity. """ dt = (rayend - raystart) / numsamples tvalues = [raystart + i dt for i in range(numsamples + 1)] # Sample density field along the ray rhot = [densityfield(pointatt(t, raystart, rayend)) for t in tvalues] # Compute total attenuation integral R = integral{t1}^{t2} rho(tau) dtau R = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): R += (rhot[i] + rhot[i+1]) / 2.0 dt # Compute Brightness integral brightness = 0.0 for i in range(numsamples): tmid = (tvalues[i] + tvalues[i+1]) / 2.0 rhomid = (rhot[i] + rhot[i+1]) / 2.0 # Compute partial attenuation integral up to tmid partialintegral = 0.0 for j in range(i + 1): if j < numsamples: partialintegral += rhot[j] dt # Guard against division by zero if rhomid < 1e-6: term = 0.0 else: term = (R / rhomid) math.exp(-partialintegral) brightness += term dt return brightness Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: The term \frac{R}{\rho(t)} requires \rho(t) \neq 0. If the density field contains zero values, a guard clause or epsilon offset is required. Precision: The nested integrals (one for attenuation, one for brightness) can accumulate floating-point errors. High-resolution sampling is recommended. Boundary Conditions: t1 and t2 must be correctly identified as the entry and exit points of the volume. Simulates light from translucent objects by treating volumetric data samples as density emitters. It sets itself apart by explicitly defining the intensity accumulation formula and mapping ray-cast statistics (max density, distance, center of gravity) to color parameters. Complexity: The method requires two nested integrations per ray, leading to O(N^2) complexity if naive integration is used, or O(N) with precomputed cumulative density arrays, where N is the number of samples per ray. Performance: The source does not provide specific measured performance metrics, hardware, or resolution data. Strengths: Allows varying light intensity based on density, unlike Blinn's fixed method. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than simple alpha blending due to the complex integrand. Sabella's method was presented by Sabella in 1988. It is a variation on the general ray-casting theme and is similar to Blinn's method [Bli82], but improves upon it by allowing varying densities where Blinn's method is fixed. The method is discussed in the context of forward projection and volume rendering overviews. An Overview of Rendering from Volume Data --- including Surface and Volume Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/download/63614.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Density Emitter Model
head: Density Emitters
body: The Density Emitter Model simulates light from translucent objects by treating volumetric data samples representing density values as a field of density emitters, where each emitter is a tiny particle that emits and scatters light. It sets itself apart from its parent, Sabella's Density Emitter, by explicitly defining the intensity accumulation formula and the mapping of ray-cast statistics (maximum density, distance, center of gravity) to color parameters for visual effects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data where samples represent density values; ray parameters (t1, t2) defining the traversal interval within the volume. Output: Pixel intensity I and optional color parameters derived from ray statistics. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Attenuation parameter \tau: Modifiable. Controls attenuation; higher values specify a medium which darkens more rapidly. Spread parameter \beta: Modifiable. Controls the spread of density values. Low values produce a diffuse cloud appearance; higher values highlight dense portions of the data. Number of density emitters: Proportional to the scalar value in that region. Steps: 1. Cast rays from the eye point through each pixel on the image plane into the volume. 2. For each ray, traverse from t1 to t2. 3. Calculate the intensity I for the pixel using the formula below. 4. If pixel opacity reaches unity, set a flag and stop processing that pixel further (front-to-back optimization). 5. Compute three additional values for the ray: maximum density value encountered, distance at which the maximum occurred, and center of gravity of density emitters along the ray. 6. Map these three values to color parameters (e.g., hue, saturation, lightness) to achieve visual effects. Formula: The intensity I is calculated by traversing the ray from t1 to t2: I = \frac{t2}{t1} \int{t1}^{t2} \frac{\rho(t)}{e^{\tau(t)}} dt Where: \rho(t) is the density at location t. \tau(t) is the attenuation parameter at location t. The term e^{-\tau(t)} represents the probability that light will be scattered before reaching the eye. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import exp def densityemittermodel(volumedata, rayorigin, raydirection, t1, t2, taufunc, betaparam, dt): """ Simulates light intensity using the Density Emitter Model. Args: volumedata: Callable returning density rho at 3D position. rayorigin: 3D vector, eye position. raydirection: 3D vector, normalized direction. t1: Start distance along ray. t2: End distance along ray. taufunc: Callable returning attenuation tau at 3D position. betaparam: Spread parameter controlling density spread. dt: Step size for integration. Returns: intensity: Float, calculated pixel intensity. maxdensity: Float, maximum density encountered. maxdist: Float, distance where max density occurred. centerofgravity: 3D vector, center of gravity of emitters. """ intensityintegral = 0.0 maxdensity = -float('inf') maxdist = t1 weightedpositionsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] totaldensityweight = 0.0 opacity = 0.0 t = t1 while t <= t2: pos = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] rho = volumedata(pos) tau = taufunc(pos) rhoeffective = rho exp(-betaparam rho) intensityintegral += (rhoeffective / exp(tau)) dt if rhoeffective > maxdensity: maxdensity = rhoeffective maxdist = t for i in range(3): weightedpositionsum[i] += rhoeffective pos[i] totaldensityweight += rhoeffective opacity += rhoeffective dt if opacity >= 1.0: break t += dt intensity = (t2 / t1) intensityintegral if totaldensityweight > 0: centerofgravity = [weightedpositionsum[i] / totaldensityweight for i in range(3)] else: centerofgravity = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t1 for i in range(3)] return intensity, maxdensity, maxdist, centerofgravity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shadowing and color variation due to differences in scattering at different wavelengths are ignored to avoid complicating the image and detracting from density variation perception. If the ray does not intersect the volume, intensity is 0. Precision issues may arise if t1 is close to 0, causing division by zero in the \frac{t2}{t1} factor. Ensure t1 > 0. None. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray. Front-to-back rendering allows early termination if opacity reaches unity. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of volumetric data. No additional large buffers mentioned beyond standard ray-casting accumulators. Strengths: Correctly models occlusion of deeper parts of the volume by closer parts. Allows for interesting visual effects by mapping ray statistics to color parameters. Limitations: Ignores shadowing and wavelength-dependent scattering, which may reduce physical accuracy but simplifies the image. When to use: When simulating translucent objects where density variation perception is prioritized over physical light transport accuracy. The Density Emitter Model is described in the context of volume visualization principles. It is related to the work of Arie Kaufman. The basic idea is that a beam of "virtual" particles is sent through the volume, with the user selecting the particle properties and the laws of interaction. Krueger [60] showed that various existing volume rendering models can be described as special cases of an underlying transport theory model of the transfer of particles in inhomogeneous media. PDF Volume Visualization: Principles and Advances, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/KaufmanVolumeVisualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Finite Layer Cloud Shape Generation
head: Layer Cloud Side Profile, Natural XY Edge Envelope
body: Finite Layer Cloud Shape Generation is a procedural method for constructing the 3D volume shapes of layer cloud types (Cirrus, Altostratus, Nimbostratus, Stratocumulus, Stratus) by assembling a chain of connected 3D ellipsoidal lobes. It solves the geometric artifact where extruding a 2D cloud contour into a column creates a degenerate cylinder along the Z-axis, instead producing a natural side edge with vertical presence variation. It differs from its siblings Cumulonimbus and Cumulus Shape Generation and IsimCloudTexture density evaluation by specifically targeting the flat, stratified structure of layer clouds rather than convective or generic volumetric structures. The method generates a signed distance field or density contour in the XY plane, modulated by a vertical Gaussian presence function, to define the cloud's lateral boundary. Inputs: x, y, z: Coordinate arrays (typically normalized -1 to 1 or similar). typeid: Integer identifier for the cloud type. Must be in LAYERCLOUDTYPEIDS (3, 5, 6, 7, 8). rng: Random number generator instance for procedural variation. edgenoise: Noise array for organic edge variation. Outputs: finalcontour: A scalar field representing the organic cloud edge, where values > 0 indicate cloud volume. Lobe Specification Tuple: (centerx, centery, radiusx, radiusy, weight, lobez, lobezradius). Shape Profile Parameters: Retrieved via layershapeprofile(typeid), returning (centerz, halfheight, topwobble, bottomwobble, thicknessvariance, captaper, sideedgevariation). LAYERCLOUDTYPEIDS: frozenset((3, 5, 6, 7, 8)). Persistent Support Values (vertical base density): Type 3: 0.36 Type 5: 0.40 Type 6: 0.50 Type 7: 0.24 Type 8: 0.44. Typical Dimensions (for generation): majorlength: Uniform(0.45, 0.72). crosswidth: Uniform(0.22, 0.46). radiusx: Uniform(0.14, 0.30). radiusy: Uniform(0.12, 0.28). 1. Generate Lobe Specifications: Determine majorangle = rng.uniform(-π, π). Calculate direction vectors: direction = (cos(majorangle), sin(majorangle)), perpendicular = (-direction[1], direction[0]). Get shape profile for typeid to obtain centerz and halfheight. Generate count (7–13) positions along the major axis: positionsalong = linspace(-0.88, 0.88, count) + rng.normal(0.0, 0.09, count). For each position: along = positionalong majorlength. cross = rng.normal(0.0, crosswidth 0.62). position = (centerx, centery) + direction along + perpendicular cross. radiusx = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.30), radiusy = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.28). lobez = centerz + rng.uniform(-0.48, 0.48) halfheight. lobezradius = rng.uniform(0.58, 1.04) halfheight. weight = rng.uniform(0.54, 0.98). Append (position[0], position[1], radiusx, radiusy, weight, lobez, lobezradius) to edgelobespecs. Add 1–3 side lobes to prevent degeneracy: along = rng.uniform(-0.58, 0.58) majorlength. cross = choice([-1, 1]) uniform(0.60, 1.18) crosswidth. Generate similar radius/weight parameters and append to edgelobespecs. 2. Evaluate Density Field: Rotate coordinates: localx, localy = rotatedxy(x, y, variation). Initialize lobefield = zeroslike(x, dtype=float32). For each lobe in edgelobespecs (cx, cy, rx, ry, w, lz, lZR): Rotate lobe center: lcx = cos(variation)cx + sin(variation)cy, lcy = -sin(variation)cx + cos(variation)cy. Calculate 2D lobe contribution: lobe = \exp\left( -\left( \frac{localx - lcx}{rx \cdot 1.15} \right)^2 - \left( \frac{localy - lcy}{ry \cdot 1.15} \right)^2 \right) Calculate vertical presence: persistent\support = \text{lookup}(type\id) vertical\presence = persistent\support + (1.0 - persistent\support) \cdot \exp\left( -\left( \frac{z - lz}{\max(lZR, 0.001)} \right)^2 \right) Add to field: lobefield += float32(w verticalpresence) lobe. 3. Apply Horizontal Taper: Get captaper from shape profile. Calculate normalizedheight = abs(z - centerz) / max(halfheight, 0.001). Calculate taper mask: captapermask = smoothstep((normalizedheight - 0.12) / 0.88). Apply taper: lobefield -= captaper captapermask. 4. Final Contour Calculation: Calculate contour: contour = lobe\field + (edge\noise - 0.5) \cdot (0.62 + 0.30 \cdot side\variation) - cap\taper\mask \cdot cap\taper Apply organic smoothing: organic = smoothstep\left( \frac{contour - 0.30}{0.48} \right) Apply final edge guard (clears only outermost voxels): screen\distance = \min(x+1, 1-x, y+1, 1-y) final\guard = safe\edge\fade(screen\distance, 0.0, 0.045) Return organic finalguard. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def finitelayercloudshapegeneration(x, y, z, typeid, rng, edgenoise, variation): """ Generates the 3D shape contour for layer clouds. x, y, z: numpy arrays of coordinates. typeid: int, cloud type ID (3, 5, 6, 7, 8). rng: numpy.random.Generator. edgenoise: numpy array of noise values. variation: float, rotation angle. """ # Step 1: Generate Lobe Specifications majorangle = rng.uniform(-np.pi, np.pi) direction = np.array([np.cos(majorangle), np.sin(majorangle)]) perpendicular = np.array([-direction[1], direction[0]]) majorlength = rng.uniform(0.45, 0.72) crosswidth = rng.uniform(0.22, 0.46) # Get shape profile parameters (simplified lookup) centerz, halfheight,,,, captaper, sideedgevariation = layershapeprofile(typeid) count = rng.integers(7, 14) positionsalong = np.linspace(-0.88, 0.88, count) + rng.normal(0.0, 0.09, size=count) edgelobespecs = [] # Main chain lobes for posalong in positionsalong: along = posalong majorlength cross = rng.normal(0.0, crosswidth 0.62) position = np.array([0.0, 0.0]) + direction along + perpendicular cross radiusx = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.30) radiusy = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.28) lobez = centerz + rng.uniform(-0.48, 0.48) halfheight lobezradius = rng.uniform(0.58, 1.04) halfheight weight = rng.uniform(0.54, 0.98) edgelobespecs.append((position[0], position[1], radiusx, radiusy, weight, lobez, lobezradius)) # Side lobes numsidelobes = rng.integers(1, 4) for in range(numsidelobes): along = rng.uniform(-0.58, 0.58) majorlength crosssign = rng.choice([-1, 1]) cross = crosssign rng.uniform(0.60, 1.18) crosswidth position = np.array([0.0, 0.0]) + direction along + perpendicular cross radiusx = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.30) radiusy = rng.uniform(0.12, 0.28) lobez = centerz + rng.uniform(-0.48, 0.48) halfheight lobezradius = rng.uniform(0.58, 1.04) halfheight weight = rng.uniform(0.54, 0.98) edgelobespecs.append((position[0], position[1], radiusx, radiusy, weight, lobez, lobezradius)) # Step 2: Evaluate Density Field localx, localy = rotatedxy(x, y, variation) lobefield = np.zeroslike(x, dtype=np.float32) persistentsupports = {3: 0.36, 5: 0.40, 6: 0.50, 7: 0.24, 8: 0.44} persistentsupport = persistentsupports.get(typeid, 0.40) # Default fallback for cx, cy, rx, ry, w, lz, lZR in edgelobespecs: # Rotate lobe center cosv = np.cos(variation) sinv = np.sin(variation) lcx = cosv cx + sinv cy lcy = -sinv cx + cosv cy # 2D Lobe dx = (localx - lcx) / (rx 1.15) dy = (localy - lcy) / (ry 1.15) lobe = np.exp(-(dx2 + dy2)) # Vertical Presence zdiff = z - lz lobezradiussafe = max(lZR, 0.001) verticalpresence = persistentsupport + (1.0 - persistentsupport) np.exp(-(zdiff / lobezradiussafe)2) lobefield += np.float32(w verticalpresence) lobe # Step 3: Horizontal Taper normalizedheight = np.abs(z - centerz) / max(halfheight, 0.001) captapermask = smoothstep((normalizedheight - 0.12) / 0.88) lobefield -= captaper captapermask # Step 4: Final Contour contour = lobefield + (edgenoise - 0.5) (0.62 + 0.30 sideedgevariation) - captaper captapermask organic = smoothstep((contour - 0.30) / 0.48) screendistance = np.minimum.reduce([x + 1.0, 1.0 - x, y + 1.0, 1.0 - y]) finalguard = safeedgefade(screendistance, 0.0, 0.045) return organic finalguard def rotatedxy(x, y, angle): cosa = np.cos(angle) sina = np.sin(angle) return x cosa - y sina, x sina + y cosa def smoothstep(t): t = np.clip(t, 0.0, 1.0) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def safeedgefade(distance, minval, maxval): # Implementation of edge fade based on distance to screen boundary # Assuming linear fade from 1.0 at maxval to 0.0 at minval fade = np.where(distance > maxval, 1.0, np.where(distance < minval, 0.0, (distance - minval) / (maxval - minval))) return fade def layershapeprofile(typeid): # Simplified profile retrieval. In source, this returns specific params. # Example for Type 6 (Nimbostratus): center=-0.03, half=0.58, topwobble=0.180, bottomwobble=0.285, thicknessvariance=0.40, captaper=0.39, sideedgevariation=1.10 profiles = { 6: (-0.03, 0.58, 0.180, 0.285, 0.40, 0.39, 1.10) } return profiles.get(typeid, (0.0, 0.5, 0.1, 0.1, 0.3, 0.3, 1.0)) Degeneracy: Without side lobes, the cloud may degenerate into a simple cylinder along the Z-axis. The method explicitly adds 1–3 side lobes to prevent this. Boundary Clearing: The final guard clears only the outermost voxels; the main contour naturally goes to zero before reaching this boundary. Division by Zero: lobezradius and halfheight must be clamped to a minimum of 0.001 to avoid division by zero in vertical presence calculations. Generates non-spherical, multi-lobed shapes for convective clouds. Choose when modeling vertical development and irregular tops/bases. Extrudes a 2D sketch into an ellipsoidal volume for database retrieval. Choose when converting artistic sketches to volumetric data for similarity matching. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and the number of lobes. The evaluation involves a loop over edgelobespecs (typically 8–16 lobes) per voxel. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storage for the coordinate arrays, noise, and the lobe specifications. No large 3D textures are generated during the shape definition phase; it outputs a scalar field. Performance: Efficient for procedural generation. The use of Gaussian functions and smoothsteps allows for fast evaluation on GPU or CPU. Strengths: Produces natural, non-degenerate layer cloud shapes with organic edge variation. Avoids the "cylinder" artifact of simple extrusion. Limitations: Specific to layer cloud types. Not suitable for convective clouds (Cumulus/Cumulonimbus) without modification. When to Use: When generating volume data for Cirrus, Altostratus, Nimbostratus, Stratocumulus, or Stratus clouds. When Not to Use: For convective clouds or when a simple cylindrical cloud shape is desired. The method originates from the "Noise-Cloud" project, an unofficial implementation of procedural cloud generation techniques. It is designed to integrate with volume rendering pipelines, specifically for Unreal Engine 5, as indicated by the volume encoding version "ue5-volume-rg-atlas-v7-undulating-finite-layer-clouds". The technique addresses the limitations of earlier procedural cloud methods that relied on simple extrusion, providing a more physically plausible shape for layer clouds. mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cumulonimbus and Cumulus Shape Generation
head: Cumulus and Cumulonimbus Shape Generation
body: Cumulonimbus and Cumulus Shape Generation is a procedural method for generating non-spherical, multi-lobed cloud shapes for Cumulus (type 9) and Cumulonimbus (type 10) clouds, creating irregular tops and bases rather than simple spheres. It differs from explicit tessellation approaches by using a parametric lobe-generation pipeline that scales with cloud type and style. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Cloud type ID (9 for Cumulus, 10 for Cumulonimbus), style offset (31009 for realistic, 41003 for cartoon), base seed, and a random number generator (RNG). Outputs: A list of 3D ellipsoidal lobes, each defined by a center position (cx, cy, cz) and radii (rx, ry, rz). Data Structures: Each lobe is stored as a tuple or struct containing cx, cy, cz (float coordinates) and rx, ry, rz (float radii). Steps: 1. Initialize RNG: Set the random seed using the formula: \text{seed} = \text{base\seed} + \text{type\id} \times 1009 + \text{style\offset} Where typeid is 9 for Cumulus and 10 for Cumulonimbus. 2. Generate Center: Generate the base center coordinates (center\x, center\y) from a uniform distribution over the interval [-0.12, 0.12]. 3. Generate Lobes based on Type: If Type 9 (Cumulus): Base Lobes: Generate 3 to 6 base lobes. cx, cy: Generated from a uniform distribution around center\x, center\y. cz: Generated from uniform distribution in [-0.42, -0.16]. rx: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.27, 0.42]. ry: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.23, 0.37]. rz: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.14, 0.25]. Tower Lobes: Generate 5 to 10 tower lobes. direction: Generated from uniform distribution in [-\pi, \pi]. radial: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.06, 0.52]. cx, cy: Offset from the center by radial in the direction direction. cz: Generated from uniform distribution in [-0.06, 0.54]. rx: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.17, 0.34]. ry: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.16, 0.32]. rz: Generated from uniform distribution in [0.18, 0.36]. If Type 10 (Cumulonimbus): Generate a sequence of lobes indexed from 0 to lobe\count - 1. Calculate progress: progress = \frac{index}{lobe\count - 1}. cx, cy: Spread increases with progress. The base spread is 0.13 + progress \times 0.08. cz: Rises from -0.58 to 0.56, calculated as -0.58 + progress \times 1.14. rx, ry: Increase with progress, calculated as 0.24 + progress \times 0.10. rz: Not given in the sources. Other Layer Clouds (Types 1, 7): Generate 3 to 10 lobes with radial from uniform [0.03, 0.52], theta from uniform [-\pi, \pi], and cz from uniform [-0.20, 0.20]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math def generatecumuluscumulonimbuslobs(typeid, styleoffset, baseseed, lobecount=15): # 1. Initialize RNG seed = baseseed + typeid 1009 + styleoffset rng = random.Random(seed) # 2. Generate Center centerx = rng.uniform(-0.12, 0.12) centery = rng.uniform(-0.12, 0.12) lobes = [] if typeid == 9: # Cumulus # Base Lobes: 3-6 numbase = rng.randint(3, 6) for in range(numbase): cx = rng.uniform(centerx - 0.12, centerx + 0.12) cy = rng.uniform(centery - 0.12, centery + 0.12) cz = rng.uniform(-0.42, -0.16) rx = rng.uniform(0.27, 0.42) ry = rng.uniform(0.23, 0.37) rz = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.25) lobes.append({'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cz': cz, 'rx': rx, 'ry': ry, 'rz': rz}) # Tower Lobes: 5-10 numtower = rng.randint(5, 10) for in range(numtower): direction = rng.uniform(-math.pi, math.pi) radial = rng.uniform(0.06, 0.52) cx = centerx + radial math.cos(direction) cy = centery + radial math.sin(direction) cz = rng.uniform(-0.06, 0.54) rx = rng.uniform(0.17, 0.34) ry = rng.uniform(0.16, 0.32) rz = rng.uniform(0.18, 0.36) lobes.append({'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cz': cz, 'rx': rx, 'ry': ry, 'rz': rz}) elif typeid == 10: # Cumulonimbus # Guard against division by zero lobecount = max(lobecount, 2) for i in range(lobecount): progress = i / (lobecount - 1) # Spread increases with progress spread = 0.13 + progress 0.08 cx = centerx + rng.uniform(-spread, spread) cy = centery + rng.uniform(-spread, spread) # CZ rises from -0.58 to 0.56 cz = -0.58 + progress 1.14 # RX, RY increase with progress rx = 0.24 + progress 0.10 ry = 0.24 + progress 0.10 # RZ not specified in sources rz = 0.20 lobes.append({'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cz': cz, 'rx': rx, 'ry': ry, 'rz': rz}) else: # Other Layer Clouds (Types 1, 7) numother = rng.randint(3, 10) for in range(numother): radial = rng.uniform(0.03, 0.52) theta = rng.uniform(-math.pi, math.pi) cx = centerx + radial math.cos(theta) cy = centery + radial math.sin(theta) cz = rng.uniform(-0.20, 0.20) rx = rng.uniform(0.27, 0.42) ry = rng.uniform(0.23, 0.37) rz = rng.uniform(0.14, 0.25) lobes.append({'cx': cx, 'cy': cy, 'cz': cz, 'rx': rx, 'ry': ry, 'rz': rz}) return lobes Parameters: styleoffset: 31009 for realistic style, 41003 for cartoon style. typeid: 9 for Cumulus, 10 for Cumulonimbus. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: In Cumulonimbus generation, if lobecount is 1, the progress calculation involves division by zero. The implementation must enforce lobecount >= 2. Precision: The source uses floating-point uniform distributions. Deterministic results require consistent RNG state across platforms. Boundary Conditions: The coordinates and radii are normalized values. The rendering pipeline must handle these normalized coordinates correctly. The Hierarchical Implicit Blob Cloud Model is a procedural method for generating the irregular, multi-lobed shapes of Cumulus and Cumulonimbus clouds by recursively layering quasi-spherical particles. It solves the problem of creating realistic cloud tops and bases with continuous furrows, distinguishing itself from explicit tessellation approaches by using a particle system to extract isosurfaces and place subsequent levels. An algorithm for generating Cumulus (type 9) and Cumulonimbus (type 10) clouds using a sparse set of 3D Gaussian-distributed pseudo-spheroid primitives. It differs from particle-based systems by requiring significantly fewer primitives (typically 35) to achieve realistic results, and from hierarchical implicit blobs by using explicit geometric primitives with pre-processing filters to optimize rendering performance. A vertical profile function that sculpts realistic 'water balloon on a table' puffy clouds using a superellipsoid shape. It sculpts voluminous, vertical structures inside getCloud3DProfile / getCloud3DSDF using a superellipsoid profile driven by eccentricity, curvature exponent, and center distance. Eccentricity determines the widest point of the cloud, decoded from the cell ID hash. Curvature exponent is a parameter driving the superellipsoid profile shape. Uses L-systems (Lindenmayer systems) with grammar rules to generate cloud shapes. It differs from Kang et al. by including a proportional random factor in sphere radius and distance between primitives in each recursive call. It uses volumetric rendering and density function from Equation (2). The host-side C++ interpreter runs before GLSL rendering, acting as a tiny interpreter for recursive generation of spheres based on an axiom and rules, generating a string of symbols. A lexical analyser processes the generated string, inserting a sphere with random radius and length for each 'X' or 'Y' item, and applying rotation angles given by '+' and '&' operators. The BNF Grammar for generation is X \rightarrow X+YF++YF-FX-XFXF-YF+/, where '+' means turn left with angle using a rotation matrix, and '&' means pitch down with angle using a different rotation matrix. Example parameters: Iterations = 7, Angle = 10° produces thin/strange spiral shapes; Angle [50°, 100°] with same grammar produces dense cumulus formations.
