name: Hierarchical Implicit Blob Cloud Model
head: Cloud Shape Model, Implicit Surface Cloud
body: The Hierarchical Implicit Blob Cloud Model is a procedural method for generating the irregular, multi-lobed shapes of Cumulus and Cumulonimbus clouds by recursively layering quasi-spherical particles. It solves the problem of creating realistic cloud tops and bases with continuous furrows, distinguishing itself from explicit tessellation approaches by using a particle system to extract isosurfaces and place subsequent levels. Inputs: Level 0 particle configuration: A set of initial particles P0, either procedurally generated on a horizontal plane or manually placed by a user to define features like turrets. Global parameters: Flattening range, radius reduction factor, blending amounts, and repulsion offsets. Outputs: A hierarchy of implicit surfaces Sl for l = 0, \dots, L, where SL defines the final cloud shape. A mesh representation of the final surface (via isosurface extraction) suitable for rendering with specific shaders. The model relies on a hierarchical list of particles. Each particle pi at level l stores: Position Pi: 3D coordinates on the surface S{l-1}. Radius ri: Scalar value, typically ri \approx \frac{1}{3} r{parent} \times (1 + \delta), where \delta \in [-0.3, 0.3]. Flattening ei: Scalar value, randomly chosen from [0.1, 1.0]. Local Potential Field: Implicit function values used for surface extraction and neighbor interaction. 1. Initialize Level 0 (l=0): If procedural: Generate a small number of particles randomly positioned on a horizontal plane or in a small subspace. If manual: Allow user placement to shape features (e.g., turrets). Define the initial surface S0 as the union of the implicit fields of these particles. 2. Iterate for Levels l = 1 to L: Extract Surface S{l-1}: Use a particle system to extract the isosurface of the previous level S{l-1}. This involves simulating particles that repel each other and grow to populate the available surface area of S{l-1}. Growth Logic: Particles grow until they reach a target radius or energy. If a particle grows too much or an area is uncrowded, split the particle. If an area is overcrowded, remove particles. Target Distance: Maintain a target inter-particle distance (typically twice the target particle radius) to ensure equilibrium. Place Level l Particles: Use the extracted isosurface points from the previous step as the initial positions for new particles at level l. Define Particle Properties: Set radius ri based on the parent radius r{parent}: ri = \frac{1}{3} r{parent} \times (1 + \text{random}(-0.3, 0.3)). Set flattening ei randomly from [0.1, 1.0]. Set blending parameters b and I based on level l (see Parameters). Compute Implicit Field: For each particle i at level l, compute its implicit field fi(P) (see Formulas). Combine Level: The surface Sl is defined by the maximum potential of all particles at level l and the previous level's surface: Sl = \{ P \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid \max(f{l-1}(P), \maxi fi(P)) = 1 \} (Note: The source defines fl(P) as \max(f{l-1}(P), \maxi fi(P)) implicitly by stating the surface is defined from this max.) 3. Render Final Shape (SL): Extract the mesh of SL. Apply a Gardner-like shader for view-dependent transparency near silhouettes. Apply Perlin solid texture for lower-scale details. (Optional) Apply "normal blending" shader to smooth furrows near the base surface S{L-1}. Implicit Surface Definition: Each particle i defines a surface Si: Si = \{ P \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid fi(P) = 1 \} where: fi(P) = gi(P) + hi(P) Base Shape gi(P): A flattened sphere: gi(P) = \exp \left( 1 - \frac{di}{ri (1 - ei d{l-1})} \right) di: Distance from point P to particle center Pi. ri: Radius of particle i. ei: Flattening factor for particle i. d{l-1}: Distance from point P to the previous level surface S{l-1}. Deformation Field hi(P): hi(P) = mi(P) + ni(P) + oi(P) 1. Repulsion Component mi(P): Prevents overlap and creates furrows: mi(P) = \sumj (1 - \epsilon - gj(P)) \min(1, gj^2(P)) Sum is over neighboring particles j. \epsilon: Offset parameter for repulsion strength. 2. Blending Component ni(P): Enlarges the blob near the base surface S{l-1} to prevent "popping". The source does not provide the explicit mathematical formula for ni(P), only its parameters. b: Blending amount parameter. I: Parameter adjusting the fraction of the bubble enlarged. 3. Floor Repulsion Component oi(P): Creates a flat bottom. The source does not provide the explicit mathematical formula for oi(P), only its parameters. h0: Reference height for the cloud floor. \alphah: Stiffness of repulsion for the flat bottom. Rendering Transparency t: Gardner-like shader for fuzzy layer: t = (1 - \alpha \vec{N} \cdot \vec{C})^{\alphas} \vec{N}: Local normal (gradient of the field). \vec{C}: Camera direction. \alpha: Controls thickness of the transparent margin. \alphas: Controls sharpness of the transparent margin. Normal Blending (Optional): Interpolates normals near the base surface S{l-1}: \vec{N}' = (1 - p \alphaN) \vec{N} + p \alphaN \vec{g} p: Normalized distance to the base surface (1 - \text{potential}). \vec{g}: Normalized gradient of S{l-1}. \alphaN: Controls the blending strength. | Parameter | Description | Typical Value / Range | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | \epsilon | Offset for repulsion in mi(P). Controls furrow size. | 0.5 | | b | Blending amount in ni(P). | 0 for levels 0, 1; 1.0 for level 2 | | I | Fraction of bubble enlarged in ni(P). | 10 | | h0 | Reference height for cloud floor. | 100 m | | \alphah | Stiffness of repulsion for flat bottom in oi(P). | 100 m | | ei | Flattening factor for particle i. | Randomly chosen between 0.1 and 1 | | ri | Radius of particles at level l. | \frac{1}{3} r{l-1} \times (1 \pm 0.3) | | \alpha | Transparency thickness control. | Not given in the sources. | | \alphas | Transparency sharpness control. | Not given in the sources. | | \alphaN | Normal blending strength. | Not given in the sources. | Furrows vs. Contact: Blobs should not stick together; real cloud blobs have furrows. The offset parameter \epsilon in mi(P) must be set >0 (e.g., 0.5) to repulse surfaces more than for simple contact. Level 0 Initialization: Level 0 has no previous surface S{-1}. It must be created procedurally or manually. Procedural generation on a horizontal plane may result in flat bases; manual placement allows for complex features like turrets. Particle Splitting/Removal: During the isosurface extraction for level l, particles must be split if they grow too much or if areas are uncrowded, and removed if overcrowded, to maintain a natural, non-uniform distribution. Formula Gaps: The explicit mathematical formulas for ni(P) and oi(P) are not provided in the source snippets, only their parameters and qualitative descriptions. Implementers must infer these from standard implicit blob techniques or the full paper. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def distance(p1, p2): return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def getdisttoprevsurface(P): """Returns distance from P to the previous level surface S{l-1}. In practice, this is evaluated using the potential field of level l-1.""" return 0.0 # Placeholder for actual distance field query def computebaseshape(P, particle): """Computes gi(P) = exp(1 - di / (ri (1 - ei d{l-1})))""" di = distance(P, particle['pos']) dlminus1 = getdisttoprevsurface(P) r = particle['radius'] e = particle['flattening'] denom = r (1 - e dlminus1) if abs(denom) < 1e-6: return 0.0 return math.exp(1 - di / denom) def computerepulsion(P, particle, neighbors): """Computes mi(P) = sumj (1 - epsilon - gj(P)) min(1, gj(P)^2).""" epsilon = 0.5 msum = 0.0 for neighbor in neighbors: gj = computebaseshape(P, neighbor) msum += (1 - epsilon - gj) min(1.0, gj 2) return msum def computedeformation(P, particle, neighbors): """Computes hi(P) = mi(P) + ni(P) + oi(P).""" mi = computerepulsion(P, particle, neighbors) # The explicit formulas for ni(P) and oi(P) are not provided in the sources. # ni(P) uses parameters b and I to enlarge the blob near the base surface. # oi(P) uses parameters h0 and alphah to create a flat bottom. ni = 0.0 oi = 0.0 return mi + ni + oi def computeimplicitfield(P, particle, neighbors): """Computes fi(P) = gi(P) + hi(P).""" gi = computebaseshape(P, particle) hi = computedeformation(P, particle, neighbors) return gi + hi def getneighbors(p, particles, radius): return [p2 for p2 in particles if distance(p['pos'], p2['pos']) < radius] def initializeparticlesonsurface(particlesprev): """Generates initial particles on the isosurface of the previous level.""" # In practice, samples points on the implicit surface of level l-1 return [] # Placeholder for surface sampling logic def extractisosurfacelevel(particlesprev, targetradius): """Extracts isosurface of S{l-1} using a particle system simulation.""" currentparticles = initializeparticlesonsurface(particlesprev) maxiterations = 100 for in range(maxiterations): converged = True for p in currentparticles: # Grow particle towards target radius p['radius'] += 0.1 if p['radius'] > targetradius 1.1: p['radius'] = targetradius 1.1 converged = False neighbors = getneighbors(p, currentparticles, radius=targetradius 2) # Simulate repulsion by adjusting radius based on neighbor density repulsion = computerepulsion(p['pos'], p, neighbors) if repulsion > 0.5: p['radius'] -= 0.05 else: p['radius'] += 0.05 # Split if too big or uncrowded if p['radius'] > targetradius 1.05 or len(neighbors) < 2: # Split logic: create new particles at p['pos'] with smaller radius pass # Remove if overcrowded if len(neighbors) > 10: pass # Remove particle logic if converged: break return currentparticles def rendercloud(mesh, cameradir): """Renders the final cloud mesh using Gardner-like shader and Perlin texture.""" for vertex in mesh.vertices: N = vertex.normal C = cameradir dotproduct = dot(N, C) alpha = 1.0 alphas = 2.0 transparency = (1 - alpha dotproduct) alphas textureval = 0.5 # Placeholder for Perlin noise evaluation color = (textureval, textureval, textureval) (1 - transparency) return color Time Complexity: Shape generation is recursive. Each level l requires extracting the isosurface of S{l-1} using a particle system simulation, which is iterative and depends on the number of particles and convergence criteria. The authors state that rendering and animation are fast because the model does not rely on volumetric representation or voxel discretization. Memory Complexity: Stores the hierarchy of particles. The number of particles increases with each level, but radii decrease by a factor of ~3, potentially limiting the total count if surface area coverage is maintained. Measured Performance: The authors state that rendering and animation are fast because the model does not rely on volumetric representation or voxel discretization. Specific hardware or resolution benchmarks are not given in the sources. Strengths: Realistic shapes with continuous furrows. No voxel discretization artifacts. Fast rendering due to explicit mesh/shader approach. Hierarchical structure allows for multi-scale detail. Limitations: Relies on heuristic parameters (e.g., \epsilon, b, I) which may require tuning. The explicit formulas for blending (ni) and floor repulsion (oi) are not fully provided in the source, making implementation ambiguous. Does not include volumetric rendering effects (e.g., light scattering) in the shape model itself, requiring additional shaders for realistic appearance. When to Use: When generating realistic Cumulus/Cumulonimbus cloud shapes for real-time rendering or animation where performance is critical. When explicit mesh output is desired for further processing or animation. When Not to Use: When volumetric light scattering or complex internal cloud structure is required (the model only defines shape). When exact mathematical continuity of blending/floor effects is critical and the missing formulas cannot be inferred. Origin: Proposed by Fabrice Neyret and A. Bouthors from EVASION-GRAVIR/IMAG-INRIA. Published in 2004 in the paper "Modeling Clouds Shape". History and Development: The model draws on and extends several previous approaches, including implicit surfaces [Gas93] and particle-based surface extraction [WH94, CA97]. It contrasts with explicit tessellation methods like [NND96] by using a particle system for level generation. The model is designed to be integrated with particle animation and advanced rendering, though the paper focuses on shape definition. Applications: Procedural generation of cloud shapes for computer graphics, particularly in real-time rendering and animation. name: 3D Gaussian Cloud Generation
head: Gaussian pseudo-spheroid generation
body: An algorithm for generating Cumulus (type 9) and Cumulonimbus (type 10) clouds using a sparse set of 3D Gaussian-distributed pseudo-spheroid primitives. It differs from particle-based systems by requiring significantly fewer primitives (typically 35) to achieve realistic results, and from hierarchical implicit blobs by using explicit geometric primitives with pre-processing filters to optimize rendering performance. Inputs: Cloud center C; number of primitives N (typically 35); scale constants tx, ty, tz; maximum radius R{max}; radius spread \sigmar. Outputs: List of N pseudo-spheroids, each defined by position Pi, orientation (implied by axis scaling), and radius ri. Data Structures: PseudoSpheroid: struct containing position (vec3), radius (float), mean (vec3), stddev (vec3). Parameters: N = 35. R{max}: Maximum possible radius of a sphere in the variant. \sigmar: Radius spread constant. tx, ty, tz: Scale constants for the normal distribution axes. Typical values for means and standard deviations are provided in Table 2 of the source, but exact numerical values are not listed in the text. Steps: 1. Generate Positions: For each primitive i from 1 to N: Sample a random variable \mathcal{N} with normal distribution for each axis x, y, z using the specific means and standard deviations defined for the cloud type. Calculate position Pi relative to cloud center C: Pi = C + \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma) Where \mu and \sigma are the mean and standard deviation vectors for the respective axes. Note: The source mentions using clamping similar to Huang et al. [1], but does not specify the clamp bounds. Implementation typically clamps sampled values to prevent outliers from extending the cloud too far, often within \pm 3\sigma. 2. Calculate Radii: For each primitive i: Calculate distance di from Pi to C: di = \| Pi - C \| Compute radius ri using Equation (16) for real cumulus generation: ri = R{max} \cdot e^{-\frac{di^2}{2\sigmar^2}} Where R{max} is the maximum radius and \sigmar is the radius spread constant. Note: Equation (15) is a variant, but Equation (16) is specified for the experiments shown. 3. Pre-processing Filter 1 (Hollow Cloud Removal): Identify spheroids within a specific range from the center that would create a hollow appearance. Remove approximately 20% of spheroids in the nucleus. Note: The exact range threshold is not given in the text. A direct implementation removes the innermost primitives by distance until approximately 20% are removed. 4. Pre-processing Filter 2 (Containment Removal): For every pair of spheroids A and B: Calculate distance d{AB} between centers PA and PB. Check if sphere A is inside sphere B: d{AB} + rA < rB If true, remove sphere A. Repeat for all pairs to ensure no primitive is fully contained within another. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def generate3dgaussiancloud(center, numprimitives=35, rmax=1.0, sigmar=0.5, means=None, stddevs=None): """ Generates a cloud using 3D Gaussian distributed pseudo-spheroids. Args: center: (x, y, z) tuple for cloud center C. numprimitives: Number of spheroids (typically 35). rmax: Maximum radius constant. sigmar: Radius spread constant. means: List of 3 floats (meanx, meany, meanz). Not given in sources. stddevs: List of 3 floats (stdx, stdy, stdz). Not given in sources. Returns: List of dicts with 'position' and 'radius'. """ # Use standard normal distribution if Table 2 values are not provided if means is None: means = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if stddevs is None: stddevs = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] primitives = [] # Step 1: Generate Positions for in range(numprimitives): x = random.gauss(means[0], stddevs[0]) y = random.gauss(means[1], stddevs[1]) z = random.gauss(means[2], stddevs[2]) # Apply clamping as mentioned in source (similar to Huang et al.) # Clamp bounds not specified; typical implementation uses ±3σ position = (center[0] + x, center[1] + y, center[2] + z) # Step 2: Calculate Radius dx = position[0] - center[0] dy = position[1] - center[1] dz = position[2] - center[2] distance = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Equation (16) for real cumulus generation radius = rmax math.exp(-(distance2) / (2 sigmar2)) primitives.append({ 'position': position, 'radius': radius }) # Step 3: Pre-processing Filter 1 (Hollow Cloud Removal) # Source states ~20% of nucleus spheroids are removed. # Exact range threshold is not given. # Implementation removes innermost primitives by distance. primitives.sort(key=lambda p: math.sqrt( (p['position'][0]-center[0])2 + (p['position'][1]-center[1])2 + (p['position'][2]-center[2])2)) primitives = primitives[int(0.2 len(primitives)):] # Step 4: Pre-processing Filter 2 (Containment Removal) finalprimitives = [] for i, pa in enumerate(primitives): iscontained = False for j, pb in enumerate(primitives): if i == j: continue # Check if A is inside B dx = pa['position'][0] - pb['position'][0] dy = pa['position'][1] - pb['position'][1] dz = pa['position'][2] - pb['position'][2] distab = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Condition: distance + radiusA < radiusB if distab + pa['radius'] < pb['radius']: iscontained = True break if not iscontained: finalprimitives.append(pa) return finalprimitives Complexity: The pre-processing computation (comparing radii and distances) is not a drawback due to the reduced number of spheres (e.g., 35) required in the Gaussian model. Performance: The pre-processing filter 1 yields a ~30% average improvement in frame rate without affecting the look of the cloud. Strengths: Requires significantly fewer primitives (typically 35) compared to particle systems (thousands). Limitations: Relies on specific parameter tuning (means, standard deviations) which are not fully detailed in the source. The method is part of a procedural volume cloud modeling approach for real-time GPU volumetric rendering. It builds on the concept of using 3D Gaussian distributions to model cumuliform cloud shapes, which naturally resemble normal distributions. The position generation uses clamping similar to the method by Huang et al. [1], but adapts it for explicit pseudo-spheroid primitives rather than particles. name: Query Shape Generation from Vertical Sketch
head: Vertical Sketch Query Shape Generation
body: This method generates a 3D query shape for cloud volume retrieval by extruding a user-sketched 2D vertical profile into a volume where every cross-section is an ellipsoid. It solves the problem of converting a simple 2D artistic sketch into a volumetric representation suitable for similarity matching against a pre-simulated database. It differs from its sibling Cumulonimbus and Cumulus Shape Generation by focusing on layer-cloud-like ellipsoidal cross-sections derived from a single vertical curve, rather than complex convective structures. It serves as the geometric foundation for Sketch-based Cloud Volume Retrieval via SVD, which uses this shape for database matching. Inputs: 1. User-specified cloud plane height H{plane}. 2. User-specified horizontal thickness parameter d. 3. User-sketched 2D curve representing the vertical shape of the desired clouds. Outputs: A 3D query shape defined by its horizontal thickness T(x, z) at any point (x, 0, z) in the local coordinate system. Data Structures: The method does not explicitly store a voxel grid or mesh in this generation phase; it defines the shape analytically via the thickness function T(x, z). The input sketch is treated as a set of points defining the height function h(x). Steps: 1. Generate Cloud Plane: Create a horizontal plane at the user-specified height H{plane}. 2. Sketch Input: The user sketches the vertical shape of the desired clouds as a single continuous curve on the screen. 3. Project Endpoints: Identify the start and end points of the sketched curve. Project the line segment connecting these two endpoints onto the cloud plane. 4. Create Vertical Plane: Construct a vertical plane that is perpendicular to the cloud plane and contains the projected line segment from Step 3. 5. Project Sketch: Project the user's sketched curve onto this vertical plane. 6. Define Local Coordinate System: Establish a local coordinate system (x, y, z) with the following properties: Origin: Center of the line segment connecting the endpoints of the sketched curve. x-axis: Coincides with the direction of the line segment. z-axis: Coincides with the normal vector of the cloud plane (pointing upwards). y-axis: Completes the right-handed system, perpendicular to both x and z. 7. Extract Height Function: Determine the height of the vertical shape at each x coordinate, denoted as h(x), based on the projected sketch in the local coordinate system. 8. Compute Thickness: For each point (x, 0, z) within the bounds of the shape, compute the horizontal thickness T(x, z) using the formula below. Formula: The horizontal thickness T(x, z) at a point (x, 0, z) is given by: T(x, z) = \pm d \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{z}{h(x)}\right)^2} \quad \text{for } 0 < z < h(x) Where: T(x, z) is the horizontal thickness at position x and height z. d is the user-specified parameter for horizontal thickness. h(x) is the height of the vertical shape at (x, 0, 0). The \pm indicates that the thickness extends symmetrically in the y direction (positive and negative y). Parameters: d: User-specified parameter used to adjust the horizontal thickness of the query shape. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Height: If h(x) = 0 at any point, the term \frac{z}{h(x)} becomes undefined. The formula is valid only for 0 < z < h(x). Implementers must handle points where the sketch height is zero or negative by excluding them or clamping. Boundary Conditions: The formula applies strictly within the vertical extent of the sketch. Outside this range, the thickness is zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatequeryshape(sketchpoints, cloudplanenormal, d): """ Generates a query shape from a vertical sketch. Args: sketchpoints: List of 2D points (x, yscreen) representing the user's sketch. These are assumed to be in a 2D projection space. cloudplanenormal: 3D vector representing the normal of the cloud plane. d: User-specified horizontal thickness parameter. Returns: A function or data structure representing the thickness T(x, z). For implementation, this typically involves storing h(x) and using the formula. """ # Step 1: Identify endpoints of the sketch if len(sketchpoints) < 2: raise ValueError("Sketch must have at least two points") startpoint = sketchpoints[0] endpoint = sketchpoints[-1] # Step 2: Project endpoints onto the cloud plane # Assuming the sketch is given in a 2D screen space, we need to map this to 3D. # The source implies a projection process. We assume the sketch points are already # projected onto the vertical plane or can be mapped to the local x-axis. # For simplicity, we assume the sketch defines h(x) directly along the x-axis # after projection. # Step 3: Define local coordinate system # Origin: Center of the line segment connecting start and end points # We need to map the 2D sketch to the local x-axis. # Let's assume the sketch points are ordered along the x-axis in the local system. # Extract x-coordinates and corresponding heights (y in 2D sketch becomes z in 3D) # Note: The source says "x and z axes coincide with the line segment and the normal vector". # The sketch is vertical, so the vertical dimension of the sketch maps to z. # The horizontal dimension of the sketch maps to x. # Re-map sketch points to local coordinates # Assume sketchpoints are (xsketch, zsketch) in the vertical plane localxcoords = [p[0] for p in sketchpoints] localzcoords = [p[1] for p in sketchpoints] # Find the center of the line segment in the local x-z plane # The line segment connects the first and last points of the sketch # Project this segment onto the cloud plane (which is horizontal, so z=constant) # The projection of the segment onto the cloud plane defines the x-axis direction. # The source says "x axis coincides with the line segment". # So the x-axis is along the chord of the sketch. # Calculate the vector of the line segment dx = endpoint[0] - startpoint[0] dz = endpoint[1] - startpoint[1] # The length of the segment segmentlength = (dx2 + dz2)0.5 # If the segment is degenerate, handle error if segmentlength == 0: raise ValueError("Start and end points are identical") # Define the local x-axis unit vector along the segment # However, the source says "x axis coincides with the line segment". # This implies the x-axis is rotated to align with the segment. # For simplicity, we can assume the sketch is already aligned or we rotate it. # Let's assume we rotate the sketch so that the segment lies on the x-axis. # Rotation angle angle = atan2(dz, dx) # Rotate sketch points to align segment with x-axis rotatedpoints = [] for p in sketchpoints: # Translate to origin px = p[0] - startpoint[0] pz = p[1] - startpoint[1] # Rotate rx = px cos(angle) + pz sin(angle) rz = -px sin(angle) + pz cos(angle) rotatedpoints.append((rx, rz)) # Shift origin to center of the segment # The segment goes from (0,0) to (segmentlength, 0) in rotated coords centerx = segmentlength / 2 centerz = 0 finalpoints = [] for p in rotatedpoints: fx = p[0] - centerx fz = p[1] - centerz finalpoints.append((fx, fz)) # Now, finalpoints are in local coordinates (x, z) # The x-axis is along the segment, z-axis is vertical (normal to cloud plane) # Step 4: Extract height function h(x) # h(x) is the maximum z value for a given x? Or the z value of the curve? # The source says "h(x) represents the height of the vertical shape at (x, 0, 0)". # This implies the sketch defines the boundary. # Since it's a single curve, h(x) is the z-coordinate of the curve at x. # However, a single curve might not be a function h(x) if it folds. # We assume the sketch is monotonic in x or we take the envelope. # For simplicity, we assume h(x) is the z-value of the curve. # Create a lookup for h(x) # Sort points by x finalpoints.sort(key=lambda p: p[0]) # Interpolate h(x) for any x def geth(x): # Find the two points surrounding x for i in range(len(finalpoints) - 1): x1, z1 = finalpoints[i] x2, z2 = finalpoints[i+1] if x1 <= x <= x2: # Linear interpolation if x2 == x1: return z1 t = (x - x1) / (x2 - x1) return z1 + t (z2 - z1) return 0.0 # Outside bounds # Step 5: Compute thickness T(x, z) def getthickness(x, z): hx = geth(x) if hx <= 0: return 0.0 if z <= 0 or z >= hx: return 0.0 # Formula: T(x, z) = +/- d sqrt(1 - (z/h(x))^2) term = 1 - (z / hx)2 if term < 0: return 0.0 return d (term0.5) return getthickness Sketch-based Cloud Volume Retrieval via SVD is a method for retrieving realistic 3D cloud volumes from a pre-simulated database by matching a user-sketched 2D shape to 3D data using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) basis vectors for efficient similarity calculation. It differs from direct voxel comparison by projecting both the query and database volumes into a low-dimensional subspace, reducing the computational cost of similarity search from proportional to the total number of voxels M to proportional to the number of basis vectors K. This method builds on Query Shape Generation from Vertical Sketch by converting the generated query shape into a volumetric representation suitable for database matching. Time and Memory Complexity: The generation of the query shape itself is O(N) where N is the number of points in the sketch, as it involves simple geometric projections and evaluations of the thickness formula. The memory complexity is low, storing only the sketch points and the parameter d. The subsequent retrieval process using SVD has a complexity proportional to the number of basis vectors K, which is much smaller than the total number of voxels M. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics for the shape generation step are not provided in the sources. However, the SVD-based retrieval process reduces storage cost to 84% of the original and accelerates retrieval. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; allows intuitive user input via sketching; generates smooth ellipsoidal cross-sections suitable for layer clouds. Limitations: Limited to shapes that can be represented by a single vertical curve; assumes ellipsoidal cross-sections which may not fit all cloud types; requires a pre-simulated database for retrieval. When to Use: Use this method when the user wants to quickly generate a cloud volume shape for layer clouds (e.g., Stratus, Altostratus) using a simple 2D sketch and intends to retrieve a similar volume from a database. When Not to Use: Do not use this method for convective clouds (e.g., Cumulonimbus) which require more complex shapes. Do not use it if a direct volumetric generation without database retrieval is required. This method was introduced in the context of a sketch-based system for cloud volume retrieval from simulated datasets for realistic image synthesis. It is part of a pipeline that allows users to interactively specify cloud shapes and retrieve realistic volumes from a database. The method relies on the assumption that cloud cross-sections can be approximated by ellipsoids. name: Sketch-based Cloud Volume Retrieval via SVD
head: SVD-based Cloud Retrieval
body: Sketch-based Cloud Volume Retrieval via SVD is a method for retrieving realistic 3D cloud volumes from a pre-simulated database by matching a user-sketched 2D shape to 3D data using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) basis vectors for efficient similarity calculation. It differs from direct voxel comparison by projecting both the query and database volumes into a low-dimensional subspace, reducing the computational cost of similarity search from proportional to the total number of voxels M to proportional to the number of basis vectors K. This method builds on Query Shape Generation from Vertical Sketch by converting the generated query shape into a volumetric representation suitable for database matching. Inputs: 1. User sketch of the cloud bottom shape on a 2D screen. 2. User-specified height for the cloud bottom. 3. A database of pre-simulated 3D cloud volumes, each normalized to a 20 \times 20 \times 20 grid. 4. Pre-computed SVD basis vectors uk derived from the database volumes. Outputs: 1. The 3D cloud volume data from the database with the smallest similarity score to the query shape. Data Structures: Cloud Plane Grid: A 2D uniform grid representing the cloud bottom plane. Each cell stores a distance value obtained from a distance transform. Initial Query Volume (D0): A 3D uniform grid (bounding box of the query shape) where each cell contains a binary value: 1 if inside the query shape, 0 otherwise. Query Vector (x0): A 1D vector containing the voxel values of D0. Basis Vectors (uk): Pre-computed vectors representing the principal components of the database volumes. Database Volumes (Dn): Normalized to a 20 \times 20 \times 20 grid. Parameters: K: The number of basis vectors used for SVD approximation. In experiments, K = M/114, where M is the total number of voxels in the volume data. M: The total number of voxels in the volume data (e.g., 20^3 = 8000 for the normalized grid). Steps: 1. Generate Cloud Plane: The user specifies the height of the cloud bottom. The system generates a horizontal plane (cloud plane) at that height. 2. Grid Subdivision: The cloud plane is subdivided into a uniform 2D grid. 3. Project Sketch: The user sketches the shape of the cloud bottom on the screen. This 2D shape is projected onto the cloud plane grid. 4. Binary Mask Creation: For each grid point on the cloud plane, assign a value of 1 if the point is inside the projected shape, and 0 otherwise, creating a binary image. 5. Distance Transform: Apply a distance transform to the binary image to compute the Euclidean distance from each grid point to the boundary of the projected shape. 6. Query Shape Height Generation: Create the 3D query shape by assuming the cloud height at each grid point (x, y) equals the distance value obtained from the distance transform at that point. 7. Bounding Box and Volume Creation: Create a bounding box for the query shape. Subdivide this bounding box into a uniform 3D grid to form the initial query volume D0. Assign 1 to grid points inside the shape and 0 to points outside. 8. Vectorization: Represent the initial query volume D0 as a vector x0 of voxel values. 9. SVD Approximation of Query: Approximate x0 as a linear combination of the K pre-computed SVD basis vectors uk: x0 \approx \sum{k=1}^{K} w{k0} uk where w{k0} are the projection coefficients. 10. Calculate Query Coefficients: Compute the coefficients w{k0} for the query vector: w{k0} = x0 \cdot uk where \cdot denotes the dot product. 11. Retrieve Database Volumes: For each cloud volume Dn in the database: a. Represent Dn as a vector xn. b. Compute the pre-calculated coefficients w{nk} for Dn (assuming these are pre-computed or computed on the fly): w{nk} = xn \cdot uk c. Calculate the approximate similarity score: scoren \approx \sum{k=1}^{K} (w{k0} - w{nk})^2. 12. Select Best Match: Extract the volume data from the database with the smallest similarity score scoren and display it to the user. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def retrievecloudvolume(usersketchpoints, cloudbottomheight, databasevolumes, basisvectors): """ usersketchpoints: List of 2D coordinates (x, y) defining the user's sketch. cloudbottomheight: Float, the height of the cloud bottom plane. databasevolumes: List of 3D arrays (volumes), each normalized to 20x20x20. basisvectors: List of 1D arrays (vectors), pre-computed SVD basis vectors. Returns: The best matching 3D volume from the database. """ # Step 1-2: Define Cloud Plane Grid # Assuming a fixed resolution for the cloud plane grid for this example. # In practice, this resolution should be sufficient to capture the sketch details. gridresolution = 64 cloudplanegrid = create2dgrid(gridresolution, gridresolution) # Step 3-4: Project Sketch and Create Binary Mask # Project usersketchpoints onto the cloud plane grid. # Create a binary mask where 1 is inside the shape, 0 is outside. binarymask = projectsketchtogrid(usersketchpoints, cloudplanegrid) # Step 5: Distance Transform # Compute distance from each grid point to the boundary. distancemap = applydistancetransform(binarymask) # Step 6-7: Create Query Shape and Initial Query Volume D0 # The query shape height at each (x,y) is the distance value. # Create a bounding box for this shape. # Subdivide bounding box into a uniform 3D grid. # Assign 1 if inside, 0 if outside. queryvolumeD0 = createqueryvolumefromdistancemap(distancemap) # Step 8: Vectorize D0 x0 = flattentovector(queryvolumeD0) # Step 9-10: Calculate Query Coefficients wk0 K = len(basisvectors) wk0 = [] for k in range(K): uk = basisvectors[k] # wk0 = x0. uk wk0.append(dotproduct(x0, uk)) # Step 11: Calculate Similarity Scores for Database Volumes bestscore = infinity bestvolume = None for volume in databasevolumes: # Vectorize database volume xn = flattentovector(volume) # Calculate coefficients wnk for this volume # Note: In a real system, these might be pre-computed and stored. wnk = [] for k in range(K): uk = basisvectors[k] wnk.append(dotproduct(xn, uk)) # Calculate approximate similarity score score = 0.0 for k in range(K): diff = wk0[k] - wnk[k] score += diff diff # Step 12: Select Best Match if score < bestscore: bestscore = score bestvolume = volume return bestvolume def create2dgrid(resx, resy): """Creates a 2D grid structure.""" return [[0 for in range(resy)] for in range(resx)] def projectsketchtogrid(sketchpoints, grid): """ Projects 2D sketch points onto the grid and fills the interior. Returns a binary mask. """ # Implementation depends on the specific projection and filling algorithm. # A common approach is to rasterize the polygon defined by sketchpoints. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a standard polygon fill algorithm. mask = create2dgrid(len(grid), len(grid[0])) #... rasterize sketchpoints into mask... return mask def applydistancetransform(binarymask): """ Applies a distance transform to a binary mask. Returns a grid of distances. """ # Implementation of Euclidean Distance Transform. #... return distancemap def createqueryvolumefromdistancemap(distancemap): """ Creates a 3D query volume D0 based on the distance map. The height of the cloud at each (x,y) is the distance value. The volume is binary (1 inside, 0 outside) within a bounding box. """ # Determine bounding box from the extent of the distance map. # Create a 3D grid for the bounding box. # For each (x,y) in the distance map, the height z goes from 0 to distancemap[x][y]. # Fill the volume with 1s in this range, 0s outside. #... return D0 def flattentovector(volume3d): """Flattens a 3D array into a 1D vector.""" return [voxel for layer in volume3d for row in layer for voxel in row] def dotproduct(v1, v2): """Computes the dot product of two vectors.""" return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Insufficient Database Size: If the database size is insufficient to cover the shape space, generated clouds may not perfectly match the user's sketch. Precision: The approximation using SVD basis vectors introduces error. The exact similarity score is |x0 - xn|^2, while the approximate score is \sum{k=1}^{K} (w{k0} - w{nk})^2. The error depends on K. Boundary Conditions: The distance transform and projection must handle the boundaries of the sketch and the grid correctly to ensure accurate query shape generation. Time Complexity: The similarity calculation cost using SVD is proportional to K, whereas direct voxel comparison is proportional to M. With K = M/114, the computational cost is reduced by a factor of 114. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the database volumes and the pre-computed SVD basis vectors. The database volumes are normalized to a 20 \times 20 \times 20 grid. Measured Performance: In experiments, the method was used to retrieve clouds from databases of size 137 (from a 96 \times 96 \times 128 simulation grid) and 83 (from a 256 \times 128 \times 128 simulation grid). Strengths: Efficient retrieval due to dimensionality reduction via SVD. Allows for intuitive user input via sketching. Limitations: Relies on the diversity and size of the pre-simulated database. May not perfectly match user sketches if the database is small. When to Use: When real-time or near-real-time retrieval of realistic cloud volumes is needed from a fixed set of pre-simulated data, and user input is sketch-based. When Not to Use: When the desired cloud shape is not represented in the database, or when high-fidelity, non-database-driven procedural generation is required. The method was proposed by as part of a sketch-based system for cloud volume retrieval from a simulated dataset for realistic image synthesis. It builds on the idea that cumulus/cumulonimbus clouds have characteristic features: a flat bottom on a plane at a certain height, and vertical thickness larger around the center than the boundary. The system was used in Autodesk Maya 2016 for rendering final images. The database was constructed by simulating dynamic cumulus clouds using computational fluid dynamics. A sketch-based system for cloud volume retrieval from simulated dataset for realistic image synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1145/2817675.2817690, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Baked Cloud Density and AO Sampling
head: 3D Worley cell volume rendering, Baked Density and AO Sampling, Direct 3D Weather Volume Rendering with Analytical SDF, Direct 3D weather volume model, Minimal Cloud Density Function Optimization, calculateCloudDensityMinimal
body: This method replaces procedural noise evaluation with precomputed 3D volume textures containing analytical cloud density and Signed Distance Fields (SDF) derived from tileable 3D Worley cells. It solves the performance bottleneck of real-time procedural cloud rendering by baking physical density and local Ambient Occlusion (AO) into a 3D texture, allowing raymarchers to sample data directly. Unlike its siblings that rely on multi-octave 2D heightmaps or procedural turbulence, this approach uses horizontal tiling and full advection support for efficient space skipping. The method consists of two phases: Baking (precomputation) and Raymarching (runtime sampling). Inputs: Weather map coordinates, world scale (props.worldScale), cellular frequency (freq = 4.0), horizontal tile count (uCloudVolumeTiles = 4.0). Outputs: A 3D volume texture where: Alpha channel (A) stores analytical physical density. Blue channel (B) stores the 3D SDF. (Note: mentions baseAlbedo and baseDensity channels for density, and B channel for shadow transmittance/AO. The primary density/SDF bake uses Alpha for density and Blue for SDF.) 3D Volume Texture: Stores density and SDF. Layout is not explicitly defined beyond channel usage (Alpha for density, Blue for SDF). Properties (props): Contains worldScale. uCloudVolumeTiles = 4.0: Governs 3D horizontal texture coordinate wrapping. freq = 4.0: Cellular frequency used for SDF scaling. SDF Multiplier = 0.4: Conservative multiplier applied to d3d in sphere tracing step size computation. Max Step Cap = 2000.0 props.worldScale: Maximum skip step size per iteration. The baking process evaluates analytical functions and writes them to the 3D texture. 1. Evaluate Analytical Cloud 3D: Call getAnalyticalCloud3D at each voxel position. This function evaluates: Tileable 3D Worley cells. 3D SDF. Physical density with vertical layer boundaries. 2. Scale SDF: Inside getAnalyticalCloud3D, divide the cellular SDF value (cellsdf) by the cellular frequency (freq = 4.0) to match meters correctly. SDF{scaled} = \frac{cell\sdf}{4.0} 3. Write to Texture: In cloud3dvolumebake.comp: Write the analytical density to the texture's Alpha channel. Write the 3D SDF to the texture's Blue channel. During rendering, the raymarcher queries the precomputed 3D texture. 1. Query SDF: Call getCloud3DSDF to query the precomputed 3D texture SDF with internal advection support. Continuity: Do not apply a distY > 100.0 props.worldScale threshold check. This ensures a mathematically continuous distance field across the entire domain. 2. Compute Step Size: Calculate the sphere tracing step size using the queried SDF (d3d): step = \max(baseStepSize, 0.4 \times d3d) Apply a cap: step = min(step, 2000.0 props.worldScale). 3. Advance Ray: If outside the cloud mass (d3d > 0.0), advance the ray by step. This skips directly to the exact boundary of the cloud mass. If inside the cloud mass, use baseStepSize or appropriate internal step size. 4. Sample Density: Read the precomputed physical density and local AO directly from the 3D volume texture (Alpha channel). Bypass old multi-octave 2D-based heightmap evaluation in calculateCloudDensity and calculateCloudDensityMinimal. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakecloudvolume(texture, props): """ Bakes analytical density and SDF into a 3D texture. texture: 3D image buffer (RGBA) props: object containing worldScale """ freq = 4.0 uCloudVolumeTiles = 4.0 for x, y, z in texture.dimensions(): # 1. Evaluate analytical cloud properties density, cellsdf = getanalyticalcloud3d(x, y, z, props, freq, uCloudVolumeTiles) # 2. Scale SDF to match meters sdfscaled = cellsdf / freq # 3. Write to texture # Alpha channel: Density texture[x, y, z].a = density # Blue channel: SDF texture[x, y, z].b = sdfscaled def getanalyticalcloud3d(x, y, z, props, freq, uCloudVolumeTiles): """ Evaluates tileable 3D Worley cells, SDF, and physical density. Returns (density, cellsdf) """ # Evaluate Worley cells and SDF based on x, y, z # Apply horizontal tiling using uCloudVolumeTiles # Apply vertical layer boundaries # Return raw cellsdf and calculated density pass def raymarchcloud(rayorigin, raydirection, texture, props): """ Raymarches through the baked cloud volume using SDF space skipping. """ baseStepSize = 10.0 # Example base step maxStepCap = 2000.0 props.worldScale sdfmultiplier = 0.4 t = 0.0 color = vec3(0.0) while t < MAXDISTANCE: # 1. Query SDF from texture (with advection) # Note: No distY threshold check is applied here pos = rayorigin + raydirection t d3d = getcloud3dsdf(pos, texture) # 2. Compute step size step = max(baseStepSize, sdfmultiplier d3d) step = min(step, maxStepCap) # 3. Advance ray t += step # 4. Sample density and AO # Read from Alpha channel (density) and potentially other channels for AO density = texture[pos].a ao = texture[pos].b # Or separate AO channel if stored differently # Accumulate color/transmittance based on density and AO #... if density < THRESHOLD: break return color def getcloud3dsdf(pos, texture): """ Queries the precomputed 3D texture SDF. No distY > 100.0 worldScale check is performed. """ # Sample texture at pos return texture[pos].b Visual Distortion: Caused by missing steps during camera movement. Resolved by succinct stepping that skips directly to the exact boundary of the cloud mass using max(baseStepSize, d3d). Viewpoint-dependent Banding: Caused by non-continuous SDF domains or overshooting boundaries due to noise domain warping and non-linear height gradients. Eliminated by: 1. Removing the distY > 100.0 props.worldScale threshold check in getCloud3DSDF. 2. Using a conservative 0.4 multiplier on d3d and a 2000.0 props.worldScale cap on step size. SDF Scaling: Incorrect meter matching if cellsdf is not divided by freq = 4.0. Performance: Massive performance gains compared to procedural evaluation because it samples precomputed data instead of evaluating noise and density. Memory: Requires storage for a 3D volume texture containing density and SDF. Strengths: Efficient space skipping, continuous SDF domain, elimination of viewpoint-dependent banding. Limitations: Requires baking phase; less flexible than procedural methods for dynamic changes not covered by advection. This method was introduced in a pull request by ricecake (via Jules) in July 2026, transitioning the volumetric cloud rendering system from a 2D weather/SDF-based model to a direct 3D weather volume model. It was further enhanced to include precomputed density, 3D AO, and shadow transmittance. It is used in the boidsish project. Transition cloud rendering to a direct 3D weather volume density and SDF model, https://github.com/ricecake/boidsish/pull/673, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Enhance volumetric clouds system with precomputed density, 3D AO and shadow transmittance, https://github.com/ricecake/boidsish/pull/708, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Atmospheric Height Gradient
head: Cloud Type Vertical Profile, GetDensityHeightGradientForPoint, GetGradientHeightFactor, Height Density Gradient, Vertical Density Profile Gradient
body: The Atmospheric Height Gradient method defines the vertical density profile for volumetric cloud layers based on cloud type (Stratus, Cumulus, Cumulonimbus, Cirrus), creating bell-shaped or plateau-shaped density distributions relative to atmosphere thickness. Inputs: altitude: Vertical position of the evaluation point in kilometers. cloudtype: Identifier for the cloud layer type (integer 0–2 or string literal). layerbounds: bottomAltitudeKm and topAltitudeKm for the specific cloud type. cloudtypeparams: Shape parameters timewidthup, starttimeup, and starttimedown. Outputs: densitygradient: Scalar vertical shape factor (typically 0.0 to 1.2). Data Structures: The method uses a preset structure CloudAltitudeLayer with fields bottomAltitudeKm (number), topAltitudeKm (number), coverage (number), densityMultiplier (number), and precipitationFactor (number). Parameters: Presets define base altitude bounds and shape parameters per cloud type: | Cloud Type | Bottom (km) | Top (km) | timewidthup | starttimeup | starttimedown | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Stratus | 1.0 | 2.2 | 0.08 | 0.08 | 0.2 | | Cumulus | 1.5 | 4.5 | 0.14 | 0.1 | 0.5 | | Cumulonimbus | 1.2 | 9.0 | 0.2 | 0.10 | 0.7 | | Cirrus | 7.0 | 10.5 | Not given in the sources. | Not given in the sources. | Not given in the sources. | Steps: 1. Boundary Check: If altitude < bottomAltitudeKm or altitude > topAltitudeKm, return 0.0. 2. Normalized Height: Calculate height fraction h = (\text{altitude} - \text{bottomAltitudeKm}) / (\text{topAltitudeKm} - \text{bottomAltitudeKm}). 3. Cloud Type Selection: Determine gradient logic based on cloudtype. In one implementation, cloudtype is derived from weatherdata.z where z < 0.1 yields 0 (Stratus), z > 0.9 yields 2 (Cumulonimbus), otherwise 1 (Cumulus). 4. Gradient Calculation: Compute the density gradient using the selected type-specific formula. Formulas: Two distinct implementations exist in the sources. Implementation A (Sine-based with linear ramps): If altitude < starttimeup, densitygradient = 0.0. If starttimeup <= altitude < starttimeup + timewidthup: \text{factor} = \frac{2.0 \cdot \pi}{2.0 \cdot \text{timewidthup}} \text{density\gradient} = 0.5 \cdot \sin(\text{factor} \cdot \text{altitude} - \frac{\pi}{2.0} - \text{factor} \cdot \text{starttimeup}) + 0.5 If starttimeup + timewidthup <= altitude < starttimedown, densitygradient = 1.0. If starttimedown <= altitude < starttimedown + timewidthup: \text{factor} = \frac{2.0 \cdot \pi}{2.0 \cdot \text{timewidthup}} \text{density\gradient} = 0.5 \cdot \sin(\text{factor} \cdot \text{altitude} - \frac{\pi}{2.0} - \text{factor} \cdot (\text{starttimedown} + \text{timewidthup})) + 0.5 If altitude >= starttimedown + timewidthup, densitygradient = 0.0. Implementation B (Normalized Height Fraction): Stratus: \text{density\gradient} = \sin(h \cdot \pi) \cdot 0.9. Cumulus: \text{density\gradient} = \sin(h^{0.7} \cdot \pi). Cumulonimbus: If h > 0.8, return 1.2; else return 0.6 + 0.4 \cdot \sin(h \cdot \pi). Cirrus: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: The following implements Implementation B, which is self-contained and uses normalized height fraction: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeverticalprofile(altitudekm: float, cloudtype: str) -> float: """Computes the vertical density gradient for a given cloud type and altitude.""" presets = { 'stratus': {'bottom': 1.0, 'top': 2.2}, 'cumulus': {'bottom': 1.5, 'top': 4.5}, 'cumulonimbus': {'bottom': 1.2, 'top': 9.0}, 'cirrus': {'bottom': 7.0, 'top': 10.5} } if cloudtype not in presets: return 0.0 layer = presets[cloudtype] bottom = layer['bottom'] top = layer['top'] if altitudekm < bottom or altitudekm > top: return 0.0 heightfraction = (altitudekm - bottom) / (top - bottom) if cloudtype == 'stratus': return math.sin(heightfraction math.pi) 0.9 elif cloudtype == 'cumulus': return math.sin(math.pow(heightfraction, 0.7) math.pi) elif cloudtype == 'cumulonimbus': if heightfraction > 0.8: return 1.2 else: return 0.6 + 0.4 math.sin(heightfraction math.pi) elif cloudtype == 'cirrus': # Specific formula not provided in the source code snippet return 0.0 else: return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When altitude is very close to bottom or top, floating-point errors might cause the normalized height to be slightly outside [0, 1]. The boundary check in Step 1 handles this by returning 0.0. Degenerate Input: If bottom equals top, division by zero occurs in the normalized height calculation. Creates a 3D envelope for layer clouds that does not touch boundaries, using independent low-frequency random height fields for top and bottom surfaces to prevent coherent tilting, and local thickness variation for natural dilution. Steps: 1. Get profile parameters: centerz, halfheight, topwobble, bottomwobble, thicknessvariation,, = layershapeprofile(typeid). 2. Calculate local half-height with thickness noise: localhalfheight = halfheight (0.84 + thicknessvariation thicknessnoise). 3. Calculate top surface: top = centerz + localhalfheight + (topsurfacenoise - 0.5) topwobble 2.0. 4. Calculate bottom surface: bottom = centerz - localhalfheight + (bottomsurfacenoise - 0.5) bottomwobble 2.0. 5. Calculate feather width: feather = np.clip(localhalfheight 0.24, 0.045, 0.16). 6. Calculate rise and fall using smoothstep: rise = smoothstep((z - bottom) / feather), fall = 1.0 - smoothstep((z - top) / feather). 7. Return clipped product: return np.clip(rise fall, 0.0, 1.0). Pitfall: Thickness noise amplitude is limited to ensure the top surface remains above the bottom surface everywhere. Time Complexity: O(1) per point evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) for preset lookup. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Analytically defined, allows easy variation of cloud types via parameters. Limitations: Does not account for horizontal variations or noise; vertical profile is static beyond cloud type selection. When to use: When rendering volumetric clouds with distinct vertical structures for different cloud types. When not to use: When horizontal variation or dynamic weather changes are required within a single cloud layer. The Atmospheric Height Gradient method originates from implementations of realtime volumetric cloud rendering, specifically in the context of procedural cloud parameterization. It is used to define the vertical density falloff for different cloud types, ensuring realistic vertical structures such as flat Stratus, fluffy Cumulus, and towering Cumulonimbus. The method is found in open-source projects such as erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes and nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl. erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, https://github.com/erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, https://github.com/nff747/volumetric-clouds-wgsl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, https://github.com/mingtu149411/Noise-Cloud, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

body: Cloud Configuration Parameters provide a structured set of inputs to control density generation, spatial bounds, lighting interaction, and rendering quality for procedural volumetric clouds. This method acts as the central data hub, passing configuration to Volumetric Cloud Raymarching for integration and Procedural Volume Cloud Modeling for noise generation. Inputs consist of physical constants, scene geometry bounds, and rendering quality flags. Outputs are validated configuration structures passed to the rendering pipeline or volume generation algorithm. Scheme A: Shader Uniforms (CloudConfig) Defined in, this structure maps directly to GPU uniforms. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. pub struct CloudConfig { pub cloudtype: f32, // 0=stratus, 0.5=stratocumulus, 1=cumulus pub coveragemultiplier: f32, pub winddirection: [f32; 3], pub windspeed: f32, pub cloudcolor: [f32; 3], pub innersphereradius: f32, pub outersphereradius: f32, pub sphereyoffset: f32, pub maxrenderdistance: f32, pub cloudtopoffset: f32, pub weathertexturescale: f32, pub basenoisescale: f32, pub highfrequencynoisescale: f32, pub highfrequencynoiseuvscale: f32, pub highfrequencynoisehscale: f32, pub quality: CloudQuality, // Low / Medium / High } Scheme B: Volume Generation Dataclass Defined in, this frozen dataclass controls the deterministic generation of volume masks. name: Cloud Mesh Generation
body: Cloud Mesh Generation constructs a planar mesh from a procedural voxel grid by identifying contiguous regions of cloud data. It differs from Procedural Volume Rendering with Noise Perturbation by outputting explicit geometry rather than shader-based volume textures, and from Chunk Generation with Base Terrain by targeting horizontal atmospheric layers. Inputs: WORLDAREA: The total spatial extent of the cloud field in world units. CHUNKSIZE: The resolution of the voxel grid per chunk. CLOUDHEIGHT: The fixed Y-coordinate for cloud rendering. worldvoxels: A 3D boolean or integer array representing the world state. Outputs: A list of vertex positions and an index buffer representing the generated cloud mesh. Data Structures: clouddata: A 1D array of size WORLDAREA CHUNKSIZE 2 storing binary cloud presence (1 for cloud, 0 for void). visited: A boolean array of the same size tracking processed cells to prevent duplicate mesh generation. Steps: 1. Voxelization: Initialize clouddata. Iterate x and z over world dimensions. If noise2(0.13 x, 0.13 z) < 0.2, skip. Otherwise, set clouddata[idx] = 1. 2. Mesh Construction: Iterate z and x. If clouddata[idx] is 0 or idx in visited, skip. 3. X-Strip Detection: Find continuous quads along X: increment xcount while clouddata is 1 and not visited. 4. Z-Strip Detection: Find continuous quads along Z for each X in the strip: store zcount in zcountlist. 5. Primitive Generation: Generate geometric primitives (quads or triangles) covering the identified rectangular regions at CLOUDHEIGHT. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatecloudmesh(worldarea, chunksize, cloudheight): griddim = worldarea chunksize totalcells = worldarea chunksize chunksize clouddata = [0] totalcells visited = [False] totalcells vertices = [] indices = [] # 1. Voxelization for x in range(griddim): for z in range(griddim): idx = x griddim + z if noise2(0.13 x, 0.13 z) < 0.2: continue clouddata[idx] = 1 # 2. Mesh Construction for z in range(griddim): for x in range(griddim): idx = x griddim + z if clouddata[idx] == 0 or visited[idx]: continue visited[idx] = True xcount = 0 currx = x while currx < griddim and clouddata[currx griddim + z] == 1 and not visited[currx griddim + z]: visited[currx griddim + z] = True xcount += 1 currx += 1 zcountlist = [] for dx in range(xcount): currz = z zcount = 0 while currz < griddim and clouddata[(x + dx) griddim + currz] == 1 and not visited[(x + dx) griddim + currz]: visited[(x + dx) griddim + currz] = True zcount += 1 currz += 1 zcountlist.append(zcount) # Generate quads for the detected strip for dx in range(xcount): zcount = zcountlist[dx] x1, x2 = x + dx, x + dx + 1 z1, z2 = z, z + zcount v0 = [x1, cloudheight, z1] v1 = [x2, cloudheight, z1] v2 = [x2, cloudheight, z2] v3 = [x1, cloudheight, z2] vertices.extend([v0, v1, v2, v3]) indices.extend([len(vertices)-4, len(vertices)-3, len(vertices)-2]) indices.extend([len(vertices)-4, len(vertices)-2, len(vertices)-1]) return vertices, indices def noise2(x, y): # Simple deterministic hash for procedural noise return (x 12.9898 + y 78.233) % 1.0 Parameters: Noise scale: 0.13. Density threshold: 0.2. Cloud Height: Fixed Y-coordinate. Edge Cases: Precision: Noise function evaluation must be deterministic across voxelization and rendering passes. Boundaries: Loop conditions must clamp to griddim to prevent out-of-bounds array access during strip detection. A technique to 'inflate' a mesh from a point cloud by applying a scalar to the inside/outside values. A pipeline for generating high-quality artifact-free volumetric and surface meshes from random noise or a reference image without postprocessing. It uses a two-level hybrid approach: a diffusion model for global shape synthesis on voxels, and a neural network plus optimization for mesh deformation and quality control. The pipeline consists of three modules: (1) Voxel generation with diffusion models to get an initial synthesis result; (2) Voxel division to convert the voxel representation into a tetrahedral mesh template; (3) Physically correct mesh deformation using a voxel-conditional neural closest point predictor and regularized projection to add details and ensure quality. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) where W, H are grid dimensions, due to single-pass voxelization and linear strip traversal. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the clouddata and visited arrays. Strengths: Reduces overdraw compared to ray-marching; allows standard rasterization pipelines and GPU instancing. Originating from procedural generation techniques in voxel-based games, this method adapts chunk-based terrain meshing for atmospheric effects. The reference implementation uses a noise-based threshold to determine cloud presence, mapping 2D noise to a planar mesh. name: Ellipsoid Fitting and Rotation for Cloud Meshes
head: Cloud Generation from 3D Meshes, Mesh Decimation and Ellipsoid Smoothing, Mesh-to-Ellipsoid conversion, Rodrigues' Rotation Formula for Cloud Geometry, Triangle-based ellipsoid cloud generation
body: This method converts high-resolution 3D meshes (e.g., from Blender or Maya) into volumetric cloud geometry by replacing triangle faces with fitted ellipsoids. It solves the problem of rendering complex, organic shapes in real-time by decimating the input mesh and approximating its surface with smooth primitives. Unlike raw mesh rendering, this approach acts as a real-time filter that produces softer, cumuliform shapes suitable for smoke and cloud simulation. It builds on Cloud Mesh Generation by providing the specific geometric fitting and optimization steps required to transform discrete triangles into continuous volumetric primitives. Inputs: A decimated 3D mesh consisting of N triangles, where each triangle has vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. Outputs: A set of ellipsoid parameters (center, radii, rotation matrix) for each triangle, ready for GPU rendering. Data Structures: Triangle: Struct containing three 3D vertex coordinates \mathbf{v}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. Ellipsoid: Struct containing: Center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 Radii (a, b, c) \in \mathbb{R}^3 Rotation Matrix \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} Steps: 1. Mesh Decimation: Reduce the input mesh to 300–700 triangles (or \le 1000) to ensure real-time performance. A decimation rate of 80–95% is acceptable. 2. Barycenter Calculation: For each triangle, compute the barycenter \mathbf{B}: \mathbf{B} = \frac{\mathbf{v}1 + \mathbf{v}2 + \mathbf{v}3}{3} \quad \text{(Eq. 22)} 3. Scaling: Scale the triangle vertices relative to the barycenter using a scale factor s. The factor s typically falls in the range (0.1, 2]. The scaled vertices \mathbf{v}'i are calculated as: \mathbf{v}'i = \mathbf{B} + s(\mathbf{v}i - \mathbf{B}) \quad \text{(Eq. 23, 24)} 4. Radii Determination: Calculate the maximum distance from the barycenter to any scaled vertex. This distance defines the maximum radius of the circumscribing ellipsoid. The radii (a, b, c) are derived from this maximum extent. 5. Rotation Optimization: Align the ellipsoid's maximum radius with the direction of the maximum distance from the barycenter to the triangle vertices to produce a softer shape. This uses Rodrigues' Rotation Formula: Axis and Angle: Calculate the rotation axis \mathbf{k} and angle \theta using cross and dot products of the relevant direction vectors: \mathbf{k} = \frac{\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u} \times \mathbf{v}\|}, \quad \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{\mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{u}\| \|\mathbf{v}\|}\right) \quad \text{(Eq. 27, 28)} (Note: \mathbf{u} and \mathbf{v} represent the initial and target direction vectors for alignment.) Skew-Symmetric Matrix: Compute matrix \mathbf{A} corresponding to the axis vector \mathbf{x} (where \mathbf{x} is the normalized rotation axis): \mathbf{A} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -xz & xy \\ xz & 0 & -xx \\ -xy & xx & 0 \end{bmatrix} \quad \text{(Eq. 30)} Rotation Matrix: Calculate \mathbf{R} using the exponential map (Rodrigues' formula): \mathbf{R} = \mathbf{I} + (\sin \theta)\mathbf{A} + (1 - \cos \theta)\mathbf{A}^2 \quad \text{(Eq. 29)} 6. GPU Transfer: Pre-calculate formulas (1)–(3) on the CPU. Only the final rotation matrix \mathbf{R} and ellipsoid parameters are passed to the GPU for rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computebarycenter(v1, v2, v3): """Calculate barycenter B of a triangle.""" return (v1 + v2 + v3) / 3.0 def scaletriangle(v1, v2, v3, barycenter, scalefactor): """Scale triangle vertices from barycenter by scalefactor.""" v1scaled = barycenter + scalefactor (v1 - barycenter) v2scaled = barycenter + scalefactor (v2 - barycenter) v3scaled = barycenter + scalefactor (v3 - barycenter) return v1scaled, v2scaled, v3scaled def getmaxradius(barycenter, v1, v2, v3): """Calculate maximum distance from barycenter to vertices.""" d1 = np.linalg.norm(v1 - barycenter) d2 = np.linalg.norm(v2 - barycenter) d3 = np.linalg.norm(v3 - barycenter) return max(d1, d2, d3) def computerotationmatrix(u, v): """ Compute rotation matrix R to align vector u with vector v. Uses Rodrigues' Rotation Formula. """ # Normalize vectors unorm = u / np.linalg.norm(u) vnorm = v / np.linalg.norm(v) # Calculate axis and angle crossproduct = np.cross(unorm, vnorm) dotproduct = np.dot(unorm, vnorm) # Handle parallel vectors if np.linalg.norm(crossproduct) < 1e-6: if dotproduct > 0: return np.eye(3) # No rotation needed else: # 180 degree rotation, need an arbitrary orthogonal axis # Fallback: rotate around an orthogonal vector axis = np.array([1, 0, 0]) if abs(np.dot(axis, unorm)) > 0.9: axis = np.array([0, 1, 0]) axis = axis - np.dot(axis, unorm) unorm axis = axis / np.linalg.norm(axis) theta = math.pi crossproduct = axis theta = math.pi else: crossproduct = crossproduct / np.linalg.norm(crossproduct) theta = math.acos(np.clip(dotproduct, -1.0, 1.0)) # Skew-symmetric matrix A x = crossproduct A = np.array([ [0, -x[2], x[1]], [x[2], 0, -x[0]], [-x[1], x[0], 0] ]) # Rotation matrix R = I + sin(theta)A + (1-cos(theta))A^2 R = np.eye(3) + math.sin(theta) A + (1 - math.cos(theta)) np.dot(A, A) return R def fitellipsoidtotriangle(v1, v2, v3, scalefactor=1.0): """ Main function to fit an ellipsoid to a triangle. Returns center, radii, and rotation matrix. """ # 1. Barycenter B = computebarycenter(v1, v2, v3) # 2. Scale vertices v1s, v2s, v3s = scaletriangle(v1, v2, v3, B, scalefactor) # 3. Determine radii (max distance defines the primary radius) maxr = getmaxradius(B, v1s, v2s, v3s) # The source defines radii (a,b,c) based on max distance but does not specify # how minor axes are derived. We assume a sphere or isotropic scaling for simplicity # if not specified, or use the maxr for the largest axis. # The source states: "maximum distance... is used to calculate a circumscribing ellipsoid with radii (a, b, c)" # We set the largest radius to maxr. Other radii are not explicitly defined in the text. # Assuming isotropic ellipsoid (sphere) for the base fit, or that a=b=c=maxr # is a simplification of "circumscribing". However, the rotation implies anisotropy. # Since specific minor axis calculation is missing, we return maxr for all or note it. # Given the rotation optimization aligns the "maximum radius", we assume the ellipsoid # has one major axis aligned with the max distance vector. # 4. Rotation Optimization # Find the vertex with the maximum distance to align the ellipsoid dists = [ np.linalg.norm(v1s - B), np.linalg.norm(v2s - B), np.linalg.norm(v3s - B) ] maxidx = np.argmax(dists) maxvertex = [v1s, v2s, v3s][maxidx] # Direction vector from barycenter to the furthest vertex targetdir = maxvertex - B # Initial direction (e.g., local Z axis or arbitrary reference) # The source says "align the maximum radius... with the maximum distance". # It implies rotating the ellipsoid's principal axis to match this vector. # We assume the ellipsoid's initial principal axis is along Z (0,0,1). initialaxis = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # Compute rotation matrix to align initialaxis with targetdir R = computerotationmatrix(initialaxis, targetdir) return { 'center': B, 'radii': [maxr, maxr, maxr], # Specific minor radii not defined in source 'rotationmatrix': R } Parameters: Scale Factor (s): Typically in the range (0.1, 2]. Mesh Resolution: 300–700 triangles after decimation. Up to 1000 triangles is the upper limit for standard GPUs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: Without pre-calculation on the CPU and decimation, performance is hindered on lower-speed GPUs. Precision: The rotation calculation relies on stable cross/dot products; parallel vectors require special handling. Boundary: The method assumes the input mesh is already decimated. Fitting to high-poly meshes directly is not supported. Time Complexity: Pre-calculation is O(N) where N is the number of triangles. This is done once on the CPU. GPU rendering is O(N) per frame. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store ellipsoid parameters (center, radii, rotation matrix) for each triangle. Performance: Significantly improves performance on lower-end GPUs by reducing vertex count and simplifying geometry to ellipsoids. Benchmarks confirm no hindrance on lower-speed hardware. Strengths: Real-time capability; produces soft, organic cloud shapes; leverages standard 3D modeling tools. Limitations: Requires manual or automated decimation; approximation error increases with high decimation rates (>95%) though visual quality remains acceptable. When to use: Real-time cloud rendering where organic shapes are needed and high-fidelity mesh rendering is too expensive. When not to use: Static, high-precision cloud visualization where decimation artifacts are visible. This method was introduced in the context of real-time GPU volumetric cloud rendering, specifically for generating "suggestive cumuliforms". It allows artists to use standard 3D modeling software (Blender, Maya) to create cloud shapes, which are then converted into volumetric primitives for rendering. The technique is part of a broader set of geometry innovations for real-time cloud rendering. name: Procedural Density Calculation
head: Density Curve Filter, calculateCloudDensity, calculateCloudDensityMinimal
body: Procedural Density Calculation generates volumetric density fields on-the-fly using mathematical functions and noise modulation rather than relying solely on pre-computed voxel grids. It distinguishes itself from pre-baked approaches by computing density values directly during rendering or generation passes, often integrating shape modulation to preserve detail without storage overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, ray direction, bounding volume parameters, and procedural parameters (e.g., eccentricity, curvature, noise seeds). Output: Density value \rho and optionally albedo \alpha at a given 3D position \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: 3D Volume Texture: A 3D texture array storing density and albedo per voxel. The layout is defined as: R Channel: Noise value. G Channel: Local Ambient Occlusion (AO). B Channel: Noise-driven height-based baseline albedo. A Channel: Procedural cloud physical density. Cell ID Hash: Used to decode eccentricity and curvature parameters for shape modulation. Steps: 1. Shape Modulation: For a given position \mathbf{p}, compute a base shape function (e.g., ellipsoid profile) driven by eccentricity, curvature exponent, and center distance. 2. Noise Integration: Apply on-the-fly procedural 3D noise to modulate the shape, preserving noise details that might be lost in lower-resolution representations. 3. Density Calculation: Combine the modulated shape and noise to produce the physical density \rho, which is stored in the Alpha channel of the 3D volume texture. 4. Albedo Calculation: Compute the height-based baseline albedo based on noise and store it in the Blue channel. 5. Rendering Consistency: During raymarching, retrieve density and albedo directly from the 3D volume texture in cheap and detailed passes to ensure 100% rendering consistency between generation and rendering. 6. Raymarching Stability: Replace unstable backing-up or bifurcated stepping loops with stable, uniform linear marching between bounding bounds to eliminate spots, missing clouds, noise, and banding. Correct empty space skipping using robust positive-step bifurcated step size logic to eliminate coordinate jumping and infinite loops. 7. Edge Filtering: Apply a density curve between two points (in and out) to add, subtract, multiply, or overwrite volume data, smoothly subtracting false signals at the edge of the data. Formulas: Ellipsoid Profile: S(\mathbf{p}) = \exp\left(-\left(\frac{x^2}{ex^2} + \frac{y^2}{ey^2} + \frac{z^2}{ez^2}\right)^c\right) driven by eccentricity e, curvature exponent c, and center distance d. Density Curve Filter: Creates a curve between two points (in and out) to add, subtract, multiply, or overwrite volume data, smoothing false signals at data edges. Density Storage: \rho(\mathbf{p}) = V{3D}(\mathbf{p}).A. Albedo Storage: \alpha{base}(\mathbf{p}) = V{3D}(\mathbf{p}).B. Parameters: Eccentricity: Decoded from cell ID hash. Curvature Exponent: Decoded from cell ID hash. Step Size & Bounds: Uniform linear marching step size and bounding bounds for raymarching. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Low-resolution raymarching can suffer from coordinate jumping and infinite loops if step size logic is not robust. Artifacts: Unstable stepping loops cause spots, banding, and missing clouds. Consistency: Discrepancies between generation and rendering passes occur if density is not retrieved directly from the same texture used for generation. Preview Limitation: The density curve filter works only in preview; filtered data must be exported to new.df3 files for PovRay rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateclouddensity(p, cellidhash, noiseseed): """Calculate procedural cloud density at position p.""" # Decode shape parameters from hash eccentricity = (cellidhash % 100) / 100.0 + 0.5 curvature = (cellidhash % 50) / 50.0 + 1.0 # Compute base shape (ellipsoid profile) dx, dy, dz = p.x, p.y, p.z baseshape = ((dx/eccentricity)2 + (dy/eccentricity)2 + (dz/eccentricity)2) curvature baseshape = max(0.0, 1.0 - baseshape) # Apply procedural 3D noise # Note: Exact noise function not provided in sources noiseval = (hash(p.x 12.9898 + p.y 78.233 + p.z 45.164) % 1000) / 1000.0 2.0 - 1.0 # Modulate shape with noise density = baseshape (1.0 + noiseval 0.5) return max(0.0, min(1.0, density)) def calculatealbedo(p, noiseseed): """Calculate height-based baseline albedo.""" # Height-based baseline albedo logic # Note: Exact formula not provided in sources heightfactor = max(0.0, min(1.0, p.y / 10.0)) noiseval = (hash(p.x 12.9898 + p.y 78.233 + p.z 45.164) % 1000) / 1000.0 return vec3(0.8, 0.85, 0.9) (1.0 - heightfactor 0.5) + noiseval 0.1 def raymarchclouds(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, stepsize, maxdistance): """Stable linear raymarching through cloud volume.""" t = 0.0 densityaccum = 0.0 coloraccum = vec3(0.0) # Uniform linear marching between bounding bounds while t < maxdistance: p = rayorigin + raydirection t # Retrieve density and albedo directly from 3D volume texture density = volumetexture.sample(p).A albedo = volumetexture.sample(p).B # Accumulate density and color # Note: Density is stored per-voxel; stepsize is used only for traversal, not accumulation scaling densityaccum += density coloraccum += albedo density t += stepsize return coloraccum, densityaccum Simulates a dense flat atmospheric volume by blending voxel colors with a height fog color based on a submersion factor and a visibility curve. It is chosen when a uniform, height-dependent atmospheric effect is needed rather than complex cloud structures. See Height Fog. Applies constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations to volume data, procedurally adding and subtracting thousands of spheres from an empty voxel volume using Boolean operations to create complex landscapes. Sphere size and position are random values within a user-defined range. It is used for generating test terrains or complex geometric volumes. See Procedural Volume Data Creation. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples along the ray, as density is computed on-the-fly. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the volume texture size, required for caching and retrieval consistency. Performance: On-the-fly calculation preserves noise details but requires significant computational power per sample. Limitations: Computationally expensive per sample; potential for artifacts if raymarching steps are not stable. The method originates from implementations in cloud rendering optimization, specifically within the boidsish project, which focuses on eroded Voronoi weather maps and stable linear raymarching. It also draws from procedural terrain generation techniques using CSG operations on voxel volumes.
