name: Smoke Source Injection
head: GenerateSmoke, SmokeSourceVolumetric
body: Smoke Source Injection initializes a volumetric smoke source at a fixed grid location by setting density and velocity values within a defined spatial region. It solves the problem of introducing initial mass and momentum into the Navier-Stokes solver domain. It differs from Smoke Advection by creating new data rather than moving existing data, and from the General Fluid Simulation Update Loop by being a boundary/initial condition step rather than a time-integration step. Inputs: Grid resolution RES (assumed uniform or defined by dimensions). Source center coordinates (centerY, centerZ). Source radius threshold, typically RES/10. Density amount dens. Velocity vector \mathbf{v}{init}. Simulation time step dt (implicit in Unity context). Outputs: Updated density field \rho. Updated velocity field \mathbf{u}. Data Structures: 3D arrays for density and velocity components (e.g., density, velX, velY, velZ) indexed by grid coordinates (i, j, k). In Unity implementations, these are often RenderTexture or ComputeBuffer objects accessed via GPU kernels. Steps: 1. Identify the grid cells belonging to the source region. The source is typically cylindrical or spherical, centered at (centerY, centerZ) in the Y-Z plane, extending along the X-axis or defined by a specific slice. 2. For each grid cell (i, j, k) within the source bounds: a. Calculate the distance from the center in the relevant plane. For the 2D slice example in, this is d = \sqrt{(i - centerY)^2 + (j - centerZ)^2}. b. If d < RES/10, inject the source values. 3. Set the density value: In, dens is generated randomly: dens = \frac{\text{rand()} \% 1000}{1000.0}. In, dens is a user-defined parameter smokeamount. 4. Set the velocity value: In, a constant X-velocity is applied: ux = 2.0. In, a user-defined vector smokeinitialvelocity is applied. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def injectsmokesource(grid, centery, centerz, radiusthreshold, densityamount, velocityvector): """ Injects smoke density and velocity into the grid. Args: grid: Object containing density and velocity arrays (velx, vely, velz). centery: Y-coordinate of the source center. centerz: Z-coordinate of the source center. radiusthreshold: Radius of the source region (e.g., RES/10). densityamount: Scalar value for density injection. velocityvector: Vector3 (vx, vy, vz) for velocity injection. """ # Determine grid dimensions if not provided resy = grid.height resz = grid.depth # Iterate over the relevant grid cells # Note: Implementation details vary between CPU (S1) and GPU (S2) for i in range(resy): for j in range(resz): # Calculate 2D distance from center in Y-Z plane dist = math.sqrt((i - centery)2 + (j - centerz)2) if dist < radiusthreshold: # Inject density # uses random density, uses fixed amount. # We use the parameter passed for generality. grid.density[i, j] = densityamount # Inject velocity # sets only X-velocity. sets full vector. grid.velx[i, j] = velocityvector.x grid.vely[i, j] = velocityvector.y grid.velz[i, j] = velocityvector.z Parameters: centerY: Y-axis center of the smoke source. Typical value: RES/4. centerZ: Z-axis center of the smoke source. Typical value: RES/2. smokeamount: Amount of density to add. Type: float. smokeinitialvelocity: Velocity vector to add. Type: Vector3. active: Boolean flag. Defined in but noted as not used in the provided snippet. Edge Cases: Precision: Random density generation in uses integer modulo arithmetic, which may introduce bias if not handled carefully. Boundaries: The source region must be clamped to the grid boundaries to avoid out-of-bounds access. What it is: Moves existing smoke density and velocity fields through the grid. Difference: Transports data; does not create new mass. When to choose: For time-stepping after injection. Link: Smoke Advection What it is: The complete time-step cycle including advection, diffusion, and pressure projection. Difference: Orchestrates the entire physics update; injection is a sub-step or initial condition. When to choose: For the main simulation loop. Link: General Fluid Simulation Update Loop Time Complexity: O(R^2) for a 2D slice injection, or O(R^3) for a 3D volume, where R is the grid resolution. The number of cells checked is proportional to the source volume. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it modifies the grid in-place. Performance: GPU implementations (e.g., Unity Compute Shaders) allow parallel injection across many threads, significantly speeding up the process for large grids. CPU implementations are simpler but slower for high resolutions. Strengths: Simple to implement; allows for dynamic source placement. Limitations: Random density in may lead to visual noise; fixed radius in may not suit all artistic needs. Smoke source injection is a fundamental component of fluid simulation, particularly in computer graphics for creating smoke effects. It originated from early grid-based fluid simulation techniques, such as those described by Jos Stam. The specific implementations cited here are from open-source projects demonstrating real-time volumetric smoke simulation. nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, https://github.com/nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Smoke Advection
head: Tracking additional quantities like density and temperature, MacCormack routine for smoke
body: Smoke advection tracks scalar fields (density, temperature, color) that are transported by the fluid velocity field to visualize the fluid's motion, as the velocity field alone lacks visual detail. It differs from velocity advection by solving the passive scalar transport equation \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} = -(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \phi using the same numerical scheme as the velocity, allowing low-resolution grids to retain visual detail. Unlike the unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian scheme, the MacCormack scheme used here is conditionally stable and requires a limiter to prevent numerical blow-up. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Velocity field \mathbf{u}, previous scalar field \phi^n, time step dt, grid dimensions. Output: Updated scalar field \phi^{n+1}. Data Structures: For each additional quantity \phi (density, temperature, color), allocate a texture/grid with the same dimensions as the velocity grid. The scalar field \phi stores values at cell centers (collocated) or staggered positions depending on the specific solver implementation, but is advected using the velocity field \mathbf{u}. Steps: 1. Source Injection: Inject a 3D Gaussian "splat" into the color or density texture each frame to provide a source of smoke. 2. Advection: Advect the scalar field \phi using the MacCormack advection scheme driven by the velocity field \mathbf{u}. The evolution is governed by: \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial t} = -(\mathbf{u} \cdot \nabla) \phi 3. Buoyancy (Optional): If temperature T is tracked, compute buoyant force to influence velocity dynamics, making hot smoke rise and cool smoke fall. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def advectsmoke(phi, u, dt, gridsize, limiterthreshold=1.0): """ Advect scalar field phi using MacCormack scheme with velocity u. phi: 3D array of scalar values (density/temperature/color) u: 3D vector field (velocity) dt: time step gridsize: (nx, ny, nz) limiterthreshold: threshold for slope limiter to prevent blow-up """ # Predictor step: Forward differencing phipred = predictorstep(phi, u, dt, gridsize) # Corrector step: Backward differencing using predicted values phicorr = correctorstep(phi, phipred, u, dt, gridsize) # Apply limiter to prevent numerical blow-up (conditional stability) phinew = applylimiter(phi, phicorr, limiterthreshold) return phinew def predictorstep(phi, u, dt, gridsize): """ Calculate temporary predicted value using forward differencing. """ phipred = copy(phi) # Advect forward: phi(x - udt) # In practice, trace back from x to x - udt and sample phi for each cell (i, j, k): traceback = (i, j, k) - u[i, j, k] dt phipred[i, j, k] = interpolate(phi, traceback) return phipred def correctorstep(phi, phipred, u, dt, gridsize): """ Determine final corrected value using backward differencing. Alternates direction to avoid bias and achieve second-order accuracy. """ phicorr = copy(phi) # Advect backward: phi(x + udt) # Use phipred for the intermediate state for each cell (i, j, k): traceback = (i, j, k) + u[i, j, k] dt phicorr[i, j, k] = 0.5 (phi[i, j, k] + interpolate(phipred, traceback)) return phicorr def applylimiter(phi, phicorr, threshold): """ Apply slope limiter to prevent numerical blow-up. """ phinew = copy(phi) for each cell (i, j, k): slope = calculateslope(phi, i, j, k) if abs(slope) > threshold: phinew[i, j, k] = clamp(phicorr[i, j, k], phi[i, j, k] - threshold, phi[i, j, k] + threshold) else: phinew[i, j, k] = phicorr[i, j, k] return phinew Parameters: dt: Time step. Must satisfy CFL condition for stability. Limiter threshold: Prevents numerical blow-up in the MacCormack scheme. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The MacCormack scheme is conditionally stable; without a limiter, it can blow up. Color values have no physical significance but create attractive swirling patterns. Temperature values influence dynamics via buoyant force. The MacCormack advection scheme is a higher-order numerical method used to advect scalar fields (such as smoke density or temperature) and vector fields (velocity) in fluid simulations, designed to reduce the numerical smoothing inherent in standard semi-Lagrangian advection. It achieves this by combining a forward semi-Lagrangian step with a backward correction step, allowing low-resolution grids to retain visual detail comparable to significantly higher-resolution grids using standard first-order methods. Unlike the unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian scheme, the MacCormack scheme is conditionally stable and requires a limiter to prevent numerical blow-up. An explicit, two-step, three-time level scheme used to solve unsteady compressible Navier-Stokes equations, second-order accurate in both time and space, chosen for ease of parallelization. Steps: 1. Predictor step: Calculate a temporary 'predicted' value using forward differencing. 2. Corrector step: Determine the final 'corrected' value using backward differencing. 3. Alternate forward and backward differencing between predictor and corrector steps to avoid bias and achieve second-order accuracy. 4. Subdivide data domain into blocks. 5. At each time level, exchange solution values at the outermost boundary layers of each block between nearest neighbors after each predictor and corrector step. 6. Application programmer writes a 'Prepare Data' routine to calculate flow properties to be visualized and store in the appropriate format for rendering. Steps: Combine low-resolution velocity projection with high-resolution density advection. Ray march density in a volume pixel shader. Pitfall: DiffUpSample reflects low-resolution difference to high-resolution field before/after projection; it is not a physical diffusion solve. Time Complexity: Depends on the advection scheme. MacCormack is second-order accurate in time and space. Memory Complexity: Requires additional texture/grid for each scalar quantity \phi with the same dimensions as the velocity grid. Performance: MacCormack scheme allows low-resolution grids to retain visual detail comparable to significantly higher-resolution grids using standard first-order methods. Strengths: Easier to parallelize and implement than more sophisticated CFD codes. Reduces numerical smoothing. Limitations: Conditionally stable, requires limiter. Not a physical diffusion solve for DiffUpSample. Origin: Fedkiw et al. 2001. History: Used in real-time simulation and rendering of 3D fluids. Also used in parallel CFD simulations on Intel Paragon. Usage: Visualizing smoke, density, and temperature in fluid simulations. PDF Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) DTIC ADA302573: Runtime Volume Visualization for Parallel CFD., https://archive.org/details/DTICADA302573, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Part4 Chapter16 Fluid Simulation Demo, https://github.com/Razria93/GraphicsStudyArchive/issues/33, fetched 2026-10-26

name: MacCormack Advection Scheme
head: MacCormack routine
body: The MacCormack advection scheme is a higher-order numerical method used to advect scalar fields (such as smoke density or temperature) and vector fields (velocity) in fluid simulations, designed to reduce the numerical smoothing inherent in standard semi-Lagrangian advection. It achieves this by combining a forward semi-Lagrangian step with a backward correction step, allowing low-resolution grids to retain visual detail comparable to significantly higher-resolution grids using standard first-order methods. Unlike the unconditionally stable semi-Lagrangian scheme, the MacCormack scheme is conditionally stable and requires a limiter to prevent numerical blow-up. The method advects a quantity \phi from time step n to n+1 using two intermediate semi-Lagrangian advection operations. The core update formula is: \begin{aligned} \hat{\phi}^{n+1} &= \mathcal{A}(\phi^n) \\ \hat{\phi}^n &= \mathcal{A}^R(\hat{\phi}^{n+1}) \\ \phi^{n+1} &= \hat{\phi}^{n+1} + \frac{1}{2}(\phi^n - \hat{\phi}^n) \end{aligned} Where \mathcal{A} is the forward semi-Lagrangian advection operator, \mathcal{A}^R is the reversed (backward) semi-Lagrangian advection operator, and \phi^n is the field value at the current time step. Inputs: \phi^n: The scalar or vector field texture at the current time step. \mathbf{u}: The velocity field texture. \Delta t: The simulation time step. Grid dimensions: textureWidth, textureHeight, textureDepth. Outputs: \phi^{n+1}: The advected field texture at the next time step. The implementation operates on 3D textures (volumetric data) where each texel stores the field value (e.g., float4 or float3). The algorithm assumes a grid-based coordinate system where cell indices map to texture coordinates via cellIndex2TexCoord. 1. Trace Backward Characteristic: For the current grid cell, sample the velocity at the cell center using point clamping to avoid interpolation artifacts. Calculate the position at the previous time step by subtracting the velocity scaled by the time step from the current cell index: npos = in.cellIndex – timestep cellVelocity. 2. Locate Sample Corner: Determine the cell corner closest to the traced-back "particle" position by adding 0.5 to the position (to align with grid corners) and flooring the result, then convert this integer grid position to a texture coordinate: npos = floor(npos + float3(0.5f, 0.5f, 0.5f)); npos = cellIndex2TexCoord(npos);. 3. Compute Half-Texel Offsets: Calculate the offset vector ht corresponding to half a texel in each dimension: ht = float3(0.5f / textureWidth, 0.5f / textureHeight, 0.5f / textureDepth). 4. Sample Neighbors for Limiter: Sample the 8 texels closest to the traced-back particle location from the current field \phi^n using point clamping at offsets relative to the cell corner: nodeValues[k] = phin.Sample(samPointClamp, npos + offset) for k=0..7. 5. Determine Valid Range: Compute the component-wise minimum (phiMin) and maximum (phiMax) of the 8 sampled neighbor values to establish the clamping bounds. 6. Forward Advection (\hat{\phi}^{n+1}): Perform a standard semi-Lagrangian advection step by sampling \phi^n at the traced-back position using linear interpolation to obtain \hat{\phi}^{n+1}. 7. Reverse Advection & Combine: Compute \hat{\phi}^n by sampling the forward-advected field \hat{\phi}^{n+1} at the original cell center using point clamping. Combine the intermediate values using the update formula: r = phin1hat.Sample(samLinear, nposTC) + 0.5 (phin.Sample(samPointClamp, in.CENTERCELL) - phinhat.Sample(samPointClamp, in.CENTERCELL)). 8. Clamp (Limiter): Clamp the result r to the range [phiMin, phiMax] to prevent overshooting and ensure stability: r = max(min(r, phiMax), phiMin). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def macCormackadvection(phin, velocity, timestep, texturewidth, textureheight, texturedepth): """ Performs MacCormack advection on a 3D grid. phin: dict mapping (x,y,z) to float, field at time n velocity: dict mapping (x,y,z) to (vx,vy,vz), velocity field timestep: float, dt texturewidth, textureheight, texturedepth: int, grid dimensions Returns: dict mapping (x,y,z) to float, field at time n+1 """ def cellindextotexcoord(index): return (index[0] / texturewidth, index[1] / textureheight, (index[2] + 0.5) / texturedepth) ht = (0.5 / texturewidth, 0.5 / textureheight, 0.5 / texturedepth) offsets = [ (-ht[0], -ht[1], -ht[2]), (-ht[0], -ht[1], ht[2]), (-ht[0], ht[1], -ht[2]), (-ht[0], ht[1], ht[2]), (ht[0], -ht[1], -ht[2]), (ht[0], -ht[1], ht[2]), (ht[0], ht[1], -ht[2]), (ht[0], ht[1], ht[2]) ] phin1 = {} for cellindex in sorted(phin.keys()): # 1. Trace back along initial characteristic cellcentertc = cellindextotexcoord((cellindex[0] + 0.5, cellindex[1] + 0.5, cellindex[2] + 0.5)) cellvelocity = velocity[cellindex] npos = (cellindex[0] - timestep cellvelocity[0], cellindex[1] - timestep cellvelocity[1], cellindex[2] - timestep cellvelocity[2]) # 2. Locate sample corner nposcorner = (math.floor(npos[0] + 0.5), math.floor(npos[1] + 0.5), math.floor(npos[2] + 0.5)) npostc = cellindextotexcoord(nposcorner) # 3. Sample 8 neighbors for limiter nodevalues = [samplepointclamp(phin, (npostc[0] + off[0], npostc[1] + off[1], npostc[2] + off[2])) for off in offsets] phimin = min(nodevalues) phimax = max(nodevalues) # 4. Forward advection: phihat^{n+1} phihatn1 = samplelinear(phin, npostc) # 5. Reverse advection & Combine phihatn = samplepointclamp(phihatn1, cellcentertc) phincenter = samplepointclamp(phin, cellcentertc) r = phihatn1 + 0.5 (phincenter - phihatn) # 6. Clamp (Limiter) r = max(min(r, phimax), phimin) phin1[cellindex] = r return phin1 def samplelinear(texture, coord): # Standard trilinear interpolation of texture at coord return texture.get(coord, 0.0) def samplepointclamp(texture, coord): # Point sampling with clamping to texture bounds return texture.get(coord, 0.0) Grid Resolution: The scheme is particularly beneficial at lower resolutions (e.g., 128x64x64) where it matches the visual quality of higher-resolution semi-Lagrangian advection (e.g., 256x128x128). Instability: The MacCormack scheme is not unconditionally stable. Without the limiter, the simulation can "blow up" (values diverge to infinity). Overshooting: The interpolation in the forward step can produce values outside the range of the input data. The limiter clamps the result to the min/max of the 8 neighboring nodes from the initial sampling position, preventing this overshoot. Interpolation Artifacts: When determining the min/max range for the limiter, point clamping must be used to access texel centers exactly to avoid getting interpolated values that would invalidate the range bounds. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On GPUs, higher-order schemes are often a better way to get improved visual detail than simply increasing the grid resolution, because arithmetic operations are cheaper than memory bandwidth. A MacCormack scheme on a 128x64x64 grid produces comparable visual detail to a semi-Lagrangian scheme on a 256x128x128 grid, saving significant memory and bandwidth costs. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. The scheme is discussed in GPU Gems 3 (Selle et al. 2007) as a method to improve visual quality in real-time GPU fluid simulations without the performance penalty of higher-resolution grids. It is applied to both velocity and smoke density fields in the referenced GPU-based fluid solver. Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids, https://wo1fsea.github.io/files/AboutNavMesh/P5GPUGems3Real-TimeSimulationandRenderingof3DFluids.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Realtime Smoke Volume (Ex1604)
body: Realtime Smoke Volume (Ex1604) is a hybrid rendering technique that combines low-resolution velocity projection with high-resolution density advection to visualize smoke in real-time. It solves the performance bottleneck of simulating and rendering dense volumetric smoke by decoupling the fluid dynamics resolution from the visual density resolution. Unlike standard full-resolution Navier-Stokes solvers, it projects velocity on a coarse grid to maintain stability and mass conservation, then advects a finer density field using the same MacCormack routine as velocity, finally ray marching the density in a volume pixel shader. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Low-resolution velocity field (projected), high-resolution density field, external sources (optional). Output: Rendered smoke volume via ray marching in a pixel shader. Data Structures: Velocity Field: Stored on a low-resolution 3D grid. Fields for u, v, w components. Density Field: Stored on a high-resolution 3D grid. Field for scalar density \rho. Texture3D: Both fields are typically uploaded to GPU textures for compute shader access and ray marching sampling. Steps: 1. Velocity Projection: Perform a projection step on the low-resolution velocity field to ensure divergence-free conditions. This maintains fluid stability at a lower computational cost. 2. Density Advection: Advect the high-resolution density field using the low-resolution velocity field. The advection uses the MacCormack scheme, consistent with the velocity advection method. 3. Ray Marching: In the volume pixel shader, ray march through the high-resolution density field to compute the final color and opacity. Pitfalls: DiffUpSample Misconception: The DiffUpSample technique reflects low-resolution differences to the high-resolution field before or after projection. It is not a physical diffusion solve. Implementers must not treat it as a substitute for actual diffusion if physical accuracy is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def realtimesmokevolumestep(lowresvelocity, highresdensity, dt): """ Performs one step of the Realtime Smoke Volume simulation. Args: lowresvelocity: 3D array of velocity vectors (u, v, w) on low-res grid. highresdensity: 3D array of scalar density values on high-res grid. dt: Time step. Returns: Updated highresdensity field. """ # Step 1: Low-resolution velocity projection # Ensure velocity is divergence-free on the low-res grid lowresvelocity = projectvelocity(lowresvelocity) # Step 2: High-resolution density advection # Advect density using the low-res velocity field via MacCormack scheme # Note: The velocity field must be interpolated to the high-res grid coordinates highresdensity = advectdensitymaccormack( highresdensity, lowresvelocity, dt) # Step 3: Return updated density for ray marching return highresdensity def projectvelocity(velocityfield): """ Projects velocity field to be divergence-free. Uses a standard projection method (e.g., Gauss-Seidel relaxation for pressure solve). Standard projection algorithm assumed as not detailed in. """ # Placeholder for projection logic # 1. Compute divergence of velocity # 2. Solve Poisson equation for pressure # 3. Subtract gradient of pressure from velocity return velocityfield def advectdensitymaccormack(density, velocity, dt): """ Advects density using the MacCormack scheme. MacCormack scheme involves predictor and corrector steps. """ # Predictor step densitypred = density - dt divergence(density velocity) # Corrector step # Interpolate velocity and densitypred to appropriate staggered grids densitycorrected = 0.5 (density + densitypred - dt divergence(velocity densitypred)) return densitycorrected A generic simulation step that updates the smoke density field by adding external sources, optionally diffusing, advecting, and applying a fixed per-cell decay. It is a more complete physical simulation step compared to the hybrid approach of Ex1604, which skips diffusion and decay in its core description. Use this when physical accuracy (diffusion, decay) is required, rather than just visual advection. Definition: Updates density field via source addition, optional diffusion, optional advection, and fixed decay. Steps: 1. Add external sources: AddSource(sd, density). 2. If compiled with DIFFUSE, swap densityTmp and density, then diffuse: Diffuse(0, densityTmp, density, diffusion). 3. If compiled with ADVECT, swap densityTmp and density, then advect using velocity components: Advect(0, densityTmp, density, velX, velY, velZ). 4. Iterate over all cells, subtract 0.001 from density, and clamp to zero if negative: FORALLCELL { density[I(k,j,i)] -= 0.001; if(density[I(k,j,i)] < 0) density[I(k,j,i)] = 0; } ENDFOR. Time Complexity: Dominated by the low-resolution velocity projection and high-resolution density advection. The projection is O(N{low}) where N{low} is the number of low-res cells. The advection is O(N{high}) where N{high} is the number of high-res cells. Ray marching is O(N{rays} \times N{steps}). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for both low-res velocity and high-res density fields. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics are not provided in the sources. Storyboard times are given for Ex1604 (4.025s, 13.417s, 22.808s frames), but these include rendering and are not isolated simulation times. Strengths: Real-time performance due to low-res velocity projection. High visual fidelity due to high-res density advection. Limitations: Not physically accurate for diffusion or decay. Relies on the quality of the low-res velocity field for stability. When to Use: Real-time visualization of smoke where performance is critical and physical accuracy of diffusion/decay is not required. When Not to Use: When physical accuracy of diffusion or decay is required. The Realtime Smoke Volume technique is presented as part of a fluid simulation demo series (Ex1604) in a graphics study archive. It builds on the MacCormack Advection Scheme [4952-maccormack-advection-scheme.md] for advection and the general Navier-Stokes Solver Components [4639-smoke-advection.md] for velocity projection. The technique is designed to balance performance and visual quality for real-time applications. name: General Fluid Simulation Update Loop
head: Fluid Simulation Update Loop
body: The General Fluid Simulation Update Loop is the core iterative process that advances a fluid simulation state from time t to t + dt. It solves the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations by sequentially applying source injection, diffusion, pressure projection, and advection to velocity and density fields. Unlike specialized variants like Stable Fluid Dynamics for Computer Graphics which approximate shallow water equations, this loop handles general 3D incompressible flow on a grid. It serves as the bridge between physical simulation and rendering, often feeding data into particle systems or volume renderers. The loop operates on a staggered or collocated grid storing velocity \mathbf{u} and scalar fields (density \rho, temperature, etc.). The standard sequence, as observed in general implementations, is: 1. Source Injection: Add external forces to velocity and sources to density. 2. Diffusion: Solve the viscous diffusion equation. 3. Projection: Enforce incompressibility (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0) by solving a Poisson equation for pressure. 4. Advection: Transport velocity and density fields by the velocity field. 5. Particle Step (Optional): If hybrid, step particles using grid velocity, sort them, and accumulate their contribution back to the grid. 6. Render: Output the density or surface field. Grid: A 3D array of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Velocity Field (\mathbf{u}): Can be collocated (scalar at each cell) or staggered (components on faces). The parent article Navier-Stokes Solver Components details the specific layout. Density Field (\rho): Scalar field per cell. Pressure Field (p): Scalar field per cell. Particle Buffer: List of particles with position \mathbf{x}, velocity \mathbf{v}, and mass/density contribution. The following pseudocode assumes a semi-Lagrangian advection scheme and a standard projection step. It integrates the steps described in and. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fluidupdateloop(grid, particles, dt, viscosity, diffusionrate): # 1. Inject Sources # Apply external forces (gravity, user input) to velocity grid.velocity += dt grid.externalforces # Add density sources (smoke, dye) grid.density += dt grid.densitysources # 2. Diffusion # Solve implicit diffusion equation: unew - dt nu laplacian(unew) = uold # This typically involves solving a linear system (e.g., Gauss-Seidel or conjugate gradient) grid.velocity = solvediffusion(grid.velocity, viscosity, dt) grid.density = solvediffusion(grid.density, diffusionrate, dt) # 3. Projection (Pressure Solve) # Enforce divergence-free constraint: div(u) = 0 # Solve Poisson equation: laplacian(p) = div(u) / dt pressure = solvepoisson(grid.velocity, dt) # Subtract pressure gradient from velocity grid.velocity -= dt gradient(pressure) # Optional: Correct velocity field using divergence and pressure iteration # This is often part of the projection solver itself. # 4. Advection # Advect velocity by itself: du/dt = -(u. grad)u # Advect density by velocity: drho/dt = -(u. grad)rho # Using semi-Lagrangian method: trace back from current cell center grid.velocity = advectsemilagrangian(grid.velocity, grid.velocity, dt) grid.density = advectsemilagrangian(grid.density, grid.velocity, dt) # 5. Particle Step (if hybrid) if particles: # Step particles from grid velocity for p in particles: p.velocity = interpolategridvelocity(grid.velocity, p.position) p.position += dt p.velocity # Sort particles by grid cell for efficient accumulation sortparticlesbycell(particles) # Accumulate particle density/velocity to grid cleargridaccumulators(grid) for p in particles: gridaccumulate(grid, p.position, p.velocity, p.mass) # Add accumulated values to main fields grid.velocity += grid.velocityaccumulator grid.density += grid.densityaccumulator # 6. Render # Render density or surface field rendervolume(grid.density) dt: Time step. Must satisfy CFL condition for explicit schemes, but implicit diffusion allows larger steps. Typical values: 0.01 to 0.1 seconds for real-time, smaller for high-accuracy offline. \nu (Viscosity): Kinematic viscosity. Typical values: 0.00001 for water, 0.0001 for oil. Diffusion Rate: For density. Often set equal to viscosity or higher for visual diffusion. Precision: Floating point errors in projection can lead to divergence drift. Re-projection or higher precision solvers may be needed. Boundaries: No-slip (velocity=0) or free-slip (normal velocity=0, tangential derivative=0) conditions must be enforced at grid boundaries. Degenerate Input: Zero velocity fields can cause division by zero in advection if not handled. Concurrency: In GPU implementations, simultaneous writes to neighboring voxels require atomic operations or double-buffering. A simplified 2D variant that updates fields sequentially: diffusion, projection, advection. It corrects velocity using divergence and pressure iteration during projection. It is chosen for real-time 2D interactive applications where performance is critical and 3D complexity is unnecessary. A method for animating water based on a stable solution of partial differential equations approximating the shallow water equations. It results in a wave equation on a height-field where wave velocity is proportional to the square root of water depth. It is solved using an alternating-direction implicit method on a uniform finite-difference grid. Each iteration consists mainly of solving a simple tridiagonal linear system for each row and column of the height field. A single iteration per frame suffices in most cases for convincing animation. It renders water using caustic shading to simulate refraction and uses a wetness map for wetting/drying of sand. The height-field representation prevents easy simulation of breaking waves, except perhaps in combination with particle-based fluid models. A discrete, grid-based approach using simple rules rather than continuous PDEs. Water gravity checks if the voxel underneath is air; if so, it moves there. Sideways movement uses a hash of position and frame number for pseudo-random direction, moving only if the target is not solid. Direction persistence stores the first successful horizontal direction until a wall is hit, with a small probability of changing direction for natural appearance. Lava logic runs the same movement code but converts lava to stone if water is found in its von Neumann neighborhood (up, down, left, right). Sand logic only falls down directly or diagonally if obstructed, pushing up liquids it falls onto. This method is used for voxel-based simulations where simplicity and parallelism are prioritized over physical accuracy. Time Complexity: O(N) per step for advection and diffusion (where N is the number of grid cells), assuming linear solvers. Projection step depends on the solver (e.g., O(N) for multigrid, O(N \log N) for FFT). Memory Complexity: O(N) for grid fields. Particle systems add O(P) where P is the number of particles. Measured Performance: Real-time 2D simulations can run at 60+ FPS on CPU. 3D simulations typically require GPU acceleration (CUDA/OpenCL) for real-time performance at reasonable resolutions (e.g., 128^3). Scaling: Scales well with grid resolution on GPUs due to parallel nature of advection and diffusion. Strengths: Physically plausible, handles complex interactions, versatile for various fluid types. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution 3D, requires careful tuning of parameters, stability issues with large time steps in explicit schemes. When to Use: General-purpose fluid simulation, smoke, fire, water. When Not to Use: When breaking waves are critical (use height-field or particle methods), or when extreme performance is needed with low accuracy (use cellular automata). The general fluid simulation update loop is rooted in the work of Jos Stam on "Stable Fluids", which introduced stable, real-time fluid simulation for computer graphics. The specific sequence of injection, diffusion, projection, and advection is a standard discretization of the Navier-Stokes equations. The hybrid particle-grid approach is seen in modern implementations like those by Razria93. Cellular automata approaches are popular in voxel-based games and simulations. name: Cellular Automata Simulation
head: Elementary Cellular Automata, Rule 110, Rule 90, Voxel-based Cellular Automata
body: Cellular automata (CA) simulation generates volume data by evolving discrete grid states through local interaction rules, producing emergent patterns such as fluid flow or geological structures. Unlike physics-based Navier-Stokes solvers, this method relies on deterministic or pseudo-random state transitions rather than differential equations, making it computationally lightweight and suitable for real-time procedural generation. It is distinct from reaction-diffusion systems by its discrete, grid-bound nature and lack of continuous field interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid representing the current state (e.g., air, water, lava, sand, stone) and a simulation time step t. Output: A 3D voxel grid representing the state at time step t+1. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D array of voxel types. To handle concurrency on the GPU, two buffers are used: currentgrid and nextgrid. Direction: A 2D vector or integer encoding horizontal movement direction (e.g., -1 for left, 1 for right). Steps: 1. Initialize Buffers: Copy currentgrid to nextgrid or allocate new buffers to prevent race conditions during parallel updates. 2. Process Water: For each water voxel at position (x, y, z): Gravity: Check the voxel directly underneath (x, y-1, z). If it is air, move the water voxel there. Sideways Movement: If gravity cannot move the voxel, compute a pseudo-random direction using a hash of the position and frame number: dir = \text{hash}(x, y, z, t) \pmod 2. If dir=0, move left; if dir=1, move right. Persistence: Store the first successful horizontal direction in a persistent state variable for the voxel. Continue moving in this direction until a solid wall is hit. Upon hitting a wall, select a new random direction. Apply a small probability p{change} to switch direction sideways to simulate natural turbulence. Boundary Check: Only move if the target voxel is not solid. 3. Process Lava: Apply the same movement logic as water. Second Pass (Reaction): For each lava voxel, check its von Neumann neighborhood (up, down, left, right) for water voxels. If any neighbor is water, convert the lava voxel to stone. 4. Process Sand: For each sand voxel at (x, y, z): Fall Down: Check (x, y-1, z). If air, move down. Diagonal Fall: If obstructed below, check diagonal neighbors (x-1, y-1, z) and (x+1, y-1, z). If either is air, move diagonally. Displacement: If sand falls onto a liquid (water/lava), push the liquid voxel up to (x, y+1, z) if it is air. 5. Swap Buffers: Assign nextgrid to currentgrid for the next iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatecellularautomata(currentgrid, nextgrid, t): # Initialize nextgrid as a copy or empty buffer depending on implementation # Note: In a real GPU implementation, this is done via kernel launches for each voxel at (x, y, z) in currentgrid: type = currentgrid[x, y, z] if type == WATER: # Gravity if currentgrid[x, y-1, z] == AIR: nextgrid[x, y-1, z] = WATER nextgrid[x, y, z] = AIR continue # Sideways Movement with Persistence # Assume persistentdirection is stored in a separate buffer or state dir = persistentdirection[x, y, z] # If no direction stored or hit wall, pick new one if dir == 0: # 0 represents 'none' or 'hit wall' hashval = hash(x, y, z, t) if hashval % 2 == 0: dir = -1 else: dir = 1 persistentdirection[x, y, z] = dir # Try to move in dir targetx = x + dir if currentgrid[targetx, y, z] == AIR: nextgrid[targetx, y, z] = WATER nextgrid[x, y, z] = AIR # Small probability to change direction for natural look if random() < pchange: persistentdirection[x, y, z] = -dir if dir == 1 else 1 else: # Hit wall, reset direction for next frame persistentdirection[x, y, z] = 0 elif type == LAVA: # Same movement as water (simplified for brevity, assume similar logic) #... (water movement code)... pass # Reaction Pass: Check von Neumann neighborhood for water neighbors = [ (x+1, y, z), (x-1, y, z), (x, y+1, z), (x, y-1, z) ] for nx, ny, nz in neighbors: if currentgrid[nx, ny, nz] == WATER: nextgrid[x, y, z] = STONE break elif type == SAND: # Fall down if currentgrid[x, y-1, z] == AIR: nextgrid[x, y-1, z] = SAND nextgrid[x, y, z] = AIR elif currentgrid[x, y-1, z] in [WATER, LAVA]: # Push liquid up if currentgrid[x, y+1, z] == AIR: nextgrid[x, y+1, z] = currentgrid[x, y-1, z] # Move liquid up nextgrid[x, y, z] = SAND nextgrid[x, y-1, z] = AIR else: # Check diagonals if currentgrid[x-1, y-1, z] == AIR: nextgrid[x-1, y-1, z] = SAND nextgrid[x, y, z] = AIR elif currentgrid[x+1, y-1, z] == AIR: nextgrid[x+1, y-1, z] = SAND nextgrid[x, y, z] = AIR # Swap buffers currentgrid = nextgrid Parameters: p{change}: Probability of changing horizontal direction for water. Value not given in sources [G: typical value 0.01-0.1]. Hash function: Any deterministic hash mapping position and time to a binary direction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concurrency: Writing to neighboring voxels simultaneously on the GPU causes race conditions. Using double-buffered textures (current/next) is required for correctness. Solid Obstacles: Movement rules must check for non-air, non-liquid solids to prevent voxels from passing through walls. Sand Stacking: Sand logic must handle diagonal falling to create natural pyramid shapes rather than flat piles. An archetypal 2D cellular automaton where each cell’s next state depends on its eight neighbors according to four rules (birth, survival, death). It is set apart by its binary state (on/off) and discrete topological neighborhood. Choose it for generating complex, self-organizing patterns like gliders and oscillators. It runs efficiently on the GPU via double-buffered textures in GLSL. For music synchronization, treat stable patterns and gliders as triggers; pre-compute a timeline of cell births aligned with BPM markers to drive particle emission or color shifts. One-dimensional cellular automata that generate complex patterns from a single seed row. Rule 110 and Rule 90 are notable for their computational universality and fractal-like structures. Choose them for generating 1D history volumes that can be extruded into 3D. They are computed using bitwise operations from a single seed row, keeping executable size minimal for 64k intros. Time Complexity: O(N) per time step, where N is the number of voxels, as each voxel is updated based on a constant number of neighbors. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing two grid buffers (current and next). Performance: Elementary CAs can run at high frame rates on CPUs (e.g., Processing 4.3 updates a 512x512 grid at 200 fps) and even higher on GPUs (4K resolution in fragment shaders). Strengths: Extremely low code size (suitable for 64k intros), no need for complex physics solvers, emergent complexity from simple rules. Limitations: Lacks physical accuracy compared to Navier-Stokes; patterns are discrete and grid-aligned; requires careful handling of concurrency on parallel hardware. When to use: Procedural art, demoscene productions, simple fluid/geology simulations where physical accuracy is not critical. When not to use: Realistic fluid dynamics, scientific simulation requiring continuous fields. Cellular automata were popularized by John Conway’s Game of Life in 1970. Elementary cellular automata, particularly Rule 110 and Rule 90, have been used in creative coding and the demoscene for generating procedural graphics. The technique is favored in size-constrained environments like 64k intros due to its minimal computational requirements and bitwise optimization potential. It is often compared to L-systems and reaction-diffusion systems in procedural art contexts. name: Grid-Based Simulation
body: Grid-Based Simulation discretizes physical sources (fluids, smoke, fire) into a volumetric representation on a structured spatial domain. It differs from particle-based siblings like Gaussian Splashing and Position Based Fluids by storing state in fixed voxel arrays, which enables efficient divergence and advection calculations via 3D textures. Builds on Simulation output. All methods in this family map a conceptual or physical source into a discrete or analytic volumetric representation suitable for rendering. The core mechanism involves establishing a spatial domain, assigning values based on physical state or geometric intersection, and storing the result in discrete arrays or computing it on-the-fly. Solves the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on a structured 3D voxel grid to simulate fire dynamics, explicitly coupling buoyancy forces driven by temperature gradients and vorticity confinement to restore curling smoke behavior. Chosen when fire-specific thermodynamic properties and smoke dynamics are required. Integrates real-time incompressible fluid simulation with sparse voxel-based rasterization on graphics hardware, leveraging Direct3D geometry shaders for rendering and compute shaders for simulation. Chosen for efficiently visualizing general fluid dynamics within a voxel engine by bypassing CPU-GPU data transfer bottlenecks through a GPU-only pipeline. Repurposes the engine's built-in grid-based fluid simulation system to render large volumetric datasets by ignoring simulation physics and utilizing the rendering pipeline and material integration. Chosen for native engine integration and material flexibility in Unreal Engine 5, despite excessive VRAM overhead and lower effective resolution. Simulates water as a volume-conserving voxel field that falls, spreads, and settles, with an infinite ocean source. Water falls, spreads, and settles within the voxel grid. The ocean acts as an infinite source that floods craters dug below sea level. Debris buoyancy is simulated: planks, logs, crates, barrels, and TNT float and right themselves, while stone, brick, and metal sink. Mixed wreckage tilts toward its heavy end, floating pieces drift on a slow current, wash ashore, or become waterlogged. Grid-based fluid simulation originates from the Eulerian approach to computational fluid dynamics. It has been adapted for real-time graphics to simulate smoke, fire, and water by leveraging GPU compute shaders for the Navier-Stokes solver. 12.8B destructible voxels rendered in the browser with Rust WASM custom engine, https://github.com/cktang88/2.5d-experiment, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel-based 3D Fire Simulation
head: 3D Texture Fire Simulation, Navier-Stokes Fire Simulation
body:
This method simulates fire and smoke by solving the Navier-Stokes equations on a 3D voxelized grid to compute velocity, pressure, temperature, and fuel density. It differs from particle-based fire by maintaining a continuous volumetric field, allowing for realistic interaction between smoke, heat, and fuel, and enabling direct volume rendering of the resulting 3D textures. It builds on Grid-Based Simulation. Inputs: Simulation domain dimensions (e.g., 128 	imes 128 	imes 128 voxels). Physical constants: P (pressure constant), m (molecular mass), g (gravity), R (gas constant), T0 (reference temperature). Simulation parameters: time step \delta t, vorticity confinement strength \epsilon, grid spacing \delta x. Outputs: Four 3D textures (or equivalent 3D arrays) storing per-voxel values: 1. Velocity vector \mathbf{u} (3 components). 2. Pressure scalar p. 3. Temperature scalar T. 4. Fuel density scalar (implied by "fuel level" in attributes). Smoke density is also tracked as an attribute. Data Structures: The spatial domain is discretized into a 3D grid of voxels. Each voxel stores scalar or vector attributes in contiguous memory, typically mapped to 3D textures for GPU access. GPU implementation uses blocks of size 16 	imes 16 	imes 16 with 512 threads per block. Formulas: The core dynamics are governed by the Navier-Stokes equation for incompressible flow:  rac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} = -(\mathbf{u} \cdot

Buoyancy Force: \mathbf{f}{buoyancy} =  rac{Pmg}{R} \left( rac{1}{T0} -  rac{1}{T}ight) \mathbf{z} Where: T is the current temperature. T0 is the reference temperature. \mathbf{z} is the unit vector in the vertical direction (gravity direction). Higher temperatures result in larger upward velocity. 2. Vorticity Confinement Force: \mathbf{f}{vc} = \epsilon (\Psi 	imes \omega) \delta x Where: \epsilon is a scaling factor. \delta x is the grid spacing. \omega is the vorticity vector (

abla |\omega| This force restores curling behavior lost due to numerical dissipation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the 3D textures for velocity, pressure, temperature, and fuel to initial conditions (e.g., zero velocity, ambient temperature). 2. For each time step: a. Compute Forces: Calculate buoyancy \mathbf{f}{buoyancy} based on current temperature T and vorticity confinement \mathbf{f}{vc} based on current vorticity \omega. b. Advection: Compute the advection term -(\mathbf{u} \cdot 
abla) \mathbf{u} based on interactions between neighboring voxels. c. Divergence/Pressure: Compute divergence and solve for pressure p to enforce incompressibility (implied by the Navier-Stokes form and "propagate changes in pressure"). d. Update Velocity: Apply forces and pressure gradient to update velocity \mathbf{u}. e. Update Scalars: Propagate changes in temperature, fuel, and smoke density based on the updated velocity field (advection of scalars). f. Store: Update the values in the respective 3D textures. 3. Render: Inject a shader into the post-processing pipeline to ray march through the 3D textures and render the fire. Pitfalls: HLSL Global Variables: In HLSL compute shaders, global variables cannot be assigned within the shader file using an assignment operator during declaration; this results in zero values without a syntax error. Solution: Manually assign these variables in the host driver script (e.g., C#) before each invocation of the compute kernels. Debugging: HLSL shaders lack print debugging capabilities. Use debug shaders that fill 3D textures with specific values when thresholds are met, or external tools like RenderDoc. Cross-validate formulas with a Python script. A variant that applies the diffusion method to the animation of fire and other gaseous phenomena. It is noted for handling complex scenes, though progressive energy shooting can be expensive, potentially requiring a hierarchical approach. Parallelism: Uses GPU blocks of 16 	imes 16 	imes 16 with 512 threads per block. Strengths: Realistic interaction between smoke, heat, and fuel; continuous volumetric representation suitable for volume rendering. Limitations: Debugging is difficult due to lack of print support in shaders. Performance scales with grid resolution and may require hierarchical approaches for very complex scenes. name: GPU-based Fluid Simulation with Voxel Rendering
head: Integrating Real-Time Fluid Simulation with a Voxel Engine, Poxels Fluid Integration
body: This method integrates real-time incompressible fluid simulation with sparse voxel-based rasterization on graphics hardware, specifically using Direct3D geometry shaders for rendering and compute shaders for simulation. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping the continuous velocity and pressure fields of a Navier–Stokes solver to a discrete voxel grid for rendering, avoiding the performance bottleneck of copying simulation data back to the CPU. It sets itself apart from its siblings by moving the voxel activation and color ramp logic entirely into the geometry shader, utilizing stream-out for deterministic primitive ordering, and relying on the Jacobi method for pressure projection due to its GPU efficiency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D simulation domain (chunk) defined by grid dimensions (e.g., N \times N \times N). External forces (static or dynamic bodies) and initial velocity/pressure fields. Output: A rendered voxel scene representing the fluid, where active voxels are determined by non-zero velocity/pressure values, colored via a ramp function. Data Structures: Velocity Textures: Three 3D textures of type float4 (single precision) storing velocity components and temporary values for advection and diffusion. Pressure Textures: Two 3D textures of type float4 storing pressure values and temporary values for the projection step. Speed Grid Texture: The final 3D texture filled with single-precision floats representing the updated velocity field, which serves as the source for the voxel engine. Activation Texture: A 3D texture containing only non-zero values from the simulation, used by the geometry shader to determine voxel presence. Staging Texture (CPU Approach only): A texture used to transfer data from GPU memory to CPU memory. Vertex Buffer: A cached buffer storing generated vertex data via stream-out. Numbered Steps: 1. Simulation Initialization: Define the processing stages for the Navier–Stokes equations: advection of the velocity field, acceleration caused by pressure, diffusion of momentum, and application of external forces. 2. Velocity Update (Advection, Diffusion, Forces): Perform three computations to update the velocity at each time step: Advection: Advect the velocity field. Diffusion: Diffuse the momentum resulting from fluid resistance. Forces: Apply external forces from static or dynamic bodies. 3. Pressure Projection: Compute the pressure field. The source specifies the use of the Jacobi method for the pressure-Poisson system. Calculate the speed divergence. Subtract the pressure gradient from the velocity field to enforce incompressibility. 4. Output Generation: The final result of the five GPU compute stages is output in a 3D speed grid texture filled with single precision floats. 5. Voxel Activation and Rendering (GPU-Optimized Approach): Activation Texture Creation: In the fluid simulation compute shader, populate a texture with only non-zero values from the simulation data. Geometry Shader Dispatch: Dispatch to the geometry shader for stream amplification. The geometry shader reads the activation texture to determine which voxels are active. Stream-Out: Continuously output vertex data from the geometry shader stage using stream-out to a cached vertex buffer. This guarantees deterministic ordering of rendered primitives. Color Ramp: Apply a color ramp function directly in the geometry shader. The function takes a float value (representing concentration or magnitude, typically between 0 and 1) and returns an RGB color. Rasterization: Perform regular triangle geometry rasterization using the generated vertex buffer. Pseudocode (GPU-Optimized Approach): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computefluidstep(velocitytextures, pressuretextures, forces): # Step 2: Velocity Update # Advection advectedvelocity = advect(velocitytextures, dt) # Diffusion diffusedvelocity = diffuse(advectedvelocity, viscosity, dt) # Forces updatedvelocity = diffusedvelocity + forces dt # Step 3: Pressure Projection # Compute Divergence divergence = computedivergence(updatedvelocity) # Solve Pressure (Jacobi Iteration) pressure = solvepressurejacobi(divergence, pressuretextures, iterations=20) # Subtract Pressure Gradient finalvelocity = updatedvelocity - gradient(pressure) # Step 4: Output # Write final velocity to speed grid texture writetexture(speedgridtexture, finalvelocity) # Create activation texture (non-zero values only) activationdata = selectnonzero(finalvelocity) writetexture(activationtexture, activationdata) def geometryshaderrender(activationtexture, speedgridtexture): # Read voxel position and value from activation texture voxelpos = read3dcoord(activationtexture) voxelvalue = read3dvalue(activationtexture, voxelpos) if voxelvalue != 0: # Apply Color Ramp # Input: float between 0 and 1 (normalized magnitude or concentration) normalizedval = clamp(voxelvalue / maxmagnitude, 0.0, 1.0) color = applycolorramp(normalizedval) # Generate Vertex Data for the voxel (e.g., cube corners) vertices = generatecubevertices(voxelpos) # Stream-out to vertex buffer streamout(vertices, color) def rasterize(): drawtriangles(vertexbuffer) Parameters: Simulation Grid Size: Must match the size of the 3D voxel staging texture (if using CPU approach) or the resolution of the activation texture. Typical tested size: 64 \times 64 \times 64 (262,144 blocks). Jacobi Iterations: Not explicitly given, but standard for pressure projection. Color Ramp Input: A float between 0 and 1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Obstacle Detection: The described simulation does not detect or respond to obstacles. Memory Alignment: If using the CPU approach, the CPU memory buffer requires appropriate memory address alignment. Precision: Uses single-precision floats for textures. A method for computing fluid velocity by discretizing the momentum equation on a fixed Eulerian grid and solving for velocity via advection, external forces, and pressure projection. It solves the problem of real-time incompressible fluid simulation on graphics hardware by leveraging 3D textures and slice-based rendering to map grid cells directly to voxels. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using the Jacobi method for the pressure-Poisson system due to its GPU efficiency, and Semi-Lagrangian advection for unconditional stability, distinguishing it from Free-Slip Boundary Condition Enforcement which handles dynamic obstacles, and GPU-based Eulerian Fluid Solver which uses half-precision textures and multigrid. Time Complexity: The simulation steps (advection, diffusion, pressure) are performed on the GPU. The CPU approach adds significant overhead due to data transfer. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for three velocity textures, two pressure textures, and the final speed grid texture, all of type float4. Measured Performance: CPU Approach (NVIDIA GeForce GTX 950M, 64x64x64 chunk): 100 FPS (10.000 ms frame time). Copy from staging texture to CPU: 23,088,969 ns. Activate voxels and render: 976,276 ns. GPU-Only Approach (NVIDIA GeForce GT540M, 64x64x64 chunk): 180 FPS (5.556 ms frame time). Performance Improvement: The GPU-only method improves performance from 30 FPS (original method, likely referring to a less optimized version or different hardware baseline mentioned in the text as "going from 30 fps... up to 1100 fps") to 1100 FPS on the tested hardware. Scaling: Frame time scales linearly with the number of voxels. Strengths: High performance due to GPU-only processing; deterministic ordering of primitives via stream-out; efficient integration with voxel engines like Poxels. Limitations: Does not handle obstacles; limited to single chunk (without extension); requires Direct3D geometry shaders and compute shaders. When to Use: When real-time fluid visualization in a voxel engine is required and obstacle interaction is not needed. When Not to Use: When obstacle collision detection is required or when running on hardware without support for geometry shader stream-out or compute shaders. This method was proposed by integrating recent results in GPU-accelerated fluid simulation (Crane et al. 2007 and Harris 2004) with voxel-based rendering (Miller et al. 2014). It is based on the Navier–Stokes differential equations (Stam 2003). The work addresses the specific hurdles of integrating these two technologies efficiently, noting that no prior work had been reported on this particular integration. It was published in the Computational Games Journal in 2016. Integrating Real-Time Fluid Simulation with a Voxel Engine, https://doi.org/10.1007/s40869-016-0020-5, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stable Fluids (GPU Implementation)
head: Jacobi Pressure Solver, Jacobi method for pressure-Poisson system, Semi-Lagrangian Advection
body:
Stable Fluids (GPU Implementation) is a method for computing fluid velocity by discretizing the momentum equation on a fixed Eulerian grid and solving for velocity via advection, external forces, and pressure projection. It solves the problem of real-time incompressible fluid simulation on graphics hardware by leveraging 3D textures and slice-based rendering to map grid cells directly to voxels. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using the Jacobi method for the pressure-Poisson system due to its GPU efficiency, and Semi-Lagrangian advection for unconditional stability. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D grid of cubical cells representing the simulation domain; initial velocity field \mathbf{u}; pressure field p; external forces \mathbf{f}; time step \Delta t. Outputs: Updated velocity field \mathbf{u}^{n+1}; updated pressure field p^{n+1}. Data Structures: State is stored in 3D textures mapping grid cells to voxels. Velocity Texture: Stores vector quantities (velocity) at cell centers. Pressure Texture: Stores scalar quantities (pressure) at cell centers. Geometry Shader Output Struct (GSOUTPUTFLUIDSIM): Used to pass neighbor coordinates to pixel shaders. python class GSOUTPUTFLUIDSIM: def init(self, cellindex, center, left, right, bottom, top, down, up, pos, rtindex): self.cellIndex = cellindex self.CENTERCELL = center self.LEFTCELL = left self.RIGHTCELL = right self.BOTTOMCELL = bottom self.TOPCELL = top self.DOWNCELL = down self.UPCELL = up self.pos = pos self.RTIndex = rtindex Numbered Steps: The momentum equation is split into successive operations: advection, application of external forces, and pressure projection. 1. Domain Discretization: Subdivide the rectilinear volume into a regular grid of cubical cells. Store scalar (pressure) and vector (velocity) quantities at cell centers. 2. Advection (Semi-Lagrangian): Trace back along the characteristic from the current cell position to find the source velocity. Calculate position: \mathbf{pos} = \mathbf{current\pos} - \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{cellVelocity}. Convert index to texture coordinates. Sample the velocity field at the traced position using linear interpolation. Note: This scheme is unconditionally stable but introduces numerical smoothing. 3. External Forces: Apply forces (e.g., gravity) to the advected velocity field using forward Euler integration: \mathbf{u}^ = \mathbf{u}^{advected} + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{f}. 4. Divergence Calculation: Compute the divergence of the intermediate velocity field \mathbf{u}^ using central differences on neighboring cell velocities.

Iterations: The number of Jacobi iterations. Adjustable based on resources. Smoke/fire may use fewer; liquids require more to prevent volume loss. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Rendering Limitation: GPUs render into 2D buffers. 3D volume kernels must be executed once per slice by iterating over slice indices and using SVRenderTargetArrayIndex. Numerical Smoothing: Semi-Lagrangian advection is unconditionally stable but introduces smoothing, making water look viscous or smoke lose detail. Volume Loss: Too few Jacobi iterations for liquids cause volume loss, making water sink through the tank bottom because pressure from the floor cannot counteract gravity. Boundary Conditions: The basic implementation stores quantities at cell centers. Staggered MAC grids are more robust for boundary conditions but are not the default in this specific implementation. This method enforces a free-slip boundary condition for fluid simulations involving dynamic obstacles represented as voxelized solids. It ensures that fluid velocity normal to the obstacle surface matches the solid's normal velocity, allowing tangential slip, while preventing mass leakage into solid interiors. It differs from no-slip conditions by retaining tangential fluid velocity and from static boundary handling by explicitly updating obstacle velocity fields and modifying the pressure solver to ignore solid cell contributions. The Projection Method enforces incompressibility on a fluid velocity field by subtracting the gradient of a pressure field, ensuring the resulting velocity is divergence-free. It serves as the incompressibility enforcement step within the Stable Fluids framework. Operator splitting decomposes the complex dynamic equations of fluid dynamics into sequential, simpler sub-steps to facilitate numerical integration on a grid. It solves the problem of enforcing incompressibility while applying external forces and advecting the fluid state. It sets itself apart from the parent Stable Fluids (GPU Implementation) by explicitly structuring the time integration into three distinct, ordered phases: advection, force application, and pressure projection. A GPU-based Eulerian fluid solver that simulates and renders volumetrics at VR resolutions and refresh rates by using operator splitting to approximately solve the Navier-Stokes equations. It distinguishes itself by integrating a custom injection kernel for source terms and a geometric multigrid pressure solver optimized for half-precision 3D textures, enabling interactive frame rates on consumer hardware. A method to advect fluid by moving particles according to their velocities, where physical quantities like mass and velocity are bound to particles. The process moves all particles according to their velocities v{t-1} (average velocity over t-1 	o t), then applies external force and pressure projection to the advected velocities to get final velocities at the next time step t. Time Complexity: The dominant cost is the pressure solve. With Jacobi iteration, the cost is O(N \cdot I), where N is the number of grid cells and I is the number of iterations. Memory Complexity: Storage is proportional to the grid size. Table 30-1 in indicates ~9 bytes per cell for simulation (velocity RGBA16, inside-outside R8, temporary RGBA16) and ~20 bytes per pixel for rendering (off-screen targets, ray data, depth). Measured Performance: Designed for real-time applications. Performance depends on the number of Jacobi iterations. Smoke/fire can tolerate fewer iterations for higher frame rates, while liquids require more. Strengths: Unconditional stability of semi-Lagrangian advection; efficient GPU implementation using 3D textures and geometry shaders; simple to implement. Limitations: Numerical smoothing from semi-Lagrangian advection; volume loss if Jacobi iterations are insufficient for liquids; cell-centered storage is less robust than staggered grids for complex boundaries. When to use: Real-time fluid simulation where unconditional stability is prioritized, particularly for smoke and fire; liquids require careful iteration tuning to prevent volume loss. When not to use: High-fidelity liquid simulation requiring strict volume conservation without excessive iterations; simulations requiring complex boundary conditions handled by no-slip or dynamic obstacles (use Free-Slip Boundary Condition Enforcement or GPU-based Eulerian Fluid Solver). The "stable fluids" method for computing velocity was introduced by Jos Stam in 1999. A GPU implementation of this method for 2D fluids was presented by Mark Harris in 2004. The 3D GPU implementation described in the sources extends these concepts to volumetric grids using Direct3D 10 features like 3D textures and geometry shaders. Alternatives to the Jacobi solver include Conjugate Gradient (Bolz et al. 2003), Multigrid (Goodnight et al. 2003), and Cyclic reduction (Kass et al. 2006). name: Free-Slip Boundary Condition Enforcement
head: Dynamic Obstacle Handling with Free-Slip Boundary
body: This method enforces a free-slip boundary condition for fluid simulations involving dynamic obstacles represented as voxelized solids. It ensures that fluid velocity normal to the obstacle surface matches the solid's normal velocity, allowing tangential slip, while preventing mass leakage into solid interiors. It differs from no-slip conditions by retaining tangential fluid velocity and from static boundary handling by explicitly updating obstacle velocity fields and modifying the pressure solver to ignore solid cell contributions. Inputs: Fluid velocity field \mathbf{u} (3D texture). Pressure field p (3D texture). Divergence field d (3D texture). Obstacle mask texture obstacles (3D texture, scalar). Obstacle velocity texture obstaclevelocity (3D texture, vector). Simulation parameters: time step \Delta t, fluid density \rho, cell spacing \Delta x. Outputs: Updated fluid velocity field \mathbf{u}'. Updated pressure field p'. Data Structures: obstacles: 3D texture where a texel value > 0.9 indicates a solid cell. obstaclevelocity: 3D texture storing the velocity vector of the solid at each cell location. Algorithm Steps: 1. Obstacle Masking: Define a helper function IsSolidCell(coords) which returns true if obstacles.Sample(coords).r > 0.9. 2. Pressure Solve (Jacobi Iteration): When solving the discrete pressure-Poisson equation for a fluid cell (i,j,k), neighbors that are solid must not contribute to the pressure gradient. The discrete system is: \frac{\Delta t}{\rho \Delta x^2} \left( \left| F{i,j,k} \right| p{i,j,k} - \sum{n \in F{i,j,k}} pn \right) = -d{i,j,k} where F{i,j,k} is the set of adjacent fluid cell indices. In practice, during Jacobi iteration, if a neighbor cell is solid, its pressure value pn is replaced by the center cell's pressure pC to nullify the solid's contribution to the Laplacian. 3. Divergence Computation: When computing the divergence of the velocity field, if a neighboring cell is solid, sample the velocity from obstaclevelocity instead of the fluid velocity field. 4. Post-Projection Enforcement: After the pressure projection step, explicitly enforce the free-slip condition. For fluid cells adjacent to solid boundaries, compute the obstacle's velocity component normal to the boundary and replace the fluid velocity's normal component at the center cell. The condition is: \mathbf{u} \cdot \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{u}{\text{solid}} \cdot \mathbf{n} where \mathbf{n} is the surface normal. Since solid-fluid boundaries are aligned with voxel faces, \mathbf{n} is axis-aligned, making the projection a simple component selection. The tangential components of the fluid velocity are retained. If two opposing faces of a fluid cell are solid boundaries, selecting one face's normal velocity is sufficient for acceptable results. 5. Advection Constraint: During advection of any quantity (e.g., density, temperature), ensure no quantity is advected into the interior of an obstacle. If the trace point of an advection step lands inside a solid cell, the advected quantity is set to zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. LEFT = (-1, 0, 0) RIGHT = ( 1, 0, 0) BOTTOM= ( 0,-1, 0) TOP = ( 0, 1, 0) DOWN = ( 0, 0,-1) UP = ( 0, 0, 1) def issolidcell(coords, obstacletexture): """Returns True if the cell at coords is solid.""" return obstacletexture.sample(coords).r > 0.9 def getobstaclevelocity(coords, obstaclevelocitytexture): """Returns the velocity of the solid at coords.""" return obstaclevelocitytexture.sample(coords) def solvepressurejacobiobstacle(pressuretexture, divergencetexture, obstacletexture, nx, ny, nz, numiterations): """ Solves the pressure Poisson equation with free-slip boundary conditions. Solid cells are ignored in the stencil by replacing their pressure with the center cell's pressure. """ p = pressuretexture.copy() d = divergencetexture for in range(numiterations): newp = [[0.0] nz for in range(ny)] for i in range(1, nx - 1): for j in range(1, ny - 1): for k in range(1, nz - 1): if issolidcell((i, j, k), obstacletexture): continue pcenter = p[i][j][k] dval = d[i][j][k] # Sample neighbors pleft = p[i-1][j][k] pright = p[i+1][j][k] pbottom = p[i][j-1][k] ptop = p[i][j+1][k] pdown = p[i][j][k-1] pup = p[i][j][k+1] # Nullify solid neighbors if issolidcell((i-1, j, k), obstacletexture): pleft = pcenter if issolidcell((i+1, j, k), obstacletexture): pright = pcenter if issolidcell((i, j-1, k), obstacletexture): pbottom = pcenter if issolidcell((i, j+1, k), obstacletexture): ptop = pcenter if issolidcell((i, j, k-1), obstacletexture): pdown = pcenter if issolidcell((i, j, k+1), obstacletexture): pup = pcenter # Jacobi update newp[i][j][k] = (pleft + pright + pbottom + ptop + pdown + pup - dval) / 6.0 p = newp return p def computedivergenceobstacle(velocitytexture, obstacletexture, obstaclevelocitytexture, dx): """ Computes divergence of velocity, using obstacle velocity for solid neighbors. Uses standard central difference discretization. """ divergence = [[0.0] nz for in range(ny)] for i in range(1, nx - 1): for j in range(1, ny - 1): for k in range(1, nz - 1): if issolidcell((i, j, k), obstacletexture): divergence[i][j][k] = 0.0 continue # Get velocities from neighbors vleft = velocitytexture.sample((i-1, j, k)) vright = velocitytexture.sample((i+1, j, k)) vbottom = velocitytexture.sample((i, j-1, k)) vtop = velocitytexture.sample((i, j+1, k)) vdown = velocitytexture.sample((i, j, k-1)) vup = velocitytexture.sample((i, j, k+1)) # Replace solid neighbor velocities with obstacle velocities if issolidcell((i-1, j, k), obstacletexture): vleft = getobstaclevelocity((i-1, j, k), obstaclevelocitytexture) if issolidcell((i+1, j, k), obstacletexture): vright = getobstaclevelocity((i+1, j, k), obstaclevelocitytexture) if issolidcell((i, j-1, k), obstacletexture): vbottom = getobstaclevelocity((i, j-1, k), obstaclevelocitytexture) if issolidcell((i, j+1, k), obstacletexture): vtop = getobstaclevelocity((i, j+1, k), obstaclevelocitytexture) if issolidcell((i, j, k-1), obstacletexture): vdown = getobstaclevelocity((i, j, k-1), obstaclevelocitytexture) if issolidcell((i, j, k+1), obstacletexture): vup = getobstaclevelocity((i, j, k+1), obstaclevelocitytexture) # Standard central difference divergence div = (vright.x - vleft.x + vtop.y - vbottom.y + vup.z - vdown.z) / (2.0 dx) divergence[i][j][k] = div return divergence def enforcefreeslipboundary(velocitytexture, obstacletexture, obstaclevelocitytexture, nx, ny, nz): """ Explicitly enforces u. n = usolid. n after pressure projection. """ for i in range(1, nx - 1): for j in range(1, ny - 1): for k in range(1, nz - 1): if issolidcell((i, j, k), obstacletexture): continue v = velocitytexture.sample((i, j, k)) solidvel = getobstaclevelocity((i, j, k), obstaclevelocitytexture) # Check each face and enforce normal component match if issolidcell((i-1, j, k), obstacletexture): v.x = solidvel.x if issolidcell((i+1, j, k), obstacletexture): v.x = solidvel.x if issolidcell((i, j-1, k), obstacletexture): v.y = solidvel.y if issolidcell((i, j+1, k), obstacletexture): v.y = solidvel.y if issolidcell((i, j, k-1), obstacletexture): v.z = solidvel.z if issolidcell((i, j, k+1), obstacletexture): v.z = solidvel.z velocitytexture.set((i, j, k), v) def advectwithobstacleconstraint(fieldtexture, velocitytexture, obstacletexture, dt, dx, nx, ny, nz): """ Advection step that prevents leaking into solids. """ newfield = [[0.0] nz for in range(ny)] for i in range(1, nx - 1): for j in range(1, ny - 1): for k in range(1, nz - 1): if issolidcell((i, j, k), obstacletexture): newfield[i][j][k] = 0.0 continue # Backtrace vel = velocitytexture.sample((i, j, k)) tracepos = (i - vel.x dt / dx, j - vel.y dt / dx, k - vel.z dt / dx) # Check if trace point is inside a solid if issolidcell(tracepos, obstacletexture): newfield[i][j][k] = 0.0 else: # Trilinear interpolation from fieldtexture at tracepos val = fieldtexture.samplebilinear(tracepos) newfield[i][j][k] = val return newfield Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Large Time Steps: Quantities can "leak" through boundaries during advection if \Delta t is large. The advection constraint (Step 5) is critical to prevent this. Opposing Boundaries: If a fluid cell is bounded by solids on opposite faces, averaging the normal velocities from both sides is an option, but selecting one is sufficient and simpler. Time Complexity: Adds constant overhead per cell for texture lookups and conditional checks during pressure solve, divergence, and advection. The nullification trick maintains the sparsity of the matrix. Memory Complexity: Requires two additional 3D textures: obstacles (scalar) and obstaclevelocity (vector). Strengths: Handles dynamic obstacles efficiently on GPU; allows tangential slip which is physically appropriate for many fluid scenarios; simple to implement using texture sampling. Limitations: Requires pre-computed obstacle velocity field. This method is described in "Real-Time Simulation and Rendering of 3D Fluids". It extends fluid simulation to dynamic obstacles using a voxel-based inside-outside representation. The approach is designed for real-time performance on GPUs, leveraging texture sampling for boundary checks.
