name: Projection Method
head: Hodge Decomposition, Pressure Projection
body: The Projection Method enforces incompressibility on a fluid velocity field by subtracting the gradient of a pressure field, ensuring the resulting velocity is divergence-free. It serves as the incompressibility enforcement step within the Stable Fluids framework. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An intermediate velocity field \mathbf{u}^ (potentially divergent) and a grid of size N \times N \times N. Output: A divergence-free velocity field \mathbf{u} and a pressure field p. Data Structures: Velocity field: 3D array of floats, dimensions N \times N \times N, indexed by (i, j, k). Pressure field: 3D array of floats, dimensions N \times N \times N. Divergence field: 3D array of floats, dimensions N \times N \times N. Steps: 1. Compute Divergence: Calculate the divergence of the intermediate velocity field \mathbf{u}^. For a cell (i, j, k), the divergence d{i,j,k} is approximated using central differences with uniform grid spacing \Delta x = \Delta y = \Delta z = 1: d{i,j,k} = \frac{u^{i+1,j,k} - u^{i-1,j,k}}{2} + \frac{v^{i,j+1,k} - v^{i,j-1,k}}{2} + \frac{w^{i,j,k+1} - w^{i,j,k-1}}{2} 2. Solve Poisson Equation: Solve for the pressure field p such that \nabla^2 p = d. This is typically done using Jacobi iteration: p^{(k+1)}{i,j,k} = \frac{1}{6} \left( p^{(k)}{i+1,j,k} + p^{(k)}{i-1,j,k} + p^{(k)}{i,j+1,k} + p^{(k)}{i,j-1,k} + p^{(k)}{i,j,k+1} + p^{(k)}{i,j,k-1} - d{i,j,k} \right) The iteration runs for a fixed number of steps, typically 20-40 iterations. 3. Subtract Gradient: Update the velocity field by subtracting the gradient of the pressure field to make it divergence-free: \mathbf{u} = \mathbf{u}^ - \nabla p Component-wise: u{i,j,k} = u^{i,j,k} - \frac{p{i+1,j,k} - p{i-1,j,k}}{2} v{i,j,k} = v^{i,j,k} - \frac{p{i,j+1,k} - p{i,j-1,k}}{2} w{i,j,k} = w^{i,j,k} - \frac{p{i,j,k+1} - p{i,j,k-1}}{2} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectionmethod(ustar, N, iterations=30): """ Enforces incompressibility on velocity field ustar. ustar: list of 3 arrays (u, v, w) of size NNN. Returns: divergence-free velocity field (u, v, w). """ # Initialize pressure field p = [[[0.0 for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] # Step 1: Compute divergence of ustar div = [[[0.0 for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for i in range(1, N-1): for j in range(1, N-1): for k in range(1, N-1): # Central differences for divergence (Δx=1) du = (ustar[0][i+1][j][k] - ustar[0][i-1][j][k]) / 2.0 dv = (ustar[1][i][j+1][k] - ustar[1][i][j-1][k]) / 2.0 dw = (ustar[2][i][j][k+1] - ustar[2][i][j][k-1]) / 2.0 div[i][j][k] = du + dv + dw # Step 2: Solve Poisson equation for pressure using Jacobi iteration for in range(iterations): newp = [[[0.0 for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for i in range(1, N-1): for j in range(1, N-1): for k in range(1, N-1): # Jacobi update: average of neighbors minus divergence newp[i][j][k] = (p[i+1][j][k] + p[i-1][j][k] + p[i][j+1][k] + p[i][j-1][k] + p[i][j][k+1] + p[i][j][k-1] - div[i][j][k]) / 6.0 p = newp # Step 3: Subtract gradient of pressure from velocity u = [[[0.0 for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] v = [[[0.0 for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] w = [[[0.0 for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for in range(N)] for i in range(1, N-1): for j in range(1, N-1): for k in range(1, N-1): # Central differences for gradient (Δx=1) u[i][j][k] = ustar[0][i][j][k] - (p[i+1][j][k] - p[i-1][j][k]) / 2.0 v[i][j][k] = ustar[1][i][j][k] - (p[i][j+1][k] - p[i][j-1][k]) / 2.0 w[i][j][k] = ustar[2][i][j][k] - (p[i][j][k+1] - p[i][j][k-1]) / 2.0 return (u, v, w) Parameters: iterations: Number of Jacobi iterations. Typical value: 20-40. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary conditions: The source code snippet shows specific handling for boundaries, including reflection for free-slip and averaging for corners. Failure to handle boundaries correctly leads to inaccurate pressure gradients at the domain edges. Precision: Floating-point errors can accumulate during iterative solving. Ensure convergence criteria are met or use a fixed sufficient number of iterations. A neural network approach that predicts velocity updates to enforce incompressibility, replacing iterative solvers. It enables differentiable simulation but requires training data. Time Complexity: O(N^3 \cdot I), where N is the grid dimension and I is the number of Jacobi iterations. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for storing velocity, pressure, and divergence fields. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the iterative solver. Performance scales with grid resolution and iteration count. GPU acceleration is commonly used for the parallelizable Jacobi iteration and gradient computation. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for incompressible flow enforcement. Limitations: Iterative nature can be slow for high-precision requirements. Convergence depends on the grid structure and boundary conditions. The Projection Method is a fundamental technique in computational fluid dynamics. It is a core component of the Stable Fluids method, which discretizes the Navier-Stokes equations on a fixed grid. The method relies on the Helmholtz-Hodge decomposition theorem, which states that any vector field can be decomposed into a divergence-free component and a curl-free component (the gradient of a scalar potential, i.e., pressure). tzhazuma/Fluidsimulation, https://github.com/tzhazuma/Fluidsimulation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Neural Pressure Projection Solver
head: Neural Euler Simulator
body: The Neural Pressure Projection Solver is a feed-forward neural network method that predicts velocity updates (\Delta u) to enforce incompressibility in fluid simulation, replacing traditional iterative pressure solvers. Unlike the Projection Method, which computes pressure via iterative linear system solving, this approach learns the mapping from advected velocity and boundary conditions directly to the divergence-free correction, enabling differentiable simulation. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: 1. Velocity field u^: The velocity field after advection and external force application. 2. Volume field V: A scalar field representing the space distribution of materials (fluid and air). 3. Boundary distance field: A scalar field where each grid cell stores the normalized distance between its center and the container boundary. Output: Velocity update \Delta u: A vector field of the same resolution as u^, used to update the velocity field. Data Structures The inputs are 3D volumetric tensors. Convolutional layers use the notation C{channels}, K{kernelsize}S{stride}: C: Number of output channels. K: Kernel size (e.g., K3 implies a 3 \times 3 \times 3 kernel). S: Stride (e.g., S1 implies stride 1). Algorithm The network consists of three parallel mini-networks for feature extraction, followed by a fusion and regression head. 1. Feature Extraction: Process each input (u^, V, and boundary distance field) through a dedicated mini-network. Each mini-network consists of two identical blocks. Each block contains a 3D convolutional layer (C32, K3S1), Batch Normalization, and LeakyReLU activation. Let Eu, EV, and EB be the output embeddings from the velocity, volume, and boundary mini-networks, respectively. 2. Concatenation: Concatenate the embeddings along the channel dimension to form a single feature tensor F: F = \text{Concat}(Eu, EV, EB) The channel dimension of F is 32 + 32 + 32 = 96. 3. Regression Head: Process F through four convolutional blocks followed by a final convolutional layer. Each of the four blocks applies a 3D convolution (C32, K3S1), Batch Normalization, and LeakyReLU activation. The final layer applies only a 3D convolution (C3, K3S1) to produce \Delta u, omitting Batch Normalization and activation functions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def conv3d(x, inch, outch, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1): """Standard 3D convolution operation.""" return x def batchnorm(x): """Standard batch normalization operation.""" return x def leakyrelu(x, slope=0.01): """Standard LeakyReLU activation operation.""" return x def concatchannels(tensors): """Concatenate a list of tensors along the channel dimension.""" return tensors[0] def neuralpressuresolver(ustar, volumefield, boundaryfield): # ustar: (B, 3, D, H, W), volumefield: (B, 1, D, H, W), boundaryfield: (B, 1, D, H, W) # Mini-network 1: Velocity x = conv3d(ustar, 3, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) x = conv3d(x, 32, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) eu = x # Mini-network 2: Volume x = conv3d(volumefield, 1, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) x = conv3d(x, 32, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) ev = x # Mini-network 3: Boundary x = conv3d(boundaryfield, 1, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) x = conv3d(x, 32, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) eb = x # Concatenate along channel dimension f = concatchannels([eu, ev, eb]) # 96 channels # Regression head: 4 blocks of Conv32 x = conv3d(f, 96, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) x = conv3d(x, 32, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) x = conv3d(x, 32, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) x = conv3d(x, 32, 32, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) x = batchnorm(x) x = leakyrelu(x) # Final output layer (Conv only) deltau = conv3d(x, 32, 3, kernel=3, stride=1, padding=1) return deltau Parameters Kernel Size: 3 \times 3 \times 3 for all convolutions. Stride: 1 for all convolutions. Channels: 32 for all intermediate layers. Activation: LeakyReLU. Batch Normalization: Applied after every convolution except the final output layer. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Boundary Conditions: The boundary distance field is explicitly provided as input to handle container boundaries, avoiding the need for implicit boundary handling within the network weights. Input Resolution: The network assumes fixed-resolution 3D grids. Differentiability: The method is fully differentiable, allowing gradients to flow back through the simulation step for inverse problems. A related method that uses the volume field V to regress density and color for rendering, but does not solve for velocity updates. Builds on NeRF. The iterative baseline that solves the Poisson equation for pressure. Builds on Projection Method. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Differentiable, avoids iterative convergence issues. Limitations: Approximate solution. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Neural Pressure Projection Solver, also referred to as the Neural Euler Simulator, was proposed in the paper "Inferring Fluid Dynamics via Inverse Rendering". It integrates fluid simulation with inverse rendering, allowing for the inference of fluid dynamics from visual data. The method replaces the traditional pressure projection step with a learned neural network, facilitating end-to-end training for inverse problems. name: Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics
head: Advection-Force-Projection Splitting, Dimensional Splitting (Fluids), Strang Splitting
body: Operator splitting decomposes the complex dynamic equations of fluid dynamics into sequential, simpler sub-steps to facilitate numerical integration on a grid. It solves the problem of enforcing incompressibility while applying external forces and advecting the fluid state. It sets itself apart from the parent Stable Fluids (GPU Implementation) by explicitly structuring the time integration into three distinct, ordered phases: advection, force application, and pressure projection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Velocity field \mathbf{u}{t-1} at time step t-1, external force field \mathbf{f}, time step size \Delta t, and volume field \phi{t-1}. Output: Velocity field \mathbf{u}t and volume field \phit at time step t. Data Structures: Velocity field: 3D grid of vectors (u, v, w). Volume field: 3D grid of scalars. Pressure field: 3D grid of scalars (intermediate). Steps: 1. Advection: Move the fluid quantities (velocity and volume field) along the velocity field \mathbf{u}{t-1}. This is performed by back-tracing particle positions using \mathbf{u}{t-1} and interpolating quantities from the source cells to the current cell. 2. Force Application: Add the external force to the advected velocity field. 3. Pressure Projection: Rectify the velocity field to make it divergence-free (\nabla \cdot \mathbf{u}t = 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def operatorsplittingstep(utminus1, f, phitminus1, dt, gridshape): # Step 1: Advection # Back-trace positions: sourcepos = currentgridcoords - utminus1 dt sourcepos = np.indices(gridshape).transpose(1,2,3,0).astype(float) - utminus1 dt # Interpolate utminus1 and phitminus1 at sourcepos using trilinear interpolation uadvected = trilinearinterpolate(utminus1, sourcepos) phit = trilinearinterpolate(phitminus1, sourcepos) # Step 2: Force Application ustar = uadvected + dt f # Step 3: Pressure Projection # Compute divergence of ustar using central finite differences divustar = computedivergence(ustar) # Solve Poisson equation Laplacian(p) = divustar / dt using an iterative solver p = solvepoisson(divustar / dt) # Compute gradient of p using central finite differences and subtract from ustar gradp = computegradient(p) ut = ustar - dt gradp return ut, phit Parameters: \Delta t: Not given in the sources. Interpolation method: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: If \mathbf{u}{t-1} is zero, advection does not move particles; values remain unchanged. Boundary conditions for the pressure projection solver are critical for correctness. Replaces the linear pressure projection solver with a ConvNet to regress velocity corrections directly from the intermediate velocity and volume field, enabling differentiable rendering and free-surface handling. Not given in the sources. The specific application in neural fluid dynamics was detailed in "Inferring Fluid Dynamics via Inverse Rendering". name: Neural Euler Fluid Simulation
head: Neural Pressure Projection Fluid Simulation
body: Neural Euler Fluid Simulation replaces the traditional linear solver for the pressure projection step in incompressible fluid dynamics with a convolutional neural network (ConvNet). While standard methods solve a Poisson equation to enforce divergence-free velocity, this method regresses the velocity correction directly from the intermediate velocity and a volume field representation. It is distinguished by its ability to handle free-surface flows (fluid and air) explicitly through the volume field input and by integrating differentiable rendering for inverse simulation. Inputs: Velocity field at previous time step: u{t-1} (3D vector field). Volume field at previous time step: V{t-1} (scalar field, range [0, 1]). Time step: \Delta t. Gravitational acceleration: g (3D vector). Container boundary geometry (used to compute distance features). Outputs: Velocity field at current time step: ut (3D vector field). Volume field at current time step: Vt (scalar field). Grid: The simulation domain is discretized into a 3D grid. Velocity Field (u): Stores 3-component vectors per grid cell. Volume Field (V): Stores a scalar per grid cell. Feature Vector: Each grid cell includes an additional input feature representing the distance to the container boundary. 1. Advection of Volume: Advect the volume field V{t-1} using the velocity field u{t-1} to obtain Vt. Vt = \text{advect}(u{t-1}, \Delta t, V{t-1}) 2. Advection of Velocity: Advect the velocity field u{t-1} using itself to obtain the intermediate velocity u^. The source specifies using the Maccormack method to reduce numerical viscosity. u^ = \text{advect}(u{t-1}, \Delta t, u{t-1}) 3. External Force Application: Apply gravity to u^ to obtain u^{}. u^{} = u^ + g \Delta t 4. Neural Pressure Projection: Input u^{}, Vt, and boundary distance features into the ConvNet F\Theta to regress the pressure-induced velocity difference \Delta u. \Delta u = F\Theta(u^{}, Vt, \text{distances}) 5. Velocity Update: Add \Delta u to u^{} to obtain the final divergence-free velocity ut. ut = u^{} + \Delta u Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neuraleulerstep(uprev, Vprev, dt, gravity, containerboundary, convnet): """Performs one time step of Neural Euler Fluid Simulation.""" # Step 1: Advect volume field Vcurr = advect(Vprev, uprev, dt) # Step 2: Advect velocity field ustar = advect(uprev, uprev, dt) # Step 3: Apply external force (gravity) udoublestar = ustar + gravity dt # Step 4: Compute boundary distance features distances = computeboundarydistances(containerboundary) # Step 5: Neural Pressure Projection deltau = convnet(udoublestar, Vcurr, distances) # Step 6: Update velocity ucurr = udoublestar + deltau return ucurr, Vcurr def advect(field, velocityfield, dt): """Semi-Lagrangian advection with backtracing and interpolation.""" result = zeroslike(field) for x in range(field.shape[0]): for y in range(field.shape[1]): for z in range(field.shape[2]): vx, vy, vz = velocityfield[x, y, z] xback = x - vx dt yback = y - vy dt zback = z - vz dt result[x, y, z] = trilinearinterpolate(field, xback, yback, zback) return result def computeboundarydistances(containerboundary): """Computes distance from each grid cell to the container boundary.""" distances = zeroslike(containerboundary.shape) for x in range(distances.shape[0]): for y in range(distances.shape[1]): for z in range(distances.shape[2]): distances[x, y, z] = distancetosurface((x, y, z), containerboundary) return distances Volume Field Range: [0, 1.0]. Time Step (\Delta t): Not given in the sources. ConvNet Architecture: Not given in the sources. Volume Loss: Incompressible simulation may suffer from volume loss. Free Surface Handling: The explicit volume field Vt is crucial for identifying the fluid-air interface, which aids both the pressure projection and the subsequent neural rendering. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles free-surface flows naturally via the volume field; differentiable, allowing for inverse simulation (learning dynamics from visual data). Limitations: Requires training data; precision depends on the ConvNet's capacity and training. When to use: When differentiable simulation is required for inverse rendering or parameter learning. The method was introduced in the paper "Inferring Fluid Dynamics via Inverse Rendering". It builds on the operator splitting framework for fluid dynamics, specifically replacing the pressure projection step. The approach leverages the differentiability of neural networks to infer fluid dynamics from visual observations, bridging the gap between physical simulation and neural rendering. name: GPU-based Eulerian Fluid Solver
head: Dense Eulerian Fluid Solver, Eulerian Fluid Simulation, Ignis Solver
body: A GPU-based Eulerian fluid solver that simulates and renders volumetrics at VR resolutions and refresh rates by using operator splitting to approximately solve the Navier-Stokes equations. It distinguishes itself by integrating a custom injection kernel for source terms and a geometric multigrid pressure solver optimized for half-precision 3D textures, enabling interactive frame rates on consumer hardware. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Voxel position, timestep (\Delta t), grid dimensions, and source definitions (density, temperature, forces). Outputs: Updated velocity, density, and temperature fields stored in 3D textures. Data Structures: State is tracked at each grid cell center. Fields: Velocity (\mathbf{u}), Density (\rho), Temperature (T). Storage: 3D textures with 16-bit float formats (half-precision). Voxel scale: 1.5 cm. Steps: 1. Injection: A custom kernel receives voxel position and timestep. It adds density and temperature to the simulation and applies arbitrary forces, such as buoyancy. 2. Advection: Uses semi-Lagrangian advection with a MacCormack backtrace. Linear sampling is used for velocity during the backtrace. Cubic interpolation is used for the final resample of all advected properties. Vorticity confinement force is optionally applied. 3. Projection: Pressure projection is solved using geometric multigrid with a single V-cycle. The V-cycle uses 1 pre-smooth and 2 post-smooth passes. Full-weight and trilinear transfer operators are used. Jacobi iteration is used for smoothing. On the 3rd, coarsest grid, red-black Gauss-Seidel with successive over-relaxation (SOR) is used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def solvestep(grid, dt): # 1. Injection # Custom kernel adds density, temperature, and forces (e.g., buoyancy) # based on voxel position and dt. injectsources(grid, dt) # 2. Advection # Semi-Lagrangian advection with MacCormack backtrace advectvelocity(grid, dt, sampletype='linear') advectproperties(grid, dt, sampletype='cubic') # Optional vorticity confinement if applyvorticityconfinement: applyvorticityconfinence(grid, dt) # 3. Projection # Geometric multigrid with single V-cycle solvepressuremultigrid(grid) def injectsources(grid, dt): # Iterates over active voxels for voxel in grid.activevoxels: # Add density and temperature grid.density[voxel] += sourcedensity(voxel.pos, dt) grid.temperature[voxel] += sourcetemperature(voxel.pos, dt) # Apply forces like buoyancy grid.velocity[voxel] += forcebuoyancy(grid.temperature[voxel], dt) def advectvelocity(grid, dt, sampletype): # Backtrace step for velocity # Uses linear sampling for velocity during backtrace oldvelocity = grid.velocity.copy() for voxel in grid: # Trace back along velocity field tracepos = voxel.pos - oldvelocity[voxel] dt # Linear sampling for velocity backtrace grid.velocity[voxel] = samplelinear(grid.velocity, tracepos) def advectproperties(grid, dt, sampletype): # Advect density and temperature # Uses cubic interpolation for final resample for field in [grid.density, grid.temperature]: oldfield = field.copy() for voxel in grid: tracepos = voxel.pos - grid.velocity[voxel] dt # Cubic interpolation for resample field[voxel] = samplecubic(oldfield, tracepos) def solvepressuremultigrid(grid): # Single V-cycle # Pre-smoothing: 1 Jacobi pass jacobismooth(grid, iterations=1) # Coarsening: Full-weight and trilinear transfer coarsegrids = createcoarsegrids(grid, levels=3) # Solve on coarsest grid (3rd level) # Red-black Gauss-Seidel with SOR solvecoarsestgrid(coarsegrids[2], method='redblackgaussseidelsor') # Prolongation and Post-smoothing for i in range(2, 0, -1): prolongateandcorrect(coarsegrids[i], coarsegrids[i-1]) jacobismooth(coarsegrids[i-1], iterations=2) # Apply correction to fine grid applypressurecorrection(grid, coarsegrids[0]) def jacobismooth(grid, iterations): for in range(iterations): for voxel in grid: # Standard Jacobi update for pressure grid.pressure[voxel] = updatejacobi(grid.pressure, voxel) def solvecoarsestgrid(grid, method): if method == 'redblackgaussseidelsor': # Red-black ordering for color in ['red', 'black']: for voxel in grid.getvoxelsbycolor(color): # Gauss-Seidel with SOR grid.pressure[voxel] = updategaussseidelsor(grid.pressure, voxel) FluidX12 is a real-time volume rendering pipeline that simulates smoke using an Eulerian grid method to solve the Navier-Stokes equations. It distinguishes itself by integrating viewport-resolution independent anti-aliased ray marching on interior faces in cube-map space, allowing for high-quality volumetric rendering at interactive frame rates. Unlike standard fluid solvers that output static data, this pipeline couples the simulation state directly with a specialized ray-marching renderer that supports both 2D and 3D domains. Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 3080, the solver achieves frame times well within the 11.11ms budget for 90 Hz VR. Smoke Rings (232x232x160): 9.63ms total. Dust Devil (160x256x160): 9.65ms total. Wall of Fire (200x200x200): 9.73ms total. Memory: Uses half-precision (16-bit float) 3D textures for velocity, density, and temperature, effectively doubling performance on bandwidth-constrained portions. Limitations: Primarily limited by low simulation resolution necessary to run in VR on current hardware. The method is presented in "Ignis: Eulerian Fluid Simulation and Rendering at VR Frame Rates" by Charlie Shenton (SIGGRAPH Asia 2023 Posters). It builds on operator splitting [Stam 1999] and MacCormack backtrace advection [Selle et al. 2008]. Ignis: Eulerian Fluid Simulation and Rendering at VR Frame Rates, https://doi.org/10.1145/3610542.3626120, fetched 2026-10-30

name: FluidX12 Simulation Pipeline
head: Eulerian Grid Smoke Simulation, FluidEZ
body: FluidX12 is a real-time volume rendering pipeline that simulates smoke using an Eulerian grid method to solve the Navier-Stokes equations. It distinguishes itself by integrating viewport-resolution independent anti-aliased ray marching on interior faces in cube-map space, allowing for high-quality volumetric rendering at interactive frame rates. Unlike standard fluid solvers that output static data, this pipeline couples the simulation state directly with a specialized ray-marching renderer that supports both 2D and 3D domains. Inputs: Grid dimensions: Nx, Ny, Nz (default 128, 128, 128). Camera parameters: Eye position, View matrix, Projection matrix. Lighting parameters: Light position, Light color, Ambient light. Simulation parameters: Time step, Base seed for noise. Rendering parameters: Maximum ray samples (N{ray}, default 192), Maximum light samples (N{light}, default 64). Outputs: Rendered image: 8-bit RGBA texture. Updated fluid state: Velocity and density/color fields for the next frame. Simulation Buffers (Ping-Pong): Two sets of textures are used for velocity and color/density to allow read/write access during updates. mvelocities[2]: Texture3D, format R16G16B16A16FLOAT, dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz), flags ALLOWUNORDEREDACCESS. mcolors[2]: Texture3D, format R16G16B16A16FLOAT, dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz), flags ALLOWUNORDEREDACCESS. mframeParity: Integer (0 or 1) tracking the current read/write buffer index. Auxiliary Textures: mincompress: Texture3D, format R32FLOAT, dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz). Used for divergence calculation or pressure projection auxiliary data. mlightMap: Texture3D, format R11G11B10FLOAT, dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz), flags ALLOWSIMULTANEOUSACCESS. Used for storing light probe or illumination data. mcubeMap: TextureCube, format R8G8B8A8UNORM, 6 faces, 5 mipmap levels. Used for environment mapping or directional lighting integration in the ray marcher. Constant Buffers: CBSimulation: TimeStep: float BaseSeed: uint32t CBPerFrame: EyePos: XMFLOAT4 (x,y,z,w) LightPos: XMFLOAT4 LightColor: XMFLOAT4 Ambient: XMFLOAT4 CBPerObject: WorldViewProjI: XMFLOAT4X4 (Inverse World-View-Projection) WorldViewProj: XMFLOAT4X4 WorldI: XMFLOAT3X4 (Inverse World) World: XMFLOAT3X4 CBSampleRes: NumSamples: uint32t HasLightProbes: uint32t (boolean flag) NumLightSamples: uint32t 1. Initialization: Create the Direct3D 12 device, command queues, and swap chain. Initialize mvelocities and mcolors ping-pong buffers with zero or initial smoke density. Initialize auxiliary textures (mincompress, mlightMap, mcubeMap). Set default parameters: N{ray}=192, N{light}=64, world scale 10.0. 2. Simulation Update (Per Frame): Advection Pass: Dispatch compute shader CSADVECT. Write to: mvelocities[1], mcolors[mframeParity]. Read from: mvelocities[0], mcolors[!mframeParity]. Thread group dimensions: (\lceil Nx/8 \rceil, \lceil Ny/8 \rceil, Nz). This step advects velocity and color/density fields using semi-Lagrangian or similar Eulerian advection. Projection Pass: Determine dimensionality: If Nz > 1, use 3D projection; else use 2D projection. Dispatch compute shader CSPROJECT3D or CSPROJECT2D. Write to: mvelocities[0] (or appropriate buffer based on parity swap). This step enforces incompressibility by projecting the velocity field onto a divergence-free space. Buffer Swap: Toggle mframeParity to swap read/write buffers for the next frame. 3. Rendering (Per Frame): Update constant buffers with current camera, light, and simulation parameters. Dispatch ray marching compute shader or pixel shader. The renderer samples the fluid density from the grid textures along view rays. Apply anti-aliasing via viewport-resolution independent techniques on interior faces. Integrate lighting using mlightMap and mcubeMap if enabled. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. gridsize = (128, 128, 128) maxraysamples = 192 maxlightsamples = 64 worldscale = (10.0, 10.0, 10.0) velocities = [Texture3D(gridsize, format=R16G16B16A16FLOAT), Texture3D(gridsize, format=R16G16B16A16FLOAT)] colors = [Texture3D(gridsize, format=R16G16B16A16FLOAT), Texture3D(gridsize, format=R16G16B16A16FLOAT)] incompress = Texture3D(gridsize, format=R32FLOAT) lightmap = Texture3D(gridsize, format=R11G11B10FLOAT, allowsimultaneousaccess=True) cubemap = TextureCube(format=R8G8B8A8UNORM, faces=6, mips=5) frameparity = 0 def simulateandrender(frameindex, eyepos, lightpos, lightcolor, ambient, worldviewproj, worldviewprojinv, world, worldinv): global frameparity # 1. Simulation Step # Advection: Read from old buffers, write to new buffers # UAVs: velocities[1], colors[frameparity] # SRVs: velocities[0], colors[!frameparity] dispatchcs(CSADVECT, numthreadsx=ceil(gridsize.x / 8), numthreadsy=ceil(gridsize.y / 8), numthreadsz=gridsize.z) # Projection: Enforce incompressibility if gridsize.z > 1: dispatchcs(CSPROJECT3D, numthreadsx=ceil(gridsize.x / 8), numthreadsy=ceil(gridsize.y / 8), numthreadsz=gridsize.z) else: dispatchcs(CSPROJECT2D, numthreadsx=ceil(gridsize.x / 8), numthreadsy=ceil(gridsize.y / 8)) # Swap parity for next frame frameparity = 1 - frameparity # 2. Rendering Step # Update Constant Buffers cbsimulation.TimeStep = dt cbsimulation.BaseSeed = seed cbperframe.EyePos = eyepos cbperframe.LightPos = lightpos cbperframe.LightColor = lightcolor cbperframe.Ambient = ambient cbperobject.WorldViewProj = worldviewproj cbperobject.WorldViewProjI = worldviewprojinv cbperobject.World = world cbperobject.WorldI = worldinv cbsampleres.NumSamples = maxraysamples cbsampleres.HasLightProbes = haslightprobes cbsampleres.NumLightSamples = maxlightsamples # Dispatch Ray Marching # The ray marcher samples velocities[0] and colors[0] (since parity was swapped) # to render the volume. dispatchraymarcher(width, height, maxraysamples, maxlightsamples) Grid Dimensions: The projection pass switches between 2D and 3D logic based on Nz > 1. If Nz=1, 2D shaders must be used to avoid invalid memory access or incorrect physics. Precision: Velocity and color are stored in R16G16B16A16FLOAT. This provides sufficient precision for smoke density and velocity but may lose detail in extreme dynamic ranges compared to R32FLOAT. Ray Sampling: The default maxRaySamples (192) and maxLightSamples (64) are tuned for viewport resolution. Increasing resolution without adjusting these may cause performance degradation or aliasing artifacts if not handled by the anti-aliasing method. World Transform: The mvolumeWorld scale (default 10.0) must match the scene scale. Mismatched scales cause the fluid to appear too small or too large relative to the camera. Time Complexity: Simulation is O(Nx Ny Nz) per frame due to grid-wide advection and projection passes. Rendering is O(W \cdot H \cdot N{ray}) where W, H are screen dimensions and N{ray} is the number of ray samples per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for storing velocity, color, and auxiliary textures. With default 128^3 grid and 16-bit floats, this is approximately 2 \times 128^3 \times 8 \text{ bytes} \approx 256 \text{ MB} for velocity and color alone, plus auxiliary textures. Performance: Designed for real-time performance at viewport resolution on modern GPUs using DirectX 12. Strengths: Real-time capability, integration of advanced ray marching anti-aliasing, support for both 2D and 3D simulations. Limitations: Grid-based methods suffer from numerical diffusion and require fine grids for high detail, which increases memory usage. The specific implementation is tied to DirectX 12 and the XUSG framework. FluidX12 is an implementation of the techniques presented in the SIGGRAPH Asia 2021 Technical Communications paper "Viewport-Resolution Independent Anti-Aliased Ray Marching on Interior Faces in Cube-Map Space". It was developed by StarsX as a demo application to showcase real-time volume rendering of smoke simulations using Eulerian grid methods. The project relies on the XUSG (Xbox Unified Shader Graphics) framework for DirectX 12 abstraction. StarsX/FluidX12, https://github.com/StarsX/FluidX12, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Niagara Fluids Volume Rendering
head: Grid-based simulation rendering, Niagara Fluids Plugin, Niagara Fluids Plugin adaptation
body: Niagara Fluids Volume Rendering is a method for rendering volumetric data in Unreal Engine 5 by repurposing the engine's built-in grid-based fluid simulation and rendering pipeline. It ignores the simulation aspect ("do nothing" simulation) and utilizes only the rendering subsystem to display volume textures. This approach offers native engine integration and flexibility via the material system but is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on the simulation grid's memory architecture, which imposes severe VRAM constraints and limits effective resolution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume textures (e.g., imported via MHD loader) containing scalar density data. Output: Rendered 2D image with lighting and transfer function application. Data Structures: Volume Texture: Stores the voxel data. The underlying simulation grid allocates memory for simulation fields in addition to the texture data, even if unused. Niagara System: Manages the rendering instances. Each chunk of the volume dataset is typically assigned to a distinct Niagara System. Transfer Function (TF): Implemented as a 1D RGBA texture or via material parameter collections. Steps: 1. Import Data: Load volume data into the engine. Note that UE5's standard 3D textures are limited to 2048^3 voxels, necessitating chunking for larger datasets. 2. Configure Niagara System: Create a Niagara System to handle the volume. Since no native Niagara Module Script existed for volume texture sampling at the time of the survey, a custom script was required. 3. Sample Volume Data: In the custom Niagara Module Script or material, sample the volume texture at the current position. The density value is extracted from the red channel of the sampled volume texture. The transfer function is applied by sampling a 1D texture using the density value as the coordinate. 4. Render: The Niagara system renders the volume. If chunking is used, each chunk is rendered independently. Pseudocode: The core sampling logic, as implemented in the material or custom script, is as follows: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. densityvalue = VolTexture.SampleLevel(VolTextureSampler, UVW, MipLevel).r tfcolor = TFTexture.SampleLevel(TFSampler, float2(densityvalue, 0.0), 0) Parameters: Internal Resolution: Must be significantly smaller than the actual data resolution to avoid VRAM crashes. For example, a per-chunk resolution of 384 was used. Max Size: Approximately 0.45 gigavoxels at low resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VRAM Exhaustion: The simulation grid allocation overhead causes heavy VRAM consumption. Even with "do nothing" simulation, the grid data is allocated on top of the texture data. This leads to out-of-VRAM crashes if the internal resolution is too high or too many chunks are rendered simultaneously. Lighting Artifacts: Chunking the dataset into multiple Niagara Systems results in lighting artifacts at chunk borders because each chunk's lighting is computed independently. Transfer Function Limitations: Authoring transfer functions is restricted to Editor mode and does not officially support Game mode or NDisplay devices for large textures. Using per-voxel evaluation for color/alpha curves is inefficient; a 4-channel RGBA-1D lookup texture is preferred. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined, but performance is limited by resolution and VRAM availability. Memory Complexity: High. The method suffers from excessive VRAM consumption due to the underlying simulation grid allocation, even when the simulation is inactive. Measured Performance: On an RTX 3050: 10-15 FPS on 512^3 data. On an RTX 5000: 15-20 FPS on 512^3 data. Visual quality is limited by the low effective rendering resolution required to avoid crashes. Strengths: Native engine integration, flexibility via the material system, and interactive authoring of simple transfer functions in the Editor. Limitations: Severe VRAM overhead, low effective resolution, lighting artifacts at chunk borders, and lack of runtime transfer function authoring. When to use: When native integration is prioritized and dataset sizes are small enough to fit within VRAM constraints without excessive chunking. When not to use: For large datasets requiring high resolution or seamless full rendering, as the VRAM overhead and chunking artifacts make it impractical. Origin: This approach was explored as part of an investigation into rendering large volume datasets (e.g., the Kolumbo seismic dataset) in Unreal Engine 5. It was identified as a potential solution due to its native integration but was ultimately deemed impractical for large-scale scientific visualization due to memory constraints. History: The method relies on UE5's Niagara Fluids plugin, which was in beta at the time of the survey, with sparse documentation. The need for a custom Niagara Module Script arose because no built-in support for volume texture sampling existed. Usage: It was used to render volume textures imported by the MHD loader of the TBRayMarcher plugin, providing qualitatively comparable results to TBRayMarcher but with significant performance and memory trade-offs. An experimental UE5 feature using OpenVDB files, storing data sparsely with a tile-based page table. It offers better memory efficiency and seamless full rendering compared to Niagara Fluids, making it the preferred solution for large datasets. Link A plugin providing dedicated nodes for volume rendering, supporting real-time manipulation of transfer functions and rendering parameters. It suffers from lighting artifacts at chunk borders similar to Niagara Fluids but offers more structured control. name: Navier-Stokes Fire Simulation
head: Full 3D Finite Difference Solution, Physical Simulation (Navier-Stokes/Lattice), Physics-Based Fire, Physics-Based Fire Simulation
body:
Navier-Stokes Fire Simulation models fire as a hot, turbulent gas by solving the physical laws of fluid dynamics, specifically the Navier-Stokes equations, to generate time-varying volumetric data. It differs from procedural or particle-based siblings by deriving motion from conservation of momentum and mass rather than noise functions or ad-hoc particle rules, providing physically accurate convection and buoyancy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D spatial domain (grid) with resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz), physical properties (viscosity, thermal expansion coefficient), and initial conditions (velocity field \mathbf{u}, temperature/density field ho). Output: A time-evolving velocity field \mathbf{u}(x,y,z,t) and scalar field (density/temperature) suitable for volume rendering. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D array storing velocity vectors \mathbf{u} and scalars (density/temperature) at cell centers or staggered locations. Resolution: Typically coarse grids are used for the simulation step to maintain efficiency. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set initial velocity \mathbf{u}0 and density/temperature fields. Enforce boundary conditions (e.g., no-slip walls, open boundaries). 2. Force Application: Calculate external forces acting on the gas. For fire, this includes: Thermal Buoyancy: Upward force proportional to temperature difference (hot air rises). Drag: Damping forces representing viscosity. Convection: Movement of fluid due to its own velocity field. 3. Advection: Transport velocity and scalar fields by the current velocity field. This represents Newton’s Laws of Motion for the gas. 4. Pressure Solve: Solve the incompressibility constraint (
abla \cdot \mathbf{u} = 0) by computing a pressure field p that corrects the velocity field to be divergence-free. This is typically done using a Poisson equation solver. 5. Projection: Subtract the pressure gradient from the velocity field to enforce incompressibility: \mathbf{u}^{new} = \mathbf{u}^{tentative} - 
abla p. 6. Diffusion: Apply viscous diffusion to the velocity field and thermal diffusion to the temperature/density field. 7. Render: Use the resulting coarse volumetric data with global illumination algorithms (e.g., photon maps, Monte Carlo volume rendering) or detail-enhancing techniques (e.g., splats texture mapped with phenomena detail) to visualize the fire. Formulas: The Navier-Stokes equations describe the change in velocity \mathbf{u} over time:  rac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} + (\mathbf{u} \cdot 
abla) \mathbf{u} = - rac{1}{ho} 
abla p + 
u 
abla^2 \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{f} Where:  rac{\partial \mathbf{u}}{\partial t} is the local acceleration. (\mathbf{u} \cdot 
abla) \mathbf{u} is the convective acceleration. - rac{1}{ho} 
abla p is the pressure gradient force. 
u 
abla^2 \mathbf{u} is the viscous diffusion term (drag). \mathbf{f} represents external forces like thermal buoyancy. Parameters: Grid Resolution: Low resolution is standard for real-time or efficient simulation. Viscosity (
u): Controls the drag/smoothness of the flow. Buoyancy Coefficient: Controls the strength of the upward thermal force. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Numerical instability can occur if the time step is too large relative to the grid resolution (CFL condition). Boundaries: Incorrect boundary conditions can cause artifacts or unrealistic flow behavior at domain edges. Detail Loss: Coarse grids lack high-frequency detail, necessitating post-processing or global illumination techniques for visual fidelity. A specific physics-based fire model using Navier-Stokes principles, often optimized for real-time rendering. Lamorlette and Foster Fire Model Detailed breakdown of the numerical solvers (pressure, advection, diffusion) used in these simulations. Navier-Stokes Solver Components The general class of methods using discrete grids for fluid dynamics, of which Navier-Stokes fire is a specific application. Grid-Based Simulation Time Complexity: High. Solving the Navier-Stokes equations requires iterative solvers (e.g., for pressure) at each time step, making it computationally expensive compared to procedural methods. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the grid volume (Nx \cdot Ny \cdot Nz), storing velocity and scalar fields. Performance: Historically slow, but modern SIMD processors and GPUs allow for significant speedups (order of magnitude or more). Strengths: Physically accurate behavior, realistic convection and buoyancy, natural turbulence. Limitations: Computationally intensive, requires post-processing (global illumination) to achieve high visual detail due to coarse grid usage. When to Use: When physical accuracy is prioritized over raw performance or procedural control. When Not to Use: When real-time performance on low-end hardware is critical without hardware acceleration, or when artistic control via noise functions is preferred. Originating from the application of fluid dynamics laws to computer graphics, this method was developed to improve upon procedural noise-based fire rendering. It represents fire as hot and turbulent gas, solving volumetric differential equations at low resolutions. The approach leverages advances in graphics hardware (SIMD processors) to make the numerical solvers feasible. name: Lamorlette and Foster Fire Model
head: Parametric Curve-Based Fire, Shrek Fire Model
body: The Lamorlette and Foster Fire Model is a mixed framework for simulating the macro-movement of fire, originally developed for the production of the motion picture Shrek. It addresses the problem of achieving a "holistic" visual appearance for fire, distinguishing it from the atomistic look of standard particle systems or the smoke-suited appearance of texture splats. The method sets itself apart by modeling individual flame elements as parametric space curves that evolve over time, rather than relying solely on discrete point particles or static volumetric fields. Inputs: A set of initial points defining the spine of flame elements. Wind field data (velocity and temperature fields). Procedural control parameters for placement, intensity, lifespan, shape, color, and size. Outputs: A set of rendered particles representing the visible flame (oxidization region). Data Structures: Parametric Curve: Defined by a sequence of control points interpolating the flame spine. Particle: A point sampled near the curve, carrying position, color, and opacity attributes. Implicit Surface: A cylindrical profile defining the oxidization region boundary. Steps: 1. Curve Initialization: Model individual flame elements as parametric space curves. Each curve interpolates a set of points defining the spine of the flame. 2. Curve Evolution: Evolve the curves over time using a combination of physics-based, procedural, and hand-defined wind fields. Physical properties are derived from statistical measurements of natural diffusion flames. The curves are frequently re-sampled to ensure continuity and to model flames generated from moving sources. Wind Dynamics: The motion is governed by the velocity of the gas rushing into surrounding air and temperature. Drag (shearing forces) causes rotation and mixing, leading to turbulent swirling. Turbulence is exaggerated if gas flows around solid objects, transitioning from smooth flow to chaotic mixing behind the object. 3. Curve Breaking: Allow curves to break, generating independently evolving flames with a limited lifespan. Engineering observations and stochastic assumptions provide heuristics for this process. 4. Implicit Surface & Sampling: Build an implicit surface representing the oxidization region (the visible part of the flame) using a cylindrical profile. Sample particles close to this region using a volumetric falloff function. 5. Buoyancy Noise: Apply procedural noise to the particles in the parameter space of the profile. Animate this noise to follow thermal buoyancy. 6. Turbulence Noise: Transform particles into the parametric space of the flame’s structural curve. Apply a second level of noise with a Kolmogorov frequency spectrum (derived from Navier-Stokes equations for turbulence) to provide turbulent detail. 7. Rendering: Render particles using either a volumetric method or a fast painterly method. Painterly Method: Simulates a painting-like quality with visible brush strokes using height and opacity maps. Color Blending: Adjust particle color based on neighbor properties to allow flame elements to visually merge in a realistic way. 8. Procedural Control: Apply procedural controls to govern placement, intensity, lifespan, and evolution in shape, color, size, and behavior of the flames. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lamorlettefosterfiremodel(initialspinepoints, windfields, controls): # Stage 1: Initialize parametric curves curves = [] for spinepts in initialspinepoints: curve = ParametricCurve.interpolate(spinepts) curves.append(curve) # Stage 2-3: Evolution and Breaking Loop for timestep in simulationtime: newcurves = [] for curve in curves: # Evolve curve using wind fields (velocity, temperature, drag) curve.evolve(windfields) # Re-sample for continuity and moving source support curve.resample() # Stochastic breaking heuristic if shouldbreak(curve, controls): # Generate independent sub-flames with limited lifespan subflames = curve.breakapart(controls.lifespan) newcurves.extend(subflames) else: newcurves.append(curve) curves = newcurves # Stage 4: Sample particles from oxidization region particles = [] for curve in curves: # Define implicit cylindrical surface for oxidization region implicitsurface = curve.buildcylindricalprofile() # Sample particles near the surface with volumetric falloff sampledpoints = implicitsurface.samplevolumetricfalloff() for pt in sampledpoints: particle = Particle(position=pt) particles.append(particle) # Stage 5: Apply buoyancy noise in profile parameter space for particle in particles: noise = proceduralnoise(particle.profileparams, timestep) noise.animatethermalbuoyancy() particle.position += noise # Stage 6: Apply turbulence noise in curve parametric space for particle in particles: # Transform to structural curve parametric space curveparams = particle.transformtocurvespace() # Kolmogorov frequency spectrum noise turbulencenoise = kolmogorovnoise(curveparams, timestep) particle.position += turbulencenoise # Stage 7: Render # Option A: Volumetric rendering # Option B: Painterly rendering for particle in particles: # Adjust color based on neighbors for visual merging neighborcolors = getneighborcolors(particle, particles) particle.color = blendcolor(particle.color, neighborcolors) if usepainterlymethod: renderpainterly(particle, heightmap, opacitymap) else: rendervolumetric(particle) return renderedimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The re-sampling of curves requires sufficient precision to maintain continuity, especially when modeling flames from moving sources. Degenerate Input: If wind fields are static or zero, the characteristic turbulent swirling may not manifest correctly, as it relies on the interaction between gas velocity and surrounding air. Boundary: The implicit surface definition must correctly bound the oxidization region to avoid sampling particles in non-visible areas. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The model involves multiple stages of curve evolution, particle sampling, and noise application, which can be computationally intensive depending on the number of curves and particles. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Storage is required for curve definitions, particle states, and wind field data. Measured Performance: The fast painterly method is described as a way to render the image quickly, but specific performance metrics (e.g., frames per second, resolution) are not provided in the sources. Strengths: Provides a holistic look for fire, superior to atomistic particle systems and better suited for fire than texture splats. Offers artistic control through procedural parameters. Limitations: Relies on heuristics and stochastic assumptions for curve breaking, which may require tuning for different fire types. When to use: When a holistic, production-quality fire appearance is needed, particularly in contexts where artistic control is prioritized over strict physical simulation. When not to use: When atomistic particle effects are desired, or when the scene primarily involves smoke or steam where texture splats are more appropriate. The Lamorlette and Foster Fire Model was developed for the motion picture Shrek by DreamWorks. It is described as a "very solid mixed framework for macro-movement of fire in a production system". The model draws on statistical measurements of natural diffusion flames and applies Navier-Stokes equations to turbulence (Kolmogorov frequency spectrum). It is cited as a key reference for realistic fire rendering in production environments. Realistic Real-Time Rendering of Fire in a Production System, https://clas.iusb.edu/math-compsci/prior-proposals/YVanzineProposal.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Image-order rendering
body: Image-order rendering generates images by iterating over pixels and computing the contribution of volumetric data along rays cast from the camera through each pixel. It sets itself apart from Object-order rendering by processing pixels rather than voxels, ensuring correct depth sorting and occlusion handling without explicit z-buffering of primitives. All image-order methods share the fundamental loop structure: for each pixel, a ray is defined in world space, intersected with the volume domain, and sampled/composited along its path. The ray is parameterized as r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. The traversal order is determined by the pixel's position in the image plane. Computes the ordered sequence of grid cells intersected by a ray, returning cell indices and entry/exit distances. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which volumetric data elements a ray passes through without performing expensive per-voxel bounding box intersection tests or fixed-distance sampling. It sets itself apart from Direct volume ray casting by providing the geometric traversal logic (the "where" and "when") rather than the shading/compositing logic (the "what"), and from Acceleration by operating on uniform or structured grids rather than hierarchical spatial partitioning structures like octrees. Choose it when precise voxel access is required for sampling or acceleration structures. Reduces computational cost by minimizing redundant sampling, skipping invisible data, or parallelizing work. It solves the bottleneck of evaluating the volume rendering integral for every ray or voxel. Unlike Image-order rendering which defines the traversal order (eye-space), acceleration methods optimize the content of that traversal—whether by skipping empty space, terminating rays early, or adapting resolution—without changing the fundamental image-order nature of the parent. Choose it when rendering high-resolution datasets or neural fields where per-voxel evaluation is prohibitive. Casts a ray through a 3D volume for every pixel, sampling scalar values, mapping them to RGBA via a transfer function, and compositing samples front-to-back using alpha blending. It differs from Isosurface and first-hit ray casting by allowing all voxels to contribute to the final image rather than stopping at the first opaque surface, and from Distance-field ray marching by using uniform step sizes rather than distance-field-guided steps. It replaces slice-stack methods by providing a solid volume appearance from any angle without edge-on gaps. Choose it for translucent media where internal structures must be visible through outer layers. Renders a volume by tracing rays from the eye and stopping at the first voxel (or interpolated point) where the scalar field crosses a specified threshold (isovalue), treating the volume as an opaque surface. Unlike Direct volume ray casting, which composites the entire ray path to simulate transparency, this method terminates traversal upon the first hit, offering higher performance for opaque structures and avoiding the visual artifacts of volume integration. It differs from Distance-field ray marching by operating on discrete scalar fields with threshold crossing rather than continuous signed distance functions, and from Ray-grid traversal by focusing on the specific intersection logic of the isosurface rather than general grid traversal optimization. Choose it for opaque structures where surface shading and lighting are prioritized over transparency. Finds surfaces by moving along a ray in repeated steps, using a signed distance field (SDF) to choose each step size adaptively, avoiding the tradeoff of fixed-step marching. Unlike naive fixed-step marching which uses a constant increment, sphere tracing uses the SDF value as the step size, ensuring the step is as large as possible without risk of overshooting. Unlike traditional rasterization, the visible shape is defined mathematically by a scene function, not by a triangle mesh. Choose it when rendering implicit geometry or procedural volumes without explicit voxel grids. Not given in the sources. Widely used in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and computer graphics for rendering volumetric datasets such as CT scans and MRI data.

name: Ray-grid traversal
head: Voxel traversal, Grid traversal, DDA traversal, Amanatides-Woo traversal
body: Ray-grid traversal determines the sequence of uniform grid cells (voxels or tiles) intersected by a ray, enabling efficient sampling and compositing in volume rendering. It solves the problem of enumerating grid intersections without missing thin cells or performing redundant work. Unlike hierarchical methods that skip empty space via tree structures, standard ray-grid traversal steps through every cell boundary along the ray path. It differs from Acceleration by focusing on the geometric stepping logic itself, and from Direct volume ray casting by providing the traversal indices required for the sampling phase. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of advancing analytically from one cell boundary to the next, avoiding fixed-distance sampling steps. The algorithm determines the next cell by comparing the distances to the upcoming boundaries on the x, y, and z axes, selecting the minimum distance to advance. Let the ray be defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized or unnormalized). The grid is defined by cell boundaries. For a uniform grid with voxel size v and dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz, the traversal calculates the distances to the next boundaries for each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: 1. Step Direction (\text{step}i): Determines the index increment direction. \text{step}i = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } di > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} If di = 0, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension, and the corresponding distance is treated as infinity. 2. Time/Distance Delta (\Delta ti or s{\Delta i}): The distance along the ray to traverse one voxel width. \Delta ti = \frac{vi}{|di|} \cdot \text{step}i \quad \text{or} \quad s{\Delta i} = \frac{\Delta xi}{|\widehat{d}i|} where vi is the voxel size and \widehat{d}i is the unit direction component. 3. Time/Distance to Next Boundary (t{max, i} or s{max, i}): The distance from the ray origin to the first boundary crossed in axis i. t{max, i} = \frac{\text{boundary}i - oi}{di} The initial boundary is determined by the starting voxel index. If the ray starts inside the grid, the initial boundary is the next one in the direction of travel. The core loop iterates while the ray remains within the grid bounds: 1. Identify the axis k with the minimum boundary distance: t{min} = \min(t{max, x}, t{max, y}, t{max, z}). 2. Record the current cell and the interval [t{entry}, t{min}]. 3. Advance the index in axis k: \text{index}k \leftarrow \text{index}k + \text{step}k. 4. Update the boundary distance for axis k: t{max, k} \leftarrow t{max, k} + \Delta tk. 5. Update t{entry} \leftarrow t{min}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddatraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsize, gridbounds): # Initialize current voxel index currentvoxel = [int(rayorigin[i] // voxelsize) for i in range(3)] currentvoxel = [max(gridbounds.min[i], min(gridbounds.max[i], currentvoxel[i])) for i in range(3)] # Step direction per axis step = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else (-1 if raydirection[i] < 0 else 0) for i in range(3)] # Distance to next boundary nextboundary = [(currentvoxel[i] + step[i]) voxelsize for i in range(3)] tmax = [(nextboundary[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] # Distance delta per axis tdelta = [voxelsize / abs(raydirection[i]) if raydirection[i] != 0 else 0.0 for i in range(3)] tentry = 0.0 while gridbounds.min[0] <= currentvoxel[0] <= gridbounds.max[0] and \ gridbounds.min[1] <= currentvoxel[1] <= gridbounds.max[1] and \ gridbounds.min[2] <= currentvoxel[2] <= gridbounds.max[2]: minidx = tmax.index(min(tmax)) texit = tmax[minidx] yield currentvoxel, tentry, texit currentvoxel[minidx] += step[minidx] tmax[minidx] += tdelta[minidx] tentry = texit Accelerates rendering by traversing a multi-dimensional hierarchy to adaptively select resolution levels based on error tolerance. A stochastic technique for unstructured tetrahedral meshes using coarse mesh hierarchies to bound extinction. Processes Matryoshka layers in front-to-back order to handle occlusion correctly. Generates a manifold mesh by traversing a dual grid constructed from a primal voxel grid. Maps 3D volumetric data to a 2D image plane by traversing rays from pixels into the volume. Accelerates rendering of irregular grids by exploiting spatial coherence via a sweep-plane paradigm. Combines analytical DDA logic with tree-aware node skipping for sparse volume trees. Advances ray origin in discrete steps using a precomputed octant mask to track traversal state. Iterates through levels of a grid mipmap to efficiently visit child voxels. Processes bundles of coherent rays through uniform grids slice-by-slice. Determines the sequence of uniform grid cells intersected by a ray. Traverses a uniform voxel grid in Z-order while compressing identical runs. Guarantees strict 4-connectivity by resolving boundary crossing ambiguities via stable sorting. Determines the sequence of nodes in a sparse voxel octree intersected by a ray. Traverses rays through multiple binary occupancy grids to generate ray intervals. Stores traversal steps as a ray template to accelerate parallel rays [Yagel-1992-DRT]. Accelerates rendering by replacing fixed-distance steps with analytical traversal. Adapts traversal algorithms to exploit GPU/SIMD architectural features. An alternative traversal algorithm that uses barycentric coordinates (u, v, w, x) to determine the child tetrahedron, avoiding explicit plane tests. The loop continues while childCounts[tetID] > 0 and rLevel ≤ maxDepth. Barycentric coordinates are calculated as u = \text{volume}(point,l,r,b)/\text{vol}, v = \text{volume}(point,t,b,r)/\text{vol}, w = \text{volume}(point,t,l,b)/\text{vol}, and x = 1 - (u + v + w). The child index is computed using boolean logic: tet = (RB × 4) + ((RB == TB) × 2) + inner, where RB is (u + v) < 0.5, TB is (v + w) < 0.5, and inner is (u < 0.5) & (v < 0.5) & (w < 0.5) & (x < 0.5). A hybrid CPU-GPU traversal strategy where the CPU traverses the KD-tree of AMR patches back-to-front, and the GPU traverses cells within a patch. Sub-patches are generated to ensure perspective-correct sorting of cells relative to the observer. The vertex shader modifies each index according to the current observer position to generate proper cell ordering. A medium traversal structure using a supergrid to allow empty and thin regions to be crossed in far fewer null collisions than paying for the densest voxel in the volume. The Medium::samplerealinteraction consumes null collisions in one fused C++ walk instead of iterating them in Python, sharing a single loop with the DDA traversal when a supergrid is used. It is faster than the global majorant approach because it avoids paying optixTrace for every null collision. The majorantresolutionfactor controls supergrid resolution (default 8), and majorantfactor is a safety factor (default 1.2). The 'homogeneous' medium type explicitly rejects the supergrid parameter. A CUDA device function that initializes the parameters for stepping through a voxel grid along a ray. A method to determine if a target isosurface lies within a ray segment defined by voxel entry/exit points, and to calculate its relative position for opacity/color contribution. Trilinear interpolation is used to get values at entry (V{in}) and exit (V{out}). Target values are classified into three categories: (1) strictly between V{in} and V{out}, (2) one endpoint within allowable window, (3) neither endpoint within window. For Category 1, the relative distance t is parameterized using linear interpolation. For Category 2, t is set to 0 or 1. Values are sorted by depth and effects calculated. A property defining the set of cells a ray can traverse to from its current cell, inspired by pixel connectivity in image processing. In 2D, there are 4-connectivity (orthogonal neighbors) and 8-connectivity (including diagonal neighbors). The Taxicab metric is |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2| and the Chebyshev metric is \max(|x1 - x2|, |y1 - y2|). An algorithm that traverses all blocks a ray intersects with, starting from closest to the camera, to measure the direct impact of block-walking on performance by writing to a scalar at each block visit. Block walking reduces the number of queries (acceleration structure accesses) by 5-10x compared to standard ray tracing, translating to a 1.5x average performance improvement in block traversal mode. However, when content becomes too sparse, block walking is not effective and can have a high cost. In blend mode, performance improvements shrink due to costly access to individual voxel values. A dispatcher function that selects the appropriate traversal variant based on the maximum range of the segment. It computes absolute deltas dx = |end.x - start.x| and dy = |end.y - start.y|, then maxRange = max(dx, dy). If maxRange < 256.0f, it calls traverseGridSegment16 (Q8.8 fixed-point); otherwise, it calls traverseGridSegment32 (Q24.8 fixed-point). A renderer for regular grids (rgridb) that separates primitive generation and rendering into two distinct steps, regenerating all primitives if the volume changes. Unlike the hgridf renderer, it does not support partial updates of dirty cells; it regenerates the entire primitive set upon volume change. All processors accumulate interpolated values along a ray independently. Contributions are sorted with respect to visibility order before composing the final image. Frame rate scales linearly with the number of processors. The foundational algorithm, known as the Amanatides-Woo algorithm or 3D DDA, was introduced by J. Amanatides and A. Woo in 'A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing', published in Eurographics '87. It was designed to efficiently list all voxel IDs traversed by a ray in a 3D grid. name: Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant
head: Woodcock tracker, stochastic ray marching with majorant
body: Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant is a stochastic ray marching technique for volume rendering on unstructured tetrahedral meshes that utilizes a coarse mesh hierarchy to compute a tighter majorant extinction value. It solves the problem of high null-collision rates in heterogeneous volumes by bounding the local extinction with a precomputed macrocell value, thereby reducing the number of rejected samples compared to using a global or loose majorant on most datasets. It differs from standard Woodcock tracking by integrating coarse mesh traversal logic to manage the majorant bounds, and from Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting by relying on stochastic free-path sampling rather than deterministic grid traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, maximum traversal distance t{\text{max}}, current coarse element ID (coarseTetID), macrocell majorant value M{\text{macro}}, and a transfer function \text{tf} mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Output: A color value if a collision occurs within t{\text{max}}, or false (transparent) if the ray exits the volume or exceeds t{\text{max}}. Data Structures: Macrocell Majorant (M{\text{macro}}): A scalar value representing the upper bound of extinction for a coarse mesh element. Tetrahedron Vertices (tetVertices): An array of four 3D coordinates defining the current tetrahedron. Sample Point (samplePoint): The 3D position in space where the scalar value is sampled. Parameters: t{\text{max}}: The maximum distance the ray is allowed to travel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Majorant: Compute the effective majorant M as the product of the transfer function's maximum opacity and the macrocell majorant: M = \text{tf.opacity} \times M{\text{macro}}. 2. Check Validity: If M \le 0, the ray is skipped and false is returned. 3. Set Exit Boundary: Initialize the exit distance for the current coarse element to the smallest representable float less than the current ray distance t to ensure the first sample is processed: t{\text{exit}} = \text{nextafter}(t, -\infty). 4. Initialize State: Set sampleTetID to 0 and tetVertices to an empty set. 5. Stochastic Step: Generate a random number r \in [0, 1). Advance the ray distance t using the Woodcock step formula: t \leftarrow t - \frac{\ln(1 - r)}{M}. 6. Check Max Distance: If t \ge t{\text{max}}, return false. 7. Calculate Sample Point: Compute the 3D position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. 8. Check Element Boundary: If t > t{\text{exit}}, the ray has crossed a coarse element boundary. Traverse the coarse mesh to find the new tetrahedron containing \mathbf{p}: (\text{sampleTetID}, \text{tetVertices}) \leftarrow \text{traverse}(\mathbf{p}, \text{coarseTetID}). Update the exit distance for the new tetrahedron by intersecting the ray with the tetrahedron faces: t{\text{exit}} \leftarrow \text{intersectFaces}(t, \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{d}, \text{tetVertices}). 9. Sample Data: Sample the scalar value s at \mathbf{p} using the current tetrahedron: s \leftarrow \text{sampleData}(\mathbf{p}, \text{sampleTetID}, \text{tetVertices}). 10. Check Transfer Function Range: If s is not within the transfer function's valid range, continue to the next iteration. 11. Get Color: Retrieve the color C and opacity \alpha from the transfer function: (C, \alpha) \leftarrow \text{tf.getColor}(s). 12. Acceptance Test: Perform the analog acceptance test. Generate a new random number r' \in [0, 1). If: \alpha \times \text{tf.opacity} \ge r' \times M return C. Otherwise, continue to the next iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def woodcocktrackingwithmacrocell(rayorigin, raydirection, tmax, coarsetetid, macrocellmajorant, tf): # 1. Initialize majorant majorant = tf.opacity macrocellmajorant if majorant <= 0: return False # 2. Initialize distance along ray t = 0.0 # 3. Set exit boundary texit = math.nextafter(t, -float('inf')) # 4. Initialize state sampletetid = 0 tetvertices = [] while True: # 5. Stochastic step r = random.random() t -= math.log(1.0 - r) / majorant # 6. Check max distance if t >= tmax: return False # 7. Calculate sample point samplepoint = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] # 8. Check element boundary if t > texit: sampletetid, tetvertices = traverse(samplepoint, coarsetetid) texit = intersectfaces(t, samplepoint, raydirection, tetvertices) # 9. Sample data scalar = sampledata(samplepoint, sampletetid, tetvertices) # 10. Check transfer function range if not tf.inrange(scalar): continue # 11. Get color color = tf.getcolor(scalar) # 12. Acceptance test rprime = random.random() if color.opacity tf.opacity >= rprime majorant: return color def traverse(point, coarsetetid): # Standard coarse mesh traversal to find the tetrahedron containing point # Returns (tetid, vertices) return coarsetetid, gettetvertices(coarsetetid) def intersectfaces(t, p, d, vertices): # Computes the exit distance of ray R(s) = p + sd from the tetrahedron # defined by vertices. Returns the smallest positive s > 0 added to t. minexit = float('inf') faces = [(0,1,2), (0,1,3), (0,2,3), (1,2,3)] for i, j, k in faces: v0, v1, v2 = vertices[i], vertices[j], vertices[k] n = cross(sub(v1, v0), sub(v2, v0)) denom = dot(n, d) if abs(denom) > 1e-9: dist = dot(n, sub(v0, p)) / denom if dist > 0: minexit = min(minexit, dist) return t + minexit def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def sampledata(point, tetid, vertices): return 0.0 # Standard point-in-tetrahedron scalar lookup Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overstepping: When using macrocell values, if the ray crosses a boundary into a denser region, the majorant may no longer be valid. The algorithm must restart traversal from the beginning of the next element to avoid missing collisions. Performance Degradation: On datasets with shallow trees or specific structures (e.g., Agulhas), macrocell optimizations can decrease performance due to the overhead of restarting element processing. Extends this method by integrating coarse mesh traversal for AMR data, using macrocell densities to provide tighter majorants than transfer function opacity alone. An alternative acceleration technique that decomposes the medium into homogeneous and heterogeneous components, allowing non-bounding control extinction. Rendering Performance: Tighter majorants reduce the number of null collisions, improving rendering times on most datasets. Memory Complexity: Low, as it primarily stores the coarse mesh structure and transfer function data. Measured Performance: On the Agulhas dataset, macrocell optimizations degraded performance due to traversal overhead. On other datasets, tighter majorants generally improved rendering times. Strengths: Reduces null collisions in heterogeneous volumes by providing tighter bounds than global majorants. Limitations: Performance can degrade on specific dataset structures (e.g., shallow trees) due to the cost of boundary traversal and restart logic. This method is described in the context of direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. It builds upon the principles of Woodcock tracking (null-collision method) and adapts them for unstructured tetrahedral meshes using a coarse mesh hierarchy to manage majorant values.
