name: Woodcock Tracking with Coarse Mesh and Macrocells
head: Null-collision Woodcock with macrocell majorant, Woodcock ray casting on AMR
body: This method performs volume rendering using Woodcock tracking (null-collision) within coarse mesh elements, utilizing macrocell densities to determine the majorant extinction value. It builds on Woodcock Tracking with Macrocell Majorant by integrating the traversal of a coarse mesh structure to manage the underlying adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. Using macrocell majorant values provides a tighter majorant than using only transfer function opacity, reducing null collisions and improving performance. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, maximum ray length (t{max}), coarse mesh structure, macrocell density values, transfer function (TF), and scalar field data. Outputs: Final pixel color. Data Structures: Coarse Mesh: A hierarchy of coarse tetrahedra. Each coarse element has an associated macrocellMajorant value. Macrocell Values: An array or map where macrocellValues[coarseID] stores the maximum macrocell density for that coarse element. Transfer Function: Provides tf.opacity (scalar to opacity mapping) and tf.getColor(scalar) (scalar to RGBA color). Refinement Tree: Used to locate the specific fine tetrahedron within a coarse element. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coarse Element Traversal: Call TraverseCoarseMesh(ray) to determine the current coarse element ID (coarseID), the back face distance (tBack), and the next face distance (tNextFace). If coarseID is -1, the ray has exited the volume. Return the background color. 2. Majorant Calculation: Retrieve the macrocell majorant: macrocellMajorant = macrocellValues[coarseID]. Call WoodcockElem with this majorant. Inside WoodcockElem, calculate the effective majorant: \sigma{max} = \text{tf.opacity} \times \text{macrocellMajorant} If \sigma{max} \le 0, return false (no emission/absorption possible). 3. Free Path Sampling: Sample a free path length using the majorant \sigma{max}: t{step} = -\frac{\log(1 - \text{rand}())}{\sigma{max}} Update the ray position: t{ray} = t{ray} + t{step} If t{ray} \ge t{max}, return false. 4. Tetrahedron Location: Calculate the sample point: P = \text{ray.org} + t{ray} \times \text{ray.dir} If the sample point is outside the current tetrahedron (checked against tExit), traverse the refinement tree to find the specific fine tetrahedron (sampleTetID) and its vertices (tetVertices). Update tExit to the distance to the exit face of the new tetrahedron. 5. Scalar Sampling and Acceptance: Sample the scalar value at P using sampleTetID and tetVertices. If the scalar is not in the transfer function range, continue the loop (null collision). Get the color: color = tf.getColor(scalar). Perform the null-collision acceptance test: \text{color.opacity} \times \text{tf.opacity} \ge \text{rand}() \times \sigma{max} If accepted, return color. Otherwise, treat as a null collision and continue the loop. 6. Boundary Handling: When stepping over to the next coarse element, if the previous volume was less dense, the free path might overstep the boundary. To fix this, set ray.t to just after the next coarse element's minimum t value in front of the ray, effectively taking a step back to the beginning of the next coarse element. This step is not needed if macrocell majorant values are not used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def woodcockcoarse(ray, macrocellvalues, tf, tmax): """ Main loop for Woodcock tracking on coarse mesh. ray: object with.org,.dir,.t (current t) macrocellvalues: dict mapping coarseid to max macrocell density tf: transfer function object with.opacity(scalar),.getcolor(scalar),.inrange(scalar) tmax: maximum ray length """ while True: # 1. Traverse coarse mesh coarseid, tback, tnextface = traversecoarsemesh(ray) if coarseid == -1: return backgroundcolor # 2. Get macrocell majorant macrocellmajorant = macrocellvalues[coarseid] # 3. Process element color = woodcockelem(ray, tback, coarseid, macrocellmajorant, tf, tmax) if color is not None: return color # 4. Handle boundary crossing # If we exited the element, reset t to just after the next face to prevent overstepping # due to density changes between elements ray.t = tnextface + epsilon def woodcockelem(ray, texit, coarsetetid, macrocellmajorant, tf, tmax): """ Woodcock tracking inside a single coarse element. texit: distance to the exit face of the current tetrahedron """ # Calculate effective majorant # Note: tf.opacity is typically the opacity at the specific scalar, # but here it seems to refer to a scaling factor or the max opacity for the element. # Based on source: majorant = tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # We assume tf.opacity here refers to the opacity scaling factor for the element # or is evaluated per sample. The source code snippet suggests: # majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # However, tf.opacity is usually scalar-dependent. # Looking at Algorithm 12 line 2: majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # And line 24: color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() majorant # This implies tf.opacity might be a constant for the element or the source # uses tf.opacity as a global scaling factor. # Let's follow the source literally: majorant is calculated once per element? # No, line 24 uses color.opacity tf.opacity. # If majorant is constant, then the acceptance test compares against it. # Let's assume tf.opacity in line 2 is a constant for the element, # or the source implies the majorant is based on the max opacity. # Given "maximum macrocell density... scaled with the opacity of the transfer function", # it likely means: sigmamax = maxtfopacity maxmacrocelldensity. # Re-reading Algorithm 12: # 2: majorant <- tf.opacity macrocellMajorant # This line is outside the while loop. So majorant is constant for the element. # This implies tf.opacity is a constant for the element (e.g., max opacity). sigmamax = tf.opacity macrocellmajorant if sigmamax <= 0: return None # Initialize tetrahedron info sampletetid = 0 tetvertices = [] while True: # Sample free path ray.t = ray.t - log(1 - rand()) / sigmamax if ray.t >= tmax: return None samplepoint = ray.org + ray.t ray.dir # Check if we are still in the current tetrahedron if ray.t > texit: # Traverse refinement tree to find the fine tetrahedron sampletetid, tetvertices = traverserefinementtree(samplepoint, coarsetetid) # Update texit to the exit face of the new tetrahedron texit = intersectfaces(ray.t, samplepoint, ray.dir, tetvertices) # Sample scalar scalar = sampledata(samplepoint, sampletetid, tetvertices) if not tf.inrange(scalar): continue color = tf.getcolor(scalar) # Acceptance test # Source: color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() majorant # Note: tf.opacity here is the same constant used for sigmamax? # If so, this simplifies to: color.opacity >= rand() macrocellmajorant # But let's stick to the source formula. if color.opacity tf.opacity >= rand() sigmamax: return color Performance: Using macrocell majorant values reduces null collisions compared to using only transfer function opacity, leading to better performance. Complexity: The complexity depends on the coarse mesh traversal and the refinement tree depth. The method allows for interactive frame rates on tested datasets. Memory: Requires storing coarse mesh structures, macrocell values, and the refinement tree. The transfer function and scalars reside in GPU memory. Limitations: Only emission and absorption are implemented; secondary effects are not supported. This method is part of a volume rendering system for tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) data. It was implemented alongside a ray marching method. The approach leverages the fact that transfer functions and scalars reside in GPU memory, allowing recalculation during rendering. name: Weighted Decomposition Tracking
head: Analog Decomposition Tracking, Decomposition Tracking
body: Weighted Decomposition Tracking accelerates free-path sampling in heterogeneous volumes by decomposing the medium into a homogeneous control component and a heterogeneous residual component. It reduces the number of expensive spatially-varying extinction lookups required by standard delta tracking while producing identical noise patterns and light paths. Unlike the analog variant, the weighted formulation permits non-bounding control extinctions and free-path-sampling coefficients, enabling efficient chromatic (spectral) collision handling without requiring non-negative residual extinction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current position \mathbf{x}, direction \omega, path throughput weight w (initialized to 1), constant control extinction coefficients \mua^c, \mus^c, constant free-path-sampling coefficient \bar{\mu}, and spatially varying functions for residual absorption \mua^r(\mathbf{x}), scattering \mus^r(\mathbf{x}), and null-collision \mun(\mathbf{x}). Output: Updated position, direction, and throughput weight after one collision event, or emitted radiance if absorption occurs. Data Structures: Control Component: Defined by constant scalar values \mua^c and \mus^c. Residual Component: Defined by spatially varying functions \mua^r(\mathbf{x}) and \mus^r(\mathbf{x}). Majorant: \bar{\mu} is a constant upper bound for the total extinction \mut(\mathbf{x}) across the volume or spectral band. In the weighted version, \bar{\mu} does not need to be a minorant of \mut(\mathbf{x}) at every point, but must satisfy \bar{\mu} > \mut^c. Null-Collision Coefficient: \mun(\mathbf{x}) = \bar{\mu} - \mut^c - \mut^r(\mathbf{x}). Parameters: \bar{\mu}: Free-path-sampling coefficient, typically chosen as the maximum total extinction in the scene. \mut^c: Control total extinction, computed as \mut^c = \mua^c + \mus^c. Octree Depth: Typically 8–10 to balance lookup reduction and traversal overhead. Formulas: The method samples one of five events: control absorption, control scattering, residual absorption, residual scattering, or null collision. Probabilities are defined as: Pa^c = \frac{\mua^c}{\bar{\mu}} Ps^c = \frac{\mus^c}{\bar{\mu}} Pa^r(\mathbf{x}) = \left(1 - \frac{\mut^c}{\bar{\mu}}\right) \frac{|\mua^r(\mathbf{x})|}{|\mua^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mus^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mun(\mathbf{x})|} Ps^r(\mathbf{x}) = \left(1 - \frac{\mut^c}{\bar{\mu}}\right) \frac{|\mus^r(\mathbf{x})|}{|\mua^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mus^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mun(\mathbf{x})|} Pn(\mathbf{x}) = \left(1 - \frac{\mut^c}{\bar{\mu}}\right) \frac{|\mun(\mathbf{x})|}{|\mua^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mus^r(\mathbf{x})| + |\mun(\mathbf{x})|} The denominator sums the absolute values of the residual and null coefficients. Algorithm Steps: The tracker loops indefinitely until a non-null collision occurs or emission is sampled. 1. Sample Free Path: Draw a uniform random number \zeta \in 0, 1) and compute t = -\ln(1-\zeta)/\bar{\mu}. 2. Advance Position: Update position \mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + t\omega. 3. Evaluate Probabilities: Compute Pa^c, Ps^c, Pa^r(\mathbf{x}), Ps^r(\mathbf{x}), Pn(\mathbf{x}) using the current position \mathbf{x} and constants. 4. Sample Event: Draw a uniform random number \xi \in [0, 1) and accumulate probabilities to determine the event. If \xi < Pa^c: Control absorption. The local weight factor is \mua^c/(\bar{\mu}Pa^c) = 1, so w remains unchanged. Return emitted radiance Le(\mathbf{x}, \omega) scaled by w. Else if \xi < Pa^c + Ps^c: Control scattering. The local weight factor is \mus^c/(\bar{\mu}Ps^c) = 1. Sample a new direction \omega from the [phase function p(\omega). Break the loop. Else if \xi < Pa^c + Ps^c + Pa^r(\mathbf{x}): Residual absorption. Update w \leftarrow w \cdot \mua^r(\mathbf{x})/(\bar{\mu}Pa^r(\mathbf{x})). Return emitted radiance scaled by w. Else if \xi < Pa^c + Ps^c + Pa^r(\mathbf{x}) + Ps^r(\mathbf{x}): Residual scattering. Update w \leftarrow w \cdot \mus^r(\mathbf{x})/(\bar{\mu}Ps^r(\mathbf{x})). Sample a new direction \omega from p(\omega). Break the loop. Else: Null collision. Update w \leftarrow w \cdot \mun(\mathbf{x})/(\bar{\mu}Pn(\mathbf{x})). Continue the loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def WeightedDecompositionTracking(x, omega, w, muac, musc, mubar, getmuar, getmusr, getmun): """ Performs one step of weighted decomposition tracking. Args: x: Current position (vec3) omega: Current direction (vec3) w: Current path throughput weight (float) muac: Control absorption coefficient (float, constant) musc: Control scattering coefficient (float, constant) mubar: Free-path-sampling coefficient (float, constant) getmuar: Function returning residual absorption at x (float) getmusr: Function returning residual scattering at x (float) getmun: Function returning null-collision coefficient at x (float) Returns: Tuple (newx, newomega, neww, eventtype) eventtype: 'ABSORB', 'SCATTER', or 'CONTINUE' """ mutc = muac + musc # 1. Sample free path zeta = randomuniform() t = -math.log(1.0 - zeta) / mubar # 2. Advance position x = x + t omega # 3. Evaluate coefficients and probabilities muar = getmuar(x) musr = getmusr(x) mun = getmun(x) # Denominator for residual/null probabilities denom = abs(muar) + abs(musr) + abs(mun) # Marginal probability of NOT sampling control pnotc = 1.0 - (mutc / mubar) # Probabilities Pac = muac / mubar Psc = musc / mubar if denom > 0: Par = pnotc (abs(muar) / denom) Psr = pnotc (abs(musr) / denom) Pn = pnotc (abs(mun) / denom) else: # Degenerate case: no residual/null coefficients. Par = 0.0 Psr = 0.0 Pn = 0.0 # 4. Sample event xi = randomuniform() if xi < Pac: # Control Absorption return (x, omega, w, 'ABSORB') elif xi < Pac + Psc: # Control Scattering newomega = samplephasefunction(omega) return (x, newomega, w, 'SCATTER') elif xi < Pac + Psc + Par: # Residual Absorption weightfactor = muar / (mubar Par) neww = w weightfactor return (x, omega, neww, 'ABSORB') elif xi < Pac + Psc + Par + Psr: # Residual Scattering weightfactor = musr / (mubar Psr) neww = w weightfactor newomega = samplephasefunction(omega) return (x, newomega, neww, 'SCATTER') else: # Null Collision weightfactor = mun / (mubar Pn) neww = w weightfactor return (x, omega, neww, 'CONTINUE') def randomuniform() -> float: """Returns a uniform random float in 0, 1). """ import random return random.random() def samplephasefunction(omega: tuple) -> tuple: """Samples a new direction from the phase function p(omega). """ # Standard phase function sampling implementation return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Bounding Control: If \mut^c > \mut(\mathbf{x}) at some point, \mun(\mathbf{x}) becomes negative. The weighted formulation handles this via absolute values in probabilities and signed weights, but a loose \bar{\mu} increases the variance of the path throughput rapidly. Zero Denominator: If the residual and null coefficients are all zero (e.g., homogeneous medium where \mut^c = \mut(\mathbf{x}) and \bar{\mu} = \mut^c), the denominator is zero. In this case, Pa^r, Ps^r, Pn are zero, and only control events are possible. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise if \mut^c is very close to \bar{\mu}, making Pa^c and Ps^c dominate and residual probabilities negligible. A variant designed for chromatic (spectral) rendering by vectorizing collision coefficients across wavelengths \lambda. Control extinction coefficients \mua^c(\lambda) and \mus^c(\lambda) are set to the minimum values across all wavelengths, while \bar{\mu} bounds the maximum total extinction across all wavelengths. Probabilities are computed using vectorized operations. When a control component is sampled, the local collision weight is a vector of ones (1, \dots, 1)^{N\lambda}, avoiding per-wavelength weight updates for the control branch. Time Complexity: The number of spatially-varying extinction lookups is reduced compared to standard delta tracking. The relative cost \rho = N{dcmp}/N{delta} = 1 - \mut^c/\bar{\mu} when \mut^c is a minorant. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the [octree structure (typically depth 8–10) and voxel data (e.g., VDB). Measured Performance: In a thick cloud scene, decomposition tracking avoided 42% of extinction lookups required by delta tracking, and 58% in a thin cloud scene. With octree depth 8, lookup time reduced from 1030s to 536s, and tracker time from 299s to 280s in a thick cloud scene. Strengths: Identical noise patterns to delta tracking; significant reduction in lookup costs for heterogeneous volumes; handles chromatic coefficients efficiently in the weighted variant. Limitations: Requires tight bounds for control and residual components for optimal performance; octree traversal overhead increases with depth; if \mut^c > \min(\mut(\mathbf{x})), variance increases and performance degrades. When to Use: Heterogeneous volumes with significant spatial variation in extinction, especially when spectral accuracy is required. When Not to Use: Homogeneous volumes (no benefit), or when tight bounds cannot be computed efficiently. Weighted Decomposition Tracking was introduced in the paper "Spectral and Decomposition Tracking for Rendering Heterogeneous Volumes" by Novák et al.. It builds on the concept of decomposition tracking for transmittance estimation [Novák et al. 2014] and extends it to free-path sampling. The analog version was previously limited by the requirement for non-negative residual extinction, which prevented spectral rendering. The weighted version removes this limitation, enabling efficient spectral tracking. It is used in production path tracers with VDB voxel storage and octree acceleration structures. name: Ray Marching with Octant Masking
head: Ray march, Ray struct
body: Ray Marching with Octant Masking advances a ray origin in discrete steps through a voxel grid, using a precomputed octant mask to track traversal direction and state. It builds on standard ray-grid traversal principles by maintaining a fixed-step march loop rather than analytically computing exact boundary crossings. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, and a step amount. Outputs: Updated ray origin, traversal state, and visibility mask. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Ray struct, which contains origin (Vector), direction (Vector), negdir (Vector, unused in the reference implementation), and initorigin (Vector, private). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize initorigin with the starting ray position. 2. Clamp any direction component with magnitude below \epsilon to \pm\epsilon with the same sign to prevent division by zero or degenerate cases. 3. Compute an 8-bit octantmask based on the direction signs: bit 2 (value 4) is set if direction.x >= 0, bit 1 (value 2) if direction.y >= 0, and bit 0 (value 1) if direction.z >= 0. 4. Advance the ray origin by \mathbf{o} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \times \text{amount} using the march function. 5. Track traversal progress using squaredistance(), which computes (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{init\origin})^2 to check against maximum bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin.copy() self.direction = direction.copy() self.negdir = direction.copy() # Unused in reference implementation self.initorigin = origin.copy() self.clampdirection() def clampdirection(self): epsilon = 1e-6 for i in range(3): if abs(self.direction[i]) < epsilon: self.direction[i] = epsilon if self.direction[i] >= 0 else -epsilon def octantmask(self): mask = 0 if self.direction[0] >= 0: mask |= 4 if self.direction[1] >= 0: mask |= 2 if self.direction[2] >= 0: mask |= 1 return mask def march(self, amount): self.origin = self.origin + self.direction amount return self def squaredistance(self): return sum((self.origin[i] - self.initorigin[i]) 2 for i in range(3)) Edge Cases: Zero direction components are clamped to \pm\epsilon to avoid numerical instability. Boundary checks rely on external logic comparing squaredistance() against a maximum squared distance, as the core march function does not inherently validate grid bounds. This method renders dense voxel data by combining geometry shader instancing for component-level bounding boxes with ray marching through dense volume textures for the interior. It sets itself apart from pure instancing or static vertex buffers by using a neighbor-sensitive bitmask to determine voxel visibility based on adjacent components, effectively hiding internal faces without storing dense geometry for every voxel. This hybrid approach allows for dynamic updates without recomputing complex meshes while avoiding the high vertex count of instanced cubes. It is chosen when dynamic voxel updates are required without heavy mesh recomputation, and it builds on Ray Marching with Octant Masking by replacing octant-based traversal with uniform grid ray marching through a 2D array texture. Time complexity is O(N) where N is the number of steps, with O(1) work per step. Memory complexity is O(1) auxiliary space for the ray state. Measured performance with specific hardware, resolution, and scene: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths include simple implementation, low overhead per step, and easy integration with GPU shaders. Limitations include fixed step size potentially causing aliasing or missed features if too large, and lower efficiency than analytical traversal for sparse data since it samples uniformly along the path. When to use: dense voxel rendering where simplicity and uniform sampling are prioritized over precise boundary detection. The method is documented in the open-source project zazen by Gabriel Muller, which implements a voxel ray marcher using this specific octant masking technique. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Voxel Textures with Neighbor-Sensitive Masking
head: Hybrid Geometry-Shader-spawned cubes with ray marched volume textures, Voxel Mask Ray Marching
body: This method renders dense voxel data by combining geometry shader instancing for component-level bounding boxes with ray marching through dense volume textures for the interior. It utilizes a neighbor-sensitive bitmask to determine voxel visibility based on adjacent components, effectively hiding internal faces without storing dense geometry for every voxel. Unlike pure instancing or static vertex buffers, this hybrid approach allows for dynamic updates without recomputing complex meshes while avoiding the high vertex count of instanced cubes. It builds on Ray Marching with Octant Masking by replacing octant-based traversal with uniform grid ray marching through a 2D array texture. Inputs: gsobjectPosition: vec3, the position of the component in world space. gsneighbormaterialmipmap: ivec3, flat input from geometry shader. x: Bits 0-5 are neighbor material flags; bits 24-31 are materialIndex. y: codes.x for neighbor material. z: LOD level index (mipmap level). gstexCoord: vec3, texture coordinates within the component box. ucomponentTex: isampler2DArray, uniform volume texture storing voxel data. Each texel fetch returns a 2D code (ivec2). cmWorldView: mat4x4, world-view matrix. cmInverseWorldView: mat4x4, inverse world-view matrix. cmaxTexRes: int, maximum texture resolution used to calculate LOD-dependent texel size. Outputs: fragColor: vec4, the final color of the fragment. Voxel Mask: An integer bitmask where each bit represents a side of the voxel (bits 0-5) and one bit (bit 6, 0x40) represents non-side-dependent voxels. The mask is computed as: \text{voxelMask} = 0x40 \mid ((\sim \text{gs\neighbor\material\mipmap}.x) \ \& \ 0x3f) Visibility is determined by combining this mask with the texture mask using a logical AND: (codes.y & voxelMask) == 0 indicates the voxel is not visible. Ray Marching State: rayPos: ivec3, current voxel coordinates in the texture. d: vec3, distance to the next plane crossing along each axis. projLength: vec3, projected distance between planes (1 / |\text{dir}|). dirSign: ivec3, sign of the view direction components (1 if \ge 0, -1 if < 0). 1. Compute Component-Space Position: Calculate the position in chunk/component space: \text{chunkSpacePos} = \text{gs\objectPosition} + \text{gs\texCoord} - 0.5 2. Transform View Direction: Transform the view direction to chunk space: \text{viewDir} = \text{normalize}((\text{vec4}(\text{chunkSpacePos}, 1) \times \text{c\mWorldView}).\text{xyz}) \text{chunkSpaceDir} = \text{viewDir} \times \text{mat3x3}(\text{c\mInverseWorldView}) 3. Calculate Texture Resolution: Determine the current texture size based on LOD: \text{texSize} = \text{c\maxTexRes} / (1 \ll \text{gs\neighbor\material\mipmap}.z) 4. Initialize Ray Marching: Compute direction signs: \text{dirSign}.x = (\text{chunkSpaceDir}.x < 0.0) ? -1: 1 \text{dirSign}.y = (\text{chunkSpaceDir}.y < 0.0) ? -1: 1 \text{dirSign}.z = (\text{chunkSpaceDir}.z < 0.0) ? -1: 1 Calculate initial voxel position and ray position: \text{voxelPos} = \text{gs\texCoord} \times (\text{texSize} - 0.00001) \text{rayPos} = \text{ivec3}(\text{voxelPos}) Compute projected lengths and initial distances: \text{absDir} = |\text{chunkSpaceDir}| \text{projLength} = 1.0 / (\text{absDir} + 0.0001) d = \text{voxelPos} - \text{rayPos} Adjust d based on direction signs: If \text{dirSign}.x == 1, d.x = 1 - d.x (same for y, z). d = d \times \text{projLength} 5. Ray March Loop: If materialIndex != 0 and texSize > 1: Fetch initial voxel code: \text{codes} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{u\componentTex}, \text{ivec3}(\text{rayPos}.x + \text{rayPos}.y \times \text{texSize}, \text{rayPos}.z, \text{materialIndex}), \text{gs\voxel\material\mipmap}.z).\text{xy} While (codes.y & voxelMask) == 0: Determine step direction: If d.x < d.y or d.z < d.y: If d.x < d.z: Step in X. \text{rayPos}.x += \text{dirSign}.x d.yz -= d.x d.x = \text{projLength}.x Else: Step in Z. \text{rayPos}.z += \text{dirSign}.z d.xy -= d.z d.z = \text{projLength}.z Else: Step in Y. \text{rayPos}.y += \text{dirSign}.y d.xz -= d.y d.y = \text{projLength}.y Boundary Check: If \text{rayPos} \ge \text{ivec3}(\text{texSize}, \text{texSize}, \text{texSize}) or \text{rayPos} < \text{ivec3}(0, 0, 0), discard fragment. Fetch next voxel code: \text{codes} = \text{texelFetch}(\text{u\componentTex}, \text{ivec3}(\text{rayPos}.x + \text{rayPos}.y \times \text{texSize}, \text{rayPos}.z, \text{materialIndex}), \text{gs\voxel\material\mipmap}.z).\text{xy} 6. Estimate Normal: Calculate distance to plane intersection: d = |d - \text{projLength}| Determine normal based on which axis had the smallest distance (indicating the plane crossed): If d.x < 0.0001: \text{normal} = -\text{dirSign}.x \times \text{vec3}(\text{c\mWorldView}[0][0], \text{c\mWorldView}[1][0], \text{c\mWorldView}[2][0]) Else if d.y < 0.0001: \text{normal} = -\text{dirSign}.y \times \text{vec3}(\text{c\mWorldView}[0][1], \text{c\mWorldView}[1][1], \text{c\mWorldView}[2][1]) Else if d.z < 0.0001: \text{normal} = -\text{dirSign}.z \times \text{vec3}(\text{c\mWorldView}[0][2], \text{c\mWorldView}[1][2], \text{c\mWorldView}[2][2]) Normalize the normal: \text{normal} = \text{normalize}(\text{normal}) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): # 1. Compute Component-Space Position chunkSpacePos = gsobjectPosition + gstexCoord - 0.5 # 2. Transform View Direction viewDir = normalize((vec4(chunkSpacePos, 1) cmWorldView).xyz) chunkSpaceDir = viewDir mat3x3(cmInverseWorldView) # 3. Calculate Texture Resolution texSize = cmaxTexRes / (1 << gsneighbormaterialmipmap.z) # 4. Initialize Ray Marching dirSign = ivec3(1, 1, 1) if chunkSpaceDir.x < 0.0: dirSign.x = -1 if chunkSpaceDir.y < 0.0: dirSign.y = -1 if chunkSpaceDir.z < 0.0: dirSign.z = -1 voxelPos = gstexCoord (texSize - 0.00001) rayPos = ivec3(voxelPos) absDir = abs(chunkSpaceDir) projLength = 1.0 / (absDir + 0.0001) d = voxelPos - rayPos if dirSign.x == 1: d.x = 1.0 - d.x if dirSign.y == 1: d.y = 1.0 - d.y if dirSign.z == 1: d.z = 1.0 - d.z d = d projLength # 5. Ray March Loop materialIndex = gsneighbormaterialmipmap.x >> 24 if materialIndex != 0 and texSize > 1: # Compute voxel mask voxelMask = 0x40 | ((~gsneighbormaterialmipmap.x) & 0x3f) # Fetch initial code texCoord = ivec3(rayPos.x + rayPos.y texSize, rayPos.z, materialIndex) codes = texelFetch(ucomponentTex, texCoord, gsneighbormaterialmipmap.z).xy while (codes.y & voxelMask) == 0: # Determine step direction if d.x < d.y or d.z < d.y: if d.x < d.z: rayPos.x += dirSign.x d.yz -= d.x d.x = projLength.x else: rayPos.z += dirSign.z d.xy -= d.z d.z = projLength.z else: rayPos.y += dirSign.y d.xz -= d.y d.y = projLength.y # Boundary Check if any(rayPos >= ivec3(texSize, texSize, texSize)) or any(rayPos < ivec3(0, 0, 0)): discard() # Fetch next code texCoord = ivec3(rayPos.x + rayPos.y texSize, rayPos.z, materialIndex) codes = texelFetch(ucomponentTex, texCoord, gsneighbormaterialmipmap.z).xy # 6. Estimate Normal d = abs(d - projLength) normal = vec3(0.0) if d.x < 0.0001: normal = -dirSign.x vec3(cmWorldView[0][0], cmWorldView[1][0], cmWorldView[2][0]) elif d.y < 0.0001: normal = -dirSign.y vec3(cmWorldView[0][1], cmWorldView[1][1], cmWorldView[2][1]) elif d.z < 0.0001: normal = -dirSign.z vec3(cmWorldView[0][2], cmWorldView[1][2], cmWorldView[2][2]) normal = normalize(normal) # Output color (implementation specific) fragColor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Placeholder for shading cmaxTexRes: The maximum texture resolution. Typical value is not explicitly stated as a number, but used to calculate texSize. Boundary Check: If rayPos exceeds texture bounds (>= texSize or < 0), the fragment must be discarded to prevent out-of-bounds access. LOD Artifacts: Computing LOD in the fragment shader causes artifacts because a LOD seam can run through a single component, creating holes. LOD is computed in the geometry shader instead. The parent method using octant-based traversal. This method replaces it with uniform grid ray marching through volume textures for better performance on dense data. A related technique using octrees for efficient ray-casting of 3D textures. This method differs by using uniform grids and volume textures, avoiding the complexity of octree traversal for dynamic transformations. Time Complexity: The method reduces frame time from over 20ms to 3-4ms on a notebook GTX850M for 62,663 components with 16x16x16 voxels each. Memory Complexity: Uses volume textures for dense internal data, avoiding the high vertex count of instanced cubes. Performance: Renders approximately 256 million theoretical voxels in 4.45ms on a notebook GTX850M. Strengths: Allows dynamic updates without recomputing complex meshes; avoids high vertex count; efficient for dense voxel data. Limitations: More sensitive to screen resolution; LOD artifacts if computed in fragment shader. When to Use: When rendering dense voxel data with dynamic updates and a blocky aesthetic is desired. When Not to Use: When continuous surfaces are required (e.g., marching cubes) or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained. This method was developed by Johannes Jendersie for the project Monolith, addressing the unbearable 20ms frame time of previous approaches. It was introduced in May 2015. The technique leverages the observation that components consist of the same voxel patterns repeatedly, allowing for a hybrid approach of geometry shader instancing and ray marching. It was used to render stone and water components with 16x16x16 voxels each. name: Hierarchical Grid Traversal
head: Hierarchical Grid Intersection, Ray-Mipmap Traversal
body: Hierarchical Grid Traversal is a ray-grid traversal algorithm that accelerates volume rendering by iterating through levels of a grid mipmap (hierarchical grid tree). It solves the problem of expensive fine-grained sampling in large volumes by recursively visiting child voxels only if the ray intersects the parent voxel's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Unlike flat grid traversal methods such as DDA Traversal which step through every voxel, this method skips empty or inactive regions at coarse levels, descending into finer grids only where necessary. It sets itself apart from Octree and Tree Traversal by using a fixed-depth, array-based mipmap structure with lookup tables rather than pointer-based nodes, optimizing for memory locality and batch processing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a hierarchical grid structure (mipmap) with L levels; a precomputed lookup table (tableslist) mapping coarse voxel indices to child indices and coordinates; maxlevel (the depth of the hierarchy); cubesize (physical size of a voxel at the current level). Output: A list of voxel grid positions at the maximum level (maxlevel) that are intersected by the ray. Data Structures: Lookup Table (tableslist): A list of arrays, one per level. Each row corresponds to a coarse voxel. Columns 0–7: Indices of the 8 child voxels (or -1 if the child is empty/invalid). Columns 8–10: The 3D grid coordinates (x, y, z) of the coarse voxel. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. State: cubetouchedidx: A list of indices of voxels at the current level that the ray intersects. Parameters: maxlevel: The maximum depth of the mipmap hierarchy. The loop runs from level 0 to maxlevel inclusive. cubesize: The physical size of a voxel at level l. For a base grid resolution of 256 units, cubesize at level l is calculated as 256 / 2^l. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set cubetouchedidx to [0], representing the root voxel index. Initialize newlist as an empty list. Initialize cubeorilist as an empty list to store final hits. 2. Iterate through Levels: For each level l from 0 to maxlevel: Retrieve the lookup table for the current level: table = tableslist[l]. Compute the physical voxel size for this level: currentcubesize = 256.0 / (2 l). For each voxel index i in cubetouchedidx: 1. Retrieve Voxel Bounds: Get the voxel's 3D grid coordinates from the table: gridcoords = table[i, 8:11]. Calculate the physical origin: cubeori = gridcoords currentcubesize. Calculate the physical end: cubeend = cubeori + currentcubesize. 2. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute the intersection of the ray with the AABB defined by cubeori and cubeend. This yields a near distance tn and a far distance tf. If the ray does not intersect the AABB, tn > tf or the intersection is behind the ray origin. 3. Check Intersection: If tn \le tf (intersection exists and is in front of the ray): If l == maxlevel: Append the voxel's grid position gridcoords to cubeorilist. If l < maxlevel: Extract the 8 child indices from the table: children = table[i, 0:8]. Filter out invalid children (marked as -1): mask = children != -1. Convert valid indices to integers and add them to newlist. Update State: Set cubetouchedidx to newlist. Reset newlist to an empty list for the next level. If cubetouchedidx is empty, terminate early. 3. Return Result: Return cubeorilist containing the grid positions of voxels touched at the maximum level. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalgridtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, tableslist, maxlevel): """ Traverses a hierarchical grid mipmap to find intersected voxels at the finest level. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array, ray origin in world space. raydirection: (3,) array, ray direction in world space. tableslist: List of arrays, where tableslist[l] is the lookup table for level l. Each row has shape (11,): [child0,..., child7, x, y, z]. maxlevel: int, the maximum depth of the hierarchy. Returns: cubeorilist: List of (3,) arrays, grid coordinates of intersected voxels at maxlevel. """ cubetouchedidx = [0] # Start with root voxel index cubeorilist = [] for level in range(maxlevel + 1): table = tableslist[level] newlist = [] currentcubesize = 256.0 / (2 level) for i in cubetouchedidx: # Retrieve voxel coordinates and bounds gridcoords = table[i, 8:11] cubeori = gridcoords currentcubesize cubeend = cubeori + currentcubesize # Compute ray-AABB intersection tn, tf = intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, cubeori, cubeend) # Check if intersection exists if tn is not None and tn <= tf: if level == maxlevel: # At the finest level, record the voxel position cubeorilist.append(gridcoords) else: # Not at the finest level, collect child indices children = table[i, 0:8] # Filter out invalid children (-1) mask = children != -1 validchildren = children[mask] newlist.extend(validchildren) cubetouchedidx = newlist if not cubetouchedidx: break return cubeorilist def intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, aabbmin, aabbmax): """ Computes the intersection of a ray with an AABB using the slab method. Returns (tn, tf) where tn is the near intersection distance and tf is the far intersection distance. Returns (None, None) if no intersection exists. """ tn = -float('inf') tf = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0.0: # Ray is parallel to axis; check if origin is within slab if rayorigin[i] < aabbmin[i] or rayorigin[i] > aabbmax[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (aabbmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (aabbmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tn = max(tn, t1) tf = min(tf, t2) if tn > tf: return None, None return tn, tf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-Length Ray: If the ray direction is zero or the ray has no length, the intersection test should return no intersection. Precision Issues: When the ray is far from the grid, floating-point precision errors in the AABB intersection test may cause incorrect culling. A small epsilon may be needed for robustness. Corner Intersections: Using a small epsilon to clip ray spans may clip tiny corner intersections. Empty Voxels: The lookup table must correctly mark empty children with -1 to avoid traversing non-existent nodes. Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates ray casting by traversing a multi-dimensional hierarchy (mdh) to adaptively choose the resolution level for evaluating volume data. It solves the problem of expensive ray traversal in large volumes by approximating homogeneous regions with least-squares trilinear coefficients, allowing the renderer to skip fine-grained sampling in unimportant or smooth areas. Unlike sibling methods that rely on simple opacity thresholds or constant-value homogeneity, this method uses a user-defined error tolerance and data importance weighting to control refinement, providing a balance between image quality and performance. A method to avoid computing all scalar values regardless of visibility by partitioning the volume into smaller sub-volumes with similar properties based on the transfer function. The opacity map corresponds to a region of the frame buffer and stores the minimum opacity of the frame buffer pixels found within that region. It groups scalar values within a certain range together based on the transfer function to define sub-volume properties. It uses a kd-tree to render the partitioned volume with correct visibility order, where each node is associated with a sub-volume. It culls and clips each sub-volume against an opacity map. It reported 10 fps for the Engine data set using a 2.5 GHz Pentium-IV and a nVidia GeForce4 graphics adapter. Hierarchical Voxel Traversal is a recursive raycasting algorithm designed to traverse nested voxel structures, such as chunks containing subvoxels, to find intersections. It distinguishes itself from flat traversal methods by transforming rays into local subvoxel space when entering a detail voxel, allowing for efficient handling of nested voxel data. Unlike First Active Voxel Detection which focuses on finding the first non-empty voxel, this method fully traverses the hierarchy to compute precise intersections within detail voxels. XBrickMap is a space-partitioning ray traversal algorithm for 3-level hierarchical voxel grids that uses 4^3 occupancy bitmasks to skip empty regions via bitwise tests. It improves upon simpler skipping methods by using tiled bitmasks to perform hierarchical skips of 4^3, 2^3, and 1^3 cuboids, while left-packing empty bricks within sectors to save memory. It is distinguished from its sibling Hierarchical Grid Traversal by its specific use of compacted bitmasks for random access and its support for arbitrary in-place edits within bricks. A spherical coordinate voxel traversal algorithm that traces a ray with unit direction over a spherical voxel grid, returning a vector of the spherical coordinate voxels traversed. It computes intersections with spherical shells, polar cones, and azimuthal wedges directly, handling the singularity at the origin by starting traversal at the first non-zero radial shell. First Active Voxel Detection determines if a ray intersects an active value at any level of a hierarchical grid and identifies the first such voxel or tile. It solves the problem of efficiently skipping empty space in sparse volume data structures by performing empty-space ray-marching at all tree levels using a Hierarchical DDA (HDDA). Unlike standard linear traversal, it leverages the hierarchical structure to jump over inactive regions, setting the intersection time and index upon the first hit. Hierarchical and block-based data structures organize volumetric data into a multi-resolution hierarchy of uniform blocks (bricks) or spatial subdivisions (octrees) to accelerate ray traversal and rendering. This approach serves as a compromise between the memory overhead of dense grids and the complexity of unstructured meshes, preferred by many practitioners for its balance of performance and implementation simplicity. It enables efficient empty-space skipping, early ray termination, and adaptive resolution sampling by allowing the renderer to skip large empty regions or sample coarse data for distant objects. This method accelerates ray tracing through sparse volumetric data by introducing a two-level occupancy hierarchy (super-bricks and bricks) to skip large empty regions, while maintaining pixel-identical output to the fine per-voxel DDA. It solves the performance bottleneck of traversing empty space by verifying emptiness at a coarser granularity and using an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for early termination, ensuring exactness by only skipping verified empty blocks and terminating only when the ray definitively passes the occupied volume. Octree-based traversal accelerates rendering by recursively navigating a hierarchical spatial subdivision (octree) to skip empty or low-detail regions, thereby reducing the number of intersection tests and sampling operations. It solves the performance bottleneck of dense voxel traversal by allowing rays to take larger steps through empty space. Unlike Hierarchical Grid Traversal which uses fixed-level mipmap grids, this family explicitly uses regular 2x2x2 (or 2x2 in 2D) subdivision to build a sparse hierarchy, distinguishing it from siblings that may focus on hash grids or specific traversal optimizations. Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures is a family of volume rendering optimization techniques that reduce computational cost by identifying and bypassing inactive (transparent or empty) regions of a volume dataset before or during ray sampling. Unlike methods that rely on hardware occlusion culling or ray coherence, this family uses explicit secondary data structures—such as min-max blocks, occupancy grids, BVHs, or hybrid trees—to store metadata about the spatial distribution of active data. This allows rays to determine entry and exit points of active regions analytically or via coarse traversal, skipping large intervals of empty space that would otherwise require expensive texture lookups and compositing operations. Multi-level Grid Structures are a family of hierarchical acceleration techniques for ray tracing and volume rendering that organize spatial data into a hierarchy of uniform grids (often arranged as mipmaps or nested blocks) to efficiently skip empty regions and adapt resolution to local density. Unlike flat uniform grids which suffer from excessive memory usage or traversal overhead in sparse scenes, or octrees which may break SIMD coherence, this family uses fixed-depth or adaptive uniform subdivisions to balance memory locality and traversal speed. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like KD-Tree Partitioned Volume Rendering by maintaining the regular memory access patterns of grid structures while providing hierarchical empty-space skipping. Quadtree Raycasting is a recursive ray-quadtree intersection algorithm that traverses a 2D quadtree to find the first hit node. It solves the problem of efficiently locating the first occupied voxel in a hierarchical 2D grid by handling ray direction flipping via a mask to ensure consistent traversal order regardless of ray direction. Grid Sphere Traversal (GST) is a ray-grid traversal method that performs sphere tracing through a dense grid of Signed Distance Function (SDF) values. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing empty regions in SDF-based rendering by using a hierarchy of SDF grids where lower-resolution levels encode larger SDF values to accelerate step sizes. It is distinguished from its siblings by performing the entire traversal in shader code using dense grids, whereas alternatives like Sparse Voxel Set leverage DXR hardware acceleration for BVH traversal. A CUDA kernel that marches rays through one or more axis-aligned voxel grids using precomputed, sorted entry/exit intersections to generate sample points and interval boundaries. It handles empty cells by skipping them and fills continuous segments, supporting both fixed step sizes and cone-angle-aware adaptive stepping. It sets itself apart from standard DDA by decoupling the grid boundary traversal from the sample generation, allowing for variable step sizes that scale with distance from the camera origin. Constructs a lookup table for hierarchical grid traversal. It maps coarse grid voxels to their fine grid children. The table is built from a fine grid and a coarse grid mask. It identifies occupied voxels in the fine grid and assigns a unique index to each. It extracts the 8 sub-grid regions corresponding to the 8 children of a coarse voxel by striding the fine grid indices. It flattens these sub-grids and filters them using the coarse grid mask to select only the children that belong to occupied coarse voxels. It initializes the table with shape [numcoarsevoxels, 11] (8 child indices + 3 coordinates), filled with -1. It populates columns 0-7 with the filtered child indices and columns 8-10 with the coarse voxel coordinates. A ray-traversal algorithm for volumetric rendering. Its time complexity is O(p \cdot r), where p is the number of pixels and r is the volume's largest dimension in voxels. Its space complexity is dependent on the size of the data volume. It uses a relative distance formula: \text{relative distance} = (\text{target} - \text{value1}) / (\text{value2} - \text{value1}). Performs raycasting in world space by transforming the ray to local voxel space, calling the generic raycast, and transforming results back. It computes the ray end in world space, transforms the ray origin and end to local space, and calculates the local direction and max distance. It handles zero-length rays by returning an empty result when the squared distance is less than 0.000001. On success, it scales the distance back to world space and transforms the normal if enabled. Time Complexity: The time complexity depends on the number of voxels visited. In the worst case (ray passes through all voxels), it is proportional to the number of voxels in the finest level. However, in sparse volumes, it is significantly faster than flat traversal due to early culling at coarse levels. Memory Complexity: The memory complexity is dominated by the storage of the hierarchical grid and the lookup tables. The lookup table size is proportional to the number of coarse voxels per level. Performance: Performance is highly dependent on the sparsity of the volume and the efficiency of the AABB intersection test. For dense volumes, the overhead of the hierarchy may not be justified. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space; suitable for sparse and multi-resolution data; good memory locality due to array-based structure. Limitations: Requires precomputation of the lookup table; less flexible than pointer-based trees for dynamic data; potential precision issues with far-away rays. When to Use: Sparse volumes, multi-resolution data, static scenes where precomputation is feasible. When Not to Use: Dense volumes with little empty space, highly dynamic data where the hierarchy needs frequent updates. Hierarchical Grid Traversal, also known as Ray-Mipmap Traversal, is a technique used in volume rendering to accelerate ray casting through hierarchical grid structures. It builds on the principles of ray-grid traversal, specifically the DDA algorithm, by adding a hierarchical layer to skip empty regions. The method is often implemented using lookup tables to map coarse voxels to fine voxels, allowing for efficient batch processing. szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, https://github.com/szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ZephirFXEC/HNanoSolver, https://github.com/ZephirFXEC/HNanoSolver, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) DTIC ADA202661: Volumetric Rendering Techniques for the Display of Three-Dimensional Aerodynamic Flow Field Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA202661, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Zylann/godotvoxel, https://github.com/Zylann/godotvoxel, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting
head: Adaptive ray casting using trilinear basis functions, Hierarchical Data Structures for Ray Casting, Hierarchical Ray Casting with Trilinear Coefficients, Hierarchically Accelerated Ray Casting with Controlled Error, Ray casting with mdh tree
body: Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates ray casting by traversing a multi-dimensional hierarchy (mdh) to adaptively choose the resolution level for evaluating volume data. It solves the problem of expensive ray traversal in large volumes by approximating homogeneous regions with least-squares trilinear coefficients, allowing the renderer to skip fine-grained sampling in unimportant or smooth areas. Unlike sibling methods that rely on simple opacity thresholds or constant-value homogeneity, this method uses a user-defined error tolerance and data importance weighting to control refinement, providing a balance between image quality and performance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin and direction; a hierarchical data structure (mdh tree) where each node stores trilinear coefficients, nodal error, and importance; a user-defined error tolerance; a data importance weighting function (transfer function). Output: Accumulated color and opacity for the pixel corresponding to the ray. Data Structures: The hierarchy uses a BON tree structure. Each node contains: 1. Data Model: Trilinear coefficients representing a least-squares fit to the data in the region covered by the node. This provides C^0 continuity at shared faces. 2. Evaluation Information: Nodal Error: The average deviation of the node's trilinear model from the actual data within the region. Importance: A user-defined value derived from a transfer function, indicating the significance of data values in that range. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Calculate the entry and exit points of the ray with respect to the volume bounds. 2. Recursive Traversal: Call rayCastRegion(ray, region, entryPt, exitPt) starting from the root region. 3. Termination Check: If the current region is at the bottom level (original data) or the nodal error is within the user-defined tolerance (weighted by importance), render the ray segment directly from entryPt to exitPt using the current region's data model. 4. Refinement: If not at the bottom level and error exceeds tolerance: Initialize subEntry to entryPt. Loop while subEntry is not equal to exitPt and rendering is not interrupted: a. Find Subregion: Determine the specific child subregion containing subEntry using findRegion(region, subEntry). For orthographic projection, a single permutation defines the front-to-back topological order. For perspective, the permutation is fixed per ray but may vary between rays. b. Find Exit: Calculate the exit point of the ray from the current subRegion using findExit(ray, subRegion, subEntry). c. Recurse: Call rayCastRegion(ray, subRegion, subEntry, subExit). d. Advance: Update subEntry to subExit. 5. Direct Rendering (Leaf or Tolerated Node): If stopping at a node higher than the bottom level: Evaluate data, color, and opacity at the intersection points of the region's bounding box using the node's trilinear coefficients. If going down to the data level: Look up the eight corner data values of the cell/voxel and compute colors and opacity at the intersection points of the cell boundary. Integration is performed directly from entry to exit point, approximating the volume rendering integral. The method uses an approximation similar to coherent projection, evaluating the "emission" contribution at the thickest point of the cell's projection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EPSILON = 1e-6 class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def length(self): return (self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2)0.5 def getitem(self, i): return (self.x, self.y, self.z)[i] class Bounds: def init(self, minpt, maxpt): self.min, self.max = minpt, maxpt @property def center(self): return Vec3((self.min.x + self.max.x)/2, (self.min.y + self.max.y)/2, (self.min.z + self.max.z)/2) def raycastregion(ray, region, entrypt, exitpt): """Recursively compute the contribution of a ray through a specified region.""" if region.isbottomlevel or region.errorwithintolerance(): return renderraydirect(ray, entrypt, exitpt, region) subentry = entrypt while (exitpt - subentry).length() > EPSILON: subregion = findregion(region, subentry) subexit = findexit(ray, subregion, subentry) if subexit is None: break contrib = raycastregion(ray, subregion, subentry, subexit) subentry = subexit return contrib def findregion(region, point): """Determine the child subregion containing the point.""" idx = 0 for axis in range(3): if point[axis] >= region.bounds.center[axis]: idx |= (1 << axis) return region.children[idx] def findexit(ray, subregion, subentry): """Calculate exit point using Snyder and Barr generalization.""" # Maintains tx, ty, tz for imminent intersections with grid planes. # In adaptive case, updates are nondestructive. # Update amount is wx dtx if tx selected, where wx is width in grid points. tmin = float('inf') for axis in range(3): if abs(ray.direction[axis]) > EPSILON: t1 = (subregion.bounds.min[axis] - subentry[axis]) / ray.direction[axis] t2 = (subregion.bounds.max[axis] - subentry[axis]) / ray.direction[axis] t = t1 if t1 > EPSILON else t2 if t > EPSILON and t < tmin: tmin = t if tmin == float('inf'): return None return subentry + ray.direction tmin def renderraydirect(ray, entrypt, exitpt, region): """Render segment directly using region's data model.""" valin = evaluateregion(region, entrypt) valout = evaluateregion(region, exitpt) # Front-to-back compositing approximation (coherent projection style) alpha = 1.0 - (1.0 - valin.opacity) (1.0 - valout.opacity) color = valin.color (1.0 - valout.opacity) + valout.color valout.opacity return color, alpha def evaluateregion(region, point): """Evaluate data at point using trilinear coefficients or corner values.""" if region.isbottomlevel: return trilinearinterpolate(region.corners, point) else: return trilinearevaluate(region.coefficients, point) def trilinearinterpolate(corners, point): # Standard 8-corner trilinear interpolation return (0.5, 0.5) def trilinearevaluate(coeffs, point): # Evaluate trilinear function defined by coeffs at point return (0.5, 0.5) Parameters: Error Tolerance: A user-defined parameter controlling the maximum allowed error in the image. Higher tolerance allows rendering at coarser levels, increasing speed. Data Importance Weighting: A user-supplied function that weights the error metric. It allows small errors in critical data ranges to be considered serious, while substantial errors are acceptable in uninteresting ranges (e.g., air). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Discontinuity: The gradient calculated using the derivative of the trilinear function may not be continuous at shared cell faces, introducing potential error. Perspective Permutations: For perspective projection, rays may require varying permutations for subregion traversal, though the permutation is fixed within an individual ray. Adaptive Volume Ray Casting is a technique that builds on Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting by using an octree structure to determine traversal depth based on camera-defined resolution limits. It produces better image quality than splatting by avoiding splatting artifacts but is more computationally intensive. A single-pass volume rendering method compatible with a hierarchical data structure, extending Scharsach's ray-casting method. It performs traversal and color accumulation in a fragment shader for each pixel using a quad covering the display surface. The vertex shader calculates ray position and direction in data space, which are interpolated to the fragment shader. Entry/exit points are calculated, and rays not intersecting the volume terminate early. Tree traversal alternates horizontal (within node grid) and vertical (between hierarchy levels) passes, using a mini-stack or stack-less algorithm. Time Complexity: Depends on the error tolerance and data importance. In homogeneous regions, traversal stops at higher levels, reducing complexity. In complex regions, it approaches regular grid ray casting. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the hierarchical tree (mdh) with trilinear coefficients and error/importance metadata for each node. Measured Performance: On an SGI Reality Engine II with four 150 MHz processors: Hipip dataset (64^3) with 10% error and no importance: 27.0 seconds (hierarchical) vs. 97.0 seconds (regular grid). CT Head dataset (256 \times 256 \times 113) with 1% error and importance: 56.0 seconds (hierarchical) vs. 205.0 seconds (regular grid). Strengths: Provides error-controlled rendering; handles perspective and orthographic projections; easily parallelizable (each ray is nearly independent). Limitations: Noticeably slower than ray casting a non-hierarchical rectilinear volume, but usually faster than regular grid ray casting on volumes where importance functions can limit traversal. When to Use: When image quality must be controlled by error tolerance and importance weighting, and when volumes have large homogeneous or unimportant regions. When Not to Use: When maximum speed is required and error control is not critical; when hardware 3D textures or coherent projection are available and sufficient. Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting was developed by Gelder, Kim, and Wilhelms at the University of California, Santa Cruz. It was described in the technical report "Hierarchically Accelerated Ray Casting for Volume Rendering with Controlled Error" (UCSC-CRL-95-31) in March 1995. The method generalizes previous work on homogeneity (which relied on nearly constant values) to least-squares fits with trilinear basis functions. It was implemented within a general system for multi-dimensional trees (mdh). name: Adaptive Volume Ray Casting
head: volume ray casting technique
body: Adaptive Volume Ray Casting is a volume rendering technique where one ray is shot through the volume for each pixel, traversing an octree to accumulate physical values along the ray path. It builds on Hierarchical Trilinear Ray Casting by using the octree structure to determine traversal depth based on camera-defined resolution limits. It produces better image quality than splatting by avoiding splatting artifacts, but is more computationally intensive. Inputs: Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Octree data structure representing the volume. Camera parameters defining the maximum resolution level. Outputs: Accumulated pixel value for each ray. Data Structures: Octree: Hierarchical structure where nodes represent spatial subdivisions. Leaf Definition: Every cell ranked with the maximum level of resolution defined by the camera is considered as a leaf. Highest level of resolution cells are discarded when these cells are too small compared to the image pixel size. The maximum octree depth level read is therefore defined by the camera. Steps: 1. Find Intersections: Determine the intersections between the grid and the ray. Using basic 3D geometry calculation, compute the coordinates (x,y,z) of the entry and exit points of the ray in the cell faces. 2. Traverse Octree: Start from the root of the octree and traverse down the tree. This top-down traversal of the tree stops when a leaf cell is found. 3. Accumulate Contribution: Multiply the cell's observed physical value by the length between the entry and exit points into the cell faces. Add every contribution along the ray to the resulting pixel value, without taking into account any ordering. 4. Post-Processing (Optional): Apply an adaptive Gaussian blur filter as an image post-processing option to avoid aliasing in coarse mesh regions by adjusting filter size to local image resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def adaptivevolumeraycasting(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot, cameramaxlevel): """ Renders a single pixel by traversing an octree and accumulating physical values. Args: rayorigin: tuple (x, y, z), origin of the ray. raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz), direction of the ray. octreeroot: dict, root node of the octree with keys: 'bbox', 'value', 'children', 'level'. cameramaxlevel: int, maximum octree depth level defined by camera. Returns: float, accumulated pixel value. """ # Step 1 & 2: Traverse octree and accumulate contributions # The sources describe a top-down traversal that stops at leaf cells. # We implement a recursive traversal that computes per-cell entry/exit distances. return traversenode(octreeroot, rayorigin, raydirection, 0.0, float('inf'), cameramaxlevel) def traversenode(node, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, cameramaxlevel): """Recursively traverse octree nodes along the ray.""" # Compute intersection of ray with current node bounding box # The exact 3D geometry calculation is not detailed in the sources. tentry, texit = rayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, node['bbox']) # If ray misses node or intersection is behind current traversal point, return 0 if tentry is None or texit <= tmin: return 0.0 # Clamp tmax to the exit point of this node texit = min(texit, tmax) # Step 2 & 3: Stop traversal at leaf cell (or max camera level) if node['level'] >= cameramaxlevel or node['children'] is None: # Step 3: Multiply cell's observed physical value by the length between # entry and exit points into this cell faces. celllength = texit - tmin contribution = node['value'] celllength # Add every contribution along the ray to the resulting pixel value, # without taking into account any ordering. return contribution # Recurse into children that intersect the ray totalcontribution = 0.0 for child in node['children']: totalcontribution += traversenode(child, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, texit, cameramaxlevel) return totalcontribution def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, bbox): """ Compute entry and exit distances (t) of a ray intersecting an axis-aligned bounding box. bbox: tuple (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) Returns (tentry, texit) or (None, None) if no intersection. Standard ray-AABB intersection logic. """ tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bbox[i] or origin[i] > bbox[i + 3]: return None, None else: t1 = (bbox[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bbox[i + 3] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax Parameters: Camera Max Level: The maximum octree depth level read is defined by the camera. Cells smaller than the image pixel size at this level are discarded. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Aliasing can be seen on coarse mesh resolution areas because low simulation resolution leads to big pixels. An adaptive Gaussian blur filter can be used to mitigate this. Ordering: Contributions are added without taking into account any ordering, which may affect transparency/opacity calculations if not handled by the physical value definition. Precision: Ray-box intersection calculations may suffer from floating-point precision issues near cell boundaries; standard epsilon guards are recommended. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given, but described as "more computationally intensive" than splatting. Memory Complexity: Not explicitly given. Performance: The software implementation is not interactive on large datasets (e.g., Milky Way simulation with ~200 million AMR cells). Strengths: Produces better image quality than splatting (no splatting artifacts). Convenient to process large datasets as the algorithm is embarrassingly parallel. Limitations: More computationally intensive than splatting. Aliasing in coarse mesh regions. When to use: When image quality is prioritized over interactive performance and splatting artifacts are unacceptable. When not to use: When interactive performance on large datasets is required. Origin: Based on volume ray casting explained by Levoy (1990). History: Described in the context of AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) simulations, specifically for visualizing large datasets like Milky Way simulations. Usage: Used in PyMSES software for volume rendering of AMR simulations. Volume Rendering of AMR Simulations, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.1210.8014, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: KD-Tree Partitioned Volume Rendering
head: Partitioned Volume Rendering, Li et al. method
body: A method to avoid computing all scalar values regardless of visibility by partitioning the volume into smaller sub-volumes with similar properties based on the transfer function. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by using a kd-tree to manage visibility order and culling sub-volumes against an opacity map, rather than traversing a uniform grid or octree. Inputs: Volume scalar field, transfer function, camera parameters, frame buffer. Outputs: Rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Partitioned Sub-volumes: The volume is divided into regions where scalar values fall within specific ranges defined by the transfer function. 2. KD-Tree: A binary space partitioning tree where each node is associated with one sub-volume. The tree structure determines the rendering order. 3. Opacity Map: A data structure corresponding to a region of the frame buffer. It stores the minimum opacity of the frame buffer pixels found within that region. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Group scalar values within a certain range together based on the transfer function to define sub-volume properties. 2. Tree Construction: Build a kd-tree to organize these sub-volumes. Each node in the tree corresponds to a sub-volume. 3. Traversal and Culling: Use the kd-tree to render the partitioned volume with correct visibility order. For each node (sub-volume): a. Clip the sub-volume against the opacity map. b. If the sub-volume is fully occluded (based on the minimum opacity in the corresponding frame buffer region), cull it and do not compute scalar values for it. c. If visible, render the sub-volume and update the opacity map with the resulting opacities. Parameters: Transfer function ranges: Define the grouping of scalar values. Not given in the sources. Opacity map resolution: Corresponds to frame buffer regions. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Degenerate sub-volumes: If a scalar range is empty, the corresponding sub-volume is empty and should be skipped. Precision: Clipping against the opacity map requires accurate comparison of opacity values. A technique introduced into the raycasting algorithm by Bruckner and Gröller to display inner occluded objects of interest by employing a force-based model to partition the volume into several segments. The partition manner is controlled by a number of forces and constraints. Performance: Reported 10 fps for the Engine data set using a 2.5 GHz Pentium-IV and a nVidia GeForce4 graphics adapter. Strengths: Avoids computing scalar values for occluded regions, potentially reducing computation time. Limitations: Requires construction and maintenance of the kd-tree and opacity map. Performance depends on the effectiveness of the partitioning and culling. When to use: When visibility is highly occluded and the transfer function allows for effective partitioning. When not to use: When the volume is transparent or the partitioning does not result in significant culling. Proposed by Li et al. [Li03] to address the inefficiency of computing all scalar values regardless of visibility. The approach combines volume partitioning with kd-tree traversal and opacity map-based culling. name: Hierarchical Voxel Traversal
head: Recursive Voxel Traversal
body: Hierarchical Voxel Traversal is a recursive raycasting algorithm designed to traverse nested voxel structures, such as chunks containing subvoxels, to find intersections. It distinguishes itself from flat traversal methods by transforming rays into local subvoxel space when entering a detail voxel, allowing for efficient handling of nested voxel data. Unlike First Active Voxel Detection which focuses on finding the first non-empty voxel, this method fully traverses the hierarchy to compute precise intersections within detail voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin, direction, transform, and optional length; a hierarchical voxel structure (e.g., VoxelWorldAccess or generic Voxel<T>); maximum iteration limits. Output: An Intersection struct containing the hit position, normal, index, and an optional inner intersection (for detail voxels). Data Structures: Ray: Contains origin (Vec3), direction (Vec3), transform (Mat4), and length (Option<f32>). Voxel: Generic type T with properties WIDTH, DY, DZ, SCALE, and COUNT. Coordinates are mapped to linear indices using i = x + y \cdot DY + z \cdot DZ. Steps: 1. World Access Entry: Calculate the world origin in float3. Compute the current ray position in chunk-local space: current = ray.origin \cdot (1.0 / self.world.scale) - origin Call the core cast function with the world access, ray, current position, direction, and max iterations (30). 2. Voxel Check (World Access): Validate coordinates are within world bounds: coord[i] \ge 0 and coord[i] < self.world.dims[i]. Compute linear index: i = coord[0] + coord[1] \cdot dims[0] + coord[2] \cdot dims[0] \cdot dims[1]. If the voxel exists and is visible: Construct a local ray by applying scaling (sc) and translation (coord sc) to the ray's transform. Recursively cast on the voxel. If the voxel is a detail voxel (has subvoxels): Return an Intersection with inner set to the sub-intersection, index set to the chunk index, and current position/normal. If the voxel does not exist (empty chunk slot): Return an Intersection with inner: None, index: 0, and current position/normal. 3. Generic Voxel Entry: Inverse the ray transform. Scale by SUBDIV (2^{SUBDIV}). Transform ray origin and direction into subvoxel space. Move ray origin to the start of the bounding box (0 to scale) if not already inside. For each axis i: If direction[i] > 0, t = (0.0 - current[i]) / direction[i]. Else if direction[i] < 0, t = (scale - current[i]) / direction[i]. If t > 0, advance current. Call core cast with the voxel, ray, current position, direction, and max iterations 6 \cdot T::WIDTH. 4. Generic Voxel Check: Validate coordinates within T::WIDTH. Compute linear index: i = coord[0] + coord[1] \cdot T::DY + coord[2] \cdot T::DZ. If the voxel is visible and is detail: Construct local ray with scaling T::SCALE and translation coord \cdot T::SCALE. Recursively cast. Return intersection with inner sub-hit. If the voxel is visible and NOT detail: Return intersection with inner: None, index: i, current position/normal. 5. Core Cast Function: Initialize integer coordinates currenti from current floor. Adjust currenti down by 1 if current is very close to an integer boundary and direction is negative. Check starting position first using raycast.check. If hit, return immediately. Loop up to iterations: Calculate distance to next grid plane intersection for each axis using intersect(currenti[i], current[i], direction[i]). Find minimum distance i[d]. Advance current by direction \cdot i[d] where d is the axis with minimum intersection distance. Decrement currenti[d] if direction[d] < 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cast(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 1: World Access Entry # current is already in chunk-local space return castvoxel(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) def castvoxel(worldaccess, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 2: Voxel Check (World Access) # Assuming worldaccess provides dims and scale # Compute linear index from current coordinates # Check bounds and existence if not worldaccess.check(current): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) voxel = worldaccess.get(current) if not voxel.visible(): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) if voxel.isdetail(): # Construct local ray sc = worldaccess.scale localray = transformray(ray, sc, current sc) # Recursively cast subhit = cast(worldaccess, localray, vec3(0), localray.direction, 30) return Intersection(inner=subhit, index=worldaccess.index(current), position=current, normal=vec3(0)) else: return Intersection(inner=None, index=worldaccess.index(current), position=current, normal=vec3(0)) def castgeneric(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 3: Generic Voxel Entry # Inverse transform and scale invtransform = inverse(ray.transform) subdiv = 2 voxel.SUBDIV ray.origin = invtransform (ray.origin subdiv) ray.direction = invtransform (ray.direction subdiv) # Move ray origin to start of bounding box scale = voxel.SCALE for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: t = (0.0 - current[i]) / direction[i] elif direction[i] < 0: t = (scale - current[i]) / direction[i] else: t = float('inf') if t > 0: current += direction t return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, 6 voxel.WIDTH) def castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 4: Generic Voxel Check # Check bounds if not voxel.check(current): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) index = voxel.coordtoindex(current) voxeldata = voxel.get(index) if not voxeldata.visible(): return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) if voxeldata.isdetail(): sc = voxel.SCALE localray = transformray(ray, sc, current sc) subhit = castgeneric(voxeldata, localray, vec3(0), localray.direction, 6 voxeldata.WIDTH) return Intersection(inner=subhit, index=index, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) else: return Intersection(inner=None, index=index, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) def corecast(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations): # Step 5: Core Cast Function # Initialize integer coordinates currenti = floor(current) # Precision fix for negative direction at integer boundaries for i in range(3): if abs(current[i] - currenti[i]) < epsilon and direction[i] < 0: currenti[i] -= 1 # Check starting position if voxel.check(current): return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) # Traverse grid for in range(maxiterations): # Calculate distance to next grid plane distances = [] for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: distances.append(float('inf')) else: # intersect function calculates distance to next integer plane # assuming currenti[i] is the current voxel index # distance = (currenti[i] + (1 if direction[i] > 0 else 0) - current[i]) / direction[i] # Note: Exact formula depends on intersect implementation details not fully specified # Using standard AET traversal logic nextplane = currenti[i] + (1 if direction[i] > 0 else 0) distances.append((nextplane - current[i]) / direction[i]) d = argmin(distances) mindist = distances[d] if mindist == float('inf'): break # Advance current current += direction mindist currenti[d] += (1 if direction[d] < 0 else -1) # Decrement if direction is negative # Check hit at new position if voxel.check(current): return castgenericvoxel(voxel, ray, current, direction, maxiterations) return Intersection(inner=None, index=0, position=current, normal=vec3(0)) Parameters: Max iterations for VoxelWorldAccess raycasting: 30. Max iterations for Voxel<T> raycasting: 6 \cdot T::WIDTH. Pitfalls: Precision issues at integer boundaries: If the ray is exactly on an integer coordinate and moving in a negative direction, the integer coordinate index must be decremented to avoid missing the voxel or double-checking. Not given in the sources. The method is implemented in the amethystvoxel project by Kurble, licensed under Apache-2.0. It is used for rendering voxel worlds with nested detail structures.
