name: Embree Mesh Acceleration Structure
head: Embree RTC, Embree-based Volume Rendering for Unstructured Meshes, RTC Mesh
body: The Embree Mesh Acceleration Structure is a volume rendering method that wraps Intel's Embree ray-tracing engine to build a triangle mesh acceleration structure and perform ray tracing. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing complex, non-uniform geometric domains by converting unstructured mesh elements into triangular polygons. It differs from sibling methods by relying on Embree's RTC API for BVH traversal rather than custom software ray marchers or grid-based traversal, enabling both surface plots and traditional accumulation rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unstructured mesh data (vertices and connectivity) and field data associated with the mesh. Output: Rendered image (surface values or accumulated field values) and hit data (intersection points, primitive IDs). Data Structures: The implementation relies on a RenderSource object that encapsulates the logic for creating the Embree polygon mesh from the datasource and performing ray tracing calls. Internally, the acceleration structure is built using the following buffers: Vertex Buffer: Allocated with RTCFORMATFLOAT3, storing vertex coordinates as 32-bit floating-point vectors. Index Buffer: Allocated with RTCFORMATUINT3, storing triangle indices as 32-bit unsigned integer triplets. Geometry: Created via standard Embree RTC geometry creation and committed. Steps: 1. Mesh Generation: Generate a triangular polygon mesh from the unstructured mesh data by breaking up faces into multiple triangles if necessary. 2. Embree Initialization: Initialize the Embree device and scene, and set the build quality to HIGH. 3. Geometry Creation: Create triangle geometry, allocate the vertex buffer (RTCFORMATFLOAT3) and index buffer (RTCFORMATUINT3), and copy the mesh data into these buffers. 4. Commit Geometry: Commit the geometry and attach it to the Embree scene. 5. Commit Scene: Commit the scene to finalize the acceleration structure build. 6. Ray Tracing: Single Ray Closest Hit: Use rtcIntersect1 with a coherent context to find the nearest intersection for a single ray. Single Ray Any Hit (Occlusion): Use rtcOccluded1 with a coherent context to determine if a ray intersects any geometry. Multiple Ray Closest Hit: Use rtcIntersect1M with a coherent context flag determined by a parameter to trace multiple rays. Multiple Ray Any Hit: Use rtcOccluded1M with a coherent context flag. 7. Rendering: Surface Plots: Calculate the value of the field at the intersection point for each ray using the hit data computed by Embree. Accumulation Rendering: Accumulate values along each ray for every element the rays intersect, allowing operations such as computing maximum intensity along the ray. Formulas and Parameters: Coherence Flag: A boolean parameter coherent passed to trace functions. If true, uses RTCINTERSECTCONTEXTFLAGCOHERENT. If false, the same flag is used in the implementation (noted as a potential bug in the source, but documented as is). Intra-element Interpolation: Implementations of various intra-element interpolation functions are required to support meshes of various types and orders, as ray intersections may occur inside elements rather than just on surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def createembreedevice(): pass def createembreescene(device): pass def setbuildquality(scene, quality): pass def creategeometry(device, type, numprimitives): pass def createbuffer(device, type, format, numelements): pass def writebuffer(buffer, offset, data): pass def setgeometryvertexbuffer(geometry, buffer, stride, offset): pass def setgeometryindexbuffer(geometry, buffer, stride, offset): pass def commitgeometry(geometry): pass def addgeometrytoscene(scene, geometry, id): pass def commitscene(scene): pass def rtcIntersect1(scene, ray, flags): pass def rtcOccluded1(scene, ray, flags): pass def rtcIntersect1M(scene, rays, flags): pass def rtcOccluded1M(scene, rays, flags): pass def interpolatefield(fielddata, point): pass class EmbreeMesh: def init(self, vertices, indices): self.device = createembreedevice() self.scene = createembreescene(self.device) setbuildquality(self.scene, "HIGH") self.geometry = creategeometry(self.device, type="TRIANGLE", numprimitives=len(indices)) self.vertexbuffer = createbuffer(self.device, type="VERTEX", format="FLOAT3", numelements=len(vertices)) writebuffer(self.vertexbuffer, 0, vertices) setgeometryvertexbuffer(self.geometry, self.vertexbuffer, stride=0, offset=0) self.indexbuffer = createbuffer(self.device, type="INDEX", format="UINT3", numelements=len(indices)) writebuffer(self.indexbuffer, 0, indices) setgeometryindexbuffer(self.geometry, self.indexbuffer, stride=0, offset=0) commitgeometry(self.geometry) addgeometrytoscene(self.scene, self.geometry, id=0) commitscene(self.scene) def traceclosest(self, ray, coherent): flags = "RTCINTERSECTCONTEXTFLAGCOHERENT" if coherent else 0 return rtcIntersect1(self.scene, ray, flags) def traceany(self, ray, coherent): flags = "RTCINTERSECTCONTEXTFLAGCOHERENT" if coherent else 0 return rtcOccluded1(self.scene, ray, flags) def traceclosestbatch(self, rays, coherent): flags = "RTCINTERSECTCONTEXTFLAGCOHERENT" if coherent else 0 return rtcIntersect1M(self.scene, rays, flags) def rendersurface(self, rays, fielddata): hits = self.traceclosestbatch(rays, coherent=True) image = [0.0] len(rays) for i, hit in enumerate(hits): if hit.valid: image[i] = interpolatefield(fielddata, hit.point) return image def renderaccumulation(self, rays, fielddata): image = [0.0] len(rays) for i, ray in enumerate(rays): accumulated = 0.0 # Sources do not specify multi-hit traversal mechanism for accumulation. # Implementation requires a custom any-hit callback or repeated tracing. image[i] = accumulated return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intra-element Interpolation: Ray intersections may occur inside elements rather than just on surfaces. Intra-element interpolation functions must be implemented to support meshes of various types and orders. Coherence Flag Bug: The source notes a potential bug where the coherent flag logic might be inverted or incorrectly applied in the false case, but it is documented as implemented. Mesh Type Support: Currently implemented for Hexahedral and Tetrahedral mesh elements. Adding support for other mesh types requires breaking up faces into triangles. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Embree is described as a "fast ray-tracing code". Strengths: Supports both surface plots and traditional accumulation rendering; flexible integration with camera paths and multiple render sources. Limitations: Requires conversion of unstructured mesh to triangular polygons; dependent on external Embree library (though a future replacement with custom ray-tracing code is planned). When to use: When rendering unstructured mesh data with complex geometry where hardware-accelerated ray tracing provides a performance benefit over software rasterization or marching. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from the yt project's enhancement proposal for unstructured mesh volume rendering. It leverages Intel's Embree ray-tracing engine, which is known for high-performance software ray tracing. The implementation was developed to support both surface plots and accumulation rendering for unstructured mesh data, integrating with the yt volume rendering refactor to allow flexible camera paths and multiple render sources. The code examples are from an unofficial repository by Mike Smith, demonstrating a C++ implementation using glm and Embree. name: Adaptive Sampling with Region Delimiters
head: Region-based Adaptive Sampling
body: Adaptive Sampling with Region Delimiters is a sampling strategy for Adaptive Block-Refined (ABR) volume data that adapts the sampling rate to the finest cell size within each region, using sample positions as delimiters to handle boundary artifacts. Unlike Ljung [23], which defines a global set of finest level samples skipped by coarseness, this method defines independent sampling intervals for each region. It solves the problem of boundary artifacts caused by successive regions sampled at different rates, where the distance between the last sample of one region and the first of the next can be smaller or larger than either region's sampling rate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: ABR region metadata (specifically the smallest cell size within the region), ray parameters (origin, direction, entry/exit points t{in}, t{out}), and a user-provided scaling parameter. Output: A sequence of sample positions and values within the region, integrated into the ray's color/opacity accumulation. Data Structures: Region Metadata: Contains the minimum cell size \rho{min} within the ABR block. Ray State: Tracks the current position t and a per-ray random offset \rho. Parameters: Base sampling rate: 2 samples per smallest cell size in the region. User-provided scaling parameter: Scales the base sampling rate to trade quality for performance. \rho: Per-ray random offset for interleaved sampling. Steps: 1. Determine Sampling Step (dt): Calculate the base sampling step dt{base} as \rho{min} / 2 to achieve two samples per smallest cell size. Apply the user scaling factor S to get the final step size dt = S \times dt{base}. 2. Calculate First Sample Position (t0): Compute the first sample distance using the formula t0 = dt \cdot \lceil \rho / dt \rceil. 3. Generate Sample Positions: Step the ray through the region, sampling at each subsequent position t{i+1} = ti + dt. 4. Define Delimiters and Sub-intervals: Treat the generated sample positions t0, t1, \dots, tn as delimiters. These delimiters split the region's overlap interval [t{in}, t{out}] into sub-intervals T0=[t{in}, t0], T1=[t0, t1], \dots, Tm=[tn, t{out}]. 5. Sample Sub-intervals: For each sub-interval Ti, sample at its midpoint (Ti[0] + Ti[1]) / 2. Weigh the sample in the opacity correction term by the interval length dti = |Ti|. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleregionwithdelimiters(rayorigin, raydirection, tin, tout, regionmincellsize, scalingfactor, rayrandomoffset): """ Samples a volume region using adaptive sampling with region delimiters. Args: rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 (normalized) tin: float (entry distance) tout: float (exit distance) regionmincellsize: float (smallest cell size in the ABR region) scalingfactor: float (user-provided scaling parameter) rayrandomoffset: float (per-ray random offset rho) Returns: list of (position, opacitycontribution, intervallength) tuples """ # Step 1: Determine Sampling Step # Base rate is 2 samples per smallest cell size, so step = size / 2 dtbase = regionmincellsize / 2.0 dt = scalingfactor dtbase # Step 2: Calculate First Sample Position t0 = dt math.ceil(rayrandomoffset / dt) t0 = max(tin, t0) # Ensure first delimiter is within region bounds # Step 3: Generate Sample Positions (Delimiters) delimiters = [] tcurrent = t0 while tcurrent < tout: delimiters.append(tcurrent) tcurrent += dt # Step 4: Define Sub-intervals allpoints = [tin] + delimiters + [tout] samples = [] # Step 5: Sample Sub-intervals for i in range(len(allpoints) - 1): tstart = allpoints[i] tend = allpoints[i+1] if tend <= tstart: continue # Midpoint sampling midpoint = (tstart + tend) / 2.0 position = rayorigin + raydirection midpoint # Interval length for weighting dti = tend - tstart # Standard volume sampling at the computed position value = samplevolume(position) # Standard transfer function mapping value to opacity alpha = transferfunction(value) # Opacity Correction: alphatilde = 1 - (1 - alpha)^(dti / dt) if alpha > 0: alphacorrected = 1.0 - (1.0 - alpha) (dti / dt) else: alphacorrected = 0.0 samples.append((position, alphacorrected, dti)) return samples def samplevolume(position): # Returns density/value at position from the volume grid return 0.0 def transferfunction(value): # Returns opacity alpha for the given density/value return 0.0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: Successive regions sampled at different rates can have distances between the last sample of one and first of the next that are smaller or larger than the region's sampling rate, causing artifacts. The delimiter method mitigates this by explicitly sampling the gap intervals. Small Overlap Intervals: The method takes at least one sample for each region hit, even if the overlap interval is small. Banding Artifacts: At lower sampling rates, biasing the sample positions (using midpoints of variable intervals) can result in slight banding artifacts. A correction factor applied to opacity to account for variable step sizes between samples, preventing incorrect opacity due to undersampling. The formula is \tilde{\alpha} = 1 - (1 - \alpha)^{s/s1}, where s is the current step size (interval length dti), s1 is the base step size (dt), and \alpha is the opacity from the transfer function. Compared to standard adaptive sampling, this correction takes one additional sample per region (for the boundary intervals) and prevents opacity decrease from undersampling, at the cost of slight banding artifacts at low sampling rates. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of sub-intervals created by the delimiters. Since each region generates samples based on its finest cell size, fine regions require more samples. The delimiter approach adds overhead by requiring sampling at the boundaries of each region (at least one sample per region hit). Memory Complexity: Low, as it is a streaming method. No additional large data structures are required beyond the region metadata and ray state. Measured Performance: The method relies on the underlying BVH traversal performance. BVH rebuilds for large datasets (e.g., Exajet) take roughly 300ms on a Titan RTX or RTX 8000 GPU. Strengths: Eliminates boundary artifacts between regions of different refinement levels; adapts sampling to local data frequency without guessing. Limitations: Can introduce banding artifacts at low sampling rates; requires at least one sample per region hit, which may be inefficient for very small overlaps. When to Use: When rendering ABR data with significant variation in cell sizes across adjacent regions, and visual continuity at region boundaries is critical. When Not to Use: When performance is paramount and slight boundary artifacts are acceptable, or when regions are very small and the overhead of boundary sampling dominates. This method was introduced in the context of ray tracing structured AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data using ExaBricks. It addresses limitations in previous multi-block adaptive sampling techniques, such as those by Ljung [23], by providing independent sampling intervals per region. The approach leverages ABR metadata to adapt sampling rates to the finest cell size, avoiding the need to guess data frequency within a region. name: BVH Pruning for Space Skipping
head: Space Skipping via BVH Pruning
body: BVH Pruning for Space Skipping is a technique that accelerates volume rendering by excluding fully transparent regions from the Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) during construction, thereby allowing hardware ray traversal to skip empty space and non-visible data without runtime checks. It differs from sibling methods like Adaptive Sampling with Region Delimiters by integrating visibility culling directly into the BVH structure rather than managing traversal state, and from Sparse Brick Set Rendering by relying on transfer-function-aware pruning rather than static sparsity masks. Inputs: A set of Adaptive Block-Refined (ABR) regions. Precomputed scalar ranges for each ABR. A transfer function mapping scalar values to opacity. Outputs: A BVH containing only regions with non-zero maximum opacity. Data Structures: BVH Primitive: Each leaf node represents an ABR. The primitive is defined by its bounding box. If the region is pruned, the bounding box is effectively empty (or the node is removed from the hierarchy). Steps: 1. Compute Maximum Opacity: For each ABR, retrieve its precomputed scalar range [min\val, max\val]. Evaluate the transfer function T(v) over this range to find the maximum opacity: \alpha{max} = \max{v \in [min\val, max\val]} T(v) 2. Prune Decision: If \alpha{max} = 0, the region is fully transparent. Discard the region from the BVH construction by returning an empty box for its primitive. If \alpha{max} > 0, the region may contain visible data. Return the region's standard bounding box for its primitive. 3. BVH Construction: Build the BVH using the resulting set of primitives (valid boxes and empty boxes). Pitfalls: Transfer Function Changes: The BVH is static with respect to the transfer function. Any change to the transfer function or iso-value requires a full BVH rebuild to ensure correct pruning. No Runtime Checks: Because inactive regions are excluded from the BVH, no validity checks are needed during traversal, but this also means the BVH does not adapt to dynamic data changes without rebuild. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildprunedbvh(abrregions, transferfunction): """ Builds a BVH where fully transparent ABRs are excluded. Args: abrregions: List of ABR objects, each having: scalarrange: tuple (minval, maxval) boundingbox: the spatial bounds of the region transferfunction: A function T(v) returning opacity for scalar v. Returns: BVH: A Bounding Volume Hierarchy containing only non-transparent regions. """ primitives = [] for region in abrregions: minval, maxval = region.scalarrange # Compute maximum opacity in the scalar range # Note: In practice, this might use a precomputed histogram or texture lookup # rather than evaluating every scalar value. alphamax = 0.0 for v in range(minval, maxval + 1): opacity = transferfunction(v) if opacity > alphamax: alphamax = opacity # Prune if fully transparent if alphamax == 0: # Return empty box or skip adding to primitives list # The source specifies "returning an empty box", which effectively # removes it from traversal if the BVH builder handles empty bounds. continue else: primitives.append(region.boundingbox) # Construct BVH from the filtered primitives bvh = BVHBuilder(primitives) return bvh A GPU-based Empty Space Skipping (ESS) technique that uses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) built from clustered active regions of a volume, traced via NVIDIA OptiX, to skip empty space during direct volume rendering. Time Complexity: BVH construction is O(N \log N) where N is the number of non-pruned regions. The cost of pruning is proportional to the number of regions and the cost of evaluating the transfer function over the scalar range. Memory Complexity: The BVH size is reduced by the number of pruned regions, saving memory proportional to the number of excluded leaves and internal nodes. Performance: Hardware ray traversal is cheap and amortized over multiple samples. Space skipping is achieved without runtime overhead. However, a full BVH rebuild on large datasets (e.g., Exajet) takes approximately 300ms on a Titan RTX or RTX 8000 GPU. Strengths: No additional structures needed for space skipping; no runtime validity checks; leverages hardware acceleration efficiently. Limitations: Requires BVH rebuild on transfer function or iso-value changes; not suitable for dynamic transfer functions without significant latency. This method is part of the ExaBricks rendering framework for Adaptive Block-Refined (ABR) data, which uses hardware-accelerated RTX BVH traversal. It was introduced to handle visibility-dependent regions more efficiently than static sparsity masks, avoiding the need for additional structures like those used by Morrical et al.. name: Region Clustered BVH Volume Rendering
head: GPU BVH ESS, OptiX DVR
body: Region Clustered BVH Volume Rendering is a GPU-based Empty Space Skipping (ESS) technique that accelerates direct volume rendering by constructing a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) from clustered active regions of a volume, which is then traced via NVIDIA OptiX to skip empty space. Unlike traditional GPU DVR methods that rely on octrees or rasterization-based occupancy geometry (such as Sparseleap), this method leverages BVHs to represent sparse or thin strands of data with fewer nodes, avoiding the need for rasterization when the camera moves. The method operates in two phases: an offline CPU-based construction phase that prepares the BVH from volume data, and an online GPU-based traversal phase using OptiX. Input: A volumetric dataset divided into fixed-size regions (bricks); a transfer function (TF) defining opacity thresholds. Output: A BVH structure containing Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) for clustered active regions, ready for ray tracing. 1. Region Flags Array: A 3D array (or bit-string) where each element corresponds to a region in the volume. The value is 1 if the region is active (contains opacity > 0 according to the TF) and 0 otherwise. 2. 3D Summed Area Table (3DSAT): A precomputed 3D array derived from the Region Flags Array. It allows O(1) queries (8 lookups) to determine the number of active regions within any rectangular sub-volume. 3. Clustered AABBs: A list of bounding boxes representing the spatial extent of each identified cluster of active regions. 1. Region Partitioning: Divide the volume into fixed-size regions (bricks). For each region, store the minimum and maximum voxel values. 2. Activity Testing: When the transfer function updates, test all regions in parallel to determine if they are active. A region is active if its min/max values indicate the presence of opacity > 0. Store the result as a 3D bit-string ActiveFlags. 3. 3DSAT Construction: Compute the 3D Summed Area Table from ActiveFlags. For any sub-volume defined by corners (x1, y1, z1) and (x2, y2, z2), the number of active regions N is calculated using 8 lookups into the 3DSAT. 4. Clustering: Identify contiguous groups of active regions to form larger cube-shaped blocks (e.g., 2\times2\times2, 3\times3\times3, 4\times4\times4) to reduce the total node count in the BVH. Maintain a ClusteredFlags bit-string to track regions already assigned to a cluster. Sweep through the volume in descending order of cluster size (e.g., checking for 64^3, then 63^3, etc.). For each candidate cluster size S, iterate through all possible positions. If a candidate block of size S consists entirely of active regions (verified via 3DSAT) and no region in the block is marked in ClusteredFlags, mark the block as a cluster and update ClusteredFlags. 5. AABB Generation: Calculate the spatial bounds (AABBs) for each identified cluster. 6. BVH Construction and Traversal: Pass the list of AABBs to NVIDIA OptiX. OptiX constructs the BVH and initiates ray tracing for the volume rendering pipeline. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildregionclusteredbvh(volumedata, transferfunction, regionsize): """ Constructs a BVH for empty space skipping using region clustering. """ # 1. Determine active regions # volumedata is a 3D array of voxels # transferfunction is a callable or lookup table activeflags = computeactiveflags(volumedata, transferfunction, regionsize) # 2. Build 3D Summed Area Table for O(1) region counting sat = build3dsummedareatable(activeflags) # 3. Cluster active regions # Max cluster size to check (e.g., 64) maxclusterdim = 64 clusteredflags = createzerobitstring(activeflags.shape) clusters = [] # Sweep in descending order of cluster size for size in range(maxclusterdim, 1, -1): # Iterate over all possible top-left corners for a cube of 'size' for x in range(0, activeflags.shape[0] - size + 1): for y in range(0, activeflags.shape[1] - size + 1): for z in range(0, activeflags.shape[2] - size + 1): # Check if this block is fully active using 3DSAT # 8 lookups into sat count = query3dsat(sat, x, y, z, x + size - 1, y + size - 1, z + size - 1) expectedcount = size size size if count == expectedcount: # Check if any region in this block is already clustered if not isanyregionclustered(clusteredflags, x, y, z, size): # Mark this block as a cluster markregionsasclustered(clusteredflags, x, y, z, size) # Calculate AABB for this cluster aabb = computeaabbfromregioncoords(x, y, z, size, regionsize) clusters.append(aabb) # 4. Build BVH from clusters bvh = optixbuildbvh(clusters) return bvh def computeactiveflags(volume, tf, regionsize): """ Returns a 3D bit-string where 1 indicates an active region. """ flags = zeroslike(volume, dtype=bool) # Parallel test of all regions for each region r in volume: minval, maxval = getregionminmax(volume, r) if tfhasopacity(minval, maxval): flags[r] = True return flags def query3dsat(sat, x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2): """ Returns the sum of active flags in the box defined by corners. Uses 8 lookups into the 3D SAT. """ # Standard 3D SAT inclusion-exclusion principle return ( sat[x2, y2, z2] sat[x1-1, y2, z2] - sat[x2, y1-1, z2] - sat[x2, y2, z1-1] + sat[x1-1, y1-1, z2] + sat[x1-1, y2, z1-1] + sat[x2, y1-1, z1-1] sat[x1-1, y1-1, z1-1]) Cluster Shapes: The method prefers cube-shaped clusters (2\times2\times2, 3\times3\times3, etc.). Future work suggests investigating non-cubed shapes (e.g., 2\times2\times8). Precision: The 3DSAT query requires exact integer arithmetic to ensure count == expectedcount. Floating-point errors in TF evaluation should be avoided. Degenerate Input: If the volume is entirely empty, the BVH will be empty, and no rays will be traced. If the volume is entirely active, the clustering may result in a single large block or a few large blocks, depending on the sweep order. Time Complexity: The clustering step involves a sweep over the volume dimensions. For a volume of size N and max cluster size K, the complexity is roughly O(N \cdot K^3) in the worst case if not optimized, but the 3DSAT allows fast validation. The BVH build time is noted as not a hindering factor. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, the active flags bit-string, the 3DSAT (same dimensions as active flags), and the BVH nodes. Performance: Tested on an Intel Xeon E5-1620 v2 CPU and NVIDIA RTX2080 GPU. The method shows performance benefits over non-clustered BVHs and avoids the rasterization overhead of Sparseleap. Strengths: Efficiently handles sparse data and thin strands with fewer BVH nodes than octrees; avoids rasterization overhead on camera move. Limitations: Build time on CPU; clustering heuristic is limited to fully active cubes in the basic implementation. Origin: The method was presented in the context of re-evaluating BVHs for GPU-based ESS for Direct Volume Rendering, leveraging NVIDIA OptiX and RTX RTCore hardware. History: BVHs were traditionally used on CPUs for full-resolution DVR (Knoll et al. 2011) but were not standard on GPUs due to build times and traversal logic. This method adapts them for GPU ESS using hardware-accelerated ray tracing. Comparison: It differs from Sparseleap (Hadwiger et al. 2018), which uses octrees to generate occupancy geometry that must be rasterized on camera move. It also differs from traditional GPU DVR octrees, which can become deep and expensive for sparse data. An Analysis of Region Clustered BVH Volume Rendering..., https://www.highperformancegraphics.org/wp-content/uploads/2019/session1/regionclusteredbvhvolumerendering.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Sparse Brick Set Rendering
head: Raytraced SDF rendering with bricks
body: Sparse Brick Set Rendering is a method for rendering Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) using hardware-accelerated raytracing against a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) of leaf bricks, where each brick contains SDF data and is intersected via software shaders and sphere-tracing. It differs from its parent ExaBricks Rendering with RTX BVH by specifically utilizing SDF sphere-tracing within leaf nodes rather than general volume integration, and from RTX BVH Ray Tracing by relying on software intersection shaders for the SDF geometry rather than hardware-native triangle or primitive intersection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of leaf bricks, each containing a 3D texture of distance values. A BVH constructed from AABBs enclosing these bricks. A camera ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Output: The intersection distance t to the nearest isosurface, the surface normal \mathbf{n}, and the object-space position \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Brick: A 3D texture of size 8^3 = 512 samples. Inner Data: The inner 6^3 samples are sphere-traced. Padding: A neighbourhood of voxels is duplicated for each brick to avoid the texture sampler crossing brick boundaries during linear filtering. Note: 58% of each brick is dedicated to adjacency data. BVH: A hierarchy of AABBs. Only leaf nodes (representing individual bricks) are stored in the final structure used for traversal; internal nodes are discarded after construction. Algorithm Steps: 1. BVH Construction: Construct an AABB for every brick and place them into a BVH for hardware-accelerated raytracing. Only leaf bricks are required; other levels are discarded after construction. 2. BVH Traversal: Perform hardware-accelerated ray-BVH traversal. When a ray potentially intersects a leaf brick's AABB, invoke a software intersection shader. 3. AABB Intersection: Calculate the entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) distances of the ray with respect to the brick's AABB. This defines the ray interval for checking intersection with the isosurface. 4. Local Coordinate Transformation: Transform the intersection point into the bounding box's local coordinate system, ranging from [0, 1]. 5. Sphere-Tracing: Iteratively find the intersection between the ray and the isosurface using sphere-tracing. 6. Distance Sampling: Sample distance values from the volume using trilinear sampling. 7. Distance Transformation: Transform sampled distances from their formatted form in the volume texture to distances in the space encoded within the AABB where sphere tracing is performed. 8. Termination: Terminate sphere-tracing upon the first intersection with the surface, as all geometry within a brick is opaque. 9. Object-Space Transformation: Transform the intersection point back into object-space to calculate the t-value of intersection as the distance between the object-space ray origin and the object-space position of intersection. 10. Normal Calculation: Calculate surface normals using central differencing to find the gradient in the distance field at the point of intersection. Parameters: Brick Size: 8^3 voxels. The inner 6^3 are used for tracing. Sphere-Trace Max Steps: Not given in the sources. Epsilon: Not given in the sources. Distance Format Transformation: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparsebricksetrender(rayorigin, raydirection, brickaabb, bricktexture, Mobjtolocal, Mlocaltoobj): # 1. Hardware BVH traversal finds leaf brick AABB intersection # Not given in the sources: hardware BVH traversal implementation. tmin, tmax = aabbintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, brickaabb) if tmax < 0: return None # 2. Transform ray to brick local space [0,1]^3 localrayorigin = transformpoint(rayorigin, Mobjtolocal) localraydir = transformdirection(raydirection, Mobjtolocal) # 3. Sphere-tracing in local space currentpos = localrayorigin maxsteps = 100 # Not given in the sources. epsilon = 1e-4 # Not given in the sources. for in range(maxsteps): # 4. Sample distance using trilinear filtering distval = sampletrilinear(bricktexture, currentpos) # 5. Transform stored distance value to local space distance # Not given in the sources: exact distance format transformation. localdist = distval # 6. Check for intersection if localdist <= epsilon: break # 7. Advance along the ray currentpos = [currentpos[i] + localraydir[i] localdist for i in range(3)] else: return None # 8. Transform intersection point back to object space objectpos = transformpoint(currentpos, Mlocaltoobj) # 9. Calculate t-value as distance between object-space ray origin and intersection t = norm([objectpos[i] - rayorigin[i] for i in range(3)]) # 10. Calculate normal using central differencing in object space delta = 1.0 / 512.0 # Approximate voxel size in object space # Not given in the sources: exact SDF query implementation depends on brick layout. # dx = (querysdf(objectpos[0]+delta, objectpos[1], objectpos[2]) - querysdf(objectpos[0]-delta, objectpos[1], objectpos[2])) / (2 delta) # dy = (querysdf(objectpos[0], objectpos[1]+delta, objectpos[2]) - querysdf(objectpos[0], objectpos[1]-delta, objectpos[2])) / (2 delta) # dz = (querysdf(objectpos[0], objectpos[1], objectpos[2]+delta) - querysdf(objectpos[0], objectpos[1], objectpos[2]-delta)) / (2 delta) dx, dy, dz = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Not given in the sources. normallen = norm([dx, dy, dz]) normal = [dx/normallen, dy/normallen, dz/normallen] return t, normal, objectpos def aabbintersect(origin, direction, aabb): # Standard slab method for AABB intersection tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < aabb.min[i] or origin[i] > aabb.max[i]: return -1.0, -1.0 else: t1 = (aabb.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (aabb.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return -1.0, -1.0 return tmin, tmax def transformpoint(p, M): return [p[0]M[0][0] + p[1]M[1][0] + p[2]M[2][0] + M[3][0], p[0]M[0][1] + p[1]M[1][1] + p[2]M[2][1] + M[3][1], p[0]M[0][2] + p[1]M[1][2] + p[2]M[2][2] + M[3][2]] def transformdirection(v, M): return [v[0]M[0][0] + v[1]M[1][0] + v[2]M[2][0], v[0]M[0][1] + v[1]M[1][1] + v[2]M[2][1], v[0]M[0][2] + v[1]M[1][2] + v[2]M[2][2]] def sampletrilinear(texture, pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation return texture[pos[0]][pos[1]][pos[2]] # Simplified for pseudocode def norm(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Each brick uses 8^3 samples, with 58% being padding. Performance: Rendering is generally much faster than construction, and consequently optimization efforts were focused on construction instead. Strengths: Simple implementation, leverages hardware BVH traversal, avoids boundary issues with texture sampling via padding. Limitations: High memory overhead due to padding (58%). Sphere-tracing is used for simplicity despite analytical intersections being potentially faster. Central differencing for normals requires 6 samples, whereas the tetrahedron technique requires only 4. The method is based on the "sparse brick set" approach described by Evans (2022). The use of 8^3 bricks matches the wavefront size of targeted GPU hardware, allowing efficient processing by thread groups of 8^3 = 512 threads. The rendering technique is similar to hardware-accelerated raytracing methods, but specifically applies to SDFs using software shaders for the intersection logic. Real-time Rendering and Construction of Signed Distance Fields, https://jambuttenshaw.github.io/devportfolio/Dissertation.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Brick Size and Octree Limit Tuning
head: Hardware-specific Bricking, Performance Optimization via Brick Size and Octree Limit Tuning, Sampling Direction Optimization
body: Brick Size and Octree Limit Tuning optimizes GPU-based volume rendering by selecting the optimal dimensions for spatial bricks and the minimum depth of the hierarchical octree structure to balance rasterization load, triangle throughput, and texture memory constraints. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by treating brick size and octree limit as orthogonal variables that must be tuned specifically for the target hardware's texture sampling characteristics and memory hierarchy, rather than relying on a single fixed subdivision strategy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, target graphics hardware specifications (texture memory size, sampling direction penalties), and rendering parameters (view direction, transfer function). Output: Optimized brick dimensions (Bx, By, Bz) and octree limit (L). Data Structures: The method operates on the existing hierarchical grid structures defined in Hierarchical and Block-Based Data Structures. The key tunable parameters are: 1. Brick Size: The dimensions of the uniform 3D texture blocks. Sizes are typically powers of 2 to align with hardware texture requirements. 2. Octree Limit: The smallest cube size allowed in the octree subdivision. Nodes smaller than this limit are not subdivided further, regardless of data sparsity. Steps for Tuning: 1. Determine Hardware Constraints: Identify the optimal texture size for the target GPU and any sampling direction penalties (e.g., linear vs. z-axis traversal). 2. Fix One Variable: Since brick size and octree limit are orthogonal, fix the octree limit to a candidate value (e.g., 8^3 voxels) while varying the brick size. 3. Measure Performance: Render the volume with different brick sizes. Observe frame rates and identify the peak performance. Note: If the viewing direction differs from the texture z-axis by more than 45°, z-direction traversal becomes inevitable. To mitigate ATi FireGL X1-style z-direction performance penalties, alternate the orientation of the textures for each consecutive brick. 4. Fix Brick Size: Set the brick size to the optimal value found in Step 3. 5. Vary Octree Limit: Render the volume with different octree limits while keeping the brick size constant. 6. Select Optimal Octree Limit: Identify the limit that balances rasterization load and triangle throughput. Pitfall: Smaller limits cause high CPU overhead and excessive triangle counts. Larger limits cause rasterization overhead due to larger, less sparse bricks. Formulas: The volume rendering integral is evaluated in discrete steps for Early Ray Termination (ERT), which requires front-to-back traversal: C{i+1} = (1 - Ai) \cdot \alphai \cdot ci + Ci A{i+1} = (1 - Ai) \cdot \alphai + Ai Where C is accumulated color, A is accumulated opacity, \alphai is sample opacity, and ci is sample color. Parameters: Brick Size: Depends on available texture memory, optimal texture size (power of 2), nature of the data set, overlap overhead, and hardware constraints. Octree Limit: Balances rasterization load and triangle throughput. Sample Rate: Typically 1.5 samples per voxel for performance measurements. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Direction: On hardware treating 3D textures as a stack of 2D slices (e.g., ATi FireGL X1), linear traversal (x or y) is much faster than z-direction traversal. Performance varies significantly based on viewing angle relative to texture axes. Optimal Values are Hardware-Specific: The optimal brick size and octree limit differ for each graphics card and sampling direction. For example, larger bricks benefit from linear traversal in the xy-plane, while smaller bricks benefit from reduced cache trashing in other directions. Sparsity: Early Ray Termination provides no performance gain for sparse data sets if the volume is already optimized for space-skipping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tunebricksandoctree(volume, hardware, viewdirection): """ Finds optimal brick size and octree limit for a given volume and hardware. """ # Step 1: Determine hardware constraints optimaltexturesize = hardware.getoptimaltexturesize() haszpenalty = hardware.hassamplingdirectionpenalty() # e.g., ATi FireGL X1 # Step 2: Fix Octree Limit and vary Brick Size fixedoctreelimit = 8 # Example: 8^3 voxels bestbricksize = None maxfps = 0 for bricksize in [4, 8, 16, 32, 64]: # Powers of 2 # If z-penalty exists and view direction is not aligned, consider orientation if haszpenalty and not isaligned(viewdirection, hardware.texturezaxis): # Alternate orientation for consecutive bricks to mitigate penalty # This is a rendering strategy, but affects effective performance pass fps = rendervolume(volume, bricksize, fixedoctreelimit, hardware) if fps > maxfps: maxfps = fps bestbricksize = bricksize # Step 3: Fix Brick Size and vary Octree Limit fixedbricksize = bestbricksize bestoctreelimit = None maxfps = 0 for octreelimit in [4, 8, 16, 32, 64]: # Smallest cube size fps = rendervolume(volume, fixedbricksize, octreelimit, hardware) if fps > maxfps: maxfps = fps bestoctreelimit = octreelimit return bestbricksize, bestoctreelimit def rendervolume(volume, bricksize, octreelimit, hardware): """ Renders the volume with specified parameters and returns frame rate. """ # Build octree with specified limit octree = buildoctree(volume, octreelimit) # Create 3D textures for bricks # If z-penalty exists, alternate texture orientations textures = createbricks(volume, bricksize, hardware) # Traverse and render starttime = time.now() for frame in range(100): # Average over 100 frames renderframe(octree, textures, hardware) endtime = time.now() return 100 / (endtime - starttime) Time Complexity: Octree build time is bounded by CPU performance. For a 512^3 volume (256MB), building octrees took 6.5ms on a Xeon 1.7GHz and 3.5ms on a Xeon 3.0GHz. Memory Complexity: Depends on brick size and available texture memory. Smaller bricks increase overlap overhead; larger bricks require more texture memory. Performance: Significant acceleration is achieved over non-optimized GPU rendering. QuadroFX 3400: 73.5 fps (optimized) vs 9.6 fps (non-optimized), 7.66x acceleration. ATi FireGL X1 (xy aligned): 83.3 fps (optimized) vs 0.23 fps (non-optimized), 362x acceleration. ATi FireGL X1 (non xy aligned): 27.4 fps (optimized) vs 0.23 fps (non-optimized), 119x acceleration. 3DLabs Wildcat 7110: 21.3 fps (optimized) vs 0.38 fps (non-optimized), 56.1x acceleration. Scaling: Performance gains are hardware-dependent. Replacing a Xeon 3.0GHz with a 1.7GHz did not significantly affect rendering frame rates, as rendering is GPU-bound. Strengths: High acceleration on sparse data; effective use of texture memory; mitigates hardware-specific bottlenecks. Limitations: Requires hardware-specific tuning; complex to implement due to varying hardware behaviors; early ray termination is ineffective for sparse data if space-skipping is already optimal. This method originates from research by Danny Ruijters, presented in "Optimizing GPU Volume Rendering". It addresses the bottlenecks in the graphics pipeline for GPU-based volume rendering, specifically focusing on data locality, cache trashing, and hardware-specific texture sampling penalties. The approach combines bricking, octree acceleration, and early ray termination to lift these bottlenecks. Optimizing GPU Volume Rendering - Danny Ruijters, https://dannyruijters.nl/docs/OptimizingGPUVolumeRenderingfinal.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Residency Octree
head: Residency-Octree Hierarchy, hybrid data structure for out-of-core volume rendering, multi-resolution page tables combined with a special octree data structure
body: The Residency Octree is a hybrid data structure for out-of-core direct volume rendering (DVR) of multi-volume datasets that decouples the cache residency of multi-resolution data from the resolution-independent spatial subdivision determined by an octree. Unlike standard octrees where each node represents exactly one brick (one-to-one node-to-brick correspondence), each residency octree node represents a geometric spatial region and references all resolution levels in a bricked volume hierarchy. This decoupling enables efficient mixing of channel resolutions, cache-miss compensation by substituting missing bricks with available resolutions, and fine-grained empty-space skipping independent of the underlying bricking granularity. It combines the flexibility of page-table hierarchies with the traversal efficiency of octrees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multi-channel bricked volume hierarchy with n total channels, a brick cache, and a user-defined approximate leaf-node size in voxels. Output: A fully pointerless octree structure stored in a GPU buffer, enabling ray-guided traversal for rendering m \le n channels. Data Structures: The residency octree is implemented as a full, pointerless octree where all nodes are pre-allocated with fixed locations in a storage buffer to remove indirection. Node Layout: Each node consists of m unsigned 32-bit integers, where m is the number of simultaneously visualized channels. Per Channel (32 bits): 16 bits: Bitmap tracking which resolution levels the node is at least partially mapped in. 8 bits: Minimum scalar value (min) in the spatial region. 8 bits: Maximum scalar value (max) in the spatial region. Multi-Channel Extension: For channels where information is not yet initialized, the node stores a special INVALID value. If INVALID, the 32-bit slot stores a pointer to the next lower subdivision level node with valid information for that channel, or UNKNOWN if none exists. This pointer replaces the metadata to reduce memory usage. Memory Scaling: Memory usage scales linearly with the number of simultaneously visualized channels m. Definitions of Mapping States: For a given octree node and resolution level: 1. Fully Mapped: Cache-resident bricks of that level fully cover the node's spatial extent. 2. Partially Mapped: At least one brick of that level spatially overlaps with the node's extent and is resident in the cache. 3. Not Mapped: No resident bricks overlap the node. Fully mapped implies partially mapped, but not vice versa. If a node is fully mapped in a resolution level, all child nodes are also fully mapped in that level. If a node is partially mapped in a resolution level, its parent node is also partially mapped. Empty or homogeneous nodes are implicitly considered fully mapped in all resolution levels. Parameters: Leaf-node size: Defined indirectly by the user at initialization as an approximate leaf-node size in voxels. Brick size: Fixed and identical across all resolution levels in the bricked volume hierarchy (e.g., 32^3 voxels). Minimum voxels: A parameter specifying the minimum number of voxels to consider when computing metadata to avoid inaccuracies from coarse resolutions. Channel importance: User-defined weights to guide resolution range selection. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Determine the number of subdivision levels by iteratively subdividing the volume until the node size in each dimension is \le the user-defined approximate leaf-node size in voxels. Pre-allocate the pointerless octree buffer. Initialize the multi-channel page table hierarchy and brick cache. 2. Incremental Construction & Update (Server/Client Sync): Metadata Update: When new metadata for a volume region is received: Create the node if it doesn't exist, or update it if it does. Initialize metadata as INVALID for all channels except the one for which metadata was received. For the received channel, check if the node is partially mapped in each resolution level and update the bitmap accordingly. Propagate metadata up the tree: Parent min = \min(child1.min, \dots, child8.min); Parent max = \max(child1.max, \dots, child8.max). Brick Residency Update: When a new brick is received: Select an available slot in the brick cache. Identify all residency octree leaf nodes whose spatial extent overlaps the brick's spatial extent. Mark these leaf nodes as partially mapped in the brick's resolution level and channel. Propagate this update up the tree to the root node. Metadata Computation (Fallback): If the server does not support metadata queries, the client must fetch bricks at a resolution sufficient to meet the minimum number of voxels requirement to compute accurate min/max values. These bricks are uploaded to the GPU and residency info is updated. 3. Ray Traversal: Start traversal at the third level (or a user-defined level) instead of the root, and resume from the parent node of the last visited node rather than restarting per sample. For each node visited: Check transfer-function independent metadata (min, max). If the isosurface threshold T lies outside [min, max], prune the subtree. Check the residency bitmap. If the node is empty or homogeneous, treat it as fully mapped and skip loading bricks. If data is missing for a node, generate a ray-guided request to the server. If a brick is missing but a lower resolution is available, substitute it (cache-miss compensation). For multi-channel rendering: Evaluate each visible channel at every sample along the ray, even if channels have different resolutions, using accumulation-level intermixing. 4. Channel Replacement: When a channel is replaced by another, all nodes storing valid data for the old channel are marked INVALID for the new channel. The pointer mechanism is used to find valid data in lower subdivision levels if available. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseray(rayorigin, raydirection, startlevel=3, lastparentidx=None): # Resume traversal from last parent if available, else start at startlevel currentidx = lastparentidx if lastparentidx is not None else getrootchildatlevel(startlevel) while currentidx is not None: node = getnode(currentidx) # 1. Empty-space skipping using min/max metadata if rayorigin.x > node.maxval or rayorigin.x < node.minval or \ rayorigin.y > node.maxval or rayorigin.y < node.minval or \ rayorigin.z > node.maxval or rayorigin.z < node.minval: currentidx = getnextsibling(currentidx) continue # 2. Check residency bitmap for current resolution level if not (node.partialmapbitmap & (1 << currentresolutionlevel)): # Fallback to lower resolution if available fallbackres = findlowestsetbit(node.partialmapbitmap) if fallbackres is not None: samplewithbrick(rayorigin, raydirection, fallbackres) else: requestbrickfromserver(node.spatialextent, currentresolutionlevel) # Sources do not specify network protocol currentidx = getnextsibling(currentidx) continue # 3. Traverse children or sample leaf if isleaf(node): samplewithbrick(rayorigin, raydirection, currentresolutionlevel) else: currentidx = getfirstchild(currentidx) continue currentidx = getnextsibling(currentidx) def updateresidencyonbrickload(brick, resolutionlevel, channel): # Sources do not specify spatial search algorithm for overlapping leaves overlappingleaves = findoverlappingleafnodes(brick.spatialextent) for leaf in overlappingleaves: leaf.partialmapbitmap |= (1 << resolutionlevel) propagatepartialmapup(leaf) def propagatepartialmapup(node): if node is root: return parent = getparent(node) if node.ispartiallymapped(): parent.partialmapbitmap |= node.partialmapbitmap propagatepartialmapup(parent) Octree-based memory virtualization is an out-of-core rendering technique for multi-channel volume datasets that utilizes operating system memory mapping to load octree nodes and bricks on demand. It distinguishes itself from the Residency Octree by enforcing full subtree residency in the cache for high-resolution rendering, whereas the Residency Octree allows partial subtree residency. Unlike Virtual Memory Volume Rendering, which uses a multi-resolution page table hierarchy to avoid pre-computed 3D hierarchies, this method relies on an explicit octree structure. Residency Octree Update is a fully GPU-implemented parallel method for maintaining the spatial residency state of volumetric data bricks within a hierarchical octree structure. It solves the problem of keeping the residency octree consistent with the dynamic brick cache during both data loading and cache eviction, enabling efficient culling of non-resident volume regions during rendering. It differs from static octree construction by being fully parallel and event-driven, updating nodes only when bricks are added or removed from the cache. It differs from simple flat caches by maintaining a hierarchical bitmap representation of partial residency across multiple resolution levels and channels. A ray-guided renderer that accesses metadata and cached volume data through the Residency Octree to enable efficient mixing of resolutions across different channels in multi-volume datasets. It is implemented as a WebGPU compute shader that evaluates each visible channel at every sample along the ray, even when channels have different resolutions, to reduce shader divergence. Uses accumulation-level intermixing to combine different channels. The residency octree is backed by a channel-agnostic brick cache where each cache entry only contains data belonging to a single channel. This allows the number of channels to not be limited by the texture format used by the brick cache implementation, unlike Brix et al.'s approach. Residency octrees support changes to the selection of visible channels at run-time by replacing only the parts of their nodes related to the affected channels. Classification of octree nodes based on cache residency of bricks covering their spatial extent at a given resolution level. A node is fully mapped if cache-resident bricks of that level fully cover the node's spatial extent. A node is partially mapped if at least one brick of that level overlaps with the node's spatial extent and is resident in the cache. Fully mapped implies partially mapped, but not vice versa. If a node is fully mapped in a resolution level, all child nodes are also fully mapped in that level. If a node is partially mapped in a resolution level, its parent node is also partially mapped. An extension where all channels share the same octree structure, but each node stores culling and residency information for up to m \le n channels. This allows using the same spatial subdivision for empty-space skipping while rendering each channel in a different resolution. When a channel is replaced by another one, all nodes storing valid data for the old channel are marked as INVALID for the new channel. If invalid, the node stores a pointer to the node in the next lower subdivision level that has valid information for that channel, or a special UNKNOWN value if no such node exists. The pointer replaces the metadata for that channel to reduce memory. Time Complexity: Ray traversal is performed for spatial regions corresponding to octree nodes instead of bricks, and this traversal is independent of the number of channels. Memory Complexity: Memory usage scales linearly with the number of simultaneously visualized channels m. This can be mitigated by combining channels via dimensionality reduction, interleaving channels in four-component textures, or using compressed texture formats. The bit-width of the brick ID data type (e.g., 32-bit or 64-bit) constrains the maximum volume size and the maximum number of channels representable by the multi-channel page table hierarchy. Performance: Implemented as a web-based, pure client-side renderer using WebGPU and WebAssembly, it is faster than prior approaches and efficient for many data channels with a flexible and adaptive choice of data resolution. Strengths: Decouples cache residency from spatial subdivision, allowing adaptive resolution mixing and cache-miss compensation without requiring all lower resolutions to be resident. Supports fine-grained empty-space skipping independent of data subdivision. Limitations: Accumulation-level intermixing (evaluating illumination per channel per sample) is computationally more expensive than image-level intermixing. If the server does not support metadata queries, metadata must be computed on the fly, requiring careful resolution selection to meet the minimum voxel count. When to use: Out-of-core DVR of large-scale volumetric data sets with a large number of channels, such as Immunofluorescence (IF) imaging data. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Residency Octree was introduced as a hybrid approach for scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedicinal datasets. It addresses the limitations of previous octree-based out-of-core methods (e.g., [CNLE09], [BPH14]) which used a one-to-one mapping between bricks and octree nodes, intrinsically coupling resolution levels to spatial subdivision. It also improves upon page-table-based approaches which lacked efficient strategies for substituting missing high-resolution data with lower-resolution data. The method is designed for multi-channel immunoﬂuorescence data, using minima/maxima for empty-space skipping instead of histograms to maintain precision for unimodal transfer functions. name: Octree-based memory virtualization
head: Crassin et al. Octree-based memory virtualization, Interactive Visualization via Memory Mapping
body: Octree-based memory virtualization is an out-of-core rendering technique for multi-channel volume datasets that utilizes operating system memory mapping to load octree nodes and bricks on demand. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Residency Octree by enforcing full subtree residency in the cache for high-resolution rendering, whereas the Residency Octree allows partial subtree residency. Unlike Virtual Memory Volume Rendering, which uses a multi-resolution page table hierarchy to avoid pre-computed 3D hierarchies, this method relies on an explicit octree structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-channel volume dataset stored on disk; octree structure where nodes and bricks store information for up to n channels. Output: Rendered image with channels mixed via alpha blending. Data Structures: Octree Nodes: Store culling metadata and pointers to bricks. For multi-channel data, a node is marked homogeneous only if its corresponding bricks in all channels are homogeneous. Bricks: Store voxel data for up to n channels. Homogeneous Optimization: If a brick is homogeneous (all voxels contain the same value up to a user-defined threshold), the node stores the average value of the brick instead of a pointer to the brick’s location in the brick cache. Parameters: n (Number of Channels): Implementation-defined and cannot be changed at run-time. In practice, limited to 4 because GPU texture formats are limited to four components. Algorithm Steps: 1. Memory Mapping: Map the binary data files containing the octree and bricks to virtual memory using the OS-provided mmap function. This avoids loading the entire structure into physical memory, ensuring efficient use of physical memory by only loading parts actually rendered during tree traversals. 2. Tree Traversal: Traverse the octree. Since the trees are stored breadth-first, this progressive loading enables fast recursive refinements. 3. Culling: For each child of the current node, perform culling tests. Ignore children that do not pass. 4. Homogeneity Check: Determine if the current node's bricks are homogeneous across all n channels. 5. Data Access: If homogeneous: Retrieve the stored average value. If not homogeneous: Load the brick from the mapped virtual memory into the brick cache. 6. Rendering: Render the leaf nodes (e.g., as splats or rays) using the loaded data. 7. Adaptive Refinement: If the current frame rate is too low, smoothly increase the minimum regular splat size (\deltar) and minimum boundary splat size (\deltab) to reduce rendering load. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumeoctree(rootnode, nchannels): # Map files to virtual memory using OS mmap virtualmemory = osmmap(datafiles) # Global parameters for adaptive refinement deltar = initialminregularsplatsize deltab = initialminboundarysplatsize traversetree(rootnode, virtualmemory, nchannels, deltar, deltab) def traversetree(node, virtualmemory, nchannels, deltar, deltab): # Adaptive refinement check if currentframerate < threshold: deltar = smoothincrease(deltar) deltab = smoothincrease(deltab) for child in node.children: # Culling test if not passesculling(child): continue # Calculate screen size of bounding sphere screensize = calculatescreensize(child.boundingsphere) if child.isleaf: # Render leaf node renderleaf(child, virtualmemory, nchannels, deltar, deltab) else: # Recurse traversetree(child, virtualmemory, nchannels, deltar, deltab) def renderleaf(leaf, virtualmemory, nchannels, deltar, deltab): # Check homogeneity for all n channels ishomogeneous = True averagevalues = [] for c in range(nchannels): brick = leaf.bricks[c] if not isbrickhomogeneous(brick): ishomogeneous = False break averagevalues.append(brick.averagevalue) if ishomogeneous: # Use stored average values data = averagevalues else: # Load brick from virtual memory into cache data = loadbrickfromvirtualmemory(leaf.brickpointers, virtualmemory) # Render using data (e.g., splatting or ray marching) renderdata(data, deltar, deltab) Extends this method to support multiple visible channels by storing pointers and culling metadata in each node. Enforces whole subtree residency, leading to higher memory footprint and worse performance for multiple channels compared to the Residency Octree. Uses a virtual memory scheme with arbitrary packing and no pre-computed 3D hierarchy, avoiding the need to hold the entire path from leaf to root in GPU memory required by this method. Memory Efficiency: High efficiency for physical memory usage because only parts of the data structure actually rendered during tree traversals are loaded into physical memory. Performance: Fast recursive refinements are enabled by the breadth-first storage of the trees. Limitations: The number of channels is limited to 4 due to GPU texture format constraints. The method requires explicit octree traversal and holding the entire path from leaf to root in memory, which can be a drawback compared to page-table methods. Adaptivity: Supports adaptive refinement by adjusting splat sizes based on frame rate. The method was introduced by Crassin et al. [CNLE09] as a scheme for out-of-core rendering. It has been implemented in the Voreen volume rendering framework [DLJL22]. Brix et al. [BPH14] extended this approach to multi-channel data sets. name: Octree-based out-of-core volume rendering
head: Octree approach, Octree reference implementation, Octree-based Out-of-Core LOD, Out-of-core octree
body: Octree-based out-of-core volume rendering is a method for rendering multi-channel volume datasets that exceed available texture memory by storing octree nodes and bricks on disk and loading them on demand. It extends the single-channel approach of Crassin et al. to support multiple visible channels by storing pointers and culling metadata in each node. Unlike the Residency Octree, which uses an octree for hierarchical culling but allows partial subtree residency, this method enforces that the whole subtree is resident in the cache for high-resolution rendering, leading to a higher memory footprint and worse performance for multiple channels compared to the author's page-table method. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Multi-channel volume dataset (up to n channels), camera parameters, transfer function, cache size limit. Output: Rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Octree Node: boundingbox: 3D bounding box of the voxel region. minvalues: Array of size m (number of visible channels), storing the minimum scalar value for each channel within this node. maxvalues: Array of size m, storing the maximum scalar value for each channel within this node. bricks: Array of size m, where each entry is a pointer (or disk offset) to the brick data for the corresponding channel. children: Pointers to 8 child nodes (if not a leaf). 2. Hierarchy Structure File: Contains connectivity information and visibility culling information (bounding boxes). Must fit in memory; trivially small. 3. Brick Cache: Fixed-size cache (e.g., 4 GB) holding resident bricks. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the hierarchy structure file into memory. Maintain a brick cache with a fixed capacity (e.g., 4 GB). Start tree traversal at the third subdivision level counting from the root node. Initialize the current traversal node to the parent node’s subdivision level in the tree structure of the last node visited for the last sample. 2. Ray Traversal and Node Loading: For each ray sample, determine the current node in the octree using a full octree implementation that allows direct access to the correct node for a ray sample in each subdivision level. For each visible channel c \in \{0, \dots, m-1\}: Check if the node's brick for channel c is in the cache. If not, load the brick from disk into the cache, evicting old bricks if necessary. Restart the tree traversal for each visible channel to ensure that the whole subtree is resident in the cache for high-resolution rendering. This means traversing from the current node down to the leaf level for channel c to guarantee all required bricks are loaded. If the brick for the desired resolution is missing, render the next lower resolution instead. 3. Culling: Use the minvalues and maxvalues stored in each node to perform visibility culling. If the scalar range of a node does not intersect with the transfer function's opacity range for any channel, skip the node and its children. Note: Bricks containing at least one non-zero value are not considered EMPTY and must be kept in memory even if transparent under current viewing conditions. 4. Rendering: Sample the loaded brick data for the current ray position. Apply transfer function and compositing. Accumulate color and opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class OctreeNode: def init(self, level, numchannels): self.level = level self.children = [None] 8 self.bricks = [None] numchannels self.minvalues = [0.0] numchannels self.maxvalues = [0.0] numchannels self.boundingbox = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction def getchildindex(node, ray): """Determines which of the 8 octree children the ray enters next.""" # Standard ray-octree child intersection logic # Returns index 0-7 based on ray direction and node center center = [(node.boundingbox[i] + node.boundingbox[i+3]) / 2.0 for i in range(3)] idx = 0 for i in range(3): if ray.direction[i] > 0: idx |= (1 << i) return idx def intersectstransferfunction(minval, maxval, tfopacitymin, tfopacitymax): """Checks if the scalar range intersects the transfer function's opacity range.""" return maxval >= tfopacitymin and minval <= tfopacitymax def samplebrick(ray, brickdata, brickorigin, bricksize): """Samples the loaded brick data for the current ray position.""" # Standard trilinear interpolation or texture lookup return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0) # Returns (R, G, B, A) def accumulate(color, opacity, currentcolor, currentopacity): """Applies front-to-back compositing.""" newopacity = currentopacity + opacity (1.0 - currentopacity) newcolor = currentcolor + color opacity (1.0 - currentopacity) return newcolor, newopacity def renderoctreeoutofcore(hierarchy, cachesize, numchannels, tfopacitymin, tfopacitymax, maxlevel): cache = {} # Simple dict-based cache: key=brickid, value=brickdata startlevel = 3 currentnode = hierarchy.root currentlevel = 0 for ray in hierarchy.rays: # Ensure we are at least at startlevel if currentlevel < startlevel: node = currentnode level = currentlevel while level < startlevel: childidx = getchildindex(node, ray) node = node.children[childidx] level += 1 currentnode = node currentlevel = level # For each visible channel, ensure full subtree residency for c in range(numchannels): node = currentnode level = currentlevel # Traverse down to leaf, loading bricks and culling while level < maxlevel: # Load brick if missing if node.bricks[c] is not None and node.bricks[c] not in cache: if len(cache) >= cachesize: cache.pop(next(iter(cache))) # Simple eviction cache[node.bricks[c]] = loadbrickfromdisk(node.bricks[c]) # Culling check if not intersectstransferfunction(node.minvalues[c], node.maxvalues[c], tfopacitymin, tfopacitymax): break # Skip this branch # Move to child containing ray childidx = getchildindex(node, ray) node = node.children[childidx] level += 1 # Sample leaf brick if node.bricks[c] in cache: brickdata = cache[node.bricks[c]] color, opacity = samplebrick(ray, brickdata, node.boundingbox, 32) currentcolor, currentopacity = accumulate(color, opacity, currentcolor, currentopacity) else: # Fallback to lower resolution if missing lowerbrick = getlowerresolutionbrick(node, c) color, opacity = samplebrick(ray, lowerbrick, node.boundingbox, 32) currentcolor, currentopacity = accumulate(color, opacity, currentcolor, currentopacity) # Update current node for next ray optimization currentnode = node currentlevel = level Parameters: Cache size: 4 GB. Brick size (and approximate leaf-node size): 32^3 voxels. Hierarchy structure file size: Must fit in memory, trivially small. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Channels Performance: For multiple channels, the octree has to be traversed for each channel to ensure that all subtrees are resident in the cache, leading to worse performance compared to single-channel rendering. Memory Footprint: Whole subtrees have to be resident in the cache for rendering the volume in high resolution, resulting in a higher memory footprint in terms of the number of bricks in the working set compared to the residency octree. Empty Space Skipping: Bricks containing at least one non-zero value are not considered EMPTY and thus have to be kept in memory even though they might be completely transparent under the current viewing conditions. Missing Bricks: In case of a missing brick in the desired resolution, render the next lower resolution instead. A GPU-driven data structure that virtualizes a bricked multi-resolution, multi-channel volume via a paged 3D address space. It solves the problem of managing brick residency and performing address translation for out-of-core volume rendering without traversing a tree structure. Unlike the Octree-based out-of-core volume rendering, which uses an octree for hierarchical culling and requires full subtree residency, the page-table hierarchy treats each brick as an independent chunk, allowing direct access to any brick in the dataset. It extends the single-channel page-table approach by maintaining one page-table hierarchy per channel, all sharing a single brick cache. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of ray samples, but with a high constant factor due to repeated tree traversals for each channel. For multiple channels, performance degrades significantly compared to single-channel rendering. Memory Complexity: High. Requires storing the entire subtree for high-resolution rendering in the cache, leading to a larger working set than the residency octree. Cache size is typically 4 GB. Measured Performance: CyCIF Small (16 channels): 122.8 ms/frame. CyCIF Medium (15 channels): 155.1 ms/frame. CyCIF Large (4 channels): 123.5 ms/frame. Kingsnake (1 channel): 11.6 ms/frame. Bonsai (1 channel): 4.5 ms/frame. Aneurism (1 channel): 4.8 ms/frame. Scaling: Performance scales poorly with the number of visible channels due to the need to restart tree traversal for each channel. Strengths: Simple hierarchical culling using min/max values; effective for single-channel rendering where it achieves comparable frame rates to other methods. Limitations: Poor performance for multiple channels; high memory footprint due to full subtree residency requirement; inefficient empty-space skipping for non-zero but transparent voxels. The octree-based out-of-core volume rendering approach is based on the out-of-core renderer presented by Crassin et al. [CNLE09] and is similar to the octree-based method discussed by Brix et al. [BPH14]. It was extended by the author of to support multiple visible channels by storing pointers and culling metadata in each node. The method is part of a broader effort to render large biomedical datasets, such as those generated by Cyclic Immunofluorescence (CyCIF) [LIW+ 18], which can exceed available texture memory. The approach is also related to techniques for visualizing unstructured grids by converting them into a hierarchy of regular grids stored in an octree.
