name: Multi-Channel Page-Table Hierarchy
head: GPU-driven page-table hierarchy, Multi-Resolution Page Directory, Multi-channel multi-resolution page table hierarchy, Page-table approach, Sarton et al. approach
body: The Multi-Channel Page-Table Hierarchy is a GPU-driven data structure that virtualizes a bricked multi-resolution, multi-channel volume via a paged 3D address space. It solves the problem of managing brick residency and performing address translation for out-of-core volume rendering without traversing a tree structure. Unlike the Residency Octree, which uses an octree for hierarchical culling, the page-table hierarchy treats each brick as an independent chunk, allowing direct access to any brick in the dataset. It extends the single-channel page-table approach by maintaining one page-table hierarchy per channel, all sharing a single brick cache. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Virtual multi-resolution, multi-channel address (l, c, p), where l is the resolution level, c is the channel index, and p \in [0, 1)^3 are normalized floating-point coordinates. Output: Physical voxel address within the brick cache, or a cache miss signal if the brick is not resident. Data Structures: 1. Page-Table Hierarchy: Stored as a single 3D texture in rgba32uint format. Each pixel represents a page (brick) for a specific channel and resolution level. RGB Channels: Store a 3D offset (ob) into the brick cache if the brick is resident. Alpha Channel: Stores a state flag: UNMAPPED (brick not resident), MAPPED (brick resident), or EMPTY (brick contains only zero values). 2. Page-Table Metadata Buffer: A GPU buffer storing an array of metadata for each page table, including its 3D offset (o{l,c}) within the main 3D texture. 3. Brick Cache: A single-channel 3D texture (e.g., r8unorm) storing the actual brick data. All bricks have the same size in voxels (b). 4. Request Buffer: A 3D texture in r32uint format with the same resolution as the page-table hierarchy. Stores the timestamp (frame number) when each page was last requested. 5. Brick ID: An unsigned 32-bit integer used to communicate cache misses to the CPU. Bits 0-7 (8 bits): Page-table index (index into the metadata buffer). Bits 8-31 (24 bits): Spatial offset (8 bits each for x, y, z coordinates) of the brick relative to the origin within its channel and resolution. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Page Address: Calculate the address of the page in the page table for resolution level l and channel c. p{vptl,c} = o{l,c} + \lfloor p \circ v{ptl} \rfloor Where: o{l,c} is the page table offset in \mathbb{Z}^3. v{ptl} is the page table extent in \mathbb{N}^3. \circ is element-wise product. \lfloor \cdot \rfloor is element-wise flooring. 2. Retrieve Brick Offset: Sample the page at p{vptl,c} from the page-table hierarchy texture. If the alpha channel indicates EMPTY or UNMAPPED, trigger a cache miss. If MAPPED, extract the brick offset ob from the RGB channels. 3. Compute Voxel Address in Brick: Calculate the local address within the brick. pb = ob + \lfloor p \circ vl \rfloor \mod b Where: vl is the volume extent at resolution level l. b is the brick size in voxels. \mod is element-wise modulo. 4. Handle Cache Misses (Asynchronous): Write the current frame timestamp to the Request Buffer at the page address. Generate a Brick ID encoding the channel, resolution, and spatial position. The CPU reads the Request Buffer asynchronously (with at least a one-frame delay) to identify bricks to load. If the mapping between GPU-resident channels and dataset channels changes, a list of mappings with timestamps is used to correctly translate local brick IDs to global brick IDs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EMPTY = 0 UNMAPPED = 1 MAPPED = 2 vptlextents = [...] vlextents = [...] bricksize = 64 metadataoffsets = [...] pagetabletexture = rgba32uint3Dtexture brickcache = r8unorm3Dtexture requestbuffer = r32uint3Dtexture currentframe = 0 def getvoxel(p, l, c): # 1. Compute page address in the 3D texture # p in [0,1)^3, vptlextents[l] is the page table extent for level l pageaddress = metadataoffsets[l] + floor(p vptlextents[l]) # 2. Sample page state and brick offset page = pagetabletexture.sample(pageaddress) state = page.a brickoffset = page.rgb if state == EMPTY or state == UNMAPPED: # 3. Record cache miss with timestamp requestbuffer.write(pageaddress, currentframe) # 4. Generate 32-bit brick ID for CPU communication # 8 bits for page-table index, 24 bits for spatial offset pagetableindex = c len(vptlextents) + l spatialoffset = pageaddress - metadataoffsets[l] brickid = (spatialoffset.x | (spatialoffset.y << 8) | (spatialoffset.z << 16)) | (pagetableindex << 24) return brickid # Signal cache miss to CPU # 5. Compute voxel address within the brick # p in [0,1)^3, vlextents[l] is volume extent, bricksize is constant localvoxel = floor(p vlextents[l]) % bricksize physicaladdress = brickoffset + localvoxel # 6. Fetch from brick cache voxeldata = brickcache.sample(physicaladdress) return voxeldata Parameters: Brick Size (b): Constant for all bricks. Simplifies cache management as each entry in the brick cache has the same size. Brick Cache Size: Determines the maximum number of bricks in the working set. Number of Channels (m): Number of channels referenced simultaneously. Brick ID Data Type: 32-bit unsigned integer. Constrains the maximum number of bricks and channels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bit-width Constraint: The 32-bit brick ID limits the total number of page tables (m \times k) to 256. Mapping Changes: If the channel mapping changes, previously generated local brick IDs may be translated incorrectly due to the one-frame delay in reading the request buffer. This is mitigated by storing a list of mappings with timestamps. Empty Space Skipping: Bricks are only marked EMPTY if all voxels are zero. This is not transfer-function aware, so empty space skipping occurs only in rare cases. Missing Bricks: If a brick is missing, all samples falling into it are skipped for that channel; the method does not substitute missing bricks with lower-resolution versions. Memory Utilization: Bricks with at least one non-zero value must be kept in memory even if transparent under the current viewing conditions, leading to worse GPU memory utilization compared to transfer-function-aware methods. A method by Sarton et al. [SCRL20] that generalizes page-table hierarchies for non-rendering purposes and processes cache misses on the GPU itself using CUDA shared memory to minimize memory transfers between CPU and GPU. It decouples cache residency management from the spatial subdivision, using a global usage buffer and an LRU buffer to keep frequently used bricks in the cache. Time Complexity: Direct access to bricks avoids tree traversal overhead, making it efficient for dense volumes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the page-table hierarchy (one 3D texture per channel/level combination, though often packed) and the brick cache. Performance: Benchmark results for the page-table hierarchy approach show: CyCIF Small (16 channels): 34.0 ms/frame; CyCIF Medium (15 channels): 40.4 ms/frame; CyCIF Large (4 channels): 24.4 ms/frame; Kingsnake (1 channel): 15.0 ms/frame; Aneurism (4 channels): 15.0 ms/frame. Strengths: More efficient data-access patterns than octrees for dense volumes; no tree traversal overhead. Limitations: Performs significantly worse than the residency octree for datasets with large transparent regions (e.g., Aneurism, Bonsai, Kingsnake) because empty space skipping is limited to zero-valued bricks. The negative effects in the single-channel case are amplified with multiple channels. The multi-channel page-table hierarchy is modeled after the fully GPU-driven approach presented by Sarton et al. [SCRL20]. It forms the base of the residency octree. The approach virtualizes a bricked multi-volume hierarchy by implementing a paged 3D address space, extending earlier single-channel methods. name: Parallel cache management with LRU
head: GPU-based cache management, Sarton et al. LRU cache management
body: A method by Sarton et al. [SCRL20] that generalizes page-table hierarchies for non-rendering purposes and processes cache misses on the GPU itself using CUDA shared memory to minimize memory transfers between CPU and GPU. It uses a global usage buffer and an LRU buffer to keep frequently used bricks in the cache. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A brick cache with N entries, a multi-channel page-table hierarchy, and a current timestamp t (e.g., frame number). Output: Updated LRU buffer order, and a list of missing brick IDs for the current timestamp. Data Structures: 1. Global Brick-Usage Buffer: An array comprising one timestamp per cache entry, storing the last timestamp at which the corresponding cache entry was accessed. 2. LRU Buffer: An array storing linear indices into the brick cache, sorted by their most recent usage times. 3. Global Request Buffer: A 3D buffer with one entry per page in the multi-channel page-table hierarchy, storing the last request timestamp for that page. 4. Request List: A dynamic list of brick IDs for pages requested at a specific timestamp t, compiled from the request buffer. Algorithm Steps: 1. Record Usage: When a brick-cache entry is accessed, write the current timestamp t to the corresponding location in the Global Brick-Usage Buffer. 2. Update LRU Buffer: Generate a boolean mask of brick-cache entries used at the current timestamp from the timestamps in the usage buffer. Use this mask to rearrange the previous LRU buffer such that the most recently used entries are moved to the front, preserving their relative order. 3. Handle Cache Misses: On GPU access to a non-resident, non-empty brick page, write the current timestamp to the page's location in the Global Request Buffer. 4. Retrieve Misses: To retrieve misses for timestamp t, read all pages from the Request Buffer with value t. 5. Compile Requests: Use a single stream compaction operation to compile a list of all brick IDs reported missing at timestamp t. 6. Stream Bricks: Read back the Request List to the CPU, which streams the missing bricks from the server. Parameters: Max Bricks per Timestamp: A limit on the number of requested bricks per timestamp to control traffic between client and server. Can be a constant or variable (e.g., decreased during user interactions like viewport changes). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Traffic Control: Excessive traffic may occur during temporally incoherent working sets if the limit is not enforced. Empty Bricks: The method distinguishes between non-resident bricks and those known to be empty; only non-empty non-resident bricks trigger requests. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. usagebuffer = [0] N # Stores last access timestamp for each cache entry lrubuffer = list(range(N)) # Indices into cache, sorted by recency requestbuffer = [0] P # Stores last request timestamp for each page requestlimit = 100 # Max bricks per timestamp cacheresident = [True] N # Tracks residency of each cache entry cacheempty = [False] N # Tracks emptiness of each cache entry pagetobrickid = [0] P # Maps page ID to brick ID def updatelru(timestamp): # Step 1: Generate mask for entries used at current timestamp mask = [usagebuffer[i] == timestamp for i in range(N)] # Step 2: Rearrange LRU buffer # Most recently used (mask is True) go to front, preserving relative order newlrufront = [idx for idx in lrubuffer if mask[idx]] # Least recently used (mask is False) go to back, preserving relative order newlruback = [idx for idx in lrubuffer if not mask[idx]] lrubuffer[:] = newlrufront + newlruback def handleaccess(cacheentryindex, pageid, brickid, timestamp): # Record usage in global buffer usagebuffer[cacheentryindex] = timestamp # Check residency and emptiness using standard cache state arrays if not cacheresident[cacheentryindex] and not cacheempty[brickid]: requestbuffer[pageid] = timestamp def processmisses(timestamp): # Find all pages requested at this timestamp requestedpages = [pid for pid, ts in enumerate(requestbuffer) if ts == timestamp] # Limit traffic if len(requestedpages) > requestlimit: requestedpages = requestedpages[:requestlimit] # Compile brick IDs (stream compaction) brickids = [pagetobrickid[pid] for pid in requestedpages] # Transfer list to CPU for streaming hosttransfer(brickids) # Clear request buffer for this timestamp for pid in requestedpages: requestbuffer[pid] = 0 An algorithm to process cache misses on the GPU and transmit brick requests to the CPU for streaming from the server. It uses a 3D Request Buffer storing the last request timestamp for each page and a Request List compiled via stream compaction for a specific timestamp. It allows limiting the number of requested bricks per timestamp to control traffic, which can be adjusted dynamically during user interactions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires additional global buffers: Usage Buffer (N integers), LRU Buffer (N integers), and Request Buffer (P integers). Performance: Minimizes CPU-GPU memory transfers by processing misses on the GPU using CUDA shared memory. Strengths: Efficient GPU-side miss processing; scalable to exascale volumes. Limitations: Requires synchronization between GPU and CPU for brick streaming; traffic control is necessary to prevent overload. Originated with Sarton et al. [SCRL20], who generalized page-table hierarchies for volumetric datasets for non-rendering purposes. The approach builds on earlier work by Fogal et al. [FSK13] who used a global hash table for reporting cache misses, but improves efficiency by processing misses on the GPU. It is used in scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. name: Virtual Memory Volume Rendering
head: Multi-Resolution Virtual Memory Scheme, Virtual Memory Architecture for Volume Rendering, Visualization-Driven Virtual Memory Volume Rendering
body: Virtual Memory Volume Rendering is an out-of-core rendering architecture that virtualizes 3D volumes by subdividing them into small 3D blocks and mapping them to a physical block cache using a multi-resolution page table hierarchy. It solves the problem of interactive exploration of petascale microscopy data streams by decoupling the construction of the 3D multi-resolution representation from data acquisition and sample access time from hierarchy size. Unlike sibling methods such as Octree-based out-of-core volume rendering which require explicit octree traversal and holding the entire path from leaf to root in GPU memory, this method avoids these drawbacks by using a virtual memory scheme with arbitrary packing and no pre-computed 3D hierarchy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A stream of 2D microscope image tiles (raw or processed into 2D mipmaps) and a camera/view state for ray-casting. Output: A rendered image from single-pass ray-casting. Data Structures: 1. Virtual Volume: The logical 3D volume subdivided into small 3D blocks of size B \times B \times B voxels. The standard block size is 32^3 voxels. 2. Multi-Resolution Page Directory: A hierarchy of page tables corresponding to resolution levels l. This is the top-level structure in the virtual memory hierarchy. 3. Page Table Cache: A cache storing page table entries (PTEs). Each PTE maps a virtual block position to a physical position in the Block Cache or is flagged as unmapped. 4. Block Cache: A large 3D texture resident in GPU memory containing the working set of currently required 3D blocks. Blocks are packed arbitrarily into this cache. 5. Cache Miss Hash Table: A structure used to track requested voxel blocks to manage cache updates. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray-Casting in Virtual Space: For each sample along a ray, the algorithm determines the multi-resolution level l and the page table entry p corresponding to the virtual voxel address. 2. Address Translation: The algorithm performs address translation using the Multi-Resolution Page Directory and the Page Table Cache to find the physical location in the Block Cache. 3. Cache Miss Detection: The system checks if the block is unmapped (not resident in the cache). Unmapped blocks produce cache misses. 4. Backward Propagation: Cache misses are propagated backwards to trigger on-demand out-of-core processing. 5. On-Demand Construction: The system fetches the required 2D sub-tiles from the input stream and stitches/resamples them into 3D blocks. 6. Cache Update: The constructed 3D blocks are stored in the Block Cache, and the Page Table Cache is updated to map the virtual address to the new physical location. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. BLOCKSIZE = 32 # voxels per dimension def raycastingloop(ray): for sample in ray.samples: # 1. Determine virtual address components levell = determineresolutionlevel(sample.position) virtualblockid = getvirtualblockid(sample.position, levell) # 2. Address Translation physicalblockindex = translateaddress( pagedirectory, pagetablecache, levell, virtualblockid) # 3. Cache Miss Detection if physicalblockindex is UNMAPPED: # 4. Propagate Cache Miss handlecachemiss(levell, virtualblockid) # Retry translation after miss handling physicalblockindex = translateaddress( pagedirectory, pagetablecache, levell, virtualblockid) # 5. Texture Fetch color = fetchblockcolor(blockcache, physicalblockindex, sample.offset) accumulatecolor(color) def handlecachemiss(levell, virtualblockid): # 6. On-Demand Construction # Fetch 2D sub-tiles corresponding to the virtual block required2dtiles = fetch2dsubtiles(virtualblockid) # Stitch and resample into 3D block new3dblock = stitchandresample(required2dtiles, BLOCKSIZE) # Allocate space in Block Cache (arbitrary packing) physicalblockindex = allocateblockincache(blockcache, new3dblock) # Update Page Table Cache updatepagetablecache( pagetablecache, levell, virtualblockid, physicalblockindex) # Record in cache miss table for consistency cachemisstable.add(virtualblockid) def translateaddress(pagedirectory, pagetablecache, levell, virtualblockid): # Check page table cache first if virtualblockid in pagetablecache: return pagetablecache[virtualblockid] # Traverse page directory hierarchy to find PTE # Not given in sources: specific traversal algorithm for multi-resolution page directory # Assuming a standard hierarchical lookup where higher levels coarsen the address pte = lookuppagedirectory(pagedirectory, levell, virtualblockid) if pte is VALID: pagetablecache[virtualblockid] = pte.physicalindex return pte.physicalindex else: return UNMAPPED Parameters: Block Size: 32^3 voxels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Data: Missing data are detected during ray-casting as cache misses. Unmapped blocks produce cache misses which must be handled by the backward propagation mechanism. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The system only stores the working set of currently required blocks in the Block Cache, avoiding the storage of the entire hierarchy in GPU memory. Measured Performance: The system is evaluated for scalability and performance on petascale microscopy data streams. Scaling: The architecture handles missing data naturally and does not pre-compute any 3D multi-resolution representation, allowing it to accept a constant stream of 2D image tiles. Strengths: Decouples construction of the 3D multi-resolution representation from data acquisition; decouples sample access time during ray-casting from the size of the multi-resolution hierarchy; avoids explicit octree traversal and holding the entire path from leaf to root in GPU memory; supports arbitrary packing of blocks in the cache. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Interactive exploration of petascale microscopy data streams where data is acquired as a stream of 2D image tiles. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Virtual Memory Volume Rendering was introduced in a 2012 paper by Hadwiger et al.. It is designed for real microscopy data from neuroscience, enabling interactive exploration of petascale volume data. The system is visualization-driven, restricting most computations to the visible volume data. It compares favorably to previous best-of-breed systems like Gigavoxels and CERA-TVR, which use explicit octree traversal. name: Residency Octree Update
head: Incremental Construction
body: Residency Octree Update is a fully GPU-implemented parallel method for maintaining the spatial residency state of volumetric data bricks within a hierarchical octree structure. It solves the problem of keeping the residency octree consistent with the dynamic brick cache during both data loading and cache eviction, enabling efficient culling of non-resident volume regions during rendering. It differs from static octree construction by being fully parallel and event-driven, updating nodes only when bricks are added or removed from the cache. It differs from simple flat caches by maintaining a hierarchical bitmap representation of partial residency across multiple resolution levels and channels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of added brick IDs, a list of removed brick IDs, and the current state of the brick cache (residency status of bricks). Output: Updated culling metadata (min/max values) and partially mapped resolution bitmasks for all affected nodes in the residency octree, up to the root. Data Structures: Residency Octree Node: cullingmin: Scalar minimum value of the volume data within this node's spatial extent. cullingmax: Scalar maximum value of the volume data within this node's spatial extent. residencybitmap: A bitmask where each bit represents a specific resolution level and/or channel. A bit is set if at least one brick at that resolution/channel is resident in the cache and overlaps the node's spatial extent. Update-Candidate Buffer: A dynamic buffer storing indices of nodes that require recomputation in the next level up. Parameters: Brick Size: Typically 32^3 voxels. Leaf-Node Size: The approximate spatial extent of leaf nodes in the residency octree. Can be decoupled from brick size (e.g., 32^3, 16^3, 8^3, or 8 \times 8 \times 4). Algorithm Steps: The update process is initiated by the application immediately after the frame's brick-cache update is completed. It proceeds in a breadth-first manner from leaf nodes up to the root, using indirect compute passes to manage workgroup dispatch and enable early termination. 1. Process Removed Bricks: For each brick ID in the "removed" list, determine the corresponding leaf nodes in the residency octree whose spatial extent overlaps the brick's extent. For each such leaf node, check if it is still partially resident in the resolution level of the removed brick. This is done by verifying if any other brick at that resolution level overlapping the node is still resident in the cache. If the node is no longer partially resident in that resolution, update its residencybitmap (clear the corresponding bit). Mark the parent node of the updated leaf node as an update candidate in the update-candidate buffer. 2. Compute Culling Metadata for New Bricks: For each scalar value in each newly added brick, determine the corresponding leaf node in the residency octree. If the scalar value is lower than the node's current cullingmin or greater than its cullingmax, update the node's metadata. Use atomic operations (atomicMin, atomicMax) to ensure concurrent updates from multiple threads are safe. Mark the parent node of the updated leaf node as an update candidate in the update-candidate buffer. 3. Process Added Bricks: For each brick ID in the "added" list, determine all leaf nodes in the residency octree whose spatial extent overlaps the brick's extent. Mark these leaf nodes as partially mapped in the brick's resolution level and channel by setting the corresponding bits in their residencybitmap. If a node's residencybitmap changed due to this operation, mark its parent node as an update candidate in the update-candidate buffer. 4. Compile Update Candidates: Process the update-candidate buffer to compile a unique list of all nodes marked as candidates for the next level up. Clear the update-candidate buffer for subsequent iterations. Use the count of candidates to control the number of workgroups dispatched for the next indirect compute pass. If no candidates remain, terminate the update process. 5. Process Update Candidates: For each candidate node, recompute its cullingmin, cullingmax, and residencybitmap from its child nodes. The residencybitmap is updated via bitwise OR of the child node bitmasks: B{parent} = B{child1} \lor B{child2} \lor \dots \lor B{child8}, where B is the bitmask. The cullingmin and cullingmax are recomputed as the minimum and maximum of the respective values from all child nodes. If any of the node's values (cullingmin, cullingmax, or residencybitmap) changed compared to the previous state, mark the node's parent as an update candidate in the update-candidate buffer. 6. Repeat: Repeat Steps 4 and 5 until the root node is reached or no update candidates remain. Early termination occurs if a node's bitmask remains unchanged by the OR operation during Step 5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def residencyoctreeupdate(addedbricks, removedbricks, brickcache, octreenodes): # Step 1: Process Removed Bricks for brickid in removedbricks: if brickcache[brickid].isresident: continue leafnodes = getleafnodesoverlappingextent(brickcache[brickid].spatialextent) for nodeidx in leafnodes: node = octreenodes[nodeidx] res = brickcache[brickid].resolution if not checkpartialresidency(nodeidx, res, brickcache): oldbitmap = node.residencybitmap node.residencybitmap = clearbit(node.residencybitmap, res) if oldbitmap != node.residencybitmap: addtocandidates(node.parentid) # Step 2: Compute Culling Metadata for New Bricks for brickid in addedbricks: if not brickcache[brickid].isresident: continue leafnodes = getleafnodesoverlappingextent(brickcache[brickid].spatialextent) for nodeidx in leafnodes: node = octreenodes[nodeidx] valmin = brickcache[brickid].minvalue valmax = brickcache[brickid].maxvalue oldmin = node.cullingmin oldmax = node.cullingmax node.cullingmin = min(node.cullingmin, valmin) node.cullingmax = max(node.cullingmax, valmax) if node.cullingmin != oldmin or node.cullingmax != oldmax: addtocandidates(node.parentid) # Step 3: Process Added Bricks (Residency Bitmap) for brickid in addedbricks: if not brickcache[brickid].isresident: continue leafnodes = getleafnodesoverlappingextent(brickcache[brickid].spatialextent) for nodeidx in leafnodes: node = octreenodes[nodeidx] res = brickcache[brickid].resolution oldbitmap = node.residencybitmap node.residencybitmap = setbit(node.residencybitmap, res) if oldbitmap != node.residencybitmap: addtocandidates(node.parentid) # Step 4 & 5: Iterative Upward Propagation candidates = list(updatecandidates) while candidates: nextcandidates = [] for nodeidx in candidates: node = octreenodes[nodeidx] newmin = float('inf') newmax = float('-inf') newbitmap = 0 for childidx in node.childids: child = octreenodes[childidx] newmin = min(newmin, child.cullingmin) newmax = max(newmax, child.cullingmax) newbitmap = newbitmap | child.residencybitmap changed = False if newmin != node.cullingmin: node.cullingmin = newmin changed = True if newmax != node.cullingmax: node.cullingmax = newmax changed = True if newbitmap != node.residencybitmap: node.residencybitmap = newbitmap changed = True if changed: addtocandidates(node.parentid, nextcandidates) candidates = nextcandidates # Step 4: Buffer cleared by reassigning candidates list # Dispatch controlled by len(candidates) def setbit(bitmap, bitindex): return bitmap | (1 << bitindex) def clearbit(bitmap, bitindex): return bitmap & ~(1 << bitindex) def addtocandidates(nodeidx, targetlist=None): if nodeidx is None: return if targetlist is None: targetlist = updatecandidates if nodeidx not in targetlist: targetlist.append(nodeidx) def checkpartialresidency(nodeidx, resolution, brickcache): # Verify if any other brick at the given resolution overlapping the node is resident bricks = getbricksoverlappingextent(getnodeextent(nodeidx)) for brick in bricks: if brick.isresident and brick.resolution == resolution: return True return False def getleafnodesoverlappingextent(extent): # Traverse octree to find leaves intersecting extent pass def getnodeextent(nodeidx): # Derived from octree structure pass def getbricksoverlappingextent(extent): # Spatial index lookup pass An optimization technique where the spatial subdivision granularity (leaf-node size) of the residency octree is decoupled from the resolution levels of the bricked volume hierarchy. This allows finer empty-space skipping than the bricking granularity. It is beneficial for anisotropic volumes and can achieve higher frame rates. Typical brick size is 32^3 voxels, while leaf-node sizes can be 32^3, 16^3, 8^3, or even 8 \times 8 \times 4. An approach where the octree is edited by a compute pass on the GPU, rather than on the CPU with deltas uploaded every frame. This is required to satisfy the constraint of no CPU readback per frame in the hot loop. Discrete events (player digs, meteor lands, explosion) may synchronise, but terrain streaming, LOD selection, or acceleration structure refits doing readback per frame remain forbidden. An octree edited on the CPU and re-uploaded every frame violates the constraint of no CPU readback per frame in the hot loop. Time Complexity: The update process is proportional to the number of changed bricks and the height of the octree. The use of indirect compute passes and early termination (when bitmasks do not change) optimizes performance by avoiding unnecessary work. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the octree nodes (culling metadata and bitmasks) and the update-candidate buffer. The buffer size is bounded by the number of affected nodes per frame. Performance: Fully GPU-implemented, allowing parallel construction and updates. Decoupling leaf-node size from brick size can improve performance by enabling finer empty-space skipping. Strengths: Efficient handling of dynamic data loading and eviction; parallel execution on GPU; early termination reduces overhead. Limitations: Requires atomic operations for culling metadata updates, which can introduce contention. Performance depends on the spatial distribution of changes and the octree structure. The method is implemented and evaluated within a scalable web-based volume rendering framework for large biomedical datasets. It is part of the Residency Octree framework, which decouples cache residency from spatial subdivision. The method was evaluated on datasets such as CyCIF Small and CyCIF Medium. name: Residency-Octree Updates
body: Residency-Octree Updates is a method for maintaining the spatial residency state of volumetric data bricks within a hierarchical octree structure, ensuring that the tree accurately reflects which data is currently resident in the GPU cache. It solves the problem of keeping the residency octree consistent with the dynamic brick cache during both data loading and cache eviction, enabling efficient culling of non-resident volume regions during rendering. It differs from static octree construction by being fully parallel and event-driven, updating nodes only when bricks are added or removed from the cache, and from simple flat caches by maintaining a hierarchical bitmap representation of partial residency across multiple resolution levels and channels. The method maintains a multi-channel residency octree where each node stores metadata and residency bitmaps. The updates are triggered by two events: receiving new metadata for a volume region and receiving a new brick (or evicting one). Residency Octree Node: metadata: Channel-specific status (e.g., INVALID, VALID). residencybitmap: A bitfield where each bit corresponds to a resolution level. A bit is set if the node is partially mapped (i.e., at least one brick at that resolution level is resident in the cache). children: Pointers to child nodes (for non-leaves). Brick Cache: Fixed-size LRU cache storing resident bricks. Each brick has a spatial extent and a resolution level. Inputs: New metadata for a volume region (channel, resolution, spatial bounds). New brick data (spatial bounds, resolution level, channel). Eviction request (brick to remove). Outputs: Updated residency octree with correct metadata and residencybitmap values. When new metadata for a volume region is received: 1. Check Node Existence: Determine if a node corresponding to the region's spatial extent exists in the octree. 2. If New Node: Create the node and add it to the octree. Initialize metadata as INVALID for all channels. Set metadata for the received channel to VALID (or appropriate state). Initialize residencybitmap by checking each resolution level to see if the node is partially mapped. This involves checking if any brick at that resolution level overlapping the node's extent is currently in the cache. 3. If Existing Node: Update the metadata for the specific channel. If this is a multi-channel volume and the node already holds metadata for another channel, re-initialize the residencybitmap for the new channel's resolution levels by checking cache residency. When a new brick is received and stored in the cache: 1. Select Slot: Choose an available slot in the brick cache. If none is available, trigger LRU Eviction (see below). 2. Identify Leaf Nodes: Find all residency-octree leaf nodes whose spatial extent overlaps with the brick's spatial extent. 3. Mark Leaves: For each identified leaf node, mark it as partially mapped in the brick's resolution level and channel. This is done by setting the corresponding bit in the node's residencybitmap. 4. Propagate Upwards: Traverse up the tree from the affected leaf nodes to the root. For each non-leaf node, update its residencybitmap by performing a bit-wise OR of its children's bitmaps. Termination Condition: If a node's residencybitmap remains unchanged after the OR operation, stop propagating updates up the tree from that branch. When a brick is evicted from the cache: 1. Identify Affected Leaves: Find all leaf nodes whose spatial extent overlaps with the evicted brick's spatial extent. 2. Check Residency: For each affected leaf node and for the resolution level of the evicted brick: Check if any other brick at that resolution level overlapping the node's extent is still resident in the cache. If no other brick is resident, the node is no longer partially mapped in that resolution level. Set the corresponding bit in the node's residencybitmap to zero. 3. Propagate Upwards: Traverse up the tree from the affected leaf nodes to the root. For each non-leaf node, update its residencybitmap by setting it to the bit-wise OR of its children's bitmaps. Terminate propagation if the bitmap is unchanged. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateresidencyonmetadata(nodeid, channel, resolutionlevels): """ Called when new metadata for a volume region is received. nodeid: Identifier for the octree node. channel: The channel index. resolutionlevels: List of resolution levels to check for partial mapping. """ node = getorcreatenode(nodeid) # Initialize metadata if node.isnew: node.metadata = {ch: INVALID for ch in allchannels} node.metadata[channel] = VALID else: node.metadata[channel] = VALID # Initialize residency bitmap for the channel's resolution levels # This checks if any brick at these levels is currently in cache for reslevel in resolutionlevels: if ispartiallymapped(node, reslevel, channel): setbit(node.residencybitmap, reslevel) else: clearbit(node.residencybitmap, reslevel) def updateresidencyonbrickadd(brick): """ Called when a new brick is stored in the cache. brick: Object with spatialextent, resolutionlevel, channel. """ # 1. Select slot (handled by cache manager, assume slot is now occupied) # 2. Find overlapping leaf nodes leafnodes = findleafnodesoverlapping(brick.spatialextent) # 3. Mark leaves for node in leafnodes: setbit(node.residencybitmap, brick.resolutionlevel) # 4. Propagate up for node in leafnodes: current = node while current is not None: parent = current.parent if parent is None: break # Bit-wise OR of children newbitmap = 0 for child in parent.children: newbitmap |= child.residencybitmap if parent.residencybitmap == newbitmap: # Unchanged, terminate propagation for this branch break else: parent.residencybitmap = newbitmap current = parent def updateresidencyoneviction(evictedbrick): """ Called when a brick is evicted from the cache. evictedbrick: Object with spatialextent, resolutionlevel. """ # 1. Find overlapping leaf nodes leafnodes = findleafnodesoverlapping(evictedbrick.spatialextent) # 2. Check and update leaves for node in leafnodes: # Check if any other brick at this resolution level is resident isstillmapped = isanybrickresident(node, evictedbrick.resolutionlevel) if not isstillmapped: clearbit(node.residencybitmap, evictedbrick.resolutionlevel) # 3. Propagate up current = node while current is not None: parent = current.parent if parent is None: break newbitmap = 0 for child in parent.children: newbitmap |= child.residencybitmap if parent.residencybitmap == newbitmap: break else: parent.residencybitmap = newbitmap current = parent def ispartiallymapped(node, resolutionlevel, channel): """ Check if any brick at the given resolution level and channel overlapping the node's extent is in the cache. """ # Implementation depends on cache lookup efficiency # In practice, this might use a spatial index or hash map for O(1) or O(log N) lookup return cache.containsbrickoverlapping(node.spatialextent, resolutionlevel, channel) def isanybrickresident(node, resolutionlevel): """ Check if any brick at the given resolution level overlapping the node's extent is in the cache. """ return cache.containsbrickoverlapping(node.spatialextent, resolutionlevel) Bitmap Size: The number of bits in residencybitmap corresponds to the number of resolution levels. Multi-channel Volumes: Residency is tracked per channel. A node may be partially mapped for one channel but not another. Precision: Bit-wise operations are exact. No floating-point precision issues. Boundaries: Spatial overlap checks must be robust to handle bricks that exactly match node boundaries or are slightly larger/smaller due to discretization. Degenerate Input: If a brick has no overlap with any node, no updates occur. A technique used in Mega-NeRF to manage octree size by bounding it to available GPU memory and pruning nodes that do not contribute to rendering. It differs from static residency updates by actively growing and shrinking the tree based on rendering visibility rather than just cache residency. Definition: Track the number of pixels visible from each node during rendering. Subdivide the top k nodes with the most visible pixels. Prune entries that have not recently contributed to reclaim space when capacity is hit. Parameters: Maximum tree size: 20M elements. Top k nodes to subdivide: 16,384. Maximum tree depth observed: roughly 12. When to choose: Use when memory is constrained and the scene has varying levels of detail that can be dynamically adjusted based on camera view, rather than when managing a fixed set of pre-computed volume bricks. Time Complexity: Metadata Update: O(1) for node creation/update, O(R) for bitmap initialization where R is the number of resolution levels. Brick Addition/Eviction: O(L \cdot D) where L is the number of leaf nodes overlapping the brick and D is the tree depth. In practice, propagation terminates early if bitmaps are unchanged. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of nodes in the octree. Each node stores a small bitmap. Strengths: Efficiently maintains hierarchical residency information. Early termination in propagation reduces update cost. Supports multi-channel volumes. Limitations: Requires frequent cache lookups to check partial mapping. Bitmap updates are not parallelized in the description, though the parent article mentions fully GPU-implemented parallel construction. When to use: When rendering large volumetric datasets with dynamic caching and hierarchical culling is required. When not to use: For static volumes where the entire dataset is resident, or for scenes where dynamic LOD based on visibility is more important than cache residency. The Residency-Octree Update method was introduced in the context of scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedicine datasets. It was designed to efficiently manage the residency of volume bricks in a GPU cache while maintaining a hierarchical octree structure for culling. The method builds on earlier work in spatial culling and LRU cache eviction. Dynamic Octree Generation was introduced in the context of Mega-NeRF for scalable construction of large-scale NeRFs. It addresses the challenge of managing octree size in memory-constrained environments by dynamically adjusting the tree based on rendering visibility. name: Mixed-Resolution Multi-Volume Renderer
body: A ray-guided renderer that accesses metadata and cached volume data through the Residency Octree to enable efficient mixing of resolutions across different channels in multi-volume datasets. It is implemented as a WebGPU compute shader that evaluates each visible channel at every sample along a ray, even when channels have different resolutions, to reduce shader divergence. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, ray direction, current node index in the full octree, channel mapping, maximum visible channels m, and user-defined parameters. Output: Computed color and opacity for the ray segment, updated ray position, and potential data streaming requests. Data Structures: Residency Octree: Provides metadata (for empty-space skipping) and cached volume data (bricks). Full Octree Layout: Nodes are accessed directly via their index without root traversal. Channel Mapping: Maps dataset channels to the m visible channels (m \le n, where n is total channels); this mapping can change at runtime. Parameters: m: Maximum visible channels, user-defined at initialization. stepScale: User-defined scaling factor to increase or decrease the sampling rate at run-time. Channel Importance: Determined by user-defined resolution ranges via UI sliders; a channel with a higher upper bound in its resolution range is considered more important. Step Size Calculation: The sampling rate is determined globally for all channels based on the channel requiring the highest sampling rate (highest resolution). The step size dt{step} is computed as follows: 1. Calculate the step size component for each dimension i \in [0, 1, 2]: dti = \frac{1}{vi \cdot si \cdot di} Where vi is the volume extent in dimension i, si is the voxel spacing in dimension i, and di is the ray direction in dimension i. 2. Compute the global step size: dt{step} = \min(dt0, dt1, dt2) \cdot stepScale Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the maximum visible channels m and channel mapping. 2. Traversal Start: Start tree traversal at a user-defined subdivision level or the parent level of the previous termination level; never start at the root. 3. Data Check: For the current node, check if metadata and cached volume data are available. If missing, generate a request for the missing data to be streamed from the server. 4. Empty-Space Skipping: Use metadata to skip empty nodes. 5. Sampling: For each sample along the ray: Compute the global step size dt{step} based on the highest-resolution visible channel. Evaluate all m visible channels at the current sample position to reduce diverging branches in the shader. Accumulate color and opacity. 6. Termination: Stop when the ray exits the volume or opacity threshold is reached. 7. Loop: Repeat for subsequent rays or frames. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, currentnodeindex, channelmapping, stepscale, maxresv, maxress): # Compute global step size based on highest-resolution channel dtcomponents = [] for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0.0: dtcomponents.append(float('inf')) # Guard for zero direction component else: dti = 1.0 / (maxresv[i] maxress[i] raydirection[i]) dtcomponents.append(dti) dtstep = min(dtcomponents) stepscale nodeidx = currentnodeindex color = vec3(0.0) opacity = 0.0 while nodeidx is not None: # Check data availability if not hasmetadata(nodeidx) or not hascacheddata(nodeidx): requeststreaming(nodeidx) # Comment: Sources do not specify streaming protocol # Proceed if data is available or wait for async completion # Empty-space skipping if isempty(nodeidx): nodeidx = getnextnode(nodeidx) # Comment: Standard octree traversal logic continue # Sample along ray segment covered by this node # Evaluate all visible channels at each sample to reduce divergence while opacity < 1.0: samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection dtstep for ch in channelmapping: val = samplevolume(ch, samplepos) # Comment: Standard trilinear interpolation tfcolor, tfalpha = transferfunction(ch, val) # Comment: Standard transfer function lookup color += tfcolor tfalpha (1.0 - opacity) opacity += tfalpha (1.0 - opacity) rayorigin = samplepos if opacity >= 1.0: break nodeidx = getnextnode(nodeidx) # Comment: Advance to next node in traversal order return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Direction Zero: If a ray direction component is zero, dti becomes infinite. Handle this by taking the minimum of non-infinite components or using a large finite value. Missing Data: Streaming requests may stall rendering. Implement asynchronous handling or fallbacks. Channel Mapping Changes: Ensure smooth transitions when channel mapping changes at runtime. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples per ray, which is determined by dt{step}. Evaluating all m channels at each sample adds a factor of m. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of cached bricks in the residency octree. Performance: Reduces shader divergence by evaluating all channels at each sample. Global step size simplifies sampling logic. Strengths: Efficient handling of multi-resolution data, reduced divergence, ray-guided data streaming. Limitations: Potential over-sampling if lower-resolution channels are evaluated at high resolution. Requires careful tuning of stepScale and channel importance. The mixed-resolution multi-volume renderer is part of a system for scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. It leverages the residency octree for data management and is implemented as a WebGPU compute shader. The CPU drives overall rendering, dispatches rendering and memory management commands to the GPU, forwards brick requests to the server, and uploads bricks received from the server to the GPU. name: Multiresolution with Octree Bricking
head: Octree-based multiresolution, Octree-based multeresolution encoding
body: Multiresolution with Octree Bricking encodes volumetric data at varying resolutions into a spatial hierarchy (octree) to enable adaptive rendering. It solves the problem of rendering large datasets efficiently by allowing the renderer to select nodes based on display resolution, distance from the camera, or user-defined importance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly linking octree depth to resolution levels (halving at each step) and using subsampling of children to generate parent node data, rather than storing independent resolution levels or using wavelet transforms. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A high-resolution volumetric dataset. Output: An octree structure where internal nodes store lower-resolution data derived from their children, and leaves store the original high-resolution data. Data Structures: The structure is an octree. Nodes: Each node represents a cubic spatial region. Resolution: The resolution of data stored in a node is determined by its depth. If the leaf level (depth D) has resolution R, a node at depth d stores data at resolution R / 2^{D-d}. Content: Internal nodes contain subsampled data from their eight children. Leaves contain the original voxel values. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Octree Construction): 1. Define the leaves of the octree as the original high-resolution data blocks. 2. Set the root node as the coarsest resolution level. 3. For each internal node, compute its data by subsampling its eight children. The resolution of the parent is half that of its children. 4. This process is performed in a single preprocessing step. 2. Frame Update (Node Selection): 1. At every frame, traverse the octree to select a subset of nodes. 2. Selection criteria include: Display resolution. Distance from the camera (high resolution for near, low for far). Center of attention or areas of interest. User-specified bias parameters or importance metrics. 3. The selected nodes form the active set for rendering. 3. Rendering: 1. Sort the selected nodes in back-to-front order relative to the camera. 2. Render the nodes using standard volume rendering techniques (e.g., ray-marching). 3. If artifacts appear due to resolution changes, modify transfer functions in lower-resolution nodes to mitigate visual discontinuities. Parameters: Image Quality: Defined as a combination of importance or user-specified bias parameters. Resolution Scaling: Each octree level halves the resolution of the next finer level. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Limits: For datasets larger than texture memory, the entire octree cannot reside in memory. An out-of-core approach is required, where nodes are loaded on demand based on the field of view. Artifacts: Abrupt transitions between resolution levels can cause visual artifacts. Mitigation involves modifying transfer functions in lower-resolution nodes. Combines offline tensor-based compression (Tucker decomposition) with an adaptive, view-dependent loader. It differs by using rank-reduced tensors for storage and on-demand reconstruction upon cache misses, enabling stack-less ray-casting. Time Complexity: Construction is a single preprocessing step. Frame time depends on the number of selected nodes and the cost of sorting them back-to-front. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of nodes stored. For out-of-core implementations, memory usage is limited to the GPU cache size, with disk I/O for on-demand loading. Strengths: Allows high-fidelity rendering in regions of interest while maintaining context at lower resolutions. Adaptable to display resolution and user focus. Limitations: Requires preprocessing. Out-of-core implementations introduce I/O latency. Artifacts may occur at resolution boundaries if transfer functions are not adjusted. When to use: Large volumetric datasets where adaptive resolution is beneficial for performance or visual clarity. When not to use: When real-time construction is required or when memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and I/O latency is unacceptable. The technique was introduced by LaMar et al. for large dataset rendering, using an octree to encode hierarchical volume "bricking". A similar approach was presented by Boada and colleagues. It is part of a broader family of multiresolution techniques that encode data into spatial hierarchies like octrees for selective querying. The method is often used in conjunction with out-of-core strategies to handle datasets exceeding texture memory limits. name: Bricked Multiresolution Tensor Approximation
head: Bricked Multiresolution TA, Multiresolution TA octree
body: Bricked Multiresolution Tensor Approximation is a data management and rendering technique for interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets. It solves the problem of limited working memory by dividing the volume into small cubical bricks, approximating each brick using rank-reduced Tucker decomposition, and organizing them into an out-of-core octree structure. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by combining offline tensor-based compression with an adaptive, view-dependent loader that maintains a GPU cache of reconstructed bricks, enabling stack-less ray-casting with on-demand reconstruction only upon cache misses. Inputs: Original volumetric dataset (scalar field); Brick width B; Rank reduction parameter R; Reconstruction rank K (optional, for interactive control). Outputs: Out-of-core octree structure containing quantized tensor decompositions; Rendered image via CUDA ray-caster. Data Structures: 1. Brick: A cubical subvolume of size B^3. Core Tensor (\mathcal{B}): A third-order tensor of size R \times R \times R. Factor Matrices (U^{(1)}, U^{(2)}, U^{(3)}): Three matrices, each of size B \times R. Binary Histogram: A 64-bit integer used for transfer-function-based culling. Quantization: The tensor and factor matrix coefficients are quantized to reduce memory usage. 2. Octree Node: Represents a brick at a specific resolution level. Contains pointers to children (if non-leaf) or the brick data (if leaf). Includes neighbor pointers for spatial indexing. 3. GPU Cache: A 3D texture storing recently used, reconstructed bricks. Parameters: Brick Width (B): Set to 32 voxels. The source formula B = (2^8 + 2 + 2) = 32 contains a typographical error (2^8=256), but the text explicitly defines B=32 with a 2-voxel overlap at each boundary for trilinear interpolation and gradient computation. Rank Reduction (R): Typically R = B/2. For B=32, R=16, resulting in a rank-(R, R, R) Tucker Approximation. Reconstruction Rank (K): User-selectable integer K \in [1, R]. Allows interactive trade-off between detail and performance. Preprocessing (Offline): The preprocessing is performed in a low-memory setting using a bottom-up process on a brick-by-brick basis. 1. Leaf Bricks: Constructed by sampling the original dataset. Each leaf brick A \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times B \times B} is approximated using a rank-reduced Tucker decomposition. 2. Tucker Decomposition: For a brick A, the decomposition is defined as: A \approx \mathcal{B} \times1 U^{(1)} \times2 U^{(2)} \times3 U^{(3)} where \mathcal{B} is the core tensor of size R \times R \times R, and U^{(n)} are the factor matrices of size B \times R. 3. Quantization: The coefficients of \mathcal{B} and U^{(n)} are quantized to reduce storage size. 4. Non-Leaf Bricks: Constructed from their eight previously constructed children. The children are dequantized and reconstructed into full B^3 volumes. These volumes are spatially averaged to form the parent brick. The parent brick is then approximated with a new rank-reduced Tucker decomposition. 5. Histogram: A 64-bit binary histogram is computed for each brick and stored alongside the decomposition. 6. Octree Assembly: Bricks are organized into an octree, where each level represents a coarser resolution. The root represents the coarsest level. Runtime (Adaptive Loading & Rendering): 1. Working Set Maintenance: An adaptive loader updates a view- and transfer-function-dependent working set of bricks. It asynchronously fetches data from the out-of-core structure and maintains the working set on CPU and GPU memory. 2. GPU Cache: The loader maintains a cache of recently used volume bricks on the GPU, stored in a 3D texture. 3. Spatial Index: At each frame, the loader constructs a spatial index for the current working set in the form of an octree with neighbor pointers. 4. Ray-Casting: A CUDA stack-less octree ray-caster traverses the octree. It uses pre-integrated scalar transfer functions and supports various shading modes. 5. Reconstruction on Miss: The ray-caster works on reconstructed bricks. Reconstruction steps occur only upon GPU cache misses. When a cache miss occurs, the quantized tensor decomposition is dequantized and reconstructed on demand by the adaptive loader on the GPU. 6. Interactive Rank Control: The user can change the reconstruction rank K during visualization. The reconstruction uses only the K most significant ranks of the tensor decomposition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def quantize(tensor): """Quantize tensor coefficients to reduce memory usage.""" # Exact quantization scheme is not provided in the source. # Standard practice rounds to a fixed-point format or clips to a range. return np.round(tensor, decimals=2) def dequantize(quantizedtensor): """Restore quantized tensor coefficients.""" # Inverse of quantization; typically identity or scaling. return quantizedtensor def compute64bithistogram(brickdata): """Compute a 64-bit binary histogram for transfer-function culling.""" # Source does not specify binning strategy. # Standard approach: map scalar values to 64 bins, set bit if occupied. minval, maxval = brickdata.min(), brickdata.max() bins = np.linspace(minval, maxval, 65) hist, = np.histogram(brickdata, bins=bins) return np.packbits(hist > 0).astype(np.uint64) def tuckerdecomposition(brickdata, rank): """ Computes rank-reduced Tucker decomposition for a brick. brickdata: numpy array of shape (B, B, B) rank: int, R Returns: coretensor (R, R, R), factormatrices [U1 (B, R), U2 (B, R), U3 (B, R)] """ # Standard Higher-Order SVD (HOSVD) or iterative ALS method. # Mode-1 unfolding U1,, = np.linalg.svd(brickdata.reshape(B, -1), fullmatrices=False) U1 = U1[:,:rank] core = np.tensordot(U1.T, brickdata, axes=1) # Mode-2 unfolding U2,, = np.linalg.svd(core.reshape(B, -1), fullmatrices=False) U2 = U2[:,:rank] core = np.tensordot(U2.T, core, axes=1) # Mode-3 unfolding U3,, = np.linalg.svd(core.reshape(B, -1), fullmatrices=False) U3 = U3[:,:rank] core = np.tensordot(U3.T, core, axes=1) return core, [U1, U2, U3] def reconstructtucker(core, factors, rankk): """ Reconstructs the brick from Tucker decomposition using only the top K ranks. core: numpy array of shape (R, R, R) factors: list of 3 matrices, each (B, R) rankk: int, K <= R Returns: numpy array of shape (B, B, B) """ # Truncate factors and core to rank K U1 = factors[0][:,:rankk] U2 = factors[1][:,:rankk] U3 = factors[2][:,:rankk] corek = core[:rankk,:rankk,:rankk] # Reconstruct: A = B x1 U1 x2 U2 x3 U3 temp1 = np.tensordot(U1, corek, axes=([1], [0])) # Shape (B, R, R) temp2 = np.tensordot(U2, temp1, axes=([1], [1])) # Shape (B, B, R) result = np.tensordot(U3, temp2, axes=([1], [2])) # Shape (B, B, B) return result def preprocessleaf(leafdata, B, R): """Preprocesses a leaf brick.""" core, factors = tuckerdecomposition(leafdata, R) quantizedcore = quantize(core) quantizedfactors = [quantize(f) for f in factors] histogram = compute64bithistogram(leafdata) return {'core': quantizedcore, 'factors': quantizedfactors, 'histogram': histogram, 'isquantized': True} def preprocessnonleaf(childrenbricks, B, R): """Preprocesses a non-leaf brick from its 8 children.""" childvolumes = [] for child in childrenbricks: core = dequantize(child['core']) factors = [dequantize(f) for f in child['factors']] vol = reconstructtucker(core, factors, R) childvolumes.append(vol) # Source states "spatially averaged". # Implementation assumes element-wise mean of the 8 child volumes. combinedvolume = np.mean(childvolumes, axis=0) core, factors = tuckerdecomposition(combinedvolume, R) quantizedcore = quantize(core) quantizedfactors = [quantize(f) for f in factors] histogram = compute64bithistogram(combinedvolume) return {'core': quantizedcore, 'factors': quantizedfactors, 'histogram': histogram, 'isquantized': True} def renderraycaster(octree, ray, transferfunction, gpucache): """CUDA stack-less octree ray-caster.""" # Traverse octree spatial index # Check GPU cache (3D texture) for current brick # If cache miss: dequantize & reconstruct on GPU # Integrate along ray using pre-integrated scalar transfer function pass Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(N \cdot B^3) for N bricks, with tensor decomposition overhead. Runtime complexity depends on the number of cache hits. Reconstruction on cache miss is O(B^3 \cdot R^3) or similar, depending on the reconstruction method. Ray-casting is O(\text{ray length} \cdot \text{samples}). Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to raw data due to Tucker decomposition and quantization. The octree structure adds overhead. The adaptive loader maintains a working set on CPU and GPU memory, asynchronously fetching from the out-of-core structure. Performance: Enables interactive visualization of large datasets. Performance scales with the number of cache hits. Higher K values increase reconstruction time and detail. Strengths: Low memory footprint, adaptive loading, interactive rank control. Limitations: Reconstruction latency on cache misses, quantization artifacts. The method was introduced in the paper "Interactive Multiscale Tensor Reconstruction for Multiresolution Volume Visualization". It builds on the MOVR approach for adaptive refinement. It is used for interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets. name: Hierarchical DDA with Super-brick Skipping
head: Exact shadow trace with super-brick skipping and occupied-box early-out
body: This method accelerates ray tracing through sparse volumetric data by introducing a two-level occupancy hierarchy (super-bricks and bricks) to skip large empty regions, while maintaining pixel-identical output to the fine per-voxel DDA. It solves the performance bottleneck of traversing empty space by verifying emptiness at a coarser granularity and using an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for early termination, ensuring exactness by only skipping verified empty blocks and terminating only when the ray definitively passes the occupied volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, volume header, brick masks, super-brick masks, and voxel data. Output: Boolean indicating if the ray hits any occupied voxel. Data Structures: The buffer layout consists of a header, bricks, brick mask, and super mask. Header: 20 words (HEADERWORDS 20). Words 12-14: Occupied box minimum coordinates (a{min}). Words 16-18: Occupied box maximum coordinates (a{max}). Word 7: Super-mask offset. Super-bricks: A grid of 4^3 bricks, containing 32^3 cells total. Each super-brick has a nonempty bitset appended after the brick mask. Bricks: The intermediate level between super-bricks and voxels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize DDA state for the ray \mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d} within the volume bounds. 2. Loop while the ray is within the volume bounds and iteration count < 768. 3. Check super-brick occupancy via its nonempty bitset. If empty, call skipbox(32) to advance the ray state by 32 units and continue to the next iteration. 4. If the super-brick is occupied, check the current brick's occupancy mask. If the brick is empty, call skipbox(8) to advance the ray state by 8 units and continue. 5. If the brick is occupied, perform the fine per-voxel DDA traversal. 6. Early-out: if the ray is monotonic per axis and the current cell index has passed the occupied box boundary on an axis it is moving toward (step \ge 0 \land cell > a{max} or step \le 0 \land cell < a{min}), return false immediately. 7. The iteration cap remains 768; skipping reduces iterations per ray but does not change the cap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceshadow(o, d, header, brickmasks, supermasks, voxeldata): # Extract occupied box bounds from header amin = header[12:15] amax = header[16:19] # Initialize standard 3D DDA state t, cell, step, tdelta, tmax = initdda(o, d) # Iteration cap unchanged by skipping maxiterations = 768 for in range(maxiterations): # Early-out check against occupied box for axis in range(3): if step[axis] >= 0 and cell[axis] > amax[axis]: return False if step[axis] <= 0 and cell[axis] < amin[axis]: return False # Determine current super-brick index (32^3 cells per super-brick) superidx = tuple(c // 32 for c in cell) # Check super-brick occupancy via nonempty bitset if not issuperbrickoccupied(superidx, supermasks): # Skip entire 32x32x32 super-brick t, cell, step = skipbox(t, d, o, cell, step, 32) continue # Determine current brick index within super-brick (8^3 cells per brick) brickidx = tuple((c // 8) % 4 for c in cell) # Check brick occupancy mask if not isbrickoccupied(brickidx, brickmasks): # Skip 8x8x8 brick t, cell, step = skipbox(t, d, o, cell, step, 8) continue # Fine per-voxel DDA traversal within occupied brick while iswithinbrick(cell): if isvoxeloccupied(cell, voxeldata): return True t, cell, step = advancedda(t, d, cell, step, tdelta, tmax) # Advance to next cell after brick traversal t, cell, step = advancedda(t, d, cell, step, tdelta, tmax) return False def initdda(o, d): # Standard DDA initialization for unit voxel size and origin 0 step = [1 if d[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] cell = [int(o[i]) for i in range(3)] tdelta = [abs(1.0 / d[i]) if d[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tmax = [tdelta[i] (cell[i] - o[i] + (0.5 if step[i] > 0 else -0.5)) for i in range(3)] return 0.0, cell, step, tdelta, tmax def advancedda(t, d, cell, step, tdelta, tmax): # Advance to the next voxel boundary along the closest axis axis = 0 if tmax[1] < tmax[axis]: axis = 1 if tmax[2] < tmax[axis]: axis = 2 t = tmax[axis] cell[axis] += step[axis] tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] return t, cell, step, tdelta, tmax def skipbox(t, d, o, cell, step, size): # Advances ray by 'size' units using the same crossing/tie logic as fine DDA tnew = t + size # Recompute cell index at new t using DDA crossing logic to maintain exactness newcell = [int(o[i] + tnew d[i]) for i in range(3)] return tnew, newcell, step def issuperbrickoccupied(idx, masks): return masks[idx] def isbrickoccupied(idx, masks): return masks[idx] def isvoxeloccupied(cell, data): return data[cell] def iswithinbrick(cell): # Check if cell is within the current 8x8x8 brick return all(0 <= (c % 8) < 8 for c in cell) Parameters: Iteration cap: 768 iterations per ray. Super-brick size: 32^3 cells. Brick size: 8^3 cells (implied by 32/4=8). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dense Scenes: In dense scenes with no empty space (e.g., sponge1m), the extra super-mask read and early-out math can cause regression compared to the fine DDA. Precision: The skipbox function must use the same crossing/tie logic as the fine DDA to ensure visited-cell decisions are identical between skipping and fine traversal. Early-Out Correctness: The early-out condition must be checked carefully to ensure it only triggers when the ray has definitively passed the occupied volume, not just the current brick/super-brick. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is reduced for sparse volumes due to skipping empty regions, while the iteration cap remains 768. Memory complexity increases slightly due to the super-brick and brick masks. Measured Performance: On M2 Metal, for the terrain1m/orbitclose scene, GPU p50 decreased from 73.11 ms to 44.55 ms (-39.1%). On M2 Metal, for the sponge1m/fit scene, GPU p50 increased from 15.16 ms to 15.24 ms (+0.5%), showing neutral performance for dense scenes. Visual regression tests on M2 Metal show 0% differing pixels and max delta 0 for all 9 stills, confirming exactness. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths include significant speedups in sparse scenes (e.g., autumn, terrain) by skipping empty regions. Limitations include regression in dense scenes due to overhead of hierarchy checks. When to Use: Use for sparse volumetric data where large empty regions are common. Do not use for dense volumetric data where empty regions are rare, as the overhead may outweigh the benefits. This method was introduced in a pull request for the voxelite voxel editor project by 0x63616c. It is part of a performance plan to create a faster exact shadow trace. The method builds on the principles of DDA traversal but adds a hierarchical occupancy check to optimize for sparsity. name: Octree-based traversal
head: Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) traversal, Octree sphere tracing, Detail-adaptive octree sampling
body: Octree-based traversal accelerates rendering by recursively navigating a hierarchical spatial subdivision (octree) to skip empty or low-detail regions, thereby reducing the number of intersection tests and sampling operations. It solves the performance bottleneck of dense voxel traversal by allowing rays to take larger steps through empty space. Unlike Hierarchical Grid Traversal which uses fixed-level mipmap grids, this family explicitly uses regular 2x2x2 (or 2x2 in 2D) subdivision to build a sparse hierarchy, distinguishing it from siblings that may focus on hash grids or specific traversal optimizations. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical spatial partitioning using octrees (or quadtrees for 2D terrain) to cull empty space. 1. Spatial Subdivision: The domain is divided recursively into 8 sub-cubes (octants). A node is classified as Empty, Leaf, or Branch. 2. Ray-Node Intersection: For each node, the ray is tested against the node's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). If the ray misses, the node is skipped. 3. Traversal Logic: Empty Nodes: Skipped immediately. The exit time (Time of Intersection, TOI) is calculated to determine the next node to visit. Branch Nodes: The ray intersection point is compared to the node's midpoint to determine which of the 8 children to descend into. Leaf Nodes: Processing occurs here. For volume rendering, this involves sampling or checking for active values. For implicit surfaces, this involves sphere tracing or distance evaluation. 4. Exit Calculation: When a node is fully traversed or missed, the exit time t{exit} for side s in dimension dim is calculated as: t{exit} = \frac{B - \mathbf{o}{dim}}{\mathbf{d}{dim}} where B is the world-space bound value and \mathbf{o}{dim} is the ray origin component. 5. Backtracking: If the ray exits a node, the traversal backtracks to the parent or sibling based on the exit side and ray direction. Sparse Voxel Traversal is a hierarchical ray-intersection method that accelerates volume rendering by recursively traversing a sparse voxel octree (SVO) to find intersections with leaf nodes or branches, skipping empty regions to reduce sampling cost. It solves the performance bottleneck of dense voxel traversal by allowing the ray to take larger steps through empty space, significantly reducing the total number of intersection tests and node visits required to reach active data. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which steps through every voxel boundary in a uniform grid, this method uses hierarchical spatial subdivision to find non-empty space faster. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit use of regular 2x2x2 subdivision and mid-plane sorting logic for interior nodes, whereas other methods may focus purely on traversal optimization or specific data structures like hash grids. Octree partitioning for sphere tracing accelerates implicit surface rendering by dividing the spatial domain into an octree, allowing the imposition of local Lipschitz bounds on the signed distance function (SDF). This yields tighter distance bounds than global bounds, enabling the culling of octree nodes guaranteed not to intersect the implicit surface, which solves slow convergence in high-gradient regions. Octree Enhancement replaces expensive distance evaluations in sphere tracing with octree parsing overhead to accelerate convergence. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by using spatial hierarchy to skip empty space, though experiments on simple scenes have shown it may not always outperform other enhancements like convexity or triangle inequality optimizations. This method organizes large-scale terrain data into a block-based quadtree index where node metadata (bounding boxes, hierarchy levels, offsets) is packed into a compact structure array residing entirely in GPU video memory. It solves the CPU traversal and assembly overhead bottleneck by executing frustum culling and occlusion determination in parallel on the GPU via compute shaders, with each thread processing one node to output a list of visible nodes and their Level of Detail (LOD) levels. It differs from CPU-side hierarchical traversal by offloading the culling logic to the GPU, leveraging parallel processing for cache-friendly Z-order storage. Detail-adaptive Octree Sampling is a method for rendering irregular or curvilinear grids by sampling the data into a detail-adaptive octree where the local height (resolution) is determined by the local granularity of the source grid. It solves the problem of fixed-resolution limitations in regular grids, which often require excessive storage and rendering time to capture the smallest cells of an irregular dataset. Unlike its siblings, which may use uniform sparse voxel grids or sphere-tracing partitioning, this method explicitly adapts the octree structure to the varying density of the input data. The concept of using octrees for ray tracing was introduced by Williams. The specific application to sparse voxel volumes for rendering was popularized by Laine and Karras. The use of octrees for sphere tracing implicit surfaces was explored by Akenine-Möller et al.. GPU-based frustum culling for quadtree terrain was detailed by.
