name: AMR Volume Ray-Casting
head: native AMR marching, ray-marching the AMR octree
body: AMR Volume Ray-Casting is a volume rendering technique that ray-marches Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) octrees directly without resampling to a uniform grid, avoiding the (2^{l{max}})^3 memory blow-up. It solves the problem of efficiently visualizing sparse, multi-resolution simulation data by storing each leaf once in a per-level hash and stepping by the local cell size, ensuring computational cost scales with the actual simulation data rather than the bounding box. Unlike uniform grid resampling, which incurs memory, time, and quality costs, this method maintains native resolution. Inputs: Simulation data (e.g., gas density, number density) structured as an AMR octree; camera parameters (position, direction, field of view); rendering mode (e.g., emission, max intensity); compositing rules (e.g., front-to-back alpha blending). Outputs: A 2D image (pixel colors and opacities). Data Structures: amrvolume: An object containing the AMR hierarchy. perlevelhash: A hash map for each refinement level, mapping leaf coordinates to leaf nodes. Each leaf is stored exactly once. leafnode: Contains the local cell size, active planes (defining which of the 8 corner values are active), and a reference to the brick (data storage). Steps: 1. Construct Volume: Create an amrvolume object from the simulation data. This builds the per-level hash of leaves. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the image, cast a ray from the camera through the scene. 3. Traversal: Traverse the AMR octree. The ray is advanced by the local cell size of the current leaf node it intersects. 4. Sampling: Sample field values at the ray position. De-blocking: To avoid piecewise-constant artifacts (blockiness) from nearest-leaf sampling, use cross-level trilinear reconstruction. This interpolates the 8 surrounding leaf values at the local cell spacing, looking up values from finest to coarsest. Active Corners: Determine which of the 8 corner values are active based on the 6 active planes of the leaf, filling them from the brick stored in the leaf. 5. Accumulation: Accumulate color and opacity using the selected mode and compositing rules. 6. Anti-Aliasing: Apply supersampling (aa) if enabled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderamrvolume(amrvolume, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, smooth=True, aa=True): """ Renders an AMR volume by ray-marching the octree. """ image = emptyimage(imagewidth, imageheight) # Pre-compute ray directions for all pixels rays = generaterays(camera, imagewidth, imageheight) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): ray = rays[y, x] color = vec3(0.0) opacity = 0.0 # Ray marching loop t = 0.0 while t < ray.maxdistance: # Find the leaf node containing the current ray position # The ray position is ray.origin + ray.direction t leaf = amrvolume.findleaf(ray.position(t)) if leaf is None: # Ray is outside the AMR data break # Step size is the local cell size of the current leaf stepsize = leaf.localcellsize # Sample the field value at the current ray position # If smooth=True, use cross-level trilinear interpolation # If smooth=False, use nearest-leaf (piecewise-constant) if smooth: value = sampletrilinearcrosslevel(amrvolume, ray.position(t), leaf) else: value = samplenearestleaf(leaf, ray.position(t)) # Compute contribution based on rendering mode (e.g., emission) # This is a placeholder for specific compositing logic contribution = computecontribution(value, stepsize) # Front-to-back compositing alpha = contribution.alpha color = color (1.0 - alpha) + contribution.color alpha opacity += alpha (1.0 - opacity) # Advance ray t += stepsize # Early exit if fully opaque if opacity >= 1.0: break # Apply anti-aliasing if enabled if aa: # Supersampling logic would go here pass image[y, x] = color return image def sampletrilinearcrosslevel(amrvolume, position, currentleaf): """ Interpolates values from 8 surrounding leaves at the local cell spacing. Looks up values from finest to coarsest. """ # Determine the 8 surrounding leaf coordinates relative to the current leaf's grid # This requires mapping the continuous position to the discrete leaf grid surroundingleaves = getsurroundingleaves(amrvolume, position, currentleaf) # Retrieve values from bricks, respecting active planes values = [] for leaf in surroundingleaves: # Check active planes to determine which corners are valid # Fill from the brick stored in the leaf val = leaf.getvalueatposition(position) values.append(val) # Perform trilinear interpolation on the 8 values return trilinearinterpolate(values, position, surroundingleaves) Parameters: smooth: Boolean. Default true. Enables cross-level trilinear reconstruction to reduce blockiness. aa: Boolean. Enables anti-aliasing via supersampling. subregion: Optional. A subset of the AMR volume to render, used for zooming large simulations. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Blockiness: Nearest-leaf sampling results in piecewise-constant fields, causing coarse cells to look blocky. Use smooth=true. Memory Blow-up: Resampling to a uniform grid causes (2^{l{max}})^3 memory blow-up. This method avoids it by storing leaves once. Active Planes: Incorrect handling of active planes can lead to sampling invalid data. Ensure only active corners are filled from the brick. A mapper that directly maps the vtkAMR structure to OSPRay's internal AMR representation without resampling, using zero-copy memory sharing where possible. Unlike previous ParaView handling which loaded data into vtkAMR and resampled it into a structured volume (incurring memory, time, and quality costs), this mapper avoids resampling. It is integrated into VTK 7.1 and ParaView 5.0. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory scales with the actual simulation data (number of leaves), not the bounding box. Computational cost scales with the simulation data, as each ray steps by the local cell size. Avoids the (2^{l{max}})^3 memory blow-up associated with uniform grid resampling. Measured Performance: Evaluated on HPC resources including dual-socket workstations and Intel Xeon Phi "Knights Landing" nodes. Results in little memory overhead compared to resampling methods. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficient memory usage for sparse data; native resolution; direct mapping to OSPRay. Limitations: Potential for blockiness if smoothing is disabled. Requires careful handling of active planes and cross-level interpolation. When to Use: Use for visualizing sparse, multi-resolution simulation data where memory efficiency and native resolution are critical. Avoid if uniform grid resampling is acceptable and simplicity of implementation is prioritized over performance. AMR Volume Ray-Casting originated from the need to visualize large-scale scientific simulations without the prohibitive memory costs of uniform grid resampling. The technique was implemented in the Mera.jl library, with a 3-D volume ray-caster added to the core in 2026. It was also integrated into the VTK/ParaView ecosystem via OSPRay, with vtkAMRVolumeMapper introduced in VTK 7.1 and ParaView 5.0. feat(immersive): 3-D volume ray-caster in core Mera (public + tested) ( feat(immersive): 3-D volume ray-caster in core Mera (public + tested) (#260), https://github.com/ManuelBehrendt/Mera.jl/commit/46c844a80e044dbde2a0042ae8311fc407fa9517, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) CPU volume rendering of adaptive mesh refinement data, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/321321949CPUvolumerenderingofadaptivemeshrefinementdata, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Varying Refinement Levels of Coarse Elements
head: Coarse mesh refinement level variation, Inserting refinement levels into coarse mesh
body: This method optimizes hierarchical volume rendering by selectively inserting elements from specific depths of the input refinement tree into the coarse mesh, rather than using a fixed depth or only leaf nodes. It addresses the trade-off between BVH traversal efficiency and the overhead of traversing the underlying refinement tree structure. By varying the refinement level of the coarse elements, the algorithm adjusts the size of the macrocells, which impacts both the spatial acceleration structure's performance and the tightness of statistical bounds (such as majorants) used in culling. It differs from standard coarse mesh traversal by allowing the coarse element granularity to be tuned independently of the finest data resolution. The method extends the standard coarse mesh construction by controlling which nodes of the input refinement tree are promoted to the coarse mesh. Inputs: The input dataset represented as a refinement tree (e.g., TET-AMR). A target refinement level L for the coarse mesh elements. The coarse mesh traversal parameters (e.g., BVH build settings). Outputs: A coarse mesh (BVH) containing elements from the specified refinement level or their ancestors if they are leaves. Rendering performance metrics dependent on L. Data Structures: Refinement Tree: A hierarchical structure where each node represents a cluster of fine primitives. Nodes have a depth level. Coarse Mesh (BVH): A bounding volume hierarchy containing the selected elements. Each leaf in the BVH corresponds to one element from the refinement tree. Algorithm Steps: 1. Traverse Refinement Tree: For each branch of the input refinement tree, traverse from the root downwards. 2. Select Element: Stop traversal when one of the following conditions is met: the current node is at the desired target refinement level L, or the current node is a leaf element (even if its level is less than L). 3. Insert into Coarse Mesh: Add the selected element to the coarse mesh. This element becomes a leaf in the BVH. 4. Build BVH: Construct the Bounding Volume Hierarchy over the collected coarse elements. 5. Render: Perform ray traversal using the coarse mesh. If a coarse element is hit, march rays through the fine data contained within that element. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildcoarsemesh(refinementtree, targetlevel): coarseelements = [] def traverse(node, currentlevel): if currentlevel == targetlevel: coarseelements.append(node) return if node.isleaf(): coarseelements.append(node) return for child in node.children: traverse(child, currentlevel + 1) traverse(refinementtree.root, 0) # Build BVH from coarseelements return coarseelements Parameters: Target Level (L): The depth in the refinement tree where elements are inserted into the coarse mesh. Typical values tested range from 0 to 5. L=0: Only the root is used (single large macrocell). L=5: Elements at depth 5 or leaves are used. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Nodes: If the refinement tree is shallower than L, leaf nodes are inserted at their actual depth. This prevents empty levels in the coarse mesh. BVH Efficiency: Increasing L increases the number of coarse elements. This can decrease BVH traversal efficiency due to increased node count and potentially poorer spatial coherence, as noted in the sources. Macrocell Size: Higher L results in smaller macrocells. This affects statistical culling methods like Woodcock tracking, where smaller cells may yield tighter majorants but increase overhead. Uses two rays to cull empty regions. Choosing varying refinement levels here affects the granularity of the culling bounds. Dual-Ray Culling A specific nested approach. Varying refinement levels in the coarse mesh changes the boundary between the coarse and fine levels. Two-level Nested Time Complexity: Build Time: Increases with the number of coarse elements. The number of elements grows exponentially with the refinement level L in uniform datasets. Traversal Time: Depends on the balance between BVH traversal cost and refinement tree traversal cost. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of coarse elements. More elements at higher L require more memory for the BVH nodes and bounding volumes. Measured Performance: Performance varies significantly by dataset and renderer. The following data is from: Engine Dataset (Non-uniform): Ray Marcher with Macrocell: Performance degrades as L increases (41.47 ms at L=0 to 87.77 ms at L=5). Ray Marcher without Macrocell: Similar degradation (41.12 ms at L=0 to 84.02 ms at L=5). Woodcock with Macrocell: Performance degrades significantly (7.14 ms at L=0 to 94.97 ms at L=5). Scaling and Trade-offs: BVH Efficiency: Increasing the number of coarse elements decreases BVH efficiency and maximum traversal depth in the TET-AMR traversal process. Refinement Tree Traversal: Higher L decreases the depth of refinement tree traversal required during rendering. In datasets with many elements and similar average tree height (like Uniform Engine), this reduction can outweigh BVH overhead at low levels (e.g., L=1). Macrocell Majorants: For Woodcock tracking, smaller macrocells (higher L) yield tighter majorants, improving performance in specific cases (Uniform Engine L=1, 2). When to Use: Use lower levels (L=0, 1) for datasets where BVH traversal is the bottleneck or where the refinement tree is shallow. Use higher levels (L=1, 2) for uniform datasets or those with deep refinement trees where reducing refinement tree traversal depth provides a net benefit. Use higher levels if using Woodcock tracking and tighter majorants are critical. When Not to Use: Avoid high L for non-uniform datasets like the Engine dataset, where it consistently degrades performance due to BVH inefficiency. This method was explored in the context of direct volume rendering of tree-based tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (TET-AMR) data. The research investigates how the granularity of the coarse mesh interacts with different rendering techniques (Ray Marching, Woodcock tracking) and macrocell optimizations. The findings highlight that there is no single optimal refinement level; it depends on the dataset structure and the rendering algorithm's sensitivity to BVH vs. refinement tree traversal costs. name: Node Omission in Ray-Tree Traversal
head: Omisión de nodos no intersecables, Pruning non-intersectable nodes
body: Node omission is an optimization for hierarchical ray-tree traversal that prevents adding child nodes to the traversal stack if it is known they will not intersect the current ray, reducing the number of intersection tests. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Leaf Collection and Point Plane Test Traversal by operating on the spatial relationship between the ray's entry/exit parameters and the node's bounding box midpoints, rather than relying on leaf-level data structures or plane-based splitting planes. The method determines which of the eight children of a current octree node are intersected by a ray by analyzing the ray's intersection interval with the parent node's axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray r, current node n. Output: A list of valid child node indices to be added to the traversal stack. Data Structures: Child nodes are indexed 1 through 8. The pruning logic relies on set membership of children relative to the midpoint planes, assuming a standard octree indexing convention where \{1,2,3,4\} and \{5,6,7,8\} occupy opposite halves along each axis. Parameters: tx0, ty0, tz0: The entry intersection factors of the ray with the node's bounding box along the x, y, and z axes, respectively. tx1, ty1, tz1: The exit intersection factors of the ray with the node's bounding box along the x, y, and z axes, respectively. txm, tym, tzm: The midpoint factors separating the children, calculated as ((tx0, ty0, tz0) + (tx1, ty1, tz1)) \times 0.5. t{min}: The entry point of the intersection between the ray and the node, calculated as \max(tx0, ty0, tz0). t{max}: The exit point of the intersection between the ray and the node, calculated as \min(tx1, ty1, tz1). Steps: 1. Calculate the intersection factors (tx0, ty0, tz0) and (tx1, ty1, tz1) for the node's bounding box with respect to the ray. 2. Calculate the midpoint factors: txm = (tx0 + tx1) \times 0.5 tym = (ty0 + ty1) \times 0.5 tzm = (tz0 + tz1) \times 0.5 3. Calculate the effective entry and exit distances for the node: t{min} = \max(tx0, ty0, tz0) t{max} = \min(tx1, ty1, tz1) 4. Initialize a list l containing the indices of all 8 children, sorted by their traversal order. 5. Apply pruning rules based on the comparison of midpoint factors (txm, tym, tzm) against t{min} and t{max}: If txm < t{min}: Mark children \{5, 6, 7, 8\} as invalid. If txm > t{max}: Mark children \{1, 2, 3, 4\} as invalid. If tym < t{min}: Mark children \{3, 4, 7, 8\} as invalid. If tym > t{max}: Mark children \{1, 2, 5, 6\} as invalid. If tzm < t{min}: Mark children \{2, 4, 6, 8\} as invalid. If tzm > t{max}: Mark children \{1, 3, 5, 7\} as invalid. 6. Filter the list l to remove all entries marked as invalid (typically represented by setting their value to -1). 7. Return the filtered list of valid child indices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nodeomission(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax): """ Determines which children of a node are intersected by a ray. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) origin of the ray. raydirection: (x, y, z) direction of the ray. boxmin: (x, y, z) minimum corner of the node's AABB. boxmax: (x, y, z) maximum corner of the node's AABB. Returns: List of valid child indices (1-8) to traverse, or empty list if no intersection. """ # 1. Calculate intersection factors for the node box def computefactors(origin, direction, bmin, bmax): # Handle zero direction components and compute per-axis entry/exit factors if direction[0] == 0: if not (bmin[0] <= origin[0] <= bmax[0]): return None tx0, tx1 = float('-inf'), float('inf') else: tx0 = (bmin[0] - origin[0]) / direction[0] tx1 = (bmax[0] - origin[0]) / direction[0] if tx0 > tx1: tx0, tx1 = tx1, tx0 if direction[1] == 0: if not (bmin[1] <= origin[1] <= bmax[1]): return None ty0, ty1 = float('-inf'), float('inf') else: ty0 = (bmin[1] - origin[1]) / direction[1] ty1 = (bmax[1] - origin[1]) / direction[1] if ty0 > ty1: ty0, ty1 = ty1, ty0 if direction[2] == 0: if not (bmin[2] <= origin[2] <= bmax[2]): return None tz0, tz1 = float('-inf'), float('inf') else: tz0 = (bmin[2] - origin[2]) / direction[2] tz1 = (bmax[2] - origin[2]) / direction[2] if tz0 > tz1: tz0, tz1 = tz1, tz0 tmin = max(tx0, ty0, tz0) tmax = min(tx1, ty1, tz1) # Standard ray-box intersection guard if tmin > tmax or tmax < 0: return None return tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1 factors = computefactors(rayorigin, raydirection, boxmin, boxmax) if factors is None: return [] tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1 = factors # 2. Calculate midpoints txm = (tx0 + tx1) 0.5 tym = (ty0 + ty1) 0.5 tzm = (tz0 + tz1) 0.5 # 3. Set tmin and tmax for the current node tmin = max(tx0, ty0, tz0) tmax = min(tx1, ty1, tz1) # 4. Initialize list with all 8 children, sorted by traversal order children = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] # 5. Apply pruning rules if txm < tmin: children = [c for c in children if c not in {5, 6, 7, 8}] if txm > tmax: children = [c for c in children if c not in {1, 2, 3, 4}] if tym < tmin: children = [c for c in children if c not in {3, 4, 7, 8}] if tym > tmax: children = [c for c in children if c not in {1, 2, 5, 6}] if tzm < tmin: children = [c for c in children if c not in {2, 4, 6, 8}] if tzm > tmax: children = [c for c in children if c not in {1, 3, 5, 7}] return children Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-intersection: If t{min} > t{max} or the ray origin is behind the box (t{max} < 0), the ray does not intersect the node's bounding box. The algorithm returns an empty list. Precision: The source uses exact comparisons for midpoint factors against t{min} and t{max} without epsilon tolerance. Implementers should be aware that floating-point precision errors near the midpoint boundaries may lead to incorrect pruning in degenerate cases. Child Indexing: The specific set of children marked invalid depends on the octree's child indexing scheme. The source assumes a specific mapping where \{1,2,3,4\} are on one side of the x-midplane and \{5,6,7,8\} on the other. Implementers must verify their octree's indexing convention matches the sets used in the pruning rules. Time Complexity: The pruning step involves a constant number of comparisons and list filtering operations, making it O(1) per node visited. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the list of children. Measured Performance: On the scene in Figure 17 of the source, adding this optimization (referred to as "Evasion" or "Omission") alongside sorting increased FPS from ~16 to ~30 and reduced peak intersection tests from ~150 to ~85. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of intersection tests and stack operations by eliminating branches that are geometrically impossible to intersect. Limitations: Requires calculating intersection factors for the parent node's box. The benefit is highest when the ray passes through many empty or non-intersecting branches of the tree. This optimization is described in the context of Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) traversal for global illumination calculations. It is presented as a follow-up to sorting optimizations, referred to as "Omisión de nodos no intersecables" or "Evasion". The method was implemented and tested as part of a thesis on SVO compression and efficiency for global illumination. name: Two-Pass Hierarchy Traversal
head: Two-Step Hierarchy Traversal, Two-pass traversal
body: Two-Pass Hierarchy Traversal is a spatial hierarchy traversal optimization that reduces computational cost by splitting the descent into a coarse initial pass and a fine subsequent pass. It sets itself apart from single-pass methods like Leaf Collection or Point Plane Test Traversal by explicitly decoupling the identification of relevant subtrees from the detailed node evaluation, allowing for significant reuse across pixel blocks. Inputs: A spatial hierarchy (e.g., octree) representing the volume. A set of rays to be evaluated. A stopping depth parameter d{stop}, defined as the number of levels above the leaves where the first traversal terminates. Outputs: A set of active nodes at depth d{stop} relative to the leaves, forming a "coarse subtree". The final traversal results (e.g., scattering contributions) for the rays. Data Structures: Coarse Subtree: A list of nodes identified at the end of the first pass. These nodes serve as the roots for the second pass. Tile Grouping: Rays are grouped into 2 \times 2 pixel blocks to facilitate sharing of the first pass results. Parameters: Stopping Depth (d{stop}): The depth relative to the leaves where the first traversal stops. A value of 3 means the first pass stops 3 levels above the leaves, producing subtrees of depth 3. Tile Size: 2 \times 2 pixels for sharing the first pass results. Algorithm Steps: 1. Group Rays: Divide the primary rays into groups of 2 \times 2 pixels. 2. First Pass (Coarse Extraction): For each unique ray group (or individual ray if sharing is disabled), traverse the hierarchy from the root. Continue traversal until the current node's depth is d{stop} levels above the leaves. Collect all visited nodes into the Coarse Subtree. If multiple rays share the same group, they share this subtree. 3. Second Pass (Fine Traversal): For each ray, restart the traversal starting from the nodes in the Coarse Subtree corresponding to its path. Continue traversing from these nodes until the node satisfies the accuracy criterion. Compute the scattering or rendering contribution for the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stopping Depth 0: If d{stop} = 0, the first pass descends through the entire hierarchy. The second pass cost is null, and performance equals the direct implementation. Secondary Rays: Do not apply the savings (sharing or two-pass structure) to secondary rays (rays that have bounced at least once). Material Edges: Do not apply the 2 \times 2 pixel sharing when the block covers an edge of the material, as the hierarchy traversal results may differ significantly between adjacent pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twopasshierarchytraversal(hierarchy, rays, stoppingdepth, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Performs two-pass hierarchy traversal with 2x2 tile sharing. """ contributions = [0.0] len(rays) tilesize = 2 numtilesx = imagewidth // tilesize numtilesy = imageheight // tilesize for ty in range(numtilesy): for tx in range(numtilesx): tilerays = [] for dy in range(tilesize): for dx in range(tilesize): ry = ty tilesize + dy rx = tx tilesize + dx rayidx = ry imagewidth + rx if rayidx < len(rays): tilerays.append((rayidx, rays[rayidx])) # Check if the 2x2 pixel block covers a material edge coversedge = False # Implementation-dependent check if coversedge: for rayidx, ray in tilerays: subtreenodes = extractsubtree(hierarchy, ray, stoppingdepth) contributions[rayidx] = secondpasstraverse(subtreenodes, ray) else: # First pass: extract coarse subtree, shared for the tile, firstray = tilerays[0] subtreenodes = extractsubtree(hierarchy, firstray, stoppingdepth) # Second pass: restart traversal from shared nodes for each ray for rayidx, ray in tilerays: contributions[rayidx] = secondpasstraverse(subtreenodes, ray) return contributions def extractsubtree(hierarchy, ray, stoppingdepth): """ Traverses from root to stoppingdepth relative to leaves. Returns list of nodes at that depth. """ currentnodes = [hierarchy.root] currentdepth = 0 targetdepth = hierarchy.maxdepth - stoppingdepth while currentnodes and currentdepth < targetdepth: nextnodes = [] for node in currentnodes: if node.isleaf: break for child in node.children: if ray.intersects(child): nextnodes.append(child) currentnodes = nextnodes currentdepth += 1 return currentnodes def secondpasstraverse(subtreenodes, ray): """ Continues traversal from subtreenodes until accuracy criterion is met. """ # Continue traversing from these nodes until the node satisfies the accuracy criterion # Compute scattering contribution for the ray # The exact accumulation and termination logic is not specified in the sources result = 0.0 return result A two-step rendering pipeline for participating media that separates ray tracing from scattering computation. In the first step, rays are traced from the camera through the scene, and each time a ray encounters translucent material, it is stored with its starting and ending points in an auxiliary buffer. In the second step, all rays from this buffer are processed to compute their single, double, and multiple scattering contributions, which are then added to the corresponding pixel values. The auxiliary buffer contains all paths through the material, including both primary rays and secondary rays that reach the material after one or more bounces. For each ray, attenuation from material absorption and BRDF reflectance is computed after each bounce, and tracing stops when attenuation exceeds a threshold. Single scattering contributions are gathered only over a material layer of thickness \ell (one mean-free-path), as they become negligible compared to multiple scattering after roughly one mean-free-path. Time Complexity: The method reduces traversal time by up to 30% compared to a naive direct implementation. The gain depends on the stopping depth. Performance: At an optimal stopping depth of 3, the two-pass method alone reduces computation time by 15%. When combined with tile sharing over 2 \times 2 pixels, the reduction reaches 30%. Overall, it provides a 20% performance improvement over naive hierarchy traversal. Memory: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant speedup for primary rays in single and multiple scattering computations. Efficient for homogeneous participating media. Limitations: Not applicable to secondary rays. Sharing is invalid near material edges. Performance gain diminishes if stopping depth is too small (approaching 0). Origin: Introduced in the GPU implementation of the point-based rendering algorithm for participating media. Paper: "Point-Based Rendering for Homogeneous Participating Media with Refractive Boundaries" (2017). Usage: Used in rendering participating media, specifically for single and multiple scattering computations. name: Adaptive Out-of-Core Single-Pass GPU Raycasting
head: Adaptive out-of-core technique, Single-pass GPU ray casting framework
body: This method enables interactive rendering of multi-gigabyte scalar volumes on desktop hardware by combining an out-of-core octree data structure with a single-pass, stackless GPU raycasting algorithm. It solves the memory capacity and bandwidth bottlenecks of in-core rendering by maintaining a view- and transfer-function-dependent working set of volumetric bricks in GPU memory, while the rest of the dataset remains on disk. Unlike separate block rendering techniques that suffer from boundary artifacts and cannot support refractive or global illumination models, this approach performs the entire volume traversal and compositing in a single fragment shader pass, adapting sampling density to the local brick resolution. Input: A massive scalar volume dataset (e.g., 2 Gvoxels, 16-bit) stored on disk. Output: A rendered 2D image (e.g., 1024 × 1024 pixels) with accumulated color and opacity, updating the frame buffer and depth buffer. The dataset is decomposed into small cubical bricks and organized into a coarse octree structure maintained out-of-core. Leaves: Store the original voxel data for the brick. Inner Nodes: Store a filtered representation of their children (aggregated data). Node Metadata: Each node stores: The range of scalar values present in the node. Optionally, precomputed gradients. Boundary Replication: To support neighbor access for interpolation and gradients, bricks are made self-contained: One layer of neighboring samples is replicated for linear interpolation support. Two layers of neighboring samples are replicated if central differences are used for gradient computation at render time. An adaptive loader on the CPU maintains a subset of bricks in GPU memory. This set is view-dependent and transfer-function-dependent. Content: Only the bricks required for the current view and transfer function are loaded. Management: Maintained via an adaptive refinement method guided by node priorities. At each frame, a compact indexing structure is encoded in a small GPU texture. Purpose: Spatially organizes the current working set into an octree hierarchy for the raycaster. Nature: It is not a multiresolution data representation; it is a spatial index. Layout: Inner Nodes: Contain pointers to children. Leaves: Refer to volume data nodes stored in the GPU memory pool (the working set). Pointers: Include neighbor pointers to facilitate on-the-fly bounding box computation and neighbor access. 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Decompose the original volumetric model into small cubical bricks. 2. Organize bricks into a coarse octree structure maintained out-of-core. 3. Store original data at leaves and filtered representations at inner nodes. 4. Store value ranges and optional precomputed gradients for each node. 5. Replicate boundary samples (1 layer for linear interpolation, 2 layers for central difference gradients) to make bricks self-contained. 2. Adaptive Loading (CPU/GPU Interaction): 1. Initialize a working set of bricks in GPU memory. 2. Compute node priorities based on view and transfer function. 3. Asynchronously fetch data from the out-of-core octree to update the working set. 4. Refine the working set incrementally based on priorities. 5. Receive feedback from the renderer regarding occlusion to avoid loading/refining occluded zones. 3. Indexing (Per Frame): 1. Encode the spatial organization of the current working set into a compact texture. 2. Populate inner nodes with pointers to children and leaves with references to GPU memory locations. 4. Single-Pass Raycasting (GPU Fragment Shader): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray into the volume. 2. Traverse the compact indexing structure (stackless octree traversal). 3. Enumerate non-empty bricks in front-to-back order. 4. Adapt sampling density to the resolution of the current brick. 5. Compute the volume rendering integral (accumulating color and opacity). 6. Stop raycasting when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. 7. Update the frame buffer and depth buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessvolume(dataset): # 1. Decompose into bricks bricks = decomposeintocubicalbricks(dataset) # 2. Build out-of-core octree octree = buildoctree(bricks) # 3. Populate node data for node in octree.traverse(): if node.isleaf(): node.data = originalvoxeldata else: node.data = filterchildrendata(node.children) node.valuerange = computevaluerange(node.data) node.gradients = computeprecomputedgradients(node.data) # Optional # 4. Replicate boundaries for self-containment if node.isleaf(): replicateneighbors(node.data, layers=1) # For linear interpolation # replicateneighbors(node.data, layers=2) # If central differences needed def updateworkingset(octree, viewparams, transferfunction): # 1. Compute priorities for nodes priorities = computenodepriorities(octree, viewparams, transferfunction) # 2. Determine working set based on memory budget and priorities workingsetnodes = selectnodesbypriority(octree, priorities) # 3. Asynchronously fetch data from disk to GPU gpumemorypool = allocategpumemory(len(workingsetnodes)) for node in workingsetnodes: gpumemorypool[node.id] = fetchdatafromdisk(node) return gpumemorypool, workingsetnodes def buildindextexture(workingsetnodes, gpumemorypool): # Create a compact texture representing the spatial hierarchy of the working set indextexture = createtexture() for node in workingsetnodes: if node.haschildreninworkingset: # Inner node: pointer to children indextexture.setpointer(node.id, node.childrenids) else: # Leaf node: reference to GPU memory indextexture.setreference(node.id, gpumemorypool[node.id].address) return indextexture def raycastfragment(rayorigin, raydirection, indextexture, gpumemorypool, transferfunction): accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 threshold = 0.95 # Example threshold # Stackless traversal of the compact octree index currentnode = indextexture.root t = rayorigin while currentnode is not None and accumulatedopacity < threshold: # 1. Traverse to next non-empty brick # Compute bounding box on-the-fly using the index structure brickbounds = computeboundingbox(currentnode, indextexture) # Intersect ray with brick bounds tenter, texit = intersectraybrick(rayorigin, raydirection, brickbounds) if tenter is None: # Ray missed this brick, move to next sibling or parent currentnode = nextnodeintraversal(currentnode, indextexture) continue t = max(t, tenter) # 2. Sample within the brick # Adapt sampling density to brick resolution stepsize = computestepsize(brickbounds) while t < texit and accumulatedopacity < threshold: samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 3. Retrieve voxel data # Access GPU memory pool using the leaf reference voxelvalue = samplevoxel(samplepos, gpumemorypool[currentnode.ref]) # 4. Transfer function color, opacity = applytransferfunction(voxelvalue, transferfunction) # 5. Front-to-back compositing alpha = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedopacity += alpha t += stepsize # 6. Move to next node in front-to-back order currentnode = nextnodeintraversal(currentnode, indextexture) return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity Hardware: NVIDIA 8800 Ultra graphics board. Resolution: 1024 × 1024 window size. Dataset Size: 2 Gvoxels, 16-bit. Performance: Interactive exploration achieved on a desktop PC. Block Boundaries: Unlike separate block rendering, this method avoids artifacts at block boundaries because it performs a full-volume traversal. Occlusion: Feedback from the renderer is used to avoid refinement and data loading of occluded zones, preventing unnecessary GPU stalls. Neighbor Access: Failure to replicate boundary samples correctly will break linear interpolation or gradient computation if neighbor voxels are accessed. Time Complexity: The traversal is stackless and exploits the regular structure of octrees to reduce costly texture memory accesses by computing bounding boxes on-the-fly. The adaptive refinement ensures that only relevant parts of the volume are processed. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by the size of the working set in GPU memory, which is dynamically adjusted based on view and transfer function dependencies. The rest of the data remains out-of-core. Performance: Enables interactive exploration of multi-gigabyte datasets (e.g., 2 Gvoxels) on desktop hardware. Strengths: Supports full-volume optical models, including refracting volumes and global illumination, which separate block rendering cannot easily handle. Adapts sampling density to brick resolution, providing visual quality proportional to data availability. Reduces GPU stalls via occlusion query feedback. Limitations: Requires a GPU capable of single-pass fragment shader execution for volume traversal. Performance depends on the efficiency of the adaptive loader and the compact indexing structure construction. Unlike flat multiresolution blocking, it does not have a constant number of blocks, which may complicate certain types of parallelization or fixed-size memory allocation strategies. Origin: The method was presented in the paper "A single-pass GPU ray casting framework for interactive out-of-core rendering of massive volumetric datasets" by E. Gobbetti, F. Marton, and J. Jallet. History: It builds upon earlier work on out-of-core volume octrees and stackless ray traversal methods for kd-trees [7, 16], extending them to GPUs for volume rendering. It addresses the limitations of previous GPU volume rendering techniques that were restricted to moderate-sized volumes fitting entirely in texture memory. Usage: Primarily used for interactive exploration of multi-gigabyte CT datasets in medical visualization and numerical simulation analysis. name: Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) Traversal
head: BVH Traversal
body: Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) traversal accelerates ray-scene intersection and distance queries by recursively testing rays against a binary tree of Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs). It is distinguished from hierarchical grid methods (like Octree Traversal) by operating directly on unstructured geometry (e.g., triangle meshes) rather than voxelized volumes, and from software-only BVHs by leveraging hardware acceleration (e.g., NVIDIA OptiX) for ray-triangle intersections. The BVH is a binary tree where internal nodes contain AABBs enclosing their descendants, and leaves contain primitive geometry (typically triangles). Traversal begins at the root. For each node, the distance from the query point (or ray origin) to the node's AABB is computed. If this distance exceeds the current best distance d{min} (for point queries) or the ray does not intersect the AABB (for ray queries), the node is pruned. If a leaf is reached, the exact primitive intersection or distance is computed, and d{min} is updated if a closer primitive is found. Mesh BVH is a GPU-accelerated BVH designed for triangle meshes to support efficient distance queries, signed distance field (SDF) computation, and ray intersection tests. It is distinguished from hierarchical grid methods by operating on unstructured triangle geometry and from software-only BVHs by leveraging NVIDIA OptiX hardware acceleration. Choose this for SDF computation or collision detection on complex meshes. Initial Upper Bound Estimation computes a tight initial upper bound to prune BVH-tree traversal during distance field computation for isosurface approximation. It differs from standard hierarchical traversal by proactively sampling the approximated surface to establish a pruning threshold before traversal begins, rather than waiting for the first leaf encounter. Choose this when traversing BVHs for isosurface distance fields to reduce node visits. Definition Uses a BVH built over a coarse tetrahedral mesh to efficiently locate the coarse element containing a sample point. Steps 1. Build a triangle BVH over the coarse mesh by inserting four triangular faces facing outside for every coarse element. 2. Trace rays into the BVH using OptiX Wrapper Library (OWL) hit and miss functions. 3. The hit function returns the hit point and the coarse tetrahedron ID. 4. The miss function reports no intersection with BVH faces. 5. Trace two rays: one with front-face culling and one with back-face culling. If the front-culling ray misses, the point is outside the coarse mesh. If the back-culling ray misses, the point is inside the last intersected element. Comparison Unlike element marching which uses connectivity, point location querying skips coarse elements not being sampled and allows varying refinement levels in the coarse mesh. BVH traversal for point location and distance queries in volume rendering contexts has been applied to tetrahedral adaptive mesh refinement (TET-AMR) data. The approach uses a BVH to locate coarse elements efficiently, allowing the renderer to skip elements not being sampled and support varying refinement levels in the coarse mesh. Implementation often utilizes NVIDIA OptiX for hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection tests. name: Mesh BVH
head: GPU BVH for Triangle Mesh, MeshBVH, TriangleMeshSDF BVH
body: Mesh BVH is a GPU-accelerated bounding volume hierarchy designed for triangle meshes to support efficient distance queries, signed distance field (SDF) computation, and ray intersection tests. It solves the problem of rapidly determining the closest point on a complex triangle mesh or the sign of a point relative to the mesh surface, which is a bottleneck in neural rendering and collision detection. It is distinguished from hierarchical grid methods (like Octree Traversal) by operating directly on unstructured triangle geometry rather than voxelized or grid-based volumes, and from software-only BVHs by leveraging NVIDIA OptiX hardware acceleration for ray-triangle intersections. Inputs and Outputs: The primary implementation takes a triangle mesh defined by vertices V \in \mathbb{R}^{Nv \times 3} (float32) and faces F \in \mathbb{Z}^{Nf \times 3} (int32 vertex indices). Queries accept a set of points P \in \mathbb{R}^{Np \times 3} (float32). Data Structures: The hierarchy is a binary tree where internal nodes contain Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) enclosing their descendants. Leaves contain individual triangles. For signed distance computation, the structure supports traversal for unsigned distance and subsequent ray casting for sign determination. Algorithm Steps: 1. Construction: Build the BVH from input vertices and faces. On GPU implementations, this is often done via a parallel cluster merging approach to avoid CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks. The builder assigns triangles to leaf nodes and computes AABBs for internal nodes by merging child bounds. 2. Unsigned Distance Query: Given a query point p, traverse the BVH to find the closest triangle. Start at the root. For each node, compute the distance from p to the node's AABB. If the distance exceeds the current best distance d{min}, prune the node. If a leaf (triangle) is reached, compute the exact distance from p to the triangle using Voronoi region tests. Update d{min} if the triangle distance is smaller. Return the minimum distance d, the closest point c, and the face ID. 3. Sign Determination (SDF): To determine if p is inside or outside the mesh: Method A (Stab Rays): Trace K=32 rays from p in directions distributed uniformly over the sphere using a Fibonacci lattice, with pseudorandom offsets per point. If any ray reaches infinity (no intersection), p is outside (sign +1). If all rays intersect the mesh, p is inside (sign -1). Method B (Normal Check): For watertight meshes, use the normal of the closest triangle found in Step 2. If the dot product of the vector (p - c) and the triangle normal is positive, p is outside; otherwise, inside. This is disabled by default due to incompatibility with non-watertight meshes. 4. Winding Number: Compute the winding number by summing the solid angle subtended by each triangle at p, or via ray casting parity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ if root is None: return currentmindist # Compute distance from p to node AABB disttoaabb = distancepointaabb(p, root.aabb) if disttoaabb >= currentmindist: return currentmindist if root.isleaf(): a, b, c = root.trianglevertices() closest = closestpointtriangle(p, a, b, c) dist = length(p - closest) return min(currentmindist, dist) # Visit children distleft = querybvhdistance(root.left, p, currentmindist) if distleft < currentmindist: currentmindist = distleft distright = querybvhdistance(root.right, p, currentmindist) return min(currentmindist, distright) def computesigneddistance(p, bvh, numstabrays=32): """ Computes signed distance using BVH for unsigned distance and stab rays for sign. """ # 1. Unsigned distance dist, closestpoint, faceid = querybvhdistance(bvh.root, p) # 2. Sign determination via stab rays # Generate directions using Fibonacci lattice directions = [] goldenratio = (1 + math.sqrt(5)) / 2 for i in range(numstabrays): theta = 2 math.pi i / goldenratio phi = math.acos(1 - 2 (i + 0.5) / numstabrays) # Add pseudorandom offset per point (omitted for brevity, assumed handled) x = math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = math.cos(phi) directions.append((x, y, z)) isoutside = False for dir in directions: # Trace ray from p in direction dir # If ray hits infinity (no intersection), point is outside if not rayintersectsmesh(p, dir, bvh): isoutside = True break sign = 1.0 if isoutside else -1.0 return sign dist Parameters: Number of stab rays: 32. Ray tracing framework: NVIDIA OptiX 7. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight meshes: Normal-based signing is unreliable and disabled by default. Stab rays are required. Precision: Floating-point errors in ray casting may cause incorrect sign determination for points very close to the surface. Degenerate triangles: The closest point algorithm handles degenerate triangles (lines/points) via the Voronoi region logic. A binary tree hierarchy over a triangle mesh where leaves are triangles and internal nodes contain a 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) over positions and a bounding cone over shading normals for all descendants. It stores position and normal information for boundary triangles to enable hierarchical pruning of refractive path searches. It is distinguished from interval-based refinement by prioritizing speed over guaranteed convergence, typically running 2 to 5 times faster while producing visually equivalent results. Voxel Mesh Ray Intersection via BVH is a raycasting method for voxel meshes that traverses a grid of oriented sub-cubes to find intersections with voxel geometry using Binary Volume Hierarchy (BVH) triangle intersection tests. It handles multiple meshes by first checking bounding boxes and then delegating to the specific mesh's BVH. This method builds on Mesh BVH by providing the specific traversal logic and data structures required to query triangle meshes stored within a voxelized world structure. This method constructs a Binary Volume Hierarchy (BVH) on the GPU by iteratively merging clusters of triangles. It solves the problem of building hierarchical acceleration structures for ray tracing without CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks by using a fully parallel, double-buffered approach involving neighbor finding, prefix scans, and reallocation. It differs from CPU-based top-down or bottom-up builders by keeping all data on the GPU and using a "merge-compact" loop that reduces the number of active clusters by half (approximately) each iteration until a single root remains. Uses a BVH to compute the unsigned distance and barycentric coordinates from interpolated UV-space positions back to the original high-resolution mesh, correcting geometric errors from simplification/remeshing. 1. Query BVH:, faceid, uvw = bvh.unsigneddistance(validpos, returnuvw=True). 2. Fetch original triangle vertices: origtriverts = vertices[faces[faceid.long()]]. 3. Reconstruct corrected position via barycentric interpolation: validpos = (origtriverts uvw.unsqueeze(-1)).sum(dim=1). A bounding volume hierarchy adapted for the management of the blending operation, used for efficient evaluation of field functions on large skeletons. A method to compute the signed distance from a 3D point to a triangle mesh efficiently using a BVH for unsigned distance and ray casting for sign determination. 1. Construct a triangle BVH for efficient unsigned distance queries, achieving O(\log N{triangles}) average complexity. 2. Trace 32 'stab rays' distributed uniformly over the sphere using a Fibonacci lattice, pseudorandomly and independently offset for every training position. 3. If any ray reaches infinity, mark the position as 'outside' and the distance as positive. Otherwise, mark it as negative. 4. Use NVIDIA ray tracing hardware via the OptiX 7 framework for ray-triangle intersections to maximize efficiency. Parameter: Number of stab rays: 32. Pitfall: For watertight meshes, signing distance based on the normal of the closest triangle is cheaper, but this is disabled by default due to incompatibility with typical non-watertight meshes found in the wild. Comparison: Using OptiX 7 is over an order of magnitude faster than using a software triangle BVH for ray-shape intersections on an RTX 3090 GPU. Time Complexity: Unsigned distance query is O(\log N{triangles}) on average. Signed distance adds O(K \cdot \log N{triangles}) for K stab rays. Hardware Acceleration: When using NVIDIA OptiX 7, performance is over an order of magnitude faster than software BVH implementations on RTX 3090 GPUs. Memory: Depends on the BVH construction method. GPU-based cluster merging requires double-buffered memory for intermediate clusters. Strengths: High performance for distance queries and SDF computation on GPUs; supports complex, non-watertight meshes; integrates well with neural rendering pipelines. Limitations: Stab ray method is probabilistic and may fail for very thin structures or if rays are not dense enough; normal-based signing is unreliable for non-watertight meshes. When to use: When computing SDFs or closest points for triangle meshes in a GPU-accelerated environment, especially for neural rendering or collision detection. When not to use: For static, watertight meshes where normal-based signing is sufficient and faster, or when CPU-only resources are available and OptiX is not an option. Mesh BVH was introduced as part of the isoext library for GPU-based signed distance field computation from triangle meshes. It has been widely adopted in neural graphics primitives, such as Instant Neural Graphics Primitives (INGP), for efficient signed distance field computation and ray marching acceleration. The method leverages NVIDIA's OptiX ray tracing API to offload triangle intersection tests to dedicated hardware. Variants like BVH-based geometric attribute correction have been developed to handle high-resolution mesh details in voxelized representations. name: Position-Normal Tree
head: Position-Normal Tree Hierarchy, Position-Normal Tree for Hierarchical Pruning
body: A binary tree hierarchy over a triangle mesh where leaves are triangles and internal nodes contain a 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) over positions and a bounding cone over shading normals for all descendants. It stores position and normal information for boundary triangles to enable hierarchical pruning of refractive path searches. It is distinguished from interval-based refinement by prioritizing speed over guaranteed convergence, typically running 2 to 5 times faster while producing visually equivalent results. Inputs: A triangle mesh boundary. Outputs: A binary tree structure for pruning refractive path searches. Data Structures: Each node contains an AABB over positions, a bounding cone over normals, child pointers for internal nodes, and a triangle reference for leaves. Memory usage is approximately 100 bytes per boundary triangle. Steps: 1. Construct the hierarchy using a bottom-up approach. 2. Perform a depth-first traversal of the tree. 3. At each node, test for pruning using the spindle test, sidedness test, and cone overlap test. 4. If any test proves no solution exists, prune the subtree. The exact merging algorithm is not given in the sources. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Refractive index (\eta) is typically 1.5 for homogeneous media in the examples. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The tree only needs to be rebuilt if the geometry is deformed. The pruning tests are heuristic and may miss a few paths near caustic cusps on rare occasions, affecting at most a few pixels per image compared to interval-based refinement. A recursive strategy to find refraction points on triangles with smooth normals by progressively splitting the triangle into smaller sub-triangles and pruning those that cannot contain a solution. It is distinguished from interval-based refinement by prioritizing speed over guaranteed convergence, typically running 2 to 5 times faster while producing visually equivalent results. Choose it when performance is critical and visually equivalent results are acceptable over strict convergence guarantees. Essential for performance on meshes with many triangles. Without hierarchical pruning, the pool scene took 1934.6s versus 59.4s with it, a 32x slowdown. Build time is very fast, taking 6ms for the glass tile model. Memory usage is approximately 100 bytes per boundary triangle. The position-normal tree and hierarchical pruning are essential for getting good performance on boundary meshes with more than a few triangles. The position-normal tree was introduced by Bala et al., building on earlier work by Snyder and Walter et al.. It is used in single scattering in refractive media with triangle mesh boundaries to efficiently compute refractive connection paths. name: Split-and-Prune for Sub-Triangle Search
head: Cone Angles Triangle Subdivision Heuristic
body: A recursive strategy to find refraction points on triangles with smooth normals by progressively splitting the triangle into smaller sub-triangles and pruning those that cannot contain a solution. It enables efficient 2D search for refractive paths where interpolated normals create complex, non-planar solution spaces. It is distinguished from interval-based refinement by prioritizing speed over guaranteed convergence, typically running 2 to 5 times faster while producing visually equivalent results. Inputs: Triangle vertices V0, V1, V2 with positions and shading normals. Light direction \hat{L} and view direction \hat{V} at the incident point P. Refraction index \eta. Outputs: A set of sub-triangles containing potential solutions, ready for 2D Newton-Raphson iteration. Data Structures: Bounding Cone: Defined by an axis vector \hat{A} and a semi-angle \theta. Spherical Triangle Bounding Box: A 3D axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing a spherical triangle on the unit sphere. Steps: 1. Compute Bounding Cone for Shading Normals (\hat{N}s): Construct the spherical triangle defined by the vertex shading normals \hat{N}0, \hat{N}1, \hat{N}2. Compute the bounding cone for this spherical triangle. All bounding cones have their apex at the origin. 2. Compute Bounding Cone for Half-Vector (\hat{H}): Compute the spherical triangles defined by the directions (\hat{L}-Vi)/\|\hat{L}-Vi\| and (\hat{V}-Vi)/\|\hat{V}-Vi\| for i=0,1,2. Compute 3D AABBs for both spherical triangles. Scale the view direction AABB by \eta. Compute the Minkowski sum of the light AABB and the scaled view AABB by adding corresponding min/max bounds. This yields an AABB for the unnormalized half-vector. Compute the bounding cone for this resulting AABB. 3. Pruning Test: Check if the bounding cone for -\hat{H} and the bounding cone for \hat{N}s overlap. If they do not overlap, prune the triangle (it cannot contain a solution). Two cones overlap if the angle between their axes is less than the sum of their bounding semiangles. 4. Subdivision or Termination: If the triangle is not pruned, check the stopping criterion. Heuristic Stopping Criterion: If the sum of the \hat{H} cone angle and the \hat{N}s cone angle is less than 30 degrees, stop subdividing and proceed to 2D Newton-Raphson iteration. If the criterion is not met, split the triangle into 4 smaller sub-triangles by splitting each edge in half. Recursively apply steps 1-4 to each sub-triangle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class AABB: def init(self, minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz): self.minx, self.maxx = minx, maxx self.miny, self.maxy = miny, maxy self.minz, self.maxz = minz, maxz class Triangle: def init(self, v0, v1, v2, n0, n1, n2): self.v0, self.v1, self.v2 = v0, v1, v2 self.n0, self.n1, self.n2 = n0, n1, n2 def midpoint(p1, p2): return ((p1[0]+p2[0])/2, (p1[1]+p2[1])/2, (p1[2]+p2[2])/2) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) if mag > 0 else (0,0,0) def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def anglebetweenvectors(v1, v2): return math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, dot(normalize(v1), normalize(v2))))) def computesphericaltriangleboundingcone(n0, n1, n2): # Standard computation: axis is normalized sum, semi-angle is max angle to vertices axis = normalize((n0[0]+n1[0]+n2[0], n0[1]+n1[1]+n2[1], n0[2]+n1[2]+n2[2])) angle = max(anglebetweenvectors(n0, axis), anglebetweenvectors(n1, axis), anglebetweenvectors(n2, axis)) return (axis, angle) def computeaabb(sphtri): xs = [p[0] for p in sphtri] ys = [p[1] for p in sphtri] zs = [p[2] for p in sphtri] return AABB(min(xs), max(xs), min(ys), max(ys), min(zs), max(zs)) def scaleaabb(box, s): return AABB(box.minxs, box.maxxs, box.minys, box.maxys, box.minzs, box.maxzs) def minkowskisum(b1, b2): return AABB(b1.minx+b2.minx, b1.maxx+b2.maxx, b1.miny+b2.miny, b1.maxy+b2.maxy, b1.minz+b2.minz, b1.maxz+b2.maxz) def computeboxboundingcone(box): # Axis is direction to box center, semi-angle is max angle to any corner cx, cy, cz = (box.minx+box.maxx)/2, (box.miny+box.maxy)/2, (box.minz+box.maxz)/2 axis = normalize((cx, cy, cz)) corners = [ (box.minx, box.miny, box.minz), (box.maxx, box.miny, box.minz), (box.minx, box.maxy, box.minz), (box.maxx, box.maxy, box.minz), (box.minx, box.miny, box.maxz), (box.maxx, box.miny, box.maxz), (box.minx, box.maxy, box.maxz), (box.maxx, box.maxy, box.maxz) ] angle = max(anglebetweenvectors(c, axis) for c in corners) return (axis, angle) def conesoverlap(cone1, cone2): # Two cones overlap if the angle between their axes is less than the sum of their bounding semiangles return anglebetweenvectors(cone1[0], cone2[0]) < (cone1[1] + cone2[1]) def splitandprunesearch(triangle, Ldir, Vdir, eta): # Step 1: Compute bounding cone for shading normals (Ns) nscone = computesphericaltriangleboundingcone(triangle.n0, triangle.n1, triangle.n2) # Step 2: Compute bounding cone for half-vector (H) # Spherical triangle for L lsphtri = [normalize((Ldir[0]-v[0], Ldir[1]-v[1], Ldir[2]-v[2])) for v in (triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2)] # Spherical triangle for V vsphtri = [normalize((Vdir[0]-v[0], Vdir[1]-v[1], Vdir[2]-v[2])) for v in (triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2)] lbox = computeaabb(lsphtri) vbox = computeaabb(vsphtri) vboxscaled = scaleaabb(vbox, eta) hbox = minkowskisum(lbox, vboxscaled) hcone = computeboxboundingcone(hbox) # Step 3: Pruning Test # Check if bounding cone for -H and Ns overlap neghcone = (-hcone[0][0], -hcone[0][1], -hcone[0][2]), hcone[1] if not conesoverlap(neghcone, nscone): return [] # Pruned # Step 4: Subdivision or Termination coneanglesumdeg = math.degrees(hcone[1] + nscone[1]) if coneanglesumdeg < 30.0: return [triangle] # Stop subdividing, proceed to Newton-Raphson else: mid01 = midpoint(triangle.v0, triangle.v1) mid12 = midpoint(triangle.v1, triangle.v2) mid20 = midpoint(triangle.v2, triangle.v0) # Interpolate normals for sub-triangles n01 = normalize((triangle.n0[0]+triangle.n1[0], triangle.n0[1]+triangle.n1[1], triangle.n0[2]+triangle.n1[2])) n12 = normalize((triangle.n1[0]+triangle.n2[0], triangle.n1[1]+triangle.n2[1], triangle.n1[2]+triangle.n2[2])) n20 = normalize((triangle.n2[0]+triangle.n0[0], triangle.n2[1]+triangle.n0[1], triangle.n2[2]+triangle.n0[2])) subtriangles = [ Triangle(triangle.v0, mid01, mid20, triangle.n0, n01, n20), Triangle(mid01, triangle.v1, mid12, n01, triangle.n1, n12), Triangle(mid20, mid12, triangle.v2, n20, n12, triangle.n2), Triangle(mid01, mid12, mid20, n01, n12, n20) ] results = [] for subt in subtriangles: results.extend(splitandprunesearch(subt, Ldir, Vdir, eta)) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The heuristic is not guaranteed to find all solutions. It may miss a few paths near caustic cusps on rare occasions, affecting at most a few pixels. Normal-mapped triangles are not supported in the original description, though bounding cones could be precomputed. A heuristic for triangle subdivision used to find refractive paths, preferred over interval-based refinement for speed in the reported results. It is typically 2 to 5 times faster than interval-based refinement test, producing visually equivalent images. It may miss a few paths near caustic cusps on rare occasions, affecting at most a few pixels. Time Complexity: Faster than interval-based refinement, typically 2 to 5 times faster depending on the scene. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Speed; produces visually good results. Limitations: Not guaranteed to find all solutions; may miss paths near caustic cusps. When to use: When visual equivalence is acceptable and speed is prioritized over guaranteed convergence. When not to use: When guaranteed convergence is required, in which case the interval-based refinement test should be used. Originated in the paper "Single Scattering in Refractive Media with Triangle Mesh Boundaries". The method addresses the difficulty of finding refraction points on triangles with interpolated normals, where the problem is 2D rather than 1D due to the potential for multiple solutions not lying within a single incidence plane. name: Voxel Mesh Ray Intersection via BVH
head: Voxel Mesh Raycasting (BVH Triangle Intersection), VoxelGeometryIntersect, VoxelMeshIntersect
body: A raycasting method for voxel meshes that traverses a grid of oriented sub-cubes to find intersections with voxel geometry using BVH triangle intersection tests. It differs from its parent Mesh BVH by adding a spatial grid traversal layer that maps ray positions to specific voxel meshes before delegating to the mesh's internal BVH. It differs from siblings like Position-Normal Tree by relying on explicit triangle intersection tests within leaf nodes rather than implicit distance fields. Inputs: Ray origin (ro), ray direction (rd), maximum distance (MAX\DISTANCE), voxel mesh data structures (indices, vertices, BVH nodes), and world bounds. Outputs: Intersection result containing hit distance (t), hit position, normal, and triangle ID. Data Structures: VoxelMesh struct (80 bytes, 4-byte aligned): state (vec4f, offset 0): x indicates active status. position (vec3f, offset 4): World position. indexOffsets (vec4f, offset 8): x = vertex offset, y = index offset, z = BVH tree offset, w = voxel index offset. minBounds (vec3f, offset 12): Axis-aligned bounding box minimum. maxBounds (vec3f, offset 15): Axis-aligned bounding box maximum. AABB struct: min (vec4f): xyz = position, w = active flag. max (vec4f): xyz = position, w = node type (1 for inner, 2 for voxel geometry). StackNode struct: { nodeId: u32, t: f32 }. Stack: Fixed-size array of 13 StackNode elements (STACKSIZE = 13). Constants: cubeSize = 16.0, subCubeSize = 8.0, halfSize = 8.0, rayLength = 16.0, VOXELNODEINDEX = 4095u. Algorithm Steps: 1. Inverse Direction Calculation: Compute inverse ray direction components to handle near-zero values and avoid division by zero: invDir.x = \frac{1.0}{\text{sign}(rd.x) \cdot \max(|rd.x|, 10^{-8})} Repeat for y and z. 2. Initialization: Set t = \infty, totalDistance = 0.0, rayPosition = ro. 3. Grid Traversal Loop: Define an oriented bounding cube relative to rayPosition using rd, a right vector, and an up vector with halfSize offset. Iterate through a 3 \times 3 \times 3 grid of sub-cubes (indices i, j, k \in [0, 2]). Calculate sub-cube center: subCubeCenter = cubeMinCorner + rd \cdot (i \cdot subCubeSize) + right \cdot (j \cdot subCubeSize) + up \cdot (k \cdot subCubeSize) Calculate sub-cube min/max corners: subCubeMin = subCubeCenter - rd \cdot \frac{subCubeSize}{2} - right \cdot \frac{subCubeSize}{2} - up \cdot \frac{subCubeSize}{2} Lookup world mesh at subCubeMin using getWorldMesh. This function checks bounds and returns the mesh index if found. Perform bounding box intersection test between ray and voxel mesh bounds using BoundingBoxIntersect, storing result in chunkT. If mesh found, chunkT < t, and chunkT < MAX\DISTANCE, call VoxelMeshIntersect with ro, rd, mesh index, and MAX\DISTANCE. If VoxelMeshIntersect returns a hit and result.t \le t, update finalResult and t. 4. BVH Traversal (VoxelMeshIntersect): Initialize stackIndex = 0, currentNodeIndex = 0, currentNodeT = 0.0. Calculate inverseDir = 1.0 / rd. Get mesh position and offset from mesh.indexOffsets.z. Loop: Fetch current node from voxelbvh[currentNodeIndex + offset]. Leaf Check: If currentNode.max.w == 2.0, it is a leaf. Call VoxelGeometryIntersect(ro, rd, currentNodeIndex - VOXELNODEINDEX, voxelMeshIndex). If hit, set intersectResult.found = true, intersectResult.t = currentNodeT, store geometry result, and break loop. Internal Node: Calculate child IDs: leftChildId = 2 currentNodeIndex + 1, rightChildId = 2 currentNodeIndex + 2. Fetch children from voxelbvh. Test left child: If leftChild.min.w >= 0, compute leftChildT = BoundingBoxIntersect(...). If leftChildT > MAXDISTANCE, set leftChildT = \infty. Test right child: If rightChild.min.w >= 0, compute rightChildT = BoundingBoxIntersect(...). If rightChildT > MAXDISTANCE, set rightChildT = \infty. Traversal Logic: If only left hit (leftChildT < \infty and rightChildT == \infty): currentNodeIndex = leftChildId, currentNodeT = leftChildT. If only right hit (rightChildT < \infty and leftChildT == \infty): currentNodeIndex = rightChildId, currentNodeT = rightChildT. If both hit: Push farther child onto stack. Check stack overflow (stackIndex >= STACKSIZE); if overflow, set intersectResult.error = true and break. Traverse closer child. 5. Triangle Intersection (VoxelGeometryIntersect): If length <= 0 (calculated as indiceOffsets.y - indiceOffsets.x), return immediately. Loop indiceIndex from 0 to length with step 3. Get vertex indices v1, v2, v3 from indices array offset by vertexOffset. Call BVHTriangleIntersect1 with transformed vertex positions (vertices[...] + position). If triResult.t < t and triResult.t != \infty: Update intersectResult.hit = true, t = triResult.t, finalTriResult = triResult, triId = indiceIndex / 3, finalIndex = indiceOffset + indiceIndex. 6. Normal Interpolation: If hit, retrieve vertex normals n1, n2, n3 and UVs uv1, uv2, uv3. Interpolate normal: interpolatedNormal = \text{normalize}(n1 \cdot (1.0 - u - v) + n2 \cdot u + n3 \cdot v) where u, v are from finalTriResult. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Inverse Direction invrd = vec3( 1.0 / (sign(rd.x) max(abs(rd.x), 1e-8)), 1.0 / (sign(rd.y) max(abs(rd.y), 1e-8)), 1.0 / (sign(rd.z) max(abs(rd.z), 1e-8))) t = float('inf') rayposition = ro cubesize = 16.0 subcubesize = 8.0 halfsize = cubesize / 2.0 # Define oriented basis vectors (simplified for example, assumes rd is aligned or basis is precomputed) # In practice, rayRight and rayUp are orthogonal to rd rayright = vec3(0, 1, 0) # Placeholder for actual orthogonal basis calculation rayup = vec3(0, 0, 1) # Placeholder for actual orthogonal basis calculation # 3.
