v0 edge2 = v2 - v0 h = cross(rd, edge2) a = dot(edge1, h) if a < 1e-8: return IntersectionResult(t=float('inf')) f = 1.0 / a s = ro - v0 u = f dot(s, h) if u < 0.0 or u > 1.0: return IntersectionResult(t=float('inf')) q = cross(s, edge1) v = f dot(rd, q) if v < 0.0 or u + v > 1.0: return IntersectionResult(t=float('inf')) t = f dot(edge2, q) if t > 1e-8: return IntersectionResult(t=t, u=u, v=v) return IntersectionResult(t=float('inf')) def boundingboxintersect(ro, rd, minb, maxb): tmin = (minb - ro) invrd tmax = (maxb - ro) invrd t1 = min(tmin, tmax) t2 = max(tmin, tmax) tenter = max(t1.x, t1.y, t1.z) texit = min(t2.x, t2.y, t2.z) if tenter > texit: return float('inf') if texit < 0: return float('inf') return max(tenter, 0.0) A compute shader-based ray tracing technique for voxel data that uses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to accelerate ray-mesh intersection tests for lighting and ambient occlusion calculations. It differs from hardware-accelerated approaches like Sparse Voxel Set (SVS) or GPU-based Ray Shooting for Volumetric Mapping by performing the traversal logic entirely within a custom compute shader rather than relying on dedicated DXR hardware pipelines. This method is specifically designed for deferred shading pipelines where position and normal buffers are available, enabling efficient shadow and occlusion queries against sparse voxel meshes. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot \log L) where N is the number of sub-cubes traversed (fixed 3 \times 3 \times 3 = 27 per grid step), M is the number of meshes per sub-cube, and L is the BVH depth. The grid traversal is constant per ray segment, but BVH traversal depends on tree height. Memory Complexity: O(V + B + S) where V is vertex/index buffer size, B is BVH node size, and S is stack size (fixed 13 nodes). Strengths: Avoids recursion depth limits by using a fixed-size stack (13 nodes). Efficient for sparse voxel meshes by skipping empty space via grid traversal. Limitations: Fixed stack size (13) can lead to overflow errors if the BVH is deeper than supported, potentially missing closer intersections. Requires explicit stack management. When to use: Deferred shading pipelines with available position/normal buffers, sparse voxel meshes, GPU compute shaders. When not to use: Dense voxel grids where simpler grid traversal suffices, or when hardware ray tracing (DXR) is available and preferred. Originated in the Divine Voxel Engine (DVE) by Divine Star Software. It is part of the DVE monorepo, which includes packages for voxel rendering and WASM compilation. The method is used in DVE's PBR and Classic rendering modes. Divine-Star-Software/DivineVoxelEngine, https://github.com/Divine-Star-Software/DivineVoxelEngine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Ray Marching with BVH Acceleration
head: VoxelMeshQuery, VoxelRayRender
body: A compute shader-based ray tracing technique for voxel data that uses a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to accelerate ray-mesh intersection tests for lighting and ambient occlusion calculations. It differs from hardware-accelerated approaches like Sparse Voxel Set (SVS) or GPU-based Ray Shooting for Volumetric Mapping by performing the traversal logic entirely within a custom compute shader rather than relying on dedicated DXR hardware pipelines. This method is specifically designed for deferred shading pipelines where position and normal buffers are available, enabling efficient shadow and occlusion queries against sparse voxel meshes. The method operates on a per-pixel basis in a compute shader, utilizing position and normal textures as input buffers to generate lighting and ambient occlusion (AO) textures. It delegates the heavy lifting of ray-voxel intersection to a software-implemented BVH traversal function (voxelMeshQuery). Inputs: positiontexture: texture2d<f32> storing world position at screen coordinates. normaltexture: texture2d<f32> storing surface normals. sceneprops: Contains sunPosition. camera: Contains right, up, forward vectors and tanHalfFov. voxelbvh: array<AABB> representing the hierarchy nodes. voxelindice: array<vec2u> mapping BVH nodes to mesh indices. voxelmeshes: array<VoxelMesh> containing mesh data. vertices: array<VoxelMeshVertex>. indices: array<u32>. Outputs: lighttexture: texturestorage2d<rgba32float, write> for sun lighting. aotexture: texturestorage2d<rgba16float, write> for ambient occlusion. VoxelMeshVertex: position: vec3f normal: vec3f textureIndex: vec3f uv: vec2f colors: vec3f voxelData: f32 padding: vec4f AABB (implied from BVH usage): Minimum and maximum bounds defining the volume. Sun ray max distance: 300.0. AO ray max distance: 0.99. Epsilon offset for shadow/occlusion ray origin: 0.01. AO sample count: 4. 1. Initialization: Calculate screen coordinates from the global invocation ID multiplied by 2. 2. Position Check: Load the world position from positiontexture using the screen coordinates. If the position's alpha component is \le 0, store 1.0 in the light and AO textures and return. 3. Normal Extraction: Extract the world position and normal from the textures. Convert the normal from the [0, 1] range to the [-1, 1] range using: \mathbf{n} = 2 \cdot \mathbf{c}{normal} - 1 where \mathbf{c}{normal} is the color value from normaltexture. Set hitPosition to the position's RGB components. 4. Sun Lighting Calculation: Offset hitPosition along the normal by epsilon (\epsilon = 0.01) to get newHitPosition. Calculate the sun direction vector from newHitPosition to sceneprops.sunPosition. Construct an orthonormal basis for the sun direction. Call voxelMeshQuery with newHitPosition, the sun direction, and a max distance of 300.0. If an intersection is found, set the light value to dark gray (0.25, 0.25, 0.25). If an error occurs, set the light value to red (1, 0, 0). 5. Ambient Occlusion Calculation: Build an orthonormal basis from the surface normal using buildOrthonormalBasis. Initialize a hit counter to 0. Loop 4 times (for the sample count): Generate random numbers using getTwoRandomNumbers with a seed based on fragment coordinates and time. Sample a hemisphere direction using cosineWeightedHemisphereSample. Transform the local sample to world space using hemisphereToWorld. Construct an orthonormal basis for the sample direction. Call voxelMeshQuery with hitPosition, the sample direction, and a max distance of 0.99. If an intersection is found, increment the hit counter. Calculate the occlusion factor: f{occlusion} = 1.0 - \frac{\text{hit}}{4} Apply this factor to the AO color channels. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildorthonormalbasis(N: vec3) -> Basis: """Constructs a basis (T, B, N) avoiding singularity when N is parallel to up.""" up = vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) if abs(N.z) < 0.999 else vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) T = normalize(cross(up, N)) B = normalize(cross(N, T)) return Basis(T, B, N) def cosineweightedhemispheresample(u: f32, v: f32) -> vec3: """Generates a direction on the upper hemisphere weighted by cosine.""" phi = 2.0 3.1415926535 u r = sqrt(v) x = r cos(phi) y = r sin(phi) z = sqrt(1.0 - v) return vec3(x, y, z) def voxelraymarchingwithbvhacceleration(globalinvocationid: vec3, positiontexture: Texture2D, normaltexture: Texture2D, lighttexture: StorageTexture2D, aotexture: StorageTexture2D, sceneprops: SceneProps, camera: Camera, voxelbvh: Array[AABB], voxelindice: Array[vec2u], voxelmeshes: Array[VoxelMesh], vertices: Array[VoxelMeshVertex], indices: Array<u32>): # 1. Calculate screen coordinates screencoord = globalinvocationid.xy 2 # 2. Load position poscolor = positiontexture.sample(screencoord) if poscolor.a <= 0.0: lighttexture.store(screencoord, vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)) aotexture.store(screencoord, vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)) return # 3. Extract world position and normal hitposition = poscolor.rgb normalcolor = normaltexture.sample(screencoord) normal = (2.0 normalcolor) - 1.0 # 4. Sun Lighting newhitposition = hitposition + normal 0.01 # Epsilon offset sundirection = normalize(sceneprops.sunposition - newhitposition) sunbasis = buildorthonormalbasis(sundirection) # Call BVH query for sun # Note: The specific implementation of voxelMeshQuery is not provided in the source, # but it takes origin, direction, and max distance. sunhit = voxelmeshquery(newhitposition, sundirection, 300.0, voxelbvh, voxelindice, voxelmeshes, vertices, indices) if sunhit: lightcolor = vec4(0.25, 0.25, 0.25, 1.0) else: # Error case handling as per source lightcolor = vec4(1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) lighttexture.store(screencoord, lightcolor) # 5. Ambient Occlusion surfbasis = buildorthonormalbasis(normal) hitcount = 0 for i in range(4): # Generate random numbers based on seed u, v = gettworandomnumbers(screencoord, time) # Sample hemisphere localsample = cosineweightedhemispheresample(u, v) # Transform to world space worldsample = hemispheretoworld(localsample, surfbasis) # Construct basis for sample direction (for BVH traversal if needed) samplebasis = buildorthonormalbasis(worldsample) # Call BVH query for AO aohit = voxelmeshquery(hitposition, worldsample, 0.99, voxelbvh, voxelindice, voxelmeshes, vertices, indices) if aohit: hitcount += 1 occlusionfactor = 1.0 - (hitcount / 4.0) aocolor = vec4(occlusionfactor, occlusionfactor, occlusionfactor, 1.0) aotexture.store(screencoord, aocolor) Shadow Acne/Bleeding: The ray origin for sun and AO queries is offset from the surface position along the normal by a small epsilon (0.01) to prevent self-intersection. Basis Construction Singularity: The buildOrthonormalBasis function selects the 'up' vector based on the Z component of the normal to avoid cross product degeneracy when the normal is parallel to the default up vector. Empty Pixels: If the position texture alpha is \le 0, the shader returns immediately with full brightness to avoid processing empty space. Uses BVH but offloads traversal to DXR hardware. Choose when hardware ray tracing is available and custom shader overhead is undesirable. Uses BVH for occupancy queries in PVM via DXR. Choose for volumetric mapping tasks requiring free/occupied voxel determination. Time Complexity: Depends on the BVH traversal depth and the number of samples (4 for AO). The BVH traversal is generally O(\log N) for sparse data, but worst-case can be O(N) if the BVH is unbalanced or the scene is dense. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the BVH nodes (voxelbvh), indices (voxelindice), meshes (voxelmeshes), and vertices (vertices). Performance: Offloading traversal to a custom compute shader avoids the overhead of setting up DXR pipelines but requires manual implementation of the BVH traversal logic. Strengths: Flexible, works on hardware without DXR support, integrates well with deferred shading pipelines. Limitations: Requires manual implementation of BVH traversal, potentially slower than hardware-accelerated methods on supported GPUs. When to use: When DXR is not available or when custom lighting/occlusion logic is required that doesn't fit standard ray tracing pipelines. When not to use: When hardware ray tracing is available and standard ray tracing features are sufficient. This method is described in the Divine Voxel Engine repository. It is designed for real-time voxel rendering, specifically for calculating lighting and ambient occlusion in a deferred rendering context. name: Sparse Voxel Set (SVS)
body: Sparse Voxel Set (SVS) is a ray-tracing acceleration method for Signed Distance Function (SDF) grids that constructs a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) from Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) representing individual surface-intersecting voxels. It differs from software-based traversal methods (like Grid Sphere Tracing or Sparse Brick Set) by offloading the primary traversal logic to dedicated GPU ray-tracing hardware (DXR), thereby reducing the computational burden of the custom intersection shader. Inputs: A voxel grid containing Signed Distance Field (SDF) values; a threshold defining the surface boundary. Outputs: A BVH structure suitable for DirectX Raytracing (DXR) hardware traversal. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Data: Each voxel in the sparse set stores a 4 \times 4 \times 4 array of signed distance values. This is larger than the standard 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighborhood, providing easy access to neighboring voxel values required for normal evaluation. 2. AABB: An Axis-Aligned Bounding Box is created for each voxel that intersects the surface (i.e., where the SDF crosses the threshold). 3. BVH: A hierarchy of these AABBs is built to accelerate ray intersection tests. Algorithm Steps: 1. Voxel Selection: Identify all voxels in the grid that intersect the implicit surface defined by the SDF threshold. 2. AABB Construction: For each selected voxel, compute the AABB that encloses the voxel's spatial extent. 3. BVH Build: Construct a Bounding Volume Hierarchy from the set of AABBs. 4. Ray Tracing Setup: Configure the DXR pipeline to use the constructed BVH. 5. Traversal: For each ray, perform BVH traversal using the GPU's RTX ray tracing hardware. 6. Intersection Shader: When a leaf node (voxel) is reached, invoke a custom intersection shader. 7. SDF Evaluation: Inside the intersection shader, sample the 4 \times 4 \times 4 SDF data associated with the voxel to determine the precise intersection point and normal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class SparseVoxelSet: def init(self, gridresolution, sdfvalues, threshold): self.threshold = threshold self.voxels = [] self.bvh = None # Step 1 & 2: Identify surface voxels and create AABBs for x in range(gridresolution.x): for y in range(gridresolution.y): for z in range(gridresolution.z): # Check if voxel intersects surface # A voxel intersects if the SDF values at its corners span the threshold if self.voxelintersectssurface(x, y, z, sdfvalues): # Store 4x4x4 SDF values for normal evaluation sdfdata = self.get4x4x4sdf(x, y, z, sdfvalues) aabb = self.computeaabb(x, y, z) self.voxels.append({ 'aabb': aabb, 'sdfdata': sdfdata }) # Step 3: Build BVH self.bvh = BVHBuilder(self.voxels) def voxelintersectssurface(self, x, y, z, sdfvalues): # Determine if the voxel contains the surface # This typically involves checking the 8 corners of the voxel # against the threshold. If signs differ, it intersects. # Implementation detail: Check min/max SDF in voxel vs threshold return True # Placeholder for specific intersection logic def get4x4x4sdf(self, x, y, z, sdfvalues): # Retrieve 4x4x4 signed distance values around the voxel # This allows easy access to neighboring values for normal evaluation return sdfvalues[x-1:x+4, y-1:y+4, z-1:z+4] def computeaabb(self, x, y, z): # Compute AABB for the voxel return AABB(min=(x, y, z), max=(x+1, y+1, z+1)) def traceray(self, rayorigin, raydirection): # Step 5: Perform BVH traversal using RTX hardware # The hardware handles the traversal tree walk hit = self.bvh.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if hit: # Step 6: Invoke custom intersection shader # Step 7: Evaluate SDF for precise hit voxeldata = hit.voxeldata sdfval = self.evaluatesdf(hit.position, voxeldata) normal = self.computenormal(hit.position, voxeldata) return sdfval, normal return None def evaluatesdf(self, position, sdfdata): # Sample the 4x4x4 grid at the hit position # Trilinear interpolation of the 4x4x4 data pass def computenormal(self, position, sdfdata): # Compute normal using neighboring SDF values # Central difference or gradient estimation using the 4x4x4 data pass Parameters: SDF Neighborhood Size: 4 \times 4 \times 4 values per voxel. Threshold: The SDF value defining the surface (typically 0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overhead: SVS has a "much more significant memory overhead" compared to other methods due to the storage of 4 \times 4 \times 4 SDF values per voxel and the BVH structure itself. Complexity: While simpler to construct than Sparse Voxel Octrees, the memory cost is a primary limitation. Performance: SVS outperformed other methods (grid sphere tracing, sparse brick set, sparse voxel octree) in general scenarios. Hardware Dependency: Performance relies heavily on the efficiency of the GPU's RTX ray-tracing hardware. Shader Workload: Requires less work in the custom software intersection shader compared to software-based traversal methods because the BVH traversal is handled by hardware. Memory: High memory usage due to the 4 \times 4 \times 4 SDF storage per voxel and BVH overhead. Construction: Simpler and faster to construct than Sparse Voxel Octrees. Scene Suitability: Effective in general scenes; however, cache coherency in complex scenes might favor other methods like Sparse Brick Set if hardware acceleration is not fully utilized or if memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Origin: The method is described in the context of real-time rendering of Signed Distance Fields, leveraging DirectX Raytracing (DXR) hardware. Development: It is presented as an alternative to software-based SDF traversal techniques such as Grid Sphere Tracing (similar to Claybook [Aaltonen 2018]) and Sparse Brick Set (SBS). Usage: Used for real-time rendering of SDF-based geometry, particularly where high performance is required and GPU ray-tracing hardware is available. name: GPU-based Ray Shooting for Volumetric Mapping
head: GPU-Accelerated Ray Shooting for Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping, GPU-based ray shooting, RTX-based ray shooting
body: This method accelerates the ray-shooting bottleneck in Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping (PVM) by mapping leaf-level octree voxels to Axis-Aligned Bounding Boxes (AABBs) and performing massively parallel ray shooting on an RTX GPU using the DirectX Raytracing (DXR) API. It replaces the CPU-based DDA ray-shooting procedure used in standard Octomap, which typically consumes ~90% of processing time. Unlike Voxel Ray Marching with BVH Acceleration, which uses BVH for lighting and AO calculations in a compute shader, this method uses the dedicated DXR ray-tracing pipeline to determine voxel occupancy (free/occupied) by intersecting rays with a BVH of AABBs. Inputs: sensorOrigin: 3D vector representing the camera/sensor position. rayDirections: Array of 3D vectors or point cloud positions defining ray endpoints. octree: The current probabilistic volumetric map on the CPU, containing leaf-level voxels labeled as occupied, free, or unknown. Outputs: intersectedVoxels: A set of finest-resolution voxels labeled as occupied or free, which are read back to the CPU to update the octree. Data Structures: 1. AABB Set: Each leaf-level voxel in the octree is converted to an individual AABB. The AABB geometry (position and size) matches the voxel exactly. Unknown Voxels: Voxels labeled "unknown" are also converted to AABBs. This ensures the AABBs fill the entire 3D workspace, preventing rays from passing through unrepresented space without intersection. 2. BVH (Bounding Volume Hierarchy): Built on the GPU from the AABB set. Bottom Level Acceleration Structure (BLAS): Contains the geometric primitives (the AABBs). Top Level Acceleration Structure (TLAS): Contains transformation matrices and rendering materials (standard DXR requirement, though materials are unused in this specific logic). Parameters: Finest Resolution Subdivision: When an AABB larger than the finest resolution is intersected, it is subdivided into typically 16 finest-resolution voxels using DDA. Ray Count: Proportional to the point cloud size. In benchmarks, 320×240 rays (76,800 rays) were used per view. Octree Depth: Maximum depth of 16 in benchmarks, corresponding to 25K–34K leaf-level voxels. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (CPU): Scan the environment to generate a point cloud. Convert all leaf-level voxels (occupied, free, unknown) from the octree into individual AABBs. 2. Upload and Build (GPU): Upload the set of AABBs to the GPU. The RTX GPU builds the BVH of these AABBs. 3. Ray Generation (GPU): In the Ray Generation Shader, set up rays. Each ray starts at sensorOrigin and ends at a point in the point cloud. The ray length is set to the distance from the sensor origin to the point cloud point. 4. Ray Shooting (GPU): Execute massively parallel ray shooting. Rays traverse the BVH. If a ray hits an AABB within its extent, the Intersection Shader is executed. If the intersected AABB size is greater than the finest resolution voxel size, subdivide the subspace traversed by the ray into finest resolution voxels (typically 16) using DDA. For all newly generated finest resolution voxels: If the voxel includes the ray's end point, set it as occupied. Else if the ray passed through the voxel, set it as free. If ray-AABB intersection no longer occurs, the Miss Shader is executed to terminate the ray shooting (the Closest Hit Shader is not used). 5. Readback (GPU to CPU): Read back the intersected voxel data from the GPU to the CPU. 6. Update (CPU): Update the octree with the new occupancy information. Merge leaf-level nodes with the same occupancy and promote them to higher-level nodes using Octomap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. blas = BuildBLAS(aabblist) tlas = BuildTLAS(blas, identitymatrices) for each point in pointcloud: rayorigin = sensorOrigin raydirection = normalize(point - sensorOrigin) raylength = length(point - sensorOrigin) # 3. BVH Traversal hit = False currentaabb = None # Traverse BVH to find first intersecting AABB # (Implementation details of DXR traversal abstracted) if RayIntersectsBVH(rayorigin, raydirection, raylength, tlas): hit = True # Identify the specific AABB hit currentaabb = GetHitAABB() # 4. Intersection Shader Logic if currentaabb.size > finestresolutionsize: # Subdivide AABB into finest resolution voxels using DDA finestvoxels = SubdivideAABB(currentaabb, rayorigin, raydirection, raylength) for voxel in finestvoxels: if voxel.contains(rayendpoint): voxel.label = OCCUPIED else: voxel.label = FREE else: # AABB is already at finest resolution if currentaabb.contains(rayendpoint): currentaabb.label = OCCUPIED else: currentaabb.label = FREE intersecteddata = ReadBackGPUBuffer() octree = LoadOctomap() for voxel in intersecteddata: octree.updatevoxel(voxel.position, voxel.label) octree.restructure() # Merge and promote nodes Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unknown Space Handling: Rays can pass anywhere in the space. If unknown voxels are not converted to AABBs, rays may pass through unrepresented subspace without being labeled. Including unknown voxels as AABBs ensures all traversed subspace is labeled. Readback Bottleneck: Reading back voxel data from GPU to CPU takes significantly longer than the ray shooting itself (e.g., 14.19 ms readback vs 1.42 ms shooting in View a). This creates a bottleneck. The method suggests updating the octree on the GPU to mitigate this, but the described implementation performs this on the CPU. Precision: The method relies on the DXR API's ray-tracing precision. No specific numerical precision constraints are given in the sources. Time Complexity: The ray shooting performance is more than three orders of magnitude faster than the state-of-the-art Octomap CPU implementation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the BVH (BLAS and TLAS) on the GPU. The size depends on the number of leaf-level voxels (25K–34K in benchmarks). Measured Performance: Hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 3700X CPU, NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU, 16GB RAM, Windows 10, DirectX DXR. Benchmark: 77K points, 25K–34K adaptive voxel grids. View (a) Stats: 25,515 voxels. CPU Ray Shooting: 886.83 ms. GPU Ray Shooting: 1.42 ms. BVH Build: 0.59 ms. Readback: 14.19 ms. With readback included, the GPU method is still two orders of magnitude faster than the CPU version. Strengths: Drastic improvement in ray shooting speed, enabling real-time or near-real-time PVM for autonomous robotics. Limitations: The octree is not maintained on the GPU; readback from GPU to CPU is a significant bottleneck (10x the shooting time). When to use: Autonomous robotic navigational tasks requiring Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping where ray shooting is the bottleneck. When not to use: When GPU memory is insufficient for the BVH, or when the overhead of readback dominates the workflow and GPU-based octree maintenance is not implemented. Probabilistic Volumetric Mapping (PVM) represents a 3D environmental map for autonomous robotic navigational tasks. Octomap is a popular implementation using an octree structure. The main bottleneck in Octomap is the massive ray-shooting required to determine voxel occupancy, which takes up about 90% of processing time. This method was proposed by Heajung Min, Kyung Min Han, and Young J. Kim to leverage RTX GPUs and the DXR API to accelerate this process. The work was presented at ICRA 2021. name: GPU BVH Construction via Cluster Merging
head: Cluster Merging BVH, GPU-based BVH Construction via Cluster Merging, VoxelFragmentML BVH Build
body: This method constructs a Binary Volume Hierarchy (BVH) on the GPU by iteratively merging clusters of triangles. It solves the problem of building hierarchical acceleration structures for ray tracing without CPU-GPU synchronization bottlenecks by using a fully parallel, double-buffered approach involving neighbor finding, prefix scans, and reallocation. It differs from CPU-based top-down or bottom-up builders by keeping all data on the GPU and using a "merge-compact" loop that reduces the number of active clusters by half (approximately) each iteration until a single root remains. Input: A set of static triangles defined by their geometry. The number of input triangles is N. Output: A BVH stored in a GPU buffer (clusterSSBO) containing 2N - 1 nodes (clusters). The final readback size is explicitly staticData.\numTriangles \times 2 - 1. BVHCluster The fundamental unit of the BVH. On the CPU, it is defined as Model3D::BVHCluster. On the GPU, it resides in a Shader Storage Buffer Object (SSBO). The exact internal fields are not specified in the source, but it represents a cluster of triangles with a bounding volume. Current Position Buffers Two CPU-side arrays of type GLuint (unsigned 32-bit integers), currentPosBuffer and currentPosBufferOut, each of size arraySize (initially N). currentPosBufferOut is initialized with sequential integers: currentPosBufferOut[i] = i for 0 \le i < arraySize. These buffers track the compacted position of valid clusters during the merge process. GPU Buffers (SSBOs) cinBuffer: Read-only cluster data for the current iteration. coutBuffer: Write-only cluster data for the next iteration (double-buffered with cinBuffer). inCurrentPosition: Read-only position data for the current iteration. outCurrentPosition: Write-only position data for the next iteration (double-buffered with inCurrentPosition). neighborIndex: Stores the index of the nearest neighbor for each cluster. prefixScan: Temporary buffer for the parallel prefix scan (reduction and up-sweep/down-sweep). validCluster: Boolean or integer flag indicating if a cluster was merged or remains valid. mergedCluster: Buffer storing details of merged clusters. numNodesCount: Buffer to store the count of remaining nodes after an iteration. arraySizeCount: Buffer to store the updated arraySize for the loop condition. clusterSSBO: The final BVH storage, sized for N \times 2 - 1 clusters. tempClusterSSBO: Temporary cluster storage, sized for arraySize. sortedFaces: Sorted triangle indices (output of Morton sort). gpuData->tempClusterSSBO: Temporary cluster data. The construction consists of three main phases: Morton Code Sorting, Cluster Building, and Iterative Merging. Triangles are sorted by Morton code to improve spatial locality before clustering. 1. Parameters: numBits = 30 (10 bits per coordinate for 3D Morton codes). 2. Loop: Iterate currentBits from 0 to numBits - 1. 3. Bit Mask: Execute bitMaskShader on mortonCodes and indicesBufferID1. This splits indices into pBitsBufferID (bit=1) and nBitsBufferID (bit=0). 4. Reduce: Perform a prefix scan on nBitsBufferID to count the number of zeros (bit=0). 5. Reset: Execute resetPositionShader on nBitsBufferID with 1 group to set the last position to zero. 6. Down Sweep: Execute downSweepShader to compute final positions for the zeros. 7. Reallocate: Execute reallocatePositionShader to reorder indicesBufferID1 into indicesBufferID2 based on the computed positions. 1. Execution: Execute buildClusterShader with buffers { staticData.groupTopologySSBO, sortedFaces, staticData->clusterSSBO, gpuData->tempClusterSSBO }. 2. Uniforms: Set arraySize to the number of triangles. 3. Groups: Execute with numGroups groups. 4. Result: Initial leaf clusters are created in tempClusterSSBO (or clusterSSBO depending on implementation flow, but notes specify tempClusterSSBO as input to build, and clusterSSBO as final output). Note: The notes state buildClusterBuffer creates clusterData of size N \times 2 - 1 and sets up clusterSSBO (write) and tempClusterSSBO (write). The core loop reduces the number of clusters until one root remains. Initialization: 1. Calculate arraySize = number of triangles N. 2. Create input buffer outCluster (CPU side). 3. Initialize currentPosBufferOut with std::iota(..., 0). 4. Set up SSBOs: cinBuffer, coutBuffer, inCurrentPosition, outCurrentPosition, neighborIndex, prefixScan, validCluster, mergedCluster, numNodesCount, arraySizeCount. Main Loop: While arraySize > 1: 1. Buffer Swapping: Swap coutBuffer and cinBuffer. Swap outCurrentPosition and inCurrentPosition. This double-buffers the cluster and position data to allow parallel reads and writes. 2. Group Size Calculation: numGroups = ComputeShader::getNumGroups(arraySize). startThreads = std::ceil(arraySize / 2.0f). numExec = std::ceil(std::log2(arraySize)). numGroups2Log = ComputeShader::getNumGroups(startThreads). 3. Neighbor Finding: Execute findNeighborShader with buffers { cinBuffer, neighborIndex }. Uniforms: arraySize, radius (search radius for nearest neighbor clusters). Execution: numGroups groups. 4. Cluster Merging: Execute clusterMergingShader with buffers { cinBuffer, staticData.clusterSSBO, neighborIndex, validCluster, mergedCluster, prefixScan, inCurrentPosition, numNodesCount }. Uniform: arraySize. Execution: numGroups groups. This step merges clusters based on neighbors, writes valid/merged status, and updates prefix scan data. 5. Prefix Scan - Reduce Phase (First Step): Build a binary tree summatory on prefixScan. Initialize iteration = 0. Loop while (iteration < numExec): Get numThreads = threadCount[threadCount.size() - 1]. Set uniforms iteration and numThreads. Execute reduceShader with numGroups2Log groups. Push std::ceil(numThreads / 2.0f) to threadCount. 6. Prefix Scan - Reset Last Position (Second Step): Execute resetPositionShader on prefixScan with 1 group to set the last position to zero. Note: This is faster than CPU modification. 7. Prefix Scan - Down Sweep Phase (Third Step): Build tree back to first level and compute final summatory on prefixScan. Initialize iteration = threadCount.size() - 2. Loop while (iteration >= 0 && iteration < numExec): Set uniforms iteration and numThreads = threadCount[iteration]. Execute downSweepShader with numGroups2Log groups. Decrement iteration. 8. Reallocation: Execute reallocClustersShader with buffers { cinBuffer, coutBuffer, validCluster, prefixScan, inCurrentPosition, outCurrentPosition }. Uniform: arraySize. Execution: numGroups groups. This compacts the valid clusters into the output buffer (coutBuffer). 9. Update Cluster Size: Execute endLoopCompShader with buffers { arraySizeCount, prefixScan, validCluster }. Uniform: arraySize. Execution: 1 group. Read back the new arraySize from arraySizeCount. Final Readback: 1. After the loop, read the final BVH cluster data from staticData.clusterSSBO into a CPU vector. 2. The size is staticData.numTriangles 2 - 1. Cleanup: 1. Delete GPU buffers: coutBuffer, cinBuffer, inCurrentPosition, outCurrentPosition, neighborIndex, prefixScan, validCluster, mergedCluster, numNodesCount, arraySizeCount. 2. Delete CPU memory: outCluster, currentPosBuffer, currentPosBufferOut, volatileGPUData. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpubvhclustermerging(triangles): """ Constructs a BVH on the GPU using cluster merging. triangles: List of triangle objects with geometry. Returns: BVH clusters as a list of BVHCluster objects. """ N = len(triangles) arraysize = N # Phase 1: Morton Code Sort mortoncodes = computemortoncodes(triangles) indices = list(range(N)) # 30-bit radix sort (10 bits per coordinate) numbits = 30 for currentbits in range(numbits): # 1. Bit Mask pbitsindices = [] nbitsindices = [] for idx in indices: if (mortoncodes[idx] >> currentbits) & 1: pbitsindices.append(idx) else: nbitsindices.append(idx) # 2. Reduce: Count zeros (nbits) # In GPU: prefixscan(nbitsindices) # Here we simulate the count logic for position calculation ncount = len(nbitsindices) # 3. Reset Last Position (GPU optimization, simulated here by logic) # 4. Down Sweep: Compute positions # Positions for nbits (0s) are 0 to ncount-1 # Positions for pbits (1s) are ncount to N-1 # 5. Reallocate newindices = [None] N nidx = 0 pidx = 0 for idx in indices: if (mortoncodes[idx] >> currentbits) & 1: newindices[ncount + pidx] = idx pidx += 1 else: newindices[nidx] = idx nidx += 1 indices = newindices # Phase 2: Build Initial Clusters # Execute buildClusterShader # Input: sorted triangles (indices), Output: initial clusters in temp buffer clusters = buildinitialclusters(triangles, indices) # Phase 3: Iterative Merging # Buffers setup cinbuffer = clusters coutbuffer = [None] (2 N) # Pre-allocate max size inpos = list(range(N)) outpos = [None] (2 N) # Initialize outpos with sequential integers for the initial arraysize for i in range(arraysize): outpos[i] = i neighborindex = [0] arraysize prefixscan = [0] (2 N) validcluster = [True] arraysize mergedcluster = [None] (2 N) while arraysize > 1: # Buffer Swapping cinbuffer, coutbuffer = coutbuffer, cinbuffer inpos, outpos = outpos, inpos # Group Size Calculation numgroups = getnumgroups(arraysize) startthreads = ceil(arraysize / 2.0) numexec = ceil(log2(arraysize)) numgroups2log = getnumgroups(startthreads) # Neighbor Finding radius = 1.0 # Typical value, source does not specify exact default findneighbor(cinbuffer, neighborindex, arraysize, radius) # Cluster Merging clustermerging(cinbuffer, neighborindex, validcluster, mergedcluster, prefixscan, inpos, numgroups) # Prefix Scan - Reduce Phase threadcount = [] iteration = 0 while iteration < numexec: numthreads = threadcount[-1] if threadcount else arraysize reduceshader(prefixscan, iteration, numthreads, numgroups2log) threadcount.append(ceil(numthreads / 2.0)) iteration += 1 # Prefix Scan - Reset Last Position resetpositionshader(prefixscan, 1) # Prefix Scan - Down Sweep Phase iteration = len(threadcount) - 2 while iteration >= 0 and iteration < numexec: numthreads = threadcount[iteration] downsweepshader(prefixscan, iteration, numthreads, numgroups2log) iteration -= 1 # Reallocation reallocclusters(cinbuffer, coutbuffer, validcluster, prefixscan, inpos, outpos, arraysize) # Update Cluster Size newarraysize = endloopcomp(prefixscan, validcluster, arraysize) arraysize = newarraysize # Final Readback finalbvh = readback(cinbuffer, N) return finalbvh radius: The search radius for finding nearest neighbor clusters during the merging phase. Passed as a uniform to findNeighborShader. numBits: The number of bits for the radix sort, set to 30 (10 bits per coordinate for 3D Morton codes). Precision: The use of double for AABB calculations (dAABBCC, dvec3) suggests high precision is required for bounding volume operations. Boundary Conditions: The loop condition arraySize > 1 ensures the process stops at a single root. The prefix scan reset step is critical for correctness in the down-sweep phase. Degenerate Input: If arraySize is 0 or 1, the loop does not execute, and the final readback handles the base case. The source does not specify behavior for empty inputs beyond the loop condition. Time Complexity: The merging loop runs O(\log N) iterations, as the number of clusters is roughly halved each time. Each iteration involves neighbor finding (O(N)), merging (O(N)), and prefix scans (O(N)). Thus, the total time complexity is O(N \log N). Memory Complexity: The algorithm uses double-buffering for clusters and positions, requiring O(N) space for buffers. The final BVH requires 2N - 1 nodes. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method is designed for GPU parallelism, using compute shaders and SSBOs. It scales with the number of GPU threads and memory bandwidth. Strengths: Fully GPU-based, no CPU-GPU synchronization during construction, parallel neighbor finding and merging. Limitations: Requires significant GPU memory for double-buffering and temporary buffers. The neighbor finding step may be expensive for large scenes if the radius is large. When to Use: When building BVHs for static triangle meshes on the GPU is required, especially in contexts where CPU-GPU transfer overhead is prohibitive. When Not to Use: For dynamic scenes where frequent rebuilds are needed, or when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Origin: The method is described in the VoxelFragmentML project by AlfonsoLRz. History: The specific implementation details are from the VoxelFragmentML repository, which appears to be an unofficial or experimental project. Usage: Used in the VoxelFragmentML project for GPU-based BVH construction. AlfonsoLRz/VoxelFragmentML, https://github.com/AlfonsoLRz/VoxelFragmentML, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Initial Upper Bound Estimation
head: Heuristic Sampling for BVH Pruning
body: Initial Upper Bound Estimation computes a tight initial upper bound to prune BVH-tree traversal during distance field computation for isosurface approximation. It differs from standard hierarchical traversal by proactively sampling the approximated surface to establish a pruning threshold before traversal begins, rather than waiting for the first leaf encounter. This allows for more aggressive pruning at the beginning of the traversal, reducing the total number of nodes visited. Inputs: A Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) tree representing the voxel grid or surface approximation. A target isosurface to approximate. A sample count N. Outputs: An initial upper bound value U{init} used to prune BVH traversal. Data Structures: The BVH tree structure is assumed to be standard (nodes containing bounding volumes and children). A set of sample points P = \{p1, p2,..., pN\} representing locations on the approximated surface. Steps: 1. Sample Surface Points: Generate N evenly distributed points on the approximated isosurface. 2. Compute Initial Upper Bound: Calculate the upper bound U{init} based on the distances or spatial extents of the sampled points relative to the BVH structure. The specific geometric formula for deriving the bound from the points is not explicitly detailed in the source, but it serves as a threshold for pruning. 3. Prune Traversal: Use U{init} during the BVH traversal. If N=0 (no samples), the traversal proceeds without this heuristic, examining nodes until the first leaf is reached. 4. Evaluate Performance: As N increases, the estimation time rises linearly, while traversal time decreases rapidly then plateaus. Parameters: Number of sample points (N): Recommended range is 1000 to 1500 for reasonable-sized datasets. A value of 1500 was selected in the evaluation to yield swift traversal across all datasets. Pitfalls: High Point Count Variables: For variables with high point counts and even spatial distribution (e.g., CHI, vorticity), increasing samples beyond 1500 causes rapid runtime increases due to convergence toward brute-force, outweighing traversal gains. Zero Samples: Without samples, traversal takes the longest time as the tree must be examined until the first leaf is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeinitialupperbound(bvhtree, isosurface, numsamples): """ Computes an initial upper bound for BVH traversal pruning. Args: bvhtree: The BVH tree structure. isosurface: The approximated isosurface geometry. numsamples: Number of points to sample (1000-1500 recommended). Returns: float: The initial upper bound value. """ if numsamples == 0: # No initial bound; traversal will proceed until first leaf return None # Step 1: Sample a fixed number of points from the approximated surface # The source specifies "evenly sampled points" but does not provide the # specific sampling algorithm for the isosurface. samplepoints = evenlysamplesurface(isosurface, numsamples) # Step 2: Compute an initial upper bound from these points # The source states the bound is computed from the points but does not # provide the exact formula. It implies a calculation based on spatial # distribution or distance metrics. initialupperbound = calculateboundfromsamples(samplepoints) return initialupperbound def evenlysamplesurface(surface, count): """ Placeholder for surface sampling logic. The source mentions "evenly sampled points" but does not define the mathematical method for generating them from the isosurface. """ # Implementation depends on the specific isosurface representation. # Common approaches include uniform sampling on parametric domains # or stratified sampling. pass def calculateboundfromsamples(points): """ Placeholder for bound calculation. The source states the bound is computed from the points to enable pruning, but the exact aggregation function (e.g., max distance, bounding box expansion) is not specified. """ # Implementation depends on the specific pruning metric used in the BVH. pass This method computes a distance field for an isosurface approximation by finding the closest point of the isosurface for every voxel in the volume using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) tree. It differs from existing approaches by initializing the upper bound before traversal using evenly sampled points, rather than waiting for the first leaf encounter, which allows for more aggressive pruning at the beginning of the traversal. Time Complexity: Estimation time increases linearly with the sample count N. Traversal time decreases rapidly as N increases from 0, then slowly approaches a minimum. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Most datasets reach minimum traversal time between 2000 and 2300 points, fluctuating by 1 ms. For variables with high point counts (CHI, vorticity), minimums are reached earlier (1200 and 1500 points respectively). Beyond these minima, running times increase rapidly (e.g., CHI: 94.58 to 380.36; vorticity: 69.25 to 248.82). Strengths: Performance gained by using a tighter upper bound usually outweighs the costs during traversal for less than 1500 sample points. Limitations: For variables with high point counts and even spatial distribution, increasing samples beyond 1500 leads to rapid runtime increases due to convergence toward brute-force. When to Use: Use when BVH traversal for distance field computation is a bottleneck and the dataset is of reasonable size. A sample count between 1000 and 1500 is generally preferable. When Not to Use: Avoid for variables with very high point counts and even spatial distribution if sample counts exceed 1500, as the cost of estimation and convergence to brute-force outweighs traversal gains. Origin: The method is described in the context of efficient GPU-accelerated computation of isosurface similarity maps. History: The approach was evaluated to demonstrate the quality of isosurface similarity maps, following the work of Bruckner and Möller. Usage: Used in the computation of distance fields for isosurface approximation within scientific visualization, specifically for combustion, hurricane, and ionization datasets. name: BVH-Based Distance Field Computation with Heuristic Initialization
head: BVH Distance Field Computation, Heuristic BVH Traversal for Distance Fields
body: This method computes a distance field for an isosurface approximation by finding the closest point of the isosurface for every voxel in the volume using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) tree. It differs from existing approaches by initializing the upper bound before traversal using evenly sampled points, rather than waiting for the first leaf encounter, which allows for more aggressive pruning at the beginning of the traversal. Inputs: An array of points approximating the isosurface. The voxel grid for which the distance field is computed. Outputs: A distance field volume where each voxel contains the distance from its center to the isosurface. Data Structures: BVH Tree: A binary tree where each internal node consists of a bounding box including all descendants. A leaf consists of a single primitive (a single point). Stack: Used for depth-first traversal. Parameters: Downscaling: The resulting distance field is downscaled to decimate the search space. Construction Algorithm: Karras’s algorithm is used to build BVH-trees in parallel. Bounding Volume: Bounding boxes are used for lower construction time. Formulas: Distance to internal node n: d(v, n) is the minimum distance from voxel v to the bounding box of n. Distance to leaf node n: d(v, n) is the distance between voxel v and the corresponding point of n. Steps: 1. Heuristic Initialization: Estimate the upper bound before traversal. Compute the distance from the voxel v to a set of sample points P evenly sampled from the approximating points array (which is in scanline order). Calculate the initial upper bound du = \min{p \in P} d(v, p). 2. Stack Initialization: Add the root of the BVH tree to a stack. 3. Traversal Loop: Pop the first node n from the stack. If n is an internal node: For each child node nc, compute d(v, nc). If d(v, nc) < du, push nc onto the stack. If n is a leaf: Compute d(v, n) between v and n. Update du with \min(du, d(v, n)). 4. Termination: Repeat Step 3 until the stack becomes empty. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedistancefield(voxelcenters, isosurfacepoints): # Build BVH using Karras's algorithm bvhroot = buildbvhparallel(isosurfacepoints) # Downscale voxel grid to decimate search space voxelcenters = downscale(voxelcenters) # Pre-compute evenly sampled points for heuristic initialization # Points are in scanline order samplepoints = evenlysample(isosurfacepoints, count=100) # count is arbitrary, needs tuning distancefield = emptyvolumelike(voxelcenters) for v in voxelcenters: # Step 1: Heuristic Initialization du = infinity for p in samplepoints: dist = distance(v, p) if dist < du: du = dist # Step 2: Stack Initialization stack = [bvhroot] # Step 3 & 4: Traversal Loop while stack is not empty: n = stack.pop() if n is internalnode: for child in n.children: dist = distancetobbox(v, child.bbox) if dist < du: stack.push(child) else: # n is leaf dist = distance(v, n.point) if dist < du: du = dist distancefield[v] = du return distancefield def distance(v, p): return length(v - p) def distancetobbox(v, bbox): # Minimum distance from point v to axis-aligned bounding box # Standard AABB distance calculation distsq = 0 for i in 0 to 2: if v[i] < bbox.min[i]: distsq += (bbox.min[i] - v[i])^2 elif v[i] > bbox.max[i]: distsq += (v[i] - bbox.max[i])^2 return sqrt(distsq) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision may affect distance calculations, especially for voxels very close to the surface. Boundaries: Voxels far from the isosurface may have large initial upper bounds, reducing pruning efficiency. Degenerate Input: If the isosurface approximation is empty, the BVH will be empty, and the distance field will remain at infinity or a default value. A heuristic sampling process that computes a tight initial upper bound to prune BVH-tree traversal during distance field computation. Builds on Initial Upper Bound Estimation. Time Complexity: Depends on the BVH traversal depth and the number of pruned nodes. Heuristic initialization improves pruning efficiency, especially at the beginning of traversal. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the BVH tree and the distance field volume. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Parallelized using CUDA threads, one per voxel. Strengths: Efficient pruning due to heuristic initialization; parallel construction and traversal. Limitations: Requires building a BVH for every isosurface approximation; bounding boxes may not be optimal for all shapes. When to Use: When computing distance fields for isosurface approximations on GPU. When Not to Use: When the isosurface approximation is very small or when memory is constrained. Origin: The method is described in "Efficient GPU-Accelerated Computation of Isosurface...". History and Development: The approach leverages BVH trees for accelerating closest point searches, a common technique in computer graphics. The specific heuristic initialization is a novel contribution to improve pruning efficiency. Usage: Used in similarity map generation by computing mutual information of corresponding distance fields. name: Octree-based Volume Rendering
head: Chamberlain's algorithm, LaMar's algorithm, Octal tree structure for volume rendering, Octree Approach (Baseline), Octree on a GPU, Octree-based Volume Rendering with Adaptive Sampling, Weiler's smoothing
body: Octree-based volume rendering accelerates the visualization of volumetric datasets by using a hierarchical octree structure to skip invisible voxels and reduce sampling in uniform areas. It solves the problem that only a small percentage of voxels contribute to the final image, while the rest remain invisible. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Hierarchical Traversal and Residency Octree Traversal, by its specific use of a one-to-one mapping of bricks to octree nodes for culling and spatial subdivision, often relying on CPU-side or unified memory traversal logic rather than specialized GPU residency caches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (scalar field), a transfer function mapping scalar values to RGBA, and camera parameters (position, orientation, field of view). Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Octree: A hierarchical tree where each parent node contains 0 or 8 children, achieving a 2x2x2 regular subdivision of the parent node into 8 equal parts or 'leaves' [Parent]. Node Metadata: Each node stores a visibilityratio, defined as the ratio of visible data to the total amount of data in the cube. At the leaf level, a node represents one cell that is either completely filled or empty. For higher levels, visibilityratio is calculated by averaging the ratios of its 8 children. Empty Cell Condition: A cell is considered completely empty only if its eight angular (corner) values are completely transparent after applying the transfer function. Parameters: Adaptive Sampling Threshold: A predefined threshold for projected size or angular difference to trigger additional sampling points. LaMar's FOV Threshold: Nodes are selected if their projected angle is less than half the field-of-view angle. Early Stopping (PlenOctree variant): Accumulated transmittance Ti < \gamma = 0.01. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Perform octree subdivision of the volumetric data. Calculate the visibilityratio for each node. This calculation depends on the transfer function and must be recalculated if the transfer function changes. For multi-channel rendering, this preprocessing is performed per channel or requires ensuring all required subtrees remain cache resident. 2. Traversal Initialization: Start traversal at the third level of the octree (or from the parent node of the last visited sample's node) to optimize performance. For each ray, determine intersections with the octree structure. 3. Node Selection and Culling: Chamberlain's Criterion: Compute the projected size of each octree node on the fly. If the size is smaller than a predefined threshold, consider the node sufficiently accurate to approximate all nodes below it. LaMar's Criterion: Use two criteria: distance (similar to Chamberlain) and field-of-view. Discard nodes that do not intersect the view frustum. Select nodes whose projected angle is less than half the field-of-view angle. Empty Space Skipping: If a node's visibilityratio indicates it is empty (all corners transparent), skip the node entirely. 4. Adaptive Sampling: Perform adaptive sampling along the ray segment within the node. Take a large step between selection points when the beam passes through uniform areas. If there is a large difference in values between two neighboring selection points, select an additional point between them. This reduces sample size in areas where opacity makes a small contribution or where the volume is uniform. 5. Rendering and Blending: Trilinear Interpolation: Define a cell as a cube whose eight corners are adjacent to voxel values. The intensity value for each position inside the cell is defined as a trilinear interpolation of angular values. Sorting: During traversal, sort children of a node in front-to-back order. Rasterization: While a node is to be drawn, slice the cuboid box corresponding to this node. Rasterize the slices and blend them into the previously drawn slices. PlenOctree Variant: For each ray, produce a sequence of segments between voxel boundaries with constant density and color, of lengths \{\deltai\}. Apply NeRF's volume rendering model: C(r) = \sum{i=0}^{N} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) ci where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=0}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj). Early Stopping: Stop rendering when the accumulated transmittance Ti is less than \gamma = 0.01. 6. Smoothing (Optional): Apply an extension (Weiler's smoothing) to smooth discontinuity artifacts at LOD boundaries caused by inconsistencies of the view-plane at different levels of detail. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderoctreevolume(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot, transferfunction, camera): # Traversal initialization: start at third level or cached parent currentnode = getcachedparentnode(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot) or octreeroot accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 nodestack = [currentnode] while nodestack: node = nodestack.pop() # 1. Frustum and Ray Intersection if not intersectsfrustum(node, camera) or not intersectsray(node, rayorigin, raydirection): continue # 2. Empty Space Skipping if isempty(node, transferfunction): continue # 3. Selection Criteria projectedsize = computeprojectedsize(node, camera) if projectedsize > camera.threshold: # Node too large: push children sorted front-to-back children = getchildren(node) children.sortbydepth(rayorigin, raydirection) nodestack.extend(children) continue # 4. Adaptive Sampling & Rendering step = computelargestep(node) t = node.mint prevvalue = None while t <= node.maxt: pos = rayorigin + raydirection t value = samplevoxel(pos, node) rgba = transferfunction(value) if rgba.a > 0: accumulatedcolor[0] += rgba.r rgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedcolor[1] += rgba.g rgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedcolor[2] += rgba.b rgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - rgba.a) # Adaptive refinement: check difference with previous sample if prevvalue is not None and abs(value - prevvalue) > thresholddiff: midt = t - step / 2.0 midpos = rayorigin + raydirection midt midvalue = samplevoxel(midpos, node) midrgba = transferfunction(midvalue) if midrgba.a > 0: accumulatedcolor[0] += midrgba.r midrgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedcolor[1] += midrgba.g midrgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedcolor[2] += midrgba.b midrgba.a accumulatedtransmittance accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - midrgba.a) prevvalue = value t += step # Early stopping if accumulatedtransmittance < 0.01: break return accumulatedcolor def isempty(node, transferfunction): # A cell is completely empty only if its eight angular values are completely transparent corners = getnodecorners(node) for corner in corners: value = samplevoxel(corner, node) if transferfunction(value).a > 0: return False return True def trilinearinterpolate(cellcorners, pos): # cellcorners: list of 8 scalar values at cube corners # pos: local position [0,1]^3 inside cell x, y, z = pos c000, c100, c010, c110, c001, c101, c011, c111 = cellcorners i0 = c000 (1-x) + c100 x i1 = c010 (1-x) + c110 x i2 = c001 (1-x) + c101 x i3 = c011 (1-x) + c111 x j0 = i0 (1-y) + i1 y j1 = i2 (1-y) + i3 y return j0 (1-z) + j1 z def computelargestep(node): # Step size proportional to node spatial extent along ray return node.extentalongray / 4.0 def getcachedparentnode(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot): # Returns parent of last visited node or third level root return octreeroot.children[0] if hasattr(octreeroot, 'children') else octreeroot def computeprojectedsize(node, camera): # Project node bounding box to screen space return node.screenarea def intersectsfrustum(node, camera): return camera.frustum.intersects(node.bbox) def intersectsray(node, rayorigin, raydirection): return node.bbox.intersectsray(rayorigin, raydirection) def getchildren(node): return node.children if hasattr(node, 'children') else [] def samplevoxel(pos, node): # Fetch scalar value at pos, using trilinear interpolation if inside a cell if node.isleaf: return node.data[pos] return trilinearinterpolate(node.corners, node.localpos(pos)) def getnodecorners(node): return node.corners if hasattr(node, 'corners') else [0.0]8 Combines an octree for spatial subdivision with 3D non-standard Haar wavelets in leaf nodes. Distinguished by enabling incremental loading and frustum-clipping-based memory management for large-scale datasets on distributed clusters. Renders cloud surfaces using opacities \rho(X)\sigmat and voxel colors I0(X) with view-dependent octree cubes based on projected area-weighted approximation errors. Distinguished by its use of least-squares approximations and hardware cell-projection compositing. Converts a trained NeRF-SH model into a sparse octree representation for real-time rendering. Uses NeRF's volume rendering model with early stopping at transmittance < 0.01. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the octree and the sparsity of the data. In sparse volumes, it achieves significant speedups by skipping empty space. In dense volumes, the overhead of tree traversal may not be compensated by empty space skipping. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the octree structure in main memory or cache. For multi-channel rendering, entire subtrees must be resident in cache, leading to higher memory overhead (overhead ratio 1/3 for anisotropic volumes vs 1/7 for others). Measured Performance: On an Intel Core 2 CPU E8400 3.0 GHz and GeForce 8800 GTX with 512^3 scenes, the optimized version achieved 80 frames per second compared to 9 frames per second for the non-optimized version. Strengths: Eliminates rasterization as a bottleneck by skipping invisible data; effective for sparse datasets. Limitations: Substantial visual artifacts at LOD boundaries due to view-plane inconsistencies; inability to reduce volumetric data size in main memory limits rendering of datasets larger than available memory; high computational cost and memory footprint in multi-channel scenarios due to per-channel tree traversal. When to use: Sparse volumetric data where empty space skipping provides significant gains; interactive applications requiring adaptive sampling. When not to use: Dense volumes where traversal overhead dominates; scenarios with limited main memory for large datasets. The octree spatial hierarchy was first proposed by Chamberlain et al. for rendering surface geometry, involving octree subdivision, recursive traversal, and on-the-fly projection size computation. LaMar et al. developed a similar technique with improved selection criteria (distance and field-of-view). Weiler et al. proposed extensions to smooth discontinuity artifacts at LOD boundaries. The method is widely used in GPU-accelerated volume rendering pipelines to optimize performance by leveraging spatial coherence and transfer function-based culling. name: Octree-based Volume Rendering with Wavelet Leaves
head: Octree space subdivision, Octree-wavelet format
body: This method renders volumetric data by combining an octree for spatial subdivision with a multi-resolution wavelet representation stored in leaf nodes. It solves the problem of rendering large-scale datasets (gigabytes) on distributed clusters with limited per-node texture memory by enabling early termination of traversal in empty space and progressive refinement of detail. It is distinguished from its sibling Octree-based Volume Rendering by the specific use of 3D non-standard Haar wavelets in leaves to support incremental loading and frustum-clipping-based memory management. Input: A volumetric dataset (e.g., CT/MRI scans) stored in an octree-wavelet format on disk; user interaction parameters (viewpoint, scale, rotation); a user-specified octree depth parameter. Output: A rendered image on a display node, progressively refined from low to high resolution. 1. Octree Structure Nodes: Internal nodes represent space subdivisions and leaf nodes contain the volume data. Empty Marking: Empty regions are marked during preprocessing to allow traversal skipping. Indexing Scheme: A fast indexing scheme uses file names to represent the octree traversal path, where numbers in the filename indicate the path (0-7) to the leaf node. 2. Brick Files (Leaf Storage) Format: 3D non-standard Haar wavelet decomposition. Layout: Data is organized for incremental loading. Start of File: Low-resolution information (highest wavelet compression). Subsequent Data: Detail coefficients for lower wavelet levels (higher resolution). Brick Size: Brick size is determined by the user-specified octree depth; deeper octrees result in more brick files, each smaller in size. 3. Fallback Texture Content: The entire dataset is loaded once at startup into the fallback texture. Storage: The fallback texture resides permanently in the graphics card’s texture memory. Detail Level: Its detail level is lower than the maximum detail achievable via clipping, chosen to maintain a predefined minimum frame rate. 1. Preprocessing: Construct the octree from the input volume and mark empty branches to enable early termination. Apply 3D non-standard Haar wavelet decomposition to leaf nodes. Organize leaf data in brick files by placing the lowest detail level (approximation coefficients) at the beginning, followed by detail coefficients in order of increasing resolution. Load the fallback texture (entire dataset at reduced detail) into GPU memory. 2. Rendering Loop (Per Frame): Check Interaction: If the user is transforming the volume (translation, rotation, scaling), switch rendering to the Fallback Texture to maintain interactivity. If Static (User Interaction Paused): 1. Frustum Clipping: Determine which parts of the scene each rendering node must display using the octree structure, disregarding parts outside the view frustum to save RAM and texture memory. 2. Traverse Octree: Use the fast file-name indexing scheme to traverse the octree to the relevant leaf nodes. 3. Skip Empty Branches: During traversal, skip branches marked as empty during preprocessing. 4. Incremental Loading: Load the lowest detail level data from the beginning of the brick file. Display the volume at this resolution. Triggered by a timer, sequentially load detail coefficients from the brick file to reconstruct higher resolution levels (i-1, i-2, \dots). 5. Progressive Refinement: Gradually refine the image up to the maximum level of detail each graphics card can display. Wavelet Reduction: The data reduction factor at wavelet level L is given by: \text{Reduction}L = \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^L L=1: 1/8th of the data remains. L=2: 1/64th of the data remains (less than 2%). Bit Depth and Levels: With 22 bits available for underflow/precision management, the algorithm can be applied 7 times before running out of bits. \left(\frac{1}{8}\right)^7 \approx 4.77 \times 10^{-7} For a typical dataset of 256^3 = 16,777,216 voxels, this reduces to 8 voxels. Parameters: Octree Depth: User-specified. Determines the size of octree bricks; deeper octrees yield more brick files of smaller size. Threshold: Used during preprocessing to determine if wavelet coefficients can be set to zero for compression. Quantization: Real numbers can be quantized (e.g., removing fraction parts), and low-frequency coefficients may be stored at higher precision than high-frequency ones. Frustum Clipping Performance: Frustum clipping involves time-consuming file operations to load new data chunks from disk, making it impossible to perform clipping at interactive rates during volume transformation. Solution to Clipping Latency: Use the fallback texture during transformation to maintain frame rate, switching back to incremental subvolume loading only when interaction pauses. Data Distribution: The method works best for datasets where the object is near the center of the data cube with an empty or nearly empty background (e.g., CT/MRI scans). Memory Constraints: Leaf data blocks may still be too large for the texture buffer depending on octree depth; the wavelet format allows determining a compression level to fit within GPU texture memory. Time Complexity: Traversal is "almost instantaneous" due to the file-name indexing scheme. Preprocessing time is lower than BSP trees. Memory Complexity: Significant savings in disk space and RAM are achieved by not storing empty areas. Per-node memory usage is limited by the texture buffer size, managed via wavelet compression levels. Performance: Octree traversal consistently outperforms Binary Space Partition (BSP) trees in both preprocessing and traversal time for typical CT/MRI datasets. Scalability: The method is designed for distributed display clusters (e.g., 25 nodes, 50 displays, 200 megapixels). Each node allocates resources only for its portion of the scene. Strengths: Early termination in empty space, progressive refinement for immediate visual feedback, and efficient memory usage via wavelet compression. Limitations: Frustum clipping is too slow for interactive transformation, preprocessing is required to build the octree and wavelet structure, and it is best suited for sparse data with empty backgrounds. Origin: Developed for large-scale multiresolution volume rendering on distributed display clusters. Hardware Context: Tested on a cluster of 25 PowerMac G5 computers with nVidia GeForce 6800 and Quadro FX4500 graphics cards, driving a 10x5 grid of 30-inch Apple Cinema Displays (2560x1600 resolution each). Comparison: Statistical analysis showed octree techniques outperform BSP trees for typical medical imaging datasets. Giga-Scale Multiresolution Volume Rendering on Distributed Display Clusters, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-19641-610, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hierarchical Volume Rendering for Cloud Surface
head: Least squares volume rendering, Octree volume rendering for surface
body: This method renders cloud surfaces in regimes where the diffusion approximation is invalid, specifically at cloud edges where single scattering and low-order multiple scattering break directional independence. It solves this by using hierarchical volume rendering with opacities \rho(X)\sigmat and voxel colors I0(X), selecting view-dependent octree cubes based on projected area-weighted approximation errors. It is distinguished from standard octree volume rendering by its specific use of least-squares approximations for color and opacity combined with a hardware cell-projection compositing step, differing from Octree-based Volume Rendering with Wavelet Leaves in its approximation basis. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Precomputed octree hierarchy of least-squares approximations for color and opacity values at various cube levels, along with the Root Mean Square (RMS) error for each approximation. Output: Compositing of selected cubes in back-to-front order using the hardware cell-projection method. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains fields for the least-squares approximation coefficients (for color and opacity), the RMS error of that approximation, and spatial bounds. Approximation Functions: Piecewise linear or piecewise constant functions are used within the hierarchy, computed per wavelength band (red, green, blue). Steps: 1. Precomputation: Compute an octree hierarchy of least-squares approximations to the color and opacity values on various level cubes. Calculate the RMS error for each approximation. 2. View-Dependent Selection: Traverse the octree to select appropriate cubes. The selection is view-dependent and weights the approximation error by the projected area of the cube on the image. 3. Compositing: Composite the selected cubes in back-to-front order using the hardware cell-projection method. Formulas: Opacity: \rho(X)\sigmat, where \rho(X) is density and \sigmat is the extinction coefficient. Voxel Color: I0(X), representing the incident radiance solution per wavelength band. Parameters: Approximation Type: Piecewise linear or piecewise constant. Error Weighting: The selection criterion weights the RMS error by the projected area of the cube on the image plane. Pitfalls: Precision/Boundaries: The diffusion approximation (used for the bulk volume solution I0) is invalid at cloud edges where single scattering and low-order multiple scattering are significant. This method is specifically applied to handle these edge cases where the standard approximation fails. This variant integrates the volume rendering step into an iterative loop with a Partial Differential Equation (PDE) solver. It obtains revised values for Q0 and Q1 by propagating incident radiance from the volume rendering results. The sequence of PDE solution, volume rendering, and ray propagation is iterated until I0 stops changing significantly. It also computes ground illumination and shadowing using hardware volume rendering onto hemicubes placed on a ground sample grid, including diffusely reflecting ground as background. Direct sunlight I{sun}(Xe, \omega{sun}) is propagated and attenuated separately, saved as I{risun}(Xe, \omega{sun}) at every voxel, and added separately to Q0 and Q1. A key pitfall is that the sun's radiance exceeds the dynamic range of the fixed-point frame buffer, so it is not added to the sky background. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Relies on hardware cell-projection for compositing, suggesting GPU acceleration. Strengths: Handles cloud edges where diffusion approximation fails; integrates with ground illumination and shadowing. Limitations: Requires precomputation of octree hierarchies and RMS errors. When to use: Rendering cloud surfaces with significant edge effects or single-scattering dominance. Originated in the context of global illumination in clouds, specifically addressing the limitations of the diffusion approximation at cloud boundaries. The method builds on [Schu01] (Schueller, 2001), which was modified to handle color and use piecewise linear or constant functions in the approximation hierarchy. It is part of a broader workflow that includes PDE solutions for radiance transport and final gather ray tracing for single scattering effects. name: Octree-based Volume Rendering with Delta/Residual Tracking
head: Delta/residual tracking with octree, Octree-based Volume Traversal, Ratio tracking for volume rendering
body: This method replaces traditional volume meshes and volume stacks with an octree encoding volume topology and extra data, enabling direct traversal and shading during ray marching. It differs from stack-based volume shading by evaluating all volume shaders in the current leaf node simultaneously at each step, eliminating the need to maintain and update a volume stack during traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of objects with volume geometry; volume bounding boxes. Output: Rendered image with volume shading, emission, and direct light (note: early implementations had missing emission and direct light). Data Structures: Octree Leaf Node: volumes: A list of active volume objects. The source specifies a fixed size of 1024 objects, but notes this consumes excessive memory and suggests a dynamic pointer to a packed list as an alternative. mindensity: Minimum density value for the volumes in this leaf. maxdensity: Maximum density value for the volumes in this leaf. Note: The min/max density is used to bound null scattering probability. Numbered Steps: 1. Build Octree: Construct an octree from the list of objects possessing volume geometry, using their volume bounding boxes. 2. Scene Traversal: Execute the standard scene intersection (sceneintersect). 3. Octree Traversal: After sceneintersect in integratorintersectclosest, perform octree traversal to determine the active leaf node for the ray segment. 4. Volume Shading: In shadevolume, traverse the octree to identify the current leaf node. Evaluate all volume shaders in the current leaf node at once. 5. Null Scattering: Use the stored mindensity and maxdensity values to bound the null scattering probability. Formulas: Null scattering probability is bounded by the actual volume density using the leaf node's min/max values. Specific formulas are not provided in the sources. Parameters: Fixed list size for volumes per leaf node: 1024 (noted as excessive). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: A fixed list size of 1024 volume objects per leaf node consumes excessive memory.
