name: Octree Neighbor Finding
head: GetNeighbors, Neighbor Retrieval, forward neighbor retrieval
body: Octree Neighbor Finding determines the adjacent leaf nodes in six cardinal directions (±X, ±Y, ±Z) for a given node in a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO). It solves the problem of traversing between non-contiguous or differently-sized nodes during ray casting or pathfinding by locating the nearest shared ancestor and performing point location to retrieve the neighbor. Inputs: currentnode: The index of the starting leaf node. direction: A vector specifying the target direction (e.g., +X, -Y). parenttrace: An array containing the indices of all parent nodes from the root to currentnode, provided by the ray traversal algorithm. depth: The depth level of currentnode. Outputs: neighborindex: The index of the adjacent leaf node, or a sentinel value (INDEXNONE) if no neighbor exists in that direction. Data Structures: Node Struct: Contains depth (7 bits), isleaf (1 bit), position (3 floats), and size (1 float). Parent Trace Array: trace[] stores the indices of parent nodes for the current ray cap, allowing upward traversal without storing explicit parent pointers in the node structure. Algorithm Steps: 1. Validation: Verify currentnode is a leaf. If not, return immediately. 2. Target Position Calculation: Compute the position just outside the current node in the specified direction by moving slightly farther than HalfSize. 3. Upward Traversal (Find Common Ancestor): Iterate up the tree using parenttrace from the origin node's parent depth down to 0. At each level, check if the target position falls within the spatial bounds of the parent node using &-masking of the origin and destination coordinates with the corresponding depth bit, followed by integer equality. 4. Point Location: Once the common ancestor is found, perform a standard point-location search from the common ancestor to the targetpos to find the leaf at the destination. 5. Neighbor Collection: If the search lands on a leaf node, return it. If the search lands on an internal node, the neighbor is one of its children. To find the specific child adjacent to the current node, use AxisMask and AxisBit to filter by the target axis and collect the four face children. Limit the search depth to the current node's depth to ensure only adjacent leaves of equal or larger size are collected, avoiding all descendants. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. INDEXNONE = -1 def getneighbor(originidx, direction, parenttrace, nodedata, maxdepth): # 1. Validation: Verify currentnode is a leaf if not (nodedata[originidx] & 0x80): return INDEXNONE originpos = nodedata[originidx].position originsize = nodedata[originidx].size origindepth = nodedata[originidx].depth # 2. Target position: move slightly farther than HalfSize in direction targetpos = originpos + direction (originsize 0.5 + 1e-6) # 3. Upward Traversal: Find common ancestor # Begin at the depth of the origin node's parent commonancestoridx = parenttrace[origindepth - 1] if origindepth > 0 else 0 for d in range(origindepth - 1, -1, -1): depthbit = 1 << (maxdepth - d) if ((targetpos.x & depthbit) == (originpos.x & depthbit)) and \ ((targetpos.y & depthbit) == (originpos.y & depthbit)) and \ ((targetpos.z & depthbit) == (originpos.z & depthbit)): commonancestoridx = parenttrace[d] break # 4. Point Location: Find leaf at destination from common ancestor neighboridx = commonancestoridx startdepth = nodedata[commonancestoridx].depth for d in range(maxdepth - startdepth, -1, -1): shift = d childidx = ((targetpos.x >> shift) & 1) | \ (((targetpos.y >> shift) & 1) << 1) | \ (((targetpos.z >> shift) & 1) << 2) neighboridx = nodedata[neighboridx].children[childidx] if neighboridx == INDEXNONE or (nodedata[neighboridx] & 0x80): break # 5. Neighbor Collection: Handle results if neighboridx != INDEXNONE and (nodedata[neighboridx] & 0x80): # Neighbor is internal. Compute 4 face child indices using AxisMask and AxisBit axismask = 0 if direction.x != 0: axismask = 1 elif direction.y != 0: axismask = 2 else: axismask = 4 # AxisBit: returns AxisMask if Side is -1, returns 0 if Side is +1 side = -1 if (direction.x < 0 or direction.y < 0 or direction.z < 0) else 1 axisbit = axismask if side == -1 else 0 # Filter children on the specific directional face facechildren = [] for c in range(8): if (c & axisbit) == axisbit: facechildren.append(c) # Traverse down to leaf level, collecting only adjacent leaves for c in facechildren: childidx = nodedata[neighboridx].children[c] if childidx == INDEXNONE: continue if nodedata[childidx] & 0x80: return childidx neighboridx = childidx return neighboridx Parameters: AxisMask: Bit mask for axis direction. X returns 001, Y returns 010, Z returns 100. AxisBit: Returns AxisMask if Side is -1, returns 0 if Side is +1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Leaf Input: The algorithm must validate that the input node is a leaf; otherwise, it returns immediately. Depth Limiting: The search must stop at a leaf or when the depth matches the current node's depth to avoid collecting all descendants of a neighbor. Memory Footprint: Parent pointers are omitted from nodes to save memory; the parenttrace array must be maintained by the caller (ray traversal). Optimization: Use static polymorphism via templates for each X, Y, Z dimension to perform only one or two equality tests per iteration. Determines the next cell in a hierarchical spatial structure by backtracing from a start coordinate to the common ancestor with a destination coordinate, then performing point location. It differs from Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration by relying on explicit parent-pointer traversal and coordinate bit-masking rather than Morton key arithmetic. Identifies and processes the eight corner vertices of leaf nodes in a sparse voxel octree by leveraging the spatial locality of Morton (Z-order) keys. It solves the dual-grid traversal problem by operating on a pre-computed or iterated list of vertex keys, using bitwise arithmetic to resolve adjacency and handle level mismatches without tree traversal recursion. Time Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the octree, due to the upward traversal and subsequent point location. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per neighbor query, assuming the parenttrace array is provided by the traversal context. Strengths: Efficient for sparse structures where explicit parent pointers are too costly; works with arbitrary node sizes. Limitations: Requires the parenttrace array to be maintained by the caller. When to Use: When memory footprint is critical (no parent pointers in nodes) or when traversing non-contiguous nodes in an SVO. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The authors rejected Frisken and Perry's exclusive "or" method for immediate neighbors because it was no cheaper than &-masking both source and destination and performing integer equality on the results. To minimize memory footprint, parent pointers were omitted from octree nodes, requiring the ray traversal algorithm to fill an index trace array containing the indices of all parent nodes for a given cap. name: Neighbor Finding
head: Octree Hashing (Neighbor-Finding)
body: Neighbor finding locates the octree node containing a destination coordinate relative to a start coordinate by backtracing up the hierarchy to a common ancestor and performing point location. It differs from sibling methods like Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration by relying on explicit coordinate masking and a parent trace array rather than arithmetic on Morton keys. Inputs: start: The 3D integer coordinates of the origin node. dest: The 3D integer coordinates of the desired neighbor. depth: The integer depth of the start node in the octree. parenttrace[]: An array storing pointers to nodes, allowing the tree to use 1-way pointers and minimizing memory footprint. childbitdepth[]: An array where childbitdepth[up] contains the bitmask for the child index at depth up. Outputs: The index or pointer to the node containing dest. Data Structures: childbitdepth[]: Implementation-specific array of bitmasks. parenttrace[]: Array of node pointers indexed by depth. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate from the current depth down to 0: for up = depth down to 0. 2. Retrieve the child bit mask for the current level: childbit = childbitdepth[up]. 3. Check if start and dest share the same bits at this depth level for all three dimensions. This is done by masking both coordinates with the corresponding depth bit and performing integer equality. Condition: (dest.x & childbit) == (start.x & childbit) AND (dest.y & childbit) == (start.y & childbit) AND (dest.z & childbit) == (start.z & childbit). 4. If the condition is true, a common parent is found at this level. Call pointlocate(dest, up, parenttrace[up]) to retrieve the leaf at dest starting from that parent. Return the result. 5. If the loop completes without returning, check the root level match using the same masking logic with childbit from the final iteration (up=0). 6. If the root check passes, call pointlocate(dest, 0, 0) to find the leaf at the root level. 7. If no match is found, return 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neighborfind(start: Vec3i, dest: Vec3i, depth: int, parenttrace: List[int], childbitdepth: List[int]) -> int: """ Finds the node containing dest starting from start by backtracing to a common ancestor. """ # Iterate from current depth down to 0 for up in range(depth, -1, -1): childbit = childbitdepth[up] # Check if start and dest share the same bits at this depth if ((dest.x & childbit) == (start.x & childbit) and (dest.y & childbit) == (start.y & childbit) and (dest.z & childbit) == (start.z & childbit)): # Common parent found; perform point location from this parent return pointlocate(dest, up, parenttrace[up]) # Root node check (if loop completes without returning) childbit = childbitdepth[0] if ((dest.x & childbit) == (start.x & childbit) and (dest.y & childbit) == (start.y & childbit) and (dest.z & childbit) == (start.z & childbit)): return pointlocate(dest, 0, 0) return 0 def pointlocate(dest: Vec3i, startdepth: int, startnode: Node) -> int: """ Standard downward traversal from startnode to find the leaf at dest. """ node = startnode for d in range(startdepth, -1, -1): childidx = ((dest.x >> d) & 1) << 2 | ((dest.y >> d) & 1) << 1 | ((dest.z >> d) & 1) if node.children[childidx] is None: return 0 node = node.children[childidx] return node.index Parameters: childbitdepth: Implementation-specific bitmask array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parent Pointers: Explicit parent pointers are omitted from node structures to minimize memory footprint. Parent indices are provided by the ray traversal algorithm filling the parenttrace[] array. Root Handling: The algorithm explicitly handles the case where the common ancestor is the root node. Optimization: Static polymorphism via templates can be used for X, Y, Z dimensions to reduce equality tests to one or two per iteration for neighbors along designated axes. Uses a rational t-value approach to locate the exit point directly, bypassing explicit direction vector calculation. Omits explicit parent pointers, using an index trace[] array and bitwise AND masking with integer equality checks to identify common parents. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the depth of the octree, O(D), where D is the maximum depth. Memory Complexity: O(D) for the parenttrace array, which is reused during traversal. Strengths: Minimizes memory footprint by avoiding explicit parent pointers in node structures. Simple to implement using coordinate masking. Limitations: Requires a valid parenttrace array populated by a prior traversal step. Performance depends on the depth of the common ancestor. When to use: Used during sparse octree ray traversal when a neighbor node is required. Originated in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The method was developed to optimize ray traversal by efficiently finding neighboring cells without storing redundant parent pointers. It builds on earlier work by Frisken and Perry, who required foreknowledge of neighbor direction (left/right) on midplanes. This implementation omits that distinction, simplifying the logic by using coordinate masking. name: Wyvill and Kunii's Ray Tracing / Neighbor Finding Algorithm
head: Rational t-value Neighbor Finding, Wyvill-Kunii Neighbor Finding
body: Wyvill and Kunii's algorithm is a ray-tracing method for hierarchical spatial structures (quadtrees and octrees) that determines the next intersected cell by calculating a specific point guaranteed to lie inside that cell, rather than computing a direction vector. It differs from sibling methods like the standard RAYTRACER by using a rational t-value approach to locate the exit point directly, bypassing explicit direction vector calculation. Inputs: Geometric parameters for each axis I \in \{X, Y, Z\}: B[I] (base coordinate), M[I] (cell size), W\B[I] (width/boundary offset), CORNER[I] (corner coordinate), and SIGN\M[I] (motion sign, 0 or 1). Outputs: POINT[I]: The coordinates of a point inside the next intersected cell. The identity of the next cell, determined by locating POINT using a spatial search procedure analogous to FIND3DBLOCK. Data Structures: NUM and DEN: Dictionaries mapping \{X, Y, Z\} to floating-point numerators and denominators for the rational t-values. POINT: An array or dictionary of floating-point coordinates for the exit point. Lookup tables (required for context in related neighbor finding routines): EDGFDIR: Maps normal plane and signs to edge direction E. VERTEXDIR: Maps signs to vertex direction V (e.g., LDB, RUF). CHANGE: Maps direction vectors to 3D components. Steps: 1. Initialize Rational T-Values: For each coordinate I \in \{X, Y, Z\}, compute the numerator and denominator of the exit t-value T[I]: NUM[I] = CORNER[I] - SIGN\M[I] \cdot W\B[I] - SIGN\M[I] DEN[I] = M[I] 2. Find Minimum Axis: Identify the axis K corresponding to the minimum t-value by initializing K = X and comparing T[K] against T[Y] and T[Z] using cross-multiplication to avoid division: python if abs(NUM[K] DEN[I]) > abs(NUM[I] DEN[K]): K = I 3. Compute Next Cell Point: Calculate the coordinates of the point POINT using the minimum t-value T[K] for all axes: POINT[I] = M[I] \cdot \frac{NUM[K]}{DEN[K]} + B[I] \quad \text{for all } I \in \{X, Y, Z\} 4. Locate Next Cell: Use a spatial search procedure (analogous to FIND3DBLOCK) to identify the cell containing POINT. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def wyvillkuniinextcell(B, M, WB, CORNER, SIGNM): """ B: dict/array [X, Y, Z] base coordinates M: dict/array [X, Y, Z] cell sizes WB: dict/array [X, Y, Z] width/boundary offsets CORNER: dict/array [X, Y, Z] corner coordinates SIGNM: dict/array [X, Y, Z] motion signs (0 or 1) Returns: POINT dict/array [X, Y, Z] """ # Step 1: Initialize rational t-values NUM = {} DEN = {} for I in ['X', 'Y', 'Z']: NUM[I] = CORNER[I] - SIGNM[I] WB[I] - SIGNM[I] DEN[I] = M[I] # Step 2: Find axis K with minimum t-value K = 'X' for I in ['Y', 'Z']: # Compare T[K] < T[I] using cross-multiplication with absolute values if abs(NUM[K] DEN[I]) > abs(NUM[I] DEN[K]): K = I # Step 3: Compute POINT using the minimum t-value T[K] POINT = {} for I in ['X', 'Y', 'Z']: tval = NUM[K] / DEN[K] POINT[I] = M[I] tval + B[I] return POINT Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Corner Passing: If a ray passes through a cell corner (e.g., SW corner of cell 5 to cell 11), applying a 2D block finder to (ax-1, ay) may report a false intersection if cell 4 is fully occupied, whereas (ax, ay-1) avoids it. Subdivision Errors: If a cell (e.g., cell 3) is subdivided like the SE quadrant of a quadtree, the algorithm may compute an incorrect point (e.g., (12, 16) instead of (12, 15)), routing to the wrong cell (cell 10 instead of cell 3). Fix Limitations: Removing the subtraction of SIGN\M[I] from the numerator does not always fix the error, as decomposing motion into separate directions can still cause false intersections due to distinct entry/exit conventions. Simultaneous Boundaries: Wyvill and Kunii claim that when a ray reaches multiple boundaries simultaneously, arbitrarily picking one boundary perpendicular to motion is sufficient, but this claim is shown to be incorrect for certain subdivisions. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simpler structure than neighbor-finding algorithms that compute exact direction vectors, and it avoids explicit direction vector calculation. Limitations: Prone to errors in specific hierarchical subdivisions (e.g., SE quadrant subdivisions) and corner cases, and the claim of robustness for simultaneous boundary crossings is incorrect. The algorithm was proposed by Wyvill and Kunii. It is discussed in the context of implementing ray tracing with octrees and neighbor finding, where it is compared against a more robust RAYTRACER algorithm. name: Octree Neighbor Finding without Parent Pointers
head: Mask-based Neighbor Finding, Neighbor Finding without Parent Pointers
body: This method locates the voxel at a coordinate direction relative to an origin node by traversing up the octree hierarchy to find a common parent, then using point location to find the destination leaf. It is distinguished from parent-pointer-based approaches by omitting explicit parent pointers to minimize memory footprint, instead relying on an index trace[] array populated during ray traversal to provide parent indices. Unlike Frisken and Perry’s method which uses exclusive OR with depth masks, this implementation uses bitwise AND masking on both source and destination coordinates followed by integer equality checks to identify common parents, as it is not more expensive. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Origin node index, origin coordinate, destination coordinate, and the index trace[] array containing indices of all parent nodes for the current cap. Output: Index of the destination leaf node. Data Structures: index trace[]: An array storing the indices of parent nodes encountered during the ray traversal up to the current cap. Coordinates: Spatial coordinates for the origin and destination nodes. Steps: 1. Masking: Apply a bitwise AND mask to both the source (origin) and destination coordinates. 2. Comparison: Perform integer equality comparison on the masked source and destination values. 3. Recursion: If the masked values are not equal, move up the tree using the index trace[] array to access the parent node indices. Repeat the masking and comparison at the parent level. 4. Common Parent: Continue until a common parent is found where the masked coordinates are equal. 5. Point Location: Once the common parent is identified, perform point location from this ancestor to find the specific leaf node at the destination coordinate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def maskcoords(coords, depth): # Masks out bits finer than the current depth level. # Assumes depth 0 is the finest level (leaf). return coords & ~((1 << depth) - 1) def findneighbor(originindex, origincoord, destcoord, indextrace, currentdepth): # Mask both coordinates at the current depth maskedorigin = maskcoords(origincoord, currentdepth) maskeddest = maskcoords(destcoord, currentdepth) # Check for equality to find common parent if maskedorigin == maskeddest: # Common parent found; perform point location from this ancestor return pointlocation(indextrace, currentdepth, destcoord) else: # Move up to the parent using the trace array parentindex = indextrace[currentdepth - 1] # Recurse to the parent level return findneighbor(parentindex, origincoord, destcoord, indextrace, currentdepth - 1) def pointlocation(trace, startdepth, targetcoord): # Traverse down from the common ancestor to find the leaf at targetcoord currentindex = trace[startdepth] for depth in range(startdepth, -1, -1): # Extract octant bits for the current depth level octant = (targetcoord >> (3 depth)) & 7 # Compute child index using standard hash-based octree layout childindex = (currentindex << 3) | octant # Standard hash-table lookup for child existence if childindex not in hashtable: return None currentindex = childindex return currentindex Parameters: currentdepth: The depth level in the octree where the comparison is performed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Integer coordinates must be handled carefully to ensure correct masking. Boundaries: If the destination coordinate is outside the octree bounds, point location should handle this gracefully. Degenerate Input: If the origin and destination are the same, the algorithm should return the origin index immediately. An algorithm to find adjacent nodes in an octree without using locational codes, utilizing case decomposition for edges/vertices and bitwise operations for optimization. It computes the 'reflection' function for the adjacent neighbor by performing a binary exclusive OR (XOR) of the current location and the direction vector in which the neighbor is sought. It then recursively traverses up the tree to find the deepest common ancestor between the current node and the reflected location. Finally, it performs point location from the deepest common ancestor to find the target neighbor node. The average cost to find an adjacent neighbor at the same depth is O(1). Time Complexity: The average cost to find an adjacent neighbor at the same depth is O(1). The general neighbor finding algorithm involves recursion up the tree, which depends on the depth of the octree. Memory Complexity: The index trace[] array requires O(D) memory where D is the depth of the octree. O(1) additional memory is required per traversal step if the array is reused. Strengths: Minimizes memory footprint by omitting parent pointers. Efficient for non-adjacent neighbors. Limitations: Requires the index trace[] array to be maintained during ray traversal. When to Use: When memory is constrained and parent pointers are undesirable. When Not to Use: When random access to parent pointers is needed without maintaining a trace array. Neighbor finding was addressed early on in octree research. Gargantini [Gar82] provided a concise algorithm for finding adjacent nodes in the linear quadtree using Morton’s [Mor66] array-based locational code. Samet [Sam82] proposed a more general scheme for adjacent neighbor-finding using only an original node and a desired direction, with no knowledge of a locational code. The algorithm was later applied to accelerating ray tracing using a pointer octree [Sam89]. Samet [Sam90] conducted rigorous analysis of the neighbor finding technique, decomposing the algorithm into cases for edge, vertex, and aligned neighbors. Frisken and Perry noted that the “reflection” function for adjacent neighbors, implemented by Samet via a switch statement, can be accomplished by a binary exclusive “or” of the current location and the direction in which we seek a neighbor. The method described here, using masking and equality checks, was proposed in as an alternative to Frisken and Perry’s method. name: Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration
head: Vertex Neighbor Iteration via Morton Keys
body:
Morton Key Vertex Neighbor Iteration identifies and processes the eight corner vertices of leaf nodes in a sparse voxel octree by leveraging the spatial locality of Morton (Z-order) keys. It solves the dual-grid traversal problem, ensuring each shared vertex is processed exactly once across up to eight adjacent leaf nodes. It differs from standard recursive neighbor finding by operating on a pre-computed list of vertex keys and using bitwise arithmetic to resolve adjacency and level mismatches without recursive tree traversal. Inputs: A sparse voxel octree implementation providing nodeexists(key), issubdivided(key), and parent() operations. An array of vertexkeys containing MortonKey values for the eight vertices of a leaf node, with invalid vertices marked as MortonKey::none(). The target level of the leaf node (vertexlv). Outputs: An array of eight resolved neighbor keys for the valid vertices of the leaf, where each entry is either a valid MortonKey of an existing node at the same level (or an ancestor if the direct neighbor is missing) or MortonKey::none(). MortonKey: A struct wrapping a u64 integer that represents a single node in a hashed octree. Its internal representation starts with 1 for the root node and appends three bits per level for the child index along the X, Y, and Z axes. MortonKey::none() returns Self(0) and MortonKey::root() returns Self(1). HashedOctree: A concurrent hash map-based storage for the octree values. Defined as pub struct HashedOctree<T: Copy> { values: DashMap<MortonKey, T, RandomState>, }. OctreeIndex: Bitflags for child indices where RIGHT = 1 << 0, TOP = 1 << 1, and FOREMOST = 1 << 2. The method relies on three 64-bit dilation constants to perform bitwise arithmetic on Morton keys. These constants have bits set at positions corresponding to the X, Y, and Z axes in the Morton interleaving. DILX = 0b001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001u64. DILY = 0b010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010u64. DILZ = 0b100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100u64. The core of the method uses dilated integer addition and dilated integer subtraction to move along grid axes in Morton space using standard integer arithmetic masked by the dilation constants. 1. Dilated Integer Addition (computes vertex keys from a leaf key): vertex\key = \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\X) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\X) ight) \ \& \ DIL\X \ \mid \ \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\Y) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\Y) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Y \ \mid \ \left( (key.0 \mid 
eg DIL\Z) + (vertex\i \ \& \ DIL\Z) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Z Where key.0 is the Morton key of the leaf node, vertex\i is the vertex index (0–7), \mid is bitwise OR, 
eg is bitwise NOT, \& is bitwise AND, and + is integer addition. 2. Dilated Integer Subtraction (computes neighbor leaf keys from a vertex key): key{node\i} = \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\X) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\X) ight) \ \& \ DIL\X \ \mid \ \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\Y) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\Y) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Y \ \mid \ \left( (dc \ \& \ DIL\Z) - (node\i \ \& \ DIL\Z) ight) \ \& \ DIL\Z Where dc is the dilated coordinate of the vertex computed as vertex\k.0 \ll (vertex\lv - vertex\k.level()) 	imes 3, and node\i is the neighbor index (0–7). The method processes a list of vertex keys to find unique neighbors. 1. Iterate Vertices: Enumerate over the vertexkeys array and stop when vertexk equals MortonKey::none(). Let the current index be vertexi and the key be vertexk. 2. Compute Neighbor Candidates: Call vert2leaf(vertexk, vertexlv) to obtain an array neighbours of eight candidate MortonKey values for the adjacent nodes. 3. Filter Neighbors: For each neighbor index neighbouri from 0 to 7: skip if neighbouri == vertexi (the node itself). Let neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri]. If !octree.nodeexists(neighbourk), continue to the next neighbor. If octree.issubdivided(neighbourk) (the neighbor is deeper than the current leaf), mark the entire vertex as skipped because the deeper node will process the shared vertex. If neighbouri < vertexi, mark the entire vertex as skipped to ensure shared vertices between same-level nodes are processed exactly once based on fixed indices rather than iteration order. 4. Resolve Keys: If the vertex passes the filter, initialize an array keys: [MortonKey; 8]. For each neighbouri from 0 to 7, let neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri]. While neighbourk != MortonKey::none() AND !octree.nodeexists(neighbourk), set neighbourk = neighbourk.parent(). Store the resolved neighbourk in keys[neighbouri]. Return keys. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. DILX = 0b001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001001 DILY = 0b010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010010 DILZ = 0b100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100100 class MortonKey: def init(self, val: int): self.0 = val @staticmethod def none(): return MortonKey(0) @staticmethod def root(): return MortonKey(1) def level(self) -> int: if self.0 == 0: raise ValueError("Cannot get level of none key") return (63 - self.0.bitlength() + 1) // 3 def parent(self) -> 'MortonKey': return MortonKey(self.0 >> 3) def leaf2vert(key: MortonKey) -> tuple[int, list[MortonKey]]: level = key.level() levelkey = 1 << (3 level) keys = [None] 8 for vertexi in range(8): vertexkey = ( ((key.0 | ~DILX) + (vertexi & DILX)) & DILX | ((key.0 | ~DILY) + (vertexi & DILY)) & DILY | ((key.0 | ~DILZ) + (vertexi & DILZ)) & DILZ) if (vertexkey >= (levelkey << 1)) or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILX) == 0 or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILY) == 0 or \ ((vertexkey - levelkey) & DILZ) == 0: keys[vertexi] = MortonKey.none() else: keys[vertexi] = MortonKey(vertexkey) return level, keys def vert2leaf(vertexk: MortonKey, vertexlv: int) -> list[MortonKey]: dc = vertexk.0 << ((vertexlv - vertexk.level()) 3) keys = [None] 8 for nodei in range(8): keys[nodei] = MortonKey( ((dc & DILX) - (nodei & DILX)) & DILX | ((dc & DILY) - (nodei & DILY)) & DILY | ((dc & DILZ) - (nodei & DILZ)) & DILZ) return keys def processvertexneighbors(vertexkeys: list[MortonKey], octree) -> list[list[MortonKey]]: results = [] for vertexi, vertexk in enumerate(vertexkeys): if vertexk == MortonKey.none(): break neighbours = vert2leaf(vertexk, vertexk.level()) shouldprocess = True for neighbouri in range(8): if neighbouri == vertexi: continue neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri] if not octree.nodeexists(neighbourk): continue if octree.issubdivided(neighbourk): shouldprocess = False break if neighbouri < vertexi: shouldprocess = False break if not shouldprocess: continue keys = [None] 8 for neighbouri in range(8): neighbourk = neighbours[neighbouri] while neighbourk != MortonKey.none() and not octree.nodeexists(neighbourk): neighbourk = neighbourk.parent() keys[neighbouri] = neighbourk results.append(keys) return results Invalid Vertex Keys: A vertex key is invalid if it falls outside the level's range (vertexkey >= levelkey << 1) or if any dilated axis difference is zero. These invalid cases return MortonKey::none(). Concurrency: When using HashedOctree (backed by DashMap), concurrent access may deadlock if a mutable reference is held while calling value(). Tie-Breaking: The condition neighbouri < vertexi ensures that shared vertices between nodes of the same level are processed only once, relying on fixed neighbor and vertex indices rather than iteration order. Time Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of valid vertices, with constant-time bitwise operations per vertex and a bounded parent-traversal loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per vertex for storing eight keys, with external octree storage. Strengths: Avoids recursive tree traversal for neighbor finding and uses fast bitwise arithmetic, making it efficient for sparse grids where many neighbors are missing. Limitations: Requires pre-computed or easily derivable vertex keys and relies on the octree implementation providing efficient nodeexists and issubdivided checks. The method is described in the dmc (Dense Marching Cuber) project by aleokdev. It is used for dual-grid traversal in volume rendering, specifically for extracting isosurfaces from sparse voxel octrees. The approach leverages the properties of Morton keys to map spatial adjacency to arithmetic operations. aleokdev/dmc, https://github.com/aleokdev/dmc, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes
head: Child Octant Traversal, Interior Node Traversal, Mid-plane Intersection Traversal, Octree Node Traversal Order, Octree Traversal (OT), Octree Traversal with Mid-Plane Sorting, e-space coordinate traversal
body: This method traverses an octree along a ray by computing the intersection order of the X, Y, and Z mid-planes that divide a parent node into its eight child octants, allowing the ray to march sequentially through children in the correct spatial order. Unlike Hierarchical Traversal, which may use bounding volume hierarchies or less structured descent, this approach explicitly sorts mid-plane intersections to determine the exact traversal sequence, exploiting binary arithmetic to minimize branching. It is distinct from Sparse Voxel Traversal in its specific focus on the mid-plane sorting logic for interior nodes, and from Ray-Octree Traversal (Gargantini and Atkinson variant) by relying on standard floating-point comparisons rather than rational arithmetic for precision. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and an octree node defined by its center \mathbf{c}, half-extent h, and depth. The ray entry (t{enter}) and exit (t{exit}) parameters relative to the node's bounding box are pre-computed. Output: A sequence of child octant indices (0–7) to visit, and potentially the values of voxels at leaf/cap nodes for isosurface reconstruction. Data Structures: Node: Contains depth, node index, and pointers to children or scalar data. axisisects[]: An array of size 3 storing the sorted t{center} intersection distances for the X, Y, and Z mid-planes. axisbit: A bitmask (integer) representing the current child octant index. Steps: 1. Ray-Node Intersection: Perform a box test to determine if the ray intersects the current node. If not, terminate. Compute t{enter} and t{exit} for the node's bounding box. 2. Mid-Plane Computation: Compute the octree-space coordinates of the three mid-planes (X, Y, Z) that divide the node into 8 equal child octants. 3. Intersection Evaluation: Evaluate the t-parameter where the ray intersects each of the three mid-planes. 4. Sorting: Sort the t{center} intersection distances and store them in axisisects[] in ascending order. 5. First Child Determination: Compute the index of the first child octant intersected by the ray using constant shifting and binary-OR operations based on the ray's position relative to the node center, identical to point location. Let this initial index be axisbit. 6. Sequential Marching: Iterate through the sorted axisisects[]. For each mid-plane intersection: Determine which axis (X, Y, or Z) corresponds to the current smallest t value in axisisects[]. Update axisbit by inverting the bit corresponding to that axis. Visit the child octant indicated by the new axisbit. 7. Leaf/Cap Handling: If a child is a leaf or cap node, handle it using specialized routines (see Subtopics). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctreenode(rayorigin, raydirection, nodecenter, nodehalfextent, tenter, texit): # Compute local ray parameters relative to node center and half-extent localorigin = [(rayorigin[i] - nodecenter[i]) / nodehalfextent for i in range(3)] localdirection = [raydirection[i] / nodehalfextent for i in range(3)] # Compute t-values for intersection with mid-planes at 0 for each axis axisisects = [] for i in range(3): if localdirection[i] == 0.0: axisisects.append((float('inf'), i)) else: axisisects.append((-localorigin[i] / localdirection[i], i)) # Sort t-values ascending to determine traversal order axisisects.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Compute first child octant index based on local origin position axisbit = 0 if localorigin[0] >= 0: axisbit |= 1 if localorigin[1] >= 0: axisbit |= 2 if localorigin[2] >= 0: axisbit |= 4 # Visit the first child childnode = getchildnode(axisbit) if childnode is not None: visitchild(childnode) # Sequentially march across child octants by crossing mid-planes for t, axis in axisisects: if t < tenter or t > texit: continue if axis == 0: axisbit ^= 1 elif axis == 1: axisbit ^= 2 elif axis == 2: axisbit ^= 4 childnode = getchildnode(axisbit) if childnode is not None: visitchild(childnode) def getchildnode(index): # Standard operation: retrieve child node from octree structure return node.children[index] if node.haschildren else None def visitchild(child): # Standard operation: process child node if child.isleaf: handleleaf(child) elif child.iscap: handlecap(child) else: # Recurse or continue traversal pass def handleleaf(leaf): # Standard operation: sample or process leaf value pass def handlecap(cap): # Standard operation: process cap node values pass Parameters: Sorting Cost: Moderate initial cost for computing and sorting mid-plane intersections. Traversal Cost: Subsequent traversal is trivial, involving only bitmask inversion. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Standard floating-point comparisons may introduce errors in t-value comparisons, potentially leading to incorrect traversal order. Cap Nodes: Between 1 and 8 voxels in the neighborhood of a ray-intersected voxel may lie within the same cap node, requiring efficient local access. Empty Nodes: The algorithm can utilize an empty octree strategy to skip nodes that do not contain the isosurface, reducing iterations. This variant explicitly sorts mid-plane intersections to march sequentially through child octants, often using neighbor-finding for non-leaf transitions. It is distinguished by its use of rational arithmetic to maintain precision in t-value comparisons, avoiding floating-point errors inherent in standard implementations. This method interprets the IEEE-754 bit representation of floating-point coordinates to determine node depth and child indices, avoiding explicit pointer chasing or coordinate division. It replaces arithmetic division and modulo operations with bitwise shifts and masks on the mantissa. A stack-based algorithm that handles arbitrary ray directions by flipping the coordinate system and ray parameters to ensure positive traversal direction. It uses an explicit stack to manage non-linear traversal paths and direction flipping to simplify child selection logic. For cap nodes, the algorithm skips the isovalue min/max range check and recursive child traversal. Instead, it determines the values of eight forward-neighbor voxels. It checks if a neighbor lies within the same cap node using the bitwise AND of the current child octant index (child) and the neighbor direction (dir): if (child & dir). If false, the value is retrieved directly from cap.scalars[diridx]. If true, neighbor-finding logic is used. A pitfall is that 1 to 8 voxels in the neighborhood may lie within the same cap node, requiring efficient local access. Time Complexity: Moderate initial cost for computing and sorting mid-plane intersections per node. Subsequent traversal is O(1) per child, involving only bitmask inversion. Memory Complexity: Low, requiring only a small array (axisisects[]) and bitmask per node traversal. Performance: On average, Octree Traversal (OT) is faster than Sphere Marching (SM) because it utilizes empty octree nodes with smaller average depth, despite potentially requiring more iterations. It produces a grid pattern in iteration counts due to dependence on node location. Strengths: Efficient skipping of empty space; simple child selection logic after initial sorting. Limitations: Floating-point precision issues in t-value comparisons; moderate initial sorting cost. The method originates from interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes, introduced by Wald et al. in 2006. It was developed to efficiently traverse sparse voxel octrees for real-time rendering, leveraging the hierarchical structure to skip empty regions and the mid-plane sorting to determine traversal order without complex branching. body: This method traverses an octree by fully sorting child octants based on the intersection order of the X, Y, and Z mid-planes, exploiting binary arithmetic on integer coordinates to determine the traversal sequence. Unlike its sibling Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes, which determines the order of mid-plane intersections to guide recursive descent, this variant explicitly sorts these intersections to march sequentially through child octants, often using neighbor-finding for non-leaf transitions or specialized routines for leaves/caps. It is distinguished by its use of rational arithmetic to maintain precision in t-value comparisons, avoiding the floating-point errors inherent in standard implementations. Inputs: Ray defined parametrically as P(t) = B + t \cdot M, where B is the origin vector and M is the direction vector. Octree root node R. World space width W, which must be a power of 2, with the origin at (0,0,0). Optional: Isovalue for scalar/cap traversal. Outputs: Traversal of octree nodes/leaves intersected by the ray. Intersection results (e.g., color, normal) if an object is found. Rational Number: A record type used to store t-values exactly. NUM: Integer numerator. DEN: Integer denominator. Cell Record: Used to track the current cell during traversal. TIN: Rational, entry t-value. TOUT: Rational, exit t-value. SIZ: Integer, cell width. PTR: Pointer to the current octree node. CORNER: Array of 3 integers, representing the furthest corner coordinates from the origin. DIRECT: Direction enum, indicating the direction to the next cell. Auxiliary Arrays: SIGNM: Array of 3 integers (0 or 1), where SIGNM[I] = 0 if M[I] > 0 else 1. axisisects: Array storing the sorted intersection distances with the X, Y, Z mid-planes. axistable: Lookup table mapping sorted axis indices to bit positions: {4, 2, 1} corresponding to X, Y, Z bits in the child index. 1. Initialization: Set pointer P to root R. Create cell record C. Compute SIGNM[I] for each axis I \in \{X, Y, Z\}. Compute the initial entry t-value T{OUT}(C) using FIRSTPOINT(W, DIR). This involves computing rational t-values for the entry planes: \text{NUM}(T[I]) = \text{SIGN\M}[I] \cdot W - B[I] \text{DEN}(T[I]) = M[I] Determine the initial direction DIR using NEXTCELLDIRECTION based on pairwise comparisons of entry t-values. Calculate the initial corner coordinates CORNER(C) and point POINT using: \text{POINT}[I] = \left\lfloor \frac{M[I] \cdot \text{NUM}(T{OUT}(C))}{\text{DEN}(T{OUT}(C))} \right\rfloor + B[I] + \text{SIGN\M}[I] \cdot \text{CHANGE}(\text{DIR}, I) where \lfloor x \rfloor denotes the floor function. Validate entry: If any POINT[I] is outside [0, W], the ray never enters the space; return immediately. Locate the initial cell using FIND3DBLOCK(P, POINT, CORNER(C), W). 2. Traversal Loop: Loop indefinitely: Set PTR(C) = P, SIZ(C) = W, TIN(C) = TOUT(C). Compute exit t-values for each plane I \in \{X, Y, Z\} using rational arithmetic: \text{NUM}(T[I]) = \text{CORNER}(C)[I] - \text{SIGN\M}[I] \cdot W - B[I] \text{DEN}(T[I]) = M[I] Perform pairwise comparisons COMPARET(T, CYX, CZX, CZY) to determine the relative order of exit t-values. Determine the minimum exit axis (MINAXIS) and the next cell direction DIRECT(C) using NEXTCELLDIRECTION. Set TOUT(C) = T[MINAXIS]. Intersection Test: Call RAYINTERSECTSOBJECTINCELL(C). If it intersects, perform reflection/refraction or return the result. Neighbor Finding: If no intersection, find the next cell using OTGTEQNEIGHBOR(P, DIRECT(C), P, W). If the neighbor pointer P is null, the ray has exited the scene; return. If the neighbor is smaller than the current cell (GRAY(P) is true), compute the entry point into the neighbor and use FIND3DBLOCK to locate the specific block. Update CORNER(C) to align with the new neighbor, handling boundary wrapping if necessary (e.g., modulo W). 3. Interior Node Traversal (Variant Optimization): For implementations that use the "variant" approach described in (often used for sparse voxel octrees or specific hashing schemes), the traversal of an interior node differs from the pure neighbor-finding approach: Retrieve the node by depth and index. Compute the octree-space coordinates of the mid-planes dividing the child octants. Evaluate penter (ray position at entry) and sort the tcenter intersection distances with the mid-planes into axisisects[]. Sequentially march across child octants using the sorted axisisects[] array. Compute the first child octant using constant shifting and binary-or operations. Move to subsequent octants by inverting the bitmask (axisbit) along the corresponding mid-plane axes traversed. If the child is a leaf, scalar leaf, or cap node, invoke the respective specialized traversal routine. Rational Arithmetic for t-values: To avoid precision errors, t-values are stored as rational numbers t = \text{NUM} / \text{DEN}. Entry Plane t-value: \text{NUM}(T[I]) = \text{SIGN\M}[I] \cdot W - B[I] \text{DEN}(T[I]) = M[I] Exit Plane t-value: \text{NUM}(T[I]) = \text{CORNER}(C)[I] - \text{SIGN\M}[I] \cdot W - B[I] \text{DEN}(T[I]) = M[I] Point Location in Cell: \text{POINT}[I] = \left\lfloor \frac{M[I] \cdot \text{NUM}(T{OUT}(C))}{\text{DEN}(T{OUT}(C))} \right\rfloor + B[I] + \text{SIGN\M}[I] \cdot \text{CHANGE}(\text{DIR}, I) Pairwise Comparison (COMPARET): \text{CYX} = |\text{NUM}(T[Y]) \cdot \text{DEN}(T[X])| - |\text{NUM}(T[X]) \cdot \text{DEN}(T[Y])| \text{CZX} = |\text{NUM}(T[Z]) \cdot \text{DEN}(T[X])| - |\text{NUM}(T[X]) \cdot \text{DEN}(T[Z])| \text{CZY} = |\text{NUM}(T[Z]) \cdot \text{DEN}(T[Y])| - |\text{NUM}(T[Y]) \cdot \text{DEN}(T[Z])| CHANGE Function: \text{CHANGE}(L, A) indicates the smallest amount, with appropriate sign, by which coordinate A changes due to motion in direction L. For example, \text{CHANGE}(\text{'RB'}, \text{'Z'}) = -1 and \text{CHANGE}(\text{'RB'}, \text{'Y'}) = 0. Unverified code. Precision Errors: Floating-point arithmetic can cause incorrect t-value comparisons, leading to missed intersections or infinite loops. Solved by using rational arithmetic (NUM/DEN) for all t-value calculations. Rational Arithmetic Growth: The number of bits required for rational parameters grows geometrically with secondary rays (reflections/refractions). The method is adequate only if secondary rays do not spawn further secondary rays. Equal t-values: When t-values are equal (e.g., CYX=0), the ray passes through an edge or vertex. NEXTCELLDIRECTION must handle these cases by checking for edge or vertex directions. Neighbor Size Differences: If the neighbor cell is smaller than the current cell, FIND3DBLOCK must be used to locate the specific block within the neighbor. Handles leaf nodes storing a single homogeneous scalar value by recursively traversing to cap depth and performing trilinear isosurface intersection. Handles the leaf-level boundary of the octree structure where explicit child pointers are absent, determining isosurface intersections using forward-neighbor voxels. Time Complexity: The initial cost involves computing and sorting mid-plane intersections for interior nodes, which is moderate. Subsequent traversal of child octants is trivial, involving only bitmask inversions. Neighbor-finding for non-leaf transitions can be costly depending on tree depth and structure. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for rational t-values and cell records. Rational arithmetic may require larger word sizes, especially for secondary rays. Performance: Single-ray techniques are preferred over SIMD/packet traversal for highly-variant scenes or large data, as coherent techniques can cause unnecessary work when pixels cover multiple voxels. Strengths: Exact precision with rational arithmetic avoids common floating-point errors in ray tracing. Efficient traversal of child octants using binary arithmetic. Limitations: Rational arithmetic precision grows with secondary rays, limiting its use in scenes with multiple reflections/refractions. Implementation complexity is high due to the need for neighbor-finding routines and boundary handling. The algorithm was introduced by Gargantini and Atkinson in 1982. It was designed for ray tracing in scenes represented by octrees or quadtrees, using neighbor finding instead of point location to traverse cells. name: Scalar Leaf Traversal
head: Scalar leaf node traversal
body: Scalar leaf traversal is the leaf-level processing step in ray traversal of sparse voxel octrees, handling nodes that contain homogeneous scalar values and no children. It determines whether an isosurface intersects the homogeneous region by checking the neighborhood of voxel values at the cap depth. It differs from cap node traversal by assuming internal homogeneity, allowing for early rejection when the neighborhood contains identical voxels. Inputs: Ray parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, current hit distance t{hit}), scalar leaf node data (homogeneous scalar value v{leaf}, bounding box), cap depth D{cap}, and octree structure for neighbor access. Outputs: Boolean indicating if an isosurface intersection occurs within the scalar leaf, and if yes, the intersection point and normal. Data Structures: The scalar leaf node stores a single scalar value v{leaf} and its spatial bounds. The neighborhood consists of the 8 corner voxels of the cell defined by the leaf's bounding box at the cap depth. Steps: 1. Recursive Traversal: Traverse the octree recursively until the current node depth equals the cap depth D{cap}. 2. Identify Node Type: Determine if the current node at D{cap} is a scalar leaf, which has no children and a homogeneous value. 3. Boundary Value Retrieval: At the borders of the scalar leaf node, retrieve the scalar values of the 8 corner voxels of the cell defined by the leaf's bounding box. To find a neighbor in direction dir \in \{0, \dots, 7\}, check if the child bit corresponding to dir is set; if false, the neighbor value is retrieved from the parent cap's scalar array at index dir; if true, proceed with standard neighbor-finding to retrieve the value. 4. Homogeneity Check: Check if the neighborhood of 8 voxels contains identical values. If all 8 corner values are identical, conclude that no isosurface is encountered within the scalar leaf. 5. Isovalue Range Check: If the neighborhood is not uniform, check if the target isovalue v lies within the minimum and maximum of the 8 corner voxel values: \min(v{corners}) \le v \le \max(v{corners}). If it does, proceed to intersection. 6. Isosurface Intersection: Perform isosurface intersection using the 8 corner voxels as the corners of the cell. Isosurface Intersection Details: The implicit surface is defined by the trilinear Lagrangian interpolant: f(x, y, z) = \left( \sum{i, j, k=\{0,1\}} xi yj zk v{ijk} \right) - v = 0 where (i, j, k) is the minimum coordinate of the cell, v is the isovalue, v{ijk} is the value of the cell vertex, and x0 = i-x, x1 = x-i (similarly for y, z with respect to j, k). The hit position is found by evaluating the ray at the first positive root of the resulting cubic polynomial. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversescalarleaf(rayo, rayd, rayisovalue, nodebounds, capdepth, currentdepth, childmask, capscalars, octree): # Step 1 & 2: Recursive traversal to cap depth is handled by parent. # This function is invoked when a scalar leaf is reached at capdepth. if currentdepth < capdepth: return None # Step 3: Boundary Value Retrieval cornervalues = [] for dir in range(8): # Check if child bit for dir is set if not (childmask & (1 << dir)): # Neighbor is simply cap.scalars[dir] val = capscalars[dir] else: # Proceed with standard neighbor-finding to retrieve the value # Standard octree neighbor-finding logic not detailed in sources val = None # Standard octree neighbor-finding logic not detailed in sources cornervalues.append(val) # Step 4: Homogeneity Check if all(v == cornervalues[0] for v in cornervalues): return None # No isosurface encountered # Step 5: Isovalue Range Check minval = min(cornervalues) maxval = max(cornervalues) if not (minval <= rayisovalue <= maxval): return None # No isosurface encountered # Step 6: Isosurface Intersection # Solve cubic polynomial for trilinear intersection; Neubauer iterative method # Hit position is evaluating the ray at the first positive root # Cubic root finding and ray evaluation not detailed in sources return None Handles cap nodes which may have children or non-homogeneous values. Chosen when the leaf node is not a scalar leaf. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use or not use: Not given in the sources. Scalar leaf traversal is part of the interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes method, introduced by Knoll et al. in 2006. It is designed to handle the leaf nodes of sparse voxel octrees efficiently, allowing for real-time rendering of large volumes. The method builds on the ray-octree traversal technique by Gargantini and Atkinson, adapting it to handle scalar leaves specifically. name: Ray-Octree Traversal (Gargantini and Atkinson variant) > Cap Node Traversal
head: Cap intersection, Ray-Octree Traversal
body: Cap node traversal is a specialized recursive algorithm used within the Gargantini and Atkinson ray-octree traversal scheme to handle the leaf-level boundary of the octree structure. It solves the problem of determining isosurface intersections when a ray reaches the deepest level of the hierarchy, where explicit child pointers are absent and data is stored in "cap" nodes. Cap intersection is identical to interior node traversal, except it replaces the recursive child traversal block with logic to determine the values of eight forward-neighbor voxels and perform a local isosurface intersection check. Scalar leaf traversal uses the same routine at the cap depth. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: The current ray (ray), the current depth (depth), the current node index (node\index), a parent trace array (parent\trace), the current cell coordinates (cell), the entry time (tenter), and the exit time (texit). Outputs: A boolean indicating whether an isosurface intersection was found. Data Structures OctNode: Contains fields childmins, childmaxs, and childoffset, accessed via node.childmins[child], node.childmaxs[child], and node.childoffset. Cap Node: Contains an array scalars storing voxel values, indexed via diridx. Axis Table: A constant array mapping sorted axis indices to bit masks: axistable = {4, 2, 1}. Child Bit Depth: An array childbitdepth where childbit = childbitdepth[depth]. Pseudocode The following pseudocode implements the cap node traversal logic, integrated into the main traversal loop as described in and. It assumes the caller has determined that depth == maxdepth - 2 (or equivalent boundary condition) and node.childoffset == -1. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversecap(ray, depth, nodeindex, parenttrace, cell, tenter, texit, isovalue, maxdepth, nodes, childbitdepth, axistable, capscalars): """ Traverses a cap node to find isosurface intersections. Returns True if intersection found, False otherwise. """ # 1. Retrieve current node and store trace node = nodes[depth][nodeindex] parenttrace[depth] = nodeindex # 2. Calculate child bit for this depth childbit = childbitdepth[depth] # 3. Calculate center of current cell center = Vec3(cell.x | childbit, cell.y | childbit, cell.z | childbit) # 4. Calculate intersection distances to center planes tcenter = Vec3( (center.x - ray.orig.x) / ray.dir.x, (center.y - ray.orig.y) / ray.dir.y, (center.z - ray.orig.z) / ray.dir.z) # 5. Calculate entry point penter = Vec3( ray.orig.x + ray.dir.x tenter, ray.orig.y + ray.dir.y tenter, ray.orig.z + ray.dir.z tenter) # 6. Initialize child cell coordinates childcell = Vec3i(cell.x, cell.y, cell.z) # 7. Determine octant of entry point tcx = 1 if penter.x >= center.x else 0 tcy = 1 if penter.y >= center.y else 0 tcz = 1 if penter.z >= center.z else 0 # 8. Encode octant index (0-7) child = (tcx << 2) | (tcy << 1) | tcz # 9. Update child cell coordinates childcell.x |= childbit if tcx else 0 childcell.y |= childbit if tcy else 0 childcell.z |= childbit if tcz else 0 # 10. Perform 3-way minimum to sort axis intersections axes = [0, 1, 2] axes.sort(key=lambda i: tcenter[i]) axisisects = axes childtenter = tenter childtexit = 0.0 # 11. Iterate through sorted axis intersections for i in range(3): axisidx = axisisects[i] # Guard: stop if the next plane is beyond the exit time if tcenter[axisidx] >= texit: break # 12. Calculate child exit time childtexit = min(tcenter[axisidx], texit) # 13. Cap node specific logic replaces recursive child traversal # Determine values of eight forward-neighbor voxels neighborvals = [] for diridx in range(8): if not (child & diridx): # Neighbor is within the same cap node val = capscalars[diridx] else: # Neighbor is outside; perform neighbor-finding # Standard sparse voxel neighbor lookup: compute target cell coordinates # by adding/subtracting childbit based on diridx bits, then hash/lookup. val = lookupneighbor(cell, diridx, childbit) neighborvals.append(val) # Check isovalue against min/max range of the 8 neighbors minval = min(neighborvals) maxval = max(neighborvals) if minval <= isovalue <= maxval: # Standard trilinear isosurface intersection on the 8 voxel corners if intersecttrilinear(neighborvals, isovalue): return True # 14. If ray has exited the volume if childtexit == texit: return False # 15. Update entry time for next iteration childtenter = childtexit # 16. Update child index and cell coordinates based on axis crossing axisbit = axistable[axisidx] if child & axisbit: child &= ~axisbit childcell[axisidx] &= ~childbit else: child |= axisbit childcell[axisidx] |= childbit return False Parameters axistable: {4, 2, 1}. maxdepth: The maximum depth of the octree. The condition for cap traversal is depth == maxdepth - 2. Note: The source contains a typo maxdepth -- 2, which is interpreted as maxdepth - 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Typo in Depth Check: The source code snippet uses maxdepth -- 2, which is a decrement operator in C-like languages. This is likely a typo for maxdepth - 2 or maxdepth == 2 depending on context. Neighbor Finding: The exact algorithm for finding neighbors when child & dir is true is not provided in the sources. It requires accessing voxels outside the current cap node. Isosurface Check Logic: The source code uses || in the condition isovalue >= node.childmins[child] || isovalue <= node.childmaxs[child]. This is logically unusual for a bounding box check (which typically uses &&). If childmins and childmaxs are valid, this condition is almost always true. Time Complexity: The traversal is recursive and depends on the ray path length through the octree. At the cap level, it performs a constant number of operations per ray segment, specifically eight neighbor lookups and an isosurface check. Memory Complexity: Cap nodes store scalar values for the voxels they represent. Strengths: Efficiently handles the boundary of the octree without requiring explicit child pointers for the deepest level. Limitations: Requires complex neighbor-finding logic for voxels at the boundary of cap nodes. The exact performance impact of neighbor finding is not quantified in the sources. Origin: The method is part of the "Interactive Isosurface Ray Tracing of Large Octree Volumes" paper by Knoll et al.. History: It is an adaptation of Gargantini and Atkinson's ray-octree traversal technique, specifically modified to handle the leaf-level "cap" nodes in their sparse voxel octree representation. Usage: Used in real-time isosurface rendering of large volumetric datasets. name: IEEE-754 Bit Manipulation Octree Traversal
head: Bitwise Octree Traversal, IEEE-754 Voxel Traversal, Mantissa-based Octree Traversal, Octree Ray Tracing with Bitwise Cell Indexing, Ray Traversal in Octree using IEEE-754 Bit Manipulation
body: This method performs ray traversal through a sparse voxel octree by interpreting the IEEE-754 bit representation of floating-point coordinates to determine node depth and child indices, avoiding explicit pointer chasing or coordinate division. It replaces arithmetic division and modulo operations with bitwise shifts and masks on the mantissa. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} in camera space (normalized device coordinates, range [-1, 1]). Octree data structure containing nodes and voxels (see Data Structures). Maximum traversal depth MAXDEPTH (default 12). Maximum iteration count MAXITERS (default 128). Epsilon EPSILON (default 10^{-4}). Outputs: Hit result: boolean hit, and if true, the color of the first occupied voxel encountered. The octree is stored in a flat array (e.g., SSBO in GPU implementations). OctreeNode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct OctreeNode { uint info; // Bit 0: leaf flag (1 if leaf, 0 if internal). Bits 1-8: child occupancy mask (8 bits). uint childPtr; // Index into the nodes or voxels array. }; If info & 1 is set, the node is a leaf. If info & 1 is clear, the node is internal. The occupancy mask in info (bits 1-8) indicates which of the 8 children exist. The offset to the i-th child is calculated by counting the number of set bits in mask & ((1 << i) - 1). OctreeVoxel Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct OctreeVoxel { uint rgb; // Packed RGB color. R in bits 24-31, G in 16-23, B in 8-15. }; Color components are extracted by shifting right by 24, 16, and 8 bits, masking with 0xFF, and dividing by 255.0. 1. Ray Initialization: Scale ray origin from camera space [-1, 1] to world space [1, 2]. Fix zero direction components: if any component of \mathbf{d} is zero, replace it with \pm \text{EPSILON} preserving the original sign. Clamp the magnitude of each component to at least EPSILON. Normalize \mathbf{d} and compute inverse direction \mathbf{invDir} = 1.0 / \mathbf{d}. Intersect ray with root AABB [1, 2]^3. Calculate t{enter} and t{exit}. If t{exit} < t{enter} or t{exit} < 0, return miss. Advance origin: \mathbf{o} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \max(t{enter}, 0.0). Clamp \mathbf{o} to [1, 1.9999999]^3 to prevent precision issues at the exact boundary. 2. Traversal Loop: Initialize mantissaBitIdx = 22 (corresponding to the root level, as the mantissa has 23 bits, index 22 is the MSB of the fractional part). Initialize nodeIdx to the root node index (last element in OctreeNodesSSBO). Loop for iter from 0 to MAXITERS: a. Quantize Position: Convert current position \mathbf{pos} to unsigned integer representation: u = \text{floatBitsToUint}(\mathbf{pos}). Create mask to zero out lower bits: mask = \sim(0u \ll \text{mantissaBitIdx}). Quantize position to cell minimum: \mathbf{cellMin} = \text{uintBitsToFloat}(u \ \& \ mask). b. Compute Cell Size: Calculate cell size using IEEE-754 exponent manipulation: \text{cellSize} = \text{uintBitsToFloat}((127 + \text{mantissaBitIdx} - 23) \ll 23) This effectively computes 2^{\text{mantissaBitIdx} - 23}. c. Calculate Child Index: Extract child index from the mantissa bits of \mathbf{pos}: \text{childIdx} = \text{getCellIdx}(\mathbf{pos}, \text{mantissaBitIdx}) This extracts 3 bits (X, Y, Z) at the current mantissa position to form a 0-7 index. d. Descend or Hit: Check if current node is a leaf (node.info & 1). If leaf: Check if the specific child voxel is occupied using the occupancy mask or direct index. If occupied, return hit with color from OctreeVoxel[nodeIdx + childIdx] (or appropriate offset). If not leaf: Check if child childIdx exists in node.info mask. If child exists: Calculate childPtr offset: offset = popcount(node.info.mask & ((1 << childIdx) - 1)). Update nodeIdx = node.childPtr + offset. Push nodeIdx to stack shStack[glLocalInvocationIndex][22 - mantissaBitIdx] if using stack-based backtracking. Decrement mantissaBitIdx by 1. Recompute childIdx for the new level. If child does not exist: Ascend: Find the common ancestor between the previous position (cellMin) and the new position (pos) using XOR and findMSB on their IEEE-754 representations. Update mantissaBitIdx to the level of the common ancestor. Update nodeIdx to the ancestor node. Continue loop. e. Advance Ray: Compute the position of the plane exiting the current cell along the ray direction: \mathbf{planePos} = \mathbf{cellMin} + \text{step}(0.0, \mathbf{d}) \cdot \text{cellSize} Where step(0.0, d) is 1.0 if di > 0 else 0.0 for each component. Calculate distance to exit plane t{max} using inverse ray direction: t{max} = (\mathbf{planePos} - \mathbf{pos}) \cdot \mathbf{invDir}. Clamp new position \mathbf{pos} to this distance: \mathbf{pos} \leftarrow \mathbf{pos} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t{max}. Clamp \mathbf{pos} to the neighbor cell's AABB to avoid precision issues at boundaries. Calculate neighborMin and neighborMax using bit manipulation to subtract the smallest epsilon. 3. body: A stack-based algorithm for traversing an octree structure along a ray, handling arbitrary ray directions by flipping the coordinate system and ray parameters to ensure positive traversal direction. It differs from Ray Traversal of Octree Nodes by using an explicit stack to manage backtracking and state, rather than relying solely on mid-plane intersection logic for control flow, and from Ray-Octree Traversal (Gargantini and Atkinson variant) by normalizing ray direction to simplify child index calculation via XOR masking. Inputs: An octree structure (Octree), a ray (Ray) defined by origin and direction, and the octree bounding box (min, max). Outputs: A sequence of visited octree nodes (leaf or internal) intersected by the ray, or a termination signal when the ray exits the octree or all children are visited. Data Structures: 1. Node: Represents an octree node. hasChild(unsigned int i) const: Returns true if child i exists. isLeaf() const: Returns true if the node has no children. childrenoffset[8]: Array storing offsets to children. NOCHILD indicates absence. childrenbase: Base index for child data. 2. TraversalNodeInfo: Stack element. const Node node: Pointer to the current octree node. vec3 t0: Entry t-values for the current voxel bounds (x, y, z components). vec3 t1: Exit t-values for the current voxel bounds (x, y, z components). vec3 tm: Midpoint t-values for the current voxel bounds (x, y, z components). int nextchild: Index of the next child to visit. -1 indicates first visit (unvisited). 0-7 indicates specific child index. 8 indicates all children visited. 3. TreeTraverser: Main traversal class. unsigned char a: Direction flip mask (3 bits, bit 0 for Z, bit 1 for Y, bit 2 for X). Octree const octree: Pointer to the octree. Ray ray: Modified ray with flipped direction/origin. Ray originalray: Original ray for position calculation. std::vector<TraversalNodeInfo> stack: Stack for traversal state. int stepcount: Counter for steps. Initialization (initTraversal): 1. Set stepcount = 0, a = 0. 2. Store originalray. 3. For each axis i (0=X, 1=Y, 2=Z): If ray.direction[i] < 0 for i=0,1 (X, Y) OR ray.direction[i] > 0 for i=2 (Z) [G: Specific sign check logic from source]: Flip ray.origin[i] = octree->size[i] - ray.origin[i]. Flip ray.direction[i] = -ray.direction[i]. Set bit i in a (bit 0 for Z, bit 1 for Y, bit 2 for X). 4. Calculate entry/exit t-values for the octree bounding box: tx0 = (octree->min[0] - ray.origin[0]) (1.0f / ray.direction[0]). tx1 = (octree->max[0] - ray.origin[0]) (1.0f / ray.direction[0]). ty0 = (octree->min[1] - ray.origin[1]) (1.0f / ray.direction[1]). ty1 = (octree->max[1] - ray.origin[1]) (1.0f / ray.direction[1]). tz0 = (octree->min[2] - ray.origin[2]) (1.0f / ray.direction[2]). tz1 = (octree->max[2] - ray.origin[2]) (1.0f / ray.direction[2]). 5. Check intersection: If max(max(tx0, ty0), tz0) < min(min(tx1, ty1), tz1): Create TraversalNodeInfo for root: node = octree->getRootNode() t0 = vec3(tx0, ty0, tz0) t1 = vec3(tx1, ty1, tz1) tm = vec3(0.5f (tx0 + tx1), 0.5f (ty0 + ty1), 0.5f (tz0 + tz1)). nextchild = -1 Push onto stack. Else, stack remains empty. Step Function: 1. POP: If stack is empty, return. If stack.back().nextchild == 8 (all children visited) or stack.back().node->isLeaf(), pop stack and return. 2. PUSH (First Visit): If stack.back().nextchild == -1: Calculate tm (already computed in init for root, or derived from t0 and t1 for children). Determine firstchild using firstNode(t0, tm). Set stack.back().nextchild = firstchild. 3. ADVANCE: Switch on stack.back().nextchild (0-7): Calculate childindex = currentcase ^ a. Check if stack.back().node->hasChild(childindex). If exists: Calculate new t0child, t1child bounds for the child voxel based on the child's spatial extent relative to t0, t1, tm. Create new TraversalNodeInfo: node = stack.back().node->getChild(childindex). t0 = newt0 t1 = newt1 tm = 0.5f (t0 + t1) nextchild = -1 Push new node onto stack. Set stack.back().nextchild to the next child to visit after this one. If not exists, continue to next case (or handle empty child). First Child Selection (firstNode): Given t0 and tm: 1. If tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0 (entering via YZ plane, i.e., X is the last axis to exit): Check if tym < tx0 (set bit 1 for Y). Check if tzm < tx0 (set bit 0 for Z). Result: bit1 | bit0. 2. Else if ty0 > tz0 (entering via XZ plane, i.e., Y is the last axis to exit): Check if txm < ty0 (set bit 2 for X). Check if tzm < ty0 (set bit 0 for Z). Result: bit2 | bit0. 3. Else (entering via XY plane, i.e., Z is the last axis to exit): Check if txm < tz0 (set bit 2 for X). Check if tym < tz0 (set bit 1 for Y). Result: bit2 | bit1. Position Calculation (getCurrentPosition): 1. t = stack.back().t0.max() (maximum of x, y, z components of t0). 2. answer = originalray.getRayPoint(t). 3. answer[2] = -answer[2] (negate Z to compensate for Z-flip). POP condition if top.nextchild == 8 or top.node.isleaf(): self.stack.pop() return False # PUSH condition (First visit) if top.nextchild == -1: tm = top.tm firstchild = self.firstnode(top.t0, tm) top.nextchild = firstchild # Update parent's nextchild to next sibling [G: Standard traversal logic] top.nextchild = currentcase + 1 else: # Child does not exist, move to next sibling top.nextchild = currentcase + 1 return True def firstnode(self, t0, tm): tx0, ty0, tz0 = t0.x, t0.y, t0.z txm, tym, tzm = tm.x, tm.y, tm.z if tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0: # Entering via YZ plane bit1 = 1 if tym < tx0 else 0 bit0 = 1 if tzm < tx0 else 0 return bit1 | bit0 elif ty0 > tz0: # Entering via XZ plane bit2 = 1 if txm < ty0 else 0 bit0 = 1 if tzm < ty0 else 0 return bit2 | bit0 else: # Entering via XY plane bit2 = 1 if txm < tz0 else 0 bit1 = 1 if tym < tz0 else 0 return bit2 | bit1 def getcurrentposition(self): if not self.stack: return None top = self.stack[-1] t = top.t0.max() pos = self.originalray.getpoint(t) pos.z = -pos.z # body: A ray casting algorithm that traverses an octree structure to locate leaf voxels intersected by a ray. It builds on Stack-based Octree Traversal with Direction Flipping by using a stack to store parent context for backtracking when the ray exits a voxel or skips empty space. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Octree root node. Maximum scale s{max}. Chunk size constant CHUNKSIZE and number of chunks CHUNKNUM. Outputs: The leaf voxel index/pointer where the ray terminates. Data Structures: parentStack: Array of tuples (Voxel, float, glm::ivec3) of size s{max} + 1 storing parent pointer, t{max} value, and lastPos for backtracking. Voxel structure contains validMask (bitmask for existing children), leafMask (bitmask for leaf children), and childPointers (array of child node pointers). Parameters: \epsilon: Minimum absolute value for ray direction components to avoid division by zero. Value: 2^{-s{max}} (e.g., 0.015625 for s{max}=6). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def traverserayoctree(origin, dir, root, smax, CHUNKNUM, CHUNKSIZE, epsilon): # 1. Clamp direction to avoid division by zero for axis in ('x', 'y', 'z'): if abs(dir[axis]) < epsilon: dir[axis] = math.copysign(epsilon, dir[axis]) # 2. Initial bounding box intersection tmin, tmax = findMinMax(origin, dir, root.bounds) if tmin != 9999: origin = origin + tmin dir tmax -= tmin tmin = 0.0 # 3. Initialize scale, size, idx, pos scale = smax - 1 size = (CHUNKNUM CHUNKSIZE) / 2 idx, pos = getIdx(origin, size) parent = root lastPos = pos h = tmax parentStack = [None] (smax + 1) # 4. Main traversal loop while scale < smax: cmin, cmax = findMinMax(origin, dir, pos, size) tmin = max(tmin, cmin) tcmax = min(cmax, tmax) if (parent.validMask & (1 << idx)) and tmin <= tcmax: if parent.leafMask & (1 << idx): return idx if cmax < h: parentStack[scale] = (parent, tmax, lastPos) lastPos = pos h = cmax tmax = cmax size /= 2 scale -= 1 pointerIndex = -1 for i in range(idx + 1): if parent.validMask & (1 << i): pointerIndex += 1 parent = parent.childPointers[pointerIndex] point = origin + (cmin + 0.00001) dir idx, pos = getIdx(point, size) continue else: # 5. Backtrack idx = convertIndex[idx] if idx & 2: pos.x -= size if idx & 4: pos.y -= size if parentStack[scale] is not None: parent, tmax, lastPos = parentStack[scale] scale += 1 size = 2 parentStack[scale] = None else: break return None Pitfalls: Division by zero in ray-box intersection if ray direction component is zero. Handled by clamping small components to epsilon with correct sign. Precision issues near voxel boundaries. Mitigated by adding a small offset (0.00001) to c{min} when calculating the next point. Time complexity is proportional to the number of visited nodes, significantly faster than dense grid traversal for sparse volumes. Memory complexity is O(s{max}) for the stack. Strengths include efficient empty space skipping and handling arbitrary ray directions via the parent method. Limitations include stack operation overhead and performance degradation on dense volumes. Use for sparse voxel octrees; avoid for dense volumes or when hardware ray tracing is preferred. Originated in academic projects for GPU-based volumetric ray casting. name: CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal
head: SVO Traversal, Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Casting, Sparse Voxel Octree Tracing, Stack-based Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal
body: CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal is a real-time ray traversal algorithm for sparse voxel octrees that uses a stack-based approach to navigate from the root to leaf voxels, calculating intersections with node boundaries to determine the next octant. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large sparse voxel datasets on the CPU by avoiding the overhead of recursive function calls and leveraging explicit state management for cache-friendly memory access. It sets itself apart from Recursive Octree Traversal by using an explicit stack instead of the call stack, and from Parametric Octree Traversal by relying on discrete slab boundaries or DDA steps rather than parametric intervals for child selection. The method traverses a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) stored in a linear block structure. It initializes a ray for each pixel, pushes the root node onto a stack, and iteratively processes nodes until a leaf voxel is hit or the stack is empty. Input: A Sparse Voxel Octree root node; a camera position; per-pixel ray directions; screen dimensions (WIDTH, HEIGHT); field of view factor (fov). Output: A rendered pixel color buffer. The SVO nodes are stored in a linear array. Two primary structures are used: 1. Voxel Node (Internal Node): leafmask: uint32t, 8-bit bitmask indicating which children are leaf voxels. validmasks: uint32t, 8-bit bitmask indicating which children exist (are not empty). childpointers: uint32t[8], indices into the root array for the 8 children. 2. Stack Entry (for Iterative/Stack-based traversal): voxel: Pointer or index to the current node in the linear block. octant: The octant index (0-7) of the child being visited within the parent node. rayorigin: float[3], current ray origin. raydirection: float[3], current ray direction. boxsize: float, size of the bounding box at the current stack level. corner: float[3], corner coordinate of the current bounding box. Note: The stack itself is an array of StackEntry with a top index tracking depth. 1. Initialize Ray: For each pixel (i, j), compute screen coordinates and ray direction. screen\x = (i \times fov) / WIDTH - 0.5 screen\y = (j \times fov) / HEIGHT - 0.5 direction = (screen\x \times scale.x, -1 \times scale.y, screen\y \times scale.z). Set ray origin to camera position. 2. Push Root: Push the root node of the octree onto the stack. Set initial boxsize to the root box size. Set initial corner to the root box corner (e.g., (-1, -1, -1)). Set initial octant to 0. 3. Traversal Loop: While the stack is not empty: a. Peek: Get the current stack entry. Let node be the current voxel, oct be the current octant. b. Check Validity: Check if the child at oct exists. valid = (node.validmasks >> oct) & 1. c. If Invalid: Compute childsize = boxsize 0.5. Compute childcorner by adjusting corner by childsize and oct. Mirror ray and corner for intersection: mask = octantmask(oct), mirrororigin = mirror(ray.origin, mask), mirrordirection = mirror(ray.direction, mask), mirrorcorner = mirror(childcorner, mask), mirrorcorner.adjustcorner(-childsize, mask). Compute intersection distances: tx = (mirror\corner.x - mirror\origin.x) / mirror\direction.x, ty = (mirror\corner.y - mirror\origin.y) / mirror\direction.y, tz = (mirror\corner.z - mirror\origin.z) / mirror\direction.z. Find smallest positive t and hit face: Initialize t = \infty, hit\face = 0. If tx > 0, t = tx, hit\face = 4. If ty > 0 and ty < t, t = ty, hit\face = 2. If tz > 0 and tz < t, t = tz, hit\face = 1. March ray: rayorigin += raydirection t. Transfer to sibling: octant ^= hitface. Continue loop. d. If Valid: Check if Leaf: isleaf = (node.leafmask >> oct) & 1. If Leaf: Retrieve leaf data. Compute lighting: lightness = 1.0 / (ray.squaredistance() + 1.0). Set pixel color: pixel[1] += (0xff - pixel[1]) / 64. Break loop. If Internal Node: Push child node to stack. Update boxsize = 0.5. Update corner by adding halfsize if octant bit is set. Set octant to 0. Continue loop. 4. Exit Condition: If stack is empty and no voxel hit, return default color 0xFF000000. Ray-Box Intersection: tx = (mirror\corner.x - mirror\origin.x) / mirror\direction.x ty = (mirror\corner.y - mirror\origin.y) / mirror\direction.y tz = (mirror\corner.z - mirror\origin.z) / mirror\direction.z t = \min(tx, ty, tz) where t > 0. Octant Masking: mask = ray.octant\mask(). Used to mirror ray components for slab intersection tests. MAXDETAILLEVEL: Maximum recursion depth, typically 20. WIDTH: Screen width, e.g., 1280. Return a default background color. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may cause rays to miss voxels or intersect incorrectly. Use epsilon values for comparisons if necessary. Zero Direction Components: Division by zero in ray-box intersection occurs if a ray direction component is exactly zero. Clamp or add a small epsilon to the denominator. Unverified code. mirrororigin[0]) / mirrordirection[0] ty = float('inf') if mirrordirection[1] == 0 else (mirrorcorner[1] - mirrororigin[1]) / mirrordirection[1] tz = float('inf') if mirrordirection[2] == 0 else (mirrorcorner[2] -
