leaf['pos'][k])2 for k in range(3)) lightness = 1.0 / (distsq + 1.0) pixelidx = j width + i buffer[pixelidx] = (0, int((0xff - buffer[pixelidx]) / 64 + buffer[pixelidx]), 0, 0xff) hit = True break else: halfsize = boxsize 0.5 newcorner = list(corner) if oct & 1: newcorner[0] += halfsize if oct & 2: newcorner[1] += halfsize if oct & 4: newcorner[2] += halfsize childnode = node['childpointers'][oct] stack.append({'voxel': childnode, 'octant': 0, 'rayorigin': rayorigin, 'raydirection': raydirection, 'boxsize': halfsize, 'corner': newcorner}) if not hit: pixelidx = j width + i buffer[pixelidx] = 0xFF000000 return buffer Parametric Octree Traversal is a top-down recursive algorithm for finding all voxels in a sparse voxel octree intersected by a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing non-uniform octrees without maintaining neighbor pointers or sorting potentially visited sub-voxels. It sets itself apart from bottom-up methods like Samet by avoiding neighbor finding, and from HERO by computing the sequence of visited sub-voxels sequentially using simple parametric comparisons rather than sorting. Iterative Octree Traversal is a method for raycasting against a 3D Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) that replaces recursive function calls with an explicit stack to comply with hardware constraints (such as HLSL recursion limits) or to optimize CPU cache behavior. It solves the problem of unbounded call stack depth by simulating the traversal state using fixed-size arrays or dynamic stacks, employing a greedy approach that prioritizes the closest node while handling false positives via backtracking. It sets itself apart from Recursive Octree Traversal by explicitly managing the call stack and from Parametric Octree Traversal by often using discrete slab boundaries or DDA steps rather than parametric intervals for child selection. Recursive Octree Traversal is a depth-first algorithm that processes a 3D sparse voxel octree by visiting nodes to either render them as geometry or process them for mesh generation. It differs from Iterative Octree Traversal by using the call stack instead of an explicit stack, and from Parametric Octree Traversal by relying on hierarchical node masks rather than parametric ray-marching. It builds on CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal by replacing the stack-based state machine with direct recursive function calls. Compact Voxel Octree Raycasting is a CPU-based ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees that optimizes memory layout and traversal logic by compacting active ray-voxel interactions and decoding node masks on-the-fly. It solves the problem of inefficient traversal in sparse structures by using an explicit stack to manage non-sequential memory layouts and a parallel "COMPACTIFY" step to filter out non-intersecting rays, ensuring that only valid ray-voxel pairs are processed in subsequent levels. Unlike recursive or parametric approaches, it relies on a linear block structure with explicit state management, making it suitable for high-performance CPU implementations where memory bandwidth and cache locality are critical. It builds on CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal and differs from Parametric Octree Traversal, Iterative Octree Traversal, Recursive Octree Traversal, and Sparse Voxel Octree Path Tracing by explicitly managing traversal state and compacting active ray lists between levels. Sparse Voxel Octree Path Tracing is a rendering technique that traverses a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) structure on the CPU to perform path tracing, writing results to a texture displayed via OpenGL. It differs from GPU-based SVO rendering by performing all ray marching and shading calculations on the host processor, using a linear block structure for the octree and a stack-based traversal mechanism. It builds on CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal by integrating the traversal logic into a full path tracing loop that handles light bounces and material reflectivity. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of nodes visited along the ray path. In sparse scenes, this is significantly less than dense voxel traversal. Memory Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the octree, for the stack. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable on CPU for moderate resolution scenes. Performance scales with the sparsity of the voxel data. Strengths: Efficient for sparse data; no need for neighbor pointers; explicit stack allows for easy optimization and debugging. Limitations: Stack management overhead; potential for cache misses if node layout is not optimized. When to Use: CPU-based rendering of large sparse voxel datasets; when GPU recursion limits are a concern. When Not to Use: Dense voxel data; when GPU acceleration is available and preferred. CPU Sparse Voxel Octree Traversal was developed as part of real-time voxel rendering experiments, notably in the voxl project by Robert Olsson and the zazen engine by Gabriel Muller. These projects aimed to bring real-time sparse voxel rendering to the CPU, inspired by commercial solutions like Euclideon. The method has been used in academic projects and open-source engines to demonstrate efficient CPU-based voxel rendering. rools/voxl, https://github.com/rools/voxl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Parametric Octree Traversal
head: Parametric Ray-Octree Traversal, Parametric Algorithm for Octree Traversal, Revelles 2000, Revelles' algorithm, Revelles Octree Traversal, An efficient parametric algorithm for octree traversal
body: Parametric Octree Traversal is a top-down recursive algorithm for finding the subset of voxels in a sparse voxel octree pierced by a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing non-uniform octrees without maintaining neighbor pointers or sorting potentially visited sub-voxels. It sets itself apart from bottom-up methods like Samet by avoiding neighbor finding, and from HERO by computing the sequence of visited sub-voxels sequentially using simple parametric comparisons rather than sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray r defined by origin p=(px, py, pz) and direction d=(dx, dy, dz), and an octree structure containing a root node and bounding box dimensions (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax). Output: The set of terminal (leaf) nodes intersected by the ray. Data Structures: Octree: Contains a pointer to the root node, dimensions (xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax), and sizes (sizeX, sizeY, sizeZ). Node: terminal: Boolean indicating if the node is a leaf. children: Array of 8 pointers to child nodes, indexed 0–7. (Optional) debugID: Integer identifier for debugging. Preprocessing (Handling Negative Directions): The algorithm assumes non-negative ray direction components for the base logic. If any component is negative, the ray is reflected across the center plane of the octree, and a bitmask a is set to track the inversion. 1. Initialize a = 0. 2. If dx < 0: px \leftarrow sizeX - px or px \leftarrow sizeX - px (Note: S1/S2 use size, S3/S4/S5 use center2 which is equivalent to size for axis-aligned bounds starting at 0). dx \leftarrow -dx. a |= 4. 3. If dy < 0: py \leftarrow sizeY - py or py \leftarrow sizeY - py. dy \leftarrow -dy. a |= 2. 4. If dz < 0: pz \leftarrow sizeZ - pz or pz \leftarrow sizeZ - pz. dz \leftarrow -dz. a |= 1. Parametric Interval Calculation: Compute inverse direction components for stability: divx = 1/dx, \quad divy = 1/dy, \quad divz = 1/dz Handle di=0 by allowing infinite values: x/0 = +\infty if x>0, -\infty if x<0. Compute initial entry/exit t-values for the octree bounding box: tx0 = (xmin - px) \cdot divx, \quad tx1 = (xmax - px) \cdot divx ty0 = (ymin - py) \cdot divy, \quad ty1 = (ymax - py) \cdot divy tz0 = (zmin - pz) \cdot divz, \quad tz1 = (zmax - pz) \cdot divz Intersection Test: Check if the ray intersects the octree: t{min} = \max(tx0, ty0, tz0) t{max} = \min(tx1, ty1, tz1) If t{min} \ge t{max}, the ray misses the octree. Otherwise, the algorithm calls procsubtree with the root node and the six parametric t-values. Traversal Logic (procsubtree): For a node with parametric bounds (tx0, ty0, tz0) to (tx1, ty1, tz1): 1. Early Exit: If tx1 < 0 or ty1 < 0 or tz1 < 0, return (ray is behind the viewer). 2. Leaf Check: If the node is terminal, process it and return. 3. Midpoints: Compute mid-plane parameters: txm = 0.5(tx0 + tx1) tym = 0.5(ty0 + ty1) tzm = 0.5(tz0 + tz1) 4. First Node: Determine the first child to visit using firstnode(tx0, ty0, tz0, txm, tym, tzm). 5. Loop: Iterate through children using a while loop while currnode < 8. firstnode Function: Determines the entry plane by finding \max(tx0, ty0, tz0). If tx0 is max (Entry YZ plane): Bit 1 set if tym < tx0. Bit 0 set if tzm < tx0. Return index formed by bits. Else if ty0 is max (Entry XZ plane): Bit 2 set if txm < ty0. Bit 0 set if tzm < ty0. Return index formed by bits. Else (Entry XY plane, tz0 is max): Bit 2 set if txm < tz0. Bit 1 set if tym < tz0. Return index formed by bits. newnode Function: Determines the next child to visit based on the exit plane (minimum of txm, tym, tzm). If txm < tym and txm < tzm: Return X-index (4, 5, 6, or 7 depending on context). Else if tym < tzm: Return Y-index (2, 3, 6, or 7). Else: Return Z-index (1, 3, 5, or 7). Note: The specific integer return values depend on the current state and are hardcoded in the switch cases below. Switch Case Logic (Iterating Children): The traversal uses a switch statement on currnode. For each case, it recursively calls procsubtree with the appropriate sub-volume bounds and updates currnode using newnode. The child index is accessed as node.children[currnode ^ a] to account for axis inversions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. a = 0 # Global bitmask for axis inversions def procterminal(node): # Process leaf node (e.g., accumulate color, add to list) pass def rayparameter(octree, ray): global a a = 0 if ray.dx < 0.0: ray.ox = octree.sizeX - ray.ox ray.dx = -ray.dx a |= 4 if ray.dy < 0.0: ray.oy = octree.sizeY - ray.oy ray.dy = -ray.dy a |= 2 if ray.dz < 0.0: ray.oz = octree.sizeZ - ray.oz ray.dz = -ray.dz a |= 1 tx0 = (octree.xmin - ray.ox) / ray.dx tx1 = (octree.xmax - ray.ox) / ray.dx ty0 = (octree.ymin - ray.oy) / ray.dy ty1 = (octree.ymax - ray.oy) / ray.dy tz0 = (octree.zmin - ray.oz) / ray.dz tz1 = (octree.zmax - ray.oz) / ray.dz if max(tx0, ty0, tz0) < min(tx1, ty1, tz1): procsubtree(tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1, octree.root) def procsubtree(tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1, node): if tx1 < 0.0 or ty1 < 0.0 or tz1 < 0.0: return if node.terminal: procterminal(node) return txm = 0.5 (tx0 + tx1) tym = 0.5 (ty0 + ty1) tzm = 0.5 (tz0 + tz1) currnode = firstnode(tx0, ty0, tz0, txm, tym, tzm) while currnode < 8: if currnode == 0: procsubtree(tx0, ty0, tz0, txm, tym, tzm, node.children[currnode ^ a]) currnode = newnode(txm, 4, tym, 2, tzm, 1) elif currnode == 1: procsubtree(tx0, ty0, tzm, txm, tym, tz1, node.children[currnode ^ a]) currnode = newnode(txm, 5, tym, 3, tz1, 8) elif currnode == 2: procsubtree(tx0, tym, tz0, txm, ty1, tzm, node.children[currnode ^ a]) currnode = newnode(txm, 6, ty1, 8, tzm, 3) elif currnode == 3: procsubtree(tx0, tym, tzm, txm, ty1, tz1, node.children[currnode ^ a]) currnode = newnode(txm, 7, ty1, 8, tz1, 8) elif currnode == 4: procsubtree(txm, ty0, tz0, tx1, tym, tzm, node.children[currnode ^ a]) currnode = newnode(tx1, 8, tym, 6, tzm, 5) elif currnode == 5: procsubtree(txm, ty0, tzm, tx1, tym, tz1, node.children[currnode ^ a]) currnode = newnode(tx1, 8, tym, 7, tz1, 8) elif currnode == 6: procsubtree(txm, tym, tz0, tx1, ty1, tzm, node.children[currnode ^ a]) currnode = newnode(tx1, 8, ty1, 8, tzm, 7) elif currnode == 7: procsubtree(txm, tym, tzm, tx1, ty1, tz1, node.children[currnode ^ a]) currnode = 8 def firstnode(tx0, ty0, tz0, txm, tym, tzm): if tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0: ans = 0 if tym < tx0: ans |= 2 if tzm < tx0: ans |= 1 return ans elif ty0 > tz0: ans = 0 if txm < ty0: ans |= 4 if tzm < ty0: ans |= 1 return ans else: ans = 0 if txm < tz0: ans |= 4 if tym < tz0: ans |= 2 return ans def newnode(txm, x, tym, y, tzm, z): if txm < tym: if txm < tzm: return x else: if tym < tzm: return y return z Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Components: Rays parallel to axes cause division by zero. Handled by IEEE floating point infinities (+\infty, -\infty). Negative Directions: Must be handled by reflection and bitmask a before traversal begins. No Intersection: The initial bounding box check prevents unnecessary traversal. Adapts the CPU-based parametric traversal for GPU execution using a mipmap hierarchy to privilege arithmetic over memory accesses, suitable for soft shadow computation. Applies the same parametric coordinate logic to 2D quadtrees, normalizing coordinates via flipping to avoid branching on direction signs. Complexity: Within a single parent node, the longest path involves 4 children (3 transitions), totaling 10 comparisons. Memory: Requires less memory than bottom-up methods like Samet-Net because it does not store neighbor voxel pointers. Performance: On a Silicon Graphics Indigo 2 (MIPS R4000), it was 10.4%, 12.7%, and 6.8% faster than binary tree traversal for scenes with 512, 4096, and 32768 spheres respectively. It outperforms bottom-up methods (Samet, SametCorner, SametNet) and is comparable to or faster than Gargantini. Strengths: Simple implementation, no neighbor finding, efficient for full or nearly full octrees. Limitations: Recursive implementation may cause stack overflow for very deep trees (though iterative stack-based versions exist). The algorithm was introduced by J. Revelles, C. Ureña, and M. Lastra in 2000. It is based on the principles of parametric methods for BSP trees and octrees, differing in the selection of the first sub-voxel using simple comparisons on parameter values. It avoids the neighbor finding process of Samet and the sorting of potentially visited sub-voxels of HERO. name: GPU Parametric Octree Traversal
head: GPU Ray Tracing for Visibility Computation, Lefebvre Octree Access, Octree Traversal for Shadow Rays, Ray-Traced Soft Shadows using Hierarchical Voxelization, Revelles GPU Traversal
body: This method performs visibility tests to compute physically plausible soft shadows by shooting rays from fragments to light source samples through an octree-like space-partitioning data structure, checking if rays intersect a voxel set to 1. It adapts the CPU-based parametric traversal of Revelles et al. for GPU execution, utilizing a mipmap hierarchy to privilege arithmetic operations over memory accesses, which is critical given that GPU ALU horsepower increases faster than memory bandwidth. Unlike regular grids that require accessing all voxels in a region, this hierarchical algorithm requires only a single memory access to check if a region is empty. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, octree bounding box, and a mipmap hierarchy representing the octree. Outputs: Boolean intersection result (hit/miss). Data Structures: The octree is stored as a mipmap hierarchy of 3D textures. Mipmap Levels: Each level L corresponds to an octree depth. Level 0 is the maximal mip-level (root). Texture Coordinates: A node at depth d is identified by coordinates Id = (x, y, z), where x and y are texture coordinates and 1-z is the mip-level, all mapped to the [0, 1] range. Voxel Storage: In the z-direction, the full resolution is stored to allow precise intersection masking. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Check if the ray intersects the octree bounding box. If not, return miss. Initialize the current node index I0 = (0, 0, 0), representing the root. Initialize the increment incr = 1.0. 2. Direction Handling: The base Revelles method assumes positive ray directions. If any component of \mathbf{d} is negative, reverse the traversal logic: Set Id = 1 - Id (reversed texture coordinates). Use a negative increment. 3. Traversal Loop: While the ray has not reached the light source, left the octree, or hit a primitive: Access Node: Map the normalized texture coordinates Id to the texture space [0, \text{mip-level.size}]^3. Intersection Masking: To determine if the current node contains geometry, compute the inner and outer intersections between the ray and the column defined by the current (x, y) position at the current mip-level. Mask Width: Define a small mask whose width equals the exact number of voxels hit by the ray in that column. This avoids unnecessary node refinements for empty regions. Sample: Read the voxel value(s) within the mask. Check Hit: If a voxel is set to 1 (primitive present), return hit. Refine or Advance: If the node is empty (all voxels in mask are 0), the region is empty. Terminate traversal for this ray (return miss). If the node is potentially occupied (or if refinement is required to distinguish empty space), refine to the next depth level: Increment the normalized texture coordinates (x, y) in the direction of the next visited node by incr. Update incr \leftarrow incr / 2 for each octree-depth refinement. Update Id to reflect the new depth (change in z coordinate corresponding to mip-level). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuparametricoctreetraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, octreemin, octreemax, mipmaptextures, maxdepth): # 1. Ray-AABB intersection tmin, tmax = float('-inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < octreemin[i] or rayorigin[i] > octreemax[i]: return False else: t1 = (octreemin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (octreemax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < tmin: return False # 2. Initialization x, y, z = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # I0 = (0, 0, 0) incr = 1.0 depth = 0 # 3. Negative direction handling if raydirection.x < 0 or raydirection.y < 0 or raydirection.z < 0: x, y, z = 1.0 - x, 1.0 - y, 1.0 - z incr = -incr # 4. Traversal loop while depth <= maxdepth: # Determine current level size levelsize = 1 << (maxdepth - depth) # Map normalized coordinates to texture space texx = x levelsize texy = y levelsize # z maps to full resolution in z-direction texz = z (1 << maxdepth) # Compute inner and outer intersections between ray and the column # The column spans the full z-resolution at the current (x,y) position zminidx = int(texz) zmaxidx = int(texz) + 1 # Sample mask hit = False for zidx in range(zminidx, zmaxidx + 1): voxelvalue = mipmaptextures[depth][int(zidx)][int(texy)][int(texx)] if voxelvalue == 1: hit = True break if hit: return True # If empty, region is empty. Terminate traversal. if not hit: return False # Refine to next depth level x += incr y += incr incr /= 2.0 depth += 1 # Boundary check: leave octree if coordinates exceed [0, 1] if x < 0 or x > 1 or y < 0 or y > 1: return False return False Parameters: Shadow rays per fragment: 128 in the illustrated soft shadow example. Octree Resolution: 128^3 in the performance tests. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Negative Ray Directions: The base Revelles method only deals with positive directions. Negative directions must be handled by reversing texture coordinates (Id = 1 - Id) and using a negative increment. Memory Consumption: Storing only a single bit per voxel, the memory footprint becomes prohibitive at high resolutions (e.g., 1GB for a 2048^3 resolution). Precision: Mapping normalized coordinates to texture space requires care to avoid sampling errors at boundaries. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays. Memory Complexity: Prohibitive for very high resolutions due to the octree structure (e.g., 1GB for 2048^3). Performance: On a Linux workstation (Core 2 Duo E6600, 4GB RAM, Geforce 8800GTX) with 1024x768 image resolution and 128^3 octree resolution: 0.029s for Knot scene with 1 ray/fragment. 12.104s for Knot scene with 512 rays/fragment. Performance decreases as octree resolution increases and captures more geometry details, requiring more recursion. Strengths: Privileges arithmetic operations over memory accesses. Only a single memory access is required to check if a region is empty, unlike regular grids. Limitations: High memory consumption for thin octree resolutions. The method is based on the parametric octree traversal algorithm proposed by Revelles et al. for the CPU, reformulated and simplified for GPU execution by Forest et al.. It leverages the Lefebvre et al. GPU-based algorithm for efficient octree cell access [Lefebvre et al. 05], though it explicitly solves the ray-traversal problem which Lefebvre's technique does not. It is used for real-time hierarchical binary-scene voxelization and ray-traced soft shadows. name: Parametric Quadtree Traversal
head: Parametric Quadtree Ray Traversal, parametric algorithm for octree traversal (2D variant), quadtree-raycast
body:
Parametric quadtree traversal is a top-down ray-quadtree intersection algorithm that uses parametric ray coordinates to determine the entry and exit points of a ray within a node and its children. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing non-uniform depth quadtrees without branching on ray direction signs for every step, by normalizing coordinates via flipping. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating on 2D spatial hierarchies (quadtrees) rather than 3D volumes (octrees), while sharing the same parametric coordinate logic as Parametric Octree Traversal. Inputs: Ray origin (startx, starty), ray direction (dirx, diry), quadtree root node, and the spatial bounds of the root node (quad\posx, quad\posy, size). Outputs: A list of leaf nodes (or nodes with no children) intersected by the ray, in traversal order. Quadtree Node: Contains a boolean or pointer indicating if it has children (children.isnone() implies leaf). If it has children, it contains an array of 4 child nodes indexed 0-3. Indexing: Children are indexed as: 0 (bottom-left), 1 (bottom-right), 2 (top-left), 3 (top-right). This is the standard raster order. EXIT: The integer constant 4, used to signal that no further children should be visited. Mask: A 2-bit integer (0-3) tracking coordinate flips. Bit 0 corresponds to X, Bit 1 to Y. 1. Coordinate Flipping (Normalization): To handle arbitrary ray directions without conditional branching inside the loop, flip the ray origin if the direction component is negative. If dirx < 0: startx \leftarrow 2 \cdot quad\posx + size - startx and mask \leftarrow mask \ | \ 1. If diry < 0: starty \leftarrow 2 \cdot quad\posy + size - starty and mask \leftarrow mask \ | \ 2. The direction vector components are used as absolute values |dirx| and |diry| for all subsequent parametric calculations. 2. Parametric Bounds Calculation: Compute the parametric distances t along the ray to the entry and exit planes of the current node. tx0 =  rac{quad\posx - startx}{|dirx|}. tx1 =  rac{quad\posx + size - startx}{|dirx|}. ty0 =  rac{quad\posy - starty}{|diry|}. ty1 =  rac{quad\posy + size - starty}{|diry|}. 3. Node Intersection Test: t{min} = \max(tx0, ty0) and t{max} = \min(tx1, ty1). If t{min} \ge t{max}, the ray does not intersect the node; return empty list. 4. Leaf Check: If the current node has no children, return a list containing the current node. 5. Midpoint Calculation: txm =  rac{tx0 + tx1}{2} and tym =  rac{ty0 + ty1}{2}. 6. Initial Child Selection: Determine the first child to visit based on the entry point (tx0, ty0) relative to the midpoints (txm, tym). If tx0 > ty0: if tx0 < tym, curr

ode = 2. Else (tx0 \le ty0): if ty0 < txm, curr
ode = 0; else curr

name: Iterative Octree Traversal
head: BaseOctreeRenderer, Non-recursive Octree Ray Tracing, Ray-Tree Traversal for Color Rendering, Ray-Tree Traversal for Depth Visualization, Rekursionsfreie Traversierung eines Octree, Stack-based Octree Traversal, WorkOctreeRenderer
body: Iterative Octree Traversal is a method for raycasting sparse voxel octrees on hardware that prohibits recursion, such as GPUs or specific CPU shader models, by replacing the call stack with an explicit data structure. It solves the problem of stack overflow and execution context limits by using a greedy approach that tracks the closest potential intersection, backtracking to parent nodes when a "false positive" (a parent hit but no child hit) occurs. It differs from Recursive Octree Traversal by managing traversal state explicitly, and from Parametric Octree Traversal by relying on slab-based distance comparisons rather than parametric coordinate mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray r defined by origin o and direction d, and a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) stored in a linear block structure. Output: The distance t to the closest intersected voxel, or -1 if no intersection is found. Data Structures: The algorithm simulates recursion using fixed-size arrays to track depth, parent indices, and positions. skipListPerDepth[4]: Integer array storing a bitmask of visited children for each depth level. Size 4 is sufficient for typical depth limits (e.g., 512^3 tree with 32^3 leaves). parentListPerDepth[4]: Integer array storing the index of the parent node at each depth level. positionListPerDepth[4]: Array of float3 storing the position of the parent node at each depth level. stackitemt (Alternative Implementation): A struct containing slab boundaries (tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1), node address (adr), and child index (idx). Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize skipListPerDepth, parentListPerDepth, and positionListPerDepth to zero/null. Set currentDepth = 0. Handle ray direction components: if any component is zero, add a small epsilon (e.g., 0.001) to avoid division by zero. If a component is negative, negate the ray origin and direction for that axis, and set a corresponding bit in dirmask (x=4, y=2, z=1). Compute initial slab boundaries for the root octree bounds [minx, maxx] \times [miny, maxy] \times [minz, maxz]: tx0 = \frac{minx - ox}{dx}, \quad tx1 = \frac{maxx - ox}{dx} ty0 = \frac{miny - oy}{dy}, \quad ty1 = \frac{maxy - oy}{dy} tz0 = \frac{minz - oz}{dz}, \quad tz1 = \frac{maxz - oz}{dz} Scale slab boundaries by a fixed-point factor (e.g., tnumscale = 10000) to convert to integer coordinates if using integer arithmetic. Initialize minDistToNode to infinity. 2. Traversal Loop: Iterate for a maximum number of steps (maxIterations). Identify the current node to process. In the greedy approach, this is the child of the current parent that has the smallest entry slab distance t{min}. Check for False Positives/Backtracking: If the current node is a leaf (e.g., size \le 32) and intersects the ray, perform voxel-level raycasting. If a hit is found at distance t{hit}, update minDistToNode if t{hit} < minDistToNode. If the current node is an internal node, compute its 8 children's slab boundaries. The midpoint slab boundaries are calculated as: txm = \frac{tx0 + tx1}{2}, \quad tym = \frac{ty0 + ty1}{2}, \quad tzm = \frac{tz0 + tz1}{2} For each child i, determine its slab boundaries based on its octant index bits. Cull children whose exit distance is less than or equal to the current traversal start distance, or whose entry distance is greater than the current best hit. If a child intersects and is closer than minDistToNode, push the current state (parent index, position, visited mask) to the depth arrays, increment currentDepth, and move to the child. Backtracking: If no valid child is found (false positive) or all children are processed: Decrement currentDepth. If currentDepth < 0, terminate (no hit). Retrieve the parent from parentListPerDepth and positionListPerDepth. Mark the current child as visited in skipListPerDepth using bit manipulation: skipListPerDepth[currentDepth] |= (1 << usedIndex). Proceed to the next unvisited child of the parent. 3. Termination: If minDistToNode remains infinity after traversal, return -1. Otherwise, return minDistToNode. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativeoctreetraversal(ray, octree, maxiterations): # Initialization skiplist = [0] 4 parentlist = [0] 4 positionlist = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] 4 currentdepth = 0 mindist = float('inf') # Handle ray direction dirmask = 0 if ray.d.x == 0: ray.d.x = 0.001 if ray.d.y == 0: ray.d.y = 0.001 if ray.d.z == 0: ray.d.z = 0.001 if ray.d.x < 0: ray.o.x = -ray.o.x ray.d.x = -ray.d.x dirmask |= 4 if ray.d.y < 0: ray.o.y = -ray.o.y ray.d.y = -ray.d.y dirmask |= 2 if ray.d.z < 0: ray.o.z = -ray.o.z ray.d.z = -ray.d.z dirmask |= 1 # Initial slab calculation for root tx0 = (octree.minx - ray.o.x) / ray.d.x tx1 = (octree.maxx - ray.o.x) / ray.d.x ty0 = (octree.miny - ray.o.y) / ray.d.y ty1 = (octree.maxy - ray.o.y) / ray.d.y tz0 = (octree.minz - ray.o.z) / ray.d.z tz1 = (octree.maxz - ray.o.z) / ray.d.z # Scale for integer traversal if needed tnumscale = 10000 tx0 = tnumscale; tx1 = tnumscale ty0 = tnumscale; ty1 = tnumscale tz0 = tnumscale; tz1 = tnumscale # Current node state currentnode = octree.root currentsize = octree.size currentpos = octree.origin currenttx0, currentty0, currenttz0 = tx0, ty0, tz0 currenttx1, currentty1, currenttz1 = tx1, ty1, tz1 for in range(maxiterations): # Check if leaf if currentsize <= 32: # Perform voxel raycast hit, thit = rayvoxeltest(ray, currentnode.data, currentpos, currentsize) if hit and thit < mindist: mindist = thit # If we found a hit, we might still need to check other branches for closer hits # But typically we break or continue to find the absolute closest break # Simplified: assume first valid leaf hit is closest in greedy order # Internal node: compute midpoints tmx = (currenttx0 + currenttx1) / 2 tmy = (currentty0 + currentty1) / 2 tmz = (currenttz0 + currenttz1) / 2 # Find best child bestchildidx = -1 bestchilddist = float('inf') bestchildtx0, bestchildty0, bestchildtz0 = 0, 0, 0 for i in range(8): # Skip if already visited if (skiplist[currentdepth] >> i) & 1: continue # Compute child slab boundaries based on octant i # Logic depends on dirmask and octant bits # Example for child 0 (0,0,0): ctx0, ctx1 = currenttx0, tmx cty0, cty1 = currentty0, tmy ctz0, ctz1 = currenttz0, tmz # Adjust for negative directions if dirmask & 4: ctx0, ctx1 = tmx, currenttx1 if dirmask & 2: cty0, cty1 = tmy, currentty1 if dirmask & 1: ctz0, ctz1 = tmz, currenttz1 # Culling: if child exit <= current start, skip # Note: current start is implicitly tracked by traversal logic # Simple cull: if min slab boundary < mindist, it might be closer childdist = min(ctx0, cty0, ctz0) if childdist < bestchilddist: bestchilddist = childdist bestchildidx = i bestchildtx0, bestchildty0, bestchildtz0 = ctx0, cty0, ctz0 bestchildtx1, bestchildty1, bestchildtz1 = ctx1, cty1, ctz1 if bestchildidx == -1: # Backtrack if currentdepth == 0: break currentdepth -= 1 # Restore parent state currentnode = getcontainer(parentlist[currentdepth]) currentpos = positionlist[currentdepth] currentsize = octree.size >> currentdepth # Re-calculate slabs for parent or store them # Mark current child as visited # Note: 'usedindex' would be tracked in a real implementation continue # Move to child # Save parent state positionlist[currentdepth] = currentpos parentlist[currentdepth] = currentnode.index skiplist[currentdepth] |= (1 << bestchildidx) currentdepth += 1 currentnode = getcontainer(currentnode.childstart + bestchildidx) currentsize /= 2 currentpos += octantvectors[bestchildidx] currentsize currenttx0, currentty0, currenttz0 = bestchildtx0, bestchildty0, bestchildtz0 currenttx1, currentty1, currenttz1 = bestchildtx1, bestchildty1, bestchildtz1 if mindist == float('inf'): return -1 return mindist This method accelerates sparse voxel octree (SVO) raycasting by enforcing a uniform leaf node size, thereby decoupling traversal depth from data sparsity and ensuring predictable memory access patterns. Unlike Iterative Octree Traversal, which may vary leaf granularity, this approach fixes the leaf volume to 32x32x32 voxels, optimizing for hardware cache efficiency and reducing branch divergence in GPU warps, albeit at the cost of increased false-positive checks in noisy or dense regions [3900-octree-traversal-with-fixed-size-leaf-volumes.md]. This method renders a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) on the CPU by traversing the hierarchy to project voxels into a color buffer, using depth-sorted traversal and hierarchical culling based on projected size. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by supporting Level of Detail (LOD) switching between constant-value nodes and textured bricks. It builds on Iterative Octree Traversal by adding specific logic for constant node handling and brick texture sampling. This method generates a list of spatial bricks ordered from closest to furthest relative to the viewpoint to avoid testing blocks behind untested unloaded blocks. It solves the problem of unnecessary data loading by ensuring that visibility tests are performed in an order where any previously reached node cannot be occluded by a subsequently reached node. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by integrating view-dependent axis prioritization directly into a depth-first traversal of the N3-tree structure, followed by a lightweight distance sort. Hierarchical Ray Marching is a sparse voxel traversal technique that dynamically switches between octree levels and voxel levels to optimize ray-marching performance. It differs from sibling methods by adjusting the traversal granularity up or down based on hit/miss status, allowing rapid skipping of empty regions at coarse levels and precise sampling at fine levels. Ray-Direction Child Ordering is an iterative traversal optimization for sparse voxel octrees that processes child nodes in a sequence determined by the ray's direction, ensuring nodes closer to the ray origin are visited first. It solves the inefficiency of standard recursive traversal, which examines all eight children and performs redundant intersection tests for non-intersected subtrees, by using a deterministic neighbor-linking strategy to skip empty or non-intersected branches. Unlike its siblings, it avoids recursion entirely within a node's children by maintaining a currNode state and computing the next neighbor based on exit plane t-values, thereby reducing the number of intersection tests and improving performance on sparse structures. Octree Iteration with Culling is a traversal method that visits only the leaf nodes of a sparse voxel octree that intersect a specified spatial region, typically an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB). It solves the problem of efficiently identifying relevant geometry for rendering or raycasting by skipping empty or non-intersecting subtrees, thereby reducing the number of nodes processed compared to a full tree traversal. It differs from sibling methods like Octree Traversal with Fixed-Size Leaf Volumes by supporting arbitrary leaf sizes and dynamic culling regions, and from Hierarchical Ray Marching by focusing on node enumeration rather than direct volume integration. A technique for traversing an octree for ray tracing by performing the entire traversal logic (including recursion simulation) within a single CUDA kernel execution per ray, rather than using multiple kernel launches for each recursion depth [15600-single-kernel-octree-traversal.md]. A port of the 'Efficient Sparse Voxel Octrees' algorithm, specifically excluding contour generation and beam optimization features. The traversal is a near 1:1 port of the original ESVO implementation. Node encoding was changed: relative pointers are 'backwards' to allow trees to be built without intermediate buffers (parent nodes appear after children), and far pointers are signaled by a reserved upper range rather than a dedicated bit. Memory cost is approximately 4 bytes per node. Nodes are very small (4 bytes each) and localized, with a z-curve layout resulting from building the tree in depth-first order. Performance is underwhelming because it takes many extra iterations to ascend and descend the tree and advance positions by DDA. Editing cost is approximately O(log m), leveraging path copying for persistent data structures. On Sponza 2k, ESVO achieves 95.0 Mrays/s for primary rays and 66.2 Mrays/s for primary + 1 diffuse bounce. Optimization to avoid adding children to the stack if they cannot possibly intersect the ray closer than the current best intersection t. It uses precomputed slab boundaries of children. If a child's minimum slab boundary t{i1} (for i \in \{x,y,z\}) is less than the current best intersection t{min}, the child is guaranteed not to intersect closer than t{min} and is skipped. Similarly, if a child's maximum slab boundary t{i0} is greater than t{max}, the child is skipped. Factors separating children of a node are defined as ((tx0, ty0, tz0) + (tx1, ty1, tz1)) \times 0.5. Time Complexity: O(log s) in the ideal case, where s is the initial size of the Octree. The leaf raycasting is O(1) as it always processes a fixed 32x32x32 volume. In the worst case (e.g., diagonal traversal through dense regions), it can approach O(s · log s). Memory Complexity: The stack simulation uses fixed-size arrays (e.g., depth 4), resulting in O(1) auxiliary memory for the traversal state itself, independent of tree depth. Measured Performance: On an integrated GPU, ESVO (a variant) achieves 95.0 Mrays/s for primary rays on the Sponza 2k scene (499k 8³ voxels). Strengths: Eliminates recursion limits; greedy approach reduces unnecessary node visits; fixed-size leaves optimize cache usage. Limitations: False positives require backtracking, which can be costly; fixed leaf size may waste memory in sparse regions; performance degrades with high branch divergence on GPUs if not optimized. When to use: When targeting hardware without recursion support (GPUs, HLSL) or when stack depth is unpredictable. When not to use: When memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and node size is large, or when the scene is extremely dense with no empty space to skip. Iterative Octree Traversal originated as a solution to the recursion limitations in HLSL (High-Level Shading Language) and GPU architectures, which do not support general method recursion. It was developed to enable real-time raycasting of sparse voxel octrees on GPUs by simulating the call stack explicitly. The method is closely related to the ESVO (Efficient Sparse Voxel Octrees) algorithm, which popularized the use of small, localized node structures for fast traversal. name: ESVO (Efficient Sparse Voxel Octrees)
head: Efficient Sparse Voxel Octree
body: ESVO is a GPU-based ray casting algorithm that uses a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to reduce voxel storage costs and enable real-time rendering of large scenes. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using a compact 4-byte node encoding with a depth-first (z-curve) memory layout, which optimizes for localized memory access patterns on the GPU. Unlike Hierarchical Ray Marching which may use larger leaf nodes or different traversal strategies, ESVO relies on a near 1:1 port of the original implementation with specific pointer encoding changes to facilitate buffer-less tree construction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Sparse Voxel Octree structure representing the voxel scene, camera parameters (origin, direction, near/far planes), and optionally a lower-resolution distance image for beam optimization. Output: A rendered image (color and/or depth) for the given camera view. Data Structures: The SVO consists of nodes stored in a linear array. Node Layout: Each node is 4 bytes (32 bits). Content: The node contains pointers to child nodes and potentially voxel data (density/color) if it is a leaf. The exact bit-field layout for children vs. data is not fully specified in the provided notes, but the total size is fixed at 4 bytes. Pointer Encoding: Pointers are relative. "Backwards" relative pointers are used, meaning parent nodes appear after their children in the memory layout. This allows the tree to be built without intermediate buffers. Far pointers (pointing to nodes outside the immediate local range) are signaled by a reserved upper range of pointer values, rather than using a dedicated bit flag. Memory Layout: The nodes are stored in a depth-first order, resulting in a Z-curve (Morton code) layout. This locality helps mitigate memory bandwidth issues despite the small node size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Beam Optimization (Optional): If enabled, render a lower-resolution distance image first. 2. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, compute the ray origin and direction. 3. Ray Start Adjustment: If beam optimization was performed, adjust the ray's starting position based on the distance image to skip empty space and begin marching closer to surfaces. 4. Octree Traversal: Start at the root node. Use a DDA-like approach to traverse the octree. At each node, determine which child (if internal) or voxel (if leaf) the ray intersects. Update the ray position and continue traversal until a leaf is reached or the ray exits the scene. Note: The traversal involves ascending and descending the tree, which can require many iterations. 5. Voxel Sampling: At leaf nodes, sample the voxel data (density/color) and accumulate the result along the ray. 6. Image Composition: Composite the accumulated color and depth into the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderesvo(scene, camera, usebeamoptimization=False, distanceimage=None): """ Render a scene using ESVO. scene: The SVO structure (array of 4-byte nodes). camera: Contains origin, direction, near, far. distanceimage: Optional lower-res distance map for beam optimization. """ image = emptyimage(camera.resolution) # Step 1: Beam Optimization (Optional) if usebeamoptimization and distanceimage is None: distanceimage = renderlowresdistance(scene, camera) for y in range(camera.resolution.height): for x in range(camera.resolution.width): # Step 2: Ray Initialization rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(x, y) tmin = camera.near tmax = camera.far # Step 3: Ray Start Adjustment if usebeamoptimization and distanceimage is not None: dist = distanceimage.getdistance(x, y) # Adjust start position to skip empty space rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection dist tmin = dist # Step 4: Octree Traversal currentnode = scene.root accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 while currentnode is not None and tmin < tmax: # Determine intersection with current node's bounding box or children # This involves DDA-like advancement hitnode, thit = traversenode(currentnode, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax) if hitnode is None: break # Ray exited scene or node tmin = thit currentnode = hitnode # If leaf, sample voxel if isleaf(currentnode): color, alpha = samplevoxel(currentnode, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax) accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha = composite(accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha, color, alpha) if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break # Fully opaque image.setpixel(x, y, accumulatedcolor) return image def traversenode(node, rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax): """ Traverse a single node. Returns the next node to visit and the t-value. Uses relative pointers and Z-curve layout. """ # Decode node to get child pointers or voxel data # Since pointers are relative and backwards, calculate absolute addresses if needed # For simplicity, assume node provides a method to find the next child along the ray # Determine which octant the ray enters octant = getrayoctant(rayorigin, raydirection, node.bbox) if node.isinternal: # Get pointer to the child in the specified octant # Pointer is relative; adjust for backwards layout if necessary childptr = node.getchildpointer(octant) if childptr is valid: # Calculate t for intersection with child's bbox thit = intersectbbox(childptr.bbox, rayorigin, raydirection) if thit >= tmin and thit < tmax: return childptr, thit else: # Ray misses this child, try other children or exit # This part is complex due to the specific ESVO traversal logic # which may involve backtracking or checking multiple children pass return None, tmax else: # Leaf node, return itself to be sampled return node, tmin Parameters: Beam Optimization: Boolean flag to enable/disable the two-pass rendering. Node Size: Fixed at 4 bytes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The traversal can be slow due to the many iterations required to ascend and descend the tree and advance positions by DDA. Memory Bandwidth: Although nodes are small (4 bytes), the performance can be underwhelming on integrated GPUs due to memory bandwidth limitations. Pointer Encoding: The use of "backwards" relative pointers and reserved upper ranges for far pointers requires careful implementation to avoid invalid memory accesses. Time Complexity: Traversal time depends on the scene density and tree depth. Editing cost is approximately O(\log m), leveraging path copying for persistent data structures. Memory Complexity: Memory cost is approximately 4 bytes per node. Measured Performance: On Sponza 2k (499k 8^3 voxels) on an integrated GPU: Primary rays: 95.0 Mrays/s. Primary + 1 diffuse bounce: 66.2 Mrays/s. Iterations per ray: 46.9. Clocks per iteration: 148.3. On Eco House 2k (448k 8^3 voxels) on an integrated GPU: Primary rays: 67.1 Mrays/s. Primary + 1 diffuse bounce: 52.7 Mrays/s. Iterations per ray: 147.1. Clocks per iteration: 147.1. On Forest Lake 2k (807k 8^3 voxels) on an integrated GPU: Primary rays: 60.6 Mrays/s. Primary + 1 diffuse bounce: 31.4 Mrays/s. Iterations per ray: 119.7. Clocks per iteration: 101.1. Scaling: Performance is expected to improve 5-10x on real hardware compared to integrated GPUs. Strengths: Low memory footprint (4 bytes/node), localized memory access (Z-curve layout), supports real-time rendering. Limitations: High iteration count due to tree traversal overhead, performance sensitive to memory bandwidth. When to use: Suitable for real-time rendering of large voxel scenes where memory bandwidth is not the primary bottleneck and a compact representation is needed. When not to use: When higher throughput is required and memory bandwidth is limited, or when the scene is primarily smooth surfaces where other octree traversal methods might perform better. ESVO was proposed by Samuli Laine and Tero Karras in 2010. It was designed to address the high storage costs of dense voxel representations and to enable real-time ray casting on the GPU. head: Fixed-Size Leaf Octree Traversal, 32x32x32 Leaf Traversal
body: This method accelerates sparse voxel octree (SVO) raycasting by enforcing a uniform leaf node size, thereby decoupling traversal depth from data sparsity and ensuring predictable memory access patterns. Unlike Iterative Octree Traversal, which may vary leaf granularity, this approach fixes the leaf volume to 32x32x32 voxels, optimizing for hardware cache efficiency and reducing branch divergence in GPU warps, albeit at the cost of increased false-positive checks in noisy or dense regions. The algorithm traverses an octree to find the first non-empty leaf node intersected by a ray. It uses a fixed leaf size to simplify the termination condition and optimize the inner loop. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Octree root node. Volume side length s (assumed cubic, s \times s \times s). Fixed leaf size L = 32 voxels. Outputs: Intersection point or null if no leaf is hit. Data Structures: Skip List (skipListPerDepth): An array of bitmasks, one per depth level. Each bit i indicates that the i-th child of a node at that depth has already been visited or determined empty for the current ray, preventing redundant checks. Node State: Each node has a state indicating if it is a leaf or internal. Current Depth Variable (currentDepthVariable): Tracks the depth of the current node in the traversal. Parameters: Leaf size L = 32. Volume side s. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set currentDepthVariable to 0. Initialize skipListPerDepth for all possible depths to 0. Start traversal at the root node. 2. Traversal Loop: While the current node is not a leaf: Determine the child index i (0-7) that the ray enters next. This is typically calculated using the ray's direction and the node's bounding box. Check if the bit i is set in skipListPerDepth[currentDepthVariable]. If set, the child has been processed; skip to the next sibling or backtrack. If not set, proceed to the child. Update Skip List: Mark the current child as visited by setting bit i in the skip list: \text{skipListPerDepth}[currentDepthVariable] \ |= \ (1 \ll i) Save the index and position of the current parent node for potential backtracking. Increment currentDepthVariable to move one level deeper. Move to the selected child node. 3. Leaf Processing: Once a leaf node is reached, examine the 32x32x32 voxel volume contained within it. Perform ray-voxel intersection tests within this fixed-size block to find the first occupied voxel. If an intersection is found, return the result. If no intersection is found in this leaf, backtrack to the parent and continue searching other siblings. Formulas: Diagonal Leaf Count: The number of leaf nodes along the main diagonal of the volume is derived from the Pythagorean theorem: tcountNodes = \frac{s}{64} \cdot 3 \cdot \left(\frac{s}{32}\right)^2 Note: The factor \frac{s}{64} and 3 likely relate to the specific geometric derivation of the diagonal path through the grid of leaves, where each leaf is 32 \times 32 \times 32. The term (\frac{s}{32})^2 represents the number of leaves along one axis squared, scaled by the diagonal factor. Worst-Case Complexity: tTotalCount = tcountNodes \cdot \log s + 3 \cdot 32^2 Asymptotically, this simplifies to O(s \cdot \log s). Pitfalls: Noise Sensitivity: Noise in volume data causes false positives, forcing the algorithm to examine unnecessary leaf nodes, significantly reducing efficiency. Precision Errors: Unpredictable precision errors may cause rays to miss voxels or return incorrect results, often requiring post-processing (e.g., median filtering). This variant uses Breadth-First Search (BFS) to traverse the octree, extracting plane parameters from leaf nodes into a Planes structure for each voxel. It initializes an empty dictionary and a queue with the root node. For each voxel, it iterates through the octree, popping nodes from the queue. If a node is a leaf (octostate == 0), it appends center, normal, distance, and complex attributes to a temporary Planes object. If not a leaf, it adds its non-None children to the queue. The resulting tensors are moved to CUDA. This method is distinct in its use of BFS and explicit plane parameter extraction, suitable for Gaussian Splatting applications. Time Complexity: Best-case: O(\log s) per voxel, where s is the volume side length. This occurs when the ray hits a leaf quickly. Worst-case: O(s \cdot \log s). This happens when every 32x32x32 leaf node along the diagonal (through the volume center) must be examined. Memory Complexity: Depends on the octree structure. Fixed leaf sizes reduce memory overhead compared to variable-sized leaves for sparse data, but larger leaf sizes increase the probability of false positives. Performance: Warp divergence is minimal because similar rays produce similar results within a warp. Divergence is further mitigated by the relatively low number of iterations for noise-free data. Larger leaf sizes improve efficiency for sparse data but increase false positives. Smaller leaf sizes reduce false positives but increase octree memory usage. Strengths: Predictable performance, reduced branch divergence, optimized for fixed-size hardware caches. Limitations: Sensitive to noise, potential for false positives in dense regions, fixed leaf size may not be optimal for all data distributions. This method is described in a thesis on raycasting-based voxel rendering, focusing on recursive-free traversal of octrees. It emphasizes complexity analysis and divergence analysis for GPU implementation. name: Octree Traversal with LOD & Constant Nodes
head: Octree Brick Traversal with LOD & Constant Nodes, VoxViz Traversal, main traversal loop
body: This method renders a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) on the CPU by traversing the hierarchy to project voxels into a color buffer, using depth-sorted traversal and hierarchical culling based on projected size. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by supporting Level of Detail (LOD) switching between constant-value nodes and textured bricks. It builds on Iterative Octree Traversal by adding specific logic for constant node handling and brick texture sampling. Inputs: rootnode: Root of the Sparse Voxel Octree. rayorigin, raydir: Ray position and direction in world space. config: Rendering configuration containing thresholds and scalars. fb: Framebuffer for output. Outputs: fb: Updated color buffer with rendered voxels. Exact node layouts, field sizes, and bit packing are not given in the sources. kMaxNodesPerPixel = 12. kNumNodeLists = 3. kNumComponentsPerList = 4. LodScalar: Scalar for LOD calculation. kBrickStepSizeScalar: Scalar for brick step size calculation. OctTreeDepthMinusOne: Constant derived from tree depth. RayStepSize: Base step size for ray marching. 1. Initialize traversal at root: octTreeNodePtr = ivec3(0), fetch root node, set nodeExtentMin/Max to volume bounds, nodeSize = 1.0f, voxelHalfSize = RootVoxelHalfSize. 2. Compute projected voxel size: projVoxelSize = ComputeVoxelSize(rayWorldPosition, voxelHalfSize) LodScalar. 3. LOD Decision: The condition PixelSize > projVoxelSize triggers LOD switching. 4. Constant Node Handling: If constant: compute sampleRatio = pow(kBrickStepSizeScalar, OctTreeDepthMinusOne - curDepth), fetch constant value, call TraverseConstant. 5. Textured Brick Handling: If textured: compute sampleRatio = pow(kBrickStepSizeScalar, OctTreeDepthMinusOne - curBrickDepth), compute worldRayStep = rayDir RayStepSize sampleRatio, call TraverseBrick. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctree(rootnode, rayorigin, raydir, config): octtreenodeptr = (0, 0, 0) node = rootnode nodeextentmin = config.volumeboundsmin nodeextentmax = config.volumeboundsmax nodesize = 1.0 voxelhalfsize = config.rootvoxelhalfsize curdepth = 0 curbrickdepth = 0 stack = [(node, curdepth, curbrickdepth, 0.0)] while stack: node, curdepth, curbrickdepth, t = stack.pop() projvoxelsize = computevoxelsize(rayorigin, voxelhalfsize) config.LodScalar if config.PixelSize > projvoxelsize: # LOD switching triggers here pass if node.isconstant(): sampleratio = config.kBrickStepSizeScalar (config.OctTreeDepthMinusOne - curdepth) constantvalue = node.data.color # TraverseConstant: fetch constant value and apply else: sampleratio = config.kBrickStepSizeScalar (config.OctTreeDepthMinusOne - curbrickdepth) worldraystep = raydir config.RayStepSize sampleratio # TraverseBrick: sample textured brick along world ray step children = getsortedchildren(node, rayorigin) for child in children: stack.append((child, curdepth + 1, curbrickdepth + 1, t)) def computevoxelsize(raypos, voxelhalfsize): return voxelhalfsize / max(1.0, raypos.z) def getsortedchildren(node, eye): stem = node.center diff = eye - stem a = (abs(diff.x), abs(diff.y), abs(diff.z)) if a[0] > a[1] and a[0] > a[2]: order = 0 elif a[1] > a[2]: order = 1 else: order = 2 return sorted(node.children, key=lambda c: dot(c.center - eye, eye)) LOD Interpolation: The condition PixelSize > projVoxelSize triggers LOD switching, but the source code shows commented-out interpolation logic (TraverseBrickInterp) intended to blend between parent/child bricks. This blending is not implemented, potentially causing visual artifacts at LOD boundaries. A CPU-based rasterizer that traverses a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to render voxels directly into a color buffer, utilizing depth-sorted traversal and hierarchical culling strategies that switch between rectangle and point primitives based on projected depth. It distinguishes itself from GPU-based SVO renderers by performing the entire traversal and rasterization pipeline on the CPU, relying on a flat node array and explicit stack management for memory efficiency. Time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. The method uses a fixed maximum of 12 nodes per pixel (kMaxNodesPerPixel = 12) to control traversal overhead. Strengths include LOD switching between constant and textured nodes and efficient culling using projected size thresholds. Limitations include the lack of LOD interpolation, which may cause visual artifacts at LOD boundaries, and CPU-bound execution, which can be slower than GPU-based ray marching for very large datasets. This method originates from the VoxViz project, a CPU-based rasterizer for Sparse Voxel Octrees. The traversal logic is designed to handle both constant-value nodes (for distant or low-detail rendering) and textured bricks (for high-detail rendering), with LOD switching based on projected voxel size. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Voxel Octree CPU Rasterizer
head: Marceline Cramer SVO, SVO CPU
body:
A CPU-based rasterizer that traverses a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) to render voxels directly into a color buffer, utilizing depth-sorted traversal and hierarchical culling strategies that switch between rectangle and point primitives based on projected depth. It distinguishes itself from GPU-based SVO renderers by performing the entire traversal and rasterization pipeline on the CPU, relying on a flat node array and explicit stack management for memory efficiency. Inputs: SVO: A Sparse Voxel Octree stored as a flat vector of Node structures. Camera: Contains eye position (Vec3A) and projection matrix. Framebuffer: A ColorBuffer with width, height, and pixel data. DrawConfig: Parameters controlling rendering thresholds (minrect, maxrect, maxtest). Outputs: Framebuffer: Updated pixel colors with alpha blending. Node Layout: Each Node is stored in a flat Vec and referenced by NodeRef (a usize index). occupancy: ChildMask (u8). Bitmask where bit i indicates if child i exists. occupancy == 0 denotes a leaf node. children: [NodeRef; 8]. Array of indices into the flat nodes vector. data: Payload. Contains color: u32 in ABGR format (Alpha bits 24-31, Red 16-23, Green 8-15, Blue 0-7). Default is 0xff0000ff. Traversal Order: HILBERTORDER: Static array defining the default child iteration order: [(0, 0x01), (1, 0x02), (3, 0x08), (2, 0x04), (6, 0x40), (7, 0x80), (5, 0x20), (4, 0x10)]. SORTEDORDERINDICES: A static 2D array [[ (ChildIndex, ChildMask); 8 ]; 48]. Generated by calcchildorders(), which combines 6 axis permutations with 8 flip variants each. Used for depth-sorted traversal. Frame Buffer: width, height: Dimensions. px: f32, minimum of width/height. data: Vec

(flat pixel array). Default resolution 1280x720. 1. Initialization: Create a fixed-size stack [(NodePtr, Vec3A, u32); 256] to hold (nodepointer, stemposition, depth). Push the root node onto the stack. 2. Traversal Loop (fastwalk): While the stack is not empty, pop the top element (nodeptr, stem, depth). Calculate the voxel center voxel: Compute offset = depthtooffset(depth). voxel = stem.extend(offset 1.73). Retrieve the node and check if it is a leaf (node.isleaf()). Callback: Invoke onnode(isleaf, &node.data, voxel). Culling/Recursion: If the callback returns true and the node is not a leaf: Calculate the sorting order order = Node::sortingorder(&eye, &stem). Iterate through children using forkidsordered(order). For each occupied child, calculate its origin (stem + indexoffset(index, offset)) and push (childref, origin, depth + 1) to the stack. 3. Voxel Rendering (drawvoxel): Projection: Project the voxel center voxel to screen space. vertex = voxel.extend(1.0) (Vec4). frag = projectionmatrix vertex. frag.z = -voxel.w (adjust depth). screenpos = frag.xyz / frag.w (Vec3A). Primitive Selection: Determine whether to draw a rectangle or a point based on isleaf and projected Z depth z: If NOT leaf: If z > maxrect: Perform culling test (testrect). Else if z > minrect: Draw rectangle (drawrect). Else: Draw point (drawpoint). If IS leaf: If z < minrect: Draw point (drawpoint). Else: Draw rectangle (drawrect). 4. Primitive Operations: testrect: Calculate projected bounds. If area < maxtest, call fb.testrect(bounds) to reserve space/cull. Returns true if culled. drawrect: Calculate projected bounds and call fb.drawrect(bounds, color). drawpoint: Get fragment XY coordinates via fb.fragxy(projected) and call fb.drawpoint(xy, color). 5. Framebuffer Blending (Target::draw): If destination pixel is 0, write new pixel. Else, extract destination alpha dsta. If dsta < 255, blend using a = 256 - dsta. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct from typing import List, Tuple, Callable class Vec3: def init(self, x: float, y: float, z: float): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def extend(self, w: float) -> 'Vec4': return Vec4(self.x, self.y, self.z, w) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def abs(self): return Vec3(abs(self.x), abs(self.y), abs(self.z)) class Vec4: def init(self, x: float, y: float, z: float, w: float): self.x, self.y, self.z, self.w = x, y, z, w class Node: occupancy: int # ChildMask (u8) children: List[int] # [NodeRef; 8] data: 'Payload' class Payload: color: int # ABGR u32 class DrawConfig: minrect: float maxrect: float maxtest: int def depthtooffset(depth: int) -> float: # Bit manipulation to convert integer exponent to IEEE 754 float exp = 126 - depth f = exp << 23 return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', f))[0] def indexoffset(index: int, offset: float) -> Vec3: offsets = [ (-offset, -offset, -offset), (offset, -offset, -offset), (-offset, offset, -offset), (offset, offset, -offset), (-offset, -offset, offset), (offset, -offset, offset), (-offset, offset, offset), (offset, offset, offset) ] return Vec3(offsets[index]) def sortingorder(eye: Vec3, stem: Vec3) -> int: # Determine dominant axis and sign bits for depth sorting s = 0 if eye.x >= stem.x: s |= 1 if eye.y >= stem.y: s |= 2 if eye.z >= stem.z: s |= 4 sx, sy, sz = s & 1, (s >> 1) & 1, (s >> 2) & 1 a = (eye - stem).abs() if a.x > a.y and a.x > a.z: if a.y > a.z: return (sx << 2) | (sy << 1) | sz else: return 8 + ((sx << 2) | (sz << 1) | sy) elif a.y > a.z: if a.x > a.z: return 16 + ((sy << 2) | (sx << 1) | sz) else: return 24 + ((sy << 2) | (sz << 1) | sx) else: if a.x > a.y: return 32 + ((sz << 2) | (sx << 1) | sy) else: return 40 + ((sz << 2) | (sy << 1) | sx) SORTEDORDERINDICES: List[List[Tuple[int, int]]] = [] # 48 entries of 8 tuples def fastwalk(svonodes: List[Node], eye: Vec3, onnode: Callable[[bool, Payload, Vec3], bool]): # Fixed-size stack for traversal stack: List[Tuple[int, Vec3, int]] = [(0, Vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0)] 256 stackptr = 1 while stackptr > 0: stackptr -= 1 noderef, stem, depth = stack[stackptr] node = svonodes[noderef] offset = depthtooffset(depth) voxel = stem.extend(offset 1.73) isleaf = (node.occupancy == 0) shouldrecurse = onnode(isleaf, node.data, voxel) if shouldrecurse and not isleaf: order = sortingorder(eye, stem) nextlevel = depth + 1 # Iterate children in sorted order for index, mask in SORTEDORDERINDICES[order]: if (node.occupancy & mask) != 0: childref = node.children[index] origin = stem + indexoffset(index, offset) stack[stackptr] = (childref, origin, nextlevel) stackptr += 1 def drawvoxel(fb: 'Framebuffer', config: DrawConfig, isleaf: bool, voxel: Vec3, color: int): # Project voxel center vertex = voxel.extend(1.0) frag = projmatrix vertex # projmatrix is external frag.z = -voxel.w screenpos = Vec3(frag.x / frag.w, frag.y / frag.w, frag.z / frag.w) z = screenpos.z if not isleaf: if z > config.maxrect: if testrect(fb, screenpos, config.maxtest): return if z > config.minrect: drawrect(fb, screenpos, color) else: drawpoint(fb, screenpos, color) else: if z < config.minrect: drawpoint(fb, screenpos, color) else: drawrect(fb, screenpos, color) def testrect(fb: 'Framebuffer', screenpos: Vec3, maxtest: int) -> bool: bounds = getbounds(screenpos) # Helper to compute screen bounds area = (bounds[2] - bounds[0]) (bounds[3] - bounds[1]) if area < maxtest: fb.testrect(bounds) return True return False def drawrect(fb: 'Framebuffer', screenpos: Vec3, color: int): bounds = getbounds(screenpos) fb.drawrect(bounds, color) def drawpoint(fb: 'Framebuffer', screenpos: Vec3, color: int): xy = fb.fragxy(screenpos) fb.drawpoint(xy, color) minrect: Minimum projected Z to draw as a rectangle. maxrect: Maximum projected Z to draw as a rectangle; beyond this, culling is tested. maxtest: Maximum pixel area for the culling test. MAXDEPTH: Constant set to 4 in procedural generation, controlling octree depth. Precision: The depthtooffset function uses bit manipulation to generate float offsets, which may introduce precision artifacts if not handled carefully. Stack Limit: The stack size is fixed at 256 entries. Culling Logic: The culling test (testrect) reserves space in the framebuffer. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of visited nodes in the SVO. Depth sorting adds overhead proportional to the number of internal nodes traversed. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the flat node array, where N is the number of nodes. The stack is fixed size (256 entries), making it memory-efficient for deep trees. Performance: Performance is measured on CPU hardware. Strengths: Efficient memory usage due to flat array and explicit stack; flexible traversal order based on camera position; hierarchical culling reduces overdraw. Limitations: Fixed stack size limits depth; CPU-bound performance may lag behind GPU rasterizers for high-resolution scenes; precision issues in depth calculation. The method originates from the marceline-cramer/svo-cpu repository, an unofficial implementation of a CPU-based Sparse Voxel Octree rasterizer. It builds upon hierarchical grid traversal techniques and adapts them for CPU execution, emphasizing depth-sorted rendering and efficient node management. marceline-cramer/svo-cpu, https://github.com/marceline-cramer/svo-cpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ordered List Generation via N3-Tree Traversal
head: Depth-first ordered traversal, View-dependent tree traversal
body: This method generates a list of spatial bricks ordered from closest to furthest relative to the viewpoint to avoid testing blocks behind untested unloaded blocks. It solves the problem of unnecessary data loading by ensuring that visibility tests are performed in an order where any previously reached node cannot be occluded by a subsequently reached node. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by integrating view-dependent axis prioritization directly into a depth-first traversal of the N3-tree structure, followed by a lightweight distance sort. Inputs: The root of the N3-tree. The viewpoint direction vector \vec{V} = (Vx, Vy, Vz). N, the number of subdivisions per node in the hierarchy. The viewpoint position \vec{P}, required for the final distance sort. Outputs: A list of bricks ordered by strict distance to the viewpoint. Data Structures: N3-tree: A hierarchical structure where each node represents a grid of children with N subdivisions along each axis. Traversal List: A dynamic array that accumulates visited nodes during the depth-first pass. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Begin a depth-first traversal at the root node. 2. View-Dependent Axis Ordering: At each node, determine the child visitation order by sorting the three axes based on the absolute values of the viewpoint direction vector components. 3. Start Element Calculation: Compute the starting grid index for each axis using the step formula. 4. Grid Traversal: Iterate through the N \times N \times N children of the current node, prioritizing the axis with the smallest view component as the outermost loop. 5. Recursion: For each child, repeat steps 2–4 until leaf nodes are reached. 6. Distance Sorting: Sort the accumulated list by Euclidean distance to the viewpoint to prioritize nearest bricks. Formulas: The starting element E{xyz} for each axis component is calculated as: E{xyz} = \text{step}(0, V{xyz}) \times (N - 1) Where \text{step}(0, V{xyz}) is defined as: \text{step}(0, V{xyz}) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } V{xyz} < 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Here, V{xyz} represents the component of the viewpoint direction vector along the respective axis, and N is the number of subdivisions of the nodes. Parameters: N: Number of subdivisions of the nodes in the hierarchy. \vec{V}: Viewpoint direction vector components Vx, Vy, Vz. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generateorderedlist(rootnode, viewvector, N, viewpointpos): """ Generates a list of bricks ordered from closest to furthest using N3-tree traversal. """ orderedlist = [] def getaxisorder(viewvec): axes = [0, 1, 2] axes.sort(key=lambda i: abs(viewvec[i])) return axes def getstartindex(axisidx, viewvec, N): vcomp = viewvec[axisidx] stepval = 0 if vcomp < 0 else 1 return stepval (N - 1) def traverse(node): if node.isleaf(): orderedlist.append(node) return sortedaxes = getaxisorder(viewvector) startindices = [getstartindex(ax, viewvector, N) for ax in sortedaxes] # The source specifies the starting element and axis priority for child traversal, # but does not detail the exact iteration pattern for the full N^3 grid. # We iterate through all children, prioritizing the axes as outer loops. a, b, c = sortedaxes starta, startb, startc = startindices for i in range(N): for j in range(N): for k in range(N): child = node.getchild(i, j, k) traverse(child) traverse(rootnode) # Sort the list by distance to the viewpoint to prioritize nearest bricks orderedlist.sort(key=lambda node: math.dist(node.center, viewpointpos)) return orderedlist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View Vector Alignment: If a component of the view vector is zero, the tie-breaking for axis order is not specified in the sources. A deterministic tie-breaker (e.g., fixed axis priority x < y < z) should be used. Boundary Conditions: The formula assumes N \ge 1. If N=1, the start index is always 0. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for V{xyz} < 0 should handle near-zero values carefully to avoid jitter in traversal order. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of nodes visited, O(M), as the ordered traversal is not more expensive than an arbitrary traversal. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of nodes in the output list, O(M), plus O(D) for the recursion stack where D is the tree depth. Performance: The method avoids unnecessary loading of occluded blocks by ensuring that visibility tests are performed in occlusion order. Strengths: The N3-tree structure allows easy traversal in occlusion order, ensuring that any node already reached cannot be occluded by a node reached later. Limitations: The initial traversal provides an occlusion order but not a strict distance order, requiring a sorting step to prioritize nearest bricks. The method originates from research on interactive exploration of procedural volumes, specifically utilizing the N3-tree structure. It was developed to optimize visibility detection by providing a list of bricks ordered from closest to furthest, thereby minimizing the loading of occluded blocks. The N3-tree structure facilitates this by allowing easy traversal in occlusion order. Sorting from a list already ordered by a close criterion allows rapid convergence of the sorting algorithm, greatly improving visibility algorithm efficiency without additional traversal cost. name: Hierarchical Ray Marching
head: March
body: Hierarchical Ray Marching is a sparse voxel traversal technique that dynamically switches between octree levels and voxel levels to optimize ray-marching performance. It differs from sibling methods by adjusting the traversal granularity up or down based on hit/miss status, allowing rapid skipping of empty regions at coarse levels and precise sampling at fine levels. Inputs: Ray origin (P0) and direction (D). Scene data containing octantSize (size of level-0 octants) and octreeHighestLevel (maximum octree depth index). A 3D voxel texture where each texel is a u32 storing four 8-bit voxel values packed in a specific layout. Outputs: A result structure containing hit position, normal, accumulated iterations, status (0=miss, 1=hit octree, 2=hit voxel, 3=out of bounds), voxel data, and UV coordinates. Data Structures: The voxel texture packs four 8-bit values per 32-bit texel. For a texel at grid coordinates (x, y, z) where x and z are even, the layout is: bits 0–7 store the voxel at (x, y, z), bits 8–15 store (x+1, y, z), bits 16–23 store (x, y, z+1), and bits 24–31 store (x+1, y, z+1). Extraction uses a shift count derived from the least significant bits of x and z to mask and shift the correct 8-bit segment. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize level = -1 (voxel level), totalIterations = 0, and rayPos = P0. 2. Loop for a maximum number of iterations. 3. Calculate unitSize: if level == -1, unitSize = 1; otherwise unitSize = octantSize << level. 4. Calculate maxIterations for the current step: if level == octreeHighestLevel, maxIterations = 1024; otherwise maxIterations = 4. 5. Perform traversal: if level == -1, call MarchThroughVoxels(rayPos, D, maxIterations); if level >= 0, call MarchThroughOctree(rayPos / unitSize, D, level, maxIterations). 6. Scale the hit position: rayHit.position = unitSize. 7. Update state: totalIterations += rayHit.iterations and rayPos = rayHit.position. 8. Adjust level based on rayHit.status: if status == 0 (miss) and level < octreeHighestLevel, increment level (coarser) and continue; if status == 1 (hit octree) and level > -1, decrement level (finer) and continue. 9. If status == 2 (hit voxel), copy position, normal, iterations, status, voxelData, and uv to the result and return. If status == 3 (out of bounds), copy position, status, and iterations to the result and return. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hierarchicalraymarching(rayorigin, raydir, octantsize, highestlevel, voxeltexture): level = -1 totaliterations = 0 raypos = rayorigin while True: unitsize = 1 if level == -1 else octantsize << level maxiter = 1024 if level == highestlevel else 4 if level == -1: hit = marchthroughvoxels(raypos, raydir, maxiter, voxeltexture) else: # Source does not provide octree traversal implementation. hit = marchthroughoctree(raypos / unitsize, raydir, level, maxiter) hit.position = unitsize totaliterations += hit.iterations raypos = hit.position if hit.status == 2: return {'position': hit.position, 'normal': hit.normal, 'iterations': totaliterations, 'status': 2, 'voxeldata': hit.voxeldata, 'uv': hit.uv} elif hit.status == 3: return {'position': hit.position, 'status': 3, 'iterations': totaliterations} elif hit.status == 0 and level < highestlevel: level += 1 continue elif hit.status == 1 and level > -1: level -= 1 continue def marchthroughvoxels(raypos, raydir, maxiter, voxeltexture): # Standard ray-box intersection for a uniform voxel grid. tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0.0: if raypos[i] < 0.0 or raypos[i] >= 1.0: return {'position': raypos, 'status': 0, 'iterations': 0} else: t1 = (0.0 - raypos[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (1.0 - raypos[i]) / raydir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax or tmax < 0.0: return {'position': raypos, 'status': 0, 'iterations': 0} for step in range(maxiter): t = tmin + step (tmax - tmin) / maxiter samplepos = raypos + t raydir voxelgridpos = [int(p) for p in samplepos] x, y, z = voxelgridpos shift = (x & 1) | ((z & 1) << 1) mask = 255 << (shift << 3) texel = voxeltexture[x >> 1, y, z >> 1] voxelval = (texel & mask) >> (shift << 3) if voxelval != 0: return {'position': samplepos, 'normal': raydir, 'iterations': step, 'status': 2, 'voxeldata': voxelval, 'uv': samplepos} return {'position': raypos + tmax raydir, 'status': 0, 'iterations': maxiter} def marchthroughoctree(raypos, raydir, level, maxiter): # Source does not provide octree traversal implementation. return {'position': raypos, 'status': 0, 'iterations': 0} Parameters: sceneData.octantSize: The size of octants at level 0. sceneData.octreeHighestLevel: The maximum octree level index. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary checks use any(octantPos >= vec3<u32>(dimAtLevel)) to exit early if the ray leaves the volume. Incorrect bit-shifting when extracting packed voxel values will yield wrong sampling results. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources.
