name: Woodcock Collision Estimation with Octree Acceleration
head: castRayWoodcockFast
body: An optimized ray marching method that combines Woodcock collision estimation with an octree traversal to skip empty regions and nodes that do not intersect the ray's current segment, reducing the number of volume samples. It differs from standard ray marching by using the octree to cull non-intersecting nodes, and from its parent Sparse Ray-Octree Intersection (DECIDE) by employing stochastic collision estimation within leaf nodes rather than deterministic traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray with origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and valid interval [ray.minT, ray.maxT]. An octree representing the volume. A random number generator sampler. Configuration settings containing stepSize and densityScale. Output: Accumulated color and opacity along the ray segment. Data Structures: State Struct: A stack element containing: Octree const node: Pointer to the current octree node. float minT: Entry distance of the ray into the node's bounding box, clamped to the ray's current valid range. float maxT: Exit distance of the ray from the node's bounding box, clamped to the ray's current valid range. int nodesMask: Bitmask tracking which of the 8 children of the current node have already been visited or checked for intersection. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an empty stack st. Compute the bounding box intersection range for the root node. If the ray intersects the root bounding box, push the root node with the intersection range onto st. Initialize ray.minT with a random offset: ray.minT \leftarrow ray.minT + (-\ln(\text{sampler.nextFloat()})) \times \text{settings.stepSize}. 2. Traversal Loop: While st is not empty and ray.minT \le ray.maxT: 1. Pop the top state from st to get node, minT, and maxT. 2. Clamp minT and maxT to the node's bounding box intersection and the current ray.minT. 3. If minT > maxT, the ray has passed this node; pop the stack and continue to the next iteration. 4. If node is not a leaf: Determine the child ID to traverse first based on the ray's position relative to the node's center: id = (sideX \ll 2) \mid (sideY \ll 1) \mid (sideZ), where sideX, sideY, sideZ indicate which half of the node the ray occupies. If id is already in nodesMask, skip it. Compute the bounding box intersection for the child node. If valid, push the child to st with its intersection range and break the inner loop to process it immediately. 5. If node is a leaf: Calculate invMaxOpacity as the inverse of the maximum opacity in the node, defaulting to 1.0 if not pre-computed. While minT \le maxT: Sample the volume and evaluate the transfer function to obtain color C and opacity \alpha (stored as out.w). Generate a random number u = \text{sampler.nextFloat()}. Test collision: if u < (\alpha \times \text{settings.densityScale}) \times \text{invMaxOpacity} \times \text{settings.stepSize}, accumulate C and \alpha into the ray's result. Advance minT: minT \leftarrow minT + (-\ln(\text{sampler.nextFloat()})) \times \text{invMaxOpacity} \times \text{settings.stepSize}. After the leaf loop, update ray.minT \leftarrow minT and pop the stack to process the next node. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castRayWoodcockFast(ray, octree, sampler, settings): stack = [] rootbbox = octree.root.boundingbox if not rootbbox.intersects(ray): return None rootmint, rootmaxt = rootbbox.getintersection(ray) stack.append({'node': octree.root, 'minT': rootmint, 'maxT': rootmaxt, 'nodesMask': 0}) ray.minT += (-math.log(sampler.nextfloat())) settings.stepsize while stack and ray.minT <= ray.maxT: state = stack.pop() node = state['node'] mint = state['minT'] maxt = state['maxT'] nodebbox = node.boundingbox if nodebbox.intersects(ray): nmint, nmaxt = nodebbox.getintersection(ray) mint = max(mint, nmint, ray.minT) maxt = min(maxt, nmaxt) else: mint = maxt + 1.0 if mint > maxt: continue if not node.isleaf: sidex = 1 if ray.origin.x >= node.center.x else 0 sidey = 1 if ray.origin.y >= node.center.y else 0 sidez = 1 if ray.origin.z >= node.center.z else 0 childid = (sidex << 2) | (sidey << 1) | sidez if not (state['nodesMask'] & (1 << childid)): state['nodesMask'] |= (1 << childid) child = node.children[childid] childbbox = child.boundingbox if childbbox.intersects(ray): cmint, cmaxt = childbbox.getintersection(ray) stack.append({'node': child, 'minT': cmint, 'maxT': cmaxt, 'nodesMask': 0}) break else: invmaxopacity = 1.0 / node.maxopacity if node.maxopacity > 0 else 1.0 while mint <= maxt: pos = ray.origin + ray.direction mint out = samplevolume(pos) u = sampler.nextfloat() collisionprob = (out.w settings.densityscale) invmaxopacity settings.stepsize if u < collisionprob: accumulateresult(out.color, out.w) mint += (-math.log(sampler.nextfloat())) invmaxopacity settings.stepsize ray.minT = mint Parameters: settings.stepSize: Base step size for sampling. Typical value: Not given in the sources. settings.densityScale: Scaling factor for density. Typical value: Not given in the sources. invMaxOpacity: Inverse of maximum opacity in the node. Default: 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Passed Node: If minT > maxT after clamping, the ray has exited the node's bounds; the algorithm must pop the stack and continue. Precision: Floating point precision in logarithmic calculations for step advancement may cause jitter or missed collisions if not handled carefully. Empty Nodes: The octree traversal naturally skips empty nodes if they are not pushed to the stack or if their intersection is invalid. A variant of the fast Woodcock method that uses a fixed step size within leaf nodes, accumulating opacity, and compares the accumulated opacity against a random threshold S derived from the exponential distribution. It computes maxOpacity per leaf node to adapt the step size. Initialization sets S = -\ln(\text{sampler.nextFloat()})) / \text{settings.densityScale} and sum = 0.0f. When skipping a node (empty or passed), needsJitter is set to true to ensure the next entry into a volume region is jittered. For leaf nodes, maxOpacity is computed by iterating through settings.maxOpacity for masks present in the node. The stepSize is calculated using linear interpolation between 1.0 and settings.stepSize based on settings.densityScale maxOpacity. If needsJitter is true, minT is jittered by sampler.nextFloat() stepSize - dT and needsJitter is set to false. The loop runs while minT <= maxT, sampling the volume and accumulating opacity: sum += settings.densityScale out.w stepSize. If sum >= S, the intersection is recorded and the function returns true. Finally, minT is advanced by stepSize. Time Complexity: Depends on the density of the volume and the octree depth; fewer samples are taken in empty regions due to octree culling. Memory Complexity: Stack depth is proportional to the octree depth. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space and reduces sampling rate in low-density regions via Woodcock estimation. Limitations: Stochastic nature introduces noise and requires careful tuning of stepSize and densityScale. When to use: Sparse volumes with large empty regions. When not to use: Dense volumes where deterministic marching might be more efficient or less noisy. Defined in the PathTracer repository by thewildnath. It adapts Woodcock collision estimation (delta tracking) for use with hierarchical voxel structures (octrees) to accelerate volume rendering. thewildnath/PathTracer, https://github.com/thewildnath/PathTracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LiNode Light Gathering with Octree Traversal
head: LiNode::gather
body: LiNode Light Gathering is a ray-surfel intersection method that traverses an octree of surfels to determine the closest hit color and distance for a given ray. It solves the problem of efficiently gathering lighting information from a sparse, hierarchical surfel representation. It differs from its siblings by operating on surfel primitives within octree leaves rather than triangles (Octree Voxel-Triangle Intersection Test), using deterministic traversal rather than stochastic estimation (Woodcock Collision Estimation with Octree Acceleration), or performing point queries (Octree Point Search for Closest Point). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin and direction, and a root LiNode (octree node) containing surfels. Output: The closest hit color and the distance to the hit point (t). Data Structures: LiNode: Inherits from OctreeNode. Contains min and max bounding box corners, surfelCount (integer), and surfelData (array of sharedptr<Surfel>). Surfel: Contains position, normal, and color data. Accessible via methods like normal() and position(). MAXSURFELCOUNT: The maximum number of surfels a leaf node can hold before subdivision. Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Initialize tmin to infinity and closest to the background color configuration. 2. Test the ray intersection with the current octree node's bounding box using OctreeNode::testintersect. 3. If no intersection is found, set t to infinity and return the background color. 4. If the node has children: Iterate through all 8 children. Recursively call gather on each child. Update tmin and closest if a child returns a hit with a smaller distance. 5. If the node is a leaf: Check if the ray origin is inside the leaf's bounding box. If so, return the background color with t set to infinity. Iterate through all surfels in surfelData (up to surfelCount). For each surfel: Transform the ray into the surfel's local space. Normalize the ray direction. Perform backface culling: if s->normal() (ray.direction -1) > 0, skip the surfel. Test for intersection between the ray and the surfel. If an intersection is found and the distance is less than tmin, update tmin and closest with the surfel's color. 6. Set t to tmin and return closest. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math INFINITY = float('inf') class Color: def init(self, r, g, b, a=1.0): self.r, self.g, self.b, self.a = r, g, b, a config = type('Config', (), {'background': Color(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)})() def transformpoint(mat, p): return (mat[0]p.x + mat[1]p.y + mat[2]p.z + mat[3], mat[4]p.x + mat[5]p.y + mat[6]p.z + mat[7], mat[8]p.x + mat[9]p.y + mat[10]p.z + mat[11]) def transformvector(mat, v): return (mat[0]v.x + mat[1]v.y + mat[2]v.z, mat[4]v.x + mat[5]v.y + mat[6]v.z, mat[8]v.x + mat[9]v.y + mat[10]v.z) def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2) if length == 0: return (0, 0, 0) return (v.x/length, v.y/length, v.z/length) def dot(a, b): return a.xb.x + a.yb.y + a.zb.z def intersectraysphere(origin, direction, center, radius): oc = (origin.x - center.x, origin.y - center.y, origin.z - center.z) a = dot(direction, direction) b = 2.0 dot(oc, direction) c = dot(oc, oc) - radius2 discriminant = b2 - 4ac if discriminant < 0: return None, None t = (-b - math.sqrt(discriminant)) / (2a) if t < 0: return None, None return t, None def gather(ray, node): # Step 1: Initialize tmin = INFINITY closest = config.background # Step 2: Node intersection test if not node.testintersect(ray): ray.t = INFINITY return config.background # Step 4: Internal node if node.haschildren(): for i in range(8): childt, childcolor = gather(ray, node.child(i)) if childt < tmin: tmin = childt closest = childcolor ray.t = tmin return closest # Step 5: Leaf node # Check if ray start is inside bounding box if node.isinside(ray.origin): ray.t = INFINITY return config.background # Iterate surfels for i in range(node.surfelCount): surfel = node.surfelData[i] # Transform ray to surfel local space localorigin = transformpoint(surfel.transforminverse(), ray.origin) localdirection = transformvector(surfel.transforminverse(), ray.direction) localdirection = normalize(localdirection) # Backface culling if dot(surfel.normal(), (-localdirection.x, -localdirection.y, -localdirection.z)) > 0: continue # Test intersection hitt, = intersectraysphere(localorigin, localdirection, surfel.position(), surfel.radius()) if hitt is not None and hitt < tmin: tmin = hitt closest = surfel.color() ray.t = tmin return closest Parameters and Edge Cases: MAXSURFELCOUNT: When a leaf node exceeds this count, it subdivides into 8 children and re-adds the surfels. Not given in the sources. Precision: Ray transformation to local space requires careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid false negatives in intersection tests. Degenerate Input: Rays originating inside a leaf node are handled by returning the background color, preventing self-intersection artifacts. This variant processes lighting information from surfels in a leaf node by projecting them onto Spherical Harmonics. It is chosen when compact lighting representation is needed for global illumination or ambient occlusion. It differs from standard LiNode gathering by aggregating lighting data rather than finding a single closest hit. Steps: 1. For each leaf node in the LiNode hierarchy, if surfelCount is zero, return immediately. 2. Collect all surfels from surfelData into a vector of shared pointers named surflist. 3. Project the lighting onto Spherical Harmonics by calling SHProject(surflist, 2, shc). Parameters: SHProject order is hardcoded to 2, resulting in 9 coefficients. Layout: shc is an array of 9 Spherical Harmonic coefficients (indices 0-8). Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case where N is the number of surfels, but typically O(\log N) due to octree pruning. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store surfels and octree nodes. Strengths: Efficient culling of non-intersecting nodes and surfels. Simple implementation. Limitations: Performance degrades if the octree is unbalanced or if rays intersect many surfels. Backface culling is simple and may not handle complex geometry well. When to use: Real-time rendering with surfel-based representations. When not to use: Scenes with high-frequency lighting variations requiring higher-order SH or precise ray-triangle intersection. LiNode Light Gathering is part of the Mr-Voxel project, an open-source voxel-based renderer. It was developed by cgibson as part of the broader effort to create a flexible volume and surfel rendering engine. The method leverages the hierarchical structure of the octree to accelerate ray-surfel intersection tests. Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree Point Search for Closest Point
head: PinholeRayTracer::evaluate (Octree)
body: This method uses an octree to efficiently find the closest point to a ray origin among all points intersected by the ray, filtering by a maximum range. Inputs: viewpoint: An Eigen::Affine3f defining the camera position and orientation. The ray origin rayo is extracted via viewpoint.translation(). octreesearch: An instance of pcl::octree::OctreePointCloudSearch<PointT> providing spatial indexing for the input point cloud. rangeMax: A float representing the maximum sensor range. Default is 100000.0f. hfov, vfov: Horizontal and vertical field of view in radians. hsize, vsize: Half-width and half-height of the image grid in pixels. Outputs: indices: A pcl::PointIndices object containing the indices of the closest valid points for each ray. Data Structures: rayds: std::vector<Eigen::Vector3f> storing ray directions. viewed: std::set<int> tracking processed point indices to avoid duplicates. pointsidx: std::vector<int> accumulating point indices from intersected voxels. voxels: Temporary storage for voxel centers intersected by the ray. Steps: 1. Initialize ray origin rayo from viewpoint.translation(). 2. Generate a vector of ray directions rayds by calling castRays(rayds). 3. Initialize a set viewed to keep track of processed point indices to avoid duplicates. 4. Loop over each ray direction rayds[i] for i from 0 to rayds.size() - 1. 5. For the current ray, get the centers of all voxels intersected by the ray using octreesearch.getIntersectedVoxelCenters(rayo, rayds[i], voxels). 6. For each intersected voxel in voxels, retrieve the indices of points within that voxel using octreesearch.voxelSearch(voxels[h], pointsidxtemp) and append them to pointsidx. 7. Initialize idxmin to -1 and distMin to 1e+6. 8. Loop over each point index idx in pointsidx. 9. Get the point pt from the cloud using pointsidx[idx] and convert to Eigen::Vector3f ept. 10. Calculate distance dist from rayo to ept. 11. If dist is less than rangeMax AND less than distMin, update idxmin to pointsidx[idx] and distMin to dist. 12. After checking all points for the ray, if idxmin is valid (>=0) and not already in viewed, add idxmin to indices.indices and insert it into viewed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def evaluateoctreepointsearch(viewpoint, octreesearch, cloud, rangemax, hfov, vfov, hsize, vsize): # Extract ray origin from viewpoint transformation rayo = viewpoint.translation() # Generate ray directions from camera parameters rayds = castRays(hfov, vfov, hsize, vsize) viewed = set() indices = [] for raydir in rayds: # Get voxel centers intersected by the ray voxels = octreesearch.getintersectedvoxelcenters(rayo, raydir) pointsidx = [] for voxelcenter in voxels: # Retrieve point indices within the voxel pointsidxtemp = octreesearch.voxelsearch(voxelcenter) pointsidx.extend(pointsidxtemp) idxmin = -1 distmin = 1e6 for idx in pointsidx: pt = cloud[idx] # Convert point to 3D vector ept = (pt.x, pt.y, pt.z) # Calculate Euclidean distance from ray origin dist = math.sqrt((ept[0]-rayo[0])2 + (ept[1]-rayo[1])2 + (ept[2]-rayo[2])2) if dist < rangemax and dist < distmin: idxmin = idx distmin = dist if idxmin >= 0 and idxmin not in viewed: indices.append(idxmin) viewed.add(idxmin) return indices def castRays(hfov, vfov, hsize, vsize): # Standard pinhole camera ray grid generation directions = [] for j in range(-vsize, vsize + 1): for i in range(-hsize, hsize + 1): x = math.tan(hfov i / hsize) y = math.tan(vfov j / vsize) z = 1.0 norm = math.sqrt(xx + yy + zz) directions.append((x/norm, y/norm, z/norm)) return directions Parameters: rangeMax: Default 100000.0f. RES: Default 0.02f (box resolution). HFOV, VFOV: Default MPI 160.0f / 180.0f (approx 2.79 rad). HSIZE, VSIZE: Default 6 and 4 in the example code, with commented alternatives 320 and 240. Edge Cases: If no points are within rangeMax or intersected by the ray, idxmin remains -1 and no index is added. Duplicate points across voxels are handled by the viewed set, ensuring each point is only recorded once per traversal. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Residency Octree Traversal
head: Author's residency octree traversal, Ray-Guided Volume Rendering with Residency Octree, Single Channel Residency Traversal
body: Residency Octree Traversal is a ray-guided method for sparse voxel volume rendering that determines which data bricks to load from a server into a local cache based on the current viewing ray. It solves the problem of efficient memory management and bandwidth reduction in large-scale volume visualization by skipping empty or homogeneous regions and only requesting bricks that are actually needed for rendering. It sets itself apart from standard octree traversal by integrating residency metadata directly into the traversal logic, allowing the renderer to decide whether to skip a node, use its aggregate value, or request specific voxel data based on cache status and resolution requirements. The method traverses a residency octree for each pixel's viewing ray to determine the sampling strategy and data requirements. It relies on leaf node metadata to identify empty, homogeneous, or unmapped regions, and uses residency information to manage brick caching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Viewing ray (origin, direction), current pixel coordinates, current sampling step size, desired resolution level (determined by viewing parameters like distance to camera), maximum traversal depth (derived from step size to prevent skipping over samples smaller than the step). Output: A decision for each ray sample: skip (empty), use node value (homogeneous), request brick (needed but not resident), or advance to next sample. Data Structures: Residency Octree: A hierarchical structure where each node contains metadata. Node Metadata: Includes flags for empty, homogeneous, and partially mapped states, as well as residency status of child bricks. The metadata for newly added bricks is set by the bit-wise OR of their child nodes’ bitmasks. Brick Cache: Stores resident voxel data bricks. Page-Table Hierarchy: Maps nodes and resolution levels to cached brick pages. Parameters: Desired Resolution Level (resolutionLevel): Chosen based on viewing parameters (e.g., distance to camera). Maximum Traversal Depth (traversalDepth): Chosen based on the current sampling step size to ensure the ray does not skip a distance smaller than the distance to the next ray sample. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: For each pixel, march along the viewing ray. Determine the desired resolution level and maximum traversal depth. 2. Traverse: Start at the root node (assumed to have metadata). Traverse the tree until the maximum traversal depth is reached or a terminal condition is met. 3. Check Node State: At the current node, check the metadata: Empty: If the node is empty, skip all samples along the ray that would fall into this node. Advance the ray to the next relevant node or sample. Homogeneous: If the node is homogeneous (all voxels hold approximately the same value), use the node's value directly for rendering for all samples falling into the node. Advance the ray to the next node. Not Partially Mapped: If the node is not even partially mapped, stop traversal for this ray segment and report a brick request. Refinement Needed: If the current subtree is not deep enough to reach the target traversal depth AND culling information does not allow skipping the current node, refine the residency octree by requesting a new node. 4. Retrieve Brick: If the target traversal depth is reached and the current node is non-empty and inhomogeneous: Attempt to retrieve the brick of the chosen resolution level from the brick cache. Cache Miss: If the brick is not resident, report a brick request. Try to load a brick from an alternative resolution level where the node is partially mapped. No Brick Found: If no brick is found in alternative resolutions, advance the ray to the next sample. 5. Adjust Sampling: Depending on the resolution level of the retrieved brick, potentially increase the sampling distance along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def residencyoctreetraversal(ray, stepsize, rootnode): resolutionlevel = chooseresolutionlevel(ray.depth) # View-dependent LOD traversaldepth = choosetraversaldepth(stepsize) # Step-to-depth mapping node = rootnode for i in range(traversaldepth + 1): if node.isempty(): ray = skipnode(node, ray) break if node.ishomogeneous(): ray = renderandskipnode(node, ray) break if not node.ispartiallymapped(): reportbrickrequest(node, ray, resolutionlevel) ray = skipnode(node, ray) break if i < traversaldepth: nextnode = getchildnode(node, ray) if nextnode is None or nextnode.cullinginfomissing: reportnoderequest(nextnode) # Child missing culling info implies whole subtree lacks it; # treat as if max depth reached and proceed to page lookup else: node = nextnode continue page = getpage(node, ray, resolutionlevel) if page.isunmapped: reportbrickrequest(node, ray, resolutionlevel) page = getalternativepage(node, ray, resolutionlevel) if page.isunmapped: skipbrick(node, ray) else: renderuntilnextboundary(page.brick, node, ray) break if i == traversaldepth: # Fixed from source typo (i > traversaldepth) reportbrickrequest(node, ray, resolutionlevel) ray = skipnode(node, ray) def chooseresolutionlevel(depth): return max(0, depth) def choosetraversaldepth(stepsize): return max(1, stepsize) def skipnode(node, ray): return ray.advancepastboundingbox(node) def renderandskipnode(node, ray): return ray.advancepastboundingbox(node) def getchildnode(node, ray): return node.children[ray.childindex(node)] def getpage(node, ray, resolution): return pagetable.lookup(node, ray, resolution) def getalternativepage(node, ray, resolution): return pagetable.lookupalternative(node, ray, resolution) def reportbrickrequest(node, ray, resolution): pass def reportnoderequest(node): pass def skipbrick(node, ray): return ray.advancepastboundingbox(node) def renderuntilnextboundary(brick, node, ray): return ray.advancetoboundary(brick, node) Extends the method to handle multiple volume channels simultaneously within a single ray. It solves the problem of efficient empty-space and homogeneous-node skipping in multi-volume rendering by requiring that a node be empty or homogeneous for all active channels before it can be skipped. Unlike single-channel traversal, which skips a node as soon as it is empty for that specific channel, this algorithm continues traversing deeper levels for non-empty channels until they also reach an empty or homogeneous state, ensuring no visible data is skipped. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Traversal stops early for empty or homogeneous nodes, reducing the number of cache lookups and server requests. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory usage depends on the number of resident bricks and stored metadata. Performance: Efficient for large-scale volumes with significant empty or homogeneous regions, as it minimizes data transfer and processing for irrelevant data. Performance degrades if the cache misses are frequent or if the volume is dense and inhomogeneous. Strengths: Reduces bandwidth and memory usage by only loading necessary data. Supports mixed-resolution rendering for different channels. Limitations: Requires maintaining residency metadata. Complex to implement for multi-channel scenarios where traversal must continue until all channels are processed. The method was introduced in the paper "Residency Octree: A Hybrid Approach for Scalable Web Volume Rendering". It is part of a broader effort to enable scalable volume rendering on the web, leveraging ray-guided techniques to manage data residency efficiently. The algorithm shares with SparseLeap the incremental construction of the underlying tree structure. name: Residency-octree traversal for multiple channels
head: Multi-Channel Residency Octree Traversal, Multi-channel octree traversal
body: This method extends residency-based octree traversal to handle multiple volume channels simultaneously within a single ray. It solves the problem of efficient empty-space and homogeneous-node skipping in multi-volume rendering by requiring that a node be empty or homogeneous for all active channels before it can be skipped. Unlike single-channel traversal, which skips a node as soon as it is empty for that specific channel, this algorithm continues traversing deeper levels for non-empty channels until they also reach an empty or homogeneous state, ensuring no visible data is skipped. Inputs: rootNode: The root of the residency octree. ray: The current ray being evaluated. numChannels: The total number of volume channels to render. noCullingInformation(node, channelIndex): Boolean function returning true if culling metadata (empty/homogeneous flags) is unavailable for the current node and channel. isEmpty(node, channelIndex): Boolean function returning true if the node is empty for the given channel. isHomogeneous(node, channelIndex): Boolean function returning true if the node is homogeneous for the given channel. isPartiallyMapped(node, channelIndex): Boolean function returning true if the node contains data that requires further subdivision or detailed rendering. node.depth: Integer, current depth of the node in the octree. node.spatialextent: Object containing the node's bounding box boundaries. next(node, ray): Returns the child node intersected by the ray, or an object with.missing = True if missing. Outputs: Node requests for missing culling information or missing child nodes. Brick requests for rendering, including the chosen resolution level for each channel. Data Structures: traversalDepth: Integer, the maximum depth to traverse. node: Reference to the current octree node. channelIndex: Integer, index of the current channel being processed (0 to numChannels - 1). emptyChannels: Integer, counter of channels found to be empty for the current node. homogeneousChannels: Integer, counter of channels found to be homogeneous for the current node. Parameters: traversalDepth: The maximum depth for traversal, determined by the ray step size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize traversalDepth based on the ray step size. 2. Set node to rootNode, channelIndex to 0, emptyChannels to 0, and homogeneousChannels to 0. 3. Loop while node.depth is less than or equal to traversalDepth AND channelIndex is less than numChannels. 4. If no culling information is available for the current node and channelIndex, report a node request for that node and channel, increment channelIndex, and continue to the next iteration. 5. If the current node is empty for the current channelIndex: Check if emptyChannels equals numChannels - 1. If so, skip the node by updating the ray based on the node's spatial extent, break the loop, and stop traversal for this ray. If not all channels are empty, increment emptyChannels, increment channelIndex, and continue to the next channel. 6. If the node is homogeneous for the current channel (logic mirrors empty nodes): Check if homogeneousChannels equals numChannels - 1. If so, skip the node using the spatial extent of the last homogeneous node encountered, break the loop, and stop traversal. If not all channels are homogeneous, increment homogeneousChannels, increment channelIndex, and continue. 7. If the node is not partially mapped for the current channel (i.e., it is fully mapped or requires rendering): Choose the resolution level for the current depth and channel. Report a brick request with the chosen resolution level. Increment channelIndex and break the loop to proceed to rendering. 8. If node.depth is less than traversalDepth: Determine the next node along the ray. If the next node is missing, report a node request for it. Otherwise, update the current node to the next node and continue the loop. 9. If the loop continues past the depth check (implying end of traversal or specific condition), choose the resolution level for the current channel, and increment channelIndex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def residencyoctreetraversalmultichannel(rootNode, ray, numChannels): # 1. Initialize traversal depth based on ray step size traversalDepth = chooseTraversalDepth(stepSize(ray)) # 2. Initialize state node = rootNode channelIndex = 0 emptyChannels = 0 homogeneousChannels = 0 # 3. Main traversal loop while node.depth <= traversalDepth and channelIndex < numChannels: # 4. Check for culling information availability if noCullingInformation(node, channelIndex): reportNodeRequest(node, channelIndex) channelIndex += 1 continue # 5. Handle empty nodes if isEmpty(node, channelIndex): if emptyChannels == numChannels - 1: # All channels are empty; skip this node # Skipped distance determined by spatial extent of last empty node encountered ray = skipNode(node, ray) break else: # Only some channels are empty; continue to next channel emptyChannels += 1 channelIndex += 1 continue # 6. Handle homogeneous nodes (mirrors empty node logic) if isHomogeneous(node, channelIndex): if homogeneousChannels == numChannels - 1: # All channels are homogeneous; skip this node # Skipped distance determined by spatial extent of last homogeneous node encountered ray = skipNode(node, ray) break else: # Only some channels are homogeneous; continue to next channel homogeneousChannels += 1 channelIndex += 1 continue # 7. Handle partially mapped / renderable nodes if not isPartiallyMapped(node, channelIndex): # Node is fully mapped or requires rendering resolutionLevel = chooseResolutionLevel(depth(ray), channelIndex) reportBrickRequest(node, ray, resolutionLevel, channelIndex) channelIndex += 1 break # 8. Move to next level if depth allows if node.depth < traversalDepth: nextNode = next(node, ray) if nextNode.missing: reportNodeRequest(nextNode) else: node = nextNode continue else: # End of traversal depth reached resolutionLevel = chooseResolutionLevel(depth(ray), channelIndex) reportBrickRequest(node, ray, resolutionLevel, channelIndex) channelIndex += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Node Skipping: Empty nodes can only be skipped if ALL channels are empty for that node. If a node is empty for one channel but not others, traversal must continue for the non-empty channels to find the subdivision level where they are empty. Skipped Distance: The skipped distance is determined by the spatial extent of the last empty (or homogeneous) node encountered during traversal. Since spatial extents of nodes strictly decrease between tree traversal steps, this strategy ensures that non-empty space is not skipped. Homogeneous Nodes: Homogeneous nodes are handled similarly to empty nodes. They are only skipped if all channels are homogeneous for that node. The values of the last homogeneous node encountered are used for rendering the node for each channel. A technique where different channels of a multi-volume dataset are rendered at different resolution levels to save memory and reduce sample evaluation, based on frequency content or importance. Each channel has a function that constrains the range of resolution levels to choose from, based on viewing parameters like distance to the camera. The resolution constraint function can consider frequency content, viewing parameters, and transfer functions. In Figure 7.2, human tissue data with 5 channels is rendered with mixed resolutions: pink channel at l3, orange channel at l5/l4/l0, and rest at l0. Time Complexity: In multi-volume settings, empty-space skipping may require more traversal steps than single-channel settings because multiple channels must be checked for each node. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty and homogeneous regions across multiple volumes without rendering unnecessary data. Limitations: Increased traversal overhead compared to single-channel rendering due to the need to check all channels before skipping. When to use: Multi-volume rendering where channels share spatial structure and empty/homogeneous regions are common. When not to use: Single-channel rendering where simpler traversal suffices. This method is described in the context of scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. It is part of a mixed-resolution multi-volume rendering framework that uses residency-based octrees to manage memory and traversal efficiently. name: PND3D Octree Rendering
head: PND3D
body: PND3D is a volume rendering method that uses a standard 8-way octree with non-leaf nodes containing child and solid masks, visited in front-to-back depth-first order to enable occlusion culling. It distinguishes itself by splitting the screen into large rectangular tiles determined by 3 vanishing points of the voxel grid projected to screen coordinates, allowing each tile to be rendered as an independent job starting from the root of the octree. This approach facilitates multithread optimization and specific hardware-accelerated occlusion queries using bit arrays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: a sparse voxel octree where non-leaf nodes are 64-bit structures, screen resolution, and camera parameters. Output: a rendered image. Intermediate Output: a 64-bit pixel buffer containing position and leaf node index. Data Structures: Non-leaf nodes are packed 64-bit structures with the following layout: chi (char): child byte mask (1=has children, 0=pure air/solid). sol (char): solid byte mask (1=pure solid, 0=not pure solid). mrk (char): alignment padding. mrk2 (char): alignment padding. ind (int): index pointer to the first child. Numbered Steps: 1. Tile Division: Divide the screen into large rectangular tiles determined by 3 vanishing points of the voxel grid projected to screen coordinates. 2. Bounding Box Calculation: For each tile, calculate the bounding box of the cubes more quickly by using only 4 of the 8 vertices of a cube, which are known in advance based on the tile's position relative to the vanishing points. 3. Tile Rendering Job: Render each tile as an independent job, clipped to the tile like a viewport, starting from the root of the octree, allowing for multithread optimization. 4. Occlusion Query: For every non-leaf node containing some solid, perform an occlusion query on its projected bounding box. If the width is larger than 32 pixels, assume it is visible and visit its children. If the bounding box width is 32 pixels or less, use a bit array (cover buffer) with 1 bit per pixel to test if the region is fully occluded using an 'and' instruction. If fully occluded, skip the node and its children. 5. Leaf Node Processing: For leaf nodes (solid surface voxels), visit each pixel of the bounding rectangle and perform 6 dot products in the inner loop using 2 'addps' and 2 'movmskps' instructions to determine if the pixel falls inside the projected cube (a 4- or 6-sided convex polygon). 6. First Pass (CPU): Write a 64-bit pixel to the screen containing 12 bits x, 12 bits y, 12 bits z, and a 28-bit index to the leaf node holding surface voxel information. 7. Second Pass (GPU): The GPU receives the voxel position and a pointer to its surface structure, raytraces to the known cube, determines the face, and performs texture mapping with filters like bilinear and mip mapping. Formulas: Pixel packing formula: P = (x \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ | \ ((y \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ll 12) \ | \ ((z \ \& \ 0xFFF) \ll 24) \ | \ ((idx \ \& \ 0xFFFFFFF) \ll 36), where x, y, z are 12-bit coordinates and idx is the 28-bit leaf index. Parameters: Occlusion query threshold: 32 pixels width. Nodes with projected bounding box width larger than this are assumed visible. Tile count: typically 16-48 tiles per screen. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Older ATI or Intel video cards may require overriding the default rendering mode with /arbasm for full GPU acceleration or /cpu for CPU-based emulation, which lacks trilinear filtering. Precision limits are imposed by the 12-bit coordinate storage in the 64-bit pixel format. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertile(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight, rootnode): tilebounds = computetilebounds(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight) bbox = computebbox4vertices(tilebounds) traversenode(rootnode, tilebounds, bbox) def traversenode(node, tilebounds, bbox): if not node.issolid(): return if bbox.width > 32: visitchildren(node, tilebounds) else: if isfullyoccluded(tilebounds): return visitchildren(node, tilebounds) def visitchildren(node, tilebounds): for child in node.children: childbbox = computechildbbox(child, tilebounds) traversenode(child, tilebounds, childbbox) def processleafnode(leaf, tilebounds): for pixel in leaf.boundingrectanglepixels: if ispixelinsidecube(pixel, leaf): writepixel(pixel.x, pixel.y, leaf.x, leaf.y, leaf.z, leaf.index) def isfullyoccluded(tilebounds): coverbuffer = allocatecoverbuffer(tilebounds) return coverbuffer.isfullyzero() def computetilebounds(tileid, screenwidth, screenheight): return {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": screenwidth, "h": screenheight} def computebbox4vertices(bounds): return {"x": bounds["x"], "y": bounds["y"], "w": bounds["w"], "h": bounds["h"]} def computechildbbox(child, tilebounds): return {"x": 0, "y": 0, "w": 16, "h": 16} def ispixelinsidecube(pixel, leaf): return True def allocatecoverbuffer(bounds): return {"isfullyzero": lambda: False} def writepixel(px, py, x, y, z, index): pixelval = (x & 0xFFF) | ((y & 0xFFF) << 12) | ((z & 0xFFF) << 24) | ((index & 0xFFFFFFF) << 36) return pixelval Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Multithread optimization through independent tile rendering; efficient occlusion culling using bit arrays for small bounding boxes; fast bounding box calculation using 4 vertices. Limitations: Requires specific hardware instructions ('addps', 'movmskps') for leaf node processing; may need override for older ATI or Intel video cards. When to use: When multithread optimization is desired and hardware supports the required instructions. When not to use: When using older ATI or Intel video cards without override, or when highest quality texture-mapping (trilinear filtering) is required on CPU-based emulation. PND3D was developed by Ken Silverman. It is used for volume rendering with sparse voxel octrees. The engine is available under a non-commercial license. gpdaniels/pnd3d, https://github.com/gpdaniels/pnd3d, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: GigaVoxels Ray Traversal and Rendering
head: Octree-Based Sparse Voxelization
body: GigaVoxels is a GPU-based volume rendering technique that uses an octree structure to manage brick-level data, performing adaptive level-of-detail (LOD) selection of lighting and material information during ray-marching of a sparse voxelized scene. It solves the problem of rendering large, sparse 3D scenes efficiently by storing only non-empty or non-constant regions in texture memory, using a hierarchical octree to index these "bricks". Unlike dense voxelization which stores the entire volume, GigaVoxels achieves sparsity by skipping empty space and using cone tracing to automatically select appropriate LODs based on camera distance, mimicking quadrilinear interpolation across different octree levels. Inputs: Triangle mesh geometry for voxelization. Camera position and viewing frustum. Octree structure containing node pointers and brick references. Brick pool: a large 3D texture memory region containing color, normal, and light data for voxels. Outputs: Final pixel color with accumulated lighting and material properties. Octree Node Layout: The octree is implemented in a linear buffer. Each node is stored as a 64-bit value (represented as uvec4 in GLSL). The layout is: Bits 0-29 (30 bits): Pointer to the first child node. The other seven children are accessed via offsets from this pointer. Bits 30-59 (30 bits): Pointer to the brick in the brick pool. Bits 60-63 (4 bits): Status flags (e.g., constant value flag, brick loaded flag). Brick Pool: A 3D texture (BrickSampler) storing voxel data. Each brick contains a region of voxels (e.g., 3 \times 3 \times 3 or 8 \times 8 \times 8). Bricks include border voxels (neighbors) to allow hardware texture interpolation, as neighboring bricks are not necessarily adjacent in memory. Parameters: RayStepSize: Step size of the ray in world coordinates. BrickStepVector: Step size of the ray in brick pool coordinates. BrickDimension: Number of texels in a brick. RootVoxelHalfSize: Size of the voxel in the root node. BrickPoolDimension: Dimensions of the brick pool texture. OctTreeDepthMinusOne: Tree depth minus one. MaxTreeTraversals: Maximum number of tree traversals allowed per ray. MaxNodesToPushThisFrame: Maximum nodes to push onto the node usage list per frame. LodScalar: Scalar used for LOD calculations. 1. Voxelization (Preprocessing): Convert triangles to voxels in a two-step process: 1. Check if the triangle's plane intersects the voxel. 2. Rasterize the triangle along its dominant axis (largest projected area) and check if fragments intersect the 2D projection of the voxel. Insert passing voxels into the octree. If a region of space is empty or has a constant value, the node in the octree does not point to a brick or any children. Static objects are voxelized once; dynamic objects every frame, differentiated by a flag preventing overwrites. 2. Octree Filtering (LOD Generation): Initially, only leaf nodes contain material information. Fill higher octree levels by averaging material properties of child bricks. This is done in separate passes for each level. For global illumination, lights rasterize the scene, writing direction/intensity to leaf nodes, which are then filtered up the octree. 3. Ray Traversal and Cone Tracing (Rendering): For each pixel, shoot a ray. The ray performs a top-down traversal of the octree to find the lowest node containing the ray. Cone Tracing: The sampling cone width adapts to distance. Close to the camera, the cone is thin, sampling leaf nodes (high detail). Far away, the cone widens, sampling higher octree levels (blurred/averaged data). LOD Interpolation: Perform linear interpolation between adjacent octree levels to get precise LOD, mimicking quadrilinear interpolation. Brick Sampling: Sample the brick associated with the current octree node. Use border voxels for hardware interpolation. 4. Ray Marching and Blending: Compute minimum ray-box intersection time (t{Min}) by iterating over 6 planes of the node extent. Update plane D values based on nodeExtentMin/Max. Only consider intersections where dirDotN > 0. Calculate numSteps = int(distToNodeBoundary / rayStepSize) + 1. Advance ray position: rayWorldPosition += rayDir (numSteps rayStepSize). Front-to-Back Blending: If the node is constant (constValue.a < 0.005f), advance ray to exit and return. Loop numSteps times: 1. Advance rayWorldPosition by worldRayStep. 2. If dst.a > 0.995f, advance remaining steps and return. 3. Sample source color/alpha (src). 4. Update source alpha: src.a = 1.0 - (1.0 - src.a)^{sampleRatio}. 5. Update source color: src.rgb = sampleRatio. 6. Update destination: dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nodeisconstant(octtreenode): """Check if node type bits indicate a constant value.""" nodetypebits = octtreenode[0] return (nodetypebits & 0x40000000) != 0 def getchildnodepointer(octtreenode): """Extract 30-bit child pointer split into 3 10-bit indices.""" childptrbits = octtreenode[0] return ( ((childptrbits >> 20) & 0x3FF), ((childptrbits >> 10) & 0x3FF), (childptrbits & 0x3FF)) def brickisloaded(octtreenode): """Check if brick loaded flag is set.""" brickloadedbits = octtreenode[0] return (brickloadedbits & 0x80000000) != 0 def getbrickpointer(octtreenode, brickpooldimension): """Extract 30-bit brick pointer and normalize to [0, 1].""" brickptrbits = octtreenode[1] uis = (brickptrbits >> 20) & 0x3FF uit = (brickptrbits >> 10) & 0x3FF uir = brickptrbits & 0x3FF return (uis / brickpooldimension[0], uit / brickpooldimension[1], uir / brickpooldimension[2]) def getconstantvalue(octtreenode): """Extract 32-bit constant color/alpha value.""" constbits = octtreenode[1] red = constbits & 0xFF constbits >>= 8 green = constbits & 0xFF constbits >>= 8 blue = constbits & 0xFF constbits >>= 8 alpha = constbits & 0xFF return (red / 255.0, green / 255.0, blue / 255.0, alpha / 255.0) def rendergigavoxels(rayorigin, raydir, rootocttreenode, brickpooldimension, raystepsize, sampleratio): dst = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentraypos = rayorigin currentnode = rootocttreenode # Compute ray-box intersection and step count disttoboundary = computerayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydir, currentnode.bounds) numsteps = int(disttoboundary / raystepsize) + 1 for in range(numsteps): currentraypos = currentraypos + raydir raystepsize if nodeisconstant(currentnode): constval = getconstantvalue(currentnode) if constval[3] < 0.005: break srca = 1.0 - (1.0 - constval[3]) sampleratio srcrgb = (constval[0] sampleratio, constval[1] sampleratio, constval[2] sampleratio) dst = ((1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[0] + dst[0], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[1] + dst[1], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[2] + dst[2], (1.0 - dst[3]) srca + dst[3]) if dst[3] > 0.995: break continue if not brickisloaded(currentnode): # The sources do not specify the brick loading mechanism. break brickptr = getbrickpointer(currentnode, brickpooldimension) src = sample3dtexture(BrickSampler, brickptr) # Standard 3D texture fetch srca = 1.0 - (1.0 - src[3]) sampleratio srcrgb = (src[0] sampleratio, src[1] sampleratio, src[2] sampleratio) dst = ((1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[0] + dst[0], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[1] + dst[1], (1.0 - dst[3]) srcrgb[2] + dst[2], (1.0 - dst[3]) srca + dst[3]) if dst[3] > 0.995: break # The sources do not specify the exact next-node selection logic for traversal. # currentnode = getnextocttreenode(currentnode, currentraypos) return dst Slow Octree Traversal: The octree is an indirect mechanism. Traversing down to find the correct node before sampling the brick can be slow. Non-automatic LOD Interpolation: Since bricks of different LODs are in the same memory pool, hardware quadrilinear interpolation cannot be used directly. Linear interpolation between levels must be implemented manually. Redundant Memory: Bricks contain neighbor voxels for interpolation, increasing memory usage by ~33% for 8 \times 8 \times 8 bricks. Filtering Complexity: Determining shared neighbors among bricks during the filtering process is encumbered. Time Complexity: Traversal time depends on the depth of the octree and the number of nodes visited per ray. Cone tracing allows for larger step sizes at distance, reducing samples. Global illumination adds cost due to multiple cone bounces (5 for diffuse, 1 for specular). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of non-empty/constant voxels. Brick pool size is determined by BrickPoolDimension and BrickDimension. Overhead from neighbor voxels in bricks. Performance: Enables real-time rendering of large sparse scenes. Performance degrades if the octree traversal is not optimized or if too many bricks are loaded/unloaded. Strengths: Sparsity: Does not store empty space. Adaptive LOD: Automatic detail selection based on distance. Global Illumination: Supports one-bounce GI efficiently. Limitations: Indirect sampling overhead. Manual LOD interpolation. Memory overhead from neighbor voxels. Origin: GigaVoxels was introduced by Cyril Crassin et al. in 2011. It is a key component of the rendering technology behind Unreal Engine 4. History: The technique was developed to address the limitations of dense voxelization and traditional ray tracing for large scenes. It builds on the concept of sparse voxel octrees and brick-based rendering. Usage: Used in real-time rendering engines, particularly for large-scale environments and global illumination effects. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) http://realtimevoxels.blogspot.fr/2012/09/introduction-to-gigavoxels-and-sparse.html, http://realtimevoxels.blogspot.fr/2012/09/introduction-to-gigavoxels-and-sparse.html, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Voxel Grid Raycasting with Occupancy Grid
head: Occupancy Grid Culling, empty block skipping
body: A volume rendering estimator that accelerates ray traversal and sampling by using a hierarchical sparse voxel grid (often implemented via VDB/NanoVDB structures) to skip empty space along rays, returning only sample locations within occupied cells. It differs from standard Voxel Grid Raycasting by replacing dense texture lookups with a hierarchical occupancy check that reduces texture reads by a factor of 3, and from Octree Traversal by using a fixed-resolution sparse grid with hierarchical levels rather than a dynamic tree structure for the primary traversal logic. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins tensor of shape (N, 3). raysd: Normalized ray directions tensor of shape (N, 3). estimator: An OccGridEstimator object containing: binaries: Boolean tensor of shape (L, Rx, Ry, Rz) storing occupancy masks for each level L. Must be contiguous on CPU before transfer to GPU. aabbs: Tensor of shape (L, 6) storing the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) for each level, where level i is enlarged by 2^i relative to the base. resolution: 3D resolution (Rx, Ry, Rz), default 128. levels: Number of hierarchical levels L. nearplane, farplane: Scalar distances, defaults 0.0 and 10^{10}. renderstepsize: Step size for marching, default 10^{-3}. coneangle: Cone angle for linearly-increased step size, default 0.0. alphathre: Alpha threshold for skipping empty space, default 0.0. earlystopeps: Early stop threshold, default 10^{-4}. sigmafn or alphafn: Optional callables taking (t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) and returning density or opacity values, used to skip invisible space. Only one should be provided. renderbkgd: Background color tensor. timestamps: Optional tensor for dynamic scenes. Outputs: rgb: Rendered RGB image. opacity: Accumulated opacity. depth: Accumulated depth. nrenderingsamples: Number of samples used. Data Structures: DensityGrid (or OccGridEstimator): Manages the VDB/NanoVDB structure. tree: The underlying VDB grid object. binaries: The occupancy mask. gridcoords: Integer coordinates for voxels. gridindices: Indices for voxels. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create nearplanes and farplanes tensors of shape (N) filled with nearplane and farplane respectively. If tmin is provided, clamp nearplanes to \max(t{min}, near\plane). If tmax is provided, clamp farplanes to \min(t{max}, far\plane). If stratified is True, add uniform random noise in 0, render\step\size) to nearplanes. Update alphathre to \min(alpha\thre, mean\occupancy) if visibility skipping is enabled. 2. Ray-AABB Intersection: Compute intersections for all rays against all level AABBs: t{mins}, t{maxs}, hits = \text{ray\aabb\intersect}(rays\o, rays\d, aabbs) If L > 1, concatenate t{mins} and t{maxs} along the last dimension and sort them to get t{sorted} and t{indices}. If L = 1, use unsorted concatenation and identity indices to maintain kernel compatibility. 3. Iterative [Ray Marching: Initialize raymask as a boolean tensor of shape (N) with all True. Initialize opacity, depth, and rgb tensors of shape (N, 1) and (N, 3) with zeros. Loop while itersamples < maxsamples and raymask.sum() > 0: a. Calculate nalive = raymask.sum(). b. Determine samples per alive ray: n{samples} = \max\left(\min\left(\frac{N}{n{alive}}, 64\right), min\samples\right) where min\samples = 1 if cone\angle == 0 else 4. c. Call traversegrids CUDA kernel with rays, binaries, aabbs, bounds, renderstepsize, coneangle, nsamples, raymask, and pre-computed t{sorted}/t{indices}/hits. This returns intervals, samples, and terminationplanes. The kernel traverses the sparse VDB structure, skipping empty blocks. d. Extract sample intervals: t{starts} = intervals.vals[intervals.is\left] t{ends} = intervals.vals[intervals.is\right] e. Extract valid ray indices: ray\indices = samples.ray\indices[samples.is\valid] f. Visibility Skipping (if sigmafn or alphafn is provided and alphathre > 0 or earlystopeps > 0): If sigmafn is provided, compute sigmas: positions = rays\o[ray\indices] + rays\d[ray\indices] \times \frac{t{starts} + t{ends}}{2} sigmas = \sigma\fn(t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) (Handle dynamic scenes with timestamps if present). If alphafn is provided (and sigmafn is not), compute alphas similarly. Compute masks using rendervisibilityfromdensity or rendervisibilityfromalpha with packedinfo (stacked chunkindices and chunkcounts) and thresholds. Filter rayindices, tstarts, tends using the masks. g. Query radiance field for RGB and sigma: rgbs, sigmas = \text{rgb\sigma\fn}(t{starts}, t{ends}, ray\indices) (Handle dynamic scenes with timestamps if present). h. Compute rendering weights: prefix\trans = 1 - opacity[ray\indices].squeeze(-1) weights = \text{render\weight\from\density}(sigmas, prefix\trans) i. Accumulate results: rgb = rgb + weights \times rgbs opacity = opacity + weights depth = depth + weights \times \frac{t{starts} + t{ends}}{2} j. Update itersamples by adding nsamples. 4. Finalization: Add background color: rgb = rgb + render\bkgd \times (1.0 - opacity) Compute final depth: depth = \frac{depth}{\max(opacity, \epsilon)} where \epsilon is machine epsilon. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersparsevoxelgrid(rayso, raysd, estimator, sigmafn=None, alphafn=None, nearplane=0.0, farplane=1e10, renderstepsize=1e-3, renderbkgd=None, coneangle=0.0, alphathre=0.0, earlystopeps=1e-4, timestamps=None): numrays = rayso.shape[0] device = rayso.device # 1. Initialization nearplanes = torch.full((numrays,), nearplane, device=device) farplanes = torch.full((numrays,), farplane, device=device) # Clamp near/far planes if needed (omitted tmin/tmax for brevity) # Update alphathre with mean occupancy if visibility skipping is active if (alphathre > 0.0 or earlystopeps > 0.0) and (sigmafn is not None or alphafn is not None): alphathre = min(alphathre, estimator.binaries.float().mean().item()) minsamples = 1 if coneangle == 0 else 4 # 2. Ray-AABB Intersection tmins, tmaxs, hits = rayaabbintersect(rayso, raysd, estimator.aabbs) ngrids = estimator.binaries.size(0) if ngrids > 1: tsorted, tindices = torch.sort(torch.cat([tmins, tmaxs], -1), -1) else: tsorted = torch.cat([tmins, tmaxs], -1) tindices = torch.arange(0, ngrids 2, device=device, dtype=torch.int64).expand(numrays, ngrids 2) # 3. Iterative Marching raymask = torch.ones(numrays, device=device).bool() opacity = torch.zeros(numrays, 1, device=device) depth = torch.zeros(numrays, 1, device=device) rgb = torch.zeros(numrays, 3, device=device) itersamples = 0 maxsamples = 10000 # Example limit while itersamples < maxsamples: nalive = raymask.sum().item() if nalive == 0: break nsamples = max(min(numrays // nalive, 64), minsamples) itersamples += nsamples # Traverse sparse grid intervals, samples, terminationplanes = traversegrids( rayso, raysd, estimator.binaries, estimator.aabbs, nearplanes, farplanes, renderstepsize, coneangle, nsamples, raymask, tsorted, tindices, hits) tstarts = intervals.vals[intervals.isleft] tends = intervals.vals[intervals.isright] rayindices = samples.rayindices[samples.isvalid] # Visibility Skipping if (alphathre > 0.0 or earlystopeps > 0.0) and (sigmafn is not None or alphafn is not None): if tstarts.shape[0] == 0: continue if sigmafn is not None: sigmas = sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) masks = rendervisibilityfromdensity(tstarts, tends, sigmas, torch.stack([intervals.chunkindices, intervals.chunkcounts], -1), earlystopeps, alphathre) elif alphafn is not None: alphas = alphafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) masks = rendervisibilityfromalpha(alphas, torch.stack([intervals.chunkindices, intervals.chunkcounts], -1), earlystopeps, alphathre) rayindices = rayindices[masks] tstarts = tstarts[masks] tends = tends[masks] if rayindices.numel() == 0: continue # Query Radiance Field rgbs, sigmas = rgbsigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices, rayso, raysd, timestamps) # Accumulate prefixtrans = 1.0 - opacity[rayindices].squeeze(-1) weights = renderweightfromdensity(sigmas, prefixtrans) rgb = rgb + weights[:, None] rgbs opacity = opacity + weights[:, None] depth = depth + weights[:, None] (tstarts + tends)[:, None] / 2.0 # 4. Finalization if renderbkgd is not None: rgb = rgb + renderbkgd (1.0 - opacity) depth = depth / torch.clampmin(opacity, torch.finfo(rgbs.dtype).eps) return rgb, opacity, depth, itersamples Accelerates the method by decoupling counting of occupied steps from sample generation, solving variable-length buffer issues in batched CUDA kernels. Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the grid and the number of occupied intervals. The hierarchical traversal reduces the number of texture reads significantly compared to dense grids. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the binaries tensor of shape (L, Rx, Ry, Rz) and the VDB structure overhead. For L=4, R=128, this is manageable on modern GPUs. Performance: Reduces texture reads by a factor of 3. In a specific implementation (lava-lamp), texture reads dropped from 17.6M to 5.9M per frame at 1080p in a default view, and from 138M to 46M in a full-screen lamp view. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space; compatible with hierarchical grids; reduces memory bandwidth pressure. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of occupancy grid; sorting of intersection times adds overhead for multi-level grids; precision issues may arise with very small step sizes or large bounding boxes. When to use: When the scene has large empty regions and the occupancy grid can be pre-computed or updated efficiently. When not to use: When the scene is fully dense, or when the overhead of maintaining the occupancy grid outweighs the traversal savings. The method originates from the use of hierarchical VDB (OpenVDB/NanoVDB) grids for volume rendering, specifically adapted for GPU acceleration. It is widely used in neural radiance field (NeRF) rendering pipelines, such as those in the nerfacc library and unofficial implementations like faster-occgrid. The concept of using an occupancy grid to cull empty blocks is also found in traditional volume rendering, such as in the lava-lamp simulation. name: Two-pass chunked ray traversal for occupancy grids
head: Chunked ray traversal with occupancy grid, Two-pass occupancy grid traversal
body: This method accelerates sparse voxel grid raycasting using a two-pass CUDA kernel launch that first counts the number of traversal steps per ray to allocate exact sample buffers, then fills those buffers with sample intervals and ray indices. It solves the problem of variable-length sample buffers per ray in a batched kernel by computing the exact number of occupied intervals each ray intersects, allocating a contiguous buffer, and then populating it with precise sample intervals. The method consists of two sequential CUDA kernel launches. The first pass counts the number of occupied voxel intervals (chunks) each ray traverses to determine buffer sizes. The second pass writes the actual sample data into pre-allocated tensors using the computed offsets. Inputs: grids: int64 array of pointers to nanovdb::MaskGrid (device memory). rayso: float array of shape [nrays, 3], ray origins. raysd: float array of shape [nrays, 3], ray directions. resolution: int32 array of shape [3], grid resolution per axis. aabbs: float array of shape [ngrids, 6], axis-aligned bounding boxes for each grid. hits: bool array of shape [nrays, ngrids], pre-computed ray-grid intersection flags. tsorted: float array of shape [nrays, ngrids2], sorted entry/exit distances per grid. tindices: int64 array of shape [nrays, ngrids2], indices into tsorted. nearplanes: float array of shape [nrays]. farplanes: float array of shape [nrays]. Outputs (allocated before launch): chunkcounts: int64 array of shape [nrays], number of occupied chunks per ray. chunkindices: int64 array of shape [nrays], starting index in the sample buffer for each ray. rayindices: int64 array of shape [nsamples], maps each sample to its originating ray. tleft: float array of shape [nsamples], entry distance of each sample interval. tright: float array of shape [nsamples], exit distance of each sample interval. The core data structure is the occupancy grid (nanovdb::MaskGrid), accessed via pointers in grids. The traversal relies on sorted entry/exit distances (tsorted) and their corresponding grid indices (tindices) to efficiently skip empty regions. The output buffers are flattened 1D arrays where samples from all rays are concatenated. chunkindices acts as an exclusive prefix sum of chunkcounts to determine write offsets. stepsize: float, fixed step length for traversal. coneangle: float, cone angle for frustum traversal. threads: int, threads per block. Typical value: 256. n: int, grid update frequency. Default: 16. 1. First Pass (Counting): Launch traversekernel with firstpass=true to compute ntrav per ray and store in chunkcounts. 2. Prefix Sum: Compute the cumulative sum of chunkcounts to get total sample count nsamples and starting indices for each ray's chunk. 3. Second Pass (Filling): Launch traversekernel with firstpass=false to write chunkindices, rayindices, tleft, and tright into pre-allocated tensors. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversekernel(rayso, raysd, resolution, aabbs, hits, tsorted, tindices, nearplanes, farplanes, chunkcounts, chunkindices, rayindices, tleft, tright, firstpass, nrays, ngrids): # Standard CUDA thread indexing threadidx = (blockIdx.x blockDim.x) + threadIdx.x if threadidx >= nrays: return rayid = threadidx count = 0 offset = 0 if not firstpass: offset = chunkindices[rayid] # Iterate through pre-sorted grid intervals for this ray # The exact occupancy check logic over tsorted/tindices is implementation-specific for i in range(0, ngrids 2, 2): tentry = tsorted[rayid, i] texit = tsorted[rayid, i + 1] gridid = tindices[rayid, i] # Skip grids the ray does not hit if not hits[rayid, gridid]: continue # Clamp interval to camera near/far planes tl = max(tentry, nearplanes[rayid]) tr = min(texit, farplanes[rayid]) if tl < tr: if firstpass: count += 1 else: tleft[offset] = tl tright[offset] = tr rayindices[offset] = rayid offset += 1 if firstpass: chunkcounts[rayid] = count Pre-allocation: The second pass requires pre-allocated output tensors for tleft, tright, and rayindices. Passing nullptr for these pointers in the first pass avoids overwriting or invalid memory access. Precision: Floating-point precision in tsorted and tleft/tright can cause gaps or overlaps if not handled carefully. Ensure consistent clamping to nearplanes and farplanes. Empty Rays: Rays with no hits should result in chunkcounts[rayid] = 0 and no writes in the second pass. Degenerate Input: If nrays is 0 or ngrids is 0, the kernel should handle this gracefully without launching. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{grids}) for the first pass (counting) and O(N{samples}) for the second pass (filling), where N{samples} is the total number of occupied intervals. The prefix sum is O(N{rays}). Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{grids}) for tsorted and tindices, plus O(N{samples}) for the output buffers. This is more memory-efficient than fixed-step methods if occupancy is sparse. Performance: Measured performance depends on hardware and scene density. The two-pass approach adds overhead for the counting pass but reduces memory bandwidth usage in the second pass by avoiding redundant writes. It is most beneficial when occupancy is highly variable across rays. Strengths: Exact buffer allocation, reduced memory waste, coalesced memory accesses in the second pass. Limitations: Requires two kernel launches and a prefix sum operation. Not suitable for real-time applications with strict latency constraints where the overhead of the first pass is prohibitive. This method is derived from implementations in the faster-occgrid repository, which adapts techniques from neural radiance field (NeRF) rendering to sparse occupancy grids. It addresses the inefficiency of fixed-step ray marching in sparse environments by dynamically allocating memory based on actual occupancy.
