The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computefrustumcutout(volumedata, TR, TE, d, r2): """ Computes the frustum cutout depth for each pixel. Args: volumedata: The volumetric dataset. TR: Texture of ray entry points. TE: Texture of ray exit points. d: Maximum search distance in X/Y for reference texel. r2: Radius limiting the top surface size. Returns: TC: Texture containing the cutout depth c for each pixel. """ # Pass 1: Generate Depth Texture TV TV = createemptytexture(width=TR.width, height=TR.height, channels=4) for y in range(TR.height): for x in range(TR.width): # Get ray entry and exit points PR = TR.gettexel(x, y) # Vector3 PE = TE.gettexel(x, y) # Vector3 # Define ray rayorigin = PR raydirection = normalize(PE - PR) # Trace ray to find deepest VOI voxel deepestvoxel = None maxla = 0.0 # Ray marching or traversal logic to find VOI intersection # This is a placeholder for the specific volume traversal algorithm # which is assumed to be provided by the parent IDVR context. hits = traceray(volumedata, rayorigin, raydirection, isvoi=True) if hits: # Find the hit with the maximum accumulated length for hit in hits: if hit.accumulatedlength > maxla: maxla = hit.accumulatedlength deepestvoxel = hit.position # (x, y, z) if deepestvoxel is not None: TV.settexel(x, y, [deepestvoxel.x, deepestvoxel.y, deepestvoxel.z, maxla]) else: TV.settexel(x, y, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Pass 2: Define Cutout TC = createemptytexture(width=TR.width, height=TR.height, channels=1) r1 = math.sqrt(d2 + d2) for y in range(TR.height): for x in range(TR.width): PR = TR.gettexel(x, y) PVtexel = TV.gettexel(x, y) # Skip if no VOI hit in this column if PVtexel[3] == 0: TC.settexel(x, y, 0.0) # Or handle as no cutout continue # Implementation 3 (Recommended for smoothness) # Find PVd: texel in TV within distance d in X/Y with highest la bestPVd = None bestla = -1.0 # Search bounds xmin = max(0, x - d) xmax = min(TV.width - 1, x + d) ymin = max(0, y - d) ymax = min(TV.height - 1, y + d) for sy in range(ymin, ymax + 1): for sx in range(xmin, xmax + 1): candidatetexel = TV.gettexel(sx, sy) if candidatetexel[3] > 0: # Calculate distance in screen space (X/Y only) distsq = (sx - x)2 + (sy - y)2 if distsq <= d2: if candidatetexel[3] > bestla: bestla = candidatetexel[3] bestPVd = candidatetexel # [x, y, z, la] if bestPVd is None: TC.settexel(x, y, 0.0) continue # PVd is bestPVd # Calculate vector PR PVd # Note: PR is in view space/clip space? The source implies PR and PV # are in the same coordinate system for distance calculation. # Assuming PR is the entry point in 3D space and PVd.xyz is the voxel position. # We need to ensure they are comparable. The source says "vector PR PVd". # Let's assume PR is the 3D position of the ray entry. PVdpos = Vector3(bestPVd[0], bestPVd[1], bestPVd[2]) vecPRPVd = PVdpos - PR lenPRPVd = length(vecPRPVd) # Calculate RVd # R is defined using congruence theorem of triangles, constructing an edge # with 90 degrees angle from the view ray to V. # This implies RVd is the projection of the vector from Ray Origin to V # onto the plane perpendicular to the ray? Or the distance from the ray axis? # "edge with an angle of 90 degrees could be constructed from the view ray to V" # This usually means the perpendicular distance from the ray to the point V. # Let's calculate the perpendicular distance from the ray (Origin, Direction) to Point V. # Ray Origin = PR # Ray Direction = normalize(PE - PR) PE = TE.gettexel(x, y) raydir = normalize(PE - PR) # Vector from Ray Origin to V vecOV = PVdpos - PR # Project vecOV onto raydir projlen = dot(vecOV, raydir) # Perpendicular component (this is likely |RVd|) # RVd is the vector component perpendicular to the ray? # The source says "If |RV| <= r2... the ray hits the top surface". # And c is the depth. # Let's assume |RVd| is the length of the perpendicular vector from the ray to V. projvec = raydir projlen perpvec = vecOV - projvec lenRVd = length(perpvec) # Determine depth c # Formula 3: c = |RVd| - |RVd| (|PR PV| - r2) / (r1 - r2) # Note: Source uses |PR PV| in the fraction, not |PR PVd|. # But logically it should be the distance to the selected point. # Source text: "c = |RVd| - |RVd| (|PR PV| - r2) / (r1 - r2)." # It uses |PR PV| generically. In Impl 3, PV is PVd. if lenRVd <= r2: # Hits top surface # The depth value c is set to the depth value of Vd? # Source: "the depth value c of the cutout for the current view ray was set to the depth value of V." # But then it gives a formula. # "If |RV| was within a radius r2... the depth value c... was set to the depth value of V." # Then it says "Otherwise... calculated as follows". # This implies if it hits the top surface, c is simply the depth of V (along the ray?). # However, the formula (3) is provided in the context of the "smoothest result". # Let's look at the structure: # "If |RV| <= r2... depth value c... set to depth value of V. Otherwise... c =..." # So if lenRVd <= r2, c = depth of Vd. # Depth of Vd along the ray is projlen. c = projlen else: # Part of frustum face # Formula 3 numerator = lenPRPVd - r2 denominator = r1 - r2 if denominator == 0: c = lenRVd # Avoid division by zero else: c = lenRVd - lenRVd (numerator / denominator) TC.settexel(x, y, c) return TC Time Complexity: Two passes over the image resolution. Pass 1 is standard volume raycasting. Pass 2 involves a local search of radius d for each pixel, making it O(W \cdot H \cdot d^2). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for TR, TE, TV, and TC. TV stores 4 floats per pixel. Strengths: Maintains correct depth perception; view-dependent; handles complex VOI structures better than conical cutouts by using a section-like plane. Implementation 3 provides smooth depth values. Limitations: Circular artifacts (Impl 1) or hard edges (Impl 2) if not using Impl 3. Performance depends on d. When to use: When detailed examination of internal structures of a VOI is required while maintaining spatial context and depth cues, specifically when the VOI has complex depth variations. The method was developed by Hänel et al. (2014) as a modification of the Importance-Driven Volume Rendering (IDVR) algorithm by Viola et al. (2004). The original IDVR used a conical cutout, which had the drawback that nearby structures at the same depth of the VOI could be covered by surrounding tissue (e.g., brain tissue). The frustum cutout expands the cutout using a section-like plane aligned with the back side of the VOI to solve this issue. It was used in the interactive 3D visualization of structural changes in the brain of a person with corticobasal syndrome. name: Volume Thinning
body:
Volume Thinning is a sparseness control technique that reduces volume visibility by progressively dissolving voxels according to their gradient magnitude and surface curvature. It enables interactive rendering of large datasets by trading visual fidelity for performance, reducing the volume to a wireframe-like structure of strong iso-surfaces and high-curvature lines. Unlike opacity modulation, which fades the entire object uniformly, Volume Thinning selectively removes voxels to preserve structural features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset V with scalar values d(v), pre-computed gradient 
abla d(v), and curvature \kappa(v). Output: A sorted voxel list L and a sparseness factor \alpha \in [0, 1] determining the render subset. Data Structures: The core data structure is a list of voxel records containing position (x, y, z), data value d, gradient magnitude |
abla d|, and curvature magnitude |\kappa|. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute gradient magnitude |
abla d| and curvature magnitude |\kappa| for all voxels. 2. Sorting: Sort voxels into list L using a two-key sort: primary key is gradient magnitude |
abla d| (descending), secondary key is curvature magnitude |\kappa| (descending). 3. Sparseness Application: Given sparseness factor \alpha (1.0 is full, 0.0 is empty), compute cutoff index k = \lfloor \alpha \cdot N{	ext{total}} floor. The active set is L[0 \dots k-1]. 4. Rendering: Render only voxels in the active set. As \alpha decreases, low-gradient regions are removed first, retaining strong iso-surfaces; further reduction removes iso-surfaces until only high-curvature areas remain. Formulas: Gradient Magnitude: |
abla d| = \sqrt{( rac{\partial d}{\partial x})^2 + ( rac{\partial d}{\partial y})^2 + ( rac{\partial d}{\partial z})^2}. Curvature Magnitude: |\kappa| is derived from the second derivatives (Hessian matrix) of the data value. Parameters: Sparseness Factor (\alpha): Controls thinning level. Typical values are 0.75, 0.5, and 0.25. Gradient Threshold: A hard threshold on gradient magnitude filters voxels before sorting in some variants. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Gradient and curvature calculations are sensitive to noise. Boundary Conditions: Derivatives at volume boundaries require padding or one-sided differences. Degenerate Input: Voxels with zero gradient and zero curvature (e.g., uniform background) sort to the end and are excluded first. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumethinningpreprocess(volume): voxels = [] for x in range(volume.width): for y in range(volume.height): for z in range(volume.depth): gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z) curvmag = computecurvaturemagnitude(volume, x, y, z) voxels.append({'pos': (x, y, z), 'value': volume[x, y, z], 'gradmag': gradmag, 'curvmag': curvmag}) return voxels def computegradientmagnitude(volume, x, y, z): dx = volume[x + 1, y, z] - volume[x - 1, y, z] if 0 < x < volume.width - 1 else 0.0 dy = volume[x, y + 1, z] - volume[x, y - 1, z] if 0 < y < volume.height - 1 else 0.0 dz = volume[x, y, z + 1] - volume[x, y, z - 1] if 0 < z < volume.depth - 1 else 0.0 return (dx2 + dy2 + dz2)0.5 def computecurvaturemagnitude(volume, x, y, z): dxx = volume[x + 1, y, z] - 2 volume[x, y, z] + volume[x - 1, y, z] if 0 < x < volume.width - 1 else 0.0 dyy = volume[x, y + 1, z] - 2 volume[x, y, z] + volume[x, y - 1, z] if 0 < y < volume.height - 1 else 0.0 dzz = volume[x, y, z + 1] - 2 volume[x, y, z] + volume[x, y, z - 1] if 0 < z < volume.depth - 1 else 0.0 return abs(dxx + dyy + dzz) def volumethinningsort(voxels): voxels.sort(key=lambda v: v['curvmag'], reverse=True) voxels.sort(key=lambda v: v['gradmag'], reverse=True) return voxels def volumethinningrender(voxels, sparsenessfactor): if sparsenessfactor <= 0: return [] numtorender = int(sparsenessfactor len(voxels)) return voxels[:numtorender] An optimization for interactive back-to-front compositing using shear-warp projection. It maintains spatial consistency to allow alpha-blending while skipping voxels with low gradient magnitude. Definition: Extracts potentially contributing voxels into a list, storing position, data value, gradient direction, and magnitude. Filters voxels by keeping only those with gradient magnitude above a threshold, typically retaining ~25% of voxels. Steps: 1. Extract voxels with |
abla d| > 	ext{threshold}. 2. Group voxels into slices for each principal viewing axis (-x, y, z). 3. Within each slice, sort voxels by gradient magnitude. 4. During rendering, skip voxels mapped to black by the gradient magnitude windowing function g(|
abla|), which are located at the end of the sorted slice list. Comparison: Compared to MIP ordering, significantly more voxels must be rendered because skipping is based only on 'surfaceness' (gradient magnitude), not the view-dependent contour term. Time Complexity: Preprocessing is O(N) for gradient/curvature computation and sorting, where N is the voxel count. Rendering is O(\alpha N) where \alpha is the sparseness factor. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the voxel list with gradient and curvature attributes. Measured Performance: Tested on datasets of resolution 512 	imes 512 	imes 87 (Leopard Gecko) and 256 	imes 256 	imes 610 (Monster Study). The method achieves high frame rates by reducing processed voxels, with only ~25% typically included in the active set for gradient-based filtering. Strengths: Preserves structural features (iso-surfaces, ridges) while removing smooth regions. Allows smooth transition from full volume to wireframe representation. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of gradient and curvature, adding preprocessing time. The visual result is view-independent, meaning the thinning pattern does not adapt to the camera position. When to use: Interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets where structural features are more important than smooth shading. When not to use: When view-dependent contour enhancement is required, or when smooth, continuous surfaces are critical. Volume Thinning was introduced in the context of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering by Viola et al. in 2004. It is part of a broader effort to enable interactive rendering of large volumetric datasets by focusing computational resources on visually important voxels. The technique sorts voxels based on gradient and curvature magnitudes to progressively dissolve iso-surfaces into high-curvature lines. name: Nonuniform Compression on Grid Models
head: Importance-based Nonuniform Compression
body: Nonuniform Compression on Grid Models is a storage optimization technique for explicit volume rendering grids that reduces model size by applying different down-sampling scales to volume density and color features. The method operates on the insight that volume density contributes more critically to rendering quality than color features. It sets itself apart from uniform compression by asymmetrically compressing attributes and combining low-resolution grids with a sparse set of high-fidelity "important" voxels to preserve high-frequency details. This method builds on Voxel Pruning by using importance scores to identify which voxels require full resolution storage. Inputs: Original explicit grid model V = \{V\sigma, Vc\}, where V\sigma is the volume density grid and Vc is the color feature grid. Outputs: Compressed representation consisting of down-sampled grids \{\hat{V}\sigma, \hat{V}c\} and a list of important voxels with their original high-resolution values. Data Structures: 1. Down-sampled Grids: \hat{V}\sigma and \hat{V}c stored at reduced resolutions. 2. Important Voxels List: A list of tuples containing the 3D coordinates (x, y, z) and the original high-resolution values (\sigma, c) for voxels identified as important. Parameters: Sc: Down-sampling ratio for color features. Typical value: 4. S\sigma: Down-sampling ratio for volume density. Typical value: 2. Ray set: A large set of rays cast across wide views for importance estimation. Steps: 1. Calculate Importance Scores: For each voxel vl in the original grid, calculate its importance score Il by casting a large set of rays across wide views and sampling points xi. The score is the sum of contributions from all sampling points influenced by the voxel: Il = \sumi \mathbb{1}{\{xi \in \iota(vl)\}} \cdot w{i,l} \cdot Ti \cdot \alphai Where xi is a sampling point on a ray. The indicator function \mathbb{1}{\{xi \in \iota(vl)\}} equals 1 if xi is within the neighborhood of voxel vl, and 0 otherwise. The neighborhood is defined as \iota(vl) = \{vl + \delta: \delta \in [-1, 1]^3\}. The term w{i,l} is the linear interpolation weight of voxel vl for point xi, determined by the distance between xi and the 8 adjacent voxels. The terms Ti and \alphai are the transmittance and opacity at point xi, computed via standard volume rendering accumulation. 2. Identify Important Voxels: Sort all voxels by their importance scores Il in decreasing order. Select a subset of voxels with the largest scores to store at full resolution. Empirical analysis shows that approximately 17% of voxels contribute to 83% of the overall importance, and 10% contribute to 66%. 3. Compress Grids: Apply down-sampling operations to the original grids using the specified ratios: \hat{V}c = \downarrow{Sc}(Vc) \hat{V}\sigma = \downarrow{S\sigma}(V\sigma) Where \downarrowS denotes the down-sampling operation by factor S. 4. Store Compressed Model: Save the down-sampled grids \{\hat{V}\sigma, \hat{V}c\} and the list of important voxels with their original values. 5. Decompression (One-time Deployment): To recover the grid for rendering, up-sample the compressed grids \{\hat{V}\sigma, \hat{V}c\} to the original grid size using tri-linear interpolation. Then, replace the values at the coordinates of the stored important voxels with their original high-resolution values to obtain the recovered grid \{\tilde{V}\sigma, \tilde{V}c\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def downsamplegrid(grid, factor): """Downsamples a 3D grid by taking every factor-th element along each axis.""" return grid[::factor,::factor,::factor] def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """Performs tri-linear interpolation at continuous coordinates (x, y, z) on a 3D grid.""" x0, y0, z0 = math.floor(x), math.floor(y), math.floor(z) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 dx, dy, dz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 # Clamp to grid bounds x0, x1 = max(0, min(x0, grid.shape[0]-1)), max(0, min(x1, grid.shape[0]-1)) y0, y1 = max(0, min(y0, grid.shape[1]-1)), max(0, min(y1, grid.shape[1]-1)) z0, z1 = max(0, min(z0, grid.shape[2]-1)), max(0, min(z1, grid.shape[2]-1)) c00 = (1-dx)grid[x0, y0, z0] + dxgrid[x1, y0, z0] c01 = (1-dx)grid[x0, y0, z1] + dxgrid[x1, y0, z1] c10 = (1-dx)grid[x0, y1, z0] + dxgrid[x1, y1, z0] c11 = (1-dx)grid[x0, y1, z1] + dxgrid[x1, y1, z1] c0 = (1-dy)c00 + dyc10 c1 = (1-dy)c01 + dyc11 return (1-dz)c0 + dzc1 def upsamplegrid(compressed, originalshape): """Upsamples a compressed grid to the original resolution using tri-linear interpolation.""" recovered = [0.0] (originalshape[0] originalshape[1] originalshape[2]) for x in range(originalshape[0]): for y in range(originalshape[1]): for z in range(originalshape[2]): cx, cy, cz = x / compressed.shape[0], y / compressed.shape[1], z / compressed.shape[2] recovered[x originalshape[1] originalshape[2] + y originalshape[2] + z] = trilinearinterpolate(compressed, cx, cy, cz) return recovered def calculateimportancescores(gridsigma, gridcolor, rays): """Calculates importance score for each voxel based on ray sampling.""" voxelcount = gridsigma.shape[0] gridsigma.shape[1] gridsigma.shape[2] importancescores = [0.0] voxelcount for ray in rays: # Sample points along the ray points = [ray.origin + t ray.direction for t in ray.sampledistances] for point in points: # Standard volume rendering accumulation for Ti and alphai sigmai, alphai, transmittancei = 0.0, 0.0, 1.0 # Simplified accumulation for demonstration; in practice, integrate along ray segment sigmai = trilinearinterpolate(gridsigma, point.x, point.y, point.z) alphai = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai ray.stepsize) transmittancei = math.exp(-sigmai ray.stepsize) # Find influencing voxels (neighbors within [-1, 1]^3) influencingvoxels = [] for dx in [-1, 0, 1]: for dy in [-1, 0, 1]: for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: nx, ny, nz = math.floor(point.x) + dx, math.floor(point.y) + dy, math.floor(point.z) + dz if 0 <= nx < gridsigma.shape[0] and 0 <= ny < gridsigma.shape[1] and 0 <= nz < gridsigma.shape[2]: influencingvoxels.append((nx, ny, nz)) for voxelidx in influencingvoxels: # Calculate interpolation weight w{i,l} weight = trilinearinterpolate(gridsigma, point.x, point.y, point.z) # Weight proportional to contribution # Map 3D index to 1D idx = voxelidx[0] gridsigma.shape[1] gridsigma.shape[2] + voxelidx[1] gridsigma.shape[2] + voxelidx[2] # Add contribution to importance score importancescores[idx] += weight transmittancei alphai return importancescores def compressgrid(originalgridsigma, originalgridcolor, importancescores, Ssigma=2, Scolor=4, topkpercent=0.17): """Compresses the grid using nonuniform downsampling and stores important voxels.""" # Step 1: Downsample grids compressedcolor = downsamplegrid(originalgridcolor, Scolor) compressedsigma = downsamplegrid(originalgridsigma, Ssigma) # Step 2: Identify important voxels voxelindices = list(range(len(importancescores))) sortedindices = sorted(voxelindices, key=lambda i: importancescores[i], reverse=True) # Select top k percent numimportant = int(len(sortedindices) topkpercent) importantvoxelindices = sortedindices[:numimportant] # Store original values for important voxels importantvoxelsdata = [] for idx in importantvoxelindices: coords = (idx // (originalgridsigma.shape[1] originalgridsigma.shape[2]), (idx // originalgridsigma.shape[2]) % originalgridsigma.shape[1], idx % originalgridsigma.shape[2]) sigmaval = originalgridsigma[coords] colorval = originalgridcolor[coords] importantvoxelsdata.append({'coords': coords, 'sigma': sigmaval, 'color': colorval}) return compressedsigma, compressedcolor, importantvoxelsdata def decompressgrid(compressedsigma, compressedcolor, importantvoxelsdata, originalshape): """Recovers the grid by upsampling and replacing important voxels.""" # Upsample compressed grids to original shape using tri-linear interpolation recoveredsigma = upsamplegrid(compressedsigma, originalshape) recoveredcolor = upsamplegrid(compressedcolor, originalshape) # Replace values at important voxel coordinates with original high-res values for voxeldata in importantvoxelsdata: coords = voxeldata['coords'] recoveredsigma[coords] = voxeldata['sigma'] recoveredcolor[coords] = voxeldata['color'] return recoveredsigma, recoveredcolor Storage Reduction: Achieves over 40x reduction in grid model storage compared to original grid models. Quality Trade-off: Maintains competitive rendering quality with less than 0.3dB drop in PSNR compared to uncompressed models. Performance: Enables real-time rendering speeds (e.g., 180 fps) due to reduced memory footprint and bandwidth. Strengths: Significant storage savings with minimal quality loss; simple one-time decompression without runtime overhead. Limitations: Requires an initial pass to calculate importance scores; relies on the assumption that density is more important than color, which may vary by scene. When to Use: When storage or bandwidth is a constraint and real-time rendering is required. When Not to Use: When maximum possible visual fidelity is required without any compression artifacts, or if the scene has high-frequency details in color that are not captured by the importance metric. This method was introduced in the paper "Compact Real-Time Radiance Fields with Neural Codebook". It addresses the high storage costs of explicit grid-based neural radiance field representations. The approach leverages the observation that a small percentage of voxels contribute to the majority of rendering importance, allowing for selective high-resolution storage. Compact Real-Time Radiance Fields with Neural Codebook, https://doi.org/10.1109/icme55011.2023.00374, fetched 2026-10-26

name: DeepBrick
head: Deep Volume Raytracing
body: DeepBrick is a ray-marching kernel for deep volume raytracing that combines empty space skipping with front-to-back alpha blending to accumulate color and transmittance. It is distinguished from standard sparse voxel traversal by its explicit support for deep rendering outputs (depth, flow) and its specific handling of hierarchical brick data loading and evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, ray direction, world position increment (wpt), voxel delta (gvdb->vdel[0]), and a pointer to the VDB leaf node. Output: A buffer (outBuf) containing 10 floats per pixel: indices 0-2 for color, 3 for mask, 4-6 for normal, 7 for depth, 8-9 for flow. Data Structures: VDB Leaf Node: Accessed via getNode and contains the voxel data. Sample Point (p): Index coordinates derived from the world position. Accumulators: val: Vector holding voxel properties (density, color components). clr: Accumulated color and transmittance. hit: Structure storing front hit point (hit.x) and weighted mean depth (hit.y). Parameters: SCNMINVAL: Threshold for skipping empty voxels during initial traversal. SCNALPHACUT: Threshold for stopping color accumulation based on current transmittance. MAXITER: Maximum iterations per ray. SCNEXTINCT: Extinction coefficient. SCNALBEDO: Albedo multiplier. SCNPSTEP: Step size. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Get the VDB leaf node using getNode. Compute the sample point in index coordinates p from the world position wp and voxel delta gvdb->vdel[0]. Compute the world position increment wpt. Initialize val and hclr (hit color) to zero. Initialize clr (accumulated color/transmittance) to zero. Record the front hit point hit.x if it is zero. 2. Empty Space Skipping: Loop while val.w < SCNMINVAL, iter < MAXITER, and p is within bounds. Fetch the voxel value and update val.w (density). If val.w < SCNMINVAL, advance p, wp, and t.x (ray parameter). Increment iter. This loop skips voxels with negligible density. 3. Color Accumulation (Ray Marching): Loop while clr.w > SCNALPHACUT, iter < MAXITER, and p is within bounds. Perform an optional depth buffer test to cull rays that have already been occluded. Transfer the current voxel's properties into val. Compute the transmittance through the current voxel step. Update hit.y using the transmittance and step size. Fetch the voxel color into hclr. Accumulate the color clr. Update clr.w by multiplying with the new voxel transmittance. Advance p, wp, and t.x. Increment iter. 4. Finalization: Clamp the final color and alpha values. Write results to outBuf. Formulas: Transmittance is computed as \tau = \exp(SCN\EXTINCT \cdot val.w \cdot SCN\PSTEP), where val.w is the voxel density, SCN\EXTINCT is the extinction coefficient, and SCN\PSTEP is the step size. (Note: The source reuses val.w for transmittance; this implementation renames it to \tau to prevent variable reuse bugs.) Color accumulation follows clr.x += val.x \cdot clr.w \cdot (1 - \tau) \cdot SCN\ALBEDO \cdot hclr.x, where val.x is the voxel color component, clr.w is current transmittance, and SCN\ALBEDO is the albedo multiplier. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def deepbrickraycast(rayorigin, raydirection, vdbleaf, outbuf, pixelidx): # Constants SCNMINVAL = 1e-6 SCNALPHACUT = 0.01 MAXITER = 1000 SCNEXTINCT = 1.0 SCNALBEDO = 1.0 SCNPSTEP = 1.0 # Step size parameter # Initialization voxeldelta = vdbleaf.vdel[0] wp = [rayorigin[i] for i in range(3)] wpt = [raydirection[i] voxeldelta for i in range(3)] p = [(wp[i] - body: Brick Traversal is a ray-marching kernel that samples a volumetric brick texture, adjusts alpha and RGB values for variable step sizes, and composites the result into a destination color using front-to-back alpha blending. It accounts for a "sample ratio" (r) between the ray step and the brick's internal resolution to adjust sampling density across hierarchical levels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin (\mathbf{O}), ray direction (\mathbf{D}), brick bounds, brick texture data, accumulated destination color/alpha (c{dst}, a{dst}), global ray step size (RayStepSize), current brick depth (curDepth), octree depth minus one (OctTreeDepthMinusOne), and brick step size scalar (k{BrickStepSizeScalar}). Output: Composite color (c{dst}) and accumulated alpha (a{dst}). Data Structures: The method operates on the following variables: dst: Accumulated destination color and alpha. src: Fetched texel color and alpha. rayWorldPosition: Current world-space ray position. curBrickRayPos: Current brick-local ray position. Parameters: r (sampleRatio): The ratio of the ray step size to the brick's effective voxel size. It is computed as r = k{BrickStepSizeScalar}^{OctTreeDepthMinusOne - curDepth} for constant nodes, or derived from curBrickDepth for textured bricks. Steps: 1. Compute Intersection: Calculate the time to exit the brick bounds (t{exit}) using a ray-box intersection routine. 2. Calculate Steps: Determine the ray step size in world space: rayStepSize = RayStepSize \times r. Calculate the number of steps: numSteps = \lfloor t{exit} / rayStepSize \rfloor + 1. 3. Initialize: Set rayWorldPosition and curBrickRayPos to the brick entry point. Initialize c{dst} = (0,0,0,0) and a{dst} = 0. 4. Loop: For i from 0 to numSteps - 1: a. Advance World Ray: Update the world position: rayWorldPosition += worldRayStep where worldRayStep = \mathbf{D} \times RayStepSize. b. Early Exit Check: If a{dst} > 0.995, subtract (i+1) from numSteps, advance rayWorldPosition by the remaining steps to the exit point, and return. c. Fetch Texel: Sample the brick texture at curBrickRayPos to get source color c{src} and alpha a{src}. d. Adjust Values: Compute adjusted alpha and color: a{adj} = 1 - (1 - a{src})^r and c{adj} = c{src} \times r. e. Composite: Update the destination using front-to-back blending: c{dst} = (1 - a{dst}) \times c{adj} + c{dst}. The accumulated alpha updates as a{dst} = a{dst} + a{adj} \times (1 - a{dst}). f. Advance Brick Ray: Update the brick-space ray position: curBrickRayPos += brickRayStep where brickRayStep = \mathbf{D} \times rayStepSize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Voxel Grid Raycasting is a rendering technique that stores scene geometry in a 3D voxel grid and traces rays through the grid by stepping from voxel to voxel to determine intersections and surface normals. It solves the problem of efficiently determining ray-voxel intersections without performing explicit geometric intersection tests against primitives. Unlike methods that expand storage to hold complete cell data or use hierarchical structures, this method relies on a uniform grid and a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) analog to traverse the volume. It is distinguished from general Volume Raycasting by its restriction to integer-valued voxel functions and discrete stepping, rather than continuous sampling and interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \vec{o}, ray direction \vec{d} (normalized), voxel grid dimensions, voxel size (or bin size), and the voxel data structure. Output: Hit position, voxel coordinates, surface normal, and optionally material/color data. Returns failure if no intersection is found within bounds or distance limits. Data Structures: The voxel grid is typically stored as a 1D array or buffer. Layout (Uniform/Chunked): A 1D storage buffer voxels: array<u32>. Each u32 represents a single voxel. A value of 0u indicates an empty voxel; non-zero values indicate occupied voxels, where the value may encode color via unpack4x8unorm. Indexing: For a chunk of width W and height H, the index for grid coordinates (x, y, z) is: index = x + y \cdot W + z \cdot (W \cdot H) Layout (Fixed Size): Alternatively, a fixed-size 1D array blocks of size Nx 	imes Ny 	imes Nz (e.g., 16 	imes 16 	imes 16) of type int. Indexing: For a 16 	imes 16 	imes 16 grid, the index is: index = (x \cdot 16 + z) \cdot 16 + y Parameters: voxelsize / binsize: The physical side length of a voxel in world units. Typical values are 0.1 or hardcoded to 1.0. epsilon: A small offset to prevent self-intersection. Typically voxelsize 0.01. maxdist: Maximum ray travel distance. Typical value 16.0 or 10.0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Normalize the ray direction: \vec{r} = 	ext{normalize}(\vec{d}). Calculate the starting voxel coordinates by flooring the start position divided by the bin size: \vec{v}{curr} = \lfloor \vec{o} / 	ext{bin\size} floor Calculate direction indicators (step signs) for each axis: 	ext{step}i =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } ri \ge 0 \ -1 & 	ext{if } ri < 0 \end{cases} Calculate the distance to traverse one full voxel width (delta): \Delta ti =  rac{	ext{bin\size}}{|ri|} \cdot 	ext{step}i \quad 	ext{if } ri 
eq 0, 	ext{ else } \infty Calculate the distance to the next voxel boundary (t{max}) for each axis. The target boundary coordinate is (\vec{v}{curr, i} + 	ext{step}i) \cdot 	ext{bin\size}. t{max, i} =  rac{	ext{target}i - oi}{ri} \quad 	ext{if } ri 
eq 0, 	ext{ else } \infty Note: If a ray component is 0, t{max} and \Delta t are set to a minimal value (e.g., FLTMIN) or infinity to effectively remove that axis from the traversal comparison logic. 2. Edge Case Handling (Negative Direction): If the ray starts in a voxel different from the target end voxel and moves in a negative direction, decrement the corresponding voxel coordinate to ensure correct traversal start. Example: If v{curr, x} 
eq v{end, x} and rx < 0, then v{curr, x} \leftarrow v{curr, x} - 1. 3. Traversal Loop: Iterate while the current voxel is within bounds and has not exceeded maxdist or iteration limits. Find the axis with the minimum t{max} value: axis = 	ext{argmin}(t{max}). Increment the grid position on that axis: v{curr, axis} \leftarrow v{curr, axis} + 	ext{step}{axis}. Update the distance traveled: dist \leftarrow t{max, axis}. Advance the t{max} for that axis to the next boundary: t{max, axis} \leftarrow t{max, axis} + \Delta t{axis}. Store the axis of entry for normal calculation. 4. Intersection Check: Load voxel data at v{curr}. If the voxel is occupied (data 
eq 0): Calculate the surface normal based on the entry axis: \vec{n} = 	ext{axis\dir
ormal}(axis, \vec{r}). Calculate the precise hit position using the t{max} values at the time of entry. Return hit data. 5. Ray Bouncing (Optional): If multiple bounces are supported, spawn a new ray from the hit position: \vec{o}{new} = \vec{o}{hit} + \epsilon \cdot \vec{n}. Re-initialize traversal state for the new ray. If the new ray is out of range, return ambient/sky color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. It establishes a dual relationship between voxels and cells by logically shifting scalar positions backward by half a voxel width, allowing the ray tracer to intersect 8-voxel cell primitives defined by the stored leaf values. Unlike methods that expand storage to hold complete cell data, this method retrieves forward neighbors at intersection time, maintaining single scalar storage per leaf. Spherical Volume Ray Walking is a fast voxel traversal algorithm for rendering volumetric data defined on a spherical coordinate grid. It extends the cartesian fast voxel traversal method by Amanatides and Woo to non-cartesian grids, iterating through radial, polar, and azimuthal voxel boundaries to determine the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which assumes axis-aligned bounding boxes, this method handles the curved boundaries of spherical sectors, using line-sphere intersection for radial steps and 2D segment intersection for angular boundaries. Plane Marching is a raymarching technique for voxel grids that advances a ray by stepping to the nearest intersection with the integer grid planes separating voxel layers. It solves the problem of traversing a dense voxel volume to find the first solid voxel by checking occupancy at each plane boundary. Unlike shape-assisted siblings such as Sphere Assisted Raymarching or Optimised Voxel Ray Marching, it does not store auxiliary distance fields or shape metadata, relying solely on the geometric structure of the grid. This makes it simple to implement but fragile in empty space, as it never skips more than one voxel per step. RLE4 Ray Tracing is a ray-marching or voxel-intersection algorithm that traverses an RLE4-compressed volume structure (Map4) to locate the first occupied voxel along a ray or to colorize a voxel based on its position. It uses slab-based RLE encoding to skip empty space efficiently. A hierarchical raycasting algorithm that traverses a sparse shadow volume texture to find the first intersection with a shadow-casting volume. It dynamically adjusts its traversal step size and level of detail (LOD) based on occupancy bits, allowing it to skip empty space efficiently compared to fixed-step hierarchical variants. It differs from siblings such as Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping, Spherical Volume Ray Walking, Plane Marching, RLE4 Ray Tracing, Regular Grid Traversal, Voxel Raytracer, and DirectVoxGO Volume Rendering by using a multi-level occupancy-bit search that refines or coarsens traversal granularity on the fly. Regular Grid Traversal is a ray-scene intersection acceleration technique that partitions a scene bounding box into a fixed-size 3D grid of cells, returning the sequence of cells intersected by a ray to minimize primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of testing every object for every ray by only testing primitives stored in intersected cells. Unlike hierarchical structures (e.g., BVH, Octree) that partition primitives into disjoint sets, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, allowing primitives to belong to multiple sub-blocks. It is distinguished by its constant-time access to cells and simple traversal logic, making it optimal for scenes with uniform data distribution or dynamic scenes requiring frequent rebuilds. A voxel raytracer renders 3D voxel models by marching rays through a 3D grid of voxels, supporting multiple bounces for diffuse reflection and a ground plane. It differs from standard voxel grid raycasting by implementing a full path-tracing loop with diffuse scattering and anti-aliasing, rather than simple direct illumination or single-pass raymarching. DirectVoxGO is a volume rendering method that accelerates neural radiance field training and inference by sampling points directly on a structured voxel grid rather than uniformly along rays. It solves the problem of inefficient ray marching in sparse scenes by using a mask cache to skip free space and a direct lookup of density and color features from the voxel grid. It sets itself apart from standard NeRF by replacing uniform sampling with grid-based point selection and from other sparse voxel methods by using a dense voxel grid with a binary mask cache for acceleration. This method accelerates the identification of the k nearest points within a cylinder of radius \delta around a query ray in a point cloud, specifically optimized for parallel GPU execution and dynamic scenes where the point cloud changes frequently. Unlike static acceleration structures such as octrees, which require O(n \log n) construction time, this voxel grid approach achieves O(n) construction, making it superior for inverse rendering and dynamic scenarios where the structure must be rebuilt every iteration. A search algorithm used by voxel resolve and GI update to find the pixel's voxel again in the brick named by the visibility buffer. It finds the cell holding the ray's point at the stored depth, then the two cells along each axis whose centers lie nearest that point (which hold the point regardless of rounding), stopping at the first cell whose hit gives the stored depth again, bit for bit. A voxel's test depends only on the ray and the voxel, ensuring every pass meets it at the same t. A narrow band strategy that does not use any solver. When the algorithm reaches a narrow band voxel, it immediately returns a hit, resulting in a voxelization of the scene. An acceleration structure using a dense octree stored in a 3D texture to skip empty space during ray traversal. The raymarcher first traverses the octree texture; once it hits a leaf node (occupied octant), it switches to the fine-grained voxel texture for detailed collision detection. The octree is stored as a 3D texture (texture3d<u32>), with data for different levels interleaved in the Z dimension. The 3D texture approach is significantly faster for ray traversal because graphics hardware is optimized for spatially local texture access. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the ray. In the worst case (ray passing through the entire grid), N is proportional to the grid dimension. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the total number of voxels in the grid. The storage is typically a single 1D array or 3D texture. Performance: Performance is highly dependent on grid density and ray direction. Axis-aligned rays are fastest as they traverse fewer voxels per unit distance. Diagonal rays traverse more voxels. The method is very fast on GPUs due to coalesced memory access patterns when traversing linear buffers or 3D textures. Strengths: Simple implementation, no complex data structure traversal overhead (like BVH/Octree node pointers), efficient for dense uniform grids, easy to parallelize on GPU. Limitations: Inefficient for sparse scenes (many empty voxels traversed), fixed resolution (aliasing artifacts at high zoom), memory usage scales with the cube of the grid dimension. When to use: Dense voxel volumes, uniform grids, real-time rendering where simplicity and parallelism are key. When not to use: Highly sparse scenes (use Sparse Voxel Traversal or Octree), scenes with complex continuous geometry (use Ray-Primitive intersection). The method is based on the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm for ray tracing, originally described by Amanatides and Woo in 1987. It is a fundamental technique in voxel-based rendering, often used in games and real-time applications for collision detection and volume visualization. head: Cell Primitive Definition, Logical Shift Mapping, Logical Shift for Ray Tracing, Scalar Field Remapping
body: Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping is a technique for ray tracing isosurfaces defined within cells of 8 voxels using an octree that stores scalar values at voxel centers. It establishes a dual relationship between voxels and cells by logically shifting scalar positions backward by half a voxel width, allowing the ray tracer to intersect 8-voxel cell primitives defined by the stored leaf values. Unlike methods that expand storage to hold complete cell data, this method retrieves forward neighbors at intersection time, maintaining single scalar storage per leaf. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree structure storing scalar values at voxel centers, where each leaf node contains a single scalar datum v. Output: Intersection points with an isosurface defined within cells formed by 8 adjacent voxels. Data Structures: Octree: Nodes contain scalar values at their centers, and leaf nodes store a single scalar value v. Cell Primitive: A box defined by 8 vertices, where the vertices correspond to the mapped positions of 8 adjacent voxels in the octree. Mapping Logic: 1. Logical Shift: The position of all scalars is logically shifted backward by half a unit of voxel width to re-map the scalar field from voxel centers to cell corners. 2. Corner Mapping: Each voxel is mapped to the lower-left corner (minimum vertex) of a cell. 3. Boundary Condition: Values outside the octree data boundary are defined to be zero. Intersection Process: When a ray traverses an octree leaf node at indices (i, j, k) with a datum v, the ray intersects a box (cell) where (i, j, k) is mapped to the minimum vertex, and the remaining 7 vertices are formed by the forward neighbors of the voxel at (i, j, k) in the octree. Neighbor Retrieval: Instead of expanding each voxel to contain its forward neighbors (which would require 8 times the storage), the method retrieves the 7 forward neighbors of a voxel at intersection time. For a volume stored in a 3D array, querying these neighbors is a trivial array index operation. For an octree, this requires point location to retrieve the voxel values of the forward neighbors, where full top-down point location from the root is O(\log(N)) but neighbor-finding techniques can significantly reduce this cost. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectcell(rayorigin, raydirection, octree, isovalue): """ Intersect a ray with an isosurface defined by voxel-cell duality. """ # Standard octree traversal to find the leaf node intersected by the ray leafnode = octree.traverse(rayorigin, raydirection) if leafnode is None: return None # Get the scalar value at the current leaf node (voxel center) vcenter = leafnode.scalarvalue # Determine the indices (i, j, k) of the current leaf node i, j, k = leafnode.indices # Helper function to get scalar value, returning 0 for out-of-bounds def getscalar(idxi, idxj, idxk): # Standard octree point location to find the node at (idxi, idxj, idxk) node = octree.pointlocation(idxi, idxj, idxk) if node is None: return 0.0 # Boundary condition: values outside octree are zero return node.scalarvalue # Retrieve the 8 corner values for the cell # The current voxel is mapped to the minimum vertex (lower-left corner) # Neighbors are at (i+1, j, k), (i, j+1, k), (i, j, k+1), etc. corners = [ getscalar(i, j, k), # Current voxel (min corner) getscalar(i+1, j, k), # Neighbor in x getscalar(i, j+1, k), # Neighbor in y getscalar(i+1, j+1, k), # Neighbor in x,y getscalar(i, j, k+1), # Neighbor in z getscalar(i+1, j, k+1), # Neighbor in x,z getscalar(i, j+1, k+1), # Neighbor in y,z getscalar(i+1, j+1, k+1) # Neighbor in x,y,z (max corner) ] # Standard trilinear ray-cube intersection or Marching Cubes is applied # to the 8 corner values to find the isosurface intersection. # The sources do not specify the exact reconstruction algorithm. Parameters: Isovalue: The threshold value for the isosurface extraction. Not given in the sources. Voxel Width: The unit of voxel width used for the logical shift. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Storage Expansion: Storing each cell completely by expanding each voxel to contain its forward neighbors requires 8 times the storage of the original volume, which contradicts the goal of ray tracing compressed data. Boundary Handling: Values outside the octree data boundary are defined to be zero. Performance: For octrees, retrieving forward neighbors requires point location, which is more intensive than array indexing. Full top-down point location is O(\log(N)), but neighbor-finding techniques can reduce this cost. Ray walking in spherical coordinates. Not given in the sources. Ray tracing on a regular grid structure. Not given in the sources. Marching planes for volume rendering. Not given in the sources. Voxel-based ray tracing for global illumination and specular reflections. Not given in the sources. Optimized voxel ray marching techniques. Not given in the sources. Time Complexity: Neighbor retrieval in an octree is more intensive than in a 3D array, with full top-down point location at O(\log(N)) reduced by neighbor-finding techniques. Memory Complexity: Single scalar storage per leaf node, avoiding the 8x storage expansion required by naive cell expansion. Strengths: Allows ray tracing of compressed octree data without expanding storage, and permits traversal of interior nodes of the octree volume. Limitations: Neighbor retrieval in octrees is more complex and potentially slower than in regular grids. When to Use: When ray tracing isosurfaces from compressed octree volumes where storage efficiency is critical. When Not to Use: When neighbor retrieval performance is critical and the data is stored in a regular grid, where array indexing is trivial. Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping was introduced in the context of interactive isosurface ray tracing of large octree volumes. The method leverages the dual relationship between voxels and cells to efficiently ray trace isosurfaces defined within cells of 8 voxels. The approach of retrieving forward neighbors at intersection time is attributed to Parker et al.. name: Spherical Volume Ray Walking
head: Amanatides and Woo extension to spherical grids, Fast Voxel Traversal Over Spherical Grids, Spherical Volume Rendering (SVR) Algorithm, walkSphericalVolume
body: Spherical Volume Ray Walking is a fast voxel traversal algorithm for rendering volumetric data defined on a spherical coordinate grid. It extends the cartesian fast voxel traversal method by Amanatides and Woo to non-cartesian grids, iterating through radial, polar, and azimuthal voxel boundaries to determine the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray. Unlike Voxel Grid Raycasting which assumes axis-aligned bounding boxes, this method handles the curved boundaries of spherical sectors, using line-sphere intersection for radial steps and 2D segment intersection for angular boundaries. Inputs: ray (origin O as bound vector, direction D as unit free vector), grid (spherical voxel grid with parameters sphereCenter, numRadialSections, numPolarSections, numAzimuthalSections, minBound, maxBound, deltaRadiiSquared(r), deltaPhi(), deltaTheta(), sphereMaxBoundAzi(), sphereMinBoundAzi(), sphereMaxBoundPolar(), sphereMinBoundPolar(), sphereMaxRadius(), pMaxPolar(i), pMaxAzimuthal(i), centerToPolarBound(i), centerToAzimuthalBound(i)), and time range tbegin, tend. Outputs: List of Voxel structs containing {radial, polar, azimuthal} indices and optional exitt. Voxel: {radial: int, polar: int, azimuthal: int, exitt: float}. HitParameters: {tMax: float, tStep: int} where tStep is -1, 0, or 1. RaySegment: {P1: BoundVec3, P2: BoundVec3, NZDI: int}. LineSegment: {P1: float, P2: float}. BoundVec3, FreeVec3, UnitVec3: 3D vector types for bound, free, and normalized coordinates respectively. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def walksphericalvolume(ray, grid, tbegin, tend): DOUBLEMAX = float('inf') PERTURBEDT = 0.1 if tend <= 0.0: return [] rsv = grid.spherecenter() - ray.pointatparameter(0.0) sedfromcenter = rsv.squaredlength() radialentrancevoxel = 0 while sedfromcenter < grid.deltaradiisquared(radialentrancevoxel): radialentrancevoxel += 1 rayoriginisoutsidegrid = (radialentrancevoxel == 0) vectorindex = radialentrancevoxel - (1 if not rayoriginisoutsidegrid else 0) entryradiussquared = grid.deltaradiisquared(vectorindex) entryradius = grid.deltaradius() (grid.numradialsections() - vectorindex) rsvd = rsv.dot(rsv) v = rsv.dot(ray.direction()) rsvdminusvsquared = rsvd - v v if entryradiussquared <= rsvdminusvsquared: return [] d = math.sqrt(entryradiussquared - rsvdminusvsquared) trayexit = ray.timeofintersectionat(v + d) if trayexit < 0.0: return [] trayentrance = ray.timeofintersectionat(v - d) currentradialvoxel = radialentrancevoxel + (1 if rayoriginisoutsidegrid else 0) Ppolar = [None] (grid.numpolarsections() + 1) Pazimuthal = [None] (grid.numazimuthalsections() + 1) # Sources do not provide the implementation for initializevoxelboundarysegments. if rayoriginisoutsidegrid: raysphere = grid.spherecenter() - ray.pointatparameter(trayentrance) elif sedfromcenter == 0.0: raysphere = rsv - ray.direction() else: raysphere = rsv currentpolarvoxel = initializeangularvoxelid(grid, grid.numpolarsections(), raysphere, Ppolar, raysphere.y, grid.spherecenter.y, entryradius) if currentpolarvoxel >= grid.numpolarsections(): return [] currentazimuthalvoxel = initializeangularvoxelid(grid, grid.numazimuthalsections(), raysphere, Pazimuthal, raysphere.z, grid.spherecenter.z, entryradius) if currentazimuthalvoxel >= grid.numazimuthalsections(): return [] voxels = [] voxels.append(Voxel(currentradialvoxel, currentpolarvoxel, currentazimuthalvoxel)) t = trayentrance (1 if rayoriginisoutsidegrid else 0) unitizedraytime = tend grid.spheremaxdiameter() + trayentrance (1 if rayoriginisoutsidegrid else 0) if rayoriginisoutsidegrid: maxt = min(trayexit, unitizedraytime) else: maxt = unitizedraytime collineartimes = [0.0, ray.timeofintersectionat(grid.spherecenter())] raysegment = RaySegment(maxt, ray) radialstephastransitioned = False while True: radial = radialhit(ray, grid, radialstephastransitioned, currentradialvoxel, v, rsvdminusvsquared, t, maxt) raysegment.updateattime(t, ray) polar = polarhit(ray, grid, raysegment, collineartimes, currentpolarvoxel, t, maxt) azimuthal = azimuthalhit(ray, grid, raysegment, collineartimes, currentazimuthalvoxel, t, maxt) if currentradialvoxel + radial.tstep == 0 or \ (radial.tmax == DOUBLEMAX and polar.tmax == DOUBLEMAX and azimuthal.tmax == DOUBLEMAX): voxels[-1].exitt = trayexit return voxels voxelintersection = minimumintersection(radial, polar, azimuthal) if voxelintersection == VoxelIntersectionType.Radial: t = radial.tmax currentradialvoxel += radial.tstep elif voxelintersection == VoxelIntersectionType.Polar: t = polar.tmax if not inboundspolar(grid, polar.tstep, currentpolarvoxel): voxels[-1].exitt = trayexit return voxels else: currentpolarvoxel = (currentpolarvoxel + polar.tstep) % grid.numpolarsections() elif voxelintersection == VoxelIntersectionType.Azimuthal: if not inboundsazimuthal(grid, azimuthal.tstep, currentazimuthalvoxel): voxels[-1].exitt = trayexit return voxels else: t = azimuthal.tmax currentazimuthalvoxel = (currentazimuthalvoxel + azimuthal.tstep) % grid.numazimuthalsections() elif voxelintersection == grid.numazimuthalsections() elif voxelintersection == VoxelIntersectionType.PolarAzimuthal: t = polar.tmax if not inboundsazimuthal(grid, azimuthal.tstep, currentazimuthalvoxel) or \ not inboundspolar(grid, polar.tstep, currentpolarvoxel): voxels[-1].exitt = trayexit return voxels else: currentpolarvoxel = (currentpolarvoxel + polar.tstep) % grid.numpolarsections() currentazimuthalvoxel = (currentazimuthalvoxel + azimuthal.tstep) % grid.numazimuthalsections() elif voxelintersection == VoxelIntersectionType.RadialPolarAzimuthal: t = radial.tmax if not inboundspolar(grid, polar.tstep, currentpolarvoxel): voxels[-1].exitt = trayexit return voxels if not inboundsazimuthal(grid, azimuthal.tstep, currentazimuthalvoxel): voxels[-1].exitt = trayexit return voxels currentradialvoxel += radial.tstep currentpolarvoxel = (currentpolarvoxel + polar.tstep) % grid.numpolarsections() currentazimuthalvoxel = (currentazimuthalvoxel + azimuthal.tstep) % grid.numazimuthalsections() voxels.append(Voxel(currentradialvoxel, currentpolarvoxel, currentazimuthalvoxel)) def radialhit(ray, grid, radialstephastransitioned, currentradialvoxel, v, rsvdminusvsquared, t, maxt): if radialstephastransitioned: db = math.sqrt(grid.deltaradiisquared(currentradialvoxel - 1) - rsvdminusvsquared) intersectiont = ray.timeofintersectionat(v + db) if intersectiont < maxt: return HitParameters(intersectiont, -1) else: previousidx = min(currentradialvoxel, grid.numradialsections() - 1) ra = grid.deltaradiisquared(previousidx - (1 if grid.deltaradiisquared(previousidx) < rsvdminusvsquared else 0)) da = math.sqrt(ra - rsvdminusvsquared) tentrance = ray.timeofintersectionat(v - da) texit = ray.timeofintersectionat(v + da) if tentrance > t and isequal(tentrance, texit): radialstephastransitioned = True return HitParameters(tentrance, 0) elif tentrance > t and tentrance < maxt: return HitParameters(tentrance, 1) elif texit < maxt: radialstephastransitioned = True return HitParameters(texit, -1) else: return HitParameters(float('inf'), 0) else: return radialhit(ray, grid, True, currentradialvoxel, v, rsvdminusvsquared, t, maxt) def polarhit(ray, grid, raysegment, collineartimes, currentpolarvoxel, t, maxt): pone = BoundVec3(grid.pmaxpolar(currentpolarvoxel).P1, grid.pmaxpolar(currentpolarvoxel).P2, 0.0) ptwo = BoundVec3(grid.pmaxpolar(currentpolarvoxel + 1).P1, grid.pmaxpolar(currentpolarvoxel + 1).P2, 0.0) umin = grid.centertopolarbound(currentpolarvoxel) umax = grid.centertopolarbound(currentpolarvoxel + 1) wmin = pone - raysegment.P1 wmax = ptwo - raysegment.P1 perpuvmin = umin.x raysegment.vector.y - umin.y raysegment.vector.x perpuvmax = umax.x raysegment.vector.y - umax.y raysegment.vector.x perpuwmin = umin.x wmin.y - umin.y wmin.x perpuwmax = umax.x wmax.y - umax.y wmax.x perpvwmin = raysegment.vector.x wmin.y - raysegment.vector.y wmin.x perpvwmax = raysegment.vector.x wmax.y - raysegment.vector.y wmax.x return angularhit(grid, ray, perpuvmin, perpuvmax, perpuwmin, perpuwmax, perpvwmin, perpvwmax, raysegment, collineartimes, t, maxt, ray.direction.y, grid.spherecenter.y, grid.pmaxpolar(), currentpolarvoxel) def azimuthalhit(ray, grid, raysegment, collineartimes, currentazimuthalvoxel, t, maxt): pone = BoundVec3(grid.pmaxazimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P1, grid.pmaxazimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel).P2, 0.0) ptwo = BoundVec3(grid.pmaxazimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P1, grid.pmaxazimuthal(currentazimuthalvoxel + 1).P2, 0.0) umin = raysegment.vector.y - umin.y raysegment.vector.x perpuvmax = umax.x raysegment.vector.y - umax.y raysegment.vector.x perpuwmin = umin.x wmin.y - umin.y wmin.x perpuwmax = umax.x wmax.y - umax.y wmax.x perpvwmin = raysegment.vector.x wmin.y - raysegment.vector.y wmin.x perpvwmax = raysegment.vector.x wmax.y - raysegment.vector.y wmax.x return angularhit(grid, ray, perpuvmin, perpuvmax, perpuwmin, isparallelmin and isequal(perpuwmin, 0.0) and isequal(perpvwmin, 0.0) isparallelmax = isequal(perpuvmax, 0.0) iscollinearmax = isparallelmax and isequal(perpuwmax, 0.0) and isequal(perpvwmax, 0.0) a, b = 0.0, 0.0 tmin = collineartimes[1 if iscollinearmin else 0] isintersectmin = False if not isparallelmin: invperpuvmin = 1.0 / perpuvmin a = perpvwmin invperpuvmin b = perpuwmin invperpuvmin if not isparallelmax: invperpuvmax = 1.0 / perpuvmax a = perpvwmax invperpuvmax b = perpuwmax invperpuvmax if not ((a < 0.0 or a > 1.0) or (b < 0.0 or b > 1.0)): isintersectmax = True tmax = raysegment.intersectiontimeat(b, ray) ttmaxeq = isequal(t, tmax) tmaxwithinbounds = t < tmax and not ttmaxeq and tmax < maxt ttmineq = isequal(t, tmin) tminwithinbounds = t < tmin and not ttmineq and tmin < maxt if not tmaxwithinbounds and not tminwithinbounds: return HitParameters(float('inf'), 0) if isintersectmax and not isintersectmin and not iscollinearmin and tmaxwithinbounds: return HitParameters(tmax, 1) if isintersectmin and not isintersectmax and not iscollinearmax and tminwithinbounds: return HitParameters(tmin, -1) if (isintersectmin and isintersectmax) or \ (isintersectmin and iscollinearmax) or \ (isintersectmax and iscollinearmin): minmaxeq = isequal(tmin, tmax) if minmaxeq and tminwithinbounds: perturbedt = 0.1 a = -ray.direction.x perturbedt b = -raydirection2 perturbedt maxradiusoverplanelength = grid.spheremaxradius() / math.sqrt(aa + bb) p1 = grid.spherecenter.x - maxradiusoverplanelength a p2 = spherecenter2 - maxradiusoverplanelength b nextstep = abs(currentvoxel - calculateangularvoxelidfrompoints(Pmax, p1, p2)) return HitParameters(tmax, nextstep if (ray.direction.x < 0.0 or raydirection2 < 0.0) else -nextstep) if tminwithinbounds and ((tmin < tmax and not minmaxeq) or ttmaxeq): return HitParameters(tmin, -1) if tmaxwithinbounds and ((tmax < tmin and not minmaxeq) or ttmineq): return HitParameters(tmax, 1) return p1 - Pmax[i].P1 Xp2diff = p2 - Pmax[i].P1 Yp1diff = p1 - Pmax[i].P2 Yp2diff = p2 - Pmax[i].P2 d1d2 = Xp1diff2 + Xp2diff2 + Yp1diff2 + Yp2diff2 d3 = Xdiff2 + Ydiff2 if d1d2 < d3 or isequal(d1d2, d3): grid.spheremaxboundpolar() >= angval >= grid.sphereminboundpolar() def inboundsazimuthal(grid, step, currentvoxel): radian = (currentvoxel + 1) grid.deltaphi() angval = radian - abs(step polar.tmax < mint: mint = polar.tmax result = VoxelIntersectionType.Polar if azimuthal.tmax < mint: mint = azimuthal.tmax result = VoxelIntersectionType.Azimuthal if polar.tmax == mint: result = VoxelIntersectionType.RadialPolar if azimuthal.tmax == mint: result = VoxelIntersectionType.RadialAzimuthal if polar.tmax == mint and azimuthal.tmax == mint: result = VoxelIntersectionType.RadialPolarAzimuthal return result def isequal(a, b): diffx = abs(a - b) return diffx <= 1e-12 or diffx <= max(abs(a), abs(b)) 1e-8 class Voxel: def init(self, radial, polar, azimuthal): self.radial = radial self.polar = polar self.azimuthal = azimuthal self.exitt = None class HitParameters: def init(self, tMax, tStep): self.tMax = tMax self.tStep = tStep class RaySegment: def init(self, maxt, ray): self.P1 = ray.pointatparameter(0.0) self.P2 = ray.pointatparameter(maxt) self.NZDI = ray.nonzerodirectionindex() self.raysegment = self.P2 - self.P1 def updateattime(self, t, ray): self.P1 = ray.pointatparameter(t) self.raysegment = self.P2 - self.P1 def vector(self): return self.raysegment def intersectiontimeat(self, intersectparameter, ray): return (self.P1[self.NZDI] + self.raysegment[self.NZDI] intersectparameter - ray.origin()[self.NZDI]) ray.invdirection()[self.NZDI] class BoundVec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, other): return FreeVec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def getitem(self, idx): return [self.x, self.y, self.z][idx] class FreeVec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def sub(self, other): return FreeVec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) def getitem(self, idx): return [self.x, self.y, self.z][idx] def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def squaredlength(self): return self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2 class UnitVec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def getitem(self, idx): return [self.x, self.y, self.z][idx] class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.inversedirection = UnitVec3(1.0/direction.x, 1.0/direction.y, 1.0/direction.z) self.NZDindex = 0 if direction.x != 0 else (1 if direction.y != 0 else 2) def pointatparameter(self, t): return BoundVec3(self.origin.x + self.direction.x t, self.origin.y + self.direction.y t, self.origin.z + self.direction.z t) def timeofintersectionat(self, discriminantv): return self.direction[self.NZDindex] discriminantv self.inversedirection[self.NZDindex] def nonzerodirectionindex(self): return self.NZDindex def invdirection(self): return self.inversedirection class VoxelIntersectionType: Radial = 1 Polar = 2 Azimuthal = 3 RadialPolar = 4 RadialAzimuthal = 5 PolarAzimuthal = 6 RadialPolarAzimuthal = 7 DOUBLEMAX: float('inf'), used as infinity for tMax when no intersection is found. perturbedt: 0.1, used to perturb the ray direction when handling degenerate cases where tmin == tmax in angular hit. Tangential radial hit: when tentrance == texit and tentrance > t, the ray is tangent to the radial sphere boundary. Handled by setting radialstephastransitioned = true and returning tStep = 0. Degenerate angular intersection: when tmin == tmax and both are within bounds, the ray intersects at a single point on the boundary. Handled by perturbing the ray direction by 0.1 units and recalculating the voxel ID to determine the step direction. Benchmarks on 8 × 1400 MHz CPUs (L1 Data 32 KiB × 4, L1 Instruction 32 KiB × 4, L2 Unified 256 KiB × 4, L3 Unified 6144 KiB × 1). 128² rays, 64³ voxels: Mean 103 ms, Median 103 ms, Std Dev 1.1 ms. 512² rays, 128³ voxels: Mean 3187 ms, Median 3180 ms, Std Dev 8.3 ms. Scaling is roughly linear with ray count and voxel count, consistent with traversal algorithms. Strengths: Handles spherical grids efficiently without converting to cartesian. Limitations: Requires precomputed boundary segments and angular voxel ID calculations, which add overhead for non-spherical scenes. Origin: Developed by Chris Gyurgyik, Ariel Kellison, and Youhan Yuan as an extension to the yt open-source data analysis and visualization package. Based on Amanatides and Woo's 1987 seminal paper on fast voxel traversal for ray tracing. Used for visualizing physical data from non-cartesian grids within yt. spherical-volume-rendering/svr-algorithm, https://github.com/spherical-volume-rendering/svr-algorithm, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Plane Marching
head: Raymarching Plane Intersections
body: Plane Marching is a raymarching technique for voxel grids that advances a ray by stepping to the nearest intersection with the integer grid planes separating voxel layers. It solves the problem of traversing a dense voxel volume to find the first solid voxel by checking occupancy at each plane boundary. Unlike shape-assisted siblings such as Sphere Assisted Raymarching or Optimised Voxel Ray Marching, it does not store auxiliary distance fields or shape metadata, relying solely on the geometric structure of the grid. This makes it simple to implement but fragile in empty space, as it never skips more than one voxel per step. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin p0 (voxel-unit space), ray direction d (voxel-unit space), voxel grid texture voxels (3D texture containing color/alpha), voxelGridSize (dimensions of the grid in voxels), maxDistToCheck (maximum traversal distance). Output: Color vec4 of the first solid voxel encountered, or transparent black if no solid voxel is found within maxDistToCheck. Data Structures: voxels: A 3D texture where each texel stores the color and alpha of a voxel. The alpha channel determines solidity (c.a > 0). The texture coordinates are normalized to [0, 1] based on voxelGridSize. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize step distance t = 0. 2. Loop while t \le \text{maxDistToCheck}: a. Calculate current position p = p0 + d \cdot t. b. Convert p to texture coordinates by dividing by voxelGridSize. c. If the sampled alpha c.a > 0, return c. d. Calculate the distance to the next integer grid plane along each axis. e. Update t by adding the smallest positive delta plus a small epsilon. Formulas: The distance to the next plane intersection along each axis is computed using the ray direction d and current position p. In voxel-unit-space (where one voxel is 1x1x1 units), the delta for each axis component is: \text{deltas}i = \frac{\text{step}(0, di) - \text{fract}(pi)}{di} Where: i \in \{x, y, z\} \text{step}(0, di) returns 1 if di \ge 0, else 0. This effectively computes \lceil pi \rceil - pi for positive directions and \lfloor pi \rfloor - pi for negative directions. \text{fract}(pi) is the fractional part of pi (pi - \lfloor pi \rfloor). di is the i-th component of the ray direction. The step size to advance is the minimum of these deltas, ensuring the ray moves to the closest plane intersection: t{\text{new}} = t + \max(\min(\text{deltas}x, \text{deltas}y, \text{deltas}z), \epsilon) Where \epsilon is a tiny constant to prevent infinite loops due to floating-point precision errors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def planemarch(p0, d, voxels, voxelgridsize, maxdisttocheck, epsilon=1e-6): # sample3dtexture is a standard trilinear 3D texture lookup returning vec4 t = 0.0 while t <= maxdisttocheck: # Calculate current position p = p0 + d t # Sample voxel color texcoords = p / voxelgridsize c = sample3dtexture(voxels, texcoords) # Check for solidity if c.a > 0: return c # Calculate deltas to next plane boundaries deltas = [] for i in range(3): stepval = 1.0 if d[i] >= 0 else 0.0 fracval = p[i] - math.floor(p[i]) deltas.append((stepval - fracval) / d[i]) # Find the minimum positive delta to step to the closest plane # Add epsilon to guarantee progress and avoid floating point errors t += max(min(deltas), epsilon) return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Parameters: epsilon: A small constant (e.g., 10^{-6}) added to the step size to guarantee progress and prevent infinite loops caused by floating-point inaccuracies. The exact value is not specified in the sources but must be "tiny". Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floating Point Errors: Accumulation of floating-point errors can cause "tunneling" (skipping voxels) and subtle artifacts. The epsilon helps but does not fully eliminate this fragility. Degenerate Performance: In empty space or when the target voxel is far away, the algorithm checks every single voxel along the ray path because it never moves more than one voxel at a time. This leads to poor performance in degenerate cases, such as a single solid voxel in the corner of a large empty grid. Fillrate Limitation: The technique is fragment shader heavy and is likely to be fillrate limited on typical hardware. Stores radius data in empty voxels to skip large distances. Choose when performance in sparse volumes is critical. Optimizes traversal logic with early exits and culling. Choose for better performance in complex scenes. Maps voxels to cells for different traversal strategies. Choose for alternative spatial indexing. Uses spherical stepping for non-axis-aligned volumes. Choose for spherical volume representations. General regular grid traversal. Choose for non-voxel regular structures. Extends ray marching for global illumination. Choose for advanced lighting. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the ray. In the worst case (empty space), N is proportional to the distance to the first solid voxel or the grid boundary. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the total number of voxels in the grid, as the entire voxel set must be loaded into a 3D texture. Memory usage is data-independent regarding sparsity; a 32x32x32 grid always consumes the same memory regardless of how many voxels are solid. Measured Performance: In a degenerate case (32x32x32 grid with a single solid voxel in the far corner), Plane Marching shows vastly worse performance compared to shape-assisted techniques. Strengths: Performant in parallelized environments (e.g., GPUs), requires little upfront computation, and is straightforward to implement. Limitations: Fragile due to floating-point errors, fillrate limited, and inefficient in empty space. When to Use: Simple voxel rendering where performance is not critical or the volume is dense. When Not to Use: Sparse volumes, large empty spaces, or when high performance is required. Plane Marching is described as one of the most interesting ways to render voxels, performant and parallelizable. It is based on the concept of raymarching plane intersections, where a ray is advanced along the planes separating voxel layers. The technique is often compared to Inigo Quilez's ray marching work, though Quilez's work primarily focuses on signed distance fields, whereas Plane Marching uses unsigned distance fields (grid planes). The method was popularized in the context of voxel rendering for real-time applications, such as Minecraft-like games, by developers like Caleb Leak.
