name: RLE4 Ray Tracing
head: Map4 Traversal
body: RLE4 Ray Tracing is a ray-marching or voxel-intersection algorithm that traverses an RLE4-compressed volume structure (Map4) to locate the first occupied voxel along a ray or to colorize a voxel based on its position. It uses slab-based RLE encoding to skip empty space efficiently. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A float position pos (x, y, z), volume dimensions vx, vy, vz, and a pre-compressed RLE4 structure map4 containing a slab pointer array map, a slab data array slabs, and the X-dimension size sx. Output: A packed 16-bit RGB value stored in the texture array if the voxel is found, or a skip indicator if not. Data Structures: The Map4 structure uses map4.map indexed by x + z map4.sx to point into map4.slabs. Each slab entry is a 16-bit integer where bits 0–9 store a Y-coordinate increment and bits 10–15 store the Y-range length. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the float position pos to integer voxel coordinates x, y, z by scaling with volume dimensions vx, vy, vz. 2. Bounds Check: Verify x and z are within bounds. 3. Slab Access: Access the slab pointer for the current XZ coordinate. 4. Read Segment Lengths: Read the lengths of the first and second slab segments to skip header data. 5. Initialize State: Set y1=0, y2=0. Set pointer pt to p+len1. Initialize texture=0. 6. Iterate Slabs: Loop s from 0 to len1-1: a. Read Slab Entry: slab = p[0]; p += 1. b. Decode Y-Range: y1 += slab & 1023; y2 = y1 + (slab >> 10). c. Check Intersection: Check if the target Y coordinate y falls within the current slab range [y1, y2). d. Advance: If not found, advance the texture pointer and Y1: texture += y2 - y1; y1 = y2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rle4traverse(pos, vx, vy, vz, map4): # 1. Coordinate conversion x = int(pos[0] vx) y = int(pos[1] vy) z = int(pos[2] vz) # 2. Bounds check if x < 0 or x >= vx or z < 0 or z >= vz: return None # 3. Slab access (pointer arithmetic simulated via index offset) p = map4.slabs + map4.map[x + z map4.sx] # 4. Read segment lengths len1 = p[0]; p += 1 len2 = p[0]; p += 1 # 5. Initialize state y1 = 0 y2 = 0 pt = p + len1 texture = 0 # 6. Iterate slabs for s in range(len1): slab = p[0]; p += 1 y1 += slab & 1023 y2 = y1 + (slab >> 10) # 6c. Check intersection if y >= y1 and y < y2: col = readcolorfromtexture(pt, texture + y - y1) r = clamp(col[0] 15 + 16, 0, 31) g = clamp(col[1] 15 + 16, 0, 31) b = clamp(col[2] 15 + 16, 0, 31) packed = int(r + (g << 5) + (b << 10)) pt[texture + y - y1] = packed return packed # 6d. Advance texture += y2 - y1 y1 = y2 return None def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def readcolorfromtexture(texturearray, offset): # Standard texture/array lookup return texturearray[offset] Parameters: Color quantization: 5 bits per channel (0–31 range). Y-range decoding: 10 bits for Y-increment, 6 bits for Y-length. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bounds: The algorithm assumes the target Y coordinate is within the volume bounds checked at the start; if the ray passes through multiple slabs, it iterates until the Y range is found. Precision: The color quantization uses 5 bits per channel, which may introduce visible banding in high-dynamic-range scenes. Empty Regions: If the Y coordinate is not found in any slab, the algorithm returns without writing, effectively skipping the voxel. This method performs GPU-based ray casting on volume data compressed using run-length encoding (RLE), storing the compressed structure in 2D textures to facilitate efficient random access. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by avoiding full decompression; instead, it uses a texture-based lookup system to determine if a sample point lies in an uncompressed surface region, an "inside" region, or an "outside" region, returning special markers for the latter two. This approach is particularly suited for scenarios where the volume geometry is sparse or has large uniform interior/exterior regions, allowing the renderer to skip volumetric integration in those areas. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of Y-slabs traversed along the ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the compressed RLE4 structure, where N is the number of occupied Y-ranges. Performance: Efficient for sparse volumes with large uniform regions, as it avoids full decompression and skips empty space. Strengths: Low memory footprint for sparse data; fast traversal of empty space; GPU-friendly texture lookups. Limitations: Color quantization limits visual fidelity to 5 bits per channel; requires pre-compression of volume data; not suitable for dense volumes where compression ratio is low. The method is documented in the OpenGL-Voxel-Splatting repository. It is used for efficient ray casting in sparse volumetric data, leveraging RLE compression to skip empty space. sp4cerat/OpenGL-Voxel-Splatting, https://github.com/sp4cerat/OpenGL-Voxel-Splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: RL-compressed GPU Ray Casting with Texture-Based Lookup
head: Run-Length Encoded GPU Renderer
body: This method performs GPU-based ray casting on volume data compressed using run-length encoding (RLE), storing the compressed structure in 2D textures to facilitate efficient random access. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by avoiding full decompression; instead, it uses a texture-based lookup system to determine if a sample point lies in an uncompressed surface region, an "inside" region, or an "outside" region, returning special markers for the latter two. This approach is particularly suited for scenarios where the volume geometry is sparse or has large uniform interior/exterior regions, allowing the renderer to skip volumetric integration in those areas. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset, compressed into a specific RLE structure. Output: A rendered 2D image generated via fragment shaders. Query: A 3D coordinate (x, y, z) requested by the ray caster to determine the voxel value or classification. Data Structures The compressed data is stored in three 2D textures created by a builder and resident in graphics memory: 1. Index Texture: Stores offsets to the beginnings of each line in the Line Texture. It allows direct access to the RLE data corresponding to a specific (y, z) plane. 2. Line Texture: Contains the run-length encoded data. It stores pairs of values (count, offset) consecutively for each row (line) of the volume. 3. Surface Texture: Stores the actual volumetric values for uncompressed regions. It is accessed via offsets provided in the Line Texture. Encoding Details: Each entry in the Line Texture is a pair: (count, offset). count: The number of voxels in the run. offset: If the run is in an uncompressed area, this is the offset into the Surface Texture where the voxel values begin. If the run is in a compressed area, the offset is fictitiously set to 0 or 1 to distinguish compressed regions from uncompressed ones. Offset 0 typically denotes "Outside" and 1 denotes "Inside" (or vice versa, as they are special markers). The data is organized such that lines of the volume are stored sequentially, with the Index Texture providing the starting position for each (y, z) line. Algorithm: Voxel Lookup When a fragment shader needs the value for a voxel at (x, y, z): 1. Locate Line: Use the Index Texture to retrieve the offset in the Line Texture corresponding to the (y, z) coordinates. 2. Iterate Runs: Read pairs (count, offset) from the Line Texture starting at the located offset. For each pair, check if the requested x coordinate falls within the current run. Let x{start} be the cumulative count of voxels processed so far in this line. The condition is: x{start} \le x < x{start} + count. If the condition is met, the run containing x is found. 3. Determine Region: If the offset of the found pair is 0 or 1 (compressed area): Return a special value: C (Inside) or O (Outside). No further lookup is performed; full decompression is avoided. If the offset is a valid texture address (uncompressed area): Calculate the specific index into the Surface Texture. The index is offset + (x - xstart). Retrieve the actual voxel value from the Surface Texture at this index. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getvoxelvalue(x, y, z, indextexture, linetexture, surfacetexture): """ Retrieves the voxel value or classification for (x, y, z). Returns: A float value if the voxel is in an uncompressed surface region. 'O' if the voxel is in a compressed Outside region. 'I' if the voxel is in a compressed Inside region. """ # Step 1: Get the start offset in the Line Texture for the (y, z) line linestartoffset = indextexture.sample(y, z) # Step 2: Iterate through the run-length pairs in the Line Texture currentoffset = linestartoffset xstart = 0 while True: # Read the next pair (count, offset) from the Line Texture count, offset = linetexture.samplepair(currentoffset) # Check if the requested x falls within this run if xstart <= x < xstart + count: # Step 3: Determine if the region is compressed or uncompressed if offset == 0 or offset == 1: # Compressed region if offset == 0: return 'O' # Outside else: return 'I' # Inside else: # Uncompressed region # Calculate the index in the Surface Texture relativex = x - xstart surfaceindex = offset + relativex return surfacetexture.sample(surfaceindex) # Advance to next pair in the line texture array currentoffset += 1 xstart += count Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The method relies on integer arithmetic for indices. Ensure that the count and offset fields are large enough to represent the volume dimensions and texture sizes without overflow. Compressed Region Semantics: The distinction between "Inside" and "Outside" is binary in compressed regions. The renderer must know which offset value (0 or 1) corresponds to which classification. Time Complexity: Lookup time is proportional to the number of runs in the line segment for the given (y, z) plane. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is the sum of the sizes of the Index Texture, Line Texture, and Surface Texture. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient for volumes with large uniform regions (inside/outside). Avoids the computational cost of decompressing the entire volume. Suitable for GPU implementation using texture lookups. Limitations: Random access to uncompressed voxels requires iterating through the Line Texture. Not as efficient as direct indexing for fully dense volumes. The distinction between compressed and uncompressed regions is rigid. This method was implemented in the VRE volume rendering engine. It was designed to illustrate how to develop new plugins requiring special memory representations on the GPU, specifically leveraging OpenGL textures for compressed data storage. The approach was tested with simple command-line interfaces and GUI applications. The VRE volume rendering engine, https://doi.org/10.1145/1925059.1925072, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Sparse Shadow Volume Raycast
head: raycastShadowVolumeSparse
body: A hierarchical raycasting algorithm that traverses a sparse shadow volume texture to find the first intersection with a shadow-casting volume. It dynamically adjusts its traversal step size and level of detail (LOD) based on occupancy bits, allowing it to skip empty space efficiently compared to fixed-step hierarchical variants. It differs from siblings such as Voxel-Cell Duality Mapping, Spherical Volume Ray Walking, Plane Marching, RLE4 Ray Tracing, Regular Grid Traversal, Voxel Raytracer, and DirectVoxGO Volume Rendering by using a multi-level occupancy-bit search that refines or coarsens traversal granularity on the fly. Inputs: origin: Ray origin in world space. dir: Ray direction (normalized). dist: Maximum ray distance. uVolOffset: Offset vector for the shadow volume texture coordinates. uVolTexelSize: Physical size of a texel in the shadow volume. uVolResolution: Resolution of the shadow volume texture (vec3). uShadowVolume: The sparse shadow volume texture. Outputs: d: Distance to the first occupied voxel. Returns dist if no intersection is found within the limit. Data Structures: uShadowVolume: A texture where each texel contains occupancy information. The algorithm samples this texture at different LODs. The exact internal structure is abstracted by the texture fetch, but the algorithm relies on the x component of the sampled value being non-zero to indicate occupancy. Steps: 1. Initialization: Translate origin by uVolOffset. Compute step as uVolTexelSize. Compute stepDir as dir invShadowVolumeResolution. Compute pos as origin invVolumeTexelSize invShadowVolumeResolution. Halve stepDir and step by multiplying by 0.5. Initialize lod to -1 and d to 0.0. 2. Traversal Loop: While d < dist: Sample c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod).x. If lod == -1 (Coarse Search): If c != 0, calculate bit index from fractional parts of pos: bit = (fract(pos.x uVolResolution.x) > 0.5 ? 1: 0) + (fract(pos.y uVolResolution.y) > 0.5 ? 2: 0) + (fract(pos.z uVolResolution.z) > 0.5 ? 4: 0). Create mask mask = 1 << bit. If (mask & c) != 0, return d. Else, advance pos += stepDir and d += step. If c == 0, increment lod, double stepDir and step, and advance pos += stepDir and d += step. If lod != -1 (Refinement): If c != 0, halve stepDir and step, decrement lod, and backtrack pos -= stepDir and d -= step. Else (c == 0), if lod < 2, sample c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod + 1).x. If that sample is 0, increment lod, double stepDir and step, and advance pos += stepDir and d += step. Formulas: invShadowVolumeResolution = 1.0 / uVolResolution invVolumeTexelSize = 1.0 / uVolTexelSize stepDir = dir invShadowVolumeResolution pos = origin invVolumeTexelSize invShadowVolumeResolution bit = (fract(pos.x uVolResolution.x) > 0.5 ? 1: 0) + (fract(pos.y uVolResolution.y) > 0.5 ? 2: 0) + (fract(pos.z uVolResolution.z) > 0.5 ? 4: 0) Parameters: uVolResolution: vec3, resolution of the shadow volume texture. uVolTexelSize: float, physical size of a texel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The algorithm assumes a maximum LOD of 2. If lod is already 2 and the sample is empty, it does not attempt to go deeper, relying on the coarse search or returning the distance limit. Precision issues may arise when calculating bit indices from fractional parts of pos if pos values are very large or small. The algorithm assumes the shadow volume texture supports textureLod with varying LOD levels. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def fract(x): return x - math.floor(x) def textureLod(tex, pos, lod): # Standard GPU texture fetch with explicit LOD bias return tex.sample(pos, lod) def raycastshadowvolumesparse(origin, dir, dist, uVolOffset, uVolTexelSize, uVolResolution, uShadowVolume): invShadowVolumeResolution = 1.0 / uVolResolution invVolumeTexelSize = 1.0 / uVolTexelSize origin = origin + uVolOffset step = uVolTexelSize stepDir = dir invShadowVolumeResolution pos = origin invVolumeTexelSize invShadowVolumeResolution stepDir = stepDir 0.5 step = step 0.5 lod = -1 d = 0.0 while d < dist: c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod).x if lod == -1: if c != 0: bit = (1 if fract(pos.x uVolResolution.x) > 0.5 else 0) + \ (2 if fract(pos.y uVolResolution.y) > 0.5 else 0) + \ (4 if fract(pos.z uVolResolution.z) > 0.5 else 0) mask = 1 << bit if (mask & c) != 0: return d else: pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step else: lod = lod + 1 stepDir = stepDir 2.0 step = step 2.0 pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step else: if c != 0: stepDir = stepDir 0.5 step = step 0.5 lod = lod - 1 pos = pos - stepDir d = d - step else: if lod < 2: c = textureLod(uShadowVolume, pos, lod + 1).x if c == 0: lod = lod + 1 stepDir = stepDir 2.0 step = step 2.0 pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step else: # If lod is already 2 and the sample is empty, it does not attempt to go deeper, relying on the coarse search or returning the distance limit pos = pos + stepDir d = d + step return dist A hierarchical raycasting algorithm for shadow volumes that uses fixed step sizes and LODs, traversing from base distance to further distances using specific LOD levels (0, 1, 2). It differs from the sparse variant by not dynamically adjusting step sizes based on occupancy bits, instead using predefined distance thresholds (baseDistance) to switch between LOD levels. It is chosen when the shadow volume is not sparse or when a simpler, fixed-step traversal is preferred. Performs a directional shadow raycast against the sparse shadow volume, including screen-space blocking check and position jittering. It first checks if the ray is blocked in screen space; if so, it returns 0.0. Otherwise, it jitters the position and calls raycastShadowVolumeSparse with the jittered position and direction. It is used to reduce aliasing and improve shadow quality. Not given in the sources. Origin: The method is described in the context of a voxel rendering project, specifically in the mainsv.cpp file of the TTFH/Voxel-Render repository. TTFH/Voxel-Render, https://github.com/TTFH/Voxel-Render, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Regular Grid Traversal
head: Grid Traversal Algorithm, 3D-DDA, Digital Differential Analyzer (for grids)
body: Regular Grid Traversal is a ray-scene intersection acceleration technique that partitions a scene bounding box into a fixed-size 3D grid of cells, returning the sequence of cells intersected by a ray to minimize primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of testing every object for every ray by only testing primitives stored in intersected cells. Unlike hierarchical structures (e.g., BVH, Octree) that partition primitives into disjoint sets, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, allowing primitives to belong to multiple sub-blocks. It is distinguished by its constant-time access to cells and simple traversal logic, making it optimal for scenes with uniform data distribution or dynamic scenes requiring frequent rebuilds. The method consists of two phases: Grid Construction (building the structure) and Ray Traversal (using the structure). 1. Initialize: Allocate a 1D array mGrid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz and set all entries to NULL. 2. Calculate Dimensions: Compute voxel dimensions and their reciprocals for fast division: dx = \frac{p2.x - p1.x}{Nx}, \quad dx{reci} = \frac{1}{dx} (Similarly for dy, dz and dy{reci}, dz{reci}). 3. Assign Primitives: For each primitive P: Get its Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) [b{min}, b{max}]. Calculate the range of grid cells overlapping this AABB. Clamp coordinates to grid bounds [0, N-1] to handle primitives outside or on the boundary: x1 = \max(0, \lfloor (b{min}.x - p1.x) \cdot dx{reci} \rfloor) x2 = \min(Nx - 1, \lfloor (b{max}.x - p1.x) \cdot dx{reci} \rfloor + 1) (Similarly for y1, y2 and z1, z2). Loop over all cells (x, y, z) in the range [x1, x2) \times [y1, y2) \times [z1, z2): Construct the AABB for the current cell. If the primitive intersects the cell AABB, add the primitive to the cell's ObjectList. Note: This mapping must be conservative; it may include more primitives than strictly necessary but never fewer. The traversal identifies the sequence of cells intersected by a ray r(t) = o + t \cdot d. 1. Ray-Grid Intersection: Intersect the ray with the grid's bounding box [p1, p2] to find entry t{enter} and exit t{exit} parameters. If t{exit} < 0 or t{enter} > t{exit}, the ray misses the grid. If t{enter} < 0, set t{enter} = 0 (ray starts inside). 2. Initialization: Determine the starting point on the ray: start\point = o + d \cdot t{enter}. Calculate the starting cell (X, Y, Z): X = \lfloor \frac{start\point.x - p1.x}{dx} \rfloor (Similarly for Y, Z). Calculate step directions: stepX = \text{sign}(d.x) \quad (\text{1 if } d.x \ge 0, -1 \text{ otherwise}) (Similarly for stepY, stepZ). Calculate delta distances (distance to cross one cell): tDeltaX = \frac{dx}{|d.x|} \text{ if } d.x \neq 0 \text{ else } \infty (Similarly for tDeltaY, tDeltaZ). Calculate initial boundary distances (tMax): If d.x > 0: tMaxX = \frac{(X + 1) \cdot dx + p1.x - start\point.x}{d.x} If d.x < 0: tMaxX = \frac{X \cdot dx + p1.x - start\point.x}{d.x} If d.x = 0: tMaxX = \infty. (Similarly for tMaxY, tMaxZ). 3. Loop: While t{enter} < t{exit}: Process the current cell (X, Y, Z): If mGrid[idx] is not NULL, iterate through the ObjectList. For each primitive, perform intersection test. Deduplication: To avoid testing the same primitive multiple times (if it spans multiple cells), use a "Mailbox" system: assign each ray a unique ID, and store the ray ID in the primitive's intersection cache. Skip tests if the cache already contains the current ray ID. Correctness Check: If an intersection is found but the point is outside the current cell, continue advancing. Advance to the nearest boundary: Find axis A \in \{X, Y, Z\} with minimum tMaxA. Update tMaxA \leftarrow tMaxA + tDeltaA. Update coordinate A \leftarrow A + stepA. If the new coordinate is out of bounds, terminate. A Regular Grid is a spatial acceleration structure that divides a scene bounding box into a fixed-size 3D grid of cells (voxels) to reduce the number of ray-primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of testing every object for every ray by only testing primitives stored in cells intersected by the ray. Unlike hierarchical structures (e.g., BVH, Octree) that partition primitives into disjoint sets, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, allowing primitives to belong to multiple sub-blocks. It is distinguished by its constant-time access to cells and simple traversal logic, making it optimal for scenes with uniform data distribution or dynamic scenes requiring frequent rebuilds. Voxel-based Ray Tracing is a global illumination (GI) and specular reflection fallback method that performs Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal through a sparse, block-occupancy voxel grid to sample indirect lighting and environment reflections. It serves as a drop-in replacement for Screen-Space Ray Tracing (SSRT) for GI and a fallback for Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) when screen-space coverage is incomplete, combining sky occlusion with Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) colour bleeding. Unlike standard voxel raycasting which often relies on volume density, this method operates on a binary block-occupancy grid to determine surface hits for lighting queries. Optimised Voxel Ray Marching is a ray traversal algorithm for voxel-based scenes that uses fixed-length steps along the ray to traverse a 3D grid of voxels, checking for occupancy at each step. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space in large voxel worlds by optimizing memory access patterns, specifically by keeping block lookups within the current working chunk to minimize bitshifts, masks, and multiplication operations. It sets itself apart from Regular Grid Traversal by using a chunked memory layout that reduces boundary calculation overhead, and from Chunked Voxel Traversal by relying on fixed-size inner grids which simplifies implementation and memory layout. The Regular Grid Traversal algorithm is a foundational technique in ray tracing, historically developed to determine the cells traversed by a ray in a grid. Algorithms for grid traversal are quite similar to rasterization algorithms (such as Bresenham line draw algorithm [Bre65]), but unlike Bresenham which produces visually acceptable lines in the shortest time without finding all pixels traversed, grid traversal must find all cells traversed by the ray segment. A naive 3D extension of Bresenham is not suitable as a grid traversal algorithm. Traversal time is a critical metric, often modeled by two constants: T{setup} (time to setup traversal algorithm) and T{step} (time spent to advance from a cell to its neighbor without checking intersection). An algorithm with low T{setup} usually performs better for low resolution grids, whereas high T{step} provides bad performance for larger grids. Sources A Survey on Exploiting Grids for Ray Tracing, https://doi.org/10.2312/localchapterevents/italchap/italianchapconf2008/089-096, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Regular Grid
head: Grid Data Structure, Grilles régulières, Regular Grid Spatial Subdivision, Uniform Grids, Uniform Spatial Subdivision
body: A Regular Grid is a spatial acceleration structure that divides a scene bounding box into a fixed-size 3D grid of cells (voxels) to reduce the number of ray-primitive intersection tests. It solves the problem of testing every object for every ray by only testing primitives stored in cells intersected by the ray. Unlike hierarchical structures (e.g., BVH, Octree) that partition primitives into disjoint sets, the Regular Grid partitions space into disjoint sub-blocks, allowing primitives to belong to multiple sub-blocks. It is distinguished by its constant-time access to cells and simple traversal logic, making it optimal for scenes with uniform data distribution on GPU. Its linear build time makes it attractive for dynamic scenes requiring frequent rebuilds. The method consists of two phases: Grid Construction (building the structure) and Ray Traversal (using the structure). Inputs: Scene primitives (with bounding boxes), scene bounding box [p1, p2], grid resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz). Outputs: A 1D array representing the grid cells, where each cell contains a list of pointers to overlapping primitives. The grid is stored as a 1D array mGrid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Each element is a pointer to an ObjectList. Index Calculation: For cell coordinates (x, y, z), the index is: idx = x + y \cdot Nx + z \cdot Nx \cdot Ny ObjectList: A linked list node containing: primitive: Pointer to the primitive object. next: Pointer to the next ObjectList in the chain. 1. Initialize: Allocate mGrid of size Nx Ny Nz and set all entries to NULL. 2. Calculate Dimensions: Compute voxel dimensions and their reciprocals for fast division: dx = \frac{p2.x - p1.x}{Nx}, \quad dx{reci} = \frac{1}{dx} (Similarly for dy, dz and dy{reci}, dz{reci}). 3. Assign Primitives: For each primitive P: Get its Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) [b{min}, b{max}]. Calculate the range of grid cells overlapping this AABB. Clamp coordinates to grid bounds [0, N-1] to handle primitives outside or on the boundary: x1 = \max(0, \lfloor (b{min}.x - p1.x) \cdot dx{reci} \rfloor) x2 = \min(Nx - 1, \lfloor (b{max}.x - p1.x) \cdot dx{reci} \rfloor + 1) (Similarly for y1, y2 and z1, z2). Loop over all cells (x, y, z) in the range [x1, x2) \times [y1, y2) \times [z1, z2): Construct the AABB for the current cell. If the primitive intersects the cell AABB, add the primitive to the cell's ObjectList. Note: This mapping must be conservative; it may include more primitives than strictly necessary but never fewer. The traversal identifies the sequence of cells intersected by a ray r(t) = o + t \cdot d. 1. Ray-Grid Intersection: Intersect the ray with the grid's bounding box [p1, p2] to find entry t{enter} and exit t{exit} parameters. If t{exit} < 0 or t{enter} > t{exit}, the ray misses the grid. If t{enter} < 0, set t{enter} = 0 (ray starts inside). 2. Initialization: Determine the starting point on the ray: start\point = o + d \cdot t{enter}. Calculate the starting cell (X, Y, Z): X = \lfloor \frac{start\point.x - p1.x}{dx} \rfloor (Similarly for Y, Z). Calculate step directions: stepX = \text{sign}(d.x) \quad (\text{1 if } d.x \ge 0, -1 \text{ otherwise}) (Similarly for stepY, stepZ). Calculate delta distances (distance to cross one cell): tDeltaX = \frac{dx}{|d.x|} \text{ if } d.x \neq 0 \text{ else } \infty (Similarly for tDeltaY, tDeltaZ). Calculate initial boundary distances (tMax): If d.x > 0: tMaxX = \frac{(X + 1) \cdot dx + p1.x - start\point.x}{d.x} If d.x < 0: tMaxX = \frac{X \cdot dx + p1.x - start\point.x}{d.x} If d.x = 0: tMaxX = \infty. (Similarly for tMaxY, tMaxZ). 3. Loop: While t{enter} < t{exit}: Process the current cell (X, Y, Z): If mGrid[idx] is not NULL, iterate through the ObjectList. For each primitive, perform intersection test. Deduplication: To avoid testing the same primitive multiple times (if it spans multiple cells), use a "Mailbox" system: assign each ray a unique ID, and store the ray ID in the primitive's intersection cache. Skip tests if the cache already contains the current ray ID. Correctness Check: If an intersection is found but the point is outside the current cell, continue advancing. Advance to the nearest boundary: Find axis A \in \{X, Y, Z\} with minimum tMaxA. Update tMaxA \leftarrow tMaxA + tDeltaA. Update coordinate A \leftarrow A + stepA. If the new coordinate is out of bounds, terminate. Unverified code. Loop while True: # Check bounds if not (0 <= X < Nx and 0 <= Y < Ny and 0 <= Z < Nz): break idx = X + Y Nx + Z Nx Ny node = grid[idx] # Process cell while node is not None: prim = node.primitive # Mailbox check: skip if already tested for this ray if not prim.istestedfor(rayid): hit = testprimitive(prim, rayorigin, raydir, rayid) if hit is not None: return hit node = node.next # Advance to nearest boundary if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: tmaxx += tdeltax X += stepx else: tmaxz += tdeltaz Z += stepz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: tmaxy += tdeltay Y += stepy else: tmaxz += tdeltaz Z += stepz return None GRIDSIZE (N): The number of cells along each axis. Total cells N^3. Voxel Density (D): Ratio of voxels to objects. D=1.0 is often inefficient; D=20.0 ("Uniform Grid Customary") is recommended for better performance in SPD scenes. Resolution: Should strive to create cubical voxels by setting Nx, Ny, Nz proportional to the scene bounding box dimensions. Intersection Outside Cell: A primitive in cell F may be intersected while the ray is in cell F, but the intersection point lies in cell G. Testing only the current cell misses this or requires redundant checks. Solution: Continue advancing to subsequent cells until the intersection point is within the current cell or a closer intersection is found. Redundant Tests: Primitives spanning multiple cells are tested multiple times. Solution: Use "Mailboxes" (ray ID caching) to skip already-tested primitives. Sparse Scenes: High memory usage due to empty cells. Not suitable for very sparse scenes. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for the grid array plus storage for primitives in lists. Computes intersections between a ray and a regular-grid mesh with O(P) complexity, exploiting structured topology for neural field rendering. Time Complexity: Build: Linear with respect to the number of primitives or grid size (O(N{prim} + N{cells})). Allows interactive rebuilds for dynamic scenes. Traversal: Depends on the number of cells traversed and primitives per cell. Setup cost T{setup} is significant; step cost T{step} degrades performance in large grids. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz) for the grid array plus storage for primitives in lists. High for sparse scenes as empty voxels consume memory. Performance: On Intel Pentium II 350 MHz, 'tree' scene (513x513, depth 4): Uniform Grid D=1.0 took 1517.0s traversal; D=20.0 took 781.3s. Outperforms hierarchical grids for some SPD scenes with high voxel density. Optimal on GPU for uniform data distribution due to cached texture accesses (100x faster). Strengths: Simple implementation, fast build time, good for dynamic scenes, constant-time access. Limitations: High memory for sparse scenes, redundant tests for large primitives, not adaptive. name: Regular-Grid Mesh Intersection
head: Ray-Mesh Quadrature
body: Regular-Grid Mesh Intersection is a method to compute intersections between a ray and a regular-grid mesh M of size P \times P \times P with O(P) complexity. It sets itself apart from general ray-mesh intersection algorithms by exploiting the structured topology of the regular grid to limit the search space to a linear number of voxels and faces, enabling efficient quadrature for neural field rendering. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Regular-grid mesh M defined on a grid of size P \times P \times P. Acceleration grid G \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times P \times P}, where each cell stores a value indicating the likelihood of containing geometry. Training stage indicator t (normalized to [0,1]) to determine pruning aggressiveness. Scene type flag (e.g., unbounded 360°). Outputs: A set of quadrature points (intersection points) between the ray and the mesh faces. Data Structures: Acceleration Grid G: A 3D array of size P \times P \times P. Each element G{i,j,k} is a real number. The sources do not specify the exact bit-packing or normalization range, but it is used as a threshold filter. Mesh M: Implicitly defined by the regular grid vertices. The mesh consists of faces incident to the voxel vertices. Parameters: \tauG = 0.1: Threshold for pruning voxels in the acceleration grid. P: Grid resolution (dimension of the regular grid). Steps: 1. Compute Intersected Voxels: Solve 3P ray-plane intersections to determine the set of voxels intersected by the ray. Using the intersection points, identify at most 3P intersected voxels. 2. Prune Empty Voxels (Conditional): Use the acceleration grid G to prune voxels unlikely to contain geometry. A voxel is kept if its corresponding value in G exceeds \tauG = 0.1. Training Stage 1 (First Quarter): Do not use G for pruning. Keep all 3P intersected voxels and all 3P intersection points. Training Stage 2 (Second Quarter): Use G to remove empty voxels. Keep at most 3P/2 non-empty voxels and the 3P/2 intersection points closest to the camera. Training Stage 3 (Rest of Training): Use G to remove empty voxels. Keep at most 3P/4 intersection points. Batch Size Adjustment: Double the training batch size each time the number of intersections is halved. 3. Compute Quadrature Points: For each kept voxel, compute intersections between the ray and the faces of M that are incident to the voxel’s vertex. This yields the final set of quadrature points. 4. Special Case for Unbounded 360° Scenes: For concentric boxes in unbounded 360° scenes, compute their intersections and keep all of them, regardless of the pruning steps above. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def regulargridmeshintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, mesh, accelgrid, P, trainingstage, isunbounded360): """ Compute intersections between a ray and a regular-grid mesh. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. mesh: Regular-grid mesh of size P x P x P. accelgrid: 3D array of size P x P x P, values indicate geometry likelihood. P: Integer, grid resolution. trainingstage: Float in [0, 1], normalized training progress. isunbounded360: Boolean, true for unbounded 360 degree scenes. Returns: list of intersection points (quadrature points). """ # Step 1: Compute intersected voxels # Solve 3P ray-plane intersections to find intersected voxels intersectedvoxels = solverayplaneintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, P) # At most 3P voxels numvoxels = len(intersectedvoxels) # Step 2: Pruning based on training stage if isunbounded360: # Special case: keep all intersections for concentric boxes keptvoxels = intersectedvoxels else: if trainingstage < 0.25: # First quarter: no pruning, keep all keptvoxels = intersectedvoxels elif trainingstage < 0.5: # Second quarter: prune using G, keep at most 3P/2 keptvoxels = prunevoxels(intersectedvoxels, accelgrid, threshold=0.1) # Keep closest 3P/2 to camera keptvoxels = keepclosest(keptvoxels, rayorigin, limit=3P/2) else: # Rest of training: prune using G, keep at most 3P/4 keptvoxels = prunevoxels(intersectedvoxels, accelgrid, threshold=0.1) # Keep closest 3P/4 to camera keptvoxels = keepclosest(keptvoxels, rayorigin, limit=3P/4) # Step 3: Compute quadrature points quadraturepoints = [] for voxel in keptvoxels: # Compute intersections between ray and faces incident to voxel's vertex points = computefaceintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, mesh, voxel) quadraturepoints.extend(points) return quadraturepoints def solverayplaneintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, P): """ Solve 3P ray-plane intersections to obtain intersected voxels. Returns a list of voxel indices or coordinates. """ # Implementation detail: The source states this involves solving 3P ray-plane intersections. # The exact geometric formulation for the planes is not provided in the text. # Assuming standard ray-box intersection logic adapted for the grid planes. # The result is at most 3P voxels. pass def prunevoxels(voxels, accelgrid, threshold): """ Remove voxels where accelgrid value is below threshold. """ kept = [] for voxel in voxels: # Access accelgrid at voxel coordinates if accelgrid[voxel] >= threshold: kept.append(voxel) return kept def keepclosest(voxels, rayorigin, limit): """ Keep the 'limit' voxels closest to rayorigin. """ # Sort voxels by distance to rayorigin sortedvoxels = sorted(voxels, key=lambda v: distance(v, rayorigin)) return sortedvoxels[:limit] def computefaceintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, mesh, voxel): """ Compute intersections between ray and faces of M incident to voxel's vertex. """ # Implementation detail: The source states this yields the final quadrature points. # The specific faces incident to the vertex are not enumerated. # Assuming standard ray-triangle intersection for the mesh faces associated with the voxel. pass Time Complexity: O(P) for computing intersections. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the acceleration grid G \in \mathbb{R}^{P \times P \times P}. Performance: The method enables efficient neural field rendering on mobile architectures by reducing the number of intersection tests. Strengths: Linear complexity with respect to grid resolution P; efficient pruning via acceleration grid. Limitations: Accuracy of the acceleration grid G is low in the first quarter of training, necessitating full voxel retention initially. The method is described in the context of MobileNeRF, which exploits the polygon rasterization pipeline for efficient neural field rendering on mobile architectures. It was introduced to address the computational cost of ray-mesh intersections in neural rendering. name: Voxel-based Ray Tracing for GI and Specular Reflections
head: ApplyVoxelRT, Voxel RT, VoxelDDA, VoxelReflectionFallback
body: Voxel-based Ray Tracing is a global illumination (GI) and specular reflection fallback method that performs Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal through a sparse, block-occupancy voxel grid to sample indirect lighting and environment reflections. It serves as a drop-in replacement for Screen-Space Ray Tracing (SSRT) for GI and a fallback for Screen-Space Reflections (SSR) when screen-space coverage is incomplete, combining sky occlusion with Light Propagation Volumes (LPV) colour bleeding. Unlike standard voxel raycasting which often relies on volume density, this method operates on a binary block-occupancy grid to determine surface hits for lighting queries. The method consists of a core 3D DDA traversal kernel (VoxelDDA), a lighting sampling function (SampleVoxelLighting), and two high-level application functions: ApplyVoxelRT for GI and VoxelReflectionFallback for specular reflections. Input Grid: A 128^3 block-occupancy grid stored in imgVoxelMask, populated every frame during the shadow pass. Input Lighting: LPV (Light Propagation Volumes) data, accessed via image load/store operations. Input Ray: Origin o, direction d, and maximum traversal distance/steps. Output GI: A blended indirect colour value combining sky occlusion and LPV bounce. Output Reflection: A specular colour sampled from the voxel grid at the hit location. Voxel Grid (imgVoxelMask): A 3D image buffer representing a 128 \times 128 \times 128 grid. Each voxel stores a binary occupancy flag (1 if a block exists, 0 otherwise). LPV Buffer: A 3D texture or image buffer storing propagated light colour and intensity values for each voxel. VOXELGISAMPLES: Number of cosine-weighted hemisphere rays for GI sampling. Default: 4. VOXELGISTEPS: Maximum number of DDA steps for GI ray traversal. VOXELREFLSTEPS: Maximum number of DDA steps for reflection ray traversal. VOXELRTREFLECTIONS: Feature flag (boolean) to enable specular reflection fallback. Default: Disabled (commented out). VOXELGI: Indirect effect mode identifier (value 6). This function performs the 3D DDA traversal to find the first occupied voxel face intersected by a ray. 1. Initialization: Calculate grid dimensions Nx=Ny=Nz=128. Determine cell size dx, dy, dz based on the world-space bounding box of the voxel grid. Compute step directions: stepX = \text{sign}(d.x), stepY = \text{sign}(d.y), stepZ = \text{sign}(d.z). Compute delta distances: tDeltaX = dx / |d.x| (if d.x \neq 0 else \infty), similarly for Y, Z. Determine starting cell (X, Y, Z) from the ray origin (clamped to entry point). Compute initial boundary distances tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ to the next grid plane in the direction of travel. Apply a small ray bias to the origin to prevent self-intersection and handle near-parallel rays gracefully. 2. Traversal Loop: Iterate up to maxsteps times. Find the axis with the minimum tMax (tMin = \min(tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ)). Check if the current cell (X, Y, Z) is occupied in imgVoxelMask. If occupied, return the hit position (face centre) and the axis-aligned normal of the face crossed. Advance the ray: Increment the coordinate of the minimum axis by its step direction. Update the corresponding tMax by adding its tDelta. If the ray exits the grid bounds or reaches maxsteps without a hit, return a miss status. 1. Given a hit position P and normal N from VoxelDDA: 2. Offset the sampling position by half a block in the direction of the normal (or opposite, depending on LPV convention) to sample the LPV data "in front" of the surface. 3. Read the indirect colour from the LPV buffer at this offset position. 1. Initialize total indirect colour C{indirect} = 0. 2. Generate VOXELGISAMPLES cosine-weighted hemisphere rays around the surface normal. 3. For each ray: Call VoxelDDA with the ray parameters and VOXELGISTEPS. If a hit is found: Call SampleVoxelLighting to get LPV colour C{lpv}. Blend C{lpv} with sky contribution (based on ray direction and sky occlusion). Accumulate into C{indirect}. If no hit, use sky contribution only. 4. Average the results from all samples. 1. Check if VOXELRTREFLECTIONS is enabled and if SSR missed (e.g., environmentReflection.a < 1). 2. Construct a specular reflection ray from the surface normal and view direction. 3. Call VoxelDDA with this ray and VOXELREFLSTEPS. 4. If a hit is found: Call SampleVoxelLighting to get the voxel colour. Scale the voxel lighting to match typical sky-reflection brightness ranges to avoid visual mismatch. Return the scaled colour as the reflection result. 5. If no hit, return transparent or black. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. GRIDSIZE = 128 VOXELGISAMPLES = 4 VOXELGISTEPS = 64 # Example default, configurable VOXELREFLSTEPS = 32 # Example default, configurable def VoxelDDA(origin, direction, maxsteps): """ Performs 3D DDA traversal on the voxel grid. Returns (hitposition, hitnormal) or None if miss. """ # 1. Initialization # Assuming grid bounds [0, 1] in world space for simplicity, # scaled by actual grid dimensions in implementation. dx = 1.0 / GRIDSIZE dy = 1.0 / GRIDSIZE dz = 1.0 / GRIDSIZE # Step directions stepX = 1 if direction.x > 0 else (-1 if direction.x < 0 else 0) stepY = 1 if direction.y > 0 else (-1 if direction.y < 0 else 0) stepZ = 1 if direction.z > 0 else (-1 if direction.z < 0 else 0) # Delta distances tDeltaX = dx / abs(direction.x) if direction.x != 0 else float('inf') tDeltaY = dy / abs(direction.y) if direction.y != 0 else float('inf') tDeltaZ = dz / abs(direction.z) if direction.z != 0 else float('inf') # Initial cell # Apply small bias to avoid self-intersection bias = 1e-4 startpoint = origin + direction bias X = floor((startpoint.x) / dx) Y = floor((startpoint.y) / dy) Z = floor((startpoint.z) / dz) # Clamp to grid bounds X = clamp(X, 0, GRIDSIZE - 1) Y = clamp(Y, 0, GRIDSIZE - 1) Z = clamp(Z, 0, GRIDSIZE - 1) # Initial tMax (distance to next boundary) # For positive direction: boundary is at (X+1)dx # For negative direction: boundary is at Xdx if direction.x > 0: tMaxX = ((X + 1) dx - startpoint.x) / direction.x elif direction.x < 0: tMaxX = (X dx - startpoint.x) / direction.x else: tMaxX = float('inf') if direction.y > 0: tMaxY = ((Y + 1) dy - startpoint.y) / direction.y elif direction.y < 0: tMaxY = (Y dy - startpoint.y) / direction.y else: tMaxY = float('inf') if direction.z > 0: tMaxZ = ((Z + 1) dz - startpoint.z) / direction.z elif direction.z < 0: tMaxZ = (Z dz - startpoint.z) / direction.z else: tMaxZ = float('inf') # 2. Traversal Loop for i in range(maxsteps): # Check bounds if X < 0 or X >= GRIDSIZE or Y < 0 or Y >= GRIDSIZE or Z < 0 or Z >= GRIDSIZE: return None # Check occupancy in imgVoxelMask if isoccupied(X, Y, Z): # Calculate hit position (face centre) # Determine which axis was crossed last mint = min(tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ) hitpos = startpoint + direction mint # Determine normal if tMaxX <= tMaxY and tMaxX <= tMaxZ: normal = vec3(-stepX, 0, 0) elif tMaxY <= tMaxX and tMaxY <= tMaxZ: normal = vec3(0, -stepY, 0) else: normal = vec3(0, 0, -stepZ) return (hitpos, normal) # Advance if tMaxX < tMaxY: if tMaxX < tMaxZ: X += stepX tMaxX += tDeltaX else: Z += stepZ tMaxZ += tDeltaZ else: if tMaxY < tMaxZ: Y += stepY tMaxY += tDeltaY else: Z += stepZ tMaxZ += tDeltaZ return None def SampleVoxelLighting(hitpos, hitnormal): """ Samples LPV data half a block in front of the hit face. """ # Offset by half a block in the direction of the normal offset = hitnormal (0.5 / GRIDSIZE) samplepos = hitpos + offset # Read from LPV buffer # Note: Actual implementation requires GLSL imageLoad or texture lookup # Assuming a function getLPVColor(pos) exists return getLPVColor(samplepos) def ApplyVoxelRT(surfacepos, surfacenormal, viewdir): """ Computes GI using cosine-weighted hemisphere sampling. """ totalcolor = vec3(0.0) count = 0 for i in range(VOXELGISAMPLES): # Generate cosine-weighted hemisphere ray raydir = cosineweightedhemispheresample(surfacenormal) # Trace ray hit = VoxelDDA(surfacepos, raydir, VOXELGISTEPS) if hit is not None: hitpos, hitnormal = hit lpvcolor = SampleVoxelLighting(hitpos, hitnormal) # Blend sky contribution with LPV bounce # Sky contribution depends on raydir and sky occlusion skycontrib = getskycontribution(raydir) indirectcolor = mix(skycontrib, lpvcolor, 0.5) # Blending factor is implementation detail totalcolor += indirectcolor count += 1 else: # No hit, use sky contribution skycontrib = getskycontribution(raydir) totalcolor += skycontrib count += 1 if count > 0: return totalcolor / count else: return vec3(0.0) def VoxelReflectionFallback(surfacepos, surfacenormal, viewdir): """ Fallback for specular reflections when SSR misses. """ # Construct reflection ray raydir = reflect(-viewdir, surfacenormal) # Trace ray hit = VoxelDDA(surfacepos, raydir, VOXELREFLSTEPS) if hit is not None: hitpos, hitnormal = hit voxelcolor = SampleVoxelLighting(hitpos, hitnormal) # Scale to match sky-reflection brightness scaledcolor = voxelcolor brightnessscalefactor return scaledcolor else: return vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Transparent Self-Intersection: A ray bias must be applied to the origin to prevent the ray from immediately hitting the voxel it started in. Near-Parallel Rays: The DDA logic must handle cases where d.x, d.y, or d.z is zero to avoid division by zero in tDelta calculations. Hardware Support: Requires GLARBshaderimageloadstore for reading the voxel mask and LPV data. If unsupported, the system must degrade to SSRT. Visual Mismatch: Voxel lighting for reflections must be scaled to match the brightness of sky reflections to avoid visual discontinuities. Precision Artifacts: On hardware with aggressive FP16 FTZ (Flush To Zero) behaviour (e.g., NVIDIA RTX 5000 series), near-zero values can become exact zeros, causing black flickering artifacts in tonemapping or TAA passes. Epsilon guards are required. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot S) per pixel, where K is the number of GI samples (VOXELGISAMPLES) and S is the maximum DDA steps (VOXELGISTEPS or VOXELREFLSTEPS). Memory Complexity: O(N^3) for the voxel grid, where N=128. The grid is stored in imgVoxelMask and LPV buffers. Performance: The method is computationally expensive due to multiple ray traces per pixel for GI. It is intended as a fallback or alternative to SSRT, which is generally cheaper but limited by screen-space coverage. Strengths: Provides global illumination and reflections in areas where screen-space methods fail (e.g., off-screen objects, transparent surfaces). Limitations: Requires LPV data, which adds complexity to the rendering pipeline. Performance scales poorly with high sample counts. Visual quality depends on the accuracy of the LPV propagation. This method was implemented by nyzxor as a pull request to the Eclipse-Shader (an edit of Chocapic13 V9 / Bliss) for Minecraft, integrated via the Iris shader mod. It was added to provide an alternative global illumination method and a specular reflection fallback, leveraging the existing voxel grid infrastructure used for shadowing. The implementation addresses specific hardware issues, such as FP16 precision artifacts on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. name: Optimised Voxel Ray Marching
head: Chunk-based Voxel Traversal, Fixed-step voxel ray marching, Optimised CPU Ray Marching, Sector's Edge, Voxel Volume Ray Tracing, VoxelsRayTracingTutorial
body: Optimised Voxel Ray Marching is a ray traversal algorithm for voxel-based scenes that uses fixed-length steps along the ray to traverse a 3D grid of voxels, checking for occupancy at each step. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space in large voxel worlds by optimizing memory access patterns, specifically by keeping block lookups within the current working chunk to minimize bitshifts, masks, and multiplication operations. It sets itself apart from Regular Grid Traversal by using a chunked memory layout that reduces boundary calculation overhead, and from Chunked Voxel Traversal by relying on fixed-size inner grids which simplifies implementation and memory layout. The method implements a fixed-step ray marcher optimized for CPU collision detection. It differs from the standard 3D-DDA traversal described in Regular Grid Traversal by maintaining a reference to the current "working chunk" and updating it only when the ray crosses a chunk boundary, thereby avoiding repeated chunk index calculations for every voxel step. Inputs: start: Ray origin in world/voxel space (Vector3). velocity: Ray direction vector (normalized). max: Maximum ray length in world units. chunks: 3D array of Chunk references indexed by [chunkIndexX, chunkIndexY, chunkIndexZ]. MAPSIZE: World dimensions (e.g., 512 \times 160 \times 512). CHUNKSIZE: Side length of a chunk in blocks (typically 32). Outputs: hit: Boolean indicating if a solid block was intersected. axis: The axis (X, Y, or Z) of the face hit (used for reflection). Chunk: Contains a 1D array data of size CHUNK\SIZE^3 (e.g., 32768 for size 32). data stores Block structs sequentially. Block: Single byte field kind. Value 0 indicates empty; non-zero indicates solid. Map: 3D array chunks[,,] of Chunk references. Chunk indices are derived from world coordinates via bit-shifting: idx = coord \gg SHIFT, where SHIFT = \log2(CHUNK\SIZE). Chunk-relative coordinates are derived via bitmask: rel = coord \& MASK, where MASK = CHUNK\SIZE - 1. EPS: 5 \times 10^{-5}, used to offset ray origins to prevent self-intersection. CHUNKSIZE: 32. SHIFT: 5. MASK: 0x1f (31). MAPSIZEX/Z: 512, MAPSIZEY: 160. 1. Initialization: Convert start to integer voxel coordinates: x = \lfloor start.x \rfloor, y = \lfloor start.y \rfloor, z = \lfloor start.z \rfloor. Check bounds: If (x, y, z) is outside MAPSIZE, return hit = false. Calculate chunk indices: cx = x \gg SHIFT, cy = y \gg SHIFT, cz = z \gg SHIFT. Retrieve current chunk: c = chunks[cx, cy, cz]. Calculate chunk-relative coordinates: i = x \& MASK, j = y \& MASK, k = z \& MASK. Calculate linear access index in chunk: access = j + i \cdot CHUNK\SIZE + k \cdot CHUNK\SIZE^2. Check start block: If c is null or c.data[access].kind == 0, return hit = false (unless start/end are same block, handled separately). 2. Direction Setup: Normalize velocity. Calculate inverted components: invX = |1/velocity.x|, invY = |1/velocity.y|, invZ = |1/velocity.z|. Initialize direction-dependent variables for each axis based on the sign of the velocity component: If velocity.axis > 0: step = 1 comparison = CHUNK\SIZE (boundary exit condition) reset = 0 accessReset = -CHUNK\SIZE (for X/Z) or -1 (for Y) accessIncrement = CHUNK\SIZE (for X) or CHUNK\SIZE^2 (for Z) or 1 (for Y) dist = (coord - start.coord + 1) If velocity.axis < 0: step = -1 comparison = -1 reset = CHUNK\SIZE - 1 accessReset = CHUNK\SIZE (for X/Z) or 1 (for Y) accessIncrement = -CHUNK\SIZE (for X) or -CHUNK\SIZE^2 (for Z) or -1 (for Y) dist = (start.coord - coord) Calculate initial distance to next boundary in t-units: tDist{axis} = velocity.axis == 0 ? \infty: inv{axis} \cdot dist{axis}. 3. Marching Loop: Initialize t = 0.0. While t \le max: Occupancy Check: If c is not null and c.data[access].kind \neq 0, set hit = true, return. Find Closest Boundary: Compare tDistX, tDistY, tDistZ. Advance Axis: Let axis be the axis with the minimum tDist. Update relative coordinate: coord{rel} += step{axis}. Update access index: access += step{axis} (for Y) or access += accessIncrement{axis} (for X/Z). Chunk Boundary Check: If coord{rel} == comparison{axis}: Reset relative coordinate: coord{rel} = reset{axis}. Update access index: access += accessReset{axis}. Update chunk index: chunkIndex{axis} += step{axis}. Check new chunk bounds: If chunkIndex{axis} is out of map bounds, return hit = false. Load new chunk: c = chunks[cx, cy, cz]. Update progress: t = tDist{axis}. Update distance to next boundary: tDist{axis} += inv{axis}. Store hit axis: axis = axis. 4. Termination: If loop completes without hit, return hit = false. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(start: Vector3, velocity: Vector3, maxdist: float, chunks: Array3D, mapsize: Vector3i, chunksize: int) -> bool: # 1. Initialization x = floor(start.x) y = floor(start.y) z = floor(start.z) # Bounds check if x < 0 or x >= mapsize.x or y < 0 or y >= mapsize.y or z < 0 or z >= mapsize.z: return False shift = log2(chunksize) mask = chunksize - 1 cx = x >> shift cy = y >> shift cz = z >> shift c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] if c is None: return False i = x & mask j = y & mask k = z & mask access = j + i chunksize + k (chunksize chunksize) # Handle single-block ray endx = floor(start.x + velocity.x maxdist) endy = floor(start.y + velocity.y maxdist) endz = floor(start.z + velocity.z maxdist) if x == endx and y == endy and z == endz: return c.data[access].kind != 0 # 2. Direction Setup velocity = normalize(velocity) invx = abs(1.0 / velocity.x) if velocity.x != 0 else infinity invy = abs(1.0 / velocity.y) if velocity.y != 0 else infinity invz = abs(1.0 / velocity.z) if velocity.z != 0 else infinity # Helper to setup axis vars def setupaxis(coord, startcoord, velcomp, size): if velcomp > 0: return { 'step': 1, 'comparison': size, 'reset': 0, 'accessreset': -size, 'accessinc': size, # Simplified for Y; X/Z use size^2 'dist': coord - startcoord + 1 } else: return { 'step': -1, 'comparison': -1, 'reset': size - 1, 'accessreset': size, 'accessinc': -size, 'dist': startcoord - coord } varsx = setupaxis(x, start.x, velocity.x, chunksize) varsy = setupaxis(y, start.y, velocity.y, chunksize) varsz = setupaxis(z, start.z, velocity.z, chunksize) # Adjust access resets/increments for X and Z dimensions varsx['accessreset'] = -(chunksize chunksize) varsx['accessinc'] = chunksize varsz['accessreset'] = -(chunksize chunksize chunksize) varsz['accessinc'] = chunksize chunksize tdistx = invx varsx['dist'] if velocity.x != 0 else infinity tdisty = invy varsy['dist'] if velocity.y != 0 else infinity tdistz = invz varsz['dist'] if velocity.z != 0 else infinity t = 0.0 hitaxis = None # 3. Marching Loop while t <= maxdist: if c is not None and c.data[access].kind != 0: return True # Find closest boundary if tdisty < tdistx: if tdisty < tdistz: # Advance Y j += varsy['step'] access += varsy['step'] if j == varsy['comparison']: j = varsy['reset'] access += varsy['accessreset'] cy += varsy['step'] if cy < 0 or cy >= mapsize.y // chunksize: return False c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] t = tdisty tdisty += invy hitaxis = 'Y' else: # Advance Z k += varsz['step'] access += varsz['accessinc'] if k == varsz['comparison']: k = varsz['reset'] access += varsz['accessreset'] cz += varsz['step'] if cz < 0 or cz >= mapsize.z // chunksize: return False c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] t = tdistz tdistz += invz hitaxis = 'Z' else: if tdistx < tdistz: # Advance X i += varsx['step'] access += varsx['accessinc'] if i == varsx['comparison']: i = varsx['reset'] access += varsx['accessreset'] cx += varsx['step'] if cx < 0 or cx >= mapsize.x // chunksize: return False c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] t = tdistx tdistx += invx hitaxis = 'X' else: # Advance Z k += varsz['step'] access += varsz['accessinc'] if k == varsz['comparison']: k = varsz['reset'] access += varsz['accessreset'] cz += varsz['step'] if cz < 0 or cz >= mapsize.z // chunksize: return False c = chunks[cx, cy, cz] t = tdistz tdistz += invz hitaxis = 'Z' return False Self-Intersection: When computing normals or shadow rays, offset the origin by n \cdot EPS to avoid hitting the surface itself. Null Chunks: Empty chunks may be represented by null references. The algorithm must check for null before accessing data. Boundary Precision: Using floor on the start position is standard, but floating-point inaccuracies at chunk boundaries can cause skipping or double-checking. The EPS offset helps mitigate this. Zero Velocity: If a velocity component is 0, the distance to the next boundary is infinity, preventing advancement on that axis. Optimizes ray marching through a voxel grid by avoiding redundant cell checks when traversing a 2x2x2 block. It steps a 2x2x2 block of grid cells; after stepping along one axis, half of the block was tested in the previous step, so it tests only the 4 cells on the leading side. This reduces the number of grid-walk calls and improves cache locality. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed. The cost per step is very low due to bitwise operations for chunk indexing. Memory Complexity: Depends on the sparse voxel grid implementation. Chunks are allocated on-demand, reducing memory usage for empty worlds. Performance: On a Ryzen 5 1600 CPU, ray marching for 1-10 blocks takes ~250 nanoseconds, allowing 64,000 rays per frame per thread at 60fps. For longer rays (200-400 blocks), it takes ~3400 nanoseconds, allowing 4,700 rays per frame. Strengths: Extremely fast for CPU-based collision detection in voxel games. Minimizes cache misses by keeping access local to the current chunk. Limitations: Fixed-step nature means it may step through empty space if the grid is sparse and chunks are not hierarchical (unlike Octree-based methods). Not suitable for high-precision continuous collision detection without sub-stepping. The method is based on "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing" by John Amanatides and Andrew Woo. It was specifically optimized for CPU implementation in the game Sector's Edge by Vercidium to handle particle and projectile collisions efficiently. The optimization focuses on reducing the computational overhead of chunk boundary checks by maintaining a "current working chunk" reference. name: Chunked Voxel Traversal
head: Chunk-based Voxel Traversal, Fixed-step voxel ray marching
body: Chunked Voxel Traversal is a hierarchical ray traversal method for sparse voxel grids that accelerates intersection testing by organizing voxels into a 3D grid of smaller 3D sub-grids called "chunks". It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space in large voxel worlds by allowing the ray to skip entire chunks that contain no geometry. It sets itself apart from pure 3D grid traversal by reducing the number of intersection checks in empty regions, and from octree-based traversal by using fixed-size inner grids which simplifies implementation and memory layout. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, outer grid occupancy data, and chunk data. Output: The first non-empty voxel hit by the ray, or null if the ray exits the world without hitting a voxel. Data Structures: The structure is a two-level hierarchy: 1. Outer Grid: A 3D array representing the world space, divided into chunks. Each entry stores a boolean or bitmask indicating if the chunk is empty. 2. Chunks: Each chunk is a fixed-size 3D array of voxels. Voxel Data: Compressed to 8 bytes per voxel on the GPU to reduce transmission size; material properties are sent separately from voxel data. Bit Packing: Voxel attributes are packed into the 8 bytes. A critical implementation detail is that bitmasks must be applied before shifting data; applying them after results in zeroed-out data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Outer Traversal: Use the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to traverse the outer 3D grid of chunks along the ray direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Chunk Check: For each chunk visited by the outer DDA, check its occupancy flag. If the chunk is marked as empty, skip it and continue to the next chunk in the outer DDA loop. 3. Inner Traversal: If the chunk is non-empty, use the DDA algorithm to traverse the identified chunk. 4. Voxel Hit Test: If a voxel is hit within the chunk, return that information to the outer DDA loop and terminate traversal. If no voxel is hit in the chunk, continue iterating the outer DDA loop to check the next chunk. Transparency Handling: For transparent voxels, a fraction of the transparent object's color is added to the color behind it. The traversal carries this transparent object information to the next voxel or chunk for final color determination. DDA Step Formula: The traversal advances along the axis with the smallest entry distance: t{next} = t{current} + \Delta t, where \Delta ti = 1/|di| for axis i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def chunkedvoxeltraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, outergrid, chunks, chunksize): step = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] tmax = [float('inf')] 3 tdelta = [abs(1.0 / raydirection[i]) if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] currentchunk = [int(rayorigin[i] // chunksize) for i in range(3)] for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] != 0: tmax[i] = ((currentchunk[i] + (1 if step[i] > 0 else 0)) chunksize - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] while True: if not outergrid[currentchunk[0]][currentchunk[1]][currentchunk[2]]: tmin = min(tmax) if tmin == float('inf'): break for i in range(3): if tmax[i] == tmin: currentchunk[i] += step[i] tmax[i] += tdelta[i] continue chunk = chunks[currentchunk[0]][currentchunk[1]][currentchunk[2]] localorigin = [rayorigin[i] - currentchunk[i] chunksize for i in range(3)] innerstep = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] innertmax = [float('inf')] 3 innertdelta = [abs(1.0 / raydirection[i]) if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] innervoxel = [int(localorigin[i]) for i in range(3)] for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] != 0: innertmax[i] = (innervoxel[i] + (1 if innerstep[i] > 0 else 0) - localorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] hitvoxel = None while True: if chunk[innervoxel[0]][innervoxel[1]][innervoxel[2]] != 0: hitvoxel = chunk[innervoxel[0]][innervoxel[1]][innervoxel[2]] break tmin = min(innertmax) if tmin == float('inf'): break for i in range(3): if innertmax[i] == tmin: innervoxel[i] += innerstep[i] innertmax[i] += innertdelta[i] if hitvoxel is not None: return hitvoxel tmin = min(tmax) if tmin == float('inf'): break for i in range(3): if tmax[i] == tmin: currentchunk[i] += step[i] tmax[i] += tdelta[i] return None Parameters: Chunk Dimensions: 8x8x8 voxels per chunk. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bitmask Order: Applying bitmasks after shifting data results in zeroed-out data. Bitmasks must be applied before shifting. Padding: Compressing voxel data to 8 bytes may require padding variables to maintain data alignment on the GPU. A per-voxel lighting method that decouples illumination calculation from the rendering pipeline to enable dynamic streaming and instant map edits. Unlike standard ray-traced voxel rendering which computes lighting per-pixel per-frame, this method accumulates diffuse lighting over multiple frames while calculating direct and specular components via fixed uniform sampling, allowing the scene to remain interactive during edits. It builds on Chunked Voxel Traversal by organizing voxels into 8x8x8 chunks to facilitate efficient skipping of empty space and targeted updates. Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the voxel grid; skips empty chunks to reduce intersection tests, behaving like standard DDA in dense regions. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for outer grid occupancy flags and chunk data, with voxels compressed to 8 bytes per voxel. Strengths: Efficient skipping of empty space; fixed-size chunks simplify memory layout. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was described in an unofficial blog post by a developer working on a voxel raytracer. The author sought a middle ground between the simplicity of a 3D grid and the efficiency of octrees, leading to the "chunked" approach. The implementation details, including the 8x8x8 chunk size and 8-byte voxel compression, were derived from practical experience in developing a real-time voxel rendering engine. name: Voxel Path Tracing with Chunked Storage
head: Chunked Voxel Path Tracing, Per-voxel lighting path tracing
body: Voxel Path Tracing with Chunked Storage is a per-voxel lighting method that decouples illumination calculation from the rendering pipeline to enable dynamic streaming and instant map edits. Unlike standard ray-traced voxel rendering which computes lighting per-pixel per-frame, this method accumulates diffuse lighting over multiple frames while calculating direct and specular components via fixed uniform sampling, allowing the scene to remain interactive during edits. It builds on Chunked Voxel Traversal by organizing voxels into 8x8x8 chunks to facilitate efficient skipping of empty space and targeted updates. Inputs: Voxel Map: A sparse grid of chunks. Each chunk contains a 3D array of voxels. Lighting Request Buffer: A std430 buffer (binding 3) containing uint chunkIndices[]. Each entry packs a chunk index (28 bits) and a voxel offset within that chunk (4 bits). Scene Data: mapSize: Uniform uvec3 defining the global map dimensions. sunDir: Normalized vector pointing to the sun. camPos: Camera position. skyCubemap: Uniform samplerCube for sky color sampling when useCubemap is true. Parameters: numDiffuseSamples: Number of diffuse samples per frame. maxDiffuseSamples: Maximum stored diffuse samples. diffuseBounceLimit: Max diffuse bounces. specularBounceLimit: Max specular bounces. shadowSoftness: Shadow softness factor. useCubemap: Boolean flag for sky sampling. CHUNKSIZE: ivec3(8, 8, 8). INVCHUNKSIZE: vec3(0.125, 0.125, 0.125). HALFINVCHUNKSIZE: vec3(0.0625, 0.0625, 0.0625). EPSILON: 0.0001. Outputs: Voxel Storage: Each voxel stores normal (vec3), material (uint), albedo (vec3), specLight (vec3), and diffuseLight (vec3). Voxel Struct: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Voxel { vec3 normal; uint material; vec3 albedo; vec3 specLight; vec3 diffuseLight; }; Chunk Indices Buffer Layout: Each uint in lightingRequestBuffer contains: Bits 0-3: Voxel offset within the chunk (4 bits). Bits 4-31: Chunk index (28 bits). Sphere Points: A constant array spherePoints[15] containing 15 pre-defined vec3 points on the unit sphere, used for soft shadows and rough reflections. 1. Initialization: Set enableRefraction = false. Determine the chunk index from the work group ID: mapIndex = chunkIndices[glWorkGroupID.x] >> 4. Retrieve the chunk's world position: mapPos = ivec3(chunks[mapIndex].pos.xyz). Calculate the local voxel number: voxNum = glLocalInvocationID.x + (chunkIndices[glWorkGroupID.x] & 15) glWorkGroupSize.x. Get the chunk-local voxel position: chunkPos = getvoxelposition(mapIndex, voxNum). Edge Case: If !inchunkbounds(chunkPos), terminate the shader invocation. 2. Voxel Decompression: Calculate global voxel index: voxelIndex = map[mapIndex].voxelIndex + voxNum. Decompress the voxel data from the map to retrieve thisVoxel and thisMaterial. Determine indirect samples: indirectSamples = float(min(chunks[mapIndex].numIndirectSamples, maxDiffuseSamples)). 3. Ray Position Calculation: If indirectSamples == 0, set firstSample = true. Calculate ray origin in world space: rayPos = INVCHUNKSIZE chunkPos + mapPos + HALFINVCHUNKSIZE. Adjust rayPos based on surface normal to avoid self-intersection: rayPos += (HALFINVCHUNKSIZE - vec3(EPSILON)) thisVoxel.normal. 4. Specular Lighting Calculation: Condition: If thisMaterial.specular > 0.0 AND dot(viewDir, thisVoxel.normal) < 0.0 AND thisMaterial.reflectType <= 1: Calculate reflection vector: reflected = reflect(normalize(viewDir), thisVoxel.normal). Initialize specLight = vec3(0.0). Loop i from 0 to 14: Sample direction: specDir = normalize(reflected thisMaterial.shininess + spherePoints[i]) + EPSILON. Call specularray(..., specLight) (see below). Average result: specLight /= 15.0. 5. Diffuse Lighting Calculation: Condition: If thisMaterial.specular < 1.0: Initialize diffuseLight = vec3(0.0). Add ambient contribution: diffuseLight += ambientStrength. Loop i from 0 to numDiffuseSamples - 1: Call diffuseray(..., diffuseLight) (see below). Call shadowray(..., diffuseLight) (see below). Accumulate with history: diffuseLight = (thisVoxel.diffuseLight indirectSamples + diffuseLight) / (indirectSamples + numDiffuseSamples). 6. Output Storage: Clamp specLight and diffuseLight to [0, 1]. Convert diffuseLight to 16-bit per channel: writeDiffuseLight = uvec3(round(diffuseLight 65535)). Split into upper/lower bytes and store albedo, specLight, diffuseLight into voxels[voxelIndex] using encodeuintRGBA. Calculates direct sunlight contribution. 1. Determine shadow direction: If firstSample is true: updatedSunDir = sunDir + EPSILON. Else: updatedSunDir = normalize(sunDir shadowSoftness + randunitsphere(seed)) + EPSILON. 2. Trace shadow: Call stepmap(updatedSunDir, 1 / updatedSunDir, rayPos, true, -1.0, tempNormal, hitVoxel, colorAdd, colorMult). 3. If stepmap returns false (no hit): Add sunlight: color += sunStrength colorMult + colorAdd. Calculates specular bounces. 1. Loop i from 0 to specularBounceLimit: Trace ray: Call stepmap(rayDir, 1 / rayDir, rayPos, true, -1.0, tempNormal, hitVoxel, colorAdd, colorMult). Hit Case: Get hitMapIndex. If map[hitMapIndex].flags & 4 is true, set map[hitMapIndex].flags |= 4. Check adjacency: dist = abs(floor(rayPos CHUNKSIZE) - floor(lastPos CHUNKSIZE)). If dot(dist, dist) <= 1, return (stop tracing). Update diffuse component: hitVoxel.diffuseLight = 1.0 - hitMaterial.specular. If hitMaterial.emissive: Add to color: color += (hitVoxel.albedo colorMult + colorAdd) multiplier albedo. Return. Update specular multiplier: multiplier = hitVoxel.albedo colorMult hitMaterial.specular. Update state: reflectType, lastPos. Reflect ray: rayDir = reflect(rayDir, hitVoxel.normal). Calculates indirect diffuse bounces. 1. Loop i from 0 to diffuseBounceLimit: Determine direction dir: If i > 0 and (rand(seed + diffuseBounceLimit + i) + 1) 0.5 < hitMaterial.specular: dir = normalize(reflect(lastDir, hitNormal) hitMaterial.shininess + randunitsphere(time + i)). Else if firstSample: dir = normalize(hitNormal) + EPSILON. Else: dir = normalize(hitNormal + randunitsphere(seed + i)) + EPSILON. Trace ray: Call stepmap(dir, 1 / dir, rayPos, true, -1.0, tempNormal, hitVoxel, colorAdd, colorMult). Update hitNormal and hitMaterial. Hit Case: Check adjacency: dist = abs(floor(lastPos CHUNKSIZE) - floor(rayPos CHUNKSIZE)). If dot(dist, dist) < 1, return. If hitMaterial.emissive: Add to color: color += newColor (hitVoxel.albedo colorMult + colorAdd). Return. Else: Update color: newColor = (hitVoxel.albedo colorMult + colorAdd). Miss Case: Add sky contribution: color += (newColor max(dot(dir, sunDir), 0.0) sunStrength colorMult + colorAdd). Return. Unverified code. EPSILON = 0.0001 def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def ivec3(x, y, z): return (int(x), int(y), int(z)) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def reflect(I, N): return (I[0] - 2dot(I, N)N[0], I[1] - 2dot(I, N)N[1], I[2] - 2dot(I, N)N[2]) def absvec(v): return (abs(v[0]), abs(v[1]), abs(v[2])) def floorvec(v): return (math.floor(v[0]), math.floor(v[1]), math.floor(v[2])) def clampvec(v, mn, mx): return (max(mn, min(mx, v[0])), max(mn, min(mx, v[1])), max(mn, min(mx, v[2]))) def rand(seed): return
