name: Hierarchical Brick-Map DDA
head: Multi-level DDA with brick map, Sparse brick-map ray marching
body: Hierarchical Brick-Map DDA is a ray traversal technique that replaces dense voxel buffers with a sparse, hierarchical structure to skip empty regions in volumetric data. It operates by maintaining a top-level grid of cells (typically stride 8 voxels) that point to allocated "bricks" containing fine-grained voxel data; if a top-level cell is empty, the ray strides over the entire cell volume, descending only into occupied bricks for local DDA. This approach significantly reduces memory footprint and traversal time for sparse volumes, such as drone airspace which is >99% empty, compared to dense voxel storage or non-hierarchical sparse methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A dense voxel grid (or SDF field) defined on a global coordinate system; ray origin O and direction D. Output: Ray-marched color/depth, with traversal skipping empty space. Data Structures: The method relies on three primary GPU buffers and a uniform structure: 1. topGrid: A sparse 3D grid where each cell contains a pointer (index) to a brick in the brickPool, or a null value if the cell is empty. The dimensions are defined by topsize. 2. brickPool: A contiguous array of occupied bricks. Each brick stores BRICK^3 voxel values. 3. counter: An atomic counter used during the build phase to allocate slots in brickPool. 4. Grid Uniform: Contains topsize (dimensions of the top-level grid) and BRICK (side length of a brick in voxels, typically 8). Parameters: BRICK: Side length of a voxel brick. Default value is 8. MAX\STEPS: Maximum number of ray marching steps. Increased to 1024 to accommodate hierarchical overhead and longer paths in sparse data (up from 512 in dense implementations). Build Phase (Compute Shader): Before traversal, the sparse structure is built from dense data: 1. For each top-level cell in the global grid: 2. Scan the BRICK^3 voxels corresponding to that cell. 3. If any voxel is non-zero (solid), atomically allocate a slot in brickPool using counter. 4. Copy the voxel data into the allocated slot. 5. Update the corresponding entry in topGrid to point to the new brick index. Traversal Phase (Ray Marching Shader): The traversal uses a multi-level Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA): 1. Initialization: Compute initial ray parameters (t{min}, t{max}) and step sizes. Initialize top-level cell coordinates (x, y, z) based on ray origin. 2. Top-Level Traversal Loop: While t < t{max} and steps < MAX\STEPS: Check if the current top-level cell (x, y, z) is occupied (pointer in topGrid is not null). If Empty: Calculate the distance to the next top-level cell boundary along the ray direction. Update t \leftarrow t + \Delta t{top}. Update (x, y, z) to the next top-level cell indices. Continue loop. If Occupied: Descent: Retrieve the brick index from topGrid. Map the ray origin and direction into the local coordinate system of the brick. Re-derive the fine-grained ray direction vector fv based on the actual ray position within the occupied brick to ensure correct sampling. Fine-Grained DDA: Perform standard voxel DDA within the brick's local bounds. Ascent: When the ray exits the brick (either hitting a surface or leaving the brick boundary): Map the exit point back to global coordinates. Recompute c{tmax} (distance to the next top-level cell boundary) for the new top cell to resume coarse traversal correctly. Update (x, y, z) to the new top-level cell. Continue loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchbrickmap(rayorigin, raydirection, topgrid, brickpool, topsize, bricksize=8, maxsteps=1024): BRICK = bricksize MAXSTEPS = maxsteps t = 0.0 steps = 0 invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0 else 1e9 for d in raydirection] step = [1 if d > 0 else -1 for d in raydirection] tx = int(rayorigin[0] // BRICK) ty = int(rayorigin[1] // BRICK) tz = int(rayorigin[2] // BRICK) tmaxtopx = (tx + step[0]) BRICK - rayorigin[0] if invdir[0] < 1e9 else 0.0 tmaxtopy = (ty + step[1]) BRICK - rayorigin[1] if invdir[1] < 1e9 else 0.0 tmaxtopz = (tz + step[2]) BRICK - rayorigin[2] if invdir[2] < 1e9 else 0.0 tmaxtop = min(tmaxtopx, tmaxtopy, tmaxtopz) inbrick = False localorigin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] localinvdir = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] localtmaxx = 0.0 localtmaxy = 0.0 localtmaxz = 0.0 while steps < MAXSTEPS: steps += 1 if not inbrick: if t >= tmaxtop: if raydirection[0] > 0: tx += 1; tmaxtopx += BRICK invdir[0] elif raydirection[0] < 0: tx -= 1; tmaxtopx -= BRICK invdir[0] if raydirection[1] > 0: ty += 1; tmaxtopy += BRICK invdir[1] elif raydirection[1] < 0: ty -= 1; tmaxtopy -= BRICK invdir[1] if raydirection[2] > 0: tz += 1; tmaxtopz += BRICK invdir[2] elif raydirection[2] < 0: tz -= 1; tmaxtopz -= BRICK invdir[2] tmaxtop = min(tmaxtopx, tmaxtopy, tmaxtopz) t += BRICK continue brickidx = topgrid[tx, ty, tz] if brickidx is None: t += tmaxtop if raydirection[0] > 0: tx += 1; tmaxtopx += BRICK invdir[0] elif raydirection[0] < 0: tx -= 1; tmaxtopx -= BRICK invdir[0] if raydirection[1] > 0: ty += 1; tmaxtopy += BRICK invdir[1] elif raydirection[1] < 0: ty -= 1; tmaxtopy -= BRICK invdir[1] if raydirection[2] > 0: tz += 1; tmaxtopz += BRICK invdir[2] elif raydirection[2] < 0: tz -= 1; tmaxtopz -= BRICK invdir[2] tmaxtop = min(tmaxtopx, tmaxtopy, tmaxtopz) continue else: inbrick = True brickoriginglobal = (tx BRICK, ty BRICK, tz BRICK) localorigin = [(rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t) - brickoriginglobal[i] for i in range(3)] localinvdir = [1.0 / raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] localtmaxx = (BRICK - localorigin[0]) localinvdir[0] if localinvdir[0] > 0 else -localorigin[0] localinvdir[0] localtmaxy = (BRICK - localorigin[1]) localinvdir[1] if localinvdir[1] > 0 else -localorigin[1] localinvdir[1] localtmaxz = (BRICK - localorigin[2]) localinvdir[2] if localinvdir[2] > 0 else -localorigin[2] localinvdir[2] continue dtlocal = min(localtmaxx, localtmaxy, localtmaxz) if dtlocal <= 0: inbrick = False t += dtlocal currentglobalpos = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] tmaxtopx = (tx + step[0]) BRICK - currentglobalpos[0] if invdir[0] < 1e9 else 0.0 tmaxtopy = (ty + step[1]) BRICK - currentglobalpos[1] if invdir[1] < 1e9 else 0.0 tmaxtopz = (tz + step[2]) BRICK - currentglobalpos[2] if invdir[2] < 1e9 else 0.0 tmaxtop = min(tmaxtopx, tmaxtopy, tmaxtopz) if raydirection[0] > 0: tx += 1; tmaxtopx += BRICK invdir[0] elif raydirection[0] < 0: tx -= 1; tmaxtopx -= BRICK invdir[0] if raydirection[1] > 0: ty += 1; tmaxtopy += BRICK invdir[1] elif raydirection[1] < 0: ty -= 1; tmaxtopy -= BRICK invdir[1] if raydirection[2] > 0: tz += 1; tmaxtopz += BRICK invdir[2] elif raydirection[2] < 0: tz -= 1; tmaxtopz -= BRICK invdir[2] tmaxtop = min(tmaxtopx, tmaxtopy, tmaxtopz) continue if localtmaxx <= localtmaxy and localtmaxx <= localtmaxz: localtmaxx += BRICK localinvdir[0] elif localtmaxy <= localtmaxx and localtmaxy <= localtmaxz: localtmaxy += BRICK localinvdir[1] else: localtmaxz += BRICK localinvdir[2] t += dtlocal return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Brick Edge Transitions: Visual popping or missing voxels can occur at brick boundaries if the transition between top-level cells and brick interiors is not handled smoothly. Validation requires toggling camera angles to ensure clean boundary-crossing transitions. Axis-Aligned Rays: The method reuses AABB (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box) clipping and safe-ray-distance primitives from dense implementations to handle axis-aligned rays and rays outside the grid volume correctly without artifacts. Sparse Ray Marching with Nested Axis-Aligned Distance Fields (NAADF) is a technique for traversing sparse voxel grids by skipping over empty space using precomputed distance fields, replacing traditional brick coordinate rasterization with a simpler pipeline suitable for g-buffer and path tracing. It differs from its sibling Hierarchical Brick-Map DDA by calculating the largest empty region along the ray's path via axis-aligned bounds, allowing it to step over multiple cells at once rather than advancing one cell boundary per iteration. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of occupied bricks intersected by the ray, plus the cost of traversing empty top-level cells. In sparse scenes, k \ll N^3 (where N is the global resolution). Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot BRICK^3) where B is the number of occupied bricks. For a heightmap stand-in with N=128, the brick count is roughly top^2 (~256 bricks) instead of the worst-case top^3 (4096). Memory savings grow with sparsity. Measured Performance: For drone airspace (>99% empty), the method significantly reduces traversal time compared to dense voxel buffers. Strengths: Significant memory reduction in sparse volumes; efficient skipping of empty space; compatible with GPU compute shaders for build phase. Limitations: Requires a build phase to construct the sparse structure; potential for visual artifacts at brick boundaries if not implemented carefully; increased MAX\STEPS may be required due to hierarchical overhead. When to Use: Sparse volumetric data (e.g., drone airspace, large outdoor scenes with sparse objects). When Not to Use: Dense volumetric data (e.g., medical CT scans with high fill rate) where the overhead of hierarchical traversal may not justify the memory savings, or when dynamic updates are frequent and costly. Hierarchical Brick-Map DDA was introduced as part of the ResQ Viz project, specifically in PR #67, to optimize ray marching for sparse volumes like drone airspace. It builds upon the concept of sparse voxel traversal and brick-based storage, adapting it for GPU-based ray marching with WebGPU. The method addresses the inefficiency of dense voxel buffers in highly sparse environments by introducing a two-level hierarchy: a coarse top-level grid and fine-grained bricks. feat(viz): hierarchical brick-map DDA for /spike.html, https://github.com/resq-software/viz/pull/67, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Ray tracing of signed distance function grids, https://www.jcgt.org/published/0011/03/06/paper-lowres.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Ray Marching with Nested Axis-Aligned Distance Fields (NAADF)
head: NAADF Ray Marching, Sparse Raymarching
body: Sparse Ray Marching with Nested Axis-Aligned Distance Fields (NAADF) is a technique for traversing sparse voxel grids by skipping over empty space using precomputed distance fields, replacing traditional brick coordinate rasterization with a simpler pipeline suitable for g-buffer and path tracing. It differs from its sibling Hierarchical Brick-Map DDA by calculating the largest empty region along the ray's path via axis-aligned bounds, allowing it to step over multiple cells at once rather than advancing one cell boundary per iteration. Inputs: Ray origin (rayorigin), ray direction (raydir), maximum traversal distance (tmax), global grid extent (gridext), voxel occupancy masks (voxelmasks), and axis-aligned distance fields (voxelaadf). Outputs: Boolean indicating if a voxel was hit (True) or if the ray exited the grid/max distance (False). The method relies on a three-level grid hierarchy: 1. Voxel Grid: The bottom level containing individual voxels. 2. Brick Grid: Each brick contains 4^3 voxels. 3. Chunk Grid: Each chunk contains 4^3 bricks. Axis-Aligned Distance Field (AADF) Layout: Each cell in the AADF stores six distances, representing the number of free (empty) cells along each axis in both positive and negative directions. These are packed into a single 32-bit unsigned integer (uint): Bits 0–4: Distance in -X direction. Bits 5–9: Distance in +X direction. Bits 10–14: Distance in -Y direction. Bits 15–19: Distance in +Y direction. Bits 20–24: Distance in -Z direction. Bits 25–29: Distance in +Z direction. Voxel Masks: A sparse structure used to quickly identify occupied bricks. The index into the mask is calculated via masklinearidx(ipos), which maps the 3D integer position to a linear index based on the brick dimensions (VXMASKEXT). 1. Initialize: Compute inverse direction invdir = 1.0 / (raydir + (raydir == 0.0) 1e-30) to guard against division by zero. Set integer position ipos = floor(rayorigin). Set local position localpos = rayorigin - ipos. Set accumulated distance distance = 0.0. 2. Loop: Iterate i from 0 to 3 gridext - 1. 3. Boundary Check: If any component of ipos is greater than or equal to gridext, return False. 4. Voxel Mask Check: Load the voxel mask at ipos // VXMASKEXT. Calculate the linear index idx using masklinearidx(ipos). If (mask & (1 << idx)) != 0, return True (a voxel was hit). 5. Load AADF: Load the AADF value at ipos. Determine shift values based on ray direction signs to extract the correct distance for the direction of travel: shiftx = 0 if raydir.x < 0 else 5. shifty = 10 if raydir.y < 0 else 15. shiftz = 20 if raydir.z < 0 else 25. 6. Extract Bounds: Extract the number of free cells for each axis by shifting and masking with 31 (5 bits): bounds.x = (aadf >> shiftx) & 31. bounds.y = (aadf >> shifty) & 31. bounds.z = (aadf >> shiftz) & 31. 7. Calculate Empty Region: Determine the minimum and maximum bounds of the empty region relative to the current cell: cellmin = max(ipos - bounds, 0). cellmax = min(ipos + 1 + bounds, gridext). Determine the exitplane coordinate for each axis: use cellmin if the ray direction is negative, otherwise use cellmax. 8. Calculate Step Distance: Calculate the distance to the exit plane in ray space: sidedist = (exitplane - ipos - localpos) invdir. Guard against zero ray direction components by setting the corresponding sidedist component to 3e+38. 9. Determine T: Find the minimum distance to any exit plane: t = min(sidedist.x, sidedist.y, sidedist.z). Add t to distance. If distance > tmax, return False. 10. Update Position: Determine which planes were crossed: crossed = step(sidedist, t). Update local position: advanced = localpos + t raydir. Calculate integer cell delta: celldelta = floor(advanced + crossed sign(raydir) 0.5). Update ipos += celldelta and localpos = advanced - celldelta. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sparseraymarch(rayorigin, raydir, tmax, gridext, voxelmasks, voxelaadf, VXMASKEXT): # Guard against division by zero invdir = tuple(1.0 / (d + (1e-30 if d == 0.0 else 0.0)) for d in raydir) # Initialize positions ipos = tuple(math.floor(p) for p in rayorigin) localpos = tuple(rayorigin[j] - ipos[j] for j in range(3)) distance = 0.0 maxiter = 3 gridext for i in range(maxiter): # Boundary check if any(p >= gridext for p in ipos): return False # Voxel mask check maskidx = tuple(p // VXMASKEXT for p in ipos) mask = voxelmasks[maskidx] idx = ipos[0] + ipos[1] VXMASKEXT + ipos[2] VXMASKEXT VXMASKEXT if (mask >> idx) & 1: return True # Load AADF aadf = voxelaadf[ipos] # Determine shifts based on ray direction shiftx = 0 if raydir[0] < 0.0 else 5 shifty = 10 if raydir[1] < 0.0 else 15 shiftz = 20 if raydir[2] < 0.0 else 25 # Extract bounds (5 bits each) bounds = ( (aadf >> shiftx) & 31, (aadf >> shifty) & 31, (aadf >> shiftz) & 31) # Calculate empty region boundaries cellmin = tuple(max(ipos[j] - bounds[j], 0) for j in range(3)) cellmax = tuple(min(ipos[j] + 1 + bounds[j], gridext) for j in range(3)) # Determine exit plane exitplane = tuple( cellmin[j] if raydir[j] < 0.0 else cellmax[j] for j in range(3)) # Calculate step distance sidedist = tuple( (exitplane[j] - ipos[j] - localpos[j]) invdir[j] for j in range(3)) # Guard against zero ray direction components sidedist = tuple(3e+38 if raydir[j] == 0.0 else sidedist[j] for j in range(3)) # Determine t t = min(sidedist) distance += t if distance > tmax: return False # Update position crossed = tuple(1.0 if sidedist[j] < t else 0.0 for j in range(3)) advanced = tuple(localpos[j] + t raydir[j] for j in range(3)) signdir = tuple(1.0 if raydir[j] > 0.0 else (-1.0 if raydir[j] < 0.0 else 0.0) for j in range(3)) celldelta = tuple(math.floor(advanced[j] + crossed[j] signdir[j] 0.5) for j in range(3)) ipos = tuple(ipos[j] + celldelta[j] for j in range(3)) localpos = tuple(advanced[j] - celldelta[j] for j in range(3)) return False Grid Compression: The implementation uses "naive" AADFs. The compression method described in the source paper is not implemented, leading to redundancy in empty space. Zero Direction: Ray direction components equal to zero are handled by adding 1e-30 to the denominator during inverse calculation and setting the corresponding sidedist to 3e+38 to prevent invalid steps. Loop Limit: The loop runs up to 3 gridext iterations. Time Complexity: The method steps over the largest empty space calculated from the AADF, potentially reducing the number of iterations compared to standard DDA which steps one cell boundary at a time. However, the overhead of AADF lookups and bit manipulation may offset gains in highly sparse but large grids. Memory Complexity: Naive AADFs consume significant memory. For a 1024^3 voxel grid, the voxel AADF alone requires 4 GiB. For a 256^3 grid, it requires 64 MiB. This makes the method less scalable for very large grids without compression. Performance: On the monu2 scene, FPS increased slightly from 144.00 to 144.05 (+0.03%), but average GPU walltime increased from 5.11 ms to 6.35 ms (+24.30%). On the sponza-1024 scene (1 billion voxels), FPS decreased from 81.41 to 64.73 (-20.48%), and average GPU walltime increased from 20.72 ms to 26.28 ms (+26.86%). Strengths: Simpler pipeline than brick coordinate rasterization; suitable for g-buffer and path tracing; effective at skipping empty space in sparse volumes. Limitations: High memory usage for large grids due to naive AADF storage; potential performance regression in complex scenes due to increased register allocation and reduced occupancy (e.g., occupancy dropped from 52.02% to 36.38% in RTAO shader tests). NAADF is inspired by the paper "Globally Illuminated Voxel Worlds Accelerated with Nested Axis‐Aligned Distance Fields". It was implemented in a voxel raytracer devlog to replace an existing DDA renderer, aiming to provide a promising method for both basic g-buffer + RTAO rendering and potential path tracing. The three-level grid hierarchy (voxel, brick, chunk) was adopted from the source paper. Voxel Raytracer Devlog // My thought repository, https://nelari.us/post/voxel-ray-tracing/, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Sparse Point Cloud Tracer
head: Packed SPC Tracer
body: The Sparse Point Cloud (SPC) Tracer is a ray-tracing method for rendering sparse point clouds by intersecting camera rays against cell centers within a structured grid hierarchy, returning the color of the nearest intersected cell without neural volume integration. It differs from its siblings, such as Voxel Grid Raycasting which renders volumetric density, and Cap Node Traversal which handles hierarchical brick structures, by treating the SPC as a set of discrete, colored points located at grid cell centers, effectively performing a nearest-neighbor lookup in 3D space projected onto the image plane. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of camera rays (origin and direction), a Neural Field (nef) containing the SPC grid structure and color lookup, a background color (bgcolor), and a Level of Detail index (lodidx). Outputs: A RenderBuffer dataclass containing tensors for depth, hit status, RGB color, and alpha for each pixel. Data Structures RaytraceResults: A structure returned by the grid backend containing: ridx: Ray indices (integers). pidx: Point indices (integers) corresponding to the SPC grid cells. depth: Intersection depths (floats). RenderBuffer: A dataclass holding: depth: Tensor of shape (N, 1), initialized to zeros. hit: Tensor of shape (N, bool), initialized to false. rgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3), initialized to zeros. alpha: Tensor of shape (N, 1), initialized to zeros. Parameters bgcolor: Background color tuple, default (0.0, 0.0, 0.0). lodidx: Level of Detail index. If None, defaults to nef.grid.blas.maxlevel. Steps 1. Initialize LOD: If lodidx is None, set lodidx = nef.grid.blas.maxlevel. 2. Ray-Grid Intersection: Call the backend raytracer nef.grid.blas.raytrace(rays, lodidx, withexit=False) to compute intersections between the input rays and the SPC grid points. This returns RaytraceResults containing ridx, pidx, and depth. 3. Identify First Hits: Use the helper function spcrender.markpackboundaries(ridx) to generate a boolean mask identifying the first hit for each unique ray index. Extract the corresponding point indices (firsthitspoint), ray indices (firsthitsray), and depths (firsthitsdepth) using this mask. 4. Retrieve Color: Query the neural field nef for the color of the intersected cells. Pass firsthitspoint.long() and the channel specifier 'rgb' to nef to obtain the RGB color values for the hit points. 5. Initialize Output Buffers: Create the RenderBuffer tensors. Initialize depth to zeros, hit to false, rgb to zeros, and alpha to ones for hit rays (or zeros initially, then updated). 6. Assign Hit Data: Set depth[firsthitsray.long()] = firsthitsdepth. Set hit[firsthitsray.long()] = True (or based on alpha threshold alpha[..., 0] > 0.0 as per source logic, though typically hit implies visibility). Set rgb[firsthitsray.long(),:3] = color. Set outalpha[firsthitsray.long()] = alpha (where alpha is derived from the hit or set to 1.0 for opaque points). 7. Return: Return the populated RenderBuffer. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tracesparsepointcloud(rays, nef, spcrender, bgcolor=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), lodidx=None): """ Trace rays against a Sparse Point Cloud grid. Args: rays: Ray origins and directions. nef: Neural field object containing the SPC grid and color lookup. spcrender: Renderer helper object with boundary marking utilities. bgcolor: Background color tuple. lodidx: Level of Detail index. Returns: RenderBuffer: Contains depth, hit, rgb, and alpha tensors. """ # Step 1: Initialize LOD if lodidx is None: lodidx = nef.grid.blas.maxlevel # Step 2: Ray-Grid Intersection # Call backend raytracer. withexit=False as per source. results = nef.grid.blas.raytrace(rays, lodidx, withexit=False) ridx = results.ridx pidx = results.pidx depth = results.depth # Step 3: Identify First Hits # Create mask for first hit per ray mask = spcrender.markpackboundaries(ridx) # Extract first hits using mask firsthitspoint = pidx[mask] firsthitsray = ridx[mask] firsthitsdepth = depth[mask] # Step 4: Retrieve Color # Query neural field for RGB color of hit points # Note:.long() converts indices to long tensor for lookup color = nef(firsthitspoint.long(), channels='rgb') # Step 5: Initialize Output Buffers N = rays.numrays # Assuming rays has a numrays attribute or similar size # Create tensors of appropriate size N outdepth = torch.zeros(N, 1) outhit = torch.zeros(N, dtype=torch.bool) outrgb = torch.zeros(N, 3) outalpha = torch.zeros(N, 1) # Step 6: Assign Hit Data # Map results back to ray indices rayindiceslong = firsthitsray.long() outdepth[rayindiceslong] = firsthitsdepth outhit[rayindiceslong] = True # Hit is true if a point was found outrgb[rayindiceslong,:3] = color # Alpha is typically 1.0 for opaque point rendering, or derived from neural field # Source mentions alpha[..., 0] > 0.0 check, assuming alpha is 1.0 for hits outalpha[rayindiceslong] = 1.0 # Step 7: Return RenderBuffer return RenderBuffer( depth=outdepth, hit=outhit, rgb=outrgb, alpha=outalpha) Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Hit: If a ray does not intersect any SPC point, the corresponding pixel remains with default values (depth 0, hit false, rgb 0). The background color bgcolor is not explicitly blended in the core tracer steps described; it may be handled by a composite pass or defaulting to black if not set. Precision: Depth values are stored as floats. Ensure sufficient precision for large scenes or distant points. Index Mapping: The mapping from ridx to pixel indices must be consistent. markpackboundaries handles the logic of selecting the first hit along the ray, which is critical for correct occlusion in point clouds. An acceleration technique that projects 3D points to a 2D image plane and uses a hash table to store all points per pixel, enabling adaptive search ranges based on viewpoint distance, rather than fixed radii or KNN. Time Complexity: Dominated by the ray-grid intersection step nef.grid.blas.raytrace. The complexity depends on the underlying grid structure (likely a hierarchical sparse voxel octree or similar) and the number of points. The color lookup is O(1) per hit. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the SPC grid structure and the color data for each point. The RenderBuffer scales linearly with the number of pixels N. Performance: Performance is highly dependent on the efficiency of the nef.grid.blas.raytrace implementation. Sparse structures allow skipping empty space, but point clouds can be dense in certain regions. Strengths: Simple rendering model (discrete points), efficient for sparse data, leverages existing hierarchical grid traversal structures. Limitations: Does not inherently handle transparency or volume integration; points are opaque. Aliasing may occur if points are smaller than a pixel. When to Use: Ideal for visualizing large, sparse 3D point clouds where discrete point representation is acceptable and performance is critical. When Not to Use: When volumetric rendering, smooth surfaces, or transparency effects are required. The Sparse Point Cloud Tracer is part of the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp framework, introduced in the SIGGRAPH 2022 demo context. It is designed to work with Structured Point Clouds (SPC) stored in a hierarchical grid format, allowing for efficient ray-tracing-based visualization of large-scale 3D data. NVIDIAGameWorks/kaolin-wisp, https://github.com/NVIDIAGameWorks/kaolin-wisp, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Hashed-point searching
head: HashPoint
body: Hashed-point searching is an acceleration technique for ray-tracing-based point cloud rendering that transforms the 3D search space into a 2D image plane for hash table lookup. Unlike traditional rasterization methods that use a z-buffer to retain only the nearest point per pixel, this method projects all points onto the image plane and preserves all points falling within each pixel, storing them in a hash table to enable swift location of point clouds near a camera ray. It is distinguished by its use of an adaptive searching range determined by the distance between points and the viewpoint, rather than relying on a fixed radius or K-nearest neighbors. Inputs: Point cloud data: A list of n 3D points \mathbf{x}^{pc}. Camera parameters: Focal length f, ray origin \mathbf{o} (optical center), and pixel dimensions in world coordinates \Delta x, \Delta y derived from calibrated camera parameters. Rendering configuration: Near clipping distance t{near}, far clipping distance t{far}, and a base radius parameter corresponding to the minimum radius at t{near}. Outputs: A hash table mapping pixel indices to lists of point indices. For a given ray, a set of candidate sample points \mathbf{x}^{sp}j projected onto the ray, filtered by an adaptive radius. Data Structures: 1. Point List: An array of size n storing the original point cloud data. The order of points may be adjusted during construction. 2. Hash Table: A dictionary or array where: Key: The integer index of a pixel on the 2D image plane. Value: A tuple or struct containing: startindex: The position (index) of the first point in the Point List that falls on this pixel. count: The number of points that fall on this pixel. Steps: 1. Projection and Z-ordering: Project all points from the point cloud onto the 2D image plane. Arrange the points falling on the same pixel in Z-order (Morton code) to ensure they are stored as closely as possible in sequence in the Point List. This ordering facilitates efficient retrieval. 2. Atomic Reordering (CUDA): Adjust the order of points in the Point List to reflect the Z-order arrangement. This positional adjustment is achieved using atomic operations in CUDA, with a time complexity of O(1) per point adjustment. 3. Hash Table Construction: Iterate through the reordered Point List. For each point, determine its pixel index. Update the Hash Table for that pixel: If the pixel index is not present in the Hash Table, initialize it with startindex set to the current point's index in the Point List and count set to 1. If the pixel index exists, increment the count. 4. Ray Traversal and Kernel Definition: For each pixel in the target ray's search kernel: Calculate the radius of the disc representing the pixel: \dot{r} = \frac{\Delta x \cdot \Delta y}{\pi} where \Delta x and \Delta y are the width and height of the pixel in world coordinates. Define a larger disc radius \ddot{r} for the searching kernel to mitigate holes caused by point cloud sparsity. Calculate the magnitude of the searching kernel s: s = 2 \cdot \dot{r}\ddot{r} + 1 This defines the spatial extent of the search around the central pixel. 5. Adaptive Radius Calculation: For a sample point candidate \mathbf{x}^{sp}j located at distance t along the ray (where \mathbf{x}^{sp}j = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}), compute the adaptive radius r: r = \frac {\|\mathbf {x^{sp}j}-\mathbf {o}\|2 \cdot f \ddot {r}}{\|\mathbf {po} - \mathbf {o}\|2 \cdot \sqrt {\left (\sqrt {\|\mathbf {po} - \mathbf {o}\|2^2-f^2}- \ddot {r}\right)^2+f^2}} where: f is the focal length. \mathbf{o} is the ray origin. \mathbf{po} is the pixel center. \mathbf{x}^{sp}j is the sample point. The minimum radius r{min} occurs at t{near} and matches the input hyperparameter radius. As t increases, r increases. 6. Search and Filtering: Traverse each pixel in the search kernel defined by s. Assess the number of associated points per pixel using the Hash Table (count) to determine if a search is needed. If required, look up the point list for the pixel using the Hash Table (startindex and count). For each point in the list, calculate its distance to the ray. If the distance is within the adaptive radius r calculated for the point's depth, include it as a candidate sample point \mathbf{x}^{sp}j. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def buildhashtable(points, cameraparams, imagewidth, imageheight): """ Constructs the hash table for hashed-point searching. Args: points: List of 3D points (n, 3). cameraparams: Dict containing 'f' (focal length), 'o' (ray origin), 'K' (intrinsic matrix or equivalent for projection), 'deltax', 'deltay' (pixel world dimensions). imagewidth: Width of the image plane in pixels. imageheight: Height of the image plane in pixels. Returns: hashtable: Dict mapping pixelindex -> {'startindex': int, 'count': int} pointlist: Reordered list of point indices. """ n = len(points) # Step 1 & 2: Project and Z-order # Note: Z-ordering requires mapping 3D coordinates to 2D pixel indices # and then sorting points within each pixel by their Morton code. # This implementation assumes a helper function 'projectandgetmorton' # which returns (pixelindex, mortoncode) for each point. pointmortondata = [] for i, p in enumerate(points): pixelidx, mortoncode = projectandgetmorton(p, cameraparams, imagewidth, imageheight) pointmortondata.append((pixelidx, mortoncode, i)) # Sort by pixel index, then by morton code pointmortondata.sort(key=lambda x: (x[0], x[1])) # Step 3: Build Hash Table hashtable = {} pointlist = [] # Stores original indices in the new Z-ordered sequence currentpixelidx = -1 startindex = 0 for idx, (pixelidx, mortoncode, originalidx) in enumerate(pointmortondata): if pixelidx != currentpixelidx: # New pixel if currentpixelidx != -1: # Finalize previous pixel hashtable[currentpixelidx]['count'] = idx - startindex currentpixelidx = pixelidx startindex = idx hashtable[currentpixelidx] = { 'startindex': idx, 'count': 0 # Will be updated or calculated at end } pointlist.append(originalidx) # Finalize last pixel if currentpixelidx != -1: hashtable[currentpixelidx]['count'] = n - startindex return hashtable, pointlist def searchpoints(rayorigin, raydirection, pixelcenter, tnear, tfar, hashtable, pointlist, points, cameraparams, searchkernelradius): """ Searches for points near a ray using the hashed-point structure. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector o. raydirection: Normalized 3D vector d. pixelcenter: 3D vector po (center of the primary pixel). tnear, tfar: Floats for clipping. hashtable: The constructed hash table. pointlist: The reordered point indices. points: Original point cloud data. cameraparams: Dict with 'f', 'deltax', 'deltay'. searchkernelradius: The radius rdoubledot (r̈) for the kernel. Returns: candidates: List of sample point candidates (3D vectors). """ f = cameraparams['f'] deltax = cameraparams['deltax'] deltay = cameraparams['deltay'] # Calculate pixel disc radius rdot rdot = (deltax deltay) / math.pi # Calculate search kernel magnitude s (not strictly needed for lookup logic # if we iterate pixels, but defines the scope) # s = 2 rdot rdoubledot + 1 candidates = [] # Determine which pixels to check based on the search kernel # This requires projecting the search kernel onto the image plane # and iterating over those pixel indices. # For simplicity, we assume a helper 'getkernelpixels' returns # a list of pixel indices within the search kernel. kernelpixelindices = getkernelpixels(pixelcenter, rayorigin, raydirection, rdot, searchkernelradius, cameraparams, imagewidth, imageheight) for pixelidx in kernelpixelindices: if pixelidx not in hashtable: continue info = hashtable[pixelidx] start = info['startindex'] count = info['count'] # Iterate over points in this pixel's bucket for i in range(start, start + count): pointidx = pointlist[i] pointpos = points[pointidx] # Project point onto ray to find t # xspj = o + t d # We need to check if the point is within the adaptive radius r # First, find the projection of the point onto the ray # t = dot(point - o, d) t = dot(pointpos - rayorigin, raydirection) if t < tnear or t > tfar: continue # Calculate the closest point on the ray to the 3D point closestpointonray = rayorigin + t raydirection distancetoray = norm(pointpos - o|| which is simply t. # Let's verify the formula components. # ||xspj - o||2 is the distance from origin to the sample point on the ray. # Since xspj = o + td, ||xspj - o|| = t. distotopoint = t distotopixelcenter = norm(pixelcenter - The method mitigates this by using a larger disc radius \ddot{r} for the searching kernel, expanding the search area beyond the immediate pixel. Precision: The adaptive radius calculation involves square roots and divisions. Numerical stability should be considered, particularly when \|\mathbf{po} - \mathbf{o}\| is close to f or when t is very small. Boundary Conditions: Points exactly on the boundary of the image plane or at t{near}/t{far} must be handled consistently with the projection and clipping logic. Time Complexity: Construction: O(n) for n points, with O(1) per point adjustment during reordering. Query: O(1) per pixel lookup. Total search complexity is O(n + mq), where m is the number of rays and q is the average number of points falling in the radius of each ray. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the point list and hash table entries. Strengths: Shifts the search paradigm from "ray seeking point" to "point seeking ray," which is efficient for sparse point clouds. Adaptive radius reduces noise from irrelevant points and avoids the fixed radius/K-NN limitations. High efficiency due to hash table lookup and atomic operations. Limitations: Requires CUDA for efficient atomic reordering (as per the source implementation). Performance depends on the distribution of points; highly clustered points may lead to hash collisions or large buckets, though the hash table structure handles this via linked lists or arrays. The method is designed for neural rendering contexts where feature aggregation is performed on the primary surface. Hashed-point searching, also known as HashPoint, was introduced in the paper "HashPoint: Accelerated Point Searching and Sampling for Neural Rendering". The method was developed to address the inefficiencies of traditional 3D point cloud searching in neural rendering pipelines. It draws inspiration from Morton code (Z-order) for spatial indexing and volume rendering techniques for sample point selection. The approach is particularly relevant for novel view synthesis and 3D Gaussian Splatting variants that rely on sparse point cloud representations. name: Octree Partitioning for Sphere Tracing
head: Octree-based sphere tracing, Spatial partitioning with Lipschitz bounds
body: Octree partitioning for sphere tracing accelerates implicit surface rendering by dividing the spatial domain into an octree, allowing the imposition of local Lipschitz bounds on the signed distance function (SDF). This yields tighter distance bounds than global bounds, enabling the culling of octree nodes guaranteed not to intersect the implicit surface, which solves slow convergence in high-gradient regions. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, maximum traversal distance t{max}, and an octree where each cell stores a local Lipschitz bound. Outputs: Intersection distance t{hit} along the ray, or a failure indicator if no intersection is found within t{max}. Data Structures: Each octree cell stores an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB), a local Lipschitz constant L{cell} representing the upper bound on \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\| within the cell, and optionally an integer index to the closest object. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize traversal distance t = 0 and set the current node to the octree root. 2. Test the ray against the current node's AABB; if the ray misses, terminate traversal or backtrack to the parent/sibling. 3. If the ray intersects, compute entry and exit distances relative to the ray origin, and update t = \max(t, t{entry}). 4. Apply culling: if the Euclidean distance from the ray to the cell center exceeds the safe step bound f(\mathbf{p})/L{cell}, skip the cell and advance t to t{exit}. 5. If the current node is a leaf, evaluate the SDF at \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}; if f(\mathbf{p}) \ge 0, advance t by \Delta t = f(\mathbf{p}) / L{cell}. 6. If the current node is a branch, determine which of the 8 child octants contains the ray and descend to that child. 7. Repeat until t \ge t{max} or f(\mathbf{p}) \approx 0 within tolerance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def octreespheretrace(rayorigin, raydir, tmax, octreeroot): t = 0.0 node = octreeroot while t < tmax: # Ray-AABB intersection (slab method) invdir = 1.0 / raydir tmin = max((node.aabb.min - rayorigin) invdir) tmaxcell = min((node.aabb.max - rayorigin) invdir) tentry = max(t, tmin) texit = tmaxcell if tentry > texit or texit < 0: break t = tentry p = rayorigin + t raydir # Culling using Lipschitz bound disttocenter = length(p - node.centroid) if disttocenter > f(p) / node.Lcell: t = texit node = backtrack(node) continue # Leaf processing if node.isleaf: dist = f(p) if dist <= 0: return t t += dist / node.Lcell # Branch descent else: childidx = determinechildoctant(p, node) node = node.children[childidx] return failure def backtrack(node): # Returns parent or sibling node based on traversal stack pass def determinechildoctant(p, node): # Returns index 0-7 based on comparing p to node center pass Formulas: Lipschitz Bound: L{cell} satisfies \|f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})\| \le L{cell} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\| for all \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} in the cell. Closest Object Test (Optional): An object Oi is the closest object to a cell C if d(\text{centroid}(C), Oi) + d(\text{centroid}(C), \text{corner}(C)) < d(\text{centroid}(C), Oj) for all other objects Oj. Parameters: L{cell}: Computed as \max{\mathbf{x} \in \text{cell}} \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|. t{max}: Scene-dependent maximum ray length. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Closest Object: Under the strict definition, some cells may not have a single closest object if distances to multiple objects are equal or geometry is complex. Precision: High gradient magnitudes require small L{cell} values, leading to small step sizes and potential performance degradation if the octree is not deep enough. Accelerates sphere tracing by partitioning the domain into an octree where each cell stores a local Lipschitz bound of the field function. This allows the ray tracer to cull empty or fully interior nodes without evaluating the implicit surface, solving the problem of slow convergence in regions with high gradient magnitudes. It differs from Segment Tracing by using static cell bounds rather than dynamic segment-specific bounds, making it susceptible to field function queries at every cell intersection. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Tighter bounds than global Lipschitz constants; efficient culling of empty space; compatible with any SDF as long as a local gradient bound can be computed. Limitations: Requires pre-computation or dynamic construction of the octree; susceptible to field function queries at every cell intersection if not optimized; some cells may not have a closest object. When to Use: Scenes with complex implicit surfaces where global bounds are too loose, leading to excessive sampling. When Not to Use: Simple scenes where global bounds are sufficient, or when dynamic scene updates make octree construction prohibitive. Octree partitioning for sphere tracing was introduced by Kalra and Barr in 1989. It builds on the geometric method of sphere tracing, which uses the signed distance function to step along the ray. The key insight was that partitioning the domain allows the imposition of local bounds on the Lipschitz constants, yielding tighter signed distance bounds. This technique was also used in polygonization [Bloomenthal, 1989] and ray tracing [Kalra & Barr, 1989] of implicit surfaces. name: Lipschitz Constant Based Ray Tracing
head: Octree-Accelerated Sphere Tracing
body: Lipschitz Constant Based Ray Tracing accelerates sphere tracing by partitioning the domain into an octree where each cell stores a local Lipschitz bound of the field function. This allows the ray tracer to cull empty or fully interior nodes without evaluating the implicit surface, solving the problem of slow convergence in regions with high gradient magnitudes. It differs from Segment Tracing by using static cell bounds rather than dynamic segment-specific bounds, making it susceptible to field function queries at every cell intersection. Inputs: Implicit field function f(\mathbf{x}), its gradient \nabla f(\mathbf{x}), and its Hessian or second derivatives (required for bound calculation). An octree structure where each node corresponds to a cubic cell C. Outputs: A set of intersection points between a ray and the implicit surface f(\mathbf{x}) = 0. Data Structures: The octree nodes store a scalar value: the local Lipschitz bound \lambda(C). Field: lambda (float): The Lipschitz constant for the cell. Geometry: Implicitly defined by the octree hierarchy; each cell C has a bounding sphere S \supset C. Method Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Octree Construction): For each cell C in the octree: a. Identify the bounding sphere S of the cubic cell C. b. Compute the local Lipschitz bound \lambda(S) for the field function over the region S. This requires evaluating the maximum magnitude of the gradient or using second derivatives to bound the rate of change. c. Store \lambda(S) in the octree node corresponding to C. 2. Ray Traversal: For a given ray \Delta: a. Traverse the octree to find all cells intersected by the ray. b. For each intersected cell C with stored bound \lambda(C): i. Evaluate the field function f(\mathbf{x}) at the entry point of the ray into C. ii. Apply the Lipschitz criterion to determine if the cell straddles the implicit surface. A cell is considered empty or completely inside if the field value does not change sign or if the Lipschitz bound indicates the surface cannot be reached within the cell given the current field value. iii. If the cell straddles the surface, perform sphere tracing within the cell using the local bound \lambda(C) to step towards the root. iv. If the cell does not straddle, prune it (skip further traversal into children or the cell interior). 3. Root Isolation: Once a straddling cell is identified, isolate the root by investigating changes in the gradient and the sign of the field function within that cell. Formulas: Lipschitz Bound: \lambda(S) = \sup{\mathbf{x} \in S} \|\nabla f(\mathbf{x})\|. The bound is computed using the query \lambda(S) where S is the bounding sphere of cell C. Sphere Tracing Step: t{next} = t{current} + \frac{f(\mathbf{x}{current})}{\lambda(C)}. The step size is a function of the current field value and the local Lipschitz constant. Parameters: Octree Depth (\delta): The depth of the octree partitioning. Typical values depend on model density. For sparse models, \delta \approx 5 may suffice. For dense models like "Temple", \delta \ge 9 is needed for competitiveness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Derivative Availability: The method requires the existence and calculability of the first and second derivatives of the field function. If these are not available, the bound cannot be computed accurately. Bound Accuracy: The bound \lambda(S) is a global bound for the sphere S containing the cell, which is less accurate than the segment-specific bound \lambda(e) used in Segment Tracing. This can lead to larger step sizes and more iterations if the bound is loose. Query Overhead: Field function queries are performed for all intersections between the ray and the cells, which can be a performance bottleneck compared to methods that minimize queries. Time Complexity: Depends on octree depth and model density. Performance improves with higher octree depths for sparse models, but dense models require deeper trees (\delta \ge 9) to be competitive with Segment Tracing. Memory Complexity: Extra memory cost of 1 to 4 MB depending on the geometry of the implicit model and octree depth. Performance: For sparse models (e.g., "Chandelier"), the octree prunes empty space effectively and performs slightly faster than Segment Tracing even at shallow depths (\delta \approx 5). For dense models, Segment Tracing is generally faster unless the octree depth is high. Strengths: Effective pruning of empty space in sparse scenes; robust convergence guaranteed by Lipschitz bounds. Limitations: Requires differentiable field functions; static bounds are less accurate than dynamic segment bounds; high memory overhead for deep octrees. When to use: Sparse implicit models where empty space pruning is beneficial; scenes where pre-processing time is acceptable. When not to use: Dense models with complex primitives unless deep octrees are feasible; scenes where field derivatives are not available or expensive to compute. The principle of Lipschitz continuity was first used by [KB89] for guaranteed localization of intersections between a ray and an implicit surface. The existence of a global Lipschitz constant for signed distance fields was used by [Har96] to define a robust ray-tracing algorithm known as sphere tracing. This method is widely used for direct content creation in shaders. The specific application of storing local Lipschitz bounds in an octree for acceleration was compared against Segment Tracing in. name: Octree Enhancement
head: Octree-based Sphere Tracing Enhancement
body: Octree Enhancement replaces expensive distance evaluations in sphere tracing with octree parsing overhead to accelerate convergence. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by using spatial hierarchy to skip empty space, though experiments on simple scenes have shown it may not always outperform other enhancements like convexity or triangle inequality optimizations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and an implicit surface defined by a distance function f(\mathbf{x}). Output: The intersection point or null if no intersection is found within the maximum distance. Data Structures: Octree: A hierarchical structure where each node represents a spatial region. Nodes are classified as Empty, Leaf, or Branch. VoxelBounds: Stores coordinates as multiples of 2^{\text{lg\size}} and the log2 of the voxel size. Steps: 1. Ray-Node Intersection: Test the ray against the current node's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). 2. Node Classification: Determine if the node is Empty, Leaf, or Branch. 3. Traversal Decision: If Empty: Skip the node. Calculate the exit time (TOI) to determine the next node to visit in the parent or sibling hierarchy. If Branch: Determine which of the 8 children the ray enters next by comparing the intersection point to the node's midpoint. If Leaf: Perform sphere tracing within the leaf's volume using the distance function. 4. Distance Evaluation: In the leaf, compute the distance t = f(\mathbf{x}). If t is small enough, the surface is hit. Otherwise, advance the ray by t. 5. Exit Calculation: When a node is fully traversed or missed, calculate the exit time t{exit} for side s in dimension dim as: t{exit} = \frac{B - \mathbf{o}{dim}}{\mathbf{d}{dim}} where B is the world-space bound value and \mathbf{o}{dim} is the ray origin component. Parameters: Maximum Depth: Not given in the sources. Threshold: Not given in the sources for the basic enhancement, but relevant for variants. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Oscillations: Echoes of the octree bounds can cause oscillations at the high end of the step-size spectrum in histograms. Performance on Simple Scenes: Experiments on simple scenes failed to demonstrate increased performance from octree enhancement compared to other techniques. A method to reduce computation burden in forward viewing by exploiting spatial coherency in voxel space. It represents the 3D volume as an octree, grouping neighboring voxels with the same or similar values (up to a threshold) into uniform cubic subvolumes, which are transformed and rendered as a single unit. The transformation of sub-octants is computed efficiently using the parent's transformation, requiring 3 divisions and 6 additions per coordinate transformation in 3D. The threshold value determines if neighboring voxels are similar enough to be grouped. Time Complexity: Replaces distance computations with octree parsing overhead. The cost of transformation in the variant is 3 divisions and 6 additions per coordinate. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the octree structure. Measured Performance: In experiments on simple scenes, octree enhancement did not demonstrate increased performance over unenhanced sphere tracing or other enhancements like convexity. Strengths: Can accelerate convergence in complex scenes with large empty spaces. Limitations: May not perform as well as techniques based on space coherence in simple scenes; oscillations in step-size histograms. When to Use: Complex scenes where empty space is significant and other enhancements are insufficient. When Not to Use: Simple scenes where other enhancements (convexity, triangle inequality) provide better performance. Originated from the geometric method of sphere tracing for antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces. The concept of using octrees to reduce computation by exploiting spatial coherency is also discussed in volume visualization tutorials. name: Block-based Quadtree Index with GPU Frustum Culling
head: Compute shader culling, GPU-side quadtree traversal
body: This method accelerates large-scale terrain rendering by storing a block-based quadtree index entirely in GPU video memory and performing frustum culling and Level-of-Detail (LOD) selection via parallel compute shaders. It differs from CPU-based hierarchical traversal Octree-based traversal by eliminating CPU-GPU synchronization overhead and from standard sparse voxel approaches Sparse Voxel Traversal by using fixed-size tile blocks with Z-order storage for cache-friendly access. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Global terrain elevation data (e.g., SRTM), camera frustum parameters, and terrain resolution parameters (L, K). Output: A list of visible nodes and their corresponding LOD levels, ready for rendering. Data Structures: The method relies on two primary buffers residing in GPU memory: 1. Quadtree Node Index Structure: A compact structure array containing per-node metadata. Fields include: Bounding boxes (AABB). Center coordinates. Hierarchy levels (depth). Offsets within the data buffer. Storage order: Z-order curve (Morton code) to ensure spatially adjacent nodes are adjacent in memory. 2. Tile Data Buffer: Contains the actual elevation samples. Layout: Tiles are written in Z-order curve order. Internal Tile Layout: Within each tile, elevation values are stored contiguously in row-major order. Texture Mapping: Texture atlases are aligned one-to-one with elevation data blocks, sharing deterministic buffer offsets to avoid secondary lookup tables. Parameters: L: Exponent defining total terrain size as 2^L \times 2^L samples. K: Exponent defining leaf node (tile) size as 2^K \times 2^K samples. Typical value K=9 (512×512 samples). D: Quadtree depth, calculated as D = L - K. Algorithm Steps: 1. Index Construction: Divide the terrain domain into fixed-size tile blocks of 2^K \times 2^K samples. Calculate quadtree depth D = L - K. Compute total number of nodes N{total} = \sum{i=0}^{D} 4^i = \frac{4^{D+1}-1}{3}. Populate the Node Index Structure with bounding boxes, centers, levels, and Z-order offsets for all N{total} nodes. Write elevation data to the Tile Data Buffer in Z-order, with row-major storage within tiles. 2. Parallel Culling (Compute Shader): Launch a compute shader with one thread per node in the index structure. Each thread reads its node's bounding box and center. Perform frustum culling: Test if the node's AABB intersects the camera frustum. Perform occlusion determination (if applicable): Check visibility against previously culled nodes or depth buffer (implementation detail varies, but cited as part of the parallel output). Determine LOD level based on distance or screen-space error (computed on GPU). Output a list of visible nodes and their LOD levels. 3. Rendering: Use the visible node list to fetch elevation and texture data from the Tile Data Buffer and Texture Atlas, respectively, using the precomputed offsets. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct NodeInfo { float3 center; float3 bboxmin; float3 bboxmax; uint level; uint dataoffset; uint zorder; } function isvisible(node: NodeInfo, frustum: Frustum) -> bool: # AABB vs Frustum intersection test # Returns true if any part of the AABB is inside the frustum for each plane in frustum: if all corners of node.bboxmin/max are outside plane: return false return true function computelod(node: NodeInfo, camera: Camera) -> uint: # Example: LOD based on distance to camera center dist = length(node.center - camera.position) # Simplified LOD logic; actual implementation may use screen-space error if dist < 1000: return 0 elif dist < 5000: return 1 else: return 2 kernel main(): nodeid = dispatchthreadid.x node = nodeindices[nodeid] if isvisible(node, camera.frustum): lod = computelod(node, camera) outputlist.append(nodeid, lod) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Capacity: For global data (e.g., 1.66 \times 10^{11} samples at 30m resolution), the number of leaf nodes (\sim 6.3 \times 10^5) and total nodes (\sim 8.4 \times 10^5) fit in GPU memory with K=9. Smaller K increases node count exponentially; larger K reduces granularity. Z-order Cache Friendliness: Deviating from Z-order storage may degrade performance due to poor cache locality during traversal. Texture Alignment: Mismatched offsets between elevation and texture buffers will cause rendering artifacts. The one-to-one alignment is critical. Time Complexity: Frustum culling is O(N) where N is the number of nodes, but executed in parallel on the GPU. The constant factor is low due to simple AABB tests. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the index structure. For global SRTM30m data with K=9, \sim 8.4 \times 10^5 nodes fit in GPU memory. Performance: Eliminates CPU-GPU transfer overhead for culling. Verified superior rendering throughput over WebGL-based methods. Strengths: Scalable to global datasets; cache-friendly storage; parallel culling. Limitations: Requires GPU memory for the entire index; less flexible for dynamic topology changes compared to CPU-managed trees. This method was proposed in the context of WebGPU terrain visualization, addressing the bottleneck of CPU-side traversal and data reorganization for large-scale datasets. It builds on prior work in WebGPU for terrain [1-5] and dynamic terrain tiling [7], leveraging space-filling curves for cache efficiency [9]. name: Detail-adaptive Octree Sampling
head: Detail-Adaptive Octree Resampling
body: Detail-adaptive Octree Sampling is a method for rendering irregular or curvilinear grids by overcoming the fixed resolution limits of regular grids. It solves the problem of excessive storage and rendering time required to resample irregular data onto a uniform grid with the smallest cell granularity. It sets itself apart from standard regular grid volume rendering by dynamically adjusting local height based on local grid granularity, allowing for time-critical rendering of complex topologies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Irregular or curvilinear grid data (e.g., tetrahedral meshes). Output: A rendered image, typically using feedforward projection methods. Data Structures: Detail-Adaptive Octree: A hierarchical spatial partitioning structure. Unlike a uniform octree, the local height (depth/size) of nodes is determined by the local granularity of the input grid. Layout: Not given in the sources. The structure supports classification of nodes as Empty, Leaf, or Branch as per the parent method's shared principles. Steps: 1. Decomposition: Sample the irregular data into a detail-adaptive octree. The resolution of the octree is not fixed globally; instead, the local height of the octree nodes is determined by the local granularity of the irregular grid. 2. Rendering: Render the grid within a time-critical framework using the octree decomposition. This typically involves feedforward (projection) methods where cells are projected onto the screen one by one. Note: The sources mention Projected Tetrahedra (PT) as a popular projection algorithm for this context, which decomposes tetrahedra into triangles based on their projected profile. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderirregulargrid(irregulardata): # Step 1: Construct the detail-adaptive octree # The local height of nodes is determined by local grid granularity octree = builddetailadaptiveoctree(irregulardata) # Step 2: Render using the octree decomposition # This allows rendering within a time-critical framework image = renderwithoctree(octree) return image Parameters: Local Granularity: The variable determining the local height of the octree nodes. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. A feedforward projection method often used with this sampling approach. It projects cells onto the screen and decomposes them into triangles, handling four classes of projections. It is chosen when rendering irregular tetrahedral grids with high accuracy is required. See Projected Tetrahedra. Time Complexity: Allows rendering within a time-critical framework, implying efficiency compared to naive resampling. Exact complexity not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Overcomes the need to fix resolution to the smallest cell, reducing storage requirements compared to a uniform high-resolution grid. Exact memory usage not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles irregular/curvilinear grids without excessive resampling overhead; supports time-critical rendering. Limitations: Requires implementation of octree decomposition and potentially complex projection logic (e.g., PT classes). When to use: When rendering irregular grids where fixed-resolution regular grids are too large for storage or rendering. When not to use: For regular, uniform grids where standard volume rendering is sufficient. The method was introduced to address the limitations of fixed-resolution regular grids when dealing with irregular data. It is discussed in the context of volume visualization and volume graphics, specifically regarding the rendering of curvilinear grids and tetrahedral meshes. The approach leverages octree decomposition to manage the complexity of irregular topologies. name: Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures
body: Empty Space Skipping via Data Structures is a family of volume rendering optimization techniques that reduce computational cost by identifying and bypassing inactive (transparent or empty) regions of a volume dataset before or during ray sampling. Unlike methods that rely on hardware occlusion culling or ray coherence, this family uses explicit secondary data structures—such as min-max blocks, occupancy grids, BVHs, or hybrid trees—to store metadata about the spatial distribution of active data. This allows rays to determine entry and exit points of active regions analytically or via coarse traversal, skipping large intervals of empty space that would otherwise require expensive texture lookups and compositing operations. The core mechanism shared by all methods in this family involves three stages: construction of a secondary acceleration structure, definition of activity, and ray-based skipping. 1. Acceleration Structure Construction: A secondary data structure is built to represent the volume. 2. Active Region Definition: A block or region is defined as "active" if it contributes to the final image. 3. Ray Query and Skip: During rendering, the algorithm queries the acceleration structure to find the entry and exit points of active regions along a ray. 4. Coordinate Mapping: Efficient mapping between ray positions and grid indices is required, typically via integer division by block size: u{\text{occ}} = \lfloor u{\text{vol}} / B \rfloor. Uses min-max block structures and rasterizes bounding geometry of active blocks to determine ray start/end points. Best for isosurface rendering with static transfer functions. Uses hardware depth/alpha tests on texture slabs to find near/far points. Best for legacy OpenGL pipelines and slab-based rendering. Uses BVH with density bounds for sphere tracing. Best for semi-transparent volumes with constant or varying density. Uses occupancy volumes for neural radiance fields (NeRF). Best for volumetric video and neural rendering. Uses flat or multi-resolution occupancy grids. Best for simple, direct indexing acceleration. Uses a leap buffer based on ray coherence. Best for close-up views with large empty foregrounds. Combines kd-tree root with uniform grid leaves. Best for large datasets requiring balanced construction cost and skipping granularity. Definition: A technique achieving extremely fine-grained empty space skipping by marching rays only through active volume cells, located efficiently with a HistoPyramid texture and rendered as point primitives. Steps: 1. Locate active volume cells using a HistoPyramid texture. 2. Render active cells as point primitives to create rays close to the isosurface. 3. Accelerate by exploiting early-depth testing: compare fragment's interpolated z-coordinate with depth buffer value; discard if occluded. 4. Rasterize primitives in front-to-back order to increase discarded fragments, achieved via CPU-based sorting of volume slices. Comparison: Considered a hybrid object-order and image-order approach, meaning it is dependent on rendering resolution. Steps: 1. Divide span space points into one of the L \times L lattice elements. 2. Assign each lattice element to a category based on its position relative to the isovalue v (see Figure 3 cases in). 3. Trivially include cells in region 2. 4. For cells in region 3, require a test against their maximum value. 5. For cells in region 4, require a test against their minimum value. 6. For cells in region 5, require a full min-max search of its cells. 7. Create search structures only at the lattice elements along the diagonal region 5. 8. Coalesce lattice elements at other regions into sorted linear arrays. 9. Build a kd-tree for each lattice element along the y = x line, since only these elements may fall into region 5 classification. Parameter: Lattice resolution L: User-defined resolution for dividing span space points. Steps: 1. Propagate current transfer function values to the leafs of the Mixture Graph. 2. Use the hierarchy for skipping longer segments. 3. If the opacity value in parent voxels falls below a certain threshold, traverse the hierarchy upwards to establish larger blocks that can be skipped. Parameter: Threshold: A low opacity threshold used to trigger skipping; typical value is 10^{-8}. Performance: Average 3x speedup compared to the same implementation without mipmaps using a threshold of 10^{-8}. Empty space skipping is a fundamental optimization in volume rendering, addressing the high cost of sampling large volumes where significant portions are transparent or empty. Early methods relied on ray coherence (Space Leaping). The use of explicit data structures for skipping evolved with GPU capabilities. Liu et al. [LCD09] introduced HistoPyramid-based skipping, followed by IsoBAS [LCD15] and Jiang et al. [JRZ16], which are considered hybrid object-order/image-order approaches. Shen et al. [14] proposed the ISSUE algorithm for isosurface extraction using lattice subdivision. More recently, hierarchical structures like Mixture Graphs have been developed to balance construction cost and skipping efficiency for large-scale datasets. name: Object-Order Empty Space Skipping
head: Block min-max culling, Front-to-back ray-casting with bounding box culling, GPU-based Ray-Casting with Object-Order Empty Space Skipping
body: Object-Order Empty Space Skipping is a volume rendering optimization technique that reduces the number of volume samples by culling transparent or irrelevant regions before raycasting begins. It differs from its siblings by performing culling during the rasterization setup phase using precomputed block statistics, rather than during ray traversal or via bounding geometry rasterization. Unlike Early Shader Termination, which stops rays dynamically during compositing, this method prevents rays from entering empty blocks entirely. Unlike Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping, it relies on scalar block bounds rather than polygonal approximations. The method combines object-order skipping (via block min-max values) with image-order skipping (per-sample checks) to accelerate front-to-back ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume texture V, isovalue threshold T, camera parameters (position c, screen coordinates (x,y)), block size B (e.g., 4^3 or 8^3 voxels). Output: Rendered image with rays skipping inactive regions. Data Structures: 1. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing voxel values. 2. Min-Max Block Structure: A secondary structure storing the minimum and maximum values for each block in the regular subdivision of the volume. The block dimensions are typically 4^3 or 8^3 voxels. 3. Bounding Geometry: Implicitly defined by the active blocks. Active blocks are those where \max(V{block}) \ge T. Steps: 1. Initialization (Pre-computation): Subdivide the volume into blocks of size B \times B \times B. For each block, compute and store the minimum and maximum voxel values in the Min-Max Block Structure. Identify active blocks: A block is active if its maximum value is greater than or equal to the isovalue threshold T. Generate bounding geometry for active blocks. This involves identifying faces of active blocks that are adjacent to inactive blocks. 2. Per-Frame Setup (Object-Order Skipping): Compute ray direction \mathbf{d}(x, y) for each pixel (x, y) from camera position c: \mathbf{p}(t, x, y) = c + t \mathbf{d}(x, y) Determine the initial ray depth range [t{start}(x, y), t{exit}(x, y)] by rasterizing the bounding geometry of active blocks: Render front faces of the active block bounding geometry with a depth test that retains the closest intersection (e.g., GLLESS) to obtain t{start}(x, y). Render back faces of the active block bounding geometry with a depth test that retains the farthest intersection (e.g., GLGREATER) to obtain t{exit}(x, y). Note: This approach does not exclude inactive blocks enclosed by active blocks from the search range [t{start}, t{exit}]. 3. Ray Casting Loop (Image-Order Skipping): For each pixel, cast a ray in front-to-back order within the range [t{start}(x, y), t{exit}(x, y)]. At each sample point, determine which block the sample belongs to using integer division: u{block} = \lfloor u{vol} / B \rfloor where u{vol} is the coordinate in the volume texture and B is the block size. Retrieve the min-max values for the current block from the Min-Max Block Structure. Skip Condition: If the current sample's value (or the block's max value, depending on implementation detail) indicates the region is inactive (e.g., block max < T for isosurface, or specific opacity criteria for volume rendering), skip the sample. For isosurface rendering, if the block is inactive, skip all samples within that block. If the block is active, perform the standard ray casting computation (e.g., texture fetch, compositing). Terminate the ray if the isosurface is found or the ray exits the volume. Parameters: Block size B: Typically 4^3 or 8^3 voxels per block. Isovalue threshold T: Determines active blocks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Enclosed Inactive Blocks: Inactive blocks enclosed by active blocks are not excluded from the search range [t{start}, t{exit}] by the bounding geometry. Samples in these blocks are skipped on a per-sample basis early in the ray-casting loop. Performance Overhead: Inactive blocks enclosed by active blocks result in per-sample checks, which adds overhead compared to fully excluded regions. Isovalue Changes: When the isovalue changes, the active status of blocks must be recomputed, and the bounding geometry updated. Early Shader Termination is an optimization technique that discards the execution of complex decoding shaders for fragments likely to represent empty space by using an early z-test in a two-pass rendering approach. It builds on Object-Order Empty Space Skipping by adding a lightweight pre-check to avoid expensive shader execution in empty regions. Compared to rendering uncompressed data, this approach initially perceives a loss in performance of a factor of 2-3 due to complex shaders and texture indirections; however, in empty regions, it results in a considerable speed-up because only one texture fetch is needed to check the mean. Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping is a volume rendering optimization technique that uses hardware-accelerated rasterization to determine the start and end positions for ray marching, thereby skipping empty space. It solves the problem of expensive tree traversal on the GPU by replacing hierarchical data structure lookups with fragment shader depth testing. It sets itself apart from Min-Max Block Culling by using explicit geometric primitives (quads/boxes) and depth buffers rather than scalar min-max values, and from Early Shader Termination by performing culling in a dedicated geometry pass rather than within the ray-marching loop. Min-Max Block Culling is an object-order empty space skipping technique that reduces the number of volume samples by culling transparent or irrelevant regions before raycasting begins. It differs from its siblings by performing culling during the rasterization setup phase using precomputed block statistics, rather than during ray traversal or via bounding geometry rasterization. Unlike Early Shader Termination, which stops rays dynamically during compositing, this method prevents rays from entering empty blocks entirely. Unlike Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping, it relies on scalar block bounds rather than polygonal approximations. A data structure for empty-space skipping in pre-integrated volume rendering. It modifies the region covered by each block so that each block covers some region of which thickness is at least the sampling distance. By overlapping the region of each block, a line segment formed by two sampling points can be tested for transparency using only one block, avoiding the overhead of determining which of multiple intersecting blocks are transparent. Definition: Each block covers a region of thickness at least the sampling distance, creating overlaps between adjacent blocks. Steps: 1. Modify the region covered by each block such that each block covers a region of thickness at least the sampling distance, creating overlaps between adjacent blocks. 2. To skip a line segment formed by two sampling points, test only the single block that contains the line segment (or overlaps it sufficiently) to determine if it is transparent. If the block is transparent, skip the sampling process for that segment. Comparison: Unlike previous methods where a line segment may intersect at most three blocks and requires testing all intersecting blocks (creating overhead to determine cases like Fig. 1a vs 1b), this method tests only one block due to the overlapping region design. Time Complexity: The object-order skipping phase is O(1) per pixel for depth range computation (via rasterization) and O(N) for ray casting, where N is the number of samples in the active range. The per-sample check for image-order skipping is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(V/B^3) for the min-max block structure, where V is the volume size and B is the block size. Measured Performance: The method reduces overhead by skipping most empty space with no cost using modified ray segments. Only a small number of samples require per-sample skipping, accelerated via adaptive sampling. Strengths: Reduces the number of volume samples significantly for sparse volumes. Simple to implement with standard GPU rasterization features. Limitations: Inactive blocks enclosed by active blocks are not excluded from the search range, leading to per-sample checks. Performance may degrade if the volume is dense or if the block size is not optimal. When to Use: Suitable for sparse volumes with clear isosurfaces or transparent regions. Effective when combined with adaptive sampling. When Not to Use: Not suitable for dense volumes where most blocks are active, as the overhead of per-sample checks may outweigh the benefits. Object-Order Empty Space Skipping was introduced in the context of GPU-based ray-casting for real-time volume rendering. It builds on the idea of using block min-max values to cull inactive regions, reducing the overhead of empty space skipping. The method has been used in various implementations of real-time volume rendering, particularly for isosurface rendering.
