name: Early Shader Termination
head: Early End of Computation, Early z-test optimization, Two-pass empty space culling
body: Early Shader Termination is an optimization technique that discards the execution of complex decoding shaders for fragments likely to represent empty space by using an early z-test in a two-pass rendering approach. It builds on Object-Order Empty Space Skipping by adding a lightweight pre-check to avoid expensive shader execution in empty regions. Compared to rendering uncompressed data, this approach initially perceives a loss in performance of a factor of 2-3 due to complex shaders and texture indirections; however, in empty regions, it results in a considerable speed-up because only one texture fetch is needed to check the mean. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A compressed volume dataset where each block (macro-cell) has an associated index texture I storing metadata (specifically the mean value in the R-component) and dependent data textures C1, C2. A slicing polygon representing the current view frustum or volume boundary. Output: A rendered image where empty space fragments are skipped, and depth values are correctly updated to allow subsequent fragments to pass depth tests. Data Structures: Index Texture I: Stores block metadata. The R-component holds the mean value of the block. Dependent Textures C1, C2: Store difference information or raw data, addressed using components of I. Steps: 1. First Pass (Empty Space Detection): Render the slicing polygon twice. In the first pass, issue a simple pixel shader program. In the shader, access index texture I and check the mean value stored in the R-component. If the mean value is zero, render the fragment with color and opacity set to zero. This does not affect the color buffer but sets the depth value in the depth buffer. If the mean value is not zero, discard the fragment using a kill instruction. This prevents the fragment from affecting the color or depth buffer. 2. Second Pass (Complex Rendering): Render the slicing polygon again with the complex shader. Set the depth test to GLGREATER in the second pass. The early z-test only lets fragments pass that were discarded in the first pass (where mean \neq 0). All other fragments (where mean = 0) are discarded before entering the complex shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyshadertermination(fragments, indextextureI, complexdecodefunc): """ Simulates the two-pass early shader termination optimization. fragments: list of objects with.coords,.blockid,.z (depth) indextextureI: dict mapping blockid to objects with.R (mean value) complexdecodefunc: callable that returns decoded color for non-empty blocks """ depthbuffer = {} # Maps fragment coordinates to depth from pass 1 pass1discarded = [] # Pass 1: Simple pixel shader for frag in fragments: meanval = indextextureI[frag.blockid].R if meanval == 0: # Empty space: write depth, zero color/opacity depthbuffer[frag.coords] = frag.z pass1discarded.append(False) else: # Non-empty space: discard via kill instruction # Depth buffer retains the last valid depth for this coordinate pass1discarded.append(True) # Pass 2: Complex shader with GLGREATER depth test finaloutput = [] for i, frag in enumerate(fragments): if not pass1discarded[i]: # Early z-test fails: GLGREATER requires frag.z > depthbuffer[frag.coords] # Since pass 1 wrote frag.z, frag.z > frag.z is false. Fragment discarded. continue # Early z-test passes for discarded fragments (mean != 0) lastdepth = depthbuffer.get(frag.coords, -float('inf')) if frag.z > lastdepth: # GLGREATER decoded = complexdecodefunc(frag, indextextureI) finaloutput.append(decoded) return finaloutput Parameters: Depth Test Function: Must be set to GLGREATER in the second pass to leverage the early z-test correctly. Mean Threshold: Zero is used as the threshold for empty space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Buffer Consistency: If a fragment is discarded in the shader (via kill), the depth value of the fragment rendered last is still valid in the depth buffer. This must be accounted for when using depth tests, as the discarded fragment does not update the depth buffer. Performance Overhead: The two-pass approach introduces overhead. The initial performance loss compared to uncompressed rendering is a factor of 2-3 due to the complexity of the shaders and texture indirections. Adds spatial coherence checks along the scanline direction to skip entire segments of empty space within a macro-cell projection. It builds on Early Shader Termination by optimizing the scope of the termination check. Time Complexity: In empty regions, the complexity is reduced to one texture fetch per block to check the mean. In non-empty regions, the full complex shader is executed. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the index texture I and dependent textures C1, C2. Measured Performance: On an Intel P4 1900 MHz machine, this approach saves another 5 percent of overall rendering time on average when combined with other optimizations like Early End of Computation. Strengths: Considerable speed-up in empty regions, which are frequent in numerical simulation results. Limitations: Initial performance loss of 2-3x compared to uncompressed rendering due to shader complexity and indirections. Requires hardware support for early z-test. The technique was proposed in the context of compression domain volume rendering to address performance losses caused by complex shader programs and texture indirections. It leverages the early z-test feature available on target graphics architectures to avoid executing pixel shaders for fragments that are likely to decode empty space. The concept of terminating computation early is also discussed in the context of cell-based first-hit ray casting, where rendering ends as soon as all pixels are covered, saving approximately 5 percent of overall rendering time. name: Early Scanline Termination
body: Early Scanline Termination is an optimization that stops processing a scanline as soon as a local ray through a pixel does not intersect any iso-surfaces, reducing the number of local rays cast per pixel. It operates within the macro-cell projection framework to skip empty segments along rows or columns of pixels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projected macro-cell bounding box, set of surface cells within the macro-cell, current scanline (row or column of pixels), image buffer, and per-pixel sequence flags. Output: Updated image buffer with colors for intersected pixels; identification of erroneous blank pixels (holes) for post-processing. Data Structures: Image Buffer: 2D array storing color values for each pixel. Sequence Flags: Two boolean flags per pixel indicating whether the pixel was recently dropped due to horizontal or vertical early scanline termination. Flags are set to True for all empty dropped pixels. The bounds of each new sequence of dropped pixels are marked by setting the sequence flags of the pixel immediately preceding the sequence and the pixel immediately following the sequence to False. A pixel through which a regular local ray has been cast has its sequence flags reset to False. Steps: 1. Identify all scanlines intersecting the macro-cell projection. 2. Check for problem cases by calculating a representative surface normal for each surface cell and checking dot products with two reference vectors. If a boundary cell prohibits termination, project its center point to the image plane. The collection of these projections forms a critical region. 3. Iterate through pixels of a scanline from one boundary to the other. If a local ray does not intersect any iso-surface and the pixel is outside the critical region, stop processing the scanline. Mark all remaining empty pixels as dropped, setting the appropriate sequence flag (horizontal or vertical) to True. Set the sequence flags of the pixel immediately preceding the first dropped pixel and the pixel immediately following the last dropped pixel to False to mark the sequence bounds. If a regular local ray is cast through a pixel, reset its sequence flags to False. 4. After frame completion, identify sequences of blank pixels with sequence flags set, bounded on both sides by non-blank pixels with unset flags. Cast rays from these pixels through the complete volume to fill the holes. Formulas: Representative normal check: N \cdot V{ref} > 0 indicates a problem case (left-facing normal or dangerous face). Critical region: Union of projected center points of all boundary cells where the dot product condition holds. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Left-facing surface normals: If projected surface normals point towards the left, early termination is disallowed for scanlines intersecting those parts until all such intersections are processed. Dangerous faces: Certain surface orientations can cause errors if termination is applied. Errors: Early scanline termination can lead to errors in about 0.017 percent of pixels on average, resulting in visible holes. These holes must be identified and filled after frame completion. Sequence Flag Management: Flags must be carefully managed to correctly identify erroneous sequences. Pixels erroneously dropped will never be part of a dropped sequence again. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyscanlinetermination(macrocell, scanlinepixels, imagebuffer, sequenceflags, ishorizontal): # Project 3D cell centers to 2D image coordinates def projecttoimage(point3d): return (point3d.x, point3d.y) # Check if a 2D point lies outside a set of projected critical points def isoutsidecriticalregion(point2d, criticalpoints): if not criticalpoints: return True minx = min(p[0] for p in criticalpoints) maxx = max(p[0] for p in criticalpoints) miny = min(p[1] for p in criticalpoints) maxy = max(p[1] for p in criticalpoints) return not (minx <= point2d[0] <= maxx and miny <= point2d[1] <= maxy) # Cast a ray through the macro-cell to find the first iso-surface intersection def castlocalray(pixel2d): # Standard ray-marching or bounding volume traversal return None # Compute color from intersection data def computecolor(intersection): return (255, 255, 255) BLANK = (0, 0, 0, 0) criticalpoints = [projecttoimage(cell.center) for cell in macrocell.surfacecells if cell.prohibitstermination] terminated = False firstdroppedidx = None lastdroppedidx = None for i, pixel in enumerate(scanlinepixels): if terminated: break intersection = castlocalray(pixel) if intersection is not None: imagebuffer[pixel] = computecolor(intersection) sequenceflags[pixel] = (False, False) else: if isoutsidecriticalregion(pixel, criticalpoints): terminated = True firstdroppedidx = i for j in range(i, len(scanlinepixels)): p = scanlinepixels[j] imagebuffer[p] = BLANK if ishorizontal: sequenceflags[p] = (True, sequenceflags[p][1]) else: sequenceflags[p] = (sequenceflags[p][0], True) lastdroppedidx = j if firstdroppedidx > 0: sequenceflags[scanlinepixels[firstdroppedidx - 1]] = (False, False) if lastdroppedidx + 1 < len(scanlinepixels): sequenceflags[scanlinepixels[lastdroppedidx + 1]] = (False, False) def fillholes(imagebuffer, sequenceflags, imageheight, imagewidth): BLANK = (0, 0, 0, 0) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if imagebuffer[y, x] == BLANK and sequenceflags[y, x] != (False, False): # Verify bounds: preceding and following pixels must be non-blank with flags (False, False) leftok = (x == 0) or (imagebuffer[y, x-1] != BLANK and sequenceflags[y, x-1] == (False, False)) rightok = (x == imagewidth-1) or (imagebuffer[y, x+1] != BLANK and sequenceflags[y, x+1] == (False, False)) if leftok and rightok: imagebuffer[y, x] = castlocalray((x, y)) Performance: Saves another 17 percent of overall rendering time on average. Reduces rays per pixel from 2.483 to 1.285 in the tested scenario. Memory Complexity: Requires two sequence flags per pixel for tracking. Limitations: Errors occur in about 0.017 percent of pixels on average, resulting in visible holes that require post-processing. Performance is dependent on the data set and the position of the view point. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping
head: Bounding Geometry Rasterization, Raster-based Bounding Box Culling, Rasterizing Bounding Geometry
body: Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping is a volume rendering optimization technique that uses hardware-accelerated rasterization to determine the start and end positions for ray marching, thereby skipping empty space. It solves the problem of expensive tree traversal on the GPU by replacing hierarchical data structure lookups with fragment shader depth testing. It sets itself apart from Min-Max Block Culling by using explicit geometric primitives (quads/boxes) and depth buffers rather than scalar min-max values, and from Early Shader Termination by performing culling in a dedicated geometry pass rather than within the ray-marching loop. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume texture containing iso values (or occupancy data), a threshold iso value, and a coarse grid definition (e.g., grid cells spanning N^3 voxels). Output: A rendered image where rays are marched only through active regions, with start and end positions derived from rasterized depth values. Data Structures: 1. gridTex: A 3D texture where each voxel stores the maximum iso value of the corresponding coarse grid cell. 2. Bounding Geometry: A set of quads (or bounding boxes) representing the boundaries between active and inactive regions in gridTex. 3. Offscreen Buffer: A depth buffer (and optionally a color buffer) used to store minimum and maximum depth values for each fragment during the first pass. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct gridTex by sampling the volume texture. Each voxel in gridTex contains the maximum iso value within its corresponding coarse grid cell. Define the coarse grid dimensions. For a volume of size Vx \times Vy \times Vz and a cell size of C^3 voxels, the grid dimensions are \lceil Vx/C \rceil \times \lceil Vy/C \rceil \times \lceil Vz/C \rceil. 2. Generate Bounding Geometry: For each pair of neighboring voxels in gridTex, determine if a boundary exists. A grid voxel is considered active if its maximum iso value is above the threshold iso value. Generate a quad (or bounding box face) if one voxel in the neighbor pair is active and the other is inactive. This process identifies the surface of the active volume data. 3. First Pass (Depth Computation): Render the generated bounding geometry to an offscreen buffer. For each fragment, store the minimum depth (front face) and maximum depth (back face) of the bounding geometry. This pass effectively projects the 3D active regions onto the 2D screen, capturing the depth extent of the volume along each ray. 4. Second Pass (Ray Marching): Render the front faces of the bounding geometry again to the main buffer. In the fragment shader, discard the fragment if it is not at the minimum depth value recorded in the first pass. This ensures that only the front-most active region is processed, preventing double-counting or processing of occluded empty space. Compute the start position of the ray using the minimum depth value and the end position using the maximum depth value from the first pass. March the ray between these start and end positions using standard volume rendering techniques (e.g., ray casting). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializegrid(volumetexture, cellsize): """ Create a coarse grid texture storing max iso values. """ griddims = ( ceil(volumetexture.width / cellsize), ceil(volumetexture.height / cellsize), ceil(volumetexture.depth / cellsize)) gridtex = create3dtexture(griddims) for z in range(griddims[2]): for y in range(griddims[1]): for x in range(griddims[0]): # Sample the volume texture for this coarse cell maxval = -infinity for dz in range(cellsize): for dy in range(cellsize): for dx in range(cellsize): vx = x cellsize + dx vy = y cellsize + dy vz = z cellsize + dz val = volumetexture.sample(vx, vy, vz) if val > maxval: maxval = val gridtex.set(x, y, z, maxval) return gridtex def generateboundinggeometry(gridtex, threshold, cellsize, volumedims): """ Generate quads for boundaries between active and inactive regions. """ quads = [] griddims = gridtex.dimensions for z in range(griddims[2]): for y in range(griddims[1]): for x in range(griddims[0]): isactive = gridtex.get(x, y, z) > threshold # Check neighbors in +x, +y, +z directions neighbors = [ (x + 1, y, z), (x, y + 1, z), (x, y, z + 1) ] for nx, ny, nz in neighbors: if nx < griddims[0] and ny < griddims[1] and nz < griddims[2]: neighboractive = gridtex.get(nx, ny, nz) > threshold if isactive != neighboractive: # Generate a quad at the boundary quad = createquadatboundary(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, cellsize, volumedims) quads.append(quad) return quads def createquadatboundary(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, cellsize, volumedims): """ Create a quad representing the boundary between two grid cells. """ # Calculate world coordinates of the boundary plane # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation depends on coordinate system boundarypos = getboundaryposition(x, y, z, nx, ny, nz, cellsize) return Quad(position=boundarypos, normal=getnormal(nx, ny, nz)) def renderfirstpass(quads, offscreenbuffer): """ Render bounding geometry to compute min/max depth. """ # Clear depth buffer offscreenbuffer.cleardepth() # Render all quads for quad in quads: # Render front and back faces to capture depth range # Store min and max depth for each fragment offscreenbuffer.render(quad, storeminmaxdepth=True) return offscreenbuffer def rendersecondpass(quads, offscreenbuffer, mainbuffer): """ Render front faces and perform ray marching. """ # Render front faces only for quad in quads: # In fragment shader: # 1. Check if current fragment depth == mindepth from first pass # 2. If not, discard # 3. If yes, compute ray start/end from min/max depth # 4. March ray and color pixel mainbuffer.render(quad, fragmentshader=raymarchingshader, depthbuffer=offscreenbuffer) def raymarchingshader(fragmentdepth, mindepth, maxdepth): """ Fragment shader for ray marching. """ # Discard if not at minimum depth if fragmentdepth != mindepth: discard() # Compute ray start and end positions from depth values raystart = depthtoworld(mindepth) rayend = depthtoworld(maxdepth) # March ray color = marchray(raystart, rayend) return color Parameters: Threshold Iso Value: The iso value above which a grid cell is considered active. Typical values depend on the data distribution. Cell Size: The number of voxels per coarse grid cell. A common example is 8^3 voxels per cell. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Iso Value Changes: The bounding geometry must be regenerated whenever the threshold iso value changes, as active regions may shift. Precision: Depth buffer precision must be sufficient to distinguish between front and back faces, especially for thin structures. Occlusion: The method relies on depth testing to handle occlusion. If the depth buffer is not properly cleared or updated, incorrect start/end positions may be computed. SparseLeap is a method for efficient empty space skipping in very large, sparse volume data, such as terabyte-sized microscopy volumes. It solves the problem of fragmented space subdivisions making empty regions hard to skip and the infeasibility of pre-computing well-adapted space subdivisions due to frequent changes in active objects. It sets itself apart from its siblings by exploiting hardware-accelerated rasterization to create per-pixel ray segment lists, thereby avoiding hierarchy traversal on the GPU during the ray-casting stage. Unlike standard octree empty space skipping, SparseLeap scales better to large, sparse data. It is agnostic of the underlying data structure used for managing volume data (e.g., page-table hierarchies or octrees). Texture Box Approximation is a method for accelerating volume rendering by approximating the volume data with a set of bounding boxes, called texture boxes, which are rasterized to efficiently clip empty space from the rendering pipeline. It differs from level-of-detail methods that rasterize lower-resolution blocks by focusing on spatial occupancy to discard empty regions entirely before fragment shader execution. Time Complexity: The complexity depends on the number of active grid cells and the cost of rasterization. Generating the bounding geometry is O(N) where N is the number of grid cells. Rasterization is generally efficient on modern GPUs. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for gridTex, the bounding geometry, and the offscreen buffer. Measured Performance: Can lead to fewer look-ups into the empty-space skipping data structure during rendering when compared to octree structures. Strengths: Avoids expensive tree traversal on the GPU; leverages hardware-accelerated rasterization. Limitations: Requires regeneration of bounding geometry when iso values change. May have overhead for generating the geometry if the volume is dense. When to Use: Suitable for scenarios where tree traversal is a bottleneck and the volume data can be approximated by coarse grid cells. When Not to Use: Not suitable for highly dynamic volumes where the active regions change frequently, as the geometry regeneration cost may outweigh the benefits. The technique was proposed by Liu et al. [LCDP13] and Hadwiger et al. [HAAB+ 18] as a way to avoid hierarchy traversal on the GPU by using rasterization hardware. name: SparseLeap Rasterization
head: SparseLeap rasterization details
body: SparseLeap is a method for efficient empty space skipping in very large, sparse volume data, such as terabyte-sized microscopy volumes. It solves the problem of fragmented space subdivisions making empty regions hard to skip and the infeasibility of pre-computing well-adapted space subdivisions due to frequent changes in active objects. It sets itself apart from its siblings by exploiting hardware-accelerated rasterization to create per-pixel ray segment lists, thereby avoiding hierarchy traversal on the GPU during the ray-casting stage. Unlike standard octree empty space skipping, SparseLeap scales better to large, sparse data. It is agnostic of the underlying data structure used for managing volume data (e.g., page-table hierarchies or octrees). SparseLeap operates in two main stages: a preprocessing/rasterization stage and a ray-casting stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An occupancy-histogram tree where each node has an occupancy class (empty, non-empty, or unknown). The tree is lazily constructed. Output: A set of ray segment lists, one per pixel, identifying non-empty regions along the viewing ray. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy-Histogram Tree: A hierarchical structure where each node stores an occupancy class. Leaf nodes store the class directly; non-leaf nodes determine their class via a majority vote over their occupancy histogram (the class occurring most often in all leaf nodes of its sub-tree). 2. Occupancy Geometry: An array of bounding boxes extracted from the tree. Each emitted box stores: Center coordinates. Size (dimensions). Node's occupancy class. Parent's occupancy class. 3. Ray Segment List: A per-pixel list of ray events (entry/exit) defining intervals (segments) with associated occupancy classes. Steps: 1. Occupancy Geometry Generation: Traverse the occupancy-histogram tree in breadth-first order, visiting child nodes in a fixed order (not visibility order). For the root node, set the parent occupancy class to invalid (not equal to any other class). The root always emits its bounding box. For each visited non-leaf node, determine its occupancy class by taking the majority vote over its occupancy histogram. For leaf nodes, use the occupancy class already stored in the node. Compare the node's occupancy class with its parent's occupancy class. If they are the same, skip emission. If they are different, emit a bounding box containing the node's center, size, its own occupancy class, and its parent's occupancy class. If the number of emitted bounding boxes exceeds a prespecified optional resource limit, stop traversal. 2. Rasterization (Object-Order Stage): Rasterize the set of fine-grained, view-independent bounding boxes generated in Step 1 using hardware-accelerated rasterization. For each pixel, compute an ordered list of stabbing boundary faces. Convert this into a ray segment list where consecutive ray segments of the same occupancy class are merged. This creates singly-linked lists of ray events per pixel. Exploit frame coherence by re-using the same bounding boxes unless the set of active objects changes. 3. Ray-Casting (Image-Order Stage): Perform ray casting independently for each pixel. Use the pre-computed ray segment lists to identify non-empty regions along the ray. Leap over empty space without hierarchy traversal by skipping segments marked as empty. Sample the non-empty volume data only within the non-empty segments. 4. Color Calculation: Apply a simple analytical lighting model to each intersection of the ray and the volume cell. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparseleaprender(occupancytree, camera, volumedata): # Step 1: Generate Occupancy Geometry boundingboxes = [] stack = [(occupancytree.root, None)] # (node, parentclass) while stack: node, parentclass = stack.pop(0) # Breadth-first traversal # Determine current node's class if node.isleaf: currentclass = node.occupancyclass else: currentclass = getmajorityvote(node.occupancyhistogram) # Geometry Emission Rule if currentclass != parentclass: box = { 'center': node.center, 'size': node.size, 'myclass': currentclass, 'parentclass': parentclass } boundingboxes.append(box) # Add children to stack for child in node.children: stack.append((child, currentclass)) # Step 2: Rasterization # Hardware rasterization of boundingboxes produces per-pixel ray segment lists # This step is typically handled by the GPU rasterizer, not explicit CPU code raysegmentlists = hardwarerasterize(boundingboxes, camera) # Step 3 & 4: Ray Casting and Color Calculation for pixel in pixels: segments = raysegmentlists[pixel] color = vec3(0.0) for segment in segments: if segment.occupancyclass == 'empty': continue # Leap over empty space # Sample volume data in non-empty segment sample = samplevolume(segment.ray, volumedata) # Apply analytical lighting model lightcolor = calculatelighting(sample, segment.ray) color += lightcolor pixel.color = color Parameters: Resource Limit: An optional prespecified maximum number of bounding boxes. If exceeded, traversal stops. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fragmentation: Some fragmentation of space still remains in the occupancy geometry, which is resolved during the subsequent rasterization of ray segment lists where consecutive ray segments of the same occupancy class are merged. Active Objects: The method relies on frame coherence. If the set of active objects changes frequently, the bounding boxes must be regenerated, incurring preprocessing cost. A view-independent process that extracts nested bounding boxes from an occupancy histogram tree to represent space occupancy, reducing spatial fragmentation compared to standard octrees. It traverses the tree in breadth-first order, emitting boxes only when the occupancy class differs from the parent's class. It allows for an optional resource limit to cap the number of emitted boxes. See Occupancy Geometry Generation for details on the subsequent conversion to ray segment lists. Time Complexity: The preprocessing stage (occupancy geometry generation) is linear with respect to the number of nodes in the occupancy-histogram tree. The rasterization stage is hardware-accelerated and efficient. The ray-casting stage is proportional to the number of non-empty samples, avoiding traversal of empty space. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the occupancy-histogram tree and the number of emitted bounding boxes. The ray segment lists are stored per pixel. Measured Performance: SparseLeap scales better to large, sparse data than standard octree empty space skipping. It optimizes both the number of look-ups into the data structure used for empty-space skipping and the number of samples along each viewing ray. Strengths: Agnostic of the underlying data structure (e.g., page-table hierarchies, octrees). Efficient for very large, sparse volumes with fine structures. Limitations: Requires hardware rasterization capabilities. Performance may degrade if the set of active objects changes frequently, requiring regeneration of bounding boxes. When to use: Large, sparse volume data (e.g., terabyte-sized microscopy volumes) where empty space skipping is critical and the active regions change frequently. When not to use: Small, dense volumes where standard traversal is sufficient, or hardware rasterization is not available. SparseLeap was introduced by Markus Hadwiger, Ali K Al-Awami, Johanna Beyer, and Hanspeter Pfister in 2017. It addresses the challenges of volume rendering for very high-resolution, large-size data, such as terabyte-sized microscopy volumes, which contain many fine and intricate structures. The method moves the major cost of empty space skipping out of the ray-casting stage and into a hybrid strategy that balances computational load between determining empty ray segments in a rasterization (object-order) stage and sampling non-empty volume data in the ray-casting (image-order) stage. name: Ray Segment List Generation
head: Rasterizing occupancy geometry for ray segments
body: Ray Segment List Generation converts the rasterized occupancy geometry of a volume into singly-linked lists of ray events per pixel, defining ray segments (intervals between events) with associated occupancy classes. It sets itself apart from hierarchical traversal methods by performing a sequential, non-hierarchical "traversal" where the occupancy class is embedded directly in the event types (entry/exit), eliminating the need for a stack to push and pop classes during parsing. Inputs: Occupancy geometry array (bounding boxes with front/back face flags and occupancy classes). Visibility order of the geometry. Volume bounding box (for initialization). Outputs: For each pixel: a singly-linked list of ray events. Each event contains Depth (1D parameter), EventType (entry/exit), and OccupancyClass (empty/non-empty/unknown). The list defines ray segments between consecutive events. Data Structures: Ray Event: A structure containing: depth: float, the 1D parameter position of the intersection with a bounding box face. eventtype: enum, ENTRY or EXIT. occclass: enum, EMPTY, NONEMPTY, or UNKNOWN. Ray Segment List: A singly-linked list of Ray Event nodes, initialized per pixel. Initialization: 1. For each pixel, initialize the ray segment list as a single segment with occupancy class UNKNOWN. 2. This segment starts at the volume bounding box front face position and ends at the back face position. 3. The list comprises two events: Event 1: eventtype=ENTRY, depth=frontfaceposition, occclass=UNKNOWN. Event 2: eventtype=EXIT, depth=backfaceposition, occclass=UNKNOWN. Rasterization Pass: 1. Rasterize the occupancy geometry array in a single rendering pass. 2. For each fragment generated, invoke a fragment shader. 3. Determine if the fragment resulted from a front face or back face rasterization to set the EventType (ENTRY or EXIT). 4. Create a new Ray Event for the fragment: depth: Intersection parameter. eventtype: Determined in step 3. occclass: If eventtype == ENTRY: Set to the occupancy class of the bounding box that generated the event. If eventtype == EXIT: Set to the occupancy class of the box's parent. Incremental Event Processing (Merging and Deletion): For each incoming event E{new}, access the tail of the current ray segment list. Let the last event in the list be E{last}. If E{last}.depth \neq E{new}.depth, append E{new} to the list. If E{last}.depth == E{new}.depth, apply the following rules to E{last} and E{new} (and potentially preceding events): 1. Merge Same Type: If E{last}.eventtype == E{new}.eventtype (both ENTRY or both EXIT): Delete E{last}. Replace E{last}'s position in the list with E{new} (or append E{new} if E{last} was the only one, effectively overwriting). The surviving event is E{new}, adopting its occclass. 2. Delete Exit-Entry Pair (Same Class): If E{last}.eventtype == EXIT and E{new}.eventtype == ENTRY: Let E{prev} be the event preceding E{last} in the list (if it exists). If E{new}.occclass == E{prev}.occclass (indicating consecutive segments of the same occupancy class): Delete both E{last} and E{new}. This merges the segment ending at E{last} and the segment starting at E{new} into one longer segment of class E{prev}.occclass. 3. Delete Entry-Exit Pair (Grazing): If E{last}.eventtype == ENTRY and E{new}.eventtype == EXIT: Delete both E{last} and E{new}, regardless of occupancy class. This handles grazing rays hitting an edge or corner, generating two events at the same depth. 4. Remove Short Empty Segments: Detect very short empty ray segments that cannot be merged because they precede a non-empty segment. Remove these segments to reduce depth complexity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class RayEvent: def init(self, depth, eventtype, occclass): self.depth = depth self.eventtype = eventtype self.occclass = occclass def processevent(raysegmentlist, newevent): """ Incrementally updates the ray segment list with a new event, applying merging and deletion rules for events at the same depth. """ if not raysegmentlist: raysegmentlist.append(newevent) return lastevent = raysegmentlist[-1] # If depths differ, simply append if lastevent.depth != newevent.depth: raysegmentlist.append(newevent) return # Depths are equal, apply rules prevevent = raysegmentlist[-2] if len(raysegmentlist) > 2 else None # Rule 1: Merge same type if lastevent.eventtype == newevent.eventtype: # Overwrite lastevent with newevent raysegmentlist[-1] = newevent return # Rule 2: Exit followed by Entry (same class) if lastevent.eventtype == "EXIT" and newevent.eventtype == "ENTRY": # Check if previous event exists and has same class as new event if prevevent is not None and prevevent.occclass == newevent.occclass: # Delete both lastevent and newevent raysegmentlist.pop() # Remove lastevent # newevent is not added return else: # Cannot merge, append newevent raysegmentlist.append(newevent) return # Rule 3: Entry followed by Exit (grazing) if lastevent.eventtype == "ENTRY" and newevent.eventtype == "EXIT": # Delete both raysegmentlist.pop() # Remove lastevent # newevent is not added return # Fallback: Append if no rule matched raysegmentlist.append(newevent) def generateraysegmentlists(occupancygeometry, volumebbox): """ Main function to generate ray segment lists for all pixels. """ # Initialize ray segment lists for all pixels raysegmentlists = {} for pixel in allpixels: # Default segment: UNKNOWN class, spanning volume bbox frontdepth = volumebbox.frontfacedepth(pixel) backdepth = volumebbox.backfacedepth(pixel) evententry = RayEvent(depth=frontdepth, eventtype="ENTRY", occclass="UNKNOWN") eventexit = RayEvent(depth=backdepth, eventtype="EXIT", occclass="UNKNOWN") raysegmentlists[pixel] = [evententry, eventexit] # Rasterize occupancy geometry # Note: Exact rasterization loop details are not provided in the sources for fragment in rasterize(occupancygeometry): pixel = fragment.pixel raysegmentlist = raysegmentlists[pixel] # Determine event type from face flag if fragment.isfrontface: eventtype = "ENTRY" else: eventtype = "EXIT" # Determine occupancy class if eventtype == "ENTRY": occclass = fragment.boundingbox.occupancyclass else: # EXIT occclass = fragment.boundingbox.parent.occupancyclass newevent = RayEvent(depth=fragment.depth, eventtype=eventtype, occclass=occclass) # Process incrementally processevent(raysegmentlist, newevent) return raysegmentlists Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grazing Rays: Rays hitting box edges/corners generate Entry/Exit pairs at the same depth. These must be deleted to avoid spurious segments. Short Empty Segments: Empty segments preceding non-empty segments that are too short to merge must be explicitly detected and removed to reduce depth complexity. Parent Class for Exit: Correctly identifying the parent box's occupancy class for exit events is critical for the merging logic. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of fragments generated during rasterization, as each fragment triggers an incremental update to the ray segment list tail. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of ray events per pixel. Strengths: Enables sequential, non-hierarchical traversal of the occupancy histogram tree without a stack, simplifying the ray-casting stage. Limitations: Performance depends on the efficiency of the fragment shader and the resulting depth complexity of the lists. Ray Segment List Generation is part of the SparseLeap algorithm for efficient empty space skipping in large-scale volume rendering. It was introduced in the paper "SparseLeap: Efficient Empty Space Skipping for Large-Scale Volume Rendering" (2018). The method builds on the concept of lazy evaluation and occupancy histogram trees, where geometry is generated on-the-fly. name: Texture Box Approximation
head: Li and Kaufman Texture Box Approximation
body: Texture Box Approximation is a method for accelerating volume rendering by approximating the volume data with a set of bounding boxes, called texture boxes, which are rasterized to efficiently clip empty space from the rendering pipeline. It differs from level-of-detail methods that rasterize lower-resolution blocks by focusing on spatial occupancy to discard empty regions entirely before fragment shader execution. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset; a hierarchical structure (e.g., octree or grid) defining leaf nodes; camera parameters. Outputs: A 2D image with empty space skipped. Data Structures: Texture Box: A 3D bounding box defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). Hierarchy: A tree where leaf nodes correspond to texture boxes. Each leaf node contains a reference to the volume data subset it bounds. Steps: 1. Construct Hierarchy: Build a hierarchical data structure (e.g., octree) over the volume data. Each leaf node represents a sub-volume. 2. Define Texture Boxes: For each leaf node, compute its 3D bounding box in world or view space. This box is the "texture box". 3. Rasterize Bounding Geometry: Project the 3D texture boxes onto the 2D screen. Rasterize these projected boxes using standard hardware rasterization. 4. Clip Empty Space: The rasterization process inherently clips pixels outside the projected boxes. Only pixels covered by at least one texture box are processed by the fragment shader. 5. Render Volume: For each covered pixel, sample the volume data within the corresponding texture box and compute the final color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def textureboxapproximation(volumedata, hierarchy, camera): # 1. Construct hierarchy (assumed pre-built) # hierarchy.leaves contains leaf nodes # 2. Define texture boxes for each leaf textureboxes = [] for leaf in hierarchy.leaves: # Compute 3D bounding box of the leaf's volume data box = compute3dboundingbox(leaf.volumedata) # Project to screen space screenbox = projecttoscreen(box, camera) textureboxes.append(screenbox) # 3. Rasterize bounding geometry # Hardware rasterizer clips pixels outside screenbox # Only pixels inside screenbox are sent to fragment shader # 4. Render volume for covered pixels for pixel in coveredpixels: # Find the texture box covering this pixel box = findcoveringbox(pixel, textureboxes) # Sample volume data within the box color = samplevolume(volumedata, box, pixel, camera) return color Parameters: Hierarchy Type: Not given in the sources. name: Min-Max Block Culling
head: Active block culling, Min-Max Bricks, Min-max blocks, Object-Order Empty Space Skipping (Min-Max Bricks)
body: Min-Max Block Culling is an object-order empty space skipping technique that reduces the number of volume samples by culling transparent or irrelevant regions before raycasting begins. It differs from its siblings by performing culling during the rasterization setup phase using precomputed block statistics, rather than during ray traversal or via bounding geometry rasterization. Unlike Early Shader Termination, which stops rays dynamically during compositing, this method prevents rays from entering empty blocks entirely. Unlike Rasterizing Bounding Geometry for Empty Space Skipping, it relies on scalar block bounds rather than polygonal approximations. Inputs: Volume dataset discretized into blocks (bricks) of fixed size. Transfer function or isovalue defining the rendering range. Camera parameters for ray generation. Outputs: A set of active blocks whose front and back faces are rasterized to initiate rays. Final composited image. Data Structures: Block Min-Max Values: For each block Bi, store two scalar values: mini and maxi. These represent the minimum and maximum scalar values contained within the block's voxel grid. Layout: A 1D array or 3D texture where each entry corresponds to a block, containing two floats (or fixed-point values). Size: One entry per block. Steps: 1. Precompute Block Statistics: Calculate mini and maxi for every block in the volume. 2. Cull Blocks: For each block Bi, check if its value range [mini, maxi] intersects the rendering range defined by the transfer function or isovalue. If the block is outside the range (e.g., maxi < \text{isovalue} or mini > \text{isovalue} for isosurface rendering), mark it as culled. If the block intersects the range, mark it as active. 3. Rasterize Active Blocks: For each active block, rasterize its front and back faces against the screen. This generates a coverage mask indicating which screen pixels have rays entering the block. Note: If the viewpoint is inside the volume, near clipping planes may be used to fill holes. 4. Ray Initialization: For each pixel covered by an active block's front face, initialize a ray starting at the intersection point with the front face. 5. Raycasting and Termination: Cast rays through the active blocks. Terminate the ray when full opacity is reached. Terminate the ray when the back face of the block is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeblockbounds(volume, blocksize): bounds = [] nx, ny, nz = len(volume[0][0]), len(volume[0]), len(volume) for z in range(0, nz, blocksize): for y in range(0, ny, blocksize): for x in range(0, nx, blocksize): minv, maxv = float('inf'), float('-inf') for dz in range(blocksize): for dy in range(blocksize): for dx in range(blocksize): if z+dz < nz and y+dy < ny and x+dx < nx: v = volume[z+dz][y+dy][x+dx] if v < minv: minv = v if v > maxv: maxv = v bounds.append((minv, maxv)) return bounds def cullblocks(bounds, isovalue): return [i for i, (minv, maxv) in enumerate(bounds) if minv <= isovalue <= maxv] def renderminmaxculling(volume, blocksize, isovalue, resx, resy): bounds = computeblockbounds(volume, blocksize) activeindices = cullblocks(bounds, isovalue) image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(resy)] # Rasterize active blocks to generate coverage mask coverage = [[False] resx for in range(resy)] for idx in activeindices: # Determine block screen bounds (simplified projection) bx = (idx % (len(volume[0][0]) // blocksize)) blocksize by = ((idx // (len(volume[0][0]) // blocksize)) % (len(volume[0]) // blocksize)) blocksize bz = (idx // ((len(volume[0][0]) // blocksize) (len(volume[0]) // blocksize))) blocksize # Project block to screen coordinates minpx, maxpx = int(bx / len(volume[0][0]) resx), int((bx + blocksize) / len(volume[0][0]) resx) minpy, maxpy = int(by / len(volume[0]) resy), int((by + blocksize) / len(volume[0]) resy) for py in range(minpy, maxpy): for px in range(minpx, maxpx): if 0 <= py < resy and 0 <= px < resx: coverage[py][px] = True for py in range(resy): for px in range(resx): if not coverage[py][px]: continue # Start ray at front face (z=0) currentz = 0.0 opacity = 0.0 step = 1.0 / resy # Terminate when back face (z=1.0) or full opacity reached while currentz < 1.0 and opacity < 1.0: vz = int(currentz len(volume)) if vz < len(volume): sample = volume[vz][int(py)][int(px)] alpha = 1.0 if sample == isovalue else 0.0 opacity += alpha (1.0 - opacity) currentz += step if opacity >= 1.0: image[py][px] = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] return image Parameters: Block Size: Not given in the sources. Isovalue/Transfer Function: Depends on the dataset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incomplete Skipping: This method does not skip all empty space, only the empty blocks culled during the rasterization setup phase. Viewpoint Inside Volume: If the camera is inside the volume, near clipping planes must be used to fill holes in the ray coverage. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for min-max values for each block, O(B). Strengths: Reduces sample count by skipping entire blocks that are transparent. Simple to implement as it relies on standard rasterization. Limitations: Does not skip all empty space; internal block emptiness is not exploited. When to Use: When the volume has large transparent regions that can be grouped into blocks. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in GPU-based volume raycasting research, specifically in the work of Markus Hadwiger and others at VRVIS Research Center, Vienna, Austria. The technique is described in the context of advanced illumination techniques for GPU-based volume raycasting. It builds on image-based ray setup and allows for viewpoint inside the volume. name: Ray Casting with Depth/Alpha Test for Empty Space Skipping
head: Empty Space Skipping via OpenGL Tests, Ray Casting using Alpha and Depth Tests, Texture Slab Volume Rendering with GPU-based Acceleration, Westermann & Sevenich Empty Space Skipping, Westermann & Sevenich Technique
body: This method accelerates ray-based volume rendering by using the graphics hardware's depth buffer and alpha test to determine the entry and exit points of the volume along each pixel's ray, thereby skipping sampling in empty space. Unlike its parent method, which relies on a pre-computed or dynamically updated secondary data structure (like an octree) to query occupancy, this technique constructs the acceleration structure (Slab Silhouette Maps) on the fly during the rendering pass using standard OpenGL state. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Space Leaping by avoiding CPU-side preprocessing and hierarchical traversal logic, instead leveraging hardware z-occlusion culling to identify active segments. The method operates in three main phases: pre-processing (gradient calculation), acceleration structure generation (Slab Silhouette Maps), and ray casting with skipping. Input: A 3D volume dataset (scalar values), a transfer function mapping scalars to color and opacity, and a camera configuration (view and projection matrices). Output: A 2D image (framebuffer) with the composited volume. 1. Volume Data: Stored in CPU memory or GPU texture memory. 2. Gradient Volume: Pre-computed gradients for each voxel, stored in CPU memory or a GPU texture (typically RGB format for normal vectors). 3. Texture Slabs: The 3D volume is sliced into 2D textures. Slices are grouped into "slabs" to reduce the number of rendering passes. 4. Depth Buffer: Used to store the near and far intersection distances. It is initialized and queried in two separate passes. 5. Slab Silhouette Maps (SSM): Implicitly stored in the depth buffer. These maps identify empty spaces and terminated rays by storing the depth values of the first and last visible fragments of each slab. 1. Pre-compute Gradients and Illumination (CPU): Calculate the gradient for each volume element using central differences. Perform illumination and shading calculations based on the lighting model and store the results in main memory or a texture. Note: This step is performed once on the CPU, unlike methods that compute lighting per-sample on the GPU. 2. Prepare Textures and Display Lists: For each axis (X, Y, Z), create 2D textures for planes parallel to that axis. Load these textures into GPU memory. Create display lists for front-to-back and back-to-front rendering orders. 3. Determine Rendering Axis: Determine the object axis with the smallest angle to the projection plane. Select the farthest texture from the camera in the corresponding set. Rotate the camera and draw the textures starting from the selected one. 4. Generate Slab Silhouette Maps (SSM) via Two Passes: The goal is to find the near (P) and far (Q) intersection points of the ray with the volume. Pass 1 (Find Near Point): Initialize the depth buffer to 1.0 (maximum value). Set depth write criterion to GLLESS. Enable the Alpha Test with GLGREATER and a reference value > 0 (e.g., 0.001) to discard fragments with zero opacity. Render the volume slabs from front to back. The depth buffer now contains the distances of the closest significant fragments to the projection plane for each pixel. Pass 2 (Find Far Point): Initialize the depth buffer to 0.0 (minimum value). Set depth write criterion to GLGREATER. Keep Alpha Test enabled (GLGREATER, ref > 0). Render the volume slabs from back to front (or front to back, depending on implementation, but the logic captures the farthest visible fragment due to GLGREATER and initialization). The depth buffer now contains the distances of the farthest significant fragments. 5. Coordinate Transformation: The depth buffer stores values in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC), range [0, 1]. Transform these NDC coordinates to world coordinates to get the ray origin P and ray end Q. For a pixel with screen coordinates (xs, ys, zs), the world coordinates (x, y, z, w) are calculated as: \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ w \end{bmatrix} = (P M)^{-1} V \begin{bmatrix} xs \\ ys \\ zs \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} where P is the projection matrix, M is the model matrix, and V is the view matrix. The near point P{world} corresponds to the depth from Pass 1, and the far point Q{world} corresponds to the depth from Pass 2. 6. Ray Casting with Empty Space Skipping: For each pixel, cast a ray between P and Q. Sample the volume only within the interval [P, Q]. Use parametric equations for t \in [0, 1]: \begin{aligned} X(t) &= Px + (Qx - Px)t \\ Y(t) &= Py + (Qy - Py)t \\ Z(t) &= Pz + (Qz - Pz)t \end{aligned} The increment in t is determined by the number of samples n per ray (e.g., \Delta t = 1/n). Composite the samples using the standard volume rendering integral, but restricted to the active segment: L(x) = \int{xA'}^{xB'} \left[ e^{-\int{xA'}^{x00} \phit(x')dx'} \epsilon(x00) dx00 \right] where xA' and xB' are the near and far points, \phit is the extinction coefficient, and \epsilon is the color. Draw the final color to the framebuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumewithdepthalphaskip(volume, transferfunction, camera): """ Renders a volume using Westermann & Sevenich's empty space skipping technique. """ # 1. Pre-compute gradients and illumination on CPU gradients = computecentraldifferencegradients(volume) illuminatedvolume = applylightingmodel(volume, gradients, transferfunction) # 2. Prepare 2D texture slabs slabs = createtextureslabs(illuminatedvolume) # 3. Determine rendering axis and order axis = getaxiswithsmallestangletoprojectionplane(camera) slaborder = getsortedslabs(slabs, axis, camera) # 4. Pass 1: Find Near Points (SSM) glcleardepth(1.0) gldepthfunc(GLLESS) glenable(GLALPHATEST) glalphafunc(GLGREATER, 0.001) # Discard zero opacity gldepthmask(GLTRUE) for slab in slaborder: # Front to back glbindtexture(slab) gldrawslab(slab) neardepthbuffer = glreaddepthbuffer() # 5. Pass 2: Find Far Points (SSM) glcleardepth(0.0) gldepthfunc(GLGREATER) # Alpha test remains enabled for slab in reversed(slaborder): # Back to front glbindtexture(slab) gldrawslab(slab) fardepthbuffer = glreaddepthbuffer() # 6. Ray Casting imagewidth, imageheight = getframebuffersize() projectionmatrix = camera.projectionmatrix modelmatrix = camera.modelmatrix viewmatrix = camera.viewmatrix invpm = inverse(projectionmatrix modelmatrix) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Get NDC depths znearndc = neardepthbuffer[y, x] zfarndc = fardepthbuffer[y, x] # Skip if no volume intersection (e.g., if depth is default or invalid) if znearndc == 1.0 or zfarndc == 0.0: continue # Transform NDC to World Coordinates # NDC x,y are in [-1, 1], z in [0, 1] # Assuming standard OpenGL viewport mapping ndcx = (2.0 x / imagewidth) - 1.0 ndcy = (2.0 y / imageheight) - 1.0 # Reconstruct world coordinates for near point nearworld = transformndctoworld(ndcx, ndcy, znearndc, invpm, viewmatrix) # Reconstruct world coordinates for far point farworld = transformndctoworld(ndcx, ndcy, zfarndc, invpm, viewmatrix) # Ray Casting between nearworld and farworld color = compositeray(nearworld, farworld, volume, transferfunction) setframebufferpixel(x, y, color) def transformndctoworld(ndcx, ndcy, ndcz, invpm, viewmatrix): """ Transforms NDC coordinates to world coordinates. Note: The exact transformation depends on the specific OpenGL pipeline state. This is a simplified representation of the matrix math described in. """ # Homogeneous NDC coordinate ndccoord = [ndcx, ndcy, ndcz, 1.0] # Apply inverse projection and model view to get view space, then inverse view to get world # The source formula: [x,y,z,w] = (PM)^-1 V [xs, ys, zs, 1] # Here xs,ys,zs are assumed to be the NDC coords if V is identity or handled separately. # A more robust implementation would unproject from NDC to World directly. # Simplified: Unproject from NDC to World # This step requires careful handling of the specific coordinate system conventions. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a helper function exists that performs # the inverse projection and view transformations correctly. return unproject(ndcx, ndcy, ndcz, invpm, viewmatrix) def compositeray(origin, end, volume, transferfunction): """ Standard front-to-back compositing for the ray segment [origin, end]. """ alpha = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Calculate step size raylength = distance(origin, end) numsamples = 100 # Or based on resolution step = raylength / numsamples currentpos = origin for i in range(numsamples): # Sample volume at currentpos scalar = samplevolume(currentpos, volume) rgba = transferfunction(scalar) # Front-to-back compositing alpha += (1.0 - alpha) rgba.alpha color += rgba.color rgba.alpha (1.0 - (alpha - rgba.alpha)) # Simplified approximation if alpha >= 0.99: # Early ray termination break currentpos += normalize(end - origin) step return color Alpha Test Reference Value: > 0 (e.g., 0.001) to discard fully transparent fragments. Depth Buffer Initialization: 1.0 for near point pass, 0.0 for far point pass. Number of Samples (n): Determined by desired image quality and ray length. Typical values range from 50 to 200 per ray segment. Coordinate System Mismatch: The depth buffer uses NDC [0, 1], while ray casting requires local/world coordinates. A transformation is necessary. High Data Dispersion: If the volume has high dispersion (many small isolated structures), the technique only skips external empty space. The ray length with skipping may be similar to the naive ray length, reducing effectiveness. Precision: Floating-point precision in the depth buffer can affect the accuracy of the near/far points, especially for thin structures. Uses external polygonal meshes instead of alpha/depth tests to define sampling intervals. Uses camera-facing quads and depth tests to cull occluded primitives before ray marching. Time Complexity: The acceleration structure generation (SSM) is very small compared to total rendering time. The ray casting time is reduced to almost a quarter of a naive ray caster. Measured Performance: 3 to 4 times faster than naive ray casting when using alpha and depth tests. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume, gradients, and 2D texture slabs. No additional hierarchical data structure (like an octree) is needed on the CPU. Strengths: No CPU-side preprocessing required; leverages hardware z-occlusion culling; simple implementation using standard OpenGL features. Limitations: Lighting is pre-computed on the CPU, making dynamic lighting difficult. Effectiveness degrades with high data dispersion. Limited to skipping external empty space; internal holes are not skipped. The method was introduced by Westermann & Sevenich in [WS01]. It is a hybrid volume rendering technique that uses 2D textures and OpenGL alpha/depth tests to discard non-contributing intervals of the volume rendering integral. It differs from Engel, Kraus & Ertl's method by performing illumination calculation on the CPU in the initial phase, whereas Engel's method does it on the GPU. name: Polygon Assisted Ray Casting
head: Empty Space Skipping via Volumetric Clipping, Empty space skipping via the volumetric clipping, Hybrid Space Leaping with Graphics Hardware, PARC, Volumetric clipping
body: Polygon Assisted Ray Casting (PARC) is an acceleration technique for volumetric ray tracing that uses graphics hardware to determine the start and end points of ray segments intersecting the volume, thereby skipping empty space. Unlike its parent method, which relies on the volume's own alpha and depth tests, PARC approximates the volume with an external polygonal mesh to define valid sampling intervals. This approach typically reduces the computation of primary rays by a factor of four. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volumetric dataset, a polygonal mesh that completely encloses all non-transparent or relevant regions of the volume, camera position and orientation, and light source positions for shadow rays. Output: A rendered image where ray sampling is restricted to segments defined by the mesh intersections. Data Structures Bounding Mesh: A polyhedral representation of the volume that must completely contain the actual volumetric objects. It may be non-convex. Distance Buffers: Two OpenGL frame buffers storing distances from the viewpoint to the mesh front and back faces. Closest-Distance Buffer: Stores the nearest intersection distance for each pixel. Farthest-Distance Buffer: Stores the farthest intersection distance for each pixel. Layout: These buffers store up to 4 ray path segments per pixel, allowing the representation of non-convex meshes with multiple entry and exit points. Steps 1. Mesh Creation: Create a polygonal representation that completely contains or encloses all important regions in the volume. 2. Buffer Initialization: Prepare two distance buffers to store the closest and farthest distances. 3. Projection (Closest and Farthest): Render the bounding mesh into the closest-distance buffer using a standard "less than" depth test, and into the farthest-distance buffer using a "greater than" depth test. 4. Shader Execution: During rendering, a specific shader program calculates the distance between the observer and the fragment position on the mesh surface for each pixel. 5. Ray Casting: For each pixel, retrieve the stored distances from the buffers. If no Z-buffer information exists for a pixel, skip intersection calculations for that ray. Use the stored distances to clip the rays, defining the segments of the ray path to be traversed. Perform volumetric ray casting only within these clipped segments. 6. Secondary Rays: For shadow rays from point and directional lights, repeat the projection steps from each light location or direction to determine occlusion. Use uniform space subdivision and bounding boxes to optimize secondary rays. 7. Refinement: The initial PARC image can be refined by continuing to follow PARC rays intersecting data according to a full volumetric ray tracing algorithm to generate shadows, reflections, and transparency. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polygonassistedraycasting(volume, mesh, camera, lightsources): # Initialize distance buffers: 2D array of lists, max 4 segments per pixel closestbuffer = [[[] for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] farthestbuffer = [[[] for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] # Project mesh to fill buffers using depth tests for face in mesh.faces: for pixel in projectfacetoscreen(face, camera): dist = distance(camera.origin, pixel.position) addtobuffer(closestbuffer, pixel.x, pixel.y, dist, min) addtobuffer(farthestbuffer, pixel.x, pixel.y, dist, max) # Ray Casting image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height camera.width)] for y in range(camera.height): for x in range(camera.width): distsclose = closestbuffer[y][x] distsfar = farthestbuffer[y][x] if not distsclose or not distsfar: continue rayorigin = camera.origin raydirection = normalize(pixel.position - camera.origin) segments = clipraysegments(rayorigin, raydirection, distsclose, distsfar) for seg in segments: # Source does not specify the volumetric ray casting algorithm itself color = volumetricraycastsegment(volume, rayorigin, seg.start, seg.end, raydirection) image[y camera.width + x] = color # Secondary Rays (Shadows) for light in lightsources: shadowclose = [[[] for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] shadowfar = [[[] for in range(camera.width)] for in range(camera.height)] for face in mesh.faces: for pixel in projectfacetoscreen(face, light): dist = distance(light.origin, pixel.position) addtobuffer(shadowclose, pixel.x, pixel.y, dist, min) addtobuffer(shadowfar, pixel.x, pixel.y, dist, max) # Use shadow buffers to determine occlusion for secondary rays pass return image def addtobuffer(buffer, x, y, dist, op): if len(buffer[y][x]) >= 4: return if op == min: if not buffer[y][x] or dist < min(buffer[y][x]): buffer[y][x].append(dist) elif op == max: if not buffer[y][x] or dist > max(buffer[y][x]): buffer[y][x].append(dist) Parameters Mesh Resolution: Not given in the sources. Must be coarse enough for fast rendering but fine enough to bound the volume accurately. Segments per Pixel: Up to 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Mesh Containment: The polygonal model must completely contain the actual volumetric objects; otherwise, rays may sample empty space or miss data. Non-Convexity: Standard Z-buffering only captures one segment. To handle non-convex meshes, the implementation must support multiple segments per pixel (up to 4). Performance: PARC typically reduces the computation of primary rays by a factor of four. Hardware Dependency: Requires graphics hardware capable of Z-buffering and texture rendering (OpenGL). Memory: Requires additional memory for the distance buffers (two buffers per view/light). Strengths: Significant speedup for primary rays; allows interactive manipulation of the bounding mesh. Limitations: Requires maintaining a separate polygonal representation; less effective if the volume is sparse or the mesh is complex. When to Use: When primary ray computation is the bottleneck and a suitable bounding mesh can be created. When Not to Use: When the volume is dense or the bounding mesh is too complex to render efficiently. Origin: Introduced by Sobierajski in 1995. History: Part of the VolVis volume visualization system, which uses a multi-algorithm progressive refinement approach. Usage: Used in VolVis after user interaction with a polyhedral representation to produce a ray-cast image. name: Occlusion Frustums
head: Occlusion volumes, Proxy geometry via first-hit image
body: Occlusion Frustums is an empty space skipping optimization for volume raycasting that reduces costly volume texture fetches by generating proxy geometry based on visibility information from previous frames. Unlike Polygon Assisted Ray Casting, which requires complex, data-dependent preprocessing and simplification, this method constructs simple pyramidal frustums on-the-fly using a first-hit image, allowing instant adaptation to transfer function changes without invalidation. It differs from point-based space leaping by operating in object space, eliminating the need for reprojection during view changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A "first-hit image" from the previous frame's rendering pass. This image contains the position of the first non-empty voxel per ray in its color channels and marks rays hitting only empty voxels in its alpha channel. Output: A set of triangle primitives (proxy geometry) representing occlusion frustums, which are rendered to a depth buffer to skip ray traversal in empty regions. Data Structures: First-Hit Image: A 2D texture where each pixel (u, v) corresponds to a ray. The RGB values encode the 3D position of the first hit voxel. The alpha value indicates emptiness. Occlusion Block: A grouping of pixels (typically 4 \times 4) in the first-hit image. If all pixels in a block are empty, the block is considered empty. Parameters: Block Size: The dimension of the pixel grid grouping. Typical value: 4 \times 4. This balances accuracy against the complexity of the generated geometry. Steps: 1. Generate First-Hit Image: During the previous frame's raycasting, render a first-hit image. For each ray, if a non-empty voxel is hit, store its 3D position in the pixel color. If the ray hits only empty space, mark the pixel alpha as empty. 2. Identify Empty Blocks: Divide the first-hit image into blocks of size B \times B (e.g., 4 \times 4). A block is marked as empty if all constituent pixels indicate empty voxels. 3. Construct Frustum Geometry: For each non-empty block (or individual pixel if block size is 1), construct a quadrilateral pyramidal occlusion frustum: Top Base: A quadrilateral located at the 3D position of the first-hit voxel corresponding to the block. Extrusion: Extrude the top base along projectors extending from the Center of Projection (COP) through the vertices of the top base quad. Depth Extent: Extend the frustum such that its bottom base lies outside the dataset's bounding box. Clipping: Clip the frustum against the dataset's bounding box (unit cube [0,1]^2 in ray parameter space) to ensure it fits within the hardware-clamped color range [0,1]. Enlargement: Slightly enlarge the clipped frustum and move it towards the camera to ensure all potentially non-empty voxels are covered. 4. Handle New Objects: To prevent skipping objects that enter the view from outside the previous frame's view frustum, subtract the previous frame's view frustum from an initial cube proxy geometry (which encloses all voxels) and add this resulting geometry to the set of occlusion frustums. 5. Render Proxy Geometry: Render the constructed frustums using a fragment shader that assigns vertex positions as fragment colors. The z-buffer handles overlapping frustums. 6. Raycasting Skip: During the current frame's raycasting, use the rendered proxy geometry to determine if a ray passes through empty space. If a ray intersects the proxy geometry, it skips sampling in that region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateocclusionfrustums(firsthitimage, blocksize=4): """ Generates proxy geometry from a first-hit image. firsthitimage: 2D array of (color, alpha) tuples. Returns: List of triangle primitives. """ frustums = [] height, width = firsthitimage.shape # Iterate over blocks for y in range(0, height, blocksize): for x in range(0, width, blocksize): # Check if block is empty isempty = True hitpos = None for dy in range(blocksize): for dx in range(blocksize): if y + dy < height and x + dx < width: color, alpha = firsthitimage[y + dy, x + dx] if alpha is not empty: # Alpha indicates emptiness isempty = False hitpos = color # Use first non-empty hit for block break if not isempty: break if not isempty: # Construct frustum for this block frustum = buildfrustum(hitpos, blocksize, x, y, width, height) frustums.append(frustum) # Add geometry for new objects (outside previous view frustum) newobjectgeometry = subtractpreviousviewfrustumfrominitialcube() frustums.extend(newobjectgeometry) return frustums def buildfrustum(hitpos, blocksize, blockx, blocky, imgwidth, imgheight): """ Constructs a clipped, enlarged occlusion frustum. hitpos: 3D position of the first hit voxel. """ # 1. Define top base quad at hitpos # Map block coordinates to 3D space relative to hitpos # Assuming hitpos is the center or representative point of the block topquad = getquadverticesatposition(hitpos, blocksize) # 2. Extrude along projectors from Center of Projection (COP) # COP is typically (0,0,0) in view space or defined by camera cop = getcenterofprojection() bottomquad = [] for vertex in topquad: # Ray from COP through vertex direction = normalize(vertex - cop) # Extrude far enough to go outside bounding box # Bounding box is [0,1]^3 in object space or similar # Extend until it exceeds max dimension extendedvertex = cop + direction largedistance bottomquad.append(extendedvertex) # 3. Clip against dataset bounding box # The frustum must fit in [0,1]^2 for ray parameter encoding clippedfrustum = clipfrustumagainstbbox(topquad, bottomquad, bbox) # 4. Enlarge and move towards camera enlargedfrustum = enlargeandshifttowardscamera(clippedfrustum) # 5. Convert to triangles triangles = quadtotriangles(enlargedfrustum) return triangles def subtractpreviousviewfrustumfrominitialcube(): """ Generates geometry for objects entering from outside the previous view. """ # Initial cube proxy geometry encloses all voxels initialcube = getboundingboxcube() previousviewfrustum = getpreviousframeviewfrustum() # Subtract previous view frustum from initial cube # This results in geometry representing regions outside the previous view newobjectgeo = booleansubtract(initialcube, previousviewfrustum) return newobjectgeo Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Undersampling: If voxels are missed due to undersampling, parts of the volume may be incorrectly identified as empty and permanently removed from the proxy geometry. This is mitigated by constant refreshing of the geometry and using occlusion blocks (all voxels in a block must be missed). Hardware Clamping: Geometry reaching outside the unit cube [0,1]^2 leads to wrong ray directions because hardware clamps colors to [0,1]. The frustum must be closed from all sides and clipped against the bounding box. New Objects: Objects appearing outside the previous view frustum are skipped if not handled. This is addressed by adding the geometry resulting from subtracting the previous view frustum from the initial cube proxy. Non-continuous View Changes: Unlike point-based methods, this technique works for non-continuous view changes and introduces no image artifacts. Time Complexity: The runtime is mainly dependent on the resulting 2D image resolution, not the 3D data set resolution. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Tested on Intel Core 2 Duo E6300 CPU and NVIDIA GeForce 8800 GT GPU. Sparse data sets (e.g., 'vertebra'): Speedup of 1.36x. Dense data sets (e.g., 'vmhead (skin)'): Speedup of 0.77x (slowdown) due to overhead. The optimization is most useful for high-resolution data sets and high-quality rendering where sampling costs are high. Scaling: Scales well to large viewport sizes (e.g., 1024^2), producing greater speed-ups than for smaller viewports (512^2) for some data sets. Strengths: No preprocessing required; adapts instantly to transfer function changes; works for non-continuous view changes; no image artifacts. Limitations: Overhead for dense data sets; potential for undersampling errors (mitigated by refresh rate and block size). Origin: Introduced by J. Mensmann, T. Ropinski, and K. Hinrichs in 2008. Paper: "Accelerating Volume Raycasting using Occlusion Frustums". History: Developed as a novel approach to empty space leaping to reduce costly volume texture fetches during ray traversal. It was implemented in OpenGL/GLSL and integrated into the Voreen volume rendering framework. Comparison: Unlike PARC [ASK92], it does not use a closely-fitted, data-dependent proxy geometry requiring simplification. Unlike point-based space leaping, no reprojection is necessary.
