name: Empty Space Map Generation
head: Empty Space Skipping Map, Ray Marching with Empty Space Map, Visibility Map Generation
body: Empty Space Map Generation is a preprocessing technique that creates a boolean map indicating which voxels in a scalar field contain no visible geometry, allowing ray marching to skip empty regions. It reduces the number of density samples and transfer function evaluations by jumping over contiguous blocks of empty space. Unlike Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage), which computes distances to occupied blocks, this method uses a binary occupancy check based on a transfer function threshold. Inputs: Scalar field data: A 3D array of density values with dimensions W \times H \times D. Transfer function: A function TF(v) that maps a scalar value v to a density or opacity value. Threshold: A tolerance value T. If any vertex of a voxel has a transfer function density > T, the voxel is considered non-empty. Outputs: Empty Space Map: A boolean array of size (W-1) \times (H-1) \times (D-1), where each element indicates if the corresponding voxel is empty. Data Structures: emptyspacemap: A flat boolean array indexed by a field offset function field->Offset(i, j, k). Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Map Generation): 1. Loop over all voxel indices (i, j, k) from 0 to \text{dims}[\text{axis}]-2 for each dimension. 2. For each voxel, evaluate the transfer function at its 8 vertices. 3. Compute the vertex index as v = vi + vj \times 2 + vk \times 4, where vi, vj, vk \in \{0, 1\}. 4. Retrieve the scalar value at (i + vi, j + vj, k + vk) and evaluate its density d = TF(\text{scalar}). 5. Mark the voxel as empty if all 8 vertices have d \le T; otherwise mark it as non-empty. 6. Store the result: emptyspacemap[field->Offset(i, j, k)] = isempty. 2. Ray Marching (Skipping): 1. Compute the current 3D voxel indices (vi, vj, vk) from the current ray position p. 2. Check if the current voxel is marked as empty in emptyspacemap using the computed indices and field offset. 3. If the voxel is empty: a. Compute the voxel minimum V{\min} and maximum V{\max} points in world space. b. Compute the intersection interval [t{\text{enter}}, t{\text{exit}}] of the ray with the voxel bounding box. c. Advance the ray parameter t by the maximum of (t{\text{exit}} - t) and marchingdelta to skip the empty voxel. d. Update the ray position p = O + t \cdot D and recompute voxel indices. e. Repeat the check for the new voxel. 4. If the voxel is not empty, proceed with standard ray marching sampling within the voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generateemptyspacemap(field, transferfunction, threshold, width, height, depth): """Generates a boolean map indicating empty voxels based on a transfer function threshold.""" w, h, d = width - 1, height - 1, depth - 1 emptyspacemap = [False] (w h d) for i in range(w): for j in range(h): for k in range(d): isempty = True # Check all 8 vertices of the voxel (i, j, k) for vi in range(2): for vj in range(2): for vk in range(2): # Global coordinates of the vertex x, y, z = i + vi, j + vj, k + vk # Evaluate transfer function density density = transferfunction(field[x][y][z]) # If any vertex exceeds threshold, voxel is not empty if density > threshold: isempty = False break if not isempty: break if not isempty: break # Store using a flat offset (equivalent to field->Offset(i, j, k)) # Implementation of field->Offset depends on memory layout; row-major assumed here. emptyspacemap[i + j w + k w h] = isempty return emptyspacemap def raymarchskip(rayorigin, raydirection, emptyspacemap, voxelorigin, voxelsize, marchingdelta, mapw, maph, mapd): """Advances a ray through empty space using the precomputed map.""" t = 0.0 # Convert ray origin to voxel coordinates vi = math.floor((rayorigin[0] - voxelorigin[0]) / voxelsize) vj = math.floor((rayorigin[1] - voxelorigin[1]) / voxelsize) vk = math.floor((rayorigin[2] - voxelorigin[2]) / voxelsize) while True: # Clamp indices to map bounds vi = max(0, min(vi, mapw - 1)) vj = max(0, min(vj, maph - 1)) vk = max(0, min(vk, mapd - 1)) if emptyspacemap[vi + vj mapw + vk mapw maph]: # Compute voxel bounds in world space vmin = [voxelorigin[0] + vi voxelsize, voxelorigin[1] + vj voxelsize, voxelorigin[2] + vk voxelsize] vmax = [voxelorigin[0] + (vi + 1) voxelsize, voxelorigin[1] + (vj + 1) voxelsize, voxelorigin[2] + (vk + 1) voxelsize] # Compute intersection interval [tenter, texit] of ray with voxel bounding box tenter = -math.inf texit = math.inf for axis in range(3): if raydirection[axis] == 0: if rayorigin[axis] < vmin[axis] or rayorigin[axis] > vmax[axis]: return rayorigin + [raydirection[0]t, raydirection[1]t, raydirection[2]t] else: t1 = (vmin[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) / raydirection[axis] t2 = (vmax[axis] - rayorigin[axis]) / raydirection[axis] tenter = max(tenter, min(t1, t2)) texit = min(texit, max(t1, t2)) if tenter > texit: return rayorigin + [raydirection[0]t, raydirection[1]t, raydirection[2]t] # Advance t: max(texit - t, marchingdelta) to ensure progress (matches FMax clamping) t = t + max(texit - t, marchingdelta) # Update ray position and recompute voxel indices raypos = [rayorigin[0] + raydirection[0]t, rayorigin[1] + raydirection[1]t, rayorigin[2] + raydirection[2]t] vi = math.floor((raypos[0] - voxelorigin[0]) / voxelsize) vj = math.floor((raypos[1] - voxelorigin[1]) / voxelsize) vk = math.floor((raypos[2] - voxelorigin[2]) / voxelsize) else: break return raypos Parameters: threshold: The density threshold for the transfer function. Typical values depend on the specific transfer function and data normalization. Not given in the sources. marchingdelta: The minimum step size to ensure progress. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision problems may occur when computing voxel intersections; the travel value is clamped using FMax to ensure progress. The map size is (W-1) \times (H-1) \times (D-1), so the scalar field must have at least 2 voxels in each dimension. Uses a pre-computed Chebyshev distance map to skip multiple empty voxels in any dimension along a ray. It replaces the binary occupancy check with a metric that quantifies the distance to the nearest occupied block, allowing the ray to jump directly to the next potential intersection. Unlike the occupancy map method, which resumes sampling after a fixed number of empty voxels, this method dynamically calculates the skip distance based on local geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method reduces the number of density samples and transfer function evaluations. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for volumes with large empty regions. Limitations: Binary check may skip over thin structures if the threshold is not carefully chosen. Precision issues can occur at voxel boundaries. This method is implemented in the SRaimondi/VolumeRender repository as a preprocessing step to accelerate ray marching in volume rendering. name: Chebyshev Distance Map Empty Space Skipping
head: Chebychev distance maps for empty-space skipping, Isotropic Chebyshev distance map
body: Chebyshev distance map empty space skipping is a ray-traversal acceleration technique that uses a pre-computed distance map to skip multiple empty voxels in any dimension along a ray. It builds on Empty Space Map Generation by replacing the binary occupancy check with a metric that quantifies the distance to the nearest occupied block, allowing the ray to jump directly to the next potential intersection. Unlike the occupancy map method, which resumes sampling after a fixed number of empty voxels, this method dynamically calculates the skip distance based on the local geometry, achieving an average speed-up of 5.3 times the baseline frame rate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An occupancy map (boolean grid indicating visible geometry based on a transfer function threshold). Output: A Chebyshev distance map texture where each voxel stores the Chebyshev distance to the nearest occupied block. Data Structures: Distance Map Texture: A 3D image texture with an unsigned 8-bit integer channel (r8ui). Layout: 3D grid of uint8 values. Constraint: Distances are limited to a maximum of 255 due to the 8-bit storage. Occupancy Map Integration: The distance map can overwrite the occupancy map texture to save memory, but a separate "swap image" of identical dimensions is required during generation. Algorithm: Distance Map Generation The transformation from an occupancy map to a Chebyshev distance map is decomposed into three 1D passes that are trivially parallelized on a GPU. The passes operate on rows (x-axis), columns (y-axis), and slices (z-axis) independently. 1. First Transformation (X-axis): For each column and slice, perform a forward pass and a backward pass along the x-dimension. Forward Pass: Initialize D1 from the occupancy map at x=0. Iterate x from 1 to dim.x-1. Update D = \min(D1 + 1, \text{occ}(x)). Store D in the distance map. Update D1 = D. Backward Pass: Iterate x from dim.x-2 down to 0. Update D = \min(D1 + 1, \text{dist}(x)). Store D in the distance map. Update D1 = D. Note: This pass can read from and write to the same texture if it is the occupancy map. 2. Second Transformation (Y-axis): For each row and slice, perform a single-pass zig-zag search along the y-dimension. Read the current distance D from the output of the first transformation. Iterate n from 1 to D-1. If y \ge n, read Dn = \text{dist}(x, y-n, z). Update D = \min(D, \max(n, Dn)). If y+n < dim.y and n < D, read Dn = \text{dist}(x, y+n, z). Update D = \min(D, \max(n, Dn)). Store the final D in the swap image. 3. Third Transformation (Z-axis): For each row and column, perform a single-pass zig-zag search along the z-dimension. Read from the swap image (output of the second transformation). Perform the same zig-zag logic as the second transformation but on the z-axis. Store the final Chebyshev distance in the distance map. Pseudocode for Generation (Python-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def firsttransformation(dist, occ, dim): # Invoked for all columns (y) and slices (z) for y in range(dim[1]): for z in range(dim[2]): pos = (0, y, z) D1 = occ[pos] # Forward pass for x in range(1, dim[0]): currentpos = (x, y, z) D = min(D1 + 1, occ[currentpos]) dist[currentpos] = D D1 = D # Backward pass for x in range(dim[0] - 2, -1, -1): currentpos = (x, y, z) D = min(D1 + 1, dist[currentpos]) dist[currentpos] = D D1 = D def secondtransformation(dist, swap, dim): # Invoked for all rows (x) and slices (z) for x in range(dim[0]): for z in range(dim[2]): pos = (x, 0, z) D = dist[pos] # Zig-zag search along y-axis for n in range(1, D): if pos[1] >= n: Dn = dist[(pos[0], pos[1] - n, pos[2])] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) if (pos[1] + n) < dim[1] and n < D: Dn = dist[(pos[0], pos[1] + n, pos[2])] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) swap[pos] = D def thirdtransformation(swap, dist, dim): # Invoked for all rows (x) and columns (y) for x in range(dim[0]): for y in range(dim[1]): pos = (x, y, 0) D = swap[pos] # Zig-zag search along z-axis for n in range(1, D): if pos[2] >= n: Dn = swap[(pos[0], pos[1], pos[2] - n)] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) if (pos[2] + n) < dim[2] and n < D: Dn = swap[(pos[0], pos[1], pos[2] + n)] D = min(D, max(n, Dn)) dist[pos] = D Ray Traversal Step Calculation: During rendering, the distance D is sampled from the distance map at the current ray position. The number of steps to the next sampling point is calculated to skip D blocks. Chebyshev Distance Definition: D{\text{Chebyshev}}(\mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2) = \max(|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2|) where \mathbf{p}1 and \mathbf{p}2 are two points. Step Calculation: The number of steps \Delta{ij} to the next sampling point D blocks away on dimension j \in \{x, y, z\} is: \Delta{ij} = \begin{cases} \lceil (D + \lfloor \mathbf{u}j \rfloor - \mathbf{u}j) / \Delta \mathbf{u}j \rceil, & \text{if } \Delta \mathbf{u}j > 0 \\ \lceil (1 - D + \lfloor \mathbf{u}j \rfloor - \mathbf{u}j) / \Delta \mathbf{u}j \rceil, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \mathbf{u} is the current ray position in block coordinates, and \Delta \mathbf{u} is the ray direction in block coordinates. Vectorized Form: \Delta \mathbf{i} = \lceil (\text{step}(-\Delta \mathbf{u}) + \text{sgn}(\Delta \mathbf{u}) \cdot D + \lfloor \mathbf{u} \rfloor - \mathbf{u}) / \Delta \mathbf{u} \rceil This vectorized equation allows skipping multiple blocks with a single sample of the distance map. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Overhead: The generation process requires a swap image, doubling the memory requirements compared to using only an occupancy map. Distance Limit: The use of 8-bit integers limits the maximum skip distance to 255 blocks. Transfer Function Dependency: Since the distance maps are transfer-function dependent, they need to be updated on transfer-function changes. Initial Skip Size: When exiting an occupied region, the initial skip distance D is small. This can be suboptimal if the next occupied region is far away. A variant that uses separate distance maps for each of the 8 directional octants (defined by the sign of the x, y, and z components) to optimize skipping when exiting occupied regions. It is generated by modifying the isotropic transformations to scan in single directions only, requiring a total of 24 transformations (2 for the first pass, 4 for the second, reusing intermediate maps). During traversal, the octant index is computed once based on the fixed ray direction, and the corresponding anisotropic distance map is indexed. Compared to the Extended Anisotropic Chebyshev Distance (Es and Işler [8]), which requires 24x the memory of the isotropic map, this isotropic approach uses significantly less memory while providing sufficient performance gains. Time Complexity: The generation of the distance map involves three 1D passes. The first pass is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. The second and third passes involve a zig-zag search that depends on the current distance value, potentially making them slower than a simple linear pass, but still parallelizable. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the distance map (1 byte per voxel) and a swap image (1 byte per voxel) during generation. Total 2 bytes per voxel for the acceleration structure. Performance: Achieves an average speed-up of 5.3 times the baseline frame rate. Strengths: Allows skipping multiple blocks in any dimension, not constrained by the block size B as in the occupancy map method. Efficiently parallelized on GPU. Limitations: Memory overhead due to the swap image. Limited to 255 block skips due to 8-bit storage. Requires regeneration on transfer function changes. When to Use: When the volume has large empty regions and the transfer function is static or changes infrequently. When memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and the 255-block skip limit is sufficient. When Not to Use: When the transfer function changes frequently, as the regeneration cost may outweigh the rendering benefits. When memory is extremely constrained and the 2x overhead is unacceptable. The technique was introduced by Deakin and Knackstedt. It builds on the work of Saito and Toriwaki [12] for transforming occupancy maps to distance maps, adapted for Chebyshev distance and GPU parallelization. The method was developed to address the limitations of the original occupancy map approach, which resumed sampling after a fixed length of empty voxels, by allowing dynamic skip distances. Deakin and Knackstedt [DK20] further improved the approach by resuming empty-space skipping after a single empty voxel instead of a fixed set length. name: Distance Field Precomputation
head: Distance Field Computation, Precomputed Distance Field Generation
body: Distance Field Precomputation involves calculating distance fields for scalar fields involved in fiber surface definitions to facilitate fast intersection detection via the rule of signs. It builds on Distance Map Computation (Multi-Stage). Unlike Empty Space Map Generation which focuses on occupancy, or Distance Transformation (Proximity Clouds) which may use proximity clouds, this method specifically targets the geometric boundaries of fiber surfaces for ray-tracing acceleration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar fields defining fiber surfaces (e.g., FSCP - Fiber Surface Control Points). Output: A precomputed 2D distance field array. Data Structures: Distance Field Array: A 2D grid. The source specifies a size of 64 \times 64. Steps: 1. Identify the relevant scalar fields defining the fiber surfaces. 2. Compute the distance field for these fields. The computation time is fixed and depends only on the distance field dimensions. 3. name: Distance Transformation (Proximity Clouds)
head: Proximity Clouds
body: Distance Transformation, also known as Proximity Clouds, accelerates ray traversal in regular grids filled with empty zones by pre-calculating distance information to the nearest full element in the grid. It differs from hierarchical structures by storing distance data in a flat 3D volume aligned with the original voxel indices, allowing for O(1) lookup during traversal without tree navigation overhead. Inputs and Outputs Input: A binary volume where cells are classified as transparent (empty) or opaque (full). Output: A distance volume (distance map) where each cell contains the distance to the nearest non-empty cell. Data Structures Distance Volume: A 3D grid with the same dimensions as the input binary volume, where each cell stores a scalar value representing the Euclidean distance between the center of the current cell and the center of the nearest non-empty cell. Algorithm Steps 1. Generate Input Binary Volume: Encode the scene geometry into a binary volume, marking cells as transparent or opaque. 2. Compute Distance Map: Calculate the distance from every cell to the nearest non-empty cell using exact metrics (City Block, Euclidean, Chessboard) or approximate methods like Chamfering. Chamfering uses a mask of local distances propagated through the volume, where larger masks yield higher accuracy but increase preprocessing time. 3. Ray Casting with Adaptive Traversal: For each ray, determine the current cell index using fixed-point arithmetic and integer division. Case A (Vicinity of Object): If the current sample is near an object, perform simple incremental ray traversal (step-by-step sampling). Case B (Empty Space): If the current sample is in empty space, use the distance value d stored in the current cell to skip the empty region. 4. Skip Calculation: Calculate the new sample location to jump to the edge of the empty zone using the formula \text{New Sample} = \text{Current Sample} + \text{Unit Ray Direction} \times (d - 1). The stepping distance is d-1 (not d) to avoid skipping beyond the free zone, because the distance is calculated from the center of the current cell. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computedistancemap(binaryvolume): """ Computes the distance map from a binary volume. binaryvolume: 3D list/array where 1 is opaque, 0 is transparent. Returns: 3D array of distances. """ # The sources do not specify the exact distance map generation algorithm. # A standard Chamfering mask pass or BFS would be used here. # Stub implementation for structural completeness. dims = (len(binaryvolume), len(binaryvolume[0]), len(binaryvolume[0][0])) return [[[0.0 for in range(dims[2])] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] def getcellindex(pos, rayorigin, voxelsize): """ Computes the grid cell index containing the given position. Uses floor division as described in the sources. """ return tuple(math.floor((pos[i] - rayorigin[i]) / voxelsize) for i in range(3)) def raycastproximityclouds(rayorigin, raydirection, distancevolume, voxelsize, maxdistance, nearobjectthreshold=1.5): """ Casts a ray using Proximity Clouds acceleration. """ t = 0.0 currentpos = [rayorigin[i] for i in range(3)] # Determine initial cell index currentcell = getcellindex(currentpos, rayorigin, voxelsize) while t < maxdistance: # Bounds check if not (0 <= currentcell[0] < len(distancevolume) and 0 <= currentcell[1] < len(distancevolume[0]) and 0 <= currentcell[2] < len(distancevolume[0][0])): break # Get distance to nearest object from the precomputed map d = distancevolume[currentcell[0]][currentcell[1]][currentcell[2]] # Check if we are in the vicinity of an object if d < nearobjectthreshold: # Simple incremental traversal stepsize = voxelsize currentpos = [currentpos[i] + raydirection[i] stepsize for i in range(3)] t += stepsize currentcell = getcellindex(currentpos, rayorigin, voxelsize) else: # Skip empty region # Formula: New sample = Current + direction (d - 1) skipdistance = max(d - 1.0, 1e-6) # Guard against zero/negative steps # Update position currentpos = [currentpos[i] + raydirection[i] skipdistance for i in range(3)] t += skipdistance # Update cell index currentcell = getcellindex(currentpos, rayorigin, voxelsize) # If we jumped past the object or out of bounds, break if not (0 <= currentcell[0] < len(distancevolume) and 0 <= currentcell[1] < len(distancevolume[0]) and 0 <= currentcell[2] < len(distancevolume[0][0])): break return currentpos, t Parameters Distance Metric: Choice between City Block, Euclidean, Chessboard, or Chamfering approximation, where the applied metric is a compromise between preprocessing and rendering times. Threshold: The value distinguishing "vicinity of an object" from "empty space" is not explicitly defined in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Stepping Distance: The stepping distance must be d-1, not d, to avoid skipping beyond the free zone because the distance is calculated from the center of the current cell. Dynamic Scenes: The method is too costly for dynamic scenes because the distance map must be recomputed for every frame. Preprocessing Time: Depends on the distance metric, where Chamfering is efficient but higher accuracy requires larger masks and longer preprocessing. Rendering Speed: Fast for scenes with large empty regions due to skipping, and the structure is considered optimal on GPUs for scenes with uniform data distribution. Memory: Requires storing an additional 3D volume for distances, in addition to the binary volume. Limitations: Not suitable for dynamic scenes due to high preprocessing cost, and avoids the additional computational cost required for traversing cells at different hierarchy levels found in other methods. Origin: Presented by Cohen and Sheffer in 1994. History: The technique was introduced to accelerate ray traversal in regular grids with empty zones, proving effective for static scenes. Usage: Applied in medical volume rendering and other domains where static scenes with significant empty space are common. name: Occupancy Mipmap Generation
body: Occupancy Mipmap Generation computes a hierarchical occupancy mipmap for a 3D grid using JAX convolutions. It builds on Occupancy Map Generation by extending a single-resolution occupancy mask into a multi-resolution pyramid. Inputs: mat: A 3D array representing the input grid, where non-zero values indicate occupied space. Dimensions are X \times Y \times Z. xdim: The width of the grid (X). Outputs: mipmap: A list of JAX arrays representing the occupancy hierarchy. Data Structures: occupancymat: A 3D binary mask of the same shape as mat, where occupancymat[i,j,k] = 1 if mat[i,j,k] > 0, else 0. data: A 4D JAX tensor with shape (1, X, Y, Z, 1) (batch size 1, channel size 1). kernel: A 5D tensor for convolution, shape (2^i, 2^i, 2^i, 1, 1). mipmap: A Python list of JAX arrays. Steps: 1. Calculate the number of hierarchical levels: L = \lfloor \log2(xdim) \rfloor. 2. Create the binary occupancy mask: occupancymat = (mat > 0).astype(float32). 3. Compute the total number of occupied points: nbofpts = sum(occupancymat). 4. Convert occupancymat to a JAX array and add batch and channel dimensions: data = occupancymat[None,:,:,:, None], resulting in shape (1, X, Y, Z, 1). 5. Initialize an empty list mipmap. 6. For each level i from 0 to L-1: a. Create a convolution kernel of ones with shape (2^i, 2^i, 2^i, 1, 1). b. Define the dimension numbers for lax.convgeneraldilated: input and output dimensions are 'NHWDC' (Batch, Height, Width, Depth, Channel), and kernel dimensions are 'HWDIO' (Kernel Height, Kernel Width, Kernel Depth, Input Channel, Output Channel). c. Apply lax.convgeneraldilated with strides (2^i, 2^i, 2^i) and 'SAME' padding. d. Remove the batch and channel dimensions from the convolution output. e. Append the resulting 3D array to mipmap. f. Update data to the stripped convolution output for the next iteration. 7. Append a final level to mipmap containing nbofpts as a single scalar tensor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax.lax import convgeneraldilated, convdimensionnumbers def generateoccupancymipmap(mat): """ Generates a hierarchical occupancy mipmap from a 3D grid. Args: mat: numpy array, shape (X, Y, Z). Non-zero values indicate occupancy. Returns: mipmap: list of jax arrays. mipmap[i] is the occupancy map at level i. mipmap[-1] is a scalar tensor with the total count of occupied voxels. """ xdim = mat.shape[0] levels = jnp.log2(xdim).astype(int) occupancymat = (mat > 0).astype(jnp.float32) nbofpts = jnp.sum(occupancymat) data = jnp.array(occupancymat) data = data[None,:,:,:, None] # Shape: (1, X, Y, Z, 1) mipmap = [] for i in range(levels): kernelsize = 2i kernel = jnp.ones((kernelsize, kernelsize, kernelsize, 1, 1)) dn = convdimensionnumbers(data.shape, kernel.shape, ('NHWDC', 'HWDIO', 'NHWDC')) # Note: The provided source code snippet only constructs kernels and dimension numbers; # the convolution call and data update are omitted. convout = convgeneraldilated( data, kernel, windowstrides=(kernelsize, kernelsize, kernelsize), padding='SAME', dimensionnumbers=dn) convout = convout[0,:,:,:, 0] # Remove batch and channel dims mipmap.append(convout) data = convout[None,:,:,:, None] # Update for next level mipmap.append(jnp.array(nbofpts)) return mipmap Parameters: mat: Input 3D grid array. xdim: Grid width. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: xdim is truncated to an integer via.astype(int) if not a power of 2, which may truncate the expected level count. The convolution sums occupancy counts, so coarser levels contain values >1 indicating multiple occupied voxels map to a single coarse voxel. Periodically refreshes a 3D occupancy grid by querying a NeRF model for density at voxel centers. It solves stale spatial caching in on-the-fly NeRF training. It differs from this method by using direct density queries rather than convolutional mipmap generation. Generates an occupancy map by counting rays passing through voxels. It differs from this method by using explicit ray traversal statistics rather than JAX convolutions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Occupancy Grid Update
head: Density-Based Grid Update, Grid Density Thresholding, Occupancy Grid Update from Density
body: Occupancy Grid Update is a method to periodically refresh a 3D occupancy grid by querying a Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) model for density at grid voxel centers and marking voxels as occupied if the density exceeds a specified threshold. It solves the problem of accelerating ray marching by skipping empty space during training and rendering. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Occupancy Map Generation via Ray Casting, by directly evaluating the neural network's output on a regular lattice rather than casting rays through the scene to infer occupancy. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A trained NeRF model (or proposal network), the 3D grid resolution, the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defining the scene bounds, and a density threshold. Outputs: A 3D boolean occupancy grid (or binary mask) indicating which voxels are occupied. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D array of shape (resolution, resolution, resolution) containing boolean values (True/False or 1/0). AABB: Defined by aabbmin and aabbmax (3D vectors). Steps: 1. Generate Grid Coordinates: Create a 3D meshgrid of integer indices from 0 to resolution - 1 for x, y, and z dimensions. \text{grid\coords} = \text{meshgrid}(0, \dots, \text{res}-1, \text{indexing}='ij').\text{reshape}(-1, 3) 2. Convert to World Positions: Map the grid indices to world coordinates using the AABB: \text{positions} = \text{aabb\min} + \left( \frac{\text{grid\indices.float()} + 0.5}{\text{resolution}} \right) \times (\text{aabb\max} - \text{aabb\min}) 3. Query Densities: Pass the world positions to the NeRF model to retrieve volume density \sigma. If the model supports forwardwithdensityonly, use it. Otherwise, call the model with dummy view directions and extract the density component. 4. Update Grid: Compare the queried densities against the threshold: \text{occupied} = \sigma > \text{threshold} Reshape the result back to (resolution, resolution, resolution). Parameters: resolution: Integer, default 128. densitythreshold: Float, default 0.01. updategridevery: Integer, iteration interval for updates (e.g., 500). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateoccupancygrid(model, aabbmin, aabbmax, resolution, threshold, updateevery, step): """ Updates the occupancy grid based on NeRF density predictions. Args: model: NeRF model with a forward method. aabbmin: Tensor (3,), minimum bounds of the scene. aabbmax: Tensor (3,), maximum bounds of the scene. resolution: int, grid resolution. threshold: float, density threshold for occupancy. updateevery: int, frequency of updates. step: int, current training step. Returns: grid: Tensor (resolution, resolution, resolution), boolean occupancy grid. """ # Only update periodically if step % updateevery != 0: # Return previous grid or None if not initialized return None # 1. Generate grid coordinates x = torch.linspace(0, resolution - 1, resolution) y = torch.linspace(0, resolution - 1, resolution) z = torch.linspace(0, resolution - 1, resolution) gridcoords = torch.stack(torch.meshgrid(x, y, z, indexing='ij'), dim=-1).reshape(-1, 3) # 2. Convert to world positions # positions = aabbmin + ((gridcoords.float() + 0.5) / resolution) (aabbmax - aabbmin) # Note: gridcoords are integers 0..res-1. Adding 0.5 centers them in voxels. positions = aabbmin + ((gridcoords.float() + 0.5) / resolution) (aabbmax - aabbmin) # 3. Query densities # Batch processing to avoid OOM batchsize = 4096 densities = [] for i in range(0, len(positions), batchsize): batchpos = positions[i:i+batchsize] if hasattr(model, 'forwardwithdensityonly'): batchdens = model.forwardwithdensityonly(batchpos) else: # Dummy directions for models requiring viewdirs dummydirs = torch.zeroslike(batchpos) # Assume model returns (rgb, sigma,...) or similar out = model(batchpos, dummydirs) # Extract density; index may vary by implementation batchdens = out[..., 0] if out.dim() > 1 else out densities.append(batchdens) alldensities = torch.cat(densities, dim=0) # 4. Update grid occupied = alldensities > threshold grid = occupied.reshape(resolution, resolution, resolution) return grid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point comparisons at the threshold boundary may cause flickering if the grid is updated frequently with noisy density estimates. Boundaries: Voxels outside the AABB must be handled explicitly (e.g., marked as empty). Degenerate Input: If the NeRF model is not trained, densities may be uniform, leading to an all-occupied or all-empty grid. This method periodically refreshes a 3D hierarchical density grid using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of newly queried densities to stabilize training and refine the representation of occupied space. It builds on Occupancy Grid Update by maintaining continuous density values per voxel alongside binary occupancy. Not given in the sources. This method adapts the occupancy grid for efficient point sampling in dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by treating voxel occupancy as a time-varying probability rather than a static binary state. It solves the problem of maintaining sampling efficiency in on-the-fly training where scene geometry changes, by applying a transition function to predict motion and a Bayesian update to incorporate new density observations. Unlike static NeRFs that cache grids or 4D space-time grids that fail to accelerate per-frame training, this method transitions the 3D grid between frames to preserve occupancy information relevant to the current time step. MERF Baking is a post-training procedure that converts a trained neural field representation into a block-sparse, texture-based format optimized for real-time web rendering. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large-scale neural scenes by evaluating the MLP outputs on discrete grids and using a binary occupancy grid to cull empty or occluded voxels. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Density Grid Update with EMA and Occupancy Grid Transition and Update, by explicitly targeting web-based delivery through texture compression and block-sparse storage, trading higher frame rates for neural field reconstruction capabilities compared to mesh rasterization methods. Unlike existing baking pipelines that do not consider the proposal-MLP and use uniformly-spaced sample points (causing fog-like artifacts and floating blobs), this method uses proposal-MLP sampling and real-time renderer step sizes for visibility culling, resulting in a lossless pipeline. When Not to Use: Do not use for highly dynamic scenes without adaptation (see Occupancy Grid Transition and Update). name: Density Grid Update with EMA
head: EMA Occupancy Grid Update
body: This method periodically refreshes a 3D hierarchical density grid using an Exponential Moving Average (EMA) of newly queried densities to stabilize training and refine the representation of occupied space. It builds on Occupancy Grid Update by maintaining continuous density values per voxel alongside binary occupancy. Inputs: step: Current training iteration integer. occevalfn: Callable taking sample locations (N, 3) and returning occupancy values (N, 1). occthre: Float threshold for binary occupancy determination (default 0.01). emadecay: Float decay factor for the EMA (default 0.95). warmupsteps: Integer number of initial steps to sample all cells (default 256). n: Integer frequency of updates (update every n steps, default 16). self.densitygrid: 3D tensor storing density values \sigma. self.occs: Tensor storing continuous occupancy values o. self.binaries: Boolean tensor indicating occupied voxels. self.resolution: Grid resolution integer. self.levels: Number of hierarchical levels. self.aabbs: Axis-aligned bounding boxes for each level, shape (levels, 6). self.cellsperlvl: Number of cells per level. self.gridcoords: Precomputed grid coordinates for all cells. self.bound: World-space bounding box size. self.density: Callable neural network returning density values. Outputs: Updated self.densitygrid. Updated self.meandensity. Updated self.binaries and self.occs. Data Structures: densitygrid: 3D tensor storing density values \sigma. occs: 1D or 3D tensor storing continuous occupancy values o. binaries: Boolean tensor indicating occupied voxels (o > \text{thre}). aabbs: Tensor of shape (levels, 6) storing [minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz] for each level. Parameters: occthre: Default 0.01. emadecay: Default 0.95. warmupsteps: Default 256. n: Update frequency, default 16. Steps: 1. Check Training State and Frequency: If not in training mode, raise RuntimeError. If step % n != 0, skip update. 2. Cell Sampling: Determine which cells to query based on the current step: If step < warmupsteps: Sample all cells uniformly using self.getallcells(). If step >= warmupsteps: Sample N = \text{self.cells\per\lvl} // 4 cells, mixing uniform and occupied cells using self.sampleuniformandoccupiedcells(N). 3. Coordinate Transformation: For each level lvl and its sampled indices: Retrieve grid coordinates: gridcoords = self.gridcoords[indices]. Add uniform random noise to jitter sampling within voxels: x{\text{local}} = \frac{\text{grid\coords} + \text{rand}(\text{grid\coords})}{\text{self.resolution}}. Transform local coordinates to world space using the level's AABB: x{\text{world}} = \text{aabbs[lvl,:3]} + x{\text{local}} \times (\text{aabbs[lvl, 3:]} - \text{aabbs[lvl,:3]}). 4. Occupancy Evaluation: Evaluate occupancy at world coordinates x{\text{world}} using occevalfn: o = \text{occ\eval\fn}(x{\text{world}}).\text{squeeze}(-1). 5. Occupancy Grid Update (EMA): Compute global cell IDs: \text{cell\ids} = \text{lvl} \times \text{self.cells\per\lvl} + \text{indices}. Update occupancy values using EMA maximum: \text{self.occs}[\text{cell\ids}] = \max(\text{self.occs}[\text{cell\ids}] \times \text{ema\decay}, o). Note: The implementation uses torch.maximum instead of scattermax for updating occupied cells, noting that empirically the results are almost the same. 6. Binary Occupancy Update: Compute the threshold for binary occupancy: \text{thre} = \text{clamp}(\text{mean}(\text{self.occs}[\text{self.occs} \ge 0]), \text{max}=\text{occ\thre}). Update binary grid: \text{self.binaries} = (\text{self.occs} > \text{thre}).\text{view}(\text{self.binaries.shape}). 7. Density Grid Update: Initialize a temporary grid: tmpgrid = torch.zeroslike(self.densitygrid). Generate coordinate lines for X, Y, Z axes using torch.linspace from -self.bound + half\grid\size to self.bound - half\grid\size, split into chunks of 128. Construct meshgrid points: xx, yy, zz = \text{meshgrid}(xs, ys, zs, \text{indexing}="ij"). Concatenate and reshape points to shape (N, 3): \text{pts} = \text{cat}([xx.\text{reshape}(-1, 1), yy.\text{reshape}(-1, 1), zz.\text{reshape}(-1, 1)], \text{dim}=-1). Add uniform noise in range [-hgs, hgs] to points: \text{pts} += (\text{rand}(\text{pts}) \times 2 - 1) \times \text{half\grid\size} where \text{half\grid\size} = \text{self.bound} / \text{resolution}. Pad points to a multiple of 128 for manual padding: \text{pad\n} = 128 - (\text{num\pts} \% 128). Query density from the network: \text{density} = \text{self.density}(\text{pts}.\text{to}(\text{tmp\grid.device}))[:\text{num\pts}].\text{reshape}(lx, ly, lz).\text{detach}(). Assign density to the temporary grid at the corresponding slice: \text{tmp\grid}[xi \times 128:\dots, yi \times 128:\dots, zi \times 128:\dots] = \text{density}. Update the density grid using EMA: \text{self.density\grid} = \max(\text{self.density\grid} \times \text{decay}, \text{tmp\grid}). Update mean density: \text{self.mean\density} = \text{mean}(\text{self.density\grid}).\text{item}(). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch class DensityGridUpdater: def init(self, densitygrid, occs, binaries, resolution, levels, aabbs, cellsperlvl, gridcoords, bound, densityfn, meandensity): self.densitygrid = densitygrid self.occs = occs self.binaries = binaries self.resolution = resolution self.levels = levels self.aabbs = aabbs self.cellsperlvl = cellsperlvl self.gridcoords = gridcoords self.bound = bound self.density = densityfn self.meandensity = meandensity self.training = True def update(self, step, occevalfn, occthre=0.01, emadecay=0.95, warmupsteps=256, n=16): if not self.training: raise RuntimeError("Update only allowed during training") if step % n != 0: return # 1. Cell Sampling if step < warmupsteps: indiceslist = self.getallcells() else: N = self.cellsperlvl // 4 indiceslist = self.sampleuniformandoccupiedcells(N) # 2. name: Voxel Prior Loss
body: Voxel Prior Loss is a regularization term for 3D Gaussian Splatting that aligns learned Gaussian primitives with a precomputed voxel grid occupancy. It solves the problem of floating artifacts in empty space and ensures Gaussians in occupied regions maintain appropriate scale and opacity. It sets itself apart from standard photometric losses by explicitly enforcing geometric priors derived from voxel occupancy, suppressing Gaussians in empty voxels and encouraging dense, correctly scaled Gaussians in occupied ones. Inputs and outputs: Inputs: gaussians: Object containing attributes for N Gaussians. position: Tensor of shape (N, 3), world coordinates. opacity: Tensor of shape (N,), scalar opacity values. scale: Tensor of shape (N, 3), scale factors along principal axes. voxelindices: Tensor of shape (N, 3), integer voxel coordinates (d, h, w) for each Gaussian. voxelgrid: 3D occupancy grid of dimensions gridsize (D, H, W), flattened to 1D for indexing. Values are binary or boolean (occupied vs. empty). voxelcenters: Tensor of shape (D \times H \times W, 3), world coordinates of voxel centers. gridsize: Tuple (D, H, W) representing the dimensions of the voxel grid. voxelsize: Scalar, the physical size of a single voxel edge. penaltyweight: Float, weight for empty voxel opacity suppression. posweight: Float, weight for empty voxel position penalty. scaleweight: Float, weight for occupied voxel scale constraint. encourageweight: Float, weight for occupied voxel opacity encouragement. eps: Small float for numerical stability in normalization. Outputs: totalloss: Scalar, the computed regularization loss. Data structures: flatvoxelgrid: 1D tensor of shape (D \times H \times W), containing occupancy status (1 if occupied, 0 if empty). flatindices: 1D tensor of shape (N), mapping each Gaussian to its corresponding voxel index in the flattened grid. emptymask: Boolean tensor of shape (N), true where flatvoxelgrid indicates empty voxels. occupiedmask: Boolean tensor of shape (N), true where flatvoxelgrid indicates occupied voxels. Steps: 1. Map Gaussians to Voxels: Convert the 3D voxel indices of each Gaussian into a linear index for the flattened grid. 2. Retrieve Voxel Properties: Get occupancy status via isoccupied = flatvoxelgrid[flatindices] and voxel center coordinates via voxelcenter = voxelcenters.view(-1, 3)[flatindices]. 3. Compute Empty Voxel Penalty (Opacity): Identify empty voxels via emptymask = ~isoccupied and calculate the penalty as the weighted sum of opacity for Gaussians in empty voxels. 4. Compute Empty Voxel Position Penalty: Calculate an exponential distance penalty for Gaussians in empty voxels based on their L2 norm. 5. Compute Occupied Voxel Scale Loss: Identify occupied voxels via occupiedmask = isoccupied and penalize Gaussians whose scale exceeds the voxel size, clamping negative differences to zero. 6. Compute Occupied Voxel Opacity Encouragement: Penalize Gaussians in occupied voxels having opacity below 0.1 using a ReLU-like function. 7. Normalize Total Loss: Sum all components and normalize by the number of Gaussians plus a small epsilon. Formulas: Linear index calculation: flat\indices = indices[:,0] \times (grid\size[1] \times grid\size[2]) + indices[:,1] \times grid\size[2] + indices[:,2], where indices is (N, 3) voxel indices and grid\size is (D, H, W). Empty voxel position penalty: penalty\position = pos\weight \times \sum \exp(-5 \times \|position[empty\mask]\|), where \|\cdot\| is the L2 norm. Occupied voxel scale loss: scale\loss = scale\weight \times \sum \max(0, scale[occupied\mask] - voxel\size), summed over all elements of the (N, 3) scale tensor. Occupied voxel opacity encouragement: opacity\loss = encourage\weight \times \sum \max(0, 0.1 - opacity[occupied\mask]). Normalized total loss: total\loss = \frac{penalty\opacity + penalty\position + scale\loss + opacity\loss}{N + eps}. Parameters: penaltyweight: Weight for empty voxel opacity suppression. Default value: 1.0. encourageweight: Weight for occupied voxel opacity encouragement. Default value: 0.5. posweight: Weight for empty voxel position penalty. Default value: 0.2. scaleweight: Weight for occupied voxel scale constraint. Default value: 0.3. Edge cases and pitfalls: Out-of-bounds Indices: If a Gaussian's position falls outside the voxel grid bounds, flatindices may be invalid. Ensure voxelindices are clamped or Gaussians outside the grid are excluded from the loss. Scale Interpretation: The source formula clamp(scale[occupiedmask] - voxelsize, min=0) is ambiguous if scale is a vector (N,3). The implementation sums over all elements of the clamped difference. Empty Mask Logic: Ensure isoccupied is boolean or castable to boolean. If the grid uses 0/1 integers, bitwise inversion ~isoccupied might invert bits incorrectly if not cast to bool first. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def norm(v): return math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) def exp(x): return math.exp(x) def clamp(x, minval): return max(minval, x) def relu(x): return max(0.0, x) def computevoxelpriorloss(gaussians, voxelgrid, voxelcenters, gridsize, voxelsize, penaltyweight=1.0, posweight=0.2, scaleweight=0.3, encourageweight=0.5, eps=1e-8): """ Computes the Voxel Prior Loss for 3D Gaussians. Args: gaussians: Object with attributes.position (N,3),.opacity (N,),.scale (N,3),.voxelindices (N,3) voxelgrid: 1D list/tensor (DHW,) of occupancy (1=occupied, 0=empty) voxelcenters: List/tensor (DHW, 3) of voxel center coordinates gridsize: Tuple (D, H, W) voxelsize: Scalar float, edge length of a voxel penaltyweight: Weight for empty voxel opacity penalty posweight: Weight for empty voxel position penalty scaleweight: Weight for occupied voxel scale penalty encourageweight: Weight for occupied voxel opacity encouragement eps: Small constant for numerical stability Returns: totalloss: Scalar float """ # 1. Map Gaussians to Voxel Indices indices = gaussians.voxelindices # Shape (N, 3) D, H, W = gridsize flatindices = [int(idx[0] (H W) + idx[1] W + idx[2]) for idx in indices] # 2. Retrieve Voxel Properties isoccupied = [bool(voxelgrid[i]) for i in flatindices] voxelcentersflat = [voxelcenters[i] for i in flatindices] # Retrieved per source, unused in loss # Extract Gaussian attributes opacity = gaussians.opacity # Shape (N,) position = gaussians.position # Shape (N, 3) scale = gaussians.scale # Shape (N, 3) # Masks emptymask = [not occ for occ in isoccupied] occupiedmask = [occ for occ in isoccupied] # 3. Empty Voxel Opacity Penalty penaltyopacity = penaltyweight sum(opacity[i] for i in range(len(opacity)) if emptymask[i]) # 4. Empty Voxel Position Penalty penaltyposition = posweight sum(exp(-5 norm(position[i])) for i in range(len(position)) if emptymask[i]) # 5. Occupied Voxel Scale Loss scaleloss = scaleweight sum(clamp(scale[i][j] - voxelsize, 0.0) for i in range(len(scale)) if occupiedmask[i] for j in range(3)) # 6. Occupied Voxel Opacity Encouragement opacityloss = encourageweight sum(relu(0.1 - opacity[i]) for i in range(len(opacity)) if occupiedmask[i]) # 7. Normalize N = len(opacity) totalloss = (penaltyopacity + penaltyposition + scaleloss + opacityloss) / (N + eps) return totalloss Regularizes visible 3D Gaussians by computing their perpendicular distance to voxel plane boundaries, weighting the distance by voxel complexity, and averaging over all voxels. It filters visible Gaussians using a visibility filter, maps positions to voxel grid coordinates via floor division by 2.0, gathers Gaussians per voxel, computes distances as |\mathbf{p}i \cdot \mathbf{n}v + dv| / \|\mathbf{n}v\|, finds the minimum distance per Gaussian, weights by voxel complexity, and divides by the number of voxels. The loss is defined as L{voxel} = \frac{1}{V} \sum{v \in V} \frac{1}{Mv} \sum{i=1}^{Mv} c{v, i} \cdot \min{j} \frac{|\mathbf{p}i \cdot \mathbf{n}v + dv|}{\|\mathbf{n}v\|}, where V is the number of voxels, Mv is Gaussians in voxel v, \mathbf{p}i is Gaussian position, \mathbf{n}v is voxel normal, dv is voxel plane offset, and c{v, i} is voxel complexity. It uses VOXELLOC to convert voxel grid keys to spatial position identifiers for indexing. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Voxel Prior Loss is a regularization term introduced within 3D Gaussian Splatting training pipelines to enforce geometric consistency via voxel occupancy priors. It operates by constraining Gaussians to align with precomputed voxel grids, suppressing empty space and fitting occupied geometry. name: Occupancy Grid Transition and Update
head: Dynamic Occupancy Grid, HMM-based Occupancy Update, Occ. Grid Transition, Probabilistic Occupancy Grid, Transition and Update of Occupancy Grid
body: This method adapts the occupancy grid for efficient point sampling in dynamic Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by treating voxel occupancy as a time-varying probability rather than a static binary state. It solves the problem of maintaining sampling efficiency in on-the-fly training where scene geometry changes, by applying a transition function to predict motion and a Bayesian update to incorporate new density observations. Unlike static NeRFs that cache grids or 4D space-time grids that fail to accelerate per-frame training, this method transitions the 3D grid between frames to preserve occupancy information relevant to the current time step. Inputs and Outputs Input: The final occupancy grid from the previous frame optimization G^J{k-1}, where k is the current frame index and J is the total number of optimization iterations per frame. Input: The volume density output \sigma(x) from the NeRF model during current frame optimization. Input: A 3D convolution kernel S representing motion probability. Output: The updated occupancy grid G^jk for the current frame at iteration j, used to guide point sampling. Data Structures Occupancy Grid (G): A 3D tensor where each element G(x) represents the probability that voxel x contains positive volume density. The values are continuous probabilities in the range [0, 1]. Kernel (S): A 3D kernel used for convolution, defined as a simple 3D Gaussian function. Steps 1. Transition (Prediction): At the start of optimizing frame k, apply a transition function to the previous frame's final grid G^J{k-1} to model potential motion. This is computed by convolving the previous grid with the kernel S: G^0k = S G^J{k-1} Here, G^0k is the initial occupancy probability for frame k before any new observations are processed. The convolution assumes a Markov property where motion is limited and local. 2. Bayesian Update (Correction): During the J optimization iterations for frame k, update the occupancy grid probability G^jk after each iteration j (where j \in [1, J]) using the NeRF's volume density output \sigma(x) at the sampled point x. The update rule is: G^jk = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \sigma(x) < G^{j-1}k \\ \sigma(x) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} This is a simplified Bayesian update P(\sigma(x) | G^{j-1}k). The condition \sigma(x) < G^{j-1}k triggers a certainty of occupancy (probability 1), while otherwise the probability is set to the observed density value. 3. Sampling: Use the updated grid G^jk to sample points only in occupied areas (where probability is significant) during the on-the-fly training process. Parameters Kernel S: A 3D Gaussian function. Its specific width/standard deviation is not given in the sources, but it is chosen to represent the probability of motion based on the Markov assumption of limited historical motion information. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Global Sampling Failure: Using global random sampling (as in Instant-NGP) to update the grid ignores previous occupancy values and transitions. In on-the-fly training with few iterations, this can miss occupied regions that have moved, resulting in "blank cubes" in rendered images. This method avoids that by updating probabilities at occupied points based on transition. Dynamic Scene Assumption: The method is designed for dynamic scenes captured by multi-view forward-facing cameras. It may not be directly applicable to monocular or 360-degree inward-facing setups without modification, as these involve different motion characteristics and hardware constraints. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateoccupancygridtransitionandupdate(Gprev, kernelS, nerfmodel, numiterations): # Gprev: 3D tensor of occupancy probabilities from previous frame (G^J{k-1}) # kernelS: 3D Gaussian kernel for motion transition # nerfmodel: The NeRF model providing volume density sigma(x) # numiterations: J, number of optimization steps per frame # Step 1: Transition (Prediction) # Convolve previous grid with motion kernel # Note: 3D convolution implementation is standard; sources do not specify details. Gcurrent = convolve3d(Gprev, kernelS) # Step 2: Bayesian Update (Correction) for j in range(1, numiterations + 1): # Sample points x based on current occupancy probabilities Gcurrent # Note: Point sampling strategy is standard; sources do not specify details. points = samplepointsfromgrid(Gcurrent) for x in points: # Get volume density from NeRF sigmax = nerfmodel.getvolumedensity(x) # Bayesian update rule from sources if sigmax < Gcurrent[x]: Gcurrent[x] = 1.0 else: Gcurrent[x] = sigmax return Gcurrent def convolve3d(grid, kernel): # Standard 3D convolution implementation # Note: sources do not specify details. return grid def samplepointsfromgrid(grid): # Standard importance sampling from probability distribution # Note: sources do not specify details. return [] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On the synthetic D-NeRF dataset, the method achieves 6 frames per second (FPS) for training and rendering combined. It significantly accelerates on-the-fly training compared to state-of-the-art algorithms while maintaining comparable rendering quality. Strengths: Maintains occupancy information across frames, avoiding the "blank cube" artifacts caused by global random sampling in dynamic scenes. Efficient for on-the-fly training with limited iterations per frame. Limitations: Relies on the Markov assumption of limited motion, which may not capture complex, long-range movements accurately without tuning the kernel S. Performance may degrade in scenes with rapid, non-local motion. Origin: Proposed in OD-NeRF: Efficient Training of On-the-Fly Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields. History: The method addresses the limitation of static NeRF occupancy grids [13, 1] and 4D space-time grids [16] which do not improve on-the-fly efficiency. It formulates the problem using a Hidden Markov Model approach to transition and update the grid. Usage: Evaluated on synthetic D-NeRF [18], real-world MeetRoom [6], and DyNeRF [8] datasets. It is particularly relevant for streaming scenarios with multi-view forward-facing cameras. name: MERF Baking
head: Baking to Discrete Grids, Proposal-MLP-aware baking pipeline
body: MERF Baking is a post-training procedure that converts a trained neural field representation into a block-sparse, texture-based format optimized for real-time web rendering. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large-scale neural scenes by evaluating the MLP outputs on discrete grids and using a binary occupancy grid to cull empty or occluded voxels. It sets itself apart from its siblings, such as Density Grid Update with EMA and Occupancy Grid Transition and Update, by explicitly targeting web-based delivery through texture compression and block-sparse storage, trading higher frame rates for neural field reconstruction capabilities compared to mesh rasterization methods. Unlike existing baking pipelines that do not consider the proposal-MLP and use uniformly-spaced sample points (causing fog-like artifacts and floating blobs), this method uses proposal-MLP sampling and real-time renderer step sizes for visibility culling, resulting in a lossless pipeline. Inputs: Trained Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) parameters. Set of training rays with associated camera poses and ground truth images. Proposal MLP parameters (used during training to sample points near surfaces). Real-time renderer step size parameter \delta (small uniform step size in contracted space). Occupancy threshold \tau = 0.005. Outputs: Binary occupancy grid A at base resolution. Mipmapped occupancy grids for empty space skipping. Baked 2D planes and 3D voxel grid in block-sparse format. Encoded textures (PNGs). Data Structures: 1. Binary Occupancy Grid (A): A 3D grid where each voxel is a binary flag (occupied/unoccupied). The base resolution is typically 4096. 2. Block-Sparse Voxel Grid: Stores the baked density/color data. Only data blocks containing at least one occupied voxel are stored. 3. Mipmapped Occupancy Grids: Lower-resolution versions of A created via max-pooling with filter sizes 16, 32, and 128. For a base resolution of 4096, this results in grids of size 256, 128, and 32. Steps: 1. Render Training Rays and Extract Weighted Points: Render all training rays using the trained Proposal MLP. Extract a set of weighted points \{(xi, wi)\}, where xi is the 3D position of a sample point and wi is the associated volume rendering weight from the volume rendering equation. wi = Ti \cdot (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where Ti is the transmittance up to point i, \sigmai is the density, and \deltai is the distance to the next sample. Note that these points cluster around surfaces because they are sampled by the proposal-MLP. 2. Compute Opacity for Culling: Compute the opacity \alphai for each point xi based on the distance between samples \delta used by the real-time renderer, not the proposal-MLP. The real-time renderer steps through contracted space with a small uniform step size \delta. \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(xi) \cdot \delta) Using the real-time step size \delta ensures aggressive culling while guaranteeing that voxels with significant opacity (\alphai > 0.005) are not culled in the final sampling scheme. The weight wi depends on densities along the entire ray (visibility), while \alphai depends only on the density at xi. 3. Populate Binary Occupancy Grid (A): Initialize grid A to all zeros. For each weighted point (xi, wi): Identify the eight voxels surrounding the position xi. Mark these eight voxels as occupied (set to 1) if both conditions are met: wi > \tau \quad \text{and} \quad \alphai > \tau where \tau = 0.005. Voxels corresponding to occluded content, regions not sampled by any training ray, or low opacity are left unoccupied (0). 4. Generate Mipmapped Occupancy Grids: Create multiple lower-resolution versions of the binary occupancy grid A using max-pooling with filter sizes 16, 32, and 128. These are used for hierarchical empty space skipping during ray traversal. 5. Bake Neural Field Outputs: Evaluate the trained MLP to compute density and color for all occupied voxels in A. Store the resulting 3D voxel grid in a block-sparse format, storing only data blocks that contain occupied voxels. Bake the three high-resolution 2D planes (used in MERF) alongside the 3D voxel grid. 6. Encode Textures: Encode the baked textures as PNGs to reduce storage size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def merfbaking(trainedmlp, proposalmlp, trainingrays, realtimestepsize, threshold=0.005, baseresolution=4096): # Step 1: Render training rays and extract weighted points weightedpoints = [] for ray in trainingrays: samples = proposalmlp.sample(ray) for sample in samples: xi = sample.position sigmai = trainedmlp.density(xi) wi = calculatevolumeweight(ray, sample, trainedmlp) alphai = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai realtimestepsize) weightedpoints.append((xi, wi, alphai)) # Step 2: Populate binary occupancy grid A occupancygrid = [[[0] baseresolution for in range(baseresolution)] for in range(baseresolution)] for (xi, wi, alphai) in weightedpoints: if wi > threshold and alphai > threshold: voxelindices = getsurroundingvoxels(xi, baseresolution) for idx in voxelindices: occupancygrid[idx[0]][idx[1]][idx[2]] = 1 # Step 3: Generate mipmapped occupancy grids mipmaps = [] for filtersize in [16, 32, 128]: mipmap = maxpool3d(occupancygrid, filtersize) mipmaps.append(mipmap) # Step 4: Bake neural field outputs bakedvoxelgrid = {} baked2dplanes = [] for voxel in getoccupiedvoxels(occupancygrid): x = voxel.center sigma = trainedmlp.density(x) color = trainedmlp.color(x) bakedvoxelgrid[voxel.blockid] = (sigma, color) # Note: The exact procedure for baking the three high-resolution 2D planes is not detailed in the sources. # Step 5: Encode textures pngtextures = encodetopng(baked2dplanes) pngvoxeldata = encodetopng(bakedvoxelgrid) return occupancygrid, mipmaps, (bakedvoxelgrid, baked2dplanes), (pngtextures, pngvoxeldata) def calculatevolumeweight(ray, sample, trainedmlp): Ti = 1.0 for prevsample in ray.samplesbefore(sample): sigmaprev = trainedmlp.density(prevsample.position) deltaprev = prevsample.distancetonext() Ti = math.exp(-sigmaprev deltaprev) sigmai = trainedmlp.density(sample.position) deltai = sample.distancetonext() return Ti (1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai deltai)) def getsurroundingvoxels(point, resolution): indices = [] for dx in [-0.5, 0.5]: for dy in [-0.5, 0.5]: for dz in [-0.5, 0.5]: ix = max(0, min(resolution - 1, int(math.floor(point[0] + dx)))) iy = max(0, min(resolution - 1, int(math.floor(point[1] + dy)))) iz = max(0, min(resolution - 1, int(math.floor(point[2] + dz)))) indices.append((ix, iy, iz)) return indices def maxpool3d(grid, filtersize): res = len(grid) newres = res // filtersize newgrid = [[[0] newres for in range(newres)] for in range(newres)] for x in range(newres): for y in range(newres): for z in range(newres): maxval = 0 for dx in range(filtersize): for dy in range(filtersize): for dz in range(filtersize): maxval = max(maxval, grid[xfiltersize+dx][yfiltersize+dy][zfiltersize+dz]) newgrid[x][y][z] = maxval return newgrid def getoccupiedvoxels(grid): occupied = [] res = len(grid) for x in range(res): for y in range(res): for z in range(res): if grid[x][y][z] == 1: occupied.append(type('Voxel', (), {'center': (x + 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5), 'blockid': (x // 16, y // 16, z // 16), 'localindex': (x % 16, y % 16, z % 16)})()) return occupied def encodetopng(data): # Sources do not specify the exact encoding pipeline beyond PNG compression. return data Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The opacity calculation must use the real-time renderer's step size \delta, not the proposal-MLP's step size, to avoid culling voxels that will be sampled in the real-time viewer. Degenerate Input: If the proposal-MLP fails to sample a region, that region will not be marked as occupied, potentially leading to missing geometry if the proposal-MLP is inaccurate. However, the method guarantees that voxels with significant opacity (\alphai > 0.005) are not culled. City-on-Web Baking is a post-training procedure that converts a neural field representation into a block-sparse, texture-based format optimized for real-time web rendering. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large-scale neural scenes by baking high-resolution 2D planes and low-resolution 3D voxel grids per block, storing only non-empty voxels. It sets itself apart from its parent, MERF Baking, by explicitly targeting web-based delivery through texture compression and block-sparse storage, trading higher frame rates for neural field reconstruction capabilities compared to mesh rasterization methods. Time Complexity: The baking process involves rendering all training rays and evaluating the MLP for occupied voxels. The complexity is proportional to the number of training rays and the number of occupied voxels. Memory Complexity: The memory usage is dominated by the block-sparse voxel grid and the 2D planes. The use of block-sparse storage and PNG compression significantly reduces memory footprint compared to dense grids. Measured Performance: The method achieves real-time rendering speeds in a web browser using three.js. The baking pipeline is almost lossless compared to the pre-baking quality. Strengths: Lossless quality compared to pre-baking; efficient empty space skipping via mipmapped occupancy grids; web-friendly format (PNGs, block-sparse). Limitations: Requires a proposal-MLP for effective sampling; baking time depends on the number of training rays and scene complexity. When to use: Real-time view synthesis in unbounded scenes, particularly for web-based applications. When not to use: Offline rendering where quality is paramount and speed is not a constraint; scenes where the proposal-MLP fails to capture geometry accurately. MERF (Memory-Efficient Radiance Fields) was introduced by Barron et al. in 2022. The baking method is a key component of MERF, enabling real-time rendering of large-scale scenes by converting the neural field into a discrete, sparse format. The method builds on the idea of using occupancy grids for empty space skipping, as seen in Occupancy Grid Update, but extends it with a proposal-MLP-aware pipeline to ensure high fidelity. It solves the problem of storing and transmitting large-scale neural scenes by baking high-resolution 2D planes and low-resolution 3D voxel grids per block, storing only non-empty voxels. It sets itself apart from its parent, MERF Baking, by explicitly targeting web-based delivery through texture compression and block-sparse storage, trading lower frame rates for neural field reconstruction capabilities compared to mesh rasterization methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained neural radiance field (NeRF) or neural rendering model, typically using multi-resolution hash encoding and MLPs for density, color, and specular features. Output: A set of compressed PNG texture assets representing baked grid attributes, organized in a block-sparse structure with Level of Detail (LOD) support. Data Structures: Block-Sparse 3D Voxel Grid: Stores only non-empty voxels. Each block has a voxel resolution of 512^3. High-Resolution 2D Planes (Triplanes): Stored as images within each block. Resolution is 2048^2 per plane. Binary Occupancy Grids (\phi^{k,l}): Identifies occupied voxels within each block. Texture Assets: Baked grid attributes stored as images to reduce memory footprint and accelerate web transmission. Steps: 1. Ray Sampling: Render all training rays to collect ray samples initially. 2. Thresholding: Retain samples with opacity and weight values above a certain threshold; discard samples below the threshold. 3. Occupancy Marking: Use the preserved samples to mark the adjacent eight grid points as occupied in the binary occupancy grids \phi^{k,l}. 4. Baking: Bake high-resolution 2D planes (triplanes) and a low-resolution 3D voxel grid within each block to derive the attribute function f^{k,l}. 5. Sparse Storage: Store only the non-empty 3D voxels using a block-sparse format. 6. LOD Generation: Downsample the occupancy grid using max-pooling to generate lower-resolution LODs for efficient rendering. 7. Compression: Compress the resulting textures into PNG format to reduce storage footprint. Parameters: Voxel resolution per block: 512^3. Triplane resolution per block: 2048^2. Encoder: 4-layer MLP with 64 hidden dimensions (after multi-resolution hash encoding). Deferred MLP: 3-layer MLP with 16 hidden dimensions for residual view-dependent color. Batch size: 16,384 rays per batch. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Web Performance: The method results in lower frame rates compared to mesh rasterization-based methods due to the use of volume rendering. LOD Management: Resource usage decreases with higher LODs, but the lowest LOD maintains high-fidelity rendering results. This variant emphasizes the specific mechanism of marking occupancy and baking. It renders training rays, retains high-opacity/weight samples, marks adjacent grid points in \phi^{k,l}, and bakes triplanes and voxel grids. It explicitly stores non-empty voxels in a block-sparse format and downsamples occupancy grids via max-pooling for LODs, compressing textures to PNG. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Significantly reduced compared to dense grids due to block-sparse storage and texture compression. The lowest LOD still maintains high-fidelity results, but resource usage increases with higher resolution blocks. Measured Performance: On the Matrix City, Campus, and Rubble datasets, the method achieves competitive PSNR, LPIPS, and SSIM scores (e.g., 25.87 PSNR on Matrix City). Scaling: The method is designed for large-scale scenes (e.g., 1200 × 800 square meters) and supports LODs to manage resource loading on web platforms. Strengths: Enables neural field reconstruction for large-scale scenes on the web; reduces memory and transmission costs via compression and sparse storage. Limitations: Lower frame rates compared to mesh rasterization methods due to volume rendering overhead. When to use: Real-time neural rendering of large-scale scenes on web platforms where neural field quality is prioritized over maximum frame rate. When not to use: Applications requiring mesh rasterization performance or where neural field reconstruction is unnecessary. City-on-Web was introduced in 2024 by F. Author et al. in the paper "City-on-Web: Real-Time Neural Rendering of Large-Scale Scenes on the Web". It builds on MERF Baking and is implemented using the nerfstudio framework with the tiny-cuda-nn extension, targeting JavaScript web applications with GLSL rendering.
