name: Occupancy Grid and Importance Sampling Fusion
head: GridNeRFSampler, Lightning-NeRF Sampler
body: A ray sampling method that fuses occupancy grid-based sparse sampling with importance sampling to generate ray samples efficiently for neural radiance fields, specifically designed for autonomous driving scenes. It builds on Occupancy Grid Update by using the grid to perform an initial coarse pass, then redistributing samples based on the resulting density weights to concentrate computation on opaque regions. Inputs: rayso: Tensor of ray origins, shape (N, 3), contiguous. raysd: Tensor of ray directions, shape (N, 3), contiguous. tmin: Optional near plane distance. If not provided, defaults to None (handled as -\infty or ignored by backend). tmax: Optional far plane distance. If not provided, defaults to 10^{10}. densityfn: Callable evaluating density \sigma at positions. If None, density checking is disabled during inference. renderstepsize: Minimum step size for coarse sampling. alphathre: Opacity threshold for skipping samples. Default 0.01. coneangle: Cone angle for adaptive raymarching. 0 for uniform marching. Typical value for real scenes is 1/256 \approx 0.004; 0.0 for Blender scenes. numfinesamples: Number of importance samples to generate per ray for the fine pass. Default 32. self.training: Boolean flag determining if stratified perturbation is applied. occupancygrid: An OccGridEstimator instance used to skip empty space. Outputs: raysamples: Object containing origins, directions, starts, ends, and pixelarea. rayindices: Tensor mapping samples back to original rays. Data Structures: packedinfo: Tensor of shape (R, 2), where R is the number of active rays. Column 0 is the start index in the flattened sample arrays, Column 1 is the count of samples for that ray. rayindices: LongTensor mapping each sample to its source ray ID. starts, ends: 1D Tensors of shape (S,) containing the t-coordinates of sample boundaries, where S is the total number of sample boundaries. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling via Occupancy Grid: Call self.occupancygrid.sampling() with rayso, raysd, tmin, tmax, sigmafn (derived from densityfn), renderstepsize, nearplane, farplane, stratified (based on self.training), coneangle, and alphathre. This returns rayindices, starts, and ends for the coarse samples. 2. Edge Case Handling: If the number of coarse samples is 0 (i.e., starts.shape[0] == 0), create a single fake sample to prevent empty tensor issues: Set rayindices to torch.zeros((1,)). Set starts and ends to torch.ones((1,)). This effectively represents a single sample on the last ray starting and ending at t=1. 3. Compact Ray Indexing: Transform dilated ray indices to compact indices: Compute uniquerayindices = torch.unique(rayindices). Compute newrayindices = torch.bucketize(rayindices, uniquerayindices, right=False). Compute newnumrays = len(uniquerayindices). 4. Pack Uniform Samples: Create packed info for the coarse samples: packedinfouniform = nerfacc.packinfo(newrayindices, newnumrays). 5. Evaluate Density: Compute positions for coarse samples: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o}{ri} + \mathbf{d}{ri} \cdot \frac{\text{starts}i + \text{ends}i}{2} where \mathbf{o} and \mathbf{d} are indexed by newrayindices. Evaluate density: \sigmai = \text{density\fn}(\mathbf{p}i). Squeeze to 1D. 6. Compute Weights: Compute weights from density using the backend's rendering function: wi = \text{render\weight\from\density}(\text{starts}, \text{ends}, \sigmai, \text{packed\info\uniform}) Add epsilon to prevent zero weights: wi \leftarrow wi + 10^{-2}. 7. Prepare for PDF Sampling: Append Trailing Zeros: Create trailingzeros of shape (\text{new\num\rays}, \dots) (zeros). Use packedappend to append these zeros to weightsuniform to serve as the PDF denominator/normalization tail. weightsuniform, packedinfomerged = packedappend(weightsuniform, trailingzeros, 1, newrayindices, packedinfouniform). Append Trailing Ends: Compute the last sample ID for each ray: \text{last\sample\id}r = \text{packed\info\uniform}[r, 0] + \text{packed\info\uniform}[r, 1] - 1 Get trailingends = ends[lastsampleid]. Use packedappend to append these trailing ends to starts to form the bins for sampling. existingbins, = packedappend(starts, trailingends, 1, newrayindices, packedinfouniform). 8. Importance Sampling (Fine Pass): Perform PDF sampling to get fine sample positions t: t{\text{fine}} = \text{packed\sample\PDF}(\text{bins}=\text{existing\bins}, \text{weights}=\text{weights\uniform}, \text{pack\infos}=\text{packed\info\merged}, \text{num\to\sample}=\text{num\fine\samples} + 1, \text{perturb}=\text{self.training}) Extract the sampled t values. 9. Merge Coarse and Fine Samples: Create Fine Ray Indices: \text{ray\indices\fine} = \text{torch.arange}(\text{new\num\rays}) \cdot \text{repeat\interleave}(\text{num\fine\samples}) packedinfofine = nerfacc.packinfo(rayindicesfine, newnumrays). Merge Starts: starts = mergetwopackssortedaligned(starts, packedinfouniform, samplest[...,:-1].reshape(-1), packedinfofine, bsorted=True, returnval=True)[0]. Merge Ends: ends = mergetwopackssortedaligned(ends, packedinfouniform, samplest[..., 1:].reshape(-1), packedinfofine, bsorted=True, returnval=True)[0]. Update Ray Indices: rayindicescomplete = packedappend(newrayindices, rayindicesfine, numfinesamples, newrayindices, packedinfouniform)[0] rayindices = uniquerayindices[rayindicescomplete]. 10. Construct Output: Extract origins and directions: \mathbf{o} = \text{rays\o}[\text{ray\indices}], \mathbf{d} = \text{rays\d}[\text{ray\indices}]. If cameraindices exists, index it similarly. Create Frustums with origins, directions, starts[..., None], ends[..., None], and pixelarea = zeros. Return raysamples and rayindices. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from typing import Tuple def occupancygridandimportancesamplingfusion( rayso: torch.Tensor, raysd: torch.Tensor, tmin: float, tmax: float, densityfn, renderstepsize: float, alphathre: float, coneangle: float, numfinesamples: int, training: bool, occupancygrid, nerfacc, nearplane: float, farplane: float) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """ Returns: rayindices, starts, ends, origins, directions """ # 1. Coarse Sampling rayindices, starts, ends = occupancygrid.sampling( rayso=rayso, raysd=raysd, tmin=tmin, tmax=tmax, sigmafn=densityfn, # Derived from densityfn renderstepsize=renderstepsize, nearplane=nearplane, farplane=farplane, stratified=training, coneangle=coneangle, alphathre=alphathre) # 2. Edge Case: Empty Samples if starts.shape[0] == 0: rayindices = torch.zeros((1,), dtype=torch.long, device=rayso.device) starts = torch.ones((1,), device=rayso.device) ends = torch.ones((1,), device=rayso.device) # Construct fake frustum and return origins = rayso[rayindices] directions = raysd[rayindices] return rayindices, starts, ends, origins, directions # 3. Compact Ray Indices uniquerayindices = torch.unique(rayindices) newrayindices = torch.bucketize(rayindices, uniquerayindices, right=False) newnumrays = len(uniquerayindices) # 4. Pack Uniform Samples packedinfouniform = nerfacc.packinfo(newrayindices, newnumrays) # 5. Evaluate Density # Compute positions: origins + dirs (starts + ends) / 2 # Note: origins and dirs must be indexed by newrayindices originscoarse = rayso[newrayindices] dirscoarse = raysd[newrayindices] # (starts + ends) / 2 midt = (starts + ends) / 2.0 positionsuniform = originscoarse + dirscoarse midt[:, None] sigmasuniform = densityfn(positionsuniform).squeeze() # 6. Compute Weights weightsuniform,, = nerfacc.renderweightfromdensity( tstarts=starts, tends=ends, sigmas=sigmasuniform, packedinfo=packedinfouniform) # Add epsilon weightsuniform = weightsuniform + 1e-2 # 7. Prepare for PDF Sampling # Append trailing zeros to weights trailingzeros = torch.zeros(newnumrays, device=weightsuniform.device) weightsuniform, packedinfomerged = packedappend( feat=weightsuniform, other=trailingzeros, numappendperpack=1, rayindices=newrayindices, packinfos=packedinfouniform) # Append trailing ends to starts lastsampleid = packedinfouniform[:, 0] + packedinfouniform[:, 1] - 1 trailingends = ends[lastsampleid] existingbins, = packedappend( feat=starts, other=trailingends, numappendperpack=1, rayindices=newrayindices, packinfos=packedinfouniform) # 8. Importance Sampling samplest = nerfacc.packedsamplepdf( bins=existingbins, weights=weightsuniform, packinfos=packedinfomerged, numtosample=numfinesamples + 1, perturb=training)[0] # 9. Merge Coarse and Fine # Create fine ray indices rayindicesfine = torch.arange(newnumrays, device=rayso.device) # Repeat interleave logic for indices: each ray index appears numfinesamples times # However, packedinfofine expects counts. # The source uses: rayindicesfine = torch.arange(newnumrays).repeatinterleave(numfinesamples) # But wait, packedinfofine is created from rayindicesfine and newnumrays? # Actually, the source says: # rayindicesfine = torch.arange(newnumrays,...).repeatinterleave(numfinesamples) # packedinfofine = nerfacc.packinfo(rayindicesfine, newnumrays) # This implies rayindicesfine has length newnumrays numfinesamples. rayindicesfine = torch.repeatinterleave(torch.arange(newnumrays, device=rayso.device), numfinesamples) packedinfofine = nerfacc.packinfo(rayindicesfine, newnumrays) # Merge Starts finestarts = samplest[...,:-1].reshape(-1) starts = nerfacc.mergetwopackssortedaligned( starts, packedinfouniform, finestarts, packedinfofine, bsorted=True, returnval=True)[0] # Merge Ends fineends = samplest[..., 1:].reshape(-1) ends = nerfacc.mergetwopackssortedaligned( ends, packedinfouniform, fineends, packedinfofine, bsorted=True, returnval=True)[0] # Update Ray Indices rayindicescomplete = packedappend( feat=newrayindices, other=rayindicesfine, numappendperpack=numfinesamples, rayindices=newrayindices, packinfos=packedinfouniform)[0] rayindices = uniquerayindices[rayindicescomplete] # 10. Construct Output origins = rayso[rayindices] directions = raysd[rayindices] return rayindices, starts, ends, origins, directions def packedappend( feat: torch.Tensor, other: torch.Tensor, numappendperpack: int, rayindices: torch.LongTensor, packinfos: torch.LongTensor) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.LongTensor]: numrays = packinfos.shape[0] newvals = feat.newempty([feat.numel() + numrays numappendperpack]) originalindices = torch.arange(feat.numel(), device=feat.device) originalaranges = torch.arange(numrays numappendperpack, device=feat.device) pidxa = originalindices + (rayindices numappendperpack) expandpackinfos = packinfos.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numappendperpack, -1).reshape(-1, 2) pidxb = expandpackinfos[:, 0] + expandpackinfos[:, 1] + originalaranges newvals.scatter(0, pidxa, feat) newvals.scatter(0, pidxb, other) newpackedinfos = packinfos.clone() newpackedinfos[:, 0] += originalaranges[::numappendperpack] newpackedinfos[:, 1] += numappendperpack return newvals, newpackedinfos Time Complexity: Dominated by the occupancy grid traversal for coarse sampling and the density evaluation at coarse sample positions. Importance sampling adds overhead proportional to numfinesamples but reduces the total number of samples needed for high-quality rendering by concentrating them in opaque regions. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active samples. The packedinfo structures and intermediate tensors (weights, bins) scale with the number of rays and samples per ray. Strengths: Significantly accelerates rendering in large-scale autonomous driving scenes by skipping empty space via the occupancy grid and reducing noise/variance via importance sampling. Limitations: Requires maintaining and updating the occupancy grid. The fusion logic adds implementation complexity compared to simple uniform or stratified sampling. Performance depends heavily on the accuracy of the occupancy grid and the density function. When to use: Neural Radiance Fields for large-scale outdoor scenes (e.g., KITTI-360, Argoverse2) where empty space is prevalent and computational efficiency is critical. When not to use: Small-scale indoor scenes with dense geometry where empty space skipping provides little benefit, or when inference speed is prioritized over quality and density checking is disabled. The method is part of the Lightning-NeRF framework, designed for efficient training and inference of neural radiance fields in autonomous driving scenarios. It leverages the nerfacc library for efficient ray marching and packing operations. The approach combines the spatial efficiency of occupancy grids with the statistical efficiency of importance sampling to handle the scale and sparsity of real-world driving data. name: Occupancy Map Generation via Ray Casting
head: DVGO Voxel Count Views
body: This method generates an occupancy map by counting the number of rays passing through each voxel in a 3D grid, identifying regions viewed by training cameras to initialize or refine the geometry mask. Inputs: rays: Tensor of ray origins and directions. worldsize: Dimensions of the 3D grid. stepsize: Distance between sample points along a ray. near, far: Clamping distances for ray segment intersection. downrate: Downsampling factor for rays if irregularshape is false. irregularshape: Boolean flag determining ray batching strategy. Outputs: count: A zero-initialized tensor with the same shape as the density grid, accumulating ray hits. Data Structures: count: 3D tensor, shape (D, H, W), dtype float32. ones: A DenseGrid object representing a 3D grid of ones, used for gradient accumulation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateoccupancymap(rays, worldsize, stepsize, near, far, downrate, irregularshape, worldbounds): count = torch.zeros(worldsize, dtype=torch.float32) if irregularshape: raybatches = [rays[i:i+10000] for i in range(0, len(rays), 10000)] else: raysdownsampled = rays[::downrate,::downrate].reshape(-1, rays.shape[-1]) raybatches = [raysdownsampled[i:i+10000] for i in range(0, len(raysdownsampled), 10000)] for batch in raybatches: ones = DenseGrid(size=1, worldsize=worldsize, bounds=worldbounds) vec = batch.direction.clone() vec[vec == 0] = 1e-6 ratea = (worldbounds.min - batch.origin) / vec rateb = (worldbounds.max - batch.origin) / vec tmin = max(min(ratea), min(rateb)) tmax = min(max(ratea), max(rateb)) tmin = clamp(tmin, near, far) tmax = clamp(tmax, near, far) Nsamples = int(np.linalg.norm(np.array(worldsize) + 1) / stepsize) + 1 interpx = torch.linspace(tmin, tmax, Nsamples) rayspts = batch.origin + interpx.unsqueeze(1) batch.direction ones.query(rayspts).backward() count += (ones.grad > 1).float() return count Formulas: Sample count per ray: N{\text{samples}} = \left\lfloor \frac{\| \text{world\size} + 1 \|}{\text{stepsize}} \right\rfloor + 1. Intersection bounds: t{\min} = \max(\min(\text{rate\a}), \min(\text{rate\b})) and t{\max} = \min(\max(\text{rate\a}), \max(\text{rate\b})), clamped to [\text{near}, \text{far}]. Parameters: far: Set to 10^9 to prevent rays from stopping early due to small bounding box limits. Nsamples: Calculated as above. Edge Cases: Division by zero in ray direction normalization is handled by replacing zeros with 10^{-6}. Small bounding box limits causing premature ray termination are mitigated by setting far to 10^9. Not given in the sources. name: Brick Occupancy Recomputation
head: Brick Occupancy Compute
body: Brick Occupancy Recomputation is a GPU compute shader routine that regenerates the occupancy status of volumetric bricks after dynamic voxel changes, ensuring the hierarchical traversal structure remains consistent with the underlying voxel data. It differs from static generation methods by being designed for frequent, localized updates in interactive simulations, relying on shared memory reduction to avoid atomic operations and global memory contention. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A texture containing voxel data (1-bit solid/air flags) organized into fixed-size bricks. Output: An occupancy map (brickmap) where each entry corresponds to a brick, storing the count of non-air voxels within that brick. Data Structures: Voxel Texture: 1-bit per voxel representation of solid vs. air. Occupancy Map: Array of unsigned integers, one per brick. Shared Memory: Array of 32 unsigned integers, one per thread in the block. Parameters: Thread Block Size: Exactly 32 threads. Voxels per Thread: 16 voxels. Brick Size: Implicitly 32 \times 16 = 512 voxels per brick. Steps: 1. Dispatch: Launch a compute shader where each thread block is assigned to process exactly one brick. 2. Load: Each of the 32 threads reads 16 voxels from its assigned segment of the brick. 3. Count: Each thread counts the number of voxels in its segment that are not air (i.e., are solid). 4. Store: Each thread writes its count to a unique index in a shared memory array of unsigned integers. 5. Sync: Execute a barrier synchronization to ensure all threads have written their partial counts to shared memory. 6. Reduce: The first thread (thread ID 0) sums the values from the shared memory array. 7. Write: Thread 0 writes the total sum to the corresponding entry in the brickmap. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def brickoccupancyrecompute(brickid, voxeltexture, occupancymap): sharedcounts = [0] 32 threadidx = getlocalthreadid() # 0 to 31 brickstart = brickid 512 voxelbase = brickstart + (threadidx 16) count = 0 for i in range(16): voxelval = voxeltexture[voxelbase + i] if voxelval & 1: # 1-bit solid/air flag count += 1 sharedcounts[threadidx] = count threadbarrier() # Synchronize all threads in the block if threadidx == 0: total = sum(sharedcounts) occupancymap[brickid] = total def getlocalthreadid(): return 0 # Thread 0 to 31 within the block def threadbarrier(): pass # Blocks until all threads in the group reach this point Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Uses a 1-bit per voxel solid/air flag; maximum count per brick is 512. Boundaries: Assumes brick boundaries align with the voxel grid and texture sampling coordinates. Degenerate Input: If the voxel texture is not properly bound or aligned, reads may return undefined values. A two-level hierarchical data structure combining an N-ary tree for hierarchy with regular voxel bricks in leaves, generalizing octree-based Brick Maps for efficient GPU traversal and filtering. See N3-tree with regular mipmapped bricks. Time Complexity: O(1) per brick, proportional to the number of voxels in the brick (512 reads, 32 writes). Memory Complexity: O(1) per brick for shared memory (32 integers). Performance: Fast due to avoidance of atomic operations and use of fast shared memory. Strengths: Low latency and no global memory contention. Limitations: Fixed brick size (512 voxels) and thread count (32). When to Use: Interactive voxel simulations where the world changes frequently and collision detection requires up-to-date occupancy data. When Not to Use: Static volumes or scenes where occupancy rarely changes. Originated in the context of voxel-based game development, specifically for the "VoxelPlayground" project by Joris Rijsdijk, to handle dynamic voxel changes in a brick-based rendering and physics system. It addresses the problem of maintaining consistency between the voxel data and the hierarchical occupancy map used for efficient traversal and collision detection. name: N3-tree with regular mipmapped bricks
head: N3-tree with regular voxel bricks, N3-tree+briques de voxels
body: The N3-tree with regular mipmapped bricks is a two-level hierarchical data structure for procedural volume exploration that combines an N-ary tree (N3-tree) for hierarchy with regular voxel bricks stored in the leaves. It links the compactness of a hierarchical structure with the efficient traversal and trilinear/quadrilinear filtering capabilities of regular grids on GPU. It generalizes the original octree-based Brick Maps to allow arbitrary subdivision of nodes (N-ary instead of binary octree) to enable efficient GPU traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A procedural volume defined by a total maximum resolution Rt on each axis, a maximum brick resolution Rb, and a node subdivision resolution N. Output: A GPU-accessible structure consisting of an indirection texture (the tree), a brick storage texture (the data), and a brick indirection storage (mip-level mapping). Data Structures: 1. Indirection Storage (The Tree): Format: 3D texture using an unsigned integer RGBA format with 32 bits per component. Layout: Each node in the N3-tree is stored as a small N^3 grid of indirection cells within this texture. Spatial Locality: The N^3 grids are organized using a Peano curve (Swizzled Walk) layout to maximize cache efficiency during tree traversal. Cell Encoding (Sub-node information): Each cell contains 32 bits packed as follows: Red (R): 3D address (X, Y, Z) of the child node or the regular brick in the brick storage. Green (G): 3D address of the parent node. Blue (B): Reserved for future use. Alpha (A): Average value of all voxels in the node's covered space. Flags: 1 bit identifies the sub-node type (brick or tree node) and 1 bit identifies an empty node flag (no descendants). Addressable Dimension: The 10-bit address per coordinate allows addressing elements in a storage of maximum dimension 1024^3. 2. Brick Storage (The Data): Format: 3D texture storing regular scalar density data or gradients. Layout: Divided into zones grouping bricks of identical resolution. Brick Structure: Each brick includes its data plus a 1-voxel border surrounding the data to allow trilinear filtering without artifacts from adjacent bricks. Filtering: Accessed in the shader by floating-point coordinates; integer coordinates from the indirection storage are transformed on the fly. 3. Brick Indirection Storage: Purpose: Links the hierarchical tree to brick data. Content: A list of addresses for each brick's data for every mip-mapping level in the brick storage. Unloaded Data: Entries marked with a negative value indicate unloaded data. Manual Mip-mapping: Hardware mip-mapping requires duplicating the 1-voxel border 2^n times for a stack of n levels and halving it at each sub-level, which is memory expensive. This method implements 3D mip-mapping manually to achieve identical performance cost but with lower memory overhead. Number of Nodes: In the worst case (full resolution, no empty space skipping), the number of nodes to store in the tree is calculated as: \sum{i=0}^{n} \left( \frac{Nb}{N^i} \right)^3 Where: n = \frac{\log(Nb)}{\log N} Nb = \frac{Rt}{Rb} Rt: Total maximum resolution on each axis. Rb: Maximum resolution of a brick. N: Resolution of each node (e.g., N=2 for octree). Parameters: Example: Rt = 1024^3, N = 4, Rb = 16. Result: An indirection storage of 64^3 is nearly sufficient. Recommended Size: A practical recommended size is 128^3. Degrees of Freedom: Node subdivision resolution (N) and regular brick resolution. These impact traversal performance and update efficiency. name: Two-stage Ray Marching with Empty-Space Skipping
head: Occupancy Map Empty Space Skipping, Occupancy-based early exit, Simple occupancy map traversal, Two-phase volumetric rendering
body: Two-stage Ray Marching with Empty-Space Skipping is a rendering optimization that accelerates ray traversal in sparse volumetric data by bypassing empty regions using a precomputed occupancy map. It splits ray traversal into two distinct phases: Stage 1 performs cheap lookups in a lower-resolution occupancy grid to locate the entry point into active volume blocks, and Stage 2 performs expensive density sampling only within those active segments. This method sets itself apart from its siblings by decoupling the traversal logic into a coarse "find entry" phase and a fine "integrate" phase, relying on a flat or sparse occupancy grid rather than hierarchical structures like octrees. It builds on the shared principles of Occupancy Grid and Map-Based Empty Space Skipping by utilizing a secondary acceleration structure to define active regions and skip empty space. The method operates by first constructing an occupancy map that indicates which blocks of the primary volume contain data. During rendering, rays traverse this map to skip empty space, then switch to high-resolution sampling upon entering an occupied block. Inputs: Primary volume data (density/opacity field) at resolution N{vol} \times N{vol} \times N{vol}. Occupancy map at resolution N{occ} \times N{occ} \times N{occ}, where N{occ} = N{vol} / B and B is the block size factor. Camera parameters: origin, direction, projection matrix, and world-to-camera transform. Volume bounds: \mathbf{B}{extent} (half-extents) and voxel resolution V{res}. Parameters: RayMaxLength, DensityMult, Smoothing, SmokeOrigin, SmokeRadius. Outputs: Final color buffer (image) with accumulated opacity and color. 1. Primary Volume Buffer: A 3D texture or structured buffer storing density/opacity values. 2. Occupancy Map: A 3D texture or structured buffer storing binary or scalar occupancy status. Layout: Flattened 1D buffer index for voxel (x, y, z) in row-major order: \text{index} = z \cdot (N{vol,x} \cdot N{vol,y}) + y \cdot N{vol,x} + x Values: Typically 0 (empty) or 1 (filled/active). Out-of-bounds queries may return -1. 3. Ray State: origin: Camera position in world space. rayVector: Normalized direction vector. length: Current distance along the ray. smokeValue: Current sampled value (used to track stage state). A compute shader generates the occupancy map. Each shader invocation evaluates a unique volume block for occupancy. For each block in the occupancy grid, sample the corresponding region in the primary volume. Determine occupancy based on a threshold (e.g., max density > 0 or opacity > \epsilon). Write the result to the occupancy map voxel. For each pixel (u, v): 1. Compute ray direction in world space: \mathbf{d}{clip} = (u \cdot 2 - 1, v \cdot 2 - 1, 0) \mathbf{d}{cam} = \text{mul}(\mathbf{M}{invProj}, \mathbf{d}{clip}) \mathbf{rayVector} = \text{normalize}(\text{mul}(\mathbf{M}{camToWorld}, \mathbf{d}{cam})) 2. Set origin to camera position. 3. Initialize length = 0, stepSize = \Delta t{vol} (volume voxel step), smokeValue = -1 (indicating Stage 1 active). Loop until an occupied block is found or the ray exits the volume: 1. Calculate current world position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{origin} + \text{length} \cdot \mathbf{rayVector} 2. Check volume bounds. If \mathbf{p} is outside \mathbf{B}{extent}, return black color (miss). 3. Query occupancy map: Convert \mathbf{p} to occupancy grid coordinates: \mathbf{u}{occ} = \lfloor \mathbf{p} / (B \cdot V{res}) \rfloor (Derived from parent principles and S1 Eq. 10) Sample smokeValue = getSmokeVoxel(p). 4. Skip Logic: If smokeValue == 0 (empty block): Calculate steps to next occupancy voxel boundary. The step count \Delta i in volume voxels is derived from the distance to the next occupancy grid cell boundary. Using the vectorized step calculation: \Delta \mathbf{i} = \lceil (\text{step}(\Delta \mathbf{u}) + \lfloor \mathbf{u} \rfloor - \mathbf{u}) / \Delta \mathbf{u} \rceil where \Delta \mathbf{u} is the ray step in occupancy space: \Delta \mathbf{u}{\text{occ}} = \frac{d{\text{vol}}}{B} \Delta \mathbf{t}{\text{vol}} The scalar step to advance is: \Delta i = \max(\min(\Delta \mathbf{i}), 1) Update length += \Delta i \cdot \Delta t{vol}. If smokeValue > 0 (occupied block): Backward Adjustment: To account for interpolation halos or boundary isosurfaces, decrement the step count to ensure the ray goes back at least one voxel length: \Delta i{\text{backward}} = -\lfloor f \rfloor where f is the sampling factor. \text{length} += \Delta i{\text{backward}} \cdot \Delta t{vol} Switch to Stage 2. Perform high-resolution integration within the occupied block. 1. Initialize stage2StepNum = 0, accumulatedDensity = 0, stage2StepMax = 40 (or until ray exit). 2. Loop while stage2StepNum < stage2StepMax: Calculate samplePoint = origin + length rayVector. Compute density: \text{density} = 1 - \text{smoothstep}(\text{Smoothing}, 1.0, \frac{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{S}{origin}\|}{\mathbf{S}{radius}}) (Note: Source uses screen UVs for noise, which is a known pitfall; correct implementation uses world position). Accumulate: accumulatedDensity += density DensityMult. Update length += stepSize. Increment stage2StepNum. 3. Resume Skipping: After Stage 2, check if the ray is still within an occupied block. If the occupancy map coordinate u{occ} changes and the previous voxel had zero opacity, resume Stage 1 skipping. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostageraymarch(origin, rayvector, volumetexture, occupancymap, params): """ params: B: Block size factor (ratio of vol res to occ res) voxelres: Resolution of primary volume voxels boundsextent: Half-extents of volume bounds raymaxlength: Maximum ray length densitymult: Scaling factor for density smoothing: Smoothstep parameter smokeorigin, smokeradius: Sphere parameters for density """ length = 0.0 stepsize = voxelres smokevalue = -1 # -1: Stage 1, >0: Stage 2 active stage2steps = 0 stage2max = 40 accumulateddensity = 0.0 # Precompute occupancy step delta # Delta uocc is the ray step in occupancy grid units # Delta tvol is the ray step in volume units # Delta uocc = (1/B) (Delta tvol / voxelres) ? # From S1 Eq 10: Delta uocc = (dvol / B) Delta tvol # Assuming dvol is 1 (voxel size in world units? No, dvol is likely 1 if tvol is in voxel units) # Let's assume tvol is in world units. # If tvol = voxelres, then uocc step = voxelres / (B voxelres) = 1/B. # We need to calculate steps to next occupancy boundary. while length < params.raymaxlength: # 1. Calculate current position pos = origin + length rayvector # 2. Bounds Check if not isinsidebounds(pos, params.boundsextent): return 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Miss # 3. Determine Stage if smokevalue <= 0: # Stage 1: Skip Empty Space # Query occupancy map occcoord = floor(pos / (params.B params.voxelres)) smokevalue = occupancymap.sample(occcoord) if smokevalue == 0: # Empty block: Skip to next occupancy voxel # Calculate steps to next boundary in occupancy space # Current u in occupancy space uocc = pos / (params.B params.voxelres) # Ray step in occupancy space deltauocc = rayvector / (params.B params.voxelres) # Calculate steps to next integer boundary for each dimension # Using S1 Eq 8 and 9 # step function: 1 if x >= 0 else 0 stepfunc = [1.0 if d >= 0 else 0.0 for d in deltauocc] # Vectorized step calculation # deltaivec = ceil((step(deltau) + floor(u) - u) / deltau) deltaivec = [] for j in range(3): if deltauocc[j] == 0: deltaivec.append(float('inf')) else: numerator = stepfunc[j] + floor(uocc[j]) - uocc[j] deltaivec.append(ceil(numerator / deltauocc[j])) # Minimum step, clamped to 1 deltai = max(min(deltaivec), 1.0) # Advance length # deltai is in volume voxel steps length += deltai params.voxelres else: # Occupied block found # Backward adjustment to handle interpolation halos # S1 Eq 11: deltaibackward = -floor(f) # f is sampling factor. Assuming f=1 for standard marching deltaibackward = -1 length += deltaibackward params.voxelres # Switch to Stage 2 smokevalue = 1 stage2steps = 0 accumulateddensity = 0.0 else: # Stage 2: Sample Density # Check if we should resume skipping (if we exited the block) occcoord = floor(pos / (params.B params.voxelres)) currentoccupancy = occupancymap.sample(occcoord) if currentoccupancy == 0: # Exited occupied block, resume Stage 1 smokevalue = -1 continue # Perform sampling samplepoint = pos distfromorigin = length(samplepoint - params.smokeorigin) normalizeddist = distfromorigin / params.smokeradius # Density calculation (Simplified from S2, ignoring screen-space noise pitfall) density = 1.0 - smoothstep(params.smoothing, 1.0, normalizeddist) accumulateddensity += density params.densitymult length += params.voxelres stage2steps += 1 if stage2steps >= params.stage2max: # End of block or max steps smokevalue = -1 # Resume skipping continue return accumulateddensity, 0.0, 0.0 # Simplified return def isinsidebounds(pos, boundsextent): return (abs(pos.x) <= boundsextent.x and abs(pos.y) <= boundsextent.y and abs(pos.z) <= boundsextent.z) def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) B (Block Size): Ratio of volume resolution to occupancy map resolution. Larger B skips more empty voxels per sample but reduces precision near occupied regions. Typical values depend on sparsity; e.g., B=4 or B=8. Step Size: Usually equal to the primary volume voxel resolution. Stage 2 Max Steps: Fixed limit (e.g., 40) or until ray exit. Smoothing: Smoothstep edge parameter for density falloff. 1. Stage 2 Bounds Ignorance: The accumulation loop may run for a fixed number of steps regardless of whether the ray has exited the voxel grid, causing smoke to bleed past the volume boundary. 2. Asymmetric Bounds Check: Incorrect bounds checking logic (e.g., position.y < -BoundsExtent.y + BoundsExtent.y) can anchor the volume incorrectly or cause out-of-bounds access. 3. Variable Shadowing: Using length as a variable name can shadow intrinsic functions like length() in HLSL/GLSL. 4. Screen-Space Noise: Sampling noise using screen UVs (uv) pins the noise pattern to the screen, causing it to "swim" as the camera moves. Correct implementation requires sampling noise using world position (samplePoint). 5. Interpolation Halos: Trilinear interpolation can cause a sampling point near the edge of an empty block to map to a non-zero opacity if a neighboring block is occupied. The backward adjustment step is necessary to prevent missing these boundary details. An image-space method that uses detector rays and space leap rays to skip empty space without pre-processing or 3D data structures. Choose when memory is constrained or transfer functions change frequently. Builds on this method by using a preprocessed occupancy map to jump directly from one non-empty voxel to the next. Choose for sparse datasets where a flat occupancy grid offers a better trade-off between memory and traversal simplicity than hierarchical structures. Time Complexity: Stage 1 is O(1) per occupancy voxel visited. Stage 2 is O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the active segment. Total time is proportional to the number of active voxels plus the number of empty blocks skipped. Memory Complexity: O(N{occ}^3) for the occupancy map, where N{occ} = N{vol} / B. This is significantly smaller than the primary volume if B > 1. Performance: Performance scales with the sparsity of the volume. Higher B values improve performance on sparse volumes but may reduce accuracy near boundaries. Strengths: Simple to implement; low memory overhead for the acceleration structure; effective for sparse data. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the occupancy map; less effective for dense volumes; fixed step size in Stage 2 may lead to over-sampling or bleeding. The method originates from efficient ray casting techniques for volumetric images, specifically utilizing distance maps and occupancy grids for empty space skipping. It is a foundational technique in GPU-based volume rendering, often implemented using compute shaders to generate the occupancy map and ray marching kernels to perform the traversal. name: PDF Light Weight Space Leaping
head: LWSL, Light Weight Space Leaping, Light Weight Space Leaping using Ray Coherence, Ray Coherence Space Leaping, Space Leaping using Ray Coherence
body: PDF Light Weight Space Leaping (LWSL) is a space-leaping acceleration technique for volume rendering that exploits ray coherence to skip empty space without requiring pre-processing or 3D data structures. It divides image-plane rays into two groups: detector rays, which perform full ray casting to determine the distance to the first non-empty cell, and space leap rays, which are accelerated by skipping empty space based on information propagated from detector rays. Unlike data-structure-based methods (e.g., DFB) or temporal coherence techniques, LWSL is an image-space method with memory and run-time complexity proportional only to the image size, making it independent of dataset complexity and transfer function changes. Inputs: Volume dataset (voxel grid). Camera parameters (eye position, image plane resolution, projection type: parallel or perspective). Sampling distance \delta. Detector pixel configuration (e.g., 1:4 zig-zag pattern). Outputs: Rendered image buffer. Data Structures: Leap Buffer: A 2D array with resolution equal to the image plane. Each element is an 8-bit or 16-bit integer storing the number of samples the ray traverses in empty space before hitting a non-empty cell. For detector pixels: Stores the sample count returned by the detector ray. For space leap pixels: Stores the minimum sample count from neighboring detector rays in their influence area. Initialization: All entries are zero (empty) before Phase 1. Detector Mask: A boolean array indicating which pixels are detector pixels. Definitions: Cell: A cubical region with voxels at all eight corners and no voxels inside. Empty Cell: A cell where the opacity of all eight corner voxels is zero (for tri-linear interpolation). For higher-order interpolation, all contributing neighboring voxels must have zero opacity. Cell Group: The set of 8 cells surrounding a single voxel. Influence Area: The set of neighboring non-detector pixels to which a detector pixel spreads its leap information. It includes all pixels that could potentially project onto the same cell group without intersecting another detector ray. Parameters: Detector Density: 1 detector ray for every 4 pixels (1:4 ratio) using a zig-zag scheme. Leap Buffer Type: 8-bit or 16-bit integer. Algorithm Steps: 1. Phase 1: Detector Ray Casting 1. Initialize the Leap Buffer to zero and the Detector Mask to false. 2. Identify detector pixels using the zig-zag pattern. 3. For each detector pixel: a. Cast a ray from the pixel into the volume. b. Traverse the ray, checking for empty cells. c. To check if a cell is empty, perform a bitwise OR operation on the opacity values of all voxels in the cell (or all contributing voxels for higher-order interpolation). If the result is non-zero, the cell is non-empty; otherwise, it is empty. d. Skip interpolation, shading, and compositing for empty cells to save time. e. Count the number of samples (N{det}) taken until the first non-empty cell is encountered. f. Store N{det} in the Leap Buffer at the detector pixel's location. g. Mark the location in the Detector Mask as true. h. Perform full ray casting (sampling, compositing, shading) for the detector ray and store the result in the image buffer. 2. Phase 2: Leap Buffer Filling (Spreading) 1. For each detector pixel: a. Identify its influence area (neighboring non-detector pixels). b. For each pixel in the influence area: i. If the neighbor's Leap Buffer value is zero (unset), store the detector pixel's N{det} value. ii. If the neighbor's value is already set, compare it with N{det} and store the minimum of the two. This ensures a conservative estimate, preventing the ray from overshooting a non-empty cell. 2. After spreading, the Leap Buffer is fully populated with the minimum empty-space traversal counts for all pixels. 3. Phase 3: Space Leap Ray Casting 1. Sweep the Leap Buffer from top to bottom (or any order) to find non-detector pixels. 2. For each non-detector pixel: a. Retrieve the leap count N{leap} from the Leap Buffer. b. Boundary Check: If N{leap} == 0, do not leap. Start ray casting from the image plane. c. Perspective Clamp (if applicable): If the projected distance exceeds the maximum accuracy distance x1xn (see Formulas), clamp N{leap} to the corresponding sample count for x1xn. d. Leap: Move the ray start point forward by N{leap} \times \delta along the ray direction. e. Backtracking Check: Sample the first point after leaping. If this point is inside a non-empty cell, backtrack the ray origin backwards by sample steps until an empty cell is found. The maximum backtracking distance is bounded by the longest edge of a cell group divided by \delta. f. Perform standard ray casting (sampling, compositing, shading) from the new start point. Early ray termination can be applied. Formulas: Minimum Projection Width (w{min}): w{min} = \sqrt{p^2 + (2p)^2} = p\sqrt{5} where p is the inter-pixel distance on the image plane in world coordinates. Maximum Inter-pixel Distance for Parallel Projection (p{max}): p{max} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} \mu{min} where \mu{min} is the length of the smallest edge of the voxel unit size. To guarantee detection of single voxels, p \le p{max}. Maximum Ray Traversal Distance for Perspective Projection (x1xn): x1xn = \left( \frac{\sqrt{2} \times \mu{min}}{\sqrt{5} \times p} - 1 \right) \times ex1 where ex1 is the distance from the eye to the image plane. Rays should not leap beyond this distance to maintain accuracy. Backtracking Limit (M{max}): M{max} = \frac{\max(\mux, \muy, \muz)}{\delta} where \mux, \muy, \muz are the cell group edge lengths (or voxel dimensions along the axes) and \delta is the sampling distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lightweightspaceleaping(volume, camera, imagewidth, imageheight, delta, bounds): # 1. Initialize Data Structures leapbuffer = [[0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] isdetector = [[False] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] imagebuffer = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight imagewidth)] # 2. Identify Detector Pixels (1:4 Zig-Zag Pattern) detectorpixels = [] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Zig-zag/Checkerboard pattern ensuring 1 detector per 4 pixels if (x % 2 == 0 and y % 2 == 0) or (x % 2 == 1 and y % 2 == 1): detectorpixels.append((x, y)) isdetector[x][y] = True # 3. Phase 1: Cast Detector Rays for (dx, dy) in detectorpixels: rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(dx, dy) samplescount = 0 currentpos = list(rayorigin) # Traverse until non-empty cell or end of volume while volume.contains(currentpos): cell = volume.getcellat(currentpos) # Check emptiness via bitwise OR of corner opacities cellopacityor = 0 for voxel in cell.corners: cellopacityor |= voxel.opacity if cellopacityor == 0: samplescount += 1 currentpos[0] += raydir[0] delta currentpos[1] += raydir[1] delta currentpos[2] += raydir[2] delta else: break # Store leap info leapbuffer[dx][dy] = samplescount isdetector[dx][dy] = True # Full ray casting for detector pixel color = castray(rayorigin, raydir, volume, delta, samplescount) imagebuffer[dy imagewidth + dx] = color # 4. Phase 2: Fill Leap Buffer (Spreading) # Influence area covers neighbors that could share a cell group projection # Exact radius depends on geometry; a 3x3 window covers immediate neighbors spreadradius = 1 for (dx, dy) in detectorpixels: leapval = leapbuffer[dx][dy] for ny in range(dy - spreadradius, dy + spreadradius + 1): for nx in range(dx - spreadradius, dx + spreadradius + 1): if 0 <= nx < imagewidth and 0 <= ny < imageheight: if not isdetector[nx][ny]: currentval = leapbuffer[nx][ny] if currentval == 0: # Unset leapbuffer[nx][ny] = leapval else: leapbuffer[nx][ny] = min(currentval, leapval) # 5. Phase 3: Cast Space Leap Rays for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if not isdetector[x][y]: leapval = leapbuffer[x][y] # Boundary check if leapval == 0: rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(x, y) color = castray(rayorigin, raydir, volume, delta, 0) imagebuffer[y imagewidth + x] = color continue # Perspective clamp maxsamples = calculatemaxsamplesforaccuracy(camera, delta) effectiveleap = min(leapval, maxsamples) rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(x, y) rayorigin = [rayorigin[i] + raydir[i] effectiveleap delta for i in range(3)] # Backtracking check backtracksteps = 0 maxbacktrack = calculatemaxsamplesforaccuracy(camera, delta) # Upper bound while volume.iscellnonemptyat(rayorigin) and backtracksteps <= maxbacktrack: rayorigin = [rayorigin[i] - raydir[i] delta for i in range(3)] backtracksteps += 1 if not volume.contains(rayorigin): break # Full ray casting from new start color = castray(rayorigin, raydir, volume, delta, 0) imagebuffer[y imagewidth + x] = color return imagebuffer def castray(origin, direction, volume, delta, startsamples): # Inline standard ray casting: sampling, compositing, shading pos = list(origin) for in range(startsamples): pos[0] += direction[0] delta pos[1] += direction[1] delta pos[2] += direction[2] delta color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while volume.contains(pos): sample = volume.sample(pos) alpha = sample.opacity # Standard front-to-back compositing color = [c (1.0 - alpha) + sample.color[i] alpha for i, c in enumerate(color)] if sum(color) > 0.99: # Early ray termination break pos[0] += direction[0] delta pos[1] += direction[1] delta pos[2] += direction[2] delta return color def calculatemaxsamplesforaccuracy(camera, delta): # x1xn = ((sqrt(2) mumin / (sqrt(5) p)) - 1) ex1 # N = x1xn / delta mumin = camera.mumin p = camera.pixeldistance ex1 = camera.eyetoplanedistance x1xn = ((math.sqrt(2) mumin) / (math.sqrt(5) p) - 1) ex1 return int(x1xn / delta) A correction mechanism applied to space leap rays to ensure that no non-transparent sample points are missed during the leap phase. It is distinguished from standard space leaping by the explicit verification of the first sample's location relative to empty space and the subsequent backward movement of the ray origin if it lands inside a non-empty cell. Time Complexity: Proportional to the image size. The number of detector rays is fixed (e.g., 1/4 of total pixels), and the spreading step is also proportional to the number of detector pixels times the influence area size. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the image size. The Leap Buffer requires 8-bit or 16-bit integers per pixel, independent of the volume dataset size. Performance: Provides significant acceleration for scenes with large empty regions. Performance scales with the amount of empty space; more empty space leads to larger leaps and fewer samples. Strengths: No pre-processing or 3D data structures required. Independent of transfer function (can be changed interactively). Works with both parallel and perspective projection. No temporal coherence required; suitable for out-of-order rendering and mosaics. Easy to implement. Limitations: Accuracy depends on the detector pixel density and the geometric bounds (p{max}). If the pixel distance is too large, small objects may be missed. In perspective projection, accuracy degrades beyond distance x1xn, requiring clamping. Requires backtracking in some cases, adding overhead. Not suitable for scenes with very small, sparse objects if the detector density is too low. PDF Light Weight Space Leaping was introduced by Sarang Lakare and Arie Kaufman at the Center for Visual Computing, Stony Brook University, in 2004. It was presented at the IEEE Visualization 2004 conference. The method was developed to address the limitations of previous space-leaping techniques, which either required complex data structures (like DFB) or depended on temporal coherence. It builds on the concept of ray coherence, where neighboring rays often traverse similar distances in empty space. name: Backtracking Space Leap Rays
head: Backtracking Correction for Space Leap Rays
body: Backtracking Space Leap Rays is a correction mechanism applied to space leap rays in volume rendering to ensure that no non-transparent sample points are missed during the leap phase. It solves the problem where a space leap ray, accelerated by a detector ray, might jump past the boundary of a non-empty cell group, thereby skipping valid data. It is distinguished from standard space leaping by the explicit verification of the first sample's location relative to empty space and the subsequent backward movement of the ray origin if it lands inside a non-empty cell. Inputs and Outputs Input: A space leap ray defined by its origin and direction, a leap buffer containing the number of samples taken by the corresponding detector ray to reach the first non-empty cell, and the volume data structure with cell group boundaries. Output: A corrected ray origin that is guaranteed to be in an empty cell, along with a temporary buffer of sample values collected during backtracking. Data Structures Leap Buffer: An array storing integer values representing the number of samples a detector ray traversed through empty space before hitting a non-empty cell. Temporary Buffer: A small array or stack used to store sample values (color and opacity) collected during the backtracking phase to avoid re-sampling. Parameters \delta: The sampling distance (step size) along the ray. \mux, \muy, \muz: The dimensions (edge lengths) of the current cell group. M{max}: The maximum number of samples to backtrack. Steps 1. Leap Check: Determine the tentative new origin of the space leap ray based on the leap buffer value. 2. Boundary Condition Check: If the leap buffer value is zero, do not leap the ray at all; proceed with standard ray marching from the previous position. 3. Leap Adjustment: When leaping, leap one sample less than the value stored in the leap buffer. This ensures that the sample immediately preceding the leap target is the last sample in an empty cell. 4. Empty Cell Verification: Evaluate the volume data at the first sample point of the (adjusted) space leap ray. 5. Backtracking Decision: If the first sample point is inside an empty cell, the ray is correctly positioned before the cell group. Proceed to standard ray marching from this point. If the first sample point is inside a non-empty cell, the ray has jumped too far and missed the object boundary. Initiate backtracking. 6. Backtracking Execution: Move the ray origin backwards by one sample distance (\delta) at a time. Sample the volume at each backtracked position. Store the resulting sample values in the temporary buffer. Continue backtracking until the sample point is located inside an empty cell. Limit: Do not backtrack beyond the limit defined by the leap buffer value, as this would move the ray behind the image plane. Upper Bound: The maximum number of backtracking steps is bounded by M{max}. 7. Compositing: After backtracking completes, composite the sample values stored in the temporary buffer into the final image buffer before continuing with the forward ray march. Formulas The upper limit for the number of samples a ray needs to backtrack is calculated as: M{max} = 2 \times \frac{\max(\mux, \muy, \muz)}{\delta} Where: \mux, \muy, \muz are the longest edges of the cell group. \delta is the sampling distance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backtrackingspaceleapray(rayorigin, raydirection, leapbuffervalue, cellgroupdims, samplingdistance, volumedata): """ Corrects a space leap ray to ensure it starts in an empty cell. Args: rayorigin: Initial origin of the space leap ray. raydirection: Unit direction vector of the ray. leapbuffervalue: Number of empty samples from the detector ray. cellgroupdims: Tuple (mux, muy, muz) of the cell group dimensions. samplingdistance: Step size delta. volumedata: Object providing volume access methods. Returns: correctedorigin: The new ray origin guaranteed to be in empty space. tempsamples: List of sample values collected during backtracking. """ # Step 2: Boundary Condition Check if leapbuffervalue == 0: # Do not leap; use original origin or previous position return rayorigin, [] # Step 3: Leap Adjustment # Leap one sample less than the buffer value to land on the last empty sample leapsamples = leapbuffervalue - 1 tentativeorigin = rayorigin + raydirection (leapsamples samplingdistance) # Step 4: Empty Cell Verification # Check if the first sample point is inside a non-empty cell isnonempty = volumedata.isnonempty(tentativeorigin) if not isnonempty: # Step 5a: First sample is in empty cell return tentativeorigin, [] # Step 5b: First sample is in non-empty cell, initiate backtracking correctedorigin = tentativeorigin tempsamples = [] # Calculate upper limit for backtracking maxedge = max(cellgroupdims) mmax = int(2 (maxedge / samplingdistance)) # Step 6: Backtracking Execution # We backtrack until we find an empty cell. # We must not backtrack beyond the leap buffer value to avoid going behind image plane. backtracklimit = min(mmax, leapbuffervalue) for i in range(1, backtracklimit + 1): # Move back one sample correctedorigin = tentativeorigin - raydirection (i samplingdistance) # Sample the volume samplevalue = volumedata.sample(correctedorigin) tempsamples.append(samplevalue) # Check if we are now in an empty cell if not volumedata.isnonempty(correctedorigin): break # Step 7: Compositing is handled by the caller using tempsamples return correctedorigin, tempsamples Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Leap Buffer: If the leap buffer value is zero, the ray must not be leaped at all. Image Plane Boundary: Backtracking must not exceed the leap buffer value, otherwise the ray origin moves behind the image plane. Off-by-One Leap: Leaping exactly the buffer value would land on the first non-empty sample. Leaping one less ensures the first sample checked is the last empty one, but if that is still non-empty (due to interpolation or data structure granularity), backtracking is required. Time Complexity: Backtracking causes no additional overhead because the ray would have been sampled at those missed points anyway. Memory Complexity: Requires a temporary buffer to store sample values during backtracking. Performance: In practice, M{max} is found to be between 1 and 3 samples. Strengths: Guarantees visual correctness by preventing missed objects. Limitations: Requires checking the volume data at the tentative leap position and storing temporary samples. Backtracking Space Leap Rays was introduced in the paper "PDF Light Weight Space Leaping using Ray Coherence" by Lakare et al. (2004). It was implemented in the Vikon system for perspective direct volume rendering, particularly for endoscopy applications such as Virtual Colonoscopy. The method addresses the coherence-based space leaping technique's vulnerability to missing small or distant objects when leap rays jump over cell group boundaries. name: Volume Occupancy Map Skip
head: Empty Voxel Skip, 空体素跳过技术
body: Volume Occupancy Map Skip is a rendering optimization that accelerates ray traversal in sparse volumetric data by bypassing empty regions. It builds on Two-stage Ray Marching with Empty-Space Skipping by using a preprocessed occupancy map to jump directly from one non-empty voxel to the next, avoiding density evaluations in empty space. Unlike PDF Light Weight Space Leaping, which typically uses hierarchical structures like octrees for space leaping, this method relies on a flat or sparse occupancy grid to identify empty voxels, offering a trade-off between memory overhead and traversal simplicity for specific sparse datasets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric dataset (density field) and a set of rays. Output: Rendered image or accumulated density/transmittance. Auxiliary: A preprocessed Volume Occupancy Map (binary mask). Data Structures: Volume Occupancy Map: A binary volume (mask) of the same dimensions as the density field. Each voxel stores a single bit or byte indicating occupancy: 1 (occupied/non-empty) or 0 (empty). specifies this as a "binary volume." refers to it generally as a "Volume Occupancy Map." Density Field: The primary volumetric data containing density values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline/Initial Stage): Analyze the volumetric dataset to determine which voxels contain non-zero density or significant content. Construct the Volume Occupancy Map. For each voxel v in the grid, set Map[v] = 1 if the voxel is occupied, else Map[v] = 0. In the context of dynamic scenes (e.g., ViSNeRF), this mask may be updated based on empty voxels determined from multiple static scenes. 2. Ray Traversal (Runtime): For each ray, perform standard ray-box intersection to find the entry point into the volume bounding box. Initialize ray parameters (position, direction, step size). Loop: a. Check the current voxel's occupancy status in the Volume Occupancy Map. b. If Empty (Map[v] == 0): Skip sampling the density function. Jump to the next non-empty voxel. The method of jumping depends on the implementation: Naive: Increment voxel coordinates until a non-empty voxel is found. Optimized: Use a precomputed list of occupied voxel indices or a sparse structure (like a linked list of occupied voxels) to jump directly. implies "jumping directly to the next non-empty voxel," suggesting an efficient lookup rather than linear scan, though the exact data structure for the "jump" is not detailed in the sources. A common implementation uses a sorted list of occupied voxel coordinates or a sparse hash map for O(1) or O(\log N) lookup. c. If Occupied (Map[v] == 1): Sample the density function at the current ray position. Accumulate color and opacity (standard volume rendering integration). Advance the ray by a step size (e.g., 0.5 voxel spacing as noted in medical imaging contexts). Update ray position. d. Termination: Stop if the ray exits the volume bounding box. Stop if transmittance drops below a threshold (early ray termination). Formulas: Occupancy Check: Occupancy(v) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \rho(v) > \epsilon \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \rho(v) is the density at voxel v and \epsilon is a small threshold. Ray Advancement: P{next} = P{current} + \Delta t \cdot \vec{d}, where \Delta t is the step size. Parameters: Step Size: Typically set to 0.5 voxel spacing to balance detail and performance in medical imaging. Threshold (\epsilon): Not given in the sources. A small value (e.g., 10^{-6}) is typical to define "empty." Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point comparisons for occupancy should use a small epsilon to avoid missing thin structures due to numerical noise. Boundaries: Ensure the occupancy map covers the entire volume bounding box. Rays exiting the box must be handled correctly. Dynamic Scenes: For dynamic scenes, the occupancy map must be updated efficiently. Sparse Data: If the data is extremely sparse, a flat occupancy map may consume significant memory. mentions "sparse clouds" and "sparse voxel" structures in comparisons, implying that for very large sparse volumes, a sparse representation of the occupancy map (e.g., using a hash table or linked list) might be necessary, though the core method described uses a "Volume Occupancy Map." An efficiency optimization used in training neural radiance fields (e.g., ViSNeRF) to skip sampling at empty voxels along valid rays. It creates a binary mask volume after an initial training stage to record empty voxels, improving subsequent training efficiency. For dynamic scenes, the mask is updated based on empty voxels from multiple static scenes. Time Complexity: Depends on the implementation of the "jump." If using a linear scan through the occupancy map, it is O(N) in the worst case (where N is the number of voxels along the ray). If using a precomputed list of occupied voxels, it is O(K) where K is the number of occupied voxels along the ray. notes that 3D-DDA (which this builds on) has complexity O(n) where n is the number of voxels traversed, compared to O(N^3) for brute force. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the total number of voxels in the grid, for the occupancy map. compares memory usage: "Low" for brute force, "High" for octrees, "Medium" for 3D-DDA, and "Extremely High" for SVO. The occupancy map adds a memory overhead proportional to the volume size. Performance: In a medical imaging project, this technique increased rendering frame rate by 3.2x. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for sparse data; reduces expensive density evaluations. Limitations: Requires preprocessing; memory overhead for the occupancy map; less effective for dense data. When to use: Sparse volumetric data (e.g., atmospheric clouds, medical CT with large empty regions). When not to use: Dense volumetric data where most voxels are occupied; memory-constrained environments. The technique is described in the context of volume rendering optimizations, specifically for sparse data like atmospheric clouds or medical imaging. cites a medical imaging project where it improved frame rates. applies a similar concept ("Voxel skipping") in the context of ViSNeRF for dynamic volumetric scenes, using a mask volume to skip empty voxels during training. name: Hierarchical Sampling with Occupancy Grid
head: FLASH Renderer, NeRF Hierarchical Sampling
body: Hierarchical Sampling with Occupancy Grid is a two-stage volume rendering method that combines empty-space skipping via an occupancy grid with importance-based hierarchical sampling to accelerate Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training and inference. It differs from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the coarse sampling phase (guided by spatial occupancy) from the fine sampling phase (guided by rendered weights), allowing for efficient refinement of high-density regions without re-evaluating empty space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o}, ray directions \mathbf{d}, near/far clipping planes (t{\text{near}}, t{\text{far}}), an occupancy grid structure, a coarse NeRF model, and a fine NeRF model. Outputs: Rendered RGB color, depth, accumulated opacity, and weights for each ray. Data Structures: OccupancyGrid: A 3D boolean grid representing the spatial distribution of active volume data. resolution: Integer, the side length of the cubic grid. aabbmin: Tensor of shape [3], minimum bounds of the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) in world space. aabbmax: Tensor of shape [3], maximum bounds of the AABB in world space. densitythreshold: Float, the density threshold used to determine if a voxel is occupied. grid: Boolean tensor of shape [resolution, resolution, resolution], where True indicates an occupied voxel. voxelsize: Tensor of shape [3], the physical size of each voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Normalize Ray Directions: Normalize the input ray directions to unit length: \mathbf{d}{\text{norm}} = \frac{\mathbf{d}}{\|\mathbf{d}\|} 2. Coarse Sampling with Empty-Space Skipping: Determine coarse sample positions t{\text{coarse}} along the ray. If an OccupancyGrid is available, query it to find occupied regions within [t{\text{near}}, t{\text{far}}] and sample points within these segments. If no occupancy grid is present, perform standard stratified sampling across the entire interval [t{\text{near}}, t{\text{far}}]. Let Nc be the number of coarse samples (default 32). 3. Coarse Rendering: Evaluate the coarse model at positions \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + t{\text{coarse}, i} \mathbf{d}{\text{norm}}. Query the coarse model for density \sigmai and color \mathbf{c}i. Compute distances between adjacent samples: di = t{\text{coarse}, i+1} - t{\text{coarse}, i}. Append a large distance (e.g., 10^{10}) for the last segment to handle the background contribution. Compute alpha opacity: \alphai = 1.0 - \exp(-\sigmai \cdot di) Compute transmittance (accumulated opacity from previous samples): Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj + \epsilon) where \epsilon = 10^{-10} is added for numerical stability. Compute weights: wi = Ti \cdot \alphai Compute coarse color and depth: \mathbf{C}{\text{coarse}} = \sum{i=0}^{Nc-1} wi \mathbf{c}i D{\text{coarse}} = \sum{i=0}^{Nc-1} wi t{\text{coarse}, i} A{\text{coarse}} = \sum{i=0}^{Nc-1} wi 4. Hierarchical Fine Sampling: Use the coarse weights wi to guide the placement of fine samples. Compute midpoints between coarse samples: t{\text{mid}, i} = \frac{t{\text{coarse}, i} + t{\text{coarse}, i+1}}{2} Construct bins for sampling: \text{bins} = [t{\text{coarse}, 0}, t{\text{mid}, 0}, \dots, t{\text{mid}, Nc-2}, t{\text{coarse}, Nc-1}] Sample Nf fine positions t{\text{fine}} from these bins, where the probability of sampling in a bin is proportional to the sum of weights of the coarse samples defining that bin. This is done via inverse transform sampling using the cumulative weights. 5. Combine and Sort: Concatenate coarse and fine samples: t{\text{combined}} = \text{sort}(t{\text{coarse}} \cup t{\text{fine}}) Let N{\text{total}} = Nc + Nf. 6. Fine Rendering: Evaluate the fine model at all positions in t{\text{combined}}. Query the fine model for density \sigma'i and color \mathbf{c}'i. Recompute di, \alphai, Ti, wi using the fine model's densities and the sorted t{\text{combined}} intervals. Compute final color: \mathbf{C}{\text{final}} = \sum{i=0}^{N{\text{total}}-1} wi \mathbf{c}'i Compute final depth: D{\text{final}} = \sum{i=0}^{N{\text{total}}-1} wi t{\text{combined}, i} Compute final accumulated opacity: A{\text{final}} = \sum{i=0}^{N{\text{total}}-1} wi 7. Background Compositing: If a white background is assumed, add the background contribution: \mathbf{C}{\text{out}} = \mathbf{C}{\text{final}} + (1.0 - A{\text{final}}) \cdot \mathbf{1} Otherwise, \mathbf{C}{\text{out}} = \mathbf{C}{\text{final}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def hierarchicalsamplingwithoccupancygrid( rayso, # [numrays, 3] raysd, # [numrays, 3] near, # float far, # float numcoarse, # int numfine, # int occupancygrid, # Optional OccupancyGrid object modelcoarse, # Coarse NeRF model modelfine, # Fine NeRF model whitebackground=True): # 1. Normalize rays raysd = torch.nn.functional.normalize(raysd, dim=-1) # 2. Coarse Sampling if occupancygrid is not None: occupiedintervals = occupancygrid.sampleoccupiedregions(rayso, raysd, near, far) tcoarse = samplefromintervals(occupiedintervals, numcoarse) else: tcoarse = samplestratified(near, far, numcoarse) # 3. Coarse Rendering positionscoarse = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + tcoarse.unsqueeze(2) raysd.unsqueeze(1) posflat = positionscoarse.reshape(-1, 3) dirflat = raysd.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numcoarse, -1).reshape(-1, 3) rgbcoarse, densitycoarse = modelcoarse(posflat, dirflat) rgbcoarse = rgbcoarse.reshape(-1, numcoarse, 3) densitycoarse = densitycoarse.reshape(-1, numcoarse) # Compute distances dists = tcoarse[:, 1:] - tcoarse[:,:-1] # Append a large distance for the last segment to handle background dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.full((dists.shape[0], 1), 1e10, device=dists.device)], dim=-1) # Compute Alpha alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densitycoarse dists) # Compute Transmittance: T[i] = prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - alpha[j] + eps) oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alpha + 1e-10 T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[:,:1]), oneminusalpha], dim=-1).cumprod(dim=-1)[:,:-1] weightscoarse = T alpha # 4. Hierarchical Fine Sampling tmid = 0.5 (tcoarse[:,:-1] + tcoarse[:, 1:]) bins = torch.cat([tcoarse[:,:1], tmid, tcoarse[:, -1:]], dim=-1) tfine = samplehierarchical(bins, weightscoarse.detach(), numfine) # 5. Combine and Sort tcombined = torch.cat([tcoarse, tfine], dim=-1) tcombined, = torch.sort(tcombined, dim=-1) # 6. Fine Rendering positionsfine = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + tcombined.unsqueeze(2) raysd.unsqueeze(1) posflatfine = positionsfine.reshape(-1, 3) dirflatfine = raysd.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, tcombined.shape[1], -1).reshape(-1, 3) rgbfine, densityfine = modelfine(posflatfine, dirflatfine) rgbfine = rgbfine.reshape(-1, tcombined.shape[1], 3) densityfine = densityfine.reshape(-1, tcombined.shape[1]) # Recompute distances for combined samples distscombined = tcombined[:, 1:] - tcombined[:,:-1] distscombined = torch.cat([distscombined, torch.full((distscombined.shape[0], 1), 1e10, device=distscombined.device)], dim=-1) alphafine = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densityfine distscombined) oneminusalphafine = 1.0 - alphafine + 1e-10 Tfine = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alphafine[:,:1]), oneminusalphafine], dim=-1).cumprod(dim=-1)[:,:-1] weightsfine = Tfine alphafine # 7. Composite rgbintegrated = torch.sum(weightsfine.unsqueeze(-1) rgbfine, dim=1) acc = torch.sum(weightsfine, dim=-1) depth = torch.sum(weightsfine tcombined, dim=-1) if whitebackground: rgbfinal = rgbintegrated + (1.0 - acc.unsqueeze(-1)) else: rgbfinal = rgbintegrated return rgbfinal, depth, acc, weightsfine def samplestratified(near, far, numsamples): """Standard stratified sampling over [near, far].""" step = (far - near) / numsamples offsets = torch.randlike(near) step return near + torch.arange(numsamples, device=near.device).float() step + offsets def samplefromintervals(intervals, numsamples): """Sample uniformly from a list of [start, end] intervals per ray.""" # intervals: list of [numrays, K] tensors # Flatten intervals to sample from starts = torch.stack([iv[:, 0] for iv in intervals], dim=-1) ends = torch.stack([iv[:, 1] for iv in intervals], dim=-1) lengths = ends - starts totallength = lengths.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) probs = lengths / (totallength + 1e-10) # Select interval index per sample u = torch.rand(numsamples, device=starts.device) cumprobs = torch.cumsum(probs, dim=-1) # Broadcast cumprobs to numsamples cumprobs = cumprobs.unsqueeze(0).expand(numsamples, -1, -1) u = u.unsqueeze(-1).unsqueeze(-1).expand(-1, cumprobs.shape[1], cumprobs.shape[2]) binindices = torch.searchsorted(cumprobs, u, right=True) binindices = torch.clamp(binindices, 0, probs.shape[1] - 1) # Sample uniformly within selected interval localu = torch.rand(numsamples, device=starts.device) selectedstarts = torch.gather(starts, 1, binindices) selectedlengths = torch.gather(lengths, 1, binindices) return selectedstarts + localu selectedlengths def samplehierarchical(bins, weights, numsamples): """Inverse transform sampling from bins weighted by coarse weights.""" # Normalize weights to probabilities prob = weights / (weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-10) # Cumulative distribution cdf = prob.cumsum(dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[:,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Generate uniform random numbers u = torch.randlike(cdf) # Find bin index for each u binindices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, right=True) - 1 binindices = torch.clamp(binindices, 0, bins.shape[1] - 2) # Interpolate within the bin binstart = bins[torch.arange(bins.shape[0]), binindices] binend = bins[torch.arange(bins.shape[0]), binindices + 1] # Map u to the specific bin's local probability bincdfstart = cdf[torch.arange(cdf.shape[0]), binindices] bincdfend = cdf[torch.arange(cdf.shape[0]), binindices + 1] localu = (u - bincdfstart) / (bincdfend - bincdfstart + 1e-10) return binstart + localu (binend - binstart) Parameters: near: Float, default 2.0. Near clipping plane distance. far: Float, default 6.0. Far clipping plane distance. numcoarsesamples: Integer, default 32. Number of samples taken along each ray in the coarse stage. numfinesamples: Integer, default 64. Number of samples taken along each ray in the fine stage. occupancygrid: Optional OccupancyGrid instance. If present, used for empty-space skipping during coarse sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero in Ray-AABB Intersection: When computing ray-box intersections for the occupancy grid, add a small epsilon (10^{-8}) to ray directions to prevent division by zero if a ray is parallel to a box face. Numerical Stability in Transmittance: Add 10^{-10} to (1 - \alpha) before computing the cumulative product to prevent NaN values due to floating-point underflow. Model Input Compatibility: If the model does not support forwardwithdensityonly, dummy zero directions may need to be passed to satisfy input shape requirements during density-only queries. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: FLASH achieves training speeds of 10-15 minutes on a single GPU for synthetic scenes, significantly faster than vanilla NeRF. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space, reducing the number of model evaluations. Hierarchical sampling focuses computational effort on high-density regions, improving image quality per sample. Limitations: Requires construction and maintenance of the occupancy grid. Performance depends on the sparsity of the scene; if the scene is dense, the occupancy grid provides less benefit. Hierarchical Sampling with Occupancy Grid is implemented in the FLASH (Fast Learning for Accurate Scene Hashing) project, an experimental implementation of Instant-NGP for Neural Radiance Fields. It was developed to enable rapid training of 3D scenes from 2D images, leveraging multi-resolution hash encoding and occupancy grids for acceleration.
