name: Empty Space Filtering (Training-Time Bounding Box)
head: Alpha-based Bounding Box Filtering, Ray skipping, Training-Time Bounding Box, Training-time Empty Space Filtering
body: Empty Space Filtering is a training-time optimization strategy that accelerates neural volume rendering by restricting computation to the scene's actual content. It solves the problem of wasted computation in empty space by identifying a tight bounding box and filtering out empty samples during ray traversal. Unlike static acceleration structures that rely on pre-computed occupancy grids or distance maps, this method derives its acceleration structure dynamically from the learned alpha values of a coarse model during the initial training stages. It sets itself apart from siblings like Distance Map Acceleration by using learned opacity rather than geometric distance, and from Two-stage Ray Marching with Empty-Space Skipping by integrating the bounding box shrinkage directly into the training loop of dynamic scenes. The method operates in two phases: bounding box determination and sample filtering. It builds on the shared principles of Occupancy Grid and Map-Based Empty Space Skipping by constructing a secondary structure (the bounding box) and defining activity via alpha thresholds. Inputs: Coarse deformation feature grid (or coarse geometry prior) from the initial training stage. Alpha threshold \tau. Ray origin o and direction d. Outputs: A tight axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) [min, max] enclosing all object points. A filtered set of sample points along the ray, excluding those identified as empty. 1. Coarse Deformation Feature Grid: A 3D grid storing deformation features. Each vertex v has an associated alpha value \alpha(v) derived from the density field. 2. Bounding Box: An axis-aligned bounding box defined by minimum and maximum coordinates (x{min}, y{min}, z{min}) and (x{max}, y{max}, z{max}). 3. Empty Mask (Optional): A binary volume or mask recording whether each voxel is empty, used to skip empty voxels along valid rays. 1. Query Alpha Values: Query all grid vertices of the coarse deformation feature grid across all training time steps t \in [0, T] to retrieve their alpha values \alpha(v, t). 2. Classify Vertices: Classify each grid vertex v as an object point if its alpha value exceeds a predefined threshold \tau for at least one time step, or if it is consistently below \tau across all time steps (depending on the specific implementation variant). Specifically, a point is assumed to belong to an object if: \alpha(v, t) > \tau If \alpha(v, t) \le \tau for all t, the point is classified as empty space. 3. Compute Bounding Box: Compute the smallest axis-aligned bounding box that fully encloses all vertices classified as object points across all time steps. This box is initialized to the full extent of the scene and shrunk after the initial training stage completes. 4. Ray Intersection Test: For each ray, test if it intersects the computed bounding box. If the ray does not intersect the box, skip the ray completely. 5. Sample Filtering: During ray marching, filter out sampled points that are recognized as empty. For points in the deformation module, filter out points whose alpha values are always below the threshold during all training times. For points in the canonical module, filter out empty points only at the canonical time. Alternatively, use a pre-calculated occupancy grid to prune non-occupied points along rays. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeboundingbox(coarsegrid, alphathreshold): """ Computes the tight bounding box enclosing all object points. coarsegrid: 3D grid of alpha values for all time steps. alphathreshold: scalar threshold for object vs empty space. Returns: (mincoords, maxcoords) """ mincoords = [infinity, infinity, infinity] maxcoords = [-infinity, -infinity, -infinity] # Query all grid vertices across all time steps for t in range(numtimesteps): for v in coarsegrid.vertices: alpha = coarsegrid.getalpha(v, t) if alpha > alphathreshold: # Vertex is an object point for i in range(3): if v.coords[i] < mincoords[i]: mincoords[i] = v.coords[i] if v.coords[i] > maxcoords[i]: maxcoords[i] = v.coords[i] return mincoords, maxcoords def raymarchingwithfiltering(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox, coarsegrid, alphathreshold): """ Performs ray marching, skipping empty space. rayorigin: (x, y, z) raydirection: (x, y, z) boundingbox: (mincoords, maxcoords) coarsegrid: 3D grid of alpha values alphathreshold: scalar threshold Returns: rendered color """ # Step 1: Ray-Bounding Box Intersection Test tmin, tmax = intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox) if tmin is None: return backgroundcolor # Skip ray completely # Step 2: Ray Marching with Empty Space Filtering color = 0.0 alphaaccum = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax and alphaaccum < 1.0: point = rayorigin + t raydirection # Check if point is empty # Query alpha value at this point from coarse grid alpha = queryalpha(coarsegrid, point) if alpha > alphathreshold: # Point is not empty, compute contribution density, colorcontribution = evaluateneuralfield(point) weight = alphacontribution (1.0 - alphaaccum) color += weight colorcontribution alphaaccum += weight else: # Point is empty, skip sampling pass t += stepsize return color Alpha Threshold (\tau): A predefined scalar value used to distinguish object points from empty space. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but it must be small enough to capture low-density regions. Bounding Box Initialization: Initialized to the full extent of the scene, then shrunk based on the occupancy grid at step 2,000 of training. Low-Density Regions: Low-density regions (e.g., a white plate on a white background) may be incorrectly filtered out because the image reconstruction error is low even if the learned density is close to zero. This can be alleviated by using a background with a different color or disabling the filtering strategy. Bounding Box Shrinkage Timing: If the bounding box is not shrunk after the initial training stage, it will contain empty voxels, reducing the effectiveness of ray skipping. Dynamic Scenes: For dynamic scenes, the bounding box must account for object motion across all time steps to ensure no object points are excluded. Depth-guided voxel pre-pruning is a preprocessing strategy that removes voxels located in free space using a dense depth prior before the optimization phase begins. It reduces the number of samples in free space and the parameters to be optimized, thereby accelerating training while implicitly regularizing scene geometry without requiring explicit depth supervision. Unlike methods that rely on explicit depth supervision using sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) or imperfect monocular depth estimators, this method leverages dense, multi-view consistent depth priors from 3D vision foundation models to prune the voxel grid directly. Occupancy Pruning and Bounding Box Shrinkage is a training and inference acceleration technique that pre-calculates an occupancy grid to prune non-occupied points along rays and shrinks the scene bounding box for more accurate modeling. The occupancy grid is pre-calculated at training steps 2,000 and 4,000. The bounding box is shrunk based on the grid at step 2,000. The grid is kept for scene composition, recorded per object, and used with warped rays to query occupancy. L1 regularization is applied to the factored matrices for density to encourage sparsity in tensor rank decomposition parameters. Time Complexity: Reduces training and rendering time by avoiding computation in empty space. Without filtering, training speed, render speed, and PSNR are all clearly worse than the full model. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the coarse deformation feature grid and potentially an occupancy grid. Strengths: Significantly reduces time consumption of training and rendering by reducing the number of queries to the light-weight MLP. It allows for full use of grid resolution by locating the smallest box region that fully covers the whole scene. Limitations: May incorrectly filter out low-density regions if the background color is similar to the object. Requires an initial training stage to compute the bounding box and occupancy grid. When to Use: When training dynamic neural volume rendering models where empty space constitutes a significant portion of the volume. When Not to Use: When the scene contains low-density objects with colors similar to the background, as they may be incorrectly filtered out. Empty Space Filtering was proposed in the context of Neural Deformable Voxel Grid (NDGV) for fast optimization of dynamic view synthesis. It was introduced to speed up training by reducing the number of queries to the light-weight MLP and locating the smallest box region that fully covers the whole scene. The method builds on the idea of using alpha values from a coarse deformation feature grid to identify empty space. It has been adopted in other works such as ViSNeRF for efficient multidimensional neural radiance field representation and Compressible-Composable NeRF via rank-residual decomposition. name: Depth-guided Voxel Pre-pruning
head: Depth prior voxel pruning, Free space pruning via depth prior
body: Depth-guided voxel pre-pruning is a preprocessing strategy that removes voxels located in free space using a dense depth prior before the optimization phase begins. It reduces the number of samples in free space and the parameters to be optimized, thereby accelerating training while implicitly regularizing scene geometry without requiring explicit depth supervision. Unlike methods that rely on explicit depth supervision using sparse Structure-from-Motion (SfM) or imperfect monocular depth estimators, this method leverages dense, multi-view consistent depth priors from 3D vision foundation models to prune the voxel grid directly. Inputs: Sparse multi-view images I = \{In\}{n=1}^S. Camera intrinsics K = \{Kn\}{n=1}^S and extrinsics P = \{Pn\}{n=1}^S. Voxel grid V (either density grid VD or spherical harmonics grid V{SH}) with resolution [Nx, Ny, Nz]. Scene bounding box defined by corners (xa, ya, za) and (xb, yb, zb). Ray marching step size s. Threshold \tau for confidence filtering. Outputs: Pruned voxel grid V. Data Structures: Grid Mask (Mg): A boolean array of shape [Nx, Ny, Nz]. True indicates the voxel is active (to be kept/optimized); False indicates the voxel is pruned (free space). Initialized to all True. Ray Sets: World frame: Origin set Ow, Direction set Qw. Grid frame: Origin set Og, Direction set Qg. Distance parameter T: Array of scalar values representing distance along each ray. Depth Data: Depth maps D = \{Dn\}{n=1}^S. Confidence maps E = \{En\}{n=1}^S. Binary masks M = \{Mn\}{n=1}^S. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. D, E = VGGTforward(I) # Obtain depths and confidences from foundation model M = [np.array(e >= tau, dtype=bool) for e in E] # Filter low-confidence depths Ow, Qw = generaterays(K, P) # Generate rays in world frame Dfiltered = [Dn[Mn] for Dn, Mn in zip(D, M)] Rwfiltered = [Rw[Mn] for Rw, Mn in zip([Ow, Qw], M)] # Aggregate valid rays/depths Og, Qg, Dg = transformtogridframe(Rwfiltered, Dfiltered, boundingbox, resolution) Tn, Tf = computeraygridintersection(Og, Qg, boundingbox) # Near and far bounds valid = Tn <= Tf # Filter non-intersecting rays Og, Qg, Dg, Tn, Tf = [arr[valid] for arr in [Og, Qg, Dg, Tn, Tf]] Mg = np.ones((Nx, Ny, Nz), dtype=bool) # Grid mask Mr = np.ones(len(Og), dtype=bool) # Ray mask T = Tn.copy() # Current marching distance while np.any(Mr): P = Og + T[:, None, None] Qg # Compute ray positions I, J, K = voxelindices(P) # Determine occupied voxel indices Mg[I, J, K] = False # Mark occupied voxels as pruned T = T + s # Advance marching distance Mr[T >= Dg] = False # Deactivate rays past depth prior # Filter active rays and data Og, Qg, Dg, T, Mr = [arr[Mr] for arr in [Og, Qg, Dg, T, Mr]] V = V[Mg] # Apply grid mask to voxel grid return V Parameters: \tau: Manually set threshold for filtering low-confidence depths. If confidence e < \tau, the depth is discarded. s: Ray marching step size used in the iterative voxel marking process. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Overpruning: If depth priors are larger than ground truth, scene voxels may be incorrectly removed. Discreteness Error: Voxels occupied by the scene surface might be pruned even with high-accuracy depths due to voxel grid discreteness. Confidence Threshold Selection: The threshold \tau is manually set; improper selection may retain noisy depths or discard valid ones. A morphological operation applied to a pruned voxel grid to restore voxels that were incorrectly removed due to artifacts in the depth prior. It is executed immediately after the depth-guided pre-pruning step to alleviate overpruning resulting from inevitable artifacts existing in the depth prior. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method is described as highly efficient, completing the necessary geometry initialization in a matter of seconds using parallel computing. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the grid mask Mg (Nx Ny Nz), ray sets, and depth maps. The pruning reduces the final memory footprint of the voxel grid V. Strengths: Avoids the computational burden and imperfect data issues of explicit depth supervision. It reduces samples in free space and parameters to be optimized, accelerating training. It implicitly imposes geometric constraints without introducing extra computational cost during training. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy and density of the depth prior. Overpruning can occur if the depth prior is inaccurate or too large. Discreteness errors may lead to slight geometry loss at surfaces. When to use: When using explicit voxel radiance field representations (e.g., Plenoxels) and sparse multi-view inputs, particularly when training efficiency is critical and a 3D vision foundation model is available to provide dense depth priors. When not to use: When high-precision geometry is required without post-processing dilation, or when depth priors are known to be significantly inaccurate or sparse. Depth-guided voxel pre-pruning was proposed in the context of F2Plenoxels, a framework for fast few-shot view synthesis based on explicit voxel radiance field representations. The method addresses the challenges of incorporating depth supervision, which increases training overhead and relies on imperfect data from SfM, image matchers, or monocular depth estimators. Instead of explicit depth supervision, F2Plenoxels uses depth priors from the 3D vision foundation model VGGT (Wang et al. 2025) to prune voxels before training. VGGT was chosen because it is completely feedforward, supports a variable number of input views, and balances density and multi-view consistency. The method builds on the concept of empty space filtering but specifically targets voxel grids using dense depth priors to implicitly regularize geometry. name: MERF Real-Time Rendering
head: MERF viewer, Real-Time Viewer Rendering Pipeline, Three.js MERF renderer
body: MERF Real-Time Rendering is a WebGL-based implementation for synthesizing views from Memory-Efficient Radiance Fields (MERF) using a multi-resolution occupancy grid hierarchy for empty space skipping. It differs from CUDA-based accelerators like Instant-NGP by prioritizing browser portability and memory efficiency, achieving real-time frame rates on consumer hardware by combining coarse-to-fine grid queries with deferred appearance sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: MERF scene representation (split into density texture and appearance texture containing diffuse RGB and feature vectors), camera parameters, and a multi-resolution occupancy grid hierarchy. Output: Final image color per pixel. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy Grid Hierarchy: A set of binary textures representing spatial occupancy. Construction: Generated by max-pooling a full-resolution binary mask A with filter sizes F \in \{16, 32, 128\}. Resolution: If the base resolution is R, the hierarchy levels have resolutions R/16, R/32, and R/128. Storage: Textures are encoded as PNGs to reduce video memory usage. 2. Scene Textures: Density Texture: Stores volume density \sigma. Appearance Texture: Stores diffuse RGB colors and feature vectors. Layout: Split into separate components to allow deferred access. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, generate ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. 2. Termination Check: Initialize transmittance T = 1.0. If T < 2 \times 10^{-4}, terminate the ray. 3. Coarse-to-Fine Query: Iterate through the occupancy grid hierarchy from coarsest to finest level. For the current sample position \mathbf{x}, compute grid indices for the current level. Query the occupancy grid at these indices. If any level indicates the voxel is empty (0), calculate the exit point of the empty block using ray-AABB intersection. Advance the ray sample position \mathbf{x} to this exit point and restart the hierarchy query from the coarsest level. 4. Scene Access: If all levels in the hierarchy indicate the voxel is occupied (1), access the MERF scene representation. Deferred Sampling: Query the Density Texture at \mathbf{x} to obtain \sigma. Compute voxel opacity contribution. If \sigma results in non-zero opacity, query the Appearance Texture at \mathbf{x} to obtain color \mathbf{c} and features. If \sigma is zero, skip reading the Appearance Texture. 5. Volume Rendering: Compute color contribution C{\text{sample}} and update transmittance T using standard volume rendering integration. Update sample position \mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x} + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{d}. 6. Loop: Repeat steps 2–5 until T < 2 \times 10^{-4} or the ray exits the scene bounds. Formulas: Opacity per step: \alpha = 1 - e^{-\sigma \Delta t} Transmittance update: T{\text{new}} = T{\text{old}} \cdot (1 - \alpha) Color accumulation: C{\text{out}} = C{\text{in}} + \alpha \cdot \mathbf{c} \cdot T{\text{old}} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, occupancygrids, densitytex, appearancetex): TTHRESHOLD = 2e-4 FILTERSIZES = [128, 32, 16] # Coarsest to finest STEPSIZE = 0.01 # Fixed step size t = 0.0 T = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while T > TTHRESHOLD: currentpos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] skip = False for levelidx in range(len(FILTERSIZES)): res = FILTERSIZES[levelidx] # Map world position to integer grid indices (coordinates assumed normalized to [0,1]) grididx = (int(currentpos[0] res), int(currentpos[1] res), int(currentpos[2] res)) # Query binary occupancy (0=empty, 1=occupied) isoccupied = occupancygrids[levelidx][grididx[0]][grididx[1]][grididx[2]] if isoccupied == 0: # Empty space detected: skip to the end of this block mincorner = [grididx[i] / res for i in range(3)] maxcorner = [(grididx[i] + 1) / res for i in range(3)] tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') raymisses = False for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0.0: if currentpos[i] < mincorner[i] or currentpos[i] > maxcorner[i]: raymisses = True break else: t1 = (mincorner[i] - currentpos[i]) / raydirection[i] t2 = (maxcorner[i] - currentpos[i]) / raydirection[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if not raymisses and tmax > t: t = tmax skip = True break # Restart hierarchy check from coarsest level at new position if skip: continue # All levels occupied: access scene representation sigma = texturelookup(densitytex, currentpos) if sigma > 0.0: color, features = texturelookup(appearancetex, currentpos) alpha = 1.0 - exp(-sigma STEPSIZE) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + T alpha color[i] for i in range(3)] T = (1.0 - alpha) t += STEPSIZE return accumulatedcolor Parameters: Transmittance Termination Threshold: 2 \times 10^{-4}. Occupancy Grid Filter Sizes: 16, 32, and 128. Base Resolution: Example given as 4096, resulting in grid sizes 256, 128, and 32. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ray-AABB intersection must correctly compute block exits to prevent sampling gaps or overlaps. Memory Layout: The MLP optimization relies on linear memory access patterns; improper texture layout can negate speed gains. Empty Space: Skipping logic must correctly handle the transition between grid levels to avoid missing thin occupied structures. Performance: On an RTX 3090 GPU at 1920x1080 resolution, MERF renders at frame rates well above 100 FPS. In contrast, Instant-NGP achieves 4 FPS on the same hardware at the same resolution. Memory: MERF consumes approximately one-fifth of the video memory of SNeRG++. Hardware: Implemented as a WebGL application (Three.js), making it portable across devices including mobile browsers, though performance varies by GPU. Optimizations: Loop unrolling of the deferred rendering MLP. Memory layout modifications for linear access. Exploitation of fast mat4 multiplication. These optimizations provide an additional 4× speed-up. Limitations: Quality reduction compared to non-real-time methods is evident in background regions (e.g., 1.24 dB PSNR reduction compared to MobileNeRF on Macbook, though MobileNeRF uses 2x memory). Origin: MERF (Memory-Efficient Radiance Fields) was introduced by to enable real-time view synthesis in unbounded scenes with limited memory. Implementation: The real-time viewer is implemented as a Javascript 3D (Three.js) web application, orchestrated by a single GLSL fragment shader. Context: It builds upon SNeRG's implementation and uses the view-dependence model introduced by Hedman et al.. It is designed to be more portable than CUDA-based solutions like Instant-NGP. name: VDBEstimator
head: Occupancy Estimator Using A VDB
body: VDBEstimator is an occupancy estimation method that uses a volumetric data base (VDB) grid, specifically the fVDB format, to perform spatial skipping of invisible space during ray marching. It maintains a mutable grid and a buffer of float occupancy values to guide sampling, allowing rays to bypass inactive regions without evaluating the volume density function. It builds on Occupancy Grid and Map-Based Empty Space Skipping by leveraging hierarchical sparse structures for efficient traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins (O) and directions (D), near/far planes (t{min}, t{max}), rendering step size, and the VDB grid state. Outputs: Ray intervals (t{starts}, t{ends}), ray indices, and updated occupancy grid state. Data Structures: The estimator maintains two main state attributes: 1. self.grid: An fVDB GridBatch object created via sparsegridfromijk with mutable=True. 2. self.occs: A torch.nn.Parameter tensor of shape [self.grid.totalvoxels] initialized to zeros, with requiresgrad=False. Parameters: renderstepsize: Default 10^{-3}. The step size for marching through the grid. earlystopeps: Default 10^{-4}. Early stop threshold for skipping invisible space. alphathre: Default 0.0. Alpha threshold for skipping empty space. occthre: Default 10^{-2}. Threshold used to binarize the occupancy grid during updates. emadecay: Default 0.95. The decay rate for Exponential Moving Average (EMA) updates of the occupancy field. warmupsteps: Default 256. During this initial stage, all cells are sampled. n: Default 16. The estimator updates the grid every n training steps. Algorithm Steps: 1. Plane Clamping: If tmin is provided, clamp nearplanes to be at least tmin. If tmax is provided, clamp farplanes to be at most tmax. 2. Stratified Sampling (Optional): If stratified is True, add jitter to nearplanes: t{near}^{\text{jittered}} = t{near} + \text{rand}() \times \text{render\step\size} where \text{rand}() is a uniform random value. 3. VDB Traversal: Call traversevdbs with rays, grid, near/far planes, step size, and cone angle to get initial tstarts, tends, and rayindices. This function computes ray-AABB intersections. For each ray-grid pair, it calculates t{min} = \max(\min(t1, t2), \text{near\plane}) and t{max} = \min(\max(t1, t2), \text{far\plane}), where t1, t2 are the intersection distances with the AABB faces. If no intersection exists (t{max} \le t{min} or t{max} \le 0), the interval is marked as invalid. 4. Alpha Threshold Capping: If skipping invisible space is enabled (alphathre > 0.0 or earlystopeps > 0.0) and a density/alpha function is provided, cap the alpha threshold: \alpha{thre} = \min(\alpha{thre}, \text{mean}(self.occs)) This prevents skipping based on an overly aggressive threshold relative to the current estimated occupancy. 5. Masking and Filtering: Generate a mask for valid intervals (where t{max} > t{min} and intersection exists). Filter rayindices, tstarts, and tends using this mask. 6. Grid Update (Training): If current training step < warmupsteps: Sample all cells using getallcells(). If step >= warmupsteps: Call sampleuniformandoccupiedcells(). This samples n = \text{total\voxels} // 4 uniform cells and n occupied cells (or all occupied if fewer than n), concatenating them for gradient updates. Update self.occs using EMA with emadecay. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch from typing import Optional, Tuple def vdbestimatorsample( grid, # fVDB GridBatch object occs: torch.Tensor, # [totalvoxels] rayso: torch.Tensor, # [nrays, 3] raysd: torch.Tensor, # [nrays, 3] nearplanes: torch.Tensor, # [nrays] farplanes: torch.Tensor, # [nrays] tmin: Optional[float] = None, tmax: Optional[float] = None, stratified: bool = False, renderstepsize: float = 1e-3, alphathre: float = 0.0, earlystopeps: float = 1e-4, step: int = 0, warmupsteps: int = 256, n: int = 16, emadecay: float = 0.95, occthre: float = 1e-2) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """ Perform ray marching with VDB-based empty space skipping. Returns: rayindices, tstarts, tends, updatedoccs """ # 1. Plane Clamping if tmin is not None: nearplanes = torch.clamp(nearplanes, min=tmin) if tmax is not None: farplanes = torch.clamp(farplanes, max=tmax) # 2. Stratified Sampling if stratified: jitter = torch.randlike(nearplanes) renderstepsize nearplanes = nearplanes + jitter # 3. VDB Traversal rayindices, tstarts, tends = traversevdbs( rayso, raysd, grid, nearplanes, farplanes, renderstepsize, coneangle=0.0) # 4. Alpha Threshold Capping if (alphathre > 0.0 or earlystopeps > 0.0) and hasattr(grid, 'densityfunc'): meanocc = occs.mean().item() alphathre = min(alphathre, meanocc) # 5. Masking and Filtering validmask = (tends > tstarts) & (tends > 0) rayindices = rayindices[validmask] tstarts = tstarts[validmask] tends = tends[validmask] # 6. Grid Update (if in training mode) # Sources do not provide the exact implementation for cell sampling and EMA updates. # if step % n == 0: # if step < warmupsteps: # cellstosample = getallcells(grid) # else: # nuniform = grid.totalvoxels // 4 # noccupied = min(nuniform, countoccupiedcells(grid, occs, occthre)) # uniformcells = sampleuniformcells(grid, nuniform) # occupiedcells = sampleoccupiedcells(grid, occs, noccupied, occthre) # cellstosample = concatenate(uniformcells, occupiedcells) # # Query density/alpha at cellstosample # # Update occs using EMA # newocc = queryocc(grid, cellstosample) # occs[cellstosample] = emadecay occs[cellstosample] + (1 - emadecay) newocc return rayindices, tstarts, tends, occs def traversevdbs( rayso: torch.Tensor, # [nrays, 3] raysd: torch.Tensor, # [nrays, 3] grid, # fVDB GridBatch object nearplanes: torch.Tensor, # [nrays] farplanes: torch.Tensor, # [nrays] stepsize: float, coneangle: float) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """ Traverses the VDB grid to find ray intervals. Returns rayindices, tstarts, tends. """ # The core traversal logic calls grids.uniformraysamples to get indices and intervals, then unbinds the intervals. intervals = grid.uniformraysamples(rayso, raysd, nearplanes, farplanes, stepsize, coneangle) rayindices, tstarts, tends = intervals.unbind() return rayindices, tstarts, tends Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Single Grid Limitation: The traversevdbs function currently asserts that only one grid is supported (assert len(grids) == 1). Boundary Constraints: There is a TODO comment indicating that endpoints of sample intervals should be restrained to be within grid boundaries, but this is not yet implemented. Precision: The use of torch.frexp for mip level computation in query assumes specific normalization and may have edge cases near zero. Uses distance transforms to skip empty space. Sets itself apart by using distance values rather than binary occupancy. Choose when smooth transitions between empty and active regions are needed. Distance Map Acceleration Uses a coarse pass to identify active regions before fine sampling. Sets itself apart by decoupling traversal from sampling. Choose for scenes with large empty volumes. Two-stage Ray Marching with Empty-Space Skipping Uses a hierarchical occupancy grid (e.g., octree) for skipping. Sets itself apart by supporting multi-resolution occupancy. Choose for highly sparse volumes. Hierarchical Sampling with Occupancy Grid Filters empty space during training using a bounding box. Sets itself apart by being a training-time optimization rather than a runtime traversal structure. Choose for static scenes with known bounds. Empty Space Filtering (Training-Time Bounding Box) Uses a hash grid for real-time rendering. Sets itself apart by focusing on real-time performance with hash-based lookups. Choose for interactive applications. MERF Real-Time Rendering Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the VDB grid. Traversal is proportional to the number of active voxels intersected by rays. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active voxels in the VDB grid plus the occupancy buffer. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with sparsity. The hierarchical nature of fVDB allows efficient traversal of large volumes with sparse active regions. Strengths: Efficient empty space skipping, mutable grid allows for dynamic updates during training. Limitations: Currently supports only a single grid. Boundary constraints are not fully implemented. When to use: Suitable for training NeRF-like models where the volume is sparse and dynamic updates to occupancy are beneficial. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes requiring multiple VDB grids or where boundary constraints are critical. VDBEstimator is part of the Taylor-NeRF project, which aims to improve NeRF training efficiency and quality. It leverages the fVDB library for efficient sparse volume representation and traversal. The method was introduced in the context of Taylor series expansion for NeRF, where efficient sampling is crucial for convergence. taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, https://github.com/taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Space Leaping
body: Space leaping is an acceleration technique for volume rendering that rapidly skips over empty or homogeneous regions of a volume to speed up rendering. It solves the problem of excessive computation in large volumes where significant portions of the ray path contribute no visible information. Unlike sibling methods that rely on hierarchical structures like octrees or occupancy grids to define active regions, space leaping often utilizes pre-computed distance information or ray coherence to determine safe skip distances. It is particularly effective in applications like virtual endoscopy where the camera is close to the object surface, leaving large empty spaces in front of the first hit. Space leaping avoids processing regions of a volume that will not contribute to the final image by using pre-computed data structures or coherence properties to determine how far a ray can advance without sampling. The technique implements distance-based skipping for empty cells or coherence-based skipping using a per-pixel leap buffer. Inputs: Volume dataset V with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Transfer function T(v) mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Ray parameters: origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Pre-computed acceleration data: either a distance transform volume D (for proximity clouds) or a leap buffer L (for ray coherence). Outputs: Final pixel color and accumulated opacity. A 3D volume D of the same resolution as V, where each empty cell stores the distance to the nearest opaque cell. Layout: Array of floats or integers matching the volume grid. Value: D[i,j,k] encodes the distance that can be safely skipped along any ray sampling the empty cell at (i,j,k). Opaque Cell: A voxel where T(V[i,j,k]) > \epsilon. A 2D buffer L of size Nx \times Ny (image plane resolution), storing the number of samples a detector ray took to reach the first non-empty cell. Layout: Array of integers. Value: L[u,v] = count of empty samples between image plane and first hit for pixel (u,v). 1. Preprocessing: Compute the distance transform D for the volume. For every empty voxel, calculate the distance to the nearest active voxel. 2. Leap Buffer Construction (Per Frame/View): Cast a sparse set of space leap rays (e.g., one out of every 4 rays) from the image plane into the volume. For each leap ray, find the first sample point inside an active cell and store the number of empty samples traversed in L at the corresponding pixel coordinates. 3. Ray Initialization: Start ray at \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}. 4. Sampling Loop: a. Sample volume value v = V(\mathbf{p}). b. If v is active (opacity > \epsilon), proceed with standard ray casting integration. c. If v is empty: i. Retrieve skip distance s = D(\mathbf{p}). ii. Advance ray: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + s \cdot \mathbf{d}. iii. Clamp \mathbf{p} to volume bounds. 5. Termination: Stop when ray exits volume or accumulated opacity exceeds threshold. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spaceleaprender(volume, accelerationdata, rayorigin, raydirection, imageplane, opacitythreshold): # accelerationdata: dict containing 'distancetransform' or 'leapbuffer' raystep = 1.0 # Normalized step size per voxel maxt = computemaxt(rayorigin, raydirection, volume.bounds) for u, v in imageplane: accumulatedopacity = 0.0 pixelcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = 0.0 # Leap Buffer Initialization (Variant B) if 'leapbuffer' in accelerationdata: skipcount = accelerationdata['leapbuffer'][u, v] if skipcount > 0: t = skipcount raystep # Backtrack if initial leap lands inside non-empty cell while t > 0 and volume.isoccupied(rayorigin + t raydirection): t -= raystep # Do not backtrack beyond original skip count to stay in front of image plane if t < 0: t = 0.0 else: t = 0.0 # Main Traversal Loop while t < maxt and accumulatedopacity < opacitythreshold: p = rayorigin + t raydirection cellidx = volume.worldtoindex(p) if not volume.isoccupied(cellidx): # Variant A: Proximity Cloud / Distance Transform if 'distancetransform' in accelerationdata: skipdist = accelerationdata['distancetransform'][cellidx] t += skipdist else: t += raystep else: # Standard sampling and front-to-back compositing val = volume.read(cellidx) op = transferfunction(val).opacity col = transferfunction(val).color pixelcolor = pixelcolor + col op (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity += op (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) t += raystep imageplane[u, v].color = pixelcolor imageplane[u, v].opacity = accumulatedopacity Opacity Threshold (\epsilon): Minimum opacity to consider a voxel active. Typical values: 0.01 to 0.05. Leap Ray Density: In the Vikon system, one out of every 4 rays is used for leap buffer construction, achieving 75% of possible acceleration. Transfer Function Changes: Content-based space leaping (using proximity clouds) requires extensive re-computation of the distance transform whenever the transfer function changes. High-Frequency Data: Techniques break down on datasets with high-frequency information (e.g., ultrasound) where most voxels are relevant, causing rendering times to increase rather than decrease. Boundary Misses: Standard space leaping may miss objects projecting only on boundary pixels. This is addressed by the Boundary Pixel Detector Ray Casting variant, which treats all boundary pixels as mandatory detector pixels. Leap Buffer Zero: If the leap buffer value is zero, the space leap ray should not be leaped at all. Post-Object Space: Space leaping is only possible between the image plane and the first object hit; empty space beyond the first hit cannot be leaped in the coherence-based method. Boundary Pixel Detector Ray Casting is a safety mechanism within Space Leaping that ensures objects projecting only on boundary pixels are not missed by considering all boundary pixels as detector pixels. It distinguishes itself from standard space leaping by treating all image boundary pixels as mandatory detector pixels, preventing the algorithm from leaping over objects located at the periphery of the view frustum. The leap buffer stores the number of samples the detector ray took to reach a non-empty cell, where the sample before that is the last sample in an empty cell. If the leap buffer value is zero, the space leap ray should not be leaped at all. The simplest form of space leaping for empty space, facilitated by enclosing the object into a set of boxes, possibly hierarchical. The algorithm quickly determines and tests the rays' intersection with each of the boxes before engaging in more time-consuming volumetric traversal of the material within only if the ray intersects the box. Time Complexity: Base volume rendering complexity is O(n^3) where n is the volume dimension. Leap Buffer Construction: O(N^2) where N \times N is the image plane size, as it scans the buffer once. Rendering: Depends on the density of active voxels. In sparse volumes, speedups are significant; in dense volumes, performance may degrade due to overhead. Memory Complexity: Proximity Cloud: O(n^3) for the distance volume. Leap Buffer: O(N^2) for the 2D buffer. Measured Performance: Speedups of up to 165% over non-space leap ray casting were achieved on a Pentium-IV, 2.6GHz PC with 1GB RAM and Linux OS. Memory usage for leap buffer was 256x256 bytes for tested datasets. Strengths: Ideal for virtual endoscopy and applications requiring camera placement close to object surface. Low memory overhead for the leap buffer variant (O(N^2)). Limitations: Cannot achieve as much empty space skipping as techniques using data structures for empty/non-empty voxel info (e.g., octrees) because it only leaps one out of every 4 rays in the coherence variant, getting 75% of possible acceleration. Performance is classification dependent; changes to opacity transfer function require lengthy re-computation for content-based methods. Ineffective for volumes with high percentage of relevant voxels (e.g., shockwave dataset). Space leaping was introduced as a method to efficiently traverse or skip empty space in volume rendering. The original approach utilized hierarchical spatial data structures like octrees or flat pyramids. The concept of using proximity clouds (distance transforms) was also explored early on. The Vikon system incorporated a specific space leaping acceleration technique using ray coherence (leap buffers) for perspective direct volume rendering, specifically for endoscopy applications like Virtual Colonoscopy. The technique is listed as a powerful method for raycasting alongside bounding volumes and multi-resolution grid traversal. name: Boundary Pixel Detector Ray Casting
head: Boundary Pixel Detection
body: Boundary Pixel Detector Ray Casting is a safety mechanism within Space Leaping [5863-space-leaping.md] that ensures objects projecting only on boundary pixels are not missed by considering all boundary pixels as detector pixels. It distinguishes itself from standard space leaping by treating all image boundary pixels as mandatory detector pixels, preventing the algorithm from leaping over objects located at the periphery of the view frustum. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Image buffer dimensions (width W, height H) and the leap buffer state. Output: A set of detector rays originating from boundary pixels that populate the leap buffer. Data Structures: Leap Buffer: A 2D array corresponding to the image buffer pixels, used to track processed or leaped pixels. Steps: 1. Identify boundary pixels of the image buffer. 2. Shoot detector rays from all identified boundary pixels to populate the leap buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shootboundarydetectorrays(W, H, leapbuffer): """Shoots detector rays from all image boundary pixels to populate the leap buffer.""" boundarypixels = [] for x in range(W): boundarypixels.append((x, 0)) boundarypixels.append((x, H - 1)) for y in range(1, H - 1): boundarypixels.append((0, y)) boundarypixels.append((W - 1, y)) for x, y in boundarypixels: # Standard ray generation maps pixel (x, y) to a view ray. # The detector ray is shot without space-leaping skips. # Results are recorded in the leap buffer to mark the pixel as processed. leapbuffer[x][y] = 1 return leapbuffer Parameters: Boundary Definition: Strictly the outermost rows and columns of the image buffer. Leap Buffer Update: The specific flag or value written to the leap buffer is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Boundary Objects: If detector rays are not shot from boundary pixels, a cell group might be leaped over and missed if the detector rays around its projection intersect another cell group further away. First Sample Rule: The general space leaping technique requires that the first sample of a space leap ray be in an empty cell to avoid missing non-transparent sample points. Boundary detector rays must adhere to this rule to ensure correctness. What it is: A rule applied to space leap rays to ensure they do not leap beyond an object boundary inside a cell group. Distinction: It focuses on intra-cell-group accuracy rather than inter-cell-group skipping. When to choose: When ensuring that no non-transparent sample points are missed within a single cell group during the leap process. Link: Backtracking Space Leap Rays Time complexity is not given in the sources. Memory complexity is not given in the sources. Strengths are not given in the sources. Limitations are not given in the sources. When to use is not given in the sources. Origin: Introduced in "Light Weight Space Leaping using Ray Coherence" by Lakare et al. (2004). History: Developed to address a specific flaw in early space leaping implementations where objects at the periphery of the view were incorrectly skipped due to the coherence-based skipping logic. Usage: Used in high-performance volume rendering systems that employ ray coherence and space leaping to optimize rendering speed. name: Hybrid kd-tree/Uniform Grid
head: Hybrid kd-tree/uniform grid structure (Zellmann et al.), Zellmann et al. Hybrid Structure
body: This method accelerates volume rendering by combining a kd-tree at the root level with a uniform grid at the leaf-node level to perform efficient empty-space skipping. It addresses the trade-off between the high construction cost of deep trees and the coarse skipping granularity of shallow trees by decoupling tree depth from skipping granularity. Unlike pure hierarchical structures, it allows for faster construction while maintaining rendering efficiency in large datasets by using the kd-tree for coarse traversal and the uniform grid for fine-grained empty-space detection within leaf nodes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset; a transfer function defining opacity/density thresholds for "active" regions. Output: A rendered image; a sorted list of non-empty leaf nodes for GPU iteration. Data Structures: 1. Hybrid Structure: Root: A kd-tree. Each node stores splitting planes and bounding boxes. Leaves: Uniform grids. Each leaf node contains a regular 3D grid of cells. Cells store metadata indicating occupancy (empty vs. active) or data values. Layout: The kd-tree nodes are stored in a flat array or pointer-based structure. Leaf nodes point to their respective uniform grid arrays. The uniform grid cells may store either a data value or "uniformity information" indicating the size of an empty octant. Steps: 1. Construction: Build a kd-tree over the volume data. The splitting criteria typically use summed-volume tables or density thresholds to balance the tree. At each leaf node of the kd-tree, subdivide the corresponding volume region into a uniform grid. Populate the uniform grid cells with occupancy metadata. A cell is marked "active" if its maximum scalar value exceeds a threshold \tau or if it contains non-zero density. For the Uniform Buffer variant, store "uniformity information" in empty voxels of the regular 3D raster, indicating the size of the empty octant to skip. 2. CPU Traversal (Pre-processing): Traverse the kd-tree on the CPU. Identify all non-empty leaf nodes. Sort these leaf nodes based on their spatial position relative to the camera or ray origin to optimize GPU processing order. 3. GPU Rendering (Ray Casting): For each ray, use the sorted list of non-empty leaf nodes to determine which regions to sample. Skip rays that do not intersect any active leaf nodes. For intersecting rays, iterate through the active leaf nodes. Within each leaf node, traverse the uniform grid. If a cell contains "uniformity information" (in the Uniform Buffer variant), leap forward to the first voxel beyond the uniform region. Sample the primary volume texture only within active cells. Formulas: Occupancy Check: A block/cell is active if \max(\text{block}) > \tau. Coordinate Mapping: Map ray position u{\text{vol}} to grid index u{\text{occ}} via u{\text{occ}} = \lfloor u{\text{vol}} / B \rfloor, where B is the block size. Leap Forward: If a voxel contains uniformity information for an octant of size S, advance the ray by S units in the ray direction. Parameters: Threshold \tau: Density/opacity threshold for activity. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Leaf Grid Resolution: Resolution of the uniform grid within each kd-tree leaf. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in ray-triangle or ray-plane intersections during kd-tree traversal may cause missed nodes or double-sampling. Boundary Conditions: Rays entering/exiting the volume must be correctly handled to avoid out-of-bounds memory access in the uniform grid. Transfer Function Changes: If the transfer function changes, the occupancy metadata may need to be recomputed, which can be costly if done per frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class KdTreeNode: def init(self, isleaf, splitaxis, splitvalue, left, right, leafgrid=None): self.isleaf = isleaf self.splitaxis = splitaxis self.splitvalue = splitvalue self.left = left self.right = right self.leafgrid = leafgrid # Uniform grid if leaf class UniformGridCell: def init(self, isactive, datavalue=None, uniformityinfo=None): self.isactive = isactive self.datavalue = datavalue self.uniformityinfo = uniformityinfo # Size of empty octant to skip def buildhybridstructure(volumedata, threshold): # Build kd-tree recursively # At leaf nodes, create uniform grid # Populate grid cells with occupancy info pass def traversekdtree(ray, node, sortedleafnodes): if node is None: return # Check intersection with node bounding box if not rayintersectsbbox(ray, node.bbox): return if node.isleaf: # Add to sorted list if active if node.leafgrid.hasactivecells(): sortedleafnodes.append(node.leafgrid) else: # Traverse children # Determine which child to visit first based on ray direction if ray.direction[node.splitaxis] >= 0: traversekdtree(ray, node.left, sortedleafnodes) traversekdtree(ray, node.right, sortedleafnodes) else: traversekdtree(ray, node.right, sortedleafnodes) traversekdtree(ray, node.left, sortedleafnodes) def renderray(ray, sortedleafnodes, volumetexture): color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 for leafgrid in sortedleafnodes: # Traverse uniform grid within leaf for cell in leafgrid: if cell.uniformityinfo is not None: # Leap forward ray.origin += ray.direction cell.uniformityinfo continue if cell.isactive: # Sample volume density = samplevolume(ray, volumetexture) opacity = transferfunction(density) # Composite color += (1.0 - alpha) opacity colormap(density) alpha += (1.0 - alpha) opacity if alpha >= 1.0: break if alpha >= 1.0: break return color Hybrid Grids is a volume rendering strategy that combines a shallow k-d tree with a global grid of macro cells to perform empty-space skipping. It solves the trade-off between the high construction cost of deep trees and the coarse skipping granularity of shallow trees by using the k-d tree for coarse traversal and the global grid for fine-grained empty space detection within leaf nodes. It sets itself apart from pure hierarchical structures by decoupling the tree depth from the granularity of empty-space skipping, allowing for faster construction while maintaining rendering efficiency in large datasets. A combination of hierarchical and regular grid advantages where uniformity information decoded by an octree is stored in the empty space of a regular 3D raster to skip empty space without tree search overhead. When a ray encounters a voxel containing 'uniformity information', instruct the ray to perform a leap forward to the first voxel beyond the uniform region. Voxels in the uniform buffer contain either a data value or information indicating to which size empty octant they belong. Traversing a hierarchical data structure is inefficient compared to regular grids; the uniform buffer avoids the time-consuming tree search for appropriate neighbors. The approach saves the need to perform a tree search for the appropriate neighbor, which is the most time-consuming operation and major disadvantage of hierarchical structures. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N \log N) for the kd-tree and O(N) for the uniform grid population, where N is the number of voxels. Rendering is O(R \cdot L \cdot G), where R is the number of rays, L is the number of active leaf nodes, and G is the average number of active cells per leaf node. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the volume data plus overhead for the kd-tree nodes and uniform grid metadata. The uniform buffer variant may have additional overhead for storing uniformity information. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Faster construction than deep trees; efficient empty-space skipping; decoupled granularity. Avoids time-consuming tree searches for neighbors. Limitations: Requires CPU-GPU synchronization for sorted leaf node lists; transfer-function dependent updates may be costly. When to Use: Large datasets with significant empty space; scenarios where construction time is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: Small datasets where overhead dominates; dynamic scenes requiring frequent structure updates. The hybrid kd-tree/uniform grid structure was presented by Zellmann et al. [ZML19] as a method for empty-space skipping in volume rendering. It builds on earlier work by Zellmann et al. [ZSL21] on kd-tree construction based on summed-volume tables, adapting it for GPU-based construction. The uniform buffer variant is described in tutorials on volume visualization techniques, highlighting the inefficiency of hierarchical structure traversal compared to regular grids. name: Hybrid Grids
body: Hybrid Grids is a rendering strategy combining a shallow k-d tree with a global grid of macro cells to perform empty-space skipping. It addresses the trade-off between the high construction cost of deep trees and the coarse skipping granularity of shallow trees by using the k-d tree for coarse traversal and the global grid for fine-grained empty space detection within leaf nodes. It sets itself apart from pure hierarchical structures by decoupling tree depth from skipping granularity, enabling faster construction while maintaining rendering efficiency in large datasets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Sparse volumetric dataset, k-d tree construction parameters (macro cell size 32^3), global grid resolution (macro cell size 16^3). Output: Rendered image with empty-space skipping applied. Data Structures: 1. Shallow k-d tree: Built using Spatial Volume Traversal (SVT) macro cells of size 32^3. Each SVT stores occupancy information for its volumetric region. 2. Global Grid: A uniform grid of macro cells derived from the SVTs. Each cell represents a 16^3 voxel region and stores occupancy status (empty or occupied). Steps: 1. Construct Shallow k-d Tree: Build a shallow k-d tree using SVT macro cells of size 32^3. 2. Derive Global Grid: Extract occupancy information from the SVTs of the k-d tree. 3. Resample Global Grid: Resample the derived grid to a macro cell size of 16^3 using constant-time operations on the SVTs. The original construction size of 32^3 is replaced by 16^3 for finer granularity. 4. Ray Traversal: Adapt the ray marching algorithm to perform full traversal per ray until a k-d tree leaf node is found. 5. Fine-Grained Skipping: Inside the k-d tree leaf node, use the global grid to skip over empty space with 16^3 granularity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderhybridgrid(volume, kdtree, globalgrid, gridorigin, gridspacing): # kdtree: shallow k-d tree with leaf nodes containing SVT occupancy # globalgrid: uniform grid of 16^3 macro cells with occupancy flags # gridorigin: (x, y, z) of global grid origin # gridspacing: 16.0 (voxel size per macro cell) for pixel in pixels: rayorigin = pixeltorayorigin(pixel) raydirection = pixeltoraydirection(pixel) # Step 1: Traverse k-d tree to find leaf # Standard k-d tree traversal logic leafnode = traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, kdtree) if leafnode is None or leafnode.isempty: continue # Step 2: Use global grid for fine-grained skipping within leaf leafmin, leafmax = leafnode.bounds # Map leaf bounds to global grid coordinates mincell = [int((leafmin[i] - gridorigin[i]) / gridspacing) for i in range(3)] maxcell = [int((leafmax[i] - gridorigin[i]) / gridspacing) for i in range(3)] # Ray-grid traversal (DDA) within leaf bounds cell = mincell[:] step = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] tdelta = [abs(1.0 / raydirection[i]) for i in range(3)] tmax = [tdelta[i] (gridspacing - (rayorigin[i] - gridorigin[i]) % gridspacing) for i in range(3)] while all(cell[i] <= maxcell[i] for i in range(3)): if not globalgrid[cell[0], cell[1], cell[2]].isempty: # Standard volume shading step rendervolumesegment(rayorigin, raydirection, cell) if tmax[0] < tmax[1] and tmax[0] < tmax[2]: cell[0] += step[0] tmax[0] += tdelta[0] elif tmax[1] < tmax[2]: cell[1] += step[1] tmax[1] += tdelta[1] else: cell[2] += step[2] tmax[2] += tdelta[2] Parameters: Macro cell size for k-d tree construction: 32^3. Macro cell size for global grid: 16^3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The global grid must be aligned with the k-d tree's SVT structure to ensure correct mapping. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. A hybrid data structure combining a kd-tree structure at the root level and a uniform grid at the leaf-node level used for empty-space skipping. Techniques for skipping empty space in volume rendering using various data structures. Traversal methods for hierarchical grid structures in volume rendering. Ray traversal techniques for grid-based volume data. Rendering methods that process pixels in image order. Techniques for rendering volumetric data. Time Complexity: Construction time is identical to shallow k-d trees. Rendering time depends on the depth of the k-d tree and the granularity of the global grid. Memory Complexity: Storage overhead is negligible as the global grid is derived from the SVTs of the k-d tree. Measured Performance: Outperforms the outer loop approach (calling a volume rendering shader per block) when using relatively deep trees. Construction performance is the same as that for shallow k-d trees. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Faster construction than deep trees, finer-grained empty space skipping than shallow trees alone, effective for large datasets near available texture memory. Limitations: Construction times are significantly higher than shallow trees when compared to deep trees, but identical to shallow trees. May not be optimal for all scene types. When to use: When data sets are large (near available texture memory) or when empty space manifests as wholes inside the volume. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Hybrid Grids was proposed in [ZML19] as an alternative rendering strategy to balance the trade-offs between deep and shallow k-d trees. It was evaluated in the context of the Virvo volume rendering library [SWWL01] and the Visionaray library [ZWL17]. The approach leverages the occupancy information stored in Spatial Volume Traversal (SVT) macro cells to derive a global grid, allowing for efficient empty-space skipping without significant additional storage overhead. name: ISSUE Algorithm
head: Modified ISSUE Algorithm
body: The ISSUE (Isosurface Extraction using Span Space Subdivision) algorithm is an image-order method for isosurface extraction that improves upon the NOISE algorithm by subdividing span space into an axis-aligned lattice. It solves the problem of efficient traversal and classification of volumetric cells relative to an isovalue, enabling parallel processing. It sets itself apart from siblings like Space Leaping by operating in span space (value domain) rather than spatial domain, allowing for coarser skipping based on data value ranges rather than just spatial occupancy. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volumetric dataset, isovalue v, lattice resolution L. Output: Isosurface geometry (triangles/points). Data Structures: 1. Lattice: An L \times L grid representing the span space (value range). Each cell (i, j) corresponds to a range of min-max values. 2. Classification Map: For each lattice element, a category (1-5) indicating its relationship to the isovalue v. 3. Search Structures: For Region 5 elements: A kd-tree built on the lattice element's cells. For other regions: Sorted linear arrays (coalesced from lattice elements). Steps: 1. Lattice Construction: Divide the span space (range of data values) into an L \times L axis-aligned lattice. Each tile contains approximately the same number of cells. 2. Classification: For each lattice element, determine its category based on its min/max bounds relative to the isovalue v: Region 1: Max value < v. Trivially exclude cells. Region 2: Min value > v. Trivially include cells. Region 3: Min value < v and Max value > v, but specific geometric condition (see Fig 3) requires test against Max value. Region 4: Min value < v and Max value > v, but specific geometric condition requires test against Min value. Region 5: Requires full min-max search of its cells. 3. Structure Building (Modified ISSUE): Identify lattice elements falling into Region 5. These lie along the diagonal y=x in the lattice. Build a kd-tree for each Region 5 lattice element. Coalesce lattice elements from Regions 1-4 into sorted linear arrays. 4. Traversal/Extraction: Query the structures to find active cells. For Region 5, use the kd-tree to find cells intersecting the isovalue. For other regions, use the sorted arrays or trivial inclusion/exclusion rules. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def issueextract(volume, isovalue, L): # 1. Build Lattice # Determine minval and maxval of volume minval = min(volume) maxval = max(volume) # Create L x L lattice lattice = [[None for in range(L)] for in range(L)] # Assign cells to lattice elements # Each cell has minc and maxc (min/max value in cell) for cell in volume.cells: # Map cell value range to lattice indices # This is a simplification; actual mapping depends on specific binning i = int((cell.maxc - minval) / (maxval - minval) L) j = int((cell.minc - minval) / (maxval - minval) L) i = min(i, L-1) j = min(j, L-1) lattice[i][j].append(cell) # 2. Classify Lattice Elements regions = {1: [], 2: [], 3: [], 4: [], 5: []} for i in range(L): for j in range(L): elem = lattice[i][j] if not elem: continue # Determine global min/max for this lattice element elemmin = min(c.minc for c in elem) elemmax = max(c.maxc for c in elem) # Classification logic based on isovalue v # Note: Exact geometric conditions for Regions 3, 4, 5 are complex # and depend on the specific lattice cell boundaries relative to v. # Simplified logic based on source description: if elemmax < isovalue: regions[1].append(elem) # Exclude elif elemmin > isovalue: regions[2].append(elem) # Include elif i == j: # Diagonal, potential Region 5 regions[5].append(elem) else: # Heuristic for 3 and 4 based on source # Region 3: test against max # Region 4: test against min # This is a simplification; real implementation requires precise boundary checks if elemmax < isovalue + threshold: # Placeholder for precise condition regions[3].append(elem) else: regions[4].append(elem) # 3. Build Search Structures (Modified ISSUE) searchstructures = {} # Build kd-trees for Region 5 for elem in regions[5]: tree = buildkdtree(elem.cells) searchstructures[elem] = tree # Coalesce other regions into sorted arrays sortedarrays = {} for r in [1, 2, 3, 4]: sortedarrays[r] = coalesceandsort(regions[r]) # 4. Extract Isosurface triangles = [] # Process Region 5 (Active search) for elem in regions[5]: tree = searchstructures[elem] # Query tree for cells intersecting isovalue activecells = querykdtree(tree, isovalue) for cell in activecells: triangles.extend(extractcell(cell, isovalue)) # Process Region 2 (Trivially include) for elem in regions[2]: for cell in elem.cells: triangles.extend(extractcell(cell, isovalue)) # Process Regions 3 and 4 (Filtered) # Note: Source says "test against max/min". Implementation requires filtering. for elem in regions[3]: for cell in elem.cells: if cell.maxc >= isovalue: # Test against max triangles.extend(extractcell(cell, isovalue)) for elem in regions[4]: for cell in elem.cells: if cell.minc <= isovalue: # Test against min triangles.extend(extractcell(cell, isovalue)) return triangles Parameters: L: Lattice resolution. User-defined. Higher L increases precision but also memory overhead. Edge Cases: Empty Lattice Elements: Skip processing. Precision: Floating point comparisons for isovalue tests must handle epsilon. Memory: The modified version increases memory usage due to kd-trees and sorted arrays. Time Complexity: O(n + k) for NOISE; ISSUE improves performance but adds overhead for lattice construction and structure building. The modified version simplifies search but adds build time. Memory Complexity: Higher than NOISE due to lattice, kd-trees, and sorted arrays. Parallelism: Easily parallelizable by dividing lattice elements among processors. Strengths: Parallelizable, efficient for large datasets with coherent value ranges. Limitations: Higher memory requirement, build time overhead. The ISSUE algorithm was proposed by Shen et al. as an improvement over the NOISE algorithm. It utilizes span space subdivision to accelerate isosurface extraction. The modified version further optimizes by focusing search structures on the diagonal region.
