name: Two-Level Grid Ray Traversal
head: Modified DDA Traversal
body: Two-Level Grid Ray Traversal is a ray-grid traversal algorithm designed for two-level hierarchical grid structures, modifying the standard Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to step through top-level cells and then treat each top cell as a uniform grid for leaf traversal. It sets itself apart from uniform grid traversal by handling hierarchical data structures while maintaining SIMD-friendly coherence, and from other hierarchical methods by reusing decision variables between levels to minimize computational overhead. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of rays Ro, where all rays originate within a given top-level grid cell o. A two-level grid structure consisting of a top-level grid and leaf grids associated with each top-level cell. Output: A sequence of intersected cells (top-level and leaf-level) for each ray in the set. Data Structures The algorithm operates on a two-level grid structure. The top level is treated as a uniform grid. Each top-level cell contains a reference to a leaf grid, which is also treated as a uniform grid. The specific layout of the leaf grids (e.g., dense array, sparse structure) is defined by the construction method [S226-two-level-grid-construction.md], but the traversal logic assumes they behave as uniform grids during the leaf phase. Numbered Steps 1. Top-Level Traversal: Step through the top level of the two-level grid structure using the standard DDA algorithm, identical to traversing a uniform grid. 2. Leaf Initialization: Upon entering a top-level cell, treat that cell as the origin for a new uniform grid traversal. Reuse decision variables from the top-level traversal to spare computations when initializing the decision variables for the leaf level. 3. Leaf Traversal: Advance through the leaf cells within the current top-level cell using the same DDA algorithm used for the top level. 4. Iteration: Repeat steps 2 and 3 for each subsequent top-level cell entered by the rays. Formulas The algorithm relies on the coherence property of DDA traversal. Let Ro be a set of rays, all of which have origin (not necessarily the same) in a given grid cell o. Statement: If a cell c is intersected by any ray r \in Ro and is the n-th cell along r counted from the origin, then c will be the n-th cell along any ray r^ \in Ro that intersects c. Proof Basis: Let o be the 0-th cell along the rays in the set. For each cell c, it holds that it is at distance (x, y, z) from o, where x, y and z are integers denoting the distance (in number of cells) along the coordinate axis with the same name. During traversal, rays advance with exactly one neighbor cell at a time, and the two cells share a side. This means that c will be traversed at x+y+z = n-th step of the traversal algorithm for any ray with origin in o if at all. Parameters Grid Density: A single grid density is determined using the Surface Area Cost Model to work well with the traversal implementation for all test scenes. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Otherwise, the algorithm is SIMD-friendly. Memory Access: A cell along the traversal path, if loaded, will be loaded exactly once from memory. This property transfers to the two-level grid structure when traversing the top level and when rays agree on the first leaf cell when they traverse the leaves. name: Macrocell Grid Traversal
head: Downscaled Grid Traversal, Macrocell or multigrids, multigrids
body: Macrocell Grid Traversal is a hierarchical acceleration technique for ray-grid traversal that superimposes a coarse grid over a base uniform fine grid to skip empty regions. It solves the problem of excessive traversal overhead in large, sparse uniform grids by allowing rays to bypass blocks of empty fine cells in single steps. Unlike Multi-Level Array Grid which may use complex indexing or variable subdivision, or Multi-Grid Ray Traversal which might involve multiple independent grids, Macrocell Grid Traversal uses a fixed, regular downsampling factor M to create a simple boolean occupancy map. This simplicity allows for trivial build times and efficient reuse of frustum setup calculations, yielding approximately 30% performance improvement over single ray grids for medium-sized animated scenes. Inputs: A base uniform fine grid of resolution N \times N \times N (or W \times H \times D). The ray parameters: origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and inverse direction \mathbf{d}^{-1}. The downsampling factor M (typically 6). Outputs: A traversal sequence of occupied fine grid cells. A boolean occupancy flag for each macrocell indicating if any underlying fine cell is occupied. The structure consists of two grids: 1. Fine Grid: The original voxel data. Cells are indexed by (i, j, k). 2. Macrocell Grid: A coarse grid of resolution \lceil N/M \rceil \times \lceil N/M \rceil \times \lceil N/M \rceil. Layout: Flat array or organized in bricks for locality. Fields: Each macrocell stores a single boolean flag occupied. Definition: A macrocell at coarse index (I, J, K) corresponds to the fine grid block defined by fine indices: i \in [I \cdot M, \min((I+1) \cdot M, N) - 1] j \in [J \cdot M, \min((J+1) \cdot M, N) - 1] k \in [K \cdot M, \min((K+1) \cdot M, N) - 1] Occupancy: macrocell[I][J][K].occupied is true if any fine cell in the corresponding block is occupied, false otherwise. M (Downsampling Factor): The side length of the cubic block of fine cells represented by one macrocell. Typical Value: M = 6. Constraints: Smaller M yields insufficient savings to justify overhead; larger M reduces the probability of finding empty regions, reducing skip benefits. 1. Initialize the macrocell grid with all flags set to false. 2. Iterate through all fine grid cells (i, j, k). 3. If fine cell (i, j, k) is occupied: Compute macrocell coordinates: I = \lfloor i / M \rfloor J = \lfloor j / M \rfloor K = \lfloor k / M \rfloor Set macrocell[I][J][K].occupied = true. 4. Handle boundary conditions where N is not a multiple of M by ensuring array bounds checks during indexing. The traversal reuses the standard ray-grid traversal logic (DDA) but operates on macrocells first to determine skip distances. 1. Frustum Setup (Coarse): Compute the initial intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of the ray with the entire scene bounding box. Compute the coarse grid step variables. Since the macrocell grid is a downscaled version, the step sizes in macrocell space are M times larger than in fine cell space. Let \Delta t{x}, \Delta t{y}, \Delta t{z} be the time to cross one fine cell. The time to cross one macrocell is M \cdot \Delta t{x}, etc. Alternatively, compute the coarse grid traversal parameters by dividing the fine grid setup values by M. 2. Coarse Traversal Loop: Initialize coarse DDA variables (I, J, K) to the macrocell containing the ray origin. While t < t{max}: Check if macrocell[I][J][K].occupied is false. If Empty: Skip the entire macrocell. Advance the coarse DDA to the next macrocell along the ray direction. Update t by adding the time to cross the current macrocell (M \cdot \Delta t). Continue loop. If Occupied: Perform fine grid traversal within this macrocell block. Determine the fine cell indices (i{start}, j{start}, k{start}) corresponding to (I, J, K). Execute standard fine grid DDA steps for cells within the block I \cdot M, (I+1) \cdot M) \times [J \cdot M, (J+1) \cdot M) \times [K \cdot M, (K+1) \cdot M). For each occupied fine cell, perform [ray-volume intersection. Update t and fine DDA variables. If the ray exits the current macrocell block, advance the coarse DDA to the next macrocell (I', J', K') and continue the coarse loop. 3. Edge Cases: Partial Macrocells: At the boundaries of the grid, macrocells may be smaller than M \times M \times M. The traversal must handle these boundary blocks correctly by checking array bounds. Ray Origin Outside: If the ray origin is outside the grid, standard frustum clipping applies before coarse traversal begins. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversemacrocellgrid(rayorigin, raydir, finegrid, macrocellgrid, M): """ rayorigin: (ox, oy, oz) raydir: (dx, dy, dz) finegrid: 3D array of booleans, size N x N x N macrocellgrid: 3D array of booleans, size ceil(N/M) x ceil(N/M) x ceil(N/M) M: downsampling factor """ # 1. Setup Fine Grid DDA # Standard ray-grid traversal setup for fine grid # Calculate tmin, tmax for the entire scene bounding box # Calculate deltat (time to cross one fine cell) # Calculate tmaxx, tmaxy, tmaxz (entry times to next cell) # Calculate stepx, stepy, stepz (direction of DDA) # Calculate currentcell (i, j, k) containing ray origin # 2. Setup Coarse Grid DDA # Coarse grid resolution Ncoarse = ceil(N / M) # Map fine cell to coarse cell coarsei = floor(i / M) coarsej = floor(j / M) coarsek = floor(k / M) # Coarse DDA parameters # Time to cross one macrocell is M deltat coarsedeltatx = M deltatx coarsedeltaty = M deltaty coarsedeltatz = M deltatz # Entry times to next coarse cell # Adjust tmaxx/y/z to align with coarse grid boundaries # If current fine cell is not at the start of a macrocell, # the first coarse step might be partial. # Simplified: Assume we jump to the next coarse cell boundary. # 3. Traversal while t < tmax: # Check if current coarse cell is empty if not macrocellgrid[coarsei][coarsej][coarsek]: # Skip this macrocell # Advance coarse DDA if stepx == 1: tmaxx += coarsedeltatx if tmaxx < tmaxy and tmaxx < tmaxz: coarsei += 1 t = tmaxx continue elif stepx == -1: tmaxx -= coarsedeltatx if tmaxx < tmaxy and tmaxx < tmaxz: coarsei -= 1 t = tmaxx continue # Similar logic for y and z steps... # Determine which axis is next if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: coarsei += stepx t = tmaxx tmaxx += coarsedeltatx else: coarsek += stepz t = tmaxz tmaxz += coarsedeltatz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: coarsej += stepy t = tmaxy tmaxy += coarsedeltaty else: coarsek += stepz t = tmaxz tmaxz += coarsedeltatz else: # Macrocell is occupied, traverse fine cells within this block # Determine the bounds of the current macrocell in fine grid istart = coarsei M jstart = coarsej M kstart = coarsek M iend = min(istart + M, N) jend = min(jstart + M, N) kend = min(kstart + M, N) # Reset fine DDA to the start of the macrocell if needed, # or continue from current fine cell if inside the block. # Standard fine grid traversal loop while t < tmax and i < iend and j < jend and k < kend: if finegrid[i][j][k]: # Perform ray-volume intersection intersect(rayorigin, raydir, i, j, k) # Advance fine DDA if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: i += stepx t = tmaxx tmaxx += deltatx else: k += stepz t = tmaxz tmaxz += deltatz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: j += stepy t = tmaxy tmaxy += deltaty else: k += stepz t = tmaxz tmaxz += deltatz # After finishing the block, advance coarse DDA # Determine which coarse axis was last crossed # This requires tracking which fine step caused the exit from the block # Simplified: Just advance to the next coarse cell in the direction of the ray # Note: The coarse DDA state (tmaxx/y/z) must be synchronized with the fine DDA # exit point. # Re-calculate coarse entry times based on current fine position # This ensures continuity coarsei = floor(i / M) coarsej = floor(j / M) coarsek = floor(k / M) # Update coarse tmax values to reflect the current position # This is a simplification; a robust implementation would maintain # coarse tmax values incrementally. tmaxxcoarse = (coarsei + 1) coarsedeltatx if stepx == 1 else coarsei coarsedeltatx #... similar for y and z # Advance coarse DDA to the next cell # (Logic similar to the empty case, but triggered after block traversal) if stepx == 1: coarsei += 1 t = tmaxxcoarse # Approximate #... Multi-Level Array Grid: Uses array-based indexing for variable depth subdivision. Choose when scene density varies significantly across different regions and a fixed M is insufficient. Multi-Grid Ray Traversal: May involve multiple distinct grids or more complex hierarchical structures. Choose when the scene has distinct geometric components that benefit from separate acceleration structures. Two-Level Grids for Ray Tracing on GPUs: Optimized specifically for GPU architectures with specific memory coalescing requirements. Choose when targeting GPU hardware with limited shared memory. Multi-resolution grids: General term for grids with varying resolution. Choose when the scene has high-frequency details in some areas and low-frequency in others, requiring adaptive refinement rather than fixed blocks. Time Complexity: Build time is O(N^3) for the fine grid, but the macrocell build is O((N/M)^3) which is trivial. Traversal time is reduced by skipping empty macrocells. The overhead of checking macrocells is minimal. Memory Complexity: Adds O((N/M)^3) bits (or bytes) for the macrocell grid. For M=6, this is roughly 1/216 of the fine grid size, which is negligible. Measured Performance: Approximately 30% improvement over single ray grids for medium-sized animated scenes. Strengths: Trivial and cheap build process. Simple traversal logic. Low memory overhead. Effective for scenes with large empty regions. Limitations: Fixed block size M may not adapt to varying density. For smaller resolutions, savings are insufficient. For larger resolutions, probability of finding empty regions decreases. Not suitable for scenes with highly varying geometric density without additional robustness. When to Use: Medium-sized animated scenes with significant empty space and uniform fine grid resolution. When Not to Use: Scenes with highly varying density where fixed blocks are inefficient, or very small grids where overhead dominates. Macrocell Grid Traversal was proposed by Parker et al. in 1999. It is a simple hierarchical optimization to a base uniform grid, often used to apply grids to scalar volume fields. The method was designed to formulate a viable grid traversal for medium-size animated scenes, balancing performance and build time. Additional levels of macrocells could further improve performance for more complex models, but were not investigated in the original work. name: Multi-resolution grids
head: Hierarchical voxel grids, JW89, Jevans and Wyvill method, Jevans and Wyvill's approach
body: Multi-resolution grids (JW89) is a recursive hierarchical subdivision algorithm for ray tracing that integrates regular and adaptive spatial subdivision methods. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both large, regularly distributed objects and small, dense clusters by allowing variable resolution across the spatial domain. Unlike fixed-resolution grids or purely octree-based approaches, voxels in recursive grids cannot overlap, so each nested grid along the ray path is tested exactly once. It uses a top-down build strategy where internal voxels maintain their own local sub-grids, enabling efficient traversal through deep recursion when paired with a hash-table indexing strategy. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of geometric primitives and a scene bounding box. Output: A hierarchical grid data structure (root voxel) and a traversal state for ray intersection. Data Structures The structure is a loosely nested recursive grid. Voxel: The fundamental unit. Type: Enum { LEAF, INTERNAL }. Leaf Voxel: Contains a list of primitives intersecting the voxel volume. Internal Voxel: Contains a local voxel grid subdivision (child voxels) and a hash table mapping child coordinates to child voxel pointers. Hash Table: Used to maintain each non-empty internal voxel, allowing direct access to child grids and enabling deep recursion without linear search overhead. Build Process (Top-Down) All primitives are initially inserted into a single root voxel. The build process is top-down. The algorithm recursively subdivides internal voxels based on one of the following criteria: 1. Octree-like: Subdivide into a 2 \times 2 \times 2 grid (8 children). 2. Maximum Depth: Stop subdivision when a predefined tree depth is reached. 3. Constant Resolution: Fix the resolution of voxel subgrids to a specific value regardless of content density. 4. Variable (Adaptive) Resolution: Subdivide based on occupancy or primitive count thresholds. Parameters Coarseness of the initial voxel grid. Depth of adaptive subdivision trees. Maximum number of polygons per voxel (termination criterion for leaf nodes). Maximum depth for grids: typically 2 or 3. Traversal 1. Intersect ray with the root voxel AABB. 2. If intersection fails, terminate. 3. If the current voxel is a Leaf, test the ray against all primitives in the leaf's list. 4. If the current voxel is Internal, use the hash table to locate the specific child voxel corresponding to the ray's current position. 5. Recursively traverse the child voxel. 6. Continue until a primitive intersection is found or the ray exits the structure. Pitfalls Without a good indexing strategy (such as the hash table used in JW89), it is not possible to use deep levels of recursion efficiently due to the cost of locating child nodes. Build cost is generally higher than general bottom-up strategies. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildgrid(primitives, bounds, depth=0, maxdepth=3, threshold=10): # Standard top-down recursive subdivision voxel = Voxel(bounds) if len(primitives) <= threshold or depth >= maxdepth: voxel.type = LEAF voxel.primitives = primitives return voxel voxel.type = INTERNAL # Subdivide bounds into 2x2x2 child cells childcells = splitbounds(bounds) childprimitives = [[] for in range(8)] for prim in primitives: for i, cell in enumerate(childcells): if intersects(prim, cell): childprimitives[i].append(prim) # Recursively build children and populate hash table hashtable = {} for i, cellprims in enumerate(childprimitives): if cellprims: childbounds = childcells[i] childvoxel = buildgrid(childprims, childbounds, depth + 1, maxdepth, threshold) hashtable[i] = childvoxel voxel.children = hashtable return voxel def traverseray(ray, voxel): # Standard ray-voxel traversal if not intersects(ray, voxel.bounds): return None if voxel.type == LEAF: return intersectprimitives(ray, voxel.primitives) # Compute child index from ray position childidx = getchildindex(ray, voxel.bounds) if childidx in voxel.children: return traverseray(ray, voxel.children[childidx]) return None Time Complexity: Build time is higher than bottom-up strategies. Traversal cost depends on recursion depth and hash table lookup. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of internal nodes and the hash table storage for non-empty voxels. Strengths: Efficiently handles mixed-scale scenes (large regular objects + small dense objects). Limitations: High build cost. Not well-suited for GPU computation due to branching and pointer chasing inherent in hash-table-based recursive traversal. When to use: CPU-based ray tracing where scene geometry has significant scale variation. When not to use: GPU ray tracing (due to branching and memory access patterns). The method was proposed by Jevans and Wyvill in 1989. It is described in detail in "A Survey on Exploiting Grids for Ray Tracing" and "Grids in Ray Tracing: A Comprehensive Survey". The approach integrates regular grid traversal with adaptive subdivision, offering a middle ground between uniform grids and octrees. name: Quadtree Raycasting
head: raycast2
body: Quadtree Raycasting is a recursive ray-quadtree intersection algorithm that traverses a 2D quadtree to find the first hit node. It solves the problem of efficiently locating the first occupied voxel in a hierarchical 2D grid by handling ray direction flipping via a mask to ensure consistent traversal order regardless of ray direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: start (Vec2, ray origin in world space), dir (Vec2, ray direction vector), node (QuadtreeNode, the root or current subtree to traverse), tx0, ty0, tx1, ty1 (f32, boundary distances in ray parameter space). Output: Optional[Tuple[QuadtreeNode, float]] representing the first hit node and the hit distance t, or None if no intersection is found within the bounds. Data Structures: The QuadtreeNode structure: isfull: bool, indicates if the node represents a fully occupied volume. children: Optional[List[QuadtreeNode]], a fixed-size array of 4 child nodes (bottom-left, bottom-right, top-left, top-right), or None if leaf. size: f32, the spatial extent (width/height) of the node in world units. position: IVec2, the integer coordinates of the node's bottom-left corner. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization and Masking: Initialize a bitmask mask to 0. If dir.x < 0: Flip start.x using start.x = 2.0 node.position.x + node.size - start.x and set mask bit 0. If dir.y < 0: Flip start.y using start.y = 2.0 node.position.y + node.size - start.y and set mask bit 1. 2. Intersection Check: Calculate intersection distances to the node boundaries: tx0 = (node.position.x - start.x) / |dir.x| ty0 = (node.position.y - start.y) / |dir.y| tx1 = (node.position.x + node.size - start.x) / |dir.x| ty1 = (node.position.y + node.size - start.y) / |dir.y| Determine intersection interval: t{min} = \max(tx0, ty0) t{max} = \min(tx1, ty1) If t{min} \ge t{max}, the ray does not intersect the node bounding box; return None. 3. Recursive Traversal (procsubtree): Call the recursive function with the current node and the calculated boundary distances (tx0, ty0, tx1, ty1). Inside procsubtree(node, tx0, ty0, tx1, ty1, mask): 1. Early Exit: If tx1 < 0 or ty1 < 0, the ray has passed the node's far boundary; return None. 2. Leaf Check: If node.children is None: If node.isfull is true, the ray hits this node. Calculate hit distance t = \max(tx0, ty0). Return (node, t). 3. Internal Node: If the node has children: Calculate midpoints: txm = (tx0 + tx1) / 2 tym = (ty0 + ty1) / 2 Determine the first child index to visit using firstnode(tx0, ty0, txm, tym) which accounts for the ray direction relative to the sub-regions. Iterate through children using a loop variable currnode starting from firstnode(...). For each child, apply the mask to the index: childidx = currnode ^ mask. This ensures the logical child index corresponds to the correct spatial quadrant regardless of ray direction. Child 0 (Bottom-Left): Recurse with bounds (tx0, ty0, txm, tym). If a hit is returned, propagate it up. Else, continue. Child 1 (Bottom-Right): Recurse with bounds (txm, ty0, tx1, tym). If a hit is returned, propagate it up. Else, continue. Child 2 (Top-Left): Recurse with bounds (tx0, tym, txm, ty1). If a hit is returned, propagate it up. Else, continue. Child 3 (Top-Right): Recurse with bounds (txm, tym, tx1, ty1). If a hit is returned, propagate it up. Else, terminate the loop. If no child returns a hit, return None. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from typing import Optional, Tuple, List class QuadtreeNode: def init(self, isfull: bool, children: Optional[List['QuadtreeNode']], size: float, position: Tuple[int, int]): self.isfull = isfull self.children = children self.size = size self.position = position def quadtreeraycast(start: Tuple[float, float], dir: Tuple[float, float], node: QuadtreeNode) -> Optional[Tuple[QuadtreeNode, float]]: # Step 1: Initialization and Masking mask = 0 currentstart = list(start) if dir[0] < 0: currentstart[0] = 2.0 node.position[0] + node.size - start[0] mask |= 1 if dir[1] < 0: currentstart[1] = 2.0 node.position[1] + node.size - start[1] mask |= 2 # Step 2: Intersection Check absdx = abs(dir[0]) if dir[0] != 0 else 1e-9 absdy = abs(dir[1]) if dir[1] != 0 else 1e-9 tx0 = (node.position[0] - currentstart[0]) / absdx ty0 = (node.position[1] - currentstart[1]) / absdy tx1 = (node.position[0] + node.size - currentstart[0]) / absdx ty1 = (node.position[1] + node.size - currentstart[1]) / absdy tmin = max(tx0, ty0) tmax = min(tx1, ty1) if tmin >= tmax: return None # Step 3: Recursive Traversal return procsubtree(node, tx0, ty0, tx1, ty1, mask) def procsubtree(node: QuadtreeNode, tx0: float, ty0: float, tx1: float, ty1: float, mask: int) -> Optional[Tuple[QuadtreeNode, float]]: # Early Exit if tx1 < 0 or ty1 < 0: return None # Leaf Check if node.children is None: if node.isfull: t = max(tx0, ty0) return (node, t) else: return None # Internal Node txm = (tx0 + tx1) / 2.0 tym = (ty0 + ty1) / 2.0 # Determine traversal order based on ray direction relative to sub-regions firstidx = firstnode(tx0, ty0, txm, tym) currnode = firstidx while currnode < 4: # Apply mask to invert child index if necessary childidx = currnode ^ mask child = node.children[childidx] # Define bounds for the specific child quadrant if childidx == 0: # Bottom-Left hit = procsubtree(child, tx0, ty0, txm, tym, mask) elif childidx == 1: # Bottom-Right hit = procsubtree(child, txm, ty0, tx1, tym, mask) elif childidx == 2: # Top-Left hit = procsubtree(child, tx0, tym, txm, ty1, mask) elif childidx == 3: # Top-Right hit = procsubtree(child, txm, tym, tx1, ty1, mask) else: hit = None if hit is not None: return hit # Move to next node in traversal order currnode += 1 return None def firstnode(tx0: float, ty0: float, txm: float, tym: float) -> int: """Determines the first child index to visit based on ray entry quadrant.""" if tx0 < txm and ty0 < tym: return 0 elif tx0 >= txm and ty0 < tym: return 1 elif tx0 < txm and ty0 >= tym: return 2 else: return 3 Parameters: start: Vec2, ray origin. dir: Vec2, ray direction. mask: u8, bitmask for child index inversion. Bit 0 set if dir.x < 0, Bit 1 set if dir.y < 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by zero if dir.x or dir.y is 0. Guard against this by using a small epsilon or handling axis-aligned rays separately. Boundaries: The algorithm assumes firstnode and nextnode correctly determine traversal order based on ray direction relative to the current bounding box sub-regions. Incorrect implementation of these helpers leads to missing hits or infinite loops. Degenerate Input: Nodes with size 0 should be handled or avoided in the quadtree construction. name: Ray Grid Traversal with Adaptive Step Sizing
head: CNC Traversal, Ray Traversal through Multiple Voxel Grids, Traverse Grids Kernel Logic
body: A CUDA kernel that marches rays through one or more axis-aligned voxel grids using precomputed, sorted entry/exit intersections to generate sample points and interval boundaries. It handles empty cells by skipping them and fills continuous segments, supporting both fixed step sizes and cone-angle-aware adaptive stepping. It sets itself apart from standard DDA by decoupling the grid boundary traversal from the sample generation, allowing for variable step sizes that scale with distance from the camera origin. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [nrays, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [nrays, 3]. raysmask: Optional boolean mask, shape [nrays], to skip specific rays. binaries: Occupancy grids, shape [ngrids, resx, resy, resz], boolean values indicating occupied cells. aabbs: Axis-aligned bounding boxes for each grid, shape [ngrids, 6] (min/max x, y, z). hits: Boolean array, shape [nrays, ngrids], indicating if a ray intersects a grid. tsorted: Sorted intersection distances, shape [nrays, ngrids 2]. tindices: Grid IDs corresponding to each intersection in tsorted, shape [nrays, ngrids 2]. nearplanes: Near plane distances, shape [nrays]. farplanes: Far plane distances, shape [nrays]. stepsize: Base step length. Default 1e-3. If <= 0.0, the kernel records steps through each voxel cell instead of marching. coneangle: Controls linear increase of step size with distance. Must be >= 0.0. A value of 0.0 means uniform marching with stepsize. traversestepslimit: Maximum number of traversal steps per ray. Enables early termination. Default None (unlimited). If <= 0, no limit is applied. overallocate: Boolean flag. If true, memory is pre-allocated based on limits for single-pass traversal. If false, a two-pass approach is used. firstpass: Boolean flag indicating if this is the counting pass (for two-pass allocation). chunkstartbin: Global offset for writing into packed output buffers. Outputs: intervals: PackedRaySegmentsSpec containing vals (start/end distances), rayindices, isleft, isright, and chunkcnts. samples: PackedRaySegmentsSpec containing vals (sample positions), rayindices, isvalid, and chunkcnts. terminateplanes: Optional array, shape [nrays], storing the final tlast for each ray. Data Structures: The algorithm relies on pre-sorted intersection arrays tsorted and tindices. tsorted contains the 2 \times n\grids intersection points for each ray, sorted by distance. tindices maps these distances to the specific grid ID. The occupancy is stored in binaries, a multi-dimensional boolean array. Parameters: stepsize: 1e-3. coneangle: 0.0 (uniform) to positive values. traversestepslimit: None. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute thread ID tid. Skip masked rays. Skip rays with zero chunk counts if not the first pass. Initialize tlast = nearplanes[tid], continuous = false, nintervals = 0, nsamples = 0. Loop over intersections i from basetsorted to basetsorted + ngrids 2 - 1. 2. Interval Bounds: Compute valid interval bounds clamped to near/far planes: thistmin = max(tsorted[i], nearplanes[tid]), thistmax = min(tsorted[i + 1], farplanes[tid]). Skip if thistmin >= thistmax. 3. Step Size & Continuity: If !continuous, set tlast = thistmin if stepsize <= 0.0f. Otherwise, compute dt = clamp(tlast coneangle, stepsize, 1e10f) and march tlast += dt in a while loop until tlast + dt 0.5f >= thistmin. Set continuous = true after the first interval. 4. AABB Setup: Create AABBSpec from aabbs + level 6. Call setuptraversal to compute delta (voxel step), tdist (distance to next grid boundary), and indices (stepindex, currentindex, finalindex). 5. Voxel Traversal: While ttraverse < thistmax: Get cellid from current indices. Empty Cell: If !binaries[cellid], set continuous = false. If stepsize <= 0.0f, set tlast = ttraverse. Otherwise, march tlast using dt until tlast + dt 0.5f >= ttraverse. Advance traversal with singletraversal. If it returns false, break. Occupied Cell: If binaries[cellid], calculate tnext. If stepsize <= 0.0f, tnext = ttraverse. Otherwise, calculate dt, check if tlast + dt 0.5f >= ttraverse (break if so), else tnext = tlast + dt. Write Samples: If !firstpass and samples.chunkcnts is not null, store sample midpoint: samples.vals[idx] = (tnext + tlast) 0.5f where idx = chunkstartbin + nsamples. Set isvalid = true. Increment nsamples. Write Intervals: If intervals.chunkcnts != nullptr and !firstpass. If !continuous, write left interval (tlast) and right interval (tnext) with isleft=true and isright=true, incrementing nintervals twice. If continuous, write right interval (tnext) with isleft set on the previous index and isright=true, incrementing nintervals once. Set tlast = tnext. Advance traversal with singletraversal. If it returns false, break. 6. Finalization: Store tlast to terminateplanes[tid] if not null. Store nintervals to intervals.chunkcnts[tid] and nsamples to samples.chunkcnts[tid] if respective chunk counts are not null. Formula: Step size calculation: dt = \text{clamp}(t \cdot \text{cone\angle}, dt{min}, dt{max}), where t is the current distance along the ray, dt{min} is stepsize, and dt{max} is 1e10. Standard CUDA kernel context: nrays, ngrids, tid, basetsorted nrays = len(rayso) ngrids = len(aabbs) tid = getthreadid() # blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x if raysmask is not None and not raysmask[tid]: return if not firstpass and intervals.chunkcnts[tid] == 0: return tlast = nearplanes[tid] continuous = False nintervals = 0 nsamples = 0 basetsorted = tid 2 # Assuming contiguous layout for simplicity for i in range(basetsorted, basetsorted + ngrids 2, 2): if i + 1 >= len(tsorted): break thistmin = max(tsorted[i], nearplanes[tid]) thistmax = min(tsorted[i + 1], farplanes[tid]) if thistmin >= thistmax: continue if not continuous: if stepsize <= 0.0: tlast = thistmin else: dt = clamp(tlast coneangle, stepsize, 1e10) while tlast + dt 0.5 < thistmin: tlast += dt continuous = True gridid = tindices[i] aabb = aabbs[gridid] # setuptraversal computes delta, tdist, stepindex, currentindex, finalindex delta, tdist, stepindex, currentindex, finalindex = setuptraversal( rayso[tid], raysd[tid], thistmin, thistmax, aabb) if delta is None: continue ttraverse = thistmin steps = 0 while ttraverse < thistmax: if traversestepslimit is not None and traversestepslimit > 0: if steps >= traversestepslimit: break steps += 1 cellid = getcellid(currentindex, binaries[gridid].shape) # Linear to 3D index conversion if not binaries[gridid][cellid]: continuous = False if stepsize <= 0.0: tlast = ttraverse else: dt = clamp(tlast coneangle, stepsize, 1e10) while tlast + dt 0.5 < ttraverse: tlast += dt if not singletraversal(tdist, currentindex, stepindex, delta): break ttraverse += tdist else: if stepsize <= 0.0: tnext = ttraverse else: dt = clamp(tlast coneangle, stepsize, 1e10) if tlast + dt 0.5 >= ttraverse: break tnext = tlast + dt if not firstpass and samples.chunkcnts is not None: idx = chunkstartbin + nsamples samples.vals[idx] = (tnext + tlast) 0.5 samples.rayindices[idx] = tid samples.isvalid[idx] = True nsamples += 1 if intervals.chunkcnts is not None and not firstpass: if not continuous: intervals.vals[nintervals] = tlast intervals.rayindices[nintervals] = tid intervals.isleft[nintervals] = True intervals.isright[nintervals] = True nintervals += 1 intervals.vals[nintervals] = tnext intervals.rayindices[nintervals] = tid intervals.isleft[nintervals] = True intervals.isright[nintervals] = True nintervals += 1 else: intervals.isleft[nintervals - 1] = True intervals.vals[nintervals] = tnext intervals.rayindices[nintervals] = tid intervals.isleft[nintervals] = False intervals.isright[nintervals] = True nintervals += 1 tlast = tnext if not singletraversal(tdist, currentindex, stepindex, delta): break ttraverse += tdist if terminateplanes is not None: terminateplanes[tid] = tlast if intervals.chunkcnts is not None: intervals.chunkcnts[tid] = nintervals if samples.chunkcnts is not None: samples.chunkcnts[tid] = nsamples def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def setuptraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, aabb): # Standard DDA AABB traversal setup not detailed in sources invdir = 1.0 / rayd tminaabb = (aabb[:3] - rayo) invdir tmaxaabb = (aabb[3:] - rayo) invdir tenter = max(max(tminaabb), tmin) texit = min(min(tmaxaabb), tmax) if tenter >= texit: return None, 0, None, None, None delta = rayd tdist = 1.0 return delta, tdist, 0, 0, 0 def singletraversal(tdist, currentindex, stepindex, delta): # Standard DDA voxel step advancement not detailed in sources return True def getcellid(index, shape): # Simple modulo arithmetic for linear to 3D index z = index // (shape[0] shape[1]) y = (index // shape[0]) % shape[1] x = index % shape[0] return (x, y, z) def getthreadid(): # Standard CUDA thread ID computation return 0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping Grids: The order of grids matters. The grid with the lower index (front) has higher priority when examining occupancy status. If they overlap, the first grid's occupancy status overwrites the second's. Invalid Intervals: If the clamped near bound is greater than or equal to the clamped far bound (e.g., due to nearplane > farplane or grid boundaries), the interval is skipped to prevent zero-length or negative-length marching segments. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when comparing tlast + dt 0.5f with boundaries. The use of 0.5f suggests a margin for error or centering logic. Two-Pass Allocation: If overallocate is false, a two-pass approach is required. The first pass counts intervals/samples, and the second pass fills them. This requires persistent storage of chunkcnts between passes. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and the number of voxels traversed per ray. The adaptive step size can reduce the number of samples for distant rays, improving performance. Memory Complexity: Depends on the output buffers. If overallocate is true, memory is allocated based on traversestepslimit 2 for intervals and traversestepslimit for samples. If false, a two-pass approach is used, requiring less initial memory but two kernel launches. Performance: Optimized for GPU execution using CUDA. Efficiently handles sparse voxel grids by skipping empty cells. Strengths: Adaptive step sizing reduces sample count for distant objects. Handles multiple grids and occupancy masks. Efficient empty space skipping. Limitations: Requires precomputed sorted intersections. Overlapping grid handling is simplistic (first grid wins). Two-pass allocation adds overhead if overallocate is false. When to Use: NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines where adaptive sampling is beneficial. When Not to Use: When uniform sampling is required and coneangle is 0. When overlapping grids with complex occlusion rules are needed. The method is implemented in the nerfacc library, a general NeRF acceleration toolbox. It is used in the CNC (Context-based Neural Compression) framework for efficient ray marching in NeRF and 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines. name: Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) Traversal
head: 3D DDA Ray Traversal, DDA Algorithm, Digital Differential Analyzer
body: Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) Traversal is a grid traversal algorithm that determines the sequence of axis-aligned grid cells (voxels or tiles) intersected by a ray. It solves the problem of efficiently locating geometry in a dense grid without performing expensive per-voxel intersection tests or suffering from the gaps and redundancies of naive fixed-step ray marching. Unlike Siddon's Algorithm, which computes exact parametric intersection lengths for integration, DDA steps discretely through grid cells using incremental comparisons, making it suitable for real-time ray casting and shadow calculation. It sets itself apart from 3D Bresenham Voxel Traversal by using floating-point t-values for boundary distances rather than integer error accumulation, allowing it to handle arbitrary ray directions and non-unit grid spacing more naturally. The algorithm advances analytically from one cell boundary to the next, avoiding fixed-distance sampling steps. The core mechanism determines the next cell by comparing the distances to the upcoming boundaries on the x, y, and z axes, selecting the minimum distance to advance. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} = (ox, oy, oz) in world or local space. Ray direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz). Grid parameters: voxel size v (or dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz and bounds). Optional: Maximum traversal distance or step limit. Outputs: A sequence of voxel indices (i, j, k) visited by the ray. Optional: Entry and exit distances t{entry}, t{exit} for each voxel. The state is maintained using three vectors of size 3 (one per axis) and a current index vector: 1. step: Integer vector \{-1, 0, 1\} indicating the direction of index increment per axis. 2. tdelta: Float vector representing the distance along the ray to traverse one voxel width. 3. tmax: Float vector representing the distance from the ray origin to the next boundary crossed in each axis. 4. currentvoxel: Integer vector (i, j, k) representing the current cell index. 1. Validate Direction: If \mathbf{d} is zero or non-finite, return error. 2. Determine Start Voxel: Compute the initial voxel index containing the ray origin. For a uniform grid with voxel size v, i = \lfloor ox / v \rfloor. If the origin lies exactly on a boundary k \cdot v, it belongs to cell k (using floor). Clamp indices to grid bounds. 3. Compute Step Direction: \text{step}i = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } di > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} If di = 0, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension. 4. Compute Delta (t{\Delta}): The distance to traverse one voxel. t{\Delta, i} = \frac{vi}{|di|} \quad \text{if } di \neq 0 If di = 0, set t{\Delta, i} = 0. 5. Compute Initial Max (t{max}): The distance to the first boundary in each axis. t{max, i} = \begin{cases} \frac{(i + 1)vi - oi}{di} & \text{if } di > 0 \\ \frac{i \cdot vi - oi}{di} & \text{if } di < 0 \\ \infty & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} If the ray starts inside the grid, the initial boundary is the next one in the direction of travel. Iterate while the ray remains within grid bounds and has not exceeded max distance/steps: 1. Identify Axis: Find the axis k with the minimum boundary distance: t{min} = \min(t{max, x}, t{max, y}, t{max, z}). 2. Record Cell: Yield or process currentvoxel with interval [t{entry}, t{min}]. 3. Advance Index: Increment the index in the selected axis: \text{current\voxel}k \leftarrow \text{current\voxel}k + \text{step}k. 4. Update Boundary: Update the boundary distance for axis k: t{max, k} \leftarrow t{max, k} + t{\Delta, k}. 5. Update Entry: Set t{entry} \leftarrow t{min}. Zero Direction Components: If di = 0, the axis never steps. t{max, i} is set to infinity, and t{\Delta, i} is 0. Coincident Crossings: If the ray hits an edge or corner (multiple t{max} values are equal), a fixed priority order (e.g., X, then Y, then Z) must be used to determine which axis steps first to ensure deterministic traversal. Precision Errors: Successive summation of t{max} can lead to floating-point error accumulation over long traversals. Some implementations recalculate t{max} analytically or use correction terms if t{max} falls behind the current ray parameter. Over-traversal: Traversal should stop at a distance of 1 voxel or a specified threshold to prevent over-traversal beyond a target point (e.g., LiDAR hit). Empty Space: Cells outside a bounded volume are treated as traversable empty space, allowing the ray to cross into the volume. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddatraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsize, gridbounds): """ Traverses a uniform grid along a ray using the DDA algorithm. Args: rayorigin: tuple (ox, oy, oz) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) voxelsize: float or tuple (vx, vy, vz) gridbounds: object with min and max voxel indices Yields: (voxelindex, tentry, texit) """ # 1. Initialize current voxel index currentvoxel = [ int(rayorigin[0] // voxelsize[0]), int(rayorigin[1] // voxelsize[1]), int(rayorigin[2] // voxelsize[2]) ] # Clamp to grid bounds currentvoxel = [ max(gridbounds.min[0], min(gridbounds.max[0], currentvoxel[0])), max(gridbounds.min[1], min(gridbounds.max[1], currentvoxel[1])), max(gridbounds.min[2], min(gridbounds.max[2], currentvoxel[2])) ] # 2. Step direction per axis step = [0, 0, 0] for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] > 0: step[i] = 1 elif raydirection[i] < 0: step[i] = -1 else: step[i] = 0 # 3. Distance to next boundary (tmax) and delta tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tdelta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] == 0: tmax[i] = float('inf') tdelta[i] = 0.0 else: # Boundary is the face between currentvoxel and the next cell # If step > 0, next boundary is at (current + 1) size # If step < 0, next boundary is at current size boundaryidx = currentvoxel[i] + (1 if step[i] > 0 else 0) nextboundary = boundaryidx voxelsize[i] tmax[i] = (nextboundary - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] tdelta[i] = voxelsize[i] / abs(raydirection[i]) tentry = 0.0 # 4. Traversal Loop while (currentvoxel[0] >= gridbounds.min[0] and currentvoxel[0] <= gridbounds.max[0] and currentvoxel[1] >= gridbounds.min[1] and currentvoxel[1] <= gridbounds.max[1] and currentvoxel[2] >= gridbounds.min[2] and currentvoxel[2] <= gridbounds.max[2]): # Find minimum boundary distance with fixed priority X, Y, Z minidx = 0 minval = tmax[0] if tmax[1] < minval: minval = tmax[1] minidx = 1 if tmax[2] < minval: minidx = 2 texit = tmax[minidx] yield currentvoxel, tentry, texit # Advance index and update boundary currentvoxel[minidx] += step[minidx] tmax[minidx] += tdelta[minidx] tentry = texit The standard Digital Differential Analyzer traversal for uniform grids, using floating-point t-values for boundary distances. Traverses a fixed 4x4x4 grid of "wide cells" within an AABB, generating bounding boxes and t-intervals to optimize octree traversal. Replaces deep octree traversal with a two-level hierarchy (coarse then fine) to skip empty space in huge voxel spaces. Uses a 64-bit bitmask per brick to skip empty voxels inside an occupied brick without additional texture lookups. Combines hierarchical traversal with narrow-band detection, halting at the first sign change in a scalar field. Samples data at voxel centers upon entry, prioritizing speed over sampling uniformity. Adapts DDA for GPUs using SIMD parallelism, shared memory caching, and register management. An algorithm that captures all discrete grid points the line passes through, implemented as a naive reference for comparison. Determines the surface normal of a voxel hit by comparing accumulated distances to x and y planes using branchless programming: compare = totalt.x <= totalt.y ? vec2(1.0,0.0): vec2(0.0,1.0). Extends DDA to handle overlapping, compactly supported B-spline basis functions by using a neural network to compute basis contributions, avoiding closed-form analytical expressions. Identifies the first cell hit via an item buffer (Z-buffer encoding of indices) and traverses subsequent cells by finding the nearest intersection among the five remaining walls of the current cell, explicitly checking for re-entry after exiting. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels traversed. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, as only the current state vectors are stored. Performance: Highly efficient for uniform grids and real-time applications. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory footprint, deterministic, and fast for dense or uniform data. Limitations: Visits every voxel along the ray path, which is inefficient for sparse data or large empty spaces compared to hierarchical methods. Precision errors can accumulate over very long traversals. When to use: Real-time ray casting, shadow mapping, uniform grids, or when hardware simplicity is prioritized. When not to use: Sparse volumes where empty space skipping is critical (use Hierarchical Grid Traversal or Octree and Tree Traversal). The 3D DDA algorithm was introduced by Amanatides and Woo in their seminal paper "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing" (1987/1988). It is widely used in ray casting and volume rendering. Variants and optimizations continue to be developed for specific hardware and data structures, such as GPU implementations and hierarchical extensions. name: DDA
head: Digital Differential Analyzer, DDA Algorithm, 3D DDA method
body: The Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) is a grid traversal algorithm used in volume rendering and ray tracing to efficiently determine the sequence of voxels or grid cells intersected by a ray. It solves the problem of locating geometry in a dense uniform grid without performing expensive per-voxel intersection tests or suffering from the precision errors and missed voxels inherent in naive fixed-step ray marching. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using incremental arithmetic to step through adjacent grid cells along the ray direction, often eliminating branching paths to optimize for GPU execution. Unlike Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal which explicitly tracks parametric distances (t-values) and deltas, standard DDA implementations often utilize an Origin-Inverse Direction (OOD) formulation or a sideDist approach to drive integer-step traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (typically normalized), and a uniform voxel grid. Output: A sequence of voxel indices (i, j, k) visited by the ray, or a boolean hit status if a specific cell is encountered. Data Structures: The core state is typically held in a structure containing: pos: Current voxel coordinates, usually vec3<i32> or vec3<int>. Initialized to \lfloor \mathbf{o} \rfloor. stepdir: Direction of movement per axis, vec3<i32>, derived from \text{sign}(\mathbf{d}). deltadist: Distance along the ray to cross one grid cell, vec3<f32>. Calculated as |\mathbf{d}^{-1}| (absolute value of inverse direction). sidedist: Distance to the next grid boundary along the ray, vec3<f32>. Initialization: 1. Compute inverse direction \mathbf{d}^{-1} = 1/\mathbf{d}. Handle zero components by setting inverse to infinity or handling separately. 2. Set current position \mathbf{pos} = \lfloor \mathbf{o} \rfloor. 3. Set step direction \mathbf{step\dir} = \text{sign}(\mathbf{d}). 4. Set delta distance \mathbf{delta\dist} = |\mathbf{d}^{-1}|. 5. Calculate initial side distances. A common robust formulation (avoiding explicit ceiling/floor logic for boundaries) is: \mathbf{side\dist} = (\text{sign}(\mathbf{d}) \cdot (\lfloor \mathbf{o} \rfloor - \mathbf{o}) + 0.5) \cdot \mathbf{delta\dist} + 0.5 \cdot \mathbf{delta\dist} Note: The exact formula varies by implementation. A simpler geometric derivation for the first boundary is: If dx > 0: t{next} = (\lceil ox \rceil - ox) / dx. If dx < 0: t{next} = (ox - \lfloor ox \rfloor) / |dx| (distance to lower bound). The sidedist represents the parametric distance t to the next crossing. Stepping Loop: 1. Determine which axis to step by finding the minimum sidedist. 2. Update sidedist for the stepped axis by adding deltadist. 3. Update pos for the stepped axis by adding stepdir. 4. Repeat until the ray exits the grid or a hit is found. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initdda(rayorigin, raydirection): # 1. Inverse direction invdir = 1.0 / raydirection # 2. Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero # If a component is 0, the ray never crosses a grid line in that axis. # We can set deltadist to infinity or handle it via masking. # For this implementation, we assume non-zero directions or use a mask. # 3. Current voxel position pos = floor(rayorigin) # 4. Step direction stepdir = sign(raydirection) # 5. Delta distance (distance along ray to cross 1 unit in grid) deltadist = abs(invdir) # 6. Side distance (distance to next grid boundary) # Formula derived from: sidedist = (sign(d) (floor(o) - o) + 0.5) deltadist + 0.5 deltadist # This effectively calculates the distance to the nearest integer boundary in the direction of travel. sidedist = (stepdir (casttofloat(pos) - rayorigin) + 0.5) deltadist + 0.5 deltadist return { 'pos': pos, 'stepdir': stepdir, 'deltadist': deltadist, 'sidedist': sidedist } def stepdda(state): # Find the axis with the minimum sidedist # Using a mask to avoid branching # mask[i] is true if sidedist[i] <= sidedist[j] and sidedist[i] <= sidedist[k] # Cyclic comparison: x vs y,z; y vs z,x; z vs x,y mask = (state['sidedist'].xyz <= min(state['sidedist'].yzx, state['sidedist'].zxy)) # Update sidedist for the stepped axis(es) # If multiple axes are equal (rare, degenerate), all are stepped state['sidedist'] += mask state['deltadist'] # Update position for the stepped axis(es) state['pos'] += mask state['stepdir'] # Return the normal of the face crossed (optional, for shading) # Normal is opposite to stepdir for the stepped axis normal = mask -state['stepdir'] return state, normal Parameters: rayorigin: vec3<f32>. raydirection: vec3<f32>, usually normalized. gridsize: vec3<i32> representing the dimensions of the voxel array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Components: If a ray direction component is zero, the ray is parallel to the grid lines in that axis. The inverse direction is infinite. The algorithm must handle this to avoid NaNs or infinite loops. A common fix is to set deltadist to infinity for that axis, ensuring it is never selected as the minimum sidedist. Rays on Boundaries: If the ray origin lies exactly on a grid line, the initial sidedist calculation might yield 0. This can cause the ray to "stutter" or process the same cell twice. Guarding against dt > 0 or adding a small epsilon can prevent this. GPU Branching: Standard implementations using if statements for determining the next axis can be inefficient on GPUs due to divergence. The mask-based approach described above eliminates branching. Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate over long traversals. Using integer arithmetic for voxel indices (as done in pos) mitigates this, while sidedist remains floating-point. TRFRay3 is a data structure and traversal algorithm for performing Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) ray marching through a voxel grid. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which voxels a ray intersects by stepping through adjacent grid cells along a ray direction. It sets itself apart from its siblings by encapsulating the ray state (origin, direction, inverse direction, and signs) into a contiguous, SIMD-friendly structure that precomputes division-heavy terms to avoid runtime division. Unlike Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal which explicitly tracks tMax and tDelta per axis, TRFRay3 often utilizes an Origin-Inverse Direction (OOD) formulation or a sideDist approach to drive the integer-step traversal. A differentiable Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) loop that traverses a grid along a ray, invoking a callback function for each visited cell. It extends standard DDA traversal by maintaining differentiable state variables, allowing gradients to flow back through the ray marching steps. Amanatides-Woo is a fast, branch-minimal algorithm for traversing a uniform 3D voxel grid along a ray, visiting only the voxels intersected by the ray in O(nx + ny + nz) time. It solves the problem of efficiently locating geometry in a dense grid without performing expensive per-voxel intersection tests or suffering from the precision errors and missed voxels inherent in naive fixed-step ray marching. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using floating-point parametric distances (t-values) to determine the next voxel boundary crossing based on the minimum time to cross any axis boundary, guaranteeing that the ray stops and tests a voxel index at exactly one of the x, y, or z dividing planes. 3D Bresenham Voxel Traversal is a discrete line algorithm used to determine the sequence of integer voxel coordinates intersected by a line segment in a 3D grid. It rasterizes a line between two integer coordinates by iterating along the dominant axis and updating the other two axes based on accumulated error terms. It differs from its parent DDA and siblings like Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal by operating entirely in integer arithmetic rather than floating-point plane intersections, making it computationally lighter but topologically distinct: it does not consider every block the ray passes through, skipping those where the ray does not get close enough to the block center. This method traverses the grid cells intersected by a line segment defined by two points, calling a visitor function for each cell in traversal order. It solves the problem of efficiently determining the sequence of axis-aligned grid cells crossed by a ray or segment, which is a fundamental step in volume rendering and ray tracing. Unlike the original Amanatides–Woo voxel traversal which is optimized for large 3D grids with high initialization costs, this specific 2D floating-point variant is designed for small grids (e.g., 2x2 cells) where its logic is adapted to minimize overhead. It builds on DDA by using a Digital Differential Analyzer approach to step through cells based on distance to grid boundaries. Hierarchical DDA Traversal extends standard DDA DDA to efficiently traverse sparse, multi-resolution volume structures by adapting step sizes to the current tree level. Unlike sibling methods that step voxel-by-voxel Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal or use fixed-resolution grids 3D Bresenham Voxel Traversal, this family skips empty internal nodes or adjusts mip-levels dynamically to balance speed and precision. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(n) where n is the number of voxels intersected by the ray. This is optimal as every intersected voxel must be visited. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory for the traversal state (position, distances, directions). Measured Performance: The DDA method is well-suited for hardware implementation and can be pipelined for maximized throughput. On GPUs, branchless implementations (using masks) significantly outperform branching versions by avoiding instruction divergence. Compared to naive ray marching (fixed small steps), DDA reduces the number of iterations from thousands to the number of intersected voxels, resulting in significantly fewer computations. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fast, branch-minimal (with mask optimization), simple to implement, works well on uniform grids. Limitations: Performance degrades on sparse grids where many empty voxels are visited. Not suitable for non-uniform grids without modification (e.g., Hierarchical DDA Traversal). Precision issues can arise with very long rays or very small voxels if floating-point precision is insufficient. When to Use: Use for uniform voxel grids in volume rendering or ray tracing where performance is critical and the grid is dense enough that the overhead of hierarchical structures is not justified. Use when GPU efficiency is a priority and branchless code is required. When Not to Use: Do not use for sparse grids; use Hierarchical DDA Traversal or Voxel Occupancy Mask instead. Do not use if the grid is non-uniform; use Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal with adaptive step sizes or a different acceleration structure. The Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm originated as a hardware or software method for interpolation of variables over an interval between start and end points, used for rasterization of lines, triangles, and polygons. In the context of 3D grid traversal, it was adapted to efficiently determine which voxels a ray intersects. The specific branchless GPU-optimized version is often cited from work by Xiao et al., which eliminates branching paths for faster GPU execution.
