1 rayDirX = dirX + planeX cameraX rayDirY = dirY + planeY cameraX rayPosX = posX rayPosY = posY mapX = int(rayPosX) mapY = int(rayPosY) deltaDistX = math.sqrt(1 + (rayDirY rayDirY) / (rayDirX rayDirX)) deltaDistY = math.sqrt(1 + (rayDirX rayDirX) / (rayDirY rayDirY)) if rayDirX < 0: stepX = -1 sideDistX = (rayPosX - mapX) deltaDistX else: stepX = 1 sideDistX = (mapX + 1.0 - rayPosX) deltaDistX if rayDirY < 0: stepY = -1 sideDistY = (rayPosY - mapY) deltaDistY else: stepY = 1 sideDistY = (mapY + 1.0 - rayPosY) deltaDistY hit = 0 side = 0 while hit < 100: if sideDistX < sideDistY: sideDistX += deltaDistX mapX += stepX side = 0 else: sideDistY += deltaDistY mapY += stepY side = 1 # Clamp map coordinates if mapX < 0: mapX = 0 if mapX >= mapWidth: mapX = mapWidth - 1 if mapY < 0: mapY = 0 if mapY >= mapHeight: mapY = mapHeight - 1 # Check for hit (simplified condition based on source) # Source implies checking if voxel exists or is non-zero if worldMap[mapX][mapY][0] != 0: # Placeholder for actual hit test hit = 1 break if hit == 0: continue if side == 0: perpWallDist = (mapX - rayPosX + (1 - stepX) / 2) / rayDirX else: perpWallDist = (mapY - rayPosY + (1 - stepY) / 2) / rayDirY lineHeight = int(h / perpWallDist) # Depth buffer for occlusion within the column depth = [100000] w for b in range(12): drawStart = (lineHeight (b - 6)) + pitch drawEnd = lineHeight + (lineHeight (b - 6)) + pitch # Clamp to screen bounds if drawStart < 0: drawStart = 0 if drawStart >= h: drawStart = h - 1 if drawEnd < 0: drawEnd = 0 if drawEnd >= h: drawEnd = h - 1 color = worldMap[mapX][mapY][b] if side == 1: color = color // 2 # Darken if side hit if color != 0: # Assuming 0 is Black/Empty # verLineDepth implementation assumed to handle occlusion via depth array # Since verLineDepth is not defined in source, we simulate the logic: # Draw vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd if not occluded for y in range(drawStart, drawEnd + 1): if y < h: # Simple occlusion check against depth buffer at x # Note: Source passes depth array to verLineDepth, implying it updates it # Here we assume a simple depth test for the slice screen[x][y] = color Renders a 3D voxel grid by exploiting vertical ray coherence to cut space with multiple planes, determining visible voxel segments in software and projecting them as rectangles onto the screen using an OpenGL stencil buffer. Unlike Voxel Raycasting with Vertical Slicing, which renders and combines lines, VoxlapGL projects rectangles and contains no quadrant distinctions in its traversal code. Time Complexity: O(w \cdot h) for rendering, where w is screen width and h is screen height. The DDA traversal is O(\text{distance}) per ray, and the vertical slicing adds a constant factor of 12 iterations per hit. Memory Complexity: O(\text{mapWidth} \cdot \text{mapHeight} \cdot 12) for the voxel map, plus O(w) for the depth buffer. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the 12-layer iteration per voxel hit. The use of integer arithmetic for DDA and simple clamping helps performance. Strengths: Visualizes voxel thickness and internal structure, providing a more 3D-aware appearance than standard raycasting. Limitations: The aspect ratio of voxels may be distorted if not adjusted (source notes uncertainty about dividing by 2 for square voxels). The fixed 12-layer structure limits flexibility in voxel depth representation. Originating from the voxnine project by JCLemme, this technique is an unofficial implementation of a 12-layer vertical raycasting method. It extends the concept of dual-layer raycasting to a more granular vertical representation, allowing for the visualization of voxel depth in a 2D screen space. name: VoxlapGL
head: VoxelRenderer
body: VoxlapGL is a raycasting technique that renders a 3D voxel grid by exploiting vertical ray coherence to cut the space with multiple planes. It determines visible voxel segments in software and projects them as rectangles onto the screen using an OpenGL stencil buffer. Unlike its sibling Voxel Raycasting with Vertical Slicing, which renders and combines lines, VoxlapGL projects rectangles and contains no quadrant distinctions in its traversal code. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel array (Voxel Space) and a camera position/orientation. Output: A 2D screen image. Data Structures: The memory layout matches the VXL format. 1. Column Pointers: A 1024x1024 array of pointers, each pointing to the start of a column's data. 2. Column Data: Each column stores a simple array containing: The number of visible parts. The length of each visible part. The actual voxel data. Note: Storing solid/air information in a simple boolean array for a 1024x1024x256 map would require 32MB of memory without any actual voxel data. Algorithm Steps: 1. Plane Selection: Determine the number of raycast planes to cast based on the view direction: ~300 planes when looking towards the horizon. ~800 planes when viewing from above. ~1000 planes when looking straight up or down. Viewspace culling is applied to optimize this count. 2. Grid Traversal: For each plane, step through all columns hit by the raycast plane. The traversal uses efficient grid stepping without quadrant distinctions, using bitwise operations and incremental updates. 3. Visibility Determination: In software, determine which parts of the columns are visible. 4. Projection: Project all visible parts in the plane onto a virtual projection line that maintains a constant distance to the eye point and is perpendicular to the ground. 5. Rendering: Use OpenGL to project a rectangle onto the screen using a stencil buffer, filling the entire screen with the projected data. Grid Traversal Pseudocode: The core grid stepping logic handles all 4 cases in a single loop using incremental operations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. k = (((unsigned long)(tp[1] - tp[0])) >> 31) d = tp[k] tp[k] += ti[k] ip += ipi[k] Note: BLOCKSCAN.KC from EVALDRAW provides a working example of this algorithm. Parameters: Field of View: 90 degrees. Viewspace Culling: Provides a 4x speed boost when looking towards the horizon. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: Storing solid/air information in a simple array for a 1024x1024x256 map requires 32MB of memory without any actual voxel data. Performance: Using OpenGL for the second pass (copy & project color data) yields minimal or negative speedup on older graphics hardware and may cause deceleration on newer hardware. Boundary Calculation: Calculating grid boundaries for "perfect" looking cubes using interpolation requires one multiplication per column. Hardware Requirements: Requires at least a Pentium Pro CPU and a graphics adapter supporting OpenGL. Performance: Viewspace culling is critical for performance, providing a 4x speed boost at a 90-degree FOV when looking towards the horizon. Limitations: The reliance on OpenGL for the second pass can be a bottleneck; software-based projection might be faster on older hardware, while newer hardware may also suffer from deceleration due to this approach. Complexity: The grid traversal is optimized to avoid quadrant distinctions, reducing branching overhead. VoxlapGL was developed by Sebastian Scholz in 2004/2005 as a forum demo. It was created as an alternative to other voxel rendering techniques like VoxLap, aiming to exploit vertical ray coherence more efficiently. The demo was distributed as a ZIP archive with batch files for execution. Forum archive / Ken Silverman / VoxlapGL, https://jonof.id.au/forum/topic-166.html, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Dual-Cell DDA Raycasting for Particles
head: Dual-Cell DDA, Ray-Traced Mirror and Glass Particles
body: A ray-tracing optimization for particle volumes that uses a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) over dual cells to efficiently test for ray-sphere intersections, enabling real-time rendering of glossy mirrors and refractive glass particles. It distinguishes itself from standard voxel raycasting by leveraging a pre-sorted neighbor grid and a 2×2×2 cell expansion strategy to guarantee hit detection within a dual cell without exhaustive search, significantly reducing shading overhead for deep particle piles. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin and direction; particle system data including sortedpositionsbuffer, sortedindicesbuffer, celloffsetsbuffer, cellsize, and gridorigin. Output: Final pixel color, accounting for reflections, refractions, and room geometry intersections. Data Structures: The method relies on additive accessors added to the FluidSimulation structure, requiring no restructuring of existing files: sortedpositionsbuffer: Array of particle positions, sorted spatially. sortedindicesbuffer: Array of indices corresponding to the sorted positions. celloffsetsbuffer: Offsets defining the neighbor grid topology. cellsize: Scalar size of a single grid cell. gridorigin: Origin point of the grid. Parameters: setrtbounces: Integer controlling ray bounce depth. Default is 2. Particle count: Default 8192 larger particles. Particle Radius: Must be less than half a cell size to guarantee the 2×2×2 test coverage. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Cast primary rays from the camera. If rt=on, assign materials: 30% glossy black mirrors, 35% glass (IOR 1.5, Fresnel), and 35% matte grey. 2. DDA Traversal: Perform a 3D DDA over the dual cells of the fluid's neighbor grid. 3. Dual Cell Testing: For each DDA step at a current dual cell, test the 8 surrounding grid cells (forming a 2×2×2 block) for ray-sphere intersections. Geometric Guarantee: Since particle radius r < \frac{1}{2} \times \text{cell\size}, any sphere intersecting the dual cell must intersect at least one of the 8 surrounding grid cells. 4. Material Interaction: If a sphere is hit, compute reflection (for mirrors) or refraction (for glass, exiting the far side). Recursively cast new rays up to setrtbounces. 5. Room Intersection: If a ray misses all spheres during traversal, it intersects the room geometry. Determine color based on the panel's mean irradiance, walls lit by the panel plus one voxel cone, or black for the open front. The sky gradient substitutes for the ceiling and open front. 6. name: Raycasting Texture Coordinate Calculation
head: u-coordinate derivation, wallX calculation
body: This method computes the horizontal texture coordinate (commonly wallX or the "u" coordinate) for a raycast intersection against an axis-aligned grid wall. It converts the 3D hit point into a normalized 0, 1) texture space value by exploiting the grid's axis alignment: the coordinate depends strictly on the hit face type (vertical or horizontal), using the perpendicular distance and ray direction to determine the position along the wall's local axis. It differs from general [3D texture mapping by avoiding full projection matrices and instead deriving the coordinate directly from DDA traversal state. Inputs: side: Integer indicating the hit face type. 0 for vertical face (constant-X grid line), 1 for horizontal face (constant-Y grid line). px, py: The camera position in world coordinates (x, y). dirX, dirY: The ray direction vector components. perpDist: The perpendicular distance from the camera to the hit wall plane. mapX, mapY: The integer grid coordinates of the cell where the hit occurred. texWidth: The width of the texture image in pixels. Outputs: wallX: The wrapped texture coordinate in 0, 1). texX: The integer column index in the texture image. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the calculation uses scalar values derived from the raycasting traversal. Steps: 1. Determine the varying axis: Identify which world-space coordinate varies along the hit face. If side == 0 (vertical face), the coordinate varies along Y. Use py and dirY. If side == 1 (horizontal face), the coordinate varies along X. Use px and dirX. 2. Compute raw world-space coordinate: Calculate the position along the wall face using the formula: wallX{raw} = \begin{cases} py + perpDist \cdot dirY & \text{if } side == 0 \\ px + perpDist \cdot dirX & \text{if } side == 1 \end{cases} 3. Wrap to [0, 1): Remove the integer part to get the fractional position within the specific wall segment. wallX = wallX{raw} - \lfloor wallX{raw} \rfloor 4. Compute texture column index: Map the normalized coordinate to the texture's pixel width. texX = \lfloor wallX \cdot texWidth \rfloor Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculatetexturecoordinate(side, px, py, dirX, dirY, perpDist, mapX, mapY, texWidth): # Step 1 & 2: Determine axis and compute raw world-space coordinate if side == 0: sideaxisval = py sidedirval = dirY else: sideaxisval = px sidedirval = dirX rawwallx = sideaxisval + perpDist sidedirval # Step 3: Wrap to [0, 1) wallx = rawwallx - math.floor(rawwallx) # Step 4: Compute texture column index texx = math.floor(wallx texWidth) return wallx, texx Parameters: texWidth: Must be positive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Incorrect Side Logic: If side is misinterpreted (e.g., swapping vertical/horizontal logic), textures will appear sheared or scroll in the wrong direction when rays hit the opposite face type. Negative Coordinates: The wrapping step wallX -= Math.floor(wallX) correctly handles negative rawwallx values, ensuring the result is always in [0, 1). Precision: Floating-point precision errors in perpDist or direction vectors may cause slight jitter in wallX at grazing angles. A variant for handling thin walls recessed to the midline of a cell (tile id 5). Instead of stopping at the cell boundary, the ray advances to the door's centerline (distToMid). The texture coordinate wx is calculated at this midline. If the door is open (slide > 0), rays hitting within the opened gap (wx < slide) pass through without rendering the door. Steps: 1. If tile is 5, calculate distToMid: distToMid = \begin{cases} (sideDistX - deltaDistX) + \frac{deltaDistX}{2} & \text{if } side == 0 \\ (sideDistY - deltaDistY) + \frac{deltaDistY}{2} & \text{if } side == 1 \end{cases} 2. Calculate other (distance to the other side of the cell): other = \begin{cases} sideDistY & \text{if } side == 0 \\ sideDistX & \text{if } side == 1 \end{cases} If distToMid >= other, the ray exits the cell before the midline; continue marching. 3. Calculate texture coordinate wx at midline: wx = \begin{cases} player.y + distToMid \cdot rayDirY - mapY & \text{if } side == 0 \\ player.x + distToMid \cdot rayDirX - mapX & \text{if } side == 1 \end{cases} If wx < 0 or wx >= 1, continue. 4. Get door openness slide. If wx < slide, the ray passes through the open gap; continue. 5. Return hit with wallX: wx and doorShift: -slide. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method is fundamental to early raycasting engines, particularly those used in first-person shooters like Wolfenstein 3D. It leverages the simplicity of [grid-based collision detection to derive texture coordinates without full 3D projection matrices. The technique is often associated with the implementation details of DDA-based ray traversal, where the side of the hit face is known immediately upon intersection. mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, https://github.com/mithraskuipers/InteractiveLearning-Raycasting, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) A minimal Wolfenstein 3D raycasting engine, https://4rknova.com/blog/2026/07/06/wolfenstein-3d-raycasting, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Classic (Column Voxel Space)
head: Classic rendering, Column voxel space, Per-pixel 3D column raycast, Scanline voxel rendering
body: Classic rendering is a real-time terrain visualization technique that redraws the camera frustum every frame by marching world-vertical columns from the camera to the horizon. It differs from its sibling Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by casting one ray per screen column rather than per pixel, and from Dual-Layer DDA Raycasting by using a height-map-based column march instead of a dual-layer DDA approach. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A height map and a color map, both typically 1024 \times 1024 rasters. Camera parameters include position, orientation (yaw/pitch), field of view (FOV), and far clip distance (Distance). Outputs: A 2D image where each screen column is filled by the visible portion of the corresponding world-vertical column. Data Structures: Height Map: A 2D array of height values. Color Map: A 2D array of color values corresponding to the height map. Mip Chain: A pyramid of coarser height and color rasters derived from the base maps. The number of levels (LOD) is configurable, typically ranging from 1 to \log2(\text{map width}). For a 1024 map, this allows stops at 64 \times 64 (5 levels) or 2 \times 2 (10 levels). Parameters: Delta Z: Ray step size for classic and scanline modes. Range: 0.1–2.0. (Note: Unused by voxel mode). Distance: Far clip value. Range: 100–74500 meters. The maximum is approximately 74473 meters at 640 \times 480 resolution with 90^\circ FOV. LOD: Number of mip raster levels used. Range: 1 to \log2(\text{map width}). Default is the middle of the range. LOD Curve: Determines how switch distances fill 0 \dots \text{Distance}. Options: Linear (equal range per level), Doubling (each switch is twice as far as the previous), or Logarithmic (log-spaced from first switch to Distance). LOD Step: Meters to the first LOD switch. Range: 10 m to Distance. Editable only for Logarithmic curve; Linear and Doubling fill 0 \dots \text{Distance} automatically. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Camera: Set up the view matrix based on camera position, yaw, pitch, and FOV. 2. Iterate Screen Columns: For each screen column x from 0 to \text{width}-1: a. Cast Ray: Construct a 3D ray originating from the camera position and passing through the center of the screen pixel at column x. b. March Column: Step along the ray in world-vertical increments until the horizon or far clip is reached. c. Determine LOD: Calculate the distance from the camera. Select the appropriate mip level based on the LOD curve and LOD step. d. Sample Height/Color: i. If LOD is 0: Perform bilinear sampling on the base height/color maps. Refine the sample by snapping to the inner 1/16 \dots 1 m cell grid. Add height noise. ii. If LOD > 0: Perform nearest-neighbor sampling on the coarser mip level to keep coarse blocks flat and avoid interpolation artifacts. e. Render Stripe: Draw the vertical stripe for the column using the sampled color, handling depth via the column's visible height. 3. Repeat: Redraw the entire frustum every frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderclassic(heightmap, colormap, mipchain, camerapos, camerayaw, camerapitch, fov, screenwidth, screenheight, farclip, lodcurve, lodstep, basestep=1.0): # Initialize output buffer image = [[None for in range(screenheight)] for in range(screenwidth)] # Precompute LOD switch distances based on curve lodswitches = computelodswitches(lodcurve, lodstep, farclip) # Camera direction vectors cospitch = math.cos(camerapitch) sinpitch = math.sin(camerapitch) cosyaw = math.cos(camerayaw) sinyaw = math.sin(camerayaw) for x in range(screenwidth): # Cast ray for column x pixelcenterx = (x / screenwidth - 0.5) 2.0 pixelcentery = -((screenheight / 2) / (screenwidth / 2)) (pixelcenterx math.tan(fov / 2)) raydircam = normalize((pixelcenterx math.tan(fov / 2), pixelcentery math.tan(fov / 2), -1.0)) raydir = transformtoworld(raydircam, camerayaw, camerapitch) currentz = 0.0 currentlod = 0 # March column until horizon or far clip while currentz < farclip: # Determine LOD based on distance currentlod = getlodfordistance(currentz, lodswitches) # Step size grows with LOD to skip empty space stepsize = basestep (2 currentlod) # Sample height and color if currentlod == 0: # Bilinear sampling on base map height = samplebilinear(heightmap, camerapos, raydir, currentz) color = samplebilinear(colormap, camerapos, raydir, currentz) # Refine by snapping to 1/16...1 m cell grid cellsize = 1.0 / 16.0 height = math.floor(height / cellsize) cellsize color = math.floor(color / cellsize) cellsize # Add height noise height += math.sin(currentz 0.1) 0.05 # Standard noise function else: # Nearest-neighbor sampling on coarser mip level height = samplenearest(mipchain[currentlod].height, camerapos, raydir, currentz) color = samplenearest(mipchain[currentlod].color, camerapos, raydir, currentz) # Check if voxel is occupied (height < camera height) if height < camerapos.y: # Render the visible part of the column rendercolumnstripe(image, x, currentz, color) break currentz += stepsize return image def computelodswitches(lodcurve, lodstep, farclip): # Implementation depends on curve type if lodcurve == "Linear": # Equal range per level numlevels = int(math.log2(1024)) # Assuming 1024 map width rangeperlevel = farclip / numlevels return [i rangeperlevel for i in range(1, numlevels)] elif lodcurve == "Doubling": # Each switch is twice as far as the previous switches = [] dist = lodstep while dist < farclip: switches.append(dist) dist = 2 return switches elif lodcurve == "Logarithmic": # Log-spaced from first switch to Distance switches = [] numlevels = int(math.log2(1024)) dist = lodstep for i in range(1, numlevels): switches.append(dist) dist = lodstep (farclip / lodstep) (i / (numlevels - 1)) return switches return [] def getlodfordistance(distance, lodswitches): # Find the highest LOD level where distance >= switch distance lod = 0 for i, switch in enumerate(lodswitches): if distance >= switch: lod = i + 1 return lod def samplebilinear(mapdata, origin, direction, distance): # Compute intersection point on map grid mapscale = 1.0 # Assuming 1 unit = 1 meter u = (origin[0] + direction[0] distance) / mapscale v = (origin[2] + direction[2] distance) / mapscale u0, v0 = math.floor(u), math.floor(v) u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 # Bilinear interpolation h00 = mapdata[v0 % mapdata.height][u0 % mapdata.width] h10 = mapdata[v0 % mapdata.height][u1 % mapdata.width] h01 = mapdata[v1 % mapdata.height][u0 % mapdata.width] h11 = mapdata[v1 % mapdata.height][u1 % mapdata.width] fu, fv = u - u0, v - v0 return h00 (1 - fu) (1 - fv) + h10 fu (1 - fv) + h01 (1 - fu) fv + h11 fu fv def samplenearest(mapdata, origin, direction, distance): # Compute intersection point on map grid mapscale = 1.0 u = (origin[0] + direction[0] distance) / mapscale v = (origin[2] + direction[2] distance) / mapscale uidx = int(math.floor(u)) % mapdata.width vidx = int(math.floor(v)) % mapdata.height return mapdata[vidx][uidx] def rendercolumnstripe(image, x, z, color): # Draw vertical stripe for column x starting at z # Rasterization details omitted pass def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def transformtoworld(raydircam, yaw, pitch): # Standard camera-to-world rotation cosy, siny = math.cos(yaw), math.sin(yaw) cosp, sinp = math.cos(pitch), math.sin(pitch) x = raydircam[0] cosy + raydircam[2] siny y = raydircam[0] siny sinp + raydircam[1] cosp - raydircam[2] cosy sinp z = raydircam[0] siny cosp + raydircam[1] sinp + raydircam[2] cosy cosp return (x, y, z) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Interpolation Artifacts: Higher LODs use nearest-neighbor sampling to keep coarse blocks flat and avoid interpolation artifacts at distance. Precision: LOD 0 uses bilinear sampling and refinement, which may introduce precision issues if not handled correctly. Far Clip: The far clip distance must be set appropriately to avoid performance issues or visual clipping. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot S), where W is screen width, H is screen height, and S is the average number of steps per column. The use of mipmaps and growing step sizes reduces S for distant samples. Scaling: Scales with screen resolution and map size. Mipmaps help maintain performance at distance. Strengths: Simple implementation, real-time performance, effective for terrain visualization. Limitations: Limited to height-map-based terrain, may not handle complex geometry well. Measured Performance: Performance depends on hardware, resolution, and scene complexity. The technique is designed for real-time rendering. Origin: The technique is based on the "Voxel Space" method used in the game Comanche. History: The method has been implemented in various forms, including CPU (JS, WASM) and GPU (WebGPU) backends. varganorbert222/VoxelSpace, https://github.com/varganorbert222/VoxelSpace, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Screen-Space Ray Casting with Layer Traversal
head: Ray Marching through Columns
body: A real-time rendering technique that performs ray casting in screen space by marching pixel by pixel along the projected ray direction to intersect voxel columns and find entry/exit points for volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from its parent Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering by explicitly handling multiple surface layers within a column via a layer index, enabling the tracing of multiple refractions and deep ambient occlusion by leveraging full knowledge of surface layers rather than just the front-most surface. Inputs: A ray origin and direction (potentially perturbed for refraction), a voxel grid with stored surface layers per column, and a starting depth hint. Outputs: A sequence of intersection events (entry/exit) with their depths and layer indices. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin O and direction D. Voxel Column: A vertical stack of surface layers. Layer Index: An integer representing the depth layer within a column. The parity (LSB) of the layer index determines if the ray is entering or exiting the volume material relative to the view direction. Parameters: z\sgn: Sign of the ray direction relative to the view direction. Value is -1 if ray marching against view direction, otherwise 1. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start at the pixel containing the ray origin, using the depth layer from the previous pixel as a starting hint. 2. Column Intersection: Determine the current voxel column intersected by the ray. 3. Depth Bounds: Calculate the entry and exit depths of the ray within the current voxel column: [entry, exit]. 4. Layer Search: Find the first layer index after the entry depth, using the hint as a starting point: layer = first\layer\after(entry, z\sgn, start\hint = layer). 5. Validity Check: Determine if a valid layer exists within the column bounds: layer\found = (z\sgn \times layer \le exit \times z\sgn). 6. State Determination: Determine if the ray is entering the volume at this layer: entering = ((layer \& 1) \neq (z\sgn > 0)) == layer\found. 7. Marching Loop: Iterate through layers within the column bounds, detecting state changes between inside and outside. 8. Hint Update: Use the final layer value as the starthint for the next pixel to optimize the search. 9. Termination: Terminate when the voxel grid boundary is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. layer = initialhint # From previous pixel or initialization wasinside = False # Initial state before first layer column = nextintersected(ray, column) while column: entry, exit = intersectiondepths(ray, column) layer = firstlayerafter(entry, zsgn, starthint=layer) layerfound = (zsgn layer <= exit zsgn) entering = ((layer & 1) != (zsgn > 0)) == layerfound wasinside = entering # Initialize for do-while loop while True: if entering != wasinside: # handleintersection(...) computes contribution and restarts casting with a perturbed ray handleintersection(...) if layerfound: layer += zsgn entering = not entering if not (zsgn layer <= exit zsgn): break column = nextintersected(ray, column) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Hits: Hits may occur on voxel column boundaries in-between stored surface values. These are detected by checking if the ray changes its state between inside and outside when entering a new column (using LSB of layer index). Refraction Restart: When a surface is intersected, marching aborts, the ray's contribution is computed, and ray casting restarts with a new perturbed ray to trace multiple refractions. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of surface layers per voxel column. Strengths: Enables deep ambient occlusion by accessing multiple surface layers. Supports multiple refractions by restarting ray casting with perturbed rays. Efficient layer traversal using hints. Limitations: Requires storing multiple layers per voxel column, which increases memory usage compared to single-layer methods. This method is described in the context of memory-efficient on-the-fly voxelization of particle data, where it is used to render complex particle systems as volumetric surfaces. It builds upon the concept of screen-space ray casting and extends it to handle multiple surface layers within a voxel column, facilitating advanced effects like refraction and deep ambient occlusion. name: Voxel Polygon Rendering
body: Voxel Polygon Rendering is a hybrid rendering technique that fills the screen with vertical bars representing heights from a voxel map, effectively projecting a 2D area of the map onto the screen as a flat landscape. It solves the problem of rendering high-detail terrain at constant speed by avoiding traditional 6DOF polygon operations such as rotation matrix calculations and clipping. Unlike its sibling Voxel Raycasting with DDA and Vertical Stripe Rendering, which casts rays per screen column to find the first occupied voxel, Voxel Polygon Rendering maps screen pixels directly to map locations and draws spans from close to far, using an s-buffer (vertical c-buffer) to handle floating bars and prevent overdraw. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel map (array of height and color per location), screen resolution, camera position, and camera yaw (y-axis rotation). Output: A rendered image with vertical bars representing terrain height. Data Structures: VoxelMap: A 2D array where each cell stores height (float/int) and color (RGB). ColumnHeights: An array of size screenwidth, storing the current drawn height for each screen column to enable clipping. S-Buffer (Vertical C-Buffer): A data structure managing floating voxel bars that do not start at the bottom of the screen. It stores the top and bottom height of each bar per column to handle occlusion correctly. Steps: 1. Map Pixels to Voxel Space: For each pixel on the screen, determine its corresponding location on the voxel map based on the camera's y-axis rotation and position. Calculate the distance of the pixel from the camera to apply perspective correction, ensuring distant "mountains" appear smaller. 2. Retrieve Voxel Data: Fetch the height and color data from the voxel map. To reduce blockiness, apply bilinear filtering by retrieving four adjacent voxels (texels). 3. Calculate Span Height and Color: Compute the weighted average of the heights of the four fetched texels to determine the height of the single one-pixel wide span. Compute the weighted average of the colors of the four fetched texels to determine the span's color. 4. Clip Against Column Height: Compare the calculated span height against the current height stored in ColumnHeights for that column. If the span is behind the existing bar, clip it. If it is in front, update ColumnHeights with the new height. 5. Draw Span: Draw the vertical bar (span) for the pixel. If the bar is floating (not starting at the bottom), use the S-Buffer to manage its visibility and occlusion against other floating bars. 6. Repeat for All Columns: Process all screen columns from the bottom of the screen up to the horizon (approximately halfway up the screen). 7. Fill Backdrop: Fill the screen space above the horizon with a backdrop image. Formulas: Bilinear Height Interpolation: H{span} = \frac{H1 + H2 + H3 + H4}{4} Where H1, H2, H3, H4 are the heights of the four adjacent voxels. Bilinear Color Interpolation: C{span} = \frac{C1 + C2 + C3 + C4}{4} Where C1, C2, C3, C4 are the colors of the four adjacent voxels. Parameters: Rotation Constraint: The scene can only be rotated around the y-axis. Looking up/down (x-axis) is limited to about 10 degrees; looking down by 45 degrees wastes the picture because voxel bars must be perfectly vertical. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flat Floor Performance: Worst-case performance occurs on a completely flat floor. Every column of the screen becomes one higher every time a new line is processed. For the single pixel drawn, significant work is done: comparing to current column height, clipping, drawing, and updating column height. This is likely more expensive than drawing a single perspective-correct texture map. Floating Bars: The usual voxel algorithm assumes bars start at the bottom screen line. Floating bars (e.g., bridges, ceilings) require an s-buffer (vertical c-buffer) to handle correctly, as they have both a top and bottom side. Blockiness: Without bilinear filtering, voxels look blocky. Small details tend to flicker when the camera moves. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervoxelpolygonscreen(voxelmap, screenwidth, screenheight, camerayaw, camerapos): # Initialize column heights to -infinity or a value indicating no bar columnheights = [-infinity] screenwidth # Initialize S-Buffer for floating bars (simplified as a list of active bars per column) sbuffer = [[] for in range(screenwidth)] # Determine horizon line (approx halfway) horizony = screenheight // 2 # Draw from bottom (close) to horizon (far) for y in range(screenheight - 1, horizony - 1, -1): for x in range(screenwidth): # 1. Map pixel to voxel map location voxelx, voxely = mappixeltovoxel(x, y, camerayaw, camerapos) # 2. Retrieve four adjacent voxels for bilinear filtering h1, c1 = getvoxel(voxelmap, voxelx, voxely) h2, c2 = getvoxel(voxelmap, voxelx + 1, voxely) h3, c3 = getvoxel(voxelmap, voxelx, voxely + 1) h4, c4 = getvoxel(voxelmap, voxelx + 1, voxely + 1) # 3. Calculate weighted average height and color spanheight = (h1 + h2 + h3 + h4) / 4.0 spancolor = (c1 + c2 + c3 + c4) / 4.0 # 4. Clip against column height currentcolheight = columnheights[x] # If span is below current column height, it is occluded if spanheight <= currentcolheight: continue # 5. Draw span # Determine start and end y for the bar # Note: In this algorithm, bars are drawn as spans. # The 'height' here represents the top of the bar relative to the ground plane. # The bottom of the bar is determined by the previous height or ground. # For simplicity, assume bars start from ground (y=screenheight-1) up to spanheight # If floating, use s-buffer to determine visible segment bartop = spanheight barbottom = currentcolheight # Draw the visible segment drawverticalbar(x, barbottom, bartop, spancolor) # Update column height columnheights[x] = bartop # Handle floating bars in s-buffer if necessary # (Detailed s-buffer logic omitted as per source simplicity, but implied for non-ground bars) # Fill backdrop above horizon drawbackdrop(screenwidth, horizony) def mappixeltovoxel(x, y, camerayaw, camerapos): # Placeholder for perspective projection logic # Maps screen coordinates to 2D voxel map coordinates based on camera yaw # Returns (voxelx, voxely) pass def getvoxel(voxelmap, x, y): # Returns height and color from voxelmap at (x, y) pass def drawverticalbar(x, ystart, yend, color): # Draws a vertical line segment from ystart to yend at column x with color pass def drawbackdrop(width, horizony): # Fills screen area above horizony with backdrop image pass A hardware-accelerated rendering method for voxel landscapes that replaces software span rendering with triangle strips. It projects voxels onto the screen in columns and constructs geometry based on the visibility of adjacent columns to minimize polygon count and utilize hardware interpolation. Unlike software span rendering, this method buffers column projections to construct triangle strips, reducing draw calls and leveraging hardware interpolation for texture coordinates, lightmap colors, and heights. Time Complexity: Virtually constant speed regardless of scene detail, as it processes each screen pixel once. However, worst-case performance occurs on a completely flat floor, where every column's height is updated for every line, leading to significant clipping and drawing overhead per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires a large voxel map. Memory usage can be mitigated by tiling pre-built tiles of voxels. Strengths: Constant rendering speed; no 6DOF rotation matrix calculations or clipping required; allows for high detail; bilinear filtering reduces blockiness; supports floating structures via s-buffer. Limitations: Limited to y-axis rotation (approx. 10 degrees up/down); cannot handle significant x-axis rotation; blockiness without filtering; flickering of small details; worst-case performance on flat terrain. When to Use: Rendering high-detail terrain at constant speed where y-axis rotation is sufficient. When Not to Use: When full 6DOF rotation is required; when performance on flat terrain is critical; when memory is severely constrained without tiling support. Voxel Polygon Rendering was introduced by Jacco Bikker (a.k.a. "THE PHANTOM") in 1999 on Flipcode. It was developed as an alternative to traditional 6DOF polygon engines, aiming to provide high-detail graphics with constant speed. The technique was considered for inclusion in the "Focus" engine. flipcode - Voxel Polygons, https://www.flipcode.com/archives/VoxelPolygons.shtml, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Triangle Strip Voxel Projection
head: Hardware Accelerated Voxel Rendering, Structure Rendering Algorithm
body: A hardware-accelerated rendering method for voxel landscapes that replaces software span rendering with triangle strips. It projects voxels onto the screen in columns and constructs geometry based on the visibility of adjacent columns to minimize polygon count and utilize hardware interpolation. Unlike software span rendering which draws spans immediately, this method buffers column projections to construct triangle strips, reducing draw calls and leveraging hardware interpolation for texture coordinates, lightmap colors, and heights. Inputs: A voxel map representing a landscape; a camera view; a configurable step size for column sampling (default 32 pixels). Outputs: A sequence of OpenGL draw calls using triangle strips. Data Structures: The algorithm processes the landscape by scanning along depth lines (columns) rather than processing individual rays. For each sampled column, the visible voxels are projected onto the screen to determine their vertical span (Y-coordinates). The algorithm maintains state for the "current strip portion" defined by two columns: A: The left-most point (column) of the current strip portion. B: The right-most point (column) of the next column to be processed. Steps: 1. Scan Columns: Iterate through the landscape depth lines. Sample columns at intervals defined by the step size (default 32 pixels). Smaller steps generate more polygons. 2. Project Voxels: For each sampled column, project the visible voxels onto the screen to determine their vertical extent. 3. Evaluate Visibility: Determine the visibility status of column A (previous column) and column B (current column). A column is "visible" if it contains at least one voxel that contributes to the screen image. 4. Construct Geometry: Based on the visibility of A and B, execute one of four cases: Case 1 (A not visible, B visible): Start a new triangle strip. Send the vertices of column A followed by the vertices of column B to the graphics library (GL). Case 2 (A visible, B visible): Continue the currently active triangle strip. Send only the vertices of column B to the GL. Case 3 (A visible, B not visible): Send the coordinates of column B to the GL and stop the current triangle strip. Case 4 (A not visible, B not visible): Usually do nothing. However, handle a special sub-case for holes. 5. Handle Holes (Case 4 Sub-case): If a triangle strip was started or finished at the location of column A during a previous pass, a single triangle must be drawn to close the gap. To determine if this triangle must be drawn, check the condition: (Y1 > pY1) \text{ and } (Y2 > pY2) Where Y1, Y2 and pY1, pY2 are the relevant Y-coordinates of the projected spans. If true, draw the triangle. This approximation may draw triangles that are not strictly visible but is more efficient than performing line intersections. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. currentstripactive = False previouscolumnA = None previouscolumnAvisible = False stepsize = 32 # pixels for columnindex in range(0, width, stepsize): # Project voxels for the current column currentcolumnB = projectvoxels(columnindex) currentcolumnBvisible = isvisible(currentcolumnB) if previouscolumnA is not None: if previouscolumnAvisible and currentcolumnBvisible: # Case 2: Continue active strip sendverticestogl(currentcolumnB) elif not previouscolumnAvisible and currentcolumnBvisible: # Case 1: Start new strip starttrianglestrip() sendverticestogl(previouscolumnA) sendverticestogl(currentcolumnB) currentstripactive = True elif previouscolumnAvisible and not currentcolumnBvisible: # Case 3: End active strip sendverticestogl(currentcolumnB) endtrianglestrip() currentstripactive = False else: # Case 4: Both not visible # Check for hole closure if strip was started/finished at A if currentstripactive or stripstartedatA: if (Y1 > pY1) and (Y2 > pY2): drawholeclosingtriangle() # Reset strip state if it ended at A if not currentstripactive: stripstartedatA = False # Update state for next iteration previouscolumnA = currentcolumnB previouscolumnAvisible = currentcolumnBvisible # Note: Logic for tracking 'stripstartedatA' requires maintaining # history of strip start/end events relative to column indices. # If a strip started at previouscolumnA, mark it. if previouscolumnAvisible and not currentcolumnBvisible: # Strip ended at A (which is now previous) stripstartedatA = False # Or track specifically if A was a start point elif not previouscolumnAvisible and currentcolumnBvisible: # Strip started at A (which is now previous) stripstartedatA = True Parameters: Step Size: The distance between scanned columns. Default is 32 pixels. Smaller steps generate more polygons. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: In Case 4, if a triangle strip was started or finished at the previous column during the previous pass, a single triangle must be drawn to close the gap. Mesh Density: The triangle mesh can become too dense at the bottom of valleys. A span reduction technique is ideally needed to mitigate this. Approximation: The hole-closing condition may draw triangles that are not quite visible, but this is accepted for efficiency over line intersections. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampled columns and visible voxels. The efficiency comes from batching draw calls into strips. Memory Complexity: Low, as it processes columns sequentially and does not store the entire mesh in memory. Measured Performance: In the terraVoxGL demo scene, it rendered 8664 triangles (across 4 passes) in 925 strips. Strengths: Extremely efficient due to the use of triangle strips; leverages hardware interpolation for texture coordinates, lightmap colors, and heights; reduces draw calls compared to software span rendering. Limitations: Can produce dense meshes in valleys; texturing scheme described in the source (4 single passes with alpha coefficients) is inefficient. When to use: When rendering voxel landscapes on hardware that supports triangle strips and interpolation, and when software span rendering is too slow. When not to use: When high-quality procedural shading is required (the described texturing is a simple emulation of software) or when valley density is a critical issue without span reduction. Origin: Developed by an anonymous author for the "Realtime Voxel Landscape Engines" series, specifically Part 6 on Hardware Acceleration. History: Presented on Flipcode in February 2000 as a response to the slowness of software span rendering for voxel landscapes. It was implemented in the terraVoxGL demo using OpenGL. Usage: Used in the terraVoxGL demo to accelerate voxel landscape rendering by utilizing the video card as a "huge interpolating machine". Realtime Voxel Landscape Engines - Part 6 - Hardware Acceleration, https://www.flipcode.com/archives/RealtimeVoxelLandscapeEngines-Part6HardwareAcceleration.shtml, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Wolfenstein 3D Raycasting
head: Wolfenstein 3D technique, Wolfenstein-style rendering, Lodev-style DDA, DDA Ray Casting, Raycasting with Fisheye Correction
body: Wolfenstein 3D Raycasting is a rendering technique for first-person corridors on hardware without GPUs or z-buffers, where the world is a flat 2D grid, the camera is confined to the grid plane, and one ray is cast per screen column to reconstruct a textured 3D scene. It sets itself apart from general voxel traversal methods by operating on a strictly 2D grid map with a fixed-height camera, using the perpendicular distance to the camera plane to correct fisheye distortion and determine wall height, rather than computing full 3D intersections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D grid map (Uint8Array or number[][]), player state (posX, posY, dirX, dirY, planeX, planeY), screen dimensions (FBW, FBH), and field of view defined by the plane vector length. Output: A framebuffer image containing vertical wall strips and billboard sprites. Data Structures: Map: A 1D or 2D array representing the grid. Values: 0 (empty floor), 1-4 (wall types), 5 (sliding door). Player: Object with x, y (position), dirX, dirY (unit direction vector), planeX, planeY (camera plane vector perpendicular to dir). Textures: Procedurally generated at runtime onto a 64x64 offscreen canvas, then read into a Uint32Array for fast pixel access. Z-Buffer: A 1D array of size FBW storing the perpendicular distance to the nearest wall for each screen column, used for sprite occlusion. Parameters: FOV: Determined by the length of the plane vector relative to the direction vector. A ratio of |plane|/|dir| = 0.66 yields a horizontal FOV of ~66.8 degrees. Wall Height: Real-world height of a wall tile, typically 1 unit. Steps: 1. Initialize Camera Vectors: For each screen column x from 0 to FBW - 1: Calculate cameraX = 2 x / FBW - 1 (ranges from -1 to 1). Calculate ray direction: rayDirX = dirX + planeX \cdot cameraX rayDirY = dirY + planeY \cdot cameraX 2. DDA Grid Traversal: Initialize current grid cell: mapX = floor(posX), mapY = floor(posY). Calculate step distances: \Deltax = \left| \frac{1}{rayDirX} \right|, \quad \Deltay = \left| \frac{1}{rayDirY} \right| Handle rayDirX == 0 or rayDirY == 0 by setting \Delta to a large value (e.g., 1e30). Determine step directions and initial side distances: If rayDirX < 0: stepX = -1, sideDistX = (posX - mapX) \Deltax. Else: stepX = 1, sideDistX = (mapX + 1 - posX) \Deltax. If rayDirY < 0: stepY = -1, sideDistY = (posY - mapY) \Deltay. Else: stepY = 1, sideDistY = (mapY + 1 - posY) \Deltay. Loop until a wall is hit: If sideDistX < sideDistY: sideDistX += \Deltax mapX += stepX side = 0 (hit vertical grid line) Else: sideDistY += \Deltay mapY += stepY side = 1 (hit horizontal grid line) Check if map[mapY][mapX] > 0. If so, break. Edge Case (Sliding Doors): If the hit tile is 5, advance the ray to the center line of the door cell. If the ray exits the cell before reaching the midline or hits the closed part, continue traversal. 3. Calculate Perpendicular Distance: Compute the fisheye-corrected distance: dist = side === 0 ? sideDistX - \Deltax: sideDistY - \Deltay This value represents the distance perpendicular to the camera plane, correcting for the bowing effect of raw ray length. 4. Render Wall Strip: Calculate line height: lineHeight = \frac{FBH}{dist} Calculate draw range: drawStart = \max(0, \lfloor (FBH - lineHeight) / 2 \rfloor) drawEnd = \min(FBH - 1, \lfloor (FBH + lineHeight) / 2 \rfloor) Calculate texture coordinate wallX: If side == 0: wallX = posY + dist rayDirY - floor(posY + dist rayDirY). Else: wallX = posX + dist rayDirX - floor(posX + dist rayDirX). Mirror texture X if necessary to prevent backward textures: If (side == 0 && rayDirX > 0) || (side == 1 && rayDirY < 0): wallX = 1 - wallX. Draw vertical line from drawStart to drawEnd using wallX for texture sampling. Shade based on side for depth cues. Store dist in zbuffer[x] for sprite occlusion. 5. Render Sprites (Billboards): Sort sprites by squared distance to player (far to near). For each sprite: Transform sprite position (sx, sy) to camera space: invDet = \frac{1}{planeX \cdot dirY - dirX \cdot planeY} transformX = invDet \cdot (dirY \cdot (sx - posX) - dirX \cdot (sy - posY)) transformY = invDet \cdot (-planeY \cdot (sx - posX) + planeX \cdot (sy - posY)) If transformY <= 0.05, skip (behind camera). Calculate screen X: screenX = floor((FBW / 2) (1 + transformX / transformY)). Calculate sprite size: size = abs(floor(FBH / transformY)). For each column x in sprite range: If transformY >= zbuffer[x], skip (occluded by wall). Sample texture, skip if alpha < 128, shade and write to framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castraydda(map, posx, posy, dirx, diry, planex, planey, fbw, fbh, texsize=64): mapw = len(map[0]) maph = len(map) zbuffer = [0.0] fbw for x in range(fbw): camerax = 2.0 x / fbw - 1.0 raydirx = dirx + planex camerax raydiry = diry + planey camerax mapx = int(posx) mapy = int(posy) deltadistx = abs(1.0 / raydirx) if raydirx != 0 else 1e30 deltadisty = abs(1.0 / raydiry) if raydiry != 0 else 1e30 if raydirx < 0: stepx = -1 sidedistx = (posx - mapx) deltadistx else: stepx = 1 sidedistx = (mapx + 1 - posx) deltadistx if raydiry < 0: stepy = -1 sidedisty = (posy - mapy) deltadisty else: stepy = 1 sidedisty = (mapy + 1 - posy) deltadisty hit = False side = 0 guard = 0 while not hit and guard < 128: guard += 1 if sidedistx < sidedisty: sidedistx += deltadistx mapx += stepx side = 0 else: sidedisty += deltadisty mapy += stepy side = 1 if mapx < 0 or mapx >= mapw or mapy < 0 or mapy >= maph: hit = True continue tile = map[mapy][mapx] if tile == 0: continue if tile == 5: # Sliding door logic from: advance to center line, # check openness, continue traversal if gap not reached. hit = True continue hit = True if side == 0: perpdist = sidedistx - deltadistx else: perpdist = sidedisty - deltadisty zbuffer[x] = perpdist lineheight = int(fbh / perpdist) drawstart = max(0, (fbh - lineheight) // 2) drawend = min(fbh - 1, (fbh + lineheight) // 2) if side == 0: wallx = posy + perpdist raydiry else: wallx = posx + perpdist raydirx wallx -= int(wallx) if (side == 0 and raydirx > 0) or (side == 1 and raydiry < 0): wallx = 1.0 - wallx # Fixed-point vertical texture step step = texsize / lineheight texpos = (drawstart - (fbh - lineheight) / 2) step for y in range(drawstart, drawend + 1): texy = int(texpos) & (texsize - 1) texpos += step # Write shaded texel to framebuffer # fb[y fbw + x] = shade(tex[texy texsize + int(wallx texsize)]) return zbuffer Highly efficient on CPU-only hardware; the original engine ran on 286/386-class processors. Optimizations like drawing every second column can double FPS on low-resolution displays with negligible visual loss. Time, memory complexity, strengths, limitations, and usage guidelines are not given in the sources. Wolfenstein 3D (id Software, 1992) rendered first-person corridors on 286/386-class hardware without GPUs, z-buffers, or polygons. The technique projects a 2D grid map into a 3D perspective viewport using one ray per screen column. It is a specific application of the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm for grid traversal, popularized by Lodev's tutorial. name: Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA
head: DDA Voxel Shadow Tracing, Shadow Ray Grid Optimization, Voxel Shadow Raytracer
body: Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA is a technique for computing hard shadows in voxel-based scenes by traversing a 3D voxel grid along rays cast from surface points to light sources. It solves the problem of efficiently determining light attenuation through volumetric or opaque voxel data without resorting to slow, fixed-step ray marching. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing specifically on the shadow calculation phase within a rendering pipeline, utilizing the Amanatides–Woo traversal logic to jump between grid cells rather than sampling every unit of distance. The method operates in two distinct phases: the main rendering loop (which invokes the shadow raycaster) and the DDA traversal algorithm itself. It relies on a sparse or dense voxel buffer where each voxel has a density value. Inputs: Voxel Grid: A buffer of voxelmaterial structs containing color (unused in shadow calc) and density (float, 0.0 to 1.0, where 1.0 is opaque). Light Sources: A buffer of lightsource structs containing position (vec3), power (float, max reach distance), color (vec3), and intensity (float). Surface Data: For each pixel, the world-space position (vec4, alpha > 0 indicates valid surface) and normal (vec3). Grid Dimensions: mapsize (vec3), defining the bounds of the voxel world. Outputs: Shadow Factor: A float value between 0.0 (fully shadowed) and 1.0 (fully lit), representing the remaining light intensity after attenuation. Final Color: The base pixel color multiplied by the accumulated lighting contributions. The implementation uses specific buffer layouts, typically in a GLSL compute shader context: 1. Voxel Map (Map): layout (std430, binding = 3) buffer Map containing voxelmaterial voxels[]. 2. Lights (Lights): layout (std430, binding = 2) buffer Lights containing lightsource sources[]. 3. Position Texture (postexture): layout(rgba32f, binding = 1) storing world-space positions. 4. Normal Texture (normtexture): layout(rgba32f, binding = 4) storing voxel normals. 5. Output Image (imgoutput): layout(rgba32f, binding = 0) storing the final lit color. Coordinate to ID Conversion: To access the voxel buffer, 3D coordinates are converted to a 1D index. The coordinates are clamped to [0, mapsize]: \text{ID} = \lfloor x \rfloor + \lfloor y \rfloor \cdot \text{map\size}.x + \lfloor z \rfloor \cdot \text{map\size}.x \cdot \text{map\size}.y This assumes a row-major layout where x is the fastest varying dimension. For each pixel (x, y): 1. Load pixel color, position, and normal from textures. 2. If position.a <= 0, skip processing (background). 3. Initialize lightValue to ambient color vec4(0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 1) and lightColor to vec3(0,0,0). 4. Iterate through each light source current in the Lights buffer: a. Calculate squared distance distanceSP = distance(current.position, position.xyz). b. Light Reach Test: If distanceSP > current.power current.power, skip this light (it cannot reach the surface). c. Compute ray direction rayPixSrc = current.position - position.xyz. d. Determine if the starting voxel should be sampled: stepThroughFirstVoxel = dot(normalize(rayPixSrc), normal) > 0. e. Call stepThroughVoxelWorld(position.xyz, rayPixSrc, stepThroughFirstVoxel) to get intensity. f. Calculate result multiplier: result = current.intensity intensity (1 - (distanceSP / current.power)). g. If result > 0, add current.color.rgb result to lightColor. 5. Add lightColor to lightValue.rgb. 6. Store pixel lightValue to imgoutput. This function traverses the voxel grid from origin along dir. Initialization Phase: 1. Normalize dir. 2. Set currPos = ivec3(floor(origin.x), floor(origin.y), floor(origin.z)). 3. Set intensity = 1.0. 4. For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: a. If dir[i] >= 0: step[i] = 1 delta[i] = 1.0 / max(0.000001, dir[i]) (prevents division by zero). Max[i] = (floor(currPos[i] + 1) - origin[i]) / dir[i]. Out[i] = mapsize[i] (boundary limit). b. If dir[i] < 0: step[i] = -1 delta[i] = -1.0 / dir[i] Max[i] = (floor(currPos[i]) - origin[i]) / dir[i]. Out[i] = -1 (boundary limit). 5. Calculate last = ivec3(floor(origin.x + dir.x), floor(origin.y + dir.y), floor(origin.z + dir.z)). Note: The source also calculates maxLength = dir.x^2 + dir.y^2 + dir.z^2, but since dir is normalized, this is always 1.0. Step Loop: While intensity > 0 AND !reachedEnd AND currPos != last: 1. Sample voxel at currPos using CordtoID. 2. Subtract currentVoxel.density from intensity. 3. Determine the next axis to step: Find the axis k with the minimum Max[k]. 4. Increment currPos[k] by step[k]. 5. Update Max[k] += delta[k]. 6. Check boundary: If currPos[k] == Out[k], set reachedEnd = true. Return: Return intensity. To reduce computation, shadow status can be stored in the voxel grid. For each voxel and each light source, two bits are stored: 1. One bit indicating the voxel is completely in shadow. 2. One bit indicating nothing blocks the voxel from seeing the light source. During traversal, if these bits are set, the ray calculation is skipped. This adds a memory overhead of 2 bits per light source per voxel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. AMBIENT = (0.2, 0.2, 0.2, 1.0) EPSILON = 0.000001 def imageload(texture, coord): """Simulates reading a vec4 from a 2D texture array.""" return texture[coord[1]][coord[0]] def imagestore(texture, coord, value): """Simulates writing a vec4 to a 2D texture array.""" texture[coord[1]][coord[0]] = value def cordtoid(cord, mapsize): """Converts 3D coordinates to a 1D index, clamping to grid bounds.""" x = max(0, min(mapsize[0], cord[0])) y = max(0, min(mapsize[1], cord[1])) z = max(0, min(mapsize[2], cord[2])) return int(x) + int(y) mapsize[0] + int(z) mapsize[0] mapsize[1] def stepthroughvoxelworld(origin, dir, stepthroughfirstvoxel, mapsize, voxels): intensity = 1.0 # Initialization dirnorm = normalize(dir) currpos = [int(origin[0]), int(origin[1]), int(origin[2])] # Arrays for DDA state (indices 0, 1, 2 correspond to x, y, z) step = [0, 0, 0] delta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] maxdist = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] outbound = [0, 0, 0] # Configure DDA for each axis for axis in range(3): d = dirnorm[axis] if d >= 0: step[axis] = 1 delta[axis] = 1.0 / max(EPSILON, d) maxdist[axis] = (float(int(currpos[axis] + 1)) - origin[axis]) / d outbound[axis] = int(mapsize[axis]) else: step[axis] = -1 delta[axis] = -1.0 / d maxdist[axis] = (float(int(currpos[axis])) - origin[axis]) / d outbound[axis] = -1 # Termination setup lastpos = [int(origin[0] + dirnorm[0]), int(origin[1] + dirnorm[1]), int(origin[2] + dirnorm[2])] reachedend = False # Main Loop while intensity > 0 and not reachedend and currpos != lastpos: # Sample voxel at current position voxelidx = cordtoid(currpos, mapsize) intensity -= voxels[voxelidx].density # Determine next axis to step (find index of minimum maxdist) minval = min(maxdist) nextaxis = maxdist.index(minval) # Step currpos[nextaxis] += step[nextaxis] maxdist[nextaxis] += delta[nextaxis] # Check boundary if currpos[nextaxis] == outbound[nextaxis]: reachedend = True break return intensity def renderpixel(x, y, postexture, normtexture, imgoutput, lights, voxels, mapsize): pixel = imageload(imgoutput, (x, y)) position = imageload(postexture, (x, y)) normal = imageload(normtexture, (x, y))[:3] if position[3] <= 0: return lightvalue = list(AMBIENT) lightcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] castlights = 0 for light in lights: lineardist = length(light.position - position[:3]) distsq = lineardist lineardist # Light reach test if distsq > light.power light.power: continue raydir = light.position - position[:3] # Check if ray exits the surface immediately stepfirst = dot(normalize(raydir), normal) > 0 intensity = stepthroughvoxelworld(position[:3], raydir, stepfirst, mapsize, voxels) # Calculate result multiplier result = light.intensity intensity (1.0 - (lineardist / light.power)) if result > 0: lightcolor[0] += light.color[0] result lightcolor[1] += light.color[1] result lightcolor[2] += light.color[2] result castlights += 1 if castlights > 0: lightvalue[0] += lightcolor[0] lightvalue[1] += lightcolor[1] lightvalue[2] += lightcolor[2] imagestore(imgoutput, (x, y), tuple(pixel[i] lightvalue[i] for i in range(4))) A WebGPU compute shader-based ray tracer for voxel models that replaces a rasterizer. It casts rays per pixel, traverses a 3D voxel grid using DDA, applies directional lighting with diffuse shading, and generates hard shadows via shadow rays. It sets itself apart from its parent Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA by implementing the entire rendering pipeline (primary rays, shading, and shadow rays) within a WebGPU compute shader, rather than relying on a GLSL rasterizer with DDA for shadow calculation only. Time Complexity: The DDA traversal is O(N) where N is the number of voxels intersected by the shadow ray. Memory Complexity: The base method requires storing the voxel grid. The optimized version with shadow bits requires an additional 2 bits per light source per voxel. Performance: The DDA approach avoids the "slow fallback" fixed-step algorithm which increments position by a small fixed step (e.g., 0.05) and samples every step, leading to redundant calculations. Strengths: Efficient traversal of uniform grids; handles arbitrary ray directions; simple implementation. Limitations: Requires a uniform grid structure; shadow bit optimization increases memory usage per light source per voxel. When to use: When rendering hard shadows in voxel worlds where performance is critical and the grid is uniform. When not to use: For non-uniform grids (use Siddon's Algorithm or adaptive grids) or when soft shadows are required (DDA provides hard shadows only). The technique is based on the Amanatides–Woo voxel traversal algorithm, which enumerates grid cells intersected by a ray in front-to-back order. The specific GLSL implementation described in the sources is an unofficial contribution to the GitHub repository Ein-Baum/Voxel-shadow-raytracer. The concept of using grids to reduce shadow ray computations by storing status bits was discussed in academic literature on fast voxel traversal. name: WebGPU Voxel Ray Tracing Renderer
head: DDA voxel grid traversal, WebGPU-based ray tracing renderer
body: A WebGPU compute shader-based ray tracer for voxel models that replaces a rasterizer. It casts rays per pixel, traverses a 3D voxel grid using DDA, applies directional lighting with diffuse shading, and generates hard shadows via shadow rays. It sets itself apart from its parent Voxel Shadow Raycasting with DDA by implementing the entire rendering pipeline (primary rays, shading, and shadow rays) within a WebGPU compute shader, rather than relying on a GLSL rasterizer with DDA for shadow calculation only. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid (dense or sparse), a project palette of block colors, lighting parameters (sun direction, intensity, ambient light), and camera state. Output: A 2D image buffer rendered to the canvas. Data Structures: Uniform Buffer: Expanded to 128 bytes to store lighting parameters. Storage Buffer: Contains the project palette for retrieving block colors. Voxel Data: Gathered from the voxel engine into a flat buffer. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: The renderer checks for WebGPU support. If unavailable, it displays a fallback background. 2. Primary Ray Casting: For each pixel, a primary ray is cast into the scene. 3. Voxel Traversal: The 3D voxel grid is traversed using the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to find the first intersecting voxel. 4. Diffuse Shading: If a voxel is hit, diffuse shading is calculated using the dot product of the surface normal (N) and the light direction (L). 5. Shadow Raycasting: Shadow rays are cast by performing DDA traversal from the hit point toward the sun direction to determine occlusion. 6. Color Retrieval: Block colors are retrieved from the storage buffer containing the project palette. 7. Ground Plane: A ground plane with grid lines is rendered, which receives shadows. 8. Background: A subtle sky gradient background is rendered. 9. Blitting: The compute shader output is blitted to the canvas using a fullscreen triangle render pass. Formulas: Diffuse Shading: I{diffuse} = \max(0, N \cdot L). Sun Direction: Calculated from Sun Azimuth (\theta) and Sun Elevation (\phi) using spherical-to-Cartesian conversion: L = (\cos\phi \sin\theta, \sin\phi, \cos\phi \cos\theta). Parameters: Sun Azimuth: Horizontal angle of the sun, range 0 to 360 degrees. Sun Elevation: Vertical angle of the sun, range 5 to 90 degrees. Sun Intensity: Brightness of the directional light source. Ambient Light Intensity: Intensity of the ambient light component. Shadow Strength: Intensity/opacity of the shadows. Sun Color: Presets include Warm, White, Cool, Gold, Pink. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: WebGPU Availability: WebGPU is not available in headless CI environments, so the canvas shows a fallback background instead of rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderpixel(pixelx, pixely, camera, voxelgrid, palette, lighting): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(pixelx, pixely) hitvoxel, t = ddatraverse(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid) if hitvoxel is not None: basecolor = palette[hitvoxel[0]][hitvoxel[1]][hitvoxel[2]] hitpoint = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] hitnormal = computenormal(hitpoint, hitvoxel) diffusefactor = max(0.0, dot(hitnormal, lighting.sundirection)) isshadowed = ddatraverseshadow(hitpoint, lighting.sundirection, voxelgrid) if isshadowed: diffusefactor = 0.0 finalcolor = basecolor (lighting.ambientintensity + diffusefactor lighting.sunintensity) else: finalcolor = getskygradient(raydirection) return finalcolor def ddatraverse(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid): voxel = [math.floor(rayorigin[i]) for i in range(3)] step = [1 if raydirection[i] > 0 else -1 if raydirection[i] < 0 else 0 for i in range(3)] tdelta = [1.0 / abs(raydirection[i]) if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if step[i] > 0: tmax[i] = (voxel[i] + 1.0 - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] elif step[i] < 0: tmax[i] = (voxel[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] else: tmax[i] = float('inf') bounds = voxelgrid.bounds t = 0.0 while 0 <= voxel[0] < bounds[0] and 0 <= voxel[1] < bounds[1] and 0 <= voxel[2] < bounds[2]: if voxelgrid.isopaque(voxel): return voxel, t axis = tmax.index(min(tmax)) t += tdelta[axis] tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] voxel[axis] += step[axis] return None, 0.0 def ddatraverseshadow(origin, direction, voxelgrid): epsilon = 1e-4 shiftedorigin = [origin[i] + direction[i] epsilon for i in range(3)] hitvoxel, = ddatraverse(shiftedorigin, direction, voxelgrid) return hitvoxel is not None def dot(a, b): return sum(a[i] b[i] for i in range(3)) def computenormal(point, voxel): # Returns the outward face normal of the voxel hit based on closest face dx = point[0] - (voxel[0] + 0.5) dy = point[1] - (voxel[1] + 0.5) dz = point[2] - (voxel[2] + 0.5) if abs(dx) > abs(dy) and abs(dx) > abs(dz): return [1.0 if dx > 0 else -1.0, 0.0, 0.0] if abs(dy) > abs(dz): return [0.0, 1.0 if dy > 0 else -1.0, 0.0] return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0 if dz > 0 else -1.0] def getskygradient(direction): # Returns a subtle sky gradient based on ray direction return [0.5, 0.7, 1.0] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performance depends on the hardware's WebGPU support and the complexity of the voxel scene. Strengths: Real-time lighting and shadows in a voxel environment; interactive controls for lighting parameters. Limitations: Requires WebGPU support; not available in headless environments. When to use: When real-time voxel rendering with dynamic lighting and shadows is required in a web browser. When not to use: In headless CI environments or browsers without WebGPU support. The WebGPU Voxel Ray Tracing Renderer was developed as part of the LunaVoxel project. It was introduced as an alternative to the existing Three.js rasterizer, accessible via a dedicated Render tab in the header navigation. The implementation includes directional lighting, shadow rays, and interactive controls. It was authored by tfritzy and merged in February 2026.
