name: Siddon's Algorithm
head: Exact discrete Beer-Lambert law, Ray casting with voxel intersection, Siddon ray tracing, exact radiological path calculation
body: Siddon's Algorithm is a method for analytically computing the exact intersection lengths of a ray with each voxel in a 3D grid by tracking parametric alpha values at which the ray crosses parallel CT planes (x, y, z). It serves as a ray-driven forward projection method that calculates the line-integral as a weighted sum of the values of intersected voxels, where weights are the length of intersection between each voxel and the ray. This method provides an exact computation of the discretized Beer-Lambert law for X-ray attenuation, calculating the integral of linear attenuation coefficients (LACs) along a ray by summing the LAC in every voxel intersected by the ray, weighted by the intersection length. It is widely used in slice-to-volume registration and differentiable rendering. Inputs and Outputs: The algorithm takes a ray defined by a source point \mathbf{s} and a target/detector point \mathbf{p}, and a discrete 3D volume \hat{\mu} (or \mathbf{V}) representing the voxel grid of Linear Attenuation Coefficients (LACs) or densities. Outputs typically include: alphas: Relative distance between start and endpoint for the intersections with the cube. l: Lengths of intersections with cubes. rho: Densities extracted from cubes. d12: Distance between start and endpoint of ray tracing. ix: Indices of hit voxels. The final rendered intensity or energy attenuation E(R) or I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r}). Data Structures: The volume is represented as a 3D grid. The ray is parameterized by \alpha \in [0, 1]. The intersections are stored as a sorted set of parametric values \{\alpha1, \dots, \alphaM\}. Steps: 1. Define the Ray: Define the ray \vec{r}(\alpha) = \mathbf{s} + \alpha(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) for \alpha \in [0, 1], where \mathbf{s} is the X-ray source position and \mathbf{p} is the detector pixel position. 2. Compute Plane Intersections: Calculate the intersection parameters of the ray with the parallel planes comprising the voxel grid. For a voxel size \Delta X in the x-direction and the location of the 0-th plane bx, the intersection with the i-th plane is: \alphax(i) = \frac{bx + i \Delta X - \mathbf{s}x}{\mathbf{p}x - \mathbf{s}x} Analogous expressions are used for \alphay(\cdot) and \alphaz(\cdot). 3. Sort Intersections: Combine the intersection parameters from all three axes and sort them to form the set \mathbf{\alpha} = \text{sort}(\mathbf{\alpha}x, \mathbf{\alpha}y, \mathbf{\alpha}z), which contains M values parameterizing the intersections. 4. Iterate and Sum: Iterate m from 1 to M-1. For each segment between \alpham and \alpha{m+1}: a. Calculate the midpoint parameter: \alpha{mid} = \frac{\alpha{m+1} + \alpham}{2}. b. Evaluate the voxel LAC at the midpoint: \hat{\mu}[\mathbf{s} + \alpha{mid} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s})]. Note: This indexing operation returns the LAC of the intersected voxel. c. Multiply by the segment length parameter difference: (\alpha{m+1} - \alpham). 5. Final Calculation: Sum these products and multiply by the ray length \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\| to get the rendered intensity: I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r}) = \| \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s} \| \sum{m=1}^{M-1} \hat{\mu} \left[ \mathbf{s} + \frac{\alpha{m+1} + \alpham}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) \right] (\alpha{m+1} - \alpham) Alternatively expressed as energy attenuation E(R): E(R) = \| \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s} \|2 \sum{m=1}^{M-1} (\alpha{m+1} - \alpham) \mathbf{V} \left[ \mathbf{s} + \frac{\alpha{m+1} + \alpham}{2} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) \right] The term \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\|2 cancels the reciprocal length units of \mathbf{V} to make E unitless. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def siddonsalgorithm(source, target, volume, voxelsize, originoffset, voxelshift=0.5): """ source: tuple (sx, sy, sz) target: tuple (px, py, pz) volume: 3D array of LACs voxelsize: float, size of one voxel in mm originoffset: tuple (bx, by, bz), location of the 0-th plane in mm voxelshift: float, 0.0 for corner-aligned, 0.5 for center-aligned voxels """ sx, sy, sz = source px, py, pz = target bx, by, bz = originoffset dx, dy, dz = voxelsize dirx = px - sx diry = py - sy dirz = pz - sz raylength = (dirx2 + diry2 + dirz2)0.5 alphas = set() eps = 1e-08 # X planes Nx = len(volume) for i in range(Nx): planex = bx + i dx if abs(dirx) > eps: alpha = (planex - sx) / dirx if 0.0 <= alpha <= 1.0: alphas.add(alpha) # Y planes Ny = len(volume[0]) for j in range(Ny): planey = by + j dy if abs(diry) > eps: alpha = (planey - sy) / diry if 0.0 <= alpha <= 1.0: alphas.add(alpha) # Z planes Nz = len(volume[0][0]) for k in range(Nz): planez = bz + k dz if abs(dirz) > eps: alpha = (planez - sz) / dirz if 0.0 <= alpha <= 1.0: alphas.add(alpha) # Add endpoints if not present alphas.add(0.0) alphas.add(1.0) sortedalphas = sorted(list(alphas)) totalintegral = 0.0 for m in range(len(sortedalphas) - 1): alpham = sortedalphas[m] alpham1 = sortedalphas[m+1] alphamid = (alpham + alpham1) / 2.0 midx = sx + alphamid dirx midy = sy + alphamid diry midz = sz + alphamid dirz # Map to voxel indices ix = int((midx - bx) / dx - voxelshift) iy = int((midy - by) / dy - voxelshift) iz = int((midz - bz) / dz - voxelshift) if 0 <= ix < Nx and 0 <= iy < Ny and 0 <= iz < Nz: mu = volume[ix][iy][iz] totalintegral += mu (alpham1 - alpham) return raylength totalintegral Parameters: voxelshift: float, default 0.5. Determines if the voxel is at the top left corner (0) or the center (0.5). mode: str, default 'nearest'. Interpolation mode for gridsample. filterintersectionsoutsidevolume: bool, default False. If True, uses alphamin/max to filter the intersections. eps: float, default 1e-08. Small constant to avoid div by zero errors. isocenterCube: The isocenter position in cube coordinates [mm]. resolution: The resolution of the cubes in mm/voxel. sourcePoint: The starting point of the ray tracing. targetPoint: The ending point of the ray tracing. cubes: A cell array of density/material cubes to trace through. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Division by zero must be handled if the ray is parallel to a grid plane. Boundaries: Intersections outside the volume should be filtered if filterintersectionsoutsidevolume is True. Degenerate Input: If the ray does not intersect the volume, the sum is zero. Accuracy: Nearest-neighbour interpolation is too simplified for most applications; the input voxel volume must be at least double the resolution in each dimension compared to the desired reconstruction resolution to maintain accuracy. Overfitting: In sparse-view settings, Siddon's method suffers from overfitting because it does not allow ground truth pixels to provide self-supervision to voxels not directly intersected by the ray. Time and Memory Complexity: Computation scales cubically with the resolution of the voxelgrid \hat{\mu} because it requires computing every plane intersection. The number of intersections M is proportional to the number of voxels intersected, which can be up to Nx + Ny + Nz for a grid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Measured Performance: On 40 test walnuts with 15 input views, Siddon's method achieved SSIM 0.923, PSNR 37.69, MSE 1.28 \times 10^{-5}, PCC 0.96, and runtime 11.3 minutes on a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU. The batch size is limited by memory constraints to |\mathcal{R}| = 5.5 \times 10^5 rays per batch. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exactly computes line integrals, leading to higher fidelity novel views compared to trilinear interpolation. It is widely used in slice-to-volume registration. Limitations: Inferior in accuracy to Joseph's and Köhler's methods when compared against ideal analytical values. It does not account for patterns of reflection and scattering present in real X-ray systems. It is more prone to overfitting in sparse views compared to trilinear interpolation. When to Use: Use when exact radiological path calculation is required for differentiable rendering or slice-to-volume registration, and computational resources allow for the cubic scaling. When Not to Use: Avoid when real-time performance is critical and approximate methods (like trilinear interpolation) are sufficient, or when sparse-view reconstruction is prone to overfitting. Siddon's Algorithm was introduced by R.L. Siddon in 1985 in the paper 'Fast calculation of the exact radiological path for a three-dimensional CT array', published in Med. Phys. 12(2):252-5. It is a parametric method to generate Digital Radiographic Reconstructions (DRRs) by modeling the geometry of an idealized projectional radiography system. It is used in medical imaging, particularly in radiation therapy planning (e.g., matRad) and CBCT reconstruction. rayTracing — matRad 3.2.3 documentation, https://matrad.readthedocs.io/en/stable/api/raytracing.html, fetched 2026-10-25 5 Forward Projection through Voxel Volumes, https://www.cvl.isy.liu.se/education/undergraduate/tsbb31/download/TurbellPhDCh5.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Differentiable Voxel-based X-ray Rendering Improves Sparse-View 3D CBCT Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2411.19224, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) renderers – diffdrr, https://vivekg.dev/DiffDRR/api/renderers.html, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Voxel Raycasting with Normal Estimation
head: Amanatides and Woo algorithm, Digital Differential Analyzer voxel traversal, Voxel Raycasting via DDA, DDA Voxel Traversal
body: Voxel Raycasting with Normal Estimation is a method for tracing a ray through a voxel grid to find the first solid voxel hit, simultaneously estimating the surface normal based on the traversal direction relative to the grid axes. It solves the problem of efficiently querying sparse or dense voxel structures for collision, occlusion, or surface detection by walking the grid directly, visiting only intersected cells. It differs from fixed-step raymarching by using precomputed distance-to-boundary parameters (tMax) to jump directly to the next voxel boundary, ensuring exactly one voxel is processed per step and eliminating redundant checks. It builds on Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal by providing the core traversal mechanism that identifies the hit voxel and entry face, which are then used for normal estimation. Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), maximum ray distance maxDist, voxel grid occupancy data, and an epsilon constant \epsilon for degenerate ray detection. Outputs: Boolean hit status, hit position P, and surface normal N. Data Structures: Ray: Contains origin (Vec3), direction (Vec3), maxDistance (float). VoxelGrid: Provides a function isSolid(x, y, z) returning boolean. HitResult: Contains hit (bool), point (Vec3), normal (Vec3). Parameters: \epsilon = 0.0001. maxDist = 6.0 (typical, scene-dependent). Algorithm Steps: 1. Degenerate Ray Check: Calculate squared magnitude |D|^2. If |D|^2 < \epsilon, return no hit. 2. Initialization: Compute step direction vector S: Sx = \text{sign}(Dx), \quad Sy = \text{sign}(Dy), \quad Sz = \text{sign}(Dz) Where \text{sign}(v) = 1 if v > 0, -1 if v < 0, and 0 if v = 0. Compute step size (reciprocal of direction magnitude): \Delta Tx = \begin{cases} 1/|Dx| & \text{if } |Dx| > \epsilon \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \Delta Ty = \begin{cases} 1/|Dy| & \text{if } |Dy| > \epsilon \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \Delta Tz = \begin{cases} 1/|Dz| & \text{if } |Dz| > \epsilon \\ \infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Determine starting voxel coordinates: Vx = \lfloor Ox \rfloor, \quad Vy = \lfloor Oy \rfloor, \quad Vz = \lfloor Oz \rfloor. Initialize distance to next boundary (T{max}) for each axis: T{maxx} = \begin{cases} (Vx + 1 - Ox) \Delta Tx & \text{if } Sx = 1 \\ (Ox - Vx) \Delta Tx & \text{if } Sx = -1 \\ \infty & \text{if } Sx = 0 \end{cases} T{maxy} = \begin{cases} (Vy + 1 - Oy) \Delta Ty & \text{if } Sy = 1 \\ (Oy - Vy) \Delta Ty & \text{if } Sy = -1 \\ \infty & \text{if } Sy = 0 \end{cases} T{maxz} = \begin{cases} (Vz + 1 - Oz) \Delta Tz & \text{if } Sz = 1 \\ (Oz - Vz) \Delta Tz & \text{if } Sz = -1 \\ \infty & \text{if } Sz = 0 \end{cases}. Initialize previous position P{prev} = O. 3. Immediate Hit Check: Check if the starting voxel (Vx, Vy, Vz) is solid. If yes, calculate the entry normal based on the closest face (determined by ray direction and local position within the voxel) and return the hit. Note: Standard Amanatides-Woo traversal assumes the ray starts outside or handles the start voxel separately; if the start voxel is solid, the normal is typically the face opposite to the dominant direction component of the ray if entering from inside, or the face corresponding to the first boundary crossed if considering the ray origin as the entry point. For simplicity in this "first hit" context, if the start voxel is solid, we treat it as the hit.. 4. DDA Loop: While T{maxx} < maxDist, T{maxy} < maxDist, and T{maxz} < maxDist: Find the minimum T{max} among T{maxx}, T{maxy}, T{maxz}. Tie-breaking priority: X > Y > Z. Update previous position: P{prev} = P{curr} (where P{curr} is the current ray position, implicitly tracked by the loop progress). Advance the voxel index along the axis with the minimum T{max}: If T{maxx} is smallest: Vx \leftarrow Vx + Sx, T{maxx} \leftarrow T{maxx} + \Delta Tx. Normal candidate N{cand} = (-Sx, 0, 0). Else if T{maxy} is smallest: Vy \leftarrow Vy + Sy, T{maxy} \leftarrow T{maxy} + \Delta Ty. Normal candidate N{cand} = (0, -Sy, 0). Else: Vz \leftarrow Vz + Sz, T{maxz} \leftarrow T{maxz} + \Delta Tz. Normal candidate N{cand} = (0, 0, -Sz). Check if the new voxel (Vx, Vy, Vz) is solid. If solid: Calculate displacement vector Diff = P{curr} - P{prev}. Estimate normal N by comparing absolute components of Diff: If |Diffx| > |Diffy| and |Diffx| > |Diffz|: N = (\text{sign}(Diffx) \cdot -1, 0, 0)? No, the source says: if Diffx > 0, normal is (-1, 0, 0), else (1, 0, 0). This matches -Sx if Sx is the step direction. Let's stick to the source formula: N = \begin{cases} (-1, 0, 0) & \text{if } Diffx > 0 \\ (1, 0, 0) & \text{if } Diffx < 0 \end{cases} Else if |Diffy| > |Diffz|: N = \begin{cases} (0, -1, 0) & \text{if } Diffy > 0 \\ (0, 1, 0) & \text{if } Diffy < 0 \end{cases} Else: N = \begin{cases} (0, 0, -1) & \text{if } Diffz > 0 \\ (0, 0, 1) & \text{if } Diffz < 0 \end{cases} Return hit with position P{curr} and normal N. If not solid, continue loop. 5. Termination: If the loop completes without hitting a solid voxel, return no hit. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def voxelraycastwithnormalestimation(origin, direction, maxdist, issolid, epsilon=0.0001): """ Traces a ray through a voxel grid to find the first solid voxel and estimate its normal. Args: origin (Vec3): Ray origin. direction (Vec3): Ray direction (assumed normalized). maxdist (float): Maximum ray length. issolid (function): Function taking (x, y, z) integers, returning True if voxel is solid. epsilon (float): Threshold for degenerate rays. Returns: dict: {'hit': bool, 'point': Vec3, 'normal': Vec3} """ # 1. Degenerate Ray Check dirsq = direction.x2 + direction.y2 + direction.z2 if dirsq < epsilon: return {'hit': False, 'point': None, 'normal': None} # 2. Initialization # Step direction stepx = 1 if direction.x > 0 else (-1 if direction.x < 0 else 0) stepy = 1 if direction.y > 0 else (-1 if direction.y < 0 else 0) stepz = 1 if direction.z > 0 else (-1 if direction.z < 0 else 0) # Step size (reciprocal of direction magnitude) absdx = abs(direction.x) absdy = abs(direction.y) absdz = abs(direction.z) deltatx = (1.0 / absdx) if absdx > epsilon else float('inf') deltaty = (1.0 / absdy) if absdy > epsilon else float('inf') deltatz = (1.0 / absdz) if absdz > epsilon else float('inf') # Starting voxel voxelx = math.floor(origin.x) voxely = math.floor(origin.y) voxelz = math.floor(origin.z) # Distance to next boundary if stepx == 1: tmaxx = (voxelx + 1.0 - origin.x) deltatx elif stepx == -1: tmaxx = (origin.x - voxelx) deltatx else: tmaxx = float('inf') if stepy == 1: tmaxy = (voxely + 1.0 - origin.y) deltaty elif stepy == -1: tmaxy = (origin.y - voxely) deltaty else: tmaxy = float('inf') if stepz == 1: tmaxz = (voxelz + 1.0 - origin.z) deltatz elif stepz == -1: tmaxz = (origin.z - voxelz) deltatz else: tmaxz = float('inf') # 3. Immediate Hit Check if issolid(voxelx, voxely, voxelz): # Estimate normal for start voxel based on ray direction # If entering from outside, normal is opposite to dominant direction component # If inside, this logic might need refinement, but standard DDA assumes start is outside or handled. # For "first hit" from origin, if origin is inside solid, we return immediately. # Normal estimation for immediate hit: closest face. absstepx = abs(stepx) absstepy = abs(stepy) absstepz = abs(stepz) # Determine closest face based on ray direction relative to voxel center? # Source says "closest face based on ray direction and local position". # Simplified: if ray is moving +X, normal is -X. normal = Vec3(-stepx, -stepy, -stepz) # Normalize to axis-aligned if abs(direction.x) > abs(direction.y) and abs(direction.x) > abs(direction.z): normal = Vec3(-stepx, 0, 0) elif abs(direction.y) > abs(direction.z): normal = Vec3(0, -stepy, 0) else: normal = Vec3(0, 0, -stepz) return {'hit': True, 'point': origin, 'normal': normal} prevpos = origin currpos = origin # 4. DDA Loop while tmaxx < maxdist and tmaxy < maxdist and tmaxz < maxdist: # Find minimum tmax if tmaxx <= tmaxy and tmaxx <= tmaxz: # Advance X voxelx += stepx tmaxx += deltatx axis = 'x' elif tmaxy <= tmaxz: # Advance Y voxely += stepy tmaxy += deltaty axis = 'y' else: # Advance Z voxelz += stepz tmaxz += deltatz axis = 'z' # Update current position (approximate, using tmax of the axis just crossed) # In a strict DDA, we track t. Here we can compute point from tmax. # However, for normal estimation, we need the displacement from prevpos. # Let's compute the intersection point for the axis that was crossed. if axis == 'x': t = tmaxx - deltatx # The t value at the start of this step # Actually, tmaxx is the t value AT the boundary. # The point at the boundary is: currpos = Vec3( origin.x + direction.x tmaxx, origin.y + direction.y tmaxx, origin.z + direction.z tmaxx) elif axis == 'y': t = tmaxy - deltaty currpos = Vec3( origin.x + direction.x tmaxy, origin.y + direction.y tmaxy, origin.z + direction.z tmaxy) else: t = tmaxz - deltatz currpos = Vec3( origin.x + direction.x tmaxz, origin.y + direction.y tmaxz, origin.z + direction.z tmaxz) # Check occupancy if issolid(voxelx, voxely, voxelz): # 5. Normal Estimation diff = currpos - prevpos absdiffx = abs(diff.x) absdiffy = abs(diff.y) absdiffz = abs(diff.z) if absdiffx > absdiffy and absdiffx > absdiffz: if diff.x > 0: normal = Vec3(-1, 0, 0) else: normal = Vec3(1, 0, 0) elif absdiffy > absdiffz: if diff.y > 0: normal = Vec3(0, -1, 0) else: normal = Vec3(0, 1, 0) else: if diff.z > 0: normal = Vec3(0, 0, -1) else: normal = Vec3(0, 0, 1) return {'hit': True, 'point': currpos, 'normal': normal} prevpos = currpos return {'hit': False, 'point': None, 'normal': None} class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def sub(self, other): return Vec3(self.x - other.x, self.y - other.y, self.z - other.z) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Rays: Rays with zero or near-zero direction components must be handled to avoid division by zero or infinite loops. Axis-Aligned Rays: If a direction component is exactly 0, the corresponding step and deltat are handled as 0 and infinity respectively, skipping traversal on that axis. Normal Accuracy: Normal estimation relies on the displacement vector between steps. If the step size is large relative to voxel size, or if the ray passes through a corner, the normal may be inaccurate or incorrectly axis-aligned. The method assumes the ray enters the voxel face corresponding to the largest component of the displacement vector. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in tmax accumulation can cause jitter or missed voxels in long rays. Using double precision or periodic re-normalization of tmax may be required. A traversal algorithm that determines the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray without explicit intersection tests, using precomputed distance-to-boundary parameters. It differs by providing the core traversal mechanism for hit voxel and entry face identification, used for normal estimation. Choose when efficient, exact voxel stepping is required for collision or surface detection. Extends basic voxel raycasting by combining grid traversal with precise geometric intersection against sub-voxel AABB hitboxes. It differs by refining the hit position and normal for non-cuboid shapes, falling back to grid face normals for solid voxels. Choose when non-cuboid collision shapes (hitboxes) are present in the voxel environment. Time Complexity: O(N + A \log A), where N is the number of voxels intersected (proportional to maxDist) and A is the number of axis crossings (typically small, O(1) per axis). The sorting of candidates in some variants dominates if A is large, but in standard DDA, it is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the voxel grid storage. Performance: On a 256x256x256 colorfield (16 million voxels), software-mode raycasting achieves decent speed at 2000x2000 resolution and real-time rates at 800x600 for dense objects. It is more efficient than PhysX raycasts for voxel grids. Strengths: Parallelizable (each ray is independent), efficient for sparse grids (visits only intersected cells), simple implementation. Limitations: Normal estimation is approximate and axis-aligned, not suitable for smooth surfaces. Performance degrades with very long rays or dense grids without spatial acceleration structures. When to Use: Collision detection, occlusion culling, and simple surface normal estimation in voxel-based games or simulations where performance is critical and high-precision normals are not required. When Not to Use: When smooth, continuous surface normals are needed, or when the voxel grid is extremely dense and hierarchical structures (like Octrees) would provide better traversal performance. The method is based on the Amanatides and Woo algorithm, a classic ray traversal algorithm for regular grids. It was popularized in the context of voxel rendering and collision detection in games. The algorithm was originally described in "A Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing" by Amanatides and Woo (1987). It has been widely adopted in voxel engines for its simplicity and efficiency. name: DN_step_map
head: Amanatides & Woo Ray Traversal, Digital Differential Analyzer raycast, Voxel Grid Raycasting (DDA), Voxel Raycasting / 3D DDA Block Traversal
body: DNstepmap is a voxel traversal algorithm that determines the sequence of voxels intersected by a ray in a regular grid without performing explicit intersection tests with voxel faces. It solves the problem of efficiently querying sparse or dense voxel structures for collision, occlusion, or surface detection by stepping through the grid along the ray direction. It differs from fixed-step raymarching by using precomputed distance-to-boundary parameters (tMax) to jump directly to the next voxel boundary, ensuring exactly one voxel is processed per step and eliminating redundant checks. It builds on Voxel Raycasting with Normal Estimation by providing the core traversal mechanism that identifies the hit voxel and entry face, which are then used for normal estimation. Inputs: rayPos: Ray origin (px, py, pz) in world or volume coordinates. rayDir: Ray direction vector (dx, dy, dz). Must be non-zero. tmax: Maximum traversal distance (parameter t). voxSize: Voxel side length (assumed 1.0 for unit grids, or explicit scalar). maxSteps: Optional integer limit to prevent infinite loops in degenerate cases (e.g., origin inside solid). Default 1024. Outputs: hitVoxel: Coordinates (i, j, k) of the first occupied voxel. hitFace: The face entered (e.g., neg-x, pos-y). prevEmptyVoxel: The voxel coordinate immediately preceding the hit, useful for block placement. hitPos: Intersection point in world coordinates. hitNormal: Surface normal at the hit location. Boolean success flag. Data Structures: current: Integer tuple (X, Y, Z) representing the current voxel index. step: Integer tuple (stepx, stepy, stepz) indicating direction of increment (1, -1, 0). tMax: Float tuple (tMaxx, tMaxy, tMaxz) representing the ray parameter t at which the ray crosses the next voxel boundary along each axis. tDelta: Float tuple (tDeltax, tDeltay, tDeltaz) representing the distance between consecutive voxel boundaries along each axis. Steps: 1. Validate Direction: Calculate direction length L = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2}. If L < \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-5}), return failure. Normalize direction: dx \leftarrow dx/L, dy \leftarrow dy/L, dz \leftarrow dz/L. 2. Initialize Voxel Index: Compute starting voxel indices: X = \lfloor px \rfloor, \quad Y = \lfloor py \rfloor, \quad Z = \lfloor pz \rfloor. Note: If the grid has an origin offset or cell size C, adjust: X = \lfloor (px - Ox)/C \rfloor. 3. Compute Step Directions: For each axis a \in \{x, y, z\}: stepa = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } da > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } da < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } da = 0 \end{cases}. 4. Compute Delta and Initial tMax: For each axis a: If da \neq 0: tDeltaa = \frac{1.0}{|da|}. Determine the next boundary coordinate Ba: Ba = \begin{cases} X + 1 & \text{if } stepa = 1 \\ X & \text{if } stepa = -1 \end{cases}. Calculate initial distance to boundary: tMaxa = \frac{(Ba - pa) \cdot C}{da}. Note: If da < 0, the formula effectively becomes \frac{(pa - X) \cdot C}{|da|}. If da = 0: tDeltaa = \infty, \quad tMaxa = \infty. This prevents division by zero and excludes the axis from traversal decisions. 5. Traverse Loop: Initialize traveldist = 0.0. Loop while traveldist < tmax and steps < maxSteps: a. Check Current Voxel: Query voxel occupancy at (X, Y, Z). If occupied, return hit data: hitVoxel = (X, Y, Z) hitPos = rayPos + rayDir \cdot travel\dist hitNormal = (-stepx, -stepy, -stepz) (inward facing normal of the entry face). prevEmptyVoxel = (X - stepx, Y - stepy, Z - stepz). Return success. Pitfall: If the ray origin is already inside an occupied voxel, the check in step 5a must occur before stepping, or the algorithm must handle the "inside" case explicitly to return the starting voxel as the hit. Standard DDA assumes entry from outside; if inside, the first step moves to a neighbor, potentially missing the start voxel if not checked pre-loop. b. Find Next Boundary: Identify the axis with the minimum tMax: axis = \arg\min{a \in \{x,y,z\}} tMaxa. If tMax{axis} > tmax, break loop (ray exits volume). c. Advance Ray: Update traveldist += tMax{axis}. Update current voxel index: current{axis} += step{axis}. Update tMax{axis}: tMax{axis} += tDelta{axis}. Record hitFace based on axis and step{axis} (e.g., if axis=x, stepx=1, face is neg-x). 6. Termination: If loop completes without hit, return failure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dnstepmap(raypos, raydir, tmax, voxsize=1.0, maxsteps=1024): # 1. Validate and normalize direction dirlen = math.sqrt(raydir.x2 + raydir.y2 + raydir.z2) if dirlen < 1e-5: return None dx = raydir.x / dirlen dy = raydir.y / dirlen dz = raydir.z / dirlen # 2. Initialize voxel indices cx = math.floor(raypos.x / voxsize) cy = math.floor(raypos.y / voxsize) cz = math.floor(raypos.z / voxsize) # 3. Compute step directions stepx = 1 if dx > 0 else (-1 if dx < 0 else 0) stepy = 1 if dy > 0 else (-1 if dy < 0 else 0) stepz = 1 if dz > 0 else (-1 if dz < 0 else 0) # 4. Compute tDelta and tMax # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero if dx != 0: tdeltax = voxsize / abs(dx) # Next boundary coordinate in world space nextbndx = (cx + (1 if stepx > 0 else 0)) voxsize tmaxx = (nextbndx - raypos.x) / dx else: tdeltax = float('inf') tmaxx = float('inf') if dy != 0: tdeltay = voxsize / abs(dy) nextbndy = (cy + (1 if stepy > 0 else 0)) voxsize tmaxy = (nextbndy - raypos.y) / dy else: tdeltay = float('inf') tmaxy = float('inf') if dz != 0: tdeltaz = voxsize / abs(dz) nextbndz = (cz + (1 if stepz > 0 else 0)) voxsize tmaxz = (nextbndz - raypos.z) / dz else: tdeltaz = float('inf') tmaxz = float('inf') traveldist = 0.0 # 5. Traverse for in range(maxsteps): # Check current voxel (Handle "inside" case) if isoccupied(cx, cy, cz): hitpos = raypos + (raydir traveldist) hitnormal = (-stepx, -stepy, -stepz) prevvoxel = (cx - stepx, cy - stepy, cz - stepz) return { 'hitVoxel': (cx, cy, cz), 'hitPos': hitpos, 'hitNormal': hitnormal, 'prevEmptyVoxel': prevvoxel } # Find minimum tMax if tmaxx <= tmaxy and tmaxx <= tmaxz: axis = 'x' tmax = tmaxx elif tmaxy <= tmaxz: axis = 'y' tmax = tmaxy else: axis = 'z' tmax = tmaxz if tmax > tmax: break # Advance traveldist = tmax if axis == 'x': cx += stepx tmaxx += tdeltax hitface = 'neg-x' if stepx < 0 else 'pos-x' elif axis == 'y': cy += stepy tmaxy += tdeltay hitface = 'neg-y' if stepy < 0 else 'pos-y' else: cz += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz hitface = 'neg-z' if stepz < 0 else 'pos-z' return None This method performs hidden surface elimination by casting a ray through a binary voxel volume to locate the first voxel where a specific data channel is non-zero. It differs from standard DDA traversal by optimizing for sparse or binary data: it processes voxels in groups of eight packed into a single byte, advancing the ray by whole bytes when the group is empty, thereby skipping large empty regions efficiently. This approach is distinct from sibling methods that use adaptive edge smoothing or neighbor-averaged interpolation, as it relies on strict bitwise presence checks rather than continuous field evaluation. This method extends standard DDA raymarching by sampling corner and edge voxel occupancy to adaptively compute volume content, eliminating stepping artifacts and spikes caused by uniform voxel traversal. Unlike standard DDA which steps uniformly through fixed voxels, this technique smooths terrain surfaces without increasing the step count or requiring geometry subdivision. It builds on DNstepmap by refining the surface normal and volume estimation at the hit voxel. A technique to compute voxel volume values at corners for smooth terrain rendering, replacing side-based volume storage with corner-based values to better represent surface geometry during raymarching. It sets apart from sibling methods by explicitly handling diagonal neighbors (NW, NE, SW, SE) and applying "surface block maxing" to clamp volumes at surface boundaries, whereas siblings like Midpoint UV Calculation focus on interpolation precision or Voxel DDA Raymarching with Adaptive Edge Smoothing focus on edge artifacts without the specific corner-maxing logic. A voxel raymarching technique that calculates smooth surface entry heights by averaging adjacent voxel volume/height values and interpolating based on the ray's entry position within the cube. It improves upon simple linear interpolation between two voxels by using neighbor-averaged face heights, though it initially ignores the center voxel's influence, leading to sharp edges. Midpoint UV Calculation computes the UV coordinates of the midpoint plane within a voxel traversal step to determine height and lighting variations for surface rendering. It sets apart from sibling methods by explicitly calculating a geometric midpoint between entry and exit UV states to drive height maps, whereas siblings like Corner-based Voxel Volume Calculation rely on corner interpolation and Voxel DDA Raymarching with Neighbor-Averaged Entry Interpolation focus on entry-point smoothing. Bresenham Voxel Traversal is a discrete voxel traversal algorithm that uses an integral error-accumulation method to step through voxels along the dominant axis of a ray. It serves as an alternative to floating-point DDA methods by relying on integer arithmetic for axis increments, which can offer performance benefits in specific hardware or software contexts. It differs from its parent DNstepmap by generating a full sequence of visited voxel coordinates rather than just the first hit, and from siblings like Voxel DDA Raymarching with Adaptive Edge Smoothing by using a strict integer-based decision logic rather than floating-point distance comparisons. Voxel Grid Ray Marching is an algorithm to traverse a 3D voxel grid along a ray, returning the IDs of all visited cells. It handles rays starting outside the grid by computing the entry point intersection with the bounding box. It builds on DNstepmap, which casts a ray into the voxel volume to find the first intersecting voxel, returning hit position, voxel data, and surface normal. Reads adjacent voxel volumes at ray entry and exit positions to adjust traversal behavior, preventing artifacts such as floating voxels, flat edges, and incorrect slope rendering. When exiting a voxel, it calculates the exit voxel's grid position by adding the current position, the step direction mask, and an offset derived from the mask. When entering a voxel, it calculates the entry voxel's grid position using the same mask-based offset logic, ensuring the offset is negative or adjusted for entry direction. It samples the volume value from the calculated adjacent voxel and uses it to modify the ray's exit behavior or skip logic. Pitfall: Reading adjacent voxels can impact performance, though the author notes it may not significantly affect frame rate on small maps. Checks the entry mask to determine which face (X, Y, or Z) the ray enters the voxel. If entering from the left/back, it sets the start UV to the back face and interpolates toward the center. If entering from the right/front, it sets the start UV to the front face and interpolates toward the right/center. Pitfall: Using integer division for UV coordinate calculations causes terrain vertices to fail to connect across voxel edges; all coordinate math must use floating-point types. Time Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of voxels traversed along the ray. Each step involves constant-time comparisons and updates. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the voxel grid storage itself. Performance: Significantly faster than fixed-step raymarching for sparse grids or when large empty regions are present, as it skips directly to boundaries. It avoids the overhead of explicit plane intersection tests. Strengths: Deterministic traversal order; efficient handling of axis-aligned grids; robust handling of parallel rays (via infinity handling). Limitations: Does not handle non-axis-aligned voxel grids (e.g., rotated or skewed) without modification. Precision issues may arise with very large coordinates or very small voxel sizes due to floating-point accumulation in tMax. Requires careful handling of ray origins inside occupied voxels. When to use: Collision detection, occlusion culling, and surface picking in voxel-based worlds. When not to use: When smooth, continuous field evaluation is required without discrete stepping (use Voxel DDA Raymarching with Adaptive Edge Smoothing instead). The algorithm is based on the Amanatides & Woo method, originally published in 1986 for ray tracing through voxel grids. It is widely implemented in voxel engines for efficient raycasting. name: Voxel Raycast (Nonzero/Color Channel)
head: Hidden Surface Elimination via Ray Casting, Visible Surface Detection, zylann::voxel_raycast with Color Predicate
body: This method performs hidden surface elimination by casting a ray through a binary voxel volume to locate the first voxel where a specific data channel is non-zero. It differs from standard DDA traversal by optimizing for sparse or binary data: it processes voxels in groups of eight packed into a single byte, advancing the ray by whole bytes when the group is empty, thereby skipping large empty regions efficiently. This approach is distinct from sibling methods that use adaptive edge smoothing or neighbor-averaged interpolation, as it relies on strict bitwise presence checks rather than continuous field evaluation. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{O} and direction \mathbf{D} (normalized). Voxel grid data structure containing binary or channel-based voxel values. Channel index c to evaluate for non-zero presence. Maximum ray distance d{max}. Outputs: Hit position \mathbf{P}{hit}. Previous position \mathbf{P}{prev} (position before the hit). Distance along ray d{hit}. Surface normal \mathbf{N}. Data Structures: The voxel data is stored in a binary array where each byte holds eight voxels. The layout assumes a specific packing order (typically least-significant bit to most-significant bit or vice versa, though the exact bit-to-voxel mapping depends on the implementation's endianness and packing convention). A predicate structure RaycastPredicateColor holds a reference to the VoxelData and the target channel index c. Steps: 1. Initialize Raycast Predicate: Create a predicate object that encapsulates the voxel data and the channel index c. The predicate's evaluation function operator() takes a ray state (containing the current hit position) and returns true if the voxel value at that position for channel c is non-zero. 2. Execute Voxel Raycast: Call the core raycasting routine (e.g., zylann::voxelraycast) with the ray origin, direction, the predicate, maximum distance, and output variables for hit/previous positions and distances. 3. Byte-Level Traversal (Optimization): Inside the traversal, the algorithm examines the voxel array along the ray's path. For rays aligned with main axes (X, Y, or ±Z), it reads one byte at a time. If the byte value is zero, it advances to the next byte, effectively skipping eight voxels simultaneously. 4. Hit Detection: If the byte value is non-zero, the algorithm identifies that a surface voxel exists within that byte. 5. Voxel Extraction: The specific surface voxel is retrieved by applying a bitmask to the non-zero byte to isolate the exact voxel corresponding to the ray's current position. 6. Result Construction: Upon a successful hit, instantiate a VoxelRaycastResult object. Set the position to the hit location, the previous position to the location before the hit, the distance to the hit distance, and compute the normal as the normalized vector from the previous position to the hit position: \mathbf{N} = \frac{\mathbf{P}{hit} - \mathbf{P}{prev}}{\|\mathbf{P}{hit} - \mathbf{P}{prev}\|}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelraycastnonzerocolor(rayorigin, raydirection, voxeldata, channelindex, maxdistance): """ Casts a ray to find the first voxel where the specified channel is non-zero. Optimized for byte-packed voxel data (8 voxels per byte). """ # Define the predicate function def predicate(raystate): # Get the current position from the ray state pos = raystate.hitposition # Retrieve the voxel value for the specific channel # defval is a default value if the position is out of bounds voxelvalue = voxeldata.getvoxel(pos, channelindex, defval=0) # Return True if the value is non-zero return voxelvalue != 0 # Initialize output variables hitposition = None prevposition = None hitdistance = None # Call the underlying voxel raycast implementation # This function handles the DDA traversal and calls the predicate success = zylannvoxelraycastimpl( rayorigin=rayorigin, raydirection=raydirection, predicate=predicate, maxdistance=maxdistance, outhitposition=hitposition, outprevposition=prevposition, outhitdistance=hitdistance) if success: # Compute normal from the step taken normal = normalize(hitposition - prevposition) result = VoxelRaycastResult( position=hitposition, previousposition=prevposition, distancealongray=hitdistance, normal=normal) return result else: return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Byte Alignment: The algorithm assumes the voxel array is stored such that each byte holds eight voxels, allowing 8 voxels to be examined simultaneously along main axes. If the data is not packed this way, the optimization fails or produces incorrect results. Bit Masking: The specific surface voxel must be correctly extracted from the byte using masking. Incorrect bit ordering (LSB vs MSB) will lead to hitting the wrong voxel within the byte. Precision: Floating-point precision in ray position calculation may cause jitter or missed hits in sparse volumes if not handled with epsilon checks. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of empty bytes traversed before a hit. In sparse volumes, this is significantly faster than per-voxel traversal. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as it operates on the existing voxel data structure. Strengths: Extremely fast for binary or sparse data where large empty regions are common. Simple to implement if the data format is known. Limitations: Only works for finding the first non-zero voxel. Not suitable for volume rendering requiring integration through the entire ray. Requires specific data packing (8 voxels/byte). When to use: Hidden surface elimination, collision detection in binary voxel worlds, visible surface detection. When not to use: Volume rendering with transparency, continuous field evaluation, or when data is not packed in 8-voxel bytes. The concept of hidden surface elimination via ray casting in binary voxel models was introduced in the late 1980s, with early implementations focusing on efficient depth cues for real-time rotation. The specific optimization of examining eight voxels per byte was described in "Hardware Support for the Display and Manipulation of Binary Voxel Models" (1988). The modern implementation in zylann::voxelraycast adapts this principle for real-time applications in engines like Godot, integrating it with general-purpose voxel data structures. name: Voxel DDA Raymarching with Adaptive Edge Smoothing
head: Adaptive voxel terrain marching, Corner-based volume smoothing
body: This method extends standard DDA raymarching by sampling corner and edge voxel occupancy to adaptively compute volume content, eliminating stepping artifacts and spikes caused by uniform voxel traversal. Unlike standard DDA which steps uniformly through fixed voxels, this technique smooths terrain surfaces without increasing the step count or requiring geometry subdivision. It builds on DNstepmap by refining the surface normal and volume estimation at the hit voxel. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, voxel grid data V, camera field of view (FOV). Outputs: Hit position, voxel data, surface normal, and adaptive volume content. The voxel grid V stores occupancy states. Each voxel has a state: AIR: Empty space. SURFACE: Solid terrain block. NON-SURFACE: Solid but not terrain (e.g., bedrock, or internal structure). EMPTY: Explicitly empty (often synonymous with AIR in this context, but distinguished by adjacency checks). The noise function generates a float value N for each voxel coordinate. Height offset H = \lfloor N \rfloor (integer part). Volume content Vc = N - H (decimal part, 0 \le Vc < 1). 1. Ray Direction Correction: Determine the ray direction based on the camera's FOV. If the camera has a negative Z FOV (looking in the negative Z direction), the ray direction \mathbf{d} must be inverted to match the coordinate system. Failure to invert results in swapped entry/exit masks and incorrect terrain rendering. 2. Corner Sampling: For the current voxel being traversed, sample the occupancy state at its four corners: Northwest (NW), Northeast (NE), Southwest (SW), and Southeast (SE). 3. Priority Volume Calculation: If any corner block is NON-SURFACE and not AIR, set the volume content to maximum (1.0). This NON-SURFACE state has the highest priority. 4. Edge Adjacency Check: If no NON-SURFACE blocks exist: Check for AIR blocks. For each corner (e.g., NW), check the adjacent orthogonal blocks (West and North). If either adjacent orthogonal block is AIR or NON-SURFACE, set the volume content to 0 (if AIR) or maximum (if NON-SURFACE). This logic prevents elevation spikes at edges where diagonal blocks are solid but orthogonal neighbors are empty. 5. Zero-Volume Smoothing: Handle voxels with zero volume to prevent visual spikes and square artifacts. Average adjacent volumes or make zero-volume voxels shallow. This ensures smooth transitions and avoids sharp edges when traversing near empty space. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getadaptivevolume(voxelcoords, grid, noisefunc): """ Computes adaptive volume content for a voxel based on corner and edge occupancy. """ # 1. Get base noise value noiseval = noisefunc(voxelcoords) heightoffset = int(noiseval) basevolume = noiseval - heightoffset # 2. Sample corner states # Assuming grid.getstate(x, y, z) returns 'AIR', 'SURFACE', or 'NON-SURFACE' nw = grid.getstate(voxelcoords.x, voxelcoords.y, voxelcoords.z) ne = grid.getstate(voxelcoords.x + 1, voxelcoords.y, voxelcoords.z) sw = grid.getstate(voxelcoords.x, voxelcoords.y + 1, voxelcoords.z) se = grid.getstate(voxelcoords.x + 1, voxelcoords.y + 1, voxelcoords.z) corners = [nw, ne, sw, se] # 3. Priority: Non-surface, non-air blocks for state in corners: if state == 'NON-SURFACE': return 1.0 # Max volume # 4. body: A technique to compute voxel volume values at corners for smooth terrain rendering, replacing side-based volume storage with corner-based values to better represent surface geometry during raymarching. Neighbor Summation: Sum the ColorIndex values of the checked neighbors (Left, Right, Front, Back, NW, NE, SW, SE). 5. head: Voxel DDA smooth terrain interpolation, Voxel terrain raymarching entry height calculation
body: A voxel raymarching technique that calculates smooth surface entry heights by averaging adjacent voxel volume/height values and interpolating based on the ray's entry position within the cube. It improves upon simple linear interpolation between two voxels by using neighbor-averaged face heights, though it initially ignores the center voxel's influence, leading to sharp edges. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray entry position within the current voxel cube (normalized u, v \in [0, 1] along the entry face axes); height values of the current voxel and its immediate neighbors (h{left}, h{right}, h{center}, etc.). Output: Smoothed entry height h{entry} at the ray's intersection point with the voxel face. Data Structures: Voxel heights are stored in a 0-7 range (3 bits). Note: The developer notes that fixing color artifacts would require sacrificing four bits, implying higher precision or additional data may be needed for production. Steps: 1. Identify Entry Face: Determine which face the ray enters the voxel cube (e.g., left side if traversing positive X). 2. Retrieve Neighbor Heights: Get the height values of the two adjacent voxels defining that face (e.g., h{left} and h{right} for an X-axis entry). 3. Calculate Base Side Height: Average the two adjacent voxel heights to define the entry face height: h{side} = \frac{h{left} + h{right}}{2} 4. Normalize Entry Coordinate: Normalize the ray's entry coordinate along the entry axis to a 0-1 range. Let this normalized value be t{raw} \in [0, 1]. 5. Scale Entry Coordinate: Adjust t{raw} to t \in [0, 1] to account for the center voxel's influence (which is not yet integrated but affects the coordinate mapping): If t{raw} < 0.5: t = t{raw} \times 2 If t{raw} \ge 0.5: t = (t{raw} - 0.5) \times 2 6. Compute Final Entry Height: Linearly interpolate between the two adjacent voxel heights using the scaled entry coordinate t: h{entry} = h{A} + (h{B} - h{A}) \cdot t where hA and hB are the heights of the voxels defining the entry face (e.g., h{left} and h{right}). Args: hleft (float): Height of the left neighbor voxel. hright (float): Height of the right neighbor voxel. traw (float): Raw entry coordinate normalized to [0, 1] along the entry axis. Returns: float: Smoothed entry height. """ # Step 3: Calculate base side height by averaging adjacent voxels hside = (hleft + hright) / 2.0 # Step 5: Scale entry coordinate to [0, 1] based on half-cube position if traw < 0.5: t = traw 2.0 else: t = (traw - 0.5) 2.0 # Step 6: Linear interpolation between adjacent voxel heights hentry = hleft + (hright - hleft) t return hentry Parameters: Voxel height values are stored in a 0-7 range (3 bits). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Center Voxel Ignorance: The center voxel's height is initially ignored in the interpolation, causing flat or incorrectly sloped surfaces. The surface should curve toward the center voxel's height to avoid sharp edges. Ambiguous Zero Height: A voxel height value of 0 is ambiguous: it may represent an empty voxel ('cold entirely') or a valid surface height of zero, causing incorrect surface deformation. Negative FOV: A negative field of view (FOV) inverts the camera's coordinate system, causing input axes (horizontal/vertical) to flip. This requires negating the input values or flipping the FOV back to positive. Time Complexity: Constant time O(1) per voxel entry, involving basic arithmetic operations (addition, division, multiplication, comparison). Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory, requiring storage for neighbor heights and entry coordinates. Strengths: Provides smoother surface transitions compared to simple linear interpolation by averaging neighbor heights. Limitations: Initial implementation ignores the center voxel, leading to sharp edges and incorrect slopes. Ambiguity in zero-height voxels can cause visual artifacts. When Not to Use: When high precision is required, or when the center voxel's influence is critical for surface continuity. body: Midpoint UV Calculation computes the UV coordinates of the midpoint plane within a voxel traversal step to determine height and lighting variations for surface rendering. It sets apart from sibling methods by explicitly calculating a geometric midpoint between entry and exit UV states to drive height maps, whereas siblings like Corner-based Voxel Volume Calculation rely on corner interpolation and Voxel DDA Raymarching with Neighbor-Averaged Entry Interpolation focus on entry-point smoothing. Inputs: southwest, southeast, northwest, northeast: 2D UV coordinate vectors representing the four corners of the current voxel face or traversal step. center: A scalar representing the central reference point of the voxel. Outputs: midpointx, midpointy: The calculated midpoint UV coordinates. Derived height values for lighting/terrain generation. Data Structures: midpoints: A list of two 2D vectors storing the Southwest and Northwest midpoint coordinates. Steps: 1. Initialize the midpoint vector structure: midpoints = load2(). 2. Calculate the Southwest midpoint UV by averaging the Southwest and Southeast UV coordinates: midpoints[0] = (southwest + southeast) / 2. 3. Calculate the Northwest midpoint UV by averaging the Northwest and Northeast UV coordinates: midpoints[1] = (northwest + northeast) / 2. 4. Apply Y min/max constraints to the midpoint Y component, ensuring the constraint is reused for both midpoints to maintain consistency. 5. If midpoints[0].y < 0.5, set midpointx = center + 0.5. 6. Otherwise, set midpointy = center. 7. The resulting midpointUV is used to calculate map height and lighting variations. Pitfalls: Rendering only functions correctly above the calculated midpoint; below it, the ray traversal lacks proper height calculations, causing incorrect visual output. The method assumes a specific traversal direction; entering from above and exiting below without explicit quadrant handling can lead to inaccurate midpoint values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def load2(): return [0.0, 0.0] def clamp(value, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(value, maxval)) def calculatemidpointuv(southwest, southeast, northwest, northeast, center): # Step 1: Initialize midpoint vector structure midpoints = [load2(), load2()] # Step 2: Calculate Southwest midpoint UV midpoints[0] = [ (southwest[0] + southeast[0]) / 2.0, (southwest[1] + southeast[1]) / 2.0 ] # Step 3: Calculate Northwest midpoint UV midpoints[1] = [ (northwest[0] + northeast[0]) / 2.0, (northwest[1] + northeast[1]) / 2.0 ] # Step 4: Apply Y min/max constraints (reused for both midpoints) midpoints[0][1] = clamp(midpoints[0][1], 0.0, 1.0) midpoints[1][1] = clamp(midpoints[1][1], 0.0, 1.0) # Step 5 & 6: Determine final midpoint components based on Y threshold if midpoints[0][1] < 0.5: midpointx = center + 0.5 midpointy = midpoints[0][1] else: midpointx = midpoints[0][0] midpointy = center return midpointx, midpointy Calculates the exact Y height where a ray intersects the midpoint plane using linear interpolation between entry and exit Y values. It determines the entry Y value (Y{entry}) and exit Y value (Y{exit}) for the current voxel step. The Y difference is calculated as \text{diff} = Y{entry} - Y{exit}. The Y offset at the midpoint is found by multiplying the difference by the normalized X position (t, typically 0.5). The intersection height is obtained by subtracting the offset from the entry Y height: Y{intersect} = Y{entry} - (Y{entry} - Y{exit}) \times t. A key pitfall is that midpoint accuracy degrades if the ray enters from above and exits below without explicit quadrant handling or proper step direction tracking. body: Bresenham Voxel Traversal is a discrete voxel traversal algorithm that uses an integral error-accumulation method to step through voxels along the dominant axis of a ray. It serves as an alternative to floating-point DDA methods by relying on integer arithmetic for axis increments, which can offer performance benefits in specific hardware or software contexts. Outputs: A list of 3D integer coordinates (i, j, k) representing the sequence of voxels visited by the ray. Integers: ii, jj, kk for voxel indices; dx, dy, dz for ray deltas; err1, err2 for error terms. Parameters: EPSILON: A small positive constant to handle precision issues and boundary conditions. Typical value: 10^{-6} or similar, depending on coordinate scale. quality: A switch case value determining the rendering mode (0-4), though the traversal logic itself is independent of this switch in the source code. If t{entry} < \text{EPSILON}, the ray does not intersect the grid (or starts inside but exits immediately in a degenerate case). Push (-1, -1, -1) to the output list and return. 2. Determine Start and End Points: Calculate the start point P{start} and end point P{end} of the ray segment within the grid. If the ray origin O is outside the grid, P{start} = O + (t{entry} + \text{EPSILON}) \cdot D. If the ray origin O is inside the grid, P{start} = O. P{end} = O + t{exit} \cdot D. The source code implies P{end} is calculated similarly to P{start} but using t{exit}. 3. Calculate Deltas and Increments: Convert P{start} and P{end} to voxel coordinates or calculate deltas in world space. The source code calculates deltas dx, dy, dz as the difference in world coordinates between P{end} and P{start}. dx = P{end}.x - P{start}.x dy = P{end}.y - P{start}.y dz = P{end}.z - P{start}.z Calculate lengths along each axis. These are likely the integer number of steps along each axis. Let Nx = \lceil Lx / s \rceil, Ny = \lceil Ly / s \rceil, Nz = \lceil Lz / s \rceil. If |dx| \ge |dy| and |dx| \ge |dz|, X is dominant. If |dy| \ge |dx| and |dy| \ge |dz|, Y is dominant. If |dz| \ge |dx| and |dz| \ge |dy|, Z is dominant. 5. Traverse Voxels: Initialize the current voxel position (i, j, k) to the voxel containing P{start}. The source code initializes point implicitly or via the loop. Case 1: X is dominant Initialize error terms: err1 = dy2 - x{length} err2 = dz2 - x{length} Loop ii from 0 to xlength (inclusive, based on ii < xlength in source? Source says ii < xlength but also pushes final point. Let's follow source: for (int ii = 0; ii < xlength; ii++)). Push current point (i, j, k) to output. If err1 > 0: j += y{inc} err1 -= dx2 If err2 > 0: k += z{inc} err2 -= dx2 err1 += dy2 err2 += dz2 i += x{inc} Push final point (i, j, k) after the loop. Case 2: Y is dominant Initialize error terms: err1 = dx2 - y{length} err2 = dz2 - y{length} Loop ii from 0 to ylength. Push current point (i, j, k) to output. If err1 > 0: i += x{inc} err1 -= dy2 If err2 > 0: k += z{inc} err2 -= dy2 err1 += dx2 err2 += dz2 j += y{inc} Push final point (i, j, k) after the loop. Case 3: Z is dominant Initialize error terms: err1 = dy2 - z{length} err2 = dx2 - z{length} Loop ii from 0 to zlength. Push current point (i, j, k) to output. Boundaries: The source code does not explicitly show boundary checks within the loop. It is assumed that the ray-cube intersection ensures the start and end points are within the grid, and the increments keep the voxel indices within bounds. However, if the ray starts exactly on a boundary, care must be taken to avoid double-counting or missing voxels. If the ray is parallel to an axis, the dominant axis logic still holds, but the error terms for the non-dominant axes will be zero, resulting in no increments along those axes. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the list of visited voxels. Performance: Integer arithmetic is generally faster than floating-point arithmetic on many hardware platforms, making this method potentially faster than DDA-based methods in software implementations. However, the lack of early-out optimizations (like stopping when a certain density threshold is reached) may lead to unnecessary computations in sparse volumes.
