The Bresenham Voxel Traversal algorithm is derived from Bresenham's line algorithm, which is a classic computer graphics algorithm for rasterizing lines using integer arithmetic. It was adapted for voxel traversal in the context of volumetric rendering, specifically in the VolumetricClouds project by dotcamdev. The method is used in the MarchRayVoxel function to generate a sequence of voxel coordinates for light transmittance calculations. dotcamdev/VolumetricClouds, https://github.com/dotcamdev/VolumetricClouds, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Grid Ray Marching
head: VoxelGridBase::rayMarch
body: Voxel Grid Ray Marching is an algorithm to traverse a 3D voxel grid along a ray, returning the IDs of all visited cells. It handles rays starting outside the grid by computing the entry point intersection with the bounding box. It builds on DNstepmap, which casts a ray into the voxel volume to find the first intersecting voxel, returning hit position, voxel data, and surface normal. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (normalized). Voxel grid bounding box defined by minimum corner B{min} and maximum corner B{max}. Grid dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz (number of voxels per axis). Voxel size s (assumed uniform across axes). Outputs: List of visited voxel indices (IDs). Data Structures: currentVoxel: Integer array of size 3, storing the current voxel index (i, j, k). steps: Integer array of size 3, storing the direction of increment for each axis (+1 or -1). deltas: Float array of size 3, storing the distance to cross one voxel boundary along each axis. ts: Float array of size 3, storing the distance from the ray origin to the next boundary crossing along each axis. finalVoxels: Integer array of size 3, storing the boundary voxel index where traversal stops for each axis. Steps: 1. Check Intersection with Bounding Box: Determine if the ray intersects the grid bounding box. If the ray origin is inside the box, the intersection point is the origin. Otherwise, compute the intersection point P{entry} with the box faces. If there is no intersection, return an empty list. 2. Clamp Start Position: Clamp the start position P{start} to ensure it lies strictly inside the last voxel to avoid boundary exclusion errors due to floating-point precision or floor operations. P{start} = \max(P{entry}, B{min}) P{start} = \min(P{start}, B{max} - \epsilon \cdot s) Where \epsilon is a small constant (e.g., 0.01). 3. Determine Current Voxel: Calculate the initial voxel index containing P{start}: currentVoxel[c] = \left\lfloor \frac{P{start}[c] - B{min}[c]}{s} \right\rfloor for each axis c \in \{x, y, z\}. 4. Calculate Step Directions: Determine the direction of traversal for each axis based on the ray direction: steps[c] = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } D[c] \ge 0 \\ -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 5. Calculate Deltas: Compute the distance to cross one voxel boundary along each axis: deltas[c] = \frac{s}{|D[c]|} If D[c] = 0, the ray is parallel to the axis boundaries; handle as a special case (e.g., set deltas[c] = \infty). 6. Calculate Fractional Distance: Compute the fractional distance from B{min} to P{start}, normalized by cell size: frac[c] = \frac{P{start}[c] - B{min}[c]}{s} - \left\lfloor \frac{P{start}[c] - B{min}[c]}{s} \right\rfloor 7. Initialize T-values and Final Voxels: Initialize the distance to the next boundary crossing ts[c] and the final voxel index finalVoxels[c] for each axis: ts[c] = \begin{cases} deltas[c] \cdot (1.0 - frac[c]) & \text{if } D[c] \ge 0 \\ deltas[c] \cdot frac[c] & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} finalVoxels[c] = \begin{cases} Nc & \text{if } D[c] \ge 0 \\ -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 8. Traverse Voxel Grid: Loop indefinitely: a. Add currentVoxel to the list of visited voxel IDs. b. Find the axis c{min} with the minimum ts value: c{min} = \arg\minc ts[c]. c. Increment the current voxel index along c{min}: currentVoxel[c{min}] += steps[c{min}]. d. If currentVoxel[c{min}] == finalVoxels[c{min}], break the loop. e. Update the t-value for axis c{min}: ts[c{min}] += deltas[c{min}]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelgridraymarching(rayorigin, raydir, boxmin, boxmax, dims, cellsize): """ Traverses a 3D voxel grid along a ray. Args: rayorigin: (3,) array-like, ray origin point. raydir: (3,) array-like, normalized ray direction vector. boxmin: (3,) array-like, minimum corner of the bounding box. boxmax: (3,) array-like, maximum corner of the bounding box. dims: (3,) array-like, number of voxels per axis (Nx, Ny, Nz). cellsize: float, size of each voxel (assumed uniform). Returns: List of voxel indices (tuples of 3 integers) visited by the ray. """ import numpy as np # Step 1: Check intersection with bounding box # Simplified intersection check; assumes ray intersects if it passes through the box # In a full implementation, compute entry point Pentry here. # For this method, we assume Pentry is computed or rayorigin is inside. # If rayorigin is outside, compute intersection with box faces. # If no intersection, return empty list. # Placeholder for intersection logic if origin is outside # Pstart = computeintersection(rayorigin, raydir, boxmin, boxmax) # If no intersection: return [] # Use rayorigin as start if inside, else use intersection point Pstart = np.array(rayorigin) # Step 2: Clamp start position epsilon = 0.01 Pstart = np.maximum(Pstart, boxmin) Pstart = np.minimum(Pstart, boxmax - epsilon cellsize) # Step 3: Determine current voxel currentvoxel = np.floor((Pstart - boxmin) / cellsize).astype(int) # Step 4: Calculate step directions steps = np.where(raydir >= 0, 1, -1) # Step 5: Calculate deltas # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero absdir = np.abs(raydir) deltas = np.where(absdir > 1e-8, cellsize / absdir, np.inf) # Step 6: Calculate fractional distance frac = ((Pstart - boxmin) / cellsize) - np.floor((Pstart - boxmin) / cellsize) # Step 7: Initialize T-values and final voxels ts = np.where(raydir >= 0, deltas (1.0 - frac), deltas frac) finalvoxels = np.where(raydir >= 0, dims, -1) visitedcells = [] # Step 8: Traverse while True: visitedcells.append(tuple(currentvoxel)) # Find axis with minimum t-value minidx = np.argmin(ts) # Increment current voxel along that axis currentvoxel[minidx] += steps[minidx] # Check if we have reached the final voxel for that axis if currentvoxel[minidx] == finalvoxels[minidx]: break # Update t-value for the axis ts[minidx] += deltas[minidx] return visitedcells Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels visited along the ray. In the worst case, N is proportional to the diagonal length of the grid in voxel units. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the output list of visited voxels. Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient for uniform grids, handles boundary conditions explicitly. Limitations: Does not handle non-uniform voxel sizes without modification. Precision issues may occur at boundaries, mitigated by clamping. When to use: When a simple, fast traversal of a uniform voxel grid is required, and all visited voxels need to be processed. When not to use: For non-uniform grids, or when only the first hit is needed (use DNstepmap). This method is derived from the implementation in the FDS-GS repository. It is a standard approach for ray-voxel intersection, often referred to as the Amanatides-Woo algorithm or DDA traversal, adapted for specific grid structures. whoiszzj/FDS-GS, https://github.com/whoiszzj/FDS-GS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Raycast with AABB Hitbox Refinement
head: Voxel Raycasting with AABB Refinement
body: This method extends basic voxel raycasting by combining axis-aligned grid traversal with precise geometric intersection against sub-voxel bounding boxes. It solves the problem of accurately determining surface contact points and normals in voxel environments where blocks may have non-cuboid collision shapes (hitboxes). Unlike its parent method, which returns only the voxel face normal for solid blocks, this algorithm refines the hit position and normal by intersecting the ray against specific AABB hitboxes for non-solid voxels, or falls back to the grid face normal for solid voxels. Inputs: Ray origin: (px, py, pz) Ray direction: (dx, dy, dz) Maximum traversal distance: t{max} Voxel grid data structure providing access to voxel definitions by integer coordinates. Configuration flags: includeNonSelectable (boolean), excludeMode (filter logic). Outputs: Hit voxel coordinates: (ix, iy, iz) Hit distance: t Hit normal: \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) Hit position: \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{p}{origin} + \mathbf{n}{dir} \cdot t (where \mathbf{n}{dir} is the normalized ray direction). Null/None if no hit is found within t{max}. Voxel Definition: Contains at minimum: id: Integer identifier. solid: Boolean indicating if the voxel is fully solid. selectable: Boolean indicating if the voxel can be targeted. hitboxes: List of AABBs. Each AABB is defined by min/max coordinates relative to the voxel origin: (minx, miny, minz) and (maxx, maxy, maxz). segmentstate: Optional integer or enum used to offset hitbox positions. epsilon: Threshold for zero-direction detection. Value: 10^{-6}. 1. Initialization: Calculate initial voxel coordinates: ix = \lfloor px \rfloor, \quad iy = \lfloor py \rfloor, \quad iz = \lfloor pz \rfloor Determine step directions for each axis: sx = \text{sign}(dx), \quad sy = \text{sign}(dy), \quad sz = \text{sign}(dz) Where \text{sign}(v) is 1 if v \ge 0 and -1 if v < 0. Calculate delta distances to cross the next voxel boundary: t{xDelta} = \begin{cases} \infty & \text{if } |dx| < \epsilon \\ \frac{1.0}{|dx|} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} t{yDelta} = \begin{cases} \infty & \text{if } |dy| < \epsilon \\ \frac{1.0}{|dy|} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} t{zDelta} = \begin{cases} \infty & \text{if } |dz| < \epsilon \\ \frac{1.0}{|dz|} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Calculate initial distance to the first boundary (t{xMax}, t{yMax}, t{zMax}): If dx \ge 0: x{dist} = (ix + 1) - px If dx < 0: x{dist} = px - ix t{xMax} = t{xDelta} \cdot x{dist} Repeat similarly for y and z axes. Initialize current distance t = 0. Initialize steppedIndex to -1 (indicating no axis stepped yet). 2. Traversal Loop: While t \le t{max}: Retrieve voxel definition at (ix, iy, iz). If voxel is null or air, return null. Selectability Check: If voxel.id is not BLOCKAIR AND (voxel.selectable is true OR includeNonSelectable is true) AND (voxel.id passes filter based on excludeMode): Proceed to hit detection. Hit Detection: Case A: Non-Solid Voxel (voxel.solid is false): Initialize closestt = \infty, closestnormal = (0,0,0). For each hitbox in voxel.hitboxes: Determine AABB bounds. If voxel.segmentstate exists, apply offset to hitbox coordinates. Perform Ray-AABB intersection test between ray (\mathbf{p}{origin}, \mathbf{d}{dir}) and AABB. If intersection exists at distance t{hit} < t{max} and t{hit} < closestt: closestt = t{hit} closestnormal = \text{intersection normal} If closestt < \infty: Return hit: voxel, t = closestt, \mathbf{n} = closestnormal. Update end position: \mathbf{p}{end} = \mathbf{p}{origin} + \mathbf{d}{dir} \cdot t. Case B: Solid Voxel (voxel.solid is true): Determine the face normal based on the last axis stepped into. If steppedIndex \ge 0: \mathbf{n} = (0, 0, 0) \mathbf{n}{steppedIndex} = -s{steppedIndex} Else: \mathbf{n} = (0, 0, 0) (or handle degenerate start case). Return hit: voxel, t, \mathbf{n}. Advance Ray: Identify the smallest boundary distance: t{next} = \min(t{xMax}, t{yMax}, t{zMax}) Update current distance: t = t{next}. Increment coordinate for the axis corresponding to the minimum: If t{xMax} is min: ix \leftarrow ix + sx, t{xMax} \leftarrow t{xMax} + t{xDelta}, steppedIndex = 0. If t{yMax} is min: iy \leftarrow iy + sy, t{yMax} \leftarrow t{yMax} + t{yDelta}, steppedIndex = 1. If t{zMax} is min: iz \leftarrow iz + sz, t{zMax} \leftarrow t{zMax} + t{zDelta}, steppedIndex = 2. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raycastvoxelaabb(porigin, ddir, tmax, voxelgrid, includenonselectable=False, excludemode=None): """ Performs voxel raycasting with AABB hitbox refinement. Args: porigin: Tuple (px, py, pz) ddir: Tuple (dx, dy, dz) tmax: Float voxelgrid: Object with method getvoxel(ix, iy, iz) includenonselectable: Boolean excludemode: Function or filter logic Returns: Tuple (voxel, t, normal) or None """ epsilon = 1e-6 # 1. Initialization ix = math.floor(porigin[0]) iy = math.floor(porigin[1]) iz = math.floor(porigin[2]) dx, dy, dz = ddir sx = 1 if dx >= 0 else -1 sy = 1 if dy >= 0 else -1 sz = 1 if dz >= 0 else -1 # Delta distances txdelta = math.inf if abs(dx) < epsilon else 1.0 / abs(dx) tydelta = math.inf if abs(dy) < epsilon else 1.0 / abs(dy) tzdelta = math.inf if abs(dz) < epsilon else 1.0 / abs(dz) # Initial max distances if dx >= 0: xdist = (ix + 1) - porigin[0] else: xdist = porigin[0] - ix txmax = txdelta xdist if dy >= 0: ydist = (iy + 1) - porigin[1] else: ydist = porigin[1] - iy tymax = tydelta ydist if dz >= 0: zdist = (iz + 1) - porigin[2] else: zdist = porigin[2] - iz tzmax = tzdelta zdist t = 0.0 steppedindex = -1 # 2. Traversal Loop while t <= tmax: voxel = voxelgrid.getvoxel(ix, iy, iz) if voxel is None: return None # Selectability Check isair = (voxel.id == "BLOCKAIR") if not isair: isselectable = voxel.selectable or includenonselectable passesfilter = True # Assume passes if excludemode is None or logic handled if excludemode is not None: passesfilter = excludemode(voxel.id) if isselectable and passesfilter: # Hit Detection if not voxel.solid: # Non-solid: Check AABBs closestt = math.inf closestnormal = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for hitbox in voxel.hitboxes: # Apply segment state offset if present offset = voxel.getsegmentoffset() if hasattr(voxel, 'getsegmentoffset') else (0,0,0) minb = (hitbox.minx + offset[0], hitbox.miny + offset[1], hitbox.minz + offset[2]) maxb = (hitbox.maxx + offset[0], hitbox.maxy + offset[1], hitbox.maxz + offset[2]) # Ray-AABB Intersection hitt, hitn = intersectrayaabb(porigin, ddir, minb, maxb) if hitt is not None and hitt < tmax and hitt < closestt: closestt = hitt closestnormal = hitn if closestt < math.inf: # Return hit return (voxel, closestt, closestnormal) else: # Solid: Return face normal normal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if steppedindex >= 0: stepdirs = [sx, sy, sz] normal[steppedindex] = -stepdirs[steppedindex] return (voxel, t, tuple(normal)) # Advance Ray if txmax < tymax: if txmax < tzmax: t = txmax ix += sx txmax += txdelta steppedindex = 0 else: t = tzmax iz += sz tzmax += tzdelta steppedindex = 2 else: if tymax < tzmax: t = tymax iy += sy tymax += tydelta steppedindex = 1 else: t = tzmax iz += sz tzmax += tzdelta steppedindex = 2 return None def intersectrayaabb(origin, direction, minb, maxb): """ Standard Ray-AABB intersection. Returns (t, normal) or (None, None). """ # Initialize tmin and tmax tmin = -math.inf tmax = math.inf # Precompute inverse direction invdir = [1.0/d if abs(d) > 1e-9 else 0.0 for d in direction] normals = [] for i in range(3): if invdir[i] >= 0: t1 = (minb[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] t2 = (maxb[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] n = [-1.0 if j == i else 0.0 for j in range(3)] else: t1 = (maxb[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] t2 = (minb[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] n = [1.0 if j == i else 0.0 for j in range(3)] if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 normals = [n] elif abs(t1 - tmin) < 1e-9: normals.append(n) if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 else: return None, None if tmin > tmax: return None, None if tmin < 0: # Ray starts inside or behind # For this algorithm, we usually want the first positive hit # However, standard DDA assumes entering from outside. # If tmin < 0, check tmax. if tmax < 0: return None, None # If inside, return the exit normal? Or ignore? # The source implies finding the "closest hit distance". # If the ray starts inside a hitbox, tmin is negative. # We should likely return the positive intersection if it exists. if tmax > 0: # Return exit normal # Re-calculate normal for tmax # Simplified: return None for complex inside cases unless specified # Given the context of voxel traversal, we usually hit from outside. return None, None # Return normal corresponding to tmin # If multiple normals have same tmin, pick one (e.g., first) if normals: return tmin, normals[0] return None, None Division by Zero: If a ray direction component is effectively zero (|di| < \epsilon), the delta distance is set to infinity. This ensures the axis is never chosen for stepping, preventing division by zero and infinite loops. Degenerate Rays: If all direction components are zero, the ray does not move. The algorithm should handle this by returning null or handling it before traversal. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in boundary calculations can cause the ray to skip voxels or re-enter the same voxel. Using epsilon for comparisons helps mitigate this. Hitbox Offsets: If a voxel has a segmentstate, hitbox coordinates must be adjusted by the offset before intersection testing. Failure to do so results in incorrect hit positions. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels traversed along the ray. For each non-solid voxel hit, an additional O(K) cost is incurred where K is the number of hitboxes in that voxel. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the voxel grid storage. Strengths: Provides accurate surface normals and hit positions for non-cuboid collision shapes within a voxel grid. Combines the speed of grid traversal with the precision of geometric intersection. Limitations: More computationally expensive than simple face-normal raycasting due to AABB intersection tests. Performance degrades if voxels have many hitboxes. When to Use: When voxel blocks have complex collision shapes (e.g., stairs, slabs, custom models) and accurate normal estimation is required for physics or rendering. When Not to Use: For simple cubic voxel worlds where face normals are sufficient, or when performance is critical and hitbox precision is not needed. This method is an extension of voxel raycasting techniques used in voxel-based games and simulations. It builds upon the Amanatides-Woo voxel traversal algorithm Parent by adding a layer of geometric precision for non-solid blocks. The specific implementation details, including the handling of segment states and hitbox offsets, are derived from the voxelcore library. MihailRis/voxelcore, https://github.com/MihailRis/voxelcore, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing
head: 3D line scan-conversion, Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing, Voxel DDA Ray Marching, voxelDDA
body: 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing is a discrete ray traversal algorithm that approximates a continuous ray as a sequence of adjacent voxels in a uniform 3D grid using integer arithmetic. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which voxels a ray intersects without computing floating-point ray-AABB intersections at every step. Unlike Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal, which calculates exact distances to voxel boundaries using floating-point division, Bresenham tracing relies on error accumulation to determine the next voxel, making it computationally cheaper and immune to division-by-zero errors for axis-aligned rays. It is distinct from Siddon's Algorithm by avoiding floating-point slab intersection calculations entirely. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \vec{o}, ray direction \vec{d}, grid dimensions (W, H, D), voxel size s (typically s=1), and a voxel grid data structure. Output: A sequence of voxel coordinates (x, y, z) visited by the ray, or a hit result containing the first occupied voxel's index, normal, and distance. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A dense 1D array or 3D array. For a grid of size W \times H \times D, the linear index for coordinate (x, y, z) in row-major order is: \text{index} = (z \cdot H + y) \cdot W + x State Variables: Current voxel coordinates (x, y, z), step directions (x{inc}, y{inc}, z{inc}) \in \{-1, 1\}, and error accumulators (c1, c2). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Determine the entry point t0 where the ray enters the grid's Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). If the ray does not intersect the grid, terminate. Calculate the initial world position: \vec{f}0 = \vec{o} + t0 \cdot \vec{d}. Compute the initial voxel index \vec{i}0 = \lfloor \vec{f}0 \rfloor (component-wise floor). This is the starting voxel (x, y, z). Calculate the target end position \vec{f}1 corresponding to the exit of the grid or a maximum distance. Compute deltas: \Delta x = |xf - xi|, \Delta y = |yf - yi|, \Delta z = |zf - zi|. Determine step directions: x{inc} = \text{sign}(xf - xi), y{inc} = \text{sign}(yf - yi), z{inc} = \text{sign}(zf - zi). Identify the dominant axis (the axis with the largest delta). Let this be D{dom} with value \Delta{dom}. Initialize error accumulators c1 = c2 = \Delta{dom} / 2. This centers the error term to handle the start voxel correctly. 2. Traversal Loop: Iterate i from 1 to \Delta{dom} (inclusive). Step on Dominant Axis: Increment the coordinate on the dominant axis by its step direction (x \leftarrow x + x{inc} if X is dominant, etc.). Update Error Accumulators: If X is dominant: c1 \leftarrow c1 + \Delta y, c2 \leftarrow c2 + \Delta z. If Y is dominant: c1 \leftarrow c1 + \Delta x, c2 \leftarrow c2 + \Delta z. If Z is dominant: c1 \leftarrow c1 + \Delta y, c2 \leftarrow c2 + \Delta x. Check Non-Dominant Axes: If c1 \ge \Delta{dom}: c1 \leftarrow c1 - \Delta{dom} Increment the corresponding non-dominant coordinate by its step direction. If c2 \ge \Delta{dom}: c2 \leftarrow c2 - \Delta{dom} Increment the other non-dominant coordinate by its step direction. Process Voxel: The current (x, y, z) is a voxel intersected by the ray. Check occupancy or perform shading. Boundary Check: If the updated coordinates exceed grid bounds [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1] \times [0, D-1], terminate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bresenhamvoxeltracing(rayorigin, raydirection, gridwidth, gridheight, griddepth, voxelsize=1.0): # 1. Calculate entry/exit t-values for the grid AABB # Simplified: assume ray intersects grid. Calculate start and end voxel coordinates. # In practice, use slab intersection to find tentry and texit. # f0 = rayorigin + tentry raydirection # f1 = rayorigin + texit raydirection # Map world coordinates to voxel indices # i0 = floor(f0 / voxelsize) # i1 = floor(f1 / voxelsize) xi, yi, zi = i0 xf, yf, zf = i1 # 2. Calculate deltas and step directions dx = xf - xi dy = yf - yi dz = zf - zi xinc = 1 if dx > 0 else -1 yinc = 1 if dy > 0 else -1 zinc = 1 if dz > 0 else -1 absdx = abs(dx) absdy = abs(dy) absdz = abs(dz) # 3. Identify dominant axis # Initialize error accumulators c1 = 0 c2 = 0 # Process start voxel yield (xi, yi, zi) # Determine dominant axis and iterate if absdx >= absdy and absdx >= absdz: # X is dominant c1 = absdx // 2 c2 = absdx // 2 for in range(absdx): xi += xinc c1 += absdy if c1 >= absdx: c1 -= absdx yi += yinc c2 += absdz if c2 >= absdx: c2 -= absdx zi += zinc yield (xi, yi, zi) elif absdy >= absdx and absdy >= absdz: # Y is dominant c1 = absdy // 2 c2 = absdy // 2 for in range(absdy): yi += yinc c1 += absdx if c1 >= absdy: c1 -= absdy xi += xinc c2 += absdz if c2 >= absdy: c2 -= absdy zi += zinc yield (xi, yi, zi) else: # Z is dominant c1 = absdz // 2 c2 = absdz // 2 for in range(absdz): zi += zinc c1 += absdy if c1 >= absdz: c1 -= absdz yi += yinc c2 += absdx if c2 >= absdz: c2 -= absdz xi += xinc yield (xi, yi, zi) Parameters: voxelsize: Typically 1.0 to eliminate division in coordinate mapping. maxsteps: Optional limit to prevent infinite loops in degenerate cases (e.g., ray parallel to grid face but outside bounds). Default 128 for a 64x64x64 grid. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Axis-Aligned Rays: If a ray direction component is zero, the standard DDA division by zero is avoided in Bresenham's integer logic. However, the dominant axis selection must handle ties (e.g., if dx=0, dy=0, dz>0, Z is dominant). Boundary Conditions: The algorithm must clamp coordinates to [0, \text{dim}-1] to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Connectivity: The standard Bresenham algorithm produces a 6-connected path in 3D (moving along one axis at a time, or diagonally across faces). A 26-connected path (allowing corner crossings) may miss intersections that a 6-connected path detects, but requires less computation. The basic integer accumulation described above yields a path that is topologically consistent with the line segment but may not visit every voxel touched by the continuous ray if the ray passes through a voxel corner. Precision: Using integer arithmetic avoids floating-point accumulation errors, but the initial mapping from world to voxel coordinates must be precise. This method implements the Amanatides and Woo voxel traversal algorithm using scaled integer arithmetic to determine the sequence of grid cells intersected by a ray, ensuring exactness and stability by avoiding floating-point operations. It serves as the core traversal loop for image-order volume rendering or ray casting. Voxel Traversal with Rounding Error Correction is a method for stepping a ray through a voxel grid that explicitly compensates for floating-point precision errors in position calculations. It builds on 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing by adding a correction step to ensure the ray enters the correct adjacent voxel, preventing misses or incorrect entries caused by rounding artifacts. The Liu Extension of Bresenham is a voxel traversal algorithm that extends the classic 2D Bresenham line algorithm to 3D grid traversal by detecting and visiting diagonal neighbors when the ray intersects a cell corner. Unlike standard Bresenham which visits only one neighbor per step, this method checks if the error exceeds a specific threshold to decide whether to visit both (x+1, y) and (x+1, y+1) in 2D, or the corresponding diagonal paths in 3D. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on a geometric intersection check against a derived threshold rather than simple integer error accumulation, offering performance advantages even on modern hardware where floating-point operations are efficient. The Zalik et al. algorithm is a voxel traversal method that corrects the topological incompleteness of standard 3D Bresenham tracing by ensuring all cells intersected by a ray are visited. It differs from its parent 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing by adding a post-processing phase to recover missed cells, whereas siblings like Integer-based Amanatides and Woo Voxel Traversal compute intersections analytically. BCC/FCC Ray Tracing is a volume rendering and object representation method that samples 3-D data on Body Centered Cubic (BCC) or Face Centered Cubic (FCC) grids instead of standard cubic grids. It solves topological defects inherent in cubic grids—specifically, the possibility of a ray passing through an object surface without intersecting any voxel—by utilizing grids with superior topological properties that guarantee closed surfaces and robust discrete curve/surface definitions. Unlike cubic grid methods such as 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing or Integer-based Amanatides and Woo Voxel Traversal, this approach defines voxels as Voronoi cells (Truncated Octahedra for BCC, Rhombic Dodecahedra for FCC) and traces rays by minimizing the cross-sectional area of the ray beam within these polyhedral structures. Template-Based Volume Viewing is a ray-grid traversal technique for parallel projection that exploits inter-ray coherence by precomputing a single sequence of voxel increments (a template) and reusing it for all rays, thereby avoiding per-ray line algorithm activation. It solves the discretization errors and performance overhead inherent in naive per-ray traversal, where varying initial positions cause voxels to be skipped or visited multiple times. Unlike siblings that recompute traversal logic per ray, this method ensures all rays share the same form regardless of length, distributing discretization error uniformly. A ray tracing method for voxel models that walks a block of a model cell by cell using the Amanatides-Woo DDA algorithm, organizing models into 8^3 blocks within a BVH to skip empty space. It cuts the model into 8^3 blocks, shrinks them to voxel representations, inserts them into a BVH, and walks the grid cell by cell. Boundary artifacts on block edges are handled by reading neighboring cells from the whole model. Memory usage is one byte per voxel cell. It is approximately 15% faster than quad-based tracing on the monu1 scene. A lighting calculation performed using the normal and position derived from the voxel traversal hit, rather than the continuous surface intersection of standard ray tracing. It calculates the real-world position of the hit using the traversal distance hitT (vec3 realPos = ro + hitT rd;), computes diffuse lighting intensity using the dot product of the hit normal and light position, applies ambient and diffuse scaling, and mixes between shadow and cube colors based on intensity. Standard ambient occlusion and shadow calculations may not work correctly because they are computed on the continuous geometry rather than the voxel grid. A shading technique used within the voxel tracer where rays bounce off voxel surfaces. It uses a probabilistic mix of perfect reflection and diffuse scattering to simulate indirect lighting and color bleeding, limited to a maximum of 3 bounces. If a random number rand > 0.9, a perfect specular reflection is performed; otherwise, a random diffuse direction is generated, reflected if it points into the surface, and attenuated by the voxel's color. The diffuse reflection correction is dir{out} = dir{rand} - 2 \cdot (dir{rand} \cdot normal) \cdot normal if dir{rand} \cdot normal < 0. The demo has very limited denoising, resulting in extremely noisy images. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels traversed, bounded by the grid dimension in the worst case (O(\max(W, H, D))). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for the traversal state, plus O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for the voxel grid. Performance: Integer arithmetic is generally faster than floating-point division, making Bresenham tracing efficient on hardware without advanced FPUs or when integer units are preferred. However, it may visit more voxels than necessary (topological incompleteness) compared to analytical methods like Amanatides-Woo or Siddon's, potentially increasing shading cost. Strengths: No division by zero issues for axis-aligned rays; simple integer logic; low memory overhead; easy to implement. Limitations: May miss voxels intersected by the ray (topological incompleteness) if the path is not 26-connected or if error accumulation is not corrected. Less precise than floating-point DDA for determining exact hit positions. The method originates from the classic Bresenham line algorithm, extended to 3D for voxelization and raycasting. It is often referred to as "Voxel DDA Ray Marching" or "3D line scan-conversion". It is used in voxel-based games (e.g., Minecraft-like engines) for collision detection and raycasting, and in medical volume rendering as a discrete approximation of ray casting. The "Fast Voxel Traversal Algorithm for Ray Tracing" by Amanatides and Woo (1987) is a related but distinct floating-point method; Bresenham's integer variant is often used as a simpler alternative or as a basis for integer-based optimizations. name: Integer-based Amanatides and Woo Voxel Traversal
head: Exact integer grid traversal, Integer-based Fast Grid Traversal, Integer-based ray marching
body: This method implements the Amanatides and Woo voxel traversal algorithm using scaled integer arithmetic to determine the sequence of grid cells intersected by a ray, ensuring exactness and stability by avoiding floating-point operations. It serves as the core traversal loop for image-order volume rendering or ray casting. Inputs: startX, startY, startZ: Integer grid coordinates of the starting voxel. originX, originY, originZ: Ray origin in world space. vx, vy, vz: Ray direction vector components, scaled to integers. cellSize: Width of a single voxel in world units. justOutX, justOutY, justOutZ: Predefined boundary values indicating the grid exit for each axis. Outputs: The first object hit in the voxel grid, or None if the ray exits the grid without hitting an object. Data Structures: X, Y, Z: Current voxel coordinates (32-bit signed integers). stepX, stepY, stepZ: Direction indicators (+1 or -1) for each axis. iDeltaX, iDeltaY, iDeltaZ: Scaled delta distances to the next boundary crossing for each axis (64-bit signed integers, long long). iMaxX, iMaxY, iMaxZ: Scaled distances to the first boundary crossing for each axis (64-bit signed integers, long long). Parameters: Typical values for cellSize depend on the scene scale. vx, vy, vz must be scaled consistently with origin and cellSize. The scaling factor S is implicitly |vx vy vz|. The algorithm avoids division by multiplying the standard floating-point t{max} formula by this factor. Steps: 1. Initialization Phase: 1. Set current voxel coordinates: X = startX, Y = startY, Z = startZ. 2. Determine step directions: stepX = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } vx \ge 0 \\ -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Repeat for stepY and stepZ). 3. Calculate the world-space coordinate of the next grid boundary for each axis: nextBoundaryX = \begin{cases} (X + 1) \cdot cellSize & \text{if } stepX > 0 \\ X \cdot cellSize & \text{if } stepX \le 0 \end{cases} (Repeat for Y and Z). 4. Compute scaled delta distances (iDelta) for each axis. These represent the change in scaled distance when crossing one voxel: iDeltaX = cellSize \cdot |vy \cdot vz| iDeltaY = cellSize \cdot |vx \cdot vz| iDeltaZ = cellSize \cdot |vx \cdot vy| Use 64-bit integers (long long) to prevent overflow during multiplication. 5. Initialize scaled max distances (iMax) to the first boundary crossing. The standard floating-point formula t{max} = \frac{boundary - origin}{v} is scaled by multiplying by |vx vy vz|. iMaxX = (nextBoundaryX - originX) \cdot vy \cdot vz If vx < 0, negate iMaxX to correct for the direction of division. If vx = 0, set iMaxX = LLONG\MAX (parallel ray). (Repeat for iMaxY and iMaxZ). 2. Incremental Phase: 1. Enter a loop. Compare iMaxX, iMaxY, and iMaxZ to find the smallest value, indicating the next axis to cross. 2. If iMaxX is the smallest: Increment X by stepX. If X == justOutX, return None (ray exited grid). Update iMaxX = iMaxX + iDeltaX. 3. Else if iMaxY is the smallest: Increment Y by stepY. If Y == justOutY, return None. Update iMaxY = iMaxY + iDeltaY. 4. Else (iMaxZ is the smallest): Increment Z by stepZ. If Z == justOutZ, return None. Update iMaxZ = iMaxZ + iDeltaZ. 5. Check the voxel list at the current (X, Y, Z) coordinates for an object hit. 6. If an object is hit, return it. Otherwise, continue the loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def integeramanatideswootraversal(startX, startY, startZ, originX, originY, originZ, vx, vy, vz, cellSize, justOutX, justOutY, justOutZ): # 1. Initialization Phase X, Y, Z = startX, startY, startZ stepX = 1 if vx >= 0 else -1 stepY = 1 if vy >= 0 else -1 stepZ = 1 if vz >= 0 else -1 nextBoundaryX = (X + 1) cellSize if stepX > 0 else X cellSize nextBoundaryY = (Y + 1) cellSize if stepY > 0 else Y cellSize nextBoundaryZ = (Z + 1) cellSize if stepZ > 0 else Z cellSize # Compute scale factors (Absolute values of cross-products) # Use 64-bit integers to prevent overflow iDeltaX = cellSize abs(vy vz) iDeltaY = cellSize abs(vx vz) iDeltaZ = cellSize abs(vx vy) # Initialize iMax (Scaled t to next boundary) # Logic: (nextBoundary - origin) (product of other two velocity components) # Correct sign for negative velocity components INF = 263 - 1 # LLONGMAX iMaxX = (nextBoundaryX - originX) vy vz if vx < 0: iMaxX = -iMaxX if vx == 0: iMaxX = INF iMaxY = (nextBoundaryY - originY) vx vz if vy < 0: iMaxY = -iMaxY if vy == 0: iMaxY = INF iMaxZ = (nextBoundaryZ - originZ) vx vy if vz < 0: iMaxZ = -iMaxZ if vz == 0: iMaxZ = INF # Check starting voxel before traversal hit = None # Placeholder for external voxel list lookup if hit is not None: return hit # 2. Incremental Phase while True: if iMaxX < iMaxY: if iMaxX < iMaxZ: # X is smallest X += stepX if X == justOutX: return None iMaxX += iDeltaX else: # Z is smallest Z += stepZ if Z == justOutZ: return None iMaxZ += iDeltaZ else: if iMaxY < iMaxZ: # Y is smallest Y += stepY if Y == justOutY: return None iMaxY += iDeltaY else: # Z is smallest Z += stepZ if Z == justOutZ: return None iMaxZ += iDeltaZ # Check voxel list at current (X, Y, Z) for an object hit hit = None # Placeholder for external voxel list lookup if hit is not None: return hit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If a velocity component is 0 (e.g., vx = 0), the corresponding iMax is set to LLONGMAX, effectively removing that axis from the minimum comparison. Integer Overflow: The intermediate calculations for iDelta and iMax involve products of velocity components and coordinates. Using 64-bit integers (long long) is necessary to prevent overflow for large grids or high-precision direction vectors. Grid Exit: The loop terminates when the incremented coordinate equals the predefined justOut boundary for that axis. This method implements the Amanatides–Woo voxel traversal algorithm using 16-bit signed fixed-point arithmetic (Q8.8 format) to avoid floating-point operations entirely. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which grid cells a line segment intersects in 2D space, serving as the core traversal loop for image-order volume rendering or ray casting. It sets itself apart from its parent Integer-based Amanatides and Woo Voxel Traversal by using fractional bits to represent sub-cell distances, allowing for exact intersection calculations without the accumulation of rounding errors inherent in pure integer DDA, while maintaining the speed benefits of integer arithmetic. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels traversed. Each iteration performs a constant number of integer comparisons and additions. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Significantly faster than floating-point Amanatides-Woo on hardware lacking efficient FPUs or where integer arithmetic is preferred for determinism. It avoids the cost of division and floating-point conversion. Strengths: Exactness (no rounding errors in traversal order), stability, and speed. Ideal for fixed-grid environments like voxel games or exact collision detection. Limitations: Requires careful scaling of input values to fit within 64-bit integer limits. Not suitable for dynamic grids where cell sizes vary per axis unless adapted. Precision is limited by the integer range; very small steps or very large grids may require higher precision types or fixed-point variants. The original Amanatides and Woo algorithm (1987) is a standard method for voxel traversal using floating-point arithmetic. This integer-based variant was proposed in an unofficial GitHub issue discussion to provide a fast, exact, and stable alternative for applications like bullet hit detection in games, where floating-point precision issues could cause rays to pass through voxels incorrectly. It mirrors the logic of the original paper but replaces floating-point operations with scaled integer arithmetic. name: Voxel Traversal with Rounding Error Correction
head: Rounding Error Corrected Voxel Traversal
body: Voxel Traversal with Rounding Error Correction is a method for stepping a ray through a voxel grid that explicitly compensates for floating-point precision errors in position calculations. It builds on 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing by adding a correction step to ensure the ray enters the correct adjacent voxel, preventing misses or incorrect entries caused by rounding artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current voxel integer position intPosition3 (3 integers), current float position floatPosition3 (3 floats), ray direction signs pstvDirComps and ngtvDirComps (3 booleans indicating positive/negative direction components), rounding status flags rightRnddComps (3 booleans indicating correctly rounded components), and sideMax (3 floats specifying the exit side of the current voxel, corresponding to tMax). Output: Updated intPosition3 reflecting the next voxel index. Data Structures: intPosition3: A 3-component integer vector representing the current voxel coordinates (i, j, k). floatPosition3: A 3-component float vector representing the ray's position in voxel space. pstvDirComps: A 3-component boolean vector where Px=1 if dx > 0, else 0. ngtvDirComps: A 3-component boolean vector where Nx=1 if dx < 0, else 0. rightRnddComps: A 3-component boolean vector where Rx=1 if the component of floatPosition3 was correctly rounded relative to the expected voxel boundary, else 0. wrongRnddComps: The logical NOT of rightRnddComps (Wx = \neg Rx). sideMax: A 3-component float vector indicating the side of the current voxel where the ray exits. The sign indicates the exit direction (e.g., (1, 0, 0) means exit on the right side, +x). Steps: 1. Calculate Correction Vector Components: Determine which components require a shift by combining direction signs and rounding error flags. For positive direction components, a shift is needed if rounding was wrong: Cx = Px \land Wx. For negative direction components, a shift is needed if rounding was correct, as this represents the same stepping problem: Cx = Nx \land Rx. Combine these using logical OR: C = (P \land W) \lor (N \land R). 2. Determine Shift Direction and Magnitude: The sign of the shift is determined by sideMax. If sideMax indicates an exit on the +x side, the shift in x is positive, moving to the higher index voxel. The sideMax vector's sign corresponds to the direction of travel for the exiting component. 3. Apply Shift: Update intPosition3 by adding the correction vector scaled by the shift direction. For each component c \in \{x, y, z\}, if Cc is true, increment or decrement intPosition3[c] by 1 based on the sign of sideMax[c]. Formula: The correction vector C is calculated as: C = (pstvDirComps \land wrongRnddComps) \lor (ngtvDirComps \land rightRnddComps) Where: pstvDirComps: Boolean vector indicating positive direction components. ngtvDirComps: Boolean vector indicating negative direction components. wrongRnddComps: Boolean vector indicating components with rounding errors. rightRnddComps: Boolean vector indicating correctly rounded components. \land: Logical AND. \lor: Logical OR. The update to intPosition3 is: intPosition3{new} = intPosition3{old} + \text{sign}(sideMax) \cdot C Where \text{sign}(sideMax) returns +1 or -1 for each component based on the sign of sideMax. Parameters: sideMax: A vector specifying the side of the current voxel where the next voxel is adjacent. Its sign specifies the exit point side (e.g., (1, 0, 0) means exit on the right side). Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rounding errors in float position calculations can cause the ray to miss the correct voxel or enter the wrong one. The case where the direction is negative and no rounding error occurred (ngtvDirComps \land rightRnddComps) presents the same stepping problem as described in reference [6]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def correctvoxeltraversal(intposition, sidemax, pstvdir, ngtvdir, rightrndd): """ Corrects voxel position for rounding errors. Args: intposition: List[int, int, int] - Current voxel indices [i, j, k] sidemax: List[float, float, float] - Exit side indicators (signs) pstvdir: List[bool, bool, bool] - True if direction component is positive ngtvdir: List[bool, bool, bool] - True if direction component is negative rightrndd: List[bool, bool, bool] - True if rounding was correct Returns: List[int, int, int] - Corrected voxel indices """ # Calculate wrong rounding flags wrongrndd = [not r for r in rightrndd] # Calculate correction vector components # C = (pstvdir AND wrongrndd) OR (ngtvdir AND rightrndd) correction = [] for c in range(3): term1 = pstvdir[c] and wrongrndd[c] term2 = ngtvdir[c] and rightrndd[c] correction.append(term1 or term2) # Apply correction newposition = list(intposition) for c in range(3): if correction[c]: # Determine shift direction from sidemax sign # sidemax sign indicates the exit side, which aligns with the travel direction shift = 1 if sidemax[c] > 0 else -1 newposition[c] += shift return newposition Uses integer arithmetic to avoid floating-point errors entirely. Choose when precision is critical and direction is constant. The base method that this correction augments. Choose for general ray-voxel intersection. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel step, as the correction involves a constant number of logical operations and additions. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for flags and temporary vectors. Strengths: Corrects for floating-point inaccuracies that can lead to incorrect voxel stepping, ensuring robustness in ray traversal. Limitations: Requires tracking rounding status for each component, adding complexity to the traversal loop. When to use: When using floating-point position calculations in voxel traversal and precision errors are observed or suspected. The method is described in a thesis on raycasting-based voxel rendering. It addresses issues found in standard Bresenham-based traversal when implemented with floating-point arithmetic. name: Liu Extension of Bresenham
head: Bresenham Extension, LZY04, Liu Extension, Liu et al. Algorithm
body: The Liu Extension of Bresenham is a voxel traversal algorithm that extends the classic 2D Bresenham line algorithm to 3D grid traversal by detecting and visiting diagonal neighbors when the ray intersects a cell corner. Unlike standard Bresenham which visits only one neighbor per step, this method checks if the error exceeds a specific threshold to decide whether to visit both (x+1, y) and (x+1, y+1) in 2D, or the corresponding diagonal paths in 3D. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on a geometric intersection check against a derived threshold rather than simple integer error accumulation, offering performance advantages even on modern hardware where floating-point operations are efficient. Inputs: Ray origin (x0, y0, z0), ray direction (dx, dy, dz), and the starting voxel (x, y, z). Outputs: A sequence of voxel coordinates visited by the ray. Data Structures: Current voxel coordinates: (x, y, z) (integers). Error accumulator: e (floating-point or fixed-point). Slope: k = dx/dy (for 2D) or analogous slopes for 3D axes. Steps: 1. Determine the intersection point of the line with the two walls of the current cell. 2. Compute the error e, defined as the difference between the chosen integer cell boundary and the real coordinate of the line intersection. 3. Compare e against a threshold. Source defines the threshold as \frac{1}{2} - \frac{dy}{2dx}, while Source contains garbled text that has been interpreted as \frac{1}{2} - \frac{1}{2dx \times dy} or 2^{1/2} dx dy, which are likely transcription errors. 4. If e > \text{threshold}, visit both (x+1, y) and (x+1, y+1). Otherwise, proceed with the standard single-step traversal. 5. Thereafter, follow the standard Bresenham approach, adjusting the algorithm to integer arithmetic by accumulating the slope k = dx/dy and subtracting 1 when the error exceeds the threshold. 6. In the three-dimensional case, identify two possible paths from cell (x, y, z) to (x+1, y+1, z+1). The specific logic for selecting between these paths is not fully detailed in the provided text. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def liubresenham2d(x0, y0, x1, y1): """Liu Extension of Bresenham for 2D grid traversal. Assumes dx > 0, dy > 0.""" dx = x1 - x0 dy = y1 - y0 k = dx / dy threshold = 0.5 - (dy / (2.0 dx)) # Formula from x, y = x0, y0 yield (x, y) e = 0.0 # Initialization for in range(dx): e += k # Cumulative slope accumulation if e > threshold: yield (x + 1, y) yield (x + 1, y + 1) e -= 1.0 # Integer adjustment else: yield (x + 1, y) x += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Threshold Formula Disagreement: Sources and provide conflicting or garbled formulas for the threshold. Implementers should verify the correct threshold against the original [LZY04] paper. Negative Directions: The algorithm assumes positive direction components. Handling negative dx, dy, dz requires mirroring the coordinate system or adjusting the neighbor selection logic. 3D Complexity: The 3D extension is described vaguely as identifying two possible paths. Implementers must derive the specific 3D diagonal traversal logic, likely involving checks against multiple thresholds for the three axes. Performance: The Liu algorithm is reported to be faster than Zalik et al.'s code-based approach and even faster than standard Bresenham on modern processors, where floating-point arithmetic is nearly as efficient as integer arithmetic. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed, and memory complexity is constant, storing only current coordinates and error terms. Strengths: Efficient diagonal traversal without complex branching; leverages floating-point precision for threshold checks. Limitations: Ambiguity in the 3D extension details; potential precision issues if the threshold formula is misinterpreted. The Liu Extension of Bresenham was proposed by Liu et al. in [LZY04]. It is an efficient extension of Bresenham's algorithm designed for ray tracing and grid traversal. It addresses the limitation of standard Bresenham by explicitly handling diagonal cell visits when the ray intersects a cell corner, improving traversal accuracy and efficiency in certain scenarios. name: Zalik et al. Algorithm
head: ZCO97, Zalik et al. code-based traversal
body: The Zalik et al. algorithm is a voxel traversal method that corrects the topological incompleteness of standard 3D Bresenham tracing by ensuring all cells intersected by a ray are visited. It differs from its parent 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing by adding a post-processing phase to recover missed cells, whereas siblings like Integer-based Amanatides and Woo Voxel Traversal compute intersections analytically. Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D, grid dimensions, and the driving axis (e.g., x). Outputs: A sequence of voxel coordinates (x, y, z) representing all cells intersected by the ray. Data Structures: currentcell: Tuple (x, y, z) of integers. nextcell: Tuple (x', y', z') of integers. error: Floating-point value tracking the deviation of the ray from the integer grid line. Steps: 1. Bresenham Phase: Execute standard 3D Bresenham algorithm along the driving axis to generate a primary sequence of cells. At each step, the algorithm selects one adjacent cell (e.g., between (x+1, y) and (x+1, y+1)) based on the error term e compared against a threshold (typically 1/2). 2. Relationship Examination Phase: For every pair of successive cells ci and c{i+1} in the Bresenham sequence, examine their geometric relationship. 3. Recovery: If the ray passes through a corner or edge shared by multiple voxels, the standard Bresenham step may skip one or more valid cells. The algorithm identifies these missing cells by analyzing the coordinate differences between ci and c{i+1} and inserts them into the traversal sequence. 4. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-3 until the ray exits the grid. Pitfalls: The algorithm requires elaborate implementation logic to determine which cells are "missed" based on the relationship between successive cells. Higher traversal time compared to simpler methods due to the additional examination phase. Time Complexity: Higher than standard Bresenham due to the second phase of examining relationships between successive cells. Memory Complexity: Low, storing only current and next voxel coordinates. Strengths: Guarantees topological correctness by visiting all intersected cells, unlike standard Bresenham. Limitations: Elaborate implementation and increased computational overhead per step. When to use: When strict topological correctness is required and performance is secondary to completeness. When not to use: When performance is critical and minor topological errors are acceptable, or when using more efficient extensions like the Liu Extension. The algorithm was proposed by Zalik et al. in 1997 (ZCO97) to address the limitation of Bresenham's algorithm, which, when a driving axis is chosen, selects only one cell between adjacent options (e.g., (x+1, y) and (x+1, y+1)) and never both, thus missing cells traversed by the ray. It is part of the family of code-based traversal algorithms. name: BCC/FCC Ray Tracing
head: BCC/FCC Ray Tracing and Object Representation, Ray-tracing in BCC and FCC grids, Smooth Object Surface representation
body: BCC/FCC Ray Tracing is a volume rendering and object representation method that samples 3-D data on Body Centered Cubic (BCC) or Face Centered Cubic (FCC) grids instead of standard cubic grids. It solves topological defects inherent in cubic grids—specifically, the possibility of a ray passing through an object surface without intersecting any voxel—by utilizing grids with superior topological properties that guarantee closed surfaces and robust discrete curve/surface definitions. Unlike cubic grid methods such as 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing or Integer-based Amanatides and Woo Voxel Traversal, this approach defines voxels as Voronoi cells (Truncated Octahedra for BCC, Rhombic Dodecahedra for FCC) and traces rays by minimizing the cross-sectional area of the ray beam within these polyhedral structures. Inputs: 1. Volume Data: A 3-D signal sampled on a BCC or FCC grid, typically resampled from a standard cubic grid using a 3-D cubic B-Spline interpolator. 2. Smooth Surface Coefficients: A signed integer coefficient for each voxel in the transition region, representing the sub-voxel distance between the voxel center and the object boundary. Values range from -128 to 127, where positive values indicate interior voxels and negative values indicate exterior voxels. 3. Ray Definition: An origin point P and a direction vector \vec{PQ}. Outputs: 1. Rendered Image: A 2-D pixel array with lighting and antialiasing. 2. Traced Ray Path: A sequence of connected voxels representing the light beam. 1. Grid Topology The grid is defined by its Voronoi cells. Connectivity is strictly defined by common faces: Two voxels are connected if they share a common face. Two faces are connected if they share a common edge. Two edges are connected if they share a common vertex. Intersection at lower dimensions (m < n-1) does not imply connectivity. 2. Smooth Object Surface Representation Object Surface: The set of faces between object voxels and non-object voxels. Due to grid properties, every face in the object surface has exactly one face connected to each of its edges, ensuring the surface is always closed. Smooth Surface Coefficients: A signed integer c \in [-128, 127] assigned to each voxel in contact with the object surface. These coefficients are computed using an edge detector operator based on geometric moments to estimate sub-voxel distances. 3. Directional Regions All possible ray directions are partitioned into regions corresponding to the yard directions perpendicular to the faces of the Voronoi polyhedron. BCC Grid: 24 directional regions. FCC Grid: 20 directional regions. Each region is defined by a basis of three vectors \{\vec{A}, \vec{B}, \vec{C}\} corresponding to faces of the Voronoi polyhedron sharing a common vertex. These vectors span a triangular pyramid with its vertex at the polyhedron center. Step 1: Compute Smooth Surface Coefficients Apply an edge detector operator based on geometric moments to the volume data. This estimates the sub-voxel distance between the voxel center and the object boundary. Result: Signed integer coefficients c \in [-128, 127]. c > 0: Interior voxel. c < 0: Exterior voxel. Step 2: Determine Directional Region Given the ray direction vector \vec{d}, identify which of the 24 (BCC) or 20 (FCC) directional regions it falls into. This is analogous to finding the octant in Bresenham's algorithm but uses the yard directions perpendicular to the Voronoi faces. Step 3: Decompose Ray Vector Decompose the line vector \vec{PQ} components \{na, nb, nc\} in the basis \{\vec{A}, \vec{B}, \vec{C}\} of the identified region. Geometrically, this means that to go from P to Q, na steps must be performed in the \vec{A} direction, nb in \vec{B}, and nc in \vec{C}. Step 4: Trace the Ray (Minimize Rhombus Area) Trace the line by advancing from one voxel to the next, minimizing the area of the rhombus R (the rhombic base of the prism containing all line beam points). 1. Project the grid points onto a plane N orthogonal to the line \vec{PQ}. The projection consists of a set of 2-D grids shifted by a constant vector. 2. At each step, select the next voxel such that the area of the rhombus R formed by the current and next beam points is minimized. 3. Advance using only integer sums. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def bccfccraytracing(origin, direction, basisvectors, coefficients, bounds): """ Traces a ray through a BCC or FCC grid. Args: origin: tuple (x, y, z) representing point P direction: tuple (dx, dy, dz) representing vector PQ basisvectors: list of 3 tuples [(Ax, Ay, Az), (Bx, By, Bz), (Cx, Cy, Cz)] coefficients: 3D array of signed integers (-128 to 127) bounds: tuple ((minx, maxx), (miny, maxy), (minz, maxz)) Returns: List of voxel indices traversed by the ray """ A, B, C = basisvectors # Step 2 & 3: Decompose direction into basis coefficients # Solve direction = naA + nbB + ncC det = A[0](B[1]C[2] - B[2]C[1]) - A[1](B[0]C[2] - B[2]C[0]) + A[2](B[0]C[1] - B[1]C[0]) na = (direction[0](B[1]C[2] - B[2]C[1]) - direction[1](B[0]C[2] - B[2]C[0]) + direction[2](B[0]C[1] - B[1]C[0])) / det nb = (A[0](direction[1]C[2] - direction[2]C[1]) - A[1](direction[0]C[2] - direction[2]C[0]) + A[2](direction[0]C[1] - direction[1]C[0])) / det nc = (A[0](B[1]direction[2] - B[2]direction[1]) - A[1](B[0]direction[2] - B[2]direction[0]) + A[2](B[0]direction[1] - B[1]direction[0])) / det # Map origin to initial voxel index currentvoxel = (int(origin[0]), int(origin[1]), int(origin[2])) path = [currentvoxel] # Step 4: Trace the ray using integer sums # Track position in basis coordinate system x, y, z = 0, 0, 0 maxsteps = int(math.ceil(math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in direction)))) for in range(maxsteps): bestvoxel = None minarea = float('inf') # Evaluate candidates in basis directions candidates = [ (x + 1, y, z, A), (x, y + 1, z, B), (x, y, z + 1, C) ] for nx, ny, nz, stepvec in candidates: # Calculate rhombus area R for the step # The rhombus R is the rhombic base of the prism containing all line beam points. # Exact geometric formula for area minimization is not given in the sources. area = 0.0 nextvoxel = (currentvoxel[0] + stepvec[0], currentvoxel[1] + stepvec[1], currentvoxel[2] + stepvec[2]) if bounds[0][0] <= nextvoxel[0] <= bounds[0][1] and bounds[1][0] <= nextvoxel[1] <= bounds[1][1] and bounds[2][0] <= nextvoxel[2] <= bounds[2][1]: if area < minarea: minarea = area bestvoxel = nextvoxel x, y, z = nx, ny, nz if bestvoxel is None: break currentvoxel = bestvoxel path.append(currentvoxel) if not (bounds[0][0] <= currentvoxel[0] <= bounds[0][1] and bounds[1][0] <= currentvoxel[1] <= bounds[1][1] and bounds[2][0] <= currentvoxel[2] <= bounds[2][1]): break return path Coefficient Range: Signed integers from -128 to 127. Directional Regions: 24 for BCC, 20 for FCC. Precision: The algorithm uses only integer sums for advancement, avoiding floating-point accumulation errors during traversal. Degenerate Input: The method assumes the ray direction is not parallel to any basis vector face normal, which would make the decomposition ambiguous. The partitioning into regions handles this by assigning directions to specific pyramids. Resampling: The input volume must be resampled to the BCC/FCC grid. The source uses a 3-D cubic B-Spline interpolator, which duplicates the number of voxels compared to the original cubic grid. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The ray tracing step uses only integer sums, making it computationally efficient, similar to Bresenham's algorithm. Memory: The method reduces information by representing objects only by their external surfaces and smooth coefficients, potentially reducing memory usage compared to full volume storage. Measured Performance: Hardware: PC-Pentium 166MHz, Linux 2.0.18. Scene: Hip joint CT reconstruction, 100x100x100 voxels, resampled to BCC. Output: 256x256 pixels. Time: 3 seconds for ray tracing, lighting (one light source), and antialiasing. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Eliminates topological problems (rays passing through surfaces without touching) common in cubic grids. Allows robust definition of discrete curves and surfaces. Enables sub-voxel deformation by changing coefficients. Reduces aliasing effects. Limitations: Requires resampling from cubic to BCC/FCC, which increases voxel count (duplicates voxels). When to Use: When topological correctness is critical (e.g., medical imaging where missing a surface is unacceptable). When sub-voxel surface representation is needed for smooth rendering or collision detection. When computational resources allow for the overhead of resampling and basis decomposition. When Not to Use: For simple scenes where cubic grid topological defects are negligible or handled by thicker rays. When real-time performance on very low-end hardware is required and the overhead of BCC/FCC processing is prohibitive. Origin: The method was introduced by Luis Ibáñez, Chafia Hamitouche, and Christian Roux from ENST-Bretagne, France. History and Development: The paper describes a ray-tracing and object description method for objects sampled in BCC and FCC grids, which are well-known in crystallography. The use of these grids is motivated by their ability to reduce the density of samples needed to represent a signal without information loss (satisfying the Shannon theorem optimally with BCC) and their better topological properties compared to the cubic grid. Usage: The method is used as a ray casting engine in a direct volume rendering program for medical imaging, specifically for hip joint CT reconstruction data. name: Template-Based Volume Viewing
head: Template-Based Ray Tracing, Parallel Projection Template Method
body: Template-Based Volume Viewing is a ray-grid traversal technique for parallel projection that exploits inter-ray coherence by precomputing a single sequence of voxel increments (a template) and reusing it for all rays, thereby avoiding per-ray line algorithm activation. It solves the discretization errors and performance overhead inherent in naive per-ray traversal, where varying initial positions cause voxels to be skipped or visited multiple times. Unlike siblings that recompute traversal logic per ray, this method ensures all rays share the same form regardless of length, distributing discretization error uniformly. Inputs and Outputs Input: Volume data (typically binary for the discrete line approach), camera parameters defining a parallel projection, and the volume bounding box. Output: A rendered image where each pixel corresponds to a ray traversing the volume using the precomputed template. Data Structures Ray Template: A fixed sequence of integer increments (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) representing the path through the voxel grid. The size of the template is determined by the maximum extent of the volume in the chosen traversal direction. Base Plane: A 2D grid parallel to one of the volume faces, used to map screen pixels to the template indices. Algorithm Steps 1. Determine the Base Plane: Select a plane parallel to one of the volume faces (e.g., z=0 or z=Z{max}) to serve as the template placement surface. This guarantees a complete and uniform tessellation of the volume. 2. Compute Projection Extent: Calculate the size of the projection plane required to cover the volume from the parallel projection viewpoint. This determines the dimensions of the base plane grid. 3. Compute Parallel Ray Template: Generate a single 3D line-voxelization path using either a 6-line or 26-line algorithm. The 6-line algorithm visits more voxels (up to twice as many as the 26-line maximum). The 26-line algorithm visits fewer voxels and uniformly samples the space. Store the sequence of voxel increments (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) for this path. This step is performed once. 4. Ray Casting (Trace the Rays): For each pixel on the screen: Map the pixel coordinate to the corresponding position on the Base Plane. Retrieve the precomputed Ray Template. Traverse the volume by applying the template increments sequentially to the current voxel index. Accumulate color/opacity along the path. 5. 2D Mapping: Map the results from the Base Plane coordinates to the final screen plane coordinates. Formulas and Parameters Discrete vs. Continuous Line: The method supports discrete line tracing (constant interpolation) and continuous line tracing (multiple samples per voxel, higher-order interpolation). Data Type Constraint: The discrete line approach is valid only for binary data. Using synthetic object voxelization with the continuous approach may yield incorrect results. Round Error Handling: A critical pitfall is that the entry point to the volume is calculated in floating point, but the discrete line algorithm is activated from the initial integer point of the grid. The template-based approach mitigates this by ensuring all rays follow the same integer-based increment sequence, eliminating the need to reactivate the line algorithm for every ray. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def templatebasedvolumerendering(volume, cameraparams): # 1. Determine Base Plane # Select a face parallel to the projection direction. # Let the base plane be a 2D grid of size (W, H) corresponding to the image. baseplane = createbaseplane(cameraparams.imagewidth, cameraparams.imageheight) # 2. Compute Projection Extent # Determine the bounding box of the volume in the base plane's coordinate system. projectionextent = computeprojectionextent(volume.boundingbox, cameraparams) # 3. Compute Parallel Ray Template # Choose between 6-line or 26-line algorithm. # 26-line is preferred for fewer voxel visits and uniform sampling. traversalalgorithm = "26-line" template = computelinevoxelization(volume.boundingbox, traversalalgorithm) # template is a list of (dx, dy, dz) increments # 4. Ray Casting image = emptyimage(cameraparams.imagewidth, cameraparams.imageheight) for y in range(cameraparams.imageheight): for x in range(cameraparams.imagewidth): # Map pixel to base plane basepos = mappixeltobaseplane(x, y, baseplane, projectionextent) # Initialize ray state currentvoxel = basepos accumulatedcolor = (0, 0, 0, 0) # Trace using precomputed template for dx, dy, dz in template: # Apply increment currentvoxel = (currentvoxel.x + dx, currentvoxel.y + dy, currentvoxel.z + dz) # Check if voxel is within volume bounds if not isinsidevolume(currentvoxel, volume.boundingbox): break # Sample volume data density = volume.sample(currentvoxel) # Accumulate (simplified constant interpolation for discrete case) accumulatedcolor = accumulatecolor(accumulatedcolor, density) image.setpixel(x, y, accumulatedcolor) return image Uses integer arithmetic to avoid floating-point division per step but still computes traversal per ray. Choose when per-ray precision is needed without template overhead. Link Addresses precision issues in standard DDA. Choose when floating-point errors in entry points are critical. Link An extension of Bresenham's algorithm for 3D. Choose for specific line-drawing optimizations. Link Optimized voxel traversal. Choose for general-purpose high-performance traversal. Link Uses Body-Centered Cubic or Face-Centered Cubic lattices. Choose for better isotropic sampling. Link Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L), where N is the number of rays (pixels) and L is the length of the ray template (volume depth). The per-ray cost is reduced to simple addition and lookup. Memory Complexity: O(L) for storing the ray template. The base plane requires O(W \cdot H) memory. Performance: On average, this method is 2 times faster than using a standard 26-line algorithm. The performance gain grows with the number of rays traced. Strengths: Eliminates per-ray algorithm activation overhead; ensures uniform discretization error distribution; avoids skipping or double-visiting voxels caused by naive per-ray traversal. Limitations: Only applicable to parallel projection; discrete line approach is restricted to binary data; requires precomputation of the template. When to Use: Parallel projection volume rendering with large images where inter-ray coherence is high. When Not to Use: Perspective projection (rays are not parallel); non-binary data requiring continuous interpolation with the discrete line method (may yield wrong results). Template-Based Volume Viewing was developed by A. Kaeli et al. (noted as YaKa in source) and presented in 1998 as part of research on inter-ray coherency in volume rendering. It addresses the inefficiencies of naive ray casting by leveraging the redundancy in parallel ray paths. The method is a foundational technique in image-order rendering for parallel projections, preceding more advanced fast volume rendering techniques.
