name: Restartable DDA for Voxel Traversal
head: DdaState, Voxel Marcher
body: Restartable DDA for Voxel Traversal is a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm designed to traverse a 3D voxel grid while allowing the ray direction to be modified mid-walk, such as during refraction events. It solves the problem of maintaining traversal state consistency when a ray changes direction, enabling efficient volume transmission calculations without restarting the entire traversal from the original origin. It is distinct from standard Amanatides and Woo traversal by its explicit support for re-initializing the state structure with a new origin and direction while preserving the grid geometry context, and it differs from 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing by using floating-point distance calculations rather than integer arithmetic. The method operates by maintaining a state structure that tracks the current position, distance to the next voxel boundary on each axis, and the step direction. The algorithm consists of an initialization phase that computes these values based on the ray origin, direction, and grid bounds, and a stepping phase that advances the ray to the nearest boundary. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D, grid bounding box [B{min}, B{max}], voxel size C, grid dimensions N. Outputs: A boolean indicating success (hit) or failure (miss/out of bounds), and the updated DdaState structure. Data Structures: The core state is held in DdaState and GridDims: DdaState: d: float3 Normalized direction components. Clamped to magnitude 10^{-8} if near zero. idx: int3 Current voxel indices (i, j, k). stp: int3 Step direction per axis (1 or -1). tmax: float3 Distance to the next voxel boundary along each axis. tdelta: float3 Distance required to cross one voxel along each axis. tcur: float Current distance along the ray from the origin. axis: int The axis of the current traversal step (0, 1, or 2). enteraxis: int The axis of entry into the grid (-1 if not set). GridDims: bmin: float3 Bounding box minimum. bmax: float3 Bounding box maximum. cell: float3 Voxel dimensions per axis. dims: int3 Voxel count per axis. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (ddainit): 1. Set t{min} = 0.0, t{exit} = 10^{30}, enter\axis = -1. 2. For each axis a \in \{0, 1, 2\}: If |D[a]| < 10^{-8}, set D[a] = \text{sign}(D[a]) \times 10^{-8} (or 10^{-8} if D[a]=0). Calculate t0 = (B{min}[a] - O[a]) / D[a] and t1 = (B{max}[a] - O[a]) / D[a]. If t0 > t1, swap t0 and t1. If t0 > t{min}, set enter\axis = a. Update t{min} = \max(t{min}, t0). Update t{exit} = \min(t{exit}, t1). 3. If t{min} > t{exit}, return false (miss). 4. Calculate starting position: P = O + D \times (t{min} + 10^{-4}). 5. For each axis a \in \{0, 1, 2\}: idx[a] = \text{clamp}(\lfloor (P[a] - B{min}[a]) / C[a] \rfloor, 0, N[a] - 1). stp[a] = D[a] > 0 ? 1: -1. Calculate next boundary: Next = B{min}[a] + (idx[a] + (stp[a] > 0 ? 1: 0)) \times C[a]. t{max}[a] = (Next - O[a]) / D[a]. t{delta}[a] = C[a] / |D[a]|. 6. Set axis = enter\axis < 0 ? 1: enter\axis. 7. Set t{cur} = t{min}. 8. Return true. 2. Stepping (ddastep): 1. Determine the axis with the smallest t{max}: If t{max}[0] < t{max}[1]: If t{max}[0] < t{max}[2], axis = 0. Else, axis = 2. Else: If t{max}[1] < t{max}[2], axis = 1. Else, axis = 2. 2. Update t{cur} = t{max}[axis]. 3. Increment idx[axis] by stp[axis]. 4. If idx[axis] < 0 or idx[axis] \ge N[axis], return false (out of bounds). 5. Update t{max}[axis] += t{delta}[axis]. 6. Return true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddainit(origin, dir, bmin, bmax, cell, dims): tmin = 0.0 texit = 1e30 enteraxis = -1 d = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for a in range(3): if abs(dir[a]) < 1e-8: d[a] = 1e-8 if dir[a] >= 0 else -1e-8 else: d[a] = dir[a] for a in range(3): t0 = (bmin[a] - origin[a]) / d[a] t1 = (bmax[a] - origin[a]) / d[a] if t0 > t1: t0, t1 = t1, t0 if t0 > tmin: enteraxis = a tmin = max(tmin, t0) texit = min(texit, t1) if tmin > texit: return False, None pos = [origin[a] + d[a] (tmin + 1e-4) for a in range(3)] state = { 'd': d, 'idx': [0, 0, 0], 'stp': [0, 0, 0], 'tmax': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'tdelta': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'tcur': tmin, 'axis': 1, 'enteraxis': enteraxis } for a in range(3): idxval = int((pos[a] - bmin[a]) / cell[a]) idxval = max(0, min(idxval, dims[a] - 1)) state['idx'][a] = idxval state['stp'][a] = 1 if d[a] > 0.0 else -1 nextval = bmin[a] + (idxval + (1 if state['stp'][a] > 0 else 0)) cell[a] state['tmax'][a] = (nextval - origin[a]) / d[a] state['tdelta'][a] = cell[a] / abs(d[a]) if state['enteraxis'] < 0: state['axis'] = 1 else: state['axis'] = state['enteraxis'] return True, state def ddastep(state, dims): tmax = state['tmax'] if tmax[0] < tmax[1]: if tmax[0] < tmax[2]: axis = 0 else: axis = 2 else: if tmax[1] < tmax[2]: axis = 1 else: axis = 2 state['axis'] = axis state['tcur'] = tmax[axis] state['idx'][axis] += state['stp'][axis] if state['idx'][axis] < 0 or state['idx'][axis] >= dims[axis]: return False state['tmax'][axis] += state['tdelta'][axis] return True Parameters and Edge Cases: Epsilon: A small value 10^{-4} is added to t{min} when calculating the initial position to ensure the ray starts strictly inside the first voxel, avoiding boundary precision issues. Direction Clamping: Direction components near zero are clamped to \pm 10^{-8} to prevent division by zero in t{max} calculations. Degenerate Direction: If the new ray direction becomes degenerate (e.g., after refraction, if \dot{rdir, rdir} < 10^{-6}), the algorithm falls back to the original direction. Restartability: The method allows re-initialization with a new origin and direction (e.g., at a refraction surface) by calling ddainit again, while reusing the grid parameters. A three-phase rendering technique for simulating light interaction with a voxel-based water surface and volume. It is distinct from full volumetric path tracing by using a deterministic ray-marching approach optimized for voxel grids, relying on Restartable DDA for Voxel Traversal to handle the change in ray direction at the surface. Time Complexity: O(1) per step for ddastep. Initialization is O(1) (constant number of arithmetic operations). Total time is proportional to the number of voxels traversed. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for the DdaState structure. Strengths: Efficient for sparse and dense voxel grids; supports mid-traversal direction changes (refraction); robust against degenerate rays and boundary cases. Limitations: Floating-point precision issues may arise for very large grids or very small voxels if not handled carefully (mitigated by epsilon and clamping). When to use: Ideal for volumetric rendering involving refraction, transmission, or any scenario where ray direction changes within the volume. When not to use: Not suitable for integer-only environments or when exact integer arithmetic is required (use 3D Bresenham Voxel Tracing instead). The Restartable DDA for Voxel Traversal is derived from the Amanatides and Woo algorithm but extended to support state restartability for refraction. It is used in the "Voxel Ocean" project for rendering transparent, refractive water over complex terrain, where it handles the transmission phase of light through the water volume. The implementation is found in the vox-ocean repository. wlim33/vox-ocean, https://github.com/wlim33/vox-ocean, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Water Refraction and Transmission
head: Phase 1-3 Water March, See-through water marcher
body: A three-phase rendering technique for simulating light interaction with a voxel-based water surface and volume. It solves the problem of rendering transparent, refractive water over a complex terrain by marching a ray from the camera to the surface, calculating surface reflections and refraction, and then transmitting light through the water volume to the background. It is distinct from full volumetric path tracing by using a deterministic ray-marching approach optimized for voxel grids, relying on Restartable DDA for Voxel Traversal to handle the change in ray direction at the surface. Inputs: Camera position (org) and direction (dir) for the current pixel. Inverse view-projection matrix (U.inv\view\proj) for ray origin reconstruction. Voxel grid description (vg) including extent, cell sizes, and bounds. Sky cube map (sky\cube) for environment reflection. Material data structure (vg) for reading voxel contents. Parameters: U.water\ior (Index of Refraction), U.depth\fog\density, U.extinction\rgb, U.deep\water\color, U.max\steps. Outputs: Final pixel color (color) after tonemapping. Data Structures: DdaState W: State structure for the DDA traversal, containing current voxel index (W.idx), current distance along ray (W.t\cur), ray direction (W.d), and the axis of the current voxel face (W.axis). This structure is re-initialized in Phase 2. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization (Camera to Surface): Construct the ray origin and direction. For perspective projection, the origin is the camera position. For orthographic projection, the origin is backed up beyond the grid AABB. p0 = U.inv\view\proj \cdot [ndcx, ndcy, 0.0, 1.0]^T p1 = U.inv\view\proj \cdot [ndcx, ndcy, 1.0, 1.0]^T near\pt = p0.xyz / p0.w dir = normalize(p1.xyz / p1.w - near\pt) org = \begin{cases} U.camera\pos & \text{if } U.ortho\backup == 0 \\ near\pt - dir \cdot U.ortho\backup & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 2. Phase 1: Surface Entry: March the ray from org along dir using the DDA until the first non-air/water cell is found. Let the entry point be entry\p and the entry axis be entry\axis. 3. Phase 2: Surface Interaction: Calculate the surface normal n{entry} based on the entry axis. Calculate the view vector V from the entry point to the camera. V = normalize(org - entry\p) Calculate Fresnel reflectance F using the Schlick approximation: nv = \max(dot(n{entry}, V), 0.0) F = 0.02 + 0.98 \cdot (1.0 - nv)^5 Calculate the reflection ray R: R = reflect(-V, n{entry}) Sample the sky cube for the reflection color, adding sun specular highlights: reflection = sky\cube.sample(R).rgb + U.sun\color \cdot \max(dot(R, sun), 0.0)^{U.sun\shininess} Calculate the refracted ray direction rdir: rdir = refract(dir, n{entry}, 1.0 / U.water\ior) Guard against degenerate refraction (total internal reflection or grazing angles): \text{if } dot(rdir, rdir) < 10^{-6} \text{ then } rdir = dir rdir = normalize(rdir) Re-initialize the DDA state W with the entry point (offset slightly along rdir to avoid self-intersection) and the refracted direction: walking = dda\init(W, entry\p + rdir \cdot 10^{-4}, rdir, G) 4. Phase 3: Volume Transmission: Initialize water\dist = 0.0, end\mat = MAT\AIR, end\axis = 1, and exited\up = false. Loop while walking and steps < U.max\steps: 1. Increment steps. 2. Read material m at W.idx. 3. If m is not MAT\AIR, MAT\WATER, or MAT\BUBBLE: Set end\mat = m, end\axis = W.axis. Break loop. 4. Record t\enter = W.t\cur. 5. Step the DDA: alive = dda\step(W, G). 6. If m == MAT\WATER: water\dist += W.t\cur - t\enter. 7. If not alive: Set exited\up = (rdir.y > 0.0). Break loop. 5. Special Material Handling: If end\mat is MAT\FISH, MAT\FIRE, or MAT\LAVA, render the material opaque and unattenuated by the water path or surface reflection. Fish: Return tonemapped terrain color for fish. Fire: Return tonemapped palette color multiplied by 3.0. Lava: Return tonemapped palette color multiplied by 1.25. 6. Background and Attenuation: Determine the background color bg behind the water: If end\mat \neq MAT\AIR: bg = terrain\color(end\mat, face\normal(end\axis, W.d), sun, U). Else if exited\up: bg = sky\cube.sample(cube\smp, rdir).rgb. Else: bg = U.deep\water\color. Apply Beer-Lambert transmission: T = \exp(-U.depth\fog\density \cdot water\dist \cdot U.extinction\rgb) refr = bg \cdot T + U.deep\water\color \cdot (1.0 - T) 7. Final Composition: Mix the refracted and reflected colors based on Fresnel reflectance: color = mix(refr, reflection, F) Apply ACES tonemapping and return. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MATAIR = 0 MATWATER = 1 MATBUBBLE = 2 MATFISH = 3 MATFIRE = 4 MATLAVA = 5 def ddainit(startpos, direction, grid): # Initialize Amanatides-Woo DDA state W = {} W['idx'] = [int((startpos[i] - grid['bmin'][i]) / grid['cell'][i]) for i in range(3)] W['tcur'] = 0.0 W['d'] = direction W['step'] = [1 if direction[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] W['tmax'] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] W['tstep'] = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): if direction[i] != 0: # Distance to next grid boundary boundary = grid['bmin'][i] + (W['idx'][i] + 1) grid['cell'][i] if direction[i] > 0 else grid['bmin'][i] + W['idx'][i] grid['cell'][i] W['tmax'][i] = (boundary - startpos[i]) / direction[i] W['tstep'][i] = grid['cell'][i] / abs(direction[i]) else: W['tmax'][i] = float('inf') W['tstep'][i] = float('inf') W['axis'] = -1 return W def ddastep(W, grid): # Advance DDA to next voxel if W['tmax'][0] < W['tmax'][1] and W['tmax'][0] < W['tmax'][2]: axis = 0 elif W['tmax'][1] < W['tmax'][2]: axis = 1 else: axis = 2 W['idx'][axis] += W['step'][axis] W['tcur'] = W['tmax'][axis] W['tmax'][axis] += W['tstep'][axis] W['axis'] = axis # Check bounds against grid dimensions if (W['idx'][0] < grid['bminidx'][0] or W['idx'][0] >= grid['bmaxidx'][0] or W['idx'][1] < grid['bminidx'][1] or W['idx'][1] >= grid['bmaxidx'][1] or W['idx'][2] < grid['bminidx'][2] or W['idx'][2] >= grid['bmaxidx'][2]): return False return True def readmaterial(vg, idx): # Read material ID from voxel grid at index return vg.materials[idx[0], idx[1], idx[2]] def marchtosurface(org, dir, vg, G, maxsteps): # Phase 1: March from camera to first non-air/water cell W = ddainit(org, dir, G) steps = 0 while steps < maxsteps: m = readmaterial(vg, W['idx']) if m != MATAIR and m != MATWATER: return [org[i] + dir[i] W['tcur'] for i in range(3)], W['axis'] alive = ddastep(W, G) if not alive: break steps += 1 return org, 1 def getsurfacenormal(axis): # Returns axis-aligned normal n = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] n[axis] = 1.0 return n def voxelwaterrefraction(ndc, invviewproj, camerapos, orthobackup, skycube, vg, G, U, sun): # 1. Ray Initialization p0 = invviewproj [ndc.x, ndc.y, 0.0, 1.0] p1 = invviewproj [ndc.x, ndc.y, 1.0, 1.0] nearpt = [p0[0]/p0[3], p0[1]/p0[3], p0[2]/p0[3]] dir = normalize([p1[0]/p1[3] - nearpt[0], p1[1]/p1[3] - nearpt[1], p1[2]/p1[3] - nearpt[2]]) if orthobackup == 0: org = camerapos else: org = [nearpt[i] - dir[i] orthobackup for i in range(3)] # Phase 1: March to surface entryp, entryaxis = marchtosurface(org, dir, vg, G, U.maxsteps) # Phase 2: Surface Interaction nentry = getsurfacenormal(entryaxis) V = normalize([org[i] - entryp[i] for i in range(3)]) nv = max(dot(nentry, V), 0.0) F = 0.02 + 0.98 pow(1.0 - nv, 5.0) R = reflect([-V[i] for i in range(3)], nentry) reflection = skycube.sample(R).rgb + \ U.suncolor pow(max(dot(R, sun), 0.0), U.sunshininess) rdir = refract(dir, nentry, 1.0 / U.waterior) if dot(rdir, rdir) < 1e-6: rdir = dir rdir = normalize(rdir) # Re-initialize DDA for refraction W = ddainit([entryp[i] + rdir[i] 1e-4 for i in range(3)], rdir, G) walking = True steps = 0 waterdist = 0.0 endmat = MATAIR endaxis = 1 exitedup = False # Phase 3: Volume Transmission while walking and steps < U.maxsteps: steps += 1 m = readmaterial(vg, W['idx']) if m != MATAIR and m != MATWATER and m != MATBUBBLE: endmat = m endaxis = W['axis'] break tenter = W['tcur'] alive = ddastep(W, G) if m == MATWATER: waterdist += W['tcur'] - tenter if not alive: exitedup = rdir[1] > 0.0 break # Special Materials if endmat == MATFISH: return acestonemap(terraincolor(MATFISH, facenormal(endaxis, W['d']), sun, U)) if endmat == MATFIRE: return acestonemap(U.palette[MATFIRE] 3.0) if endmat == MATLAVA: return acestonemap(U.palette[MATLAVA] 1.25) # Background if endmat != MATAIR: bg = terraincolor(endmat, facenormal(endaxis, W['d']), sun, U) elif exitedup: bg = skycube.sample(rdir).rgb else: bg = U.deepwatercolor # Beer-Lambert T = [exp(-U.depthfogdensity waterdist U.extinctionrgb[i]) for i in range(3)] refr = [bg[i] T[i] + U.deepwatercolor[i] (1.0 - T[i]) for i in range(3)] color = [refr[i] (1.0 - F) + reflection[i] F for i in range(3)] return acestonemap(color) Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed in the water volume and the distance to the surface. Bounded by U.max\steps. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), aside from the voxel grid storage. Strengths: Efficiently handles refraction and reflection in a single pass without recursive ray tracing. Correctly handles complex terrain occlusion behind the water. Limitations: Does not simulate subsurface scattering or multiple bounces within the water. Accuracy depends on voxel resolution. When to use: Real-time rendering of voxel-based water bodies where performance is critical and full volumetric path tracing is too expensive. Originating from the "Vox-Ocean" project by wlim33, this method implements a specialized water rendering pipeline for voxel dioramas. It combines standard ray-marching techniques with specific optimizations for voxel grids, such as the restartable DDA for handling refraction. name: Naive Voxel Ray Traversal
head: Fixed-step raycast, Naive Voxel Raycasting, RLV Rendering, Ray Line Voxelization, Ray marching on voxel data, Raymarching Voxel Rendering, Step-based voxel raycasting, Voxel Ray Tracing
body: Naive Voxel Ray Traversal is a brute-force method for rendering voxel data by stepping a ray forward in fixed increments along its direction vector, checking for occupied voxels at each step. It solves the problem of determining which voxels a ray intersects without transforming volumetric data into triangle meshes, allowing for high fidelity (smaller voxel sizes) without the performance cost of rendering thousands of triangles. Unlike Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal, which calculates exact voxel boundary crossings, this method uses a constant step size, making it simple to implement but prone to missing voxels and aliasing artifacts. Inputs: rayorigin: 3D vector (Ox, Oy, Oz), typically the camera position. raydirection: 3D vector (Dx, Dy, Dz), normalized. voxelgrid: 3D array or sparse structure storing voxel states (empty/filled or color data). voxelsize: Fixed step size \Delta t (often equal to the physical size of a voxel in world units). maxdistance: Maximum ray length before termination. Outputs: Pixel color: Color of the first non-empty voxel hit, or background color if no hit occurs within maxdistance. Data Structures: The voxel grid is accessed via integer coordinates (i, j, k). Continuous ray positions are mapped to grid indices using rounding or flooring. A common mapping is i = \lfloor x + 0.5 \rfloor, which maps continuous coordinates to the nearest integer grid center. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: Set current position pos to rayorigin. Set hit flag to false. Set temp (distance traveled) to 0. 2. Loop: While temp < maxdistance: a. Query Voxel: Convert pos to integer voxel coordinates (i, j, k). Check if the voxel at (i, j, k) is occupied. b. Check Hit: If the voxel is occupied: Set hit to true. Record the hit position and voxel data. Break the loop. c. Advance Ray: Update pos by adding raydirection voxelsize. Increment temp by voxelsize. 3. Termination: If the loop completes without a hit, the ray has exited the grid or reached maxdistance. 4. Output: If hit is true, set pixel color to the voxel's color. Otherwise, set pixel color to the background color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def naivevoxeltraverse(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, voxelsize, maxdistance): pos = rayorigin temp = 0.0 hitvoxel = None while temp < maxdistance: # Map continuous position to integer voxel coordinates # Using floor(pos + 0.5) to round to nearest voxel center ix = floor(pos.x + 0.5) iy = floor(pos.y + 0.5) iz = floor(pos.z + 0.5) # Query voxel occupancy voxel = voxelgrid.get(ix, iy, iz) if voxel is not None and voxel.isfilled(): hitvoxel = voxel break # Advance ray by fixed step pos = pos + raydirection voxelsize temp = temp + voxelsize if hitvoxel is not None: return hitvoxel.color else: return backgroundcolor Parameters: voxelsize: The fixed step size. Often set to the physical size of a voxel in the grid. In some implementations, a smaller step like 0.1f is used to reduce tunneling, though this increases iteration count. maxdistance: Maximum ray length in world units. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tunneling/Missing Voxels: The method can completely miss voxels that the ray should intersect, especially if the step size is large relative to the voxel size or if the ray passes through corners. Decreasing the step size reduces this risk but does not eliminate it and significantly increases computation time. Aliasing Artifacts: Fixed-step sampling causes visible aliasing artifacts because the sampling points are not aligned with the voxel grid boundaries. Double Processing: Some voxels may be processed twice due to the stepping logic and coordinate rounding. Performance: The method processes many empty voxels even if the ray does not hit anything, wasting computation. An optimization that tracks object identifiers during traversal to skip redundant intersection tests for the same object. During traversal, a rayID is assigned or checked for each voxel to record which objects have already been tested, ensuring each object is intersected at most once per ray. Its effectiveness scales with grid subdivision level, as higher subdivision causes objects to cover more voxels, increasing the probability of repeated visits. In test scenes with high object counts, it can reduce ray intersections significantly (e.g., from 6.6 to 3.8 per ray). A compromise approach where sampling occurs only when the ray intersects voxel boundaries (faces in 3D, edges in 2D). It attempts to balance speed and accuracy. In 2D, 1 interpolation is necessary per sample; in 3D, 3 interpolations are necessary per sample (e.g., along Y, then Y again, then X). Pitfalls include unequal sampling distances, which can lead to clusters of samples very close together, causing extra computation without improving visual quality, and lower accuracy compared to regular sampling due to uneven spacing. It is faster than regular sampling but less accurate, and more accurate than nearest neighbor but slower. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of voxels along the ray path per pixel. Performance is generally unacceptable for real-time without optimization. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel grid storage. Naive traversal itself uses constant extra memory. Measured Performance: Rendering a 80x80x100 voxel grid (640k total voxels) at 700x444 resolution takes approximately 20 seconds per frame on an AMD Phenom II X6 @ 3.4 GHz using a single thread. Strengths: Simple to implement; does not require complex data structures like octrees for basic traversal; renders only visible voxels, avoiding CPU-GPU transfer overhead compared to geometry shader approaches. Unlike triangle mesh rendering, the number of rays remains constant per pixel regardless of voxel resolution. Limitations: Prone to tunneling and aliasing artifacts; inefficient for sparse grids as it processes empty space; performance degrades quickly with multiple rays per pixel (shadows, AO). When to Use: Educational purposes, simple voxel rendering, or as a baseline for comparison. Not suitable for real-time applications with high-resolution voxel grids without significant optimizations. When Not to Use: When high fidelity and artifact-free rendering are required, or when performance is critical. Naive Voxel Ray Traversal is one of the earliest and simplest methods for rendering voxel data. It is often cited in early game development forums and tutorials as a starting point for voxel rendering before more efficient algorithms like Amanatides-Woo are introduced. The method is discussed in the context of "Ray Line Voxelization" (RLV) and is compared to other ray traversal techniques such as Regular Sampling and Nearest Neighbor. It highlights the fundamental trade-off between implementation simplicity and rendering accuracy/performance in voxel-based graphics. name: DDA Skip
head: DDA Skip Kernel, Skipping DDA
body: DDA Skip is a ray-sampling kernel that bypasses all leading empty voxels in a sparse grid before initiating the standard marching process through occupied regions. It is distinguished from its sibling DDA Branch by deferring occupancy checks until an occupied voxel is guaranteed to be found, rather than branching per voxel. This method is adopted by Instant-NGP. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, near plane t{min}, far plane t{max}, sparse grid G (occupancy map), and step size \Delta t. Outputs: List of sample points buf along the ray within [t{min}, t{max}] where G is occupied. Data Structures: buf: List of floats (sample distances t). t{last}: Float, current sampling position, initialized to t{min}. ijk: Integer triplet, current voxel coordinates. t0, t1: Floats, entry and exit distances of the current voxel along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddaskip(ray, tmin, tmax, grid, deltat): buf = [] tlast = tmin while tlast <= tmax: t1 = tmin while True: ijk, t0, t1 = ddastep(ray, t1) # Advances DDA state to next voxel boundary if grid.at(ijk): break while tlast <= t0: tlast += deltat while tlast <= t1: buf.append(tlast) tlast += deltat return buf Parameters: \Delta t: Step size. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Floating-point errors may cause discrepancies in rendering results compared to other samplers. If the ray never hits an occupied voxel, the inner repeat loop may run indefinitely or until t{max} is exceeded depending on implementation bounds. Performance: DDA Skip performs poorly with standard DDA, offering no speedup or even slowing down rendering. However, when combined with VDB grids and Hierarchical DDA (HDDA), it renders faster than the baseline. Strengths: Reduces computational overhead in threads when using hierarchical structures like VDB. Limitations: Ineffective with dense or standard DDA traversals. DDA Skip was introduced in the context of accelerating occupancy grid-based NeRF rendering. It is specifically adopted by Instant-NGP. The method contrasts with "DDA Branch" (used in NerfAcc), which synchronizes traversal and branches based on occupancy per voxel. name: Occupancy-aware DDA Traversal
head: Active Voxel DDA, Branching DDA, DDA Branch, DDA Branch Kernel, Occupancy-based DDA
body: Occupancy-aware DDA Traversal is a ray-sampling kernel variant that traverses a voxel grid using standard Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) logic but branches execution based on the occupancy status of each visited voxel. Unlike sibling methods that skip empty space entirely (e.g., DDA Skip), this method synchronizes traversal across all workers and processes every voxel, conditionally recording samples only for active voxels while advancing time for inactive ones. It is primarily adopted in the NerfAcc library for accelerating occupancy grid-based NeRF rendering. The method builds on Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal by using a standard DDA or Hierarchical DDA (HDDA) analyzer to determine voxel intervals, then branching execution based on occupancy. The core distinction is that the traversal interval [t0, t1] for the current voxel is determined first, and then the algorithm iterates through this interval, checking occupancy at each step. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin o, ray direction d, near plane t{min}, far plane t{max}, voxel size, grid origin, and a voxel grid data structure supporting an occupancy query grid.at(ijk) which returns a boolean. Outputs: A buffer buf containing a list of sample positions t along the ray. Data Structures: buf: A dynamic list or array of floats storing sample distances t. grid: A dense or VDB grid structure. The source specifies grid.at(ijk) returns whether the voxel at index ijk is occupied. Analyzer: A helper function (DDA or HDDA) that returns the voxel index ijk and the entry/exit t-values [t0, t1] for the next voxel intersected by the ray starting from a given t. Parameters: \Delta t: The step size for sampling within a voxel. The source notes a "linearly increasing stepsize" for specific datasets like Mip-NeRF 360, but the algorithm structure uses a constant \Delta t per iteration. t{last}: The current position along the ray, initialized to t{min}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize buf as an empty list. 2. Set t{last} \leftarrow t{min}. 3. While t{last} \le t{max}: a. Call Analyzer(ray, tlast) to obtain the current voxel index ijk and the interval [t0, t1] where the ray is inside this voxel. b. Pre-voxel gap: While t{last} \le t0: i. t{last} \leftarrow t{last} + \Delta t. c. Voxel traversal: While t{last} \le t1: i. Check occupancy: isactive = grid.at(ijk). ii. If isactive is true: 1. Append t{last} to buf. iii. t{last} \leftarrow t{last} + \Delta t. 4. Return buf. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddabranch(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, voxelsize, gridorigin, gridat, dt): """ Occupancy-aware DDA Traversal. Args: rayo: Ray origin (3,) rayd: Ray direction (3,) tmin: Near plane distance tmax: Far plane distance voxelsize: Uniform voxel edge length gridorigin: World-space origin of the voxel grid gridat: Function returning boolean occupancy for voxel index ijk dt: Step size for sampling Returns: buf: List of sample distances t """ buf = [] tlast = tmin while tlast <= tmax: # Compute current voxel index and entry/exit t-values (Amanatides-Woo step) ijk = tuple(int((rayo[i] + rayd[i] tlast - gridorigin[i]) / voxelsize) for i in range(3)) t0 = tlast t1 = tmax for axis in range(3): if rayd[axis] > 0: t0 = max(t0, (gridorigin[axis] + ijk[axis] voxelsize - rayo[axis]) / rayd[axis]) t1 = min(t1, (gridorigin[axis] + (ijk[axis] + 1) voxelsize - rayo[axis]) / rayd[axis]) elif rayd[axis] < 0: t0 = max(t0, (gridorigin[axis] + (ijk[axis] + 1) voxelsize - rayo[axis]) / rayd[axis]) t1 = min(t1, (gridorigin[axis] + ijk[axis] voxelsize - rayo[axis]) / rayd[axis]) else: t0 = max(t0, tlast) t1 = min(t1, tlast) # Advance tlast to enter the current voxel while tlast <= t0: tlast += dt # Traverse inside the current voxel while tlast <= t1: if gridat(ijk): buf.append(tlast) tlast += dt return buf Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The source does not specify floating-point precision handling. Implementers should ensure t{last} comparisons are robust against floating-point drift, especially when \Delta t is small. Empty Voxels: Unlike DDA Skip, this method does not skip empty voxels. It iterates through them, performing the occupancy check and advancing t{last} without recording samples. Multi-resolution: When using multi-resolution VDB grids (e.g., for Mip-NeRF 360), the Analyzer must prioritize finer voxels if multiple voxels are intersected at the same time. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The method synchronizes traversal across all workers, which can be beneficial for GPU parallelism but may cause divergence if occupancy is highly irregular. Strengths: Simple integration with existing DDA/HDDA analyzers; consistent synchronization across threads. Limitations: Processes every voxel regardless of occupancy, branching execution to record samples only for active voxels. The method was introduced in the supplementary material of "Plug-and-Play Acceleration of Occupancy Grid-based NeRF Rendering using VDB Grid and Hierarchical Ray Traversal". It is named "DDA branch" to distinguish it from "DDA skip" (used by InstantNGP) and is adopted by the NerfAcc library. The approach leverages standard DDA or Hierarchical DDA (HDDA) as the underlying analyzer. name: Voxel Raymarching with DDA and Bounding Box Culling
head: Voxel Raymarching, Voxel Raymarching with DDA
body: Voxel Raymarching with DDA and Bounding Box Culling is an image-order rendering technique for sparse, segmented voxel models. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large voxel volumes by treating the model as a bounding box mesh where the fragment shader ignores the geometry and instead casts a ray from the eye through the pixel. The ray intersects the box analytically to find the entry point, then steps through the voxel grid using Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal until it finds a non-empty voxel or leaves the box. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly decoupling the ray origin from the box surface intersection to avoid floating-point boundary errors, and by using a segment directory to manage sparse 3D texture arrays. Inputs: Voxel Data: A sparse voxel model split into 128×128×128 voxel segments (bricks). Each segment is stored as an R8 3D texture (one byte per voxel, holding a palette index). Segment Directory: A 2D texture listing active segments. Each entry contains the segment's 3D grid coordinates (X, Y, Z) and its index in the bound texture array. Palette: A 256×1 RGBA8 texture mapping palette indices to colors. Camera State: Eye offset, screen UV, projection matrix, view matrix, and inverse model matrix. Bounding Box: boxcenter (Vector3) and boxsize (Vector3) defining the volume in voxel space. Lighting: lightposition in voxel space. Outputs: Albedo: The color of the first hit voxel, lit by the point light. Depth: The depth of the hit voxel surface in clip space. Segment Brick Textures: An array of Texture3D objects. Each texture is 128³ voxels, R8 format. The array order matches the directory entries. Segment Directory: A 2D texture where each texel i stores (segX, segY, segZ, textureSlot) as floats. The textureSlot is the index into the segmentvoxels array. Palette Texture: 256×1 RGBA8. Colors are stored as uint 0xRRGGBBAA, reversed to 0xAABBGGRR so little-endian memory bytes are R, G, B, A. Read as sRGB in the shader. Bounding Box Uniforms: boxcenter and boxsize passed to the shader. 1. Compute Per-Eye Ray Origin and Direction: Transform EYEOFFSET (per-eye offset in midpoint view space) to world space: \text{camera\world} = (\text{INV\VIEW\MATRIX} \times \text{vec4}(\text{EYE\OFFSET}, 1.0)).\text{xyz} Unproject SCREENUV through the inverse projection matrix into view space, normalize the vector from EYEOFFSET to the unprojected point, then transform direction to world space: \text{view\frag} = \text{INV\PROJECTION\MATRIX} \times \text{vec4}(\text{SCREEN\UV} \times 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) \text{view\frag} /= \text{view\frag}.w \text{ray\dir\view} = \text{normalize}(\text{view\frag}.xyz - \text{EYE\OFFSET}) \text{ray\world\dir} = \text{normalize}((\text{INV\VIEW\MATRIX} \times \text{vec4}(\text{ray\dir\view}, 0.0)).xyz) Transform ray origin and direction to voxel space using the inverse model matrix: \text{camera\voxel} = (\text{inv\model\matrix} \times \text{vec4}(\text{camera\world}, 1.0)).xyz + \text{box\center} \text{ray\dir} = \text{normalize}((\text{inv\model\matrix} \times \text{vec4}(\text{ray\world\dir}, 0.0)).xyz) Compute box bounds in voxel space: \text{box\min} = \text{box\center} - \text{box\size} \times 0.5 \text{box\max} = \text{box\center} + \text{box\size} \times 0.5 2. March Through the Box: Perform a ray-AABB slab test to find the entry point tentry and exit point texit of the ray with the bounding box. If the ray misses the box, discard the pixel. Start DDA traversal from the entry point. The traversal steps through voxels along the ray path. For each voxel visited, sample the corresponding 3D texture from the segmentvoxels array using the segment directory to find the correct texture index. If a non-empty voxel (palette index > 0) is found, record the hit position, normal, and material ID. If the ray exits the box without finding a non-empty voxel, discard the pixel. 3. Compute Lighting: Calculate point light lighting with 30% ambient and 70% diffuse: \text{to\light} = \text{normalize}(\text{light\position} - \text{hit\pos}) \text{lighting} = \max(\text{dot}(\text{normal}, \text{to\light}), 0.0) \times 0.7 + 0.3 Clamp back-facing normals to 0. 4. Output Albedo: Retrieve the palette color by material index: \text{ALBEDO} = \text{get\material\color}(\text{material}) \times \text{lighting} 5. Write Depth: Transform hitpos from voxel space to mesh-local (subtract boxcenter), then to world (MODELMATRIX), then to clip space (PROJECTIONMATRIX VIEWMATRIX), and write normalized depth: \text{hit\clip} = \text{PROJECTION\MATRIX} \times \text{VIEW\MATRIX} \times \text{MODEL\MATRIX} \times \text{vec4}(\text{hit\pos} - \text{box\center}, 1.0) \text{DEPTH} = \text{hit\clip}.z / \text{hit\clip}.w Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. fragmentshader(SCREENUV, EYEOFFSET, INVPROJECTIONMATRIX, INVVIEWMATRIX, MODELMATRIX, INVMODELMATRIX, PROJECTIONMATRIX, boxcenter, boxsize, segmentdirectory, segmentvoxels, palette, lightposition): # 1. Compute Per-Eye Ray Origin and Direction cameraworld = (INVVIEWMATRIX vec4(EYEOFFSET, 1.0)).xyz viewfrag = INVPROJECTIONMATRIX vec4(SCREENUV 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) viewfrag = viewfrag / viewfrag.w raydirview = normalize(viewfrag.xyz - EYEOFFSET) rayworlddir = normalize((INVVIEWMATRIX vec4(raydirview, 0.0)).xyz) cameravoxel = (INVMODELMATRIX vec4(cameraworld, 1.0)).xyz + boxcenter raydir = normalize((INVMODELMATRIX vec4(rayworlddir, 0.0)).xyz) boxmin = boxcenter - boxsize 0.5 boxmax = boxcenter + boxsize 0.5 # 2. March Through the Box tentry, texit, normal, hitpos, materialid = marchbox(cameravoxel, raydir, boxmin, boxmax, segmentdirectory, segmentvoxels) if materialid == 0: discard # Miss # 3. Compute Lighting tolight = normalize(lightposition - hitpos) lighting = max(dot(normal, tolight), 0.0) 0.7 + 0.3 # 4. Output Albedo albedo = getmaterialcolor(materialid, palette) lighting # 5. Write Depth hitclip = PROJECTIONMATRIX VIEWMATRIX MODELMATRIX vec4(hitpos - boxcenter, 1.0) depth = hitclip.z / hitclip.w return albedo, depth marchbox(origin, raydir, boxmin, boxmax, segmentdirectory, segmentvoxels): # Ray-AABB Slab Test invraydir = 1.0 / raydir t0 = (boxmin - origin) invraydir t1 = (boxmax - origin) invraydir tnear = max(max(min(t0.x, t1.x), min(t0.y, t1.y)), min(t0.z, t1.z)) tfar = min(min(max(t0.x, t1.x), max(t0.y, t1.y)), max(t0.z, t1.z)) if tnear > tfar or tfar < 0: return 0, 0, vec3(0), vec3(0), 0 # Miss # Start DDA at tnear currentpos = origin + raydir tnear currentvoxel = floor(currentpos) # DDA Step Calculation stepx = sign(raydir.x) stepy = sign(raydir.y) stepz = sign(raydir.z) tmaxx = (boxmin.x if stepx < 0 else boxmax.x - currentvoxel.x) / raydir.x tmaxy = (boxmin.y if stepy < 0 else boxmax.y - currentvoxel.y) / raydir.y tmaxz = (boxmin.z if stepz < 0 else boxmax.z - currentvoxel.z) / raydir.z tdeltax = abs(1.0 / raydir.x) tdeltay = abs(1.0 / raydir.y) tdeltaz = abs(1.0 / raydir.z) while tnear <= tfar: # Sample voxel segmentid = getsegmentid(currentvoxel) textureindex = gettextureindex(segmentid, segmentdirectory) if textureindex != -1: voxeldata = texelFetch(segmentvoxels[textureindex], currentvoxel % 128).r if voxeldata > 0: # Hit found hitpos = origin + raydir tnear normal = computenormal(currentvoxel, hitpos, raydir) return tnear, tfar, normal, hitpos, voxeldata # Advance DDA if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: currentvoxel.x += stepx tnear += tdeltax tmaxx += tdeltax else: currentvoxel.z += stepz tnear += tdeltaz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: currentvoxel.y += stepy tnear += tdeltay tmaxy += tdeltay else: currentvoxel.z += stepz tnear += tdeltaz tmaxz += tdeltaz # Check bounds if not insidebox(currentvoxel, boxmin, boxmax): break return 0, 0, vec3(0), vec3(0), 0 # Miss getsegmentid(voxel): # Voxel coordinates are Z-up (MagicaVoxel) # Segment grid coordinates are multiplied by 128 X = voxel.x >> 7 Y = voxel.z >> 7 # Note: Z-up storage, Y-up world conversion handled in CPU Z = voxel.y >> 7 return (X << 18) | (Y << 9) | Z gettextureindex(segmentid, directory): # Directory is a 2D texture, segmentid maps to a specific texel # Return the texture slot stored in the directory pass # Implementation depends on directory layout computenormal(voxel, hitpos, raydir): # Approximate normal based on which face was entered pass # Implementation details not fully specified in sources insidebox(voxel, boxmin, boxmax): return all(voxel >= boxmin) and all(voxel <= boxmax) Segment Size: 128×128×128 voxels per segment. View Distance: Camera positioned at 2.5 times the model's largest dimension from the model center. Light Position: Default vec3(50.0, 50.0, 25.0) in voxel space. Inv Model Matrix: Inverse of the MeshInstance's GlobalTransform, precomputed on the CPU every frame. Bounds Update: When model bounds change, the bounding box mesh size and position must be updated, and shader uniforms boxcenter and boxsize must be refreshed. Otherwise, rays will start in the wrong place. Ray Origin Precision: Starting the ray at the interpolated box-surface position causes fuzzy faces, wrong first-hit lighting, and vanishing faces for faces at coordinate 0 due to floor() boundary float errors. This is solved by intersecting the ray with the box analytically and clamping the origin just inside it. Depth Buffer: Without writing depth at the hit voxel surface, the depth buffer holds the depth of the box's back face. This causes other geometry to intersect the model as if it were a solid box, and in VR the OpenXR compositor uses depth for reprojection, warping a flat box as a plane and canceling per-eye parallax. Coordinate Systems: Voxel data uses Z-up (MagicaVoxel). Godot uses Y-up. C# code converts voxel coordinates (x, y, z)zup to world coordinates (x, z, y)yup. The shader converts back when reading voxels. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels traversed along the ray. The DDA traversal is efficient for sparse volumes as it skips empty space. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active segments. Each segment is a 128³ R8 texture (2 MB). The directory texture is small. Strengths: Efficient for sparse voxel models. Avoids floating-point boundary errors by using analytical ray-box intersection. Works well in VR due to correct depth writing. Limitations: Requires precomputed inverse model matrix. Performance depends on the density of the voxel model. When to Use: Sparse voxel models with large empty spaces. VR applications requiring correct depth for reprojection. When Not to Use: Dense voxel models where ray traversal becomes expensive. Models with frequent dynamic changes requiring frequent bound updates. This method is implemented in the Voxel2Pixel graphics library by Ben McLean. It is designed for use in Godot Engine for rendering voxel models in VR and desktop environments. The method builds on the Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal algorithm for efficient ray traversal through voxel grids. name: 3D Bresenham Voxel Traversal
head: 3D Bresenham Algorithm, 3D Digital Differential Analyzer, CW88, Cleary and Wyvill Algorithm, Integer Ray Stepping, Three-Dimensional Digital Difference Analyzer
body: 3D Bresenham Voxel Traversal is a discrete line algorithm used to determine the sequence of integer voxel coordinates intersected by a line segment in a 3D grid. It rasterizes a line between two integer coordinates by iterating along the dominant axis and updating the other two axes based on accumulated error terms. It differs from its parent DDA and siblings like Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal by operating entirely in integer arithmetic rather than floating-point plane intersections, making it computationally lighter but topologically distinct: it does not consider every block the ray passes through, skipping those where the ray does not get close enough to the block center. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Start voxel coordinates (xi, yi, zi), end voxel coordinates (xf, yf, zf), and implicitly the grid structure. Output: A sequence of integer voxel coordinates (x, y, z) representing the voxels traversed by the line segment. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains the following state variables: x, y, z: Current voxel coordinates (integers). dx, dy, dz: Absolute differences in coordinates (|xf - xi|, etc.). xinc, yinc, zinc: Step directions (1 if xf > xi, else -1). ey, ez: Error terms (used in the Liu-Cheng variant). c1, c2: Accumulator terms (used in the accumulator variant). Numbered Steps: The algorithm determines the sequence of crossing types by comparing distances to the next wall crossings. Two equivalent integer implementations exist: the accumulator method (handles any dominant axis) and the Liu-Cheng error-term method (requires a dominant axis assumption). 1. Initialization: Set current position: x = xi, y = yi, z = zi. Calculate absolute differences: dx = |xf - xi|, dy = |yf - yi|, dz = |zf - zi|. Determine step directions: xinc = \text{sign}(xf - xi), yinc = \text{sign}(yf - yi), zinc = \text{sign}(zf - zi). Process the starting voxel (x, y, z). 2. Iteration (Accumulator Variant): The loop structure depends on the dominant axis. Case 1: X is dominant (dx \ge dy and dx \ge dz): 1. Initialize error accumulators: c1 = \lfloor dx / 2 \rfloor, c2 = \lfloor dx / 2 \rfloor. 2. Loop i from 1 to dx: 1. Increment x by xinc. 2. Add dy to c1. If c1 \ge dx, subtract dx from c1 and increment y by yinc. 3. Add dz to c2. If c2 \ge dx, subtract dx from c2 and increment z by zinc. 4. Process voxel (x, y, z). Case 2: Y is dominant (dy \ge dx and dy \ge dz): 1. Initialize error accumulators: c1 = \lfloor dy / 2 \rfloor, c2 = \lfloor dy / 2 \rfloor. 2. Loop i from 1 to dy: 1. Increment y by yinc. 2. Add dx to c1. If c1 \ge dy, subtract dy from c1 and increment x by xinc. 3. Add dz to c2. If c2 \ge dy, subtract dy from c2 and increment z by zinc. 4. Process voxel (x, y, z). Case 3: Z is dominant (dz \ge dx and dz \ge dy): 1. Initialize error accumulators: c1 = \lfloor dz / 2 \rfloor, c2 = \lfloor dz / 2 \rfloor. 2. Loop i from 1 to dz: 1. Increment z by zinc. 2. Add dy to c1. If c1 \ge dz, subtract dz from c1 and increment y by yinc. 3. Add dx to c2. If c2 \ge dz, subtract dz from c2 and increment x by xinc. 4. Process voxel (x, y, z). Liu-Cheng Variant (Integer Error Terms): An alternative formulation by Liu and Cheng assumes \Delta X \geq \Delta Y \geq 0 and \Delta X \geq \Delta Z \geq 0 (X is dominant). It uses explicit error terms ey and ez. 1. Initialization: ey = 2\Delta Y - \Delta X. ez = 2\Delta Z - \Delta X. x = X0, y = Y0, z = Z0. 2. Loop: While x \leq X1 (or x \neq X1 for negative direction): 1. Set voxel at (x, y, z). 2. Increment x by 1. 3. If ey \geq 0: Increment y by 1. Update ey = ey + 2(\Delta Y - \Delta X). Else: Update ey = ey + 2\Delta Y. 4. If ez \geq 0: Increment z by 1. Update ez = ez + 2(\Delta Z - \Delta X). Else: Update ez = ez + 2\Delta Z. Pseudocode (Accumulator Variant): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bresenham3daccumulator(xi, yi, zi, xf, yf, zf): dx = abs(xf - xi) dy = abs(yf - yi) dz = abs(zf - zi) xinc = 1 if xf > xi else -1 yinc = 1 if yf > yi else -1 zinc = 1 if zf > zi else -1 x, y, z = xi, yi, zi # Process start voxel # Process voxel (x, y, z) if dx >= dy and dx >= dz: c1 = c2 = dx // 2 for in range(dx): x += xinc c1 += dy if c1 >= dx: c1 -= dx y += yinc c2 += dz if c2 >= dx: c2 -= dx z += zinc # Process voxel (x, y, z) elif dy >= dx and dy >= dz: c1 = c2 = dy // 2 for in range(dy): y += yinc c1 += dx if c1 >= dy: c1 -= dy x += xinc c2 += dz if c2 >= dy: c2 -= dy z += zinc # Process voxel (x, y, z) else: c1 = c2 = dz // 2 for in range(dz): z += zinc c1 += dy if c1 >= dz: c1 -= dz y += yinc c2 += dx if c2 >= dz: c2 -= dz x += xinc # Process voxel (x, y, z) Parameters: Grid Resolution: Implicitly defined by the integer coordinates. Connectivity: Standard Bresenham produces 18- or 26-connected lines. For strict 6-connectivity, see Integer Bresenham Voxelization with 6-Connectivity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missed Voxels: The algorithm may miss blocks that the ray barely passes through, specifically those where the ray does not get close enough to the block center. For example, a block 3rd down and 3rd right from the top-left corner in a reference diagram is passed through by the line but not hit by Bresenham's algorithm. Dominant Axis Assumption: The Liu-Cheng variant requires the dominant axis to be X. If this is not the case, the axes must be permuted, or the accumulator-based method should be used. Generates a 6-connected sequence of integer voxel coordinates intersected by a line segment, ensuring that every consecutive pair of voxels shares a face. It solves the connectivity gap in standard Bresenham algorithms, which may skip voxels or produce 18/26-connected lines, making it essential for applications requiring strict topological continuity such as interior filling of triangles in scanline voxelization. It differs from 26-connected traversal by being slower but more accurate for small features. Line drawing algorithms where lines are symmetric around the center, allowing drawing two symmetric pixels at a time. The traversal algorithm starts from the midpoint (pixel) and goes through the two outermost points, or vice versa, starts from outermost pixels and goes through the midpoint. Performance: Significantly reduces positional computation time compared to floating-point methods but sacrifices grid flexibility. Grid Requirements: Requires the ray's origin and destination points to be located exactly at the center of volume cells. Requires all grid cells to have constant length along each axis direction; cells need not be cubic but must be uniform per axis. Cannot be applied to arbitrary or irregular grids; strictly requires pre-constrained, regularly spaced input data. Strengths: Extremely fast, no floating-point operations (in the integer variant), low memory footprint. Limitations: Does not guarantee visiting every voxel the ray physically intersects (topological incompleteness compared to DDA/Amanatides-Woo). Produces 18- or 26-connected lines by default, which may be undesirable for certain rendering or voxelization tasks requiring 6-connectivity. When to use: Suitable for simple voxel games or when approximate traversal is acceptable. When not to use: When strict topological continuity (6-connectivity) is required, or when the ray must visit every voxel it touches (e.g., precise volume rendering where missing a thin voxel causes artifacts). In such cases, use Amanatides-Woo Voxel Traversal or Integer Bresenham Voxelization with 6-Connectivity. The 3D Bresenham algorithm is an extension of Bresenham's line algorithm, originally developed for 2D rasterization. The 3D version presented by Liu and Cheng follows the original Bresenham algorithm closely, introducing a second error term to handle the third dimension. It is widely used in voxel-based games and simple 3D rasterization tasks due to its integer-only arithmetic. name: Integer Bresenham Voxelization with 6-Connectivity
head: 6-Connected Bresenham Algorithm Modification, 6-connected Bresenham, Discrete Ray Traversal, Modified Bresenham
body: This method generates a 6-connected sequence of integer voxel coordinates intersected by a line segment, ensuring that every consecutive pair of voxels shares a face. It solves the connectivity gap in standard Bresenham algorithms, which may skip voxels or produce 18/26-connected lines, making it essential for applications requiring strict topological continuity such as interior filling of triangles in scanline voxelization. It differs from 26-connected traversal by being slower but more accurate for small features. Inputs: Start voxel (X0, Y0, Z0), end voxel (X1, Y1, Z1), and a callback or iterator interface SetVoxel(voxel). Outputs: A sequence of voxels visited along the line. Data Structures: dx, dy, dz: Absolute differences |X1 - X0|, |Y1 - Y0|, |Z1 - Z0|. sx, sy, sz: Step directions (1 or -1) for each axis; 0 if the difference is zero. A: Index of the dominant axis (0 for X, 1 for Y, 2 for Z). i1, i2: Indices of the secondary axes, calculated as (A + 1) \pmod 3 and (A + 2) \pmod 3. e1, e2: Error accumulators for the secondary axes. C: Array of current voxel coordinates [x, y, z]. D: Array of absolute differences [dx, dy, dz]. S: Array of step signs [sx, sy, sz]. Parameters: Typical values are derived directly from input coordinates. No fixed constants are used other than 2 and 3 in modulo arithmetic. Steps: 1. Initialization: Calculate absolute differences: \Delta X = |X1 - X0|, \Delta Y = |Y1 - Y0|, \Delta Z = |Z1 - Z0|. Determine step signs: sx = \text{sign}(X1 - X0), sy = \text{sign}(Y1 - Y0), sz = \text{sign}(Z1 - Z0). Determine dominant axis A: A = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \Delta X \ge \Delta Y \text{ and } \Delta X \ge \Delta Z \\ 1 & \text{if } \Delta Y > \Delta X \text{ and } \Delta Y \ge \Delta Z \\ 2 & \text{if } \Delta Z > \Delta X \text{ and } \Delta Z > \Delta Y \end{cases} Calculate secondary indices: i1 = (A + 1) \pmod 3, i2 = (A + 2) \pmod 3. Map values to arrays for uniform access: D = [\Delta X, \Delta Y, \Delta Z], S = [sx, sy, sz], C = [X0, Y0, Z0]. Initialize error terms for secondary axes using standard 2D Bresenham logic adapted for 3D: e1 = 2 D[i1] - D[A], e2 = 2 D[i2] - D[A]. Set current coordinates C[0]=X0, C[1]=Y0, C[2]=Z0. 2. Iteration: Yield the starting voxel (X0, Y0, Z0). Iterate along the dominant axis A until the current coordinate equals the target coordinate. In each iteration, increment the dominant axis coordinate by its step sign. Check the error condition for the first secondary axis i1: If e1 \ge 0: If e1 \ge D[i1], yield the voxel with the secondary axis i1 incremented: (C[0], C[1], C[2]) with C[i1] + S[i1]. Otherwise, yield the current voxel (C[0], C[1], C[2]). Increment the secondary axis coordinate C[i1] += S[i1]. Update error: e1 = e1 + 2(D[i1] - D[A]). Else: Update error: e1 = e1 + 2 D[i1]. Check the error condition for the second secondary axis i2 using the same logic as for i1. The algorithm may generate up to three voxels per dominant axis iteration, requiring an iterator or buffer to handle multiple outputs per step. 3. Termination: After the loop, explicitly yield the final voxel at (X1, Y1, Z1) to resolve the pitfall where the loop condition misses the last voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def integerbresenham6connected(x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1): dx = abs(x1 - x0) dy = abs(y1 - y0) dz = abs(z1 - z0) sx = 1 if x1 > x0 else (-1 if x1 < x0 else 0) sy = 1 if y1 > y0 else (-1 if y1 < y0 else 0) sz = 1 if z1 > z0 else (-1 if z1 < z0 else 0) if dx >= dy and dx >= dz: A = 0 elif dy >= dx and dy >= dz: A = 1 else: A = 2 i1 = (A + 1) % 3 i2 = (A + 2) % 3 D = [dx, dy, dz] S = [sx, sy, sz] C = [x0, y0, z0] e1 = 2 D[i1] - D[A] e2 = 2 D[i2] - D[A] target = [x1, y1, z1][A] yield tuple(C) while C[A] != target: C[A] += S[A] if e1 >= 0: if e1 >= D[i1]: voxel = list(C) voxel[i1] += S[i1] yield tuple(voxel) C[i1] += S[i1] e1 += 2 (D[i1] - D[A]) else: yield tuple(C) C[i1] += S[i1] e1 += 2 (D[i1] - D[A]) else: e1 += 2 D[i1] if e2 >= 0: if e2 >= D[i2]: voxel = list(C) voxel[i2] += S[i2] yield tuple(voxel) C[i2] += S[i2] e2 += 2 (D[i2] - D[A]) else: yield tuple(C) C[i2] += S[i2] e2 += 2 (D[i2] - D[A]) else: e2 += 2 D[i2] yield tuple(C) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Last Voxel: The loop condition C[A] != target excludes the final voxel. It must be explicitly appended after the loop. Multiple Voxels: The algorithm can generate up to three voxels per dominant axis iteration. This conflicts with algorithms expecting a single next voxel. Implementers must use an iterator or buffer to handle this. Negative Directions: Handled by absolute differences and sign variables. Zero Difference: If a difference is zero, the step is 0, and the axis does not change. The error term logic still applies but will not trigger steps if the dominant axis is not that axis. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the length of the line in the dominant axis. Each iteration performs constant work, but may emit up to 3 voxels. Memory Complexity: O(1) if implemented as an iterator/generator. O(V) if storing all voxels, where V is the number of voxels (up to 3N). Performance: Slower than 26-connected traversal due to stricter connectivity checks and potential multiple emissions per step. Strengths: Guarantees 6-connectivity, ensuring no gaps in voxelized lines. Essential for filling interiors of triangles. Limitations: More complex to implement than standard Bresenham. Requires handling multiple outputs per step. The algorithm originates from a thesis on optimal scanline voxelization algorithms. It was developed to address the lack of 6-connectivity in standard 3D Bresenham algorithms, which are insufficient for filling triangle interiors in integer-based voxelization. The modification adapts the classic Bresenham line algorithm to 3D and enforces face-sharing connectivity between consecutive voxels. A Comparison of Optimal Scanline Voxelization Algorithms, https://liu.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:1459330/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Chapter 7 - Advanced Computer Graphics - VTK, https://examples.vtk.org/site/VTKBook/07Chapter7/, fetched 2026-10-29 (book)

name: Amanatides–Woo grid traversal
head: Line walk traversal on extended grid lines, traverseGridSegmentFloat
body:
This method traverses the grid cells intersected by a line segment defined by two points, calling a visitor function for each cell in traversal order. It solves the problem of efficiently determining the sequence of axis-aligned grid cells crossed by a ray or segment, which is a fundamental step in volume rendering and ray tracing. Unlike the original Amanatides–Woo voxel traversal which is optimized for large 3D grids with high initialization costs, this specific 2D floating-point variant is designed for small grids (e.g., 2x2 cells) where its logic is adapted to minimize overhead. It builds on DDA by using a Digital Differential Analyzer approach to step through cells based on distance to grid boundaries. Inputs: start: A 2D point (start.x, start.y) representing the beginning of the line segment. end: A 2D point (end.x, end.y) representing the end of the line segment. visitor: A callable object with a method visit(int, int) that is invoked for each traversed cell (x, y). Outputs: The visitor.visit function is called for every grid cell intersected by the segment, in the order they are encountered from start to end. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required for the core traversal loop. The algorithm uses scalar variables for coordinates, deltas, and t-max values. Note: A related conceptual approach for small grids involves a 4x4 array of areas where each entry stores delimiting lines for north, east, south, and west sides, but the standard floating-point implementation described here uses direct arithmetic. Parameters: FLFLTMAX: A large floating-point constant representing infinity, used when a component of the direction vector is zero to prevent division by zero. Steps: 1. Compute Initial Cell Coordinates: Determine the grid cell indices containing the start and end points: x0 = \lfloor start.x floor, \quad y0 = \lfloor start.y floor x1 = \lfloor end.x floor, \quad y1 = \lfloor end.y floor 2. Compute Step Directions: Determine the direction of traversal along each axis: stepX =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } x1 > x0 \ -1 & 	ext{if } x1 < x0 \ 0 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} stepY =  egin{cases} 1 & 	ext{if } y1 > y0 \ -1 & 	ext{if } y1 < y0 \ 0 & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} 3. Compute Direction Deltas: Calculate the total displacement of the segment: dx = end.x - start.x dy = end.y - start.y 4. Compute T-Deltas (Inverse Step Size): Calculate the change in parameter t required to cross one grid cell in each direction. If the direction component is zero, the t-delta is set to infinity: tDeltaX =  egin{cases} \left|  rac{1}{dx} ight| & 	ext{if } dx 
eq 0 \ FL\FLT\MAX & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} tDeltaY =  egin{cases} \left|  rac{1}{dy} ight| & 	ext{if } dy 
eq 0 \ FL\FLT\MAX & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} 5. Compute Next Intersection Coordinates: Determine the coordinate of the next grid boundary to cross in each direction. If stepping positively, the next boundary is the integer immediately following the start coordinate; otherwise, it is the integer at the start coordinate (assuming the start is not exactly on an integer boundary, or handling the degenerate case where step=0): nextX =  egin{cases} \lfloor start.x floor + 1 & 	ext{if } stepX > 0 \ \lfloor start.x floor & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} nextY =  egin{cases} \lfloor start.y floor + 1 & 	ext{if } stepY > 0 \ \lfloor start.y floor & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} 6. Compute Initial T-Max Values: Calculate the parameter t at which the ray first intersects the next grid boundary in each direction. If the direction component is zero, the t-max is infinity: tMaxX =  egin{cases} \left|  rac{nextX - start.x}{dx} ight| & 	ext{if } dx 
eq 0 \ FL\FLT\MAX & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} tMaxY =  egin{cases} \left|  rac{nextY - start.y}{dy} ight| & 	ext{if } dy 
eq 0 \ FL\FLT\MAX & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} 7. Initialize Loop State: Set the maximum valid t to 1.0 (the end of the segment). Initialize current cell coordinates to the start cell: maxT = 1.0 currentX = x0 currentY = y0 8. Traversal Loop: Repeat the following steps until the end of the segment is reached: a. Call visitor.visit(currentX, currentY). b. Find the minimum t-max: t = \min(tMaxX, tMaxY). c. If t > maxT, break the loop. d. If tMaxX < tMaxY: Increment tMaxX by tDeltaX: tMaxX \leftarrow tMaxX + tDeltaX. Increment currentX by stepX: currentX \leftarrow currentX + stepX. e. Else (if tMaxY \le tMaxX): Increment tMaxY by tDeltaY: tMaxY \leftarrow tMaxY + tDeltaY. Increment currentY by stepY: currentY \leftarrow currentY + stepY. 9. Final Cell Check: After the loop, if the current cell is not the end cell (x1, y1), explicitly visit the end cell to ensure it is included: If currentX 
eq x1 or currentY 
eq y1, call visitor.visit(x1, y1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversegridsegmentfloat(startx, starty, endx, endy, visitor): # 1. Compute Initial Cell Coordinates x0 = floor(startx) y0 = floor(starty) x1 = floor(endx) y1 = floor(endy) # 2. Compute Step Directions if x1 > x0: stepx = 1 elif x1 < x0: stepx = -1 else: stepx = 0 if y1 > y0: stepy = 1 elif y1 < y0: stepy = -1 else: stepy = 0 # 3. Compute Direction Deltas dx = endx - startx dy = endy - starty # 4. Compute T-Deltas if dx != 0.0: tdeltax = abs(1.0 / dx) else: tdeltax = FLFLTMAX if dy != 0.0: tdeltay = abs(1.0 / dy) else: tdeltay = FLFLTMAX # 5. Compute Next Intersection Coordinates if stepx > 0: nextx = floor(startx) + 1 else: nextx = floor(startx) if stepy > 0: nexty = floor(starty) + 1 else: nexty = floor(starty) # 6. Compute Initial T-Max Values if dx != 0.0: tmaxx = abs((nextx - startx) / dx) else: tmaxx = FLFLTMAX if dy != 0.0: tmaxy = abs((nexty - starty) / dy) else: tmaxy = FLFLTMAX # 7. Initialize Loop State maxt = 1.0 currentx = x0 currenty = y0 # 8. Traversal Loop while True: visitor.visit(currentx, currenty) t = min(tmaxx, tmaxy) if t > maxt: break if tmaxx < tmaxy: tmaxx += tdeltax currentx += stepx else: tmaxy += tdeltay currenty += stepy # 9. Final Cell Check if currentx != x1 or currenty != y1: visitor.visit(x1, y1) FLFLTMAX should be defined as a sufficiently large float (e.g., 1e30 or float('inf')) to represent infinity. floor returns the largest integer less than or equal to the argument. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Component: If dx=0 or dy=0, the corresponding t-delta and t-max are set to infinity to prevent division by zero and ensure the loop only steps in the non-zero direction. End Cell Inclusion: The loop may terminate before visiting the final cell (x1, y1) if the segment ends exactly at a boundary or if the t-max logic skips the last step. The explicit check at the end ensures the end cell is always visited. Degenerate Segment: If start equals end, dx=0 and dy=0. The loop will visit the start cell once and then break, as tMaxX and tMaxY are infinity, and t > maxT will be false initially? No, if dx=0, tMaxX = \infty. t = \min(\infty, \infty) = \infty. If maxT=1.0, t > maxT is true, so it breaks after visiting the start cell. This is correct behavior for a point segment. Implements the algorithm using 32-bit signed integers with 8 fractional bits (Q24.8) to improve performance and avoid floating-point precision issues. Compiles the per-ray traversal logic into a tight loop using Numba, eliminating global ray state array overhead. Extends the 2D DDA to calculate Z-coordinates for culling in 2.5D height-field representations. Applies the traversal logic to a logical height map for exact, deterministic picking in 2D grid-based environments. Time Complexity: The traversal time is proportional to the number of cells intersected by the segment. Each step involves constant-time arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as only scalar variables are used. Performance: The floating-point variant is efficient for general use. However, for small grids (e.g., 2x2), the initialization cost of the general Amanatides–Woo algorithm is considered high, making this specific optimized variant or fixed-point variants more suitable. Strengths: Simple implementation, no complex data structures, handles arbitrary segment directions. Limitations: Floating-point precision issues may arise in specific hardware or with very large coordinates; fixed-point variants are preferred in such cases. The Amanatides–Woo algorithm was originally introduced for voxel traversal in ray tracing. The specific 2D floating-point variant described here is implemented in libraries such as FastLED for grid traversal tasks. It is a standard technique in computer graphics for accelerating ray-grid intersection tests. Fast axis aligned cell traversal algorithm, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/13700625, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) FastLED: fl/traversegrid.h Source File, https://fastled.io/docs/d9/d42/traversegrid8hsource.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)
