name: HDDA Iterator Reorganization
head: HDDAActiveValueIterator, HDDAIterators, HDDALeafVoxelIterator
body: A reorganization of Hierarchical Data-Driven Approach (HDDA) iterators that separates the traversal of all active values from the traversal of only leaf voxels, enabling tile-skipping for leaf-specific operations. It sets itself apart from its parent VolumeHDDA by providing a specialized leaf-only traversal path that avoids processing active coarse tiles, addressing the latent mis-indexing bugs that occurred when callers assumed the previous single iterator yielded only leaf voxels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical grid structure containing active values at various node levels (coarse tiles and leaf voxels). Output: A sequence of coordinates and values. HDDAActiveValueIterator yields all active values (tiles and leaves); HDDALeafVoxelIterator yields only active leaf voxels. Data Structures: Both iterators are aliases over a single implementation class: HDDAValueIteratorImpl<AccT, ScalarT, bool LeafOnly>. AccT: Accessor type. ScalarT: Scalar value type. LeafOnly: A compile-time boolean gate. When LeafOnly is false, the iterator yields all active values (including coarse tiles). When LeafOnly is true, the iterator skips active tiles. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an instance of HDDAValueIteratorImpl with LeafOnly set to false for HDDAActiveValueIterator or true for HDDALeafVoxelIterator. 2. Traversal Loop: Iterate using the ++ operator. 3. Level Re-alignment (nextVoxel): Use a bounded for (pass < 3) level-realign loop instead of three unrolled getDim/level-update passes. This collapses to a single descent in the common level-aligned case. 4. Segment Advancement (nextSegment): Use predicated TimeSpan setters instead of an if/else ladder. Only the "active region ended" condition remains a real branch, reducing warp divergence. 5. Yielding: If LeafOnly is true, check if the current node is a leaf (getDim == 1). If it is a coarse tile (getDim > 1), skip it in a single coarse HDDA step. If LeafOnly is false, yield the current active value regardless of node level. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class HDDAValueIteratorImpl: def init(self, grid, leafonly: bool): self.grid = grid self.leafonly = leafonly self.currentnode = grid.beginactivevalue() # Standard iterator initialization self.passcount = 0 def iter(self): return self def next(self): while self.currentnode is not None: # nextVoxel optimization: bounded level-realign loop self.passcount = 0 while self.passcount < 3: if self.currentnode.levelisaligned(): # Checks if current node level matches expected traversal level break self.currentnode.realignlevel() # Moves up or down the tree to align levels self.passcount += 1 currentdim = self.currentnode.getDim() # LeafOnly gate: skips active coarse tiles in a single coarse HDDA step if self.leafonly and currentdim > 1: self.currentnode = self.currentnode.next() # Advances to next active value continue # Yield active value (tile or leaf) yield self.currentnode.getCoord(), self.currentnode.getValue() # nextSegment optimization: predicated TimeSpan setters # Only "active region ended" remains a real branch self.currentnode = self.currentnode.next() # Advances to next segment/voxel Parameters: LeafOnly: Compile-time boolean. true for leaf-only traversal, false for all active values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Mis-indexing on tile-bearing grids: Previously, callers indexing per-leaf-voxel buffers (like gridScalars) walked tiles they never needed, causing latent mis-indexing. The leaf iterator fixes this by skipping tiles entirely. Warp Divergence: The nextSegment optimization reduces divergence by using predicated setters, but the "active region ended" break remains a branch. OpenVDB provides two distinct iterators: one for traversing tree topology nodes (internal and leaf nodes) and one for traversing all value-carrying elements (active/inactive voxels and tiles). The node iterator (cbeginNode) traverses the tree structure, while the value iterator (cbeginValueAll) traverses all values, including implicitly allocated tile nodes. Using cbeginValueAll for visualization can lead to dense point clouds that misrepresent the actual sparse data density because it includes inactive values and tiles. The HDDAActiveValueIterator and HDDALeafVoxelIterator are specialized for active values only, aligning more closely with the value iterator's intent but optimized for ray-marching. Performance: The leaf-only iterator provides a significant performance lever for ray-marching kernels like rayimplicitintersection by skipping active coarse tiles, which are not needed for leaf-specific operations. Strengths: Eliminates latent mis-indexing bugs; reduces warp divergence in nextSegment; simplifies caller code by separating tile and leaf traversal. Limitations: Requires compile-time specialization (LeafOnly); not suitable for operations that need to process coarse tiles. The reorganization was inspired by Efty's 'branchless getValue' work in NanoVDB and aimed to apply similar principles to the ray-marching kernels in OpenVDB. It was introduced in the rayimplicitintersection improvements PR. The change addresses issues where the previous HDDAVoxelIterator yielded active values at any node level, forcing callers to branch on getDim() to distinguish between tiles and leaves, which led to inefficiencies and bugs. rayimplicitintersection improvements, https://github.com/openvdb/fvdb-core/pull/663, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Question/doubt about VDB allocation, https://github.com/fzi-forschungszentrum-informatik/vdbmapping/issues/2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-level DDA with Adaptive Mip Selection
head: DDA-based volume sampling routine, Multi-level traversal scheme
body: This method is a ray traversal and sampling algorithm for volume rendering that combines Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) brick traversal with delta tracking, using multiple mip levels of a majorant texture to adaptively balance step size and sampling accuracy. It solves the problem of inefficient sampling in sparse or heterogeneous volumes by allowing large steps in empty regions (coarse mip levels) while maintaining precision near density changes (fine mip levels). It sets itself apart from standard DDA by dynamically adjusting the spatial resolution of the majorant lookup per step without branching, and from pure delta tracking by using DDA to skip empty space more efficiently. The algorithm traverses a ray through a volume hierarchy of bricks, using a majorant texture to estimate the probability of interaction. It maintains a target optical thickness (tauToGo) and steps through the volume, dynamically selecting the mip level for the majorant lookup based on a heuristic that increases resolution as the ray progresses and decreases it upon collision detection. Inputs: Ray origin (rayOrigin), ray direction (rayDir), volume data (density texture, majorant texture hierarchy), initial distance t (usually 0 or start of volume). Outputs: Collision point, type of collision (real or null), updated ray state. Majorant Texture Hierarchy: A set of mip levels (0 to 3) of a texture storing the majorant density. The source specifies 3 mip levels are computed. Brick Geometry: Bricks are dilated by 0.5 voxels in the direction of travel to improve numerical stability and reduce step counts. The brick dimension at mip level m is dim = 8 << m. Initial Mip Level: 3.0 (coarsest). Mip Increment: 0.33 per iteration. Mip Decrement on Collision: 2.0. Mip Bounds: Clamped between 0.0 and 3.0. Brick Dilation: 0.5 voxels. 1. Initialize the target optical thickness tauToGo by sampling a uniform random number r and computing tauToGo = -log(1.0 - r). 2. Initialize the mip level mip = 3.0. 3. Enter the volume traversal loop (while inside the volume): a. Calculate the current ray position: pos = rayOrigin + t rayDir. b. Lookup the majorant density at pos using the current mip level, rounded to an integer: majorant = lookupMajorant(pos, round(mip)). c. Compute the next DDA step distance nextt using the stepDDA function with the current mip level. d. Increment the mip level: mip = min(3.0, mip + 0.33). e. Calculate the step distance dt = nextt - t and the optical thickness traversed dtau = majorant dt. f. Update the current distance t = nextt. g. Subtract the traversed optical thickness from the target: tauToGo -= dtau. h. If tauToGo > 0, continue to the next iteration (no collision yet). i. If tauToGo <= 0 (collision detected): i. Decrement the mip level: mip = max(0.0, mip - 2.0). ii. Step back to the exact collision point using linear interpolation: t += dt (tauToGo / dtau). iii. Lookup the actual density at the collision point: density = lookup(rayOrigin + t rayDir). iv. Perform Russian roulette for real vs. null collision: if random() majorant < density, handle a real collision; otherwise, treat as a null collision. v. For a null collision, restart the traversal by sampling a new target optical thickness: tauToGo = -log(1.0 - random()). Target Optical Thickness: tauToGo = -log(1.0 - random()). Brick Dimension: dim = 8 << mip. DDA Offset: ofs = ri (((ri >= 0.0) ? dim + 0.5: -0.5) - ro). Where ri is the ray inverse direction (1.0 / rayDir) and ro is the ray origin relative to the brick. DDA Step Distance: tmax = floor(pos (1.0 / dim)) dim ri + ofs. The final step distance is min(tmax.x, min(tmax.y, tmax.z)). Collision Point Refinement: tcollision = tprev + dt (tauToGoremaining / dtautraversed). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def stepdda(ro, ri, pos, mip): """ Compute the next DDA step distance using dilated brick boundaries. ro: Ray origin relative to brick (float3) ri: Ray inverse direction (float3) pos: Current ray position (float3) mip: Current mip level (float) """ dim = 8 << int(mip) # Calculate offset based on direction and dilation # If ri component >= 0, offset is (dim + 0.5) - ro # If ri component < 0, offset is -0.5 - ro # This is applied component-wise ofsx = ri.x (((dim + 0.5) - ro.x) if ri.x >= 0 else (-0.5 - ro.x)) ofsy = ri.y (((dim + 0.5) - ro.y) if ri.y >= 0 else (-0.5 - ro.y)) ofsz = ri.z (((dim + 0.5) - ro.z) if ri.z >= 0 else (-0.5 - ro.z)) # Calculate tmax for each dimension tmaxx = math.floor(pos.x (1.0 / dim)) dim ri.x + ofsx tmaxy = math.floor(pos.y (1.0 / dim)) dim ri.y + ofsy tmaxz = math.floor(pos.z (1.0 / dim)) dim ri.z + ofsz return min(tmaxx, min(tmaxy, tmaxz)) def multilevelddaadaptivemip(rayorigin, raydir, volumedata): """ Main traversal loop. rayorigin: float3 raydir: float3 volumedata: Object containing lookupMajorant and lookup functions """ # Initialize target optical thickness r = random.random() tautogo = -math.log(1.0 - r) # Initialize mip level mip = 3.0 # Assume t starts at 0 or entry point t = 0.0 # Precompute inverse ray direction invraydir = 1.0 / raydir while True: # Loop until collision handled or ray exits volume # Calculate current position pos = rayorigin + t raydir # Lookup majorant at current mip level # round(mip) ensures integer index for texture lookup majorant = volumedata.lookupmajorant(pos, int(round(mip))) # Compute next DDA step nextt = stepdda( rayorigin, invraydir, pos, mip) # Increment mip level mip = min(3.0, mip + 0.33) # Calculate step distance and optical thickness dt = nextt - t dtau = majorant dt # Update current distance t = nextt # Update remaining optical thickness tautogo -= dtau # Check for collision if tautogo > 0: continue # No collision, continue to next step # Collision detected # Decrement mip level mip = max(0.0, mip - 2.0) # Step back to exact collision point # Note: dt is the step size taken in the previous iteration # dtau is the optical thickness traversed in that step # tautogo is the remaining optical thickness before this step (negative or zero now) # The fraction of the step to go back is tautogo / dtau # Since tautogo <= 0, this is a negative fraction t += dt (tautogo / dtau) # Lookup actual density at collision point collisionpos = rayorigin + t raydir density = volumedata.lookup(collisionpos) # Russian roulette for real vs null collision r = random.random() if r majorant < density: # Handle real collision return {"type": "real", "position": collisionpos, "density": density} else: # Null collision # Restart traversal with new target r = random.random() tautogo = -math.log(1.0 - r) # Continue loop to step forward again Numerical Instability on Brick Boundaries: Ray intersections falling exactly on brick boundaries can cause numerical issues. This is mitigated by dilating brick boundaries by 0.5 voxels in the direction of travel, ensuring the DDA oversteps into each brick. Execution Divergence on GPUs: Implementing separate loops for each mip level causes execution divergence on SIMT devices (GPUs). The adaptive mip selection is computed dynamically per step without branching to avoid this. Precision: The mip level is rounded to an integer for texture lookup, but maintained as a float for the heuristic increment/decrement. A sibling method that uses a hierarchical DDA structure. It differs in its specific implementation of the hierarchy and traversal logic. HDDA A sibling method, likely an extension or variant of HDDA for volume rendering. VolumeHDDA Time Complexity: The number of steps is reduced compared to regular DDA due to larger steps in empty space and dilated boundaries. For example, the adaptive DDA achieved 3.9ms on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 for one sample per pixel at 1920x1080 with 3 bounces on the Moana cloud scene. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is 86.7MB for the Moana cloud scene with BC4 compression. Strengths: Reduces the number of volume and majorant lookups, especially in empty space regions. Improves numerical stability. Avoids execution divergence on GPUs. Limitations: Requires computation of multiple mip levels of the majorant texture. The heuristic for mip selection may not be optimal for all scenes. When to Use: Suitable for GPU-based unbiased volume path tracing where performance and numerical stability are critical. When Not to Use: If the volume is very dense and homogeneous, the overhead of mip level management may not be justified. If CPU rendering is required, the GPU-specific divergence avoidance is less relevant. The method was introduced in "Efficient Unbiased Volume Path Tracing on the GPU". It builds on the principles of Hierarchical DDA Traversal [17026-hierarchical-dda-traversal.md] and adapts them for volume rendering by integrating delta tracking and adaptive mip selection. The approach was inspired by techniques used in screen-space reflections. Efficient Unbiased Volume Path Tracing on the GPU, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4842-7185-843, fetched 2026-10-24 (book)

name: Wide DDA Cell Traversal
body:
Wide DDA Cell Traversal is an algorithm for traversing a fixed 4x4x4 grid of "wide cells" within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) approach. It generates bounding boxes and t-intervals for each cell to optimize octree traversal by visiting occupied child cells in ray order. Inputs: boundsmin, boundsmax: AABB defining the 4x4x4 grid region (vec3). origin: Ray origin point (vec3). direction: Ray direction vector (vec3). maxs: Maximum traversal distance parameter (float). baset: Base parameter for t-interval calculation (float). reverse: Boolean flag controlling t-interval sign convention (bool). visitor: Callback function bool visitor(cell) that receives the current cell data. Outputs: Sequence of WideDdaCell structures passed to the visitor, representing occupied cells in traversal order. Data Structures: WideDdaCell: childindex (int): Packed index of the cell within the 4x4x4 grid. Layout: cellx | (celly << 2) | (cellz << 4). boundsmin, boundsmax (vec3): Local bounding box of the cell. tnear (float): Entry distance along the ray. tfar (float): Exit distance along the ray. Constants: kEpsilon: Small floating-point tolerance for boundary comparisons (exact value not given in the sources). cellsize: Dimensions of each wide cell, calculated as (boundsmax - boundsmin) 0.25. Steps: 1. Initialize Cell Indices: Map the ray origin to local cell coordinates (cellx, celly, cellz) using localcellforposition, which handles boundary conditions and rounding with kEpsilon tolerance. Compute local coordinate: local = (origin - bounds\min) / cell\size. Compute rounded value: rounded = round(local). Check boundary: If |local - rounded| \le 8.0 	imes kEpsilon, the position is on a boundary. Clamp boundary to [0, 3]. If boundary \le 0, return 0. If boundary \ge 4, return 3. Otherwise, return boundary - 1 if walk\direction < -kEpsilon, else boundary. Otherwise, return clamp(floor(local), 0, 3). Note: walk\direction is the sign of the ray direction component (-1 or 1). 2. Setup Axis Parameters: For each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: Determine step direction: stepi = sign(directioni). If |directioni| \le kEpsilon, set stepi = 0. Calculate delta distance: delta\si = cell\size / |directioni| if |directioni| > kEpsilon, else \infty. Calculate next intersection distance: next\si. If stepi = 0, set next\si = \infty. Otherwise, compute the distance to the next cell boundary along axis i from the current cell index. 3. Iterate: Loop up to 96 times. a. Check Bounds: If cellx 
otin 0, 4) or celly 
otin [0, 4) or cellz 
otin [0, 4) or current\s > max\s + kEpsilon, break loop. b. Determine Next Cell: Calculate next\s = \min(next\sx, next\sy, next\sz, max\s). Determine child\index = cell\x \mid (cell\y \ll 2) \mid (cell\z \ll 4). c. Compute Cell Bounds: child\min = bounds\min + cell\size 	imes vec3(cell\x, cell\y, cell\z). child\max = child\min + cell\size. d. Compute t-intervals: If reverse is true: t
ear = base	 - next\s. t ar = base	 - current\s. Else: t
ear = base	 + current\s. t ar = base	 + next\s. e. Visit Cell: Construct WideDdaCell with childindex, childmin, childmax, tnear, tfar. Call visitor(cell). If it returns false, terminate traversal immediately. f. Check Termination: If next\s \ge max\s - kEpsilon, break loop. g. Advance: Update current\s = next\s. Advance the axis with the smallest next\si. If next\sx \le next\sy + kEpsilon and next\sx \le next\sz + kEpsilon, advance x. Else if next\sy \le next\sz + kEpsilon, advance y. Else, advance z. Use advanceaxis to update the corresponding cell index and next\si. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class WideDdaCell: def init(self, childindex, boundsmin, boundsmax, tnear, tfar): self.childindex = childindex self.boundsmin = boundsmin self.boundsmax = boundsmax self.tnear = tnear self.tfar = tfar def wideddacelltraversal(boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, maxs, baset, reverse, visitor): kEpsilon = 1e-6 # Not given in the sources, standard tolerance cellsize = (boundsmax - boundsmin) 0.25 # Initialize cell indices (scalar per axis as walkdirection is per-axis) dirxsign = 1.0 if direction.x > 0 else (-1.0 if direction.x < 0 else 0.0) dirysign = 1.0 if direction.y > 0 else (-1.0 if direction.y < 0 else 0.0) dirzsign = 1.0 if direction.z > 0 else (-1.0 if direction.z < 0 else 0.0) cellx = localcellforposition(origin.x, boundsmin.x, cellsize, dirxsign, kEpsilon) celly = localcellforposition(origin.y, boundsmin.y, cellsize, dirysign, kEpsilon) cellz = localcellforposition(origin.z, boundsmin.z, cellsize, dirzsign, kEpsilon) # Setup axis parameters stepx, nextsx, deltasx = axissetup(direction.x, cellsize, cellx, boundsmin.x, origin.x, kEpsilon) stepy, nextsy, deltasy = axissetup(direction.y, cellsize, celly, boundsmin.y, origin.y, kEpsilon) stepz, nextsz, deltasz = axissetup(direction.z, cellsize, cellz, boundsmin.z, origin.z, kEpsilon) currents = 0.0 for in range(96): if not (0 <= cellx < 4 and 0 <= celly < 4 and 0 <= cellz < 4): break if currents > maxs + kEpsilon: break nexts = min(nextsx, nextsy, nextsz, maxs) childindex = cellx | (celly << 2) | (cellz << 4) childmin = vec3(boundsmin.x + cellsize cellx, boundsmin.y + cellsize celly, boundsmin.z + cellsize cellz) childmax = vec3(childmin.x + cellsize, childmin.y + cellsize, childmin.z + cellsize) if reverse: tnear = baset - nexts tfar = baset - currents else: tnear = baset + currents tfar = baset + nexts cell = WideDdaCell(childindex=childindex, boundsmin=childmin, boundsmax=childmax, tnear=tnear, tfar=tfar) if not visitor(cell): return if nexts >= maxs - kEpsilon: break currents = nexts if nextsx <= nextsy + kEpsilon and nextsx <= nextsz + kEpsilon: cellx, nextsx = advanceaxis(stepx, deltasx, nextsx) elif nextsy <= nextsz + kEpsilon: celly, nextsy = advanceaxis(stepy, deltasy, nextsy) else: cellz, nextsz = advanceaxis(stepz, deltasz, nextsz) def localcellforposition(pos, minbound, cellsize, walkdirection, kEpsilon): local = (pos - minbound) / cellsize rounded = round(local) if abs(local - rounded) <= 8.0 kEpsilon: boundary = max(0, min(3, rounded)) if boundary <= 0: return 0 if boundary >= 4: return 3 if walkdirection < -kEpsilon: return boundary - 1 else: return boundary else: return max(0, min(3, floor(local))) def axissetup(dirval, cellsize, cellidx, minbound, origin, kEpsilon): if abs(dirval) <= kEpsilon: return 0, float('inf'), float('inf') step = 1 if dirval > 0 else -1 deltas = cellsize / abs(dirval) local = (origin - minbound) / cellsize if step > 0: nexts = (cellidx + 1 - local) cellsize / dirval else: nexts = (cellidx - local) cellsize / dirval return step, nexts, deltas def advanceaxis(step, deltas, currentnexts): return currentnexts + step, currentnexts + deltas [Wide Node DDA Cell Calculation is a helper function that maps a continuous position to a discrete cell index (0-3) within a 4x4x4 wide node, handling boundary cases where the position falls exactly on a cell edge. It is used by Wide DDA Cell Traversal to initialize the starting cell indices. It differs from standard floor-based mapping by using an 8kEpsilon tolerance window and the walkdirection parameter to break ties, ensuring consistent DDA stepping. Time Complexity: O(1) per wide cell visited, with a maximum of 96 iterations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, storing only current cell indices and axis parameters. Strengths: Handles near-zero ray directions by setting step to 0 and distances to infinity, preventing division by zero and infinite loops. Handles boundary cases robustly using kEpsilon and walkdirection. Limitations: Limited to 4x4x4 grids. When to use: When traversing wide octree nodes or fixed-size blocks where occupancy is high and ray order is important. When not to use: For sparse grids or when the grid size is not a multiple of 4. Wide DDA Cell Traversal is part of the svo (Sparse Voxel Octree) rendering pipeline, specifically designed for efficient traversal of wide nodes in a GPU-based renderer. hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, https://github.com/hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Wide Node DDA Traversal
head: Wide Node DDA
body: Wide Node DDA Traversal traverses a 4x4x4 grid of wide cells within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) approach to visit occupied child cells in ray order. It generates bounding boxes and t-intervals for each cell to optimize octree traversal. It builds on Wide DDA Cell Traversal by providing a visitor callback mechanism and mask-based filtering required for wide octree nodes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: boundsmin, boundsmax: The AABB of the wide node as 3D vectors. origin, direction: Ray origin and direction vectors. tnear, tfar: The ray segment interval to traverse. reverse: Boolean flag for traversal direction. nodeindex: Index of the wide node in the octree structure. octree: The global octree data structure containing widenodes(), maxdepth(), and payloadbase(). depthremaining: Current recursion depth counter. best: Current best hit record containing hit and t for pruning. Outputs: bool: Indicates traversal success or early termination. Side effects: Calls considerleaf or recursive traversal for valid children. Data Structures: WideNodeDescriptor: childmask: std::uint64t, bitmask of occupied child cells. leafmask: std::uint64t, bitmask of children that are leaves. internalchildmask: std::uint64t, bitmask of children that are internal nodes. payloadbase: Implied offset for leaf payloads. childbase: Implied offset for child nodes. Cell Info: childindex: Index of the cell within the 4x4x4 grid (0-63). boundsmin, boundsmax: Bounding box of the specific wide cell. tnear, tfar: T-interval of the ray intersection with the cell. Helper Functions: countbits(mask): Counts set bits in mask. prefixrank(mask, childindex): Returns the rank (index among set bits) of childindex in mask. childindexfordepth(x, y, z, childdepth): Computes the 3-bit child index from coordinates. containspoint(minbound, maxbound, point): Checks if point is inside bounds. Numbered Steps: 1. Boundary Check: If nodeindex is out of bounds or depthremaining <= 0, return immediately. 2. Descriptor Retrieval: Retrieve WideNodeDescriptor from octree.widenodes()[nodeindex]. 3. DDA Iteration: Call visitwidecellsdda with boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, tnear, tfar, reverse, and a lambda visitor. Note: visitwidecellsdda iterates through the 4x4x4 grid using DDA logic, invoking the visitor for each cell intersected by the ray. 4. Visitor Logic (executed for each cell): a. Get childindex from cell.childindex. b. Compute childbit as 1 << childindex. c. Occupancy Check: If childbit is not in childmask, skip this cell. d. Pruning: If best.hit is true and max(cell.tnear, 0.0) > best.t + kEpsilon, skip this cell. e. Leaf Processing: If childbit is in leafmask: i. Compute leafid using descriptor.payloadbase() and prefixrank(leafmask, childindex). ii. Compute depth as octree.maxdepth() - depthremaining + 2. iii. Call considerleaf(cell.boundsmin, cell.boundsmax, leafid, depth). f. Internal Node Processing: If childbit is in internalchildmask (and not leaf), recursively call traversewidenode with updated depthremaining - 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversewidenode(nodeindex, depthremaining, octree, best, boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, tnear, tfar): # Step 1: Boundary Check if nodeindex >= octree.numwidenodes() or depthremaining <= 0: return False # Step 2: Descriptor Retrieval descriptor = octree.widenodes()[nodeindex] childmask = descriptor.childmask leafmask = descriptor.leafmask internalchildmask = descriptor.internalchildmask # Step 3: DDA Iteration def visitor(cell): # Step 4a: Get childindex childindex = cell.childindex # Step 4b: Compute childbit childbit = 1 << childindex # Step 4c: Occupancy Check if not (childbit & childmask): return # Step 4d: Pruning if best.hit and max(cell.tnear, 0.0) > best.t + kEpsilon: return # Step 4e: Leaf Processing if childbit & leafmask: leafrank = prefixrank(leafmask, childindex) leafid = descriptor.payloadbase() + leafrank depth = octree.maxdepth() - depthremaining + 2 considerleaf(cell.boundsmin, cell.boundsmax, leafid, depth) # Step 4f: Internal Node Processing elif childbit & internalchildmask: childnodeindex = descriptor.childbase + childindex traversewidenode(childnodeindex, depthremaining - 1, octree, best, cell.boundsmin, cell.boundsmax, origin, direction, cell.tnear, cell.tfar) visitwidecellsdda(boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, tnear, tfar, False, visitor) return True def visitwidecellsdda(boundsmin, boundsmax, origin, direction, tnearglobal, tfarglobal, reverse, visitor): # Standard 3D DDA for a 4x4x4 grid invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0.0 else float('inf') for d in direction] step = [1 if d > 0 else -1 for d in direction] # Clamp origin to bounds to find starting cell t = [(boundsmin[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmax = [(boundsmax[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] # Initial cell coordinates ix = int((origin[0] - boundsmin[0]) invdir[0]) if direction[0] != 0 else 0 iy = int((origin[1] - boundsmin[1]) invdir[1]) if direction[1] != 0 else 0 iz = int((origin[2] - boundsmin[2]) invdir[2]) if direction[2] != 0 else 0 ix = max(0, min(3, ix)) iy = max(0, min(3, iy)) iz = max(0, min(3, iz)) # DDA state tmaxx = tmax[0] if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = tmax[1] if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxz = tmax[2] if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') tnextx = tmaxx if step[0] == 1 else t[0] tnexty = tmaxy if step[1] == 1 else t[1] tnextz = tmaxz if step[2] == 1 else t[2] # Precompute cell size cellsize = [boundsmax[i] - boundsmin[i] for i in range(3)] cellsize = [s / 4.0 for s in cellsize] # Visit cells in DDA order for in range(64): # Compute t-interval for current cell cellmin = [boundsmin[i] + ix cellsize[i] for i in range(3)] cellmax = [cellmin[i] + cellsize[i] for i in range(3)] tentry = max((cellmin[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) texit = min((cellmax[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)) tnear = max(tentry, tnearglobal) tfar = min(texit, tfarglobal) if tnear < tfar: childindex = ix + 4 iy + 16 iz visitor({'childindex': childindex, 'boundsmin': cellmin, 'boundsmax': cellmax, 'tnear': float(tnear), 'tfar': float(tfar)}) # Step DDA if tnextx < tnexty: if tnextx < tnextz: ix += step[0] tnextx += tmaxx else: iz += step[2] tnextz += tmaxz else: if tnexty < tnextz: iy += step[1] tnexty += tmaxy else: iz += step[2] tnextz += tmaxz if not (0 <= ix <= 3 and 0 <= iy <= 3 and 0 <= iz <= 3): break def prefixrank(mask, childindex): if childindex <= 0: return 0 lowermask = (1 << childindex) - 1 return countbits(mask & lowermask) def countbits(mask): count = 0 while mask != 0: count += mask & 1 mask = mask >> 1 return count def considerleaf(boundsmin, boundsmax, leafid, depth): # Processes leaf hit; implementation depends on downstream rendering logic pass kEpsilon = 1e-6 Parameters: kEpsilon: Small float value for pruning comparison. maxdepth: Maximum depth of the octree. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point comparisons for t-intervals and pruning require epsilon tolerance. Boundaries: nodeindex out of bounds must be checked to prevent memory access violations. Degenerate Input: depthremaining <= 0 stops recursion to prevent infinite loops or invalid accesses. Zero Direction Components: DDA must handle zero direction components by clamping to inf and skipping steps to avoid division by zero. Traverses a wide octree node by iterating over 4x4x4 wide cells using visitwidecellsdda and processing each cell's children based on masks. It distinguishes itself by handling both leaf and internal node children within the same traversal loop, using childmask, leafmask, and internalchildmask to determine the action for each cell. Choose this when you need to traverse a wide octree node with mixed leaf and internal children efficiently. Link: Octree Node Traversal (Wide). Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Proportional to the number of wide cells intersected by the ray, filtered by occupancy masks. Memory: O(1) additional memory per node traversal, excluding the octree structure itself. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of wide cells and the depth of the octree. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Efficiently visits only occupied cells in ray order, reducing unnecessary checks. Limitations: Requires pre-computed masks and descriptors. When to Use: Use when traversing wide octree nodes with sparse occupancy. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Wide Node DDA Traversal is part of the sparse voxel octree rendering pipeline. It originates from the hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels repository, which implements efficient wide-node traversal for volume rendering. hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, https://github.com/hectorpiteau/sparse-voxels, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Two-Step Discrete Ray Tracing
head: Two-step DDA, Two step ray tracing, Fujimoto et al. 3DDDA, Three-dimensional DDA, Discrete Ray-Tracing DDA, Two-Step Discrete Ray Tracing with Octree
body: Two-Step Discrete Ray Tracing is a ray traversal optimization for huge voxel spaces that replaces a single deep octree traversal with a two-level hierarchy of coarser and finer grids. It solves the performance penalty of traversing empty space at high resolution by first stepping through a coarse grid, then transitioning ray parameters into a finer sub-grid only when an occupied coarse voxel is hit. It differs from single-step discrete ray-tracing by using an octree to represent the scene at several resolutions, bypassing memory limits and optimizing traversal time. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree representing the voxel space; a ray defined by origin O and direction D; the total number of octree levels L{total}. Output: A sequence of occupied voxels (or object lists) encountered by the ray, ordered by distance. Data Structures: Octree Cell: A simple array of eight elements, each identifying a sub-octant and containing a pointer to a descendent cell or a null pointer if the sub-octant is empty. XYZ Register: A single integer variable containing the three coordinates of the current voxel packed into one register. The width of each coordinate in bits corresponds to the number of levels in the current step. Fixed-Point Variables: 64-bit integers used to represent real values (l1, l2, q1, q2) to maintain precision beyond the 53-bit mantissa limit of double-precision floats. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization (Step 1): Calculate inverse slopes for the coarse resolution. Determine signs of increments inc1, inc2, incd based on direction components. Calculate initial intersection distances l1 and l2 using heights h1, h2 and slopes. Convert l1, l2, q1, q2 to 64-bit fixed-point notation. Initialize XYZ and mask. Set XYZ{ant} = XYZ and end\condition = mask \ll 1. 2. Step 1 Traversal (Coarse Octree): Loop while the current voxel's octant parent bits remain unchanged from the initial value (XYZ{ant}). If no incremental axis transition is imminent (d \ge limit), increment the driving axis coordinate (XYZ += inc{drive}), increment d (d++), and check for octant exit. If an incremental axis transition is imminent (d < limit), select the nearest incremental axis (i1 or i2), increment that axis coordinate, update the intersection distance (l += q), update the limit, and check for octant exit. If the ray exits the empty octant (parent bits change), break the loop. 3. Transition to Step 2: If a non-empty voxel is reached in Step 1, initialize Step 2 parameters. Convert ray parameters (d', i'1, i'2) to the finer resolution (second step). If Step 2 does not reach a non-empty voxel, continue tracing in Step 1. 4. Step 2 Traversal (Fine Sub-grid): Execute a three-dimensional DDA within the fine sub-grid. Advance axes based on minimum tMax values (tMaxX, tMaxY, tMaxZ). After advancing, retrieve the object list: list = ObjectList[X][Y][Z]. Loop while list == NIL. Formulas: Slope calculation for incremental steps: q1 = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta i1} and q2 = \frac{\Delta d}{\Delta i2}, where \Delta d is the ray step size and \Delta i1, \Delta i2 are voxel grid spacings. Parameters: Step 1 Levels (L1): Optimal value is 6. Step 2 Levels (L2): L{total} - L1. Connection Type: Algorithm must use 6-connected neighborhood for continuity in the second step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Error: Standard double precision (53-bit mantissa) propagates errors rapidly in incremental calculus. Fixed-point notation is required to maintain precision for connection-6 continuity. Transition Errors: The transition between the two levels is calculated in floating-point arithmetic, requiring high precision for correctness. Resolution Scaling: The advantage of the two-step process decreases for lower screen resolutions due to floating-point calculation errors during the transition between the two steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostepddaoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, octreeroot, totallevels, gridbounds): L1 = 6 # Optimal levels for first step L2 = totallevels - L1 bits = L1 SHIFT = 32 dx, dy, dz = raydirection absdx, absdy, absdz = abs(dx), abs(dy), abs(dz) # Determine driving axis and incremental axes if absdx >= absdy and absdx >= absdz: drive, i1, i2 = 0, 1, 2 elif absdy >= absdx and absdy >= absdz: drive, i1, i2 = 1, 0, 2 else: drive, i1, i2 = 2, 0, 1 dprime = abs(dx); i1prime = abs(dy); i2prime = abs(dz) if i1prime == 0: i1prime = 1.0 if i2prime == 0: i2prime = 1.0 spacing = 1.0 dprime /= spacing; i1prime /= spacing; i2prime /= spacing q1 = dprime / i1prime; q2 = dprime / i2prime inc1 = 1 if dx > 0 else -1; inc2 = 1 if dy > 0 else -1 if drive == 0: incdrive = 1 if dx > 0 else -1 elif drive == 1: incdrive = 1 if dy > 0 else -1 else: incdrive = 1 if dz > 0 else -1 x0, y0, z0 = int(rayorigin[0]//spacing), int(rayorigin[1]//spacing), int(rayorigin[2]//spacing) h1 = (x0 + (1 if inc1 > 0 else 0)) spacing - rayorigin[i1] h2 = (y0 + (1 if inc2 > 0 else 0)) spacing - rayorigin[i2] d = int(dprime); i1v = int(i1prime); i2v = int(i2prime) if dprime < 0: l1 = h1 q1 - dprime; l2 = h2 q2 - dprime d = -d; incq1 = -q1; incq2 = -q2; incd = -1 else: l1 = h1 q1 + dprime; l2 = h2 q2 + dprime incq1 = q1; incq2 = q2; incd = 1 l1fp = int(l1 (1<<SHIFT)); l2fp = int(l2 (1<<SHIFT)) q1fp = int(incq1 (1<<SHIFT)); q2fp = int(incq2 (1<<SHIFT)) XYZ = (x0 << 2bits) | (y0 << bits) | z0 mask = (1 << bits) - 1 XYZant = XYZ & mask # Step 1 Loop (Coarse Traversal) while (XYZ & mask) == XYZant: limit = min(l1fp >> SHIFT, l2fp >> SHIFT) if d >= limit: if drive == 0: x0 += incdrive elif drive == 1: y0 += incdrive else: z0 += incdrive XYZ = (x0 << 2bits) | (y0 << bits) | z0 d += incd else: if l1fp < l2fp: if i1 == 0: x0 += inc1 elif i1 == 1: y0 += inc1 else: z0 += inc1 XYZ = (x0 << 2bits) | (y0 << bits) | z0 l1fp += q1fp else: if i2 == 0: x0 += inc2 elif i2 == 1: y0 += inc2 else: z0 += inc2 XYZ = (x0 << 2bits) | (y0 << bits) | z0 l2fp += q2fp if (XYZ & mask) != XYZant: XYZant = XYZ & mask break # Transition & Step 2 (Fine Traversal) occupied = octreeroot.checkoccupied(x0, y0, z0, L1) if occupied: finespacing = spacing / (1 << L2) # Recalculate DDA variables for fine grid using finespacing # Fixed-point conversion and loop follow identical structure to Step 1 # Step 2 uses Amanatides & Woo tMax advancement for object retrieval tMaxX = (x0 + (1 if dx > 0 else 0)) / abs(dx) if abs(dx) > 0 else float('inf') tMaxY = (y0 + (1 if dy > 0 else 0)) / abs(dy) if abs(dy) > 0 else float('inf') tMaxZ = (z0 + (1 if dz > 0 else 0)) / abs(dz) if abs(dz) > 0 else float('inf') tDeltaX = 1.0 / abs(dx) if abs(dx) > 0 else float('inf') tDeltaY = 1.0 / abs(dy) if abs(dy) > 0 else float('inf') tDeltaZ = 1.0 / abs(dz) if abs(dz) > 0 else float('inf') while True: if tMaxX < tMaxY and tMaxX < tMaxZ: x0 += (1 if dx > 0 else -1) if x0 == gridbounds.maxx: return None tMaxX += tDeltaX elif tMaxY < tMaxZ: y0 += (1 if dy > 0 else -1) if y0 == gridbounds.maxy: return None tMaxY += tDeltaY else: z0 += (1 if dz > 0 else -1) if z0 == gridbounds.maxz: return None tMaxZ += tDeltaZ objlist = octreeroot.getobjectlist(x0, y0, z0) if objlist is not None: return objlist else: continuestep1() # Continue Step 1 if Step 2 didn't find anything Hierarchical DDA is a ray traversal optimization for huge voxel spaces that replaces a single deep octree traversal with a two-level hierarchy of coarser and finer grids. It solves the performance penalty of traversing empty space at high resolution by first stepping through a coarse grid, then transitioning ray parameters into a finer sub-grid only when an occupied coarse voxel is hit. It differs from standard DDA by preserving inverse slopes across the level boundary to avoid recalculation, and from Two-Step Discrete Ray Tracing by explicitly defining the coordinate conversion and limit calculation logic required for the transition. Time Complexity: Reduces global time by about 50% over previous implementations by keeping the DDA in a closed loop in empty regions. Achieves a five-fold reduction in time compared to a single-step implementation. For the largest 3D grid (2048^3) and largest image resolution, it takes one-fifth of the single-step process time. Memory Complexity: Uses an octree to represent the scene at several resolutions, bypassing memory limits of high-resolution 3D grids. Performance: Optimal performance is achieved with 6 levels in the first step. The advantage decreases for lower screen resolutions due to floating-point calculation errors during the transition between the two steps. Strengths: Ideal for very high resolution 3D grids and large images. Uses integer/fixed-point arithmetic for efficiency and accuracy. Limitations: Precision errors can occur if standard double precision (53-bit mantissa) is used; fixed-point notation is required. The transition between levels is calculated in floating-point arithmetic, requiring high precision. Origin: Proposed by Fujimoto et al.. History: Developed to address the memory and performance problems of discrete ray-tracing in huge voxel spaces. It builds on the 3DDDA method by Fujimoto et al. [7] and improves upon Sung's algorithm by eliminating the "ComplexSkipParent" procedure. Usage: Used for visualizing huge volumetric data realistically, ideal for very high resolution 3D grids and large images. Discrete Ray-Tracing of Huge Voxel Spaces - doczz.net, https://doczz.net/doc/7276913/discrete-ray-tracing-of-huge-voxel-spaces, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical DDA / Multi-step DDA
head: Level transition, Second Step Transition, Sub-octree entry
body: Hierarchical DDA converts ray parameters when entering a finer resolution sub-grid from a coarser voxel, preserving inverse slopes to avoid recalculation. It solves the performance penalty of traversing deep octrees over empty regions by stepping through a coarse grid first, then initializing a second three-dimensional DDA inside the occupied coarse voxel. It sets apart from standard DDA by explicitly defining the coordinate conversion and limit calculation logic required for the level transition. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D, coarse grid dimensions Nc, fine grid dimensions Nf (per coarse voxel), and the current coarse voxel index (Xc, Yc, Zc). Output: Initialized state for the fine-grid DDA: local coordinates (X2, Y2, Z2), inverse slopes (inv\q1, inv\q2), and step limits (limit2). Data Structures: The grid is logically subdivided into two steps. A total resolution of 1024^3 is represented as a 32^3 first step, where each voxel contains a 32^3 second step sub-grid. The octree has 10 levels: the first 5 levels belong to the first step, and the second 5 levels belong to the second step. Algorithm Steps: 1. Determine Ray Type: Check if the ray is a "secondary ray in the first voxel" (i.e., the ray origin is inside the first voxel of the second step, indicated by XYZ == XYZ{ant}). 2. Calculate Inverse Slopes: For primary rays or secondary rays not in the first voxel, calculate inverse slopes once per ray: inv\q1 = \frac{i1}{d} inv\q2 = \frac{i2}{d} where i1, i2 are incremental axis indices and d is the driving axis step. 3. Coordinate Conversion: Convert global integer coordinates to second-step local coordinates using modulo and integer division to map global voxel indices to local sub-grid indices. 4. Calculate Limits: Convert l21, l22 to fixed-point and set limit2 to the integer part of the smaller l value. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode implements the transition logic described in. It defines modf to return the fractional part of a number. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modf(x): """Returns the fractional part of x.""" return x - int(x) def hierarchicalddatransition(raydir, dprime, iprime21, iprime22, drivingaxisidx, issecondaryfirstvoxel, coarsevoxelidx, finesize, i1, i2): """ Initializes the second-step DDA state. raydir: direction vector (dx, dy, dz) dprime: local depth offset from previous step iprime21, iprime22: local incremental offsets drivingaxisidx: 0, 1, or 2 issecondaryfirstvoxel: True if XYZ == XYZant coarsevoxelidx: (Xc, Yc, Zc) finesize: size of the second-step sub-grid (e.g., 32) i1, i2: incremental axis steps (typically 1) """ if issecondaryfirstvoxel: # Secondary ray in 1st voxel: calculate l21, l22 directly if raydir[drivingaxisidx] > 0: l21 = (iprime21 / raydir[drivingaxisidx]) - dprime l22 = (iprime22 / raydir[drivingaxisidx]) - dprime else: l21 = (iprime21 / raydir[drivingaxisidx]) + dprime l22 = (iprime22 / raydir[drivingaxisidx]) + dprime XYZ2 = {'d': dprime, 'i1': iprime21, 'i2': iprime22, 'l21': l21, 'l22': l22} else: # Primary/other ray: calculate inverse slopes once invq1 = i1 / raydir[drivingaxisidx] invq2 = i2 / raydir[drivingaxisidx] # Coordinate conversion to 2nd step local intd = coarsevoxelidx[drivingaxisidx] inti1 = coarsevoxelidx[1 - drivingaxisidx] inti2 = coarsevoxelidx[2 - drivingaxisidx] intd2 = intd % finesize inti12 = inti1 % finesize inti22 = inti2 % finesize # Calculate limits for incremental axes fraci1 = modf(inti12) fraci2 = modf(inti22) if inti12 < 0: l21 = -invq1 fraci1 + intd2 else: l21 = invq1 (1.0 - fraci1) + intd2 if inti22 < 0: l22 = -invq2 fraci2 + intd2 else: l22 = invq2 (1.0 - fraci2) + intd2 # Convert to fixed point and set limit limit2 = int(min(l21, l22)) XYZ2 = {'d': intd2, 'i1': inti12, 'i2': inti22, 'l21': l21, 'l22': l22, 'limit2': limit2} return XYZ2 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The procedure must consider error estimations to guarantee 53-bit precision on 64-bit machines. Direction Sign: The calculation of l21 and l22 depends on the sign of the ray direction components (d > 0 or d < 0). Boundary Conditions: When the intersection point is at a higher voxel boundary (d < 0), the local coordinate d2 is set to 0. Optimizes traversal by detecting uniform materials and terminating the DDA early without descending the hierarchy. CPU passes detect 4^3 bricks and 16^3 tiles filled with a single opaque material and publish packed byte LUTs. During DDA, the ray terminates at the cell's entry face when a uniform region is hit, skipping further hierarchy descent. Time Complexity: Reduces traversal time for huge voxel spaces by skipping empty regions at the coarse level. The transition cost is low due to preserved inverse slopes. Memory Complexity: Requires storing two levels of octree data. For a 1024^3 grid, this is represented as a 32^3 coarse grid with 32^3 fine sub-grids. Performance: Tested on an SGI Crimson workstation (R4000+R4010, 100MHz, 128Mb). Limitations: Requires careful error estimation to maintain precision. Less effective if the coarse grid has many occupied voxels. The method was introduced in "Discrete Ray-Tracing of Huge Voxel Spaces". It addresses the inefficiency of traversing deep octrees for large voxel datasets by using a two-step process. Discrete Ray-Tracing of Huge Voxel Spaces, https://doczz.net/doc/7276913/discrete-ray-tracing-of-huge-voxel-spaces, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Occupancy Mask
head: Bitmask Brick Traversal
body: Voxel Occupancy Mask is an optimization for brick-level ray traversal that replaces per-brick occupancy flags with a 64-bit bitmask representing the occupancy of every voxel within a small brick. This allows the renderer to skip empty voxels inside an occupied brick without performing additional texture lookups for occupancy data. It differs from the parent Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) Traversal by introducing a finer-grained brick structure (4×4×4) and explicit bit-level occupancy checks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, direction, inverse direction, DDA delta values, current brick cell coordinates, and texture/buffer resources. Output: Palette index of the first occupied voxel hit, or 0 if the brick is empty or the ray exits without hitting occupied voxels. Data Structures: Texture3D<uint2> voxelmasks: A 3D texture where each texel corresponds to a brick. The value is a uint2 (64 bits total), storing the occupancy bits for the 64 voxels in that brick. The layout is linear: voxel index i maps to bit i within the 64-bit integer formed by the two 32-bit words. Texture3D<uint> voxels: The voxel color/opacity grid. StructuredBuffer<uint> palettergba: The color palette. Parameters: VXBRICKEXT: The side length of a brick in voxels. Set to 4 in this implementation, yielding 4^3 = 64 voxels per brick. Steps: 1. Load Mask: Load the 64-bit occupancy mask for the current brick from voxelmasks. \text{mask} = \text{voxel\masks.Load}(\text{brick\cell}, 0).\text{rg} 2. Check Brick Occupancy: If both 32-bit words of the mask are zero, the brick is empty and can be skipped. \text{if } (\text{any}(\text{mask} \neq \text{uint2}(0u, 0u))) 3. Trace Brick: Perform DDA traversal within the brick bounds, using the loaded mask for occupancy checks. 4. Inside Traversal Loop: a. Calculate the linear voxel index for the current local cell within the brick: \text{voxel\idx} = \text{local\cell}.x + \text{local\cell}.y \times \text{VX\BRICK\EXT} + \text{local\cell}.z \times \text{VX\BRICK\EXT}^2 b. Determine which 32-bit word and bit corresponds to this voxel: \text{word} = \text{mask}[\text{voxel\idx} \gg 5u] \text{bit} = 1u \ll (\text{voxel\idx} \& 31u) c. Check if the bit is set: \text{if } ((\text{word} \& \text{bit}) \neq 0u) d. If occupied, load the voxel color from the voxels texture at the brick-minimum plus local cell offset and return the palette index. e. If not occupied, advance the DDA to the next voxel within the brick. 5. Exit Condition: If the ray exits the brick without finding an occupied voxel, return 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxeloccupancymasktraversal(origin, dir, brickcell, voxelmasks, voxels, palettergba): VXBRICKEXT = 4 brickmin = [brickcell[i] VXBRICKEXT for i in range(3)] brickmax = [brickmin[i] + VXBRICKEXT for i in range(3)] # Handle zero direction components invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0.0 else 0.0 for d in dir] step = [1 if d > 0 else -1 if d < 0 else 0 for d in dir] # Compute brick entry/exit t tentry = max((brickmin[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] if invdir[i] != 0 else (float('inf') if origin[i] < brickmin[i] else float('-inf')) for i in range(3)) texit = min((brickmax[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] if invdir[i] != 0 else (float('-inf') if origin[i] >= brickmax[i] else float('inf')) for i in range(3)) if texit < 0 or tentry > texit: return 0 t = max(tentry, 0.0) voxel = [int(origin[i] + t dir[i]) for i in range(3)] # Precompute next boundary and tmax nextboundary = [brickmin[i] + step[i] if step[i] != 0 else brickmin[i] for i in range(3)] tmax = [abs(nextboundary[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] if invdir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] while t < texit: if not all(brickmin[i] <= voxel[i] < brickmax[i] for i in range(3)): break # Load mask mask = voxelmasks[brickcell] if mask[0] == 0 and mask[1] == 0: return 0 # Calculate linear voxel index local = [voxel[i] - brickmin[i] for i in range(3)] voxelidx = local[0] + local[1] VXBRICKEXT + local[2] VXBRICKEXT VXBRICKEXT # Check occupancy bit word = mask[voxelidx >> 5] bit = 1 << (voxelidx & 31) if (word & bit) != 0: return voxels[voxel[0], voxel[1], voxel[2]] # Advance DDA mint = min(tmax) t += mint for i in range(3): if tmax[i] == mint: voxel[i] += step[i] nextboundary[i] += step[i] tmax[i] = abs(nextboundary[i] - origin[i]) invdir[i] if invdir[i] != 0 else float('inf') return 0 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Bitwise operations on large indices must be handled carefully to avoid overflow. The shift amount voxelidx & 31 ensures the shift is within 0–31. Boundaries: The DDA traversal must correctly handle brick boundaries. If the ray enters or exits a brick, the localcell calculation must be accurate. Degenerate Input: If the ray is parallel to an axis, invdir may be infinite or zero. Standard DDA handling applies. Time Complexity: O(1) per brick for the occupancy check. Traversal within an occupied brick is proportional to the number of voxels traversed, but empty voxels are skipped without texture lookups. Memory Complexity: Adds a Texture3D<uint2> for masks. For a 4×4×4 brick, this is 64 bits per brick, which is very compact. Performance: In the specific implementation cited, this method performed worse than the parent commit in every scene. The smaller brick granularity (4×4×4) resulted in more bricks being visited along the ray, slowing down rendering, especially when viewing the model from afar. Strengths: Eliminates texture lookups for occupancy checks within bricks. Limitations: Increased number of bricks visited due to smaller size. The overhead of managing smaller bricks outweighed the benefit of skipping empty voxels in the tested scenes. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. name: Zero-Crossing DDA Traversal
head: Zero Crossing Detection, ZeroCrossing, ZeroCrossingNode
body: Zero-Crossing DDA Traversal performs empty-space ray-marching at all levels of a hierarchical grid using a Hierarchical Digital Differential Analyzer (HDDA) to detect the first voxel where a scalar field changes sign relative to the entry voxel's value. It solves the problem of efficiently skipping empty or uniform regions by combining coarse hierarchical traversal with narrow-band voxel-level detection. Unlike standard DDA methods that visit every voxel, this method returns immediately upon detecting a sign change, making it suitable for isosurface extraction or narrow-band volume rendering. It builds on Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) Traversal and differs from DDA, Two-Step Discrete Ray Tracing, Voxel Occupancy Mask, Parallel 3D-DDA, and Nearest Neighbor Ray Traversal by halting traversal at the first sign change rather than sampling all active voxels. Inputs: ray (object with clip(bbox), t0(), t1(), invDir(), and operator()(time)), acc (accessor with root().bbox(), getDim(ijk, ray), isActive(ijk), and getValue(ijk)), ijk (coordinate reference), v (value reference), t (time reference). Outputs: Boolean indicating success; ijk, v, and t updated on success. HDDA: State machine for hierarchical stepping. Maintains mDelta (time delta to next voxel boundary) and mNext (next voxel coordinates). Provides step() to advance, time() to get current ray parameter, voxel() to get current voxel index, dim() to get current node dimension, init() to initialize, and update() to reinitialize with a new dimension. Coord: Integer coordinate type. RoundDown<Coord>(pos) or Coord::Floor(pos) computes the voxel index containing a 3D position. Delta: Constant 1.0001 used to offset the ray position when determining the next voxel index after a step, ensuring the next voxel is correctly identified and avoiding boundary precision issues. 1. Ray Clipping: Clip the ray to the root bounding box. If clipping fails or ray.t1() > 1e20, return false. 2. Initialization: Set Delta = 1.0001. Compute initial ijk = RoundDown<Coord>(ray.start()). Initialize HDDA with ray and acc.getDim(ijk, ray). Read v0 = acc.getValue(ijk). 3. Hierarchical Traversal: While hdda.step() returns true: Compute ijk = RoundDown<Coord>(ray(hdda.time() + Delta)). Update hdda.update(ray, acc.getDim(ijk, ray)). If hdda.dim() > 1 (tile value) or !acc.isActive(ijk) (inactive voxel), continue to the next step. 4. Narrow-Band Traversal: While hdda.step() returns true and acc.isActive(hdda.voxel()) is true: Read v = acc.getValue(hdda.voxel()). Check for zero-crossing: If v v0 < 0: Set ijk = hdda.voxel(). Set t = hdda.time(). Return true. 5. Termination: If the loops complete without finding a zero-crossing, return false. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def zerocrossingdda(ray, acc): # 1. Ray Clipping if not ray.clip(acc.root().bbox()) or ray.t1() > 1e20: return False, None, None, None Delta = 1.0001 ijk = math.floor(ray.start()) # 2. Initialize HDDA hdda = HDDA(ray, acc.getdim(ijk, ray)) v0 = acc.getvalue(ijk) # 3. Hierarchical Traversal Loop while hdda.step(): ijk = math.floor(ray(hdda.time() + Delta)) hdda.update(ray, acc.getdim(ijk, ray)) # Skip tiles or inactive voxels if hdda.dim() > 1 or not acc.isactive(ijk): continue # 4. Narrow-Band Traversal Loop while hdda.step() and acc.isactive(hdda.voxel()): v = acc.getvalue(hdda.voxel()) if v v0 < 0: ijk = hdda.voxel() t = hdda.time() return True, ijk, v, t return False, None, None, None Precision: The Delta offset of 1.0001 prevents sampling the same voxel twice due to floating-point inaccuracies at voxel boundaries. Inactive Voxels & Tiles: The algorithm explicitly skips inactive voxels and hierarchical tiles (dim() > 1) to ensure voxel-level precision for the zero-crossing check. Fixed Reference Value: The sign change is always compared against v0 (the value at the entry voxel), not the previous voxel's value, meaning it only detects the first crossing relative to the ray origin's sign. No Zero-Crossing: If the ray passes through a region where the sign never changes relative to v0, the function returns false. Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the zero-crossing. In empty space, HDDA skips large volumes efficiently. In dense narrow bands, it behaves like standard DDA but stops at the first sign change. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as it uses iterative stepping without recursion or large stacks. Strengths: Efficient for sparse volumes; avoids unnecessary voxel visits in empty regions; precise voxel-level localization. Limitations: Only detects the first zero-crossing relative to the entry point value; may miss multiple zero-crossings in a single ray pass; requires active voxel data. The method is implemented in the NanoVDB library as part of the OpenVDB ecosystem, which is widely used in visual effects and scientific visualization for large-scale volumetric data. The HDDA class is designed for hierarchical grids, allowing efficient traversal of multi-resolution data structures. openvdb/nanovdb/nanovdb/math/HDDA.h at master, https://github.com/AcademySoftwareFoundation/openvdb/blob/master/nanovdb/nanovdb/math/HDDA.h, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) nanovdb/util/HDDA.h File Reference - OpenVDB, https://academysoftwarefoundation.github.io/openvdb/HDDA8h.html, fetched 2026-10-25 ZephirFXEC/HNanoSolver, https://github.com/ZephirFXEC/HNanoSolver, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Nearest Neighbor Ray Traversal
head: Scan Conversion, Nearest Neighbor Interpolation
body: Nearest Neighbor Ray Traversal is a volume rendering method that samples data values at the center of each voxel immediately upon entry, requiring zero interpolation. It prioritizes maximum speed over sampling uniformity, making it the fastest but least accurate traversal approach. Inputs: A ray defined by origin P and direction g, a step size d, and a voxel grid where data values are stored at cell centers. Outputs: A sequence of sampled intensity values along the ray path. Data Structures: The voxel grid is pre-shifted by 0.5 units in all dimensions so that data values reside at the geometric centers of the grid cells rather than the corners. This allows direct indexing of the center value for any visited voxel. Steps: 1. Calculate the sample point Q = P + k \times V, where V = d \times g. 2. Round Q to the nearest integer voxel coordinates. 3. Retrieve the data value stored at the center of the current voxel. 4. Check if the voxel is on the boundary by comparing its value against a threshold. 5. If the voxel is on the boundary, perform shading/compositing. 6. Increment k and repeat from Step 1 until the ray exits the volume. Parameters: Interpolation Count: 0 interpolations are required in both 2D and 3D. Grid Shift: The grid must be shifted by half a unit (0.5) to align data with voxel centers. Pitfalls: Jagged Artifacts: The method produces jagged sampling artifacts because the distance between effective data samples is not uniform. Non-Uniform Density: Large gaps in sampling density occur as the ray traverses cells, leading to lower accuracy compared to regular sampling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nearestneighbortraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, grid, threshold=0.0): """ Performs Nearest Neighbor Ray Traversal on a pre-shifted grid. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple representing P. raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) tuple representing g (normalized). stepsize: float d, the distance between consecutive samples. grid: 3D array where data is stored at voxel centers. threshold: float, value used to determine boundary voxels. Returns: List of sampled values along the ray. """ samples = [] k = 0 # Step vector V = d g V = (stepsize raydirection[0], stepsize raydirection[1], stepsize raydirection[2]) while True: # Step 1: Calculate sample point Q qx = rayorigin[0] + k V[0] qy = rayorigin[1] + k V[1] qz = rayorigin[2] + k V[2] # Step 2: Round Q to nearest integer voxel coordinates ix = int(round(qx)) iy = int(round(qy)) iz = int(round(qz)) # Boundary check for grid bounds if not (0 <= ix < grid.shape[0] and 0 <= iy < grid.shape[1] and 0 <= iz < grid.shape[2]): break # Step 3: Retrieve value at center of current voxel value = grid[ix, iy, iz] # Step 4 & 5: Check boundary and perform shading if value > threshold: value = applyshading(value) samples.append(value) # Step 6: Increment k and repeat k += 1 return samples def applyshading(value): """Applies a basic shading/compositing operation to boundary voxels.""" # Standard compositing or shading logic; returns the processed value return value Samples at uniform intervals along the ray, requiring interpolation. It is more accurate but slower than Nearest Neighbor. Choose it when visual fidelity and uniform sampling density are prioritized over speed. Regular Sampling Samples at voxel boundaries or edges. It is a compromise between speed and accuracy, requiring fewer interpolations than regular sampling. Choose it when a balance between traversal speed and sampling consistency is needed. Blocked Intersection Approach Speed: Fastest among ray traversal methods due to zero interpolation cost. Accuracy: Least accurate due to jagged sampling and non-uniform distances between effective data samples. Memory: Requires a pre-shifted grid structure to store data at centers. Use Case: Suitable for real-time applications where speed is critical and visual fidelity regarding sampling uniformity is secondary. The method is described in the context of Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) ray-casting pipelines, where data is typically defined at voxel corners and interpolated. The specific "Nearest Neighbor" traversal approach, also referred to as "Scan Conversion," is highlighted in educational materials comparing traversal strategies. It is often contrasted with Tuy's ray-casting pipeline which uses interpolation. name: Hardware/Implementation Optimization
body: Hardware/Implementation Optimization adapts Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) ray traversal algorithms for execution on parallel hardware, primarily GPUs. It solves performance bottlenecks of naive ray marching, such as branch divergence, memory latency, and low shader occupancy, by restructuring data layouts, unifying control flow, and optimizing register usage. This family focuses on low-level execution characteristics (warps, registers, cache lines) rather than mathematical traversal logic, distinguishing it from algorithmic variants like Parallel 3D-DDA and GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing via DDA. 1. Branch Unification: Divergent branches from different ray quadrants or entry points are eliminated to maintain SIMD efficiency, typically by permuting axes or unifying logic so all threads in a warp execute the same instruction stream. 2. Memory Coalescing and Caching: Global memory access patterns are coalesced, often using Structure of Arrays (SoA) layouts for ray data and caching voxel tiles in shared memory for threads accessing nearby voxels. 3. Occupancy Management: Shader occupancy is critical; high register allocation and excessive state carried across loops reduce concurrent warps and cause memory stalls. Optimizations reduce register pressure and deduplicate calculations. 4. Implicit Clipping: Expensive explicit clipping is avoided by structuring tests so out-of-bounds accesses return sentinel values (e.g., zero depth) that naturally terminate iteration. A GPU-optimized implementation of the DDA algorithm that maps logical traversal steps to hardware warps for high-throughput SIMD execution. It sets itself apart from CPU-based per-pixel renderers by prioritizing warp-level parallelism and shared memory caching over strict per-pixel ordering. Choose this method when processing millions of rays simultaneously on modern graphics hardware. An efficient GPU solution for screen-space 3D ray tracing against a depth buffer, adapting perspective-correct DDA line rasterization. It sets itself apart from linear 3D marching by ensuring sampled pixels form a contiguous set with no oversampling, placing each pixel adjacent to the previous one. Choose this method when tracing against a depth buffer requires contiguous pixel sampling without gaps or duplicates. An empirical evaluation of DDA traversal optimizations within the Bend voxel renderer, categorizing techniques by retained or rejected status based on performance regressions. It sets itself apart from algorithmic variants by focusing on implementation-level micro-optimizations and their measurable impact on CPU/GPU workloads rather than changing traversal logic. Choose this reference when evaluating whether specific micro-optimizations justify their overhead in compressed voxel structures. A method that optimizes the DDA ray traversal shader to increase GPU occupancy by reducing register allocation and minimizing state carried across loops. It sets itself apart from general execution configuration tuning by focusing on internal variable management and instruction deduplication within the shader code itself. Choose this method when high register pressure limits concurrent warps and causes memory stalls in complex traversal logic. The optimization of DDA traversal for hardware emerged with the rise of GPU-based ray tracing and voxel rendering. Early implementations suffered from severe performance penalties due to branch divergence and inefficient memory access patterns. Specific techniques, such as those in Shader Occupancy Optimization for DDA, were developed and profiled within the "vxray" voxel raytracer context. The screen-space DDA approach leverages the hardware rasterizer's inherent line-drawing capabilities to avoid the overhead of 3D marching. name: Shader Occupancy Optimization for DDA
head: DDA Shader Register Optimization, Optimizing 2-Level DDA Shader, Shader Occupancy Optimization
body: This method increases GPU shader occupancy for Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) ray-grid traversal by reducing register pressure and minimizing state carried across nested loops. It addresses the performance degradation caused by low occupancy (e.g., 35.43%) and high register allocation (e.g., 92 registers) in unoptimized 2-level DDA shaders, which leads to memory stalls despite high ALU usage. Unlike general occupancy tuning, it specifically targets the variable bloat inherent in nested loop structures for voxel traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An unoptimized 2-level DDA shader implementation containing separate mincell and maxcell variables and redundant tdelta calculations. Output: An optimized shader with reduced register allocation and higher occupancy. Data Structures: localcell: A single int3 variable representing the current voxel coordinates. VXBRICKEXT: A constant defining the brick dimensions (e.g., 8 or 16). voxelmask: An array of uint values used for sparse voxel access. Steps: 1. Variable Consolidation: Replace the pair of variables mincell and maxcell with a single local variable localcell. 2. Bounds Checking: Implement bounds checking using a unified comparison against the brick extent: cpp if (any((uint3)localcell >= (uint)VXBRICKEXT)) { // Handle out-of-bounds or termination } 3. Deduplication: Remove redundant tdelta calculations and unnecessary work within the nested loops. 4. Loop State Reduction: Ensure that fewer variables are carried over the loops into registers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizedddaloop(rayorigin, raydirection, brickmin, brickmax, voxelmask, voxels): # Initialize localcell based on ray entry localcell = computeinitialcell(rayorigin, raydirection, brickmin) # Pre-calculate tdelta once if possible, or deduplicate if computed per axis # Note: Exact tdelta deduplication logic depends on specific DDA variant, # but the key is avoiding recomputation or storing redundant deltas in registers. while True: # Bounds check using single variable and brick extent if any((uint3)localcell >= (uint)VXBRICKEXT): break # Compute voxel index voxelidx = localcell.x + localcell.y VXBRICKEXT + localcell.z VXBRICKEXT VXBRICKEXT # Sparse voxel access word = voxelmask[voxelidx >> 5u] bit = 1u << (voxelidx & 31u) if (word & bit) != 0u: # Load voxel data return voxels.Load(int4(brickmin + localcell, 0)).r # Advance ray localcell = advanceddastep(localcell, raydirection) # Check for brick exit or other termination conditions if isbrickexit(localcell, brickmax): break Parameters: VXBRICKEXT: Brick dimension. Typical values are 8 or 16. Not given in the sources. Target Register Allocation: < 72 registers (achieved 72 vs 92). Target Occupancy: > 40% (achieved 42.37% vs 35.43%). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Occupancy: Unoptimized shaders may have occupancy as low as 35.43% with 92 registers, causing memory stalls. Register Pressure: Carrying excessive state across nested loops increases register allocation, reducing the number of concurrent warps. Focuses on thread block/grid dimensions and shared memory to maximize occupancy, accounting for branch divergence in ray-grid traversal. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Reduced register usage (from 92 to 72 registers). Time: Performance improvements vary by scene complexity. Measured Performance: monu2-1 (128³): FPS 143.20 -> 144.00 (+0.56%), Walltime 6.58 ms -> 5.37 ms (-18.32%). sponza-256-1: FPS 59.78 -> 72.83 (+21.83%), Walltime 28.39 ms -> 22.51 ms (-20.71%). sponza-256-2: FPS 109.53 -> 143.94 (+31.42%), Walltime 13.40 ms -> 7.32 ms (-45.33%). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant walltime reduction in complex scenes (up to 45.33% faster). Limitations: Modest FPS gains in simpler scenes (0.56%). When to Use: Use when DDA shader occupancy is low (<40%) and register allocation is high (>80 registers). Originated from development logs of a voxel raytracer, specifically addressing the performance drop in 2-level DDA shaders compared to naive DDA. The unoptimized 2-level DDA shader had an occupancy of 35.43% and 92 registers, compared to 71.39% and 42 registers for the naive DDA. name: CUDA Execution Configuration Optimization
head: Block Size and Grid Size Tuning, GPU Occupancy Optimization
body: CUDA Execution Configuration Optimization is the process of selecting thread block dimensions, grid dimensions, and shared memory allocation to maximize GPU occupancy and rendering performance for ray-casting volume rendering. It addresses the problem that performance varies significantly (up to 265%) based on these parameters, with no single optimal configuration for all datasets or algorithms. Unlike general occupancy tuning, this method specifically accounts for the high branch divergence and load imbalance inherent in ray-grid traversal, where threads within a warp often execute different code paths or terminate at different times. Inputs: Volume dataset dimensions (e.g., Nx, Ny, Nz). Target resolution (image width W, height H). GPU hardware capabilities (max threads per block, max warps per SM, register file size). Algorithmic characteristics (branching density, early ray termination usage, memory access pattern). Outputs: Optimal block dimensions (Bx, By, Bz) such that Bx \times By \times Bz is the total threads per block. Optimal grid dimensions (Gx, Gy) such that Gx \times Gy \ge W \times H. Shared memory size (if applicable). Data Structures: Execution Configuration: A tuple (Bx, By, Bz, Gx, Gy, S{mem}). Occupancy Metric: O = \frac{N{active\warps}}{N{max\warps\per\SM}}. Parameters: Block Size (B): The number of threads per block. Common benchmarked sizes include 4\times4, 4\times8, 4\times16, 4\times32, 8\times8, 8\times16, 8\times32, 16\times16. Minimum Threads: CUDA blocks require a minimum of 32 threads to saturate computational throughput in a standard SIMT model, but smaller blocks (e.g., 16) perform well in raycasting due to divergence. Exclusion Threshold: Configurations with fewer than 4 threads per block are excluded because a warp requires at least 4 clock cycles to schedule, guaranteeing under-utilization. Typical Optimal Size: Empirically, the "sweet spot" is 16 or 32 threads per block, depending on memory ordering and Early Ray Termination (ERT) status. Steps: 1. Map Pixels to Threads: Assign one thread per pixel. The grid size is calculated as Gx = \lceil W / Bx \rceil and Gy = \lceil H / By \rceil. 2. Select Block Dimensions: Choose Bx, By from the set of candidate sizes. The product B{total} = Bx \times By determines the block size. 3. Calculate Occupancy: Use the CUDA occupancy calculator or hardware limits to determine the maximum number of warps per SM for the given kernel register and shared memory usage. 4. Benchmark Performance: Render standard datasets (e.g., Bucky 32^3, Engine 256^3, Porsche 559\times1024\times347) for each candidate configuration. 5. Analyze Trade-offs: Compare frames per second (FPS) against L2 cache miss rates and divergence metrics. 6. Select Optimal Configuration: Choose the configuration with the highest FPS, balancing warp saturation and cache utilization. Formulas: Occupancy: O = \frac{\text{Number of active warps}}{\text{Maximum warps allowed per multiprocessor}} Grid Dimensions: Gx = \left\lceil \frac{W}{Bx} \right\rceil, \quad Gy = \left\lceil \frac{H}{By} \right\rceil Pitfalls: Load Imbalance: Larger thread blocks exhibit greater load imbalance because the variation in ray lengths increases with block size. Divergence: Threads in a warp (32 threads) are executed in subsets of 8. If threads do not share a common instruction (e.g., due to conditionals like empty-space skipping or ERT), they diverge and execute serially. Cache vs. Saturation Trade-off: Small blocks may have fewer L2 cache misses but fail to saturate the warp scheduler. Large blocks saturate the scheduler but may cause more cache misses and load imbalance. The optimal size is a trade-off between these two factors. Dataset Dependency: The optimal block size for one problem is not the same as for another, even on the same platform. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizecudaexecutionconfig(volumedims, imagedims, gpuprops): """ Determine optimal CUDA execution configuration for volume rendering. """ W, H = imagedims candidates = [ (4, 4), (4, 8), (4, 16), (4, 32), (8, 8), (8, 16), (8, 32), (16, 16) ] bestconfig = None maxfps = 0 for Bx, By in candidates: # Exclude blocks with < 4 threads to avoid guaranteed under-utilization if Bx By < 4: continue # Calculate grid dimensions Gx = (W + Bx - 1) // Bx Gy = (H + By - 1) // By # Calculate occupancy based on GPU props (registers, shared mem) # This step typically uses CUDA Occupancy Calculator logic occupancy = calculateoccupancy(gpuprops, Bx By) # Benchmark rendering performance # In practice, this involves launching the kernel and measuring FPS fps = benchmarkrendering(Bx, By, Gx, Gy, volumedims) if fps > maxfps: maxfps = fps bestconfig = { 'block': (Bx, By), 'grid': (Gx, Gy), 'occupancy': occupancy, 'fps': fps } return bestconfig Focuses on reducing register allocation and minimizing state carried across loops to allow more warps per SM. This is a prerequisite for effective execution configuration tuning, as it defines the register/shared memory constraints used in occupancy calculations [Parent]. An algorithmic optimization that can change the optimal block size. ERT introduces conditionals that increase divergence, potentially favoring smaller block sizes (e.g., 16 threads) to mitigate load imbalance. Time Complexity: The optimization process itself is offline (benchmarking). The runtime cost of the kernel is O(N) where N is the number of pixels, but the constant factor varies significantly with configuration. Memory Complexity: Depends on shared memory usage and register allocation per thread. The configuration selection aims to maximize occupancy without exceeding hardware limits. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA GTX280 with an Intel Core 2 Quad 2.33GHz processor and 4GB memory: Bucky (32\times32\times32): 61 FPS with block sizes 4\times16, 4\times32, 8\times8, 8\times16, 8\times32. Engine (256\times256\times256): 31 FPS with block sizes 4\times16, 4\times32, 8\times8, 8\times16, 8\times32. Porsche (559\times1024\times347): 21 FPS with block sizes 4\times16, 4\times32, 8\times8, 8\times16, 8\times32. The 16\times16 block size yielded lower performance (21 FPS on Engine, 20 FPS on Porsche) compared to 8\times8/8\times16/8\times32 (31 FPS on Engine, 21 FPS on Porsche). Performance Variation: Performance varies by as much as 265% depending on thread block size. Strengths: Maximizes hardware utilization by aligning thread counts with warp scheduler capabilities and cache hierarchy. Limitations: Highly sensitive to dataset characteristics (ray length distribution) and algorithmic details (branching). Requires empirical benchmarking for each new dataset or algorithm variant. When to Use: When deploying ray-casting volume rendering on CUDA GPUs, especially for datasets with varying complexity or when enabling/disabling optimizations like ERT. When Not to Use: For simple, uniform workloads where a fixed, sub-optimal configuration is acceptable for simplicity, or when the overhead of benchmarking outweighs the performance gain. The method originated from research into GPU-accelerated voxel traversal and ray-casting volume rendering in the late 2000s. Key studies by Braley et al. (2010) and subsequent work by researchers at the University of North Texas highlighted the significant impact of execution configuration on performance. The NVIDIA CUDA Programming Guide recommends experimentation due to the kernel-dependent nature of execution configuration effects. The findings were validated on NVIDIA GTX280 hardware, establishing benchmarks for block sizes and occupancy metrics that remain relevant for understanding SIMT execution characteristics.
