name: Parallel 3D-DDA
head: SIMD Ray Marching, 并行化改造方案
body: Parallel 3D-DDA is a GPU-optimized implementation of the 3D Digital Differential Analyzer traversal algorithm, designed to process large batches of rays simultaneously using Single Instruction, Multiple Data (SIMD) parallelism. It solves the performance bottleneck of naive ray marching by leveraging modern GPU architectures to achieve high throughput, processing approximately 28 million rays per second on an NVIDIA A100. Unlike its parent Hardware/Implementation Optimization which outlines general principles, this method specifically details the warp-level parallelization and mixed-precision strategies required to maintain efficiency in volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N rays, each defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and step size \Delta s. The volume data is stored in a 3D grid (Structure of Arrays or Structure of Structures). Output: Computed color and opacity for each ray, or traversal termination status. Data Structures: Ray Data: Stored in a Structure of Arrays (SoA) layout to ensure coalesced global memory access. Each ray requires fields for current position, step size, and remaining distance. Voxel Data: Cached in shared memory to reduce global memory latency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Warp Partitioning: Divide the set of N rays into groups of 32 (one warp per GPU thread block or subgroup). Each thread within a warp processes exactly one ray. 2. Initialization: For each ray, calculate the initial intersection with the volume bounding box. Determine the entry voxel and the direction of traversal (sign of \mathbf{d} components). 3. Shared Memory Loading: Load the relevant voxel tile or chunk into shared memory for the warp. 4. Traversal Loop: a. Sample the voxel at the current ray position. b. Update ray position: \mathbf{p}{new} = \mathbf{p}{old} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \Delta s. c. Check for termination (exit volume or opacity threshold reached). d. If not terminated, update voxel indices based on direction signs. 5. Termination: Write results to global memory. Mixed Precision Strategy: To balance precision and performance, the algorithm employs a two-stage precision approach: 1. Initial Stage: Use 32-bit floating-point numbers (FP32) for the first few steps to ensure accurate entry point calculation and initial sampling. 2. Deep Penetration Stage: Switch to 16-bit floating-point numbers (FP16) as the ray penetrates deeper into the medium to accelerate calculation. Parameters: Step Size: Typically set to 0.5 voxel spacing to balance detail and performance. Warp Size: 32 threads (standard NVIDIA GPU warp size). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: Using FP16 for initial entry calculations can cause jitter or incorrect voxel hits. The switch to FP16 should only occur after the ray is firmly inside the volume. Memory Coalescing: Non-coalesced access patterns in global memory can severely degrade performance. SoA layout is critical. Occupancy: High register pressure from carrying per-ray state can reduce occupancy. State should be minimized or stored in registers efficiently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallel3dddawarp(rayindices): # 1. Load ray data into registers origins = [raydata.origin[i] for i in rayindices] directions = [raydata.direction[i] for i in rayindices] steps = [raydata.step[i] for i in rayindices] # 2. Initialize traversal state # Calculate entry voxel and step signs based on direction entryvoxels = computeentryvoxel(origins, directions) stepsigns = sign(directions) tmax = computedistancetoexit(origins, directions, volumebounds) # 3. Shared memory cache for voxels sharedvoxelcache = allocatesharedmemory() for stepcount in range(MAXSTEPS): # 4. Load voxel data into shared memory if needed # (Optimization: Load tile covering current voxel coordinates) currentvoxels = loadvoxelsintosharedmemory(entryvoxels) # 5. Sample and update for i in range(32): # Unrolled or loop over warp if tmax[i] <= 0: continue # Ray terminated # Determine precision based on step count if stepcount < PRECISIONSWITCHTHRESHOLD: precision = FP32 else: precision = FP16 # Sample voxel voxelvalue = samplevoxel(currentvoxels[i], precision) # Update position origins[i] += directions[i] steps[i] tmax[i] -= steps[i] # Update voxel index entryvoxels[i] += stepsigns[i] # Check termination if tmax[i] <= 0 or isoutofbounds(entryvoxels[i]): tmax[i] = 0 # 6. Write results writeresults(rayindices, origins, tmax) A variant that dynamically switches from FP32 to FP16 during traversal. It uses FP32 for initial steps to ensure precision and FP16 for deeper penetration to accelerate calculation. This strategy increased computational throughput by 40% in game engine practice while maintaining visual effects. A CPU-based method that performs strict per-pixel traversal order over a brickmap. It serves as a clean-room alternative to column-coherent raycasting, enabling correct compositing of transparent voxels without depth sorting or Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) schemes. Unlike the parallel GPU method, it focuses on traversal order correctness on CPU architectures. Throughput: On an NVIDIA A100 GPU, the parallelized 3D-DDA implementation can process 28 million rays per second. Sampling Efficiency: The average sampling count is reduced by 99.7% compared to brute-force traversal. Performance Gains: Empty voxel skipping techniques can increase rendering frame rates by 3.2x in medical imaging projects. Memory Usage: Medium memory footprint compared to brute-force (low) or SVO (extremely high). Strengths: High throughput on modern GPUs; suitable for dynamic volume data and large-scale scenes. Limitations: Requires careful management of shared memory and precision; less efficient for extremely sparse data without occupancy maps. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering, medical CT visualization, and meteorological cloud rendering where high performance is critical. When Not to Use: Extremely sparse data where SVO or octree acceleration is more appropriate; static scenes where precomputed acceleration structures are viable. The method originates from the need to optimize volume rendering on modern GPU architectures. It builds upon the foundational 3D-DDA algorithm, adapting it for SIMD execution. The specific implementation details, including warp partitioning and mixed-precision strategies, are documented in practical engineering guides for volume rendering. It is used in medical CT 3D reconstruction, meteorological cloud simulation, and game engines. 体渲染中的体素遍历技术:从理论到实践, https://developer.baidu.com/article/detail.html?id=6975905, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer
head: Brickmap 3D-DDA, CPU-based 3D-DDA Renderer
body: The Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer is a CPU-based volume rendering method that performs a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal per pixel over a brickmap. It serves as a clean-room alternative to column-coherent raycasting, specifically designed for the roxlap engine. Unlike its parent Parallel 3D-DDA which focuses on general parallelization strategies, this method implements a strict per-pixel traversal order that enables correct compositing of transparent voxels without depth sorting or Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) schemes. The method takes a brickmap, camera parameters, and a frame buffer as input, and outputs a rendered image frame buffer. Data Structures: Brickmap: The spatial data structure storing voxel data. It supports runtime editing (carve/fill spans, cubes, rectangles, spheres) via roxlapformats::edit::. Material Palette: A 256-entry palette used to drive per-instance, per-voxel, and world-terrain material properties, supporting mixed opaque-frame and glass models. Color Callbacks: Closure-based functions replacing global state, supporting constant, jittered, position-dependent, and texture-mapped color functions. Steps: 1. Frame Partitioning: The renderer splits the frame into row strips for parallel processing using the rayon library. 2. Ray Initialization: For each pixel in a strip, compute the ray origin and direction from camera parameters. 3. 3D-DDA Traversal: Traverse the brickmap along the ray. The traversal must visit voxels strictly front-to-back. 4. Empty Space Skipping: Skip empty cells to optimize performance. A regression test ensures no leaks occur in empty space handling. 5. Voxel Sampling: Sample the voxel at the current DDA step. Retrieve the material ID and use the closure-based color callback to compute color, avoiding global state management. 6. Compositing: Composite the voxel color into the pixel buffer using front-to-back accumulation. Volumetric opacity is weighted by the ray's path length. 7. Termination: Stop traversal when the ray exits the brickmap bounds or the accumulated transmittance drops below a threshold. Formulas: Volumetric Weighting: Opacity is weighted by the ray's path length, causing filled clouds to appear denser at their core. Front-to-Back Compositing: For a sequence of voxels i with transmittance Ti and color Ci, the final color C{final} is computed as: C{final} = \sum{i} Ci \cdot \alphai \cdot \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) where \alphai is the effective opacity of voxel i. Parameters: Material Palette Size: 256 entries. Parallelism: Controlled by RAYONNUMTHREADS environment variable. Pitfalls: Empty Space Leaks: Incorrect implementation of empty space skipping can lead to visual artifacts (leaks). A specific regression test is required to ensure correctness. Global State: Avoid global state for color functions; use closure-based callbacks to prevent state management issues. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(brickmap, camera, framebuffer, materialpalette): # Split frame into row strips for parallel processing stripheight = max(1, framebuffer.height // 4) strips = [(y, min(y + stripheight, framebuffer.height)) for y in range(0, framebuffer.height, stripheight)] for ystart, yend in strips: for y in range(ystart, yend): for x in range(framebuffer.width): # Initialize ray for pixel (x, y) rayorigin, raydir = camera.getray(x, y) raydir = normalize(raydir) # Initialize compositing state acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 # 3D-DDA Initialization # Assume brickmap bounds are in voxel indices boundsmin = brickmap.bounds.min boundsmax = brickmap.bounds.max voxelpos = [int(rayorigin[i]) for i in range(3)] step = [1 if raydir[i] > 0 else -1 for i in range(3)] tmax = [ (voxelpos[i] + (1 if step[i] == 1 else 0) - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] if raydir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3) ] tdelta = [step[i] / raydir[i] if raydir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] # 3D-DDA Traversal loop while boundsmin[0] <= voxelpos[0] <= boundsmax[0] and \ boundsmin[1] <= voxelpos[1] <= boundsmax[1] and \ boundsmin[2] <= voxelpos[2] <= boundsmax[2]: # Advance to next voxel axis = 0 if tmax[1] < tmax[axis]: axis = 1 if tmax[2] < tmax[axis]: axis = 2 tmax[axis] += tdelta[axis] voxelpos[axis] += step[axis] # Empty space skipping if not brickmap.isvoxelfilled(voxelpos): continue # Sample voxel properties matid = brickmap.getmaterialid(voxelpos) material = materialpalette[matid] colorfunc = material.getcolorcallback() voxelcolor = colorfunc(voxelpos, matid) voxelalpha = material.alpha # Volumetric weighting by path length pathlength = tdelta[axis] effectivealpha = voxelalpha min(1.0, pathlength) # Front-to-back compositing for i in range(3): acccolor[i] += voxelcolor[i] effectivealpha transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - effectivealpha) acccolor[3] = 1.0 - (1.0 - acccolor[3]) (1.0 - effectivealpha) if transmittance < 0.01: break framebuffer.setpixel(x, y, acccolor) A compositing strategy for transparent voxels (alpha-blended, additive, Beer–Lambert volumetric) that relies on front-to-back traversal order, eliminating the need for depth sorting or Order-Independent Transparency (OIT) schemes. It supports constant, jittered, position-dependent, and texture-mapped color functions via closure-based callbacks, replacing the global-state dance of the original engine. Volumetric opacity is weighted by the ray's path length, causing filled clouds to appear denser at their core. It uses a 256-entry material palette to drive per-instance and per-voxel material properties, supporting mixed opaque-frame and glass models. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the average number of voxels traversed per ray. Parallelized across CPU cores using rayon. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Feature-complete CPU renderer with per-arch SIMD support (SSE2 / NEON / wasm simd128). Correctness is validated against a dense per-voxel reference walk. Strengths: Clean-room implementation independent of Voxlap C source; deterministic on CPU; supports complex material palettes and closure-based color functions. Limitations: CPU-bound; performance depends on brickmap traversal efficiency; empty space skipping must be carefully implemented to avoid leaks. When to Use: When a deterministic, CPU-based volume renderer is needed for brickmap data, especially for transparent voxels requiring correct front-to-back compositing. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The Per-pixel 3D-DDA Renderer is part of the roxlap project, an independent Rust implementation inspired by Ken Silverman's Voxlap engine. It was developed as a clean-room alternative to Voxlap's column-coherent raycaster. The renderer is part of the roxlap-cli crate, published on crates.io. The project includes documentation on porting, multicore performance, and scene graph integration. roxlap-cli 0.32.0, https://docs.rs/crate/roxlap-cli/latest, fetched 2026-10-29

name: GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing via DDA
head: Efficient GPU Screen-Space Ray Tracing via DDA, Linear 2D Iteration, Perspective-Correct DDA Ray Tracing, Thin-line Rasterization for Ray Casting
body: This method provides an efficient GPU solution for screen-space 3D ray tracing against a depth buffer by adapting the perspective-correct Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) line rasterization algorithm. It solves the inefficiency and missing intersections inherent in linear 3D marching by ensuring that sampled pixels form a contiguous set with no oversampling. Unlike linear 3D ray marching, which projects 3D points to screen space and can skip pixels or oversample the same pixel multiple times, this method places each sampled pixel adjacent (in x, y, or diagonally) to the previous one and samples each pixel at most once. Inputs: csOrig: Camera-space ray origin. csDir: Camera-space ray direction. proj: Projection matrix. nearPlaneZ: Negative near plane Z value. csZBuffer: Depth buffer texture. csZBufferSize: Dimensions of the depth buffer. csZBufferIsHyperbolic: Boolean flag indicating if the depth buffer stores hyperbolic (perspective-correct) depth values. csZThickness: Camera-space z-thickness ascribed to each point in the depth buffer. maxDistance: Maximum trace distance in camera-space. maxSteps: Maximum number of steps allowed during the trace. stride: Controls spacing between samples. stride = 1.0 produces thin-line rasterization. jitter: A value in the range [0, 1] used to bump the ray in pixels to conceal banding artifacts introduced by spaced samples. Outputs: Boolean indicating if a surface was hit. hitPixel: Coordinates of the hit pixel. hitLayer: Index of the hit layer in the depth buffer (if multiple layers are supported). csHitPoint: Camera-space position of the hit. The method operates on a depth buffer (csZBuffer) accessed via texelFetch. The depth buffer stores depth values which may be hyperbolic (perspective-correct) or linear, determined by csZBufferIsHyperbolic. The algorithm assumes a right-handed camera space where +z is out of the screen. 1. Unify DDA Cases: The classic DDA has eight cases (4 quadrants \times 2 iteration directions). These are unified by permuting axes and taking derivatives relative to the sign of \Delta x, ensuring iteration is always performed along the x-axis. A matrix permutation compensates for this in the vertical case, allowing all subsequent code to assume iteration in x. This eliminates divergent execution on GPUs. 2. Clip Far End: Clip only the far end of the ray against the near plane. The caller ensures the ray origin lies within the view frustum, eliminating the need for complex frustum clipping logic. 3. Implicit Viewport Clipping: Structure the test so that a zero value returned by texelFetch for an out-of-bounds depth-buffer sample terminates iteration. 4. Iterate and Sample: Perform the DDA iteration. At each step, calculate the 3D point corresponding to the current 2D screen point and test for intersection with the depth buffer. The 3D point Q' corresponding to a 2D screen point (x, y) is calculated as: Q'(x,y) = \frac{(Q \otimes k)(x,y)}{k(x,y)} where k = 1/(H \otimes (0,0,0,1)) is the reciprocal of the homogeneous w component, and Q \otimes k interpolates linearly in 2D. The following pseudocode implements the core DDA loop. It assumes the axis permutation has already been applied so that iteration proceeds along the x-axis. It uses conditional assignment instead of branches to maintain SIMD efficiency. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceRay(csOrig, csDir, proj, nearPlaneZ, csZBuffer, csZBufferSize, csZBufferIsHyperbolic, csZThickness, maxDistance, maxSteps, stride, jitter): # 1. Calculate screen-space endpoints P0 and P1 # P0 is the screen position of csOrig (already in frustum) # P1 is the screen position of csOrig + csDir maxDistance # Note: Division by w is handled via perspective-correct interpolation # 2. Determine delta and slope for DDA # dx = P1.x - P0.x # dy = P1.y - P0.y # The algorithm unifies cases by ensuring iteration is along x # If |dx| < |dy|, axes are permuted so that the major axis is x # 3. Initialize DDA state # t = 0.0 # currentx = P0.x # currenty = P0.y # stepx = sign(dx) stride # stepy = (dy/dx) stepx # Precomputed slope # Add jitter to initial position to conceal banding currentx += jitter stepx currenty += jitter stepy # 4. Iterate for step in range(maxSteps): # Check bounds implicitly: if out of bounds, texelFetch returns 0 # which terminates the loop in the intersection test # Calculate 3D point from screen coordinates # Use perspective-correct interpolation for depth if csZBufferIsHyperbolic: # Depth is stored as 1/w or similar hyperbolic value # Interpolate 1/w linearly, then invert invw = interpolateinvw(currentx, currenty) depth = 1.0 / invw else: depth = texelFetch(csZBuffer, int(currentx), int(currenty)).z # Intersection test # Compare ray depth at current screen position with depth buffer # Ray depth is derived from csOrig and csDir raydepth = calculateraydepth(csOrig, csDir, currentx, currenty) # Check if ray hits surface # Account for zThickness for robustness if raydepth <= depth + csZThickness: # Hit found csHitPoint = reconstruct3dpoint(currentx, currenty, raydepth) return True, (currentx, currenty), 0, csHitPoint # Advance DDA t += 1.0 currentx += stepx currenty += stepy # Check if we have exceeded max distance or steps if t > maxDistance or step >= maxSteps: break return False, (0, 0), 0, (0, 0, 0) stride: Controls spacing between samples. stride = 1.0 produces thin-line rasterization. Larger values space samples for efficiency at the cost of quality. jitter: A value in the range [0, 1] used to bump the ray in pixels to conceal banding artifacts introduced by spaced samples (stride > 1.0). csZBufferIsHyperbolic: Boolean encoding flag for the depth buffer. Determines if the depth buffer stores hyperbolic (perspective-correct) depth values. csZThickness: Camera-space z-thickness ascribed to each point in the depth buffer, used for robustness in intersection testing. maxDistance: Maximum trace distance in camera-space. maxSteps: Maximum number of steps allowed during the trace. Branch Divergence: Classic DDA implementations suffer from divergent execution on GPUs due to branching for different quadrants and iteration directions. This method avoids this by unifying cases via axis permutation. Banding Artifacts: Banding artifacts appear when using stride > 1.0 for efficiency. This is handled by applying a jitter value in [0, 1] to the ray. Out-of-Bounds Access: The method relies on implicit clipping to the viewport. If the depth buffer does not return zero for out-of-bounds accesses, the iteration may not terminate correctly. Time Complexity: The method performs a fixed number of steps up to maxSteps or maxDistance. Each step involves simple arithmetic operations (FMUL) and a texture lookup. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory is required beyond the depth buffer. The algorithm is designed to minimize register count and instruction cache pressure. Measured Performance: Used in production for reflections in ripply water, achieving 2 ms at 1080p on GeForce 650M. Strengths: Ensures sampling at a contiguous set of pixels with no oversampling, addressing the inefficiency and missing intersections of linear 3D marching. Efficient on GPUs due to branch unification and simple arithmetic. Limitations: Quality decreases with larger stride values, requiring jitter to mitigate banding. Relies on the caller to ensure the ray origin is within the view frustum. When to Use: Suitable for screen-space effects like reflections in ripply water where performance is critical and the depth buffer is available. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes requiring global illumination or complex ray-object intersections beyond the depth buffer. The underlying method of 2D iteration is about 20 years old, evolving from Bresenham's algorithm through DDA. Recent games brought details for reflection tracing and GPU optimizations. Wronski [2014a, 80][2014b] and Valient [2014b, 90][2014a] sketched algorithms in presentations. The method has been proven in production of recent major game titles. Efficient GPU screen-space ray tracing, https://jcgt.org/published/0003/04/04/paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: DDA Optimizations (Rejected/Retained)
head: Boundary event counts, DDA region traversal, Explicit zero-event guards, Per-ray subtree caching, Redundant floor removal
body: This family article catalogs specific algorithmic modifications to the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) ray traversal, evaluating their impact on CPU and GPU performance to determine which optimizations are retained in the final implementation. It distinguishes between successful optimizations that reduce computational overhead and rejected variants that introduce complexity or overhead that outweighs their benefits. The primary goal is to refine the traversal loop's efficiency by minimizing redundant calculations, improving cache locality, and reducing branch divergence, while maintaining exact surface intersection correctness. The optimizations in this family operate under the constraints of the parent family's shared principles: branch unification, memory coalescing, occupancy management, and implicit clipping. All retained optimizations must preserve the exact geometric correctness of surface intersections and image byte accumulation. Rejected optimizations are those where the reduction in traversal steps (e.g., fewer tree visits or skipped empty regions) was offset by increased per-step overhead, such as complex ownership checks, repeated CPU costs, or negative impacts on GPU warp efficiency. The evaluation methodology involves comparing cumulative CPU costs, actual work counters, and complete-frame measurements across CPU and GPU workloads, often using specific benchmark configurations (e.g., CPU1, CPU6, CPU12, GPU fork-seven) to isolate the impact of each change. This optimization compares upstream world representations to optimize how the DDA crosses compressed uniform regions. It aims to reduce the number of steps taken when traversing large empty or uniform volumes by leveraging the hierarchical structure of the world data. The optimization is documented in the region DDA profile, which records cumulative CPU costs and actual work counters. It is a retained optimization that improves performance by reducing unnecessary traversal steps in uniform areas. This optimization replaces the baseline binary search for event detection with a bounded estimate followed by an exact plane correction. This approach reduces the computational cost of finding the next voxel boundary while maintaining accuracy. It has been shown to provide repeated gains on CPU12 and separate GPU measurements. It is a retained optimization that improves traversal efficiency by avoiding the overhead of binary search. This optimization attempts to cache subtree information on a per-ray basis to reduce the number of tree visits required during traversal. However, it was rejected because the reduction in tree visits did not offset the added overhead of managing ownership and cache coherence. The retained DDA implementation remains unchanged, indicating that the baseline traversal is more efficient than this cached approach. This optimization involves checking for short-circuiting conditions where no events (intersections or exits) are expected, allowing the traversal to skip certain calculations. Four prototypes were tested. Broader guards were found to regress performance on the GPU, while the smallest guard avoided advancement plane calculations but introduced a repeated CPU cost. Consequently, the retained DDA implementation remains unchanged, as the trade-offs were not favorable. This optimization simplifies the retained event estimate by removing redundant floor operations. It preserves exact surfaces and image bytes while improving performance. GPU fork-seven measurements show improvements in two batches, although parallel CPU samples favor the baseline. It is a retained optimization that reduces computational overhead in the event estimation step. This optimization reuses the known integer limit for axes leaving a region to optimize boundary event detection. It preserves exact surfaces and image bytes and has been shown to improve performance on CPU1, CPU6, and CPU12 in repeated complete-window measurements. However, GPU gains remain inconclusive. It is a retained optimization that leverages known limits to reduce calculation overhead. The optimizations described in this family are derived from the development and profiling of the Bend voxel renderer, specifically focusing on the DDA traversal component. The work is documented in a series of internal reports and documentation files within the aivv73/bend-voxel repository, including docs/dda-optimization.md, docs/dda-profile.md, docs/dda-estimate.md, docs/dda-cursor.md, docs/dda-zero.md, docs/dda-floor.md, and docs/dda-boundary.md. The evaluation involves a mix of CPU and GPU benchmarks, with specific attention to the trade-offs between algorithmic complexity and runtime performance. The goal is to identify the most efficient traversal strategy for rendering large voxel datasets. aivv73/bend-voxel, https://github.com/aivv73/bend-voxel, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Voxel DDA Raymarching with Midpoint Interpolation
head: DDA ray marching, sphere tracing (referenced as alternative), triangular prism method
body: Voxel DDA Raymarching with Midpoint Interpolation is a ray-terrain intersection technique for smooth heightfields represented by voxel corner volumes. It computes surface heights at voxel midpoints from adjacent corner values and linearly interpolates the ray's intersection point along the traversal edge. Unlike standard DDA which steps through discrete cells, this method refines the intersection within a single voxel using midpoint geometry, offering a balance between the speed of coarse traversal and the accuracy of continuous surface tracing. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D. Voxel grid of corner heights H{corner}(i,j,k). Voxel size V{size}. Entry UV coordinates on the voxel face where the ray enters. Outputs: Intersection UV coordinate u{intersect}. Intersection height y{intersect}. Boolean flag indicating hit or miss. Data Structures: midpoints: A vector or struct containing height values at the midpoints of voxel edges. Specifically, midpoints.y represents the height at the midpoint of the edge being traversed. entryuv: The UV coordinate where the ray enters the current voxel face. paralleluv: The UV coordinate parallel to the ray's primary traversal direction along the voxel face. perpendicularuv: The UV coordinate perpendicular to the ray's primary traversal direction, used for logic switching in the upper half of the voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Midpoint Height: For the edge being traversed, calculate the height at the midpoint using the two adjacent corner volumes: h{mid} = \frac{h{corner1} + h{corner2}}{2} 2. Determine Traversal Logic Branch: Check the Z-component of the entry UV coordinate (entry\uv.z) to determine the traversal logic branch. If entry\uv.z < 0.5: Use "normal" logic (lower half). If entry\uv.z \ge 0.5: Use "perpendicular" logic (upper half). 3. Calculate Intersection Percentage: Determine how far along the voxel edge the ray intersects the surface. This is done by comparing the ray's Y-coordinate (ray\y) against the side value (h{side}) and the midpoint value (h{mid}). p = \frac{ray\y - h{side}}{h{mid} - h{side}} Note: h{side} is the height of the corner at the start of the edge segment being considered. 4. Compute Final Intersection UV: Interpolate between the entry UV and the parallel UV using the calculated percentage p. u{intersect} = entry\uv + p \times (parallel\uv - entry\uv) Alternatively, using the specific formula provided in sources: u{intersect} = entry\uv + \frac{midpoints.y - entry\uv.y}{midpoints.y - midpoints.x.y} \times (parallel\uv - entry\uv) Clarification: The source formula notation is ambiguous. The logical interpretation is linear interpolation based on height difference. 5. Ray Height Comparison: Compare the ray's Y-coordinate at the current step against the intersection height. If ray\y > h{intersect}: The ray is above the surface. Continue marching to the next voxel/step. If ray\y \le h{intersect}: The ray has hit or passed below the surface. Return the color at u{intersect} and break. 6. Logic Switching (Upper Half): If the traversal logic branch is "perpendicular" (entry\uv.z \ge 0.5): Switch from using paralleluv to perpendicularuv for the interpolation direction. Adjust the starting point reference to ensure consistent reading direction regardless of ray entry angle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelddamidpointinterpolation(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, voxelsize): """ Performs Voxel DDA Raymarching with Midpoint Interpolation. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) voxelgrid: 3D array of corner heights voxelsize: float, size of one voxel Returns: intersectionuv: (u, v) or None if no hit """ # Initialize ray parameters t = 0.0 currentpos = rayorigin # Determine initial voxel and entry UV # Standard DDA initialization to find first voxel intersection voxelcoords = worldtovoxel(currentpos) entryuv = computeentryuv(currentpos, raydirection, voxelcoords, voxelsize) while True: # 1. Compute Midpoint Height # Identify the two corners defining the edge being traversed # Logic to select corner1 and corner2 based on traversal direction and entryuv corner1height = getcornerheight(voxelgrid, voxelcoords, cornerindex1) corner2height = getcornerheight(voxelgrid, voxelcoords, cornerindex2) midpointheight = (corner1height + corner2height) / 2.0 # 2. Determine Traversal Logic Branch isupperhalf = entryuv.z >= 0.5 # 3. Calculate Intersection Percentage # Get the side value (height at the start of the edge segment) sideheight = getsideheight(voxelgrid, voxelcoords, isupperhalf) # Get ray Y at current t rayy = rayorigin.y + raydirection.y t # Avoid division by zero denom = midpointheight - sideheight if abs(denom) < 1e-6: # Degenerate case: flat surface percentage = 0.0 else: percentage = (rayy - sideheight) / denom # Clamp percentage to [0, 1] for safety percentage = max(0.0, min(1.0, percentage)) # 4. Compute Final Intersection UV if isupperhalf: # Use perpendicular UV logic paralleluv = entryuv.perpendicularuv # Adjust entry point reference if necessary # Ensure consistent start/end reference baseuv = entryuv.paralleluv # Switched base else: # Use normal logic paralleluv = entryuv.paralleluv baseuv = entryuv intersectuv = baseuv + percentage (paralleluv - baseuv) # 5. Ray Height Comparison # Calculate the height of the surface at the intersection point # Interpolate surface height at intersectuv using corner heights surfaceheight = interpolatesurfaceheight(voxelgrid, voxelcoords, intersectuv) if rayy > surfaceheight: # Ray is above surface, continue marching # Advance ray to next voxel boundary t = advanceraytonextvoxel(rayorigin, raydirection, t, voxelcoords, voxelsize) voxelcoords = updatevoxelcoords(voxelcoords, raydirection) entryuv = computeentryuv(rayorigin + raydirection t, raydirection, voxelcoords, voxelsize) else: # Ray has hit the surface return intersectuv, surfaceheight Parameters: entryuv: The UV coordinate where the ray enters the voxel face. paralleluv: The UV coordinate parallel to the ray's traversal direction along the voxel face. perpendicularuv: The UV coordinate perpendicular to the ray's traversal direction, used when switching logic for the upper voxel half. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Entry Direction Ambiguity: The algorithm must consistently read from the same starting point to the same ending point regardless of whether the ray enters from above, below, or the side. Failure to fix the start/end reference causes incorrect interpolation. Boundary Threshold at 0.5: The entryuv.z < 0.5 check splits the voxel traversal logic. Crossing this threshold requires switching from parallel UV to perpendicular UV and adjusting the entry point reference, otherwise the intersection math breaks. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel step, with a constant number of arithmetic operations for midpoint calculation and interpolation. Total complexity depends on the number of voxels traversed, similar to standard DDA. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as it only stores current voxel coordinates and UV values. Strengths: Provides smoother terrain representation than nearest-neighbor methods by using midpoint interpolation. Simpler to implement than full continuous ray marching. Limitations: Accuracy is limited by the voxel resolution and the linear interpolation assumption. May exhibit artifacts if the terrain has high-frequency details smaller than the voxel size. When to Use: Suitable for real-time terrain rendering where performance is critical but some smoothness is desired. When Not to Use: Not suitable for highly detailed or non-smooth terrains where higher-order interpolation or continuous ray marching is required. The method is described in an unofficial video tutorial on smooth terrain rendering using voxel DDA raymarching. It references sphere tracing as an alternative approach but focuses on a DDA-based traversal with midpoint interpolation for terrain heightfields. The technique appears to be a practical implementation for game development or real-time graphics, emphasizing simplicity and performance over theoretical optimality. name: Z-order curve traversal with run-length encoding
head: Morton order traversal, Z-curve RLE stream
body: This method traverses a uniform voxel grid in Z-order (Morton) sequence while compressing contiguous runs of identical voxel values into run-length encoded (RLE) records, thereby skipping redundant sampling steps. It uses a flat, stack-based iteration over a padded power-of-two grid structure rather than ray-based advancement or hierarchical tree navigation. Inputs: A uniform voxel grid of dimensions W \times H \times D. Outputs: A stream of IndexedLeaf records, each containing a voxel value and the starting linear index of the run. Data Structures: The traversal state is maintained in a ZStream object and a stack of ZFrame objects. 1. ZFrame struct: size (unsigned int): The side length of the current cube in the Z-order hierarchy. offset (3-component integer vector): Stores the x, y, z coordinates of the cube's origin. i (uint8t): An iterator counter (0–7) tracking which of the 8 children of the current node has been visited. 2. ZStream class fields: model (pointer to voxel data): Reference to the voxel data source. index (unsigned integer): The current linear index in the Z-order stream. open (bool): Flag indicating if the stream has more data. streamleaf (voxel value): The value of the most recently fetched voxel. stack (stack of ZFrame): The traversal stack. power (unsigned int): The exponent such that 2^{power} is the padded grid dimension. streamsize (unsigned integer): The total number of voxels in the padded grid (2^{3 \cdot power}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute power as \lceil \log2(\max(W, H, D)) \rceil and streamsize as 2^{3 \cdot power}. 2. Initialize the stack with a root ZFrame: size = 2^{power}, offset = (0,0,0), i = 0. 3. Initialize index = 0, open = true, and fetch the first voxel using nextcoords() to populate streamleaf. 4. Loop while open is true: call nextcoords() to get the next voxel position and fetch its value from model. 5. If the fetched value equals streamleaf, increment index and repeat the fetch until a different value is found or the stream ends. 6. If the value differs from streamleaf or the stream ends, return an IndexedLeaf containing the previous streamleaf value and the index where that run started, then update streamleaf to the new value and increment index. 7. Coordinate Generation (nextcoords): If frame.size == 1, return frame.offset, pop the frame, backtrack by popping frames where top.i >= 8, set open = false if the stack becomes empty, and increment index. Otherwise, compute childsize = frame.size / 2, determine the child offset by adding childsize to the x, y, or z axis if bits 4, 2, or 1 of frame.i are set, increment frame.i, push a new ZFrame with size = childsize, offset = childoffset, i = 0, and recurse. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nextcoords(stack, indexref): """Generates the next coordinate in Z-order traversal using a stack. Returns the coordinate tuple (x, y, z). Modifies stack and indexref.""" while True: frame = stack[-1] # Base case: leaf node if frame['size'] == 1: coord = frame['offset'] stack.pop() # Backtrack if all 8 children of the parent have been visited while len(stack) > 0 and stack[-1]['i'] >= 8: stack.pop() indexref[0] += 1 return coord # Recursive step: determine child childsize = frame['size'] // 2 childidx = frame['i'] # Calculate child offset based on bits 4, 2, 1 of frame.i offset = list(frame['offset']) # [x, y, z] if childidx & 4: offset[2] += childsize # z-axis if childidx & 2: offset[1] += childsize # y-axis if childidx & 1: offset[0] += childsize # x-axis frame['i'] += 1 # Push new frame for the child newframe = { 'size': childsize, 'offset': tuple(offset), 'i': 0 } stack.append(newframe) # Continue to the next level (simulating recursion) # Loop back to process the new top of the stack def traverserle(model, width, height, depth): """Main traversal function. Returns a list of (value, startindex) tuples.""" power = math.ceil(math.log2(max(width, height, depth))) streamsize = 2 (3 power) stack = [{'size': 2power, 'offset': (0, 0, 0), 'i': 0}] indexref = [0] # Mutable container for index open = True # Fetch first voxel firstcoord = nextcoords(stack, indexref) prevleaf = model.at(firstcoord) results = [] while open: currcoord = nextcoords(stack, indexref) currleaf = model.at(currcoord) if currleaf != prevleaf: results.append((prevleaf, indexref[0])) prevleaf = currleaf # If stack is empty, open becomes false inside nextcoords if not stack: open = False # Append the final run results.append((prevleaf, indexref[0])) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Power-of-Two Dimensions: The grid is padded to the next power of two with implicit empty voxels. Stack Depth: The traversal uses a stack-based iterative approach to simulate recursion, and the stack depth is bounded by the 8-children-per-node limit. Run Compression: If all voxels are identical, the RLE stream contains a single entry; if no runs exist, performance degrades to standard Z-order traversal overhead. Time Complexity: O(N) where N = 2^{3 \cdot power} is the number of voxels in the padded grid. Memory Complexity: O(\log N) for the traversal stack. Performance: Highly efficient for volumes with large homogeneous regions; performance degrades if the volume is noisy or lacks contiguous runs. Strengths: Simple stack-based implementation, predictable cache-friendly traversal pattern, and effective compression for coherent data. Limitations: Requires power-of-two padding which wastes memory for non-aligned dimensions, and is unsuitable for highly sparse data without significant overhead. The method is derived from the Zazen project by Gabriel Müller, which implements a Z-order curve traversal with run-length encoding for volume rendering. It leverages the spatial locality of Morton order to provide a predictable traversal pattern while compressing redundant data. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Octree and Tree Traversal
body: Octree and Tree Traversal methods determine which nodes of a hierarchical spatial structure (typically an octree or sparse voxel octree) a ray intersects, enabling efficient rendering of sparse volumetric data by skipping empty space. Unlike uniform grid ray marching which samples every voxel, these methods use the tree hierarchy to jump over empty regions, reducing computational cost. They differ from BVH-based approaches by operating directly on the octree structure without an intermediate bounding volume hierarchy, although some implementations may convert the SVO to a BVH for specific traversal optimizations. They build on the parent's Shared principles of analytically advancing from one cell boundary to the next. Tree traversal adds hierarchical navigation: 1. Child Selection: For a node with center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s, the ray position \mathbf{p} determines the child index k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(px \ge cx) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(py \ge cy) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(pz \ge cz) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 2. Empty Space Skipping: If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree. This is achieved by advancing the ray parameter t to the exit of the current node or using neighbor pointers to jump to the next potentially occupied node. 3. Leaf Handling: Upon reaching a leaf node, the method typically switches to a fixed-step traversal (like DDA) within the leaf's voxel grid to sample the volume data. 4. Backtracking: Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch. This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU). Precisely locates isosurface intersections on the edges of an adaptive octree's leaf cells and computes surface normals. It solves geometric inaccuracy in dual contouring by refining intersection positions to sub-cell accuracy for Quadratic Error Function (QEF) vertex placement, unlike Octree Path Computation which focuses on traversal efficiency. Eliminates the explicit stack data structure in hierarchical volume traversal by recalculating Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) parameters at every descent and ascent step. It trades increased computational cost for zero stack memory usage, making it advantageous in memory-constrained environments like early GPU architectures. Decouples branch-intensive octree traversal from the raycasting loop using a rasterization pass to identify active volume regions and a shadow mapping pass for lighting. It solves performance bottlenecks on sparse data by moving empty-space culling into a graphics pipeline stage, achieving 2 to 4 times faster rendering than state-of-the-art algorithms on large out-of-core datasets. Extends the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) algorithm to N-ary hierarchical trees for GPU shader implementation. It solves efficient traversal of sparse voxel structures by maintaining a small, fixed-size stack of DDA states, allowing descent and ascent without dynamic memory allocation. Minimizes computational cost for time-varying volume rendering by rendering only modified data subtrees and compositing them with retained partial images of unmodified data. It differs from standard incremental rendering by maintaining a persistent hierarchical structure that mirrors the data's compressed octree, enabling efficient spatial updates without full re-rendering. A hierarchical ray traversal algorithm designed to step a ray through a generic grid structure (such as OpenVDB) to identify intersections with active nodes. It solves efficient navigation of sparse, multi-resolution volumetric data by skipping empty subtrees and returning precise intersection intervals for occupied nodes, bridging coarse hierarchical culling and fine-grained voxel sampling. Constructs a spatial hierarchy by recursively splitting nodes based on the proximity of visible camera centers to the node's center. It solves efficient mapping of 3D space into local warp spaces for multi-view rendering by ensuring regions near cameras are represented with higher resolution, using camera-centric distance metrics rather than data density. Performs type resolution and function routing at Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation time, inlining traversal, type checks, and address lookups to eliminate switch statements and runtime overhead. It sets itself apart from standard dynamic dispatch by making access time independent of the number of elemental node types, as specialized code paths are baked into the executable. A family of hierarchical methods that determine the sequence of nodes or cells intersected by a ray within a spatial data structure, primarily to accelerate volume rendering and surface intersection tests. This family is distinguished from Stackless Traversal by its explicit reliance on parent-child pointer relationships and backtracking logic rather than encoding traversal state into a bitstream. Generates a manifold isosurface from an adaptive octree by constructing a dual simplicial partition. It solves self-intersections and non-manifold vertices inherent in adaptive octrees by creating a dual structure that ensures convexity and manifold topology, unlike Dual Marching Tetrahedra (DMC) which can produce self-intersecting flaps. A GPU-based volume rendering technique for interactive visualization of dynamic particle systems (e.g., SPH) that reconstructs a scalar field via raycasting without preprocessing. It solves the performance bottleneck of gathering particle contributions by using three GPU-managed caches: a node-cache for accelerated tree traversal, an influence-cache for fast particle access, and a slab-cache for intermediate compositing. A hierarchical level-of-detail method for real-time large-scale Gaussian Splatting that reduces rendering cost by aggregating primitives into equivalent planks based on a pixel-footprint budget. It solves rendering millions of Gaussians in real-time by dynamically selecting between raw primitives, fine equivalent planks, or coarse aggregate planks depending on distance and scale relative to the camera. Accelerates ray-volume intersection by traversing a sparse octree structure to identify contiguous segments of active data. It solves inefficiently sampling empty space in large volumetric datasets by skipping inactive nodes and resolving hits at the node level rather than the individual voxel level, providing entry and exit times for line-integration. Optimizes volume rendering by identifying and discarding geometry that does not contribute to the final image, thereby reducing computational load. This family distinguishes itself from sibling traversal methods by decoupling visibility determination from the core sampling loop, often serving as a pre-pass or integrated filter to limit the working set of voxels, splats, or bricks. Defines how hierarchical volume data (typically octrees) is organized in memory and accessed during ray traversal. It solves efficiently mapping spatial coordinates to volume samples while minimizing memory bandwidth and traversal overhead, focusing on storage layout and connectivity required to support traversal algorithms. Generates signed-distance function (SDF) samples from a sparse octree acceleration structure constructed from a single mesh shape. It limits sampling to occupied octree cells, supports equal distribution of samples per cell, and allows online resampling via a cached narrowband pool, optionally including RGB data derived from mesh textures. Organizes volumetric or geometric primitives into a tree structure to accelerate ray intersection tests and point location. They solve the problem of O(N) linear scans by enabling O(\log N) traversal, reducing the number of samples required to render a volume, and adapt to data sparsity by skipping empty regions entirely. Accelerates volume rendering by using hierarchical error metrics stored in non-leaf octree nodes to skip or approximate low-entropy regions. Unlike standard traversal which visits all occupied nodes, this method dynamically adjusts traversal granularity based on a user-defined error tolerance or time budget, trading visual fidelity for performance in smooth or transparent areas. Store incoming radiance from a light source in the octree leaves by rendering the scene from the light's view using standard rasterization to output a world position map (light-view map), where each pixel represents a photon. Photons are splatted using a fragment shader with one thread per light-view-map pixel, storing them as a direction distribution and energy proportional to the subtended solid angle of the pixel as seen from the light. Atomic add operations are used to handle multiple photons ending up in the same voxel, though they are currently only available for integer textures, requiring a 16-bit normalized texture format denormalized upon access. Voxels are repeated for adjacent bricks for fast hardware-supported filtering, but copying photons directly to all required locations in adjacent bricks leads to many thread collisions and bandwidth issues. A rendering strategy that uses the tree representation to perform selective rendering efficiently, reducing I/O costs and enabling distribution of data and calculations to multiple workstations. It examines the encoded data to identify partial images built from subtrees which have not changed, and reuses the identified unchanged partial images in the following time steps. A smaller leaf-node size leads to less overlap of node lists between image tiles, but increases storage and traversal overhead. A storage format where the volume is stored as a flat hierarchy of bricks of size n^3 to improve cache-coherence, derived from fully expanded octrees. It uses an efficient indexing scheme to quickly find the memory address of voxels located in the 8-neighborhood required for trilinear interpolation. The use of octrees for volume rendering originated as a method to handle sparse data efficiently, reducing memory usage and traversal time compared to uniform grids. Early implementations focused on minimizing the number of transparent voxels during accumulation. The concept of using hierarchical structures for time-varying data was explored to reduce I/O costs and enable selective rendering, allowing unchanged subtrees to be reused across time steps. Modern implementations often combine these hierarchical traversal techniques with GPU-specific optimizations, such as stackless traversal or mini-stacks, to handle the parallel nature of volume rendering on graphics hardware. name: Stackless Traversal
head: Algorithme sans pile, Parcours sans pile, Parent-link traversal, Stack-less Tree Traversal
body: Stackless Traversal is a method for traversing hierarchical volume structures (such as N3-trees or octrees) that eliminates the need for an explicit stack data structure by recalculating Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) parameters at every descent and ascent. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack by relying on parent pointers stored within the hierarchy to navigate, trading memory usage for computational cost. This approach is particularly advantageous in memory-constrained environments, such as early GPU architectures where dynamic array indexing forced stack data into slow local memory. The algorithm traverses a hierarchical grid by maintaining the current ray state and navigating the tree structure using explicit parent links. Unlike stack-based methods that push and pop nodes, this method recalculates the ray's entry point and DDA deltas whenever it moves between a parent and child node. Input: Ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; Hierarchical volume structure where each node stores a pointer to its parent and its spatial bounds; Grid resolution and voxel size. Output: A sequence of visited nodes (bricks) and their corresponding traversal intervals [t{entry}, t{exit}] for volume integration. The hierarchical structure must support: 1. Parent Pointer: Each node contains a reference to its immediate parent node. 2. Child Pointer: Each node contains references to its children (if not a leaf). 3. Spatial Bounds: Each node stores its minimum and maximum coordinates (or index ranges) to define its voxel extent. 4. Node Type/Status: Flags indicating if the node is empty, a leaf (brick), or an internal node. For a uniform grid with voxel size v and dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz, the traversal relies on three key precomputed values per axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: 1. Step Direction (\text{step}i): \text{step}i = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } di > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} 2. Time/Distance Delta (\Delta ti): \Delta ti = \frac{vi}{|di|} \cdot \text{step}i If di = 0, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension, and the corresponding distance is treated as infinity. 3. Time/Distance to Next Boundary (t{max, i}): t{max, i} = \frac{\text{boundary}i - oi}{di} The initial boundary is determined by the starting voxel index. 1. Initialization: Compute initial DDA parameters (\text{step}, \Delta t, t{max}) for the ray origin within the root node's bounds. Identify the starting leaf node containing the ray origin. 2. Process Current Node: If the current node is empty, skip it and proceed to the next step (ascent). If the current node is a leaf (brick): Perform ray marching within the brick's volume. If data is unavailable (e.g., dynamic loading failure), use the stored average and accumulate it based on the distance traversed by the ray in that brick (pre-integration). If the current node is an internal node, proceed to navigation. 3. Navigation (Descent/Ascent): Ascent: If the ray exits the current node, use the parent pointer stored in the structure to move to the parent node. This link points directly to the exact sub-node of the parent, allowing extraction of the current cell information in the parent's grid without recalculation. Descent: If the ray enters a child node, recalculate all DDA parameters (\text{step}, \Delta t, t{max}) for the new node. 4. Loop: Repeat steps 2-3 until the ray exits the entire volume hierarchy. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stacklesstraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, voxelsize): # DDA initialization step = [1 if d > 0 else (-1 if d < 0 else 0) for d in raydirection] tdelta = [voxelsize / abs(d) if d != 0 else float('inf') for d in raydirection] # Find initial leaf node containing rayorigin currentnode = findleaf(rootnode, rayorigin) currentrayt = 0.0 while currentnode is not None: # Compute distance to next boundary on each axis for current node tmax = computetmax(rayorigin, raydirection, currentnode.bounds, step, tdelta) # Exit time from current node texit = min(tmax) # Process node based on type if currentnode.isempty: # Skip empty node, advance ray to exit currentrayt += texit rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection texit # Ascent: move to parent via stored pointer currentnode = currentnode.parent continue if currentnode.isleaf: # Ray march within brick bounds processbrick(currentnode, rayorigin, raydirection, texit) currentrayt += texit rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection texit # Ascent: move to parent via stored pointer currentnode = currentnode.parent continue # Internal node: descend to child containing ray # Child index from ray position relative to node center center = currentnode.center childidx = 4 (rayorigin.x >= center.x) + 2 (rayorigin.y >= center.y) + (rayorigin.z >= center.z) # Descent: move to child currentnode = currentnode.children[childidx] # Recalculate all DDA parameters for the new child node tmax = computetmax(rayorigin, raydirection, currentnode.bounds, step, tdelta) # Advance ray to child entry point tentry = min(tmax) currentrayt += tentry rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection tentry return def findleaf(root, point): node = root while not node.isleaf: center = node.center idx = 4 (point.x >= center.x) + 2 (point.y >= center.y) + (point.z >= center.z) node = node.children[idx] return node def computetmax(origin, direction, bounds, step, tdelta): tmax = [] for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: tmax.append(float('inf')) else: boundary = bounds.max[i] if step[i] > 0 else bounds.min[i] tmax.append((boundary - origin[i]) / direction[i]) return tmax def processbrick(leaf, origin, direction, texit): # Standard fixed-step sampling within leaf bounds [tentry, texit] pass Conditional Block Size: Limit the size of if...then...else bodies to reduce divergent threads on GPU multiprocessors. Register Usage: Limit the number of registers used to allow multiprocessors to handle more parallel threads, better covering texture access latency. GPU Memory Latency: On architectures like the NVIDIA G80, dynamically indexed arrays are placed in "local" memory (device memory), which is uncached and up to 50x slower than registers. This negatively impacts performance compared to register-based stack access. Local memory accesses incur maximum latency and transfer cost from graphics memory. Zero Direction Components: When di = 0, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension, and the corresponding distance is treated as infinity to prevent division by zero. A variant for BVHs that uses a bit-array to track processed subtrees, allowing complete stack exhaustion without state loss. Choose this when memory is extremely constrained and restarts are frequent. Time Complexity: Higher per-node computational cost due to DDA recalculation at every ascent/descent. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary stack space (excluding the tree structure itself). Performance: On the NVIDIA G80 GPU, the stackless algorithm was approximately 50% faster than the mini-stack algorithm. This result is attributed to the G80's shader compiler placing dynamically indexed arrays (used for the stack) in slow, uncached local memory, whereas the stackless method kept data in registers or faster memory spaces. Strengths: No stack overflow risk; minimal memory footprint; efficient on hardware with slow local memory for dynamic arrays. Limitations: Higher arithmetic intensity per node visit; requires parent pointers in the data structure. When to Use: Memory-constrained environments (e.g., embedded systems, early GPUs); scenarios where stack depth is unpredictable or large. When Not to Use: Hardware with fast, cached local memory and efficient stack operations; scenes with very shallow hierarchies where recalculation overhead outweighs stack costs. The Stackless Traversal algorithm was developed and tested for traversing hierarchical volume structures (N3-tree/octree). It was designed to address the limitations of stack-based methods on early GPU architectures (specifically the G80) where dynamic memory indexing was penalized by the hardware compiler. The method leverages parent pointers stored in the hierarchical structure to navigate without a stack, recalculating DDA parameters to maintain correctness. name: Restart Trail
head: Generalized Restart Trail, Restart Trail for Wide BVHs, Short Stack BVH Traversal, Short stack traversal with restart trail, Wide BVH Traversal with Short Stack, Wide BVH Traversal with a Short Stack
body: Restart Trail is a stackless or short-stack traversal algorithm for Bounding Volume Hierarchies (BVHs) that enables traversal restarts from the root by storing one bit of data per hierarchy level to track which parts of the tree have been processed. It sets itself apart from standard short-stack traversal by allowing the stack to be completely exhausted without losing traversal state, using a compact bit-array (the "trail") to resume from the correct point, whereas methods like Stack Culling trade a small increase in traversal steps for reduced primitive intersections using only 1 bit of extra storage per stack entry. It solves the problem of memory-constrained traversal (e.g., in hardware or GPUs) where a full stack is too large, by replacing the stack with a fixed-size short stack and a restart mechanism that avoids re-entering already processed subtrees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray, an N-wide BVH (where N is the number of children per internal node), and a short stack of fixed size (typically 5 entries). Output: The closest intersection (for closest-hit) or all intersections (for any-hit), traversing the BVH. Data Structures: 1. Restart Trail (trail): An array of bits (for binary BVHs) or counters (for N-wide BVHs) with one entry per hierarchy level. For binary BVHs: trail is a single register (trailReg) of 32 or 64 bits. trail[0] is a sentinel. trail[i] corresponds to the node at level i. For N-wide BVHs: trail[i] is a counter ranging from 0 to N-1. trail[i] stores the number of children at level i already processed. N-1 indicates the current subtree is the last child at that level. 2. Level Register (levelReg): A register with exactly one bit set, corresponding to the bit position in trailReg pointing to the parent of the current node. Initialized to 10000... (1 followed by zeros) for the sentinel. 3. Short Stack: A fixed-size array of node references. Each entry may include a reserved bit to mark if the entry corresponds to the last child of its parent node. 4. Pop Level (popLevel): An integer tracking the level where the last stack pop would have taken the traversal. Initialized to NONE. Parameters: N: The width of the BVH (number of children per internal node). Short Stack Size: A small fixed number of entries (e.g., 5) stored in on-chip memory. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set node to ROOT. Set trail to all zeros (or counters to 0). Set level to 0. Set shortstack to empty. Set popLevel to NONE. 2. Traversal Loop: While the current node is not a leaf: a. Intersect Children: Intersect the ray against all children of node. Let H be the list of intersecting children. b. Sort: Sort H by increasing hit distance to obtain sorted list S. c. Handle Multiple Hits (Binary BVH Logic): If both children are intersected: Identify near child (smaller t{min}) and far child (greater t{min}). Increment level (shift levelReg right by 1). If trail[level] is 1 (bit set): Set node to far. (The near child has been fully processed or skipped). Else: Set node to near. Push far onto the short stack. If only one child is intersected: Increment level. If level \neq popLevel: Set trail[level] to 1. Set node to the intersected child. Else (level == popLevel): Invoke POP(). This handles the case where the far child was culled during the processing of the near child. If no children are intersected: Invoke POP(). d. Handle Multiple Hits (N-wide BVH Logic): Let k = \text{trail}[\text{level}]. If k = N-1: Remove all but the last entry in S to form Q. (Current subtree is the last one). Else: Remove the first k entries in S to form Q. (Skip already processed children). If Q is empty: Call POP(trail, level). Else: Set node to the first entry in Q. Remove the first entry from Q. If Q is empty: Set trail[level] to N-1. Else: Mark the last entry in Q as the "last child" and push remaining entries in Q onto the short stack (back-to-front order). 3. Leaf Processing: Intersect the ray against primitives in the leaf node. If a closer primitive is found, shorten the ray at the end. Invoke POP(). 4. POP() Operation: Find Parent Level: Scan the restart trail upwards from the current level. Skip levels with the max count value (N-1 for wide BVHs, or bit=1 for binary BVHs where it indicates completion). Find the largest i \le \text{level} such that trail[i] is 0 (binary) or < N-1 (wide). If no such level exists (all scanned levels are maxed), the stack is empty and traversal is complete. Update Trail: Increment trail[parentLevel] (wide BVH) or set trail[parentLevel] to 1 (binary BVH). Clear all counters/bits below parentLevel to 0. Update State: If short stack is empty: Set node to ROOT, level to 0. Restart traversal. Else: Pop from short stack. If popped node is tagged as "last child": Set trail[parentLevel] to N-1 (wide BVH). If popped node is tagged as "parent node" (Stack Culling extension): Set level to parentLevel. Else: Set level to parentLevel + 1. Save Pop Level: If a node's near child is marked as fully processed (bit set in trail for binary, or counter incremented for wide), save the level of that node into popLevel. Pseudocode (N-wide BVH, generalizing): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def restarttrailtraverse(ray, root, bvhwidth, maxdepth, shortstacksize=5): # Initialization trail = [0] maxdepth level = 0 node = root shortstack = [] while True: # Traverse down while not node.isleaf(): # Intersect children hits = [] for child in node.children: t = ray.intersect(child.bvhnode) if t is not None: hits.append((t, child)) # Sort by hit distance hits.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Skip already processed children k = trail[level] if k == bvhwidth - 1: # Current subtree is the last one, keep only the last child q = hits[-1:] if hits else [] else: # Skip first k children q = hits[k:] if not q: # Stack underflow, pop node, level, shortstack, done = pop(trail, level, shortstack, bvhwidth, root) if done: return None continue # Proceed to next node node = q[0][1] q.pop(0) if not q: trail[level] = bvhwidth - 1 else: # Mark last child and push to stack q[-1][1].islastchild = True # Push back-to-front for childnode, in reversed(q): if len(shortstack) < shortstacksize: shortstack.append(childnode) # Leaf processing tleaf, primitive = ray.intersectleaf(node) if tleaf is not None and tleaf < ray.tmax: ray.tmax = tleaf # Pop after leaf node, level, shortstack, done = pop(trail, level, shortstack, bvhwidth, root) if done: return None # Check if we restarted to root and finished if level == 0 and node == root and trail[0] == bvhwidth - 1: break def pop(trail, level, shortstack, bvhwidth, root): # Find parent level: scan upwards from level-1, skip levels with max count parentlevel = -1 for i in range(level - 1, -1, -1): if trail[i] < bvhwidth - 1: parentlevel = i break if parentlevel < 0: return root, 0, [], True # Stack empty, traversal complete # Increment counter at parent level trail[parentlevel] += 1 # Clear counters below parent level for i in range(parentlevel + 1, len(trail)): trail[i] = 0 if not shortstack: # Restart from root return root, 0, [], False else: node = shortstack.pop() if node.islastchild: trail[parentlevel] = bvhwidth - 1 level = parentlevel + 1 return node, level, shortstack, False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Traversal Order: Must be front-to-back (closest first) for closest-hit searches. If a child is culled because a closer hit was found, it must not be counted as 'processed' in the restart trail counter, otherwise the restart will skip it incorrectly. Culled Far Child: When a node has two intersecting children, but the far child becomes culled during the processing of the near child (due to ray shortening), the algorithm must detect this via popLevel to avoid re-entering the near branch. If level equals popLevel in the single-child branch, it indicates the far child was culled, and POP() must be invoked. Precision: Care must be taken to ensure that equal t values after a restart do not cause re-entering already processed branches, leading to infinite loops. A technique that pushes the parent node onto the stack instead of multiple children when multiple children intersect and at least one is a leaf. The parent is re-intersected later to cull children with hit distances greater than the current closest hit. It sets itself apart from standard short-stack traversal by trading a small increase in traversal steps (1-7%) for a reduction in primitive intersections (2-14%), using only 1 bit of extra storage per stack entry instead of storing hit distances for every entry. Time Complexity: Traversal steps increase by 1-10% for closest-hit queries and 0-5% for any-hit queries compared to a full stack. Stackless traversal (no short stack) visits approximately 2.2–2.4 times as many nodes as ordinary traversal with a full stack. A short stack with just one entry reduces this multiplier to 1.3–1.4. Memory Complexity: Uses ~3x less memory than a full stack. For a short stack of 5 entries, storage is < 44 bytes (Root: 64 bits, Current Node: 32 bits, Restart Trail: 3x32 bits, Current Depth: 5 bits, Short Stack: 5x32 bits). A full stack for a max depth of 32 requires 136 bytes. Performance: Preliminary tests on NVIDIA G80 and GT200 hardware indicate that memory bandwidth benefits of short stacks may not outweigh costs of restarts, SIMD divergence, and extra instructions. However, it is well-suited for hardware hierarchy traversal units where registers are limited. Strengths: Compact memory footprint, no need for parent pointers or hash lookups in BVH nodes, simpler implementation than stackless backtracking methods. Limitations: Restart overhead increases with smaller stack sizes. Slightly higher extraneous node visits compared to kd-trees due to BVH child overlap causing more stack pushes. Restart Trail was introduced by Tero Laine in 2010. It generalizes the restart trail algorithm for binary BVHs to BVHs of arbitrary widths, as proposed by Scheuermann et al.. It is used in real-time ray tracing, particularly in hardware acceleration units and GPU ray cast kernels where memory bandwidth and on-chip storage are critical constraints. name: Stack Culling (Parent Node Re-intersection)
head: Short Stack Culling
body: Stack culling is a technique for stackless or short-stack ray traversal that reduces expensive ray-primitive intersection tests by deferring the processing of multiple intersecting children. Instead of pushing all intersecting children onto the stack, the algorithm pushes the parent node itself when multiple children intersect and at least one is a leaf. The parent is re-intersected later to cull children with hit distances greater than the current closest hit. It sets itself apart from standard short-stack traversal by trading a small increase in traversal steps (1-7%) for a reduction in primitive intersections (2-14%), using only 1 bit of extra storage per stack entry instead of storing hit distances for every entry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray, BVH (N-wide), short stack, restart trail. Output: Closest hit distance (for closest-hit) or all hits (for any-hit). Data Structures: Short Stack: Stores node references. Each entry includes a flag bit to mark if the node is a "parent node". Restart Trail: An array of counters, one per hierarchy level, tracking how many children at each level have been processed. Current Depth: Tracks the current level in the tree. Steps: 1. Intersection Check: For an internal N-wide node, compute intersections between the N child bounding boxes and the ray to find a list H of intersecting children. 2. Sorting: Sort H based on increasing hit distance to obtain a sorted list S. 3. Restart Handling: If traversal restarts from the root, remove the first k nodes from S (where k is the count value at the current level in the restart trail) to avoid re-traversing previously processed children. 4. Stack Culling Decision: If the number of intersecting children is greater than 2 AND at least one child is a leaf: Push the parent node onto the short stack, tagged as a "parent node". Continue traversal with the closest child (first in S). Otherwise: Push the intersecting children onto the short stack in back-to-front order (excluding the closest child, which is traversed next). Tag the last child pushed as the "last child" to update the restart trail correctly. 5. Stack Pop (Re-intersection): When popping from the stack, if the node is tagged as a "parent node": Set the current depth to the depth of the parent node. Re-intersect the parent node's children against the ray. Use the restart trail to skip children that were already traversed. Cull any child whose hit distance is greater than the current closest hit distance found so far. If the node is not a parent node, proceed with standard traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseray(ray, bvh, shortstack, restarttrail, maxlevel): # Initialize currentnode = bvh.root currentlevel = 0 while True: # Get children intersections children = currentnode.children intersections = [] for child in children: hitdist = rayintersectbvhbox(ray, child.bbox) if hitdist is not None: intersections.append((hitdist, child)) # Sort by distance intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Apply restart trail to skip already processed children k = restarttrail[currentlevel] validintersections = intersections[k:] if not validintersections: # No new children to process, pop from stack if not shortstack: return None # No more hits node, isparent, islast = shortstack.pop() if isparent: # Re-intersect parent node currentlevel = findparentlevel(restarttrail, currentlevel) restarttrail[currentlevel] += 1 resettrail(restarttrail, currentlevel + 1, maxlevel) # Re-evaluate children of this parent # Note: In a real implementation, this might loop back to intersection step # or directly process the re-intersection results. # For simplicity, we assume the loop continues to re-evaluate 'node' currentnode = node continue else: if islast: restarttrail[currentlevel] = len(children) - 1 currentnode = node currentlevel += 1 continue # Stack Culling Logic # If > 2 children intersect and at least one is a leaf if len(validintersections) > 2 and any(child.isleaf for, child in validintersections): # Push parent instead of children shortstack.append((currentnode, isparent=True, islast=False)) # Continue with closest child nextdist, nextnode = validintersections[0] currentnode = nextnode currentlevel += 1 else: # Standard short stack push # Push remaining children in back-to-front order for dist, child in reversed(validintersections[1:]): islast = (child == validintersections[-1][1]) shortstack.append((child, isparent=False, islast=islast)) # Continue with closest child nextdist, nextnode = validintersections[0] currentnode = nextnode currentlevel += 1 # Update restart trail if this is the last child if nextnode == validintersections[-1][1]: restarttrail[currentlevel] = len(children) - 1 def findparentlevel(trail, currentlevel): # Find the highest level with a non-max count to determine parent level # Simplified logic based on for i in range(currentlevel, -1, -1): if trail[i] < len(bvh.childrencount[i]) - 1: return i return -1 def resettrail(trail, startlevel, maxlevel): for i in range(startlevel, maxlevel + 1): trail[i] = 0 Parameters: Short stack size: Typically 5 entries. Additional storage: 1 bit per stack entry. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Front-to-back ordering: Strictly required for closest-hit searches to ensure culling logic remains consistent with restart trail counters. Not required for any-hit searches. Precision: Re-intersection may introduce slight numerical differences, but the culling logic relies on distance comparisons. Degenerate Input: If all children are leaves, the culling condition (>2 children and at least one leaf) may not trigger, falling back to standard behavior. An extension that culls leaf node entries on the stack when a closer intersection has been found, skipping expensive primitive intersection tests for further nodes. During traversal, the current hit distance is updated every time a ray intersects a leaf node. Subsequent child node intersections at a distance greater than the current hit distance are culled. When an internal node is re-visited after a restart, children that previously intersected the ray but are now further than the current hit are also culled. Front-to-back ordering is strictly required for closest-hit searches to ensure culling logic remains consistent with restart trail counters. It is not required for any-hit searches. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Approximately 3x less than a full stack. With a short stack of 5 entries, storage is less than 44 bytes (root 64 bits, current node 32 bits, restart trail 3x32 bits, current depth 5 bits, stack entries 5x32 bits). A full stack with max depth 32 requires 136 bytes. Time: Overhead in traversal steps is 1-10% for closest-hit queries and 0-5% for any-hit queries with a short stack of 5 entries. Quad intersections are reduced by 2-14%. Measured Performance: Evaluated with different path traced scenes. Restart overhead is at most 10% with a short stack of 5 entries. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant memory reduction, reduced primitive intersections. Limitations: Slight increase in traversal steps, requires front-to-back ordering for closest-hit. When to Use: Use when memory is constrained and primitive intersection cost is high. Not recommended when traversal step overhead is unacceptable or when any-hit queries are the primary use case (though it still works, the benefit is less pronounced). Originated in the paper "Wide BVH Traversal with a Short Stack". The technique leverages the generalized restart trail mechanism to cull leaf node entries on the stack for closest-hit searches. It addresses the trade-off between memory usage and traversal efficiency in BVH ray casting.
