name: GPU Octree Volume Rasterization with Shadow Mapping
head: asvo renderer, voxel-based octree traversal
body: This method implements high-performance GPU volume rendering by decoupling the branch-intensive octree traversal from the raycasting loop, using a rasterization pass to identify active volume regions and a shadow mapping pass for lighting. It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional raycasting on sparse data by moving empty-space culling into a graphics pipeline stage, achieving 2 to 4 times faster rendering speeds than state-of-the-art algorithms on large out-of-core datasets. Unlike sibling methods that rely on pure ray-tracing traversal or fixed-step DDA, this approach uses view-dependent proxy geometry rasterization to generate a per-pixel list of penetrated bricks, ensuring front-to-back processing and tighter ray segments. It builds on Octree and Tree Traversal and relates to Stackless Traversal and DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack. The method operates in two main phases: a traversal/rasterization phase to identify active volume regions, and a rendering phase that may include a shadow map pass. Inputs: Octree structure composed of bricks, where each brick is split into regular macrocells. Frame dimensions: mwindowWidth, mwindowHeight. Camera and light parameters. Job queue for parallel traversal managed via a device pointer. Outputs: Final color buffer (via PBO/Texture). Shadow map (if shadow pass is enabled). Traversal Queue: A device pointer dTravQueuePtr used to manage parallel traversal jobs. It is initialized to hEndIndex before traversal begins. Depth Buffer Texture: Configured with cudaTextureDesc: addressMode[0] = cudaAddressModeClamp. filterMode = cudaFilterModePoint. normalizedCoords = false. readMode = cudaReadModeElementType. Shadow Map: Stores minimum depth values. Initialized with minDepth = 2147483647. 1. Initialization: Set hStartIndex = 0 and hEndIndex = obj.data()->jobs().size(). Initialize dTravQueuePtr[0] = hEndIndex. Initialize octreeLevel to 0. 2. Traversal Loop: While hEndIndex - hStartIndex > 0: 1. Launch the traverse kernel with job range [hStartIndex, hEndIndex) and current octreeLevel. 2. Update hStartIndex = hEndIndex. 3. Update hEndIndex = dTravQueuePtr[0]. 4. Increment octreeLevel. Pitfall: If dTravQueuePtr[0] is not updated correctly by the kernel, the loop may infinite loop or terminate prematurely. 3. Rendering Pass: If shadowPass is true: 1. Launch drawShadowMap kernel. 2. Pitfall: If no voxels are found, minDepth remains 2147483647 and shadowMap[index] is not written. Else: 1. Launch draw kernel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. dtravqueueptr = [0] def renderframe(model, camera, light, windowwidth, windowheight): # 1. Initialize traversal state hstartindex = 0 hendindex = model.jobs().size() dtravqueueptr[0] = hendindex octreelevel = 0 # 2. Parallel Traversal Loop while hendindex - hstartindex > 0: # Launch traverse kernel for current job range and depth traversekernel( jobstart=hstartindex, jobend=hendindex, level=octreelevel, camera=camera, model=model, queueptr=dtravqueueptr) # Update indices based on device queue pointer hstartindex = hendindex hendindex = dtravqueueptr[0] octreelevel += 1 # 3. Rendering Pass shadowpassenabled = True # Controlled by application state if shadowpassenabled: # Shadow map generation drawshadowmapkernel( camera=camera, light=light, model=model, mindepthinit=2147483647) else: # Direct volume rendering drawkernel( camera=camera, light=light, model=model) def traversekernel(jobstart, jobend, level, camera, model, queueptr): # Standard GPU kernel launch pattern # Processes jobs in [jobstart, jobend) at given octree depth # Updates queueptr[0] with next batch index upon completion pass def drawshadowmapkernel(camera, light, model, mindepthinit): # Standard GPU kernel launch pattern # Renders shadow map using mindepthinit as initial depth value pass def drawkernel(camera, light, model): # Standard GPU kernel launch pattern # Renders final color buffer pass A GPU-based high-quality volume rendering approach for large out-of-core volume data that reduces rendering time by moving branch-intensive accelerating structure traversal out of the GPU raycasting loop and introducing efficient empty-space culling via rasterization. It stores the volume in an octree of bricks, further splitting every brick into regular macrocells. The method rasterizes proxy geometry of a view-dependent cut of octree nodes to capture penetrated bricks in a per-pixel list in front-to-back order. This allows raycasting to occur only inside tighter ray segments, achieving two levels of empty space skipping (brick and macrocell). It achieved 2 to 4 times faster rendering speed than current state-of-the-art algorithms across various datasets. Performance: Achieves 2 to 4 times faster rendering speed than state-of-the-art algorithms on large out-of-core datasets. Complexity: Reduces branch divergence by moving traversal out of the raycasting loop. Memory: Requires storage for octree bricks and macrocells. Strengths: Efficient empty-space culling, suitability for large out-of-core data, reduced GPU branch intensity. Limitations: Complexity of managing rasterization-based culling and proxy geometry generation. When to use: Large out-of-core volume datasets where traditional raycasting traversal is a bottleneck. The method originates from research on GPU-based high-quality volume rendering of large out-of-core volume data, focusing on reducing rendering time by optimizing ray traversal costs. The "asvo" implementation provides a CUDA-based reference for this approach. denniskb/asvo, https://github.com/denniskb/asvo, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) accelerating high-quality out-of-core GPU volume rendering, https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22778151/, fetched 2026-10-29 (abstract only, unofficial)

name: Tile-based Octree Traversal
head: Tile-based rendering with octree
body: Tile-based Octree Traversal accelerates volume rendering by grouping rays into image tiles and pre-computing the set of octree nodes intersecting each tile. Unlike standard per-ray traversal, it reduces redundant node visits by sharing traversal state across rays within a tile, leveraging spatial coherence. It builds on Octree and Tree Traversal by batching the hierarchical descent. Inputs: An octree structure (root node, child pointers, empty-space flags), volume data (at leaf nodes), image resolution, tile dimensions (e.g., 8 \times 8 or 16 \times 16 pixels). Outputs: Rendered image buffer. Data Structures: 1. Octree Node: Contains a bounding box (min/max or center/half-extent), a flag indicating if the node is empty/uniform, and pointers to children (or a leaf data pointer). 2. Tile Node List: A list of pointers to octree nodes that intersect the tile's frustum. This list is pre-computed or updated incrementally. Steps: 1. Tile Frustum Construction: For each tile, define a viewing frustum based on the camera parameters and the tile's pixel coordinates. 2. Tile Node List Generation: Traverse the octree to find all nodes intersecting the tile frustum. Store these nodes in the tile's node list. Optimization: Use the empty-space skipping principle from the parent. If a node is empty and does not intersect the tile frustum, skip its subtree. Leaf Size Trade-off: A smaller leaf-node size results in less overlap of node lists between adjacent tiles, reducing redundant processing, but increases storage and traversal overhead for the lists themselves. 3. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the tile, generate a ray from the camera origin through the pixel center. 4. Tile-Aware Traversal: For each ray, traverse the octree using the pre-computed tile node list as a starting point or constraint. Use the child selection formula from the parent to descend. Skip empty nodes. Sample volume data at leaf nodes. 5. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. 6. Backtracking: Return to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch, using an explicit stack or recursion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertile(tile, octreeroot, volumedata): # 1. Generate tile node list tilenodelist = [] traversefortile(octreeroot, tile.frustum, tilenodelist) # 2. Process rays in the tile for pixel in tile.pixels: ray = generateray(pixel) color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = ray.origin # 3. Traverse using tile node list # Note: In practice, the tile node list might be used to skip # irrelevant parts of the tree or to initialize the traversal stack. # Here, we assume a standard traversal constrained by the tile's bounds. stack = [octreeroot] while stack: node = stack.pop() # Check intersection with tile frustum (optimization) if not intersects(node.bbox, tile.frustum): continue # Empty space skipping if node.isempty: continue # Leaf handling if node.isleaf: color, alpha = samplevolume(ray, node, volumedata, color, alpha) continue # Child selection childindex = getchildindex(ray, node.center, node.halfextent) if node.children[childindex] is not None: stack.append(node.children[childindex]) tile.imagebuffer[pixel.coords] = color def traversefortile(node, frustum, nodelist): if node is None: return if not intersects(node.bbox, frustum): return if node.isempty: return # Skip subtree nodelist.append(node) if not node.isleaf: for child in node.children: traversefortile(child, frustum, nodelist) Parameters: Tile Size: Common sizes are 8 \times 8 or 16 \times 16 pixels. Larger tiles increase coherence but may lead to larger node lists and cache misses. Smaller tiles reduce list overlap but increase overhead. Leaf Node Size: Smaller leaf sizes reduce node list overlap between tiles but increase storage and traversal overhead. Edge Cases: Degenerate Tiles: Tiles with no intersecting nodes should be skipped entirely. Precision: Floating-point precision issues in ray-node intersection tests can lead to missed nodes or double-counting. Use epsilon values for comparisons. Memory: Large node lists for complex tiles can exceed cache limits, leading to performance degradation. Extends tile-based traversal by dynamically adjusting the octree structure per tile to optimize for local complexity. Choose when scene complexity varies significantly across the image. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L), where N is the number of rays (pixels) and L is the average number of nodes visited per ray. Tile-based traversal reduces L by sharing traversal work, but adds overhead for node list generation. Memory Complexity: O(N{nodes} + N{tiles} \cdot L{avg}), where N{nodes} is the number of octree nodes and L{avg} is the average tile node list size. Performance: Generally faster than per-ray traversal for large, sparse volumes due to reduced redundant node visits. Performance degrades if tile node lists are large or if the scene is highly uniform (where simple DDA might be faster). Strengths: Efficient for sparse volumes, reduces overdraw, leverages spatial coherence. Limitations: Increased memory usage for node lists, complexity in dynamic scenes where the tree changes frequently. When to Use: Large, static, sparse volumes where spatial coherence is high. When Not to Use: Highly dynamic scenes, very dense volumes, or when memory is constrained. Tile-based rendering with octrees was popularized by Wang et al. [WBD+ 21] for scalable web-based volume rendering of large biomedical datasets. It addresses the scalability issues of traditional raycasting by combining tile-based rendering techniques with hierarchical data structures. name: TileTree Rendering
head: TileTree
body: TileTree Rendering is a method for storing and accessing high-resolution texture data on octree-structured volumes, enabling seamless interpolation and adaptive resolution. It differs from standard octree texturing by storing separate tile maps for each face of the octree leaves and using a weighted blending scheme based on surface normal direction to eliminate visible seams at tile boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D position p and a surface normal IN.Nrm. Output: A 4D color value (RGBA) representing the texture at p. Data Structures: Each octree leaf node stores: 1. A 6-bit bit vector marking tile presence on each of the 6 faces (positive/negative X, Y, Z). 2. Two 16-bit integers storing the coordinates of the top-left corner of the tiles within the global tile map. 3. An 8-bit integer storing the resolution of the tiles tileres. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Lookup: Perform an octree lookup at position p to retrieve the leaf node data. 2. Decode Face Presence: Decode the 6-bit presence vector into two 3D vectors: facep (positive X, Y, Z) and facen (negative X, Y, Z), where components are 1 if the tile is present and 0 otherwise. 3. Local Coordinates: Compute local coordinates within the node by scaling p by the node's level size (lvlsize) and taking the fractional part: local = \text{frac}(p \times lvlsize) 4. UVW Alignment: Decode the tile resolution tileres from the leaf. Compute UVW coordinates aligned on leaf boundaries to ensure seamless interpolation: uvw = local \times \frac{tileres - 1.0}{tileres} + \frac{0.5}{tileres} 5. Face Selection: Normalize the input normal IN.Nrm to get nrm. Compute view vectors for positive and negative faces: vp = facep \times nrm vn = facen \times (-nrm) Select the active face ID based on the view direction. If vp > 0, use idp = (XP, YP, ZP); otherwise, if vn > 0, use idn = (XN, YN, ZN); otherwise, the ID is -1. Store the result in faceid. 6. Tile Access: Initialize colors clr0, clr1, clr2 to 0. Access tile data for present tiles using the tileLkup function: If faceid.x > -1, clr0 = \text{tileLkup}(leaf, faceid.x, uvw.yz). If faceid.y > -1, clr1 = \text{tileLkup}(leaf, faceid.y, uvw.xz). If faceid.z > -1, clr2 = \text{tileLkup}(leaf, faceid.z, uvw.xy). 7. Sample Usage Vector: Compute the alpha usage vector \alpha{xyz} from the alpha channels (w component) of the sampled colors, adding a small epsilon (10^{-6}) for robustness: \alpha{xyz} = 10^{-6} + \text{float3}(clr0.w, clr1.w, clr2.w) 8. Damping Factor: Compute the damping factor for seamless interpolation. Calculate anrm = |nrm|. Compute: damp = \frac{anrm}{\max(anrm.x, \max(anrm.y, anrm.z))} Multiply \alpha{xyz} by damp. 9. Weight Computation: Compute weights w for blending. Calculate inv = 1 - \alpha{xyz}. Compute: w = \alpha{xyz} \times inv.yzx \times inv.zxy 10. Final Color: Compute the final color by the weighted sum of clr0, clr1, clr2 using weights w.x, w.y, w.z, divided by the dot product of w and 1: \text{return } \frac{clr0 \times w.x + clr1 \times w.y + clr2 \times w.z}{\text{dot}(w, 1)} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tileTreeLookup(p, INNrm, octreelookup, decodeposfacepresence, decodenegfacepresence, decodetileresolution, tileLkup, lvlsize): # 1. Octree Lookup leaf = octreelookup(p) # 2. Decode Face Presence facep = decodeposfacepresence(leaf) facen = decodenegfacepresence(leaf) # 3. Local Coordinates local = frac(p lvlsize) # 4. UVW Alignment tileres = decodetileresolution(leaf) uvw = local ((tileres - 1.0) / tileres) + (0.5 / tileres) # 5. Face Selection nrm = normalize(INNrm) vp = facep nrm vn = facen (-nrm) idp = float3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # XP, YP, ZP indicators (assuming 1 if present in facep) idn = float3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # XN, YN, ZN indicators (assuming 1 if present in facen) # Note: The source uses facep and facen as masks. # The logic implies idp and idn are indices or masks. # Based on source: "if faceid.x > -1". # We assume facep and facen contain 1.0 for present, 0.0 for absent. # The source code: float3 idp = float3(XP,YP,ZP); # This implies XP, YP, ZP are specific identifiers or the presence mask itself. # Given the context "Select the active face ID... if vp > 0", # and the subsequent access "tileLkup(leaf, faceid.x,...)", # faceid.x must be a valid index or flag. # The source code sets faceid = (vp > 0) ? idp: -1. # If idp is the presence mask, this logic is slightly ambiguous in isolation, # but the standard interpretation in this context is that idp/n are the presence vectors themselves # or indices derived from them. However, the source explicitly defines: # float3 idp = float3(XP,YP,ZP); # Let's stick to the source's variable names for the mask logic. # Actually, looking at "vp = facep nrm", facep is the presence mask. # The selection logic checks if the dot product is positive. # The source code: float3 faceid = (vp > 0) ? idp: -1; # This suggests idp is a vector of indices or flags. # For implementation, we treat idp and idn as the presence masks (1.0/0.0) # or specific indices if the API requires. # Given "tileLkup(leaf, faceid.x,...)", faceid.x is likely an index. # However, the source does not define XP, YP, ZP as variables but as placeholders for indices. # We will assume faceid.x/y/z are the indices of the tiles on the respective faces. # The source code snippet is: # float3 idp = float3(XP,YP,ZP); # This implies XP, YP, ZP are constants or variables representing the tile indices for the positive faces. # Since the leaf stores "coordinates of the top left corner", the indices are likely derived or stored. # For the purpose of this article, we follow the source's structure exactly. faceid = float3(-1.0, -1.0, -1.0) if vp.x > 0: faceid.x = XP # Placeholder for actual index logic from source if vp.y > 0: faceid.y = YP if vp.z > 0: faceid.z = ZP if vn.x > 0: faceid.x = XN if vn.y > 0: faceid.y = YN if vn.z > 0: faceid.z = ZN # Re-evaluating source: "float3 faceid = (vp > 0) ? idp: -1; faceid = (vn > 0) ? idn: faceid;" # This is component-wise or scalar? The source uses float3 comparisons. # In GLSL/HLSL, (vp > 0) is component-wise. # So faceid is a vector where each component is either the corresponding idp/n or -1. faceid = select(vp > 0, idp, float3(-1,-1,-1)) faceid = select(vn > 0, idn, faceid) # 6. Tile Access clr0 = float4(0,0,0,0) clr1 = float4(0,0,0,0) clr2 = float4(0,0,0,0) if faceid.x > -1: clr0 = tileLkup(leaf, faceid.x, uvw.yz) if faceid.y > -1: clr1 = tileLkup(leaf, faceid.y, uvw.xz) if faceid.z > -1: clr2 = tileLkup(leaf, faceid.z, uvw.xy) # 7. In a concrete implementation, these would be extracted from the leaf data or derived from the face presence bits. The select operation is assumed to be component-wise. This variant refers to the core shader logic described in the main method, specifically focusing on the octree traversal, face selection, UV calculation, and tile access steps. It emphasizes the extraction of sample usage flags (alpha) from tile colors with epsilon addition for robustness. Due to the tile resolution being 2k+1, standard MIP-mapping cannot be directly applied to the tile map. This variant uses a strategy where a separate tile map is computed for each resolution level. One tile coordinate per level is stored in the octree leaves. During rendering, the appropriate MIP level is computed and the color is fetched from the corresponding tile map; two levels may be accessed for linear interpolation between MIP levels. Additionally, the tree itself may be MIP-mapped in cases of extreme undersampling. Time and Memory Complexity: The method requires an octree lookup and a fixed number of tile lookups (up to 3) per sample. The memory footprint is efficient; for example, an Armadillo model textured at 1024^3 resolution fits in 11.4 MB, and a Dragon model fits in 11.3 MB. Strengths and Limitations: The primary strength is seamless interpolation and adaptive resolution, eliminating visible seams at tile boundaries. The limitation is the complexity of handling non-power-of-two tile resolutions (2k+1) for MIP-mapping, requiring separate tile maps per level. When to Use: Use when high-resolution texture storage is required on sparse volumes with the need for seamless interpolation and adaptive resolution. name: Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision
head: Frustum-Based Octree Subdivision, Octree Space Subdivision
body: Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision is a scene representation method that constructs a hierarchical spatial partitioning based on camera visibility rather than geometric occupancy. It solves the problem of efficiently organizing large-scale scenes with arbitrary camera trajectories by subdividing space only where cameras are present and close enough to require detail. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack by focusing on the construction of the octree structure driven by camera positions, whereas siblings focus on the traversal of an existing structure. It differs from Octree Texture Subdivision by operating in geometric world space rather than texture coordinate space. The method constructs an octree where leaf nodes define regions for warping functions. The construction is driven by the positions and frustums of visible cameras. Inputs: Set of camera centers \mathcal{C} = \{c1, \dots, cN\}. Set of camera view frustums \mathcal{F} = \{f1, \dots, fN\}. Parameters: \lambda = 3 (subdivision threshold multiplier), nc = 4 (max cameras per leaf). Outputs: An octree structure with leaf nodes \{Si\}. For each leaf node Si, a subset of selected cameras \mathcal{C}{Si} \subseteq \mathcal{C} with |\mathcal{C}{Si}| \le nc. Data Structures: Octree Node: center: \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (world coordinates). sidelength: s \in \mathbb{R} (scalar). children: Array of 8 child nodes (or null if leaf). selectedcameras: List of camera indices (only for leaves). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Root: Compute the bounding box \mathcal{B}{cam} of all camera centers \mathcal{C}. Let W be the side length of \mathcal{B}{cam}. Create root node with side length s{root} = 512 \cdot W. Center the root node to encompass \mathcal{B}{cam} with significant margin. 2. Recursive Subdivision: Define function Subdivide(node, cameras): Let s be node.sidelength. Let \mathbf{c} be node.center. Filter cameras to keep only those whose view frustum fj intersects node's bounding box. Let this set be \mathcal{C}{vis}. If \mathcal{C}{vis} is empty, mark node as leaf with no cameras and return. Check subdivision condition: For each camera cj \in \mathcal{C}{vis}, calculate distance dj = \|cj - \mathbf{c}\|. If \exists cj such that dj \le \lambda \cdot s: Subdivide node into 8 children. Each child has side length s/2. Center each child appropriately relative to \mathbf{c}. For each child, call Subdivide(child, cameras). Else: Mark node as leaf. If |\mathcal{C}{vis}| > nc: Select a subset \mathcal{C}{sel} \subseteq \mathcal{C}{vis} of size nc such that the minimal pairwise distance between selected cameras is maximized. Store \mathcal{C}{sel} in node.selectedcameras. Else: Store all \mathcal{C}{vis} in node.selectedcameras. Return. 3. Camera Selection Strategy (for leaves with > nc cameras): Given a set of K > nc visible cameras, find indices I \subset \{1, \dots, K\} with |I|=nc. Optimize: \max{I} \min{i, j \in I, i \neq j} \|ci - cj\|. Note: The exact optimization algorithm is in supplementary material. A greedy approach or k-means-like clustering can be used as an approximation. Parameters: \lambda = 3: Threshold for subdivision. If a camera is within 3s of the node center, subdivide. nc = 4: Maximum number of cameras associated with a single leaf node for warping function construction. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Root Size: The root must be sufficiently large (512 \times camera bounding box) to contain far-away objects like sky. Failure to do so causes clipping of distant geometry. Empty Nodes: Nodes with no intersecting frustums should be pruned or marked as empty to save memory. Precision: Distance calculations dj should use double precision if the scene scale is large to avoid incorrect subdivision decisions due to floating-point error. Operates on texture coordinate space rather than geometric voxel grid, allowing hardware texture interpolation to handle hierarchical sampling. Choose when working with texture-mapped volumes or when hardware interpolation is desired. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N \cdot L) where N is the number of cameras and L is the average number of nodes visited per camera during the check-and-subdivide process. The depth of the tree depends on the distribution of cameras and the \lambda threshold. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of leaf nodes and the number of cameras stored per leaf. The large root bounding box ensures no spatial gaps but may increase initial memory allocation if not managed carefully. Strengths: Efficiently handles large scenes with sparse camera coverage by not subdividing empty regions. Adapts resolution to camera density. Limitations: The subdivision is static based on camera positions; it does not adapt to scene geometry complexity directly. The choice of \lambda and nc significantly impacts the tree structure and subsequent warping accuracy. When to use: Large-scale scene reconstruction with known camera trajectories (e.g., NeRF training with free camera paths) where spatial organization is needed for efficient warping or sampling. The method originates from F2-NeRF, a technique for fast Neural Radiance Field training with free camera trajectories. It was introduced to handle the computational challenges of large-scale scenes by organizing the space based on camera visibility rather than static geometry. The approach allows for the construction of warping functions tailored to local camera configurations, improving training speed and reconstruction quality for dynamic or large-scale environments. F2-NeRF: Fast Neural Radiance Field Training with Free Camera Trajectories, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00404, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Octree Texture Subdivision
head: Octree texture subdivision (Boada et al, LaMar et al.)
body: Octree Texture Subdivision is a method that subdivides the texture space into an octree to skip empty regions and use lower-resolution textures for distant or low-interest regions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating directly on the texture coordinate space rather than the geometric voxel grid, allowing hardware texture interpolation to handle the hierarchical sampling. Inputs: A 3D scalar field volume, a camera view, and an octree structure defined over the texture coordinate space [0,1]^3. Outputs: A rendered image. Data Structures: The method maintains an octree where each node corresponds to a sub-volume in texture space. Node fields: level: Integer depth of the node (0 is root). resolution: The side length of the voxel grid represented by this node's texture. texturehandle: Reference to a 3D texture object of size 2^{level} \times 2^{level} \times 2^{level} (or similar power-of-two scaling). empty: Boolean flag indicating if the node contains no significant data. Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the octree over the texture space. Populate leaf nodes with 3D textures sampled from the original volume data. Mark nodes as empty if their contained data falls below a significance threshold. 2. Traversal: For each pixel, cast a ray. Traverse the octree from the root. 3. Culling: If a node is marked empty, skip it entirely. 4. Subdivision: If the ray intersects a node and the node is not a leaf, or if the node is a leaf but the ray requires higher precision (e.g., near the camera or in high-interest regions), subdivide the node. 5. Sampling: If the current node is a leaf, sample the associated 3D texture using hardware interpolation. The texture coordinates for sampling are derived from the ray's intersection with the node's bounding box in texture space. 6. Classification/Compositing: Apply volume classification and front-to-back or back-to-front compositing using the sampled values. 7. Adaptation: Dynamically adjust the octree depth based on view distance and interest. Use lower-resolution textures (shallower nodes) for regions far from the viewpoint or of lower interest. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderoctreetexturevolume(volumedata, camera, octreeroot): # Initialize octree with full-resolution textures at leaves octree = buildoctree(volumedata) for each pixel (x, y): ray = camera.castray(x, y) color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Traverse octree node = octreeroot t = ray.origin while node is not None: if node.isempty: break # Skip empty regions # Check if we need to go deeper or sample if node.isleaf or shouldsubdivide(node, ray): # Sample from the node's associated 3D texture # Texture coordinates are mapped from ray intersection within node bounds texcoords = mapraytotexturecoords(ray, node.bounds) value = hardware3dtexturesample(node.texturehandle, texcoords) # Classification and compositing alpha, rgb = classifyandcomposite(value, color) color = (rgb, alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break t += ray.stepsize # Advance ray else: # Subdivide or move to child node = getnextnode(node, ray) setpixelcolor(x, y, color) Parameters: Empty threshold: Not given in the sources. Interest metric: Not given in the sources. Edge cases: Precision: Hardware interpolation may introduce artifacts if the texture resolution is too low for the ray step size. Boundaries: Texture coordinates must be clamped to [0,1] to avoid out-of-bounds access. Time and memory complexity: Depends on the octree depth and the sparsity of the volume. Memory is reduced by storing lower-resolution textures for distant/empty regions. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with hardware texture interpolation capabilities. Strengths: Reduces memory bandwidth by skipping empty regions and using lower-resolution textures for less important areas. Limitations: Relies on hardware 3D texture support and interpolation quality. When to use: When hardware supports 3D texture interpolation and the volume has significant empty or low-interest regions. When not: When high precision is required everywhere or hardware support is lacking. Origin: Proposed by Boada et al. and LaMar et al.. History: Emerged with the advent of programmable vertex shaders and advanced PC graphics hardware (NVIDIA, ATI, 3DLabs), making texture-mapped volume rendering accessible to a broader community at less than 2% of the cost of previous workstations. Usage: Used in texture-mapped volume rendering pipelines. Overview of Volume Rendering, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/papers/volvisOverview.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Volume Visualization and Volume Graphics, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/teaching/cse332/volvisChapter.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (book)

name: JIT Type Specialization
head: JIT Member Function Evaluation
body: JIT Type Specialization is a technique where type resolution and function routing are performed at Just-In-Time (JIT) compilation time, inlining the traversal, type check, and address lookup into the final function to eliminate switch statements and runtime type resolving overhead. It sets itself apart from standard dynamic dispatch by making access time independent of the number of different elemental node types, as the specialized code paths are baked directly into the executable. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A key (e.g., coordinate or ray parameter) and a root node reference. Output: The result of the specialized function call for the element found at the key. Data Structures: Compact Array (acomp): Stores type identifiers and pointers (addresses) for elements. Types are encoded as distinct identifiers (e.g., colors like green, orange, blue). Specialized Functions: Individual functions for each element type that operate on the element's data. Numbered Steps: 1. Standard Runtime Dispatch: Perform a tree traversal to locate the element index, look up the element structure in acomp, and use a runtime switch statement to route the call to the specialized function based on the element type. 2. JIT Inlining: The JIT compiler generates a specialized version of the function that inlines the traversal logic, type checks, and address lookups. This eliminates the compact array lookup and switch statements. 3. Execution: The generated code directly compares keys against tree-specific thresholds to determine the path and calls the specific function with a pre-resolved address. Formulas: The method relies on conditional comparisons for traversal rather than closed-form mathematical equations. The logic follows the pattern: if (key < threshold) traverse left; else if (key > threshold) traverse right; else call specialized function. Thresholds are derived from the specific tree structure (e.g., 106, 8, 4, 13 in the source example). Parameters: Element Types: Encoded as distinct identifiers in the compact array. Thresholds: Specific to the tree structure being traversed. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: JIT Overhead: JIT compilation overhead is incurred once per function or tree configuration, not per access. Memory Fetches: The technique eliminates memory fetches in the top-level traversal code by inlining the logic, reducing memory-bound performance bottlenecks. Code Specificity: The generated code is specific to the tree structure and element types present at JIT time. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the difference between the standard runtime dispatch approach and the JIT-specialized approach. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. ADDR0, ADDR1, ADDR2, ADDR3 = 0x1000, 0x1008, 0x1010, 0x1018 ADDR4, ADDR5, ADDR6, ADDR7 = 0x1020, 0x1028, 0x1030, 0x1038 def foogreen(address): return f"greendataat{address}" def fooorange(address): return f"orangedataat{address}" def fooblue(address): return f"bluedataat{address}" def find(key, root): # Standard recursive or iterative tree traversal logic return 0 def fooruntime(key, root, acomp): index = find(key, root) e = acomp[index] if e.type == "green": return foogreen(e.address) elif e.type == "orange": return fooorange(e.address) elif e.type == "blue": return fooblue(e.address) def foojit(key): # Inlined traversal and type specialization # Compare key to root key if key < 106: # Traverse left subtree if key < 8: # Traverse left-left subtree if key < 4: return foogreen(ADDR0) elif key > 4: return foogreen(ADDR2) else: return foogreen(ADDR1) else: # Traverse left-right subtree if key < 13: return foogreen(ADDR4) elif key > 13: return fooorange(ADDR6) else: return foogreen(ADDR5) else: # Traverse right subtree # Code omitted for brevity in source # Follows same pattern of key comparisons and direct address calls return fooorange(ADDR7) Time Complexity: Access time is independent of the number of different elemental node types. The overhead of resolving types is eliminated. Memory Complexity: Requires a compact array to store types and pointers. Strengths: Eliminates runtime type resolving overhead and switch statements. Reduces memory-bound performance issues during tree traversal. Limitations: Requires a JIT compiler infrastructure. The generated code is specific to the tree structure and element types at JIT time. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. JIT Type Specialization, also known as JIT Member Function Evaluation, is described in the context of the JiTTree, a just-in-time compiled sparse GPU volume data structure. It is designed to improve the performance of data processing algorithms by making access less memory-bound. The technique allows an arbitrary number of different kinds of sparse data structures to improve overall quality without introducing new memory fetches. name: Ray Traversal Algorithms
body: Ray Traversal Algorithms are a family of hierarchical descent methods used to efficiently determine which nodes of a sparse voxel octree (SVO) or similar tree structure intersect a given ray. They solve the problem of avoiding redundant intersection tests in large, sparse volumetric datasets by skipping empty subtrees and jumping directly to occupied leaf nodes or boundary cells. This family is distinguished from sibling methods like GPU Octree Volume Rasterization by its reliance on explicit ray-tree intersection logic rather than rasterization primitives, and from Camera-Driven Octree Subdivision by its focus on per-ray traversal state rather than global view-dependent subdivision. See Octree and Tree Traversal for shared principles. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent. The traversal begins at the root of the octree and determines which of the eight children (octants) the ray intersects. This is typically done by comparing the ray's position relative to the center of the current node's bounding box. 1. Child Selection: For a node with center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s, the ray position \mathbf{p} determines the child index k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(px \ge cx) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(py \ge cy) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(pz \ge cz) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 2. Empty Space Skipping: If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree. This is achieved by advancing the ray parameter t to the exit of the current node or using neighbor pointers to jump to the next potentially occupied node. 3. Leaf Handling: Upon reaching a leaf node, the method typically switches to a fixed-step traversal (like DDA) within the leaf's voxel grid to sample the volume data. 4. Backtracking: Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch. This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, maxdepth): """ Generic hierarchical ray traversal for octree families. rayorigin: (x, y, z) ray origin. raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) normalized ray direction. rootnode: Root octree node object. maxdepth: Maximum traversal depth. Returns: List of visited leaf nodes or samples. """ stack = [] currentnode = rootnode depth = 0 scale = rootnode.size while depth < maxdepth: # Child Selection center = currentnode.center k = 4 (rayorigin.x >= center.x) + 2 (rayorigin.y >= center.y) + 1 (rayorigin.z >= center.z) # Fetch child node child = currentnode.children[k] # Empty Space Skipping if child.isempty: texit = computeexitt(rayorigin, raydirection, currentnode.bounds) rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection texit # Backtrack if stack: depth -= 1 currentnode = stack.pop() scale /= 2 else: return [] # Ray exited tree continue # Descend stack.append(currentnode) currentnode = child depth += 1 scale /= 2 # Leaf Handling return sampleleaf(currentnode, rayorigin, raydirection) Octree Path Computation is the algorithmic process of determining the sequence of child nodes (the "path") traversed by a ray or frustum as it descends from the root of an octree to a specific leaf or target node. It solves the problem of efficiently identifying which spatial subdivisions a ray intersects without performing redundant geometric intersection tests at every level. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal by focusing on the explicit encoding and decoding of the traversal sequence itself, often for purposes such as neighbor finding, path caching, or coordinate reconstruction, rather than just the final sampling step. Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) Ray Traversal is a hierarchical raycasting technique that renders volumetric data stored in a 3D sparse octree structure by traversing the tree along ray paths to find occupied leaf nodes (voxels). It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large, sparse 3D datasets without the memory overhead of dense voxel grids by skipping empty space via axis-aligned slab intersection logic. Unlike standard ray-triangle rasterization, it uses a single draw call to fire one ray per pixel, descending the octree to find the first hit, and differs from GigaVoxels by not relying on a fixed-resolution texture-based cache, operating directly on the octree structure. Rational Ray Parameterization for Octree Traversal is a method for tracing rays through an octree using exact rational arithmetic to avoid floating-point precision errors during cell boundary crossing and neighbor finding. It solves the problem of determining the next cell intersected by a ray when the ray parameters are not integers, which typically occurs when the viewplane is in an arbitrary position in space. Unlike sibling methods that rely on floating-point comparisons or pre-computed structures, this method guarantees robustness by representing ray parameters as rational numbers (numerator/denominator pairs) and using integer arithmetic for all comparisons and boundary tests. Ray-Occlusion Traversal in Octree is a hierarchical ray-intersection algorithm that traverses an octree structure to determine if a ray intersects any solid voxel or leaf node, primarily used for shadow ray computation and early termination in volume rendering. It differs from its siblings by explicitly handling rays starting inside or outside the root bounding box via plane intersection logic and using a fixed-depth descent loop with explicit parent-boundary checks to manage traversal state, rather than relying solely on neighbor-finding or bottom-up approaches. This method extends the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) grid traversal algorithm to N-ary hierarchical trees for GPU shader implementation. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing sparse voxel structures by maintaining a small, fixed-size stack of DDA states, allowing the ray to descend into child nodes and ascend back to parent nodes without dynamic memory allocation. It is distinguished from standard DDA by its hierarchical boundary handling and from other tree traversals by its reliance on a statically allocated mini-stack indexed via Shader Model 4.0 features. Presence Acceleration is a ray traversal technique that uses a binary pyramid to skip empty regions in a volume by identifying cells containing at least one opaque voxel. It solves the problem of inefficiently traversing large transparent areas in volume data. Unlike pointer-based octrees, it relies on a fixed-resolution, pointerless grid hierarchy that allows for simple, predictable memory access patterns. Boundary Cell-Based Ray Casting (BC-RC) is a fast serial ray casting algorithm that accelerates volume rendering by skipping empty space using boundary cells. It improves upon the PARC algorithm by obtaining a more accurate object boundary estimation with less computational overhead using incremental parallel projection for each boundary cell. Unlike PARC, which uses pre-calculated sub-volumes whose projection is expensive when small, BC-RC uses tiny grid cells for more accurate boundary estimation and employs fast incremental parallel projection with templates to reduce projection overhead. An algorithm to find all octants in a pointer-based octree that intersect with a given ray, returning them sorted by distance (closest first). It uses parametric ray representation (t-values) to traverse the octree structure efficiently. It distinguishes itself from Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal by focusing on discrete octant traversal logic for pointer-based structures rather than dense voxel sampling, and from Ray-Octree Boundary Intersection by operating on the internal hierarchy rather than just the root bounding box. This method renders hierarchical point-cloud or sparse volume data by traversing an octree in screen-space order, prioritizing nodes that project largest on the display. It solves the problem of maintaining visual fidelity while adhering to a strict rendering budget (e.g., maximum point count or fill rate) by dynamically adjusting the level of detail (LOD) based on camera distance and frustum visibility. Unlike fixed-depth traversal, it stops refining nodes once the budget is exhausted, ensuring consistent performance regardless of scene complexity. Hierarchical Tree Node Traversal is a method for accelerating ray-volume intersection by traversing a sparse octree structure to identify contiguous segments of active data. It solves the problem of inefficiently sampling empty space in large volumetric datasets by skipping inactive nodes and resolving hits at the node level rather than the individual voxel level. Unlike sibling methods that may compute precise Hermite data or rasterize shadows, this approach focuses on robust, thread-safe ray marching against a generic grid, providing entry and exit times for line-integration. The implementation does not use SIMD or packet tracing. Coherent techniques (like frustum-based traversals) are avoided because highly-variant scenes and pixels covering multiple voxels cause unnecessary work and potential performance decreases compared to single-ray techniques. Perform an additional intersection test for every leaf voxel found in the hierarchy traversal using the raymarching algorithm. If the ray does not intersect the distance field, continue ray traversal. Add a premature stop when the valid mask is set to zero (no children) to render the model from various levels of detail dynamically. If the premature intersection with the distance field fails, continue traversal. Stops traversing the octree when the projected area of the next intersected child voxel is smaller than the projected area of the pixel on the screen, skipping ray-isosurface intersection tests. Implement a version similar to cone tracing, approximating the radius of a cone around the ray. Exploit the fact that finite difference normal calculation can be evaluated at any point in the voxel. Voxelized normals are only rendered when the entire projected voxel area is smaller than the pixel to remove aliasing effects. A ray-tracing system designed to address two basic problems in generating continuous-tone images: speed and aliasing. The scheme is based on the coherency of an auxiliary data structure imposed on the original object domain. Investigate simple spatial enumeration and a hybrid octree approach as the auxiliary data structures. Develop 3DDDA, a 3D line generator for efficient traversing of both the spatial enumeration and hybrid octree structures. Remove jags from edges by implementing a scheme for identifying edge orientation and distance from pixel center to true edge. Antialiasing time depends on the total length of the edges encountered. 3DDDA provides an order of magnitude improvement in processing speed compared to other known ray-tracing methods. Processing time is virtually independent of the number of objects involved in the scene. For large numbers of objects, the method actually becomes faster than scan-line methods. Antialiasing time is normally only a fractional addition to the time needed to produce the scene without antialiasing. The foundational work for efficient octree traversal in ray tracing was established by Wald et al. in 2006, who introduced optimized single-ray traversal techniques for large octree volumes, noting that coherent techniques like frustum-based traversal could degrade performance on large, sparse datasets due to excessive work on pixels covering multiple voxels. The 3DDDA algorithm, introduced by Williams et al., provided an early framework for using 3D DDA on hybrid octree structures to achieve significant speedups and antialiasing. More recent developments include dynamic LOD traversal strategies that skip ray-isosurface intersection tests based on projected voxel area. name: Octree Path Computation
body: Octree Path Computation determines the sequence of child nodes traversed by a ray or frustum as it descends from the root of an octree to a target node. It identifies spatial subdivisions without redundant geometric intersection tests at every level. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal by focusing on the explicit encoding and decoding of the traversal sequence for neighbor finding, path caching, or coordinate reconstruction. Inputs: Target grid coordinates (rx, ry, rz) or ray parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Octree metadata: maximum depth D, current level lv, and bounding box. Optional: Pre-computed path from root to a reference node (e.g., u,v-minimal ray). Outputs: A path vector or integer representing the sequence of octant indices from root to leaf. Voxel coordinates (i, j, k) at a specific level. Path Vector: A list or array of integers, where each element pl \in \{0, \dots, 7\} represents the octant index at level l. Bit-Path Integer: A single integer where 3 bits are allocated per level, totaling 3 \times D bits. Voxel Coordinates: 3D integer vector (i, j, k) representing the position within the voxel grid at level lv. 1. Path Encoding (Forward Computation): To compute the path for a point or ray: a. Initialize an empty path vector P and a scale variable s = 2^{D-1}. b. For each depth level l from 0 to D-1: i. Determine the octant bits by comparing the current grid coordinates (rx, ry, rz) against the scale s. ii. Calculate the octant index k using the child selection formula: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(rx \ge s) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(ry \ge s) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(rz \ge s). iii. Subtract s from the coordinate if the bit is set: rx \leftarrow rx - s \cdot \mathbb{I}(rx \ge s), ry \leftarrow ry - s \cdot \mathbb{I}(ry \ge s), rz \leftarrow rz - s \cdot \mathbb{I}(rz \ge s). iv. Append k to P. v. Right-shift the scale: s \leftarrow s / 2. 2. Path Decoding (Coordinate Reconstruction): To reconstruct voxel coordinates from a stored path integer or vector: a. Let lv be the target level and MAX\NUM\LEVELS be the maximum depth. b. Shift the octpath right by 3 \times (MAX\NUM\LEVELS - lv) bits to remove irrelevant higher-level bits. c. Iterate l from 0 to lv-1: i. Extract the lowest 3 bits of the current path to get the octant index. ii. Decode the octant into local coordinates (dx, dy, dz) using bit masks: dx = (idx \gg 2) \& 1, dy = (idx \gg 1) \& 1, dz = idx \& 1. iii. Accumulate the global coordinates: i = (i \ll 1) + dx, j = (j \ll 1) + dy, k = (k \ll 1) + dz. iv. Shift the path right by 3 bits. Voxel Size: The physical size of a voxel at level lv is computed as: s = \text{scene\extent} \times 2^{-lv}. MAX\NUM\LEVELS: Maximum depth of the octree, typically 16. D: The depth of the current node or target leaf. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. Returns: List of octant indices [k0, k1,..., k{maxdepth-1}] """ path = [] scale = 1 << (maxdepth - 1) # 2^(maxdepth - 1) for in range(maxdepth): k = 0 if rx >= scale: k += 4 rx -= scale if ry >= scale: k += 2 ry -= scale if rz >= scale: k += 1 rz -= scale path.append(k) scale >>= 1 # Right shift by 1 return path def decodevoxelfrompath(pathint, lv, maxnumlevels=16): """ Decodes voxel coordinates from a bit-packed path integer. pathint: Integer containing the path bits. lv: Target level to decode to. maxnumlevels: Maximum depth of the octree. Returns: Tuple (i, j, k) """ shift = 3 (maxnumlevels - lv) pathint >>= shift i, j, k = 0, 0, 0 for in range(lv): idx = pathint & 0x7 pathint >>= 3 dx = (idx >> 2) & 1 dy = (idx >> 1) & 1 dz = idx & 1 i = (i << 1) + dx j = (j << 1) + dy k = (k << 1) + dz return (i, j, k) An algorithm to find the adjacent cell a sharing a specific face f with a given cell c in a generalized octree, handling cases where the neighbor might be at a different subdivision level. It solves the problem of inefficient random access patterns in large datasets by learning local access traffic, specifically the frequent appearance of predecessor-current-successor node sequences. Subdivide a node into 32 children if too many objects are associated with it or the cell is too large. Associate objects with one or more children. 6. head: Get Neighbour Algorithm
body: An algorithm to find the adjacent cell a sharing a specific face f with a given cell c in a generalized octree, handling cases where the neighbor might be at a different subdivision level. Inputs: A cell c and a face f for which the neighbor is sought. Outputs: The adjacent cell a sharing face f with c, or null if no valid neighbor exists. Data Structures: Cell Representation: Defined by spatial coordinates and a Morton code (Z-order curve). Level: The subdivision depth of the cell. Offset: An integer variable tracking the search depth relative to the cell's level. Steps: 1. Determine the level of cell c, denoted as Lc. 2. Identify the coincident face f' corresponding to the input face f. 3. Initialize an offset variable k = 1. 4. Loop while k \le Lc: a. Compute the candidate neighbor using GetAdjacentCellByFace(c, f, k). b. Check if the candidate cell a exists in the octree structure. c. If a exists: i. Retrieve the geometric limit of cell c in the direction of face f, denoted Limitc. ii. Retrieve the geometric limit of cell a in the direction of the coincident face f', denoted Limita. iii. If Limitc == Limita, the cells share the exact same boundary plane. Return a. iv. Else, the limits do not match. Increment k by 1 and continue the loop. d. If a does not exist, increment k by 1 and continue the loop. 5. If the loop completes without returning a cell, no valid neighbor exists. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def GetNeighbor(c, f, storage): level = c.level coincidentFace = (f + 3) % 6 # Opposite face mapping offset = 1 while offset <= level: candidatemorton = GetAdjacentCellByFace(c, f, offset, storage) if candidatemorton is not None: a = storage.get(candidatemorton) if a is not None: cellLimitC = GetCellLimitByFace(c, f) cellLimitA = GetCellLimitByFace(a, coincidentFace) if cellLimitC == cellLimitA: return a offset += 1 return None def GetAdjacentCellByFace(cell, face, offset, storage): # Obtain spatial coordinates, add offset in direction, convert to Morton code coords = list(cell.coords) if face == 0: coords[0] += offset elif face == 1: coords[0] -= offset elif face == 2: coords[1] += offset elif face == 3: coords[1] -= offset elif face == 4: coords[2] += offset elif face == 5: coords[2] -= offset morton = coordstomorton(coords) # If no neighbouring cell exists, look at parent by shifting 3 LSBs if morton not in storage: morton = cell.morton >> 3 return morton def GetCellLimitByFace(cell, face): # Return boundary coordinate along face axis if face < 2: return cell.coords[0] if face < 4: return cell.coords[1] return cell.coords[2] def coordstomorton(coords): # Standard Morton/Z-order encoding x, y, z = coords return (x << 2) | (y << 1) | z Parameters: offset: Starts at 1. The maximum value is bounded by the depth of the octree, as anisotropic subdivision usually occurs at the deepest levels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Anisotropic Subdivision: The algorithm is designed for generalized octrees where cells may have different sizes. The offset loop handles cases where the neighbor is at a different subdivision level. Precision: Geometric limit comparison must use exact equality. Floating-point errors in limit calculation could cause false negatives. Boundary Conditions: If the cell is on the boundary of the domain, Exists will return false for external neighbors, and the loop will terminate correctly. Indirect Neighbor Search computes the set of neighbors for the three faces of a cell c that are not covered by direct neighbors. These neighbors are separated from c by splitting planes located deeper in the octree hierarchy. While Direct Neighbor Search handles the immediate vicinity resulting from the last three splitting steps, Indirect Neighbor Search handles the remaining faces by traversing the tree structure to find cells or planes on the opposite side of bounding splitting planes. It is the second phase of the complete neighborhood computation in generalized octrees. Generates fragments corresponding to rays intersecting the cell. This approach is used for efficient classification of cells in volume rendering contexts, where sub-volumes are projected onto the image plane and fragments are generated for rays intersecting the cell. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles generalized (anisotropic) octrees efficiently without requiring regular grid structures. Limitations: Performance degrades if the octree has very deep levels and neighbors are sparse, requiring many offset increments. The algorithm was introduced by Ricardo Uribe Lobello, Florence Denis, and Florent Dupont in their work on adaptive surface extraction from anisotropic volumetric data using generalized octrees. It addresses the need for efficient neighbor access in non-uniform octrees where standard bitwise neighbor calculations fail due to varying cell sizes. name: Indirect Neighbor Search
body: Indirect Neighbor Search computes the set of neighbors for the three faces of a cell c that are not covered by direct neighbors. These neighbors are separated from c by splitting planes located deeper in the octree hierarchy. While Direct Neighbor Search handles the immediate vicinity resulting from the last three splitting steps, Indirect Neighbor Search handles the remaining faces by traversing the tree structure to find cells or planes on the opposite side of bounding splitting planes. It is the second phase of the complete neighborhood computation in generalized octrees. Inputs: Cell index bd (binary representation). The set of direct neighbors N{direct}(c) computed in the previous step. Cell coordinates (x, y, z) for geometric tests. Outputs: The set of indirect neighbors N{indirect}(c). The complete neighborhood N(c) = N{direct}(c) \cup N{indirect}(c). Data Structures: Cell index bd: A binary integer where every third bit corresponds to a dimension (x0, x1, x2). The least significant bits correspond to the root level, and higher bits to deeper levels. N(c): A set of indices (integers) representing splitting planes and leaf cells. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify Bounding Splitting Planes: For each dimension d \in \{0, 1, 2\}, determine the splitting plane that bounds cell c on the face not covered by direct neighbors. Extract the bits of bd corresponding to dimension d by considering every third bit starting from the least significant bit (LSB) for that dimension. Scan these bits from LSB to MSB (root to leaf). Find the first bit swap (transition from 0 to 1 or 1 to 0) in this sequence. If the first swap occurs at subsequence index j (where j=0 is the LSB), the index of the bounding splitting plane is b{dj} = bd \gg (3j) (right shift by 3j). If no bit swap occurs in a dimension, the cell lies entirely on one side of all division planes in that dimension relative to the root, and there is no bounding plane in that direction for indirect neighbors. 2. Recursive Search for Indirect Neighbors: For each identified bounding plane p found in Step 1: Perform a recursive search in the subtree starting from p to find cells or planes on the opposite side of p relative to c. The recursion logic for a currentnode (which is a splitting plane) is as follows: 1. If currentnode splits in the same dimension as p: Continue with the subtree of currentnode that is adjacent to c (the side containing c). 2. Else (if currentnode splits in a different dimension): Check if currentnode has a common point with c. This check requires comparing the coordinates of c against the pivot value of the splitting plane. If they have a common point: Add currentnode to N(c). Continue with both subtrees of currentnode. If they do not have a common point: Continue with the subtree of currentnode that is adjacent to c. The recursion stops when leaf nodes (cells) are reached. These leaf cells are added to N(c). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findindirectneighbors(cellindex, cellcoords, directneighbors): """ Computes indirect neighbors for cell c with binary index b. Assumes directneighbors N(c) is already computed. """ indirectneighbors = set() # Dimensions are interleaved in Morton code: bits 0,3,6... for dim 0; 1,4,7... for dim 1; 2,5,8... for dim 2 for dim in range(3): # Extract bits for this dimension bits = [] temp = cellindex while temp > 0: bits.append((temp >> dim) & 1) temp >>= 3 # Scan from LSB (index 0) to MSB to find first swap firstswapidx = -1 for k in range(1, len(bits)): if bits[k] != bits[k-1]: firstswapidx = k break if firstswapidx != -1: # The plane index is the cell index right-shifted by 3j planeindex = cellindex >> (3 firstswapidx) # Step 2: Recursive search searchsubtree(planeindex, cellindex, cellcoords, indirectneighbors, dim) return indirectneighbors def searchsubtree(currentplane, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp): """ Recursive search for indirect neighbors. currentplane: index of a splitting plane. cellindex: binary index of the target cell c. cellcoords: (x, y, z) coordinates of c. neighborset: set to add found neighbors to. dimp: split dimension of the initial bounding plane p. """ # Leaf detection: check tree-specific flag or mask indicating a leaf node if isleaf(currentplane): neighborset.add(currentplane) return # Determine split dimension of currentplane (Morton code: dim 0 at bit 0, dim 1 at bit 1, dim 2 at bit 2) dimcurrent = currentplane & 3 if dimcurrent == dimp: # Continue with subtree next to c nextnode = getchildtowardsc(currentplane, cellcoords) if nextnode is not None: searchsubtree(nextnode, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp) else: # Different dimension: check if current plane has a common point with c if hascommonpoint(currentplane, cellcoords): neighborset.add(currentplane) # Continue with both subtrees leftchild = currentplane << 1 rightchild = (currentplane << 1) | 1 searchsubtree(leftchild, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp) searchsubtree(rightchild, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp) else: # Continue with subtree next to c nextnode = getchildtowardsc(currentplane, cellcoords) if nextnode is not None: searchsubtree(nextnode, cellindex, cellcoords, neighborset, dimp) def getchildtowardsc(nodeindex, cellcoords): """ Returns the child node of 'nodeindex' that is on the same side as cell c. Uses coordinate comparison as specified by the source. """ dim = nodeindex & 3 coord = cellcoords[dim] # Retrieve pivot value for the splitting plane; implementation depends on tree storage pivot = getpivot(nodeindex) if coord < pivot: return nodeindex << 1 else: return (nodeindex << 1) | 1 def hascommonpoint(planeindex, cellcoords): """ Checks if the cell c has a common point with the splitting plane. This test uses the coordinates of c when comparing it to the pivot value of the splitting plane. """ dim = planeindex & 3 coord = cellcoords[dim] pivot = getpivot(planeindex) # Exact boundary check return abs(coord - pivot) < 1e-9 Parameters: None explicitly defined. The algorithm is deterministic based on the tree structure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Bit Swap: If no bit swap is found in a dimension during Step 1, there is no bounding plane in that direction, and no indirect neighbors are searched for that face. Coordinate Dependency: Only the test for whether a plane has a common point with c uses the coordinates of c. All other operations (bit scanning, XOR, recursion path selection) use the binary representation of indices for speed. Worst Case Complexity: The worst-case number of indirect neighbors is O(\sqrt[3]{n^2}), where n is the number of cells. This occurs only for a small number of cells. Average Case: In 3D, the average case has up to 9 neighbors per face, leading to 27 indirect neighbors per cell. Computes the set of direct neighbors N(c) for a cell c with index bd. Direct neighbors include splitting planes and cells resulting from the last three splitting steps. It identifies direct splitting planes at indices b{d1}, b{d2}, b{d3} (right shifts by 1, 2, 3 bits) and adjacent cells using bitwise XOR with 1d, 10d, 100d. It also checks four additional splitting planes beyond the direct ones using specific criteria to complete the neighborhood. This method covers half of the faces of c and includes at least three and at most seven cells plus the respective splitting planes in between. Time Complexity: The search performance is similar to nearest-neighbor search in kd-trees due to the heavy use of binary operations. The worst-case complexity for indirect neighbors is O(\sqrt[3]{n^2}). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast execution due to bitwise operations; avoids coordinate comparisons except for the final geometric test. Limitations: Worst-case complexity can be high for specific cell configurations, though rare. When to use: When a complete neighborhood of a cell in a generalized octree is required for isosurface extraction or other volume rendering techniques. The method was introduced by P. Rosenthal and L. Linsen in their 2006 paper "Direct Isosurface Extraction from Scattered Volume Data". It is part of a two-step process for computing the neighborhood of a cell in a generalized octree, which is used for direct isosurface extraction from scattered volume data. name: SVO Pathfinder with Lazy Theta* and LOS Recovery
head: Lazy Theta* Pathfinding on SVO
body: This method performs 3D pathfinding on a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by combining A search with Lazy Theta logic, where line-of-sight (LOS) checks are performed optimistically during neighbor expansion to allow straight-line shortcuts, with a recovery step if LOS fails. It differs from standard A on octrees by reducing path length and node visits through direct parent-to-current-node connections when possible, and differs from pure ray-casting pathfinding by caching collision results to avoid expensive per-step ray-marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Start and End world positions, Agent Radius, SVO structure (node array, depth, traversal data). Output: Sequence of nodes forming the path, or failure if no path exists. Data Structures: Node Array: Flat array of SVO nodes. Collision Test Cache: Stores result per node: 0 (no test performed), -1 (collision detected), +1 (no collision). Cost Array: Stores cumulative cost g(n) for each node index. Parent Array: Stores parent node index for each node. Open Array: Priority queue of nodes to expand, ordered by f(n) = g(n) + h(n). Closed Array: Boolean flag array indicating if a node has been expanded. InlineAllocator: Used for neighbor collection; behaves like a fixed allocator but switches to heap allocation if the set capacity is exceeded. Parameters: AgentRadius: Radius of the agent. Clamped to prevent invalid access. MaxDepth: Maximum depth of the SVO. Typical values: 6 or 8. AxisBit: Bit mask for neighbor calculation. Points to 1 when Side is negative, because when the current node faces the positive direction, the neighboring node is adjacent in the negative direction. Steps: 1. Initialize and Validate: Clamp AgentRadius. Get nodes at Start and End positions by accessing the node Array. Verify traversability using cached collision test results. If Start or End nodes are not traversable (result \neq +1), return failure. If Start and End are the same node, return immediately. 2. Neighbor Collection: Iterate from 0 to 7 to collect neighbor indices based on target axis (0 or 1). Traverse the tree using DFS to collect all leaf nodes. Keep only passable nodes (collision test result +1). 3. Pathfinding (Lazy Theta): Initialize Cost, Parent, Open, and Closed arrays. While Open is not empty, pop node u with lowest f(u). If u is End, reconstruct path and return. For each neighbor v, calculate tentative g(v). Perform LOS check between parent of u (or u if u is Start) and v. If LOS is clear, set parent of v to parent of u (or u) and update g(v) using direct distance. Else, set parent of v to u and update g(v) using distance from u to v. 4. LOS Method: Perform a simple collision test between two points. Can be implemented with ray-marching using SVO, but simple collision test is used for lower code complexity with negligible performance loss. Pitfalls: Agent Radius vs Node Size: Simple comparison of octree node size with AgentRadius is insufficient. Example: AgentRadius 700, octree alley sizes 200, 400, 200. It cannot pass through the 400-sized node despite the gap, requiring explicit collision testing. Collision Test Cache: Running a collision test every time is expensive. Only run it when AgentRadius is larger than the node size, and cache the result for each node. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import heapq import math def findpath(svonodes, startpos, endpos, agentradius, maxdepth): # 1. Initialize and Validate agentradius = max(0.0, agentradius) # Clamp to non-negative startidx = getnodeatposition(svonodes, startpos, maxdepth) endidx = getnodeatposition(svonodes, endpos, maxdepth) if startidx is None or endidx is None: return None if svonodes[startidx].collisioncache != 1 or svonodes[endidx].collisioncache != 1: return None if startidx == endidx: return [startidx] numnodes = len(svonodes) cost = [float('inf')] numnodes parent = [-1] numnodes closed = [False] numnodes openset = [] # (fscore, nodeidx) cost[startidx] = 0.0 heapq.heappush(openset, (heuristic(startpos, endpos), startidx)) while openset: fu, u = heapq.heappop(openset) if u == endidx: return reconstructpath(parent, u) if closed[u]: continue closed[u] = True # 2. Neighbor Collection neighbors = collectneighbors(svonodes, u, agentradius, maxdepth) for v in neighbors: if closed[v] or svonodes[v].collisioncache != 1: continue tentativeg = cost[u] + distance(svonodes[u].pos, svonodes[v].pos) # 3. Pathfinding (Lazy Theta) parentu = parent[u] if parent[u] != -1 else u if lineofsight(svonodes, parentu, v): newparent = parentu newg = cost[parentu] + distance(svonodes[parentu].pos, svonodes[v].pos) else: newparent = u newg = tentativeg if newg < cost[v]: cost[v] = newg parent[v] = newparent heapq.heappush(openset, (newg + heuristic(svonodes[v].pos, endpos), v)) return None def getnodeatposition(nodes, pos, maxdepth): # Accesses the node Array to find the leaf containing pos for i, node in enumerate(nodes): if node.containspoint(pos): return i return None def collectneighbors(nodes, nodeidx, agentradius, maxdepth): # Uses InlineAllocator behavior: starts fixed, switches to heap if exceeded neighbors = [] for i in range(8): neighboridx = calculateneighborindex(nodeidx, i) if neighboridx is not None and neighboridx < len(nodes): leaves = traversetree(nodes, neighboridx) for leaf in leaves: if nodes[leaf].collisioncache == 1: neighbors.append(leaf) return neighbors def calculateneighborindex(nodeidx, i): # AxisBit points to 1 when Side is negative return nodeidx + (1 << i) def traversetree(nodes, startidx): # DFS to collect all leaf nodes stack = [startidx] leaves = [] while stack: curr = stack.pop() if nodes[curr].isleaf: leaves.append(curr) else: stack.extend(nodes[curr].children) return leaves def lineofsight(nodes, startidx, endidx): # Perform a simple collision test between two points # Exact implementation details are not provided in the sources return True def heuristic(posa, posb): return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(posa, posb))) def distance(posa, posb): return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(posa, posb))) def reconstructpath(parent, endidx): path = [] curr = endidx while curr != -1: path.append(curr) curr = parent[curr] return path[::-1] Time Complexity: Depends on SVO depth and branching factor. At MaxDepth 6, BuildSVO takes 700 microseconds, FindPath takes 300 microseconds. At MaxDepth 8, BuildSVO takes 14 milliseconds, FindPath takes 4 milliseconds. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of nodes in the SVO. Performance: Parallelization improves performance for simple repetitive tasks like BuildSVO. At MaxDepth 6, ParallelFor took 0.7ms, while a regular loop took 1.9ms. Strengths: Reduces path length and node visits through LOS checks. Caching collision results avoids expensive per-step ray-marching. Limitations: Code complexity increases with parallelization. Simple collision test may not be optimal for all scenarios. This method was developed for Unreal Engine 5 (UE5) as a simple SVO pathfinder for 3D pathfinding. It was presented in a tutorial video by an unofficial source. The method leverages the SVO structure for efficient spatial queries and combines A with Lazy Theta for optimal pathfinding. It solves the problem of inefficient random access patterns in large datasets by learning local access traffic, specifically the frequent appearance of predecessor-current-successor node sequences. Unlike the Ray Driven Predictor (RDP), which assumes spatial continuity along a ray, APP does not require nodes to be on the same line or in the same neighborhood, allowing it to accommodate diverse rendering features such as refraction and space leaping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A new sample point s; two recent octree nodes N{last} (the node accessed before N{cur}) and N{cur} (the node currently being accessed). Output: The predicted next node N{new} and cache precaching instructions. Data Structures: Octree Node Metadata: Each octree node stores four pairs of predecessor-successor records, where each record consists of a predecessor node identifier (N{p,i}) and a successor node identifier (N{s,i}). Storage Constraint: Knowledge acquisition and storage are limited to leaf nodes only, which reduces computational costs and utilizes the eight unused child addresses in each leaf node. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set N{new} \leftarrow \text{NULL}. 2. Check Current Node: If s is in N{cur}, set N{new} \leftarrow N{cur} and terminate prediction. 3. Phase I: Access Path Prediction: If N{new} is NULL, iterate through each recorded predecessor N{p,i} of N{cur}. If N{last} == N{p,i} and s is in N{p,i}, set N{new} \leftarrow N{p,i}. 4. Phase II: Historical Successor Prediction: If N{new} is NULL, iterate through each recorded successor N{s,i} of N{cur}. If s is in N{s,i}, set N{new} \leftarrow N{s,i} and return N{new}. 5. Phase III: Fallback Navigation: If N{new} is NULL, set N{new} \leftarrow \text{OctreeNavigation}(N{cur}, s). 6. Update Knowledge: Replace the oldest (N{p,i}, N{s,i}) pair in N{cur} with (N{last}, N{new}). 7. Precaching: If N{cur} is a recorded predecessor of N{new}, set N{next} to the corresponding successor in N{new} and precache N{next} with high priority. Otherwise, precache all four successors in N{new} with low priority. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def AccessPathPredictor(s, Nlast, Ncur): """Predicts the next octree node to access based on learned access patterns.""" Nnew = None # Step 2: Check if sample point is already in the current node if contains(Ncur, s): Nnew = Ncur return Nnew # Step 3: Phase I - Prediction using Access Path for i in range(4): pred = Ncur.predecessors[i] if pred is not None and Nlast == pred and contains(pred, s): Nnew = pred break # Step 4: Phase II - Prediction using Historical Successors if Nnew is None: for i in range(4): succ = Ncur.successors[i] if succ is not None and contains(succ, s): Nnew = succ return Nnew # Step 5: Phase III - Fallback to standard octree navigation if Nnew is None: Nnew = OctreeNavigation(Ncur, s) # Step 6: Update knowledge in Ncur (shift oldest pair out, insert new pair) for i in range(3): Ncur.predecessors[i] = Ncur.predecessors[i+1] Ncur.successors[i] = Ncur.successors[i+1] Ncur.predecessors[3] = Nlast Ncur.successors[3] = Nnew # Step 7: Precaching if Ncur in Nnew.predecessors: idx = Nnew.predecessors.index(Ncur) Nnext = Nnew.successors[idx] # Instruct cache manager to load Nnext with high priority else: for child in Nnew.children: # Instruct cache manager to load child with low priority return Nnew def contains(node, point): """Returns True if point is within the spatial bounds of the node.""" return all(node.min[k] <= point[k] < node.max[k] for k in range(3)) def OctreeNavigation(currentnode, targetpoint): """Standard octree traversal to find the leaf node containing targetpoint.""" if currentnode.isleaf(): return currentnode childindex = getchildindex(currentnode, targetpoint) if currentnode.children[childindex] is not None: return OctreeNavigation(currentnode.children[childindex], targetpoint) return currentnode def getchildindex(node, point): """Determines the index (0-7) of the child containing the point.""" mid = node.center index = 0 if point.x >= mid.x: index |= 1 if point.y >= mid.y: index |= 2 if point.z >= mid.z: index |= 4 return index Parameters: History Depth: Each node stores four predecessor-successor pairs. Storage Scope: Leaf nodes only. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Node Limitation: Knowledge is restricted to leaf nodes to reduce computational costs and utilize the eight unused child addresses in each leaf node. A knowledge-based algorithm that removes the assumption of specific predecessor-current-successor patterns, relying entirely on historic records of nodes required immediately after a visit. It utilizes the eight unused child addresses in each leaf node to store up to eight potential successors. When visiting a node, it pre-caches all known potential successors. If more than eight successors are identified, the oldest is replaced. A key pitfall is that pre-caching up to eight nodes to load one may generate excessive disk traffic. A prediction-based algorithm closely coupled with a discrete ray-tracing engine. It assumes that octree nodes following the ray and along its path will likely be accessed subsequently. Given a ray and current sampling position sc, it determines a predicted sampling point sp on the ray just outside the current octree node. It then navigates the octree to reach the node containing sp, instructing the lower layer to prefetch any nodes not already in the cache during this navigation. This process repeats for each sampling point. Time Complexity: Prediction phases run in O(1) time relative to the fixed history size of four pairs. Octree navigation complexity is not given in the sources. Memory Overhead: Four predecessor-successor pairs per leaf node. Performance: Effective for applications with regular access patterns such as ray tracing, marching cubes, and feature tracking. Limitations: Less effective for highly irregular or random access patterns where historical patterns do not repeat. Comparison: Unlike RDP, APP does not assume spatial continuity, making it more robust for refraction and space leaping. Unlike HAP, APP uses specific path patterns rather than immediate successors, potentially reducing unnecessary pre-caching. The Access Path Predictor was introduced by D. Chisnall, M. Chen, and C. Hansen in 2006 as part of their work on knowledge-based out-of-core algorithms for data management in visualization. It is part of a suite of predictors including the Ray Driven Predictor and History-based Access Predictor, designed to work within a discrete ray-tracing engine.
