name: Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal (State Machine)
head: Fixed-Point SVO Traversal, SVO Raycasting
body: A deterministic software ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) implemented as a finite state machine using fixed-point arithmetic, originally designed to emulate an FPGA hardware raycaster. It differs from recursive or stack-based traversals by using explicit goto-based control flow and a circular buffer stack to manage backtracking, ensuring predictable execution paths suitable for hardware synthesis or deterministic software rendering. Inputs: Ray origin r.o, ray direction r.d, SVO data structure (compact nodes), traversal parameters. Outputs: Hit point, depth, or traversal status. Data Structures: CNode (Compact Node): 32-bit packed structure. Bits 0-7: validmask (8 bits, child validity). Bits 8-15: leafmask (8 bits, child leaf status). Bits 16-30: childptr (15 bits, offset to children). Bit 31: farptr flag (1 bit, indicates if children are at a far address). OctreeCursor: Contains pointer to CNode data, current CNode node, current address adr, current level, and a Cache pointer. StackItem: cur: OctreeCursor. tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1: Fixed-point intersection times (tnum). idx: Current child index being processed. Stack: Circular buffer of StackItem with top index, length, and size ss. Push wraps top modulo ss and increments length (capped at ss). Pop decrements top (wrapping if negative) and decrements length. Parameters: terminLevel: Maximum depth before forcing leaf termination. Default: 10. tnumscale: Fixed-point scaling factor. Value: 65536 (2^{16}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Direction Normalization: If any component of r.d is zero, add 0.001 to that component to prevent division by zero. If any component of r.d is negative, flip the ray origin component (r.o.x \leftarrow -r.o.x) and negate the direction component (r.d.x \leftarrow -r.d.x). Record these flips in dirmask (bit 4 for X, bit 2 for Y, bit 1 for Z). 2. Initial Bounding Box Intersection: Compute intersection times with the unit cube [-1, 1]^3: tx0 = \frac{-1 - r.o.x}{r.d.x}, \quad tx1 = \frac{1 - r.o.x}{r.d.x} ty0 = \frac{-1 - r.o.y}{r.d.y}, \quad ty1 = \frac{1 - r.o.y}{r.d.y} tz0 = \frac{-1 - r.o.z}{r.d.z}, \quad tz1 = \frac{1 - r.o.z}{r.d.z} Calculate entry and exit times: t{enter} = \max(tx0, \max(ty0, tz0)) t{exit} = \min(tx1, \min(ty1, tz1)) If t{enter} \ge t{exit}, the ray misses the bounding box; terminate. 3. Fixed-Point Conversion: Scale times by tnumscale: tnum = t \times 65536. Clip values to [tnum\min + 1000, tnum\max - 1000] to prevent overflow. 4. State Machine Loop: The traversal uses goto-based control flow. Initialization: Initialize cur to root. level = 0. Compute Midpoints: txm = (tx0+tx1)/2, tym = (ty0+ty1)/2, tzm = (tz0+tz1)/2. Set Entry Time: Set t{enter} = \max(tx0, \max(ty0, tz0)). Select Initial Child Index: idx = (txm < t{enter}) \ll 2 \mid (tym < t{enter}) \ll 1 \mid (tzm < t{enter}). Compute Child Bounds: tx0{child} = (idx \& 4) ? txm: tx0, tx1{child} = (idx \& 4) ? tx1: txm (similarly for Y and Z). Calculate Child Exit Time: t{exit\child} = \min(tx1{child}, \min(ty1{child}, tz1{child})). Flip Index for Direction: idx{flip} = idx \oplus dir\mask. Check Exit: If t{exit\child} \le t{start} (current traversal start time), skip this node. Jump to next index. Check Leaf/Termination: If cur.childIsFilled(idxflip) OR level == terminLevel: mark as leaf hit and finish. Check Validity: If cur.childIsValid(idxflip): push current state (cur, bounds, idx) to Stack. Update cur to child: cur = cur.getChild(idxflip). Update bounds to child bounds. Increment level. Continue traversal. Handle Node Exit/Backtrack: If exiting node and level==0, finish. If stack is empty, restart traversal from t{exit\child}. Otherwise, pop stack, decrement level, and continue traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversesvostatemachine(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, nodedata, cache, terminlevel=10, tnumscale=65536): # 1. Handle Ray Direction dirmask = 0 ro = list(rayorigin) # [x, y, z] rd = list(raydirection) for i in range(3): if rd[i] == 0: rd[i] = 0.001 if rd[i] < 0: ro[i] = -ro[i] rd[i] = -rd[i] if i == 0: dirmask |= 4 elif i == 1: dirmask |= 2 elif i == 2: dirmask |= 1 # 2. Initial Bounding Box Intersection tx0 = (-1.0 - ro[0]) / rd[0] tx1 = (1.0 - ro[0]) / rd[0] ty0 = (-1.0 - ro[1]) / rd[1] ty1 = (1.0 - ro[1]) / rd[1] tz0 = (-1.0 - ro[2]) / rd[2] tz1 = (1.0 - ro[2]) / rd[2] tenter = max(tx0, max(ty0, tz0)) texit = min(tx1, min(ty1, tz1)) if tenter >= texit: return None # Miss # 3. Fixed-Point Conversion & Clipping tnummax = 231 - 1 # tnummin = -231 # def totnum(t): val = int(t tnumscale) return max(tnummin + 1000, min(tnummax - 1000, val)) tx0, tx1 = totnum(tx0), totnum(tx1) ty0, ty1 = totnum(ty0), totnum(ty1) tz0, tz1 = totnum(tz0), totnum(tz1) # Data Structures class StackItem: def init(self, cur, tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1, idx): self.cur = cur self.tx0, self.ty0, self.tz0 = tx0, ty0, tz0 self.tx1, self.ty1, self.tz1 = tx1, ty1, tz1 self.idx = idx stackstore = [None] 256 # ss stacktop = 0 stacklen = 0 def pushstack(item): nonlocal stacktop, stacklen stackstore[stacktop] = item stacktop = (stacktop + 1) % len(stackstore) if stacklen < len(stackstore): stacklen += 1 def popstack(): nonlocal stacktop, stacklen if stacklen == 0: return None stacklen -= 1 stacktop = (stacktop - 1) % len(stackstore) if stacktop < 0: stacktop += len(stackstore) return stackstore[stacktop] class OctreeCursor: def init(self, data, node, adr, level, cache): self.data = data self.node = node self.adr = adr self.level = level self.cache = cache def childIsFilled(self, idx): return (self.node.leafmask >> idx) & 1 def childIsValid(self, idx): return (self.node.validmask >> idx) & 1 def getChild(self, childidx): childptr = self.node.childptr & ~(1 << 15) if self.node.childptr & (1 << 15): faradr = self.adr + childptr childnode = self.data[faradr] else: childnode = self.data[self.adr + childptr] return OctreeCursor(self.data, childnode, self.adr + childptr, self.level + 1, self.cache) # Initialize cur = OctreeCursor(nodedata, rootnode, 0, 0, cache) level = 0 tstart = 0 idx = 0 texitchild = 0 while True: # Compute midpoints & entry time txm = (tx0 + tx1) // 2 tym = (ty0 + ty1) // 2 tzm = (tz0 + tz1) // 2 tentercurr = max(tx0, max(ty0, tz0)) # Select initial child index on first node if level == 0 and idx == 0: idx = ((txm < tentercurr) << 2) | ((tym < tentercurr) << 1) | (tzm < tentercurr) while idx < 8: # Compute child bounds ctx0 = txm if (idx & 4) else tx0 ctx1 = tx1 if (idx & 4) else txm cty0 = tym if (idx & 2) else ty0 cty1 = ty1 if (idx & 2) else tym ctz0 = tzm if (idx & 1) else tz0 ctz1 = tz1 if (idx & 1) else tzm texitchild = min(ctx1, min(cty1, ctz1)) idxflip = idx ^ dirmask # Check Exit if texitchild <= tstart: idx += 1 continue # Check Leaf/Termination if cur.childIsFilled(idxflip) or level == terminlevel: return {"hit": True, "depth": texitchild, "node": cur.node} # Check Validity if cur.childIsValid(idxflip): pushstack(StackItem(cur, tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1, idx)) cur = cur.getChild(idxflip) tx0, ty0, tz0 = ctx0, cty0, ctz0 tx1, ty1, tz1 = ctx1, cty1, ctz1 level += 1 idx = 0 break # Restart loop for new node else: idx += 1 # Handle Node Exit/Backtrack if level == 0: return None # Finish if stacklen == 0: # Restart from texitchild tstart = texitchild cur = OctreeCursor(nodedata, rootnode, 0, 0, cache) level = 0 tx0, tx1 = totnum((-1.0 - ro[0]) / rd[0]), totnum((1.0 - ro[0]) / rd[0]) ty0, ty1 = totnum((-1.0 - ro[1]) / rd[1]), totnum((1.0 - ro[1]) / rd[1]) tz0, tz1 = totnum((-1.0 - ro[2]) / rd[2]), totnum((1.0 - ro[2]) / rd[2]) idx = 0 continue popped = popstack() cur = popped.cur tx0, ty0, tz0 = popped.tx0, popped.ty0, popped.tz0 tx1, ty1, tz1 = popped.tx1, popped.ty1, popped.tz1 idx = popped.idx + 1 level -= 1 Not given in the sources. The method originates from the svo-workbench project by skyfex, which implements a software ray tracer for Sparse Voxel Octrees. It was specifically designed to model a Verilog-based hardware raycaster, allowing the same traversal logic to be used in both software and FPGA implementations. The project demonstrates caching strategies and rendering into a shared framebuffer. skyfex/svo-workbench, https://github.com/skyfex/svo-workbench, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Animated Sparse Voxel Octrees (ASVO)
head: Animated Sparse Voxel Octree Renderer with X-Toon Shading, SVO renderer, XToonVolume
body: ASVO is a GPU-based raycasting method for rendering animated sparse voxel octrees (SVOs) using X-Toon shading. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering voxel-based characters and models that undergo rigid transformations or skinning by animating rigid octree parts via a keyframed skeleton and placing them in a per-frame top-level bounding volume hierarchy (BVH). Unlike static SVO renderers, ASVO dynamically updates the spatial acceleration structure every frame to account for bone-driven deformation, allowing for real-time animation of complex voxel models. The method consists of an octree builder, an animation system, a traversal kernel, and a shading/draw kernel. It is implemented using OpenGL 4.5 compute shaders. Inputs: Sparse Voxel Octree data: Inner nodes, leaf nodes (visual data), and animation bone matrices. Scene data: Camera position, view/projection matrices, light position, and texture maps (diffuse, illumination, normal, specular). Animation frame index. Outputs: Color buffer (final rendered image). Depth buffer (for visibility culling). The implementation uses parallel arrays to store the octree and job queue. Inner Nodes (BFSInnerNode): mask: Bitmask indicating which of the 8 children are occupied. childPtr: Index offset to the first child in the inner node array. Leaf Nodes (VisualData): boneWeights: Array of 4 floats representing skinning weights. If boneWeights.x > 0, the leaf is skinned. boneIndex0-3: Indices of the 4 bones influencing this leaf. normal: Surface normal vector. pos: Packed position/size data (used for screen-space checks). tangent, texCoord, eyeVec, originalCenter: Additional visual data. Jobs (BFSJob): index: Index of the node in the inner node array. x, y, z: Subscript within the parent node (0-7). Animation Buffer: animation: Array of float4x4 matrices. Size is mframeCount mboneCount. 1. Octree Building (Pre-processing): Build the octree from Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) or raw volumes using a Morton-sorted, bottom-up approach. Prefilter color and normal data during construction. Perform size checks on nodes. 2. Animation Update: Update the current animation frame based on elapsed time. Rigid octree parts are animated by a keyframed skeleton. Construct a per-frame top-level BVH containing the animated parts. 3. Traversal Kernel (Job Queue Processing): Each thread processes one job from a shared queue. Grid Cell Calculation: Calculate the dimensions of the voxel at the current octree level: gridCellDim = \frac{dimension}{2^{octreeLevel}} gridCellHalfDim = gridCellDim \times 0.5 Skinning Application: Compute the voxel center in world space. If the leaf node has bone weights (node.vd.boneWeights.x > 0), interpolate the center position using up to 4 bone transformations from the animation buffer based on boneIndex0-3 and boneWeights.x-w. Otherwise, use the original center. Dimension Adjustment: Resize the voxel half-dimension to counteract stretching during skinning: gridCellHalfDim \times= \min(2.0, \text{involvedBones}) Transformation to Clip Space: Transform the center and dimensions into clip space by multiplying by world, view, and projection matrices. Compute the eye vector: eyeVec = \text{normalize}(camPos - center) Culling: Perform frustum culling: The voxel is visible if its clip-space bounds are within [-1, 1]. Perform back-face culling: If the octree level is greater than 8, the voxel is visible only if: \text{dot}(node.vd.normal, eyeVec) \ge -0.4 Screen Projection and Queueing: Project the voxel center to screen coordinates (x, y) and compute depth: depth = center.z \times \text{INT\MAX} If the voxel has children (dgetChildCountFromMask(node.mask) != 0) and spans more than 1 pixel (dimVec.x > 1.0), add child jobs to the queue using atomicAdd on sharedTravQueuePtr. Otherwise, update the depth buffer: atomicMin(depthBuffer + index, depth) Visual Data Writing: If the voxel was drawn (w==1) and its depth matches the updated depth buffer value, write its visual data (normal, tangent, position, texCoord, eyeVec, originalCenter) to the voxelBuffer at the screen index. 4. Draw Kernel (Shading): For each pixel, scan a 3x3 neighborhood in the depth buffer to find the voxel with the minimum depth that covers the pixel. A voxel covers the pixel if: |vd.pos.x - 0.5 - x| \le vd.pos.z \quad \text{and} \quad |vd.pos.y - 0.5 - y| \le vd.pos.w Lighting: Transform the voxel center to light space. Check shadow mapping against shadowMap. Compute diffuse and specular lighting using textures for diffuse, illumination, normal, and specular maps. Update the color buffer. Unverified code. centerworld) # Culling if not isinfrustum(centerclip): return if octreelevel > 8: if dot(vd.normal, eyevec) < -0.4: return # Project to screen xscreen, yscreen = projecttoscreen(centerclip) depth = centerclip.z INTMAX # Check if leaf or has children childcount = getchildcountfrommask(node.mask) dimvec = getdimensionvector(node) if childcount != 0 and dimvec.x > 1.0: # Add children to queue for i in range(8): if (node.mask & (1 << i)) != 0: newjob = BFSJob(node.childptr + i, (job.x 2) + (i & 1), (job.y 2) + ((i & 2) >> 1), (job.z 2) + ((i & 4) >> 2)) atomicadd(sharedtravqueueptr, 1) jobqueue[atomicadd(sharedtravqueueptr, -1)] = newjob # Push to queue else: # Update depth buffer index = getscreenindex(xscreen, yscreen) olddepth = atomicmin(depthbuffer + index, depth) # If we won the depth test (or it was the first write) if depth == depthbuffer[index]: # Write visual data voxelbuffer[index] = VisualData(vd.normal, vd.tangent, centerworld, vd.texcoord, eyevec, vd.originalcenter) def drawkernel(depthbuffer, voxelbuffer, shadowmap, diffusemap, illummap, specmap, normalmap, colorbuffer): x, y = getpixelcoordinates() # Scan 3x3 neighborhood for min depth mindepth = INTMAX bestvoxel = None for dy in range(-1, 2): for dx in range(-1, 2): idx = getscreenindex(x + dx, y + dy) d = depthbuffer[idx] if d < mindepth: mindepth = d bestvoxel = voxelbuffer[idx] if bestvoxel is None: return # Check coverage if abs(bestvoxel.pos.x - 0.5 - x) <= bestvoxel.pos.z and abs(bestvoxel.pos.y - 0.5 - y) <= bestvoxel.pos.w: # Lighting lightspacepos = transformtolightspace(bestvoxel.originalcenter) shadow = checkshadowmapping(lightspacepos, shadowmap) diffuse = sampletexture(diffusemap, bestvoxel.texcoord) illum = sampletexture(illummap, bestvoxel.texcoord) spec = sampletexture(specmap, bestvoxel.texcoord) normal = sampletexture(normalmap, bestvoxel.texcoord) color = computediffusespecularlighting(normal, bestvoxel.eyevec, lightspacepos, shadow, diffuse, illum, spec) colorbuffer[x, y] = color Graphics API: OpenGL 4.5 compute shaders. Back-face Culling Threshold: dot(normal, eyeVec) >= -0.4 for levels > 8. Skinning Stretch Compensation: min(2.0, involvedBones). Divide by Zero: In the original 2016 shader, a divide by zero error occurred when r = 1 in the X-Toon log formula. This must be guarded against. Light Direction: The original shader incorrectly used the light position as a direction vector. It must be converted to a direction (light position - surface position). Negative Dot Product: Using pow on a negative n.v (normal dot view) caused issues. Ensure the base is non-negative or handle negative results appropriately. Unsigned Gradients: Ensure gradients are handled as signed values if required by the shading model, as unsigned gradients caused artifacts in the original version. GLREPEAT: Issues with GLREPEAT texture wrapping were present in the original shader and must be fixed. Time Complexity: The traversal is hierarchical DDA with pixel-footprint LOD. The complexity depends on the depth of the octree and the number of visible voxels. The use of a job queue allows for parallel processing on the GPU. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for inner nodes, leaf nodes, animation matrices, and the BVH. The BVH is rebuilt per frame, which adds overhead but allows for efficient culling of animated parts. Performance: The implementation includes unit tests for traversal and BVH against brute force, and a --compare mode that checks GPU output against the CPU renderer, ensuring correctness. Strengths: Efficiently handles animated voxel models using skinning and hierarchical culling. The per-frame BVH allows for efficient culling of non-visible animated parts. Limitations: The per-frame BVH construction adds overhead. The method is specific to OpenGL 4.5 compute shaders in the provided implementation. ASVO was introduced as part of a thesis project on animated sparse voxel octrees. The original implementation was in CUDA/C++ with an XNA/C# prototype for design. A later rebuild by Andre Rogers added an OpenGL 4.5 compute shader implementation with X-Toon shading, fixing several shader bugs from the original 2016 version. The method is demonstrated with scenes such as a crowd of walkers sharing limb octrees and a bonsai tree. name: SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation
head: SVO Ray March, SVO Ray Marcher, Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Tracing
body: SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation is a ray traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) that uses an explicit stack to manage traversal state, enabling efficient navigation through the hierarchical structure to find voxel intersections. It differs from parent methods by decoupling the traversal logic from the ray's parametric distance, using a fixed-point-like scale representation to step through the tree levels, and explicitly managing node validity and corner positions via a stack of nodeinfot elements. This approach allows for robust handling of empty space and early termination based on pixel error thresholds. Inputs: raypos: The origin of the ray (\mathbf{p}). raydir: The direction of the ray (\mathbf{d}), normalized. svotree: The Sparse Voxel Octree data structure. minraylength2: A minimum ray length constant added to the calculated distance. rayScale2: A parameter related to ray step size or resolution, used for pixel error calculation. Outputs: outt: The distance to the hit voxel along the ray. outnormal: The normal of the hit voxel face. bool: True if a hit was found, false otherwise. The algorithm relies on a stack to store traversal state. nodeinfot parent: Index or pointer to the parent node in the SVO. corner: A 3-bit integer (or equivalent) representing the corner of the current node within its parent. lower: A 3D vector (\mathbb{R}^3) representing the absolute lower bound of the current node in world space. Stack A dynamic array or linked list of nodeinfot elements. Operations: push, pop, back (access top element), size (get current depth). rayScale2: Used in svovoxelpixelerror to determine the threshold for pixel error. minraylength2: A minimum ray length constant added to the calculated distance. 1. Initialization: Initialize an empty stack stack. Determine the root node of the SVO. Calculate the initial lower bound for the root node (typically the origin of the SVO space). Push the root node onto the stack. Set rayisoutside = false. 2. Traversal Loop: While stack.size > 0: Let level = stack.size. Calculate scale = 1.0 / (1 << level). Let current = stack.back(). Determine node validity: Check if the node is null using svotreeisnull. Check if the node is a leaf using svotreeisleaff3. Check if the node has children using svotreehaschildren. Check if the node contains a voxel using svotreevoxelexists. If rayisoutside is true: Pop the stack: svostackpop(&stack). If the stack is empty, break and return false. Retrieve the new current from stack.back(). Adjust lower: lower -= cornerincrement0 scale, where cornerincrement0 is the unit vector corresponding to the popped node's corner. Attempt to move to the next corner in the outface direction: nextcorner1 = movecorner(current.corner, outface). If nextcorner1 is valid: Set rayisoutside = false. Update current.parent and current.corner to the popped node's parent and nextcorner1. Adjust lower: lower -= cornerincrement0 scale; lower += cornerincrement1 scale, where cornerincrement1 corresponds to nextcorner1. Continue to the next iteration. If nextcorner1 is invalid (boundary of parent): Set rayisoutside = true. Continue to the next iteration (loop will pop again). If the current node has a voxel (svotreevoxelexists) and the ray intersects the voxel data (svointersectsvoxeldataf3): Calculate direction bounds: dirbounds = svocalculatedirboundsf3(lower, lower + scale, raydir). Check for pixel error: error = svovoxelpixelerror(sdistancef3(raypos, dirlower), rayScale2, level). If error < threshold: Record hit distance: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirlower). Compute normal from the opposite face of outface. Return true. If the node is a leaf (svotreeisleaff3): Record hit distance and normal. Return true. If the node has children (svotreehaschildren): Push the current node onto the stack: svostackpush(&stack, &current). Calculate the next corner for the child node: nextcorner = svopushcalculatenextcornerf3(cubenormalizeddir, dirlower, scale, t1). Update lower for the child node: nextlower = lower + (cornerincrement childscale), where childscale = 1.0 / (1 << (level + 1)). Get the child node descriptor: current = svotreegetchild(addressspace, current, nextcorner). Update lower = nextlower. Continue to the next iteration. 3. Termination: If the stack is empty and no hit was found, return false. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def svoraymarchstackbased(raypos, raydir, svotree, minraylength2, rayScale2): stack = [] rootnode = svotree.getroot() rootlower = svotree.getlowerbound() current = NodeInfo(parent=None, corner=0, lower=rootlower) stack.append(current) rayisoutside = False while len(stack) > 0: level = len(stack) scale = 1.0 / (1 << level) current = stack[-1] isnull = svotreeisnull(svotree, current) isleaf = svotreeisleaff3(svotree, current) haschildren = svotreehaschildren(svotree, current) hasvoxel = svotreevoxelexists(svotree, current) if rayisoutside: stack.pop() if len(stack) == 0: return False, None, None current = stack[-1] cornerincrement0 = getcornerunitvector(current.corner) current.lower -= cornerincrement0 scale outface = getoutface(raydir, current.corner) nextcorner1 = movecorner(current.corner, outface) if nextcorner1 is not None: rayisoutside = False current.corner = nextcorner1 cornerincrement1 = getcornerunitvector(nextcorner1) current.lower -= cornerincrement0 scale current.lower += cornerincrement1 scale continue else: rayisoutside = True continue if hasvoxel and svointersectsvoxeldataf3(svotree, current): dirbounds = svocalculatedirboundsf3(current.lower, current.lower + scale, raydir) error = svovoxelpixelerror(sdistancef3(raypos, dirbounds.dirlower), rayScale2, level) if error < threshold: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirbounds.dirlower) outnormal = computenormalfromface(oppositeface(outface)) return True, outt, outnormal if isleaf: outt = minraylength2 + sdistancef3(raypos, dirbounds.dirlower) outnormal = computenormalfromface(oppositeface(outface)) return True, outt, outnormal if haschildren: stack.append(current) nextcorner = svopushcalculatenextcornerf3(cubenormalizeddir, dirbounds.dirlower, scale, t1) childscale = 1.0 / (1 << (level + 1)) nextlower = current.lower + (cornerincrement childscale) current = svotreegetchild(addressspace, current, nextcorner) current.lower = nextlower continue return False, None, None realazthat/landscapes, https://github.com/realazthat/landscapes, fetched 2026-10-26 name: Octree Voxel Raycasting for Hover (Closest Active Voxel)
head: Octree Closest Hit Tracing
body: This method traces rays against a GPU-accessible octree to find the closest intersections with active voxels. It tracks both the nearest active leaf node and the nearest empty space node to support hover interactions. It differs from standard SVO ray tracing [2989-sparse-voxel-octree-ray-tracing.md] by prioritizing closest-hit detection and empty-space fallback for interaction rather than full volume integration. Inputs: rays (GPU buffer of Ray structs, size resolution resolution), octree (GPU-accessible sparse voxel octree), resolution (grid width and height). Outputs: hits (GPU buffer of Hit structs, size resolution resolution), hosthits (host std::vector<Hit> of size resolution resolution for downloaded results). Data Structures: Ray: Origin and direction vectors. Hit: Intersection results including distance, position, and normal. OctreeNode: isLeaf (bool), isActive (bool), position (vec3), size (vec3), color (vec3), children (array of 8 pointers). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceclosestkernel(rays, hits, octree, resolution, currentdepth): for idx in range(resolution resolution): ray = rays[idx] closesthitdistance = float('inf') closestemptydistance = float('inf') foundactivevoxel = False hoverinfo = {"hashit": False, "node": None, "distance": float('inf'), "position": None, "normal": None} node = octree.root depth = 0 while node is not None: hitdistance, hitposition, hitnormal = computeintersection(ray, node) if hitdistance < float('inf'): if node.isActive and node.isLeaf: if hitdistance < closesthitdistance: closesthitdistance = hitdistance foundactivevoxel = True hits[idx].distance = closesthitdistance hits[idx].position = hitposition hits[idx].normal = hitnormal elif not foundactivevoxel and depth >= currentdepth and hitdistance < closestemptydistance: closestemptydistance = hitdistance hoverinfo["hashit"] = True hoverinfo["node"] = node hoverinfo["distance"] = closestemptydistance hoverinfo["position"] = hitposition hoverinfo["normal"] = hitnormal # Advance traversal logic node = getnextnode(node, ray, depth) depth += 1 hits[idx].hoverinfo = hoverinfo Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Reset closestHitDistance to infinity, closestEmptyDistance to infinity, and foundActiveVoxel to false when depth == 1. Reset hoverInfo.hasHit to false. 2. Dispatch: Call octree->traceclosest(rays->data(), hits->data(), resolution, resolution) on the GPU. 3. Traversal: For each ray, traverse the octree. If an active leaf is intersected, update closestHitDistance and record the hit. If an empty/internal node is intersected and !foundActiveVoxel and depth >= currentDepth and hitDistance < closestEmptyDistance, compute position and normal, update hoverInfo to point to the empty space node, set closestEmptyDistance = hitDistance, and set hoverInfo.hasHit = true. 4. Download: Transfer hits to host memory via hits->download(hosthits.data()). Parameters: resolution: Width and height of the ray grid. currentDepth: Maximum traversal depth limit. Edge Cases: No Hit: If no active voxel is intersected, foundActiveVoxel remains false and hoverInfo.hasHit indicates empty-space fallback. Precision: Floating-point comparisons for distance thresholds may require epsilon guards. Boundaries: Ray origins exactly on node boundaries require consistent half-open interval handling. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of rays (W \times H) and D is the average octree traversal depth. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the rays and hits GPU buffers. Strengths: Parallel GPU execution efficiently resolves closest-hit queries for interaction. Limitations: Requires host-device synchronization for result downloads and GPU memory allocation. When to Use: Hover interactions, picking, or closest-hit queries in SVO-based renderers. When Not to Use: Full volume integration, ray marching with accumulation, or CPU-only pipelines. The method originates from GPU-based voxelization pipelines that dispatch ray tracing tasks via a stream and thread pool architecture. It builds on Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Tracing by specializing the traversal for closest active voxel detection and empty-space hover feedback. name: Octree Ray Marching with Brick Interpolation and Early Termination
head: Brick-based SVO Ray Marching, GigaVoxels-style Ray Traversal
body: This method performs volume rendering on a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) by traversing the tree structure and sampling data stored in "bricks" (small, fixed-size blocks of voxels) rather than individual leaf voxels. It solves the problem of inefficient memory access and cache thrashing in large-volume rendering by grouping data into bricks, which improves texture cache utilization and reduces traversal overhead compared to single-voxel stepping. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SVO Ray Marching with Stack-Based Navigation by explicitly handling interpolation between bricks of different resolutions and using early termination based on accumulated opacity to skip empty space, whereas Octree Voxel Raycasting for Hover (Closest Active Voxel) focuses on finding the nearest surface rather than full volume integration. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D in world coordinates. SVO root node pointer. Volume bounding box extents V{min} and V{max}. Current camera projection parameters (to compute projected voxel size). Brick dimensions (Bx, By, Bz) and border sizes. Maximum nodes to push per frame (MaxNodesToPushThisFrame) and reset threshold (maxNodesPerPixelBlock). Outputs: Final color C and opacity \alpha for the pixel. Updated node usage statistics for asynchronous brick loading. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains a pointer to the next node in the hierarchy, a pointer to the brick data (if leaf), and metadata (depth, size). Brick Data: A 3D texture or buffer containing color and optionally gradient values for a block of voxels. Node Usage List: A queue of nodes recently traversed, used to trigger asynchronous GPU upload of their brick data. Parameters: projVoxelSize: Projected voxel size in world units. parentVoxelSize: Voxel size at the parent octree level. k{ChildNodeSizeScalar}: Scalar multiplier for node size on descent (typically 0.5 for octrees). MaxNodesToPushThisFrame: Limit on asynchronous work per frame. maxNodesPerPixelBlock: Threshold for resetting the per-block traversal counter. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set current node N to root. Set current extents E{min} = V{min}, E{max} = V{max}. Set current node size S = 1.0 (normalized) or root voxel size. Set voxel half-size h = RootVoxelHalfSize. Reset traversal counters: traversalCount = 0, nodeListTraversalCount = 0. Initialize accumulated color C = (0,0,0,0) and transmittance T = 1.0. 2. Ray-Volume Intersection Test: Compute containment: test1 = \text{sign}(O - V{min}) test2 = \text{sign}(V{max} - O) inside = \text{dot}(test1, test2) If inside < 3, the ray origin is outside the volume bounding box. Handle entry point calculation or terminate if the ray does not intersect the bounding box. 3. Traversal Loop: While T > \epsilon and N is valid: a. Increment Counters: traversalCount \leftarrow traversalCount + 1 nodeListTraversalCount \leftarrow nodeListTraversalCount + 1 If nodeListTraversalCount \ge maxNodesPerPixelBlock, reset nodeListTraversalCount = 0. b. Node Management (Asynchronous Loading): If nodeListTraversalCount is within startPushingNodes, stopPushingNodes) and pushedNodeCount < MaxNodesToPushThisFrame: Increment pushedNodeCount. Call AddToNodeUsageList(N). This schedules the brick data associated with N for asynchronous GPU upload if not already present. c. Interpolation Decision: Check if interpolation is enabled: Condition: projVoxelSize > parentVoxelSize (or similar scale check), curDepth \neq 0, and interpolation factor > 0.001. If true, compute previous brick ray position and call TraverseBrickInterp. Otherwise, call TraverseBrick. Note: Interpolation is disabled at the root node (curDepth == 0) to prevent invalid ratios when parentVoxelSize equals projVoxelSize. d. Descent (if moving to child): Compute brick offset: brickOffset = rayBrickPosition \times k{TreeN} (where k{TreeN} is the number of children, typically 8). Clamp to child index: childOffset = \text{clamp}(\text{uvec3}(brickOffset), 0, 1). Update ray position within brick: rayBrickPosition = brickOffset - vec3(childOffset). Update extents: E{min} += (vec3(childOffset) \times S) E{max} -= ((vec3(1.0) - vec3(childOffset)) \times S) Fetch next node: N = \text{texelFetch}(OctTreeSampler, N.ptr, 0). e. [Brick Traversal (TraverseBrick): Sample the brick data at the current ray position. Compute density/color \rho, c. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \times (1 - \rho \cdot \Delta s). Update color: C \leftarrow C + T \cdot c \cdot \rho \cdot \Delta s. Advance ray by step size \Delta s. f. Brick Interpolation (TraverseBrickInterp): Sample surrounding bricks or interpolate within the brick based on the interpolation factor derived from projVoxelSize and parentVoxelSize. Apply the same color/opacity accumulation as above. Pitfall: Interpolation factor is clamped to [0.0, 1.0] and thresholded at 0.001 to avoid division by zero. g. Early Termination: If accumulated opacity > 0.995 AND the current step actually traversed a brick or constant value (not empty space): Terminate loop. This prevents premature cutoff during initialization or in empty space. 4. Reset State: After ray completion, reset N to root, extents, and sizes for the next ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydir, rootnode, volumeextentsmin, volumeextentsmax, projvoxelsize, parentvoxelsize, maxnodesperblock, maxnodesperframe): # Initialization currentnode = rootnode nodesize = 1.0 # Normalized or root voxel size voxelhalfsize = rootvoxelhalfsize extentsmin = volumeextentsmin extentsmax = volumeextentsmax accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 traversalcount = 0 nodelisttraversalcount = 0 pushednodecount = 0 curdepth = 0 # Ray-Volume Intersection Check test1 = sign(rayorigin - volumeextentsmin) test2 = sign(volumeextentsmax - rayorigin) inside = dot(test1, test2) if inside < 3.0: # Handle ray outside volume or compute entry point pass while transmittance > 0.001 and currentnode is not None: traversalcount += 1 nodelisttraversalcount += 1 # Reset counter if threshold reached if nodelisttraversalcount >= maxnodesperblock: nodelisttraversalcount = 0 # Asynchronous Node Loading if (startpushingnodes <= nodelisttraversalcount < stoppushingnodes) and \ (pushednodecount < maxnodesperframe): pushednodecount += 1 addtonodeusagelist(currentnode) # Determine Interpolation Mode interpfactor = computeinterpolationfactor(projvoxelsize, parentvoxelsize) enableinterp = (projvoxelsize > parentvoxelsize) and (curdepth != 0) and (interpfactor > 0.001) if enableinterp: prevbrickraypos = computeprevbrickraypos() color, alpha, newtransmittance = traversebrickinterp(currentnode, rayorigin, raydir, prevbrickraypos, interpfactor, nodesize, extentsmin, extentsmax) else: color, alpha, newtransmittance = traversebrick(currentnode, rayorigin, raydir, nodesize, extentsmin, extentsmax) # Update Accumulators accumulatedcolor += transmittance color transmittance = newtransmittance # Early Termination Check if transmittance < 0.005 and alpha > 0.0: # Opacity > 0.995 implies transmittance < 0.005 # Ensure we actually traversed something if alpha > 0.0: break # Descent Logic (Simplified for single step) # In a real implementation, this happens inside traversebrick/interp or as a separate step # if moving to a child node: # brickoffset = raybrickposition 8 # childoffset = clamp(uvec3(brickoffset), 0, 1) # raybrickposition = brickoffset - vec3(childoffset) # extentsmin += vec3(childoffset) nodesize # extentsmax -= (vec3(1.0) - vec3(childoffset)) nodesize # currentnode = fetchnextnode(currentnode, childoffset) # nodesize = 0.5 # curdepth += 1 return accumulatedcolor This variant accelerates rendering by using sparse octrees to store caches, enabling raytracing to skip empty space and terminate rays missing the object. It converts the density cache to a signed distance function (SDF) by thresholding at 0.0, optionally downsamples the SDF, and generates a collision mesh using marching cubes. Rays are traced against the BVH of this mesh to find occupied voxels, skipping empty space efficiently. For rays hitting occupied voxels, volume integration uses cached components. It uses BVH/ray-triangle intersection instead of hierarchical DDA to leverage hardware acceleration, allow easy mesh deformation/downsampling, and enable compositing of fake shadows/bouncelight. Cache resolutions are typically 1024^3 (8 components) for NeRF Synthetic 360 scenes (except ship: 768^3) and 768^3 (6 components) for LLFF. This method performs volume rendering via ray-casting that traverses the octree hierarchy to skip empty space and march rays near the surface. It uses multi-resolution interpolation to handle variable resolution blocks at boundaries, avoiding complex synchronization issues. The hierarchy is traversed to skip empty space and advance the ray as close as possible to the surface. In the proximity of the surface, the ray is marched in steps proportional to the distance from the zero-crossing. At each step, the SDF field is sampled via tri-linear interpolation. The accurate 3D position of the surface is computed when the ray transitions from positive to negative space. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of visible voxels/bricks along the ray. Early termination reduces the effective N significantly in sparse volumes. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the total volume of the SVO, but only active bricks are loaded into GPU memory. The node usage list adds O(M) overhead where M is the number of nodes traversed per frame. Performance: Improves cache coherency by accessing brick-sized blocks rather than scattered leaf voxels. Asynchronous loading hides memory latency. Strengths: Efficient handling of large, sparse volumes; reduced memory bandwidth usage; supports dynamic transfer functions without texture regeneration (unlike some bricking techniques). Limitations: Interpolation artifacts at brick boundaries if not handled carefully; complexity in managing asynchronous loading and node usage lists; early termination may cause visual artifacts if not tuned properly. When to use: Large-scale volume rendering where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and the volume is sparse. When not to use: Dense volumes where brick overhead outweighs benefits, or when exact surface reconstruction is required without post-processing. The method originates from the GigaVoxels project, which introduced bricking as a technique to optimize volume rendering on GPUs by grouping voxels into bricks to improve cache performance. The specific combination of octree traversal, brick interpolation, and early termination is detailed in the VoxViz thesis, which describes the implementation of GigaVoxels in a real-time rendering context. The technique addresses the limitations of traditional ray marching on dense textures and the overhead of pure octree traversal on leaf nodes. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) FastNeRF by Garbin et al., https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.10380, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Adaptive-resolution octree-based volumetric SLAM, https://www.doc.ic.ac.uk/~sleutene/publications/Vespa3DV19.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Two-staged Space-Skipping with Bricking and Octrees
head: Bricking with octree refinement, Two-stage space-skipping
body: This method balances GPU rendering bottlenecks by dividing space-skipping into two distinct stages: coarse division using bricking to address bus and texture cache limitations, and fine division using octrees within bricks to address the rasterization bottleneck. It solves the problem of inefficient memory access and load balancing in large volume rendering by allowing runtime transfer function changes without texture regeneration, unlike Tong et al.'s bricking technique which requires regenerating textures for every transfer function change. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar voxel volume dataset, potentially exceeding available texture memory. Output: A rendered image with optical properties (RGB\alpha) mapped via a transfer function. Data Structures: 1. Bricks: The volume is divided into 3D chunks called bricks. Layout: Each brick contains unmodified scalar voxel values. Size: Brick dimension b (in voxels) must be \le the size of available texture memory. If volume dimensions do not divide evenly by b, additional partially empty bricks or smaller rest-bricks are added. Overlap: Adjacent bricks overlap by n voxels in every direction to support interpolation. Nearest neighbor: n=0. Trilinear interpolation: n=1. Pre-integrated rendering or on-the-fly gradient calculation: n \ge 2 (increased by another voxel). Memory Overhead: Approximately (3 \cdot n / b) \cdot 100\%. 2. Octrees: Stored within each brick. Layout: Sparse representation of the brick's interior, marking empty regions. Purpose: Enables skipping empty regions at a finer granularity than the brick level. 3. Transfer Function: Applied in the fragment shader. Mechanism: RGB\alpha values are looked up post-interpolatively based on the current scalar value, allowing runtime changes without regenerating textures. Numbered Steps: 1. Stage 1: Coarse Division (Bricking) Divide the volume dataset into bricks of size b \times b \times b. Load bricks sequentially from main memory into texture memory if the volume exceeds available texture memory. Apply early ray termination to each brick to alleviate fragment shader load, particularly beneficial for highly-filled datasets. 2. Stage 2: Fine Division (Octree Traversal) Employ an octree within each loaded brick. Use the octree to skip empty regions at a finer granularity than the brick level. Perform ray casting within the non-empty octree nodes. 3. Rendering and Transfer Function Application Store unmodified scalar voxel values in the brick textures. In the fragment shader, lookup RGB\alpha values post-interpolatively based on the scalar value and the current transfer function. Formulas: Memory Overhead: \text{Overhead} \approx \frac{3 \cdot n}{b} \cdot 100\%. b: Brick dimension in voxels. n: Overlap in voxels in every direction. Parameters: Brick Size (b): Must be equal to or smaller than the size of the available texture memory. Overlap (n): Depends on the interpolation kernel. For trilinear, n=1. For pre-integration/gradient calculation, n \ge 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Triangle Throughput Bottleneck: Space-skipping techniques may increase the amount of triangles considerably. If the triangle count becomes too high, it becomes a limiting factor for frame rate, potentially overloading the triangle throughput bottleneck when the rasterization bottleneck is lifted. Bottleneck Balance: The two stages (bricking and octree) must be balanced because lifting one bottleneck may overload another (e.g., rasterization vs. triangle throughput). Texture Memory Limits: If the amount of data in textures exceeds available texture memory, textures are swapped between main memory and texture memory, which can impact performance. Power of 2 Constraints: Many graphics cards require 3D texture sizes to be a power of 2 in every direction. Non-divisible dimensions require additional layers or rest-bricks. Quaternary Tree Volume Traversal is a hybrid rendering technique that offloads coarse spatial partitioning to the CPU and fine-grained ray-object intersection to the GPU. It solves the problem of inefficient memory access and load balancing in volume rendering by dividing the rendering pipeline into two distinct stages: geometric culling on the CPU and ray casting on the GPU. Unlike pure GPU ray tracers, this method leverages the CPU's flexibility to build a quaternary tree for early space-skipping, reducing the number of rays processed by the GPU. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Memory overhead for bricks is approximately (3 \cdot n / b) \cdot 100\%. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Addresses bus and texture cache bottlenecks via bricking. Addresses rasterization bottleneck via fine-grained octree skipping. Allows runtime transfer function changes without texture regeneration by storing scalar values and using fragment shader lookup. Early ray termination alleviates fragment shader load. Limitations: Risk of triangle throughput bottleneck if space-skipping increases triangle count too much. Requires balancing between coarse and fine division stages to avoid overloading other bottlenecks. Texture compression methods (S3TC, FXT1, etc.) are unsuitable for 12- or 16-bit scalar medical data, necessitating this approach for large sparse datasets. When to Use: Large volume datasets exceeding texture memory, especially those with sparse regions (e.g., vessels occupying 1% to 8% of the volume) where space-skipping provides significant benefit. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method was introduced in 2006 in Plzen, Czech Republic. History: It builds upon earlier bricking techniques by Eckhardt [Eck98] and Wang et al. [WWE04], and specifically addresses limitations in Tong et al.'s bricking technique [TWTT99] which required texture regeneration for transfer function changes. It also responds to the unsuitability of standard texture compression for high-bit scalar data. Usage: Used in GPU volume rendering to handle large datasets and optimize performance by addressing specific graphics pipeline bottlenecks (bus, texture cache, rasterization, triangle throughput). name: Quaternary Tree Volume Traversal

body: Quaternary Tree Volume Traversal is a two-stage rasterization process distributed between a central processor and a graphics processing unit. The CPU divides object space using a quaternary tree to find intersections, and the GPU performs ray casting and shading. Inputs: An implicit function defining the object surface. Camera parameters, with the GPU ray direction fixed along the Z-axis. A target tile size parameter that terminates the CPU subdivision. Outputs: A rendered image with smooth shading and lighting. Z-coordinates and surface normals for each pixel. Data Structures: Quaternary Tree: Each node represents a square region in the XY plane and branches into four children corresponding to the quadrants of the parent region. Fragment List: A list of geometric primitives generated by the CPU, containing the bounding boxes of tiles where the object intersects the volume. Algorithm Steps: 1. CPU: Divide the current cube region into four equal parts in the XY plane. 2. CPU: Test each part for intersection with the object. 3. CPU: If a part does not intersect the object, neglect it; if it intersects, repeat the division procedure on that part. 4. CPU: Stop recursion when the current part corresponds to a tile of the predefined size. 5. CPU: Generate a list of fragments representing the geometric objects intersecting with the tiles. 6. GPU: Feed the fragment list to the GPU input. 7. GPU: For each pixel, test the relevant fragment for intersection with a ray directed along the Z-axis. 8. GPU: Perform a binary search along the ray to find the nearest intersection point, defined as the first point where the object function vanishes. 9. GPU: Determine the z-coordinate and surface normal for each pixel. 10. GPU: Apply a local lighting model using the coordinates and normals to compute the final pixel color. region.xmin < tilesize and region.ymax - region.ymin < tilesize): if intersectsobject(region): fragments.append(Fragment(region)) return fragments midx = (region.xmin + region.xmax) / 2 midy = (region.ymin + region.ymax) / 2 quadrants = [ Region(region.xmin, midx, region.ymin, midy, region.zmin, region.zmax), Region(midx, region.xmax, region.ymin, midy, region.zmin, region.zmax), Region(region.xmin, midx, midy, region.ymax, region.zmin, region.zmax), Region(midx, region.xmax, midy, region.ymax, region.zmin, region.zmax) ] for quad in quadrants: if intersectsobject(quad): fragments.extend(buildquaternarytree(quad, tilesize)) return fragments def evaluatescalarfield(point): # Placeholder for the implicit surface function f(x,y,z) return point.z - 0.5 def binarysearchintersection(origin, direction, fragment): zlow = fragment.region.zmin zhigh = fragment.region.zmax maxiterations = 32 epsilon = 1e-4 for in range(maxiterations): zmid = (zlow + zhigh) / 2 point = (origin[0] + direction[0] zmid, origin[1] + direction[1] zmid, zmid) value = evaluatescalarfield(point) if abs(value) < epsilon: return zmid if value > 0: zhigh = zmid else: zlow = zmid return None def calculatenormal(point): # Approximate normal using central finite differences h = 1e-5 dx = evaluatescalarfield((point[0]+h, point[1], point[2])) - evaluatescalarfield((point[0]-h, point[1], point[2])) dy = evaluatescalarfield((point[0], point[1]+h, point[2])) - evaluatescalarfield((point[0], point[1]-h, point[2])) dz = evaluatescalarfield((point[0], point[1], point[2]+h)) - evaluatescalarfield((point[0], point[1], point[2]-h)) length = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz)0.5 return (dx/length, dy/length, dz/length) def applylighting(point, normal): # Simple diffuse lighting model return (0.5 + 0.5 max(0, normal[2])) def renderfragments(fragments, imagewidth, imageheight, tilesize): image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): origin = (float(x), float(y), 0.0) direction = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) relevantfragment = None for frag in fragments: if (frag.region.xmin <= x < frag.region.xmax and frag.region.ymin <= y < frag.region.ymax): relevantfragment = frag break if relevantfragment is not None: zintersect = binarysearchintersection(origin, direction, relevantfragment) if zintersect is not None: point = (origin[0], origin[1], zintersect) normal = calculatenormal(point) image[y][x] = applylighting(point, normal) return image Parameters: Tile Size: The size of the fragments generated by the CPU. Ray Direction: Assumed to be along the Z-axis for the GPU stage. name: Stackless GPU Raycasting with Octree Traversal
head: Adaptive out-of-core volume rendering, GPU ray-casting with octree, Out-of-Core GPU Volume Ray Casting, Stackless octree traversal on the GPU
body: This method performs volume rendering by traversing a Sparse Voxel Octree (SVO) on the GPU without using a stack, computing the volume rendering integral in front-to-back order. It solves the problem of efficient memory access and traversal overhead in sparse volumetric data by combining space-skipping (via empty node detection) with adaptive sampling density. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Two-staged Space-Skipping with Bricking and Octrees by performing neighbor lookups implicitly on-the-fly using the octree's regular structure, rather than relying on precomputed neighbor pointers or a two-stage bricking pipeline. It builds on the concepts of Octree Ray Marching with Brick Interpolation and Early Termination but replaces explicit brick interpolation with adaptive sampling based on leaf resolution. The algorithm maintains the state of the current ray segment (entry point t{min}, current node pointer, current bounding box, and octree level) in registers. It traverses the octree from the root to the leaf containing the current sampling point, accumulates color and opacity if the leaf is non-empty, and moves to the next leaf via implicit neighbor calculation when the ray exits the current box. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (in texture coordinates, normalized to [0,1]^3). Spatial Index Texture: A 3D texture storing the octree structure. Leaf Data Texture: A 3D texture storing the actual volume data (density/color) for non-empty leaves. Transfer Function: A 2D texture mapping density and octree level to color and opacity. Outputs: fragment.color: Accumulated RGBA color. fragment.depth: Depth of the first opaque surface encountered (or far plane). Spatial Index Texture Texel Layout (float4): xyz: Pointer to the first child node (for inner nodes) or to the leaf data (for leaf nodes). Stored as a 3D coordinate offset in the texture. w: Tag/Status. If w indicates an Inner Node: The xyz components point to children. The children are stored consecutively in the texture. The offset to the i-th child (where i \in [0,7]) is calculated as dot3(s, float3(1, 2, 4)) texelsz, where s is the child index vector. If w indicates a Leaf Node: The xyz components point to the leaf data in the Leaf Data Texture. The w component of a leaf node's index texel stores the octree level of the neighbor in the direction of the exit face. Empty Node: A specific marker (e.g., w=0 or null pointer) indicating no children or data. Null Pointer: Used to terminate traversal. Neighbor Pointers: Leaf nodes use RGB components to point to leaf information, and 6 consecutive texels store pointers to neighbors. The stackless traversal logic relies on implicit neighbor calculation for the exit face to avoid extra texture fetches. Early Termination Threshold: Opacity \alpha{thresh} = 0.99. If accumulated opacity exceeds this, the ray terminates. Box Normalization: All computations are done in texture coordinates. The octree subdivides the unit cube [0,1]^3. Sampling: Adaptive. Step size is determined by the resolution of the current leaf (box dimension). The following pseudocode implements the fragment shader logic. It assumes standard vector operations and texture sampling. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. color = float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) depth = FAR nodeptr = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) octreelevel = 0 boxmin = float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) boxdim = float3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) tmin = ray.tnear while not isnull(nodeptr) and color.a < 1.0: # 1. Find leaf containing current sampling point P P = ray.origin + ray.direction tmin # Fetch current node node = tex3d(spatialindex, nodeptr) # 2. Down Traversal: Descend to the leaf containing P while isinner(node.w): boxdim = boxdim / 2.0 boxmid = boxmin + boxdim # s[i] = 1 if P[i] >= boxmid[i], else 0 s = step(boxmid, P) boxmin = boxmin + s boxdim childoffset = dot3(s, float3(1.0, 2.0, 4.0)) texelsz nodeptr = node.xyz + float3(childoffset, 0.0, 0.0) node = tex3d(spatialindex, nodeptr) octreelevel += 1 # 3. Clip ray to current leaf box to find exit face (boxtmax, exitfaceidx, exitdir) = boxclip(ray, tmin, ray.tfar, boxmin, boxdim) # 4. Accumulate if non-empty if not isempty(node.w): dataptr = node.xyz (color, depth) = accumulate(color, ray, tmin, boxtmax, dataptr, boxmin, boxmin + boxdim) # Check for early termination if color.a >= 0.99: break # 5. Move to Neighbor if ray exits current block if tmin >= boxtmax: # Fetch neighbor pointer. Neighbors are stored at 6 consecutive texels after data pointer. neighboroffset = float3(1.0 + exitfaceidx, 0.0, 0.0) texelsz neighbor = tex3d(spatialindex, node.xyz + neighboroffset) nodeptr = neighbor.xyz octreelevel = neighbor.w boxdim = exp2(-octreelevel) boxmin = floor(boxmin / boxdim) boxdim tmin = boxtmax else: tmin = boxtmax def boxclip(ray, tmin, tfar, boxmin, boxdim): t0 = (boxmin - ray.origin) / ray.direction t1 = (boxmin + boxdim - ray.origin) / ray.direction tenter = max(min(t0.x, t1.x), min(t0.y, t1.y), min(t0.z, t1.z)) texit = min(max(t0.x, t1.x), max(t0.y, t1.y), max(t0.z, t1.z)) tmax = min(texit, tfar) # Determine exit face index and direction if texit == max(t0.x, t1.x): exitfaceidx = 0 if ray.direction.x > 0 else 3 exitdir = float3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) if ray.direction.x > 0 else float3(-1.0, 0.0, 0.0) elif texit == max(t0.y, t1.y): exitfaceidx = 1 if ray.direction.y > 0 else 4 exitdir = float3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) if ray.direction.y > 0 else float3(0.0, -1.0, 0.0) else: exitfaceidx = 2 if ray.direction.z > 0 else 5 exitdir = float3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) if ray.direction.z > 0 else float3(0.0, 0.0, -1.0) return (tmax, exitfaceidx, exitdir) def accumulate(color, ray, tstart, tend, dataptr, boxmin, boxmax): stepsize = boxdim.x / 8.0 # Standard brick resolution t = tstart while t < tend: samplepos = ray.origin + ray.direction t density = tex3d(leafdata, dataptr + (samplepos - boxmin) / boxdim brickres) tfcolor, tfalpha = tex2d(transferfunc, float2(density, octreelevel)) alpha = tfalpha stepsize color = color + (1.0 - color.a) tfcolor alpha t += stepsize return (color, depth) def step(edge, x): return 0.0 if x < edge else 1.0 def dot3(a, b): return a.x b.x + a.y b.y + a.z b.z def tex3d(tex, coord): return tex[coord] def isinner(w): return w != 0 def isempty(w): return w == 0 def isnull(ptr): return ptr == float3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Null Pointers: The last leaf data texel always contains a NULL pointer. This is used to simplify handling of rays that do not exit from the current box (e.g., terminate due to opacity threshold). If traversal reaches a null pointer, the loop terminates. Coarser Neighbors: When moving to a neighbor with a coarser octree level, the current box must be coarsened. This is done by updating boxdim to 2^{-\text{neighbor\level}} and snapping boxmin to the neighbor's grid: \lfloor \text{box\min} / \text{box\dim} \rfloor \cdot \text{box\dim}. Termination: Rays that terminate due to the opacity threshold (0.99) must not continue to neighbors. The null pointer check and the opacity check inside the loop handle this. Time Complexity: O(k) per ray, where k is the number of non-empty leaves traversed. The traversal is stackless, reducing memory overhead and instruction count compared to stack-based methods. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the octree structure, where N is the number of nodes. The spatial index is stored in a 3D texture. Performance: The method is efficient for sparse data because it skips empty space. Adaptive sampling reduces the number of texture fetches for large empty or uniform regions. The on-the-fly neighbor calculation reduces texture memory bandwidth usage compared to methods storing explicit neighbor pointers for all nodes. Strengths: No stack required; efficient memory access; adaptive sampling; early termination. Limitations: Requires a well-constructed octree; implicit neighbor calculation assumes regular octree structure; may have branch divergence on GPU if rays traverse different paths. The method was introduced in "A single-pass GPU ray casting framework for interactive out-of-core volume rendering" (2008) by. It extends stackless ray traversal techniques previously used for kd-trees [7,16] to octrees. The key innovation is the implicit computation of neighbor bounding boxes using the octree's regular structure, avoiding the need for explicit neighbor pointers in the index structure for all nodes, thus saving memory and texture fetches. It is used in interactive volume rendering systems where out-of-core data handling and high performance are required. body: A raycasting method that traverses an octree structure stored in a GPU buffer to render voxels, handling both solid nodes and leaf nodes containing 8x8x8 voxel bricks using a 3D texture for brick data storage. It differs from standard sparse voxel octree traversal by packing leaf node data into a 3D texture and encoding brick coordinates within the node's color data, allowing for efficient brick-level raymarching. Inputs and Outputs Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), world bounds, octree node buffer, 3D texture voxelBlocks containing 8x8x8 voxel bricks. Output: Accumulated color and opacity for the pixel. Data Structures The octree is stored as a flat array of octreeNode structs in a GPU buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct octreeNode { uint childData; // Encodes leaf/solid flags and child offset uint colorData; // Encodes color for solids or brick coordinates for leaves }; Bit Packing in childData LEAFMASK (0x80000000): Indicates leaf node. SOLIDMASK (0x40000000): Indicates solid node. FINALMASK (0xA0000000): LEAFMASK | SOLIDMASK. If (childData & FINALMASK) == FINALMASK, the node is a leaf or solid. CHILDMASK (0x3FFFFFFF): Stores the index of the first child node if not a leaf. Bit Packing in colorData (Leaf Nodes) For leaf nodes, colorData stores the brick coordinates packed as a uint. COORDMASK (0x000003FF): Extracts 10-bit coordinates. Brick X: Bits 20-29. Calculated as (loc >> 20) & COORDMASK. Brick Y: Bits 10-19. Calculated as (loc >> 10) & COORDMASK. Brick Z: Bits 0-9. Calculated as loc & COORDMASK. Voxel Data Storage Voxel data is stored in a uniform 3D texture voxelBlocks (sampler3D). Each voxel is a vec4 (RGBA). Parameters MAXDEPTH: Maximum octree depth allowed, set to 10. If depth exceeds this, treat as leaf/solid. BRICKSIZE: Size of voxel bricks, defined as 8. MAXSTEPS: Maximum traversal steps, set to 200. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize Ray Traversal: Normalize direction D. Compute inverse direction D{inv} = 1/D. Compute delta T = |D{inv}|. Determine entry/exit parameters s{min}, s{max} based on world bounds and ray origin. 2. Traverse Octree: Initialize current node index to root (0), depth to 0, and bounds (x{min}, dim) to world bounds. Loop with maxSteps = 200. Check if current node is leaf/solid: if ((nodes[node].childData & FINALMASK) == FINALMASK). If true, process leaf/solid logic (Step 3). If false, descend to child node (Step 4). 3. Raymarch through the 8x8x8 brick using DDA-like stepping. Loop through voxels in the brick using stepTmax comparisons to determine which axis to step next. Check voxel alpha; if non-zero, blend color and accumulate alpha. Break if line position goes out of [0, 8) bounds. 4. If depth == 0, return accumulated color. Otherwise, reset traversal to root. Compute next node index: python nextNode = (nodes[node].childData & CHILDMASK) + (subNodeLoc.x << 2) + (subNodeLoc.y << 1) + subNodeLoc.z Increment depth, halve dim, update xMin. name: SVO Walk (Traversal)
body: SVO Walk is a depth-first traversal algorithm for Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO) that visits nodes in an order determined by the eye position, invoking a callback for each visited node. It differs from pure SVO traversal by explicitly managing a stack to control visitation order based on eye position, and from BVH-based approaches by operating directly on the octree structure without an intermediate bounding volume hierarchy. Inputs: SVO root node, eye position, and a callback function onnode. Outputs: Execution of onnode for each visited node in traversal order. Data Structures: Stack: Stores tuples (noderef, stem, depth). noderef: Pointer or index to the current octree node. stem: A 3D integer vector representing the node's origin coordinates at the current depth. depth: The current octree depth level (integer). Formulas: Offset: The physical size of a voxel at a given depth. \text{offset} = 2^{-\text{depth}} Implemented via bit manipulation for efficiency: python exp = 126 - depth f = exp << 23 offset = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', f))[0] # bit-cast to float Voxel Position: The world-space position of the voxel corner. \text{voxel} = \text{stem} \times \text{offset} Child Origin: For a child at index i (0-7) in the octree: \text{new\origin} = \text{stem} + \text{index\offset}(i, \text{offset}) Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the stack with (ROOTNODE, (0,0,0), 0). 2. While the stack is not empty: a. Pop (noderef, stem, depth) from the stack. b. Retrieve the node from noderef. c. Calculate offset using the bit-manipulation method above. d. Calculate voxel = stem offset. e. Call onnode(isleaf, data, voxel). f. If onnode returns true AND the node is not a leaf: i. Calculate the sorting order of the 8 children based on the eye position and stem. ii. For each child in the sorted order: 1. Determine the child's index i. 2. Calculate neworigin = stem + indexoffset(i, offset). 3. Push (childref, neworigin, depth + 1) to the stack. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import struct import math def svowalk(rootnode, eyeposition, onnode): stack = [(rootnode, (0, 0, 0), 0)] while stack: noderef, stem, depth = stack.pop() # offset = 2^(-depth) via bit manipulation exp = 126 - depth f = exp << 23 offset = struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', f))[0] # bit-cast to float # voxel = stem.extend(offset) voxel = (stem[0] offset, stem[1] offset, stem[2] offset) isleaf = noderef.isleaf() data = noderef.data if onnode(isleaf, data, voxel): if not isleaf: children = noderef.children # Sort children indices 0-7 based on distance to eyeposition def childorigin(i): return (stem[0] + ((i & 1) offset), stem[1] + (((i >> 1) & 1) offset), stem[2] + (((i >> 2) & 1) offset)) sortedchildren = sorted(range(8), key=lambda i: math.dist(eyeposition, childorigin(i))) for i in sortedchildren: neworigin = childorigin(i) stack.append((children[i], neworigin, depth + 1)) Fast Walk Variant: Uses a fixed-size stack array of 256 elements. Uses raw pointers for node access to minimize overhead. Calculates voxel using offset 1.73 (approx \sqrt{3}) in some implementations, though the standard formula is 2^{-\text{depth}}. Edge Cases: Stack Overflow: The fixed-size stack (256 elements) may overflow in deep or complex scenes. Precision: The bit-manipulation method for offset calculation is efficient but limited to specific depth ranges where 126 - \text{depth} yields a valid IEEE 754 exponent. A hybrid variant combining BVH coarse culling with SVO fine-grained evaluation. It reduces visited nodes compared to pure SVO traversal and maintains SVO memory efficiency at the leaves compared to pure BVH traversal. Iterates through all nodes using a PreOrderTraversal to compute global active states. If a node's local state is INACTIVE, it sets activeGlobal to FALSE and marks inactiveAncestors as TRUE; otherwise it inherits inactiveAncestors from the parent. If the node is globally active, it increments the numActiveGlobal counter. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of visited nodes. Memory Complexity: O(D) for the stack, where D is the maximum depth of the tree. The fixed-size stack variant uses constant memory (256 elements). The SVO Walk algorithm is described in the svo-cpu repository by marceline-cramer. marceline-cramer/svo-cpu, https://github.com/marceline-cramer/svo-cpu, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Lipschitz Pruning: Hierarchical Simplification of Primitive‐Based SDFs, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70057, fetched 2026-10-26
