name: Octree-based Raycasting
head: Raycasting mit Octree-Beschleunigungsstruktur, Voxel-Raycasting mit Octree
body: Octree-based raycasting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates ray traversal by utilizing an octree structure to skip empty space regions. It solves the performance bottleneck of naive raycasting, which scales linearly with the number of voxels O(n), by culling large volumes of empty space. It differs from its parent Ray-Occlusion Traversal in Octree by explicitly maintaining voxel counts per node to support dynamic updates, and from Bottom-up Neighbor-Finding Ray Traversal by relying on top-down parametric analysis rather than neighbor-finding for traversal. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, octree root node, voxel data buffer. Outputs: Intersection points, accumulated color/opacity. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains a boolean exists flag and an integer voxelcount. Voxel Buffer: Stores density/color values for active voxels. StructuredBuffer: GPU buffer holding node data, declared globallycoherent for atomic operations. Steps: 1. Initialization: Start traversal at the root node. If the ray originates inside the root, compute entry point; otherwise, intersect ray with root bounding box planes [Parent]. 2. Node Evaluation: For the current node, check exists. If false, terminate traversal for this branch. 3. Voxel Count Check: Read voxelcount. If voxelcount is 0, deactivate the node (set exists to false). 4. Ray-Node Intersection: Compute parametric intersection of the ray with the current node's bounding box. If the ray misses or the intersection distance exceeds the current closest hit tmax, terminate this branch. 5. Leaf/Interior Decision: If leaf: Sample voxel data at the intersection point. If interior: Compute child bounding boxes. Determine which children intersect the ray within tmax. 6. Recursive Traversal: For each intersecting child, recursively call the raycasting function with the child's exit distance as the new tmax. Return the closest hit found. 7. Dynamic Update (On Modification): When a voxel is deleted, decrement voxelcount of all ancestor nodes. If voxelcount reaches 0, mark the node as inactive. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MAXDEPTH = 5 # Typical tree depth def raycastoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, node, depth, tmax): # Check if node exists if not node.exists: return None # Check if node contains voxels if node.voxelcount == 0: node.exists = False return None # Ray-AABB intersection for current node hit, tmin, texitnode = rayaabbintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, node.bboxmin, node.bboxmax) if not hit: return None if tmin < 0: tmin = 0.0 # Handle ray origin inside node if tmin >= tmax: return None # Base case: Leaf node if depth == MAXDEPTH: return samplevoxel(rayorigin, raydirection, node.voxeldata, tmin) # Recursive case: Interior node childrentovisit = [] for i in range(8): childmin, childmax = getchildbbox(node.bboxmin, node.bboxmax, i) childhit, childtmin, childtexit = rayaabbintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, childmin, childmax) if childhit and childtmin < tmax: childrentovisit.append((i, childtmin, childtexit)) # Sort by tmin for early exit optimization childrentovisit.sort(key=lambda x: x[1]) closesthit = None for childidx, childtmin, childtexit in childrentovisit: childnode = node.children[childidx] hit = raycastoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, childnode, depth + 1, childtexit) if hit is not None: if closesthit is None or hit.distance < closesthit.distance: closesthit = hit if closesthit.distance <= childtmin: break # Early exit: closer hit found return closesthit def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, bboxmin, bboxmax): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0.0: if origin[i] < bboxmin[i] or origin[i] > bboxmax[i]: return False, 0.0, 0.0 else: invd = 1.0 / direction[i] t1 = (bboxmin[i] - origin[i]) invd t2 = (bboxmax[i] - origin[i]) invd if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if tmin > tmax: return False, 0.0, 0.0 return True, tmin, tmax def getchildbbox(parentmin, parentmax, childidx): childmin = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] childmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(3): half = (parentmax[i] - parentmin[i]) / 2.0 if (childidx >> i) & 1: childmin[i] = parentmin[i] + half childmax[i] = parentmax[i] else: childmin[i] = parentmin[i] childmax[i] = parentmin[i] + half return childmin, childmax def samplevoxel(rayorigin, raydirection, voxeldata, thit): # Standard texture lookup at parametric distance thit return {"distance": thit, "density": 0.0, "color": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]} Parameters: MAXDEPTH: Depth of the octree. Typical value D=5 for large datasets. voxelcount: Integer field in node structure. tmax: Tracks the current branch exit distance along the ray to prune further traversal. Edge Cases: Empty Root: If the root has voxelcount 0, no traversal occurs. Dynamic Updates: Concurrent writes to voxelcount require atomic operations to prevent data races. Zero Direction Components: Handled by checking ray origin against axis bounds before division. A technique to prevent data races during concurrent writes to voxelcount in the octree nodes. It uses HLSL intrinsics InterlockedAdd for atomic addition/subtraction on the voxelcount variable. The StructuredBuffer must be declared with the globallycoherent qualifier to ensure visibility across warps. This is necessary because multiple voxels in the same node may be deleted simultaneously, leading to inconsistent data if not synchronized. A top-down parametric raycasting technique that combines a voxel traversal algorithm with octree traversal. It uses a 3D supercover DDA line algorithm to iterate over octants in the highest LOD grid along the ray's 3D line. For each octant identified, it performs recursive top-down parametric raycasting to find entry and exit planes, using child existence masks to accelerate search. Pitfall: The highest LOD grid has no coarser parent, so no meta information exists. A hash map must be queried for every octant in this grid, and empty space cannot be skipped on this level. Performance: Raycasting 1,048,576 spheres takes >65ms with a naive approach, but <0.5ms with the octree approach (tree depth D=5). Time Complexity: Naive raycasting scales as O(n). Octree traversal complexity is Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(n) for storing voxel data plus overhead for octree nodes. Measured Performance: Raycasting 1,048,576 spheres takes <0.5ms with octree (depth D=5) vs >65ms naive. Strengths: Significant speedup for sparse volumes; supports dynamic updates with atomic operations. Limitations: Overhead for maintaining voxelcount and atomic operations; highest LOD grid requires hash map queries, preventing empty space skipping. Originated in the context of raycasting-based voxel rendering, where acceleration structures are necessary due to the O(n) complexity of naive raycasting. The approach was developed to handle dynamic volume modifications, requiring the octree to track voxel counts per node. Atomic operations using HLSL intrinsics were introduced to handle concurrent updates. The hybrid approach with voxel traversal was proposed to handle the highest LOD grid where meta-information is unavailable. name: DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack
head: Mini-stack traversal, Stack-based hierarchical traversal
body: This method extends the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) grid traversal algorithm to N-ary hierarchical trees for GPU shader implementation. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing sparse voxel structures by maintaining a small, fixed-size stack of DDA states, allowing the ray to descend into child nodes and ascend back to parent nodes without dynamic memory allocation. It is distinguished from standard DDA by its hierarchical boundary handling and from other tree traversals by its reliance on a statically allocated mini-stack indexed via Shader Model 4.0 features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, hierarchical tree structure with N-ary nodes, maximum tree depth D{max}, and node accessors. Output: Sequence of leaf voxels visited by the ray, along with their entry and exit distances. Data Structures: Mini-Stack: A fixed-size array of length D{max} (compile-time constant). Each entry at index level stores: tmax[3]: Distance to the next boundary for each axis (x, y, z) within the current node's local grid. tdelta[3]: Distance increment per voxel step for each axis. step[3]: Direction of index increment (+1 or -1) for each axis. currentindex[3]: Current voxel coordinates (i, j, k) within the current node's local grid. nodeaddr: Memory address or index of the node in the indirection pool. Stack Pointer: An integer variable tracking the current depth in the stack, initially 0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute DDA parameters for the root node's bounding box. Push the root's DDA state onto the stack at index 0. Set stackptr = 0. 2. Descent Phase: While the current node is not a leaf, identify the child node intersected by the ray using the current DDA state. Compute DDA parameters for the child node's local grid (the entry distance into the child equals the exit distance from the parent's current cell). Update the stack entry at stackptr with the new DDA parameters and the child's node address. Increment stackptr. Repeat until a leaf node is reached. 3. Horizontal Advance: Within the current node (leaf or internal), advance the DDA: find the axis k with the minimum tmax[k]. Record the voxel at currentindex and the interval [t{entry}, t{max}[k]]. Advance currentindex[k] by step[k]. Update tmax[k] += tdelta[k]. Update tentry = tmax[k]. If the new currentindex is within the node's bounds, continue processing the next voxel. If outside, proceed to Vertical Ascent. 4. Vertical Ascent: Decrement stackptr. If stackptr < 0, the ray has exited the entire tree; terminate. Retrieve the DDA state from the stack at the new stackptr. Resume the Horizontal Advance loop from the point where the descent occurred, using the stored DDA parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ddatreetraversalministack(rayorigin, raydirection, rootnode, maxdepth, getnode, isleaf, getbounds, voxelsize=1.0): # Initialize DDA parameters for a bounding box def initdda(origin, direction, bounds): step = [0, 0, 0] tmax = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tdelta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentindex = [0, 0, 0] for i in range(3): if direction[i] > 0: step[i] = 1 currentindex[i] = int((origin[i] - bounds.min[i]) / voxelsize) nextboundary = (currentindex[i] + 1) voxelsize + bounds.min[i] tmax[i] = (nextboundary - origin[i]) / direction[i] tdelta[i] = voxelsize / direction[i] elif direction[i] < 0: step[i] = -1 currentindex[i] = int((origin[i] - bounds.min[i]) / voxelsize) nextboundary = currentindex[i] voxelsize + bounds.min[i] tmax[i] = (nextboundary - origin[i]) / direction[i] tdelta[i] = -voxelsize / direction[i] else: step[i] = 0 tmax[i] = float('inf') tdelta[i] = 0.0 return step, tmax, tdelta, currentindex stack = [None] maxdepth stackptr = 0 # Initialization: root node bounds = getbounds(rootnode) step, tmax, tdelta, currentindex = initdda(rayorigin, raydirection, bounds) stack[0] = {'step': step, 'tmax': tmax, 'tdelta': tdelta, 'currentindex': currentindex, 'nodeaddr': rootnode.address} tentry = 0.0 while True: state = stack[stackptr] node = getnode(state['nodeaddr']) bounds = getbounds(node) if isleaf(node): # Horizontal Advance for leaf while True: minidx = 0 minval = state['tmax'][0] for i in range(1, 3): if state['tmax'][i] < minval: minval = state['tmax'][i] minidx = i texit = minval yield state['currentindex'], tentry, texit state['currentindex'][minidx] += state['step'][minidx] state['tmax'][minidx] += state['tdelta'][minidx] tentry = texit # Check bounds if not (bounds.min[0] <= state['currentindex'][0] <= bounds.max[0] and bounds.min[1] <= state['currentindex'][1] <= bounds.max[1] and bounds.min[2] <= state['currentindex'][2] <= bounds.max[2]): break else: # Internal node: find child to descend minidx = 0 minval = state['tmax'][0] for i in range(1, 3): if state['tmax'][i] < minval: minval = state['tmax'][i] minidx = i texit = minval # Child indexing depends on tree layout (e.g., octree Morton order) childnode = getchild(node, state['currentindex']) if childnode is None: pass # No child in this direction, proceed to ascent else: # Compute DDA for child node childbounds = getbounds(childnode) childorigin = [rayorigin[i] + texit raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] childstep, childtmax, childtdelta, childcurrentindex = initdda(childorigin, raydirection, childbounds) stackptr += 1 stack[stackptr] = {'step': childstep, 'tmax': childtmax, 'tdelta': childtdelta, 'currentindex': childcurrentindex, 'nodeaddr': childnode.address} tentry = texit continue # Vertical Ascent stackptr -= 1 if stackptr < 0: break Parameters: Stack Size: Fixed at compile time, equal to the maximum depth of the hierarchical structure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Components: If a ray direction component is zero, the corresponding tdelta is set to 0.0 and tmax to \infty, ensuring the ray never advances in that axis. Precision Errors: Floating-point precision issues may cause the ray to miss small voxels or re-enter previously visited cells. Using epsilon offsets or robust geometric predicates is recommended. Empty Nodes: If a node has no children in the ray's path, the algorithm must correctly ascend without attempting to access non-existent child nodes. This method extends the DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack to support Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs (SSVDAGs), a compression format that exploits geometric symmetries to reduce memory footprint. It solves the problem of correctly traversing a DAG where child nodes and leaf voxels may be mirrored relative to their parent's coordinate system. The key distinction from standard octree DDA is the maintenance of a 3-bit mirrormask that tracks reflection transformations, allowing the algorithm to map logical voxel indices to physical storage locations without decompressing the geometry. Time Complexity: Constant per traversal step, with total time proportional to the number of visited cells plus the number of hierarchical transitions. Memory Complexity: O(D), where D is the maximum tree depth, due to the fixed-size mini-stack. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to the use of statically allocated arrays and minimal branching. The fixed stack size avoids dynamic memory allocation overhead. Strengths: Fast traversal, low memory overhead, suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs. Limitations: Requires compile-time knowledge of maximum tree depth; less flexible for dynamically changing tree structures. The method was proposed for the interactive exploration of procedural volumes. It extends the classic DDA algorithm to N-ary trees, leveraging Shader Model 4.0 features for dynamic indexing of local arrays. name: Optimized Octree DDA Traversal for SSVDAGs
body: This method extends the DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack to support Symmetry-aware Sparse Voxel DAGs (SSVDAGs), a compression format that exploits geometric symmetries to reduce memory footprint. It solves the problem of correctly traversing a DAG where child nodes and leaf voxels may be mirrored relative to their parent's coordinate system. The key distinction from standard octree DDA is the maintenance of a 3-bit mirrormask that tracks reflection transformations, allowing the algorithm to map logical voxel indices to physical storage locations without decompressing the geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray r (origin, direction), ray.tmin, ray.tmax, and a projection factor projfactor for resolution checks. Output: The intersection distance t or a sentinel value indicating no intersection. Data Structures: Stack: Stores tuples (nodeidx, innerhdr, mirrormask, level) to restore state when moving up the tree. Inner Header (innerhdr): Contains voxel occupancy bits and child pointers. Leaf Data (leafdata): Contains voxel occupancy bits for leaf nodes. Mirror Mask (mirrormask): A 3-bit integer indicating which reflections (X, Y, Z axes) must be applied to indices. Helper Functions: DDAinit(): Initializes DDA state for the root node. Returns (voxidx, ddastate). DDAnext(ddastate): Advances DDA to the next voxel at the current level. Returns updated (voxidx, ddastate). DDAdown(ddastate): Adjusts DDA state to descend into a child node. Returns updated (voxidx, ddastate). isinbounds(voxidx, level): Checks if voxidx is within the valid range for the current tree level. innervoxelbit(mirroredvoxidx, innerhdr): Checks if the voxel at mirroredvoxidx is full in the inner header. leafvoxelbit(mirroredvoxidx, leafdata): Checks if the voxel at mirroredvoxidx is full in the leaf data. fetchinnerhdr(nodeidx): Loads the inner header for the given node index. fetchleafdata(nodeidx): Loads the leaf data for the given node index. fetchtaggedptr(innerhdr, nodeidx, mirroredvoxidx): Retrieves the child node index and symmetry mask m from the header using a manually unrolled loop to compute offsets for tagged pointers (0, 2, or 4 bytes). mirror(mask, voxidx, level): Applies reflections from mask to voxidx based on level. resolutionok(t, cellsize, projfactor): Determines if the current voxel size is sufficient for the desired resolution. stackisempty(), stackpush(), stackpop(): Standard mini-stack operations implemented as list operations. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set t = \text{ray.t\min}. Set mirrormask = 0. Set level = 0. Set cellsize = 0.5. Initialize DDA: (voxidx, ddastate) = DDAinit(). Set nodeidx = 0. Set leafdata = 0. Load root header: innerhdr = fetchinnerhdr(nodeidx). Compute initial mirrored index: mirroredvoxidx = mirror(mirrormask, voxidx, level). 2. Traversal Loop: Execute at least once, then repeat while t < \text{ray.t\max}: 1. Check Occupancy: If level < MAXLEVEL: isfullvoxel = innervoxelbit(mirroredvoxidx, innerhdr). Else: isfullvoxel = leafvoxelbit(mirroredvoxidx, leafdata). 2. If Empty (!isfullvoxel): Advance DDA: (voxidx, ddastate) = DDAnext(ddastate). Check Bounds: If !isinbounds(voxidx, level): If Stack is Empty: Return NOINTERSECTION. Else: Save oldlevel = level. Pop Stack: (nodeidx, innerhdr, mirrormask, level) = stackpop(). Update Cell Size: cellsize = (1 << (oldlevel - level)). Advance DDA: (voxidx, ddastate) = DDAnext(ddastate). 3. If Full (isfullvoxel): Check Termination: If level == MAXLEVEL or resolutionok(t, cellsize, projfactor): Return t (Intersection Found). Else (Refine): If isinbounds(voxidx, level): Push current state (nodeidx, innerhdr, mirrormask, level) to stack (corrected from source typo). Fetch Child: (m, nodeidx) = fetchtaggedptr(innerhdr, nodeidx, mirroredvoxidx). Update Mask: mirrormask ^= m. Increment Level: level += 1. Halve Cell Size: cellsize = 0.5. Descend DDA: (voxidx, ddastate) = DDAdown(ddastate). Load Child Data: If level < MAXLEVEL - 1: innerhdr = fetchinnerhdr(nodeidx). Else (Leaf): Increment Level: level += 1. Halve Cell Size: cellsize = 0.5. Descend DDA: (voxidx, ddastate) = DDAdown(ddastate). Load Leaf Data: leafdata = fetchleafdata(nodeidx). 4. Update Mirrored Index: mirroredvoxidx = mirror(mirrormask, voxidx, level). 3. Termination: If loop exits without returning, return NOINTERSECTION. Parameters: MAXLEVEL: The maximum depth of the octree. Not given in the sources. projfactor: Scaling factor for resolution check. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Leaf Refinement: Leaves are treated as 4x4 blocks, requiring an extra level increment and DDA descent step compared to inner nodes. Pointer Size: Child pointers are tagged and can be 0, 2, or 4 bytes, requiring specific offset calculation logic in fetchtaggedptr. Mirror Mask Restoration: The mirrormask must be pushed to the stack and restored upon popping to ensure correct index mapping when backtracking. Source Typo Fix: The original listing contains if (isinbounds(DDAnext())), which prematurely advances the DDA state. This is corrected to if isinbounds(voxidx, level) to check bounds on the current voxel before descending. The original listing also contains a colon typo oldlevel = level: (nodeidx,...) = stackpop();, corrected to a semicolon. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traceray(r, projfactor, MAXLEVEL): t = r.tmin mirrormask = 0 level = 0 cellsize = 0.5 voxidx, ddastate = DDAinit() # Standard DDA initialization nodeidx = 0 leafdata = 0 innerhdr = fetchinnerhdr(nodeidx) # mirroredvoxidx = mirror(mirrormask, voxidx, level) # stack = [] # Mini-stack implementation while True: if level < MAXLEVEL: isfullvoxel = innervoxelbit(mirroredvoxidx, innerhdr) # else: isfullvoxel = leafvoxelbit(mirroredvoxidx, leafdata) # if not isfullvoxel: voxidx, ddastate = DDAnext(ddastate) # if not isinbounds(voxidx, level): # if not stack: # return NOINTERSECTION oldlevel = level nodeidx, innerhdr, mirrormask, level = stack.pop() # cellsize = (1 << (oldlevel - level)) # voxidx, ddastate = DDAnext(ddastate) # else: if level == MAXLEVEL or resolutionok(t, cellsize, projfactor): # return t if isinbounds(voxidx, level): # Fixed source typo stack.append((nodeidx, innerhdr, mirrormask, level)) # m, nodeidx = fetchtaggedptr(innerhdr, nodeidx, mirroredvoxidx) # mirrormask ^= m # level += 1 cellsize = 0.5 voxidx, ddastate = DDAdown(ddastate) # if level < MAXLEVEL - 1: innerhdr = fetchinnerhdr(nodeidx) # else: level += 1 cellsize = 0.5 voxidx, ddastate = DDAdown(ddastate) # leafdata = fetchleafdata(nodeidx) # mirroredvoxidx = mirror(mirrormask, voxidx, level) # if t >= r.tmax: break return NOINTERSECTION Precomputes a lookup table to accelerate octree child pointer indirection during traversal, reducing branching or pointer chasing. Allocates a 65536×8 byte array of sl::int8t. Layout is column-major over children: data[j 65536 + i] stores child j's indirection for node index i. Uploaded to GPU as a GLTEXTUREBUFFER with internal format GLR8I. The indirection value is computed as valj(i) = \sum{k=j+1}^{7} \min\left(\left\lfloor \frac{i}{2^{2k}} \right\rfloor \bmod 4, 2\right) where i \in [0, 65535] is the node index and j \in [0, 7] is the child index. Generation iterates i from 0 to 65535 and j from 0 to 7, summing masked bits of i from bit 14 down to 2j+2, clamped to 2, and storing the result. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels visited along the ray path, including backtracking steps. The overhead of mirrormask updates and tagged pointer fetching is constant per node visit. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the mini-stack depth, which is bounded by the tree height. The stack stores (nodeidx, innerhdr, mirrormask, level) per level. Strengths: Significantly reduces memory bandwidth and storage by leveraging symmetries (SSVDAG compression). Avoids explicit decompression of mirrored nodes. Limitations: Requires careful handling of mirrored indices and tagged pointers. Performance may degrade if the symmetry compression ratio is low. When to Use: High-resolution scenes with significant geometric symmetries where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: Scenes with little symmetry, or when hardware lacks efficient support for the required bitwise operations and stack management. SSVDAGs were introduced by Kämpe et al. in 2013 as a compression technique for sparse voxel grids. The optimized DDA traversal for SSVDAGs was presented in a 2017 paper by Albertojaspe, extending the original SVDAG traversal to support more efficient GPU-based ray tracing by integrating symmetry-aware index mapping directly into the DDA loop. name: Presence Acceleration
head: Binary Pyramid Ray Traversal, Binary pyramid traversal, Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration, Levoy's octree acceleration
body: Presence Acceleration is a ray traversal technique that uses a binary pyramid to skip empty regions in a volume by identifying cells containing at least one opaque voxel. It solves the problem of inefficiently traversing large transparent areas in volume data. Unlike pointer-based octrees, it relies on a fixed-resolution, pointerless grid hierarchy that allows for simple, predictable memory access patterns. Inputs: A volume dataset of resolution N \times N \times N where N = 2^M + 1 for some integer M \ge 1. A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: A set of samples taken along the ray within non-empty elementary cells, used for compositing. The method constructs a Binary Pyramid, which is a set of M + 1 volumes indexed by level m = 0, \dots, M. Level V0: Measures (N - 1) \times (N - 1) \times (N - 1) cells. Each cell represents the rectangular region bounded by eight neighboring voxels in the original volume data. Value: A cell value is 1 if at least one of its eight corner voxels has opacity > 0. Otherwise, the value is 0. Level Vm (m > 0): Measures (N - 1)/2^m cells on each side. Value: A cell at level m is 0 if all four corner cells at level m-1 are 0. Otherwise, the value is 1. Level VM: A single cell (1 \times 1 \times 1) representing the entire volume. The pyramid is "complete" and "pointerless," meaning the children of any cell at level m are located at fixed offsets in the array V{m-1}. 1. Pyramid Construction: Compute V0 by checking the opacity of the 8 corner voxels for each cell. Compute higher levels Vm iteratively. For each cell in Vm, check the 4 corner cells in V{m-1}. If all are 0, set Vm cell to 0; else set to 1. 2. Ray Initialization: Calculate the entry point of the ray into the single cell at the top level VM. Let this be the current position \mathbf{p} and the current level m = M. 3. Traversal Loop: While m \ge 0: Check the value of the current cell in Vm at position \mathbf{p}. If the cell value is 0 (Empty): Calculate the intersection point of the ray with the boundary of the current cell. Advance the ray to this intersection point. Determine the next cell at the same level m that the ray will enter. Parent Check: If the parent of this next cell differs from the parent of the previous cell, move up to the parent level (m \leftarrow m + 1) and investigate the parent cell. If the parent cell is also empty (0), skip it and continue iterating upwards until a non-empty parent is found or the root is reached. If the parent is non-empty, move down to the appropriate child at level m. If the cell value is 1 (Non-Empty): If m > 0, move down one level (m \leftarrow m - 1). Determine which child cell at level m-1 encloses the current ray position. Update the current position to the entry point of the ray into this child cell. Repeat the loop for the new level. If m = 0, the ray has reached an elementary cell (a cell in V0) that contains at least one opaque voxel. 4. Sampling and Compositing: Once an elementary cell at level 0 is identified, take samples at evenly spaced locations along the ray within this cell. Perform volume compositing using these samples. After compositing, the ray continues from the exit point of this elementary cell, and the traversal resumes from the current level (typically re-evaluating the current cell or moving to the next cell in V0). pos[axis]) / rayd[axis] if tcandidate > 0 and tcandidate < texit: texit = tcandidate t += texit pos = rayo + rayd t # Determine next cell index at same level nextidx = list(idx) for axis in range(3): if rayd[axis] > 0: nextidx[axis] += 1 elif rayd[axis] < 0: nextidx[axis] -= 1 nextidx = tuple(nextidx) # Parent check currparent = tuple(i // 2 for i in idx) nextparent = tuple(i // 2 for i in nextidx) if currparent != nextparent: # Move up to parent level level += 1 # Re-evaluate parent while level <= M: pidx = tuple(i // 2 for i in idx) if pyramid[level][pidx] == 0: level += 1 currparent = tuple(i // 2 for i in currparent) else: # Found non-empty parent, move down to child level -= 1 childsize = (N - texit + (texit / (numsamples + 1)) (k + 1) samples.append(rayo + rayd st) composite(samples) # Advance to next cell in V0 nextidx = list(idx) for axis in range(3): if rayd[axis] > 0: nextidx[axis] += 1 elif rayd[axis] < 0: nextidx[axis] -= 1 idx = tuple(nextidx) level = 0 Volume Resolution: Must be N = 2^M + 1. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in ray-cell intersection calculations can lead to missed cells or double-sampling. Robust intersection tests are recommended. Homogeneity: Presence Acceleration only detects "presence" of opacity. It does not handle homogeneous transparent regions efficiently. For that, Denskin and Hanrahan's Homogeneity Acceleration (using range pyramids) is an extension. Time Complexity: Construction visits all cells, taking O(N^3) time. Traversal time is proportional to the number of non-empty cells visited. Memory Complexity: The pyramid requires storage proportional to the sum of cells across all levels: \sum{m=0}^{M} ((N-1)/2^m)^3. Strengths: Simple implementation, no pointers, cache-friendly due to regular grid structure, effective for sparse volumes with large empty regions. Limitations: Requires specific volume resolution (2^M+1). Less efficient than sparse octrees for extremely sparse data where the overhead of the pyramid is high. Does not handle homogeneous regions as well as range pyramids. Presence Acceleration was introduced by Marc Levoy in 1991. It is also known as Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration. The method exploits the discrete nature of volume data to create a pointerless octree representation (binary pyramid) that allows for rapid traversal of empty space. It was later extended by Denskin and Hanrahan in 1992 with Homogeneity Acceleration, which used range pyramids to approximate homogeneous regions. name: Boundary Cell-Based Ray Casting
head: BC-RC, Cell-Based Ray Casting, Improved PARC
body: Boundary Cell-Based Ray Casting (BC-RC) is a fast serial ray casting algorithm that accelerates volume rendering by skipping empty space using boundary cells. It improves upon the PARC algorithm by obtaining a more accurate object boundary estimation with less computational overhead using incremental parallel projection for each boundary cell. Unlike PARC, which uses pre-calculated sub-volumes whose projection is expensive when small, BC-RC uses tiny grid cells for more accurate boundary estimation and employs fast incremental parallel projection with templates to reduce projection overhead. The algorithm consists of three main steps: (1) detect boundary cells in a preprocessing stage; (2) project the boundary cells onto the image plane to produce intersection distance values for each pixel; and (3) for each viable pixel that intersects the object, sample and composite starting from the intersection. Inputs: Volumetric data set: A regular grid of volume elements (voxels) with scalar values. Camera parameters: View direction and image plane dimensions for parallel projection. Outputs: Rendered image: Computed via ray traversal from closest to farthest intersection. Z-buffers: Front (Zn) and Rear (Zr) buffers storing intersection distances. 1. Boundary Cell Flag Array (F): Layout: A 3D array indexed by cell coordinates (i, j, k). Content: Binary flag F(i, j, k). Value 1 indicates the cell contains the object boundary; 0 indicates empty or fully inside/outside (not a boundary cell). 2. Front Z-Buffer (Zn): Layout: 2D array indexed by image pixel coordinates. Content: Stores the closest intersection distance to the object boundary for each pixel. 3. Rear Z-Buffer (Zr): Layout: 2D array indexed by image pixel coordinates. Content: Stores the farthest intersection distance to the object boundary for each pixel. Grid Cell: The volume contained within the rectangular box bounded by eight corner voxels from two adjacent parallel slices. Boundary Cell: A grid cell containing the object boundary inside the volume. Parallel Projection: A projection method where the projected area of every cell has the same shape and size in the image plane. Only the projected position and the distance of the cell center to the image plane differ from cell to cell. 1. Boundary Cell Detection (Offline Preprocessing): Scan the volume data. For each grid cell C(i, j, k), determine if it contains the object boundary. If a boundary cell is found, set its flag F(i, j, k) = 1. If not, set F(i, j, k) = 0. Note: This information is viewpoint-independent. 2. Boundary Cell Projection (Online): Initialize front z-buffer Zn and rear z-buffer Zr for all pixels to infinity/empty. Project boundary cells onto the image plane using parallel projection. Only cells with F(i, j, k) = 1 are projected. Incremental Projection: Project the first cell C(0, 0, 0) onto the image plane to obtain its initial projected position and depth. Calculate the projected positions and depths of remaining cells using incremental vectors with only addition operations. Note: This avoids expensive per-cell projection calculations. Z-Buffer Update: For each projected boundary cell, determine the intersection distances along the rays cast from the image pixels. Update Zn with the closest intersection distance. Update Zr with the farthest intersection distance. 3. Ray Traversal: Iterate over each pixel in the image plane. Check if the pixel is viable: if Zn and Zr indicate an intersection (i.e., not empty). For viable pixels, cast a ray. Traverse the ray from the closest intersection distance (Zn) to the farthest intersection distance (Zr). Sample and composite the volume data along the ray. Incorporate optimizations such as adaptive image sampling and early ray termination. Unverified code. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values representing the volume. imagewidth: Width of the output image in pixels. imageheight: Height of the output image in pixels. cellsize: Size of a grid cell (assumed uniform). viewdirection: Normalized vector representing the view direction for parallel projection. Returns: renderedimage: 2D array of color values. """ # Step 1: Boundary Cell Detection (Offline) # Determine dimensions of the volume grid griddims = volumedata.shape numcellsx, numcellsy, numcellsz = griddims # Initialize boundary cell flags # F[i, j, k] = 1 if cell (i,j,k) is a boundary cell, else 0 F = np.zeros((numcellsx, numcellsy, numcellsz), dtype=np.uint8) # Scan volume to detect boundary cells # A cell is a boundary cell if it contains the object boundary. # This typically involves checking if the cell's bounding box intersects # the isosurface or if there is a transition in scalar values across the cell. # For implementation, this requires a specific boundary detection criterion. # Here we assume a helper function exists. for i in range(numcellsx): for j in range(numcellsy): for k in range(numcellsz): if isboundarycell(volumedata, i, j, k, cellsize): F[i, j, k] = 1 # Step 2: Boundary Cell Projection # Initialize Z-buffers # Zn stores closest intersection distance, Zr stores farthest Zn = np.full((imageheight, imagewidth), np.inf) Zr = np.full((imageheight, imagewidth), -np.inf) # Project boundary cells using incremental parallel projection # Determine pixel size and image plane origin based on viewdirection and dimensions # This part depends on specific camera setup. Assuming standard parallel projection setup. pixelsizex =... # Derived from image dimensions and view frustum pixelsizey =... # Derived from image dimensions and view frustum imageorigin =... # Top-left or center of image plane in world coordinates # Project first cell C(0,0,0) to get base position and depth # Cell center for C(0,0,0) cellcenter000 = getcellcenter(0, 0, 0, cellsize) # Project cellcenter000 onto image plane # This yields initial pixel coordinates (u0, v0) and depth d0 u0, v0, d0 = projectparallel(cellcenter000, viewdirection, imageorigin, pixelsizex, pixelsizey) # Incremental vectors for moving to adjacent cells # In parallel projection, moving from C(i,j,k) to C(i+1,j,k) # shifts the projected position by a constant vector and changes depth by a constant amount. deltau =... # Incremental shift in u for +1 in i deltav =... # Incremental shift in v for +1 in j deltad =... # Incremental shift in depth for +1 in i (example) # Note: The exact incremental vectors depend on the orientation of the grid relative to the view direction. # For simplicity, assume grid axes are aligned or precomputed. # Iterate over all cells for i in range(numcellsx): for j in range(numcellsy): for k in range(numcellsz): if F[i, j, k] == 1: # Calculate projected position and depth incrementally # Current cell center cellcenter = getcellcenter(i, j, k, cellsize) # Project to image plane # Using incremental approach: # u = u0 + ideltaui + jdeltauj + kdeltauk # v = v0 + ideltavi + jdeltavj + kdeltavk # d = d0 + ideltadi + jdeltadj + kdeltadk # For this pseudocode, we assume precomputed incremental steps for each axis u = u0 + i deltaui + j deltauj + k deltauk v = v0 + i deltavi + j deltavj + k deltavk d = d0 + i deltadi + j deltadj + k deltadk # Determine intersection distances for the cell # The cell has a front and back face along the view direction. # Calculate min and max depth of the cell along the ray celldepthmin, celldepthmax = getcelldepthrange(cellcenter, cellsize, viewdirection) # Map projected position (u, v) to pixel coordinates # This requires mapping the continuous image plane coordinates to discrete pixels pixelu, pixelv = maptopixel(u, v, imageorigin, pixelsizex, pixelsizey) if 0 <= pixelu < imagewidth and 0 <= pixelv < imageheight: # Update Z-buffers # The intersection distances are relative to the camera/origin # Assuming d is the depth of the center, adjust for cell extent distfront = d - celldepthmin/2 # Approximation distback = d + celldepthmax/2 # Approximation # Update front z-buffer (closest) if distfront < Zn[pixelv, pixelu]: Zn[pixelv, pixelu] = distfront # Update rear z-buffer (farthest) if distback > Zr[pixelv, pixelu]: Zr[pixelv, pixelu] = distback # Step 3: Ray Traversal renderedimage = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if Zn[y, x] == np.inf: # No intersection, background color renderedimage[y, x] = backgroundcolor continue # Cast ray from closest to farthest intersection tstart = Zn[y, x] tend = Zr[y, x] # Sample and composite along the ray # Use adaptive sampling and early termination color = compositeray(tstart, tend, viewdirection, volumedata, cellsize) renderedimage[y, x] = color return renderedimage def isboundarycell(volumedata, i, j, k, cellsize): """ Determines if a grid cell contains the object boundary. This is a placeholder for the specific boundary detection logic. """ # Example: Check if scalar values at the 8 corners of the cell # span the isovalue threshold. # This requires defining an isovalue and checking the corners. # Corners of cell (i,j,k) are defined by the 8 voxels bounding it. # Implementation details depend on the specific volume representation. return False # Placeholder def getcellcenter(i, j, k, cellsize): """ Returns the 3D coordinates of the center of cell (i,j,k). """ # Assuming cell (0,0,0) starts at origin return np.array([i cellsize, j cellsize, k cellsize]) def projectparallel(point, viewdirection, imageorigin, pixelsizex, pixelsizey): """ Projects a 3D point onto the image plane using parallel projection. Returns (u, v, depth). """ # Vector from image origin to point vec = point - imageorigin # Depth is the projection of vec onto the view direction depth = np.dot(vec, viewdirection) # Projected position on image plane # This requires a basis for the image plane perpendicular to viewdirection # Simplified: assume viewdirection is along Z, image plane is XY # u = vec.x / pixelsizex # v = vec.y / pixelsizey # This is a simplified example. Real implementation needs proper basis vectors. u = vec[0] / pixelsizex v = vec[1] / pixelsizey return u, v, depth def getcelldepthrange(cellcenter, cellsize, viewdirection): """ Returns the minimum and maximum depth of a cell along the view direction. """ # The cell is a box. The min/max depth are at the corners. # Calculate all 8 corners, project onto viewdirection, find min/max. # Simplified: assume cell is aligned with axes and view is along Z # Min depth is center.z - cellsize/2, Max is center.z + cellsize/2 # For general view direction, this requires more complex calculation. mind = -cellsize / 2 maxd = cellsize / 2 return mind, maxd def maptopixel(u, v, imageorigin, pixelsizex, pixelsizey): """ Maps continuous image plane coordinates to discrete pixel indices. """ # Assuming u, v are in pixels relative to origin pixelu = int(u) pixelv = int(v) return pixelu, pixelv def compositeray(tstart, tend, viewdirection, volumedata, cellsize): """ Samples and composites the volume along the ray from tstart to tend. """ # Implementation of ray marching with adaptive sampling and early termination # This is a placeholder for the actual compositing logic. return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) Flag F: Binary flag for each cell C(i,j,k). Value 1 indicates the cell contains the object boundary; 0 indicates empty or fully inside/outside (not a boundary cell). Cell Size: The size of the grid cells, which determines the resolution of the boundary estimation. Isovalue: (Implicit) The scalar value threshold used to define the object boundary within the volume data. Precision: Incremental projection relies on addition operations, which can accumulate floating-point errors over large volumes. Boundaries: The algorithm assumes a regular grid of volume elements. Irregular grids may require adaptation. Degenerate Input: If the volume data is empty or contains no boundary cells, the Z-buffers will remain empty, and no rays will be cast. Uses octrees to compute ray paths, offering a different hierarchical structure compared to the grid-based boundary cells of BC-RC. Choose when memory efficiency for sparse data is critical. Octree Path Computation Traverses sparse voxel octrees, providing better handling of large, sparse datasets than the regular grid approach of BC-RC. Choose for very large, sparse volumes. Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal Uses rational parameterization to improve traversal accuracy in octrees, addressing precision issues that may arise in BC-RC's incremental projection. Choose when high precision is required. Rational Ray Parameterization for Octree Traversal Focuses on occlusion culling within octrees, which can complement BC-RC's boundary cell skipping. Choose when occlusion is a major performance bottleneck. Ray-Occlusion Traversal in Octree Eliminates the need for a stack during traversal, which can be beneficial for GPU implementations, unlike the serial nature of BC-RC. Choose for GPU acceleration. Stackless Traversal Accelerates traversal by checking for the presence of data, similar to BC-RC's boundary cell flags but potentially more efficient. Choose for faster empty space skipping. Presence Acceleration A general term for ray casting using octrees, which BC-RC improves upon by using boundary cells. Choose when a hierarchical structure is preferred. Octree Raycasting Traverses hierarchical tree nodes, offering a flexible structure compared to the fixed grid of BC-RC. Choose for complex hierarchical data. Hierarchical Tree Node Traversal Time Complexity: The preprocessing step (boundary cell detection) is O(N) where N is the number of cells. The projection step is O(B) where B is the number of boundary cells. The ray traversal step is O(P \cdot L) where P is the number of viable pixels and L is the average ray length within the object. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, the boundary cell flags (O(N)), and the Z-buffers (O(P)). Measured Performance: The algorithm is described as "fast" and improves upon PARC by reducing projection overhead and providing more accurate boundary estimation. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of boundary cells and viable pixels. Adaptive image sampling can help manage complexity in high-detail regions. Strengths: Fast serial rendering, accurate boundary estimation, reduced projection overhead via incremental projection, viewpoint-independent preprocessing. Limitations: Serial algorithm, may not be as efficient for very large sparse datasets as octree-based methods, incremental projection can accumulate errors. When to Use: Suitable for time-critical volume rendering where accuracy and speed are important, and the data is not extremely sparse. When Not to Use: For very large, sparse datasets where octree-based methods are more efficient, or for parallel/GPU implementations where stackless traversal is preferred. Boundary Cell-Based Ray Casting was proposed as an improvement on the PARC algorithm. It was developed in the context of time-critical volume rendering, aiming to accelerate the ray casting procedure by skipping over empty space in volume datasets. The algorithm was part of a broader effort to establish hierarchical level-of-detail representation of 3D data sets and develop user interfaces for interactive exploration. name: Octree Raycasting
head: Ray-Octant Intersection
body: An algorithm to find all octants in a pointer-based octree that intersect with a given ray, returning them sorted by distance (closest first). It uses parametric ray representation (t-values) to traverse the octree structure efficiently. It distinguishes itself from Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal by focusing on discrete octant traversal logic for pointer-based structures rather than dense voxel sampling, and from Ray-Octree Boundary Intersection by operating on the internal hierarchy rather than just the root bounding box. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a pointer-based octree node; pre-computed entry/exit t-values for the current node's bounding box (tx0, ty0, tz0 for entry; tx1, ty1, tz1 for exit). Output: A list of intersected octants sorted by distance from the ray origin. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains a pointer to children (array of 8 nodes or null) and a bitmask/flag RaycastingFlags to handle child reordering or symmetry. RaycastingFlags: A static constant holding a single value value used as a bitmask or index modifier for child array access. Steps: 1. Intersection Check: Verify if the ray intersects the current octant. Calculate the mean t-values for the center of the current octant: txm = 0.5 \cdot (tx0 + tx1), \quad tym = 0.5 \cdot (ty0 + ty1), \quad tzm = 0.5 \cdot (tz0 + tz1) Check if the ray is behind the current octant or does not intersect it by verifying if tx1 < 0.0, ty1 < 0.0, or tz1 < 0.0. If any are negative, return immediately. 2. Entry Octant Determination: Determine the index of the first octant the ray enters within the current node using findEntryOctant(tx0, ty0, tz0, txm, tym, tzm). This function maps ray-parametric intersections to discrete octant indices using axis-aligned comparisons. 3. Traversal Loop: Loop through octants starting from currentOctant (the entry index) while currentOctant < 8. For each octant, recursively call raycastOctant with the appropriate t-value bounds for that child octant. Update currentOctant to the next intersected octant using findNextOctant(currentOctant, txm, tym, tzm). 4. Child Access: Access the child node using the RaycastingFlags mask. For octants i \in \{1, \dots, 7\}, the child index is children[f ^ i], where f is the flag value. Octant 0 uses children[f]. 5. Termination: Octant 7 (far top right) is the last possible octant reachable from the entry point in this traversal order. After processing octant 7, the loop terminates by setting currentOctant = 8. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastoctant(node, tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1, result): # Check if ray is behind or misses the current octant if tx1 < 0.0 or ty1 < 0.0 or tz1 < 0.0: return # Calculate mean t-values for the center of the current octant txm = 0.5 (tx0 + tx1) tym = 0.5 (ty0 + ty1) tzm = 0.5 (tz0 + tz1) # Determine the entry octant index (0-7) currentoctant = findentryoctant(tx0, ty0, tz0, txm, tym, tzm) # Loop through octants starting from the entry point while currentoctant < 8: # Determine child index based on RaycastingFlags # f is a static constant bitmask for symmetry/reordering childidx = children[f ^ currentoctant] if currentoctant > 0 else children[f] # Recursively process the child octant # Note: t-bounds for the child are derived from tx0/tx1 and the octant's spatial position # For octant 0 (closest), bounds are (tx0, ty0, tz0) to (txm, tym, tzm) # For octant 7 (farthest), bounds are (txm, tym, tzm) to (tx1, ty1, tz1) # Intermediate octants use mixed bounds based on their axis alignment if childidx is not None: raycastoctant(childidx, childtx0, childty0, childtz0, childtx1, childty1, childtz1, result) # Move to the next intersected octant if currentoctant == 7: currentoctant = 8 # Termination condition else: currentoctant = findnextoctant(currentoctant, txm, tym, tzm) Parameters: tx0, ty0, tz0: The ray projection parameters (t-values) at the entry point of the current octant for the x, y, and z axes respectively. tx1, ty1, tz1: The ray projection parameters (t-values) at the exit point of the current octant for the x, y, and z axes respectively. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Octant 7 Termination: Octant 7 is the last possible octant reachable from the entry point. The loop must explicitly terminate after processing it by setting currentOctant = 8. Child Reordering: The RaycastingFlags mask must be applied correctly to handle potential child reordering or symmetry in the octree structure. Zero Direction Components: If the ray direction has zero components, division by zero may occur in intersection logic. This is typically handled by normalizing the ray direction to be strictly positive or using epsilon comparisons. Calculates the entry and exit distances of a ray relative to the bounding box of an octree root node. It serves as the core intersection test within the broader Octree Raycasting framework, determining if a ray intersects the octree's spatial bounds before initiating traversal. Determines the index of the first octant a ray enters within a local 2×2×2 block of an octree, and the index of the subsequent octant the ray traverses. It maps ray-parametric intersections to discrete octant indices using axis-aligned comparisons. Finds specific points within a pointer-based octree that intersect with a given ray by iterating through all octants intersected by the ray and testing the points contained within those octants. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on discrete point data rather than continuous volume density or boundary surfaces. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of intersected octants. In the worst case (ray passing through all occupied nodes), it is O(N) where N is the number of nodes. However, empty space skipping reduces this significantly for sparse data. Memory Complexity: O(D) where D is the depth of the octree, due to recursion stack. On GPU, an explicit stack is required. Strengths: Efficient for sparse data; avoids sampling empty space; returns intersected octants in sorted order (closest first). Limitations: Requires pointer-based octree structure; recursion depth can be an issue on hardware with limited stack size; not optimized for dense volume rendering without additional leaf-level sampling strategies. When to Use: When discrete octant intersection is required (e.g., for point clouds, boundary detection, or as a pre-pass for volume rendering). When Not to Use: For dense volume rendering where voxel-level sampling is needed; consider Sparse Voxel Octree Ray Traversal instead. Originated from the sparse-octree module by vanruesc. The method is designed for efficient ray intersection with pointer-based octrees, commonly used in computer graphics for spatial partitioning of sparse data. sparse-octree module, https://github.com/vanruesc/sparse-octree, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Octree Boundary Intersection
head: intersectOctree
body: Calculates the entry and exit distances of a ray relative to the bounding box of an octree root node. It normalizes the ray direction to be strictly positive to simplify intersection logic and handles zero-direction components to prevent division by zero. This method serves as the core intersection test within the broader Octree Raycasting framework. Inputs: ray: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. octree: An octree structure with defined bounds. flags: A RaycastingFlags object (integer) to store axis flip information. Outputs: An array [tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1] if the ray hits the octree, where t{x0}, t{y0}, t{z0} are entry distances and t{x1}, t{y1}, t{z1} are exit distances for each axis. null if the ray does not intersect the octree. Data Structures: RaycastingFlags: An integer where Bit 0 (value 1) indicates Z flip, Bit 1 (value 2) indicates Y flip, and Bit 2 (value 4) indicates X flip. Steps: 1. Translate Extents: Translate the octant extents to the scene origin by setting min to (0, 0, 0) and max to octree.max - octree.min. 2. Calculate Dimensions: Compute dimensions and half-dimensions of the octree: \text{dimensions} = \text{octree.getDimensions()} \text{halfDimensions} = \text{dimensions} \times 0.5 3. Translate Origin: Translate the ray origin to the center of the octant: \text{origin} = \text{ray.origin} - \text{octree.getCenter()} + \text{halfDimensions} 4. Reset Flags: Reset raycasting flags to 0. 5. Normalize Direction (Flip): For each axis (x, y, z): If direction[axis] < 0: Flip the origin coordinate: \text{origin}[axis] = \text{dimensions}[axis] - \text{origin}[axis]. Negate the direction: \text{direction}[axis] = -\text{direction}[axis]. Set the corresponding flag bit: x \rightarrow 4, y \rightarrow 2, z \rightarrow 1. 6. Handle Zero Direction: For each axis, if direction[axis] == 0, set direction[axis] to Number.EPSILON to prevent division by zero. 7. Compute Inverse Directions: \text{invDir}x = 1.0 / \text{direction}x, \quad \text{invDir}y = 1.0 / \text{direction}y, \quad \text{invDir}z = 1.0 / \text{direction}z 8. Calculate Intersection Parameters: For each axis, calculate entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances: t{x0} = (\text{min}x - \text{origin}x) \times \text{invDir}x, \quad t{x1} = (\text{max}x - \text{origin}x) \times \text{invDir}x 9. Check Intersection: \text{hit} = \max(t{x0}, t{y0}, t{z0}) < \min(t{x1}, t{y1}, t{z1}) Return [tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1] if hit, else null. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intersectoctree(rayorigin, raydirection, octreemin, octreemax, octreecenter, flags): # Step 1: Translate extents to scene origin minext = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] maxext = [octreemax[i] - octreemin[i] for i in range(3)] # Step 2: Calculate dimensions and half-dimensions dimensions = [maxext[i] - minext[i] for i in range(3)] halfdimensions = [d 0.5 for d in dimensions] # Step 3: Translate ray origin to center of octant origin = [rayorigin[i] - octreecenter[i] + halfdimensions[i] for i in range(3)] # Step 4: Reset flags flags = 0 # Step 5: Normalize direction (Flip) for i in range(3): if raydirection[i] < 0: origin[i] = dimensions[i] - origin[i] raydirection[i] = -raydirection[i] # Set flag bit: x=4, y=2, z=1 if i == 0: flags |= 4 elif i == 1: flags |= 2 else: flags |= 1 # Step 6: Handle zero direction EPSILON = 1e-8 # Number.EPSILON equivalent direction = [raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0 else EPSILON for i in range(3)] # Step 7: Compute inverse directions invdir = [1.0 / direction[i] for i in range(3)] # Step 8: Calculate intersection parameters tx0 = (minext[0] - origin[0]) invdir[0] tx1 = (maxext[0] - origin[0]) invdir[0] ty0 = (minext[1] - origin[1]) invdir[1] ty1 = (maxext[1] - origin[1]) invdir[1] tz0 = (minext[2] - origin[2]) invdir[2] tz1 = (maxext[2] - origin[2]) invdir[2] # Step 9: Check intersection tenter = max(tx0, ty0, tz0) texit = min(tx1, ty1, tz1) if tenter < texit: return [tx0, ty0, tz0, tx1, ty1, tz1] else: return None Parameters: flags: A RaycastingFlags object used to store axis flip information. Bit 0 (value 1) indicates Z flip, Bit 1 (value 2) indicates Y flip, Bit 2 (value 4) indicates X flip. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction Components: Rays with zero direction components cause division by zero. The implementation replaces 0.0 with Number.EPSILON. Grazing Boundaries: Exact boundary contacts may produce t{\text{enter}} = t{\text{exit}}. The comparison uses < to strictly follow the source definition. Rays Behind the Box: Rays originating outside the box and pointing away yield negative t{\text{exit}}. A guard rejects these cases. This algorithm determines whether a ray intersects an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) representing an octree node and prepares the necessary parameters for traversing its subtrees. It distinguishes itself by normalizing the ray direction to be strictly positive through coordinate flipping, which simplifies the subsequent intersection logic and traversal order determination. This method serves as the core intersection test within the broader Ray-Octree Boundary Intersection framework. Not given in the sources. name: Ray-AABB Intersection for Octree Traversal
head: Ray-Parameter Function, Revelles, Urena and Lastra Octree Traversal
body: This algorithm determines whether a ray intersects an axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) representing an octree node and prepares parameters for traversing its subtrees. It distinguishes itself by normalizing the ray direction to be strictly positive through coordinate flipping, which simplifies the subsequent intersection logic and traversal order determination. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d (3D vectors). Octree node bounds: minimum corner \min, maximum corner \max, and node size \size. Outputs: Boolean indicating intersection. If intersecting, calls processSubtree with entry/exit distances and a bitmask. Data Structures: a: Unsigned integer bitmask (3 bits) indicating which axes were flipped. t0: Vector of entry distances per axis. t1: Vector of exit distances per axis. t: Scalar tracking the maximum entry distance (closest entry point). Steps: 1. Initialize bitmask a = 0. 2. Copy ray origin o and direction d. 3. For each axis i \in \{0, 1, 2\}: If d[i] < 0: Flip origin: o[i] = \size[i] - o[i]. Negate direction: d[i] = -d[i]. Set bit i in a: a \ |= \ (1 \ll (2-i)). Specifically: bit 2 (value 4) for axis 0, bit 1 (value 2) for axis 1, bit 0 (value 1) for axis 2. 4. Compute entry distances: t0 = (\min - o) / d. 5. Compute exit distances: t1 = (\max - o) / d. 6. Initialize t = \infty (maximum double value). 7. Check intersection: If \max(t0) < \min(t1), the ray intersects the box. Call processSubtree(t0, t1, r, t, sd, a). Otherwise, return false. Formulas: Origin flip: o[i] = \size[i] - o[i]. Entry distance: t0[i] = (\min[i] - o[i]) / d[i]. Exit distance: t1[i] = (\max[i] - o[i]) / d[i]. Intersection condition: \max(t0) < \min(t1). Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Incorrect traversal logic or misinterpretation of \size can cause rendering artifacts, such as only the upper-right part of the image being rendered while the rest is rejected. The formula o[i] = \size[i] - o[i] is specific to the implementation cited. Standard implementations often use o[i] = \max[i] - o[i] or similar depending on coordinate space. Sources indicate ambiguity in \size: it is either \size = \max - \min or \size = (\max - \min) / 2. Implementers must verify the definition of \size in their specific octree structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayaabbintersect(octnode, ray): # Inputs: octnode with attributes min, max, size # ray with attributes origin (o), direction (d) a = 0 o = [ray.origin[0], ray.origin[1], ray.origin[2]] d = [ray.direction[0], ray.direction[1], ray.direction[2]] # Normalize ray direction to be positive if d[0] < 0: o[0] = octnode.size[0] - o[0] d[0] = -d[0] a |= 4 # Bit 2 if d[1] < 0: o[1] = octnode.size[1] - o[1] d[1] = -d[1] a |= 2 # Bit 1 if d[2] < 0: o[2] = octnode.size[2] - o[2] d[2] = -d[2] a |= 1 # Bit 0 # Compute intersection distances t0 = [(octnode.min[i] - o[i]) / d[i] for i in range(3)] t1 = [(octnode.max[i] - o[i]) / d[i] for i in range(3)] t = float('inf') # Check for intersection if max(t0) < min(t1): # processsubtree(t0, t1, ray, t, sd, a) is not defined in the sources; # it handles child traversal using bitmask a and distance t. return True else: return False Time Complexity: O(1) per node visit. The intersection test involves a constant number of arithmetic operations and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simplifies traversal logic by ensuring positive ray directions, allowing consistent ordering of child node visits based on the bitmask. Limitations: Relies on correct interpretation of node size and bounds. Incorrect implementation can lead to significant rendering errors (e.g., missing image regions). When to use: When traversing an octree where node bounds are axis-aligned and the traversal order needs to be determined by the ray's entry/exit points relative to the node's children. This method is based on the "Efficient Parametric Algorithm for Octree Traversal" by Revelles, Urena, and Lastra. The specific implementation details and pitfalls discussed in the sources stem from a community discussion on Stack Overflow regarding an implementation of this algorithm. The algorithm is a standard technique in volume rendering and ray tracing for efficient spatial subdivision traversal. name: Ray-Octant Traversal (Entry)
head: findEntryOctant, findNextOctant
body: Determines the index of the first octant a ray enters within a local 2×2×2 block of a pointer-based octree, and the index of the subsequent octant the ray traverses. It maps ray-parametric intersections to discrete octant indices using axis-aligned comparisons. Inputs: tx0, ty0, tz0: Ray projection parameters at the start of the current segment. tx1, ty1, tz1: Ray projection parameters at the end of the current segment. txm, tym, tzm: Ray projection parameters at the midpoint of the current octant along each axis. Outputs: entryIndex: Integer 0–7 representing the octant index the ray enters. nextOctant: Integer 0–7 representing the next octant to visit. Data Structures: octantTable: An 8 \times 3 array of integers 0–7, where octantTable[currentOctant][exit] returns the next octant index. The exit dimension uses 0 for the YZ-plane, 1 for the XZ-plane, and 2 for the XY-plane. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize entry = 0. 2. Compare start parameters to find the largest: If tx0 is the largest (tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0): the ray enters through the YZ-plane (index 0). If tym < tx0, set bit 2: entry |= 2. If tzm < tx0, set bit 1: entry |= 1. Else if ty0 is larger than tz0: the ray enters through the XZ-plane (index 1). If txm < ty0, set bit 2: entry |= 4. If tzm < ty0, set bit 1: entry |= 1. Else (tz0 is largest): the ray enters through the XY-plane (index 2). If txm < tz0, set bit 2: entry |= 4. If tym < tz0, set bit 1: entry |= 2. 3. Return entry. 4. Compare exit parameters tx1 and ty1. 5. If tx1 < ty1, set mint = tx1 and exit = 0 (YZ-plane). 6. Else, set mint = ty1 and exit = 1 (XZ-plane). 7. If tz1 < mint, set exit = 2 (XY-plane). 8. Return octantTable[currentOctant][exit]. Formulas: Midpoint parameters: txm = 0.5 \times (tx0 + tx1), tym = 0.5 \times (ty0 + ty1), tzm = 0.5 \times (tz0 + tz1). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findentryoctant(tx0, ty0, tz0, txm, tym, tzm): entry = 0 if tx0 > ty0 and tx0 > tz0: if tym < tx0: entry |= 2 if tzm < tx0: entry |= 1 elif ty0 > tz0: if txm < ty0: entry |= 4 if tzm < ty0: entry |= 1 else: if txm < tz0: entry |= 4 if tym < tz0: entry |= 2 return entry def findnextoctant(currentoctant, tx1, ty1, tz1, octanttable): if tx1 < ty1: mint = tx1 exitplane = 0 else: mint = ty1 exitplane = 1 if tz1 < mint: exitplane = 2 return octanttable[currentoctant][exitplane] OCTANTTABLE = [ [1, 2, 4], [0, 3, 5], [0, 3, 6], [2, 1, 7], [0, 5, 6], [4, 7, 1], [4, 7, 2], [6, 5, 3] ] Parameters: tx0, ty0, tz0: Start t-values. txm, tym, tzm: Midpoint t-values. tx1, ty1, tz1: End t-values. octantTable: 8 \times 3 integer array. Edge Cases: Ray origin exactly on a plane boundary: The strict comparisons (>, <) determine the entry. Exact equality may lead to arbitrary but consistent selection depending on implementation. Degenerate ray (zero length): tx0 == tx1, etc. The logic still holds but txm == tx0. Outside-in rays: The algorithm assumes tx0, ty0, tz0 represent parametric distances to the current node's faces; negative directions are handled correctly by the midpoint comparisons. Time Complexity: O(1) for both entry and next octant calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the lookup table (24 integers). Strengths: Branch-minimized entry calculation; fast traversal step. Limitations: Requires pre-computed or maintained lookup table; specific to pointer-based octree traversal where children are accessed via flags. Used in efficient raycasting through sparse octrees where nodes are stored in arrays and accessed via bit flags. sparse-octree module, https://github.com/vanruesc/sparse-octree, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree Raycasting (Point Intersection)
head: PointOctant
body: This method finds specific points within a pointer-based octree that intersect with a given ray by iterating through all octants intersected by the ray and testing the points contained within those octants. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on discrete point data rather than continuous volume density or boundary surfaces, serving as the intersection logic for PointOctree structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A raycaster (defining origin and direction) and a PointOctree instance. Output: A list of RayPointIntersection objects, sorted by distance from the ray origin. Data Structures: PointOctree<T>: Extends Octree<PointOctant<T>>. Fields: bias: Number. Octant boundary bias. If > 0, the octree is "loose". maxPoints: Number. Maximum distinct points per leaf octant before a split occurs. Default: 8. maxDepth: Number. Maximum tree depth level (starting at 0). Default: 8. PointOctant<T>: Represents a node in the octree. Field: pointData. Contains the points stored in this octant. Can be null if empty or not yet populated. RayPointIntersection: The result object returned for each hit point. Parameters: bias: Default 0.0. Must be \ge 0. maxPoints: Default 8. Must be \ge 1. maxDepth: Default 8. Must be \ge 0. Steps: 1. Initialize an empty list result of type RayPointIntersection. 2. Retrieve the list of octants intersecting the ray by calling the parent method super.getIntersectingNodes(raycaster). 3. If the list of intersecting octants is not empty: a. Iterate through each octant in the list. b. Check if the octant has point data (pointData !== null). c. If point data exists, call pointData.testPoints(raycaster, result) to identify specific points within the octant that intersect the ray and add them to result. 4. Return the result list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointoctreeraycast(raycaster, octree): # 1. Initialize result list result = [] # 2. Get intersecting octants from parent traversal logic # super.getIntersectingNodes(raycaster) returns a list of PointOctant objects intersectingoctants = super.getIntersectingNodes(raycaster) # 3. Iterate through octants if intersectingoctants is not empty: for octant in intersectingoctants: # 4. Check for point data if octant.pointData is not null: # 5. Test points within this octant against the ray # This modifies the result list in place or returns new intersections octant.pointData.testPoints(raycaster, result) # 6. Return results return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinity Depth: Allowing maxDepth to be infinite can result in poor performance due to infinitely small octants. Bias: The bias parameter must be non-negative. It affects the "looseness" of the octree boundaries. Empty Octants: Octants without pointData are skipped, optimizing traversal for sparse data. A GPU-based technique extending this method by adding recursive shading for non-opaque surfaces to simulate transparent and reflective materials. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of intersecting octants and the number of points per octant. The traversal is efficient due to the octree structure, but point testing is linear with respect to points in the leaf octants. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of points stored in the octree. Strengths: Efficient for sparse point data; avoids testing points in non-intersecting octants. Limitations: Performance degrades if maxDepth is too high or if octants contain excessive points. Not suitable for continuous volume rendering without modification. This method is part of the sparse-octree module, which implements a pointer-based octree for storing and querying points in 3D space. It is designed to work with the PointOctant class to provide efficient raycasting against discrete point sets. sparse-octree module, https://github.com/vanruesc/sparse-octree, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Octree Raycasting with Refraction and Reflection
head: CUDA Octree Raycasting with Refraction and Reflection
body: A GPU-based volume rendering technique that traverses an octree using CUDA kernels to compute ray-surface intersections, handling refraction and reflection recursively to simulate transparent and reflective materials. It extends Octree Raycasting (Point Intersection) by adding recursive shading for non-opaque surfaces, distinguishing itself from sibling methods that only handle point intersection or single-bounce reflections. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree data structure representing the volume, camera parameters (position, projection matrix), viewport dimensions (width \times height), and rendering flags (enablereflection, enablerefraction, depth buffer enabled). Output: A color buffer (image) and optionally a depth buffer. Data Structures: The method relies on specific structures to track traversal state and hit information: 1. StackEntry: Used for parent voxel tracking during traversal. parent: const int32t pointer to the parent node. tmax: float maximum t-value for the current voxel. 2. RaycastHit: Stores the result of a raycast intersection. hitt: float distance to the hit. hitpos: glm::vec3 world position of the hit. hitparent: const int32t pointer to the parent node. hitidx: int32t child index. hitposinternal: glm::vec3 internal position within the voxel. hitscale: int32t scale/depth of the hit node. Parameters: MAXSCALE: The maximum depth of the octree, defined as 23, corresponding to the number of bits in a single precision float. THREADSPERBLOCKSQUARE: The number of threads per block in each dimension, set to 32, which is a multiple of the warp size. HALFSQRT2: A constant used for origin offsetting (value \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} or 0.7071...). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize CUDA Kernel Grid: Calculate block size as dim3(32, 32) and grid size as dim3((width + 31) / 32, (height + 31) / 32) to cover the viewport dimensions. 2. Compute Eye Ray: For each pixel (x, y): Check if x \ge width or y \ge height. If so, return early to prevent writing to invalid memory. Normalize coordinates to [0, 1]. Convert to NDC [-1, 1]. Multiply by the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. Normalize the resulting vector to get the ray direction. Set ray origin to the camera position. 3. Initial Raycast: Call raycast(tree, &eyeray, stack, &raycastHit) to find the first surface intersection in the octree. 4. Handle Hit: If raycastHit.hitscale < MAXSCALE: Calculate NDC depth from hitpos using the MVP matrix. Clamp depth to [-1, 1]. Write to the depth buffer if enabled. Decompress raw attachment to get shading attributes. 5. Shade Fragment: Call shade<0>(renderingattributes, eyeray, raycastHit, stack, tree) to compute the initial color. This function handles recursive refraction and reflection. Recursive Shading Logic (shade<recursions>): Refraction Handling: If enablereflection is false but refraction is active: Calculate the surface normal. Adjust for the dot product sign (normal orientation relative to ray). Compute refracted direction using indices of refraction (IOR). Refraction Origin Offset: To prevent self-intersection, set the new ray origin: \text{refraction\ray.origin} = \text{hit\pos} + \text{direction} \times \text{HALF\SQRT\2} \times \exp2(\text{hit.hit\scale} - \text{MAX\SCALE}) This offsets the origin along the ray direction based on the hit scale. Perform recursive raycast for the refracted ray. If refractionhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE: Recursively call shade<recursions+1>. Add result to output weighted by oneminusalpha. Else: Add ambient color weighted by oneminusalpha. Reflection Handling: Perform recursive raycast for the reflected ray. If reflectionhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE: Recursively call shade<recursions+1>. Add result to output weighted by reflectivity. Else: Add clear color weighted by reflectivity 6. Unmap Resources and Render: Unmap CUDA resources. Bind Pixel Buffer Objects (PBOs) to OpenGL textures. Draw a fullscreen quad to display the result. Optionally blit the depth buffer to the main framebuffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors.
