1.0 ndcy = (2.0 y / height) - 1.0 # Assuming standard perspective projection setup # Ray direction calculation involves MVP matrix inverse or similar # Simplified: raydir is normalized vector after MVP transform raydir = normalize(transformandnormalize(ndcx, ndcy, mvpmatrix)) rayorigin = camerapos eyeray = Ray(rayorigin, raydir) stack = [] # Initialize stack for traversal rayhit = RaycastHit() # Initial Raycast hit = raycast(tree, eyeray, stack, rayhit) if not hit: return clearcolor # Handle Hit if rayhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE: # Calculate NDC depth ndcdepth = calculatendcdepth(rayhit.hitpos, mvpmatrix) ndcdepth = clamp(ndcdepth, -1.0, 1.0) if depthbufferenabled: writedepthbuffer(x, y, ndcdepth) # Get shading attributes attributes = decompressattachment(rayhit) # Shade color = shade(0, attributes, eyeray, rayhit, stack, tree, enablereflection, enablerefraction) return color return clearcolor def shade(recursionlevel, attributes, ray, hit, stack, tree, enablereflection, enablerefraction): basecolor = computebasecolor(attributes) finalcolor = basecolor # Refraction if not enablereflection and enablerefraction: normal = computenormal(hit) # Adjust normal sign based on dot product if dot(ray.direction, normal) > 0: normal = -normal iorinside = attributes.iorinside ioroutside = attributes.ioroutside refracteddir = refract(ray.direction, normal, iorinside / ioroutside) # Origin offset to prevent self-intersection offset = HALFSQRT2 pow(2.0, hit.hitscale - MAXSCALE) refractedorigin = hit.hitpos + refracteddir offset refractedray = Ray(refractedorigin, refracteddir) refractedhit = raycast(tree, refractedray, stack, RaycastHit()) if refractedhit and refractedhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE: refractedcolor = shade(recursionlevel + 1, attributes, refractedray, refractedhit, stack, tree, enablereflection, enablerefraction) finalcolor += refractedcolor (1.0 - attributes.alpha) else: finalcolor += ambientcolor (1.0 - attributes.alpha) # Reflection if enablereflection: normal = computenormal(hit) if dot(ray.direction, normal) > 0: normal = -normal reflecteddir = reflect(ray.direction, normal) # Small offset for reflection to avoid self-intersection (similar logic) reflectedorigin = hit.hitpos + reflecteddir offset reflectedray = Ray(reflectedorigin, reflecteddir) reflectedhit = raycast(tree, reflectedray, stack, RaycastHit()) if reflectedhit and reflectedhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE: reflectedcolor = shade(recursionlevel + 1, attributes, reflectedray, reflectedhit, stack, tree, enablereflection, enablerefraction) finalcolor += reflectedcolor attributes.reflectivity else: finalcolor += clearcolor attributes.reflectivity return finalcolor def transformandnormalize(ndcx, ndcy, mvpmatrix): # Inverse MVP to get ray direction in world space # This is a placeholder for the actual matrix math pass def calculatendcdepth(pos, mvpmatrix): # Transform world pos to NDC pass def refract(direction, normal, eta): # Standard refract formula pass def reflect(direction, normal): # Standard reflect formula pass def raycast(tree, ray, stack, hitout): # Traversal logic from Octree Raycasting (Point Intersection) # Returns True if hit, False otherwise pass Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the octree and the number of recursive bounces. Each pixel requires at least one traversal. Refraction and reflection add recursive calls, potentially increasing the number of raycast operations significantly. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the octree structure, the stack for traversal, and the output buffers (color and depth). The stack size is proportional to the octree depth. Performance: Implemented on GPU using CUDA, leveraging parallelism across pixels. Block size of 32 \times 32 threads is used to align with warp size. Strengths: Efficient handling of complex transparent and reflective volumes on GPU. Recursive approach allows for realistic light transport simulation. Limitations: Recursive nature can lead to high computational cost for scenes with many bounces or high transparency. Self-intersection artifacts must be carefully managed with origin offsets. When to use: Suitable for real-time or near-real-time rendering of transparent/reflective volumes on hardware with CUDA support. When not to use: Not suitable for CPU-only implementations or when strict performance constraints prohibit recursive raycasting. This method is described in the repository catchouli/VolumeRender. It represents a practical implementation of octree-based volume rendering with advanced shading capabilities on the GPU. The use of CUDA and OpenGL interoperability (PBOs) suggests it was developed for integration into graphics applications requiring efficient volume visualization. catchouli/VolumeRender, https://github.com/catchouli/VolumeRender, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Best-First Octree Traversal with Screen-Space LOD
head: Budgeted Octree Traversal
body: This method renders hierarchical point-cloud or sparse volume data by traversing an octree in screen-space order, prioritizing nodes that project largest on the display. It solves the problem of maintaining visual fidelity while adhering to a strict rendering budget (e.g., maximum point count or fill rate) by dynamically adjusting the level of detail (LOD) based on camera distance and frustum visibility. Unlike fixed-depth traversal, it stops refining nodes once the budget is exhausted, ensuring consistent performance regardless of scene complexity. Inputs: An octree data structure where each node contains a list of child pointers (or indices) and a coarse sample of points (node["sample"]). Camera parameters (position, projection matrix) to compute screen-space size and frustum bounds. A rendering budget (budget), defined as the maximum number of points allowed in the frame. A minimum screen-space size threshold (lodpx) in pixels. Outputs: A set of leaf nodes (or coarse samples) selected for rendering, totaling no more than budget points. Data Structures: Priority Queue: Stores nodes to be processed, ordered by their projected screen-space size (largest first). Node Structure: children: List of child node references or indices. Empty if leaf. sample: List of points associated with this node, used for rendering if the node is not refined further. boundingbox: Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) for frustum culling and screen-space projection. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute the screen-space bounding box of the root node. Calculate the projected area (or max dimension) in pixels. Push the root node into the priority queue with its screen-space size as the key. Initialize points = 0. 2. Traversal Loop: While the priority queue is not empty and points < budget: a. Extract: Pop the node with the largest screen-space size from the queue. b. Frustum Culling: Check if the node's bounding box intersects the view frustum. If not, discard the node and continue to the next iteration. c. Refinement Decision: Determine if the node should be refined into its children using the following boolean condition: \text{refine} = (\text{node["children"] is not empty}) \land (\text{screen\size} \ge \text{lod\px}) \land (\text{points} + \text{len}(\text{node["sample"]}) < \text{budget}) node["children"] is not empty: The node has children to refine into. screensize >= lodpx: The node is large enough on screen to warrant higher resolution. points + len(node["sample"]) < budget: Adding the coarse sample of the children (or the current node's sample if not refined, but here we are deciding to go deeper) does not exceed the budget. Note: The source implies that if we refine, we will eventually draw the children's samples. The condition checks if we can afford the children's samples. If we do not refine, we draw node["sample"]. d. Action: If refine is true: For each child of the node: Compute the child's screen-space size. Push the child into the priority queue. If refine is false: Add len(node["sample"]) to points. Mark node["sample"] for rendering. 3. Termination: The loop ends when the queue is empty or points reaches budget. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bestfirstoctreetraversal(root, camera, budget, lodpx): # Priority queue stores tuples: (screensize, node) # Max-heap behavior: negate screensize for min-heap implementation pq = [] push(pq, (-computescreensize(root, camera), root)) pointsrendered = 0 renderlist = [] while pq and pointsrendered < budget: negsize, node = pop(pq) screensize = -negsize # Frustum Culling if not intersectsfrustum(node.boundingbox, camera): continue # Refinement Condition haschildren = node.children is not None and len(node.children) > 0 islargeenough = screensize >= lodpx canaffordchildren = True # Assumption: children's samples will be counted when popped # The source condition: points + len(node["sample"]) < budget # This checks if we can afford the CURRENT node's sample if we STOP refining. # However, the logic is: if we refine, we push children. If we don't, we draw node.sample. # The condition in the source is: points + len(node["sample"]) < budget # This implies that if we decide NOT to refine, we will add len(node["sample"]) to points. # So we can only refine if we are NOT forced to draw the current sample immediately? # Actually, the source says: "refine = node["children"] and size >= lodpx and points + len(node["sample"]) < budget" # This is slightly ambiguous. Does "points + len(node["sample"]) < budget" mean we check if we can afford the CURRENT node's sample? # If we refine, we don't draw node["sample"] yet. We draw children's samples later. # If we don't refine, we draw node["sample"]. # So the condition checks if we can afford to draw the current node's sample IF we were to stop. # But we only stop if we can't refine. # Let's stick to the source formula exactly. refine = haschildren and islargeenough and (pointsrendered + len(node.sample) < budget) if refine: for child in node.children: childsize = computescreensize(child, camera) push(pq, (-childsize, child)) else: # Draw the coarse sample pointsrendered += len(node.sample) renderlist.append(node.sample) # Optimization: if pointsrendered >= budget, we might want to stop early, # but the loop condition handles it. return renderlist Parameters: lodpx: Minimum screen-space size in pixels. Typical values depend on resolution and desired detail, e.g., 1-5 pixels. budget: Maximum number of points to render. Typical values depend on hardware capabilities, e.g., 60,000 points. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Budget Exhaustion: If the budget is reached before the queue is empty, the traversal stops, potentially leaving large background areas unrendered or coarsely rendered. Small Nodes: Nodes smaller than lodpx are never refined, even if they are in the foreground, ensuring a minimum LOD. Frustum Culling: Incorrect frustum culling can lead to rendering off-screen nodes or missing visible nodes. Precision: Screen-space size calculation must be robust to avoid jitter or incorrect ordering due to floating-point errors. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) in the worst case, where N is the number of nodes in the octree, due to priority queue operations. In practice, it is faster as many nodes are culled. Memory Complexity: O(D), where D is the depth of the octree, for the priority queue and recursion stack (if implemented recursively, though this method uses an explicit queue). Performance: On a 2.18 million point room scan, a far camera drew ~60,000 points coarsely, while a near camera drew ~60,000 points densely on foreground surfaces. Strengths: Consistent performance, adaptive LOD, efficient culling. Limitations: Requires a priority queue, which can be expensive on GPU if not implemented carefully. This method was described in an unofficial source discussing point cloud level of detail using octrees. It emphasizes a "best-first" approach driven by screen-space size and budget constraints. name: Topology-Caching for Dynamic Particle Volume Raycasting
head: GPU-based volume raycasting for particle systems, Topology-Cached Raycasting, Topology-Caching
body: Topology-Caching is a GPU-based volume rendering technique for the interactive visualization of dynamic particle systems (e.g., SPH) that reconstructs a scalar field via raycasting without preprocessing. It solves the performance bottleneck of gathering particle contributions for field reconstruction by using three GPU-managed caches: a node-cache for accelerated tree traversal, an influence-cache for fast particle access, and a slab-cache for intermediate compositing. Unlike scattering approaches that cause memory collisions or splatting techniques that require sorting, this method uses a gathering principle with coherent ray packets and stackless traversal to achieve interactive frame rates for hundreds of thousands of particles. The method operates on a data-parallel octree that is rebuilt every frame to organize the dynamic particle set. It processes the image plane using ray packets organized into slabs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Dynamic particle set \{\mathbf{p}i, qi\} where \mathbf{p}i is position and qi is scalar quantity; camera parameters; proxy geometry defining the entry point into the particle volume. Output: Composited image with alpha values. Data Structures: 1. Data-Parallel Octree: Hierarchical structure of nodes. Each node stores pointers to children and neighbors. Supports Level-of-Detail (LOD) where particles are merged into larger particles on coarser levels. 2. Node-Cache: Stores a local subset of octree nodes relevant for the current slab's spatial extent. 3. Influence-Cache: A reference array within each node storing pointers to particles whose support radius h overlaps the node. Particles are redundantly assigned to up to 8 neighboring nodes. 4. Slab-Cache: Stores intermediate reconstruction results (weighted field values) for all rays in a packet across all slices of the current slab. Parameters: Support radius h: Finite support of the kernel function. Ray Packet Size: 4 rays per packet. Slices per Slab: 3. Slab Size: 8 \times 8 pixels. Early Ray Termination Threshold: \alpha = 0.99. Octree Depth: 8. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Construction: Rebuild the data-parallel octree in each frame using level-order traversals to exploit GPU parallelism. 2. LOD Construction: Perform bottom-up construction of a particle LOD hierarchy. Particles are added to the next coarser tree level and merged into larger particles, accumulating quantities. 3. Influence-Cache Creation: Assign each particle (including LOD particles) to a reference array in up to 8 neighboring nodes if the particle's support radius h overlaps the node. 4. Ray Packet Initialization: Subdivide the viewing plane into 8 \times 8 pixel regions. Define ray packet origins. Use a proxy geometry to determine the entry point (smallest distance t{entry}) for the first slab for all rays in the packet. 5. Main Loop (Slab Traversal): 5.1. Node Fetching (Node-Cache Filling): Calculate the mid-point of the current slab to determine the current leaf-node of interest. Determine the respective node for each point of the slab (border points may need neighboring nodes). Restrict slab spatial extent to be smaller than the size of a leaf-node. Load the current leaf-node and all relevant neighboring nodes into the Node-Cache. 5.2. Field Reconstruction (Slab-Cache Population): For each slice in the slab (3 slices): For each ray in the packet: Determine the evaluation point \mathbf{x} along the ray. Identify the node containing \mathbf{x} from the Node-Cache. Access particles contributing to \mathbf{x} via the Influence-Cache of that node. Compute scalar field q(\mathbf{x}) using kernel interpolation: q(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{\sum{\mathbf{p}i \in Ni} qi K(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i\|, h)}{\sum{\mathbf{p}i \in Ni} K(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i\|, h)} where Ni is the set of particles in the node, K is a radial symmetric kernel, and h is the support radius. Store the result in the Slab-Cache. Optimization: If adjacent points along a ray require the same node, the node's particles contribute directly to multiple points, reducing global memory reads. 5.3. Compositing: Composite the slices of the slab in front-to-back order using the values in the Slab-Cache. 5.4. Traversal Decisions: Empty Space Skipping: If the current node is empty, skip the whole ray packet to the next node intersection. Early Ray Termination: Compare individual compositing results among rays in the packet. If all composited values are above \alpha = 0.99, stop packet traversal. Advance: Advance rays to the next slab. Update t{entry} using the proxy geometry for the new slab. 6. Final Composition: Compute the resulting image by compositing the slices of all slabs in front-to-back order. Stackless Traversal Details (for Node Fetching): When traversing to find the required node for a slab's mid-point: 1. If the previously required node is at leaf-level and a valid pointer to the neighboring node exists, load the neighboring node. 2. If the pointer to the neighboring node is invalid (no neighbor at leaf-level), traverse upward following parent links until a valid neighboring node at another tree-level is found. This node is an empty-node, suitable for empty space skipping. 3. If the previous node is at intermediate-level and a valid pointer to the neighboring node exists, traverse following child-pointers until a node at leaf-level is reached. 4. If there is no node at leaf-level available, load the node closest to the leaf-level, which is also suited for empty space skipping. Gradient Computation (Optional for Isosurface): Compute gradients in eye space using the Slab-Cache. Adjust step-size \Delta x of central differences for each slice because adjacent rays are not parallel: \Delta x = \alpha \cdot w \cdot n with the pixel-size w and the distance to the near plane n. Overlapping slabs by border-rays solves discontinuities at slab borders. Pitfalls: Image Quality Approximation: LOD particles cause approximation error, but it is hardly noticeable (<3% difference in white regions vs dark regions). Shared Memory Constraints: The slab size (8 \times 8) and slices (3) are chosen to fit shared memory (16KB on GTX 280). High register count (45) limits occupancy to 31.3% on older GPUs. Time Complexity: Interactive frame rates for up to several 10^5 particles. Memory Complexity: High shared memory usage (~1900 bytes per packet). Node-cache (~300 bytes), Slab-cache (~1536 bytes for weighted results). Performance: GTX 280, 800x600 resolution: T-Sensor (50k particles, 10k nodes): 25ms. Fountain (60k particles, 6k nodes): 21ms. Dam (130k particles, 25k nodes): 45ms. GTX 480 (48KB shared memory): T-Sensor: 132ms. Fountain: 251ms. Dam: 274ms. Scaling: Occupancy improves on GPUs with larger shared memory (e.g., GTX 480 has 48KB vs 16KB on GTX 280), resulting in better performance as noted in the source. Strengths: No preprocessing required; handles dynamic particle sets; fast neighbor access via influence-cache; reduced memory reads via slab-cache; interactive frame rates. Limitations: Approximation error from LOD (though negligible); high register usage limits occupancy on older GPUs; requires rebuilding octree every frame. The method was presented by Jens Orthmann, Maik Keller, and Andreas Kolb from the University of Siegen, Germany. It builds on data-parallel octrees by Zhou et al. [ZGHG10] and stackless traversal techniques by Popov et al. [PGSS07]. It is designed for ad-hoc visualization of SPH fluid simulations directly after each simulation step. Topology-Caching for Dynamic Particle Volume Raycasting, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe/vmv/vmv10/147-154, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Budgeted-GS Factoring LOD
head: Budget-Centered Training (BCT) context, Factored LOD
body: Budgeted-GS Factoring LOD is a hierarchical level-of-detail (LOD) method for real-time large-scale Gaussian Splatting that reduces rendering cost by aggregating primitives into equivalent planks based on a pixel-footprint budget. It solves the problem of rendering millions of Gaussians in real-time by dynamically selecting between raw primitives, fine equivalent planks, or coarse aggregate planks depending on their distance and scale relative to the camera. Unlike standard compression methods that operate in an over-budgeted regime with flat error curves, this method achieves a steeper error reduction (slope approaching -0.5) by using a "floor law" to select the optimal budget, allowing for significant size reduction (119× smaller than input) while maintaining visual fidelity. The method consists of a construction phase that builds a hierarchical octree of equivalent planks and a rendering phase that selects the appropriate LOD tier for each node. Inputs: A set of N trained 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by mean \mui, rotation Ri, scale \sigmai, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic (SH) color coefficients. Camera parameters: position p and focal length f (in pixels). Budget parameter c (scalar). Outputs: An octree structure where each node (leaf or internal) contains a list of equivalent planks, organized by scale bands. Rendered image using the selected tier for each visible primitive/plank. The scene is partitioned using a GPU octree. Leaf Capacity: Each leaf node holds at most 4096 primitives. Primitive Representation (Plank): Each primitive is converted to a "plank" defined by (\mu, R, h=3\sigma, \alpha). Equivalent Plank: An aggregate representation defined by (c^, R^, h^, w^) and SH coefficients. Scale Bands: Within each leaf, planks are grouped into bands \ell based on their maximum height s = \max(h). Bucket: Within a (leaf, band) group, planks are split into consecutive buckets of at most 256 planks. 1. Primitive Conversion: Convert each Gaussian primitive i with scale \sigmai into a plank with height hi = 3\sigmai. The primitive is now represented as (\mui, Ri, hi, \alphai). 2. Octree Construction: Partition the scene bounding box into a GPU octree with a leaf capacity of 4096 primitives. 3. Scale Banding: For each leaf node, determine the base scale s{base} as the 5% quantile of the height s across the entire scene. For each plank in the leaf with maximum height s, compute the scale band index: \ell = \lfloor \log2 (s/s{base}) \rfloor Group planks by their (leaf, band) pair. 4. Factoring (Moment Matching): For each (leaf, band) group: a. Order the planks by Morton code to ensure spatial locality. b. Split the ordered planks into consecutive buckets, each containing at most 256 planks. c. For each bucket, compute the equivalent plank parameters by conserving weighted volume W, centroid c^, and inertia tensor T^. Weighted Volume: W = \sumi \alphai |Vi| where |Vi| is the volume of the i-th plank. Centroid: c^ = \frac{\sumi \alphai |Vi| \mui}{W} Inertia Tensor: T^ = \sumi \alphai |Vi| \left( (\mui - c^)(\mui - c^)^\top + \frac{1}{3} Ri \text{diag}(hi)^2 Ri^\top \right) where Ri is the rotation and hi is the height of the i-th plank. Equivalent Plank Derivation: Perform eigendecomposition on T^ to derive the equivalent plank's rotation R^ and height h^. The weight w^ is calculated as: w^ = W/|V^| \in [0,1] where |V^| is the volume of the equivalent plank. Color Handling: Colors are handled as opacity-weighted first moments of the SH coefficients, computed separately for DC and higher bands. 5. Bottom-Up Aggregation: Apply the same factoring treatment to internal nodes of the octree. Every (node, band) pair owns one equivalent plank. Raw planks are retained in Morton order within leaf nodes for the finest tier. 6. Rendering Tier Selection: At render time, for a camera at position p with focal length f, calculate the threshold t for each (leaf, band) group: t = c \cdot \frac{d}{f} where d is the distance from the camera to the centroid of the group. Determine the tier based on the mean scale \bar{s} and equivalent-plank scale \bar{h}: Raw Tier: If \bar{s} \ge t, members are individually resolvable. Render the original Gaussians. Fine Tier: If \bar{s} < t \le \bar{h}, the cluster is resolvable but members are not. Render the fine equivalent planks. Coarse Tier: If \bar{h} < t, the content is sub-pixel. Render the single aggregate plank of the (leaf, band). Bucket Size: 256 planks per bucket. Budget Parameter c: Controls the aggressiveness of LOD. c=1: Exactly resolvable (reference tier). c>1: Collapses sub-pixel content (scale truncation). c<1: Super-resolving regime (keeps members below pixel scale). Typical value for distant aerial cameras: c \approx 0.3. Precision: The inertia tensor calculation involves summing weighted outer products, which may require double precision for large scenes to avoid numerical instability. Boundary Conditions: The Morton code ordering ensures spatial locality, but extreme anisotropy in primitive scales may lead to inefficient bucketing if the scale banding is not fine-grained enough. Degenerate Input: If a bucket contains fewer than 256 planks, the moment matching still applies to the available planks. Time Complexity: Construction takes seconds on multi-million-primitive scenes on a single GPU. Rendering is real-time, with tier selection being O(1) per node. Memory Complexity: The aggregate representation is 119× smaller than the input. Performance: Achieves a steeper error curve (slope approaching -0.5) compared to published compression methods (slopes [-0.28, +0.09]). Strengths: Real-time performance on large-scale scenes, certified compression headroom, and significant size reduction. Limitations: Requires a construction phase; effectiveness depends on the accuracy of the "floor law" estimation. Budgeted-GS Factoring LOD was introduced in the paper "Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD". It builds on the principles of octree traversal and Gaussian splatting, extending them with a hierarchical factoring mechanism based on moment matching. The method addresses the limitations of existing compression techniques by operating in a budgeted regime that aligns with the perceptual floor of the scene. Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03162, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical Tree Node Traversal
head: VolumeRayIntersector
body: Hierarchical Tree Node Traversal accelerates ray-volume intersection by traversing a sparse octree to identify contiguous segments of active data. It solves the problem of inefficiently sampling empty space by skipping inactive nodes and resolving hits at the node level rather than the individual voxel level. Unlike sibling methods that rasterize shadows or compute precise Hermite data, this approach focuses on robust ray marching against a generic grid, providing entry and exit times for line-integration. The method is implemented via the VolumeRayIntersector class template, which encapsulates the logic for intersecting a ray with a generic volume grid using an internal boolean tree. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A GridT (the volume data), an optional dilationCount (integer, default 0), and an optional explicit bounding box CoordBBox. Output: Boolean flags indicating ray validity, and updated time parameters t0 and t1 representing the entry and exit points of active regions along the index ray. Data Structures: TreeT: A boolean tree derived from the input grid's root type, converted to store bool values. This tree is used to accelerate ray marching and may be dilated based on dilationCount. CoordBBox: The axis-aligned bounding box of the active voxels in index space, cached for efficient ray-box intersection tests. ValueAccessor: An internal accessor for the tree, which is not thread-safe and must be copied per thread. Parameters: NodeLevel (template int, default GridT::TreeType::RootNodeType::ChildNodeType::LEVEL): Specifies the tree node level at which traversal and hit resolution occur. dilationCount (int, default 0): The number of voxel dilations performed on a boolean copy of the input grid to account for interpolation kernel sizes. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the intersector with the grid and optional dilation count or bounding box. The constructor validates that grid voxels are uniform and the grid is not empty, throwing a RuntimeError otherwise. 2. Thread Safety Setup: For multi-threaded execution, create a new instance for each computational thread using the shallow copy constructor. This ensures thread safety by duplicating the non-thread-safe ValueAccessor and cached CoordBBox efficiently. 3. Ray Setup: Call setIndexRay or setWorldRay with the ray to traverse. If the ray misses the grid's bounding box, the method returns false, indicating no further marching is required. 4. Marching Loop: Call march(t0, t1) in a loop. This function performs the hierarchical descent. It returns true if the ray intersects active values (active voxels or tiles). 5. Hit Resolution: Upon a successful march, t0 and t1 are updated with the entry and exit times along the INDEX ray. These times are resolved at the node level (e.g., LeafNode) rather than for individual active voxels. 6. Coordinate Conversion: Convert the index-space hit times to world coordinates using getIndexPos(time), getWorldPos(time), and getWorldTime(time). 7. Hit List Generation: Optionally, call hits(list) to populate a container of RayType::TimeSpan objects with all detected hits along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. throws RuntimeError if not uniform or empty self.grid = grid self.dilationcount = dilationcount self.bbox = bbox if bbox else self.computeactivebbox(grid) self.tree = self.buildbooltree(grid, dilationcount) self.accessor = self.createaccessor(self.tree) self.indexray = None def computeactivebbox(self, grid): return CoordBBox(grid.minindex, grid.maxindex) def buildbooltree(self, grid, dilationcount): # Creates boolean tree from grid, dilated by dilationcount # Not given in the sources. return [] def createaccessor(self, tree): return {} def setindexray(self, ray): self.indexray = ray return rayintersectsbbox(ray, self.bbox) def march(self, t0, t1): # Performs hierarchical descent through the boolean tree # Updates t0 and t1 with entry/exit times along the INDEX ray # Returns True if ray intersects active values (tiles or leaves) # Not given in the sources. return False def getindexpos(self, time): return [self.indexray.origin[i] + time self.indexray.direction[i] for i in range(3)] def getworldpos(self, time): # Converts index-space time to world position using grid transform # Not given in the sources. return self.getindexpos(time) def getworldtime(self, time): # Converts index-space time to world-space time # Not given in the sources. return time def hits(self, listout): # Populates list with RayType::TimeSpan objects # Not given in the sources. pass intersector = VolumeRayIntersector(grid, dilationcount=0) threadintersector = VolumeRayIntersector(intersector) ray = Ray(origin=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], direction=[1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) if not threadintersector.setindexray(ray): pass t0 = 0.0 t1 = 0.0 while threadintersector.march(t0, t1): worldposstart = threadintersector.getworldpos(t0) worldposend = threadintersector.getworldpos(t1) # Perform line-integration between t0 and t1 hitslist = [] threadintersector.hits(hitslist) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thread Safety: The class is not thread-safe due to its internal ValueAccessor and cached CoordBBox. Using a single instance across threads causes race conditions. Always use the copy constructor for each thread. Coordinate Space: t0 and t1 are computed in index space, not world space. Client code must use getIndexPos or maintain an index ray instance for coordinate conversion. Uniform Voxels: Constructors throw a RuntimeError if the grid voxels are not uniform or the grid is empty. Node-Level Resolution: Hits are resolved at the node level (e.g., LeafNode), not individual active voxels. This means t0 and t1 represent the bounds of a node, not necessarily the exact bounds of every active voxel within it. Time Complexity: Depends on the depth of the octree and the sparsity of the volume. Hierarchical traversal skips empty space, reducing the number of samples compared to fixed-step DDA. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the boolean tree (TreeT) and the bounding box cache. The shallow copy constructor ensures that per-thread memory overhead is limited to the accessor and bbox structures. Strengths: Thread-safe design via copying; handles generic grids; accounts for interpolation kernel sizes via dilation; robust bounding box checks. Limitations: Not thread-safe without copying; requires uniform voxels; hit resolution is at the node level, which may be coarser than voxel-level precision. When to Use: When rendering large, sparse volumetric datasets on multi-threaded CPU or GPU systems where thread safety and efficient empty space skipping are critical. When Not to Use: When the grid has non-uniform voxels, as the constructor throws a RuntimeError. It provides a standardized API for ray-volume intersection within the OpenVDB ecosystem, leveraging the library's sparse data structures for performance. name: Frustum and Visibility Culling
head: Frustum Culling, Visibility Culling, Frustum-Occlusion Culling
body: Frustum and Visibility Culling methods optimize volume rendering by identifying and discarding geometry that does not contribute to the final image, thereby reducing computational load. This family distinguishes itself from sibling traversal methods by decoupling visibility determination from the core sampling loop, often serving as a pre-pass or integrated filter to limit the working set of voxels, splats, or bricks. Unlike Octree and Tree Traversal which focuses on hierarchical descent, these methods focus on spatial containment relative to the camera. This method renders hierarchical shell and solid volumetric structures by traversing a bounding-sphere tree and adaptively controlling the frame rate through dynamic adjustment of minimum splat sizes. It distinguishes itself from standard octree traversal by replacing fixed-resolution voxel sampling with screen-space splat rendering, where the granularity of the visual output is directly tied to performance feedback. Unlike sibling methods that rely on geometric bounding boxes for culling, this approach uses bounding spheres and hierarchical normal cones to optimize visibility tests for point-based primitives. Choose when adaptive performance control for point-based primitives is needed. See Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control. Frustum Culling Integration is a visibility optimization technique applied during the progressive loading and rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. It filters out splats that lie outside the user's current viewing frustum to prioritize the transmission and rendering of visible geometry. It differs from its sibling Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control by focusing on spatial visibility rather than frame-rate stability, and from Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal by typically operating on a pre-ordered list of splats rather than a hierarchical tree structure during the culling phase. Choose for optimizing transmission and rendering of visible Gaussian splats. See Frustum Culling Integration. This method identifies a set of visible voxels by traversing an octree hierarchy and culling nodes that do not intersect the camera's view frustum or whose projected screen area is smaller than a single pixel. It serves as a visibility pre-pass for voxel rasterization, automatically determining the Level of Detail (LOD) for rendering. Unlike standard ray-marching which samples volume density, this approach outputs a list of 3D bounding boxes (voxels) to be rasterized as geometry using hardware instancing. It is distinct from Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control by using explicit frustum intersection tests rather than frame-rate driven depth limits, and from Frustum Culling Integration by specifically targeting octree structures for voxel-based rendering pipelines. Choose when targeting octree structures for voxel-based rendering pipelines. See Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal. Frustum culling for octree nodes is a hierarchical visibility test that discards entire octree subtrees if their axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) lies completely outside the view frustum. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which parts of a sparse volumetric or point-cloud structure are visible, avoiding per-element processing for millions of points with a single bounding box test. Unlike sibling methods that may integrate occlusion or frame-rate control, this method focuses purely on geometric containment within the six clipping planes, serving as the primary "existence" decision before traversal begins. Choose as a primary existence decision before traversal begins. See Frustum Culling for Octree Nodes. Visibility is determined during ray traversal, providing implicit view frustum culling without extra steps. The method provides implicit occlusion culling without extra steps or occlusion buffers. Rays determine the working set directly by writing out a list of bricks they require (intersect) in front-to-back order. It uses modern OpenGL extensions such as GLARBshaderstoragebufferobject. Introduced by Crassin et al. in 2009. The concept of culling visible geometry is fundamental to computer graphics. In the context of volume rendering, early approaches relied on explicit pre-passes to determine the "working set" of bricks or voxels. As hardware capabilities evolved, particularly with the advent of shader storage buffer objects, methods like Ray-Guided Volume Rendering integrated culling directly into the rendering pipeline. The specific techniques described in the subtopics represent specialized applications of these principles to different data structures (octrees, splats, bounding-sphere trees) and rendering paradigms (rasterization, ray-casting). name: Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control
head: Adaptive Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control, Visibility Culling Tests
body: This method renders hierarchical shell and solid volumetric structures by traversing a bounding-sphere tree and adaptively controlling the frame rate through dynamic adjustment of minimum splat sizes. It distinguishes itself from standard octree traversal by replacing fixed-resolution voxel sampling with screen-space splat rendering, where the granularity of the visual output is directly tied to performance feedback. Unlike sibling methods such as Frustum Culling Integration, Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal, and Frustum Culling for Octree Nodes that rely on geometric bounding boxes for culling, this approach uses bounding spheres and hierarchical normal cones to optimize visibility tests for point-based primitives. The algorithm traverses a hierarchical tree (Shell or Solid) using a recursive descent. It combines visibility culling tests with a feedback loop that adjusts rendering parameters to maintain a target frame rate. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Root node of the bounding-sphere tree; current camera parameters (view frustum); current frame rate measurement. Output: Rendered image composed of splats. Global Parameters: \deltar (minimum regular splat size in pixels), \deltab (minimum boundary splat size in pixels). Data Structures: The tree nodes store bounding sphere attributes. These attributes are compressed and decompressed on-the-fly using table lookups during traversal to save memory and bandwidth. Shell Nodes: Store hierarchical normal vectors and bounding normal cones. Solid Nodes: Do not store normal information during traversal; normals are derived from a CSG probe at render time. Numbered Steps: 1. Frame-Rate Feedback: Measure the current frame rate. If it is too low, smoothly increase \deltar and \deltab. If the frame rate is too high (after a completed traversal), allow \deltar and \deltab to decrease. In the original implementation, these parameters are only allowed to decrease after a fully completed tree traversal has led to too high frame rates. 2. Traverse Tree: Call TraverseTree on the root node. 3. Culling Tests: For each child of the current node, perform the following tests in order. If a test fails, the child and its subtree are ignored. View-Frustum Culling: If the bounding sphere is completely outside the viewing frustum, ignore the node and all children. If the bounding sphere intersects any plane of the view frustum, traverse to the children. If the bounding sphere is completely inside the view frustum, disable this culling test for all children. Back-Face Culling (Shell): Use the hierarchically encoded normal vectors and bounding normal cones to eliminate branches where all nodes point entirely away from the camera. Back-Face Culling (Solid): Hierarchical culling is not performed during traversal because normals depend on the CSG probe. Instead, back-face culling is performed before rendering individual Solid splats using normals derived from the CSG probe. Occlusion Culling: Hierarchical occlusion culling is considered too hard for point-based primitives. Instead, enable the z-buffer algorithm in the graphics hardware for occlusion culling. 4. Splat Sizing: Calculate the screen size S of the child's bounding sphere in pixels. 5. Leaf/Node Handling: If the child is a leaf node, render it as a splat of size S pixels. If the child is a regular node and S < \deltar, render it as a splat of size \deltar pixels. If the child is a boundary node and S < \deltab, render it as a splat of size \deltab pixels. Otherwise, recursively call TraverseTree(child). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. deltar = 1.0 # Minimum regular splat size in pixels deltab = 1.0 # Minimum boundary splat size in pixels traversalcompleted = True # Flag to permit delta decrease def updateframeratecontrol(currentframerate, targetframerate): """Adjusts deltar and deltab based on frame rate feedback.""" nonlocal deltar, deltab, traversalcompleted if currentframerate < targetframerate: deltar = 1.1 # Increase smoothly deltab = 1.1 elif currentframerate > targetframerate and traversalcompleted: # Only allow decrease after a fully completed traversal deltar = max(1.0, deltar 0.9) deltab = max(1.0, deltab 0.9) traversalcompleted = True def traversetree(node): """Recursively traverses the bounding-sphere tree.""" nonlocal traversalcompleted traversalcompleted = False # Decompress attributes on-the-fly using table lookups # Fast on-the-fly table lookup implementation for child in node.children: # 1. View-Frustum Culling # Standard sphere vs 6-plane frustum test frustumstatus = "OUTSIDE" if sphereoutsidefrustum(child.boundingsphere) else ("INSIDE" if sphereinsidefrustum(child.boundingsphere) else "INTERSECTS") if frustumstatus == "OUTSIDE": continue # Ignore node and children elif frustumstatus == "INTERSECTS": pass # Traverse to children, keep culling active elif frustumstatus == "INSIDE": pass # Disable frustum culling for children # 2. Back-Face Culling (Shell specific) if node.type == "SHELL": # Uses hierarchical normal vectors and bounding normal cones if dot(child.normalcone.axis, cameraposition - child.normalcone.center) < -child.normalcone.radius: continue # Eliminate branch # 3. Calculate screen size # Projects bounding sphere radius to screen space S = 2.0 child.boundingsphere.radius camera.focallength / distance(camera.position, child.boundingsphere.center) # 4. Leaf or Node Handling if child.isleaf: # Rasterizes a point/splat at center with screen size drawpoint(child.center, S) elif child.type == "REGULAR" and S < deltar: drawpoint(child.center, deltar) elif child.type == "BOUNDARY" and S < deltab: drawpoint(child.center, deltab) else: traversetree(child) traversalcompleted = True def drawpoint(center, size): # Rasterizes a point/splat at center with screen size pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter Adjustment: \deltar and \deltab are only allowed to decrease after a fully completed tree traversal has led to too high frame rates. This prevents oscillation during partial traversals. Solid Node Normals: Solid nodes lack hierarchical normal information. Back-face culling must be deferred to the splat rendering stage using the CSG probe, which adds overhead compared to Shell nodes. Occlusion: Hierarchical occlusion culling is not implemented due to the point-based nature of the primitives. Relying on the hardware z-buffer is the only option, which may be less efficient for highly overlapping structures. Time Complexity: Depends on the tree depth and the selectivity of the culling tests. The adaptive frame-rate control ensures that the number of rendered splats is bounded by the performance target, effectively capping the rendering cost. Memory: The tree is stored breath-first, allowing progressive loading of only the parts of the data structure actually rendered during traversal. Attributes are compressed and decompressed on-the-fly. Strengths: Real-time performance is guaranteed through adaptive refinement. The use of bounding spheres and normal cones allows for efficient visibility culling. Limitations: Occlusion culling is limited to hardware z-buffering. Solid nodes require additional computation for normal derivation. The method was introduced by Museth and Lombeyna in 2004 as part of the TetSplat system for real-time rendering and volume clipping of large volumetric datasets. It was designed to handle both shell (surface) and solid (volume) representations efficiently by leveraging hierarchical tree structures and adaptive rendering techniques. name: Frustum Culling Integration
head: Base+Frustum culling
body: Frustum Culling Integration is a visibility optimization technique applied during the progressive loading and rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. It filters out splats that lie outside the user's current viewing frustum to prioritize the transmission and rendering of visible geometry. It differs from its sibling Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control by focusing on spatial visibility rather than frame-rate stability, and from Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal by operating on a pre-ordered list of splats rather than a hierarchical tree structure during the culling phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of 3D Gaussians (splats) with their mean positions, the current camera view and projection matrices, and a frustum margin parameter. Output: A filtered subset of splats that are considered visible (inside the frustum). Data Structures: Splat List: An array of Gaussian objects containing mean positions and screen-space projections. Steps: 1. Global Ordering (Pre-requisite): Frustum culling is applied after a global ordering of splats has been determined. This means the culling step filters the list rather than re-ordering it. 2. Frustum Margin Application: Define the viewing frustum boundaries (left, right, bottom, top, near, far) and increase them by 30%. 3. Projection and Filtering: Project all splats onto the image plane. Filter the splats that fall outside the expanded frustum boundaries. 4. Selection: Retain only those splats where the projected center lies within the expanded frustum. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def frustumcullsplats(splats, viewmatrix, projmatrix, marginfactor=0.3): """ Filters a list of splats based on the viewing frustum with a margin. Args: splats: List of Gaussian objects with 'mean' (vec3). viewmatrix: 4x4 view matrix. projmatrix: 4x4 projection matrix. marginfactor: Percentage to expand frustum boundaries (e.g., 0.3 for 30%). Returns: List of splats inside the expanded frustum. """ visiblesplats = [] vpmatrix = projmatrix @ viewmatrix margin = marginfactor # Standard NDC frustum bounds are [-1, 1] for x and y. # Increasing boundaries by marginfactor expands the visible region. xmin = -1.0 (1.0 + margin) xmax = 1.0 (1.0 + margin) ymin = -1.0 (1.0 + margin) ymax = 1.0 (1.0 + margin) for gaussian in splats: # Standard perspective projection and NDC conversion poshomogeneous = vec4(gaussian.mean, 1.0) clippos = vpmatrix @ poshomogeneous if clippos.w <= 0.0: continue ndcx = clippos.x / clippos.w ndcy = clippos.y / clippos.w if xmin <= ndcx <= xmax and ymin <= ndcy <= ymax: visiblesplats.append(gaussian) return visiblesplats Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion Ignorance: Frustum culling occurs after global ordering and does not account for occlusions from the current viewpoint. Small Background Splats: If more than 10% of splats are visible within the frustum, small background splats may still not be selected for high-quality loading because the culling happens after the initial priority list is formed. Gaussian Extent: Since Gaussians cover areas rather than points on the image plane, a Gaussian with a mean outside the frustum might still contribute to the image. The margin mitigates this by counting Gaussians inside the expanded frustum. A technique to fine-tune the ordering of splats based on the user's initial pose, selecting a percentage of splats from within the viewing frustum to allow for rapid movement while focusing on visible content. It involves projecting all splats onto the image plane and filtering those outside the frustum. A typical parameter is the frustum margin, set to 30% to increase frustum boundaries. This variant is chosen when user-specific view information is available to improve perceived quality during camera movement. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The complete approach (octree + frustum culling) performs better when user-specific view information is available. However, if more than 10% of splats are visible, the benefit is reduced for background details. Strengths: Reduces the number of splats processed by excluding clearly invisible geometry. Limitations: Does not handle occlusion; relies on pre-computed ordering; margin parameter requires tuning. When to use: When user view direction is known and the scene has significant geometry outside the current view. When not to use: When occlusion is the primary bottleneck or when the view is fully contained within the scene (high visibility percentage). The method originates from the PRoGS (Progressive Rendering of Gaussian Splats) paper. It was developed to address the bandwidth and rendering costs of progressive 3D Gaussian Splatting by leveraging user view information to prioritize visible splats. The approach builds on the base progressive rendering method by adding a visibility filter. name: Frustum-Occlusion Culling for Octree Traversal
head: Frustum-octant traversal, Voxel LOD selection, Voxel LOD selection via Frustum Culling, Voxel Rasterization via Frustum Culling and Instancing
body: This method identifies a set of visible voxels by traversing an octree hierarchy and culling nodes that do not intersect the camera's view frustum or whose projected screen area is smaller than a single pixel. It serves as a visibility pre-pass for voxel rasterization, automatically determining the Level of Detail (LOD) for rendering. Unlike standard ray-marching which samples volume density, this approach outputs a list of 3D bounding boxes to be rasterized as geometry using hardware instancing. Inputs: Camera view frustum, octree hierarchy with axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs), global AABB, screen resolution (W, H). Outputs: Buffer of visible voxels, each containing position and size. Data Structures: Octree node with AABB and 8-bit occupancy mask. Voxel buffer storing {position: vec3, size: float}. Algorithm: 1. Frustum Intersection Test: Approximate octant-AABB intersection as a frustum-sphere intersection for efficiency. The sphere diameter equals the octant's AABB diagonal. If the sphere does not intersect the frustum, cull the branch. 2. Projected Area Test (LOD Selection): Calculate the octant's projected area on the screen. If the area is less than one pixel, halt traversal for this branch. 3. Termination: Halt traversal if the node has no further subdivisions (leaf). 4. Buffer Population: When halted (LOD cutoff, leaf, or frustum exit), append the voxel's position and size to the buffer. These attributes are derived implicitly from the node's AABB within the global coordinate space. 5. Rasterization: After traversal, pass the buffer to a hardware instancing pipeline to rasterize the voxels. Formulas: Sphere center: \mathbf{c} = \frac{\mathbf{aabb}{min} + \mathbf{aabb}{max}}{2} Sphere radius: r = \frac{\|\mathbf{aabb}{max} - \mathbf{aabb}{min}\|}{2} LOD condition: A{screen} < 1.0 pixel Parameters: Canonical voxel template: cube with c{min} = (-1, -1, -1) and c{max} = (+1, +1, +1). LOD threshold: projected area < 1 pixel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numeric precision degrades at extreme subdivision depths. Over-subdivision wastes memory when LOD would naturally halt at coarser levels. Sphere approximation may cause false positives (culling fewer nodes than strict AABB test) but never false negatives. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traverseoctree(node, frustum, screenwidth, screenheight, voxelbuffer): # 1. Frustum Culling via Sphere Approximation center = (node.aabb.min + node.aabb.max) / 2.0 radius = length(node.aabb.max - node.aabb.min) / 2.0 if not frustum.intersectssphere(center, radius): return # 2. Projected Area / LOD Check projectedarea = calculateprojectedarea(node.aabb, frustum.viewmatrix, frustum.projmatrix, screenwidth, screenheight) if projectedarea < 1.0 or node.isleaf(): voxelbuffer.append({'position': center, 'size': length(node.aabb.max - node.aabb.min)}) return # 3. Recurse into children for child in node.children: if child is not None: traverseoctree(child, frustum, screenwidth, screenheight, voxelbuffer) def calculateprojectedarea(aabb, viewmatrix, projmatrix, w, h): # Transform 8 AABB corners to clip space corners = [] for x in [aabb.min.x, aabb.max.x]: for y in [aabb.min.y, aabb.max.y]: for z in [aabb.min.z, aabb.max.z]: corners.append(vec4(x, y, z, 1.0)) clipcorners = [projmatrix (viewmatrix c) for c in corners] # Convert to NDC [-1, 1] and find screen-space bounding box ndcx = [(c.x / c.w) for c in clipcorners] ndcy = [(c.y / c.w) for c in clipcorners] minx, maxx = min(ndcx), max(ndcx) miny, maxy = min(ndcy), max(ndcy) # Map NDC to screen pixels screenw = max(0.0, (maxx - minx) 0.5 w) screenh = max(0.0, (maxy - miny) 0.5 h) return screenw screenh Time Complexity: Worst-case O(N) for a full octree. Average case visits only visible and LOD-relevant nodes. Memory Complexity: Octree stored breadth-first with 1 byte per node mask. Buffer size scales with visible voxel count. Performance: Profiled at 1920x1280 resolution with 25%–85% pixel coverage on Intel Core i5-2540M / NVIDIA Quadro 3000M / Windows 7 / OpenGL 4.2. Voxel rasterization times (ms) for 'basketball' dataset at depth 10: Geometry Shader 3.454, Uniform Buffer 2.549, Hardware Texture Buffer 2.773, Instancing Vertex Buffer 5.599. Strengths and Limitations: Automatic LOD selection and efficient frustum culling. Geometry Shader is slowest for voxels due to hardware optimization for quads; Uniform Buffer is fastest. Described in the context of hardware-accelerated geometry instancing for surfel and voxel rendering of scanned 4D media. Highlights trade-offs between GPU instancing techniques for voxel data. name: Frustum Culling for Octree Nodes
head: AABB-in-frustum test, Positive-vertex test
body: Frustum culling for octree nodes is a hierarchical visibility test that discards entire octree subtrees if their axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) lies completely outside the view frustum. It solves the problem of efficiently determining which parts of a sparse volumetric or point-cloud structure are visible, avoiding per-element processing for millions of points with a single bounding box test. Unlike sibling methods that may integrate occlusion or frame-rate control, this method focuses purely on geometric containment within the six clipping planes, serving as the primary "existence" decision before traversal begins. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An octree node defined by its axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) and the view frustum defined by six planes. Output: A boolean value indicating whether the node's bounding box intersects the frustum (True) or is completely outside (False). Data Structures: Node: Represented by two 3D vectors: bmin (minimum corner) and bmax (maximum corner). Planes: A list of six plane definitions. Each plane is defined by the equation ax + by + cz + d = 0, where (a, b, c) is the normal vector and d is the distance from the origin. Algorithm Steps: 1. For each of the six frustum planes, identify the corner of the node's bounding box that is farthest along the plane's normal vector. This corner represents the "best case" for visibility against that specific plane. 2. The coordinates of this farthest corner (px, py, pz) are selected as follows: px = \text{bmax}[0] if a \ge 0, else \text{bmin}[0] py = \text{bmax}[1] if b \ge 0, else \text{bmin}[1] pz = \text{bmax}[2] if c \ge 0, else \text{bmin}[2] 3. Evaluate the plane equation for this corner: val = a \cdot px + b \cdot py + c \cdot pz + d. 4. If val < 0 for any of the six planes, the entire bounding box is outside the frustum relative to that plane. Return False (cull the node). 5. If the condition is not met for all six planes, the bounding box intersects the frustum. Return True. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def aabbinfrustum(node, planes): """ True if the node's box is at least partly inside the frustum (positive-vertex test). Args: node: Dictionary or object with 'min' and 'max' fields, each a 3D vector (bmin, bmax). planes: List of six tuples (a, b, c, d) representing plane equations ax + by + cz + d = 0. Returns: bool: True if the node intersects the frustum, False otherwise. """ bmin = node["min"] bmax = node["max"] for a, b, c, d in planes: # Select the corner farthest along the plane's normal px = bmax[0] if a >= 0 else bmin[0] py = bmax[1] if b >= 0 else bmin[1] pz = bmax[2] if c >= 0 else bmin[2] # Test if this best-case corner is outside the plane if a px + b py + c pz + d < 0: return False return True Parameters: Planes: The six coefficients (a, b, c, d) for the view frustum planes. Node Bounds: bmin and bmax define the spatial extent of the octree node. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Conservatism: The test is conservative; it never hides a point that should be shown. This ensures correctness but may result in keeping some nodes that are mostly outside the frustum but have at least one corner inside. Precision: Standard floating-point arithmetic is sufficient, but care should be taken with near-zero plane distances or degenerate boxes. Time Complexity: O(1) per node, specifically costing six comparisons (one per frustum plane) to decide the existence of the entire subtree. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, requiring only local variables for the corner selection and plane evaluation. Strengths: Extremely fast hierarchical culling; discards millions of points with a single box test; simple implementation. Limitations: Conservative nature may lead to over-culling (keeping nodes that are mostly outside); does not account for occlusion by other geometry. When to Use: As a first-pass visibility filter for sparse volumes or point clouds where hierarchical structure is available. When Not to Use: When occlusion by other geometry is significant (use Frustum-Occlusion Culling) or when frame-rate control is the primary concern (use Bounding-Sphere Tree Traversal with Frame-Rate Control). Frustum culling for octree nodes originates from the need to efficiently render large-scale point clouds and sparse volumes. The technique leverages the hierarchical nature of octrees to perform coarse-grained visibility tests. It is a fundamental component in point cloud level-of-detail systems and out-core rendering pipelines. The method is often referred to as the "positive-vertex test" because it tests the most positive vertex relative to each plane normal. name: Octree Sampled SDF Dataset
body: A dataset class that generates signed-distance function (SDF) samples from a sparse octree acceleration structure constructed from a single mesh shape. It limits sampling to occupied octree cells, supports equal distribution of samples per cell, and allows online resampling via a cached narrowband pool. It optionally includes RGB data derived from mesh textures. Inputs: occupancystruct (OctreeAS): An octree acceleration structure initialized from a mesh. samplemode (List[str]): Sampling scheme supporting 'tracer' (on surface), 'near' (near surface), and 'rand' (uniform in occupied grid cells). Default: ['rand', 'rand', 'near', 'near', 'trace']. numsamples (int): Number of data points kept in the working set at any given time. Default: 100,000. samplespervoxel (int): Number of samples to generate per octree grid cell to create a preliminary equally distributed pool. Default: 32. sampletex (bool): Whether to include RGB from mesh textures. Outputs: A dataset of points with associated SDF values and optionally RGB, formatted for neural field training. Data Structures: blas: The OctreeAS object containing points (coordinates), pyramid (hierarchy), and extent (metadata). datapool: A cached pool of narrowband values used for online resampling. data: The current working set of samples. Steps: 1. Extract Geometry and Level: Retrieve vertices, faces, and the maximum octree level from the acceleration structure. \text{vertices} = \text{blas.extent['vertices']}, \quad \text{faces} = \text{blas.extent['faces']}, \quad \text{level} = \text{blas.max\level} 2. Compute Voxel Corners: Determine the corner coordinates for the target octree level. \text{corners} = \text{spc\ops.unbatched\get\level\points}(\text{blas.points}, \text{blas.pyramid}, \text{level}) 3. Generate Initial Points: Based on samplemode, generate point sets. For 'near' modes: Sample points near the surface with variance inversely proportional to the level. \text{variance} = \frac{1}{2^{\text{level}}} For 'trace' modes: Sample points directly on the surface. For 'rand' modes: Sample uniformly in occupied cells. 4. Filter by Narrowband: Concatenate all generated points and query the acceleration structure to keep only those within the narrowband (occupied cells). \text{query\results} = \text{blas.query}(\text{pts}, 0) \text{pts} = \text{pts}[\text{query\results.pidx} > -1] 5. Compute SDF and RGB: If sampletex is True, compute RGB using texture mapping. Otherwise, compute SDF distances. 6. Resample (Online): During training, resample the working set from the cached datapool to maintain diversity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def getlevelcorners(points, pyramid, level): """Extract grid coordinates for a specific octree level.""" # Standard implementation: index points using the pyramid hierarchy for the target level return points[pyramid[level]] def samplenearsurface(vertices, faces, numpts, variance): """Generate points near the surface with specified variance.""" # Standard implementation: sample random barycentric coordinates on triangles, # then add Gaussian noise scaled by sqrt(variance) triidx = torch.randint(0, len(faces), (numpts,)) bary = torch.rand(numpts, 3) bary /= bary.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) surfacepts = (bary[:, None,:] vertices[faces[triidx]]).sum(dim=1) noise = torch.randnlike(surfacepts) torch.sqrt(torch.tensor(variance)) return surfacepts + noise def samplesurface(vertices, faces, numpts): """Generate points directly on the surface.""" # Standard implementation: sample random barycentric coordinates on triangles triidx = torch.randint(0, len(faces), (numpts,)) bary = torch.rand(numpts, 3) bary /= bary.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) return (bary[:, None,:] vertices[faces[triidx]]).sum(dim=1) def computesdf(vertices, faces, pts): """Compute signed distance from points to mesh.""" # Standard implementation: find closest point on mesh triangles # For brevity, returns Euclidean distance to nearest vertex as a proxy dists = torch.cdist(pts, vertices) return dists.min(dim=1).values def sampletexture(vertices, faces, texv, texf, mats, pts): """Compute RGB from mesh textures.""" # Standard implementation: project points to mesh, interpolate texture coordinates # Returns dummy RGB for self-containment rgb = torch.zeroslike(pts) hitpts = pts d = torch.zeros(len(pts)) return rgb, hitpts, d def initoctreesdfdataset(occupancystruct, samplemode=['rand', 'rand', 'near', 'near', 'trace'], numsamples=100000, samplespervoxel=32, sampletex=True): """Initialize the Octree Sampled SDF Dataset.""" # 1. Extract mesh geometry and octree level vertices = occupancystruct.extent['vertices'] faces = occupancystruct.extent['faces'] level = occupancystruct.maxlevel # 2. Compute voxel corners for the target level corners = getlevelcorners(occupancystruct.points, occupancystruct.pyramid, level) # 3. Generate points based on samplemode allpts = [] numptspermode = numsamples // len(samplemode) for mode in samplemode: if mode == 'near': variance = 1.0 / (2 level) pts = samplenearsurface(vertices, faces, numptspermode, variance) allpts.append(pts) elif mode == 'trace': pts = samplesurface(vertices, faces, numptspermode) allpts.append(pts) elif mode == 'rand': # Uniform sampling in occupied grid cells # Standard implementation: generate random points within bounding boxes of active octree cells pts = torch.rand(numptspermode, 3) (occupancystruct.bounds.max - occupancystruct.bounds.min) + occupancystruct.bounds.min allpts.append(pts) else: raise Exception(f"Sampling mode {mode} not implemented") # Concatenate all generated points pts = torch.cat(allpts, dim=0) # 4. Filter out points outside the narrowband queryresults = occupancystruct.query(pts, 0) validmask = queryresults.pidx > -1 pts = pts[validmask] # 5. Compute distances and optionally RGB if sampletex: rgb, hitpts, d = sampletexture(vertices, faces, occupancystruct.texv, occupancystruct.texf, occupancystruct.mats, pts) else: d = computesdf(vertices, faces, pts) rgb = None # 6. Initialize the working set and pool datapool = { 'pts': pts.clone().detach(), 'sdf': d.clone().detach(), 'rgb': rgb.clone().detach() if rgb is not None else None } poolsize = datapool['pts'].shape[0] if poolsize > numsamples: idx = torch.randperm(poolsize, device='cuda')[:numsamples] data = {k: v[idx.to(v.device)] for k, v in datapool.items() if v is not None} else: data = datapool return { 'data': data, 'datapool': datapool, 'numsamples': numsamples } def resampleworkingset(datasetobj): """Resample the working set from the cached pool.""" datapool = datasetobj['datapool'] numsamples = datasetobj['numsamples'] poolsize = datapool['pts'].shape[0] # Fixed off-by-one: use poolsize instead of poolsize - 1 idx = torch.randperm(poolsize, device='cuda') # Truncate to numsamples if needed if numsamples < poolsize: idx = idx[:numsamples] # Resample newdata = {k: v[idx.to(v.device)] for k, v in datapool.items() if v is not None} datasetobj['data'] = newdata return datasetobj Parameters: occupancystruct: Must be an OctreeAS initialized from a mesh. If not, supportsblas returns False and validate raises RuntimeError. samplemode: List of strings. Unrecognized strings raise Exception(f"Sampling mode {mode} not implemented"). Pitfalls: The acceleration structure must be an OctreeAS initialized from a mesh. Unrecognized samplemode strings raise an exception. Precision and boundary conditions depend on the narrowband query threshold and variance scaling. Memory: The preliminary pool size scales with samplespervoxel per occupied cell, while the active working set is strictly capped at numsamples. Performance: Sampling is executed on mesh faces and limited to occupied octree cells, making it efficient for sparse representations. Strengths: Supports online resampling via a cached narrowband pool to maintain training diversity. Limitations: Limited to single mesh shapes. This method is part of the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp library, specifically designed for neural field training with sparse octree representations. name: Selective and Budgeted Rendering
head: Compositing Tree Rendering, Octree-based Entropy Rendering
body: Selective and Budgeted Rendering accelerates volume rendering by leveraging hierarchical data structures to avoid redundant computation, either by reusing unchanged partial images over time or by skipping low-complexity regions based on error metrics. It differs from standard hierarchical traversal by introducing temporal persistence (compositing trees) or statistical bounds (entropy) to control rendering budget, whereas siblings like DDA Tree Traversal with Mini-Stack focus on spatial traversal efficiency without temporal or statistical pruning. This family shares the parent's core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent. All methods utilize an octree structure where nodes represent spatial subdivisions. The traversal logic relies on the parent's child selection, empty space skipping, leaf handling, and backtracking mechanisms. Specific to this family, nodes may store auxiliary data (partial images or entropy metrics) that influence the traversal path or the final pixel value computation. A time-varying volume rendering strategy that avoids re-rendering unmodified data by retaining partial images of static subtrees and incrementally compositing them with newly rendered partial images from modified regions. It differs from standard incremental rendering by maintaining a persistent pointer-based octree structure (the compositing tree) that mirrors the data compression structure, allowing for efficient splicing of new branches and recomposition of ancestors, whereas methods like Octree-based Entropy Rendering focus on spatial resolution adaptation rather than temporal delta-compositing. Octree-based Entropy Rendering accelerates volume rendering by traversing a hierarchical octree decomposition where non-leaf nodes store entropy metrics or error measures. It solves the problem of redundant computation in low-entropy occupied space by allowing rays to skip or coarsely sample regions based on these metrics. Unlike sibling methods like Compositing Tree Rendering which may focus on specific compositing structures, this method explicitly uses statistical variance or error bounds to control traversal depth. A rendering strategy that uses the tree representation to perform selective rendering efficiently, reducing I/O costs and enabling distribution of data and calculations to multiple workstations. Examine the encoded data to identify partial images built from subtrees which have not changed. Reuse the identified unchanged partial images in the following time steps. Selective and Budgeted Rendering originated in the context of time-varying volume data visualization, where inter-frame delay and storage space were significant bottlenecks. The approach was developed to leverage hierarchical data structures for both compression and rendering acceleration. Preliminary tests showed reductions of up to 90% in storage space and inter-frame delay. The method is particularly relevant for scientific visualization of dynamic datasets where significant portions of the volume remain constant between time steps.
