The pyramid has levels m = 0, \dots, M. Cell Size: The size of cells on level m is 2^m times the spacing between voxels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coordinate Alignment: Voxel (1,1,1) is placed at the front-lower-right corner of cell (1,1,1) on level 0. Cell (1,1,1) on level 0 encloses the space between voxels (1,1,1) and (2,2,2). Care must be taken to align ray coordinates with this cell-based indexing. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when computing ray-cell intersections, especially at higher levels where cell sizes are large. Boundary Conditions: Rays entering or exiting the volume must be handled correctly, especially when moving up the pyramid levels. Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination is a ray tracing algorithm that uses a pyramidal data structure of binary volumes to skip empty regions and an adaptive termination criterion to stop tracing when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. Unlike geometric ray tracing, which uses bounding volumes or spatial subdivision with lists of primitives, this method uses a hierarchical binary volume structure, which is more efficient for volume data because volume datasets have tens of millions of spatially ordered cells with single samples, whereas geometric scenes have hundreds of cells with many primitives. An optimization that uses a binary octree to avoid unnecessary resampling of voxels in transparent regions of the volume. A hierarchical spatial data structure (quadtree recursively subdivided down to pixel size) where empty space uniformity information is stored in the empty voxels of the 3D volume grid. The structure is a quadtree recursively subdivided down until pixel size. Gray squares denote voxels with volume data; white squares denote empty voxels storing the octree level. Time Complexity: The cost of ray tracing volumetric data using a hierarchical enumeration grows linearly with the size of the image, logarithmically with the length of each ray, and linearly with the depth complexity of the data. Memory Complexity: The pyramid requires storing M+1 binary volumes. The total number of cells is \sum{m=0}^{M} ((N-1)/2^m)^3. For large N, this is dominated by the base level V0, which has (N-1)^3 cells. Thus, memory usage is O(N^3), same as the original dataset, but with a smaller constant factor (1 bit per cell vs. multiple bits per voxel). Performance: Speedups of an order of magnitude have been observed for datasets of useful size and complexity. The method saves time by quickly advancing across empty regions of space using the binary pyramid structure. Strengths: Efficiently skips large empty regions; suitable for image-order rendering; simple binary structure. Limitations: Requires O(N^3) memory for the pyramid; construction time is non-trivial; less flexible than condensed octrees for highly irregular data. When to use: When rendering large, sparse volumetric datasets with significant empty regions using image-order rendering. When not to use: When memory is constrained and the dataset is dense; when object-order rendering is preferred. Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization was introduced by Marc Levoy in the late 1980s as part of his work on efficient volume rendering algorithms. It was one of the first techniques to exploit spatial coherence in volumetric data for acceleration. The method is based on the observation that many datasets contain coherent regions of uninteresting voxels (opacity zero). It differs from earlier methods like [25] (likely referring to a condensed octree representation) by using a pyramid of binary volumes/complete octree rather than a condensed representation, and by rendering in image order rather than object order. name: Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination
head: Combined Hierarchical Enumeration and Adaptive Termination, Levoy's Ray Tracing Optimizations, Pyramidal Volume Traversal, TraceRay2
body: Hierarchical Volume Traversal with Adaptive Termination is a ray tracing algorithm that uses a pyramidal data structure of binary volumes to skip empty regions and an adaptive termination criterion to stop tracing when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. Unlike geometric ray tracing, which uses bounding volumes or spatial subdivision with lists of primitives, this method uses a hierarchical binary volume structure, which is more efficient for volume data because volume datasets have tens of millions of spatially ordered cells with single samples, whereas geometric scenes have hundreds of cells with many primitives. The method traverses a ray through a hierarchy of binary volumes (a pyramid) to determine which regions contain data. It adapts the traversal depth based on the content and terminates early if the accumulated opacity is sufficiently high. Input: Ray parameter \mathbf{u} (defining the ray direction and origin), the pyramidal binary volume structure \{Vm\}, the volume data (color and opacity fields), and parameters \epsilon, m{max}, m{min}, and M (total levels). Output: Final ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) and accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}). The core data structure is a pyramid of binary volumes. Binary Volumes Vm: For each level m \in \{0, \dots, M\}, Vm is a 3D grid of bits. V0 is the base level, and Vm for m > 0 is derived from V{m-1}. Memory layout: (2^{M+1} - 1)/7 bits total for the pyramid. Volume Data: Monochrome color and opacity fields. Memory layout: 2N^3 bytes for color and opacity per voxel. Output Image: Memory layout: P^2 bytes. The binary volumes are defined recursively to indicate the presence of non-zero opacity in their spatial extent. Base Level (V0): V0(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } \alpha(\mathbf{i} + \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{for } \mathbf{i} \in \{1, 2, \dots, N-1\}^3 \text{ and any } \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \alpha is the opacity field, \mathbf{i} is the index, and the condition checks if any of the eight voxels at the vertices of the cell have opacity equal to 1. Higher Levels (Vm, m > 0): Vm(\mathbf{i}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } V{m-1}(2\mathbf{i} - \Delta\mathbf{i}) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} for \mathbf{i} \in \{1, 2, \dots, \frac{N-1}{m+1}\}^3 and any \Delta\mathbf{i} \in \{0, 1\}^3. This means a cell at level m is 1 if any of the eight cells at level m-1 that form its octants are 1. \epsilon: Threshold for significant color change. Default value 0.05. Higher values reduce rendering time, lower values reduce artifacts. m{max}: Starting level for traversal. Set to M - 2 for all values of M to minimize traversal costs. m{min}: Lowest level to descend to before rendering. Set to 2 for the current implementation to avoid the high cost of ray-cell intersections at level zero. M: Total number of levels in the pyramid. The algorithm processes each ray \mathbf{u} as follows: 1. Initialize ray color \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) and opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}) to 0. 2. Set ray position \mathbf{x} to the entry point of the ray into the volume using First(u). 3. Set current level m to m{max}. 4. Loop while the ray position \mathbf{x} is in bounds (InBounds(x)) and accumulated opacity \alpha(\mathbf{u}) is less than or equal to 1 - \epsilon: a. Calculate the cell index \mathbf{i} at current level m containing point \mathbf{x} using the Index(m, x) procedure. b. If the cell value Vm(\mathbf{i}) is 1 and m > m{min}: i. Decrement level m by 1 (m:= m - 1) and repeat the loop. c. Else (if cell is 1 and at min level, or cell is 0): i. If the cell value Vm(\mathbf{i}) is 1: 1. Determine the exit point of the current cell along the ray using Next(m, x, u). 2. Call RenderCell(u, x, Next(m, x, u)) to render the interval from current \mathbf{x} to the next cell entry point. ii. Advance to the next cell on the same level. iii. While the parent of the new cell differs from the parent of the old cell and m < M: 1. Move up to the parent cell (\mathbf{i}:= \text{Parent}(m, \mathbf{i})). 2. Increment level m (m:= m + 1). iv. Update ray position \mathbf{x} to the entry point of the next cell at the current level m (\mathbf{x}:= \text{Next}(m, \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})). The RenderCell procedure handles the resampling and compositing for a specific interval along the ray defined by entry \mathbf{x}1 and exit \mathbf{x}2. 1. Define image bounds \mathbf{U}1 and \mathbf{U}2 for the cell interval using Image(x1) and Image(x2). 2. Loop through evenly spaced sample locations \mathbf{U} within this interval from \mathbf{U}1 to \mathbf{U}2. Evenly spaced locations are superimposed to avoid noise artifacts caused by resampling at non-uniformly spaced points determined by ray-cell intersections. 3. For each sample \mathbf{U}: a. Get object space coordinates \mathbf{x} using Object(U). b. Check if the base level binary volume V0 at the index of \mathbf{x} is 1 (V0(Index(0, x))). c. If 1: i. Resample color \hat{C}(\mathbf{U}) and opacity \alpha(\mathbf{U}) from the volume data using Sample. ii. Composite the sample into the ray: \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}):= \hat{C}(\mathbf{u}) + \hat{C}(\mathbf{U})(1 - \alpha(\mathbf{u})) \alpha(\mathbf{u}):= \alpha(\mathbf{u}) + \alpha(\mathbf{U})(1 - \alpha(\mathbf{u})). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def TraceRay2(u, epsilon, mmax, mmin, M, V, bounds): # u = (origin, direction), V = [V0, V1,..., VM], bounds = (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) Cray = 0.0 alpharay = 0.0 x = First(u, bounds) m = mmax while InBounds(x, bounds) and alpharay <= 1.0 - epsilon: i = Index(m, x, bounds) if V[m][i] == 1 and m > mmin: m -= 1 continue else: if V[m][i] == 1: xexit = Next(m, x, u, bounds) Cray, alpharay = RenderCell(u, x, xexit, Cray, alpharay, V, bounds) xnext = Next(m, x, u, bounds) while m < M and Parent(m, Index(m, xnext, bounds)) != Parent(m, i): i = Parent(m, i) m += 1 x = xnext return Cray, alpharay def RenderCell(u, x1, x2, Cray, alpharay, V, bounds): U1 = Image(x1) U2 = Image(x2) for y in range(U1[1], U2[1] + 1): for x in range(U1[0], U2[0] + 1): U = (x, y) objx = Object(U) if V[0][Index(0, objx, bounds)] == 1: Csample = Sample(V.color, objx) alphasample = Sample(V.opacity, objx) Cray = Cray + Csample (1.0 - alpharay) alpharay = alpharay + alphasample (1.0 - alpharay) return Cray, alpharay def First(u, bounds): o, d = u tmin = 0.0 for k in range(3): if d[k] == 0.0: if o[k] < bounds[2k] or o[k] > bounds[2k+1]: return None else: t1 = (bounds[2k] - o[k]) / d[k] t2 = (bounds[2k+1] - o[k]) / d[k] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) return o + tmin d def InBounds(x, bounds): return all(bounds[2k] <= x[k] <= bounds[2k+1] for k in range(3)) def Index(m, x, bounds): cellsize = (bounds[1] - bounds[0]) / (2m) return tuple(int((x[k] - bounds[2k]) / cellsize) for k in range(3)) def Next(m, x, u, bounds): o, d = u cellsize = (bounds[1] - bounds[0]) / (2m) tmax = float('inf') for k in range(3): if d[k] != 0.0: t = (bounds[2k] + cellsize - x[k]) / d[k] if t > 0.0: tmax = min(tmax, t) return x + tmax d def Parent(m, i): return tuple(i[k] // 2 for k in range(3)) def Image(x): return (int(x[0]), int(x[1])) def Object(U): return (float(U[0]), float(U[1]), 0.0) def Sample(field, x): # Standard trilinear interpolation of field at object-space x ix, iy, iz = x fx, fy, fz = ix - int(ix), iy - int(iy), iz - int(iz) def v(x, y, z): return field[int(x)][int(y)][int(z)] c00 = v(ix, iy, iz) (1-fx) + v(ix+1, iy, iz) fx c01 = v(ix, iy, iz+1) (1-fx) + v(ix+1, iy, iz+1) fx c10 = v(ix, iy+1, iz) (1-fx) + v(ix+1, iy+1, iz) fx c11 = v(ix, iy+1, iz+1) (1-fx) + v(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) fx return c00 (1-fy) + c01 fy Resampling Artifacts: Resampling at non-uniformly spaced points (determined by ray-cell intersections) adds noise artifacts to the image. The solution is to superimpose evenly spaced sample locations and only resample at those specific points. Level Zero Descent: Descending to level zero is inefficient for orthographic projections because ray-cell intersection costs exceed simple differencing. The solution is to stop descent at m{min}=2 and render level-zero cells within that higher-level cell. Zero Direction Components: Ray directions with zero components must be handled in Next to avoid division by zero when computing cell exit distances. Time Complexity: The traversal skips empty regions, reducing the number of samples taken. The adaptive termination stops tracing when accumulated opacity exceeds 1 - \epsilon, further reducing work. The cost of traversal is minimized by starting at m{max} = M - 2. Performance time is proportional to the number of rays cast. Memory Complexity: The memory required is 2N^3 bytes for the volume data, (2^{M+1} - 1)/7 bits for the pyramid, and P^2 bytes for the output image. Strengths: Efficient for volume data with large empty regions. The hierarchical structure allows skipping large empty areas. The adaptive termination reduces work for opaque regions. Combining termination and octree optimizations achieves savings of more than an order of magnitude. Limitations: Inefficient if the volume is mostly opaque or has no empty regions, as the hierarchy may not provide significant skipping. Descending to level zero is inefficient for orthographic projections due to high intersection costs. Precise selection of parameters is crucial for the adaptive rendering algorithm. When to Use: Suitable for volume datasets with significant empty space and where ray-cell intersection costs are high (e.g., orthographic projections). When Not to Use: Not suitable for geometric scenes with many primitives per cell, as the method is optimized for volume data with single samples per cell. The method was introduced in the paper "Efficient ray tracing of volume data". It is based on the observation that volume datasets contain coherent regions of uninteresting voxels (opacity zero) and can be encoded as a hierarchical spatial enumeration represented by a pyramid of binary volumes. The method is also known as Pyramidal Volume Traversal or TraceRay2. It builds on earlier work in adaptive rendering based on estimated image complexity at sample regions of the image plane. name: Jiang et al. Acceleration Structure
head: JRZ*16 method
body: The Jiang et al. acceleration structure is a hybrid object-order and image-order method designed to efficiently locate active cells for both direct and indirect volume visualization. It differs from pure image-order ray casting by leveraging hierarchical structures to skip empty space, while remaining dependent on rendering resolution like other hybrid approaches. Inputs: Scalar volume data; rendering resolution; ray origin and direction. Outputs: Rendered image with active cells rendered via ray marching. The method constructs a hierarchical acceleration structure to identify active cells (non-empty or relevant data regions). The traversal logic follows the shared principles of hierarchical descent. 1. Structure Construction: Build a hierarchical data structure (e.g., octree) from the volume data, marking nodes that contain active cells. 2. Ray Traversal: For each pixel, cast a ray into the volume. Traverse the hierarchy starting from the root. 3. Active Cell Identification: Use the structure to skip empty subtrees, identifying only the active cells intersected by the ray. 4. Ray Marching: Once active cells are located, perform ray marching within those regions to compute the final color. Parameters: Hierarchy depth: Not given in the sources. Threshold for "active": Not given in the sources. Edge cases: Resolution dependence: As a hybrid approach, performance and behavior depend on the rendering resolution. An acceleration structure introduced by Liu et al. [LCD15] for faster identification of active cells with less memory overhead than previous methods. It is cited as a precursor or related work to the Jiang et al. method in the context of hybrid approaches. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficiently locates active cells for direct and indirect visualization. Limitations: Dependent on rendering resolution, classifying it as a hybrid object-order and image-order approach. Use cases: Direct and indirect volume visualization where active cell identification is a bottleneck. The method was proposed by Jiang et al. [JRZ16] as part of research into efficient volume rendering techniques. It is situated in the context of hybrid rendering approaches that combine object-order preprocessing with image-order rendering. name: Silhouette Image Space Acceleration Structure (Mip Pyramid)
head: Hierarchical Voxelization Acceleration Structure
body: This method accelerates voxel coverage queries in image-based modeling by using a hierarchical mip pyramid over silhouette images to provide conservative bounds on voxel visibility. It solves the problem of efficiently determining whether a voxel intersects the visual hull without sampling every pixel, thereby reducing computation and data access for culling decisions. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its direct inspiration from the hierarchical z-buffer, storing min/max bounds of texel blocks to ensure no small features are missed or holes created in the voxelization. Inputs: A set of n silhouette images, one per camera view. A voxel v defined by its 8 corners in Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) space. The n pre-generated silhouette image pyramids. Outputs: A conservative lower bound (min) and upper bound (max) on the silhouette value \mathcal{S}(\mathbf{p}) for all points \mathbf{p} within voxel v. If the lower bound is 0, the voxel is outside the visual hull. Data Structures: Silhouette Image Pyramid: For each of the n views, a pyramid of texture levels is stored. Level 0: Original smoothed silhouette image. Level l+1: Each texel stores the minimum and maximum values of the 2 \times 2 block of texels from level l that it covers. Format: Two-channel texture (min, max) per texel. Algorithm: sampleSilhouette(v, i) Given voxel v and camera view i: 1. Project Corners: Project the 8 NDC space corners of voxel v into the 2D image space of camera i. 2. Bounding Rectangle: Compute the axis-aligned bounding rectangle (minX, minY, maxX, maxY) that encloses all projected corners. 3. Determine Level: Calculate the sampling level L in the mip pyramid: L = \lfloor \log2(\max(maxX - minX, maxY - minY)) \rfloor At this level L, the bounding rectangle covers at most a 2 \times 2 block of texels. 4. Sample Texels: Sample the texels at the corners of the bounding rectangle (minX, minY), (maxX, minY), (minX, maxY), and (maxX, maxY) from level L of the pyramid for view i. Let these values be (mink, maxk) for k \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}. 5. Compute Bounds: min\boundi = \min{k} (mink) max\boundi = \max{k} (maxk) These provide a conservative bound on the silhouette value \mathcal{I}i(\mathbf{C}i(\mathbf{p})) for all \mathbf{p} within v. Global Voxel Bound: To determine if the voxel is inside the visual hull, combine bounds across all n views: min\bound{total} = \prod{i=1}^{n} min\boundi max\bound{total} = \prod{i=1}^{n} max\boundi If min\bound{total} > 0, the voxel is fully inside. If max\bound{total} = 0, it is fully outside. Otherwise, further sampling is required. Generation: The n image pyramids are generated by a compute kernel launched immediately after silhouette image smoothing. Pitfalls: Conservative bounds ensure no small features are missed and no holes are created in voxelization, as bounds are conservatively correct. Precision issues in projection or log calculation may affect level selection; ensure robust handling of edge cases where the bounding box size is very small or zero. This method acquires and preprocesses silhouette images from raw camera data to create smooth, calibrated binary masks used for visual hull approximation. It solves the problem of converting raw, distorted Bayer-pattern sensor data into high-quality silhouette inputs for hierarchical acceleration structures. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its unified compute kernel approach that simultaneously handles lens distortion, demosaicing, and chroma-keying, followed by separable Gaussian filtering to control surface smoothness. Time Complexity: The query time is O(1) per voxel per view, as it involves a constant number of projections and texture lookups (4 samples) regardless of voxel size or image resolution. Memory Complexity: Requires storing n mip pyramids. Each pyramid level reduces the image size by half in each dimension, so the total memory is proportional to 4/3 of the original image size per view (sum of geometric series 1 + 1/4 + 1/16 + \dots). Performance: Greatly reduces the amount of computation and data accesses needed by the oracle kernel to make a culling decision for a given voxel. Strengths: Conservative bounds prevent holes in voxelization; efficient culling of empty space. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of silhouette images and pyramids; performance depends on the number of views n. The method was introduced in the context of real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization for image-based modeling. It is inspired by the well-known hierarchical z-buffer [Greene et al. 1993], adapting the concept of hierarchical depth testing to silhouette coverage queries. The acceleration structure is part of a pipeline that includes silhouette image acquisition, filtering, and voxel rendering as screen-space splats. name: Silhouette Image Acquisition and Filtering
head: Chroma-keyed silhouette generation, Gaussian-filtered silhouette images
body: This method acquires and preprocesses silhouette images from raw camera data to create smooth, calibrated binary masks used for visual hull approximation. It solves the problem of converting raw, distorted Bayer-pattern sensor data into high-quality silhouette inputs for hierarchical acceleration structures. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its unified compute kernel approach that simultaneously handles lens distortion, demosaicing, and chroma-keying, followed by separable Gaussian filtering to control surface smoothness. Inputs: Raw Bayer pattern image data from a camera; camera parameters for distortion correction; chroma key color range. Outputs: Calibrated silhouette images (2D arrays of 0s and 1s); filtered silhouette images. Data Structures: Input Texture: 2D texture array storing raw Bayer data (8 bits per pixel). Output Texture: 2D texture array storing silhouette values (float or integer, 0 or 1). Filter Kernel: Separable Gaussian kernel with unit integral. Steps: 1. Upload Data: Upload raw Bayer pattern data to the GPU as a 2D texture array, reducing camera bus and CPU/GPU bandwidth usage compared to higher-bit formats. 2. Compute Kernel Launch: Launch a single GPU compute kernel where each thread or thread block processes a portion of the image. 3. Distortion Correction: Remove radial lens distortion from the pixel coordinates to produce calibrated silhouette images. 4. Demosaicing: Convert the Bayer pattern data to full RGB or luminance values. 5. Chroma Keying: Segment foreground and background pixels. Foreground pixels are assigned a value of 0, and background pixels are assigned a value of 1. This creates the initial binary silhouette image \mathcal{I}i. 6. Filtering: Apply a separable Gaussian filter to the binary silhouette images. The filter has a unit integral, and the kernel width is a parameter. Increasing the width increases blur, resulting in a smoother visual hull surface S(\mathbf{p}). Implementation uses a thread block per row/column strategy to fit the entire image row or column in shared memory, leveraging separability for performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def correctradialdistortion(x, y, intrinsics): # Standard radial distortion correction using camera intrinsics cx, cy, fx, fy = intrinsics['cx'], intrinsics['cy'], intrinsics['fx'], intrinsics['fy'] k1, k2 = intrinsics['k1'], intrinsics['k2'] unorm = (x - cx) / fx vnorm = (y - cy) / fy r2 = unorm2 + vnorm2 scale = 1.0 + k1 r2 + k2 r22 return unorm scale fx + cx, vnorm scale fy + cy def demosaicbayer(u, v, bayerdata): # Bilinear interpolation of Bayer pattern to RGB x, y = int(u), int(v) # Assuming standard RGGB pattern r = (bayerdata[y, x] + bayerdata[y+1, x+1]) / 2.0 g = (bayerdata[y, x+1] + bayerdata[y+1, x]) / 2.0 b = bayerdata[y+1, x+1] return r, g, b def isinchromarange(r, g, b, chromarange): # Check if color falls within the specified foreground chroma range return (chromarange['rmin'] <= r <= chromarange['rmax'] and chromarange['gmin'] <= g <= chromarange['gmax'] and chromarange['bmin'] <= b <= chromarange['bmax']) def creategaussian1d(width): # Create 1D Gaussian kernel with unit integral sigma = width / 6.0 kernel = [] for i in range(-int(width/2), int(width/2) + 1): val = math.exp(-(i2) / (2 sigma2)) kernel.append(val) norm = sum(kernel) return [v / norm for v in kernel] def apply1dfilter(image, kernel, axis='horizontal'): # Apply 1D separable filter using shared memory per row/column height, width = len(image), len(image[0]) output = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for i in range(height): row = image[i] # Simulate shared memory load with padding for boundary handling shared = [0.0] (width + len(kernel)) for j in range(width): shared[j + len(kernel)//2] = row[j] for j in range(width): acc = 0.0 for k in range(len(kernel)): acc += shared[j + k] kernel[k] output[i][j] = acc if axis == 'vertical': return [[output[j][i] for j in range(height)] for i in range(width)] return output def processsilhouettepipeline(bayerdata, intrinsics, chromarange, kernelwidth): # Steps 1-5: Acquire and chroma-key silhouette = [[0.0] len(bayerdata[0]) for in range(len(bayerdata))] for y in range(len(bayerdata)): for x in range(len(bayerdata[0])): u, v = correctradialdistortion(x, y, intrinsics) r, g, b = demosaicbayer(u, v, bayerdata) silhouette[y][x] = 0.0 if isinchromarange(r, g, b, chromarange) else 1.0 # Step 6: Filter temp = apply1dfilter(silhouette, creategaussian1d(kernelwidth), 'horizontal') filtered = apply1dfilter(temp, creategaussian1d(kernelwidth), 'vertical') return filtered Parameters: Kernel Width: Controls the amount of blur. Larger values produce smoother surfaces S(\mathbf{p}). Not given in the sources. Chroma Range: The color threshold for segmentation. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using 8-bit Bayer data reduces bandwidth but may limit color precision for chroma keying. Boundaries: Shared memory usage requires careful handling of image boundaries during the separable filter passes. A technique that exploits slab silhouette maps and an early depth test to skip empty spaces along the direction normal to the texture slice. It is used to optimize volume rendering by avoiding computation in non-transparent regions. It is distinguished by its specific application of early depth testing in conjunction with slab-based silhouette data for empty space skipping. Time Complexity: The compute kernel runs in O(N) time for N pixels, with the filtering step also being O(N) due to separability. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the input Bayer texture array and output silhouette textures. Shared memory is used for filter rows/columns to increase convolution performance. Performance: The single compute kernel approach and shared memory usage for filtering provide high performance on GPUs. Strengths: Reduces data bandwidth; produces smooth surfaces suitable for visual hull approximation; efficient GPU implementation. Limitations: Requires camera calibration for distortion correction. When to use: When real-time or high-resolution silhouette acquisition from raw camera data is needed for visual hull-based volume rendering. When not to use: When high-precision color segmentation is required beyond chroma keying capabilities, or when camera calibration is unavailable. This method is described in the context of real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization and image-based modeling. It was introduced by the authors of the source paper to efficiently generate silhouette inputs for visual hull oracle kernels. The use of chroma keying and Gaussian filtering for silhouette smoothing is a standard technique in image-based modeling to create smooth visual hull surfaces. The concept of using slab silhouette maps for empty space skipping was explored by Keleş et al.. name: Visual Hull Oracle Kernel
body: The Visual Hull Oracle Kernel performs binary culling of voxels to determine if they intersect the visual hull surface S(p) = 0.5. It identifies which voxels in a sparse voxel grid contribute to the final volume by leveraging hierarchical mip pyramids over silhouette images to compute conservative bounds on voxel coverage. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific use of component-wise multiplication of conservative bounds across multiple camera views to make a definitive KEEP or CULL decision, building on the silhouette acquisition and filtering techniques described in Silhouette Image Acquisition and Filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of voxels (VoxelListIn), n filtered silhouette images, n corresponding mip pyramids, and coordinate transforms from Novel View Camera (NVC) space to silhouette image space and screen space. Output: A decision array (oracleOutput) where each entry is either CULL or KEEP. Data Structures: VoxelListIn: Array of voxel structures, indexed by threadID. oracleOutput: Array of integers, indexed by threadID. boundsx and boundsy: Scalars storing the lower and upper limits of the conservative bound on the silhouette coverage for a voxel. Parameters: numCameras: The number of input camera views. boundsx: Lower limit of the conservative bound on S(p). boundsy: Upper limit of the conservative bound on S(p). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize DECISION to CULL. 2. Read the current voxel v from VoxelListIn[threadID]. 3. Check if the voxel is outside the viewing frustum of the novel view using outsideFrustum(v). If outsideFrustum(v) is true, skip further processing for this voxel and write CULL to oracleOutput[threadID]. If outsideFrustum(v) is false, proceed to step 4. 4. Initialize boundsx and boundsy to 1.0. 5. Loop through each camera index i from 0 to numCameras - 1: Call sampleSilhouette(v, i) to retrieve the conservative bound of voxel v's projection into silhouette image i. Update boundsx and boundsy by performing component-wise multiplication with the returned values. 6. After the loop, evaluate the final boundsx and boundsy: If boundsx < 0.5 AND boundsy > 0.5, set DECISION to KEEP. Otherwise, DECISION remains CULL. 7. Write DECISION to oracleOutput[threadID]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. CULL = 0 KEEP = 1 def visualhulloraclekernel(threadID, VoxelListIn, oracleOutput, numCameras, outsideFrustum, sampleSilhouette): DECISION = CULL v = VoxelListIn[threadID] if not outsideFrustum(v): boundsx = 1.0 boundsy = 1.0 for i in range(numCameras): cambounds = sampleSilhouette(v, i) boundsx = cambounds[0] boundsy = cambounds[1] if boundsx < 0.5 and boundsy > 0.5: DECISION = KEEP oracleOutput[threadID] = DECISION Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Frustum Culling: Voxels outside the viewing frustum of the novel view are automatically culled via the outsideFrustum(v) check to avoid unnecessary computation. Precision: The method relies on conservative bounds; if the mip pyramid levels are too coarse, the bounds may be inaccurate, potentially leading to false positives (keeping voxels that should be culled) or false negatives (culling voxels that should be kept). Surface Definition: The decision is based on the intersection with the surface S(p) = 0.5, making the thresholds 0.5 specific to this definition. A voxel-based approach that retrieves the photo-hull of a shape using a view-dependent plane-sweeping strategy. It differs from the standard Visual Hull Oracle by combining rendering and reconstruction into a single step, producing no explicit volume. A key pitfall is that it performs photo-consistency checks on each fragment regardless of rejection by silhouette/background tests due to a lack of branching support at the time. Performance achieves rendering frame rates of 2-3 frames per second. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels processed, as each voxel culling decision is independent and assigned to a single thread. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for n silhouette images and n mip pyramids, where n is the number of cameras. Performance: The hierarchical, coarse-to-fine manner of processing accelerates computation. Specific frame rates for the oracle kernel alone are not given, but related GPU-based photo-hull methods achieve 2-3 fps. Strengths: Efficient culling of voxels outside the frustum and those not intersecting the visual hull surface. Limitations: Requires pre-computed mip pyramids and silhouette images. The Visual Hull Oracle Kernel was introduced in the context of real-time high-resolution sparse voxelization for image-based modeling. It builds upon hierarchical z-buffer concepts and uses mip pyramids to accelerate voxel/silhouette coverage queries. The approach is part of a broader shift towards GPU-based processing for volumetric reconstruction, following earlier work on GPU-based visual hull rendering. name: Pixel separation for bright foreground
head: Bright pixel separation, Split scattering image
body: Pixel separation for bright foreground is a technique used in silhouette image acquisition and filtering to correct the incorrect blurring of bright pixels located at low depths (foreground) against dark backgrounds. It solves the problem where standard luminance-weighted blurring causes bright foreground objects to lose intensity or blend incorrectly by splitting the input scattering image into two separate components: one for separated bright pixels (L{\text{ssc}}) and one for the rest (L{\text{sc}}). Inputs: Original scattering image \mathbf{L}. Original depth image \mathbf{D}'. Original luminance image \mathbf{Y}^{[0]} derived from \mathbf{L}. MIP chain depth K. Separation parameters: Ty (min luminance), \varepsilony (luminance width), T{d'} (max depth), \varepsilon{d'} (depth width), k{ssc} (fixed MIP level for fetching). Outputs: Separated blurred scattering image \mathbb{L}'{\text{SSC}}. Remaining blurred scattering image \mathbb{L}'{\text{SC}} (constructed via standard luminance-weighted MIP chain on L{sc}). Data Structures: \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[0...K]}: MIP chain for separated scattering, built using simple Gaussian blurring. \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}^{[0...K]}: Depth MIP chain for separated pixels, built using luminance-weighted averaging. \mathbb{L}{\text{sc}}^{[0...K]}: MIP chain for remaining pixels, built using standard luminance-weighted technique. Steps: 1. Compute Separation Mask M: Calculate the mask based on high luminance and low depth using smoothstep functions: M = \text{smoothstep}(Ty, Ty + \varepsilony, \mathbf{Y}^{[0]}) \cdot \left( 1 - \text{smoothstep}(T{d'} - \varepsilon{d'}, T{d'}, \mathbf{D}'^{[0]}) \right) where \mathbf{Y}^{[0]} is the luminance of the original scattering image and \mathbf{D}'^{[0]} is the original depth image. 2. Split Scattering Image: Divide the original scattering image \mathbf{L} into two images using the mask M: L{\text{ssc}} = e^{-Ca \cdot P} \cdot \left( 1 - e^{-Cs \cdot P} \right) \cdot M \cdot L L{\text{sc}} = e^{-Ca \cdot P} \cdot \left( 1 - e^{-Cs \cdot P} \right) \cdot (1 - M) \cdot L The term e^{-Ca \cdot P} \cdot (1 - e^{-Cs \cdot P}) represents the original weight applied to the scattering image. The sum L{\text{ssc}} + L{\text{sc}} equals the original unmasked scattering image, ensuring no information loss. 3. Build MIP Chain for Separated Pixels (L{ssc}): Construct the MIP chain \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[0...K]} using simple Gaussian blurring without luminance weighting or masking, allowing bright pixels to propagate: \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} = \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[k-1]} \mathcal{G} where \mathcal{G} is the Gaussian kernel and \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[0]} = L{\text{ssc}}. 4. Build Depth MIP Chain for Separated Pixels: Construct the depth MIP chain \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}^{[0...K]} using luminance-weighted averaging to prioritize the depth of bright separated pixels: D{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} = \frac{\left( \gamma{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} \cdot D{\text{ssc}}^{[k-1]} \right) \mathcal{U}}{\gamma{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} \mathcal{U}} where \gamma{\text{ssc}}^{[k]} is the luminance of \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[k]}, \mathcal{U} is the uniform averaging kernel, and D{\text{ssc}}^{[0]} = \mathbf{D}'. 5. Build MIP Chain for Remaining Pixels (L{sc}): Filter L{sc} using the standard luminance-weighted MIP chain technique. 6. Fetch Final Separated Image: Determine the level \ell' from the fixed MIP level k{ssc} using the depth chain \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}: \ell' = \ell \left( \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}^{[k{\text{SSC}}]} \right) \mathbb{L}'{\text{SSC}} = \mathbb{L}^{[\ell']}{\text{SSC}} where \ell(\cdot) denotes the level selection function based on depth values. Parameters: Ty: Minimum luminance threshold for separation. Set experimentally. \varepsilony: Luminance threshold width. Set experimentally. T{d'}: Maximum depth threshold for separation. Set experimentally. \varepsilon{d'}: Depth threshold width. Set experimentally. k{ssc}: Fixed MIP level index for fetching from the separated chain (0 \le k{ssc} \le K). Typical value k{ssc} = 0.7 \cdot K. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter values (Ty, \varepsilony, T{d'}, \varepsilon{d'}, k{ssc}) must be carefully set based on experiments for individual scenes and media combinations. Incorrect parameter settings may result in incorrect blurring or loss of bright pixel energy. The choice of k{ssc} heavily depends on the number of pixels actually separated in the scene. Time Complexity: Adds overhead for mask computation, image splitting, and construction of a separate MIP chain for bright pixels. The depth chain construction involves additional luminance-weighted averaging. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the additional MIP chains \mathbb{L}{\text{ssc}}^{[0...K]} and \mathbb{D}'{\text{SSC}}^{[0...K]}. Strengths: Correctly preserves the intensity and appearance of bright foreground objects that would otherwise be incorrectly blurred or suppressed. Limitations: Requires manual tuning of parameters per scene. The fixed level k{ssc} is arbitrary and may not be optimal for all scenes. When to use: When bright foreground objects are present against dark backgrounds and standard luminance-weighted blurring causes visual artifacts. The technique was introduced by Tomas Davidovic in his 2012 thesis "Real-Time Light Transport in Analytically Integrable Participating Media". PDF Real-Time Light Transport in Analytically Integrable Participating Media, https://cgg.mff.cuni.cz/~tomas/publications/pub-thesis-real-time-scattering/thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Flex-block tree
head: Cell-tree, Flex-block partition
body: The flex-block tree is a hierarchical data structure derived from a kd-tree partition, designed primarily for load balancing in distributed volume rendering (both ray casting and ray tracing). It partitions a volume into "flex-blocks," which are cells containing tightly cropped subvolumes that do not necessarily occupy the entire cell volume. Unlike traditional space subdivision methods, the flex-block partition does not restrict partition cuts to alternate between axes, allowing it to handle scenes with disproportionate dimensions effectively. It serves as a dependency graph that determines the deterministic depth order of blocks for image compositing in ray casting and accelerates ray traversal by indicating potential neighbor cells in ray tracing. The method constructs a tree where internal nodes define partition boundaries and leaf nodes represent the data containers (flex-blocks). The construction involves preprocessing the volume to remove empty space, partitioning the remaining data using a modified kd-tree algorithm, and extracting view-dependent ordering information. Inputs: Raw volume data (slices or voxels). Optional mask volume defining regions of interest. Number of render-nodes (for distributed systems). View directions (typically 8 quantized directions). Outputs: A flex-block tree (dependency graph). Cropped volume data (bricks) distributed to render-nodes. Look-up tables mapping view directions to flex-block traversal orders. Flex-block Tree Node Internal nodes in the tree store partitioning information similar to a traditional binary tree: cutplane: The position and normal of the splitting plane. children: Pointers or indices to the left and right child nodes. Flex-block (Leaf Node) Each leaf node represents a cell in the partition: bbox: A tightly cropped axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) enclosing the non-empty data within the cell. dataref: Reference to the subvolume data (brick) stored in memory or on disk. dependencies: Information used for ray-task scheduling and traversal speedup. 1. Empty Space Reduction: If a mask volume is not provided, perform out-of-core region growing on raw data slices to create a mask. Crop each slice to bounding rectangles of non-empty regions defined by the mask. Align a tight AABB around cohesive non-empty areas of the volume to eliminate empty space. 2. Partitioning (Moving Walls): Apply a "moving walls" algorithm to partition the scene. This algorithm moves partition walls to simultaneously accommodate non-empty subvolume boundaries and balance the load across render-nodes. This step generates a partition structure that respects the data distribution requirements. 3. kd-tree Extraction: Extract a kd-tree from the output of the moving walls procedure. Unlike standard kd-trees, this partition does not enforce alternating axis cuts. The cut axis is chosen to optimize load balancing and accommodate disproportionate scene dimensions. 4. Dynamic Programming for Load Balancing: Use a dynamic programming (DP) algorithm to group bricks and solve the Load Balanced Network Distribution (LBND) problem. The DP evaluates a cost function to minimize end-to-end rendering time, which is a function of the slowest render-node, image composition time, and network communication time. This step creates the final flex-blocks within the kd-tree-like partition. 5. Dependency Graph Construction: For each of the eight quantized view directions, extract the image priority order (depth order) of the flex-blocks from the kd-tree. Store these orders in look-up tables. These tables form the dependency graph of flex-blocks. This graph is used for: Ray Casting: Determining the order for compositing images from different nodes. Ray Tracing: Accelerating traversal by indicating potential neighbors a ray may enter. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildflexblocktree(volumedata, mask=None, numnodes=1, viewdirections=8): """ Constructs a flex-block tree for distributed volume rendering. Args: volumedata: Raw volume slices or voxels. mask: Optional mask volume. If None, generated via region growing. numnodes: Number of render-nodes for load balancing. viewdirections: Number of quantized view directions (typically 8). Returns: flexblocktree: The constructed tree structure. dependencytables: Look-up tables for view-dependent traversal orders. croppeddata: Cropped volume bricks distributed to nodes. """ # Step 1: Empty Space Reduction if mask is None: # Out-of-core region growing to create mask mask = regiongrowing(volumedata) # Crop slices to bounding rectangles of non-empty regions croppedslices = cropslices(volumedata, mask) # Align tight AABBs around cohesive non-empty areas # This reduces data size and simplifies partitioning volumedatareduced = aligntightbboxes(croppedslices) # Step 2: Partitioning with Moving Walls # Moves walls to balance load across numnodes and respect data boundaries partitionstructure = movingwallsalgorithm(volumedatareduced, numnodes) # Step 3: Extract kd-tree # Does not restrict cuts to alternate axes kdtree = extractkdtree(partitionstructure) # Step 4: Dynamic Programming for Load Balancing # Solves LBND problem to minimize end-to-end render time # Cost function considers slowest node, composition time, and network time flexblocks = dynamicprogrammingpartition(kdtree, numnodes) # Step 5: Construct Dependency Graph dependencytables = {} for direction in getquantizedviewdirections(viewdirections): # Extract depth order of flex-blocks for this view order = getimagepriorityorder(kdtree, flexblocks, direction) dependencytables[direction] = order # Build the final tree structure # Internal nodes: cutplane, children # Leaf nodes: flex-block (bbox, dataref, dependencies) flexblocktree = buildtreestructure(kdtree, flexblocks) return flexblocktree, dependencytables, flexblocks View Directions: Typically 8 quantized directions are used to extract image priority orders. Render-nodes: The number of processing units in the distributed system, used to balance the partition. Disproportionate Scenes: Standard kd-trees may perform poorly on scenes with disproportionate dimensions. The flex-block partition addresses this by not restricting cut axes. NP-Completeness: Determining the optimum order for caching cells in ray tracing is NP-Complete. The method uses heuristics and dynamic programming approximations. Data Movement: Reducing empty space early in the pipeline reduces run-time for preprocessing and network data movement. Failure to crop empty space effectively can lead to inefficient load balancing. A compact representation of ray dependencies between cells, where a cell is a flex-block. It is used for ray-task scheduling and ray traversal speedup in ray tracing. The underlying data distribution method derived from the flex-block tree. It defines how data is split among render-nodes and how bricks are scheduled. Time Complexity: The construction involves region growing, partitioning, and dynamic programming. The DP solution for LBND is optimized to minimize end-to-end rendering time, which depends on the slowest node, composition time, and network communication. The exact complexity of the DP step is not specified, but the problem of optimal caching order is NP-Complete. Memory Complexity: The cell-tree (dependency graph) is described as being several orders of magnitude smaller than the number of dependencies it represents. Strengths: Effective load balancing for distributed rendering. Handles scenes with disproportionate dimensions. Automates space skipping by using data extents of flex-blocks. Reduces data movement by cropping empty space early. Limitations: Requires preprocessing (region growing, cropping, partitioning). Dynamic task scheduling is complex due to the NP-Complete nature of optimal caching. When to Use: Suitable for distributed volume visualization of massive datasets where load balancing and efficient data distribution are critical. The flex-block tree was introduced in the context of massive data management for distributed volume visualization. It addresses the limitations of traditional space subdivision methods, which do not adequately handle load balancing in distributed rendering environments. The method was developed to support both software ray tracing and hardware ray casting in a distributed cluster setting. It builds upon concepts from kd-trees and dynamic programming for load balanced network distribution (LBND). name: Data Structure and Indexing
head: Hierarchical Data Structures Indexing
body: This family defines the memory layout, pointer encoding, and traversal logic for hierarchical acceleration structures (primarily octrees) used in volume rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently navigating sparse 3D data by mapping tree topology to linear memory or GPU textures, enabling fast empty-space skipping and neighbor-based boundary crossing. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the low-level representation of the tree hierarchy itself (e.g., texture encoding, point storage) rather than high-level traversal optimizations or specific acceleration heuristics. All methods in this family share the core mechanism of hierarchical descent and ascent. The traversal begins at the root of the octree and determines which of the eight children (octants) the ray intersects. This is typically done by comparing the ray's position relative to the center of the current node's bounding box. 1. Child Selection: For a node with center \mathbf{c} and half-extent s, the ray position \mathbf{p} determines the child index k \in \{0, \dots, 7\}: k = 4 \cdot \mathbb{I}(px \ge cx) + 2 \cdot \mathbb{I}(py \ge cy) + 1 \cdot \mathbb{I}(pz \ge cz) where \mathbb{I}(\cdot) is the indicator function. 2. Empty Space Skipping: If the selected child is marked as empty (or uniform), the traversal skips the subtree. This is achieved by advancing the ray parameter t to the exit of the current node or using neighbor pointers to jump to the next potentially occupied node. 3. Leaf Handling: Upon reaching a leaf node, the method typically switches to a fixed-step traversal (like DDA) within the leaf's voxel grid to sample the volume data. 4. Backtracking: Because octrees are sparse and irregular, traversal often requires backtracking to the parent node when a ray exits a subtree or encounters an empty branch. This is implemented using an explicit stack (on GPU) or recursion (on CPU). A spatial index structure that augments a branch-on-need octree with links to allow direct traversal to adjacent nodes, used to accelerate ray traversal in volume rendering. It differs from full 26-neighbor structures by maintaining only x-neighbor pointers, reducing memory overhead while enabling efficient skipping of empty space and boundary crossing. The structure is encoded into an 8-bit RGBA 3D texture. Each octree node is encoded in 8 consecutive texels arranged in the x-direction. The layout uses a tagged pointer scheme where the Alpha (A) component determines the node kind: A=1.0 for inner nodes, A=0.5 for data nodes (leaves with data), and A=0.0 for empty nodes. Inner node RGB components point to the first of 8 children, arranged consecutively in the x-direction. Leaf node RGB components point to leaf info, consisting of a data pointer and 6 consecutive texels storing neighbor pointers for the 6 faces. The last leaf data texel contains a NULL pointer. Neighbor pointers use their A value to encode the octree level of the neighbor. Construction involves initializing top-level nodes (typically two levels below the root) and establishing x-neighbor pointers, propagating these pointers down to child nodes that share boundaries but have different parents, and finally encoding the structure into a 3D texture. Boundary nodes link to the smallest node enclosing all adjacent nodes if multiple exist. Traversal stops before reaching a single root node at the top level to optimize performance. See Octree with Neighbor Pointers. A Point Octree is a recursive hierarchical data structure designed to manage a dynamic set of 3D points, supporting insertion, removal, movement, and spatial queries such as nearest neighbor and radius search. It differs from voxel-based octrees by storing data only at leaf nodes corresponding to occupied regions, allowing for efficient handling of sparse point clouds without allocating memory for empty space. The tree consists of nodes containing an array of up to 8 child octants and a PointData object at leaves. PointData uses two parallel arrays: points (Vector3[]) and data (T[]). Key parameters include maxPoints (leaf capacity), maxDepth (recursion limit), and bias (padding for boundary checks). Insertion recursively finds the leaf, updates existing points, or splits the node if full, redistributing points to children using a bias for containment checks. Radius search recursively traverses intersecting octants and filters leaves by squared distance. Movement updates positions in place or removes/reinserts if the octant changes. See Point Octree. A hybrid CPU-GPU traversal strategy where the CPU traverses the KD-tree of AMR patches back-to-front, and the GPU traverses cells within a patch. Sub-patches are generated to ensure perspective-correct sorting of cells relative to the observer. The CPU traverses the KD-tree hierarchy in back-to-front fashion, choosing the appropriate order at each internal node until a leaf node (patch) is found. The vertex shader modifies each index according to the current observer position to generate proper cell ordering, ensuring perspective-correct sorting. Transfers gradient octrees computed on the server side to a rendering client to reduce network traffic and avoid the need to compute gradients on the client. A simple binary tree indexing scheme to identify and organize patches in a breadth-first manner (coarse to fine). Allows quick identification of cousin patches. View-dependent mesh generation uses recursive traversal over the patch hierarchy by indexing into a fixed-size 1D array of patches, accumulating patch IDs for later decompression and rendering. The use of hierarchical data structures for volume rendering dates back to the early 1990s, with octrees being a primary choice for representing sparse volumetric data. Early work focused on CPU-based traversal using linked lists or arrays. With the advent of GPUs, texture-based encodings became prevalent to leverage hardware texture units for pointer chasing and empty-space skipping. The specific encoding of octrees into 3D textures with tagged pointers was developed to facilitate efficient traversal on graphics hardware. Neighbor pointer techniques were introduced to handle boundary crossings efficiently without backtracking. Point octrees are widely used in computer graphics for managing particle systems and dynamic point clouds. AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) structures, often indexed via binary trees or KD-trees, are used in scientific visualization to handle multi-resolution data. name: Octree with Neighbor Pointers
head: Octree Construction with X-Neighbor Pointers, Octree with neighbors structure
body: A spatial index structure that augments a branch-on-need octree with links to allow direct traversal to adjacent nodes, used to accelerate ray traversal in volume rendering. It differs from full 26-neighbor structures by maintaining only x-neighbor pointers, reducing memory overhead while enabling efficient skipping of empty space and boundary crossing. Inputs: A view-dependent branch-on-need octree. Outputs: A 3D texture acting as a spatial index, encoded with tagged pointers and neighbor links. Data Structures: The structure is encoded into an 8-bit RGBA 3D texture. Each octree node is encoded in 8 consecutive texels arranged in the x-direction. The layout uses a tagged pointer scheme where the Alpha (A) component determines the node kind: A=1.0: Inner node. A=0.5: Data node (leaf with data). A=0.0: Empty node. Inner Node Layout: The RGB components point to the first of 8 children, which are arranged consecutively in the x-direction. Leaf Node Layout: The RGB components point to leaf info, consisting of: 1. A data pointer (if not empty). 2. 6 consecutive texels storing neighbor pointers for the 6 faces. The last leaf data texel contains a NULL pointer. Neighbor pointers use their A value to encode the octree level of the neighbor. Construction Steps: 1. Top-Level Initialization: Create all nodes at the top level n (typically two levels below the root to speed up traversal) and establish x-neighbor pointers for all adjacent nodes at this level. 2. Pointer Propagation: Propagate x-neighbor pointers from nodes in level i to their child nodes in level i-1. Specifically, link adjacent level-(i-1) nodes that have different parent nodes. 3. Texture Encoding: Encode the resulting structure into a 3D texture. Update the GPU texture using glTexSubImage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildoctreewithneighbors(octree): # Step 1: Initialize top level toplevel = octree.getlevel(n) # n is typically rootlevel - 2 for node in toplevel: node.neighborsx = findxneighbors(node, toplevel) # Step 2: Propagate pointers down for level in range(n, 0, -1): currentlevelnodes = octree.getlevel(level) childlevelnodes = octree.getlevel(level - 1) for parent in currentlevelnodes: children = parent.getchildren() # Link children that share a boundary but have different parents for i, child in enumerate(children): # Find adjacent children in the same level # Logic depends on Morton ordering or spatial adjacency adjacentchildren = findadjacentchildren(child, childlevelnodes) for adjchild in adjacentchildren: if adjchild.parent != parent: child.setneighbor(adjchild) # Step 3: Encode to 3D texture texture = create3dtexture(width, height, depth) for node in octree.allnodes(): encodenodetotexture(node, texture) return texture def findxneighbors(node, levelnodes): # Returns pointer to the node immediately adjacent in the +x direction # at the same level pass def encodenodetotexture(node, texture): # Determine node type if node.isempty: alpha = 0.0 rgb = NULL elif node.isleaf: alpha = 0.5 # RGB points to data pointer # Next 6 texels store neighbor pointers # Last texel is NULL else: alpha = 1.0 # RGB points to first child (8 children follow in x) pass Edge Cases: Boundary Nodes: Neighbor pointers link to the smallest node enclosing all adjacent nodes if there are multiple ones. Depth Limit: Traversal stops before reaching a single root node at the top level to optimize performance. Memory: Uses a 3D texture with 8-bit RGBA components. Each node occupies 8 texels. The addressing space can potentially address 16 \times M nodes, which is several orders of magnitude larger than needed. Performance: On-the-fly construction at each frame allows for view-dependent optimization. Comparison: Differs from Zhou et al. [2010] by storing different payload (mesh vs point cloud) and maintaining only x-neighbor pointers instead of pointers to all 26 neighbors. Originated in the context of GPU-based volume rendering and voxelization. The structure was introduced to accelerate ray casting by providing direct access to adjacent nodes, avoiding backtracking. It shares similarities with bottom-up breadth-first construction using Morton ordering. name: Point Octree
body: A Point Octree is a recursive hierarchical data structure designed to manage a dynamic set of 3D points, supporting insertion, removal, movement, and spatial queries such as nearest neighbor and radius search. It differs from voxel-based octrees by storing data only at leaf nodes corresponding to occupied regions, allowing for efficient handling of sparse point clouds without allocating memory for empty space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D points \mathbf{p}i with associated user data Di. Output: A tree structure enabling O(\log N) average-case spatial queries and updates. Data Structures: The tree consists of nodes (octants). Each node contains: children: An array of up to 8 child octants (or null if leaf). data: A PointData<T> object (or null if internal node). PointData<T> layout: Two parallel arrays: points: Vector3[]: Stores the coordinates of points in this leaf. data: T[]: Stores the associated user data for each point. Parameters: maxPoints: Maximum number of points allowed in a leaf before splitting (default not specified in sources). maxDepth: Hard limit on recursion depth to prevent infinite subdivision. bias: A padding value added to octant boundaries during containment checks to handle points near boundaries or sphere intersections. Algorithm Steps: 1. Insertion (set): Recursively traverse from the root to find the leaf octant containing the point \mathbf{p}. Check if \mathbf{p} already exists in the leaf's points array. If yes, update the corresponding entry in data. If the leaf is full (number of points \ge maxPoints) and current depth < maxDepth, call split() and redistribute(). Otherwise, append \mathbf{p} to points and D to data in the leaf. 2. Splitting and Redistribution: split(): Create 8 empty child octants. redistribute(bias): Iterate through all points in the current node's data. For each point, determine which child octant contains it (using contains(point, bias)). Move the point and its data to the child's PointData. Set the current node's data to null. 3. Radius Search (findPoints): Recursively traverse child octants that intersect the query sphere (defined by center \mathbf{c} and radius r). Intersection is checked using contains(center, r). In leaf nodes, compute squared distance d^2 = \|\mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{c}\|^2 for each point. Filter points where d^2 \le r^2. 4. Movement (move): If the point and new position are in the same octant, update the position in place. If they diverge, remove the point from the old location and insert it at the new location. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class PointData: def init(self): self.points = [] # List of Vector3 self.data = [] # List of T class PointOctant: def init(self, minbound, maxbound): self.min = minbound self.max = maxbound self.children = None # List of PointOctant or None self.data = None # PointData or None def contains(self, point, bias=0): """Check if point is inside octant boundaries with optional bias.""" return (point.x >= self.min.x - bias and point.x <= self.max.x + bias and point.y >= self.min.y - bias and point.y <= self.max.y + bias and point.z >= self.min.z - bias and point.z <= self.max.z + bias) def split(self): """Create 8 children.""" mid = (self.min + self.max) / 2 self.children = [] for i in range(8): # Determine child bounds based on bit index i # x: (i>>2)&1, y: (i>>1)&1, z: i&1 xbit = (i >> 2) & 1 ybit = (i >> 1) & 1 zbit = i & 1 newmin = Vector3( self.min.x if xbit == 0 else mid.x, self.min.y if ybit == 0 else mid.y, self.min.z if zbit == 0 else mid.z) newmax = Vector3( self.max.x if xbit == 0 else mid.x, self.max.y if ybit == 0 else mid.y, self.max.z if zbit == 0 else mid.z) self.children.append(PointOctant(newmin, newmax)) self.data = None def redistribute(self, bias): """Move points to children.""" if self.data is None or self.children is None: return for i in range(len(self.data.points)): p = self.data.points[i] d = self.data.data[i] for child in self.children: if child.contains(p, bias): if child.data is None: child.data = PointData() child.data.points.append(p) child.data.data.append(d) break self.data = None def set(self, point, dataentry, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth, bias): """Insert or update a point.""" if currentdepth >= maxdepth: # Hard limit reached, append anyway or handle error if self.data is None: self.data = PointData() self.data.points.append(point) self.data.data.append(dataentry) return if self.children is None: # Leaf node if self.data is None: self.data = PointData() # Check for existing point for i in range(len(self.data.points)): if self.data.points[i].equals(point): self.data.data[i] = dataentry return # If full, split and redistribute if len(self.data.points) >= maxpoints: self.split() self.redistribute(bias) # Now recurse into children for child in self.children: if child.contains(point, bias): child.set(point, dataentry, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1, bias) return else: self.data.points.append(point) self.data.data.append(dataentry) else: # Internal node, recurse for child in self.children: if child.contains(point, bias): child.set(point, dataentry, maxpoints, maxdepth, currentdepth + 1, bias) return def findpoints(self, center, radius, bias, results): """Find points within radius.""" if self.data is None: return # Check if octant intersects sphere if not self.contains(center, radius): return if self.children is None: # Leaf node for i in range(len(self.data.points)): dsq = self.data.points[i].distancesquared(center) if dsq <= radius radius: results.append((self.data.points[i], self.data.data[i])) else: # Internal node for child in self.children: child.findpoints(center, radius, bias, results) Uses an octree (or kDTree) to accelerate spatial queries like nearest neighbor and radius search, avoiding O(N^2) brute-force comparisons. On a 1.42 million point indoor scan, building a cKDTree index took 417 ms. For 300k points, 16-Nearest Neighbor queries took 4.1 ms with the tree vs 5,071 ms brute force (1,224x speedup). Radius search (r=0.15m) took 26 ms vs 3,246 ms (126x speedup). Brute force is faster for single lookups, but the tree amortizes build cost over many queries. Used for normal estimation, segmentation, and ground filtering. Time Complexity: Average case for insertion, deletion, and spatial queries is O(\log N). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of points and the tree depth. No memory is allocated for empty space. Performance: On a 1.42M point scan, index build took 417 ms. 16-NN query on 300k points: 4.1 ms (tree) vs 5,071 ms (brute force). Strengths: Efficient for sparse data; supports dynamic updates (insert/remove/move). Limitations: maxDepth is a hard limit that may prevent perfect balancing for very dense clusters. Build cost is non-trivial for large static datasets if queries are few. The Point Octree is a standard recursive octree implementation for managing 3D points. It is widely used in point cloud processing for tasks requiring spatial indexing, such as normal estimation and segmentation. The specific implementation details (parallel arrays, bias-based containment) are derived from the sparse-octree library. sparse-octree module, https://github.com/vanruesc/sparse-octree, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Point Cloud Level of Detail: Octrees and Out-of-Core..., https://learngeodata.eu/point-cloud-level-of-detail-octree/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Spatial Hierarchies
head: Spatial Tree Structures
body: Spatial Hierarchies organize data into tree structures to accelerate point location via recursive search. They solve the problem of inefficient traversal in sparse scenes by reducing intersection tests. Unlike sibling methods such as Hierarchical Spatial Enumeration Optimization or Jiang et al. Acceleration Structure, they dynamically partition space rather than relying on fixed grids or image-order traversal. For the shared family principles, see Hierarchical Data Structures. Insertion into spatial hierarchies refers to the algorithmic process of adding primitives into an existing or growing hierarchical data structure. Unlike static build methods that analyze the entire scene at once, insertion methods process primitives one by one, allowing for incremental updates. This makes it suitable for dynamic environments, though it is highly sensitive to the order of insertion. It is chosen when scenes require frequent updates or when building from unsorted data. Spatial hierarchies such as octtrees, BSP trees, and KD trees were developed to optimize point location by recursive search. name: Insertion into Spatial Hierarchies
head: Incremental Insertion, Dynamic Insertion
body: Insertion into spatial hierarchies refers to the algorithmic process of adding primitives (such as triangles or voxels) into an existing or growing hierarchical data structure, such as an octree or bounding volume hierarchy (BVH). It solves the problem of maintaining spatial coherence and query efficiency in dynamic scenes or when building structures from unsorted data. Unlike static build methods that analyze the entire scene at once, insertion methods process primitives one by one, allowing for incremental updates. The primary distinction from sibling methods like Median-Cut or Surface Area Heuristic (SAH) builds is that insertion does not require a full re-sorting or re-partitioning of the dataset, making it suitable for dynamic environments, though it is highly sensitive to the order of insertion. The method varies significantly depending on the specific insertion strategy (e.g., recursive subdivision vs. iterative sifting). Below are the two primary approaches documented in the sources. This approach is typical for octrees where nodes are subdivided based on a primitive count threshold. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A node in the hierarchy, a primitive (e.g., bounding box or triangle). Output: The modified hierarchy with the primitive added. Data Structures: node: Contains a bounding volume (bound), a list of primitives (prims), a count of primitives (nprims), a depth level (depth), and child pointers. leaf(node): A boolean check returning true if the node has no children. Parameters: MAXDEPTH: The maximum allowed depth of the tree. Typical value: 16. MAXPRIMS: The maximum number of primitives allowed in a leaf before subdivision. Typical range: 2 to 8. Steps: 1. Check if the primitive overlaps with the current node's bounding volume. If not, terminate. 2. If the node is a leaf: If nprims exceeds MAXPRIMS AND depth is less than MAXDEPTH: Subdivide the node into children. Recursively insert the primitive into all children that overlap it. Else: Append the primitive to the node's primitive list. 3. If the node is not a leaf: Recursively insert the primitive into all children that overlap it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def insertrecursive(node, primitive): # Check overlap between primitive and node bounding volume if not overlap(node.bound, primitive): return if isleaf(node): # Leaf node logic if node.nprims > MAXPRIMS and node.depth < MAXDEPTH: # Subdivide if capacity exceeded and depth limit not reached subdivide(node) for child in node.children: insertrecursive(child, primitive) else: # Add to leaf list node.prims.append(primitive) node.nprims += 1 else: # Internal node logic for child in node.children: insertrecursive(child, primitive) This method builds a BVH by sifting primitives down to leaves, potentially restructuring the tree dynamically. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An existing BVH (initially an empty root), a new primitive. Output: The updated BVH. Steps: 1. Start with an empty root node. 2. For each new primitive: Let the primitive "sift" from the root towards the leaves. At each internal node, decide whether to: Attach the primitive to the current internal node's list. Pass the primitive to the left or right child subtree. If the primitive arrives at a leaf node: Replace the leaf with an internal node. Attach the existing primitive (from the leaf) and the new primitive as children of this new internal node. During sifting, update the bounding volumes of intermediate nodes to encompass the new primitive if necessary. Pitfalls: The order of insertion has a very large influence on the quality of the resulting tree. Poor ordering can lead to unbalanced trees with poor traversal performance. A dynamic insertion method introduced by Goldsmith and Salmon in 1987. It differs from static builds by inserting primitives one by one, sifting them to the bottom of the BVH. If a leaf is reached, it is split into an internal node with the old and new primitives as children. It is chosen for incremental scene updates or when the dataset is not available all at once. Its main limitation is sensitivity to insertion order, which affects tree balance and quality. Time Complexity: Insertion of a single primitive is O(D) where D is the depth of the tree, assuming constant-time overlap tests. However, frequent subdivisions and bounding volume updates can add overhead. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives and the tree depth. Dynamic splitting increases node count. Performance: Performance is highly dependent on the insertion order. Experiments show that sorted insertion or specific shuffling can significantly reduce the number of intersection tests per ray compared to random or model-load order. Strengths: Supports dynamic scenes; no need to rebuild the entire tree for new objects. Limitations: Tree quality degrades with poor insertion order; may require periodic rebalancing or rebuilding for optimal performance. The concept of inserting primitives into spatial hierarchies is fundamental to dynamic ray tracing and collision detection. The recursive subdivision approach is common in octree implementations for volume rendering and voxel data. The Iterative Insert method was specifically introduced by Goldsmith and Salmon in 1987 for building BVHs incrementally. It was designed to handle scenes where objects are added or removed over time, avoiding the cost of full rebuilds. name: Brick-of-Bricks Decomposition
head: Flat hierarchy of bricks
body: Brick-of-Bricks Decomposition is a storage format for hierarchical volume data where the volume is stored as a flat hierarchy of bricks of size n^3 to improve cache-coherence in volume traversal. It arises from not fully expanding an octree into single-voxel leaf nodes. It sets itself apart from fully expanded octrees by reducing pointer overhead and improving spatial locality for raycasting very large volumes. Inputs: An octree structure that is not fully expanded (i.e., non-leaf nodes may have children that are also non-leaf nodes, and leaf nodes may represent blocks of voxels rather than single voxels). Outputs: A flat array of bricks, where each brick is a contiguous block of n^3 voxels, along with an indexing scheme to map ray traversal steps to brick memory addresses. Data Structures: 1. Brick Array: A 1D array storing the voxel data. Each brick contains n^3 voxels. The layout is typically row-major or column-major within the brick, but the specific internal layout is not given in the sources. 2. Hierarchy Index: A structure mapping the octree topology to the flat brick array. This allows efficient calculation of the memory address for any voxel in the 8-neighborhood required for trilinear interpolation. Steps: 1. Construct Hierarchy: Build an octree where nodes are not necessarily expanded to single voxels. Non-leaf nodes store aggregate information (e.g., average, entropy, error metrics). 2. Flatten to Bricks: Traverse the octree and group nodes into bricks of size n^3. The value of n is not given in the sources. 3. Indexing Scheme: Implement an efficient indexing scheme to quickly find the memory address of voxels located in the 8-neighborhood required for trilinear interpolation. This scheme maps the hierarchical position (brick ID, offset within brick) to the flat array index. 4. Raycasting: During traversal, use the indexing scheme to access voxel data for shading and interpolation. Parameters: n: The side length of a brick in voxels. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: The indexing scheme must correctly handle bricks at the boundaries of the volume or irregular octree structures. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation requires access to 8 neighboring voxels. If a neighbor crosses a brick boundary, the indexing scheme must correctly locate the adjacent brick and the relative offset within it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getvoxelvalue(brickarray, hierarchyindex, brickid, x, y, z, n): """ Get the value of a voxel at local coordinates (x, y, z) in brickid. n is the brick size. """ # Calculate global offset within the brick # Assuming row-major order: x + ny + nnz offset = x + n y + n n z # Get the base address of the brick from the hierarchy index # The exact method to compute base address from hierarchy is not given baseaddress = hierarchyindex.getbrickbaseaddress(brickid) return brickarray[baseaddress + offset] def getneighborvalue(brickarray, hierarchyindex, currentbrickid, x, y, z, n, dx, dy, dz): """ Get the value of a neighbor voxel at (x+dx, y+dy, z+dz). Handles brick boundary crossing. """ nx, ny, nz = x + dx, y + dy, z + dz # Check if neighbor is within the current brick if 0 <= nx < n and 0 <= ny < n and 0 <= nz < n: return getvoxelvalue(brickarray, hierarchyindex, currentbrickid, nx, ny, nz, n) else: # Determine the adjacent brick ID # The exact logic for determining adjacent brick ID is not given adjacentbrickid = hierarchyindex.getadjacentbrickid(currentbrickid, dx, dy, dz) # Calculate local coordinates in the adjacent brick # This depends on the direction of the neighbor localx = (nx % n + n) % n localy = (ny % n + n) % n localz = (nz % n + n) % n return getvoxelvalue(brickarray, hierarchyindex, adjacentbrickid, localx, localy, localz, n) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves cache-coherence in volume traversal compared to fully expanded octrees. Strengths: Better cache performance for large volumes due to flat storage and reduced pointer overhead. Limitations: Requires an efficient indexing scheme for neighbor access, which can be complex to implement. Brick-of-Bricks Decomposition was introduced by Parker et al. for raycasting very large volumes. It is derived from the observation that octrees do not have to be balanced nor fully expanded into single-voxel leaf nodes.
