name: kD-Tree Traversal
head: kdt traversal
body: kD-Tree Traversal is a ray traversal algorithm for binary spatial partitioning structures where nodes split space using arbitrary axis-aligned planes, offering more flexible geometry adaptation than fixed-center octrees. It solves the problem of efficiently intersecting rays with complex, non-uniform geometry distributions by recursively descending a binary tree, determining which child node (near or far) the ray intersects relative to the splitting plane, and performing early termination upon finding the first hit. Unlike octrees, which subdivide at the center of cells, kD-trees allow subdivision in all directions via single splitting planes, adapting better to the distribution of geometry. Inputs: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), and a root node of the kD-tree. Outputs: The distance t{hit} to the closest intersection with a primitive in the scene, or \infty if no intersection is found. Data Structures: The kD-tree is a binary tree. Each node contains: 1. Splitting Plane: Defined by an axis index axis \in \{0, 1, 2\} (representing x, y, or z) and a split position s along that axis. 2. Children: Pointers to two child nodes (left and right). 3. Primitives: A list of geometry primitives (e.g., triangles) stored only in leaf nodes. 4. Bounding Box: Implicitly defined by the path from the root. The root encloses the entire scene. Each child's bounding box is the parent's box clipped by the splitting plane. Explicit storage of bounding boxes is not required for traversal if the split position and axis are known. Construction (Brief): 1. Given a cell (axis-aligned BBox) and a list of primitives, choose an axis-aligned splitting plane perpendicular to one coordinate axis. 2. Distribute geometry among the two children. Polygons straddling the plane must be assigned to both children. 3. Recurse until a stopping criterion is met (e.g., max depth, number of objects, or cost function threshold). 4. Splitting Plane Selection: To minimize traversal cost, use the Surface-Area-Heuristic (SAH). Try all 3 axes. For each axis, evaluate the cost function at finite points (borders of bounding boxes of primitives) using a plane sweep. Choose the axis and split position with the minimum cost. SAH Cost Function: C(B) = Area(B1) \cdot N(B1) + Area(B2) \cdot N(B2) where Area(Bi) is the surface area of child box i and N(Bi) is the number of triangles in child box i. This assumes rays have a far-away origin and hit the root bounding volume. Cost Ratio: The ratio of time for one ray-primitive test (ti) to one ray-splitting-plane intersection test (tt) is typically 80:1. Approximation: For large scenes (>500,000 polygons), sort polygons into buckets and evaluate SAH only at bucket borders. Traversal Algorithm (Recursive): The traversal determines the intersection of the ray with the splitting plane to identify the "near" child (containing the ray origin) and the "far" child. 1. Leaf Check: If the current node is a leaf, intersect the ray with each primitive in the node's object list. Discard intersections with t > t{max}. Return the closest intersection t{hit} if found, otherwise return \infty. 2. Splitting Plane Intersection: Calculate t{split}, the signed distance along the ray to the splitting plane of the current node. t{split} = \frac{s - o{axis}}{d{axis}} where s is the split position, o{axis} is the ray origin component along the split axis, and d{axis} is the ray direction component along the split axis. If d{axis} = 0, the ray is parallel to the plane; handle as a special case (e.g., treat as intersecting both or neither based on origin position). 3. Child Determination: If d{axis} > 0, the ray moves in the positive direction of the axis. The "near" child is the left child (if split position s is the boundary) or determined by comparing o{axis} to s. Specifically, the child containing the origin is determined by \mathbb{I}(o{axis} < s). Let near be the child containing the origin, and far be the other child. 4. Traversal Logic: If t{split} > t{max}: The splitting plane is beyond the current search range. Traverse only the near child with t{min}, t{max}. If t{split} < t{min}: The splitting plane is before the current search range. Traverse only the far child with t{min}, t{max}. Otherwise (t{min} \le t{split} \le t{max}): The ray intersects the splitting plane within the range. 1. Recursively traverse the near child with t{min}, t{split}. Let the result be t{hit}. 2. If t{hit} < t{split}: A hit was found in the near subtree before the splitting plane. Return t{hit} (early termination). 3. Else: Traverse the far child with t{split}, t{max}. Return the result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, node, tmin, tmax): """ Recursively traverse a kD-tree. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple raydirection: (x, y, z) tuple node: Current node object tmin: Minimum t value for intersection test tmax: Maximum t value for intersection test Returns: thit: Distance to closest intersection, or infinity if none """ # 1. Leaf Handling if node.isleaf: thit = infinity for primitive in node.primitives: t = intersectrayprimitive(rayorigin, raydirection, primitive) if tmin <= t < thit: thit = t return thit # 2. Splitting Plane Intersection axis = node.axis splitpos = node.splitposition oaxis = rayorigin[axis] daxis = raydirection[axis] # Handle parallel ray case if daxis == 0: # Ray is parallel to splitting plane # Determine which side the origin is on if oaxis < splitpos: nearchild = node.left farchild = node.right else: nearchild = node.right farchild = node.left # Traverse both? Or just the one containing origin? # Standard kD-tree traversal for parallel rays usually requires checking both # if the ray is inside the node's volume, but typically we treat tsplit as infinity # or handle via the logic below. # If daxis is 0, tsplit is undefined. # We can treat tsplit as infinity if the ray is moving away, or -infinity if towards. # However, a robust implementation checks if the ray origin is on one side. # If the ray is parallel, it will never cross the plane. # So we only traverse the child containing the origin? # No, if the ray is inside the node, it might exit the node's volume through a face # not defined by this split. But for binary tree traversal, we assume the split # divides the space. If parallel, it stays on one side. # Let's use the standard logic: if daxis == 0, tsplit is effectively infinity # if moving away from the split, or -infinity if moving towards. # But simpler: determine near/far based on origin position. # And since tsplit is not crossed, we only traverse the near child? # Actually, if the ray is parallel, it never crosses the plane, so it stays in one subtree. # So we only traverse the child containing the origin. thit = traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, nearchild, tmin, tmax) return thit tsplit = (splitpos - oaxis) / daxis # 3. Child Determination # Determine which child contains the ray origin if daxis > 0: if oaxis < splitpos: nearchild = node.left farchild = node.right else: nearchild = node.right farchild = node.left else: # daxis < 0 if oaxis < splitpos: nearchild = node.right farchild = node.left else: nearchild = node.left farchild = node.right # 4. Traversal Logic if tsplit > tmax: # Splitting plane is beyond the current search range return traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, nearchild, tmin, tmax) elif tsplit < tmin: # Splitting plane is before the current search range return traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, farchild, tmin, tmax) else: # Ray intersects the splitting plane within the range # Traverse near child first thitnear = traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, nearchild, tmin, tsplit) if thitnear < tsplit: # Hit found in near subtree before the splitting plane return thitnear # Traverse far child return traversekdtree(rayorigin, raydirection, farchild, tsplit, tmax) Optimized Iterative Traversal (for Shadow Rays): For shadow rays where any hit is sufficient, the tree can be transformed to allow pure Depth-First Search (DFS) using a linear array and skip pointers. 1. Transform the tree into a linear array where nodes are ordered for DFS. 2. Each node has a skipNode pointer to the next node to visit if the current node has no primitives or no hit. 3. Algorithm: python def traverseshadowray(ray, root): node = root stopnode = root.skipnode while node < stopnode: if intersectsraynode(ray, node): if node.hasprimitives: if intersectsrayprimitive(ray, node.primitives): return intersection node = node.skipnode return "no intersection" Oversized Object Handling: If objects are very large (e.g., in architectural models), they can hinder the finding of good splitting planes. 1. Before each splitting, filter out "oversized objects". 2. If many oversized objects exist, build a separate kD-tree for them. 3. Otherwise, store them in a simple list attached to the node or scene. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Straddling Polygons: In regular kD-trees, polygons straddling the splitting plane must be stored in both subtrees, leading to 2-3 times more pointers to triangles than triangles exist. This increases memory usage and traversal time. Precision: Floating-point precision issues can arise when calculating t{split}, especially when the ray is nearly parallel to the splitting plane (d{axis} \approx 0). Boundary Conditions: Ensure correct handling of ray origins exactly on the splitting plane. A variant of the kD-tree using 2 parallel splitting planes per node (also known as BoxTree or Bounding Interval Hierarchy, BIH). It solves the straddling polygon problem by ensuring that polygons are not stored in both subtrees; instead, the space between the two planes is shared. However, because the child boxes overlap, traversal cannot stop as soon as a hit is found in the 'near' subtree; the 'far' subtree must also be checked if the hit is within the overlap region. Time Complexity: Average case O(\log N) for balanced trees, but can degrade to O(N) for poorly constructed trees or specific ray directions. Traversal cost is dominated by the number of nodes visited. Memory Complexity: O(N) for N primitives, but with a constant factor overhead due to storing straddling polygons in multiple nodes (2-3x pointers). SKD-Trees reduce this overhead but increase node size (2 planes vs 1). Performance: Very fast ray traversal due to simple node structure (8 bytes per node: axis + split position). SAH construction is O(N \log N) or O(N^2) depending on implementation, but plane sweep optimization reduces it. Strengths: Adaptive subdivision, compact nodes, simple and fast traversal, good for static scenes. Limitations: Memory intensive due to straddling polygons, construction can be slow for large scenes, not ideal for dynamic scenes due to frequent rebuilds. When to use: Static scenes with complex geometry distribution where adaptive subdivision is beneficial. When not to use: Dynamic scenes requiring frequent updates, or when memory is extremely constrained. kD-trees were introduced as an acceleration structure for ray tracing to address the inflexibility of octrees, which always subdivide at the center of cells. The concept of kD-trees for spatial partitioning dates back to the 1970s, but their application to ray tracing and the use of SAH for construction were popularized in the 1990s and 2000s. The "best known method" for static scenes was highlighted in a Siggraph Course in 2006. The Spatial KD-Tree (SKD-Tree) or BIH variant was proposed in 1987, 2002, and 2006 to mitigate the straddling polygon issue. Advanced Computer Graphics, https://cgvr.cs.uni-bremen.de/teaching/cg213/folien/03%20-%20Acceleration%20data%20structures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Ray Template Traversal
head: Ray Template, Template-Based Rendering, Template-Based Volume Viewing, Template-based ray casting, Templated Ray Casting
body: Ray Template Traversal is a discrete ray casting technique for parallel projections (orthographic viewing) that accelerates rendering by storing the traversal steps through the volume as a single "ray template". Unlike standard DDA methods that compute step directions for every ray, this method precomputes a 26-connected line sequence once and reuses it for all parallel rays. It sets itself apart by requiring rays to be cast from a specific "base plane" within the volume rather than the image plane, ensuring uniform tessellation where each voxel is visited exactly once, followed by a 2D resampling step to map the result to the screen. The method relies on the fact that in parallel viewing, all rays have the same geometric form. The algorithm consists of three phases: Initialization, Ray Casting, and 2D Mapping. Inputs: Volume data grid V with dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Orthographic camera parameters: viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and the image plane extent. (Optional) Supersampling configuration (number of sub-pixel offsets). Outputs: Rendered image on the screen plane. 1. Ray Template (T): A list of discrete steps. Each step is an integer vector (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) where components are in \{-1, 0, 1\}. The template represents a 26-connected path through the voxel grid. For standard zero-order interpolation, the template contains integer voxel indices. For higher-order interpolation (multiple samples per voxel), the template may contain floating-point offsets or weights. 2. Base Plane: A 2D plane within the volume grid, parallel to one of the volume faces (e.g., z=0 or z=Nz-1), chosen such that it is the plane of the volume buffer most parallel to the image plane. 3. Base Image (I{base}): A 2D buffer storing the accumulated ray values (color/opacity) for each pixel in the base plane. Generate the ray template using a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or Bresenham-like algorithm. 1. Define the viewing direction \mathbf{d} = (dx, dy, dz). 2. Compute the step direction for each axis: \text{step}i = \begin{cases} +1 & \text{if } di > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } di < 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } di = 0 \end{cases} 3. Generate the sequence of voxel indices visited by a ray starting at (0,0,0) with direction \mathbf{d}. Store the relative increments (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z) between consecutive voxels in the list T. Note: If supersampling is used, multiple templates are generated, one for each relative sub-pixel origin position. Cast rays from the base plane to populate the base image. 1. Identify the base plane coordinates. If the image plane is defined by pixel coordinates (u, v), map these to the base plane. For example, if the base plane is z=0, the base plane coordinates correspond to the (x, y) positions of the rays. 2. For each pixel (u, v) in the image extent: a. Determine the starting voxel index \mathbf{p}{start} on the base plane corresponding to (u, v). b. Initialize accumulation variables: C{acc} = 0, \alpha{acc} = 0. c. Iterate through the steps in the template T: i. Update current voxel index: \mathbf{p}{curr} \leftarrow \mathbf{p}{curr} + T[k]. ii. Check if \mathbf{p}{curr} is within volume bounds. iii. Sample the volume value v{val} = V(\mathbf{p}{curr}). iv. Compute color c and opacity \alpha using transfer functions. v. Perform front-to-back compositing: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) vi. If \alpha{acc} exceeds a user-defined threshold, break. d. Store (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) in I{base}(u, v). Map the warped image from the base plane to the screen plane. 1. The base image I{base} is geometrically distorted relative to the final image because it was generated on a plane parallel to the volume face, not the image plane. 2. For each pixel (u, v) in the final image: a. Calculate the corresponding coordinates (u', v') in the base plane coordinate system using the inverse of the projection transformation. b. Sample I{base}(u', v') using bilinear interpolation. c. Assign the interpolated value to the final image pixel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raytemplatetraversal(volume, imagewidth, imageheight, viewdirection, baseplaneaxis): """ volume: 3D array [Nx, Ny, Nz] imagewidth, imageheight: int viewdirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) baseplaneaxis: 'x', 'y', or 'z', indicating which volume face is parallel to the image plane """ # Phase 1: Initialization # Generate the ray template (sequence of voxel steps) template = generateddatemplate(viewdirection) # Base plane is at z=0 for simplicity, mapping image (u,v) to volume (x,y,0) # We assume volume dimensions are large enough to cover the image extent baseimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] for row in baseimage: row[:] = [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0] imagewidth # Phase 2: Ray Casting for u in range(imagewidth): for v in range(imageheight): currentvoxel = (u, v, 0) acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for step in template: currentvoxel = (currentvoxel[0] + step[0], currentvoxel[1] + step[1], currentvoxel[2] + step[2]) if not (0 <= currentvoxel[0] < volume.shape[0] and 0 <= currentvoxel[1] < volume.shape[1] and 0 <= currentvoxel[2] < volume.shape[2]): break val = volume[currentvoxel[0]][currentvoxel[1]][currentvoxel[2]] color, alpha = applytransferfunctions(val) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor[0] += color[0] weight acccolor[1] += color[1] weight acccolor[2] += color[2] weight accalpha += alpha (1.0 - accalpha) if accalpha > 0.95: break baseimage[v][u] = (tuple(acccolor), accalpha) # Phase 3: 2D Mapping finalimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] for row in finalimage: row[:] = [(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0] imagewidth for u in range(imagewidth): for v in range(imageheight): baseu, basev = maptobaseplane(u, v, viewdirection, baseplaneaxis) finalimage[v][u] = bilinearinterpolate(baseimage, baseu, basev) return finalimage def generateddatemplate(direction): """ Generates a list of integer steps (dx, dy, dz) representing a 26-connected line. Uses a standard 3D DDA or Bresenham algorithm. """ dx, dy, dz = direction steps = [] cx, cy, cz = 0, 0, 0 # Standard 3D DDA to generate steps until a sufficient length is reached # This covers the maximum possible depth in the viewing direction maxsteps = 1000 # Sufficient for typical volume depths for in range(maxsteps): steps.append((dx, dy, dz)) # In a real implementation, DDA would compute exact boundary crossings # and append the correct step vector (e.g., (1,0,0), (1,1,0), etc.) # Here we assume direction components are normalized to step increments pass return steps def applytransferfunctions(val): # Standard transfer function lookup color = (val, val, val) alpha = 0.1 return color, alpha def maptobaseplane(u, v, viewdirection, baseplaneaxis): # Inverse orthographic projection: maps screen coords to base plane coords # Simplified affine transform return float(u), float(v) def bilinearinterpolate(image, u, v): # Clamp coordinates to valid range h, w = len(image), len(image[0]) u = max(0.0, min(float(w) - 1.0, u)) v = max(0.0, min(float(h) - 1.0, v)) u0, v0 = int(u), int(v) u1, v1 = u0 + 1, v0 + 1 du, dv = u - u0, v - v0 # Handle boundary cases u1 = min(u1, w - 1) v1 = min(v1, h - 1) p00 = image[v0][u0] p10 = image[v0][u1] p01 = image[v1][u0] p11 = image[v1][u1] # Interpolate color color = ( (1-du)(1-dv)p00[0][0] + du(1-dv)p10[0][0] + (1-du)dvp01[0][0] + dudvp11[0][0], (1-du)(1-dv)p00[0][1] + du(1-dv)p10[0][1] + (1-du)dvp01[0][1] + dudvp11[0][1], (1-du)(1-dv)p00[0][2] + du(1-dv)p10[0][2] + (1-du)dvp01[0][2] + dudvp11[0][2]) alpha = (1-du)(1-dv)p00[1] + du(1-dv)p10[1] + (1-du)dvp01[1] + dudvp11[1] return (color, alpha) Base Plane Selection: The base plane must be chosen parallel to one of the volume faces. If rays are cast from the image plane instead, voxels will be missed or double-counted. Supersampling: To support supersampling, multiple templates are required, one for each sub-pixel offset. For 4x supersampling, 4 templates are generated. Higher-Order Interpolation: For trilinear interpolation, the template can be extended to include floating-point weights for the 8 surrounding voxels, precomputed for the specific sub-pixel position. Illumination: The method supports on-the-fly shading (e.g., Phong model) during the ray casting phase. Empty Space: Adaptive variations can use different templates for empty and dense regions. Time Complexity: The template generation is O(1) (or O(L) where L is the template length, computed once). The ray casting phase is O(N{pixels} \cdot L), where L is the average number of steps per ray. Since the template is reused, the per-ray cost is reduced to simple integer additions and array lookups. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, plus O(L) for the template storage. The base image requires O(N{pixels}) memory. Performance: The method is significantly faster than naive DDA per ray. Yagel and Kaufman reported a 3x speedup over previous algorithms for a resolution image. Supersampling increases time linearly (e.g., 4 rays/pixel takes 4x longer). Strengths: Extremely efficient for parallel projections; avoids redundant floating-point calculations per ray; guarantees uniform sampling. Limitations: Only applicable to orthographic (parallel) projections; requires a 2D resampling step which adds complexity; not suitable for perspective views without modification. Ray Template Traversal was introduced by R. Yagel and A. Kaufman in "Template-Based Volume Viewing" (1992). It was developed to address the computational expense of discretizing every ray individually in parallel volume rendering. name: Ray Structure
head: Ray Data Structure, Ray Representation, Ray3D
body: A Ray Structure is a geometric primitive class representing a ray in 3D space, defined by an origin point and a direction vector. It serves as the fundamental unit for image-order volume rendering traversal, providing methods to evaluate points along the ray path. It differs from sibling structures like the Ray Bundle by managing a single ray's state rather than batched metadata, and from the Hit Record Structure by representing the query vector rather than the intersection result. Inputs and Outputs: The structure takes an origin \mathbf{o} and a direction \mathbf{v} as inputs. It outputs a point \mathbf{p} on the ray for a given scalar parameter t, or a normalized direction vector. Data Structures and Layout: The core layout consists of two 3D vectors: 1. orig: The ray origin, typically a point3 or vec3 type (3 floating-point values). 2. dir: The ray direction, a vec3 type (3 floating-point values). Some implementations extend this with additional metadata for traversal context: depth: An unsigned 32-bit integer (u32) representing traversal depth. time: A 32-bit float (f32) for time-varying scenes. rangemin / rangemax: Floating-point bounds for the valid parameter t. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Default constructor: Initialize orig to (0,0,0) and dir to (0,0,-1). Parameterized constructor: Accept orig and dir. Normalize dir to unit length. Set rangemin to 10^{-5} and rangemax to 10^{30}. Length setting: If a specific ray length L is required, normalize dir and scale it: \mathbf{v}{new} = \frac{\mathbf{v}}{\|\mathbf{v}\|} \times L. 2. Point Evaluation: Compute the point at parameter t using the linear equation: \mathbf{p}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{v} This operation assumes \mathbf{v} is normalized if t represents Euclidean distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Ray: def init(self, origin=None, direction=None): if origin is None: self.orig = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: self.orig = list(origin) if direction is None: self.dir = [0.0, 0.0, -1.0] else: self.dir = list(direction) self.normalizedirection() # Default range bounds self.rangemin = 1e-5 self.rangemax = 1e30 def normalizedirection(self): """Normalize direction vector to unit length.""" x, y, z = self.dir length = (x2 + y2 + z2)0.5 if length > 0: self.dir[0] /= length self.dir[1] /= length self.dir[2] /= length def setraylength(self, length): """Scale direction vector to a specific Euclidean length.""" x, y, z = self.dir currentlength = (x2 + y2 + z2)0.5 if currentlength > 0: scale = length / currentlength self.dir[0] = scale self.dir[1] = scale self.dir[2] = scale def at(self, t): """ Compute point on ray at parameter t. Formula: p = orig + t dir """ return [ self.orig[0] + t self.dir[0], self.orig[1] + t self.dir[1], self.orig[2] + t self.dir[2] ] def getpoint(self, t): """Alias for at(t).""" return self.at(t) Parameters: RAYMINT: Minimum valid t value, typically 10^{-5} to avoid self-intersection or precision errors. RAYMAXT: Maximum valid t value, typically 10^{30} or scene bounds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction: If the input direction is (0,0,0), normalization fails. Implementations should guard against this or treat it as a degenerate ray. Precision: Using unnormalized directions with t as distance leads to incorrect sampling positions. Always normalize or use t as a scalar multiplier of the raw vector. Range Clipping: In traversal, t must be clamped to [range\min, range\max] to prevent sampling outside the volume or at the camera plane. A Ray Bundle is a container data structure that groups ray origins, directions, and associated sampling parameters (sample points and lengths) into a single object, typically implemented as a collection of aligned tensors. It solves the problem of managing batched ray data for volume rendering and neural rendering pipelines, allowing efficient vectorized operations and memory transfers. It differs from a RayBatch container by explicitly bundling sampling metadata (sample points/lengths) alongside geometric ray data, and from a Hit Record Structure by focusing on input ray generation rather than output intersection results. The RayBatch container is a NumPy-style data structure for storing and sampling ray batches during training, supporting efficient indexing, slicing, and conversion to Mitsuba tensor types. It provides batch-level operations and explicit conversion logic to Mitsuba 3, distinguishing it from the generic Ray Structure and the Ray Bundle. A hit record structure stores the geometric and material properties of a ray-surface intersection. It passes intersection context (position, normal, distance, and material reference) from traversal to shading. It is distinguished from sibling structures like the Ray Bundle or RayBatch container by focusing on the state of a single intersection event rather than the propagation or batching of rays themselves. Plücker Ray Embedding parameterizes a 3D ray using Plücker coordinates to create a scale-, position-, and focal-length-independent representation. It maps a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{v} into a 16-dimensional multivector, enabling robust modulation of camera poses to image features in neural rendering frameworks. Unlike extrinsic/intrinsic matrix parameterizations, this method relies on the cross product \mathbf{o} \times \mathbf{v}. The Z-list-buffer Ray Representation is a volume data storage format that stores voxel data as an array of rays, where each ray contains a list of sample points (position and normal) defining regions. It replaces traditional scalar fields to reduce storage and preserve sharp features, supporting any cell-based triangulation method. It is distinguished from sibling structures by its specific generation method using orthographic projection and a Z-buffer with a Z-list, which is faster than modified ray tracing for axis-aligned rays. Ray Segments Spec is a data structure designed to represent ray segments efficiently, particularly in the context of volume rendering and neural radiance fields. It stores segment values, endpoint flags, validity, chunking information, and ray mappings. It differs from sibling structures like Ray Bundle by focusing on explicit segment-level metadata rather than raw ray parameters, and from RayBatch container by providing granular control over segment validity and chunking. Definition: Core geometric primitives used for ray tracing and scene representation: Ray (origin, direction, depth, time), DifferentialRay (extends Ray with perturbation origins/directions), and BBox (min/max points). Layout: Ray: ori (Point3): 12 bytes. dir (Vec3): 24 bytes. depth (u32): 4 bytes. time (f32): 4 bytes. Total: 44 bytes. BBox: minP, maxP (Point3). Initialized to {INFINITY, INFINITY, INFINITY} and {-INFINITY, -INFINITY, -INFINITY} respectively. Code: Point evaluation follows the standard linear interpolation \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v}.(Note: No dedicated article exists for this variant, so it is listed here as a minor variant without a specific link, or linked to the closest sibling if applicable. As per instructions, minor variants have no article of their own.) Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: O(1) per ray. Typically 24 bytes (origin + direction) or 44 bytes with metadata. Time: Point evaluation is O(1), involving 3 multiplications and 3 additions. Measured Performance: Performance is dominated by the cost of the evaluation function when called millions of times during traversal. Vectorization (SIMD) benefits are realized when using Ray Bundle or RayBatch container structures that align multiple rays in memory. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Minimal memory footprint, simple arithmetic, hardware-friendly layout. Limitations: Does not handle batch operations natively (requires external containers), lacks metadata for complex traversal states (e.g., hit records). When to use: Use for single-ray queries, basic traversal kernels, or as a building block for batched structures. Avoid for neural rendering pipelines requiring batched tensor operations; use Ray Bundle instead. The Ray Structure is a fundamental concept in computer graphics, originating from standard ray tracing literature. It is widely implemented in open-source volume rendering projects such as cpuvoxelraycaster, lidar-sphere-tracing, and volumerenderer. Variants with extended metadata (depth, time) are found in real-time rendering demos like SVODemo. name: Ray Bundle
head: Ray Bundle Data Structure, Ray Bundle Generation
body: A Ray Bundle is a container data structure that groups ray origins, directions, and associated sampling parameters (sample points and lengths) into a single object, typically implemented as a collection of aligned tensors. It solves the problem of managing batched ray data for volume rendering and neural rendering pipelines, allowing efficient vectorized operations and memory transfers. It differs from a RayBatch container by explicitly bundling sampling metadata (sample points/lengths) alongside geometric ray data, and from a Hit Record Structure by focusing on input ray generation rather than output intersection results. Inputs: Tensors for ray origins, ray directions, sample points along rays, and distances of sample points from origins. Outputs: A structured object (class instance) containing these tensors, supporting indexing, reshaping, and device transfer. The RayBundle class wraps four per-ray tensors: 1. origins: Tensor of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of rays. Stores the 3D coordinates of ray origins. 2. directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3). Stores the normalized direction vectors of the rays. 3. samplepoints: Tensor of shape (N, n{pts}, 3), where n{pts} is the number of sample points per ray. Stores the 3D coordinates of sample points along each ray. 4. samplelengths: Tensor of shape (N, n{pts}, 1). Stores the distance of each sample point from the ray origin. 1. Initialization: Create a RayBundle instance by passing the four tensors (origins, directions, samplepoints, samplelengths) to the constructor. 2. Indexing: Access a subset of rays using getitem(idx). This returns a new RayBundle with sliced tensors for all four fields at index idx. 3. Reshaping: Use the reshape method to change the batch dimensions while preserving the last dimensions: origins and directions to (args, 3), sample points to (args, n{pts}, 3), and sample lengths to (args, n{pts}, 1). 4. Viewing: Use the view method to return a new RayBundle with viewed tensors, preserving the same last dimension constraints as reshape. 5. Replacement: Use replace(kwargs) to update specific attributes (e.g., origins) and return the modified bundle. 6. Device Transfer: Use to(device) to move all tensors to a specified device (e.g., GPU). 7. Property Access: shape: Returns origins.shape[:-1], representing the batch dimensions. sampleshape: Returns samplepoints.shape[:-1], representing the batch and sample dimensions. device: Returns samplepoints.device. Camera-Space Directions: For a camera with width W, height H, and focal length f, pixel coordinates (i, j) are used to compute camera-space directions: x = \frac{i - W/2}{f} y = -\frac{j - H/2}{f} z = -1 World-Space Directions: Transform camera-space directions to world space using the rotation matrix R from the camera-to-world transform, then normalize: \mathbf{d}{world} = \text{normalize}(R \cdot [x, y, z]^T) Ray Origins: Set to the camera position extracted from the camera-to-world matrix. N: Number of rays (batch size). Not given in the sources. n{pts}: Number of sample points per ray. Not given in the sources. W, H: Image width and height. Not given in the sources. f: Focal length. Not given in the sources. Precision: Tensor operations assume standard floating-point precision. No specific pitfalls mentioned. Boundaries: The reshape and view methods must preserve the last dimensions (3 for origins/directions/sample points, 1 for sample lengths). Mismatched dimensions will cause errors. Degenerate Input: Empty tensors or mismatched batch sizes between origins, directions, sample points, and sample lengths will cause initialization or indexing failures. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch class RayBundle: def init(self, origins: torch.Tensor, directions: torch.Tensor, samplepoints: torch.Tensor, samplelengths: torch.Tensor): """ Initialize a RayBundle with ray data. Args: origins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) directions: Tensor of shape (N, 3) samplepoints: Tensor of shape (N, npts, 3) samplelengths: Tensor of shape (N, npts, 1) """ self.origins = origins self.directions = directions self.samplepoints = samplepoints self.samplelengths = samplelengths @property def shape(self): """Returns the batch dimensions.""" return self.origins.shape[:-1] @property def sampleshape(self): """Returns the batch and sample dimensions.""" return self.samplepoints.shape[:-1] @property def device(self): """Returns the device of the samplepoints tensor.""" return self.samplepoints.device def getitem(self, idx): """Returns a new RayBundle with sliced tensors.""" return RayBundle( origins=self.origins[idx], directions=self.directions[idx], samplepoints=self.samplepoints[idx], samplelengths=self.samplelengths[idx]) def reshape(self, args): """Reshapes tensors, preserving last dimensions.""" neworigins = self.origins.reshape(args, 3) newdirections = self.directions.reshape(args, 3) newsamplepoints = self.samplepoints.reshape(args, self.samplepoints.shape[-2], 3) newsamplelengths = self.samplelengths.reshape(args, self.samplelengths.shape[-2], 1) return RayBundle(neworigins, newdirections, newsamplepoints, newsamplelengths) def view(self, args): """Views tensors, preserving last dimensions.""" neworigins = self.origins.view(args, 3) newdirections = self.directions.view(args, 3) newsamplepoints = self.samplepoints.view(args, self.samplepoints.shape[-2], 3) newsamplelengths = self.samplelengths.view(args, self.samplelengths.shape[-2], 1) return RayBundle(neworigins, newdirections, newsamplepoints, newsamplelengths) def replace(self, kwargs): """Updates attributes based on kwargs.""" for key, value in kwargs.items(): if hasattr(self, key): setattr(self, key, value) return self def to(self, device): """Moves all tensors to the specified device.""" return RayBundle( origins=self.origins.to(device), directions=self.directions.to(device), samplepoints=self.samplepoints.to(device), samplelengths=self.samplelengths.to(device)) A 2D temporary buffer used to store slanted Projection Ray Planes (PRPs), allowing parallel access for storing horizontal beams and parallel retrieval of vertical viewing rays. It is physically divided into n modules and diagonally skewed to allow conflict-free writing of an entire horizontal beam and conflict-free retrieval of an entire vertical ray. The slanted PRP is loaded one beam at a time, from closest to furthest, with each beam shifted left or right to align viewing rays vertically. Retrieved vertical rays are transferred to the Ray Projection Tree (RPT), shifting rays during transfer to position the closest voxel correctly. Pitfalls include neighborhood access (requiring multiple parallel 2DSBs and processing rays only after the succeeding slanted PRP is loaded) and pipeline overlap (using a fourth plane to load the next slanted PRP while three extract the 27-voxel cube). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of rays N and sample points per ray n{pts}, specifically O(N \cdot n{pts}) for sample points and lengths, and O(N) for origins and directions. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with batch size N and number of samples n{pts}. Strengths: Efficient vectorized operations, easy indexing and reshaping, device transfer support. Limitations: Requires careful dimension management during reshape/view operations. When to Use: When managing batched ray data for volume rendering or neural rendering pipelines. When Not to Use: When individual ray processing is required without batching, or when memory constraints are tight and N \cdot n{pts} is very large. The Ray Bundle data structure is commonly used in modern neural rendering and volume rendering frameworks, such as those based on VolSDF and NeRF. It facilitates the efficient handling of ray data for differentiable rendering. The 2D Skewed Buffer variant originates from hardware-based volume visualization systems for arbitrary parallel projection, designed to handle slanted projection ray planes efficiently. omkarchittar/NeuralSurfaces, https://github.com/omkarchittar/NeuralSurfaces, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) samirangode/Volume-Rendering-and-Neural-Radiance-Fields, https://github.com/samirangode/Volume-Rendering-and-Neural-Radiance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, https://github.com/Fhz2346/Neural-Volume-Rendering-and-Surface-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) InanXR/FLASH, https://github.com/InanXR/FLASH, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) An Extended Volume Visualization System for Arbitrary Parallel Projection, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh92/064-069, fetched 2026-10-29

name: RayBatch container
head: RayBatch
body: The RayBatch container is a NumPy-style data structure for storing and sampling ray batches during training, supporting efficient indexing, slicing, and conversion to Mitsuba tensor types. It provides batch-level operations and explicit conversion logic to Mitsuba 3, distinguishing it from the generic Ray Structure and the Ray Bundle. Inputs and Outputs: Input: NumPy arrays for ray origins, directions, and colors, plus optional arrays for masks, sensor indices, and pixel coordinates. Output: A RayBatch object that supports indexing and slicing, and a method to convert its contents into Mitsuba mi.Ray3f and mi.Color3f objects. Data Structures: The container holds the following fields, all sharing a common batch dimension N: origins: np.ndarray, shape (N, 3). directions: np.ndarray, shape (N, 3), normalized. colors: np.ndarray, shape (N, 3). masks: np.ndarray, shape (N, 1) or (N,), optional. sensorindices: np.ndarray, shape (N,), optional. pixelcoords: np.ndarray, shape (N, 2), optional. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Construct the container by passing the NumPy arrays for origins, directions, and colors. 2. Validation: Verify that origins and directions have shape (N, 3), colors has shape (N, 3), and masks (if present) have shape (N, 1) or (N,). 3. Sampling: To sample a subset of rays, generate random indices using rng.choice(self.numrays, size=numrays, replace=False) and index the internal arrays. 4. Conversion: Convert the batch to Mitsuba types by mapping origins to mi.Point3f, directions to mi.Vector3f, and colors to mi.Color3f. Formulas: Ray count: N = \text{origins.shape}[0]. Parameters: numrays: Implicitly defined by the batch dimension N. replace: Boolean for sampling (default False). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shape Mismatches: If origins, directions, and colors do not share the same batch dimension N, assertion errors will be raised. Mask Reshaping: Masks provided as 1D arrays (N,) must be explicitly reshaped to (N, 1) before assignment to avoid broadcasting issues. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from typing import Tuple, Optional import mitsuba as mi class RayBatch: def init( self, origins: np.ndarray, directions: np.ndarray, colors: np.ndarray, masks: Optional[np.ndarray] = None, sensorindices: Optional[np.ndarray] = None, pixelcoords: Optional[np.ndarray] = None): assert origins.shape == (origins.shape[0], 3), "Origins must be (N, 3)" assert directions.shape == (directions.shape[0], 3), "Directions must be (N, 3)" assert colors.shape == (colors.shape[0], 3), "Colors must be (N, 3)" assert origins.shape[0] == directions.shape[0] == colors.shape[0], "Batch dimensions must match" self.numrays = origins.shape[0] self.origins = origins self.directions = directions self.colors = colors if masks is not None: if masks.ndim == 1: masks = masks.reshape(-1, 1) assert masks.shape[0] == self.numrays, "Mask batch dimension must match" self.masks = masks self.sensorindices = sensorindices self.pixelcoords = pixelcoords def sample(self, numrays: int, rng: np.random.Generator) -> 'RayBatch': indices = rng.choice(self.numrays, size=numrays, replace=False) neworigins = self.origins[indices] newdirections = self.directions[indices] newcolors = self.colors[indices] newmasks = self.masks[indices] if self.masks is not None else None newsensorindices = self.sensorindices[indices] if self.sensorindices is not None else None newpixelcoords = self.pixelcoords[indices] if self.pixelcoords is not None else None return RayBatch( origins=neworigins, directions=newdirections, colors=newcolors, masks=newmasks, sensorindices=newsensorindices, pixelcoords=newpixelcoords) def tomitsuba(self) -> Tuple[mi.Ray3f, mi.Color3f]: originsmi = mi.TensorXf(self.origins) directionsmi = mi.TensorXf(self.directions) rays = mi.Ray3f( o=mi.Point3f(originsmi[:, 0], originsmi[:, 1], originsmi[:, 2]), d=mi.Vector3f(directionsmi[:, 0], directionsmi[:, 1], directionsmi[:, 2])) colorsmi = mi.Color3f( mi.Float(self.colors[:, 0]), mi.Float(self.colors[:, 1]), mi.Float(self.colors[:, 2])) return rays, colorsmi Not given in the sources. name: Hit Record Structure
head: FrontFace Determination, Hit Data Structure, Hit Record & Face Normal Orientation, HitRecord, Ray Hit Data Structure, RayHit
body: A hit record structure stores the geometric and material properties of a ray-surface intersection. It passes intersection context (position, normal, distance, and material reference) from traversal to shading. It is distinguished from sibling structures like the Ray Bundle or RayBatch container by focusing on the state of a single intersection event rather than the propagation or batching of rays themselves. Input: A ray (origin, direction), a geometric primitive (e.g., sphere, plane, splat), and optionally a material reference. Output: A populated Hit Record instance containing the hit point, oriented normal, distance along the ray, and material data. Sources define the exact field layouts differently based on the rendering context: Gaussian Splats: origin (THREE.Vector3), normal (THREE.Vector3), distance (number, initialized to 0), splatIndex (number, initialized to 0). Solid Primitives: point (Point3), normal (Vector3), t (double), frontface (bool), material (Material), transmittance (double, initialized to 1.0), istransmission (bool). Go Tracer: P (Vector), Normal (Vector), T (float64), FrontFace (bool), Mat (Material). Voxel Octrees: color (Color), voxelObjPos (Vector3), voxelObjSize (float), objPos (Vector3), worldPos (Vector3), attributesPtr (int), faceNormal (Vector3). 1. Compute the dot product of the ray direction D and the geometric outward normal N{\text{out}}. 2. Set frontface to true if N{\text{out}} \cdot D < 0. 3. Set the oriented normal N to N{\text{out}} if frontface is true, otherwise set N to -N{\text{out}}. Formula: N = \begin{cases} N{\text{out}} & \text{if } N{\text{out}} \cdot D < 0 \\ -N{\text{out}} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where N{\text{out}} is the geometric outward normal and D is the ray direction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Vector3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def negate(self): return Vector3(-self.x, -self.y, -self.z) def copy(self, other): self.x = other.x self.y = other.y self.z = other.z class HitRecord: def init(self): self.point = Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.normal = Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) self.distance = 0.0 self.frontface = False self.material = None self.transmittance = 1.0 self.istransmission = False self.splatIndex = 0 def setfacenormal(self, raydirection, outwardnormal): dotproduct = raydirection.dot(outwardnormal) self.frontface = dotproduct < 0 if self.frontface: self.normal.copy(outwardnormal) else: self.normal.copy(outwardnormal.negate()) def set(self, origin, normal, distance, splatindex=0): self.point.copy(origin) self.normal.copy(normal) self.distance = distance self.splatIndex = splatindex def clone(self): hitclone = HitRecord() hitclone.point.copy(self.point) hitclone.normal.copy(self.normal) hitclone.distance = self.distance hitclone.splatIndex = self.splatIndex hitclone.frontface = self.frontface hitclone.material = self.material hitclone.transmittance = self.transmittance hitclone.istransmission = self.istransmission return hitclone Precision: The dot product comparison dotproduct < 0 is sensitive to floating-point precision. In degenerate cases where the ray is parallel to the surface, the dot product is near zero. Boundaries: The distance (t) must be checked against tmin and tmax before populating the Hit Record to ensure the hit is within the valid ray segment. Initialization: The transmittance field is initialized to 1.0 (fully opaque/start of path). The distance and splatIndex fields are initialized to 0. A variant used in voxel-based ray tracers where hit state routing relies on sentinel values rather than explicit material pointers. It distinguishes between analytic primitives, TLAS instances, and world voxels by checking ray.mvoxel against specific bit flags (e.g., 0x40000000 for bit 30, 0x20000000 for bit 29, 0x80000000 for bit 31). Choose this variant when working with hybrid acceleration structures that encode primitive types directly in traversal data to avoid pointer indirection during shading. Each dispatch path returns a BounceResult containing direct lighting, throughput scaling, and a continuation flag for iterative trace loops. Time Complexity: O(1) per intersection for record population and front-face determination, as it processes only the closest hit found by traversal. Memory Complexity: O(1) per record; size varies by context (e.g., adding splatIndex adds 4–8 bytes, transmittance adds 8 bytes). Strengths: Decouples traversal from shading and guarantees consistent normal orientation for lighting calculations. Limitations: Storing full records for all potential hits before discarding non-closest intersections can cause memory bandwidth bottlenecks on GPUs; early-z or discard logic is often required. When to use: Standard in any ray-traced or ray-marched renderer requiring surface properties for shading. When not to use: Not needed for pure volume rendering without surface intersections or when using implicit shading without explicit hit records. name: Plücker Ray Embedding
body: Plücker Ray Embedding parameterizes a 3D ray using Plücker coordinates to create a representation independent of scale, camera position, and focal length. It maps a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{v} into a 16-dimensional multivector using the cross product between the camera location and ray direction. Unlike extrinsic/intrinsic matrix parameterizations, this method enables robust modulation of camera poses to image features in neural rendering frameworks. Inputs: plueckerray: Tensor of shape [..., 6]. The last dimension contains the ray parameters, with indices 0–2 representing the cross product components and indices 3–5 representing the direction \mathbf{v}. Outputs: multivector: Tensor of shape [..., 16]. Data Structures: The multivector is a 16-element vector where specific indices store the direction and permuted/negated cross product components. Steps: 1. Initialize mv as a zero tensor of shape [..., 16] with the same device and dtype as plueckerray. 2. Assign the direction vector \mathbf{v} (from input indices 3:6) to multivector indices 5:8. 3. Assign the cross product components to multivector indices 8, 9, 10 using the explicit index mapping: index 8 receives input index 2, index 9 receives negative input index 1, and index 10 receives input index 0. 4. Indices 0–4 and 11–15 remain zero as per initialization and lack of assignment in the source. Extracting Plücker Ray from Multivector: To reverse the embedding, concatenate mv[..., 10], -mv[..., 9], mv[..., 8], and mv[..., 5:8] to reconstruct the original 6D ray tensor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def embedplueckerray(plueckerray: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Embeds a ray [mx, my, mz, vx, vy, vz] into a 16D multivector. Follows the index mapping from. """ shape = plueckerray.shape[:-1] mv = torch.zeros(shape, 16, device=plueckerray.device, dtype=plueckerray.dtype) # Assign direction v (input indices 3:6) to multivector indices 5:8 mv[..., 5] = plueckerray[..., 3] mv[..., 6] = plueckerray[..., 4] mv[..., 7] = plueckerray[..., 5] # Assign cross product components via explicit index mapping mv[..., 8] = plueckerray[..., 2] # input index 2 mv[..., 9] = -plueckerray[..., 1] # negative input index 1 mv[..., 10] = plueckerray[..., 0] # input index 0 return mv def extractplueckerray(mv: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Extracts ray [mx, my, mz, vx, vy, vz] from 16D multivector. Follows the extraction logic from. """ mx = mv[..., 10] my = -mv[..., 9] mz = mv[..., 8] vx = mv[..., 5] vy = mv[..., 6] vz = mv[..., 7] return torch.cat([mx.unsqueeze(-1), my.unsqueeze(-1), mz.unsqueeze(-1), mv[..., 5:8]], dim=-1) Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. A collection of rays sharing a common origin or structure. Chosen when processing multiple rays simultaneously for batched rendering. See Ray Bundle. A data structure for batching ray parameters for efficient GPU processing. Chosen for high-throughput rasterization or ray marching. See RayBatch container. Stores intersection details (point, normal, distance) for a ray. Chosen when ray-object intersection results need to be retained for shading. See Hit Record Structure. Defines sub-segments of a ray for adaptive traversal. Chosen when ray length varies significantly or adaptive sampling is required. See Ray Segments Spec. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Invariant to camera scale, position, and focal length. Facilitates feature fusion in multi-view transformers. Limitations: The specific index mapping for the cross product components differs from the standard geometric formula \mathbf{o} \times \mathbf{v} = (oy vz - oz vy, oz vx - ox vz, ox vy - oy vx), requiring strict adherence to the source's layout. The 16D vector is sparse, with only 6 elements populated. When to use: When integrating camera rays into neural networks that require geometric invariance. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Plücker coordinates provide a homogeneous representation of lines in 3D space. In computer vision and rendering, they are used to parameterize rays independently of the camera's intrinsic and extrinsic parameters. This allows for robust feature fusion across multiple views in neural reconstruction models, such as the Fusion ViT described in. The specific 16D multivector embedding and index mapping originates from the GAI-GS repository, while the theoretical motivation for using Plücker rays for scale/position invariance is detailed in X-GRM. name: Z-list-buffer Ray Representation
head: Z-list-buffer, Ray Representation, Ray-Rep, Array of Rays
body: The Z-list-buffer Ray Representation is a volume data storage format that stores voxel data as an array of rays, where each ray contains a list of sample points (position and normal) defining regions. It replaces traditional scalar fields to reduce storage and preserve sharp features, supporting any cell-based triangulation method. It is distinguished from sibling structures by its specific generation method using orthographic projection and a Z-buffer with a Z-list, which is faster than modified ray tracing for axis-aligned rays. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Hermite data (position and normal) at a fine resolution grid of size nk \times nk \times nk. Output: Three arrays of rays (one for each axis: x, y, z), where each array has a resolution of (nk + 1) \times (nk + 1). Data Structures: 1. Sample: A structure containing: position: 3D point (x, y, z). normal: 3D vector (nx, ny, nz). 2. Ray: A list of Sample objects. Samples are classified as left bounding (marks the left boundary of a region) or right bounding (marks the right boundary of a region). A pair of samples defines a region: the first sample is the left boundary, the second is the right boundary. 3. Ray Array: An array of Ray objects. The resolution is (nk + 1) \times (nk + 1). Three such arrays are maintained, one for each axis. Algorithm Steps: 1. Acquire Hermite data at a uniform nk \times nk \times nk grid resolution. 2. Shoot axis-aligned rays along the x, y, and z axes. 3. For each ray, compute all intersection points with the volume data and their corresponding normals. 4. Store these intersection points as Sample objects in the corresponding Ray list. 5. Classify each sample as left or right bounding based on the region it defines. 6. Use orthographic projection and a Z-buffer with a Z-list for each entry to perform scan conversion, which is faster than modified ray tracing for this specific axis-aligned case. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatezlistbuffer(hermitedata, nk): """ Generates Z-list-buffer Ray Representation from Hermite data. Args: hermitedata: 3D grid of (position, normal) pairs at resolution nk x nk x nk. nk: Integer, finest resolution of the input grid. Returns: raysx, raysy, raysz: Three 2D arrays of Ray objects, each of size (nk + 1) x (nk + 1). """ # Initialize arrays of rays. Each ray is a list of samples. # Resolution is (nk + 1) x (nk + 1) raysx = [[[] for in range(nk + 1)] for in range(nk + 1)] raysy = [[[] for in range(nk + 1)] for in range(nk + 1)] raysz = [[[] for in range(nk + 1)] for in range(nk + 1)] # Step 1 & 2: Shoot axis-aligned rays and compute intersections # Note: The source specifies using orthographic projection and Z-buffer with Z-list # for faster scan conversion than modified ray tracing. # This implies a rasterization-like approach rather than analytical ray marching. # For each axis, we iterate through the grid cells to determine ray intersections. # Since the input is Hermite data (implicit surface), we must find where rays intersect the surface. # Example for X-axis rays: # Rays are parallel to X-axis. For each (y, z) coordinate in the (nk + 1) x (nk + 1) grid: for y in range(nk + 1): for z in range(nk + 1): # Define the ray: origin (xmin, y, z), direction (1, 0, 0) # xmin and xmax are the bounds of the volume rayorigin = (0.0, y, z) # Assuming normalized coordinates or grid indices raydirection = (1.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Find all intersection points of this ray with the volume defined by hermitedata # This step typically involves evaluating the implicit function or using the Hermite data # to determine surface crossings. intersections = findintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, hermitedata) # Step 3 & 4: Store intersection points and normals as samples raysamples = [] for i, point in enumerate(intersections): # point is (x, y, z) # normal is computed from Hermite data at the intersection normal = computenormal(point, hermitedata) # Step 5: Classify as left or right bounding # In 1D, samples alternate: left, right, left, right... # The first sample in the list is the left boundary of the first region. if i % 2 == 0: sampletype = "leftbounding" else: sampletype = "rightbounding" sample = { "position": point, "normal": normal, "type": sampletype } raysamples.append(sample) # Store in the corresponding ray array raysx[y][z] = raysamples # Repeat for Y and Z axes similarly #... (code for Y and Z axes omitted for brevity, following same logic) return raysx, raysy, raysz def findintersections(rayorigin, raydirection, hermitedata): """ Finds all intersection points of a ray with the volume defined by hermitedata. This is a placeholder for the specific intersection algorithm, which may involve evaluating the implicit function derived from Hermite data. """ # Implementation detail: This function would evaluate the implicit surface # defined by the Hermite data along the ray and find roots. # The source notes that this is done via scan conversion using orthographic projection # and a Z-buffer with a Z-list, which suggests a rasterization-based approach # rather than analytical root finding. # However, the core concept is finding the intersection points. return [] # Placeholder def computenormal(point, hermitedata): """ Computes the normal vector at a given point using the Hermite data. """ # Implementation detail: The normal is typically the gradient of the implicit function. # Hermite data provides both position and normal, so interpolation might be used. return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Placeholder Parameters: nk: The finest resolution of the input Hermite data grid. Typical values are not specified, but the example uses a 512^3 grid for comparison. Average number of samples per ray: ~2.86 for a dragon model, ~2.05 for a fandisk model. This is significantly lower than the 512 samples required for a 512^3 distance field. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundancy: The representation is redundant and requires regularization. Regularization: Separate blocks of voxel terrain are best stored as triangular meshes and converted to Ray-Rep and back as needed. Precision: The source notes that the representation is precise, but does not specify numerical precision issues. In practice, floating-point precision may affect intersection calculations, especially for thin features. Time Complexity: Not explicitly given. The generation is faster than modified ray tracing due to the use of orthographic projection and Z-buffer with Z-list. Memory Complexity: Redundant, requiring regularization. However, it reduces storage compared to scalar fields. For a 512^3 distance field, it reduces the number of samples per ray from 512 to approximately 2. Measured Performance: Average of ~2.86 samples per ray for a dragon model and ~2.05 for a fandisk model. Strengths: High speed for triangulation using dual methods, preserves sharp features, reduces storage compared to scalar fields. Limitations: Redundant, requires regularization, higher storage than compressible formats. When to use: When fast rendering from polygonal representation and fast CSG operations are required, such as in virtual world sculpting. When not to use: When storage space is a critical constraint and compression is available for other formats. Origin: The concept was introduced in the paper "Detail sculpting using cubical marching squares". The term "Z-list-buffer" was used in the same paper to describe the generation method. History: The GPU implementation of Ray-Rep with normals is called Layered Depth-Normal Images (LDNI). Before GPGPU, layered depth images (LDI) used texture arrays to store depth and normal. With CUDA, OpenCL, and compute shaders, it became possible to build lists of points for each image fragment on the GPU. Usage: Used in virtual world sculpting, which involves continuous subtraction operations on target objects. It is also used for voxel terrain storage in VR system design. name: Grid Sphere Traversal
body: Grid Sphere Traversal (GST) is a ray-grid traversal method that performs sphere tracing through a dense grid of Signed Distance Function (SDF) values. It solves the problem of efficiently traversing empty regions in SDF-based rendering by using a hierarchy of SDF grids where lower-resolution levels encode larger SDF values to accelerate step sizes. It is distinguished from its siblings by performing the entire traversal in shader code using dense grids, whereas alternatives like Sparse Voxel Set leverage DXR hardware acceleration for BVH traversal. Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, SDF grid hierarchy (mipmap levels), grid resolution per level. Outputs: Intersection distance or null. Data Structures: SDF Grid: A 3D texture or array storing SDF values. Value Encoding: SDF values are clamped to [-1, 1]. A value of 1 encodes a distance of 2.5 interior voxel diagonals. This allows storage as 8-bit signed normalized (snorm) integers. Hierarchy: A set of grid levels L0, L1, \dots, Ln. Level L0 is the highest resolution. Lower-resolution levels (higher index) encode larger SDF values to represent empty space more coarsely. Steps: 1. Initialize: Start at the root level (lowest resolution, highest index) of the SDF hierarchy. 2. Traverse Hierarchy: For the current ray, determine the position in the current grid level. 3. Sample SDF: Sample the SDF value at the current ray position from the current grid level. 4. Adaptive Resolution Selection: Use the sampled SDF value to determine if the ray is in empty space. If the SDF value indicates sufficient empty space (larger distance), the algorithm may step forward by a larger amount or switch to a lower-resolution level to maximize step size safely. If the ray is close to the surface (small SDF value), switch to a higher-resolution level to reduce step size and maintain precision. 5. Sphere Trace: Perform sphere tracing steps. The step size is determined by the SDF value at the current position, scaled appropriately for the grid resolution and encoding. 6. Intersection Check: If the SDF value is below a threshold (surface hit), return the intersection distance. If the ray exits the grid or exceeds max distance, return null. 7. Shader Execution: The entire traversal logic is implemented in shader code (e.g., GLSL/HLSL). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gridspheretraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, sdfgrids, gridbounds, maxsteps, epsilon, levelswitchthreshold): # sdfgrids: list of 3D textures/arrays, index 0 is lowest resolution (coarsest) # gridbounds: (mincorner, maxcorner) defining the world-space extent of the grids # levelswitchthreshold: multiplier for voxelsize to decide when to change resolution t = 0.0 currentlevel = 0 pos = rayorigin for in range(maxsteps): # Check if ray has exited the grid bounds if not isinsidegrid(pos, gridbounds): return None # Compute physical voxel size for current level # Assuming cubic grids with side length L at level 0, scaled by 2^level levelscale = 2 currentlevel gridside = gridbounds[1][0] - gridbounds[0][0] voxelsize = gridside / (sdfgrids[0].shape[0] levelscale) # Sample SDF value at current position # Coordinates normalized to [0, 1] for texture lookup uv = (pos - gridbounds[0]) / (gridbounds[1] - gridbounds[0]) uv = clamp(uv, 0.0, 1.0) sdfsnorm = texturesample(sdfgrids[currentlevel], uv) # Decode 8-bit snorm to physical distance # snorm 1.0 -> 2.5 sqrt(3) voxelsize physicaldist = sdfsnorm 2.5 sqrt(3) voxelsize # Surface intersection check if physicaldist < epsilon: return t # Sphere tracing step step = max(epsilon, physicaldist) t += step pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Adaptive resolution selection # Large empty space (large SDF) -> coarser level (higher index) # Near surface (small SDF) -> finer level (lower index) if physicaldist > levelswitchthreshold voxelsize and currentlevel < len(sdfgrids) - 1: currentlevel += 1 elif physicaldist < 0.5 levelswitchthreshold voxelsize and currentlevel > 0: currentlevel -= 1 return None def isinsidegrid(point, bounds): return all(bounds[0][i] <= point[i] <= bounds[1][i] for i in range(3)) def clamp(v, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(maxval, v)) def texturesample(grid, uv): # Standard trilinear interpolation of 3D texture at normalized coordinates # Returns value in [-1, 1] return grid[uv] Parameters: SDF Encoding: 8-bit snorm, range [-1, 1], mapping 1.0 to 2.5 interior voxel diagonals. Max Steps: Not given in the sources. Epsilon: Not given in the sources. Level Switch Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Using 8-bit snorm may introduce quantization errors. The mapping of 1.0 to 2.5 diagonals is a specific design choice to maximize the range of representable distances. Boundaries: Ray must be clamped to the grid bounds. Degenerate Input: Empty space far from surface may require many steps if the hierarchy is not deep enough or if the adaptive resolution selection is not optimal. A grid traversal algorithm used in Claybook (Aaltonen, 2018) where every voxel is uniquely associated with a raytracing bounding box. It performed best in open and simple scenes compared to sparse brick set and sparse voxel octree. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of steps in sphere tracing and the depth of the hierarchy. Adaptive resolution selection aims to reduce steps in empty space. Memory Complexity: Dense grid storage. All voxels are stored, including those without SDF surface. Performance: Performed best in open and simple scenes. Outperformed by sparse voxel set in general due to DXR hardware acceleration, but GST has better cache coherency due to compact data storage. Strengths: Simple implementation in shader code, good cache coherency, effective in open scenes. Limitations: Dense storage is memory-intensive. Less effective in complex scenes compared to sparse methods. Grid Sphere Traversal was evaluated in the context of ray tracing signed distance function grids. It is similar to the technique used in Claybook by Aaltonen (2018). The method was compared against sparse voxel set, sparse brick set, and sparse voxel octree.
