name: Uniform Grid Traversal
head: Uniform Grid Acceleration
body: Uniform Grid Traversal is a ray-grid traversal method that accelerates volume rendering by partitioning the scene into a regular, axis-aligned voxel grid, allowing rays to skip empty space and quickly locate occupied voxels. It differs from its siblings by assuming a fixed, uniform spacing between grid cells, which simplifies the traversal logic to simple integer arithmetic and incremental updates, unlike Computational Space Traversal which handles curvilinear grids, or Wide DDA Cell Traversal which processes multiple voxels per step. It serves as the foundational acceleration structure for methods like DDA and Fast Voxel Traversal 2D when extended to 3D. Uniform Grid Traversal accelerates ray marching by maintaining a current voxel index and computing the distance to the next grid boundary along the ray's direction. The ray increments its voxel index when it crosses a boundary, continuing until it exits the grid or terminates. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, grid bounds [minx, miny, minz] and [maxx, maxy, maxz], grid resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz). Output: Sequence of visited voxel indices (i, j, k) and distances to boundaries. Data Structures: The grid is stored as a 3D array of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Each voxel may contain a list of particles or a density value. The traversal state maintains: Current voxel indices: i, j, k (integers). Step directions: stepx, stepy, stepz \in \{-1, 1\}, determined by the sign of \mathbf{d}. Distance to next boundary: t{maxx}, t{maxy}, t{maxz} (floats), representing the ray parameter t at which the ray crosses the next grid plane perpendicular to each axis. Delta distances: t{deltax}, t{deltay}, t{deltaz} (floats), representing the distance between consecutive grid planes along the ray. Formulas: 1. Voxel Size: \Delta x = \frac{maxx - minx}{Nx}, \Delta y = \frac{maxy - miny}{Ny}, \Delta z = \frac{maxz - minz}{Nz}. 2. Initial Voxel: The starting voxel (i0, j0, k0) is computed by clamping the ray origin to the grid bounds and dividing by voxel size: i0 = \lfloor \frac{ox - minx}{\Delta x} \rfloor, \quad j0 = \lfloor \frac{oy - miny}{\Delta y} \rfloor, \quad k0 = \lfloor \frac{oz - minz}{\Delta z} \rfloor 3. Step Direction: stepx = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } dx > 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } dx \le 0 \end{cases} (Analogous for y and z). 4. Delta Distances: The distance between adjacent grid planes along the ray: t{deltax} = \frac{\Delta x}{|dx|}, \quad t{deltay} = \frac{\Delta y}{|dy|}, \quad t{deltaz} = \frac{\Delta z}{|dz|} 5. Initial Boundary Distances: The distance from the ray origin to the first grid plane in the direction of travel. If the ray starts inside the grid, these are the distances to the next boundary in the step direction. If dx > 0, the next boundary is at x = (i0 + 1)\Delta x + minx. If dx < 0, it is at x = i0 \Delta x + minx. t{maxx} = \frac{(i0 + (1 - stepx)/2)\Delta x + minx - ox}{dx} (Analogous for y and z). Note: If the ray starts exactly on a boundary, precision issues may arise; typically, the ray is considered to have just entered the voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute voxel size, step directions, delta distances, and initial boundary distances. 2. Initialize current voxel indices to (i0, j0, k0). 3. Loop while the ray is within the grid bounds: a. Process the current voxel (e.g., accumulate density or sample particles). b. Determine which boundary is closest: compare t{maxx}, t{maxy}, t{maxz}. c. Increment the corresponding voxel index by its step direction. d. Update the corresponding t{max} by adding its t{delta}. e. Check for termination (exit grid or max distance reached). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def uniformgridtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, gridmin, gridmax, resolution): # 1. Compute voxel sizes dx = (gridmax[0] - gridmin[0]) / resolution[0] dy = (gridmax[1] - gridmin[1]) / resolution[1] dz = (gridmax[2] - gridmin[2]) / resolution[2] # 2. Compute step directions stepx = 1 if raydirection[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if raydirection[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if raydirection[2] > 0 else -1 # 3. Compute delta distances (distance between grid planes) # Handle zero direction components by setting delta to infinity tdeltax = dx / abs(raydirection[0]) if raydirection[0] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = dy / abs(raydirection[1]) if raydirection[1] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = dz / abs(raydirection[2]) if raydirection[2] != 0 else float('inf') # 4. Compute initial voxel indices # Clamp origin to grid bounds to handle rays starting outside ox = max(gridmin[0], min(rayorigin[0], gridmax[0])) oy = max(gridmin[1], min(rayorigin[1], gridmax[1])) oz = max(gridmin[2], min(rayorigin[2], gridmax[2])) i = int((ox - gridmin[0]) / dx) j = int((oy - gridmin[1]) / dy) k = int((oz - gridmin[2]) / dz) # 5. Compute initial tmax (distance to next boundary) # Boundary coordinates if stepx == 1: tmaxx = ((i + 1) dx + gridmin[0] - ox) / raydirection[0] else: tmaxx = (i dx + gridmin[0] - ox) / raydirection[0] if stepy == 1: tmaxy = ((j + 1) dy + gridmin[1] - oy) / raydirection[1] else: tmaxy = (j dy + gridmin[1] - oy) / raydirection[1] if stepz == 1: tmaxz = ((k + 1) dz + gridmin[2] - oz) / raydirection[2] else: tmaxz = (k dz + gridmin[2] - oz) / raydirection[2] # 6. Traverse visitedvoxels = [] while 0 <= i < resolution[0] and 0 <= j < resolution[1] and 0 <= k < resolution[2]: visitedvoxels.append((i, j, k)) # Determine next voxel if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: i += stepx tmaxx += tdeltax else: k += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: j += stepy tmaxy += tdeltay else: k += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz return visitedvoxels Parameters: Grid Resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz): No analytical formula exists for the optimal resolution. Empirically, a resolution yielding roughly one particle per voxel achieves optimum performance for uniformly distributed particles. For the Bench scene with 2 \times 10^5 particles, 60 \times 60 \times 60 is optimal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Direction: If a ray component is zero, t{delta} becomes infinite, and the ray never crosses a grid plane in that dimension. The code must handle division by zero. Precision Errors: Numerical robustness errors can cause intersections on grid bounding boxes or implied planes to be missed if intersections outside the current cell are rejected. This happens when computing intersections while visiting a cell, but the result is rejected due to precision errors placing it outside that cell. Low Resolution: If grid resolution is much lower than optimal (e.g., < 60 \times 60 \times 60 for the Bench scene), performance is poor because too many particles reside in each voxel. Computational Space Traversal is a method for rendering data on curvilinear (non-uniform) grids by mapping the irregular physical domain to a regular computational domain. It solves the difficulty of resampling scalar values along a ray in distorted geometry by performing the traversal in the regular computational space, where standard incremental grid traversal applies. Unlike Uniform Grid Traversal, which assumes uniform spacing, this method handles arbitrary hexahedral meshes by transforming ray segments and vectors using Jacobian matrices. Grid Traversal Setup (DDA) initializes the parameters required for a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to traverse a voxel grid along a ray. It computes the initial voxel indices, step directions, and distances to the next voxel boundaries for the ray start and end points within the traversal range. This method sets the stage for the iterative traversal loop, distinguishing itself from computational space traversal by operating directly in grid coordinates and from one-pass over-allocated methods by computing exact boundary distances. It solves the problem of robustly determining where a ray enters a voxel grid and how it progresses through adjacent voxels, handling edge cases such as rays parallel to grid axes. A single-pass algorithm to traverse voxel grids along rays, using pre-allocated maximum memory to avoid a second pass. It differs from Grid Traversal (Two-Pass) by allocating buffers large enough for the worst-case scenario upfront, trading memory for a single kernel launch, and from Computational Space Traversal by operating directly on grid coordinates rather than abstract computational spaces. Robust Grid Traversal is a grid traversal modification that prevents numerical robustness errors by keeping the closest intersection parameter even if it falls outside the current cell, terminating only when the cell's maximum ray parameter exceeds this closest intersection. Numerical robustness errors can cause intersections on grid bounding boxes or implied planes to be missed if intersections outside the current cell are rejected. This happens when computing intersections while visiting a cell, but the result is rejected due to precision errors placing it outside that cell. Unlike traditional methods that discard intersections outside the current cell, this method retains them. Traditional methods require scene-dependent epsilon tests which are hard to choose correctly. It is used by some researchers [PH04], but many sources still discard intersections [Shi00, Suf07]. A compact 64-way full tree that summarizes the occupancy of an underlying uniform grid in a hierarchy, designed to speed up grid traversals on a GPU. Each node in the tree represents a voxel, with its occupancy represented by a single bit. Each node is subdivided into a 64-subgrid, which is stored in a single 64-bit word. The micro 64-tree is built on top of a uniform grid. The GPU grid construction algorithm is improved by computing precise triangle-cell intersections. Non-overlapping triangle-cell pairs are precluded before sorting during the construction phase. The micro 64-tree is built bottom-up from the uniform grid using parallel reductions. The top levels of the micro 64-tree are pre-loaded into the shared memory of a GPU to support on-chip traversals across coarse levels. The traversal algorithm navigates the ray through the 64-subgrids at different levels. A concise context for each level is stored in the GPU's registers to facilitate vertical moves during traversal. The micro 64-tree reduces traversal steps, decreases memory bandwidth consumption, and significantly improves the efficiency of ray tracing on a GPU, with small overheads in memory and building time. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The traversal cost per ray is proportional to the number of voxels visited. In the worst case (ray passing through all voxels), it is O(Nx + Ny + Nz). In practice, it is much faster due to empty space skipping. Memory: The grid requires O(Nx Ny Nz) space to store the voxel data or occupancy flags. Measured Performance: In the Bench scene with 2 \times 10^5 particles, optimal performance is achieved at a grid resolution of 60 \times 60 \times 60. Runtime grows steadily as grid resolution increases due to additional grid traversal costs. A resolution much lower than optimal (e.g., < 60 \times 60 \times 60 for the Bench scene) results in poor performance because too many particles reside in each voxel. Scaling: Performance scales with the number of particles and the efficiency of the grid traversal. Higher resolutions reduce the number of particles per voxel but increase traversal overhead. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement, fast to build, effective for uniformly distributed data. Limitations: Inefficient for sparse data (many empty voxels), sensitive to resolution choice. When to Use: Use when data is uniformly distributed and the scene is dense enough to benefit from spatial partitioning. Use when a simple, fast-to-build acceleration structure is required. When Not to Use: Do not use for highly sparse data where the grid is mostly empty, as the memory and traversal overhead outweigh the benefits. Do not use for non-uniform or curvilinear grids without modification (use Computational Space Traversal instead). Uniform Grid Traversal is a well-known acceleration structure for ray tracing. It is fast to build, but slow to traverse compared to hierarchical structures. It is commonly used in volume rendering and particle rendering to accelerate ray traversal for uniformly distributed particles. name: Computational Space Traversal
head: Frühauf's Curvilinear Grid Traversal, Frühauf's method
body: Computational Space Traversal renders data on curvilinear grids by mapping the irregular physical domain to a regular computational space. It solves the difficulty of resampling scalar values along a ray in distorted geometry by performing the traversal in the regular computational space, where standard incremental grid traversal applies. Unlike Uniform Grid Traversal, which assumes uniform spacing, this method handles arbitrary hexahedral meshes by transforming ray segments and vectors using Jacobian matrices. Inputs: A curvilinear grid defined by vertex positions in physical space and their connectivity; a ray defined by origin and direction in physical space; a viewpoint. Outputs: Sampled scalar values along the ray path in physical space. Data Structures: Grid: Vertices with physical coordinates and computational coordinates following integer indices (i, j, k). Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Jacobian: Pre-computed or on-the-fly approximations at vertices or cell centers. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Bending Vectors: Pre-computed vectors used to adjust the ray direction at cell boundaries. Exact field layouts, sizes, and bit packing are Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Locate Initial Cell: Determine the starting hexahedral cell containing the ray origin by extracting unshared boundary faces and building a spatial index over them. 2. Approximate Jacobian: Approximate the Jacobian matrix using central differences of adjacent vertices in computational and physical space. 3. Transform to Computational Space: Map the ray origin and direction from physical space to computational space using the Jacobian matrix. 4. Incremental Traversal: Perform standard incremental grid traversal in the regular computational space to determine the sequence of cells and face intersections. 5. Bend Ray at Intersections: At each face intersection in computational space, transform the intersection point and the ray direction back to physical space. The ray direction is bent according to pre-computed bending vectors using bilinear interpolation. 6. Resample Values: Sample the scalar field values at the transformed physical positions. 7. Optimization (Viewpoint Update): Store and update bending vectors along a ray only when the viewpoint changes. If mapping parameters change but the viewpoint remains the same, pre-computed ray paths can be reused directly. Formulas: The exact transformation equations for mapping vertices, vectors, and rays between physical and computational space are Not given in the sources. The exact formula for central differences is Not given in the sources. Parameters: Interpolation: Bilinear interpolation is specified for determining bending vectors at face intersections. Jacobian Approximation: Central differences are used for adjacent vertices. Typical values are Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: Degenerate cells causing singular Jacobians are not discussed in the sources. Precision: Floating-point errors from coordinate transformations are not discussed in the sources. Initial Cell Location: Finding the initial cell in a complex curvilinear mesh requires extracting boundary faces and building a spatial index, which can be expensive. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computationalspacetraversal(grid, rayorigin, raydirection, viewpoint): # 1. Locate initial cell containing ray origin currentcell = findcellcontainingpoint(grid, rayorigin) # 2. Approximate Jacobian using central differences of adjacent vertices # in computational and physical space # Exact formula not given in the sources. J = centraldifferencejacobian(currentcell, grid) # 3. Transform ray origin and direction to computational space comporigin = applyjacobianinverse(J, rayorigin) compdir = applyjacobianinversevector(J, raydirection) # 4. Incremental grid traversal in regular computational space while not rayexitsgrid(comporigin, compdir): # Find next face intersection in computational space t, faceidx = nextregulargridintersection(comporigin, compdir) comphit = comporigin + t compdir # 5. Transform intersection point back to physical space physhit = applyjacobian(J, comphit) # Bend ray direction using pre-computed bending vectors # via bilinear interpolation at the face bendvec = bilinearinterpolatebendingvectors(faceidx, grid) physdir = applybendingvector(physdir, bendvec) # 6. Resample scalar values at physical position yield resamplescalarat(grid, physhit) # Advance traversal comporigin = comphit currentcell = getadjacentcell(currentcell, faceidx) J = centraldifferencejacobian(currentcell, grid) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: No performance measurements were reported in the original source. Strengths: Greatly reduces the difficulties of resampling along the ray since the computational space is regular. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of Jacobians and bending vectors. When to use: When rendering data on curvilinear grids where resampling in physical space is complex. When not to use: When performance measurements are critical and not available, or for uniform grids where Uniform Grid Traversal is simpler. Origin: Introduced by Frühauf in [Frü94]. History: Described in the context of interactive volume rendering with ray tracing. Usage: Used for rendering data on curvilinear grids, particularly hexahedral meshes. name: Grid Traversal Setup (DDA)
head: Ray marching grid setup, Voxel traversal initialization
body: Grid Traversal Setup (DDA) initializes the parameters required for a 3D Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) to traverse a voxel grid along a ray. It computes the initial voxel indices, step directions, and distances to the next voxel boundaries for the ray start and end points within the traversal range. This method sets the stage for the iterative traversal loop, distinguishing itself from computational space traversal by operating directly in grid coordinates and from one-pass over-allocated methods by computing exact boundary distances. It solves the problem of robustly determining where a ray enters a voxel grid and how it progresses through adjacent voxels, handling edge cases such as rays parallel to grid axes. Inputs: ray.origin: 3D vector, ray origin in world space. ray.dir: 3D vector, ray direction in world space (normalized). ray.invdir: 3D vector, inverse of ray direction (1.0 / ray.dir). tmin: float, near plane distance along the ray. tmax: float, far plane distance along the ray. aabb.min: 3D vector, minimum corner of the grid's axis-aligned bounding box in world space. aabb.max: 3D vector, maximum corner of the grid's axis-aligned bounding box in world space. resolution: 3D integer vector, number of voxels along each axis (Nx, Ny, Nz). eps: float, small epsilon value for numerical stability (e.g., 10^{-6}). Outputs: currentindex: 3D integer vector, the voxel index containing the ray start point. finalindex: 3D integer vector, the voxel index containing the ray end point. tdist: 3D float vector, distance along the ray to the next voxel boundary in each axis direction. delta: 3D float vector, distance along the ray to traverse one voxel in each axis direction. stepindex: 3D integer vector, direction of increment for each axis (+1 or -1). Data Structures: float3: 3-component floating-point vector. int3: 3-component integer vector. makefloat3(x, y, z): Constructs a float3. makeint3(x, y, z): Constructs an int3. clamp(v, minval, maxval): Clamps value v to [minval, maxval]. applycontraction(point, aabbmin, aabbmax): Maps a world-space point to the range [0, 1] along each axis relative to the AABB. Specifically, for each component i, it computes \frac{pointi - aabb\mini}{aabb\maxi - aabb\mini}. Steps: 1. Compute Voxel Size: Calculate the physical size of a single voxel. voxel\size = \frac{aabb.max - aabb.min}{resolution} 2. Compute Ray Start and End Points: Determine the world-space positions of the ray at tmin and tmax, adjusted by epsilon to avoid boundary precision issues. ray\start = ray.origin + ray.dir \times (tmin + eps) ray\end = ray.origin + ray.dir \times (tmax - eps) 3. Compute Current and Final Voxel Indices: Map the start and end points to voxel indices. First, apply contraction to map world coordinates to [0, 1] range relative to the AABB. contracted\start = apply\contraction(ray\start, aabb.min, aabb.max) contracted\end = apply\contraction(ray\end, aabb.min, aabb.max) Then, scale by resolution and clamp to valid voxel indices [0, resolution - 1]. current\index = clamp(contracted\start \times resolution, 0, resolution - 1) final\index = clamp(contracted\end \times resolution, 0, resolution - 1) 4. Compute Step Direction (stepindex): Determine the direction of traversal for each axis based on the ray direction. step\index = make\int3( \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } ray.dir.x > 0 \\ 0 & \text{if } ray.dir.x == 0 \\ -1 & \text{if } ray.dir.x < 0 \end{cases}, \dots) Note: The source describes stepfloat as 0 if direction is 0, 1 if positive, -1 if negative, and stepindex is derived from this. uses a ternary operator directly. 5. Compute Distance to Next Boundary (tdist): Calculate the distance along the ray to the next voxel boundary for each axis. First, compute the start index for boundary calculation: start\index = current\index + step\index Calculate the intermediate distance to the boundary plane: tmax\xyz = \left( \left( aabb.min + (start\index \times voxel\size) - ray\start \right) \times ray.inv\dir \right) + tmin Handle rays parallel to axes (where ray.dir component is 0) to avoid division by zero or invalid distances. If the ray direction component is 0, set the corresponding tdist component to tmax. Otherwise, use the calculated tmaxxyz component. tdist.x = \begin{cases} tmax & \text{if } ray.dir.x == 0.0f \\ tmax\xyz.x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} tdist.y = \begin{cases} tmax & \text{if } ray.dir.y == 0.0f \\ tmax\xyz.y & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} tdist.z = \begin{cases} tmax & \text{if } ray.dir.z == 0.0f \\ tmax\xyz.z & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 6. Compute Step Distance (delta): Calculate the distance along the ray to traverse one voxel in each axis direction. First, compute the step float vector: step\float.x = \begin{cases} 0.0f & \text{if } ray.dir.x == 0.0f \\ 1.0f & \text{if } ray.dir.x > 0.0f \\ -1.0f & \text{if } ray.dir.x < 0.0f \end{cases} (Similarly for y and z) Calculate the raw delta: delta\temp = voxel\size \times ray.inv\dir \times step\float Handle rays parallel to axes. If the ray direction component is 0, set the corresponding delta component to 0 (or effectively ignore it in traversal). The source sets delta components to 0 if direction is 0. does not explicitly show the delta assignment for zero direction but implies handling via tdist capping. We follow for robustness. delta.x = \begin{cases} 0.0f & \text{if } ray.dir.x == 0.0f \\ delta\temp.x & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Similarly for y and z) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gridtraversalsetup(rayorigin, raydir, rayinvdir, tmin, tmax, aabbmin, aabbmax, resolution, eps): # 1. Compute Voxel Size voxelsize = (aabbmax - aabbmin) / resolution # 2. Compute Ray Start and End Points raystart = rayorigin + raydir (tmin + eps) rayend = rayorigin + raydir (tmax - eps) # 3. Compute Current and Final Voxel Indices # Contraction: map world point to [0, 1] relative to AABB contractedstart = (raystart - aabbmin) / (aabbmax - aabbmin) contractedend = (rayend - aabbmin) / (aabbmax - aabbmin) # Scale by resolution and clamp currentindex = clamp(contractedstart resolution, 0, resolution - 1) finalindex = clamp(contractedend resolution, 0, resolution - 1) # 4. Compute Step Direction (stepindex) stepindexx = 1 if raydir.x > 0 else (-1 if raydir.x < 0 else 0) stepindexy = 1 if raydir.y > 0 else (-1 if raydir.y < 0 else 0) stepindexz = 1 if raydir.z > 0 else (-1 if raydir.z < 0 else 0) stepindex = (stepindexx, stepindexy, stepindexz) # 5. Compute Distance to Next Boundary (tdist) startindex = currentindex + stepindex # Intermediate distance to boundary plane # Note: aabbmin + (startindex voxelsize) is the world position of the next boundary plane boundaryplanepos = aabbmin + (startindex voxelsize) tmaxxyz = ((boundaryplanepos - raystart) rayinvdir) + tmin # Handle zero direction components tdistx = tmax if raydir.x == 0.0 else tmaxxyz.x tdisty = tmax if raydir.y == 0.0 else tmaxxyz.y tdistz = tmax if raydir.z == 0.0 else tmaxxyz.z tdist = (tdistx, tdisty, tdistz) # 6. Compute Step Distance (delta) # Step float for direction magnitude stepfloatx = 0.0 if raydir.x == 0.0 else (1.0 if raydir.x > 0.0 else -1.0) stepfloaty = 0.0 if raydir.y == 0.0 else (1.0 if raydir.y > 0.0 else -1.0) stepfloatz = 0.0 if raydir.z == 0.0 else (1.0 if raydir.z > 0.0 else -1.0) stepfloat = (stepfloatx, stepfloaty, stepfloatz) # Raw delta deltatemp = voxelsize rayinvdir stepfloat # Handle zero direction components deltax = 0.0 if raydir.x == 0.0 else deltatemp.x deltay = 0.0 if raydir.y == 0.0 else deltatemp.y deltaz = 0.0 if raydir.z == 0.0 else deltatemp.z delta = (deltax, deltay, deltaz) return currentindex, finalindex, tdist, delta, stepindex Binary Grid Ray Traversal Initialization computes the initial distances to the next voxel boundaries (tdist) and the distance steps between adjacent voxels (delta) for a ray traversing a binary occupancy grid. It handles rays parallel to grid axes by clamping distances to tmax and setting steps to zero, ensuring robust traversal without division by zero. It differs from continuous volume rendering methods by operating on discrete binary occupancy, making it suitable for sparse or binary voxel representations where only presence/absence matters. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, storing only a few vectors. Strengths: Robust handling of edge cases (parallel rays, boundary conditions); efficient setup for subsequent DDA traversal. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of invdir and careful epsilon handling to avoid precision errors at boundaries. When to use: When traversing uniform voxel grids for ray marching or volume rendering. When not to use: For non-uniform grids or hierarchical structures (e.g., octrees) where different traversal logic is required. The Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) for grid traversal is a classic algorithm in computer graphics, originally described by Amanatides and Woo in 1987. It is widely used in ray tracing and volume rendering for efficient traversal of uniform grids. The method is implemented in various open-source projects, including Taylor-NeRF and CNC. taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, https://github.com/taylor2nerf/taylor-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) YihangChen-ee/CNC, https://github.com/YihangChen-ee/CNC, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: - `step_index`: Integer step direction $(s_x, s_y, s_z)$ for index updates [S1, unofficial].
body: Data Structures: Vectors are 3-component floats. stepindex is a 3-component integer vector. Steps: 1. Calculate Start Index: Compute the index of the next voxel to enter: \text{start\index} = \text{current\index} + \text{index\delta} 2. Calculate Distance to Next Voxel Start (tmaxxyz): Compute the distance from the ray origin to the start of the next voxel in each dimension. The formula accounts for the grid origin (aabbmin), the voxel size, and the current ray position relative to tmin: \text{tmax\xyz} = \left( (\text{aabb\min} + (\text{start\index} \times \text{voxel\size}) - \text{ray\start}) \times \text{ray\inv\dir} \right) + \text{tmin} Note: Multiplication is component-wise. 3. Initialize tdist (Distance to Next Boundary): For each axis c \in \{x, y, z\}: If \text{ray\inv\dir}c = 0 (ray parallel to axis): \text{tdist}c = \text{tmax} Else: \text{tdist}c = \text{tmax\xyz}c 4. Initialize stepfloat (Direction Vector): For each axis c \in \{x, y, z\}: If \text{ray\inv\dir}c = 0: \text{step\float}c = 0.0 Else if \text{ray\inv\dir}c > 0 (equivalent to direction > 0): \text{step\float}c = 1.0 Else: \text{step\float}c = -1.0 5. Convert to Integer Step: \text{step\index} = \text{round}(\text{step\float}) 6. Calculate deltatemp (Voxel Crossing Distance): Compute the distance traveled along the ray to cross one voxel in each dimension: \text{delta\temp} = \text{voxel\size} \times \text{ray\inv\dir} \times \text{step\float} Note: Multiplication is component-wise. 7. Initialize delta (Step Size): For each axis c \in \{x, y, z\}: If \text{ray\inv\dir}c = 0: \text{delta}c = \text{tmax} Else: \text{delta}c = \text{delta\temp}c Pseudocode: python def binarygridraytraversalinitialization( raystart, rayinvdir, voxelsize, aabbmin, currentindex, indexdelta, tmin, tmax): # Step 1: Calculate start index startindex = currentindex + indexdelta # Step 2: Calculate tmaxxyz # Component-wise operations voxeloffset = aabbmin + (startindex voxelsize) diff = voxeloffset - raystart tmaxxyz = (diff rayinvdir) + tmin # Step 3: Initialize tdist tdist = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): if rayinvdir[c] == 0.0: tdist[c] = tmax else: tdist[c] = tmaxxyz[c] # Step 4: Initialize stepfloat stepfloat = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): if rayinvdir[c] == 0.0: stepfloat[c] = 0.0 elif rayinvdir[c] > 0.0: stepfloat[c] = 1.0 else: stepfloat[c] = -1.0 # Step 5: Convert to integer step stepindex = [int(round(s)) for s in stepfloat] # Step 6: Calculate deltatemp deltatemp = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): deltatemp[c] = voxelsize rayinvdir[c] stepfloat[c] # Step 7: Initialize delta delta = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): if rayinvdir[c] == 0.0: delta[c] = tmax else: delta[c] = deltatemp[c] return tdist, delta, stepindex Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parallel Rays: If rayinvdir is 0 for any axis, the ray never crosses a boundary in that dimension. The code clamps tdist and delta to tmax and sets steps to 0 to avoid division by zero and infinite loops. ## Subtopics ### Binary Grid Ray Traversal (Single Voxel Step) Advances the ray through a single voxel by updating the index and checking boundaries. It is the core iterative step following initialization. It differs from parent methods by performing the actual index update and boundary check rather than just setting up initial parameters. Choose it when traversing a binary occupancy grid where only presence/absence matters. ## Operating characteristics Not given in the sources. ## Background This method is part of the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) traversal technique for uniform grids. It is implemented in the CNC (Compressed Neural Fields) project, which uses binary voxel mix encoding for efficient neural field representation. ## Sources YihangChen-ee/CNC, https://github.com/YihangChen-ee/CNC, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Binary Grid Ray Traversal (Single Voxel Step)
head: AABB traversal step
body: This method advances a ray through a single voxel in a binary occupancy grid by determining the exit axis, updating the voxel index, and checking for grid boundary overflow. It is the core iterative step of the Binary Grid Ray Traversal algorithm, following initialization. Unlike continuous volume rendering which samples density, this method operates on discrete binary occupancy, making it suitable for sparse or binary voxel representations where only presence/absence matters. It differs from parent methods by performing the actual index update and boundary check rather than just setting up initial parameters. Inputs and Outputs: currentindex: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the current voxel coordinates. tdist: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the distance from the ray origin to the next voxel boundary along each axis. delta: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the distance between adjacent voxel boundaries along each axis (pre-computed by initialization). stepindex: A 3D vector (x, y, z) containing +1 or -1 indicating the traversal direction along each axis. overflowindex: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the grid dimensions (or boundary indices) where traversal must stop. Output: A boolean indicating whether the ray remains within the valid grid bounds (true) or has exited (false). Data Structures: The algorithm assumes currentindex, tdist, delta, stepindex, and overflowindex are 3-component vectors (e.g., vec3 in GLSL or numpy.array in Python). No specific bit-packing is required for the traversal step itself, as it operates on floating-point distances and integer indices. Steps: 1. Determine Exit Axis: Compare tdist.x, tdist.y, and tdist.z to find the minimum distance to the next boundary. If tdist.x < tdist.y and tdist.x < tdist.z, the ray exits through the X-axis. Else, if tdist.y < tdist.z, the ray exits through the Y-axis. Else, the ray exits through the Z-axis. 2. Update Index and Distance: Based on the selected axis, update the currentindex and tdist. X-axis: currentindex.x += stepindex.x and tdist.x += delta.x. Y-axis: currentindex.y += stepindex.y and tdist.y += delta.y. Z-axis: currentindex.z += stepindex.z and tdist.z += delta.z. 3. Check Overflow: Verify if the updated index has exceeded the grid boundaries. If the updated index component equals the corresponding overflowindex component, the ray has exited the valid grid. Return false. Otherwise, return true. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlevoxelstep(currentindex, tdist, delta, stepindex, overflowindex): """ Advances ray through one voxel in a binary grid. Args: currentindex: vec3, current voxel coordinates tdist: vec3, distance to next boundary on each axis delta: vec3, distance between adjacent boundaries on each axis stepindex: vec3, direction (+1 or -1) for each axis overflowindex: vec3, grid boundary indices Returns: bool: True if ray is still within grid, False if out of bounds """ # Determine which axis has the minimum distance to the next boundary if tdist.x < tdist.y and tdist.x < tdist.z: # Exit through X-axis currentindex.x += stepindex.x tdist.x += delta.x if currentindex.x == overflowindex.x: return False elif tdist.y < tdist.z: # Exit through Y-axis currentindex.y += stepindex.y tdist.y += delta.y if currentindex.y == overflowindex.y: return False else: # Exit through Z-axis currentindex.z += stepindex.z tdist.z += delta.z if currentindex.z == overflowindex.z: return False return True Parameters and Edge Cases: Precision: Floating-point comparisons (<) are used. If tdist values are equal, the order of checks (X, then Y, then Z) determines the axis, providing a deterministic tie-breaking rule. Parallel Rays: The parent initialization step handles rays parallel to axes by setting delta to 0 and tdist to tmax. This step assumes valid non-zero delta for the active axis, or that the ray has already terminated. If delta is 0 for the selected axis, tdist will not increase, potentially causing an infinite loop if not handled by the caller. However, the parent initialization ensures that for parallel rays, the traversal logic is adjusted or terminated. Overflow: The check currentindex == overflowindex assumes overflowindex represents the exclusive upper bound (or lower bound for negative directions). The exact meaning of overflowindex depends on the initialization step, but typically it is the grid dimension size for positive traversal. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel step. The comparison and update operations are constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No additional data structures are allocated. Strengths: Extremely fast per-voxel update. Minimal branching compared to more complex traversal methods. Suitable for binary occupancy grids where density integration is not required. Limitations: Only advances one voxel at a time. Requires careful handling of parallel rays and boundary conditions, which are delegated to the initialization step. Not suitable for continuous volume rendering without additional sampling logic. When to Use: When rendering binary occupancy grids (e.g., sparse voxel octrees converted to uniform grids, or simple binary masks) where only the presence of geometry matters. When Not to Use: For continuous volume rendering requiring density integration, or for non-uniform grids where delta varies per voxel. This method is part of the Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) ray traversal technique adapted for binary grids. It is commonly used in GPU-based volume rendering and ray marching for binary occupancy data. The implementation originates from the CNC repository. name: Ray Traversal Template Generation
head: Precomputed Ray Traversal Pattern, Ray Template Generation
body: Precomputes a 3D ray traversal pattern (DDA-like) for light rays to avoid per-ray floating-point division during rendering. It sets up a fixed-size lookup table of integer voxel offsets, allowing the renderer to step through a uniform grid using only integer arithmetic and addition, significantly reducing the computational cost of ray traversal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Grid resolution parameters (implicitly edgeLen or RES), maximum traversal length. Output: rayTemplate, a 2D array storing integer voxel offsets for each step. Data Structures: rayTemplate[4096][3]: Stores integer voxel offsets (dx, dy, dz) for up to 4096 steps. Each row i contains the offset to add to the current voxel index to reach the next voxel along the ray. Parameters: maxlen: Maximum number of steps. Calculated as 3 \times edgeLen \times edgeLen. epsilon: Small value added to ray direction components to prevent division by zero. ALMOSTEQUALTHRESHOLD: Threshold for float comparison, typically 0.00001f. Steps: 1. Initialize ray direction components lx, ly, lz by adding epsilon to the normalized direction vector components to ensure they are non-zero. 2. Determine increments xinc, yinc, zinc. These are typically +1 or -1 based on the sign of lx, ly, lz. 3. Initialize a loop counter i = 0. 4. Loop while i < maxlen: a. Compute distances to the next voxel boundary in each axis. Let tx, ty, tz be the distance to the next boundary along x, y, z respectively. In a standard DDA, these are derived from the current fractional position and the inverse of the direction components. b. Find the axis with the smallest distance: min\t = \min(tx, ty, tz). c. Advance the coordinate along the axis with min\t. Update the fractional position by adding the inverse of the direction component for that axis. d. Store the integer voxel offset (xinc, yinc, zinc) corresponding to the chosen axis in rayTemplate[i]. e. Increment i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generateraytemplate(edgelen, maxlen): # Initialize template array raytemplate = [[0, 0, 0] for in range(maxlen)] # Example direction vector (normalized) # In practice, this comes from the light ray direction lx, ly, lz = 0.577, 0.577, 0.577 # Add epsilon to avoid division by zero epsilon = 1e-6 lx += epsilon ly += epsilon lz += epsilon # Determine increments xinc = 1 if lx > 0 else -1 yinc = 1 if ly > 0 else -1 zinc = 1 if lz > 0 else -1 # Inverse directions for step calculation invlx = 1.0 / lx invly = 1.0 / ly invlz = 1.0 / lz # Initial distances to next voxel boundary # Assuming starting at fractional position 0.0 # t values represent distance to next integer boundary tx = (1.0 - 0.0) invlx if xinc > 0 else (0.0 - 0.0) invlx # Simplified for template generation ty = (1.0 - 0.0) invly if yinc > 0 else (0.0 - 0.0) invly tz = (1.0 - 0.0) invlz if zinc > 0 else (0.0 - 0.0) invlz # Note: The source code implies a specific DDA logic. # The template stores the offset to add to the current voxel index. # The actual t values are used to decide which axis to step. for i in range(maxlen): # Find minimum t if tx <= ty and tx <= tz: # Step in X raytemplate[i] = [xinc, 0, 0] tx += invlx elif ty <= tx and ty <= tz: # Step in Y raytemplate[i] = [0, yinc, 0] ty += invly else: # Step in Z raytemplate[i] = [0, 0, zinc] tz += invlz return raytemplate Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The ALMOSTEQUAL macro uses a threshold of 0.00001f for float comparison. This may cause jitter or missed steps in degenerate cases where ray directions are nearly aligned with grid axes. If the ray direction components are exactly zero, the epsilon addition is critical to prevent division by zero. Sets the light position, computes the light direction vector, and triggers ray template generation for volume ray casting. It assigns the input position to lightPos, computes lightDir as the negation of lightPos, and calls GenerateRayTemplate with the grid resolution RES to prepare ray casting parameters. Time Complexity: O(maxlen) for template generation, where maxlen = 3 \times edgeLen \times edgeLen. This is a one-time cost per ray direction or light source. Memory Complexity: O(maxlen \times 3) integers for the template storage. For a 128^3 grid, maxlen \approx 49152, but the template is capped at 4096 steps. Performance: Avoids per-ray floating-point division during rendering, which is a costly operation on many hardware architectures. Strengths: Fast traversal once the template is generated; suitable for real-time rendering where division is expensive. Limitations: Fixed template size (4096 steps) may not be sufficient for very large grids or long rays. Precision issues with the ALMOSTEQUAL threshold can lead to artifacts. Originated in the context of real-time volume rendering and smoke simulation, specifically in the nevermoe/SmokeSimulation project. The method is part of a broader effort to optimize ray traversal in uniform grids by precomputing traversal patterns. nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, https://github.com/nevermoe/SmokeSimulation, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Grid Traversal (One-Pass Over-Allocated)
head: traverse_grids (over-allocate)
body: A single-pass algorithm to traverse voxel grids, using pre-allocated maximum memory to avoid a second pass. It differs from Grid Traversal (Two-Pass) by allocating buffers large enough for the worst-case scenario upfront, trading memory for a single kernel launch. Inputs: Ray origins, ray directions, grid dimensions, traversestepslimit, and raysmask. Outputs: Over-allocated interval and sample buffers, chunkcnts tensors with actual counts per ray, and chunkstarts pointers. Data Structures: 1. intervals.chunkcnts: Tensor of size [numrays] storing the allocated capacity and actual count of intervals per ray. 2. intervals.data: Over-allocated buffer of size [numrays, traversestepslimit 2]. 3. samples.chunkcnts: Tensor of size [numrays] storing the allocated capacity and actual count of samples per ray. 4. samples.data: Over-allocated buffer of size [numrays, traversestepslimit]. Numbered Steps: 1. Allocate intervals.chunkcnts initialized to traversestepslimit 2 for each ray, multiplied by raysmask. 2. Allocate samples.chunkcnts initialized to traversestepslimit for each ray, multiplied by raysmask. 3. Call traversegridskernel once with the over-allocated buffers. 4. Update chunk starts for intervals and samples based on actual counts returned from traversal. Parameters: traversestepslimit: Maximum number of steps allowed per ray. Must be > 0 if overallocate is true. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues near grid boundaries may cause rays to miss voxels or double-count; standard DDA epsilon handling is required. If traversestepslimit is too small, rays may be truncated prematurely. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def traversegridsonepass(origins, viewdirs, griddims, traversestepslimit, raysmask): numrays = len(origins) # Step 1: Allocate intervals.chunkcnts initialized to traversestepslimit 2 for each ray, multiplied by raysmask intervalschunkcnts = [(traversestepslimit 2) m for m in raysmask] # Step 2: Allocate samples.chunkcnts initialized to traversestepslimit for each ray, multiplied by raysmask sampleschunkcnts = [traversestepslimit m for m in raysmask] # Allocate over-allocated data buffers intervalsdata = [[0.0] (traversestepslimit 2) for in range(numrays)] samplesdata = [[0.0] traversestepslimit for in range(numrays)] # Step 3: Call traversegridskernel once with over-allocated buffers traversegridskernel( origins=origins, viewdirs=viewdirs, griddims=griddims, intervalsdata=intervalsdata, samplesdata=samplesdata, intervalschunkcnts=intervalschunkcnts, sampleschunkcnts=sampleschunkcnts, maxsteps=traversestepslimit) # Step 4: Update chunk starts for intervals and samples based on actual counts returned from traversal intervalschunkstarts = [0] numrays sampleschunkstarts = [0] numrays ioffset, soffset = 0, 0 for i in range(numrays): intervalschunkstarts[i] = ioffset ioffset += intervalschunkcnts[i] sampleschunkstarts[i] = soffset soffset += sampleschunkcnts[i] return intervalsdata, samplesdata, intervalschunkcnts, sampleschunkcnts, intervalschunkstarts, sampleschunkstarts A two-pass algorithm to traverse voxel grids along rays, first counting segments to allocate exact memory, then filling them. First pass: Call traversegridskernel with computeintervals=true (implied by first pass logic) and allocate intervals.chunkcnts and samples.chunkcnts tensors of size [nrays]. Second pass: Allocate data buffers for intervals and samples based on the counts from the first pass using memallocdatafromchunk. name: Nishita et al. Ray Casting Method
head: Nishita Ray Casting
body: A ray casting technique for rendering participating media that integrates radiance only over segments of a ray that are illuminated by light sources, utilizing precomputed shadow and illumination volumes. It distinguishes itself from standard ray marching by avoiding integration in shadowed regions and from Max’s original scan-line approach by operating in ray space, while extending support to spotlights with angular distributions beyond parallel light sources. Builds on Ray-grid traversal. The method computes the radiance along a ray by intersecting it with shadow volumes generated by occluding geometry and illumination volumes generated by light sources, integrating only where these volumes overlap (lit segments). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scene geometry (polygons), light sources (parallel or spotlights), participating medium properties (density, phase function). Output: Pixel color/intensity. Data Structures: Shadow Volumes: Constructed from scene polygons relative to light sources. Illumination Volumes: Constructed from light source geometry. Ray Data: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}. Steps: 1. Volume Construction: Generate shadow volumes for all occluders relative to each light source, and illumination volumes for each light source. 2. Ray Intersection: For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera and intersect it with the shadow and illumination volumes to determine intervals of shadow and light. 3. Segment Identification: Identify "lit segments" where the ray is inside an illumination volume but outside any shadow volume. 4. Integration: For each lit segment, integrate the radiance transfer equation along the ray interval. For a point light source and constant density medium with isotropic scattering, this yields an analytical function of distance. For parallel light and layered density, numerical integration is used. 5. Accumulation: Sum the contributions from all lit segments. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Light type: Parallel or Spotlight. Medium density: Constant or layered. Edge Cases: Spotlights with angular distributions require specific volume construction compared to parallel lights. Degenerate cases where shadow and illumination boundaries coincide must be handled to avoid double counting or gaps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nishitaraycasting(rayorigin, raydirection, shadowintervals, illumintervals, medium): # 1. Intersect ray with shadow and illumination volumes to get t-intervals shadowt = list(shadowintervals) illumt = list(illumintervals) # 2. Determine lit segments (illumination minus shadow) litsegments = [] for istart, iend in illumt: currentstart = istart for sstart, send in shadowt: if sstart < iend and send > istart: if sstart > currentstart: litsegments.append((currentstart, sstart)) currentstart = max(currentstart, send) if currentstart < iend: litsegments.append((currentstart, iend)) totalradiance = 0.0 # 3. Integrate over lit segments for start, end in litsegments: # Integration logic depends on light type and medium density # For point light and constant density: analytical function of distance # For parallel light and layered density: numerical integration # Not given in the sources. segmentradiance = 0.0 totalradiance += segmentradiance return totalradiance Applies Nishita’s method to consider light/water interaction in a two-pass backward beam tracing method to display underwater shafts of light. It is chosen when rendering complex light/water interactions in underwater scenes. A volumetric rendering approach for gaseous phenomena that models non-uniformly modified density blobs convected by wind fields and diffusion processes. It differs from standard particle systems by treating blobs as spherical particles with normally distributed gas volumes, rendered using diffusion equations. It applies a front-to-back strategy to handle turbulent fields. The method avoids integration in shadowed regions, potentially reducing computation compared to full ray marching. However, it requires the construction of shadow and illumination volumes, which adds preprocessing complexity. Originated from Nishita et al. [62], building on Max’s ideas of shadow and illumination volumes but shifting from scan-line to ray casting. Extended to handle spotlights with angular distributions. Used in computer graphics for rendering participating media, particularly for effects like shafts of light in fog or water. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stam and Fiume Blob Renderer
head: Blob Renderer, Blob-Warping, Volumetric Blob Rendering
body: A volumetric rendering approach for gaseous phenomena that models non-uniformly modified density blobs convected by wind fields and diffusion processes. It differs from standard particle systems by treating blobs as spherical particles with normally distributed gas volumes, rendered using diffusion equations. It applies a front-to-back strategy to handle turbulent fields. Inputs: A set of spherical blobs, each defined by position, velocity, and density parameters; a wind field; and diffusion parameters. Outputs: A rendered image of the gaseous phenomenon. Data Structures: Blob: A structure containing position vector \mathbf{p}, velocity vector \mathbf{v}, radius r, and density distribution parameters. Wind Field: A function or grid returning velocity \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}, t) at position \mathbf{x} and time t. Steps: 1. Initialize blob positions and velocities based on physical properties (convection, pressure, drag). 2. For each frame, update blob positions using Newton’s Laws of Motion, accounting for convection, drag, and thermal buoyancy. 3. Model the gas density within each blob as normally distributed over its spherical volume. 4. Apply diffusion equations to modify the density distribution over time. 5. Render the scene using a front-to-back ray casting strategy. 6. For each pixel, cast a ray and integrate the density contributions of intersecting blobs, considering the normally distributed gas volume. 7. Compute lighting and scattering effects based on the integrated density. Formulas: Gas density distribution: \rho(\mathbf{x}) = \rho0 \exp\left(-\frac{|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}|^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), where \rho0 is peak density, \mathbf{p} is blob center, and \sigma is spread parameter. Position update: \mathbf{p}{t+1} = \mathbf{p}t + \mathbf{v}t \Delta t. Velocity update: \mathbf{v}{t+1} = \mathbf{v}t + (\mathbf{u}(\mathbf{p}t, t) - \mathbf{v}t) \Delta t + \mathbf{a}{buoyancy} \Delta t. Parameters: \sigma: Spread parameter for density distribution. Not given in the sources. \Delta t: Time step. Not given in the sources. \rho0: Peak density. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision issues in density calculation for distant blobs. Use early ray termination if density falls below threshold. Boundary handling for wind fields. Clamp or interpolate wind velocities at domain boundaries. Degenerate input: Blobs with zero radius or density. Skip such blobs during rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderblobrenderer(blobs, windfield, diffusionparams, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): ray = camera.castray(x, y) color = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 for blob in blobs: if rayintersectsblob(ray, blob): density = computedensity(ray, blob, diffusionparams) absorption = density ray.stepsize color += (1.0 - transmittance) lighting(ray, blob) transmittance = exp(-absorption) if transmittance < 0.01: break image[y, x] = color return image def computedensity(ray, blob, diffusionparams): # Compute intersection point and distance # Apply diffusion equation to modify density # Return density value pass def lighting(ray, blob): # Compute lighting based on blob properties and wind field pass Time complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of blobs. Memory complexity: O(M) for storing blob data. Performance depends on the number of blobs and the complexity of the wind field. Strengths: Realistic modeling of turbulent gases. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large numbers of blobs. When to use: For realistic gaseous effects like smoke or fire. When not to use: For real-time applications with limited computational resources. Origin: Stam and Fiume. History: Applied to turbulent fields in gaseous phenomena. Usage: Rendering of gaseous effects like smoke and fire. name: TomoSphero Raytracer
head: Spherical Grid Raytracer, TomoSphero
body: TomoSphero is a differentiable raytracer designed for tomographic reconstruction on spherical grids, specifically targeting planetary and solar atmospheric modeling where spherical symmetry is prevalent. Unlike Cartesian ray-grid traversal methods that assume uniform voxel sizes and axis-aligned boundaries, TomoSphero explicitly computes intersections with spherical (radial), conical (elevational), and planar (azimuthal) boundaries to handle non-uniform and partial spherical domains. It solves the problem of efficiently computing line integrals (Fredholm integrals of the first kind) for optically thin media by precomputing voxel indices and intersection lengths, enabling fast GPU-accelerated forward and backward passes for gradient-based optimization. The method discretizes the continuous line integral of an object \rho along a ray into a weighted sum of voxel values, where weights are the intersection lengths of the ray with each voxel. The algorithm operates in four distinct phases: intersection computation, region indexing, sorting/length calculation, and integration. Inputs: Ray: Origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Grid: Defined by shape (Nr, Ne, Na) representing radial, elevational, and azimuthal dimensions. Radial boundaries: Nr + 1 spheres. Elevational boundaries: Ne + 1 cones. Azimuthal boundaries: Na + 1 planes. Object: 3D volume \rho defined on the spherical grid. Outputs: Measurements: Scalar projection values for each ray. Operator Data: Arrays of voxel indices (regs) and intersection lengths (lens) for use in reconstruction. The core data structure is a table (list of rows) where each row corresponds to a segment of the ray intersecting a specific voxel. For a single ray, the table has N rows, where N = 2(Nr + 1) + 2(Ne + 1) + (Na + 1). Each row contains: 1. Voxel Indices: A tuple (ri, ei, ai) representing the radial, elevational, and azimuthal indices of the voxel. 2. Intersection Length: \Delta li, the distance along the ray within that voxel. The implementation stores these as parallel arrays accessible via.regs (indices) and.lens (lengths). Step 1: Compute Ray-Boundary Intersections For each boundary type, compute the intersection points of the ray with all boundaries and their distances l from the ray origin \mathbf{o}. Radial (Spheres) and Elevational (Cones): Assume an upper bound of 2(Nr + 1) intersections for spheres/cones and Na + 1 for planes. Azimuthal (Planes): Each ray intersects each of the Na + 1 planar boundaries at most once. No Intersection Handling: If a boundary does not intersect the ray, store the coordinate but set the distance l to \infty. Step 2: Determine Crossing Direction and Region Indices For each intersection point, determine if the ray crosses the boundary in a "positive" (increasing index) or "negative" (decreasing index) direction. The direction depends on the crossing point coordinate and the ray direction \mathbf{d}. Convert boundary indices to region indices: If the crossing direction is negative, decrement the boundary index to get the region index. Step 3: Sort and Compute Intersection Lengths 1. Collect all region indices from Step 2 into a single list. 2. Sort all intersection points by their distance l from the ray start. 3. Compute the intersection length \Delta li for each segment as the difference between adjacent sorted distances: \Delta li = l{i+1} - li. Note: If li = \infty, \Delta li becomes \infty or \text{NaN}. 4. Construct the 3D voxel index table: Start with the voxel index of the ray origin. Insert the sorted region indices into the table. Fill in missing indices from the previous row to form complete 3D tuples (r, e, a). The total number of rows is N = 2(Nr + 1) + 2(Ne + 1) + (Na + 1). 5. Invalid Row Handling: Set \Delta li = 0 for any row where: The region index is invalid (less than 0 or \ge the grid dimension size). \Delta li is \infty or \text{NaN}. This ensures invalid segments contribute zero to the final sum. Step 4: Line Integration Compute the projection measurement y as the inner product of the object values and the intersection lengths: y = \sum{i=1}^{N} \rho(ri, ei, ai) \cdot \Delta li where \rho(ri, ei, ai) is the value of the object at the voxel indices (ri, ei, ai). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def intersectsphere(o, d, radius): """Standard ray-sphere intersection. Returns list of distances or [inf].""" oc = o b = 2.0 sum(d[i] oc[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(oc[i]2 for i in range(3)) - radius2 disc = b2 - 4.0 c if disc < 0: return [float('inf')] sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / 2.0 t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / 2.0 return [t for t in (t1, t2) if t >= 0] if t1 >= 0 else ([t2] if t2 >= 0 else [float('inf')]) def intersectcone(o, d, apex, axis, halfangle): """Standard ray-cone intersection. Returns list of distances or [inf].""" # Simplified standard quadratic solver for ray-cone v = [o[i] - apex[i] for i in range(3)] cosa = math.cos(halfangle) a = sum(d[i]axis[i] for i in range(3))2 - cosa2 sum(d[i]2 for i in range(3)) b = 2.0 (sum(d[i]axis[i] for i in range(3)) sum(v[i]axis[i] for i in range(3)) - cosa2 sum(v[i]d[i] for i in range(3))) c = sum(v[i]axis[i] for i in range(3))2 - cosa2 sum(v[i]2 for i in range(3)) disc = b2 - 4.0 a c if disc < 0 or abs(a) < 1e-9: return [float('inf')] sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) return [t for t in (t1, t2) if t >= 0] if t1 >= 0 else ([t2] if t2 >= 0 else [float('inf')]) def intersectplane(o, d, point, normal): """Standard ray-plane intersection. Returns list of distances or [inf].""" denom = sum(d[i] normal[i] for i in range(3)) if abs(denom) < 1e-9: return [float('inf')] t = sum((point[i] - o[i]) normal[i] for i in range(3)) / denom return [t] if t >= 0 else [float('inf')] def getcrossingdirection(dist, raydir, boundarytype, boundaryidx, grid): """Determines if crossing increases or decreases the region index.""" # Standard logic: positive if moving towards higher index, negative otherwise return 'positive' if raydir[0] > 0 else 'negative' def getvoxelindex(origin, grid): """Maps ray origin to initial voxel indices.""" return (0, 0, 0) # Placeholder for coordinate-to-index mapping def raytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, grid, objectvolume): # Step 1: Compute intersections rdists = [] for rbound in grid.radialboundaries: rdists.extend(intersectsphere(rayorigin, raydirection, rbound)) edists = [] for ebound in grid.elevationalboundaries: edists.extend(intersectcone(rayorigin, raydirection, ebound.apex, ebound.axis, ebound.halfangle)) adists = [] for abound in grid.azimuthalboundaries: adists.extend(intersectplane(rayorigin, raydirection, abound.point, abound.normal)) # Step 2: Determine crossing direction and region indices regions = [] for i, dist in enumerate(rdists): if dist == float('inf'): continue direction = getcrossingdirection(dist, raydirection, 'radial', i, grid) regionidx = i if direction == 'positive' else i - 1 regions.append(('r', regionidx, dist)) for i, dist in enumerate(edists): if dist == float('inf'): continue direction = getcrossingdirection(dist, raydirection, 'elevational', i, grid) regionidx = i if direction == 'positive' else i - 1 regions.append(('e', regionidx, dist)) for i, dist in enumerate(adists): if dist == float('inf'): continue direction = getcrossingdirection(dist, raydirection, 'azimuthal', i, grid) regionidx = i if direction == 'positive' else i - 1 regions.append(('a', regionidx, dist)) # Step 3: Sort and compute lengths regions.sort(key=lambda x: x[2]) segments = [] for i in range(len(regions) - 1): distcurr = regions[i][2] distnext = regions[i+1][2] length = distnext - distcurr if distcurr != float('inf') and distnext != float('inf') else float('inf') segments.append({'type': regions[i][0], 'regionidx': regions[i][1], 'length': length}) # Build 3D voxel table by propagating indices currentvoxel = list(getvoxelindex(rayorigin, grid)) voxeltable = [] prevdist = 0.0 for seg in segments: dim = seg['type'] idx = seg['regionidx'] if dim == 'r': currentvoxel[0] = idx elif dim == 'e': currentvoxel[1] = idx elif dim == 'a': currentvoxel[2] = idx voxeltable.append({'voxel': tuple(currentvoxel), 'length': seg['length']}) # Validate and zero invalid rows for entry in voxeltable: r, e, a = entry['voxel'] length = entry['length'] if (r < 0 or r >= grid.Nr or e < 0 or e >= grid.Ne or a < 0 or a >= grid.Na): entry['length'] = 0.0 continue if math.isinf(length) or math.isnan(length): entry['length'] = 0.0 # Step 4: Line Integration total = 0.0 for entry in voxeltable: r, e, a = entry['voxel'] length = entry['length'] rho = objectvolume[r, e, a] total += rho length return total Grid Shape (Nr, Ne, Na): Determines the resolution and number of boundaries. Data Types: The implementation uses int64 for indices and float64 for distances and values to ensure precision. No Intersection: If a boundary does not intersect the ray, the distance is set to \infty, and the corresponding segment is handled in validation. Parallel Boundaries: Numerically degenerate cases, such as a line of sight parallel to an azimuthal boundary plane, must be tested for consistency. Memory Limits: The algorithm does not support out-of-core operation. If the simultaneous computation for all rays exceeds available memory (VRAM), the algorithm fails. Invalid Indices: Rays passing outside the grid or crossing boundaries with no intersection result in invalid region indices, which are zeroed out to prevent contribution to the sum. Time Complexity: The algorithm involves computing intersections for all boundaries (O(Nr + Ne + Na) per ray), sorting them (O(K \log K) where K is the number of intersections), and integrating (O(K)). Since K \approx 2(Nr + 1) + 2(Ne + 1) + (Na + 1), the complexity is dominated by sorting and intersection computation. Memory Complexity: Peak memory usage is approximately (2Nr + 2Ne + Na) \cdot 6 \cdot N{rays} \cdot 8 / 10^9 GB, accounting for 6 arrays per ray (voxel indices for r/e/a, lengths, values, and temporary arrays) using 8-byte types. Performance: Validation tests on a unit sphere with a (50, 50, 50) grid showed measurements within 0.00001\% of the true value, approaching machine epsilon for float32. Strengths: Efficient for spherical symmetries; differentiable via PyTorch; supports arbitrary projection geometries (cone, parallel). Limitations: High memory usage for large grids and many rays; no out-of-core support; requires precomputation of intersections. TomoSphero was introduced to address the limitations of Cartesian discretization in tomographic reconstruction for planetary and solar atmospheres, where spherical symmetry is common. It is implemented in PyTorch to leverage GPU acceleration and automatic differentiation for gradient-based optimization. The method is used in atmospheric tomography, such as modeling the Carruthers Geocorona Observatory surveying Earth's exosphere. name: Ray Casting via Grid Line Intersection
head: DDA Raycasting, Vertical/Horizontal Collision Casting
body: This method is a 2D raycasting technique that computes intersections with vertical and horizontal grid lines to step cell-by-cell along a ray until a non-zero map cell is found. It distinguishes itself by explicitly calculating vertical and horizontal traces separately, selecting the closest hit between the two, and using Euclidean distance for the final result. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 2D grid map (content), player position (player.position.x, player.position.y), ray angle (angle), grid cell size (assumed 1 unit in source). Output: Hit object containing side (0 or 1), map coordinates (mapX, mapY), perpendicular wall distance (perpWallDist), and final intersection coordinates (finalX, finalY). Data Structures: content: A 2D array representing the grid. content[x][y] holds the cell value. Non-zero values indicate walls. player: Object with position (x, y) and other properties not directly used in the core DDA logic shown. Parameters: angle: Ray direction in radians. mapX, mapY: Current grid coordinates. sideDistX, sideDistY: Distance to the next vertical/horizontal grid line. stepX, stepY: Step direction (+1 or -1) for x and y. deltaDistX, deltaDistY: Distance to travel in x/y to reach the next grid line. Steps: 1. Initialize Vertical Trace: Compute vertical ray direction: right = Math.abs(Math.floor((angle - Math.PI / 2) / Math.PI) % 2). Compute first vertical grid line intersection X: firstX = right ? Math.floor(player.position.x / 1) 1 + 1: Math.floor(player.position.x / 1) 1. Compute corresponding Y: firstY = player.position.y + (firstX - player.position.x) Math.tan(angle). Set step vectors: xA = right ? 1: -1, yA = xA Math.tan(angle). Initialize loop variables: nextX = firstX, nextY = firstY. 2. Step Vertical Trace: Loop: cellX = right ? Math.floor(nextX / 1): Math.floor(nextX / 1) - 1. cellY = Math.floor(nextY / 1). Check bounds: If cellY < 0 or cellY >= map height or cellX < 0 or cellX >= map width, break. Check cell: If content[cellX][cellY] == 0, nextX += xA, nextY += yA. Else, hit found. Calculate distance: distance = sqrt((player.position.x - nextX)^2 + (player.position.y - nextY)^2). Return hit with side 0 (vertical hit). 3. Initialize Horizontal Trace: Compute horizontal ray direction: up = Math.abs(Math.floor(angle / Math.PI) % 2). Compute first horizontal grid line intersection Y: firstY = up ? Math.floor(player.position.y / 1) 1: Math.floor(player.position.y / 1) 1 + 1. Compute corresponding X: firstX = player.position.x + (firstY - player.position.y) / Math.tan(angle). Set step vectors: yA = up ? -1: 1, xA = yA / Math.tan(angle). Initialize loop variables: nextX = firstX, nextY = firstY. 4. Step Horizontal Trace: Loop: cellX = Math.floor(nextX / 1). cellY = up ? Math.floor(nextY / 1) - 1: Math.floor(nextY / 1). Check bounds: If cellY < 0 or cellY >= map height or cellX < 0 or cellX >= map width, break. Check cell: If content[cellX][cellY] == 0, nextX += xA, nextY += yA. Else, hit found. Calculate distance: distance = sqrt((player.position.x - nextX)^2 + (player.position.y - nextY)^2). Return hit with side 1 (horizontal hit). 5. Select Closest Hit: Compare distances from vertical and horizontal traces. Return the hit with the smaller distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastingviagridlineintersection(mapcontent, playerpos, angle): # Initialize vertical trace right = abs(math.floor((angle - math.pi / 2) / math.pi) % 2) firstx = (math.floor(playerpos.x / 1) 1 + 1) if right else (math.floor(playerpos.x / 1) 1) firsty = playerpos.y + (firstx - playerpos.x) math.tan(angle) xstep = 1 if right else -1 ystep = xstep math.tan(angle) nextx, nexty = firstx, firsty # Step vertical trace while True: cellx = math.floor(nextx / 1) if right else (math.floor(nextx / 1) - 1) celly = math.floor(nexty / 1) if not (0 <= celly < len(mapcontent) and 0 <= cellx < len(mapcontent[0])): break if mapcontent[cellx][celly] == 0: nextx += xstep nexty += ystep else: verticalhitdist = math.sqrt((playerpos.x - nextx)2 + (playerpos.y - nexty)2) verticalhit = (0, cellx, celly, verticalhitdist) break # Initialize horizontal trace up = abs(math.floor(angle / math.pi) % 2) firsty = (math.floor(playerpos.y / 1) 1) if up else (math.floor(playerpos.y / 1) 1 + 1) firstx = playerpos.x + (firsty - playerpos.y) / math.tan(angle) ystep = -1 if up else 1 xstep = ystep / math.tan(angle) nextx, nexty = firstx, firsty # Step horizontal trace while True: cellx = math.floor(nextx / 1) celly = (math.floor(nexty / 1) - 1) if up else math.floor(nexty / 1) if not (0 <= celly < len(mapcontent) and 0 <= cellx < len(mapcontent[0])): break if mapcontent[cellx][celly] == 0: nextx += xstep nexty += ystep else: horizontalhitdist = math.sqrt((playerpos.x - nextx)2 + (playerpos.y - nexty)2) horizontalhit = (1, cellx, celly, horizontalhitdist) break # Select closest hit if verticalhitdist < horizontalhitdist: return verticalhit else: return horizontalhit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero when tan(angle) is undefined (angle = 0, pi, etc.). Handle separately or use alternative calculations. Boundary checks are crucial to avoid out-of-bounds array access. Precision issues with floating-point arithmetic may affect hit detection. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of cells traversed by the ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Simple to implement, efficient for uniform grids. Limitations: Explicitly calculates two traces, which may be less efficient than a single DDA traversal. Not given in the sources for measured performance. Origin: Not given in the sources. History and development: Not given in the sources. Where it is used: Not given in the sources. name: Rendering Strategy and Optimization
body: Rendering Strategy and Optimization is a family of techniques that accelerate volume rendering by optimizing the efficiency of ray-grid traversal and determining optimal data structures for a given scene. It addresses the computational bottleneck of evaluating every voxel or primitive along a ray, which is often redundant due to empty space or coarse sampling. Unlike sibling methods that define specific traversal algorithms (e.g., DDA, Octree), this family focuses on how to execute traversal more efficiently (via hardware awareness or algorithmic shortcuts) and what resolution to use (via cost models) to minimize total rendering time. All methods in this family build on Ray-grid traversal, which advances analytically from one cell boundary to the next. The core mechanism determines the next cell by comparing distances to upcoming boundaries on the x, y, and z axes, selecting the minimum distance to advance. Optimization and cost models do not alter this fundamental geometric logic but instead optimize the cost of executing it or the parameters (like grid resolution) under which it runs. This family accelerates ray-grid traversal by exploiting spatial coherence among ray bundles or by enforcing strict topological connectivity rules to resolve boundary ambiguities. Unlike standard cell-by-cell methods like Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) Traversal which process rays individually and may suffer from divergence or diagonal jumps, this family processes rays as coherent frustums or resolves tie-breaking conditions explicitly. It solves the problem of packet divergence in coherent ray tracing and normal inaccuracies in uniform grid traversal. Rendering Order and Strategy defines the sequence in which volumetric cells are processed during ray-grid traversal to ensure correct optical compositing (typically front-to-back) and efficient occlusion culling. It solves the problem of determining which cells contribute to the final pixel color and in what order, distinguishing itself from sibling methods by decoupling the geometric traversal logic (handled by the parent Ray-grid traversal) from the semantic processing order required for correct alpha blending or visibility determination. This family encompasses techniques that accelerate volume rendering by optimizing the efficiency of ray-grid traversal and determining optimal data structures for a given scene. It addresses the computational bottleneck of evaluating every voxel or primitive along a ray, which is often redundant due to empty space or coarse sampling. Unlike sibling methods that define specific traversal algorithms (e.g., DDA, Octree), this family focuses on how to execute traversal more efficiently (via hardware awareness or algorithmic shortcuts) and what resolution to use (via cost models) to minimize total rendering time.
