name: Coherent and Connectivity Traversal
body: This family accelerates ray-grid traversal by exploiting spatial coherence among ray bundles or by enforcing strict topological connectivity rules to resolve boundary ambiguities. It solves the problem of packet divergence in coherent ray tracing and normal inaccuracies in uniform grid traversal. All methods in this family build on Ray-grid traversal, which advances analytically from one cell boundary to the next [Parent]. Optimization and cost models do not alter this fundamental geometric logic but instead optimize the cost of executing it or the parameters under which it runs [Parent]. Processes bundles of coherent rays as frustums, advancing slice-by-slice along a dominant axis rather than cell-by-cell. It sets itself apart from its sibling Rendering Order and Strategy and standard 3DDDA by avoiding expensive packet splitting and merging operations, allowing the grid to be rebuilt from scratch every frame for dynamic scenes while maintaining performance competitive with kd-trees. Choose it when rendering dynamic scenes with large coherent ray packets where packet divergence would break cell-by-cell traversal. Guarantees strict 4-connectivity by explicitly resolving boundary crossing ambiguities via stable sorting of intersection distances. It sets itself apart from its sibling Coherent Grid Traversal and standard DDA by explicitly testing a 2x2 cell neighborhood and using axis-priority sorting to prevent diagonal jumps, ensuring that rays crossing grid lines do so one axis at a time. Choose it when topological consistency and correct normal calculation are required, particularly for primary rays hitting silhouettes or when diagonal jumps cause artifacts. A property defining the set of cells a ray can traverse to from its current cell, inspired by pixel connectivity in image processing. Taxicab metric distance between P1=(x1, y1) and P2=(x2, y2) is |x1 - x2| + |y1 - y2|. Chebyshev metric distance between P1=(x1, y1) and P2=(x2, y2) is \max(|x1 - x2|, |y1 - y2|). In 2D, there are 4-connectivity (orthogonal neighbors) and 8-connectivity (including diagonal neighbors). The concept of connectivity in ray traversal was formalized in a thesis by Hur, which analyzed the behavior of rays crossing voxel corners. The thesis noted that standard DDA methods might traverse through corners, leading to 8-connectivity, whereas specific algorithms aim for 4-connectivity to ensure correct normal calculation and topological consistency. versal algorithm for ray tracing Hur man gör en hierarkisk..., https://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:2069409/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Coherent Grid Traversal
head: CGT (Coherent Grid Traversal), CGT algorithm, Ize et al. traversal, Slice by slice algorithm
body: Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) is a ray tracing acceleration technique for uniform grids that traverses bundles (frustums) of coherent rays slice-by-slice along a dominant axis, abandoning cell-by-cell traversal to avoid expensive packet splitting and merging operations. It sets itself apart from its sibling Hero-like 4-Connectivity (H4T) and standard 3DDDA by processing entire slices of cells as a coherent whole, allowing the grid to be rebuilt from scratch every frame for dynamic scenes while maintaining performance competitive with kd-trees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A packet of N \times N coherent rays (spanning an angle < \pi/2) defined by origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d}; a uniform grid of dimensions Nx \times Ny \times Nz; the grid's bounding box. Output: A sequence of grid cells (or bricks) overlapped by the ray packet frustum, in traversal order along the major axis. Data Structures: Canonical Grid Space: Rays are transformed such that the grid maps to [0, Nx) \times [0, Ny) \times [0, Nz). Cell coordinates are computed by truncating floating-point positions to integers. Frustum Representation: Defined by four bounding planes in the minor axes (\tilde{U}, \tilde{V}) and near/far planes in the major axis (\tilde{K}). For primary rays, these are derived from the four corner rays of the packet. Overlap Box B(i): A 2D axis-aligned box in the \tilde{U}, \tilde{V} plane representing the frustum's intersection with slice i along \tilde{K}. Stored as four floats: [u{min}, v{min}, u{max}, v{max}]. Bricked Volume (Optional): For volume rendering, the volume is stored as "bricks" referenced by 3 maps (one per principal axis). Empty bricks are not stored for compression. Parameters: Packet Size: Typically 4 \times 4 or 8 \times 8 rays. Major Axis \tilde{K}: Determined by the dominant component (\pm X, \pm Y, \pm Z) of the first ray's direction. All rays must have the same sign along \tilde{K} to allow front-to-back traversal. Minor Axes \tilde{U}, \tilde{V}: The remaining two dimensions. Steps: 1. Transform: Convert all rays in the packet to canonical grid space. 2. Select Major Axis: Identify \tilde{K} as the axis with the maximum absolute direction component of the first ray. Verify all rays have the same sign along \tilde{K}. 3. Compute Frustum Planes: Calculate the slopes and offsets of the four bounding planes in \tilde{U} and \tilde{V} based on the extremal rays (or all rays for secondary packets). 4. Clip to Grid: Intersect the frustum with the grid's bounding box to determine the first slice index k{min} and last slice index k{max} along \tilde{K}. If the interval is empty, terminate. 5. Initialize Overlap Box: Compute the initial overlap box B(0) for slice k{min} by finding the min/max \tilde{U} and \tilde{V} coordinates of the frustum's entry and exit points at that slice. 6. Traverse Slices: For each slice k from k{min} to k{max}: a. Convert to Cell IDs: Truncate the min/max coordinates of B(k) to integers to get the cell range [i0..i1] \times [j0..j1] in the \tilde{U}, \tilde{V} plane. b. Intersect: Intersect all rays in the packet with all primitives (triangles or volume data) in the cells defined by the range. c. Increment Overlap Box: Compute B(k+1) = B(k) + \Delta B, where \Delta B = (du{min}, du{max}, dv{min}, dv{max}) are the slopes of the bounding planes in grid space. This requires four floating-point additions. 7. Early Termination: If all rays have intersected their targets, stop traversal. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coherentgridtraversal(rays, griddims, gridbounds): # 1. Transform rays to canonical grid space (assumed pre-computed) # 2. Select major axis K firstray = rays[0] absd = [abs(firstray.d[i]) for i in range(3)] kaxis = absd.index(max(absd)) uaxis = (kaxis + 1) % 3 vaxis = (kaxis + 2) % 3 # Check coherence: all rays must have same sign along K ksign = 1 if firstray.d[kaxis] > 0 else -1 for ray in rays: if ray.d[kaxis] ksign <= 0: raise ValueError("Rays are not coherent along major axis K") # 3. Compute Frustum Planes (slopes and offsets in grid space) slopes = [] offsets = [] for ray in rays: if ray.d[kaxis] == 0: continue du = ray.d[uaxis] / ray.d[kaxis] dv = ray.d[vaxis] / ray.d[kaxis] slopes.append((du, dv)) # U(K) = offsetu + K du => offsetu = U(0) - 0 du # Using ray origin projected to K=0 plane: offsetu = ray.o[uaxis] - ray.o[kaxis] du offsetv = ray.o[vaxis] - ray.o[kaxis] dv offsets.append((offsetu, offsetv)) dumin = min(s[0] for s in slopes) dumax = max(s[0] for s in slopes) dvmin = min(s[1] for s in slopes) dvmax = max(s[1] for s in slopes) offsetumin = min(o[0] for o in offsets) offsetumax = max(o[0] for o in offsets) offsetvmin = min(o[1] for o in offsets) offsetvmax = max(o[1] for o in offsets) # 4. Clip to Grid to find kmin and kmax # Frustum K-extent is clipped to [0, griddims[kaxis]) # Assuming frustum near/far in canonical space are known or derived from ray origins frustumkmin = max(0.0, min(ray.o[kaxis] for ray in rays)) frustumkmax = max(ray.o[kaxis] + ray.d[kaxis] 1000.0 for ray in rays) # Simplified far plane kmin = max(0, int(frustumkmin)) kmax = min(griddims[kaxis] - 1, int(frustumkmax)) if kmin > kmax: return # 5. Initialize Overlap Box B(0) for slice kmin bumin = offsetumin + kmin dumin bumax = offsetumax + kmin dumax bvmin = offsetvmin + kmin dvmin bvmax = offsetvmax + kmin dvmax deltab = (dumin, dumax, dvmin, dvmax) # 6. Traverse Slices for k in range(kmin, kmax + 1): # Convert to cell IDs via truncation i0 = int(bumin) i1 = int(bumax) j0 = int(bvmin) j1 = int(bvmax) # Clamp to grid bounds i0 = max(0, min(i0, griddims[uaxis] - 1)) i1 = max(0, min(i1, griddims[uaxis] - 1)) j0 = max(0, min(j0, griddims[vaxis] - 1)) j1 = max(0, min(j1, griddims[vaxis] - 1)) # Yield cells in this slice for i in range(i0, i1 + 1): for j in range(j0, j1 + 1): yield (i, j, k) # Incremental update for next slice: B(k+1) = B(k) + ΔB bumin += deltab[0] bumax += deltab[1] bvmin += deltab[2] bvmax += deltab[3] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Divergence: If rays span an angle > \pi/2, they may have different signs along the traversal axis, violating the front-to-back assumption. Mitigation: Ensure packet coherence or split packets only when hit points are too distant (silhouettes), as general splitting deteriorates to single-ray traversal. Silhouette Hit Points: If primary rays hit object silhouettes, hit points can be distant, creating a wide frustum where the method breaks down. Mitigation: Split the packet into subpackets if min/max hit distances are too large. Roll Angle: When the "roll" angle of the bundles to the volume angle is close to \pi/4, block fetches can double. Redundant Intersections: Grids do not conform tightly to geometry, and filling cells with bounding boxes exacerbates redundant triangle intersections. Mitigation: Use SIMD frustum culling and mailboxing. Straddling Triangles: Large triangles or small triangles straddling boundaries may appear in multiple cells. Mitigation: Mailboxing. An optimization for glyph-based particle visualization that eliminates data duplication by storing each particle in exactly one grid cell, traversing an enlarged frustum to ensure containment. Choose it when visualizing large particle datasets to avoid redundant intersection tests and storage overhead. Extends CGT to large volumes using a recursive hierarchy of macrocells (2^3 children) to amortize traversal costs, using an iterative stack. Choose it when flat CGT performance degrades on massive datasets, as it maintains slice-based traversal while managing spatial hierarchy. A parallelization scheme assigning processing elements to slices of the volume, requiring explicit data structures to map bundles to slices. Choose it when reducing redundant block fetches from neighboring bundles is prioritized over direct bundle processing. A parallelization scheme where bundles of rays are processed in parallel, distributing work across processing elements. Choose it for straightforward implementation on multi-core systems, accepting potential redundant block fetches from neighboring bundles. A culling technique for spheres that checks if the sphere center is contained within an enlarged bounding frustum, avoiding unnecessary intersection tests. Choose it for particle-based visualization where planar shaft culling is inapplicable. A hierarchical grid structure that divides densely populated regions more finely, using parameter range culling for early-out tests. Choose it when aggressive early-out tests on particle properties are needed to replace simple empty/non-empty flags. Time Complexity: The traversal cost per step is independent of the number of rays in the packet, encouraging larger packets. The incremental update of the overlap box requires only four floating-point additions (one SIMD instruction) and one float-to-int conversion (one SIMD instruction) per slice. Memory Complexity: The grid is uniform and simple to build, making it suitable for per-frame rebuilds in dynamic scenes. For volume rendering, a "bricked" volume structure reduces memory overhead by not storing empty bricks. Measured Performance: On a dual 3.2 GHz Xeon, rendering a 174K triangle animated scene at 1024x1024 achieves 1.4 fps with shading/textures/shadows, and 3.4 fps excluding them. CGT outperforms single-ray 3DDDA by a factor of 6.75 to 20.9x. It performs competitively with kd-trees (e.g., 1.0M vs 0.82M ray-triangle intersections in the 'toys' scene). Scaling: Sublinear scaling in screen resolution is observed because higher resolutions enable larger packets, amortizing traversal costs. Strengths: Simple grid construction allows for full per-frame rebuilds, ideal for dynamic/animated scenes. Avoids expensive packet splitting and merging. Cache-friendly for volume rendering. Limitations: Uniform grids are ill-suited for highly complex scenes with high variation in geometry size and density (e.g., Boeing 777). Performance degrades if the roll angle is close to \pi/4. Coherent Grid Traversal was introduced in 2006 by Wald, Ize, Kensler, Knoll, and Parker in "Ray Tracing Animated Scenes using Coherent Grid Traversal" published in ACM Transactions on Graphics (SIGGRAPH). It was developed to address the limitations of packet-based kd-tree traversal for dynamic scenes, where rebuilding the kd-tree is expensive. The algorithm abandons cell-by-cell traversal (3DDDA) in favor of slice-by-slice traversal to maintain coherence within ray packets. It has been used in systems for interactive visualization of large particle datasets and volume rendering. name: Sphere-Center Method
head: Sphere-center grid
body: The Sphere-Center Method is an optimization for glyph-based particle visualization within the Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) framework that eliminates data duplication and redundant intersection tests by storing each particle in exactly one grid cell. It achieves this by traversing an enlarged frustum that accounts for the maximum particle radius, ensuring that any sphere intersecting the original view volume has its center contained within the traversal bounds. Unlike standard grid approaches that require mailboxes or reference lists to handle primitives overlapping multiple cells, this method guarantees single storage and single intersection per particle. The method exploits the property that particle radii are either uniform or fall within a well-defined range. By using the maximum radius across all particles, the algorithm constructs a frustum large enough to contain the centers of all potentially intersecting spheres, thereby allowing a simple "center-in-cell" storage scheme. Inputs: Particle dataset: A collection of spheres defined by center coordinates (x, y, z) and radius r. Ray packet frustum F: Defined by bounding planes and near/far clipping planes. Grid resolution: Determines the cell size in world units. Outputs: A grid structure where each sphere is stored in exactly one cell. An enlarged frustum Fr used for traversal. Grid: A multi-level grid structure (as defined in Coherent Grid Traversal). Cell Content: Each cell stores a list of particle indices or direct particle data. Unlike standard grids, no duplicate entries or mailbox structures are required. Particle Storage: Particles are stored directly in the finest level of the grid. The conversion from floating-point center coordinates to grid cell indices is performed via truncation. r{max}: The maximum radius across all particles in the dataset. This value is determined once during initialization and cached for subsequent build and traversal steps. dU: The direction vector component of the normal to a bounding plane of the frustum. 1. Initialization: Compute r{max} by iterating over all particles and finding the maximum radius. Cache r{max} for use in grid construction and traversal. 2. Grid Construction: For each particle with center C = (x, y, z), compute its grid cell coordinates by truncating the floating-point values of its center in the grid coordinate space to integers. Store the particle in the list of the identified cell. This process replaces expensive primitive/cell or bounding box/cell overlap tests with a single float-to-int truncation per particle. 3. Frustum Enlargement: Compute the shift distance s for the side bounding planes of the frustum. The distance s is calculated based on r{max} and the plane normal direction dU: s = r{max} \sqrt{1 + dU^2} Derivation: The condition that a sphere of radius r{max} intersects a bounding plane defined by normal direction dU is equivalent to the sphere's center being within distance r{max} of the plane. Geometrically, this requires shifting the plane by s such that the projection of the shift vector onto the normal equals r{max}. The scalar projection formula yields r{max} = \frac{\langle -dU, 1 \rangle \cdot \langle 0, s \rangle}{|\langle -dU, 1 \rangle|}, which solves to s = r{max} \sqrt{1 + dU^2}. Adjust the bounding planes: Add s to the u0 parameter for the maximum bounding plane and subtract s for the minimum bounding plane. Adjust the near and far planes: Shift the near plane by r{max} in the -\mathbf{K} direction and the far plane by r{max} in the +\mathbf{K} direction, where \mathbf{K} is the viewing direction. The resulting structure is the enlarged frustum Fr. 4. Traversal: Traverse the grid using the enlarged frustum Fr instead of the original frustum F. For each cell visited, intersect the rays in the packet against all spheres stored in that cell. Because the frustum is enlarged by r{max}, any sphere intersecting the original frustum F is guaranteed to have its center inside Fr. Thus, intersecting only spheres whose centers are in the visited cells covers all potential intersections. 5. Early Ray Termination: Adjust early ray termination criteria to account for spheres whose centers lie in the next slice but whose geometry extends into the current slice due to the enlarged frustum. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raysphereintersect(rayo, rayd, spherec, radius): """Standard ray-sphere intersection check.""" oc = [rayo[i] - spherec[i] for i in range(3)] a = sum(rayd[i] rayd[i] for i in range(3)) b = sum(oc[i] rayd[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(oc[i] oc[i] for i in range(3)) - radius radius return b b - a c >= 0 def spherecenterbuild(particles, frustumplanes, frustumnear, frustumfar, viewdir, cellsize): rmax = max(p.radius for p in particles) grid = {} for i, p in enumerate(particles): gx = int(p.center[0] / cellsize) gy = int(p.center[1] / cellsize) gz = int(p.center[2] / cellsize) grid.setdefault((gx, gy, gz), []).append(i) enlargedplanes = [] for plane in frustumplanes: dU = plane['normal'][0] s = rmax math.sqrt(1.0 + dU dU) newu0 = plane['u0'] + (s if plane['ismax'] else -s) enlargedplanes.append({'normal': plane['normal'], 'u0': newu0, 'ismax': plane['ismax']}) enlargednear = frustumnear - rmax enlargedfar = frustumfar + rmax return grid, enlargedplanes, enlargednear, enlargedfar, viewdir def traverse(grid, planes, near, far, viewdir, particles, rays): for cellkey, indices in grid.items(): cellmin = [c 1.0 for c in cellkey] cellmax = [m + 1.0 for m in cellmin] if not boxintersectsfrustum(cellmin, cellmax, planes, near, far, viewdir): continue for idx in indices: p = particles[idx] for ray in rays: if raysphereintersect(ray.origin, ray.dir, p.center, p.radius): pass def boxintersectsfrustum(boxmin, boxmax, planes, near, far, viewdir): """Checks if an axis-aligned box intersects the frustum planes.""" for plane in planes: n = plane['normal'] u0 = plane['u0'] # Check if box is completely outside the plane if (boxmin[0] n[0] + boxmin[1] n[1] + boxmin[2] n[2] < u0 and boxmax[0] n[0] + boxmax[1] n[1] + boxmax[2] n[2] < u0): return False if boxmin[2] < near or boxmax[2] > far: return False return True Wide Radius Range: If particle radii span several orders of magnitude, using r{max} causes the enlarged frustum to be excessively large. This results in traversing many empty cells and intersecting many unnecessary spheres, potentially outweighing the benefits of single storage. Frustum culling is typically required to mitigate this performance loss. Non-Uniform Radii: The method assumes radii are uniform or within a small range. If this assumption is violated, the performance gain diminishes. Plane Normal Definition: The calculation of s depends on the definition of dU. The sources define dU as the direction vector of the given plane's normal in a reduced 2D context where the normal is \langle -dU, 1 \rangle. Implementers must ensure dU is extracted correctly from the frustum plane definitions. Uses a macrocell hierarchy to skip empty space efficiently within the CGT framework. Choose when the scene has large regions of empty space and hierarchical skipping is beneficial. See Macrocell Hierarchical CGT. Parallelizes the processing of slices within the CGT traversal. Choose when hardware supports parallel execution across slices. See Slice Parallelisation. Parallelizes ray packets across multiple cores. Choose when ray-level parallelism is preferred over slice-level. See Bundle Parallelisation. Uses SIMD instructions to efficiently cull spheres against frusta. Choose when CPU SIMD capabilities are available to accelerate culling operations. See SIMD Sphere/Frustum Culling. Time Complexity: Grid construction is O(N) where N is the number of particles, due to the simple truncation operation. Traversal complexity depends on the number of cells visited by the enlarged frustum and the number of spheres per cell. Memory Complexity: Memory footprint is reduced significantly because each particle is stored exactly once. For the BulletTorso dataset (35M particles), storage dropped from 3.11 GB (with references) to 1.04 GB. Measured Performance: Speed-up over standard grid: 1.02x to 1.27x on various datasets (Cylinder, JP8, Bullet, Thunder, Foam, BulletTorso). Grid construction time improvement: Up to 3.07x faster insertion phase (e.g., JP8 dataset: 797.71 ms to 260.13 ms). Total construction time improved from 1407.27 ms to 510.96 ms (factor of 2.75). Strengths: Eliminates data duplication and mailbox overhead. Improves locality of reference. Simplifies grid construction by avoiding overlap tests. Efficient frustum computation using SIMD (5 operations). Limitations: Performance degrades if particle radii vary widely. Requires a priori knowledge of r{max}. Enlarged frustum may traverse more cells than necessary if r{max} is large relative to particle density. When to Use: Ideal for particle-based simulation data with uniform or narrowly distributed radii, where interactive performance and low memory footprint are critical. When Not to Use: When particle radii vary by several orders of magnitude, unless combined with effective frustum culling. The Sphere-Center Method was introduced in the context of interactive ray tracing for particle-based simulation data, specifically for visualizing material point method (MPM) simulations. It was presented as an optimization to the Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) algorithm to address classic grid problems: duplicate data, lack of locality of reference, and redundant intersection tests. The method draws inspiration from offset surfaces used in collision detection. It was evaluated on datasets such as Cylinder, JP8, Bullet, Thunder, Foam, and BulletTorso, demonstrating improvements in both frame rate and memory usage. The approach is applicable to other primitive types, such as triangles, though primarily designed for spherical glyphs. name: Macrocell Hierarchical CGT
head: Hierarchical CGT, Recursive CGT with Array Stack
body: Macrocell Hierarchical CGT extends Coherent Grid Traversal [2987-coherent-grid-traversal.md] to handle large volumes by introducing a recursive hierarchy of macrocells, where each parent block contains 2^3 children. It solves the performance degradation of flat CGT on large datasets by amortizing traversal costs across multiple levels of granularity, using an array stack to manage the hierarchy iteratively rather than recursively. It differs from Sphere-Center Method by maintaining slice-based frustum traversal and from Bundle Parallelisation by focusing on spatial hierarchy management rather than ray packet parallelism. Inputs: A ray packet with bounding frustum defined by axes U, V, K; a volume with a hierarchical macrocell structure; a target isovalue. Outputs: A list of visited cells or traversal state updates. Data Structures: The core structure is an Array Stack that replaces recursive function calls. For a hierarchy of depth L, the stack stores: 1. uslice, vslice: Current slice coordinates for each level l \in [0, L-1]. 2. uinc, vinc: Increment values for U and V axes for each level. 3. currentslice: The current slice index within the active macrocell level. 4. returnslice: The slice index at which to resume parent macrocell traversal. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the stack for the root macrocell level. Set initial U, V slices and increments based on the frustum intersection with the root volume. Set currentslice to the starting K-slice. Let l be the current macrocell level (initially 0). 2. Loop: While the stack is not empty and rays have not exited the volume: a. Culling Test: Check if the current macrocell at uslice[l], vslice[l] contains the target isovalue by comparing it against the macrocell's precomputed min/max range. b. Traversal Decision: i. If the macrocell is empty (isovalue not in min/max range), skip to the next slice or parent level. ii. If the macrocell is non-empty and l < L-1 (not leaf), push state for child level l+1 onto the stack. Child coordinates are derived from parent coordinates as M-multiples. iii. If the macrocell is non-empty and l = L-1 (leaf level), traverse the full slice of volume cells within this macrocell using standard CGT logic. c. Advance: Increment currentslice for level l. If currentslice exceeds the macrocell boundary, pop the stack to return to the parent level l-1, setting currentslice to returnslice[l-1]. 3. Termination: Stop when all rays have intersected or exited the root macrocell. Formulas: Child coordinate mapping: C{child} = M \times C{parent}. Next macrocell slice (for binary subdivision, M=2): Slice{next} = Slice{current} + 2. Parameters: M: Macrocell width multiple. Typically M=2 for octree alignment. L: Number of macrocell layers. A 3-deep hierarchy is effective for volumes > 256^3. Edge Cases: Implicit Macrocells: When using an octree, macrocells are implicit. Min/max pairs are retrieved from octree interior nodes, but to avoid costly lookups, the path from the octree root to the current node along the U,V-minimal ray of the frustum is stored. Leaf Node Mapping: A single coarse scalar leaf node in the octree may cover multiple finer-level implicit macrocells. The algorithm must find the deepest octree child mapping to the implicit macrocell coordinate to perform the isovalue cull. A variant where the macrocell hierarchy is implicit in the octree structure, retrieving min/max pairs from octree interior nodes instead of explicit macrocell blocks. It uses a common coordinate space [0, 2^{d{max}}] for all octree node depths, where d{max} is the maximum tree depth. This allows optimization for binary subdivision: multiplying the K-slice by macrocell width M=2 is replaced by a bitwise left-shift, and computing the next macrocell slice requires a simple +2 addition. It is chosen when the volume is naturally stored as an octree, avoiding the overhead of explicit macrocell data structures. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of visited cells, but with a significantly reduced constant factor for large volumes due to early culling at macrocell levels. Memory Complexity: O(L) for the stack, where L is the hierarchy depth. Additional memory for octree storage if implicit. Performance: A recursive 3-level macrocell hierarchy yields best performance for volumes larger than 256^3. Strengths: Handles large volumes efficiently; avoids recursion overhead; compatible with octree structures. Limitations: Requires precomputed min/max values for macrocells; complex implementation due to stack management and implicit node mapping. When to use: Large volumetric datasets (> 256^3) where flat CGT is too slow. When not to use: Small volumes where overhead outweighs benefits; non-octree data without explicit macrocell construction. Developed by Knoll et al. as an extension of Coherent Grid Traversal [2987-coherent-grid-traversal.md] to handle larger volumes, building on Parker et al.'s work. It was implemented to address the limitations of two-level hierarchies for volumes as small as 30^3, finding that deeper hierarchies (equivalent to full octrees) were necessary for robustness. It is used in interactive ray tracing of implicit surfaces and volumetric visualization. name: Slice Parallelisation
head: Data Parallel, Data Parallel / Slice-Parallel Rendering, Ray-slice-sweeping, Slice-Parallel Rendering
body: Slice Parallelisation is a parallelisation scheme for Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) where processing elements are assigned to slices of the volume rather than individual rays or bundles. It solves the problem of determining which ray bundles intersect a given slice when traversal is not incremental, requiring explicit data structures to map bundles to slices. Unlike Bundle Parallelisation, it reduces redundant block fetches from neighbouring bundles by organizing work per slice. Inputs: A set of ray bundles defined by their entry and exit points. The volume grid structure. The dominant traversal axis k. Outputs: For each slice s, a list of bundles that intersect it, ready for processing. Data Structures: The method maintains two sets of structures to track bundle-slice intersections: 1. Primary Vectors and Tables: Vector A: Stores references to bundles that start at the beginning of the volume (k=0). Vector D: Stores references to bundles that end at the end of the volume (k=k{\text{max}}). Table P: Index table corresponding to A. P[i] stores the slice index s where bundle A[i] starts. Table Q: Index table corresponding to D. Q[j] stores the slice index s where bundle D[j] ends. 2. Secondary Lists and Tables: List S: Stores references to "remaining" bundles (those that do not start at k=0 and do not end at k=k{\text{max}}). List E: Stores references to the same "remaining" bundles. Table M: Index table corresponding to S. M[i] stores the slice index s where bundle S[i] first intersects the volume. Table N: Index table corresponding to E. N[j] stores the slice index s where bundle E[j] last intersects the volume. List S is sorted by the values in M (ascending). List E is sorted by the values in N (ascending). Algorithm Steps: 1. Classification: During tracing, classify every bundle into one of three categories: starters (k=0), finishers (k=k{\text{max}}), and remaining bundles. 2. Population: Add starters to vector A and record their starting slice index in table P. Add finishers to vector D and record their ending slice index in table Q. Add remaining bundles to lists S and E, recording their first intersecting slice in M and last intersecting slice in N. Sort S by M and E by N. 3. Slice Processing: For a processing element assigned to slice s, identify all intersecting bundles using the following logic: Identify Starters: Retrieve all bundles from A where P[i] == s. Identify Finishers: Retrieve all bundles from D where Q[j] == s. Identify Remaining: Find bundles in S where M[i] \le s and bundles in E where N[j] \ge s. The intersection of these two sets gives the remaining bundles active in slice s. Combine: The total set of bundles for slice s is B(s) = B{\text{start}}(s) \cup B{\text{end}}(s) \cup B{\text{mid}}(s). 4. Traversal: For each bundle in B(s), perform the CGT traversal steps for the cells within slice s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processslice(s, A, D, P, Q, S, E, M, N): # Identify starters: bundles starting exactly at slice s Bstart = [A[i] for i in range(len(A)) if P[i] == s] # Identify finishers: bundles ending exactly at slice s Bend = [D[j] for j in range(len(D)) if Q[j] == s] # Identify remaining bundles: those that span across slice s # S is sorted by M (ascending), E is sorted by N (ascending) # Sources state we must run through both lists to find the intersection Bmid = [] for i in range(len(S)): if M[i] <= s: bundle = S[i] for j in range(len(E)): if E[j] is bundle and N[j] >= s: Bmid.append(bundle) break return Bstart + Bend + Bmid Formulas: B{\text{start}}(s) = \{ A[i] \mid P[i] == s \} B{\text{end}}(s) = \{ D[j] \mid Q[j] == s \} B{\text{mid}}(s) = \{ S[i] \mid M[i] \le s \} \cap \{ E[j] \mid N[j] \ge s \} Parameters: k{\text{max}}: The maximum index along the dominant traversal axis. Average percentage of "Remaining" bundles: ~14%. Maximum percentage of "Remaining" bundles: 33%. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Locality: If vectors A and D fit in cache/local store, identifying bundles for a slice requires 0 memory reads beyond the cache. If they do not fit, exactly 2 memory reads are required to fetch the relevant index tables. Redundant Fetches: While Slice Parallelisation is less likely to exhibit redundant block fetches from neighbouring bundles compared to other methods, it is still possible. Roll Angle: When the "roll" angle of the bundles relative to the volume angle is close to \pi/4, the number of block fetches can double. A solution is noted as "not yet published" in the source. A slice-parallel technique that processes consecutive data slices parallel to a face of the volume data set. It partitions object space rather than screen space, assigning tasks to processors that request new tasks upon completion. Introduced by de Boer et al., this variant divides the volume into horizontal sections processed in turn. This reduces the slice face area and hence the size of the slice buffers. A two-dimensional array of SIMD processing elements used for parallel segmentation. The volume is distributed so that a complete beam of voxels along the z-axis is stored on each processing element, allowing conflict-free access to any z-slice with only a single clock cycle delay between slices. Complexity: The identification of bundles for a slice s requires constant time for starters and finishers (2 memory reads). The identification of remaining bundles requires scanning lists S and E. Since the remaining bundles are a small fraction (avg 14%, max 33%), this overhead is considered negligible and "does not hit performance". Memory: Requires storage for vectors A, D and lists S, E, plus index tables P, Q, M, N. Strengths: Trivial to implement (e.g., 1 line of OpenMP code in C++). Reduces redundant block fetches compared to bundle parallelisation. Limitations: Traversal is not incremental, requiring explicit tracking of bundle-slice intersections. Performance may degrade if the roll angle is near \pi/4. Slice Parallelisation is a parallelisation strategy developed for the Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) algorithm for volume rendering. It was presented by researchers at the UCL Department of Computer Science. The method addresses the non-incremental nature of slice-based traversal by introducing explicit data structures to map bundles to slices. name: Bundle Parallelisation
head: GPU Integration Optimization, Ray Compaction and Sorting Optimization
body: Bundle parallelisation is a parallelization scheme for coherent grid traversal where bundles of rays are processed in parallel. It distributes the processing of ray bundles across multiple processing elements to accelerate volume rendering. Unlike slice parallelisation, which requires complex index tables to map bundles to slices, bundle parallelisation processes bundles directly, though it may result in redundant block fetches from neighbouring bundles. Inputs: Ray bundles, depth map, shadow map, and image dimensions. Outputs: Rendered image pixels with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: Bundle: A collection of rays sharing a common traversal path or depth range. Shadow Map: Depth buffer used for visibility prefiltering. Partial Sum Tree: Stores accumulated transmittance and color for a slice. Thread Blocks: Allocated per slice. Steps: 1. Rectification: Perform a data-parallel operation on the depth and shadow maps to prepare data for visibility queries. One thread is assigned per output pixel. 2. Sorting and Prefiltering: Combine visibility prefiltering and sorting into a single kernel. This step coalesces groups of 4 rays based on their depth information from the shadow map. A modified GPU radix sort is used to coalesce rays with similar depths as it walks over the input shadow map. 3. Integration: Allocate one thread block of 32 threads per slice. Assign one thread per slice for the integration phase because partial sum trees are too large to fit into shared memory. Store the partial sum trees in global memory. Execute the inner loop using the while-if-if strategy (UPDATE-TREE and QUERY-TREE) to minimize instruction divergence, ensuring at least half the threads in a warp perform useful work. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bundleparallelisation(bundles, depthmap, shadowmap, imagewidth, imageheight): # Step 1: Rectification # Data-parallel operation on depth and shadow maps. # One thread per output pixel. rectifieddata = [] for y in range(imageheight): row = [] for x in range(imagewidth): row.append((depthmap[y][x], shadowmap[y][x])) rectifieddata.append(row) # Step 2: Sorting and Prefiltering # Combine visibility prefiltering and sorting into a single kernel. # Coalesce groups of 4 rays based on depth from shadow map. # Modified GPU radix sort coalesces rays with similar depths walking over shadow map. sortedbundles = [] for bundle in bundles: groups = [] for i in range(0, len(bundle), 4): group = bundle[i:i+4] # Sort group by shadow map depth to coalesce similar rays group.sort(key=lambda ray: rectifieddata[ray.y][ray.x][1]) groups.append(group) sortedbundles.append(groups) # Step 3: Integration # Allocate one block of 32 threads per slice. # Assign one thread per slice because partial sum trees are too large for shared memory. # Store trees in global memory. numslices = imageheight // 32 globalmemorytrees = [None] numslices renderedimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight imagewidth)] for sliceidx in range(numslices): # One thread per slice handles this slice tree = globalmemorytrees[sliceidx] for group in sortedbundles: # while-if-if strategy for UPDATE-TREE and QUERY-TREE # Ensures at least half threads in warp do useful work while group: # UPDATE-TREE: accumulate transmittance and color # QUERY-TREE: sample and composite # Implementation details for tree operations not given in sources. pass return renderedimage Parameters: Block Size: 32 threads per slice. Ray Grouping: Groups of 4 rays coalesced during sorting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Redundant Fetches: Some blocks may be fetched multiple times from neighbouring bundles. Memory Constraints: Partial sum trees are too large for shared memory on current hardware, necessitating global memory storage. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Global memory usage for partial sum trees due to size constraints. Performance: The method is described as "trivial" to implement on CPU with OpenMP (1 line of code). On GPU, it uses specific optimizations like the while-if-if strategy to ensure at least half the threads in a warp do useful work. name: SIMD Sphere/Frustum Culling
head: Sphere/Frustum Culling
body: A culling technique to reject non-overlapping spheres by checking if the sphere center is contained within an enlarged bounding frustum, thereby avoiding unnecessary ray/sphere intersection tests caused by discretization artifacts or spheres smaller than the maximum radius r{max}. It sets itself apart from the SIMD shaft culling used in the original Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) by being appropriate for spheres, which lack the planar edges required for shaft culling. Inputs: A packet of rays bounded by an original bounding frustum \mathcal{F}. A set of spheres, each defined by a center \mathbf{c} and radius r. An enlarged bounding frustum \mathcal{F}', constructed by shifting the planes of \mathcal{F} outward by r{max} (the maximum possible sphere radius in the dataset). This enlarged frustum is typically a by-product of the Sphere-Center Method. Outputs: A subset of spheres that potentially intersect the original frustum \mathcal{F}, requiring further ray/sphere intersection testing. Data Structures: The frustum is represented by its six planes. The "shifted bounding planes" from the Sphere-Center method define \mathcal{F}'. Steps: 1. For each sphere in the current cell or packet: a. Determine if the sphere center \mathbf{c} is contained within the enlarged frustum \mathcal{F}'. b. The containment test checks if the distance from \mathbf{c} to any plane of \mathcal{F}' is greater than the sphere's radius r; if so, the rays bounded by the frustum cannot intersect the sphere. Specifically, if the center is not contained by \mathcal{F}', the sphere is culled. c. If the center is contained by \mathcal{F}', the sphere is not culled and an intersection test is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isculled(spherecenter, enlargedfrustumplanes): """ spherecenter: vector (x, y, z) enlargedfrustumplanes: list of 6 plane definitions (normal, distance) Returns True if the sphere is culled (center outside enlarged frustum). """ for plane in enlargedfrustumplanes: # plane.normal is normalized vector pointing inward # plane.distance is scalar d # Signed distance from center to plane dist = dot(plane.normal, spherecenter) - plane.distance # If distance is negative, center is outside this plane if dist < 0: return True return False Parameters: r{max}: The maximum radius of any sphere in the dataset, used to compute the enlarged frustum \mathcal{F}'. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Small Spheres: This approach does not cull spheres with radii r < r{max} that are contained by the enlarged frustum \mathcal{F}' but do not overlap the original frustum \mathcal{F}. These spheres require an intersection test. Discretization Artifacts: Spheres may lie within a cell through which the enlarged frustum passes, but the sphere does not overlap either the original or the enlarged frustum. The culling detects this if the center is outside \mathcal{F}', but if the center is inside \mathcal{F}' due to the expansion, the test proceeds. Complexity: The culling check requires only one SIMD operation on modern CPUs per sphere, as it involves simple distance-to-plane comparisons. Performance: Efficient frustum culling significantly reduces the number of ray/sphere intersection tests. In tests with 16 threads, the number of tests skipped ranged from 38.40% to 81.34% across datasets, improving interactive performance (frame rate) by a factor of 1.17 to 1.68. Cylinder: 61.84% skipped, 1.40x speed-up. JP8: 81.34% skipped, 1.68x speed-up. Bullet: 67.22% skipped, 1.41x speed-up. Thunder: 58.34% skipped, 1.40x speed-up. Foam: 55.61% skipped, 1.47x speed-up. BulletTorso: 38.40% skipped, 1.17x speed-up. Strengths: It cancels the behavior of uniform grids requiring more primitive intersection tests than adaptive structures like kd-trees or BVHs by reducing the number of actual tests performed. It is simpler than shaft culling and appropriate for spheres. Limitations: It cannot cull small spheres (r < r{max}) that are inside the expanded frustum but outside the original frustum. The technique is described in a paper on a coherent grid traversal approach for visualizing particle-based simulation data. It was developed to replace SIMD shaft culling, which relies on planar edges and is thus inappropriate for spheres. The technique leverages the shifted bounding planes generated by the Sphere-Center Method. name: Hierarchical Grid with Macrocells
head: Macrocell hierarchy, Two-level hierarchy
body: A hierarchical grid structure that divides densely populated regions of space more finely than empty regions by imposing a coarser grid over the previous level, where each macrocell corresponds to an M \times M \times M block of cells in the underlying level. It sets itself apart from the original Coherent Grid Traversal (CGT) by replacing simple Boolean empty/non-empty flags with parameter range culling, storing minimum and maximum values for multiple particle properties to enable more aggressive early-out tests. Inputs: Particle dataset containing position, radius, and up to four additional properties; macrocell resolution M; grid dimensions. Outputs: Hierarchical grid structure consisting of macrocells containing bounds for underlying cells. Data Structures: 1. Macrocell: Stores minimum and maximum values for eight parameters: position x, y, z, radius, and up to four additional particle properties. This replaces the Boolean empty/non-empty flag used in the original CGT algorithm. 2. Underlying Grid: Standard CGT grid cells, organized into blocks of size M \times M \times M corresponding to macrocells. Construction Algorithm (Sort-Middle): 1. Distribute construction tasks for disjoint sections of the grid statically among all system threads. 2. Each thread performs a coarse parallel bucket sort of particles by their cell location, inserting them into its local set of buckets. 3. Regions for each bucket are disjoint, avoiding write conflicts and the need for mutexes. 4. Each thread inserts its particles into the appropriate grid cells within its assigned disjoint region. 5. Aggregate the grid data to form macrocells by computing the min/max of the eight parameters across all particles contained in each underlying M \times M \times M block of cells. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildhierarchicalgrid(particles, M, numthreads, gridmin, gridmax, cellsize): # 1. Static distribution of grid sections to threads threadranges = [] for t in range(numthreads): start = gridmin + t (gridmax - gridmin) // numthreads end = gridmin + (t + 1) (gridmax - gridmin) // numthreads threadranges.append((start, end)) # 2. Parallel bucket sort per thread localbuckets = [[] for in range(numthreads)] for particle in particles: cellidx = int((particle.pos - gridmin) / cellsize) threadid = 0 for t, (start, end) in enumerate(threadranges): if start <= cellidx < end: threadid = t break localbuckets[threadid].append(particle) # 3. Insert into grid cells numcells = int((gridmax - gridmin) / cellsize) gridcells = [[] for in range(numcells)] for t in range(numthreads): for particle in localbuckets[t]: cellidx = int((particle.pos - gridmin) / cellsize) gridcells[cellidx].append(particle) # 4. Build Macrocells macrocells = [] nummacrocells = numcells // (M M M) for mcidx in range(nummacrocells): mcmin = [float('inf')] 8 mcmax = [float('-inf')] 8 basecell = mcidx M M M for c in range(basecell, basecell + M M M): for particle in gridcells[c]: # Parameters: x, y, z, radius, prop1, prop2, prop3, prop4 for i in range(8): val = particle.props[i] if i < len(particle.props) else 0.0 mcmin[i] = min(mcmin[i], val) mcmax[i] = max(mcmax[i], val) macrocells.append({'min': mcmin, 'max': mcmax}) return macrocells, gridcells Parameters: Macrocell resolution (M): The size of the macrocell block in cells. Typical value: 6 \times 6 \times 6. Lambda (\lambda): A parameter affecting performance in modified algorithms. Value \lambda = 1 provides best performance for tested datasets. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Write Conflicts: Avoided by using disjoint regions for each thread during construction. Parameter Tuning: Performance varies widely with \lambda for extremely large particle counts; \lambda=1 is recommended. Frustum Overlap: Ray packet size impacts performance; larger packets overlap more cells, increasing intersection cost per step. A hierarchical grid building method that handles very complex scenes by organizing primitives into a structure for efficient traversal of empty spaces. Unlike top-down adaptive subdivision, it uses a bottom-up construction via filtering and clustering. It builds upon the hierarchical grid with macrocells concept by structuring the hierarchy through local grid clusters rather than a single global recursive subdivision. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N) with parallel bucket sort, where N is the number of particles, due to disjoint thread regions. Traversal benefits from parameter range culling, potentially reducing intersection tests compared to Boolean flags. Memory Complexity: Higher than original CGT due to storing 8 min/max values per macrocell instead of a single Boolean flag. Performance: \lambda = 1 and M = 6 \times 6 \times 6 yield reasonable performance for tested datasets. Performance is sensitive to \lambda for very large particle counts. Strengths: Efficient traversal via parameter range culling; parallel construction without synchronization. Limitations: Performance sensitivity to \lambda for extremely large particle counts. Originated from the macrocell hierarchy described by Parker et al. [17] and adapted for particle-based simulation data visualization. The construction algorithm uses the sort-middle approach described by Ize et al. [9] to quickly rebuild the grid each frame. It builds on the original CGT algorithm but modifies the macrocell data structure to support parameter range culling. name: Loosely Nested Grids
head: Bottom-up hierarchical grid construction, Cazals et al. hierarchical grid
body: Loosely Nested Grids is a hierarchical grid building method designed to handle very complex scenes by organizing primitives into a structure that allows efficient traversal of empty spaces. Unlike top-down adaptive subdivision methods, it employs a bottom-up construction approach via filtering and clustering steps. It builds on Hierarchical Grid with Macrocells by structuring the hierarchy through local grid clusters rather than a single global recursive subdivision. Inputs: A set of geometric primitives defining the scene. Outputs: A hierarchical grid data structure, viewed as a loosely nested recursive grid. Data Structures: The structure consists of a hierarchy of grids where each level contains clusters of primitives, and each cluster is associated with a local grid. The hierarchy connects these local grids to enable traversal that skips empty regions. Algorithm Steps: The construction follows a four-step bottom-up process: 1. Organize Primitives: Divide the scene primitives into subsets of similar size. 2. Cluster Neighbors: For each group of primitives identified in Step 1, group neighboring primitives into clusters. 3. Construct Local Grids: For each cluster formed in Step 2, construct a local grid. 4. Construct Hierarchy: Build a hierarchy of these local grids. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildlooselynestedgrids(primitives): # Step 1: Organize primitives into subsets of similar size # The specific partitioning algorithm is not detailed in the sources. subsets = [primitives[i:i+1] for i in range(0, len(primitives), 1)] clusters = [] # Step 2: Group neighbors into clusters for each subset # The specific clustering metric is not detailed in the sources. for subset in subsets: clusters.append(subset) localgrids = [] # Step 3: Construct a grid for each cluster # The resolution and cell size of the local grid are not specified. for cluster in clusters: localgrids.append(None) # Step 4: Construct a hierarchy of these grids # The specific linking mechanism is not detailed in the sources. hierarchy = localgrids return hierarchy Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Build Cost: The method has a greater build cost compared to general bottom-up strategies. Complexity: While designed for complex scenes, the multi-step clustering and hierarchy construction may introduce overhead for simpler scenes. Scalability: Suitable for very complex scenes due to the hierarchical organization. Strengths: Bottom-up construction avoids the pitfalls of top-down adaptive subdivision; effective for complex scenes with dense regions. name: Adaptive grid data structure (Klimaszewski and Sederberg)
head: Adaptive grid (Klimaszewski and Sederberg), KS97 adaptive grid, Klimaszewski and Sederberg adaptive grid
body: The adaptive grid data structure, proposed by Klimaszewski and Sederberg [KS97], is a hierarchical grid building method that constructs local grids acting as bounding boxes in densely populated areas. It is characterized by a fast bottom-up construction approach, contrasting with top-down adaptive subdivision methods. The resulting structure is viewed as a loosely nested recursive grid. Inputs: A set of geometric primitives. Outputs: A hierarchical structure of local grids. Data Structures: The structure consists of a hierarchy of bounding boxes. Each node in the hierarchy contains a local grid. The hierarchy is built such that boxes act as bounding volumes for the primitives they contain. Algorithm Steps: The construction follows a specific bottom-up sequence: 1. Bounding Box Creation: For each primitive, surround it with a bounding box. 2. Merging: For all bounding boxes, merge close boxes to form a structured grid. 3. Tree Insertion: For all remaining boxes, insert the box into the tree using a minimum surface criterion. 4. Local Grid Construction: For all bounding boxes in the hierarchy, build a local grid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeboundingbox(primitive): # Standard operation: returns axis-aligned bounding box enclosing primitive return primitive.aabb def mergecloseboxes(boxes): # Standard operation: merges spatially close boxes into a single box # The exact threshold for "close" is not specified in the sources. if not boxes: return [] merged = [boxes[0]] for box in boxes[1:]: # Distance check placeholder; threshold not given in sources if distance(merged[-1].center, box.center) < threshold: merged[-1] = union(merged[-1], box) else: merged.append(box) return merged def buildhierarchy(boxes): # Standard operation: inserts boxes into a tree structure # The minimum surface criterion is used to determine parent-child relationships. # The specific formula is not given in the sources. tree = Node() for box in boxes: tree.insert(box, criterion="minimumsurface") return tree def buildlocalgrid(box): # Standard operation: creates a grid structure within the bounding box return Grid(box) def buildks97adaptivegrid(primitives): boxes = [computeboundingbox(p) for p in primitives] mergedboxes = mergecloseboxes(boxes) tree = buildhierarchy(mergedboxes) for node in tree.nodes(): node.localgrid = buildlocalgrid(node.boundingbox) return tree Parameters: Minimum Surface Criterion: Used during tree insertion. The specific formula or threshold for "minimum surface" is not given in the sources. Merge Threshold: The definition of "close" for merging boxes is not specified in the sources. Memory: The structure is described as a "loosely nested recursive grid". Specific memory layout details for this method are not provided in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast bottom-up construction; handles densely populated areas via local grids. Limitations: Higher build cost. The adaptive grid data structure was proposed by Klimaszewski and Sederberg in 1997. It is part of the broader field of grid-based ray tracing acceleration structures. name: Hero-like 4-Connectivity (H4T)
body: Hero-like 4-Connectivity (H4T) is a ray traversal algorithm for uniform grids that guarantees strict 4-connectivity by resolving boundary crossing ambiguities through a stable sort of candidate cell entries. It differs from standard DDA and its sibling Coherent Grid Traversal by explicitly testing a 2x2 cell neighborhood and using axis-priority sorting to prevent diagonal jumps, ensuring that rays crossing grid lines do so one axis at a time. H4T determines the sequence of voxels visited by a ray by identifying the entry point into a 2x2 block of cells and then advancing through them while maintaining connectivity. The method relies on a stable sorting mechanism to break ties between axis crossings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, grid dimensions, voxel size v. Output: A sequence of voxel indices (i, j, k) visited by the ray. Data Structures: Candidate List: A list of tuples containing (t, \text{axis\id}), where t is the distance to the next boundary and \text{axis\id} identifies the axis (0 for x, 1 for y). Note: The source specifies axis numbers 0 and 1, implying a 2D projection or specific handling for the primary axes in the 2x2 test context. Steps: 1. 2x2 Cell Test: Identify the candidate cells the ray passes through in the current 2x2 block. This involves determining which of the four adjacent cells the ray enters first based on the ray's position relative to the grid boundaries. 2. Associate Axis IDs: For each candidate boundary crossing distance t, associate it with an axis identifier. The source specifies storing 0 for the x-axis and 1 for the y-axis. 3. Stable Sort: Sort the candidate list using a stable sorting algorithm. The sort key is primarily the axis identifier, and secondarily the t-value. This ensures that if t-values for the x and y axes are equal (a tie), the x-axis (0) is processed before the y-axis (1). 4. Advance: Select the first entry in the sorted list as the next cell. Update the ray's position and repeat the process for the next block. The grid position must be floored before reading the grid data, as the method may produce fractional position values during intermediate calculations. Pseudocode: The source notes that the C code is too long to include and describes the logic conceptually. The following pseudocode implements the described stable sort logic for the 2x2 test resolution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def h4ttraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsize, gridbounds): # Determine initial voxel currentvoxel = [int(rayorigin[i] // voxelsize) for i in range(3)] # Calculate distances to next boundaries for x and y (primary axes for 2x2 test) # Note: Standard DDA calculates tmax for all axes. H4T focuses on resolving # the tie between x and y planes specifically. # Calculate tmax for x and y axes tmaxx = (currentvoxel[0] + (1 if raydirection[0] > 0 else 0)) voxelsize - rayorigin[0] tmaxx /= raydirection[0] if raydirection[0] != 0 else float('inf') tmaxy = (currentvoxel[1] + (1 if raydirection[1] > 0 else 0)) voxelsize - rayorigin[1] tmaxy /= raydirection[1] if raydirection[1] != 0 else float('inf') # Create candidate list with axis IDs: 0 for x, 1 for y candidates = [] if raydirection[0] != 0: candidates.append((tmaxx, 0)) if raydirection[1] != 0: candidates.append((tmaxy, 1)) # Stable sort: first by axisid, then by t-value # Python's sort is stable. We sort by (axisid, tvalue) candidates.sort(key=lambda x: (x[1], x[0])) # The first candidate is the next cell to enter # This ensures x-axis crossings are prioritized over y-axis crossings on ties nextt, nextaxis = candidates[0] # Advance in the chosen axis step = 1 if raydirection[nextaxis] > 0 else -1 currentvoxel[nextaxis] += step # Update tmax for the advanced axis if nextaxis == 0: tmaxx += voxelsize / abs(raydirection[0]) else: tmaxy += voxelsize / abs(raydirection[1]) # Re-evaluate candidates for the next step # In a full implementation, this loop continues, updating candidates # based on the new voxel position and re-sorting or merging the sorted lists. # The source emphasizes the sorting mechanism for tie-breaking. yield currentvoxel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ties: The critical pitfall is the handling of equal t-values for different axes. Without stable sorting by axis ID, the traversal may jump diagonally, violating 4-connectivity. The source explicitly states that sorting by axis number first preserves 4-connectivity. Fractional Positions: The method may result in fractional grid positions during calculation. The grid must be accessed using floored coordinates. Code Length: The source notes that the full implementation is complex and lengthy, suggesting careful handling of the candidate list management. Correctness: H4T achieved 100% correctness for both position and normal in randomized testing (100,000,000 cases) and specific test cases (2,883,496 cases), outperforming HP4T and HP8T which had error rates of 99.99% and 97.66% respectively. Complexity: The source does not provide explicit time or memory complexity metrics. However, the requirement for stable sorting of candidates suggests a slight overhead compared to simple min-selection, but this is negligible for the 2x2 test scope. Strengths: Highest accuracy among tested methods; guarantees 4-connectivity. Limitations: Implementation complexity is high; the source code was not published due to length. name: Hierarchical Planes 4-Connectivity (HP4T)
body: Hierarchical Planes 4-Connectivity (HP4T) is a ray traversal algorithm for hierarchical grids, such as Octrees or Sparse Voxel Octrees (SVO), that ensures strict 4-connectivity by preventing diagonal jumps between cells. It distinguishes itself from its sibling Hierarchical Planes 8-Connectivity (HP8T) by applying clamping logic to the non-hit axis, thereby avoiding the surface normal ambiguities and connectivity errors inherent in 8-connected approaches. HP4T calculates the intersection of a ray with the bounding planes of the current cell to determine the next cell. It uses the plane positions directly to compute the new grid coordinates, ensuring that the ray does not skip adjacent cells diagonally. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin (rayposition), ray direction (raydir), inverse ray direction (invdir), current grid position (gridposition), current cell size (cellsize), and grid dimensions (gridwidth, gridheight). Outputs: Updated gridposition for the next cell, and the traversal distance t to that cell. Data Structures The method operates on 2D grid positions (x, y) representing the current cell indices in the hierarchical level. gridposition: A 2D vector (x, y) of integer or floating-point coordinates. rayposition: A 2D vector (x, y) representing the ray origin projected or relevant to the current plane. raydir: A 2D vector (x, y) representing the ray direction. invdir: A 2D vector (x, y) where each component is the reciprocal of the corresponding component in raydir. cellsize: A scalar representing the physical size of the cell at the current hierarchy level. Parameters cellsize: The size of the cell in world units, determined by the hierarchy level L as 2^L. For example, at level 0, cellsize is 1; at level 1, it is 2; at level 2, it is 4. invdir: Defined as the element-wise reciprocal of raydir, retaining the sign of the direction rather than using absolute values. isdirpos(x): A helper function returning 1 if x \ge 0, else 0, used to determine the offset of the next plane in the positive direction. isdirneg(x): A helper function returning 0 if x \ge 0, else 1, used to determine the offset of the next plane in the negative direction. signdir(x): A helper function returning the sign of x (1 if x \ge 0, -1 if x < 0). Steps 1. Calculate Plane Positions: Compute the world coordinates of the planes bounding the current cell in both axes using component-wise operations: \text{planes} = (\lfloor \text{grid\position} / \text{cellsize} \rfloor + \text{is\dir\pos}(\text{ray\dir})) \times \text{cellsize} Here, \lfloor \cdot \rfloor denotes the floor function applied component-wise, and the final multiplication is a Hadamard (pairwise) product. 2. Calculate Total T: Compute the distance along the ray to each plane using component-wise multiplication: \text{total\t} = (\text{planes} - \text{ray\position}) \times \text{inv\dir} This yields the parametric distance to the X and Y planes respectively. 3. Determine Hit Axis: Compare totalt.x and totalt.y to identify which plane the ray intersects first. 4. If totalt.x <= totalt.y (X-plane hit first): a. Set t = \text{total\t.x}. b. Update X position: \text{grid\position.x} = \text{planes.x} - \text{is\dir\neg}(\text{ray\dir.x}) This moves the grid index to the next cell in the direction of travel. c. Store the old Y position: \text{old\grid\pos\y} = \text{grid\position.y} d. Calculate the candidate new Y position based on ray intersection: \text{grid\position.y} = \lfloor \text{ray\dir.y} \times t + \text{ray\position.y} \rfloor e. Apply 4-connectivity clamping to Y. First, ensure no backward movement: \text{grid\position.y} = \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times \max(0.0, \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times (\text{grid\position.y} - \text{old\grid\pos\y})) Second, ensure the new Y does not skip the adjacent cell defined by the plane: \text{grid\position.y} = \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times \min(\text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times (\text{planes.y} - \text{is\dir\pos}(\text{ray\dir.y})), \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.y}) \times (\text{grid\position.y} + \text{old\grid\pos\y})) This clamping prevents diagonal jumps by restricting the Y update to the immediate neighbor. 5. Else (totalt.x > totalt.y, Y-plane hit first): a. Set t = \text{total\t.y}. b. Update Y position: \text{grid\position.y} = \text{planes.y} - \text{is\dir\neg}(\text{ray\dir.y}) c. Update X position using simplified clamping logic: \text{grid\position.x} = \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.x}) \times \min(\text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.x}) \times \text{planes.x} - \text{is\dir\pos}(\text{ray\dir.x}), \max(0.0, \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.x}) \times (\lfloor \text{ray\dir.x} \times t + \text{ray\position.x} \rfloor - \text{grid\position.x})) + \text{sign\dir}(\text{ray\dir.x}) \times \text{grid\position.x}) This mirrors the X-hit case logic, calculating a candidate position, clamping to prevent backward movement, and clamping to prevent skipping the plane neighbor. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hp4tstep(gridposition, rayposition, raydir, invdir, cellsize, gridwidth, gridheight): def isdirpos(x): return 1 if x >= 0 else 0 def isdirneg(x): return 0 if x >= 0 else 1 def signdir(x): return 1 if x >= 0 else -1 # 1. Calculate plane positions (component-wise) planesx = (math.floor(gridposition.x / cellsize) + isdirpos(raydir.x)) cellsize planesy = (math.floor(gridposition.y / cellsize) + isdirpos(raydir.y)) cellsize # 2. Calculate totalt (component-wise) totaltx = (planesx - rayposition.x) invdir.x totalty = (planesy - rayposition.y) invdir.y if totaltx <= totalty: # X plane hit first t = totaltx # Update X gridposition.x = planesx - isdirneg(raydir.x) # Clamp Y oldgridposy = gridposition.y candidatey = math.floor(raydir.y t + rayposition.y) # Clamp 1: prevent backward movement gridposition.y = signdir(raydir.y) max(0.0, signdir(raydir.y) (candidatey - oldgridposy)) # Clamp 2: prevent skipping plane gridposition.y = signdir(raydir.y) min( signdir(raydir.y) (planesy - isdirpos(raydir.y)), signdir(raydir.y) (gridposition.y + oldgridposy)) else: # Y plane hit first t = totalty # Update Y gridposition.y = planesy - isdirneg(raydir.y) # Clamp X sx = signdir(raydir.x) candidatex = math.floor(raydir.x t + rayposition.x) gridposition.x = sx min( sx planesx - isdirpos(raydir.x), max(0.0, sx (candidatex - gridposition.x)) + sx gridposition.x) return gridposition, t Pitfalls Precision and connectivity errors in naive implementations using compare variables and t + eps can cause 8-connectivity (diagonal jumps) and incorrect surface normals. HP4T avoids this by using the explicit clamping logic described above. Removes the clamping logic of HP4T to allow 8-connectivity (diagonal jumps), simplifying the update code but requiring careful handling of surface normals and fractional positions. Choose HP8T when performance is critical and normal accuracy can be handled via post-processing or alternative methods. Time Complexity: Constant time per cell traversal step, involving basic arithmetic operations (floor, multiply, add, min, max). Memory Complexity: Constant space, requiring only a few temporary variables for the current step. Performance: In randomized testing of 100,000,000 cases, HP4T achieved a 99.99% chance of correct position and a 99.99% chance of correct surface normal. Strengths: Ensures strict 4-connectivity, avoiding diagonal jumps that can cause artifacts in hierarchical grids. Limitations: Slightly more complex logic than HP8T due to clamping, and achieves 99.99% accuracy rather than the 100% accuracy of H4T in randomized testing. When to use: When traversing hierarchical grids (Octrees/SVO) and strict 4-connectivity is required to avoid skipping cells or producing incorrect normals, and the slight performance overhead of clamping is acceptable. When not to use: If 100% geometric correctness is required and the overhead of H4T is acceptable, or if maximum performance is needed and 8-connectivity artifacts can be mitigated elsewhere. HP4T is part of a family of ray traversal methods for hierarchical grids, including H4T and HP8T. The "T" stands for "total," referring to the total summation concept from earlier chapters in the source material, and "HP" stands for Hierarchical Planes. The method was developed to address precision and connectivity errors found in naive implementations that use compare variables and t + eps for level switching, which can result in 8-connectivity and incorrect surface normals. The author notes that such issues may be a reason for surface normal errors in games like Teardown, which uses a similar flawed compare variable optimization.
