name: Hierarchical Planes 8-Connectivity (HP8T)
body: Hierarchical Planes 8-Connectivity (HP8T) is a ray traversal algorithm for hierarchical grids that simplifies the update logic of Hierarchical Planes 4-Connectivity (HP4T). While HP4T enforces strict 4-connectivity by clamping the non-hit axis, HP8T removes this clamping to allow 8-connectivity, permitting diagonal jumps between cells. This simplification reduces computational overhead but requires flooring fractional grid positions before data access and introduces ambiguities in surface normal calculation when using simple comparison variables. HP8T builds on Hierarchical Planes 4-Connectivity (HP4T) by modifying the update step for the axis that is not currently being hit by the ray plane intersection. Inputs: rayposition: The starting position of the ray in world space. raydir: The normalized direction vector of the ray. invdir: The reciprocal of raydir (1.0 / ray\dir). cellsize: The side length of the uniform grid cells. isdirpos: A vector indicating the positive direction of traversal for each axis (typically 1.0 if raydir > 0, else 0.0). israyneg: A vector indicating the negative direction (typically -1.0 if raydir < 0, else 0.0), used to adjust the plane position. gridwidth, gridheight: The dimensions of the 2D grid slice being traversed. gridposition: The current continuous position of the ray within the grid. Outputs: Updated gridposition for each step. t: The distance to the next plane intersection. Not given in the sources. 1. Calculate Planes: Determine the world coordinates of the next grid planes for the X and Y axes based on the current gridposition. planes = (\lfloor grid\position / cellsize \rfloor + is\dir\pos) \times cellsize 2. Calculate Total T: Compute the distance along the ray to reach these planes. total\t = (planes - ray\position) \times inv\dir 3. Determine Hit Axis: Compare totalt.x and totalt.y. If totalt.x <= totalt.y: The ray hits the X plane first. Else: The ray hits the Y plane first. 4. Update Position: If X is hit: Update X coordinate to the plane position: gridposition.x = planes.x - israyneg.x. Update Y coordinate by adding the delta corresponding to the travel time totalt.x: gridposition.y += raydir.y max(0.0, totalt.x - (gridposition.y - rayposition.y) invdir.y). Set t = totalt.x. If Y is hit: Update Y coordinate to the plane position: gridposition.y = planes.y - israyneg.y. Update X coordinate by adding the delta corresponding to the travel time totalt.y: gridposition.x += raydir.x max(0.0, totalt.y - (gridposition.x - rayposition.x) invdir.x). Set t = totalt.y. 5. Access Grid: Before reading the grid data at the new position, floor the gridposition components to obtain integer indices. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def traversehp8t(rayposition, raydir, invdir, cellsize, isdirpos, israyneg, gridwidth, gridheight, gridposition): while 0 <= gridposition[0] < gridwidth and 0 <= gridposition[1] < gridheight: planesx = (math.floor(gridposition[0] / cellsize) + isdirpos[0]) cellsize planesy = (math.floor(gridposition[1] / cellsize) + isdirpos[1]) cellsize totaltx = (planesx - rayposition[0]) invdir[0] totalty = (planesy - rayposition[1]) invdir[1] if totaltx <= totalty: gridposition[0] = planesx - israyneg[0] gridposition[1] += raydir[1] max(0.0, totaltx - (gridposition[1] - rayposition[1]) invdir[1]) t = totaltx else: gridposition[1] = planesy - israyneg[1] gridposition[0] += raydir[0] max(0.0, totalty - (gridposition[0] - rayposition[0]) invdir[0]) t = totalty cellsize: The resolution of the underlying uniform grid. isdirpos, israyneg: Derived from raydir. isdirpos is 1.0 where raydir > 0, else 0.0. israyneg is -1.0 where raydir < 0, else 0.0. Fractional Positions: Unlike HP4T, gridposition retains fractional values and must be floored before accessing grid data to avoid reading incorrect cells or causing memory errors. Surface Normal Ambiguity: HP8T allows diagonal jumps. If surface normals are calculated using a simple compare variable, the calculation will be incorrect for diagonal transitions because the compare value cannot distinguish between entering a cell from the side versus entering from a corner. A post-processing step analyzing surrounding cells is required to determine the correct normal. Boundary Checks: The loop condition checks gridposition against gridwidth and gridheight. Accuracy: In randomized testing (100,000,000 cases), HP8T achieved a 99.99% chance of correct position and 99.99% chance of correct normal. This is slightly lower than the 100% accuracy of Hero-like 4-Connectivity (H4T). Strengths: Simpler calculation for the non-hit axis compared to HP4T, as it avoids the complex clamping logic. Limitations: 8-connectivity introduces potential errors in surface normal determination if not handled with additional logic. The lack of clamping means the ray can "jump" diagonally, which may be undesirable for algorithms requiring strict 4-connectivity. HP8T is described in a thesis. It is presented as a variant of HP4T, designed to simplify the traversal logic by removing the clamping step for the non-hit axis. The method was evaluated against HP4T and H4T using randomized and specific test cases. versal algorithm for ray tracing Hur man gör en hierarkisk..., https://kth.diva-portal.org/smash/get/diva2:2069409/FULLTEXT01.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial)

name: Rendering Order and Strategy
body: Rendering Order and Strategy defines the sequence in which volumetric cells are processed during ray-grid traversal to ensure correct optical compositing and efficient occlusion culling. It solves the problem of determining which cells contribute to the final pixel color and in what order, distinguishing itself from sibling methods by decoupling the geometric traversal logic (handled by the parent Ray-grid traversal) from the semantic processing order required for correct alpha blending or visibility determination. The family shares the fundamental requirement that cell processing must respect the viewing direction to correctly accumulate opacity and color. While the parent Ray-grid traversal provides the geometric sequence of voxel indices visited by a ray, the rendering strategy determines how these visits are mapped to the final image buffer. The core principle is that for standard volume rendering with absorption, processing must occur from the camera towards the volume interior (front-to-back) to allow early termination when the ray becomes fully opaque. Strategies may also involve spatial partitioning (e.g., layers, octants) to group cells for batch processing or to handle complex hierarchical data structures where implicit occlusion rules replace per-ray depth sorting. Front-to-Back Layer Traversal is a rendering order strategy for Matryoshka-like hierarchical data structures that processes cells in front-to-back order along the viewing direction to handle occlusion correctly. It operates on pre-defined layers composed of six planes, classifying them into closest and furthest groups relative to the camera to ensure outer cells occlude inner cells without per-ray depth sorting. It builds on Ray-grid traversal but applies a specific plane-grouping logic to manage the visibility of nested structures. Choose this method when rendering hierarchical "Matryoshka" data structures where cells are grouped into concentric layers, and efficient occlusion culling of inner layers by outer layers is required without sorting every cell individually. See Front-to-Back Layer Traversal. Backward Projection (also known as Backward Mapping or image-order rendering) is a volume rendering technique that iterates over all pixels of the output image to determine the contribution of the volume data to each pixel. It solves the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to a 2D image plane by reversing the projection direction: instead of sampling the volume and projecting to the image (forward mapping), it traces rays from the camera through the image plane into the volume. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Front-to-Back Layer Traversal, by its explicit iteration over the output image grid, which ensures every pixel is addressed exactly once and simplifies handling of non-uniform sampling or sparse data structures. Choose this method when uniform pixel coverage is required, or when the rendering pipeline is driven by the output image resolution rather than the volume data structure. See Backward Projection. A ray-casting algorithm on rectilinear grids using object-order processing, randomized high sampling rate, and trilinear interpolation. The sampling rate variable (\Delta s) is initialized to 0.5, allowing between two and four samplings along a ray within a cell. Pixel subdivisions and precomputed rays are fixed to 16^2 (256 subdivisions), allowing up to 4x zoom without visible noise. The implementation targets 512x512 pixel images to maintain high quality. The algorithm lacks perspective projection, which is a drawback for stereo viewing or VR, though parallel projection is often preferred in scientific visualization. The distinction between object-order (volume-driven) and image-order (pixel-driven) rendering strategies has been fundamental since the early days of volume visualization. Object-order methods, such as the randomized sampling approach described by, emerged to leverage the efficiency of traversing the volume data structure directly, often achieving interactive frame rates for isosurface visualization. Image-order methods, like backward projection, became standard for ensuring consistent pixel coverage and simplifying the compositing logic, particularly as hardware acceleration for ray-box intersection and texture sampling improved. The development of hierarchical strategies like Front-to-Back Layer Traversal addresses the specific needs of complex, nested data structures where traditional linear traversal is inefficient for occlusion culling. name: Front-to-Back Layer Traversal
head: Layer-based Front-to-Back Traversal
body: Front-to-Back Layer Traversal is a rendering order strategy for Matryoshka-like hierarchical data structures that processes cells in front-to-back order along the viewing direction to handle occlusion correctly. It operates on pre-defined layers composed of six planes, classifying them into closest and furthest groups relative to the camera to ensure outer cells occlude inner cells without per-ray depth sorting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Matryoshka layer lm defined by six planes, a viewing direction (camera position), and an auxiliary buffer for marking drawable cells. Output: A sequence of cell processing instructions ordered front-to-back. Data Structures: Layer Definition: A layer consists of six planes classified into two groups based on the camera position. Closest Planes: The three planes closest to the camera, defined by binary indices kx, ky, kz \in \{0, 1\}. Furthest Planes: The three planes furthest from the camera, defined by the opposite indices k'x, k'y, k'z. Auxiliary Buffer: A memory structure used to mark cells as "drawable" during a first pass, allowing them to be processed in the correct order during a second pass. Parameters: kx, ky, kz: Binary values (0 or 1) determined by the viewing camera to define which planes are closest to the camera position. k'x, k'y, k'z: The opposite values of kx, ky, kz (i.e., 1-kx, etc.), defining the furthest planes. Steps: 1. Classify Planes: Determine kx, ky, kz based on the camera's viewing direction to identify the closest planes. 2. Process Closest Planes: Identify planes X=X{kx}, Y=Y{ky}, Z=Z{kz}. Within this group, apply intra-plane ordering: cells from X=X{kx} that also belong to Y=Y{ky} are treated before any cells from Y=Y{ky}, and plane Z=Z{kz} is processed last among the three closest planes. Mark these cells as drawable in the auxiliary buffer. 3. Process Inner Layers: If lm is not the last layer, process the next inner layer l{m+1} using the same logic. 4. Process Furthest Planes: Identify planes X=X{k'x}, Y=Y{k'y}, Z=Z{k'z}. Within this group, apply inverted intra-plane ordering: plane Z=Z{k'z} is processed first because it may occlude cells in Y=Y{k'y}, which in turn may occlude cells in X=X{k'x}. Process the cells marked in the auxiliary buffer in this specific order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobacklayertraversal(layer, cameraposition, auxiliarybuffer): # Determine closest planes based on camera position # The sources do not specify the exact coordinate transformation logic kx, ky, kz = 0, 0, 0 # Placeholder for implementation detail kpx, kpy, kpz = 1 - kx, 1 - ky, 1 - kz # Step 1: Process closest planes # Intra-plane order: Xkx, then Yky, then Zkz (last among closest) auxiliarybuffer.clear() auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planex[kx]) auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planey[ky]) auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planez[kz]) # Process cells in the buffer according to the specified plane order # The sources do not specify the exact cell iteration logic for plane in [layer.planex[kx], layer.planey[ky], layer.planez[kz]]: for cell in plane: if cell in auxiliarybuffer: processcell(cell) # Step 2: Process inner layers if not the last layer if not layer.islastlayer(): fronttobacklayertraversal(layer.nextinnerlayer, cameraposition, auxiliarybuffer) # Step 3: Process furthest planes # Intra-plane order: Zkpz first, then Ykpy, then Xkpx (last among furthest) auxiliarybuffer.clear() auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planez[kpz]) auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planey[kpy]) auxiliarybuffer.extend(layer.planex[kpx]) for plane in [layer.planez[kpz], layer.planey[kpy], layer.planex[kpx]]: for cell in plane: if cell in auxiliarybuffer: processcell(cell) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shared Cells: Cells at the intersection of planes (edges/corners) must be handled carefully to avoid double processing or incorrect occlusion. The intra-plane ordering rules specifically address this. Camera Position: The values of kx, ky, kz depend on the camera position. If the camera moves, these values may change, requiring a re-evaluation of the plane grouping. Auxiliary Buffer: Requires sufficient memory to store the drawable cells for each layer. A specific ordering rule for processing cells within the same plane group to handle shared cells (edges/corners) correctly, ensuring correct occlusion between planes. For closest planes, cells from X=X1 belonging to Y=Y1 are processed before Y=Y1, and Z=Z1 is last. For furthest planes, Z=Z0 is first, occluding Y=Y0, which occludes X=X0. The sources do not provide measured performance, hardware specifics, or explicit time/memory complexity formulas. Strengths include correct occlusion handling for nested Matryoshka structures without per-ray depth sorting, and efficiency for parallel projections with fixed viewing directions. Limitations include the requirement for an auxiliary buffer and dependency on camera position for plane classification, which may require re-evaluation if the camera moves frequently. It is suitable for rendering Matryoshka-like data structures with parallel projection where correct occlusion is required, but not for structures that do not fit the Matryoshka layer model or when auxiliary buffer memory is constrained. The method is described in the context of the Matryoshka algorithm for visualizing active cells in hierarchical data structures. It addresses the challenge of maintaining correct front-to-back rendering order for occlusion by leveraging the geometric properties of layer planes relative to the camera position. name: Backward Projection
head: Backward Mapping, Backward and forward texture mapping algorithms, Backward texture mapping, Forward texture mapping, image-order algorithms
body: Backward Projection (also known as Backward Mapping or image-order algorithms) is a volume rendering strategy that iterates over all pixels of the output image and determines the contributions of the volume integral to the current pixel. It solves the problem of mapping 3D volumetric data to a 2D image by casting rays from the camera through the volume for each pixel, yielding a simple and visually accurate mechanism for volume rendering. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Front-to-Back Layer Traversal, by its explicit iteration over the image space (pixels) rather than the volume space (voxels). Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset V (scalar or vector values), a camera model (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d} per pixel), and transfer functions mapping volume values to color c and opacity \alpha. Output: A 2D image buffer I with dimensions H \times W \times C (where C is channels, typically 3 for RGB). Data Structures: Volume V: A 3D array of size Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Values are accessed via trilinear interpolation. Image Buffer I: A 2D array of size H \times W \times C. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the image buffer I to zero. 2. For each pixel (i, j) in the image grid (0 \le i < H, 0 \le j < W): a. Compute the ray origin \mathbf{o}{i,j} and direction \mathbf{d}{i,j} from the camera model. b. Determine the entry and exit points of the ray with the volume bounding box. Let the parametric range be [t{start}, t{end}]. c. Initialize the accumulated color C{acc} = (0,0,0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. d. Iterate along the ray from t{start} to t{end} with step size \Delta t (typically the voxel spacing or diagonal): i. Compute sample position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}{i,j} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}{i,j}. ii. Sample the volume value v = V(\mathbf{p}) using trilinear interpolation. iii. Map v to color c and opacity \alpha using transfer functions. iv. Apply the front-to-back compositing equation: C{acc} = C{acc} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) e. Store C{acc} in I[i, j]. Formulas: The volume rendering integral is approximated using a Riemann sum. The compositing equation for each sample l is: I(\hat{x}) = \sum{l=1}^{L} c(xl) \alphal \prod{j=1}^{l-1} (1 - \alphaj) where c(xl) is the color and \alphal is the opacity at sample position xl. Parameters: \Delta t: Step size. Typical value: distance between voxel centers or voxel diagonal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point precision errors in ray marching can cause gaps or overlaps if \Delta t is not chosen carefully relative to voxel size. Boundaries: Rays missing the volume entirely must be handled to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Degenerate Input: Empty volumes or volumes with zero opacity everywhere result in a black or background image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backwardprojection(volume, camera, height, width, channels, transferfunc, dt=1.0): """ volume: 3D numpy array (Dx, Dy, Dz) camera: object with method getray(i, j) returning (origin, direction) height, width: int channels: int (e.g., 3 for RGB) transferfunc: function mapping scalar value to (color, alpha) dt: float, step size along the ray """ image = np.zeros((height, width, channels), dtype=np.float32) Dx, Dy, Dz = volume.shape for i in range(height): for j in range(width): origin, direction = camera.getray(i, j) # Compute ray bounds with volume bounding box [0, Dx] x [0, Dy] x [0, Dz] tmin = -np.inf tmax = np.inf nointersect = False for k in range(3): if direction[k] == 0: if origin[k] < 0 or origin[k] > [Dx, Dy, Dz][k]: nointersect = True break else: t1 = (0.0 - origin[k]) / direction[k] t2 = ([Dx, Dy, Dz][k] - origin[k]) / direction[k] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if nointersect or tmin > tmax: continue acccolor = np.zeros(channels) accalpha = 0.0 t = tmin while t <= tmax: pos = origin + t direction x, y, z = pos if 0 <= x < Dx and 0 <= y < Dy and 0 <= z < Dz: # Trilinear interpolation x0, y0, z0 = int(x), int(y), int(z) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 fx, fy, fz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 def clamp(v, dim): return max(0, min(v, dim - 1)) v000 = volume[clamp(x0, Dx), clamp(y0, Dy), clamp(z0, Dz)] v100 = volume[clamp(x1, Dx), clamp(y0, Dy), clamp(z0, Dz)] v010 = volume[clamp(x0, Dx), clamp(y1, Dy), clamp(z0, Dz)] v110 = volume[clamp(x1, Dx), clamp(y1, Dy), clamp(z0, Dz)] v001 = volume[clamp(x0, Dx), clamp(y0, Dy), clamp(z1, Dz)] v101 = volume[clamp(x1, Dx), clamp(y0, Dy), clamp(z1, Dz)] v011 = volume[clamp(x0, Dx), clamp(y1, Dy), clamp(z1, Dz)] v111 = volume[clamp(x1, Dx), clamp(y1, Dy), clamp(z1, Dz)] c00 = v000 (1 - fx) + v100 fx c10 = v010 (1 - fx) + v110 fx c01 = v001 (1 - fx) + v101 fx c11 = v011 (1 - fx) + v111 fx c0 = c00 (1 - fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1 - fy) + c11 fy val = c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz color, alpha = transferfunc(val) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor += color weight accalpha += weight t += dt image[i, j] = acccolor return image GPU Backprojection is a rendering pass that visualizes detected scale-space blobs by mapping projection data back into a 3D reconstruction volume. It solves the problem of efficiently computing weighted contributions of scale-space features to image pixels by parallelizing the accumulation over the output space (voxels or pixels) on NVIDIA GPUs. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific application to scale-space blob visualization and its implementation as a CUDA kernel that decouples the expensive scale-space computation from the frequent backprojection step, unlike Ray Segment Projection to Image which projects geometric primitives, or Cone Beam Forward Projection with Trilinear Interpolation which performs the forward mapping. This method computes the bounding segment of a ray (defined by origin and direction) that overlaps with a canonical image frame, returning the parametric t-range and the 2D xy coordinates at the entry and exit points. It solves the problem of determining which parts of a 3D ray are visible within the 2D image plane boundaries, which is a prerequisite for subsequent rasterization or sampling in backward projection pipelines. It differs from GPU Backprojection by explicitly computing geometric bounds rather than relying on hardware rasterization, and from Cone Beam Forward Projection with Trilinear Interpolation by operating on individual rays rather than volumetric integration. Cone Beam Forward Projection computes the line integrals of a 3D volume along rays defined by a source and a 2D detector array, simulating the acquisition of projection data (sinograms) for cone-beam geometry. It differs from its sibling GPU Backprojection by integrating volume values along rays rather than distributing detector values into the volume, and from Ray Segment Projection to Image by explicitly handling the 3D-to-2D perspective projection geometry with trilinear interpolation. It is the primary forward operator for iterative reconstruction algorithms like Differentiable Forward Projection (Mesh) and 3D Siddon's Method for Intercept Matrix Calculation. Circular Integral Convolution generates a blurred image from a scan by integrating ray values across all angles for each point, effectively filtering the true image with a 1/r-weighted kernel. It serves as a pre-processing step for deconvolution-based reconstruction rather than a full reconstruction method itself. Gaussian Texture Filtering via Jacobian Back-projection is a technique to compute the color of a screen pixel by integrating a texture signal against a Gaussian filter, where the filter is back-projected from screen space to texture space using the local affine approximation (Jacobian) of the texture mapping. It solves the problem of aliasing in texture mapping by ensuring that the frequency content of the projected texture is properly band-limited before sampling. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on pre-filtered mipmaps or simple box filters, this method explicitly models the pixel footprint as a Gaussian and adapts its shape in texture space based on the local distortion of the surface mapping. Visibility Thresholding for Scale Backprojection is a method to prevent scale information from being backprojected to voxels that correspond to vessels, giving a better classification of the brain. A voxel is determined to be not visible from the Laplacian of Gaussian (LoG) extrema if, at some point along the ray connecting the two positions, the intensity is below the threshold \tau. Alternatively, thresholding can be based on gradient magnitude. The parameter \tau (tau) is a visibility parameter used to control the sensitivity of the visibility test, based on scalar value or gradient magnitude. This is a fast approximation; more accurate results can be obtained with a region growing approach added as a post-process based on the initial size-based classification. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot N), where H, W are image dimensions and N is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume and O(H \cdot W) for the image buffer. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the efficiency of the ray-volume intersection and interpolation. The source framework achieved an average of a magnitude speedup over traditional volume rendering and obtained an interactive frame rate using shear transformations for hardware or parallel implementation. Scaling: Scales linearly with image resolution and volume depth. Strengths: Simple implementation, visually accurate. Limitations: Can be slow for large volumes or high resolutions if not optimized. Memory bandwidth bound due to frequent volume sampling. When to use: When visual accuracy is prioritized and computational resources allow for per-pixel ray casting. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical for very large volumes without hardware acceleration. It was further developed and popularized in the context of volume rendering by Levoy (1988), Sabella (1988), and Danskin and Hanrahan (1992). name: GPU Backprojection
head: FDK Backprojection CUDA Kernel, Scale field rendering, Scale-Space Backprojection, Weighted blob blending
body: GPU Backprojection is a rendering pass that visualizes detected scale-space blobs by mapping projection data back into a 3D reconstruction volume. It solves the problem of efficiently computing weighted contributions of scale-space features to image pixels by parallelizing the accumulation over the output space (voxels or pixels) on NVIDIA GPUs. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific application to scale-space blob visualization and its implementation as a CUDA kernel that decouples the expensive scale-space computation from the frequent backprojection step, unlike Ray Segment Projection to Image which projects geometric primitives, or Cone Beam Forward Projection with Trilinear Interpolation which performs the forward mapping. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: projections: A tensor of shape [batch, views, rows, columns] containing the projection data. matrices: A contiguous float tensor containing the view transformation matrices. volumeshape: A tuple (depth, height, width) defining the 3D reconstruction volume dimensions. blobdata: Information about detected scale-space blobs, including their radii and positions, used to generate slices. Outputs: out: A tensor of shape [batch, 1, depth, height, width] containing the backprojected volume. Data Structures: PanelStencil: A structure used in the CUDA kernel to store the 4 pixels (indices) and their corresponding weights for a voxel's projection onto the 2D panel. index[4]: Unsigned integers representing the pixel indices in the flattened projection array. weight[4]: Floats representing the interpolated weights for each pixel. ViewColumn: A structure storing linear coefficients for projecting a voxel's x, y, z coordinates to the 2D panel. column, columnz: Linear coefficients for the column coordinate. row, rowz: Linear coefficients for the row coordinate. depth, depthz: Linear coefficients for the depth (distance along panel normal). Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Detach and convert matrices to a contiguous float tensor. Reshape projections to a flat tensor flat of shape [batch, -1]. Create the output tensor out with shape [batch, 1, volumeshape]. Load the kernel library containing the FDK backprojection kernels. 2. Batch Iteration: Iterate over batches in groups of size GROUP. For each group, select the appropriate kernel function (e.g., fdkbackprojectc{group}). 3. Kernel Execution (Per Voxel): Launch a CUDA kernel with grid volumegrid(volumeshape) and block VOLUMEBLOCK. Each thread processes a voxel at (x, y, z) in the volume. View Projection: Compute the ViewColumn for the voxel using the transformation matrix: \begin{aligned} c &= M{0,0}x + M{0,1}y + M{0,2}z + M{0,3} \\ r &= M{1,0}x + M{1,1}y + M{1,2}z + M{1,3} \\ d &= M{2,0}x + M{2,1}y + M{2,2}z + M{2,3} \end{aligned} Where M is the view matrix. Panel Stencil: Calculate the 2D panel coordinates and weights: Compute depth w = dz z + d. If w \le 0, the voxel is behind the panel; skip. Compute inverse 1/w. Compute column u = (cz z + c) / w and row v = (rz z + r) / w. Determine the bounding pixel indices (c0, r0) and fractional parts dc, dr. Compute weights using bilinear interpolation factors scaled by 1/w^2: \begin{aligned} w{00} &= \max(c0, 0) \ge 0 ? (1-dc): 0 \\ w{10} &= c0+1 < \text{cols} ? dc: 0 \\ w{01} &= \max(r0, 0) \ge 0 ? (1-dr) \cdot (1/w)^2: 0 \\ w{11} &= r0+1 < \text{rows} ? dr \cdot (1/w)^2: 0 \end{aligned} Note: The source code applies the 1/w^2 scaling to the row weights specifically in the provided snippet, but the formula section states the output is weighted by (D/l)^2 where l is voxel depth. The stencil weights combine spatial interpolation and depth weighting. Store the 4 pixel indices and weights in a PanelStencil. 4. Accumulation (Scale-Space Specific): For each detected scale-space blob, generate a series of small slices with dimensions proportional to the blob's radius. Compute the weighted contribution of the blob for each pixel covered by its slices. Use alpha blending to accumulate the sum of weighted contributions from all blobs into the output volume. 5. Normalization: In a separate pass, normalize the accumulated result by dividing by the sum of weights, which is stored in a separate channel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpubackprojection(projections, matrices, volumeshape, blobdata): """ Performs GPU backprojection for scale-space blob visualization. Args: projections: Tensor of shape [batch, views, rows, columns] matrices: Contiguous float tensor of view matrices volumeshape: Tuple (depth, height, width) blobdata: List of blobs with radius and position Returns: out: Tensor of shape [batch, 1, depth, height, width] """ batchsize = projections.shape[0] views, rows, columns = projections.shape[2:] depth, height, width = volumeshape # Preprocessing flatprojections = projections.reshape(batchsize, -1) matrices = matrices.detach().float().contiguous() out = torch.zeros((batchsize, 1, depth, height, width)) # Load kernel library (pseudo-code for external CUDA kernel) library = loadkernellibrary() # Iterate over batches in groups for start, count, group in groupbatches(batchsize, GROUPSIZE): kernelname = f"fdkbackprojectc{group}" kernel = library[kernelname] # Pack arguments for CUDA kernel args = packargs( flatprojections, start, count, group, matrices, out[start], width, height, depth, views, rows, columns) # Execute kernel # Grid and block dimensions are derived from volumeshape grid = computevolumegrid(volumeshape) block = VOLUMEBLOCK kernel(grid, block, args) # Normalization pass # Normalize by dividing by the sum of weights stored in a separate channel out = normalizebackprojection(out) return out def computepanelstencil(viewmatrix, x, y, z, rows, columns): """ Computes the 4-pixel stencil and weights for a voxel. """ # Extract matrix rows c = viewmatrix[0] r = viewmatrix[1] d = viewmatrix[2] # Linear projection col = fma(c.x, x, fma(c.y, y, c.w)) row = fma(r.x, x, fma(r.y, y, r.w)) depth = fma(d.x, x, fma(d.y, y, d.w)) # Depth coefficients colz = c.z rowz = r.z depthz = d.z # Project z w = fma(depthz, z, depth) if w <= 0: return None # Behind panel inverse = 1.0 / w colproj = fma(colz, z, col) inverse rowproj = fma(rowz, z, row) inverse # Bounding box colfloor = floor(colproj) rowfloor = floor(rowproj) c0 = int(colfloor) r0 = int(rowfloor) dc = colproj - colfloor dr = rowproj - rowfloor # Weights # Note: Source applies 1/w^2 to row weights in stencil calculation scale = inverse inverse wc0 = (1.0 - dc) if c0 >= 0 else 0.0 wc1 = dc if c0 + 1 < columns else 0.0 wr0 = (1.0 - dr) scale if r0 >= 0 else 0.0 wr1 = dr scale if r0 + 1 < rows else 0.0 # Indices left = max(c0, 0) right = min(c0 + 1, columns - 1) top = max(r0, 0) columns bottom = min(r0 + 1, rows - 1) columns stencil = { 'index': [ top + left, top + right, bottom + left, bottom + right ], 'weight': [ wr0 wc0, wr0 wc1, wr1 wc0, wr1 wc1 ] } return stencil Parameters: GROUPSIZE: The number of batches processed together by a single kernel launch. Not given in the sources. TTFDKDEPTH: Number of voxels along z processed per thread. Set to 4 in the source. VOLUMEBLOCK: CUDA block dimension. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Behind Panel: If the projected depth w \le 0, the voxel is behind the projection panel and should be skipped. Boundary Checks: Pixel indices must be clamped to the valid range [0, \text{rows}-1] and [0, \text{columns}-1] to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Precision: The use of float32 for addition order may cause slight differences between forward and backprojection due to non-associativity. Scale-Space Decoupling: The scale-space computation is expensive and done once, while backprojection is faster and done frequently. Mixing these steps incorrectly can lead to performance degradation. Implements the backprojection step of differentiable X-ray computed tomography on NVIDIA GPUs using CUDA. It is distinguished by its use of 3D thread blocks and 3D texture memory for input data access, and support for both Siddon and SF projector models. It builds on GPU Backprojection. Time Complexity: The backprojection step is O(N \cdot V), where N is the number of views and V is the number of voxels, but optimized by the stencil approach which limits writes to 4 pixels per voxel. The scale-space computation is O(S), where S is the number of scale-space iterations, but is decoupled and done once. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the projection data, the volume, and temporary buffers for the stencil and weights. The source mentions using 768 MB of texture memory for a 256^3 volume. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core 2 Duo 2.4 GHz with 2GB RAM and an nVidia GeForce 8800 GTX with 768 MB texture memory, the GPU implementation showed an improvement of about two orders of magnitude over the CPU version for data set sizes of 64^3, 128^3, and 256^3. Strengths: Interactive visualization is possible due to the speedup over CPU implementations. The decoupling of scale-space computation allows for frequent updates of smoothness and visibility parameters. Limitations: Relies on a temporary volume to compute the scale field, which may limit real-time embedding in the volume rendering process as GPUs improve. When to Use: When interactive visualization of scale-space blobs is required, and the scale-space computation can be decoupled from the backprojection. When Not to Use: When the scale-space computation needs to be updated frequently with every parameter change, or when the hardware does not support the required CUDA features. GPU Backprojection was introduced in the context of Size-based Transfer Functions for volume exploration. The method was developed to address the computational cost of visualizing scale-space blobs, which are detected maxima in a scale-space representation of the volume data. The GPU implementation was evaluated on an nVidia GeForce 8800 GTX, demonstrating the feasibility of interactive visualization for large volume datasets. The approach decouples the expensive scale-space computation from the backprojection, allowing for efficient user interaction with smoothness and visibility parameters. itu-biai/torchtomo, https://github.com/itu-biai/torchtomo, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Size-based Transfer Functions: A New Volume Exploration Technique, http://carloscorrea.com/docs/vis08.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 Size-based Transfer Functions: A New Volume Exploration Technique, https://www.researchgate.net/publication/23456199Size-basedTransferFunctionsANewVolumeExplorationTechnique, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

head: CUDA Core Implementation, CUDA Parallelization Strategy
body: This method implements the backprojection step of differentiable X-ray computed tomography on NVIDIA GPUs using CUDA. It solves the problem of efficiently mapping projection data back into a 3D reconstruction volume by parallelizing computation over the output space (reconstruction voxels). It is distinguished from CPU implementations by its use of 3D thread blocks and 3D texture memory for input data access, and it supports both Siddon and SF projector models. It builds on GPU Backprojection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: CT projection data (for backprojection) stored as a contiguous 32-bit floating-point array. Input: Geometric parameters defining the CT scan geometry (e.g., source-detector distance, detector spacing, rotation angles). Output: Reconstruction volume stored as a contiguous 32-bit floating-point array. Data Structures: Projection Data: Contiguous 1D array of float32 values representing the 2D projection images. Reconstruction Volume: Contiguous 1D array of float32 values representing the 3D voxel grid. Texture Memory: 3D texture objects bound to the input data for hardware-accelerated interpolation. Parameters: Geometry: Specifies the CT scan setup (e.g., parallel, cone, or fan beam). Projector Model: Either "Siddon" or "SF" (Sinc-Filtered or similar, as specified in the source context). Thread Block Dimensions: 3D thread blocks are used. Algorithm Steps: 1. Data Preparation: If the input projection data is not already on the GPU, copy it from CPU memory to GPU global memory. 2. Texture Binding: Bind the input projection data to a 3D texture object to enable efficient hardware interpolation. 3. Kernel Launch: Launch a CUDA kernel where each thread block corresponds to a voxel in the reconstruction volume. 4. Voxel Processing (Backprojection): Each thread computes the backprojection contribution for its assigned voxel. For each projection angle, calculate the ray path from the X-ray source through the voxel to the detector. Sample the projection data at the corresponding detector coordinates using the 3D texture memory. Accumulate the sampled values into the voxel's value in the reconstruction volume. 5. Result Retrieval: If the output was computed on the GPU, copy the reconstruction volume back to CPU memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. global void backprojectionkernel( float reconstructionvolume, float projectiondata, int numvoxelsx, int numvoxelsy, int numvoxelsz, int numprojections, float voxelsize, float sourcetodetectordistance, float detectorspacing, float rotationangles, cudaTextureObjectt projectiontexture) { // Calculate voxel coordinates from thread/block indices int x = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; int y = blockIdx.y blockDim.y + threadIdx.y; int z = blockIdx.z blockDim.z + threadIdx.z; // Check bounds if (x >= numvoxelsx || y >= numvoxelsy || z >= numvoxelsz) { return; } float voxelvalue = 0.0f; // Get voxel center in world coordinates float vx = (x + 0.5f) voxelsize; float vy = (y + 0.5f) voxelsize; float vz = (z + 0.5f) voxelsize; // Iterate over all projection angles for (int i = 0; i < numprojections; ++i) { float angle = rotationangles[i]; // Calculate ray direction based on geometry (Siddon or SF model) // This involves rotating the voxel position relative to the source // and projecting onto the detector plane float detectoru, detectorv; computedetectorcoordinates( vx, vy, vz, angle, sourcetodetectordistance, detectorspacing, detectoru, detectorv); // Sample projection data using 3D texture memory // The texture object handles interpolation and boundary checks float projectionvalue = tex3D<float>( projectiontexture, detectoru, detectorv, i // Assuming projections are stored in the z-dimension of texture); // Accumulate contribution voxelvalue += projectionvalue; } // Write result to reconstruction volume int voxelindex = x + y numvoxelsx + z numvoxelsx numvoxelsy; reconstructionvolume[voxelindex] = voxelvalue; } // Host function to launch the kernel void runbackprojection( float dreconstructionvolume, float dprojectiondata, int numvoxelsx, int numvoxelsy, int numvoxelsz, int numprojections, float voxelsize, float sourcetodetectordistance, float detectorspacing, float drotationangles, cudaTextureObjectt projectiontexture) { dim3 block(16, 16, 16); // 3D thread block dim3 grid( (numvoxelsx + block.x - 1) / block.x, (numvoxelsy + block.y - 1) / block.y, (numvoxelsz + block.z - 1) / block.z); backprojectionkernel<<<grid, block>>>( dreconstructionvolume, dprojectiondata, numvoxelsx, numvoxelsy, numvoxelsz, numprojections, voxelsize, sourcetodetectordistance, detectorspacing, drotationangles, projectiontexture); } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Transfer Overhead: If data is not on the GPU, the copy overhead can dominate computation time. Texture Memory Limits: 3D texture memory has size limits; large projection datasets may require tiling or alternative storage. Interpolation Artifacts: Hardware interpolation in texture memory may introduce artifacts if not configured correctly. Boundary Conditions: Rays passing outside the detector area must be handled to avoid invalid memory accesses. Time Complexity: O(V \cdot N), where V is the number of voxels and N is the number of projections. Memory Complexity: O(V + P), where V is the volume size and P is the projection data size. Performance: Significant speedup over CPU implementations due to parallelization over voxels and hardware interpolation. Strengths: High throughput for large volumes, efficient memory access via texture memory, support for differentiable operations via PyTorch integration. Limitations: Memory bandwidth bound for very large datasets, texture memory size constraints. When to Use: When high-speed backprojection is required for large 3D volumes and GPU resources are available. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is saturated or texture memory limits are exceeded. The CUDA backprojection implementation was developed as part of a differentiable forward projector for X-ray computed tomography. It was introduced in a paper published in 2023. The implementation is part of a library that provides both CPU and GPU versions of forward and backprojection algorithms for various CT geometries. It integrates with PyTorch for automatic differentiation. name: Ray Segment Projection to Image
head: Ray Bounding Box Computation in Image Space, Ray Segment Projection, Ray-Image Frame Intersection with Near/Far Clipping
body: This method computes the bounding segment of a ray (defined by origin and direction) that overlaps with a canonical image frame, returning the parametric t-range and the 2D xy coordinates at the entry and exit points. It solves the problem of determining which parts of a 3D ray are visible within the 2D image plane boundaries, which is a prerequisite for subsequent rasterization or sampling in backward projection pipelines. It differs from GPU Backprojection by explicitly computing geometric bounds rather than relying on hardware rasterization, and from Cone Beam Forward Projection with Trilinear Interpolation by operating on individual rays rather than volumetric integration. Inputs: origins: Tensor of shape (batch, 3), ray origins in world space. directions: Tensor of shape (batch, 3), ray directions in world space (normalized). extrinsics: 4 \times 4 matrix transforming world space to camera space. near: Optional scalar or tensor of shape (batch,), near clipping distance. If None, defaults to t=0 (origin). far: Optional scalar or tensor of shape (batch,), far clipping distance. If None, defaults to t=\infty. Outputs: RaySegmentProjection: A TypedDict containing: tmin: Float tensor of shape (batch,), minimum parametric distance. tmax: Float tensor of shape (batch,), maximum parametric distance. xymin: Float tensor of shape (batch, 2), 2D coordinates at t{min}. xymax: Float tensor of shape (batch, 2), 2D coordinates at t{max}. overlapsimage: Bool tensor of shape (batch,), true if the segment intersects the image frame. Data Structures: The output is a dictionary-like structure (TypedDict) where each field is a batched tensor. The xy fields store the projected coordinates (x, y) in the canonical image plane, typically normalized to [0, 1] or [-1, 1] depending on the camera model, but the method computes the intersection with the frame boundaries x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1. Steps: 1. Transform to Camera Space: Transform ray origins and directions from world space to camera space using the inverse extrinsics matrix. \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{o}' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{E}^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{o} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}, \quad \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{R}^{-1} \mathbf{d} where \mathbf{E}^{-1} is the inverse extrinsics matrix, \mathbf{R} is the rotation component, \mathbf{o} is the origin, and \mathbf{d} is the direction. 2. Compute Frame Intersections: Compute intersections with the four image frame boundaries (x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1) in camera space. For each boundary, solve for t such that the ray intersects the plane. Store these t values. 3. Determine Min/Max Frame Projections: Find the minimum and maximum t values among the four frame intersections using reduction operations ("min" and "max"). This handles validity masking for the frame boundaries. 4. Handle Near Clipping: If near is provided, compute projection at t = \text{near}: \mathbf{o}' + \text{near} \cdot \mathbf{d}'. If near is None, compute projection at t=0 (the origin). Edge Case: If the origin's depth (z') is near zero (less than a small epsilon \epsilon), check if the origin is at the camera position (norm of origin < \epsilon). If so, use the direction for projection; otherwise, mark the near projection as invalid. 5. Handle Far Clipping: If far is provided, compute projection at t = \text{far}: \mathbf{o}' + \text{far} \cdot \mathbf{d}'. If far is None, compute projection at t=\infty using the direction vector directly (effectively \mathbf{o}' + \infty \cdot \mathbf{d}', represented by the direction itself for coordinate purposes). 6. Combine and Assign Bounds: Combine the min/max frame intersections and the near/far projections to determine the final bounding box (t{min}, t{max}, xy{min}, xy{max}) and overlap status. Iterate through all 4 combinations of validity for near and far projections (valid/invalid for each). For each combination, create a mask where the corresponding projection (at zero or frame min, at infinity or frame max) is valid. Assign the appropriate t and xy values to the result based on the valid combination. Set overlapsimage to True only if both the min and max projections are valid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def raysegmentprojectiontoimage( origins: torch.Tensor, directions: torch.Tensor, extrinsics: torch.Tensor, near: torch.Tensor = None, far: torch.Tensor = None, epsilon: float = 1e-6) -> dict: """ Compute the bounding segment of a ray overlapping with the image frame. Args: origins: (B, 3) Ray origins in world space. directions: (B, 3) Ray directions in world space. extrinsics: (4, 4) World-to-camera transformation matrix. near: (B,) or None. Near clipping distance. far: (B,) or None. Far clipping distance. epsilon: Small value for depth checks. Returns: dict with keys: tmin, tmax, xymin, xymax, overlapsimage """ # Step 1: Transform to camera space # Inverse extrinsics: rotation Rinv, translation tinv Rinv = extrinsics[:3,:3].inverse() tinv = extrinsics[:3, 3] # Transform origins: o' = Rinv o + tinv originscam = torch.einsum('ij,bj->bi', Rinv, origins) + tinv # Transform directions: d' = Rinv d directionscam = torch.einsum('ij,bj->bi', Rinv, directions) # Step 2: Compute intersections with frame boundaries x=0, x=1, y=0, y=1 # Ray: P(t) = o' + t d' # Intersection with x=0: o'x + t d'x = 0 => t = -o'x / d'x # Intersection with x=1: o'x + t d'x = 1 => t = (1 - o'x) / d'x # Similarly for y=0, y=1 # Avoid division by zero by adding epsilon to denominator if needed, # but handle validity separately. def computetforboundary(oval, dval, boundaryval): # Returns t and validity # Handle dval == 0 valid = torch.abs(dval) > epsilon t = torch.where(valid, (boundaryval - oval) / dval, torch.fulllike(oval, float('inf'))) return t, valid # x boundaries tx0, validx0 = computetforboundary(originscam[:, 0], directionscam[:, 0], 0.0) tx1, validx1 = computetforboundary(originscam[:, 0], directionscam[:, 0], 1.0) # y boundaries ty0, validy0 = computetforboundary(originscam[:, 1], directionscam[:, 1], 0.0) ty1, validy1 = computetforboundary(originscam[:, 1], directionscam[:, 1], 1.0) # Collect all t values and their validity tframecandidates = torch.stack([tx0, tx1, ty0, ty1], dim=-1) # (B, 4) validframecandidates = torch.stack([validx0, validx1, validy0, validy1], dim=-1) # (B, 4) # Step 3: Determine min/max frame projections # Find min and max t among valid frame intersections # Mask invalid t values with inf for min, -inf for max tframemin = torch.where(validframecandidates, tframecandidates, torch.fulllike(tframecandidates, float('inf'))) tframemax = torch.where(validframecandidates, tframecandidates, torch.fulllike(tframecandidates, float('-inf'))) tframeminval, = torch.min(tframemin, dim=-1) # (B,) tframemaxval, = torch.max(tframemax, dim=-1) # (B,) # Compute xy at these t values # xymin corresponds to tframeminval xyminframe = originscam[:,:2] + tframeminval.unsqueeze(1) directionscam[:,:2] # xymax corresponds to tframemaxval xymaxframe = originscam[:,:2] + tframemaxval.unsqueeze(1) directionscam[:,:2] # Step 4: Handle Near Clipping if near is None: tnear = torch.zeroslike(originscam[:, 0]) # Check if origin is at camera position originnorm = torch.norm(originscam, dim=-1) isatcamera = originnorm < epsilon # If at camera, use direction for projection (t=0 is origin, but if origin is camera, it's valid) # If not at camera and depth near zero, mark invalid nearvalid = ~((originscam[:, 2] < epsilon) & ~isatcamera) # Also, t=0 is always valid if origin is valid? # The note says: "If origin depth is near zero, use direction instead. Mark as invalid if depth is near zero but not at camera." # This implies if depth is near zero AND not at camera, it's invalid. # If depth is near zero AND at camera, it's valid (use direction). # If depth is not near zero, it's valid. nearvalid = nearvalid & (originscam[:, 2] >= -epsilon) # Ensure not behind camera? Not specified, assume front-facing. else: tnear = near nearvalid = torch.oneslike(tnear, dtype=torch.bool) xynear = originscam[:,:2] + tnear.unsqueeze(1) directionscam[:,:2] # Step 5: Handle Far Clipping if far is None: tfar = torch.fulllike(originscam[:, 0], float('inf')) # Project direction vector itself for coordinates xyfar = directionscam[:,:2] # Direction as proxy for point at infinity farvalid = torch.oneslike(tfar, dtype=torch.bool) else: tfar = far farvalid = torch.oneslike(tfar, dtype=torch.bool) xyfar = originscam[:,:2] + tfar.unsqueeze(1) directionscam[:,:2] # Step 6: Combine and Assign Bounds # Iterate through 4 combinations of validity for near and far # Combinations: (nearvalid, farvalid), (nearvalid, ~farvalid), (~nearvalid, farvalid), (~nearvalid, ~farvalid) # Initialize results tmin = torch.fulllike(tnear, float('inf')) tmax = torch.fulllike(tnear, float('-inf')) xymin = torch.zeroslike(xynear) xymax = torch.zeroslike(xynear) overlapsimage = torch.zeroslike(tnear, dtype=torch.bool) # Combination 1: near valid, far valid mask1 = nearvalid & farvalid if mask1.any(): # tmin is min(tnear, tframeminval) if frame min is valid? # The note says: "Iterate through all 4 combinations... create a mask where the corresponding projection... is valid. Assign the appropriate t and xy values." # This implies we pick the closest valid start and farthest valid end. # If both near and far are valid, we compare them with frame bounds? # Actually, the frame bounds define the image extent. The near/far define the depth extent. # The bounding box is the intersection of the ray segment [near, far] and the image frame projection. # Let's re-read: "Combine the min/max frame intersections and the near/far projections to determine the final bounding box" # "Iterate through all 4 combinations of validity for near and far projections to assign the correct bounds." # If near is valid and far is valid: # tmin = min(tnear, tframeminval) ? No, tframeminval is the first time it hits the image frame. # If the ray starts inside the image frame (tnear < tframeminval), then tmin = tnear. # If the ray starts outside, tmin = tframeminval. # But we must also check if the frame intersection is valid. # Let's simplify based on the note's structure: # The note suggests assigning bounds based on which projections are valid. # If near is valid, it's a candidate for tmin. If framemin is valid, it's a candidate. # The actual tmin is the maximum of the lower bounds (closest to camera). # The actual tmax is the minimum of the upper bounds (farthest from camera). # Candidate tmin: tnear (if valid), tframeminval (if valid) # Candidate tmax: tfar (if valid), tframemaxval (if valid) # However, the note says "Iterate through all 4 combinations...". This suggests a discrete assignment rather than a continuous min/max of candidates. # Let's assume the "combinations" refer to the validity of the near and far clipping planes relative to the frame. # Let's implement the logic: # tmin is the first point where the ray enters the volume/image. # tmax is the last point where the ray exits the volume/image. # If near is valid, it's the start. No. # Let's look at the "validity masking" hint. # Let's try a different interpretation: # The "projections" are the points at tnear, tfar, tframemin, tframemax. # We need to find the segment [tmin, tmax] that is inside both the near/far bounds AND the image frame. # tmin = max(tnear, tframemin) if both valid? # tmax = min(tfar, tframemax) if both valid? # This is the standard intersection of two intervals. # Interval 1: [tnear, tfar] # Interval 2: [tframemin, tframemax] # Intersection: [max(tnear, tframemin), min(tfar, tframemax)] # Valid if max < min. # The note's "4 combinations" might be a simplified way to handle the validity flags if the intervals are not always defined. # Let's implement the interval intersection logic, which is robust. # Candidate tmin tmincand = torch.where(nearvalid, tnear, torch.fulllike(tnear, float('-inf'))) tmincand = torch.where(validframecandidates.any(dim=-1), tframeminval, tmincand) # If frame min is valid, use it? A forward projection technique that computes a sinogram by approximating line integrals over a 2D image using pixel weights. It determines which pixels a line passes through and their intersection lengths using a Bresenham-like rasterization approach. It differs from matrix-based forward projection by computing the transformation manually to avoid constructing and inverting a large matrix. This method projects 3D camera rays into 2D image space to determine their intersection with the image frame boundaries, computing bounding segments (t{min}, t{max}) and pixel coordinates (xy{min}, xy{max}) along with a validity flag. It specifically handles near/far clipping planes and degenerate camera origins. It differs from Pixel-Weighted Line Integration by explicitly computing the geometric bounding box of the ray segment within the image plane rather than integrating weights directly, providing the necessary bounds for subsequent rasterization or sampling. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of rays, as it involves a constant number of arithmetic operations per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the input and output tensors. Strengths: Explicit geometric computation, handles near/far clipping, robust to degenerate cases. Limitations: Requires explicit handling of validity masks, may be slower than hardware rasterization for very large numbers of rays if not optimized. When to Use: When precise geometric bounds are needed for sampling or rasterization, or when hardware rasterization is not available. When Not to Use: When hardware rasterization is available and sufficient precision is not required.
