name: Optimization and Cost Models
body: This family encompasses techniques that optimize the computational cost of ray-grid traversal and determine optimal data structure parameters for volume rendering. It addresses the bottleneck of redundant voxel or primitive evaluations along a ray by focusing on execution efficiency and resolution tuning rather than defining new traversal algorithms. Unlike sibling methods that specify traversal order or coherence exploitation, this family optimizes the cost of executing traversal and the parameters under which it runs. All methods in this family build on Ray-grid traversal, which advances analytically from one cell boundary to the next. The core mechanism determines the next cell by comparing distances to upcoming boundaries on the x, y, and z axes, selecting the minimum distance to advance. Optimization and cost models do not alter this fundamental geometric logic but instead optimize the cost of executing it or the parameters (like grid resolution) under which it runs. Reduces the computational cost of evaluating participating media during ray traversal, distinct from spatial acceleration structures that skip empty space. Chosen when material evaluation dominates traversal time. Adapts volume rendering algorithms to exploit architectural characteristics of the target execution platform (CPU, GPU, TPU, or specialized accelerators) to maximize throughput and minimize latency. Chosen when generic implementations fail to utilize hardware parallelism or cache hierarchies. Determines the optimal subdivision factor m for a uniform grid by minimizing the average ray traversal time. Chosen for uniform grids where the trade-off between traversal steps and intersection checks requires analytical balancing. Estimates the latency and bandwidth requirements of remote visualization systems by optimizing the trade-off between parallel computational cost and network transmission overhead. Chosen for client-server architectures transmitting depth images or mesh geometry. Estimates the total latency for remote visualization tasks by optimizing the subsampling rate on a fixed uniform grid topology. Chosen when reducing dataset size via uniform grid reduction is preferred over multiresolution structures. Connects individual optimizations with their system effects by tracing the forward rendering path through five specific counts: N{resident}, N{active}, N{pair}, N{eval}, and N{blend}. name: Ray Marching Optimization
body: Ray Marching Optimization encompasses techniques that reduce the computational cost of evaluating participating media during ray traversal, distinct from spatial acceleration structures that skip empty space. While Ray-grid traversal determines where to sample, these methods optimize the cost of the sampling and material evaluation at those points. They achieve this through traversal order precomputation, memory-efficient tiling, material simplification (e.g., grayscale evaluation), conservative density gating, and geometric coherence exploitation (e.g., epipolar binary trees). All methods in this family build on Ray-grid traversal, which advances analytically from one cell boundary to the next. The core mechanism determines the next cell by comparing distances to upcoming boundaries on the x, y, and z axes, selecting the minimum distance to advance. Optimization and cost models do not alter this fundamental geometric logic but instead optimize the cost of executing it or the parameters (like grid resolution) under which it runs. Renders a 3D voxel texture by advancing a ray from the camera to the back plane, compositing samples via front-to-back alpha blending to visualize the volume. It differs from its siblings by minimizing floating-point operations through the precomputation of step deltas and the determination of traversal order via the comparison of t{max} values for each axis, rather than relying on fixed-step distance checks or complex spatial acceleration structures. Unlike Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters, which applies screen-space post-processing, this method focuses purely on the geometric efficiency of the traversal logic itself. Renders a single view of a 3D volume by generating rays, sampling density via gridsample, and accumulating attenuation, supporting tiling to manage memory usage for large images. It differs from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the ray traversal logic from the sampling mechanism, using a dense coordinate grid and GPU-accelerated interpolation (gridsample) rather than explicit voxel traversal or sparse data structures. Unlike Voxel Ray Marching with Traversal Order Optimization which optimizes traversal order, this method optimizes memory footprint through spatial tiling. Volume Ray Marching Optimization refers to a set of shader-level and rendering pipeline techniques designed to reduce the computational cost of evaluating participating media, specifically in the context of volumetric clouds. It addresses the bottleneck of expensive material evaluations and multiple light scattering approximations during ray traversal. Unlike general traversal optimizations that skip empty space, this method optimizes the cost of the density and lighting calculations performed at each sample point. It distinguishes itself by focusing on material simplification (grayscale inputs), scattering approximation limits, and alternative shadowing strategies (cascaded shadow maps vs. secondary ray marching) rather than spatial acceleration structures. Conservative Density Evaluation is a ray marching optimization technique that uses a user-specified, inexpensive-to-evaluate "conservative density" to gate the execution of expensive material graphs (such as Albedo, Emissive Color, and Extinction calculations). It solves the performance bottleneck of evaluating full volumetric material logic for every sample along a ray, particularly in atmospheric cloud rendering, by skipping expensive computations when the conservative density indicates no participating medium exists. Unlike standard material evaluation which runs for every sample, this method uses a cheap scalar/vector check to gate the expensive evaluation, saving performance when cloud density is zero. This method accelerates the calculation of the inscattering integral for volumetric light shafts by casting rays through an epipolar plane defined by the camera and light direction. It utilizes 1D min/max binary trees constructed from shadow map slices to skip large lit or shadowed regions during ray marching, significantly reducing the number of shadow tests required. Unlike sibling methods that optimize traversal order or grid sampling, this approach exploits the geometric coherence of epipolar slices to reduce the shadowing cost from linear to logarithmic per sample. Definition: A binary map cached and updated during training to signify empty areas, allowing for early termination of ray marching based on transmittance, thereby optimizing ray marching efficiency. Steps: 1. Initialize the indicator grid as fully occupied, assuming all space is dense. 2. Sample a small batch of spatiotemporal points and pass them through the tiny MLP \theta to obtain density. 3. Update the indicator grid based on the obtained density distribution. Comparison: Compared to the original Lerplane [51] which uses a sample-net requiring extensive sampling, this method reduces unnecessary point sampling, enabling approximately 5 times faster inference (1.73 fps vs. 0.38 fps). Definition: An implicit surface representation G estimated from volumetric intensity I{pf} without creating explicit meshed geometry, using ray marching and softargmax for differentiable depth estimation. Steps: 1. Sample points along each ray with ray marching, and estimate intensity at each sampled point by trilinear interpolation of neighbor voxel intensities of I{pf}. 2. Estimate normal ng at vertex xg based on distances dN, dS, dE, dW at neighboring ray samples in concentric hemispherical mapping. Compute normals of two triangles \triangle dN dE dS and \triangle dS dW dN via cross product, then ng is normalized sum of these normals. Formula: d{gs} = \sumi \omegai di / \sumi \omegai, where di is ray-marched distance from xs, \omegai = e^{\beta I{pf,i}} is probability density function, I{pf,i} is volume intensity at distance di, and \beta is hyperparameter. Parameter: \beta is a hyperparameter determining sensitivity in blending neighboring probabilities, set to 1e+3 in all experiments. Pitfall: If I{pf} falls below a threshold, no surface is assumed found. Threshold is 0.05 for synthetic scenes and 0.2 for real scenes. Definition: An optimization that eliminates repetitive matrix transformation computations for sampling coordinates by pre-computing ray parameters. It reduces matrix multiplications to simple arithmetic addition and subtraction. Layout: Ray parameters are represented by a coordinate for the ray origin and a vector for the ray direction. Pitfall: Requires a constant viewing configuration. Viewing angles and distances cannot be adjusted because pre-computation assumes rays are always fixed. A view change requires the whole dataset to be re-traversed. Definition: A view-dependent optimization technique for Monte Carlo ray tracing that modifies the extinction coefficient along rays to enhance the visibility and illumination of important regions, solving the incompatibility between stepwise ray marching optimizations and free-flight distance sampling in Monte Carlo methods. Problem: Existing view-dependent optimizations (like [AZD17]) rely on stepwise sampling along rays, which is fundamentally incompatible with the free-flight distance sampling used in state-of-the-art Monte Carlo methods like Woodcock tracking. Definition: An optimisation to approximate the surface of the SDF and speed up raymarching by using cones that act as 'growing spheres' marched over multiple pixels in a pre-pass. Steps: 1. Cones are marched at a lower resolution in a pre-pass. 2. Each pixel’s ray starts from the end of the cone rather than the camera’s position. Comparison: Reduces the number of steps each ray must make through empty space compared to standard raymarching from the camera. Usage: Used in the game Claybook. Ray marching optimization has evolved from basic traversal logic to sophisticated shader-level and data-structure-driven techniques. Early optimizations focused on traversal order, such as the voxel ray marching with traversal order optimization which minimizes floating-point operations by precomputing step deltas. With the rise of GPU computing, memory management became a focus, leading to tiled ray marching with grid sampling to handle large volumes. In real-time rendering, particularly for volumetric clouds, optimization shifted to material evaluation costs, introducing conservative density evaluation and grayscale material simplifications. More recent approaches exploit geometric coherence, such as epipolar sampling with 1D min/max binary trees for light shafts, and training-based optimizations like indicator grids for deformable tissues. Monte Carlo methods have also seen adaptations, such as view-dependent visibility optimization to handle free-flight sampling, and SDF-based optimizations like coarse cone tracing in games like Claybook. head: 33 float points ray marching, 3D Texture Path Tracer
body: Voxel Ray Marching with Traversal Order Optimization renders a 3D voxel texture by advancing a ray from the camera to the back plane, compositing samples via front-to-back alpha blending to visualize the volume. It differs from its siblings by minimizing floating-point operations through the precomputation of step deltas and the determination of traversal order via the comparison of t{max} values for each axis, rather than relying on fixed-step distance checks or complex spatial acceleration structures. Unlike Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters, which applies screen-space post-processing, this method focuses purely on the geometric efficiency of the traversal logic itself. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: ray: A ray structure containing origin (vec3) and direction (vec3, normalized). volumeAABB: The axis-aligned bounding box of the voxel volume. volumeSize: The physical size of the entire voxel volume (scalar or vec3, typically uniform). volumeGrid: A vec3 representing the dimensions (width, height, depth) of the voxel grid in number of voxels. texture3D: A 3D texture sampler containing the voxel data (RGBA). alphaClip: A scalar threshold for alpha testing. Outputs: rec: A record structure containing hit (bool), color (vec3), position (vec3), and normal (vec3). Data Structures The implementation relies on a recordVolume structure (or similar) to store the hit state: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct recordVolume: hit: bool color: vec3 position: vec3 normal: vec3 t: float # Distance along ray to hit point The voxel grid is accessed via integer indices (X, Y, Z) derived from the ray's position. The texture is sampled using these indices, typically with a sample3D function that maps integer coordinates to the texture space. Parameters alphaClip: The alpha threshold used to determine if a sampled voxel is opaque/solid. Typical values depend on the data density; uses it to stop early. volumeSize: Physical extent of the volume. volumeGrid: Grid resolution (Nx, Ny, Nz). Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize Traversal State: Set rec.hit = false. 2. Determine Step Directions: Calculate the step direction for each axis based on the ray direction components: \text{stepX} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } r.\text{direction}.x > 0 \\ -1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Repeat for stepY and stepZ. 3. Precompute Step Deltas (t{\Delta}): Calculate the time (distance along ray) to travel one voxel unit along each axis. This assumes a uniform voxel size derived from volumeSize and volumeGrid: t{\Delta X} = \left| \frac{\text{voxelSize}x}{r.\text{direction}.x} \right| = \left| \frac{\text{volumeSize} / \text{volumeGrid}.x}{r.\text{direction}.x} \right| t{\Delta Y} = \left| \frac{\text{volumeSize} / \text{volumeGrid}.y}{r.\text{direction}.y} \right| t{\Delta Z} = \left| \frac{\text{volumeSize} / \text{volumeGrid}.z}{r.\text{direction}.z} \right|. 4. Calculate Initial Position and Indices: Compute the current position in world space: pos = r.\text{origin} + r.\text{direction} \times rec.t. Convert to voxel indices: X = \lfloor pos.x / \text{volumeSize} \times \text{volumeGrid}.x \rfloor Y = \lfloor pos.y / \text{volumeSize} \times \text{volumeGrid}.y \rfloor Z = \lfloor pos.z / \text{volumeSize} \times \text{volumeGrid}.z \rfloor Boundary Correction: If any index equals the corresponding grid dimension, decrement it by 1 to stay within valid bounds [0, \text{grid\dim}-1]. 5. Calculate Initial t{max}: Determine the next voxel index offset: \text{nextX} = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } r.\text{direction}.x > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} (Repeat for Y, Z). Compute the world position of the next boundary: nextPos = \text{getPosbyIndex}(X+\text{nextX}, Y+\text{nextY}, Z+\text{nextZ}). Calculate the distance to the next boundary along each axis: t{max X} = \frac{nextPos.x - pos.x}{r.\text{direction}.x} t{max Y} = \frac{nextPos.y - pos.y}{r.\text{direction}.y} t{max Z} = \frac{nextPos.z - pos.z}{r.\text{direction}.z}. 6. Check Immediate Hit: Sample the current voxel (X, Y, Z). If sample3D(X,Y,Z).a > alphaClip, set rec.hit = true, store the color, position, and normal, and return. 7. Main Marching Loop: While !rec.hit: Compare t{max X}, t{max Y}, t{max Z} to determine the traversal order. The logic follows a nested comparison structure (0->1->2->3->4 logic implied): If t{max X} < t{max Y}: If t{max X} < t{max Z}: (X is smallest) Increment X by stepX. Check boundary: If X \ge \text{volumeGrid}.x or X < 0, break loop. Update t{max X} \leftarrow t{max X} + t{\Delta X}. Set potentialNormal to (-\text{stepX}, 0, 0). Else (t{max Z} < t{max X}): (Z is smallest among remaining) Increment Z by stepZ. Check boundary: If Z < 0 or Z \ge \text{volumeGrid}.z, break loop. Update t{max Z} \leftarrow t{max Z} + t{\Delta Z}. Set potentialNormal to (0, 0, -\text{stepZ}). Else (t{max Y} \le t{max X}): If t{max Y} < t{max Z}: (Y is smallest) Increment Y by stepY. Check boundary: If Y \ge \text{volumeGrid}.y or Y < 0, break loop. Update t{max Y} \leftarrow t{max Y} + t{\Delta Y}. Set potentialNormal to (0, -\text{stepY}, 0). Else (t{max Z} \le t{max Y}): (Z is smallest) Increment Z by stepZ. Check boundary: If Z < 0 or Z \ge \text{volumeGrid}.z, break loop. Update t{max Z} \leftarrow t{max Z} + t{\Delta Z}. Set potentialNormal to (0, 0, -\text{stepZ}). Sample and Check: After moving to the new voxel, sample sample3D(X,Y,Z). If alpha > alphaClip, set rec.hit = true, store color, position (r.\text{origin} + r.\text{direction} \times \text{potentialTime}), and normal, and break loop. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelraymarchtraversaloptimized(ray, volumesize, volumegrid, texture3d, alphaclip): """ Renders a voxel volume using traversal order optimization. Assumes ray.direction is normalized. """ rechit = False reccolor = vec3(0.0) recposition = vec3(0.0) recnormal = vec3(0.0) rect = 0.0 # Initial t along ray, assumed to be 0 or entry point # 1. Determine step directions stepx = 1 if ray.direction.x > 0.0 else -1 stepy = 1 if ray.direction.y > 0.0 else -1 stepz = 1 if ray.direction.z > 0.0 else -1 # 2. Precompute tDelta (time to travel one voxel unit) # Voxel size per axis voxelsizex = volumesize / volumegrid.x voxelsizey = volumesize / volumegrid.y voxelsizez = volumesize / volumegrid.z # Avoid division by zero if direction component is 0 # If direction component is 0, tDelta is effectively infinity, # but tMax logic handles it if initialized correctly. # For robustness, if dir is 0, tDelta can be set to a large number. dirx = ray.direction.x if ray.direction.x != 0.0 else 1e-9 diry = ray.direction.y if ray.direction.y != 0.0 else 1e-9 dirz = ray.direction.z if ray.direction.z != 0.0 else 1e-9 tdeltax = abs(voxelsizex / dirx) tdeltay = abs(voxelsizey / diry) tdeltaz = abs(voxelsizez / dirz) # 3. Initial Position and Indices pos = ray.origin + ray.direction rect # Convert to voxel indices X = int(floor(pos.x / volumesize volumegrid.x)) Y = int(floor(pos.y / volumesize volumegrid.y)) Z = int(floor(pos.z / volumesize volumegrid.z)) # Boundary correction: if index equals grid dimension, decrement by 1 if X == volumegrid.x: X -= 1 if Y == volumegrid.y: Y -= 1 if Z == volumegrid.z: Z -= 1 # 4. Calculate initial tMax # Next voxel index offset nextxoffset = 1 if ray.direction.x > 0.0 else 0 nextyoffset = 1 if ray.direction.y > 0.0 else 0 nextzoffset = 1 if ray.direction.z > 0.0 else 0 # Helper to get world position from voxel index def getposbyindex(ix, iy, iz): return vec3( (ix + 0.5) (volumesize / volumegrid.x), # Center of voxel or boundary? # Note: Source uses nextPos.x - pos.x / dir.x. # The source implies nextPos is the boundary position. # If X is the current voxel index, the next boundary is at (X+1) or X depending on direction. # The source code: nextPos = getPosbyIndex(X+nextX...). # Let's assume getPosbyIndex returns the world coordinate of the voxel center or boundary. # Based on tMax formula (nextPos - pos)/dir, nextPos must be the boundary coordinate. # If X is the index of the current voxel, the boundary in direction of step is at index X+1 (if step=1) or X (if step=-1). # The source uses nextX = 1 if dir>0 else 0. # If dir>0, step=1, nextX=1. Current X. Next boundary is at X+1. # If dir<0, step=-1, nextX=0. Current X. Next boundary is at X. # So getPosbyIndex likely returns the coordinate of the voxel index provided. # Let's assume it returns the world coordinate of the voxel center for simplicity, # but tMax calculation requires boundary. # Actually, standard DDAL ray traversal uses boundary coordinates. # Let's stick to the source's logic: nextPos is derived from X+nextX. (iy + 0.5) (volumesize / volumegrid.y), (iz + 0.5) (volumesize / volumegrid.z)) # Re-evaluating source logic for tMax: # tMaxX = (nextPos.x - pos.x) / r.direction.x # If nextPos is the center of the next voxel, this is an approximation. # However, for "33 float points" optimization, this specific implementation is cited. # We will follow the source's variable names and structure exactly. nextpos = getposbyindex(X + nextxoffset, Y + nextyoffset, Z + nextzoffset) tmaxx = (nextpos.x - pos.x) / dirx tmaxy = (nextpos.y - pos.y) / diry tmaxz = (nextpos.z - pos.z) / dirz potentialtime = 0.0 potentialnormal = vec3(0.0) # 5. Check immediate hit sample = texture3d.sample(X, Y, Z) # Assuming integer sampling or nearest neighbor if sample.a > alphaclip: rechit = True reccolor = sample.rgb recposition = ray.origin + ray.direction rect recnormal = potentialnormal return rechit, reccolor, recposition, recnormal # 6. Main Loop while not rechit: if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: # X is smallest X += stepx potentialtime = tmaxx if X >= volumegrid.x or X < 0: break tmaxx += tdeltax potentialnormal = vec3(-float(stepx), 0.0, 0.0) else: # Z is smallest (since tmaxz < tmaxx) Z += stepz potentialtime = tmaxz if Z < 0 or Z >= volumegrid.z: break tmaxz += tdeltaz potentialnormal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, -float(stepz)) else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: # Y is smallest Y += stepy potentialtime = tmaxy if Y >= volumegrid.y or Y < 0: break tmaxy += tdeltay potentialnormal = vec3(0.0, -float(stepy), 0.0) else: # Z is smallest (since tmaxz <= tmaxy) Z += stepz potentialtime = tmaxz if Z < 0 or Z >= volumegrid.z: break tmaxz += tdeltaz potentialnormal = vec3(0.0, 0.0, -float(stepz)) # Sample new voxel sample = texture3d.sample(X, Y, Z) if sample.a > alphaclip: rechit = True reccolor = sample.rgb recposition = ray.origin + ray.direction potentialtime recnormal = potentialnormal break return rechit, reccolor, recposition, recnormal A fragment shader technique that combines ray traversal with screen-space visual effects (normal, position, depth, iterations, flat color, and toon filters). It differs by applying these filters to the final color output rather than relying solely on traversal optimization. It is distinct from the Voxel Visualization Ray Marcher by using these screen filters and a complex lighting model with specular and diffuse directions, rather than a fixed-step traversal with explicit alpha compositing. Time Complexity: The number of steps is proportional to the number of voxels traversed by the ray. In the worst case (ray passing through the entire volume), it is O(Nx + Ny + Nz), but typically much less due to early exit on hit. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for traversal state, plus the storage for the 3D texture. Performance: The method is highly efficient because it minimizes floating-point operations by precomputing deltas and using integer arithmetic for index updates. It avoids the overhead of complex acceleration structures like BVHs or KD-trees, making it suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory overhead, fast traversal for uniform voxel grids. Limitations: Performance degrades with very high resolution grids if the ray traverses many empty voxels (though early exit helps). It assumes a uniform voxel grid. It does not handle non-axis-aligned volumes or complex geometry directly. When to use: Real-time rendering of voxel-based data (e.g., medical imaging, voxel art) where the grid is uniform and axis-aligned. When not to use: Non-uniform grids, complex implicit surfaces, or scenes requiring hierarchical acceleration. The method originates from the implementation of a voxel path tracing engine, specifically described in "A Voxel PathTracing Engine" by Jiayu He. The technique is noted for its efficiency, requiring only "33 float points calculations" for the traversal logic, which is comparable to BVH collision detection efficiency. It builds on the principles of Ray-grid traversal, optimizing the cost of executing the traversal by precomputing step deltas and determining the order of axis crossings via t{max} comparisons. The approach is also referenced in the context of Metal-based voxel cone tracing implementations. kakashidinho/VoxelConeTracingMetal, https://github.com/kakashidinho/VoxelConeTracingMetal, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Voxel PathTracing Engine - Jiayu He - GitHub Pages, https://iota11.github.io/2024/01/10/voxelRender/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

head: Voxel Transparency Shader
body: Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters is a fragment shader technique for rendering voxelized data that combines ray traversal through a 3D texture with screen-space visual effects. It differs from its parent Voxel Ray Marching with Traversal Order Optimization by applying screen-space filters (normal, position, depth, iterations, flat color, and toon) to the final color output rather than relying solely on traversal optimization. It is distinct from the Voxel Visualization Ray Marcher by using these screen filters and a complex lighting model with specular and diffuse directions, rather than a fixed-step traversal with explicit alpha compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin, ray direction, scene data (including worldWidth, time, screenFilter flag, tonemap flag), camera data (prevPosition, prevRotation), previous depth texture, color texture, position texture. Outputs: Final color written to colorTexture, velocity written to velocityTexture, depth written to currentDepthTexture. Data Structures: RayHit: Contains status (int), position (vec3<f32>), normal (vec3<f32>), voxelData (u32), uv (vec2<f32>), worldUV (vec2<f32>), iterations (u32). VoxelData (u32): Packed 32-bit integer. Bits 7–4 store albedoIndex (4 bits). Bits 3–0 store materialIndex (4 bits). Material: Contains emissive (bool), specular (float). SceneData: Contains worldWidth (int), time (float), screenFilter (int), tonemap (int). CameraData: Contains position (vec3<f32>), prevPosition (vec3<f32>), prevRotation (mat4x4<f32>). name: Voxel Visualization Ray Marcher
head: 3D Texture Visualizer, Simple Fragment Shader Path Tracer
body: A fragment shader technique that ray marches through a 3D texture to visualize voxelized data by accumulating color along a ray until opacity saturates or the ray exits the volume. It differs from its parent, Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters, by using a fixed-step march with pre-computed ray origins rather than screen-space filtering. Unlike Voxel Visualization Ray Casting, which relies on pre-computed intersection textures for ray initialization, this method computes the ray direction dynamically from front and back intersection points. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: textureCoordinateFrag (in vec2, fragment screen-space coordinates), textureFront (sampler2D, stores ray origin coordinates), textureBack (sampler2D, stores ray direction endpoints), texture3D (sampler3D, contains the voxelized volume data), cameraPosition (vec3, world-space camera position), and state (int, mipmap level, default 0). Outputs: color (out vec4, final accumulated color). Data Structures Uniforms: STEPLENGTH (float, fixed distance advanced per step, default 0.005), INVSTEPLENGTH (float, computed as 1.0 / STEPLENGTH). Textures: textureFront and textureBack are 2D textures mapping screen fragments to 3D space points, and texture3D is a 3D texture containing voxel colors and alpha. Parameters STEPLENGTH: 0.005. INVSTEPLENGTH: 200.0 (derived). state: 0. cameraPosition: Provided by application. Algorithm 1. Initialize Ray Origin: Check if cameraPosition is inside the unit cube with a margin of 0.2f. If inside, set origin = cameraPosition. Otherwise, sample origin from textureFront using textureCoordinateFrag. Pitfall: The origin must avoid invalid positions; using the front buffer ensures valid ray starting points when the camera is outside the volume. 2. Calculate Total Steps: Sample backPoint from textureBack using textureCoordinateFrag. Compute direction = backPoint - origin. Normalize direction to ensure STEPLENGTH represents a fixed world distance. Compute rayLength = length(direction). Compute numberOfSteps = uint(INVSTEPLENGTH rayLength). 3. Initialize Accumulator: Set color = vec4(0.0). 4. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate step from 0 to numberOfSteps inclusive. Early Exit: If color.a >= 0.99, break the loop. Compute Position: currentPoint = origin + STEPLENGTH float(step) direction. Sample Volume: Scale and bias currentPoint to the [0, 1] range. Sample texture3D at the scaled point using state as the mipmap level. Accumulate Color: Apply alpha compositing c{out} = c{in} + (1.0 - c{in}.a) \times s, where c{in} is the accumulated color, c{in}.a is its alpha, and s is the sampled voxel color. Update color = color + (1.0 - color.a) currentSample. 5. Gamma Correction: Apply sRGB gamma correction to the RGB channels by raising to the power of 1/2.2. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vec3(x, y, z): return (x, y, z) def vec4(r, g, b, a): return (r, g, b, a) def length(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def normalize(v): l = length(v) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) if l > 0 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def sample2d(tex, uv): return vec4(0.0) def sample3d(tex, uv, mip): return vec4(0.0) def isinsideunitcube(pos, margin=0.2): return all(-margin <= c <= 1.0+margin for c in pos) def voxelraymarcher(textureCoordinateFrag, textureFront, textureBack, texture3D, cameraPosition, state=0): STEPLENGTH = 0.005 INVSTEPLENGTH = 1.0 / STEPLENGTH # Step 1: Initialize Ray Origin if isinsideunitcube(cameraPosition, margin=0.2): origin = cameraPosition else: origin = sample2d(textureFront, textureCoordinateFrag)[:3] # Step 2: Calculate Total Steps backPoint = sample2d(textureBack, textureCoordinateFrag)[:3] rawdirection = (backPoint[0]-origin[0], backPoint[1]-origin[1], backPoint[2]-origin[2]) direction = normalize(rawdirection) rayLength = length(rawdirection) numberOfSteps = int(INVSTEPLENGTH rayLength) # Step 3: Initialize Accumulator color = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Step 4: Ray Marching Loop for step in range(numberOfSteps + 1): if color[3] >= 0.99: break currentPoint = (origin[0] + STEPLENGTH step direction[0], origin[1] + STEPLENGTH step direction[1], origin[2] + STEPLENGTH step direction[2]) # Scale and bias to [0, 1] currentPoint = (max(0.0, min(1.0, currentPoint[0])), max(0.0, min(1.0, currentPoint[1])), max(0.0, min(1.0, currentPoint[2]))) currentSample = sample3d(texture3D, currentPoint, state) color = (color[0] + (1.0 - color[3]) currentSample[0], color[1] + (1.0 - color[3]) currentSample[1], color[2] + (1.0 - color[3]) currentSample[2], color[3] + (1.0 - color[3]) currentSample[3]) # Step 5: Gamma Correction color = (pow(color[0], 1.0/2.2), pow(color[1], 1.0/2.2), pow(color[2], 1.0/2.2), color[3]) return color A fragment shader technique that visualizes a 3D voxel grid by casting rays from the camera through a unit cube, using pre-computed front and back intersection textures to determine the ray origin and direction. Unlike traditional mesh rendering which requires draw calls per object, this method holds geometric complexity in 3D voxel textures and renders the entire structure in a single draw call using only a few triangles. It differs from its parent, Voxel Visualization Ray Marcher, by explicitly utilizing pre-computed intersection textures for ray initialization rather than computing intersections or marching from a generic camera position. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) per fragment for the shader state, plus storage for the 3D texture and front/back 2D textures. Performance: Performance depends on STEPLENGTH and ray length. Strengths: Simple implementation, single draw call, works with any 3D texture. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missed details if STEPLENGTH is too large. When to use: Real-time visualization of voxel data where simplicity is preferred over optimization. When not to use: Large volumes with sparse data. Originating from unofficial implementations, this method provides a straightforward approach to rendering voxel data using fragment shaders. It builds on the concept of ray marching through 3D textures, a common technique in volume rendering. name: Voxel Visualization Ray Casting
head: Voxel Ray Casting
body: Voxel Visualization Ray Casting is a fragment shader technique that visualizes a 3D voxel grid by casting rays from the camera through a unit cube, using pre-computed front and back intersection textures to determine the ray origin and direction. Unlike traditional mesh rendering which requires draw calls per object, this method holds geometric complexity in 3D voxel textures and renders the entire structure in a single draw call using only 12 triangles. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: textureFront: A 2D texture (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGB16F) storing the front intersection point of the ray with the unit cube for each screen coordinate. textureBack: A 2D texture (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGB16F) storing the back intersection point of the ray with the unit cube for each screen coordinate. texture3D: A 3D texture containing the voxel data (density, color, material index). textureCoordinateFrag: The current fragment's texture coordinates (screen space UV). cameraPosition: The world-space position of the camera. STEPLENGTH: A constant defining the step size for ray traversal (0.005f). Outputs: Fragment color, depth, and normal data derived from the first voxel intersection. Data Structures: FBO Structure: The front and back textures are generated from a Framebuffer Object (FBO) containing width, height, a textureBuffer (GLRGB16F), and a renderBuffer (GLDEPTHCOMPONENT24). Texture Parameters: GLNEAREST filtering and GLREPEAT wrapping are used for the intersection textures. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Determine the ray origin and direction based on the camera's position relative to the unit cube. If the cameraPosition is inside the unit cube (checked with an epsilon of 0.2f), set the ray origin to cameraPosition. Otherwise, sample the front intersection texture at the current fragment coordinates to get the origin: origin = texture(textureFront, textureCoordinateFrag).xyz. Calculate the direction by sampling the back intersection texture and subtracting the origin: direction = texture(textureBack, textureCoordinateFrag).xyz - origin. 2. Ray Marching: Step along the ray direction using STEPLENGTH. 3. Intersection Test: Sample the texture3D at the current ray position. 4. Termination: If an intersection is found (e.g., non-empty voxel), stop marching and return the color index, depth, and normal data. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. STEPLENGTH = 0.005 EPSILONINSIDE = 0.2 def sample2d(sampler, uv): # Standard 2D texture lookup returning a vec3 return sampler[uv.x][uv.y] # Standard texture sampling def sample3d(sampler, xyz): # Standard 3D texture lookup returning a vec3/vec4 return sampler[xyz] # Standard texture sampling def voxelvisualizationraycasting(textureCoordinateFrag, cameraPosition, textureFront, textureBack, texture3D): # Step 1: Ray Initialization # Check if camera is inside the unit cube [0, 1]^3 isinside = all(0.0 <= c <= 1.0 for c in cameraPosition) # Standard bounds check if isinside: origin = cameraPosition else: origin = sample2d(textureFront, textureCoordinateFrag) backpoint = sample2d(textureBack, textureCoordinateFrag) direction = backpoint - origin direction = normalize(direction) # Normalize for consistent step length # Step 2 & 3: Ray Marching and Intersection currentpos = origin maxsteps = 1000 # Safety limit to prevent infinite loops for i in range(maxsteps): voxeldata = sample3d(texture3D, currentpos) # Check for intersection (e.g., non-empty voxel) if voxeldata.x > 0.0: # Standard active voxel check colorindex = voxeldata.x depth = length(currentpos - origin) normal = normalize(voxeldata.yz) # Standard normal extraction return colorindex, depth, normal currentpos += direction STEPLENGTH # Boundary check if not (0.0 <= currentpos.x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= currentpos.y <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= currentpos.z <= 1.0): break return 0.0, 0.0, vec3(0.0) Parameters: STEPLENGTH: 0.005f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Camera Inside Volume: The method explicitly handles the case where the camera is inside the unit cube by using the camera position as the origin, avoiding incorrect front-face intersections. Precision: The use of GLRGB16F for intersection textures may introduce precision errors in ray origin/direction calculation, potentially causing gaps or artifacts in the voxel visualization. Degenerate Input: If the front/back textures are not correctly generated for the current camera view, rays may miss the volume entirely or intersect incorrectly. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps taken along the ray until an intersection is found or the ray exits the volume. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D voxel texture and the two 2D intersection textures. Performance: Renders complex structures in a single draw call (e.g., 12 triangles for a sign that would otherwise require 891 draw calls for meshes). Strengths: High performance for large voxel datasets; simple geometry (single quad) for rendering. Limitations: Step size is fixed, potentially leading to aliasing or missed thin structures if STEPLENGTH is too large; requires pre-computation of intersection textures. When to use: Real-time visualization of voxel-based environments where geometry is dense and static or semi-static. When not to use: When high-precision ray tracing is required without aliasing, or when the volume is sparse and sparse traversal algorithms would be more efficient. The technique is used in the game Teardown, where it allows for the real-time rendering of destructible voxel environments. The method was implemented in the repository stormouse/voxel-cone-tracing-cs580. The method leverages the efficiency of fragment shaders to replace traditional mesh-based rendering for voxel data. stormouse/voxel-cone-tracing-cs580, https://github.com/stormouse/voxel-cone-tracing-cs580, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Teardown Render Techniques - GitHub Pages, https://zacxalot.github.io/rendering/9-teardown/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Ray Marching with Sector-Based Indexing
head: NoiseSDFCompute Voxel Marching, VoxelScene Ray Marching
body: A ray marching algorithm for rendering voxel scenes that utilizes a sector-based storage layout to index voxels and a bounding box intersection test to step through the volume. It builds on Voxel Raymarching with Screen Filters by organizing voxel data into fixed-size sectors for spatial indexing. Inputs and Outputs Input: ray origin (O), ray direction (D), voxel data array (voxelData), world dimensions (WX, WY, WZ), sector dimensions (SX, SY, SZ), world offset (O{world}), maximum steps (maxSteps), maximum distance (maxDist), minimum step size (minDist). Output: hit distance or miss indicator. Data Structures Voxel data is stored in a flat array of 32-bit unsigned integers (u32). Each u32 word stores the solidity status of 32 voxels as individual bits. The layout is organized into sectors to facilitate spatial indexing. Indexing Logic To determine if a voxel at world position P is solid: 1. Convert world position to voxel coordinates: vx = \lfloor Px - O{world\x} \rfloor, vy = \lfloor Py - O{world\y} \rfloor, vz = \lfloor Pz - O{world\z} \rfloor. 2. Check bounds: if 0 \le vx < WX, 0 \le vy < WY, 0 \le vz < WZ, proceed. 3. Calculate sector index: idx{sector} = \lfloor vz / SZ \rfloor + N{sectors\Z} \times \lfloor vx / SX \rfloor. 4. Calculate local index within the sector: idx{local} = (vz \pmod{SZ}) + SZ \times ((vx \pmod{SX}) + SX \times vy). 5. Calculate global index in the flat array: idx{global} = idx{sector} \times (SX \times SY \times SZ) + idx{local}. 6. Check bit value: \text{solid} = (\text{voxelData}[\lfloor idx{global} / 32 \rfloor] \gg (idx{global} \pmod{32})) \& 1. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize totalDist = 0.0. 2. Loop i from 0 to maxSteps: a. Calculate pos = O + D \times totalDist. b. Calculate distance to nearest solid voxel (or SDF) from pos. c. If distance < minDist, return hit. d. If totalDist > maxDist, return miss. e. totalDist += distance. Ray-Box Intersection Calculate inverse direction: D{inv} = 1.0 / D. Calculate near and far intersections: near = (B{min} - O) \times D{inv}, far = (B{max} - O) \times D{inv}. Calculate t0 = \max(\max(nearx, neary), nearz) and t1 = \min(\min(farx, fary), farz). If \max(t0, 0.0) > t1, return \infty (miss), else return t0. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelraymarch(origin, direction, voxeldata, worldsize, sectorsize, worldoffset, maxsteps, maxdist, mindist): wx, wy, wz = worldsize sx, sy, sz = sectorsize ox, oy, oz = worldoffset sectorsx = wx // sx sectorsz = wz // sz invdirx = 1.0 / direction[0] invdiry = 1.0 / direction[1] invdirz = 1.0 / direction[2] nearx = (ox - origin[0]) invdirx neary = (oy - origin[1]) invdiry nearz = (oz - origin[2]) invdirz farx = (ox + wx - origin[0]) invdirx fary = (oy + wy - origin[1]) invdiry farz = (oz + wz - origin[2]) invdirz t0 = max(max(nearx, neary), nearz) t1 = min(min(farx, fary), farz) if max(t0, 0.0) > t1: return None totaldist = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if totaldist > maxdist: return None posx = origin[0] + direction[0] totaldist posy = origin[1] + direction[1] totaldist posz = origin[2] + direction[2] totaldist vx = int(posx - ox) vy = int(posy - oy) vz = int(posz - oz) if not (0 <= vx < wx and 0 <= vy < wy and 0 <= vz < wz): return None sectorindex = (vz // sz) + sectorsz (vx // sx) localindex = (vz % sz) + sz ((vx % sx) + sx vy) sectorvolume = sx sy sz globalindex = sectorindex sectorvolume + localindex wordindex = globalindex // 32 bitindex = globalindex % 32 issolid = (voxeldata[wordindex] >> bitindex) & 1 if issolid: return totaldist dist = computedisttosolid(posx, posy, posz, direction, voxeldata, worldsize, sectorsize, worldoffset) if dist < mindist: return totaldist totaldist += dist return None def computedisttosolid(px, py, pz, dir, voxeldata, worldsize, sectorsize, worldoffset): # The source notes state "Calculate dist to nearest solid voxel (or SDF)" without specifying the exact method. # A standard implementation computes the distance to the next voxel boundary along the ray direction. stepx = (1.0 if dir[0] > 0 else 0.0) - (px - worldoffset[0]) stepy = (1.0 if dir[1] > 0 else 0.0) - (py - worldoffset[1]) stepz = (1.0 if dir[2] > 0 else 0.0) - (pz - worldoffset[2]) return min(stepx / dir[0], stepy / dir[1], stepz / dir[2]) Parameters WORLD\SIZE\X, WORLD\SIZE\Y, WORLD\SIZE\Z: 256. SECTOR\SIZE\X: 16, SECTOR\SIZE\Y: 256, SECTOR\SIZE\Z: 16. WORLD\OFFSET\X: -128, WORLD\OFFSET\Y: 0, WORLD\OFFSET\Z: -128. maxSteps: 128. maxDist: 100.0. minDist: 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision errors may accumulate over many steps; using double precision for totalDist is recommended. Zero direction components cause division by zero in D{inv}; clamp or handle axis-aligned rays explicitly. Out-of-bounds voxel coordinates must be rejected before indexing to prevent array overflows. Time complexity is O(maxSteps) per ray, bounded by the maximum iteration count. Memory complexity is O(WX \times WY \times WZ / 32) for the voxel data array. Sector-based indexing improves cache locality for spatially coherent rays. Binary voxel data limits shading to simple hit/miss queries. Distance calculation requires an SDF or neighbor search, which is not detailed in the source. It is suitable for real-time rendering of binary voxel scenes where memory bandwidth is a constraint. It is not suitable for scenes requiring complex shading, transparency, or non-binary voxel data. The method is documented in an open-source repository. It is part of a suite of voxel rendering techniques aimed at efficient real-time rendering of voxel worlds. name: Tiled Ray Marching with Grid Sampling
head: Python-loop renderer, Tiled rendering
body: Renders a single view of a 3D volume by generating rays, sampling density via gridsample, and accumulating attenuation, supporting tiling to manage memory usage for large images. It differs from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the ray traversal logic from the sampling mechanism, using a dense coordinate grid and GPU-accelerated interpolation (gridsample) rather than explicit voxel traversal or sparse data structures. Unlike Voxel Ray Marching with Traversal Order Optimization which optimizes traversal order, this method optimizes memory footprint through spatial tiling. Inputs: Camera view matrix (camera-to-world or world-to-camera). Volume geometry transform (ijk2ras) mapping voxel indices to world space. Volume density tensor of shape (C, W, H, D) or (1, C, W, H, D). Image dimensions H \times W. Parameters: raysamples (int), tileh, tilew (int), usebeerlambert (bool), densityfactor (float), margin (float, default 30.0). Outputs: Rendered color/alpha image. Optional optical depth (\tau). Data Structures: dirscam: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) storing normalized camera-space view directions. dirsijk: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) storing world-space directions transformed to IJK space. originijk: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) storing camera position in IJK space. ijk: Tensor of shape (H, W, \text{ray\samples}, 3) storing sample coordinates in IJK space. Steps: 1. Initialize Camera Directions: Compute vertical field of view (fov) to populate dirscam. Directions are normalized. 2. Extract Camera Pose: Determine if the input cameramatrix is camera-to-world or world-to-camera by checking the norm of the translation vector. If the norm is < 1.0, invert the matrix to obtain camera-to-world. Extract rotation R{cam} and position P{cam} from the camera-to-world matrix. 3. Compute Volume Bounds: Generate 8 corners of the volume bounding box in IJK space: (0,0,0) to (W-1, H-1, D-1). Transform corners to RAS (world) space using ijk2ras. Project vectors from P{cam} to each corner along the view direction to find min/max distances. Set near and far clipping planes: \text{near} = \min(\text{distances}) - \text{margin} \text{far} = \max(\text{distances}) + \text{margin} Clamp near to \ge 0.1. 4. Transform to IJK Space: Extract rotation R{ijk} and translation t{ijk} from ijk2ras. Compute scale factor: s = \frac{2.0}{\max(W, H, D) - 1} Transform world-space directions to IJK space: \vec{d}{ijk} = \vec{d}{world} R{ijk}^T Transform camera position to IJK space: P{ijk} = P{cam} R{ijk}^T + t{ijk}. 5. Generate Sample Coordinates: Create depth values along the ray: \text{depths}i = \text{near} + (\text{far} - \text{near}) \frac{i}{\text{ray\samples} - 1}, \quad i \in [0, \text{ray\samples}-1] Compute IJK coordinates for all samples for all pixels: \text{ijk}{h,w,i} = s \cdot (P{ijk,h,w} + \vec{d}{ijk,h,w} \cdot \text{depths}i) - 1 Resulting shape: (H, W, \text{ray\samples}, 3). 6. Tiled Rendering Loop: If image dimensions exceed 2 \times \text{tile\h} \times 2 \times \text{tile\w}, iterate over tiles (th, tw). For each tile, extract the corresponding sub-grid of ijk coordinates. 7. Density Sampling: Prepare density tensor for gridsample by adding batch/channel dimensions if necessary, resulting in shape (1, C, W, H, D). Sample density using bilinear/trilinear interpolation: \text{dens}{tile} = \text{grid\sample}(\text{density}, \text{ijk}{tile}, \text{align\corners}=\text{False}). 8. Accumulation: Compute step size: \Delta = \frac{\text{far} - \text{near}}{\text{ray\samples}}. Mode A: Beer-Lambert Law (usebeerlambert=True): Compute optical depth: \tau = \sum{i=0}^{\text{ray\samples}-1} \text{dens}{tile}[i] \cdot \Delta. Apply Poisson noise to \tau if applypoisson is True. Return 1 - e^{-\tau} (transmission) or \tau. Mode B: Cumulative Product (usebeerlambert=False): Compute per-sample contribution: di = \text{density\factor} \cdot \frac{\text{dens}{tile}[i]}{\text{ray\samples}}. Compute transmission: Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - dj). Compute weight: wi = di \cdot Ti. Compute alpha: \alpha = 1 - \prod{j=0}^{\text{ray\samples}-1} (1 - dj). Return weighted sum normalized by sum of weights. 9. Scatter Channels: If scatter is defined, process scatter channels separately using DepthAwareScatter and concatenate with non-scatter results. 10. Composite: Concatenate tile outputs along height and width axes to form the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def tiledraymarchingwithgridsampling( density: torch.Tensor, cameramatrix: torch.Tensor, ijk2ras: torch.Tensor, h: int, w: int, raysamples: int, tileh: int = 256, tilew: int = 256, usebeerlambert: bool = True, densityfactor: float = 1.0, margin: float = 30.0) -> torch.Tensor: """ Renders a volume using tiled ray marching with grid sampling. """ device = density.device dtype = density.dtype # 1. Prepare Density Tensor for gridsample # gridsample expects (N, C, H, W) or (N, C, D, H, W) # density input is assumed (C, W, H, D) or (1, C, W, H, D) if density.ndim == 4: density = density.unsqueeze(0) # Add batch dim # Ensure shape is (1, C, W, H, D) assert density.ndim == 5, "Density must be 5D" # 2. Extract Camera Info # Determine if cameramatrix is world-to-camera or camera-to-world testpos = cameramatrix[:,:3, 3] translationnorm = torch.norm(testpos, dim=1) needsinvert = translationnorm < 1.0 camtoworld = torch.inverse(cameramatrix) camposras = torch.where(needsinvert.view(-1, 1), camtoworld[:,:3, 3], cameramatrix[:,:3, 3]) viewdircam = torch.where(needsinvert.view(-1, 1), camtoworld[:,:3, 2], cameramatrix[:,:3, 2]) # Normalize view directions viewdircam = viewdircam / torch.norm(viewdircam, dim=1, keepdim=True) # 3. Compute Near/Far # Get volume shape,, volw, volh, vold = density.shape cornersijk = torch.tensor([ [0, 0, 0], [volw-1, 0, 0], [0, volh-1, 0], [volw-1, volh-1, 0], [0, 0, vold-1], [volw-1, 0, vold-1], [0, volh-1, vold-1], [volw-1, volh-1, vold-1] ], dtype=dtype, device=device) cornershomog = torch.cat([cornersijk, torch.ones(8, 1, device=device)], dim=1) cornersras = (ijk2ras @ cornershomog.T).T[:,:3] tocorners = cornersras.unsqueeze(0) - camposras.unsqueeze(1) distances = torch.sum(tocorners viewdircam.unsqueeze(1), dim=2) near = torch.min(distances, dim=1).values - margin far = torch.max(distances, dim=1).values + margin near = torch.clamp(near, min=0.1) # 4. Transform to IJK Space Rijk = ijk2ras[:3,:3] tijk = ijk2ras[:3, 3] scale = 2.0 / (max(volw, volh, vold) - 1) # dirscam is (H, W, 3), need to transform each pixel's direction # viewdircam is (B, 3), assume B=1 for single view or broadcast # For simplicity, assume single camera for this pseudocode structure matching S1 dirsworld = viewdircam.unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, hw, -1).reshape(h, w, 3) dirsijk = dirsworld @ Rijk.T camposijk = camposras[0] @ Rijk.T + tijk # Assuming single camera # 5. Generate Sample Coordinates depths = near[0] + (far[0] - near[0]) torch.linspace(0, 1, raysamples, device=device) # depths shape: (raysamples,) # originijk shape: (1, 1, 3) originijk = camposijk.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) # dirsijk shape: (H, W, 3) # depths shape: (raysamples,) # ijk shape: (H, W, raysamples, 3) ijk = scale (originijk + dirsijk.unsqueeze(2) depths.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(3)) - 1 # 6. Tiled Rendering # Determine tile bounds tileheff = tileh if h > 2 tileh else h tileweff = tilew if w > 2 tilew else w outcolor = torch.zeros(h, w, 3, dtype=dtype, device=device) outalpha = torch.zeros(h, w, dtype=dtype, device=device) for ty in range(0, h, tileheff): for tx in range(0, w, tileweff): tyend = min(ty + tileheff, h) txend = min(tx + tileweff, w) # Extract tile coordinates ijktile = ijk[ty:tyend, tx:txend,:,:] # (tileh, tilew, raysamples, 3) # Sample density # gridsample expects normalized coordinates in [-1, 1] # density shape: (1, C, W, H, D) # ijktile shape: (Ht, Wt, S, 3) -> (Ht, Wt, S, 3) # gridsample input: (N, C, H, W) or (N, C, D, H, W) # We need to reshape for gridsample # gridsample takes (N, Hin, Win, 2) or (N, Din, Hin, Win, 3) # Here density is (1, C, W, H, D). We treat W,H,D as spatial dims. # gridsample expects coordinates in last dim. # Reshape density to (1, C, D, H, W) if necessary? # S1 says densityb shape (1, C, W, H, D). # gridsample with aligncorners=False maps [-1,1] to [0, size-1]. denstile = F.gridsample( density, ijktile.unsqueeze(0), # Add batch dim: (1, Ht, Wt, S, 3) aligncorners=False, mode='trilinear') # denstile shape: (1, C, S, Ht, Wt) -> transpose to (1, C, Ht, Wt, S) denstile = denstile.squeeze(0).permute(0, 3, 4, 1, 2) # (C, Ht, Wt, S) ? # Actually gridsample output is (N, C, Hout, Wout) or (N, C, Dout, Hout, Wout) # Input coords: (N, Hout, Wout, 3) or (N, Dout, Hout, Wout, 3) # If density is (1, C, W, H, D), gridsample treats W,H,D as spatial. # Output shape: (1, C, S, Ht, Wt) if we pass (1, Ht, Wt, S, 3)? No. # Let's follow S1 logic: denstile = gridsample(densityb, coordstile) # S1 implies denstile has shape compatible with accumulation. # Simplified accumulation logic based on S1 formulas stepsize = (far[0] - near[0]) / raysamples if usebeerlambert: tau = torch.sum(denstile stepsize, dim=-1) # Sum over samples # Apply Poisson noise here if needed transmission = torch.exp(-tau) color = 1.0 - transmission alpha = 1.0 - transmission else: d = densityfactor denstile / raysamples # Cumprod trans = torch.cumprod(1.0 - d, dim=-1) weight = d trans alpha = 1.0 - torch.prod(1.0 - d, dim=-1) # Weighted sum wsum = torch.sum(weight, dim=-1) color = torch.sum(weight, dim=-1) / (wsum + 1e-6) # Store results outcolor[ty:tyend, tx:txend] = color outalpha[ty:tyend, tx:txend] = alpha return outcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point errors in coordinate transformation can cause sampling artifacts at volume boundaries. Using aligncorners=False in gridsample maps coordinates to the center of pixels, which may require careful scaling. Boundary Conditions: The margin parameter ensures rays intersect the volume. If margin is too small, rays may miss the volume entirely, resulting in black images. Memory: Large images require tiling. If tileh and tilew are too small, overhead increases; if too large, memory overflow occurs. Accelerates the sampling step of vcrendertifxyz surface rendering by offloading trilinear sampling and pyramid generation to a CUDA or ROCm GPU, while maintaining byte-identical output to the CPU reference implementation. It differs from native integration by using LDPRELOAD interposition to intercept the CPU sampling function, allowing the existing C++ renderer to remain unchanged. Choose this when you need GPU acceleration for sampling without modifying the core rendering pipeline. The Naive PyTorch Baseline Renderer is a reference implementation for differentiable rendering that processes all primitives for every pixel sequentially using standard PyTorch tensor operations. It serves as a performance baseline to demonstrate the efficiency gains of optimized CUDA implementations, which utilize tile-based culling, per-pixel parallelism, and FP16 optimization. Unlike its siblings, it lacks spatial optimization, tile-based binning, or specialized kernels, resulting in significant memory and computational overhead. Choose this for debugging and correctness verification, not for production performance. Iterates over each tile, then each ray through the tile, then each ray step. If the neighbors of the current step are not located on the local node, it fetches the required macro(s) from other nodes. If the neighbors of the current step have not been shaded, it shades them. This variant is designed for distributed memory systems where volume data is partitioned across multiple compute nodes. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot \text{ray\samples}) for sampling and accumulation. Tiling does not change asymptotic complexity but adds overhead for tile management. Memory Complexity: O(\text{tile\h} \cdot \text{tile\w} \cdot \text{ray\samples}) for intermediate tensors during tiling. Without tiling, O(H \cdot W \cdot \text{ray\samples}). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with image resolution and number of samples. Tiling allows rendering of images larger than available GPU memory. Strengths: Simple implementation using standard PyTorch operations; leverages GPU-accelerated gridsample for interpolation; memory-efficient via tiling. Limitations: Not optimized for sparse volumes; interpolation artifacts may occur if raysamples is low; tiling overhead for small images. When to use: When using dense volume data and PyTorch-based differentiable rendering pipelines. When not to use: For sparse volumes where traversal-based methods are more efficient; when strict real-time performance is required without GPU acceleration. Originated in the context of differentiable volume rendering using PyTorch, specifically in the flashdrr project. The method leverages standard computer graphics techniques (ray generation, coordinate transformation) combined with deep learning primitives (gridsample) to enable gradient-based optimization of volume parameters. The tiling strategy is a common technique in image processing to manage memory constraints. pcarnah/flashdrr, https://github.com/pcarnah/flashdrr, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DTIC ADA236632: Taxonomy and Algorithms for Volume Rendering on Multicomputers, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA236632, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Opt-in GPU Sampling for tifxyz Rendering
head: vc_render_tifxyz GPU sampling
body: This method accelerates the sampling step of vcrendertifxyz surface rendering by offloading trilinear sampling and pyramid generation to a CUDA or ROCm GPU, while maintaining byte-identical output to the CPU reference implementation. It differs from native integration by using LDPRELOAD interposition to intercept the CPU sampling function, allowing the existing C++ renderer to remain unchanged. The method consists of two phases: a CPU dump phase and a GPU sampling phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A surface directory, a volume path (OME-Zarr format), and environment variables controlling execution. Output: A Zarr directory containing pyramid levels L0–L5, byte-identical to the CPU-only render. Data Structures: The shim intercepts specific C++ symbols to extract rendering geometry. The intercepted data consists of tile sample positions, defined as base points and step directions for each tile. These are dumped to a directory specified by RENDERSHIMDIR. Parameters: RENDERGPU: Environment variable. Set to 1 to enable the GPU path; otherwise, the normal CPU render runs. RENDERSHIMDIR: Environment variable specifying the directory where the shim dumps tile sample positions. PyTorch: Required dependency for rendergpu.py, must be built with CUDA or ROCm support. Steps: 1. CPU Dump Phase: The CPU renderer (vcrendertifxyz) is executed with LDPRELOAD pointing to rendershim.so. The shim intercepts the sampleTileSlices function (specifically the u8 specialization) and VcDataset::writeChunkSkipEmpty by mangled name. Instead of performing actual sampling, it dumps the tile sample positions (base points and step directions) to the directory specified by RENDERSHIMDIR. The vccore library must be a shared library to allow this interposition. 2. GPU Sampling Phase: The Python script rendergpu.py reads the dumped sample positions and the volume data. Memory Management: Volume chunks are kept in GPU memory across surfaces to optimize I/O. Computation: The GPU performs trilinear sampling and pyramid generation using fp32 arithmetic to reproduce the CPU sampler's output exactly. Output: The GPU-generated pyramid levels (L0–L5) are written into the zarr directory structure created by the initial C++ run. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import os import torch import numpy as np def rungpusampling(shimdir, zarroutput, volumepath): # 1. Load dumped sample positions from shim directory tiledata = [] for filename in sorted(os.listdir(shimdir)): filepath = os.path.join(shimdir, filename) # Parse dump files containing base points and step directions. # The exact binary/text format is implementation-specific to rendershim.so. tiledata.append(parsedumpfile(filepath)) if not tiledata: raise ValueError("No tile data found. Shim dump may be empty or signatures changed.") # 2. Load volume chunks into GPU memory chunks = [] for chunkfile in sorted(os.listdir(volumepath)): chunks.append(np.fromfile(chunkfile, dtype=np.uint8)) volumenp = np.concatenate(chunks) volumechunks = torch.fromnumpy(volumenp).to(torch.float32).cuda() # 3. Perform trilinear sampling and pyramid generation on GPU pyramidlevels = [] for level in range(6): # L0 to L5 outputshape = calculateoutputshape(tiledata, level) outputtensor = torch.zeros(outputshape, dtype=torch.float32, device="cuda") # Custom CUDA/ROCm kernel iterates over all sample points. # For each point (x, y, z): # ix, iy, iz = floor(x), floor(y), floor(z) # fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz # v000 = volume[ix, iy, iz], v100 = volume[ix+1, iy, iz],... # val = (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz)v000 + fx(1-fy)(1-fz)v100 + (1-fx)fy(1-fz)v010 + fxfy(1-fz)v110 + # (1-fx)(1-fy)fzv001 + fx(1-fy)fzv101 + (1-fx)fyfzv011 + fxfyfzv111 # outputtensor[...] = val # The kernel is launched with tiledata and volumechunks as arguments. # Sources do not specify the exact kernel launch syntax; standard PyTorch CUDA kernel launch is used. # Pyramid generation for levels > 0 uses average pooling. if level > 0: kernelsize = 2 level # Reshape to apply pooling, compute mean over kernel, reshape back # Standard downsampling operation outputtensor = torch.nn.functional.avgpool3d(outputtensor, kernelsize=kernelsize, stride=kernelsize) pyramidlevels.append(outputtensor) # 4. Write results to Zarr directory structure for levelidx, leveldata in enumerate(pyramidlevels): npdata = leveldata.cpu().numpy() leveldir = os.path.join(zarroutput, f"level{levelidx}") os.makedirs(leveldir, existok=True) import zarr z = zarr.open(os.path.join(leveldir, "data.zarr"), mode="w") z[:] = npdata def parsedumpfile(filepath): # Implementation depends on the exact dump format. with open(filepath, 'rb') as f: data = f.read() # Unpack data based on known structure. pass def calculateoutputshape(tiledata, targetlevel): # The shape depends on the number of tiles and the downsampling factor. numtiles = len(tiledata) # Assume a 2D grid of tiles for simplicity. return (numtiles, 1, 1) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Symbol Signature Changes: If the signatures of the intercepted symbols (sampleTileSlices<u8> and VcDataset::writeChunkSkipEmpty) change, the dump output will be empty, and rendergpu.py will stop with an error. It does not produce a wrong render. Shared Library Requirement: The shim requires vccore to be a shared library (the default) to allow LDPRELOAD interposition. Precision: The GPU uses fp32 arithmetic to ensure byte-identical output with the CPU sampler. Time Complexity: Most GPU time is spent reading volume chunks from disk; sampling and pyramid generation take about 5 seconds for 10 wraps. Memory Complexity: Volume chunks are kept in GPU memory across surfaces to optimize I/O. Measured Performance: Radeon AI PRO R9700: Rendering 10 PHerc0800 wraps took 28–47 seconds with the GPU tool compared to 64–82 seconds with the stock CPU render. AMD Instinct MI50: The median time for 20 rounds of 10 wraps was 49.5 seconds (range 35.9–70.0) for the GPU path versus 64.2 seconds (range 48.3–104.5) for the CPU path. RTX 3080: Rendering wraps 030-035 took 8.7/6.3/5.8 seconds across three rounds compared to 14.1/12.1/13.9 seconds for CPU. Accuracy: Parity checks confirmed byte-identical output at all six pyramid levels (L0–L5) for 20 of 20 PHerc0800 wraps on an AMD Instinct MI50. On an RTX 3080, 150 tiles of wrap w030 were byte-identical to the CPU render at L0. Strengths: Significant speedup on GPU hardware; byte-identical output to CPU reference. Limitations: Relies on LDPRELOAD interposition, which is a workaround that may break if symbol signatures change. Requires PyTorch with CUDA or ROCm support. This method was developed by phippsrtyler and submitted as a pull request to the Vesuvius Challenge monorepo (ScrollPrize/villa) in October 2026. It is used for rendering PHerc0800 wraps of the Villa dei Papiri scrolls. The technique was introduced to accelerate the vcrendertifxyz surface rendering process, which is a critical step between fitted surface generation and final visualization. volume-cartographer: opt-in GPU sampling for vcrendertifxyz (scripts/rendergpu), https://github.com/ScrollPrize/villa/pull/2225, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Naive PyTorch Baseline Renderer
head: Sequential CPU loop, Standard tensor operations renderer
body:
The Naive PyTorch Baseline Renderer is a reference implementation for differentiable rendering that processes all primitives for every pixel sequentially using standard PyTorch tensor operations. It serves as a performance baseline to demonstrate the efficiency gains of optimized CUDA implementations, which utilize tile-based culling, per-pixel parallelism, and FP16 optimization. Unlike its siblings, it lacks spatial optimization, tile-based binning, or specialized kernels, resulting in significant memory and computational overhead. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of N primitives as input, where each primitive i is defined by parameters \{(xi, yi, si, 	hetai, 
ui, ci)\}{i=1}^N. Here, (xi, yi) is the center, si is the scale, 	hetai is the rotation angle, 
ui is a density parameter, and ci is the base color. A mask texture Mi is associated with each primitive. The method outputs a rendered image tensor I of size H{canvas} 	imes W{canvas}. Data Structures: The implementation uses two 2D tensors X and Y of shape (H{canvas}, W{canvas}) to represent the normalized coordinates of each pixel. It maintains two accumulator tensors I (image) and T (transparency), both of shape (H{canvas}, W{canvas}), initialized to zeros and ones respectively. During execution, full-canvas tensors are allocated for \Delta x, \Delta y, u, v, and mask for each primitive. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate coordinate grids X, Y over the canvas dimensions H{canvas}, W{canvas} using torch.meshgrid. 2. Initialize the output image I to zeros and the transparency mask T to ones. 3. Iterate through each primitive i from 0 to N-1. 4. Compute displacement vectors: \Delta x = X - xi and \Delta y = Y - yi. 5. Transform coordinates to the primitive's local space by rotating and scaling \Delta x, \Delta y by angle 	hetai and scale si to obtain local coordinates u, v. 6. Sample the primitive's mask texture Mi at (u, v) using torch.gridsample to get the mask value. 7. Compute opacity \alphai and color ci using the defined formulas. 8. Update the image and transparency using alpha compositing: I \leftarrow I + T \cdot \alphai \cdot ci and T \leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai). 9. Return the final image I. Formulas: \alphai = \alpha{max} \cdot \sigma(
ui) \cdot 	ext{mask} ci = \sigma(ci) where \sigma denotes the sigmoid function, \alpha{max} is a maximum opacity constant, and 	ext{mask} is the sampled texture value. Parameters: The parameter \alpha{max} controls the maximum opacity scaling. Typical values for \alpha{max} are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method allocates full-canvas tensors for every primitive in the loop, which causes massive memory allocation. For 1000 primitives on a 512 	imes 512 canvas, this results in approximately 5 GB of memory allocation at FP32 precision due to intermediate tensors \Delta x, \Delta y, u, v, and mask. Every primitive is evaluated at all H 	imes W pixels, even if the primitive contributes nothing to the final image, yielding 262 million wasted evaluations for the 1000-primitive example. The Python for loop prevents primitive-level parallelism and forces repeated kernel launches, significantly slowing down execution compared to GPU-optimized approaches. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def naivepytorchrenderer(primitives, Hcanvas, Wcanvas, alphamax=1.0): # 1. Create meshgrid X, Y over canvas dimensions y, x = torch.meshgrid( torch.linspace(-1, 1, Hcanvas, device=primitives[0]['x'].device), torch.linspace(-1, 1, Wcanvas, device=primitives[0]['x'].device), indexing='ij') # 2. Initialize output image I to zeros and transparency mask T to ones I = torch.zeros((Hcanvas, Wcanvas), device=primitives[0]['x'].device) T = torch.ones((Hcanvas, Wcanvas), device=primitives[0]['x'].device) N = len(primitives) # 3. Loop i from 0 to N-1 for i in range(N): prim = primitives[i] xi, yi = prim['x'], prim['y'] si, thetai = prim['s'], prim['theta'] nui, ci = prim['nu'], prim['c'] Mi = prim['masktexture'] # 4. Compute deltas ∆x = X - xi, ∆y = Y - yi dx = x - xi dy = y - yi # 5. Rotate/scale deltas by primitive angle θi and scale si to get u, v costheta, sintheta = torch.cos(thetai), torch.sin(thetai) u = (dx costheta + dy sintheta) / si v = (-dx sintheta + dy costheta) / si # 6. Sample mask from primitive's mask texture Mi at (u, v) using torch.gridsample grid = torch.stack([u, v], dim=-1).unsqueeze(0) mask = F.gridsample(Mi, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros', aligncorners=True).squeeze() # 7. Compute opacity αi = αmax · σ(νi) · mask and color ci = σ(ci) alphai = alphamax torch.sigmoid(nui) mask ci = torch.sigmoid(ci) # 8. Update image I = I + T · αi · ci and transparency T = T · (1 - αi) I = I + T alphai ci T = T (1 - alphai) # 9. Return I return I The time complexity is O(N 	imes H 	imes W) because every primitive is evaluated at all H 	imes W pixels. The memory complexity is O(N 	imes H 	imes W) per iteration because each primitive creates full-canvas tensors for intermediate calculations. The naive version is 30-50x slower than the optimized CUDA implementation. Its strengths include a simple implementation using standard PyTorch operations and its role as a clear baseline for comparison. Its limitations are massive memory allocation, sequential processing, lack of spatial culling, and generic interpolation operations. It should only be used for small-scale testing or as a reference for correctness against optimized renderers. It should not be used for large scenes, high-resolution images, or any performance-critical application. The Naive PyTorch Baseline Renderer was introduced in the paper "DiffBMP: Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives". It was designed to demonstrate the efficiency of a custom CUDA implementation by comparing it against a straightforward PyTorch-based renderer that uses standard tensor operations without tile-based culling or specialized kernels. The paper highlights the major bottlenecks of this approach, including no spatial culling, massive memory allocation, sequential loops, and generic operations.
