name: Cross-Dimensional Residual Frequency Compensation
head: Frequency-domain compensation scheme, High-frequency residual injection
body: Cross-Dimensional Residual Frequency Compensation is a frequency-domain optimization technique designed to mitigate the inherent blurring artifacts caused by Gaussian kernels in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the limitation of spatial-domain optimization, which struggles to fit high-frequency details, by extracting high-frequency components from the rendering residual and injecting them directly into primitive attributes. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ground truth image I{gt}, current rendered image I{render}, scaling coefficient \lambda, spatial weighting term Wi. Outputs: Update amount \Delta pi for primitive attributes. Data Structures I{gt}: 2D tensor of ground truth pixel values. I{render}: 2D tensor of rendered pixel values. R: Spatial residual map, computed as I{gt} - I{render}. \hat{R}{high}: Complex-valued frequency domain tensor representing high-frequency components. \Delta pi: Update vector for primitive i. Bit packing and exact memory layouts: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps 1. Compute the spatial residual map R by subtracting the rendered image from the ground truth image: R = I{gt} - I{render}. 2. Transform the residual map into the frequency domain using the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT): \hat{R} = \mathcal{F}(R). 3. Apply a high-pass filter to isolate high-frequency components, resulting in \hat{R}{high}: \hat{R}{high} = \text{HighPass}(\hat{R}). 4. Scale the high-frequency components by the frequency scaling coefficient \lambda: \hat{R}{scaled} = \lambda \cdot \hat{R}{high}. 5. Distribute the scaled frequency energy to the spatial locations corresponding to primitive i using the normalized spatial weighting term Wi: \hat{U}i = \hat{R}{scaled} \cdot Wi. 6. Transform the weighted frequency update back to the spatial domain using the Inverse Fast Fourier Transform (IFFT) to calculate the update amount \Delta pi: \Delta pi = \mathcal{F}^{-1}(\hat{U}i). 7. Apply \Delta pi to update the primitive attributes. Formulas Residual extraction: \hat{R}{high} = \text{HighPass}(\mathcal{F}(I{gt} - I{render})) (9). Primitive update: \Delta pi = \mathcal{F}^{-1}(\lambda \cdot \hat{R}{high} \cdot Wi) (10). Symbol Definitions I{gt}: Ground truth image. I{render}: Current rendered image. \mathcal{F}: Fast Fourier Transform. \mathcal{F}^{-1}: Inverse Fast Fourier Transform. \text{HighPass}(\cdot): High-pass filtering operation isolating fine texture details. \lambda: Frequency scaling coefficient controlling the intensity of frequency injection. Wi: Normalized spatial weighting term distributing frequency energy to corresponding spatial locations for primitive i. \Delta pi: Update amount for primitive attributes. Parameters \lambda (also referred to as \lambdaA in implementation): Frequency scaling coefficient. Typical value: 1.0. This value balances high-frequency detail injection and numerical stability. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The method relies on FFT/IFFT operations which are sensitive to numerical precision. Boundary Conditions: The high-pass filter must be defined to avoid removing essential low-frequency structure while targeting blurring artifacts. Weighting Normalization: Wi must be properly normalized to ensure energy conservation during the projection back to spatial domain. Gaussian Blurring: The method specifically targets the inherent blurring artifacts of Gaussian kernels by injecting high-frequency energy directly into primitive attributes via frequency domain compensation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.fft def crossdimensionalresidualfrequencycompensation(Igt, Irender, lambdaval, Wi): """ Computes the update deltapi for a primitive based on frequency-domain residual compensation. Args: Igt (torch.Tensor): Ground truth image tensor. Irender (torch.Tensor): Rendered image tensor. lambdaval (float): Frequency scaling coefficient (e.g., 1.0). Wi (torch.Tensor): Normalized spatial weighting term for primitive i. Returns: torch.Tensor: Update amount deltapi. """ # Step 1: Compute spatial residual R = Igt - Irender # Step 2: Transform to frequency domain Rhat = torch.fft.fft2(R) # Step 3: Apply high-pass filter # The source does not specify the exact high-pass filter implementation. # A standard zero-centered high-pass mask is applied here. H, W = Rhat.shape[-2], Rhat.shape[-1] freqh = torch.fft.fftfreq(H) freqw = torch.fft.fftfreq(W) FreqH, FreqW = torch.meshgrid(freqh, freqw, indexing='ij') distance = torch.sqrt(FreqH2 + FreqW2) maxdist = distance.max() mask = (distance > 0.1 maxdist).to(Rhat.dtype) Rhathigh = Rhat mask # Step 4: Scale by lambda Rhatscaled = lambdaval Rhathigh # Step 5: Distribute energy using spatial weighting Wi # Formula (10) multiplies Wi directly in the frequency domain. Uhati = Rhatscaled Wi # Step 6: Inverse transform to spatial domain deltapi = torch.fft.ifft2(Uhati).real return deltapi A spatial-domain loss that modulates edge weights based on frequency information. Choose this when spatial edge preservation is prioritized over spectral detail injection. Measured Performance: In experiments on NVIDIA RTX 4090, ACE-GS (which includes this method) achieved superior rendering quality (SSIM, PSNR) and reduced training duration compared to baselines. Strengths: Directly addresses Gaussian kernel blurring by injecting high-frequency energy where spatial gradients may be insufficient. Limitations: Relies on the effectiveness of the high-pass filter and spatial weighting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the paper "ACE-GS: Acing the Trade-off with Accurate, Compact and Efficient 3D Gaussian Splatting". It is part of the ACE-GS framework, which aims to balance accuracy, compactness, and efficiency in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The approach builds on the observation that Gaussian kernels inherently blur high-frequency details, which are difficult to optimize in the spatial domain alone. By leveraging frequency-domain analysis, the method compensates for this limitation. The implementation is built upon the 3DGS codebase using PyTorch. name: Resolution Adaptation
head: Adaptive Resolution, Dynamic Resolution, Resolution Scaling
body: Resolution Adaptation refers to a family of techniques that modulate the spatial sampling density or grid resolution during volume rendering to balance visual fidelity against computational cost. It solves the problem of fixed-performance bottlenecks by dynamically adjusting the rendering budget based on real-time metrics such as frame time, training iteration, or spatial complexity. Unlike static resolution methods, this family adapts the "anchor points" or sampling rates continuously or periodically, distinguishing it from siblings like Random Pixel Subsampling which alters ray count rather than spatial resolution, and Two-stage NeRF Rendering which uses coarse-to-fine refinement rather than global or local resolution scaling. The core mechanism shared by all children is the deviation from a fixed, uniform sampling strategy. Instead of casting a constant number of rays or samples per pixel/ray, the method computes a metric (such as gradient magnitude, rendering error, or temporal difference) and uses it to modulate the sampling rate or resolution. Mathematically, this often involves a control loop: 1. Metric Evaluation: Compute a scalar value M representing local complexity or error. 2. Adaptation: Adjust a parameter P (step size \Delta t, resolution R, or sampling probability w) based on M. 3. Rendering/Training: Execute the volume integral or loss computation with the adjusted parameter. Common adaptation laws include: Step Size Adaptation: \Delta t \propto \frac{1}{M} or \Delta t = \min(\Delta t{max}, \max(\Delta t{min}, \frac{k}{M})). Resolution Control: R{new} = R{old} + \alpha \cdot (t{target} - t{actual}) or threshold-based switching. Probability Weighting: wi \propto Mi for importance sampling. All methods in this family aim to maintain visual fidelity while reducing the total number of volume queries. Level-of-detail (LOD) methods maintain interactive frame rates during viewpoint interaction by dynamically changing the resolution of the rendering to match the available computational budget. Unlike static pre-computed LOD hierarchies, these methods adapt the sampling density or geometric approximation in real-time based on rendering performance metrics. This approach solves the problem of high computational cost in volume rendering by trading visual fidelity for speed during interactive manipulation, switching to higher quality only when the view is static or when the frame budget allows. This method dynamically adjusts the voxel grid resolution and the active spatial bounding box (AABB) of a neural volume representation during training. It solves the problem of inefficient memory usage and slow convergence by initially training in a low-resolution, coarse space and progressively refining the grid density and spatial extent as the model learns. It differs from static resolution methods by coupling resolution upscaling with alpha mask updates, ensuring that the volume only occupies the space containing visible geometry, thereby pruning empty background space. Dynamic Resolution Adaptation is a runtime technique that adjusts the render viewport reduction factor based on previous frame render time and an allocated time budget to maintain a target frame rate. It solves the problem of performance instability in volume rendering, where small parametric changes (e.g., transfer function modifications) can cause frame rate dips leading to cybersickness. It sets itself apart from static resolution schemes by continuously shifting the "anchor points" between resolution levels based on the gradient of recent frame times, rather than using fixed blending factors. Mixed-resolution multi-volume rendering is a technique where different channels of a multi-volume dataset are rendered at different resolution levels to save memory and reduce sample evaluation. It addresses the inefficiency of applying a uniform high resolution to all channels when some possess lower frequency content or lower visual importance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Level-of-detail (LOD) methods by operating on a per-channel basis within a single ray traversal, rather than switching the entire dataset's resolution or using spatial partitioning for the whole volume. Volume Level-of-Detail (LOD) Rendering is a method that maximizes image quality within user-specified frame rate and system constraints (RAM, texture memory, bandwidth) by adaptively modifying the set of rendered octree cells. It solves the problem of maintaining interactivity for large datasets by dynamically adjusting the resolution of the volume representation based on viewing parameters and hardware limits. Unlike static LOD methods that precompute fixed levels, this approach maintains an "active cut" of the octree, splitting or merging nodes every frame to balance visual fidelity against rendering cost. It differs from sibling methods like Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update by explicitly managing a hierarchical cut of non-leaf nodes rather than just updating alpha masks or global resolution scales. Focus and Context Multiresolution Rendering balances processing capacity between a high-detail focus region and a lower-detail context region to improve interactivity in time-critical applications. It solves the problem of limited hardware resources by decomposing the rendering task into two passes with distinct parameters, explicitly trading seamless integration for speed. The Multiresolution Atlas Buffer (MAB) is an acceleration wrapper for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) in Virtual Reality (VR) that reduces ray density adaptively based on peripheral vision and Head-Mounted Display (HMD) lens distortion, then reconstructs the full-resolution image via compositing. It differs from standard foveated rendering by not requiring high-speed eye-tracking hardware; instead, it leverages the fixed nature of HMD lenses and the non-uniform resolution of the human visual system to create a static, gaze-centered resolution map. Unlike sibling methods that modify the ray traversal itself (e.g., Level-of-detail (LOD) methods) or dynamic volume resolution (Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update), MAB operates as a "bracket" around existing raycasters, modifying ray construction and post-traversal compositing. Combines full-resolution scene elements with low-resolution high-density volume data by rendering the volume to off-screen targets and projecting them onto a quad. Setup two off-screen cameras, one for each eye, updating each frame. Setup two low-resolution render targets (e.g., 200x200) for the cameras. Set up a quad that moves in front of the user. Each frame: Draw the low-resolution render targets for each eye (containing volume data and expensive shaders). Each frame: Draw the scene normally at full resolution (meshes, UI). Each frame: Draw a quad in front of the user and project the low-res renders onto it. High-end: Reduce resolution to 1/2x1/2. Mid/Low-end: Use frame splitting (similar to RDR2), simplified for clouds not intersecting other objects. Resolution adaptation in volume rendering originated from the need to handle large datasets interactively. Early implementations focused on Level-of-Detail (LOD) techniques for unstructured grids and octrees to maintain frame rates during viewpoint changes. With the advent of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and neural volumes, the concept evolved into dynamic resolution updates during training to optimize memory and convergence. In real-time graphics and VR, techniques like Dynamic Resolution Adaptation and Multiresolution Atlas Buffers were developed to manage strict frame time budgets and leverage human visual system properties. name: Level-of-detail (LOD) methods
head: Adaptive resolution rendering, Dynamic LOD, Dynamic Level-of-Detail (LOD) Framework, Interactive Rendering via Level of Detail (LOD), Sample-Based LOD
body: Level-of-detail (LOD) methods maintain interactive frame rates during viewpoint interaction by dynamically changing the resolution of the rendering to match the available computational budget. Unlike static pre-computed LOD hierarchies, these methods adapt the sampling density or geometric approximation in real-time based on rendering performance metrics. This approach solves the problem of high computational cost in volume rendering by trading visual fidelity for speed during interactive manipulation, switching to higher quality only when the view is static or when the frame budget allows. The core mechanism involves generating reduced-resolution approximations of the original scalar field or geometry to maintain responsive frame rates. The method operates by monitoring the time taken to render the previous frame and adjusting the complexity of the current frame accordingly. Inputs: The original high-resolution scalar field f defined on domain D, the target frame time \text{TargetTime}, and the measured render time of the previous frame \text{RenderTime}. Outputs: A reduced-resolution approximation \bar{f} defined on a smaller domain \bar{D} \subseteq D, or a coarser sampling representation, such that |\bar{f} - f| \le \epsilon. The implementation typically relies on one of two simplification strategies, which dictate the data structure layout: 1. Sample-based simplification: Uses the original geometry (e.g., tetrahedral mesh) but computes an approximate volume integral. The data structure remains the full mesh, but a subset of faces is selected for rendering. 2. Domain-based simplification: Approximates the domain geometry first (e.g., via edge collapses on a tetrahedral mesh) and then computes the exact integral over the simplified geometry. The data structure is a hierarchical mesh with connectivity information allowing incremental culling of simplices. The following steps describe the adaptive control loop, primarily derived from the sample-based approach for unstructured grids: 1. Initialize: Set \text{TargetTime} to the desired frame time for interactive viewing (typically 0.01 seconds). 2. Measure: Record \text{RenderTime}, the time taken to render the previous frame. 3. Calculate Selection Count: Determine the number of internal faces |I| to include in the current LOD pass using the formula: |I|{new} = \frac{|I|{prev} \times \text{TargetTime}}{\text{RenderTime}} Where |I|{prev} is the number of internal faces selected in the previous frame. The source formula uses |I| on both sides, implying an iterative update where the new count is proportional to the previous count scaled by the time ratio. 4. Select Faces: Choose |I| internal faces from the mesh based on mesh geometry and scalar values to maximize visual smoothness when the viewpoint changes. 5. Render: If using sample-based simplification: Render the selected faces I combined with the boundary faces B (where B \cup I \subseteq F, and F is the full face set). If using domain-based simplification: Render the simplified mesh where simplices have been removed based on error criteria. If using coarse sampling (texture slicing): Render every k-th slice (e.g., every fourth slice) instead of all slices. If using ray casting: Use larger step sizes or cast fewer rays. 6. Fallback: If high-quality volume rendering (HAVS) is unavailable, render only the outer faces of the unstructured grid as a translucent surface. Alternatively, generate a smaller image via ZSWEEP or ray casting and render it as a texture-mapped polygon with bilinear interpolation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time def lodrenderloop(mesh, targettime=0.01): """ Adaptive LOD rendering loop for unstructured grids. mesh: Object containing faces F, boundary faces B, and internal faces Iall. targettime: Desired frame time in seconds. """ prevrendertime = targettime # Initialize to targettime to avoid division by zero numinternalfaces = len(mesh.Iall) while True: # Loop continues until application exits starttime = time.monotonic() # 1. Calculate selection count based on previous frame's performance # Formula: |I|new = (|I|prev TargetTime) / RenderTime if prevrendertime > 0: numinternalfaces = int((numinternalfaces targettime) / prevrendertime) else: numinternalfaces = len(mesh.Iall) # Clamp to valid range [0, len(Iall)] numinternalfaces = max(0, min(numinternalfaces, len(mesh.Iall))) # 2. Select faces # Standard operation: sort faces by error metric or geometric priority, take top N selectedfaces = mesh.Iall[:numinternalfaces] # 3. Render # Combine boundary faces (always rendered) with selected internal faces renderablefaces = mesh.B + selectedfaces # Standard volume rendering: rasterize faces, apply transfer function, and accumulate color/opacity along rays image = rasterizeandaccumulate(renderablefaces) # 4. Update timing prevrendertime = time.monotonic() - starttime # 5. Display # Standard operation: present frame buffer to display presentframe(image) TargetTime: The amount of time desired for each frame for interactive viewing. Typical value: 0.01 seconds. Step Size / Ray Count: For ray-casting LOD, the step size \Delta t is increased or the number of rays is decreased. Slice Interval: For texture slicing, the interval between sampled slices (e.g., every fourth slice). Oscillation: Rapid changes in view complexity can cause the LOD level to oscillate between high and low resolutions. The source notes that face selection should be based on mesh geometry and scalar values to maximize visual smoothness when the viewpoint changes. Fallback Quality: If HAVS is unavailable, rendering only outer faces may result in significant loss of internal structure visibility. Approximation Error: Sample-based simplification provides different results than domain-based simplification. Sample-based uses the original geometry to compute an approximate integral, while domain-based approximates the geometry first. Frustum-based LOD Selection determines the appropriate resolution level for a volume entity by calculating the distance from the camera to the entity relative to the camera's frustum faces. It solves the problem of maintaining responsive frame rates for large-scale datasets by selecting lower resolutions for distant or peripheral rays, thereby minimizing memory bandwidth and sample counts. Unlike Footprint-based LOD Selection, which relies on the actual projected footprint of the data to select the coarsest level satisfying a pixel threshold, this method uses distance-to-frustum-face metrics to drive LOD selection. View-Dependent Adaptive Refinement is a technique for displaying large-volume data at interactive frame rates by adaptively refining meshes in regions of interest (close to the viewpoint or line of sight) while using lower resolution for distant regions. It solves the problem of rendering high-fidelity volume data in real-time by balancing approximation error against distance from the viewer. It differs from Frustum-based LOD Selection by using a continuous, error-driven subdivision criterion based on distance rather than discrete frustum culling or static LOD levels. This variant uses an auxiliary texture analysis to dynamically adjust the resolution of the rendering. The algorithm analyzes the rendered image to count "lone texels" (texels containing the isosurface with no neighbors also containing it) and "tooth texels" (texels containing the isosurface with only one neighbor also containing it). The ratio Si of these texels to the total texels in the auxiliary texture T determines the resolution factor n for the next frame. Formula: n{i+1} = \begin{cases} ni & \text{if } S{min} \le Si \le S{max} \\ ni - 1 & \text{if } Si > S{max} \\ ni + 1 & \text{if } Si < S{min} \end{cases} Parameters: n: The resolution reduction factor for the auxiliary texture. Range is [2, 5]. Lower n means higher resolution (n=1 is full size). S{max}: User-defined quality threshold. S{min}: Set to S{max} / 2. Si: The ratio of (lone texels + tooth texels) to total texels in the auxiliary texture T for frame i. Implementation Note: To increase performance, the auxiliary texture analysis is done on the CPU in parallel with the second step of the rendering process (e.g., ray casting), increasing frame time only by the time taken to copy texture data from GPU to CPU. Time Complexity: The complexity is adaptive. The rendering time is bounded by \text{TargetTime} during interaction. Memory Complexity: Sample-based simplification requires storing the full mesh but only rendering a subset, so memory usage remains high but constant. Domain-based simplification may require storing hierarchical mesh structures, potentially increasing memory overhead. Performance: Provides substantial improvements in interactivity for large unstructured grids, especially on GPUs which are efficient for rendering large scenes of polygons. Strengths: Maintains interactive frame rates during user manipulation; simple data structures for sample-based approaches; easy return to full quality by selecting all internal faces. Limitations: Visual quality may degrade significantly if the LOD is too aggressive; sample-based simplification may produce artifacts if the transfer function is not accounted for in face selection. When to use: Interactive visualization of large scalar fields where user manipulation is frequent. LOD techniques for volume rendering originated from the need to visualize large scalar fields represented as tetrahedral meshes interactively. Early methods proposed hierarchically simplifying the tetrahedral mesh using edge collapses, similar to triangle-based simplification, using connectivity information to incrementally cull simplices. The distinction between sample-based and domain-based simplification was highlighted in early works, with sample-based approaches favored for their simplicity in dynamic LOD implementation. The concept was further popularized in textbooks and practical applications like ParaView, where LOD is used to provide interactive rendering rates for unstructured data. name: Frustum-based LOD Selection
head: Auto Level of Detail (LOD), Distance-based LOD, Frustum Face Distance LOD, Multi-resolution volumes (LOD), Simple LOD
body: Frustum-based LOD Selection determines the appropriate level of detail (LOD) depth for a volumetric entity by calculating the distance from the camera to the entity's frustum faces, ensuring that the projected voxel size remains smaller than a screen pixel. Unlike View-Dependent Adaptive Refinement, which refines resolution based on local scalar variance or error metrics, this method relies on distance-driven selection to choose lower LODs for distant or peripheral rays, thereby minimizing sample counts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera world-space position, camera inverse MVP matrix, entity world-space position and scale, array of depth thresholds, screen width. Outputs: Selected LOD integer level. Data Structures: depthTresholds: An array of floats where each element corresponds to a LOD depth. The value is calculated as 1.0f / 2^{depth} for depths 1 to maxSvoDepth. cameraposition: World-space position of the camera. transformComponent: Contains the entity's world-space position and scale. Steps: 1. Calculate Camera-to-Entity Distance: Compute the Euclidean distance between the camera position and the entity's transformed position. d = \| \text{camera\position} - \text{entity\position} \| 2. Determine Frustum Face Positions: To account for the angular spread of the frustum, calculate the positions of the left and right frustum faces at the depth of the entity. Define Normalized Device Coordinate (NDC) points representing the left and right edges of the view volume, e.g., A = (-1, 0, 0, 1) and B = (1, 0, 0, 1). Transform these NDC points to view space using the inverse Model-View-Projection matrix (MVP^{-1}): VA = MVP^{-1} \cdot A, \quad VB = MVP^{-1} \cdot B Scale these vectors by the camera-to-entity distance d and add the camera position to find the world-space positions of the frustum faces at that depth: P{left} = \text{camera\position} + VA \cdot d P{right} = \text{camera\position} + VB \cdot d 3. Calculate Normalized Frustum Width: Compute the distance between the left and right frustum face positions and normalize it by the screen width W: D{norm} = \frac{\| P{left} - P{right} \|}{W} 4. Select LOD Level: Iterate through the depthTresholds array to find the first threshold that the calculated distance d exceeds. For each index i from 0 to depthTresholds.size() - 1: Let depth = i + 1. Let Ti be depthTresholds[i]. If d > Ti \times \text{entity\scale}, then set LOD = depth and break. If no threshold is exceeded, the finest LOD (1) is used. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectfrustumlod(camerapos, entitypos, entityscale, depththresholds, inversemvp): """ Selects LOD based on distance to frustum faces. Args: camerapos: vec3, world position of camera entitypos: vec3, world position of entity entityscale: float, scale of the entity depththresholds: list of float, precomputed thresholds [1/2^1, 1/2^2,...] inversemvp: mat4, inverse model-view-projection matrix Returns: int: Selected LOD level (1-based index) """ # Step 1: Calculate camera-to-entity distance cameratoentitydist = sqrt( (camerapos.x - entitypos.x)2 + (camerapos.y - entitypos.y)2 + (camerapos.z - entitypos.z)2) # Step 2: Determine Frustum Face Positions # Define NDC points for left and right edges pointandc = ( -1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) pointbndc = ( 1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Transform NDC points to view space viewveca = inversemvp @ pointandc viewvecb = inversemvp @ pointbndc # Calculate left and right frustum face positions at the entity's depth leftfrustumfacepos = camerapos + viewveca.xyz cameratoentitydist rightfrustumfacepos = camerapos + viewvecb.xyz cameratoentitydist # Step 4: Iterate through depth thresholds for i in range(len(depththresholds)): depth = i + 1 threshold = depththresholds[i] # Check if distance exceeds threshold scaled by entity scale if cameratoentitydist > threshold entityscale: return depth # Default to finest LOD if no threshold exceeded return 1 Parameters: depthTresholds: Array of floats with typical values 1.0/2^d for d \in [1, \text{max\depth}]. lod: Integer uniform variable controlling the active LOD state in the shader. cameraposition: World-space position of the camera. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in matrix inversion or distance calculation can cause jittering at threshold boundaries. Clamping the distance or using a small epsilon when comparing against thresholds mitigates this. Boundaries: If the entity is partially outside the frustum, the distance calculation might need to account for the closest visible face rather than the center. Degenerate Input: If screenwidth is zero, the normalized distance calculation fails. Ensure screen width is at least 1. Determines LOD by ensuring the projected voxel size does not exceed a pixel threshold, using the actual projected footprint rather than just distance to frustum faces. Retains full-resolution voxels only within a radius defined by the camera's pixel footprint, using concentric clipmap rings. Time Complexity: O(1) for LOD selection per entity, as it involves a fixed number of vector operations and a loop over a small, fixed number of LOD levels. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the multi-resolution volume data (MIP-map pyramid), where N is the number of voxels in the finest resolution. Performance: Significantly reduces memory bandwidth and sample counts for large-scale datasets by skipping distant regions. Strengths: Effective for large volumes where distant details are less perceptible. Limitations: Does not account for local scalar variance; relies solely on distance-driven selection. When to use: Large-scale volumetric datasets (e.g., geophysical simulations) where performance is critical and visual quality degradation at distance is acceptable. When not to use: Scenes requiring high-fidelity detail throughout the volume or where scalar variance is a better indicator of needed resolution. Frustum-based LOD selection is a technique used in volume ray casting to optimize rendering performance by adapting resolution based on ray distance from the viewer. It is commonly used in conjunction with hierarchical representations such as octree-based voxel MIP-map pyramids. The method is particularly suited for large-scale datasets like geophysical simulations, where it cuts memory and sample requirements significantly while maintaining perceptual quality. name: Footprint-based LOD Selection
head: Additive Ladder Level Selection, Coarsest substitutive level selection
body: Footprint-based LOD Selection determines the appropriate level of detail for volumetric entities by ensuring that the projected size of a voxel (or splat) on the screen does not exceed a specific pixel threshold, thereby preventing aliasing and excessive memory bandwidth usage. Unlike its parent Frustum-based LOD Selection, which relies on distance to frustum faces, this method uses the actual projected footprint of the data, selecting the coarsest level in an additive ladder that satisfies the constraint. It is distinguished from Cone-Footprint LOD and Step Sizing by its use of a fixed median footprint threshold rather than sample density proportional to screen content. Inputs: A list of nodes/chunks in an additive ladder structure. Camera projection matrix and viewport dimensions. Stamped footprint dimensions for each node, or bounding box geometry. Ordering of splats (Greedy or Self-energy). Outputs: Selected LOD level index for each node. Fetch requests for the corresponding data chunks. Data Structures: Node: Contains bounding box, stamped footprint dimensions (width, height), and a list of LOD levels. Additive Ladder: A hierarchical structure where each level contains a subset of the data, ordered for efficient streaming. Steps: 1. Project Footprint: For each node, calculate the projected size of its footprint on the screen. If stamped footprint dimensions are available and match the display context, use them. Otherwise, calculate the screen-area fraction of the node’s bounding box. 2. Check Constraint: Compare the projected median splat footprint against the threshold of 1.5 CSS pixels. 3. Select Level: Select the coarsest substitutive level in the additive ladder whose projected median splat footprint is \le 1.5 CSS pixels. If no level satisfies the constraint, select the finest level. 4. Apply Hysteresis: To prevent flickering between levels during camera movement, apply a 10% margin against coarsening. 5. Frustum Cull: Frustum-cull partition tiles so that coarse or off-screen regions are never fetched at full detail. 6. Ordering: If the number of splats is \le 5,000, use Greedy ordering. If the number of splats is > 5,000, use O(N \log N) self-energy ordering. Greedy ordering lowers the residual area under the loading curve by 0.2–2.6% relative to self-energy ordering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def projectfootprint(stampedfootprint, boundingbox, camera, viewport): """Projects footprint to screen space. Uses stamped dimensions if valid, else bounding box area.""" if stampedfootprint is not None and stampedfootprint.matchesdisplay(): return stampedfootprint.project(camera, viewport) return boundingbox.projectscreenarea(camera, viewport) def calculatemediansplatfootprint(projectedfootprint, levelindex): """Estimates median splat footprint for a given LOD level index.""" # Standard scaling: footprint scales inversely with level index return projectedfootprint / (2 levelindex) def selectlodlevel(node, camera, viewport, previouslevelindex, threshold=1.5, hysteresismargin=0.10): """ Selects the LOD level for a node based on its projected footprint. Args: node: Object containing boundingbox, stampedfootprint (optional), and levels (list of LOD levels). camera: Camera object with projectionmatrix and viewmatrix. viewport: Viewport dimensions (width, height). previouslevelindex: Index of the level used in the previous frame. threshold: Maximum allowed footprint in CSS pixels (default 1.5). hysteresismargin: Margin against coarsening (default 0.10). Returns: int: Index of the selected LOD level. """ # Step 1: Calculate projected footprint projectedfootprint = projectfootprint(node.stampedfootprint, node.boundingbox, camera, viewport) # Step 2 & 3: Find coarsest level satisfying constraint selectedlevelindex = -1 for levelindex, level in enumerate(node.levels): medianfootprint = calculatemediansplatfootprint(projectedfootprint, levelindex) if medianfootprint <= threshold: selectedlevelindex = levelindex break # If no level satisfies, select finest if selectedlevelindex == -1: selectedlevelindex = len(node.levels) - 1 # Step 4: Apply hysteresis against coarsening # Only allow switching to a coarser level (lower index) if footprint is sufficiently smaller if selectedlevelindex < previouslevelindex: if medianfootprint > threshold (1 - hysteresismargin): selectedlevelindex = previouslevelindex return selectedlevelindex Parameters: Footprint Threshold: 1.5 CSS pixels. Hysteresis Margin: 10% against coarsening. Ordering Threshold: 5,000 splats (Greedy below, Self-energy above). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Stamped Footprint: If no footprint is stamped or dimensions do not match, fall back to screen-area fraction of the bounding box. No Satisfying Level: If no level meets the footprint constraint, the finest level is selected. Flickering: Without hysteresis, rapid changes in camera distance can cause flickering between LOD levels. A 10% margin is applied to prevent this. A technique replacing fixed step counts with sample density proportional to screen content (cone footprint) rather than camera distance, to reduce stationary-shimmer/aliasing. It differs from Footprint-based LOD Selection by using a dynamic footprint based on cone projection rather than a fixed median splat threshold. Choose this when aliasing in static scenes is a primary concern. See Cone-Footprint LOD and Step Sizing. Applies a per-chunk exponent to counteract brightness loss from downsampling averaging, which destroys color-opacity correlation. The exponent multiplies the gamma exponent. The formula is exponent = base\exponent + \log2(downsample) \times scale\factor. The old law used lift proportional to (downsample - 1), which was incorrect because averaging reduces the same 2x2x2 neighborhood per level, making it one comparable step per level. Default refit is 0.08 per level. Seam response is monotonic across the whole slider (-33.0% at 0, -10.1% at 0.08). Pitfall: Old form caused level-6 bricks to ask for exponent -0.386 on a seven-level pyramid; the 0.25 clamp caught it, causing artifacts. Measured +35.7% at default against -34.0% with compensation off, overshooting null by 6x. Floor sat pinned at clamp, causing pale flash on zoom. Time Complexity: Level selection is O(L) per node, where L is the number of levels. Ordering is O(N) for Greedy (up to 5,000 splats) and O(N \log N) for Self-energy (above 5,000 splats). Memory Complexity: Depends on the additive ladder structure and caching strategy (multi-level cache with decoded per-slice geometry, decoded chunks, compressed chunks, and HTTP range requests). Performance: Greedy ordering lowers the residual area under the loading curve by 0.2–2.6% relative to self-energy ordering. Strengths: Prevents aliasing by controlling projected footprint size; reduces memory bandwidth by fetching only necessary detail; hysteresis prevents visual flickering. Limitations: Requires stamped footprint data for optimal performance; fallback to bounding box may be less accurate; ordering complexity increases for large scenes. When to Use: Interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets where aliasing and memory bandwidth are concerns. When Not to Use: When stamped footprint data is unavailable and bounding box fallback is insufficient for quality requirements. Footprint-based LOD Selection is used in scalable interactive web visualization of multidimensional scientific data, specifically in the Luxar project for Gaussian splatting microscopy data. It is part of a broader system that includes additive ladders, multi-level caching, and prefetching to handle large datasets efficiently. name: Cone-Footprint LOD and Step Sizing
head: cone LOD, cone-footprint LOD
body: Cone-Footprint LOD replaces fixed step counts with sample density proportional to the screen-space footprint of a voxel rather than camera distance, effectively reducing stationary shimmer and aliasing. It sets itself apart from distance-based LOD methods by dynamically matching the sampling rate to the projected pixel area at the current march distance. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D, entry distance t{min}, exit distance t{max}, voxel size in world units V{world}, pyramid mip levels L=0 \dots N, and tuning parameters STEP\QUALITY and SKIP\CHECK\STRIDE. Outputs: A sequence of sample positions and values along the ray, terminated when t \ge t{max} or a skip condition is met. Data Structures Pyramid Mips: A hierarchy of voxel grids where level l has texel size V{world} \cdot 2^l. Ray State: Current distance t, current LOD level lod, and iteration counter i. Parameters STEP\QUALITY = 2.0: Multiplier for the base step size to ensure sufficient oversampling. SKIP\CHECK\STRIDE = 4: Frequency of pyramid skip checks. STEP\COUNT = 256: Maximum iteration safety cap, increased from 128. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization: Set t = t{min}, i = 0. Compute initial LOD: lod = coneLod(t, O, D, V{world}), which returns the mip level l such that the texel size at level l approximates the screen-space footprint of a pixel at distance t. 2. Main Loop: While t < t{max} and i < STEP\COUNT: a. Skip Check: If i \pmod{SKIP\CHECK\STRIDE} == 0, check if the ray is inside a skip region (e.g., empty space or low-contrast volume) using the pyramid data at the current lod. If the skip condition is met: Calculate the exit distance of the current skip cell, t{skip\exit}. Jump t to t{skip\exit} and apply a jitter offset to prevent ray synchronization. Update lod based on the new t. Increment i and continue to the next iteration without sampling. b. Step Sizing: Compute the base step length from the current LOD: lod\step = V{world} \cdot 2^{lod} \cdot STEP\QUALITY. Compute the safety floor to prevent truncation at large tiers: floor\step = \frac{t{max} - t}{STEP\COUNT - i}. Determine the actual step length: step\length = \max(lod\step, floor\step). c. Sampling: Sample the volume texture at position P = O + t \cdot D using the current lod. d. Advance: t = t + step\length, i = i + 1. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def conefootprintmarch(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, voxelsizelocal, pyramid, stepquality=2.0, skipcheckstride=4, stepcount=256): t = tmin i = 0 lod = conelod(t, rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsizelocal) while t < tmax and i < stepcount: if i % skipcheckstride == 0: if pyramid.isskipregion(t, lod): tskipexit = pyramid.cellexitt(t, lod) t = tskipexit + hash(rayorigin, i) 1e-6 lod = conelod(t, rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsizelocal) i += 1 continue lodstep = voxelsizelocal (2 lod) stepquality remainingsteps = stepcount - i floorstep = (tmax - t) / remainingsteps steplength = max(lodstep, floorstep) sampleposition = rayorigin + t raydirection value = pyramid.samplelod(sampleposition, lod, mipmapfilter='linear') t += steplength i += 1 return samples Edge Cases and Pitfalls Truncation: STEP\COUNT=256 can truncate a ray mid-cube at large tiers because honest LOD-driven steps near the camera are voxel-sized, and 256 of them fall short of a large-tier cube's diagonal. The per-iteration step floor guarantees every ray reaches t{max}. Banding: The skip-jump's direct t = skipExitT + \epsilon re-synchronizes every ray that skipped the same pyramid cell onto that cell's exit plane, causing stationary banding. Re-jittering on resume with the ray's own hash, salted by iteration count, breaks this correlation. Mipmap Filtering: The WebGPU default mipmapFilter: 'nearest' causes fractional cone-LOD to snap between mips instead of blending, creating hard detail-shell edges. The sampler must be set to mipmapFilter: 'linear' to fix this. Redundant Checks: Near the camera, LOD-0 steps are voxel-sized, making re-testing membership every step redundant. Throttling the skip check to every 4th iteration (SKIP\CHECK\STRIDE=4) optimizes performance without quality loss. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples, but N is now adaptive. The skip check adds a constant overhead every SKIP\CHECK\STRIDE iterations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the pyramid storage, which is stored in deviation space. Performance: In paired A/B testing against a baseline with fixed steps, this method recovered most of the performance regression caused by aggressive skipping in previous tasks. For example, in a "volume-inside" scenario, total merged time dropped from 2.2ms (Task 5) to 1.4ms (Task 6). Strengths: Eliminates stationary shimmer by aligning sample density with screen content. Adaptive skipping reduces cost in empty regions. Limitations: Requires a pyramid structure. Tuning parameters (STEP\QUALITY, SKIP\CHECK\STRIDE) are critical for performance/quality balance. STEP\QUALITY=1.0 was found to increase cost by 68% with no visible quality gain compared to 2.0. This method was developed as part of the Skymap project's volume raymarch acceleration efforts, specifically addressing aliasing and performance in GPU-based volume rendering. It was introduced in Pull Request #556 by rulkens, co-authored with Claude Fable, in August 2026. The technique builds on earlier work in GPU pyramids and TF-adaptive skipping. feat(volumes): raymarch acceleration — GPU pyramids, TF-adaptive skipping, cone LOD, https://github.com/rulkens/skymap/pull/556, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Pixel-Sized Clipmap LOD for Voxels
head: Clipmap rings, Pixel-sized LOD
body: Pixel-Sized Clipmap LOD is a level-of-detail strategy where full-resolution voxels are retained only within a radius defined by the camera's pixel footprint, with coarser resolutions arranged in concentric clipmap rings. It differs from footprint-based methods by strictly tying the LOD boundary to the angular size of a single pixel at the current resolution and field of view, ensuring that the finest detail is never over-sampled relative to the screen. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Voxel size s (world units per voxel), camera vertical field of view \theta{v}, screen height H (pixels), and the desired number of LOD rings L. Outputs: A set of clipmap rings, where ring i contains voxels of size s \cdot 2^i spanning a specific radial distance from the camera. Data Structures The data is organized into concentric rings around the camera position. Each ring i (where i=0 is the innermost full-resolution ring) stores voxels at resolution si = s \cdot 2^i. Ring i Bounds: Spans radial distance [R{i-1}, Ri] where Ri = R0 \cdot 2^i. Voxel Count per Ring: Each ring holds approximately 0.75 \times N0 voxels, where N0 is the voxel count in the central disk. Storage Format: Voxels can be stored in a compact format (e.g., 3.3 bytes/voxel) or raw format (e.g., 8 bytes/voxel). Algorithm Steps 1. Calculate Pixel Angular Size: Determine the angular span of one pixel. For a vertical FOV \theta{v} and screen height H: \alpha = \frac{\theta{v}}{H} Typical value for 1440p at 70° vertical FOV: \alpha \approx 8.48 \times 10^{-4} radians. 2. Determine Full-Resolution Radius (R0): Calculate the distance at which a single voxel of size s subtends exactly one pixel. R0 = \frac{s}{\alpha} \approx 1180 \cdot s For s=2 cm, R0 \approx 24 m. For s=25 cm, R0 \approx 295 m. 3. Calculate Central Disk Voxels (N0): Compute the number of voxels required to fill the disk of radius R0 at resolution s. N0 = \frac{\pi R0^2}{s^2} = \pi \left(\frac{1180 \cdot s}{s}\right)^2 = \pi \cdot 1180^2 \approx 4.4 \times 10^6 If a roughness factor k=2 is applied, N0 \approx 8.7 \times 10^6. 4. Define Clipmap Rings: For each subsequent ring i from 1 to L: Voxel Size: si = s \cdot 2^i. Outer Radius: Ri = R0 \cdot 2^i. Voxel Count: Ni = 0.75 \times N0. 5. Total Resident Voxels: The total number of voxels resident in memory for L rings is: N{total} = N0 \cdot (1 + 0.75 \cdot L) Example: For L=6, N{total} \approx 4.8 \times 10^7. Parameters and Typical Values LOD Levels (L): To reach distances of 1–5 km from R0: s=2 cm: 5–8 levels. s=5 cm: 4–6 levels. s=10 cm: 3–5 levels. s=25 cm: 2–4 levels. Memory Footprint: 6 rings: 160 MB (compact) / 390 MB (raw). 8 rings: 200 MB (compact) / 500 MB (raw). 12 rings: 290 MB (compact) / 710 MB (raw). High-Quality Headroom: For path-traced detail at 2 voxels per pixel, multiply resident memory by 4 (approx. 0.6–2.8 GB). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: At 2 cm resolution, a 32-bit integer voxel coordinate spans \approx 85,900 km, which is ample. Float32 positions at 5 km from origin have a step of 0.49 mm, which is sufficient for camera-relative coordinates. Full-Resolution Region: The region within R0 must remain full-resolution regardless of pixel size for dynamic elements like edits, debris, fluids, and collisions. For a 64 m radius per player, this costs 211 MB (compact) at 2 cm resolution. Memory Scaling: While the clipmap scales logarithmically, the full-resolution dynamic region scales with the square of the voxel size. Smaller s significantly increases the cost of the central dynamic region. A Level of Detail scheme covering all-voxel to orbit views using camera-centred rings where each level is twice as coarse as the one inside it, using the same brick format at each mip level. It employs approximately 19–20 levels, ranging from 10 cm resolution out to the Planet-disc Zoom level. Unlike hybrid approaches, it uses no heightfield or mesh fallback, relying entirely on voxel data for all distances. Downsampling is performed such that a coarse voxel is solid if at least 4 of its 8 children are solid, taking the most common solid child's material. Edits propagate up all levels immediately. Time Complexity: The number of LOD levels grows logarithmically with distance. On-demand generation cost scales with voxel density; for example, 2 cm resolution requires 25× more voxel evaluations than 10 cm resolution for the same area. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by the number of rings L. Total voxels scale linearly with L (N0 \cdot (1 + 0.75 \cdot L)). Performance: The method fits within 8–12 GB of VRAM, leaving room for path-tracing buffers and lighting caches. Aokana keeps only ~2–17% of a scene resident with distance LOD, confirming the efficiency of this bounded memory approach. Strengths: Bounded memory usage; efficient coverage of large distances; simple ring-based data structure. Limitations: Requires significant memory for high-resolution dynamic regions near the camera; quality headroom for high-fidelity rendering (2 voxels/pixel) increases memory demands substantially. This method is described in the context of voxel data structures for large-scale environments, specifically in the "bhayanakvoxel" project research documentation. It is also referenced in discussions regarding voxel data structure and LOD scheme selection for all-voxel to orbit views. voxel-data-structures.md, https://github.com/theHimanshuShekhar/bhayanakvoxel/blob/research/voxel-data-structures/docs/research/voxel-data-structures.md, fetched 2026-10-28 Choose voxel data structure & LOD scheme #9, https://github.com/theHimanshuShekhar/bhayanakvoxel/issues/9, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: View-Dependent Adaptive Refinement
head: Distance-dependent Mesh Refinement, Error-based Adaptive Refinement
body: View-Dependent Adaptive Refinement is a technique for displaying large-volume data at interactive frame rates by adaptively refining meshes in regions of interest (close to the viewpoint or line of sight) while using lower resolution for distant regions. Decisions on resolution levels are automatically made by applying error metrics and viewing parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multiresolution mesh hierarchy (typically tetrahedral), a viewpoint position, a maximum sight distance d{max}, a maximum approximation error E{max}, and a decline rate parameter \alpha. Output: A refined mesh where tetrahedra are subdivided or kept coarse based on their distance-dependent error threshold. Data Structures: Mesh Hierarchy: The method uses a hierarchy of tetrahedra created via longest-edge bisection. This structure supports both regular and irregular tetrahedral meshes. Constraint: The subdivision process must not generate mesh inconsistencies such as hanging nodes. The method is independent of the specific subdivision method used to create the hierarchy, provided continuity is maintained. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate over each tetrahedron T in the visible region, optionally restricted to a view frustum defined by d{max} and a maximum deviation angle from the line of sight. 2. Compute the distance d(T) from the tetrahedron T to the viewpoint. 3. Compute the approximation error E(T) for the tetrahedron T using an appropriate error metric for the scalar field. 4. Compute the distance-dependent threshold. 5. If E(T) exceeds the threshold, subdivide tetrahedron T. 6. Repeat the process iteratively until no further subdivisions are required or a maximum depth is reached. Formula: E(T) > \frac{d(T)}{d{max}} \alpha E{max} where E(T) is the approximation error for tetrahedron T, d(T) is the distance from T to the viewpoint, d{max} is the maximum distance from the viewpoint (range of sight), E{max} is the maximum approximation error, and \alpha determines how quickly resolution decreases with distance. Parameters: E{max}: Maximum approximation error. Application-specific and user-controlled. d{max}: Maximum distance from the viewpoint (range of sight). Application-specific and user-controlled. \alpha: Parameter determining how quickly resolution decreases with distance. Typical values correspond to linear or quadratic decline. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hanging Nodes: The subdivision method must ensure that adjacent tetrahedra do not create hanging nodes, which would break mesh continuity. Frustum Restriction: To optimize performance, subdivision can be restricted to regions within a view frustum defined by d{max} and a maximum deviation angle from the line of sight. Error Metric Dependency: The accuracy of the refinement depends on the quality of the error metric E(T) used. Precision and Boundaries: The threshold scales linearly or quadratically with distance, requiring careful handling of floating-point precision near d{max}. Degenerate Input: Tetrahedra with zero volume or coincident vertices must be filtered before error computation to avoid division by zero or invalid distances. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def viewdependentadaptiverefinement(tetrahedra, viewpoint, dmax, Emax, alpha): """ Refines a tetrahedral mesh based on view-dependent error. Args: tetrahedra: List of tetrahedron objects, each with attributes: error: Approximation error E(T) center: Center point of the tetrahedron viewpoint: 3D vector representing the camera position dmax: Maximum distance from viewpoint (range of sight) Emax: Maximum approximation error threshold alpha: Rate of resolution decline with distance Returns: Refined list of tetrahedra """ refinedtetrahedra = [] for T in tetrahedra: # Compute Euclidean distance from tetrahedron center to viewpoint dT = ((T.center.x - viewpoint.x)2 + (T.center.y - viewpoint.y)2 + (T.center.z - viewpoint.z)2)0.5 if dT > dmax: refinedtetrahedra.append(T) continue ET = T.error threshold = (dT / dmax) alpha Emax if ET > threshold: # Subdivide T via longest-edge bisection; sources do not specify the exact implementation # children = T.subdivide() # refinedtetrahedra.extend(children) pass else: refinedtetrahedra.append(T) return refinedtetrahedra A view-dependent LOD algorithm that dynamically generates an optimal triangulation for terrain meshes per frame based on the camera viewpoint. It solves high CPU overhead of continuous LOD methods by using a bottom-up approach that maintains mesh continuity without global remeshing. It differs from top-down LOD methods by starting from a coarse mesh and refining only where necessary. Choose it for real-time terrain rendering where mesh continuity and low CPU overhead are prioritized. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides high resolution near the viewpoint while maintaining performance in distant regions. Limitations: Subdivision overhead can be significant if many tetrahedra exceed the threshold. When to use: Interactive fly-through exploration of large volume datasets where visual fidelity near the viewer is critical. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from research on adaptive multi-valued volume data visualization. It builds on the concept of using error metrics and viewing parameters to automatically determine resolution levels. The approach is based on earlier work referenced as [30] in the source. It is particularly relevant for 3D fly-through-like navigation through datasets. Adaptive Multi-Valued Volume Data Visualization using Data-Dependent Error Metrics, https://doi.org/10.2316/journal.205.2005.2.205-4291, fetched 2026-10-26

name: ROAM (Real Time Optimally Adapting Meshes)
head: Serial Tessellation Algorithm
body: ROAM is a view-dependent level-of-detail algorithm that dynamically generates an optimal triangulation for a terrain mesh for each frame based on the camera viewpoint. It solves the high CPU overhead of continuous LOD methods by adaptively refining meshes in regions of interest while maintaining a consistent triangulation across the visible surface. It differs from top-down LOD methods by starting from a coarse mesh and refining only where necessary, building on View-Dependent Adaptive Refinement. Input: A height map defining the terrain surface; a camera position; a pool of pre-allocated vertices; an adaptive tolerance parameter t (distance-dependent). Output: A continuous, adaptive triangulation of the visible terrain for the current frame. Bintree Patch: The terrain is subdivided into patches, each managed by a Bintree (Binary Tree) structure. Triangle: Each triangle stores pointers to its three neighbors. Vertex Pool: A finite pool of vertices. When a new vertex is introduced, it is removed from the pool. If the pool is empty, no further refinement is possible. Height Map: Provides the z-coordinate (height) for any (x, y) position. 1. Initialization: Initialize the landscape with a coarse mesh. 2. Frame Rendering Loop: a. Tessellation: Perform adaptive view-dependent tessellation for each visible patch. i. Traversal: Recursively traverse the two Bintree structures in each visible patch. ii. Refinement Decision: For each triangle T in the Bintree: 1. Calculate the adaptive tolerance t based on the distance of the triangle's center to the observer. 2. Compute the distance d between the middle point of the triangle's base edge and the corresponding point in the height map. 3. Split Condition: If d > t, the triangle must be split. iii. Split Execution: To split triangle T without creating cracks: 1. Identify the Longest Edge Propagation Path (LEPP) starting from T. 2. Recursively split all triangles along the LEPP until a terminal edge is found (a base edge shared by two adjacent triangles or a border edge of the mesh). 3. Perform the Split operation: Replace triangle T and its adjacent neighbor (forming a diamond) with four new triangles by introducing a new vertex at the center of the diamond. This new vertex is taken from the vertex pool. 3. Render: Render the resulting mesh. Split Condition: d(\text{middle\point}(base), \text{height\map\point}) > t Where: base: The base edge of the triangle T. \text{middle\point}(base): The midpoint of the base edge. \text{height\map\point}: The height value from the height map at the (x, y) coordinates of the midpoint. t: Adaptive tolerance parameter, dependent on the distance of the point to the observer. t: Adaptive tolerance parameter. It varies based on the distance of the point to the observer. Closer points have smaller t, requiring finer detail. Cracks: Splitting a triangle T while its base neighbor Tb is at a coarser level creates a crack. The LEPP mechanism ensures Tb is split first, propagating the refinement to maintain continuity. Vertex Pool Exhaustion: If the pre-allocated vertex pool is exhausted, no further refinement is possible. CPU Overhead: The tessellation process is the most CPU-expensive part of the algorithm due to recursive traversal and pointer management. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def midpoint(self, other): return Vec3((self.x+other.x)/2, (self.y+other.y)/2, (self.z+other.z)/2) class Edge: def init(self, v0, v1, neighbor=None): self.v0, self.v1, self.neighbor = v0, v1, neighbor def midpoint(self): return self.v0.midpoint(self.v1) class Triangle: def init(self, v0, v1, v2, baseedge=None): self.v0, self.v1, self.v2 = v0, v1, v2 self.baseedge = baseedge if baseedge else Edge(v0, v1) def center(self): return Vec3((self.v0.x+self.v1.x+self.v2.x)/3, (self.v0.y+self.v1.y+self.v2.y)/3, (self.v0.z+self.v1.z+self.v2.z)/3) def getapex(self): return self.v2 def roamtessellation(visiblepatches, camerapos, heightmap, vertexpool, tolerancefunc): for patch in visiblepatches: traversebintree(patch.root, camerapos, heightmap, vertexpool, tolerancefunc) def traversebintree(node, camerapos, heightmap, vertexpool, tolerancefunc): if node is None or node.triangle is None: return tri = node.triangle center = tri.center() dist = math.sqrt((center.x-camerapos.x)2 + (center.y-camerapos.y)2 + (center.z-camerapos.z)2) t = tolerancefunc(dist) basemid = tri.baseedge.midpoint() heightval = heightmap.getheight(basemid.x, basemid.y) d = math.sqrt((basemid.z - heightval)2) if d > t: lepp = findlepp(tri) for trisplit in lepp: splittriangle(trisplit, heightmap, vertexpool) def findlepp(starttri): path = [] current = starttri while not isterminaledge(current): path.append(current) current = current.baseedge.neighbor path.append(current) return path def isterminaledge(tri): neighbor = tri.baseedge.neighbor if neighbor is None: return True if neighbor.baseedge == tri.baseedge: return True return False def splittriangle(tri, heightmap, vertexpool): if tri.baseedge.neighbor is None or not vertexpool.hasvertices(): return neighbor = tri.baseedge.neighbor newvertex = vertexpool.pop() apex1 = tri.getapex() apex2 = neighbor.getapex() newvertex.x = (apex1.x + apex2.x) / 2 newvertex.y = (apex1.y + apex2.y) / 2 newvertex.z = heightmap.getheight(newvertex.x, newvertex.y) # Replace the diamond (tri and neighbor) with four new triangles sharing newvertex # Update Bintree nodes and neighbor pointers accordingly Time Complexity: The tessellation process is the most CPU-expensive part due to recursive traversal and pointer management. Parallelization can reduce time if decoupled, but recursive nature causes vertex allocation conflicts. Memory Complexity: Depends on the pre-allocated vertex pool size and Bintree structures. Strengths: Provides optimal triangulation for the camera viewpoint; maintains mesh continuity via LEPP. Limitations: High CPU overhead; requires a finite pre-allocated vertex pool; parallelization is complex due to synchronization needs. When to use: Interactive frame rates for large terrain datasets where CPU resources are available for tessellation. When not to use: When GPU-based tessellation is preferred or vertex pool management is too restrictive. ROAM was introduced by Duchaineau et al. in 1997. It was designed to address the high CPU overhead of continuous LOD methods by providing a view-dependent, optimally adapting mesh. The algorithm has been extended to parallel implementations to leverage multiprocessor architectures. name: Dynamic Volume Resolution & Alpha Mask Update
head: Dynamic Resolution and Mask Update
body: This method dynamically adjusts the voxel grid resolution and the active spatial bounding box (AABB) of a neural volume representation during training. It solves the problem of inefficient memory usage and slow convergence by initially training in a low-resolution, coarse space and progressively refining the grid density and spatial extent as the model learns. It differs from static resolution methods by coupling resolution upscaling with alpha mask updates, ensuring that the volume only occupies the space containing visible geometry, thereby pruning empty background space. The method operates as a periodic control loop triggered at specific training iterations. It manages two distinct resources: the spatial resolution of the voxel grid and the spatial extent of the volume (defined by its AABB). Inputs: iteration: Current training step index. updateAlphaMasklist: List of integers specifying iterations where the alpha mask and AABB should be updated. upsamplist: List of integers specifying iterations where the voxel resolution should be increased. args: Configuration object containing hyperparameters (see Parameters). tensorf: The neural volume object holding the grid, optimizer, and AABB. allrays, allrgbs: The dataset of rays and corresponding ground truth colors. Outputs: Updated tensorf with new resolution, new AABB, and reinitialized optimizer. Filtered allrays and allrgbs if rays fall outside the new bounding box. AABB (Axis-Aligned Bounding Box): Defined by two 3D vectors, min and max, representing the corners of the volume. Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor of density and color features. Its dimensions are determined by resocur. Optimizer State: Typically Adam or RAdam, storing momentum buffers for each parameter. updateAlphaMasklist: List of iteration numbers. upsamplist: List of iteration numbers. args.lrupsamplereset: Boolean. If True, resets learning rate to args.lrinit on upsample; otherwise applies decay. args.lrdecaytargetratio: Float. Multiplier for LR decay if lrupsamplereset is False. args.nSamples: Integer. Maximum samples per ray before dynamic adjustment. args.stepratio: Float. Controls sample density relative to resolution during upscaling. args.lrinit, args.lrbasis: Floats. Initial learning rates for main and basis parameters. args.ndcray: Boolean. If True, rays are in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC), bypassing spatial culling. args.L1weightrest: Float. L1 regularization weight used after the first shrink. 1. Check for Alpha Mask Update: If iteration is in updateAlphaMasklist: 1. Determine mask resolution resomask. If resocur[0] resocur[1] resocur[2] < 2563, set resomask = resocur to cap mask resolution. 2. Update the alpha mask: newaabb = tensorf.updateAlphaMask(tuple(resomask)). 3. Shrink Volume: If this is the first update, shrink the volume to the new newaabb: tensorf.shrink(newaabb). 4. Update Regularization: Switch the L1 regularization weight: L1regweight = args.L1weightrest. 5. Filter Rays (Conditional): If args.ndcray is False AND this is the second update iteration: Filter rays outside the new bounding box: allrays, allrgbs = tensorf.filteringrays(allrays, allrgbs). Reinitialize the sampler: trainingSampler = SimpleSampler(allrgbs.shape[0], args.batchsize). Note: NDC rays bypass spatial bounding box culling, so filtering is skipped for them. 2. Check for Resolution Upsampling: If iteration is in upsamplist: 1. Pop the next target voxel count: nvoxels = Nvoxellist.pop(0). 2. Convert voxel count to resolution: resocur = Ntoreso(nvoxels, tensorf.aabb). 3. Update Samples per Ray: Calculate the new number of samples per ray: nSamples = min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(resocur, args.stepratio)). 4. Upsample Grid: Upsample the volume grid to the new resolution: tensorf.upsamplevolumegrid(resocur). 5. Calculate Learning Rate Scale: If args.lrupsamplereset is True: lrscale = 1. Else: lrscale = args.lrdecaytargetratio (iteration / args.niters). 6. Reinitialize Optimizer: Get new parameter groups with scaled learning rates: gradvars = tensorf.getoptparamgroups(args.lrinit lrscale, args.lrbasis lrscale). Reinitialize the optimizer: optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(gradvars, betas=(0.9, 0.99)). Pitfall: This discards all momentum states from previous steps, which may cause training instability if not intended. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stepdynamicresolutionandmask( iteration, updateAlphaMasklist, upsamplist, args, tensorf, allrays, allrgbs, Nvoxellist): """ Performs dynamic resolution and alpha mask updates for a neural volume. """ # Track update counts if not stored in tensorf if not hasattr(tensorf, 'alphaupdatecount'): tensorf.alphaupdatecount = 0 if not hasattr(tensorf, 'hasbeenshrunk'): tensorf.hasbeenshrunk = False # --- Alpha Mask Update --- if iteration in updateAlphaMasklist: currentvoxelcount = tensorf.resocur[0] tensorf.resocur[1] tensorf.resocur[2] if currentvoxelcount < 2563: resomask = tensorf.resocur else: resomask = tensorf.resocur newaabb = tensorf.updateAlphaMask(tuple(resomask)) if not tensorf.hasbeenshrunk: tensorf.shrink(newaabb) tensorf.hasbeenshrunk = True tensorf.L1regweight = args.L1weightrest if not args.ndcray and tensorf.alphaupdatecount == 1: allrays, allrgbs = tensorf.filteringrays(allrays, allrgbs) trainingSampler = SimpleSampler(len(allrgbs), args.batchsize) tensorf.alphaupdatecount += 1 # --- Resolution Upsampling --- if iteration in upsamplist: if not Nvoxellist: raise ValueError("No more voxel counts in Nvoxellist") nvoxels = Nvoxellist.pop(0) resocur = Ntoreso(nvoxels, tensorf.aabb) nSamples = min(args.nSamples, calnsamples(resocur, args.stepratio)) tensorf.upsamplevolumegrid(resocur) if args.lrupsamplereset: lrscale = 1.0 else: lrscale = args.lrdecaytargetratio (iteration / args.niters) gradvars = tensorf.getoptparamgroups( args.lrinit lrscale, args.lrbasis lrscale) # Reinitialize optimizer (standard Adam implementation) optimizer = StandardAdamOptimizer(gradvars, lr=1e-3, betas=(0.9, 0.99)) tensorf.resocur = resocur tensorf.nSamples = nSamples return allrays, allrgbs, tensorf, optimizer def Ntoreso(nvoxels, aabb): """ Converts a total number of voxels to a 3D resolution tuple, preserving the aspect ratio of the AABB. """ sidelength = round(nvoxels (1/3)) mincorner = aabb.min maxcorner = aabb.max dims = [maxcorner[i] - mincorner[i] for i in range(3)] maxdim = max(dims) aspect = [d / maxdim for d in dims] resox = max(1, round(sidelength aspect[0])) resoy = max(1, round(sidelength aspect[1])) resoz = max(1, round(sidelength aspect[2])) return (resox, resoy, resoz) def calnsamples(reso, stepratio): """ Calculates the number of samples per ray based on resolution and step ratio. """ return int(sum(reso) stepratio) def filteringrays(rays, rgbs): """ Filters out rays that fall outside the current AABB. """ # Standard implementation: keep rays where intersection with AABB is valid return rays, rgbs class SimpleSampler: def init(self, numrays, batchsize): self.numrays = numrays self.batchsize = batchsize class StandardAdamOptimizer: """ Minimal Adam optimizer implementation to avoid library internals. """ def init(self, params, lr, betas): self.params = params self.lr = lr self.betas = betas self.state = {} Optimizer Reinitialization: Reinitializing the optimizer discards momentum states. This can lead to training instability or slower convergence if the learning rate schedule is not adjusted accordingly. NDC Rays: If args.ndcray is True, rays are not filtered by the AABB. This means the volume may be trained on empty space if the AABB is shrunk, leading to wasted computation. Ray Filtering Timing: Ray filtering is only applied on the second alpha mask update. The first update does not filter rays, which may leave rays in empty space during initial training. Resolution Capping: The mask resolution is capped only when the total voxel count is below 256^3; otherwise resomask remains equal to resocur. Alpha Mask Generation creates a binary occupancy grid from a dense density field to prune empty space and enable adaptive resolution. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly combining density thresholding with multi-scale max pooling to smooth the mask boundaries before updating the active bounding box. Limitations: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Alpha Mask Generation
head: Density Thresholding, TensorBase Alpha Mask Update, Alpha Mask Update & Volume Resolution Adjustment, Dense Alpha Mask Generation, getDenseAlpha, updateAlphaMask
body: Alpha Mask Generation creates a binary occupancy grid from a dense density field to prune empty space and enable adaptive resolution. It differs from sibling methods by explicitly combining density thresholding with multi-scale max pooling to smooth mask boundaries before updating the active bounding box. Inputs: Dense density field (implicitly accessed via self.computealpha). Current bounding box self.aabb (min/max coordinates). Current resolution resocur. Update schedule updateAlphaMasklist. Grid size gridSize (default: (200, 200, 200)). Threshold alphaMaskthres for binarizing alpha values. Outputs: AlphaGridMask object containing the binary mask and the new active bounding box newaabb. Data Structures: AlphaGridMask: Contains a 3D binary tensor (voxels) and the AABB bounds. resocur: Tuple (x, y, z) representing current voxel counts. Steps: 1. Initialization Check: If the current iteration is not in updateAlphaMasklist, skip. If resocur[0] resocur[1] resocur[2] < 256^3, set resomask = resocur. 2. Mask Update: Call tensorf.updateAlphaMask(tuple(resomask)) to obtain newaabb. 3. Shrinkage (First Update): If this is the first update time, call tensorf.shrink(newaabb) and set L1regweight = args.L1weightrest. 4. Coordinate Grid Generation: Generate a 3D grid of normalized coordinates (0 \dots 1) using torch.meshgrid with resolution gridSize. 5. World Space Mapping: Map normalized coordinates to world space densexyz using linear interpolation between self.aabb[0] and self.aabb[1]. 6. Alpha Computation: Iterate over the first dimension of the grid to compute alpha values for each slice using self.computealpha. 7. Smoothing (Coarse): Apply 3D max pooling with kernel size 5 and padding 2 to the alpha values. 8. Thresholding: Binarize alpha values: set to 1 if \ge alphaMaskthres, else 0. 9. Smoothing (Fine): Apply 3D max pooling with kernel size 3 and padding 1 to the binarized mask. 10. AABB Recalculation: Calculate the new bounding box based on the min and max coordinates of voxels where alpha > 0.5. 11. Finalization: Create and return an AlphaGridMask object with the final mask and newaabb. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F class AlphaGridMask: def init(self, mask, aabb): self.mask = mask self.aabb = aabb def generatealphamask(self, iteration, updateAlphaMasklist, args, gridsize=(200, 200, 200)): # Step 1: Check update schedule if iteration not in updateAlphaMasklist: return None # Step 2: Determine resolution voxelcount = self.resocur[0] self.resocur[1] self.resocur[2] if voxelcount < 2563: resomask = self.resocur else: resomask = self.resocur # Step 3: Initial mask update to get AABB newaabb = self.tensorf.updateAlphaMask(tuple(resomask)) # Step 4: Handle first update shrinkage if iteration == updateAlphaMasklist[0]: self.tensorf.shrink(newaabb) self.L1regweight = args.L1weightrest # Step 5: Generate normalized coordinate grid x = torch.linspace(0, 1, gridsize[0]) y = torch.linspace(0, 1, gridsize[1]) z = torch.linspace(0, 1, gridsize[2]) gridx, gridy, gridz = torch.meshgrid(x, y, z, indexing='ij') # Step 6: Map to world space densexyz = torch.stack([ gridx (self.aabb[1][0] - self.aabb[0][0]) + self.aabb[0][0], gridy (self.aabb[1][1] - self.aabb[0][1]) + self.aabb[0][1], gridz (self.aabb[1][2] - self.aabb[0][2]) + self.aabb[0][2] ], dim=-1) # Step 7: Compute alpha values alphavalues = [] for i in range(gridsize[0]): slicexyz = densexyz[i,:,:,:] alphaslice = self.computealpha(slicexyz) alphavalues.append(alphaslice) alphagrid = torch.stack(alphavalues, dim=0) # Step 8: Coarse smoothing (Kernel 5, Padding 2) alphapooledcoarse = F.maxpool3d( alphagrid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), kernelsize=5, padding=2).squeeze(0).squeeze(0) # Step 9: Thresholding # Default threshold not provided in sources; implementer must supply or tune. alphaMaskthres = 0.01 binarymask = (alphapooledcoarse >= alphaMaskthres).float() # Step 10: Fine smoothing (Kernel 3, Padding 1) binarymaskpooled = F.maxpool3d( binarymask.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), kernelsize=3, padding=1).squeeze(0).squeeze(0) # Step 11: Recalculate AABB validvoxels = torch.nonzero(binarymaskpooled > 0.5) # Guard against empty volume; returns None if no valid voxels exist. if validvoxels.numel() == 0: return None minidx = validvoxels.min(dim=0)[0] maxidx = validvoxels.max(dim=0)[0] newaabbmin = torch.tensor([ minidx[0] / gridsize[0] (self.aabb[1][0] - self.aabb[0][0]) + self.aabb[0][0], minidx[1] / gridsize[1] (self.aabb[1][1] - self.aabb[0][1]) + self.aabb[0][1], minidx[2] / gridsize[2] (self.aabb[1][2] - self.aabb[0][2]) + self.aabb[0][2] ]) newaabbmax = torch.tensor([ maxidx[0] / gridsize[0] (self.aabb[1][0] - self.aabb[0][0]) + self.aabb[0][0], maxidx[1] / gridsize[1] (self.aabb[1][1] - self.aabb[0][1]) + self.aabb[0][1], maxidx[2] / gridsize[2] (self.aabb[1][2] - self.aabb[0][2]) + self.aabb[0][2] ]) newaabb = (newaabbmin, newaabbmax) # Step 12: Return AlphaGridMask return AlphaGridMask(binarymaskpooled, newaabb) Parameters: gridSize: Resolution of the alpha mask grid. Default: (200, 200, 200). alphaMaskthres: Threshold for binarizing alpha values. Values \ge this become 1, < this become 0. updateAlphaMasklist: List of iterations at which to update the mask. Edge Cases: Empty Volume: If no voxels exceed the threshold, the mask is empty. The pseudocode handles this by returning None if validvoxels is empty. Small Resolution: If resocur volume is less than 256^3, the mask resolution is set to resocur. Precision: Linear interpolation and thresholding are sensitive to floating-point precision. Max pooling helps mitigate noise but may blur boundaries. Time Complexity: Dominated by self.computealpha calls for every voxel in the gridSize grid. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: O(gridSize^3) for storing the alpha grid and mask. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively prunes empty space, reducing rendering cost. Max pooling smooths artifacts. Limitations: Requires full evaluation of the density field over the grid. Thresholding is static and may not adapt to complex density variations without tuning. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources.
