name: Adaptive Volume Renderer (AVR)
head: Adapted version of differentiable ray marching algorithm, RM-LSTM based adaptive sampling
body: The Adaptive Volume Renderer (AVR) is a rendering procedure that combines adaptive ray sampling with standard volume rendering to reduce computational cost while maintaining visual quality. It addresses the high latency of standard volume rendering by using a recurrent neural network (RM-LSTM) to predict a surface intersection point, then samples points around that prediction for volume rendering. It sets itself apart from its sibling Raymarcher by performing volume rendering around the predicted depth rather than outputting a single point, achieving comparable quality to standard volume rendering but approximately 7 times faster. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Latent features extracted from a CNN encoder (specifically a pretrained ResNet 34 as used in PixelNeRF). Output: Final RGB color value for the pixel. Data Structures: RM-LSTM State: Hidden state and cell state for the LSTM. Feature Vector: Input to the LSTM, dimension matching the CNN encoder's output. Depth: Scalar value representing the distance along the ray. Parameters: RM-LSTM Feature Channels: 512. RM-LSTM Steps: 10. Volume Rendering Sample Count (n): 10. Sampling Neighborhood Radius: \pm 0.05 around the predicted depth. Depth Bounds: Near plane d{min} = 0.5, Far plane d{max} = 2.0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Feature Extraction: Extract latent features F from the CNN encoder for the input view. 2. Initialization: Initialize the RM-LSTM hidden state h0 and cell state c0 to zeros. Initialize current depth d0 = 0.0. 3. LSTM Prediction Loop: For step t from 1 to 10: Input the latent features F and current depth d{t-1} into the RM-LSTM. Compute new hidden state ht and cell state ct. Predict step length \Delta dt and update depth dt = d{t-1} + \Delta dt. Note: The exact mapping from LSTM output to \Delta dt is a learned transformation not specified in the source. 4. Depth Regularization: If the final predicted depth d{10} falls outside [0.5, 2.0], apply a penalty to the reconstruction loss during training. 5. Sampling: Generate n=10 sample points uniformly distributed within the neighborhood [d{10} - 0.05, d{10} + 0.05]. 6. Volume Rendering: Perform standard discrete volume rendering (alpha compositing) along these 10 sampled points using the neural field to obtain RGB values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def adaptivevolumerenderer(latentfeatures, rmlstmchannels, rmlstmsteps, nsamples, radius, nearplane, farplane): """ Renders a pixel using the Adaptive Volume Renderer method. Args: latentfeatures: Tensor from CNN encoder (ResNet 34). rmlstmchannels: Number of feature channels in RM-LSTM (512). rmlstmsteps: Number of LSTM steps (10). nsamples: Number of volume rendering samples (10). radius: Sampling neighborhood radius (0.05). nearplane: Near plane bound (0.5). farplane: Far plane bound (2.0). Returns: rgb: Final RGB color value. """ # Step 1: Latent features F are extracted from the CNN encoder F = latentfeatures # Step 2: Initialize RM-LSTM hidden and cell states to zeros h = [0.0] rmlstmchannels c = [0.0] rmlstmchannels currentdepth = 0.0 # Initial ray depth # Step 3: RM-LSTM Prediction Loop for t in range(rmlstmsteps): # RM-LSTM internal computation is a learned mapping not specified in the source # It takes F and currentdepth, outputs a step length deltad deltad = 0.0 # Placeholder for learned step prediction currentdepth += deltad # Step 4: Depth regularization penalizes final depth outside [0.5, 2.0] during training loss # Step 5: Sample n points around predicted depth sampledepths = [currentdepth - radius + i (2 radius / (nsamples - 1)) for i in range(nsamples)] # Step 6: Standard volume rendering (discrete alpha compositing) transmittance = 1.0 rgb = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(nsamples): # Query neural field for density sigma and color at sampledepths[i] sigma, color = 0.0, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for neural field query # Compute step size between consecutive samples step = sampledepths[i+1] - sampledepths[i] if i < nsamples - 1 else radius # Update transmittance and accumulate color alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma step) rgb[0] += transmittance alpha color[0] rgb[1] += transmittance alpha color[1] rgb[2] += transmittance alpha color[2] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return rgb Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Bounds: If the predicted depth falls outside [0.5, 2.0], the model may produce incorrect results; the source specifies a regularization term to penalize this during training, but does not define inference-time clamping. Precision: The small neighborhood size (\pm 0.05) requires accurate depth prediction; errors in LSTM prediction may lead to sampling in empty space or incorrect surface regions. Computational Constraints: The number of LSTM steps is fixed at 10 due to computational constraints, which may limit the accuracy of depth prediction for complex scenes. Time Complexity: Approximately 7 times faster than standard volume rendering, achieving 4.2 fps compared to 0.4 fps on the ShapeNet cars dataset. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the LSTM state and the latent features from the CNN encoder; the RM-LSTM uses 512 feature channels. Quality: Achieves comparable quality to standard volume rendering (PSNR 23.22 vs 23.34, SSIM 0.9056 vs 0.9048, LPIPS 0.108 vs 0.111). Comparison to Raymarcher: AVR is slower than the Raymarcher variant (4.2 fps vs 34.9 fps) but achieves better quality (PSNR 23.22 vs 23.02). Strengths: Maintains high visual fidelity while reducing computational cost. Limitations: Requires training a separate LSTM module; performance is dependent on the accuracy of the LSTM depth prediction. The Adaptive Volume Renderer was proposed by Philipp Henzler, Jeremy Reizenstein, Patrick Labatut, Roman Shapovalov, Tobias … as an adaptation of the differentiable ray marching algorithm. It builds on the PixelNeRF architecture, which uses a CNN encoder (pretrained ResNet 34) to extract latent features. The method was evaluated on the ShapeNet cars dataset, with 2150 training cars and 352 test cars, using 8 views per scene. The work was presented in an unofficial source, likely a project report or preprint. name: Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Sampling
head: Hierarchical Sampling, Two-Stage Sampling, Coarse-Fine NeRF
body: Coarse-to-Fine Hierarchical Sampling is a strategy that improves the learning of high-frequency details in Neural Radiance Fields by performing two tiers of volume sampling. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling, where most samples fall in empty space, by using a coarse network to identify opaque regions and then clustering a second set of samples near those regions to train a fine network. It sets itself apart from standard uniform sampling by adaptively concentrating computational effort on visible geometry, and from its sibling TermiNeRF by not explicitly modeling termination probabilities but rather relying on opacity-based importance sampling. The family shares the deviation from a fixed, uniform sampling strategy. Instead of casting a constant number of rays or samples per pixel/ray, the method computes a metric (such as gradient magnitude, rendering error, or temporal difference) and uses it to modulate the sampling rate or resolution. Mathematically, this often involves a control loop: 1. Metric Evaluation: Compute a scalar value M representing local complexity or error. 2. Adaptation: Adjust a parameter P (step size \Delta t, resolution R, or sampling probability w) based on M. 3. Rendering/Training: Execute the volume integral or loss computation with the adjusted parameter. Common adaptation laws include: Step Size Adaptation: \Delta t \propto \frac{1}{M} or \Delta t = \min(\Delta t{max}, \max(\Delta t{min}, \frac{k}{M})). Resolution Control: R{new} = R{old} + \alpha \cdot (t{target} - t{actual}) or threshold-based switching. Probability Weighting: wi \propto Mi for importance sampling. All methods in this family aim to maintain visual fidelity while reducing the total number of volume queries. Uses a coarse MLP to generate weights, then samples fine points from the resulting PDF. It sets itself apart by using a separate fine network trained jointly with the coarse one, relying on density-based heuristics rather than learned proposals. Choose when you need a simple, effective baseline for high-frequency detail recovery without complex architectural changes. Trains a dedicated sampling network to predict importance weights for fixed bins, replacing the heuristic coarse-to-fine step. It sets itself apart by using a single evaluation of a sampling network per ray to predict weights, rather than hierarchical refinement. Choose when you want to eliminate the non-differentiable sampling step and optimize the sampling distribution directly. Replaces heuristic sampling with a differentiable 'proposer' module that outputs fine sample locations from coarse features. It sets itself apart by enabling end-to-end training of the entire system (coarse, proposer, fine) to improve view synthesis quality. Choose when you need a fully differentiable pipeline that learns optimal sampling locations rather than relying on opacity-based PDFs. The concept was introduced in the original NeRF paper (Mildenhall et al., 2020) as a way to mitigate the inefficiency of uniform sampling. It became a standard component in subsequent NeRF variants due to its ability to allocate samples to geometrically relevant regions. Mildenhall, B., et al. name: Coarse-to-Fine NeRF
head: Coarse-Fine NeRF, Hierarchical Rendering (Original NeRF), Two-Stage NeRF
body: Coarse-to-Fine NeRF is a hierarchical sampling strategy that improves the learning of high-frequency details in Neural Radiance Fields by performing two tiers of volume sampling. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling, where most samples fall in empty space, by using a coarse network to identify opaque regions and then clustering a second set of samples near those regions to train a fine network. It sets itself apart from standard uniform sampling by adaptively concentrating computational effort on visible geometry, and from its sibling TermiNeRF by not explicitly modeling termination probabilities but rather relying on opacity-based importance sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray directions \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3, near bound t{near}, far bound t{far}, number of coarse samples Nc, number of fine samples Nf. Outputs: Rendered RGB color \mathbf{C}(\mathbf{r}), depth map, accumulated alpha, and weights for both coarse and fine passes. Data Structures: Networks: Two separate Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs), networkcoarse and networkfine. Both share the same architecture (hidden dimensions, layers) but have distinct parameters. Positional Encoding: Input coordinates are encoded using positional encoding with poslevels (default 10) and view directions with dirlevels (default 4). Raw Output Tensor: For each sample, the network outputs a tensor of shape (raycount, samplecount, 4). The first 3 channels are RGB (sigmoided to [0,1]), and the 4th channel is the raw volume density \sigma. Parameters: ncoarse: Number of coarse samples per ray. Default: 64. nfine: Number of fine samples per ray. Default: 128. perturb: Boolean flag to enable stratified jittering during coarse sampling. Default: True. rawnoisestd: Standard deviation of uniform noise added to volume density before ReLU. Default: 0. whitebkgd: Boolean flag. If True, adds unaccounted transmittance to RGB assuming a white background. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Generate Nc depth values tc uniformly spaced between t{near} and t{far}. If perturb is True, apply stratified sampling by adding uniform noise \mathcal{U}[0, 1] to break symmetry and reduce aliasing. 2. Coarse Query: Convert depth values to 3D points \mathbf{p}c = \mathbf{o} + tc \mathbf{d}. Query networkcoarse with \mathbf{p}c and encoded directions to obtain raw outputs \mathbf{raw}c. 3. Coarse Rendering: Convert \mathbf{raw}c to alpha compositing weights wc using volume rendering equations. Compute the coarse RGB color \mathbf{C}c and depth. 4. Hierarchical Sampling: Use the coarse weights wc to define a probability distribution. Sample Nf new depth values tf from this distribution using inverse transform sampling (or samplepdf). Pitfall: The sampling step is non-differentiable. Gradients must not flow back through this step to the coarse network. The coarse samples/weights used for fine sampling must be detached from the computation graph. 5. Fine Sampling Preparation: Concatenate coarse and fine depth values: t{fine\all} = \text{sort}([tc, tf]). Convert these to 3D points \mathbf{p}{fine\all}. 6. Fine Query: Query networkfine with \mathbf{p}{fine\all} and encoded directions to obtain \mathbf{raw}f. 7. Fine Rendering: Convert \mathbf{raw}f to weights wf and compute the final RGB color \mathbf{C}f. Formulas: Distance between samples: \deltai = z{i+1} - zi An infinite distance (10^{10}) is appended to the last column to ensure the opacity of the last segment is 1. Alpha (Opacity): \alpha = 1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \delta) Where \sigma is the volume density from the network output, optionally perturbed by noise \mathcal{U}[0,1] if rawnoisestd > 0, and passed through ReLU. Transmittance: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) Computed as the cumulative product of (1 - \alpha), prepended with 1. The last column is discarded. Weights: wi = \alphai \cdot Ti RGB Rendering: \mathbf{C} = \sum{i=1}^{N} wi \mathbf{c}i If whitebkgd is True: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C} + (1 - \sum wi) \cdot \mathbf{1}. Loss Function: L = L{coarse} + L{fine} L{coarse} = \text{mean}((\mathbf{C}{coarse} - \mathbf{C}{target})^2) L{fine} = \text{mean}((\mathbf{C}{fine} - \mathbf{C}{target})^2) Both networks are supervised against the target pixel color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def raw2outputs(raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd=0, whitebkgd=False): """ Converts raw network outputs to radiance and weights. raw: (raycount, samplecount, 4) -> RGB (0-1) and sigma zvals: (raycount, samplecount) raysd: (raycount, 3) """ # Calculate distances between samples dists = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] # Append infinite distance for the last segment dists = torch.cat([dists, torch.fulllike(dists[...,:1], 1e10)], dim=-1) # Scale by ray direction norm dists = dists torch.norm(raysd[..., None,:], dim=-1) # Extract RGB and Sigma rgb = torch.sigmoid(raw[...,:3]) sigmaraw = raw[..., 3] # Add noise to sigma if specified noise = 0. if rawnoisestd > 0.: noise = torch.randnlike(sigmaraw) rawnoisestd # Apply ReLU and compute alpha sigma = F.relu(sigmaraw + noise) alpha = 1. - torch.exp(-sigma dists) # Compute transmittance T # Ti = prod{j<i} (1 - alphaj) transmittanceprev = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(alpha[...,:1]), 1. - alpha + 1e-10], dim=-1) T = torch.cumprod(transmittanceprev, dim=-1)[...,:-1] # Compute weights weights = alpha T # Render RGB rgbmap = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgb, dim=-2) # Render Depth depthmap = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=-1) # Accumulated Alpha accmap = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) # White background if whitebkgd: rgbmap = rgbmap + (1. - accmap[..., None]) return rgbmap, depthmap, accmap, weights def stratifiedsample(near, far, Nc, rayo, rayd, perturb=True): """ Uniform stratified sampling along rays. Returns: pts (B, Nc, 3), dirs (B, Nc, 3), tvals (B, Nc) """ device = rayo.device tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, Nc, device=device) tvals = tvals.expand(rayo.shape[:-1], Nc) if perturb: mid = (tvals[...,:-1] + tvals[..., 1:]) / 2.0 upper = torch.cat([mid, tvals[..., -1:]], dim=-1) lower = torch.cat([tvals[...,:1], mid], dim=-1) tvals = lower + (upper - lower) torch.randlike(tvals) pts = rayo.unsqueeze(-2) + rayd.unsqueeze(-2) tvals.unsqueeze(-1) dirs = rayd.unsqueeze(-2).expandas(pts) return pts, dirs, tvals def samplepdf(bins, weights, Nf, perturb=True): """ Hierarchical sampling based on coarse weights. bins: (B, Nc) sorted depth values from coarse pass weights: (B, Nc) alpha compositing weights from coarse pass Returns: tfine (B, Nf) """ # Get midpoints of coarse bins for PDF definition # weights[i] corresponds to the segment between bins[i] and bins[i+1] # We need to handle the last segment or use the provided bins as boundaries # Calculate PDF from weights # weights shape: (B, Nc). bins shape: (B, Nc) # The weight wi is for the interval [bins[i], bins[i+1]]? # In standard NeRF implementation, weights are computed for samples at bins. # We construct a CDF from weights and sample from it. # Normalize weights to sum to 1 per ray weights = weights + 1e-5 # prevent NaN pdf = weights / torch.sum(weights, dim=-1, keepdim=True) cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Sample uniform values u = torch.rand(cdf.shape[:-1], Nf, device=weights.device) # Inverse transform sampling # Find indices where cdf < u indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf[...,:-1], u, right=True) # Clamp indices indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, cdf.shape[-2] - 2) # Linear interpolation within bins g = indices.float() binlow = bins[torch.arange(cdf.shape[0]).unsqueeze(-1), indices] binhigh = bins[torch.arange(cdf.shape[0]).unsqueeze(-1), indices + 1] # Normalize u to the bin's CDF range cdflow = cdf[torch.arange(cdf.shape[0]).unsqueeze(-1), indices] cdfhigh = cdf[torch.arange(cdf.shape[0]).unsqueeze(-1), indices + 1] t = binlow + (binhigh - binlow) ((u - cdflow) / (cdfhigh - cdflow + 1e-5)) if perturb: # Add jitter dists = binhigh - binlow t = t + torch.randlike(t) dists return t def renderrays(rayso, raysd, networkcoarse, networkfine, near, far, ncoarse=64, nfine=128, rawnoisestd=0, whitebkgd=False, perturb=True): """ Full coarse-to-fine rendering pipeline. """ # 1. Coarse Sampling ptscoarse, dirscoarse, tcoarse = stratifiedsample( near, far, ncoarse, rayso, raysd, perturb) # 2. Coarse Query # Assume network takes (pts, dirs) and returns raw (B, N, 4) rawcoarse = networkcoarse(ptscoarse, dirscoarse) # 3. Coarse Rendering rgbcoarse, depthcoarse, acccoarse, weightscoarse = raw2outputs( rawcoarse, tcoarse, raysd, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd) # 4. Hierarchical Sampling # Detach to prevent gradient flow from fine to coarse sampling logic weightscoarsedetached = weightscoarse.detach() tcoarsedetached = tcoarse.detach() tfine = samplepdf(tcoarsedetached, weightscoarsedetached, nfine, perturb) # 5. Fine Sampling Preparation tfineall = torch.cat([tcoarsedetached, tfine], dim=-1) tfineall, = torch.sort(tfineall, dim=-1) ptsfineall = rayso.unsqueeze(-2) + raysd.unsqueeze(-2) tfineall.unsqueeze(-1) dirsfineall = raysd.unsqueeze(-2).expandas(ptsfineall) # 6. Fine Query rawfine = networkfine(ptsfineall, dirsfineall) # 7. Fine Rendering rgbfine, depthfine, accfine, weightsfine = raw2outputs( rawfine, tfineall, raysd, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd) return { 'rgbcoarse': rgbcoarse, 'depthcoarse': depthcoarse, 'rgbfine': rgbfine, 'depthfine': depthfine, 'weightscoarse': weightscoarse, 'weightsfine': weightsfine } A variant that uses a single MLP with parameters \Theta for both coarse and fine stages, enabled by Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) which explicitly encodes scale into input features. Unlike standard NeRF which requires two distinct MLPs because standard PE only models one scale, this approach allows one MLP to learn a multiscale representation. The optimization balances coarse and fine losses using a hyperparameter \lambda (default 0.1). A strategy that selectively increases the sampling rate only within the bounding box of an object area to ensure detailed sampling without significantly increasing overall computational cost. It addresses the pitfall where standard uniform sampling results in sparse points on small objects relative to the scene, causing missing areas in rendered images due to inaccurate PDF in the fine stage. A method used in DONeRF to translate depth oracle classification outputs into sample locations. It treats the classified depth output vector from a single oracle network evaluation as a piecewise-constant Probability Density Function (PDF) and samples from its Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF). Unlike standard NeRF which builds a PDF from opacity outputs of a coarse shading network evaluated at multiple locations, this uses the oracle's direct output. Time Complexity: O(Nc + Nf) network queries per ray, where Nc is coarse samples and Nf is fine samples. Typically Nc=64, Nf=128. Memory Complexity: Stores outputs for both coarse and fine passes. The compute graph must be static; the coarse-to-fine edge is cut via.detach() to prevent cyclic definitions. Performance: Improves detail learning by clustering samples near opaque regions, unlike evenly distributed sampling. It prevents dense sampling at fine scales in empty space, improving computational efficiency compared to uniformly dense sampling. Strengths: Better reconstruction of high-frequency details; efficient use of samples by focusing on geometry. Limitations: Requires two network passes (or two networks); non-differentiable sampling step breaks gradient flow from fine to coarse. Coarse-to-Fine NeRF, also known as Hierarchical Rendering, was introduced in the original NeRF paper by Mildenhall et al.. It was designed to improve computational efficiency and rendering quality by using a coarse network to guide the sampling of a fine network. The method has become a standard component in many subsequent NeRF variants. name: Hexagonal Multisampling Pattern Derivation
head: Conical frustum multisampling, Cylindrical multisampling pattern
body: This method constructs a multisampling pattern for a conical frustum by first generating a zero-mean, identity-covariance pattern for a cylinder and then warping it to match the frustum's analytical mean and covariance. It ensures uniform distribution along the ray and in angles around the ray while minimizing the number of samples for efficiency. It differs from siblings like DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering by explicitly matching statistical moments of the conical frustum rather than filtering depth estimates, and from Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts by using a fixed hexagonal geometry derived from cylindrical symmetry rather than hemispherical wavefronts. Inputs: n: Number of samples (fixed to 6). \mathbf{c}: Center of the conical frustum (mean position). \mathbf{\Sigma}: Covariance matrix of the conical frustum. \mathbf{R}: Rotation matrix aligning the cylinder's local z-axis with the ray direction. Outputs: \mathbf{x}j \in \mathbb{R}^3: The j-th sample position in world space, for j = 0, \dots, n-1. Data Structures: theta1: Array of 6 angles [0, 2\pi/3, 4\pi/3, \pi, 5\pi/3, \pi/3]. cylsamples: Array of 6 vectors \mathbf{y}j \in \mathbb{R}^3 representing the canonical cylinder pattern. Steps: 1. Construct Canonical Cylinder Pattern: Generate n=6 points \mathbf{y}j in a local coordinate system where the cylinder axis aligns with the z-axis. The coordinates are defined as: \mathbf{y}j = \begin{bmatrix} \cos (\thetaj)/\sqrt {3} \\ \sin (\thetaj)/\sqrt {3} \\ \frac {j - (n-1)/2}{\sqrt {n(n^2-1)/12}} \end{bmatrix} where \thetaj are taken from theta1. This pattern has a mean of \mathbf{0} and a covariance of I3 (identity matrix). 2. Compute Warping Parameters: Determine the scaling and translation required to map the canonical cylinder to the target conical frustum. The target frustum has mean \mathbf{c} and covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}. The canonical cylinder has mean \mathbf{0} and covariance I3. 3. Warp Samples: Transform each canonical sample \mathbf{y}j to the world space sample \mathbf{x}j. The transformation aligns the cylinder's principal axes with the eigenvectors of \mathbf{\Sigma} and scales them by the square roots of the eigenvalues, then translates by \mathbf{c}. Specifically, if \mathbf{\Sigma} = \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{\Lambda} \mathbf{Q}^T is the eigendecomposition, the transformation is: \mathbf{x}j = \mathbf{c} + \mathbf{Q} \mathbf{\Lambda}^{1/2} \mathbf{R} \mathbf{y}j where \mathbf{R} rotates the canonical cylinder's z-axis to align with the primary direction of the frustum (typically the ray direction). In the context of mip-NeRF, the frustum is oriented along the ray, so \mathbf{R} aligns the local z-axis with the ray direction vector. 4. Return Samples: Return the set \{\mathbf{x}0, \dots, \mathbf{x}{n-1}\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def hexagonalmultisamplingpattern(n=6): """ Generates the canonical hexagonal multisampling pattern for a cylinder. Returns the n sample coordinates in local cylinder space. """ # Angles from theta1 theta1 = np.array([0, 2np.pi/3, 4np.pi/3, np.pi, 5np.pi/3, np.pi/3]) samples = [] for j in range(n): # x component x = np.cos(theta1[j]) / np.sqrt(3) # y component y = np.sin(theta1[j]) / np.sqrt(3) # z component (along the cylinder axis) z = (j - (n - 1) / 2) / np.sqrt(n (n2 - 1) / 12) samples.append([x, y, z]) return np.array(samples) def warptoconicalfrustum(cylsamples, mean, cov, raydirection): """ Warps canonical cylinder samples to match a conical frustum defined by mean and covariance. Args: cylsamples: (n, 3) array of canonical cylinder samples. mean: (3,) array, center of the frustum. cov: (3, 3) array, covariance matrix of the frustum. raydirection: (3,) array, unit vector along the ray. Returns: (n, 3) array of warped samples in world space. """ # Eigendecomposition of the frustum covariance eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(cov) # Square root of eigenvalues for scaling sqrteigenvalues = np.sqrt(eigenvalues) # Construct scaling matrix S = np.diag(sqrteigenvalues) # Rotation matrix to align canonical cylinder z-axis with ray direction canonicalz = np.array([0, 0, 1]) if np.allclose(raydirection, canonicalz): R = np.eye(3) elif np.allclose(raydirection, -canonicalz): # Rotate 180 degrees around x-axis R = np.diag([1, -1, -1]) else: # General case: rotate canonicalz to raydirection using Rodrigues' formula v1 = canonicalz v2 = raydirection cross = np.cross(v1, v2) dot = np.dot(v1, v2) skew = np.array([ [0, -cross[2], cross[1]], [cross[2], 0, -cross[0]], [-cross[1], cross[0], 0] ]) R = np.eye(3) + skew + skew @ skew (1 / (1 + dot)) # Combined transformation matrix: T = Q S R T = eigenvectors @ S @ R # Transform samples: x = mean + T @ y warpedsamples = (cylsamples @ T.T) + mean return warpedsamples Parameters: n=6: The number of samples. This is the smallest number that allows for a zero-mean, identity-covariance pattern with the specified angular distribution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No samples are placed exactly along the ray; they are distributed at a distance proportional to the cone radius. The full covariance matrices of the samples and the frustum are not necessarily identical, but variance along the ray and total variance perpendicular to the ray are equal. The mismatch goes to zero as t \gg \dot{r}. The pattern relies on specific angular choices (\theta1 or \theta2) to maintain the zero-mean and identity-covariance property for n=6. Using other angles or n values will break these properties. Filters depth estimates to improve sampling. Choose when depth uncertainty is high and analytical covariance is less reliable. Samples hemispherical wavefronts. Choose when rendering scenes with significant hemispherical illumination or when the conical frustum approximation is insufficient for large angles. Time Complexity: O(n) where n=6. The warping involves a fixed number of matrix-vector multiplications. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store the samples. Strengths: Efficient (only 6 samples), matches analytical moments of the conical frustum, ensures uniform angular and axial distribution. Limitations: Does not place samples on the ray axis, which may be suboptimal for some scenes. The covariance mismatch, though small, exists. When to use: When rendering with conical frustums and efficiency is critical, and the frustum is not extremely wide (t \gg \dot{r}). When not to use: When high accuracy on the ray axis is required, or when the frustum is very wide and the covariance mismatch becomes significant. The method was introduced in the context of Mip-NeRF to improve the accuracy of volume rendering by better approximating the integral over a conical frustum. It is based on the Unscented Transform, which uses a minimal set of samples to capture the mean and covariance of a random variable. The specific hexagonal pattern was derived to satisfy the criteria of uniform distribution and moment matching with the smallest number of points. name: DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering
head: Classified Depth Oracle, Depth smoothing filter, Neighborhood filter
body: DONeRF Depth Oracle Filtering is a preprocessing step applied to the training targets of the depth oracle network to improve surface detection consistency and reduce false negatives. It operates by smoothing classification targets in image and depth space, unlike Hexagonal Multisampling Pattern Derivation which derives sampling patterns directly, and unlike Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts which focuses on wavefronts. Trade-offs are detailed in Operating characteristics. The method filters the ground-truth classification targets generated for the depth oracle network. The oracle predicts a likelihood for each discretized segment along a ray, where a high value indicates the segment should receive samples and a low value indicates it should be skipped. Input: The unfiltered one-hot classification target C{x,y}(z) for each pixel (x,y) and discretized depth segment z. Output: The filtered classification target \hat{C}{x,y}(z) used for training the depth oracle network. Note: Filtering is applied only to training targets; no filtering is performed during inference. The classification target is a 3D array indexed by pixel coordinates (x,y) and depth segment index z. C{x,y}(z): Binary value (0 or 1). ds: Depth of the first surface along the ray. dz, d{z+1}: Discretization boundaries for segment z. The unfiltered target is a one-hot encoding: C{x,y}(z) = \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } dz \leq ds < d{z+1} \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where ds is the depth of the first surface, and dz, d{z+1} are the boundaries of the discretized segment z. The filtering consists of two stages: a 2D spatial neighborhood filter and a 1D depth-axis smoothing filter. 1. 2D Neighborhood Filter (Radial): Applies a radial filter to include values from neighboring rays with a contribution weighted by their distance. For a filter size K, the intermediate target \hat{C}{x,y}(z) is computed as: \hat{C}{x,y}(z) = \max{i,j \in \pm \lfloor K/2 \rfloor} \left( C{x+i,y+j}(z) - \frac{\sqrt{2+j^2}}{\sqrt{2 \cdot \lfloor K/2 \rfloor}} \right) Here, i and j are offsets in the x and y directions. The term \frac{\sqrt{2+j^2}}{\sqrt{2 \cdot \lfloor K/2 \rfloor}} represents the distance penalty. For a 5 \times 5 filter (K=5), rays at distances 3, 2, 1, 0 pixels contribute 0, ≈0.30, ≈0.65, 1 respectively. For multiple depth values with the same discretization result, the maximum result is taken to ensure the largest value is placed at the actual surface. 2. 1D Depth Smoothing Filter: Applies a 1D triangle filter along the depth axis with kernel size Z: \hat{C}(z) = \min \left( \sum{i=-\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor}^{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor} \hat{C}(z+i) \frac{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1 - |i|}{\lfloor Z/2 \rfloor + 1}, 1 \right) This acts as label smoothing, blurring depth values to help the oracle predict consistent outputs at depth discontinuities. Filter Size K: Size of the 2D spatial filter. Example: K=5. Kernel Size Z: Size of the 1D depth filter. Example: Z=5. Loss Function: Binary Cross-Entropy (BCE). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def filterdepthoracletargets(C, K, Z): """ Filters the depth oracle classification targets. Args: C: 3D list of shape (H, W, D) containing binary classification targets. C[x][y][z] is 1 if the surface is in segment z, else 0. K: Integer, size of the 2D spatial filter (must be odd). Z: Integer, size of the 1D depth filter (must be odd). Returns: filteredC: 3D list of shape (H, W, D) with filtered targets. """ H, W, D = len(C), len(C[0]), len(C[0][0]) # Step 1: 2D Neighborhood Filter step1 = [[[-float('inf')] D for in range(W)] for in range(H)] halfK = K // 2 denom2d = math.sqrt(2 halfK) for x in range(H): for y in range(W): for z in range(D): maxval = -float('inf') for i in range(-halfK, halfK + 1): for j in range(-halfK, halfK + 1): nx, ny = x + i, y + j if 0 <= nx < H and 0 <= ny < W: weight = math.sqrt(2 + j2) / denom2d val = C[nx][ny][z] - weight if val > maxval: maxval = val step1[x][y][z] = maxval # Step 2: 1D Depth Smoothing Filter filteredC = [[[0.0] D for in range(W)] for in range(H)] halfZ = Z // 2 for x in range(H): for y in range(W): for z in range(D): sumval = 0.0 for i in range(-halfZ, halfZ + 1): nz = z + i if 0 <= nz < D: weight = (halfZ + 1 - abs(i)) / (halfZ + 1) sumval += step1[x][y][nz] weight filteredC[x][y][z] = min(sumval, 1.0) return filteredC Filter Size: Using an even larger filter size than recommended (e.g., K > 5) may reduce overall quality because it places many samples in empty space rather than on the surface. False Positives vs Negatives: Filtering increases false positives (sampling regions that do not need samples) but decreases false negatives (missing surfaces). This is acceptable because the local raymarching network handles empty space (no image contribution), while missing surfaces clearly reduces image quality. Inference: No filtering is done during inference; the filter is strictly for training target generation. Performance Gain: The neighborhood filter adds 1.3 dB–1.8 dB to PSNR, and the depth smoothing filter adds 0.1 dB, measured on test scenes with configuration K=5, Z=5, I=128 compared to the baseline. Cost: The filtering adds no inference cost as it is applied only to training targets. Scaling: The method scales with the filter sizes K and Z during target generation; larger filters increase computational cost and may degrade quality if too large. DONeRF (Depth Oracle Networks) was introduced to enable real-time rendering of compact neural radiance fields. The depth oracle filtering technique was developed to address the difficulty of training the oracle to predict consistent outputs at depth discontinuities by providing a multi-class target that is filtered in image-space and along the depth axis. name: Hierarchical Sampling for Hemispherical Wavefronts
head: Coarse-to-Fine Hemispherical Sampling, NeTF Hierarchical Sampling
body: This method is a coarse-to-fine sampling scheme for 2D hemispherical wavefronts used in Non-Line-of-Sight (NLOS) imaging to balance reconstruction quality and computational overhead. It addresses the intractability of explicit volumetric resampling on a hemisphere by using a differentiable hierarchical approach, distinct from the 1D ray sampling used in NeRF. Inputs: Detection spot coordinates (x', y') and time t. Coarse network parameters. Fine network parameters. Number of coarse samples Nc^2. Number of fine samples Nf. Radius r of the hemispherical wavefront. Outputs: Estimated transient \tau(x', y', t). Data Structures: Coarse samples: Set of Nc^2 uniform points on the hemisphere, defined by spherical coordinates (\theta, \phi). Fine samples: Set of Nf points generated via Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), defined by (\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f). PDF K(\theta, \phi): Probability density function estimated by the coarse network for importance sampling. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc^2 uniform scene points in the hemisphere. 2. Coarse Evaluation: Evaluate the coarse network at these points using the estimated PDF k(\theta, \phi) to compute the coarse integral \tauc(x', y', t). 3. Fine Sampling (MCMC): Employ the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm with a conditional Gaussian distribution for state transition of the Markov chain to produce Nf fine scene points along hemispherical wavefronts intersecting the NLOS scene. 4. Fine Evaluation: Compute the fine integral \tauf(x', y', t) using the fine samples and the PDF K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f). 5. Combination: Combine coarse and fine samples (Nc^2 + Nf) to re-evaluate reconstruction quality from the fine network, calculating the final transient as the average of the coarse and fine integrals. Formulas: The final transient is the average of the coarse and fine estimates: \tau(x', y', t) = \frac{\tauc(x', y', t) + \tauf(x', y', t)}{2} The fine integral is estimated as: \tauf(x', y', t) = \frac{1}{r^4} \sum{i,j} \frac{\sigma(r, \theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f) \rho(r, \theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f)}{K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f)} Where: \tauc(x', y', t) is the integral estimated with coarse samples Nc^2. \tauf(x', y', t) is the transient estimated with Nf samples from MCMC. K(\theta{ij}^f, \phi{ij}^f) is the PDF used for importance sampling in the MCMC fine sampling step. \sigma and \rho are volume density and emission/reflectance properties evaluated at the fine sample points. r is the radius of the hemispherical wavefront. head: Proposal Sampling, Proposal sampler, Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Network
body: Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling is a multi-level volumetric rendering strategy that uses a cascade of proposal networks to sample ray intervals, dilating weights to reduce aliasing, and integrating positional encoding (IPE) via Gaussian casting. It solves the problem of aliasing and inefficient sampling in unbounded scenes by learning a density function that guides the placement of fine samples toward opaque regions, while using a specific resampling procedure to ensure fine intervals cover the support of coarse histograms. The method consists of a proposal network \Theta{\text{prop}} and a main NeRF network \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. The proposal network learns a mapping from 3D positions to density, \Theta{\text{prop}}: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, \vec{p} \mapsto \sigma, which is optimized concurrently with the main NeRF to bound the weights produced by \Theta{\text{NeRF}}. The sampling process operates in levels. For each ray, the algorithm performs multiple rounds of proposal sampling followed by a final NeRF rendering round. Inputs: Ray origins, directions, near/far bounds. Camera intrinsics (for ray warping). Training fraction (for annealing). Hyperparameters: numlevels, numpropsamples, numnerfsamples, dilationbias, dilationmultiplier, annealslope, resamplepadding, singlejitter, stoplevelgrad, nearannealrate, nearannealinit. Outputs: Rendered color and auxiliary variables (depth, normal, etc.) for the final level. History of distances and weights from all levels for gradient computation. Distances (sdist): Tensor of shape (batch, 2 numsamples + 1) representing the endpoints of intervals in normalized distance space s \in [0, 1]. The values are sorted. Weights (weights): Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples) representing the opacity contribution of each interval. Proposal Network (propmlp): A small MLP with 4 layers and 256 hidden units, mapping 3D coordinates to density \sigma. If singlemlp is True, this shares weights with nerfmlp. Ray Warp Function (stot): A mapping from normalized distance s to metric distance t, computed using the ray distance function and near/far bounds. 1. Initialization: Compute the ray warp function stot mapping normalized distance s to metric distance t. Initialize initsnear to 0.0 if nearannealrate is None, otherwise initsnear = clip(1 - train\frac / near\anneal\rate, 0, near\anneal\init). Set initsfar to 1.0. Concatenate initsnear and initsfar to form initial sdist with shape (batch, 2). Initialize weights to ones with shape (batch,). Set prodnumsamples = 1. 2. Iterate over Levels: Loop over level index ilevel from 0 to numlevels - 1. Determine if current level is a proposal level: isprop = ilevel < (numlevels - 1). Set numsamples: if isprop, use numpropsamples (default 64); else use numnerfsamples (default 32). 3. Dilate Weights (if not first level): If ilevel > 0 and dilation is active (dilationbias > 0 or dilationmultiplier > 0): Calculate dilation factor: dilation = dilationbias + dilationmultiplier (initsfar - initsnear) / prodnumsamples. Update prodnumsamples = numsamples. Dilate weights: Call stepfun.maxdilateweights(sdist, weights, dilation, domain=(initsnear, initsfar), renormalize=True). Slice sdist and weights to remove first and last elements: sdist = sdist[..., 1:-1], weights = weights[..., 1:-1]. 4. Compute Annealing Factor: If annealslope > 0: Define bias function: \text{bias}(x, s) = \frac{s \cdot x}{(s - 1) \cdot x + 1}. Compute anneal = bias(trainfrac, annealslope). Else, anneal = 1.0. 5. Compute Resampling Logits: Calculate logits for sampling new intervals: \text{logits\resample}i = \begin{cases} \text{anneal} \cdot \log(\text{weights}i + \text{resample\padding}) & \text{if } \text{sdist}{i+1} > \text{sdist}i \\ -\infty & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where resamplepadding is added for stability (default 0.0). 6. Sample New Intervals (Resampling): Split RNG key. Call stepfun.sampleintervals(key, sdist, logitsresample, numsamples, singlejitter=singlejitter, domain=(initsnear, initsfar), usegpuresampling=usegpuresampling). This function samples n sorted values from the coarse histogram weights. It uses the midpoints of each adjacent sample pair as the endpoints of the new set of "fine" intervals. It reflects the first and last sample around the first and last endpoint to deal with boundary conditions. If stoplevelgrad is True, apply sdist = jax.lax.stopgradient(sdist). 7. Convert to Metric Distance: Compute tdist = stot(sdist). 8. Cast Rays and Evaluate MLP: Cast rays to Gaussians using tdist, origins, directions, and rayshape (default 'cone'). Split RNG key. Evaluate MLP (propmlp if proposal, nerfmlp if final): Input: Gaussian cast positions, view directions (if useviewdirs), image plane, exposure. Output: Density \sigma and RGB color. 9. Compute Alpha Weights: Compute weights using the formula: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where Ti = \exp(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj) is the transmittance, \sigmai is the density, and \deltai is the distance between sample points. Call computealphaweights(density, tdist, directions, opaquebackground). 10. Determine Background Color: If bgintensityrange[0] == bgintensityrange[1], bgrgbs is that scalar. Else if rng is None, bgrgbs is the midpoint. Else, sample bgrgbs uniformly from the range. 11. Volumetric Rendering: Call volumetricrendering(rgb, weights, tdist, bgrgbs, far, computeextras, extras). 12. Store History: Append rendering to renderings. Copy sdist and weights to rayresults. Append rayresults to rayhistory. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def mipnerf360proposalsampling( origins, directions, near, far, viewdirs, imageplane, exposurevalues, nerfmlp, propmlp, config, trainfrac, rng): batchsize = origins.shape[0] # 1. Initialization # Ray warp: linear mapping from normalized s to metric t def stot(s): return near + s (far - near) if config.nearannealrate is None: initsnear = 0.0 else: initsnear = np.clip(1.0 - trainfrac / config.nearannealrate, 0.0, config.nearannealinit) initsfar = 1.0 sdist = np.concatenate([np.full((batchsize, 1), initsnear), np.full((batchsize, 1), initsfar)], axis=-1) weights = np.ones(batchsize) prodnumsamples = 1 renderings = [] rayhistory = [] # 2. Iterate over levels for ilevel in range(config.numlevels): isprop = ilevel < (config.numlevels - 1) numsamples = config.numpropsamples if isprop else config.numnerfsamples # 3. Dilate weights (if not first level) if ilevel > 0 and (config.dilationbias > 0 or config.dilationmultiplier > 0): dilation = config.dilationbias + config.dilationmultiplier (initsfar - initsnear) / prodnumsamples prodnumsamples = numsamples # Dilate intervals and renormalize weights midpoints = (sdist[:,:-1] + sdist[:, 1:]) / 2.0 halfwidths = (sdist[:, 1:] - sdist[:,:-1]) / 2.0 newhalfwidths = halfwidths + dilation newsdist = np.concatenate([ np.maximum(midpoints - newhalfwidths, initsnear), np.minimum(midpoints + newhalfwidths, initsfar) ], axis=-1) weights = weights / np.sum(weights) sdist = newsdist # Slice to remove first and last elements sdist = sdist[:, 1:-1] weights = weights[1:-1] # 4. Compute Annealing Factor if config.annealslope > 0: bias = lambda x, s: (s x) / ((s - 1) x + 1) anneal = bias(trainfrac, config.annealslope) else: anneal = 1.0 # 5. Compute Resampling Logits valid = sdist[:, 1:] > sdist[:,:-1] logitsresample = np.where( valid, anneal np.log(weights + config.resamplepadding), -np.inf) # 6. Sample New Intervals (Resampling) # Split RNG key (simplified for pseudocode) rng, key = np.random.RandomState(), np.random.RandomState() # Resampling procedure from: probs = logitsresample - np.max(logitsresample, axis=-1, keepdims=True) probs = np.exp(probs) probs = probs / np.sum(probs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) indices = np.random.choice(sdist.shape[1] - 1, size=numsamples, p=probs, replace=True) indices = np.sort(indices, axis=-1) newsdist = (sdist[:, indices] + sdist[:, indices + 1]) / 2.0 newsdist[:, 0] = 2.0 sdist[:, 0] - newsdist[:, 0] newsdist[:, -1] = 2.0 sdist[:, -1] - newsdist[:, -1] newsdist = np.clip(np.sort(newsdist, axis=-1), initsnear, initsfar) sdist = newsdist if config.stoplevelgrad: sdist = sdist.copy() # 7. Convert to Metric Distance tdist = stot(sdist) # 8. Cast Rays and Evaluate MLP gaussians = tdist mlp = propmlp if isprop else nerfmlp rayresults = mlp(gaussians, viewdirs=viewdirs if config.useviewdirs else None, imageplane=imageplane, exposure=exposurevalues) # 9. Compute Alpha Weights density = rayresults['density'] deltas = np.diff(tdist, axis=-1) transmittance = np.exp(-np.cumsum(density[:,:-1] deltas, axis=-1)) transmittance = np.concatenate([np.ones((batchsize, 1)), transmittance], axis=-1) weights = transmittance (1.0 - np.exp(-density deltas)) # 10. Determine Background Color if config.bgintensityrange[0] == config.bgintensityrange[1]: bgrgbs = config.bgintensityrange[0] elif rng is None: bgrgbs = (config.bgintensityrange[0] + config.bgintensityrange[1]) / 2.0 else: bgrgbs = np.random.uniform(config.bgintensityrange[0], config.bgintensityrange[1], size=(batchsize, 3)) # 11. Volumetric Rendering rendering = np.sum(weights[:,:, np.newaxis] rayresults['rgb'], axis=1) + bgrgbs # 12. Store History renderings.append(rendering) rayresults['sdist'] = sdist rayresults['weights'] = weights rayhistory.append(rayresults) return renderings, rayhistory numpropsamples: 64. numnerfsamples: 32. numlevels: 3 (2 proposals, 1 NeRF). dilationmultiplier: 0.5. dilationbias: 0.0025. annealslope: 10. stoplevelgrad: True. resamplepadding: 0.0. singlejitter: True. rayshape: 'cone'. nearannealinit: 0.95. nearannealrate: None (optional). Boundary Conditions: The resampling procedure reflects the first and last sample around the first and last endpoint to handle boundary conditions, preventing aliasing that occurs when samples do not span the extent of coarse histogram bins. Precision: resamplepadding is added to weights before taking the log to prevent numerical instability when weights are zero or very small. Gradient Flow: stoplevelgrad prevents gradients from flowing back through the sampling process of previous levels, stabilizing training. Near Bound Annealing: If nearannealrate is set, the near bound initsnear anneals from 0 to nearannealinit over the course of training, helping to stabilize early training. The Dynamic Optimal Sampling Layer is a three-stage sampling strategy (coarse, optimal, fine) that inserts an optimal sampling layer between coarse and fine sampling to adaptively adjust the number and locations of new sample points based on priorities from the previous stage, targeting high-weight regions. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling by replacing uniform or fixed-density refinement with a priority-driven allocation mechanism that uses dilation to expand coverage in high-density areas, thereby improving sampling efficiency and rendering quality in sparse reconstruction scenarios. NeRF-Casting is a differentiable volume rendering method that extends NeRF with explicit reflection modeling to handle glossy surfaces and consistent view-dependent appearance. It solves the problem of inaccurate specular highlights and inconsistent reflections in standard neural radiance fields by introducing a reflection-dependent color MLP and a modified proposal sampling scheme. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling and Zip-NeRF by adapting their adaptive sampling and hash grid structures to support reflected rays. MCBlock is a dynamic-resolution ray-sampling algorithm for Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training that partitions training images into pixel blocks of varying sizes based on texture intensity, using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to optimize the partition during training. It accelerates training by focusing high-frequency sampling on complex regions and low-frequency sampling on simple regions, addressing the inefficiency of uniform pixel-wise sampling and the artifacts of static multi-resolution methods. Unlike its siblings, it combines active sampling with dynamic block partitioning and block-wise novel view synthesis to eliminate high-frequency flaws in simple-texture regions. Sampling strategy for depth in the GeNeRF component, using uniform sampling in inverse-depth space. Number of inverse-depth samples: 64 for IBRNet and DBARF. 128 for BARF and GARF. Time Complexity: The proposal network is small (4 layers, 256 units) compared to the main NeRF MLP, making the sampling rounds efficient. Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storing distances and weights for all levels. The proposal network uses significantly less memory than the main NeRF due to its smaller architecture. Measured Performance: In unbounded scenes, this method reduces aliasing compared to using sampled points directly as endpoints. The dilation helps reduce aliasing by expanding intervals in high-weight regions. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling was introduced in "Mip-NeRF 360: Unbounded Anti-Aliased Neural Radiance Fields". It builds on the original Mip-NeRF by adding a proposal network to guide sampling in unbounded scenes. The method is implemented in the MultiNeRF codebase. It is used in various NeRF variants, including Zip-NeRF and NeRF-Casting. name: Dynamic Optimal Sampling Layer
body: The Dynamic Optimal Sampling Layer is a three-stage sampling strategy (coarse, optimal, fine) that inserts an optimal sampling layer between coarse and fine sampling to adaptively adjust the number and locations of new sample points based on priorities from the previous stage, targeting high-weight regions. It builds on the conical ray and fine sampling concepts from Mip-NeRF. Inputs: Ray parameters (origin, direction, near/far planes), coarse sample weights, and hyperparameters (random offset range, dilation ratio, weight smoothing factor, dynamic padding parameters). Outputs: A set of sample points along the ray distributed across three stages, which are used to query the radiance field. Coarse Samples: A list of sample points along the ray depth with associated weights and conical volumes. Exact layout not given in the sources. Priority Map: A normalized weight distribution derived from coarse samples, indicating high-priority (high-density/high-weight) regions. Exact layout not given in the sources. Optimal Samples: A dynamically allocated list of sample points where the count and location in each interval are determined by the priority map. Exact layout not given in the sources. Fine Samples: A list of sample points refined from the optimal layer's output. Exact layout not given in the sources. 1. Coarse Sampling: Adopt conical rays as in Mip-NeRF. Stratify sampling along the depth direction, distributing sample points from near to far planes. Introduce a moderate random offset \delta in each interval to achieve a more uniform initial distribution. \delta is randomly generated within the [0,1) range. Compute weights wi for each coarse sample by querying the radiance field. 2. Optimal Sampling: Determine the sampling priority for each region based on the weights wi from the coarse layer. Apply a weight smoothing factor to the priorities to ensure a smoother weight distribution and prevent over-concentration in certain areas, which could lead to overfitting. Dynamically determine the number of sampling points in each region based on the smoothed priority, concentrating points in high-density/high-priority areas and reducing points in low-priority areas to save computational resources. Apply dynamic padding parameters to the allocated points to prevent detail loss. Perform a dilation operation to expand sampling points in high-priority regions along the depth direction by a specified ratio, increasing coverage and diversity while reducing the likelihood of missing subtle variations. Output a set of dilated sample points with associated weights. 3. Fine Sampling: Use the dilated sampling points from the optimal layer as input for the fine sampling stage. Refine sampling locations based on the weights along the ray, following the original Mip-NeRF approach. Capture local details by refining the sampling locations around the high-weight regions identified in the previous stages. Random Offset: \delta \sim U[0, 1). This is prevented by introducing a weight smoothing factor to ensure smoother weight distribution and maintain a relatively balanced sampling pattern. Detail Loss: Detail loss can occur if sampling is too sparse in critical regions. This is mitigated by combining dynamic padding parameters with the weight smoothing factor. Sparse Reconstruction Challenges: Traditional methods may suffer from unstable rendering quality in scenes with specular reflections or low lighting. The three-stage strategy addresses these challenges by adaptively adjusting sampling density. Unverified code. near)) coarsepoints = [rayorigin + d raydirection for d in coarsedepths] coarseweights = [radiancefieldquery(p) for p in coarsepoints] # Stage 2: Optimal Sampling # Compute priority from coarse weights totalw = sum(coarseweights) if totalw == 0: smoothedpriorities = [1.0 / numcoarse] numcoarse else: normalized = [w / totalw for w in coarseweights] # Apply weight smoothing factor (formula not given in sources) smoothedpriorities = [w smoothingfactor for w in normalized] totalsmooth = sum(smoothedpriorities) smoothedpriorities = [p / totalsmooth for p in smoothedpriorities] # Dynamic sampling allocation based on priority numoptimalperinterval = [] for p in smoothedpriorities: base = max(1, int(p numcoarse)) numoptimalperinterval.append(base + padding) # Dynamic padding parameters # Generate optimal samples within intervals optimalpoints = [] optimalintervalindices = [] for i in range(numcoarse - 1): n = numoptimalperinterval[i] for j in range(n): delta = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) t = (j + delta) / n depth = coarsedepths[i] + t (coarsedepths[i+1] - coarsedepths[i]) optimalpoints.append(rayorigin + depth raydirection) optimalintervalindices.append(i) # Dilation operation: expand points in high-priority regions along depth by ratio dilatedpoints = [] for i, p in enumerate(optimalpoints): dilatedpoints.append(p) # Dilate points belonging to high-priority intervals (exact threshold not given in sources) if smoothedpriorities[optimalintervalindices[i]] > 0.5: dilatedpoints.append(p + dilationratio raydirection) dilatedpoints.append(p - dilationratio raydirection) # Query weights for dilated points dilatedweights = [radiancefieldquery(p) for p in dilatedpoints] # Stage 3: Fine Sampling # Refine based on weights using Mip-NeRF fine sampling finepoints = [] totaldw = sum(dilatedweights) if totaldw > 0: probs = [w / totaldw for w in dilatedweights] # Sample more points near high weights for in range(numcoarse): idx = random.choices(range(len(dilatedpoints)), weights=probs, k=1)[0] finepoints.append(dilatedpoints[idx]) else: finepoints = dilatedpoints[:] return coarsepoints + dilatedpoints + finepoints Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. head: NeRF-Casting, Improved View-Dependent Appearance with Consistent Reflections
body: NeRF-Casting is a differentiable volume rendering method that extends NeRF with explicit reflection modeling to handle glossy surfaces and consistent view-dependent appearance. It solves the problem of inaccurate specular highlights and inconsistent reflections in standard neural radiance fields by introducing a reflection-dependent color MLP and a modified proposal sampling scheme. It builds on Mip-NeRF 360 Proposal Sampling and Zip-NeRF by adapting their adaptive sampling and hash grid structures to support reflected rays. Inputs: Camera poses and intrinsic parameters. Training images (resolution 3504 \times 2336, downsampled by 4). Masked images (background removal). Outputs: Rendered RGB images for given camera poses. Predicted normals \tilde{\mathbf{n}}. Predicted roughness \rho. Density field \tau. Hash Grids (NGP): The method uses separate hash grids for different feature types. Appearance Model Grid: Resolutions 2^0, \dots, 2^9 with 2 dimensions each. Final Sampling Grids: Three separate NGP features queried in the final round: 1. Roughness: 1 dimension. 2. Normals: 3 dimensions. 3. Density/Bottleneck/Mixing: 4 dimensions. Proposal Grids: Used for adaptive sampling. Round i uses a hash grid with resolutions 2^{a1}, \dots, 2^{ai}, where a1=9, a2=11, a3=13. Each grid has a maximum of 2^{21} elements. MLPs: View-dependent Color MLP (Mc): Two-layer MLP, hidden dimension 128, output logistic sigmoid. Reflection-dependent Color MLP (Mr): Two-layer MLP, hidden dimension 128, output logistic sigmoid. Feature Decoders: Two-layer MLPs, hidden dimension 64, for roughness, normals, density, and mixing coefficients. 1. Initialization: Initialize hash grids for proposal sampling and appearance modeling. Initialize MLP weights. Set optimization progress t=0. 2. Ray Casting: For each training pixel, cast a primary camera ray. Compute reflected rays based on predicted normals and view directions. 3. Adaptive Proposal Sampling: Perform 3 rounds of proposal sampling. Round 1: Resolution 2^9, 64 samples for camera rays, 64 for reflected rays. Round 2: Resolution 2^{11}, 64 samples for camera rays, 64 for reflected rays. Round 3: Resolution 2^{13}, 32 samples for camera rays. No reflected rays in this round. Generate samples along the ray using the proposal distribution. 4. Feature Querying: For each sample point \mathbf{x}, query the hash grids. Apply coarse-to-fine windowing to the features \mathbf{f} using the windowing function \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{v}, t): \mathbf{f}' = \mathbf{f} \odot \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{v}, t) where \mathbf{v} is the resolution vector, t \in [0,1] is optimization progress, and: \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{v}, t) = \frac{1 - \cos(\pi \xi(\mathbf{v}, t))}{2} \xi(\mathbf{v}, t) = \text{clip}(\log2(m) - \log2(\mathbf{v}) - 1 + st) with m = 16\sqrt{2} and s = 25. 5. Feature Decoding: Decode raw NGP features into physical properties: Roughness: \rho = \text{softplus}(\text{MLP}(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}\rho) - 1). Normals: \tilde{\mathbf{n}} = \text{normalize}(\text{MLP}(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}n)). Density: \tau = \exp(\text{MLP}(\hat{\mathbf{f}}b) + 2). Mixing Coefficients: \beta = \text{sigmoid}(\text{MLP}(\tilde{\mathbf{f}}b)). 6. Color Prediction: View-dependent Color: Input to Mc: position \mathbf{x}, bottleneck vector \mathbf{b}, normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{d}, and camera position \mathbf{o} encoded as (\cos(\mathbf{o}), \sin(\mathbf{o}), \cos(2\mathbf{o}), \sin(2\mathbf{o})). Reflection-dependent Color: Input to Mr: position \mathbf{x}, bottleneck \mathbf{b}, normal \mathbf{n}, dot product \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}, reflected ray direction \mathbf{d}', feature vector \bar{\mathbf{f}}, and camera position encoding. 7. Volume Rendering: Accumulate color and density along the ray using standard volume rendering equations. Apply stop-gradient operators when accumulating normal vectors and intersection points to prevent gradients from affecting weights. 8. Loss Computation: Reconstruction Loss: MSE between rendered and ground truth images. Proposal Supervision: Modify Zip-NeRF's spline-based loss. Blur each NeRF interval by a rectangular pulse whose radius is the weighted geometric mean of the proposal distribution intervals overlapping with the NeRF interval. Compute by taking log-widths of proposal intervals, interpolating into a step function, averaging log-widths, and exponentiating. Distortion Loss: Apply distortion loss from mip-NeRF 360 to both camera rays and reflected rays to prevent 'floater' artifacts. Orientation Loss: Apply orientation loss from Ref-NeRF to normal vectors with weight 10^{-3}. 9. Optimization: Update parameters using Adam optimizer. Unverified code. name: MCBlock
head: MCTS-based Dynamic-Resolution Ray Sampling
body: MCBlock is a dynamic-resolution ray-sampling algorithm for Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) training that partitions training images into pixel blocks of varying sizes based on texture intensity, using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) to optimize the partition during training. It accelerates training by focusing high-frequency sampling on complex regions and low-frequency sampling on simple regions, addressing the inefficiency of uniform pixel-wise sampling and the artifacts of static multi-resolution methods. Unlike its siblings, it combines active sampling with dynamic block partitioning and block-wise novel view synthesis to eliminate high-frequency flaws in simple-texture regions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of training images with known camera poses; a cone-tracing NeRF model (e.g., Mipnerf, Zipnerf); hyperparameters \lambda (temperature coefficient), \epsilonL (pruning threshold), \epsilon{init} (initialization variance threshold), \epsilonC (complexity threshold). Outputs: A trained NeRF model; accelerated training time; novel view images rendered in a block-wise manner. Data Structures: Monte-Carlo Quadtree: Each training image has an associated quadtree. Root Node: Represents the entire image of size H \times W. Internal Node: Represents a rectangular pixel block. Has four children representing evenly divided sub-blocks (e.g., (H/2, W/2), (H/4, W/4), etc.). Leaf Node: Represents a pixel block currently selected for training. Node Fields: |Bi|: Size of block i (height \times width). Li: Loss value of block i. For leaf nodes, Li = \|C{Bi} - C^c{Bi}\|2 (MSE between average color C{Bi} and recently rendered color C^c{Bi}). Ui: UCT value. For leaf nodes, Ui = Li \cdot e^{\lambda \cdot Oi} \cdot |Bi|, where Oi is the time interval since last sampling. For internal nodes, Uj = \sum{k \in Chj} Uk. Oi: Expired time (time since last sampling). Reset to 0 upon sampling. Parameters: \lambda: Temperature coefficient controlling the influence of the expired time term in UCT calculation. Typical value: Not explicitly given, but used in formulas. \epsilonL: Threshold for scaled loss during pruning. Typical value: 10^{-2}. \epsilon{init}: Threshold for texture variance during initialization. Typical value: 10^{-3}. \epsilonC: Threshold for complexity/expansion. Typical value: 10^{-4}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: For each training image, compute color variance. Initialize the quadtree structure based on texture intensity. Regions with variance below \epsilon{init} are assigned larger initial blocks; complex regions are assigned smaller blocks. All leaf nodes form the initial block partition. 2. Block Selection (Tree Walk): Start at the root node. At each internal node j, select a child node k with probability proportional to its UCT value relative to the sum of UCT values of all children: P(k) = \frac{Uk}{\sum{m \in Chj} Um}. Continue until a leaf node j is selected. 3. Block Rendering and Loss Calculation: Render the selected leaf block Bj using the cone-tracing NeRF model. Calculate the rendering loss Lj = \|C{Bj} - C^c{Bj}\|2. Perform backpropagation through the NeRF model to update weights. 4. Backpropagation and Pruning: Multiply all UCT values in the tree by e^\lambda to simulate the increment of expired time O. For each leaf node j in the current batch: Set Oj = 0. Set Uj = Lj \cdot |Bj|. Walk up from each leaf node to the root: For each internal node j encountered: Update Uj = \sum{k \in Chj} Uk. Update Lj = \frac{1}{|Chj|} \sum{k \in Chj} Lk. If batch size is S{batch} and image size is S{image}, this process contains complex operations for \log4(S{image}) \cdot S{batch} nodes and simple multiplications for all nodes, ensuring high efficiency. Pruning: Prune children of internal nodes if their scaled loss falls below \epsilonL to promote training efficiency. Note: The exact pruning condition formula is not explicitly provided in the text, but it relies on \epsilonL and loss values. 5. Expansion: If the selected leaf node j has high loss (indicating complex texture or high-frequency flaws), split its block into four equal sub-blocks (children). Assign the UCT value (scaled by block size) and loss value of node j to the new child nodes to bypass expensive initial loss calculations. Randomly add one of the newly expanded nodes to the training batch for the current iteration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The source describes texture-based initialization to boost speed. Exact recursive splitting logic is not provided in code form. """ root = Node(height, width) # Placeholder for recursive variance-based splitting logic return root def selectleaf(root): """Select a leaf node using UCT probabilities.""" node = root while node.children: sumuct = sum(child.UCT for child in node.children) if sumuct == 0: node = node.children[0] else: r = random.uniform(0, sumuct) cumulative = 0.0 for child in node.children: cumulative += child.UCT if cumulative >= r: node = child break return node def renderblock(blocknode, nerfmodel): """ Render a block using cone-tracing NeRF. Returns average color and rendered color tensor. """ avgcolor, renderedcolors = nerfmodel.forward(blocknode) return avgcolor, renderedcolors def calculateloss(avgcolor, renderedcolors): """Calculate MSE loss between average color and rendered colors.""" return float(((avgcolor - renderedcolors) 2).mean()) def backpropagateandprune(root, batchleaves, lambdaparam, epsilonL): """ Update UCT and loss values, and prune nodes. """ # Multiply all UCT values by e^lambda def updateexpiredtime(node): node.UCT = math.exp(lambdaparam) for child in node.children: updateexpiredtime(child) updateexpiredtime(root) # Reset expired time and update UCT for batch leaves for leaf in batchleaves: leaf.expiredtime = 0 leaf.UCT = leaf.loss (leaf.height leaf.width) # Walk up and update internal nodes for leaf in batchleaves: current = leaf while current.parent: parent = current.parent parent.UCT = sum(child.UCT for child in parent.children) parent.loss = sum(child.loss for child in parent.children) / len(parent.children) current = parent # Pruning logic (simplified based on description) # If a node's loss is below threshold, it might be pruned (merged with siblings) # The exact pruning condition is not fully specified in the source text. pass def expandnode(node, batch): """ Split a leaf node into four children if loss is high. """ h, w = node.height, node.width newh, neww = h // 2, w // 2 # Create four children children = [] for in range(4): child = Node(newh, neww, parent=node) # Assign UCT and loss from parent. Source says "scaled by block size". child.UCT = node.UCT / 4 child.loss = node.loss children.append(child) node.children = children node.UCT = 0 node.loss = 0 # Randomly add one expanded node to batch batch.append(random.choice(children)) def trainmcblock(nerfmodel, images, poses, lambdaparam, epsilonL, epsiloninit, epsilonC, batchsize, numiterations): root = initializetree(computevariance(images[0]), images[0].shape[0], images[0].shape[1], epsiloninit) for iteration in range(numiterations): batchleaves = [] # Selection and Expansion for in range(batchsize): leaf = selectleaf(root) # Render and calculate loss avgcolor, renderedcolors = renderblock(leaf, nerfmodel) loss = calculateloss(avgcolor, renderedcolors) leaf.loss = loss # Backpropagate through NeRF nerfmodel.backward(loss) batchleaves.append(leaf) # Expansion if loss is high if loss > epsilonC: expandnode(leaf, batchleaves) # Backpropagate UCT and Loss in the tree backpropagateandprune(root, batchleaves, lambdaparam, epsilonL) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High-frequency flaws in simple-texture regions: Without block splitting, simple regions may lack supervision for high-frequency parameters, leading to artifacts like floaters. Novel view synthesis artifacts: Rendering novel views pixel-wise can expose faulty parameters. MCBlock uses block-wise rendering, warping the training view block partition to the novel view, to avoid rendering high-frequency flaws. Testing view performance: MCBlock performance on testing views may be slightly worse than baselines because the estimated block partition for testing views is not precise. Precision and Boundaries: The algorithm relies on accurate cone-tracing and IPE. Time Complexity: The backpropagation and UCT update process involves complex operations for \log4(S{image}) \cdot S{batch} nodes and simple multiplications for all nodes, ensuring high efficiency. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the quadtree structure for each training image, with node counts proportional to the image resolution and the depth of the tree. Measured Performance: Achieves up to 2.33x training acceleration on the Blender dataset (LPIPS = 0.030) compared to random sampling. Achieves up to 1.66x acceleration on outdoor Mipnerf360 scenes (LPIPS = 0.145) and 1.6x on indoor Mipnerf360 scenes (LPIPS = 0.035) compared to random sampling. Reduces training time to 47.5% of random ray selection on Mipnerf/lego and 51.3% on Zipnerf/bicycle. Overhead is 5.9% of total iteration time for Zipnerf and 4.1% for Mipnerf on RTX 4090. Strengths: Accelerates training significantly, especially in early stages; eliminates high-frequency artifacts in simple-texture regions; works with any cone-tracing NeRF model. Limitations: Slightly worse performance on testing views due to imprecise block partition estimation; advantage over other methods diminishes in later training stages as loss values become outdated. When to use: When training speed is a priority and the scene contains regions with varying texture complexity (e.g., outdoor scenes with sky/background). Not recommended when testing view quality is the sole metric and computational resources are not a constraint. MCBlock was proposed by Yunpeng Tan, Junlin Hao, Jiangkai Wu, Liming Liu, Qingyang Li, and Xinggong Zhang. It is implemented in Nerfstudio and tested on Mipnerf360 and Blender datasets. The method builds on the concept of cone-tracing NeRFs (like Mipnerf) which use Integrated Positional Encoding (IPE) to handle low-resolution rendering, and active ray sampling methods like ActRay, which sample pixels based on fitting difficulty. MCBlock extends this by using MCTS to dynamically partition images into blocks of different sizes, addressing the limitations of uniform block sizes in PyNeRF and pixel-wise sampling in ActRay. name: ENeRF
head: Cascade Cost Volume NeRF
body: ENeRF is a method for efficient neural radiance field training that replaces uniform ray sampling with geometry-aware sampling guided by a cascade cost volume. It builds on Coarse-to-Fine NeRF by introducing a 3D feature volume to predict coarse depth and confidence maps, allowing the fine network to sample points near the scene surface. This reduces the number of sample points per ray by up to 128× while maintaining competitive accuracy. Inputs: A set of calibrated multi-view images with known camera poses. Outputs: A fine radiance field model and associated geometry-aware features. Data Structures: 1. Cascade Cost Volume (3D Feature Volume): A 3D grid storing features derived from multi-view image patches, used to predict coarse geometry. 2. Depth Map: A 2D tensor predicting the distance to the scene surface for each pixel. 3. Confidence Map: A 2D tensor indicating the reliability of the depth prediction. Steps: 1. Build Cascade Cost Volume: Construct a 3D feature volume from the input multi-view images by aggregating geometric information across views. 2. Predict Coarse Geometry: Use the 3D feature volume to predict a coarse depth map and a confidence map for each input view. 3. Sample Near Surface: For each ray, use the predicted depth and confidence to sample a small number of points located near the estimated scene surface. This reduces sample points compared to uniform or hierarchical sampling. 4. Train Radiance Field: Train the fine radiance field MLP using the samples from Step 3. The 3D feature volume also provides rich geometry-aware features to aid in constructing the generalizable radiance field. Parameters: Sample count per ray: Reduced by up to 128× compared to baseline methods. Thresholds for depth/confidence: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method struggles without high-quality depth supervision. Precision issues may arise in the depth prediction step if the cost volume resolution is insufficient. The 3D feature volume provides rich geometry-aware features # Not given in the sources. radiancefield = None return radiancefield A 3D feature volume used to predict coarse geometry. It aggregates geometric information across views to construct a generalizable radiance field. Sampling points near the predicted surface depth. It differs from uniform sampling by focusing computational effort on relevant geometry, reducing sample counts by up to 128×. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is significantly improved due to reduced sample counts (up to 128× reduction). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 3D feature volume (cascade cost volume). Strengths: High rendering speed, competitive accuracy, uses multi-view geometry to reduce sampling overhead. Limitations: Requires high-quality depth supervision for optimal performance. When to use: When multi-view input is available and reducing sample counts is prioritized. When not to use: When depth supervision is unavailable or low-quality. ENeRF was introduced in "Efficient Neural Radiance Fields for Interactive Free-viewpoint Video" (SIGGRAPH Asia 2022). It was inspired by deep learning techniques for multiview stereo. It addresses the limitations of earlier cost volume methods that were not end-to-end trainable and struggled without high-quality depth supervision.
