name: TermiNeRF
head: Ray Termination Prediction, TermiNeRF Sampling Distribution Learning
body: TermiNeRF is a method for efficient neural rendering that jointly trains a sampling network and a color network to predict the distribution of ideal sampling locations along a viewing ray. By concentrating samples where opacity is high and skipping free space, it significantly reduces the number of color network evaluations required per pixel. It sets itself apart from its siblings, Coarse-to-Fine NeRF and NeRF-ID, by using a single evaluation of a dedicated sampling network per ray to predict importance weights for a fixed set of bins, rather than relying on hierarchical coarse-to-fine refinement or implicit density-based adaptive step sizes. TermiNeRF splits the standard NeRF architecture into two components: a Sampling Network that predicts sample importance, and a Shading (Color) Network that renders the final color. The method operates in three phases: pre-training the color network, training the sampling network, and joint fine-tuning. Input: A viewing ray defined by origin \mathbf{O} and direction \mathbf{d}. Output: A rendered pixel color C and, during training, gradients for both networks. 1. Ray Parameterization: Rays are discretized into a fixed set of bins using a "centered-logarithmic" sampling scheme to ensure constant segment lengths and avoid ambiguity in ray representation. The ray segment is defined by two boundary points A and B such that |\mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A}| = \ell. The direction is \vec{d} = \mathbf{B} - \mathbf{A}. The midpoint of the segment is the closest point to the scene origin: \mathbf{O}{mid} = \frac{\mathbf{A}+\mathbf{B}}{2}. The segment length \ell is set to 4.0. Sample points are placed at: \{ \mathbf{A}, \mathbf{A} + s2 \cdot \vec{d}, \dots, \mathbf{A} + s{N-1} \cdot \vec{d}, \mathbf{B} \} where the positions si are formed by concatenating two sequences l and u: li = 1 - 2^{\frac{1-i}{N/2-1}}, \quad i \in \{1, \dots, N/2 - 1\} uj = 2^{\frac{j-N/2}{N/2-1}}, \quad j \in \{1, \dots, N/2\} The full set of sample positions is \{l1, \dots, l{N/2-1}, u1, \dots, u{N/2}\}. 2. Sampling Network: An MLP with 8 hidden layers, 256 units per layer, and a skip connection to the fifth layer. It takes the ray parameters (derived from A, B) and outputs N raw weights. 3. Shading Network: The original NeRF color network (pre-trained). 1. Train the standard NeRF (color and density networks) using the original hierarchical sampling strategy (e.g., 64 coarse + 128 fine samples) until convergence. 1. Generate Ground Truth Weights: For each ray, evaluate the pre-trained fine NeRF network at N{gt} points (e.g., 196 points: 64 coarse + 128 fine + 64 additional) to obtain tuples (zi, \sigmai). 2. Compute Raw Weights: Calculate the volumetric rendering weight wi for each sample i using the standard volume rendering equation: wi = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) where \deltai = z{i+1} - zi is the distance between neighboring samples. 3. Normalize Weights: Normalize the weights so they sum to 1: \hat{w}i = \frac{wi}{\sum{j=0}^{N} wj} 4. Distribution Matching (Max-Resampling): The ground truth weights are defined at arbitrary zi locations, but the sampling network predicts weights for fixed bins defined by the centered-logarithmic points. To align them: Define new bins bj delimited by [\hat{z}j, \hat{z}{j+1}] based on the fixed sample positions. Assign weight \hat{w}j to bin bj using max-resampling: \hat{w}j = \max \{ wi \mid \hat{z}j \le zi \le \hat{z}{j+1} \} \cup \{ w'j, w'{j+1} \} where w'j is the linear interpolation of weights from the old distribution at \hat{z}j. 5. Gaussian Blurring: Smooth the resampled weights to reduce noise from the NeRF estimation. Use a Gaussian blur window of size K=9 and \sigma=3.0. The Euclidean distance covered by the window is d = \frac{K}{N{samples}} \cdot \ell. 6. Normalize Blurred Weights: Re-normalize the blurred weights to sum to 1. 7. Train Sampling Network: Train the sampling network using Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss between its predicted normalized weights and the processed ground truth weights. Use Adam optimizer with learning rate 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. 1. Sampling Strategy: For each ray, sample N{pred} points (e.g., 128) stochastically according to the distribution predicted by the sampling network. 2. Add Equidistant Samples: To ensure the sampling network learns geometry in unsampled regions (free space), add N{eq} equidistantly sampled points (e.g., 64) along the whole ray between near and far z-values. 3. Evaluate Color Network: Evaluate the shading network at all sampled points (predicted + equidistant) to get (\mathbf{c}i, \sigmai). 4. Render: Aggregate colors using volumetric rendering. 5. Update: Alternate updates of the color and sampling networks using Adam optimizer. Learning rate for the sampling network is 5 \cdot 10^{-4} and for the color network is 5 \cdot 10^{-5}. Input: Ray parameters (derived from A, B). Output: N raw weights. """ def init(self, N): super().init() self.N = N # Architecture details inferred from self.layers = nn.ModuleList([ nn.Linear(3, 256), # Assuming 3D input for simplicity, actual input is ray param nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), # 5th layer nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(256, N) ]) self.skiplayeridx = 4 # 0-indexed, corresponds to 5th layer def forward(self, rayinput): x = rayinput for i, layer in enumerate(self.layers): x = layer(x) if i == self.skiplayeridx: skip = x if i > self.skiplayeridx: x = x + skip return x def getcenteredlogarithmicsamples(N, A, B): """ Generates N sample positions along segment A->B. Returns list of positions si relative to A. """ # Find indices surrounding ztarget # This is a simplified placeholder for the actual interpolation logic # In practice, use torch.searchsorted or similar pass def trainsamplingnetwork(colornet, samplingnet, dataloader, Nsamples=128, Neq=64): """ Phase 2: Train Sampling Network against pre-trained Color Net. """ optimizer = optim.Adam(samplingnet.parameters(), lr=5e-4) samplingnet.train() colornet.eval() for ray, gtcolor in dataloader: # 1. Get ground truth weights from Color Net # Evaluate fine NeRF at 196 points (64 coarse + 128 fine + 64 extra) zgt, sigmagt = evaluatefinenerf(colornet, ray, numpoints=196) # 2. Compute raw weights delta = zgt[1:] - zgt[:-1] transmittance = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigmagt[:-1] delta, dim=0)) raww = transmittance (1 - torch.exp(-sigmagt[:-1] delta)) # 3. Max-Resample # Note: The paper describes resampling to match the bins defined by the fixed points # We need to map oldz to new bin centers/boundaries neww = maxresample(zgt, raww, newz) # 6. Blur neww = gaussianblur(neww, K=9, sigma=3.0) # 7. Normalize again neww = neww / neww.sum() # 8. Forward pass through Sampling Network rayinput = getrayinput(ray) # Extract A, B, etc. predraww = samplingnet(rayinput) predw = predraww / predraww.sum() # 9. Loss loss = nn.MSELoss()(predw, neww) optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() def renderterminerf(colornet, samplingnet, ray, Npred=128, Neq=64): """ Phase 3: Joint Fine-Tuning / Inference. """ samplingnet.eval() colornet.eval() # 1. Predict distribution rayinput = getrayinput(ray) predraww = samplingnet(rayinput) predw = predraww / predraww.sum() # 2. Sample Npred points stochastically from predw # Map probabilities to positions along the ray sampledz = samplefromdistribution(predw, Npred) # 3. Add Neq equidistant points A, B = getrayboundaries(ray) eqz = torch.linspace(A, B, Neq) # 4. Combine and sort allz = torch.cat([sampledz, eqz]).sort()[0] # 5. Evaluate Color Network # Get sigma and color at allz sigma, color = evaluatecolornet(colornet, ray, allz) # 6. Volumetric Rendering delta = allz[1:] - allz[:-1] transmittance = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(sigma[:-1] delta, dim=0)) finalcolor = (transmittance color[:-1] delta).sum() # Simplified aggregation return finalcolor Segment Length (\ell): 4.0. Blur Window Size (K): 9. Blur Sigma (\sigma): 3.0. Sampling Network Learning Rate: 5 \cdot 10^{-4}. Color Network Learning Rate: 5 \cdot 10^{-5}. Samples per Ray (Training): 128 predicted + 64 equidistant. Samples per Ray (Inference): Variable, e.g., 32. Uneven Segment Lengths: Using sphere intersection representations creates uneven segment lengths, which puts computational pressure on the network. This is mitigated by enforcing a constant length segment \ell. Arbitrary Training Signals: Training both networks jointly from the start is inefficient because the sampling network receives arbitrary signals from an untrained color network. The color network must be pre-trained first. Free Space Learning: If only predicted samples are used, the sampling network may never learn geometry in unsampled regions (free space). Adding equidistant samples ensures density values are acquired for these regions. False Positives: A false-positive sampling network misprediction (predicting a sample in free space) poses no issue for the color network, as the density will be low. Speed: Rendering time reduced to \le 1 second for an image. Achieves a 14x speedup relative to standard NeRF. Quality: Achieves similar or higher PSNR/LPIPS than NeRF with significantly fewer forward passes (e.g., 7.32x speedup for TermiNeRF 32 vs NeRF 8+16). Fine-Tuning: Scenes can be fine-tuned up to the penultimate step in only three minutes on a GTX1080. Memory: Requires storing the sampling network in addition to the color network. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained NeRF to initialize the color network for best results. TermiNeRF was introduced by Martin Piala and Ronald Clark from Imperial College London in 2021. It addresses the slow rendering times of neural radiance fields (NeRF) by learning a direct mapping from camera rays to locations along the ray that are most likely to influence the pixel's final appearance. The method is cited in later surveys on learning-based 3D representations as a key example of splitting NeRF into a sampling network and a shading network. name: NeRF-ID
head: NeRF in detail
body: NeRF-ID (NeRF in detail) is a method that replaces the heuristic coarse-to-fine sampling of NeRF with a differentiable 'proposer' module, enabling end-to-end training of the entire system (coarse network, proposer, and fine network) to improve view synthesis quality. It solves the limitation of vanilla coarse-to-fine approaches where the sample proposal procedure is handcrafted and not trained for the specific task. Unlike Coarse-to-Fine NeRF which relies on density-based heuristics, NeRF-ID uses a learnable neural network to directly output fine sample locations from coarse features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin and direction. Output: A rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}} for the ray. Data Structures: Coarse Samples: Nc points ti equally spaced along the ray interval [0, 1] (normalized near to far). Coarse Features: For each coarse sample i, a feature vector \mathbf{f}i extracted from the coarse network (last activations before the density projection). Proposer: A neural network taking \{\mathbf{f}i, ti\}{i=1}^{Nc} as input and outputting Nf scalar positions. Fine Samples: Nf points t'j proposed by the proposer. Numbered Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Query the coarse network on Nc equally spaced samples along the ray to obtain densities \sigmai and features \mathbf{f}i. 2. Proposal Generation: Pass the coarse features \mathbf{f}i and their normalized positions ti \in [0, 1] through the proposer network. 3. Position Clamping: The proposer outputs Nf scalars. Pass these through a sigmoid function to constrain them to [0, 1]. 4. Fine Sampling: Query the fine network on the union of the Nc coarse samples and the Nf proposed fine samples. 5. Rendering: Compute the final ray color using the standard volume rendering equation with all Nc + Nf samples. Formulas: The rendering equation for ray color \hat{\mathbf{C}} is: \hat{\mathbf{C}} = \sum{i=1}^N wi \mathbf{c}i where N = Nc + Nf, and for each sample i: wi = Ti \left( 1 - \exp(-\sigmai(t{i+1} - ti)) \right) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj(t{i+1} - ti)\right) Here \sigmai is density, \mathbf{c}i is color, and ti is the location along the ray for the i-th sample. Parameters: Nc: Number of equally spaced samples queried from the coarse network. Nf: Number of additional samples proposed by the proposer for the fine network. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Training Instability: Training the proposer from scratch can be unstable due to lack of supervision. Feature Extraction: The proposer requires specific internal features (last activations before density projection) from the coarse network, not just the final density output. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nerfidrender(rayorigin, raydirection, coarsenet, proposernet, finenet, Nc, Nf): # Step 1: Coarse Sampling # Generate Nc equally spaced points in [0, 1] coarset = linspace(0, 1, Nc) # Query coarse network # coarsenet returns features and densities # Assume coarsenet returns (features, densities) coarsefeatures, coarsedensities = coarsenet(rayorigin, raydirection, coarset) # Step 2 & 3: Proposal Generation # Prepare input for proposer: features and positions # Proposer input shape: (Nc, featuredim) and (Nc,) proposedtsigmoid = proposernet(coarsefeatures, coarset) # Clamp to [0, 1] via sigmoid (already done in proposer output definition) # Note: The source states output is passed through sigmoid to get [0,1] proposedt = proposedtsigmoid # Step 4: Fine Sampling # Union of coarse and fine samples allt = concatenate([coarset, proposedt]) allt.sort() # Ensure sorted order for volume rendering # Query fine network on all samples finecolors, finedensities = finenet(rayorigin, raydirection, allt) # Step 5: Rendering # Compute weights and transmittance # t{i+1} - ti calculation dt = allt[1:] - allt[:-1] # Pad dt to match number of samples? Standard NeRF uses intervals. # Assuming allt has N samples, we need N-1 intervals or handle boundaries. # Standard implementation usually assumes t{N+1} or handles last sample. # For simplicity, we follow the formula structure. # Transmittance Ti # T1 = 1 # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj dtj) # Note: dtj corresponds to interval before sample j? # Formula: Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj(t{i+1} - ti)) # Wait, formula indices in source: Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj(t{i+1} - ti)) # This implies dtj = t{j+1} - tj. # Calculate cumulative sum of sigma dt sigmadt = finedensities[:-1] dt # sigma for first N-1 samples? # Actually, standard NeRF rendering: # Ti = exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj (t{j+1} - tj)) # wi = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai (t{i+1} - ti))) # Let's align indices carefully. # Samples: 1 to N. # Intervals: 1 to N-1? Or N intervals? # Source formula: sum{j=1}^{i-1}. If i=1, sum is empty, T1=1. # If i=N, sum is 1 to N-1. # So we need N-1 intervals. # Re-evaluate dt size. If allt has N elements, we have N-1 intervals. # But finedensities has N elements. # The last sample's density is often unused for transmittance of itself, # but used for its own weight? # wi uses sigmai and (t{i+1} - ti). # For i=N, t{N+1} is undefined. Usually t{N+1} = far plane or ignored. # In practice, often N samples cover [near, far]. # Let's assume standard implementation where last interval is handled or N is large enough. # Simplified rendering loop for clarity T = 1.0 color = zeros(3) for i in range(N): # Interval length if i < N - 1: deltat = allt[i+1] - allt[i] else: deltat = 0.0 # Or handle boundary # Weight # wi = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai deltat)) # Note: Source formula uses t{i+1} - ti. # If i=N, t{N+1} is not in allt. # We assume the source implies standard volume rendering where last sample # contributes but doesn't cast shadow forward, or deltat is 0. weight = T (1 - exp(-finedensities[i] deltat)) color += weight finecolors[i] # Update Transmittance for next sample # T{i+1} = Ti exp(-sigmai deltat) T = T exp(-finedensities[i] deltat) return color Uses a transformer encoder to process input features and a transformer decoder with Nf learned queries to produce proposals via cross-attention. Chosen when high accuracy in feature interaction is needed. Sums point features with positional encodings, passes through an FC layer and ReLU, averages to form a ray representation, then decodes via an FC. Chosen for lower computational overhead compared to Transformers. Applies a single MLPMix block to stacked point features (sorted by position), followed by average pooling and an FC decoder. Chosen as a middle-ground between Pool and Transformer complexity. Time Complexity: Adds the computational cost of the proposer network to the standard NeRF rendering time. The proposer is designed to be small relative to coarse/fine networks to have negligible overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing coarse features for all Nc samples to pass to the proposer. Performance: Achieves superior view synthesis quality over NeRF and state-of-the-art on synthetic Blender benchmarks and comparable performance on real LLFF-NeRF scenes. Strengths: End-to-end differentiability allows learning optimal sampling strategies; can achieve 25% computation savings by filtering low-importance samples without quality loss. Limitations: Training from scratch is unstable; requires a two-stage training strategy. NeRF-ID was introduced in the paper "NeRF in detail: Learning to sample for view synthesis". It addresses the limitation of vanilla NeRF's coarse-to-fine sampling, which relies on a heuristic piece-wise constant PDF computed from coarse densities. The method was developed to enable end-to-end training of the sampling mechanism, improving view synthesis quality. name: Fixed-Resolution Surface Rendering with View Bounds
head: 2 mm however long rendering, Surface Rendering with Adaptive Voxel Sampling and View Bounds, qc_surfaces surface rendering
body: This method renders medical volumes (CT, MR, PET, RT Dose) as surfaces at a fixed spatial resolution of 2 mm, regardless of the volume's length, provided it stays within strict physical bounds. It solves the problem of coarse sampling in long volumes (e.g., whole-body scans), where previous methods limited the voxel count per side to 256, resulting in resolutions as coarse as ~7 mm for a 1,800 mm long scan. Unlike Two-stage NeRF Rendering which adapts resolution based on neural network confidence, or Resolution Adaptation which varies pixel density, this method enforces a uniform 2 mm grid for visual consistency in medical review, specifically ensuring facial features are rendered with the same fidelity in whole-body scans as in head scans. Inputs: A medical volume dataset (voxel grid with physical spacing). Outputs: Six surface render views (Front, Back, Left, Right, Top, Bottom) and associated projection data. Data Structures: Volume: Contains physical dimensions (Lx, Ly, Lz) in mm and voxel spacing (sx, sy, sz). Surface: Boolean flag large. If true, the volume is rejected. Crossings: 16-bit integers representing ray-surface intersections. Batch: A chunk of 64 slices processed simultaneously. Parameters: MINIMUMVOXEL: 2 mm. The target sampling resolution. LONGEST: 2,000 mm. Maximum allowed extent along the head-to-foot axis (Z). WIDEST: 1,000 mm. Maximum allowed extent along the other two axes (X, Y). BATCHSIZE: 64 slices. Steps: 1. Bound Check: Calculate the volume's physical extent along the head-to-foot axis (Ez) and the maximum extent of the other two axes (E{xy} = \max(Ex, Ey)). If Ez > \text{LONGEST} OR E{xy} > \text{WIDEST}: Set Surface.large = true. Return: No mask, no image, no projection. Slices beyond the cine strip are held (not decoded). Ensure the volume orientation is known to identify the head-to-foot axis correctly. 2. Determine Sampling Resolution: Calculate the effective voxel spacing s{eff}: s{eff} = \min(s{min}, \text{MINIMUM\VOXEL}) where s{min} = \min(sx, sy, sz) is the smallest physical spacing of the input volume. If the volume is already finer than 2 mm, use its native spacing to preserve detail, but do not upsample. 3. Generate Views: Define six viewing directions. Five are standard orthogonal views. The sixth is the "From Behind" view. From Behind Configuration: Rotate the view by 180 degrees around the vertical axis. The patient's left remains on the viewer's left. Rays travel along the voxels in the same direction as the frontal view (head-to-foot or foot-to-head depending on convention, but consistent with frontal). 4. Render Crossings (Batch Processing): For each of the six views: a. Initialize a row of crossings for the view width. b. Iterate through the volume slices in batches of BATCHSIZE (64 slices). c. For each batch: i. Step rays for the current slice batch alone. ii. Calculate surface intersections (crossings) for the rays. iii. Store crossings as 16-bit integers to save memory. d. Combine results from all batches into the final row. e. For the "From Behind" view, add a tile to each row but do not create new rows of crossings, as its rays are reversed frontal rays. 5. Handle Edge Cases: Edge Marks: The "From Behind" view draws edges facing the back. This ensures that a mark within two voxels of the slice edge is shown face-on rather than edge-on, correcting a previous pitfall where such marks were only visible as edges from front/side views. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersurface(volume, minvoxel=2.0, longest=2000.0, widest=1000.0, batchsize=64): # 1. Bound Check extentz = volume.extentz extentx = volume.extentx extenty = volume.extenty if extentz > longest or max(extentx, extenty) > widest: return None, None, None # Large volume, hold slices # 2. Determine Resolution minspacing = min(volume.spacingx, volume.spacingy, volume.spacingz) stepsize = min(minspacing, minvoxel) # 3. Generate Views views = [ View("Front", direction=(0, 0, 1)), View("Back", direction=(0, 0, -1)), View("Left", direction=(1, 0, 0)), View("Right", direction=(-1, 0, 0)), View("Top", direction=(0, 1, 0)), View("Bottom", direction=(0, -1, 0)), View("FromBehind", direction=(0, 0, 1), rotation=180) # Patient left on viewer left ] results = {} for view in views: crossings = [] numslices = volume.numslices # 4. Batch Processing for startslice in range(0, numslices, batchsize): endslice = min(startslice + batchsize, numslices) batch = volume.getslices(startslice, endslice) # Step rays for this batch batchcrossings = stepraysforbatch(batch, view, stepsize) crossings.extend(batchcrossings) results[view.name] = crossings return results The five standard views (Front, Back, Left, Right, Top). Used for general anatomical overview. Choose when standard DICOM viewer compatibility is required. The sixth view, rotated 180 degrees. Sets itself apart by showing posterior surfaces face-on, resolving edge-case visibility issues. Choose when reviewing posterior features or ensuring consistent facial preview in whole-body scans. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels in the volume, O(N), where N is the total voxel count within the bounds. The fixed resolution means the number of samples per ray is constant relative to the volume's physical depth, not its voxel count. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the volume data itself. The largest rendered volume (1,000x1,000x2,000 mm) peaks at approximately 1.4 GB memory usage. Using 16-bit integers for crossings reduces intermediate memory overhead compared to 64-bit floats. Measured Performance: In a whole-body MR Otsu threshold calculation, memory usage dropped from 911 MB (with float64 copy) to 355 MB (direct comparison/chunked). Strengths: Consistent visual detail for medical review regardless of volume length; prevents coarse sampling artifacts in long volumes; memory efficient through batching and 16-bit integer storage. Limitations: Volumes exceeding 2,000 mm in length or 1,000 mm in width are not rendered at all; fixed resolution may be overkill for small volumes or under-resolving for very high-resolution small volumes (though native spacing is used if finer). When to use: Medical QC packs, contour sheets, and previews where consistent facial/anatomical detail is critical across varying scan lengths. When not to use: Volumes exceeding the physical bounds; real-time interactive rendering where memory is extremely constrained and the volume is very large. This method was introduced in the pymedphys project to address gaps in the QC pack's surface rendering capabilities. Prior to this change, volumes longer than 510 mm were coarsened to maintain a 256-voxel limit per side, leading to resolutions as coarse as ~7 mm for whole-body CTs. The change, documented in pull request #2434, added a "from behind" view and removed the voxel-side limit, enforcing a 2 mm sampling resolution for volumes within strict bounds. It is used in medical physics QC tools for verifying contour accuracy and dose distributions. name: Two-stage NeRF Rendering
head: Coarse and Fine Sampling, Proposal Network Sampler, Rendering Sampling Strategy
body: Two-stage NeRF Rendering is an acceleration technique for Neural Radiance Fields that decouples the estimation of scene density from the detailed evaluation of color and density. It solves the problem of high computational cost in volume rendering by first using a coarse pass to identify high-density regions, then using those results to importance-sample a fine pass. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by concentrating computational effort on relevant geometry, and from single-stage methods by explicitly separating the rough density estimation from the detailed evaluation. The method consists of two distinct rendering passes: a coarse pass to estimate the transmittance and density distribution along rays, and a fine pass that refines the color and density estimates using samples concentrated in high-density regions identified by the coarse pass. Inputs: Ray bundle (origin o, direction d), near/far bounds (tn, tf), coarse network Nc, fine network Nf. Outputs: Rendered color C(r), depth, and optionally opacity for each ray r. Ray Samples: A list of 3D points ti along the ray. Network Outputs: For each point, the network returns density \sigma and color c. Weights: Importance weights wi derived from the coarse pass transmittance. 1. Coarse Sampling: Sample Nc points uniformly or stratified along the ray interval [tn, tf]. Query the coarse network Nc at these points to obtain density \sigmac and color cc. Compute transmittance Ti and weights wi for the coarse samples: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmac(tj) \Delta tj\right) wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmac(ti) \Delta ti)) Normalize weights if necessary for stability, though standard volume rendering formulas handle this naturally. 2. Fine Sampling: Use the coarse weights wi to define a probability distribution for sampling. Sample Nf points from this distribution (importance sampling). Query the fine network Nf at these points to obtain density \sigmaf and color cf. Compute final color: C(r) = \sum{i=1}^{Nf} wi^f cf(ti) where wi^f are the importance weights derived from the fine samples' contribution to the volume integral, often re-weighted by the coarse transmittance to ensure unbiased estimation. Coarse samples per ray (Nc): Typically 64. Fine samples per ray (Nf): Typically 192 (64 initial + 128 additional). Total samples per ray: 256. Initial Sampler: Can be uniform or piecewise; defaults to uniform if specified. Update Schedule: Determines how often proposal networks are updated during training. Precision: Floating-point precision in transmittance calculation can lead to underflow in long rays. Use log-space computations for stability. Boundaries: Ensure near/far planes are tight to avoid sampling empty space. Adaptive near/far planes can be used. Degenerate Input: If density is zero everywhere, weights become uniform, and the fine pass may waste samples. A fallback to uniform sampling is recommended. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostagerender(rayorigins, raydirections, tnear, tfar, coarsenet, finenet): # Step 1: Coarse Sampling # Sample Nc points uniformly or stratified coarsesamples = stratifiedsample(tnear, tfar, numsamples=64) # Query coarse network coarsedensity, coarsecolor = coarsenet(coarsesamples) # Compute coarse weights and transmittance coarsetransmittance = computetransmittance(coarsedensity) coarseweights = computeweights(coarsetransmittance, coarsedensity) # Step 2: Fine Sampling # Use coarse weights to sample fine points finesamples = importancesample(coarsesamples, coarseweights, numsamples=192) # Query fine network finedensity, finecolor = finenet(finesamples) # Compute fine weights and final color finetransmittance = computetransmittance(finedensity) fineweights = computeweights(finetransmittance, finedensity) # Re-weight by coarse transmittance for unbiased estimation # Note: In practice, this often involves reusing coarse transmittance at fine sample locations # or interpolating coarse transmittance to fine sample locations. # For simplicity, we assume fine weights are computed relative to the start of the ray, # but weighted by the coarse transmittance at the start of the fine segment. finalcolor = sum(fineweights finecolor) return finalcolor Combined sampling stacks an occupancy grid on top of a proposal network to reduce the number of rays processed and shrink the near-far plane for remaining rays. It leverages transmittance estimation from both structures to skip empty space more effectively than either method alone. It differs from VF-NeRF Rendering Pipeline by using a learned proposal network for initial density estimation rather than a fixed grid, and from Coarse-Fine Sampling by explicitly combining a sparse spatial index with a neural density prior to prune rays before the final fine sampling stage. The VF-NeRF rendering pipeline is a two-stage volume rendering method that uses a vector field network to predict surface normals, features, and Jacobians for density estimation and shading. It differs from standard NeRF by deriving density from the directional derivative of the vector field rather than a direct scalar field prediction, enabling explicit surface representation within the implicit volume. It builds on Two-stage NeRF Rendering by integrating vector field-based density computation into the coarse and fine sampling passes. Coarse-Fine Sampling is a two-pass rendering technique for Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) that improves image quality and sampling efficiency by first estimating the scene's density distribution with a coarse pass, then using that distribution to importance-sample a fine pass. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by concentrating computational effort on high-density regions identified in the first pass, and from single-stage methods by decoupling the rough density estimation from the detailed color/density evaluation. Semantic Loss Computation computes the cross-entropy loss over coarse and fine semantic predictions for query rays to train a generalizable semantic field. It differs from standard photometric NeRF losses by enforcing semantic consistency across views via ray-based feature projection, allowing the model to learn contextual geometry for semantic information rather than just color. It is a core component of the Two-stage NeRF Rendering pipeline, specifically enabling the training of the semantic head alongside the geometry-aware network. One-Step NeRF Rendering is a volume rendering method that eliminates the multi-stage sampling pipeline by using only stratified sampling for both foreground and background components. It solves the computational overhead of importance sampling and proposal networks by treating the background as an outer volume, similar to the NeRF++ approach. It differs from Two-stage NeRF Rendering by removing the fine-stage refinement and from Coarse-Fine Sampling by using a single uniform depth distribution for all samples. Base-NeRF uses a hierarchical proposal network structure. Proposal 1 queries 128 linearly spaced samples. Proposal 2 queries 96 samples using probability density sampling. The final NeRF model queries 48 samples using probability density sampling. At test time, final NeRF sampling is increased to 192 points for higher rendering quality. The architecture uses Hash Grids and MLPs: Proposal 1 (Hash Grid 5/17/16/64, MLP 1/16), Proposal 2 (Hash Grid 5/17/16/256, MLP 1/16), NeRF (Hash Grid 5/19/16/2048, MLP 1/64). On the Blender dataset, rays corresponding to background can be heavily pruned, yielding large speedups. NeRF-ID renders views up to 50% faster while achieving better results than NeRF†. HeadNeRF computes a low-resolution 2D feature map IF from ray samples to serve as input for a subsequent 2D neural rendering module. It samples 64 points per ray. The output feature map IF dimensions are R^{256 \times 32 \times 32}. Hierarchical volume sampling is removed to speed up inference, accepting potential quality trade-offs for real-time performance. A method to balance appearance and geometric continuity in NeRF synthesis by searching patches in two phases, significantly enhancing speed. In the first phase, search patches for density only. Speedup comparison: For 100^2 size, Baseline 163.47s vs Two-phase 14.99s (10.90x); for 200^2, 270.70s vs 23.62s (11.46x); for 300^2, 454.41s vs 38.46s (11.82x); for 400^2, 714.64s vs 59.57s (12.00x). NeRSTF combines Signed Distance Fields (SDF) and Texture Fields (TF) or a combined NeRSTF model, using a two-pass rendering approach (coarse stratified, fine importance) to produce backpropagable views. Steps: 1. Query the model (sdf/tf or nerstf) for density, signed distance, and channels at query points. 2. Render rays with coarse, stratified samples using StratifiedRaySampler. 3. Render rays with fine, importance-weighted samples using the sampler from the coarse pass. 4. Scale output channels by channelscale (default 255.0). 5. If separatesharedsamples is true, include coarse results in the output dictionary. Parameters: ncoarsesamples, nfinesamples, separatesharedsamples. Time Complexity: O(Nc + Nf) network queries per ray, where Nc and Nf are the number of coarse and fine samples. Memory Complexity: O(Nc + Nf) to store intermediate densities and colors. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA V100, rendering a realistic synthetic dataset (640k rays/image) or real scenes (762k rays/image) takes approximately 30 seconds per frame, resulting in 150-200 million network queries per image. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with the number of rays and samples. Strengths: Significant reduction in network queries compared to uniform sampling; improved image quality by focusing on high-density regions. Limitations: Increased implementation complexity; potential for artifacts if coarse sampling is insufficient. When to use: When computational resources are limited but high-quality novel view synthesis is required. When not to use: For real-time applications requiring very low latency without hardware acceleration, or for scenes with uniform density where uniform sampling is sufficient. Two-stage NeRF Rendering was introduced in the original NeRF paper by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It has since become a standard technique in NeRF-based rendering pipelines, with various extensions and optimizations proposed in subsequent works.
