name: Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer
head: PackedRFTracer
body: The Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer is a differentiable rendering method for sparse, packed radiance fields that generates a variable number of samples per ray, packed into a flat tensor structure. It solves the inefficiency of standard ray marching by using a sparse acceleration structure to sample only within occupied cells, resulting in a custom number of samples per ray rather than a fixed grid. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly manages the "packed" data layout where rays with different intersection counts share a single contiguous buffer, requiring specific reduction operations to handle boundaries between rays. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A neural field (nef) with an attached grid/BLAS, a batch of rays (origin, direction), configuration parameters (raymarchtype, numsteps, bgcolor), and optional extra channels. Outputs: Computed RGB color, depth, alpha, and hit status for each ray in the batch. Data Structures: Packed Tensor: A 1D tensor containing samples for all rays concatenated. Pack Info: Metadata indicating the start index and count of samples for each ray in the packed tensor. Boundary: A boolean or integer mask indicating the end of valid samples for each ray in the packed tensor. Parameters: raymarchtype (str): 'voxel' (intersects acceleration structure cells, samples numsteps times per cell) or 'ray' (samples numsteps along ray, culls outside occupied cells). numsteps (int): Number of samples per intersected cell (for 'voxel') or per ray before culling (for 'ray'). stepsize (float): Currently unused. bgcolor (Tuple[float, float, float]): Background color, default (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Steps: 1. Initialization: Store bgcolor as a float32 tensor. Assert that the neural field has a grid attribute. 2. LOD Selection: If lodidx is None, set it to nef.grid.numlods - 1 (highest detail). 3. Ray Marching: Call nef.grid.raymarch() with rays, activelods[lodidx], numsteps, and raymarchtype. This returns ridx (ray indices), samples (coordinates), deltas (distances), depths, packinfo, and boundary. 4. Preparation: Extract results. Set prevnumsamples to samples.shape[0]. Get hit ray directions using rays.dirs.indexselect(0, ridx). 5. Neural Field Query: Query nef at samples with hitrayd and lodidx for channels ["rgb", "density"]. Reshape density to (numsamples, 1) to prevent squeezing. 6. Buffer Initialization: Initialize output buffers: depth (N, 1), rgb (N, 3) initialized to bgcolor, hit (N, bool), outalpha (N, 1). 7. Optical Thickness: Compute tau = density deltas. Delete density and deltas to free memory. 8. Exponential Integration: Compute raycolors and transmittance using spcrender.exponentialintegration(color, tau, boundary, exclusive=True). 9. Depth Computation (Optional): If 'depth' is requested, compute raydepth = spcrender.sumreduce(depths.reshape(numsamples, 1) transmittance, boundary). Assign depth[ridxhit,:] = raydepth. 10. Alpha and Hit Status: Compute alpha = spcrender.sumreduce(transmittance, boundary). Assign outalpha[ridxhit] = alpha and hit[ridxhit] = alpha[...,0] > 0.0. 11. Color Composition: For hit rays, compute rgb[ridxhit] = (self.bgcolor (1.0-alpha)) + raycolors. 12. Extra Channels: For each extra channel, query nef, perform exponentialintegration, compute compositedfeats = alpha rayfeats, and assign to outfeats[ridxhit]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def trace(self, rays, nef, lodidx=None, channels=None): # 1. Assert grid exists assert hasattr(nef, 'grid') # 2. Determine LOD if lodidx is None: lodidx = nef.grid.numlods - 1 # 3. Ray Marching via Sparse Grid raymarchresults = nef.grid.raymarch( rays=rays, activelods=[lodidx], numsteps=self.numsteps, raymarchtype=self.raymarchtype) ridx, samples, deltas, depths, packinfo, boundary = raymarchresults prevnumsamples = samples.shape[0] # 4. Get directions for hit rays hitrayd = rays.dirs.indexselect(0, ridx) # 5. Query Neural Field color, density = nef( coords=samples, rayd=hitrayd, lodidx=lodidx, channels=["rgb", "density"]) # Protect against squeezed return shape if density.dim() == 1: density = density.unsqueeze(1) # 6. Initialize Output Buffers N = rays.dirs.shape[0] device = rays.dirs.device depthout = torch.zeros((N, 1), device=device) rgbout = torch.tensor(self.bgcolor, dtype=torch.float32, device=device).expand(N, -1).clone() hitout = torch.zeros(N, dtype=torch.bool, device=device) outalpha = torch.zeros((N, 1), device=device) # 7. Compute Optical Thickness tau = density deltas del density, deltas # 8. Exponential Integration raycolors, transmittance = exponentialintegration(color, tau, boundary, exclusive=True) # 9. Depth Computation if 'depth' in channels: depthsreshaped = depths.reshape(prevnumsamples, 1) raydepth = sumreduce(depthsreshaped transmittance, boundary) hitmask = transmittance[:, 0] > 0.0 ridxhit = ridx[hitmask] depthout[ridxhit] = raydepth[hitmask] # 10. Alpha and Hit Status alpha = sumreduce(transmittance, boundary) ridxhit = ridx[transmittance[:, 0] > 0.0] outalpha[ridxhit] = alpha[hitmask] hitout[ridxhit] = alpha[hitmask, 0] > 0.0 # 11. Color Composition if hitmask.any(): bgcontrib = torch.tensor(self.bgcolor, dtype=torch.float32, device=device) (1.0 - alpha[hitmask]) rgbout[ridxhit] = bgcontrib + raycolors[hitmask] # 12. Extra Channels if channels: outfeats = torch.zeros(N, 1, device=device) # Placeholder for channel dimension for ch in channels: if ch in ['rgb', 'density', 'depth']: continue feats, = nef(coords=samples, rayd=hitrayd, lodidx=lodidx, channels=[ch]) rayfeats, = exponentialintegration(feats, tau, boundary, exclusive=True) compositedfeats = alpha rayfeats outfeats = torch.cat([outfeats, compositedfeats], dim=1) # Assign composited features to output buffer (structure depends on extrachannels layout) return rgbout, depthout, outalpha, hitout def sumreduce(arr, boundary): """Sums elements between boundaries, returning per-ray sums.""" out = torch.zeroslike(arr[:,:1]) currentsum = torch.zeroslike(out) for i in range(arr.shape[0]): currentsum += arr[i] if boundary[i]: out[i] = currentsum currentsum = torch.zeroslike(currentsum) return out def exponentialintegration(color, tau, boundary, exclusive=True): """Computes transmittance and ray colors for volume rendering.""" numsamples = tau.shape[0] transmittance = torch.zeroslike(color) raycolors = torch.zeroslike(color) currentT = torch.ones(color.shape[0], device=color.device).unsqueeze(1) for i in range(numsamples): if exclusive: transmittance[i] = currentT sigmadelta = tau[i, 0] Tstep = torch.exp(-sigmadelta) raycolors[i] = currentT (1.0 - Tstep) color[i] currentT = currentT Tstep else: sigmadelta = tau[i, 0] Tstep = torch.exp(-sigmadelta) transmittance[i] = currentT Tstep raycolors[i] = currentT (1.0 - Tstep) color[i] currentT = currentT Tstep if boundary[i]: currentT = torch.ones(color.shape[0], device=color.device).unsqueeze(1) return raycolors, transmittance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: bgcolor must be stored as float32 to ensure consistency during accumulation. Shape Squeezing: Density output from the neural field may be squeezed to 1D if batch size is 1; explicit reshaping to (N, 1) is required. Boundary Handling: The boundary parameter is critical for sumreduce and exponentialintegration to correctly handle rays with varying sample counts in the packed tensor. The parent method that provides the underlying sparse acceleration structure and training-time sampling logic. Sparse Ray Marching (Training) An alternative implementation using CUDA kernels for NGP-style grids, likely offering lower-level performance optimization but potentially less flexibility in packed tensor handling compared to the Python-based tracer. CUDA Ray Marching (IDDR-NGP Backend) A simplified tracer used only for forward passes during training, lacking the full differentiable integration and packed tensor management of the inference tracer. Training Ray Marching (Forward Only) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Differentiable, handles variable sample counts efficiently, integrates with sparse acceleration structures. Limitations: Requires a compatible neural field and grid structure. 'stepsize' is currently unused, limiting control over sampling density in some modes. When to Use: When rendering sparse radiance fields or SDFs where most of the volume is empty, and differentiability is required. When Not to Use: For dense volumes where fixed-step ray marching might be more cache-friendly, or when hardware acceleration for sparse structures is not available. The Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer is part of the NVIDIA Kaolin-Wisp framework, introduced in the context of SIGGRAPH 2022 demos for interactive neural rendering. It builds upon the concept of "packed" tensors for variable-length data, a technique popularized in libraries like Kaolin for efficient batched operations on sparse data. The method is designed to work with Neural Geometric LODs and sparse occupancy structures (BLAS) to enable real-time rendering of high-fidelity neural fields. name: Sparse Grid Volume Rendering (Foreground)
head: Plenoxel Ray Tracing (Forward)
body: Sparse Grid Volume Rendering (Foreground) is a CUDA-based volume rendering method that traces rays through a sparse voxel grid to compute final color and log-transmittance using volume rendering with spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. It differs from its siblings by explicitly managing warp-level parallelism for SH basis evaluation and accumulation, utilizing shared memory for warp-local data to minimize global memory traffic, and employing early termination based on transmission thresholds. Unlike CUDA Ray Marching (IDDR-NGP Backend) which uses hash encoding, or Sparse Packed Radiance Field Tracer which may use different interpolation schemes, this method relies on trilinear interpolation over a sparse connectivity structure. Inputs: rays: Array of ray origins and directions. grid: A PackedSparseGridSpec structure containing sparse voxel data. opt: RenderOptions structure controlling marching parameters. outv: Output buffer for rendered colors. outlogtransmit: Optional output buffer for log-transmittance. Outputs: outv: Rendered color per ray. outlogtransmit: Log-transmittance per ray (if provided). PackedSparseGridSpec: links: Sparse connectivity structure for voxel lookup. stridex: Stride for density data lookup. size[3]: Grid dimensions (width, height, depth). densitydata: Density values (\sigma) stored in a sparse format. shdata: Spherical Harmonics coefficients for color. shdatadim: Number of SH bands/dimensions (typically 9 for 3rd order). basisdim: Number of SH basis functions per color channel. backgroundnlayers: Number of background layers (0 implies simple background). backgroundbrightness: Scalar background color value. SingleRaySpec: origin[3]: Ray origin coordinates. dir[3]: Ray direction vector. tmin: Near bound of the ray segment within the grid. tmax: Far bound of the ray segment within the grid. pos[3]: Current ray position. l[3]: Integer voxel coordinates. worldstep: Step size in world units. RenderOptions: stepsize: Fixed step size for ray marching. sigmathresh: Density threshold below which samples are skipped. stopthresh: Transmission threshold below which ray marching terminates early. lastsampleopaque: Boolean flag; if true, sets worldstep to 10^9 for the last sample. backgroundbrightness: Scalar background color. randomize: Boolean flag for randomization (not used in forward pass logic described). randomsigmastd: Float for randomization (not used in forward pass logic described). The kernel launches with TRACERAYCUDATHREADS = 128 threads per block, processing TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK = 4 rays per block (since WARPSIZE = 32). 1. Initialization: Compute thread ID tid = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x. Compute rayid = tid >> 5 (integer division by 32). Compute laneid = threadIdx.x & 0x1F (modulo 32). If laneid >= grid.shdatadim, return early. Copy rays.origins[rayid] and rays.dirs[rayid] into shared memory rayspec[rayblkid] where rayblkid = tid / 32. Compute ray bounds tmin and tmax using rayfindbounds(rayspec[rayblkid], grid, opt, rayid). If tmin > tmax, the ray is outside the grid. Output backgroundbrightness if grid.backgroundnlayers == 0, else 0. Set logtransmit = 0 if outlogtransmit is not null. 2. Shared Memory Allocation: shared float sphfuncval[4][9] for SH basis values. shared SingleRaySpec rayspec[4] for ray data. shared typename WarpReducef::TempStorage tempstorage[4] for warp reductions. 3. Spherical Harmonics Evaluation: Compute SH basis values for the ray direction rayspec[rayblkid].dir using calcsphfunc(grid, laneid, rayid, rayspec[rayblkid].dir, sphfuncval[rayblkid]). This fills sphfuncval[rayblkid] with 9 values (assuming 3rd order SH). Synchronize warp: syncwarp((1U << grid.shdatadim) - 1) to ensure all lanes have computed SH values. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize t = rayspec[rayblkid].tmin. While t <= rayspec[rayblkid].tmax: a. Position Computation: ray.pos[j] = fmaf(t, rayspec[rayblkid].dir[j], rayspec[rayblkid].origin[j]) for j=0,1,2. Clamp ray.pos[j] to [0, grid.size[j] - 1]. Compute integer voxel coordinates: ray.l[j] = min(staticcast<int32t>(ray.pos[j]), grid.size[j] - 2). Compute fractional part: ray.pos[j] -= staticcast<float>(ray.l[j]). b. Density Sampling: Sample density \sigma using trilinear interpolation: \sigma = \text{trilerp\cuvol\one}(grid.links, grid.densitydata, grid.stridex, grid.size[2], 1, ray.l, ray.pos, 0). c. Threshold Check: If \sigma \le opt.sigma\thresh, skip sampling and continue to next step (advance t). d. Color Sampling: Sample SH color coefficients: lane\color = \text{trilerp\cuvol\one}(grid.links, grid.shdata, grid.stridex, grid.size[2], grid.sh\data\dim, ray.l, ray.pos, lane\id). Multiply by SH basis value: lane\color = sphfunc\val[ray\blk\id][lane\id]. e. Weight Computation: Compute optical depth increment: pcnt = ray\spec[ray\blk\id].world\step \times \sigma. Compute weight: weight = \exp(log\transmit) \times (1 - \exp(-pcnt)). Update log-transmittance: log\transmit -= pcnt. f. Accumulation: Reduce lanecolor across the warp using WarpReducef::HeadSegmentedSum with mask lanecolorgrpid == 0 (where lanecolorgrpid groups lanes by SH basis index). Let result be lanecolortotal. Add to output: outv += weight \times \max(lane\color\total + 0.5f, 0.f). This clamps the color to non-negative values. g. Last Sample Handling: If opt.last\sample\opaque is true and t + opt.step\size > ray\spec[ray\blk\id].tmax, set ray\spec[ray\blk\id].world\step = 10^9 to make the last sample fully opaque. h. Step Advancement: t += opt.step\size. i. Early Termination: If \exp(log\transmit) < opt.stop\thresh, set log\transmit = -1000.0f and break the loop. 5. Background Addition: If grid.background\nlayers == 0, add background contribution: outv += \exp(log\transmit) \times opt.background\brightness. 6. Output: If laneid == 0, write out[laneid] = outv and if outlogtransmit is not null, write outlogtransmit = logtransmit. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraykernel(rays, grid, opt, outv, outlogtransmit): tid = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x rayid = tid // 32 laneid = threadIdx.x % 32 rayblkid = threadIdx.x // 32 # 0 to 3 # Early exit if laneid exceeds SH dimensions if laneid >= grid.shdatadim: return # Shared memory for ray data and SH basis sharedrayspec = shared SingleRaySpec[4] sharedsphfuncval = shared float[4][9] sharedtempstorage = shared WarpReducef::TempStorage[4] # Initialize ray data in shared memory sharedrayspec[rayblkid].origin = rays.origins[rayid] sharedrayspec[rayblkid].dir = rays.dirs[rayid] # Compute ray bounds tmin, tmax = rayfindbounds(sharedrayspec[rayblkid], grid, opt, rayid) # Handle rays outside grid if tmin > tmax: if grid.backgroundnlayers == 0: outv[rayid] = opt.backgroundbrightness else: outv[rayid] = 0.0 if outlogtransmit is not None: outlogtransmit[rayid] = 0.0 return # Compute SH basis values calcsphfunc(grid, laneid, rayid, sharedrayspec[rayblkid].dir, sharedsphfuncval[rayblkid]) syncwarp((1 << grid.shdatadim) - 1) # Initialize ray marching t = tmin logtransmit = 0.0 outcolor = 0.0 worldstep = opt.stepsize while t <= tmax: # Position computation pos = sharedrayspec[rayblkid].origin + t sharedrayspec[rayblkid].dir pos = clamp(pos, 0.0, grid.size - 1.0) l = floor(pos) frac = pos - l l = min(l, grid.size - 2) # Density sampling sigma = trilerpcuvolone(grid.links, grid.densitydata, grid.stridex, grid.size[2], 1, l, frac, 0) # Threshold check if sigma <= opt.sigmathresh: t += opt.stepsize continue # Color sampling lanecolor = trilerpcuvolone(grid.links, grid.shdata, grid.stridex, grid.size[2], grid.shdatadim, l, frac, laneid) lanecolor = sharedsphfuncval[rayblkid][laneid] # Weight computation pcnt = worldstep sigma weight = exp(logtransmit) (1.0 - exp(-pcnt)) logtransmit -= pcnt # Warp reduction for color lanecolortotal = WarpReducef(sharedtempstorage[rayblkid]).HeadSegmentedSum(lanecolor, laneid == 0) # Accumulation outcolor += weight max(lanecolortotal + 0.5, 0.0) # Last sample handling if opt.lastsampleopaque and t + opt.stepsize > tmax: worldstep = 1e9 # Step advancement t += opt.stepsize # Early termination if exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh: logtransmit = -1000.0 break # Background addition if grid.backgroundnlayers == 0: outcolor += exp(logtransmit) opt.backgroundbrightness # Output if laneid == 0: outv[rayid] = outcolor if outlogtransmit is not None: outlogtransmit[rayid] = logtransmit grid.basisdim: Number of SH basis functions per color channel. opt.stepsize: Fixed step size for ray marching. opt.sigmathresh: Density threshold below which samples are skipped. opt.stopthresh: Transmission threshold below which ray marching terminates early. opt.lastsampleopaque: Boolean flag; if true, sets worldstep to 10^9 for the last sample. If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, the ray is outside the grid. Output backgroundbrightness if grid.backgroundnlayers == 0, else 0. Set logtransmit to 0 if outlogtransmit is not null. Precision issues may arise from repeated floating-point additions in the ray marching loop; using fmaf helps maintain precision. The SH basis evaluation must be synchronized across the warp before color accumulation to ensure correct reduction. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of rays and M is the number of steps per ray. The number of steps is determined by the grid size and stepsize. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the number of voxels in the sparse grid. Shared memory usage is constant per block (4 \times 9 floats for SH basis, 4 \times ray spec, 4 \times temp storage). Measured Performance: On RTX 3090, Instant-NGP implemented in JNeRF achieves about 133 iterations per second for the lego dataset. Strengths: Efficient use of shared memory and warp-level parallelism for SH evaluation. Early termination reduces computation for transparent regions. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence in complex scenes. Sparse grid lookup overhead may dominate for very sparse grids. When to Use: Real-time rendering of sparse voxel-based radiance fields. When Not to Use: Scenes requiring high-frequency details that cannot be captured by fixed step size or SH basis. Sparse Grid Volume Rendering (Foreground) is derived from Plenoxels, which introduced the use of sparse voxel grids with spherical harmonics for radiance field representation. The implementation in NeRF-Factory and JNeRF adapts this for efficient CUDA execution, leveraging warp-level operations for SH evaluation. The method is part of the broader effort to accelerate NeRF rendering through sparse representations and efficient memory access patterns. kakaobrain/nerf-factory, https://github.com/kakaobrain/nerf-factory, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Jittor/JNeRF, https://github.com/Jittor/JNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Chunked Volume Rendering
head: Chunked Volume Rendering with Early Stopping, Memory-efficient chunked rendering, NeRF-style Volume Rendering, TBRayMarcher Plugin, Volume Rendering (NeRF-style), VolumeRenderer, VolumeRendererChunk
body: Chunked Volume Rendering is a memory-efficient inference technique that integrates color and density along rays by processing sampled points in fixed-size batches (chunks). It solves the GPU memory bottleneck associated with rendering large scenes or high-resolution implicit fields by allowing a trade-off between memory usage and computational throughput. It differs from its parent Inference Ray Marching and Integration by explicitly batching the forward pass to constrain VRAM, and from its sibling Inference Ray Compositing by focusing on the chunked accumulation of radiance rather than just the compositing logic. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A raybundle containing origins, directions, and pre-sampled points (shape [B, Npts, 3]); an implicit function implicitfn to query density and features; a sampler to generate points; and configuration parameters (chunksize, raymarchingtolerance, whitebackground). Output: A dictionary containing feature (rendered color, shape [B, 3]) and depth (rendered depth, shape [B, 1]). Data Structures: chunkfeatures: List of tensors storing rendered features for each chunk. chunkdepths: List of tensors storing rendered depths for each chunk. accumulatedfreeenergy: Tensor tracking the cumulative free energy (opacity) for early stopping. Parameters: chunksize: Number of rays (or samples) processed per iteration. Default is 65,536 (1024 64) for training, or chunksize // 1024 for inference. raymarchingtolerance: Threshold for early stopping. If > 0, rays terminate when accumulated free energy exceeds -log(tolerance). whitebackground: Boolean. If True, background is white; otherwise black. Formulas: 1. Segment Lengths (Deltas): \delta = [d2-d1, \dots, dn-d{n-1}, 10^{10}] where di are the distances of sample points from the origin. The last delta is set to a large value to ensure termination. 2. Hit and Empty Probabilities: Let ft be the "free energy" (density \times delta) at step t. at = 1 - \exp(-ft) \quad \text{(Probability of hit at step } t \text{)} bt = \exp\left(-\sum{k=0}^{t-1} fk\right) \quad \text{(Probability of empty space up to step } t \text{)} \text{probs}t = at \times bt 3. Rendering: \text{color} = \sumt \text{texture}t \times \text{probs}t \text{depth} = \sumt \text{sampled\depth}t \times \text{probs}t \text{missed} = 1 - \sumt \text{probs}t Algorithm: 1. Initialize accumulatedfreeenergy to zeros, chunkfeatures and chunkdepths to empty lists. 2. Determine total rays N. Iterate chunkstart from 0 to N with step chunksize. 3. Slice raybundle for the current chunk: curraybundle = raybundle[chunkstart: chunkstart + chunksize]. 4. Call the parent forward method (or forwardonce) with curraybundle to get curfeature and curdepth. Note: If the implementation uses explicit accumulation within the chunk loop (as in), iterate through sample indices i. Compute weights wt = \text{probs}t. Update accumulatedfreeenergy. If accumulatedfreeenergy > -log(raymarchingtolerance), mask out subsequent hits for those rays. 5. Append curfeature to chunkfeatures and curdepth to chunkdepths. 6. Concatenate all chunks: \text{feature} = \text{cat}(chunk\features, \text{dim}=0) \text{depth} = \text{cat}(chunk\depths, \text{dim}=0) 7. If whitebackground is True, add (1 - missed) 1.0 to color. 8. Return feature and depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def chunkedvolumerender(raybundle, implicitfn, sampler, chunksize=65536, raymarchingtolerance=0.0, whitebackground=False): # raybundle: dict with 'origins' [B, 3], 'directions' [B, 3], 'points' [B, N, 3] # Returns: feature [B, 3], depth [B, 1] B = raybundle['origins'].shape[0] chunkfeatures = [] chunkdepths = [] # Handle edge case: no rays if B == 0: return torch.zeros((0, 3)), torch.zeros((0, 1)) for chunkstart in range(0, B, chunksize): # Slice current chunk endidx = min(chunkstart + chunksize, B) curraybundle = { 'origins': raybundle['origins'][chunkstart:endidx], 'directions': raybundle['directions'][chunkstart:endidx], 'points': raybundle['points'][chunkstart:endidx] } # Sample points if not provided, or use provided points # Assuming sampler returns points [Bchunk, N, 3] and deltas [Bchunk, N] points = sampler(curraybundle) deltas = computedeltas(points) # [Bchunk, N] # Query implicit function for density and color # density [Bchunk, N, 1], color [Bchunk, N, 3] density, color = implicitfn(points) # Compute probabilities # freeenergy = density deltas freeenergy = density.squeeze(-1) deltas # [Bchunk, N] # Shifted free energy for transmittance # bt = exp(-cumsum(shiftedfreeenergy)) shiftedfreeenergy = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(freeenergy[:,:1]), freeenergy[:,:-1]], dim=1) transmittance = torch.exp(-torch.cumsum(shiftedfreeenergy, dim=1)) # Alpha and weights alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-freeenergy) weights = alpha transmittance # Render Color and Depth # color = sum(weights color) renderedcolor = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(-1) color, dim=1) # depth = sum(weights depthsamples) # depthsamples are distances of points from origin depthsamples = torch.norm(points - curraybundle['origins'].unsqueeze(1), dim=-1) # [Bchunk, N] rendereddepth = torch.sum(weights depthsamples, dim=1) # Missed probability missed = 1.0 - torch.sum(weights, dim=1) # Apply background if whitebackground: renderedcolor = renderedcolor + (1.0 - missed.unsqueeze(-1)) 1.0 else: renderedcolor = renderedcolor # Black background (0) chunkfeatures.append(renderedcolor) chunkdepths.append(rendereddepth.unsqueeze(-1)) # Concatenate results finalfeature = torch.cat(chunkfeatures, dim=0) finaldepth = torch.cat(chunkdepths, dim=0) return finalfeature, finaldepth def computedeltas(points): # points [B, N, 3] # deltas [B, N] diffs = points[:, 1:] - points[:,:-1] deltas = torch.norm(diffs, dim=-1) # Append large value for last segment largedelta = torch.oneslike(deltas[:,:1]) 1e10 return torch.cat([deltas, largedelta], dim=1) The pseudocode above implements the standard NeRF-style integration. The source mentions an accumulatedfreeenergy variable used for early stopping within a loop over samples. The logic for early stopping is: if raymarchingtolerance > 0, maintain a running sum of freeenergy. If the sum exceeds -log(raymarchingtolerance), set alpha to 0 for all subsequent steps for that ray. This is omitted in the clean vectorized pseudocode for brevity but is a critical pitfall for memory-constrained implementations. This method accelerates volume rendering by combining chunked ray batching with an occupancy grid estimator to skip empty space. It solves the performance bottleneck of uniform ray marching in sparse or large scenes by only sampling regions where the radiance field has non-zero density. It differs from its parent Chunked Volume Rendering by integrating a specific hierarchical occupancy grid for adaptive sampling, and from its sibling Block-based Volume Rendering Strategy by using a continuous grid-based estimator rather than discrete block structures. Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation provides the mathematical foundation for distributing volumetric rendering across multiple disjoint spatial segments (partitions) along a ray. It solves the problem of correctly accumulating color, transmittance, and auxiliary losses (such as distortion) when a ray traverses multiple independent volume tiles, which may be processed by different compute units. It sets itself apart from standard single-volume ray marching by explicitly decomposing global integrals into sums of local segment integrals weighted by upstream transmittance, enabling parallel prefix-scan accumulation. A rendering strategy for large scenes partitioned into blocks, where each block uses a separate shader due to web texture unit limits. It solves the problem where standard volume rendering fails because sampling points across a ray may belong to different blocks loaded by different shaders, breaking 3D consistency and correct occlusion. It sets itself apart from its siblings by enforcing sequential rendering and post-hoc accumulation rather than attempting to load all resources into a single pass or using occupancy grids to skip empty space. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot B), where N is the number of samples per ray and B is the number of rays. Chunking does not change the asymptotic complexity but increases overhead due to loop iterations. Memory Complexity: O(B{chunk} \cdot N), where B{chunk} is the chunksize. This allows rendering scenes with B \gg B{chunk} by trading memory for time. Performance: In Unreal Engine, chunking allows rendering datasets >1 gigavoxel, but introduces visual artifacts at chunk borders if lighting is computed independently per chunk. A workaround using a "4-in-1" material can achieve seamless lighting but drops framerates to ~1fps. Strengths: Enables rendering of very large scenes or high-resolution implicit fields on GPUs with limited VRAM. Limitations: Chunking can introduce artifacts if not handled correctly (e.g., lighting discontinuities). Early stopping requires careful tolerance tuning to avoid premature termination. Chunked Volume Rendering is based on the volume rendering equations defined in [Mildenhall et al. 2020] (NeRF). It has been implemented in various contexts, including the TBRayMarcher plugin for Unreal Engine, the NSVF framework by Facebook Research, and web-based viewers like Niivue. The technique is essential for real-time inference of large neural radiance fields and volumetric datasets. name: Chunked Volume Rendering with Occupancy Grid Estimator
head: OccGrid Estimator Rendering Loop, OccGridEstimator Rendering
body: This method accelerates volume rendering by combining chunked ray batching with an OccGridEstimator to sample along rays, query a radiance field for density and color at sample midpoints, and composite the result per chunk. It differs from its parent Chunked Volume Rendering by integrating a hierarchical occupancy grid for adaptive sampling, and from its sibling Block-based Volume Rendering Strategy by using a continuous grid-based estimator rather than discrete block structures. Inputs: Ray origins: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3). View directions: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3). Radiance field: Object with querydensity(positions) and querycolor(positions) methods. OccGridEstimator: Object with sampling(...) method. Parameters: nearplane, farplane, renderstepsize, alphathre, coneangle, testchunksize. Outputs: RGB image: Shape (H, W, 3). Depth image: Shape (H, W). Opacity image: Shape (H, W). Extras: Additional per-sample data. Data Structures: RaySamples: Contains vals (flattened sample data), rayindices (mapping samples to rays), and packedinfo (chunk boundaries). OccGrid: Hierarchical grid storing occupancy probabilities, updated via exponential moving average. Steps: 1. Reshape Rays: If ray origins and directions are 3D tensors of shape (H, W, 3), reshape them to 2D tensors of shape (N, 3) where N = H \times W. Store the original shape for final reshaping. 2. Chunking: Divide the N rays into chunks of size testchunksize. If in training mode, use max(int32) to process all rays at once. 3. Define Density Function: For each chunk, define a function sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices) that calculates sample midpoints: pos = origins[ray\indices] + dirs[ray\indices] \times \frac{t\starts + t\ends}{2.0}, and queries the radiance field for density: \sigma = radiance\field.query\density(pos). If temporal scenes are supported, pass timestamps to the query. 4. Sampling: Call estimator.sampling(sigmafn, nearplane, farplane, renderstepsize, stratified, coneangle, alphathre). This returns rayindices, tstarts, and tends. 5. Rendering: Call the rendering composite function with tstarts, tends, rayindices, nrays, and a combined function rgbsigmafn (which queries both color and density). This returns rgb, opacity, depth, and extras for the chunk. 6. Concatenation: Concatenate results from all chunks along dimension 0. 7. Reshape: Reshape the concatenated results back to the original image dimensions (H, W, 3) for RGB, (H, W) for depth/opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def renderimagewithoccgridtest( radiancefield, estimator, origins, viewdirs, nearplane=0.0, farplane=1e10, renderstepsize=1e-3, alphathre=0.0, coneangle=0.0, testchunksize=8192, istraining=False): # 1. Reshape rays if origins.dim() == 3: raysshape = origins.shape[:-1] origins = origins.view(-1, 3) viewdirs = viewdirs.view(-1, 3) else: raysshape = (origins.shape[0],) origins = origins.view(-1, 3) viewdirs = viewdirs.view(-1, 3) nrays = origins.shape[0] # 2. Chunking chunksize = 231 - 1 if istraining else testchunksize allrgb = [] alldepth = [] allopacity = [] allextras = [] for i in range(0, nrays, chunksize): chunkend = min(i + chunksize, nrays) chunkorigins = origins[i:chunkend] chunkdirs = viewdirs[i:chunkend] # 3. Define sigmafn for this chunk def sigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices): midpoints = chunkorigins[rayindices] + chunkdirs[rayindices] (tstarts + tends) / 2.0 densities = radiancefield.querydensity(midpoints) return densities # 4. Sampling rayindices, tstarts, tends = estimator.sampling( sigmafn=sigmafn, nearplane=nearplane, farplane=farplane, renderstepsize=renderstepsize, stratified=True, coneangle=coneangle, alphathre=alphathre) # 5. Rendering (explicit front-to-back volume compositing) def rgbsigmafn(tstarts, tends, rayindices): midpoints = chunkorigins[rayindices] + chunkdirs[rayindices] (tstarts + tends) / 2.0 densities = radiancefield.querydensity(midpoints) colors = radiancefield.querycolor(midpoints) return colors, densities nsamples = len(tstarts) chunkraycount = chunkend - i chunkrgb = torch.zeros(chunkraycount, 3, device=origins.device) chunkopacity = torch.zeros(chunkraycount, device=origins.device) chunkdepth = torch.zeros(chunkraycount, device=origins.device) # Sort samples by tstarts for each ray in the chunk sortedindices = torch.argsort(tstarts) tstartss = tstarts[sortedindices] tendss = tends[sortedindices] rayidxs = rayindices[sortedindices] colorss, densitiess = rgbsigmafn(tstartss, tendss, rayidxs) alphass = 1.0 - torch.exp(-densitiess (tendss - tstartss)) transmittances = torch.ones(chunkraycount, device=origins.device) for k in range(nsamples): r = rayidxs[k] alpha = alphass[k] # Use transmittance BEFORE this sample chunkrgb[r] += colorss[k] alpha transmittances[r] chunkopacity[r] += alpha transmittances[r] chunkdepth[r] += tstartss[k] alpha transmittances[r] # Update transmittance for NEXT samples transmittances[r] = (1.0 - alpha) chunkdepth = torch.where(chunkopacity > 0, chunkdepth / chunkopacity, chunkdepth) allrgb.append(chunkrgb) alldepth.append(chunkdepth) allopacity.append(chunkopacity) allextras.append({}) # 6. Concatenation finalrgb = torch.cat(allrgb, dim=0) finaldepth = torch.cat(alldepth, dim=0) finalopacity = torch.cat(allopacity, dim=0) # 7. Reshape finalrgb = finalrgb.view(raysshape, 3) finaldepth = finaldepth.view(raysshape) finalopacity = finalopacity.view(raysshape) return finalrgb, finaldepth, finalopacity, allextras Parameters: nearplane: Float, default 0.0. Minimum distance for ray marching. farplane: Float, default 1e10. Maximum distance for ray marching. renderstepsize: Float, default 1e-3. Base step size for sampling. alphathre: Float, default 0.0. Alpha threshold for filtering samples. coneangle: Float, default 0.0. Cone angle for adaptive sampling. testchunksize: Int, default 8192. Number of rays per chunk during inference. Edge Cases: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation
head: Distributed Volume Rendering Equations
body: Partitioned Volume Rendering Derivation provides the mathematical foundation for distributing volumetric rendering across multiple disjoint spatial segments (partitions) along a ray. It solves the problem of correctly accumulating color, transmittance, and auxiliary losses (such as distortion) when a ray traverses multiple independent volume tiles, which may be processed by different compute units. It sets itself apart from standard single-volume ray marching by explicitly decomposing global integrals into sums of local segment integrals weighted by upstream transmittance, enabling parallel prefix-scan accumulation. The method relies on decomposing the continuous volume rendering integral into discrete segments [tk, t{k+1}] defined by the boundaries of spatial partitions. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin o, direction d, and a set of N partition boundaries t1, t2, \dots, t{N+1} along the ray parameter t. For each segment k, the local density \sigma(t) and color c(t) are available. Outputs: Global accumulated color C(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}), global distortion loss \mathcal{L}{dist}(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}), and intermediate terms required for parallel reduction. Data Structures The derivation assumes the ray is divided into N segments. Each segment k corresponds to a spatial tile. The key intermediate values computed per segment are: A(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}): Accumulated weight (alpha) within the segment. D(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}): Accumulated depth-weight within the segment. T(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}): Transmittance through the segment. Formulas Let w(t) = T(t1 \rightarrow t) \sigma(t) be the contribution weight at t. The standard volume rendering equation for color is: C(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = \int{t1}^{t{N+1}} w(t) c(t) dt This is decomposed into a sum over N segments: C(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = \sum{k=1}^N T(t1 \rightarrow tk) C(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}) where the local segment color is: C(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}) = \int{tk}^{t{k+1}} T(tk \rightarrow t) \sigma(t) c(t) dt Here, T(t1 \rightarrow tk) is the transmittance from the ray origin to the start of segment k, acting as a weight for the local result. For distortion loss, we define the accumulated weight A and accumulated depth D over an interval [ta, tb] as: A(ta \rightarrow tb) = \int{ta}^{tb} w(t) dt D(ta \rightarrow tb) = \int{ta}^{tb} w(t) t dt The global distortion loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{dist}(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = 2 \int{t1}^{t{N+1}} w(t) \left( t - \frac{D(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1})}{A(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1})} \right) A(t1 \rightarrow t) dt (Note: The source defines the loss via the decomposition of \mathcal{L}1 and \mathcal{L}2 terms). The derivation shows this global loss can be computed from local segment losses using an intermediate term S: S(t1 \rightarrow tk) = D(tk \rightarrow t{k+1})A(t1 \rightarrow tk) - A(tk \rightarrow t{k+1})D(t1 \rightarrow tk) The final decomposed distortion loss is: \mathcal{L}{dist}(t1 \rightarrow t{N+1}) = 2 \sum{k=1}^N T(t1 \rightarrow tk) S(t1 \rightarrow tk) + \sum{k=1}^N T(t1 \rightarrow tk)^2 \mathcal{L}{dist}(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}) where \mathcal{L}{dist}(tk \rightarrow t{k+1}) is the local distortion loss within segment k. Parameters N: The number of segments (partitions) along the ray, corresponding to the number of tiles the ray intersects. Pseudocode The following pseudocode computes the global color and distortion loss from pre-computed local segment statistics. It assumes localA[k], localD[k], localC[k], and localLdist[k] are computed independently for each segment k \in [0, N-1]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partitionedrendering(localsegments): """ localsegments: list of N dicts, each containing: 'A': accumulated weight A(tk -> t{k+1}) 'D': accumulated depth D(tk -> t{k+1}) 'C': local color C(tk -> t{k+1}) 'Ldist': local distortion loss Ldist(tk -> t{k+1}) 'Tprev': transmittance from ray origin to tk, T(t1 -> tk) """ N = len(localsegments) globalcolor = 0.0 globaldistloss = 0.0 # Precompute global A and D for the entire ray to handle edge cases if needed, # though the formula relies on prefix products of T. for k in range(N): seg = localsegments[k] Tprev = seg['Tprev'] Alocal = seg['A'] Dlocal = seg['D'] Clocal = seg['C'] Ldistlocal = seg['Ldist'] # 1. Accumulate Color # Cglobal += T(t1 -> tk) C(tk -> t{k+1}) globalcolor += Tprev Clocal # 2. Compute Intermediate Term S # S(t1 -> tk) = D(tk -> t{k+1}) A(t1 -> tk) - A(tk -> t{k+1}) D(t1 -> tk) # Note: A(t1 -> tk) and D(t1 -> tk) are the accumulated values from segments 0 to k-1. # These must be maintained in a running prefix sum. Aprefix = seg['Aprefix'] # A(t1 -> tk) Dprefix = seg['Dprefix'] # D(t1 -> tk) S = Dlocal Aprefix - Alocal Dprefix # 3. Accumulate Distortion Loss # Term 1: 2 T(t1 -> tk) S(t1 -> tk) term1 = 2.0 Tprev S # Term 2: T(t1 -> tk)^2 Ldist(tk -> t{k+1}) term2 = (Tprev 2) Ldistlocal globaldistloss += term1 + term2 return globalcolor, globaldistloss The pseudocode assumes Aprefix and Dprefix are provided or computed via a parallel prefix scan (e.g., using NerfAcc) over the segments. Tprev is the product of transmittances of all preceding segments. Performs volumetric rendering over a partition of possible t values in the union of rendering volumes, combining results from disjoint volume integrals and a void model for empty space. It sets itself apart from standard single-volume ray marching by explicitly handling multiple disjoint volume bounds and accumulating transmittance across partitions, ensuring correct alpha compositing when rays traverse empty space between volumes. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of segments N for the accumulation step, assuming local segment computations are parallelized. The parallel prefix scan for transmittance and accumulated A/D adds a logarithmic factor or linear factor depending on the reduction implementation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing intermediate A, D, C, L{dist} for each segment. The memory footprint scales with N and the number of rays. Strengths: Enables efficient distribution of rendering work across multiple GPUs by minimizing communication (only per-ray aggregates need reduction). Limitations: Requires precise spatial partitioning and handling of empty space/void models to ensure correct transmittance accumulation. When to use: Large-scale NeRF training/inference where a single GPU cannot hold the volume or process all rays efficiently. The derivation originates from NeRF-XL, which scales NeRFs with multiple GPUs. It builds on the spatial partitioning scheme described in Appendix A.3, where space is divided recursively using CDF-based splitting to create nearly cubic partitions. The method allows distributed NeRFs to compute global integrals from local segment results, facilitating batched asynchronous send/receive operations and parallel prefix scans. name: Partitioned Volumetric Rendering with RayVolumeIntegral
head: Partitioned Volumetric Rendering
body: Partitioned Volumetric Rendering with RayVolumeIntegral performs volumetric rendering over a partition of possible t values in the union of rendering volumes, combining results from disjoint volume integrals and a void model for empty space. It sets itself apart from standard single-volume ray marching by explicitly handling multiple disjoint volume bounds and accumulating transmittance across partitions, ensuring correct alpha compositing when rays traverse empty space between volumes. Inputs: rays: Origin and direction vectors for each pixel. resultsi: A sequence of RayVolumeIntegralResults objects, each containing volumerange (start/end t), raw (raw network outputs like density/color), and transmittance. voidmodel: A function or model that queries background color/transmittance for empty space. origin, direc: Ray origins and directions. importancesamplingoptions: Configuration for the sampler. Outputs: results: A combined RayVolumeIntegralResults object containing the final rendered channels and transmittance. RayVolumeIntegral A dataclass holding the rendering configuration: model: NeRFModel instance. volume: Volume instance. sampler: RaySampler instance. nsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray segment. RayVolumeIntegralResults Holds the state of integration for a specific volume partition: volumerange: Defines the t interval [t0, t1]. raw: Raw outputs from the neural network (density, color, etc.). transmittance: Scalar or tensor representing transmittance at the end of the interval. output: Rendered channels (e.g., RGB). 1. Initialization: Initialize origin, direc from rays. Set prevrawoutputs to a list of Nones. Initialize samplers list, rawoutputs list, t0 to None, and results to None. 2. Loop over Volume Partitions: For each resultsi in the sequence of volume results: a. Sampler Creation: Create an ImportanceRaySampler using resultsi.volumerange, resultsi.raw, and importancesamplingoptions. Append this sampler to samplers. b. Raw Output Storage: Append resultsi.raw to rawoutputs. c. Update Start Time: Update t0 to resultsi.volumerange.nextt0(). d. Combine Results: If results is None, set results = resultsi. Otherwise, update results by combining it with resultsi using the partitioned combination rule. 3. Void Background Addition: After the loop, add the void background to the final result: \text{results.output.channels} = \text{results.output.channels} + \text{results.transmittance} \cdot \text{void\model}(\text{Query}(origin, direc)). This method handles the sampling and integration for a single volume partition defined by self.volume. 1. Intersection and Sampling: Intersect rays with the volume: vrange = self.volume.intersect(origin, direction, t0lower=t0). Sample t values: ts = self.sampler.sample(vrange.t0, vrange.t1, self.nsamples). 2. Position and Interval Calculation: Compute sample positions: positions = origin.unsqueeze(-2) + ts directions. Compute midpoints: mids = (ts[..., 1:,:] + ts[...,:-1,:]) / 2. 3. Model Query: Query the neural network model with positions, optional directions, and interval bounds: python tmin = torch.cat([vrange.t0[..., None,:], mids], dim=-2) tmax = torch.cat([mids, vrange.t1[..., None,:]], dim=-2) raw = Query(position=positions, direction=optionaldirections, tmin=tmin, tmax=tmax). 4. Integration: Call self.integratesamples(vrange, raw) to obtain output and transmittance. 5. Masking Non-Intersected Rays: Mask transmittance: transmittance = torch.where(vrange.intersected, transmittance, torch.oneslike(transmittance)). Mask output tensors: output = output.map(mapfn=maskfn, shouldmap=istensor) where maskfn returns torch.where(vrange.intersected, tensor, torch.zeroslike(tensor)). This method computes the discrete volume integral approximation. 1. Density and Transmittance Calculation: Calculate interval lengths: dt = volumerange.partition(raw.ts). Compute optical depth increments: ddensity = raw.density dt. Compute cumulative optical depth: mass = torch.cumsum(ddensity, dim=-2). Compute final transmittance: transmittance = torch.exp(-mass[..., -1,:]). Compute per-sample alphas: alphas = 1.0 - torch.exp(-ddensity). Compute per-sample transmittances Ts: Ts = \exp\left(\text{cat}([0, -\text{mass}[...,:-1,:]], \text{dim}=-2)\right). Compute weights: weights = alphas Ts. 2. Weighted Summation: Integrate using integrate(key, samples, weights) which returns torch.sum(samples weights, dim=-2) for keys other than 'density'. Handle auxiliary losses with detached weights if noweightgradauxlosses is enabled: use weights.detach(). When combining results from disjoint volume partitions [t0, t1] and [t1, t2], the integral over [t0, t2] is the sum of the integral over [t0, t1] and the transmittance at t1 times the integral over [t1, t2]: \int{t0}^{t2} = \int{t0}^{t1} + \text{transmittance}(t1) \cdot \int{t1}^{t2} Implemented as: prevval + prevtransmittance curval. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def renderpartitionedvolumes(rays, volumeresultslist, voidmodel, cfg): """ Renders volumes by partitioning the ray space and combining results. Args: rays: Tuple of (origins, directions). volumeresultslist: List of RayVolumeIntegralResults objects. voidmodel: Function to query background color. cfg: Configuration object. Returns: Combined RayVolumeIntegralResults. """ origins, directions = rays prevrawoutputs = [None] len(volumeresultslist) samplers = [] rawoutputs = [] t0 = None results = None for i, resultsi in enumerate(volumeresultslist): # Step 2a: Create Importance Ray Sampler sampler = ImportanceRaySampler( volumerange=resultsi.volumerange, raw=resultsi.raw, options=cfg.importancesamplingoptions) samplers.append(sampler) # Step 2b: Store raw outputs rawoutputs.append(resultsi.raw) # Step 2c: Update t0 t0 = resultsi.volumerange.nextt0() # Step 2d: Combine results if results is None: results = resultsi else: # Combine using the partitioned rule: prev + prevtrans cur # Assuming resultsi has 'output' (channels) and 'transmittance' combinedchannels = results.output.channels + results.transmittance resultsi.output.channels # Transmittance updates to the end of the current partition combinedtransmittance = results.transmittance resultsi.transmittance # Reconstruct results object (simplified) results = RayVolumeIntegralResults( volumerange=resultsi.volumerange, # Or unioned range raw=resultsi.raw, output=CombinedOutput(channels=combinedchannels), transmittance=combinedtransmittance) # Step 3: Add void background # Query void model at ray origin/direction voidcolor = voidmodel(Query(origin=origins, direction=directions)) # Add void contribution weighted by final transmittance finalchannels = results.output.channels + results.transmittance voidcolor # Update final results with combined channels results.output.channels = finalchannels return results def integratesamples(vrange, raw, nsamples): """ Integrates raw network outputs along a ray segment. Args: vrange: Volume range object with t0, t1, and intersected mask. raw: Dict of raw outputs (density, color, etc.) with ts (sample t values). nsamples: Number of samples. Returns: output: Rendered channels. transmittance: Final transmittance. name: Block-based Volume Rendering Strategy
head: Multi-shader Block Accumulation, Sequential Block Rendering
body: A rendering strategy for large scenes partitioned into blocks, where each block uses a separate shader due to web texture unit limits. It solves the problem where standard volume rendering fails because sampling points across a ray may belong to different blocks loaded by different shaders, breaking 3D consistency and correct occlusion. It sets itself apart from its siblings by enforcing sequential rendering and post-hoc accumulation rather than attempting to load all resources into a single pass or using occupancy grids to skip empty space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of M scene blocks, each associated with a dedicated shader instance containing its specific texture resources. Output: The final composite color Cr for the pixel. Data Structures: Block List: A list of M blocks, each containing a reference to its shader and its spatial position. Shader State: Each shader instance holds the texture units required to render its specific block. Steps: 1. Depth Sorting: Sort all M scene blocks relative to the camera viewpoint to determine the rendering order from back to front. 2. Sequential Rendering: Iterate through the sorted blocks. For each block k: Activate the dedicated shader for block k. Render the block to obtain its local color ck and opacity \alphak. Store ck and \alphak for accumulation. 3. Accumulation: Combine the results using the volume rendering equation: Cr = \sum{k=1}^{M} \left( \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj) \right) ck Where: Cr is the final composite color. M is the total number of blocks. ck is the color output by the shader for block k. \alphak is the opacity output by the shader for block k. The term \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphaj) represents the transmittance from all preceding blocks j < k. Parameters: Texture Unit Limit: Typically no more than 16 texture units can be loaded into a single web shader. This constraint necessitates the separation of blocks into different shaders. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Web Platform Limits: Web platforms limit texture units to ~16, preventing loading all block resources into a single shader. 3D Consistency: Using different shaders per block breaks standard volume rendering because sampling points across a ray may belong to different blocks/shaders. This method ensures correctness by rendering sequentially and combining results. Memory Usage: Loading all blocks for rendering is impractical due to excessive memory usage on standard consumer devices. Training Pipeline Consistency is a strategy to minimize the discrepancy between the training and inference phases of block-based volume rendering by enforcing the identical rendering pipeline during both stages. It solves the problem where training with a continuous, global coordinate system leads to artifacts or quality degradation when the model is deployed in a constrained, block-based rendering environment. It sets itself apart from standard neural rendering methods by explicitly simulating the discrete, hardware-bound constraints of the target rendering hardware (such as texture unit limits and quantization) during the optimization process. A memory-saving rendering strategy for high-resolution volumes that splits the spatial dimensions into overlapping patches, renders them independently, and merges the results to scale to arbitrary image resolutions. Unlike full-volume rendering which requires memory proportional to H \times W, the patch-based approach trades redundant computation in overlapping regions for drastically reduced memory footprint, enabling scaling to arbitrary resolutions. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of blocks M for the sorting and accumulation steps, plus the cost of rendering each block. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active blocks loaded into shaders, constrained by the texture unit limit (typically 16). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Supports dynamic loading of resources via Level-of-Detail (LOD) generation to handle large scenes on consumer devices. Strengths: Enables rendering of large-scale scenes on web platforms with limited texture unit resources. Ensures correct occlusion and 3D consistency. Limitations: Requires sequential rendering, which may be slower than parallel approaches if not optimized. Limited by the number of texture units available per shader. When to use: When rendering large scenes on web platforms with strict texture unit limits. When not: When high parallelism is required and texture unit limits are not a constraint. Originated in the "City-on-Web" paper. The method addresses challenges associated with resource-independent block-based rendering on the web, specifically the limitation on the number and resolution of texture units that can be loaded into a shader. It draws inspiration from traditional graphics techniques for Level-of-Detail (LOD) generation. name: Training Pipeline Consistency
head: Simulated finite grid approach, Training-time block rendering
body: Training Pipeline Consistency is a strategy to minimize the discrepancy between the training and inference phases of block-based volume rendering by enforcing the identical rendering pipeline during both stages. It solves the problem where training with a continuous, global coordinate system leads to artifacts or quality degradation when the model is deployed in a constrained, block-based rendering environment. It sets itself apart from standard neural rendering methods by explicitly simulating the discrete, hardware-bound constraints of the target rendering hardware (such as texture unit limits and quantization) during the optimization process. The method ensures that the data flow, sampling logic, and integration order during training are identical to those used in the final web-based rendering stage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray \boldsymbol{r}(t), scene bounding box, block partitioning parameters, proposal MLPs \psi^k, and attribute MLPs f^k for each block k. Output: Final rendered color and opacity for the ray. Data Structures: Blocks (Bk): The scene is partitioned into spatial blocks, each with an associated proposal MLP \psi^k and attribute MLP f^k. Ray Samples: Points sampled along the ray \boldsymbol{r}(t) between near and far boundaries. Numbered Steps: 1. Uniform Sampling: For a given ray \boldsymbol{r}(t), uniformly sample points between the near and far boundaries defined by the scene’s bounding box. 2. Block Determination: For each sample point, determine which block Bk it resides in using an xy-coordinate projection, referred to as Eq. (4) in the source. 3. Proposal Sampling: Query the proposal MLP \psi^k corresponding to the determined block Bk to sample probability distributions along the ray. 4. Attribute Querying: Query the attribute MLP f^k corresponding to block Bk to obtain the rendering attributes for the sample points. 5. Sequential Rendering: Render each block sequentially to obtain the color and opacity for the ray in Bk. 6. Final Composition: Use Eq. (5) to derive the final rendering result by combining the block contributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderrayconsistent(rayorigin, raydirection, scenebboxmin, scenebboxmax, blocksize, proposalmlps, attributemlps): """ Renders a ray using the same pipeline as the training stage to ensure consistency. Args: rayorigin: 3D array/tuple of ray origin coordinates. raydirection: 3D array/tuple of ray direction vector. scenebboxmin: 3D array/tuple of bounding box minimum coordinates. scenebboxmax: 3D array/tuple of bounding box maximum coordinates. blocksize: Width/height of each spatial block. proposalmlps: Dictionary mapping block index to proposal MLP function. attributemlps: Dictionary mapping block index to attribute MLP function. Returns: finalcolor: Rendered color for the ray. finalopacity: Rendered opacity for the ray. """ # Step 1: Uniform sampling between near and far boundaries tmin = max((scenebboxmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)) tmax = min((scenebboxmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydirection[i] if raydirection[i] != 0 else float('-inf') for i in range(3)) tnear = max(tmin, 0.0) tfar = tmax if tnear >= tfar: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0 numsamples = 128 # Typical value for volume rendering; not explicitly given in S1 tsamples = [tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] points = [[rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] for t in tsamples] finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaaccum = 0.0 # Group points by block blockpoints = {} for i, point in enumerate(points): # Step 2: Determine block Bk using xy-coordinate projection (Eq. 4) blockidx = getblockindexfromxy(point[0], point[1], scenebboxmin, scenebboxmax, blocksize) if blockidx not in blockpoints: blockpoints[blockidx] = [] blockpoints[blockidx].append((i, point)) # Process blocks in order (assuming blocks are ordered along the ray or spatially) # Note: The exact ordering logic for sequential block rendering is not detailed in S1 sortedblockindices = sorted(blockpoints.keys()) for blockidx in sortedblockindices: if blockidx not in blockpoints: continue pointsinblock = blockpoints[blockidx] proposalmlp = proposalmlps[blockidx] attributemlp = attributemlps[blockidx] # Step 3: Query proposal MLP to sample probability distributions proposalweights = proposalmlp(pointsinblock) # Step 4: Query attribute MLP to obtain attributes attributes = attributemlp(pointsinblock) colors = [attr[:3] for attr in attributes] densities = [attr[3] for attr in attributes] # Step 5: Render block sequentially for idxinblock, (globali, point) in enumerate(pointsinblock): # Calculate delta distance if idxinblock == 0: deltat = tsamples[pointsinblock[1][0]] - tsamples[globali] if len(pointsinblock) > 1 else 0.0 elif idxinblock == len(pointsinblock) - 1: deltat = tsamples[globali] - tsamples[pointsinblock[-2][0]] else: deltat = (tsamples[pointsinblock[idxinblock + 1][0]] - tsamples[pointsinblock[idxinblock - 1][0]]) / 2.0 # Convert density to opacity alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-densities[idxinblock] deltat) # Compositing weight = alpha (1.0 - alphaaccum) finalcolor[0] += weight colors[idxinblock][0] finalcolor[1] += weight colors[idxinblock][1] finalcolor[2] += weight colors[idxinblock][2] alphaaccum += weight if alphaaccum >= 1.0: break return finalcolor, alphaaccum def getblockindexfromxy(x, y, bboxmin, bboxmax, blocksize): # Assuming a simple grid-based partitioning based on xy-coordinate projection # as described in the source for Eq. (4). width = bboxmax[0] - bboxmin[0] height = bboxmax[1] - bboxmin[1] cols = int(width / blocksize) rows = int(height / blocksize) col = int((x - bboxmin[0]) / blocksize) row = int((y - bboxmin[1]) / blocksize) return row cols + col Parameters: Number of Samples: Not given in the sources. Loss Weights: The training loss includes \lambda1 \mathcal{L}{\text{s3im}}, \lambda2 \mathcal{L}{\text{prop}}, \lambda3 \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}, \lambda4 \mathcal{L}{\text{s}}, and \lambda5 \mathcal{L}{\text{opacity}}. Specific values for \lambdai are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on simulating quantization during training to mimic discrete texture lookups. Failure to accurately simulate this can lead to a gap between training and rendering. Boundaries: The method assumes a well-defined scene bounding box for uniform sampling. Block Assignment: The block determination (Eq. 4) must be consistent between training and rendering. A memory-optimized rendering pipeline that combines a low-resolution sparse voxel representation with high-resolution 2D triplanes, bridging training and rendering by simulating grid and quantization constraints during training. It reduces memory requirements compared to SNeRG by replacing the dense 3D voxel grid with a hybrid sparse voxel and 2D triplane representation. During training, it simulates a finite grid approach by querying MLPs at virtual grid corners instead of continuous coordinates, and simulates quantization to closely mimic the discrete texture lookup behavior of the actual rendering pipeline. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The MERF variant reduces memory requirements compared to SNeRG by using a hybrid sparse voxel and 2D triplane representation. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Minimizes the gap between training and rendering quality by ensuring pipeline consistency. The MERF variant offers significant memory reduction. Limitations: The block-based approach is constrained by web texture unit limits, requiring sequential rendering [Parent]. When to use: When deploying neural radiance fields on web platforms with strict hardware constraints (texture unit limits) and where training-inference consistency is critical for quality. The method originates from the "City-on-Web" project, which focuses on real-time neural rendering of large-scale scenes on the web. It was developed to address the limitations of existing methods like SNeRG, which demand substantial memory. name: Patch-based Volume Rendering
head: Patch-based rendering strategy
body: A memory-saving rendering strategy for high-resolution volumes that splits the spatial dimensions into overlapping patches, renders them independently, and merges the results to scale to arbitrary image resolutions. Unlike full-volume rendering which requires memory proportional to H \times W, the patch-based approach trades redundant computation in overlapping regions for drastically reduced memory footprint, enabling scaling to arbitrary resolutions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target image resolution H \times W, a volume representation (coarse and fine models), and a patch grid configuration P \times P. Output: A rendered image of resolution H \times W. Data Structures: The method relies on the standard volume representation used in MuRF: Coarse Volume: Resolution H/8 \times W/8 \times D1 \times C1. Fine Volume: Resolution H \times W \times D2 \times C2. Patches: The spatial dimensions (H, W) are divided into a grid of P \times P overlapping patches. Parameters: P \times P: Grid size of overlapping patches along the spatial dimensions. Typical value: 4 \times 4 (yielding 16 patches). D1: Number of sampling points per ray for the coarse model. Value: 64. D2: Number of sampling points per ray for the fine model. Value: 16. C1: Feature dimension of the coarse volume representation. Value: 128. C2: Feature dimension of the fine volume representation. Value: 16. Steps: 1. Partition: Split the volume's first two spatial dimensions into a grid of P \times P overlapping patches. 2. Render: Render each patch independently using the standard volume rendering pipeline. 3. Merge: Combine all patch results into a full image. Overlapping regions are combined with simple averaging. name: BRDF Evaluation Kernel
body: The BRDF Evaluation Kernel evaluates a Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) for a batch of rays during inference ray marching and integration. It transforms geometric and material inputs into final pixel colors. It is distinct from compositing operations, focusing solely on the local reflection model evaluation. Inputs and Outputs: rgba: Input RGBA tensor (material color/opacity data). position: Input position tensor (3D coordinates). gradient: Input gradient tensor (normals or density gradients). rayDir: Input ray direction tensor. virtualsize: Dimensions of the virtual batch grid. rgbaOutput: Output RGBA tensor containing the computed color. Data Structures: The kernel operates on flat tensors indexed by a linear batch index b. The layout assumes contiguous memory access for the input tensors and the output tensor. Steps: 1. Initialize the loop over the batch using KERNEL1DLOOP with bounds determined by virtualsize.x virtualsize.y virtualsize.z. 2. For each batch index b: a. Fetch rgba, position, gradient, and rayDir from their respective input tensors at index b. b. Set batch = 0. c. Call brdf.eval(rgba, position, gradient, rayDir, batch) to compute the reflected color. d. Write the resulting color to rgbaOutput at index b. Formulas: Not given in the sources. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def brdfevalkernel(rgba, position, gradient, rayDir, virtualsize, rgbaOutput): totalelements = virtualsize[0] virtualsize[1] virtualsize[2] for b in range(totalelements): currentrgba = rgba[b] currentposition = position[b] currentgradient = gradient[b] currentrayDir = rayDir[b] batch = 0 # The source does not provide the internal BRDF formula. color = brdfeval(currentrgba, currentposition, currentgradient, currentrayDir, batch) rgbaOutput[b] = color def brdfeval(rgba, position, gradient, rayDir, batch): # The source does not provide the internal BRDF formula. return rgba Parameters: virtualsize: Defines the batch dimension. Typical values depend on the resolution of the volume and the number of rays processed per frame. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The kernel assumes valid inputs for all tensors. Degenerate inputs (e.g., zero-length gradients) are not explicitly handled in the source description. Precision issues may arise if the evaluation function involves complex trigonometric or normalization operations on the gradient and ray direction vectors. EPBRR is a variant proposed by Poirier-Ginter et al. [2025] as an improvement to 3DGRT's ray tracer. It introduces various optimizations to the ray tracing process. However, it used a crude custom implementation of Depth Importance (DI), summarized as "binning the depth maps". Experiments in EDGS argued against this specific DI approach. Furthermore, EPBRR techniques were not tested against proper dense initialization and were not included in a full ray-tracing solution. They offered only limited comparisons to 3DGRT, which excluded DI and trained at reduced iteration counts without Spherical Harmonics (SH). The method was not validated individually. head: Inference Module
body: The Inference Pipeline renders images from a trained dense point cloud and new camera poses without requiring further optimization. It differs from its sibling Inference Ray Compositing by handling the complete forward evaluation loop from input data structures to final image output, whereas the sibling focuses specifically on the ray-compositing mathematics. It is distinct from Sparse Ray Marching (Training) as it operates on a fully trained, dense representation rather than a sparse, evolving one. Inputs: 1. DensePointCloudWithExtraFeatures: The trained set of 3D points with associated features. 2. NewCameraPose: The target view parameters. Outputs: 1. Image: The rendered output. The rasterizer outputs the final Image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inferencepipeline(densepointcloud, camerapose): """Renders an image from a trained dense point cloud and camera pose.""" # Step 1: Load inputs # densepointcloud and camerapose are provided to the module. # Step 2: Rasterization # Pass the point cloud and camera pose to a rasterizer. # The sources do not specify the internal rasterization algorithm. # Standard rasterization projects primitives to screen space, sorts them by depth, and composites them. projectedprimitives = projecttoscreen(densepointcloud, camerapose) sortedprimitives = sortbydepth(projectedprimitives) image = alphacomposite(sortedprimitives) # Step 3: Output Image # The rasterizer outputs the final image. return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: View-Dependent Color: The color MLP must be re-evaluated whenever the viewing angle shifts to account for scene colors changing with viewing direction. Bounding Box Cropping: For inference, an enlarged bounding box around the projected mesh on the image plane is cropped, and only pixels inside the bounding box are rendered. Renders a set of views from a trained dense point cloud, prunes points occluded by or too close to the camera, and saves rendered images, depth maps, and colored depth maps. It differs from the parent Inference Pipeline by focusing specifically on the extraction and visualization of depth data and the pruning of invalid geometry, rather than the full evaluation loop including FPS calculation and video generation. After training, uses only the forward flow to render images. Passes a control encoding to the MLPs to determine the object to be rendered at runtime. Invokes the MLPs whenever a change in the encoding is necessary. Re-evaluates the color MLP whenever the viewing angle shifts to account for scene colors changing with viewing direction. For other MLPs, predicts k parameters for each anchor point instead of inferring for every viewing direction. 3D embeddings are decoded from shallow to deep levels using level-wise context models. The last 3D level is utilized to generate dimension-wise context for 2D embeddings. 2D embeddings are decoded in a coarse-to-fine order with the assistance of the dimension-wise context. Once the embeddings are decoded, all rendering processes are the same as INGP, requiring no additional time. For inference, an enlarged bounding box around the projected SMPL mesh on the image plane is cropped, and only pixels inside the bounding box are rendered. For unseen test poses, the latent code Z of the last training frame is used as input. Encoding/Decoding Time: Approximately 1 second. Rendering Time: After decoding, rendering requires no additional time beyond the base INGP process. For a 512 × 512 image, rendering takes 10-20 seconds depending on the bounding box size of the subject. Joint Root-Finding Time: Approximately 1 second. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability; supports context translation via control encoding without retraining. Limitations: Requires a trained representation; control encoding changes may require MLP re-evaluation. When to use: When real-time rendering of trained models is required, especially with dynamic context or style changes. When not to use: When optimization during inference is needed. The Inference Pipeline is a component of Gaussian Splatting rendering systems, enabling real-time visualization of trained models without the computational overhead of training or optimization.
