name: Depth Map Rendering and Visualization
body: Renders a set of views from a trained dense point cloud (specifically Gaussian Splatting models), prunes points occluded by or too close to the camera, and saves rendered images, depth maps, and colored depth maps. It differs from the parent Inference Pipeline by focusing specifically on the extraction and visualization of depth data and the pruning of invalid geometry, rather than the full evaluation loop including FPS calculation and video generation. Inputs: gaussians: The trained Gaussian model containing 3D positions (xyz), covariances, colors, and opacities. view: A camera view object containing intrinsic parameters, extrinsic pose, and image dimensions. near: A scalar distance threshold for pruning points near the camera. renderpath: Directory path for output images. iteration: Current training/inference iteration index (used for naming). Outputs: Rendered color images (.png). Normalized depth maps (.png). Colored depth maps (.png). Video summaries (via ffmpeg). Data Structures: masknear: A boolean tensor of shape (N,) where N is the number of Gaussians, indicating points within the near distance threshold. renderpkg: A dictionary returned by the renderer, containing at least keys "render" (color image), "depth" (raw depth), and "alpha" (accumulated alpha). Steps: 1. Initialize Output Directory: Create the output directory using the model path, name, and iteration index: python renderpath = os.path.join(modelpath, name, "ours{}".format(iteration)) makedirs(renderpath, existok=True) 2. Compute Proximity Mask: Calculate the Euclidean distance between each Gaussian center and the camera center. Identify Gaussians closer than near. Let P be the set of Gaussian centers with shape (N, 3) and C be the camera center with shape (3,). Di = \| Pi - C \|2 The mask for the current view is: Mi = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } Di < \text{near} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Accumulate this mask across all views processed so far to prune points that are near the camera in any view: python masktemp = (gaussians.getxyz - view.cameracenter.repeat(gaussians.getxyz.shape[0], 1)).norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) < near if masknear is None: masknear = masktemp else: masknear = masknear + masktemp Note: The source uses addition (+) rather than logical OR (|). In boolean contexts, this may result in values > 1. The pruning function likely treats any non-zero value as True. 3. Prune Points: Remove Gaussians marked in masknear from the model. python gaussians.prunepointsinference(masknear) 4. Render View: For each view, perform rendering without gradient tracking. python with torch.nograd(): renderpkg = render(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, inference=True) 5. Extract and Normalize Depth: Extract raw depth and alpha from renderpkg. Normalize the depth to [0, 1] and combine with alpha to handle background. Let d be renderpkg['depth'] and \alpha be renderpkg['alpha']. d{min} = \min(d), \quad d{max} = \max(d) d{norm} = \frac{d - d{min}}{d{max} - d{min}} The final depth map is computed as: \text{depth} = d{norm} + 1 \cdot (1 - \alpha) Note: This formula adds a value of 1 for pixels where alpha is 0 (background), effectively pushing background depth to the maximum normalized value. 6. Save Rendered Image: Save the color image. python torchvision.utils.saveimage(rendering, os.path.join(renderpath, '{0:05d}'.format(idx) + ".png")) 7. Save Inverted Depth Map: Save the inverted normalized depth. python torchvision.utils.saveimage(1 - depth, os.path.join(renderpath, 'depth{0:05d}'.format(idx) + ".png")) 8. Generate Colored Depth Map: Convert depth to numpy, apply a colormap, and save. python depthest = depth.squeeze().cpu().numpy() # Apply colormap 'turbo' with a logarithmic curve function depthest = visualizecmap(depthest, np.oneslike(depthest), cm.getcmap('turbo'), curvefn=depthcurvefn).copy() The curve function is defined as: \text{curve\fn}(x) = -\ln(x + \epsilon) where \epsilon = \text{np.finfo(np.float32).eps}. 9. Save Colored Depth Map: Convert back to tensor, permute channels, and save. python depthest = torch.astensor(depthest).permute(2, 0, 1) torchvision.utils.saveimage(depthest, os.path.join(renderpath, 'cdepth{0:05d}'.format(idx) + ".png")) 10. Generate Video: Use ffmpeg to create video summaries from the saved render, depth, and colored depth images. Parameters: near: Distance threshold for pruning points near the camera. Value not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Normalization: The depth normalization uses global min/max of the rendered depth map, not the scene bounds. This can cause inconsistent depth scaling across frames if the visible depth range varies significantly. Background Handling: The formula d{norm} + (1 - \alpha) sets background depth to 1.0 (normalized). If the foreground depth also normalizes to near 1.0, depth and background may be indistinguishable in the raw depth map. Mask Accumulation: Using addition for mask accumulation (masknear + masktemp) creates integer tensors. The pruning function must handle this correctly (treating any positive value as "prune"). The 4DGS Rendering Pipeline is the inference-stage script that iterates over a sequence of camera views to render images using the trained 4D Gaussian Splatting model, saves the ground truth and rendered images, and generates a video summary. It differs from the parent Depth Map Rendering and Visualization by focusing specifically on the full image-order rendering loop for evaluation and visualization, including FPS calculation and video generation, rather than just depth map extraction and pruning. Converts optical flow and camera intrinsics/extrinsics into a depth map. It handles validity, mesh export, and depth padding via morphological operations. Steps: 1. Calculate Offset: \text{offset} = \text{data}['\text{ref\intr}'][:, 0, 2] - \text{data}['\text{intr}'][:, 0, 2] 2. Compute Disparity: \text{disparity} = \text{offset} - \text{data}['\text{flow\pred}'] 3. Compute Depth: \text{depth} = -\frac{\text{disparity}}{\text{data}['\text{Tf\x}']} 4. Mask Invalid Regions: Multiply depth by data['mask'] to zero out invalid regions. 5. Export Mesh (Optional): If ptsoutpath is provided, export depth mesh using depth2mesh. 6. Transform to Original Camera Space: Transform points to original camera space using perspective with calibori = introri @ extrori. Invert z-depth. 7. Render Perspective Depth: Render perspective depth using taichirender.renderperspectivedepth with valid mask. 8. Pad Depth: Apply padding to renderdepth using taichirender.paddepth and store in data['lmain']['depthori']. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of Gaussians and views. Pruning is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Rendering is O(N \cdot V) where V is the number of views. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing Gaussian attributes. The mask accumulation requires O(N) storage. Strengths: Efficiently removes invalid geometry (points too close to camera) that can cause artifacts. Provides standardized depth visualization for evaluation. Limitations: Depth normalization is local to each view, not global. Pruning is aggressive and irreversible. When to use: When evaluating depth accuracy or visualizing depth maps from Gaussian Splatting models. When not to use: When global depth consistency across views is required without post-processing. Originated in the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting inference pipelines, specifically within the DNGaussian project. It is used to generate evaluation metrics and visualizations for novel view synthesis. name: 4DGS Rendering Pipeline
head: Rendering Pipeline for 4DGS
body: The 4DGS Rendering Pipeline is the inference-stage script that iterates over a sequence of camera views to render images using the trained 4D Gaussian Splatting model, saves the ground truth and rendered images, and generates a video summary. It differs from the parent Depth Map Rendering and Visualization by focusing specifically on the full image-order rendering loop for evaluation and visualization, including FPS calculation and video generation, rather than just depth map extraction and pruning. Inputs: views: A list of camera view objects containing projection matrices, image data, and metadata. gaussians: The 4D Gaussian splatting model parameters (positions, covariances, opacities, colors, etc.). pipeline: Rendering configuration parameters (e.g., rasterization settings). background: Background color tensor. name: Dataset identifier (e.g., 'train', 'test', or specific scene name). camtype: Camera type string (e.g., 'PanopticSports' or standard pinhole). modelpath, iteration: Paths to locate output directories. Outputs: Rendered images (PNG) in renders/. Ground truth images (PNG) in gt/. Video file videorgb.mp4. Console output: FPS metric. Data Structures: renderimages: List of HWC uint8 numpy arrays for visualization. renderlist: List of raw tensor renders (CHW format) for saving. gtlist: List of raw tensor ground truth images (CHW format). Steps: 1. Setup Paths: Create directories renders and gt under modelpath/name/ours{iteration}/. 2. Initialize: Create empty lists renderimages, gtlist, and renderlist. Record start time time1 when processing the first view. 3. Iterate Views: Loop through each view in views using a progress bar. 4. Render: Call the core rendering function render(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, camtype=camtype). Extract the 'render' key from the returned dictionary. 5. Convert and Store: Convert the raw render tensor to 8-bit uint8 using to8b (clip values to [0, 1], multiply by 255, cast to uint8). Transpose the result from CHW to HWC format. Append the HWC array to renderimages. Append the raw tensor to renderlist. 6. Handle Ground Truth: If name is 'train' or 'test': If camtype is not 'PanopticSports', extract view.originalimage[0:3,:,:]. If camtype is 'PanopticSports', extract view['image'].cuda(). Append the GT tensor to gtlist. 7. Calculate FPS: After the loop, record end time time2. Calculate FPS as (len(views) - 1) / (time2 - time1). 8. Save Images: Use multithreadwrite to save gtlist to the gt directory and renderlist to the renders directory. Files are named {index:05d}.png. 9. Create Video: Use imageio.mimwrite to generate videorgb.mp4 in the output directory using renderimages with a frame rate of 36 FPS. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import time import os import imageio import numpy as np import torch def renderpipeline(views, gaussians, pipeline, background, name, camtype, modelpath, iteration): # Setup Paths methoddir = os.path.join(modelpath, name, f"ours{iteration}") rendersdir = os.path.join(methoddir, "renders") gtsdir = os.path.join(methoddir, "gt") os.makedirs(rendersdir, existok=True) os.makedirs(gtsdir, existok=True) renderimages = [] gtlist = [] renderlist = [] # Iterate Views for idx, view in enumerate(views): if idx == 0: time1 = time.time() # Render # Note: render() is assumed to be defined in the parent context or imported rendering = render(view, gaussians, pipeline, background, camtype=camtype)["render"] # Convert and Store # to8b clips to [0,1], multiplies by 255, casts to uint8 renderuint8 = to8b(rendering) # Transpose from CHW to HWC renderhwc = renderuint8.transpose(1, 2, 0) renderimages.append(renderhwc) renderlist.append(rendering) # Handle Ground Truth if name in ["train", "test"]: if camtype != "PanopticSports": gt = view.originalimage[0:3,:,:] else: gt = view['image'].cuda() gtlist.append(gt) time2 = time.time() # Calculate FPS fps = (len(views) - 1) / (time2 - time1) print(f"FPS: {fps}") # Save Images # multithreadwrite is a helper function for parallel I/O multithreadwrite(gtlist, gtsdir) multithreadwrite(renderlist, rendersdir) # Create Video videopath = os.path.join(methoddir, "videorgb.mp4") imageio.mimwrite(videopath, renderimages, fps=36) Parameters: fps for video: 36. resolution: Performance metrics provided for 800x800 and 1352x1014. Edge Cases: If name is not 'train' or 'test', ground truth is not collected. If camtype is 'PanopticSports', the GT extraction logic differs, requiring access to view['image'] instead of view.originalimage. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of views N. Measured Performance: 82 FPS at 800x800 resolution for synthetic data; 30 FPS at 1352x1014 resolution for real datasets. Strengths: Provides standardized evaluation metrics (SSIM, PSNR, LPIPS) and visualization outputs for 4DGS models. Limitations: Performance is resolution-dependent and varies between synthetic and real-world datasets. The 4DGS Rendering Pipeline originates from the 4D Gaussian Splatting method for dynamic scene reconstruction. It is part of the evaluation and visualization suite provided in the official/unofficial implementation repository. name: DVGO Volume Rendering Forward
body: Performs volume rendering for a batch of rays, including sampling, density/alpha computation, transmittance calculation, color estimation, and ray marching. It computes the final rendered color, distance, accumulation, and weights from RGB, density, tvals, directions, and background color assumption. It differs from NeRF Volume Rendering by using a pre-allocated 3D voxel grid for density and color storage, enabling faster training and inference via direct memory access, while maintaining the volume rendering integral formulation. Inputs: raypts: Ray origins and directions (or sampled points along rays). tvals: Sample positions along the ray. dirs: Ray directions. density: Density values from the density network/grid. rgb: RGB color values associated with samples. maskcache: Optional mask for known free space. usefouriergrid: Boolean flag for Fourier grid usage. fastcolorthres: Threshold for early filtering. rgbnet: Optional network for view-dependent color. rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag for direct RGB output. rgbnetfullimplicit: Boolean flag for implicit RGB features. whitebkgd: Boolean flag for white background assumption. renderdepth: Boolean flag for depth output. bg: Background color. N: Total number of samples. Outputs: comprgb: Computed RGB color. distance: Accumulated distance/depth. acc: Accumulated alpha/opacity. weights: Rendering weights. Data Structures: tmids: Midpoint distances between samples. Layout: (batch, numsamples-1). tdists: Distances between consecutive samples. Layout: (batch, numsamples-1). delta: Segment lengths scaled by direction norm. Layout: (batch, numsamples-1). densitydelta: Product of density and delta. Layout: (batch, numsamples-1). trans: Transmittance values. Layout: (batch, numsamples). weights: Rendering weights. Layout: (batch, numsamples). Steps: 1. Sample Points: Sample points on rays using self.sampleray. 2. Compute Midpoints: Compute t{mids} as 0.5 \times (t{vals}[:,:-1] + t{vals}[:, 1:]). 3. Free Space Masking: If maskcache exists and usefouriergrid is false, filter raypts, rayid, and stepid by the mask. 4. Compute Distances: Compute t{dists} as t{vals}[:, 1:] - t{vals}[:,:-1]. 5. Query Density: Query density from the density network/grid. 6. Compute Delta: Compute \delta as t{dists} multiplied by the norm of dirs. 7. Activate Density: Activate density to alpha using self.activatedensity. 8. Compute Density Delta: Compute densitydelta as density[:, 0] delta. 9. Fast Color Filtering: If fastcolorthres > 0 and usefouriergrid is false, filter points where alpha > fastcolorthres. 10. Compute Transmittance: Compute trans by concatenating zeros with cumsum of densitydelta[:,:-1], then exp of the negative. trans = \exp(-\text{cumsum}(\text{density\delta}[:,:-1])) (Note: trans is typically padded with 1.0 at the start or end depending on implementation details, here described as concatenating zeros then exp negative). 11. Compute Weights: Compute accumulated transmittance weights using Alphas2Weights.apply with alpha, rayid, and N. weights = \alpha \times trans 12. Compute RGB: Compute comprgb as sum of weights[:, None] rgb along axis -2. 13. Fast Color Filtering (Weights): If fastcolorthres > 0 and usefouriergrid is false, filter points where weights > fastcolorthres. 14. Compute Accumulation: Compute acc as sum of weights along axis -1. 15. Query Color Feature: Query color feature k0 from the k0 network if rgbnetfullimplicit is false. 16. Compute Distance: Compute distance as sum of weights tmids along axis -1, divided by acc. 17. View-Dependent Color: If rgbnet exists, compute view-dependent color. If rgbnetdirect is true, use k0 as view feature; otherwise split k0 into diffuse (first 3 channels) and view (remaining channels). 18. Clip Distance: Clip distance using nantonum (replacing inf with inf) and clipping to [t{vals}[:, 0], t{vals}[:, -1]]. 19. View Direction Embedding: Compute positional embedding for viewdirs: flatten viewdirs, multiply by viewfreq, concatenate sin/cos embeddings, then flatten and index by rayid. 20. Background Addition: If whitebkgd is True, add (1. - acc[:, None]) to comprgb. 21. RGB Network: Concatenate k0view and viewdirsemb, pass through rgbnet to get rgblogit. 22. Final RGB: Compute final RGB: if rgbnetdirect, \text{sigmoid}(rgb\logit); else \text{sigmoid}(rgb\logit + k0\diffuse). 23. Marched RGB: Compute marched RGB using segmentcoo: sum of (weights \times rgb) grouped by rayid, plus background contribution (alphainv\last \times bg). 24. Depth Output: If renderdepth is true, compute depth using segmentcoo: sum of (weights \times step\id) grouped by rayid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def dvgovolumerenderingforward( raypts, tvals, dirs, density, rgb, maskcache=None, usefouriergrid=False, fastcolorthres=0.0, rgbnet=None, rgbnetdirect=False, rgbnetfullimplicit=False, whitebkgd=False, renderdepth=False, bg=None, N=None, viewfreq=1): """ Performs volume rendering for a batch of rays. Args: raypts: Tensor of ray points. tvals: Tensor of sample positions along rays. Shape: (batch, numsamples). dirs: Tensor of ray directions. Shape: (batch, numsamples, 3). density: Tensor of density values. Shape: (batch, numsamples, 1). rgb: Tensor of RGB values. Shape: (batch, numsamples, 3). maskcache: Optional mask for free space. usefouriergrid: Boolean flag. fastcolorthres: Threshold for early filtering. rgbnet: Optional network for view-dependent color. rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag for direct RGB output. rgbnetfullimplicit: Boolean flag for implicit RGB features. whitebkgd: Boolean flag for white background. renderdepth: Boolean flag for depth output. bg: Background color. N: Total number of samples. viewfreq: Frequency for positional embedding. Returns: comprgb: Computed RGB color. distance: Accumulated distance/depth. acc: Accumulated alpha/opacity. weights: Rendering weights. """ # Step 2: Compute Midpoints tmids = 0.5 (tvals[:,:-1] + tvals[:, 1:]) # Step 3: Free Space Masking (Placeholder for specific mask logic) if maskcache is not None and not usefouriergrid: # Filter raypts, rayid, stepid by mask # This step is implementation-specific and depends on the maskcache structure pass # Step 4: Compute Distances tdists = tvals[:, 1:] - tvals[:,:-1] # Step 6: Compute Delta delta = tdists torch.norm(dirs, dim=-1) # Step 7: Activate Density (Placeholder for specific activation logic) # self.activatedensity is called here # Assuming density is already activated or this step modifies it # density = self.activatedensity(density) # Step 8: Compute Density Delta densitydelta = density[:,:, 0] delta # Step 9: Fast Color Filtering (Placeholder) if fastcolorthres > 0 and not usefouriergrid: # Filter points where alpha > fastcolorthres # alpha = 1 - torch.exp(-densitydelta) # mask = alpha > fastcolorthres # densitydelta = densitydelta[mask] #... filter other tensors accordingly pass # Step 10: Compute Transmittance # Concatenate zeros with cumsum of densitydelta[:,:-1], then exp of the negative # Note: The exact indexing might vary, assuming standard cumulative product logic cumsumdensity = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(densitydelta[:,:1]), torch.cumsum(densitydelta[:,:-1], dim=-1)], dim=-1) trans = torch.exp(-cumsumdensity) # Step 11: Compute Weights # alpha = 1 - exp(-densitydelta) alpha = 1 - torch.exp(-densitydelta) # weights = alpha trans # Note: trans needs to be aligned with alpha. Usually trans[i] is transmittance BEFORE sample i. # If trans is computed as above, it might need adjustment. # Assuming trans is aligned such that trans[:, i] is transmittance before sample i. # The pseudocode in S2 says "concatenating zeros with cumsum of densitydelta[...,:-1]". # This implies trans shape is (batch, numsamples-1). # weights shape is (batch, numsamples-1). weights = alpha trans # Step 12: Compute RGB comprgb = torch.sum(weights[:,:, None] rgb[:,:-1], dim=-2) # Step 13: Fast Color Filtering (Weights) (Placeholder) if fastcolorthres > 0 and not usefouriergrid: # Filter points where weights > fastcolorthres pass # Step 14: Compute Accumulation acc = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) # Step 15: Query Color Feature k0 = None # Placeholder for k0 network query if not rgbnetfullimplicit: # k0 = k0network(...) pass # Step 16: Compute Distance # distance = sum(weights tmids) / acc # Handle division by zero distance = torch.sum(weights tmids, dim=-1) / (acc + 1e-8) # Step 17: View-Dependent Color if rgbnet is not None: if rgbnetdirect: k0view = k0 k0diffuse = None else: k0diffuse = k0[:,:,:3] k0view = k0[:,:, 3:] # Step 19: View Direction Embedding # Flatten viewdirs, multiply by viewfreq, concatenate sin/cos embeddings viewdirs = dirs[:, 0] # Example: use first direction or mean viewdirsflat = viewdirs.view(-1, 3) freqbands = 2 torch.arange(viewfreq).to(viewdirs.device) viewdirsemb = torch.cat([torch.sin(viewdirsflat freqbands), torch.cos(viewdirsflat freqbands)], dim=-1) viewdirsemb = viewdirsemb.view(viewdirs.shape[0], -1) # Step 21: RGB Network # Concatenate k0view and viewdirsemb, pass through rgbnet if k0view is not None: rgbinput = torch.cat([k0view, viewdirsemb], dim=-1) else: rgbinput = viewdirsemb rgblogit = rgbnet(rgbinput) # Step 22: Final RGB if rgbnetdirect: rgbfinal = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit) else: rgbfinal = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit + k0diffuse) # Recompute comprgb with final RGB comprgb = torch.sum(weights[:,:, None] rgbfinal[:,:-1], dim=-2) # Step 20: Background Addition if whitebkgd: comprgb = comprgb + (1. - acc[:, None]) # Step 18: Clip Distance distance = torch.clamp(distance, min=tvals[:, 0], max=tvals[:, -1]) distance = torch.nantonum(distance, nan=float('inf')) # Step 23: Marched RGB (Placeholder for segmentcoo) # This step aggregates results by rayid # comprgb = segmentcoo(weights rgb, rayid) + alphainvlast bg pass # Step 24: Depth Output (Placeholder) if renderdepth: # depth = segmentcoo(weights stepid, rayid) pass return comprgb, distance, acc, weights Parameters: interval: Calculated as renderkwargs['stepsize'] self.voxelsizeratio. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero in distance calculation when acc is zero. Mitigated by adding a small epsilon or handling zero accumulation separately. Precision issues with cumulative sums and exponentials for transmittance. Boundary conditions for ray sampling and masking. NeRF Volume Rendering is a differentiable method for synthesizing photorealistic novel views of a scene by estimating volume density and RGB color along camera rays using a neural network. It solves the problem of continuous 3D scene representation and rendering by parameterizing the scene as an implicit function, typically implemented via Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Unlike explicit voxel-based methods such as DVGO, which store features in a grid and use interpolation, the classical NeRF approach queries a continuous field directly at sampled points along the ray. This allows for high-fidelity view-dependent effects but incurs significant computational costs due to the large number of MLP queries required. This method performs the forward pass for Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO), computing the final RGB color, depth, and optional segmentation masks for a batch of rays by marching through a dense voxel grid. It differs from NeRF Volume Rendering by using a pre-allocated 3D voxel grid for density and color storage, enabling faster training and inference via direct memory access, while maintaining the volume rendering integral formulation. It builds on DVGO Volume Rendering Forward. A CUDA kernel that traverses rays through a data structure, accumulating color and transmittance with early ray marching termination when transmittance drops below a threshold. It launches a kernel with one thread per ray, exits if thread index exceeds numrays, loads ray origin and direction, initializes color to zero and transmittance T to 1.0, loops over a fixed number of samples (e.g., 100), looks up density sigma from shared memory, computes segment length delta (e.g., 0.01f), computes alpha using the Beer-Lambert law approximation, computes sample color (placeholder spherical harmonics), accumulates color using standard volumetric integration, updates transmittance, checks early termination condition and breaks loop if met, and writes final accumulated color to output buffer. Parameters include earlyThreshold (transmittance threshold, e.g., 0.01f), numsamples (fixed number of traversal steps, e.g., 100), and delta (dummy segment length, e.g., 0.01f). The layout uses a struct float3 { float x, y, z; } for raysorigin, raysdirection, and outputcolors. Not given in the sources. name: NeRF Volume Rendering
head: NeRF Rendering Equation, Neural Radiance Field rendering, Vanilla NeRF Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering from Voxel Grid, classical volume rendering with MLP
body: NeRF Volume Rendering is a differentiable method for synthesizing photorealistic novel views of a scene by estimating volume density and RGB color along camera rays using a neural network. It solves the problem of continuous 3D scene representation and rendering by parameterizing the scene as an implicit function, typically implemented via Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs). Unlike explicit voxel-based methods such as DVGO, which store features in a grid and use interpolation, the classical NeRF approach queries a continuous field directly at sampled points along the ray. This allows for high-fidelity view-dependent effects but incurs significant computational costs due to the large number of MLP queries required. Inputs: Camera pose: Origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and view direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit vector). Neural Network Model \mathcal{F}\Phi (or \mathcal{H}\Theta): An MLP that maps spatial coordinates and view directions to density and color. Sampling parameters: Number of sample points K (or N) and the distribution of samples along the ray. Outputs: Pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) \in \mathbb{R}^3 for the ray \mathbf{r}. MLP Network \mathcal{F}\Phi: A feed-forward neural network. Input: Concatenated spatial coordinate \mathbf{x} = (x, y, z) and view direction \mathbf{d}. Output: Density \sigma \in \mathbb{R} and color \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Sample Points: A list of K 3D coordinates \{\mathbf{x}1, \dots, \mathbf{x}K\} along the ray. 1. Ray Generation: For a given pixel, generate a camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. 2. Sampling: Sample K points \mathbf{x}i along the ray within a defined interval [t{near}, t{far}]. The points are typically spaced by a distance \deltai. 3. MLP Query: For each sampled point \mathbf{x}i, query the MLP \mathcal{F}\Phi with input (\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) to obtain the volume density \sigmai and the RGB color \mathbf{c}i. 4. Transmittance Calculation: Compute the accumulated transmittance Ti for each sample point i. Ti represents the probability that the ray travels from the camera origin to sample i without being absorbed or scattered. Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \deltaj is the distance between sample j and j+1. For the first sample, T1 = 1. 5. Alpha Compositing: Compute the weight \alphai for each sample, representing the probability that the ray is absorbed at sample i: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). 6. Color Accumulation: Compute the final pixel color C(\mathbf{r}) as a weighted sum of the colors of the sampled points: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{K} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}i = \sum{i=1}^{K} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i. Continuous Formulation: The process can also be viewed as a discretization of the continuous volume rendering integral: C(\mathbf{r}) = \int{t1}^{t2} T(t) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(t)) \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t), \mathbf{d}) \, dt where T(t) = \exp\left(-\int{t1}^{t} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(u)) \, du\right). Ray: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Transmittance: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Segment Transmittance: \omegai = \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). Alpha (Absorption Probability): \alphai = 1 - \omegai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). Final Color: C(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{K} Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i. Loss Function: The model is trained by minimizing the photometric loss (MSE) between rendered color C(\mathbf{r}) and ground truth color C{gt}(\mathbf{r}): L{NeRF} = \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| C(\mathbf{r}) - C{gt}(\mathbf{r}) \|^2. K (or N): Number of sample points per ray. A typical value is 192. \deltai: Distance between adjacent samples xi and x{i+1}. \mathbf{x}: Spatial coordinate (x, y, z). \mathbf{d}: View direction. Can be represented as a 3D Cartesian unit vector or spherical coordinates (\phi, \theta). \sigma: Volume density (non-negative scalar). \mathbf{c}: RGB color (3D vector). Precision: The exponential function in transmittance calculation can lead to underflow if density is high or distances are large, resulting in Ti \approx 0. Boundaries: The sampling interval [t{near}, t{far}] must be chosen to encompass the scene. Points outside this range are ignored. Degenerate Input: If \sigmai = 0 for all samples, the color is black (or background color if explicitly handled). Computational Cost: The method requires a large number of MLP queries, leading to high training and rendering times. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def nerfvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, mlpnetwork, numsamples, near, far): """ Renders a single pixel color using NeRF volume rendering. Args: rayorigin (tuple): (ox, oy, oz) camera origin. raydirection (tuple): (dx, dy, dz) unit view direction. mlpnetwork (function): MLP function Fphi(x, d) -> (sigma, color). numsamples (int): Number of sample points K. near (float): Near clipping plane distance tnear. far (float): Far clipping plane distance tfar. Returns: tuple: (r, g, b) final pixel color. """ # Step 1: Sample points along the ray tvals = [near + i (far - near) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples)] # Step 2: Initialize accumulators accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(numsamples): # Calculate 3D point position t = tvals[i] point = ( rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) # Step 3: Query MLP for density and color sigma, color = mlpnetwork(point, raydirection) # Step 4: Compute delta (distance to next sample) if i < numsamples - 1: delta = tvals[i+1] - tvals[i] else: # For the last sample, delta is undefined by the formula. # Standard practice uses the previous interval or a small epsilon. delta = tvals[i] - tvals[i-1] if i > 0 else 0.01 # Step 5: Compute alpha and accumulate color alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha finalcolor[0] += weight color[0] finalcolor[1] += weight color[1] finalcolor[2] += weight color[2] # Step 6: Update transmittance for next sample accumulatedtransmittance = math.exp(-sigma delta) # Early termination optimization if accumulatedtransmittance < 1e-4: break return tuple(finalcolor) DVGO Volume Rendering Forward: Uses a voxel grid to store features and trilinear interpolation, reducing MLP queries. Choose when memory is constrained and high resolution is needed, but view-dependent effects are less critical or approximated. DVGO Instant NGP: Uses multi-resolution hash encoding to accelerate NeRF training and rendering. Choose when fast training and real-time rendering are required. Instant NGP TensoRF: Decomposes the feature grid into low-rank factors for storage efficiency. Choose when memory footprint is a primary concern. TensoRF Time Complexity: Training and rendering times are typically very large due to the infinite and continuous nature of space requiring a multitude of giant MLP queries. Each pixel requires K MLP forward passes. Memory Complexity: The MLP weights are stored in memory. The size depends on the network architecture. No explicit voxel grid is stored in the classical NeRF formulation. Measured Performance: With K=192 samples, rendering high-resolution images can be slow without acceleration techniques. Strengths: High-quality view-dependent effects due to direct MLP query of color based on view direction. Continuous representation allows for arbitrary resolution. Limitations: Slow rendering speed. High memory usage for large networks. Requires significant computational resources for training. When to use: When photorealism and view-dependent effects are paramount, and computational resources are available. When not to use: When real-time rendering is required, or memory is severely constrained. NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) was introduced by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It uses MLP networks to learn the radiance field of arbitrary scenes. Once sufficiently optimized, NeRF can estimate both the volume density \sigma and RGB color \mathbf{c} of the continuous function that describes the radiance field. It is then able to reconstruct a photorealistic view from an unseen pose using a differentiable volume rendering method. The method has become a foundational technique in 3D computer vision and graphics, inspiring numerous acceleration methods and applications in novel view synthesis, geometry reconstruction, and stylization. name: DVGO Ray Sampling and Rendering
head: DVGO forward pass, Direct Voxel Grid Optimization rendering
body: This method performs the forward pass for Direct Voxel Grid Optimization (DVGO), computing the final RGB color, depth, and optional segmentation masks for a batch of rays by marching through a dense voxel grid. It differs from NeRF Volume Rendering by using a pre-allocated 3D voxel grid for density and color storage, enabling faster training and inference via direct memory access, while maintaining the volume rendering integral formulation. It builds on DVGO Volume Rendering Forward. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [N, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [N, 3]. viewdirs: Normalized view directions, shape [N, 3]. renderkwargs: Dictionary containing near, far, stepsize, bg (background color), inversey, flipx, flipy, ndc. model: The DVGO model instance containing: xyzmin, xyzmax: Bounding box of the voxel grid. voxelsize: Physical size of one voxel. voxelsizeratio: Ratio used for step calculation. density: Voxel density grid. k0: Voxel color/density feature grid (if rgbnetfullimplicit is false). rgbnet: MLP for view-dependent color (optional). rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag for direct color output. segmaskgrid: Segmentation mask grid (optional). dualsegmaskgrid: Dual segmentation mask grid (optional, used in 'fine' mode). maskcache: Binary cache for valid voxels (optional). numobjects: Number of segmentation classes. mode: 'fine' or other. fastcolorthres: Minimum threshold for color filtering. renderfct: Threshold for alpha/weight filtering (default 0). Outputs: rgbmarched: Rendered RGB colors, shape [N, 3]. depth: Rendered depth (if requested). alphainvlast: Transmittance at the end of the ray, shape [N]. weights: Rendering weights for sampled points (filtered). segmaskmarched: Segmentation masks, shape [N, \text{num\objects}]. dualsegmaskmarched: Dual segmentation masks (if 'fine' mode). rawalpha, rawrgb, rayid, stepid: Intermediate filtered data. Data Structures: Voxel Grids: Dense 3D tensors. density stores raw density values. k0 stores raw color features (RGB + optional diffuse/specular components). segmaskgrid stores per-object probabilities. Ray Data: Batched tensors for origins, directions, and view vectors. Steps: 1. Ray-Bounding Box Intersection: Compute the intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] of each ray with the voxel grid bounding box [xyz{min}, xyz{max}]. Let vec = rays\d. rate\a = \frac{xyz{min} - rays\o}{vec} rate\b = \frac{xyz{max} - rays\o}{vec} t{min} = \text{clamp}(\max(\min(rate\a, rate\b), \text{axis}=2), \text{min}=near, \text{max}=far) t{max} = \text{clamp}(\min(\max(rate\a, rate\b), \text{axis}=2), \text{min}=near, \text{max}=far) If t{min} \ge t{max}, the ray does not intersect the box or is outside the near/far planes. 2. Point Sampling: Calculate the step distance for sampling. step = stepsize \times voxel\size \times rng where rng is a random variable uniform in [0, 1] for jittering. Compute interpolation positions along the ray: interpx = t{min} + \frac{step}{\|rays\d\|} Compute ray points: rays\pts = rays\o + rays\d \times interpx 3. Filtering by Bounding Box and Cache: Use a CUDA kernel sampleptsonrays to: Determine which points lie within [xyz{min}, xyz{max}] and [near, far]. Generate maskoutbbox (points outside). Assign rayid and stepid to each valid point. Return Nsteps (number of valid steps per ray). Filter to maskinbbox = ~maskoutbbox. If maskcache exists, further filter points using maskcache(rayspts[maskinbbox]). 4. Alpha Thresholding (Optimization): If renderfct > 0: Compute alpha for all points. Create mask mask = (alpha > renderfct). Filter raypts, rayid, stepid, density, alpha by this mask. Note: renderfct is set to \max(render\fct, fast\color\thres). 5. Alpha to Weight Conversion: Compute rendering weights from alpha values using the Alphas2Weights function, which implements the standard volume rendering accumulation: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \Deltai) wi = \alphai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) This is implemented efficiently using Alphas2Weights.apply(alpha, rayid, N). If renderfct > 0, filter weights, alpha, raypts, rayid, stepid by mask = (weights > renderfct). 6. Segmentation Mask Query: If segmaskgrid.grid.requiresgrad: Enable gradient tracking. Query maskpred = segmaskgrid(rayspts). If mode == 'fine', also query dualmaskpred = dualsegmaskgrid(rayspts). If not requiring grad, query directly. 7. Color Query: Query raw color features k0 from the voxel grid: k0 = k0(rayspts). If rgbnet is None: rgb = \text{sigmoid}(k0) If rgbnet exists: Determine view-dependent input: If rgbnetdirect: k0view = k0. Else: k0view = k0[:, 3:], k0diffuse = k0[:,:3]. Compute view direction embedding: viewdirs\emb = \text{concat}([viewdirs, \sin(viewdirs \times \pi \times 2^{\text{freq}}), \cos(viewdirs \times \pi \times 2^{\text{freq}})]) (Frequency multiplication is applied as per standard positional encoding). Flatten and index viewdirsemb by rayid. Concatenate features: rgbfeat = concat([k0view, viewdirsemb], dim=-1). Compute logit: rgblogit = rgbnet(rgbfeat). Compute final RGB: If rgbnetdirect: rgb = sigmoid(rgblogit). Else: rgb = sigmoid(rgblogit + k0diffuse). 8. RGB Accumulation: Accumulate RGB using scatter sum: rgb\marched = \text{segment\coo}(src = weights \times rgb, index = ray\id, out = \text{zeros}([N, 3]), reduce = \text{'sum'}) 9. Segmentation Accumulation: If numobjects == 1: seg\mask\marched = \text{segment\coo}(src = weights \times mask\pred, index = ray\id, out = \text{zeros}([N, 1]), reduce = \text{'sum'}) If mode == 'fine', also compute dualsegmaskmarched. If numobjects != 1: seg\mask\marched = \text{segment\coo}(src = weights \times mask\pred, index = ray\id, out = \text{zeros}([N, num\objects]), reduce = \text{'sum'}) If mode == 'fine', also compute dualsegmaskmarched. 10. Background Addition: rgb\marched += alphainv\last \times bg Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ device = rayso.device N = rayso.shape[0] near = renderkwargs['near'] far = renderkwargs['far'] stepsize = renderkwargs['stepsize'] bg = renderkwargs['bg'] xyzmin = model.xyzmin xyzmax = model.xyzmax voxelsize = model.voxelsize voxelsizeratio = model.voxelsizeratio renderfct = model.renderfct fastcolorthres = model.fastcolorthres # Step 1: Ray-Bounding Box Intersection vec = raysd ratea = (xyzmin - rayso) / vec rateb = (xyzmax - rayso) / vec tmin = torch.minimum(ratea, rateb).amax(dim=-1) tmax = torch.maximum(ratea, rateb).amin(dim=-1) tmin = torch.clamp(tmin, min=near, max=far) tmax = torch.clamp(tmax, min=near, max=far) # Handle rays that don't intersect or are outside near/far validmask = tmin < tmax if not validmask.any(): # Return zeros or background for all rays return { 'rgbmarched': torch.zeros(N, 3, device=device), 'alphainvlast': torch.ones(N, device=device), 'depth': torch.zeros(N, device=device), 'weights': torch.zeros(0, device=device), 'rawalpha': torch.zeros(0, device=device), 'rawrgb': torch.zeros(0, device=device), 'rayid': torch.zeros(0, dtype=torch.long, device=device), 'segmaskmarched': torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device), 'dualsegmaskmarched': torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device) if model.mode == 'fine' else None } # Step 2: Point Sampling # Generate random jitter for each step # Note: In practice, Nsteps is determined by the CUDA kernel # Here we simulate the logic for clarity, assuming we have a way to get Nsteps # The actual implementation uses a CUDA kernel to determine valid points # Step 3: Filter by Bounding Box and Cache # Call CUDA kernel: sampleptsonrays # Returns: raypts, maskoutbbox, rayid, stepid, Nsteps, tmin, tmax # For pseudocode, we assume these are computed # raypts, maskoutbbox, rayid, stepid, Nsteps, tmin, tmax = sampleptsonrayscuda(...) # Since we can't call CUDA, we describe the logic: # 1. Compute step distance: step = stepsize voxelsize rng # 2. Compute interpx = tmin + step / ||raysd|| # 3. Compute rayspts = rayso + raysd interpx # 4. Filter points within xyzmin/xyzmax and near/far # 5. Apply maskcache if exists # For the sake of the pseudocode, we assume we have filtered points # rayptsvalid, rayidvalid, stepidvalid, Nstepsvalid =... # Step 4: Alpha Thresholding # Compute alpha from density # density = model.density(rayptsvalid) # shift = model.shift # Assuming shift is a parameter # interval = stepsize voxelsizeratio # alpha = 1 - (1 + torch.exp(density + shift))(-interval) # This is equivalent to: alpha = 1 - torch.exp(-torch.nn.functional.softplus(density + shift) interval) # If renderfct > 0, filter if renderfct > 0: renderfct = max(renderfct, fastcolorthres) # mask = (alpha > renderfct) # Filter raypts, rayid, stepid, density, alpha by mask # Step 5: Alpha to Weight Conversion # weights, alphainvlast = Alphas2Weights.apply(alpha, rayid, N) # If renderfct > 0, filter weights, alpha, raypts, rayid, stepid by (weights > renderfct) # Step 6: Segmentation Mask Query segmaskmarched = torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device) dualsegmaskmarched = None if model.segmaskgrid is not None: if model.segmaskgrid.grid.requiresgrad: model.segmaskgrid.grid.requiresgrad(True) maskpred = model.segmaskgrid(rayptsvalid) if model.mode == 'fine': dualmaskpred = model.dualsegmaskgrid(rayptsvalid) else: maskpred = model.segmaskgrid(rayptsvalid) if model.mode == 'fine': dualmaskpred = model.dualsegmaskgrid(rayptsvalid) # Accumulate segmentation masks if model.numobjects == 1: segmaskmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) maskpred.unsqueeze(-1)), index=rayidvalid, out=torch.zeros(N, 1, device=device), reduce='sum') if model.mode == 'fine': dualsegmaskmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) dualmaskpred.unsqueeze(-1)), index=rayidvalid, out=torch.zeros(N, 1, device=device), reduce='sum') else: segmaskmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) maskpred), index=rayidvalid, out=torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device), reduce='sum') if model.mode == 'fine': dualsegmaskmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) dualmaskpred), index=rayidvalid, out=torch.zeros(N, model.numobjects, device=device), reduce='sum') # Step 7: Color Query k0 = model.k0(rayptsvalid) if model.rgbnet is None: rgb = torch.sigmoid(k0) else: if model.rgbnetdirect: k0view = k0 else: k0view = k0[:, 3:] k0diffuse = k0[:,:3] # View direction embedding # Assuming freqmult is a parameter or fixed freqmult = 1 # Placeholder for actual frequency multiplication logic viewdirsemb = torch.cat([ viewdirs, torch.sin(viewdirs freqmult torch.pi), torch.cos(viewdirs freqmult torch.pi) ], dim=-1) # Flatten and index by rayid # Note: viewdirsemb needs to be indexed by rayidvalid viewdirsembindexed = viewdirsemb[rayidvalid] rgbfeat = torch.cat([k0view, viewdirsembindexed], dim=-1) rgblogit = model.rgbnet(rgbfeat) if model.rgbnetdirect: rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit) else: rgb = torch.sigmoid(rgblogit + k0diffuse) # Step 8: RGB Accumulation rgbmarched = segmentcoo( src=(weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb), index=rayidvalid, out=torch.zeros(N, 3, device=device), reduce='sum') # Step 10: Background Addition rgbmarched += (alphainvlast.unsqueeze(-1) bg) return { 'rgbmarched': rgbmarched, 'depth': None, # Depth computation depends on specific implementation 'alphainvlast': alphainvlast, 'weights': weights, 'rawalpha': alpha, 'rawrgb': rgb, 'rayid': rayidvalid, 'segmaskmarched': segmaskmarched, 'dualsegmaskmarched': dualsegmaskmarched } def segmentcoo(src, index, out, reduce='sum'): """ PyTorch scatter operation equivalent to COO segment sum. """ # This is a simplified representation. In practice, torch.scatteradd is used. # out.scatteradd(dim=0, index=index.unsqueeze(-1).expandas(src), src=src) # For multi-dimensional out, we need to handle each channel separately or use advanced indexing. # Here we assume a simple 1D index for rays. for i in range(out.shape[1]): out[:, i].scatteradd(0, index, src[:, i]) return out Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point precision issues can arise when computing ratea and rateb for rays nearly parallel to the bounding box faces. Clamping to near and far helps. Boundaries: Rays that do not intersect the bounding box must be handled to avoid invalid memory access or NaN values. Degenerate Input: Empty batches or rays with zero length should be checked. Memory: Large batches can exhaust GPU memory. Splitting rays into chunks (e.g., 8192) is recommended. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of rays and S is the number of samples per ray. The dominant cost is the voxel grid lookups and the scatter operations. Memory Complexity: O(V + N \cdot S), where V is the number of voxels. The voxel grids are stored in memory, and intermediate tensors for ray points and features are allocated per batch. Measured Performance: DVGO is generally faster to train than NeRF due to the dense voxel grid allowing for efficient memory access and parallelization. Inference speed is comparable to NeRF but can be faster with optimized voxel traversal. Strengths: Fast training, efficient memory access, supports view-dependent effects. Limitations: Memory usage scales with voxel resolution, which can be high for large scenes. Less flexible than NeRF for representing complex geometry without high resolution. When to Use: When training speed is a priority and the scene can be represented well with a voxel grid. Suitable for real-time applications if optimized. When Not to Use: For scenes with very fine details that require extremely high voxel resolution, or for scenes with complex topology that is better represented by implicit functions. DVGO was introduced in the paper "Direct Voxel Grid Optimization for Super-Resolution Compact 3D Gaussian Splatting" (Note: The source refers to "SegmentAnythingin3D" which uses DVGO, but the original DVGO paper is "Direct Voxel Grid Optimization" by Yu et al., 2021. The notes provided are from the GitHub repository which implements DVGO for segmentation). The method was developed to address the slow training times of NeRF by using a dense voxel grid instead of a neural network for density and color representation. It has been used in various 3D reconstruction and segmentation tasks. Jumpat/SegmentAnythingin3D, https://github.com/Jumpat/SegmentAnythingin3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Light-space opacity precomputation
head: Light-point-of-view ray marching, Light-volume accumulation
body: Light-space opacity precomputation accelerates non-collocated view and light rendering by precomputing the accumulated opacity along light rays, thereby avoiding expensive per-shading-point light-ray marching. It differs from naive non-collocated rendering by precomputing light-transport opacity from the light's point of view and reusing it for any view direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume representation of the scene and the light source position/direction. Output: A precomputed 3D volume storing accumulated opacity (transmittance) from the light's perspective. Data Structures: Precomputed Volume: A 3D grid storing accumulated opacity values. Layout: 3D array of floating-point values. Size: 128^3 voxels, restricted by available GPU memory. Coordinate System: The scene is normalized such that the object center is at the origin and scaled to fit within the [-1, 1]^3 cube. Steps: 1. Scene Normalization: Translate the object center to the origin and scale the bounding box to fit into the [-1, 1]^3 cube. 2. Light-View Ray Marching: Ray march from the light's point of view through the volume. 3. Opacity Accumulation: Accumulate opacity along each light ray at each spatial position of the volume. The accumulated opacity (transmittance) T(\mathbf{p}) at position \mathbf{p} is computed as: T(\mathbf{p}) = \exp\left(-\sum{i} \sigmai \Delta si\right) where \sigmai is the extinction coefficient at sample i and \Delta si is the step size along the ray from the light source to \mathbf{p}. 4. Storage: Store the accumulated opacity in a precomputed volume. 5. Rendering Sampling: During rendering, sample the precomputed accumulated opacity volume directly for each shading point's connection to the light source. Parameters: Volume Resolution: 128^3. Scene Normalization: Object center translated to origin, scaled to fit into the [-1, 1]^3 cube. Training Image Resolution: 400 \times 500 to 1100 \times 1100. Training Iterations: ~450,000 total, converges in ~200,000. Rendering Resolution: 700 \times 700. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: SfM Registration Failure: Structure from Motion (SfM) may fail to register certain views, reducing the actual number of training images to 300 to 385 per scene. Resolution Limits: A 128^3 volume resolution may fail to fully reproduce geometry and appearance for scenes with highly complex surface normal variations and texture details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precomputelightopacity(volumequery, lightpos, gridsize=128, boundsmin=-1.0, boundsmax=1.0): """ Precomputes accumulated opacity (transmittance) from the light's point of view. Args: volumequery: Callable that returns the extinction coefficient sigma at a 3D point. lightpos: 3D tuple/list, position of the light source. gridsize: Resolution of the precomputed volume (default 128). boundsmin, boundsmax: Normalized bounds of the volume (default -1 to 1). Returns: lightopacityvolume: 3D list of shape (gridsize, gridsize, gridsize) """ # Initialize output volume lightopacityvolume = [[[0.0] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] for in range(gridsize)] stepsize = (boundsmax - boundsmin) / gridsize marchsteps = 64 marchsteplen = stepsize marchsteps # Total distance covered per voxel ray for z in range(gridsize): for y in range(gridsize): for x in range(gridsize): # Voxel center in normalized space [-1, 1]^3 p = (boundsmin + (x + 0.5) stepsize, boundsmin + (y + 0.5) stepsize, boundsmin + (z + 0.5) stepsize) # Ray direction from light to voxel dirvec = (p[0] - lightpos[0], p[1] - lightpos[1], p[2] - lightpos[2]) length = math.sqrt(dirvec[0]2 + dirvec[1]2 + dirvec[2]2) if length == 0: lightopacityvolume[z][y][x] = 1.0 continue # Normalize direction dirvec = (dirvec[0] / length, dirvec[1] / length, dirvec[2] / length) # Discrete accumulation from light to p accumulatedsigmads = 0.0 currentpos = list(lightpos) # March from light towards p for step in range(marchsteps): # Sample extinction coefficient at currentpos sigma = volumequery(currentpos) accumulatedsigmads += sigma marchsteplen # Advance along ray currentpos = (currentpos[0] + dirvec[0] marchsteplen, currentpos[1] + dirvec[1] marchsteplen, currentpos[2] + dirvec[2] marchsteplen) # Compute transmittance T = exp(-integral of sigma) t = 1.0 if accumulatedsigmads == 0 else math.exp(-accumulatedsigmads) lightopacityvolume[z][y][x] = t return lightopacityvolume Accelerates the computation of multiple scattering in participating media by precomputing the visibility of the light source from the perspective of the volume into a 2D texture map. It solves the problem of expensive per-shading-point light-ray marching by storing light visibility modulated by source intensity, allowing efficient blur-based approximation of indirect illumination. It differs from the parent method by specifically targeting the visibility component via a 2D orthographic projection of the volume's bounding box, rather than storing full 3D light-segment integrals for every voxel. A geometry shader-based method to generate optimized entry-points for light-space illumination by projecting first/last hit point pairs from camera space to light space. Line segments are formed based on each first and last hit point pair derived from the visibility pass and projected as seen from the light source using a geometry shader operating on hit point pairs. Representing line segments as cuboids avoids degeneration to points when the light direction is collinear with the camera direction, which would cause holes; cuboid depth corresponds to the distance between first and last hit points, and width/height are calculated based on pixel size and distance to the light source. No specific rasterization is required as synchronization is per-pixel based. Multiple light sources are handled by projecting instantiated geometry to multiple output targets using respective light source projection matrices. Generating optimized exit-points yields no performance improvement with early ray-termination. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On 4 NVIDIA 2080Ti RTX GPUs, training takes ~450,000 iterations (~2 days), converging in ~200,000 iterations. Rendering a 700 \times 700 image takes ~0.8s for collocated view and light, and ~2.3s for non-collocated view and light using this precomputation. Strengths: Significantly reduces rendering time for arbitrary light and view directions compared to naive per-point light-ray marching. Limitations: High memory usage restricts volume resolution to 128^3, which may fail to reproduce complex surface normal variations and texture details. SfM registration failures can reduce the number of available training images. When to use: Relighting and novel view synthesis under arbitrary light and view directions. When not to use: Scenes requiring high-fidelity reproduction of complex surface normal variations and fine texture details beyond the 128^3 resolution limit. This method was introduced in the context of deep reflectance volumes for relightable reconstructions from multi-view photometric images. It addresses the computational bottleneck of non-collocated rendering where the light and camera are not at the same position, requiring expensive light-ray marching for each shading point. The approach leverages the observation that light-transport opacity can be precomputed from the light's perspective and reused for any view direction. name: LightImage Precomputation
head: LightImage
body: LightImage Precomputation accelerates the computation of multiple scattering in participating media by precomputing the visibility of the light source from the perspective of the volume into a 2D texture map. It solves the problem of expensive per-shading-point light-ray marching by storing light visibility modulated by source intensity, allowing efficient blur-based approximation of indirect illumination. It differs from its parent method, Light-space opacity precomputation, by specifically targeting the visibility component via a 2D orthographic projection of the volume's bounding box, rather than storing full 3D light-segment integrals for every voxel. Inputs: Static volume density field \sigmat(x) (or scattering coefficient b(x)). Static light source direction \omega{light} and intensity distribution Li(\omega). Scene geometry (occluders). Volume bounding box. Outputs: A 2D texture map (LightImage) storing visibility values. A 3D texture map (light volume) storing integrated light segment lengths. 1. light Volume (3D Texture) Format: GLLUMINANCE floating-point texture. Orientation: The 3D volume is oriented such that the z-axis is aligned with the light direction \omega{light}. Extents: Large enough to completely contain the density volume. Content: Each voxel stores \ell{light} = \int b(x) ds, the integral of the scattering coefficient along the straight line from the voxel to the light. Wavelength Handling: If b depends on wavelength, wavelength-averaged values are used to save storage and computation. 2. LightImage (2D Texture) Format: 2D texture map. Orientation: Perpendicular to the light direction, mapped onto the bounding box of the light volume. Content: Pixels store visibility of the light source from the volume, modulated by the light source's spatial intensity distribution. Value 1: Light is visible. Value 0: Light is completely blocked. Intermediate values: Partial visibility or intensity modulation. Mipmap Pyramid: A mipmap pyramid is constructed to allow efficient computation of radiance blurred over a width w using GLLINEARMIPMAPLINEAR filtering. 1. Compute light Volume: For every volume cell, integrate the scattering coefficient b along the light direction from the cell to the light source. Store the result in the 3D texture oriented with the z-axis aligned to the light. 2. Determine Maximum Blur Width: Calculate the maximum blur width w{max} required for the mipmap pyramid. Formula: w{max} = w(\ell{max}, s{max}). Where s{max} is the length of the volume diagonal. And \ell{max} = s{max} \bar{b}, where \bar{b} is the average scattering coefficient. 3. Render LightImage Base Level: Orient an orthographic camera in the direction of the light. Render all scene objects (occluders) in black. Render the bounding box of the medium in white. The resulting image represents the visibility of the light source from the volume's perspective. Note: Objects completely inside the volume do not affect the LightImage and are ignored in multiple scattering calculations, though they affect single scattering. Edge Case: If no objects obscure the volume, the LightImage has a uniform constant value of 1. 4. Construct Mipmap Pyramid: Generate a Gaussian mipmap pyramid for the LightImage. Blur widths increase linearly from 0 (lowest level, original LightImage) to w{max} (final level). Implementation options: Software Gaussian filtering (accurate). Hardware Gaussian filter [Jargstorff 2004]. GLSGISgeneratemipmap (box filter, cheaper in software but expensive in hardware). Light Segment Integral: \ell{light} = \int b(x) ds Integrated along the straight line from the voxel to the light. Maximum Blur Width: w{max} = w(\ell{max}, s{max}) Where s{max} is the volume diagonal length and \ell{max} = s{max} \bar{b}. Average Scattering Coefficient (\bar{b}): Used to estimate \ell{max}. Blur Width Function (w): Maps \ell{max} and s{max} to a pixel width. Mipmap Levels: Determined by the linear increase from 0 to w{max}. Dynamic Data: If volume density or light direction changes, the light volume and LightImage must be updated. Internal Occluders: Objects completely inside the volume do not affect the LightImage. They are ignored in multiple scattering calculations but still affect single scattering. No Occlusion: If no objects obscure the volume, the LightImage is a uniform constant value of 1. Color Dependence: The light volume uses wavelength-averaged scattering coefficients. This is considered sufficiently accurate for most participating media, which are rarely strongly colored. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precomputelightimage(volumedensity, lightdirection, sceneobjects, volumebbox): # Step 1: Compute light Volume # Orient 3D volume such that z-axis aligns with lightdirection lightvolume = [[0.0 for in range(volumebbox.depth)] for in range(volumebbox.height)] for z in range(volumebbox.depth): for y in range(volumebbox.height): for x in range(volumebbox.width): # Integrate scattering coefficient along the line from voxel to light rayorigin = volumebbox.origin + volumebbox.step (x, y, z) raydirection = lightdirection pathlength = volumebbox.extentalong(raydirection) integral = 0.0 stepsize = volumebbox.step[0] for t in range(0, int(pathlength), stepsize): point = rayorigin + raydirection t integral += volumedensity[point] stepsize lightvolume[z][y][x] = integral # Step 2: Determine Maximum Blur Width smax = volumebbox.diagonallength() # Average scattering coefficient barb barb = sum(sum(sum(cell for cell in row) for row in plane) for plane in volumedensity) / volumedensity.size lmax = smax barb # Exact formula for w(lmax, smax) not given in sources. wmax = lmax # Step 3: Render LightImage Base Level # Orient orthographic camera in direction of light camerawidth, cameraheight = volumebbox.resolution2d baseimage = [[0.0 for in range(camerawidth)] for in range(cameraheight)] for y in range(cameraheight): for x in range(camerawidth): ray = camera.castray(x, y, lightdirection) if volumebbox.intersects(ray): baseimage[y][x] = 1.0 # Objects completely inside the volume do not affect the LightImage # Objects outside the volume block the light (value remains 0) # Step 4: Construct Mipmap Pyramid lightimage = generatemipmappyramid(baseimage, maxblurwidth=wmax) return lightvolume, lightimage def generatemipmappyramid(image, maxblurwidth): # Standard Gaussian mipmap generation levels = [image] current = image numlevels = math.ceil(math.log2(min(len(image[0]), len(image)))) for i in range(1, numlevels): # Blur widths increase linearly from 0 to wmax blursigma = (i / numlevels) maxblurwidth blurred = applygaussianfilter(current, blursigma) downsampled = [[blurred[j][k] for k in range(0, len(blurred[0]), 2)] for j in range(0, len(blurred), 2)] levels.append(downsampled) current = downsampled return levels def applygaussianfilter(image, sigma): # Standard separable Gaussian convolution kernelsize = int(math.ceil(4 sigma)) kernel = [math.exp(-0.5 (x / sigma) 2) for x in range(-kernelsize, kernelsize + 1)] kernelsum = sum(kernel) kernel = [k / kernelsum for k in kernel] # Apply horizontal pass hpass = [[sum(image[r][c - k] kernel[k] for k in range(len(kernel))) for c in range(len(image[0]))] for r in range(len(image))] # Apply vertical pass vpass = [[sum(hpass[r - k][c] kernel[k] for k in range(len(kernel))) for c in range(len(hpass[0]))] for r in range(len(hpass))] return vpass Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales with the resolution of the light volume and the LightImage. The mipmap pyramid allows efficient lookup at different blur widths. Strengths: Accelerates multiple scattering computation by avoiding per-shading-point light-ray marching. Simple to implement using standard OpenGL texture and rendering features. Handles non-uniform light source intensity. Limitations: Assumes static light and volume density. Updates are required for dynamic scenes. Objects inside the volume are ignored in multiple scattering, which may lead to inaccuracies if such objects are significant. Approximation via Gaussian blur may lose high-frequency details. When to Use: Static scenes with participating media where multiple scattering is significant and performance is critical. When Not to Use: Dynamic scenes with changing light or density, or scenes with significant internal occluders affecting multiple scattering. Origin: The method was introduced in "A lighting model for general participating media" by Premože et al.. History: It is described as a variation of a deep shadow map [Lokovic and Veach 2000]. Usage: Used in OpenGL pipelines with NVIDIA CG for real-time rendering of participating media. name: Inference Acceleration Strategies
head: Inference Optimization Strategies
body: Inference Acceleration Strategies is a set of techniques designed to boost the efficiency of real-time volume rendering inference with minimal quality degradation. It addresses the computational bottleneck of evaluating neural networks and processing rays during the G-Buffer and shading passes. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining algorithmic optimizations (such as step size and early termination) with hardware-specific acceleration (cooperative vectors) to achieve significant speedups over software-based implementations. The method integrates two distinct categories of acceleration: algorithmic ray marching optimizations and hardware-accelerated neural inference. Inputs: Scene data (voxel grids, neural codebooks), camera parameters, ray batches. Outputs: Rendered images with reduced latency. 1. Ray Batch: A collection of rays processed in parallel. 2. Tile Classification: Tiles of pixels (e.g., 8 \times 4) classified as: Non-neural (gray). Neural with a single MLP (green). Neural with mixed MLPs (red). 3. MLP Parameters: Multi-Layer Perceptron weights, where hidden dimensions D are tested at 16, 32, and 64. The following steps are applied during the inference pass: 1. Combine Thread: Group threads to optimize memory access patterns and reduce overhead. 2. Prefetch Neighbor: Pre-fetch adjacent voxel or feature data to hide memory latency. 3. Larger Step: Increase the step size along the ray to reduce the number of evaluations, accepting a slight quality trade-off. 4. Early Termination: Stop ray marching when opacity accumulates to a threshold, skipping unnecessary computations. 5. Hardware-Accelerated MLP Inference: Fetch block-compressed latent features using the texture unit with hardware-accelerated anisotropic filtering. Execute MLP layer inference using cooperative vectors. Use column-major layout for matrix multiplication. Group pixels within the same workgroup to share the same base matrix, ensuring cooperative vector efficiency. The following pseudocode illustrates the integration of algorithmic and hardware strategies. Note that hardware-specific instructions (cooperative vectors) are abstracted as hwmatmul for clarity, as the specific API calls depend on the graphics driver. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderinferenceaccelerated(rays, scene, config): """ Render a batch of rays using inference acceleration strategies. Args: rays: List of Ray objects (origin, direction). scene: Scene data containing voxel grid and neural codebooks. config: Configuration dictionary with parameters. Returns: List of color values for each ray. """ results = [] # Step 1: Combine Thread (Group rays for parallel processing) # Implementation detail: Group rays into workgroups/batches. workgroups = groupraysintoworkgroups(rays, config.threadgroupsize) for workgroup in workgroups: # Step 2: Tile Classification (For hardware acceleration context) # Classify tiles to determine if cooperative vectors are beneficial. # If mixed MLPs, repack pixels to uniform tiles to avoid divergence. tiles = classifytiles(workgroup) for tile in tiles: if tile.ismixed: repacktiletouniform(tile) # Step 3: Hardware-Accelerated MLP Inference (if neural) if tile.isneural: # Fetch block-compressed latent features # Use texture unit with hardware-accelerated anisotropic filtering latentfeatures = fetchblockcompressedfeatures(tile.pixels, scene.codebooks) # Execute MLP using cooperative vectors # Use column-major layout. Threads in same workgroup use same base matrix. # Tested MLP hidden dimensions D: 16, 32, 64. # Assume MLP layers are defined in scene. for layer in scene.mlplayers: # hwmatmul represents the cooperative vector matrix multiplication # This replaces software FMA for D >= 32 latentfeatures = hwmatmul(latentfeatures, layer.weights, layout='columnmajor') latentfeatures = applyactivation(latentfeatures, layer.activation) tile.color = decodeoutput(latentfeatures) else: # Non-neural shading (e.g., simple lighting) tile.color = computesimpleshading(tile.pixels, scene) # Step 4: Algorithmic Ray Marching Optimizations # These are applied during the ray marching phase, potentially before or after # the neural evaluation depending on the specific pipeline integration. # Step 5: Larger Step # Increase step size to reduce evaluations. stepsize = config.basestepsize config.stepmultiplier # Step 6: Early Termination # Terminate ray if opacity threshold is reached. opacitythreshold = 0.99 # Step 7: Prefetch Neighbor # Pre-fetch neighbor data to hide latency. # Implementation detail: Issue prefetch instructions for adjacent voxels. for ray in tile.rays: color = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 t = ray.origin while t < ray.end and transmittance > 1e-4: # Fetch voxel data at current position voxel = samplevoxel(scene, t) # Evaluate color and opacity # If neural, use the pre-computed tile color or evaluate MLP if tile.isneural: c, o = evaluateneuralmaterial(voxel, tile.color) else: c, o = evaluatesimplematerial(voxel) # Composite contribution = c o transmittance color += contribution transmittance = (1.0 - o) # Early Termination Check if transmittance < opacitythreshold: break # Move along ray with Larger Step t += ray.direction stepsize # Prefetch Neighbor Check # Issue prefetch for next voxel position prefetchvoxel(scene, t) results.append(color) return results MLP Hidden Dimensions (D): Tested values are 16, 32, and 64. Wider MLPs (D \ge 32) show significant speedup with cooperative vectors. Step Multiplier: Controls the "Larger Step" strategy. Opacity Threshold: Controls "Early Termination". Mixed Tiles: When a tile contains pixels requiring different MLPs, divergence occurs. The solution is to repack pixels into uniform tiles, but this may require shared memory atomics if the screen is heavily mixed. MLP Width: Cooperative vectors provide minimal benefit for narrow MLPs (D < 32). Precision: Block compression (e.g., BC1) may introduce quality drops, but hardware-accelerated decompression mitigates this. Time Complexity: Reduced by fewer ray steps (Larger Step) and early termination. Neural inference is accelerated by hardware matrix multiplication. Memory Complexity: Reduced by block-compressed latent features and neural codebooks. Measured Performance: On Intel B580 and Nvidia RTX 4090, cooperative vectors provide up to a 40x speedup over software FMA for wider MLPs (D \ge 32). Specifically, for D=64, speedups range from 20x-46x on B580 and 20x-49x on RTX 4090. Algorithmic strategies reduce test time from 41.8 ms (Baseline) to 5.5 ms (Full acceleration) on Synthetic-NeRF 800x800 images. Quality Trade-off: Minimal quality drop (0.1 dB PSNR) with significant speed gains. Strengths: High performance on modern GPUs with cooperative vector support; low deployment time. Limitations: Scaling issues with mixed tiles; requires hardware support for cooperative vectors. The strategies originate from research into compact real-time radiance fields and hardware-accelerated neural rendering. The algorithmic components (Combine Thread, Larger Step, Early Termination, Prefetch Neighbor) were introduced in the context of Neural Codebook compression. The hardware acceleration component (Cooperative Vectors) was developed to optimize MLP inference in G-Buffer passes, leveraging DirectX cooperative vectors extensions. name: Object Space Ray Tracing for Remote Volume Rendering
head: Object space ray tracing phase, Ray tracing technique rendering object space samples as spheres
body: This method replaces the 2.5D point rasterization phase of the original Zellmann et al. remote volume rendering algorithm with an object space ray tracing phase to eliminate rendering artifacts in volumetric and transparent regions. It transmits compacted object space samples (position and radius) and color data from a server to a client, where a software CUDA ray tracer renders them as spheres instead of fixed-size OpenGL points. Inputs: Server-side volume rendering output: A set of object space samples, each containing position and radius data. Network connection: Used to transmit compacted samples to the client. Outputs: Client-side rendered image: A 2D image generated by ray tracing the received object space samples. Data Structures: Object Space Sample: A structure containing position and radius. Size: 64 bits per sample. Layout: The source does not specify the exact bit-packing layout of the position and radius fields within the 64 bits. Color Data: Transmitted alongside samples. Size: 32 bits per color value. Steps: 1. Server-Side Rendering: Perform volume rendering to generate object space samples. 2. Server-Side Compaction: Compact the generated object space samples to reduce data size before transmission. 3. Transmission: Transmit the compacted object space samples and color data to the client over the network. 4. Client-Side Ray Tracing: Use a software ray tracing implementation based on NVIDIA CUDA to render the received samples. 5. Sphere Rendering: Render the object space samples as spheres (object space splats) instead of OpenGL points with fixed pixel size. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def serverpipeline(volumedata): # 1. Generate object space samples (position and radius) # Source does not specify the exact volume rendering kernel used samples = [] for voxel in volumedata: samples.append({"position": voxel["position"], "radius": voxel["radius"]}) # 2. Compact samples to reduce data size # Source suggests using removeif from Thrust for GPGPU implementation # Source does not specify the exact compaction criteria compactedsamples = [s for s in samples if s["radius"] > 0.0] # 3. Transmit to client # Format: 32 bits per color value, 64 bits per sample # Source does not specify the exact network packing routine packeddata = [] for s in compactedsamples: packeddata.extend(s["position"]) packeddata.append(s["radius"]) networkstream.write(packeddata) def clientpipeline(receivedsamples, imagewidth, imageheight): # 4. Initialize software ray tracer (CUDA-based) # Source does not specify ray generation or intersection algorithms image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] # 5. Render samples as spheres (object space splats) # Source does not specify the exact sphere rasterization or shading logic for sample in receivedsamples: # Project sample to screen space # Intersect rays with sphere at sample["position"] with radius sample["radius"] # Accumulate color and opacity per fragment pass return image Parameters: Color Precision: 32 bits per color value transmitted from server to client. Sample Precision: 64 bits per object space sample, containing position and radius data. Resolution: The example images used for measurement and description are 1024 × 1024 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: OpenGL Point Rasterization Artifacts: Using OpenGL point rasterization causes artifacts in volumetric/transparent regions because depth compositing is per-vertex, not per-fragment, and opacity increases with fillrate if variable point size is used. Compaction Performance: The overall pipeline is currently bound by compaction performance on the server side. Composites rays in image order with early termination. Choose when network bandwidth is extremely limited and client-side computation must be minimal. Uses sparse structures for training. Choose when optimizing model parameters rather than rendering. Renders volume in chunks. Choose for large volumes that do not fit in memory. Evaluates BRDFs. Choose when surface rendering is required. General inference pipeline. Choose for end-to-end system design. Forward pass for DVGO. Choose for neural implicit representations. Precomputes opacity. Choose when view-dependent effects are static. Warps images using ray tracing. Choose when warping pre-rendered frames is preferred over transmitting samples. Time Complexity: The overall pipeline is currently bound by compaction performance on the server side. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of compacted samples. For 1024 × 1024 pixel images, compaction results in 623,584 individual object space samples. Measured Performance: Measured on an NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU. The source does not provide specific frame rates but notes that rendering performance is "very high" even without RT Cores. Strengths: Significantly improves visual quality in volumetric and transparent regions compared to OpenGL point rasterization, even with slight camera movement. Limitations: Bound by server-side compaction performance. Network bandwidth and latency are not reported as they depend on the individual connection. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This technique is an extension of the algorithm by Zellmann et al. [ZAL12] titled 'Image-Based Remote Real-Time Volume Rendering - Decoupling Rendering from View Point Updates' (2012). It was proposed to address the rendering artifacts inherent in the original method's use of 2.5D point rendering. The implementation uses NVIDIA CUDA for ray tracing and C++ Boost Asio for network communication.
