name: Ray Tracing-Based Image Warping for Remote Volume Rendering
head: Object-space splatting with ray tracing, Sphere-based reprojection
body: This method decouples volume rendering computation from display by transmitting object-space samples (position and color) from a server to a client, where they are rendered as semi-transparent spheres using first-hit ray tracing. It replaces the rasterized point primitives of the base image-warping method to eliminate reprojection artifacts caused by fixed-size point primitives, effectively implementing a distance-aware splatting technique. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data, camera parameters (origin o, direction \tilde{d}), and a representative depth heuristic value ti derived from the server-side ray marcher. Output: A stream of compacted object-space samples (packed 64-bit positions and radii) and associated volume-rendered colors sent to the client, which produces the final image via ray tracing. Data Structures: Server Output Buffer: A screen-sized buffer storing object-space samples. Each sample consists of a quantized 64-bit value packing the object-space coordinate p and the footprint radius, and an associated volume-rendered color value. Client Data Structure: A list of semi-transparent spheres defined by center position p and radius r, with a constant color attribute. Steps: 1. Server: Ray Marching and Depth Estimation. Render the volume using a ray marcher. For each pixel, determine a representative depth value ti using a heuristic (e.g., from Zellmann et al.). 2. Server: Compute Object-Space Coordinate. Calculate the object-space coordinate p for the representative depth using the formula: p = o + \tilde{d} ti where o is the ray origin, \tilde{d} is the direction vector, and ti is the ray parameter associated with the representative depth. 3. Server: Assign Footprint Radius. Determine the radius r for the sample: if the ray hit the volume and integrated a color with non-zero opacity, r = 0.5 \times \text{voxel\diagonal}; otherwise, r = 0. 4. Server: Quantize and Pack. Quantize the object-space coordinate p and pack it together with the radius r into a single 64-bit value. 5. Server: Compact Buffer. Move all samples with a radius of zero to one side of the buffer. Send only the samples with non-zero radius to the client to reduce bandwidth. 6. Client: Receive Data. Receive the buffers containing the packed object-space samples and their associated colors. 7. Client: Build BVH. Reinterpret the received object-space samples as semi-transparent spheres. Build a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) over these sphere positions using the LBVH algorithm. 8. Client: Ray Trace. Render the point cloud using first-hit ray tracing. Each sphere is colorized according to its designated pixel color with no additional shading. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def serverrender(volume, rayorigins, raydirections, voxelsize): samples = [] for o, d in zip(rayorigins, raydirections): # Step 1: Volume marching heuristic to find ti, hit, and color ti, hit, color = volumemarch(o, d, volume) if not hit or color.opacity == 0: continue # Step 2: Compute object-space coordinate p = o + d ti # Step 3: Assign footprint radius voxeldiagonal = voxelsize math.sqrt(3) r = 0.5 voxeldiagonal if hit and color.opacity > 0 else 0.0 # Step 4: Quantize and pack into 64-bit value packed = pack64bit(p, r) samples.append((packed, color)) # Step 5: Compact buffer (move zero-radius samples to one side) compacted = [(p, c) for p, c in samples if unpackradius(p) > 0] return compacted def volumemarch(o, d, volume): # Standard volume ray marching stub returning (ti, hit, color) return 1.0, True, (1.0, 0.5, 0.2, 0.8) def pack64bit(p, r): # Quantize coordinates and radius, pack into 64-bit integer qx, qy, qz = int(p.x 1000), int(p.y 1000), int(p.z 1000) qr = int(r 1000) return (qx << 48) | (qy << 32) | (qz << 16) | qr def unpack64bit(packed): # Extract position and radius from 64-bit value qx = (packed >> 48) & 0xFFFF qy = (packed >> 32) & 0xFFFF qz = (packed >> 16) & 0xFFFF qr = packed & 0xFFFF return (qx / 1000.0, qy / 1000.0, qz / 1000.0), qr / 1000.0 def clientrender(receivedsamples): # Step 6: Receive data (already in receivedsamples) # Step 7: Reinterpret as spheres and build BVH spheres = [] for packed, color in receivedsamples: p, r = unpack64bit(packed) spheres.append({'center': p, 'radius': r, 'color': color}) # Step 7: Build LBVH from positions bvh = buildbvh(spheres) # Step 8: Ray trace image = [] for pixel in screenpixels: ray = {'origin': pixel.origin, 'direction': pixel.direction} hit = firsthitquery(bvh, ray) if hit: image.append(hit.color) else: image.append((0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) return image def buildbvh(spheres): # Standard LBVH construction algorithm if not spheres: return None # Simplified recursive BVH builder for demonstration center = sum(s['center'] for s in spheres) / len(spheres) left = [s for s in spheres if (s['center'][0] - center[0]) < 0] right = [s for s in spheres if (s['center'][0] - center[0]) >= 0] return {'left': buildbvh(left), 'right': buildbvh(right), 'spheres': spheres} def firsthitquery(bvh, ray): # Standard first-hit ray tracing query if not bvh: return None closest = None mint = float('inf') for s in bvh['spheres']: t = raysphereintersect(ray, s) if t is not None and t < mint: mint = t closest = s if bvh['left']: tl = raysphereintersect(ray, bvh['left']) if tl is not None and tl < mint: closest = bvh['left'] mint = tl if bvh['right']: tr = raysphereintersect(ray, bvh['right']) if tr is not None and tr < mint: closest = bvh['right'] return closest def raysphereintersect(ray, sphere): # Standard ray-sphere intersection oc = (ray['origin'][0] - sphere['center'][0], ray['origin'][1] - sphere['center'][1], ray['origin'][2] - sphere['center'][2]) a = ray['direction'][0]2 + ray['direction'][1]2 + ray['direction'][2]2 b = 2.0 (oc[0]ray['direction'][0] + oc[1]ray['direction'][1] + oc[2]ray['direction'][2]) c = oc[0]2 + oc[1]2 + oc[2]2 - sphere['radius']2 discriminant = b2 - 4ac if discriminant < 0: return None t = (-b - math.sqrt(discriminant)) / (2a) return t if t > 0 else None screenpixels = [{'origin': (0, 0, 0), 'direction': (0, 0, 1)}] Parameters: Footprint Radius: Set to half the size of a voxel’s diagonal for valid volume hits; zero otherwise. Data Packing: Object space coordinate and radius are packed into 64 bits. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Rasterization Artifacts: Fixed-size point primitives cause artifacts because their size does not vary with distance. This is avoided by using solid spheres where the footprint decreases with increasing distance to the viewer. Multi-hit Ray Tracing: Multi-hit ray tracing was experimented with but yielded mixed image quality results, so first-hit was chosen for simplicity and consistency. Time Complexity: Server-side complexity is dominated by volume ray marching. Client-side complexity includes LBVH construction and ray tracing. The sources report LBVH construction taking 11 ms and compaction taking 23 ms for a point cloud of 623,584 samples. Memory Complexity: The server sends only non-zero radius samples, reducing bandwidth. The client stores the BVH and sphere data. Measured Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 2080 GPU, rendering five views with a viewport of 1024 \times 1024 pixels resulted in frame rates ranging from 229 FPS to 408 FPS, depending on the view. Strengths: Eliminates reprojection artifacts associated with rasterized point primitives; reduces bandwidth by compacting zero-radius samples. Limitations: Requires real-time ray tracing hardware (e.g., NVIDIA RTX); LBVH construction adds latency on the client side. When to use: Remote volume rendering where visual quality (artifact-free reprojection) is prioritized over minimal client-side latency, and hardware supports real-time ray tracing. When not to use: Hardware without ray tracing support; scenarios where network bandwidth is extremely constrained and compaction is insufficient. The method was proposed by Zellmann as an augmentation to the image-warping-based remote volume rendering algorithm by Zellmann et al. [ZAL12]. It shifts from an image-based approach to an object-order approach based on real-time ray tracing. The implementation uses NVIDIA CUDA for rendering and Boost Asio for network communication. Augmenting Image Warping-Based Remote Volume Rendering with Ray Tracing, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2006.14726, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Raw Volume Rendering
head: Single Rendering Algorithm, vpRenderRawVolume
body: Raw Volume Rendering is a direct rendering routine that processes raw voxel data and stores the result in the current image array, optionally accelerating the process if an octree is present in the context. It is designed for scenarios where the volume data or the opacity transfer function changes between renderings, distinguishing it from preclassified rendering which requires fixed classification. The variant that skips precomputation entirely is significantly slower and useful only for single renderings. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel array containing raw scalar or vector data, a classification function (opacity transfer function), view parameters, and shading parameters. Output: The composited image stored in the current image array. Data Structures: Voxel Array: The raw volume data. The layout and field specifications must be valid; otherwise, VPERRORBADVOXEL is returned. Intermediate Image: An internal work buffer used to hold temporary results during rendering. Octree (Optional): If present in the context (created via vpCreateMinMaxOctree), it is used to accelerate rendering by skipping empty space. The variant that does not use any precomputed data structures skips octree construction entirely. Parameters: Maximum Opacity Threshold (VPMAXRAYOPACITY): A value specifying the threshold for pixel opacity. If reached, no more voxels are composited. Default is 1.0. A typical good value is 0.95. Values closer to 1.0 result in longer rendering times but less error. Intermediate Image Hints (VPINTWIDTHHINT, VPINTHEIGHTHINT): Specify the maximum size of the internal work buffer to avoid reallocation overhead. If no scaling is present, the max dimension is twice the largest volume dimension. Intermediate Image Queries (VPINTERMEDIATEWIDTH, VPINTERMEDIATEHEIGHT): Used to find the precise bound for the intermediate image size required for rendering with current viewing parameters. Steps: 1. Load the volume data. 2. (Optional) Precompute the min-max octree with vpCreateMinMaxOctree() if acceleration is desired and the volume is static. If this step is skipped, the rendering is significantly slower and suitable only for single renderings. 3. Choose the classification function (opacity transfer function). 4. Set the view and shading parameters. 5. Render with vpRenderRawVolume(). Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the usage pattern for Raw Volume Rendering without precomputed acceleration structures, as described in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrawvolume(vpc, volumedata, classificationfunction, viewparams, shadingparams): # 1. Load volume data # Sources do not specify exact API for loading; assume context is initialized setvolumeparameters(vpc, volumedata) # 2. Choose classification function setclassificationfunction(vpc, classificationfunction) # 3. Set view and shading parameters setviewparameters(vpc, viewparams) setshadingparameters(vpc, shadingparams) # 4. Set maximum opacity threshold (optional, default 1.0) # Typical value: 0.95 setmaxrayopacity(vpc, 0.95) # 5. Render result = vpRenderRawVolume(vpc) if result != VPOK: handleerror(result) return result def setvolumeparameters(vpc, data): vpc.volumesize = data.shape vpc.voxelsize = data.voxelsize vpc.voxelfields = data.fields if not vpc.volumesize or not vpc.voxelsize: return VPERRORBADVOLUME if not vpc.voxelfields: return VPERRORBADVOXEL return VPOK def setclassificationfunction(vpc, func): vpc.opacitytables = func.tables vpc.fieldmapping = func.fieldmapping if not vpc.opacitytables or not vpc.fieldmapping: return VPERRORBADCLASSIFIER return VPOK def setviewparameters(vpc, params): vpc.viewmatrix = params.viewmatrix if not ismatrixnonsingular(vpc.viewmatrix): return VPERRORSINGULAR return VPOK def setshadingparameters(vpc, params): vpc.shadingtables = params.shadingtables vpc.materialtypes = params.materialtypes if not vpc.shadingtables or not vpc.materialtypes: return VPERRORBADSHADER return VPOK def setmaxrayopacity(vpc, threshold): vpc.maxrayopacity = threshold return VPOK def vpRenderRawVolume(vpc): # Simulates the rendering routine return VPOK def handleerror(code): raise RuntimeError(f"Rendering failed with error code {code}") def ismatrixnonsingular(matrix): # Standard linear algebra check return abs(matrix.det()) > 1e-9 VPOK = 0 VPERRORBADVOLUME = 1 VPERRORBADVOXEL = 2 VPERRORBADCLASSIFIER = 3 VPERRORSINGULAR = 4 VPERRORBADSHADER = 5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shading Lookup Tables Error (VPERRORBADSHADER): Occurs if tables are sized incorrectly, voxel fields used to index are invalid, or the number of material types is invalid. Singular Matrix Error (VPERRORSINGULAR): Occurs if one of the current view transformation matrices is singular. Bad Volume Error (VPERRORBADVOLUME): Occurs if volume size has not been set or is invalid, or there is no volume data. Bad Voxel Error (VPERRORBADVOXEL): Occurs if voxel size or voxel fields have not been specified or have been incorrectly specified. Bad Classifier Error (VPERRORBADCLASSIFIER): Occurs if opacity transfer function tables have invalid sizes, are associated with invalid voxel fields, or have been incorrectly specified. This error is specific to vpRenderRawVolume. Bad Shadow Error (VPERRORBADSHADOW): Occurs if the angle between the shadow light vector and the viewing direction is too large (must be less than 45 degrees). Either change light direction or disable shadows. Performance: Raw Volume Rendering is significantly slower than rendering with a precomputed min-max octree or using vpRenderClassifiedVolume. Acceleration: Rendering with an octree is significantly faster than without, but still slower than rendering with vpRenderClassifiedVolume. Use Cases: It is useful only for single renderings from a volume. vpRenderClassifiedVolume is preferred when the same volume is rendered multiple times with the same opacity transfer function. Memory: Uses an intermediate image work buffer. The size of this buffer depends on the volume size and view transformation. Reallocation overhead can be avoided by setting size hints (VPINTWIDTHHINT, VPINTHEIGHTHINT). Raw Volume Rendering is part of the VolPack library, a software library for volume rendering. It is one of three main rendering algorithms provided by VolPack, alongside vpRenderClassifiedVolume and the Min-Max Octree algorithm. The method is implemented via the vpRenderRawVolume routine. vpRenderRawVolume(3), https://www.mankier.com/3/vpRenderRawVolume, fetched 2026-10-27 VolPack User's Guide, http://www-graphics.stanford.edu/software/volpack/vpuserguide.html, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Exploiting Temporal Coherence (C-Buffer)
head: C-Buffer, C-Buffer Temporal Coherence, Coherent Volume Rendering, Coordinates-buffer
body: Exploiting Temporal Coherence via a C-Buffer (Coordinates-buffer) accelerates volume rendering in animations by storing the 3D coordinates of the first non-transparent voxel hit by each ray, allowing subsequent frames to start ray casting closer to the surface rather than from the volume boundary. It estimates the new ray start points by transforming the stored coordinates according to the new viewing parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, camera/view parameters, and the C-Buffer from the previous frame. Output: Rendered image, updated C-Buffer. Data Structures: C-Buffer (C): A 2D array of size W \times H (image resolution). Each entry stores the 3D coordinates of the first non-transparent voxel hit by the ray corresponding to that pixel. Format: (x, y, z) representing voxel indices or normalized coordinates within the volume grid. Empty State: A special flag or value indicates no hit was recorded for that pixel in the previous frame. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization (First Frame): Perform standard ray casting for all pixels from the volume entry point to the exit point. Identify the first non-transparent voxel hit at coordinates (x{hit}, y{hit}, z{hit}). Store (x{hit}, y{hit}, z{hit}) in the C-Buffer entry for that pixel. Render the image. 2. Subsequent Frames (Ray Start Determination): For each pixel, retrieve the stored coordinates from the C-Buffer. Case A: Empty Entry: If the C-Buffer entry is empty, start the ray at the volume boundary (standard approach). Case B: Valid Entry: Use the stored coordinates as the starting point for ray casting. The stored coordinate serves as an estimate of where the new rays should start their volume traversal. 3. C-Buffer Update (Rotation Handling): If the world space rotates (or camera rotates relative to volume), the voxel coordinates stored in the C-Buffer must be transformed to align with the new view. Let R be the rotation matrix applied to the world space. For each entry containing (x, y, z): 1. Transform the voxel coordinates to world space (if stored in voxel space) or apply rotation directly if stored in world space. Let the transformed coordinates be (x', y', z'). 2. Project (x', y', z') back to screen space (i', j') using the current view and projection matrices. 3. Map the value from the old C-Buffer entry to the new screen coordinate (i', j'). Collision Detection (Hidden Voxels): If multiple previous entries map to the same new screen coordinate (i', j'), it indicates a change in depth ordering (occlusion). Specifically, if the relative order of projected voxels changes, the deeper voxel is potentially hidden. These entries possibly have to be removed. 4. Rendering and Final Update: Render the frame using the updated C-Buffer for ray starts. Update the C-Buffer with the new first-hit coordinates for the current frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderwithcbuffer(volume, volmin, volmax, cbuffer, frameindex, viewmatrix, projmatrix): H, W = cbuffer.shape newcbuffer = [[None] W for in range(H)] image = [[None] W for in range(H)] # 1. Handle C-Buffer transformation if view changed if frameindex > 0: cbuffer = updatecbufferonrotation(cbuffer, viewmatrix, volmin, volmax, H, W) for j in range(H): for i in range(W): rayorigin, raydir = generateray(i, j, viewmatrix, projmatrix, volmin, volmax) prevhit = cbuffer[j][i] if prevhit is not None: hit = traceraystartingat(volume, rayorigin, raydir, prevhit, volmin, volmax) else: hit = tracerayfromboundary(volume, rayorigin, raydir, volmin, volmax) if hit is not None: image[j][i] = samplecolor(volume, rayorigin, raydir, hit) newcbuffer[j][i] = hit else: image[j][i] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) newcbuffer[j][i] = None return image, newcbuffer def updatecbufferonrotation(cbuffer, viewmatrix, volmin, volmax, H, W): tempmap = {} for j in range(H): for i in range(W): voxel = cbuffer[j][i] if voxel is None: continue # Transform voxel coordinates to world space worldpos = list(voxel) # Apply rotation/view matrix rotatedpos = applymatrix(viewmatrix, worldpos) # Project back to screen screenpos = worldtoscreen(rotatedpos, H, W) inew, jnew = screenpos if 0 <= inew < W and 0 <= jnew < H: if (inew, jnew) not in tempmap: tempmap[(inew, jnew)] = [] tempmap[(inew, jnew)].append(voxel) newcbuffer = [[None] W for in range(H)] for (inew, jnew), voxels in tempmap.items(): if len(voxels) == 1: newcbuffer[jnew][inew] = voxels[0] else: newcbuffer[jnew][inew] = None return newcbuffer def tracerayfromboundary(volume, origin, direction, volmin, volmax): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for k in range(3): if abs(direction[k]) < 1e-6: if origin[k] < volmin[k] or origin[k] > volmax[k]: return None else: t1 = (volmin[k] - origin[k]) / direction[k] t2 = (volmax[k] - origin[k]) / direction[k] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return None step = [1 if direction[k] > 0 else -1 for k in range(3)] tdelta = [abs(1.0 / direction[k]) if abs(direction[k]) > 1e-6 else float('inf') for k in range(3)] tmax = [tdelta[k] (step[k] (volmin[k] if step[k] < 0 else volmax[k]) - origin[k]) for k in range(3)] currentvoxel = [int((origin[k] + tmin direction[k] - volmin[k]) / (volmax[k] - volmin[k]) 100.0) for k in range(3)] currentvoxel = [max(0, min(99, currentvoxel[k])) for k in range(3)] t = tmin while t <= tmax: if volume[currentvoxel[0]][currentvoxel[1]][currentvoxel[2]] > 0.0: return currentvoxel if tmax[0] < tmax[1] and tmax[0] < tmax[2]: t = tmax[0]; tmax[0] += tdelta[0]; currentvoxel[0] += step[0] elif tmax[1] < tmax[2]: t = tmax[1]; tmax[1] += tdelta[1]; currentvoxel[1] += step[1] else: t = tmax[2]; tmax[2] += tdelta[2]; currentvoxel[2] += step[2] return None def traceraystartingat(volume, origin, direction, startvoxel, volmin, volmax): step = [1 if direction[k] > 0 else -1 for k in range(3)] tdelta = [abs(1.0 / direction[k]) if abs(direction[k]) > 1e-6 else float('inf') for k in range(3)] tmax = [tdelta[k] (step[k] (volmin[k] if step[k] < 0 else volmax[k]) - origin[k]) for k in range(3)] currentvoxel = list(startvoxel) tstart = 0.0 for k in range(3): if abs(direction[k]) > 1e-6: tstart = max(tstart, (currentvoxel[k] - (origin[k] - volmin[k]) / (volmax[k] - volmin[k]) 100.0) tdelta[k]) t = tstart while t <= tmax[0] + tmax[1] + tmax[2]: if 0 <= currentvoxel[0] < 100 and 0 <= currentvoxel[1] < 100 and 0 <= currentvoxel[2] < 100: if volume[currentvoxel[0]][currentvoxel[1]][currentvoxel[2]] > 0.0: return currentvoxel if tmax[0] < tmax[1] and tmax[0] < tmax[2]: t = tmax[0]; tmax[0] += tdelta[0]; currentvoxel[0] += step[0] elif tmax[1] < tmax[2]: t = tmax[1]; tmax[1] += tdelta[1]; currentvoxel[1] += step[1] else: t = tmax[2]; tmax[2] += tdelta[2]; currentvoxel[2] += step[2] return None def generateray(i, j, viewmatrix, projmatrix, volmin, volmax): # Standard ray generation from screen coordinates to world space return (volmin, [1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) def applymatrix(matrix, point): # Homogeneous transformation return point def worldtoscreen(worldpos, H, W): # Project world pos to screen coords return (0, 0) def samplecolor(volume, origin, direction, hit): # Sample transfer function at hit location return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Parameters: Blend Factor: Not applicable (geometric caching, not color blending). Invalidation Threshold: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Entries: If a C-buffer entry is empty, the ray must start at the volume boundary. Rotation Collisions: When the world rotates, multiple voxel coordinates may map to the same C-buffer entry. This indicates potentially hidden voxels. These entries possibly have to be removed. Depth Order Change: If the relative order of projected voxels changes, the deeper voxel is hidden. The C-buffer must detect this and invalidate the entry. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H) per frame for buffer update and ray casting. Ray casting is accelerated by starting closer to the surface, reducing the number of samples per ray in coherent regions. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the C-Buffer. Strengths: Significant speedup in animations with small camera or volume movements. Reduces overdraw in transparent volumes. Limitations: Requires handling of rotation and occlusion changes. Performance degrades if the scene changes rapidly or if there is large camera motion between frames. When to Use: Volume animations with smooth camera motion or slow volume updates. When Not to Use: Scenes with rapid, discontinuous changes in geometry or camera position. The C-Buffer technique was introduced in the context of Direct Volume Rendering for animations. It exploits the temporal coherence of the first-hit surface in volume rendering. The method was reported by Yagel and Shi for speeding up the process of volume rendering a sequence of images. name: Photometric Optimization
head: Albedo/Emission/Extinction optimization, EgoNeRF Training, Property reconstruction, Volume Optimization
body: Photometric optimization is an inverse rendering technique that recovers latent scene parameters—such as 3D geometry, pose, texture, and lighting—by minimizing the photometric difference between a target image and a rendered image. It formulates the problem as an unconstrained optimization task, leveraging gradients estimated via differentiable rendering pipelines to update parameters using gradient descent. Unlike methods that rely on discrete candidate light sources or explicit shadow detection, this approach performs continuous optimization of scene properties, often utilizing regularizers to constrain the solution space. The method minimizes a photometric loss function to update scene parameters. The standard emission-absorption model computes the color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for a ray \mathbf{r} as, building on Radiance-field optimization: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^N Ti (1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai)) \mathbf{c}i where \sigmai is the density, \deltai is the step size, \mathbf{c}i is the color, and Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) is the transmittance. Inputs: A set of target images (ground truth colors C(\mathbf{r})), initial scene parameters (e.g., voxel grid densities \sigma, albedo \mathbf{a}, emission \mathbf{e}, or neural network weights), and camera poses. Outputs: Optimized scene parameters that minimize the difference between rendered and target images. Voxel Grid: Stores volume properties such as extinction, albedo, and emission. Feature Grids: In methods like EgoNeRF, balanced spherical grids G\sigma, Ga store density and appearance features. Ray Batch: A set of randomly sampled rays \mathcal{R} for each optimization step. 1. Ray Sampling: Sample a batch of rays \mathcal{R} from the target images. 2. Volume Rendering: Compute the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for each ray \mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R} using the current scene parameters and the volume rendering equation. 3. Loss Computation: Calculate the photometric loss \mathcal{L} between the rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and the ground-truth color C(\mathbf{r}): \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2 4. Regularization (Optional): Apply regularization terms to improve stability and reduce artifacts. Laplacian Regularizer: In, a weak Laplacian regularizer is applied to introduce diffusion between neighboring voxels, reducing stripe and edge artifacts without smoothing intricate detail. Total Variation (TV) Loss: In, TV loss is applied to feature grids to reduce noise, especially for real-world datasets with imperfect camera poses. 5. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients of the total loss with respect to the scene parameters. 6. Parameter Update: Update the scene parameters using an optimizer (e.g., Conjugate Gradient for, or automatic differentiation/Adam for). 7. Iteration: Repeat steps 1–6 until convergence. Photometric Loss: \mathcal{L} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|} \sum{\mathbf{r} \in \mathcal{R}} \| \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) - C(\mathbf{r}) \|2^2. Histogram Matching Loss (for cloud synthesis): \arg \min{L0, La} \sum{n=1}^{nL} [h(I{ph}, n) - h(I(L0, La), n)]^2, where nL is the number of intensity levels, h(I, n) is the normalized n-th histogram of image I, and I(L0, La) is the rendered image using parameters L0 and La. Ray Marching Steps: In, twice the number of ray marching steps for the length of the diagonal as the number of voxels along an axis is a good choice. Convergence: The process converges after three to five conjugate gradient steps. Emission Constraint: Emission can only lighten the appearance. Albedo Constraint: Albedo can only darken the appearance. Insufficient Views: May induce stripe patterns into the volume because constraint pixels affect only voxels along their corresponding ray. Edges Between Regions: Edges can appear between constrained and unconstrained regions if only parts of the object are specified in target images. Emission/Albedo Constraints: If only emission is optimized, the result cannot fully match desired appearance as light is only added. If only albedo is optimized, light is only removed, preventing perfect matching. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Ray: def init(self, cameraid, origin, direction, u, v): self.cameraid = cameraid self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.u = u self.v = v def photometricoptimization(sceneparams, targetimages, cameraposes, numiterations): """ Optimizes scene parameters to match target images using photometric loss. """ for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Ray Sampling rays = samplerays(targetimages, cameraposes) # 2. Volume Rendering renderedcolors = volumerender(rays, sceneparams) # 3. Loss Computation gtcolors = getgroundtruthcolors(rays, targetimages) loss = meansquarederror(renderedcolors, gtcolors) # 4. Regularization if sceneparams.uselaplacian: loss += laplacianregularization(sceneparams) if sceneparams.usetv: loss += totalvariationloss(sceneparams) # 5. Gradient Computation gradients = computegradients(loss, sceneparams) # 6. Parameter Update sceneparams = updateparameters(sceneparams, gradients) return sceneparams def samplerays(images, poses, batchsize=256): """Sample rays uniformly from the image plane for each pose.""" rays = [] for in range(batchsize): poseidx = random.randint(0, len(poses) - 1) u, v = random.uniform(0, 1), random.uniform(0, 1) origin = poses[poseidx].camtoworld[:3, 3] direction = poses[poseidx].camtoworld[:3,:3] @ np.array([u - 0.5, v - 0.5, 1.0]) rays.append(Ray(poseidx, origin, direction, u, v)) return rays def volumerender(rays, params): """Computes color using alpha compositing along each ray.""" colors = [] for ray in rays: T = 1.0 color = np.zeros(3) for step in range(params.numsteps): t = step params.stepsize pos = ray.origin + ray.direction t sigma, c = params.query(pos) alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma params.stepsize) color += T alpha c T = (1.0 - alpha) colors.append(color) return np.array(colors) def getgroundtruthcolors(rays, images): """Retrieve ground truth colors for sampled pixels.""" return np.array([images[ray.cameraid][ray.u, ray.v] for ray in rays]) def meansquarederror(rendered, groundtruth): return np.mean((rendered - groundtruth) 2) def laplacianregularization(params): """Weak Laplacian regularizer for diffusion between neighboring voxels.""" grid = params.grid diffx = np.diff(grid, axis=0) diffy = np.diff(grid, axis=1) diffz = np.diff(grid, axis=2) return np.sum(diffx 2) + np.sum(diffy 2) + np.sum(diffz 2) def totalvariationloss(params): """Total variation loss to reduce noise in feature grids.""" grid = params.grid diffx = np.diff(grid, axis=0) diffy = np.diff(grid, axis=1) diffz = np.diff(grid, axis=2) return np.sum(np.abs(diffx)) + np.sum(np.abs(diffy)) + np.sum(np.abs(diffz)) def computegradients(loss, params): """Computes gradients via automatic differentiation or conjugate gradient solver.""" return params.computegradient(loss) def updateparameters(params, gradients): """Updates parameters using conjugate gradient or Adam optimizer.""" return params.applyoptimizer(gradients) Image-based reconstruction optimization is an inverse rendering technique that recovers latent scene parameters—such as 3D geometry, pose, texture, and lighting—by minimizing the photometric difference between a target image and a rendered image. It formulates the problem as an unconstrained optimization task, leveraging gradients estimated via differentiable rendering pipelines to update parameters using gradient descent. Unlike methods that rely on discrete candidate light sources or explicit shadow detection, this approach performs continuous optimization of scene properties, often utilizing regularizers to constrain the solution space. NeRFLiX is a post-processing method for novel view synthesis that removes native rendering artifacts from Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) by learning degradation-driven multiview blending. It distinguishes itself from standard photometric optimization by explicitly modeling the degradation process via a NeRF-style degradation simulator and a multiview mixer, rather than solely optimizing scene parameters. Joint Optimization of Scene and Renderer is a photometric optimization method that simultaneously refines the geometric and appearance attributes of a scene representation alongside the parameters of a neural renderer. It solves the problem of reconstructing high-quality novel views from a sparse set of input images by treating per-pixel attributes (color, depth, normal, uncertainty, and latent features) as learnable parameters. It differs from Image-based reconstruction optimization by explicitly optimizing the scene's underlying point-based representation attributes rather than just camera poses or static geometry, and it differs from Gradient-Based SE(3) Optimization by focusing on per-view attribute refinement rather than global camera pose estimation. Adaptive IOR Optimization is a training procedure for neural radiance fields that iteratively searches for the optimal Index of Refraction (IOR) to minimize the reconstruction error of transparent foreground objects. It solves the problem of unknown or inaccurate IOR values in refractive scene reconstruction by decoupling background training from foreground IOR selection. It differs from sibling methods like Image-based reconstruction optimization by explicitly treating IOR as a discrete search parameter rather than a continuous gradient-based variable, and from Gradient-Based SE(3) Optimization by focusing on material properties rather than camera pose. Optimization parameters used during the explicit mesh shading pass to refine geometry and scene elements (materials, lighting). Removing the per-vertex deformation vector \Delta v causes floating noisy points in the reconstructed mesh, which degrades lighting quality. Both \Delta v and \Delta m are crucial for high-quality reconstruction; ablation results show the full model significantly outperforms variants without \Delta v or \Delta m on both NeRF-synthetic and RefNeRF-synthetic datasets. A technique to determine parameters L0 and La by minimizing the difference between the histogram of the input photograph and the histogram of rendered example cloud volumes. Solves the nonlinear least square problem using a quasi-Newton method. Formula: \arg \min{L0, La} \sum{n=1}^{nL} [h(I{ph}, n) - h(I(L0, La), n)]^2, where nL is the number of intensity levels, h(I, n) is the normalized n-th histogram of image I, and I(L0, La) is the rendered image using L0 and La. Optimized parameters are denoted L^0, L^a. Applies volume optimization on the result of light optimization to better match desired appearance using the same target images. Light optimization is theoretically redundant if emission is allowed, but useful when volume properties must not change or emission is to be avoided. Light optimization has a more global character as each light source affects the entire volume, connecting appearance to the rest of the scene. Used for rapid preview with a single view without introducing high-frequency artifacts from low input image counts. Methods to find noise parameters from an example image, often by analyzing the Fourier transform or power spectrum. Approaches set parameters of existing procedural shaders from an example image to make the shader produce an image resembling the example. Steps include computing the Fourier transform of the example image, thresholding the magnitude to select sine waves, extending the 2D function to 3D, and refining for directional aspects. Other approaches identify main frequencies in 1D noise profiles, perform histogram matching, and extend to 2D/3D. Automatically compute weights of band-pass isotropic noise octaves to resemble an example image. Randomize the phase spectrum of a given texture to obtain homogeneous noise with the same power spectrum. Search for closest matches in a database of shader-generated images or optimize shader parameters using a genetic algorithm. Alternates between camera correction (improving rendering gradient consistency) and token refinement (improving geometry for subsequent camera updates). Concludes with a short joint photometric refinement of tokens and poses. Uses up to four alternating rounds followed by at most 96 joint refinement steps with an L1 objective. Adds approximately 1.6 s per scene at 16 views on an RTX 4090. Time Complexity: Scales with the number of voxels, ray marching steps, and number of views. For 128^3 voxels, 256 ray marching steps, and 460K constraint pixels (2 views), the result is computed in less than two seconds. With 2.3M constraint pixels (10 views), computation takes seven seconds. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Optimizing for 16 light coefficients on a 128^3 volume with 2.3M constraint pixels (10 views) takes around three seconds. Scaling: Volume optimization can reconstruct higher frequencies than light optimization because it modifies the volume locally. EgoNeRF does not need a coarse-to-fine reconstruction approach for robust optimization because the balanced feature grid guarantees a nearly uniform ray-grid hitting rate. Strengths: Can reconstruct high frequencies locally. Limitations: Insufficient views may induce stripe patterns. Edges can appear between constrained and unconstrained regions. Emission-only or albedo-only optimization cannot perfectly match desired appearance. When to Use: When high-frequency details need to be reconstructed, or when specific volume properties (like albedo or emission) need to be stylized or corrected. When Not to Use: When only global lighting changes are needed, or when volume properties must remain unchanged. Photometric optimization for volume rendering was introduced in the context of volume stylization and property manipulation. The method was proposed by for static volume stylization using a painting metaphor, allowing users to modify albedo, emission, and extinction to match target images. It has since been applied to various domains, including cloud synthesis, egocentric view synthesis, dynamic scene representation, and inverse rendering. It is used for adding imprinted logos to smoke volumes, modifying volcano smoke appearance, and reconstructing extinction for refractive volumes. name: Image-based reconstruction optimization
head: Chair reconstruction optimization, Differentiable rendering optimization, Face reconstruction optimization, Inverse Rendering Optimization, Shape reconstruction via gradient descent, Single image chair reconstruction
body: Image-based reconstruction optimization is an inverse rendering technique that recovers latent scene parameters—such as 3D geometry, pose, texture, and lighting—by minimizing the photometric difference between a target image and a rendered image. It formulates the problem as an unconstrained optimization task, leveraging gradients estimated via differentiable rendering pipelines to update parameters using gradient descent. Unlike methods that rely on discrete candidate light sources or explicit shadow detection, this approach performs continuous optimization of scene properties. It distinguishes itself from finite difference methods by providing cleaner, unbiased derivative estimations, and from feed-forward networks by allowing explicit control over geometry and lighting through iterative refinement. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: One or more target images (I{target} or I), and optionally initial guesses for scene parameters. For single-image reconstruction, a pre-trained autoencoder prior may be required. Outputs: Optimized scene parameters \pi^ (or specific subsets like shape z, pose \theta, texture \phi, lighting \eta). Data Structures: Latent Shape Vector (z0): A fixed-dimensional vector representing 3D geometry. Dimensions vary by application: 200 for face reconstruction, 250 for chair reconstruction. Pose Parameter (\theta): Typically defined by azimuth and elevation angles. Texture Vector (\phi0): Latent representation of surface color/texture. Lighting Parameter (\eta): Parameters defining light source position, intensity, or environment map. Decoders: g(z0): Autoencoder decoder mapping latent shape vector to 3D geometry (e.g., mesh vertices). h(\phi0): Texture decoder mapping latent vector to texture. Renderer (f): A differentiable rendering function that takes geometry, pose, texture, and lighting to produce an image. Optimization Objective: The general objective is to find parameters \pi^ that minimize the difference between the rendered image I(\pi) and the target image I{target}: \pi^ = \arg \min\pi \| I(\pi) - I{target} \| The norm \| \cdot \| is the L2 difference between Gaussian pyramids of the images to reduce sensitivity to local minima. For specific applications, the objective function includes regularization terms: 1. Face Reconstruction: \min{z0, \theta, \phi0, \eta} \| I - f(g(z0), \theta, h(\phi0), \eta) \|^2 2. Chair Reconstruction (with Shape Prior): \min{z, \theta} \alpha \| I - f(g(z0), \theta) \|^2 + \beta (z - \mu)^T \Sigma^{-1} (z - \mu) Where \mu and \Sigma are the mean and covariance of z0 estimated from a training set, and \alpha, \beta are loss weights. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam [Kingma and Ba 2014] is used for gradient descent. Loss Weights: \alpha = 5, \beta = 1 for chair reconstruction. Learning Rate: Not explicitly given in sources; relies on Adam defaults or specific configurations in cited works. Batching: Mini-batch gradient descent may be used, rendering only a subset of input images per iteration. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize pose parameters \theta by subdividing the pose space into a grid. For faces, azimuth and elevation are in [0, 180] degrees; for chairs, azimuth is [0, 360] and elevation is [0, 180] degrees. 2. Initialization: Initialize multiple sets of parameters (z0, \theta, \phi0, \eta) (e.g., 5 sets) to avoid local minima. 3. Gradient Estimation: Render the current scene parameters using the differentiable renderer f. 4. Gradient Estimation: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the parameters using boundary integral techniques or differentiable Monte Carlo path tracing. Use Multiple Importance Sampling (MIS) and edge sorting to reduce variance in gradient estimates. 5. Parameter Update: Update parameters using the Adam optimizer. For mesh-based methods, update vertex positions using estimated gradients. 6. Refinement: If using grid-based pose initialization, further subdivide the grid around the current best pose parameters. 7. Re-initialization: Re-initialize parameters with the current best ones after a fixed number of steps (e.g., every 200 steps) to escape local minima. 8. Convergence: Continue optimization until convergence. Typical step counts are ~1800 steps for face reconstruction and ~2000 steps for chair reconstruction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import copy import random def imagebasedreconstructionoptimization(targetimages, initialparams, renderer, optimizerconfig): """ Optimizes scene parameters to match target images. Args: targetimages: List of target RGB images. initialparams: Initial guess for parameters (z0, theta, phi0, eta). renderer: Differentiable rendering function f(geometry, pose, texture, lighting). optimizerconfig: Configuration for Adam optimizer. Returns: Optimized parameters pi. """ # 1. Initialization # Subdivide pose space into a grid if not provided if initialparams.get('theta') is None: azimuthrange = initialparams.get('azimuthrange', [0, 360]) elevationrange = initialparams.get('elevationrange', [0, 180]) initialparams['theta'] = {'azimuth': (azimuthrange[0] + azimuthrange[1]) / 2, 'elevation': (elevationrange[0] + elevationrange[1]) / 2} # Initialize multiple sets of parameters to avoid local minima numinit = 5 paramsets = [copy.deepcopy(initialparams) for in range(numinit)] bestloss = float('inf') bestparams = None prevbestloss = float('inf') maxsteps = 2000 reinitinterval = 200 convergencethreshold = 1e-6 for step in range(maxsteps): currentloss = float('inf') currentbestparams = None for i in range(numinit): params = paramsets[i] # Render current parameters renderedimage = renderer( geometry=params['z0'], pose=params['theta'], texture=params['phi0'], lighting=params['eta']) # Compute Loss (L2 difference between Gaussian pyramids) loss = computegaussianpyramidl2loss(renderedimage, targetimages) # Compute Gradients using differentiable rendering pipeline gradients = computegradients(loss, params, renderer) # Update Parameters using Adam optimizer params = adamstep(params, gradients, optimizerconfig) paramsets[i] = params if loss < currentloss: currentloss = loss currentbestparams = copy.deepcopy(params) # Update all parameter sets with the best found in this iteration for i in range(numinit): paramsets[i] = copy.deepcopy(currentbestparams) if currentloss < bestloss: bestloss = currentloss bestparams = copy.deepcopy(currentbestparams) # Re-initialize around best parameters to refine search if step > 0 and step % reinitinterval == 0: paramsets = [perturbaround(params=bestparams, scale=0.1) for in range(numinit)] # Check for convergence if step > 100 and abs(bestloss - prevbestloss) < convergencethreshold: break prevbestloss = bestloss return bestparams def computegaussianpyramidl2loss(renderedimage, targetimages): """Computes L2 loss between Gaussian pyramids of rendered and target images.""" totalloss = 0.0 for target in targetimages: renderedpyramid = buildgaussianpyramid(renderedimage) targetpyramid = buildgaussianpyramid(target) for rimg, timg in zip(renderedpyramid, targetpyramid): totalloss += sum((r - t) 2 for r, t in zip(rimg, timg)) return totalloss def buildgaussianpyramid(image, levels=3): """Standard image downsampling to create Gaussian pyramid.""" pyramid = [image] current = image for in range(levels - 1): # Simple 2x2 average pooling for downsampling current = [[(current[r][c] + current[r][c+1] + current[r+1][c] + current[r+1][c+1]) / 4 for c in range(0, len(current[0]), 2)] for r in range(0, len(current), 2)] pyramid.append(current) return pyramid def computegradients(loss, params, renderer): """Backpropagation through the differentiable renderer.""" return renderer.backward(loss, params) def adamstep(params, gradients, config): """Minimal Adam optimizer update.""" lr = config.get('lr', 0.001) beta1, beta2, eps = 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8 # Simplified update step; maintains m and v in config or params in practice for key in params: params[key] -= lr gradients[key] return params def perturbaround(params, scale): """Re-initialize parameters around the best ones with small random noise.""" newparams = copy.deepcopy(params) for key in newparams: if isinstance(newparams[key], (int, float)): newparams[key] += (random.uniform(-1, 1) scale) return newparams Recovers latent scene parameters (camera pose, light placement, surface color) by minimizing photometric error using a differentiable renderer based on the Blinn-Phong model. It specifically estimates the 3D position and intensity of a punctual light source by minimizing photometric error between a rendered image and an observed RGBD image. It distinguishes itself from alternatives by relying on a completely differentiable renderer that explicitly includes cast shadows, thereby increasing robustness against imperfect reflectance estimation. Unlike methods that use discrete candidate light sources or explicit shadow detection, it performs continuous optimization of light position and renders a shadow map at each iteration. Reconstructs 3D geometry, texture, pose, and lighting from a single image by optimizing a latent representation of a pre-trained 3D auto-encoder decoder, regularizing the reconstruction to prevent noisy results. It explicitly reconstructs 3D geometry, pose, lighting, and texture, allowing for higher resolution (512x512 vs 150x150) and better control in out-of-plane rotation and re-texturing compared to methods that learn a disentangled graphics code. Simultaneously reconstructs 3D geometry, diffuse/specular reflectance, and environment lighting from multi-view photography by minimizing photometric error in a differentiable rendering pipeline. It solves the inverse problem of inferring latent scene parameters from observed images by treating the renderer as a differentiable function that maps parameters to pixels, enabling gradient-based optimization. It sets itself apart by explicitly handling the joint optimization of geometry, BRDF parameters, and lighting sources using a physically-based Monte Carlo path tracer (Mitsuba2) with alternating parameter updates to manage memory constraints. An optimization process where scene parameters are updated to minimize the distance between the frozen neural network's latents for the current rendered scene and the target scene. It renders n views of the current scene using the differentiable renderer f(\pi), passes each rendered view through a frozen neural network NN(\cdot), and updates scene parameters \pi to minimize the distance between the network's latents for the current scene and for the target scene. The experiment stops if the loss does not improve for 50 epochs. Baseline reconstructions optimize the same scene parameters but against an image-space loss instead of a network latent, used only to calibrate the metamer criterion. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of iterations and the cost of gradient estimation. Convergence takes around 2000 steps for chair reconstruction. Performance statistics show CPU core minutes per iteration ranging from 7.6 to 31 for various scenes. Memory Complexity: Depends on the resolution of the images and the complexity of the scene representation (e.g., mesh vertices, latent vectors). The latent shape vector dimension is 200–250. Strengths: Produces cleaner and unbiased derivative estimations compared to finite difference methods. Can handle complex scenes with participating media and translucent objects. Shape priors help regularize the solution space for challenging geometries. Limitations: Reconstructing objects with large pose search spaces (e.g., chairs with 360-degree azimuth) and high geometric variance (thin parts) is challenging. Requires a differentiable renderer, which can be computationally expensive. May converge to local minima if not initialized properly. When to Use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of geometry, lighting, and texture is required from images, and differentiable rendering infrastructure is available. Suitable for single-image or multi-view reconstruction tasks where explicit ground-truth lighting is not available. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical, as optimization can be slow. When the object geometry is not well-represented by the chosen prior or parameterization. Image-based reconstruction optimization is rooted in the field of inverse rendering, which seeks to infer scene parameters from observed images. The method has been demonstrated on face reconstruction and chair reconstruction, as well as general inverse rendering with differentiable ray tracing. Key developments include the use of boundary integral techniques for gradient estimation, the integration of deep learning priors via autoencoders, and the application of differentiable Monte Carlo path tracing. The method builds on earlier work in differentiable rendering and optimization, such as Zhang et al. [2020] for interior terms and Nicolet et al. [2021] for mesh updates. name: Inverse Rendering with Differentiable Ray Tracing
head: Differentiable Rendering Optimization, Gradient-based Inverse Rendering, Robust Point Light Source Estimation Using Differentiable Rendering
body:
Inverse rendering recovers latent scene parameters—such as camera pose, light placement, and surface color—that produce a given target photograph by formulating the problem as an unconstrained optimization task using gradients from the rendering pipeline. This method solves the problem of estimating 3D illumination (specifically punctual light source position and intensity) and material properties by minimizing the photometric error between a rendered image and an observed RGBD image. It distinguishes itself from alternatives like Inverse Rendering with Shape Prior by relying on a completely differentiable renderer based on the Blinn-Phong model that explicitly includes cast shadows, thereby increasing robustness against imperfect reflectance estimation. Unlike methods that use discrete candidate light sources or explicit shadow detection, it performs continuous optimization of light position and renders a shadow map at each iteration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry G = (X, N, C), where X is a 3D point cloud, N is the surface normals, and C is the camera pose; material properties M = (kd, ks, \alpha) (diffuse reflectance, specular reflectance, shininess); and an observed target image I^. Outputs: Optimized lighting parameters L = (Li, I{L,i}), where Li is the 3D location and I{L,i} is the scalar intensity of the punctual light source. Data Structures: Geometry G: Represented as an oriented point cloud. X contains 3D coordinates for each point. N contains the corresponding normal vectors. C contains camera pose parameters. Lighting L: Parametrized by a 3D vector for position Li and a scalar for intensity I{L,i}. Image I: A tensor of shape H 	imes W 	imes C, normalized to [0, 1]. Illumination Model: The total image intensity I at a point x is the sum of ambient, diffuse, and specular terms: I = Ia + Id + Is 1. Ambient Term: Calculated as the product of diffuse reflectance kd and ambient illumination La: Ia = kd 	imes La 2. Diffuse Term: Proportional to the dot product of the surface normal N and the light vector (Li - X), scaled by the shadow term Si, diffuse reflectance kd, and light intensity I{L,i}: Id = kd 	imes Si 	imes (Li - X)^t 	imes N 	imes I{L,i} 3. Specular Term: A factor of the scalar product between the normal N and the halfway vector H (between the viewer C-X and the light source Li-X), scaled by specular reflectance ks, shininess \alpha, shadow term Si, and light intensity I{L,i}: Is = ks 	imes Si 	imes (H^t N)^\alpha 	imes I{L,i} 4. Shadow Term Si: Equals 1 when the light illuminates the point X and 0 otherwise. Optimization Objective: The problem minimizes the squared L2 norm of the difference between the rendered image I(G, M, L) and the observed image I^ with respect to the lighting parameters L: \hat{L} = \arg \minL E = \arg \minL \|I(G, M, L) - I^\|2^2 The mean squared error (MSE) loss used is: L(	heta) =  rac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} (Ii(	heta) - Ti)^2 where I(	heta) \in [0, 1]^{H 	imes W 	imes C} is the rendered image, T \in [0, 1]^{H 	imes W 	imes C} is the target image, and N = H \cdot W \cdot C is the total number of pixel-channel values. Algorithm: The optimization uses the Adam optimizer. The update step for parameters 	heta (which may include light position, intensity, or material properties) is: \hat{m}t =  rac{mt}{1 -  eta1^t}, \quad \hat{v}t =  rac{vt}{1 -  eta2^t} 	heta{t+1} = 	hetat - \eta  rac{\hat{m}t}{\sqrt{\hat{v}t + \epsilon}} where mt, vt are biased first and second moment estimates, and \eta,  eta1,  eta2, \epsilon are optimizer hyperparameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inverserenderingoptimization(geometry, materials, targetimage, maxiterations, losstolerance): """ Optimizes lighting parameters (and optionally materials) to match a target image. Args: geometry: Tuple (X, N, C) representing point cloud, normals, camera pose. materials: Tuple (kd, ks, alpha) representing diffuse, specular reflectance, shininess. targetimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, C) normalized to [0, 1]. maxiterations: Integer Nmax. losstolerance: Float epsilon for convergence. Returns: Optimized lighting parameters L. """ # Initialize lighting parameters randomly or with a prior L = initializelightingparameters() # Adam optimizer state m = 0 v = 0 t = 0 converged = False itercount = 0 while not converged and itercount < maxiterations: # 1. Forward Pass: Render image with current parameters # The renderer computes I = Ia + Id + Is using the Blinn-Phong model # and differentiable ray tracing to compute shadows. renderedimage = render(geometry, materials, L) # 2. Compute Loss # MSE loss over all pixels and channels loss = meansquarederror(renderedimage, targetimage) # 3. Compute Gradients # Gradients are propagated through the differentiable renderer # to compute d(loss)/d(L) and optionally d(loss)/d(materials) gradients = computegradients(loss, L, geometry, materials) # 4. Update Parameters using Adam t += 1 m = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) gradients v = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) (gradients 2) mhat = m / (1 - beta1 t) vhat = v / (1 - beta2 t) L = L - learningrate mhat / (sqrt(vhat) + epsilon) # Optional: Project material parameters back to [0, 1] if optimizing materials # materials = projecttorgbcube(materials) # 5. Check Convergence if loss < losstolerance: converged = True itercount += 1 return L Parameters: Adam Hyperparameters: \eta,  eta1,  eta2, \epsilon are used consistently across tasks. Specific values are not listed in the sources but were selected for stable, monotone convergence. Diffuse Reflectance (kd): Coefficient for diffuse term. Specular Reflectance (ks): Coefficient for specular term. Shininess (\alpha): Exponent for specular term. Ambient Illumination (La): Constant ambient light term. Finite Difference Perturbation (h): Used for verification, h = 1 	imes 10^{-5} relative to parameter value (\Delta 	hetai = h \cdot |	hetai| for 	hetai 
eq 0, and \Delta 	hetai = h for 	hetai = 0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Imperfect Reflectance: The method handles imperfect reflectance estimation by including cast shadows, which increases robustness compared to methods that do not use shadows or explicitly separate diffuse/specular components. Gradient Verification: Gradient approximation error E{grad} is measured as  rac{\|
abla{AD} L - 
abla{FD} L\|2}{\|
abla{FD} L\|2 + \epsilon}, where 
abla{AD} is the AD gradient and 
abla{FD} is the finite-difference gradient with h=10^{-5} and \epsilon = 10^{-8}. Material Bounds: When optimizing material properties (RGB colors), a Euclidean projection onto the RGB cube [0, 1]^3 is applied after every iteration to ensure valid colors. Extracts imaging parameters (illumination, camera positions, sea colors) from observed images by iteratively optimizing lighting parameters using the differentiable renderer. It reconstructs surface normal and roughness first, then optimizes lighting parameters (color of sky light, color of sunlight, direction of sunlight) incrementally using gradient propagation. In experiments, optimization ran for 400 iterations using Adam, reducing loss to 10^{-6} and converging to ground truth values. Time Complexity: The computational cost scales with the number of operations in the forward pass rather than with the number of parameters, making it substantially more efficient for high-dimensional optimization problems. Measured Performance: Camera Calibration: MSE loss fell from >5700 to <100 within 150 iterations. Final position error 0.008 ± 0.002 units (0.20 ± 0.05% relative error). Converged in 147 ± 12 iterations over 10 runs. Light Estimation: Converged in <500 iterations. Position error <2% of ground truth. Intensity error <5% of true value. Material Estimation: Final MSE < 1e-4 in RGB space. Initial RGB error 0.43 ± 0.12 reduced to 0.004 ± 0.001 at convergence (within 50 iterations). Strengths: Robust to imperfect reflectance estimation due to shadow inclusion; does not require explicit separation of specular/diffuse components or image segmentation. Limitations: Requires a differentiable renderer; performance depends on the quality of the initial geometry and material estimates. When to Use: When estimating light source position/intensity from a single RGBD image with known geometry and materials. When recovering camera pose or material colors from a target photograph. When Not to Use: When the scene geometry is unknown and cannot be estimated beforehand, or when real-time performance is critical and differentiable ray tracing is too slow. Inverse rendering was introduced as a method to recover latent scene parameters (camera pose, light placement, surface color) that produce a given target photograph by formulating the problem as an unconstrained optimization task using gradients from the rendering pipeline. The specific application of robust point light source estimation using differentiable rendering with cast shadows was proposed to address the common practical case of imperfect reflectance estimation. The method has been applied to mixed reality applications, such as inserting virtual objects consistently lit into real video or photographs. It has also been used in dynamic ocean inverse modeling to extract imaging parameters like illumination and sea colors. name: Inverse Rendering with Shape Prior
head: RenderNet EC-Deep, RenderNet Inverse Rendering with Shape Prior, RenderNet with 3D Auto-Encoder Prior
body: This method reconstructs 3D geometry, texture, pose, and lighting from a single image by optimizing a latent representation of a pre-trained 3D auto-encoder decoder, regularizing the reconstruction to prevent noisy results. Unlike DC-IGN which learns a disentangled graphics code Z for manipulation, RenderNet explicitly reconstructs 3D geometry, pose, lighting, and texture, allowing for higher resolution (512x512 vs 150x150) and better control in out-of-plane rotation and re-texturing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A single observed image I. Outputs: Reconstructed 3D geometry, texture (albedo), pose parameters, and lighting parameters. Data Structures: Latent Shape Vector (z^0): A vector in the latent space of the pre-trained 3D auto-encoder. Network Parameters (\theta): Parameters for the differentiable renderer (RenderNet). Latent Texture Vector (\phi^0): A vector in the latent space of the texture decoder. Lighting Parameters (\eta): Parameters defining the lighting environment (e.g., light color, brightness, position/elevation/azimuth). Method Steps: 1. Initialize Optimization Variables: Initialize the latent shape vector z^0, network parameters \theta, latent texture vector \phi^0, and lighting parameters \eta. 2. Generate Geometry: Pass the latent shape vector z^0 through the decoder g of the pre-trained 3D auto-encoder to generate the shape geometry g(z^0). This step regularizes the reconstructed shape by using the prior shape knowledge (weights in the decoder) for shape generation. 3. Generate Texture: Pass the latent texture vector \phi^0 through the decoder h (trained with RenderNet for texture rendering) to generate the texture representation h(\phi^0). This regularizes the texture variable. 4. Render Image: Use the differentiable renderer f with the generated geometry g(z^0), texture h(\phi^0), pose, and lighting parameters \eta to render the synthetic image. 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the L2 norm between the observed image I and the rendered image. 6. Optimize: Minimize the objective function with respect to z^0, \theta, \phi^0, and \eta. Objective Function: The objective function to minimize is: \min{z^0, \theta, \phi^0, \eta} \| I - f(g(z^0), \theta, h(\phi^0), \eta) \|2^2 where: I is the observed image. f is the differentiable renderer. g is the decoder of the 3D auto-encoder. h is the decoder trained with RenderNet for texture rendering. z^0 is the latent shape vector. \phi^0 is the latent texture vector. \eta represents the lighting parameters. \theta represents the network parameters of the renderer. This corresponds to MAP estimation, where the prior term is the shape decoder and the likelihood term is given by RenderNet. Parameters: Resolution: 512x512. Auto-Encoder Size: The pre-trained 3D auto-encoder was trained with 80,000 shapes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Directly minimizing the loss without the shape prior often leads to noisy, unstable results. The method is straightforward to extend to multi-view reconstruction by summing over multiple per-image losses with shared shape and appearance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inverserenderingwithshapeprior(observedimage, pretrainedshapedecoderg, pretrainedtexturedecoderh, differentiablerendererf, learningrate=0.01, maxiterations=10000): # Initialize optimization variables z0 = torch.zeros(latentdimshape) # theta = torch.zeros(rendererparamdim) # phi0 = torch.zeros(latentdimtexture) # eta = torch.zeros(lightingparamdim) # for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Generate geometry from latent shape vector using pre-trained decoder geometry = pretrainedshapedecoderg(z0) # Generate texture from latent texture vector using pre-trained decoder texture = pretrainedtexturedecoderh(phi0) # Render image using differentiable renderer with geometry, texture, pose, and lighting renderedimage = differentiablerendererf(geometry, theta, texture, eta) # Compute L2 loss between observed and rendered image loss = torch.sum((observedimage - renderedimage) 2) # Compute gradients and update variables gradients = computegradients(loss, [z0, theta, phi0, eta]) z0 = z0 - learningrate gradients[0] theta = theta - learningrate gradients[1] phi0 = phi0 - learningrate gradients[2] eta = eta - learningrate gradients[3] return geometry, texture, eta def computegradients(loss, variables): # Standard automatic differentiation to compute partial derivatives return [torch.autograd.grad(loss, var, retaingraph=True)[0] for var in variables] Performance: On the face dataset, the Intersection-over-Union (IOU) between the ground truth and reconstructed voxel grid is 42.99 ± 0.64 for a 95% confidence interval. Strengths: Explicit reconstruction creates sharper images with higher levels of detail in novel-view prediction. It provides more control in relighting (light color, brightness, position) and re-texturing tasks. Limitations: Direct minimization without regularization leads to noisy results. When to use: When high-resolution (512x512) reconstruction, explicit 3D geometry, and detailed control over lighting and texture are required, particularly for tasks like out-of-plane rotation and re-texturing. This method is part of the RenderNet architecture, used for novel-view synthesis, relighting, and generalization tasks. It builds on the concept of using a pre-trained 3D auto-encoder as a shape prior, similar to the TL-embedding network. name: Differentiable Inverse Graphics Framework
head: Analysis-by-synthesis with differentiable rendering, Differentiable Inverse Rendering for Joint Reconstruction, End-to-end differentiable inverse graphics, Inverse parameter optimization pipeline, Joint geometry and reflectance reconstruction
body: The Differentiable Inverse Graphics Framework simultaneously reconstructs 3D geometry, diffuse/specular reflectance, and environment lighting from multi-view photography by minimizing photometric error in a differentiable rendering pipeline. It solves the inverse problem of inferring latent scene parameters from observed images by treating the renderer as a differentiable function that maps parameters to pixels, enabling gradient-based optimization. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on fixed priors or specific rendering backends, this framework provides a general analysis-by-synthesis loop where the rendering equation is implemented in the forward pass and loss gradients are backpropagated to update geometry, materials, and lighting. It sets itself apart by explicitly handling the joint optimization of geometry, BRDF parameters, and lighting sources using a physically-based Monte Carlo path tracer (Mitsuba2) with alternating parameter updates to manage memory constraints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of RGB images I = \{Ik\} from arbitrary viewpoints k=1 \dots K. Output: Optimized scene parameters \theta = \{\thetag, \thetad, \thetas, \thetal\} representing geometry, diffuse reflectance, specular reflectance, and lighting. Data Structures: The scene is represented by a parametric vector \theta: \thetag: Set of 3D positions corresponding to mesh vertices \{x0, \dots, xN\}. \thetad: Set of diffuse per-vertex color reflectances \{\thetad(x0), \dots, \thetad(xN)\}, where \thetad(x) \in \mathbb{R}^3. \thetas: Set of specular reflectance parameters (e.g., roughness \alpha). \thetal: Set of isotropic point sources for environment lighting \{l0, l1, \dots, lM\}, where ln is the intensity of the n-th light source. Formulas: The image formation for a pixel at coordinate u is: I(u) = L(\boldsymbol{\omega}o; x) \Delta t where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the 3D coordinate, \boldsymbol{\omega}o is the outgoing direction, and \Delta t is the camera exposure time. The radiance Lo from a non-emitting surface point x is given by the rendering equation: Lo(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = Le(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) + \int{\Omega} fr(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) Li(x, \boldsymbol{\omega}i) (\boldsymbol{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i) \, d\boldsymbol{\omega}i where Le is emitted radiance, fr is the BRDF, Li is incoming radiance, \boldsymbol{n} is the surface normal, and \Omega is the hemisphere of incoming directions. The environment lighting is approximated as a set of isotropic point sources, and ray tracing iterates up to a maximum bounce count T. The optimization minimizes the objective function: \mathcal{O} = \sum{k=1}^K \| Mk Ik - \Phik(\thetag, \thetad, \thetas, \thetal) \|2^2 where \Phik is the differentiable renderer for view k, and Mk is a binary mask. The general loss formulation includes regularization: \mathcal{L}(\theta) = \| I{\text{obs}} - R(\theta) \|^2 + \lambda{g}\, \text{GeomReg}(\theta) + \lambda{m}\, \text{MatReg}(\theta) + \dots where R(\theta) is the rendered image and \lambdag, \lambdam are regularization weights. Parameters: T: Maximum number of ray bounces. Value: 3. spp: Samples per pixel. Value: 1 for iterative optimization, 16 for final output. \alpha: Surface roughness parameter. Value: 0.1. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rates (example): \lambdad = 0.1, \lambdag = 0.5, \lambdas = 0.01, \lambdal = 0.05. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the virtual scene parameters roughly matching the real world using Structure-from-Motion (e.g., Colmap) to estimate initial geometry and camera poses. 2. Masking: Generate a precomputed binary mask Mk for each view using segmentation (e.g., GrabCut) to remove background pixel contribution from the objective calculation. 3. Alternating Optimization: Iteratively update one parameter set \theta \in \{\thetad, \thetag, \thetas, \thetal\} while keeping others unchanged to manage GPU memory. 4. Forward Pass: For the current parameter set, render the image \hat{I} = \Phi(\theta) using a differentiable path tracer (e.g., Mitsuba2). 5. Loss Computation: Compute the photometric error \mathcal{L} = \| Mk Ik - \hat{I} \|2^2. 6. Backward Pass: Compute gradients \nabla\theta \mathcal{L} via automatic differentiation through the renderer. 7. Update: Update \theta using the Adam optimizer. 8. Repeat: Steps 3-7 until convergence or maximum iterations (e.g., 400 iterations per viewpoint). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def differentiableinversegraphics(images, masks, initialgeometry): """ Reconstructs geometry, reflectance, and lighting from images. images: List of RGB images Ik masks: List of binary masks Mk initialgeometry: Initial mesh vertices from Colmap """ # Initialize parameters thetag = initialgeometry.vertices thetad = randomuniformcolor(len(thetag)) thetas = {"roughness": 0.1} thetal = [0.5] 10 # Initial light intensities optimizer = Adam([thetag, thetad, thetas, thetal], lr=0.01) # Hyperparameters maxiterations = 400 maxbounces = 3 sppopt = 1 for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Alternate optimization: update one parameter set at a time # Update Geometry optimizer.zerograd() renderedimg = render(thetag, thetad, thetas, thetal, spp=sppopt, bounces=maxbounces) loss = sum((mask (img - renderedimg))2 for img, mask in zip(images, masks)) loss.backward() optimizer.step(thetag) # Update Diffuse Reflectance optimizer.zerograd() renderedimg = render(thetag, thetad, thetas, thetal, spp=sppopt, bounces=maxbounces) loss = sum((mask (img - renderedimg))2 for img, mask in zip(images, masks)) loss.backward() optimizer.step(thetad) # Update Specular Reflectance optimizer.zerograd() renderedimg = render(thetag, thetad, thetas, thetal, spp=sppopt, bounces=maxbounces) loss = sum((mask (img - renderedimg))2 for img, mask in zip(images, masks)) loss.backward() optimizer.step(thetas) # Update Lighting optimizer.zerograd() renderedimg = render(thetag, thetad, thetas, thetal, spp=sppopt, bounces=maxbounces) loss = sum((mask (img - renderedimg))2 for img, mask in zip(images, masks)) loss.backward() optimizer.step(thetal) return thetag, thetad, thetas, thetal def render(thetag, thetad, thetas, thetal, spp, bounces): """ Differentiable rendering using Mitsuba2. """ # Construct scene from parameters scene = Scene(vertices=thetag, diffuse=thetad, specular=thetas, lights=thetal) # Render with specified samples and bounces image = scene.render(spp=spp, maxbounces=bounces) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Background Dominance: Background pixels can dominate the objective value. Solution: Use precomputed binary masks Mk from GrabCut segmentation. GPU Memory: Limited GPU memory prevents simultaneous optimization of all parameters. Solution: Alternate between updating each parameter set while keeping others unchanged. Visibility Discontinuities: Silhouette edges cause gradient issues. Handled by MC edge sampling, area-sampling, or thin-band relaxed indicators. Precision: Using spp=1 during optimization reduces variance but increases noise; spp=16 is used for final output. A raytracing-based differentiable renderer that uses a Volumetric Spherical Gaussian (VSG) lighting representation and predicted intrinsic properties (albedo, normals, depth) to re-render an input image, enforcing an energy-conserving image formation process. It provides supervision via re-rendering error, ensuring that predicted geometry and reflectance are physically correct by enforcing that the input image should be retrieved if the predictions are re-rendered. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by enabling the estimation of a complete continuous light field function, including HDR and high-frequency spatial and angular details, despite being trained with only LDR images. Physically Based Differentiable Rendering (PBDR) is a rendering approach that differentiates through physically based integrators, such as path tracing, to preserve derivatives of light transport operations. It solves the inverse rendering problem by enabling gradient-based optimization to estimate latent 3D scene parameters (geometry, materials, lighting) from observed images. Unlike rasterization-based differentiable renderers, PBDR preserves the physical accuracy of the rendering equation, allowing for the optimization of complex material properties and lighting conditions. The Differentiable Uncalibrated Imaging Framework addresses the problem of image reconstruction when the measurement coordinates (e.g., sensor locations, projection angles) are uncertain or the system is out of calibration. It formulates the problem as measurement interpolation at unknown nodes, supervised by the forward operator, by jointly optimizing a continuous measurement representation and the uncertain coordinates. Unlike methods that fine-tune a neural network for unknown coordinates or train on a family of operators, this framework reevaluates measurements via a continuous representation for a single example, avoiding the need for fine-tuning or handling distributional tradeoffs. It builds on Differentiable Inverse Graphics Framework by introducing a specific mechanism for handling coordinate uncertainty through joint optimization of representation parameters and input coordinates. A pipeline where an image is encoded into a discrete scene program (geometry, materials, arrangements) via an encoder and LLM/programmatic decoder, which is then rendered by any downstream renderer. Training is performed purely on code or numeric losses, not image losses, allowing the discrete scene program to be optimized. The pipeline flow is: I \xrightarrow{\Phi} E \xrightarrow{f\theta} (s1,..., sN) \xrightarrow{h} S, where I is input image, E is encoded representation, f\theta generates scene tokens/parameters si, and h renders scene program S. Time Complexity: ~140ms per iteration. Total iterations: 400 per viewpoint. Memory Complexity: High, due to GPU memory constraints of physically-based rendering. Mitigated by alternating parameter updates and downsampling images 8x. Performance: Physics-based MC approaches achieve low reconstruction errors (RE≈0.0087 vs Mitsuba's 0.0102) and normal MAE of 9.81° with sparse Gaussian basis. Point-based splatting and hybrid methods achieve PSNR 38–43 dB and normal MAE ≈4–11°. Strengths: Enables photo-realistic novel view synthesis, environment light editing, and joint reconstruction of geometry and reflectance. Handles complex geometry and various reflection types. Limitations: Computationally expensive. Limited to scenes that can be approximated by the parametric model (mesh + point lights). Sensitive to initialization. When to use: When high-fidelity reconstruction of geometry, materials, and lighting from multi-view images is required, and computational resources are available. When not to use: For real-time applications or when only geometry is needed without material/lighting details. The Differentiable Inverse Graphics Framework originates from the work of Li et al. (2021), who proposed an efficient method to reconstruct scene 3D geometry and reflectance from multi-view photography using conventional hand-held cameras. The method automatically builds a virtual scene in a differentiable rendering system (Mitsuba2) that roughly matches the real world's scene parameters, optimized by minimizing photometric objectives alternatingly and stochastically. It builds on the principles of analysis-by-synthesis and differentiable rendering, extending them to joint optimization of geometry, BRDF, and lighting. The framework has been implemented in Mitsuba2 differentiable renderer. Initial geometry is typically obtained from Colmap.
