name: Image-Based Rendering for Volume Surfaces
head: Image-based framework, Image-based volume rendering with keyview caching, Keyview IBR, Keyview-based rendering, Surface IBR
body: Image-Based Rendering (IBR) for Volume Surfaces is an acceleration technique that caches a fully volume-rendered view (the keyview) and reuses it for novel views by texture-mapping it to a geometric iso-surface model, only ray-casting newly visible regions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Temporal Differential Rendering by explicitly constructing an intermediate geometric surface to project the cached image, rather than relying solely on pixel-space reprojection or buffer accumulation. This approach is particularly effective for large static volumes where camera motion is incremental, such as in virtual colon navigation. The method reduces computational cost by reusing a previously rendered image for the majority of the screen, leveraging temporal coherence between adjacent frames. Inputs: V: A 3D volume dataset. T: A transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity. C{key}: The camera pose of the cached keyview. C{novel}: The camera pose of the current novel view. I{key}: The fully volume-rendered image buffer from the keyview. Outputs: I{novel}: The rendered image for the novel view. 1. Iso-Surface Model (M): A geometric mesh representing the iso-surface extracted from V. Iso-value (v{iso}): Derived from the transfer function T. Generation: Extracted using a levels-of-detail algorithm optimized for regular volumes. 2. Keyview Cache: Image (I{key}): A 2D texture buffer containing the color/opacity data from the previous full render. Camera Pose (C{key}): Stored to compute the transformation to the novel view. 1. Iso-Surface Extraction: Construct the geometric model M from volume V using the iso-value v{iso} deduced from T. 2. Keyview Rendering: If no keyview exists, perform a full volume render of V using camera C{key} to generate I{key}. 3. Texture Mapping: Projectively texture-map the image I{key} onto the geometric model M. The source notes the use of backward and forward processing orders for high-quality texture mapping. 4. Novel View Projection: Render the textured model M using the novel camera pose C{novel}. 5. Identify Newly Visible Regions: Determine which pixels in the novel view correspond to volume data that was occluded or hidden in the keyview but is now visible. 6. Ray Casting for New Regions: For each pixel in the newly visible regions, cast a ray through the volume V using the novel camera C{novel}. 7. Composite Image: Initialize I{novel} with the projected image, then replace the pixel values in the newly visible regions with the results from the ray casting step. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rendernovelview(volume, transferfunction, keyviewimage, keyviewcamera, novelcamera, isovalue): """ Renders a novel view using Image-Based Rendering for Volume Surfaces. """ # Step 1: Extract iso-surface model M from volume V using isovalue # Source does not specify the exact extraction algorithm; standard LOD/marching cubes meshvertices, meshfaces = extractisosurface(volume, isovalue) # Step 2: Texture map keyview image onto mesh M # Source mentions backward/forward processing orders but not exact implementation texturedmesh = texturemapmesh(meshvertices, meshfaces, keyviewimage, keyviewcamera) # Step 3: Project textured mesh to novel view camera # Rasterization produces a depth buffer and a color buffer projectedcolor, projecteddepth = rasterizemesh(texturedmesh, novelcamera) # Step 4: Identify newly visible pixels # Compare depth of M in novel view against keyview visibility # Pixels where novel depth < projected depth are newly visible newpixelmask = identifynewlyvisiblepixels(projecteddepth, keyviewcamera, novelcamera) # Step 5: Ray cast only the new pixels newcolors = np.zeroslike(projectedcolor) for u, v in np.argwhere(newpixelmask): rayorigin, raydirection = computeray(novelcamera, u, v) color = volumeraycast(volume, transferfunction, rayorigin, raydirection) newcolors[u, v] = color # Step 6: Composite result novelviewimage = projectedcolor.copy() novelviewimage[newpixelmask] = newcolors[newpixelmask] return novelviewimage def extractisosurface(volume, isovalue): """Returns (vertices, faces) for the iso-surface at isovalue.""" # Standard implementation omitted for brevity; returns mesh data return np.array([]), np.array([]) def texturemapmesh(vertices, faces, keyviewimage, camera): """Projects keyviewimage onto vertices using camera projection.""" # Assigns texture coordinates to vertices based on keyview projection return {"vertices": vertices, "faces": faces, "texcoords": np.zeroslike(vertices)} def rasterizemesh(mesh, camera): """Renders textured mesh to screen, returning color and depth buffers.""" # Standard GPU rasterization logic return np.zeros((100, 100, 3)), np.zeros((100, 100)) def identifynewlyvisiblepixels(depthbuffer, keyviewcamera, novelcamera): """Returns boolean mask of pixels requiring new ray casting.""" # Compares visibility between keyview and novel view return np.ones((100, 100), dtype=bool) def computeray(camera, u, v): """Computes ray origin and direction from camera and pixel coordinates.""" return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]), np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) def volumeraycast(volume, transferfunction, origin, direction): """Performs standard volume integration along the ray.""" # Standard ray marching implementation return np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]) Volume Size: The method targets large volumes, specifically those over 1024^3 where traditional rendering is too slow. It has been successfully tested on 512^3 datasets. Camera Motion: The method assumes small camera movements between frames. Fallback: If the camera motion is too large, the newly visible region may cover the entire image, negating the speedup. In such cases, fall back to a full volume render and update the keyview cache. Time Complexity: The cost is proportional to the number of pixels in newly visible regions multiplied by the average ray length through the volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, the surface model, and the keyview image buffer. Performance: Provides an average speedup of an order of magnitude (10x) over traditional volume rendering. Achieves interactive frame rates for 512^3 datasets in virtual colon navigation. Strengths: Significant reduction in ray casting operations when camera motion is small; leverages existing hardware rasterization for the bulk of the image. Limitations: Requires construction and maintenance of a geometric iso-surface model; quality depends on the accuracy of the iso-surface approximation; not suitable for highly dynamic volumes or large camera jumps. The method was proposed in the context of interactive volume rendering for large biomedical and geoscience datasets. It was introduced by Baoquan Chen in a dissertation and subsequent Eurographics 2001 paper. The work addresses the computational bottleneck of ray casting large volumes by exploiting temporal coherence between adjacent frames in navigation sequences. It extends the concept of image-based rendering from surface models to volumetric data by using an intermediate iso-surface representation. name: Temporal Differential Rendering
head: Dirty-brick partial re-render, Dirty-row flush
body: Temporal differential rendering reduces per-frame computational cost by skipping the rendering of screen regions that have not changed since the previous frame. It solves the problem of redundant ray-marching or shading work in dynamic scenes where only small portions of the volume or camera view update between iterations. Unlike Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation, which blends historical buffers to reduce noise, this method performs a binary check for change and completely bypasses the rendering pipeline for clean regions, offering higher fidelity at the cost of strict temporal consistency requirements. The method operates by maintaining a representation of the previous frame's state and comparing it against the current frame to identify "dirty" regions. Two primary implementations exist: tile-based dirty-brick tracking for GPU-accelerated volume rendering and row-based hashing for CPU-based or console rendering. Inputs: Current frame data: Volume state, camera parameters, or canvas content. Previous frame data: Rendered buffer, hash values, or dirty region masks. Change indicators: Physics updates, user edits, or camera movement vectors. Outputs: Rendered image for dirty regions only. Updated previous frame buffer/hash state. 1. Dirty Region Map: A boolean or integer array mapping screen tiles (e.g., 8×8 pixels) or rows to their dirty status. 2. Previous Frame Buffer: A texture or array storing the color/opacity values from the previous frame for comparison or fallback. 3. Hash Table (Row-based): An array of hash values, one per row, used to detect changes in console/ASCII rendering. This variant, described in, projects dirty bricks (from physics or edits) into screen tiles. 1. Dirty Brick Projection: On the CPU, identify bricks that have changed due to physics, edits, or camera movement. Project these bricks into 8×8 screen tiles to mark them as "dirty". 2. Tile Hashing/Check: For each 8×8 tile, determine if it contains any dirty bricks. If a tile is clean, mark it as "unchanged". 3. Early-Out: In the compute shader, check the tile status. If the tile is clean, skip the ray-marching and shading steps for all pixels in that tile. 4. Rendering: For dirty tiles, perform the standard rendering pass (e.g., distance LOD, DDA traversal). 5. Update State: Update the dirty tile map for the next frame based on new changes. This variant, described in, uses per-row hashing to detect changes in a character canvas. 1. Initialization: Initialize the previous canvas buffer and row hash array. Set FNV offset constant H{offset} = 2166136261u and FNV prime constant H{prime} = 16777619u. 2. Dimension Check: If the current canvas dimensions differ from the previous buffer dimensions, reinitialize the previous buffers to match. 3. Row Hashing: For each row y from 0 to H-1: Initialize hash h = H{offset}. For each column x from 0 to W-1: Get character ch = \text{canvas}[y, x]. Update hash: h = (h \oplus \text{ushort}(ch)) \times H{prime}. Get color string col = \text{colors}[y, x]. Get color hash colId = \text{col} \text{ is null } ? 0: \text{RuntimeHelpers.GetHashCode}(col). Update hash: h = (h \oplus \text{uint}(colId)) \times H{prime}. Store h as \text{rowHash}[y]. 4. Change Detection: Compare \text{rowHash}[y] with \text{prevRowHash}[y]. If they are equal, the row is clean; skip rendering for this row. 5. Flush Dirty Rows: If the row is dirty: Initialize a string builder for ANSI escape sequences. Append cursor move sequence: \x1b[{y+1};1H. For each column x from 0 to W-1: Get color col = \text{colors}[y, x]. If col \neq \text{lastColor}, append color code (or reset code if null) to builder. Set \text{lastColor} = col. Get character ch = \text{canvas}[y, x]. Append ch (or space if null) to builder. Write the accumulated string to the console. 6. Update State: Copy current canvas and colors to previous buffers. Update \text{prevRowHash}[y] with the new hash. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FNVOFFSET = 2166136261 FNVPRIME = 16777619 def computerowhash(canvasrow, colorsrow): """Compute FNV-1a hash for a single row.""" h = FNVOFFSET for x in range(len(canvasrow)): ch = canvasrow[x] # Convert char to ushort (assuming ASCII/UTF-16 compatible) chval = ord(ch) if ch else 0 h ^= chval h = FNVPRIME col = colorsrow[x] # Get hash of color string; 0 if null colid = hash(col) if col is not None else 0 h ^= colid h = FNVPRIME return h def temporaldifferentialrender(canvas, colors, prevcanvas, prevcolors, prevrowhashes, width, height): """ Render only dirty rows using temporal differential rendering. canvas: 2D array of characters [height][width] colors: 2D array of color strings [height][width] prevcanvas: 2D array of previous characters prevcolors: 2D array of previous colors prevrowhashes: 1D array of previous row hashes """ # Check dimensions if len(canvas) != len(prevcanvas) or len(canvas[0]) != len(prevcanvas[0]): prevcanvas = [[None for in range(width)] for in range(height)] prevcolors = [[None for in range(width)] for in range(height)] prevrowhashes = [0] height outputlines = [] anywrites = False for y in range(height): # Compute current row hash currenthash = computerowhash(canvas[y], colors[y]) # Check if row changed if currenthash == prevrowhashes[y]: # Row is clean, skip rendering continue # Row is dirty, render it anywrites = True linebuffer = [] # Move cursor to start of row (1-based indexing for ANSI) linebuffer.append(f"\x1b[{y+1};1H") lastcolor = None for x in range(width): col = colors[y][x] if col != lastcolor: if col is None: linebuffer.append("\x1b[0m") # Reset else: linebuffer.append(col) # Assume col is ANSI code lastcolor = col ch = canvas[y][x] if ch == '\0': ch = ' ' linebuffer.append(ch) outputlines.append("".join(linebuffer)) # Update previous state prevcanvas[y] = canvas[y][:] prevcolors[y] = colors[y][:] prevrowhashes[y] = currenthash if anywrites: print("".join(outputlines)) else: # No changes, could skip entirely or just copy buffers pass Tile Size: 8×8 pixels is used in. Hash Constants: FNV-1a offset 2166136261u and prime 16777619u are used in. Safety Margin: A 16-voxel safety margin is used in the distance LOD pass to prevent popping artifacts when fast-forwarding rays. Precision: Hash collisions are possible but rare with FNV-1a. In high-contrast scenes, false positives (rendering clean rows) are acceptable; false negatives (skipping dirty rows) cause visual artifacts. Boundaries: Dimension mismatches between frames require buffer reinitialization. Degenerate Input: Empty rows or null characters must be handled explicitly to avoid hash mismatches. A variant where a partial volume rendering pass is performed between visibility detection passes to update occluding data with newly loaded bricks. The frequency of total scene rendering must be chosen carefully as it is expensive. Future work suggests storing ray state (position, direction, hierarchy position, DDA state) in image space buffers for progressive rendering resumption. A heuristic to prevent flicker in static regions by freezing primitives whose bounding boxes do not intersect the inter-frame difference mask D. For each primitive i, if Bi \cap \text{support}(D) = \emptyset, set \text{freeze}i = 1. Only primitives with \text{freeze}i = 0 are updated during optimization, preventing spurious updates in static areas. The specific implementation using per-row FNV hashing to detect changes in console/ASCII rendering, as detailed in the main algorithm. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of dirty tiles/rows. Clean regions are skipped entirely, reducing effective work to O(D) where D is the number of dirty regions. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for storing previous frame buffers and hash arrays. Performance: In scenes with high temporal coherence, performance scales linearly with the number of changes. In static scenes, rendering cost approaches zero. Strengths: Eliminates redundant computation; high fidelity (no temporal blending artifacts); simple implementation. Limitations: Requires strict temporal consistency; cannot handle large camera movements or scene changes without full re-render; hash collisions may cause artifacts. When to Use: Dynamic scenes with small, localized changes (e.g., voxel games, fluid simulations). When Not to Use: Scenes with large, global changes or high-frequency noise where temporal accumulation is more appropriate. Temporal differential rendering originated in the context of voxel-based real-time rendering and console-based graphics. The dirty-brick approach was implemented in the voxelG project by mstampfli, leveraging GPU compute shaders for efficient tile-based culling. The dirty-row hashing approach was developed for console canvas rendering in csRaymarching by 0gecco, using FNV hashing for efficient row-level change detection. The concept of partial updates and freezing for flicker reduction has also been explored in differentiable rendering of bitmap primitives (DiffBMP) and procedural volume exploration. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) 0gecco/csRaymarching, https://github.com/0gecco/csRaymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Représentation et algorithmes pour l'exploration interactive de volumes procéduraux étendus et détaillés, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00598406v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DiffBMP: Differentiable Rendering with Bitmap Primitives, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2602.22625, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation
head: Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) via reprojection
body: Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation stabilizes voxel and volume rendering over time by blending the current frame's color with an accumulated color buffer from the previous frame, using camera motion vectors to align pixels. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by operating directly on the final radiance image in screen space, leveraging temporal coherence to reduce noise and aliasing without requiring per-voxel state caching or complex model coefficient tracking. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current frame color (colourattachment), current frame world position (positionattachment), previous frame accumulated color (accumulationattachment), camera transformation matrices (traceuniforms.lastcamera), and control uniforms (reprojectionfactor, indirectlighting). Outputs: Final output color for the current pixel. Data Structures: colourattachment: texture2d<f32>, binding 3. Stores the current frame's computed color. positionattachment: texturestorage2d<rgba32float, readwrite>, binding 3. Stores the world-space position for each pixel, used for reprojection. accumulationattachment: texturestorage2d<rgba16float, readwrite>, binding 1. Stores the temporally accumulated color from previous frames. Algorithm Steps: 1. Load Current State: Read the current frame's color C{curr} from colourattachment at sample position (u, v) and the world position P{curr} from positionattachment at (u, v). 2. Check Reprojection Conditions: If indirectlighting is zero or reprojectionfactor \le 0.0, skip reprojection and output C{curr} directly. 3. Compute Local Bounds (Edge Detection): To prevent ghosting across edges, compute local color bounds using C{curr} and its 8 immediate neighbors (C0 to C8) in a 3x3 grid. Calculate the 'plus' bounds (cross pattern: center, top, bottom, left, right) and 'square' bounds (full 3x3). Compute C{min} and C{max} as the average of the minimums and maximums of the 'plus' and 'square' bounds respectively. 4. Reproject Position: Transform P{curr} into the previous frame's clip space using traceuniforms.lastcamera. 5. Convert to Texture Coordinates: Convert the clip space coordinates to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) range [-1, 1], then map to texture coordinates (u{prev}, v{prev}) for the accumulationattachment. 6. Validate Projection: If the projected coordinates are outside the NDC range [-1, 1] (indicating the pixel is newly visible or occluded), the history sample is invalid. Skip blending and output C{curr}. 7. Fetch History: Load the accumulated color C{hist} from accumulationattachment at (u{prev}, v{prev}). 8. Blend: Compute the mixed color C{mix} using the reprojectionfactor \alpha: C{mix} = C{curr} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha) + C{hist} \cdot \alpha 9. Clamp: Clamp C{mix} to the local bounds [C{min}, C{max}] to prevent bleeding across high-frequency details or edges. 10. Output: Return C{mix} as the final color. Accumulation Step: After the reprojection pass, a separate accumulation shader stores the final output color of the current frame into accumulationattachment for use in the next frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reprojectionpass(u, v, colourattachment, positionattachment, accumulationattachment, lastcamera, reprojectionfactor, indirectlighting): # 1. Load current state Ccurr = colourattachment[u, v] Pcurr = positionattachment[u, v] # 2. Check conditions if indirectlighting == 0 or reprojectionfactor <= 0.0: return Ccurr # 3. Compute local bounds # Get 3x3 neighborhood colors neighbors = [colourattachment[u+du, v+dv] for du in [-1, 0, 1] for dv in [-1, 0, 1]] # Plus pattern indices: center(4), top(1), bottom(7), left(3), right(5) plusindices = [4, 1, 7, 3, 5] squareindices = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8] plusmin = min(neighbors[i] for i in plusindices) plusmax = max(neighbors[i] for i in plusindices) squaremin = min(neighbors[i] for i in squareindices) squaremax = max(neighbors[i] for i in squareindices) Cmin = (plusmin + squaremin) / 2.0 Cmax = (plusmax + squaremax) / 2.0 # 4. Reproject position # Transform Pcurr to previous frame clip space Pclip = lastcamera.transformpoint(Pcurr) # 5. Convert to NDC and texture coordinates # Assuming perspective projection, divide by w if Pclip.w == 0: return Ccurr ndcx = Pclip.x / Pclip.w ndcy = Pclip.y / Pclip.w # Map NDC [-1, 1] to texture coordinates [0, 1] uprev = (ndcx + 1.0) / 2.0 vprev = (ndcy + 1.0) / 2.0 # 6. Validate projection if not (0.0 <= uprev <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= vprev <= 1.0): return Ccurr # 7. Fetch history Chist = accumulationattachment[uprev, vprev] # 8. Blend alpha = reprojectionfactor Cmix = Ccurr (1.0 - alpha) + Chist alpha # 9. Clamp to local bounds Cfinal = clamp(Cmix, Cmin, Cmax) # 10. Output return Cfinal def accumulationpass(u, v, outputcolor, accumulationattachment): accumulationattachment[u, v] = outputcolor Parameters: reprojectionfactor: Float uniform controlling the blend weight between current and accumulated frames. Typical values are between 0.0 and 1.0. If \le 0.0, reprojection is skipped. indirectlighting: Unsigned integer uniform. Reprojection is only performed if this value is non-zero. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Projection: If the projected previous position is outside the NDC range [-1, 1], the pixel is considered invalid (e.g., newly visible or occluded) and must not be blended with the accumulation buffer to avoid ghosting. Edge Bleeding: Without local bound clamping, blending across object boundaries causes "ghosting" artifacts where colors from adjacent objects bleed into each other over time. Temporal Reprojection for Linear Models exploits temporal coherence by reprojecting linear model coefficients and features rather than raw pixel colors, allowing the model to react immediately to abrupt changes in camera, light, or transfer functions. Unlike standard temporal reprojection which caches constant values per pixel, this method uses linear regression to predict gradual changes while maintaining robustness against sudden shading variations, thereby avoiding the need for Monte Carlo (MC) integration resets. Temporal Gradient Denoising is a technique that reduces noise in volume rendering by applying temporal reprojection and blending to gradient images rather than the final radiance image. It solves the problem of high noise levels in Monte Carlo volume rendering, particularly in high-order scattering-dominant media, while avoiding the visible bias and artifacts that occur when denoising the original image directly. It sets itself apart from standard temporal accumulation by operating on the derivative of the radiance with respect to a source parameter (albedo), leveraging the fact that denoising artifacts in the gradient domain are not directly visible in the final color. Alpha-Max Quasi-Depth Motion Vector is a method to compute screen-space motion vectors for direct volume rendering (DVR) by using the 3D position of the point with maximum alpha along the ray as a proxy for depth, enabling temporal reprojection despite the lack of a single surface depth value. For each pixel at current frame coordinates (u, v), it identifies the point p in world space where the alpha value is maximum along the ray passing through the volume. It then reprojects p back to the previous frame's coordinate system using previous camera transformation matrices to obtain coordinates (u', v'). The screen-space motion vector is calculated as the difference between (u, v) and (u', v'). This heuristic provides an acceptable approximation for motion vector estimation because the point of maximum alpha has the maximum contribution to the final accumulated sample. Frame Averaging at Rest is a post-processing technique where, when the camera stops, consecutive frames are averaged with tiny sub-pixel offsets so the image settles into a clean still. It involves detecting camera stop and then averaging frames with tiny sub-pixel offsets to refine the image quality during static periods. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel per frame, as it involves a constant number of texture lookups, arithmetic operations, and a single matrix transformation per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the accumulation buffer, where W and H are the screen dimensions. The accumulationattachment typically uses rgba16float to balance precision and memory usage. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with screen resolution. The method is highly parallelizable on GPUs due to its per-pixel nature. Strengths: Effectively reduces temporal noise and aliasing; simple to implement as a post-processing pass; robust against minor camera jitter. Limitations: Prone to ghosting artifacts if motion vectors are inaccurate or if objects move rapidly; requires accurate position buffers for reprojection; clamping can introduce slight blurring at edges. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering where temporal stability is desired and camera motion is relatively smooth. When Not to Use: Scenes with rapid, large-scale object movement or significant disocclusions where ghosting is unacceptable without complex history management. Reprojection with Temporal Accumulation is a technique used in voxel and volume rendering to stabilize images over time. It is closely related to Temporal Anti-Aliasing (TAA) used in rasterization. The method leverages the correlation between consecutive frames to reduce noise and improve visual quality. Variants such as Alpha-Max Quasi-Depth Motion Vector address specific challenges in volume rendering, such as the lack of a single depth value. Frame Averaging at Rest is used in progressive loading scenarios to refine static images. ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, https://github.com/ria8651/bevy-voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Deep Learning Based Super-Resolution for Medical Volume Visualization with Direct Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-20713-68, fetched 2026-10-26 Volume rendering: progressive multiscale loading, sorted compositing, lighting and more from a histotomography fork (2.8 TB volume @ 16bits) - what, if anything, would be worth upstreaming?, https://github.com/google/neuroglancer/issues/1134, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Temporal Reprojection for Linear Models
body: Temporal Reprojection for Linear Models exploits temporal coherence by reprojecting linear model coefficients and features rather than raw pixel colors, allowing the model to react immediately to abrupt changes in camera, light, or transfer functions. Unlike standard temporal reprojection which caches constant values per pixel, this method uses linear regression to predict gradual changes while maintaining robustness against sudden shading variations, thereby avoiding the need for Monte Carlo (MC) integration resets. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current frame's noisy MC estimates \tilde{I}j(t), camera view matrix, per-pixel world coordinates, and the history buffer from the previous frame. Outputs: Denoised color values derived from the linear model, updated feature vectors zj(t), and linear model coefficients. Data Structures: History Buffer: Stores the feature vector zj \in \mathbb{R}^3 for each pixel j. The vector corresponds to pixel color (RGB) and is constructed using all three channels simultaneously to avoid color-shift effects, even though denoising is performed per channel. Linear Model: Maintains coefficients for linear regression at each pixel. The specific coefficient update logic is handled by Weighted Recursive Least Squares (wRLS), which allocates high weights to samples with lower noise variance. Steps: 1. Estimate Velocities: Calculate per-pixel velocity vectors \upsilonj = (\upsilonx, \upsilony) using the camera view matrix and per-pixel world coordinates. 2. Reproject Coordinates: Define the reprojection operation \pi(\upsilonj) to map the current pixel index j to the corresponding coordinate q in the previous frame: q \leftarrow \pi(\upsilonj) = j + \upsilonj If \upsilonj = 0 (e.g., static camera), q = j. 3. Retrieve History: Access the history feature zq(t-1) from the reprojected coordinate q in the previous frame's history buffer. 4. Rectify History (Clamping): Apply the neighborhood clamping operator \Psi[\cdot] to the reprojected history zq(t-1) using the current noisy estimate \tilde{I}j(t). This rectification reduces artifacts caused by stale history data when the scene content has changed. 5. Update Feature Vector: Construct the new feature vector zj(t) by combining the rectified history and the current estimate. The update uses an exponentially weighted history buffer: zj(t) = \alpha \Psi[zq(t-1), \tilde{I}j(t)] + (1 - \alpha)\tilde{I}j(t) where \alpha is a weight controlling the balance between history and the current estimate. 6. Linear Regression: Use the updated feature vector zj(t) as input to the linear model (specifically Weighted RLS) to predict the denoised output. The wRLS variant handles temporally varying noise inherent in DVR images generated with small sample counts. Parameters: \alpha: Exponential decay weight for the history buffer. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but it controls the trade-off between temporal stability and responsiveness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Abrupt Changes: Standard reprojection of pixel colors fails to adapt to changes in lighting or transfer functions. Linear model reprojection reacts immediately to these changes, avoiding MC integration resets. Color Shifts: Denoising is performed per channel, but the feature zj(t) must be constructed using all three color channels simultaneously to avoid undesired color-shift effects. Stale History: Without the clamping operator \Psi[\cdot], reprojected history can introduce artifacts if the underlying scene has changed significantly between frames. A feature vector zj(t) constructed from an exponentially weighted history buffer of MC estimates, used as input to the linear model to provide temporal stability and reduce noise variance. It updates via zj(t) = \alpha\Psi[zq(t-1), \tilde{I}j(t)] + (1-\alpha)\tilde{I}j(t), where \Psi[\cdot] is a neighborhood clamping operator that relies on the current-frame input estimate \tilde{I}j(t) to reduce artifacts from stale history data. It is chosen when temporal stability is required without sacrificing responsiveness to lighting changes. It differs from simple color accumulation by integrating clamping and multi-channel construction to prevent color shifts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method involves per-pixel velocity estimation, reprojection, clamping, and weighted RLS updates. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the history buffer zj \in \mathbb{R}^3 per pixel, in addition to the linear model coefficients. Strengths: Reacts immediately to abrupt changes in shading, lighting, or transfer functions, avoiding MC integration resets. More robust than caching constant values per pixel. Limitations: Requires estimation of per-pixel velocities (optical flow) and additional storage for history buffers. Performance: Demonstrated on real-time VPT. Specific hardware or resolution metrics are not given in the sources. This method was introduced in the context of real-time volumetric path tracing (VPT) for direct volume rendering. It addresses the limitations of conventional temporal reprojection, which reprojects pixel colors and struggles with dynamic scene changes. The approach builds on exponentially weighted history buffers and weighted recursive least squares (wRLS) to handle heterogeneous noise in DVR images. name: Temporal Gradient Denoising
head: Temporal denoising of gradient image, Temporal denoising on gradients
body: Temporal Gradient Denoising is a technique that reduces noise in volume rendering by applying temporal reprojection and blending to gradient images rather than the final radiance image. It solves the problem of high noise levels in Monte Carlo volume rendering, particularly in high-order scattering-dominant media, while avoiding the visible bias and artifacts that occur when denoising the original image directly. It sets itself apart from standard temporal accumulation by operating on the derivative of the radiance with respect to a source parameter (albedo), leveraging the fact that denoising artifacts in the gradient domain are not directly visible in the final color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sequence of rendered gradient images Gk for k \in [0, N-1], where k=0 is the target frame; motion vectors d and velocities vd in screen space; smoothing factor wa; number of frames N; time t. Outputs: A denoised gradient image G{\text{denoised}} for the target frame. Data Structures: Gradient Image: A 2D array of floating-point values representing the gradient of radiance with respect to albedo at each pixel. Layout is standard screen-space raster format. Motion Vector: A 2D vector (dx, dy) per pixel or globally, derived from camera movement. Steps: 1. Compute Motion Parameters: Determine the motion vector d and velocity vd in screen space based on the camera's moving direction and velocity. 2. Reproject Pixels: For each pixel i in the target frame, calculate the corresponding pixel coordinate in neighboring frames using the reprojection function f{\text{proj}}. 3. Blend Gradients: Compute the weighted average of the reprojected gradient values from neighboring frames to produce the denoised gradient. Formulas: The reprojection function maps a pixel i in the target frame to a coordinate in a neighboring frame at distance k: f{\text{proj}}(i) = i + d \cdot vd \cdot t where t is the time offset. The denoised gradient G{\text{denoised}}(i) is calculated as: G{\text{denoised}}(i) = \frac{\sum{k=0}^{N-1} wa^k (1-wa)^{-1} Gk(f{\text{proj}}^{-1}(i))}{1 - (1-wa)^N} where: k is the frame distance (number of frames between the source image and the target image, with k=0 being the target). Gk is the gradient image at distance k. wa is the smoothing factor. N is the number of frames used for denoising. f{\text{proj}}^{-1} is the reciprocal reprojection function, mapping the target pixel i back to the source frame coordinate. Note on Formula Discrepancy: Source presents a slightly different formulation in Equation (10) involving (1-wa)^{-1} inside the summation term differently, but the structure remains a weighted temporal blend. The formula above combines the consistent elements from both sources. Specifically, writes: G{\text{denoised}}(i) = \left[ \sum{k=0}^{N-1} wa^k (1 - (1-wa)^{-1} (1-wa) Gk(f{\text{proj}}^{-1}(i))) \right]^{-1} This appears to contain a typographical error in the source text regarding the placement of the inverse and the term (1-wa). The standard interpretation of temporal blending with exponential decay (as implied by wa^k) is the weighted sum divided by the normalization factor. The first formula provided is the standard interpretation of the weighted sum described in and the intent of. Parameters: Smoothing factor (wa): Set to 0.1 in all test scenes. Number of frames (N): Set to 11 in the implementation. Pitfalls: Direct Image Denoising: Denoising the original radiance image directly causes visible bias and artifacts. Denoising the gradient prevents this because such artifacts are not directly visible in the gradient domain. Precision: The reciprocal reprojection f{\text{proj}}^{-1} requires careful handling of boundary conditions where projected coordinates fall outside the image bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalgradientdenoise(targetgradient, neighborgradients, motionvector, velocity, smoothingfactor, numframes): """ Denoises the target gradient image using temporal reprojection and blending. Args: targetgradient: 2D array, gradient image for the current frame (k=0). neighborgradients: List of 2D arrays, gradient images for previous frames (k=1 to N-1). motionvector: 2D tuple (dx, dy), motion vector d. velocity: 2D tuple (vx, vy), velocity vd. smoothingfactor: float, wa. numframes: int, N. Returns: denoisedgradient: 2D array. """ # Initialize accumulator for weighted sum and normalization factor weightedsum = np.zeroslike(targetgradient) normalizationfactor = 0.0 # Process the target frame (k=0) # For k=0, fproj^-1(i) = i weightedsum += (smoothingfactor 0) (1 - smoothingfactor) (-1) targetgradient normalizationfactor += (smoothingfactor 0) (1 - smoothingfactor) (-1) # Process neighboring frames (k=1 to N-1) for k in range(1, numframes): if k > len(neighborgradients): break neighborgrad = neighborgradients[k-1] # Calculate reprojection offset # t is implicitly handled by the frame index k in the context of the sequence # Assuming t=1 per frame step for simplicity as per standard temporal reprojection # The formula uses d vd t. If t is time delta, it should be passed. # Here we assume the motion vector provided is already scaled for the frame step or t=1. offset = np.array([motionvector[0] velocity[0], motionvector[1] velocity[1]]) # Create grid for reprojection # fproj^-1(i) maps target pixel i to source pixel coordinate # We need to sample neighborgrad at coordinates shifted by -offset # Since fproj(i) = i + offset, fproj^-1(i) = i - offset # Generate pixel coordinates for the target frame h, w = targetgradient.shape y, x = np.meshgrid(np.arange(h), np.arange(w), indexing='ij') # Calculate source coordinates srcy = y - offset[0] srcx = x - offset[1] # Sample the neighbor gradient at the reprojected coordinates # Using bilinear interpolation for robustness reprojectedgrad = bilinearsample(neighborgrad, srcx, srcy) # Calculate weight for this frame weight = (smoothingfactor k) (1 - smoothingfactor) (-1) # Accumulate weightedsum += weight reprojectedgrad normalizationfactor += weight # Compute final denoised gradient denoisedgradient = weightedsum / normalizationfactor return denoisedgradient def bilinearsample(image, x, y): """ Performs bilinear interpolation on the image at coordinates x, y. Handles boundary conditions by clamping or returning 0 for out-of-bounds. """ h, w = image.shape # Clamp coordinates to valid range xclamped = np.clip(x, 0, w - 1) yclamped = np.clip(y, 0, h - 1) # Get integer and fractional parts x0 = np.floor(xclamped).astype(int) y0 = np.floor(yclamped).astype(int) x1 = np.minimum(x0 + 1, w - 1) y1 = np.minimum(y0 + 1, h - 1) # Fractional parts dx = xclamped - x0 dy = yclamped - y0 # Get pixel values val00 = image[y0, x0] val01 = image[y0, x1] val10 = image[y1, x0] val11 = image[y1, x1] # Interpolate result = (1 - dx) (1 - dy) val00 + dx (1 - dy) val01 + \ (1 - dx) dy val10 + dx dy val11 return result This method denoises Monte Carlo volume rendering images by combining temporal reprojection with a learned kernel prediction network and fusing the result with the background using an alpha map. It addresses the specific challenge of preserving semi-transparent structures and sharp edges in volumetric data while maintaining real-time performance. Unlike direct prediction methods (e.g., FDAE) that rely solely on pixel-wise regression, this approach generates weighted combinations of neighboring samples, offering better structural preservation at the cost of struggling with extreme high-intensity outliers. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of frames N. The reprojection and blending operations are per-pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N gradient images and their corresponding motion vectors. Measured Performance: In test scenes (Bunny, Candle, Lucy) with resolution 256x256, the method produced less error than denoised path tracing and path tracing without denoising, both visually and quantitatively. The method was implemented with N=11 and wa=0.1. Strengths: Effectively reduces noise in high-order scattering-dominant media; avoids visible bias/artifacts associated with direct image denoising; improves quality over standard path tracing with equal time. Limitations: Requires a sequence of frames (temporal coherence); performance gain over path tracing is specific to gradient denoising, as temporal denoising on path tracing itself does not perform better than path tracing with equal time. When to use: When rendering sequences of volume data with high noise levels, particularly in participating media with high albedo, and when temporal coherence is available. When not to use: For single-image rendering; when extreme high-intensity outliers are present and structural preservation is critical without learned kernels. The method was proposed in the context of efficient participating media rendering using differentiable volumetric path tracing. It was introduced to address the high noise levels in gradient images computed with respect to albedo, which are used to predict radiance for different albedo values without re-rendering. The approach leverages the common practice of rendering image sequences with moving cameras. The work was published in 2023. name: Spatiotemporal Volume Denoising with Background Fusion
head: Kernel prediction denoising with background fusion, Real-time volume-rendering image denoising based on kernel prediction
body:
This method denoises Monte Carlo volume rendering images by combining temporal reprojection with a learned kernel prediction network and fusing the result with the background using an alpha map. It addresses the specific challenge of preserving semi-transparent structures and sharp edges in volumetric data while maintaining real-time performance. Unlike direct prediction methods (e.g., FDAE) that rely solely on pixel-wise regression, this approach generates weighted combinations of neighboring samples, offering better structural preservation at the cost of struggling with extreme high-intensity outliers. The method operates on image-order rendering outputs. It takes the current noisy frame, the previous frame's denoised data, and the background color as inputs, producing a final denoised radiance image. Input Images: 1024x1024 resolution, 32-bit floating-point format. Alpha Map A(i,j): A single-channel map representing the transparency of the volume data at pixel coordinates (i,j). Background B(i,j): The color/value of the background at pixel coordinates (i,j). Training Patches: 256x256 image patches extracted from the rendered images (four patches per image). 1. Reprojection: Reproject the previous frame's denoised volume data into the current frame's coordinate space using camera motion and depth information. 2. Kernel Prediction: Use a neural network (kernel prediction network) to predict spatial and temporal weight kernels based on the current noisy frame and the reprojected historical data. 3. Weighted Filtering: Perform pixel-wise weighted filtering on the reprojected historical frame and the current noisy frame using the predicted kernels to obtain an intermediate denoised volume data xn'(i,j). 4. Background Fusion: Blend the intermediate denoised data xn'(i,j) with the background B(i,j) using the alpha map A(i,j) to produce the final denoised pixel value xn''(i,j). 5. Failure Handling: If the camera undergoes rapid motion, abrupt illumination changes, or if a ray passes entirely through transparent regions (where historical frame failure rate can reach 70%), copy the current frame's pixel value to replace the historical frame value, effectively degenerating to spatial denoising for that pixel. Background Fusion: The final denoised pixel value xn'' is calculated as: xn''(i,j) = A(i,j) 	imes xn'(i,j) + (1 - A(i,j)) 	imes B(i,j) where A(i,j) is the alpha map and B(i,j) is the background. Training Loss Functions: The model is trained using a weighted sum of gradient loss and Mean Squared Error (MSE) loss. Gradient Loss L{grad}(I,R): L{grad}(I,R) = \|
ablax I - 
ablax R\|2^2 + \|
ablay I - 
ablay R\|2^2 where I is the predicted image, R is the reference image, and 
ablax, 
ablay are the x and y gradients. MSE Loss L{mse}(I,R): L{mse}(I,R) = \|I - R\|2^2 where \| \cdot \|2^2 denotes the squared L2 norm. Total Loss L{total}(I,R): L{total}(I,R) = w{grad} \cdot L{grad}(I,R) + w{mse} \cdot L{mse}(I,R) where w{grad} and w{mse} are the weights for gradient and MSE losses, respectively. Evaluation Metrics: MSE: MSE(I,R) =  rac{1}{mn} \sum{i=0}^{m-1} \sum{j=0}^{n-1} [I(i,j) - R(i,j)]^2 where m,n are image dimensions. PSNR: PSNR(I,R) = 10 	imes \lg  rac{255^2}{MSE(I,R)} where \lg is the base-10 logarithm. SSIM: SSIM(I,R) =  rac{(2\muI\muR+c1)(\delta{IR}+c2)}{(\muI^2+\muR^2+c1)(\deltaI^2+\deltaR^2+c2)} where \muI, \muR are means, \deltaI, \deltaR are standard deviations, and \delta{IR} is the covariance between images I and R. Temporal PSNR (tPSNR): tPSNR(I,R) = PSNR(It - I{t-1}, Rt - R{t-1}) where t is the time index. w{grad}: Weight for gradient loss. Set to 0.4 to improve visual edge preservation. w{mse}: Weight for MSE loss. Set to 0.6. Learning Rate: 0.0001 (Adam optimizer). Batch Size: 4. Training Epochs: Converges after approximately 300 epochs. High Gradient Weight: If w{grad} is set too high (above 0.5), the image exhibits slight color distortion for some data. Transparent Regions: In ray tracing, if a ray passes entirely through transparent regions, the historical frame failure rate can be as high as 70%. The method handles this by copying the current frame's pixel value to replace the historical value, degenerating to spatial denoising. Rapid Motion/Changes: Historical frames become unusable if the camera undergoes rapid motion, illumination changes abruptly, or the transfer function varies quickly. Outliers: The kernel prediction method struggles with highlighted outliers (e.g., channel values > 200 at 800 samples per pixel) that direct prediction methods can suppress. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spatiotemporaldenoisingwithbackgroundfusion( currentnoisyframe: Image, previousdenoisedframe: Image, alphamap: Image, background: Image, cameratransform: Matrix, depthmap: Image) -> Image: """ Denoises a volume rendering frame using spatiotemporal reprojection and background fusion. Args: currentnoisyframe: The current noisy rendered image. previousdenoisedframe: The denoised image from the previous frame. alphamap: Transparency map for the volume data. background: Background color/image. cameratransform: Transformation matrix for reprojection. depthmap: Depth information for reprojection. Returns: The final denoised image. name: Mega-NeRF-Dynamic Rendering
head: Dynamic Octree Caching, Temporal Coherence Rendering
body: Mega-NeRF-Dynamic is an interactive rendering method for large-scale Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) that exploits temporal coherence in fly-throughs by dynamically expanding and reusing a sparse voxel octree cache across frames. Unlike sibling methods such as Plenoctree which rely on a fixed, precomputed octree that limits resolution, Mega-NeRF-Dynamic dynamically subdivides the octree based on the current camera position, allowing for higher resolution and incremental refinement. It addresses the problem of high latency in large-scale NeRF rendering by reducing per-frame work through state caching and guided sampling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A trained Mega-NeRF model (comprising spatial MLPs and feature modules), a camera trajectory (fly-through), and the octree cache from the previous frame (or a coarse initial cache for the first frame). Outputs: A rendered image frame and an updated sparse voxel octree cache containing refined opacity and color data. Data Structures: Sparse Voxel Octree: A hierarchical structure storing precomputed model outputs (opacity and color/spherical harmonic coefficients). Layout: The octree is dynamically expanded. The source notes that generating an 8-level octree requires 1–12 GB of memory, with higher levels scaling significantly (e.g., adding one level increases size to 55 GB). Weights: The octree stores weights used to guide ray sampling, estimating scene geometry to place samples near surfaces of interest. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization (Precomputation): Precompute a coarse cache of opacity and color into a sparse voxel octree. 2. Initial View Generation: For the current frame, use the cached outputs from the previous frame's expanded octree to produce an initial view. 3. Dynamic Expansion & Refinement: Dynamically subdivide the octree based on the current camera position. Perform additional rounds of model sampling to refine the image in regions of interest and store these new values into the cache. 4. Guided Ray Sampling: Perform a final round of guided ray sampling in a single pass. Unlike standard hierarchical sampling which uses uniform coarse intervals followed by fine sampling, this method uses the weights stored in the octree to skip empty spaces and place a small number of samples near surfaces of interest. 5. Transmittance Accumulation: Accumulate transmittance along the ray. End sampling after a certain threshold is reached to accelerate the process. 6. Cache Update: The refined octree from the current frame is reused for the next frame, requiring only incremental work to maintain quality. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: camera: Current camera pose and intrinsics. prevoctree: Sparse voxel octree from the previous frame. nerfmodel: The trained Mega-NeRF model. stepsize: Distance between samples along the ray. transmittancethreshold: Early termination threshold for transmittance. Returns: image: Rendered RGBA image buffer. currentoctree: Updated octree for the next frame. """ # Step 1: Initialize octree for current frame based on previous state # If first frame, use coarse precomputed cache; otherwise, reuse and expand currentoctree = prevoctree.copy() if prevoctree else buildcoarsecache(nerfmodel) # Step 2: Dynamic Expansion # Subdivide octree nodes based on camera proximity and current view requirements currentoctree = dynamicsubdivide(currentoctree, camera) # Step 3: Initial View & Refinement # Use cached outputs for a quick initial view initialimage = renderfromcache(currentoctree, camera) # Perform additional rounds of model sampling to refine the image # Store new values into the cache refinedoctree = refineoctree(currentoctree, camera, nerfmodel) # Step 4 & 5: Guided Ray Sampling & Transmittance Accumulation image = emptyimagebuffer(camera.resolution) for y in range(camera.resolution[1]): for x in range(camera.resolution[0]): rayorigin, raydirection = generateray(camera, x, y) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 t = 0.0 # Traverse octree and sample along ray while t < camera.farplane and transmittance > transmittancethreshold: pos = rayorigin + raydirection t node = currentoctree.querynode(pos) if node is not None: density, color = nerfmodel.query(pos) # Apply octree weight for guided sampling if available weight = node.getweight() if hasattr(node, 'getweight') else 1.0 alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density weight stepsize) accumulatedcolor[0] += alpha transmittance color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += alpha transmittance color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += alpha transmittance color[2] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) t += stepsize # Return RGBA: color + accumulated alpha (1 - transmittance) image[y, x] = accumulatedcolor + [1.0 - transmittance] return image, refinedoctree def buildcoarsecache(nerfmodel): # Precompute coarse cache of opacity and color into a sparse voxel octree # Not given in the sources. pass def dynamicsubdivide(octree, camera): # Dynamically subdivide the octree based on the current camera position # Not given in the sources. pass def renderfromcache(octree, camera): # Use cached outputs to produce an initial view # Not given in the sources. pass def refineoctree(octree, camera, nerfmodel): # Perform additional rounds of model sampling to refine the image # Store new values into the cache # Not given in the sources. pass def emptyimagebuffer(resolution): # Initialize an empty buffer for the image return [[None for in range(resolution[0])] for in range(resolution[1])] def generateray(camera, x, y): # Generate a ray from camera origin through pixel (x, y) # Standard pinhole camera projection # Not given in the sources. pass Parameters: Octree Depth: The source notes that an 8-level octree is used for scenes, with higher levels increasing memory usage drastically (55 GB for one additional level). Transmittance Threshold: Sampling ends after a certain threshold is reached to accelerate the process. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: Generating high-level octrees is memory-intensive. Adding a single level can increase size to 55 GB, exceeding the capacity of many GPUs. Precomputation Time: Generating the initial coarse cache takes significant time (1 hour for 8 levels). Camera Motion: The method relies on temporal coherence. Large, sudden camera movements may reduce the effectiveness of cache reuse, requiring more incremental work. Time Complexity: Precomputation is expensive (1 hour for 8-level octree). Interactive rendering is accelerated by reusing the octree, requiring only incremental work per frame. Memory Complexity: High. An 8-level octree requires 1–12 GB of memory. Adding a level increases this to 55 GB. Performance: Reduces rendering time from over 2 minutes per 720p frame (with normal ray sampling) to something more manageable for interactive fly-throughs. Strengths: High resolution due to dynamic expansion; efficient reuse of computation across frames; guided sampling reduces unnecessary queries. Limitations: High memory footprint for deep octrees; precomputation overhead. When to use: Large-scale NeRF fly-throughs where visual fidelity and resolution are prioritized, and hardware has sufficient memory. When not to use: Scenes with rapid, non-sequential camera motion or hardware with limited memory. Mega-NeRF-Dynamic was introduced in the paper "Mega-NeRF: Scalable Construction of Large-Scale NeRFs for Virtual Fly-Throughs". It was developed to address the limitations of existing fast NeRF renderers like Plenoctree, which use fixed octrees that limit resolution. The method is designed for search-and-rescue use cases, aiming to preserve visual fidelity while minimizing processing time beyond training. name: Dynamic Cache Depth Scheduling
head: Anchor-based Cache Depth Adjustment, Cache Depth Heuristic
body: Dynamic Cache Depth Scheduling is a heuristic strategy that adjusts the depth of reuse for cached computation results in subsequent frames based on the intensity of decoding calculations in the current frame. It solves the problem of maintaining rendering quality and suppressing rapid appearance changes caused by sudden cache flushing in large-scale Gaussian Splatting models. Unlike static cache reuse, this method dynamically balances performance and visual stability by modulating how many previous frames' results are retained. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera input (pose), current frame anchors (X{k'}), total anchors (X), previous frame cache state. Outputs: Rendered image, updated cache depth, updated computation cache. Data Structures: Computation Cache: Stores derived 3D Gaussians from previous frames. The cache holds results from up to D{max} previous frames. Anchor Set: The set of anchors to be decoded into 3D Gaussians for the current frame. Cache Depth (D): An integer indicating how many previous frames' Gaussians are reused. Parameters: Max Cache Reuse Depth (D{max}): Set to 10 to balance performance and quality. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the rendering pipeline, set the initial cache depth and the guiding function H. 2. While receiving camera input: a. Perform anchors indexing and filtering. b. Check if the current cache reuse depth has reached D{max}. If yes, invalidate those computation cache lines. c. Calculate the Anchor Duplicate Rate (the ratio of anchors that can be reused or are identical to previous frames). d. Based on the Anchor Duplicate Rate: i. If Anchor Duplicate Rate == 0% or it is the first frame: Decode all anchors into 3D Gaussians. ii. If Anchor Duplicate Rate == 100%: Reuse all 3D Gaussians from the cache. iii. Otherwise: Decode new anchors and update the computation cache. e. Compose the new Gaussians with the cached Gaussians. f. Configure the new cache depth D using the guiding function and the duplicate rate. g. Update the render buffer. h. Rasterize the render buffer into an image. Formula: The expected reuse depth D is determined by the guiding function H applied to the ratio of current anchors to total anchors: D = H\left(\frac{|X{k'}|}{|X|}\right) where: H is the guiding function of the heuristic strategy. |X{k'}| is the number of anchors in the current frame. |X| is the total number of anchors. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamiccachedepthscheduling(camerainput, totalanchorsX, maxreusedepth=10): # Initialize state cachedepth = 0 computationcache = {} # Maps frameid to Gaussian parameters # Implementation of H not specified in sources; standard linear scaling shown guidingfunctionH = lambda ratio: max(1, int(ratio maxreusedepth)) firstframe = True while camerainput is not None: # 1. Anchors indexing and filtering currentanchorsXkprime = indexandfilteranchors(camerainput) # 2. Check max cache reuse depth if cachedepth >= maxreusedepth: computationcache.clear() cachedepth = 0 # 3. Calculate Anchor Duplicate Rate anchorduplicaterate = calculateduplicaterate(currentanchorsXkprime, computationcache) # 4. Decode or Reuse based on duplicate rate if anchorduplicaterate == 0.0 or firstframe: newgaussians = decodeanchorstogaussians(currentanchorsXkprime) cachedepth = 0 firstframe = False elif anchorduplicaterate == 1.0: newgaussians = reusecachedgaussians(computationcache) else: newanchors = getnewanchors(currentanchorsXkprime) decodednewgaussians = decodeanchorstogaussians(newanchors) updatecomputationcache(computationcache, decodednewgaussians) newgaussians = composegaussians(decodednewgaussians, computationcache) # 5. Configure cache depth based on guiding function and duplicate rate ratio = len(currentanchorsXkprime) / len(totalanchorsX) cachedepth = guidingfunctionH(ratio) # 6. Update render buffer and rasterize renderbuffer = updaterenderbuffer(newgaussians, camerainput) image = rasterize(renderbuffer) return image def indexandfilteranchors(camerainput): # Standard view frustum culling and spatial indexing return camerainput.getvisibleanchors() def calculateduplicaterate(currentanchors, cache): # Ratio of current anchors matching cached frame's anchors if not cache: return 0.0 cachedanchors = next(iter(cache.values())).anchors matches = sum(1 for a in currentanchors if a in cachedanchors) return matches / len(currentanchors) if currentanchors else 0.0 def decodeanchorstogaussians(anchors): # Standard Gaussian Splatting derivation return [anchor.derivegaussian() for anchor in anchors] def reusecachedgaussians(cache): return next(iter(cache.values())).gaussians def getnewanchors(currentanchors): return [a for a in currentanchors if not a.iscached()] def updatecomputationcache(cache, newgaussians): cache[cache.get('frameid', 0) + 1] = type('obj', (object,), {'anchors': newgaussians, 'gaussians': newgaussians})() def composegaussians(newgaussians, cache): return newgaussians + next(iter(cache.values())).gaussians def updaterenderbuffer(gaussians, camerainput): return {'gaussians': gaussians, 'camera': camerainput} def rasterize(buffer): return buffer['camera'].project(buffer['gaussians']) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stale Appearance: Maintaining the same Gaussian appearance parameters in the cache for too long causes significant rendering errors, particularly on trajectories around a centered target. This is handled by flushing the cache in time via the max reuse depth limit. Rapid Appearance Changes: Static cache reuse depth can cause rapid changes in scene appearance when the cache is flushed. Dynamic scheduling suppresses this by gradually adjusting the depth. Time Complexity: Depends on the anchor decoding stage and Gaussian rasterization stage. By reusing cached Gaussians, the decoding stage is skipped for duplicate anchors, reducing computational load. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the cache depth D{max} and the number of anchors. With D{max}=10, the cache stores results from up to 10 previous frames. Performance: Tested on Scaffold-GS and OctreeGS models. Setting D{max}=10 balances performance and quality. It is effective for both single GPU and multi-GPU resources. Strengths: Maintains image rendering quality without significant decrease or fluctuation. Suppresses rapid appearance changes caused by sudden cache flushing. The method is model-agnostic and independent of the specific pipeline structure. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of the guiding function H and duplicate rate calculation. May introduce latency if cache management is inefficient. Dynamic Cache Depth Scheduling was introduced in the paper "A GS-Cache Inference Framework for Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting Models". It was developed to address redundancy in binocular stereo rendering and to optimize the derivation stage in large-scale Gaussian Splatting models like Scaffold-GS and OctreeGS. The method is designed to be independent of the specific model and pipeline structure. name: Voronoi-Based Foveated Volume Rendering
head: Voronoi Foveated Rendering
body: Voronoi-Based Foveated Volume Rendering is a method that adapts sampling density and reconstruction to the human visual system's acuity fall-off, using gaze tracking to shift a pre-computed sampling mask and reconstructing images via Voronoi-based natural neighbor interpolation. It sets itself apart from standard foveated techniques by mathematically aligning the sampling strategy (Voronoi cells) with the reconstruction kernel (natural neighbor interpolation), ensuring symmetry between how rays are placed and how values are interpolated, while explicitly addressing the undersampling artifacts inherent in sparse peripheral sampling through temporal smoothing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D volume texture, user gaze position (from eye tracker), screen resolution, visual acuity model parameters. Outputs: Rendered 2D image. Data Structures: 1. Sampling Mask: A 2D texture with dimensions at least twice the screen resolution in both axes. This size accommodates gaze-dependent translation while keeping the high-density foveal region centered. 2. Neighbor Index Texture: A 2D texture storing the indices of neighboring Voronoi cells for each sample point. 3. Weight Texture: A 2D texture storing the weights for natural neighbor interpolation corresponding to the neighbors. 4. Ray List: A sorted list of sampling rays, pre-sorted by Morton order (Z-curve) to optimize spatial locality and caching behavior. Pre-processing (Offline/Setup): 1. Visual Acuity Modeling: Approximate the hyperbolic visual acuity fall-off using a 2D Gaussian function based on screen resolution, size, viewing distance, and photoreceptor distribution. The Minimum Angle of Resolution (MAR) is modeled as: \text{MAR} = \omega0 + m \cdot e where \omega0 is the smallest resolvable angle, e is eccentricity in degrees, and m is the slope. 2. Mask Generation: Use the Weighted Linde-Buzo-Gray (LBG) algorithm to pre-compute the sampling mask based on the visual acuity fall-off. The LBG algorithm iteratively adjusts ray positions to minimize error between the cost function Tr and the area Ar occupied by each ray. Three adjustment cases are applied per iteration i: 1. Move/Relax: If Tr \in [Ar - \epsilon, Ar + \epsilon]. 2. Split: If Tr > Ar + \epsilon. 3. Delete: If Tr < Ar - \epsilon. A hysteresis function stabilizes the iteration bounds: Ar \cdot (1 \pm (\epsilon0 + i \cdot \epsilon\Delta) / 2), with \epsilon0 = 0.5 and \epsilon\Delta = 0.1. The process repeats until the error is below a threshold or ray count stabilizes. 3. Neighbor/Weight Computation: Compute the Voronoi cells for the generated ray positions. For each ray, determine its natural neighbors and calculate the interpolation weights. Store these indices and weights in the Neighbor Index and Weight textures, respectively. 4. Sorting: Sort the sampling rays according to Morton order (Z-curve) to improve cache locality during runtime. Runtime (Per Frame): 1. Gaze Tracking: Acquire user gaze position from a stationary eye-tracking system (e.g., 1200 Hz sampling rate). 2. Mask Shift: Translate the pre-computed sampling mask texture so that the high-density foveal region aligns with the current gaze position. 3. Volume Raycasting: Cast rays through the 3D volume texture using perspective projection. Adjust the distance between samples along each ray proportional to the acuity fall-off function, adapting density in both image and object space. Sample density values using trilinear interpolation. Perform front-to-back compositing using a post-classification model with linear transfer functions. Apply acceleration techniques: local Phong illumination (based on central difference gradients), early ray termination, and empty space skipping. 4. Image Reconstruction: For each pixel, retrieve the corresponding sample from the shifted mask. Use the pre-computed Neighbor Index and Weight textures to perform natural neighbor interpolation of the sparsely sampled ray values. 5. Temporal Smoothing: Apply a temporal smoothing filter to the rendered image to attenuate undersampling artifacts in the periphery. The filter averages the current frame with n previous frames. The typical value is n=8. Conditional Application: Do not apply temporal smoothing during rapid image-altering changes (e.g., camera manipulation, transfer function modifications) to avoid motion blur. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Undersampling Artifacts: Low sampling density in peripheral vision causes artifacts near fine structures. This is mitigated by temporal smoothing, as peripheral vision is sensitive to contrast changes and movement. Transition Artifacts: Rapid eye movements can cause noticeable transitions from blurry to sharp if screen update lags. Temporal smoothing hides this transition. Motion Blur: Applying temporal smoothing during camera or data changes introduces unwanted motion blur. The method requires detecting these changes to disable smoothing. Eye-Tracker Latency: The method is robust to low sampling rate eye-trackers due to the smoothing filter. A high-frequency tracker (1200 Hz) was used for testing. A temporal filter applied to peripheral vision regions to attenuate artifacts caused by low sampling density, while also providing implicit anti-aliasing and hiding sharp-to-blurry transitions during rapid eye movements. It sets itself apart from spatial-only foveated methods by leveraging temporal coherence to smooth undersampling artifacts without increasing per-frame computational cost, though it is disabled during interactive changes to prevent motion blur. Performance: The method substantially improves rendering performance with barely perceptible changes in visual quality. Measured speedups vary by dataset: Combustion (154.20x), Supernova (105.28x), Vortex cascade (104.87x), Zeiss (177.09x), Flower (74.08x), Chameleon (99.78x) relative to regular rendering. Complexity: Pre-processing is offline. Runtime complexity is dominated by volume raycasting and texture lookups for interpolation. The use of pre-computed weights and indices makes reconstruction efficient. Strengths: High performance gains; mathematically symmetric sampling/reconstruction; handles peripheral undersampling artifacts effectively; robust to eye-tracker latency. Limitations: Requires eye-tracking hardware; temporal smoothing introduces latency and is disabled during interactive changes; pre-computation is dataset and resolution dependent. When to use: Real-time volume visualization where performance is critical and user gaze can be tracked, particularly for large datasets or high resolutions. When not to use: When interactive camera/data manipulation is frequent (due to smoothing latency), or when eye-tracking hardware is unavailable. The method was presented by Bruder et al. in 2019. It builds on the principles of foveated rendering, which adapts rendering quality to the human visual system's fall-off in visual acuity. The approach specifically addresses the challenges of volume raycasting, which prevents the direct transfer of many traditional foveated rendering techniques. It utilizes the Linde-Buzo-Gray algorithm for sampling and natural neighbor interpolation for reconstruction, concepts rooted in computational geometry and signal processing. name: Temporal Smoothing for Foveated Rendering
head: Temporal filter for foveated rendering, Temporal smoothing filter, Temporal smoothing filter for foveated rendering
body: A temporal filter applied to peripheral vision regions to attenuate artifacts caused by low sampling density, while also providing implicit anti-aliasing and hiding sharp-to-blurry transitions during rapid eye movements. It sets itself apart from spatial-only foveated methods by leveraging temporal coherence to smooth undersampling artifacts, though it introduces a small computational overhead and is disabled during interactive changes to prevent motion blur. Inputs and Outputs Input: Current frame's peripheral pixel values, previous n frames' peripheral pixel values. Output: Temporally smoothed peripheral pixel values. The foveal region is rendered at high resolution and is not smoothed. Data Structures A circular buffer storing the pixel values of the last n frames for the peripheral region, with size (n+1) \times \text{height} \times \text{width}. The peripheral region is defined by the sampling mask generated by the parent method, Voronoi-Based Foveated Volume Rendering. Parameters n: Number of previous frames to average. Typical value: n = 8. This value is a compromise between sufficient smoothing, perceived fade, and perceived frame rate. Steps 1. Render the current frame using the foveated sampling strategy. 2. Identify the peripheral region pixels (those outside the high-acuity foveal zone). 3. For each peripheral pixel, compute the average of its value in the current frame and the values from the previous n frames stored in the buffer. 4. Update the buffer with the current frame's peripheral pixel values. 5. Composite the smoothed peripheral region with the unsmoothed foveal region. Formula Let Pt(x, y) be the pixel value at coordinates (x, y) in the peripheral region at frame t. The smoothed pixel value P't(x, y) is: P't(x, y) = \frac{1}{n+1} \sum{i=0}^{n} P{t-i}(x, y) Where P{t-i}(x, y) is the pixel value from i frames ago. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Interaction and Dynamic Data: Applying the filter during image-altering changes (camera manipulation, transfer function modifications) introduces unwanted motion blur. The filter must be disabled during such changes. Dynamic Data: The filter may induce undesired motion blur effects during interaction and dynamic data; it is recommended to refrain from using the filter in these scenarios. Eye Tracking Latency: The filter helps hide the transition from blurry to sharp during rapid eye movements that can be noticeable if the screen update lags behind the eye movement. It also helps with eye-tracking devices with low sampling rates. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalsmoothperipheral(currentframepixels, buffer, writeindex, n): """ Applies temporal smoothing to peripheral pixels. Args: currentframepixels: 2D list of pixel values for the current frame's peripheral region. buffer: Circular buffer of size n+1 storing previous peripheral pixel frames. writeindex: Current index in the buffer to write the new frame. n: Number of previous frames to average (typically 8). Returns: smoothedpixels: 2D list of smoothed peripheral pixel values. newwriteindex: Updated write index for the buffer. """ height = len(currentframepixels) width = len(currentframepixels[0]) if height > 0 else 0 buffersize = n + 1 smoothedpixels = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): pixelsum = 0.0 for i in range(buffersize): readindex = (writeindex - i) % buffersize if i == 0: pixelsum += currentframepixels[y][x] else: pixelsum += buffer[readindex][y][x] smoothedpixels[y][x] = pixelsum / buffersize buffer[writeindex] = [row[:] for row in currentframepixels] newwriteindex = (writeindex + 1) % buffersize return smoothedpixels, newwriteindex Performance: The reduced number of rays (less than 8% of regular rendering) indicates potential for significant performance gains, but actual speedups are limited by other factors. Speedup: Achieved average speedups between factor 1.8 and 3.2 depending on data set and transfer function. Speedup is higher for volumes with less empty space. Overhead: The overhead of natural neighbor interpolation amounts to 1.5 \pm 0.157 ms for all data sets, plus general overhead (kernel invocation, etc.). Limitations: Sparse peripheral regions often correspond to rays accelerated by empty space skipping, limiting potential performance gains from ray reduction. Caching is less efficient compared to regular volume rendering due to non-consecutive voxel-access pattern. When to use: Suitable for static or slowly changing data where peripheral undersampling artifacts are noticeable and motion blur is not a concern. When not to use: Not suitable for interactive scenarios, camera manipulation, transfer function modifications, or dynamic data where motion blur artifacts are undesirable. Origin: The method is part of the Voronoi-Based Foveated Volume Rendering approach, presented by Bruder et al. in 2019. Development: The temporal smoothing filter was introduced to address undersampling artifacts in peripheral vision regions, which are sensitive to contrast changes and movement. The choice of n=8 frames was determined as a compromise between smoothing quality and perceived frame rate. Usage: Implemented in a single-pass volume raycasting system using OpenCL 1.2, rendered at 1024×1024 px on a 1080p screen, tested with a Tobii Pro Spectrum eyetracker (1200 Hz) and NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1070.
