name: Ray-guided volume rendering with missing brick reporting
head: Ray-guided methods
body: Ray-guided volume rendering with missing brick reporting is an out-of-core rendering technique where the working set (the minimal subset of volume data required to render an image) is determined dynamically during the ray-casting process rather than in advance. It solves the problem of memory bottlenecks in large-scale volume rendering by streaming only the bricks actually accessed by rays, ensuring optimal accuracy by never loading data that will not be used. Unlike sibling methods that may estimate working sets conservatively or use fixed traversal patterns, this approach minimizes memory utilization by reporting missing bricks on the GPU for subsequent frame loading. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, volume brick hierarchy (multiple resolutions), current brick cache state, and previous frame's resume state (rayResumeColor, rayResumePos). Output: Final accumulated color for the pixel, updated brick request list for the CPU/disk subsystem, and updated resume state for the next frame. Data Structures: 1. Brick Cache: A 3D texture or buffer storing individual bricks of different resolutions in GPU memory in an unordered manner. 2. Residency Map: A data structure storing whether each brick in the global volume is currently resident in the cache. This is used for address translation, mapping sample locations in reference space (e.g., normalized [0, 1]^3) to texture coordinates within the specific brick in the cache. 3. Missing Brick Hash Table: A lock-free, set-based, linearly-probed hash table stored in an image load store buffer (e.g., using GLARBshaderimageloadstore). It records brick identifiers to coordinate disk access. 4. Ray State: rayResumeColor: Accumulated color from previous frames. rayResumePos: The position in the volume where the first missing brick occurred, used to resume rendering. terminated: Boolean flag indicating if a missing brick has been encountered for the current ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set color = rayResumeColor and terminated = true (assuming the ray will finish if no missing bricks are found). 2. Ray Loop: Repeat until the ray exits the volume or saturates: a. Compute Level of Detail (LoD): Determine the required LoD based on the current ray depth. b. Get Brick: Call GetBrick(ray) to retrieve the brick and its associated samplingRate. GetBrick always returns some data, potentially at a lower resolution than requested. c. Address Translation: Retrieve the offsets for the brick from the pool using PoolOffsets(brick). d. Check Resolution: If samplingRate is not equal to RequiredSamplingForLOD(LoD), the data is undersampled. i. Report Missing: Call ReportMissingBrick(brick) to add the brick to the hash table. ii. Record Resume Point: If terminated is true (indicating this is the first missing brick encountered for this ray), set terminated = false and store the current ray position in rayResumePos. e. Raycast: Perform the raycasting step using the ray, stepSize, and offsets. 3. Update State: Set rayResumeColor = color. If the ray completed successfully (no missing bricks), set rayResumePos = FINISHED. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayguidedrendering(ray, rayresumecolor, rayresumepos): color = rayresumecolor terminated = True # Assume ray will finish unless a missing brick is found # Resume position if we stopped due to missing data currentray = ray if rayresumepos != FINISHED: currentray = rayresumepos else: currentray = ray while currentray.depth < exitdepth and not currentray.saturated: # 1. Determine required resolution lod = computelod(currentray.depth) # 2. Retrieve brick and its actual sampling rate brick, samplingrate = getbrick(currentray) # 3. Get offsets for address translation within the cache offsets = pooloffsets(brick) # 4. Check if the retrieved brick matches the required LOD requiredsampling = requiredsamplingforlod(lod) if samplingrate != requiredsampling: # Data is undersampled; report missing brick reportmissingbrick(brick) # Record the position of the first missing brick for resumption if terminated: terminated = False rayresumepos = currentray # 5. Perform the raycasting step color = raycaststep(currentray, offsets) # Advance ray currentray.advance() # Update resume state for next frame rayresumecolor = color if terminated: rayresumepos = FINISHED return color, rayresumecolor, rayresumepos Parameters: rayResumePos: Stores the position in the volume where the first missing brick occurred. terminated: Boolean flag indicating if a missing brick has been encountered for the current ray. GLARBshaderimageloadstore: OpenGL extension used for atomic operations and independent image buffers in the hash table implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Undersampling: If data is undersampled, the renderer displays a coarser version initially but progressively refines regions with finer resolution data until sampled at a single voxel per pixel or the maximum data resolution. Write Hazards: The lock-free hash table must handle concurrent writes from multiple rays requesting the same brick. Linear probing with atomic operations is used to mitigate hazards. Termination: The terminated flag ensures that rayResumePos is only set once per ray per frame, at the first missing brick encountered. The Greedy Brick Request Strategy is a data-loading heuristic in ray-guided volume rendering that requests all intermediate levels of detail (LoD) along a ray's path when a higher-resolution brick is unavailable, rather than waiting for the final required resolution. Unlike the Global strategy, which only requests the final necessary brick, the Greedy strategy floods the request hash table with intermediate bricks. This prioritizes iterative visual refinement and faster convergence of image quality over minimizing the total number of unique brick requests per frame. It produces more responsive, iteratively-refined images and may converge in fewer frames because it allows rays to sample at final resolution quickly, triggering earlier ray termination. The Global Brick Request Strategy is a data-loading heuristic where a ray only requests the bricks absolutely required to satisfy the final rendering request, leaving space in the hash table for other rays. When a brick is missing, it increments the LoD and looks up the brick at the new resolution, continuing until a missing brick is no longer reported. Unlike the 'Greedy' strategy, the Global strategy does not request intermediate bricks. It generates the final correct image quickest in terms of raw completion but may produce less pleasing intermediate progress. A subsystem for recording missing bricks identified during ray-casting on the GPU, using a lock-free hash table stored in an image load store buffer to coordinate disk access and update the volume pool. It uses the GLARBshaderimageloadstore extension (core in OpenGL 4.2) to create an image buffer independent of the current rendering buffer. It implements a set-based linearly-probed lock-free hash table using atomic load/store operations. Hashing is based on the brick identifier so that multiple rays requesting the same brick hash to the same position, keeping the table size small and avoiding duplicate values inherent in multiple render target approaches. Time Complexity: The per-frame cost is dominated by ray casting and hash table insertions. Hash table operations are O(1) amortized due to linear probing and atomic operations. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of resident bricks in the cache plus the size of the hash table. The hash table size is kept small by hashing on brick IDs, which exploits spatial coherency (neighboring rays request similar bricks). Measured Performance: The greedy strategy was found to converge in the fewest number of frames and produce more pleasing progress information, despite flooding the hash table, because it enables earlier ray termination. The global strategy generates the final correct image quickest in raw completion time but offers less responsive intermediate progress. Strengths: Minimizes working-set size by only streaming accessed bricks. Ensures optimal accuracy by never loading unused data. Scales to extremely large data sets. Limitations: Requires complex GPU-side logic for missing brick reporting and hash table management. Previous approaches using conservative working-set estimates led to sub-optimal memory utilization. When to use: Large-scale volume rendering where data exceeds GPU memory capacity and interactive or progressive refinement is desired. When not to use: When data fits entirely in GPU memory, or when the overhead of hash table management and frame-to-frame resumption is unacceptable compared to simpler in-core methods. Ray-guided volume rendering was introduced to address the limitations of early approaches that produced conservative estimates of the working set, leading to sub-optimal memory utilization. Key early works include [CNLE09], [HBJP12], [FSK13], and [BPH14]. The specific technique of missing brick reporting with GPU-based hash table coordination was detailed by Crassin et al. (PMC4260263). The method builds on the principle of address translation using octrees or page-table hierarchies. The use of GLARBshaderimageloadstore for lock-free hash tables was adopted to overcome the limitations of multiple render targets, which ignore spatial coherency and lead to duplicate values and larger texture reads back. name: Greedy Brick Request Strategy
head: Greedy algorithm
body: The Greedy Brick Request Strategy is a data-loading heuristic in ray-guided volume rendering that requests all intermediate levels of detail (LoD) along a ray's path when a higher-resolution brick is unavailable, rather than waiting for the final required resolution. Unlike the Global strategy, which only requests the final necessary brick, the Greedy strategy floods the request hash table with intermediate bricks. This prioritizes iterative visual refinement and faster convergence of image quality over minimizing the total number of unique brick requests per frame. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The current ray state, the current Level of Detail (LoD) index, and a missing brick report function. Output: A sequence of missing brick reports for all intermediate resolutions up to the first available brick. Data Structures: Hash Table: A table used to accumulate brick requests from all active rays, which is read back from the GPU at the end of a frame to fill the volume pool. Level of Detail (LoD): An integer index representing the resolution of the brick, where higher indices indicate finer resolution. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize the current LoD to the base resolution required for the current sample or the last known available resolution. 2. Enter a loop that continues as long as a brick is missing. 3. Increment the LoD index. 4. Look up the brick corresponding to the current ray position and the new LoD. 5. Check if the brick is missing (not resident in memory). 6. If the brick is missing: Report the missing brick to the hash table. Continue the loop to request the next higher resolution. 7. If the brick is found (not missing): Terminate the loop. Proceed with rendering using the found brick. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def greedybrickrequest(ray, currentlod, lookupbrick, ismissing, reportmissing): """ Requests all intermediate bricks from currentlod up to the first available brick. """ lod = currentlod while True: lod += 1 brick = lookupbrick(ray, lod) if ismissing(brick): reportmissing(brick) else: return brick Parameters: LoD Increment: Increments by 1 at each step, moving from coarser to finer resolutions. Hash Table Saturation: Because the Greedy strategy requests all intermediate bricks, it can flood the request hash table with many requests per ray. Convergence Behavior: The strategy allows a ray to sample at its final resolution quickly, which can cause earlier ray termination and faster convergence in fewer frames. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Termination: If the ray exits the volume bounds before finding a resident brick, the loop must terminate to prevent infinite execution. Hash Table Contention: Flooding the hash table with intermediate requests per ray may cause contention or overflow if the table size is not sufficiently large. Lookup Precision: The lookup function must correctly map ray positions to brick indices at each LoD to avoid missing bricks or requesting invalid resolutions. An alternative strategy that performs brick lookup once per brick rather than every sample, maintaining a simple ray-marching core. It differs from the Greedy strategy by using an out-of-core, progressive rendering methodology that breaks the GPU-memory-size barrier, whereas Greedy focuses on iterative refinement via intermediate requests. Time Complexity: The number of lookups and potential hash table writes per ray is proportional to the number of missing intermediate levels of detail. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is dominated by the request hash table, which accumulates more requests per frame than the Global strategy. Performance: The Greedy strategy converges in fewer frames to a visually pleasing result compared to the Global strategy. This is because it allows rays to sample at their final resolution more quickly, which can cause earlier ray termination and faster accumulation of high-frequency details. Strengths: Produces more responsive, iteratively-refined images with more densely-packed intermediate progress. Limitations: Higher memory usage for the request table due to flooding the hash table with intermediate requests. When to use: When visual responsiveness and smooth convergence are critical. When not to use: When the goal is to minimize the total number of disk I/O operations regardless of visual convergence speed, as the Global strategy generates the final correct image quickest. The Greedy Brick Request Strategy was introduced in the context of scalable GPU-based ray-guided volume rendering. It was compared against the "Global" strategy, which only requests the final required brick. The authors found that the Greedy approach, despite its higher request volume, converged faster and produced more pleasing progress information, surprising initial expectations that the Global strategy would be more efficient. name: Ray-Guided Grid Leaping
head: Out-of-core ray-guided rendering, Ray-guided volume rendering
body: Ray-Guided Grid Leaping is an out-of-core volume rendering technique that couples the rendering process with the identification of which sub-volumes ('bricks') must be loaded, using ray-sampling characteristics to determine future data requirements in concert with standard ray traversal and accumulation. It differs from Hadwiger et al. by performing brick lookup once per brick rather than every sample, maintaining a simple ray-marching core, and utilizing an out-of-core, progressive rendering methodology that breaks the GPU-memory-size barrier. Inputs: Input volume data existing at a single resolution. Transfer function. Camera parameters. Outputs: Rendered image. Updated GPU texture pool with paged-in bricks. Data Structures: 1. Multiresolution Hierarchy: A preprocess built from the single-resolution input data, consisting of simple multiresolution Cartesian grids (bricks). 2. Lookup Table: Stores the status for each brick index. It has three states: Empty Non-empty and present on the GPU Non-empty and absent 3. GPU Hash Table: A lock-free hash table used to record missing bricks for feedback to the I/O layer. Parameters: Pixel Error Threshold: The level of detail is computed to maintain a pixel error of less than one. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Build a multiresolution hierarchy as a preprocess for input data which exist at only one resolution. 2. Ray Processing (Per Ray): a. Compute the level of detail (LOD) required to maintain a pixel error of less than one. b. Compute a brick index from the LOD and the position in the volume. c. Use the brick index to fetch information from the lookup table to identify the brick's state: i. If the brick is empty, skip the brick and repeat the process at the brick’s exit point. ii. If the brick is non-empty and present on the GPU, ray-cast that brick. iii. If the brick is non-empty and absent from GPU memory, return the finest coarser level available and add the missing entry to the GPU hash table. 3. End of Frame: a. Read back the GPU hash table to host memory. b. Use the read-back data to page in bricks from disk or cache. c. Upload paged-in bricks to a GPU texture pool. 4. Subsequent Frame: Use the portion of the brick pool for sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EMPTY = 0 NONEMPTYPRESENT = 1 NONEMPTYABSENT = 2 def rayguidedgridleapingraykernel(rayorigin, raydirection, volumemaxt, lookuptable, brickpool, missingbrickshashtable): """ Processes a single ray using Ray-Guided Grid Leaping. rayorigin: vec3, start of the ray raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the ray volumemaxt: float, maximum distance along the ray within the volume bounds lookuptable: dict, maps brickidx to status (EMPTY, NONEMPTYPRESENT, NONEMPTYABSENT) brickpool: dict, maps brickidx to brick data missingbrickshashtable: lock-free hash table, records missing bricks """ t = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 while t < volumemaxt: # 1. Compute Level of Detail (LOD) to maintain pixel error < 1 # Sources do not provide the exact LOD computation formula. lod = computelodforpixelerrorthreshold(t, threshold=1.0) # 2. Compute Brick Index from LOD and position position = rayorigin + raydirection t brickidx = computebrickindex(lod, position) # 3. Lookup Brick Status status = lookuptable.get(brickidx) if status == EMPTY: # Skip empty brick and jump to exit point # Sources do not provide the exact exit point calculation. t = getbrickexitpoint(brickidx, position, raydirection) continue elif status == NONEMPTYPRESENT: # Ray-cast the present brick brickdata = brickpool.get(brickidx) color, alpha, t = raycastbrick(rayorigin, raydirection, t, brickdata, color, alpha) elif status == NONEMPTYABSENT: # Return finest coarser level available # Add missing entry to GPU hash table for I/O feedback missingbrickshashtable.insert(brickidx) # Use coarser level for sampling coarserbrickidx = getcoarserbrick(brickidx) coarserdata = brickpool.get(coarserbrickidx) color, alpha, t = raycastbrick(rayorigin, raydirection, t, coarserdata, color, alpha) return color def endofframeprocessing(missingbrickshashtable, brickpool, diskcache): """ Handles I/O for missing bricks identified during the frame. """ # 1. Read back GPU hash table to host memory missingbricks = missingbrickshashtable.readbacktohost() # 2. Page in bricks from disk or cache pagedbricks = [] for brickidx in missingbricks: data = diskcache.load(brickidx) pagedbricks.append((brickidx, data)) # 3. Upload paged-in bricks to GPU texture pool for brickidx, data in pagedbricks: brickpool.upload(brickidx, data) # 4. Clear hash table for next frame missingbrickshashtable.clear() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The level of detail calculation must ensure pixel error remains below one to maintain visual fidelity while optimizing performance. Boundaries: When skipping empty bricks, the algorithm must correctly calculate the exit point to resume marching. Missing Data: If a brick is non-empty but absent, the system must gracefully degrade to the finest coarser level available rather than failing. A strategy where a ray requests intermediate levels of detail (bricks) along its path when a resolution is missing, flooding the hash table with requests. This produces more responsive, iteratively-refined images and converges in fewer frames. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The renderer is designed to render massive datasets extremely fast on commodity GPU hardware. It breaks the GPU-memory-size barrier that limits data sizes in prior work. Scaling: The methodology allows graceful scaling down to consumer-level graphics cards. Strengths: Performs brick lookup once per brick instead of every sample, maintaining a simple and familiar ray-marching core. Utilizes modern GPU features to implement a lock-free feedback data structure, enabling the implementation to spend more time computing on the GPU and less time pushing data around. Out-of-core, progressive rendering methodology breaks the GPU-memory-size barrier. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When rendering massive datasets on commodity GPU hardware where GPU memory is insufficient to hold the entire volume. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Ray-Guided Grid Leaping is reminiscent of the recent work of Hadwiger et al. [2] and Engel’s CERA-TVR [26], which in turn is based on the Gigavoxels system [3]. It shares with Hadwiger et al. the requirement of a set of simple multiresolution Cartesian grids and an OpenGL-based table to report missing bricks. From the CERA-TVR system, it inherits the idea to only recompute and request grid cells at boundaries. The work provides new depth to discussions of parameters relevant in the development of a ray-guided direct volume renderer, including strategies for loading higher resolution data, issues surrounding bricking and brick sizes, and the effect of brick layout strategies on large volume access times. An Analysis of Scalable GPU-Based Ray-Guided Volume Rendering, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4260263/, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Depth Sampling with Voxel Layer Alignment
head: Layered Interpolation, Optimal Interpolation, Optimal Interpolation for Ray Casting
body: Adaptive Depth Sampling with Voxel Layer Alignment is an acceleration technique for ray traversal that reduces the computational cost of trilinear interpolation by aligning sample points with voxel layers to enable bilinear interpolation, while skipping intermediate samples via adaptive depth sampling. It differs from standard trilinear interpolation by exploiting ray direction to align samples with voxel layers, allowing bilinear interpolation (lower cost) for half the points, and skipping intermediate points via adaptive depth sampling. The method operates on a regular 3D grid where voxels are aligned to integer coordinates. It assumes the ray traversal has already determined the entry and exit points within the volume. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Volume bounding box [x{min}, x{max}] \times [y{min}, y{max}] \times [z{min}, z{max}]. Grid dimensions Nx, Ny, Nz. Voxel spacing \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z (assumed uniform for simplicity, or incorporated into \mathbf{d}). Outputs: A sequence of sample positions \mathbf{p}i and their corresponding interpolated values. Data Structures: The volume data is stored in a 3D array or texture. No auxiliary structures are required beyond the ray parameters and volume bounds. Steps: 1. Determine the reference axis: Identify the axis perpendicular to the parallel voxel layers that are traversed fastest by the current ray. This is the axis corresponding to the largest component of the ray direction vector \mathbf{d}. Let this axis be k \in \{x, y, z\}. 2. Decide the first sampling position: Calculate the position where the ray enters the volume. Adjust this entry point slightly if necessary to ensure the first sample lies on a voxel layer along the reference axis k, or calculate the offset to the nearest voxel layer. 3. Calculate sampling interval l: Determine the sampling interval l along the ray such that every alternate sampling point lies exactly on a voxel layer perpendicular to the reference axis k. If the voxel spacing along axis k is \Deltak, and the ray direction component along k is dk, the distance between adjacent voxel layers along the ray is \Deltak / |dk|. To have every alternate point on a layer, the interval l is set to 2 \cdot (\Deltak / |dk|). 4. Sample and Interpolate: For sample points lying exactly on a voxel layer (every other point starting from the first), use bilinear interpolation in the two axes perpendicular to the reference axis k. This is significantly cheaper than trilinear interpolation. For sample points lying between voxel layers, use simplified trilinear interpolation. Apply adaptive depth sampling to skip the time-consuming points between layers. Specifically, skip every other sample point along the ray. Since the points on the layers are already sampled with bilinear interpolation, and the points between layers are skipped, the algorithm effectively samples only the points on the voxel layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivedepthsamplingraycasting(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds, volumedata, griddims, voxelspacing): # 1. Determine reference axis (axis of fastest traversal) absd = abs(raydirection) refaxis = argmax(absd) # 0 for x, 1 for y, 2 for z # 2. Calculate distance between voxel layers along the ray for the reference axis # Voxel spacing along the reference axis deltak = voxelspacing[refaxis] # Component of ray direction along reference axis dk = raydirection[refaxis] # Distance between adjacent voxel layers along the ray distbetweenlayers = deltak / abs(dk) # 3. Calculate sampling interval l for every alternate point on a layer # We want every 2nd point to be on a layer, so we skip one layer's worth of distance l = 2 distbetweenlayers # 4. Determine entry point into volume tentry = computerayvolumeintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) # Adjust entry point to align with first voxel layer if desired, # or simply start at tentry and let the first sample be the "layer" sample. # The method states "decide the first sampling position when the ray reaches the volume". # We assume the first sample is at tentry. samples = [] t = tentry while t < computerayvolumeexit(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds): # Calculate sample position samplepos = rayorigin + t raydirection # Check if samplepos is on a voxel layer along refaxis # A point is on a layer if its coordinate along refaxis is an integer multiple of deltak # relative to the volume origin. # Let's assume volume origin is (0,0,0) for simplicity, or adjust accordingly. coordk = samplepos[refaxis] isonlayer = isclosetointeger(coordk / deltak) if isonlayer: # Use bilinear interpolation in the other two axes val = bilinearinterpolation(samplepos, volumedata, griddims, voxelspacing, refaxis) else: # This point is skipped by adaptive depth sampling in the "skip every other" strategy. # However, the description says "use simplified trilinear interpolation for the other sampling points". # But then it says "skipping over every other sample point". # The optimization is to SKIP the points between layers. # So we do NOT process points between layers. pass # Adaptive Depth Sampling: Skip the next point (which would be between layers) # We advance by 2 distbetweenlayers, so the next point is on a layer. t += l samples.append((samplepos, val)) return samples def isclosetointeger(val, epsilon=1e-6): return abs(val - round(val)) < epsilon def bilinearinterpolation(pos, volumedata, griddims, voxelspacing, refaxis): # Interpolate in the two axes NOT equal to refaxis # This is a standard bilinear interpolation in 3D space, fixing the refaxis coordinate # Implementation details omitted for brevity, but standard bilinear interp. pass Parameters: Sampling interval l: Calculated as 2 \cdot \Deltak / |dk|. Adaptive depth factor: Skip every other sample point (factor of 2). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray parallel to a voxel layer: If dk \approx 0, the ray is parallel to the voxel layers of axis k. The distance between layers becomes infinite. This case must be handled separately, likely by choosing a different reference axis or falling back to standard trilinear interpolation. Precision: Floating-point errors may cause points that should be on a layer to be slightly off. Use a tolerance \epsilon when checking isonlayer. Boundary conditions: Ensure the ray entry and exit calculations are robust to avoid sampling outside the volume. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of interpolation operations by half (skipping every other point) and reduces the cost of the remaining interpolations from trilinear to bilinear. The sources state that the algorithm saved about 70% of ray traversal time by skipping over every other point along each ray. Memory Complexity: No additional memory structures are required beyond the volume data and ray parameters. Strengths: Significant speedup in ray traversal time. Exploits the regular structure of the voxel grid. Limitations: Only applicable to regular 3D grids. Requires careful handling of ray direction to determine the reference axis. May introduce artifacts if the skipping rate is too high for the scene's frequency content, though the sources do not discuss this trade-off explicitly. When to use: When rendering regular 3D volumes with high performance requirements and the ray traversal is a bottleneck. Particularly effective when combined with other acceleration techniques like boundary cell-based ray casting. The method was proposed in the context of high-performance parallel volume rendering, specifically as part of a fast serial ray casting algorithm. It is described in the NASA Technical Reports Server publication "Time-Critical Volume Rendering". The technique is somewhat similar to Levoy's optimization of adaptive image sampling within the image plane. Time-Critical Volume Rendering, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19990040407/downloads/19990040407.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) NASA Technical Reports Server (NTRS) 19990040407: Time-Critical Volume Rendering, https://archive.org/details/NASANTRSArchive19990040407, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Optimized Ray Casting
head: Adaptive Ray Casting, Boundary cell projection, Fast Ray Casting Algorithm, Octtree Ray Casting
body: Optimized Ray Casting is a volume rendering algorithm that accelerates image-order rendering by combining hierarchical data structures (octrees) with adaptive sampling and early ray termination. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard ray casting, which processes every voxel along a ray regardless of transparency or redundancy. It sets itself apart from siblings like Lazy Sweep Ray Casting by using explicit octtree traversal to skip transparent regions rather than relying on sweep-line or slab-based accumulation, and from Ray-guided volume rendering with missing brick reporting by focusing on single-volume hierarchical traversal rather than distributed brick management. Inputs: 3D scalar volume dataset (regular grid); camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}); rendering parameters (opacity threshold, sample region size, color/density difference thresholds). Outputs: 2D color image. Data Structures: 1. Octree: Hierarchical representation of the volume. Each node represents a macro-block (e.g., 8 \times 8 \times 8 voxels). Nodes are tagged as "fully transparent" if all constituent voxels are transparent. 2. Backstore: Pixel memory storing intermediate results for parallel renderers. Parameters: Alpha Cutoff: Opacity threshold for early ray termination. Typical values: 92% (electric field), 98% (neghip, brain). Sample Region Size: Square grid for adaptive sampling. Typical value: 3 \times 3 pixels. Color Difference Threshold: Max allowed difference for bilinear interpolation of adjacent pixels. Typical values: 10 (electric field), 40 (neghip), 30 (brain). Density Difference Threshold: Max allowed difference for adaptive ray density along a ray. Typical values: 30 (electric field), 80 (neghip), 5 (brain). Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline): Construct the octree from the volume data. Tag macros containing only transparent voxels. Detect boundary cells for traversal optimization. 2. Ray Initialization: For each pixel in the image, define ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. If a cut plane is defined, start the ray at the intersection with the plane instead of the dataset boundary. 3. Adaptive Ray Casting Loop: Coarse Pass: Cast rays on a coarse grid (e.g., every 3rd pixel). Refinement: For each coarse pixel, check adjacent pixels. If the color difference exceeds the threshold, cast additional rays for the intermediate pixels. Final Image Formation: Form the final image by bilinear interpolation of the ray-cast pixels. 4. Ray Traversal and Compositing (Per Ray): Traverse the octree to find the entry and exit points of the ray within the volume. Initialize accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0 and color C{acc} = 0. While \alpha{acc} < \text{Alpha Cutoff} and ray is within volume: Use the octree to skip over transparent regions. If a node is fully transparent, advance t past it. Sample the voxel value V at current t. Check density difference against previous sample. If difference > Threshold, ensure sufficient sampling density (cast additional rays if in adaptive mode). Compute transmittance T = \exp(-\sigma \Delta t) and opacity contribution \alpha = 1 - T. Update accumulated color: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{voxel} \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). Update accumulated opacity: \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). Advance t by step size \Delta t. If \alpha{acc} \ge \text{Alpha Cutoff}, terminate ray (Early Ray Termination). 5. Parallel Execution (Optional): Master GPU controls slave GPUs via a finite state automaton. Slaves render image tiles (e.g., 128 \times 128) independently. Macros are fetched asynchronously to slave pixel memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def optimizedraycasting(volumedata, camera, params): """ volumedata: 3D array of voxel values camera: object with origin o, direction d, and image dimensions params: dict with alphacutoff, colorthresh, densitythresh, regionsize """ # Preprocessing octree = buildoctree(volumedata) tagtransparentmacros(octree) imagewidth = camera.width imageheight = camera.height image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) # Adaptive Sampling: Coarse Grid step = params['regionsize'] # e.g., 3 coarsepixels = [] for y in range(0, imageheight, step): for x in range(0, imagewidth, step): ray = Ray(camera.o, normalize(camera.d + offset(x, y, camera))) color = castray(ray, octree, params) image[y, x] = color coarsepixels.append((x, y, color)) # Refinement: Interpolate missing pixels for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if (y % step != 0) or (x % step != 0): # Check neighbors for color difference neighbors = getneighbors(image, x, y) if any(abs(c - neighbors[0]) > params['colorthresh'] for c in neighbors): ray = Ray(camera.o, normalize(camera.d + offset(x, y, camera))) image[y, x] = castray(ray, octree, params) else: image[y, x] = bilinearinterpolate(image, x, y) return image def castray(ray, octree, params): alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = 0.0 t = ray.entryt prevval = None while alphaacc < params['alphacutoff'] and t < ray.exitt: # Octtree Skip node = octree.getnodeat(ray, t) if node.istransparent: t = node.exitt continue # Sample val = samplevolume(ray, t) # Adaptive Density Check if prevval is not None and abs(val - prevval) > params['densitythresh']: # In a full implementation, this might trigger sub-stepping # For this algorithm, it ensures we don't undersample high-contrast areas pass # Compositing alpha = computeopacity(val) color = computecolor(val) coloracc = coloracc + color alpha (1.0 - alphaacc) alphaacc = alphaacc + alpha (1.0 - alphaacc) prevval = val t += ray.stepsize return coloracc Accelerates direct illumination in Monte Carlo volume rendering by optimizing extinction estimates along light rays. Unlike the parent method which optimizes camera rays, this handles stochastic scattering vertices, requiring data structure rebuilding per light ray set. Visualizes CFD density/refractive index fields on distributed supercomputers. Converts curilinear grids to rectilinear multi-block voxel fields to avoid integral errors from overlapping grids, distributing voxels for efficient parallel ray-casting. Progressive ray casting that decomposes the image into screen-space tiles, sorts them by cost, and renders them in batches within a time budget. Optimizes GPU cache locality by processing tiles rather than individual rays, avoiding stalls on mobile/low-performance devices. Considers optical effects (caustics, shafts of light) in water modeled as a uniform particle density medium. Uses analytical functions for scattered light intensity based on distance, avoiding numerical integration and ray-tracing in favor of scanline Z-buffer and accumulation buffer techniques. Replaces real-time gradient calculation during raycasting with a pre-computed 3D RGBA texture lookup. Saves 6 extra texture fetches per sample by trading memory for computation speed, advantageous for VR hardware like HTC Vive. Modifies ray casting to reslice a volume along an arbitrary plane ax + by + cz + d = 0. Implemented by starting the ray search at the z-coordinate determined by the plane equation or continuing until the x-coordinate value, effectively removing voxels on one side of the plane. Time Complexity: Depends on the sparsity of the volume and the effectiveness of the octtree. In the worst case (fully opaque), it approaches O(N) where N is the number of voxels along the ray. With transparent regions, it is significantly faster due to skipping. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data plus O(M) for the octree, where M is the number of macro blocks. Measured Performance: On 16-processor SGI Power Challenge: Electric field (50^3) 0.04s, Neghip (68^3) 0.15s, Brain (256 \times 256 \times 124) 0.09s. On 4 processors: Electric field 0.39s, Neghip 1.02s, Brain 0.17s. On 8 processors: Electric field 0.11s, Neghip 0.93s, Brain 0.12s. On 12 processors: Electric field 0.06s, Neghip 0.28s, Brain 0.11s. More than 10 frames per second achieved on 16 processors for all datasets. Slave GPU rendering of 128 \times 128 tile for 128^3 dataset: 100-240 ms. Strengths: High performance on sparse/transparent volumes; interactive frame rates achievable on parallel hardware; adaptive sampling reduces aliasing without uniform high resolution. Limitations: Overhead of octtree construction and traversal for dense volumes; adaptive sampling may introduce artifacts if thresholds are poorly chosen. When to use: Sparse volumetric data (e.g., medical CT, scientific simulations); interactive applications requiring real-time feedback; parallel rendering architectures. When not to use: Dense, fully opaque volumes where octtree skipping provides little benefit; hardware with limited VRAM for octree storage. Originated in the late 1980s and early 1990s with work by Levoy and others on hierarchical volume representation. The specific "Fast Ray Casting Algorithm" with boundary cell projection and adaptive sampling was demonstrated on SGI workstations and parallel clusters in the early 1990s. It builds on Parent by introducing specific optimizations for hierarchical data traversal and adaptive sampling rates. Time-Critical Volume Rendering, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19990040407/downloads/19990040407.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) DTIC ADA236718: Achieving Direct Volume Visualization with Interactive Semantic Region Selection, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA236718, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Rendering and Interacting With Volume Models in Immersive Environments, https://doi.org/10.2312/ceig.20181153, fetched 2026-10-26 Hardware Support for the Display and Manipulation of Binary Voxel Models, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh88/103-117, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Light Ray Extinction Optimization
head: Light Ray Visibility Optimization, Direct Illumination Extinction Optimization
body: Light Ray Extinction Optimization accelerates the computation of direct illumination in Monte Carlo volume rendering by optimizing the extinction coefficient estimates along rays connecting scattering vertices to light sources. While the parent method, Optimized Ray Casting, focuses on visibility along camera rays, this technique extends the optimization to the light transport path, reducing variance in shadowed or complex volumetric regions. It is distinct from camera-ray optimization because the scattering locations are stochastic, requiring the data structure to be rebuilt for each set of light rays rather than updated progressively. Inputs: The scene's volume density field (implicit or explicit). The phase function for scattering events. The light source geometry and emission profile. The data structure used for visibility optimization (typically a hierarchical structure like a tree or grid-based structure capable of merging segments, as described in Optimized Ray Casting). Outputs: Optimized extinction coefficient \mu'(y) at any point y along a light ray. Transmittance estimates between a scattering vertex and the light source. Data Structures: The method reuses the same data structure employed for camera-ray visibility optimization. This structure maintains a set of segments representing intervals of constant or approximated extinction. Key operations include: insert(list, candidate): Inserts a new segment or sample point into the structure. merge(): Combines adjacent or redundant segments to reduce structure size. evaluate(y): Queries the structure to retrieve the optimized extinction coefficient \mu'(y) at a specific location y. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sample Light Rays: For each scattering vertex y determined during the rendering process (via delta tracking on camera rays), cast a ray towards the light source. 2. Stratified Sampling: Draw a fixed number of stratified samples along the light ray segment between y and the light source. The number of samples is a parameter; 200 samples are recommended as a trade-off between accuracy and speed. 3. Build Data Structure: Insert the stratified samples into the optimization data structure. Since scattering locations change stochastically across frames or passes, the data structure is built from scratch for each set of light rays rather than updated incrementally. Note: Splitting of existing segments or discarding of redundant samples is only necessary for progressive updates. For a standard per-pass build, these operations can be omitted to simplify implementation. 4. Compute Optimized Extinction: When estimating transmittance or sampling collisions for the light ray, query the data structure to obtain the optimized extinction coefficient \mu'(y) at the current position. 5. Delta Tracking with Optimized Coefficients: Use \mu'(y) to compute the decision probabilities for the delta tracking algorithm along the light ray. This allows for more efficient sampling of scattering events compared to using the raw or unoptimized density. 6. Handle Multiple Scattering (Optional): If multiple scattering is supported, sample additional rays at new scattering locations according to the phase function. Apply the same optimization process to these new light rays. 7. Ratio Tracking (Advanced): In implementations using ratio tracking [NSJ14], multiple vertices are produced during transmittance estimation. Each vertex requires an optimized extinction value, necessitating repeated queries to the data structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelightrayextinction(scatteringvertex, lightsource, datastructure, numsamples=200): """ Optimizes extinction estimation for a ray from a scattering vertex to a light source. Args: scatteringvertex: The 3D position y where scattering occurred. lightsource: Object defining the light's position and emission. datastructure: The hierarchical structure for extinction optimization. numsamples: Number of stratified samples to draw (default 200). Returns: The optimized data structure ready for transmittance queries. """ # 1. Define the ray segment from scattering vertex to light source # Note: For area lights, this may involve multiple rays or a representative direction. rayorigin = scatteringvertex raydirection = normalize(lightsource.position - rayorigin) raylength = distance(rayorigin, lightsource.position) # 2. Generate stratified samples along the ray # Stratified sampling ensures uniform coverage of the path samplepositions = generatestratifiedsamples(rayorigin, raydirection, raylength, numsamples) # 3. Evaluate raw extinction at sample positions # This assumes a function getdensity(p) exists from the volume dataset rawextinctions = [getdensity(p) for p in samplepositions] # 4. Build the data structure from scratch # Since scattering locations are stochastic, we do not merge with previous frames # We insert samples into the structure. # Optimization: Skip segment splitting/discarding if not doing progressive updates. datastructure.clear() for i in range(len(samplepositions)): datastructure.insert(samplepositions[i], rawextinctions[i]) # 5. Merge redundant segments if the structure supports it # This step reduces memory usage and query time datastructure.merge() return datastructure def queryoptimizedextinction(position, datastructure): """ Retrieves the optimized extinction coefficient at a given position. Args: position: The 3D point y to query. datastructure: The built optimization structure. Returns: muprimestar: The optimized extinction coefficient. """ return datastructure.evaluate(position) def renderlightcontribution(scatteringvertex, lightsource, datastructure): """ Computes the direct illumination contribution using optimized extinction. """ # Rebuild structure for this specific light ray optimizedstructure = computelightrayextinction(scatteringvertex, lightsource, datastructure) # Use delta tracking along the light ray # The decision probabilities are computed using the optimized extinction currentpos = scatteringvertex transmittance = 1.0 while currentpos is within light source bounds: # Get optimized extinction at current position muopt = queryoptimizedextinction(currentpos, optimizedstructure) # Compute decision probability for delta tracking # P(scatter) = muopt / mumax (where mumax is the majorant) # P(absorb) = 1 - P(scatter) # Sample event event = sampledeltatrackingevent(muopt) if event == SCATTER: # Compute scattering contribution contribution = transmittance lightsource.emission phasefunction(currentpos, lightsource) return contribution elif event == ABSORB: break else: # Move to next collision distance = sampledistance(muopt) currentpos += raydirection distance transmittance = exp(-muopt distance) return 0.0 Parameters: Number of samples: 200 samples per light ray is recommended as a good trade-off between accuracy and speed. Progressive Updates: Splitting of segments or discarding of samples is optional and only required for progressive rendering updates. For standard per-pass builds, these can be left out. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Stochastic Scattering Locations: Because scattering vertices are determined stochastically, the data structure cannot be reused across frames. It must be rebuilt from scratch for each set of light rays. Long Transport Paths: Optimizing extinction along very long transport paths (e.g., multiple scattering events far from the camera) is computationally costly and may yield no visual improvement. Memory Allocation: The method requires a static allocation for light ray optimization (e.g., 156MB as reported for the HEPTANE dataset) plus per-pixel allocations for structure sizes and offsets. Time Complexity: The cost is dominated by building the data structure for each light ray. With 200 samples, the overhead is low. On the HEPTANE dataset with 5000 samples per pixel, render times dropped from 51.7s (reference) to 21.47s–37s depending on the number of samples used for optimization. Memory Complexity: Requires a static allocation independent of resolution (e.g., 156MB) plus per-pixel allocations for the data structure. Strengths: Significantly reduces variance in direct illumination, especially in shadowed regions or complex volumetric scenes. Improves visualization quality without excessive computational cost. Limitations: Cannot be easily integrated into progressive rendering due to the stochastic nature of scattering locations. Optimizing for multiple scattering events far from the camera is inefficient. When to Use: When direct illumination variance is high and the scene contains complex shadowing or participating media. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained, or when the scene is optically thin and variance is already low. Light Ray Extinction Optimization was introduced in the context of view-dependent visibility optimization for Monte Carlo volume visualization. It builds upon the idea of optimizing camera-ray visibility by extending the same hierarchical data structure techniques to light rays. The method addresses the challenge of efficiently computing transmittance in participating media, where standard delta tracking can be inefficient due to high variance in dense regions. By optimizing the extinction coefficient estimates, the method allows for more efficient sampling of light transport paths. View‐Dependent Visibility Optimization for Monte Carlo Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70064, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Parallel Volume Rendering for Computational Flow Imaging
head: CFI Parallel Volume Rendering, Preprocessed Raytracing for CFI
body: Parallel Volume Rendering for Computational Flow Imaging (CFI) is a method for visualizing refractive index or density fields from Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations on distributed-memory supercomputers. It solves the problem of integral errors caused by intersecting or overlapping curvilinear CFD grids by converting them into rectilinear multi-block voxel fields. Unlike cell projection, which double-counts overlapping segments, or simple resampling, which creates unmanageably large regular grids, this method uses preprocessing to distribute voxels into balanced, regular regions for efficient parallel ray-casting. Inputs: Curvilinear, multi-zone, overlapping CFD grid data (e.g., hexahedral cells) representing flow fields (density, refractive index). Outputs: Rendered images (shadowgraph, schlieren, or interferometric) or field data. Data Structures: 1. Voxel Grid: A set of voxels derived from the continuous CFD geometry. Each voxel stores the physical property value (e.g., density \rho) and its position. 2. Region Block: A regular sub-region of the flow field, defined by equal divisions along the x and y coordinates. Each block is assigned to a specific processor in the distributed system. Parameters: Integration Rule: Trapezoidal rule. Communication: MPI (Message Passing Interface). Hardware: Distributed-memory architecture (e.g., Beowulf cluster with switch-based interconnect). Language: C++. Steps: 1. Voxelization: Convert the continuous geometric representation of the curvilinear CFD grids into a discrete set of voxels. This step maps the irregular grid cells to a voxel representation, avoiding the need for high-rate resampling to a single regular grid. 2. Region Division: Divide the entire flow field into regular regions by equally partitioning the domain along the x and y coordinates. 3. Load Balancing: Distribute the voxels into these regions such that each region contains approximately the same number of voxels. This mitigates load imbalances caused by the varying sizes and shapes of the original CFD cells, which can differ by several orders of magnitude due to adaptive mesh refinement. 4. Distribution: Assign each region (block of voxels) to a different processor in the parallel distributed-memory system using MPI. 5. Rendering (Ray-Casting): For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. The ray traversal is performed locally on the processor holding the relevant blocks. Each line integral process searches through all voxels in its assigned block. Formulas: The optical intensity I is calculated via line-of-sight integration. The integration is performed according to the trapezoidal rule over n segments along the light path. For Shadowgraph systems, which respond to the second derivative of flow density \rho, the intensity is proportional to: I \propto \int \left( \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial x^2} + \frac{\partial^2 \rho}{\partial y^2} \right) dz Discretized for n segments, this involves summing the contributions of the second derivatives at specific points. For Schlieren systems, which respond to the first derivative, the intensity depends on the orientation of the knife-edge or color filter: Vertical knife-edge: I \propto \int \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial x} dz Horizontal knife-edge: I \propto \int \frac{\partial \rho}{\partial y} dz For Interferometric systems (e.g., Mach-Zehnder), the light intensity is proportional to the fringe shift, which relates to the line integral of the refractive index (or density). """ # Step 1: Voxelization # Convert continuous curvilinear CFD grids into a set of voxels. # Each voxel contains position (x, y, z) and property value (e.g., density). allvoxels = voxelize(cfdgrids) # Step 2: Region Division & Step 3: Load Balancing # Divide the flow field into regular regions along x and y. # Distribute voxels to regions such that each region has ~equal voxel count. # This balances the load across processors despite varying cell sizes. regions = createbalancedregions(allvoxels) # Step 4: Distribution # Assign regions to processors. # In a real MPI implementation, this involves gathering voxels for this rank. myvoxels = getvoxelsforcurrentrank(regions) # Step 5: Rendering # Initialize output image image = new Image(imagewidth, imageheight) # Parallelize over pixels or blocks for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Cast ray for this pixel ray = castray(x, y) # Perform line-of-sight integration # The ray searches through all voxels in the assigned blocks intensity = integrateray(ray, myvoxels) image.setpixel(x, y, intensity) return image def voxelize(cfdgrids): """ Converts curvilinear CFD cells into a set of voxels. Returns a list of Voxel objects. """ voxels = [] for cell in cfdgrids: # Map the continuous geometric representation of the cell to voxels. # The specific voxelization algorithm (e.g., grid-based sampling) # is not detailed in the source, but the goal is to eliminate # overlap errors inherent in cell projection. cellvoxels = mapcelltovoxels(cell) voxels.extend(cellvoxels) return voxels def createbalancedregions(allvoxels): """ Divides the flow field into regular regions along x and y. Distributes voxels to ensure each region has approximately the same number of voxels. """ # Determine bounds of the flow field minx, maxx = getminmax(allvoxels, 'x') miny, maxy = getminmax(allvoxels, 'y') # Equally divide the field along x and y coordinates # The number of divisions is determined by the number of processors or desired block size numprocessors = MPICommsize() # Simple grid division strategy divisionsx = int(sqrt(numprocessors)) divisionsy = int(sqrt(numprocessors)) regions = [] for i in range(divisionsx): for j in range(divisionsy): region = { 'xstart': minx + i (maxx - minx) / divisionsx, 'xend': minx + (i + 1) (maxx - minx) / divisionsx, 'ystart': miny + j (maxy - miny) / divisionsy, 'yend': miny + (j + 1) (maxy - miny) / divisionsy, 'voxels': [] } regions.append(region) # Distribute voxels into regions for voxel in allvoxels: for region in regions: if region['xstart'] <= voxel.x < region['xend'] and \ region['ystart'] <= voxel.y < region['yend']: region['voxels'].append(voxel) break # Re-balance if necessary to ensure equal voxel counts per region # (Implementation detail: redistribute voxels from over-loaded to under-loaded regions) regions = balanceregions(regions) return regions def getvoxelsforcurrentrank(regions): """ Returns the voxels assigned to the current MPI rank. """ rank = MPICommrank() # Assuming regions are distributed round-robin or by contiguous blocks to ranks # The source states: "voxels in different regions are distributed into different parts" # and "every processor requires the same amount of storage space" return regions[rank]['voxels'] def castray(x, y): """ Creates a ray vector for pixel (x, y). """ # Ray origin and direction depend on camera setup # Not specified in detail, assumed standard perspective/orthographic projection return Ray(origin=(x, y, 0), direction=(0, 0, 1)) def integrateray(ray, voxels): """ Performs line-of-sight integration using the trapezoidal rule. """ # Sort voxels along the ray direction (z-axis) sortedvoxels = sortvoxelsbyz(voxels, ray) # Trapezoidal rule integration # Sum contributions of segments along the ray path integral = 0.0 for i in range(len(sortedvoxels) - 1): v1 = sortedvoxels[i] v2 = sortedvoxels[i+1] # Calculate integrand value (e.g., density derivative for schlieren) # The specific derivative (1st or 2nd) depends on the CFI mode val1 = getintegrand(v1) val2 = getintegrand(v2) # Distance between voxels along the ray dz = abs(v2.z - v1.z) # Trapezoidal rule: (val1 + val2) / 2 dz integral += (val1 + val2) / 2.0 dz return integral def getintegrand(voxel): """ Returns the appropriate integrand value based on the CFI mode. Shadowgraph: 2nd derivative of density. Schlieren: 1st derivative of density. Interferometry: Density/Refractive index. """ # Placeholder for specific derivative calculation # The source notes that the algorithm calculates values of the appropriate integrand # at certain points. return voxel.density # Simplified; actual implementation requires derivative computation def balanceregions(regions): """ Ensures each region has approximately the same number of voxels. """ # This step addresses the load imbalance caused by varying voxel sizes/shapes. # Voxels are moved between regions to equalize counts. # Exact rebalancing algorithm is not specified in the source. # A simple approach is to sort all voxels by a space-filling curve # and assign them to regions in order, ensuring balanced counts. allvoxels = [v for r in regions for v in r['voxels']] allvoxels.sort(key=lambda v: v.x + v.y) # Simple heuristic newregions = [] voxelsperregion = len(allvoxels) // len(regions) for i, region in enumerate(regions): startidx = i voxelsperregion endidx = startidx + voxelsperregion if i < len(regions) - 1 else len(allvoxels) region['voxels'] = allvoxels[startidx:endidx] newregions.append(region) return newregions Time Complexity: The preprocessing (voxelization and distribution) has a cost, but the rendering speed is improved by having fewer voxels to search in each block. The total searching speed increases as more blocks with fewer voxels are created, despite the distribution cost. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of voxels. This method avoids the excessive memory requirements of resampling to a high-resolution regular grid. Performance: Tested on a Beowulf cluster (9 nodes, 800 MHz Pentium III, 100 Mb/s Ethernet) with datasets of ~0.5 million hexahedral cells. The method showed significant performance improvement over cell projection and simple resampling. Strengths: Eliminates integral errors from overlapping grids; balances load across processors; efficient for large-scale distributed systems. Limitations: Requires preprocessing overhead; load imbalances are unavoidable but reduced; performance depends on the efficiency of the voxelization and distribution steps. Computational Flow Imaging (CFI) is a technique for flow visualization that simulates optical wave interaction with flow fields to generate digital images (shadowgraph, schlieren, interferometric). Traditional methods like cell projection suffer from integral errors when dealing with intersecting or overlapping curvilinear CFD grids. Simple resampling to a regular grid is inefficient due to high storage and rendering costs. This parallel volume rendering method was developed to address these issues on distributed-memory supercomputers, specifically implemented in C++ using MPI. name: STiles (Sorted Tiles)
head: Sorted Tiles, Sorting Tiles
body: STiles is a progressive ray casting technique that decomposes the image space into screen-space tiles, sorts them by estimated rendering cost, and renders them in batches across subsequent frames until a fixed time budget is reached. It addresses the problem of interactive volume rendering on mobile and low-performance devices by avoiding the stall caused by rendering high-resolution images in a single frame. Unlike FBSlabs, which renders fixed slabs across the entire image, STiles groups tiles of similar cost to efficiently utilize the GPU within a strict time budget, leveraging 3D texture cache locality by processing tiles rather than individual rays. The method operates in three phases: an interaction phase, a sorting phase, and a progressive rendering phase. Input: High-resolution volume dataset, transfer function, camera parameters, viewport dimensions. Output: Final high-resolution rendered image. Intermediate Data: T{low}: A 2D texture storing low-resolution color (RGB) and ray cost (Alpha). T{high}: A 2D texture storing high-resolution color for rendered tiles. Correlation Maps: Two 2D textures mapping sorted tile indices to unsorted tile coordinates and vice versa. 1. T{low}: A 2D texture where: RGB channels: Low-resolution ray casting color. Alpha channel: Ray cost, defined as the number of ray samples taken during the low-resolution pass. 2. Correlation Maps: Two textures generated during sorting. They allow translation between the sorted order of tiles and their original screen positions. 3. Tile Grid: The viewport is divided into square tiles of fixed size S \times S. Tile Size (S): 8x8 pixels. This size balances 3D texture cache locality against visual blockiness during the transition from low to high resolution. Time Budget (T{budget}): 0.1 seconds per frame. The maximum time allowed for rendering high-resolution tiles in a single frame. 1. Low Resolution Ray Casting (Interaction Phase): While the user interacts (rotates/zooms), perform standard low-resolution ray casting in a fragment shader. For each pixel, store the resulting color in the RGB channels of T{low} and the number of ray samples taken in the Alpha channel of T{low}. This alpha value serves as the estimated rendering cost for the corresponding high-resolution tile. 2. Tile Sorting (Sorting Phase): Triggered once user interaction stops. a. Tile Division: Split the viewport into tiles of size S \times S. b. Cost Estimation: For each tile, estimate its cost by querying the Alpha channel of T{low} at the tile's center pixel. c. GPU Radix Sort: Sort the tiles by their estimated cost using a GPU radix sort implemented in three compute shader steps: i. Group Counting: Classify tiles into groups based on cost and count the number of tiles in each group. ii. Group Offset Setting: Scan the counters to establish start offsets for each group in the output texture. iii. Sorting: Place tiles into the output texture according to the offsets. d. Correlation Maps: Generate two coordinate maps during sorting to translate between sorted tile indices and unsorted screen coordinates. 3. Progressive High Resolution Ray Casting (Rendering Phase): Render tiles in the sorted order into T{high}. a. Budget Management: Determine the number of tiles N to render in the current frame. The algorithm uses a decreasing tile budget per frame to compensate for the non-linear increase in accumulated time (as later tiles may be more expensive or cache misses increase). b. Rendering Loop: Render N tiles from the sorted list. After rendering each tile (or batch), measure elapsed time. If the time budget (0.1s) is exceeded, stop rendering for that frame. c. Ray Casting: In the fragment shader for high-resolution tiles, discard rays that do not intersect the proxy geometry. This allows empty or nearly empty tiles to complete instantly, even if their cost estimate was non-zero. 4. Compositing: For each pixel in the final image: If the pixel belongs to a tile that has been rendered in T{high}, use the high-resolution color from T{high}. Otherwise, use the low-resolution color from T{low}. This compositing is performed every frame, progressively replacing low-resolution pixels with high-resolution ones. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 3 and 4 in successive frames until all tiles are rendered and T{high} contains the complete high-resolution image. Unverified code. TILESIZE = 8 TIMEBUDGET = 0.1 # seconds Tlow: Texture2D # RGB: Low-res color, A: Ray cost (sample count) Thigh: Texture2D # RGB: High-res color for rendered tiles SortedTiles: Array[Tuple[int, int]] # List of (x, y) tile coordinates sorted by cost CorrMapSortedToUnsorted: Texture2D CorrMapUnsortedToSorted: Texture2D def initialize(): # 1. Low Resolution Ray Casting # Perform during user interaction renderlowres(Tlow) def oninteractionstops(): # 2. Tile Sorting numtilesx = viewportwidth // TILESIZE numtilesy = viewportheight // TILESIZE # Estimate costs from Tlow alpha at tile centers tilecosts = [] for y in range(numtilesy): for x in range(numtilesx): centerx = x TILESIZE + TILESIZE // 2 centery = y TILESIZE + TILESIZE // 2 cost = Tlow.getalpha(centerx, centery) tilecosts.append((cost, x, y)) # Sort tiles by cost (ascending) tilecosts.sort(key=lambda item: item[0]) # Extract sorted coordinates global SortedTiles SortedTiles = [(item[1], item[2]) for item in tilecosts] # Generate correlation maps using GPU radix sort compute shaders # Step i: Group counting # Step ii: Group offset setting # Step iii: Sorting # Output: CorrMapSortedToUnsorted and CorrMapUnsortedToSorted generatecorrelationmaps(tilecosts) def progressiverenderingloop(): global currenttileindex currenttileindex = 0 while currenttileindex < len(SortedTiles): starttime = getcurrenttime() # Determine number of tiles to render this frame # Budget decreases in later frames to compensate for non-linear time increase tilestorender = estimatetilebudget(currenttileindex, len(SortedTiles)) for i in range(tilestorender): if currenttileindex >= len(SortedTiles): break tilecoord = SortedTiles[currenttileindex] renderhighrestile(tilecoord, Thigh) currenttileindex += 1 # Check time budget if getelapsedtime(starttime) > TIMEBUDGET: break # Composite current image compositeimage(Tlow, Thigh, CorrMapSortedToUnsorted) # Wait for next frame waitforvsync() def renderhighrestile(tilecoord, targettexture): x, y = tilecoord # Render fragment shader for this tile region # Fragment shader discards rays not intersecting proxy geometry pass def compositeimage(Tlow, Thigh, corrmap): for each pixel (px, py): # Determine if this pixel is in a rendered high-res tile # Use correlation maps to check if (px, py) is covered by Thigh if ispixelinrenderedtile(px, py, corrmap): color = Thigh.getcolor(px, py) else: color = Tlow.getcolor(px, py) display(color) def estimatetilebudget(currentindex, totaltiles): # Heuristic: Render more tiles in early frames, fewer in later frames # to maintain stable frame time despite increasing complexity/cost # Exact formula not specified, but based on empirical charts # Returns an integer N return max(1, totaltiles - currentindex) # Placeholder logic, actual logic is heuristic Empty Tiles: Tiles with zero cost (empty regions) are rendered first. The fragment shader discards rays not intersecting proxy geometry, allowing these tiles to complete instantly. Cost Estimation Accuracy: Tile cost is estimated from a single sample at the tile center in T{low}. This is not perfectly reliable for the entire tile, but the impact is mitigated by the fast completion of empty tiles. Sorting Granularity: Sorting individual rays yields poorer performance than sorting tiles. Packing rays into tiles leverages the 3D texture cache. Visual Transition: The transition from low to high resolution is visible. Tile size 8 \times 8 is a compromise between cache performance and visual blockiness. Time Budget Exceedance: If the time budget is exceeded, rendering stops for that frame. The next frame resumes from where it left off. Time Complexity: The sorting phase is O(N \log N) or O(N) depending on the radix sort implementation, where N is the number of tiles. This is performed once per interaction session. The rendering phase is proportional to the number of tiles rendered per frame, bounded by the time budget. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for T{low}, T{high}, and correlation maps. Memory usage is O(W \times H), where W, H are viewport dimensions. Measured Performance: On Nexus 6, STiles achieved average completion times of 8.84s (Vix), 9.73s (Head), 8.83s (Obelix), 9.75s (Chamaleon), and 8.65s (Melanix). This is approximately half the time of FBSlabs. On Nexus 6P, times were 16.52s (Vix), 16.20s (Head), 17.06s (Obelix), 16.89s (Chamaleon), and 19.73s (Melanix). Strengths: Maintains interactivity by bounding frame time. Efficiently utilizes GPU cache by processing tiles. Faster completion than slab-based methods. Limitations: Requires multiple frames to reach full resolution. Visual transition artifacts. Sorting overhead (though negligible). When to Use: Mobile and low-performance devices where interactive frame rates are critical and full-resolution rendering cannot be completed in a single frame. When Not to Use: High-performance desktops where full-resolution rendering is feasible in one frame, or where visual continuity is more important than interactivity. STiles was introduced in the paper "Progressive Ray Casting for Volumetric Models on Mobile Devices". The work was motivated by the need to render large medical volume datasets (resolutions > 512^3) on mobile devices at full resolution while maintaining interactive frame rates. The method builds on the observation that rendering time increases non-linearly when rendering a fixed number of tiles per frame, necessitating a decreasing tile budget per frame. It was developed as an alternative to Front-to-back Slabs (FBSlabs) and Simple progressive ray casting, offering better performance and cache utilization.
