name: Prediction Buffer Voxel Traversal
head: Local Traversal, Modified Depth Buffer Traversal, Prediction Buffer, Sparse Traversal
body: Prediction Buffer Voxel Traversal is a GPU-accelerated dataset traversal technique that exploits frame-to-frame coherence during camera rotation to accelerate isosurface volume rendering. It uses a modified depth buffer, called the prediction buffer, to store ray-cast results from the previous frame, allowing the renderer to skip large portions of the volume or refine local searches instead of performing a full traversal for every pixel. Unlike C-buffer or image cache techniques that store coordinates or iso-maps and suffer from aliasing or lack data parallelism on GPUs, the prediction buffer stores depth distances and is designed for high-performance GPU parallelism. Inputs: Ray \mathbf{R} for each pixel, defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Volume dataset with bounding box defined by t{min} and t{max}. Isosurface value \rho{iso}. Prediction buffer from the previous frame. Step size parameter dt (adaptive based on data variance). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray where \rho(t) = \rho{iso}. Updated prediction buffer for the current frame. Prediction Buffer: A 2D array (one value per pixel) storing a single floating-point value d{ij} for pixel p{ij}. The value represents the distance from the eye to the interaction point along the ray. The value types are: 1. Positive number (d{ij} > 0): The ray hit the isosurface in the previous frame. The value is the distance to that hit. 2. Negative flag (d{hitBoxMissSurf}): The ray missed the isosurface but hit the volume bounding box in the previous frame. 3. Negative flag (d{missBox}): The ray missed the volume bounding box completely in the previous frame. 4. No information (d{noInfo}): No data available (e.g., first frame). \kappa{max}, \kappa{min}: Experimentally determined constants for adaptive step size. Typical values are \kappa{max} = 0.3 and \kappa{min} = 0.1. \alpha: Frequency of full traversal to correct errors. Typical value is \alpha = 10 (perform full traversal every 10 frames). dt: Step size for sparse traversal, calculated based on local data variance. 1. Ray Casting: Cast one ray for each pixel in the final rendered image. 2. Prediction Retrieval: Retrieve the prediction buffer value d{ij} for the current pixel from the previous frame. 3. Traversal Mode Selection: If d{ij} = d{missBox} or d{ij} = d{noInfo}, perform Full Traversal (standard DDA or dense sampling). If d{ij} = d{hitBoxMissSurf}, perform Local Traversal (refine search near bounding box entry). If d{ij} > 0, perform Sparse Traversal (skip to predicted depth). Note: Every \alpha frames, force Full Traversal for all pixels to prevent error accumulation. 4. Adaptive Step Size Calculation: Calculate dt using the variance v of the data in the current brick/region, and global min/max variances v{min}, v{max}: dt = \kappa{min} + (\kappa{max} - \kappa{min}) \frac{v - v{min}}{v{max} - v{min}} 5. Traversal Execution: Sparse Traversal: Start at t{start} = t{min} + d{ij}. Use the algorithm below to find the intersection. Local Traversal: Start at t{start} = d{ij}. Search in both forward and backward directions from t{start} until the isosurface is found or volume bounds are exceeded. 6. Prediction Buffer Update: Store the result of the current frame's ray cast into the prediction buffer for the next frame. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictionbuffertraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, predictionbuffer, framecount, alpha): """ Main entry point for prediction buffer voxel traversal. """ pixelid = getpixelidfromray(rayo, rayd) # Force full traversal periodically to correct drift if framecount % alpha == 0: return fulltraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso) # Retrieve prediction dprev = predictionbuffer[pixelid] # Determine traversal mode if dprev == dmissBox or dprev == dnoInfo: return fulltraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso) elif dprev == dhitBoxMissSurf: return localtraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, dprev) else: # dprev > 0 (hit isosurface) return sparsetraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, dprev) def sparsetraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, dprev): """ Sparse traversal starting from predicted depth. """ # Calculate adaptive dt based on variance (pseudo-code for variance calc omitted) dt = calculateadaptivedt(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax) # Start traversal from the predicted hit point # Note: The source describes starting at tmin + dt for the loop, # but using dprev to skip. We align tprev and tcurr around the predicted hit. # However, the provided Algorithm 2 in initializes tprev = tmin. # To implement the "skip" behavior described in text: tstart = tmin + dprev # We need to sample around tstart. # The source algorithm 2 is a standard DDA loop. # For sparse traversal, we jump to tstart. tprev = tstart tcurr = tstart + dt # Ensure we don't exceed bounds if tprev < tmin: tprev = tmin if tcurr > tmax: tcurr = tmax rhoprev = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tprev) rhocurr = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurr) while tcurr <= tmax: if rhoiso is between rhoprev and rhocurr: return bisectionfind(tprev, tcurr, rhoiso) tprev = tcurr tcurr = tprev + dt rhoprev = rhocurr rhocurr = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurr) return -1.0 def localtraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso, dprev): """ Local traversal starting from predicted depth, searching both forward and backward. """ dt = calculateadaptivedt(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax) tstart = dprev # Forward search tcurrfwd = tstart + dt tprevfwd = tstart rhoprevfwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tprevfwd) rhocurrfwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurrfwd) while tcurrfwd <= tmax: if rhoiso is between rhoprevfwd and rhocurrfwd: return bisectionfind(tprevfwd, tcurrfwd, rhoiso) tprevfwd = tcurrfwd tcurrfwd = tprevfwd + dt rhoprevfwd = rhocurrfwd rhocurrfwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurrfwd) # Backward search (if forward failed) tcurrbwd = tstart - dt tprevbwd = tstart rhoprevbwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tprevbwd) rhocurrbwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurrbwd) while tcurrbwd >= tmin: if rhoiso is between rhoprevbwd and rhocurrbwd: return bisectionfind(tcurrbwd, tprevbwd, rhoiso) tprevbwd = tcurrbwd tcurrbwd = tprevbwd - dt rhoprevbwd = rhocurrbwd rhocurrbwd = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tcurrbwd) return -1.0 def fulltraversal(rayo, rayd, tmin, tmax, rhoiso): """ Standard dense traversal (e.g., DDA). """ # Implementation of standard voxel traversal pass def trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, t): """ Sample volume data at ray position t. """ pos = rayo + rayd t return volumetexturesample(pos) def bisectionfind(ta, tb, rhoiso): """ Find exact intersection using bisection. """ for i in range(10): # Fixed iterations for convergence tmid = (ta + tb) / 2 rhomid = trilinearsample(rayo, rayd, tmid) if abs(rhomid - rhoiso) < epsilon: return tmid if (rhomid - rhoiso) (rhoa - rhoiso) < 0: tb = tmid rhob = rhomid else: ta = tmid rhoa = rhomid return (ta + tb) / 2 Skipping Isosurface: Sparse traversal may skip an isosurface if dt is too large, introducing artifacts. This is minimized by choosing dt based on data variance. Local Traversal Failure: Local traversal may fail to find the isosurface if the surface moves significantly between frames or if the local search exits volume bounds before finding the surface, producing incorrect results compared to Full Traversal. Error Accumulation: To remedy the risk of missing surfaces due to coherence errors, the method performs a full traversal every \alpha frames. Time Complexity: Significantly faster than full traversal during camera rotation due to skipped voxels. Sparse traversal contains no branching, yielding higher performance on CUDA architectures compared to regular traversal which has divergent branching penalties. Memory Complexity: Requires one additional floating-point value per pixel for the prediction buffer. Performance: The method can double the rendering speed compared to standard techniques. Performance is influenced by block size, shared memory usage, and texture vs. global memory access patterns. Strengths: High parallelism on GPUs; no divergent branching in sparse traversal; effective for interactive rotation. Limitations: Not suitable for large camera movements (coherence breaks); potential for visual artifacts if dt is poorly chosen or if the surface moves rapidly; requires periodic full traversal to correct errors. When to use: Interactive volume rendering with small camera rotations on GPU architectures. When not to use: Large viewpoint changes, static scenes with no coherence, or when strict visual accuracy is required without periodic correction. Origin: The technique was proposed by Braley et al. in "GPU Accelerated Voxel Traversal using the Prediction Buffer". History: It builds upon earlier work on C-buffers and image caches [Yoon et al. 1997], which were not suited for GPU architectures due to lack of data parallelism. It also relates to temporal coherence techniques by Klein et al. [2005]. Usage: Implemented using NVIDIA's CUDA toolkit (version 2.2 in the source) for massively parallel isosurface volume rendering. name: LLO-based Ray-casting
head: LLO ray-casting, Linear Level Octree ray-casting
body: LLO-based ray-casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates image-order rendering by utilizing a Linear Level Octree (LLO) spatial data structure to skip empty space and facilitate early ray termination. It differs from brute-force ray-casting by replacing uniform voxel traversal with hierarchical octree traversal, and from other acceleration structures by encoding the octree in a linear array to optimize cache residency and memory access patterns. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (voxel grid), a camera position, a camera orientation, and a homogeneous threshold value for LLO generation. Output: A 2D rendered image. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Linear Level Octree (LLO). The LLO is a hierarchical representation of the volume where each node represents an octant (a sub-volume). Node Classification: Each octant is classified based on the voxel values within it. The classification determines if the octant is "empty," "opaque," or "semi-transparent." Homogeneous Threshold: A threshold value is used to determine voxel classification during LLO generation. A value of 10 is used in the cited implementation. Linear Layout: The octree nodes are stored in a linear array. The specific indexing scheme allows for efficient traversal without explicit pointer chasing, leveraging spatial locality. Build the octree hierarchy by grouping voxels into octants. Mark octants as empty if they contain no significant data (below threshold) or as opaque/semi-transparent based on content. Store the resulting octree in a linear array. 2. Ray Casting Loop (for each pixel): Compute the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for the current pixel. Initialize ray parameter t = t{entry} (start of volume). Traversal: Start at the root of the LLO. Determine which octant the ray currently intersects. If the octant is empty: Skip the entire octant. Update t to the exit point of the octant. Move to the next intersected octant in the linear structure. If the octant is opaque: Perform standard ray-casting within this octant. name: Empty Space Skipping via Acceleration Structures
head: Acceleration Structure-Based Empty Space Skipping, Hierarchical Skipping
body: Empty space skipping via acceleration structures accelerates volume rendering by identifying and bypassing transparent or empty regions of the volume data before expensive sampling and compositing occur. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on geometric proxies [16346-progressive-ray-casting-for-volumetric-models-on-mobile-devi.md] or orthogonal opacity maps [990-occlusion-clipping-with-orthogonal-opacity-map.md], this family constructs explicit hierarchical or grid-based metadata structures (e.g., octrees, BVHs, min/max grids) to determine ray visibility [13062-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structure.md]. It sets itself apart from SparseLeap by typically using scalar min/max values or occupancy flags rather than rasterized segment lists, and from Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping by employing fixed-grid brick structures or specific tree traversals rather than generic bounding box hierarchies [13062-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structure.md]. The core mechanism shared by all children is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity or global performance budgets. Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. SparseLeap is a hybrid object-order (rasterization) and image-order (ray-casting) method for efficient empty space skipping in large, sparse volumes with fine structures. It solves the problem of high computational cost and space fragmentation inherent in standard hierarchical empty space skipping (e.g., octrees) by decoupling the empty space skipping data structures from the underlying volume representation. Unlike standard octree methods that suffer from fragmentation and high traversal costs, SparseLeap rasterizes view-independent occupancy geometry to generate per-pixel linked lists of ray segments, enabling "as-long-as-possible" skipping via simple linear list traversal without hierarchy traversal. This method accelerates traditional ray casting for large-scale aerosol visualization (smoke, fog, dust) by combining a Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree (BVH) for empty voxel skipping, early termination of light compositing, and grouped linear interpolation to reduce computational load. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like SparseLeap and Efficient Space Skipping & Adaptive Sampling of Unstructured Volumes Using H.W. Accel. Ray Tracing by specifically employing a BVH constructed from an octree traversal to avoid the overhead of recording empty nodes, which increases complexity in pure octree-based approaches, while offering dynamic update capabilities superior to K-D trees. SparseLeap is a ray-guided volume rendering technique that separates meta-data for empty space skipping from the volume data itself, using a ray segment list to process rays. It extends standard ray-casting by introducing an outer loop over ray segments and handling 'occupancy misses' to delay the determination of whether a brick is empty or non-empty until it is actually needed. Unlike octree-based skipping which incurs high depth complexity due to fragmented space subdivision, SparseLeap limits depth complexity by generating fewer, longer ray segments. Space skipping and empty volume culling are acceleration techniques in image-order volume rendering that reduce computational load by identifying and bypassing regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its primary focus on geometric or scalar-based determination of "visible" vs. "invisible" primitives (cells, voxels, or rays) before expensive integration occurs, whereas methods like Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control operate during the ray-marching process itself. This method accelerates direct volume rendering by using a hierarchical min/max acceleration structure to skip transparent regions of the volume data. It reduces the number of ray samples taken by allowing rays to jump over blocks that do not contain visible data, typically achieving a 1.5–2x speedup. It differs from sibling methods like Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping by using a fixed-grid brick structure rather than a tree of bounding boxes, and from SparseLeap by relying on scalar min/max values rather than occupancy or sparse data structures. Empty Space Skipping (ESS): Rays start sampling at the boundaries of a proxy geometry that roughly adjusts to non-transparent regions of the volume model, discarding transparent regions. Definition: A method to skip empty space using a hierarchical formulation to reduce computational impact, and a quadratic term on visibility to mitigate smoke-like artifacts in real scenes. Step: For each hierarchical level above the first, store the voxel grid of the previous level. If the density value for a voxel in that grid is smaller than a threshold \lambdav = 1.0, skip the voxel and treat it as empty. Formula: Auxiliary loss Ls = \lambdas (-4(T - 0.5)^2 + 1), where T is the total visibility for each ray, and \lambdas = 0.1. This term helps mitigate smoke-like artifacts and keeps real scenes sparse. Parameter: \lambdas = 0.1. The concept of empty space skipping is fundamental to efficient volume rendering, particularly for large-scale datasets where most of the volume is transparent or empty. Early implementations relied on simple grid-based checks or octrees [13062-empty-space-skipping-via-acceleration-structure.md]. The use of hierarchical bounding box trees (BVH) for aerosol visualization was developed to handle large-scale smoke and fog [8182-hierarchical-bounding-box-tree-for-empty-space-skipping.md]. SparseLeap was introduced to address the fragmentation issues in standard octree-based skipping by decoupling the skipping data from the volume representation [5152-sparseleap.md]. The auxiliary terms for smoke mitigation were introduced in the context of view-dependent radiance fields to address shape-radiance ambiguity. name: SparseLeap
head: Empty Space Skipping via Rasterized Ray Segment Lists, SparseLeap-an effective empty space skipping technique
body: SparseLeap is a hybrid object-order (rasterization) and image-order (ray-casting) method for efficient empty space skipping in large, sparse volumes with fine structures. It decouples empty space skipping data structures from the underlying volume representation, avoiding the space fragmentation and hierarchy traversal overhead typical of standard octree-based approaches. By rasterizing view-independent occupancy geometry into per-pixel linked lists of ray segments, it moves the major cost of empty space skipping from the ray-casting shader to GPU hardware rasterization. SparseLeap operates in four main stages: building an occupancy histogram tree, generating occupancy geometry, rasterizing ray segment lists, and performing ray-casting with linear list traversal. Inputs: Volume data (grid, octree, etc.) and segmentation labels. Current transfer function and set of active (enabled) objects. Camera view parameters (position, orientation). Outputs: Rendered image with empty space skipped. Updated occupancy histogram tree (if grown/pruned). Occupancy Histogram Tree Node (CPU): Child pointers (standard tree structure). Histogram: Three integer counts representing the number of leaf nodes in the sub-tree for each occupancy class: countempty, countnonempty, countunknown. Leaf nodes may store metadata (min/max scalar value, contained objects) for culling. Occupancy Geometry (GPU): A set of nested bounding boxes. Each box has an associated occupancy class (empty, non-empty, unknown). Boxes are emitted only when the occupancy class changes during a top-down tree traversal. Ray Segment List Buffer (GPU): Two arrays per pixel resolution: 1. Linked List Elements: Array of size screenwidth screenheight maxdepthcomplexity. Each element is 12 bytes. Layout: start (float, ray parameter), end (float, ray parameter), class (uint8, occupancy class) [G: inferred from 12-byte size and segment definition]. 2. Linked List Heads: Array of size screenwidth screenheight. Each head is 16 bytes. Layout: headindex (int32, index into elements array), count (uint32, number of segments) [G: inferred from 16-byte size and linked list header definition]. 1. Build/Update Occupancy Histogram Tree: Traverse the tree recursively in depth-first order starting at the root. For leaf nodes, determine occupancy class by comparing metadata against the current transfer function and active object set: If all contained objects are disabled or min/max scalar value results in zero opacity: empty. Otherwise: non-empty. If metadata is missing or culling is delayed: unknown. For non-leaf nodes, compute histogram as the sum of children's histograms. 2. Generate Occupancy Geometry: Traverse the occupancy histogram tree top-down. Emit a bounding box for a node only if its occupancy class differs from its parent's class. Box sizes decrease from root to leaves. Re-use previously generated geometry if occupancy classes have not changed (e.g., only light direction changed). 3. Rasterize Ray Segment Lists: Rasterize the occupancy geometry onto the screen. For each pixel, generate a linked list of ray segments corresponding to the intersections with the bounding boxes. Merge consecutive segments of the same occupancy class into a single segment. The rasterization order ensures segments are sorted from front to back along the ray. Re-use existing ray segment lists if the view has not changed (e.g., only lighting changed). 4. Ray-Casting with Linear List Traversal: For each pixel, retrieve its ray segment list. Traverse the list from front to back. Skip segments with class empty. For segments with class non-empty or unknown: Sample the volume data within the segment. If class is unknown, generate an occupancy miss. Perform standard front-to-back compositing for sampled segments [G: standard volume rendering loop]. Occupancy Histogram Propagation: For a non-leaf node N with children C1, C2, \dots, Ck: HN = \sum{i=1}^{k} H{Ci} where HN is the histogram vector (count\empty, count\non\empty, count\unknown) for node N. Ray-Casting Loop: C{acc} = 0, \alpha{acc} = 0 \text{for each segment } S \text{ in ray segment list:} \quad \text{if } S.class == \text{empty: continue} \quad \text{if } S.class == \text{unknown:} \quad \quad \text{trigger occupancy miss for } S \quad \quad \text{continue} \quad \text{sample volume along } S \quad C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \quad \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \quad \text{if } \alpha{acc} > \text{threshold: break} Occupancy Classes: empty, non-empty, unknown. List Element Size: 12 bytes. List Head Size: 16 bytes. Screen Resolution: 1,200×1,200 (used in implementation examples). Unknown Class Handling: If a ray encounters a segment of class unknown, the ray-caster generates an occupancy miss. This triggers asynchronous culling or tree growth. Sparsity Requirement: The technique is only efficient if the volume is sufficiently sparse, as storing and computing metadata incurs overhead that must be amortized. Tree Growth/Pruning: If an occupancy miss corresponds to a non-existent node, the tree is grown to include it. Unused nodes are pruned using a least-recently used strategy. NeRF Dependency: When used with NeRF, the effectiveness of empty space skipping depends on the quality of the NeRF output, as accurate volume density information improves skipping. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class OccupancyNode: def init(self): self.children = [] self.histogram = [0, 0, 0] # [empty, nonempty, unknown] self.metadata = None # min/max scalar, objects self.class = None # leaf class def buildoccupancytree(root, transferfunction, activeobjects): def dfs(node): if node is leaf: node.class = determineleafclass(node, transferfunction, activeobjects) else: for child in node.children: dfs(child) node.histogram = sum(child.histogram for child in node.children) dfs(root) def determineleafclass(leaf, transferfunction, activeobjects): if leaf.metadata is None: return 'unknown' if allobjectsdisabled(leaf.metadata, activeobjects): return 'empty' if zeroopacity(leaf.metadata, transferfunction): return 'empty' return 'nonempty' def generateoccupancygeometry(root): geometry = [] def traverse(node, parentclass): if node.class != parentclass: geometry.append(BoundingBox(node.spatialextent, node.class)) for child in node.children: traverse(child, node.class) traverse(root, 'empty') return geometry def rasterizeraysegmentlists(geometry, camera, screenwidth, screenheight): # Initialize buffers elements = [] # List of (start, end, class) heads = [None] (screenwidth screenheight) # Rasterize geometry for box in geometry: if box.class == 'empty': continue # Skip empty boxes for rasterization? No, rasterize all to get segments # Rasterize box onto screen for pixel in pixelsintersectingbox(box, camera): segment = (box.raystart, box.rayend, box.class) if heads[pixel] is None: heads[pixel] = [] heads[pixel].append(segment) # Merge consecutive segments of same class for pixel in range(screenwidth screenheight): if heads[pixel] is not None: merged = mergesegments(heads[pixel]) heads[pixel] = merged return elements, heads def mergesegments(segments): if not segments: return [] merged = [segments[0]] for seg in segments[1:]: if seg.class == merged[-1].class: # Merge: extend end of last segment merged[-1] = (merged[-1].start, seg.end, seg.class) else: merged.append(seg) return merged def raycast(screenwidth, screenheight, heads, volumesampler): image = zeros((screenheight, screenwidth, 3)) for y in range(screenheight): for x in range(screenwidth): ray = getray(x, y) segments = heads[y screenwidth + x] if segments is None: continue Cacc = 0 alphaacc = 0 for seg in segments: if seg.class == 'empty': continue if seg.class == 'unknown': # Trigger occupancy miss continue # Sample volume along segment Csample, alphasample = volumesampler.sample(ray, seg.start, seg.end) # Composite alphaterm = alphasample (1 - alphaacc) Cacc += Csample alphaterm alphaacc += alphaterm if alphaacc > 0.99: break image[y, x] = Cacc return image Uses a hierarchical tree of bounding boxes for empty space skipping. Choose when a strict hierarchy is preferred over rasterization. Extends SparseLeap with dynamic tree growth and pruning based on occupancy misses. Choose when volume sparsity changes dynamically. Traditional space skipping using bounding volumes. Choose for simpler implementations without rasterization. General acceleration structure-based skipping. Choose for generic volume representations. Focuses on mobile performance with progressive rendering. Choose for mobile devices. Time Complexity: Rasterization is O(G) where G is the number of occupancy geometry primitives. Ray-casting is O(S) where S is the number of non-empty segments per ray. Memory Complexity: GPU memory for ray segment lists is O(W \cdot H \cdot D) where W, H are screen dimensions and D is average depth complexity. Occupancy geometry is significantly smaller than equivalent octrees (kilobytes vs megabytes). Measured Performance: On a Geforce Titan X with 1,200×1,200 resolution, SparseLeap achieved higher frame rates than octree-based methods for sparse volumes. For the Lego dataset (100x100 resolution), SparseLeap skipped 31.96% of empty space and achieved a PSNR of 22.23 with N=32 samples per ray, compared to 20.60 for hierarchical sampling. Strengths: Avoids space fragmentation, decouples empty space skipping from volume sampling, leverages GPU rasterization, supports dynamic transfer functions and object sets. Limitations: Requires sufficient sparsity to amortize overhead, dependent on NeRF quality for NeRF-based rendering. When to Use: Large, sparse volumes with fine structures, dynamic transfer functions, or active object sets. When Not to Use: Dense volumes where sparsity is low, or when hardware rasterization is not available. SparseLeap was introduced by Hadwiger et al. in 2018. It was designed to address the limitations of standard octree empty space skipping, which suffers from space fragmentation and high traversal costs for large, finely detailed volume data. The method has been applied to various datasets including SEM Mouse Cortex, Aneurysm, Stag Beetle, and Xmas Tree. It is also used in conjunction with Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to improve rendering efficiency. head: Accelerated Ray Casting with BVH and Early Termination, Large-Scale Aerosols Visualization via Accelerated Ray Casting, Large-scale Aerosols Visualization Method, Ray Casting Acceleration Algorithm
body: This method accelerates traditional front-to-back ray casting for large-scale volumetric data (specifically aerosols like smoke, fog, and dust) by combining a Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree (BVH) for empty-space culling, early termination of the compositing loop, and adaptive sampling with grouped linear interpolation. It addresses the low efficiency and high resource consumption of standard ray casting when processing large scalar fields. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on octrees or sparse grids, this approach uses a BVH to avoid recording numerous empty nodes, thereby reducing computational complexity and allowing for dynamic updates when the dataset changes. Input: A 3D scalar field representing volume data (e.g., density/opacity values for aerosols); camera parameters (viewpoint, direction, field of view); rendering parameters (early termination threshold, sampling intervals). Output: A 2D image where each pixel color is computed via front-to-back compositing, skipping empty regions and terminating rays that are sufficiently opaque. An AABB is defined by two 3D vectors: min and max, representing the minimum and maximum coordinates along the x, y, and z axes. The six faces are parallel to the xy, xz, and yz planes. The BVH is a binary tree used to store the shape of bounding boxes. Root Node: Represents the largest bounding box encompassing the entire volume data. Internal Nodes: Each internal node has exactly two child nodes, representing two sub-bounding boxes that partition the parent's space. Leaf Nodes: Each leaf node corresponds to a sub-block of the volume data. Node Attributes: Empty: The sub-block contains no valid data (or values below a significance threshold). Non-Empty: The sub-block contains valid data. Unknown: The status is not yet determined or requires further traversal (used during construction). Proportion: For non-leaf nodes, an attribute representing the proportion of child nodes that are non-empty, used to assign the node's primary attribute. 1. Subdivision: The volume data is subdivided into blocks. Each leaf node corresponds to one such block. 2. Boundary Expansion: To avoid interpolation errors at block boundaries (where interpolated values might exceed the original block's min/max), each sub-data block is expanded by one voxel in all directions during the construction phase. 3. Min/Max Storage: The minimum and maximum values of each sub-data block are counted and stored in the bounding box structure to facilitate 3D texture generation and culling decisions. 4. Octree Pre-processing: The data is recursively divided into eight parts to form an octree. Leaf nodes of this octree are marked as Empty, Non-Empty, or Unknown. Non-leaf nodes are assigned the attribute of their children that has the highest proportion. 5. BVH Generation: A breadth-first search is performed on the octree. Bounding boxes are constructed for volume data blocks whose attributes differ from their parent nodes. These boxes form the BVH. 1. Divide the volume data into initial blocks. 2. For each block, expand the data by one voxel to handle boundary interpolation safety. 3. Compute the minimum and maximum scalar values for each expanded block. 4. Build an underlying octree by recursively dividing blocks into eight children. 5. Label octree leaves as Empty, Non-Empty, or Unknown based on data presence. 6. For each octree internal node, calculate the proportion of Non-Empty children. Assign the node's attribute to the majority label (e.g., if >50% children are Non-Empty, label the parent Non-Empty). 7. Traverse the octree (BFS). Identify blocks where the attribute differs from the parent. 8. Construct AABBs for these differing blocks. 9. Organize these AABBs into a binary BVH structure, where internal nodes represent the union of their children's AABBs, and leaves represent the specific data blocks. For each pixel, cast a ray from the camera through the pixel into the volume. 1. Ray-BVH Intersection: Determine the entry and exit points of the ray into the BVH. 2. Traversal: Traverse the BVH from the root. If the ray does not intersect a node's AABB, skip the entire subtree. If the ray intersects a leaf node's AABB: Check the leaf's attribute. If Empty, skip sampling within this block. If Non-Empty, proceed to sample. 3. Merging and Deletion: As the ray passes through multiple bounding boxes, merge overlapping valid ranges and delete empty ranges to determine the final valid sampling intervals. Standard ray casting uses a fixed sampling interval. This method adapts the interval and interpolation based on the ray's position and data validity. 1. Adaptive Interval: Initialize a base sampling interval \Delta. As the ray traverses the volume: If an invalid (empty) sampling point is encountered, increase the sampling interval (reduce resampling frequency). If a valid (non-empty) sampling point is encountered, restore the interval to the base value. 2. Grouped Linear Interpolation: Divide all resampling points on the ray into three levels based on their distance from the viewpoint: Level 1: Closest to the viewpoint. Level 2: Intermediate distance. Level 3: Farthest from the viewpoint. Apply different linear interpolation complexities for each level. The amount of interpolation calculation decreases from Level 1 to Level 3. This reduces computational load without significantly reducing image authenticity. During the front-to-back compositing loop, check the cumulative opacity \alpha{acc} after each sample. 1. Condition: If \alpha{acc} > T{term}, where T{term} is the early termination threshold, terminate the ray calculation. 2. Rationale: As \alpha{acc} approaches 1, the pixel value becomes saturated, and further sampling has minimal effect on the final color. 3. Threshold: The specific numerical value for T{term} is not given in the sources. Unverified code. Initialize compositing variables alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = vec3(0.0) currentpos = ray.origin stepsize = BASEINTERVAL distancefromviewpoint = 0.0 # 3. Iterate through valid ranges for startt, endt in validranges: # Adjust step size based on validity (Adaptive Sampling) # Note: In this simplified loop, we assume we are already in a valid range. # The logic from implies stepsize increases when hitting invalid points # and resets when hitting valid ones. Since we are iterating validranges, # we reset to BASEINTERVAL at the start of each valid range. stepsize = BASEINTERVAL # Sample within this valid range t = startt while t < endt: samplepos = ray.origin + ray.direction t # Get sample value (density/opacity) # Note: Actual implementation requires trilinear interpolation of volumedata sample = volumedata.sample(samplepos) # Calculate sample opacity and color contribution # Assuming sample is density, convert to alpha via transfer function alphasample = transferfunction(sample) colorsample = illuminationmodel(sample, samplepos, ray.direction) # Front-to-back compositing # Cacc = Cacc + Csample alphasample (1 - alphaacc) # alphaacc = alphaacc + alphasample (1 - alphaacc) weight = alphasample (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc += colorsample weight alphaacc += weight # Early Termination Check if alphaacc > TTERM: break # Adaptive Step Size Logic (Simplified for valid range traversal) # If we encounter an "invalid" point inside a range (e.g. below threshold), # we might increase step size. However, the BVH culling handles empty blocks. # The adaptive sampling in seems to apply to the continuous traversal. # Here, we assume validranges are dense enough or we check individual points. # Grouped Interpolation Level Selection distancefromviewpoint = length(samplepos - camera.origin) interplevel = getinterpolationlevel(distancefromviewpoint) # The interpolation complexity is handled in the volumedata.sample() call # based on the level. # Advance position t += stepsize if alphaacc > TTERM: break return coloracc def getvalidrangesbvh(ray, bvh): """ Traverses the BVH to find valid (non-empty) sampling intervals. Merges and deletes empty ranges as per. """ validranges = [] stack = [bvh.root] while stack: node = stack.pop() # Check intersection with AABB if not rayintersectsaabb(ray, node.aabb): continue if node.isleaf: if node.attribute == NONEMPTY: # Calculate intersection interval with the leaf's AABB tmin, tmax = rayaabbintersection(ray, node.aabb) if tmin < tmax: validranges.append((tmin, tmax)) else: # Push children to stack (order doesn't strictly matter for correctness, # but front-to-back is better for early termination) stack.append(node.right) stack.append(node.left) # Merge overlapping ranges and sort by tmin validranges = mergeranges(validranges) validranges.sort(key=lambda r: r[0]) return validranges def getinterpolationlevel(distance): """ Divides resampling points into 3 levels based on distance from viewpoint. Level 1: Closest Level 2: Intermediate Level 3: Farthest """ # Exact thresholds are not given in sources # This is a placeholder for the logic described if distance < LEVEL1RANGE: return 1 elif distance < LEVEL2RANGE: return 2 else: return 3 Early Termination Threshold (T{term}): A value for cumulative opacity \alpha{acc} above which the ray calculation is terminated. The sources state "a threshold can be set" but do not specify a numerical value. Sampling Interval: Base interval for resampling. Increased when invalid points are encountered, restored when valid points are found. Boundary Interpolation Errors: Interpolating values at the edges of sub-data blocks can result in values greater than the maximum or smaller than the minimum of the original block. This is mitigated by expanding each sub-data block by one voxel during BVH construction. Empty Node Overhead: Unlike octrees, the BVH construction avoids recording many empty nodes, which reduces computational complexity. However, if the BVH is not constructed efficiently, traversal overhead may negate benefits. Dynamic Data: The BVH can be dynamically updated if the dataset changes frequently, unlike some static structures. The sources note that compared to octree-based methods, this BVH method avoids recording many empty nodes, which increases computational complexity in those alternative methods. Rendering: The time complexity per ray is reduced by skipping empty spaces and early termination. The adaptive sampling and grouped interpolation further reduce the cost of interpolation calculations. Hardware: AMD Ryzen 5 5600H with Radeon Graphics 3.30 GHz, Windows 10 64-bit, 16GB memory. Software: Visual Studio 2019, Unity3D, C#, HLSL. Results: The method reduces unnecessary space debris, lowering hardware load and improving rendering speed, meeting real-time rendering requirements for large-scale aerosols. It significantly shortens total interpolation calculation time compared to traditional algorithms. Strengths: Avoids recording many empty nodes compared to octree-based methods. Not heavily dependent on the spatial position of non-empty voxels. Can be dynamically updated if the dataset changes frequently. Reduces hardware load and improves rendering speed for large-scale aerosols. Limitations: The specific numerical values for parameters (like T{term} and interpolation level ranges) are not provided, requiring empirical tuning. The method is tailored for large-scale aerosols; performance on other types of volumetric data is not explicitly detailed. The method was proposed in the paper "Large-scale Aerosols Visualization Based on the Accelerated Ray Casting Algorithm". It was developed to address the disadvantages of traditional ray casting algorithms, such as low efficiency, slow speed, and large resource consumption when rendering aerosol data (smoke, fog, dust) in 3D scenes. The method combines several optimization techniques: 1. BVH for Empty-Space Skipping: Uses a hierarchical bounding box tree to cull empty voxels. 2. Early Termination: Stops compositing when cumulative opacity exceeds a threshold. 3. Adaptive Sampling: Adjusts sampling intervals based on data validity. 4. Grouped Linear Interpolation: Reduces interpolation cost by varying complexity based on distance from the viewpoint. name: SparseLeap Ray-Casting with Occupancy Misses
head: Ray-guided volume rendering with empty space skipping
body: SparseLeap is a volume rendering technique that separates meta-data for empty space skipping from the volume data itself, using a ray-guided framework where ray segments are processed in a list. It extends standard ray-casting by adding an outer loop over ray segments and handling 'occupancy misses' to delay the determination of whether a brick is empty or non-empty until it is actually needed. Unlike octree-based skipping which incurs high depth complexity due to fragmented space subdivision, SparseLeap limits depth complexity significantly by substituting homogeneous sub-trees in the occupancy histogram tree on-the-fly. SparseLeap operates within a ray-guided volume rendering framework that relies on lazy evaluation. The method augments the standard front-to-back compositing loop with an outer loop that iterates over a list of ray segments. These segments are derived from an occupancy histogram tree, which tracks the empty/non-empty status of volume bricks. Inputs: Ray segment list: A list of segments along each view ray, each tagged with an occupancy class (empty, nonempty, or unknown). Volume data: Stored in bricks, managed by an out-of-core memory system. Occupancy Histogram Tree: A hierarchical structure representing the occupancy status of volume bricks. Outputs: Rendered image pixel colors. Updated occupancy histogram tree (with homogeneous sub-trees substituted and unused nodes retired). Ray Segment Each entry in the ray segment list represents a contiguous portion of a ray. start: Ray parameter t{start} (float). end: Ray parameter t{end} (float). occupancyclass: Enum or integer code. 0: Empty (skip). 1: Nonempty (sample). 2: Unknown (resolve miss). Occupancy Histogram Tree Node occupancyclass: The dominant occupancy class of the sub-tree. ishomogeneous: Boolean flag indicating if all children share the same occupancy class. children: References to child nodes (if not a leaf). usagecount: Integer for LRU eviction tracking. 1. Initialization: For each pixel, cast a view ray. Generate an initial ray segment list covering the ray's path through the volume. Initially, segments may be marked as unknown if their occupancy is not yet determined. 2. Outer Loop (Segment Iteration): Iterate through the ray segment list linearly. Process consecutive overlapping pairs of ray events to define segments. 3. Segment Classification: If occupancyclass is empty: Skip the segment. Advance the ray position to t{end} of the current segment. Continue to the next segment. If occupancyclass is nonempty: Proceed to sampling. If occupancyclass is unknown: Generate an occupancy miss. 4. Occupancy Miss Resolution: When an occupancy miss occurs, trigger culling to determine the actual occupancy class of the underlying volume brick. If the brick is determined to be empty: Update the segment's class to empty and skip. If the brick is determined to be nonempty: Update the segment's class to nonempty and proceed to sampling. Delayed Update: Bricks never intersected by view rays (occluded or outside frustum) do not have their occupancy class determined, saving computation and memory bandwidth. 5. Sampling: If the segment is nonempty, perform standard ray-casting sampling within the segment bounds. Data Cache Miss Handling: If the volume data for the current brick is not in cache, generate a data cache miss to load it. If the class is unknown, do not generate a data cache miss immediately. Resolve the occupancy miss first. Only load data if the resolution confirms the brick is nonempty. If the class is empty or unknown (and resolved as empty), no data cache miss is generated. 6. Homogeneous Sub-tree Substitution: After occupancy updates, check the occupancy histogram tree for sub-trees where all nodes have the same occupancy class. Substitute these homogeneous sub-trees with a single node of that class. This is determined efficiently using occupancy histograms. 7. Memory Management (LRU): The ray-caster reports usage of volume bricks to the out-of-core memory management system. Unused nodes in the occupancy histogram tree are retired regularly using a Least-Recently Used (LRU) scheme based on this usage information. This scales the tree size to the current working set rather than the whole volume. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sparseleapraycast(ray, segmentlist, occupancytree, volumecache): """ Renders a single ray using SparseLeap logic. """ color = vec4(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 # Iterate through segments in the list for segment in segmentlist: tstart = segment.start tend = segment.end occclass = segment.occupancyclass # Step 3: Classify segment if occclass == EMPTY: # Skip empty segments continue elif occclass == UNKNOWN: # Step 4: Resolve occupancy miss actualclass = resolveoccupancymiss(segment, occupancytree) if actualclass == EMPTY: continue elif actualclass == NONEMPTY: occclass = NONEMPTY else: # Should not happen if resolution is correct, but handle as skip continue # Step 5: Sampling if occclass == NONEMPTY: # Check if data is in cache if not volumecache.contains(segment.brickid): # Generate data cache miss (only if nonempty) volumecache.load(segment.brickid) # Perform standard ray-casting integration for this segment # This involves stepping through samples within [tstart, tend] samplecolor, samplealpha = standardraycastsegment( ray, tstart, tend, volumecache, segment.brickid) # Front-to-back compositing alphacontribution = samplealpha transmittance color += samplecolor alphacontribution transmittance = (1.0 - samplealpha) # Early termination check (standard optimization) if transmittance < EPSILON: break return color def resolveoccupancymiss(segment, occupancytree): """ Determines if a brick is empty or nonempty. Updates the occupancy tree if necessary. """ brickid = segment.brickid # Check tree for existing classification if occupancytree.isclassified(brickid): return occupancytree.getclass(brickid) # Perform culling computation (expensive, but only done when needed) isempty = performculling(brickid) newclass = EMPTY if isempty else NONEMPTY # Update tree occupancytree.setclass(brickid, newclass) # Step 6: Check for homogeneous sub-trees and substitute occupancytree.substitutehomogeneoussubtrees(brickid) return newclass Empty Space Skipping Granularity: Can be as small as 4^3 blocks for terabyte-sized volumes. This allows finer granularity than the brick size used for memory management (e.g., 32^3 blocks). Block Sizes for Culling: Evaluated sizes include 4^3, 8^3, 16^3, and 32^3 blocks. Order-Dependent Rasterization: The rasterization of occupancy geometry into ray segment lists must process fragments in the same order as they are submitted to OpenGL. This is handled using the ARBfragmentshaderinterlock capability. Short Empty Segments: Very short empty ray segments that cannot be merged into a longer empty segment because they precede a non-empty segment are detected and removed to reduce depth complexity. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of samples processed by skipping empty space. The complexity depends on the depth complexity of the ray segment list. Memory Complexity: The occupancy histogram tree scales with the current output size (working set) rather than the whole volume, thanks to LRU retirement of unused nodes. Measured Performance: On the SEM Mouse Cortex dataset, SparseLeap had an average of 3.84 segments per ray (min 1, max 31), while octree traversal had an average of 13.44 intersected nodes (min 4, max 45). Strengths: Limits depth complexity significantly compared to octree-based skipping. Scales better to finely detailed, sparse data. Output-sensitive culling avoids processing occluded regions. Limitations: Requires implementation of fragment shader interlock for correct rasterization order. Culling computation is deferred, which may cause latency spikes if many misses occur simultaneously. When to Use: Large-scale, sparse volume datasets where empty space skipping is critical for performance. When Not to Use: Dense volumes where empty space skipping provides little benefit, or hardware lacking ARBfragmentshaderinterlock. SparseLeap was introduced in the paper "SparseLeap: Efficient Empty Space Skipping for Large-Scale Volume Rendering". It is implemented using OpenGL with GLSL shaders and integrated with a large-scale out-of-core raycasting system. Evaluation was performed on an NVIDIA GeForce Titan X (Pascal) GPU with 12 GB RAM. name: Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling
head: Empty Space Skipping, Volume Culling
body: Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling refers to a family of acceleration techniques in volume rendering that reduce computational load by identifying and excluding primitives, voxels, or ray segments that do not contribute to the final image. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping by encompassing a broader range of strategies, including geometric bounding volumes, visibility masks, and parallel segment lists, rather than relying solely on hierarchical tree traversal. It differs from Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control by focusing on pre-computed or geometrically derived exclusion zones rather than just dynamic ray state termination. The core mechanism shared by all children is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity or global performance budgets. Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists is a distributed-memory and shared-memory parallel volume rendering algorithm that accelerates ray casting by precomputing lists of occupied volume segments to skip empty space. It distributes image rows across MPI ranks and OpenMP threads, calculating sampling points based on a derived step length. It differs from siblings like SparseLeap by using explicit segment lists derived from volume geometry rather than sparse voxel octree traversal or occupancy misses, and from Visibility Culling by operating at the ray-segment level rather than tile or view-frustum level. See Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists. Visibility Culling is a family of acceleration techniques in volume rendering that reduces computational load by identifying and excluding primitives, voxels, or ray segments that do not contribute to the final image. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling by focusing on optical or geometric visibility relative to the camera, rather than purely on geometric emptiness, and from Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control by often operating on pre-computed or screen-space visibility masks rather than just dynamic ray state. See Visibility Culling. Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling restricts volume reconstruction computation to the "effective" reconstruction area by calculating an initial bounding volume and slicing it according to the viewing direction, using these slices as a depth buffer to guide reconstruction. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Hierarchical Bounding Box Tree for Empty-Space Skipping by using a simple geometric approximation (truncated shapes) rather than a hierarchical tree structure, and from Occupancy Mask Culling by being an approximation rather than an exact mask of projection data shadows. See Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling. Definition: A rendering optimization that infers ray-BBox intersection to sample query points only within the scene bounding box, applicable only to bounded scenes. Steps: Fuse approximately ten point-wise operations for the forward and backward pass of the density-to-alpha function conversion. In the volume rendering accumulation, halt tracking a ray once the accumulated transmittance falls below 10^{-3}. Definition: Acceleration methods that localize the surface interface and concentrate samples only in relevant regions, effectively skipping empty space, because only 10-20% of evaluated samples have non-zero density. Steps: Refine the sampling strategy to focus solely on the localized surface. Comparison: Standard volumetric rendering is inefficient because it samples the entire ray; surface localization reduces the number of required MLP evaluations by skipping empty space. Definition: Optimization to avoid visiting every volume at every step. Previously, the march visited every volume at every step just to ask cellindex whether it was inside, and almost always was not. The new method builds an active list up front, so a step only visits volumes whose t-range contains it. Comparison: Differs from the previous approach which visited every volume at every step. The new approach is pure work elimination and produces byte-identical output. The concept of skipping empty space in volume rendering dates back to the early days of ray casting, where the primary goal was to avoid sampling voxels with zero density. Early methods relied on simple bounding boxes or grid-based occupancy flags. As rendering hardware evolved, more sophisticated structures like hierarchical bounding box trees and sparse voxel octrees were introduced to handle larger and more complex datasets. The rise of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and implicit representations has renewed interest in these techniques, leading to methods like parsimonious ray sampling and surface localization acceleration that integrate culling directly into the learning and rendering pipeline. Parallel implementations have further optimized these techniques for distributed and multi-threaded environments, enabling real-time rendering of large-scale volumetric data. name: Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists
body:
Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists is a parallel rendering algorithm that distributes image rows across MPI ranks and OpenMP threads to accelerate volume rendering. It uses segment lists to skip empty space and calculates sampling points based on a step length. It builds on Space Skipping and Empty Volume Culling by explicitly generating a list of active ray segments to bypass empty regions before sampling. Inputs: Image dimensions (width, height), camera parameters (position, direction, field of view), volume data structure (with block/brick layout), configuration (sampling rate, thread counts, MPI size). Outputs: Rendered image (pixel colors). Data Structures: raytracer struct: Fields mstartx, mstarty, mendx, mendy, mwidth, mheight, mdepth, mwriter, mthreadId. Segment: Pair of floats (sbeg, send) representing the start and end distances of an active ray segment within the volume. pointlist: List of floats representing sampling positions along the ray. seglist: List of Segment objects returned by the volume structure. Parameters: samplingrate: Controls step length. Typical value 1.0. threadnums: Number of OpenMP threads. Default 4. commsize: Number of MPI ranks. Steps: 1. Calculate Step Length: step\len =  rac{1.0}{samplingate \cdot \|dims\|} where dims is the volume dimension vector. 2. Determine Job Count: If config::multithreading is true, jobs = config::corecount config::corethreadcount; else jobs = 1. 3. Calculate Row Distribution: line

The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parallelraycastingsegmentlists(width, height, campos, raydir, volume, config): # Step 1: Calculate step length dims = volume.getdimensions() samplingrate = config.get('samplingrate', 1.0) steplen = 1.0 / (samplingrate norm(dims)) # Step 2: Determine job count if config.get('multithreading', True): jobs = config.get('corecount', 1) config.get('corethreadcount', 1) else: jobs = 1 # Step 3: Calculate row distribution commsize = config.get('commsize', 1) threadnums = config.get('threadnums', 4) linenums = ceil(height / commsize) tlinenums = ceil(linenums / threadnums) # Step 4: Precompute block offsets (simplified) bufbase = volume.getbaseaddress() blockoffsets = {} for k in range(volume.getdepth()): for j in range(volume.getheight()): for i in range(volume.getwidth()): block = volume.getblock(k, j, i) if block is None: blockoffsets[(k, j, i)] = -1 else: blockoffsets[(k, j, i)] = block.data - seg.x) / steplen) steplen currentpos = alignedbeg while currentpos <= send: pointlist.append(currentpos) currentpos += steplen # Render pixel using pointlist renderpixel(row, col, campos, raydir, pointlist, volume) Uses visibility information to skip rays that do not intersect the volume. Visibility Culling Uses bounding volumes to cull empty space. Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of active samples. The parallelization reduces wall-clock time by a factor proportional to the number of threads and MPI ranks, subject to communication overhead. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels and the number of segments. The segment list size depends on the volume's empty space ratio. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of MPI ranks and OpenMP threads. Strengths: Efficiently skips empty space, reducing the number of samples per ray. Parallelization improves performance on multi-core and multi-node systems. Limitations: Requires precomputation of segment lists. Performance depends on the efficiency of the segment list generation and the distribution of work across threads. When to use: When rendering large volumes with significant empty space on parallel hardware. When not: When the volume is dense and empty space skipping provides little benefit, or when the overhead of segment list generation is high. name: Visibility Culling
body: Visibility Culling is a family of acceleration techniques in volume rendering that reduces computational load by identifying and bypassing data or primitives that do not contribute to the final image. It sets itself apart from its siblings by encompassing a broad range of strategies—from geometric frustum tests to optical termination and screen-space feedback—unlike Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling which focuses strictly on geometric emptiness, or Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists which focuses on parallelization efficiency. The core mechanism shared by all children is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying computational effort based on local coverage (e.g., skipping full screen regions) or global completion (e.g., terminating when all pixels are covered). Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control are acceleration techniques that reduce the computational cost of volume rendering by halting the ray-marching integration loop when the remaining contribution to the pixel is deemed negligible. Unlike Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map which culls based on pre-computed opacity maps, or Empty-space skipping which skips geometrically empty regions, these methods operate on the accumulated state of the ray during traversal. They set themselves apart from Bounding Volume Culling by relying on optical properties (opacity/transmittance) rather than geometric bounds, and from Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping by focusing on the termination of the integration path rather than the step size. Probabilistic Culling is a rendering optimization that intentionally allows false-negatives in intersection tests to reduce duplicated fragments and rendering time, particularly in virtual reality (VR) and high-resolution contexts. It sets itself apart from conservative culling methods by trading strict geometric accuracy for performance, relying on the fact that resulting visual artifacts are imperceptible. Visibility Feedback with Screen Space Subdivision is an out-of-core volume rendering optimization that uses visibility information gathered during the current frame to prevent the loading and refinement of occluded data in subsequent frames. Unlike standard early ray termination, which only skips computation after data has already been loaded into the GPU working set, this method feeds visibility results back to the loader to reduce GPU memory usage and bandwidth. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining occlusion queries with a screen-space subdivision strategy to interleave query processing with rasterization, thereby hiding the latency inherent in asynchronous occlusion query results. Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping is an acceleration technique for direct volume rendering that combines space leaping (empty voxel skipping) with adaptive variable step-size sampling. It solves the problem of redundant computation in large datasets containing significant empty space, such as medical CT scans, by bypassing empty regions entirely and adjusting sampling density based on local voxel occupancy. Unlike traditional equidistant ray casting, this method reduces computational overhead without altering the input data structure. A preprocessing technique that decomposes the domain of viewing directions into 24 regions on a directional cube to extract a lower number of potentially visible voxels compared to the standard 6-region decomposition, improving extraction rate and rendering speed. Frustum culling is a visibility culling technique that reduces rendering load by filtering out faces, chunks, or primitives that lie outside the camera's viewing frustum. It solves the problem of unnecessary computation for geometry that does not contribute to the final image by performing a conservative intersection test between bounding volumes and the six planes defining the view frustum. It operates on spatial extent relative to the camera orientation and projection, distinguishing it from depth-based occlusion or transmittance-termination methods. This method prevents infinite rendering loops in interactive volume visualization by detecting when the rendering pipeline exceeds the frame budget and forcing a quality reduction on the subsequent frame. It acts as a safety mechanism distinct from standard early termination, which stops individual rays based on opacity Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control. The Visible Zone Algorithm is a conservative visibility computation method that determines which primitives are potentially visible from a set of viewpoints by projecting them into screen space and retaining only those within a specified depth thickness. It sets itself apart from approximate visibility methods by guaranteeing correct visibility with less than one pixel of screen-space deviation. The Occlusion-Aware Visibility Filter replaces the standard view-frustum test in 3D Gaussian Splatting densification with a rendering-based signal that restricts statistical updates to Gaussians that actually contribute to the final image. Unlike sibling methods that rely on binary flags or pixel counts, this method uses the sum of blending weights to determine visibility, ensuring that occluded Gaussians do not accumulate densification statistics. Definition: An optimization dividing image space into equal-sized squares of n \times n pixels to reduce overhead from per-pixel visibility testing. If a screen region is full, rasterization skips to the next boundary. Performance: Screen regions save another 3 percent of overall rendering time on average. Definition: A GPU-based visibility test using a 2^D Boolean lookup table to cull cells that do not intersect the transfer function's opacity range, reducing load on the rendering stage. Steps: Geometry shader computes the minimum and maximum of the 8 cell corner values. These two values are used as table lookup indices to fetch a visibility value. If the cell is deemed visible, the geometry shader instantiates its 6 faces. Parameters: Visibility Lookup Table: A 2^D table where D is the number of scalar value bins. For each pair of values s1 and s2, the table holds 1 if there exists at least an opacity which is non-zero for scalar values in [s1, s2], otherwise 0. Performance: On a PC with two Xeon E5345 processors, 4GB memory, GeForce 8800 GTX (768MB), using the 'meteorite' dataset (2,377,878 cells), removing the look-up table drops performance to <1 fps (specifically 0.76 fps). Adding the look-up table increases framerate to ~3.48 fps. Adding the hybrid CPU-GPU mesh traversal mechanism to the look-up table optimization increases the framerate to 3.62 fps. Visibility culling in volume rendering has evolved from simple geometric checks to complex, view-dependent, and feedback-driven mechanisms. Early implementations focused on reducing overhead in ray casting by dividing image space into screen regions to skip full areas. As rendering moved to GPU-based pipelines, techniques like scalar range lookup tables were introduced to cull cells based on transfer function opacity ranges, significantly improving performance for AMR datasets. The family also includes safety mechanisms like Interactive Render Quality Estimation & Cancellation to prevent infinite loops in real-time applications, and view-dependent preprocessing such as 24-Region View-Dependent Visibility Preprocessing and feedback loops like Visibility Feedback with Screen Space Subdivision to manage out-of-core data loading. name: Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control
head: Early Ray Termination, Probabilistic Termination, Russian Roulette in Volume Rendering
body: Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control are acceleration techniques that reduce the computational cost of volume rendering by halting the ray-marching integration loop when the remaining contribution to the pixel is deemed negligible. Unlike Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map which culls based on pre-computed opacity maps, or Empty-space skipping which skips geometrically empty regions, these methods operate on the accumulated state of the ray during traversal. They set themselves apart from Bounding Volume Culling by relying on optical properties (opacity/transmittance) rather than geometric bounds, and from Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping by focusing on the termination of the integration path rather than the step size. The core mechanism shared by all methods in this family is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity or global performance budgets. Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. Proactively skips intervals of the ray path before sampling, often using auxiliary data structures like octrees, bounding volumes, or occupancy grids. It sets itself apart from Early Stop by operating on the internal structure of the volume data rather than accumulated opacity. Limits raymarching to a specific geometric boundary, dropping rays that exceed a certain distance from the eye or miss the volume entirely. It differs from this family's core termination logic by using hard geometric constraints to discard rays before or during traversal. A randomized early-out technique that removes the statistical bias introduced by deterministic early termination. It probabilistically terminates rays with low contribution weights while scaling up the weights of surviving paths to maintain an unbiased expectation of the final pixel color. Limits the computation of noise frequencies in procedural volumes by breaking the evaluation loop as soon as the ray position is determined to be outside the bounding volume of the current frequency level. It builds on this family by applying early loop breaks specifically to hierarchical noise evaluation. A GPU-based technique that combines single-pass fragment shader execution with dynamic branching, transmittance-based early termination, and dithered starting positions to hide staircase effects. Skips fragment shader execution for rays that have already accumulated sufficient opacity by performing a depth test before the main volume rendering pass, deferring the termination decision to the rasterizer's depth buffer. Adjusts the near and far bounds of volumetric ray sampling using a learned depth prior (disparity map) to restrict integration to relevant depth ranges, reducing floating artifacts and unnecessary computation. Halts the front-to-back ray integration loop once the accumulated opacity exceeds a predefined threshold. It differs from Russian Roulette by using a deterministic cutoff rather than a probabilistic one, which introduces a systematic bias in exchange for reduced noise and computational cost. Terminates ray integration early once the accumulated color change between consecutive samples falls below a defined threshold, monitoring the rate of change in the accumulated color rather than just opacity saturation. A mechanism that allows a query coordinate to be finalised early (not processed further) when its predicted uncertainty is less than a certain threshold, avoiding unnecessary calculations. During training, sample points can exit at multiple stages. During inferencing, points exit only once at a specific stage. Points found earlier to be reliable immediately exit and are rendered. Which branch is taken depends on clustering results. The concept of early termination in volume rendering has evolved from simple opacity thresholds to sophisticated probabilistic and uncertainty-aware methods. Early implementations relied on deterministic checks against accumulated opacity or transmittance to skip remaining samples. The introduction of Russian Roulette addressed the bias inherent in deterministic cutoffs by providing an unbiased statistical alternative. More recent developments, such as Recursive-NeRF, incorporate uncertainty prediction to dynamically decide when a query point is reliable enough to terminate processing, enabling efficient rendering of complex scenes by clustering uncertain points into sub-networks. name: Empty-space skipping
head: ESS, Empty Region Skipping, Empty space culling
body: Empty-space skipping (ESS) is a volume rendering acceleration technique that reduces computational cost by identifying and bypassing regions of the volumetric dataset that are transparent or contain no relevant data. It solves the problem of wasted computation when ray marching through empty space, which constitutes a significant portion of the rendering time in sparse volumes. Unlike Early Stop, which terminates rays based on accumulated opacity, ESS proactively skips intervals of the ray path before sampling, often using auxiliary data structures like octrees, bounding volumes, or occupancy grids. It sets itself apart from Bounding Volume Culling by operating on the internal structure of the volume data rather than just external object bounds. The method modifies the standard ray-marching loop by inserting checks against an acceleration structure or occupancy map to determine if a segment of the ray lies within empty space. If empty, the ray is advanced to the next non-empty boundary; if not, standard sampling proceeds. Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, volume dataset V, acceleration structure A (e.g., octree, occupancy grid, min-max bricks), transfer function TF. Output: Accumulated color C{acc} and opacity \alpha{acc} for the pixel. The specific layout depends on the variant, but common structures include: 1. Occupancy Grid: A 3D texture or array where each voxel stores a binary value (occupied/empty). 2. Min-Max Bricks/Texture: A coarse 3D texture storing the minimum and maximum scalar values of disjoint blocks from the original volume. For example, a block size of 8^3 might be stored in a texture 1/8 the size of the original volume, with R-channel for min and G-channel for max. A secondary 2D texture (CT) may map (min, max) pairs to boolean occupancy based on the transfer function. 3. Distance/Occupancy Map: A texture storing the distance to the nearest non-empty voxel or a binary occupancy flag, often indexed by ray direction to handle anisotropy. 4. Octree/BSP Tree: Hierarchical nodes storing statistical bounds (min/max) for child regions. The following pseudocode implements a generic ESS loop using a distance/occupancy map, following the Block and Chebyshev variants from. Unverified code. Typical values depend on resolution; higher factors yield coarser sampling. alphathre: Opacity threshold below which a region is considered empty. Typical value: 10^{-2}. earlystopeps: Transmittance threshold for early termination. Typical value: 10^{-4}. esstype: Integer flag selecting the ESS variant. 1 = Block Empty Space Skipping; 2 = Chebyshev Empty Space Skipping. Degenerate Rays: Rays with infinite length, NaN components, or length > \sqrt{3} (in normalized space) should be terminated immediately to prevent performance regressions.
