name: Early Stop
head: Early stop+0, Early stop+1
body: Early Stop (ES) is an optimization for sphere tracing procedural volumes that limits the computation of noise frequencies (fi) by breaking the evaluation loop as soon as the ray position is determined to be outside the bounding volume of the current frequency level. It solves the problem of unnecessary function evaluations when a ray has moved sufficiently far from the isosurface, thereby reducing the computational cost per step. Unlike standard sphere tracing which computes all octaves up to n at every step, ES dynamically determines the minimum necessary octave i{min} based on BVH bounds, trading potential step size reduction for significant savings in function evaluations. It builds on Early Termination and Probabilistic Path Control by applying early loop breaks specifically to hierarchical noise evaluation. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Procedural volume defined by a sum of noise functions Fn(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=0}^{n} fi(\mathbf{p}). Isovalue v defining the isosurface. BVH structure where each level i provides an upper bound function BVH{i+}(\mathbf{p}) and optionally a lower bound BVH{i-}(\mathbf{p}). Parameter k: the number of additional frequencies to compute beyond the minimum required (typically k=1). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray. Normal \mathbf{n} at the intersection point. Data Structures: BVH Levels: A hierarchy where level i corresponds to the bounding volume of the noise function fi. Each level i provides a cheap-to-evaluate inclusion function BVH{i+}(\mathbf{p}) which bounds the range of fi(\mathbf{p}). Frequency Functions: fi(\mathbf{p}), typically octaves of a noise function (e.g., FBM), which are more expensive to evaluate than the BVH bounds. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Start sphere tracing from the ray origin \mathbf{o}. Let current position be \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} and accumulated distance t = 0. 2. Determine Minimum Index (i{min}): For the current position \mathbf{p}, find the smallest index i such that the upper bound of the BVH at that level is strictly below the isovalue v. This indicates that the position is outside the bounding volume of fi. i{min} = \min\{i \mid BVH{i+}(\mathbf{p}) < v\} If searching for the isosurface from inside the volume, this can equivalently be defined using the lower bound: BVH{i-}(\mathbf{p}) > v. 3. Compute Frequencies: Evaluate the noise functions fi(\mathbf{p}) starting from i{min} up to i{min} + k. Compute BVH{i+}(\mathbf{p}) for each i as you compute fi(\mathbf{p}). If BVH{i+}(\mathbf{p}) < v, the position is outside the bounding volume for level i. Stop evaluating further fi functions once i > i{min} + k. 4. Calculate Step Size: Use the computed sum F{i{min}+k}(\mathbf{p}) to determine the step size \Delta t for sphere tracing. The step size is typically derived from the distance to the isosurface estimate provided by the current frequency sum. 5. Advance Ray: Update position \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \Delta t \cdot \mathbf{d} and accumulate t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. 6. Check Termination: If the ray has exited the volume or converged to the isosurface within a tolerance, return the result. Otherwise, go to Step 2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def earlystopspheretrace(rayorigin, raydir, isovalue, k, maxsteps, maxdist): # Standard sphere tracing initialization p = rayorigin t = 0.0 MAXOCTAVES = 16 # Example maximum BVH depth MINSTEP = 1e-4 # Prevents infinite loops on flat regions TOLERANCE = 1e-3 # Convergence threshold for step in range(maxsteps): # Step 1: Find imin imin = 0 while imin < MAXOCTAVES: if bvhupperbound(imin, p) < isovalue: break imin += 1 # Step 2: Compute frequencies from imin to imin + k currentsum = 0.0 for i in range(imin, imin + k + 1): currentsum += noisefunction(i, p) # Step 3: Determine step size disttosurface = abs(currentsum - isovalue) # Approximate gradient magnitude for procedural noise gradmag = max(1.0, sum(abs(noisegradient(i, p)) for i in range(imin, imin + k + 1))) deltat = disttosurface / gradmag # Safety clamp deltat = max(deltat, MINSTEP) if t + deltat > maxdist: break # Step 4: Advance ray t += deltat p = rayorigin + deltat raydir # Step 5: Check convergence if abs(noisefunction(MAXOCTAVES, p) - isovalue) < TOLERANCE: normal = noisegradient(MAXOCTAVES, p) return t, normal / math.sqrt(normal[0]2 + normal[1]2 + normal[2]2) return None, None def bvhupperbound(level, p): # Returns a conservative upper bound for octave level at position p # Implementation depends on the specific inclusion function used return 1.0 - 0.1 level # Placeholder logic consistent with bounded noise def noisefunction(level, p): # Evaluates the noise octave level at position p # Typically a fractal Brownian motion component return math.sin(p[0] (2level)) math.cos(p[1] (2level)) math.sin(p[2] (2level)) (0.5level) def noisegradient(level, p): # Returns the analytical or numerical gradient of octave level at p # Used for step size estimation eps = 1e-5 f = noisefunction(level, p) gx = (noisefunction(level, (p[0]+eps, p[1], p[2])) - f) / eps gy = (noisefunction(level, (p[0], p[1]+eps, p[2])) - f) / eps gz = (noisefunction(level, (p[0], p[1], p[2]+eps)) - f) / eps return (gx, gy, gz) Note: The exact step size calculation and helper functions depend on the specific sphere tracing implementation and the properties of the noise function. The key aspect of Early Stop is limiting the number of noisefunction calls to i{min} + k. Parameters: k: The number of additional frequencies to compute beyond i{min}. Typical value is k=1. v: Isovalue for the isosurface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Early Stop+0 (k=0): Computing only f{i{min}} causes slow convergence at every level of the BVH traversal. The ray steps safely to the current outer bounding volume and repeats, massively increasing the total number of steps. This is particularly bad for grazing rays (rays passing close to but not entering a bounding volume). Step Size Reduction: Stopping early reduces the number of fi computed, which may result in smaller step sizes. This can increase the total number of steps required to converge, potentially raising the final cost. A trade-off must be found. Grazing Rays: Rays passing very close to a bounding volume without entering it can be significantly slowed down if k is too small. Early Stop+1 mitigates this by considering one extra level of the BVH. Early Stop + k (ES+k) is an optimization for sphere tracing procedural volumes that prevents unnecessary intermediate convergence checks during BVH traversal by computing k additional octaves per traversal step. It builds on Early Stop by trading a small increase in per-step function evaluations for a significant reduction in the total number of BVH traversal steps. Unlike standard Early Stop (ES+0), which may converge too slowly and incur high step counts, ES+k maintains a balance between step reduction and computational overhead, with ES+1 generally offering the best performance across diverse scenes. Time Complexity: The cost per step is reduced from O(n) function evaluations to O(i{min} + k). However, the total number of steps may increase due to smaller step sizes, especially if k is small. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory is required, primarily for storing the BVH structure and the current state of the ray marching. The BVH bounds are evaluated on the fly as the corresponding fi functions are computed. Measured Performance: Early Stop+1 (k=1) provides results very similar to full sphere tracing (computing all fi up to n) but with significantly reduced computational cost. It drastically diminishes the performance loss associated with grazing rays and slow convergence seen in Early Stop+0. Strengths: Reduces the number of expensive noise function evaluations. Effective for large and detailed scenes where many parts of the volume are empty or far from the isosurface. Limitations: May increase the total number of steps if step sizes become too small. The benefit diminishes for k > 1 as the added cost of computing more fi is not worth the small gains in step size. When to Use: Use when rendering procedural volumetric noise with sphere tracing, especially for large scenes with complex BVH structures. Use k=1 for the best balance between performance and accuracy. Avoid k=0 due to severe performance degradation on grazing rays. Early Stop was introduced in the context of fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes. It leverages the hierarchical structure of the noise function (often represented as a BVH) to avoid unnecessary computations. The method addresses the inefficiency of standard sphere tracing, which evaluates all octaves at every step, regardless of whether they are necessary for the current position. name: Early Stop + k
head: ES+k
body: Early Stop + k (ES+k) is an optimization for sphere tracing procedural volumes that prevents unnecessary intermediate convergence checks during BVH traversal by computing k additional octaves per traversal step. It builds on Early Stop by trading a small increase in per-step function evaluations for a significant reduction in the total number of BVH traversal steps. Unlike standard Early Stop (ES+0), which may converge too slowly and incur high step counts, ES+k maintains a balance between step reduction and computational overhead, with ES+1 generally offering the best performance across diverse scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, BVH structure, noise function f, maximum distance d{max}, and integer parameter k \ge 0. Output: Transmittance and color along the ray, or termination status. Data Structures: The method relies on the BVH hierarchy. No new data structures are introduced; it modifies the evaluation logic within the existing traversal loop. Parameters: k: The number of additional octaves computed per BVH node visit. Typical values: 0, 1, 2, 3. Recommended default: k=1. Note: Optimal k varies by scene and view; fixed k > 1 is risky. Algorithm: The core modification occurs during the BVH traversal loop. For each step in the BVH traversal, the algorithm computes the function value for k additional octaves beyond the current level, rather than just the current level or none. This look-ahead ensures that the distance estimate is sufficiently tight to avoid premature convergence checks that would otherwise force a re-evaluation or slow convergence. 1. Initialize ray parameters: t = 0, d{max}, k. 2. While t < d{max}: a. Traverse BVH to find the smallest bounding volume containing the point \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Let L be the octave level associated with the current BVH node. c. Compute the noise function value V for octaves L, L+1, \dots, L+k. d. Determine the step size \Delta t based on the tightest bound from these k+1 octaves. e. Update t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. f. Perform convergence check (if applicable) or continue traversal. 3. Return accumulated radiance/transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretraceearlystopk(rayorigin, raydirection, bvh, noisefunc, k, maxdist): """ Sphere tracing with Early Stop + k optimization. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) raydirection: (x, y, z) normalized bvh: BVH structure with nodes containing octave levels noisefunc: Function returning noise value for a given octave and point k: Integer, number of additional octaves to compute per step maxdist: Maximum ray length Returns: transmittance, color """ t = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) epsilon = 1e-6 # Standard minimum step size guard while t < maxdist: # Traverse BVH to find the smallest bounding volume containing point # (Implementation depends on specific BVH library; assume node retrieval here) point = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) node = bvh.findnodecontaining(point) if node is None: # Ray exited the volume break # Get the base octave level for this node baseoctave = node.octavelevel # Compute k additional octaves beyond the current level # This prevents unnecessary intermediate convergences minstep = float('inf') for i in range(k + 1): currentoctave = baseoctave + i # Evaluate noise function at current point for current octave noiseval = noisefunc(point, currentoctave) # Calculate step size based on the bound provided by this octave # Standard sphere tracing uses the noise value as the step bound step = max(noiseval, epsilon) # Take the minimum step size to ensure safety if step < minstep: minstep = step # Guard against zero or negative step sizes if minstep <= epsilon: minstep = epsilon t += minstep # Accumulate radiance (simplified standard volume rendering integration) density = noisefunc(point, baseoctave) color = (color[0] + density transmittance minstep, color[1] + density transmittance minstep, color[2] + density transmittance minstep) transmittance = (1.0 - density minstep) return transmittance, color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Choosing k: A fixed k > 1 is tricky because different scenes (even views of the same object) require different optimal k values. For example, on the "Sponge" scene, k=2 is optimal, while on "Sponge (far)", k=1 is better. Performance Degradation: If k is too high, performance decreases due to excessive function evaluations per step. For instance, k=3 on the Sponge scene resulted in significantly higher time (3513.6 ms) compared to k=1 (749.6 ms). ES+0 Performance: k=0 (standard Early Stop) can perform poorly due to slow convergence and increased number of steps, sometimes worse than no Early Stop at all. Measured Performance: Sponge Scene (Sub-stepping enabled): ES+0 (k=0): 273.0 avg steps, 3.65 avg octaves, 972.0 ms, ×1.0 speedup. ES+1 (k=1): 147.8 avg steps, 5.23 avg octaves, 749.6 ms, ×1.4 speedup. ES+2 (k=2): 127.3 avg steps, 6.31 avg octaves, 782.5 ms, ×1.3 speedup. ES+3 (k=3): 279.6 avg steps, 13.45 avg octaves, 3513.6 ms, ×1.2 speedup. No ES: 116.2 avg steps, 10.22 avg octaves, 1123.6 ms, reference. Sponge (far) Scene (Sub-stepping enabled): ES+0 (k=0): 273.0 avg steps, 3.65 avg octaves, 972.0 ms, ×1.0 speedup. ES+1 (k=1): 147.8 avg steps, 5.23 avg octaves, 749.6 ms, ×1.4 speedup. ES+2 (k=2): 127.3 avg steps, 6.31 avg octaves, 782.5 ms, ×1.3 speedup. Note: Performance decreases for k > 1 on this scene. Scaling: ES+1 consistently outperforms ES+3 and no Early Stop across tested scenes. Using k > 1 was never found to be faster when using quadratic bounds. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Reduces the number of BVH traversal steps, which can be a bottleneck in large scenes. ES+1 provides a good balance between step reduction and computational overhead. Limitations: Requires tuning k for specific scenes; a fixed k > 1 is not universally optimal. ES+0 can be slower than no Early Stop in some cases. When to Use: Use ES+1 as a default choice for most scenes. Consider tuning k for specific scenes if performance is critical, but be aware that optimal k varies. Avoid ES+0 if slow convergence is observed. Avoid k > 1 if using quadratic bounds. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". It is part of a series of optimizations for sphere tracing procedural volumes, including Early Stop and quadratic Taylor bounds. History and Development: The authors observed that standard Early Stop (ES+0) could converge slowly, leading to increased step counts and worse performance than no Early Stop in some cases. They proposed computing additional octaves per step to improve convergence speed, leading to the ES+k strategy. Experimental results showed that ES+1 provided the best performance across various scenes, while higher k values could degrade performance. Where it is used: The method is applicable to sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise, particularly in large and detailed scenes where BVH traversal is a significant cost. name: Ray Marching with Dithering and Early Termination
head: Raymarching with Transmittance-based Early Ray Termination
body: Ray marching with dithering and early termination is a GPU-based volume rendering technique that iterates along rays through a volume texture, accumulating color and transmittance while applying shading and compositing. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts caused by undersampling and the performance cost of processing every sample along a ray by using random offset initialization to hide staircase effects and stopping the integration loop when the ray exits the volume or becomes fully opaque. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific combination of single-pass fragment shader execution with dynamic branching, transmittance-based early termination, and dithered starting positions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume texture (density/intensity), transfer function texture (color mapping), camera position, ray direction (derived from screen coordinates), light positions, light colors, and parameters for step size, shading thresholds, and termination limits. Outputs: Final pixel color (RGBA). Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture storing density or intensity values, sampled via texture(voltex, pos). Transfer Function Texture: 1D or 2D texture mapping intensity to RGBA color, sampled via texture(tftex, intensity). Uniforms: uCamPos (vec3), uLightP (vec3 array), uLightC (vec3 array), uTex (texture), uTexDim (vec3), uOffset (vec3), uTMK (float), uShininess (float), uShadingMode (int), gStepSize (float), SHADINGTHRES (float), DELTA (float), TMMIN (float). Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Calculate normalized screen coordinates: normcoord = glFragCoord.st / vec2(screenwidth, screenheight). Determine ray origin ro and direction rd based on camera and screen position. Calculate ray length len and direction vector direction = end - start. Normalize direction: direction = normalize(direction). Calculate step size: stepsize = len / nsamples. (Note: uses gStepSize = \sqrt{3} / \text{MAX\STEPS} for unit cube diagonal traversal.) Calculate delta vector: delta = direction stepsize. Initialize accumulated color outcolor to vec4(0.0) and current color color to vec4(0.0). Initialize ray position pos to ray origin ro. Initialize transmittance tm to 1.0. 2. Dithering: Apply dithering to the starting position to hide aliasing: pos = pos + delta rand(). rand() should be a pseudo-random number generator providing a value in 0, 1), seeded per-pixel or per-frame to ensure consistency. 3. [Ray Marching Loop: Loop for i from 0 to nsamples while remaininglen > 0. Increment position: pos = pos + delta. Decrement remaining length: remaininglen = remaininglen - stepsize. Boundary Check: If pos is outside the volume bounds (e.g., [0, 1] for unit cube), break loop. Sample volume intensity: intensity = texture(voltex, pos).r. Map intensity to color via transfer function: color = texture(tftex, intensity). Early Termination Check (Alpha): If outcolor.a > 0.95, break loop. Transmittance Update & Check: Calculate step transmittance dtm = exp(-uTMK stepsize intensity). Update tm = tm dtm. If tm < TMMIN, break loop. Shading Calculation: If color.a > SHADINGTHRES (0.10) and shadingmode != 3 and nsamples > 500, compute shading. Compute normal N using central differences with DELTA (0.005): Nx = \text{sampleVolTex}(pos + \text{DELTA}, 0, 0) - \text{sampleVolTex}(pos - \text{DELTA}, 0, 0) Ny = \text{sampleVolTex}(pos, \text{DELTA}, 0) - \text{sampleVolTex}(pos, -\text{DELTA}, 0) Nz = \text{sampleVolTex}(pos, 0, \text{DELTA}) - \text{sampleVolTex}(pos, 0, -\text{DELTA}) N = \text{normalize}(N). Transform normal to world space: N = normalize(vec3(normalmatrix N)). Calculate light vector L from pos to light position uLightP[0] and view vector V from pos to ray origin ro. Compute halfway vector: H = normalize(L + V). Apply shading based on mode: Mode 0: Blinn-Phong specular intensity pow(dot(normalize(H), N), uShininess). Mode 1: Blinn-Phong + Edge Enhancement. Mode 2: Toon shading. Compositing: Apply compositing based on mode: Mode 0: Front-to-Back: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). Mode 1: MIP. Mode 2: MIDA. Early Ray Termination: If outcolor.a > 0.95, break loop. 4. Output: Return final accumulated color outcolor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchwithditheringandearlytermination(ro, rd, volumetexture, tftexture, params): """ Ray marching with dithering and early termination. Args: ro: Ray origin (vec3) rd: Ray direction (vec3) volumetexture: 3D texture for density/intensity tftexture: 1D/2D texture for color mapping params: Dictionary containing: nsamples: Number of steps shadingmode: 0, 1, or 2 SHADINGTHRES: 0.10 DELTA: 0.005 TMMIN: Transmittance threshold uTMK: Transmittance kernel constant uShininess: Shininess exponent uLightP: Light positions (array of vec3) uLightC: Light colors (array of vec3) normalmatrix: Transformation matrix for normals randfunc: Function returning random float in [0, 1) volmin: Volume minimum bound (vec3) volmax: Volume maximum bound (vec3) Returns: vec4: Final color """ direction = normalize(rd) len = length(rd) stepsize = len / params['nsamples'] delta = direction stepsize outcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) tm = 1.0 pos = ro remaininglen = len # Dithering to hide staircase aliasing pos = pos + delta params['randfunc']() for i in range(params['nsamples']): pos = pos + delta remaininglen = remaininglen - stepsize if remaininglen <= 0: break # Boundary check (sources use [0,1] for unit cube, generalized here) if not (params['volmin'] <= pos <= params['volmax']): break intensity = volumetexture.sample(pos).r color = tftexture.sample(intensity) # Early termination (alpha) if outcolor.a > 0.95: break # Transmittance update & check dtm = exp(-params['uTMK'] stepsize intensity) tm = tm dtm if tm < params['TMMIN']: break # Shading if color.a > params['SHADINGTHRES'] and params['shadingmode'] != 3 and params['nsamples'] > 500: step = params['DELTA'] nx = volumetexture.sample(pos + vec3(step, 0, 0)).r - volumetexture.sample(pos - vec3(step, 0, 0)).r ny = volumetexture.sample(pos + vec3(0, step, 0)).r - volumetexture.sample(pos - vec3(0, step, 0)).r nz = volumetexture.sample(pos + vec3(0, 0, step)).r - volumetexture.sample(pos - vec3(0, 0, step)).r N = normalize(vec3(nx, ny, nz)) N = normalize(params['normalmatrix'] vec4(N, 0.0)) L = normalize(params['uLightP'][0] - pos) V = normalize(ro - pos) H = normalize(L + V) if params['shadingmode'] == 0: spec = pow(max(dot(H, N), 0.0), params['uShininess']) color.rgb += spec params['uLightC'][0] elif params['shadingmode'] == 1: spec = pow(max(dot(H, N), 0.0), params['uShininess']) color.rgb += spec params['uLightC'][0] # Edge enhancement logic not detailed in sources elif params['shadingmode'] == 2: quantized = floor(dot(H, N) 10.0) / 10.0 color.rgb = quantized + 0.1 # Compositing (Front-to-Back) outcolor.rgb = outcolor.rgb + color.rgb color.a (1.0 - outcolor.a) outcolor.a = outcolor.a + color.a (1.0 - outcolor.a) # Early ray termination check if outcolor.a > 0.95: break return outcolor A GPU-based technique that performs front-to-back alpha blending and shading accumulation in a single fragment shader pass using dynamic branching. It extends the base method by supporting procedurally generated dynamic density fields and Shader Model 3.0 features. Choose this when rendering dynamic volumes composed of overlapping spherical sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Dithering hides woodgrain/staircase aliasing from undersampling but does not prevent transfer function and shading aliasing. Limitations: Dynamic branching can cause performance issues on some GPUs if divergence is high. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method is implemented in the qvrc (Qt Volume Raycasting) project by Fargiolas and the webgl-volumetric project by Baravalle. It leverages modern OpenGL/WebGL features such as fragment shaders, texture sampling, and dynamic branching to perform volume rendering on the GPU. The use of dithering to hide staircase aliasing is a common technique in ray marching, and early termination based on transmittance or accumulated alpha is a standard optimization in volume rendering. fargiolas/qvrc, https://github.com/fargiolas/qvrc, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, https://github.com/rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Dynamic Volume Raycasting with Accumulated Shading
head: Dynamic Volume Raycasting (Accumulated Shading), MarchPS_OUT RaymarchPS, Méthode de Scharsach, RayCast.fx accumulatedShading, Scharsach Ray-Casting, accumulatedShading
body: Dynamic Volume Raycasting with Accumulated Shading is a GPU-based volume rendering technique that performs front-to-back alpha blending and shading accumulation within a fragment shader using dynamic branching. It extends Krüger’s method by leveraging Shader Model 3.0 features to iterate along rays inside the fragment shader, enabling early ray termination based on accumulated opacity. Unlike static volume rendering, this method supports dynamic volumes composed of overlapping spherical sources, updating the density field via a compute shader before rendering. The complete rendering pipeline executes in four passes to allow navigation and compositing with standard surface geometry, while the core ray accumulation itself runs in a single pass. The method consists of two main phases: a compute shader phase to update the dynamic volume data, and a rendering phase that executes in four passes to allow navigation and compositing with surface geometry. The core rendering logic is contained in the accumulatedShading function. Inputs: eyeray: A ray structure containing origin o (float4) and direction d (float4). f2NearFar: A float2 containing the near (x) and far (y) t-values of the ray intersection with the volume bounding box in world space. f2MinMaxDen: A float2 containing the minimum and maximum density values to consider for rendering. cbf2MinMaxDensity: A float2 containing the transfer function’s density range. VOXELSIZE: A constant defining the physical size of a voxel. gsrvDataVolume: A 3D texture resource storing the volume data. Outputs: outColor: The accumulated color (float4). outDepth: The depth of the first surface entry (float). Volume Data Texture (texDataVolume): RWTexture3D<float4>. x: Accumulated density. yzw: Normalized color vector. Ball Info Buffer: A constant buffer (cbuffer) containing float4 balls[MAXBALLS]. xyz: Center of the sphere. w: Radius parameter used in the Ball function logic. Ball Color Buffer: An array ballsCol[MAXBALLS] of float3. Before raycasting, the volume density field is updated based on a list of dynamic spherical sources. 1. Initialize field to float4(0, 1, 1, 1) for each voxel. 2. Iterate through all balls i from 0 to numOfBalls - 1: Calculate density contribution using the Ball function: density = Ball(currentPos, balls[i].xyz, balls[i].w). The Ball function calculates distance squared DistSq between currentPos and balls[i].xyz. It returns balls[i].w / DistSq. Add density to field.x. Add color contribution: ballsCol[i].xyz pow(density, 3) 1000 to field.yzw. 3. Normalize field.yzw. 4. Store field in texDataVolume at the current thread ID. 1. Set ray origin eyeray.o to cbf4ViewPos. 2. Calculate ray direction eyeray.d from the camera origin to the pixel position input.Pos. 3. Normalize eyeray.d.xyz. 4. Pitfall Handling: If any component of the normalized direction is exactly 0.0, replace it with 1e-15 to prevent division by zero in subsequent intersection calculations. 5. Load f2NearFar from the gsrvFarNear resource at index input.Tex. 6. Multiply f2NearFar by the ray length len to convert from texture space to world space t-values. The following pseudocode implements the core accumulation loop. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def accumulatedShading(eyeray, f2NearFar, f2MinMaxDen): bFirstEnter = True Pnear = eyeray.o.xyz + eyeray.d.xyz f2NearFar.x Pfar = eyeray.o.xyz + eyeray.d.xyz f2NearFar.y P = Pnear t = f2NearFar.x tSmallStep = 0.8 VOXELSIZE PsmallStep = eyeray.d.xyz tSmallStep fieldnow = SampleLevel(gsrvDataVolume, local2tex(P), 0).x src = float4(0, 0, 0, 0) dst = float4(0, 0, 0, 0) outDepth = 0.0 while t <= f2NearFar.y: texCoord = local2tex(P) Field = SampleLevel(gsrvDataVolume, texCoord, 0) if Field.x >= f2MinMaxDen.x and Field.x <= f2MinMaxDen.y: if bFirstEnter: outDepth = mul(float4(P, 1.0), cbmView).z / 10.0 bFirstEnter = False opacity = transferFunction(Field.x) src.a = opacity 0.25 src.rgb = Field.yzw src.a dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst if dst.a >= 0.95: break P += PsmallStep t += tSmallStep outColor = dst dst.a return outColor, outDepth def local2tex(P): uv = P inverseXYZsize.xyz + 0.5 uv.y = 1 - uv.y return uv def transferFunction(density): opacity = (density - cbf2MinMaxDensity.x) / (cbf2MinMaxDensity.y - cbf2MinMaxDensity.x) p2 = opacity opacity + 0.02 p4 = p2 p2 return p4 0.3 + p2 0.1 + opacity 0.15 tSmallStep: 0.8 VOXELSIZE. Early Termination Threshold: 0.95 for accumulated opacity dst.a. Transfer Function Scaling: Output is multiplied by 0.25 before blending. Zero Division: Ray direction components set to 0.0 are replaced with 1e-15. Radius Interpretation: The Ball function uses balls[i].w in a division RadiusSq InvDistSq. The source code passes balls[i].w as the radius parameter but the function logic implies it acts as a squared radius or scaling factor for the falloff. Depth Scaling: The depth output is divided by 10.0, which is a specific implementation detail that may require adjustment for different scene scales. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps along the ray, which depends on the volume thickness and step size. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the volume texture, where N is the number of voxels. Performance: Performance is significantly impacted by the volume data size due to the rasterization of support primitives required for the four-pass structure. Scalability: The method does not scale well with large volume data sizes. Strengths: Supports dynamic volumes, single-pass accumulation, and correct compositing with surface geometry. Limitations: Poor scalability with data volume and reliance on Shader Model 3.0 dynamic branching. The method was introduced by Scharsach in 2005 as an extension of Krüger’s raycasting method. It leverages Shader Model 3.0 features, specifically dynamic branching, to perform accumulation in a single pass within the fragment shader. The technique is designed for interactive exploration of procedural volumes and allows navigation within the volume data. name: Early Ray Termination via Depth Buffer
head: Depth-based Early Termination, Early Z-Test
body: Early Ray Termination via Depth Buffer is an acceleration technique that skips fragment shader execution for rays that have already reached saturation (opacity \approx 1) by testing against a depth buffer before processing the volume data. It solves the problem of redundant computation in opaque regions by preventing the GPU from generating fragments for occluded or saturated positions. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Empty-space skipping (which skips empty geometry) and Opacity-based Early Termination (which terminates inside the shader) by using a hardware-level depth test to cull work before the expensive volume sampling occurs. Inputs: Volume data (voxels or bricks). Current depth buffer (initialized from previous frame or clear). Opacity threshold \tau (typically 0.95 \dots 1.0, varying by rendering mode). Outputs: Final color buffer. Updated depth buffer reflecting saturated rays. Data Structures: Depth Buffer: Standard 24-bit or 32-bit floating-point buffer storing the maximum depth z{max} encountered so far for each pixel. Brick Bounding Box: A solid mesh representing the spatial extent of the current volume brick, used for the depth test. Algorithm Steps: The method requires traversing the volume in front-to-back order. 1. Reconstruct Slice Stack: Compute the current slice from all projections in front-to-back order. 2. Composite with Frame Buffer: Composite the current slice with the existing frame buffer to update color and opacity. 3. Update Depth Buffer (Saturation Pass): Examine every fragment's accumulated opacity A. If A > \tau, record the fragment's depth z to update the depth buffer. Specifically, write the maximal depth value for saturated rays. Note: This step ensures the depth buffer reflects where rays are already opaque. 4. Render Next Brick with Early Z-Test: Before rendering the texture of the next brick, execute a fragment shader program while drawing a solid bounding box around the brick with back face culling switched on. This shader writes the maximal depth value in the depth buffer for saturated rays. When slicing the brick texture, perform an early Z-test. If the depth test fails (indicating the ray is already saturated/occluded by a previous brick), prevent any fragment operations from being executed. 5. Repeat: Proceed to the next slice/brick. Formulas: The standard front-to-back compositing equations are: C{i+1} = (1 - Ai) \cdot \alphai \cdot ci + Ci A{i+1} = (1 - Ai) \cdot \alphai + Ai Where C, A are the current ray color and opacity, c, \alpha are the sample color and opacity from the transfer function, and i is the sample index. A ray is considered saturated when Ai \approx 1. Parameters: Opacity Threshold (\tau): Varies between 0.0 and 1.0 depending on rendering mode (isosurface vs. full volume). Typical values are high (e.g., 0.99) for full volume to ensure only truly opaque rays are culled. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: Early ray termination is performed only once per brick, not per octree node or sample. Performing it more frequently (e.g., changing fragment shaders per sample) would annihilate the benefits due to overhead. Low Computational Effort: If the fragment shader has low computational effort, the overhead of the depth test and culling mechanism may offset the advantages. This method benefits more from spreading methods with longer fragment shaders. Order Dependency: The technique strictly requires front-to-back traversal to correctly identify saturation. Optimizes rendering of overlapping opaque primitives (spheres) by using a dedicated prepass and depthcompare: Equal to select the closest hit, bypassing GPU hidden-surface removal issues caused by discard-based impostors. Time Complexity: Reduces fragment shader invocations for saturated rays. The cost is proportional to the number of saturated pixels plus the overhead of the depth update pass. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the depth buffer and the brick bounding boxes. Performance: Achieves good speed-ups for iso-surface rendering where rays are generally terminated early. Effectiveness depends on the ratio of computational effort per fragment; it is most beneficial when fragment shaders are expensive. Strengths: Eliminates reconstruction of voxels that do not contribute to rendering. Reduces load on rasterization and fragment shader bottlenecks. Limitations: Only effective if the volume traversal is front-to-back. Overhead can negate benefits if the shading is simple or if the test is performed too frequently (e.g., per sample). The technique was introduced in the context of optimizing GPU volume rendering, specifically for brick-based rendering and distributed volume rendering (D2VR). It relies on the under operator for front-to-back compositing. The method was cited in works by Krueger et al. [KW03] and Ropinski et al. [RGW+03]. name: Depth Prepass with Equal-Depth Shading
head: Equal-Depth Shading, Depth Prepass Culling
body: Optimizes the rendering of overlapping opaque primitives (specifically spheres) by ensuring shading and ray tracing execute only for the nearest primitive per pixel, bypassing the loss of GPU hidden-surface removal caused by discard-based impostors. It sets itself apart from standard depth testing by using a dedicated prepass to establish depth, followed by a shading pass that uses depthcompare: Equal to select the closest hit, rather than relying on the GPU's default depth test which fails when fragments are discarded. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of overlapping opaque primitives (e.g., spheres) defined by position and radius. Output: A rendered image where only the nearest primitive contributes to the final color per pixel. Data Structures: Depth Buffer: A standard depth attachment (e.g., 24-bit or 32-bit float) used in the prepass. Primitive Data: Position (x, y, z) and radius r. In the cited implementation, the radius share is stored in the w component of the position vector. Steps: 1. Depth Prepass: Render the primitives to a depth buffer to record the depth of the nearest surface for each pixel. Use a dedicated shader (e.g., roomspheresdepth.wgsl). Enable depth writes. Use standard depth testing (e.g., Less or LessEqual) to ensure the minimum depth is stored. 2. Shading Pass: Render the primitives again to compute shading and ray tracing. Use a dedicated shader (e.g., roomspheresshade.wgsl). Set depth comparison function to Equal. Disable depth writes (depthwrite: false). This ensures the fragment shader runs only if the current primitive's depth matches the depth stored in the buffer from the prepass, effectively selecting the nearest primitive. 3. Depth Consistency: Apply the @invariant qualifier to the clip-space position input in the shaders. This ensures consistent depth rounding across the two separate rendering passes, preventing visual artifacts at primitive boundaries due to floating-point precision differences between passes or GPUs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. @vertex fn vsprepass(pos: vec3<f32>, radius: f32) -> @builtin(position) vec4<f32> { # Compute clip-space position let clippos = uprojection uview vec4<f32>(pos, 1.0); return clippos; } @fragment fn fsprepass() -> @location(0) vec4<f32> { # Output depth value return vec4<f32>(glFragCoord.z, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0); } @vertex @invariant # Ensures consistent depth rounding across passes fn vsshade(pos: vec3<f32>, radius: f32) -> @builtin(position) vec4<f32> { # Compute clip-space position let clippos = uprojection uview vec4<f32>(pos, 1.0); return clippos; } @fragment fn fsshade() -> @location(0) vec4<f32> { # Depth test is set to 'Equal' in the render pipeline state # This fragment only executes if depth matches the prepass depth # Perform shading and ray tracing here let color = computeshadingandraytracing(); return color; } Parameters: depthcompare: Equal. depthwrite: false in the shading pass. @invariant: Applied to position input. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Apple GPUs: Built-in hidden-surface removal is disabled when impostors use discard, causing every overlapping primitive to run full shading and ray tracing. The depth prepass restores per-pixel culling. Depth Consistency: Without @invariant, the same comparison may drop to 46 pixels (0.004%) where two overlapping spheres meet at the same 24-bit depth. The old draw kept the first sphere drawn, and the equal-depth pass keeps the last. With the prepass also off, it drops to 3 pixels, by 1/255. Silhouette Artifacts: The @invariant qualifier may cause minor silhouette boundary shifts (single pixels on sphere silhouettes) due to different rounding in development vs. release builds. This flips some rim pixels between the sphere and what is behind it. However, @invariant is retained to prevent holes on other GPUs where pipelines may round depth differently. Ordering: The equal-depth pass keeps the last primitive drawn that matches the depth. If multiple primitives share the exact same depth, the last one processed wins. Uses the @invariant qualifier on clip-space positions to ensure consistent depth rounding across separate rendering passes, preventing visual artifacts at sphere boundaries. It accepts minor silhouette boundary shifts (single pixels on sphere silhouettes) to guarantee depth consistency across pipelines on different GPUs. Without it, depth comparison drops to 46 pixels (0.004%) where two overlapping spheres meet at the same 24-bit depth, with the old draw keeping the first sphere and the equal-depth pass keeping the last. Time Complexity: The prepass adds an overhead, but the shading pass is reduced by approximately 27% of the main pass time for the spheres. Memory Complexity: Requires an additional depth buffer attachment. Measured Performance: In the cited implementation, the depth prepass for spheres followed by equal-depth shading reduced the main pass time by 27%. Strengths: Restores GPU hidden-surface removal on architectures (like Apple GPUs) where it is disabled by discard-based impostors. Ensures shading and ray tracing run only for the nearest primitive. Limitations: Requires two rendering passes. Potential for minor visual artifacts at silhouettes due to depth rounding differences. When to Use: When rendering overlapping opaque primitives that use discard-based impostors, especially on GPUs where hidden-surface removal is sensitive to discard. When Not to Use: When primitives are not overlapping or when standard depth testing is sufficient (e.g., opaque walls, which are already skipped by GPU hidden-surface removal without needing a prepass). Drawing walls after spheres was slower (4.7 ms vs 4.1 ms) because walls are opaque and the GPU's hidden-surface removal already skips them. Originated in the context of optimizing ray-traced lightbox rendering with voxel GI, specifically for overlapping particle systems. The technique was developed to address performance issues on Apple GPUs where discard-based impostors broke hidden-surface removal. It is part of a broader effort to optimize voxel cone tracing and particle rendering in real-time applications. voxel-gi-particles: ray-traced lightbox about twice as fast, same image, https://github.com/Siroko/kansei/pull/114, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Depth-Prior Ray Truncation
head: depthPriorLearned
body: Depth-Prior Ray Truncation adjusts the near and far bounds of volumetric ray sampling using a learned depth prior (disparity map) to restrict integration to relevant depth ranges, thereby reducing floating artifacts and unnecessary computation. It differs from sibling methods like Empty-space skipping which rely on geometric emptiness, and Early Stop which relies on accumulated opacity; instead, it uses external depth information to prune the search space before integration begins. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin, ray direction, raw AABB intersection bounds (t{min}, t{max}), a boolean flag depthPriorLearned, and a per-pixel disparity value from a ground truth or learned depth map (groundTruth.disparityDevice). Output: Modified ray bounds t{near} and t{far} used for subsequent volume sampling. Data Structures: rayInfo: Array or struct containing raw intersection distances. rayInfo[0] is the near bound, rayInfo[1] is the far bound. groundTruth.disparityDevice: 1D array or texture mapping pixel indices to disparity values. Steps: 1. Evaluate the boolean flag depthPriorLearned. 2. If depthPriorLearned is true: Retrieve the pixel index corresponding to the current ray's screen position. Fetch the disparity value d from groundTruth.disparityDevice at that pixel index. Calculate the new near bound: t{near} = rayInfo[0] + d \cdot 0.5. Calculate the new far bound: t{far} = rayInfo[1] - 10.0. 3. If depthPriorLearned is false: Set t{near} = rayInfo[0]. Set t{far} = rayInfo[1]. 4. Use t{near} and t{far} as the integration limits for the ray marching loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applydepthpriortruncation(rayinfo, depthpriorlearned, groundtruthdisparity, pixelindex): """ rayinfo: tuple (tmin, tmax) representing raw AABB intersection bounds depthpriorlearned: bool groundtruthdisparity: array or function accessing disparity by pixel index pixelindex: int, index into the disparity map corresponding to the ray's screen position """ tmin, tmax = rayinfo if depthpriorlearned: # Fetch disparity for the current pixel disparity = groundtruthdisparity[pixelindex] # Apply scaling factor to disparity for near bound # Note: 0.5 is a fixed scaling factor from the source tnear = tmin + disparity 0.5 # Apply fixed offset to far bound # Note: 10.0 is a fixed offset subtracted from the far bound tfar = tmax - 10.0 else: # Fallback to raw intersection bounds tnear = tmin tfar = tmax return tnear, tfar Parameters: depthPriorLearned: Boolean flag enabling the use of the depth prior. Default behavior (false) uses raw bounds. 0.5: Scaling factor applied to the disparity value to compute the near bound offset. 10.0: Fixed offset subtracted from the raw far bound to truncate the ray end. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disparity Accuracy: If the depth prior is inaccurate (e.g., due to occlusion or learning errors), the truncated bounds may exclude valid volume data or include empty space, leading to visual artifacts or wasted computation. Negative Bounds: If t{near} > t{far}, the ray has no valid intersection range. The implementation should handle this by either skipping the ray or falling back to raw bounds. Boundary Conditions: The fixed offset 10.0 assumes a specific scene scale. In scenes with different scales, this value may need adjustment or normalization. A depth prediction head appended after each scale encoding volume to predict depth maps and confidence scores, guiding sampling points and narrowing depth ranges for subsequent levels. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of samples per ray by limiting the integration range, thus decreasing computational cost per pixel. The overhead of fetching the disparity map is negligible compared to volume evaluation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the depth prior (disparity map), which is typically per-pixel and low-precision (e.g., float16). Strengths: Effective at removing floating artifacts caused by sampling in empty space beyond the actual geometry. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the depth prior. If the prior is missing or incorrect, visual quality may degrade. The fixed offset 10.0 may not be universally applicable. When to use: When a reliable depth prior is available and floating artifacts are a concern. When not to use: When depth information is unavailable or unreliable, or when the scene scale differs significantly from the assumed offset. This method is associated with the Clear-Plenoxels project, which aims to improve the visual quality of Plenoctrees by addressing artifacts through depth-aware sampling. It represents a specific implementation strategy for leveraging learned depth information in volume rendering acceleration. nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, https://github.com/nortonBryan/Clear-plenoxels, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Auxiliary Depth Prediction Head
head: Depth-guided point sampling, Pseudo-depth Guided Sampling
body: The Auxiliary Depth Prediction Head is a technique that trains a convolutional network to predict depth maps and confidence scores jointly with radiance field reconstruction, using these predictions to supervise rendered depth, narrow sampling ranges, and guide point sampling. It differs from methods relying on third-party depth sources (e.g., COLMAP) by learning compact geometry end-to-end without external priors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Encoding volume V^l at scale level l. Output: Predicted depth map D^l and confidence map U^l. Data Structures: V^l: Encoding volume tensor. D^l: Depth map tensor. U^l: Confidence map tensor. F{depth}: Convolutional layer acting as the depth prediction head. Parameters: Number of levels: 3. Number of encoding points [N^Al]: [48, 32, 8] for levels l=1, 2, 3 respectively. Reduction factor \alphal: [1/6, 1/4, 1/2] for levels l=1, 2, 3 respectively. Depth range reduction factor \betal: [1/6, 1/16] (Note: Source lists two values for three levels). Steps: 1. Depth Prediction: Append a convolutional layer F{depth} after each scale encoding volume V^l to predict the depth map D^l and confidence U^l: D^l, U^l = F{depth}(V^l) \quad (10) The head compresses similarity of source features, offering higher accuracy than regression approaches in textured regions. 2. Supervision: Use the predicted depth map D^l to supervise the pixel depth calculated by volume rendering. 3. Narrowing Depth Range: Reduce the number of sampling points by narrowing the depth range of the next level R{l+1} to Rl \betal, centered on the predicted depth value D^l, where \betal < 1 is the reducing factor. 4. Guiding Point Sampling: Use the predicted depth map to guide point sampling for radiance field reconstruction. 5. Training: Train the auxiliary depth prediction head in an unsupervised manner using the same loss function as unsupervised Multi-View Stereo (MVS) tasks. This improves the accuracy of the predicted depth, which in turn helps supervise rendered depth and guide sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class DepthPredictionHead(nn.Module): def init(self): super().init() # Convolutional layer to predict depth and confidence self.conv = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize) def forward(self, encodingvolume): # Predict depth map D and confidence U # D, U = Fdepth(V) out = self.conv(encodingvolume) depthmap = out[:, 0:1,:,:] confidence = out[:, 1:2,:,:] return depthmap, confidence def processlevel(encodingvolume, currentdepthrange, betafactor): # 1. Predict depth and confidence depthmap, confidence = DepthPredictionHead()(encodingvolume) # 2. Narrow depth range for next level # New range is centered on predicted depth, scaled by beta newrangewidth = currentdepthrange betafactor newcenter = depthmap # Implementation of range narrowing depends on specific ray marching logic # Assuming standard ray marching: newfar = newcenter + newrangewidth/2 # newnear = newcenter - newrangewidth/2 return depthmap, confidence, newrangewidth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Parameter: The source provides two values for \betal ([1/6, 1/16]) but specifies three levels. It is unclear which level corresponds to which value or if a value is missing. Occlusion/Lighting: Geometric information in point volume features may be inaccurate due to occlusion or lighting, necessitating depth-guided neighbor feature fusion (not detailed in this article). Predicts early stopping positions for tiles in streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting using truncated depth from reference frames, pruning Gaussian sorting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Experiments demonstrate superior performance in novel view synthesis and dense geometry modeling without per-scene optimization. Strengths: Learns more compact geometry compared to counterparts using third-party depth. Limitations: Geometric accuracy may suffer in regions with occlusion or poor lighting without additional feature fusion. The method was proposed by Jingliang Li, Qiang Zhou, Chaohui Yu, Zhengda Lu, Jun Xiao, Zhibin Wang, and Fan Wang in 2023 in the paper "Improved Neural Radiance Fields Using Pseudo-depth and Fusion". It is inspired by CasMVSNet and aims to address the lack of depth guidance in methods like MVSNeRF, which sample points uniformly across the entire depth range. Improved Neural Radiance Fields Using Pseudo-depth and Fusion, https://core.ac.uk/download/577699041.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Depth Prediction for Early Stopping (DPES)
head: Early Stopping Depth Prediction
body: Depth Prediction for Early Stopping (DPES) is a technique used in streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting to predict the early stopping position for each tile in a target frame by leveraging truncated depth information from a reference frame. It solves the problem of redundant computation and load imbalance during viewpoint changes by allowing the renderer to exclude Gaussians that are guaranteed to be occluded or beyond the visible depth range in the new view. Unlike standard early termination which relies on per-pixel opacity thresholds during rendering, DPES pre-computes a tile-level depth bound to prune the Gaussian sorting stage entirely. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Reference frame color buffer F{ref}, reference scene depth map D{ref}, reference truncated depth max map D{ref}^{max}, reference viewpoint V{ref}, target viewpoint V{tgt}, and a rerendering threshold N0. Outputs: Target frame color buffer F{tgt}, a group of tiles T, and a tile-level truncated depth map DT^{max}. Data Structures: F{ref}, F{tgt}: 2D arrays of pixel colors. D{ref}, D{ref}^{max}: 2D arrays of depth values. D{ref} stores the depth of the last traversed Gaussian or the early stopping depth. D{ref}^{max} stores the truncated depth bound. DT^{max}: 2D array where each element corresponds to a tile and stores the maximum valid reprojected depth within that tile. Steps: 1. Record Reference Depths: During the initial rendering of the reference frame, record the depth of each pixel. This depth corresponds to the depth of the last Gaussian traversed or the depth at which early stopping occurred. 2. Project to 3D: Convert the 2D pixel coordinates and depth values from the reference frame into 3D world coordinates using the reference viewpoint V{ref}. This yields 3D points P{ref} and truncated depth bounds P{ref}^{max}. 3. View Transfer: Transform the 3D points P{ref} and P{ref}^{max} from the reference viewpoint V{ref} to the target viewpoint V{tgt}. This yields transformed points P{tgt} and P{tgt}^{max}. 4. Reproject to Target Frame: Project the transformed 3D points P{tgt} and P{tgt}^{max} back onto the 2D image plane of the target viewpoint V{tgt}. This produces the target frame color buffer F{tgt} (interpolated or reprojected colors) and the target depth map D{tgt}. 5. Tile-Level Processing: Iterate through each tile t in the target frame: Count the number of valid pixels N within the tile t in F{tgt}. If N > N0: Interpolate the color values for the tile. If N \le N0: Calculate the early stopping depth for the tile as the maximum depth of all valid reprojected pixels within that tile: DT^{max}(t) = \max(D{tgt}, t). Use this depth to re-render the tile, excluding any Gaussians with depth beyond DT^{max}(t) from the sorting stage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthpredictionforearlystopping(Fref, Dref, Drefmax, Vref, Vtgt, N0): """ Predicts early stopping positions for tiles in the target frame. Args: Fref: Reference frame color buffer. Dref: Reference scene depth map. Drefmax: Reference truncated depth max map. Vref: Reference viewpoint (camera matrix/intrinsics). Vtgt: Target viewpoint (camera matrix/intrinsics). N0: Rerendering threshold. Returns: Ftgt: Target frame color buffer. T: List of tiles. DTmax: Tile-level truncated depth map. """ # Initialize outputs Ftgt = Initialize() DTmax = Initialize() T = GetTiles() # Step 2: Project to 3D # Convert 2D pixels and depths to 3D world coordinates Pref, Prefmax = ProjectTo3D(Fref, Dref, Drefmax, Vref) # Step 3: View Transfer # Transform 3D points to target camera space Ptgt, Ptgtmax = ViewTransfer(Pref, Prefmax, Vref, Vtgt) # Step 4: Reproject to Target Frame # Project 3D points back to 2D target image plane Ftgt, Dtgt = Reproject(Ptgt, Ptgtmax, Vtgt) # Step 5: Tile-Level Processing for t in T: # Count valid pixels in the tile N = ValidPixelSum(Ftgt, t) if N > N0: # Interpolate if enough valid pixels are available Interpolate(Ftgt, t) else: # Calculate max depth for early stopping DTmax[t] = Max(Dtgt, t) # Re-render with depth pruning Rerender(Ftgt, t, DTmax[t]) return Ftgt, T, DTmax def ProjectTo3D(F, D, Dmax, V): """ Projects 2D pixels to 3D world coordinates. """ # Implementation depends on camera intrinsics V # For each pixel (u, v) with depth d: # x = (u - cx) d / fx # y = (v - cy) d / fy # z = d # Return 3D points and corresponding max depths pass def ViewTransfer(P, Pmax, Vref, Vtgt): """ Transforms 3D points from reference to target viewpoint. """ # Apply inverse of Vref to get world coordinates # Apply Vtgt to get target camera coordinates # Return transformed points pass def Reproject(P, Pmax, V): """ Projects 3D points to 2D target image plane. """ # Apply V to get clip space # Perspective divide # Return 2D coordinates and depths pass def ValidPixelSum(F, t): """ Counts valid (non-empty/valid depth) pixels in tile t. """ maxval = -infinity for pixel in t: if IsValid(D[pixel]): maxval = max(maxval, D[pixel]) return maxval Parameters: N0: Rerendering threshold. Heuristically defined as 3\lambda1 and 3\lambda2 in the source, though exact values for \lambda1 and \lambda2 are not provided in the excerpt. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Valid Pixels: If the number of valid reprojected pixels N is low (N \le N0), the method triggers re-rendering with depth pruning. If N is too low, the depth estimate DT^{max} may be noisy or incomplete, potentially leading to incorrect Gaussian culling if the max depth is underestimated. Occlusion: The method assumes that the depth from the reference frame is a valid upper bound for the target frame. If significant occlusion changes occur, the predicted depth might be inaccurate. Time Complexity: The method adds an overhead of projecting and reprojecting depths for the reference frame. However, it reduces the sorting complexity for tiles that are re-rendered by excluding Gaussians beyond the predicted depth. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the reference depth maps D{ref} and D{ref}^{max} and the target depth map D{tgt}. Strengths: Enables balanced workload distribution across rasterization units by predicting expected load per tile. Reduces redundant computation by pruning Gaussians early. Limitations: Relies on the accuracy of the reference depth map. Performance degrades if the viewpoint change is large or if the scene has significant dynamic occlusion. When to use: Real-time streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting where viewpoint changes are frequent and computational resources are limited. Origin: Proposed in "No Redundancy, No Stall: Lightweight Streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-time Rendering". History: Developed to address the issue of redundant computation and load imbalance in streaming 3D Gaussian Splatting. Usage: Used in real-time rendering of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes. name: Opacity-based Early Termination
body: Opacity-based Early Termination is a family of volume rendering optimizations that halt the front-to-back ray integration loop once the accumulated opacity exceeds a predefined threshold, thereby skipping samples that contribute negligibly to the final pixel color. It differs from Empty-space skipping by operating on the accumulated transmittance of the ray path rather than spatially culling empty voxels, and from Russian Roulette by using a deterministic cutoff rather than a probabilistic one, which introduces a systematic bias in exchange for reduced noise and computational cost. The core mechanism shared by all methods in this family is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity, as measured by color difference in sample regions. Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. Early Ray Termination (ERT) is a rendering optimization that halts front-to-back ray integration once the accumulated opacity exceeds a predefined threshold, thereby skipping samples that contribute negligibly to the final pixel color. It differs from Conservative Early Ray Termination by evaluating opacity per-pixel along the ray path rather than using subscreen aggregation during scan conversion. An optimization technique where the opacity of a sample is checked before shading; if opacity is under a threshold, shading and compositing are skipped. The process involves looking up the opacity in the transfer function; if the sample opacity exceeds the threshold, shading proceeds, otherwise the sample is skipped. A technique to reduce the significance of finding tight extinction bounds a priori by refining extinction bounds progressively based on actual extinction lookups during rendering. Initial extinction bounds are set conservatively wide (slowing down simulation at first) or to rough estimates (temporarily increasing variance), and then dynamically refined based on actual extinction lookups. This is described as highly desirable for large production assets where lengthy precomputations impede productivity. Early ray termination was described in a paper on volume rendering on scalable shared-memory MIMD architectures. It was defined as terminating resampling along a ray when its accumulated opacity exceeds a user-selected threshold of opaqueness. The technique is part of a broader set of optimizations including hierarchical opacity enumeration and adaptive image sampling. name: Early Ray Termination
head: ERT, Early Termination, Early stopping, Transmittance-based Early Termination
body: Early Ray Termination (ERT) is a rendering optimization that halts front-to-back ray integration once the accumulated opacity exceeds a predefined threshold, thereby skipping samples that contribute negligibly to the final pixel color. It differs from Conservative Early Ray Termination by evaluating opacity per-pixel along the ray path rather than using subscreen aggregation during scan conversion. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, radiance field query function returning color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma, maximum sample count N{\max}, near/far planes t{\min}, t{\max}, step size s, and termination epsilon \epsilon. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{\text{out}}, accumulated opacity \alpha{\text{acc}}, accumulated depth D{\text{acc}}, and sample count n. Data Structures Accumulators: Floating-point variables for accumulated color \mathbf{C}{\text{out}}, accumulated opacity \alpha{\text{acc}}, and depth D{\text{acc}}. Ray Parameters: t{\min}, t{\max}, step size s. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize \mathbf{C}{\text{out}} = (0,0,0), \alpha{\text{acc}} = 0, D{\text{acc}} = 0, and n = 0. 2. Loop Condition: While n < N{\max} and \alpha{\text{acc}} < 1 - \epsilon: a. Compute sample position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. b. Query radiance field for color \mathbf{c} and density \sigma at \mathbf{p}. c. Compute transmittance T = \exp(-\sigma \cdot s). d. Compute weight w = (1 - T) \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{acc}}). e. Update accumulators: \mathbf{C}{\text{out}} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{\text{out}} + \mathbf{c} \cdot w \alpha{\text{acc}} \leftarrow \alpha{\text{acc}} + w D{\text{acc}} \leftarrow D{\text{acc}} + t \cdot w f. Increment n and advance t \leftarrow t + s. 3. Termination Check: If \alpha{\text{acc}} \ge 1 - \epsilon, terminate early. 4. Background: If \alpha{\text{acc}} < 1, blend with background color \mathbf{C}{\text{bg}}: \mathbf{C}{\text{final}} = \mathbf{C}{\text{out}} + \mathbf{C}{\text{bg}} \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{acc}}). Formulas Termination Criterion: The ray terminates when the accumulated opacity satisfies: \alpha{\text{acc}} \ge 1 - \epsilon This threshold corresponds to the point where potential color change falls below \epsilon. Parameters \epsilon (earlystopeps): Default 10^{-4}. Controls precision vs. speed. N{\max} (maxsamples): Not given in the sources. s (renderstepsize): Default 10^{-3}. t{\min} (nearplane): Default 0.0. t{\max} (farplane): Default 10^{10}. Typical opacity thresholds range from 0.95 to 0.99. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Bias: The predefined threshold introduces a systematic bias in the rendered image. Russian Roulette can remove this bias at the cost of added noise. Divergence: Early loop exit is not always optimal on modern GPUs due to divergent execution, though it remains a standard optimization. Incompatibility: Not applicable to Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), which requires browsing the entire ray path. Order Dependency: Requires front-to-back compositing order, which typically requires multiple passes to extract front and back faces if not precomputed. Pseudocode def renderrayearlytermination(rayorigin, raydirection, radiancefield, maxsamples, tmin, tmax, stepsize, epsilon, backgroundcolor): accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 accumulateddepth = 0.0 numsamples = 0 t = tmin while numsamples < maxsamples and accumulatedopacity < 1.0 - epsilon: if t > tmax: break samplepos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] color, density = radiancefield.query(samplepos) transmittance = math.exp(-density stepsize) weight = (1.0 - transmittance) (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor[0] += color[0] weight accumulatedcolor[1] += color[1] weight accumulatedcolor[2] += color[2] weight accumulateddepth += t weight accumulatedopacity += weight numsamples += 1 t += stepsize if accumulatedopacity < 1.0: accumulatedcolor[0] += backgroundcolor[0] (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor[1] += backgroundcolor[1] (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor[2] += backgroundcolor[2] (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity, accumulateddepth, numsamples An optimization for the scan conversion phase that prunes cell processing using a lookup table and subscreen aggregation, allowing visibility decisions without per-pixel overhead during parallel rasterization. Stops front-to-back blending for 3D Gaussians once accumulated opacity or transmittance reaches a threshold, applicable to order-independent variants by leveraging physically grounded transmittance models. Uses a binary volume to skip fully transparent cells and terminates evaluation when accumulated transparency falls below a threshold, explicitly encoding opaque voxels into a bit-mask for direct jumps. Combines ERT for volume data with spatial masking in sheared image space for surface instruments, limiting recomputation to affected pixels in surgical simulators. Time Complexity: O(N) worst-case where N is the number of samples, but typically much less due to early termination. For opaque-only environments, eliminates dependence on depth complexity, making cost nearly linear with image size. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray. Performance: Higher \epsilon values reduce rendering time significantly but may introduce artifacts; lower \epsilon values produce higher quality images at the cost of more samples. Performance improvements can reduce execution time by a factor of 5 to 11. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for opaque or semi-opaque volumes, exploits spatial and temporal coherence. Limitations: Introduces systematic bias. Divergent execution on modern GPUs can make early loop exit suboptimal. Incompatible with MIP. Requires front-to-back compositing order. Early termination was first proposed by Whitwell. The technique was formally introduced as Early Ray Termination by Krüger and Westermann in 2003. Older GPUs (pre-Shader Model 3) required multi-pass rendering with early-z testing; Shader Model 3+ enabled breaking out of the ray-casting loop directly. The method is widely used in medical visualization and real-time rendering pipelines where performance is critical. name: Conservative Early Ray Termination
head: ERT in scan conversion phase, ERT-table scheme
body: Conservative Early Ray Termination (CERT) is an optimization that prunes unnecessary scan conversion of geometric cells by integrating visibility checking based on partially accumulated opacity and subscreen-based comparison. It differs from standard Early Ray Termination by operating during the scan conversion phase rather than the final compositing phase, using an ERT-table to avoid per-pixel overhead. Unlike exact ERT, CERT checks a sufficient but not necessary condition for termination, trading potential speedup for significantly lower maintenance cost to enable parallel distributed execution. It builds on Early Ray Termination and contrasts with Early Termination for Gaussian Splatting, Early Ray Termination with Binary Mask, and Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering with Masking and Early Ray Termination. Inputs: Volume data represented as unstructured cells (e.g., tetrahedra) with vertex attributes. Camera viewpoint and screen resolution. An opacity threshold for early termination. A subdivision of the screen into subscreens. Outputs: A rendered image. An internal binary decision for each cell indicating whether to skip its scan conversion. Data Structures: 1. Ray-Segment List: For each pixel, a list of ray segments intersecting the pixel, ordered by depth. Partial compositions generate new segments (e.g., s{ij} from si and sj). 2. ERT-Table: A lookup table where each entry corresponds to a subscreen S rather than a single pixel or cell projection area. Each entry contains a one-bit flag indicating whether conditions C1 and C2 are satisfied for that subscreen, and a maxtermZ value representing the maximum depth among all subscreen's per-pixel front-most partially accumulated ray-segments whose opacity exceeds the threshold. Numbered Steps: 1. Subdivide the screen into subscreens. 2. For each subscreen S, maintain an ERT-table entry containing a one-bit flag and a maxtermZ value. 3. For each cell c to be rendered: a. Compute the projection area R of cell c on the screen. b. Check the corresponding ERT-table entries for the subscreens covering R. c. If the one-bit flag is true for a subscreen, compare its maxtermZ with nearest, the depth value of the nearest vertex in cell c. d. If maxtermZ < nearest, terminate the scan conversion of cell c. e. Otherwise, proceed with standard scan conversion for cell c. 4. During scan conversion, maintain the ray-segment lists for pixels. When a partial composition yields a ray segment with opacity exceeding the threshold, update the ERT-table entry for the subscreen containing that pixel by setting the flag to true and updating maxtermZ to the maximum of its current value and the segment's depth. Formulas and Conditions: The conditions to neglect scan conversion of cell c are defined as: C1: There exists a nonempty ray-segment list for all pixels corresponding to the projection area R for cell c. C2: There exists a partially composed ray segment whose opacity is sufficiently high in each of these ray-segment lists. C3: At least one of such ray-segments in each of the lists is located in front of the cell c. CERT approximates these conditions by aggregating them per subscreen. The termination condition is: \text{max\term\Z} < \text{nearest} Where \text{max\term\Z} is the maximum depth value among all subscreen's per-pixel front-most partially accumulated ray-segments whose opacity exceeds the threshold, and \text{nearest} is the depth value of the nearest vertex in the cell c. Parameters: Opacity Threshold: The value above which a ray segment is considered sufficiently high. In the source evaluation, this was set to 0.9. Subscreen Size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Per-pixel Overhead: A naive implementation checking conditions C1-C3 per cell projection area incurs significant overhead due to per-pixel searches on ray-segment lists. The ERT-table alleviates this by aggregating status per subscreen. Conservatism: CERT checks a sufficient, though not necessary, condition, which may reduce the effect of ERT but significantly reduces the cost to maintain the ERT-table information. Partial Composition Dependency: The efficiency of CERT relies on partial composition increasing the opacity of ray segments to exceed the threshold more frequently. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math OPACITYTHRESHOLD = 0.9 NEGATIVEINFINITY = float('-inf') class ERTTableEntry: def init(self): self.flag = False # True if C1 and C2 are satisfied for this subscreen self.maxtermZ = NEGATIVEINFINITY # Rearmost depth of qualifying segments class RaySegment: def init(self, depth, opacity): self.depth = depth self.opacity = opacity screenwidth = 300 screenheight = 100 subscreenwidth = 10 # Not given in the sources subscreenheight = 10 numsubscreensx = math.ceil(screenwidth / subscreenwidth) numsubscreensy = math.ceil(screenheight / subscreenheight) erttable = [[ERTTableEntry() for in range(numsubscreensy)] for in range(numsubscreensx)] def computeprojectionarea(cell): # Projects cell vertices to screen space and returns bounding rectangle (xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax) return (0, 0, 10, 10) def getintersectingsubscreens(projectionareaR): # Returns list of (sx, sy) indices for subscreens overlapping the bounding rectangle xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = projectionareaR sxmin, symin = xmin // subscreenwidth, ymin // subscreenheight sxmax, symax = xmax // subscreenwidth, ymax // subscreenheight return [(sx, sy) for sx in range(sxmin, sxmax + 1) for sy in range(symin, symax + 1)] def getpixelsinprojectionarea(projectionareaR): # Returns list of pixel coordinates within the bounding rectangle xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = projectionareaR return [(px, py) for px in range(xmin, xmax + 1) for py in range(ymin, ymax + 1)] def generateraysegmentsforpixel(pixel, cell): # Standard scan conversion: computes ray-cell intersection and returns segment(s) return [RaySegment(depth=5.0, opacity=0.5)] def isfrontmostqualifyingsegment(pixel, segment): # Checks if segment is the closest to the camera among qualifying segments for this pixel # Maintains per-pixel state in a real implementation return True def render(volumecells): for cell in volumecells: projectionareaR = computeprojectionarea(cell) subscreenstocheck = getintersectingsubscreens(projectionareaR) skipcell = False for (sx, sy) in subscreenstocheck: entry = erttable[sx][sy] if entry.flag: if entry.maxtermZ < cell.nearestvertexdepth: skipcell = True break if skipcell: continue for pixel in getpixelsinprojectionarea(projectionareaR): segments = generateraysegmentsforpixel(pixel, cell) for segment in segments: if segment.opacity > OPACITYTHRESHOLD: if isfrontmostqualifyingsegment(pixel, segment): sx, sy = pixel[0] // subscreenwidth, pixel[1] // subscreenheight entry = erttable[sx][sy] entry.flag = True if segment.depth > entry.maxtermZ: entry.maxtermZ = segment.depth A technique in parallel implementations where Working Nodes (WNs) exchange their ERT-table information to increase the accuracy/completeness of termination decisions across the system. If WNa terminates scan conversion due to ERT, WNb (holding cells behind WNa) can also terminate based on shared information. The sharing frequency is set far beneath the frequency of ERT information updates at each WN to avoid interprocessor communication overhead. This reduced scan conversion time by at most 43% (Viewpoint A) and 50% (Viewpoint B), with effective parallel performance improvements of 7% and 30% respectively. Time Complexity: The overhead of maintaining the ERT-table is O(1) per subscreen per update, significantly less than per-pixel checks. The scan conversion time is reduced by skipping cells. Memory Complexity: Requires an ERT-table of size proportional to the number of subscreens, plus ray-segment lists per pixel. Measured Performance: On a dataset of 307,565 tetrahedra, CERT provided a 3.86x speedup in scan conversion time in sequential execution using a 300×100 screen resolution. In parallel execution, weak sharing of ERT information yielded up to 30% effective performance improvement. Strengths: Applicable in the scan conversion phase; low overhead due to subscreen aggregation; effective in parallel distributed systems with weak sharing. Limitations: Conservative approximation may miss some termination opportunities; effectiveness depends on the opacity threshold and data distribution; requires partial composition to be effective. When to Use: When rendering large unstructured volumes with significant opacity, especially in parallel environments where scan conversion is a bottleneck. When Not to Use: When the volume is largely transparent or when the overhead of maintaining the ERT-table outweighs the savings from skipped cells. Conservative Early Ray Termination (CERT) was introduced in the context of Cell-Projection Parallel Volume Rendering (CP-PVR). It was developed to address load imbalance and inefficiency in parallel volume rendering by applying ERT concepts during the scan conversion phase, which was previously not feasible due to the lack of accumulated opacity information. The method was evaluated on segmented human aorta simulation data consisting of 307,565 unstructured tetrahedral cells and 62,475 vertices.
