name: Early Termination for Gaussian Splatting
head: Early Termination (ET), Early term, Full early termination
body: Early Termination (ET) is a rendering acceleration method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that stops the front-to-back blending process for a pixel once its accumulated opacity or transmittance reaches a predefined threshold, thereby eliminating unnecessary computation for distant or occluded Gaussians. Unlike its parent method, Early Ray Termination, which relies on strict depth sorting to ensure correct alpha-blending order, ET in Gaussian Splatting can be applied to order-independent or sort-free variants by leveraging physically grounded transmittance models that decay similarly to standard alpha-blending. It sets itself apart from siblings like Conservative Early Ray Termination by potentially offering higher throughput gains at the cost of slight visual approximations, as it may terminate rays even if the strict transmittance threshold hasn't been fully met in non-physical blending kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians projected onto the image plane, sorted or grouped by tile/pixel; accumulated color C and transmittance T per pixel; a termination threshold \epsilon (typically matching the value used in vanilla 3DGS). Output: Final pixel color C{final} and a termination ratio r^{\text{ET}}. Data Structures: Per-Pixel State: Accumulated color C = (R, G, B) and accumulated transmittance T. Initialized to C = (0,0,0) and T = 1.0. Gaussian List: A list of Gaussians intersecting the pixel's tile or ray, ordered by depth (for sorted methods) or processed in arbitrary order (for sort-free methods with physical transmittance). Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel in the tile, initialize accumulated color C = (0,0,0) and transmittance T = 1.0. 2. Iteration: Iterate through the Gaussians associated with the pixel. For each Gaussian i: a. Contribution Calculation: Compute the color contribution \Delta Ci and opacity \alphai based on the Gaussian's properties and the ray intersection. b. Alpha Blending Update: Update the accumulated color and transmittance: C{new} = C{old} + \Delta Ci \cdot T{old} T{new} = T{old} \cdot (1 - \alphai) c. Termination Check: Check if the accumulated transmittance T{new} (or accumulated opacity 1 - T{new}) meets the termination condition. In standard 3DGS-style ET: If T{new} < \epsilon, terminate processing for this pixel. In Cell-Based ET: If cell-level transmittance T{cell}^n < \epsilon, halt blending for the cell. d. Update State: If not terminated, update C \leftarrow C{new} and T \leftarrow T{new}. 3. Finalization: The final pixel color is C{final} = C. Formulas: Termination Ratio: The efficiency of ET is measured by the ratio of skipped Gaussians: r^{\text{ET}} = 1 - \frac{N^{\text{rendered}}}{N^{\text{val}}} where N^{\text{rendered}} is the number of Gaussians contributing to the final color, and N^{\text{val}} is the total number of valid Gaussians interacted along the ray. Parameters: Threshold (\epsilon): The transmittance threshold for early termination. Sources indicate this is maintained at the same value as used in vanilla 3DGS. Specific numerical values are not given in the sources, but it is described as an empirical threshold. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Order Independence: In sort-free methods (e.g., LC-WSR), transmittance does not strictly decrease with depth, which can lead to popping artifacts if not handled. Duplex-GS resolves this by using physically grounded transmittance that decays similarly to alpha-blending, allowing ET without explicit ordering. RaySplats Cap: In RaySplats, capping the maximum number of Gaussians can trigger early termination even if the transmittance threshold is not reached. This requires gradient correction during training to stabilize. Compression Impact: In compressed models, the ratio of unused Gaussians due to ET may decrease (e.g., from ~50% in uncompressed 3DGS to 24.3% in compressed models), reducing the potential savings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyterminationrender(gaussians, tilesize=16, epsilon=0.05): """ Renders a tile using Early Termination. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects projected to the tile. tilesize: Size of the tile (e.g., 16x16). epsilon: Transmittance threshold for early termination. """ # Initialize per-pixel accumulators # Assuming a flat array for simplicity, size = tilesize tilesize numpixels = tilesize tilesize acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] numpixels acctransmittance = [1.0] numpixels # Sort Gaussians by depth if required by the specific ET variant # For sort-free variants with physical transmittance, sorting may not be needed gaussianssorted = sortbydepth(gaussians) for gaussian in gaussianssorted: # Identify pixels covered by this Gaussian coveredpixels = getcoveredpixels(gaussian, tilesize) for idx in coveredpixels: # Skip if already terminated if acctransmittance[idx] < epsilon: continue # Calculate contribution alpha = gaussian.computealpha(idx) deltacolor = gaussian.computecolor(idx) # Update accumulation # Cnew = Cold + deltacolor Told # Tnew = Told (1 - alpha) told = acctransmittance[idx] cold = acccolor[idx] acccolor[idx] = [ cold[0] + deltacolor[0] told, cold[1] + deltacolor[1] told, cold[2] + deltacolor[2] told ] acctransmittance[idx] = told (1 - alpha) # Check for termination if acctransmittance[idx] < epsilon: # Mark as terminated to skip future Gaussians for this pixel # In a real implementation, this might be handled by a mask or flag pass return acccolor A rendering optimization that halts the front-to-back blending process at the cell level once the cell-level transmittance T{cell}^n decays below a predefined threshold \epsilon, eliminating transparency artifacts and accelerating rendering. Unlike prior Weighted Splatting/Rendering (WSR) methods, this formulation constrains the opacity parameter \sigma{n,k} to the physically plausible range of [0, 1], allowing the empirical threshold to be directly transferred and facilitating more effective pruning and regularization. The blending is halted when T{cell}^n < \epsilon. A rasterization module subdivided into alpha-pruning, early termination, and color accumulation stages to optimize rendering by reducing point processing. The alpha-pruning stage excludes unnecessary Gaussian points based on their alpha values. The early termination stage performs multiplication and subtraction operations followed by a comparison to determine if the accumulated pixel color has reached a saturation point, beyond which further processing would not significantly alter the final output. In compressed models, this results in 24.3% of Gaussian points being unused due to early termination, saving around 24% of computational resources in subsequent stages. A method that accelerates ray tracing by capping the maximum number of Gaussians accumulated along each ray, allowing storage in a fixed-size local memory array. To stabilize training under this approximation, it continues accumulating additional Gaussians beyond the cap and uses their contributions to correct the gradients of the front-most Gaussians. A key pitfall is that the cap may trigger early termination even when the transmittance threshold has not yet been reached. Throughput Gain: Early Termination increases throughput significantly. In one implementation, it raised FPS from 97.7 to 129.0 at 1080p, a 1.32× gain (75.70% to 100.00% throughput). In another evaluation on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, enabling ET resulted in 155 FPS compared to 212 FPS when disabled, with a PSNR of 27.66 vs 26.60. Complexity: Reduces the number of Gaussian points processed in the volume rendering and sorting stages. In uncompressed 3DGS, approximately 50% of Gaussian points are unused due to ET, while in compressed models, this ratio is 24.3%. Strengths: Eliminates unnecessary blending work, especially for distant or occluded Gaussians. It is compatible with both sorted and sort-free rendering pipelines if physically grounded transmittance is used. Limitations: In sort-free methods, lack of strict depth order can cause popping artifacts if transmittance is not physically grounded. Capping the number of Gaussians (as in RaySplats) can lead to premature termination and requires gradient correction. When to Use: Use when real-time performance is critical and slight visual approximations are acceptable. Particularly effective in scenes with high occlusion or large depth ranges. When Not to Use: Avoid in scenarios requiring strict order-independent transparency without physical transmittance constraints, or when the highest possible PSNR is required without any approximation. Early Termination for Gaussian Splatting was introduced as an optimization to accelerate the rendering pipeline of 3D Gaussian Splatting. It builds on the alpha-blending principles of the original 3DGS method. The method has been adapted and extended in various forms, such as Cell-Based 3DGS (Duplex-GS) to support order-independent rendering, and hardware accelerators to reduce gate count and power consumption. RaySplats introduced a capped accumulation approach for ray tracing. name: Early Ray Termination with Binary Mask
head: Alpha-blending with binary skip
body: Early Ray Termination with Binary Mask is an acceleration technique for alpha-blending volume rendering that combines empty space skipping via a binary mask with opacity-based early termination. It solves the problem of wasting computational resources on fully transparent regions and redundant compositing steps by using a precomputed binary structure to jump directly to opaque voxels and stopping the front-to-back evaluation once accumulated transparency drops below a threshold. It sets itself apart from standard early ray termination by explicitly skipping empty cells via bit manipulation, and from conservative early ray termination by allowing termination based on a strict transparency threshold rather than a conservative bound [1949-conservative-early-ray-termination.md]. The method operates on a volume grid of size X \times Y \times Z. It uses a binary mask structure to store the presence of opaque voxels and a volume data structure to store their optical properties. Inputs and Outputs Input: volume: A 3D array of voxels. Each voxel v contains color (RGB) and opacity (float in [0, 1]). mask: A 3D array of integers (typically 32-bit) with dimensions imax \times Y \times X, where imax = \lceil Z / 32 \rceil. Each integer represents a "segment" of 32 voxels along the Z-axis for a specific (x, y) coordinate. The k-th bit of the integer corresponds to the voxel at z = 32 \cdot i + k. threshold: A pre-defined double value for accumulated transparency. If accumulated transparency falls below this value, the ray terminates. Output: color: The final composited RGB color for the pixel at (x, y). Data Structures Binary Mask: The mask is organized as mask[i][y][x]. The i-th dimension corresponds to blocks of 32 Z-slices. The bits within the integer are packed such that bit 0 corresponds to the first voxel in the block, and bit 31 to the last. A set bit indicates an opaque voxel; a cleared bit indicates a transparent voxel. Voxel: Contains color (e.g., float[3]) and opacity (e.g., float). Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize trans (accumulated transparency) to 1.0 and color to BLACK (zero vector). 2. Calculate imax as (Z + 31) / 32 using integer division. 3. Loop i from 0 to imax - 1: a. Retrieve segment = mask[i][y][x]. b. While segment is non-zero: i. Call Depth(segment) to find the position of the least significant set bit (or next non-zero bit). Let this bit offset be z (0 \le z < 32). ii. Calculate the global Z-coordinate: z{global} = 32 \cdot i + z. iii. Retrieve the voxel v = volume[z{global}][y][x]. iv. Update accumulated transparency: trans = trans \times (1.0 - v.opacity). v. Check termination: If trans < threshold, return color immediately. vi. Composite color: color = color + v.color \times v.opacity \times trans. vii. Clear the processed bit in segment: segment = segment & ~(0x80000000 >> z). This operation deletes the bit at position z so the next Depth call finds the subsequent opaque voxel. 4. Return color. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphablendingbinarymask(x, y, volume, mask, threshold, Z): """ Renders a pixel (x, y) using Early Ray Termination with Binary Mask. Args: x, y: Pixel coordinates. volume: 3D array of voxels with.color and.opacity attributes. mask: 3D array of integers, shape (imax, Y, X). threshold: Float, transparency threshold for early termination. Z: Integer, total depth of the volume. Returns: rgb: Tuple or array of 3 floats representing the final color. """ # Constants BLACK = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Initialization trans = 1.0 color = BLACK imax = (Z + 31) // 32 for i in range(imax): segment = mask[i][y][x] while segment != 0: # Find the position of the next set bit (least significant bit) # This is equivalent to counting trailing zeros or using a bit scan instruction z = depthoffirstsetbit(segment) # Calculate global Z coordinate zglobal = 32 i + z # Retrieve voxel data v = volume[zglobal][y][x] # Update accumulated transparency trans = (1.0 - v.opacity) # Early termination check if trans < threshold: return color # Front-to-back compositing # color += v.color v.opacity trans color = ( color[0] + v.color[0] v.opacity trans, color[1] + v.color[1] v.opacity trans, color[2] + v.color[2] v.opacity trans) # Clear the processed bit to find the next one # 0x80000000 is 1 << 31. Shifting right by z gives a mask for bit z. # NOTing it gives a mask with 0 at bit z and 1 elsewhere. # ANDing with segment clears bit z. segment &= ~(0x80000000 >> z) return color def depthoffirstsetbit(segment): """ Returns the index of the least significant set bit (0-31). Implements a simple bit scan for clarity. """ for z in range(32): if segment & (1 << z): return z return 0 # Should not be reached if segment != 0 Parameters threshold: A pre-defined value for accumulated transparency. Typical values are small positive numbers (e.g., 10^{-3} to 10^{-5}) depending on the desired visual fidelity and performance trade-off. imax: Derived from volume depth Z. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Accumulated transparency trans is a product of values in [0, 1]. It can underflow to zero for very long rays or high-opacity volumes. The threshold check prevents unnecessary computation but must be chosen carefully to avoid premature termination artifacts. Bit Manipulation: The bit clearing operation segment &= ~(0x80000000 >> z) assumes a 32-bit integer and a specific bit ordering. If the hardware or language handles bit shifts differently (e.g., arithmetic vs. logical, or different endianness), this must be adjusted. Boundary Conditions: The loop runs up to imax. If Z is not a multiple of 32, the last segment may contain unused bits. The mask should be initialized such that unused bits are 0 to prevent false positives. A cache attached at the beginning of the volume raycasting pipeline to skip resampling and compositing in cells where all eight samples are classified as transparent, addressing remaining transparent regions not skipped by block/octree entry points. It is chosen when the binary mask or octree does not reach down to the cell level, leaving small transparent gaps. The cache layout uses one bit per cell, storing combined information for eight samples. It is more efficient than transfer function lookups for large zoom factors because one bit stores info for eight samples, avoiding repeated lookups for multiple rays hitting the same cell. The cache size is 32^3 bits = 4096 bytes. It is initialized with all cells visible; as rays classify cells as invisible, their bits are set. The cache remains valid until transfer function modifications occur. Time Complexity: The algorithm skips transparent regions entirely, reducing the number of compositing steps to the number of opaque voxels along the ray. In the worst case (fully opaque volume), it performs Z iterations, but with bit manipulation, the inner loop runs only for opaque voxels. The Depth function and bit clearing are O(1) or O(\log Z) depending on implementation, but typically optimized to O(1) with hardware support. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the binary mask, which is X \times Y \times \lceil Z/32 \rceil integers. For a 512 \times 512 \times 512 volume, this is 512 \times 512 \times 16 \times 4 bytes \approx 16 MB, significantly less than the raw volume data. Measured Performance: The technique is well-known in volume rendering literature for accelerating alpha-blending. It is particularly effective for sparse volumes or volumes with large transparent regions. Strengths: Precise skipping of empty regions; efficient bit-level manipulation; simple integration with standard alpha-blending. Limitations: Requires precomputation of the binary mask; less effective for dense volumes with few transparent regions; threshold selection can impact visual quality. When to use: Sparse volumes, interactive rendering where performance is critical, and when the volume has large transparent regions. When not to use: Dense volumes with minimal transparency, or when memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and mask generation is expensive. The technique is based on the concept of early ray termination, a well-known acceleration method in volume rendering literature. The specific use of binary masks for empty space skipping was described in the context of interactive volume rendering for medical data visualization. The cell invisibility cache variant was introduced to handle remaining transparent regions in octree-based rendering, improving performance for large medical datasets. Interactive Volume-Rendering Techniques for Medical Data Visualization, https://doi.org/10.2312/diss.20018138, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Efficient Volume Visualization of Large Medical Datasets, https://old.cescg.org/CESCG-2004/web/Bruckner-Stefan/html/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Surface-Volume Rendering with Masking and Early Ray Termination
head: Fast Surface and Volume Rendering Based on Shear-Warp Factorization, Masking in Sheared Image Space, Spine Biopsy Simulator (SBS) rendering method
body: This method accelerates the hybrid rendering of a volume-rendered organ and a surface-rendered instrument by combining early ray termination for the volume data with spatial masking in the sheared image space for the instrument. It solves the performance bottleneck of real-time surgical simulators where a moving instrument must be composited over a large volume dataset. Unlike standard early ray termination which only stops volume traversal, this method explicitly tracks the instrument's motion in 2D sheared space to limit recomputation to only the affected pixels, achieving speed-ups of up to 2.84x compared to full recomputation. Inputs: Volume dataset: 3D array of voxel values, typically sized 256 \times 256 \times 256. Instrument geometry: Surface model defined by vertices (x, y, z). View parameters: View direction defined by angles (\theta, \phi). Previous frame state: Previous mask N{t-1}(u,v). Outputs: Combined image C(K,v) containing the volume-rendered organ and the surface-rendered instrument. 1. Volume Data: 3D array of voxel values. 2. Instrument Geometry: List of vertices (x, y, z) and surface normals/faces. 3. Mask Nt(u,v): 2D binary array of size equal to the image resolution. Nt(u,v) = 1 if the pixel (u,v) requires update (instrument present or changed), 0 otherwise. 4. Shear Coefficients: sx = \tan\theta, sy = \tan\phi. 5. Accumulated Opacity a{acc}(u,v): 2D array storing the accumulated opacity of the volume ray traversal up to the termination point. 1. Calculate Shear Coefficients: Determine the shear coefficients based on the view direction (\theta, \phi). The first rotation is counterclockwise about the y-axis by \theta, and the second is counterclockwise about the x-axis by \phi: sx = \tan\theta sy = \tan\phi 2. Transform Instrument to Sheared Space: Transform the instrument's 3D geometry (x, y, z) into the 3D sheared space (xs, ys, zs) using an affine transform matrix for shear. This allows the depth of the instrument to be represented simply by the z-coordinate in the sheared space. 3. Update Mask: Determine the region of the image that needs updating based on the instrument's motion. If the instrument position changes, identify the pixels (u,v) where the instrument exists at time t. Update the mask Nt(u,v) using binary OR with the previous mask N{t-1}(u,v): Nt(u,v) = N{t-1}(u,v) \text{ OR } Nt(u,v) \quad \text{if the instrument exists at } (u,v) \text{ at time } t Nt(u,v) = N{t-1}(u,v) \quad \text{otherwise} This ensures that once a pixel is marked as requiring an update, it remains marked until the viewer position changes or the mask is reset. 4. Volume Rendering with Early Ray Termination: For each pixel (u,v) in the image: If Nt(u,v) == 1, perform ray casting through the volume. Terminate the ray when the accumulated opacity exceeds a given threshold OR when the ray intersects the surface of the instrument. Assume instrument opacity is 1; once the ray meets the instrument, no further volume computation is needed for that ray. Calculate the depth of the organ intersection d{org} and the accumulated opacity a{acc}(u,v) up to the termination point ZB(u,v). 5. Depth Comparison: Compare the depth of the instrument d2 (in the 3D sheared space, d2 = zs) with the depth of the organ d{org} (Euclidean distance d1 or sheared depth). If the organ depth is longer than the instrument depth, the instrument is in front of the organ. The depth d2 is used instead of Euclidean distance d1 to reduce computation time. Euclidean distance is defined as: d1 = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2} where dx, dy, dz are distances along the axes between the voxel and the pixel. 6. Composite Instrument and Volume: Combine the surface-rendered instrument image f{inst}(u,v) with the volume-rendered organ image I{org}(u,v) using alpha-blending. The instrument's contribution is weighted by the remaining accumulated opacity of the organs. Sources differ on the exact weighting formula; S1 proposes C(K,v) = f{inst}(u,v) + (1 - a{inst}(u,v)) \cdot I{org}(u,v) / a{acc}(u,v), while S2 uses C(K,v) = f{inst}(u,v) + I{org}(u,v) \cdot (1 - a{acc}(u,v)). Where: C(K,v) is the combined image pixel. f{inst}(u,v) is the pixel value of the 2D instrument image. I{org}(u,v) is the pixel value of the volume-rendered organ image from ray traversal up to ZB(u,v). a{acc}(u,v) is the accumulated opacity of the organs. As a{acc}(u,v) increases, the weight of the instrument decreases. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def hybridrender(volumedata, instrumentgeometry, viewtheta, viewphi, prevmask, imagewidth, imageheight, threshold=0.95): # 1. Calculate Shear Coefficients sx = math.tan(viewtheta) sy = math.tan(viewphi) # 2. Transform Instrument to Sheared Space # Apply shear transformation: xs = x + sx z, ys = y + sy z, zs = z instrumentsheared = [] for vertex in instrumentgeometry: x, y, z = vertex instrumentsheared.append((x + sx z, y + sy z, z)) # 3. Update Mask # Determine current instrument projection in 2D image space currentinstrumentpixels = getinstrumentpixelmask(instrumentsheared, imagewidth, imageheight) # Binary OR with previous mask newmask = [[prevmask[v][u] | currentinstrumentpixels[v][u] for u in range(imagewidth)] for v in range(imageheight)] # 4. Initialize Output Image combinedimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(imagewidth)] for in range(imageheight)] # 5. Render Pixels for v in range(imageheight): for u in range(imagewidth): if newmask[v][u] == 0: continue # Ray casting through volume accumulatedopacity = 0.0 organcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] terminationdepth = float('inf') instrumenthit = False # Traverse ray through volume for sampledepth in range(0, 100, 1): # Check for instrument intersection if checkinstrumentintersection(u, v, sampledepth, instrumentsheared): terminationdepth = sampledepth instrumenthit = True break # Early termination condition if accumulatedopacity > threshold: terminationdepth = sampledepth break # Volume compositing (front-to-back) color, opacity = samplevolumecolor(volumedata, u, v, sampledepth) weight = (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity organcolor = [organcolor[i] + color[i] weight for i in range(3)] accumulatedopacity += weight # Get instrument color if it was in front instrumentcolor = getinstrumentcoloratdepth(u, v, terminationdepth, instrumentsheared) if instrumenthit else None # 6. Composite if instrumentcolor is not None: remainingopacity = 1.0 - accumulatedopacity combinedimage[v][u] = [ instrumentcolor[i] + organcolor[i] remainingopacity for i in range(3) ] else: combinedimage[v][u] = organcolor return combinedimage, newmask def getinstrumentpixelmask(instrumentsheared, width, height): mask = [[0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] if not instrumentsheared: return mask minx = min(v[0] for v in instrumentsheared) maxx = max(v[0] for v in instrumentsheared) miny = min(v[1] for v in instrumentsheared) maxy = max(v[1] for v in instrumentsheared) for y in range(int(miny), int(maxy) + 1): for x in range(int(minx), int(maxx) + 1): if 0 <= y < height and 0 <= x < width: mask[y][x] = 1 return mask def checkinstrumentintersection(u, v, depth, instrumentsheared): # Standard ray-surface intersection logic in sheared space # Returns True if instrument surface is at this depth along the ray return False def samplevolumecolor(volumedata, u, v, depth): # Standard trilinear interpolation and transfer function application return ([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 0.0) def getinstrumentcoloratdepth(u, v, depth, instrumentsheared): # Standard surface shading and lighting calculation return None Threshold: Accumulated opacity threshold for early ray termination. Not given in the sources. Data Size: 256 \times 256 \times 256 voxels. Hardware: 400-MHz Pentium PC with 256 MB memory. Overhead: Rendering time does not decrease proportionally to the voxel count reduction because the compositing function has overheads, such as determining the masking region and the voxel-skipping procedure with ray termination in the intermediate image. Resampling: The shear-warp algorithm involves two resampling steps: every slice is resampled during compositing, and the intermediate image is resampled. Viewer Position Change: The mask is only updated based on instrument motion. If the viewer's position changes, the mask must be reset or recomputed for the entire image. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of voxels contributing to volume rendering from ~2,650,000 to ~20,000-35,000 (about 1% of the total) when the instrument moves 7.03 mm in x- and z-directions. Measured Performance: Torso Scene (Skin, Lung, Spine): Color rendering time reduced from 0.91 s to 0.32 s (2.84x faster). Spine Only Scene (Half Needle Overlap): Color rendering time reduced from 0.36 s to 0.22 s (1.64x faster). Strengths: Significant speed-up for hybrid rendering of moving instruments over large volumes. Effective for simulators requiring real-time feedback. Limitations: Speed-up is limited by the overhead of mask management and shear-warp resampling. Performance gain decreases when the volume rendering region is smaller (e.g., spine only vs. full torso). When to Use: Real-time surgical simulators or medical training systems where a surface-rendered instrument (e.g., needle) must be interactively moved over a volume-rendered organ dataset. When Not to Use: Static scenes where the instrument does not move, or scenes where the viewer position changes frequently, as the mask optimization becomes less effective or requires full recomputation. This method was developed for the Spine Biopsy Simulator (SBS) system, which helps medical students train for spine biopsy procedures virtually. The system combines volume-rendered organs and a surface-rendered needle image to provide realistic visualization and haptic feedback. The approach leverages the shear-warp factorization algorithm for fast volume rendering and extends it with masking and early ray termination to handle the dynamic instrument. The work was supported by the Korea Ministry of Information and Communication under the 98-10 grant. Fast Surface and Volume Rendering Based on Shear-Warp Factorization for a Surgical Simulator, https://doi.org/10.1002/igs.10050, fetched 2026-10-26 Fast surface and volume rendering based on shear-warp factorization for a surgical simulator., https://www.scienceopen.com/document?vid=077fb90e-0925-455c-85c6-4927cdfc1199, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Adaptive Termination
body: Adaptive Termination is a volume rendering acceleration technique that terminates ray integration early once the accumulated color change between consecutive samples falls below a defined threshold \epsilon. It identifies the last sample along a ray that significantly changes the color, defined as C{out} - C{in} > \epsilon, and stops further sampling when the change is no longer significant or when opacity exceeds 1 - \epsilon. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray parameters (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}), volume data, transfer functions (opacity \alpha, color C), step size \Delta t, and termination threshold \epsilon > 0. Output: Final pixel color C{final} and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Data Structures: Accumulated color C{acc} (initialized to [0,0,0]). Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} (initialized to 0). Previous accumulated color C{prev} (initialized to [0,0,0]). Threshold \epsilon (small positive constant). Steps: 1. Cast a ray through the volume and compute its intersection interval [t{min}, t{max}] with the volume bounds. 2. Sample equidistant points along the ray segment within the volume bounds using step size \Delta t. 3. For each sample i: a. Retrieve sample color C{sample} and opacity \alpha{sample} from transfer functions. b. Compute the contribution to the accumulated color: \Delta C = C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). c. Update accumulated color: C{acc} = C{acc} + \Delta C. d. Update accumulated opacity: \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}). e. Check termination condition: if \alpha{acc} \ge 1 - \epsilon or |C{acc} - C{prev}| \le \epsilon, terminate. f. Set C{prev} = C{acc}. 4. Return C{acc}. Parameters: \epsilon: Termination threshold. Higher values reduce rendering time but may increase artifacts; lower values reduce artifacts and produce higher quality images. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The comparison |C{acc} - C{prev}| \le \epsilon is sensitive to floating-point precision. If \epsilon is too small relative to the precision of C{acc}, the condition may never trigger, negating the benefit. Boundary: The condition \alpha{acc} \ge 1 - \epsilon ensures that rays passing through fully opaque regions terminate correctly, even if color changes are minimal due to occlusion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivetermination(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds, stepsize, epsilon): # 1. Intersect ray with volume bounding box tmin, tmax = 0.0, 0.0 invdir = [1.0 / d if d != 0 else float('inf') for d in raydirection] for i in range(3): t1 = (volumebounds[2 i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] t2 = (volumebounds[2 i + 1] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Ray misses volume # 2. Initialize accumulators acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 prevcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = tmin # 3. March along ray segment while t <= tmax: # Sample volume at current position pos = [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] t for i in range(3)] samplecolor, sampleopacity = volumedata.sample(pos) # Front-to-back compositing weight = sampleopacity (1.0 - accopacity) acccolor = [acccolor[j] + samplecolor[j] weight for j in range(3)] accopacity = accopacity + sampleopacity (1.0 - accopacity) # 4. Check termination conditions if accopacity >= 1.0 - epsilon: break colordiff = sum(abs(acccolor[j] - prevcolor[j]) for j in range(3)) if colordiff <= epsilon: break prevcolor = acccolor t += stepsize return acccolor + [accopacity] Time Complexity: O(N) in the worst case (no early termination), but typically O(K) where K \ll N is the number of samples processed before termination. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it only stores current and previous color/opacity states. Strengths: Reduces computation in homogeneous or low-contrast regions where opacity accumulates slowly but color change is minimal. Complements opacity-based termination by handling cases where opacity is high but color is stable. Limitations: Requires computing the difference between consecutive accumulated colors, adding a small per-sample overhead. May introduce artifacts if \epsilon is set too high, causing premature termination in regions with subtle but important details. When to use: When the volume has regions of low contrast or homogeneous density where color changes are negligible despite remaining samples. When not to use: When high-frequency color details are critical and \epsilon cannot be set low enough without performance loss. Adaptive Termination was introduced in the context of Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) techniques, specifically within ray-casting algorithms. It is described in educational resources on volume rendering, such as presentations on ray-casting methods. The technique leverages the observation that once the accumulated color stabilizes (i.e., changes by less than a small threshold \epsilon), further samples contribute negligibly to the final image, allowing for early termination. Terminates based on a fixed number of samples or a global budget, not local color change [1790-early-stop.md]. Terminates solely when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold, ignoring color change magnitude [7920-opacity-based-early-termination.md]. Probabilistically terminates rays based on transmittance, used for stochastic paths rather than deterministic ray casting [1371-russian-roulette.md]. name: Probabilistic Culling
head: Approximate Intersection Culling, Approximate Tile-Wise Culling, Ibrahim et al, Probabilistic Culling for Particle Rendering
body: Probabilistic Culling is a rendering optimization that intentionally allows false-negatives in intersection tests to reduce duplicated fragments and rendering time, particularly in virtual reality (VR) and high-resolution contexts. It sets itself apart from conservative culling methods by trading strict geometric accuracy for performance, relying on the fact that resulting visual artifacts are imperceptible. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of view-dependent primitives (e.g., splats or tiles) and their bounding volumes. Output: A subset of primitives passed to the rasterization stage, with some occluded primitives incorrectly classified as visible (false-negatives). Data Structures: The method operates on tile-wise or primitive-level bounding boxes. Steps: 1. Bounding: Compute tight bounding boxes for each tile or primitive group. 2. Approximate Intersection Test: Perform an intersection test between the view frustum (or camera ray) and the bounding box; unlike conservative culling, this test may return visible even if the primitive is occluded, justifying false-negatives to reduce duplicated fragments. 3. Fragment Generation: Pass the visible primitives to the rasterizer; approximate culling reduces the amount of staged fragments compared to tight bounding boxes. 4. Rendering: Render the fragments; image difference metrics confirm the visual impact is negligible. Formulas: The method modifies the culling condition rather than compositing. Conservative culling ensures V = \text{true} \implies \text{primitive is visible}. Probabilistic culling allows V = \text{true} \implies \text{primitive is processed, potentially introducing false-negatives}. Parameters: Bounding Box Tightness: Controls the trade-off between culling overhead and fragment reduction. Framebuffer Resolution: The benefit increases with resolution and is especially prominent in VR. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Resolution: At default framebuffer sizes (e.g., 1920×1080), performance gains are minimal because the reduction in sorting/rasterization workload is offset by a slight increase in fragment creation duration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def probabilisticcull(primitives, frustumbounds): """ Cull primitives using approximate intersection tests. frustumbounds: dict with keys 'minx', 'maxx', 'miny', 'maxy', 'minz', 'maxz' """ visibleprimitives = [] for prim in primitives: # Compute tight bounding box for the primitive bboxmin = [min(v[i] for v in prim.vertices) for i in range(3)] bboxmax = [max(v[i] for v in prim.vertices) for i in range(3)] # Perform approximate intersection test # Standard AABB vs view frustum check isvisible = True if bboxmax[0] < frustumbounds['minx'] or bboxmin[0] > frustumbounds['maxx']: isvisible = False elif bboxmax[1] < frustumbounds['miny'] or bboxmin[1] > frustumbounds['maxy']: isvisible = False elif bboxmax[2] < frustumbounds['minz'] or bboxmin[2] > frustumbounds['maxz']: isvisible = False # Probabilistic culling allows false-negatives by skipping strict occlusion checks if isvisible: visibleprimitives.append(prim) return visibleprimitives A runtime optimization that isolates particle subsets by culling particles whose simulation property values do not overlap a user-defined valid range. It sets itself apart by allowing interactive range changes, unlike static culling. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: The culling step is O(N) where N is the number of primitives/tiles, reducing the workload for sorting and rasterization. Memory: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Berlin Scene (Desktop): Fragments reduced from 6.3M to 5.9M; rendering time from 2.7ms to 2.6ms. Berlin Scene (VR): Fragments reduced from 12.8M to 9.8M; rendering time from 5.6ms to 5.2ms. Visual Quality: Image difference metrics show renderings are virtually indistinguishable (Berlin PSNR 41.83 dB, SSIM 0.9996, FLIP 0.0010, LPIPS 0.0021). Scaling: The impact increases with framebuffer size and is especially prominent in VR rendering, where the pixel count is significantly higher (e.g., 4.36 times more pixels in VR vs. desktop). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant performance gains in VR and high-resolution rendering; imperceptible visual quality loss. Limitations: Little impact at low resolutions; potential for a slight increase in fragment creation duration. Probabilistic Culling, also known as Approximate Tile-Wise Culling, was proposed by Ibrahim et al. [IRR22] for efficient particle rendering using task and mesh shader pipelines. It is used in contexts where real-time performance is critical, such as VR, and where the visual cost of false-negatives is acceptable. name: Parameter Range Culling
head: PIC culling, PR culling, Property Range Culling, Run Time Parameter Culling
body: Parameter Range Culling is a runtime optimization that isolates particle subsets by culling particles whose simulation property values do not overlap a user-defined valid range. It solves the problem of visualizing specific behaviors within large particle datasets by avoiding unnecessary ray/sphere intersection tests for particles outside the range of interest. It sets itself apart from static culling methods by allowing the valid range to be changed interactively at runtime, providing flexibility for data analysis, albeit with some computational overhead compared to pre-cropped data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A particle dataset organized in a macrocell hierarchy (see Coherent Grid Traversal), where each particle has a position, radius, and up to four additional simulation properties (e.g., density, velocity). The user specifies a valid range for these properties. Output: A subset of particles that lie within the valid range, which are then subjected to ray/sphere intersection tests. Data Structures: Macrocell: Each macrocell stores the minimum and maximum values for each of the eight parameters (four properties \times two bounds: min/max) across all particles it contains. Particle: Each particle stores its position, radius, and the values for the four additional properties. Numbered Steps: 1. Macrocell Culling: During grid traversal, check if the macrocell's stored min/max range for each of the eight parameters overlaps the user-specified valid range. If the macrocell range does not overlap the user-specified range, skip the macrocell and cull all contained particles. This check requires eight SIMD operations: four comparisons, two Boolean AND operations, and two masking operations. 2. Particle Culling: If at least one particle in a macrocell lies within the valid range, the macrocell cannot be skipped. Apply the same range check to individual particles before performing the intersection test. If any of the particle's values lie outside the user-specified range, skip the intersection test and cull the particle. This also requires eight SIMD operations per sphere: four comparisons, two Boolean AND operations, and two masking operations. Formulas: Let Pi be a particle with property values v{i,1}, v{i,2}, v{i,3}, v{i,4}. Let [Lk, Uk] be the user-specified valid range for property k. Let [min{c,k}, max{c,k}] be the stored min/max range for property k in macrocell c. A macrocell c is culled if for any property k \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}: max{c,k} < Lk \quad \text{or} \quad min{c,k} > Uk A particle i is culled if for any property k \in \{1, 2, 3, 4\}: v{i,k} < Lk \quad \text{or} \quad v{i,k} > Uk Parameters: Number of Properties: Up to four additional properties per particle. SIMD Operations: 16 SIMD operations total for macrocell and particle range checking (8 for macrocell, 8 for particle). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: The range check is inclusive/exclusive depending on implementation, but the sources define culling based on non-overlap. Degenerate Input: If the user specifies an empty range, all particles are culled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def parameterrangeculling(macrocell, userranges, particles): """ macrocell: object with minmaxproperties (array of 4 tuples, each tuple is (min, max)) userranges: array of 4 tuples, each tuple is (lowerbound, upperbound) particles: list of particle objects, each with properties (array of 4 values) """ # Step 1: Macrocell Culling for k in range(4): cellmin, cellmax = macrocell.minmaxproperties[k] lower, upper = userranges[k] # Check for non-overlap if cellmax < lower or cellmin > upper: return [] # Cull entire macrocell # Step 2: Particle Culling validparticles = [] for particle in particles: isvalid = True for k in range(4): val = particle.properties[k] lower, upper = userranges[k] if val < lower or val > upper: isvalid = False break if isvalid: validparticles.append(particle) return validparticles Culls particles outside the view frustum. Sets it apart by using geometric bounds rather than simulation properties. Choose it for basic visibility optimization. Frustum Culling Culls particles based on ray/axis-aligned bounding box intersections. Sets it apart by using ray-specific bounds. Choose it for ray-based acceleration. Ray/Box Culling Time Complexity: The cost of range checking is amortized over the number of particles in a macrocell and is significantly less than the ray/sphere intersection tests. However, the 16 SIMD operations add computational overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing min/max values for 8 parameters per macrocell. Measured Performance: Thunder dataset: 43.06 fps (PR cull) vs 59.55 fps (Pre-crop). Total processing time reduced by 43.00%, mean culling rate 14.23%, max culling rate 43.06%. BulletTorso dataset: 11.18 fps (PR cull) vs 25.49 fps (Pre-crop). Total processing time reduced by 34.17%, mean culling rate 3.17%, max culling rate 11.18%. Performance degradation compared to preprocessed data: Factor of 1.38–2.28. Strengths: Provides interactive flexibility for data analysis by allowing runtime range changes. Limitations: Adds computational overhead due to SIMD operations, resulting in lower frame rates compared to pre-cropped data. When to use: When interactive exploration of specific simulation properties is required. When not to use: When maximum performance is needed and the particle subset is static (use pre-cropping instead). Parameter Range Culling was introduced in the context of coherent grid traversal for visualizing particle-based simulation data. It was developed to allow investigators to isolate particles with specific parameter values (e.g., density, velocity) to gain insight into simulation behavior. The method is part of a broader suite of culling techniques including frustum culling and ray/box culling. name: Visibility Feedback with Screen Space Subdivision
head: Occlusion Culling Feedback, Visibility Feedback for Occlusion Culling, Visibility-based Node Refinement
body: Visibility Feedback with Screen Space Subdivision is an out-of-core volume rendering optimization that uses visibility information gathered during the current frame to prevent the loading and refinement of occluded data in subsequent frames. Unlike standard early ray termination, which only skips computation after data has already been loaded into the GPU working set, this method feeds visibility results back to the loader to reduce GPU memory usage and bandwidth. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by combining occlusion queries with a screen-space subdivision strategy to interleave query processing with rasterization, thereby hiding the latency inherent in asynchronous occlusion query results. The method operates on an octree data structure where nodes represent bricks of volume data. It modifies the standard rendering loop by introducing a feedback cycle that updates node visibility status based on rasterization results. Input: An octree of volume bricks, a camera view, and a transfer function. Output: A rendered image and an updated visibility status for each octree node. Octree Node: Contains a 3D bounding box, a refinement status flag, and a boolean visible flag indicating whether the node was marked visible in the previous frame. Visibility Query List: A list of 2D screen-space bounding rectangles for non-empty leaf nodes selected for occlusion testing. Screen Tiles: A recursive partition of the viewport used to schedule queries and separate queried blocks from others. 1. Initialization: Start with the octree root. Mark all nodes as potentially visible. 2. Refinement and Rendering: Refine only nodes marked as visible from the previous frame. Perform front-to-back ray casting for the current frame. In the fragment shader, write the depth of the last visited sample to the depth buffer. Accumulate color and opacity using standard front-to-back compositing. Terminate rays when the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (early ray termination). 3. Screen Space Subdivision: Collect the 2D screen-space projections (bounding rectangles) of all non-empty leaf nodes that were rendered. Recursively partition the screen into tiles using a 2D binary space subdivision (BSP) to separate blocks for which visibility will be queried from others. At each subdivision step, place a split plane along one of the axes (X or Y) at the position that separates the set of blocks into two equally sized subsets. Select one of the two resulting tiles as containing the subset of nodes to be occlusion queried. Continue subdividing only the selected tile until its size falls below a threshold or the query budget is met. Rotate the selection strategy (e.g., alternate which half-space is queried) across frames to ensure all nodes are covered within a minimum number of frames. 4. Occlusion Query Execution: Issue rendering commands for the tiles. For the tile selected for querying, issue an occlusion query for the bounding box of the non-empty leaves contained within it. The query is issued immediately after the rendering command for the first tile to interleave query processing with the rasterization of other tiles, reducing end-to-end latency. 5. Visibility Update: After the frame completes, retrieve occlusion query results. If the number of visible pixels for a node's bounding box is below a visibility threshold (typically 4 pixels), mark the node as not visible. Propagate visibility up the tree: an inner node is considered visible if and only if at least one of its children is visible. Store these visibility flags for use in the next frame's refinement cycle. The method modifies the standard front-to-back compositing loop by introducing early termination conditions and visibility feedback: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) where C{acc} and \alpha{acc} are the accumulated color and opacity, and C{sample} and \alpha{sample} are the color and opacity of the current sample. Rays terminate when \alpha{acc} exceeds a predefined threshold. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(octree, camera, transferfunction, prevvisibilityflags): # 1. Refinement: only refine nodes marked visible in the previous frame visiblenodes = [node for node in octree.nodes if prevvisibilityflags[node.id]] workingset = [] for node in visiblenodes: if node.isleaf: workingset.append(node) else: workingset.extend(node.children) # 2. Rendering: front-to-back ray casting with early termination for node in workingset: if node.isleaf: # Standard front-to-back compositing loop for a leaf brick acccolor, accalpha = 0.0, 0.0 for sample in node.samples: Cs, alphas = sample.color, sample.alpha acccolor += Cs alphas (1.0 - accalpha) accalpha += alphas (1.0 - accalpha) if accalpha > 0.99: break # Write depth of last visited sample to the depth buffer writedepthtobuffer(sample.z) # 3. Screen Space Subdivision: collect 2D projections of non-empty leaves leafprojections = [] for node in workingset: if node.isleaf: rect = project2drect(node.boundingbox, camera) leafprojections.append({'node': node, 'rect': rect}) # Partition screen into tiles using 2D BSP tiles, queriednodes = screenspacesubdivide(leafprojections) # 4. Issue Occlusion Queries: render tiles, query selected subset for tile in tiles: if tile in queriednodes: # Issue hardware occlusion query for the tile's bounding box issueocclusionquery(tile.boundingbox) else: # Render the tile without occlusion query rendertile(tile) # 5. Visibility Feedback: retrieve results (delayed by N+1 frames) queryresults = getocclusionqueryresults() newvisibilityflags = {} # Process leaves first to ensure children are evaluated before parents for node in octree.nodes: if node.isleaf: if node in queriednodes: visiblepixels = queryresults.get(node.id, 0) newvisibilityflags[node.id] = visiblepixels >= VISIBILITYTHRESHOLD else: newvisibilityflags[node.id] = True # Not queried, assume visible else: # Propagate up: node visible if at least one child is visible newvisibilityflags[node.id] = any(newvisibilityflags[child.id] for child in node.children) return newvisibilityflags def screenspacesubdivide(projections): if not projections: return [], [] mid = len(projections) // 2 leftprojections = projections[:mid] rightprojections = projections[mid:] # Select one tile for querying (strategy rotates per frame) queriednodes = [p['node'] for p in leftprojections] if len(leftprojections) > THRESHOLD: subtiles, subqueried = screenspacesubdivide(leftprojections) return subtiles, subqueried else: return [Tile(leftprojections)], queriednodes def project2drect(bbox, camera): corners = [project3dto2d(p, camera) for p in bbox] return {'minx': min(c[0] for c in corners), 'maxx': max(c[0] for c in corners), 'miny': min(c[1] for c in corners), 'maxy': max(c[1] for c in corners)} def project3dto2d(point, camera): x, y, z = point cx, cy, cz = camera.position fx, fy = camera.focallength return ((x - cx) fx / (z - cz), (y - cy) fy / (z - cz)) THRESHOLD = 10 VISIBILITYTHRESHOLD = 4 Visibility Threshold: The number of visible pixels below which a node is marked as not visible. Typical value: 4 pixels. Visibility Incorporation Delay: The number of frames between issuing a query and using its result. Calculated as N + 1, where N is the number of partitions required to cover all blocks. Typical value: 2 to 4 frames. Pipeline Latency: Occlusion query results are not available immediately due to the delay between issuing the query and rasterizer processing. A straightforward implementation issuing queries for all nodes is inefficient. The screen space subdivision mitigates this by interleaving queries with rasterization. Semitransparent Materials: Visibility culling is less effective for semitransparent materials because more samples are accumulated, leading to higher texture memory needs and reduced working set reduction. Degenerate Input: If the screen space subdivision results in tiles smaller than the threshold but still containing nodes, the recursion stops, and the query is issued for the entire tile. Working Set Reduction: Reduces the working set by approximately 50% in semitransparent cases and by approximately 60% when surfaces are more opaque. Memory Occupation: Isosurface rendering: Average 1560 bricks, peak 1820 bricks. Direct Volume Rendering (DVR): Average 1890 bricks, peak 2450 bricks. Minimum texture memory occupation for both: ~475 octree bricks (corresponding to distant views). Performance: Isosurface rendering: Average 20 Hz, peak 40 Hz. DVR: Average 12-30 Hz (varies by transfer function). Scaling: On a 1024x1024 window, performance slows down by a factor of 3 compared to 640x480, roughly corresponding to the pixel count increase. Strengths: Significantly reduces GPU memory bandwidth and memory usage by preventing the loading of occluded data. Effective for opaque surfaces. Limitations: Less effective for highly semitransparent volumes. Requires asynchronous query handling to hide latency. Adds complexity to the rendering pipeline due to screen space subdivision and feedback delay. This method was introduced in the context of out-of-core GPU ray casting for interactive volume rendering. It addresses the limitation of standard early ray termination, which discovers occlusion only after data is loaded, by incorporating visibility feedback into the loader. The technique relies on the spatial and temporal coherence of volume rendering to schedule occlusion queries efficiently. name: Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping
head: Improved Ray Casting with Empty Voxel Skipping and Multi-Step Length, Space leap empty voxel ray-casting algorithm, Three-step jump algorithm
body: Adaptive Multi-Step Empty Voxel Skipping is an acceleration technique for direct volume rendering that combines space leaping (empty voxel skipping) with adaptive variable step-size sampling. It solves the problem of redundant computation in large datasets containing significant empty space, such as medical CT scans, by bypassing empty regions entirely and adjusting sampling density based on local voxel occupancy. Unlike traditional equidistant ray casting, this method reduces computational overhead without altering the input data structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (e.g., CT scan), camera parameters, and ray generation state. Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: The algorithm is implemented by inheriting the VTK base class vtkVolumeRayCastingFunction to create a new class vtkMyVolumeRayCastFunction that encapsulates the improved logic. The core data structure tracks the ray's current position along the ray and its current operational mode. Ray States: The ray operates in one of two mutually exclusive states: 1. Search State: The ray traverses empty voxels to find the next non-empty voxel without compositing. 2. Accumulation State: The ray samples non-empty voxels, accumulating color and transparency. Algorithm Steps: 1. Pre-check Validity: Detect if any non-empty voxels exist along the ray direction. If no non-empty voxels are detected, mark the ray as invalid and skip all operations, proceeding to the next ray. 2. Initialize Ray State: Set the ray to the Search State. 3. Adaptive Step Selection: Determine the sampling step length based on local voxel density at the current ray position. If the area contains many empty voxels, set a longer step value. If voxel density is high, set a shorter step value to increase accuracy. 4. Traverse and Compositing Loop: While the ray is within the volume bounds, sample the current voxel. If in Search State and the voxel is empty, advance the ray position by the current step length and repeat. If in Search State and the voxel is non-empty, switch to Accumulation State. If in Accumulation State, sample the voxel, accumulate color and transparency using front-to-back compositing, advance the ray position by the step length, and re-evaluate local density to adjust the step length for the next iteration. 5. Resample and Synthesize: Perform resampling and compositing only on the identified non-empty voxels using the selected step length, skipping invalid computations on empty regions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, volumebounds): # Check if ray intersects volume bounds if not intersectsvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Pre-check: Detect if any non-empty voxels exist along the ray direction # The sources do not specify the exact acceleration structure for this check. if not hasnonemptyvoxelsalongray(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds, volumedata): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Initialize ray state currentpos = rayorigin raystate = "SEARCH" # SEARCH or ACCUMULATE accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Initial step length (default or derived from global density) steplength = getinitialsteplength(volumedata) while isinsidevolume(currentpos, volumebounds): voxelvalue = samplevoxel(currentpos, volumedata) if raystate == "SEARCH": if isempty(voxelvalue): # Skip empty voxel currentpos = currentpos + raydirection steplength steplength = adaptivesteplength(currentpos, volumedata) else: # Found non-empty voxel, switch to accumulation raystate = "ACCUMULATE" # Fall through to accumulation logic for this voxel if raystate == "ACCUMULATE": color, alpha = transferfunction(voxelvalue) # Front-to-back compositing accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + (color alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity)) accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + (alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity)) # Advance ray and adjust step length based on new position's density currentpos = currentpos + raydirection steplength steplength = adaptivesteplength(currentpos, volumedata) return accumulatedcolor def intersectsvolume(origin, direction, bounds): # Standard ray-AABB intersection test pass def hasnonemptyvoxelsalongray(origin, direction, bounds, data): # The sources do not specify the exact acceleration structure for this check. pass def getinitialsteplength(data): # The sources do not specify the exact initialization logic. pass def isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): # Standard bounds check pass def samplevoxel(pos, data): # Standard trilinear/trilinear interpolation or direct lookup pass def isempty(value): # Standard threshold comparison pass def transferfunction(value): # Standard opacity/color mapping pass def adaptivesteplength(pos, data): # The sources do not specify the exact density evaluation function. pass Parameters: Step Length (s): A variable step size. It is not fixed. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Porphyritic Artifacts: The combination of empty voxel jumping and uneven (adaptive) sampling can cause a patchy or mottled appearance in the rendered image, particularly noticeable during rotation interactions. Boundary Conditions: Rays that do not intersect the volume or pass entirely through empty space must be handled efficiently to avoid unnecessary computation. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of samples per ray by skipping empty voxels. The complexity depends on the sparsity of the volume. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data and potentially auxiliary structures for empty voxel detection. The VTK implementation inherits from vtkVolumeRayCastingFunction, implying minimal additional memory overhead beyond the base class. Measured Performance: Tested on Windows 7, Visual Studio 2010, VTK 5.10.1, using virtual human head CT scan data. Rendering speed was measured by rotation time. The method achieved significant speedup compared to traditional ray casting. Strengths: Reduces computational overhead without changing the input 2D sequence images. Maintains visual quality almost identical to the original method, despite artifacts. Limitations: Can introduce visual artifacts (porphyritic appearance) due to uneven sampling. When to Use: Suitable for large-volume datasets with significant empty space, such as medical CT scans. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Origin: The method was proposed in a paper titled "The research of improved ray casting algorithm on VTK". History: It builds upon the traditional ray-casting algorithm proposed by Marc Levoy. The algorithm was implemented using the Visualization Toolkit (VTK). Development: The method combines space leaping (empty voxel skipping) with adaptive multi-step length sampling. It was tested on VTK 5.10.1. Usage: Primarily used in medical image visualization, specifically for CT scan data. name: 24-Region View-Dependent Visibility Preprocessing
body: A preprocessing technique that decomposes the domain of viewing directions into 24 regions on a directional cube to extract a lower number of potentially visible voxels compared to the standard 6-region decomposition, improving extraction rate and rendering speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset V of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, where each voxel has a binary boundary indicator b(i, j, k) (1 if boundary, 0 otherwise). Output: A set of precomputed visibility masks Mr for each of the 24 regions r, where Mr(i, j, k) = 1 if voxel (i, j, k) is potentially visible from direction r, and 0 otherwise. Data Structures: b(i, j, k): Binary grid storing boundary indicators. v(i, j, k): Binary visibility grid computed for a specific viewing direction region. Mr: Array of visibility grids, one for each of the 24 regions. Steps: 1. Decompose Viewing Directions: Divide the viewing direction domain into 24 regions based on the signs of the x and y components, assuming the principal component of the viewing direction is the z coordinate. 2. Compute Visibility for Each Region: For each of the 24 regions, compute the visibility function v(i, j, k) using the boundary grid. 3. Select Region at Render Time: During rendering, determine the current viewing direction, identify which of the 24 regions it falls into, and select the corresponding precomputed visibility mask Mr. Formula: For the case where the x and y components of the viewing direction are both positive, the visibility function v(i, j, k) is defined as: v(i, j, k) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } k = 0 \\ 1 & \text{if } \exists l, m \text{ s.t. } i - 1 \leq l \leq i, \ j - 1 \leq m \leq j, \ v(l, m, k - 1) = 1, \ b(l, m, k - 1) = 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} k=0: Voxels on the front-most slice (along the principal axis) are visible. Recursive step: A voxel (i, j, k) is visible if there exists a neighbor (l, m) in the previous slice (k-1) such that the neighbor is visible (v(l, m, k-1)=1) and the neighbor is not a boundary voxel (b(l, m, k-1)=0). This condition checks only four voxels that could hide the current voxel from the specific viewing direction. This condition is stronger than the general 6-region case (which checks 9 voxels), resulting in fewer extracted voxels. Parameters: Number of regions: 24. Principal axis: z (assumed for the formula, but the method applies to any principal axis). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Preprocessing Time: Decomposing into 24 regions increases preprocessing time compared to 6 regions. Storage: Requires storing 24 visibility masks instead of 6, increasing memory usage. Direction Mapping: The viewing direction must be accurately mapped to one of the 24 regions to select the correct precomputed data structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevisibilityquadrant(boundary): """ Computes visibility mask for the viewing direction quadrant where x>0 and y>0. boundary: 3D list of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) with 1 for boundary, 0 otherwise. Returns: 3D list of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) with 1 for visible, 0 otherwise. """ Nx, Ny, Nz = len(boundary[0][0]), len(boundary[0]), len(boundary) vis = [[[0] Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] # Base case: k=0 is visible for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): vis[i][j][0] = 1 # Recursive step for k > 0 for k in range(1, Nz): for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): isvisible = False # Check the 4 neighbors in the previous slice: (i-1,j-1) to (i,j) for l in range(max(0, i - 1), min(Nx, i + 1)): for m in range(max(0, j - 1), min(Ny, j + 1)): if vis[l][m][k - 1] == 1 and boundary[l][m][k - 1] == 0: isvisible = True break if isvisible: break vis[i][j][k] = 1 if isvisible else 0 return vis def computeall24regions(boundary): """ Computes visibility masks for all 24 regions. The exact angular subdivision per sign quadrant is implementation-specific. This function demonstrates the core logic for one quadrant; others follow by flipping neighbor offsets. """ masks = {} # Compute for the positive quadrant (x>0, y>0) masks['pospos'] = computevisibilityquadrant(boundary) # Other 23 regions are computed similarly with sign-adapted neighbor ranges return masks def renderwith24regionculling(volumedata, viewingdirection, visibilitymasks): """ Renders volume using precomputed 24-region visibility masks. """ # Map viewing direction to one of the 24 regions based on sign combinations regionid = getregionid(viewingdirection) mask = visibilitymasks[regionid] # Standard front-to-back compositing loop for pixel in pixels: ray = generateray(pixel, viewingdirection) alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = 0.0 for t in ray: voxel = samplevolume(ray, t) if mask[voxelcoords] == 0: continue # Skip invisible voxel alphasample = voxel.opacity colorsample = voxel.color alphaacc += alphasample (1 - alphaacc) coloracc += colorsample alphasample (1 - alphaacc) if alphaacc > 0.99: break # Early termination setpixelcolor(pixel, coloracc) A lightweight preprocessing step performed by each input processor (not rendering processor) before local rendering to optimize the subsequent image compositing step and select the appropriate octree level for adaptive rendering. It involves quantization (32-bit to 8-bit), central differencing for gradient vectors (lighting), and one-side differencing for temporal domain enhancement. The octree level is chosen based on image resolution, data resolution, and a user-specified limit on elements projected per pixel. This variant focuses on data preparation and level-of-detail selection rather than directional visibility culling. Time Complexity: Preprocessing time increases with the number of regions, requiring more time than the 6-region method. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 24 visibility masks instead of 6, increasing memory usage. Performance: On a low resolution dataset, decomposing into 24 regions extracts 1.8% of voxels, compared to 3.4% for 6 regions. On a high resolution volume, it extracts 0.9% compared to 1.8% for 6 regions. This significant reduction in extracted voxels leads to faster rendering. Strengths: Higher extraction rate efficiency (fewer voxels processed) compared to 6-region decomposition. Limitations: Increased preprocessing time and storage requirements. Proposed to improve the extraction rate of potentially visible voxels by refining the directional decomposition beyond the standard 6-region approach. name: Frustum Culling
head: View Frustum Culling, markVisible
body: Frustum culling is a visibility culling technique that reduces rendering load by filtering out faces, chunks, or primitives that lie outside the camera's viewing frustum. It solves the problem of unnecessary computation for geometry that does not contribute to the final image by performing a conservative intersection test between bounding volumes and the six planes defining the view frustum. It operates on spatial extent relative to the camera orientation and projection, distinguishing it from depth-based occlusion or transmittance-termination methods. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Spatial entities (chunks, blocks, segments, or points) defined by bounding volumes (spheres or axis-aligned boxes). Camera parameters: view matrix (V), projection matrix (P), near plane distance (n), and far plane distance (f). Outputs: A boolean tensor or mask indicating which entities are visible within the frustum. Data Structures: Bounding Sphere: Defined by center ck = (xk, yk, zk) and radius rk. Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB): Defined by minimum and maximum corner vectors bmin = (bmin[0], bmin[1], bmin[2]) and bmax = (bmax[0], bmax[1], bmax[2]). Frustum Planes: Six planes derived from the combined projection-view matrix M = P \cdot V, each represented by coefficients (a, b, c, d) for the plane equation ax + by + cz + d = 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Extract the six frustum planes from the combined matrix M = P \cdot V. 2. For each entity, compute its signed distance to every frustum plane. 3. Apply the sphere or AABB intersection test against all six planes. 4. If the entity fails any single plane test, mark it as culled; otherwise, mark it as visible. 5. For hierarchical structures, test the node's bounding volume first; if the node is fully outside, discard the entire subtree; if fully inside, accept all descendants; if intersecting, recurse into children. Formulas: Sphere Frustum Test: For a plane with coefficients (a, b, c, d) and sphere center (xk, yk, zk), the signed distance is dist = a xk + b yk + c zk + d. The sphere is culled if dist < -rk for any plane. AABB Frustum Test (Positive-Vertex Test): For each plane (a, b, c, d), select the box corner farthest along the plane's normal: px = bmax[0] if a \ge 0 else bmin[0], py = bmax[1] if b \ge 0 else bmin[1], pz = bmax[2] if c \ge 0 else bmin[2]. Evaluate val = a \cdot px + b \cdot py + c \cdot pz + d. If val < 0 for any plane, the box is culled. Active Block Set (Two-Level Variant): \mathcal{K}t = \bigcup{c \in \mathcal{B}t} \{k \mid \text{visible}(k, c)\}, where \mathcal{B}t is the camera batch and k is a block. Parameters: Camera Configuration: Typical helper implementations use FOV 20°, aspect ratio 1.77, near plane 0.5, and far plane 5. Depth Tolerance: When combined with depth-based visibility, a relative tolerance \epsilon = 0.15 is used to account for Gaussian mean positions and depth smoothing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Chunk Center Accuracy: Incorrect calculation of chunk centers during map loading can cause valid chunks to disappear erroneously. Boundary Definitions: Using spherical boundaries for frustum culling alongside Euclidean distance for proximity culling can produce visible artifacts or inconsistencies. Mutual Exclusivity: Some implementations cannot run frustum and proximity culling simultaneously due to conflicting state management. Conservatism: The positive-vertex AABB test is conservative; it never hides a point that should be shown, but may retain nodes that are mostly outside the frustum yet have a corner inside. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def multiplymatrices(A, B): """Multiplies two 4x4 matrices (row-major layout).""" C = [[0.0]4 for in range(4)] for i in range(4): for j in range(4): for k in range(4): C[i][j] += A[i][k] B[k][j] return C def normalizeplane(plane): """Normalizes plane coefficients (a,b,c,d) so the normal vector has unit length.""" a, b, c, d = plane length = math.sqrt(aa + bb + cc) if length == 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return (a/length, b/length, c/length, d/length) def extractfrustumplanes(viewmatrix, projmatrix): """Extracts 6 planes from the combined projection-view matrix M = P V.""" M = multiplymatrices(projmatrix, viewmatrix) planes = [] # M is stored as row-major list of rows. Standard OpenGL extraction uses columns: # Left: M[3] + M[0], Right: M[3] - M[0], Bottom: M[3] + M[1], Top: M[3] - M[1], Near: M[3] + M[2], Far: M[3] - M[2] planes.append(normalizeplane((M[0][3] + M[0][0], M[1][3] + M[1][0], M[2][3] + M[2][0], M[3][3] + M[3][0]))) # Left planes.append(normalizeplane((M[0][3] - M[0][0], M[1][3] - M[1][0], M[2][3] - M[2][0], M[3][3] - M[3][0]))) # Right planes.append(normalizeplane((M[0][3] + M[0][1], M[1][3] + M[1][1], M[2][3] + M[2][1], M[3][3] + M[3][1]))) # Bottom planes.append(normalizeplane((M[0][3] - M[0][1], M[1][3] - M[1][1], M[2][3] - M[2][1], M[3][3] - M[3][1]))) # Top planes.append(normalizeplane((M[0][3] + M[0][2], M[1][3] + M[1][2], M[2][3] + M[2][2], M[3][3] + M[2][3]))) # Near planes.append(normalizeplane((M[0][3] - M[0][2], M[1][3] - M[1][2], M[2][3] - M[2][2], M[3][3] - M[2][3]))) # Far return planes def spherefrustumtest(center, radius, planes): """Tests if a sphere intersects the frustum. Returns True if visible.""" for a, b, c, d in planes: dist = acenter[0] + bcenter[1] + ccenter[2] + d if dist < -radius: return False return True def aabbfrustumtest(bmin, bmax, planes): """Tests if an AABB intersects the frustum using the positive-vertex test.""" for a, b, c, d in planes: px = bmax[0] if a >= 0 else bmin[0] py = bmax[1] if b >= 0 else bmin[1] pz = bmax[2] if c >= 0 else bmin[2] if apx + bpy + cpz + d < 0: return False return True def frustumcullentities(entities, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """ entities: List of dicts with 'type' ('sphere' or 'aabb'), 'center', 'radius', 'bmin', 'bmax'. Returns a boolean list indicating visibility. """ planes = extractfrustumplanes(viewmatrix, projmatrix) visiblemask = [] for entity in entities: if entity["type"] == "sphere": visiblemask.append(spherefrustumtest(entity["center"], entity["radius"], planes)) elif entity["type"] == "aabb": visiblemask.append(aabbfrustumtest(entity["bmin"], entity["bmax"], planes)) else: # Not given in the sources. visiblemask.append(False) return visiblemask An optimization technique specifically for segment-based tetrahedral meshing. It rejects segments lying outside the view frustum early in the rendering pipeline to counteract over-refinement caused by Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) dependencies, thereby reducing mesh size and computational load. A hierarchical approach used in out-of-core 3D Gaussian Splatting (TideGS). Level 1 (CPU) computes an active block set \mathcal{K}t = \bigcup{c \in \mathcal{B}t} \{k \mid \text{visible}(k, c)\} for a camera batch \mathcal{B}t using coarse bounding spheres with center ck and radius rk. It applies a 6-plane frustum test and culls a sphere if its signed distance to any plane satisfies d < -rk. Level 2 (GPU) materializes selected resident blocks Rt in VRAM, runs the standard 3DGS projection/rasterization pipeline, determines the final contributing set It, and restricts the forward/backward pass to only Gaussians in It. Level 1 is conservative and may admit extra blocks, while Level 2 applies exact pipeline semantics. A helper class implementation that uses a camera's frustum to cull an octree and visualizes intersecting octants with an InstancedMesh. It constructs a PerspectiveCamera with FOV 20°, aspect 1.77, near 0.5, and far 5, and initializes camera position using spherical coordinates (radius 5, phi \pi/3, theta \pi \cdot 1.75). It computes the frustum from projectionMatrix matrixWorldInverse, iterates through octree nodes, and updates an InstancedMesh (BoxGeometry 1,1,1, capacity 2500) with the center and dimensions of intersecting octants. A selection method for error feature aggregation that combines frustum and depth tests to ensure only views observing a token's surface are used. The frustum test transforms the token mean position pj into the camera frame to obtain depth d{jn}, projects it to pixel u{jn}, and passes the view if d{jn} > 0 and 0 \le u < W, 0 \le v < H. The depth test samples the expected depth Dn at u{jn} and keeps the view if d{jn} \le (1 + \epsilon) Dn(u{jn}) with \epsilon = 0.15. The tolerance handles Gaussian mean offsets and depth smoothing at discontinuities. Time Complexity: O(N) for flat entity lists, where N is the number of bounding volumes. O(\log N) or better for balanced hierarchical structures, as entire subtrees are discarded with a single box test. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store bounding volumes and visibility masks. Performance: Significantly reduces GPU and PCIe/SSD transfer costs by filtering blocks before data movement. Prevents performance bottlenecks from over-refined meshes outside the view in segment-based rendering. Strengths: Simple to implement, highly effective for large sparse scenes, and conservative (never hides visible geometry). Limitations: Conservative bounding volumes may admit extra geometry; accuracy depends on precise bounding volume generation; some implementations cannot combine it with proximity culling. Frustum culling is a fundamental computer graphics optimization technique originally developed to avoid processing geometry outside the camera's field of view. Møller and Haines discuss several algorithms for volume/frustum intersection. It is widely applied in out-of-core visualization, voxel rendering, and modern 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines to manage memory and processing loads.
