name: Interactive Render Quality Estimation & Cancellation
head: Interactive quality fallback, Octree render cancellation
body: This method prevents infinite rendering loops in interactive volume visualization by detecting when the rendering pipeline exceeds the frame budget and forcing a quality reduction on the subsequent frame. It acts as a safety mechanism distinct from standard early termination, which stops individual rays based on opacity. Inputs: Not given in the sources. Outputs: Not given in the sources. Data Structures: renderingRequired: Container holding the boolean flag OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED. OCTREEINTERACTIVERENDERINGPOINTTHRESHOLD: Scalar threshold used to estimate a safe render quality when interactive traversal is canceled. Steps: 1. After octree traversal, check if OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED is set in renderingRequired. 2. If the flag is set, unlock the rendering API. 3. Estimate a lower interactive render quality using OCTREEINTERACTIVERENDERINGPOINTTHRESHOLD. 4. Return early to avoid a rendering loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(octree, camera, renderingstate): # Check if previous frame exceeded time budget if renderingstate.renderingrequired.OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED: # Unlock the API to prevent deadlock # Release rendering context locks # Estimate lower interactive render quality using threshold # Compute reduced step size or sample count based on OCTREEINTERACTIVERENDERINGPOINTTHRESHOLD return estimatedquality # Standard front-to-back volume integration loop renderingstate.renderingrequired.OCTREERENDERINGCANCELED = False return result Parameters: OCTREEINTERACTIVERENDERINGPOINTTHRESHOLD: Threshold used to estimate a safe render quality when interactive traversal is canceled. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Loop: Overestimating render quality when the cancellation flag is set can cause an infinite rendering loop, as the system continues to request more work than the hardware can deliver. The cancellation check and forced quality estimation prevent this by guaranteeing a lower computational load on the next frame. A preprocessing step that computes view-dependent visibility coefficients for each octree leaf, used by the Prioritized-Layered Projection (PLP) algorithm to prioritize visible nodes at runtime. It estimates the likelihood of a node blocking light by rasterizing its contents against its bounding box from multiple sample viewpoints. Steps: 1. For each octree leaf, place an arbitrary number of sample viewpoints around the leaf. 2. Select viewpoints such that the entire node is visible towards its center, maximizing the projected screen area of the node's bounding box. 3. For each sample viewpoint: rasterize the node's bounding box in green; rasterize the node's contents in red over a black background without depth tests; read back the frame buffer; count green pixels (ng) and red pixels (nr). 4. Compute the visibility coefficient as nr / (nr + ng). 5. At runtime, select the coefficient whose corresponding sampling direction is closest to the current viewing direction. Parameters: numcoefficients: The number of visibility coefficients stored per node. Typical value is 20. Time Complexity: The cancellation check is O(1). Quality estimation is O(1). Actual rendering cost is reduced significantly by skipping the full traversal loop. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory for the flag and threshold. Visibility coefficients add constant memory per node. Performance: Guarantees frame completion by degrading quality, preventing hangs. Strengths: Robust against infinite loops; simple to implement. Limitations: Visual quality may fluctuate between frames; does not optimize the current frame's quality, only ensures completion. The method originates from interactive visualization systems for large datasets, specifically those using octree structures for out-of-core rendering. The cancellation mechanism is documented in the iVoxel repository. The visibility coefficient variant is described in Wagner Correa's thesis on out-of-core visualization techniques. larsxschneider/iVoxel, https://github.com/larsxschneider/iVoxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) New Techniques for Out-Of-Core Visualization of Large Datasets, https://ctsilva.github.io/thesis/wagner-correa-thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Visible Zone Algorithm
head: ComputeVisibilityMask, Hall-Holt and Rusinkiewicz Visible Zone Algorithm, Visibility Mask Computation
body: The Visible Zone Algorithm is a conservative visibility computation method that determines which primitives are potentially visible from a set of viewpoints by projecting them into screen space and retaining only those within a specified depth thickness. It sets itself apart from approximate visibility methods by guaranteeing correct visibility with less than one pixel of screen-space deviation. The algorithm computes a binary visibility matrix O of size N \times K, where N is the number of input points and K is the number of viewpoints. It operates by projecting all points from each viewpoint, grouping them by pixel, sorting by depth, and marking the top \tau points as visible. Inputs: P: Set of N points (e.g., Gaussian centroids or voxel centers). V: Set of K viewpoints. \tau: Thickness parameter, defining the number of visible layers per pixel. Outputs: O: N \times K visibility matrix, where O[i, j] = 1 if point i is visible from viewpoint j, else 0. Data Structures: M: A dictionary mapping pixel coordinates (u, v) to a list of points projected to that pixel. M^: A set of points identified as visible for the current viewpoint. Steps: 1. Initialize O with zeros. 2. For each viewpoint j from 1 to K: a. Let c be the current viewpoint. b. Retrieve extrinsic matrix d and intrinsic matrix K{intr} for c. c. Initialize empty map M. d. For each point i from 1 to N: i. Let p be point P[i]. ii. Compute 2D projection xc = (u, v) using forward projection with d and K{intr}. iii. Add p to the list M{u,v} associated with pixel (u, v) in M. e. Initialize empty set M^. f. For each list M{u,v} in M: i. Sort M{u,v} by depth z (ascending). ii. For i from 1 to \tau: add M{u,v}[i] to M^. g. For each point i from 1 to N: i. If P[i] is in M^, set O[i, j] = 1. 3. Return O. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevisibilitymask(P, V, tau): """ Compute visibility mask for points P from viewpoints V with thickness tau. P: List of N points, each with 3D coordinates (x, y, z). V: List of K viewpoints, each with extrinsic (d) and intrinsic (Kintr) matrices. tau: Integer, number of visible layers per pixel. Returns: N x K matrix O. """ N = len(P) K = len(V) O = [[0] K for in range(N)] for j in range(K): c = V[j] d = c.extrinsicmatrix Kintr = c.intrinsicmatrix M = {} # Project all points for i in range(N): p = P[i] u, v = forwardprojection(p, d, Kintr) if (u, v) not in M: M[(u, v)] = [] M[(u, v)].append(p) Mstar = set() # Determine visible points per pixel for pointlist in M.values(): # Sort by depth z pointlist.sort(key=lambda pt: pt.z) # Pick first tau points (bounds to available points if tau exceeds list length) for k in range(min(tau, len(pointlist))): Mstar.add(pointlist[k]) # Update visibility matrix for i in range(N): if P[i] in Mstar: O[i][j] = 1 return O def forwardprojection(p, d, Kintr): """ Project 3D point p using extrinsic d and intrinsic Kintr. Returns (u, v) pixel coordinates. """ # Transform to camera coordinates pcam = transformpoint(p, d) # Perspective divide and project to pixel coordinates x, y, z = pcam.x, pcam.y, pcam.z if z <= 0: return None u = Kintr.fx (x / z) + Kintr.cx v = Kintr.fy (y / z) + Kintr.cy return int(u), int(v) def transformpoint(p, d): """ Apply 4x4 extrinsic matrix d to 3D point p. Returns transformed Point object. """ wx = d[0][0]p.x + d[0][1]p.y + d[0][2]p.z + d[0][3] wy = d[1][0]p.x + d[1][1]p.y + d[1][2]p.z + d[1][3] wz = d[2][0]p.x + d[2][1]p.y + d[2][2]p.z + d[2][3] return Point(wx, wy, wz) Parameters: \tau: Thickness. Defines the number of visible layers per pixel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If \tau exceeds the number of points projected to a pixel, the selection loop bounds to the available points. Precision in projection and sorting affects depth ordering and which points are considered "in front". The algorithm assumes points are distinct; overlapping points at the same depth may require deterministic tie-breaking logic. A method to compute approximate visibility for line drawings from volume data by reducing the number of vertices checked for occlusion, trading accuracy for performance. It sets itself apart from the exact visibility algorithm Visible Zone Algorithm by sacrificing worst-case correctness for a predictable speedup factor, making it suitable for large datasets where interactive frame rates are prioritized over perfect occlusion handling. The algorithm achieves real-time frame rates for 2D and 2.5D datasets. The precomputation cost can be high; for a model with 13 million triangles, the accuracy guarantee costs 128 hours of precomputation on a cluster of 16 PCs. It is suitable for scenarios where conservative visibility is critical and precomputation time is acceptable. It is less suitable for dynamic scenes where viewpoints change frequently, as the mask must be recomputed. The Visible Zone Algorithm was developed by Hall-Holt and Rusinkiewicz. It is designed for conservative visibility computation with incremental updates. It is used to interactively render large datasets with less than one pixel of screen-space deviation. name: Approximate Visibility Algorithm
head: Stride-based Visibility Sampling
body: A method to compute approximate visibility for line drawings from volume data by reducing the number of vertices checked for occlusion, trading accuracy for performance. It sets itself apart from the exact visibility algorithm Visible Zone Algorithm by sacrificing worst-case correctness for a predictable speedup factor, making it suitable for large datasets where interactive frame rates are prioritized over perfect occlusion handling. Input: A loop of vertices V = \{v0, v1, \dots, v{N-1}\} representing a contour or cutting plane intersection, and a stride parameter k. Output: A visibility mask M for each vertex in the loop, where M[i] indicates whether vertex vi is visible or occluded. Visibility Array: An array of boolean values or flags, size N, corresponding to the vertices in the loop. Stride Parameter: Integer k \ge 1. 1. Initialize the visibility status for all vertices in the loop as "unknown". 2. Iterate through the loop indices i with a step size of k (i.e., i = 0, k, 2k, \dots). 3. For each sampled vertex vi: perform the exact visibility test to determine if vi is visible, and store the result in M[i]. 4. For each interval between two consecutive sampled vertices vi and v{i+k}: if M[i] \neq M[i+k] (a transition is detected), iterate through all intervening vertices j where i < j < i+k and perform the exact visibility test for each vj to determine the exact transition point. If M[i] == M[i+k] (no transition detected), assume all intervening vertices j where i < j < i+k have the same visibility as M[i] and set M[j] = M[i] for all such j. 5. Return the visibility mask M. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximatevisibility(vertices, k, visibilitytestfunc): """ Compute approximate visibility for a loop of vertices. Args: vertices: List of vertex objects or indices. k: Stride length for sampling. visibilitytestfunc: Function that returns True if vertex is visible, False otherwise. Returns: List of booleans representing visibility status for each vertex. """ n = len(vertices) visibility = [None] n # Step 1: Sample every k-th vertex for i in range(0, n, k): visibility[i] = visibilitytestfunc(vertices[i]) # Step 2: Check intervals between consecutive sampled vertices for i in range(0, n - k, k): start = i end = i + k if visibility[start] != visibility[end]: for j in range(start + 1, end): visibility[j] = visibilitytestfunc(vertices[j]) else: for j in range(start + 1, end): visibility[j] = visibility[start] # Handle remaining vertices if n is not a multiple of k (wrap-around for closed loops) lastsampled = (n - 1) // k k if lastsampled < n - 1: if visibility[lastsampled] != visibility[0]: for j in range(lastsampled + 1, n): visibility[j] = visibilitytestfunc(vertices[j]) else: for j in range(lastsampled + 1, n): visibility[j] = visibility[lastsampled] return visibility k: The stride length for sampling vertices. Typical values tested: 1, 2, 4, 8. k=1 corresponds to the exact visibility algorithm. Narrow occluders: If the stride k is too large, narrow occluders may be missed, causing visible artifacts (mislabeled vertices). Guarantee: The method guarantees that no details larger than k voxels are missed. Precision: The method relies on the visibility test function being consistent. Inconsistent tests may lead to false transitions. Time Complexity: Reduces the algorithm's running time by a factor of at most k compared to checking every vertex. The exact visibility algorithm is O(n^2) for a volume of size n^3. Strengths: Significant speedup for large datasets where many vertices share the same visibility status. Limitations: May mislabel vertices if narrow occluders are present and k is large. Not suitable for real-time rendering if high accuracy is required for narrow features. When to use: Large datasets where interactive frame rates are needed and narrow occluders are not critical. When not to use: When exact visibility is required, or when the dataset contains many narrow occluders and k must be small. Origin: Developed as part of a system for line drawings from volume data. History: Introduced in the context of line drawings from volume data, specifically for handling visibility of contours and cutting planes. Usage: Used in the aneurysm dataset rendering to handle narrow occluders, though video sequences were created without it. name: Occlusion-Aware Visibility Filter
head: Weight-based Visibility Filter
body: The Occlusion-Aware Visibility Filter replaces the standard view-frustum test in 3D Gaussian Splatting densification with a rendering-based signal that restricts statistical updates to Gaussians that actually contribute to the final image. Unlike sibling methods that rely on binary flags or pixel counts, this method uses the sum of blending weights to determine visibility, ensuring that occluded Gaussians do not accumulate densification statistics. The method operates during the training loop of 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically modifying the Adaptive Density Control (ADC) phase. It ensures that gradient and radius statistics are only accumulated for Gaussians that are not fully occluded by front-facing primitives. Input: The set of 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G}, the current camera view parameters, and the rendered image. Output: A boolean visibility mask or accumulated contribution metric for each Gaussian, used to gate densification statistics. Gaussian State: Each Gaussian i maintains a state including its position \mui, covariance \Sigmai, opacity \alphai, and color ci. Contribution Accumulator: A scalar value Wi per Gaussian, initialized to zero at the start of each view or epoch, accumulating the sum of blending weights. Statistics Buffer: Buffers for positional gradients g{i,v} and other ADC metrics, which are conditionally updated based on the filter's output. 1. Rendering: For each pixel p in the view, render the image using front-to-back compositing. The contribution of Gaussian i to pixel p is determined by its blending weight w{i,p}. 2. Blending Weight Calculation: Calculate the blending weight for Gaussian i at pixel p: w{i,p} = \alpha{i,p} \cdot T{i,p} where \alpha{i,p} is the per-pixel opacity of the Gaussian and T{i,p} is the transmittance (fraction of light reaching the Gaussian from the camera). 3. Accumulation: For each Gaussian i that contributes to any pixel, add its blending weight to its total contribution accumulator Wi: Wi = \sum{p \in \text{pixels}} w{i,p} Note: Rendering typically terminates early when transmittance T{i,p} falls below a threshold (e.g., 10^{-4}), meaning Gaussians behind this point are not rendered and contribute zero. 4. Visibility Determination: After processing all pixels for the view, determine if Gaussian i is visible: If Wi > 0, the Gaussian is considered visible (it participated in rendering). If Wi = 0, the Gaussian is considered occluded (it did not contribute to the image). 5. Statistics Gating: During the Adaptive Density Control (ADC) event: If Gaussian i is visible (Wi > 0), accumulate its positional gradient g{i,v} = \partial L / \partial \mui and other statistics for densification decisions. If Gaussian i is occluded (Wi = 0), exclude it from densification statistics. The raw view count normalizer is replaced by an average-contribution normalizer based on these filtered statistics. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def occlusionawarefilter(gaussians, view): """ Filters Gaussians based on their actual contribution to the rendered view. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects, each with attributes: id: Unique identifier wtotal: Accumulated blending weight (initialized to 0.0 per view) view: Camera view parameters and pixel grid. Returns: visiblegaussians: List of Gaussians with wtotal > 0. """ visiblegaussians = [] # Step 1 & 2: Render and Accumulate Blending Weights # Note: In a real rasterizer, this happens during the forward pass. # Here we simulate the accumulation logic described in the source. for gaussian in gaussians: gaussian.wtotal = 0.0 # Iterate over pixels where this Gaussian might contribute. # In practice, this is handled by the rasterizer's tile-based approach. # We assume the rasterizer provides the list of pixels p and their # corresponding blending weights w{i,p} for this Gaussian. for pixel, blendingweight in getrenderingcontributions(gaussian, view): gaussian.wtotal += blendingweight # Step 4: Determine Visibility for gaussian in gaussians: if gaussian.wtotal > 0: visiblegaussians.append(gaussian) return visiblegaussians def updatedensificationstatistics(gaussians, gradients, visiblegaussians): """ Updates ADC statistics only for visible Gaussians. Args: gaussians: All Gaussians. gradients: Pre-computed gradients for all Gaussians. visiblegaussians: List of Gaussians determined to be visible. """ # Create a set for fast lookup visibleset = set(g.id for g in visiblegaussians) for gaussian in gaussians: if gaussian.id in visibleset: # Accumulate gradient and other stats for densification accumulategradient(gaussian, gradients[gaussian.id]) # The normalizer for the average contribution criterion is updated # using only these visible Gaussians else: # Reset or ignore statistics for occluded Gaussians resetstatistics(gaussian) Transmittance Threshold: Rendering terminates when T{i,p} < 10^{-4}. This is a standard 3DGS parameter that implicitly defines the occlusion boundary. Zero Contribution: A Gaussian with Wi = 0 is strictly excluded. This handles cases where a Gaussian is within the frustum but completely behind other opaque geometry. Precision: The sum of blending weights Wi is a floating-point accumulation. While small contributions might be lost to precision, the binary nature of the filter (zero vs. non-zero) makes it robust to minor numerical noise, provided the threshold is strictly >0. Time Complexity: The visibility filter adds negligible overhead as it reuses data already computed during the forward rendering pass (blending weights). The main cost is the conditional update of statistics, which is O(N) where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Requires storing one scalar Wi per Gaussian per view or epoch, which is minimal compared to the Gaussian state itself. Performance: In occlusion-heavy scenes, this method reduces the number of Gaussians required by up to 63% compared to occlusion-blind baselines, while improving image quality metrics (e.g., up to 6% lower LPIPS). Strengths: Prevents under-densification in occluded regions by ignoring irrelevant Gaussians. It is more nuanced than binary flags because it uses the magnitude of contribution. Limitations: It is specific to the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework and its densification pipeline. It does not accelerate the forward rendering itself, but rather the training efficiency and final model compactness. The Occlusion-Aware Visibility Filter was introduced in the paper "Counting Contributions, Not Views: Occlusion-Aware Densification for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses a limitation in standard 3D Gaussian Splatting where densification statistics are based on view-frustum tests, which count Gaussians that are potentially visible but may be fully occluded in specific views. This leads to inefficient densification in complex, occlusion-heavy scenes. The method replaces the frustum-based filter with a rendering-based signal, specifically the sum of blending weights, which is also used in the proposed "Average Contribution Criterion" for densification decisions. It is integrated into a framework based on StopThePop. name: Bounding Volume Empty-Space Culling
head: Bounding volume strategy
body: Bounding volume empty-space culling restricts volume reconstruction and rendering computation to the "effective" area where voxel values are valid, bypassing empty space outside this region. It differs from its sibling Parallel Ray Casting with Segment Lists by using a geometric bounding volume as a depth buffer to guide the pipeline, rather than explicit segment lists, and from Visibility Culling by focusing on the validity of the reconstruction domain itself rather than fragment-level occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Projection data (sinogram), viewing direction, and volume grid dimensions. Output: A depth buffer defining the valid reconstruction bounds for the current view, used to cull invalid voxels during reconstruction and rendering. Data Structures: Bounding Volume: A geometric primitive (truncated circle for 2D, truncated cylinder for 3D) representing the effective reconstruction area. Depth Buffer: A buffer storing the slice boundaries of the bounding volume, used to restrict computation. Steps: 1. Calculate Initial Bounding Volume: Determine the effective reconstruction area based on the assumption of parallel beam reconstruction. For a 2D square volume slice, this is a truncated circle; for a 3D cubic volume, it is a truncated cylinder. 2. Slice Bounding Volume: Slice the calculated bounding volume according to the current viewing direction. 3. Generate Depth Buffer: Use the resulting bounding volume slices to create a depth buffer. 4. Restrict Computation: Use the depth buffer to guide the reconstruction pipeline, ensuring that computation is restricted to the effective area throughout the entire process. Formulas: The effective area is defined by the geometry of the projection system. For parallel beam reconstruction, the valid voxel region is bounded by the projection of the object's extent. No explicit formula is provided in the sources for the truncation, but it is described as a truncated circle (2D) or truncated cylinder (3D). Parameters: Viewing direction: Determines the slicing of the bounding volume. Reconstruction grid: Defines the resolution of the volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes parallel beam reconstruction; deviations may affect accuracy. The bounding volume is an approximation; it may include some empty space or exclude valid voxels if the object shape is highly irregular. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateboundingvolume(griddims, projectiontype): """ Calculate the initial bounding volume based on parallel beam assumption. Returns a geometric primitive (truncated circle/cylinder). """ if projectiontype == "2D": # Truncated circle for 2D square volume slice radius = max(griddims.x, griddims.y) / 2.0 return TruncatedCircle(radius) elif projectiontype == "3D": # Truncated cylinder for 3D cubic volume radius = max(griddims.x, griddims.y) / 2.0 height = griddims.z return TruncatedCylinder(radius, height) else: raise ValueError("Unsupported projection type") def sliceboundingvolume(boundingvolume, viewingdirection): """ Slice the bounding volume according to the viewing direction. Returns a list of slice boundaries. """ # Implementation depends on the specific geometry and viewing direction # This step generates the depth buffer slices return sliceboundaries def restrictreconstruction(depthbuffer, reconstructionpipeline): """ Use the depth buffer to restrict computation within the effective area. """ for slice in reconstructionpipeline: if slice is within depthbuffer: process(slice) else: skip(slice) A sophisticated preprocessing scheme that reconstructs a volume mask labeling all voxels in the shadow of non-zero projection data, which is then sliced per frame to drive reconstruction more accurately than a bounding sphere. It is equivalent to empty space skipping, with the bounding volume method being a good approximation for many cases, while the occupancy mask is more accurate. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of voxels processed by culling those outside the effective area. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the bounding volume and depth buffer. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective for regular object shapes. Limitations: Approximation may not be accurate for complex or irregular object shapes. Originated in the context of GPU-accelerated Direct Volume Rendering (D2VR). The method is described in the paper "GPU-Accelerated D2VR". name: Empty-space skipping via Acceleration Structure
head: Empty space skipping via the acceleration structure
body: This method accelerates direct volume rendering by using a hierarchical min/max acceleration structure to skip transparent regions of the volume data. It reduces the number of samples taken per ray by jumping over blocks that contain no visible data, distinct from sibling methods that may use sparse voxel grids or hierarchical bounding box trees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source volumetric dataset (e.g., 512 \times 512 \times 512) and a pre-computed acceleration structure. Output: A rendered image with reduced computational cost. Data Structures: The acceleration structure is a small two-channel volumetric dataset. Dimensions: 16 \times 16 \times 16 cells. Layout: Each cell corresponds to a 32 \times 32 \times 32 block in the source dataset. Content: Each cell stores the minimum and maximum values found within its corresponding source block. Alternative Layout: Some implementations use a per-field min/max structure organized in 32 \times 32 \times 32 bricks. Algorithm Steps: 1. For each ray, determine the intersection with the acceleration structure grid. 2. Traverse the acceleration structure cells along the ray path. 3. For each cell, retrieve the stored minimum and maximum values. 4. Check if the space corresponding to the cell is transparent. This is determined by comparing the min/max values against the transfer function's opacity threshold or visibility criteria. 5. If the cell is transparent (i.e., contains no visible data), skip the entire 32 \times 32 \times 32 block and advance the ray to the next cell. 6. If the cell is not transparent, sample the source data within that block and perform standard front-to-back compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, accelstructure): # Determine initial entry point into the acceleration structure grid tmin, tmax = intersectaccelgrid(rayorigin, raydirection) # Traverse acceleration structure cells while tmin < tmax: # Get current cell coordinates in the 16x16x16 structure cellcoords = getcellcoords(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin) # Retrieve min/max values for this cell minval, maxval = accelstructure[cellcoords] # Check if the block is transparent if istransparent(minval, maxval): # Skip this 32x32x32 block tmin += stepsizeaccelcell(raydirection) else: # Process the block in the source volume blockorigin = getblockorigin(cellcoords) blocksamples = sampleblock(blockorigin, rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata) composite(blocksamples) # Advance ray past this block tmin += stepsizeaccelcell(raydirection) return accumulatedcolor def istransparent(minval, maxval): # Implementation depends on transfer function; # typically true if maxval < opacitythreshold return maxval < OPACITYTHRESHOLD Parameters: Block Size: 32 \times 32 \times 32 voxels. Acceleration Structure Resolution: 16 \times 16 \times 16 cells. Source Resolution Example: 512 \times 512 \times 512. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Min/max values must accurately represent the range of the source block to avoid false negatives (skipping visible data) or false positives (skipping empty data). Boundary Conditions: Ray traversal must correctly handle entry and exit from the acceleration structure grid. Uses sparse voxel octrees for skipping; chosen for highly sparse data. Uses AABB trees; chosen for complex geometry integration. Extends SparseLeap with occupancy misses; chosen for dynamic scenes. Uses bounding volumes; chosen for static volumes with large empty regions. Adaptive sampling; chosen for mobile performance. Performance: Accelerates visualization by 1.5-2 times compared to non-skipping methods. Complexity: Time complexity is reduced proportional to the fraction of empty space skipped. Memory complexity is dominated by the acceleration structure, which is significantly smaller than the source volume (16^3 vs 512^3). Strengths: Simple to implement on GPU; effective for volumes with large transparent regions. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the acceleration structure; less effective for dense volumes. This technique is an extension of CPU-based empty space skipping methods to GPU implementations. It is used in direct volume rendering to optimize ray casting by avoiding unnecessary sampling of transparent regions. name: Progressive Ray Casting for Volumetric Models on Mobile Devices
body: This method addresses the computational constraints of interactive volume rendering on mobile devices by combining multiresolution data structures with acceleration techniques. It solves the trade-off between frame rate and visual fidelity by using a lower-resolution dataset for exploration and progressively refining high-resolution details in regions of interest. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by explicitly targeting mobile hardware limitations and integrating Empty Space Skipping (ESS) and Early Ray Termination (ERT) within a progressive refinement framework. The core mechanism shared by all children is the reduction of work units (samples, voxels, or pixels) processed per frame while maintaining acceptable visual fidelity. This is achieved through three primary strategies: 1. Culling/Skipping: Identifying regions of the volume or ray path that do not contribute to the final image (e.g., empty space, occluded voxels) and bypassing their evaluation. 2. Termination: Halting the integration loop when the accumulated contribution becomes negligible (e.g., high opacity, low transmittance). 3. Adaptation: Varying the computational effort based on local scene complexity or global performance budgets. Mathematically, these methods modify the standard front-to-back compositing loop: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) by introducing conditions that break the loop early, skip iterations, or reduce the number of C{sample} queries. This family does not define distinct algorithmic subtopics in the provided notes; rather, it describes a system-level approach. The primary components are: Uses a lower-resolution dataset for interactive exploration and a high-resolution dataset for progressive refinement of regions of interest. Incorporates ESS and ERT to reduce sampling overhead. Origin: The method was proposed in a paper titled "Progressive Ray Casting for Volumetric Models on Mobile Devices". History and Development: The work focuses on the limitation of GPU horsepower on mobile devices, noting that while models might fit in memory, frame rates can be inefficient for interactivity. It builds upon acceleration techniques described by Krüger and Westermann. Usage: It is designed for medical image inspection, where orthographic projections are the standard view. name: Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map
head: Orthogonal Opacity Map Occlusion Clipping, Orthogonal Opacity Map Occlusion Culling, Opacity Culling and Clipping, Occlusion Culling and Clipping, Empty Space Skipping and Occlusion Clipping
body: Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map is an acceleration technique for texture-based volume rendering that skips occluded voxels by maintaining a low-resolution 2D opacity map on a plane orthogonal to a major dataset axis. It differs from per-voxel early ray termination by testing occlusion at the sub-volume level, allowing it to cull entire bounding boxes or clip their geometry against the opacity map to avoid rendering thousands of voxels hidden behind opaque surfaces. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D texture dataset, transfer function, viewing parameters, sub-volume bounding boxes (axis-aligned). Output: Final image, updated opacity map. Data Structures: 1. Orthogonal Opacity Map: A 2D map orthogonal to the major axis of the dataset most parallel to the viewing direction. Each pixel represents the minimum opacity accumulated in the corresponding region of the frame buffer. 2. Hierarchical CPU Map: A CPU-side structure built from the GPU-obtained low-resolution opacity map to accelerate culling queries. 3. Sub-volume Bounding Boxes: Axis-aligned boxes defining regions of the volume to be rendered. Parameters: Opacity Threshold (T{op}): Typically 95% of the maximum opacity. Desired Updates (k): Initial empirically determined number of map updates per frame (typically 9). DeltaVoxels (Dv): Number of voxels rendered before an opacity map update. Calculated as Dv = \lfloor \text{Total Voxels in non-empty boxes} / (k + 1) \rfloor. Constant (c): Used in performance function, typically 0.02. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set opacity map to invalid. Render textures as if clipping is not used. Initialize voxel counter V{count} = 0. 2. Rendering Loop (per sub-volume): If opacity map is invalid, render sub-volume normally. Increment V{count} by the number of voxels in the sub-volume. If V{count} \ge Dv: Update Opacity Map (see Step 3). Reset V{count} = 0. If opacity map is valid: 1. Project the front and back faces of the sub-volume's bounding box onto the orthogonal opacity map. Since the box is axis-aligned, projections are rectangles. For perspective projection, apply scaling and translation; for parallel, only translation. 2. Combine the two projections to determine the total projected area. 3. Search for transparent pixels in the map covering the projected rectangle Rp. Pixels with opacity < T{op} are transparent. 4. If Rp falls outside the map border, add that area to visible regions. 5. Compute the bounding rectangle Rv of all visible regions. 6. Back-project: Project Rv back to the front and back faces of the sub-volume (parallel to the opacity map) to get R{vpf} and R{vpb}. 7. Compute union R{vp} = R{vpf} \cup R{vpb}. 8. If R{vp} is empty, cull the sub-volume (skip rendering). 9. Otherwise, use R{vp} as the new front/back faces to create a clipped bounding box and render only the visible portion. 3. Opacity Map Update: Project the current frame buffer onto the object-aligned plane orthogonal to the major axis. Down-sample the result to a low-resolution image to reduce GPU-to-CPU transfer costs and comparison overhead. Each pixel in the map stores the minimum opacity of the corresponding frame buffer region. Note: Opacity values in the map increase monotonically during the rendering of the same frame. Formula: Projection Distance: When projecting a slice parallel to the opacity map, the distance between adjacent voxels d becomes d': d' = d \frac{l1 + l2}{l1} where l1 is the distance from the camera to the slice, and l2 is the slice thickness. Pitfalls: Resolution Trade-off: Low-resolution maps reduce accuracy of occlusion detection but improve efficiency. CPU Bottleneck: Current implementations require CPU involvement and data transfer across the AGP/PCIe bus, limiting performance. This method creates a 2D opacity map on a plane orthogonal to a major axis by projecting the rendered frame buffer onto that plane and downsampling the result. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a low-resolution occlusion mask for volume rendering culling, minimizing data transfer costs between graphics and main memory while preserving sufficient occlusion information. It differs from hierarchical approaches by using a fixed-resolution, multi-pass averaging strategy rather than a tree structure. See Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation. Hidden Volume Removal (HVR) is an occlusion culling optimization for object-order volume rendering that eliminates a large fraction of cells and octree nodes within the opacity range, particularly effective for isosurface visualization. It compensates for the lack of early ray termination inherent in object-order rendering by using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps (HOMs) to skip hidden nodes in the min-max octree. Unlike its sibling Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation, which relies on orthogonal projections and neighbor finding, HVR uses a hierarchical map structure to approximate node visibility, providing superior skipping efficiency at the cost of some artifacts due to approximation. See Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps. An adaptive system to adjust the number of opacity map updates (k) per frame based on performance history to balance rendering speed and occlusion detection overhead. Polling: Every n-th frame (e.g., n=10), poll performance using the number in range [k-hw, k+hw] that has not been updated for the longest. Increment age of all slots by 1 except the polled one. Update k: When all slots are valid, pick the slot with best performance as the new center. Change k to this new center and shift performance statistics accordingly. Performance function: p = v - c \cdot k, where v is the percentage of voxels culled and clipped, k is the actual number of map updates, and c is a constant (0.02 for tested datasets). Parameter: k: Initial empirically determined number of map updates (typically 9). A technique to save time by culling points that are occluded by opaque volume material in front of their footprint. Require front-to-back rendering to maintain an opacity image (occlusion map). Check if the volume material in front of the point's footprint is opaque; if so, the point is not visible. Mueller '00 method: After compositing, convolve the opacity image with a box filter sized to the projected footprint. If a pixel value in the convolved map is > threshold, the entire footprint neighborhood is > threshold, allowing fast culling by checking only the pixel nearest to the projected point center. Lee '00 method: Keep points in an octree and maintain a visibility map as a quadtree. Check the projection of an octree node against the corresponding level of the visibility map quadtree. Cull occluded octree nodes; subdivide if not occluded; rasterize points that fail the occlusion test. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sub-volumes and the cost of projecting bounding boxes onto the opacity map. The adaptive update mechanism adjusts the optimal number of opacity map updates to balance accuracy and performance. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the low-resolution opacity map and the CPU-side hierarchical map. Measured Performance: On average, 50-60% of non-empty voxels are excluded from rendering. The average speedup factor for Empty Space Skipping + Occlusion Clipping (ESS+CC) vs conventional is 3.3x. For the 'Knee' dataset, ESS+CC achieves a speedup of 4.7x over Basic, with 63.8% of voxels skipped. Strengths: Highly effective when there are many non-empty voxels and significant occlusion, complementing Empty Space Skipping which is better for large amounts of empty voxels. Limitations: Requires CPU involvement and data transfer across the bus, which limits performance. Low-resolution maps trade off accuracy for efficiency. The technique was introduced by Mueller et al. in 2004. It extends earlier work on empty space skipping and is related to hardware occlusion queries used for visibility culling in opaque surfaces, as described by Govindraju et al. in 2003. It is designed specifically for texture-based volume rendering, where primitives contain thousands of voxels, making per-voxel tests inefficient. name: Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation
body: This method creates a 2D opacity map on a plane orthogonal to a major axis by projecting the rendered frame buffer onto that plane and downsampling the result. It solves the problem of efficiently generating a low-resolution occlusion mask for volume rendering culling, minimizing data transfer costs between graphics and main memory while preserving sufficient occlusion information. It differs from hierarchical approaches by using a fixed-resolution, multi-pass averaging strategy rather than a tree structure. Inputs: Current frame buffer FB containing color/opacity data. Desired low-resolution map dimensions n \times n (typical value: 64 \times 64). Camera projection and view matrices defining the current frame's geometry. High-resolution map side length N (derived from projection geometry so each FB pixel maps to at least one pixel in the high-resolution buffer). Outputs: A low-resolution opacity map of size n \times n in main memory. Data Structures: T{FB}: Texture copy of the frame buffer FB. PB{hm}: High-resolution pixel buffer (optional intermediate; see Optimization). T{hm}: Texture bound to PB{hm}, holding the high-resolution opacity map. PBm: Low-resolution pixel buffer of size n \times n. Steps: 1. Frame Buffer Copy: Copy the current frame buffer FB into a texture T{FB}. 2. Projective Texturing: Imagine a rectangle R parallel to the object-aligned orthogonal plane, oriented orthogonal to the camera. Apply projective texturing: treat T{FB} as a slide projected from the camera position onto R. 3. High-Resolution Projection: Orthogonally project the textured rectangle R onto a high-resolution pixel buffer PB{hm}. The resolution of PB{hm} must be sufficient so that each pixel in FB maps to at least one pixel in PB{hm}. Bind PB{hm} to texture T{hm}. 4. Multi-Pass Downsampling: Initialize PBm (size n \times n). Calculate the number of passes required: P = \left\lceil \frac{(N/n)^2}{4} \right\rceil where N is the side length of the high-resolution map (N \times N) and n is the side length of the low-resolution map (n \times n). For pass k from 0 to P-1: Set the blending function to MIN. Configure texture coordinates so that each pixel in PBm aligns with the center of 4 neighboring texels in T{hm} and uses linear interpolation to fetch their average. Translate the texture coordinates (or view volume) so that each pixel in PBm maps to the center of another 4 uncontributed texels in T{hm}. Render T{hm} to PBm using the configured coordinates and MIN blending. Repeat until all texels in T{hm} have contributed. 5. Readback: Read the contents of PBm to main memory. Optimization: Combine projection and downsampling into a single step by targeting projective texturing directly to PBm (the low-resolution pixel buffer) instead of creating T{hm} explicitly. Since hardware auto-generated texture coordinates (TexGen) cannot be translated for downsampling in this direct path, apply a translation to the view volume using glOrtho() in OpenGL to shift the sampling region for each pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def createorthogonalopacitymap(FBtexture, N, n=64): """ Creates a low-resolution orthogonal opacity map from the frame buffer. FBtexture: 2D list/array of shape (N, N) containing the projected frame buffer data. N: Side length of the high-resolution projected map (N x N). n: Side length of the low-resolution output map (n x n). Returns: 2D list of shape (n, n) containing opacity values. """ # Calculate number of multi-pass rendering steps P = math.ceil((N / n) 2 / 4) # Initialize low-resolution pixel buffer PBm = [[0.0] n for in range(n)] for k in range(P): # Calculate grid offset for this pass. # Shifts the 2x2 sampling window by 0.5 units in x/y to cover # the next set of uncontributed texels per output pixel. dx = (k % 2) 0.5 dy = (k // 2) 0.5 # Simulate GPU projective texturing and downsampling: for i in range(n): for j in range(n): # Map PBm pixel center to projected texture coordinates u = (i + dx) / n v = (j + dy) / n # Sample 4 neighboring texels in the high-res projected image texu = u N texv = v N # Bilinear interpolation of 4 texels x0, y0 = math.floor(texu), math.floor(texv) x1, y1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1 fx, fy = texu - x0, texv - y0 # Fetch texels (clamp to boundaries as standard for opacity) t00 = FBtexture[min(y0, N-1)][min(x0, N-1)] t01 = FBtexture[min(y0, N-1)][min(x1, N-1)] t10 = FBtexture[min(y1, N-1)][min(x0, N-1)] t11 = FBtexture[min(y1, N-1)][min(x1, N-1)] avg = (t00 (1-fx)(1-fy) + t01 fx(1-fy) + t10 (1-fx)fy + t11 fxfy) # MIN blending: keep the smaller opacity value PBm[i][j] = min(PBm[i][j], avg) return PBm Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Coverage: The translation step ensures complete coverage of the high-resolution map without gaps or overlaps that would skew the average. Precision: Linear interpolation is used for averaging 4 texels; standard floating-point precision is sufficient for opacity values. Not given in the sources: Degenerate input handling, exact time/memory complexity, and specific boundary conditions beyond the translation coverage. Uses a hierarchical tree structure for occlusion culling, offering better adaptability to varying density but higher complexity. Choose when scene density varies significantly. The parent method that uses this opacity map for culling. Choose this when simple, fast culling along a major axis is sufficient. Performance: Typical low-resolution map size is 64 \times 64. Downsampling reduces the resolution to limit transfer costs from graphics to main memory and reduces the amount of comparisons required for occlusion clipping. Strengths: Simple implementation on GPU; effective for orthogonal views; reduces data transfer overhead. Limitations: Fixed resolution; requires multiple passes for downsampling. Not given in the sources: Exact time and memory complexity, measured performance on specific hardware, or scaling laws. Originated in the context of texture-based volume rendering for empty space skipping and occlusion clipping. The method was proposed by Mueller et al. in "Empty Space Skipping and Occlusion Clipping for Texture-based Volume Rendering". It is used in real-time volume rendering applications where culling occluded voxels improves performance. name: Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps
head: HOM-based Occlusion Culling, Hidden Volume Removal (HVR), Hierarchical Occlusion Map Occlusion Clipping
body: Hidden Volume Removal (HVR) is an occlusion culling optimization for object-order volume rendering that eliminates a large fraction of cells and octree nodes within the opacity range, particularly effective for isosurface visualization. It compensates for the lack of early ray termination inherent in object-order rendering by using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps (HOMs) to skip hidden nodes in the min-max octree. Unlike its sibling Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation, which relies on orthogonal projections and neighbor finding, HVR uses a hierarchical map structure to approximate node visibility, providing superior skipping efficiency at the cost of some artifacts due to approximation. Inputs: An octree representation of the volume data. A camera view using orthogonal projection. A rendering image plane of width m. Outputs: A rendered image with hidden nodes skipped. Updated HOM structures reflecting current opacity. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchical Occlusion Maps (HOMs): A hierarchy of images where pixels store an integer value in the range [0, 16] and are initialized to 0. Multiple hierarchy levels exist, with the first map size being 1/4 of the image area and the last representing a single pixel. The finest map (Level 0) has a side length of m/2. The coarsest map (Level L) has a side length of 1. A pixel in HOM level k covers a 2^k \times 2^k area of the finest map. 2. Octree: Standard min-max octree structure where each node has a projected center. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize all HOM pixels to 0. Determine the mapping between octree levels and HOM levels. For each octree level, find the finest HOM level such that a single HOM pixel can include the entire projection of the octree node. 2. HOM Update Process: Triggered when a pixel on the image plane becomes opaque during rendering. Identify the corresponding pixel in the finest HOM (Level 0). Increment this pixel and its 3 nearest neighbors in the map (forming a 2 \times 2 block centered on the opaque pixel's projection). Recursive Propagation: If any HOM pixel reaches the maximum value of 16: Increment the corresponding pixel in the superior (coarser) HOM level. Repeat the neighbor incrementation and check for 16 in the superior level. Continue recursively up the hierarchy until no pixel reaches 16 or the top level is reached. 3. Visibility Test: For each octree node to be processed: Project the center of the node onto the image plane. Identify the HOM level associated with the node's octree level (as determined in Step 1). Find the pixel in that HOM level corresponding to the projected center. Test: If the pixel value equals 16, the node is considered hidden and skipped. A value of 16 indicates that an extended square around the pixel (made of 16 quarter-pixels) is opaque. If the value is less than 16, the node is visible and processed. Note: An additional opacity test must be added for every treated ray to handle cases where the HOM approximation is insufficient. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math MAXHOMVALUE = 16 def initializehoms(imagewidth): """Initialize HOM hierarchy with zeros. Finest map (level 0) size is imagewidth/2. Coarsest map (level L) size is 1x1. """ numlevels = int(math.log2(imagewidth)) homs = [] for level in range(numlevels): side = imagewidth // (2 (level + 1)) homs.append([[0] side for in range(side)]) return homs def updatehoms(homs, imagex, imagey): """Update HOMs when an image plane pixel (imagex, imagey) becomes opaque.""" # Map image pixel to finest HOM (level 0) # Finest HOM pixel covers 2x2 image pixels homx = imagex // 2 homy = imagey // 2 propagateupdate(homs, 0, homx, homy) def propagateupdate(homs, level, x, y): """Recursively increment HOM pixels and propagate when MAXHOMVALUE is reached.""" if level >= len(homs): return levelhoms = homs[level] levelh = len(levelhoms) levelw = len(levelhoms[0]) for dx in (0, 1): for dy in (0, 1): nx = x + dx ny = y + dy if 0 <= nx < levelw and 0 <= ny < levelh: levelhoms[ny][nx] += 1 if levelhoms[ny][nx] == MAXHOMVALUE: if level + 1 < len(homs): propagateupdate(homs, level + 1, nx // 2, ny // 2) def computehomlevelforoctreelevel(octreelevel, homlevelmap): """Return the precomputed HOM level for a given octree level.""" return homlevelmap[octreelevel] def isnodehidden(node, homs, homlevelmap): """Check if an octree node is hidden using HOMs.""" homlevel = computehomlevelforoctreelevel(node.octreelevel, homlevelmap) levelhoms = homs[homlevel] levelh = len(levelhoms) levelw = len(levelhoms[0]) # Map projected center to HOM coordinates side = len(levelhoms) homx = int(node.projectedcenterx / side) homy = int(node.projectedcentery / side) if 0 <= homx < levelw and 0 <= homy < levelh: return levelhoms[homy][homx] == MAXHOMVALUE return False Parameters: HOM Max Value: 16. HOM Resolution: Finest map is 1/4 of the image area. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation Artifacts: The visibility test is an approximation, and big block skipping is rare due to the low accuracy of the occlusion maps. Some hidden nodes far beyond the visible surface may still be encountered. Non-Optimal Traversal: The recursive run of the octree does not optimize HVR efficiency optimally, and some hidden nodes are processed unnecessarily. Neighbor Finding: The approach relies on trees that do not allow efficient neighbor finding, which is a limitation compared to other methods. A proposed extension to exploit the hierarchy for accelerating occlusion tests, using the model from [BWPP04] to hierarchically test occlusion of visible nodes without latency from waiting for parent node results. However, the hierarchy is not exploited in the current algorithm to accelerate occlusion tests. Time Complexity: The update complexity is m^2 \cdot \log2(m), where m is the image width. Performance: HVR is more efficient than the method by Lee and Ihm [9]. For similar renderings, Lee and Ihm achieve 25% occluded splats for the head dataset and 67% for the brain dataset, whereas HVR achieves higher occlusion ratios (e.g., 91.70% for Head (a)). Throughput: The algorithm delivers an approximately constant cell throughput (between 1.4 and 2.1 millions cells per second). Strengths: Eliminates a large fraction of cells and octree nodes within the opacity range, particularly effective for isosurface visualization. It is an efficient alternative to the lack of early ray termination in object-order volume rendering. Produces better image quality than some competitors (e.g., Ultravis). Limitations: Big block skipping is rare due to low accuracy of occlusion maps. Some hidden nodes far beyond the visible surface may still be encountered. The recursive run of the octree does not optimize HVR efficiency. When to Use: Effective for isosurface visualization where early ray termination is not available or effective. When Not to Use: When high accuracy in skipping distant hidden nodes is required, or when semi-transparent transfer functions are used (trilinear interpolation becomes predominant, reducing HVR efficiency). Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps was introduced in the paper "A new object-order ray-casting algorithm". It was developed to address the inefficiencies of previous occlusion culling methods in object-order volume rendering, specifically those that relied on trees without efficient neighbor finding. The method builds on the concept of Hierarchical Occlusion Maps [35] to provide superior skipping of hidden nodes in the octree. A proposed extension to exploit the hierarchy further was discussed in a thesis, but was not implemented in the original algorithm. name: Fine-Scale Occlusion Map Culling
head: Average occlusion map, Fine-Scale Occlusion Map
body: Fine-Scale Occlusion Map Culling is a visibility culling technique that determines voxel rasterization eligibility using an occlusion map where each pixel represents the average opacity of a box-neighborhood footprint. It provides finer-grained culling than octree-based space skipping by operating on a per-voxel basis rather than per-node, allowing for the retention of high-frequency volume content that hierarchical decomposition might discard. Input: A volume dataset, a pre-computed orthogonal opacity map (from Occlusion Clipping with Orthogonal Opacity Map), and the screen-space projection parameters for the current view. Output: A boolean mask or rasterization decision for each voxel indicating whether it contributes to the final image. Occlusion Map: A 2D grid aligned with the screen. Each cell (u, v) stores a scalar value representing the average opacity of the volume within the footprint associated with that pixel. Footprint: A box-shaped neighborhood in screen space corresponding to the projection of a voxel or a group of voxels. 1. Construct the Average Occlusion Map: For each pixel in the target resolution, calculate the average opacity of all voxels whose screen-space projections fall within the pixel's footprint. This averaging process smooths the opacity data, creating a coarse representation of occlusion. 2. Index the Map for Voxel Culling: For each voxel to be rendered, determine its screen-space coordinate (uv, vv). 3. Evaluate Occlusion: Retrieve the value from the occlusion map at index (uv, vv). 4. Rasterization Decision: If the retrieved occlusion map value indicates that the footprint is fully opaque (or exceeds a specific threshold), the voxel is culled. Otherwise, the voxel must be rasterized. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finescaleculling(voxelscreencoords, occlusionmap, threshold=1.0): """ Determine if a voxel should be rasterized based on the fine-scale occlusion map. Args: voxelscreencoords: List of (u, v) tuples representing screen coordinates of voxels. occlusionmap: 2D array where each cell contains the average opacity of its footprint. threshold: Opacity value above which a voxel is considered occluded. Returns: List of booleans indicating whether each voxel should be rasterized. """ cullingresults = [] for u, v in voxelscreencoords: # Ensure coordinates are within bounds if 0 <= u < occlusionmap.width and 0 <= v < occlusionmap.height: # Index the occlusion map with the voxel's screen-space coordinate avgopacity = occlusionmap[u][v] # Check if the footprint must be rasterized # If average opacity is below threshold, the voxel is not fully occluded if avgopacity < threshold: cullingresults.append(True) # Rasterize else: cullingresults.append(False) # Cull else: # Out of bounds, typically rasterize or handle as error cullingresults.append(True) return cullingresults Threshold: The opacity value used to decide culling. Not given in the sources. Footprint Size: The size of the box-neighborhood averaged per pixel. Not given in the sources. Boundary Conditions: Voxels projecting outside the screen bounds must be handled explicitly. Precision: Averaging may introduce precision errors if not managed, though specific bit-packing is not detailed. Degenerate Input: If the volume has no opacity, the map will be all zeros, and no culling occurs. The prerequisite step that generates the base opacity map. It sets up the orthogonal projection used by this method. Orthogonal Opacity Map Creation A sibling method that uses hierarchical decomposition (octrees) for culling. Fine-Scale Occlusion Map Culling is chosen when preserving high-frequency content is more important than the large-scale culling efficiency of octrees. Hidden Volume Removal using Hierarchical Occlusion Maps Time Complexity: Depends on the number of voxels and the cost of indexing the occlusion map. The sources do not provide a formal complexity class. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the occlusion map. The size depends on the screen resolution and footprint size. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Retains volume frequency content better than hierarchical decomposition by using averaging rather than binary culling at node levels. Limitations: May be less efficient for large-scale culling compared to octree-based methods. When to use: When fine-scale visibility culling is needed without losing high-frequency details, potentially in combination with octree culling. When not to use: When large-scale culling efficiency is the primary concern and high-frequency detail is less critical. The method was described in the context of volume rendering acceleration, offering an alternative to octree-based space skipping. It was proposed to benefit from both large-scale culling (via octrees) and fine-scale culling (via average occlusion maps). The concept is discussed in academic overviews and textbooks on volume visualization. name: Early Z-Test Acceleration
head: Early z-test
body: Early Z-Test Acceleration is a hardware optimization applied before the fragment shader executes for a particular fragment to avoid shader execution, enabling the fragment processor to immediately process the next incoming fragment. It is used to integrate early ray termination and empty-space skipping into the rendering pipeline. Unlike software-based checks that still invoke the shader, this method discards occluded fragments at the hardware level, yielding performance gains of up to a factor of 3 for typical volumetric datasets on hardware such as the ATI 9700. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A depth buffer containing depth values from prior rendering passes; a fragment with an associated depth value. Output: The fragment is discarded if it fails the depth test, or passed to the fragment shader if it passes. Data Structures: Depth Buffer: A 2D array of depth values per screen coordinate, storing the closest surface depth encountered so far. Prerequisites and Constraints: 1. The depth test must be enabled in the graphics state. 2. Depth values must have been written to the depth buffer in prior rendering passes. 3. All other per-fragment tests (e.g., stencil, alpha) must be disabled. 4. The fragment's depth value must not be modified in the fragment shader. Algorithm Steps: 1. The rasterizer assigns a depth value z{\text{frag}} to each fragment based on its view-space position. 2. The hardware compares z{\text{frag}} against the stored depth value z{\text{buffer}} at the corresponding screen coordinate. 3. If z{\text{frag}} fails the depth test, the fragment is discarded immediately without shader execution. 4. If z{\text{frag}} passes, the fragment shader executes to compute color and opacity. 5. If the fragment passes and the depth buffer is writable, z{\text{buffer}} is updated to z{\text{frag}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyztest(zfrag, zbuffer): # Hardware depth comparison performed before shader execution. # Returns True if fragment passes, False if discarded. return zfrag <= zbuffer def fragmentshader(): # Shader executes only if earlyztest returns True. # Must not modify output depth; hardware relies on implicit zfrag. # Standard front-to-back compositing loop would run here. return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth modification in the shader disables the early z-test, forcing fallback to standard execution order. Enabling other per-fragment tests (stencil, alpha) disables the optimization. A hardware acceleration technique used to speed up parity counting by using a z-buffer. Based on an idea originally by Emil Praun. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Reduces shader execution time proportionally to the area of occluded fragments. Memory: Requires a depth buffer. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated performance gains of up to a factor of 3 for typical renditions of volumetric data sets on the ATI 9700 graphics card. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in shader invocations for occluded regions; leverages existing hardware depth testing logic. Limitations: Only effective when there is opaque occlusion in front of the volume. Strict constraints on shader behavior (no depth modification, no other per-fragment tests) limit its applicability in complex rendering pipelines. When to Use: Use when rendering volumes behind opaque geometry or when a previous pass has established a depth buffer. Do not use if the volume is the first object rendered or if the shader requires depth modification. The technique was described in the context of GPU-based volume rendering acceleration, specifically leveraging DirectX9-level hardware capabilities. It exploits the programmable graphics hardware's ability to perform per-fragment operations, using the early z-test to terminate fragment processing once sufficient opacity has been accumulated or to skip empty space along rays of sight. The work was published in 2003/2004 by researchers including R. Westermann, focusing on real-time methods for large volumetric scalar fields. name: Direct volume ray casting
head: DVR, ray marching, front-to-back compositing, image-order volume rendering
body: Direct volume ray casting (DVR) is an image-order rendering technique that synthesizes a 2D image from a 3D scalar volume by casting a ray through each pixel, sampling the volume along the ray, and integrating the optical properties (color and opacity) using the volume rendering integral. It solves the problem of visualizing the internal structure of semi-transparent volumetric data without extracting explicit geometry, allowing all voxels to potentially contribute to the final image. Unlike surface-based methods (e.g., Isosurface and first-hit ray casting) that stop at the first opaque boundary, DVR accumulates contributions from the entire ray segment within the volume, preserving depth cues and transparency. All direct volume ray casting methods share the following core mechanism: 1. Ray Definition: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane, a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. The ray is intersected with the volume bounding box to determine the entry parameter t{near} and exit parameter t{far}. 2. Sampling: The ray segment [t{near}, t{far}] is discretized into N samples at positions ti = t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t, where \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N. At each sample position \mathbf{p}i = r(ti), the scalar volume value V(\mathbf{p}i) is retrieved, typically via trilinear interpolation of the surrounding voxels. 3. Classification (Transfer Function): The scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i) is mapped to optical properties: a color vector \mathbf{c}i (RGB) and an opacity scalar \alphai (A). This mapping is defined by a transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). The opacity is often corrected for the step size \Delta t to approximate continuous attenuation, using models such as Beer-Lambert: \alphai = 1 - e^{-\sigmai \Delta t}, where \sigmai is the extinction coefficient derived from V(\mathbf{p}i). 4. Compositing (Integration): The samples are composited into the final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out} using the front-to-back volume rendering equation: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) In iterative form, for each sample i: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai where \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} are initialized to (0, 0). 5. Shading: At each sample, a shading model (e.g., Phong, Blinn-Phong) may be applied to compute the base color \mathbf{c}i based on the local gradient \nabla V(\mathbf{p}i), which serves as the surface normal. Generates a 2D projection by processing 3D data as 2D slices, applying transfer functions, and compositing. Slower than direct ray casting due to slice-based overhead. Addresses visual artifacts from undersampling by smoothing transitions between discrete samples and continuous geometry across different scales. Synthesizes novel views by querying a neural network along camera rays and integrating outputs using classical volume rendering techniques. Stabilizes stochastic or noisy results by blending the current frame with a history buffer, specifically selecting the closest hit to preserve depth boundaries. Renders multiple volume datasets simultaneously by extending single-volume mappers to accept multiple datasets and properties, using GPU shaders for traversal. Defines how continuous scalar fields are approximated from discrete voxel data, trading computational cost, visual smoothness, and aliasing artifacts. Projects each voxel directly onto the image plane, relying on data traversal order for hidden surface removal, contrasting with image-order ray casting. Processes a stack of parallel planes instead of individual pixels, propagating light and view rays across layers to accumulate color and opacity. Represents view-dependent color and opacity data using SH coefficients stored in a voxel grid to solve expensive per-sample shading. Integrates a pre-computed volume to apply position-dependent modifications to visualization parameters, such as gamma correction. Converts 3D volumetric data into 2D polygonal slices rasterized and composited by standard graphics hardware for efficient large-volume rendering. Implements direct volume ray casting on programmable graphics hardware using a multi-pass stream model to solve CPU performance bottlenecks. Dynamically slices a 3D dataset using a semi-transparent geometric plane to reveal internal structures occluded by opaque outer layers. Treats volume datasets and geometric objects as Volume-of-Interests (VOIs) in a unified rendering framework with priority-based compositing. Generates volumetric data or manages rendering performance dynamically using procedural evaluation instead of static pre-computed textures. Deviates from standard front-to-back compositing to address specific requirements like projective diagnostic imaging, medical photo-realism, and neural scene composition. Offloads computationally intensive sampling and compositing stages to the GPU, utilizing programmable shaders and texture hardware for interactive frame rates. A lightweight, CPU-based ray-tracing tool for fast visualization of point-like data from cosmological simulations, solving large-scale particle dataset rendering. Replaces 2D texture atlases with a single 3D volume texture for raymarching, allowing larger volumes and simplifying edge handling. Visualizes datasets with non-uniform spatial resolution by leveraging hierarchical structures to reduce computational and memory overhead. Approximates complex light-material interactions by pre-computing SH coefficients for material and light functions on the CPU for GPU ray marching. Reconstructs particle density on-demand in screen space at viewport resolution, combining splatting, texture slicing, and ray casting to avoid aliasing. Utilizes fixed-point arithmetic for ray traversal and compositing in VTK, particularly suited for rendering medical images. The foundational technique generating images by casting rays from the camera, sampling a 3D scalar field at regular intervals, and accumulating via front-to-back compositing. Divides space into independent blocks, rendering each separately and blending results to solve resource isolation in distributed environments. Applies stylized, non-photorealistic shading effects including tone detail and specular highlights using discrete tone mapping. Addresses stair-stepping artifacts at volume boundaries by introducing a smaller final segment to complete the ray march. Replaces per-voxel trilinear interpolation with a two-stage process of calculating ray-plane intersections and interpolating between them. Optimized for large-scale regular 3D spatial data fields, prioritizing rendering speed and high-frequency component preservation over physical lighting accuracy. Decomposes the workload into multiple passes to decouple computational stages like light attenuation and color compositing. Extends standard compositing to support Full, Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), and XRay rendering modes. Defines how scalar data is mapped to color and opacity, enabling visualization of internal structures by assigning transparency. A rendering technique for unsorted cell projection using optical models that lead to a commutative blend function, allowing compositing in arbitrary order. Models allowing arbitrary order compositing include maximum intensity projection and restrictions of the full volume density model to either the source term or the absorption term. Implements the Svox1 rendering formula using nearest-neighbor interpolation with infinitely many steps, including forward, backward, and fused variants. An optimization for ray casting that uses the extracted isosurface as an opaque barrier to terminate rays early, rendering the isosurface's 3D texture coordinates into the exit point texture. To counteract the last incorrect sample, it weights it by the fraction of the step that is outside of the surface. Straightforward integration causes aliasing/banding artifacts because the isosurface coordinates may not lie exactly on the sample point of a marching ray. Rendering directly from the binary Mixture Graph representation at interactive rates on the GPU, supporting real-time transfer function editing across all scales of the mipmap. The rendering uses a direct volume raymarcher sampling at 0.5 voxels. Pre-computed normals derived from the method cause artifacts in the form of caps around the medial axis where segments leave the domain. Lighting contributions are computed without knowledge of position, restricting the method to light and camera at infinity. Used for real-time visual analysis applications in neuroscience and material science. A technique to render multiple volumes by taking the value of the texture itself as the color, bypassing the colormap lookup, using a 4D array (z, y, x, 4) passed directly to the texture. Requires colormaps that can work in Python on Numpy arrays. Implemented in the vispy-multivol repository as the RGBAVolumeVisual class. A strategy to break the stripe pattern of onion ring artifacts by varying sample locations of rays in adjacent pixels, either by using variable sample distances or a random offset at the beginning of each ray. Result is a more 'dithered' image where errors are randomly distributed over pixels. Solves transport for multiple rays in parallel on CPU by iterating over rays and calling the single-ray solver for each. Input arrays sigma, source, initialintensity are row-major [ray][sample]. Computes unique frustum block coordinates for the camera viewpoint to determine which volume blocks need to be rendered. Performs ray casting on the volume blocks using intrinsic, extrinsic, width, height, and render attributes. Extracts voxel indices and interpolation ratios from the ray cast results to reconstruct color via weighted interpolation of volume attributes. Reconstructs color by multiplying the volume color attribute at the hit indices by the interpolation ratios, summing over the 8 corner voxels of the hit cell, and normalizing by 255. Direct volume ray casting was introduced by Marc Levoy in his seminal 1988 paper "Display of Surfaces from Volume Data". Levoy coined the term "direct volume rendering" and defined the pipeline of classification, shading, and compositing, emphasizing the visualization of weak or fuzzy surfaces with smooth silhouettes. The method is based on the volume rendering equation, which integrates radiative energy along rays of sight. Early implementations were software-based, but the advent of programmable graphics hardware enabled GPU-accelerated ray casting, significantly improving performance. The technique is used in scientific visualization and computer graphics for visualizing semi-transparent materials.
