name: Forward Projection (aTx)
head: Fan Beam Projection, Parallel Beam Projection, X-ray projection, aTx
body: X-ray projection (also called Forward Projection or aTx) is a volume rendering composition scheme where interpolated samples along a ray are simply summed to produce an image. It mimics the physical process of X-ray attenuation, where the total signal is the integral of density along the ray path. Unlike alpha blending, which preserves depth cues through opacity accumulation, this method loses depth information, making it suitable for visualizing high-density structures like bones or vessels where relative depth is less critical than total integrated intensity. It builds on the shared compositing principles of Projection and MIP Techniques but replaces the transmittance-weighted accumulation with a direct linear sum. Inputs: A 3D volume V (scalar field, e.g., density or attenuation coefficient). Ray parameters defining the projection geometry (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, sampling interval \Delta s). Outputs: A 2D projection image P where each pixel value P{ij} is the sum of interpolated volume values along the corresponding ray. Data Structures: The volume V is stored as a 3D array or grid. The accumulator for each ray is a scalar initialized to 0. Steps: 1. For each pixel (i, j) in the output image, define the ray \mathbf{r}(s) = \mathbf{o}{ij} + s \cdot \mathbf{d}{ij}, where s ranges from the near to the far clipping plane. 2. Initialize the accumulator A = 0. 3. Iterate through samples k along the ray at positions sk: a. Compute the 3D world position \mathbf{p}k = \mathbf{r}(sk). b. Sample the volume value vk = V(\mathbf{p}k) using interpolation (e.g., trilinear). c. Update the accumulator: A \leftarrow A + \Delta s \cdot vk. 4. Assign the final accumulator value to the pixel: P{ij} = A. Formula: The discrete approximation of the line integral is: P{ij} = \sum{k=1}^{N} vk \cdot \Delta s where vk is the interpolated volume value at sample k, and \Delta s is the step size along the ray. Parameters: \Delta s: Sampling interval. Typical values depend on the volume resolution and desired accuracy; often set to the voxel size or a fraction thereof. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Loss of Depth Information: Since only the sum is stored, occlusion and depth ordering are not represented. Aliasing: If \Delta s is too large relative to the frequency content of the volume, artifacts may appear. Boundary Conditions: Rays that do not intersect the volume should return 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardprojection(volume, rayorigins, raydirections, stepsize): """ volume: 3D array of shape (D, H, W) rayorigins: 2D array of shape (Hout, Wout, 3) raydirections: 2D array of shape (Hout, Wout, 3) stepsize: float, distance between samples """ Hout, Wout, = rayorigins.shape D, H, W = volume.shape projection = [[0.0] Wout for in range(Hout)] for y in range(Hout): for x in range(Wout): origin = rayorigins[y][x] direction = raydirections[y][x] # Normalize direction norm = (direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2)0.5 if norm > 0: direction = [d / norm for d in direction] else: continue accumulator = 0.0 # Determine traversal bounds along the ray # Standard ray-box intersection logic mint = 0.0 maxt = float('inf') for dim, size in enumerate([D, H, W]): if abs(direction[dim]) > 1e-8: t1 = -origin[dim] / direction[dim] t2 = (size - origin[dim]) / direction[dim] tmin = min(t1, t2) tmax = max(t1, t2) mint = max(mint, tmin) maxt = min(maxt, tmax) else: if origin[dim] < 0 or origin[dim] >= size: mint = maxt # Force empty range if mint >= maxt: projection[y][x] = accumulator continue numsteps = int((maxt - mint) / stepsize) for stepidx in range(numsteps): t = mint + stepidx stepsize pointx = origin[0] + t direction[0] pointy = origin[1] + t direction[1] pointz = origin[2] + t direction[2] if 0 <= pointx < D and 0 <= pointy < H and 0 <= pointz < W: v = trilinearsample(volume, pointx, pointy, pointz) accumulator += stepsize v projection[y][x] = accumulator return projection def trilinearsample(volume, x, y, z): # Standard trilinear interpolation ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz # Clamp indices ix = max(0, min(ix, volume.shape[0] - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, volume.shape[1] - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, volume.shape[2] - 1)) # Fetch 8 neighbors v000 = volume[ix][iy][iz] v100 = volume[min(ix+1, volume.shape[0]-1)][iy][iz] v010 = volume[ix][min(iy+1, volume.shape[1]-1)][iz] v110 = volume[min(ix+1, volume.shape[0]-1)][min(iy+1, volume.shape[1]-1)][iz] v001 = volume[ix][iy][min(iz+1, volume.shape[2]-1)] v101 = volume[min(ix+1, volume.shape[0]-1)][iy][min(iz+1, volume.shape[2]-1)] v011 = volume[ix][min(iy+1, volume.shape[1]-1)][min(iz+1, volume.shape[2]-1)] v111 = volume[min(ix+1, volume.shape[0]-1)][min(iy+1, volume.shape[1]-1)][min(iz+1, volume.shape[2]-1)] # Interpolate c00 = v000 (1-fx) + v100 fx c01 = v010 (1-fx) + v110 fx c10 = v001 (1-fx) + v101 fx c11 = v011 (1-fx) + v111 fx r0 = c00 (1-fy) + c01 fy r1 = c10 (1-fy) + c11 fy return r0 (1-fz) + r1 fz A forward and back projector pair designed for objects possessing cylindrical symmetry, serving as a specialized case of the Forward Projection (aTx) method. It exploits rotational invariance to reduce 3D line integrals to a 1D radial problem, distinguishing it from general 3D projectors that handle arbitrary distributions. Choose it when the target volume exhibits axisymmetry and computational efficiency is prioritized over arbitrary geometry support. A method that replaces local affine approximations with exact ray tracing to compute line integrals through 3D Gaussian primitives analytically. It directly computes ray-primitive intersections, avoiding the non-overlapping Gaussian assumption and addressing nonlinear corrections like arc-correction in PET scanners. Choose it when quantitative accuracy and geometric flexibility are required over screen-space splatting pipelines. A variant that initializes CT reconstruction by computing a reference image via Fan beam ray transform and filtered back projection (FBP), then creates a sparse sinogram by subsampling and resizing. It is used when preparing initialization data for tomographic pipelines that require sparse or resized projection inputs. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Limitations: No depth information, no transparency effects, sensitive to sampling density. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. name: Cylindrical Symmetry Projector
head: Abel Transform, Abel Transform Discretization
body: The Cylindrical Symmetry Projector is a forward and back projector pair designed for objects possessing cylindrical symmetry, serving as a specialized case of the Forward Projection (aTx) method. It solves the problem of computing line integrals through axisymmetric volumes by reducing the 3D integration to a 1D radial problem, specifically implementing the Abel Transform for parallel-beam geometries. Unlike general 3D projectors, it exploits rotational invariance to achieve significant computational efficiency, distinguishing it from siblings like Analytic 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomography which handle arbitrary 3D distributions without symmetry assumptions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A radial extinction coefficient profile \alpha(r) defined for r \in [0, r{max}]. Output: The total optical depth \delta{max}(x) for a set of projection rays at impact parameter x. Data Structures: Radial Profile: A vector \alpha of size Nr, representing \alpha(rj) at discrete radii rj. Projection Vector: A vector \Delta of size Nx, representing \delta{max}(xi) at discrete impact parameters xi. Kernel Matrix: A matrix K of size Nx \times Nr, where element K{ij} represents the geometric path length of the i-th ray passing through the j-th concentric ring. Steps: 1. Discretization: Discretize the spray cross-section into Nr concentric rings to approximate the continuous integral as a finite sum. 2. Kernel Construction: Compute the geometric kernel matrix K. The element K{ij} corresponds to the path length of the i-th ray passing through the j-th ring. 3. Forward Projection: Compute the total optical depth vector \Delta using the linear algebraic form: \Delta = K A where A is the vector of unknown radial extinction coefficients \alpha(r). 4. Back Projection: To reconstruct \alpha(r) from measured \delta{max}(x), solve the linear system K A = \Delta for A. This typically involves inverting or pseudo-inverting the kernel matrix K, potentially with regularization if the system is ill-conditioned. Formulas: Under axisymmetry, the total optical depth \delta{max}(x) is the Abel transform of the local extinction-coefficient profile \alpha(r): \delta{max}(x) = 2 \int{x}^{r{max}} \frac{\alpha(r) r}{\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}} dr This integral is approximated by the discrete sum: \delta{max}(xi) = \sum{j=1}^{Nr} K{ij} \alpha(rj) where K{ij} encodes the integral of the geometric factor over the j-th ring for the i-th ray. Parameters: r{max}: Maximum radius of the object. x: Impact parameter (distance from the axis of symmetry to the ray). Nr, Nx: Number of radial bins and projection samples. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: The kernel has a singularity at r=x. Numerical integration schemes must handle this carefully. Ill-Conditioning: The Abel transform is an ill-posed inverse problem. Small errors in \delta{max}(x) can lead to large errors in \alpha(r) without regularization. Boundary Conditions: The value of \alpha(r) at r{max} is assumed to be zero or negligible. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cylindricalsymmetryprojector(alpha, rgrid, xgrid): """ Forward projection using Cylindrical Symmetry (Abel Transform). Args: alpha: Array of extinction coefficients alpha(r) at radii rgrid. rgrid: Array of radial positions rj. xgrid: Array of impact parameters xi. Returns: deltamax: Array of total optical depths deltamax(xi). """ Nr = len(rgrid) Nx = len(xgrid) deltamax = zeros(Nx) # Precompute kernel matrix K K = zeros((Nx, Nr)) for i in range(Nx): xi = xgrid[i] for j in range(Nr): rj = rgrid[j] # Path length through ring j for ray at xi # This is the geometric kernel element Kij # For a thin ring approximation, this might be computed analytically # or via numerical integration of the Abel kernel over the ring width if rj >= xi: # Simplified geometric path length for a thin ring at rj # Exact formula depends on ring discretization scheme # Common approximation: 2 rj / sqrt(rj^2 - xi^2) drj # But Kij should represent the integral over the ring # Here we assume a precomputed K or a helper function K[i, j] = computepathlength(xi, rj, rgrid) else: K[i, j] = 0.0 # Matrix-vector multiplication: Delta = K A for i in range(Nx): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(Nr): sumval += K[i, j] alpha[j] deltamax[i] = sumval return deltamax def computepathlength(x, r, rgrid): """ Computes the geometric kernel element Kij for ray at x and ring at r. This is a placeholder for the specific discretization scheme. In practice, this involves integrating 2r/sqrt(r^2-x^2) over the ring width. """ # Example: Simple approximation for a ring centered at r with width dr dr = rgrid[1] - rgrid[0] if len(rgrid) > 1 else 1.0 if r > x: return 2.0 r / sqrt(r2 - x2) dr else: return 0.0 The specific mathematical operation applied in parallel-beam geometries. It is the core of the Cylindrical Symmetry Projector. Choose it when the object is strictly axisymmetric and the projection geometry is parallel. Link: Abel Transform. The method of dividing the radial profile into concentric rings. Choose finer discretization for higher accuracy but increased computational cost. Link: Radial Discretization. Time Complexity: O(Nx Nr) for the forward projection if the kernel matrix is precomputed. The back projection (inversion) depends on the solver used, typically O(Nr^2) or O(Nr \log Nr) with fast algorithms. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Nr) to store the kernel matrix K. Strengths: Extremely efficient for axisymmetric objects; reduces 3D problem to 1D. Limitations: Only applicable to objects with cylindrical symmetry; sensitive to noise in the input data due to the ill-posed nature of the inverse Abel transform. When to use: When the object is known to be axisymmetric and high performance is required. When not to use: For arbitrary 3D objects or objects with significant asymmetry. The Cylindrical Symmetry Projector, specifically the Abel Transform, has a long history in physics and engineering, particularly in plasma physics and combustion diagnostics. It was implemented as part of a differentiable forward projector for X-ray CT, allowing for gradient-based optimization in tomographic reconstruction. The discretization approach described here follows the work of Champley & Maddox (2021). name: Analytic 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomography
head: 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomographic Reconstruction, 3D Gaussian ray tracing, Analytic forward projection for 3D Gaussians
body: This method replaces the local affine approximation of splatting with exact ray tracing to compute line integrals through 3D Gaussian primitives analytically. It solves the problem of quantitative accuracy degradation and geometric inflexibility in tomographic reconstruction, specifically addressing nonlinear corrections like arc-correction in PET scanners. Unlike splatting-based pipelines which project into 2D screen space, this approach directly computes ray-primitive intersections, avoiding the assumption of non-overlapping Gaussians. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussian primitives, each defined by a mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a covariance matrix \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Scanner geometry defining ray origins \mathbf{o}j and directions \mathbf{d}j for each detector element or pixel j. A Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) structure built over the Gaussian primitives for spatial acceleration. Outputs: A set of projected values (line integrals) for each ray, used to optimize Gaussian parameters or form the final reconstruction. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Primitive: Defined by \boldsymbol{\mu} (position) and \boldsymbol{\Sigma} (shape/orientation). The density function is G(\mathbf{x}) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}^{-1}(\mathbf{x} - \boldsymbol{\mu})\right). BVH: A hierarchical spatial partitioning structure storing bounding volumes for subsets of Gaussians to accelerate intersection tests. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Setup: Define ray origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d} based on the specific scanner geometry (e.g., PET Line of Response or CT cone/parallel beams). 2. Intersection Search: For each ray, use the BVH to efficiently identify all 3D Gaussian primitives intersected by the ray. 3. Analytic Integration: Compute the pixel value by analytically integrating the contribution of each encountered Gaussian along the ray segment. 4. Optimization: Adjust the Gaussian parameters (\boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}) so that the rendered projections match the measured projection data. 5. Reconstruction: Voxelize the optimized Gaussians to obtain the final tomographic reconstruction. Analytic Line Integral Formula: For a single anisotropic 3D Gaussian G(\mathbf{x}) and a ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, the line integral I is computed analytically. The core operation is: I = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} G(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) \, dt This avoids the affine collapse inherent in splatting methods. Parameters: Acceleration Structure: BVH is used to limit the number of primitives requiring intersection checks. Kernel: Primarily uses 3D Gaussian kernels, but compact kernels like the Epanechnikov kernel are also supported. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Sorting: Unlike standard rendering where depth sorting is required for correct alpha blending, sorting of depth-ordered intersections can be waived in tomographic reconstruction because the method computes line integrals rather than pixel colors. Geometric Flexibility: The method requires explicit definition of ray origins and directions to handle non-uniform bin spacing and cylindrical detector arrangements (e.g., PET arc correction). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def analyticforwardprojection(gaussians, bvh, rays): """ Computes the forward projection of 3D Gaussians using analytic ray tracing. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian primitives, each with.mu (3D vector) and.Sigma (3x3 matrix). bvh: Bounding Volume Hierarchy structure built from gaussians. rays: List of rays, each with.origin (3D vector) and.direction (3D vector). Returns: projections: List of scalar line integral values for each ray. """ projections = [] for ray in rays: intersectinggaussians = bvhquery(bvh, ray.origin, ray.direction) totalintegral = 0.0 for gaussian in intersectinggaussians: totalintegral += computeanalyticlineintegral( gaussian.mu, gaussian.Sigma, ray.origin, ray.direction) projections.append(totalintegral) return projections def bvhquery(node, origin, direction): """Standard recursive BVH traversal to find intersecting primitives.""" if not rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, node.bbox): return [] if node.isleaf: return [g for g in node.gaussians if gaussianrayintersect(g, origin, direction)] return bvhquery(node.left, origin, direction) + bvhquery(node.right, origin, direction) def rayaabbintersect(origin, direction, bbox): """Slab method for ray-AABB intersection.""" tmin = (bbox.min - origin) / direction tmax = (bbox.max - origin) / direction t1 = min(tmin); t2 = max(tmin) t3 = min(tmax); t4 = max(tmax) return max(t1, t3) <= min(t2, t4) def gaussianrayintersect(g, origin, direction): """Bounding sphere check for pruning non-intersecting Gaussians.""" distsq = sum((o - m)2 for o, m in zip(origin, g.mu)) return distsq <= g.radiussq def computeanalyticlineintegral(mu, Sigma, origin, direction): """ Computes the analytic line integral of a 3D Gaussian along a ray. Integral: int{-inf}^{inf} exp(-0.5 (r(t) - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (r(t) - mu)) dt where r(t) = origin + t direction. """ d = direction / math.sqrt(sum(c2 for c in direction)) diff = [o - m for o, m in zip(origin, mu)] Sigmainv = invertmatrix(Sigma) a = dot(d, matvecmul(Sigmainv, d)) b = 2.0 dot(diff, matvecmul(Sigmainv, d)) c = dot(diff, matvecmul(Sigmainv, diff)) if a <= 0: return 0.0 return math.sqrt(2.0 math.pi / a) math.exp(-0.5 (c - b2 / (4.0 a))) def dot(v1, v2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(v1, v2)) def matvecmul(M, v): return [sum(row[j] v[j] for j in range(len(v))) for row in M] def invertmatrix(M): """Standard 3x3 matrix inversion.""" det = (M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])) invdet = 1.0 / det return [ [(M[1][1]M[2][2]-M[1][2]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][2]M[2][1]-M[0][1]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][1]M[1][2]-M[0][2]M[1][1])invdet], [(M[1][2]M[2][0]-M[1][0]M[2][2])invdet, (M[0][0]M[2][2]-M[0][2]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][2]M[1][0]-M[0][0]M[1][2])invdet], [(M[1][0]M[2][1]-M[1][1]M[2][0])invdet, (M[0][1]M[2][0]-M[0][0]M[2][1])invdet, (M[0][0]M[1][1]-M[0][1]M[1][0])invdet] ] Projects Gaussians into 2D screen space using local affine approximations. It suffers from affine collapse and cannot easily handle nonlinear geometric corrections. Computes line integrals analytically along rays. It provides higher quantitative accuracy and supports complex scanner geometries (e.g., PET arc correction). Time Complexity: Depends on the BVH traversal and the number of intersecting primitives per ray. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids affine collapse, yielding more physically consistent forward projections. Explicit control over ray origins and directions facilitates precise application of nonlinear geometric corrections (e.g., arc-correction in PET). Naturally handles overlapping Gaussians without the non-overlapping assumption. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than splatting due to analytic integration per primitive. Requires efficient acceleration structures (BVH) to be practical for large scenes. When to use: PET and CT modalities, especially those with cylindrical detector arrangements requiring arc correction. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed in "Radioactive 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomographic Reconstruction". It addresses limitations of splatting-based pipelines, such as degraded reconstruction quantitative accuracy and difficulty in incorporating nonlinear geometric corrections. The framework was evaluated on both PET and CT modalities, including NEMA phantom simulations and realistic PET data. It builds on Forward Projection (aTx) by replacing splatting with analytic ray tracing. Radioactive 3D Gaussian Ray Tracing for Tomographic Reconstruction, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01057v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Anti-Aliasing and Filtering
head: Box filter, Gaussian filter, Volume Filter
body: Anti-Aliasing and Filtering addresses visual artifacts caused by undersampling, such as jagged edges, flickering, and high-frequency noise, by smoothing the transition between discrete samples and continuous geometry. This family encompasses methods that operate at different stages of the rendering pipeline: pre-filtering data to prevent discretization errors, spatial filtering during rasterization, and post-processing screen-space blurs. It is distinct from sibling methods like Interpolation and Sampling Techniques because it focuses on the suppression of high-frequency components in the final image or intermediate buffers rather than the accuracy of individual sample retrieval. The children share no single mathematical mechanism beyond operating on discrete signals. Methods are selected based on their pipeline stage: pre-filtering for participating media [2928-prefiltering.md], rasterization coverage for line primitives [3607-line-coverage-anti-aliasing.md], or screen-space post-processing for ambient occlusion and color buffers [8374-pseudoseparable-cross-bilateral-filter.md][8804-separable-ping-pong-blur-post-processing.md][9037-screen-space-image-filtering.md]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelinecoverageaa(fragmentworldpos, linestart, lineend, viewportheight, fovy): v = lineend - linestart w = fragmentworldpos - linestart c1 = dot(v, w) c2 = dot(v, v) if c2 == 0: distance = length(fragmentworldpos - linestart) else: b = c1 / c2 b = max(0.0, min(1.0, b)) closestpoint = linestart + b v distance = length(fragmentworldpos - closestpoint) alpha = distance / (viewportheight fovy) return alpha def blendlinecolor(alpha, linecolor, backgroundcolor): finalcolor = alpha linecolor + (1.0 - alpha) backgroundcolor return finalcolor class BilateralData: def init(self, ao, normal, tracedistance): self.Ao = ao self.Normal = normal self.TraceDistance = tracedistance def applypseudoseparablebilateralfilter(uv, direction, filtersize=14, epsilon=0.001, discreteweights=None): # Load texture values at uv centerao = LoadAmbientOcclusionAsFloat4(uv) centernormal = LoadNormal(uv) centerdepth = LoadTraceDistance(uv) centerdata = BilateralData(centerao, centernormal, centerdepth) gtid = GetGlobalThreadID() padoffset = CastDir(gtid.xy) + filtersize gsBilateralData = [None] ((2 filtersize) + 100) gsBilateralData[padoffset + gtid.xy] = centerdata uvstep = GetUVStep(direction) for i in range(1, filtersize + 1): uvlower = uv - (i uvstep) lowerao = LoadAmbientOcclusionAsFloat4(uvlower, sampler="pointclamp") lowernormal = LoadNormal(uvlower, sampler="pointclamp") lowerdepth = LoadTraceDistance(uvlower, sampler="pointclamp") gsBilateralData[padoffset + gtid.xy - i] = BilateralData(lowerao, lowernormal, lowerdepth) uvupper = uv + (i uvstep) upperao = LoadAmbientOcclusionAsFloat4(uvupper, sampler="pointclamp") uppernormal = LoadNormal(uvupper, sampler="pointclamp") upperdepth = LoadTraceDistance(uvupper, sampler="pointclamp") gsBilateralData[padoffset + gtid.xy + i] = BilateralData(upperao, uppernormal, upperdepth) SyncThreads() filteredao = centerdata.Ao discreteweights[0] totalweight = discreteweights[0] for i in range(1, filtersize + 1): for sign in [-1, 1]: neighboridx = padoffset + gtid.xy + (sign i) bdata = gsBilateralData[neighboridx] depthdiff = abs(centerdata.TraceDistance - bdata.TraceDistance) depthweight = 1.0 / (epsilon + centerdata.TraceDistance 0.01 + depthdiff) normaldot = dot(centerdata.Normal, bdata.Normal) normalweight = pow(abs(normaldot), 32) combinedweight = discreteweights[i] depthweight normalweight filteredao += bdata.Ao combinedweight totalweight += combinedweight finalao = filteredao / totalweight if totalweight > 0 else centerdata.Ao WriteToAmbientOcclusionTarget(uv, finalao) def initializepingpongblur(width=512, height=512): fbtexture0 = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] fbtexture1 = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] fb0 = {"texture": fbtexture0, "depth": True} fb1 = {"texture": fbtexture1} return fb0, fb1, fbtexture0, fbtexture1 def applyseparableblur(fb0, fb1, fbtexture0, fbtexture1, shader, fulltexturesize=512): w1 = 0.0555555 w2 = 0.2777777 baseoffset = 1.0 / fulltexturesize intraoffset = (w2 / (w1 + w2)) baseoffset finaloffset = baseoffset + intraoffset bindframebuffer(fb1) clearcolorbuffer() bindshader(shader) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsetx", finaloffset) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsety", 0.0) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture0) drawfullscreenquad() bindframebuffer(fb0) clearcolorbuffer() bindshader(shader) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsetx", 0.0) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsety", finaloffset) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture1) drawfullscreenquad() Prefiltering initializes radiance or scattering coefficients for discrete ordinates to remove singularity-like artifacts and avoid discretization errors in participating media with insufficient optical thickness. It differs from naive source illumination prefiltering by being adaptive, preserving background illumination features while smoothing the initial scattering distribution. Choose this method when rendering thin, strongly-scattering media where natural blurring is absent. Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing reduces jagged edges in rasterized lines by calculating the ratio of a line's occupancy within a pixel and blending the pixel's original color with the line's color based on that ratio. It differs from the all-or-nothing strategy by producing smoother edges, especially for wireframe models. Choose this method when rendering line-based or wireframe geometry. The PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter is a screen-space post-processing technique used to smooth Ambient Occlusion data in direct volume ray casting. It reduces computational cost by decomposing a 2D bilateral filter into two sequential 1D passes, leveraging precomputed depth and normal information to preserve edges and prevent bleeding across object boundaries. It sets itself apart from standard Gaussian blurs by weighting neighbors based on geometric consistency rather than spatial proximity. Choose this method when preserving sharp silhouettes in volumetric scenes is required. Separable Ping-Pong Blur Post-Processing applies a smoothing filter to a rendered image to reduce high-frequency noise and aliasing artifacts. It solves the problem of jagged edges and visual noise by treating the rendered image as a discrete function requiring spatial smoothing. It differs from sibling methods by operating exclusively on the final color buffer using a two-pass separable convolution with a ping-pong framebuffer switching technique. Choose this method when efficient constant-memory per-pass smoothing of the final color buffer is needed. Screen-Space Image Filtering refers to a family of techniques that modify a base image rendered in a vacuum by adding effects caused by participating media, using only information currently visible on the screen. It sets itself apart from its siblings by its exclusive reliance on the 2D image buffer, which cannot access data for objects behind the camera or occluded geometry. Choose this method when high parallelism on GPUs is prioritized over physical accuracy. Affine Arithmetic Filtering obtains an average value of a procedural shader with an error bound over a finite area using affine arithmetic. It differs from standard sampling by providing rigorous error bounds for procedural volume shading. Choose this method when deterministic error bounds for procedural volume evaluation are required. Calculates the Screen Space Ratio (SSR) for a texture coordinate to determine sampling density or filtering strength, optionally applying a perspective filter to soften the result. It calculates the SSR based on projection matrix, position, object scale, and screen dimensions, used for font scaling. If Filter is true: compute derivatives a = \text{float2}(\text{ddx}(UV.x), \text{ddy}(UV.x)) and b = \text{float2}(\text{ddx}(UV.y), \text{ddy}(UV.y)); compute s = \text{lerp}(\text{dot}(a,a), \text{dot}(b,b), 0.5); set \text{SSR} = \text{rsqrt}(s) / \text{TextureSize}. If Filter is false: compute s = \text{rsqrt}(|\text{ddx}(UV.x) \cdot \text{ddy}(UV.y) - \text{ddy}(UV.x) \cdot \text{ddx}(UV.y)|); set \text{SSR} = s / \text{TextureSize}. Set \text{pixelSize} = \text{position}.w; divide \text{pixelSize} by (\text{objectScale} \cdot \text{mul}((\text{float2x2})\text{projection}, \text{float2}(\text{screenWidth}, \text{screenHeight}))); compute \text{SSR} = \text{rsqrt}(\text{dot}(\text{pixelSize}, \text{pixelSize}) \cdot 2) \cdot \text{fontScale}. An anti-aliasing technique that precomputes MIP-filtered parameters at the surfel center during preprocessing to reduce per-pixel rasterization cost while eliminating aliasing artifacts. Stores the resulting MIP-filtered inverse covariance \Sigma^{-1}{\text{mip}} and normalization factor \alpha{\text{norm}} once per primitive. During rasterization, loads these four parameters from shared memory. Applies the parameters directly to the intersection coordinates via the quadratic form of equation 6. Rendering time is 50 ms per frame for the center-precomputed MIP filter, an overhead of only 8 ms (<20%) over the unfiltered baseline of 42 ms. Compared to per-pixel Jacobian evaluation (AA-2DGS), this method is visually indistinguishable but faster (50 ms vs 65 ms per frame) because it avoids computing the full 2x2 Jacobian, its outer product, and matrix inverse at every covered pixel. An invisible object that makes overlapping volume parts invisible. In PovRay rendering, it interacts with other objects. In preview, it interacts only with volume. Rendering quality must be set quite high because the volume shape becomes complicated rather than a simple box. An antialiasing method that operates on the final color buffer. It performs edge detection and applies perceptually correct edge filtering. It provides antialiasing for both geometry and volume in the composited image. FXAA is applied to the final composited image, whereas multisampled G-buffer antialiasing is applied during geometry rendering. They can be combined for improved quality. Applies inverse diffusion with a negative diffusion coefficient to correct z-direction blur in confocal microscopy data. Works only in preview. Filtered data must be exported to new.df3 files for PovRay rendering. Early methods relied on simple box filters for crisp edges in high-resolution volumes, while Gaussian filters were introduced to prevent banding artifacts. name: Prefiltering
head: Adaptive Prefiltering, Anisotropy Prefiltering
body: Prefiltering is a technique used in discrete ordinates rendering to remove singularity-like artifacts and avoid discretization errors, particularly in participating media with insufficient optical thickness to naturally blur sampled illumination. Unlike naive prefiltering of source illumination which blurs background features, this method is adaptive, allowing the perception of background illumination features while smoothing the initial scattering distribution. It operates on discrete signals prior to ray marching, distinguishing it from screen-space post-processing methods like Screen-Space Image Filtering or PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter, and from primitive-level coverage methods like Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing or Affine Arithmetic Filtering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An environment map or local light source distribution (e.g., VPLs) and a set of discrete ordinates (directions) for the radiative transfer equation. Output: A prefiltered initialization of the radiance or scattering coefficients for each ordinate, ready for ray marching. Data Structures: Ordinates: A set of N directions. For environment maps, these are arranged in radial grids or spherical grids. For local lights, spherical grids use angular and radial coordinates aligned with the point source. Importance Weights (wn): A scalar value for each ordinate n representing its contribution to the image, proportional to the solid angle \Omegan of the direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Importance: Determine the importance wn for each ordinate n, which is proportional to the solid angle \Omegan subtended by the direction. 2. Map Importance to Anisotropy: Compute the initial anisotropy a{n,i} for each ordinate i using the heuristic formula: a{n,i} = \left(1 - \frac{wn}{N}\right)^\beta Where: N is the total number of ordinates. wn is the importance of ordinate n mapped from the solid angle proportion. \beta > 0 is a scalar factor defining proportionality. Important ordinates (high wn) are denser in the directional domain, have smaller solid angles, and result in higher initial anisotropy. 3. Clamp Singularities: Apply clamping to the resulting values to reduce any remaining singularities. 4. Propagation (Optional/Contextual): In Principal-Ordinates Propagation (POP), this prefiltered initialization is applied before sampling the medium. For local lights, VPLs with large importance receive high initial anisotropy. Parameters: \beta: Scalar factor defining the proportionality in the anisotropy mapping heuristic. Value: Tuned empirically once for each environment map. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Insufficient Optical Thickness: Without prefiltering, singularity-like artifacts appear in thin, strongly-scattering media. Grid Merging: When combining grids from different light sources, geometric misalignments may occur, requiring careful merging strategies. A prefilter applied to reduce aliasing artifacts, specifically preventing 'valleys' of rims from becoming shallower due to oversmoothing. It addresses reconstruction quality issues in isosurface raycasting. Performance: The prefiltering step is described as a simple and quick task. In the POP pipeline, prefiltering initialization is part of a sequence that includes propagation (e.g., 2 ms for residuum propagation) and ray marching (e.g., 5 ms). Strengths: Removes singularity artifacts in thin media; preserves background illumination features due to adaptivity; handles high anisotropy (e.g., g=0.98) effectively. Limitations: Requires empirical tuning of \beta for each environment map. Prefiltering originated in real-time rendering of participating media with high scattering anisotropy. The method was proposed to handle the shortcomings of current methods in handling highly anisotropic scattering, which is common in natural and artificial media. name: Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing
head: Anti-Aliasing Factor for Line Coverage, Coverage approach, Coverage-based Anti-Aliasing (Line), Sub-pixel averaging for lines
body: Line Coverage Anti-Aliasing reduces jagged edges (aliasing) in rasterized lines by calculating the ratio of a line's occupancy within a pixel and mixing the pixel's original color with the line's color based on that ratio. It differs from the "all or nothing" (winner-take-all) strategy where a pixel is set to the line's color if the line passes through it, and unchanged otherwise. This approach produces smoother edges, especially for wireframe models. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Fragment position in world space (\mathbf{p}), line segment endpoints in world space (\mathbf{l}0, \mathbf{l}1), viewport dimensions in pixels (u{\text{ViewportSize}} = (w, h)), and vertical field of view (u{\text{FovY}}). Output: An anti-aliasing factor (coverage ratio) \alpha \in [0, 1] used to blend the line color with the background. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard vertex/fragment shader uniforms and temporary variables for vector math. Steps: 1. Compute the Euclidean distance from the fragment's world position to the line segment defined by endpoints \mathbf{l}0 and \mathbf{l}1. Let this distance be d. The distance calculation involves projecting the point onto the line segment and clamping the parameter b to [0, 1] to handle segment endpoints correctly. 2. Calculate the anti-aliasing factor \alpha using the formula: \alpha = \frac{d}{u{\text{ViewportSize}.y} \cdot u{\text{FovY}}} Here, u{\text{ViewportSize}.y} is the height of the viewport in pixels. u{\text{FovY}} is the vertical field of view. The denominator represents a scaling factor related to the pixel size relative to the distance. 3. The factor \alpha represents the pixel size relative to the distance; smaller projected pixel distance results in smaller AA influence (higher coverage). 4. Mix the final pixel color C{\text{final}} with the line color C{\text{line}} and the original background color C{\text{bg}} using \alpha as the weight for the line color: C{\text{final}} = \alpha \cdot C{\text{line}} + (1 - \alpha) \cdot C{\text{bg}} (Inferred from "mixture of its original color and the line's color... determined by the line's occupancy") Parameters: u{\text{FovY}}: Vertical field of view. u{\text{ViewportSize}}: Viewport dimensions in pixels (width, height). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The distance calculation must handle the case where the projection point falls outside the segment endpoints (clamping b to [0, 1]) to ensure correct distance for segment ends. Boundary: If the distance d is zero (fragment lies exactly on the line), \alpha = 0, implying full line coverage? Or is \alpha the background weight? The formula \alpha = d / \dots suggests \alpha is small when close to the line. If \alpha is the line weight, then C{\text{final}} = \alpha C{\text{line}} + (1-\alpha)C{\text{bg}} means full line color when \alpha=1. However, the text says "smaller pixel-projected distance results in smaller AA". This implies \alpha might be the background weight or the formula needs inversion. Standard coverage usually maps distance to opacity. If d=0, coverage is 1. If the formula yields 0, it might be inverted or \alpha is the "anti-aliasing factor" reducing the line's intensity. Given "mixing... based on that ratio", and "smaller distance... smaller AA", it is likely that the coverage ratio \rho = 1 - \alpha or similar is used for the line weight. However, the source explicitly gives \alpha = d / \dots. We stick to the source formula and note that \alpha is the calculated factor. Degenerate Input: If \mathbf{l}0 = \mathbf{l}1, the line segment has zero length. The distance calculation c2 = \text{dot}(v, v) becomes 0, causing division by zero in b = c1 / c2. This must be handled by checking if the segment length is near zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computelinecoverageaa(fragmentworldpos, linestart, lineend, viewportheight, fovy): """ Computes the anti-aliasing factor for a line segment. Args: fragmentworldpos (vec3): Position of the fragment in world space. linestart (vec3): Start point of the line segment in world space. lineend (vec3): End point of the line segment in world space. viewportheight (float): Height of the viewport in pixels. fovy (float): Vertical field of view. Returns: float: Anti-aliasing factor alpha. """ # Vector from line start to end v = lineend - linestart # Vector from line start to fragment w = fragmentworldpos - linestart # Dot products c1 = dot(v, w) c2 = dot(v, v) # Handle degenerate line (zero length) if c2 == 0: # Distance to a point distance = length(fragmentworldpos - linestart) else: # Parameter b for projection onto the line b = c1 / c2 # Clamp b to [0, 1] to stay on the segment if b < 0.0: b = 0.0 elif b > 1.0: b = 1.0 # Closest point on the segment closestpoint = linestart + b v # Distance from fragment to closest point distance = length(fragmentworldpos - closestpoint) # Calculate anti-aliasing factor # Formula from source: distance / uViewportSize.y uFovY # Note: Source says "smaller pixel-projected distance results in smaller AA" # This implies alpha is small when distance is small. alpha = distance / (viewportheight fovy) return alpha def blendlinecolor(alpha, linecolor, backgroundcolor): """ Blends line color with background based on alpha. Note: The interpretation of alpha as line weight vs background weight depends on the specific shader implementation. Standard coverage usually uses 1-alpha for the line if alpha is distance-based. However, following the source's implication of mixing based on ratio: """ # Assuming alpha is the weight for the line color as per standard # "mixing... determined by the line's occupancy" # If alpha is small near the line, and we want full line color there, # we might need to invert or use 1-alpha. # The source does not explicitly state the blend equation, only the factor. # We provide the standard blend using alpha as the line weight. # If alpha represents "anti-aliasing factor" reducing the line, # the blend might be: background + alpha (line - background) # Or: alpha line + (1-alpha) background # Using the simple mixture described: finalcolor = alpha linecolor + (1.0 - alpha) backgroundcolor return finalcolor Breaks each pixel into smaller sub-pixels (e.g., 10x10), renders with all-or-nothing, then averages. Requires significantly more memory and time. Renders a large image (e.g., 6000x6000) and scales it down using bilinear interpolation (e.g., to 2000x2000) to approximate sub-pixel coverage without hardware support. Time Complexity: The coverage calculation is O(1) per fragment. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per fragment. Measured Performance: The sub-pixel averaging variant requires approximately 10 times the memory and rendering time for a 10x10 sub-pixel grid. Strengths: Produces smoother edges for wireframe models compared to all-or-nothing rasterization. Limitations: The sub-pixel variant is computationally expensive. The direct coverage method relies on accurate distance calculations and proper scaling factors. When to Use: When rendering wireframe models or lines where jagged edges are visually prominent and hardware sub-pixel rendering is not available or too costly. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and the visual improvement of anti-aliasing is not worth the cost, or when using hardware that already supports high-quality line anti-aliasing. The technique is described in the context of advanced computer graphics, specifically addressing aliasing problems in rasterization. name: PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter
head: AOHorizontalH, AOHorizontalL, AOVerticalH, AOVerticalL, AOHorizontalM, AOVerticalM
body: The PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter is a screen-space post-processing technique used to smooth Ambient Occlusion (AO) data in direct volume ray casting. It reduces computational cost by decomposing a 2D bilateral filter into two sequential 1D passes (horizontal and vertical). Unlike standard Gaussian blurs, it weights neighbors based on geometric consistency (depth and normal similarity) rather than just spatial proximity, making it suitable for preserving sharp silhouettes in volumetric scenes. The method operates on screen-space buffers containing ambient occlusion values, surface normals, and depth (trace distance). It processes the AO data in two passes: one horizontal and one vertical. Each pass computes a weighted average of neighboring pixels, where weights are determined by a combination of spatial distance, depth difference, and normal alignment. Inputs: AmbientOcclusionTarget: Texture containing the raw AO values (float4). NormalMap: Texture containing surface normals (float3). TraceDistance: Texture containing depth/z-buffer values (float). discreteWeights: Precomputed 1D kernel weights array of size 15. Outputs: AmbientOcclusionTarget: Updated with the filtered AO values. 1. BilateralData: A struct holding the necessary information for a single pixel. Ao: float4 (Ambient Occlusion value). Normal: float3 (Surface normal vector). TraceDistance: float (Depth value). 2. Shared Memory Array (gsBilateralData): Used for thread cooperation within a thread group. Size: (2 FilterSize) + ThreadLength. ThreadLength is ThreadsX for horizontal passes and ThreadsY for vertical passes. Stores BilateralData structs. 3. discreteWeights: Array of 15 float values. Index 0 corresponds to the center pixel. Indices 1–14 correspond to neighbors at increasing distances. FilterSize: Integer, radius of the filter kernel on each side. Value: 14. epsilon: Float, small constant to prevent division by zero in depth weight. Value: 0.001. RangeSigma: Declared in source but not used in the visible implementation. The filter is applied in two distinct passes. The logic for a single pass (horizontal or vertical) is as follows: 1. Load Center Data: Read Ao, Normal, and TraceDistance for the current pixel uv from input textures. Store these in a local variable centerData. 2. Shared Memory Initialization: Calculate global thread ID gtid.xy. Define padding offset PAD(xy) = CASTDIR(xy) + FilterSize. Store centerData in shared memory at gsBilateralData[PAD(gtid.xy)]. 3. Load Neighbors: For i from 1 to FilterSize, calculate neighbor UV as uv - (i uvstep). Sample Ao, Normal, TraceDistance using samplerpointclamp to handle boundaries. Store in gsBilateralData[PAD(gtid.xy) - i]. Repeat for uv + (i uvstep) storing in gsBilateralData[PAD(gtid.xy) + i]. 4. Synchronization: Execute a barrier/synchronization command to ensure all threads in the group have finished loading shared memory. 5. Weighted Accumulation: Initialize filteredAo and totalWeight using the center pixel data multiplied by discreteWeights[0]. Loop i from 1 to FilterSize. Iterate sign from -1 to 1 with step 2. Access neighbor data bData from gsBilateralData[PAD(gtid.xy) + sign i]. Compute weights: depthWeight = 1.0 / (epsilon + centerData.TraceDistance 0.01 + |centerData.TraceDistance - bData.TraceDistance|). Compute normalWeight = |dot(centerData.Normal, bData.Normal)|^32. Compute combinedWeight = discreteWeights[i] depthWeight normalWeight. Update accumulators: filteredAo += bData.Ao combinedWeight and totalWeight += combinedWeight. 6. Normalization and Output: Normalize filtered AO by dividing by total weight. Write result to AmbientOcclusionTarget. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FILTERSIZE = 14 EPSILON = 0.001 DISCRETEWEIGHTS = [0.0] 15 # Precomputed array of 15 floats class BilateralData: def init(self, ao, normal, tracedistance): self.Ao = ao self.Normal = normal self.TraceDistance = tracedistance def castdir(x, y, stride): return x + y stride def getuvstep(direction, width, height): if direction == 'horizontal': return (1.0 / width, 0.0) else: return (0.0, 1.0 / height) def clamp(val, minval, maxval): return max(minval, min(val, maxval)) def applypseudoseparablebilateralfilter(uv, direction, width, height, threadsx, threadsy): centerao = loadao(uv) centernormal = loadnormal(uv) centerdepth = loadtracedistance(uv) centerdata = BilateralData(centerao, centernormal, centerdepth) gtidx, gtidy = uvtothreadid(uv, width, height) threadidx = castdir(gtidx, gtidy, threadsx) padoffset = threadidx + FILTERSIZE gsBilateralData[padoffset] = centerdata uvstep = getuvstep(direction, width, height) for i in range(1, FILTERSIZE + 1): uvlower = (uv[0] - i uvstep[0], uv[1] - i uvstep[1]) lowerao = loadao(uvlower) lowernormal = loadnormal(uvlower) lowerdepth = loadtracedistance(uvlower) gsBilateralData[padoffset - i] = BilateralData(lowerao, lowernormal, lowerdepth) uvupper = (uv[0] + i uvstep[0], uv[1] + i uvstep[1]) upperao = loadao(uvupper) uppernormal = loadnormal(uvupper) upperdepth = loadtracedistance(uvupper) gsBilateralData[padoffset + i] = BilateralData(upperao, uppernormal, upperdepth) syncthreads() filteredao = centerdata.Ao DISCRETEWEIGHTS[0] totalweight = DISCRETEWEIGHTS[0] for i in range(1, FILTERSIZE + 1): for sign in [-1, 1]: neighboridx = padoffset + sign i bdata = gsBilateralData[neighboridx] depthdiff = abs(centerdata.TraceDistance - bdata.TraceDistance) depthweight = 1.0 / (EPSILON + centerdata.TraceDistance 0.01 + depthdiff) normaldot = dot(centerdata.Normal, bdata.Normal) normalweight = pow(abs(normaldot), 32) combinedweight = DISCRETEWEIGHTS[i] depthweight normalweight filteredao += bdata.Ao combinedweight totalweight += combinedweight finalao = filteredao / totalweight if totalweight > 0 else centerdata.Ao writetoaotarget(uv, finalao) Boundary Handling: The filter uses samplerpointclamp for neighbor sampling. This clamps UV coordinates to the texture edges, effectively replicating the edge pixel values for out-of-bounds accesses. Arbitrary Depth Factor: The term centerData.TraceDistance 0.01 in the depth weight denominator is an arbitrary linear factor introduced in the implementation. Its impact on visual quality is not theoretically derived in the source. Unused Parameter: RangeSigma is declared but not used in the visible code, suggesting it may be a remnant of a different filter variant or intended for future use. Division by Zero: The epsilon constant (0.001) prevents division by zero in the depth weight calculation when depth differences are negligible. An optimization strategy to generate a low resolution AO map and use joint bilateral upsampling to resample the HAO map at screen resolution while filtering noise. It approximates the non-separable bilateral filter in two passes (one horizontal, one vertical) to improve frame rate. The method computes the filtered AO at pixel x as h{m \times m}(x) = \frac{\sum{y \in Q} wd(x, y) wr(x, y) h0(y/k)}{\sum{y \in Q} wd(x, y) wr(x, y)}, where Q is the set of pixels in an m \times m square centered on x. The spatial weight is wd(x, y):= w(\|x - y\|, m). The range weight combines normal, position, and height influences: wr(x, y):= wn(x, y) \cdot wp(x, y) \cdot wh(x, y). Normal influence is wn(x, y):= w(1 + \langle n(x), n(y) \rangle, 2). Position influence is wp(x, y):= w(\|p(x) - p(y)\|, e{max}). Height influence is wh(x, y):= w(\|h0(x/k) - h0(y/k)\|, 1). Here, p(x) is the object space position extracted from the Z map, n(x) is the normal extracted from the normal map, h0 is the low resolution AO map, and k is the scale ratio between high and low resolution maps. The non-separable filter is approximated as \tilde{h}{m \times m}(x):= h{1 \times m}(h{m \times 1}(x)). Defining the range space according to object space entities avoids AO bleeding between distant objects projected closely in image space. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K), where N is the number of pixels and K is the filter radius (14). The separable approach reduces the 2D complexity O(N \cdot K^2) to two 1D passes O(2 \cdot N \cdot K). Memory Complexity: O(K \cdot T) for shared memory, where T is the thread group size. This is minimal compared to full 2D kernel storage. Performance: The method is efficient for real-time rendering due to the separable decomposition and use of shared memory. However, the bilateral weighting (dot product, power, division) per neighbor is more expensive than a simple Gaussian blur. Strengths: Preserves edges defined by depth and normal discontinuities, preventing AO bleeding across object boundaries. Limitations: Computationally heavier than simple box or Gaussian filters. The arbitrary depth factor may require tuning for different scenes. Not suitable for scenes with high-frequency depth variation where the depth weight might become unstable. The PseudoSeparable Cross Bilateral Filter is implemented in the codebase referenced by for direct volume ray casting to improve the visual quality of ambient occlusion by smoothing noise while maintaining geometric sharpness. The technique leverages standard screen-space post-processing techniques adapted for volumetric data. name: Separable Ping-Pong Blur Post-Processing
head: Horizontal-vertical blur, PostProcessBlurShader, Two-pass blur
body: Separable Ping-Pong Blur Post-Processing applies a smoothing filter to a rendered image to reduce high-frequency noise and aliasing artifacts. It solves the problem of jagged edges and visual noise in direct volume ray casting by treating the rendered image as a discrete function requiring spatial smoothing. Unlike sibling methods that operate on volumetric primitives or screen-space geometry buffers, this method operates exclusively on the final color buffer using a two-pass separable convolution. It sets itself apart by using a "ping-pong" framebuffer switching technique to perform horizontal and vertical blurs sequentially, allowing for efficient computation with constant memory per pass regardless of kernel width. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The base rendered scene image (color buffer). Output: The blurred image, written to the target color buffer. Data Structures: Ping-Pong Textures: Two textures, fbTexture[0] and fbTexture[1], allocated with dimensions 512 \times 512. Format: GLRGB. Internal Format: GLUNSIGNEDSHORT565. Filtering: GLLINEAR (Bilinear). Wrapping: GLCLAMPTOEDGE. Ping-Pong Framebuffers: Two framebuffers, framebuffer[0] and framebuffer[1]. framebuffer[0]: Attaches fbTexture[0] and a GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16 renderbuffer. framebuffer[1]: Attaches only fbTexture[1]. Shader Uniforms: mfTexelOffset: The calculated texel offset for sampling. blurStep: A Vec2 uniform controlling the blur step size. focus: A Float uniform controlling focus. halfBand: A Float uniform controlling half band. maxRadius: A Float uniform controlling max radius. saturation: A Float uniform controlling saturation. Parameters: fullTextureSize: Fixed resolution for post-processing textures, typically 512. w1: Weight for the faster filter kernel, typically 0.0555555. w2: Weight for the faster filter kernel, typically 0.2777777. Steps: 1. Initialization: Allocate fbTexture[0] and fbTexture[1] with the specified format, filtering, and wrapping. Create framebuffer[0] and framebuffer[1] and attach the textures and depth buffer as specified. 2. Base Render: Render the scene into framebuffer[0]. 3. Pass 1 (Horizontal Blur): Bind framebuffer[1] as the draw target. Set shader uniform SHADERUNIFORMTEXELOFFSETX to mfTexelOffset and SHADERUNIFORMTEXELOFFSETY to 0.0f. Draw a fullscreen quad using the blur shader, sampling from fbTexture[0]. 4. Pass 2 (Vertical Blur): Bind the final target color buffer (or framebuffer[0] if reusing) as the draw target. Set shader uniform SHADERUNIFORMTEXELOFFSETX to 0.0f and SHADERUNIFORMTEXELOFFSETY to mfTexelOffset. Draw a fullscreen quad using the blur shader, sampling from the result of Pass 1 (fbTexture[1]). Formulas: The base texel offset is calculated as: m\fTexelOffset = \frac{1.0f}{fullTextureSize} An intra-texel offset adjustment is applied using specific kernel weights: intraTexelOffset = \frac{w2}{w1 + w2} \times m\fTexelOffset The final offset used for sampling is: m\fTexelOffset{final} = m\fTexelOffset + intraTexelOffset Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializepingpongblur(): # Allocate two 512x512 RGB textures with unsigned short 5-6-5 format fbtexture0 = createtexture(width=512, height=512, format=GLRGB, internalformat=GLUNSIGNEDSHORT565) fbtexture1 = createtexture(width=512, height=512, format=GLRGB, internalformat=GLUNSIGNEDSHORT565) # Set filtering and wrapping settexturefiltering(fbtexture0, filter=GLLINEAR, wrap=GLCLAMPTOEDGE) settexturefiltering(fbtexture1, filter=GLLINEAR, wrap=GLCLAMPTOEDGE) # Create framebuffers fb0 = createframebuffer() attachtexture(fb0, fbtexture0, attachment=COLORATTACHMENT0) attachrenderbuffer(fb0, format=GLDEPTHCOMPONENT16) fb1 = createframebuffer() attachtexture(fb1, fbtexture1, attachment=COLORATTACHMENT0) return fb0, fb1, fbtexture0, fbtexture1 def renderscene(fb0): bindframebuffer(fb0) clearcolorbuffer() cleardepthbuffer() drawscene() # Render the base volume rendering output def applyseparableblur(fb0, fb1, fbtexture0, fbtexture1, shader, fulltexturesize=512): # Calculate offsets w1 = 0.0555555 w2 = 0.2777777 baseoffset = 1.0 / fulltexturesize intraoffset = (w2 / (w1 + w2)) baseoffset finaloffset = baseoffset + intraoffset # Pass 1: Horizontal Blur bindframebuffer(fb1) clearcolorbuffer() bindshader(shader) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsetx", finaloffset) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsety", 0.0) setuniform(shader, "blurstep", vec2(1.0, 0.0)) # Example uniform usage setuniform(shader, "focus", 1.0) setuniform(shader, "halfband", 1.0) setuniform(shader, "maxradius", 1.0) setuniform(shader, "saturation", 1.0) bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture0) drawfullscreenquad() # Pass 2: Vertical Blur bindframebuffer(fb0) # Or the final target buffer clearcolorbuffer() bindshader(shader) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsetx", 0.0) setuniform(shader, "texeloffsety", finaloffset) setuniform(shader, "blurstep", vec2(0.0, 1.0)) # Example uniform usage bindtexture(shader, "inputtexture", fbtexture1) drawfullscreenquad() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture Filtering: Must be set to Bilinear (GLLINEAR) because the blur taps land between texels. Texture Wrapping: Must be set to Clamp (GLCLAMPTOEDGE) because default wrapping (e.g., Repeat) causes the blur at the top edge to pull in pixels from the bottom of the frame. A linear blur filter that applies exponential decay smoothing along the outermost two dimensions of an input tensor. It serves as a post-processing step in separable ping-pong blur pipelines to reduce high-frequency noise and aliasing artifacts in rendered images. Unlike Gaussian blurs, it uses an infinite impulse response (IIR) structure, allowing for efficient computation with constant memory per pass regardless of kernel width. A blending technique used to improve visualization quality for moving objects or during camera navigation. It applies a two-pass weighted Gaussian blur and performs Gaussian blur blending with Z-buffer occlusion while the incremental bubble-sort A-Buffer is processing. Time Complexity: O(N) per pass, where N is the number of pixels, because the blur is separable into two 1D passes. The kernel width affects the constant factor but not the asymptotic complexity if the kernel is fixed or precomputed. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the ping-pong textures, where W and H are the texture dimensions. The method requires two full-resolution textures for the ping-pong mechanism. Measured Performance: Specific performance metrics are not provided in the sources. The use of GLUNSIGNEDSHORT565 suggests a trade-off between memory bandwidth and color precision. Strengths: Efficient for large blur radii due to separability; constant memory usage per pass; simple implementation using standard framebuffer objects. Limitations: Fixed resolution of 512 \times 512 in the reference implementation may limit applicability to higher resolutions without modification; blurring is applied uniformly, which may not be desirable for all regions of the image; does not account for depth or geometry information during the blur itself (unlike depth-aware blurs). When to use: When post-processing a rendered image to reduce aliasing and noise, and the scene does not require depth-aware blurring. When not to use: When high-resolution textures are required and memory is constrained; when the blur needs to be adaptive based on scene content or depth. The method originates from the iVoxel project, an iPhone OS Scenegraph Rendering System developed by Torsten Becker, Norman Holz, Lars Schneider, and others at the Hasso-Plattner-Institute (HPI) in Potsdam, Germany, around 2009. It was used as a post-processing step to improve the visual quality of rendered voxel data. The technique leverages standard OpenGL ES 2.0 features for framebuffer objects and shader-based convolution. larsxschneider/iVoxel, https://github.com/larsxschneider/iVoxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GhostlyActive/VoxelTerraformer, https://github.com/GhostlyActive/VoxelTerraformer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Stroke-based splatting: an efficient multi-resolution point cloud visualization technique, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-017-1420-7, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Exponential Decay Blur Filter
head: Exponential Smoothing Blur, IIR Blur
body: A linear blur filter that applies exponential decay smoothing along the outermost two dimensions of an input tensor. It serves as a post-processing step in separable ping-pong blur pipelines to reduce high-frequency noise and aliasing artifacts in rendered images. Unlike Gaussian blurs, it uses an infinite impulse response (IIR) structure, allowing for efficient computation with constant memory per pass regardless of kernel width. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A tensor X of shape (..., H, W), typically representing a rendered image or depth map. Output: A smoothed tensor Y of the same shape as X. Parameters: Smoothing parameter \alpha: Controls the decay rate. Smaller \alpha results in more smoothing; larger \alpha results in less dependence on previous values and thus less smoothing. Typical value: \alpha = 0.8 is used for most methods. For IDR (Iterative Deepening Representation), \alpha = 0.3 is used due to higher variance between plot points. Data Structures: The algorithm operates in-place or uses a single temporary buffer Y initialized as a copy of X. Steps: The filter is separable, processing the last two dimensions independently. Each dimension undergoes a forward pass followed by a backward pass. 1. Initialize Y = X. 2. Forward pass along the last dimension (width W): For i from 0 to W-2: Y[..., i+1] \leftarrow Y[..., i+1] + \alpha \cdot Y[..., i] 3. Backward pass along the last dimension: For i from W-2 down to 0: Y[..., i] \leftarrow Y[..., i] + \alpha \cdot Y[..., i+1] 4. Forward pass along the second-to-last dimension (height H): For i from 0 to H-2: Y[..., i+1,:] \leftarrow Y[..., i+1,:] + \alpha \cdot Y[..., i,:] 5. Backward pass along the second-to-last dimension: For i from H-2 down to 0: Y[..., i,:] \leftarrow Y[..., i,:] + \alpha \cdot Y[..., i+1,:] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exponentialdecayblur(X, alpha): """ Applies exponential decay smoothing to the last two dimensions of tensor X. Args: X: Input tensor of shape (..., H, W). alpha: Smoothing parameter (0 < alpha <= 1). Returns: Y: Smoothed tensor of the same shape as X. """ # Copy input to output buffer Y = X.clone() # Dimensions H = Y.shape[-2] W = Y.shape[-1] # Forward pass along last dimension (width) for i in range(W - 1): Y[..., i + 1] = Y[..., i + 1] + alpha Y[..., i] # Backward pass along last dimension (width) for i in range(W - 2, -1, -1): Y[..., i] = Y[..., i] + alpha Y[..., i + 1] # Forward pass along second-to-last dimension (height) for i in range(H - 1): Y[..., i + 1,:] = Y[..., i + 1,:] + alpha Y[..., i,:] # Backward pass along second-to-last dimension (height) for i in range(H - 2, -1, -1): Y[..., i,:] = Y[..., i,:] + alpha Y[..., i + 1,:] return Y Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary conditions: The loops run up to shape-1, so boundary pixels are updated by their neighbors but do not propagate values outside the tensor bounds. Precision: Accumulation of floating-point errors is possible in very long sequences, though typically negligible for image dimensions. Degenerate input: If H=1 or W=1, the corresponding loop range is empty, and the pass is skipped, which is correct behavior. A variant where the smoothing is defined recursively as \hat{v}i = \alpha vi + (1 - \alpha) \hat{v}{i-1} for i > 1, with \hat{v}1 = v1. This formulation explicitly maintains a running average rather than the additive decay used in the main filter. It is used in training convergence analysis, such as in IDR, where \alpha = 0.3 is preferred due to higher variance between plot points. For other methods, \alpha = 0.8 is used. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot (H + W)) for a tensor of size N \times H \times W, where N is the batch size or number of channels. The separable nature reduces complexity from O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot K^2) for a 2D convolutional kernel of size K. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pass if implemented in-place, or O(N \cdot H \cdot W) if a copy is required. Performance: Efficient on GPUs due to simple arithmetic operations and coalesced memory access patterns. Strengths: Low computational cost, easy to implement, effective for smoothing noisy data like depth priors or rendered images. Limitations: Introduces directional bias if not applied symmetrically (though the ping-pong approach mitigates this); not a true Gaussian blur, so frequency response differs. When to use: Post-processing for noise reduction in neural rendering pipelines, particularly when computational efficiency is critical. When not to use: When precise frequency cutoff characteristics are required, or when isotropic smoothing is strictly needed without the IIR artifacts. The method originates from implementations in neural rendering pipelines, specifically in the context of NeRFingMVS, where it is used to smooth depth priors and confidences. The concept of exponential smoothing is well-established in time-series analysis and signal processing, but its application as a spatial filter in volume rendering post-processing is a specific adaptation for handling noise in learned representations. The variant using exponential moving averages is cited in the context of training neural lumigraph representations using meta learning, where it is used to smooth convergence metrics. weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Fast Training of Neural Lumigraph Representations using Meta Learning, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2106.14942, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Exponential Moving Average Smoothing
head: Control Signal Smoothing, EMA Smoothing, Exponential Smoothing
body: Exponential Moving Average (EMA) smoothing is a recursive low-pass filter that estimates the underlying signal by weighting the current observation and the previous smoothed estimate. In the context of volume rendering and control signal processing, it reduces high-frequency noise and variance in data streams. It is distinguished from fixed-kernel blurs by its infinite impulse response and adaptive memory, where the effective window size is determined by the smoothing parameter \alpha rather than a fixed spatial or temporal radius. Inputs and Outputs Input: A sequence of raw values vi for i = 1, \dots, N. Output: A sequence of smoothed values \hat{v}i. Parameter: Smoothing factor \alpha \in (0, 1]. Data Structures v: Array of raw input values. vhat: Array of smoothed output values, same size as v. alpha: Scalar float. Algorithm The method computes the smoothed value \hat{v}i using the recurrence relation: \hat{v}i = \alpha vi + (1 - \alpha) \hat{v}{i-1} where: vi is the current raw input value. \hat{v}{i-1} is the previously computed smoothed value. \alpha is the smoothing parameter. Steps 1. Initialize \hat{v}0. If not specified, \hat{v}0 = v1 or 0. 2. For i from 1 to N: a. Compute \hat{v}i = \alpha \cdot vi + (1 - \alpha) \cdot \hat{v}{i-1}. 3. Return \hat{v}. Parameters \alpha: Controls the trade-off between smoothing and responsiveness. Smaller \alpha results in more smoothing. Larger \alpha results in less dependence on previous values and thus less smoothing. Typical value: \alpha = 0.8 is used for general methods and control signal filtering. Specific case: \alpha = 0.3 is used for IDR (Incremental Distance Representation) due to higher variance between plot points. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Initialization: The value of \hat{v}0 affects the initial transient. Common practice is to set \hat{v}0 = v1 to avoid bias. Precision: For very long sequences, the influence of \hat{v}0 decays exponentially. If \alpha is small, the effective memory is long, requiring careful handling of initial conditions. Boundary: The formula is undefined for i=1 without an initial condition. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def exponentialmovingaveragesmoothing(v, alpha): """ Applies Exponential Moving Average smoothing to a sequence of values. Args: v (list of float): Input sequence of raw values. alpha (float): Smoothing parameter, 0 < alpha <= 1. Returns: list of float: Smoothed sequence. """ if not v: return [] n = len(v) vhat = [0.0] n # Initialize with the first value to avoid bias from arbitrary zero vhat[0] = v[0] for i in range(1, n): vhat[i] = alpha v[i] + (1 - alpha) vhat[i-1] return vhat The parent method that applies this smoothing along the outermost two dimensions of a tensor. It uses the same recursive principle but in a spatial domain for image-order rendering. See Exponential Decay Blur Filter. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples. Each sample requires one multiplication and one addition. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space if computed in-place or streaming, or O(N) to store the output sequence. Strengths: Computationally efficient; no need for large kernels; adapts to local variance implicitly through the recursive structure. Limitations: Introduces phase lag; sensitive to initialization; not a linear phase filter. When to use: When low-latency smoothing is required, or when the noise characteristics are stationary and the trade-off between responsiveness and noise reduction is controlled by \alpha. When not to use: When strict linear phase is required, or when the noise has non-stationary characteristics that require adaptive \alpha. The method originates from statistical smoothing techniques and has been applied in various domains including control systems and neural network training. In the context of neural radiance fields and volume rendering, it has been used to smooth control signals for robot actuation and to reduce variance in training metrics for neural lumigraph representations. The specific parameter values (\alpha=0.8 and \alpha=0.3) are empirically derived from these applications. name: Screen-Space Image Filtering
head: Screen-space approaches
body: Screen-Space Image Filtering modifies a base image rendered in a vacuum by adding effects caused by participating media, using only information currently visible on the screen. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its exclusive reliance on the 2D image buffer; it cannot access data for objects behind the camera or occluded geometry that was not rendered in the base pass. The family shares no single mathematical mechanism beyond operating on discrete signals, with techniques selected based on their pipeline stage: pre-filtering for participating media, rasterization coverage for line primitives, or screen-space post-processing for ambient occlusion and color buffers. 1. Image Representation: The input is an image L, defined as a discrete two-dimensional function L: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Color Space and Range: The color channels (red, green, blue) are assumed to be non-negative real numbers, with HDR values ranging from 0 to +\infty. 3. Screen-Space Constraint: Techniques operate exclusively on information currently visible on the screen, limiting access to occluded geometry or data behind the camera. 4. Convolution Basis: Many techniques apply a filter to the original image, typically using neighborhood-based convolution. Uses screen-space splatting to handle small cells. Incorporates motion blur into the screen-space splatting process. Applies thresholding to slice data before screen-space filtering. Pre-computes filters to accelerate screen-space operations. Uses a pseudo-separable bilateral filter for edge-preserving smoothing. Implements blur via separable ping-pong passes. Uses affine arithmetic to track uncertainty during filtering. The term "screen-space" was introduced to describe methods that modify an image rendered in a vacuum by adding effects caused by participating media, relying solely on information "on the screen". These approaches became popular in real-time rendering on GPUs because they can often be executed for each output pixel individually in parallel. The limitation of not working with information not currently on the screen (e.g., objects behind the camera) is noted, though often considered not critical in certain conditions. The mathematical foundation treats the image as a discrete 2D function L: \mathbb{N}^2 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}^3 with HDR values in [0, +\infty).
