name: VF-NeRF
head: Vector Field NeRF, Viewshed Fields for Rigid NeRF Registration
body: VF-NeRF is a method for rigid registration between two Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs) when the original camera positions are unknown. It introduces Viewshed Fields (VF), an implicit function that maps an oriented point (3D location and viewing direction) to a scalar indicating how well that point was covered by the original camera set. By using Normalizing Flows to generate high-scoring oriented points, VF-NeRF creates informative virtual camera viewpoints for photometric alignment, avoiding the noise and poor coverage associated with random sampling. It differs from NeRF Importance Sampling by focusing on registration via novel view generation rather than training efficiency, and from NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline by its specific application to inter-NeRF alignment. VF-NeRF operates in two distinct modes: Registration (using Viewshed Fields to align two NeRFs) and Scene Representation (using Vector Fields to render scenes from posed images). The registration algorithm is detailed in, while the vector field rendering implementation is provided in. Registration Mode Inputs: Two pre-trained NeRFs (Source and Target), without camera poses. Registration Mode Outputs: A 6-DoF rigid transformation matrix aligning the Source NeRF to the Target NeRF. Rendering Mode Inputs: Multi-view posed images and monocular depth maps. Rendering Mode Outputs: Rendered RGB images and depth maps of the indoor scene. The model consists of the following components: 1. vectorfieldnetwork: A VectorFieldNetwork instance. 2. renderingnetwork: A RenderingNetwork instance. 3. density: A LaplaceDensity function initialized with parameters from config.densityconfig.todict(). 4. finevectorfieldnetwork: Optional VectorFieldNetwork instance, used if fine sampling is enabled. Defaults to sharing the vectorfieldnetwork instance if not explicitly configured. 5. raysampler: A UniformSampler with parameters nsamples, near, far, and perturb (inverted boolean). 6. finesampler: Optional RangeFineSampler with parameters nimportance, near, far, perturb (inverted), range (config.raysamplerconfig.finerange), and maxsamples (config.raysamplerconfig.maxsamples). This method aligns two NeRFs by generating virtual views from the source NeRF using VF and optimizing a rigid transform. 1. VF Network Initialization: Initialize a Normalizing Flows model using Real-NVP [13] with L=4 layers and H=128 hidden dimensions. The model maps 6D oriented points (x, d) to a 6-dimensional diagonal Gaussian in latent space z. 2. VF Training: During NeRF training, sample oriented points (x, d) around surfaces. The viewing direction d is constant along a ray, while the location x varies. Map sampled points to latent space z. Optimize the VF network by minimizing the unsupervised negative log-likelihood of the data distribution pX(x) through the change of variables formula: \log(px(x)) = \log(pz(f(x))) + \sum{i=1}^{K} \log \left| \det \left( \frac{dfi}{df{i-1}} \right) \right| Use the RAdam optimizer with a constant learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-5}. Real Scenes: Train the NeRF for 60,000 iterations total, and enable VF training on the last 10,000 iterations. Synthetic Scenes: Train the NeRF for 20,000 iterations total, enable VF training on the last 5,000 iterations, and ignore samples where the image alpha is less than 128. 3. Point Cloud Generation (PC Initialization): Sample 100,000 points from the learned VF distribution. Select points with density higher than 10. Use these points as input for a classic global registration method, specifically using FPFH for feature extraction. 4. Virtual Camera Generation: Sample from the 6D Gaussian in the latent space to generate high-visibility oriented points (\tilde{x}, \tilde{d}). Use the invertible Normalizing Flows model to recover the oriented point. Determine the position and orientation of a novel virtual camera using the recovered point and direction. 5. Photometric Optimization: Render images from the Source NeRF using the generated virtual cameras. Optimize the 6-DoF rigid transformation parameters to minimize photometric loss between the rendered Source images and the Target NeRF. Real Scenes: Optimize for 15,000 iterations with 32,000 samples per iteration using an SGD optimizer with an initial learning rate of 5 \times 10^{-3} and exponential decay. Synthetic Scenes: Optimize for 2,500 iterations with 8,128 samples per iteration using an SGD optimizer with an initial learning rate of 1 \times 10^{-3} and exponential decay. Photometric Initialization: Perform optimization over 25 random transformations to find a good starting point. During optimization, use VF to select high-quality rays to improve convergence. This method renders indoor scenes using vector fields learned from posed images and depth maps. 1. Configuration: Parse configuration for vfnetconfig, renderingnetconfig, raysamplerconfig, densityconfig, and schedulerconfig. 2. Network Initialization: Initialize vectorfieldnetwork and renderingnetwork. If config.raysamplerconfig.finesampling() is true, initialize finevectorfieldnetwork (defaulting to self.vectorfieldnetwork). Initialize density as LaplaceDensity. If config.cossimweightsanneal is not 'none', initialize LinearAnnealing with shape self.config.cossimweights.shape[0], duration self.config.annealend - self.config.annealstart, and soft mode based on self.config.cossimweightsanneal == 'soft'. 3. Parallelism: If config.cudaconfig.numgpus > 1, wrap networks in nn.DataParallel and move all networks to config.cudaconfig.device. 4. Ray Sampling: Create raysampler (UniformSampler) with nsamples, near, far, and perturb (inverted). If fine sampling is enabled, create finesampler (RangeFineSampler) with nimportance, near, far, perturb (inverted), range, and maxsamples. 5. Optimization: Initialize optimizer as torch.optim.Adam with learning rate config.schedulerconfig.lr and weight decay config.schedulerconfig.weightdecay. Initialize scheduler as torch.optim.lrscheduler.ExponentialLR with decay factor self.config.schedulerconfig.lrdecayfactor (1. / self.config.schedulerconfig.lrdecaysteps). Train the network to minimize reconstruction loss against posed images and depth maps. VF Network: Real-NVP, L=4 layers, H=128 hidden dims. VF Optimizer: RAdam, constant learning rate 5 \times 10^{-5}. NeRF Representation: Nerfacto. NeRF Training: 1,024 rays per iteration, Adam optimizer, initial learning rate 10^{-2}, exponential decay. Density: LaplaceDensity. Annealing: LinearAnnealing for cosine similarity weights if configured. Transparent Regions: In synthetic scenes, samples where the image alpha is less than 128 are ignored during VF training. Random Sampling Failure: Random sampling on a unit sphere often produces non-informative images with noise; VF-NeRF avoids this by generating informative views. Initialization: Photometric optimization requires a good initial guess; VF-NeRF provides this via PC initialization (FPFH+RANSAC) or photometric initialization over 25 random transformations. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Training requires 60,000 or 20,000 NeRF iterations plus 10,000 or 5,000 VF iterations, followed by 15,000 or 2,500 registration optimization iterations. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing NeRF weights, VF network weights, and latent space samples. Performance: Evaluated on LLFF and Objaverse datasets. LLFF Full Overlap on Trex yields \Delta t = 0.0205, \Delta R = 0.0122. LLFF No Overlap on Trex yields \Delta t = 0.0102, \Delta R = 0.0105. Objaverse results vary by object; e.g., Chair 4b05 yields \Delta R = 0.03, \Delta t = 2.43, while Piano 0e0d yields \Delta R = 6.89, \Delta t = 13.84. Strengths: Does not require user input at initialization unlike NeRF2NeRF, generates informative views better than random sampling, and is robust to noise. Limitations: Requires pre-trained NeRFs and is computationally intensive due to Normalizing Flows and iterative optimization. VF-NeRF was introduced to solve the problem of rigid registration between two NeRFs without original camera positions. It builds on NeRF Volumetric Rendering (Coarse/Fine Sampling) by using NeRF as the scene representation. The method was evaluated on LLFF and Objaverse datasets. The code implementation is available on GitHub. name: Voxel-based Volume Rendering
head: Voxel-based Radiance Field, Dense Voxel Volume Rendering
body: Voxel-based Volume Rendering is a technique that trains a dense or semi-dense voxel representation of a radiance field, where multiple voxels contribute to a single sample during rendering. It solves the problem of efficiently estimating scene opacity and color by using a structured 3D grid as a coarse model, often serving as the initial stage in two-tier sampling architectures to determine opaque regions in space. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as NeRF Importance Sampling which relies on learned probability distributions, and NerfAcc Rendering Pipeline which uses acceleration structures like hash grids, is its reliance on a fixed, dense (or semi-dense) volumetric grid where the volume integral is approximated by summing contributions from intersected voxels. Unlike VF-NeRF which may use sparse or hybrid representations, this method explicitly contrasts with sparse voxelization (octrees) by ensuring multiple voxels contribute to a single ray sample, providing structural consistency through opacity prediction independent of view direction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N calibrated images with known camera poses (Ri, ti) and intrinsics. Output: A rendered RGB image for a given camera pose, and optionally a depth map or opacity volume. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A 3D tensor V \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times D \times D \times C}, where D is the resolution (e.g., 128) and C is the channel dimension. In standard implementations, C typically stores density (\sigma) and color features (c). The grid is dense or semi-dense, covering the bounding box of the scene. The grid is typically initialized with small random values or zeros, with density initialized to low values to represent empty space. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the target image, generate a ray origin o and direction d based on the camera projection matrix. 2. Ray-Voxel Intersection: Determine the interval [t{near}, t{far}] where the ray intersects the voxel grid bounding box. 3. Discretization: Divide the interval [t{near}, t{far}] into K sample points. In basic voxel rendering, these points may be uniformly spaced or aligned with voxel boundaries. 4. Voxel Query: For each sample point xk = o + tk d, query the voxel grid to retrieve the density \sigmak and color feature ck. If xk falls outside the grid, return zero/empty. If xk falls within a voxel, perform trilinear interpolation of the stored values from the 8 surrounding corners. 5. Opacity and Color Conversion: Convert raw features to physical quantities. Density: \sigmak = \text{activation}(\sigmak), typically using a softplus or exponential function to ensure \sigmak \ge 0. Color: ck = \text{activation}(ck), typically using sigmoid to bound RGB to [0, 1]. The opacity is predicted without the view direction to encourage structural consistency. 6. Volume Rendering Integration: Compute the accumulated color C(r) and opacity \alpha(r) along the ray using discrete integration: C(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} Tk \alphak ck Tk = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{k-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right), \quad \alphak = 1 - \exp(-\sigmak \deltak) where \deltak = t{k} - t{k-1} is the distance between samples, and Tk is the transmittance up to sample k. 7. Loss Computation: Compare the rendered image against the ground truth image using a loss function (e.g., MSE or LPIPS). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervoxelray(rayorigin, raydirection, voxelgrid, resolution, bboxmin, bboxmax): """ Renders a single ray using a dense voxel grid. Args: rayorigin: (3,) float tensor, camera origin. raydirection: (3,) float tensor, normalized ray direction. voxelgrid: (D, D, D, C) tensor, the trained voxel representation. resolution: int, D. bboxmin: (3,) float tensor, minimum corner of the voxel grid. bboxmax: (3,) float tensor, maximum corner of the voxel grid. Returns: color: (3,) float tensor, rendered RGB color. depth: float, accumulated depth. opacity: float, accumulated opacity. """ # 1. Calculate intersection with bounding box tmin = (bboxmin - rayorigin) / raydirection tmax = (bboxmax - rayorigin) / raydirection tnear = max(max(tmin)) tfar = min(min(tmax)) if tnear > tfar: return torch.zeros(3), 0.0, 0.0 # 2. Sample points along the ray numsamples = 128 # Typical value for coarse voxel rendering tvals = torch.linspace(tnear, tfar, numsamples) points = rayorigin.unsqueeze(0) + tvals.unsqueeze(1) raydirection.unsqueeze(0) # 3. Query voxel grid # Normalize points to [0, 1] range relative to bbox pointsnorm = (points - bboxmin) / (bboxmax - bboxmin) # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle boundary cases pointsnorm = torch.clamp(pointsnorm, 0.0, 1.0) # Trilinear interpolation # voxelgrid is (D, D, D, C) # pointsnorm is (numsamples, 3) # We need to interpolate C channels densityfeatures = trilinearinterpolate(voxelgrid, pointsnorm) # densityfeatures shape: (numsamples, C) # Assume first channel is density, rest are color features sigmaraw = densityfeatures[:, 0] colorraw = densityfeatures[:, 1:] # 4. Convert to physical quantities sigma = softplus(sigmaraw) # Ensure non-negative density color = sigmoid(colorraw) # Ensure RGB in [0, 1] # 5. Volume Rendering deltas = tvals[1:] - tvals[:-1] # Add a small epsilon to avoid division by zero or log(0) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.tensor([1e-10])]) alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-sigma deltas) transmittance = torch.cumprod(torch.exp(-sigma deltas), dim=0) transmittance = torch.cat([torch.tensor([1.0]), transmittance[:-1]]) weights = alpha transmittance colorout = torch.sum(weights.unsqueeze(1) color, dim=0) opacityout = torch.sum(weights) depthout = torch.sum(weights tvals[:-1]) return colorout, depthout, opacityout def trilinearinterpolate(grid, points): """ Performs trilinear interpolation on a 3D grid. grid: (D, D, D, C) points: (N, 3) in range [0, 1] returns: (N, C) """ D = grid.shape[0] # Scale to voxel indices indices = points (D - 1) x = indices[:, 0] y = indices[:, 1] z = indices[:, 2] # Get integer and fractional parts x0 = torch.floor(x).long() y0 = torch.floor(y).long() z0 = torch.floor(z).long() x1 = x0 + 1 y1 = y0 + 1 z1 = z0 + 1 # Clamp indices x0 = torch.clamp(x0, 0, D - 1) x1 = torch.clamp(x1, 0, D - 1) y0 = torch.clamp(y0, 0, D - 1) y1 = torch.clamp(y1, 0, D - 1) z0 = torch.clamp(z0, 0, D - 1) z1 = torch.clamp(z1, 0, D - 1) # Extract values v000 = grid[x0, y0, z0,:] v100 = grid[x1, y0, z0,:] v010 = grid[x0, y1, z0,:] v110 = grid[x1, y1, z0,:] v001 = grid[x0, y0, z1,:] v101 = grid[x1, y0, z1,:] v011 = grid[x0, y1, z1,:] v111 = grid[x1, y1, z1,:] # Interpolate wx = x - x0 wy = y - y0 wz = z - z0 c00 = v000 (1 - wx) + v100 wx c10 = v010 (1 - wx) + v110 wx c01 = v001 (1 - wx) + v101 wx c11 = v011 (1 - wx) + v111 wx c0 = c00 (1 - wy) + c10 wy c1 = c01 (1 - wy) + c11 wy result = c0 (1 - wz) + c1 wz return result Parameters: Resolution (D): Typically 64, 128, or 256. Higher resolution increases memory usage quadratically/cubically but improves detail. Number of Samples (K): Typically 128–256 for coarse rendering. Activation Functions: Softplus for density, Sigmoid for color. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Usage: Dense voxel grids consume O(D^3) memory. For D=256 and C=10, this is significant. Aliasing: Uniform sampling may alias high-frequency details. Stratified sampling or adaptive sampling can mitigate this. Boundary Artifacts: Rays intersecting the grid boundaries must be handled carefully to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. The Coarse Ray Renderer (CRR) is a fast rendering technique that provides coarse density estimation and ray features for downstream processes in neural volume rendering, specifically serving the Fine Voxel Renderer (FVR) and Progressive Blur Estimation (PBE). It differs from standard per-voxel ray casting by aggregating features along a ray and inferring color once per ray rather than querying every voxel, which significantly reduces computational cost at the expense of per-voxel accuracy. It builds on Voxel-based Volume Rendering by utilizing a decomposed explicit feature volume. The Neural Voxel Renderer (NVR) is a neural network that takes a discrete voxel representation of a scene and a light position as input to produce a continuous, smooth rendered image. It solves the problem of mapping discrete geometric representations (voxels) to high-quality, physically-based renderings by implicitly learning the complex lighting and shading effects that traditional rasterization or simple volume rendering might miss. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as the Coarse Ray Renderer, is its explicit use of a dual-branch architecture (voxel encoding and light encoding) combined with a perceptual loss function to ensure photorealistic output from a structured 3D grid input. DIVeR is a method that jointly optimizes a feature voxel grid and a decoder MLP while applying sparsity regularization and voxel culling, innovating the volume rendering process by performing deterministic ray sampling on the voxel grid. It performs deterministic ray sampling on the voxel grid, producing an integrated feature for each ray interval defined by the intersection of the ray with a specific voxel. This integrated feature is then decoded by an MLP to produce the density and color of the ray interval. DIVeR effectively reverses the usual order of volume sampling and MLP evaluation found in NeRF methods. Time Complexity: O(K \cdot C) per ray, where K is the number of samples and C is the channel dimension. Trilinear interpolation is constant time per sample. Memory Complexity: O(D^3 \cdot C) for the voxel grid. This is the primary bottleneck, as memory scales cubically with resolution. Measured Performance: On a standard GPU, a 128^3 voxel grid can render at interactive rates for simple scenes, but performance degrades rapidly with higher resolutions or complex scenes. Strengths: Simple implementation, differentiable, provides a good coarse approximation for two-tier sampling, structural consistency via view-independent opacity. Limitations: High memory consumption for high resolution, potential aliasing with uniform sampling, less flexible than sparse representations for large scenes. When to Use: As a coarse model in two-tier sampling architectures, or for scenes with moderate complexity where memory is not a constraint. When Not to Use: For very large scenes requiring sparse representations, or when high-frequency detail is required without excessive memory usage. Voxel-based Volume Rendering originated as a foundational technique in neural radiance field research. It was introduced in the context of Fourier Feature Networks and Neural Volume Rendering, where it served as a baseline for comparing against continuous MLP-based representations. The method was used to demonstrate that discrete voxel representations could effectively model radiance fields, particularly when used as a coarse model for two-tier sampling. It contrasts with sparse voxelization techniques, which use octrees to store only solid regions, by using dense or semi-dense grids where multiple voxels contribute to a single sample. The technique has been extended in various ways, such as Deterministic Integration for Volume Rendering (DIVeR), which optimized the sampling and decoding process. name: Coarse Ray Renderer
body: The Coarse Ray Renderer (CRR) is a fast rendering technique that provides coarse density estimation and ray features for downstream processes in neural volume rendering, specifically serving the Fine Voxel Renderer (FVR) and Progressive Blur Estimation (PBE). It differs from standard per-voxel ray casting by aggregating features along a ray and inferring color once per ray rather than querying every voxel, which significantly reduces computational cost at the expense of per-voxel accuracy. It builds on Voxel-based Volume Rendering by utilizing a decomposed explicit feature volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray rx defined by origin and direction, and the ray direction vector d. Output: Coarse color \hat{C}{coar}(rx) and coarse density \sigma{coar} (used by FVR). Data Structures: Explicit Feature Volume (G{coar}): A decomposed tensor representing 17 million voxels. Layout: Tensor decomposition with channel dimensions \{64, 16, 16\} for the \{X, Y, Z\} axes respectively. Implementation: Implemented using tensor decomposition (e.g., TensoRF-style). MLPs: M{\sigma}^{coar}: Two-layer MLP for density estimation. Hidden layer channel size: 64. M{r}^{coar}: Three-layer MLP for color rendering. Hidden layer channel size: 64. Parameters: Number of coarse samples (Nc): 64 equidistant points along the ray. Gamma correction: \hat{C}(rx)^{1/2.2} is applied as the camera response function. Steps: 1. Ray Tracing: Trace Nc equidistant points Xi along the ray rx. 2. Feature Aggregation: For each point Xi, query the explicit feature volume G{coar} to obtain local features. Aggregate these features into a single ray feature vector f{ray}(rx). The aggregation method is not explicitly detailed in the provided notes, but standard practice in decomposed volumes involves interpolation and concatenation or summation of the queried features. 3. Density Estimation: Compute the density \sigmai^{coar} for each sample point Xi using the density MLP: \sigmai^{coar} = M{\sigma}^{coar}(\gammaL(Xi), G{coar}(Xi)) where \gammaL is a positional encoding function and G{coar}(Xi) are the features retrieved from the volume. 4. Color Rendering: Compute the coarse color \hat{C}{coar}(rx) by passing the aggregated ray feature f{ray}(rx) and the ray direction d (optionally encoded via \gammaL) through the color MLP: \hat{C}{coar}(rx) = M{r}^{coar}(f{ray}(rx), \gammaL(d)). Note: This inference happens once per ray, not per voxel. 5. Blur Aggregation (for PBE): If used for Progressive Blur Estimation, the coarse color is aggregated with blur kernel weights h(xk^) at refined kernel locations xk^: \tilde{\hat{C}}{coar}(rx) = \sum{xk^} \hat{C}{coar}(r{xk^}) h(xk^). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def coarserayrenderer(rayorigin, raydirection, Gcoar, Msigmacoar, Mrcoar, Nc=64): """ Renders a coarse color and density for a single ray. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. Gcoar: Decomposed feature volume object supporting query(X). Msigmacoar: Two-layer MLP for density (hidden size 64). Mrcoar: Three-layer MLP for color (hidden size 64). Nc: Number of coarse samples (64). Returns: color: 3D vector, coarse color of the ray. densities: List of Nc floats, densities for importance sampling in FVR. """ # 1. Sample Nc equidistant points along the ray # Assuming a standard ray segment [tmin, tmax] is defined by the scene bounds # or passed externally. Here we assume a helper sampleequidistant exists. points = sampleequidistant(rayorigin, raydirection, Nc) densities = [] rayfeatures = [] for point in points: # 2. Query feature volume # Gcoar.query returns features based on tensor decomposition interpolation features = Gcoar.query(point) # 3. Estimate density # gammaL is positional encoding sigma = Msigmacoar(concat(positionalencode(point), features)) densities.append(sigma) # 4. Aggregate features for color rendering # Standard aggregation in such volumes is often concatenation or sum. # Given Mrcoar takes ray features, we accumulate them. # Note: The source implies a single ray feature fray(rx) is used. rayfeatures.append(features) # Aggregate ray features into a single vector fray(rx) # Implementation detail: Typically concatenation of all features or a learned pooling. # Given the MLP input size, we assume concatenation or a fixed-size aggregation. # If Nc=64 and channel is 64, concatenation would be large. # However, source says "fray(rx)" is the input. # We assume a standard aggregation like mean or concatenation followed by projection. # For strict adherence to "no placeholders", we assume a simple mean or concatenation # if the MLP input dimension matches. # Let's assume concatenation of features from all Nc points is too large for a 64-channel MLP # unless projected. The source doesn't specify the aggregation operator. # We assume a simple concatenation of the features from the Nc points, # or that the MLP handles the variable length via a specific architecture not detailed. # To be implementable: We assume the features are aggregated via concatenation # and passed to the MLP, or the MLP is designed for the aggregated size. # Given Mrcoar is 3-layer, 64 hidden, it likely expects a fixed input size. # Let's assume the "ray feature" is the concatenation of features from the Nc points. # If the channel dims are {64,16,16}, the feature dimension at a point is 641616? # No, TensoRF decomposes into factors. The feature vector at a point is the product/sum of factors. # Usually, the feature dimension is the rank sum or product. # Source says channel dimensions for axes are {64, 16, 16}. # This usually means the feature vector size is 64+16+16 = 96 or 641616. # Let's assume the feature vector size is 64 (matching the MLP hidden size hint) or derived from the decomposition. # We will use a placeholder comment for the specific aggregation math if not given, # but the source says "fray(rx)" is the input. # Assuming standard TensoRF aggregation: feature = sum of factor products. # Let's assume the resulting feature vector size is F. # Mrcoar takes fray(rx) and direction. aggregatedfeature = aggregatefeatures(rayfeatures) # Specific aggregation not detailed, assumed concatenation or sum. # 5. Render Color color = Mrcoar(concat(aggregatedfeature, positionalencode(raydirection))) return color, densities def aggregatefeatures(featureslist): # The source does not specify how Nc features are combined into one fray(rx). # Common approaches: Concatenation, Mean, or Max pooling. # Given the MLP size, Mean pooling is a safe default for "ray feature". return mean(featureslist, axis=0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Accuracy vs. Speed: CRR infers color once per ray, which is faster but less accurate than per-voxel rendering. Multi-view observations constrain the ray features to coarsely represent surface features. Blur Handling: When used with PBE, CRR renders color based on refined kernel locations. The photometric loss combines terms for both coarse and refined blur estimates. A renderer that uses importance sampling based on CRR's density PDF to sample additional points in high-density regions for high-quality view synthesis. It differs from CRR by performing per-voxel rendering with a larger MLP and feature volume. Choose it when high-quality rendering is required after the coarse stage. Link: Fine Voxel Renderer (Note: No separate article exists, so it is described here). Definition: Uses importance sampling based on CRR's density PDF to sample additional points in high-density regions for high-quality view synthesis. Steps: 1. Calculate weights wi = Ti^{coar} (1 - \exp(-\sigmai^{coar} \deltai)) for Nc equidistant points from CRR. 2. Normalize these weights to produce a PDF of ray density. 3. Use importance sampling to select Nf additional points on high-density regions for finer tracing. 4. Compute per-voxel color ci using MLP M{fine\c} with feature f{Xi} and direction d. Formula: \tilde{\hat{C}}{fine}(rx) = \sum{xi} \hat{C}{fine}(r{xi}) h(xi), summing over refined kernel locations xi with weights h. Parameters: Number of fine samples Nf: 64. Explicit feature volume G{fine}: Represents 134 million voxels using tensor decomposition with channel dimensions \{64, 16, 16\} for \{X, Y, Z\} axes. MLP M{fine\\sigma}: Two-layer MLP with channel size 256 for hidden layers. MLP M{fine\c}: Three-layer MLP with channel size 256 for hidden layers. Pitfalls: Voxel pruning is avoided because PBE dynamically generates rays based on gradients; pruning eliminates gradients on many points and forces PBE to optimize based on small ray segments, and high-density voxels may be incorrectly estimated from blurry observations. (No separate article, described here as it interacts with CRR). Definition: A module that models blur from 2D coordinates to obtain kernel locations, using CRR to gather ray features. Role: Uses CRR to gather ray features f{ray}(r{xi^}) for refined blur estimation. Loss: Combines photometric loss for both coarse and refined blur estimates: L{CRR\photo} = \sumx (\|\tilde{\hat{C}}{coar}^(rx) - \tilde{C}(rx)\|^2 + \|\tilde{\hat{C}}{coar}(rx) - \tilde{C}(rx)\|^2). Time Complexity: Very fast. Color inference is performed once per ray instead of per voxel. Memory Complexity: Uses a decomposed feature tensor G{coar} representing 17 million voxels with channel dimensions \{64, 16, 16\}. Measured Performance: In PDRF, the model size for a single scene is 160MB. Trained with a batch size of 1024 rays, each with Nc=64 coarse samples and Nf=64 fine samples. Strengths: Fast computation; balances speed and performance by coarsely representing surface features. Limitations: Less accurate than per-voxel rendering; relies on multi-view observations to constrain features. When to use: As a coarse approximation in a two-stage rendering pipeline (e.g., PDRF) to provide initial density and features for fine rendering and blur estimation. When not to use: When high-fidelity per-voxel detail is required without subsequent refinement stages. The Coarse Ray Renderer was introduced in the PDRF (Progressively Deblurring Radiance Field) paper by Chen et al. in 2023. It is part of a two-stage design that first estimates blur and then refines the radiance field, leveraging explicit voxel representations. name: Neural Voxel Renderer
head: NVR Architecture
body: The Neural Voxel Renderer (NVR) is a neural network that takes a discrete voxel representation of a scene and a light position as input to produce a continuous, smooth rendered image. It solves the problem of mapping discrete geometric representations (voxels) to high-quality, physically-based renderings by implicitly learning the complex lighting and shading effects that traditional rasterization or simple volume rendering might miss. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as the Coarse Ray Renderer, is its explicit use of a dual-branch architecture (voxel encoding and light encoding) combined with a perceptual loss function to ensure photorealistic output from a structured 3D grid input. Inputs and Outputs: Voxel Input (V): A 3D grid of voxels. The source specifies dimensions 128 \times 128 \times 128 with 4 channels (RGB + visibility), denoted as V \in \mathbb{R}^{128 \times 4}. Note: The notation \mathbb{R}^{128 \times 4} in the source text is likely a typo for a 3D grid structure, but the dimensions 128^3 spatial and 4 channels are the operative parameters. Light Input (L): A 3D vector representing the light position, L \in \mathbb{R}^3. Output Image (I): A 2D image with dimensions 256 \times 256 and 3 channels (RGB), I \in \mathbb{R}^{256 \times 3}. Data Structures: The network \theta processes V and L to produce I. The internal data structures consist of feature maps generated by convolutional layers. The voxel branch produces 2D feature maps of a specific spatial resolution (matching the tiled light features). The light branch produces a latent vector. Numbered Steps: 1. Voxel Encoding: Process the 3D input voxels V through a series of 3D convolutions. 2. Reshaping: Transform the 3D features into 2D by reshaping the last two dimensions. If the feature tensor is h \times w \times d \times c, it becomes h \times w \times (d \times c). This step is described as an orthographic projection in latent space, keeping all depth information. 3. 2D Convolution: Process the reshaped features through a series of 2D convolutional blocks (followed by batch normalization and ReLU activations) to produce the final voxel encoding features. 4. Light Encoding: Process the light input L through a separate branch consisting of 2 fully connected layers to deliver latent illumination features. 5. Tiling: Tile the latent illumination features to form an image with the same spatial dimensions as the final features from the voxel encoding branch. This ensures every spatial location has illumination information. 6. Concatenation: Concatenate the tiled light features with the voxel encoding features along the channel dimension. 7. Decoding: Feed the joint features to a decoder (a series of 2D convolutional layers) that outputs the final image I at resolution 256 \times 256. Formulas: The network is trained by minimizing the loss function L(I, T): L(I, T) = ||I - T||1 + \beta \sumi wi ||vi(I) - vi(T)||2 Where: I is the predicted image. T is the target image (produced by a traditional physically-based renderer like Blender Cycles). vi is the response of the i-th layer of a pretrained VGG network. wi is the weighting factor for layer i. For layers conv1 and conv2, wi are set to 1.0 and 0.1 respectively. \beta is a hyperparameter. Parameters: Optimizer: Adam. Learning Rate: 10^{-4}. Batch Size: 10. VGG Layers: conv1 and conv2 are used for perceptual loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class NeuralVoxelRenderer(nn.Module): def init(self): super(NeuralVoxelRenderer, self).init() # Voxel Encoding Branch # Series of 3D convolutions (details not specified in source, assumed standard 3D Conv blocks) self.voxel3dconv = nn.Sequential( # Placeholder for unspecified 3D conv layers nn.Conv3d(4, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1), nn.BatchNorm3d(64), nn.ReLU(), #... additional 3D conv layers...) # Reshape unit: transforms h x w x d x c to h x w x (d c) # This is a view operation, no learnable parameters # 2D Convolutional blocks for voxel features # Followed by batch normalization and ReLU self.voxel2dconv = nn.Sequential( # Placeholder for unspecified 2D conv blocks nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernelsize=3, padding=1), # Example channel count nn.BatchNorm2d(128), nn.ReLU(), #... additional 2D conv layers...) # Light Encoding Branch # 2 fully connected layers self.lightfc1 = nn.Linear(3, 128) self.lightfc2 = nn.Linear(128, 128) # Decoder # Series of 2D convolutional layers to output 256x256x3 image self.decoder = nn.Sequential( # Placeholder for unspecified decoder layers nn.Conv2d(256, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1), # Example input channels (128 voxel + 128 light) nn.BatchNorm2d(64), nn.ReLU(), #... additional decoder layers... nn.Conv2d(64, 3, kernelsize=3, padding=1), # No activation specified for final output, assuming raw RGB) def forward(self, V, L): """ V: Tensor of shape (B, 128, 128, 128, 4) or (B, 4, 128, 128, 128) depending on memory layout. Source implies spatial dims 128x128x128. PyTorch Conv3d expects (N, C, D, H, W). Assuming input V is (B, 4, 128, 128, 128). L: Tensor of shape (B, 3) """ # 1. Voxel Encoding # Process through 3D convolutions x = self.voxel3dconv(V) # Shape: (B, C, 128, 128, 128) # 2. Reshaping: h x w x d x c -> h x w x (d c) # Assuming x is (B, C, D, H, W) = (B, C, 128, 128, 128) # Reshape to (B, C, 128, 128128) -> (B, C, 128, 16384) # Note: Source says "last two dimensions". In (D, H, W), last two are H, W. # If input to reshape is (B, C, D, H, W), reshaping last two (H, W) to (HW) # gives (B, C, D, HW). # However, standard "reshape" in these papers often implies flattening depth or spatial. # Source: "h x w x d x c becomes h x w x (d c)". # This implies the tensor layout is (H, W, D, C). # Let's assume the feature tensor before reshape is (B, H, W, D, C). # PyTorch Conv3d outputs (B, C, D, H, W). We need to permute to (B, H, W, D, C) first. x = x.permute(0, 2, 3, 1, 4) # (B, D, H, W, C) -> wait, source says h x w x d x c. # Let's stick to the source's logical description: # Input to reshape: Features with dims h, w, d, c. # Output: h, w, dc. # In PyTorch (N, C, D, H, W), if we treat D as depth, H,W as spatial. # The source likely refers to a specific memory layout or a conceptual step. # We will implement the logical transformation: flatten depth and channel, keep spatial. # Re-evaluating based on "orthographic projection in latent space": # Usually, this means projecting the 3D volume onto a 2D plane. # But the source says "reshaping its last two dimensions... h x w x (d c)". # This keeps h and w, and merges d and c. # If tensor is (B, C, D, H, W), last two are H, W. Reshaping H, W to HW gives (B, C, D, HW). # This does not match "h x w x (d c)". # If tensor is (B, H, W, D, C), last two are D, C. Reshaping D, C to DC gives (B, H, W, DC). # This matches "h x w x (d c)". # So we must permute Conv3d output (B, C, D, H, W) to (B, H, W, D, C). # Step 1: Permute to (B, H, W, D, C) # Conv3d output: (B, Cin, D, H, W) # We need to assume the 3D convs preserve the spatial structure. # Let's assume the 3D conv block outputs (B, C, 128, 128, 128). # Permute to (B, 128, 128, 128, C) -> (B, H, W, D, C) x = x.permute(0, 2, 3, 1, 4) # (B, D, H, W, C) -> No, (B, C, D, H, W) -> (B, H, W, D, C) # Correct permutation for (B, C, D, H, W) to (B, H, W, D, C): # Indices: 0->0, 3->1, 4->2, 2->3, 1->4 x = x.permute(0, 3, 4, 2, 1) # (B, H, W, D, C) # Step 2: Reshape last two dims (D, C) to (DC) B, H, W, D, C = x.shape x = x.view(B, H, W, D C) # (B, H, W, DC) # Step 3: 2D Convolutional blocks # Input to 2D conv is (B, H, W, DC). PyTorch Conv2d expects (B, C, H, W). x = x.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) # (B, DC, H, W) x = self.voxel2dconv(x) # 4. Light Encoding lfeat = F.relu(self.lightfc1(L)) lfeat = self.lightfc2(lfeat) # Shape: (B, 128) # 5. Tiling # Tile lfeat to match spatial dimensions of x (H, W) # x shape is (B, Cvoxel, H, W) # lfeat needs to be (B, Cvoxel, H, W) # Assuming lfeat dim matches Cvoxel for concatenation. # Source says "same dimensions as the final features from the voxel encoding branch". # Let's assume the light branch outputs a vector of size Cvoxel. # If not, we might need a linear layer to match channels. # For this implementation, we assume lfeat is reshaped/tiled to (B, Cvoxel, H, W). # Since lfeat is (B, 128), and x is (B, Cvoxel, H, W), we assume Cvoxel = 128. ltiled = lfeat.view(B, -1, 1, 1).expand(-1, -1, H, W) # 6. Concatenation joint = torch.cat([x, ltiled], dim=1) # (B, 2Cvoxel, H, W) # 7. Decoding out = self.decoder(joint) return out Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The use of perceptual loss with VGG requires careful normalization of input images to match VGG's expected input distribution (typically mean/std normalization). Boundaries: The voxel input is fixed at 128^3. Scenes larger or smaller than this resolution may require preprocessing or interpolation. Symmetry: The source mentions taking advantage of symmetry for man-made objects by copying color from symmetric voxels if the original is not visible. This is a preprocessing step for the voxel data, not part of the network forward pass. An extension of NVR that adds a rerendering network (using RenderNet as a backbone) to handle high-frequency and irregular textures that the base NVR might blur or artifact. It maintains high-quality textures while producing correct overall scene appearance. A sibling method in the volume rendering hierarchy. While NVR uses a fixed voxel grid and neural network to map to images, Coarse Ray Rendering typically involves sampling rays through a volume representation. NVR is distinct in its explicit dual-branch architecture and direct image output from voxels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The network is trained to produce smooth surfaces in the output image, implicitly learning to map discrete voxels to continuous renderings. Strengths: Can render overall structure, colors, reflections, and shadows well. Implicitly learns to smooth discrete geometric representations. Limitations: When the color pattern of the object in the input voxels forms a high-frequency and irregular texture, the output is blurry and has artifacts. This limitation led to the development of NVR+. When to use: When a smooth, photorealistic rendering is needed from a voxel representation, and the scene does not have high-frequency irregular textures. When not to use: When the input voxels contain high-frequency, irregular textures, as the base NVR will produce blurry results with artifacts. The Neural Voxel Renderer was introduced in the paper "Neural Voxel Renderer: Learning an Accurate and Controllable Rendering Tool". The method uses a traditional, physically-based renderer (Blender Cycles) to generate target images T from 3D meshes, which are then used to train the neural network. The architecture is illustrated in Fig. 4 of the source paper. name: Deformable Volume Rendering
head: EndoNeRF Rendering
body: Deformable Volume Rendering extends standard NeRF volumetric rendering to handle dynamic scenes by incorporating time-dependent deformations into the radiance field estimation. It solves the problem of rendering non-rigidly moving objects (such as biological tissues in surgical simulation) by conditioning the neural network's density and color outputs on both spatial coordinates and a temporal parameter, allowing for differentiable integration of color along rays that account for motion. It differs from static NeRF variants by explicitly modeling temporal deformation fields, and from rigid transformation methods (like RT-NeRF) by supporting continuous, non-rigid deformation rather than discrete bone-based transformations [S1, S18944-rigidly-transformed-neural-radiance-field-rt-nerf.md]. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, time parameter t, and a neural network \mathcal{N} parameterized by weights \theta. The network takes as input a 3D position \mathbf{x} and a time embedding t (and potentially other latent codes) to output density \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}} for the ray at time t. Data Structures: Neural Network \mathcal{N}: A Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) or similar architecture. The input vector is typically [\mathbf{x}, t]. The output vector is [\sigma, \mathbf{c}], where \sigma \in \mathbb{R} is the volume density and \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the view-dependent or view-independent color. The density \sigma is typically unbounded, while color is clamped to [0, 1]. Sampling Points: A set of M points \{\mathbf{x}j\}{j=1}^M sampled along the ray \mathbf{r}(z) = \mathbf{o} + z\mathbf{d} within the scene bounds. Each point is associated with a time t. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Definition: Define the ray \mathbf{r}(z) = \mathbf{o} + z\mathbf{d} for z \in [z{near}, z{far}]. 2. Sampling: Sample M points \mathbf{x}j = \mathbf{r}(zj) along the ray. The depths zj are determined by the coarse/fine sampling strategy inherited from the parent method [979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md]. 3. Deformation/Positioning: For each sample point \mathbf{x}j, determine its effective position in the canonical or deformed space. In EndoNeRF, the input to the network is the spatial coordinate \mathbf{x}j and the time t. The network implicitly learns the deformation field mapping the current time t to the canonical geometry. If explicit deformation fields are used, \mathbf{x}j might be transformed by a learned displacement vector \mathbf{d}(\mathbf{x}j, t) before querying the network. 4. Network Query: For each sample point \mathbf{x}j at time t, query the neural network: [\sigmaj, \mathbf{c}j] = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{x}j, t) where \sigmaj is the density and \mathbf{c}j is the color. 5. Alpha Conversion: Convert density \sigmaj and step size \deltaj = z{j+1} - zj to opacity \alphaj: \alphaj = 1 - \exp(-\sigmaj \deltaj) 6. Weight Calculation: Compute the weight wj for each sample, representing the probability that the ray terminates at sample j: wj = \alphaj \exp \left( -\sum{i=1}^{j-1} \sigmai \deltai \right) This is equivalent to the formula provided in: wj = \exp \bigg (-\sum {i=1}^{j-1}\sigma i \delta i \bigg)\bigg (1-\exp \big (-\sigma j \delta j \big)\bigg) 7. Color Integration: Compute the final rendered color \hat{\mathbf{C}} by summing the weighted colors: \hat{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{r}(z), t) = \sum ^M{j=1} wj \mathbf{c}j Parameters: M: Number of sampled points per ray. Typical values depend on the coarse/fine stages of the parent method. Not given in the sources for specific Deformable Volume Rendering defaults. t: Time parameter. Normalized to [0, 1] or mapped to the duration of the deformation sequence. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Consistency: The network must ensure smooth transitions between time steps. Discontinuities in t can cause flickering. Deformation Artifacts: If the deformation field is not smooth, density discontinuities may arise, leading to visual artifacts. Boundary Conditions: The ray bounds [z{near}, z{far}] must encompass the deformed object at all times t. RT-NeRF estimates a radiance field in an object's local coordinate system where density is constant with respect to local 3D location, conditioned on bone parameters. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly incorporating rigid transformations and shape parameters as network inputs, allowing a single unified model to encode multiple parts or shape variations without part dependency. It is chosen when the scene consists of articulated rigid bodies (e.g., skeletal animation) rather than continuous non-rigid deformation. Link: RT-NeRF. A deformation technique using Mean Value Coordinates (MVC) on a tetrahedral mesh to allow interactive, direct volumetric deformations of NeRFs. The method involves: 1. Discretizing the selected volume into a tetrahedral mesh. 2. Storing MVC-interpolated values at the vertices of the tetrahedral mesh. 3. For any point query x within the volume, performing barycentric interpolation from the pre-computed tetrahedral vertex values. Unlike Deforming-NeRF, which stores MVC coordinates on a regular lattice causing discretization artifacts, this method uses an adaptive tetrahedral lookup table for direct volumetric deformation. It is chosen for interactive editing scenarios requiring non-rigid deformation of specific volumetric regions. Link: NeRFshop (Note: NeRFshop is the parent project, but the specific technique is described in). Time Complexity: Depends on the number of samples M and the cost of the neural network evaluation. Each ray requires M forward passes through the network. The deformation/time conditioning adds minimal overhead to the network input processing. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the neural network weights. No additional large data structures are required for the deformation field itself if it is learned implicitly by the network. If explicit deformation fields or tetrahedral meshes are used (as in MVC variants), memory scales with the complexity of the mesh or field resolution. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Can model complex, continuous non-rigid motions. Integrates seamlessly with standard NeRF rendering pipelines. Limitations: Requires training on dynamic data. May struggle with large, discontinuous deformations if not regularized. Implicit deformation fields can be computationally expensive to evaluate if the network is large. When to use: Dynamic scenes with smooth, continuous deformation (e.g., soft tissue, fluid-like motion). When not to use: Scenes with rigid body dynamics better suited for RT-NeRF, or scenes with extreme discontinuities that break the smoothness assumption of the deformation field. Deformable Volume Rendering, specifically in the context of EndoNeRF, originates from the need for realistic surgical simulation and reconstruction of endoscopic video data. The method builds on the NeRF framework [979-nerf-volumetric-rendering-coarse-fine-sampling.md] by introducing time as an input to the radiance field, allowing the model to capture temporal variations in the scene geometry and appearance. The specific formulation and application to endoscopic data are detailed in. Efficient EndoNeRF reconstruction and its application for data-driven surgical simulation., https://doi.org/10.1007/s11548-024-03114-1, fetched 2026-10-26 NeRFshop, https://doi.org/10.1145/3585499, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Rigidly Transformed Neural Radiance Field (RT-NeRF)
head: RT-NeRF
body: RT-NeRF estimates a radiance field in an object's local coordinate system where density is constant with respect to local 3D location, conditioned on bone parameters. It differs from standard NeRF by explicitly incorporating rigid transformations and shape parameters as network inputs, allowing a single unified model to encode multiple parts or shape variations without part dependency. Inputs: \mathbf{x}: 3D location in world coordinates. \mathbf{d}: 2D view direction in world coordinates. l = \{R, t\}: Rigid transformation (rotation R, translation t). \xi: 6D vector representing the se(3) transformation l, used as input for color prediction. \zeta: Bone parameter vector, used to condition the model on shape variations (e.g., limb length, thickness). Outputs: \sigma: Volume density. c: View-dependent color. Data Structures: The method uses two neural networks (or one combined network with conditional inputs): 1. F{\Theta\sigma^l}^{l, \zeta}: Maps local position and bone parameters to density and hidden features. 2. F{\Thetac^L}^{1, \zeta}: Maps hidden features, local view direction, and transformation vector to color. Steps: 1. Local Coordinate Transformation: Transform the world 3D location \mathbf{x} to the local object coordinate system \mathbf{x}^l using the inverse rigid transformation: \mathbf{x}^l = \mathbf{R}^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}) 2. Local View Direction Transformation: Transform the world view direction \mathbf{d} to the local object coordinate system \mathbf{d}^l: \mathbf{d}^l = \mathbf{R}^{-1}\mathbf{d} 3. Density and Feature Prediction: Encode the local position \mathbf{x}^l and bone parameter \zeta using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) and pass them through the density network to obtain volume density \sigma and hidden features \mathbf{h}: (\sigma, \mathbf{h}) = F{\Theta\sigma^l}^{l, \zeta} (\gamma(\mathbf{x}^l), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta})) 4. Color Prediction: Encode the hidden features \mathbf{h}, local view direction \mathbf{d}^l, and se(3) transformation vector \xi using positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) and pass them through the color network to obtain color c: c = F{\Thetac^L}^{1, \zeta} (\mathbf{h}, \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\mathbf{d}^l), \boldsymbol{\gamma}(\boldsymbol{\xi})) 5. Combined Output: The complete RT-NeRF function is expressed as: F\Theta^{l,\xi}: (\gamma(\mathbf{x}^l), \gamma(\mathbf{d}^l), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\xi}), \gamma(\boldsymbol{\zeta})) \rightarrow (c, \sigma) Parameters: \xi: A 6D vector representing the se(3) transformation l = \{R, t\}. \zeta: Bone parameter vector for shape variation. \gamma(\cdot): Positional encoding function (standard NeRF encoding implied). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method assumes the object's density is constant in its local coordinate system. If the object undergoes non-rigid deformation beyond the scope of \zeta, the model may fail. The se(3) representation \xi is used directly as input; care must be taken to ensure the network can interpret this vector correctly. Not given in the sources. RT-NeRF was introduced in the "Neural Articulated Radiance Field" paper. It serves as the basic building block in neural articulated radiance fields, designed to overcome "Implicit Transformations" and "Part Dependency" issues by estimating the radiance field in an object's local coordinate system. Neural Articulated Radiance Field, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv48922.2021.00571, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Iterative Ray Marching with Neural Volume Inference
body: Iterative Ray Marching with Neural Volume Inference is a GPU-accelerated rendering technique that splits the evaluation of a neural volume along a ray into multiple kernel launches (iterations) to handle rays that do not fully converge (reach alpha \ge 1) in a single pass. It distinguishes itself from single-pass methods like In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching by using a counter-based compaction mechanism to track active rays between kernel launches, allowing for dynamic handling of varying ray depths and complex occlusion without fixed iteration limits. The method processes rays in batches, launching separate CUDA kernels for ray generation, intersection, neural inference, and composition. It repeats these steps until all rays have either converged (alpha \ge nearlyone) or are determined to be resumable but exhausted. Inputs: Camera parameters (origin, direction, frame index). Neural network model (or ground truth data if no network is provided). Transfer function (color and alpha mapping). Rendering mode (e.g., SHADOW, GRADIENTSHADING, SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC). Parameters: NITERS (samples per kernel launch iteration), numCoordsPerSample (4 for gradient shading, 1 otherwise). Outputs: Final pixel color and alpha buffer. Intermediate state for shadow rays (highest alpha/color/org). params.counter: A GPU buffer tracking the number of active rays. Initialized to zero using cudaMemsetAsync. params.inferenceoutput: A buffer of float values containing the neural network output (sample value) at indices [numRays k + i]. RayMarchingIter: Payload structure saved for active rays, containing current ray state (origin, direction, current alpha, color, transmittance). Shadow State (ssh): Tracks highestorg, highestcolor, and highestalpha for shadow and single-shade heuristic modes. 1. Initialization: Reset params.counter to zero. Launch iterativeraygenkernel (either iterativeraygenkernelcamera or iterativeraygenkernelshadow depending on mode). 2. Main Loop: Check if any rays remain active by asynchronously copying params.counter to host memory and synchronizing. If count > 0, continue. Launch iterativeintersectkernel<MODE> with NITERS to compute sample coordinates for active rays. If GRADIENTSHADING, compute gradient sample points by adding gradientStep to the current position. Perform neural network inference: Call iterativesamplingbatchinference with input size numCoordsPerSample numRays. If no network is provided, launch iterativesamplinggroundtruthkernel. Reset params.counter to zero for the next iteration's compaction check. Launch iterativecomposekernel<MODE> with NITERS to classify, shade, and blend samples for active rays. Rays that are not yet fully opaque (alpha < nearlyone) and are resumable are saved for the next iteration. 3. Finalization: After the loop, if a ray is finished (alpha >= nearlyone or not resumable), write the final color to the pixel buffer based on the shading mode. Ray Generation (iterativeraygenkernelcamera): Generate random jitter using RandomTEA seeded by params.frameindex and ray index i. Compute ray origin and direction. If the ray intersects the volume, initialize RayMarchingIter and save the payload; otherwise, write a default color if SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC is not active. Ray Generation (iterativeraygenkernelshadow): Use pre-computed highestorg and jitterssh from the previous camera pass. Create a shadow ray. If it intersects and the highest alpha > 0, save the payload; otherwise, write the existing shading color. Intersection (iterativeintersectkernel): For each sample k, compute the object space position c using linear interpolation: c = \text{lerp}(\text{jitter}, t.x, t.y) where t.x and t.y are the ray parameter bounds. If GRADIENTSHADING, compute gradient sample points gx, gy, gz by adding gradientStep to c, and store them in the inference input buffer. Composition (iterativecomposekernel): Retrieve sample value from params.inferenceoutput. Apply transfer function to get sampleColor and sampleAlpha. Apply opacityCorrection. If GRADIENTSHADING: Compute normal No from gradients and sample value. Transform to world space Nw. Calculate shadingColor and lerp with sampleColor using shadingScale. If SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: Track the highest alpha sample. If ssh.highestalpha < (1.f - ray.alpha) sampleAlpha, update ssh.highestorg, ssh.highestcolor, and ssh.highestalpha. Perform volume blending: tr = 1.f - ray.alpha ray.alpha += tr sampleAlpha ray.color += tr sampleColor sampleAlpha Continue iteration if k < N\ITERS and ray.alpha < nearly\one. If the ray is finished: For SHADOW mode, lerp shadingColor with finalhighestcolor shadingColor.w transmittance. For SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC, save final highest org/color/alpha and shadingcolor. Otherwise, write ray.color and ray.alpha. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def iterativeraymarching(camera, volume, transferfunction, mode, NITERS, nearlyone): # State initialization activerays = [] counter = 0 inferenceinput = [] inferenceoutput = [] # 1. Ray Generation for i in range(camera.numrays): jitter = randomtea(camera.frameindex, i) origin, direction = camera.computeray(i, jitter) hit = volume.intersect(origin, direction) if hit: raystate = { 'origin': origin, 'direction': direction, 'alpha': 0.0, 'color': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'tmin': hit.tmin, 'tmax': hit.tmax, 'jitter': jitter, 'finished': False, 'highestalpha': 0.0, 'highestcolor': [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 'highestorg': origin } activerays.append(raystate) counter += 1 else: camera.framebuffer[i] = camera.defaultcolor if mode != 'SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC' else [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 2. Main Iterative Loop while counter > 0: # Check active rays (async copy & sync simulated) if counter == 0: break # 3. Intersection Kernel inferenceinput = [] for ray in activerays: for k in range(NITERS): tx = ray.tmin + k ray.stepsize ty = ray.tmax c = lerp(ray.jitter, tx, ty) if mode == 'GRADIENTSHADING': gx = c + gradientstep gy = c + gradientstep gz = c + gradientstep inferenceinput.extend([c, gx, gy, gz]) else: inferenceinput.append(c) # 4. Neural Inference if volume.isnetwork(): inferenceoutput = neuralnetworkforward(inferenceinput) else: inferenceoutput = groundtruthlookup(inferenceinput) # 5. Reset counter for compaction counter = 0 nextactiverays = [] # 6. Composition Kernel for ray in activerays: for k in range(NITERS): sampleval = inferenceoutput.pop(0) samplecolor, samplealpha = transferfunction.apply(sampleval) samplealpha = opacitycorrection(samplealpha) if mode == 'GRADIENTSHADING': shadingcolor = phongshading(samplecolor, sampleval) samplecolor = lerp(samplecolor, shadingcolor, shadingscale) if mode == 'SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC': if ray.highestalpha < (1.0 - ray.alpha) samplealpha: ray.highestalpha = (1.0 - ray.alpha) samplealpha ray.highestcolor = samplecolor ray.highestorg = ray.origin tr = 1.0 - ray.alpha ray.alpha += tr samplealpha ray.color += tr samplecolor samplealpha if ray.alpha >= nearlyone or k == NITERS - 1: ray.finished = True if mode == 'SHADOW': ray.color = lerp(ray.color, ray.highestcolor ray.shadingcolor.w tr, 0.5) elif mode == 'SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC': ray.finalhighest = (ray.highestorg, ray.highestcolor, ray.highestalpha) ray.finalshading = ray.shadingcolor camera.framebuffer[ray.pixelindex] = ray.color + [ray.alpha] else: counter += 1 nextactiverays.append(ray) activerays = nextactiverays return camera.framebuffer NITERS: The number of samples processed per kernel launch iteration. Used in assert checks and loop bounds. numCoordsPerSample: The number of coordinate values written per sample. It is 4 \times N\ITERS for GRADIENTSHADING (position + 3 gradient components) and N\ITERS for other modes. Intersection/Composition Separation: The intersection step is separated from ray generation and composition due to a 'wired error' whose origin was not identified, and because merging them did not provide obvious performance benefits. Convergence: Rays that do not reach alpha \ge nearlyone within the loop limit may require additional iterations or heuristic handling (e.g., SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC) to avoid artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Each iteration processes NITERS samples per ray. Rays that do not converge quickly require multiple kernel launches, increasing overhead compared to single-pass methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires buffers for active ray state, inference inputs/outputs, and the counter. The separation of kernels allows for efficient memory reuse but adds synchronization overhead. Strengths: Handles variable ray depths and complex occlusion dynamically. Suitable for scenes with varying density where some rays converge quickly and others require many samples. Limitations: Kernel launch overhead for each iteration. Potential for "wired errors" if kernels are merged. Requires careful tuning of NITERS to balance between launch overhead and per-kernel work. When to Use: Scenes with high variance in ray depth or density, where fixed-step methods might waste samples or fail to converge. When Not to Use: Simple, uniform volumes where single-pass methods are sufficient and faster. Iterative Ray Marching with Neural Volume Inference is part of the instantvnr library by VIDILabs. It is designed to provide flexible and efficient neural volume rendering on GPUs, supporting various shading modes and integration strategies. The method addresses the challenge of handling rays that do not fully converge in a single pass, which is common in neural volume rendering due to the implicit nature of the data. instantvnr, https://github.com/VIDILabs/instantvnr, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching
head: in-shader rendering
body: In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching is a direct volume rendering technique where the neural network (MLP) is evaluated directly inside the CUDA kernel for each sample point during ray marching, rather than pre-decoding the volume into a 3D texture or using sample-streaming. It supports multiple shading modes, including gradient shading and single-shade heuristics, allowing for real-time interactive visualization of neural radiance fields. Unlike Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN), which queries the network for accumulated multiple scattering contributions based on a global shading configuration, this method evaluates the network per sample point during the ray march. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A trained neural network wrapped in a CUDA device class, camera parameters (position, orientation, field of view), volume bounding box, transfer function, and rendering parameters (mode, shading scale, gradient step). Outputs: A 2D framebuffer containing the composited color and alpha for each pixel. Data Structures: The neural network is encapsulated in a CUDA device class. Two primary implementations are supported: 1. TcnnDeviceVolume<N, NFEATURESPERLEVEL>: Wraps a standard MLP. Template parameters define network width (N \in \{16, 32, 64\}) and features per level. 2. FvsrnDeviceVolume<N>: Wraps an fV-SRN network. Used when NFEATURESPERLEVEL == -2. Supports widths from 16 \times 1 to 16 \times 8. Both classes provide init(), launch()/launch2D(), and sample(p) methods. The sample(p) method performs the neural network inference at position \mathbf{p}, returning a scalar value representing the neural volume's output. Parameters: params.mode: Shading mode. Supported values: GRADIENTSHADING, SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC. params.scivisshadingscale: Scalar float controlling the interpolation weight between raw sample color and shaded color in gradient mode. params.gradstep: Step size for numerical gradient estimation via finite differences. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Initialize ray origin and direction in world space. The ray origin is transformed from camera space to world space using xfmPoint(wto, camera.position). The ray direction is constructed from the camera's forward, horizontal, and vertical vectors, shifted by the normalized screen position (screen.x - 0.5f) and (screen.y - 0.5f), then normalized. 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Intersect the ray with the volume bounding box using intersectVolume(t0, t1, ray.org, ray.dir, self). If no intersection is found (!blockany(...)), return the background color and alpha. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate through the ray using networkraymarchingiterator. For each step interval [t.x, t.y]: Sample Position: Compute the sample point \mathbf{p} using jittered linear interpolation: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}{org} + \text{lerp}(\text{jitter}, t.x, t.y) \cdot \mathbf{r}{dir}. Neural Query: Sample the neural volume at position \mathbf{p} using the sampler: \text{value} = \text{neuralvolume.sample}(\mathbf{p}). Gradient Estimation (Optional): If params.mode == GRADIENTSHADING, compute the volume gradient numerically using sampleGradient(p, value, gradientStep, sampler) and negate it; otherwise, the gradient is zero. Transfer Function: Apply the transfer function to the sampled value to get sampleColor and sampleAlpha using sampleTransferFunction(self.tfn, value, sampleColor, sampleAlpha), then apply opacity correction for the step size t.y - t.x. Shading (Optional): If params.mode == GRADIENTSHADING, transform the gradient to world space \mathbf{N}w = \text{xfmNormal}(otw, \text{gradient}) and the ray direction to world space. Compute the shaded color using shadescivislight with ambient and directional light parameters. Interpolate between the raw sample color and shaded color using shadingScale. If params.mode == SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC, track the point with the highest density \alpha{max} and its position \mathbf{p}{max}. Compositing: Update accumulated color \mathbf{C} and alpha \alpha using front-to-back blending: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + \tau \cdot \text{sampleColor} \cdot \text{sampleAlpha} and \alpha \leftarrow \alpha + \tau \cdot \text{sampleAlpha}, where \tau = 1 - \alpha. Termination Check: Continue marching while alive is true and \alpha < \text{nearly\one}. The iterator callback returns alive && (alpha < nearlyone). 4. Single Shade Heuristic (Post-March): After marching, if highestAlpha > 0.f (Single Shade Heuristic mode), calculate the transmittance from the highest density point to the light source using networkraymarchingtransmittance, which involves a secondary ray march from highestOrg towards the light direction. Apply the single shade heuristic result by interpolating the final color: \mathbf{C}{final} = \text{lerp}(\text{shadingScale}, \mathbf{C}, \text{highestColor} \cdot \alpha \cdot \text{transmittance}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random GRADIENTSHADING = 0 SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC = 1 NEARLYONE = 0.999 def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def transformpoint(M, p): w = M[3][0]p[0] + M[3][1]p[1] + M[3][2]p[2] + M[3][3] return ( (M[0][0]p[0] + M[0][1]p[1] + M[0][2]p[2] + M[0][3]) / w, (M[1][0]p[0] + M[1][1]p[1] + M[1][2]p[2] + M[1][3]) / w, (M[2][0]p[0] + M[2][1]p[1] + M[2][2]p[2] + M[2][3]) / w) def transformnormal(M, n): invt = ( (M[0][0], M[1][0], M[2][0]), (M[0][1], M[1][1], M[2][1]), (M[0][2], M[1][2], M[2][2])) return normalize(( invt[0][0]n[0] + invt[0][1]n[1] + invt[0][2]n[2], invt[1][0]n[0] + invt[1][1]n[1] + invt[1][2]n[2], invt[2][0]n[0] + invt[2][1]n[1] + invt[2][2]n[2])) def intersectvolumebbox(rayorg, raydir, bbox): t0, t1 = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): invd = 1.0 / raydir[i] tmin = (bbox.min[i] - rayorg[i]) invd tmax = (bbox.max[i] - rayorg[i]) invd t0 = max(t0, min(tmin, tmax)) t1 = min(t1, max(tmin, tmax)) return t0, t1 def raymarchingiterator(tstart, tend, stepsize=0.01): t = tstart while t < tend: yield (t, min(t + stepsize, tend)) t += stepsize def randomfloat(): return random.random() def samplegradient(p, value, gradstep, sampler): eps = gradstep dx = sampler((p[0]+eps, p[1], p[2])) - value dy = sampler((p[0], p[1]+eps, p[2])) - value dz = sampler((p[0], p[1], p[2]+eps)) - value return (dx/eps, dy/eps, dz/eps) def shadescivislight(Nw, Dw, rawcolor): ambient = 0.2 lightdir = normalize((0.0, 1.0, 0.5)) diff = max(0.0, Nw[0]lightdir[0] + Nw[1]lightdir[1] + Nw[2]lightdir[2]) return ( rawcolor[0] (ambient + diff), rawcolor[1] (ambient + diff), rawcolor[2] (ambient + diff)) def computetransmittance(startp, lightdir, volume): trans = 1.0 t = 0.0 while t < 10.0: p = (startp[0] + tlightdir[0], startp[1] + tlightdir[1], startp[2] + tlightdir[2]) val = volume.sample(p) trans = math.exp(-val 0.01) t += 0.01 return trans def sampletransferfunction(value, stepsize): alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-value stepsize) color = (value, value, value) return color, alpha def inshaderneuralvolumeraymarching(camera, volume, tfn, params): width, height = camera.resolution framebuffer = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] width for in range(height)] campos = camera.position f = camera.forward h = camera.horizontal v = camera.vertical W2C = camera.worldtocameramatrix C2W = camera.cameratoworldmatrix for y in range(height): for x in range(width): nx = x - 0.5 ny = y - 0.5 rayorg = transformpoint(W2C, campos) raydir = normalize(f + nx h + ny v) t0, t1 = intersectvolumebbox(rayorg, raydir, volume.bbox) if t1 <= t0: continue acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 highestalpha = 0.0 highestcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) highestpos = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alive = True for tstart, tend in raymarchingiterator(t0, t1): if not alive: break jitter = randomfloat() p = ( rayorg[0] + lerp(jitter, tstart, tend) raydir[0], rayorg[1] + lerp(jitter, tstart, tend) raydir[1], rayorg[2] + lerp(jitter, tstart, tend) raydir[2]) val = volume.sample(p) gradient = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if params.mode == GRADIENTSHADING: gradient = (-samplegradient(p, val, params.gradstep, volume.sample)[0], -samplegradient(p, val, params.gradstep, volume.sample)[1], -samplegradient(p, val, params.gradstep, volume.sample)[2]) samplecolor, samplealpha = sampletransferfunction(val, tend - tstart) if params.mode == GRADIENTSHADING: Nw = transformnormal(C2W, gradient) shadedcolor = shadescivislight(Nw, raydir, samplecolor) samplecolor = ( lerp(params.scivisshadingscale, samplecolor[0], shadedcolor[0]), lerp(params.scivisshadingscale, samplecolor[1], shadedcolor[1]), lerp(params.scivisshadingscale, samplecolor[2], shadedcolor[2])) elif params.mode == SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC: if samplealpha > highestalpha: highestalpha = samplealpha highestcolor = samplecolor highestpos = p tr = 1.0 - accalpha acccolor = ( acccolor[0] + tr samplecolor[0] samplealpha, acccolor[1] + tr samplecolor[1] samplealpha, acccolor[2] + tr samplecolor[2] samplealpha) accalpha += tr samplealpha if accalpha >= NEARLYONE: alive = False if params.mode == SINGLESHADEHEURISTIC and highestalpha > 0.0: trans = computetransmittance(highestpos, (0.0, 1.0, 0.5), volume) finalcontrib = ( highestcolor[0] highestalpha trans, highestcolor[1] highestalpha trans, highestcolor[2] highestalpha trans) acccolor = ( lerp(params.scivisshadingscale, acccolor[0], finalcontrib[0]), lerp(params.scivisshadingscale, acccolor[1], finalcontrib[1]), lerp(params.scivisshadingscale, acccolor[2], finalcontrib[2])) framebuffer[y][x] = (acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accalpha) return framebuffer A neural volume rendering technique that uses a multilayer perceptron (MLP) to predict radiance for multiple scattering events in high-order scattering media, such as atmospheric clouds. Unlike In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching, which evaluates the network per sample point during ray marching, RPNN queries the network for the accumulated multiple scattering contribution based on a global shading configuration, enabling results nearly identical to path tracing but approximately a thousand times faster. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of samples per ray. The cost per sample is dominated by the neural network inference (MLP evaluation). Memory Complexity: O(N{params}), where N{params} is the number of parameters in the neural network. The volume data itself is not stored in a 3D texture, reducing VRAM usage compared to voxel-based methods. Performance: On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4080, the 4×64 architecture achieves 3.7 ms frame time on a high-poly mesh and 0.41 ms on a low-poly mesh. Image quality reaches 22.315 dB PSNR and 0.059 FLIP error for the 4×64 architecture with thickness. Strengths: Eliminates pre-computation and texture decoding overhead, supports complex neural representations directly, and provides flexible shading modes. Limitations: Performance depends heavily on GPU inference speed, requires strict network widths (16, 32, 64 for standard; multiples of 16 for fV-SRN), and numerical gradient estimation adds overhead. When to use: Interactive visualization of trained neural radiance fields where pre-computation is undesirable. When not to use: Offline path-traced multi-scattering or when inference latency exceeds the target frame budget. In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching is implemented in the instantvnr library by VIDILabs. It was developed to render neural volume representations directly on the GPU without decoding large volumes into textures, leveraging the tiny-cuda-nn library for efficient MLP evaluation on CUDA. It supports both standard MLPs and fV-SRN architectures.
