name: Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN)
head: Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN) for clouds
body: Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN) is a neural volume rendering method that approximates complex light scattering within clouds and their interaction with atmospheric illumination by evaluating a multilayer perceptron (MLP) per pixel on mesh geometry, avoiding explicit volumetric integration. It sets itself apart from its sibling In-Shader Neural Volume Ray Marching by specifically decomposing the radiance prediction into direct and indirect components to handle soft shadow boundaries and multiple scattering, which earlier neural shading methods struggled with. Unlike Neural Volume Scattering Prediction, which uses sampling templates to solve the radiative transfer equation, RPNN predicts final pixel colors directly based on shading configurations. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D shading point p, sun direction (\theta, \phi), and cloud thickness \delta. Outputs: Predicted color \tilde{c} and transparency \alpha. Data Structures: Triplane Feature Maps: Three learnable parameter tensors F{XY}, F{YZ}, F{XZ} representing features on orthogonal planes. MLP: A multilayer perceptron with fully connected layers. Hidden layers use ReLU activation. The output layer uses an exponential activation function g(x) = e^{x-3}. Steps: 1. Encode Position: Project the 3D shading point p onto three orthogonal planes. Sample features F{XY}, F{YZ}, F{XZ} from each plane using bilinear interpolation. Sum these features to form the spatial encoding. 2. Form Input Vector: Concatenate the summed triplane features, the 2D sun direction vector (\theta, \phi), and the thickness parameter \delta. \theta, \phi: Spherical coordinates for azimuth and elevation angles, mapping to the sun direction in a sky model. \delta: The thickness of the cloud along the view direction at point p, computed by mirroring back-camera positions and subtracting front-camera positions. 3. Evaluate MLP: Pass the input vector through the MLP. The network outputs two RGB colors cD and cI, and a transparency value \alpha. cD: Color of the shading point when directly lit by the light source. cI: Indirect shading color when the shading point is occluded from the light source. 4. Compute Visibility: Calculate a soft visibility value v from the diffuse direct light pass. Convert the diffuse direct pass to grayscale using the luminosity method. Apply a smoothstep function (cubic Hermite interpolation) with lower threshold t{min}=0.0 and upper threshold t{max}=0.1. 5. Interpolate Color: Interpolate between cD and cI based on the visibility value v to obtain the final predicted color \tilde{c}: \tilde{c} = v \cdot cD + (1 - v) \cdot cI 6. Output: Return \tilde{c} and \alpha. Training: 1. Dataset Generation: Generate supervised data using Blender. Render physically-based, path-traced clouds under varying viewing and lighting conditions. Extract mesh representation from volumetric density field. Filter out fully transparent pixels. 2. Loss Function: Apply logarithmic transformation \log(x + 1) to both predictions (\tilde{c}, \alpha) and ground-truth RGBA values. Compute L2 loss. 3. Optimization: Use Adam optimizer. Initial learning rate 10^{-3}, halved every 50 epochs. Batch size 1024^2 samples. Train for 250 epochs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class TriplaneEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self, featuredim, planesize): super().init() # Three learnable parameter tensors for XY, YZ, XZ planes self.FXY = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(planesize, planesize, featuredim)) self.FYZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(planesize, planesize, featuredim)) self.FXZ = nn.Parameter(torch.randn(planesize, planesize, featuredim)) def forward(self, p): # p is (N, 3) tensor of 3D points # Project p onto planes and sample features # Note: Exact projection and bilinear sampling implementation details # are not fully specified in sources, assuming standard triplane sampling logic. # For implementation, one would typically normalize p to [-1, 1] and use gridsample. # Placeholder for specific bilinear interpolation logic based on source # FXYsample = bilinearinterpolate(self.FXY, p[:, [0, 1]]) # FYZsample = bilinearinterpolate(self.FYZ, p[:, [1, 2]]) # FXZsample = bilinearinterpolate(self.FXZ, p[:, [0, 2]]) # Sum features # features = FXYsample + FYZsample + FXZsample # Return dummy for structure completeness as exact sampling code is not in source return torch.zeroslike(p[:,:3]) class RPNN(nn.Module): def init(self, featuredim, hiddendims=[256, 256, 256]): super().init() self.encoder = TriplaneEncoder(featuredim, 64) # Example size # Input dim: featuredim + 2 (sun dir) + 1 (thickness) inputdim = featuredim + 3 layers = [] for dim in hiddendims: layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim, dim)) layers.append(nn.ReLU()) inputdim = dim # Output: 2 RGB colors (6 channels) + 1 alpha layers.append(nn.Linear(inputdim, 7)) self.mlp = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, p, sundir, thickness): # 1. Encode position features = self.encoder(p) # 2. Form input vector # sundir is (N, 2) theta, phi # thickness is (N, 1) inputvec = torch.cat([features, sundir, thickness], dim=-1) # 3. Evaluate MLP # Output: [cDr, cDg, cDb, cIr, cIg, cIb, alpha] rawoutput = self.mlp(inputvec) # 4. Apply output activation g(x) = exp(x - 3) # Apply to all 7 outputs output = torch.exp(rawoutput - 3.0) cD = output[:,:3] cI = output[:, 3:6] alpha = output[:, 6:7] # 5. Compute visibility (requires external diffuse pass data) # This step is performed outside the network forward pass in the renderer # using precomputed visibility values v. # For the sake of this self-contained pseudocode, we assume v is passed in. # In practice, v is derived from the diffuse direct light pass. pass def computefinalcolor(self, cD, cI, visibility): # 6. Interpolate color # visibility v is (N, 1) ctilde = visibility cD + (1 - visibility) cI return ctilde, cD, cI, visibility def computeloss(predc, predalpha, gtrgba): # Log transformation predclog = torch.log(predc + 1) gtclog = torch.log(gtrgba[:,:3] + 1) predalphalog = torch.log(predalpha + 1) gtalphalog = torch.log(gtrgba[:, 3:4] + 1) # L2 loss lossc = F.mseloss(predclog, gtclog) lossalpha = F.mseloss(predalphalog, gtalphalog) return lossc + lossalpha Uses sampling templates to predict scattering distribution and solve the radiative transfer equation, addressing RPNN's inability to handle shadows and large sampling requirements. Solves the radiative transfer equation using neural networks, differing from RPNN's direct color prediction. Time Complexity: Rendering is approximately a thousand times faster than path tracing. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for triplane feature maps and MLP weights. Training batch size is 1024^2 samples. Measured Performance: Rendering results are almost identical to path tracing. Training time is about 20 minutes on an NVIDIA A100 GPU. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability, handles multiple scattering, soft shadow boundaries via visibility interpolation. Limitations: Requires mesh geometry extraction from volumetric density field. View direction is not used as input, limiting view-dependent effects. When to use: Real-time cloud rendering where visual fidelity close to path tracing is needed. When not to use: Scenes requiring explicit view-dependent effects not captured by the triplane encoding. RPNN was proposed by Kallweit et al.. It represents radiance for each shading configuration, including location, direction, light source, and density structure. The method uses a hierarchy of point stencils to represent varying scales of cloud density. The specific implementation described in uses a triplane representation and is trained on data generated with Blender. name: Neural Volume Scattering Prediction
head: Backbone Neural Network for Volume Rendering, Deep scattering for volumes, Radiance-predicting neural network for volumes
body: Neural Volume Scattering Prediction is a method for rendering participating media that uses a neural network to predict the scattering distribution at the centers of sampling templates, which is then used to solve the radiative transfer equation. It sets itself apart from its sibling Neural Radiative Transfer Equation Solver and the earlier Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN) by decomposing input features into density, transmission, and phase, and by using specific sampling templates (diffuse and highlight) to simplify the network structure and input parameters. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Sampling features: Pre-calculated density, transmission, and phase features derived from particle position coordinates and template points. Configuration parameters: Asymmetry parameters of the Henyey-Greenstein (HG) phase function (g): 1, 2, or 3 parameters depending on material type. Albedo (\etac): A 3D vector for RGB channels, range 0–1, assumed homogeneous within the same material. Gaseous materials: 0 to 0.5. Solid, liquid, and skin materials: 0.5 to 1. Angle (\alpha): Between viewing direction (\omega) and light direction (l), calculated as \alpha = \cos^{-1}(\omega, l). Dataset: Annotated data Z = \{(F1, F(u1, l1)),..., (FN, F(uN, lN))\}, where N is the dataset size, Fi(p, l) is the annotation value, and T^c(F) is the estimated value. Outputs: Scattering distribution F(p, l) for the center point of each sampling template. These values are brought into the radiative transfer equation to render the volume medium. Data Structures Sampling Templates: Total of 4129 templates. Diffuse reflection sampling template: 8 layers. Specular (highlight) reflection sampling template: 4 layers. Feature Vectors: For the i-th layer input feature Hi^\tau, where \tau \in \{\rho, f, T\} represents density, phase function, and transmission field respectively: Average pooling: Bi^\tau = \frac{1}{ni} \sum{j=1}^{ni} H{i,j}^\tau. Maximum pooling: fi^\tau = \max H{i,j}^\tau. ni: Total number of points in the i-th layer template. Attention vector vi: 8-dimensional vector constructed from layer inputs: vi = \{Bi^\rho, Bi^f, Bi^T, fi^\rho, fi^f, fi^T, g, \alpha\}. Algorithm Steps The method uses a backbone neural network divided into two separate networks with identical structures: one for diffuse reflection and one for specular reflection. If density, transmittance, and phase are included, there are 6 identical network modules (2 per feature type: diffuse/specular). 1. Input Layer: Input sampling features (density, transmission, phase) from the pre-calculation table based on particle position and template points. Features are input in batches. There are 4129 sampling templates, so the network processes them 4129 times (or in parallel using multiple models). 2. Hidden Layer Processing (Layer-by-Layer): For each feature type (density, transmission, phase), process features layer-by-layer through identical network structures. Diffuse Reflection: Process 8 layers. Specular Reflection: Process 4 layers. Per Layer Operation: 1. Fuse current layer sampling features (e.g., density) with configuration parameters (g, \etac, \alpha). 2. Input the fused vector into an Attention Module (implemented as SENet) to determine channel importance. Construct vi from the current layer's pooled features and configuration parameters. Calculate weight coefficient wi^\tau = S(R(vi)), where R(vi) = \max(vi, 0) (ReLU) and S(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} (Sigmoid). Apply weights to features: Hi^\tau = wi^\tau \cdot \sum Hi^\tau. 3. Fuse the attention module output with the next layer's sampling features using Fully Connected layer FC-1 to match dimensions. 4. Pass the fused vector through Fully Connected layer FC-2. 5. Fuse the result with the current layer's sampling feature and output. 3. Merge Diffuse and Specular: Merge the diffuse reflection sampling density features (after 8 iterations) and specular reflection sampling density features (after 4 iterations) via a full connection. 4. Final Prediction: Input sampling transmission features and sampling phase features layer-by-layer (12 times each total across diffuse/specular paths). Fuse transmission and phase features together. Input the fused features into a Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Output the scattering distribution of the center point of the sampling template. 5. Rendering: Sample all 4129 volume medium particle points with the template. Predict output in parallel to obtain scattering distributions for all 4129 centers. Bring predicted scattering distribution values into the radiative transfer equation to render the volume medium. Loss Function The network is trained using a mean square error loss with logarithmic transformation to compress the radiation range and speed up training. LS = \frac{1}{B} \sum{i \in B} \left( \log \frac{T^c(F)}{\etac \gamma} + 1 - \log \frac{Fi(p, l)}{\etac \gamma} + 1 \right)^2 B: Batch size. T^c(F): Estimated value of the neural network. Fi(p, l): Annotation value of the scattering distribution. \etac: Albedo for RGB channel c. \gamma: Hyperparameter, typically \gamma = 4. c: RGB color channel. The total loss is minimized over the annotated dataset Z: L{total} = \argmin \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} LS. Pseudocode Unverified code. Fuse current layer features with configuration parameters # Exact fusion operation not specified; assumed concatenation or addition fusedconfig = features[0] + config # 2. FC-1: Fuse attention output with next layer features to match dimensions # Next layer features are not available in this single-layer function; # in practice, FC-1 projects the attention output to the dimension of the next layer nextlayerdim = len(features[0]) fc1out = fclayer(wi, nextlayerdim) # 4. FC-2 fc2out = fclayer(fc1out, nextlayerdim) # 5. Fuse with current layer feature and output output = [fc2out[k] + features[0][k] for k in range(nextlayerdim)] return output def neuralvolumescatteringprediction(densityfeats, transfeats, phasefeats, config): # config = [g, alpha, albedor, albedog, albedob] nlayersdiffuse = 8 nlayersspecular = 4 # Diffuse reflection path (8 layers) diffusefeats = densityfeats for in range(nlayersdiffuse): diffusefeats = processlayer(diffusefeats, config, isdiffuse=True) # Specular reflection path (4 layers) specularfeats = densityfeats for in range(nlayersspecular): specularfeats = processlayer(specularfeats, config, isdiffuse=False) # Merge diffuse and specular density features via FC mergeddensity = fclayer(diffusefeats, len(specularfeats)) # Transmission and phase features layer-by-layer (12 times each) transfeats12 = transfeats for in range(12): transfeats12 = processlayer(transfeats12, config, isdiffuse=True) phasefeats12 = phasefeats for in range(12): phasefeats12 = processlayer(phasefeats12, config, isdiffuse=True) # Fuse transmission and phase features fusedtransphase = [transfeats12[k] + phasefeats12[k] for k in range(len(transfeats12))] # Multilayer Perceptron (MLP) # Standard MLP with learned weights and ReLU activations mlpout = fclayer(fusedtransphase, 3) # Output 3 channels for RGB scattering scatteringdistribution = [max(0.0, v) for v in mlpout] return scatteringdistribution def computeloss(estimated, annotation, albedo, gamma=4): # LS = 1/B sum( (log(T^c(F)/(etacgamma)) + 1 - log(Fi(p,l)/(etacgamma)) + 1)^2) loss = 0.0 for c in range(3): # RGB channels term1 = math.log(estimated[c] / (albedo[c] gamma)) + 1.0 term2 = math.log(annotation[c] / (albedo[c] gamma)) + 1.0 loss += (term1 - term2) 2 return loss / 3.0 A real-time volume rendering method that uses a neural network to simulate the iterative integration process of solving the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), replacing traditional path tracing to achieve real-time performance for high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering. name: Neural Radiative Transfer Equation Solver
head: Neural network-based real-time volume rendering method, RPNN variant with hierarchical transmittance and sampling templates
body: A real-time volume rendering method that uses a neural network to simulate the iterative integration process of solving the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE), replacing traditional path tracing to achieve real-time performance for high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering. It sets itself apart from its sibling Neural Volume Scattering Prediction and the earlier Radiance-Predicting Neural Networks (RPNN) by decomposing input features into density, transmission, and phase, and by using specific sampling templates (diffuse and highlight) to simplify the network structure and input parameters, thereby addressing RPNN's inability to handle shadows and its requirement for large sampling. Inputs: 1. Original 3D volumetric media density field, represented as a point cloud or voxel grid with resolution 1024 \times 1024 \times 1024. 2. Incident light direction (implied by the highlight template geometry). Outputs: 1. Scattering distribution for the center points of all sampling templates, which contributes to the final radiance calculation. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchical Density Fields: A set of 11 density fields \rhoi at resolutions Ri. i=0: 1024^3 i=1: 512^3 i=2: 256^3 i=3: 128^3 i=4: 64^3 (Note: Source text contains typo '624 64 64', corrected to 64^3 based on sequence). i=5: 32^3 i=6: 16^3 i=7: 8^3 i=8: 4^3 (Note: Source text contains typo '4 4 4 4', corrected to 4^3 based on sequence). i=9: 2^3 i=10: 1^3 2. Hierarchical Transmission Fields: A set of 11 transmission fields Ti(p, y), one for each density level. 3. Transmission Feature: A single feature map resulting from the 3D-CNN processing of the 11 transmission fields. 4. Diffuse Reflection Sampling Template (S{diff}): A set of 182 points distributed in a sphere around a center point, divided into 8 layers. Layer 0: 6 points (1 center, 5 inside). Layer 1: 8 points. Layer 2: 12 points. Layer 3: 16 points. Layer 4: 24 points. Layer 5: 32 points. Layer 6: 48 points. Layer 7: 48 points. Points in layers 1-7 are evenly distributed in the spherical shell between the current layer's surface and the previous layer's surface. 5. Highlight Sampling Template (S{high}): A set of 72 points distributed along the direction of incident light, divided into 4 layers. Layer 0: 32 points. Layer 1: 16 points. Layer 2: 16 points. Layer 3: 8 points. Points are evenly distributed by distance from the center. Parameters: \lambda{i+1}: Coefficient for transmittance calculation, range [0, 1], specific value 0.6. Steps: 1. Data Processing (Hierarchical Transmittance): For each density level i from 0 to 10: a. Obtain the density field \rhoi(x) at resolution Ri. b. Calculate the transmission field Ti(p, y) using the formula: Ti(p, y) = e^{-\int{p}^{y} \lambda{i+1} \rhoi(x) dx} where p is the starting point, y is the ending point along the path, and \lambda{i+1} = 0.6. c. Store the 11 transmission fields T0, \dots, T{10}. 2. Transmission Feature Extraction: a. Input the 11 hierarchical transmission fields into a 3D Convolutional Neural Network (3D-CNN). b. The 3D-CNN assigns a weight to each level of transmission field and superimposes them to produce a single combined transmission feature. 3. Sampling Template Generation: a. Create the diffuse reflection sampling template S{diff} using a sphere divided into 8 layers. b. Create the highlight sampling template S{high} divided into 4 layers along the incident light direction. 4. Feature Sampling: For a given center point in the volume: a. Sample the density features using both S{diff} and S{high} templates. b. Sample the transmission features (from the combined feature map generated in Step 2) using both S{diff} and S{high} templates. c. Sample the phase features (scattering phase function values) using both S{diff} and S{high} templates. d. This results in sampled phase features, sampled density features, and sampled transmission features for each template layer. 5. Network Input Preparation: a. Layer the three types of sampled features (density, transmission, phase) according to the layers of the diffuse reflection sampling template and the highlight sampling template. b. The sampled features of each layer are sent into the network for internal scattering estimation. 6. Attention Mechanism: a. Pass the layered features through an attention module. b. The module selects important channel features to pay more attention to light scattering, highlights, and shadows. 7. Scattering Prediction: a. Feed the attended features into the backbone neural network. b. Predict the scattering distribution for the center points of all sampling templates (S{diff} and S{high}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def downsample(volume, targetres): """Downsamples a 3D volume to targetres using average pooling.""" srcres = len(volume) stride = srcres // targetres downsampled = [[[0.0 for in range(targetres)] for in range(targetres)] for in range(targetres)] for z in range(targetres): for y in range(targetres): for x in range(targetres): sumval = 0.0 count = 0 for dz in range(stride): for dy in range(stride): for dx in range(stride): sumval += volume[z stride + dz][y stride + dy][x stride + dx] count += 1 downsampled[z][y][x] = sumval / count return downsampled def computetransmittancefield(densityfield, lambdacoeff): """ Computes transmission field Ti(p, y) = exp(-intp^y lambda rhoi(x) dx). Assumes a standard ray-marching integration along the viewing direction. """ # Source does not specify the exact integration path discretization. # Implementing a simplified per-voxel optical depth accumulation along the z-axis. res = len(densityfield) transmissionfield = [[[0.0 for in range(res)] for in range(res)] for in range(res)] for z in range(res): for y in range(res): opticaldepth = 0.0 for x in range(res): opticaldepth += lambdacoeff densityfield[z][y][x] transmissionfield[z][y][x] = math.exp(-opticaldepth) return transmissionfield def generatediffusetemplate(): """Generates the diffuse reflection sampling template Sdiff (182 points, 8 layers).""" layers = [6, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32, 48, 48] template = [] baseradius = 1.0 for i, numpoints in enumerate(layers): points = [] if i == 0: # Layer 0: 1 center, 5 inside points.append([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) for k in range(5): theta = math.sqrt(k + 1) math.pi phi = 2 math.pi k / 1.618 r = 0.2 points.append([r math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi), r math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi), r math.cos(theta)]) else: # Layers 1-7: Evenly distributed in spherical shell prevr = baseradius (i - 1) / 7.0 currr = baseradius i / 7.0 for k in range(numpoints): theta = math.sqrt(k + 1) math.pi phi = 2 math.pi k / 1.618 r = (prevr + currr) / 2.0 points.append([r math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi), r math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi), r math.cos(theta)]) template.append(points) return template def generatehighlighttemplate(): """Generates the highlight sampling template Shigh (72 points, 4 layers).""" layers = [32, 16, 16, 8] template = [] for i, numpoints in enumerate(layers): points = [] z = (i + 1) 0.25 for k in range(numpoints): theta = math.sqrt(k + 1) math.pi phi = 2 math.pi k / 1.618 r = 0.5 x = r math.sin(theta) math.cos(phi) y = r math.sin(theta) math.sin(phi) points.append([x, y, z]) template.append(points) return template def samplefeatures(densityfield, transmissionfeature, phasefield, template): """Samples density, transmission, and phase features at template points using trilinear interpolation.""" sampled = [] res = len(densityfield) for layerpoints in template: layersamples = [] for point in layerpoints: # Normalize point to [0, 1] px, py, pz = point[0] / 2.0 + 0.5, point[1] / 2.0 + 0.5, point[2] / 2.0 + 0.5 # Trilinear interpolation (simplified) d = densityfield[int(pz res)][int(py res)][int(px res)] t = transmissionfeature[int(pz res)][int(py res)][int(px res)] p = phasefield[int(pz res)][int(py res)][int(px res)] layersamples.append([d, t, p]) sampled.append(layersamples) return sampled def threedcnnforward(transmissionfields): """Superimposes 11 transmission fields with learned weights.""" # Source does not specify exact weights or architecture. # Assuming a simple weighted sum as described: "adds a weight to each level... superimposes". combined = [[[0.0 for in range(len(transmissionfields[0]))] for in range(len(transmissionfields[0][0]))] for in range(len(transmissionfields[0][0][0]))] weights = [0.1] 11 for i, field in enumerate(transmissionfields): for z in range(len(field)): for y in range(len(field[0])): for x in range(len(field[0][0])): combined[z][y][x] += weights[i] field[z][y][x] return combined def attentionforward(features): """Selects important channel features.""" # Source does not specify attention mechanism details. # Applying a simple channel-wise scaling factor. return [[f 1.2 for f in layer] for layer in features] def backboneforward(attendedfeatures): """Predicts scattering distribution.""" # Source does not specify backbone architecture. # Flattening and applying a linear transformation. flat = [val for layer in attendedfeatures for point in layer for val in point] return [val 0.5 for val in flat] def neuralradiativetransfersolver(densityfield1024): """Main pipeline for the Neural Radiative Transfer Equation Solver.""" resolutions = [1024, 512, 256, 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1] densityfields = [downsample(densityfield1024, res) for res in resolutions] lambdacoeff = 0.6 transmissionfields = [computetransmittancefield(field, lambdacoeff) for field in densityfields] transmissionfeature = threedcnnforward(transmissionfields) sdiff = generatediffusetemplate() shigh = generatehighlighttemplate() # Phase field generation is not detailed in the source. # Assuming a constant phase field or derived from density. phasefield = [[[1.0 for in range(len(densityfields[0]))] for in range(len(densityfields[0][0]))] for in range(len(densityfields[0][0][0]))] sampleddiff = samplefeatures(densityfields[0], transmissionfeature, phasefield, sdiff) sampledhigh = samplefeatures(densityfields[0], transmissionfeature, phasefield, shigh) # Layer the features as described inputfeatures = sampleddiff + sampledhigh attendedfeatures = attentionforward(inputfeatures) scatteringdistribution = backboneforward(attendedfeatures) return scatteringdistribution A technique to represent optical depth at multiple resolutions to capture both fine details and global lighting effects efficiently. It sets itself apart by using a fixed coefficient \lambda=0.6 to scale density before integration, simplifying the transmittance calculation compared to full path tracing. Choose it when rendering large volumes with varying density scales. Link to Hierarchical Transmittance A spherical sampling pattern designed to capture isotropic scattering contributions. It sets itself apart from the highlight template by focusing on general scattering rather than directional highlights. Choose it for rendering the bulk appearance of participating media. Link to Diffuse Template A directional sampling pattern aligned with the light source to capture specular-like highlights and shadowing effects. It sets itself apart from the diffuse template by focusing on the light direction. Choose it when accurate highlights and shadows are critical. Link to Highlight Template Time Complexity: Real-time performance is claimed, significantly faster than traditional path tracing. The complexity is dominated by the 3D-CNN inference and the sampling operations, which are constant per pixel/voxel based on the fixed template sizes (182 + 72 = 254 points). Memory Complexity: Requires storing 11 hierarchical density fields and 11 transmission fields. Measured Performance: The source claims "greatly increase the rendering speed while maintaining rendering quality" and "outperforms previous methods". Specific FPS or hardware details are not given. Strengths: Real-time rendering, handles high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering, better handling of shadows and highlights compared to RPNN, simplified network structure. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of hierarchical fields, relies on neural network approximation which may not generalize to all material types, specific template geometry limits flexibility. When to use: Real-time applications requiring realistic volumetric rendering of participating media like clouds, smoke, or translucent materials. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from a paper titled "A real-time rendering method for high albedo anisotropic materials with multiple scattering". It was developed to address the limitations of previous Neural Radiance Prediction Neural Networks (RPNN), which only accepted density features, required large sampling, and struggled with shadows. The work builds on the concept of using neural networks to solve the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) iteratively, as introduced in earlier works on neural volume rendering. name: DVGO Volume Rendering Forward Pass
head: DVGO forward, Direct Voxel Grid Optimization rendering
body: The DVGO forward pass renders a 3D scene represented by a direct voxel grid of density and color features into a 2D image by querying the grid along camera rays and compositing the results. It differs from standard NeRF by replacing the multi-layer perceptron (MLP) with a direct lookup in a 3D texture (voxel grid), enabling significantly faster training and inference while maintaining view-dependent color through auxiliary feature vectors. Inputs: rayso: Origin of each ray, shape (N, 3), where N is the number of pixels (rays). raysd: Direction of each ray, shape (N, 3). near, far: Near and far clipping planes for ray marching. stepsize: Distance between sample points along the ray. renderkwargs: Dictionary containing optional flags (renderfeatures, renderdiffuse, renderdepth) and background color bg. Outputs: rgbmarched: Final rendered RGB image, shape (N, 3). alphainvlast: Accumulated transmittance at the end of the ray, shape (N). weights: Per-sample weights used for compositing, shape (M), where M is the number of valid samples. rawalpha: Raw alpha values before weighting, shape (M). rawrgb: Raw RGB values before weighting, shape (M, 3). rayid: Mapping from sample index to ray index, shape (M). depth (optional): Weighted average depth, shape (N). diffusemarched (optional): Rendered diffuse color, shape (N, 3). Density Grid (V\sigma): A 3D tensor of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz) storing raw density values. Color Feature Grid (Vc): A 3D tensor of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz, k0) storing feature vectors. k0 is the feature dimension. RGB Network (\text{rgbnet}): A small MLP (optional) that maps color features and view direction to final RGB. Diffuse Color Grid (Vd): A 3D tensor of shape (Dx, Dy, Dz, 3) storing diffuse color components (if usediffusecolor is enabled). Mask Cache: A boolean grid or hash map indicating free space, used to skip empty regions. interval: Sampling interval for density-to-alpha conversion. Calculated as stepsize voxelsizeratio. actshift: Shift parameter for the density activation function (e.g., sigmoid shift). fastcolorthres: Threshold for early ray termination. If alpha or weight exceeds this, subsequent samples are skipped. usediffusecolor: Boolean flag to enable diffuse color rendering. rgbnetfullimplicit: Boolean flag determining if view direction is concatenated with features before the RGB network. rgbnetdirect: Boolean flag determining if diffuse color is added directly to the network output. 1. Ray Sampling: Generate sample points along each ray. For each ray i \in [0, N-1], compute sample positions \mathbf{x}j = \mathbf{o}i + tj \mathbf{d}i, where tj are evenly spaced between near and far with spacing stepsize. Collect all points into raypts of shape (M, 3), along with corresponding rayid and stepid (index along the ray). 2. Free Space Culling: If maskcache is present, filter raypts, rayid, and stepid to keep only points where maskcache(raypts) is true. 3. Density Query: Query the density grid V\sigma at raypts using trilinear interpolation. Let \sigmaj be the raw density value for sample j. 4. Density to Alpha Conversion: Convert raw density \sigmaj to alpha \alphaj using the Raw2Alpha function: \alphaj = 1 - \exp(-(\sigmaj + \text{act\shift}) \cdot \text{interval}). 5. Early Termination (Alpha): If fastcolorthres > 0, filter samples where \alphaj > \text{fast\color\thres}. Remove these samples from raypts, rayid, stepid, density, and alpha. 6. Weight Computation: Compute accumulated transmittance Tj and weights wj for each sample. T1 = 1, T{j} = T{j-1} \cdot (1 - \alpha{j-1}) for j > 1 (assuming sorted by depth). wj = Tj \cdot \alphaj. Compute alphainvlast (total transmittance at the end of the ray): T{M+1} = TM \cdot (1 - \alphaM). 7. Early Termination (Weight): If fastcolorthres > 0, filter samples where wj > \text{fast\color\thres}. Remove these samples. 8. Color Query: Query the color feature grid Vc at raypts to get features \mathbf{k}j \in \mathbb{R}^{k0}. If usediffusecolor is true, query the diffuse color grid Vd to get \mathbf{d}j \in \mathbb{R}^3. 9. RGB Computation: If rgbnet is None, set \mathbf{c}j = \text{sigmoid}(\mathbf{d}j) (if diffuse is used) or use features directly. If rgbnet is not None, compute positional encoding of view direction \mathbf{d}i for the ray containing sample j, concatenate with \mathbf{k}j, pass through rgbnet, and apply sigmoid. If rgbnetdirect is true, add diffuse color: \mathbf{c}j = \mathbf{c}j + \mathbf{d}j. 10. Compositing: Compute final RGB for each ray i: \text{rgb}i = \sum{j \in \text{ray } i} wj \cdot \mathbf{c}j + T{M+1} \cdot \mathbf{bg}, where \mathbf{bg} is the background color. 11. Optional Outputs: If renderfeatures: Sum weights kj grouped by rayid. If renderdiffuse: Sum weights sigmoid(dj) grouped by rayid. If renderdepth: Sum weights stepid grouped by rayid. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def dvgoforwardpass(rayso, raysd, near, far, stepsize, model, renderkwargs): N = rayso.shape[0] # 1. Ray Sampling numsamples = int((far - near) / stepsize) tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., numsamples, device=rayso.device) tvals = near + tvals (far - near) raypts = rayso.unsqueeze(1) + raysd.unsqueeze(1) tvals.unsqueeze(2) M = N numsamples rayptsflat = raypts.reshape(-1, 3) rayid = torch.arange(N, device=rayso.device).unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, numsamples).reshape(-1) stepid = torch.arange(numsamples, device=rayso.device).unsqueeze(0).expand(N, -1).reshape(-1) # 2. Free Space Culling if model.maskcache is not None: validmask = model.maskcache(rayptsflat) rayptsflat = rayptsflat[validmask] rayid = rayid[validmask] stepid = stepid[validmask] M = rayptsflat.shape[0] if M == 0: return { 'rgbmarched': torch.zeros(N, 3, device=rayso.device) + renderkwargs['bg'], 'alphainvlast': torch.ones(N, device=rayso.device), 'weights': torch.zeros(0, device=rayso.device), 'rawalpha': torch.zeros(0, device=rayso.device), 'rawrgb': torch.zeros(0, 3, device=rayso.device), 'rayid': torch.zeros(0, dtype=torch.long, device=rayso.device) } # 3. Density Query normpts = (rayptsflat - model.xyzmin) / (model.xyzmax - model.xyzmin) normpts = torch.clamp(normpts, 0.0, 1.0) density = F.gridsample( model.densitygrid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), normpts.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), aligncorners=True).squeeze() # 4. Density to Alpha interval = stepsize model.voxelsizeratio alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-(density + model.actshift) interval) # 5. Early Termination (Alpha) if model.fastcolorthres > 0: keepmask = alpha > model.fastcolorthres rayptsflat = rayptsflat[keepmask] rayid = rayid[keepmask] stepid = stepid[keepmask] density = density[keepmask] alpha = alpha[keepmask] M = rayptsflat.shape[0] # 6. Weight Computation # Sort by rayid and stepid to ensure correct order per ray sortidx = torch.argsort(rayid 100000 + stepid) rayid = rayid[sortidx] stepid = stepid[sortidx] alpha = alpha[sortidx] # Compute transmittance T per ray T = torch.ones(M, device=rayso.device) oneminusalpha = 1.0 - alpha cumprod = torch.cumprod(oneminusalpha, dim=0) # T[j] = 1 if j is start of ray, else cumprod[j-1] raystarts = torch.zeros(N, dtype=torch.long, device=rayso.device) counts = torch.bincount(rayid, minlength=N) raystarts = torch.cat([torch.tensor([0], device=rayso.device), torch.cumsum(counts[:-1], dim=0)]) T[raystarts] = 1.0 T[raystarts[1:]] = cumprod[raystarts[1:] - 1] weights = T alpha # alphainvlast per ray is T at the last sample (1 - alpha at last sample) lastindices = raystarts + counts - 1 alphainvlastperray = T[lastindices] (1 - alpha[lastindices]) # 7. Early Termination (Weight) if model.fastcolorthres > 0: weightmask = weights > model.fastcolorthres rayptsflat = rayptsflat[weightmask] rayid = rayid[weightmask] stepid = stepid[weightmask] alpha = alpha[weightmask] weights = weights[weightmask] T = T[weightmask] M = rayptsflat.shape[0] counts = torch.bincount(rayid, minlength=N) raystarts = torch.cat([torch.tensor([0], device=rayid.device), torch.cumsum(counts[:-1], dim=0)]) lastindices = raystarts + counts - 1 alphainvlastperray = T[lastindices] (1 - alpha[lastindices]) # 8. Color Query normptsfiltered = (rayptsflat - model.xyzmin) / (model.xyzmax - model.xyzmin) normptsfiltered = torch.clamp(normptsfiltered, 0.0, 1.0) colorfeatures = F.gridsample( model.colorgrid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), normptsfiltered.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), aligncorners=True).squeeze() rgb = torch.zeros(M, 3, device=rayso.device) diffuse = torch.zeros(M, 3, device=rayso.device) if model.usediffusecolor: diffuse = F.gridsample( model.diffusegrid.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), normptsfiltered.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), aligncorners=True).squeeze() if model.rgbnet is None: if model.usediffusecolor: rgb = torch.sigmoid(diffuse) else: if colorfeatures.shape[1] == 3: rgb = colorfeatures else: rgb = torch.zeros(M, 3, device=rayso.device) else: viewdirs = raysd[rayid] viewdirspe = positionalencoding(viewdirs) inputcolor = torch.cat([colorfeatures, viewdirspe], dim=-1) rawrgb = model.rgbnet(inputcolor) rgb = torch.sigmoid(rawrgb) if model.rgbnetdirect and model.usediffusecolor: rgb = rgb + torch.sigmoid(diffuse) # 9. Compositing rgbmarched = segmentcoo( src=weights.unsqueeze(-1) rgb, index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 3, device=rayso.device), reduce='sum') bg = renderkwargs['bg'].to(rayso.device) rgbmarched = rgbmarched + alphainvlastperray.unsqueeze(-1) bg # 10. Optional Outputs extras = {} if renderkwargs.get('renderfeatures', False): extras['featuresmarched'] = segmentcoo( src=weights.unsqueeze(-1) colorfeatures, index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, colorfeatures.shape[1], device=rayso.device), reduce='sum') if model.usediffusecolor and renderkwargs.get('renderdiffuse', False): extras['diffusemarched'] = segmentcoo( src=weights.unsqueeze(-1) torch.sigmoid(diffuse), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 3, device=rayso.device), reduce='sum') if renderkwargs.get('renderdepth', False): extras['depth'] = segmentcoo( src=weights.unsqueeze(-1) stepid.unsqueeze(-1).float(), index=rayid, out=torch.zeros(N, 1, device=rayso.device), reduce='sum').squeeze(-1) return { 'rgbmarched': rgbmarched, 'alphainvlast': alphainvlastperray, 'weights': weights, 'rawalpha': alpha, 'rawrgb': rgb, 'rayid': rayid, extras } def positionalencoding(x, mindeg=0, maxdeg=10, scale=1, basefreq=2.0): """Standard sinusoidal positional encoding.""" numbands = maxdeg - mindeg freqbands = scale (2.0 torch.arange(mindeg, maxdeg, device=x.device).float()) scaledx = x.unsqueeze(-1) freqbands.unsqueeze(0) encoded = torch.cat([torch.sin(scaledx), torch.cos(scaledx)], dim=-1) return encoded.reshape(x.shape[0], -1) def segmentcoo(src, index, out, reduce='sum'): """PyTorch segment reduction using scatteradd.""" if reduce == 'sum': out = out.expandas(src) out.scatteradd(0, index.unsqueeze(-1).expandas(out), src) return out else: raise NotImplementedError("Only 'sum' reduction is supported.") Zero Density Initialization: DVGO initializes the density grid with zeros, resulting in nearly zero entropy initially. This prevents guiding the agent to choose the next-best view with highest information gain in active vision tasks. Precision: Trilinear interpolation in the voxel grid can introduce artifacts if the grid resolution is too low. Boundaries: Ray points outside the voxel grid bounds must be clamped or filtered to avoid out-of-bounds memory access. Early Termination Threshold: Setting fastcolorthres too high may skip valid samples, leading to inaccurate rendering. Setting it too low may not provide performance benefits. An additional entropy volume V(E,c) introduced to overcome the zero-entropy initialization issue of DVGO's density volume, allowing information gain calculation at the start. It stores \alpha(E,c), initialized with 0.5 to represent highest entropy. For voxels of V(\sigma,c) that have been updated in the reconstruction stage, \alpha(E,c) is synchronized with \alpha(\sigma,c). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples per ray. The lookup is O(1) per sample, making it faster than MLP-based methods which are O(N \cdot S \cdot D) where D is the MLP depth. Memory Complexity: O(Dx \cdot Dy \cdot Dz \cdot (1 + k0 + 3)), where Dx, Dy, Dz are the grid dimensions, k0 is the color feature dimension, and 3 is for diffuse color. This is significantly less than storing a full radiance field MLP weights for high-resolution scenes. Performance: Faster training and inference compared to NeRF due to the direct voxel grid lookup. However, it may suffer from aliasing artifacts if the grid resolution is not high enough. Strengths: Fast training, efficient memory usage for high-resolution scenes, easy to integrate with existing voxel-based pipelines. Limitations: Lower quality than NeRF in complex scenes due to the discrete nature of the voxel grid. View-dependent effects are limited by the feature dimension k0. DVGO (Direct Voxel Grid Optimization) was introduced as a method to accelerate NeRF training by replacing the MLP with a direct voxel grid. It builds on the principles of neural volume rendering. The method was developed to address the computational bottleneck of MLP queries in NeRF, enabling real-time or near-real-time training and rendering. gkouros/ref-dvgo, https://github.com/gkouros/ref-dvgo, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) ActiveRMAP: Radiance Field for Active Mapping And Planning, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2211.12656, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Primitive Radiance Field Integrator
body: The Volumetric Primitive Radiance Field Integrator is a path-tracing method for rendering scattering and emissive media represented by mixtures of kernel-based volumetric primitives (e.g., Gaussians, Epanechnikov) rather than voxel grids or point clouds. It modifies standard volumetric path tracing by replacing medium interaction routines with primitive-specific transmittance evaluation, free-flight distance sampling, and albedo evaluation. It distinguishes itself from its sibling, the Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator, by supporting scattering and emissive media via multiple importance sampling with PDF balancing, whereas the tomography integrator integrates density with no scattering. The integrator inherits from RBIntegrator and operates on a scene containing EllipsoidMesh primitives. Each primitive is defined by a center, rotation, scale, and opacity, optionally accompanied by spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients for emission. The method supports both primal (forward) and adjoint (backward) modes for differentiable rendering. Input: A scene graph containing EllipsoidMesh primitives. Each primitive stores geometric parameters (center \mathbf{c}, rotation matrix \mathbf{R}, scale vector \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and optionally SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH} for emission. Output: Radiance L (primal) or differential radiance \delta L (adjoint). Primitive Attributes: center: 3D vector \mathbf{c}. rotation: 3 \times 3 rotation matrix \mathbf{R}. scale: 3D vector \mathbf{s}. opacity: Scalar \alpha \in [0, 1]. shcoeffs: Array of spherical harmonic coefficients. State Variables (per ray): L: Radiance accumulator. \delta L: Differential radiance accumulator (adjoint). \beta: Path throughput. depth: Current path depth. active: Boolean mask for active rays. maxdepth (int): Maximum path depth. -1 indicates no limit, mapped to 0xFFFFFFFF internally. rrdepth (int): Minimum path depth before enabling Russian roulette. -1 indicates no limit, mapped to 0xFFFFFFFF. kerneltype (str): Name of the kernel to use for rendering the volumetric primitives, one of ['gaussian', 'epanechnikov']. srgbprimitives (bool): If true, converts sRGB light transport to linear color space at the end. userr (bool): Whether to use Russian Roulette. Determined by rrdepth >= 0 and (rrdepth < maxdepth or maxdepth == -1). 1. Initialization: Set maxdepth to 0xFFFFFFFF if input is -1. Set rrdepth to 0xFFFFFFFF if input is -1. Determine userr based on rrdepth and maxdepth. Initialize kernel with kernelfullrange=True and kernelnormalized=True. For each pixel/ray: Initialize L = 0 (or state input), \delta L = 0 (or state input), \beta = 1.0, depth = 0. Generate ray \mathbf{r}. Set active mask to true for all rays. 2. Ray Intersection Loop: While active is not empty: Perform ray intersection with scene using scene.rayintersect with flags All | BackfaceCulling and coherent intersection for depth == 0. Filter active rays to only those intersecting ellipsoids: \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ (\text{si.is\valid}() \ \& \ (\text{si.shape.shape\type}() == \text{ShapeType.Ellipsoids})) If no active rays remain, break loop. 3. Primitive Evaluation: For active rays intersecting ellipsoids: Evaluate Transmission: Gather ellipsoid parameters: center \mathbf{c}, rotation \mathbf{R}, scale \mathbf{s}, opacity \alpha. Transform ray origin and direction to local space: \mathbf{o}' = \mathbf{R}^T (\mathbf{r}.o - \mathbf{c}) / \mathbf{s} \mathbf{d}' = \mathbf{R}^T \mathbf{r}.d / \mathbf{s} Compute peak location along ray: t{peak} = -\frac{\mathbf{o}' \cdot \mathbf{d}'}{\mathbf{d}' \cdot \mathbf{d}'} Evaluate density at peak: \rho = \text{density}(t{peak}) based on kerneltype (Gaussian or Epanechnikov). Compute transmission: \text{transmission} = 1.0 - \min(\alpha \cdot \rho, 0.9999) Note: Clamping to 0.9999 avoids numerical issues with 1.0 - 1.0. Evaluate Emission: Gather SH coefficients \mathbf{c}{SH}. Compute SH degree: n = \sqrt{\text{sh\coeffs.shape}[0] / 3 - 1}. Evaluate SH basis for viewing direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{sh\dir\coef} = \text{sh\eval}(\mathbf{d}, n). Compute emission: \text{emission} = \max(\sum (\mathbf{c}{SH} \odot \mathbf{sh\dir\coef}) + 0.5, 0.0) Note: Adding 0.5 before clamping handles potential negative values from SH evaluation. Clamp Infinite Values: Le[\sim \text{dr.is\finite}(Le)] = 0.0 4. Accumulation and Throughput Update: Compute local emission contribution: Le = \beta \cdot (1.0 - \text{transmission}) \cdot \text{emission} Update radiance accumulator: L[\text{active}] = L[\text{active}] + Le \quad (\text{if primal}) L[\text{active}] = L[\text{active}] - Le \quad (\text{if adjoint}) Update path throughput: \beta[\text{active}] = \text{transmission} 5. Adjoint Indirect Radiance (Adjoint Mode Only): Compute differentiable reflected indirect radiance: L{r\ind} = L \cdot \text{transmission} / \text{dr.detach}(\text{transmission}) Compute total local contribution: Lo = Le + L{r\ind} Select finite values: Lo = \text{dr.select}(\text{active} \ \& \ \text{dr.is\finite}(Lo), Lo, 0.0) Propagate gradients: If Backward: dr.backwardfrom(δL Lo) If Forward: δL += dr.forwardto(Lo) 6. Ray Propagation and Termination: Spawn new ray origin to avoid self-intersection: \mathbf{r}.o[\text{active}] = \text{si.p} + \mathbf{r}.d \cdot 10^{-4} Update active mask and depth: \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ \text{si.is\valid}() \text{depth}[\text{active}] += 1 Kill paths with insignificant contribution: \beta{max} = \text{dr.max}(\beta) \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ (\beta{max} > 0.01) Russian Roulette (if primal and userr): Calculate probability: p{rr} = \max(\beta{max}, 0.1) Identify candidates: \text{rr\active} = (\text{depth} \ge \text{rr\depth}) \ \& \ (\beta{max} < 0.1) Scale throughput: \beta[\text{rr\active}] = 1.0 / p{rr} Determine continuation: \text{rr\continue} = \text{sample\rr} < p{rr} Update active: \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ \text{rr\continue} Limit recursion depth: \text{active} \leftarrow \text{active} \ \& \ (\text{depth} < \text{max\depth}) 7. Final Output: If srgbprimitives is true, convert L to linear space: L = \text{mi.math.srgb\to\linear}(L). Return L if primal, else \delta L. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolprimprb(scene, rayso, raysd, mode='primal', maxdepth=-1, rrdepth=-1, kerneltype='gaussian', srgbprimitives=True): # Initialize parameters if maxdepth == -1: maxdepth = 0xFFFFFFFF if rrdepth == -1: rrdepth = 0xFFFFFFFF userr = (rrdepth >= 0) and ((rrdepth < maxdepth) or (maxdepth == 0xFFFFFFFF)) N = len(rayso) L = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] deltaL = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(N)] beta = [1.0] N depth = [0] N active = [True] N kernel = Kernel(kerneltype, fullrange=True, normalized=True) while any(active): # Ray intersection si = scene.rayintersect(rayso, raysd, flags=ALL | BACKFACECULLING, coherent=(depth[0] == 0)) # Filter for ellipsoids isvalid = [si.isvalid(i) for i in range(N)] isellipsoid = [si.shape.shapetype(i) == SHAPEELLIPSOID for i in range(N)] active = [a & v & e for a, v, e in zip(active, isvalid, isellipsoid)] if not any(active): break idxs = [i for i in range(N) if active[i]] centers = [si.shape.centers[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] rotations = [si.shape.rotations[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] scales = [si.shape.scales[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] opacities = [si.shape.opacities[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] shcoeffs = [si.shape.shcoeffs[si.primitiveindex(i)] for i in idxs] # Transform to local space localo = [scalevector(dotproduct(transpose(rot), subtract(o, c)), 1.0/s) for rot, o, c, s in zip(rotations, [rayso[i] for i in idxs], centers, scales)] locald = [scalevector(dotproduct(transpose(rot), d), 1.0/s) for rot, d, s in zip(rotations, [raysd[i] for i in idxs], scales)] # Compute peak location tpeak = [-dotproduct(lo, ld) / dotproduct(ld, ld) for lo, ld in zip(localo, locald)] # Evaluate density at peak density = [kernel.evaluatedensity(lo, ld, tp) for lo, ld, tp in zip(localo, locald, tpeak)] # Compute transmission transmittance = [1.0 - min(op den, 0.9999) for op, den in zip(opacities, density)] # Evaluate emission emission = [] for i in range(len(idxs)): shdeg = sqrt(len(shcoeffs[i]) / 3.0 - 1.0) shbasis = sheval(raysd[idxs[i]], shdeg) val = sum(c b for c, b in zip(shcoeffs[i], shbasis)) + 0.5 emission.append(max(val, 0.0)) emission = [0.0 if not isfinite(e) else e for e in emission] # Compute local contribution Le = [beta[idxs[i]] (1.0 - transmittance[i]) emission[i] for i in range(len(idxs))] # Update radiance accumulator if mode == 'primal': for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): L[idx] = addvectors(L[idx], Le[i]) else: for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): L[idx] = subtractvectors(L[idx], Le[i]) # Update throughput for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): beta[idx] = transmittance[i] # Adjoint indirect radiance if mode == 'adjoint': Lrind = [] for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): Lrind.append(scalevector(addvectors(L[idx], Le[i]), transmittance[i] / transmittance[i])) Lo = [addvectors(Le[i], Lrind[i]) for i in range(len(idxs))] Lo = [0.0 if not isfinite(v) else v for v in Lo] for i, idx in enumerate(idxs): deltaL[idx] = addvectors(deltaL[idx], Lo[i]) # Spawn new ray origin for idx in idxs: rayso[idx] = addvectors(si.p[idx], scalevector(raysd[idx], 1e-4)) active[idx] = active[idx] & si.isvalid(idx) depth[idx] += 1 # Kill insignificant paths betamax = max(beta) for idx in range(N): active[idx] = active[idx] & (betamax > 0.01) # Russian Roulette if userr and any(active): rrprob = max(betamax, 0.1) rractive = [(depth[idx] >= rrdepth) and (beta[idx] < 0.1) for idx in range(N)] rrcandidates = [idx for idx in range(N) if active[idx] and rractive[idx]] for idx in rrcandidates: beta[idx] /= rrprob rrcontinue = [random() < rrprob for in rrcandidates] for i, idx in enumerate(rrcandidates): active[idx] = active[idx] & rrcontinue[i] # Limit depth for idx in range(N): active[idx] = active[idx] & (depth[idx] < maxdepth) # Convert to linear space if needed if srgbprimitives: L = [srgbtolinear(c) for c in L] return L if mode == 'primal' else deltaL def Kernel(kerneltype, fullrange, normalized): class K: def evaluatedensity(self, o, d, t): # Placeholder for kernel-specific density evaluation return 1.0 return K() def sheval(d, degree): # Standard spherical harmonic basis evaluation return [1.0] (degree + 1)2 def srgbtolinear(c): return [max(0, (x/12.92) if x <= 0.04045 else ((x+0.055)/1.055)2.4) for x in c] def scene.rayintersect(o, d, flags, coherent): class SI: def isvalid(self, i): return True def shape(self): class S: def shapetype(self, i): return SHAPEELLIPSOID def centers(self, i): return [0,0,0] def rotations(self, i): return [[1,0,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] def scales(self, i): return [1,1,1] def opacities(self, i): return 1.0 def shcoeffs(self, i): return [1.0] return S() def p(self, i): return [0,0,0] return SI() ALL, BACKFACECULLING, SHAPEELLIPSOID = 1, 2, 10 def transpose(m): return [list(row) for row in zip(m)] def subtract(a, b): return [a[i]-b[i] for i in range(3)] def scalevector(v, s): return [xs for x in v] def dotproduct(a, b): return sum(xy for x, y in zip(a, b)) def addvectors(a, b): return [a[i]+b[i] for i in range(3)] def subtractvectors(a, b): return [a[i]-b[i] for i in range(3)] def isfinite(x): return x == x def random(): return 0.5 Numerical Stability: Transmission calculation clips opacity density to 0.9999 to avoid 1.0 - 1.0 numerical issues. SH Emission: Emission calculation adds 0.5 before clamping to 0.0 to handle potential negative values from SH evaluation. Self-Intersection: Ray origin is offset by 10^{-4} along the ray direction to prevent self-intersection after scattering. The Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator is a simplified rendering method for volumetric primitives that accounts exclusively for absorption, ignoring scattering and emission. It is designed for tomography applications where the goal is to visualize density or attenuation rather than photometric appearance. Unlike its sibling Volumetric Primitive PRB Integrator, which handles scattering media, this integrator treats the volume as a purely absorbing medium. The Volumetric Primitive PRB Integrator is a path tracing method for rendering scattering and emissive media represented by mixtures of kernel-based volumetric primitives (e.g., Gaussians, Epanechnikov) rather than voxel grids or point clouds. It modifies standard volumetric path tracing by replacing medium interaction routines with primitive-specific transmittance evaluation, free-flight distance sampling, and albedo evaluation. It distinguishes itself from its sibling, the Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator, by supporting scattering and emissive media via multiple importance sampling with PDF balancing, whereas the tomography integrator integrates density with no scattering. The Epanechnikov kernel variant uses a closed-form solution for transmittance calculation. Free-flight distance sampling requires numerical root-finding methods (e.g., Newton-Raphson) due to the complexity of the analytical solution for multiple primitives. The 3D Epanechnikov kernel is defined as: Ei(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \frac{15}{8\pi} (\frac{7}{3} |\Sigmai|)^{1/2} [1 - \frac{1}{7} d(\mathbf{x})] & \text{if } d(\mathbf{x}) \le 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where d(\mathbf{x}) = (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}i)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{c}i). The Epanechnikov kernel has finite support, generating more compact primitive shells than Gaussian, enabling more efficient acceleration structures and faster rendering, especially suitable for modeling sharp edges. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is generally faster than MLP-based neural volume rendering (e.g., Instant-NGP) because it avoids expensive MLP evaluations per sample. The Epanechnikov kernel is faster than the Gaussian kernel due to its finite support and compact shells. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of primitives and their associated attributes (geometry, opacity, SH coefficients). It is significantly more memory-efficient than dense voxel grids for high-resolution scenes. Strengths: Physically based rendering (PBR) integration, supporting global illumination, soft shadows, and complex camera models. High compression rate compared to explicit voxel-based methods. Flexible control over quality vs. performance via max primitive depth. Limitations: Requires numerical root-finding for free-flight sampling in complex overlapping scenarios. Not directly compatible with rasterization pipelines without modification (unlike 3D Gaussian Splatting). When to Use: Suitable for applications requiring physically accurate rendering of scattering/emissive media with high quality and flexibility, such as scientific visualization, VFX, and PBR-based training data generation. When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time rasterization pipelines where extreme speed is required and physical accuracy is secondary (consider 3D Gaussian Splatting). Not suitable for tomography where only absorption is needed (consider Volumetric Primitive Tomography Integrator). The Volumetric Primitive Radiance Field Integrator originates from the work on volumetric primitives for modeling and rendering scattering and emissive media. It was developed to address the limitations of MLP-based neural radiance fields (slow evaluation) and explicit voxel-based methods (lack of PBR support). The method builds on the principles of neural volume rendering but replaces the implicit MLP representation with a mixture of kernel-based volumetric primitives. It is implemented in the volprim library by Meta Platforms, Inc.. facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, https://github.com/facebookresearch/volumetricprimitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Don’t Splat your Gaussians: Volumetric Ray-Traced Primitives for Modeling and Rendering Scattering and Emissive Media (2025), https://qiita.com/matumu20/items/67b33681dc97ccbcc849, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
