name: Learned Fields Prediction with Clamping
head: Clamped Field Output Prediction
body: This method predicts field outputs from a neural network model and applies clamping to log density (\log ne) and log temperature (\log T) based on configured bounds. It serves as the final output layer in neural volume rendering pipelines, ensuring that physically impossible or numerically unstable values are constrained before further processing. It differs from raw field output prediction by enforcing hard bounds on specific physical quantities, addressing the instability of unconstrained neural network outputs in tomographic reconstruction. Inputs and Outputs Input: A batch of 3D positions x{AABB} mapped to an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). Output: Clamped log density \log ne and clamped log temperature \log T. Data Structures The method relies on a configuration object containing: clamp: Boolean flag enabling/disabling clamping. lognemin, lognemax: Float bounds for log density. logtempmin, logtempmax: Float bounds for log temperature. boundsdict: Dictionary containing global bounds for density (ne), temperature (temp), and radius (r) used to validate constraints. Steps 1. Predict Raw Outputs: Call the underlying prediction function self.predictfieldoutputs(xAABB) to obtain raw outputs outs. This function returns a structure containing logne and logtemp. 2. Extract Log Density: Extract logne = outs.logne. 3. Clamp Log Density: If self.clamp is True, clamp logne to the range [self.lognemin, self.lognemax]. The clamping operation is defined as: \log ne^{clamped} = \text{clamp}(\log ne, \log n{e, min}, \log n{e, max}) where \text{clamp}(v, min, max) = \min(\max(v, min), max). 4. Extract Log Temperature: Extract logtemp = outs.logtemp. 5. Clamp Log Temperature: If logtemp is not None and self.clamp is True, clamp logtemp to the range [self.logtempmin, self.logtempmax]. The clamping operation is defined as: \log T^{clamped} = \text{clamp}(\log T, \log T{min}, \log T{max}). 6. Return Results: Return the processed outs, logne, and logtemp. Parameters lognemin, lognemax: Derived from boundsdict["ne"]["globalboundlo"] and boundsdict["ne"]["globalboundhi"]. logtempmin, logtempmax: Derived from boundsdict["temp"]["globalboundlo"] and boundsdict["temp"]["globalboundhi"]. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but bounds are printed with 6 decimal places precision. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Invalid Bounds: If boundsdict["temp"]["globalboundlo"] >= boundsdict["temp"]["globalboundhi"], a ValueError is raised, indicating invalid temperature bounds after combining PSI and atomic constraints. None Temperature: If logtemp is None, clamping is skipped for temperature. Precision: Bounds are stored and processed as float64 in grid construction, suggesting high precision requirements for boundary definitions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictwithclamping(self, xAABB): # Step 1: Predict raw outputs outs = self.predictfieldoutputs(xAABB) # Step 2: Extract log density logne = outs.logne # Step 3: Clamp log density if enabled if self.clamp: logne = max(self.lognemin, min(logne, self.lognemax)) # Step 4: Extract log temperature logtemp = outs.logtemp # Step 5: Clamp log temperature if enabled and present if self.clamp and logtemp is not None: logtemp = max(self.logtempmin, min(logtemp, self.logtempmax)) # Step 6: Return results return outs, logne, logtemp A baseline method using a positional encoder and MLP for density reconstruction. It differs from the main clamping method by using a specific MLP architecture for density only, without explicit temperature clamping logic in the description. Choose this for simple density-only reconstruction tasks. Definition: Input is 3D Cartesian position mapped to AABB. Parameters: Final-layer bias is initialized to the midpoint of the log ne clamp range. Layout: Input is concatenation of raw position, axis-wise Fourier positional encoding (L=6 bands, freq 2^0 \dots 2^5, 36 dims), and spherical-harmonic encoding (degree 2, 9 dims), totaling 48 dims. MLP has 4 hidden layers, width 256, SiLU activations, and a linear final layer outputting a single scalar \log{10} ne. Total parameters: 210,177. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of prediction points, dominated by the underlying predictfieldoutputs call. Memory Complexity: Minimal, only storing bounds and intermediate tensors. Strengths: Prevents numerical instability and unphysical values in neural volume rendering. Limitations: Hard clamping may introduce discontinuities if the network output frequently exceeds bounds. When to use: When physical bounds are known and strict adherence is required. When not to use: When soft constraints or differentiable relaxation is preferred. Originated in the CoroNeRF project for neural tomographic reconstruction. Developed to handle the joint reconstruction of electron density and temperature in plasma imaging. The clamping mechanism addresses the challenge of ensuring physically plausible outputs from neural networks trained on sparse or noisy tomographic data. name: MLP Model (Density Baseline)
head: positional encoder + MLP
body: A baseline neural volume representation that maps 3D Cartesian positions to density using a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with explicit positional encoding. It serves as a reference for density reconstruction capabilities in neural tomography, distinct from hash-grid or latent-feature approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Cartesian position vector \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3, typically mapped to an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). Output: A single scalar representing the base-10 logarithm of the number density, \log{10} ne. Data Structures and Layout: The input to the MLP is a concatenated vector of dimension 48, formed by: 1. Raw Position: 3 dimensions. 2. Fourier Positional Encoding: Axis-wise Fourier features with L=6 bands. Frequencies are 2^0, \dots, 2^5. For each axis, this generates \sin(2^k \pi x) and \cos(2^k \pi x) for k \in \{0, \dots, 5\}. Total dimensions: 2 \text{ (sin/cos)} \times 3 \text{ (axes)} \times 6 \text{ (bands)} = 36 dimensions. 3. Spherical Harmonic Encoding: Degree 2 spherical harmonics of the unit position direction. Total dimensions: (2+1)^2 = 9 dimensions. MLP Architecture: Hidden Layers: 4 layers, each with width 256. Activation: SiLU (Sigmoid Linear Unit) for hidden layers. Output Layer: Linear layer producing a single scalar. Initialization: The final layer bias is initialized to the midpoint of the configured \log ne clamp range. Total Parameters: 210,177. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Normalize or map the input 3D position \mathbf{x} to the AABB. 2. Compute the Fourier positional encoding \mathbf{f}{fourier}(\mathbf{x}) using the specified frequencies and axes. 3. Compute the spherical harmonic encoding \mathbf{f}{sh}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) where \hat{\mathbf{x}} is the normalized direction of \mathbf{x}. 4. Concatenate the raw position, Fourier encoding, and SH encoding: \mathbf{v} = [\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{f}{fourier}(\mathbf{x}), \mathbf{f}{sh}(\hat{\mathbf{x}})]. 5. Pass \mathbf{v} through the MLP: \mathbf{h}1 = \text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}1 \mathbf{v} + \mathbf{b}1) \mathbf{h}2 = \text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}2 \mathbf{h}1 + \mathbf{b}2) \mathbf{h}3 = \text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}3 \mathbf{h}2 + \mathbf{b}3) \mathbf{h}4 = \text{SiLU}(\mathbf{W}4 \mathbf{h}3 + \mathbf{b}4) \log{10} ne = \mathbf{w}5 \cdot \mathbf{h}4 + b5 6. Apply clamping to \log{10} ne based on configured bounds (as per parent method Parent). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def fourierencoding(x, numbands=6): """ Computes axis-wise Fourier positional encoding. x: (3,) array Returns: (36,) array """ freqs = np.array([2k for k in range(numbands)]) # 2^0 to 2^5 # x is (3,), freqs is (6,) # We want sin(2 pi freq xaxis) and cos(...) # Expand dims: x -> (1, 3), freqs -> (6, 1) # Result shape: (6, 3) for sin, (6, 3) for cos # Flatten to (36,) # Calculate arguments: 2 pi freqk xi # Using broadcasting: (6, 1) (1, 3) -> (6, 3) args = 2.0 math.pi np.outer(freqs, x) sinvals = np.sin(args).flatten() cosvals = np.cos(args).flatten() return np.concatenate([sinvals, cosvals]) def sphericalharmonicdegree2(x): """ Computes degree 2 spherical harmonics for the direction of x. x: (3,) array Returns: (9,) array """ # Normalize x to get direction norm = np.linalg.norm(x) if norm == 0: return np.zeros(9) d = x / norm # Degree 2 SH basis functions (real spherical harmonics) # Y0^0 y00 = 0.5 math.sqrt(1.0 / math.pi) # Y1^-1, Y1^0, Y1^1 y1m1 = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 math.pi)) d[1] # -y y10 = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 math.pi)) d[2] # z y11 = math.sqrt(3.0 / (4.0 math.pi)) d[0] # x # Y2^-2, Y2^-1, Y2^0, Y2^1, Y2^2 # Standard real SH definitions y2m2 = math.sqrt(15.0 / math.pi) d[0] d[1] y2m1 = math.sqrt(15.0 / math.pi) d[1] d[2] y20 = math.sqrt(5.0 / (16.0 math.pi)) (3 d[2]2 - 1) y21 = math.sqrt(15.0 / math.pi) d[2] d[0] y22 = math.sqrt(15.0 / math.pi) (d[0]2 - d[1]2) return np.array([y00, y1m1, y10, y11, y2m2, y2m1, y20, y21, y22]) def mlpmodelforward(x, weights, biases): """ Forward pass of the MLP baseline. x: (3,) raw position weights: list of 5 weight matrices [W1, W2, W3, W4, W5] biases: list of 5 bias vectors [b1, b2, b3, b4, b5] Returns: scalar log10ne """ # 1. Encode rawpos = x fourierfeat = fourierencoding(x) shfeat = sphericalharmonicdegree2(x) # 2. Concatenate inputvec = np.concatenate([rawpos, fourierfeat, shfeat]) # (48,) # 3. MLP Layers h = inputvec for i in range(4): # Linear + SiLU h = np.dot(h, weights[i]) + biases[i] h = h / (1 + np.exp(-h)) # SiLU approximation or explicit SiLU function # 4. Output Layer log10ne = np.dot(h, weights[4]) + biases[4] return log10ne Parameters: Fourier bands L=6. MLP hidden width: 256. MLP hidden layers: 4. Final layer bias initialization: Midpoint of \log ne clamp range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero in spherical harmonic calculation if \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{0}. Precision issues with high-frequency Fourier features if positions are not normalized to the AABB. A variant where the expression vector ei and encoded position \boldsymbol{\mu} are fed directly into an MLP \boldsymbol{\rho}(\boldsymbol{\mu}) to predict color and opacity, without a basis of latent features. It uses 5 linear layers with leaky ReLU activations. On the INSTA dataset with 295k Gaussians, it achieves 32.08 PSNR with 0.010s rendering time. It is slower than the proposed HeadGaS method despite lacking MLP computation during rendering, due to the significantly larger number of Gaussians (295k vs 28k). Complexity: The model has 210,177 parameters. The forward pass involves fixed-size matrix multiplications and trigonometric evaluations, making it independent of scene complexity (number of objects) but dependent on query frequency. Performance: Not given in the sources for this specific baseline in isolation, but compared to HeadGaS (which uses 28k Gaussians and 0.004s rendering), the HeadGaS Baseline (295k Gaussians) takes 0.010s. The MLP density baseline is used in neural tomography contexts where field fidelity is prioritized. Strengths: Simple architecture, explicit control over frequency bands via positional encoding. Limitations: High parameter count relative to simple functions; requires careful initialization of the final bias. Originated as a baseline in neural tomography research to evaluate density reconstruction capabilities using positional encoders and MLPs. It contrasts with more complex representations like multiresolution hash grids. name: Sigma Network Layer
body: The Sigma Network Layer is a reparameterization technique used in neural volume rendering to subdivide the output channels of color and density samples by modifying the last layer of each subnetwork, ensuring that the final rendered colors remain unaffected by the subdivision. It builds on the RGB Network Layer by extending the reparameterization strategy to the density prediction branch, allowing for increased model capacity or parallelism without altering the underlying radiance field representation. The method operates in two distinct phases: a static reparameterization of network weights and biases to support channel subdivision, and a dynamic execution of the forward pass using shared memory optimizations for density computation. Inputs: orgweight: Original weight tensor of shape [N, d{out}, d{in}], where N is the number of subnetworks. orgbias: Original bias tensor of shape [N, d{out}]. xyzsembedding: Input coordinate embeddings of shape [N, d{in}]. Outputs: modifiedweight: Reparameterized weight tensor. modifiedbias: Reparameterized bias tensor. density: Computed density values \sigma. The implementation relies on specific tensor layouts to facilitate the channel splitting and concatenation operations described in the sources. 1. Bias Rearrangement: The bias tensor [N, d{out}] is rearranged into [N, d{out}/4, 4] by splitting the output dimension d{out} into c=4 channels. This is achieved via a permutation operation. 2. Weight Rearrangement: The weight tensor [N, d{out}, d{in}] is rearranged into [N, d{out}/2, 2, d{in}] by splitting the output dimension d{out} into c=2 channels. blockdim: Thread block dimension. sigmaninput: Number of input neurons. sigmamodelsize: Model size parameter. netwidth: Width of the hidden layer. sigmasmpreload: Number of weight elements preloaded to shared memory. sigmanoutput: Number of output neurons (typically 1 for density). sigmalayer1base: Base index for the second hidden layer weights. This phase modifies the network parameters to allow for channel subdivision while preserving the original function output. 1. Bias Transformation: Rearrange orgbias from [N, d{out}] to [N, d{out}/4, 4]. Concatenate the rearranged bias along the channel dimension (dim=2) with itself. Rearrange the result back to [N, d{out}]. 2. Weight Transformation: Rearrange orgweight from [N, d{out}, d{in}] to [N, d{out}/2, 2, d{in}]. Concatenate the rearranged weight along the channel dimension (dim=2) with itself. Rearrange the result back to [N, d{out}, d{in}]. 3. Return: The modified weight and bias. This phase computes the density \sigma using a multi-threaded approach, likely on a GPU using a compute shader or similar parallel execution model (e.g., Taichi). 1. Initialization: Iterate over subnetworks sn in self.paddblocknetwork[None]. Calculate thread ID tid = sn % blockdim. 2. Weight Preloading: Preload network weights into shared memory weight array: weight[k] = self.sigmaweights[k] for k in range(self.sigmasmpreload). 3. Input Loading: Load input embeddings into shared memory inputval: inputval[i, tid] = self.xyzsembedding[sn, i] for i in range(self.sigmaninput). Synchronize threads: ti.simt.block.sync(). 4. First Hidden Layer: If sn < didlaunchnum, compute the first hidden layer. For each neuron i in range(self.netwidth), compute the dot product of input and weights: \text{temp} = \sum{j} \text{input\val}[j, \text{tid}] \times \text{weight}[i \times \text{sigma\n\input} + j] Store result in hid1[i, tid]. 5. Second Hidden Layer (Output): Compute the density output. For each output i in range(self.sigmanoutput), apply ReLU activation to hid1 and compute the dot product with the second layer weights: \text{temp} = \sum{j} \text{data\type}(\max(0.0, \text{hid1}[j, \text{tid}])) \times \text{weight}[\text{sigma\layer1\base} + i \times \text{net\width} + j] Store in hid2[i, tid]. 6. Final Density: Compute the final density using the exponential function: \sigma = \exp(\text{hid2}[0, \text{tid}]) Store the result: self.out1[self.temphit[sn]] = datatype(ti.exp(hid2[0, tid])). 7. Storage: Store all hidden layer outputs: self.finalembedding[sn, i] = hid2[i, tid]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def reparameterizesigmalayer(orgweight, orgbias): """ Reparameterizes the sigma network layer to support channel subdivision. orgweight: Tensor of shape [nsubnetworks, dout, din] orgbias: Tensor of shape [nsubnetworks, dout] Returns: modifiedweight, modifiedbias """ # Bias transformation # Rearrange bias from [N, dout] to [N, dout/4, 4] bias = rearrange(orgbias, 'n (d c) -> n d c', c=4) # Concatenate bias with itself along channel dimension bias = concatenate([bias, bias], dim=2) # Rearrange back to [N, dout] bias = rearrange(bias, 'n d c -> n (d c)') # Weight transformation # Rearrange weight from [N, dout, din] to [N, dout/2, 2, din] weight = rearrange(orgweight, 'n (d c) i -> n d c i', c=2) # Concatenate weight with itself along channel dimension weight = concatenate([weight, weight], dim=2) # Rearrange back to [N, dout, din] weight = rearrange(weight, 'n d c i -> n (d c) i') return weight, bias def computesigmadensity(sn, tid, xyzsembedding, sigmaweights, netwidth, sigmaninput, sigmanoutput, sigmalayer1base, hid1, hid2, out1, temphit, finalembedding): """ Computes the density for a specific subnetwork and thread. """ # Load input embeddings into shared memory for i in range(sigmaninput): inputval[i, tid] = xyzsembedding[sn, i] # Synchronize threads ti.simt.block.sync() # First hidden layer computation if sn < didlaunchnum: for i in range(netwidth): temp = 0.0 for j in range(sigmaninput): temp += inputval[j, tid] sigmaweights[i sigmaninput + j] hid1[i, tid] = temp # Second hidden layer (output layer for sigma) for i in range(sigmanoutput): temp = 0.0 for j in range(netwidth): # ReLU activation activated = max(0.0, hid1[j, tid]) temp += datatype(activated) sigmaweights[sigmalayer1base + i netwidth + j] hid2[i, tid] = temp # Final density computation density = datatype(ti.exp(hid2[0, tid])) out1[temphit[sn]] = density # Store hidden layer outputs for i in range(sigmanoutput): finalembedding[sn, i] = hid2[i, tid] Precision: The use of datatype suggests potential precision issues if not explicitly defined. Standard floating-point precision (FP32) is typical, but FP16 may be used for performance, requiring careful handling of underflow/overflow in the exponential function. Boundary Conditions: The condition sn < didlaunchnum implies that not all subnetworks may be active in every launch. Proper initialization of hid1 and hid2 for inactive threads is necessary to avoid garbage values. Shared Memory Synchronization: The ti.simt.block.sync() call is critical to ensure all threads have loaded their input embeddings before proceeding to the computation phase. Failure to synchronize can lead to race conditions. Time Complexity: The reparameterization step is O(N \cdot d{out} \cdot d{in}) and is performed once. The density computation is O(N \cdot \text{net\width} \cdot d{in}) per ray sample. Memory Complexity: The reparameterized weights and biases have the same size as the original parameters. Shared memory usage is proportional to sigmasmpreload and sigmaninput. Performance: The use of shared memory and parallel thread execution allows for efficient computation of density values, particularly on GPU architectures. Strengths: Allows for increased model capacity without changing the final rendered output. Efficient parallel execution. Limitations: Requires careful management of shared memory and synchronization. The reparameterization adds complexity to the model implementation. The Sigma Network Layer is part of the neural volume rendering pipeline, specifically within the context of progressively-connected light field networks. It was introduced to address the need for efficient view synthesis by subdividing output predictions while maintaining consistency with the original network's output. The implementation details provided in the notes are from an unofficial Taichi-based renderer. Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, https://github.com/Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Progressively-connected Light Field Network for Efficient View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2207.04465, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Subdivision of Output Layers
head: Subdiv output layers
body: Subdivision of Output Layers is a reparameterization technique used in neural volume rendering to increase the number of depth samples (output layers) during training without altering the final rendered color or density of existing rays. It modifies the last layer of each subnetwork by duplicating and rearranging weight and bias tensors, ensuring that the network's output remains consistent with the previous, coarser resolution. This method is distinct from Subdivision of Input Layers, which preserves input ray colors by modifying the first and last layers to handle increased input dimensionality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Original weight tensor W{org} of shape [n{subnetworks}, d{out}, d{in}] and bias tensor B{org} of shape [n{subnetworks}, d{out}]. Output: Modified weight tensor W{new} and bias tensor B{new} with the same shapes as the inputs, but with reparameterized values. Data Structures: The method operates on PyTorch-style tensor layouts where dimensions are explicitly split and concatenated. n{subnetworks}: Number of subnetworks. d{out}: Original output dimension (number of depth samples/channels). d{in}: Input dimension. Steps: 1. Bias Rearrangement: Split the output dimension d{out} of the bias tensor into c=4 channels. The shape [n{subnetworks}, d{out}] becomes [n{subnetworks}, d{out}/4, 4]. 2. Bias Duplication: Concatenate the rearranged bias with itself along the channel dimension (dim=2). The shape becomes [n{subnetworks}, d{out}/4, 8]. 3. Bias Reshape: Rearrange the concatenated bias back to the original output dimension structure [n{subnetworks}, d{out}]. 4. Weight Rearrangement: Split the output dimension d{out} of the weight tensor into c=2 channels. The shape [n{subnetworks}, d{out}, d{in}] becomes [n{subnetworks}, d{out}/2, 2, d{in}]. 5. Weight Duplication: Concatenate the rearranged weight with itself along the channel dimension (dim=2). The shape becomes [n{subnetworks}, d{out}/2, 4, d{in}]. 6. Weight Reshape: Rearrange the concatenated weight back to the original output dimension structure [n{subnetworks}, d{out}, d{in}]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def subdivoutputlayers(orgweight, orgbias): """ Reparameterizes the last layer of neural subnetworks to subdivide output layers. Args: orgweight: Tensor of shape [nsubnetworks, dout, din] orgbias: Tensor of shape [nsubnetworks, dout] Returns: weight: Modified weight tensor of shape [nsubnetworks, dout, din] bias: Modified bias tensor of shape [nsubnetworks, dout] """ # Step 1-3: Subdivide Bias # Rearrange bias from [n, dout] to [n, dout/4, 4] # Note: dout must be divisible by 4 bias = rearrange(orgbias, 'n (d c) -> n d c', c=4) # Concatenate with itself along dim=2 (channel dimension) bias = concatenate([bias, bias], dim=2) # Rearrange back to [n, dout] bias = rearrange(bias, 'n d c -> n (d c)') # Step 4-6: Subdivide Weight # Rearrange weight from [n, dout, din] to [n, dout/2, 2, din] # Note: dout must be divisible by 2 weight = rearrange(orgweight, 'n (d c) i -> n d c i', c=2) # Concatenate with itself along dim=2 (channel dimension) weight = concatenate([weight, weight], dim=2) # Rearrange back to [n, dout, din] weight = rearrange(weight, 'n d c i -> n (d c) i') return weight, bias Parameters: c=4 for bias splitting. c=2 for weight splitting. These constants are fixed in the source description. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Divisibility: The original output dimension d{out} must be divisible by 4 for the bias operation and by 2 for the weight operation. If d{out} is not divisible by 4, the bias rearrangement will fail. Precision: The method relies on exact tensor reshaping and concatenation. No averaging or scaling factors are applied to the output layers, unlike the input layer subdivision which uses a factor of 0.5. A reparameterization technique to maintain unchanged input ray colors after depth subdivision by modifying the weight matrices and bias vectors of the first and last layer functions of the networks. It splits the input dimension d{in} into c=2 channels, duplicates the weights, and averages them by multiplying by 0.5 to ensure hidden features remain unaffected. The bias remains unchanged. This validates that the color of each input ray is kept unchanged. Time and Memory Complexity: The operation is O(n{subnetworks} \cdot d{out} \cdot d{in}) for weights and O(n{subnetworks} \cdot d{out}) for biases, as it involves tensor rearrangement and concatenation. Memory usage remains constant as the output tensor shapes are identical to the input shapes. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: The method allows for progressive refinement of depth samples (Dk = D \times 2^k) during training stages. It scales with the number of subnetworks and the depth resolution. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Ensures consistency of rendered colors and densities when increasing depth resolution, preventing artifacts from sudden changes in sampling density. Limitations: Requires d{out} to be divisible by 4 for bias operations. Only applies to the last layer of the subnetworks. When to use it and when not: Use when progressively increasing the number of depth samples in a neural volume rendering pipeline to improve rendering quality without disrupting the learned representation. Do not use if the output dimension is not divisible by 4 or if the goal is to modify input ray properties rather than output depth samples. Originated in the "Progressively-connected Light Field Network for Efficient View Synthesis" paper (2022). The technique is part of a broader strategy involving progressive connection and depth subdivision to enhance rendering quality in neural view synthesis. It is used in conjunction with consistency losses for regularization. name: CNN Post-Processing Network
head: Lightweight CNN
body: A post-processing convolutional neural network applied to MLP-decoded results to reduce boundary artifacts. It sets itself apart from its siblings by focusing on spatial consistency of the final image rather than field prediction or sigma estimation, using neighboring regions to improve texture detail without causing multiview inconsistency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The rendered image (or feature map) produced by the preceding MLP-based volume rendering step. Output: The refined image with reduced boundary artifacts and enhanced texture detail. Data Structures: The CNN consists of five convolution layers, each with 32 channels. No skip connections are added. The network is shallow, typically 3 layers in some implementations. Steps: 1. Input Padding: Apply "reflectance" padding to the input features to handle boundary conditions for convolution. 2. Convolutional Processing: Pass the padded input through the convolutional layers. Each layer uses 3x3 kernels and ReLU activations. 3. Output Trimming: Remove the padding values from the outputs of the convolutional layers to prevent checkerboard artifacts. 4. Feature-to-RGB Conversion: Apply a feed-forward perceptron layer to convert the representation from feature space to RGB space. Formulas: Loss Function (for training): Mean Squared Error (MSE) between the MLP-decoded results and the ground-truth (GT) volume. L = \text{MSE}(I{MLP}, I{GT}) Where I{MLP} is the image decoded by the MLP and I{GT} is the ground truth. Parameters: CNN Architecture: 5 convolution layers, 32 channels each. Kernel Size: 3x3. Activation: ReLU. Quantization: 9 bits applied at the end of CNN training without subsequent fine-tuning. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Checkerboard Artifacts: Prevented by removing padding values in the outputs. Multiview Inconsistency: Avoided because the CNN is very shallow and performs no upsampling. Artifact Removal Limit: Limited capacity does not guarantee removal of boundary artifacts when distortion is significant; remaining artifacts may still negatively impact rendering quality. Training Overhead: Adds approximately 5 minutes to encoding time and 100 KB to model size. Decoding Overhead: Adds approximately 50 seconds to decoding time due to sequential inference. A specific application of the CNN to mitigate rendering artifacts caused by inconsistent outputs between adjacent disjoint volumetric blocks along their boundaries. It sets itself apart by targeting the multiscale spatiotemporal representation's block-boundary issues. Choose this when using ECNR or similar block-based neural representations. It applies a lightweight CNN module to the output of the finest scale MLPs. The CNN consists of five convolution layers, each with 32 channels, with no skip connections. It is trained using an MSE loss between MLP-decoded results and ground-truth volume. After training, quantization with 9 bits is applied without fine-tuning. Boundary Artifact Mitigation A technique where the super-resolution network accepts multiple feature maps alongside the low-resolution color image to improve reconstruction quality, specifically adapted for volumetric rendering. It sets itself apart from standard image super-resolution by incorporating volumetric-specific auxiliary data (depth, color-opacity vectors) to resolve ambiguities inherent in volume rendering, such as undefined depth in transparent regions. Supplementary Feature Input for Super-Resolution 2D Refinement Layers is an optional post-processing module applied to rendered images to enhance texture detail and prevent "texture sticking" artifacts under viewpoint changes. It builds on CNN Post-Processing Network by specifically employing alias-free convolutional layers to ensure temporal and spatial consistency when the camera moves. It addresses the limitation of standard CNNs where high-frequency details may appear to stick to the image plane rather than the 3D geometry. 2D Refinement Layers Time Complexity: Decoding adds approximately 50 seconds due to sequential inference. Despite this, it remains significantly faster than neurcomp. Memory Complexity: Adds approximately 100 KB to model size. Strengths: Reduces boundary artifacts; improves texture detail; avoids multiview inconsistency; prevents checkerboard artifacts. Limitations: Limited capacity may not remove significant distortion artifacts; adds sequential inference time; does not process each timestep independently in multiscale representations. When to Use: When using block-based neural representations (like ECNR) where boundary artifacts are prominent, and multiview consistency is critical. When Not to Use: When extreme distortion exists that exceeds the CNN's capacity to correct, or when minimal decoding overhead is required. Originated in the context of Efficient Compressive Neural Representation (ECNR) for time-varying volumetric datasets. It was introduced to address the issue of inconsistent outputs between adjacent blocks in multiscale spatiotemporal representations. The method was also explored in AligNeRF for high-fidelity neural radiance fields. ECNR: Efficient Compressive Neural Representation of Time-Varying Volumetric Datasets, https://doi.org/10.1109/pacificvis60374.2024.00017, fetched 2026-10-26 AligNeRF: High-Fidelity Neural Radiance Fields via Alignment-Aware Training, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52729.2023.00013, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Supplementary Feature Input for Super-Resolution
head: Multi-Channel Input for SR Network
body: A technique where the super-resolution network accepts multiple feature maps alongside the low-resolution color image to improve reconstruction quality, specifically adapted for volumetric rendering. It sets itself apart from standard image super-resolution by incorporating volumetric-specific auxiliary data (depth, color-opacity vectors) to resolve ambiguities inherent in volume rendering, such as undefined depth in transparent regions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of feature maps concatenated along the channel dimension. Output: A single high-resolution RGB image. Data Structures: The input tensor has shape (H, W, C{total}), where H and W are the spatial dimensions and C{total} is the sum of channels from all supplementary features. The specific layout of the input channels is: 1. Final Rendered Color: 3 channels (RGB). 2. Depth Map: 1 channel. 3. Color-Opacity Vector: 4 channels (RGBA) at the position of maximum alpha along the ray, though the opacity channel is not shown in the source figures. 4. Motion Vector Image: 2 channels (typically u, v displacement components). Numbered Steps: 1. Render the standard RGB volume image. 2. Compute the depth value at the position of maximum alpha along each ray, as standard depth is not well-defined for volumetric data and this point contributes most to the final rendering. 3. Save the color and opacity values at this same maximum-alpha position. 4. Compute motion vectors between consecutive frames. 5. Concatenate the RGB image, depth map, color-opacity vector, and motion vectors into a single multi-channel tensor. 6. Pass the concatenated tensor through the CNN Post-Processing Network [7179-cnn-post-processing-network.md] to convert the feature space to RGB space. 7. Output the reconstructed high-resolution RGB image. Formulas: Let I{LR} be the low-resolution RGB image (3 channels). Let D be the depth map (1 channel). Let C{op} be the color-opacity vector at max alpha (4 channels). Let M be the motion vector field (2 channels). The input to the SR network is F{in} = \text{Concat}(I{LR}, D, C{op}, M). The output is I{HR} = \text{SR\Network}(F{in}). Parameters: Neighborhood Clamping: A 3 \times 3 neighborhood clamping is applied, which produced reasonably effective results for the volume rendering case. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Ambiguity: Standard depth is not well-defined for volumetric data, so using depth at maximum alpha mitigates ambiguity by selecting the most visually significant surface. Opacity Visibility: The opacity channel in the color-opacity vector is included in the input structure but is not visually distinct or explicitly shown in the source figures. This method is a deep learning pipeline for super-resolving volume-rendered images by supplementing the network with auxiliary volumetric features (depth, color, opacity at max alpha) and using temporal warping with a reweighting network to handle motion and lighting changes. It sets itself apart from standard image super-resolution by generating low-resolution inputs directly from the volume renderer without anti-aliasing and by incorporating volumetric-specific auxiliary features to resolve depth ambiguity inherent in volume rendering. It builds on Supplementary Feature Input for Super-Resolution by adding temporal consistency mechanisms. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Improves reconstruction quality by providing geometric and volumetric context that RGB alone lacks. Limitations: Requires rendering additional auxiliary buffers, increasing rendering time and memory bandwidth. Depth is still an approximation for complex volumetric structures. Developed for medical volume visualization using direct volume rendering. It builds on previous works showing that reconstruction networks for surface data benefit from depth inputs. It adapts these surface-based insights to volumetric data by using max-alpha depth as a proxy for surface depth. Deep Learning Based Super-Resolution for Medical Volume Visualization with Direct Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-20713-68, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Volumetric Super-Resolution with Auxiliary Features and Temporal Warping
head: Deep Learning Based Super-Resolution for Medical Volume Visualization, SR-Volume
body: This method is a deep learning pipeline for super-resolving volume-rendered images by supplementing the network with auxiliary volumetric features (depth, color, opacity at max alpha) and using temporal warping with a reweighting network to handle motion and lighting changes. It sets itself apart from standard image super-resolution by generating low-resolution inputs directly from the volume renderer without anti-aliasing and by incorporating volumetric-specific auxiliary features to resolve depth ambiguity inherent in volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current low-resolution rendered frame, N previous low-resolution rendered frames, and auxiliary feature maps for all frames. Outputs: One high-resolution frame. Data Structures and Layouts: 1. Input Feature Images: For each frame, the following are provided: Final rendered color image: 3 channels (RGB). Depth: 1 channel. Defined as the depth at the point of maximum alpha value along the ray. Color-opacity vector: 4 channels (RGBA). Color and opacity values at the point of maximum alpha along the ray. Motion vector image: 2 channels (horizontal and vertical displacement) between the current frame and the previous frame. 2. Residual Block: Consists of two 3x3 convolutional layers, each followed by a ReLU activation. A 1x1 convolutional layer in the skip connection transforms the input shape for addition. The output of the second convolution is added to the input before the final ReLU. 3. Reweighting Network: A 3-layer convolutional network that generates a pixel-wise reweighting channel for each previous frame. 4. Autoencoder: A fully convolutional encoder-decoder hierarchy with skip connections, adopted from Hofmann et al.. Numbered Steps: 1. Generate Input Features: Render the volume to get a final color image (RGB). Calculate depth at the point of maximum alpha along the ray. Save color and opacity values at this same point. Generate a screen-space 2D motion vector image (2 channels) between current and previous frames. 2. Feature Extraction: Pass all input frames (current and previous, excluding motion vector) through a Residual Block to extract features. 3. Zero Upsampling: Upsample low-resolution input frames and extracted feature maps to the target high-resolution resolution using zero upsampling, where every low-res pixel is surrounded by zero values in high-res space. 4. Warping: Backward warp the upsampled previous frames and their feature maps to align with the current frame using the motion vectors. 5. Concatenation: Concatenate all warped previous frames/features with the current frame's features. 6. Reweighting: Pass concatenated data through a 3-layer Convolutional Reweighting Network to generate a pixel-wise reweighting channel for each previous frame. 7. Elementwise Product: Multiply each previous frame's feature maps (after zero upsampling and warping) by its corresponding reweighting channel. 8. Autoencoder Reconstruction: Concatenate the reweighted previous frames with the current frame's feature map and feed into an Autoencoder (fully convolutional encoder-decoder with skip connections) to produce the final high-resolution output. Formulas: The loss function used for training is the Charbonnier loss: L = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \rho(yi - zi) where: N is the number of pixels. yi is the output pixel value. zi is the ground truth high-resolution pixel value. \rho(x) = \sqrt{x^2 + \epsilon^2}. \epsilon = 1 \times 10^{-8} is the Charbonnier epsilon for numerical stability. Parameters: Charbonnier epsilon (\epsilon): 1 \times 10^{-8}. Input Resolution: Low-resolution inputs are rendered at 480x480, 240x240, or 120x120 without temporal anti-aliasing. Target Resolution: High-resolution ground truth and output resolution is 1920x1920. Upsampling Ratios: The network supports 4x4, 8x8, and 16x16 super-resolution. Temporal History: The network accepts N previous frames, with experiments using N=1, 2, \text{and } 3. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Depth Ambiguity: Depth is not well-defined for volumetric data. The method resolves this by using the depth at the point of maximum alpha value along the ray, as this point contributes most to the final rendering. Motion Vector Limitations: Motion vectors do not reflect shading and lighting changes between frames, nor do they handle disocclusion and ghosting directly. The reweighting network is used to weed out inconsistent samples caused by these factors. Low-Level Feature Loss: As the upsampling ratio increases (e.g., 16x16), the quality of reconstructed images deteriorates, and the network struggles to reconstruct low-level features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. ResidualBlock(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels, outchannels): super(ResidualBlock, self).init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu1 = nn.ReLU() self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(outchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu2 = nn.ReLU() self.skipconv = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, outchannels, kernelsize=1) def forward(self, x): identity = self.skipconv(x) out = self.relu1(self.conv1(x)) out = self.conv2(out) out = out + identity out = self.relu2(out) return out class ReweightingNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels): super(ReweightingNetwork, self).init() self.conv1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, 32, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu1 = nn.ReLU() self.conv2 = nn.Conv2d(32, 16, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu2 = nn.ReLU() self.conv3 = nn.Conv2d(16, 1, kernelsize=3, padding=1) def forward(self, x): out = self.relu1(self.conv1(x)) out = self.relu2(self.conv2(out)) out = self.conv3(out) return torch.sigmoid(out) class Autoencoder(nn.Module): def init(self, inchannels, outchannels): super(Autoencoder, self).init() self.enc1 = nn.Conv2d(inchannels, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.enc2 = nn.Conv2d(64, 128, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.dec1 = nn.Conv2d(128, 64, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.dec2 = nn.Conv2d(64, outchannels, kernelsize=3, padding=1) self.relu = nn.ReLU() self.skipconv1 = nn.Conv2d(64, 64, kernelsize=1) self.skipconv2 = nn.Conv2d(128, 128, kernelsize=1) def forward(self, x): e1 = self.relu(self.enc1(x)) e2 = self.relu(self.enc2(e1)) d1 = self.relu(self.dec1(e2) + self.skipconv1(e1)) out = self.dec2(d1) return out def zeroupsample(x, scalefactor): h, w = x.shape[2], x.shape[3] newh, neww = h scalefactor, w scalefactor upscaled = torch.zeros((x.shape[0], x.shape[1], newh, neww), device=x.device) upscaled[:,:,::scalefactor,::scalefactor] = x return upscaled def backwardwarp(features, motionvectors): B, C, H, W = features.shape gridy, gridx = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H), torch.arange(W), indexing='ij') gridy = gridy.float().unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(B, 1, H, W).to(features.device) gridx = gridx.float().unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(B, 1, H, W).to(features.device) flow = motionvectors.permute(0, 2, 3, 1) grid = torch.stack((gridx, gridy), dim=-1) grid = grid / torch.tensor([W - 1, H - 1], device=features.device) 2 - 1 grid = grid + flow / torch.tensor([W - 1, H - 1], device=features.device) 2 warped = F.gridsample(features, grid, mode='bilinear', paddingmode='zeros') return warped def trainstep(currentlrfeatures, previouslrfeatures, motionvectors, groundtruthhr, scalefactor): N = len(previouslrfeatures) currentfeatures = ResidualBlock(8, 64)(currentlrfeatures) previousfeatures = [ResidualBlock(8, 64)(prev) for prev in previouslrfeatures] currentfeaturesup = zeroupsample(currentfeatures, scalefactor) previousfeaturesup = [zeroupsample(prev, scalefactor) for prev in previousfeatures] warpedpreviousfeaturesup = [backwardwarp(prev, motionvectors) for prev in previousfeaturesup] concatfeatures = torch.cat([currentfeaturesup] + warpedpreviousfeaturesup, dim=1) reweightingnet = ReweightingNetwork(concatfeatures.shape[1]) reweightingchannels = [] for i in range(N): startch = 64 + i 64 endch = startch + 64 reweightingchannels.append(reweightingnet(concatfeatures[:, startch:endch,:,:])) reweightedpreviousfeatures = [prev rew for prev, rew in zip(warpedpreviousfeaturesup, reweightingchannels)] finalinput = torch.cat([currentfeaturesup] + reweightedpreviousfeatures, dim=1) autoencoder = Autoencoder(finalinput.shape[1], 3) outputhr = autoencoder(finalinput) epsilon = 1e-8 loss = torch.mean(torch.sqrt((outputhr - groundtruthhr)2 + epsilon2)) return loss, outputhr Time and Memory Complexity: The method involves multiple convolutional operations (Residual Blocks, Reweighting Network, Autoencoder) and warping operations. The complexity is dominated by the convolutional layers and the number of previous frames N. Memory usage increases with N due to storing and processing previous frames. Measured Performance: CTA-Cardio (8x8): With additional RGBA features, PSNR 38.09 dB, SSIM 0.9705. Without, PSNR 37.07 dB, SSIM 0.9683. Manix (16x16): PSNR 33.65 dB, SSIM 0.9471. Runtime: 10 fps (0.1018 seconds per frame) on the current implementation. Scaling: Performance gains are observed with additional previous frames (N=1, 2, 3). However, as the upsampling ratio increases (e.g., 16x16), the quality of reconstructed images steadily deteriorates. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Incorporates volumetric-specific auxiliary features to handle depth ambiguity. Uses temporal warping and reweighting to handle motion and lighting changes. Generates low-res inputs directly from the volume renderer, avoiding artifacts from blurring/downscaling. Limitations: Designed for offline application; runtime performance is not optimized (10 fps). Quality deteriorates at high upsampling ratios (16x16). When to use it: Medical volume visualization where high-quality super-resolution is needed and offline processing is acceptable. When not to use it: Real-time applications requiring higher frame rates without hardware acceleration (e.g., TensorRT). Origin: The method was introduced by S. Devkota et al. in the paper "Deep Learning Based Super-Resolution for Medical Volume Visualization with Direct Volume Rendering". History and Development: The reconstruction network architecture was inspired by Xiao et al. [21], and the autoencoder architecture was adopted from Hofmann et al. [8]. The method was developed to address the specific challenges of super-resolving volume-rendered images, such as depth ambiguity and the lack of standard anti-aliasing in volume rendering. Usage: Used for medical volume visualization on datasets such as CTA-Cardio, Manix, and CTA Abdomen Panoramix. name: 2D Refinement Layers
head: Alias-free 2D CNN Refinement
body: 2D Refinement Layers is an optional post-processing module applied to rendered images to enhance texture detail and prevent "texture sticking" artifacts under viewpoint changes. It builds on CNN Post-Processing Network by specifically employing alias-free convolutional layers to ensure temporal and spatial consistency when the camera moves. It addresses the limitation of standard CNNs where high-frequency details may appear to stick to the image plane rather than the 3D geometry. Inputs and Outputs Input: The rendered RGB image I{rendered} of resolution H \times W. Output: The refined RGB image I{refined} of resolution H \times W. Data Structures The refinement network is a shallow 2D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN). Architecture: 2 hidden layers. Layer Dimension: 16 channels per layer. Kernel Size: 3 \times 3. Activation: Not specified in sources, but standard for such shallow networks (e.g., ReLU or LeakyReLU). Assuming ReLU for non-linearity between layers. Sampling: Critical sampling is used to maintain alias-free properties. Steps 1. Input Preparation: Take the rendered image I{rendered}. 2. First Convolutional Layer: Apply a 3 \times 3 convolution with 16 output channels to the input. The convolution uses alias-free layers with critical sampling. 3. Non-linearity: Apply a non-linear activation function (e.g., ReLU) to the output of the first layer. 4. Second Convolutional Layer: Apply a 3 \times 3 convolution with 16 output channels to the result of step 3. This layer also uses alias-free layers with critical sampling. 5. Final Convolution: Apply a 3 \times 3 convolution with 3 output channels (RGB) to produce the final refined image. The source mentions "2 hidden layers," implying the final layer is the output layer. 6. Output: Return I{refined}. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def refineimage(renderedimage): # renderedimage: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) # Using a hypothetical alias-free conv implementation # Layer 1: 3x3 conv, 16 channels, alias-free, critical sampling x = aliasfreeconv2d(renderedimage, outchannels=16, kernelsize=3, sampling='critical') x = relu(x) # Standard activation assumed # Layer 2: 3x3 conv, 16 channels, alias-free, critical sampling x = aliasfreeconv2d(x, outchannels=16, kernelsize=3, sampling='critical') x = relu(x) # Standard activation assumed # Output Layer: 3x3 conv, 3 channels (RGB) refinedimage = aliasfreeconv2d(x, outchannels=3, kernelsize=3, sampling='critical') return refinedimage Parameters Hidden Layers: 2 Hidden Layer Dimension: 16 Kernel Size: 3 Sampling: Critical sampling (alias-free) Edge Cases and Pitfalls Texture Sticking: Standard CNNs may cause textures to stick to the 2D image plane during viewpoint changes. Using alias-free layers with critical sampling mitigates this. Optional Application: The refinement is optional and depends on the dataset. It may not be necessary for all scenes or datasets. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. However, as a shallow CNN with small kernel sizes and low channel dimensions, it is computationally lightweight compared to the volume rendering process itself. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The network has a small number of parameters (16 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 + 16 \times 16 \times 3 \times 3 + 16 \times 3 \times 3 \times 3 weights, plus biases), fitting easily in memory. Strengths: Prevents texture sticking artifacts under viewpoint changes; improves texture detail. Limitations: Optional; may not be needed for all datasets; adds a post-processing step. When to use: When rendering images that exhibit texture sticking artifacts or when higher texture fidelity is required. When not to use: When computational resources are extremely limited and the visual improvement is negligible, or for datasets where the base rendering is already sufficient. The 2D Refinement Layers method was introduced in the context of VoxGRAF: Fast 3D-Aware Image Synthesis with Sparse Voxel Grids. It leverages alias-free layers [21] to ensure that the refinement does not introduce artifacts that are inconsistent with 3D geometry. The approach is part of a broader effort to improve the visual quality of neural volume rendering methods. name: Textured Mesh Refinement
head: Deep Shading, Mesh Rendering Refinement
body: Textured Mesh Refinement is a neural rendering baseline that renders a geometric mesh approximation of a scene and refines the resulting image using a neural network to recover missing details and correct shading errors. It differs from voxel-based rerendering methods by using a mesh representation to estimate UV maps via projective texturing, though it faces similar limitations regarding GAN artifacts and shadow estimation. Inputs: 1. A textured mesh of the scene (vertices, faces, and texture coordinates). 2. Target camera viewpoint parameters. 3. Light position. 4. Target image T (for optimization/training). Outputs: Refined image I{refined} that approximates the target image T, with missing regions completed and fine details enhanced. Data Structures: Mesh: Defined by vertex positions, face connectivity, and UV coordinates. Buffers: Diffuse color buffer and depth buffer rendered from the mesh. Network: A Pix2Pix network (or similar image-to-image translation network) takes the rendered buffers and light position as input channels. Steps: 1. Estimate UV Map: Use projective texturing to estimate the UV map of the mesh relative to the target camera viewpoint. 2. Position Mesh: Place the mesh in the desired position corresponding to the target camera view. 3. Render Buffers: Render the scene to generate: Diffuse color buffer C{diffuse}. Depth buffer D. 4. Prepare Input Tensor: Concatenate C{diffuse}, D, and the light position (as an additional channel or encoded feature) to form the input tensor I{input}. 5. Neural Refinement: Pass I{input} through a neural network (e.g., Pix2Pix) to predict the refined image I{refined}. 6. Optimization: Optimize the network parameters to minimize the difference between I{refined} and the target image T. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Regions: The re-projected textured mesh may have missing regions (e.g., due to occlusion or incomplete reconstruction) which the network must complete. Artifacts: The method may produce typical GAN artifacts and fail to estimate shadows properly, similar to Image Translation models. Detail Loss: While it completes missing regions, the refined result may have less detail compared to more advanced methods like Neural Point Cloud Rendering. Performance: On 'scene0010 00', the PSNR and SSIM of the refined images (re-projected textured mesh) are 22.208 and 0.86, respectively. This is lower than the proposed Neural Point Cloud Rendering method (PSNR 24.421, SSIM 0.901). Strengths: Can complete missing regions in the re-projected textured mesh. Limitations: Faces similar limitations to Image Translation, including GAN artifacts and poor shadow estimation, despite using a mesh representation instead of voxels. The results may lack fine details compared to other neural rendering approaches. Textured Mesh Refinement is used as a comparison method in neural rendering research to evaluate the effectiveness of mesh-based representations versus point cloud or voxel-based representations. It is also referred to as "Deep Shading" in some contexts, where it is compared against voxel-based rerendering methods. What it is: A specific implementation of Textured Mesh Refinement that uses projective texturing to estimate UV maps and a Pix2Pix network for refinement. Differentiation: Uses a mesh representation instead of voxels. When to choose: When a mesh representation is preferred over voxels, but similar limitations to image translation apply. name: MLP with Positional Encoding and IOR Activation
head: MLP with Skip Connections and Refractive Index Activation
body: A multi-layer perceptron that maps 3D coordinates to a scalar field (e.g., refractive index) using positional encoding, residual skip connections, and a domain-specific activation function to constrain output ranges. It is distinguished by a post-processing activation function that maps the MLP's raw output to a positive range [1, \infty), ensuring physical validity for light propagation. Inputs: x: Input feature vector, typically the positional encoding of 3D coordinates (x, y, z). degpoint: Integer degree for positional encoding. netdepth: Integer depth of the hidden layers. netwidth: Integer width of the hidden layers. doskip: Boolean flag for skip connections. activation: Choice of activation function (ReLU or ELU). iorden: Denominator for the IOR scaling factor. Outputs: eta: Scalar field representing the refractive index at the input position. Data Structures: The MLP consists of a sequence of dense (fully connected) layers. Weights are initialized using He uniform initialization. The final layer outputs a single scalar value (outchannel = 1). Parameters: netdepth: Default 4. netwidth: Default 128 (for dark matter simulations) or 256 (for gas/neural field simulations). degpoint: Default 4 or 6. iorden: Default 400. doskip: Default True for dark matter, False for gas/neural fields. activation: nn.relu for dark matter, nn.elu for gas/neural fields. Algorithm: 1. Positional Encoding: Apply positional encoding to the input coordinates x. Let x{enc} = \text{posenc}(x, \text{deg\point}). 2. Skip Connection Storage: Store the encoded input for potential skip connections: inputs = x{enc}. 3. Hidden Layers: Iterate i from 0 to \text{net\depth} - 1: a. Apply a dense layer with width \text{net\width}: x = \text{Dense}{\text{net\width}}(x). b. Apply the chosen activation function: x = \text{Activation}(x). c. Skip Connection Logic: If doskip is true, and i > 0, and i is a multiple of \lfloor \text{net\depth} / 2 \rfloor: i. Concatenate the current representation x with the original encoded input inputs along the feature axis: x = \text{concat}(x, inputs). 4. Output Layer: Apply a final dense layer with 1 output channel: y = \text{Dense}1(x). 5. IOR Activation: Apply the refractive index activation function to constrain the output: \eta = \frac{\text{softplus}(y - 2)}{\text{ior\den}} + 1 Where \text{softplus}(z) = \ln(1 + e^z). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jax.numpy as jnp from jax import nn def posenc(x, degpoint): """Standard positional encoding.""" scales = jnp.array([2.0 (2 i / degpoint) for i in range(degpoint // 2)]) x = jnp.expanddims(x scales, axis=-1) return jnp.concatenate([jnp.sin(x), jnp.cos(x)], axis=-1) def denselayer(x, weight, bias): """Standard fully connected layer.""" return x @ weight + bias def mlpwithioractivation(x, params, degpoint, netdepth, netwidth, doskip, activationfn, iorden): """ x: Input coordinates, shape (..., 3) params: Dictionary containing weights and biases for the MLP degpoint: Degree of positional encoding netdepth: Number of hidden layers netwidth: Width of hidden layers doskip: Boolean, use skip connections activationfn: JAX activation function (e.g., nn.relu or nn.elu) iorden: Denominator for IOR scaling """ # 1. Positional Encoding xenc = posenc(x, degpoint) # 2. Store inputs for skip connections inputs = xenc # 3. Hidden Layers currentx = xenc skipinterval = netdepth // 2 for i in range(netdepth): # Apply dense layer with He uniform initialization (handled by params) currentx = denselayer(currentx, params[f'layer{i}weight'], params[f'layer{i}bias']) # Apply activation currentx = activationfn(currentx) # Skip connection logic if doskip and i > 0 and i % skipinterval == 0: # Concatenate with original encoded input currentx = jnp.concatenate([currentx, inputs], axis=-1) # 4. Final Dense Layer y = denselayer(currentx, params['outputweight'], params['outputbias']) # 5. IOR Activation eta = nn.softplus(jnp.squeeze(y) - 2) / iorden + 1.0 return eta Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The softplus function is numerically stable, but subtracting 2 before applying it is critical for the specific scaling used in the source implementation. Boundaries: The output \eta is strictly greater than 1.0 because \text{softplus}(z) > 0 for all real z, and \text{ior\den} > 0. This ensures the refractive index is physically valid (greater than vacuum). Degenerate Input: If netdepth is 0 or 1, the skip connection logic may not trigger or may behave unexpectedly depending on the modulo arithmetic. The default depth is 4. A dark matter variant of the MLP that uses netwidth=128, doskip=True, and activation=relu. It is distinguished from the gas variant by its shallower width and enabled skip connections, which optimize it for capturing the diffuse scattering properties of dark matter fields. Choose this variant when simulating dark matter distributions. See MLPactdm. A gas/neural field variant of the MLP that uses netwidth=256, doskip=False, and activation=elu. It is distinguished from the dark matter variant by its increased width, disabled skip connections, and ELU activation, which better model the continuous density gradients of gas. Choose this variant when simulating gas or neural field volumes. See MLPactgas. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. This method originates from the rtnf (Refractive Neural Fields) project, an unofficial implementation for neural volume rendering with refractive effects. It adapts the standard MLP architecture used in NeRF-like models to predict refractive index fields instead of color or density. The specific activation function is designed to map unconstrained neural network outputs to the physical domain of refractive indices. brandonyzhao/rtnf, https://github.com/brandonyzhao/rtnf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Neural Radiance Caching
head: NRC, Neural Surface Cache
body: Neural Radiance Caching (NRC) is a neural rendering technique that uses a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict photorealistic pixel colors from per-pixel feature buffers containing world-space positions and auxiliary features. It enables real-time rendering by continuously overfitting to the current lighting and geometry using sparse light paths spawned from the camera view, operating within a strict training budget. Unlike sibling methods that may require scene-specific retraining or lack dynamic support, NRC processes each pixel independently, allowing feature buffers to be treated as per-pixel feature vectors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Per-pixel feature buffers containing the world-space position \mathbf{x} and additional auxiliary encoded dimensions (e.g., view direction). Output: Predicted photorealistic pixel color (RGB). Data Structures: Feature Buffer: A per-pixel array storing the concatenated encoded position and auxiliary features. Multi-resolution Hash Encoding: A data structure mapping input coordinates to feature vectors across multiple grid resolutions. The encoding uses the same representational capacity as Neural Irradiance Volume (NIV). MLP: A non-convolutional network processing each pixel independently. Parameters: MLP Architecture: 2 hidden layers with 64 neurons each. Training Budget: 1 millisecond per frame to support animated content. Encoding: Multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22]. Steps: 1. Feature Buffer Construction: For each pixel, retrieve the world-space position \mathbf{x} and any additional auxiliary features (e.g., view direction). 2. Position Encoding: Encode the world-space position \mathbf{x} using multi-resolution hash encoding. 3. Feature Concatenation: Encode the auxiliary features using the same encoding scheme and concatenate them with the encoded position. 4. MLP Inference: Feed the concatenated vector into the MLP to predict the pixel color. 5. Online Training: Continuously update the MLP using sparse light paths spawned from the camera view, adhering to the 1 ms per frame training budget. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def concatenate(vectors): """Concatenate a list of 1D vectors into a single 1D vector.""" result = [] for v in vectors: result.extend(v) return result def neuralradiancecachingpixel(xworld, auxfeatures, mlp, hashencoder): """ Predicts color for a single pixel using Neural Radiance Caching. Args: xworld: World-space 3D position vector. auxfeatures: List of auxiliary feature vectors (e.g., view direction). mlp: The trained MLP model. hashencoder: Multi-resolution hash encoder instance. Returns: Predicted RGB color. """ # Step 2: Encode position encodedpos = hashencoder.encode(xworld) # Step 3: Encode auxiliary features and concatenate encodedaux = [hashencoder.encode(feat) for feat in auxfeatures] inputvector = concatenate([encodedpos] + encodedaux) # Step 4: MLP Inference color = mlp.forward(inputvector) return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Collisions: Hash collisions cause microstructure artifacts at the finest grid resolution, which do not disappear with longer training times. Model Capacity: Increasing the MLP capacity reduces bias but does not significantly improve quality because variance is the dominant error source in related deferred variants. Training Budget: The 1 ms per frame constraint requires efficient encoding and small network sizes to maintain real-time performance. Time Complexity: Runtime overhead is approximately 0.7 ms at 1920x1080 resolution, including both training and inference costs. Memory Complexity: Uses 2 or 4 grid levels, consuming 0.16 to 1.20 MB of memory. Measured Performance: Achieves 133 FPS with multi-resolution hash encoding versus 147 FPS with triangle wave encoding at 1920x1080 resolution. Strengths: Real-time performance, online adaptability to dynamic scenes, and high quality for static scenes. Limitations: Hash collisions produce persistent microstructure artifacts, and the method requires careful budget management to stay within the 1 ms training limit. When to Use: Suitable for real-time rendering of scenes with static geometry and dynamic objects where online adaptation is needed. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes where hash collision artifacts are unacceptable or where hardware acceleration for the specific encoding is unavailable. Neural Radiance Caching was introduced by Müller et al. in 2021. It builds on the concept of neural surface caches but adapts it for real-time rendering with online learning. The method was later augmented with multi-resolution hash encoding [MESK22] to improve quality and performance. It is used in real-time rendering applications, particularly within the instant neural graphics primitives framework. name: Temporal Accumulation (Closest Hit)
body: Temporal Accumulation (Closest Hit) stabilizes stochastic or noisy direct volume ray casting results by blending the current frame with a history buffer of previous frames. Unlike simple frame averaging, this method specifically selects the "closest hit" (the sample with the smallest depth/opacity weight) between the current frame and the accumulated history to maintain geometric stability and reduce ghosting artifacts during camera movement. The method executes as a multi-pass rendering pipeline or fragment shader logic block that manages a history buffer. It requires the current frame's color/depth and the previous frame's reprojection data. Inputs: currentframe: Current render pass output (color and depth/opacity). currentdepth: Depth value for the current pixel. historybuffer: Accumulated data from previous frames. cameramatrices: Current and previous View-Projection matrices (V{curr}, P{curr}, V{prev}, P{prev}). cameraposition: World-space camera origin. Outputs: accumulatedframe: The final stabilized color buffer. The history is typically stored in a texture array or a circular buffer to save memory. 1. History Texture Array (historyframes): Dimensions: \{width, height, N\HISTORY\ACC\}. Format: RGBA32Float or equivalent surface format. Usage: RENDERATTACHMENT | TEXTUREBINDING. Indexing: Layer index is framecount % NHISTORYACC. 2. Normal/Depth Texture (normaldepthtexture): Dimensions: \{width, height, 1\}. Format: RGBA32Float. Stores depth and potentially normal/opacity info for reprojection. 3. Uniforms (for shader passes): uCurrent: Sampler for current frame. uCurrentDepth: Sampler for current depth. uHistory: Sampler for history buffer. uInvViewProj: Inverse of current View-Projection matrix. uPrevViewProj: Inverse of previous View-Projection matrix. uCamPos: Camera world position. uBlend: Blending weight (0.0 to 1.0). uHistoryValid: Boolean flag (0 or 1) indicating if history is valid. uInvFrameNumber: Inverse of current frame count (for running average). uMix: Mixing factor for accumulator/frame blend. 1. Initialization (Closest Hit Texture Initialization): Reset the accumulation buffer to a value indicating "no hit" (e.g., vec4(-1)) when the scene changes or at startup. Clear uHistoryValid to 0. 2. Ray Pass (Current Frame Generation): Render the volume using standard ray casting. Output the result to historyframes at layer framecount % NHISTORYACC and to normaldepthtexture. Store the current frame's depth/opacity in the w component of the color vector for closest-hit comparison. 3. Reprojection and Blending (Temporal Pass): Check Validity: If uHistoryValid == 0, output currentframe directly and set uHistoryValid = 1. World Position Reconstruction: Compute ray direction in world space from NDC coordinates (u, v): \mathbf{ndc} = (2u - 1, 2v - 1) \mathbf{p}{near} = V{curr}^{-1} P{curr}^{-1} (\mathbf{ndc}x, \mathbf{ndc}y, -1, 1) \mathbf{p}{far} = V{curr}^{-1} P{curr}^{-1} (\mathbf{ndc}x, \mathbf{ndc}y, 1, 1) \mathbf{rd} = \text{normalize}\left(\frac{\mathbf{p}{far}.xyz}{\mathbf{p}{far}.w} - \frac{\mathbf{p}{near}.xyz}{\mathbf{p}{near}.w}\right) Fetch depth d from uCurrentDepth. Compute world position \mathbf{worldPos}: \mathbf{worldPos} = \mathbf{uCamPos} + \mathbf{rd} \cdot (d > 0 ? d: 200000.0) Pitfall: Pixels with no cloud (d \le 0) cause large parallax errors during reprojection; substituting a far distance (200000.0) handles this. Project to Previous Frame: Transform \mathbf{worldPos} to previous clip space: \mathbf{prevClip} = V{prev} P{prev} (\mathbf{worldPos}, 1) Compute previous UV: \mathbf{prevUv} = \left(\frac{\mathbf{prevClip}.xy}{\mathbf{prevClip}.w}\right) \cdot 0.5 + 0.5 Boundary Check: Evaluate screen validity: onScreen = prevClip.w > 0.0 && all(greaterThanEqual(prevUv, vec2(0.0))) && all(lessThanEqual(prevUv, vec2(1.0))). If !onScreen (i.e., prevClip.w <= 0.0 or prevUv outside [0, 1]), output currentframe. Closest Hit Selection: Sample current frame: \mathbf{frame} = \text{texture}(\mathbf{uCurrent}, \mathbf{vUv}). Sample history: \mathbf{acc} = \text{texture}(\mathbf{uHistory}, \mathbf{prevUv}). Let w{frame} and w{acc} be the opacity/depth weights (typically the w component). If w{frame} > 0 and w{acc} > 0: \mathbf{oClosest} = (w{frame} < w{acc}) ? \mathbf{frame}: \mathbf{acc} If only w{frame} > 0: \mathbf{oClosest} = \mathbf{frame}. If only w{acc} > 0: \mathbf{oClosest} = \mathbf{acc}. If neither: \mathbf{oClosest} = \mathbf{acc}. Noise Clamping and Blending: Compute 3x3 neighborhood min/max of current sample to bound noise: \mathbf{lo} = \min{x,y \in \{-1,0,1\}} \text{texture}(\mathbf{uCurrent}, \mathbf{vUv} + (x,y)\Delta\mathbf{uv}) \mathbf{hi} = \max{x,y \in \{-1,0,1\}} \text{texture}(\mathbf{uCurrent}, \mathbf{vUv} + (x,y)\Delta\mathbf{uv}) Pad bounds: \mathbf{lo}' = \mathbf{lo} - (\mathbf{hi} - \mathbf{lo}) \cdot 0.25 - 0.002 \mathbf{hi}' = \mathbf{hi} + (\mathbf{hi} - \mathbf{lo}) \cdot 0.25 + 0.002 Clamp history sample: \mathbf{hist} = \text{clamp}(\mathbf{acc}, \mathbf{lo}', \mathbf{hi}') Blend: \mathbf{oColor} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{hist}, \mathbf{oClosest}, \mathbf{uBlend}) Alternative: Use running average: \mathbf{oColor} = \mathbf{acc} + (\mathbf{frame} - \mathbf{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{uInvFrameNumber}. Alternative: Use mixing factor: \mathbf{oColor} = \text{mix}(\mathbf{acc}, \mathbf{frame}, \mathbf{uMix}). 4. Final Output: Present the accumulated frame to the screen. Unverified code. Noise Clamping texelsize = vec2(1.0 / currentframetex.width, 1.0 / currentframetex.height) lo = currentframetex[currentframeuv] hi = currentframetex[currentframeuv] for y in [-1, 0, 1]: for x in [-1, 0, 1]: neighbor = texture(currentframetex, currentframeuv + vec2(x, y) texelsize) lo = min(lo, neighbor) hi = max(hi, neighbor) pad = (hi - lo) 0.25 + 0.002 loclamped = lo - pad hiclamped = hi + pad histclamped = max(loclamped, min(hiclamped, historysample)) # 8. Blend result = mix(histclamped, closest, ublend) return result NHISTORYACC: Number of history frames stored. Must be >0. uBlend: Interpolation factor between clamped history and current closest hit. uMix: Blending factor between accumulator and frame. uInvFrameNumber: Inverse of current frame number for running average. uHistoryValid: Flag to skip reprojection on first frame or scene change. Disocclusion/Ghosting: Caused by camera movement or object animation. Handled by clamping history samples to the padded min/max neighborhood of the current frame. Empty Pixels: Depth \le 0 causes large parallax errors. Substitute a far distance (e.g., 200000.0). Buffer Overflow: If framecount overflows or NHISTORYACC is 0, layer indexing fails. Use modulo arithmetic framecount % NHISTORYACC. Scene Changes: Camera/object transformations invalidate history. Clear the buffer and reset uHistoryValid. Memory Limits: Multi-frame buffers require dynamic memory modification, which is limited. Single-buffer overwrite (circular buffer) is preferred. A fragment shader pass that initializes the closest hit texture to a value indicating no hit (e.g., vec4(-1)). This resets the accumulation buffer when scene conditions change or at startup. A rendering pass that blends an accumulated buffer with a new frame using a mixing factor. It samples the accumulator and current frame, selects the closest depth/position (smaller w value) if both are valid, and blends them using uMix. A technique to combine frames over time to reduce noise, using an exponential moving average or simple frame blending based on frame count. It updates the accumulator as acc + (frame - acc) uInvFrameNumber. A fragment shader pass that averages color values across multiple layers of a 2D texture array. It loops through all layers, sums the values, and divides by the number of layers. Used for temporal accumulation or history blending. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel per frame, assuming constant number of history layers and fixed neighborhood size for clamping. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times N\HISTORY\ACC) for the history buffer. Single-buffer overwrite reduces this to O(W \times H) if only the immediate previous frame is stored. Performance: Significantly reduces noise in stochastic ray casting, allowing for fewer samples per frame. Strengths: Stabilizes flickering, reduces noise, maintains sharp edges via closest-hit selection. Limitations: Ghosting artifacts during rapid motion or disocclusion if clamping is insufficient. Requires reprojection matrices and depth buffers. Temporal accumulation has been used in volume rendering to stabilize stochastic results, such as those from sparse voxel octrees or cloud rendering. The "Closest Hit" variant specifically addresses the issue of selecting the most relevant historical data to prevent ghosting of occluded geometry.
