name: vtkSlicerGPURayCastVolumeMapper
head: GPGPU Ray Cast Mapper
body: Renders a volume using ray casting on a 3D texture. It distinguishes itself by exposing parameters for distance-based color blending and ICPE scaling, building on GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper which manages the general GPU-accelerated pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D scalar field data, transfer functions, camera parameters, and bounding box definition. Output: 2D rendered image. Data Structures: The mapper maintains the following internal state and OpenGL handles: double VolumeBBoxVertices[8][3]: Stores the 8 vertices of the volume's bounding box, each with 3 coordinates. double VolumeBBoxVerticesColor[8][3]: Stores the 8 vertices of the bounding box with associated color values, each with 3 coordinates. GLfloat ParaMatrix[16]: A 4x4 matrix uniform passed to the shader for ray casting parameters. GLfloat ParaMatrix1[16]: A second 4x4 matrix uniform for additional ray casting parameters. GLuint Volume1Index: OpenGL handle for the volume texture. GLuint ColorLookupIndex: OpenGL handle for the color lookup table (CLUT). GLuint RayCastVertexShader: OpenGL handle for the vertex shader. GLuint RayCastFragmentShader: OpenGL handle for the fragment shader. GLuint RayCastProgram: OpenGL handle for the shader program linking the vertex and fragment shaders. Parameters: DistanceColorBlending (float, default 0.0): Controls brightness falloff with distance; positive values make closer voxels brighter and farther voxels darker. DepthPeelingThreshold (float): Threshold value used for depth peeling operations to handle transparency ordering. ICPEScale (float): Scale parameter for Intensity Contrast Preserving Enhancement (ICPE), used to adjust contrast during rendering. Clipping (int): Boolean flag (0 or 1) to enable or disable clipping planes. Technique (int): Integer selector for the specific rendering technique or mode to be used by the shader. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create OpenGL shaders (vertex and fragment) and link them into RayCastProgram. Generate textures for the volume data (Volume1Index) and the color lookup table (ColorLookupIndex). 2. Parameter Setup: Populate VolumeBBoxVertices with the 8 corners of the input volume's bounding box. Populate VolumeBBoxVerticesColor with corresponding colors if applicable. 3. Matrix Calculation: Compute ParaMatrix and ParaMatrix1 based on the current camera view, projection, and volume bounding box. These matrices define the ray origins and directions in texture space. 4. Shader Uniforms: Upload ParaMatrix, ParaMatrix1, DistanceColorBlending, DepthPeelingThreshold, ICPEScale, Clipping, and Technique to the shader program uniforms. 5. Rendering: Bind the volume texture and CLUT. Draw a geometry that triggers the ray casting in the fragment shader. The fragment shader samples the 3D texture along the rays defined by the matrices, applies the transfer functions, and composites the result. 6. Post-Processing: Apply depth peeling if enabled, using DepthPeelingThreshold to determine transparency handling. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Support: Hardware rendering is unsupported if the input data has more than one independent component or if the hardware lacks required OpenGL extensions. A volume rendering technique implemented in VTK.js that uses a volume actor, volume mapper, and transfer functions (color and opacity) to render 3D scalar field data (volumes) in a WebGL/WebGPU context. It provides a declarative JavaScript API for configuring piecewise transfer functions and gradient-based opacity modulation directly within the browser environment, building on vtkSlicerGPURayCastVolumeMapper which handles the underlying GPU ray casting execution. An abstract superclass for GPU volume rendering using 3D texture mapping in the fragment shader. Actual rendering work is delegated to vtkSlicerGPURayCastVolumeTextureMapper3D. It supports any data type with one component, or two/four non-independent components. Composite blending and intermixed opaque geometry are supported. Multiple volumes can be rendered if sorted back-to-front. Internal volume resolution is resampled to a power of two in each direction, capped at 128x256x256 voxels for 1 or 2 component data, or 128x128x256 voxels for 4 component data. Resolution limits are hardcoded after a GLPROXYTEXTURE3D check because some graphics drivers falsely report support despite lacking texture memory. It does not support more than one independent component or maximum intensity projection. Renders the KDE-generated density volume interactively on the GPU using raycasting, integrating shading models and user-defined opacity emphasis ranges. 1. Create a 3D floating-point texture with normalized gradient in RGB channels and scaled density in the alpha channel. 2. For each sample along the ray, look up the density value in the 3D texture. 3. Calculate color by using the density value as an index into a color map. 4. Combine the color and normalized gradient with either Phong or Gooch shading model to compute the shaded color for the sample. 5. Compute alpha value α based on density ρ and emphasis range (ρmin, ρmax) with multipliers α1 (in-range) and α2 (out-of-range). Values inside the range are scaled by α1. Values outside are scaled by a linear interpolation of α1 and α2. Parameters: α1 (in-range opacity multiplier), α2 (out-of-range opacity multiplier), ρmin and ρmax (density range of emphasis). Opacity formula: \alpha = \begin{cases} \rho \alpha1 & \rho{\min} < \rho < \rho{\max} \\ \rho \left( \left(1 - \frac{\rho}{\rho{\min}}\right) \alpha2 + \frac{\rho}{\rho{\min}} \alpha1 \right) & \rho \le \rho{\min} \\ \rho \left( \left(1 - \frac{\rho - \rho{\max}}{1 - \rho{\max}}\right) \alpha1 + \frac{\rho - \rho{\max}}{1 - \rho{\max}} \alpha2 \right) & \rho \ge \rho{\max} \end{cases} Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performance depends on hardware capabilities and the specific OpenGL extensions supported. Strengths: Provides specific controls for distance-based color blending and ICPE. Limitations: Does not support more than one independent component or maximum intensity projection. Hardware rendering fails if required extensions are missing. When to use: Use for GPU-accelerated volume rendering of scalar fields with single or non-independent multi-component data where distance-based blending or ICPE is desired. When not to use: Do not use for data with multiple independent components or when maximum intensity projection is required. It is designed to work within the CTK (Common Toolkit) and VTK ecosystem, leveraging Qt for the UI and VTK for data handling. jszgz/VolumeRenderer, https://github.com/jszgz/VolumeRenderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Illustrative Rendering of Particle Systems, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe.vmv.vmv13.177-185, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: VTK.js Volume Rendering with Transfer Functions
head: GPU Volume Rendering via VTK, VTK Volume Rendering with Transfer Functions, VTK.js Volume Rendering
body:
A volume rendering technique implemented in VTK.js that uses a volume actor, volume mapper, and transfer functions (color and opacity) to render 3D scalar field data (volumes) in a WebGL/WebGPU context. It provides a declarative JavaScript API for configuring piecewise transfer functions and gradient-based opacity modulation directly within the browser environment, building on vtkSlicerGPURayCastVolumeMapper which handles the underlying GPU ray casting execution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D scalar field data (e.g., DICOM volumes, VTI files) loaded via vtkHttpDataSetReader or similar IO modules. Output: A rendered 2D image displayed in a fullscreen WebGL/WebGPU render window. Data Structures: The method relies on VTK.js object instances rather than raw memory layouts. Key objects include: vtkVolume: The actor representing the volume in the scene graph. vtkVolumeMapper: The mapper responsible for ray casting. vtkColorTransferFunction: Stores RGB points mapping scalar values to colors. vtkPiecewiseFunction: Stores scalar-to-opacity mappings. vtkVolumeProperty: Holds the configuration for shading, interpolation, and transfer functions. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the render context by creating a fullscreen render window with a black background and retrieving the renderer. 2. Instantiate the volume actor and the volume mapper objects. 3. Configure the ray casting step size by setting the sample distance on the volume mapper. 4. Connect the data pipeline by linking the data reader's output port to the volume mapper, and the mapper to the volume actor. 5. Define the color transfer function by creating a vtkColorTransferFunction and adding RGB points. 6. Define the opacity transfer function by creating a vtkPiecewiseFunction and adding points mapping scalar values to opacity. 7. Apply the transfer functions by assigning the CTF and OTF to the volume property for component 0. 8. Configure additional volume properties including interpolation type, gradient opacity modulation, and Phong shading parameters. 9. Add the volume actor to the renderer, reset the camera and clipping range to fit the volume, and trigger the render loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupvolumerendering(reader, renderwindow, renderer): # 1. Initialize render context fullscreenrenderwindow = vtkfullscreenrenderwindow.newinstance(background=[0, 0, 0]) renderer = fullscreenrenderwindow.getrenderer() # 2. Create volume objects actor = vtkvolume.newinstance() mapper = vtkvolumemapper.newinstance() actor.setmapper(mapper) # 3. Configure ray casting step size mapper.setsampledistance(1.1) # 4. Connect data pipeline mapper.setinputconnection(reader.getoutputport()) # 5. Define Color Transfer Function (CTF) ctfun = vtkcolortransferfunction.newinstance() ctfun.addrgbpoint(0, 85 / 255.0, 0, 0) ctfun.addrgbpoint(95, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) ctfun.addrgbpoint(225, 0.66, 0.66, 0.5) ctfun.addrgbpoint(255, 0.3, 1.0, 0.5) # 6. Define Opacity Transfer Function (OTF) ofun = vtkpiecewisefunction.newinstance() ofun.addpoint(0.0, 0.0) ofun.addpoint(255.0, 1.0) # 7. Apply transfer functions to component 0 actor.getproperty().setrgbtransferfunction(0, ctfun) actor.getproperty().setscalaropacity(0, ofun) # 8. Configure volume properties actor.getproperty().setscalaropacityunitdistance(0, 3.0) actor.getproperty().setinterpolationtypetolinear() actor.getproperty().setusegradientopacity(0, True) actor.getproperty().setgradientopacityminimumvalue(0, 2) actor.getproperty().setgradientopacityminimumopacity(0, 0.0) actor.getproperty().setgradientopacitymaximumvalue(0, 20) actor.getproperty().setgradientopacitymaximumopacity(0, 1.0) actor.getproperty().setshade(True) actor.getproperty().setambient(0.2) actor.getproperty().setdiffuse(0.7) actor.getproperty().setspecular(0.3) actor.getproperty().setspecularpower(8.0) # 9. Add to scene and render renderer.addvolume(actor) renderer.resetcamera() renderer.resetcameraclippingrange() renderwindow.render() Formulas: Gradient Opacity Modulation: The opacity O{final} is modulated by the gradient magnitude |
abla f| using a piecewise linear function defined by minimum/maximum values and opacities. If |
abla f| < V{min}, O{grad} = O{min}. If |
abla f| > V{max}, O{grad} = O{max}. Otherwise, O{grad} is linearly interpolated between O{min} and O{max} based on |
abla f| between V{min} and V{max}. Parameters: V{min}=2, O{min}=0.0, V{max}=20, O{max}=1.0. Parameters with Typical Values: sampleDistance: 1.1 (controls ray step size). scalarOpacityUnitDistance: 3.0 (world units between samples). interpolationType: Linear. useGradientOpacity: true. gradientOpacityMinimumValue: 2. gradientOpacityMinimumOpacity: 0.0. gradientOpacityMaximumValue: 20. gradientOpacityMaximumOpacity: 1.0. shade: true. ambient: 0.2. diffuse: 0.7. specular: 0.3. specularPower: 8.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: RGB values in addRGBPoint must be normalized to [0, 1] if provided as 0-255 integers. Boundaries: resetCameraClippingRange() is critical to ensure the volume is not clipped by the near/far planes. Degenerate Input: If the scalar range of the data does not match the transfer function points, the volume may appear black or fully opaque. The OTF example maps 0.0 to 0.0 and 255.0 to 1.0, assuming 8-bit unsigned integer data. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a high-level JavaScript API for complex transfer function configuration and gradient-based opacity modulation in the browser. Limitations: Performance depends on WebGL/WebGPU capabilities and the complexity of the transfer functions and shading models. When to use: When rendering 3D scalar fields in a web browser with customizable color and opacity mappings. When not: When high-performance, real-time ray casting of massive datasets is required without browser constraints. This method is based on examples from VTK.js, specifically demonstrating volume rendering of human skull and chest models using React elements. It leverages the vtkVolumeMapper and vtkVolume classes to implement direct volume rendering with hardware acceleration via WebGL/WebGPU. osama51/VTK-Volume-Rendering, https://github.com/osama51/VTK-Volume-Rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Screen-space ambient occlusion for volume rendering
head: SSAO for volumes, VTK volume SSAO
body: Integrates Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO) into volume rendering by extracting per-fragment depth, world position, and surface normals from the volume ray-casting fragment shader, then feeding them into a standard SSAO pass to compute ambient occlusion for semi-transparent volumes. It differs from standard SSAO by handling the extraction of geometric proxies (position/normal) from volumetric ray-casting data rather than opaque surface geometry, and requires bypassing the standard SSAO API's opaque-pass limitation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, camera matrices (projection, model-view, volume, texture dataset), scalar opacity transfer function, volume property with shading enabled. Outputs: Final color buffer with SSAO darkening, SSAO auxiliary buffers (Position in glFragData[1], Normal in glFragData[2], Depth in glFragDepth). Data Structures: The method relies on VTK's shader replacement hooks to inject variables into the fragment shader pipeline. The following global variables are declared in the shader context: gdataPos: World-space position of the current fragment (from ray-casting). gdataNormal: World-space normal of the current fragment (from ray-casting). gsrcColor: Current fragment color including opacity. gskip: Boolean flag indicating if the fragment should be skipped. lopaqueFragPos: vec3 storing the position of the first opaque fragment found. Initialized to vec3(-1.0). lopaqueFragNormal: vec3 storing the normal of the first opaque fragment found. lupdateDepth: bool flag, initialized to true, ensuring only the first fragment with opacity > 0 writes depth. Numbered Steps: 1. Enable Shading: Ensure the volume property has shading enabled (ShadeOn()). Without this, the modified shader fails to compile. 2. Inject Shader Replacements: Add five fragment shader replacements to the VTK pipeline at specific hooks: //VTK::ComputeLighting::Dec, //VTK::RenderToImage::Dec, //VTK::RenderToImage::Init, //VTK::RenderToImage::Impl, and //VTK::RenderToImage::Exit. 3. Extract First Opaque Fragment: In the Impl hook, check if the current fragment has opacity greater than 0.0 and if depth update is allowed. If so, store the current fragment's position and normal, and disable further depth updates for this frame. 4. Compute and Write Geometry: In the Exit hook, if a valid fragment was found (position != vec3(-1.0)), compute the clip-space depth and world-space position/normal, then write them to the output buffers. If no fragment was found, write default values to avoid artifacts. 5. SSAO Pass: The standard SSAO pass reads the position (glFragData[1]), normal (glFragData[2]), and depth (glFragDepth) buffers to compute ambient occlusion. Note that the standard SSAO API only enables the opaque pass; therefore, the renderer pass must be managed directly (e.g., using vtkRenderStepPass or commenting out depth buffer blits for surfaces) to prevent the volume from disappearing or causing depth conflicts. Formulas: Depth Mapping: The depth value is mapped from clip space to framebuffer space: gl\FragDepth = 0.5 \times (gl\DepthRange.far - gl\DepthRange.near) \times depthValue.z + 0.5 \times (gl\DepthRange.far + gl\DepthRange.near) Where depthValue is the clip-space position transformed by projection, model-view, volume, and texture dataset matrices, then divided by w. World Position: gl\FragData[1] = in\modelViewMatrix \times in\volumeMatrix[0] \times in\textureDatasetMatrix[0] \times vec4(l\opaqueFragPos, 1.0) World Normal: gl\FragData[2] = vec4(normalize(l\opaqueFragNormal), 0.0) Parameters: SSAO Size Scale (Radius): Controls the spatial extent of the occlusion kernel. Small values highlight small irregularities; medium values simulate drop shadows; large values blur the effect until it becomes useless. Opacity Transfer Function Shape: A ramp function with adjustable steepness and maximum is recommended. A step function causes edge artifacts. Opacity Threshold: Default is gsrcColor.a > 0.0. A configurable threshold is suggested to prevent writing depth for nearly transparent voxels, which causes a 'shell' artifact. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. declare vec3 gdataNormal; declare vec3 lopaqueFragNormal; declare vec3 lopaqueFragPos; declare bool lupdateDepth; lopaqueFragPos = vec3(-1.0); lupdateDepth = true; if (not gskip and gsrcColor.a > 0.0 and lupdateDepth): lopaqueFragPos = gdataPos; lopaqueFragNormal = gdataNormal; lupdateDepth = false; if (lopaqueFragPos == vec3(-1.0)): # No fragment found, write defaults to avoid artifacts glFragDepth = 1.0; # glFragData[1] and [2] remain unchanged or set to safe defaults else: # Compute clip-space depth depthValue = inprojectionMatrix inmodelViewMatrix involumeMatrix[0] intextureDatasetMatrix[0] vec4(lopaqueFragPos, 1.0); depthValue = depthValue / depthValue.w; # Map depth to framebuffer range glFragDepth = 0.5 (glDepthRange.far - glDepthRange.near) depthValue.z + 0.5 (glDepthRange.far + glDepthRange.near); # Write world-space position glFragData[1] = inmodelViewMatrix involumeMatrix[0] intextureDatasetMatrix[0] vec4(lopaqueFragPos, 1.0); # Write world-space normal (normalized) glFragData[2] = vec4(normalize(lopaqueFragNormal), 0.0); Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unnormalized Normals: Failing to normalize the extracted normal causes grainy/dark artifacts in the SSAO texture. Fix: Apply normalize() to lopaqueFragNormal before writing. Shell Artifact: Writing depth for any voxel with opacity > 0 causes a 'shell' effect with high transparency. Fix: Use a higher opacity threshold or only write depth for the front-most opaque fragment. Depth Buffer Conflicts: Standard SSAO pass expects an opaque-only render pass, causing the volume to disappear or depth buffer conflicts. Workaround: Comment out the depth buffer blit required for surfaces to occlude the volume, or switch to vtkRenderStepPass. Shading Disabled: If shading is not enabled on the volume property, the modified shader fails to compile. Time Complexity: Adds one additional post-processing pass (SSAO) after volume ray-casting. Complexity depends on the SSAO kernel size and resolution. Memory Complexity: Requires additional framebuffers for position (glFragData[1]), normal (glFragData[2]), and depth (glFragDepth). Performance: Performance impact depends on the SSAO implementation and hardware. The extraction step is minimal (per-fragment). Strengths: Adds depth cues and realism to volume rendering, especially for complex internal structures. Limitations: Requires modifying the renderer pass directly; not compatible with standard SSAO API out-of-the-box; potential artifacts from semi-transparent depth writing. When to Use: When depth cues are needed for volumetric data and standard surface SSAO is not applicable. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and SSAO overhead is unacceptable, or when standard opaque surface SSAO is sufficient. Originated from discussions in the 3D Slicer community regarding the feasibility of implementing SSAO for volume rendering in VTK/3DSlicer. The method was developed as a workaround to extend SSAO capabilities to volumetric data, which typically lacks explicit surface geometry. Screen-space ambient occlusion for volume rendering, https://discourse.slicer.org/t/screen-space-ambient-occlusion-for-volume-rendering/32323, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Interpolation and Sampling Techniques
head: Trilinear Interpolation (DRR), Trilinear rendering
body: Interpolation and Sampling Techniques approximate continuous scalar fields from discrete voxel data during ray casting, determining the trade-off between computational cost and visual smoothness. This family is distinguished from Anti-Aliasing and Filtering by focusing on spatial reconstruction of the volume function rather than post-processing, and from Neural volume rendering by typically relying on explicit geometric kernels or lookup tables. A prominent example is trilinear interpolation, which offers significant speed advantages over exact intersection methods like Siddon's method for low sample counts. All methods in this family approximate a continuous scalar field V(\mathbf{p}) from discrete samples Vi at grid positions \mathbf{p}i. The core mechanism involves: 1. Query Positioning: Determining the 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} where a value is needed. 2. Kernel/Weight Application: Computing weights wi(\mathbf{p}) based on the distance between \mathbf{p} and sample centers \mathbf{p}i to calculate V(\mathbf{p}) = \sumi wi(\mathbf{p}) Vi. 3. Coordinate Transformation: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the volume's local coordinate system before interpolation. Transforms sampled depth values (z\vals) along a camera ray into physical segment lengths (dists) between consecutive samples. This conversion is necessary because uniform sampling in depth space does not correspond to uniform physical spacing in 3D space, particularly under perspective projection. It accounts for the geometric relationship between the ray direction and the viewing angle, ensuring that volume rendering integration weights samples correctly by their true spatial extent. Unlike NDC Points to Distance, which operates in Normalized Device Coordinates, this method operates directly on camera-space depth values. Samples voxel data with jittered step offsets to reduce banding, and composites the result using front-to-back alpha blending. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by perturbing sample locations with random offsets, transforming structured aliasing into less visually noticeable noise. It is particularly effective when using low sample counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation, where regular grid patterns are most visible. Warps 3D space towards the view cell center using radial distortion to bring the background closer for positional encoding, dampening high frequencies in the background while preserving foreground detail. It sets itself apart from its parent Interpolation and Sampling Techniques by explicitly warping the 3D coordinate space before encoding, and from its sibling NDC Warping by using a radial distortion function rather than a linear NDC squash. Approximates a continuous scalar field and its gradients from discrete samples (regular or irregular) using Moving Least Squares (MLS) approximation. It solves the problem of high-quality visualization of arbitrary volumetric datasets by providing a unified framework for function reconstruction that supports adaptive preintegration. Unlike Radial Basis Functions (RBFs), MLS does not require solving a global system of equations, making it more efficient for large datasets. It sets itself apart from standard interpolation methods by allowing tunable smoothing and interpolation control through basis and weighting functions, and from standard ray casting by integrating adaptive subdivision based on preintegration tables to handle the computational cost of the scalar field evaluation. Approximates a continuous volumetric field V(\mathbf{p}) from discrete samples Vi located at grid positions \mathbf{p}i to determine values along viewing rays. This family is distinguished from sibling methods like Depth to Distance Conversion and Sampling and Jittering by its exclusive focus on the spatial weighting and blending of data values, rather than coordinate mapping or noise reduction. It sets itself apart from Kernel-based Resampling by encompassing a broader range of techniques including non-kernel approaches (e.g., nearest neighbor, gradient-based splatting) and specialized hardware-accelerated primitives. A high-quality sampling technique for direct volume ray casting that improves reconstruction accuracy by compensating for the low-pass filtering effect of the cubic B-spline kernel. Unlike standard cubic B-spline interpolation, which can cause excessive blurring, this method pre-processes the voxel data to invert the kernel's frequency response, allowing for sharper results without increasing memory footprint. It is chosen when visual fidelity is prioritized over the raw performance of hardware-accelerated tri-linear interpolation. A direct volume ray casting technique that improves visual accuracy by interpolating the product of opacity and material color, rather than interpolating color and opacity separately. This method calculates the material color at a resampling point using opacity weighting before interpolation and computes lighting directly on the resampled points using interpolated normals, thereby avoiding color distortion and Mach band artifacts common in methods that interpolate shaded voxel colors. It sets itself apart from standard trilinear interpolation by preventing "intermediate colors" at material interfaces where transparent media would otherwise inappropriately influence the final color. A visibility optimization technique for Monte Carlo volume rendering that maps volume data to a discrete set of importance values after interpolation, rather than before. It solves the problem of accurately visualizing small, thin structures (e.g., bone periosteum) which are often lost or blurred by pre-interpolative importance functions due to smoothing artifacts. Unlike pre-interpolative methods that apply importance to continuous scalar values, this method creates a step function along the ray, preserving fine details and eliminating the need for smoothing discontinuities. Defines the computational framework for evaluating the volume rendering equation along a viewing ray, converting discrete volumetric data into a final pixel color. This family encompasses methods that determine where to sample the volume (stochastic vs. deterministic spacing) and how to aggregate those samples (compositing, projection, or approximation). It is distinguished from Interpolation and Sampling Techniques by focusing on the integration logic and sampling distribution rather than the spatial interpolation kernel, and from Ray Marching and Discretization by encompassing both the sampling strategy and the reduction phase. A technique to extend pre-integrated volume rendering to multidimensional transfer functions. A grid of irradiance samples is taken throughout the scene; at render time, the volume is queried and near-by irradiance samples are interpolated to estimate the global illumination at a point. The use of trilinear interpolation for volume rendering, particularly in the context of Digital Radiographic Reconstructions (DRR), has been highlighted for its significant speed advantage over exact intersection methods like Siddon's method. For instance, with 25 sample points, trilinear rendering takes approximately 737 μs, whereas Siddon's method takes ~25 ms; the costs match only when the sample count reaches ~2,000 points. name: Depth to Distance Conversion
head: Depth to Distance, depth2dist, z_vals to dists
body: Depth to Distance Conversion transforms sampled depth values (z\vals) along a camera ray into the physical segment lengths (dists) between consecutive samples. This conversion is necessary because uniform sampling in depth space does not correspond to uniform physical spacing in 3D space under perspective projection. It accounts for the geometric relationship between the ray direction and the viewing angle. Unlike NDC Points to Distance, which operates in Normalized Device Coordinates, this method operates directly on camera-space depth values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: zvals, a tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}) containing the depth values for each sample point along each ray. Output: dists, a tensor of shape (N{rays}, N{samples}) containing the physical distance between consecutive samples. Data Structures: The input zvals is a contiguous tensor where zvals[i, j] represents the depth of the j-th sample along the i-th ray. The values are assumed to be sorted in increasing order of depth (near to far). Steps: 1. Compute Raw Differences: Calculate the difference between consecutive depth values to get the raw segment lengths. For a ray with samples z0, z1, \dots, z{N-1}, the raw distance between sample j and j+1 is z{j+1} - zj. 2. Handle Boundary: Append a large constant value (10^{10}) to the end of the distance array to represent the segment after the last sample. This ensures the output tensor has the same shape as the input zvals. 3. Cosine Scaling: Scale the raw distances by the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the viewing direction. This step corrects for the perspective projection effect where depth intervals do not linearly map to Euclidean distances along the ray. Formulas: Let z{i,j} be the depth of the j-th sample on the i-th ray. The raw distance d'{i,j} between sample j and j+1 is: d'{i,j} = z{i,j+1} - z{i,j} For the last sample j = N{samples}-1, the distance is set to a large constant C = 10^{10}. The final distance d{i,j} is scaled by \cos \thetai, where \thetai is the angle between the ray direction \mathbf{d}i and the viewing direction (or the axis along which depth is measured): d{i,j} = d'{i,j} \cdot \cos \thetai If the rays are parallel to the viewing axis (orthographic), \cos \theta = 1. For perspective rays, this factor varies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def depthtodistance(zvals, cosangle): """ Convert depth values (zvals) to distances between samples. Args: zvals: Tensor of shape (Nrays, Nsamples) containing depth values. cosangle: Tensor of shape (Nrays,) or (Nrays, 1) containing the cosine of the angle between the ray and the viewing direction. Returns: dists: Tensor of shape (Nrays, Nsamples) containing segment distances. """ # Step 1: Compute raw differences between consecutive samples distsraw = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] # Step 2: Append a large constant to the last segment to match input shape largeconstant = torch.tensor(1e10, device=zvals.device, dtype=zvals.dtype) lastsegment = largeconstant torch.oneslike(distsraw[...,:1]) dists = torch.cat([distsraw, lastsegment], dim=-1) # Step 3: Scale by cosine of the angle if cosangle.dim() == 1: cosangle = cosangle.unsqueeze(-1) dists = dists cosangle return dists Parameters: largeconstant: 10^{10}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Shape Mismatch: Ensure cosangle is broadcastable to the last dimension of dists. If cosangle is per-ray, it must be unsqueezed to shape (N{rays}, 1). Last Segment: The last segment's distance is arbitrary since there is no next sample. The large constant is a convention to maintain tensor shape. Cosine Angle Definition: The exact definition of \cos \theta depends on the coordinate system. In many implementations, if the ray direction is normalized and the depth is measured along the camera's z-axis, this factor accounts for the projection geometry. Converts sampled Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) points to segment distances between consecutive samples along a ray, accounting for the cosine of the viewing angle. It operates directly in NDC space, where uniform sampling steps do not correspond to uniform physical distances, unlike linear depth-to-distance methods. Time Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}). The operation involves simple subtraction and multiplication, which are linear in the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(N{rays} \cdot N{samples}) for the output tensor dists. Strengths: Simple, efficient, and numerically stable. It correctly accounts for perspective projection effects when combined with the cosine scaling. Limitations: Assumes that the depth values are sorted and correspond to samples along a single ray. It does not handle non-linear depth mappings or complex coordinate transformations beyond the cosine scaling. When to Use: When using depth-based sampling in volume rendering or neural radiance fields where samples are generated in camera space. Not given in the sources. name: NDC Points to Distance
head: NDC to Distance, NDC to Distance Conversion, ndc2dist, ndc_pts to dists
body: Converts sampled Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) points to segment distances between consecutive samples along a ray, accounting for the cosine of the viewing angle. It operates directly in NDC space, where uniform sampling steps do not correspond to uniform physical distances, unlike linear depth-to-distance methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: ndcpts, a tensor of shape [Nray, Nsample, 3] containing 3D points in NDC space, ordered along the ray. Input: cosangle, a tensor of shape [Nray] representing the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the view direction. Output: dists, a tensor of shape [Nrays, Nsamples] containing the segment distances. Data Structures: ndcpts: Float tensor. Coordinates are in NDC space. dists: Float tensor. Steps: 1. Compute the Euclidean distance between consecutive NDC points along the ray: dists = torch.norm(ndcpts[:, 1:] - ndcpts[:,:-1], dim=-1). 2. Append a large value scaled by cosangle to the end of the distance array: dists = torch.cat([dists, 1e10 cosangle.unsqueeze(-1)], -1). Formulas: Let \mathbf{p}i be the i-th point in ndcpts for a given ray. The segment distance for i = 0, \dots, N-2 is: di = \|\mathbf{p}{i+1} - \mathbf{p}i\|2 The final distance is: d{N-1} = 10^{10} \cdot \cos(\theta) where \theta is the angle between the ray and the view direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def ndcptstodists(ndcpts, cosangle): # ndcpts: [Nray, Nsample, 3] # cosangle: [Nray] # Step 1: Compute Euclidean distances between consecutive points diffs = ndcpts[:, 1:] - ndcpts[:,:-1] dists = torch.norm(diffs, dim=-1) # Shape: [Nray, Nsample - 1] # Step 2: Append large value scaled by cosangle # cosangle.unsqueeze(-1) makes it [Nray, 1] for broadcasting sentinel = 1e10 cosangle.unsqueeze(-1) dists = torch.cat([dists, sentinel], dim=-1) # Shape: [Nray, Nsample] return dists Parameters: 1e10: A large constant appended to the distance array. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cosine Angle: If cosangle is zero, the sentinel becomes zero, which may affect integration logic. Standard forward-facing camera setups typically yield cosangle > 0. Batch Dimensions: The pseudocode assumes batched inputs [Nray,...]. For a single ray, unsqueeze dimensions appropriately before calling, or adjust slicing. Time and Memory Complexity: O(N) time and memory per ray, where N is the number of samples, dominated by vectorized tensor operations. Strengths and Limitations: Accurately computes physical distances from NDC samples for forward-facing scenes. Requires points to be in NDC space and does not apply to linear depth or world-space sampling without prior conversion. Originated in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and tensor-based variants for forward-facing scene reconstruction, where NDC space compresses the infinite depth range into a unit cube. The conversion is a standard step in the volume rendering pipeline to compute correct weights for alpha compositing. name: Sampling and Jittering
head: Jittered Ray Casting, Jittered Sampling Volume Rendering, RayCaster, Volume Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling and Front-to-Back Blending
body: Sampling and Jittering is a direct volume ray casting technique that casts rays from the camera through the volume, samples voxel data with jittered step offsets to reduce banding, and composites the result using front-to-back alpha blending. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by perturbing sample locations with random offsets, transforming structured aliasing into less visually noticeable noise. It is particularly effective when using low sample counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation, where regular grid patterns are most visible. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position (\mathbf{o}), ray direction (\mathbf{d}), volume texture (V), jitter texture (J), volume bounding box ([\mathbf{VolExtentMin}, \mathbf{VolExtentMax}]), lighting parameters (\mathbf{k}{Ambient}, \mathbf{k}{Diffuse}, \mathbf{k}{Specular}, k{Shininess}), and control flags (ComputeLighting). Outputs: Final fragment color (\mathbf{dst}). Data Structures: Voxel Sampler: A 3D texture storing scalar or RGBA volume data. Jitter Texture: A 2D texture storing pre-computed random offsets. The width and height are defined by JitterTexSize. The red channel is used for the jitter value. Ray State: Current position \mathbf{p}, direction \mathbf{d}, step size s. Parameters: NumSamples: Maximum iterations per ray. RayStepSize: Distance between consecutive samples (s). JitterTexSize: Dimension of the jitter texture. ComputeLighting: Boolean flag for shading. \mathbf{k}{Ambient} = (0.05, 0.05, 0.05) \mathbf{k}{Diffuse} = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) \mathbf{k}{Specular} = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) k{Shininess} = 100.0 Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set destination color \mathbf{dst} = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0). Calculate ray direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{frag} - \mathbf{o}). Calculate step vector \mathbf{s} = \mathbf{d} \times RayStepSize. 2. Jitter Application: Determine texture coordinate from fragment coordinates modulo JitterTexSize. Fetch jitter value j from the red channel of J. Update ray position: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{s} \times j. 3. Boundary Check: Check if \mathbf{p} is inside the volume bounds. Using the bounding box defined by \mathbf{VolExtentMin} and \mathbf{VolExtentMax}, compute test vectors. If \text{dot}(\mathbf{test1}, \mathbf{test2}) \ge 3.0, the point is inside. 4. Sampling: Sample the volume at \mathbf{p} to get source color/alpha \mathbf{src}. 5. Lighting (Optional): If ComputeLighting is true: Estimate gradient normal using central differences on the alpha channel (a) of \mathbf{src}. Use offsets ivec4(1, 0, 0, -1) and permutations (yxz, yzx, wyz, ywz, yzw) to sample neighbors. Calculate \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{sample2} - \mathbf{sample1}). If \mathbf{n} is NaN, skip shading. Apply Phong shading to \mathbf{src}.rgb using ambient, diffuse, and specular components. 6. Compositing: Update destination using front-to-back blending: \mathbf{dst} = (1.0 - \mathbf{dst}.a) \times \mathbf{src} + \mathbf{dst} 7. Termination: If \mathbf{dst}.a > 0.95, break the loop (early ray termination). 8. Advance: Update \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{s}. Re-evaluate boundary check. Repeat until NumSamples is reached or ray exits. 9. Output: Return \mathbf{dst}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Initialize dst = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) raydir = normalize(rayposition - cameraposition) raystep = raydir raystepsize # 2. Jitter offset application # Get 2D texture coordinate from fragment coordinates modulo JitterTexSize fragcoords = getfragmentcoords() # Implementation detail: derived from screen position jitteruv = vec2(fragcoords.x % jittertexsize, fragcoords.y % jittertexsize) / jittertexsize jittervalue = texture(jittertex, jitteruv).r currentpos = rayposition + raystep jittervalue for i in range(numsamples): # 3. Boundary Check # Check if currentpos is inside volume bounds # Using sign functions and dot product logic from source test1 = vec3(sign(currentpos - volextentmin)) test2 = vec3(sign(volextentmax - currentpos)) if dot(test1, test2) < 3.0: # Point is outside, advance and continue or break depending on implementation # Source implies re-evaluating inside condition for the loop currentpos += raystep continue # 4. Sample Voxel Data src = texture(voxeltex, currentpos) # 5. Lighting if computelighting: # Estimate gradient normal using central differences on alpha channel # Offsets: ivec4(1, 0, 0, -1) and permutations (yxz, yzx, wyz, ywz, yzw) # Note: Source implies specific neighbor sampling logic for gradient sample1 = texture(voxeltex, currentpos + vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Placeholder for specific neighbor logic sample2 = texture(voxeltex, currentpos + vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Placeholder for specific neighbor logic # Actual implementation requires fetching specific neighbors based on permutations # For the sake of self-contained pseudocode, we assume a gradient function exists normal = estimategradientnormal(voxeltex, currentpos) if not isnan(normal): tocamera = normalize(cameraposition - currentpos) tolight = normalize(lightposition - currentpos) src.rgb = shading(src.rgb, normal, tocamera, tolight) # 6. Front-to-Back Blending dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst # 7. Early Ray Termination if dst.a > 0.95: break # 8. Advance Ray currentpos += raystep return dst def shading(rgb, normal, tocamera, tolight): halfway = normalize(tolight + tocamera) diffuselight = max(dot(tolight, normal), 0.0) diffuse = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) specular = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) if diffuselight > 0.0: diffuse = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) rgb diffuselight # kDiffuse specularlight = pow(max(dot(halfway, normal), 0.0), 100.0) # kShininess specular = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) rgb specularlight # kSpecular ambient = vec3(0.05, 0.05, 0.05) rgb # kAmbient return ambient + diffuse + specular Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NaN Normals: Gradient calculation may result in NaN if sample1 equals sample2 or if values are identical. This is handled by checking isnan(normal) and skipping shading. Early Termination: Early ray termination occurs when accumulated alpha exceeds 0.95, potentially missing faint structures behind dense ones. Stochastic jittering is a sampling technique used in direct volume ray casting to mitigate banding and quantization artifacts caused by regular, uniformly spaced sample positions. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by perturbing sample locations with random offsets, transforming structured aliasing into less visually noticeable noise. It is particularly effective when using low sample counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation, where regular grid patterns are most visible. Hierarchical sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) is a method for generating importance samples along a ray in volume rendering by inverting the cumulative distribution function (CDF) of the rendering contribution, which is mathematically equivalent to the transmittance function. It solves the problem of efficiently placing sample points in regions of high density without redundant radiance queries, enabling differentiable end-to-end optimization of neural radiance fields. Unlike standard hierarchical sampling which samples from a piecewise constant probability density defined by coarse weights, this method uses inverse transform sampling on a piecewise approximated density field (constant or linear), allowing gradients to back-propagate through the sampling process to the density parameters. It builds on Sampling and Jittering by providing a deterministic or stratified mechanism to concentrate fine samples where the coarse pass indicated high opacity. Uniform Ray Sampling generates sample points along camera rays at equal distances between a near and far clipping plane to discretize the volume for integration. It assumes every point along the ray contributes equally to the final rendering, implying a constant probability density function (PDF) and linearly decaying transmittance. This method sets itself apart from its siblings by using fixed, deterministic spacing without adaptive logic or stratification, making it the simplest to implement but often the least efficient for scenes with large empty regions. It serves as the baseline for NeRF-style rendering. Slab-based ray sampling is an image-order caching mechanism for direct volume ray casting that groups rays into rectangular screen regions to form stacked slabs, storing voxel samples in shared memory to optimize neighborhood access for lighting and compositing. Unlike object-order bricking, which struggles with GPU hardware mapping due to per-brick lists, this method leverages the regular structure of rays within a slab to reduce memory bandwidth and latency when calculating gradients or performing ambient occlusion. It is distinct from sibling methods like Uniform Ray Sampling by explicitly managing spatial locality in shared memory across multiple rays, and from Stochastic Jittering by prioritizing deterministic cache coherence over variance reduction. Supersampling is a technique to minimize aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel and averaging the results. It handles high-frequency components in transfer functions by performing dense quadrature of the volume render integral, assuming linearity of the scalar field between sample points but not linearity of the integral itself. Unlike pre-integration, which requires equidistant sample points and fails for nonlinear integrals, supersampling accounts for the nonlinearity of the volume render integral while avoiding oversampling of the scalar field. It differs from Stochastic Jittering by using deterministic, fixed offsets for low sample counts (1x–4x) rather than random or stratified patterns, and from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering by relying on simple arithmetic averaging rather than importance-weighted integration. Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering is a technique to increase rendering performance by reducing the number of particles used during rendering, using a non-uniform sampling strategy based on data importance and view-dependent criteria. It solves the problem of high computational cost when rendering large, unstructured Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) datasets by ensuring that particles in complex regions (e.g., phase interfaces, vortices) are sampled more densely than those in homogeneous areas. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by avoiding equal-time high-error trade-offs. Epipolar sampling is a technique for aggregating features from multiple views by sampling along epipolar lines rather than along the camera ray in 3D space. It solves the problem of scale ambiguity in 3D reconstruction from sparse views, where camera poses are scaled by an arbitrary factor, preventing the inference of metric depth from a single view. Unlike standard volume rendering which samples along a ray, this method samples features from a reference pixel and correlates them with features sampled along the corresponding epipolar line in a second view, augmented with positionally encoded depths. Warp-based Sampling is a GPU optimization strategy for direct volume ray casting that improves texture cache performance by reorganizing thread warps to align sampling directions with the volume's memory strides. Unlike standard sampling where a warp processes a block of pixels, Warp Marching assigns a single warp to a single ray, marching through the volume in chunks equal to the warp size. This approach minimizes memory stride within the atomic scheduling unit (the warp), making it particularly effective for rendering large dynamic volumes at low resolutions where view-independent performance is critical. Hierarchical sampling is a two-stage strategy for volume rendering that improves image quality by concentrating samples in regions of high geometric or color complexity, thereby addressing the sensitivity of neural radiance fields to sparse initial sampling. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by using a coarse network to estimate density and guide importance sampling for a fine network, and from Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling) by explicitly defining the coarse-to-fine pipeline as the primary mechanism for efficiency, often implemented via the inverse-CDF of coarse weights. Resampling techniques align geometry and color between scenes along corresponding rays. Uniform sampling points evenly along the ray but can lead to misalignment. A strategy exists where points are valid only if density exceeds a threshold in both scenes, without resampling. Density-based resampling identifies density peaks along each ray and adjusts sampling to align key points in both scenes, ensuring improved color-geometry consistency. Consistent Ray Sampling ensures that ray sample intervals are consistent across all subvolumes to allow correct reconstruction of the original volume and prevent feature loss or enhancement. The starting sample location for each subvolume is calculated such that the distance between the first sample of the new subvolume and the last sample of the previous subvolume equals the predetermined interval. Incorrect calculation of sample locations causes small features in the data to be lost or enhanced erroneously. Ray Direction Jitter improves generalizability by applying sub-pixel jitter to ray directions. Instead of shooting in the pixel centers, a jitter \psi is applied such that: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti (\mathbf{d} + \psi) where \psi is sampled uniformly such that the resulting ray still confines to the boundaries of its designated pixel. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray (NumSamples) and the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume texture size and the jitter texture size (JitterTexSize^2). Strengths: Reduces banding artifacts significantly compared to uniform sampling, especially at low sample counts. Simple to implement in shaders. Limitations: Early ray termination may miss faint structures. Gradient estimation can be noisy or produce NaNs. When to use: When visual quality (reduction of banding) is prioritized over strict physical accuracy or when using low sample counts. When not to use: When high precision is required for faint structures behind dense ones, or when deterministic sampling is strictly required for reproducibility without random seeds. The method originates from direct volume ray casting techniques that utilize jittered sampling to mitigate aliasing. The specific implementation details, including the jitter texture lookup and Phong shading integration, are documented in the VoxViz thesis. Consistent sampling across subvolumes for parallel rendering was discussed in early parallel ray tracing algorithms. Ray direction jitter for generalizability in neural rendering contexts was introduced in NeRF for Outdoor Scene Relighting. apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, https://github.com/apecoraro/VoxVizThesis, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Generalized TensoRF: Efficient Multi-Scene Radiance Fields and View-Consistent 3D Editing, https://doi.org/10.1145/3722564.3728385, fetched 2026-10-29 A data distributed, parallel algorithm for ray-traced volume..., https://www.cs.ucdavis.edu/~ma/papers/PRS93.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 NeRF for Outdoor Scene Relighting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19787-135, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stochastic Jittering
head: Jittered Ray Sampling, Ray Jittering, Stochastic Sample Jittering
body: Stochastic jittering is a sampling technique used in direct volume ray casting to mitigate banding and quantization artifacts caused by regular, uniformly spaced sample positions. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by perturbing sample locations with random offsets, transforming structured aliasing into less visually noticeable noise. It is particularly effective when using low sample counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation, where regular grid patterns are most visible. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Base step size \Delta t. A pre-computed jitter texture (2D noise texture). Pixel coordinates (u, v) or screen-space position. Maximum noise factor \alpha (optional, controls jitter magnitude). Outputs: Perturbed sample positions along the ray. Data Structures: Jitter Texture: A 2D texture storing noise values. Dimensions: Typically N \times N (e.g., 64 \times 64). Format: Single channel or RGB, sampled with nearest-neighbor filtering. Filtering: GLNEAREST (or equivalent) to preserve sharp noise patterns without interpolation. Wrapping: GLREPEAT to allow seamless tiling. Source: Often blue noise for better perceptual quality. Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: Compute the entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) parameters along the ray where it intersects the volume bounding box. 2. Loop for Samples: For each sample index n = 0, 1, 2, \dots: a. Fetch Jitter Value: Sample the jitter texture at coordinates derived from the pixel's screen position to obtain a value j \in [0, 1]. b. Compute Sample Position: Calculate the perturbed parameter along the ray: t{sample} = t{near} + \Delta t \cdot (n + j \cdot \alpha) \mathbf{p}{sample} = \mathbf{o} + t{sample} \cdot \mathbf{d} This places the sample at a random position within the segment [t{near} + n\Delta t, t{near} + (n+1)\Delta t]. c. Sample Volume: Evaluate the volume data at \mathbf{p}{sample} to retrieve color and opacity. d. Composite: Accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing: C{out} = C{in} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - T), T{out} = T{in} + \alpha \cdot (1 - T{in}), where c and \alpha are the sample's color and opacity, and T is the accumulated transmission. e. Advance: If the ray exits the volume (t{sample} \ge t{far}) or accumulated transmission drops below a threshold (e.g., 0.01), break. Otherwise, continue to the next n. Parameters: Jitter Texture Size (N): Typical value: 64. Max Noise Factor (\alpha): Typical value: 0.75. Controls the maximum displacement relative to step size. Noise Type: Blue noise is preferred over white noise because it is intrinsically tileable and easier to blur out, reducing visible dither patterns. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetnearfar(rayorigin, raydir, volmin, volmax): """Standard slab method for AABB intersection.""" tnear = -float('inf') tfar = float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < volmin[i] or rayorigin[i] > volmax[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (volmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (volmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tnear: tnear = t1 if t2 < tfar: tfar = t2 if tnear > tfar: return None, None return tnear, tfar def stochasticjitteredraycast(rayorigin, raydir, volumedata, stepsize, jittertexture, pixeluv, maxnoisefactor=1.0, volmin=None, volmax=None, threshold=0.01): """ Casts a ray through a volume using stochastic jittering to reduce banding. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the ray. raydir: vec3, normalized direction of the ray. volumedata: function, samples volume at (x,y,z) returning (color, opacity). stepsize: float, base distance between samples. jittertexture: function, samples 2D noise texture at (u,v) returning float in [0,1]. pixeluv: vec2, screen-space coordinates of the pixel. maxnoisefactor: float, multiplier for jitter magnitude (default 1.0). volmin, volmax: vec3, volume bounding box corners. threshold: float, transmission cutoff to break early. Returns: vec4, final accumulated color with alpha. """ if volmin is None or volmax is None: raise ValueError("Volume bounding box must be provided.") tnear, tfar = computetnearfar(rayorigin, raydir, volmin, volmax) if tnear is None: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) transmission = 1.0 sampleindex = 0 # Fetch jitter value once per pixel/ray jitterval = jittertexture.sample(pixeluv.x, pixeluv.y) while tnear + stepsize (sampleindex + jitterval maxnoisefactor) < tfar and transmission > threshold: tsample = tnear + stepsize (sampleindex + jitterval maxnoisefactor) samplepos = rayorigin + tsample raydir color, opacity = volumedata(samplepos) alpha = opacity transmission accumulatedcolor += color alpha transmission -= alpha sampleindex += 1 return vec4(accumulatedcolor, 1.0 - transmission) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Banding vs. Noise: Jittering replaces visible banding artifacts with noise. While visually more pleasing, it introduces noise that may require further reduction techniques (e.g., temporal filtering). Sampling Rate Dependence: Ray jittering provides a slight improvement at low sampling rates (0.25, 0.5) but the benefit vanishes with higher sampling rates. Isosurface Errors: Without refinement, isosurface rendering errors are inevitable if sample distance is not reduced; jittering makes these artifacts less visible but does not eliminate them. Precision: At high sampling rates, the benefit of jittering vanishes as the regular sampling is sufficient to capture volume details. Slice Artifact Reduction is a stochastic sampling technique used in direct volume ray casting to mitigate "wood grain" artifacts—visible slice boundaries caused by regular ray start positions and discrete voxel grids. It differs from standard ray casting by randomizing the initial ray origin along the viewing direction and performing a localized "solidity check" to verify that a sampled voxel is truly part of the volume rather than an edge artifact. This method effectively breaks the regularity of sampling patterns that cause visible artifacts, regardless of the ray step size relative to voxel dimensions. Temporal Filtering and Jittering is a technique that smooths out noise and improves perceived volume resolution without extra raymarching steps. It addresses spatial banding artifacts caused by coarse slice resolution by combining sub-voxel depth jittering with temporal reprojection. It distinguishes itself from static spatial filters by leveraging camera motion vectors to blend frames, and from pure spatial sampling methods by accumulating jittered samples over time to improve perceived resolution without additional raymarching steps. Random Jitter with Reprojection is a technique to reduce banding artifacts caused by low sample counts in volume rendering by introducing stochastic jitter during ray marching and subsequently reducing the resulting noise via temporal accumulation. It distinguishes itself from pure spatial jittering methods by leveraging temporal coherence, projecting a pseudo-hit position from the current frame into the previous frame's screen space to blend the current result with a history buffer, thereby allowing for lower per-frame sample counts while maintaining visual stability. Ray Casting with Jittered Sampling is a direct volume rendering technique that casts rays through a 3D voxel grid to accumulate color and opacity along the ray path. It distinguishes itself from uniform ray sampling by perturbing sample positions with a pre-computed jitter texture to break up regular grid patterns and reduce aliasing artifacts. Unlike stochastic methods, it uses deterministic offsets stored in a 2D texture rather than runtime random number generation. An extension where sampling occurs at a lower resolution to reduce texture bandwidth requirements, combined with varying the sample pattern with stochastic sampling to reduce regular pattern artifacts where sampling density is reduced. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Jittering adds negligible overhead (texture fetch and addition) compared to the volume sampling itself. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) for the jitter texture, where N is the texture dimension (e.g., 64 \times 64 floats = 16 KB). Measured Performance: On typical hardware, jittering has minimal impact on frame rate. The benefit is visual quality rather than speed. Scaling: The benefit of ray jittering vanishes with higher sampling rates (e.g., s \ge 2.0). It provides a slight improvement at low sampling rates (e.g., s = 0.25, 0.5). Strengths: Effectively reduces banding and wood-grain artifacts; simple to implement; works well with nearest-neighbor interpolation. Limitations: Introduces noise; does not improve accuracy, only visual quality; ineffective at high sample counts. When to Use: When using low sample counts, nearest-neighbor interpolation, or when banding artifacts are prominent. When Not to Use: When high sample counts are available, or when noise is unacceptable without temporal filtering. name: Slice Artifact Reduction
head: Initial rays’ start positions randomization, Ray Start Position Randomization, Ray start jittering, Ray start jittering with solidity check, Wood grain artifact reduction
body: Slice Artifact Reduction is a stochastic sampling technique used in direct volume ray casting to mitigate "wood grain" artifacts—visible slice boundaries caused by regular ray start positions and discrete voxel grids. It differs from standard ray casting by randomizing the initial ray origin along the viewing direction and performing a localized "solidity check" to verify that a sampled voxel is truly part of the volume rather than an edge artifact. This method effectively breaks the regularity of sampling patterns that cause visible artifacts, regardless of the ray step size relative to voxel dimensions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset, transfer function parameters (Threshold), ray start position P{start}, ray direction vector \vec{d}, step length L, noise texture N, fragment coordinates (x, y), and far plane distance. Output: Final accumulated color dst for the pixel. Data Structures: Noise Texture: A 2D texture N of size 256 \times 256 containing random values in [0, 1]. Volume Data: Accessible via a sampling function returning scalar density V at a given position. Parameters: Threshold: Density threshold for voxel solidity. Typical value: Not given in the sources. StepLength (L): Distance between sampling points. Typical value: Not given in the sources. Noise Scale: Division factor for fragment coordinates to sample the noise texture. Typical value: 256. Algorithm Steps: 1. Jitter Ray Start: Calculate a random offset using the noise texture sampled at a scaled fragment coordinate. Add this offset to the ray start position along the view direction. P{start}' = P{start} + \vec{s} \cdot N(x/256, y/256) where \vec{s} is the step vector and N is the noise value. 2. Initialize Ray: Set current position P = P{start}', remaining ray length R = R{total}, and accumulated color dst = (0, 0, 0, 0). 3. Ray Casting Loop: While dst.a < 1 and R > 0: a. Sample density V = \text{lookup}(P). b. If V > \text{Threshold}: i. Solidity Check: Perform a localized check to ensure the voxel is solid. Move back by half-step: P \leftarrow P - \vec{s} \cdot 0.5, V \leftarrow \text{lookup}(P). If V > \text{Threshold}, scale offset forward by quarter-step: \vec{s}{offset} \leftarrow \vec{s}{offset} \cdot 0.5. Else, scale offset backward by quarter-step: \vec{s}{offset} \leftarrow \vec{s}{offset} \cdot (-0.5). Update position and sample: P \leftarrow P + \vec{s}{offset}, V \leftarrow \text{lookup}(P). ii. If V > \text{Threshold}, proceed with lighting calculations and accumulate color. Break loop if opaque. c. Advance ray: P \leftarrow P + \vec{s}, R \leftarrow R - L. 4. Temporal Accumulation (Optional): If the viewpoint is static, accumulate multiple frames over time to average out the stochastic noise. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sliceartifactreduction(rayorigin, raydirection, steplength, threshold, noisetexture, fragcoord, farplanedist): # Compute step vector from direction and length stepvector = raydirection steplength # Jitter ray start position along view direction noiseval = noisetexture.sample(fragcoord / 256.0) rayorigin += stepvector noiseval pos = rayorigin raylength = farplanedist dst = vec4(0.0) # Standard volume sampling: returns density at pos def lookup(p): return volumedata.sample(p) while dst.a < 1.0 and raylength > 0: V = lookup(pos) if V > threshold: # Solidity check s = -stepvector 0.5 pos += s V = lookup(pos) if V > threshold: s = 0.5 else: s = -0.5 pos += s V = lookup(pos) if V > threshold: # Lighting calculations (gradient estimation, diffuse lighting) # src = vec4(color, 1.0) # dst = (1.0 - dst.a) src + dst break pos += stepvector raylength -= steplength return dst Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors may cause the solidity check to fail incorrectly if the step size is very small relative to the voxel size. Boundaries: Ensure the ray start jitter does not push the ray outside the volume bounding box. A specific variant focusing solely on randomizing the initial ray origin to break regularity, effective for low step counts or nearest-neighbor interpolation. Uses temporal accumulation to average out the noise introduced by stochastic jittering, requiring a static viewpoint. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of sampling steps per ray. The solidity check adds a constant overhead (2-3 extra samples) per voxel hit. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, plus the noise texture storage. Measured Performance: Reduces visible artifacts significantly without requiring a reduction in step size, thus maintaining performance compared to high-resolution sampling. Strengths: Effective against "wood grain" artifacts; simple to implement; works well with low step counts. Limitations: Introduces stochastic noise, requiring temporal accumulation for a clean image if the viewpoint is static. When to Use: When regular sampling patterns cause visible artifacts, such as with nearest-neighbor interpolation or limited step counts. When Not to Use: When high performance is critical and artifacts are acceptable, or when using high-resolution sampling with trilinear/tricubic interpolation. The technique was popularized in the context of GPU-based volume rendering, specifically in tutorials and implementations such as "Volumetric Splatting at The Little Grasshopper". It addresses a common issue in early volume renderers where regular sampling patterns led to visible slice boundaries. The concept of randomizing ray start positions to break regularity was also discussed in academic literature on GPU volume rendering. name: Temporal Filtering and Jittering
head: Temporal Filtering, Temporal Supersampling
body: Temporal Filtering and Jittering is a technique that smooths out noise and improves perceived volume resolution without extra raymarching steps. It addresses spatial banding artifacts caused by coarse slice resolution by combining sub-voxel depth jittering with temporal reprojection. It distinguishes itself from static spatial filters by leveraging camera motion vectors to blend frames, and from pure spatial sampling methods by accumulating jittered samples over time to improve perceived resolution without additional raymarching steps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current frame’s 3D texture (or accumulated volume data), previous frame’s 3D texture, camera motion vectors, and a pseudo-random sequence (e.g., blue noise or Halton sequence). Outputs: A final filtered 3D texture. Data Structures: 3D Texture: Stores volumetric data (e.g., transmittance, in-scattered light). Layout is not explicitly defined in sources, but standard hardware trilinear interpolation (GLLINEAR) is used for sampling. Motion Vectors: 2D vectors per pixel representing the displacement of scene points between frames, used for reprojection. Jitter Offset: A sub-voxel offset derived from the pseudo-random sequence. Steps: 1. Depth Jittering: Each frame, apply a sub-voxel offset to ray positions. The offset is derived from a pseudo-random sequence such as blue noise or a Halton sequence. This offsets the sampling positions to break up spatial aliasing patterns. 2. Raymarching/Accumulation: Execute the volume rendering pass (raymarching) using the jittered ray positions to generate the current frame’s 3D texture data. 3. Temporal Reprojection Compute Pass: Blend the current frame’s 3D texture with the previous frame's 3D texture using camera motion vectors. This step effectively smooths out noise by accumulating information over time. 4. Final Composition (Post-processing): The accumulated volumetric data is applied to the scene during post-processing or forward-lighting: Retrieve the linear depth of the opaque scene fragment from the scene's depth buffer. Convert the fragment's screen coordinates and linear depth into 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) using the exponential depth equation. Sample the integrated 3D texture using hardware trilinear interpolation. Add the sampled in-scattered light to the scene color and attenuate the scene color by the sampled transmittance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalfilteringandjittering(currentframetexture, previousframetexture, motionvectors, frameindex): """ Implements Temporal Filtering and Jittering for volume rendering. Args: currentframetexture (ndarray): Raw accumulated volume data for the current frame. previousframetexture (ndarray): The filtered 3D texture from the previous frame. motionvectors (ndarray): 2D motion vectors for the current frame. frameindex (int): Index of the current frame for jitter sequence lookup. Returns: ndarray: The final filtered 3D texture for the current frame. """ height, width = currentframetexture.shape[:2] filteredtexture = np.zeroslike(currentframetexture) # Step 1: Generate jitter offset for the current frame # Standard pseudo-random sequence lookup (e.g., blue noise or Halton sequence) jitteroffset = np.array([0.0, 0.0]) # Step 2 & 3: Temporal Reprojection and Blending for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Reproject previous frame's pixel to current screen space mv = motionvectors[y, x] prevx = int(x + mv[0]) prevy = int(y + mv[1]) # Clamp to bounds prevx = max(0, min(width - 1, prevx)) prevy = max(0, min(height - 1, prevy)) prevvalue = previousframetexture[prevy, prevx] currvalue = currentframetexture[y, x] # Blend current and previous data # Simple temporal accumulation blend; exact weights depend on implementation filteredvalue = 0.5 currvalue + 0.5 prevvalue filteredtexture[y, x] = filteredvalue return filteredtexture def finalcomposition(filteredtexture, scenedepthbuffer, screencoordinates, scenecolor): """ Applies the filtered volumetric data to the final scene. Args: filteredtexture (ndarray): The output from temporalfilteringandjittering. scenedepthbuffer (ndarray): Linear depth of the opaque scene. screencoordinates (tuple): Fragment's screen coordinates (u, v). scenecolor (tuple): Opaque scene color. Returns: tuple: The final scene color with volumetric effects. """ # Retrieve linear depth of the opaque scene fragment lineardepth = scenedepthbuffer[screencoordinates] # Convert screen coordinates and linear depth to 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) # using the exponential depth equation # Standard exponential depth mapping: w = exp(-depth scale) normalized to [0,1] u, v = screencoordinates w = np.exp(-lineardepth 0.1) # Placeholder scale factor # Sample the integrated 3D texture using hardware trilinear interpolation # Standard trilinear interpolation over the 3D texture sampledlight = np.zeros(3) # Placeholder for trilinear sample # Sample transmittance (assumed to be stored in the same 3D texture or a companion texture) # Assuming transmittance is stored in the same 3D texture or a companion texture transmittance = 1.0 # Placeholder for trilinear transmittance sample # Add in-scattered light to scene color and attenuate by transmittance finalcolor = tuple(c transmittance + s for c, s in zip(scenecolor, sampledlight)) return finalcolor Parameters: Jitter Sequence: Blue noise or Halton sequence. Interpolation: Hardware trilinear interpolation (GLLINEAR). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Motion Vectors: Incorrect or missing motion vectors will cause ghosting or blurring in the temporal reprojection step. Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Edge-Preserving Kawase Blur is a post-processing technique designed to remove dither patterns introduced by blue noise jittering in volume rendering while preserving cloud edge details. It distinguishes itself from standard box blurs by using edge-aware weighting to prevent the smoothing of sharp volumetric boundaries, and from temporal accumulation methods by operating on a single frame without requiring reprojection of previous frames. A post-processing technique that smooths noise artifacts from blue noise dithering by calculating a new pixel value using a cubic polynomial over 16 neighboring pixels. It is applied as a separate post-processing pass using Frame Buffer Objects (FBOs) to render the main scene into a texture, which is then sampled by a bicubic filtering material on a fullscreen triangle. A technique to replace weighted volume lookups (trilinear interpolation) with a single stochastically jittered sample to speed up rendering while maintaining unbiased results. It provides a roughly 3.5x speedup compared to trilinear filtering. At 32 samples per pixel, the PSNR difference between stochastic and trilinear filtering is less than 0.1 dB compared to a converged reference. It is virtually indistinguishable from trilinear filtering in converged images (PSNR 56.23 dB) but is significantly faster. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Stochastic filtering (a variant) provides a roughly 3.5x speedup compared to trilinear filtering. Timings were measured on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU at 1920 × 1080 resolution with three bounces of multiple (isotropic) scattering, using a Moana cloud at 1000 × 680 × 1224 voxel resolution. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Smooths out noise and improves perceived volume resolution without extra raymarching steps. Stochastic filtering variant is significantly faster. Limitations: Requires motion vectors for temporal reprojection. Stochastic filtering may introduce noise at low sample counts, though the difference is negligible at 32 samples per pixel. When to use: When spatial banding artifacts are visible due to coarse slice resolution and extra raymarching steps are undesirable. When not to use: When motion vectors are unavailable or unreliable. Origin: The technique is described in the context of volumetric fog using 3D textures in OpenGL and efficient unbiased volume path tracing on the GPU. History and Development: The use of depth jittering with blue noise or Halton sequences to hide spatial banding artifacts is a known technique in volume rendering. The integration of temporal reprojection for noise smoothing is an extension of this approach. Stochastic filtering as a replacement for trilinear interpolation was introduced to improve performance in volume path tracing. Where it is used: Real-time volumetric rendering, particularly for clouds and fog.
