name: Occupancy Proposal Sampling
head: Occupancy Proposal Network Sampling
body: Occupancy Proposal Sampling is a ray sampling strategy that queries a lightweight occupancy proposal network at uniform intervals along each camera ray, then selects additional samples based on the initial samples to accelerate rendering. It differs from its parent, Proposal Network Sampling, by specifically utilizing an occupancy-based (binary or thresholded) signal rather than a continuous density estimate to drive the adaptive sampling, often employing separate static and dynamic branches for temporal scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray r, current time t (for dynamic scenes), and the lightweight proposal network parameters. Output: A set of sample positions \{ti\} and associated weights \{wi\} along the ray r for volume rendering integration. Data Structures: The proposal network is modeled with separate hash table-backed static and dynamic branches. Static Branch: Stores geometry that does not change over time. Dynamic Branch: Stores geometry that changes over time. Hash Table: Used for efficient spatial hashing of features in both branches. Steps: 1. Uniform Query: Query the lightweight occupancy proposal network at uniform intervals along the camera ray r within the viewing frustum (typically t0 \in [-1, 1]). 2. Sample Selection: Pick additional samples based on the initial samples. The occupancy values (or derived probabilities) from the proposal network guide the placement of these additional samples, concentrating them in regions of high occupancy. 3. Branch Separation: The proposal network maintains separate static and dynamic branches, each backed by a hash table. 4. Histogram Loss Training: Train each branch of the proposal network using histogram loss. The loss is computed using the weights of the respective branch of the main model as the target distribution. The histogram loss Lh is defined as: Lh(r) = \sum{t0 \in [-1,1]} |F(r) - \hat{F}{t0}(r)| where F(r) is the cumulative opacity from the main model and \hat{F}{t0}(r) is the cumulative opacity from the proposal network. 5. Distortion Loss Regularization: Regularize the resulting sample distances and weights using distortion loss. This encourages the samples to be evenly spaced in terms of optical depth, reducing artifacts. The distortion loss Ld is typically: Ld(r) = \sum{i} wi \hat{w}i (ti - \bar{t})^2 where \bar{t} is the expected depth. Parameters: Speedup Factor: 2-4x compared to uniform sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Hash table collisions may affect accuracy in high-density regions. Boundaries: The uniform query range must cover the entire visible scene; clipping errors can occur if the frustum is not correctly defined. Degenerate Input: If the scene is empty or fully transparent, the proposal network may return uniform occupancy, degrading to uniform sampling. A generalizable learned sampler conditioned on cheap low-resolution information to enable full-resolution rendering during training, replacing dense uniform sampling. The sampler is a scene-conditional proposal network that generalizes across scenes, inspired by density estimators, instead of being category-specific or optimized per-scene. It operates on a per-ray basis to adaptively accelerate rendering. The sampler allows the method to operate with just 20 samples per ray, compared to existing 3D GANs which must use at least 96 samples per ray. The approach uses up to 5 times fewer depth samples than dense sampling methods. Unlike acceleration structures like octrees which are limited to coarse or category-specific acceleration, this sampling-based method generalizes to every new scene. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of uniform query points plus the number of additional samples. The hash table lookups are O(1) on average. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the hash tables for the static and dynamic branches. Measured Performance: Provides a 2-4x speedup compared to uniform sampling. Scaling: Scales well with dynamic scenes due to the separation of static and dynamic branches. Strengths: Significant speedup without sacrificing quality; handles dynamic scenes effectively. Limitations: Requires training the proposal network; may introduce artifacts if the proposal network is poorly trained. When to Use: When rendering speed is critical and the scene has significant empty space or occluders. When Not to Use: When the scene is uniformly dense, as the overhead of the proposal network may not be justified. Originated in the context of scalable urban dynamic scenes, specifically in the SUDS method. It builds on the idea of using lightweight networks to guide sampling, extending it to dynamic scenes with separate static and dynamic branches. name: RangeFineSampler
body: RangeFineSampler is a hierarchical sampling technique for direct volume ray casting that refines coarse samples by generating a dense uniform grid around the coarse sample with the highest weight, supplemented by random samples across the full ray extent. It addresses missing high-frequency details between coarse samples by concentrating computational effort near the most significant signal while maintaining global coverage through random jittering. Unlike Inverse Opacity Calculation which derives samples from opacity gradients, or Proposal Network Sampling which uses learned neural networks to predict sample locations, RangeFineSampler relies on a deterministic geometric expansion around the peak weight index combined with stochastic uniform sampling. The method processes batched inputs of coarse sample depths and corresponding importance weights. It outputs a refined set of sample positions along each ray. Inputs: coarsezvals: Tensor of shape (numrays, numcoarse) containing the depth positions of coarse samples. coarseweights: Tensor of shape (numrays, numcoarse) containing the importance weights for each coarse sample. near: Float, the near plane distance of the ray. far: Float, the far plane distance of the ray. maxsamples: Integer, the maximum number of fine samples allowed per ray. Nsamples: Integer, the target number of fine samples to generate around the peak. range: Float, the width parameter controlling the interval around the max weight z-value (default 0.5). deterministic: Boolean, whether to use stratified sampling or pure random jittering. Outputs: zvalsret: Tensor of shape (numrays, numtotalsamples) containing the sorted, refined sample positions. Data Structures: The implementation uses batched tensor indexing and sorting operations. Steps: 1. Determine Effective Sample Count: Calculate the number of fine samples to generate around the peak. This is bounded by maxsamples and Nsamples. N{fine} = \min(\text{max\samples}, N{samples}) 2. Find Peak Weight Index: Identify the index of the coarse sample with the maximum weight for each ray. \text{max\indices} = \text{argmax}{dim=-1}(\text{coarse\weights}) 3. Retrieve Peak Z-Value: Get the depth value corresponding to the peak weight for each ray. \text{max\z\vals} = \text{coarse\z\vals}[\text{arange}(\text{num\rays}), \text{max\indices}] 4. Generate Uniform Samples Around Peak: Create a uniform grid of N{fine} samples centered around maxzvals. The source documentation defines range as the total width, but the implementation formula uses 2 range, effectively treating it as a half-width. The formula distributes points evenly across this interval. z{fine} = \text{max\z\vals}[:, \text{None}] - \text{range} + \frac{2 \cdot \text{range}}{N{fine} - 1} \cdot \text{arange}(N{fine}) 5. Apply Stratified Sampling (Optional): If deterministic is False, apply stratified jittering to the uniform samples to reduce aliasing. Compute midpoints between adjacent uniform samples: \text{mids} = 0.5 \cdot (z{fine}[:, 1:] + z{fine}[:,:-1]) Define intervals: \text{lower} = \text{concat}([z{fine}[:,:1], \text{mids}], \text{dim}=-1) \text{upper} = \text{concat}([\text{mids}, z{fine}[:, -1:]], \text{dim}=-1) Generate random jitter: t{rand} = \text{rand}(z{fine}.shape) Jitter the samples: z{fine} = \text{lower} + (\text{upper} - \text{lower}) \cdot t{rand} If deterministic is True, z{fine} remains the uniform grid from Step 4. 6. Combine and Sort (Global): Concatenate the original coarse samples with the random samples z{add} and sort them. z{vals\ret} = \text{sort}(\text{concat}([\text{coarse\z\vals}, z{add}], \text{dim}=-1), \text{dim}=-1)[0] 8. Inject Fine Samples for Non-Edge Rays: For rays where the peak index is not at the very beginning (index > 0), concatenate the structured fine samples z{fine} with the coarse samples and sort. \text{mask} = \text{max\indices} > 0 z{vals\ret}[\text{mask}] = \text{sort}(\text{concat}([\text{coarse\z\vals}[\text{mask}], z{fine}[\text{mask}]], \text{dim}=-1), \text{dim}=-1)[0] For rays where maxindices == 0, the sorted combination of coarse and random samples (z{vals\ret}) is retained. 9. Args: coarsezvals: (numrays, numcoarse) Tensor of coarse sample depths. coarseweights: (numrays, numcoarse) Tensor of coarse sample weights. near: Float, near plane. far: Float, far plane. maxsamples: Int, max fine samples per ray. Nsamples: Int, target number of fine samples around peak. rangeval: Float, width parameter around peak. deterministic: Bool, use stratified sampling. Returns: zvalsret: (numrays, numtotal) Tensor of sorted sample depths. The implementation must handle this by returning the single peak value. Boundary Conditions: The random samples zadd are strictly within [near, far]. Limitations: The fixed range parameter may not adapt well to varying scene densities; the lack of clamping for zfine can lead to out-of-bounds samples; the logic for maxindices == 0 may result in suboptimal sampling at the ray start. name: Inverse Sampling for Fine Rays
head: FineSampler
body: Inverse Sampling for Fine Rays is a hierarchical sampling technique in volume rendering that generates fine-grained sample positions along a ray by leveraging the probability distribution derived from a prior coarse rendering pass. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling in regions of high radiance or opacity by concentrating samples where they contribute most to the final image. It differs from its parent, Hierarchical Sampling (Inverse CDF Sampling), by explicitly defining the construction of the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF) from coarse weights, and the specific noise-injection step required to map discrete indices back to continuous depth space. It differs from Inverse Opacity Calculation by operating on pre-computed coarse weights rather than deriving probabilities from opacity accumulation during the fine pass. Inputs and Outputs: Input: zvals (coarse sample depths, shape [batch, numcoarsesamples]), weights (coarse sample importance weights, shape [batch, numcoarsesamples]), numfinesamples (integer, number of fine samples to generate per ray). Output: zvalsfine (fine sample depths, shape [batch, numfinesamples]). Data Structures: zvals: 1D array of depths along the ray. weights: 1D array of non-negative importance weights corresponding to zvals. Steps: 1. Normalize Weights: Compute the probability mass function (PMF) by normalizing the coarse weights. pi = \frac{wi}{\sum{j} wj} where wi is the weight at index i. If \sum wj = 0, use uniform distribution pi = 1/N. 2. Compute CDF: Compute the cumulative distribution function (CDF) from the PMF. ci = \sum{k=0}^{i} pk Ensure c{N-1} = 1.0 to handle floating-point errors. 3. Generate Uniform Random Numbers: Generate M uniform random numbers u \sim \mathcal{U}(0, 1) for each ray in the batch. 4. Inverse CDF Sampling: For each random number u, find the index i such that c{i-1} < u \le ci. Interpolate between zi and z{i+1} to find the continuous depth. z{fine} = zi + \frac{u - ci}{c{i+1} - ci} (z{i+1} - zi) If u > c{N-1}, clamp to z{N-1}. 5. Sort and Concatenate: Sort the generated fine samples. Concatenate with original coarse samples if required by the parent class RaySampler logic, then sort the combined set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def inversesamplingfinerays(zvals, weights, numfinesamples): """ zvals: [batch, numcoarse] weights: [batch, numcoarse] numfinesamples: int """ batchsize, numcoarse = zvals.shape # Step 1: Normalize weights to get PMF # Add small epsilon to avoid division by zero eps = 1e-10 pmf = weights / (weights.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) + eps) # Step 2: Compute CDF cdf = pmf.cumsum(dim=1) # Ensure last element is 1.0 cdf[:, -1] = 1.0 # Step 3: Generate uniform random numbers # Shape: [batch, numfinesamples] u = torch.rand(batchsize, numfinesamples, device=zvals.device) # Step 4: Inverse CDF Sampling # Find indices where cdf < u # We need to find the bin index for each u # Using searchsorted to find the right index indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, right=True) - 1 indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, numcoarse - 2) # Get lower and upper bounds for interpolation zlow = zvals.gather(1, indices) zhigh = zlow + 1e-6 # Placeholder for z[i+1], need to gather properly # Correct gathering for zhigh indiceshigh = indices + 1 zhigh = zvals.gather(1, indiceshigh) # Get CDF values for interpolation cdflow = cdf.gather(1, indices) cdfhigh = cdf.gather(1, indiceshigh) # Interpolate # Avoid division by zero if cdflow == cdfhigh denom = cdfhigh - cdflow denom = torch.where(denom == 0, torch.oneslike(denom), denom) zfine = zlow + (u - cdflow) / denom (zhigh - zlow) return zfine Edge Cases: Zero weights: Handled by adding epsilon or falling back to uniform distribution. Flat CDF: Interpolation denominator becomes zero; handled by clamping or fallback. Boundary conditions: Clamping indices to valid range. This method generates secondary sample positions along a ray by leveraging the probability distribution derived from a prior coarse rendering pass. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling in regions of high radiance or opacity by concentrating samples where they contribute most to the final image. It differs from its parent, Inverse Sampling for Fine Rays, by explicitly defining the construction of the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF) from coarse weights, and the specific noise-injection step required to map discrete indices back to continuous depth space. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for sorting if concatenation is used, or O(M) for inverse sampling where M is the number of fine samples. Memory Complexity: O(N + M) for storing coarse and fine samples. Strengths: Reduces noise in high-variance regions by concentrating samples where they matter. Limitations: Requires a prior coarse pass. Performance depends on the quality of coarse weights. When to use: When coarse samples are available and high-frequency details are expected. When not to use: When memory is constrained or coarse pass is not feasible. The FineSampler inherits from RaySampler and uses coarse samples and weights to perform inverse sampling. name: Importance Sampling (Fine)
head: Fine Importance Sampling, Fine Ray Importance Sampling
body: This method generates secondary sample positions along a ray by leveraging the probability distribution derived from a prior coarse rendering pass. It solves the problem of inefficient uniform sampling in regions of high radiance or opacity by concentrating samples where they contribute most to the final image. It differs from its parent, Inverse Sampling for Fine Rays, by explicitly defining the construction of the probability density function (PDF) and cumulative distribution function (CDF) from coarse weights, and the specific noise-injection step required to map discrete indices back to continuous depth space. Inputs: Coarse weights wi for i \in \{0, \dots, N{coarse}-1\}, representing the contribution of each coarse sample to the ray's color/depth. Number of fine samples to generate, Kf - K{fd} (denoted as N{fine} in sources). Number of coarse samples, N{coarse}. Ray depth bounds (near/far) or disparity bounds. Outputs: N{fine} sample positions (depths or disparities) along the ray. Data Structures: weights: Array of size N{coarse}. pdf: Array of size N{coarse}. cdf: Array of size N{coarse} + 1. u: Array of size N{fine} containing uniform random numbers in 0, 1). indices: Array of size N{fine} containing integer indices into the CDF. zsteps: Array of size N{fine} containing normalized positions in [0, 1). Steps: 1. Regularize Weights: Add a small epsilon \epsilon = 10^{-5} to all coarse weights to prevent division by zero. w'i = wi + \epsilon 2. Compute PDF: Normalize the regularized weights along the ray dimension to form a probability distribution. \text{pdf}i = \frac{w'i}{\sum{j=0}^{N{coarse}-1} w'j} 3. Compute CDF: Compute the cumulative sum of the PDF. Prepend a zero to the CDF array to handle the first interval correctly, resulting in an array of size N{coarse} + 1. \text{cdf}0 = 0 \text{cdf}{i+1} = \text{cdf}i + \text{pdf}i \quad \text{for } i \in \{0, \dots, N{coarse}-1\} 4. Generate Random Numbers: Generate N{fine} uniform random numbers uk \in [0, 1) for k \in \{0, \dots, N{fine}-1\}. 5. Find Indices: Use binary search (searchsorted) to find the index idxk in the CDF such that \text{cdf}{idxk} \le uk < \text{cdf}{idxk+1}. 6. Clamp Indices: Ensure indices are valid, [clamping to a minimum of 0. idxk = \max(0, idxk) 7. Compute Normalized Steps: Add uniform noise to the index to break ties and map to a continuous normalized position zk \in 0, 1). The source specifies adding uniform noise to the index and dividing by N{coarse}. zk = \frac{idxk + \text{uniform}(0, 1)}{N{coarse}} Note: This step effectively interpolates within the bin defined by the coarse sample. 8. Map to Depth/Disparity: Map the normalized step zk to the actual depth or disparity space using the same transformation logic used in the coarse sampling stage (e.g., [linear interpolation between near and far planes, or disparity-to-depth conversion). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def importancesamplingfine(weights, ncoarse, nfine, near, far): """ Perform fine importance sampling based on coarse weights. Args: weights: np.ndarray of shape (Ncoarse,), coarse rendering weights. ncoarse: int, number of coarse samples. nfine: int, number of fine samples to generate. near: float, near plane distance. far: float, far plane distance. Returns: np.ndarray of shape (Nfine,), sample depths. """ # 1. Regularize weights epsilon = 1e-5 weightsreg = weights + epsilon # 2. Compute PDF pdf = weightsreg / np.sum(weightsreg) # 3. Compute CDF (prepend zero) cdf = np.zeros(ncoarse + 1) cdf[1:] = np.cumsum(pdf) # 4. Generate uniform random numbers u = np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=nfine) # 5. Find indices in CDF # searchsorted finds the index where u[i] should be inserted to maintain order # This corresponds to the lower bound index in the CDF indices = np.searchsorted(cdf, u, side='left') # 6. Clamp indices to minimum 0 indices = np.maximum(indices, 0) # 7. Compute normalized zsteps # Add uniform noise to the index and divide by ncoarse noise = np.random.uniform(0, 1, size=nfine) zsteps = (indices + noise) / ncoarse # 8. Map zsteps to depth space # Assuming linear depth interpolation for this example # If disparity space is used, the mapping logic would differ depths = near + zsteps (far - near) return depths Parameters: N{coarse}: Number of coarse samples. Typical value: 64. N{fine}: Number of fine samples. Typical value: 64. \epsilon: Epsilon for weight regularization. Typical value: 10^{-5}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Weights: If all coarse weights are zero, the PDF becomes undefined. The epsilon addition prevents this. Index Out of Bounds: searchsorted may return an index equal to the length of the CDF if uk is very close to 1. Clamping to the maximum valid index (or handling the last bin explicitly) is required. The source specifies clamping to minimum 0, but does not explicitly mention clamping to maximum. Standard implementation should clamp to N{coarse}-1 or handle the last bin. Precision: Floating point precision in cumulative sum can lead to slight inaccuracies in CDF normalization. Disparity vs Depth: The mapping step (8) depends on whether the ray is parameterized by depth or disparity. The source states "using the same logic as coarse sampling," implying consistency with the coarse sampling method's parameterization. The general technique of using inverse transform sampling to generate fine samples based on a probability distribution. Importance Sampling (Fine) is a specific implementation of this technique using coarse weights. Link Time Complexity: O(N{coarse} + N{fine}) for computing PDF, CDF, and sampling. The searchsorted operation is O(\log N{coarse}) per sample, leading to O(N{fine} \log N{coarse}) for the sampling step. Overall complexity is dominated by O(N{coarse} + N{fine} \log N{coarse}). Memory Complexity: O(N{coarse}) to store the CDF. Strengths: Reduces variance in regions of high radiance or opacity by concentrating samples where they matter. Improves convergence rate compared to uniform fine sampling. Limitations: Requires a prior coarse pass to generate weights. Adds computational overhead for computing PDF/CDF and sampling. Performance gain depends on the scene's complexity and the quality of the coarse estimate. When to Use: When computational budget allows for a two-pass approach (coarse then fine) and the scene has significant variation in radiance/opacity. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained (due to CDF storage) or when the coarse estimate is poor (leading to poor fine sampling). This method is part of the hierarchical sampling strategy used in Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and related methods. It was introduced in the context of PixelNeRF and VolRecon. The approach builds on the idea that a coarse sampling pass can provide a rough estimate of the scene's structure, which can then be used to guide a more detailed fine sampling pass. This technique has become standard in many NeRF variants to improve rendering quality and efficiency. sxyu/pixel-nerf, https://github.com/sxyu/pixel-nerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) [PDF] VolRecon: Volume Rendering of Signed Ray Distance Functions for..., https://openaccess.thecvf.com/content/CVPR2023/papers/RenVolReconVolumeRenderingofSignedRayDistanceFunctionsforGeneralizableCVPR2023paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Discrete Distribution Sampler
head: Discrete Distribution Sampling, DistributionSampler
body: The Discrete Distribution Sampler selects indices from a finite set of choices based on associated weights, mapping a uniform random number to a specific bin via cumulative probability. It serves as the core selection mechanism in hierarchical sampling pipelines, enabling volume rendering algorithms to concentrate samples in high-density regions defined by per-bin weights. Unlike continuous interpolation methods, it operates on discrete probability mass functions, making it suitable for selecting from pre-computed bin structures or proposal distributions. The method supports two primary modes: stochastic sampling for unbiased estimation and deterministic top-k selection for stable training or debugging. The input is a set of choices with associated weights (or a probability density function tensor) and a uniform random variable u \in [0, 1). Inputs: choices: A list or tensor of items, each with an associated weight wi \ge 0. u: A uniform random number in [0, 1). deterministic: A boolean flag. If true, selects top-k indices; if false, samples stochastically. numsamples: The number of indices to select (used in deterministic mode). Outputs: index: The selected index or indices. densities: The probability density values at the selected indices. Weighted Choice: A structure containing an identifier and a float weight. PDF Tensor: In tensor-based implementations, the input is a float tensor of shape Float[batch, bucket], where bucket represents the number of discrete bins. Index Tensor: The output is an int64 tensor of shape Int64[batch, sample]. 1. Calculate Total Weight: Compute the sum of all weights: W{total} = \sum{i} wi 2. Scale Random Number: Map the uniform random variable u to the range [0, W{total}): u' = u \times W{total} 3. Iterative Subtraction: Iterate through the choices in order. For each choice i with weight wi: u' \leftarrow u' - wi If u' \le 0, return the current choice's index. 4. Fallback: If the loop completes without returning (due to floating-point precision issues where u' remains slightly positive), return the last element's index. 1. Sort and Select: Sort the probability densities (weights) in descending order and select the top k indices. 2. Gather Values: Retrieve the corresponding values from the target tensor using the selected indices. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def samplediscretedistributionstochastic(choices, u): """ Samples a single index from a list of weighted choices using inverse CDF sampling. Args: choices: List of objects with attribute 'weight' (float >= 0). u: Uniform random number in [0, 1). Returns: index: The index of the selected choice. """ # Step 1: Calculate total weight totalw = sum(choice.weight for choice in choices) # Guard against zero total weight if totalw == 0: return 0 # Default to first index or handle error # Step 2: Scale u uscaled = u totalw # Step 3: Iterate and subtract for i, choice in enumerate(choices): uscaled -= choice.weight if uscaled <= 0.0: return i # Step 4: Fallback return len(choices) - 1 Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gatherdiscretevalues(target, index, bucketdim): """ Gathers values from a target tensor using an index tensor, handling broadcasting. Args: target: Tensor of shape [..., bucketsize,...]. index: Int64 tensor of shape [..., samplesize]. bucketdim: The dimension in target corresponding to the buckets. Returns: gathered: Tensor with values selected by index. """ # Determine bucket dimension as second-to-last dimension of index # Note: Source specifies bucketdim = index.ndim - 1, but gather is along target's bucketdim. # We assume index aligns with the bucket dimension of the target. # Expand index dimensions to match target dimensionality while len(index.shape) < len(target.shape): index = index[..., None] # Broadcast index to match target shape, preserving bucket dimension size # This step ensures index can be used for gathering along the specific bucketdim broadcastedindexshape = list(target.shape) # The index tensor must be broadcastable. # If target's bucket dim is 1, reset index to zeros to handle broadcasting correctly if target.shape[bucketdim] == 1: index = torch.zeroslike(index) # Perform gather operation # Note: In PyTorch, gather requires index to have same number of dims as input # and indices to be broadcastable to input shape. return target.gather(dim=bucketdim, index=index) A variant that samples from a piecewise-constant probability density function defined by bin endpoints t and weight logits w{logits}. It supports deterministic center sampling (using linspace with padding) or stochastic sampling with uniform jitter. It uses an inverse CDF function (invertcdf) to map uniform samples to bin coordinates. Key parameters include singlejitter (same jitter for all samples along a ray) and usegpuresampling (uses gather instruction for speed). A utility function that selects n indices from a weight distribution, switching between PyTorch and NumPy implementations to handle large tensor sizes (specifically when numelements > 2^{24}). It normalizes weights, converts to NumPy for np.random.choice, and converts back to a Tensor. Samples indices from a discrete probability mass function (PMF) with replacement. It computes the cumulative distribution function (CDF) along the support dimension, generates uniform random numbers, and uses searchsorted to find corresponding indices in the CDF. Indices are clamped to the valid range [0, \text{support\size} - 1]. Time Complexity: O(N) for stochastic sampling where N is the number of bins, as it requires a linear scan to subtract weights. Deterministic top-k selection is O(N \log N) due to sorting. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the weights and cumulative sums (if precomputed). Precision: The iterative subtraction method is susceptible to floating-point precision errors if weights vary significantly in magnitude or if N is very large, potentially causing the loop to complete without u' \le 0. Using cumulative sums and binary search (searchsorted) can mitigate this but increases implementation complexity. Strengths: Simple to implement, unbiased (in stochastic mode), and flexible with arbitrary weight distributions. Limitations: Linear scan is slow for large N; deterministic mode loses stochasticity. The Discrete Distribution Sampler is a fundamental component in Monte Carlo rendering and hierarchical sampling strategies. It originates from the general technique of inverse transform sampling applied to discrete domains. In the context of volume rendering, it is used to select sample positions along a ray based on pre-computed density or opacity weights, enabling efficient hierarchical sampling. name: Hierarchical 3D Sampling
head: Hierarchical Poisson-disk Sampling, Ordered 3D Dithering
body: Hierarchical 3D Sampling generates a sequence of points within a unit cube such that any prefix \{P0, \dots, P{n-1}\} maintains uniform density and a minimum inter-point distance. This property enables density control for volume rendering, serving as an alternative to opacity control or managing the level of detail (LOD) by selecting a subset of pre-computed points. The method provides hierarchical point sets where the priority of a point is defined by its serial number (index) in the generation sequence. Ordered dithering produces regular patterns, while Poisson-disk variants produce irregular patterns to mitigate aliasing. Inputs: Target number of points n. Sampling domain: A unit cube [0,1]^3 with periodic boundary conditions (each face treated identically to its opposite). Source data: Voxel grid for scalar value retrieval. Outputs: A sequence of 3D coordinates \{P0, P1, \dots, P{n-1}\} representing the hierarchical point set. Pre-computed histogram h(s): The count of sampled points falling into each scalar value bin s, used for estimating the total number of rendered primitives. 1. Point List: An array of 3D vectors storing coordinates (x, y, z). The index k corresponds to the priority number; smaller k implies higher priority. 2. Histogram: An array indexed by scalar value s, storing the integer count h(s) of points whose interpolated scalar value equals s. 1. Generate Point Set: Create the sequence of points using either Ordered 3D Dithering or Hierarchical Poisson-disk Sampling. 2. Interpolate Scalar Values: For each point Pk, calculate the scalar value sk by linear interpolation from the original voxel data. 3. Update Histogram: Increment the count h(sk) in the histogram for the calculated scalar value. 4. Estimate Total Points: Use the histogram to estimate the total number of candidates N for density control. This is the simplest implementation, extending 2D ordered dithering (digital halftoning) directly to 3D. Method: Divide the unit cube into a grid. Assign points to grid centers. Sort the grid cells based on a 3D dithering matrix value. The first n points in this sorted order form the subset \{P0, \dots, P{n-1}\}. Properties: Points are evenly distributed. The serial number k determines priority. Proposed by McCool and Fiume, this method creates irregular patterns to avoid aliasing. Parameters: Failure threshold T{\text{fail}} = 1000. Radius reduction factor \alpha = 0.99. Initial minimum distance limit L{\text{init}}: Not given in the sources. Procedure: 1. Initialize an empty list of placed points. 2. Set current limit length L = L{\text{init}}. 3. Repeat until n points are placed: a. Attempt to place a new point P{\text{new}} randomly in the unit cube. b. Check distance to all previously placed points. c. If distance to any existing point is less than L, discard P{\text{new}} and increment failure counter C. d. If C < T{\text{fail}}, repeat step 3a. e. If C \ge T{\text{fail}}, reduce L \leftarrow L \times \alpha and reset C = 0. f. If L becomes too small to place any point, terminate or adjust L{\text{init}}. Scalar Interpolation: The scalar value s at point P is calculated by linear interpolation from the original voxel data. s = \text{LinearInterpolate}(VoxelData, P) Note: Higher degree interpolation or interpolation from irregular meshed data is also possible. Total Candidate Estimation: For a density function dm(s), the estimated total number of points N is: N = \sum{s=s{\min}}^{s{\max}} dm(s) h(s) where s{\min} and s{\max} are the minimum and maximum scalar values, and h(s) is the histogram count. For other density functions requiring gradient magnitude, an approximation is used: N = \sum{s=s{\min}}^{s{\max}} \bar{g}(s) h(s) where \bar{g}(s) is the average gradient magnitude at scalar value s. Density Adjustment: If the number of candidates N is too large for interactivity, the actual point density d(x) is reduced: d(x) = dm(x) \min(1, S/N) where S represents a target scaling factor. name: Uniform Ray Sampling
head: Fixed-step Ray Sampling, Regular Sampling, Uniform Distance Sampling, Uniform Point Sampling, Uniform Point Sampling along Rays, Uniform Sampling
body: Uniform Ray Sampling is a ray traversal approach where samples are taken at equal distances along the ray as it passes through volume data stored on a regular grid. It serves as the baseline sampling method in NeRF, assuming every point along the ray contributes equally to the final rendering when no transmittance estimator is available. It sets itself apart from Stochastic Jittering by using fixed intervals rather than random offsets, and from Slab-based Ray Sampling by ignoring voxel boundaries and maintaining a constant step size regardless of scene geometry. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (3D vector). Ray direction \mathbf{d} (unit-norm 3D vector). Near clipping plane distance t{near} (scalar). Far clipping plane distance t{far} (scalar). Number of samples N (integer). Outputs: Sample positions \mathbf{x}i for i \in [0, N-1] (3D vectors). Sample depths ti (scalars). Segment lengths \Delta ti (scalars). Data Structures: tvals: 1D tensor/array of size N containing linearly spaced depth values. samplepoints: 3D tensor/array of shape (N, 3) containing the 3D coordinates of the samples. samplelengths: 1D tensor/array of size N (or (N, 1)) containing the distance between consecutive samples. Steps: 1. Generate N linearly spaced depth values ti between t{near} and t{far}: ti = t{near} + i \cdot \frac{t{far} - t{near}}{N - 1}, \quad i = 0, 1, \dots, N-1 Note: Some implementations use N+1 points or exclude endpoints depending on the integration rule, but the core spacing remains uniform. 2. Compute the 3D sample positions by scaling the ray direction by the depth values and adding the ray origin: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \cdot \mathbf{d} 3. Calculate the segment lengths (deltas) for integration. For i < N-1: \Delta ti = t{i+1} - ti = \frac{t{far} - t{near}}{N - 1} For the last sample, \Delta t{N-1} is often set to a large value or equal to the previous step depending on the transmittance calculation. 4. Evaluate the volume density \sigma(\mathbf{x}i) and color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}i) at each sample position. 5. Compute opacity \alphai using the segment length and density: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i) \cdot \Delta ti) 6. Render using front-to-back compositing: C = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ti \alphai \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}i), \quad Ti = \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def uniformraysampling(rayorigins, raydirections, near, far, numsamples): """ Generate uniform samples along rays. Args: rayorigins: Tensor of shape (N, 3) raydirections: Tensor of shape (N, 3), unit-norm near: Scalar or Tensor of shape (N,) far: Scalar or Tensor of shape (N,) numsamples: Integer Returns: samplepoints: Tensor of shape (N, numsamples, 3) samplelengths: Tensor of shape (N, numsamples, 1) """ # Step 1: Generate linearly spaced depth values # tvals shape: (numsamples,) tvals = torch.linspace(near, far, numsamples) # Broadcast tvals to match ray batch dimension # tvals shape: (1, numsamples, 1) tvals = tvals.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1) # Step 2: Compute 3D sample positions # rayorigins shape: (N, 1, 3) # raydirections shape: (N, 1, 3) # samplepoints shape: (N, numsamples, 3) samplepoints = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + tvals raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # Step 3: Compute segment lengths # deltas shape: (numsamples - 1,) deltas = tvals[0, 1:, 0] - tvals[0,:-1, 0] # Append a large value for the last segment to handle transmittance correctly # Or repeat the last delta. Here we append a large value as per common practice lastdelta = torch.full((1,), 1e10, device=deltas.device) deltas = torch.cat([deltas, lastdelta], dim=0) # Reshape deltas to (N, numsamples, 1) samplelengths = deltas.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(-1) return samplepoints, samplelengths Parameters: numsamples (N): Number of points to sample along each ray. Typical value: 64. near (t{near}): Near clipping plane distance. Defined in config. far (t{far}): Far clipping plane distance. Defined in config. stepsize (\Delta t): Fixed distance between samples, calculated as (t{far} - t{near}) / (N - 1). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: If the step size is too large, features are missed and a banding effect appears. Mitigation: Add small random noise to sample positions (stratified sampling). Computational Cost: High computational cost due to the maximum number of interpolations required per sample point, especially in 3D where 7 interpolations are needed per sample for trilinear interpolation. Empty Space: Uniform sampling evaluates empty space equally to occupied space, leading to low efficiency compared to spatial skipping or PDF-based methods. This method ensures even spacing along rays within a voxel cell by using preprocessed ray data and a 4-bit depth-sampling indicator stored in the pixel opacity. It solves the problem of efficiently computing sampling coordinates for trilinear interpolation and evaluating the Riemann sum in front-to-back order. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by relying on a shared set of preprocessed rays and a stateful depth indicator to maintain sampling continuity across cells. Uniform NDC Point Sampling generates a fixed number of points uniformly distributed along each ray in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) space, mapping the ray parameter t from 0 to 1. Unlike standard uniform sampling which depends on scene bounding boxes or depth ranges, this method assumes a canonical camera frame, making it suitable for neural rendering pipelines that require consistent positional encoding inputs regardless of scene scale. It sets itself apart from Uniform Ray Sampling by decoupling sample density from physical depth, and from Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling by providing a linear sampling curve in NDC space that corresponds to a 1/x disparity distribution in original space. Local Sampling is a ray sampling strategy that concentrates evaluation points around a known surface representation (e.g., a depth texture) to minimize empty-space evaluations in volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Uniform Ray Sampling by leveraging geometric priors to achieve high quality with significantly fewer samples, though it relies on the availability of ground truth depth during training. Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling is a sample placement strategy that distributes points along a view ray using a logarithmic function to concentrate density near the camera while maintaining coverage over large depth ranges. It addresses the limitation of uniform sampling in large scenes, where linear spacing causes excessive evaluations in the distance or insufficient resolution near the viewer. Pixel-guided ray sampling is a non-uniform sampling strategy that calculates a prior probability distribution based on the color variation (standard deviation) within pixel neighborhoods to identify high-information regions. It solves the problem of inefficient ray casting in uniform sampling by concentrating computational resources on pixels with sharp color differences, which typically correspond to rich texture details or sharp density variations in the scene. Context-based Probability Ray Sampling is a non-uniform ray sampling strategy that allocates more rays to image regions with high visual complexity (edges, texture) and fewer rays to trivial regions (uniform backgrounds). It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by sampling more rays in areas with large probability (complex shapes/colors) and fewer rays in trivial areas (white background, walls, floors) rather than uniformly. Stratified sampling is a family of techniques that reduce variance and aliasing in volume rendering by dividing the ray integration interval into discrete bins and sampling one point per bin, ensuring better coverage than pure uniform random sampling. It sets itself apart from Uniform Ray Sampling by replacing fixed intervals or pure randomness with controlled jitter within defined strata, breaking up regular patterns while guaranteeing no gaps in the depth range. Samples points forward along the ray from the surface to get SDF values inside the object, used when latent space is not pretrained. It asserts numforwardsampling > 0, extracts valid camera rays and z-depths, and computes grid values to generate point samples at validzdepth + grid. When the camera ray reaches the translucent material after diffuse interactions, sample the ray randomly with a small number of samples, as low as one sample per camera ray. It computes k{max} sample points Pk using the formula: dk = -\frac{1}{\sigmat} \log \left( 1 - \frac{|k(1 - e^{-\sigmat d{\max}})|}{k{\max}} \right) where \sigmat is the extinction coefficient, k is the sample index, and k{max} is the total number of samples. This ensures exactly k{max} samples are placed, preventing undersampling for small object widths. Selects N\theta azimuthal directions and N\phi elevational directions to uniformly cover the sphere, then evenly places Nr points between near and far bounds for each direction, querying the network at N\theta \times N\phi \times Nr points. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. The cost is linear with respect to the number of samples and independent of scene complexity. Memory Complexity: O(N) per ray to store sample positions and densities. Performance: On RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell, 1M rays, dragon dataset, fp32, cone=0: Speedup 1.06x (2.953ms -> 2.790ms) with optimizations. For a dataset with 1-unit grid spacing, a 0.1 step size took nearly 10 times as long as a 1.0 step size, which took twice as long as a 2.0 step size. Strengths: Simple to implement, accurate for regular grids, guaranteed even spacing. Limitations: Low efficiency in empty space, high computational cost due to interpolations, prone to aliasing if step size is large. When to use: Baseline for neural rendering (NeRF), small scenes, or when no transmittance estimator is available. When not to use: Large scenes with significant empty space, where spatial skipping or importance sampling is preferred. Uniform Ray Sampling originated as the default sampling strategy in NeRF. It is based on the assumption that every point along the ray contributes equally to the final rendering, leading to a constant PDF and linearly decaying transmittance. It is widely used in neural radiance field rendering and direct volume rendering on regular grids. name: Evenly Spaced Sampling with Preprocessed Rays and Depth Indicators
head: Depth Indicator Sampling, Preprocessed Ray Structure Sampling
body: This method ensures even spacing along rays within a voxel cell by using preprocessed ray data and a 4-bit depth-sampling indicator stored in the pixel opacity. It solves the problem of efficiently computing sampling coordinates for trilinear interpolation and evaluating the Riemann sum in front-to-back order. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by relying on a shared set of preprocessed rays and a stateful depth indicator to maintain sampling continuity across cells. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A RAY structure containing entry coordinates (xyz) and a precomputed Length parameter representing the maximum number of Unit Translation Vectors (UTVs) that fit within the cell. A PIXEL structure containing a density field. An integer samplingrate in the range [1, 16]. Output: Updated PIXEL.density with accumulated luminance/density and the updated depth indicator. Data Structures: 1. Preprocessed Ray Structure: Stores 3 entry coordinates (x, y, z) as 16-bit unsigned integers representing values in the range [0, 1], plus an additional ray.Length parameter representing the maximum number of UTVs that can be added to the entry point before exiting the cell. 2. Pixel Structure: Contains a density field. The lower 4 bits (mask 0xF) store the depth-sampling indicator (next sampling offset). The upper bits (mask 0xFFF0) store accumulated density/luminance values as 16-bit unsigned integers. Unit Translation Vector (UTV): The UTV is parallel to the viewing direction. It is defined as 1/16 of the longest vector crossing the cell. Consequently, its coordinate on the major projection axis is also equal to 1/16. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Extract the lower 4 bits of pixel.density to get nextsampling, a discrete integer index representing the number of UTVs to add. 2. Loop: While nextsampling is less than ray.Length: a. Calculate the sampling position: \text{xyz} = \text{ray.xyz} + \text{next\sampling} \times \text{UTV.xyz}. b. Interpolate the volume data at xyz and accumulate the result into the pixel. c. Increment nextsampling by samplingrate. 3. Finalize: Subtract ray.Length from nextsampling to wrap the indicator for the next traversal or frame. 4. Update: Clear the lower 4 bits of pixel.density and add the new nextsampling value to it. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def accumulate(ray, pixel, samplingrate, utv): # Extract lower 4 bits for depth indicator (discrete integer index) nextsampling = pixel.density & 0xF # Iterate while within the cell's precomputed length while nextsampling < ray.Length: # Calculate sampling position using preprocessed ray entry and UTV xyz = ray.xyz + nextsampling utv # Interpolate volume data at xyz and accumulate into pixel # (Standard trilinear interpolation and front-to-back compositing) # Implementation depends on volume data structure # Advance to next sampling point nextsampling += samplingrate # Wrap the indicator for the next cell traversal or frame nextsampling -= ray.Length # Update pixel density: keep upper bits (accumulated data), set lower bits (new indicator) pixel.density = (pixel.density & 0xFFF0) + nextsampling Parameters: samplingrate: An arbitrary integer value within the range [1, 16]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation: Sampling positions and trilinear weights are approximated due to the limited set of preprocessed rays, limited projection lists, and the 4-bit depth indicator. Accuracy vs. Performance: Accuracy can be improved by increasing table sizes and depth bits, but this increases cache misses and reduces randomizing, trading noise for aliasing. A technique to reduce aliasing by using incoherent sampling depths between neighboring pixels. Half of the depth indicators are initialized to zero, and the others to half the sampling rate, ensuring every pixel differs from its four nearest neighbors. Unlike usual rectilinear sampling which causes staircase effects even at high rates, interleaving depth indicators clearly reduces aliasing. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampling points per ray within the cell, as each step performs a constant-time lookup and accumulation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the preprocessed ray table and the projection lists. The pixel structure is compact, storing 16-bit density with an embedded 4-bit state. Strengths: Efficient computation of sampling coordinates avoids complex ray-cell intersection calculations per sample. Reduces aliasing through interleaving. Limitations: Approximation errors due to limited preprocessed rays and 4-bit depth indicator. Increasing table sizes and depth bits increases cache misses and reduces randomizing, trading noise for aliasing. When to use: When rendering volumes with regular grid structures where even spacing is desired and computational efficiency is prioritized over perfect geometric accuracy. When not to use: When high precision is required and cache misses are acceptable, or when the volume has highly irregular structures that do not align well with the UTV approximation. This method originates from a new object-order ray-casting algorithm. It addresses the difficulties of computing sampling coordinates quickly and ensuring even spacing for Riemann sum evaluation in front-to-back ray casting. The technique leverages the incoherency between rays to improve rendering accuracy, building on earlier work by Theufll et al.. name: Uniform NDC Point Sampling
head: NDC Ray Sampling, NDC Sampling
body: Uniform NDC Point Sampling generates a fixed number of points uniformly distributed along each ray in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) space, mapping the ray parameter t from 0 to 1. Unlike standard uniform sampling which depends on scene bounding boxes or depth ranges, this method assumes a canonical camera frame, making it suitable for neural rendering pipelines that require consistent positional encoding inputs regardless of scene scale. It sets itself apart from Uniform Ray Sampling by decoupling sample density from physical depth, and from Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling by providing a linear sampling curve in NDC space that corresponds to a 1/x disparity distribution in original space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray origins in the average camera frame. raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray directions in the average camera frame. Nsamples: Integer, the fixed number of samples per ray. xyzmin, xyzmax: Tensors of shape (3), defining the bounding box for validity checks (optional but common in implementations like DirectVoxGO). ndcnearplane: Float, default 1.0, defining the near clipping plane in NDC space. Outputs: rayspts: Tensor of shape (N, N\samples, 3), the 3D coordinates of the sampled points. maskoutbbox: Tensor of shape (N, N\samples), boolean mask indicating points outside the bounding box. Data Structures: The method operates on standard floating-point tensors. The ray parameter t (or dist) is a scalar value in [0, 1]. Steps: 1. Transform to Average Camera Frame: Before sampling, rays must be transformed into an "average" camera frame. This involves rotating and translating the ray origins and directions such that the camera poses are centered and aligned. This step is critical; if the original rays are not in this frame, the NDC assumption fails. 2. Compute Normalized Distance: For each ray i and sample index j (where j \in \{0, \dots, N\samples-1\}), compute the normalized distance dist: dist = \frac{j}{N\samples - 1} This maps the samples linearly from t=0 to t=1. 3. Compute 3D Coordinates: Calculate the 3D point p for each sample using linear interpolation along the ray: px = ox + dx \times dist py = oy + dy \times dist pz = oz + dz \times dist where (ox, oy, oz) and (dx, dy, dz) are the components of the ray origin and direction in the average camera frame. 4. Bounding Box Check (Optional): If xyzmin and xyzmax are provided, check if any coordinate of p is less than the corresponding min or greater than the corresponding max. Set the corresponding bit in maskoutbbox to true if the point is outside. 5. Distance Scaling (Variant): In implementations like TensoRF, if NDC sampling is enabled, inter-sample distances are computed and scaled by the ray direction norm to approximate Euclidean distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def uniformndcpointsampling(rayso, raysd, Nsamples, xyzmin=None, xyzmax=None): """ Samples Nsamples uniformly spaced points along each ray in NDC space. Args: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray origins in average camera frame. raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3), ray directions in average camera frame. Nsamples: Integer, number of samples per ray. xyzmin: Tensor of shape (3), minimum bounding box coordinates. xyzmax: Tensor of shape (3), maximum bounding box coordinates. Returns: rayspts: Tensor of shape (N, Nsamples, 3), sampled points. maskoutbbox: Tensor of shape (N, Nsamples), True if point is outside bbox. """ N = rayso.shape[0] # Step 2: Compute normalized distance # dist ranges from 0.0 to 1.0, matching j / (Nsamples - 1) dists = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, Nsamples, device=rayso.device) # Expand dimensions for broadcasting # rayso: (N, 3) -> (N, 1, 3) # raysd: (N, 3) -> (N, 1, 3) # dists: (Nsamples,) -> (1, Nsamples, 1) raysoexp = rayso.unsqueeze(1) raysdexp = raysd.unsqueeze(1) distsexp = dists.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(2) # Step 3: Compute 3D coordinates # p = o + d dist rayspts = raysoexp + raysdexp distsexp maskoutbbox = torch.zeros((N, Nsamples), dtype=torch.bool, device=rayso.device) # Step 4: Bounding box check if xyzmin is not None and xyzmax is not None: # Check if any coordinate is less than min or greater than max # xyzmin: (3,) -> (1, 1, 3) # xyzmax: (3,) -> (1, 1, 3) xyzminexp = xyzmin.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) xyzmaxexp = xyzmax.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0) outmin = rayspts < xyzminexp outmax = rayspts > xyzmaxexp # Any dimension out of bounds outbbox = outmin | outmax # Reduce over the last dimension (x, y, z) maskoutbbox = outbbox.any(dim=-1) return rayspts, maskoutbbox Parameters: Nsamples: The fixed number of samples per ray. ndcnearplane: Default 1.0. Defines the near clipping plane in NDC space. Used in distance scaling variants. dmin: 1. Lower bound for NDC depth. dmax: \infty. Upper bound for NDC depth. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Average Camera Frame: The method is only applicable if all samples lie strictly in the front hemisphere of the average camera frame. Large deviations from this frame lead to high non-linear perspective distortions, which can negatively impact the learning process. Ray Direction Norm: In NDC space, the ray direction norm may vary. If Euclidean distance accuracy is required, distances must be scaled by the ray direction norm. Bounding Box: If the bounding box is not provided, the method does not filter out-of-bounds points, which may lead to sampling empty space or invalid regions. A variant that computes inter-sample distances and scales them by the ray direction norm to approximate Euclidean distance in NDC space. It uses parameters ndcnearplane (default 1.0), simulateeuclidsample (bool), and simulateeucliddepth (float) to control depth simulation. This variant is chosen when accurate depth-based weighting is needed despite using NDC sampling. Time Complexity: O(N \times N\samples), where N is the number of rays and N\samples is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N \times N\samples \times 3) for storing the sampled points. Performance: NDC sampling only surpasses uniform sampling in quality at 128 samples in ablation studies. Strengths: Consistent sample distribution regardless of scene scale; simple linear interpolation; compatible with positional encoding that expects NDC inputs. Limitations: Requires transformation to an average camera frame; sensitive to large deviations from the average frame; less effective than logarithmic or local sampling for foreground-focused scenes with low sample counts. When to Use: When using positional encodings designed for NDC space; when a fixed number of samples is required regardless of depth. When Not to Use: When the scene cannot be easily transformed to an average camera frame; when samples must remain strictly in the front hemisphere of the average camera frame; when depth-aware sampling (e.g., logarithmic) is preferred. Uniform NDC Point Sampling was introduced in the context of NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) to address positional encoding applied equally to foreground and background frequencies. The method transforms rays into an average camera frame and samples uniformly in NDC space, allowing the network to learn consistent features regardless of the original camera configuration. It was proposed as an alternative to logarithmic sampling, offering a linear sampling curve in NDC space that corresponds to a 1/x disparity distribution in original space. The approach is detailed in the original NeRF paper and subsequent works like DONeRF. name: Local Sampling
head: Surface-aware Sampling
body: Local Sampling is a ray sampling strategy that concentrates evaluation points around a known surface representation (e.g., a depth texture) to minimize empty-space evaluations in volume rendering. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Uniform Ray Sampling by leveraging geometric priors to achieve high quality with significantly fewer samples, though it relies on the availability of ground truth depth during training. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera ray parameters, a trained neural radiance field (NeRF) or similar implicit representation, and a ground truth depth texture (or depth oracle network output) representing the scene surface. Output: A set of sample positions along the ray and the corresponding volume rendering result (color and alpha). Data Structures: Depth Texture: A 2D array storing the distance from the camera origin to the nearest surface intersection for each pixel. Ray: Defined by origin o and direction d. Steps: 1. Depth Retrieval: For a given pixel, retrieve the ground truth depth z{gt} from the depth texture. 2. Sample Placement: Place a fraction of the total samples N locally around z{gt}. The remaining samples are distributed uniformly or according to another strategy in the empty space before and after the surface. 3. Volume Rendering: Evaluate the neural network at the sample positions to obtain density \sigma and color c, then perform standard volume integration. Formulas: The depth z{gt} is used to define the local region. If N is the total number of samples, and N{local} is the number of samples placed locally, the positions are clustered around z{gt}. The exact distribution within the local cluster is not specified beyond "around the surface". Parameters: N: Total samples per ray. Tested values: [2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128]. N{local}: Number of samples placed locally. Can be as low as 2 with nearly no decrease in quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Depth Discontinuities: A depth oracle network with a single depth output may smooth depth around discontinuities, causing local sampling to mix foreground and background features and distort the result. Inference Availability: Ground truth depth is often unavailable during inference due to memory/computational constraints and the need for reprojection for novel views. NDC Sampling: Sampling in Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) reaches competitive results only at high sample counts (>64) and falls behind uniform sampling at lower counts because the network must reconstruct the nonlinear transformation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def localsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, depthtexture, nerfmodel, totalsamples=64): # Get ground truth depth for the current pixel # Note: In practice, this requires a depth oracle or pre-computed depth map depthz = depthtexture[rayorigin.x, rayorigin.y] # Determine local sample range around depthz # The exact width of the local region is not specified in the source # Assuming a small epsilon range around depthz for demonstration epsilon = 0.1 localstart = max(0, depthz - epsilon) localend = depthz + epsilon # Place Nlocal samples locally nlocal = 2 localsamples = linspace(localstart, localend, nlocal) # Place remaining samples uniformly in the rest of the ray nuniform = totalsamples - nlocal # Assuming mindepth and maxdepth are defined for the scene uniformsamples = linspace(0, maxdepth, nuniform) # Combine samples allsamples = concatenate([uniformsamples, localsamples]) # Evaluate NeRF and render colors, alphas = volumerender(rayorigin, raydirection, allsamples, nerfmodel) return colors, alphas Uses mesh boundaries to localize surface evaluation, requiring only two samples per ray. It is efficient and applicable as a post-processing step to existing NeRF models. Time Complexity: Reduced compared to uniform sampling due to fewer total samples needed for equivalent quality. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the depth texture or depth oracle network. Performance: With local sampling, the number of samples can be reduced to two with nearly no decrease in quality. Log+warp adds about 1.3 dB in quality over uniform for local sampling. Strengths: Significant gains in quality-speed tradeoff given an ideal sampling oracle. Limitations: Ground truth depth is often not available during inference, making it a niche scenario without an oracle network. Originated in the context of NeRF optimization, specifically in the DONeRF paper, which explores using depth oracle networks to enable local sampling for real-time rendering of compact neural radiance fields. DONeRF: Towards Real‐Time Rendering of Compact Neural Radiance Fields using Depth Oracle Networks, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14340, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mesh-based Sampling
head: Wan et al. Mesh-based Sampling
body: Mesh-based Sampling localizes surface evaluation by estimating the volume density or Signed Distance Field (SDF) to define an inner and outer mesh boundary, using learned features attached to mesh vertices to estimate radiance. It builds on Local Sampling by placing samples around a known ground truth surface representation to reduce empty space evaluations. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by requiring only two samples per ray, significantly improving runtime efficiency while remaining applicable as a post-processing step to any existing NeRF models. Inputs: An implicit representation (volume density or SDF) defining the object geometry. Two meshes (inner and outer) derived from the implicit representation. Learned features attached to the vertices of these meshes. A viewing direction vector \mathbf{d} for the ray. Outputs: Estimated radiance for the ray. Data Structures: Inner Mesh: A triangular mesh representing the inner boundary of the surface region, with vertices storing learned feature vectors. Outer Mesh: A triangular mesh representing the outer boundary of the surface region, with vertices storing learned feature vectors. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Steps: 1. Ray-Mesh Intersection: Compute the intersection points of the viewing ray with both the inner mesh and the outer mesh. Let these intersection points be \mathbf{p}{\text{in}} and \mathbf{p}{\text{out}} respectively. 2. Feature Interpolation: At each intersection point (\mathbf{p}{\text{in}} and \mathbf{p}{\text{out}}), interpolate the learned features from the surrounding mesh vertices. This yields feature vectors \mathbf{f}{\text{in}} and \mathbf{f}{\text{out}}. 3. Radiance Estimation: Feed the interpolated features (\mathbf{f}{\text{in}}, \mathbf{f}{\text{out}}) and the viewing direction \mathbf{d} into a shallow convolutional network. 4. Output: The network outputs the estimated radiance. Formulas: Feature interpolation: \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}) = \text{Interpolate}(\mathcal{M}, \mathbf{p}), where \mathcal{M} is the mesh and \mathbf{p} is the intersection point. Radiance estimation: L = \mathcal{N}(\mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}{\text{in}}), \mathbf{f}(\mathbf{p}{\text{out}}), \mathbf{d}), where \mathcal{N} is the shallow convolutional network. Parameters: Number of samples per ray: 2. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray-mesh intersection precision must be handled carefully to avoid missing thin surface regions or producing incorrect \mathbf{p}{\text{in}}/\mathbf{p}{\text{out}} ordering. The shallow convolutional network architecture must be explicitly designed to accept two spatial feature vectors and a direction vector as joint inputs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def meshbasedsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, innermesh, outermesh, network): # 1. Ray-mesh intersection pin = intersectraymesh(rayorigin, raydirection, innermesh) pout = intersectraymesh(rayorigin, raydirection, outermesh) # 2. Feature interpolation fin = interpolatefeatures(innermesh, pin) fout = interpolatefeatures(outermesh, pout) # 3. Radiance estimation radiance = network(fin, fout, raydirection) return radiance A query point sampling strategy where points are distributed along a displacement trajectory from a voxel grid to the surface closest point, designed to be more efficient than uniform or Gaussian sampling for mesh deformation tasks. It maintains performance with fewer query points (75k vs 200k) and is more efficient for mesh deformation. In unconstrained chair point cloud generation, Trajectory 75k achieved CD=56.12 and EMD=53.30, outperforming Uniform 75k (CD=56.88, EMD=54.93) and Gaussian 75k (CD=56.46, EMD=53.97). Compared to uniform sampling (query points uniformly from voxel shape space) and Gaussian sampling (points sampled with Gaussian distribution, mean=ground truth surface, variance=0.1 and 0.01), trajectory sampling maintains performance with fewer query points (75k vs 200k) and is more efficient for mesh deformation. Efficiency: Requires only two samples per ray, significantly improving runtime efficiency compared to methods that require dense sampling or multiple evaluations. Generality: Can be applied as a post-processing step to any existing NeRF models, making it a versatile addition to existing pipelines. Performance: Specific quantitative performance metrics (e.g., FPS, memory usage) for the Wan et al. method are not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Wan et al. [WRB 23] as a way to localize the surface between an inner and outer mesh using volume density or SDF estimates from an implicit representation. It is cited in recent surveys on learning-based 3D representations as a technique that improves runtime efficiency by minimizing the number of samples per ray. name: Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling
head: Logarithmic Sampling, Logarithmic Sampling for Volumetric Clouds, Logarithmic depth sampling
body: Non-linear (Logarithmic) Sampling is a sample placement strategy that distributes points along a view ray using a logarithmic function to concentrate density near the camera while maintaining coverage over large depth ranges. It addresses the limitation of uniform sampling in large scenes, where linear spacing causes excessive evaluations in the distance or insufficient resolution near the viewer. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Minimum depth d{min}, maximum depth d{max}, and the number of samples N. Outputs: A sequence of N depth values \tilde{d}i for i \in [0, N-1]. Data Structures: A contiguous array of floating-point numbers storing the computed depth values. Parameters: d{min}: The start of the ray segment (typically camera near plane). d{max}: The end of the ray segment (typically camera far plane). N: The total number of samples per ray. Formulas: The method first generates uniform depth indices di and then warps them logarithmically. 1. Uniform Depth Generation: di = d{min} + \frac{i}{N-1} (d{max} - d{min}) where i is the sample index from 0 to N-1. 2. Logarithmic Warping: \tilde{d}i = d{min} + \frac{\log(di - d{min} + 1)}{\log(d{max} - d{min} + 1)} \cdot (d{max} - d{min}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatelogarithmicsamples(dmin, dmax, nsamples): """ Generates nsamples depth values along a ray from dmin to dmax using logarithmic non-linearity. Args: dmin (float): Minimum depth (near plane). dmax (float): Maximum depth (far plane). nsamples (int): Number of samples to generate. Returns: list[float]: List of warped depth values. """ if nsamples <= 0: return [] if dmax <= dmin: return [dmin] nsamples if nsamples == 1: return [dmin] samples = [] depthrange = dmax - dmin # Logarithmic base is arbitrary as long as numerator and denominator match logdenom = math.log(depthrange + 1) for i in range(nsamples): # Step 1: Calculate uniform depth di di = dmin + (i / (nsamples - 1)) depthrange # Step 2: Apply logarithmic warping numerator = math.log(di - dmin + 1) warpeddepth = dmin + (numerator / logdenom) depthrange samples.append(warpeddepth) return samples Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The addition of 1 inside the logarithm ensures the argument remains positive when di = d{min}. Balance: If the sampling density along the z-axis is not balanced with the x-y plane coverage, lighting will appear incorrect when the camera rotates, even if the static render looks acceptable. The goal is to keep the frustum covered by a single sample roughly cubic. Under-sampling: To maintain performance, the number of samples along the z-axis is typically set to approximately 10 times fewer than the number of samples covering the x-y plane area. Uses stratified sampling to reduce variance in radiance estimation. [1373-stratified-monte-carlo-radiance-estimate.md] Precomputes ray depths to ensure even spacing. [2335-evenly-spaced-sampling-with-preprocessed-rays-and-depth-indi.md] Samples in Normalized Device Coordinates. [2395-uniform-ndc-point-sampling.md] Applies stratification across batches of rays. [2730-batch-stratified-sampling.md] Stratifies the ray space directly. [3014-stratified-ray-sampling.md] Samples around a specific depth (e.g., ground truth or previous estimate). [5532-local-sampling.md] Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: In ablation studies, logarithmic sampling increases PSNR by 1.3 dB per doubling of N, compared to 1.8 dB for uniform sampling. Strengths: Reduces network evaluations in large depth ranges without losing quality near the camera. Limitations: Lower PSNR efficiency per sample compared to uniform sampling; requires careful balancing with x-y sampling density to avoid lighting artifacts. When to use: Large scenes with significant depth ranges; volumetric clouds; neural radiance fields where near-field detail is critical. When not to use: Small scenes with limited depth range; scenarios where uniform distribution is strictly required for theoretical guarantees. Non-linear logarithmic sampling was introduced in the context of compact neural radiance fields, specifically in the DONeRF paper. It was proposed as an intuitive first step to reduce network evaluations by focusing samples on objects closer to the camera. The technique was further popularized and adapted for real-time volumetric cloud rendering in game engines, where it is described as the "most important optimization for large scenes" to balance sample frustums.
