name: Pixel-guided ray sampling
head: Color-guided sampling, Pc sampling
body: Pixel-guided ray sampling is a non-uniform sampling strategy that calculates a prior probability distribution based on the color variation (standard deviation) within pixel neighborhoods to identify high-information regions. It solves the problem of inefficient ray casting in uniform sampling by concentrating computational resources on pixels with sharp color differences, which typically correspond to rich texture details or sharp density variations in the scene. Inputs: Source view image Ii with dimensions Hi \times Wi. Pixel coordinates (u, v) where u \in [0, Hi] and v \in [0, Wi]. Neighborhood size parameter n (default 3). Threshold scaling factor 0.01. Outputs: A set of sampled rays ri(u, v) for the image, where the probability of selecting a ray at (u, v) is proportional to the computed probability density P'c(u, v). Data Structures: The probability map Pc is a 2D array of size Hi \times Wi storing the raw standard deviation values. The normalized probability map P'c is a 2D array of size Hi \times Wi storing the final sampling weights. Steps: 1. For each pixel (u, v) in image Ii, compute the mean color \bar{c} of the n \times n neighborhood centered at (u, v). 2. Compute Pc(u, v) as the standard deviation of colors in that neighborhood. 3. Find the maximum value \max(Pc(u, v)) across the image. 4. Calculate threshold s = 0.01 \times \text{mean}(Pc), where \text{mean}(Pc) is the average of all Pc values across the image. 5. Apply normalization: P'c(u, v) = \text{clamp}(Pc(u, v), s, \max(Pc(u, v))) / \max(Pc(u, v)). 6. Sample rays ri(u, v) from pixel coordinates (u, v) according to the probability distribution P'c(u, v). Formulas: Raw probability calculation: Pc(u, v) = \text{std}(c(u, v)) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n^2} \sum{x', y'} [c(x', y') - \bar{c}]^2}, where c(u,v) is the pixel color, n is the neighborhood size (default 3), x' \in [u - \frac{n-1}{2}, u + \frac{n-1}{2}], y' \in [v - \frac{n-1}{2}, v + \frac{n-1}{2}], and \bar{c} is the mean color of the n \times n neighborhood. Computational implementation using variance identity: \text{std}(c(u, v)) = \sqrt{E(c(x', y')^2) - E(c(x', y'))^2}. Note: The source text contains a typo repeating E(c(x', y')^2), but the standard identity implies subtracting the square of the mean. Normalization to prevent underfitting: P'c(u, v) = \frac{\text{clamp}(Pc(u, v), s, \max(Pc(u, v)))}{\max(Pc(u, v))}, where s = 0.01 \times \text{mean}(Pc). Values below s are clamped to s. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pixelguidedraysampling(image: list, n: int = 3) -> list: """ Computes the normalized probability distribution for pixel-guided ray sampling. Args: image: 2D list of scalar color values (H, W). n: Neighborhood size (default 3). Returns: Pprimec: Normalized probability distribution (H, W). """ H = len(image) W = len(image[0]) halfn = (n - 1) // 2 meancolor = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] meansqcolor = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for u in range(H): for v in range(W): ustart = max(0, u - halfn) uend = min(H, u + halfn + 1) vstart = max(0, v - halfn) vend = min(W, v + halfn + 1) count = (uend - ustart) (vend - vstart) sumc = 0.0 sumsq = 0.0 for i in range(ustart, uend): for j in range(vstart, vend): val = image[i][j] sumc += val sumsq += val val meancolor[u][v] = sumc / count meansqcolor[u][v] = sumsq / count Pc = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for u in range(H): for v in range(W): var = meansqcolor[u][v] - meancolor[u][v] 2 Pc[u][v] = max(var, 0.0) 0.5 maxPc = max(max(row) for row in Pc) meanPc = sum(sum(row) for row in Pc) / (H W) s = 0.01 meanPc Pprimec = [[0.0] W for in range(H)] for u in range(H): for v in range(W): val = Pc[u][v] if val < s: val = s if val > maxPc: val = maxPc Pprimec[u][v] = val / maxPc return Pprimec Parameters: n: The size of the pixel neighborhood for computing standard deviation. Default value: 3. Threshold scaling factor: The multiplier for the lower bound threshold s. Default value: 0.01. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: Not given in the sources. Implementers typically clamp indices to image bounds. Zero Variance: If a pixel and its neighborhood have identical colors, Pc(u, v) = 0. The clamping step ensures this value is raised to s, preventing zero probability. Precision: The variance identity E(c^2) - E(c)^2 can suffer from catastrophic cancellation if the color values are large and the variance is small. Using float64 for intermediate calculations is recommended. A ray sampling strategy that uses the standard deviation of depth values in pixel neighborhoods to guide ray sampling, targeting areas with abrupt depth changes. It obtains the depth probability volume Pi(u, v) from an ENeRF coarse-to-fine approach, computes the expected depth D(u, v) = \sum{i=1}^{Nd} Pi(u, v) \cdot Li(u, v) where Li are depth planes sampled from [L{min}, L{max}] and Nd is the number of sampled depth planes. It then computes Pd(u, v) = \text{std}(D(u, v)) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n^2} \sum{x', y'} [D(x', y') - \bar{D}]^2} over an n \times n neighborhood, applies the same normalization as pixel-guided sampling to get P'd(u, v), and fuses it with the color-guided distribution via P{samp}(u, v) = \beta P'c(u, v) + (1 - \beta)P'd(u, v) during training. Time Complexity: O(H \cdot W \cdot n^2) for computing the probability map, where H and W are image dimensions and n is the neighborhood size. Sampling rays is O(H \cdot W) assuming efficient sampling from the distribution. Memory Complexity: O(H \cdot W) to store the probability maps Pc and P'c. Strengths: Focuses computational resources on pixels with sharp color differences, which correspond to rich texture details or sharp density variations in the scene. Limitations: Requires an initial pass to compute statistics. When to use: When training radiance fields or volume renderers where computational efficiency is critical and the scene has significant texture variation. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Pixel-guided ray sampling was introduced in the context of efficient ray sampling for radiance fields reconstruction. It is based on the intuition that pixels with identical colors to their neighborhood contain less information, while those with substantial color differences encompass more scene details. The method replaces the uniform distribution of sampled rays during training with a probability density function derived from color variation. Efficient ray sampling for radiance fields reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cag.2023.11.005, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Context-based Probability Ray Sampling
head: Context-based probability distribution sampling, Probability-based sampling function, context-based ray allocation, probability sampling
body: Context-based Probability Ray Sampling is a non-uniform ray sampling strategy that allocates more rays to image regions with high visual complexity (edges, texture) and fewer rays to trivial regions (uniform backgrounds). It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by sampling more rays in areas with large probability (complex shapes/colors) and fewer rays in trivial areas (white background, walls, floors) rather than uniformly. Inputs: Input image Ii with height Hi and width Wi. Color channel data c(x, y) for each pixel. Threshold parameter s. Outputs: A set of rays ri(u, v) sampled from pixel coordinates (u, v) according to a probability distribution. Data Structures: A 2D probability map g'(u, v) of size Hi \times Wi, normalized to [0, 1]. A cumulative distribution function (CDF) derived from g'(u, v) for sampling. Steps: 1. Compute Local Mean Color: For each pixel (u, v), calculate the mean color \bar{c} of the 3 \times 3 patch centered at (u, v). The patch includes pixels (x, y) where x \in \{u-1, u, u+1\} and y \in \{v-1, v, v+1\}. 2. Compute Standard Deviation (Context Metric): Calculate the standard deviation g(u, v) of the color values within the same 3 \times 3 patch. This metric represents the local color variance, where high values indicate edges or texture and low values indicate uniform areas. 3. Normalize and Clamp: Normalize g(u, v) to the interval [0, 1] and apply a lower-bound clamp to prevent trivial areas from receiving zero rays. 4. Sample Rays: Generate rays ri(u, v) for pixel (u, v) by sampling from the distribution g'(u, v). In practice, this involves constructing a CDF from g' and using inverse transform sampling or stratified sampling to select ray origins or densities. Formulas: Mean color: \bar{c} = \frac{1}{9} \sum{x,y} c(x, y), where x \in \{u-1, u, u+1\} and y \in \{v-1, v, v+1\}. Context probability: g(u, v) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{9} \sum{x,y} [c(x, y) - \bar{c}]^2}. Normalized probability: g'(u, v) = \frac{\text{clamp}(s, g(u, v))}{\max(g)}, where \text{clamp}(s, g(u, v)) replaces any value in g(u, v) less than s with s. The result is distributed in [0, 1]. Ray sampling: ri(u, v) \sim g'(u, v) for u \in [0, Hi] and v \in [0, Wi]. Parameters: Threshold s: Ensures minimum ray allocation to avoid sampling too few rays in trivial areas. Typically s = 0.01 \times \text{mean}(g(u, v)). Patch Size: The spatial neighborhood scale used to calculate context information. The source primarily uses 3 \times 3 but tests 5 \times 5, 7 \times 7, 9 \times 9, 11 \times 11. Context Metric: The method uses Standard Deviation as the context metric. Alternatives tested include Entropy and Variance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Pixels: The formula requires neighbors outside the image for edge pixels. The source does not specify padding; implementers must choose a strategy (e.g., zero, replicate, or ignore). Uniform Regions: Without clamping s, uniform regions (e.g., white walls) would have g(u, v) \approx 0, leading to no rays being sampled and potential training instability. Metric Choice: Standard Deviation was selected over tested alternatives (Entropy, Variance). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def computeprobabilitymap(image, patchsize=3, thresholdfactor=0.01): H, W, C = image.shape probmap = np.zeros((H, W)) half = patchsize // 2 padded = np.pad(image, half, mode='reflect') # for u in range(H): for v in range(W): patch = padded[u:u+patchsize, v:v+patchsize,:] meanc = np.mean(patch) stdc = np.std(patch) # Matches sqrt(1/9 sum((c-mean)^2)) probmap[u, v] = stdc maxg = np.max(probmap) meang = np.mean(probmap) s = thresholdfactor meang probmap = np.clip(probmap, s, maxg) / maxg # return probmap def samplerays(probmap, numrays): flatprobs = probmap.flatten() flatprobs /= flatprobs.sum() # pixelindices = np.random.choice(flatprobs.size, size=numrays, p=flatprobs) # rays = np.unravelindex(pixelindices, probmap.shape) # return rays Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluated on Plenoxels, it significantly improves performance over methods without probability sampling. Reduces training time by sampling fewer rays in trivial areas while maintaining accuracy in complex regions. Hardware, resolution, and scene specifics are not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple to implement; leverages existing image data; reduces computational load in low-information areas. Limitations: Requires access to the input image context; may not adapt to 3D geometry changes that do not affect 2D image variance; boundary handling is ambiguous. Originated in the paper "Fast Learning Radiance Fields by Shooting Much Fewer Rays" (2023). The method was evaluated as an ablation study on the Plenoxels radiance field method to demonstrate the benefit of context-aware ray allocation. It addresses the inefficiency of uniform sampling in neural radiance fields by recognizing that not all pixels contribute equally to the reconstruction of complex 3D structures. name: Stratified Sampling
head: Discrete Volume Rendering, Fragmental Approximate Volume Rendering Method
body: Stratified Sampling partitions the ray depth interval [tn, tf] into k equal-sized bins and generates one sample per bin, avoiding the clustering and gaps inherent in pure uniform random sampling. It sets itself apart from its parent Uniform Ray Sampling by guaranteeing coverage of the entire depth range, and from its siblings by providing a structured variance reduction technique for the volume rendering integral. The method divides the integration interval [tn, tf] into k equal-sized bins. The boundaries ti for i=0, \dots, k are defined as: ti = tn + i \cdot \frac{tf - tn}{k} For each bin i (where i=1, \dots, k), a sample \taui is generated. In the randomized (unbiased) variant, a uniform random number ui \sim U[0, 1] is drawn, and the sample is computed as: \taui = t{i-1} + ui \cdot (ti - t{i-1}) In the deterministic (midpoint) variant, the center of the bin is used: \taui = 0.5 \cdot (t{i-1} + ti) The 3D position \mathbf{p}i for each sample is calculated from the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + \taui \mathbf{d} The rendered color is approximated by summation: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{k} Ti \alphai ci where ci is the color contribution at \taui, and \alphai and Ti are the opacity and transmittance, respectively: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) where \sigmai is the density at sample i, and \deltai = ti - t{i-1} is the distance between neighboring sampling points. Focuses on the variance reduction of the radiance integral along a single ray segment. Optimizes for batched execution and GPU-accelerated neural rendering pipelines by vectorizing bin boundary and sampling operations. Extends stratification to support linear disparity sampling (lindisp) for scenes with large depth variations. Originating from the Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) framework, this method was proposed to approximate the continuous volume rendering integral by dividing the ray segment into parts and uniformly randomly sampling within each part. It addresses the limitation of fixed offline sampling locations by ensuring better coverage of the ray space. Neural Radiance Field-based Visual Rendering: a Comprehensive Review, https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/abstract/document/11455380, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Stratified Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate
head: RVS Stratified Estimate
body: The Stratified Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate is an unbiased radiance estimation technique that reduces variance compared to uniform sampling, particularly effective for degenerate distributions. It sets itself apart from its sibling Batch Stratified Sampling by focusing on the specific integration of radiance along a single ray's path segment using stratified bins, and from Stratified Ray Sampling by operating on the distance parameter t along the ray rather than stratifying the ray origins or directions themselves. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, near clipping plane tn, far clipping plane tf, and number of samples k. Outputs: Estimated radiance \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: The method requires storing the bin boundaries and the sampled distances. In implementation, these are often stored in structures like RayBundle.samplepoints (3D positions) and RayBundle.samplelengths (distances ti). Steps: 1. Define Bin Boundaries: Divide the integration interval [tn, tf] into k equal-sized bins. The boundaries ti for i=0, \dots, k are defined as: ti = tn + i \cdot \frac{tf - tn}{k} where t0 = tn and tk = tf. 2. Generate Samples: For each bin i (where i=1, \dots, k), generate a sample \taui within the interval [t{i-1}, ti]. Randomized (Unbiased): Draw a uniform random number ui \sim U[0, 1] and compute: \taui = t{i-1} + ui \cdot (ti - t{i-1}) Deterministic (Midpoint): Use the center of the bin: \taui = 0.5 \cdot (t{i-1} + ti) 3. Compute 3D Positions: Calculate the 3D position \mathbf{p}i for each sample distance \taui: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + \taui \mathbf{d} 4. Evaluate Density and Color: Evaluate the volume density \sigmai and color contribution ci at each position \mathbf{p}i. 5. Compute Opacity and Transmittance: The distance between neighboring sampling points is \deltai = ti - t{i-1}. The opacity \alphai for the segment is: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) The transmittance Ti from the ray origin to the start of bin i is: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right) 6. Accumulate Radiance: Compute the final radiance estimate by summing the contributions: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{k} Ti \alphai ci Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z) raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), assumed normalized tnear: float, near clipping plane distance tfar: float, far clipping plane distance numsamples: int, number of stratified bins k densityfunc: function(p) -> float, returns density sigma at position p colorfunc: function(p) -> float, returns color contribution c at position p Returns: float, estimated radiance C(r) """ # Step 1: Define bin boundaries # ti = tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / k # We need t0 to tk binwidth = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples # Precompute boundaries to avoid repeated multiplication # tbounds[i] corresponds to ti tbounds = [tnear + i binwidth for i in range(numsamples + 1)] totalradiance = 0.0 currenttransmittance = 1.0 # Step 2-6: Iterate over each bin for i in range(1, numsamples + 1): tprev = tbounds[i-1] tcurr = tbounds[i] # Step 2: Generate sample taui # Using randomized uniform sampling for unbiased estimate ui = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) taui = tprev + ui (tcurr - tprev) # Step 3: Compute 3D position pi = ( rayorigin[0] + taui raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + taui raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + taui raydirection[2]) # Step 4: Evaluate density and color sigmai = densityfunc(pi) ci = colorfunc(pi) # Step 5: Compute opacity and transmittance deltai = tcurr - tprev alphai = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigmai deltai) # Ti is the transmittance from origin to tprev # It is updated iteratively: Ti = T{i-1} exp(-sigma{i-1} delta{i-1}) # However, the formula in defines Ti as exp(-sum{j=1}^{i-1} sigmaj deltaj) # which is exactly the transmittance arriving at the start of bin i. # Step 6: Accumulate radiance # Contribution of bin i is Ti alphai ci contribution = currenttransmittance alphai ci totalradiance += contribution # Update transmittance for the next bin # T{i+1} = Ti exp(-sigmai deltai) currenttransmittance = math.exp(-sigmai deltai) return totalradiance Parameters: k (numsamples): The number of stratified bins. Typical values vary by scene complexity. In a 'Foggy' field experiment, k=32 matched the performance of k=256 uniform samples. In a 'Wall' field experiment, only k=4 samples were needed to match the baseline. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Distributions: The method is particularly effective for degenerate distributions where uniform sampling performs poorly. Precision: When \sigmai \deltai is very small, 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) can suffer from catastrophic cancellation. Use expm1 or Taylor expansion if necessary. Boundary Conditions: Ensure tn < tf and k > 0. If tn = tf, the interval is empty and radiance is 0. Antithetic sampling is a variance reduction technique for estimating the derivative of a BSDF with respect to scene parameters when the integrand approximates an odd function. It exploits the symmetry of Normal Distribution Functions (NDFs) to make the derivative term an odd function, allowing paired samples to cancel out noise. It sets itself apart from general stratified sampling by targeting the specific symmetry of microfacet derivatives, whereas its sibling Decomposed sampling addresses cases where derivatives are even functions. A stochastic integrator that distributes samples at equal distance, jittered by noise, combined with a ratio estimator using analytic unoccluded radiance. It uses the basic framework of stratified sampling paired with analytic unoccluded radiance computation. REES yields better convergence in unoccluded parts of the scene but leads to overall poor distribution of samples in occluded parts compared to MCWVDS. A technique to reduce variance from rare outliers in importance sampling by using a sample trimmed mean over each pixel, discarding extreme samples. It stores multiple independent, intermediate (low sample count) results. For each pixel, it discards the top 1-5% and bottom 1-5% of samples, then averages the remaining samples. This trades a slight bias for a large reduction in variance, reducing overall error. The estimator remains consistent because the distribution approaches Gaussian for large sample counts, making the bias zero for symmetric distributions. Time Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of samples per ray. Each sample requires a density and color evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray if transmittance is updated iteratively, or O(k) if storing all sample points and lengths explicitly. Measured Performance: In field experiments, the stratified estimate significantly reduces the required sample count for convergence. For a 'Foggy' scene, k=32 stratified samples matched the variance of k=256 uniform samples. For a 'Wall' scene, k=4 stratified samples were sufficient. Strengths: Unbiased estimate. Lower variance than uniform sampling, especially for degenerate distributions. Simple to implement. Limitations: Variance reduction is dependent on the smoothness of the integrand. If the integrand has sharp discontinuities not aligned with bin boundaries, variance may not be optimal. When to Use: When variance reduction is needed for volume rendering along rays, particularly in scenes with smooth or degenerate density distributions. When Not to Use: When computational budget is extremely tight and a biased approximation is acceptable, or when the integrand is highly oscillatory and not aligned with the stratification grid. name: Antithetic Sampling
head: Antithetic BSDF Sampling
body: Antithetic sampling is a variance reduction technique for estimating the derivative of a BSDF with respect to scene parameters when the integrand approximates an odd function. It exploits the symmetry of Normal Distribution Functions (NDFs) to make the derivative term an odd function, allowing paired samples to cancel out noise. It sets itself apart from general stratified sampling by targeting the specific symmetry of microfacet derivatives, whereas its sibling Decomposed sampling addresses cases where derivatives are even functions. Inputs: Outgoing direction \boldsymbol{\omega}o. Scene parameter \pi (e.g., roughness, position). NDF model D (assumed symmetric, e.g., Beckmann, GGX). Outputs: Two antithetic samples for the derivative estimate. Data Structures: Local coordinate system defined by the surface normal \mathbf{n} and tangent \mathbf{t}. Half-way vectors \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,1}, \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,2}. Steps: 1. Draw first half-way vector: Sample a half-way vector \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,1} based on the NDF D. 2. Generate antithetic half-way vector: Set \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,2} to be symmetric to \boldsymbol{\omega}{h,1} with respect to the z-axis in the local coordinate system. 3. Compute incident directions: Calculate the corresponding incident directions \boldsymbol{\omega}{i,1} and \boldsymbol{\omega}{i,2} using the reflection relation \boldsymbol{\omega}{h} = (\boldsymbol{\omega}i + \boldsymbol{\omega}o) / \|\boldsymbol{\omega}i + \boldsymbol{\omega}o\|. 4. Evaluate derivative: Compute the BSDF derivative \frac{\partial fs^{(0)}}{\partial \pi} for both samples. Formulas: The microfacet BSDF decomposes into: fs^{(0)}(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = D(\boldsymbol{\omega}h) fs^{(0)}(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) where fs^{(0)} represents other terms (e.g., Fresnel) and \boldsymbol{\omega}h:= (\boldsymbol{\omega}i + \boldsymbol{\omega}o) / \|\boldsymbol{\omega}i + \boldsymbol{\omega}o\|. The derivative with respect to parameter \pi follows the chain rule: \frac{\partial fs^{(0)}}{\partial \pi} = \frac{\partial D}{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}h} \frac{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}h}{\partial \pi} fs^{(0)} + D \frac{\partial fs^{(0)}}{\partial \pi} The first term dominates for glossy BSDFs. If D is symmetric, \frac{\partial D}{\partial \boldsymbol{\omega}h} is an odd function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def antitheticbsdfsample(outgoingdirection, parameter, ndfmodel, localbasis): """Generates two antithetic samples for BSDF derivative estimation.""" normal, tangent, bitangent = localbasis # Step 1: Draw first half-way vector based on NDF omegah1 = ndfmodel.importancesample(outgoingdirection, localbasis) # Step 2: Generate antithetic half-way vector symmetric w.r.t. z-axis (normal) z1 = dot(omegah1, normal) x1 = dot(omegah1, tangent) y1 = dot(omegah1, bitangent) omegah2 = normal z1 - tangent x1 - bitangent y1 # Step 3: Compute incident directions omegai1 = reflectacrosshalfway(omegah1, outgoingdirection) omegai2 = reflectacrosshalfway(omegah2, outgoingdirection) # Step 4: Evaluate derivative deriv1 = computebsdfderivative(omegai1, outgoingdirection, parameter, ndfmodel, localbasis) deriv2 = computebsdfderivative(omegai2, outgoingdirection, parameter, ndfmodel, localbasis) return [(omegai1, deriv1), (omegai2, deriv2)] def reflectacrosshalfway(halfway, outgoing): """Computes incident direction from half-way and outgoing vectors.""" return 2.0 dot(halfway, outgoing) halfway - outgoing def computebsdfderivative(incident, outgoing, parameter, ndfmodel, localbasis): """Evaluates the derivative using the chain rule formula.""" wh = normalize(incident + outgoing) Dval = ndfmodel.value(wh) dDdwh = ndfmodel.gradient(wh) dwhdpi = computehalfwayjacobian(incident, outgoing, parameter) Fother = ndfmodel.otherterms(incident, outgoing) dFotherdpi = ndfmodel.othertermsgradient(incident, outgoing, parameter) return dot(dDdwh, dwhdpi) Fother + Dval dFotherdpi def computehalfwayjacobian(incident, outgoing, parameter): """Standard Jacobian for half-way vector w.r.t. parameter.""" return normalize(outgoing - incident) (1.0 / norm(incident + outgoing)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Exponential Path Growth: Applying antithetic sampling to every light bounce on glossy surfaces in scenes with multiple glossy surfaces causes exponential growth in the number of light paths. Even Functions: Antithetic sampling is not effective if the BSDF derivative is an even function (e.g., derivative w.r.t. roughness of GGX), as it produces high variance in such cases. A technique for cases where BSDF derivatives are even functions, where antithetic sampling fails. The parent method that provides the stratified framework within which antithetic sampling is applied to reduce variance. Variance Reduction: Significantly lowers variance when estimating the interior integral for glossy BSDFs where the NDF is symmetric. Complexity: Doubles the number of samples per bounce if applied naively, leading to exponential path counts in complex scenes with multiple glossy surfaces. Limitations: Ineffective for even-function derivatives (e.g., GGX roughness derivative). Usage Strategy: For complex scenes, apply antithetic sampling only once per light path, merge branched paths after a few bounces (when the surface is no longer glossy), and repeat the path k times to sample k different glossy surfaces. Antithetic sampling for BSDF derivatives was formally discussed by Zhang et al. [ZDDZ21], building on earlier mentions in [LHJ19] and [ZSGJ21]. It is a key technique in differentiable rendering to stabilize gradients for glossy materials. name: Batch Stratified Sampling
head: Uniform Stratified Sampling
body: Batch Stratified Sampling partitions the ray depth interval [tn, tf] into Nc evenly-spaced bins and perturbs sample positions within each bin to reduce aliasing artifacts during volume rendering. It builds on Stratified Sampling by vectorizing the bin boundary and sampling operations to process multiple rays simultaneously, which is essential for GPU-accelerated neural rendering pipelines. Unlike pure uniform sampling, it ensures one sample per stratum, avoiding clustering and gaps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins \mathbf{o} (shape [R, 3]), ray directions \mathbf{d} (shape [R, 3]), near plane tn (scalar or [R]), far plane tf (scalar or [R]), number of samples Nc (integer), and a boolean flag perturb (default True). Outputs: Sample depths \tau (shape [R, Nc]) and 3D positions \mathbf{p} (shape [R, Nc, 3]). Data Structures: Tensors are used for all data. Depths are stored as floating-point values. Positions are stored as 3D vectors. Steps: 1. Normalize and Expand Bounds: If tn and tf are scalars, they are broadcast to match the batch dimension R. If they are 1D arrays, they are reshaped to [R, 1]. 2. Compute Bin Boundaries: Generate Nc + 1 evenly spaced depth values in the normalized interval [0, 1] using linear spacing. Let these be ui for i=0, \dots, Nc, where u0=0 and u{Nc}=1. 3. Interpolate to World Space: Map the normalized boundaries to the ray-specific near and far planes. For each ray r, the boundaries t^{(r)}i are computed as: t^{(r)}i = tn^{(r)} \cdot (1 - ui) + tf^{(r)} \cdot ui This results in a tensor of shape [R, Nc + 1]. 4. Compute Bin Midpoints: Calculate the midpoints between adjacent boundaries. For i=0, \dots, Nc-1: m^{(r)}i = 0.5 \cdot (t^{(r)}i + t^{(r)}{i+1}) This results in a tensor of shape [R, Nc]. 5. Define Interval Bounds: Lower Bounds (L): Concatenate the first boundary t^{(r)}0 with the midpoints m^{(r)}. L^{(r)} = [t^{(r)}0, m^{(r)}0, \dots, m^{(r)}{Nc-1}] Shape: [R, Nc]. Upper Bounds (U): Concatenate the midpoints m^{(r)} with the last boundary t^{(r)}{Nc}. U^{(r)} = [m^{(r)}0, \dots, m^{(r)}{Nc-1}, t^{(r)}{Nc}] Shape: [R, Nc]. 6. Sample Within Bins: Generate Nc random uniform numbers v^{(r)}i \sim U[0, 1] for each ray and bin. If perturb is True, compute the sample depth \tau^{(r)}i as: \tau^{(r)}i = L^{(r)}i + v^{(r)}i \cdot (U^{(r)}i - L^{(r)}i) If perturb is False, use the midpoint: \tau^{(r)}i = 0.5 \cdot (L^{(r)}i + U^{(r)}i) This results in a tensor of shape [R, Nc]. 7. Compute 3D Positions: For each sample, compute the 3D position \mathbf{p}^{(r)}i: \mathbf{p}^{(r)}i = \mathbf{o}^{(r)} + \tau^{(r)}i \cdot \mathbf{d}^{(r)} This results in a tensor of shape [R, Nc, 3]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def batchstratifiedsampling(rayso, raysd, near, far, numsamples, perturb=True): """ rayso: [R, 3] raysd: [R, 3] near: scalar or [R] far: scalar or [R] numsamples: int perturb: bool """ # 1. Normalize and Expand Bounds # Ensure near and far are [R, 1] if near.ndim == 0: near = near.expand(rayso.shape[0], 1) else: near = near.unsqueeze(-1) if far.ndim == 0: far = far.expand(rayso.shape[0], 1) else: far = far.unsqueeze(-1) # 2. Compute Bin Boundaries in normalized space [0, 1] # Create Nc + 1 points u = torch.linspace(0, 1, numsamples + 1, device=rayso.device) # 3. Interpolate to World Space # tvals shape: [R, Nc + 1] tvals = near (1.0 - u) + far u # 4. Compute Bin Midpoints # mids shape: [R, Nc] mids = 0.5 (tvals[:,:-1] + tvals[:, 1:]) # 5. Define Interval Bounds # Lower bounds: [t0, m0,..., m{Nc-1}] lower = torch.cat([tvals[:,:1], mids], dim=-1) # Upper bounds: [m0,..., m{Nc-1}, t{Nc}] upper = torch.cat([mids, tvals[:, -1:]], dim=-1) # 6. Sample Within Bins if perturb: # Generate random uniform numbers [R, Nc] randvals = torch.randlike(lower) # Sample uniformly within each interval zvals = lower + (upper - lower) randvals else: # Use midpoints zvals = 0.5 (lower + upper) # 7. Compute 3D Positions # rayso: [R, 3], zvals: [R, Nc], raysd: [R, 3] # Expand for broadcasting raysoexp = rayso.unsqueeze(1) # [R, 1, 3] raysdexp = raysd.unsqueeze(1) # [R, 1, 3] zvalsexp = zvals.unsqueeze(2) # [R, Nc, 1] pts = raysoexp + zvalsexp raysdexp # [R, Nc, 3] return zvals, pts Parameters: numsamples (Nc): The number of stratified bins. Typical values range from 32 to 128 in neural rendering. perturb: Boolean flag. True for unbiased randomized sampling, False for deterministic midpoint sampling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When tn \approx tf, the bin width becomes very small, potentially leading to numerical instability or duplicate samples. A small epsilon check or clamping of the bin width may be required. Boundary Conditions: The method assumes tn < tf. If tn \ge tf, the interval is invalid. The implementation should validate this input. Batch Dimensions: The method requires consistent batch dimensions for rayso, raysd, near, and far. Mismatched shapes will cause broadcasting errors. Generates a regular grid of samples per pixel with independent uniform random offsets within each grid cell to reduce aliasing while maintaining stratification. It is used in light sampling contexts, such as generating sample positions on a light source surface by looping over grid cells and adding random offsets to the base grid coordinates. A stratified sampling method where the unit interval is partitioned into c strata based on non-zero bins of a predicted distribution, and samples are allocated unevenly to strata based on the predicted probability mass to handle multimodal distributions. It allocates \lfloor s/c \rfloor samples to each stratum and distributes the remainder to bins with maximal predicted probability. It clips the distance between adjacent intra-stratum samples to the bin width to prevent outsized contributions from endpoints. It is biased if the sample budget s < c, but implementations ensure s \ge c via regularization. Typical sample budget s is 17.6 samples per ray at high resolutions. Time Complexity: O(R \cdot Nc), where R is the number of rays and Nc is the number of samples per ray. The operations are vectorizable, making it highly efficient on GPUs. Memory Complexity: O(R \cdot Nc) for storing the sample depths and positions. Performance: In neural rendering benchmarks (e.g., Blender dataset), hierarchical sampling with Nc=64 coarse and Nf=128 fine samples per ray is commonly used, achieving high PSNR with mixed precision on CUDA. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts compared to uniform sampling; efficient batch processing; simple to implement. Limitations: Does not adapt to scene complexity; may waste samples in empty space if not combined with hierarchical or adaptive strategies. When to Use: Standard direct volume rendering or neural rendering where uniform coverage is desired and computational efficiency is key. When Not to Use: Scenes with high variance or complex geometry where adaptive sampling is needed. Batch Stratified Sampling is a fundamental technique in volume rendering and neural rendering, popularized by its use in NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) and related works. It is a vectorized implementation of stratified sampling, designed for efficient execution on GPUs using frameworks like PyTorch. The method is widely used in training pipelines for neural radiance fields, where it serves as the base sampling strategy for coarse and fine passes. emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/emmanueladutwum123/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) megvii-research/cv-master-ex, https://github.com/megvii-research/cv-master-ex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) InanXR/FLASH, https://github.com/InanXR/FLASH, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, https://github.com/wangyuehi/VolumeSingleScattering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) What You See is What You GAN: Rendering Every Pixel for High-Fidelity Geometry in 3D GANs, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02148, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Stratified Ray Sampling
head: Jittered Uniform Sampling, Ray Sampling for Acoustic Volume Rendering, Stratified Sample
body: Stratified Ray Sampling is a technique for discretizing the integration interval along a camera ray in volume rendering by dividing it into equal-sized bins and drawing one sample uniformly at random from each bin. It solves the problem of aliasing and high variance associated with purely uniform or purely random sampling by ensuring that the entire depth range is covered without gaps. Unlike Stratified Monte Carlo Radiance Estimate, which focuses on general integral estimation, this method is specialized for the geometric discretization of rays in volumetric scenes. It differs from Batch Stratified Sampling by operating on individual rays rather than optimizing sample distributions across batches. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (3D vector). Ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized 3D vector). Near plane distance tn (scalar). Far plane distance tf (scalar). Number of samples per ray k (integer). Optional: lindisp (boolean, whether to sample in disparity space). Optional: perturb (boolean, whether to add random jitter). Outputs: Array of sample depths \taui for i=1, \dots, k. Array of 3D sample positions \mathbf{p}i for i=1, \dots, k. Data Structures: zvals: A 1D array of size k storing the depth values along the ray. samplepoints: A 2D array of shape (k, 3) storing the Cartesian coordinates of the samples. Steps: 1. Define Interval and Bins: Determine the total length of the integration interval: L = tf - tn The boundaries of the k equal-sized bins are defined as: ti = tn + i \cdot \frac{L}{k}, \quad \text{for } i = 0, \dots, k where t0 = tn and tk = tf. 2. Compute Base Depths (Linear or Disparity): If lindisp is False (standard depth sampling), compute the midpoints or boundaries linearly. If lindisp is True, compute in disparity space (1/t). Linear Depth: Generate k evenly spaced values between tn and tf. Let t{vals} be the boundaries: t{vals}[i] = tn + i \cdot \frac{tf - tn}{k}, \quad i=0,\dots,k Disparity Depth: Compute boundaries in disparity space d = 1/t: d{vals}[i] = \frac{1}{tn} + i \cdot \frac{\frac{1}{tf} - \frac{1}{tn}}{k}, \quad i=0,\dots,k Convert back to depth: t{vals}[i] = \frac{1}{d{vals}[i]}. 3. Generate Stratified Samples: For each bin i from 1 to k: Identify the bin boundaries: [t{i-1}, ti]. Draw a uniform random number ui \sim U[0, 1]. Compute the sample depth \taui: \taui = t{i-1} + ui \cdot (ti - t{i-1}) Note on Perturbation: In some implementations (e.g., NeRF), jitter is applied to the midpoints of the bins rather than the boundaries to avoid sampling exactly at the edges, which can cause artifacts if the density function is discontinuous. If perturb is True: 1. Compute midpoints mi = 0.5 \cdot (t{i-1} + ti) for i=1, \dots, k-1. 2. Define upper and lower bounds for jitter: \text{lower} = [t0, m1, \dots, m{k-1}] \text{upper} = [m1, \dots, m{k-1}, tk] 3. Draw random t{rand} \sim U[0, 1] of size k. 4. Compute \taui = \text{lower}[i] + t{rand}[i] \cdot (\text{upper}[i] - \text{lower}[i]). 4. Compute 3D Positions: For each sample depth \taui, compute the 3D position \mathbf{p}i: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + \taui \mathbf{d}. 5. Render (Integration): The color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) for the ray is approximated by volume rendering integration using the samples: \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^{k} Ti \alphai ci where: ci is the color contribution at \mathbf{p}i. \sigmai is the density at \mathbf{p}i. \deltai = ti - t{i-1} is the distance between bin boundaries (or \taui - \tau{i-1} if using sample-to-sample integration, but standard stratified uses bin width for opacity calculation consistency with the bin definition). Note: In standard NeRF implementations, \deltai is often approximated as the distance between consecutive samples \taui - \tau{i-1}, but the theoretical definition relies on the bin width L/k for unbiased estimation of the integral over the bin. Opacity: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai). Transmittance: Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj\right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def stratifiedraysampling(origins, directions, near, far, numsamples, lindisp=False, perturb=True): """ Generates stratified samples along rays. Args: origins: Tensor of shape (Nrays, 3) directions: Tensor of shape (Nrays, 3) near: Float, near plane distance far: Float, far plane distance numsamples: Int, number of samples per ray (k) lindisp: Bool, if True sample in disparity space perturb: Bool, if True add uniform jitter within bins Returns: zvals: Tensor of shape (Nrays, numsamples) samplepoints: Tensor of shape (Nrays, numsamples, 3) """ device = origins.device # Step 1: Define bin boundaries # Create linspace for boundaries: 0 to 1, size numsamples + 1 tvals = torch.linspace(0.0, 1.0, numsamples + 1, device=device) # Step 2: Compute depths based on lindisp if lindisp: # Sample linearly in disparity (1/depth) # dnear = 1/near, dfar = 1/far # dvals = dnear (1 - t) + dfar t # zvals = 1 / dvals # Note: tvals here are the boundaries for the linspace # We need to handle the division by zero if near=0, but typically near > 0 dnear = 1.0 / near dfar = 1.0 / far dvals = dnear (1.0 - tvals) + dfar tvals zvals = 1.0 / dvals else: # Sample linearly in depth zvals = near (1.0 - tvals) + far tvals # zvals has shape (numsamples + 1) # We need to expand to (Nrays, numsamples + 1) zvals = zvals.unsqueeze(0).expand(origins.shape[0], -1) if perturb: # Step 3: Stratified Sampling with Perturbation # Compute midpoints of the bins # mids[i] = 0.5 (zvals[:, i] + zvals[:, i+1]) for i=0..numsamples-1 mids = 0.5 (zvals[:, 1:] + zvals[:,:-1]) # Define lower and upper bounds for each sample # lower[i] = zvals[:, i] # upper[i] = zvals[:, i+1] # But for jitter, we use midpoints to define the range # lowerbound = [zvals[:, 0], mids[:, 0],..., mids[:, -1]] # upperbound = [mids[:, 0],..., mids[:, -1], zvals[:, -1]] lower = torch.cat([zvals[:,:1], mids], dim=1) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[:, -1:]], dim=1) # Draw random numbers trand = torch.randlike(zvals[:,:numsamples]) # Compute final zvals zvals = lower + (upper - lower) trand else: # Deterministic or simple uniform without perturbation logic described in S4 # If no perturbation, we might just pick the midpoint or a random point in the bin # Standard stratified without perturbation usually implies picking a random point in the bin # defined by the original tvals boundaries. # However, S4 implies perturb=True is the standard "stratified" in NeRF context. # If perturb=False, we can just use the midpoints or random in bins. # Let's stick to the random in bin definition from S1/S5 if perturb is false but stratified is true. # But S4 specifically links perturb to the stratified implementation. # If perturb is False, we can simply use the midpoints or uniform random in the original bins. # For consistency with S1/S5: # trand = torch.randlike(zvals[:,:numsamples]) # lower = zvals[:,:numsamples] # upper = zvals[:, 1:] # zvals = lower + (upper - lower) trand # This is effectively the same as perturb=True but using bin edges instead of midpoints. # We will assume perturb=True is the primary method for "Stratified Ray Sampling" in modern contexts. pass # Step 4: Compute 3D positions # origins: (Nrays, 3), directions: (Nrays, 3), zvals: (Nrays, numsamples) # samplepoints = origins[:, None,:] + directions[:, None,:] zvals[...,:, None] # Expand dimensions for broadcasting # origins: (Nrays, 1, 3) # directions: (Nrays, 1, 3) # zvals: (Nrays, numsamples, 1) originsexp = origins.unsqueeze(1) directionsexp = directions.unsqueeze(1) zvalsexp = zvals.unsqueeze(2) samplepoints = originsexp + directionsexp zvalsexp return zvals, samplepoints Parameters: numsamples (k): Typically 64 for coarse networks and 128 for fine networks in hierarchical schemes. near (tn): Minimum depth. Not given in the sources as a specific value, but defined in cfg.mindepth. far (tf): Maximum depth. Not given in the sources as a specific value, but defined in cfg.maxdepth. lindisp: Boolean. False by default. perturb: Boolean. True by default in many implementations to reduce aliasing. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near Zero Depth: If tn = 0, disparity sampling (1/t) results in division by zero. Ensure tn > 0 for disparity sampling. Bin Width vs Sample Distance: The opacity calculation \alphai uses \deltai. If using stratified sampling, \deltai should ideally be the bin width L/k to maintain the unbiased nature of the integral over the bin, rather than the distance between random samples \taui - \tau{i-1}, which varies. However, many implementations use sample-to-sample distances for simplicity. Boundary Sampling: Without perturbation, samples might fall exactly on bin boundaries, which can cause artifacts if the density function is discontinuous at those points. A refinement technique that uses coarse stratified samples to guide the placement of fine samples in high-density regions. It builds on Stratified Ray Sampling by adding an adaptive, importance-driven refinement layer. Choose this when scene geometry is complex and uniform sampling is inefficient. Time Complexity: O(k) per ray, where k is the number of samples. Generating random numbers and computing positions is linear in the number of samples. Memory Complexity: O(k) per ray to store sample depths and positions. Performance: Provides a good balance between variance and coverage. It reduces aliasing compared to uniform sampling and provides better coverage than pure random sampling. Strengths: Simple to implement, unbiased (if random), ensures full coverage of the ray interval. Limitations: Does not adapt to scene content; may waste samples in empty space or under-sample in high-frequency regions. When to Use: As a baseline sampling strategy, particularly in the coarse stage of hierarchical rendering. When Not to Use: When the scene has highly variable density and computational resources are limited; importance sampling or hierarchical methods are preferred. Stratified sampling is a fundamental technique in Monte Carlo integration and computer graphics. In the context of volume rendering and Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF), it was popularized by the original NeRF paper and subsequent implementations. It is used in various domains including acoustic volume rendering and neural surface reconstruction. The method is often employed in the coarse training stage to capture general scene structure before refining with importance sampling. name: Hierarchical Stratified Sampling
head: Importance Stratified Sampling
body: Hierarchical Stratified Sampling divides a camera ray into equally spaced bins, draws uniform samples from each, and adaptively refines regions that contributed to the final color using a probabilistic function. It builds on Stratified Ray Sampling by adding an importance-driven refinement layer to improve reconstruction quality and prevent overfitting. Inputs: Camera ray geometry (origin, direction, t{min}, t{max}), a volume representation, and a target number of initial strata N. Outputs: A sorted list of sample positions t along the ray used to predict the pixel color. Data Structures: 1. Ray Data Structure: One instance per camera ray tracking segment locations where the importance value changes. 2. Sample List: A sorted list of sample positions t and their corresponding contributions. Steps: 1. Initial Stratified Sampling: Divide the camera ray into N equally spaced bins. Draw one sample uniformly at random from each bin. 2. Contribution Analysis: Render the scene using the initial samples to identify which samples contributed to the final color. 3. Adaptive Refinement: Sample more points around the high-contribution regions using a probabilistic function to determine the expected color value along the ray. Maintain one data structure per ray and alternate between uniform strata sampling and adaptive sampling in subsequent progressive rendering passes. Adaptive sampling targets non-sampled regions between segments, within segments to detect splits, and non-sampled regions close to the begin and end of the ray. 4. Aggregation: Combine the initial stratified samples and the refined adaptive samples to predict the pixel color. Parameters: N: Number of initial strata. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Number of adaptive passes: In experiments, one uniform sampling pass followed by three adaptive sampling steps yielded extremely fast accuracy increases. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overfitting: Using stratified samples generally improves reconstructions by helping to prevent overfitting. View Dependency: NeRFs may produce incorrect depth maps if they rely on all spatial points behind a reflecting surface rather than explaining view-dependent appearance directly. Precision: The accuracy of the estimated integral \tilde{k}(t) depends on the number of adaptive steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def hierarchicalstratifiedsampling(raymint, raymaxt, numinitialstrata=64, numadaptivepasses=3): # Step 1: Divide the camera ray into equally spaced bins and draw a uniform sample from each bin binsize = (raymaxt - raymint) / numinitialstrata samples = [] for i in range(numinitialstrata): t = raymint + i binsize + random.uniform(0, binsize) samples.append(t) # Step 2-3: Maintain one data structure per camera ray # Alternate between uniform strata sampling and adaptive sampling in progressive passes for in range(numadaptivepasses): # Identify which samples contributed to the final color # Sample more points around those regions using a probabilistic function to determine the expected color value along the ray # Adaptive sampling targets: non-sampled regions between segments, within segments to detect splits, and non-sampled regions close to the begin and end of the ray newsamples = [] # The sources do not specify the exact probabilistic function or segment tracking algorithm for t in samples: # Placeholder for probabilistic refinement step pass samples.extend(newsamples) samples.sort() # Step 4: Aggregate samples to predict the pixel color # The exact aggregation weights are not specified in the sources return samples This variant maintains one data structure per camera ray and uses stratified sampling by dividing the ray into N equally-sized regions to obtain a sorted list of new samples. It alternates between uniform strata sampling and adaptive sampling in subsequent progressive rendering passes. Adaptive sampling targets non-sampled regions between segments, within segments to detect splits, and non-sampled regions close to the begin and end of the ray. In experiments, accuracy of \tilde{k}(t) increased extremely fast when performing one uniform sampling, followed by three adaptive sampling steps in subsequent progressive rendering passes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method requires multiple progressive rendering passes, with experimental results showing fast convergence after one uniform pass and three adaptive passes. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing one data structure per camera ray and a sorted list of samples. Strengths: Reduces overfitting and improves reconstruction quality. Allows for progressive refinement and fast accuracy increases in adaptive passes. Limitations: More complex to implement than uniform or simple stratified sampling. Requires multiple passes for optimal results. When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction is needed and computational resources allow for multiple sampling passes. Hierarchical Stratified Sampling was introduced in the context of 3D geometric reconstruction and evaluation of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs). It addresses the limitations of NeRFs in handling view-dependent appearance and incorrect depth maps by leveraging hierarchical sampling strategies. The method has been further developed in the context of view-dependent visibility optimization for Monte Carlo volume visualization. name: Slab-based Ray Sampling
head: Image-order caching, Slab Definition and Sampling, Slab Sampling, Slab-based approach
body: Slab-based ray sampling is an image-order caching mechanism for direct volume ray casting that groups rays into rectangular screen regions to form stacked slabs, storing voxel samples in shared memory to optimize neighborhood access for lighting and compositing. Unlike object-order bricking, which struggles with GPU hardware mapping due to per-brick lists, this method leverages the regular structure of rays within a slab to reduce memory bandwidth and latency when calculating gradients or performing ambient occlusion. It is distinct from sibling methods like Uniform Ray Sampling by explicitly managing spatial locality in shared memory across multiple rays, and from Stochastic Jittering by prioritizing deterministic cache coherence over variance reduction. Inputs: 3D volume texture (scalar field). Camera parameters (view matrix, projection type: orthogonal or perspective). Screen resolution and subdivision grid (rectangular regions). Slab depth parameter sd (number of samples written to cache per ray at once). Step length d (distance between samples). Outputs: Final pixel color and opacity via front-to-back compositing. Slab Cache: A three-dimensional array stored in GPU shared memory. Dimensions: [N{slices}, N{rays}, N{samples\per\slice}]. N{rays}: Number of rays in the slab (threads in the block). N{slices}: Determined by slab depth sd and ray length. N{samples\per\slice}: Determined by ray length and step size. Layout: Rays with the same distance to the camera lie on the same slice in the slab. Slab Definition: A slab of thickness 2d is defined by three successive samples (sf, sm, sb). The next slab is indexed by (sf, sm, sb) with the correlation sf = sb (front sample of the next slab equals the back sample of the current slab). d: Step length between samples. sd: Slab depth, controlling the number of samples written into the cache per ray simultaneously. Typical values: Not given in the sources. 1. Screen Subdivision and Slab Creation: The screen is subdivided into rectangular regions. For each region, a slab is created. For orthogonal projection, the slab is a cuboid; for perspective projection, it is a frustum. 2. Start Point Preprocessing: To ensure voxels adjacent in texture space lie close together in the cache, all ray start points in a slab are modified to have the same distance to the camera as the closest ray. Use shared memory and thread synchronization to find the minimum camera distance among all rays in the block. Move each ray's start point to this minimum distance. Pitfall: If the view plane is not parallel to one side of the proxy geometry cube, ray start positions have different distances, causing adjacent voxels to lie on different slices in the cache, resulting in incorrect gradients. Modifying start points resolves this. Texture coordinates will lie outside [0,1]^3; checks must be performed before each 3D texture fetch. 3. Main Loop Part 1 (Cache Filling): Traverse the ray from the modified start point. Retrieve scalar values for the current sample position from the 3D volume texture. Write the sample result into the shared memory slab cache. The slab depth sd controls how many samples are written per ray at a time. Border Handling: For rays adjacent to the slab boundary, execute only Part 1 to write samples into the cache. This ensures inner rays have access to neighbor voxels for gradient calculation, avoiding discontinuities (grid patterns). 4. Thread Synchronization: Perform a barrier synchronization after Part 1 to ensure all samples are written to shared memory before reading. 5. Main Loop Part 2 (Lighting and Compositing): Restart ray traversal from the beginning of the slab. Read samples directly from the shared memory cache instead of the texture. Gradient Calculation: Calculate gradients in eye space using adjacent samples on the same slice from top, left, bottom, and right rays (as seen from the viewpoint), and the next/previous samples on the current ray. Transform gradients to object space for lighting. Compositing: Apply lighting and front-to-back compositing. For pre-integration methods, fetch color/opacity from a 3D pre-integration table using the retrieved scalar values. 6. Early Ray Termination (ERT): ERT cannot stop a single ray independently because data sampled by one ray is used for gradient calculation in adjacent rays. Determine if all rays in the slab have reached the required alpha threshold. Use a flag in shared memory for synchronization to terminate further traversal for the entire slab if the condition is met. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def syncthreads(): """Thread block synchronization barrier.""" pass def texturefetch(tex, coord): """3D texture lookup with boundary check.""" if 0.0 <= coord[0] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= coord[1] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= coord[2] <= 1.0: return tex.sample(coord) return 0.0 def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) return [c/l for c in v] if l > 0 else v def length(v): return math.sqrt(sum(cc for c in v)) def slabbasedraycasting(rays, volumetexture, viewtoobjmatrix, transferfunc, sd, d): # rays: list of (origin, direction, isborderray) # sd: slab depth, number of samples written to cache per ray at once # d: step length between samples numrays = len(rays) # Shared memory cache layout: [sliceindex][rayindex][sampleindex] # sliceindex groups rays by distance to camera # Exact cache dimensions depend on ray length and d; not given in sources cache = [[[0.0] sd for in range(numrays)] for in range(2)] # 1. Start Point Preprocessing mindist = float('inf') for i in range(numrays): dist = length(rays[i][0]) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist syncthreads() for i in range(numrays): currentdist = length(rays[i][0]) if currentdist > mindist: dirnorm = normalize(rays[i][1]) rays[i] = ( [rays[i][0][j] + (mindist - currentdist) dirnorm[j] for j in range(3)], rays[i][1], rays[i][2]) syncthreads() # 2. Main Loop Part 1: Cache Filling for rayidx in range(numrays): origin, direction, isborder = rays[rayidx] stepvec = [direction[j] d for j in range(3)] currentpos = origin for sampleidx in range(sd): val = texturefetch(volumetexture, currentpos) dist = length(currentpos) sliceidx = int(dist / d) % 2 cache[sliceidx][rayidx][sampleidx] = val currentpos = [currentpos[j] + stepvec[j] for j in range(3)] syncthreads() # 3. Main Loop Part 2: Lighting and Compositing for rayidx in range(numrays): origin, direction, isborder = rays[rayidx] stepvec = [direction[j] d for j in range(3)] currentpos = origin color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] opacity = 0.0 rayalive = True for sampleidx in range(sd): if not rayalive: break dist = length(currentpos) sliceidx = int(dist / d) % 2 val = cache[sliceidx][rayidx][sampleidx] if not isborder: # Gradient Calculation in eye space # Adjacent samples on same slice from top, left, bottom, right rays # and next/previous samples on current ray # Exact neighbor indexing depends on block layout gradeye = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Left/Right rays (same slice, different rayidx) if rayidx > 0: gradeye[0] += cache[sliceidx][rayidx-1][sampleidx] - val if rayidx < numrays-1: gradeye[0] += cache[sliceidx][rayidx+1][sampleidx] - val # Top/Bottom rays (different sliceidx, same rayidx) if sliceidx > 0: gradeye[1] += cache[sliceidx-1][rayidx][sampleidx] - val if sliceidx < 1: gradeye[1] += cache[sliceidx+1][rayidx][sampleidx] - val # Next/Previous samples on current ray if sampleidx > 0: gradeye[2] += cache[sliceidx][rayidx][sampleidx-1] - val if sampleidx < sd-1: gradeye[2] += cache[sliceidx][rayidx][sampleidx+1] - val # Transform gradient to object space for lighting gradobj = [ viewtoobjmatrix[0][0]gradeye[0] + viewtoobjmatrix[0][1]gradeye[1] + viewtoobjmatrix[0][2]gradeye[2], viewtoobjmatrix[1][0]gradeye[0] + viewtoobjmatrix[1][1]gradeye[1] + viewtoobjmatrix[1][2]gradeye[2], viewtoobjmatrix[2][0]gradeye[0] + viewtoobjmatrix[2][1]gradeye[1] + viewtoobjmatrix[2][2]gradeye[2] ] # Apply lighting and front-to-back compositing # Standard volume rendering step using transferfunc and gradobj alpha = transferfunc(val, gradobj) color = [color[j] + (1.0 - opacity) alpha color[j] for j in range(3)] opacity = opacity + (1.0 - opacity) alpha # Early Ray Termination check if opacity >= 0.99: rayalive = False currentpos = [currentpos[j] + stepvec[j] for j in range(3)] # Early Ray Termination: determine if all rays reached required alpha threshold # Synchronization performed using a flag in shared memory # if allraysterminated(): break pass return color, opacity Incorrect Gradients: If the view plane is not parallel to one side of the proxy geometry cube, ray start positions have different distances to the camera. This causes voxels adjacent in the volume to lie on different slices in the slab cache, leading to incorrect gradients. Solution: Modify all ray start points in a slab to have the same distance to the camera as the closest one. Discontinuities (Grid Pattern): Ignoring voxels not accessible through the cache for gradient calculation leads to discontinuities, visible as a grid pattern. Solution: Include surrounding voxels by adding all rays adjacent to the slab to the cache. For these border rays, only Part 1 of the main loop is executed. Texture Coordinates: Moving start points may result in texture coordinates outside [0,1]^3. Checks must be performed before each 3D texture fetch. Perspective Projection: Rays are not parallel, so the distance between sample points differs, making the relation between adjacent samples in the cache irregular. An approximation of the neighborhood is often sufficient. Memory: Uses shared memory for the slab cache. The size depends on the number of rays in a block, slab depth sd, and samples per slice. It avoids large global memory allocations for bricking lists. Time: Two passes per slab (fill cache, then read/composite). This doubles the traversal cost for the cached portion but saves memory bandwidth for gradient calculations. Implemented in the Voreen volume rendering framework (Meyer-Spradow et al., 2009) for CUDA version 2.1. Specific performance numbers are not provided in the sources, but it is noted to be better adapted to CUDA architecture features than bricking. Performance advantage is realized when lighting techniques (ambient occlusion, gradient calculation) access the same sample position multiple times. Caching provides no advantage if samples are accessed only once. Strengths: Efficient use of shared memory for image-order processing; reduces memory bandwidth for neighborhood-dependent lighting; avoids object-order bricking inefficiencies on GPUs. Limitations: Requires synchronization; ERT is slab-wide, not per-ray; irregular cache layout in perspective projection; increased complexity in border handling. Use when gradient-based lighting or ambient occlusion is required and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Use when targeting GPU architectures with efficient shared memory access. Do not use if samples are accessed only once (no caching benefit) or if per-ray early termination is critical without slab-wide synchronization overhead. Introduced as an alternative to bricking (object-order) for CUDA implementation. Implemented in the Voreen volume rendering framework (Meyer-Spradow et al., 2009). Described in "An Advanced Volume Raycasting Technique Using GPU Stream Processing". Used in the Voreen volume rendering framework. Applicable to both orthogonal and perspective projections. An Advanced Volume Raycasting Technique Using GPU Stream Processing, https://www.scitepress.org/PublishedPapers/2010/28432/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Second Order Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering, https://people.freedesktop.org/~marcheu/pacificvis08.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Supersampling
head: Dense Quadrature Supersampling, Hardware Supersampling, Multi-sampling, NeRF-SR Supersampling, Oversampling, Sub-pixel Supersampling
body: Supersampling is a technique to minimize aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel and averaging the results. It handles high-frequency components in transfer functions by performing dense quadrature of the volume render integral, assuming linearity of the scalar field between sample points but not linearity of the integral itself. Unlike pre-integration, which requires equidistant sample points and fails for nonlinear integrals, supersampling accounts for the nonlinearity of the volume render integral while avoiding oversampling of the scalar field. It differs from Stochastic Jittering by using deterministic, fixed offsets for low sample counts (1x–4x) rather than random or stratified patterns, and from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering by relying on simple arithmetic averaging rather than importance-weighted integration. Inputs: Volume data set V with voxel spacing \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z. Camera parameters defining the view ray \gamma(s) for each pixel. Supersampling factor k (number of samples per pixel or per slice). Outputs: Final pixel color C{\text{pixel}}. Data Structures: Sample positions: A set of offsets \{oi\}{i=1}^{k} within the pixel area or along the ray depth. Accumulator: Sum of ray contributions S = \sum{i=1}^{k} Ci. Steps: 1. Define Sample Pattern: Determine the spatial distribution of k sample points within the pixel footprint (x-y plane) or along the ray depth (z-direction). 2. Cast Rays: For each sample point i, cast a ray \gammai(s) through the volume. 3. Sample & Composite: Evaluate radiance along the ray and perform front-to-back or back-to-front compositing to obtain the color Ci for that specific sample ray. 4. Average: Compute the final pixel color by averaging the contributions: C{\text{pixel}} = \frac{1}{k} \sum{i=1}^{k} Ci Parameters: Sampling Rate: Typically 5 samples per pixel in software implementations. Max Supersampling Factor: In hardware (VolumePro), the maximum supersampling factor in the z-direction is eight. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nonlinearity: Pre-integration fails if sample points are not equidistant because the volume render integral is nonlinear. Regular Spacing: Regular spacing where the distance between sample points in the x- and y-directions can result in aliasing; uniform distribution is desired. Hardware Limitations: Hardware supersampling is supported only in the z-direction in some architectures (e.g., VolumePro). Performance: Supersampling increases computational load. In VolumePro, supersampling by a factor of k reduces the rendering rate of a 256^3 data set to 30 frames per second. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesampleoffsets(k): """Generate k deterministic sample offsets within a unit square pixel.""" if k == 5: # Divide pixel into 4 parts, cast from centers and pixel center return [(-0.25, -0.25), (0.25, -0.25), (-0.25, 0.25), (0.25, 0.25), (0.0, 0.0)] # Standard stratified grid for arbitrary k n = int(k0.5) if n n < k: n += 1 offsets = [] for i in range(n): for j in range(n): if len(offsets) >= k: break offsets.append(((2 i + 1) / (2 n) - 0.5, (2 j + 1) / (2 n) - 0.5)) return offsets[:k] def castrayandcomposite(volume, origin, direction, tmax): """Standard front-to-back volume compositing.""" color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 step = 1.0 / volume.resolution # Simplified step size while t < tmax and alpha < 1.0: sample = volume.sample(origin + direction t) c, a = sample.color, sample.opacity transmittance = 1.0 - alpha color = tuple(c1 + c2 a transmittance for c1, c2 in zip(color, c)) alpha += a transmittance t += step return color def supersamplevolumeraycasting(volume, camera, pixel, k=5): """Renders a single pixel using supersampling.""" offsets = computesampleoffsets(k) totalcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for dx, dy in offsets: rayorigin, raydirection = camera.getray(pixel.x + dx, pixel.y + dy) color = castrayandcomposite(volume, rayorigin, raydirection, camera.farplane) totalcolor = tuple(c1 + c2 for c1, c2 in zip(totalcolor, color)) return tuple(c / k for c in totalcolor) Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing (MSAA) via Ray Distribution is an image-order rendering technique that reduces aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel, distributed within the pixel area, and averaging the resulting color values. It solves the problem of jagged edges caused by abrupt intensity changes along object silhouettes, which occur when a single ray per pixel fails to capture the scene's high-frequency details. Unlike post-processing convolution filters, this method performs supersampling directly during ray traversal, offering higher quality at the cost of increased computational load. It differs from Stochastic Jittering by using deterministic, fixed offsets for low sample counts (1x–4x) rather than random or stratified patterns, and from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering by relying on simple arithmetic averaging rather than importance-weighted integration. Z-direction supersampling is a hardware-accelerated technique that reduces aliasing artifacts by increasing the number of sample slices per volume in the z-direction, interpolating additional sample slices between existing voxel slices. It is distinct from its sibling Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution because it operates by spatial interpolation of volume data along the view ray's depth axis rather than distributing multiple rays per pixel in the image plane. A technique to mitigate interpolation artifacts in sliced-based volume rendering by adjusting the super-sampling level per slab based on its distance to the viewpoint. It assigns a higher super-sampling level to slabs located closer to the viewpoint and a lower level to slabs farther away. VolumePro uses uniform super-sampling across all slabs, causing performance degradation; SWF VRS uses differential levels to balance image quality and rendering speed. A software-based technique to achieve supersampling in x and y directions by rendering the volume multiple times with sub-pixel offsets and blending the results. It renders the volume several times with slightly different sub-pixel accurate initial offsets of the base plane in the x and y dimensions, then blends the resulting images in software to create a smoother final supersampled image. The initial offsets of the base plane must be sub-pixel accurate. A technique to improve image quality by supersampling a 3D data set using a high-quality reconstruction filter in a pre-processing step, then rendering the higher-resolution data set using trilinear interpolation. This approach yields noticeable quality improvements without necessarily increasing rendering time, addressing the low quality of standard trilinear interpolation. A small Gaussian prefilter applied along each ray, sized to the sample step, to remove moiré artifacts and improve biological detail rendering. It applies a Gaussian prefilter along each ray, sized to the sample step, and pairs with hardware-filtered data textures to eliminate the kernel's cost: using R8 for uint8, and R16 via EXTtexturenorm16 for uint16, falling back to the integer path when the extension is missing. Each lookup performs one filtered fetch instead of eight, making the kernel's cost mostly disappear. It extends to float32 next; 32- and 64-bit integers stay on the exact integer path. On integer textures with manual trilinear filtering, the kernel is expensive (about 3–4× the GPU time per frame). Images produced by the filtered path match the integer path to within one 8-bit step. An antialiasing technique that renders geometry into a multisampled G-buffer where attributes like normals and view positions are evaluated at each subsample of a fragment. This allows specular lighting to be computed at a higher effective resolution, reducing specular aliasing that standard MSAA cannot fix. Unlike standard graphics hardware multisampling which only reduces aliasing at polygon edges, this method specifically targets aliased specular highlights introduced by the fragment shader by evaluating normals per subsample. Time Complexity: Increases linearly with the number of samples k per pixel. In hardware (VolumePro), supersampling by a factor of k reduces the rendering rate of a 256^3 data set to 30 frames per second. Memory Complexity: No additional memory required for the sampling pattern itself, but hardware implementations may require additional slice buffers for interpolation. Measured Performance: CUDA implementation capable of rendering 60 frames per second with high-end hardware. Strengths: Reduces wood-grain artifacts and increases image quality by capturing high frequencies of the transfer function. Minimizes aliasing effects significantly. Limitations: Increased computational load. Regular spacing can result in aliasing if not uniform. When to Use: When high image quality is required and computational resources allow. Particularly useful for reducing artifacts along silhouette edges. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and aliasing artifacts are acceptable. Supersampling originated as a general computer graphics technique to combat aliasing caused by coarse granularity of per-pixel sampling. In volume rendering, it was adopted to handle high-frequency components in transfer functions and reduce wood-grain artifacts. The VolumePro system implemented hardware-supported supersampling in the z-direction. CUDA implementations have demonstrated its effectiveness in real-time volume rendering.
