name: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution
head: MSAA via Ray Distribution, Multi-ray AA, Multi-sample AA, Multi-sampling for rendering, Ray Distribution AA
body: Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution is an image-order rendering technique that reduces aliasing artifacts by casting multiple rays per pixel, distributed within the pixel area, and averaging the resulting color values. It solves the problem of jagged edges caused by abrupt intensity changes along object silhouettes, which occur when a single ray per pixel fails to capture high-frequency scene details. Unlike post-processing convolution filters, this method performs supersampling directly during ray traversal, offering higher quality at the cost of increased computational load. It differs from Stochastic Jittering by using deterministic, fixed offsets for low sample counts (1x–4x) rather than random patterns, and from Monte Carlo Volume Rendering by relying on simple arithmetic averaging rather than importance-weighted integration. Inputs: Pixel coordinates (x, y) from the rasterizer (e.g., glFragCoord). A uniform integer parameter AA selecting the sampling mode (1, 2, 3, or 4). A rendering function render(uv) that traces a single ray for a given normalized UV offset within the pixel and returns a vec3 color. Outputs: A single vec3 color value representing the averaged result of all distributed rays for the pixel. No complex data structures are required. The method uses scalar arithmetic for offset calculation and accumulation, and stores the AA mode selector as an integer uniform. 1. Select Mode: Determine the number of samples N based on the AA uniform. If AA is not 1, 2, or 3, default to 4. 2. Generate Offsets: Calculate 2D UV offsets (\delta u, \delta v) for each of the N rays. The offsets depend on the mode and, for 2x and 3x, the parity of the pixel coordinates. 3. Trace Rays: For each offset i \in \{0, \dots, N-1\}, pass the offset to getUV and call render to obtain color Ci. 4. Average: Sum all color values Ci and divide by N to produce the final pixel color. AAx1 (N=1): Offset: (0, 0). AAx2 (N=2): Let b{xy} = (x + y) \pmod 2. Let n{bxy} = 1 - b{xy}. Offsets: (0.33 \cdot n{bxy}, 0) and (0.33 \cdot b{xy}, 0.66). AAx3 (N=3): Let b{xy} = (x + y) \pmod 2. Let n{bxy} = 1 - b{xy}. Offsets: (0.66 \cdot n{bxy}, 0), (0.66 \cdot b{xy}, 0.66), and (0.33, 0.33). AAx4 (N=4): Define vector e = (0.125, -0.125, 0.375, -0.375). Offsets: (e.x, e.z), (e.y, e.w), (e.w, e.x), and (e.z, e.y). Averaging: C{final} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} Ci where Ci is the color returned by render(getUV(offseti)). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderaa(x: int, y: int, aamode: int, renderfunc) -> tuple: if aamode not in (1, 2, 3): aamode = 4 if aamode == 1: return renderfunc((0.0, 0.0)) elif aamode == 2: bxy = (x + y) & 1 nbxy = 1 - bxy c1 = renderfunc((0.33 nbxy, 0.0)) c2 = renderfunc((0.33 bxy, 0.66)) return ((c1[0] + c2[0]) / 2.0, (c1[1] + c2[1]) / 2.0, (c1[2] + c2[2]) / 2.0) elif aamode == 3: bxy = (x + y) & 1 nbxy = 1 - bxy c1 = renderfunc((0.66 nbxy, 0.0)) c2 = renderfunc((0.66 bxy, 0.66)) c3 = renderfunc((0.33, 0.33)) return ((c1[0] + c2[0] + c3[0]) / 3.0, (c1[1] + c2[1] + c3[1]) / 3.0, (c1[2] + c2[2] + c3[2]) / 3.0) elif aamode == 4: ex, ey, ez, ew = 0.125, -0.125, 0.375, -0.375 c1 = renderfunc((ex, ez)) c2 = renderfunc((ey, ew)) c3 = renderfunc((ew, ex)) c4 = renderfunc((ez, ey)) return ((c1[0] + c2[0] + c3[0] + c4[0]) / 4.0, (c1[1] + c2[1] + c3[1] + c4[1]) / 4.0, (c1[2] + c2[2] + c3[2] + c4[2]) / 4.0) Performance: This technique significantly reduces framerate due to the increased ray count, as rendering time increases linearly with the number of samples. Optimization: To mitigate performance loss, an optimization is to only perform AA if the iteration count (e.g., ray marching steps) is above average, as this likely indicates the ray is near an object edge. Precision: The source code uses floating-point literals 0.33 and 0.66 rather than exact fractions like 1/3 or 2/3. Boundary Conditions: The offsets are passed directly to getUV for coordinate transformation. Uses random offsets to break up regular aliasing patterns. Sets it apart by avoiding the fixed pattern bias of MSAA. Choose when you need to avoid structured artifacts. Link Uses cumulative distribution functions for importance sampling. Sets it apart by adapting to scene density and lighting. Choose when the scene has varying density or lighting that benefits from non-uniform sampling. Link Samples at regular grid points. Sets it apart by offering simplicity and predictability at the cost of potential moiré patterns. Choose for simplicity and predictability. Link Uses random sampling with statistical integration. Sets it apart by handling complex media and global illumination with higher variance. Choose for high-quality global illumination or complex media, accepting higher variance. Link Combines jittering with temporal reprojection for temporal anti-aliasing. Sets it apart by reducing flickering over time in dynamic scenes. Choose for dynamic scenes to reduce flickering over time. Link General term for sampling at higher resolution. Sets it apart as the parent category, with MSAA via Ray Distribution implementing it using fixed offsets. Choose when high-quality anti-aliasing is required and performance is not the primary constraint. Link Specialized sampling for Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics. Sets it apart by targeting particle-based fluid rendering. Choose for particle-based fluid rendering. Link Uses jittered offsets to reduce aliasing. Sets it apart by balancing regularity and randomness. Choose when you want a balance between regularity and randomness. Link Uses warp-level parallelism for sampling. Sets it apart by optimizing for GPU massive parallel contexts. Choose for GPU optimization in massive parallel contexts. Link Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples per pixel. Rendering time increases linearly proportional to the number of samples because the same number of interpolations are required for each sample. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as only the accumulated color sum is stored before averaging. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. However, it is noted that the technique "wrecks your framerate" if not optimized. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with N. AAx4 is 4x slower than AAx1. Strengths: Effective at removing jagged edges and aliasing artifacts, particularly along silhouette edges where intensity changes abruptly. Simple to implement. Limitations: High computational cost. Fixed offsets may not adapt to scene complexity, potentially wasting samples in uniform regions. When to Use: When high-quality anti-aliasing is required and performance is not the primary constraint, or when combined with edge-detection optimizations. When Not to Use: In real-time applications with strict performance budgets, or when the scene is largely uniform and aliasing is minimal. The technique is described in the context of raymarching distance fields and volume rendering. It is a form of supersampling, which is defined as sampling the scene at a higher resolution than displayed to combat aliasing. The specific offset patterns for 2x, 3x, and 4x sampling are derived from implementations in GLSL shaders, as seen in the kushchevd/RayMarching repository. The theoretical basis for supersampling as a method to reduce undersampling artifacts is discussed in literature on volume visualization. name: Z-direction Supersampling
head: Supersampling in z, VolumePro Supersampling
body: Z-direction supersampling is a hardware-accelerated technique that reduces aliasing artifacts by increasing the number of sample slices per volume in the z-direction, interpolating additional sample slices between existing voxel slices. It is distinct from its sibling Multi-Sample Anti-Aliasing via Ray Distribution because it operates by interpolating additional sample slices between existing voxel slices along the volume's z-axis, rather than distributing multiple rays per pixel in the image plane. Inputs: Volume dataset stored in voxel memory; viewing parameters (viewing angle, sample spacing). Outputs: Rendered image with reduced aliasing artifacts. Data Structures: The volume data is stored in voxel memory. The hardware pipeline includes an Interpolation unit that processes slices in order. Steps: 1. Interpolation: The hardware interpolates additional sample slices between existing voxel slices in the z-direction. This is done by performing several interpolations from the same pair of adjacent voxel slices before moving to the next slice pair. Samples pass from the Interpolation unit in slice-by-slice order. 2. Opacity Correction: The software automatically corrects opacity according to the viewing angle and the new sample spacing by reloading the opacity table. 3. Rendering: The interpolated slices are composited along the ray. If the supersampling factor is k, the total number of sample slices exceeds the number of voxel slices by a factor of k. Parameters: Supersampling Factor (k): The maximum supersampling factor in z is eight. Typical values include 2x and 3x. Pitfalls: Pipeline Stall: The voxel memory stages of the pipeline must stall and wait for the additional, supersampled slices to clear, which reduces the rendering rate. Performance: For a 256^3 data set, supersampling reduces the rendering rate to 30 frames per second. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zdirectionsupersampling(volume, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, supersamplingfactor): """ volume: 3D list [Z][Y][X] of (R, G, B, alpha) tuples. rayorigin: (ox, oy, oz) raydirection: (dx, dy, dz) stepsize: float (original voxel spacing) supersamplingfactor: int k (max 8) Returns: (R, G, B, alpha) """ # Opacity correction handled by reloading the opacity table based on viewing angle and spacing def applyopacitycorrection(alpha, viewingangle, samplespacing, k): # Standard correction scales opacity by the ratio of original to supersampled spacing return alpha (samplespacing / (samplespacing / k)) # Linear interpolation between two adjacent voxel slices def interpolateslices(slicea, sliceb, fraction): return ( slicea[0] (1.0 - fraction) + sliceb[0] fraction, slicea[1] (1.0 - fraction) + sliceb[1] fraction, slicea[2] (1.0 - fraction) + sliceb[2] fraction, slicea[3] (1.0 - fraction) + sliceb[3] fraction) # Initialize compositing state alphaout = 0.0 colorout = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Volume dimensions volz = len(volume) voly = len(volume[0]) volx = len(volume[0][0]) # Ray parameters ox, oy, oz = rayorigin dx, dy, dz = raydirection # Effective step size in z accounts for supersampling factor k stepz = stepsize / supersamplingfactor t = 0.0 while True: x = ox + dx t y = oy + dy t z = oz + dz t # Check bounds if not (0 <= x < volx and 0 <= y < voly and 0 <= z < volz): break # Get voxel indices ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) # Clamp indices to valid interpolation range if ix < 0: ix = 0 if iy < 0: iy = 0 if iz < 0: iz = 0 if ix >= volx - 1: ix = volx - 2 if iy >= voly - 1: iy = voly - 2 if iz >= volz - 1: iz = volz - 2 # Z-supersampling interpolation between adjacent slices fz = z - iz c1 = volume[iz][iy][ix] c2 = volume[iz + 1][iy][ix] sample = interpolateslices(c1, c2, fz) # Apply opacity correction for supersampling a = applyopacitycorrection(sample[3], 0.0, stepsize, supersamplingfactor) # Front-to-back compositing alphaout += a (1.0 - alphaout) colorout[0] += sample[0] a (1.0 - alphaout) colorout[1] += sample[1] a (1.0 - alphaout) colorout[2] += sample[2] a (1.0 - alphaout) if alphaout >= 1.0: break t += stepz return colorout[0], colorout[1], colorout[2], alphaout Time Complexity: Rendering time increases with the supersampling factor k due to the increased number of slices to process and the pipeline stall. Memory Complexity: Requires storing additional interpolated slices in the pipeline buffer, causing stalls. Performance: For a 256^3 dataset, rendering rate drops to 30 fps with supersampling. For a 152 \times 261 \times 200 CT scan, 3x supersampling reduces artifacts caused by insufficient sampling rate of high frequencies on the foot surface. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated, effective at reducing aliasing artifacts caused by insufficient sampling rate of high frequencies. Limitations: Limited to z-direction in hardware. Supersampling in x and y requires software-based multi-pass rendering and blending. Pipeline stalls reduce throughput. When to use: When aliasing artifacts are visible due to coarse z-sampling, especially for high-frequency surfaces. When not to use: When performance is critical and artifacts are acceptable, or when supersampling in x/y is required (requires software workaround). Z-direction supersampling was introduced in the VolumePro real-time ray-casting system. VolumePro is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering system. The technique was designed to address aliasing artifacts in real-time volume rendering by increasing the sampling density along the volume's z-axis. It is part of the VolumePro hardware's support for high-quality volume visualization. name: Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering
head: Non-uniform particle sampling, Stochastic Sampling for SPH Rendering, Stochastic sampling
body: Importance Sampling for SPH Rendering is a technique to increase rendering performance by reducing the number of particles used during rendering, using a non-uniform sampling strategy based on data importance and view-dependent criteria. It solves the problem of high computational cost when rendering large, unstructured Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) datasets by ensuring that particles in complex regions (e.g., phase interfaces, vortices) are sampled more densely than those in homogeneous areas. It differs from Uniform Ray Sampling by avoiding equal-time high-error trade-offs. Inputs and Outputs: Input: SPH particle dataset (positions, attributes, phases), camera parameters, transfer functions, and sampling parameters p{min} and p{max}. Output: Rendered image with reduced noise and artifacts in critical regions, achieved by selectively accessing a subset of particles per ray. Data Structures: Particle Data: Standard SPH structure containing position \mathbf{x}i, attributes (e.g., density, temperature), and phase identifier. Data Importance Grid/Array: A precomputed value pi for each particle i, representing the static importance of that particle based on local attribute complexity and phase interface presence. View-Dependent Criterion: A dynamic value pt calculated per pixel or ray segment based on view-dependent factors (e.g., opacity, occlusion). Parameters: p{min}: Minimal sampling probability. Controls render time significantly. Recommended value is 0.01 to avoid high sampling error at phase interfaces. p{max}: Maximal sampling probability. Controls rendering error with least effect on render times. Should be assigned to high values to increase the range of sampling probabilities. Steps: 1. Precompute Data Importance (pi): Calculate a static importance value for each particle. This value is low for homogeneous areas and high for complex regions like phase interfaces and vortices. This step is fast (<30ms) compared to volume resampling preprocessing. 2. Determine Sampling Probability (p): For each ray marching step, combine the precomputed data importance pi with the view-dependent criterion pt to determine the per-pixel particle access probability p. The specific combination formula is not provided, but it results in varying probabilities. 3. Stochastic Particle Selection: Based on the calculated probability p, randomly decide whether to access and render the current particle. If accessed, use the particle's attributes for shading. 4. Handle Phase Interfaces and Shading: If a phase transition leading to surface shading is detected during ray marching, use a constant sampling probability of one (p=1) for the iterative search for the surface position xs and the resampling of SPH attributes at xs for shading. For single scattering occlusion rays cast from a sampling point in a volumetric area, reduce the particle sampling probability by a factor of 10% (i.e., p{new} = 0.9 \times p{old}). Do not reduce the probability if an occlusion ray stems from a ray segment containing surface shading, because surfaces have higher opacity and use irradiance influenced by occlusion for shading. 5. Render: Accumulate the contributions of sampled particles to form the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random def rendersphimportancesampling(particles, camera, pmin, pmax): # Precompute static data importance pi for each particle # Not given in the sources. Typically involves analyzing local attribute variance and phase interfaces. pi = [0.0] len(particles) image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height)] for u in range(camera.width): for v in range(camera.height): ray = camera.generateray(u, v) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 while transmittance > 0.001 and ray.t < camera.maxdistance: # Find relevant particles near the current ray position # Not given in the sources. Typically uses spatial hashing or kd-tree. relevantparticles = findparticlesnearray(ray, particles) if not relevantparticles: ray.t += ray.stepsize continue selectedparticle = None for particle in relevantparticles: # Calculate view-dependent criterion pt # Not given in the sources. Typically relates to accumulated opacity or depth. pt = 1.0 - transmittance # Combine pi and pt to get sampling probability p # Formula not provided in the sources p = pi[particle.id] pt p = max(pmin, min(pmax, p)) # Stochastic selection if random.random() < p: selectedparticle = particle break if selectedparticle is None: ray.t += ray.stepsize continue # Check for phase transition if isphasetransition(selectedparticle, ray): # Use constant probability 1 for surface shading search surfacepos = findsurfaceposition(selectedparticle, ray) attributes = resamplesphattributes(surfacepos, particles) color = shadesurface(attributes, ray) transmittance = 0.0 break else: attributes = getparticleattributes(selectedparticle) # Reduce probability for secondary occlusion rays from volumetric areas if issecondaryocclusionray(ray): # Probability reduction factor of 10% applied to subsequent steps pass volumecolor = shadevolume(attributes, ray) color = [c + v transmittance for c, v in zip(color, volumecolor)] transmittance = (1.0 - selectedparticle.opacity) ray.t += ray.stepsize image[v][u] = color return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If p{min} approaches p{max}, the method collapses to uniform sampling, omitting performance advantages. Setting p{min} = 0 can lead to high sampling error at phase interfaces that were not correctly identified in the data importance pi. Therefore, p{min} should be set to at least 0.01 for high-quality renders. Temporal noise: Particle sampling and preprocessing do not currently consider temporal properties, so sampling noise may change between frames in time-dependent data. SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling is a precomputation technique that assigns sampling probabilities to SPH particles based on the local information complexity of their attributes and the presence of phase interfaces. It solves the problem of high-frequency shading errors and subsampling artifacts at phase boundaries by ensuring that regions with high attribute variation or discontinuous phase transitions are sampled more densely. It differs from naive random discarding by using a structured, data-driven importance grid that accounts for the spatial support of the SPH kernel, and it differs from its sibling Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data by explicitly computing entropy to quantify attribute variation rather than relying solely on stochastic selection heuristics. A direct volume rendering technique for large, unstructured smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) data that avoids intermediate grid representations by stochastically sampling a subset of particles during ray marching. It differs from standard DVR by using view-dependent and spatial-complexity-based probabilities to select particles, enabling continuous scaling from interactive previews to high-quality renders. It specifically addresses multi-phase flows by reconstructing interfaces between different fluid types using a combined volumetric and surface shading model. This method approximates Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) scalar fields along viewing rays using piecewise polynomial functions of higher order, addressing the challenge of rendering SPH data which has highly varying spatial resolution. It sets itself apart from linear or constant approximations by minimizing the L^2 distance between the approximation and the exact particle kernel contribution for each particle individually, allowing the representation resolution to adapt to the data resolution. Unlike sibling methods that focus on sampling strategies or entropy-based selection, this technique focuses on the mathematical fidelity of the field representation along the ray. This variant adapts sampling probabilities based on the type of shading being performed. If a phase transition leading to surface shading is detected during ray marching, it uses a constant sampling probability of one for the iterative search for the surface position xs and the resampling of SPH attributes at xs for shading. For single scattering occlusion, it reduces particle sampling probability by a factor of 10% if an occlusion ray is cast from a sampling point in a volumetric area. However, it does not reduce the probability if an occlusion ray stems from a ray segment containing surface shading, because surfaces have higher opacity and use irradiance influenced by occlusion for shading. Single scattering occlusion is low frequency and impervious to subsampling compared to surface shading, allowing reduced sampling probability for secondary rays which perform the majority of SPH approximations. Time Complexity: Rendering time is linearly dependent on the number of particle accesses. By reducing particle accesses through non-uniform sampling, performance is significantly improved. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for particle data and precomputed importance values pi. No intermediate grid representation is needed, unlike volume resampling. Measured Performance: Spray Nozzle (43.2M particles): Fast rendering <1s, High-quality 8s, No sampling 45s. Bubble (4.3M particles): Aggressive subsampling <1s, Reference >10s. Turbine: Equal-time rendering (5.3s) with uniform sampling had significantly higher error than the non-uniform sampling method. Preprocessing: Negligible preprocessing time (<30ms) compared to volume resampling which can take several minutes. Strengths: Handles dense multi-phase data with accurate phase interface reconstruction; avoids discretization errors associated with grid-based resampling; allows interactive exploration due to low preprocessing time. Limitations: Temporal noise may be visible in time-dependent data; requires careful tuning of p{min} and p{max} to balance error and performance. When to Use: When rendering large, unstructured SPH datasets with complex phase interfaces where uniform sampling is too slow or produces high error. When Not to Use: When temporal consistency is critical and preprocessing for temporal coherence is not implemented; when the dataset is very small and preprocessing overhead dominates. Originating from the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data", this method was developed to address the challenges of rendering large, unstructured SPH data without the need for expensive intermediate grid representations. It builds on the principles of direct volume ray casting and importance sampling, adapting them to the specific characteristics of SPH data, such as varying particle densities and multi-phase interfaces. The method has been applied to various SPH datasets, including spray nozzles, bubble flows, and turbine simulations, demonstrating significant performance improvements over uniform sampling and volume resampling. name: SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling
head: Data importance precomputation, Entropy-based importance
body: SPH Attribute Entropy for Importance Sampling is a precomputation technique that assigns sampling probabilities to SPH particles based on the local information complexity of their attributes and the presence of phase interfaces. It solves the problem of high-frequency shading errors and subsampling artifacts at phase boundaries by ensuring that regions with high attribute variation or discontinuous phase transitions are sampled more densely. It differs from naive random discarding by using a structured, data-driven importance grid that accounts for the spatial support of the SPH kernel, and it differs from its sibling Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data by explicitly computing entropy to quantify attribute variation rather than relying solely on stochastic selection heuristics. The method operates in two phases: a precomputation phase that builds an importance grid from the particle data, and a runtime phase that queries this grid during ray marching to determine particle sampling probabilities. Inputs: A particle set \mathcal{P} where each particle i has position \mathbf{x}i, phase \pii, and attribute values for the visualized SPH attribute A. The rendering SPH kernel function with finite support radius h. The importance grid resolution and bounds covering the spatial extent of the SPH data. The number of histogram bins N{\text{bins}} for entropy calculation. The dilation kernel width (in grid cells) and number of dilation iterations. Outputs: An importance grid storing scalar importance values pi(\mathbf{x}) for each cell. The runtime sampling probability p(\mathbf{x}) for any position \mathbf{x} during rendering. 1. Importance Grid: A 3D regular grid where each cell stores a single floating-point value representing the data importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) at the cell center \mathbf{x}c. The grid resolution is chosen to cover the bounding box of the particle set. 2. Histogram: A temporary array of size N{\text{bins}} used to compute the entropy of attribute values for particles within a local neighborhood. The precomputation determines the initial importance for each grid cell and then filters these values to account for the SPH kernel's spatial support and interface detection. 1. Initialize Grid: Create an importance grid of sufficient resolution to cover the particle domain. Initialize all cells to 0. 2. Compute Initial Importance: For each grid cell c with center \mathbf{x}c: a. Identify the set of particles \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) lying within this cell. b. If \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) is empty, set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = 0. c. If \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) contains particles with different phases (i.e., \exists i, j \in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) such that \pii \neq \pij), set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = 1. d. Otherwise, if all particles in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) have the same phase, compute the entropy of attribute A for these particles: i. Bin the attribute values of particles in \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c) into a normalized histogram h(b) with N{\text{bins}} bins. ii. Compute the entropy: \mathbb{H}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A) = - \sum{b=0}^{N{\text{bins}}-1} h(b) \log2 h(b) iii. Normalize the entropy to be independent of histogram size: \overline{\mathbb{H}}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A) = \frac{2^{\mathbb{H}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A)}}{N{\text{bins}}} iv. Set pi(\mathbf{x}c) = \mathbb{H}{\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)}(A). 3. Filter with Maximum Dilation: Apply a 3D maximum dilation filter to the importance grid to propagate importance values to neighboring cells, compensating for the fact that SPH approximation at a sampling point depends on particles in neighboring cells. a. Define a dilation kernel with width equal to the number of grid cells covered by the finite support of the SPH kernel function used in rendering. b. For each cell in the grid, update its importance value to the maximum importance value found in any cell within the dilation kernel. c. Interface Detection: During dilation, if more than half of the cells in the dilation kernel do not contain any particles, the cell is expected to contain a free-surface interface. In this case, set the cell's importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) to 1. 4. Iterate Dilation: Repeat the dilation step for a user-specified number of iterations. In practice, 1 or 2 iterations are sufficient. During ray marching, for a sampling position \mathbf{x}: 1. Query the precomputed importance value pi(\mathbf{x}) from the importance grid cell containing \mathbf{x}. 2. Combine pi(\mathbf{x}) with the view-dependent transmittance factor pt(\mathbf{x}) to determine the particle sampling probability p(\mathbf{x}) according to Equation 9 of the parent article. The exact combination formula depends on the parent article's definition of pt(\mathbf{x}). 3. Use p(\mathbf{x}) to stochastically select particles for the SPH approximation at \mathbf{x}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from collections import defaultdict class Particle: def init(self, x, y, z, phase, attr): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z self.phase = phase self.attr = attr def computeentropy(attributevalues, nbins): """Computes entropy for a set of attribute values per Eq. 11.""" if not attributevalues: return 0.0 minval = min(attributevalues) maxval = max(attributevalues) if minval == maxval: return 0.0 binwidth = (maxval - minval) / nbins hist = [0.0] nbins for v in attributevalues: b = int((v - minval) / binwidth) if b >= nbins: b = nbins - 1 hist[b] += 1.0 total = sum(hist) entropy = 0.0 for count in hist: if count > 0: p = count / total entropy -= p math.log2(p) return entropy def precomputeimportancegrid(particles, gridbounds, gridresolution, nbins, dilationradius): """Precomputes the importance grid for SPH attribute entropy sampling.""" nx, ny, nz = gridresolution (minx, maxx), (miny, maxy), (minz, maxz) = gridbounds dx = (maxx - minx) / nx dy = (maxy - miny) / ny dz = (maxz - minz) / nz importancegrid = [[[0.0] nz for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] hasparticles = [[[False] nz for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] cellparticles = defaultdict(list) for p in particles: i = int((p.x - minx) / dx) j = int((p.y - miny) / dy) k = int((p.z - minz) / dz) i = max(0, min(nx - 1, i)) j = max(0, min(ny - 1, j)) k = max(0, min(nz - 1, k)) cellparticles[(i, j, k)].append(p) hasparticles[i][j][k] = True for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): if (i, j, k) in cellparticles: plist = cellparticles[(i, j, k)] phases = set(p.phase for p in plist) if len(phases) > 1: importancegrid[i][j][k] = 1.0 else: attrs = [p.attr for p in plist] importancegrid[i][j][k] = computeentropy(attrs, nbins) for in range(dilationradius): newgrid = [[[0.0] nz for in range(ny)] for in range(nx)] for i in range(nx): for j in range(ny): for k in range(nz): imin = max(0, i - dilationradius) imax = min(nx - 1, i + dilationradius) jmin = max(0, j - dilationradius) jmax = min(ny - 1, j + dilationradius) kmin = max(0, k - dilationradius) kmax = min(nz - 1, k + dilationradius) emptycount = 0 maximp = 0.0 totalcells = (imax - imin + 1) (jmax - jmin + 1) (kmax - kmin + 1) for ii in range(imin, imax + 1): for jj in range(jmin, jmax + 1): for kk in range(kmin, kmax + 1): if not hasparticles[ii][jj][kk]: emptycount += 1 else: if importancegrid[ii][jj][kk] > maximp: maximp = importancegrid[ii][jj][kk] if emptycount > totalcells / 2: newgrid[i][j][k] = 1.0 else: newgrid[i][j][k] = maximp importancegrid = newgrid return importancegrid N{\text{bins}}: Number of histogram bins for entropy calculation. Not given in the sources. Dilation kernel width: Equal to the number of grid cells covered by the finite support of the SPH kernel function used in rendering. Dilation iterations: User-specified number of iterations for the filtering process; 1 or 2 iterations are sufficient in practice. Phase Interface Discontinuity: The approximation of phases is discontinuous, leading to edge cases where false distinct phases may be assigned to a sampling point, causing poor surface shading due to high-frequency specular highlights and high opacities. Subsampling Errors at Interfaces: Regions with different phases contain phase interfaces provoking surface shading; small SPH subsampling errors lead to poor surface shading due to dependency on normals and high opacities. Empty Cells: Cells with no particles are assigned importance 0, which is handled correctly by the interface detection logic during dilation. Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling reduces overall sampling error in SPH rendering by selecting well-distributed particle subsets within an acceleration structure's cells. It differs from naive random discarding by enforcing a structured selection process based on cell and position importance, ensuring that the statistical properties of the particle neighborhood are preserved more accurately during ray marching. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data". It addresses the challenges of rendering SPH data with multiple phases, where traditional uniform sampling can lead to artifacts at phase boundaries. The use of entropy to measure attribute variation is based on information theory [Sha48], and the normalization of entropy follows Wei et al. [WDS18]. name: Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling
head: Stratification of particle samples
body: Stratified Stochastic Particle Sampling reduces overall sampling error in SPH rendering by selecting well-distributed particle subsets within an acceleration structure's cells. It differs from naive random discarding by enforcing a structured selection process based on cell and position importance, ensuring that the statistical properties of the particle neighborhood are preserved more accurately during ray marching. Inputs: Particle set \mathcal{P} organized in a uniform grid acceleration structure. Data importance grid pi(\mathbf{x}c), precomputed for each cell center \mathbf{x}c. Sampling position \mathbf{x} within the volume. Probability bounds p{\min} and p{\max}. Outputs: A subset of particles chosen from the relevant acceleration structure cells to evaluate the SPH approximation at \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: The acceleration structure is a uniform grid storing particles, aligned with the data importance grid. Both grids share equal cell sizes and perfect overlap, ensuring overlapping cells share the same center point \mathbf{x}c. Parameters: p{\min} and p{\max} define the sampling probability bounds. Grid resolution determines cell size; optimal cell width equals the kernel function support for efficient particle access. Finer grids increase the stratification factor but may decrease performance. Algorithm: 1. Identify all cells in the acceleration structure that contribute to the SPH approximation at \mathbf{x}. Let \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}) be this set. 2. For each cell center \mathbf{x}c \in \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}): a. Retrieve the particle count |\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)| in the cell. b. Retrieve the cell importance pi(\mathbf{x}c). c. Compute the position importance pi(\mathbf{x}) for the sampling location. d. Calculate the target number of particles n using n = p{\min} + (p{\max} - p{\min}) pi(\mathbf{x}c) pi(\mathbf{x}) |\mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c)|. e. Select \lfloor n \rfloor particles from \mathcal{P}(\mathbf{x}c). f. Select one additional particle with probability n - \lfloor n \rfloor. (The source's "(n - n)" is a typographical error for the fractional part.) 3. Aggregate the selected particles from all cells in \mathcal{C}(\mathbf{x}) to perform the SPH approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def stratifiedstochasticsampling(particlesgrid, importancegrid, x, pmin, pmax, kernelradius): """ Selects particles for SPH approximation at position x using stratification. """ selectedparticles = [] cellsize = particlesgrid.cellsize # 1. Identify contributing cells for SPH approximation at x # Standard SPH kernel support determines which grid cells overlap the kernel sphere. startidx = (math.floor((x[0] - kernelradius) / cellsize), math.floor((x[1] - kernelradius) / cellsize), math.floor((x[2] - kernelradius) / cellsize)) endidx = (math.floor((x[0] + kernelradius) / cellsize), math.floor((x[1] + kernelradius) / cellsize), math.floor((x[2] + kernelradius) / cellsize)) # Precompute position importance pi(x) # Exact formula for position importance is not provided in the sources. positionimportance = 1.0 for i in range(startidx[0], endidx[0] + 1): for j in range(startidx[1], endidx[1] + 1): for k in range(startidx[2], endidx[2] + 1): xc = (i + 0.5) cellsize cellparticles = particlesgrid.getparticlesatcenter(xc) Nc = len(cellparticles) if Nc == 0: continue cellimportance = importancegrid.getvalueatcenter(xc) # 2d. Calculate target number n n = pmin + (pmax - pmin) cellimportance positionimportance Nc # 2e & 2f. Select integer part nint = math.floor(n) if nint > 0: indices = random.sample(range(Nc), min(nint, Nc)) selectedparticles.extend([cellparticles[idx] for idx in indices]) # 2g. Probabilistic additional particle remainder = n - nint if remainder > 0 and nint < Nc: if random.random() < remainder: remainingindices = [idx for idx in range(Nc) if idx not in indices] if remainingindices: selectedparticles.append(cellparticles[random.choice(remainingindices)]) return selectedparticles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Cell Access: At each sampling position, multiple cells are accessed. The position importance pi(\mathbf{x}) remains constant across all accessed cells, but the cell importance pi(\mathbf{x}c) can differ between these cells during a single SPH approximation. Grid Alignment: The method assumes the acceleration structure and the data importance grid have equal cell sizes and perfect overlap, sharing the same center point \mathbf{x}c. Performance vs. Stratification: Using a finer grid resolution increases the stratification factor but can decrease performance. The optimal cell width is equal to the kernel function support. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of contributing cells and particles per cell. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the uniform grid acceleration structure and the data importance grid. Strengths: Reduces overall sampling error by ensuring well-distributed samples in the neighborhood. It avoids the variance associated with purely random discarding of particles. Limitations: Performance can degrade if the grid resolution is too fine. It requires precomputation of importance values. When to use: Used in SPH rendering to reduce sampling error in neighborhoods. The method is described in the context of stochastic volume rendering of multi-phase SPH data. It builds upon the concept of importance sampling using SPH attribute entropy [3626-sph-attribute-entropy-for-importance-sampling.md]. The technique was introduced to handle the high-frequency nature of surface shading and phase interfaces in SPH rendering. Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi‐Phase SPH Data, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14121, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data
head: Coalesced Memory Access Sampling, GPU Ray Marching Implementation, OpenCL SPH Renderer
body: A direct volume rendering technique for large, unstructured smoothed-particle hydrodynamics (SPH) data that avoids intermediate grid representations by stochastically sampling a subset of particles during ray marching. It differs from standard DVR by using view-dependent and spatial-complexity-based probabilities to select particles, enabling continuous scaling from interactive previews to high-quality renders. It specifically addresses multi-phase flows by reconstructing interfaces between different fluid types using a combined volumetric and surface shading model. Inputs: SPH particle dataset containing positions, masses, densities, phase IDs, and attributes. Camera parameters: eye position, view direction, and projection matrix. Rendering parameters: number of ray march steps, kernel type (cubic spline or Epanechnikov), maximum number of particles to sample per cell, and a precomputed random value table. Transfer functions for volumetric opacity and color. Light sources for shading calculations. Outputs: Rendered image with color and opacity per pixel. 1. Particle Storage Flat array of particles grouped by the grid cell they reside in. Each particle i stores: \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. mi: Mass. \rhoi: Density. \phii: Phase ID (integer). Other attributes (e.g., temperature Ti). 2. Acceleration Structure (3D Uniform Grid) A 3D uniform grid covering the simulation domain. Each cell stores a reference (pointer/index) to a contiguous block of memory in the Particle Storage array containing all particles within that cell. This structure allows O(1) access to the list of particles in a specific spatial region. The grid is used only for querying particles, not as a discrete signal for traversal. 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, generate a primary ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate along the ray for a fixed number of steps or until the ray exits the domain. a. Determine Sampling Position: Calculate the current sampling point \mathbf{x} on the ray. b. Identify Relevant Grid Cell: Find the grid cell containing \mathbf{x}. c. Stochastic Particle Sampling: i. Retrieve the list of particles in the current cell from the acceleration structure. ii. Select a subset of these particles using stochastic sampling. The probability of selecting a particle is determined by an importance measure based on view-dependent factors and spatial complexity. iii. To ensure coalesced memory access on GPUs, all threads in a work group share the same random offset, but their local work group index is added as an offset to the selection. The selected subset is always a contiguous block of particles in memory. d. SPH Evaluation: i. For each selected particle j, compute the kernel weight W(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}j) using the chosen kernel function (cubic spline or Epanechnikov). ii. Estimate the field value (e.g., density, phase indicator) at \mathbf{x} by summing contributions from selected particles. iii. Determine the dominant phase at \mathbf{x} based on the phase IDs of the contributing particles. iv. Compute gradients if needed for surface reconstruction. e. Shading: i. Volumetric Shading: If the ray segment is within a homogeneous phase, use pre-integrated transfer functions [EKE01] for opacity and color accumulation. Pre-integration assumes fixed segment length and cannot handle phase transitions. ii. Surface Shading: If the ray segment crosses a phase interface, use a multi-material model. Apply Blinn-Phong BRDF for surface shading. iii. Single Scattering: Optionally perform stochastic single scattering to improve spatial perception of phase interfaces. f. Accumulation: Accumulate color and opacity along the ray using standard volume rendering integral equations. 3. Final Color: Output the accumulated color for the pixel. SPH Kernel Functions: The exact mathematical expressions for the kernel functions are Not given in the sources. The cubic spline kernel is smoother but has twice the support width of the Epanechnikov kernel, requiring more particle accesses. Importance Sampling Probability: The probability Pi of selecting particle i is proportional to an importance measure Ii. The exact formula for Ii is Not given in the sources, but it is derived from view-dependent factors and spatial complexity. Pre-integrated Transfer Function: For homogeneous segments, the transmittance T and color C are pre-computed in a 2D texture based on segment length L and optical depth \tau = \int \sigmat ds [EKE01]. This is not applicable to segments with phase transitions. Kernel Function: User-specified. Options: Cubic spline (smoother, wider support, more accesses) or Epanechnikov. Shading Model: Blinn-Phong BRDF for surface, Henyey-Greenstein phase function for volume. Number of Particles to Sample: Controls quality vs. performance. Higher values yield more accurate results. Random Values: Precomputed pseudo-random values are used instead of generating them on the GPU. Random Number Generation: Generating pseudo-random numbers on GPUs is difficult and slow. The method uses precomputed random values to avoid this. Phase Transitions: Pre-integrated transfer functions cannot be used for ray segments that cross phase boundaries because they assume fixed segment length and homogeneous material. Grid Usage: The uniform grid is only for particle querying. Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or higher-order traversal methods are not applicable because the grid does not represent a discrete signal. Memory Coalescing: To ensure efficient GPU memory access, the selected subset of particles must be contiguous in memory. This is achieved by sharing a random offset across a work group and adding the local work group index. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersphvolume(rayorigin, raydir, grid, particles, randomtable, numsteps, kerneltype, maxsamplespercell, workgroupid, localid, transferfunc): # Initialize accumulation variables color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 t = 0.0 # Ray marching loop for step in range(numsteps): # 1. Determine sampling position x = rayorigin + t raydir # 2. Identify relevant grid cell cellidx = grid.querycell(x) cellparticles = grid.cells[cellidx].particleblock # 3. Stochastic particle sampling if len(cellparticles) == 0: continue # Use precomputed random table with work-group offset for coalesced access baseoffset = randomtable[workgroupid] offset = baseoffset + localid sampleidx = offset % len(cellparticles) # Select contiguous block of particles k = min(maxsamplespercell, len(cellparticles)) subset = cellparticles[sampleidx: sampleidx + k] # 4. SPH evaluation density = 0.0 phaseid = -1 gradient = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for p in subset: r = distance(x, p.position) w = evaluatekernel(r, p.h, kerneltype) density += p.mass w / p.density if phaseid == -1 or p.phaseid == phaseid: phaseid = p.phaseid gradient += p.mass w (x - p.position) / p.density # 5. Shading # Check for phase transition or homogeneous segment if isphasetransition(phaseid, previousphase): # Surface shading with Blinn-Phong BRDF shading = computesurfaceshading(x, gradient, lightsources) else: # Volumetric shading with pre-integrated transfer functions opticaldepth = computeopticaldepth(density, steplength) shading = lookuppreintegratedtransfer(opticaldepth, transferfunc) # Optional stochastic single scattering if enablesinglescattering: shading += computesinglescattering(x, raydir, subset) # 6. Accumulation color += shading alpha (1.0 - alpha) alpha += (1.0 - alpha) shading.alpha t += steplength if alpha >= 1.0: break return color Time Complexity: Depends on the number of particles sampled per step. By sampling a subset, it reduces the complexity from O(N) per step to O(k) where k \ll N. The overall complexity is O(R \cdot S \cdot k) where R is the number of rays, S is the number of steps per ray, and k is the number of sampled particles per step. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing particles and the grid. The grid adds minimal overhead as it only stores references. Performance: Scales continuously from fast, interactive previews to high-quality rendering by adjusting the number of sampled particles. Strengths: Minimal preprocessing, no intermediate grid representation, handles large datasets, supports multi-phase flows, efficient GPU implementation with coalesced memory access. Limitations: Stochastic sampling introduces noise; requires careful tuning of the importance measure and number of samples for quality. Pre-integration is limited to homogeneous segments. When to Use: Large SPH datasets where preprocessing time and memory are constraints, and interactive or semi-interactive visualization is desired. Particularly suitable for multi-phase flows. Origin: The method was introduced in the paper "Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi-Phase SPH Data". History: It builds on previous work in SPH visualization and stochastic rendering. It addresses the computational complexity of rendering large, unstructured particle data by avoiding intermediate representations and using importance sampling. Usage: Used in scientific visualization for fluid dynamics, particularly for multi-phase flows like gas-liquid interactions. Stochastic Volume Rendering of Multi‐Phase SPH Data, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14121, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation for DVR
head: Higher-order SPH field approximation, Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation, Piecewise polynomial SPH approximation
body: This method approximates Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) scalar fields along viewing rays using piecewise polynomial functions of higher order, addressing the challenge of rendering SPH data which has highly varying spatial resolution. It sets itself apart from linear or constant approximations by minimizing the L^2 distance between the approximation and the exact particle kernel contribution for each particle individually, allowing the representation resolution to adapt to the data resolution. Unlike sibling methods that focus on sampling strategies or entropy-based selection, this technique focuses on the mathematical fidelity of the field representation along the ray [S1, 3626-importance-sampling-for-sph-rendering.md, 3638-stochastic-volume-rendering-of-multi-phase-sph-data.md]. Inputs: SPH particle dataset: positions \chi, mass \mu, target field value \alpha, density \rho, smoothing radius \zeta. Viewing rays defined by base point b and unit direction vector v. Approximation parameters: maximum polynomial degree D and number of non-trivial pieces K. SPH kernel function w(r) (typically cubic B-spline). Outputs: Rendered image with scalar field values. 1. Look-up Table (LUT) for Optimal Approximations: Precomputed for equidistant values of \Lambda (normalized distance from particle to ray). Stores localized difference coefficients \hat{a}{kd} for the optimal approximation of the unit particle contribution B\Lambda. Structure: Array indexed by \Lambda, containing sequences of knots (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}). 2. Ray Contribution List: For each ray, a list of contributions from particles. Each contribution is encoded as a sequence of knots: (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}). tk: Ray parameter (knot position). \hat{a}{kd}: Localized difference coefficients representing the change in polynomial behavior at tk. 1. Precomputation: For the chosen kernel, generate closed-form symbolic formulas for inner products \langle A, B\Lambda \rangle for variable knot positions \thetak and distance \Lambda. For a range of equidistant \Lambda values, perform non-linear optimization to find optimal knot positions \thetak that minimize E\Lambda. For each \Lambda and its optimal knots, compute the orthogonal basis \mathcal{A} and the optimal approximation S\Lambda. Encode S\Lambda as a sequence of knots (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}) and store in LUT. 2. Pass 1: Particle Approximation: For each particle i with parameters \mui, \alphai, \rhoi, \zetai, \chii: For each viewing ray j: Compute t{\chi, ij} (closest point parameter) and \Lambda{ij} = \frac{1}{\zetai} \|\chii - xj(t{\chi, ij})\|. If \Lambda{ij} is within kernel support: Retrieve precomputed localized difference coefficients \hat{a}{kd} from LUT for \Lambda{ij}. Scale and translate coefficients to match particle parameters and ray position. The contribution is \frac{\mui\alphai}{\rhoi\zetai^3} B{\Lambda{ij}}\left(\frac{t - t{\chi, ij}}{\zetai}\right). The encoding in terms of knots (tk, \hat{a}{kd}) must be adjusted for scaling by \zetai and translation by t{\chi, ij}, and amplitude scaling by \frac{\mui\alphai}{\rhoi\zetai^3}. Add the encoded contribution (knots and coefficients) to the ray's contribution list. 3. Pass 2: Sorting: For each ray, sort all contributions in its list by knot position tk in increasing order. 4. Pass 3: Accumulation and Compositing: For each ray: Initialize current polynomial coefficients a{kd} = 0 for all d. Iterate through sorted knots (tk, \hat{a}{k0}, \dots, \hat{a}{kD}): Update coefficients for the current piece k using the update rule: a{kd} = \hat{a}{kd} + \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} a{(k-1)j} (tk - t{k-1})^{j-d} for d = 0, \dots, D, where t{-1} is the ray start or previous knot, and a{(k-1)j} are coefficients from the previous piece. Evaluate the polynomial Ak(t) = \sum{d=0}^D a{kd} (t - tk)^d at sample points within [tk, t{k+1}] (or integrate if using quadrature) to get the field value. Accumulate the field value along the ray for compositing (e.g., using standard DVR compositing equations with the computed field value as the density/opacity source). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def particlewisesphdvr(particles, rays, lut, D, K, raystart, rayend): # Data structures rayknots = {ray.id: [] for ray in rays} # Pass 1: Particle Approximation for p in particles: for ray in rays: tchi = closestpointparam(ray, p.pos) Lambda = norm(p.pos - ray.pointat(tchi)) / p.zeta if Lambda < lut.maxlambda: # Retrieve precomputed knots and localized difference coefficients knots, hata = lut.query(Lambda) # Scale and translate knots and coefficients for tk, coeffs in zip(knots, hata): scaledt = p.zeta tk + tchi scaledcoeffs = [p.amplitude c for c in coeffs] rayknots[ray.id].append((scaledt, scaledcoeffs)) # Pass 2: Sorting for rayid in rayknots: rayknots[rayid].sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Pass 3: Accumulation and Compositing for ray in rays: a = [0.0] (D + 1) prevt = raystart fieldvalue = 0.0 for tk, hata in rayknots[ray.id]: # Update coefficients using the constant-complexity rule for d in range(D + 1): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(d, D + 1): sumval += comb(j, d) a[j] (tk - prevt)(j - d) a[d] = hata[d] + sumval # Evaluate polynomial at sample points within [tk, t{k+1}] # (Standard DVR sampling step) fieldvalue = sum(a[d] (tsample - tk)d for d in range(D + 1)) # Accumulate field value for compositing # (Standard DVR compositing step) prevt = tk SPH Kernel: The cubic B-spline kernel is used: w(r) = \frac{1}{4\pi} \begin{cases} (2-r)^3 - 4(1-r)^3, & 0 \leq r < 1 \\ (2-r)^3, & 1 \leq r < 2 \\ 0, & 2 \leq r \end{cases} where r is the normalized distance. Particle Contribution: A particle's contribution to a scalar field at position x is: \frac{\mu\alpha}{\rho\zeta^3} w\left(\frac{\|x - \chi\|}{\zeta}\right) Normalized Particle Contribution on a Ray: For a ray x(t) = b + tv, let t\chi be the parameter of the point on the ray closest to particle position \chi. Let \Lambda = \frac{1}{\zeta} \|\chi - x(t\chi)\|. The normalized contribution (unit mass, density, field attribute, smoothing radius) is: B\Lambda(t) = w\left(\sqrt{\Lambda^2 + t^2}\right) The actual contribution of a data particle is: \frac{\mu\alpha}{\rho\zeta^3} B\Lambda\left(\frac{t - t\chi}{\zeta}\right) Polynomial Representation: A polynomial A(t) of order D is represented by coefficients ad: A(t) = \sum{d=0}^D ad t^d Localized coefficients ad at t are computed from standard coefficients aj as: a{d} = \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} aj t^{j-d} Such that A(t) = \sum{d=0}^D a{d} (t - t)^d. Piecewise Polynomial Encoding: A continuous piecewise polynomial function is defined by knots tk and localized difference coefficients \hat{a}{kd} such that the difference between polynomials Ak (right of tk) and A{k-1} (left of tk) is: Ak(t) - A{k-1}(t) = \sum{d=0}^D \hat{a}{kd} (t - tk)^d Summing piecewise polynomials reduces to sorting their joint knots. The localized coefficients a{kd} for piece k are updated from piece k-1 using: a{kd} = \hat{a}{kd} + \sum{j=d}^D \binom{j}{d} a{(k-1)j} (tk - t{k-1})^{j-d} \quad \text{for } d = 0, \dots, D Optimal Approximation: The goal is to minimize the L^2 distance error: E\Lambda(S) = \|S - B\Lambda\|2 = \left( \int{\mathbb{R}} [S(t) - B\Lambda(t)]^2 dt \right)^{\frac{1}{2}} The space \mathcal{S} consists of even, continuous, piecewise polynomial functions with compact support, maximal degree D, and K non-trivial pieces. The dimension of \mathcal{S} is \lfloor \frac{KD}{2} \rfloor. Basis Construction: 1. Define non-orthogonal basis \tilde{\mathcal{A}} = \{\tilde{A}{kd}\} where \mathcal{J} is the set of pairs (k, d) with k \leq \lceil K/2 \rceil and d \leq D, excluding (1, d) for uneven d if K is uneven. 2. Basis functions are: \tilde{A}{kd}(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } |t| \leq \theta{k-1} \\ 1 - \left( \frac{|t| - \theta{k-1}}{\thetak - \theta{k-1}} \right)^d & \text{if } \theta{k-1} \leq |t| \leq \thetak \\ 0 & \text{if } |t| \geq \thetak \end{cases} where \theta0 = 0 and \thetak are positive knot positions. 3. Convert to orthogonal basis \mathcal{A} using Gram-Schmidt in lexicographical order: A{k^d^} = \tilde{A}{d^k^} - \sum{\substack{(k,d) \in \mathcal{J} \\ k < k^ \vee (k = k \wedge d < d^)}} \text{proj}{A{kd}}(\tilde{A}{d^k^}) where \text{proj}B(A) = \frac{\langle A, B \rangle}{\langle B, B \rangle} B and \langle A, B \rangle = \int{\mathbb{R}} A(t) B(t) dt. Optimal Knot Positions: Find \theta1, \dots, \theta{\lceil K/2 \rceil} by minimizing E\Lambda via non-linear optimization over 0 < \theta1 < \dots < \theta{\lceil K/2 \rceil}. The objective function E\Lambda is computed using closed-form symbolic formulas for inner products \langle A, B\Lambda \rangle, generated once per kernel type using computer algebra systems. For \Lambda close to the upper bound, multiple precision arithmetic (e.g., GNU MPFR) is required for stability. The optimal approximation S\Lambda for fixed knots is the orthogonal projection of B\Lambda onto \mathcal{S}: S\Lambda = \sum{A \in \mathcal{A}} \text{proj}A(B\Lambda) D: Maximum polynomial degree (order of approximation). K: Number of non-trivial polynomial pieces per particle. Continuity and Symmetry: Approximation candidates must be continuous, even functions with compact support to match the target B\Lambda. Numerical Stability: For \Lambda close to the upper bound of the kernel support, evaluation of symbolic formulae becomes unstable. Use multiple precision arithmetic (e.g., GNU MPFR) for precomputation. Degenerate Input: If \zeta = 0, the particle contribution is undefined. Guard against zero smoothing radius. Time Complexity: The summation of piecewise polynomials reduces to a sorting task. The update rule for coefficients has constant complexity per piece, irrespective of the number of particles contributing. Precomputation is done offline. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the LUT (size depends on \Lambda resolution, D, K) and per-ray contribution lists. Strengths: Higher-order approximation provides better accuracy than linear/constant methods, adapting to data resolution. Efficient summation via sorting. Limitations: Precomputation is complex and requires computer algebra systems. Numerical instability for large \Lambda. When to use: When high-fidelity rendering of SPH data is required, and precomputation time is acceptable. When not to use: For real-time rendering with strict latency constraints where precomputation is not feasible, or for very low-resolution approximations where linear methods suffice. The method is based on the paper "Particle-Wise Higher-Order SPH Field Approximation for DVR". SPH was introduced by Gingold and Monaghan (1977) and Lucy (1977). Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) has a long-standing tradition (Drebin et al., 1988). The cubic B-spline kernel is referenced from Rosswog (2009).
