name: Epipolar Sampling
head: Epipolar Line Sampling, Epipolar Light Shaft Sampling
body: Epipolar sampling is a technique that places sample points along epipolar lines (rays emanating radially from a light source's projection on the screen or feature correspondences between views) to exploit the smooth variation of inscattered light or cross-view features along these lines. This reduces the number of expensive ray-marching or feature-interpolation steps required compared to uniform sampling. In volume rendering, it optimizes light shaft computation by leveraging the observation that light intensity varies smoothly orthogonally to epipolar rays. In multi-view reconstruction, it enables cross-view feature aggregation without full 3D volume rendering by correlating features along epipolar lines. The method varies significantly depending on the application domain (light scattering vs. multi-view feature aggregation). The following describes the two primary implementations found in the sources. This variant optimizes the computation of inscattered light (light shafts) in participating media. Inputs: Screen resolution. Projected position of the light source on the screen (Lx, Ly). Depth buffer (z-buffer) of the scene. Number of initial ray-marching samples (N{init}) and interpolation samples (N{interp}) per line. Outputs: Ins scattered light intensity for each screen pixel. Auxiliary textures storing sample indices and coordinates. Data Structures: 1. Epipolar Texture: A 2D texture where each row corresponds to one epipolar line and each column to a sample location on that line. 2. Auxiliary Integer Texture: A two-channel texture storing the indices of the two closest ray-marching samples from the same slice for each interpolation sample. Steps: 1. Epipolar Line Generation: Determine the entry point E as the projected light position on the screen. If the light is behind the camera, E is the point at infinity where rays converge. If the light is on the screen: Equidistantly place a user-defined number of exit points along the screen border. Connect E to each exit point to form epipolar lines. If the light is outside the screen: Cull lines completely outside the visible area. Truncate remaining lines against screen borders. Boundary Adjustment: If the light is close to the screen boundary, rescale epipolar lines by advancing the exit point to strive for a 1:1 correspondence between samples and screen pixels, reducing redundant computations on short lines. 2. Sample Placement: Place N{init} initial ray-marching samples equidistantly along each epipolar line to capture low-frequency variations. Detect depth breaks (discontinuities) in the depth buffer along each epipolar line. Place additional ray-marching samples directly before and after each depth break to capture high-frequency details. Fill the remaining positions with interpolation samples. 3. Ray Marching: Perform expensive ray marching only at the initial and depth-break samples to compute inscattered light intensity. 4. Interpolation: For interpolation samples, compute intensity by linearly interpolating between the intensities of the two closest ray-marching samples. Use the auxiliary integer texture to retrieve the indices of the bounding ray-marching samples for efficient lookup. 5. Pixel Computation: For each screen pixel, cast an epipolar line through the pixel and compute its location in the epipolar texture. Perform bilateral filtering on the gathered inscattered light values. If no appropriate samples exist for filtering, mark the sample in a stencil and perform an additional ray-marching pass with fewer steps. This variant samples features from other views along epipolar lines for a given ray, enabling cross-view feature aggregation. Inputs: Image rays (origins, directions) for each pixel in the source view. Camera extrinsics and intrinsics for all views. Number of samples per epipolar line segment (s). Outputs: Aggregated features from other views. Data Structures: EpipolarSampling dataclass containing: features: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, otherview, ray, sample, channel). valid: Bool Tensor of shape (batch, view, otherview, ray). xyray: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, 2). xysample: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, otherview, ray, sample, 2). origins: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, 3). directions: Float Tensor of shape (batch, view, ray, 3). Steps: 1. Ray Generation: Generate image rays for each pixel in the source view using sampleimagegrid and getworldrays. 2. Projection: Project rays onto all other views using projectrays with extrinsics, intrinsics, and near/far planes. Obtain xymin, xymax, and overlapsimage masks. Clamp xymin and xymax to zero for infinite values and mask with overlapsimage. 3. Sample Depth Generation: Compute sample depths linearly spaced between 0 and 1: \text{sample\depth} = \frac{\text{torch.arange}(s) + 0.5}{s} 4. Coordinate Interpolation: Interpolate sample coordinates in the target view: \text{xy\sample} = \text{xy\min} + \text{sample\depth} \times (\text{xy\max} - \text{xy\min}) 5. Feature Sampling: Transpose sample coordinates so the 'view' dimension refers to the target view. Exclude the diagonal (self-view) using precomputed indices. Sample image features at xysample coordinates using bilinear gridsample with zero padding. The Epipolar Encoder is a two-view (or multi-view) neural module that resolves scale ambiguity in 3D reconstruction by aggregating cross-view features along epipolar lines. It solves the problem where camera poses are scaled by an arbitrary factor si, preventing the inference of metric depth from a single view. Unlike standard volume rendering which samples along a ray, this method samples features from a reference pixel and correlates them with features sampled along the corresponding epipolar line in a second view, augmented with positionally encoded depths. This allows the encoder to memorize the correct depth consistent with the scene's arbitrary scale, which is then used for subsequent Gaussian parameter prediction. An extension of the rectification mapping for perspective cameras and local spot lights. The \gamma coordinate is set to the angle the light ray makes with the direction from the light to the camera. This results in nonuniform sampling density along the camera ray, causing the ds/d\gamma term in the integral I(\gamma, \beta) to vary with both \gamma and \beta, unlike directional lights where it varies only with \beta. Light Scattering: Dramatically reduces computation time by minimizing expensive ray-marching steps. Rescaling epipolar lines reduces redundant computations on short lines and results in a more natural circular-shaped distribution of samples. Multi-View Aggregation: Enables cross-view feature aggregation without full 3D volume rendering during the encoding phase. Limitations: If the light source is close to the screen boundary, epipolar line lengths vary significantly, causing dense sampling on short lines and redundant computations if not rescaled. Epipolar sampling for light scattering was proposed by Engelhardt and Dachsbacher to optimize the rendering of light shafts by exploiting the smooth variation of inscattered light along epipolar lines. The application of epipolar sampling to multi-view feature aggregation was introduced in pixelSplat to resolve scale ambiguity in 3D Gaussian Splatting from sparse views. dcharatan/pixelsplat, https://github.com/dcharatan/pixelsplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) High-Performance Light Scattering Rendering, https://www.scribd.com/document/748135031/822368Yusov-Egor-Practical-Implementation-of-Light, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) A hierarchical volumetric shadow algorithm for single scattering, https://doi.org/10.1145/1866158.1866200, fetched 2026-11-03

name: Epipolar Encoder
body: The Epipolar Encoder is a two-view (or multi-view) neural module that resolves scale ambiguity in 3D reconstruction by aggregating cross-view features along epipolar lines. It solves the problem where camera poses are scaled by an arbitrary factor si, preventing the inference of metric depth from a single view. Unlike standard volume rendering which samples along a ray, this method samples features from a reference pixel and correlates them with features sampled along the corresponding epipolar line in a second view, augmented with positionally encoded depths. This allows the encoder to memorize the correct depth consistent with the scene's arbitrary scale, which is then used for subsequent Gaussian parameter prediction. The method operates on a pair of reference views, denoted as I (reference) and \tilde{I} (secondary), though it extends to N views. The core mechanism is epipolar cross-attention, which aligns features from I with potential correspondences in \tilde{I} using geometric depth constraints. Inputs: Reference image I and secondary image \tilde{I}. Camera poses for I and \tilde{I} (extrinsics E, \tilde{E} and intrinsics K, \tilde{K}). Feature volumes \mathbf{F} and \tilde{\mathbf{F}} of shape (H, W, C), where H, W are image dimensions and C is the feature dimension. These are produced by a per-image feature encoder applied to I and \tilde{I} separately. Outputs: Updated feature volume \mathbf{F}' of shape (H, W, C), where each pixel \mathbf{F}'[\mathbf{u}] contains aggregated cross-view information and encoded depth consistent with the scene scale. Feature Volumes: \mathbf{F}, \tilde{\mathbf{F}} \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times C}. Embedding Matrices: \mathbf{Q}, \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{V} \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times C{head}}. These are learnable linear projection matrices. Positional Encoding: \gamma: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^{C{enc}}. A standard positional encoding function (e.g., sine/cosine or learned) mapping a scalar depth to a vector. Per-Image Embeddings: \mathbf{e}i \in \mathbb{R}^{C{emb}} for each view i (used in multi-view variant). 1. Per-Image Encoding: Encode each input view into a feature volume. \mathbf{F} = \text{Encoder}(I), \quad \tilde{\mathbf{F}} = \text{Encoder}(\tilde{I}) 2. Epipolar Line Computation: For each pixel \mathbf{u} = (ux, uy) in I, compute the epipolar line \ell in \tilde{I} induced by \mathbf{u}'s camera ray. 3. Epipolar Sampling: Sample pixel coordinates \{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l\} along the epipolar line \ell in \tilde{I}. 4. Depth Triangulation: For each sample \tilde{\mathbf{u}}l, compute the distance \tilde{d}{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l} from the sample to I's camera origin by triangulating \mathbf{u} and \tilde{\mathbf{u}}l. 5. Feature Augmentation: For each sample \tilde{\mathbf{u}}l, create an augmented feature vector \mathbf{s}: \mathbf{s} = \tilde{\mathbf{F}}[\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l] \oplus \gamma(\tilde{d}{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l}) where \oplus denotes concatenation. 6. Attention Projection: Compute query, key, and value vectors for the epipolar attention: \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{Q} \cdot \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}], \quad \mathbf{k}l = \mathbf{K} \cdot \mathbf{s}, \quad \mathbf{v}l = \mathbf{V} \cdot \mathbf{s} 7. Epipolar Cross-Attention: Update the feature \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] using softmax attention over the epipolar samples: \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] \leftarrow \mathbf{F}[\mathbf{u}] + \text{Att}(\mathbf{q}, \{\mathbf{k}l\}, \{\mathbf{v}l\}) where \text{Att} denotes softmax attention and + denotes a skip connection. 8. Per-Image Self-Attention: Apply a self-attention layer to the entire feature volume \mathbf{F}: \mathbf{F} \leftarrow \mathbf{F} + \text{SelfAttention}(\mathbf{F}) Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F import math class PositionalEncoding(nn.Module): def init(self, dim): super().init() self.dim = dim def forward(self, d): # d: (B, N, L) scalar depths divterm = torch.exp(torch.arange(0, self.dim, 2, dtype=torch.float).log() -(math.log(10000.0) / self.dim)) pe = torch.zeroslike(d).unsqueeze(-1) pe[..., 0::2] = torch.sin(d.unsqueeze(-1) divterm) pe[..., 1::2] = torch.cos(d.unsqueeze(-1) divterm) return pe def getpixelcoordinates(H, W, device): y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(H, device=device), torch.arange(W, device=device), indexing='ij') return torch.stack([x.float(), y.float()], dim=-1) def computeepipolarlines(ucoords, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde): # ucoords: (B, N, 2) uhom = torch.cat([ucoords, torch.oneslike(ucoords[...,:1])], dim=-1) # (B, N, 3) RI, tI = poseI[:,:,:3,:3], poseI[:,:,:3, 3] Rt, tt = posetilde[:,:,:3,:3], posetilde[:,:,:3, 3] # Essential matrix E = [tt]x Rt RI^T def skew(v): x, y, z = v.unbind(dim=-1) return torch.stack([torch.zeroslike(x), -z, y, z, torch.zeroslike(x), -x, -y, x, torch.zeroslike(x)], dim=-1).view(v.shape[0], 3, 3) E = torch.bmm(skew(tt), torch.bmm(Rt, RI.transpose(1, 2))) # Fundamental matrix F = Ktilde^-T E K^-1 Fmat = torch.bmm(torch.inverse(Ktilde).transpose(1, 2), torch.bmm(E, torch.inverse(K))) # Epipolar lines ltilde = F uhom ltilde = torch.bmm(Fmat, uhom.transpose(1, 2)).transpose(1, 2) # (B, N, 3) return ltilde def samplelinepoints(l, H, W, L): # l: (B, N, 3) line coefficients (a, b, c) ys = torch.linspace(0, H, L, device=l.device).unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).expand(l.shape[0], l.shape[1], -1) xs = (-l[:,:, 1:2] ys - l[:,:, 2:3]) / (l[:,:, 0:1] + 1e-8) xs = torch.clamp(xs, 0, W - 1) ys = torch.clamp(ys, 0, H - 1) return torch.stack([xs, ys], dim=-1) # (B, N, L, 2) def triangulatedepths(ucoords, utildesamples, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde): # ucoords: (B, N, 2), utildesamples: (B, N, L, 2) # Unproject to rays in camera frames def unproject(u, K): uhom = torch.cat([u, torch.oneslike(u[...,:1])], dim=-1) rays = torch.bmm(uhom.unsqueeze(1), torch.inverse(K).unsqueeze(0)).squeeze(1) return F.normalize(rays, dim=-1) rI = unproject(ucoords, K) # (B, N, 3) rt = unproject(utildesamples, Ktilde) # (B, N, L, 3) # Transform to world frame RI, tI = poseI[:,:,:3,:3], poseI[:,:,:3, 3] Rt, tt = posetilde[:,:,:3,:3], posetilde[:,:,:3, 3] OI = -torch.bmm(RI.transpose(1, 2), tI.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2).unsqueeze(1).expand(-1, rI.shape[1], -1) DI = torch.bmm(RI.transpose(1, 2), rI.transpose(1, 2)).transpose(1, 2) Ot = -torch.bmm(Rt.transpose(1, 2), tt.unsqueeze(2)).squeeze(2).unsqueeze(1).unsqueeze(2).expand(-1, rt.shape[1], rt.shape[2], -1) Dt = torch.bmm(Rt.transpose(1, 2), rt.transpose(2, 3)).transpose(2, 3) # Triangulation: solve for depth dI along DI diff = Ot - OI.unsqueeze(2) # (B, N, L, 3) crossprod = torch.cross(DI.unsqueeze(2), Dt, dim=3) # (B, N, L, 3) crossprodsq = torch.sum(crossprod 2, dim=3, keepdim=True) + 1e-8 numerator = torch.sum(diff crossprod, dim=3, keepdim=True) depths = numerator.squeeze(3) / crossprodsq.squeeze(3) # (B, N, L) return depths def samplefeaturesatcoords(F, coords, H, W): # F: (B, H, W, C), coords: (B, N, L, 2) in [0, W]x[0, H] Fperm = F.permute(0, 3, 1, 2) # (B, C, H, W) x = coords[..., 0] / (W - 1) 2 - 1 y = coords[..., 1] / (H - 1) 2 - 1 grid = torch.stack([x, y], dim=-1) # (B, N, L, 2) B, N, L, = coords.shape sampled = F.gridsample(Fperm.view(BN, Fperm.shape[1], H, W), grid.view(BN, L, 1, 2), aligncorners=True) # (BN, C, L, 1) return sampled.view(B, N, L, F.shape[-1]) class EpipolarEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self, featuredim, headdim=64, numheads=8, numsamples=64): super().init() self.numsamples = numsamples self.numheads = numheads self.headdim = headdim self.qproj = nn.Linear(featuredim, numheads headdim) self.kproj = nn.Linear(featuredim + 64, numheads headdim) self.vproj = nn.Linear(featuredim + 64, numheads headdim) self.selfattn = nn.MultiheadAttention(featuredim, numheads, batchfirst=True) self.posenc = PositionalEncoding(64) def forward(self, F, Ftilde, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde, H, W): B, H, W, C = F.shape ucoords = getpixelcoordinates(H, W, F.device) ucoordsflat = ucoords.view(1, 1, HW, 2).expand(B, -1, -1, -1) ltilde = computeepipolarlines(ucoordsflat, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde) utildesamples = samplelinepoints(ltilde, H, W, self.numsamples) depths = triangulatedepths(ucoordsflat, utildesamples, poseI, posetilde, K, Ktilde) Ftildesamples = samplefeaturesatcoords(Ftilde, utildesamples, H, W) depthenc = self.posenc(depths) s = torch.cat([Ftildesamples, depthenc], dim=-1) q = self.qproj(F.view(B, -1, C)) k = self.kproj(s) v = self.vproj(s) q = q.view(B, HW, self.numheads, self.headdim).transpose(1, 2) k = k.view(B, HW, self.numsamples, self.numheads, self.headdim).transpose(1, 3).transpose(2, 3) v = v.view(B, HW, self.numsamples, self.numheads, self.headdim).transpose(1, 3).transpose(2, 3) attnweights = F.softmax(torch.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / math.sqrt(self.headdim), dim=-1) attnoutput = torch.matmul(attnweights, v) attnoutput = attnoutput.transpose(1, 2).view(B, HW, self.numheads self.headdim) Fflat = F.view(B, -1, C) Fupdatedflat = Fflat + attnoutput Fupdated = Fupdatedflat.view(B, H, W, C) Fselfinput = Fupdated.view(B, HW, C) Fselfout, = self.selfattn(Fselfinput, Fselfinput, Fselfinput) Ffinal = Fupdated + Fselfout Ffinal = Ffinal.view(B, H, W, C) return Ffinal Number of samples (L): Typically 64. Feature dimension (C): Depends on the backbone (e.g., 256, 512). Head dimension (C{head}): Typically 64. Positional Encoding: Standard sine/cosine or learned. Missing Correspondences: Pixels in I that have no match in \tilde{I} (occlusions, boundaries) will have no valid epipolar samples. The per-image self-attention layer propagates depth estimates from neighboring pixels to these regions. Triangulation Instability: If the rays from I and \tilde{I} are nearly parallel, the triangulation depth \tilde{d}{\tilde{\mathbf{u}}l} becomes noisy. This is mitigated by the attention mechanism, which learns to down-weight unreliable samples. Scale Ambiguity: Without the positional encoding of depth, the encoder cannot resolve the arbitrary scale factor si. The depth augmentation is critical. A multi-view encoder component that resolves scale ambiguity by finding cross-view pixel correspondences and associating them with positionally encoded depth values, allowing the inference of the per-scene scale factor si. It compares features belonging to a ray's corresponding pixel on one view with features sampled along the epipolar line on the other view. Epipolar samples are augmented with their positionally-encoded depths along the ray. Recorded depths are later used for depth prediction. Extends the epipolar encoder from pairs to an arbitrary number of reference views by taking epipolar samples from any number of images and using their union. For a given pixel coordinate, epipolar samples are taken from any number of images. The union of these samples is used in place of a single epipolar line's samples. A learnable per-image embedding is added to each sampled feature to allow the epipolar transformer to distinguish between samples taken from different views. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot L \cdot C^2) per pixel for the cross-attention, where N is the number of pixels, L is the number of epipolar samples, and C is the feature dimension. The self-attention layer adds O(N^2 \cdot C) if applied globally, but is typically applied per-image with linear complexity or reduced heads. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot L \cdot C) to store the epipolar samples and intermediate features. Performance: In 3-view settings, PSNR improves from 26.09 to 28.31 on the Real Estate 10k dataset, with SSIM improving from 0.863 to 0.908. Strengths: Resolves scale ambiguity without explicit depth supervision; leverages geometric constraints for robust feature aggregation. Limitations: Requires accurate camera poses; performance degrades if epipolar geometry is incorrect; self-attention may blur details in textureless regions. The Epipolar Encoder was introduced in "PixelSplat: 3D Gaussian Splats from Image Pairs for Scalable Generalizable 3D Reconstruction" (CVPR 2024). It addresses the limitation of diffusion models that rescale 3D scenes according to heuristics on depth statistics. By using an epipolar transformer, the method infers the scene scale directly from cross-view correspondences. It builds on the concept of epipolar attention [16] and is used in conjunction with 3D Gaussian Splatting [19] for novel view synthesis. name: Multi-View Epipolar Encoder
head: Multi-View Epipolar Extension
body: The Multi-View Epipolar Encoder extends the standard epipolar encoder from pairs of images to an arbitrary number of reference views. It solves the problem of limited geometric context in two-view reconstruction by aggregating epipolar samples from multiple input images. It differs from its parent, the Epipolar Encoder, by replacing the single epipolar line's samples with the union of samples from N views and introducing view-specific embeddings to disambiguate the source of each sample. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A target pixel coordinate (u, v), N reference images with known camera poses, and the corresponding epipolar geometry. Output: A feature tensor representing the aggregated epipolar context for the target pixel, ready for the epipolar transformer. Data Structures: Learnable Per-Image Embedding: A vector ei \in \mathbb{R}^d for each reference image i \in \{1, \dots, N\}. These are trainable parameters shared across all pixels. Sampled Features: For each reference image i, a set of features Fi sampled along the epipolar line corresponding to (u, v). Steps: 1. Epipolar Sampling: For each reference image i \in \{1, \dots, N\}, compute the epipolar line in image i corresponding to the target pixel (u, v) in the reference view. Sample features Fi along this line using the same sampling strategy as the base Epipolar Encoder. 2. View Embedding Addition: For each sampled feature f \in Fi, add the learnable per-image embedding ei to f. This allows the subsequent transformer to distinguish which reference image a sample originated from. f'i = fi + ei 3. Union Aggregation: Collect all modified features from all N images into a single set. \mathcal{F}{union} = \bigcup{i=1}^{N} F'i 4. Transformer Input: Pass \mathcal{F}{union} as the input sequence to the epipolar transformer. The transformer processes these samples to produce the final encoded representation. Parameters: N: Number of reference views. The method supports arbitrary N, though the source demonstrates N=3. Learning Rate: The source notes a reduction to 1 \times 10^{-4} from the default 3 \times 10^{-4} to prevent training collapse, but this is a training hyperparameter, not a method parameter. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: The number of samples grows linearly with N. If the sampling density is high, memory and compute requirements increase significantly. Ambiguity: Without the learnable embeddings, the transformer cannot distinguish between samples from different views, leading to potential confusion in feature aggregation. The Plane Sweep Volume (PSV) is a 5D tensor representation that encodes the epipolar geometry between a set of input views and a target view by projecting input images onto a series of depth planes. It differs from standard volume representations by structuring data such that adjacent camera rays have adjacent encodings, allowing local operators to process epipolar lines efficiently. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of reference views N and the number of samples per view. Memory Complexity: Linear in N and the number of samples. Performance: The 3-view variant achieves higher PSNR (28.31 vs 26.09) and SSIM (0.908 vs 0.863) on the Real Estate 10k dataset compared to the 2-view baseline. Strengths: Improved reconstruction quality with additional views; scalable to arbitrary numbers of views. Limitations: Increased computational cost with more views; potential for training instability if learning rate is not adjusted. The Multi-View Epipolar Encoder was introduced in the PixelSplat paper (2024) as an extension to the original two-view epipolar encoder. It was developed to leverage more reference views for scalable generalizable 3D reconstruction from images. name: Plane Sweep Volume (PSV)
head: Plane Sweep Volume (PSV) Averaging
body: The Plane Sweep Volume (PSV) is a 5D tensor representation that encodes the epipolar geometry between a set of input views and a target view by projecting input images onto a series of depth planes. It differs from standard volume representations by structuring data such that adjacent camera rays have adjacent encodings, allowing local operators to process epipolar lines efficiently. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of V input images Iv with known camera intrinsics Kv and extrinsics (Rv, tv) relative to a target view. The target view has intrinsics K and normal n. A set of D depth planes is defined parallel to the target image plane, specified by distances \{ad\}{d=1}^D from the target camera center. Output: A 5D tensor X \in \mathbb{R}^{D \times V \times 3 \times H \times W}, where dimensions correspond to depth, view, color channels, height, and width. Data Structures The PSV tensor X is indexed as X{d,v,c,h,w}. d \in \{1, \dots, D\}: Depth plane index. v \in \{1, \dots, V\}: Input view index. c \in \{1, 2, 3\}: Color channel. h, w: Pixel coordinates in the target image plane. Steps 1. Define Depth Planes: Establish D planes parallel to the target image plane with normal n. The distance ad of each plane from the target camera center is chosen to cover the scene's depth range. 2. Compute Homographies: For each input view v and depth plane d, compute the homography matrix H{dv} that maps points from the target image plane to the input view plane at depth ad. Assuming the world origin is at the target camera center (R = I, t = 0), the homography is: H{dv} = Kv (Rv - tv n^T) K^{-1} where Kv, K are intrinsic matrices, and Rv, tv are the rotation and translation of view v relative to the target. 3. Project Images: Apply the homography H{dv} to each input image Iv to generate a projected image X{dv} for each depth plane. This involves warping Iv according to H{dv}. 4. Construct Tensor: Assemble the projected images into the 5D tensor X. The slice r{hw} for a target pixel (h,w) contains pixels sampled along the epipolar lines in all input views at all depths. Specifically: r{hw} = \left\{ \{ X{dv,c,h,w} \}{c=1}^3 \right\}{d=1}^D \right\}{v=1}^V This structure ensures that operations along the depth dimension correspond to operations along individual epipolar lines, and operations along the view dimension correspond to operations between corresponding epipolar lines. Averaging Variants Mean PSV: Average the tensor X over the view dimension V to obtain a tensor of shape \mathbb{R}^{D \times 3 \times H \times W}. This highlights epipolar geometry: parts of objects lying on a specific depth plane appear in focus, while others appear blurry. Blurry Estimate: Average X over both view and depth dimensions to produce a blurry estimate of the target view. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Depth Coverage: The distances \{ad\} must be chosen such that the scene of interest is adequately covered. Insufficient depth range leads to missing data. Homography Assumption: The homography formula assumes planar projection or infinitesimal depth variation relative to the camera baseline. For large depth variations within a single plane, perspective distortion may occur. Memory: The 5D structure requires significant memory, scaling as O(D \cdot V \cdot H \cdot W). Memory Complexity: O(D \cdot V \cdot H \cdot W). The tensor size grows linearly with the number of depth planes, views, and image resolution. Strengths: Encodes epipolar geometry explicitly, allowing efficient local processing via convolutions. Adjacent rays have adjacent encodings, facilitating the use of simple local operators. Limitations: High memory consumption for large D and V. Requires accurate camera calibration and known depth bounds. When to Use: Novel view synthesis where generalizable models are needed, and epipolar consistency is important. Particularly effective when combined with convolutional architectures like ConvGLR. The Plane Sweep Volume was introduced in the context of generalizable novel view synthesis, specifically in the Global Latent Neural Rendering framework. The concept of averaging the PSV to highlight depth planes is closely related to the original plane sweep algorithm by Collins for depth estimation. The PSV generalizes the 4D tensor (single view) to a 5D tensor (multiple views) to leverage multi-view epipolar geometry. name: Warp-based Sampling
head: 1D Warp Marching, 2D Warp Marching, DBShuffle, SBShuffle, Warp Marching
body: Warp-based Sampling is a GPU optimization strategy for direct volume ray casting that improves texture cache performance by reorganizing thread warps to align sampling directions with the volume's memory strides. Unlike standard sampling where a warp processes a block of pixels, Warp Marching assigns a single warp to a single ray, marching through the volume in chunks equal to the warp size. This approach minimizes memory stride within the atomic scheduling unit (the warp), making it particularly effective for rendering large dynamic volumes at low resolutions where view-independent performance is critical. Inputs and Outputs Input: 3D volume texture (density field), transfer function (density to RGBA), viewing parameters (camera position, direction, projection). Output: Final pixel color (RGBA) for each frame. Data Structures Thread Organization: Threads are grouped into warps of 32 consecutive threads, which form the atomic scheduling unit in CUDA. Shared Memory: Used for intermediate color accumulation. SBShuffle (Single Buffer Shared Warp Marching): Requires 9 float4 variables per warp (8 for thread-local samples + 1 for intermediate reduction result). DBShuffle (Double Buffer Shared Warp Marching): Uses a double-buffering accumulation scheme to enhance GPU resource utilization. Binary Mask: Each thread maintains a single binary bit indicating if its current sample has non-zero alpha. Warp Shapes and Orientations A warp of 32 threads can be organized into three shapes: 32 \times 1, 16 \times 2, and 8 \times 4. 1D Warp Marching: Uses the 32 \times 1 shape. The warp takes 32 samples along the depth (Z) direction and 1 sample along the horizontal (X) direction, yielding orientation zx. 2D Warp Marching: Uses 16 \times 2 or 8 \times 4 shapes. Orientation Naming: Major direction axis followed by minor direction axis (e.g., zx, xz). Generating Orientations: zx and xz are generated by changing the marching step (shuffling width) in the depth direction. For a warp size of 32: marching 8 samples in depth creates zx orientation (8 depth, 4 horizontal). Marching 4 samples in depth creates xz orientation (8 horizontal, 4 depth). Standard sampling is a special case of Warp Marching with a marching step of 1 in depth, resulting in xy orientation (16 horizontal, 2 vertical for a 16 \times 16 block). Row-Major vs. Column-Major: Default is row-major sampling. Changing thread-pixel mapping allows column-major sampling, generating the remaining three orientations. Optimal Alignment: The major sampling direction should always be aligned with the X dimension of the volume because the X dimension has the smallest memory stride in 3D textures. Algorithm Steps 1. Warp Initialization: Assign one warp to one ray. Initialize shared memory buffers. 2. Marching Loop: a. Sample: Each thread in the warp samples the volume along the ray. The step size corresponds to the warp shape dimensions. b. Transfer Function: Map density to RGBA color. c. Pre-integration (Optional): If using pre-integrated rendering, each thread takes two density values (front and back of a slab) and shuffles the sample to its neighbor using shfldown(). d. Binary Masking: Set binary bit to 1 if alpha > 0, else 0. e. Warp Voting: Use ballot() to determine if any thread in the warp has non-zero alpha. f. Skip Check: If ballot() returns 0, skip blending for this step. g. Reduction Blending: If not skipped, perform front-to-back alpha blending in a reduction manner within the warp, leveraging the associative property of blending. h. Accumulation: Copy the final reduction result to a "safe" place (shared memory or extra memory unit) and accumulate as rays march further. 3. Final Output: After marching through the volume, write the accumulated color to the frame buffer. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from typing import List, Tuple class Float4: def init(self, r: float, g: float, b: float, a: float): self.r, self.g, self.b, self.a = r, g, b, a def blendrgba(c1: Float4, c2: Float4) -> Float4: """Front-to-back alpha blending: c1 + c2 (1 - c1.a)""" return Float4( c1.r + c2.r (1.0 - c1.a), c1.g + c2.g (1.0 - c1.a), c1.b + c2.b (1.0 - c1.a), c1.a + c2.a (1.0 - c1.a)) def samplevolume(rayorigin: Tuple[float, float, float], raydirection: Tuple[float, float, float], t: float, volume: List) -> float: """Returns scalar density at parameter t along the ray.""" idx = int(t) % len(volume) return volume[idx] def transferfunction(density: float) -> Float4: """Maps scalar density to Float4 RGBA.""" return Float4(density, density, density, density) def warpballot(predicate: bool, laneid: int, warpsize: int) -> int: """Simulates ballot(): returns bitmask of active threads in the warp.""" mask = 0 for i in range(warpsize): if predicate: mask |= (1 << i) return mask def warpshfldown(value: Float4, offset: int, laneid: int, warpsize: int, buffer: List[Float4]) -> Float4: """Simulates shfldown(): returns value from thread (laneid + offset).""" neighborid = laneid + offset if neighborid < warpsize: return buffer[neighborid] return Float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def warpmarchingkernel(rayorigin: Tuple[float, float, float], raydirection: Tuple[float, float, float], raylength: float, volume: List, transferfn, warpsize: int = 32) -> Float4: """ Simulates a single warp processing one ray using Warp Marching. laneid is the thread's index within the warp (0..31). """ laneid = 0 # Each thread executes this with a unique laneid sharedaccumulators = [Float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0)] 9 # SBShuffle layout stepsize = raylength / warpsize rayt = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = Float4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) while rayt < raylength: # 1. Sample and Transfer (parallel across lanes) samplecolors = [transferfn(samplevolume(rayorigin, raydirection, rayt + i stepsize, volume)) for i in range(warpsize)] hasalpha = [c.a > 0.0 for c in samplecolors] # 2. Warp Voting warpstate = warpballot(hasalpha[laneid], laneid, warpsize) if warpstate != 0: # 3. Reduction Blending localcolor = samplecolors[laneid] for offset in [16, 8, 4, 2, 1]: neighborcolor = warpshfldown(localcolor, offset, laneid, warpsize, samplecolors) if hasalpha[laneid]: localcolor = blendrgba(localcolor, neighborcolor) # 4. Accumulate to shared memory if laneid == 0: sharedaccumulators[0] = localcolor # 5. Read accumulated and blend with current step result prevaccum = sharedaccumulators[0] finalwarpcolor = blendrgba(prevaccum, localcolor) if laneid == 0: sharedaccumulators[0] = finalwarpcolor # 6. Advance ray rayt += stepsize return sharedaccumulators[0] Parameters Warp Size: 32 consecutive threads. Warp Shapes: 32 \times 1 (1D), 16 \times 2 and 8 \times 4 (2D). Marching Step: Determines orientation. E.g., 8 samples depth for zx, 4 samples depth for xz. Dataset Examples: vhfhead (spacing 1:1:1), vhmbody (spacing 1:1:3). Resolution: 1024 × 1024. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Viewing Direction: Performance varies significantly with viewing direction. Standard sampling is best when facing the XY plane, but Warp Marching is superior when facing the ZY plane (up to 4x speedup). Cache Coherence: If the major sampling direction is not aligned with the volume's X dimension, texture cache hit rates drop. Pre-integration: Requires two density values per thread (front and back of slab) and specific shuffling logic (shfldown). Dynamic Warp Marching is a GPU sampling strategy for direct volume ray casting that optimizes texture cache performance by dynamically aligning the sampling direction of a thread warp with the volume's X-dimension, which has the minimum memory stride. It integrates the Warp Marching concept with a dynamic viewing-direction adjustment, overcoming the limitation of the original Dynamic approach which could only sample along horizontal or vertical directions. Performance: Warp Marching is view-independent and outperforms existing empty space skipping techniques in scenarios requiring rendering of large dynamic volumes in low resolution images. Speedup: When facing the ZY plane, Warp Marching achieves more than 4 times the speedup of the Standard method. When facing the XY plane, Standard method achieves higher frame rates, but Warp Marching is not extremely poor. DBShuffle vs SBShuffle: DBShuffle performs better than SBShuffle regardless of viewing direction for both tested datasets. Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the number of samples per ray, but with reduced memory latency due to cache optimization. Memory complexity is low, relying on shared memory for intermediate results. Strengths: High texture cache hit rates, stable frame rates during volume exploration, effective for dynamic volumes. Limitations: May underperform Standard sampling when viewing direction aligns with the volume's natural memory stride (e.g., XY plane). Warp-based Sampling was introduced to address texture cache performance issues in GPU-based volume rendering. It builds on the concept of breaking a ray into segments and compositing them, as described by Ma et al. (1993). The method leverages warp-level GPU operations (voting and shuffling) introduced in the NVIDIA Kepler architecture. It is designed to replace the Standard sampling strategy in texture-based volume rendering algorithms. name: Dynamic Warp Marching
head: 3D Warp Marching, Dynamic approach
body: Dynamic Warp Marching is a GPU sampling strategy for direct volume ray casting that optimizes texture cache performance by dynamically aligning the sampling direction of a thread warp with the volume's X-dimension, which has the minimum memory stride. It integrates the Warp Marching concept with a dynamic viewing-direction adjustment, overcoming the limitation of the original Dynamic approach which could only sample along horizontal or vertical directions. Inputs: Volume data texture. Viewing direction (defined by the camera orientation relative to the volume axes). Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Outputs: Sampled voxel values along the ray path. Composited color and opacity for the pixel. Data Structures: Warp Shape: 32 \times 1. A single warp (32 threads) is responsible for one ray, with all 32 threads taking samples along the X-dimension of the volume. Thread Block Shape: Not given in the sources for the Dynamic method. Steps: 1. Determine Viewing Direction: Identify the current viewing direction relative to the volume axes (e.g., XY, YZ, ZX, etc.). 2. Adjust Sampling Direction: Unlike the Static method which aligns the major sampling direction with the horizontal direction of the view, the Dynamic method adjusts the major direction of the warp to always be parallel to the X-dimension of the volume. 3. Sample Along X: All 32 threads in the warp take samples along the X-dimension of the volume. This is done because the X-dimension has the minimum memory stride, ensuring best texture cache performance. 4. Integrate Warp Marching: The method integrates Warp Marching to allow sampling along any direction, overcoming the limitation of Standard sampling which only supports horizontal or vertical directions. Formulas: Number of voxels covered along a dimension = (distance between samples along that dimension) × (number of samples taken along that dimension). Let Vd be the voxels covered, Ds be the sampling distance, and Ns be the number of samples. Then Vd = Ds \times Ns. Parameters: Warp shape: 32 \times 1. Block shape: Not given in the sources. Sampling distance: 0.5 voxel length between samples along rays. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Viewing Direction XY or XZ: When the view is facing XY or XZ, the major warp sampling direction of the Static method is already aligned with the X-dimension of the volume. Therefore, the performance of the Static and Dynamic approaches is similar. Viewing Direction YX: The Dynamic approach is better than the Static approach when facing YX. Ray Distance/Volume Image Ratio: The performance difference between Dynamic and Static approaches is notable in datasets with larger ray distances (e.g., vhmbody) but marginal in datasets with smaller ray distances (e.g., vhfhead). This is due to different volume image ratios. Zero X-direction component: If the ray direction's X-component is zero, stepping along X requires a fallback to another axis or a small epsilon to avoid division by zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dynamicwarpmarching(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, volumedims): # Initialize compositing state color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] opacity = 0.0 alphacontribution = 0.0 # Step size along X dimension (0.5 voxel length per evidence) stepx = 0.5 dx = raydirection[0] dy = raydirection[1] dz = raydirection[2] # Handle zero X-component to avoid division by zero if abs(dx) < 1e-6: dx = 1e-6 # Calculate step in t and corresponding Y/Z increments stept = stepx / dx stepy = dy stept stepz = dz stept # Current position posx = rayorigin[0] posy = rayorigin[1] posz = rayorigin[2] # Iterate through 32 samples (warp size) for i in range(32): # Check volume boundaries if not (0 <= posx < volumedims[0] and 0 <= posy < volumedims[1] and 0 <= posz < volumedims[2]): break # Sample voxel value (standard texture fetch operation) voxel = volumetexture.sample(posx, posy, posz) # Standard front-to-back compositing alphacontribution = voxel (1.0 - opacity) color[0] += voxel[0] alphacontribution color[1] += voxel[1] alphacontribution color[2] += voxel[2] alphacontribution opacity += alphacontribution # Early ray termination if opacity >= 0.95: break # Advance position along X dimension posx += stepx posy += stepy posz += stepz return color, opacity Performance: Significant performance improvements when the view is facing YZ, ZX, or ZY. When facing XY or XZ, performance is similar to the Static method. When facing YX, the Dynamic approach is better than the Static approach. Scaling: Performance difference is notable in datasets with larger ray distances (e.g., vhmbody) but marginal in datasets with smaller ray distances (e.g., vhfhead). Strengths: Optimizes texture cache performance by aligning sampling with the X-dimension, which has the minimum memory stride. Allows sampling along any direction by integrating Warp Marching. Limitations: Performance gain is dependent on the viewing direction and dataset characteristics (ray distance/volume image ratio). The Dynamic approach was introduced by Sugimoto et al. (2014) to adjust sampling direction according to viewing direction for best texture cache performance. The method integrates Warp Marching to overcome the limitation of the original Dynamic approach, which could only sample along horizontal or vertical directions due to the limitation of Standard sampling. A cache-friendly sampling strategy for texture-based volume rendering on GPU, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.visinf.2017.08.001, fetched 2026-10-26 Uses Standard sampling with a fixed thread block shape (16 \times 16) and aligns the major sampling direction with the horizontal direction of the view. Choose when the viewing direction is already aligned with the X-dimension (XY or XZ views) for similar performance to Dynamic. Static Warp Marching Only supports horizontal or vertical sampling directions. Choose when dynamic adjustment is not needed or when the viewing direction is fixed and favorable. Standard Sampling

name: Hierarchical Sampling
head: Coarse and Refined Stage Sampling, Importance Sampling for NeRF, Multi-Stage Voxel Sampling, Two-Stage Sampling
body: Hierarchical sampling is a two-stage strategy for volume rendering that improves image quality by concentrating samples in regions of high geometric or color complexity, addressing the bottleneck of point sampling in neural radiance fields. It sets itself apart from uniform sampling by using a coarse network to estimate density and guide importance sampling for a fine network. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, near/far bounds [tn, tf], number of coarse samples N{coarse}, number of fine samples N{fine}, coarse neural network fc, fine neural network ff. Outputs: Rendered color \hat{C}(\mathbf{r}) and depth/transmittance for the ray \mathbf{r}. Data Structures: Sample Depths: Arrays of size N{coarse} and N{fine} storing scalar distances t along the ray. Density/Color: Tensors of shape (N, 4) or (N, 3) storing volume density \sigma and color \mathbf{c} for each sample point. CDF: Cumulative distribution array of size N{coarse}, normalized to [0, 1]. Parameters: N{coarse}: Number of coarse samples. Typical value: 64. N{fine}: Number of fine samples. Typical value: 64 or 128. Steps: 1. Coarse Sampling: Uniformly sample N{coarse} points along the ray interval [tn, tf]. 2. Coarse Pass: Evaluate the coarse network fc at each sample to predict volume density \sigmac and color \mathbf{c}c. 3. Weight Computation: Compute the weight wi for each coarse sample, representing its expected color contribution: wi = Tc(t{c,i}) \left( 1 - \exp\left(- \sigmac(t{c,i}) \Delta t{c,i}\right) \right) where Tc(t{c,i}) = \exp\left(-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmac(t{c,j}) \Delta t{c,j}\right) is the transmittance up to sample i, and \Delta t{c,i} = t{c,i+1} - t{c,i} is the interval length. 4. CDF Construction: Construct the cumulative distribution function (CDF) from the weights wi. 5. Fine Sampling (Importance Sampling): Sample N{fine} points from the CDF. 6. Fine Pass: Evaluate the fine network ff at each fine sample to predict density \sigmaf and color \mathbf{c}f. 7. Rendering: Combine coarse and fine samples (typically by concatenating and sorting them by depth) and perform volume rendering integration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def hierarchicalsample(rayorigins, raydirections, tnear, tfar, ncoarse, nfine, coarsenet, finenet): """ Performs hierarchical sampling for a batch of rays. Args: rayorigins: (B, 3) Tensor of ray origins. raydirections: (B, 3) Tensor of ray directions (normalized). tnear: (B,) Tensor of near bounds. tfar: (B,) Tensor of far bounds. ncoarse: int, number of coarse samples. nfine: int, number of fine samples. coarsenet: Module, coarse neural network. finenet: Module, fine neural network. Returns: tcoarse: (B, ncoarse) Tensor of coarse sample depths. sigmacoarse: (B, ncoarse, 1) Tensor of coarse densities. ccoarse: (B, ncoarse, 3) Tensor of coarse colors. tfine: (B, nfine) Tensor of fine sample depths. sigmafine: (B, nfine, 1) Tensor of fine densities. cfine: (B, nfine, 3) Tensor of fine colors. """ B = rayorigins.shape[0] # 1. Coarse Sampling: Uniform stratified sampling ucoarse = torch.linspace(0, 1, ncoarse, device=rayorigins.device).unsqueeze(0) # (1, ncoarse) noise = torch.rand(B, ncoarse, device=rayorigins.device) ucoarse = ucoarse + noise / ncoarse ucoarse = torch.clamp(ucoarse, 0, 1) tcoarse = tnear.unsqueeze(1) + ucoarse (tfar.unsqueeze(1) - tnear.unsqueeze(1)) # (B, ncoarse) # Get 3D points (positional encoding applied internally by network) ptscoarse = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + tcoarse.unsqueeze(2) raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # (B, ncoarse, 3) # 2. Coarse Pass ptscoarseflat = ptscoarse.view(-1, 3) sigmacoarseflat, ccoarseflat = coarsenet(ptscoarseflat) sigmacoarse = sigmacoarseflat.view(B, ncoarse, 1) # (B, ncoarse, 1) ccoarse = ccoarseflat.view(B, ncoarse, 3) # (B, ncoarse, 3) # 3. Weight Computation # Calculate intervals explicitly to handle boundaries correctly dtcoarse = torch.zeroslike(tcoarse) dtcoarse[:, 0] = tcoarse[:, 0] - tnear.unsqueeze(1) dtcoarse[:, 1:-1] = tcoarse[:, 1:] - tcoarse[:,:-1] dtcoarse[:, -1] = tfar.unsqueeze(1) - tcoarse[:, -1] # Transmittance Ti = exp(-sum{j<i} sigmaj dtj) alphadtcoarse = sigmacoarse.squeeze(2) dtcoarse # (B, ncoarse) cumalphacoarse = torch.cumsum(alphadtcoarse, dim=1) # (B, ncoarse) Tcoarse = torch.exp(-torch.cat([torch.zeros(B, 1, device=tcoarse.device), cumalphacoarse[:,:-1]], dim=1)) # (B, ncoarse) # Weight wi = Ti (1 - exp(-sigmai dti)) sigmasqueezed = sigmacoarse.squeeze(2) weightscoarse = Tcoarse (1 - torch.exp(-sigmasqueezed dtcoarse)) # (B, ncoarse) # 4. CDF Construction weightssum = weightscoarse.sum(dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-10 # (B, 1) weightsnorm = weightscoarse / weightssum # (B, ncoarse) cdfcoarse = torch.cumsum(weightsnorm, dim=1) # (B, ncoarse) # 5. Fine Sampling: Inverse CDF sampling ufine = torch.rand(B, nfine, device=rayorigins.device) # (B, nfine) # Find indices in CDF: cdf[i-1] < u <= cdf[i] indices = torch.searchsorted(cdfcoarse, ufine, right=True) # (B, nfine) indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, ncoarse - 1) # Interpolate t values lowerindices = indices - 1 lowerindices = torch.clamp(lowerindices, 0, ncoarse - 1) cdflower = torch.gather(cdfcoarse, 1, lowerindices) # (B, nfine) cdfupper = torch.gather(cdfcoarse, 1, indices) # (B, nfine) tlower = torch.gather(tcoarse, 1, lowerindices) # (B, nfine) tupper = torch.gather(tcoarse, 1, indices) # (B, nfine) # Linear interpolation denom = cdfupper - cdflower + 1e-10 tfine = tlower + (tupper - tlower) (ufine - cdflower) / denom # (B, nfine) # Get 3D points for fine samples ptsfine = rayorigins.unsqueeze(1) + tfine.unsqueeze(2) raydirections.unsqueeze(1) # (B, nfine, 3) # 6. Fine Pass ptsfineflat = ptsfine.view(-1, 3) sigmafineflat, cfineflat = finenet(ptsfineflat) sigmafine = sigmafineflat.view(B, nfine, 1) # (B, nfine, 1) cfine = cfineflat.view(B, nfine, 3) # (B, nfine, 3) return tcoarse, sigmacoarse, ccoarse, tfine, sigmafine, cfine Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Flow: The sampling step (inverse CDF lookup) is non-differentiable with respect to the coarse model's output. Degenerate CDF: If all coarse weights are zero (e.g., empty space), the CDF is flat. Boundary Conditions: The last interval \Delta t for the coarse samples must be handled carefully, as there is no subsequent sample. Controls rendering density using a hierarchy of sampled data to maintain constant frame rates, generating coarse density estimates on-the-fly via convolution rather than a separate pre-allocated grid. Restricts fine network evaluation to regions of significant geometric presence using a fixed density threshold, skipping empty space entirely. Improves sampling efficiency by learning a continuous density distribution (mixture of truncated Gaussians) within each ray interval, replacing discrete weight normalization with parametric Gaussian estimation. Time Complexity: O(N{coarse} + N{fine}) network evaluations per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N{coarse} + N{fine}) per ray for storing sample positions, densities, and colors. Measured Performance: In NeRF-like settings, using N{coarse}=64 and N{fine}=64-128 provides a significant quality improvement over uniform sampling with similar total sample counts, or allows for higher quality with the same computational budget. Strengths: Efficiently allocates samples to complex regions, reducing noise and aliasing in detailed areas while maintaining speed in smooth regions. Limitations: Requires two network passes (coarse and fine), increasing latency per ray, and the quality of the fine sampling is dependent on the accuracy of the coarse network's density predictions. When to Use: When rendering scenes with high-frequency details or varying opacity, and computational resources allow for two network evaluations per ray. When Not to Use: In real-time applications with strict latency constraints where a single network pass is required, or in scenes with uniform density where uniform sampling is sufficient. Hierarchical sampling was introduced as a core component of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) by Mildenhall et al. in 2020. It was designed to address the issue that uniform sampling along rays is inefficient for scenes with complex geometry, as it wastes samples in empty space and under-samples detailed regions. The method builds on the idea of importance sampling, using a coarse estimate of the scene's density to guide the placement of finer samples. It has since become a standard technique in neural volume rendering and is used in many subsequent works, including DDNeRF and Hu et al. Density-based Sampling. name: Hierarchical Density Adaptation
head: On-the-fly coarse sampling, Point Selection Criteria
body: Hierarchical Density Adaptation is a sampling strategy for volume rendering that controls rendering density using a hierarchy of sampled data to maintain constant frame rates. It serves as an alternative to opacity-based adaptive sampling, trading image smoothness for rendering speed by controlling the total number of rendered primitives per frame. It distinguishes itself from standard hierarchical sampling by generating the coarse density estimate on-the-fly from the dense grid via convolution, rather than relying on a separate, pre-allocated coarse network or grid. The method integrates with a hierarchical sampling framework where a coarse estimate predicts rough density, and a fine estimate predicts precise color using additional samples placed where coarse density was high [Parent]. The core mechanism generates the coarse density estimate on-the-fly to avoid memory overhead and ensure surface regions are not skipped. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Dense density grid G\sigma, ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d}, maximum ray distance D{\text{max}}, number of coarse samples Nc, number of fine samples Nf. Outputs: Pixel color \hat{C}. Data Structures: Dense Density Grid (G\sigma): A 3D grid storing volume density \sigma. In EgoNeRF, this is a balanced spherical feature grid. Convolution Kernel (K): A non-learnable average pooling kernel used to smooth the dense grid. Steps: 1. Obtain Coarse Density Estimate: Apply a non-learnable convolution kernel K (average pooling) to the dense density grid G\sigma to create a coarser estimate on the fly. This prevents skipping important surface regions that might occur if the dense grid were sampled directly at coarse intervals. \sigma(\mathbf{x}{\text{coarse}}) = \mathcal{T}(K G\sigma, \mathbf{x}{\text{coarse}}) where \mathcal{T} denotes trilinear interpolation. 2. Sample Coarse Points: Sample Nc points along the ray. In standard implementations, these are distributed uniformly. However, in variants with exponentially increasing grid resolution (e.g., spherical grids), they are distributed exponentially. 3. Calculate Importance Sampling Weights: Compute weights for the coarse samples based on their contribution to the ray integral. The weight wi for the i-th coarse sample is: wi = \taui (1 - e^{-\sigmai \deltai}) where: \sigmai is the coarse density at sample i. \deltai is the distance between coarse samples i and i+1 (or the step size). \taui = e^{-\sum{j=1}^{i-1} \sigmaj \deltaj} is the accumulated transmittance up to sample i. 4. Sample Fine Points: Sample Nf fine points from the probability distribution defined by the normalized weights wi. This is importance sampling, concentrating samples in regions of high density [Parent, S2]. 5. Render: Evaluate the fine network (or feature grid) at all Nc + Nf sample locations to obtain density \sigma and color c. Accumulate the color using the volume rendering equation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def hierarchicaldensityadaptation(rayorigin, raydirection, densegrid, maxdist, Nc, Nf, kernelsize=3): # 1. On-the-fly coarse density via average pooling coarsegrid = averagepool3d(densegrid, kernelsize) # 2. Sample Nc coarse points uniformly along ray [0, maxdist] coarsets = [i maxdist / Nc for i in range(Nc)] coarsepoints = [(rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) for t in coarsets] # 3. Evaluate coarse density at these points coarsedensities = [trilinearinterpolate(coarsegrid, p) for p in coarsepoints] # 4. Calculate weights for importance sampling delta = maxdist / Nc transmittances = [0.0] Nc transmittances[0] = 1.0 for i in range(1, Nc): transmittances[i] = transmittances[i-1] math.exp(-coarsedensities[i-1] delta) weights = [transmittances[i] (1.0 - math.exp(-coarsedensities[i] delta)) for i in range(Nc)] # Normalize weights to probability distribution wsum = sum(weights) if wsum == 0: probdist = [1.0 / Nc] Nc else: probdist = [w / wsum for w in weights] # 5. Sample Nf fine points from the probability distribution (Inverse CDF) cdf = [0.0] Nc cdf[0] = probdist[0] for i in range(1, Nc): cdf[i] = cdf[i-1] + probdist[i] finets = [] for in range(Nf): u = random.uniform(0, 1) idx = 0 for i in range(Nc): if u <= cdf[i]: idx = i break tmin = idx delta tmax = (idx + 1) delta finets.append(random.uniform(tmin, tmax)) # 6. Combine and sort all points by depth allts = sorted(coarsets + finets) allpoints = [(rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) for t in allts] # 7. Evaluate fine density and color at all points results = [evaluatefine(allpoints[i], densegrid) for i in range(len(allpoints))] sorteddensities = [r[0] for r in results] sortedcolors = [r[1] for r in results] # 8. Volume rendering accumulation totaltransmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(len(allpoints)): sigma = sorteddensities[i] color = sortedcolors[i] if i < len(allpoints) - 1: deltai = math.sqrt(sum((allpoints[i+1][j] - allpoints[i][j])2 for j in range(3))) else: deltai = delta alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma deltai) weight = totaltransmittance alpha accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[j] + weight color[j] for j in range(3)] totaltransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) return accumulatedcolor def averagepool3d(grid, kernelsize): """Applies average pooling to a 3D grid.""" # Standard downsampling implementation omitted for brevity pass def trilinearinterpolate(grid, point): """Performs trilinear interpolation on a 3D grid.""" # Standard interpolation implementation omitted for brevity pass def evaluatefine(point, densegrid): """Returns (sigma, color) from the fine representation.""" # Standard fine network/grid evaluation omitted for brevity pass Parameters: Nc: Number of coarse samples along the ray. Nf: Number of fine samples along the ray. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Skipping Surface Regions: Evaluating density directly from the dense grid G\sigma at coarse points might skip important surface regions if the coarse sampling interval is larger than the feature thickness. This is handled by convolving the grid with an average pooling kernel to create a coarser estimate on the fly. Precision: Accumulated transmittance \taui can underflow for long rays with high density. Use log-space accumulation if necessary. Boundary Conditions: Ensure ray clipping is handled correctly when calculating \deltai for the last sample. A variant used for outdoor or large indoor environments where the feature grid is bounded by a maximum radius R{\text{max}}. It integrates an equirectangular environment map to represent visibility at almost infinite distance. What it is: Extends the rendering equation to include an environment map term for rays that exit the feature grid. What sets it apart: Handles infinite background without requiring an infinitely large feature grid. When to choose it: For egocentric view synthesis or large indoor environments where distant visibility is needed. Link: Environment Map Integration Details: Sampling: Distribute Nc coarse samples exponentially along the ray rather than uniformly, because the feature grid size increases exponentially along the radial direction. Rendering Equation: \hat{C} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \taui (1 - e^{-\sigma(\mathbf{x}i)\deltai}) c(\mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{d}) + \tau{N+1} c{\text{env}}(\mathbf{d}) where N = Nc + Nf, \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}, and c{\text{env}} is the environment map color. Environment Map Fetch: c{\text{env}}(\mathbf{d}) = \mathcal{E}(u, v; \mathbf{d}) where (u, v) are sampling positions dependent only on viewing direction \mathbf{d}. Parameter: E \in \mathbb{R}^{H \times W \times 3}: An equirectangular environment map representing visibility at almost infinite distance. Time Complexity: O(Nc + Nf) per ray, where Nc and Nf are the number of coarse and fine samples. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the volume of the dense grid. No additional memory is allocated for a separate coarse grid. Strengths: Memory efficient (no extra coarse grid), adaptive to local density, enables constant frame rate rendering. Limitations: Requires a dense grid that stores physically meaningful volume density for the convolution to be effective. When to use: When avoiding additional memory allocation for a coarse grid is required, and the density grid stores physically meaningful values. When not to use: When the density grid stores abstract neural features rather than physical density, as convolution would not yield a meaningful coarse estimate. Origin: The concept of density control for real-time previewing was introduced as "Point Selection Criteria" to control rendering density using a hierarchy of sampled data. The specific implementation of "on-the-fly coarse sampling" using convolution on a dense grid was introduced in EgoNeRF. History: Early volume rendering used opacity control for image smoothness. Density control was proposed as an alternative for rendering speed. Neural volume rendering revived hierarchical sampling, and EgoNeRF adapted it for spherical grids with on-the-fly coarse estimation. Usage: Used in real-time volume visualization and egocentric view synthesis.
