name: Trilinear Interpolation
head: 3D Linear Interpolation, Interpolação trilinear, Linear Interpolation (Trilinear), Trilinear Interpolant, Trilinear Sampling, Voxel Trilinear Interpolation
body: Trilinear interpolation estimates the scalar value at an arbitrary point within a voxel grid by computing a weighted average of the values of the 8 surrounding voxels, based on their distances to the sample point. It solves the problem of discretization artifacts (blockiness) inherent in nearest-neighbor sampling by providing a continuous, first-order approximation of the underlying scalar field. It produces softer, higher-quality images than nearest-neighbor interpolation but requires approximately 5 times more computation time. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field defined on a regular grid with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz, and a query position \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z) in voxel space. Output: A single scalar value V(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: The volume data is stored in a 3D array (or flattened 1D array with row-major indexing). For a query point, the algorithm accesses the 8 corner values of the containing voxel: \begin{aligned} v{000} &= \text{Grid}(i0, j0, k0) \\ v{100} &= \text{Grid}(i1, j0, k0) \\ v{010} &= \text{Grid}(i0, j1, k0) \\ v{110} &= \text{Grid}(i1, j1, k0) \\ v{001} &= \text{Grid}(i0, j0, k1) \\ v{101} &= \text{Grid}(i1, j0, k1) \\ v{011} &= \text{Grid}(i0, j1, k1) \\ v{111} &= \text{Grid}(i1, j1, k1) \end{aligned} where i1 = i0 + 1, j1 = j0 + 1, k1 = k0 + 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate System Alignment: Depending on the grid's coordinate convention, an offset (e.g., -0.5) may be applied to align voxel centers with integer coordinates. Standard implementations assume voxel corners at integer indices and skip this step. \mathbf{p}{\text{aligned}} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c} \quad (\text{where } \mathbf{c} \text{ is typically } (0,0,0) \text{ or } (0.5,0.5,0.5)) 2. Index Calculation: Compute the integer indices of the lower-left corner of the containing voxel using the floor function. i0 = \lfloor p{\text{aligned}, x} \rfloor, \quad j0 = \lfloor p{\text{aligned}, y} \rfloor, \quad k0 = \lfloor p{\text{aligned}, z} \rfloor 3. Boundary Clamping: Clamp the lower indices to prevent out-of-bounds access if the query point lies on the grid boundary. If i0 = Dx - 1, set i0 = Dx - 2 (and similarly for y, z). 4. Fractional Weights: Calculate the fractional offset (weights) within the voxel. wx = p{\text{aligned}, x} - i0, \quad wy = p{\text{aligned}, y} - j0, \quad wz = p{\text{aligned}, z} - k0 These weights lie in the range [0, 1]. 5. Interpolation: Perform linear interpolation sequentially along the x, y, and z axes. X-axis: Interpolate pairs along the x-dimension for the bottom (k0) and top (k1) faces. \begin{aligned} c{00} &= v{000}(1 - wx) + v{100}wx \\ c{10} &= v{010}(1 - wx) + v{110}wx \\ c{01} &= v{001}(1 - wx) + v{101}wx \\ c{11} &= v{011}(1 - wx) + v{111}wx \end{aligned} Y-axis: Interpolate the results from the X-step along the y-dimension. \begin{aligned} c0 &= c{00}(1 - wy) + c{10}wy \\ c1 &= c{01}(1 - wy) + c{11}wy \end{aligned} Z-axis: Interpolate the results from the Y-step along the z-dimension to get the final value. V(\mathbf{p}) = c0(1 - wz) + c1 wz Expanded Formula: The result can also be expressed as a weighted sum of the 8 corners: \begin{aligned} V(\mathbf{p}) = & \ v{000}(1-wx)(1-wy)(1-wz) + v{100}wx(1-wy)(1-wz) + \\ & \ v{010}(1-wx)wy(1-wz) + v{110}wx wy (1-wz) + \\ & \ v{001}(1-wx)(1-wy)wz + v{101}wx(1-wy)wz + \\ & \ v{011}(1-wx)wy wz + v{111}wx wy wz \end{aligned} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterpolation(grid, p, dims): """ grid: 3D array of shape (Dz, Dy, Dx) p: tuple (x, y, z) in voxel space dims: tuple (Dx, Dy, Dz) """ x, y, z = p # 1. Compute lower indices i0 = int(x // 1) if x >= 0 else int(x // 1) - (1 if x != int(x) else 0) j0 = int(y // 1) if y >= 0 else int(y // 1) - (1 if y != int(y) else 0) k0 = int(z // 1) if z >= 0 else int(z // 1) - (1 if z != int(z) else 0) # 2. Handle boundaries: clamp lower index to valid range [0, dim-2] i0 = max(0, min(i0, dims[0] - 2)) j0 = max(0, min(j0, dims[1] - 2)) k0 = max(0, min(k0, dims[2] - 2)) i1 = i0 + 1 j1 = j0 + 1 k1 = k0 + 1 # 3. Compute fractional weights wx = x - i0 wy = y - j0 wz = z - k0 # 4. Fetch 8 corner values (assuming grid is indexed as [z, y, x]) v000 = grid[k0, j0, i0] v100 = grid[k0, j0, i1] v010 = grid[k0, j1, i0] v110 = grid[k0, j1, i1] v001 = grid[k1, j0, i0] v101 = grid[k1, j0, i1] v011 = grid[k1, j1, i0] v111 = grid[k1, j1, i1] # 5. Interpolate along X c00 = v000 (1 - wx) + v100 wx c10 = v010 (1 - wx) + v110 wx c01 = v001 (1 - wx) + v101 wx c11 = v011 (1 - wx) + v111 wx # 6. Interpolate along Y c0 = c00 (1 - wy) + c10 wy c1 = c01 (1 - wy) + c11 wy # 7. Interpolate along Z result = c0 (1 - wz) + c1 wz return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: If the query point lies exactly on the upper boundary of the grid, the upper neighbor index would exceed the array bounds. Clamping the lower index to dim - 2 ensures valid access. Zero-Width Voxels: If the grid has degenerate voxels (width 0), division by zero may occur if using explicit division for weights. The fractional weight calculation w = p - i0 avoids this, but boundary clamping is still necessary. Coordinate System Mismatch: Applying a -0.5 offset when the grid uses corner-aligned coordinates (or vice versa) shifts the sampling grid, causing incorrect interpolation weights and visual artifacts. Uses trilinear interpolation on a sparse grid of spherical harmonic coefficients to enable gradient-based optimization, differing from standard scalar trilinear interpolation by storing directional radiance data. Implements trilinear interpolation via a stack of 2D textures and dependent texturing to approximate 3D sampling on hardware that lacks native 3D texture support, relying on the Piecewise Regular Interval (PRI) data structure. Uses trilinear interpolation to define the scalar field within hexahedral cells but replaces uniform ray marching with analytical integration of the piecewise-linear function to avoid isosurface artifacts. Uses trilinear interpolation to approximate the line integral of the Linear Attenuation Coefficient for differentiable X-ray rendering, trading geometric precision for speed and regularization. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, requiring exactly 8 memory fetches and 7 linear interpolations (14 multiplications, 7 additions). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: Produces significantly higher quality images than nearest-neighbor interpolation but takes approximately 5 times longer to compute. It is faster than higher-order methods like tri-cubic interpolation. Strengths: Simple to implement, hardware-supported (via 3D texture sampling units in GPUs), and provides smoother results than nearest-neighbor. Limitations: Introduces blurring and high-frequency artifacts (false edges or "star patterns") due to the infinite extent of the triangular pulse kernel's Fourier transform. It is not suitable for applications requiring sharp feature preservation or exact geometric reconstruction. When to use: General-purpose volume rendering where visual smoothness is prioritized over sharpness, and computational resources are limited compared to higher-order methods. When not to use: When exact geometric intersection is required, as it approximates values rather than computing precise voxel boundaries. Trilinear interpolation is the direct 3D extension of bilinear interpolation, defined as the linear interpolation of two bilinear interpolations. It was widely adopted in early volume rendering techniques to improve upon the blocky artifacts of nearest-neighbor sampling. The method is fundamental to many volume rendering pipelines, including those implemented in OpenVDB and standard GPU texture sampling hardware. It is also used in related fields such as fluid simulation. name: Plenoxels Interpolation Methods
head: Plenoxel Grid with Trilinear Interpolation, Trilinear Plenoxel
body: Plenoxels interpolation methods define a continuous radiance field over a sparse 3D voxel grid by storing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients and opacity at voxel centers, enabling stable optimization and higher effective resolution than discrete voxel assumptions. It distinguishes itself from nearest-neighbor Plenoxels by providing a continuous function approximation that is critical for successful gradient-based optimization, and from tricubic methods by offering a favorable trade-off between smoothness and computational cost. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse 3D voxel grid containing optimized parameters; a 3D sample point \mathbf{p}; a viewing direction \mathbf{v}. Output: Radiance color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) and opacity \sigma(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: The grid stores data at voxel centers. For each active voxel, the layout is: Opacity: 1 scalar value (\sigma). Spherical Harmonics Coefficients: 27 values (9 coefficients per color channel for degree 2 SH). Note: The sources specify storing RGB channels (zero-order SH) for background spheres to conserve memory. Parameters: Spherical Harmonics Degree: 2. This requires 9 coefficients per color channel, totaling 27 harmonic coefficients per voxel plus 1 opacity coefficient. Resolution: Typical synthetic scenes use 128^3 to 512^3. Steps: 1. Locate Neighbors: Identify the 8 nearest voxel centers surrounding the sample point \mathbf{p}. Let these centers be \mathbf{c}i for i \in \{0, \dots, 7\}. 2. Compute Weights: Calculate trilinear interpolation weights wi based on the relative position of \mathbf{p} within the unit cube defined by the 8 neighbors. 3. Interpolate Opacity: Compute the opacity \sigma(\mathbf{p}) by trilinearly interpolating the opacity values \sigmai from the 8 neighbors: \sigma(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=0}^{7} wi \sigmai 4. Interpolate SH Coefficients: For each color channel k \in \{R, G, B\}, trilinearly interpolate the 9 SH coefficients C{i,j,k} (where j indexes the 9 coefficients) from the 8 neighbors to obtain the interpolated coefficients \hat{C}{j,k}: \hat{C}{j,k} = \sum{i=0}^{7} wi C{i,j,k} 5. Evaluate Radiance: Evaluate the spherical harmonic basis functions Yj(\mathbf{v}) for the viewing direction \mathbf{v}. Compute the radiance for channel k as: ck(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{j=0}^{8} \hat{C}{j,k} Yj(\mathbf{v}) The final color is \mathbf{c} = [cR, cG, cB]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearplenoxelsample(grid, p, v): # 1. Find 8 nearest voxel centers and weights # grid is a sparse structure mapping voxelindex -> (opacity, shcoeffs[27]) # p is a 3D vector neighbors = get8neighbors(grid, p) weights = computetrilinearweights(p, neighbors.corners) # 2. Interpolate opacity sigma = 0.0 for i, neighbor in enumerate(neighbors): sigma += weights[i] neighbor.opacity # 3. Interpolate SH coefficients (Degree 2 -> 9 coeffs per channel) # shcoeffs layout: [R0..R8, G0..G8, B0..B8] interpsh = [0.0] 27 for i, neighbor in enumerate(neighbors): for k in range(27): interpsh[k] += weights[i] neighbor.shcoeffs[k] # 4. Evaluate SH for viewing direction v # Y is a function returning 9 basis values for direction v yvals = evaluateshbasis(v, degree=2) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for channel in range(3): channeloffset = channel 9 radiance = 0.0 for j in range(9): radiance += interpsh[channeloffset + j] yvals[j] color[channel] = radiance return color, sigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Nearest Neighbor Instability: Using nearest-neighbor interpolation produces a discontinuous model that is difficult to optimize and less stable with respect to learning rate variations. Tricubic Cost: Tricubic interpolation offers continuous and smooth approximation but incurs substantial computation with negligible quality gain compared to trilinear. Initialization: Coefficients are optimized directly without special initialization or pretraining with a neural network. This variant extends Plenoxels to real, unbounded scenes, including forward-facing and 360° settings. For forward-facing scenes, it uses normalized device coordinates (NDC) for the sparse voxel grid structure. For 360° scenes, it augments the foreground with a multisphere image (MSI) background model using learned voxel colors and opacities with trilinear interpolation. It places 64 spheres linearly in inverse radius from 1 to \infty, pre-scaling the inner scene to be approximately contained in the unit sphere. To conserve memory, the background stores only RGB channels (zero-order SH) and uses opacity thresholding for sparse storage. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Scales with the number of active voxels. Each voxel stores 28 scalars (1 opacity + 27 SH coefficients). Background spheres store only 3 scalars (RGB) per voxel. Time: Trilinear interpolation is significantly faster than tricubic, which incurs substantial computation. Measured Performance: On 8 NeRF synthetic scenes, Trilinear Plenoxels at 128^3 resolution (PSNR 28.46, SSIM 0.926, LPIPS 0.100) outperform Nearest Neighbor at 256^3 resolution (PSNR 27.17, SSIM 0.914, LPIPS 0.119). Trilinear interpolation at 256^3 achieves PSNR 30.57, SSIM 0.950, LPIPS 0.065. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Increases effective resolution by representing sub-voxel variations; produces a continuous function approximation critical for successful optimization; more stable with respect to learning rate variations than nearest neighbor. Limitations: Tricubic offers smoother approximation but with negligible quality gain and higher cost. When to Use: Use trilinear interpolation for stable optimization and higher quality than nearest neighbor at lower resolutions. Avoid nearest neighbor if optimization stability is a concern. Avoid tricubic unless smoothness is strictly required and computational budget allows, as quality gain is negligible. Plenoxels were introduced in the paper "Plenoxels: Radiance Fields without Neural Networks". The method builds on PlenOctrees but replaces the constant-voxel assumption with trilinear interpolation to enable direct optimization of opacity and SH coefficients without neural networks. The use of degree 2 spherical harmonics was adopted from PlenOctrees, as higher orders confer minimal benefit. The method supports coarse-to-fine optimization strategies, resizing grids between arbitrary resolutions using trilinear interpolation. name: Multi-Texture Trilinear Estimation
head: Axis-aligned/View-aligned slicing, Basic Slice-based Rendering with Trilinear Interpolation, Multi-Texture Trilinear Interpolation, PRI reconstruction, Rezk-Salama Multi-Texture Trilinear
body: Multi-Texture Trilinear Estimation is a slice-based volume rendering technique that reconstructs scalar values from a Piecewise Regular Interval (PRI) representation using trilinear interpolation, implemented via a stack of parallel quads textured with scalar information. It solves the problem of visualizing space data defined on a 3D rectilinear grid by substituting direct 3D texture sampling with a two-stage interpolation process (two bilinear and one linear interpolation) to improve image quality over basic 2D texture rendering while maintaining speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Piecewise Regular Interval (PRI) representation of the volume data, consisting of an index texture and a knots texture (storing scalar values and knot distances). The PRI is constructed along a specific sampling direction. Output: A 2D image with color and opacity values computed via front-to-back or back-to-front alpha compositing. Data Structures: Index Texture: A 2D texture where each texel corresponds to a pixel on the PRI's sampling plane. It stores the identifier or pointer to the linear spline associated with that grid location. Knots Texture: Stores the linear splines. In the implementation described, this is stored as two separate textures with float format for high precision: one for scalar values and one for the distance values of the knots. The knots of each spline are sorted in depth. Steps: The algorithm reconstructs a trilinearly interpolated scalar value at a pixel fragment located at (x, y, z) in the PRI coordinate space through three main steps: 1. Projection and Neighbor Identification: Parallel project the position of the pixel fragment to the PRI's sampling plane by dropping the z coordinate. Identify the four pixels on the sampling plane that surround the projection point (x, y), i.e., the four nearest neighbors. 2. Spline Search: Search each of the four linear splines associated with the neighborhood of pixels identified in Step 1 to find the specific spline segment that overlaps the pixel fragment's z location. 3. Interpolation: Perform trilinear interpolation by executing four linear interpolations in the z direction using the four spline segments found in Step 2, followed by bilinear interpolation in the x and y directions. Implementation Details (Slicing Strategies): The method supports two slicing paradigms: Axis-Aligned Slicing: The stack of slices is positioned perpendicular to the PRI's sampling direction. To map the index texture to each rendering slice, texture coordinates at the four corners are set to (0, 0), (0, h), (w, h), and (w, 0), where w and h are the pixel dimensions of the index texture. This avoids inverse mapping from eye space to object space. View-Aligned Slicing: The stack of slices is positioned parallel to the image plane. The inverse mapping from eye space to object space is performed using OpenGL's TexGen operation, similar to shadow mapping. Shader Execution: The shader program retrieves the four nearest texels in the index texture and accesses each associated linear spline in the knots texture via dependent texturing. Since the knots are sorted in depth, the search for the spline segment including the pixel fragment's z location is performed with a binary search. Finally, the shader computes the trilinear interpolation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderprislices(indextexture, knotstexture, viewmatrix, resolution): """ Renders volume using Multi-Texture Trilinear Estimation. indextexture: 2D texture mapping (u,v) to spline IDs. knotstexture: 2D texture storing knot distances and scalar values per spline. viewmatrix: defines slice orientation (axis-aligned or view-aligned). resolution: (width, height) of the output image. """ image = createemptyimage(resolution) w, h = indextexture.width, indextexture.height # Determine slicing strategy based on view direction strategy = "axis-aligned" if isaxisaligned(viewmatrix) else "view-aligned" for slice in generateslicestack(viewmatrix, resolution): for pixel in slice.pixels: # Step 1: Project to sampling plane by dropping z, find 4 neighbors projx, projy = pixel.x, pixel.y neighbors = findfournearestneighbors(projx, projy, indextexture) zinterpolated = [] for n in neighbors: # Access spline ID via dependent texturing splineid = indextexture.sample(n.u, n.v) # Retrieve knot data for this spline knots = knotstexture.getspline(splineid) # Binary search for segment overlapping pixel.z segidx = binarysearchsortedknots(knots, pixel.z) # Linear interpolation in z d0, d1 = knots[segidx].distance, knots[segidx+1].distance s0, s1 = knots[segidx].scalar, knots[segidx+1].scalar t = (pixel.z - d0) / (d1 - d0) zinterpolated.append(lerp(s0, s1, t)) # Step 3: Bilinear interpolation in x and y fx = projx - floor(projx) fy = projy - floor(projy) # Neighbors ordered: [0]=floorx,floory, [1]=ceilx,floory, [2]=floorx,ceily, [3]=ceilx,ceily v00, v10, v01, v11 = zinterpolated[0], zinterpolated[1], zinterpolated[2], zinterpolated[3] top = lerp(v00, v10, fx) bottom = lerp(v01, v11, fx) scalar = lerp(top, bottom, fy) # Classification and compositing color, opacity = classifyscalar(scalar) image.compositefronttoback(pixel.position, color, opacity) return image def createemptyimage(resolution): return Image(resolution[0], resolution[1]) def isaxisaligned(viewmatrix): # Returns True if view direction aligns with PRI axes, False for view-aligned return True # Standard view-direction check against PRI axes def generateslicestack(viewmatrix, resolution): # Standard slice generation producing quads with pixel positions return [Slice() for in range(resolution[1])] def findfournearestneighbors(projx, projy, texture): # Returns 4 neighbor coordinates in texture space fx, fy = floor(projx), floor(projy) return [ (fx, fy), (fx+1, fy), (fx, fy+1), (fx+1, fy+1) ] def binarysearchsortedknots(knots, z): # Standard binary search over sorted knot distances low, high = 0, len(knots) - 2 while low <= high: mid = (low + high) // 2 if knots[mid].distance <= z < knots[mid+1].distance: return mid elif z < knots[mid].distance: high = mid - 1 else: low = mid + 1 return low def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def classifyscalar(scalar): # Standard transfer function mapping scalar to (color, opacity) return (scalar, 1.0) Parameters and Edge Cases: Binary Search: The search for the spline segment is a binary search over sorted knots. Precision: Knots texture is stored as two separate float textures (scalar and distance) to ensure high precision. View Direction: If the view direction changes more than 45 degrees, switching artifacts may occur if multiple PRIs are not used. Performance Bottleneck: The binary search and dependent texturing create a computational bottleneck on current GPUs. An optimization that eliminates the need for multiple data copies by reconstructing volumetric data on-the-fly, storing only one stack of original data. It is beneficial when GPU texture memory is insufficient for three copies but sufficient for one. However, it introduces a severe performance drop-off. If the data exceeds texture memory, paging or out-of-core rendering is needed. Examined by Engel et al.. Time Complexity: The algorithm requires four spline searches per pixel fragment, contributing to a considerable computational bottleneck on current GPU technology due to costly searches and interpolation. Memory Complexity: The basic algorithm requires three copies of the volumetric data set in main memory to eliminate switching artifacts when the view direction changes more than 45 degrees. This limits the algorithm to very small data sets. Strengths: Improved image quality compared to plain 2D texture-based rendering without losing too much rendering speed. View-aligned slicing requires only a single PRI at a minimum. Limitations: High storage requirements. Computational bottleneck due to binary search and dependent texturing. When to use: When image quality is prioritized over raw speed and data sets are small enough to fit in memory with three copies. When not to use: When GPU texture memory is limited and on-the-fly reconstruction causes unacceptable performance drops, or when data sets are too large for out-of-core techniques. The method was introduced by Rezk-Salama et al.. It was developed as an improvement over basic 2D texture-based rendering, aiming to substitute trilinear interpolation with two bilinear interpolations and one linear interpolation to achieve better image quality. The approach is part of the broader field of image-based volume rendering using PRI representations. name: Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering with Trilinear Interpolation
head: Analytical Integration with Trilinear Reconstruction, Köhler's Method, Semi-Analytical Preintegration for Hexahedral Cells, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering, Trilinear Preintegration
body: Semi-analytical volume rendering with trilinear interpolation is a direct volume ray casting technique for hexahedral cells that eliminates topological artifacts such as discontinuities and holes in isosurfaces by analytically determining optimal sampling points along the ray. It sets itself apart from standard trilinear interpolation [1531-trilinear-interpolation.md] by replacing uniform sampling with a piecewise-linear approximation over monotonic intervals defined by the analytical extrema of the reconstructed signal, ensuring no isovalue is missed. Inputs: Scalar field values s{ijk} at the 8 corners (i,j,k) \in \{0,1\}^3 of a hexahedral cell. Ray entry point (x0, y0, z0) and exit point (x1, y1, z1) in normalized cell coordinates [0,1]^3. Transfer functions: color c(s) and opacity \tau(s). Outputs: Accumulated color intensity I for the ray segment traversing the cell. Data Structures: Coefficients a, b, c, d of the cubic polynomial s(t). List of valid extrema R = \{r1, r2, \dots\} within [0,1]. Monotonic intervals defined by sorted sampling points T = \{0, r1, r2, 1\}. Steps: 1. Ray Parametrization: Compute the direction vector components as differences between exit and entry coordinates: vx = x1 - x0, \quad vy = y1 - y0, \quad vz = z1 - z0 The ray is parametrized as x(t) = x0 + t vx, y(t) = y0 + t vy, z(t) = z0 + t vz for t \in [0,1]. 2. Signal Reconstruction (Cubic Polynomial): Substitute the ray parametrization into the trilinear interpolation formula to obtain s(t) = a t^3 + b t^2 + c t + d. The coefficients are linear combinations of the corner values s{ijk} and ray parameters: a = (s{100} - s{000} + s{010} + s{001} + s{111} - s{110} - s{011} - s{101}) vx vy vz Coefficients b, c, d are derived similarly by collecting terms of t^2, t^1, t^0 respectively, resulting in sums of 8 terms each involving s{ijk} multiplied by products of x0, y0, z0 and vx, vy, vz. 3. Extrema Calculation: Compute the derivative s'(t) = 3a t^2 + 2b t + c. Find the roots of this quadratic equation: t = \frac{-2b \pm \sqrt{4b^2 - 12ac}}{6a} If a=0, solve the linear equation 2b t + c = 0. If a=0 and b=0, the function is constant and has no extrema. 4. Pruning and Sorting: Discard any roots t such that t < 0 or t > 1. Sort the remaining valid extrema ri in ascending order. Define the sampling points T = [0, r1, r2, \dots, 1]. 5. Interval Approximation: For each consecutive pair of sampling points ti, t{i+1} in T, approximate the signal s(t) as a linear interpolation between the values at the endpoints: s{lin}(t') = (1-t') s(ti) + t' s(t{i+1}), \quad t' \in [0,1] where t' is the local parameter within the normalized interval [0,1]. Let Li = t{i+1} - ti be the length of the interval. 6. Preintegration: Compute the contribution of each interval using preintegration functions C and \alpha. The total intensity is accumulated using front-to-back alpha compositing: I \approx C(s(0), s(r1), L0) + (1 - \alpha(s(0), s(r1), L0)) C(s(r1), s(r2), L1) + \dots where C(a, b, L) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) L e^{-\int0^{t'} \tau((1-u) a + u b) L du} dt' \alpha(a, b, L) = 1 - e^{-\int0^1 \tau((1-t') a + t' b) L dt'} In practice, these integrals are evaluated via numerical quadrature or lookup tables. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def semianalyticaltrilinearrender(scorners, x0, y0, z0, x1, y1, z1, cfunc, taufunc): """ scorners: list of 8 floats [s000, s100, s010, s001, s101, s011, s110, s111] x0,y0,z0: entry point in [0,1]^3 x1,y1,z1: exit point in [0,1]^3 cfunc: color transfer function (returns RGB tuple) taufunc: opacity transfer function (returns float) """ vx, vy, vz = x1 - x0, y1 - y0, z1 - z0 a, b, c, d = computecubiccoefficients(scorners, x0, y0, z0, vx, vy, vz) roots = solvequadratic(3a, 2b, c) validextrema = sorted([r for r in roots if 0.0 <= r <= 1.0]) samplingpoints = [0.0] + validextrema + [1.0] accumulatedalpha = 0.0 accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(len(samplingpoints) - 1): tstart, tend = samplingpoints[i], samplingpoints[i+1] L = tend - tstart sstart, send = evalcubic(a, b, c, d, tstart), evalcubic(a, b, c, d, tend) intervalcolor, intervalalpha = preintegrateinterval(sstart, send, L, cfunc, taufunc) accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[k] + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) intervalcolor[k] for k in range(3)] accumulatedalpha += (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) intervalalpha return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha def evaltrilinear(scorners, x, y, z): return (scorners[0](1-x)(1-y)(1-z) + scorners[1]x(1-y)(1-z) + scorners[2](1-x)y(1-z) + scorners[3](1-x)(1-y)z + scorners[4]x(1-y)z + scorners[5](1-x)yz + scorners[6]xy(1-z) + scorners[7]xyz) def computecubiccoefficients(scorners, x0, y0, z0, vx, vy, vz): # Coefficients for s(t) = at^3 + bt^2 + ct + d # a is explicitly defined a = (scorners[1] - scorners[0] + scorners[2] + scorners[3] + scorners[7] - scorners[6] - scorners[5] - scorners[4]) vx vy vz # b, c, d are computed similarly as linear combinations of corner values # We evaluate s(t) at t=0, 1/3, 2/3, 1 and solve the linear system tpts = [0.0, 1.0/3.0, 2.0/3.0, 1.0] spts = [evaltrilinear(scorners, x0 + tvx, y0 + tvy, z0 + tvz) for t in tpts] # Solve Vandermonde system for b, c, d (a is known) # Using Cramer's rule or Gaussian elimination for 3x3 system # Simplified: solve for b, c, d given a # t^3 coefficients are known, so we solve for remaining M = [[t2 for t in tpts], [t for t in tpts], [1.0 for in tpts]] rhs = [s - at3 for s, t in zip(spts, tpts)] b, c, d = solvelinearsystem(M, rhs) return a, b, c, d def evalcubic(a, b, c, d, t): return ((at + b)t + c)t + d def solvequadratic(A, B, C): if abs(A) < 1e-9: return [-C/B] if abs(B) > 1e-9 else [] disc = BB - 4AC if disc < 0: return [] sqrtdisc = disc0.5 return [(-B - sqrtdisc)/(2A), (-B + sqrtdisc)/(2A)] def solvelinearsystem(M, rhs): n = len(rhs) for i in range(n): maxrow = i for k in range(i+1, n): if abs(M[k][i]) > abs(M[maxrow][i]): maxrow = k M[i], M[maxrow] = M[maxrow], M[i] rhs[i], rhs[maxrow] = rhs[maxrow], rhs[i] for k in range(i+1, n): factor = M[k][i] / M[i][i] for j in range(i, n): M[k][j] -= factor M[i][j] rhs[k] -= factor rhs[i] x = [0.0]n for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): x[i] = rhs[i] for j in range(i+1, n): x[i] -= M[i][j] x[j] x[i] /= M[i][i] return x def preintegrateinterval(sstart, send, L, cfunc, taufunc, steps=16): colorintegral = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] tauintegral = 0.0 dt = 1.0 / steps accumulatedopacity = 0.0 for i in range(steps): tprime = (i + 0.5) dt sval = (1.0 - tprime)sstart + tprimesend cval = cfunc(sval) tauval = taufunc(sval) tauintegral += tauval dt accumulatedopacity += tauval dt weight = L (1.0 - tprime) colorintegral = [colorintegral[k] + weight cval[k] math.exp(-accumulatedopacity L) for k in range(3)] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-tauintegral L) return colorintegral, alpha This method extends semi-analytical volume rendering by incorporating local Phong diffuse shading into the integration process. It solves the problem of accurate lighting in volume rendering by reconstructing the shading function as a quadratic polynomial along the ray, allowing for analytical integration of the light contribution. It sets itself apart from scalar-only semi-analytical methods by requiring at most one additional sampling point per cell to capture the shading extremum, while maintaining the topological accuracy of the underlying trilinear interpolation. A technique to handle hybrid cells in Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) by propagating cell splits from the lower level cell to the higher level cell to ensure continuity across cell faces. It identifies hybrid cells (sharing an edge/face with a different level cell) and propagates splits by adding 'source split points' (using the higher-level cell's value) and 'destination split points' (using bilinearly interpolated values from a shared face) to the lower-level cell. This ensures continuity across cell faces either by using the neighbor's value or by matching the interpolation scheme of the neighbor cell, avoiding artifacts. Time Complexity: The method requires solving a quadratic equation and evaluating preintegration functions for each monotonic interval. The number of intervals is small (at most 3), making it faster than high-frequency uniform sampling for preserving topology. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for preintegration tables or numerical quadrature routines. Performance: Efficient on current graphics hardware when combined with a hybrid CPU-GPU mesh traversal technique. Strengths: Guarantees topological accuracy of isosurfaces; avoids missing isovalues; handles arbitrary transfer functions. Limitations: As the topology is consistent from one frame to another, the only remaining kind of artifacts is wobbling of the surfaces and structures inside the cells as the viewpoint changes. Complex coefficient calculation for the cubic polynomial. When to use: High-quality visualization of AMR datasets with hexahedral cells where topological accuracy is critical. Originated in a 2009 paper by titled "High-Quality, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering for AMR...", this method was developed to address the challenges of visualizing Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) datasets. It builds on the need for view-order cell traversal and high-quality rendering of hexahedral cells in AMR meshes, which often suffer from discontinuities in isosurfaces due to piecewise linear approximations. The method extends standard trilinear interpolation by leveraging the analytical properties of the reconstructed signal to determine sampling points. 5 Forward Projection through Voxel Volumes, https://www.cvl.isy.liu.se/education/undergraduate/tsbb31/download/TurbellPhDCh5.pdf, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) High-Quality, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering for AMR..., https://people.freedesktop.org/~marcheu/vis09-amr.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Local Phong Shading with Semi-Analytical Integration
head: Quadratic Shading Integration, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering with Shading
body:
This method extends semi-analytical volume rendering by incorporating local Phong diffuse shading into the integration process. It solves the problem of accurate lighting in volume rendering by reconstructing the shading function as a quadratic polynomial along the ray, allowing for analytical integration of the light contribution. It sets itself apart from scalar-only semi-analytical methods by requiring at most one additional sampling point per cell to capture the shading extremum, while maintaining the topological accuracy of the underlying trilinear interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Trilinear interpolation coefficients for the scalar field s(x,y,z) within a hexahedral cell; light direction vector \vec{L} = (lx, ly, lz); preintegration tables C{front}, C{back}, and \alpha; ray segment parameters t{start}, t{end} within the cell. Outputs: Integrated color contribution I for the ray segment, accounting for shading. Data Structures: The method relies on the trilinear coefficients s{ijk} (where i,j,k \in \{0,1\}) defining the scalar field s(x,y,z) in the unit cube. The shading function is represented by quadratic coefficients e, f, g for d(t) = e t^2 + f t + g. Steps: 1. Compute the analytical gradient 
abla s(x,y,z) from the trilinear coefficients. Compute the diffuse shading function d(x,y,z) = 
abla s(x,y,z) \cdot \vec{L}. 2. Parametrize the ray as x(t), y(t), z(t) for t \in [0, L] (local cell coordinates). Substitute into d(x,y,z) to obtain the quadratic form d(t) = e \cdot t^2 + f \cdot t + g, where e, f, g are computed from the gradient coefficients and ray parameters. For a parametrized ray inside a cell, the gradient variation over this ray is thus a quadratic form in t. 3. Find the local extremum r of d(t) by setting the derivative to zero: r = -f / (2e). Since d(t) is a quadratic polynomial, there is at most a single local extremum r. 4. Sample the shading function at the cell entry (t=0), cell exit (t=L), and the local extremum r (if 0 < r < L). This requires at most one additional sampling point per cell compared to the scalar-only method. 5. Split the ray segment [0, L] at the extremum r into [0, r] and [r, L] (if r is within the interval). The integral becomes: I = \int0^r c(s(t))d(t)e^{-\int0^t 	au(s(u))du} dt + \intr^L c(s(t))d(t)e^{-\int0^t 	au(s(u))du} dt. 6. Approximate the scalar field s(t) as linear between sample points. For the full cell with extremum r, the total integral is approximated using preintegration functions: I \approx d(s(0)) C{front}(s(0), s(r), r) + d(s(r)) C{back}(s(0), s(r), r) + (1 - \alpha(s(0), s(r), r)) [ d(s(r)) C{front}(s(r), s(L), L-r) + d(s(L)) C{back}(s(r), s(L), L-r) ]. 7. Preintegration functions are defined as: C{back}(a, b, l) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) t' e^{-\int0^{t'} 	au((1-t') a + t' b) l du} dt' C{front}(a, b, l) = \int0^1 c((1-t') a + t' b) (1-t') e^{-\int0^{t'} 	au((1-t') a + t' b) l du} dt' \alpha(a, b, l) = 1 - e^{-\int0^1 	au((1-t') b + t' a) l dt'} where a, b are scalar values at interval endpoints, l is the interval length, and c(\cdot), 	au(\cdot) are the color and absorption transfer functions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def integratelocalphongshading(scoeffs, Lvec, tstart, tend, Cfront, Cback, alpha, cfunc, taufunc): # 1. Compute quadratic coefficients e, f, g for d(t) from gradient and ray e, f, g = computeshadingquadratic(scoeffs, Lvec) # 2. Find local extremum r of d(t) = et^2 + ft + g if abs(e) > 1e-9: r = -f / (2.0 e) else: r = None # Linear case, no internal extremum # 3. Determine integration intervals based on extremum if r is not None and tstart < r < tend: t1, t2, t3 = tstart, r, tend else: t1, t2, t3 = tstart, tend, tend # 4. Sample shading function d(t) at interval boundaries d1 = et1t1 + ft1 + g d2 = et2t2 + ft2 + g d3 = et3t3 + ft3 + g # 5. Compute scalar values s(t) at boundaries (linear interpolation assumed) s1 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t1) s2 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t2) s3 = samplescalar(scoeffs, t3) # 6. Compute interval lengths l1 = t2 - t1 l2 = t3 - t2 # 7. Evaluate preintegration functions cf1 = Cfront(s1, s2, l1) cb1 = Cback(s1, s2, l1) a1 = alpha(s1, s2, l1) cf2 = Cfront(s2, s3, l2) cb2 = Cback(s2, s3, l2) # 8. Apply split-interval approximation formula I = d1 cf1 + d2 cb1 if l2 > 0: I += (1.0 - a1) (d2 cf2 + d3 cb2) return I Pitfalls: Discontinuity: The reconstructed scalar field is only C^0 continuous across cell faces. Consequently, the gradient 
abla s is discontinuous, causing shading discontinuities across cell boundaries. Extremum Handling: If the extremum r lies outside the cell interval [0, L], the shading function is monotonic within the cell, and no split is needed. Complexity: Adds at most one additional sample per cell compared to scalar-only semi-analytical rendering. Performance: Not given in the sources for specific hardware performance metrics. Strengths: Captures local lighting variations within cells. Limitations: Shading discontinuities at cell faces may be visible due to C^0 continuity of the scalar field. This method is an extension of the semi-analytical volume rendering approach for AMR (Adaptive Mesh Refinement) data, presented by Marchesin et al. in 2009. It builds on the trilinear interpolation-based semi-analytical integration described in the parent article. High-Quality, Semi-Analytical Volume Rendering for AMR..., https://people.freedesktop.org/~marcheu/vis09-amr.pdf, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Trilinear Interpolation for X-ray Attenuation Approximation
head: Fast approximation of X-ray attenuation, Interpolatory quadrature via the rectangular rule
body: This method approximates the line integral of the Linear Attenuation Coefficient (LAC) along an X-ray beam using trilinear interpolation and the rectangular rule, serving as a differentiable forward model for sparse-view Cone-Beam CT (CBCT) reconstruction. It sets itself apart from exact geometric methods like Siddon's method by trading precise voxel intersection calculations for speed and a regularization effect where rendered pixels influence non-intersected voxels, thereby preventing overfitting in sparse-view scenarios. Inputs: Ray defined by source position \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and detector pixel position \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Voxel grid of LAC values \hat{\mu}, sampled via trilinear interpolation. Number of sample points M along the ray. Outputs: Approximated X-ray intensity I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r}). Data Structures: \hat{\mu}: Scalar field defined on a 3D rectilinear grid. Trilinear interpolation \hat{\mu}[\mathbf{x}] returns the weighted average of the 8 corner voxels surrounding coordinate \mathbf{x}. \alpham: Scalar parameters for evenly spaced points along the ray segment from source to pixel. Steps: 1. Define the ray parametric equation \vec{r}(\alpha) = \mathbf{s} + \alpha(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}) for \alpha \in [0, 1]. 2. Sample M evenly spaced points \alpha1, \dots, \alphaM along the ray such that \alpha1 = 0 and \alphaM = 1. 3. Initialize the sum S = 0. 4. Iterate m from 1 to M-1: a. Evaluate the LAC at the start point of the segment using trilinear interpolation: \hat{\mu}m = \hat{\mu}[\mathbf{s} + \alpham(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s})]. b. Calculate the weighted segment length factor: wm = \frac{\alpha{m+1} - \alpha{m-1}}{2}. For the first segment (m=1), \alpha0 is undefined in the source; a standard boundary convention for this fast approximation is to clamp \alpha0 = \alpha1. c. Accumulate the product: S \leftarrow S + \hat{\mu}m \cdot wm. 5. Multiply the accumulated sum by the total ray length: I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r}) = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\| \cdot S. Formula: I{\hat{\mu}}(\vec{r}) \approx \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}\| \sum{m=1}^{M-1} \hat{\mu} [\mathbf{s} + \alpham(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s})] \frac{(\alpha{m+1} - \alpha{m-1})}{2} where: \hat{\mu}[\cdot] is the trilinear interpolation of the voxel grid. \alpham are evenly spaced parameters in [0, 1]. M is the number of sample points. Parameters: M = 500 sample points per ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearxrayattenuation(s, p, mugrid, M=500): """ Approximates X-ray attenuation using trilinear interpolation and rectangular rule. Args: s: Source position (3D vector) p: Detector pixel position (3D vector) mugrid: Trilinear interpolator for the voxel grid LAC M: Number of sample points along the ray Returns: Approximated intensity Imu(r) """ # 1. Define ray direction and length raydir = (p[0] - s[0], p[1] - s[1], p[2] - s[2]) raylength = (raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2)0.5 # 2. Sample M evenly spaced points alpha1... alphaM # alpha1 = 0, alphaM = 1 alphas = [i / (M - 1) for i in range(M)] # 3. Initialize sum totalsum = 0.0 # 4. Iterate m from 1 to M-1 for m in range(1, M): # Map formula indices (1-based) to list indices (0-based) alpham = alphas[m - 1] alphamplus1 = alphas[m] alphamminus1 = alphas[0] if m == 1 else alphas[m - 2] # Calculate weight weight = (alphamplus1 - alphamminus1) / 2.0 # Evaluate trilinear interpolation at s + alpham (p - s) point = (s[0] + alpham raydir[0], s[1] + alpham raydir[1], s[2] + alpham raydir[2]) muval = mugrid.interpolate(point) # Calls standard trilinear interpolation from parent article # Add to sum totalsum += muval weight # 5. Multiply by ray length intensity = raylength totalsum return intensity Time Complexity: Linear in the number of sample points M (O(M)). It is faster than Siddon's method, which scales cubically with the resolution of the voxel grid \hat{\mu} due to plane intersection calculations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the voxel grid \hat{\mu} and the ray batch size. The batch size for trilinear interpolation was set to 1.8 \times 10^6 rays, larger than Siddon's 5.5 \times 10^5 due to lower memory overhead per ray. Measured Performance: On a dataset of 40 walnuts with 15 input views, using a single NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, the method achieved SSIM 0.912, PSNR 37.23, MSE 1.43 \times 10^{-5}, and PCC 0.96. The reconstruction runtime was 10.0 minutes for this specific configuration. For 60-view reconstruction, the runtime was 39.1 minutes. Strengths: Faster than Siddon's method; prevents overfitting in sparse-view settings by allowing ground truth pixels to supervise more voxels (including those not directly intersected); approximates second-order effects like X-ray scatter. Limitations: Provides modestly lower quality than Siddon's method in novel view synthesis, particularly in very sparse-view settings (5-20 views) where Siddon's exact geometry yields higher fidelity. This method was introduced in the DiffVox framework for differentiable CBCT reconstruction. It addresses the computational bottleneck of exact ray-voxel intersection (Siddon's method) in differentiable rendering pipelines. By using interpolatory quadrature, it enables a fully differentiable forward model that is linear in sample count, facilitating faster optimization of the voxel grid \hat{\mu}. Differentiable Voxel-based X-ray Rendering Improves Sparse-View 3D CBCT Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2411.19224, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Radial Basis Function Interpolation
head: Kernel-based Interpolation, RBF Interpolation, Radial basis functions (RBFs)
body: Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolation is a method for approximating scalar fields from non-uniform, scattered 3D data points without requiring a structured grid. It solves the problem of visualizing or deforming space data where the underlying domain is irregular or sparse, enabling flexible surface reconstruction and deformation. Unlike grid-dependent trilinear methods, RBFs handle irregular domains effectively by using kernel-based weighting centered at each data site. However, this flexibility comes at the cost of higher computational expense, as exact interpolation requires solving dense linear systems. Inputs: A set of N scattered data points (sites) \mathbf{x}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 with associated scalar values fi (or vector displacements \mathbf{d}i for deformation). Outputs: An interpolated value f(\mathbf{x}) or displacement \mathbf{u}(\mathbf{x}) at any query point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: 1. Sites: Array of N points \mathbf{x}i. 2. Values: Array of N scalar or vector values fi. 3. Kernel Matrix: A dense N \times N matrix \Phi where \Phi{ij} = \phi(\|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{x}j\|). 4. Coefficients: Array of N coefficients \alphai (and potentially polynomial coefficients if a polynomial term is included). Method: The RBF interpolant is defined as a linear combination of radial basis functions centered at the data sites: f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai \phi(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\|) + p(\mathbf{x}) where \phi is the radial basis function kernel, and p(\mathbf{x}) is a low-degree polynomial (often constant or linear) added to ensure solvability and approximation power. Steps: 1. Construct Kernel Matrix: Compute the pairwise distances between all sites and populate the matrix \Phi using the chosen kernel \phi. Common kernels include the Gaussian \phi(r) = e^{-(\epsilon r)^2} or the Multiquadric \phi(r) = \sqrt{1 + (\epsilon r)^2}. 2. Formulate Linear System: For exact interpolation, enforce f(\mathbf{x}j) = fj for all j=1 \dots N. If a polynomial term p(\mathbf{x}) of degree k is used, additional constraints are added to ensure uniqueness (e.g., \sum \alphai = 0 for constant polynomials). The system takes the form: \begin{pmatrix} \Phi & P \\ P^T & 0 \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{\alpha} \\ \mathbf{c} \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \mathbf{f} \\ \mathbf{0} \end{pmatrix} where \mathbf{f} is the vector of target values, \boldsymbol{\alpha} are the RBF coefficients, \mathbf{c} are the polynomial coefficients, and P is a matrix of polynomial basis functions evaluated at the sites. 3. Solve System: Solve the dense linear system for \boldsymbol{\alpha} and \mathbf{c}. This step scales as O(N^3) for direct solvers. 4. Evaluate: For a query point \mathbf{x}, compute the distance vector \mathbf{r}i = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i, evaluate the kernel \phi(\|\mathbf{r}i\|) for all i, and sum the weighted contributions plus the polynomial term: f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai \phi(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\|) + \mathbf{c}^T \mathbf{p}(\mathbf{x}) Parameters: Shape Parameter (\epsilon): Controls the flatness or steepness of the kernel. Typical values depend on the data scale; too small causes ill-conditioning, too large causes over-smoothing. Polynomial Degree: Usually 0 (constant) or 1 (linear). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Computational Cost: Solving the dense system is O(N^3) in time and O(N^2) in memory, making it infeasible for very large N without approximations (e.g., Partition-of-Unity). Ill-conditioning: As the shape parameter \epsilon decreases (flatter basis functions), the condition number of \Phi increases, leading to numerical instability. Boundary Effects: RBFs are global; points far from data sites still contribute, which can cause oscillations or "ringing" artifacts near boundaries of sparse datasets. Multi-level Partition-of-Unity RBF Interpolation (MPU-RBF) is a method for constructing a global scalar field approximation from scattered 3D data points by blending local Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolants. It adapts the algorithmic structure of the Multi-level Partition-of-Unity (MPU) implicits method, replacing the original piecewise quadric approximations with local RBF interpolants to leverage their high interpolation quality at low computational cost. Unlike global RBF methods that require solving a dense linear system over all data points, this method partitions data into manageable clusters using an octree, ensuring scalability for large datasets. A technique to enforce rigid or similarity transformations in RBF interpolation by linearizing non-linear constraints on the polynomial coefficients, preventing the default affine 'squashing' effect during rotations. To enforce similarity, add linear constraints to the RBF system: \gamma0 = \lambda1 and \gamma1 = -\lambda0, where \gammai and \lambdai are polynomial coefficients for x and y components. To correct the scaling factor, regularize the deformation by adjusting the scaling after solving the RBF equations, following [IMH05]. The transformation is defined as x0 = Mx + T, where M^T M = \rho^2 I for similarity (uniform scaling \rho) and M^T M = I for rigid transformation. The linearized constraint vectors are \kappa1 = [1, 0, 0] and \kappa2 = [0, 1, 0]. Rigidity is only loosely enforced due to linearization, and the result contains a uniform scaling factor. A method to simulate cuts and discontinuous deformations by dividing the domain into continuity regions (IP, IQ) and solving separate RBF systems for each, modulated by region indicators. Divide control points into sets \{x1, \dots, xn\} and \{y1, \dots, ym\} corresponding to regions IP and IQ. Solve for coefficients ai and bj in the same way as standard RBF, but apply the resulting displacement only within their respective continuity regions. The displacement D(x) is given by: D(x) = \begin{cases} \sum{i=1}^n ai \phi(\|x - xi\|) + pk(x) & \text{if } IP(x) = 1 \\ \sum{j=1}^m bj \phi(\|x - yj\|) + qk(x) & \text{if } IQ(x) = 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where IP(x) and IQ(x) are indicator functions for the regions. A transparency map A(x) is used to modulate opacity at the cut boundary. A method to fix specific parts of a dataset (rigid features) by modifying the RBF kernel using the unsigned distance transform of the rigid region. The modified kernel is \phiR(x, xi) = D(x)D(xi)\phi(\|x - xi\|), where D(x) is the unsigned distance transform of the rigid part (zero inside the rigid part). This ensures that all points within a rigid part have an RBF contribution of zero, effectively freezing them during deformation. Time Complexity: O(N^3) for solving the dense linear system for N points. Evaluation is O(N) per query point. Memory Complexity: O(N^2) to store the dense kernel matrix \Phi. Measured Performance: Significantly slower than trilinear interpolation due to the dense system solve and lack of grid locality. Strengths: Handles irregular, scattered, and unstructured data; provides smooth, high-quality interpolation; capable of complex deformations (similarity, rigidity, cuts). Limitations: High computational cost and memory usage for large datasets; global support causes slow evaluation and boundary artifacts; sensitive to shape parameter \epsilon. When to Use: Sparse or unstructured datasets where trilinear's regularity assumption fails; applications like mesh deformation, surface reconstruction from scattered points, or when high-quality smooth interpolation is required over irregular domains. When Not to Use: Large-scale structured grid data where trilinear or higher-order grid-based methods are faster and sufficient; real-time applications with very large N without approximation techniques like MPU-RBF. Radial Basis Function interpolation originated in the field of scattered data approximation and has been applied to volume rendering and deformation. It is particularly noted in the context of volume deformation, where it allows for flexible manipulation of volumetric data without a fixed grid. The method is preferred in applications like mesh deformation and biomedical imaging where data is inherently unstructured. The use of linearized constraints for rigidity and distance-modulated kernels for rigid parts was developed to address specific deformation artifacts in volumetric data. trilinear interpolation, https://grokipedia.com/page/Trilinearinterpolation, fetched 2026-10-26 Volume Deformation via Scattered Data Interpolation, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg07/091-098, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Multi-level Partition-of-Unity RBF Interpolation
head: Local RBF Interpolation, MPU Implicit with RBF
body: Multi-level Partition-of-Unity RBF Interpolation (MPU-RBF) is a method for constructing a global scalar field approximation from scattered 3D data points by blending local Radial Basis Function (RBF) interpolants. It adapts the algorithmic structure of the Multi-level Partition-of-Unity (MPU) implicits method, replacing the original piecewise quadric approximations with local RBF interpolants to leverage their high interpolation quality at low computational cost. Unlike global RBF methods that require solving a dense linear system over all data points, this method partitions data into manageable clusters using an octree, ensuring scalability for large datasets. Inputs: A set of scattered sample points P = \{pi\} with associated scalar values \{fi\}, and an octree structure built for regularization. Outputs: A continuous scalar field function F(x) defined for any query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures: Octree Node: Contains the cell centroid, the number of points contained within the cell, and the sphere of influence radius r. Interpolation Node: A selected octree node whose centroid serves as the center for a local RBF interpolant. Local Point Set S: The subset of original sample points pi located within the sphere of influence of an interpolation node. Parameters: \alpha = 0.75: Scaling factor for the sphere of influence radius. c = 0.025: Hardy’s constant for the RBF kernel. N = 100: Maximum number of points allowed in a local matrix solver. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Construction and Radius Calculation: Construct an octree for the data. For each node, compute the number of points in the cell and the radius r of the sphere of influence centered at the node's centroid. The radius is defined as: r = \alpha d where d is the length of the octree node’s diagonal. 2. Local Point Set Collection: For a given interpolation node, identify the set S of original sample points pi that lie within the sphere of influence (distance \le r from the centroid). 3. Threshold Enforcement: If |S| > N, traverse the octree deeper to refine the partition. If a leaf node still contains too many points, augment the tree with further subdivisions until the problem size for the local matrix solver is \le N. 4. Local Interpolant Construction: For each interpolation node, solve for the coefficients \lambdai using the points in S. The local interpolant H(x) is defined by Hardy’s multiquadric RBF: H(x) = \sum{i=1}^{|S|} \lambdai \phii(x) where the basis function is: \phii(x) = \sqrt{|x - pi|^2 + c^2} The coefficients \lambdai are determined by solving the linear system A\lambda = f, where A{ij} = \phij(pi) and f is the vector of scalar values at points in S. 5. Global Approximation Evaluation: To evaluate F(x) at a query point: Identify all interpolation nodes whose spheres of influence contain x. Calculate the contribution Hk(x) of each local interpolant k. Accumulate the sum of weights W(x) = \sumk wk(x) and the sum of weighted contributions C(x) = \sumk wk(x) Hk(x). Normalize the result: F(x) = \frac{C(x)}{W(x)} The weights wk(x) are typically derived from the partition-of-unity property, ensuring smooth blending between local approximations. 6. Efficient Evaluation: The global approximation is evaluated using a recursive routine that traverses the octree, achieving O(\log m) time complexity, where m is the number of interpolation nodes. Pitfalls: Precision: The square root in Hardy’s kernel requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially for points very close to sample locations. Boundary Conditions: The method relies on overlapping spheres of influence to guarantee domain cover; insufficient overlap may lead to gaps in the reconstructed field. Data Usage: Only original sample points are used; no resampling is performed, which avoids bias introduction but requires the original data to be accessible during evaluation. Time Complexity: Evaluation is O(\log m), where m is the number of interpolation nodes. Construction involves solving local linear systems of size at most N \times N, which is constant time relative to the total dataset size. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of interpolation nodes and the storage of the octree and original points. Strengths: High interpolation quality with relatively low computational cost compared to global RBF methods; handles non-uniform, scattered data without requiring a structured grid; scalable to large datasets due to local solving. Limitations: Requires an octree structure; performance depends on the choice of parameters \alpha, c, and N. When to Use: Suitable for isosurface generation and scalar field visualization from large-scale scattered data where global methods are too expensive. The method is based on the Multi-level Partition-of-Unity (MPU) implicits method by Ohtake et al.. It adapts this framework by substituting local quadric approximations with Hardy’s multiquadric RBF interpolants. The approach was developed to address the domain cover problem in isosurface generation for large-scale scattered data visualization. name: Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation
head: 3D Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) Interpolation, Inverse Distance Weighting
body:
Inverse Distance Weighted (IDW) Interpolation is a spatial interpolation method that estimates the value of a continuous scalar field at a query point by computing a weighted average of nearby sample values, where the influence of each sample decreases as its distance from the query point increases. It is chosen when a smooth, non-linear reconstruction is required from sparse or irregular data points (such as drill-hole assays) and when the computational cost of higher-order schemes like tri-linear or tri-cubic interpolation is prohibitive or when the underlying data structure is not a regular grid. Unlike Trilinear Interpolation, which assumes a regular grid and guarantees C^0 continuity along interior faces, IDW is grid-agnostic and does not guarantee continuity across cell boundaries unless extended to neighboring cells. Inputs: A set of N sample points \{Pi\} with associated scalar values \{Vi\}, where Pi = (xi, yi, zi) and Vi is the value at Pi. A query point Q = (xq, yq, zq). Parameters: power: The IDW exponent controlling the rate of decay. Typical value: 2. searchRadius: The maximum Euclidean distance to consider samples. Typical value: 60 world units. maxNeighbors: The maximum number of nearest neighbors to include. Typical value: 16. Outputs: The interpolated scalar value V(Q). Data Structures: A spatial index (e.g., 3D Hash Grid, KD-Tree, or Octree) to efficiently retrieve neighbors within searchRadius or the maxNeighbors closest points. If using the cell-based approach described in, the data is structured as a grid of hexahedral cells, and the query point is first located within a specific cell. Steps: 1. Neighbor Retrieval: Find all sample points Pi such that the Euclidean distance di = \|Q - Pi\| is less than or equal to searchRadius. If maxNeighbors is specified, select only the k \le 	ext{maxNeighbors} points with the smallest di from the retrieved set. If no samples are found within the radius, return a nodata sentinel value (e.g., < -10^{29}). 2. Exact Hit Check: If any sample point Pj coincides exactly with Q (i.e., dj = 0), return Vj immediately. 3. Weight Calculation: For each neighbor i, compute the weight wi using the inverse distance formula: wi =  rac{1}{di^{	ext{power}}} Note: If using the specific cell-based formulation from (where neighbors are the 8 vertices of the containing cell), the weights are computed as: wi =  rac{\prod{k=0, k 
eq i}^{7} [dk(Q)]^2}{\sum{j=0, j 
eq i}^{7} \prod{l=0, l 
eq j}^{7} [dl(Q)]^2} where dk(Q) is the Euclidean distance between the k-th vertex of the cell and Q. This formulation ensures that if Q is at vertex j, wj=1 and all other wi=0. 4. Normalization and Interpolation: Compute the sum of weights W = \sum{i} wi. Compute the interpolated value: V(Q) =  rac{\sum{i} wi Vi}{W} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def idwinterpolate(querypoint, samples, spatialindex, power=2, searchradius=60, maxneighbors=16): """ querypoint: tuple (x, y, z) samples: list of tuples (point, value) spatialindex: object with queryradius and queryknearest methods power: float, IDW exponent searchradius: float, max distance to consider maxneighbors: int, max number of neighbors to use """ # Step 1: Retrieve neighbors # Try to get k-nearest neighbors first if maxneighbors is small and efficient # Otherwise, get all within radius and sort/filter candidates = spatialindex.queryradius(querypoint, searchradius) if not candidates: return -1e30 # Nodata sentinel # If we have more candidates than maxneighbors, select the closest ones if len(candidates) > maxneighbors: # Sort by distance to querypoint candidates.sort(key=lambda s: distance(querypoint, s.point)) candidates = candidates[:maxneighbors] # Step 2: Exact Hit Check for sample in candidates: if distance(querypoint, sample.point) == 0: return sample.value # Step 3 & 4: Weight Calculation and Interpolation totalweight = 0.0 weightedsum = 0.0 for sample in candidates: d = distance(querypoint, sample.point) # Avoid division by zero, though exact hit check above should catch d=0 if d == 0: return sample.value w = 1.0 / (d power) totalweight += w weightedsum += w sample.value if totalweight == 0: return -1e30 # Should not happen if candidates exist and d > 0 return weightedsum / totalweight def distance(p1, p2): return ((p1[0]-p2[0])2 + (p1[1]-p2[1])2 + (p1[2]-p2[2])2)0.5 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Continuity: The basic scheme does not guarantee C^0 continuity along interior faces of the grid. This can be minimized by including all vertices of all cells that contain a point on an interior face, effectively extending the neighbor set beyond the single containing cell. Local Sparsity: Considering only surrounding cells ignores contributions from cells in the original volume that do not include the interpolated point, which can lead to sparse sampling artifacts. Arbitrary Hexahedra: If the underlying cells are arbitrary hexahedra, vertices may be far from the query point, potentially degrading accuracy compared to regular grids. Time Complexity: O(N) for naive search, or O(\log N + k) for spatial index search, where N is the total number of samples and k is the number of neighbors (typically small, e.g., 8-16). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the sample points and the spatial index. Performance: Predictable performance for static datasets using hash grids or KD-trees. The method is computationally lightweight per query compared to tri-cubic interpolation, making it suitable for real-time or interactive visualization of sparse data. Strengths: Works with irregular, non-grid data; simple to implement; computationally efficient; handles sparse data well. Limitations: Does not guarantee continuity across cell boundaries; sensitive to the choice of power and searchRadius; may produce "bullseye" artifacts around sample points if power is too high. When to use: When data is sparse, irregular, or not on a regular grid; when real-time performance is critical; when a smooth, non-linear interpolation is desired without the complexity of higher-order schemes. When not to use: When high-order continuity is required; when the data is on a regular grid and higher-order interpolation (like Trilinear Interpolation) is feasible and preferred for accuracy. Inverse Distance Weighted Interpolation was originally proposed for distance-weighted interpolation schemes in the context of volume rendering and spatial data analysis. The specific weighting scheme used in the cell-based implementation is presented in [BS84]. It has been applied to computational fluid dynamics simulations, such as the "blunt fin" from NASA-Ames Research Center. More recently, it has been implemented in web-based 3D visualization libraries for rendering sparse assay data (e.g., gold assays) as volumetric textures. name: Lanczos Resampling
head: Lanczos kernel
body: Lanczos resampling is an interpolation technique used to resample (downsample or upsample) volumetric data by replacing each selected sample with a translated copy of the Lanczos kernel, which is a limited Sinc function. It is chosen when higher fidelity than linear or cubic interpolation is required, particularly in medical imaging contexts where preserving high-frequency details during compression or reconstruction is critical. It distinguishes itself from its siblings, such as Interpolation Schemes for Volume Rendering and Interpolation Functions for Resampling, by using a windowed sinc function that balances sharpness (low blurring) with the suppression of ringing artifacts compared to a pure sinc filter. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A discrete set of volumetric samples Vi located at grid positions \mathbf{p}i. Query Position: A 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} where the value is needed. Output: The interpolated scalar value V(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: Kernel Order (a): An integer parameter defining the radius of the kernel in voxels. Typical values are a=2 or a=3. Sample Grid: The input volume texture or array. Formula: The Lanczos kernel L(x) is defined as: L(x) = \begin{cases} \text{sinc}\left(\frac{\pi x}{a}\right) \text{sinc}(\pi x) & \text{if } |x| < a \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where: x is the distance from the query position \mathbf{p} to the sample center \mathbf{p}i (i.e., x = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}i\| in the relevant dimension). a is the Lanczos order (radius). \text{sinc}(u) = \frac{\sin(u)}{u}. Note that \text{sinc}(0) = 1. Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Map the world-space or camera-space query position \mathbf{p} to the local coordinate system of the volume data (e.g., normalized [-1, 1] or [0, 1] ranges) to determine the continuous voxel coordinates [Parent]. 2. Neighbor Selection: Identify all sample indices i such that the distance |x| between the query position and the sample center \mathbf{p}i is less than the kernel order a. For a 3D volume, this typically involves a cubic neighborhood of size (2a-1)^3. 3. Weight Calculation: For each selected neighbor i, calculate the distance x along each axis (if separable) or the radial distance. Compute the weight wi = L(x) using the formula above. 4. Summation: Compute the interpolated value: V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i} wi Vi [Parent] Pitfalls: Ringing Artifacts: Like all sinc-based filters, Lanczos resampling can introduce Gibbs phenomenon (ringing) near sharp edges if the kernel order is too high or if the signal is not band-limited. Boundary Conditions: The kernel is zero outside |x| < a. Care must be taken at volume boundaries to avoid accessing out-of-bounds memory or applying incorrect weights. Precision: The \text{sinc}(0) case must be handled explicitly to avoid division by zero. A technique to perform 3D Lanczos resampling on GPUs that lack native 3D render targets by decomposing the 3D filter into sequential 1D filters along the major axes, using 2D render targets and texture shifting. This approach is necessary because native 3D render targets were not supported at the time of the source's writing. Steps (for Lanczos Order N=3): 1. Z-Axis Pass: Use the 3D input texture six times, shifted each time by one voxel along the z-axis. Use two weighting textures for the six weights. Sum the weighted input voxels and store the result in a 6 \times 6 \times 6 intermediate output texture. 2. Y-Axis Pass: Perform the same operation for the y-axis using the 6 previously generated intermediate textures, leading to six new intermediate output textures. 3. X-Axis Pass: Use these textures, each shifted by one pixel along the x-axis, leading to the final texture. Parameters: Lanczos Order N: Determines the number of passes and texture shifts. For N=3, 43 passes are required (36+6+1). For N=2, 21 passes are required. Pitfalls: Hardware Limitations: The split-axis approach is a workaround for GPU limitations regarding 3D render targets. It requires significant memory bandwidth and multiple rendering passes, which can be computationally expensive. Time Complexity: O(a^3) per sample, where a is the kernel order. The high-quality GPU variant requires O(N^3) passes for order N if implemented naively, but the split-axis method reduces this to a fixed number of passes per axis (e.g., 43 passes for N=3). Memory Complexity: O(1) for standard CPU/GPU texture sampling. The split-axis GPU method requires storing intermediate textures, increasing memory usage proportional to the number of passes and texture dimensions. Performance: Provides higher PSNR (Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio) compared to lower-order interpolations, making it suitable for high-resolution medical image compression and reconstruction. However, it is computationally more expensive than linear or cubic interpolation. Strengths: Sharp reconstruction with minimal blurring; good balance between aliasing and smoothing. Limitations: Susceptible to ringing artifacts; computationally intensive for high orders or large volumes. Lanczos resampling is named after the mathematician Cornelius Lanczos. It is widely used in signal processing and image resampling. In the context of volume rendering, it has been applied to compress high-resolution medical images using Implicit Neural Representations (INRs) like SIREN, where it serves as a preprocessing step to downsample HR images before neural network training. It has also been used in Fourier volume rendering on the GPU to implement windowed-sinc functions for frequency space extraction. A Novel Implicit Neural Representation for Volume Data., https://eprints.bournemouth.ac.uk/38355/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Fourier volume rendering on the GPU using a split-..., https://www.researchgate.net/publication/220838994FouriervolumerenderingontheGPUusingasplit-stream-FFT, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial)

name: Interpolation Functions for Resampling
head: Cubic-spline
body: This family defines the mathematical kernels used to estimate continuous volume values V(\mathbf{p}) from discrete samples Vi for edge reconstruction and shading. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific focus on the trade-off between grey-value reconstruction fidelity and edge location accuracy, particularly in medical imaging contexts where negative values or gradient errors produce visible artifacts. All methods in this family operate on the principle that a continuous function V(\mathbf{p}) must be approximated from a discrete set of samples Vi located at grid positions \mathbf{p}i. The core mechanism involves: 1. Query Positioning: Determining the 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} where a value is needed. This may involve converting depth parameters to physical distances or warping coordinates for neural encodings. 2. Kernel/Weight Application: Computing weights wi(\mathbf{p}) based on the distance between \mathbf{p} and the sample centers \mathbf{p}i. The interpolated value is: V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i} wi(\mathbf{p}) Vi The choice of kernel (e.g., linear, cubic, inverse distance) determines the spatial extent (number of neighbors) and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring). 3. Coordinate Transformation: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the local coordinate system of the volume data (e.g., normalized [-1, 1] or [0, 1] ranges) before interpolation. Linear interpolation uses a triangular kernel with support over two adjacent voxels. It provides a balance between computational speed and smoothness. In the context of edge location estimation, linear interpolation performs better than cubic-spline but worse than quadratic re-sampling. It does not produce negative values in step responses, making it safe for data where the modulus operator is applied (e.g., MR data). Quadratic re-sampling employs a kernel with support over three voxels. It is characterized by lower sensitivity to noise compared to linear and cubic-spline functions. Crucially, for edge location estimation, quadratic re-sampling yields the smallest error, outperforming both linear and cubic methods. However, standard quadratic kernels may not be interpolatory (i.e., they may not pass exactly through the sample points) depending on the specific formulation used in the source. Cubic-spline interpolation uses a kernel with support over four voxels, offering higher-order continuity. While often considered the "best" for general grey-value reconstruction fidelity, it is problematic for edge location accuracy and specific data types. It causes overshoot in step responses, producing negative values which are invalid for MR data due to the complex modulus operator. Consequently, it yields the largest edge location error among the compared functions. This is not a kernel itself, but a specific evaluation method and application of interpolation functions for determining the position of a 1D step edge. Definition: It estimates the edge position by finding the coordinate where the re-sampled grey-value equals the arithmetic mean of the grey-values on both sides of the step. Steps: 1. Re-sample discrete samples across the step using an interpolation function. 2. Compute the mean of the grey-values on the low and high sides of the step. 3. Locate the coordinate where the re-sampled curve intersects this mean value. Comparison: Quadratic re-sampling yields the smallest edge location error, linear interpolation performs better than cubic-spline but worse than quadratic, and cubic-spline interpolation yields the largest error. The analysis of these interpolation functions originated in the context of medical image processing, specifically for iso-surface volume rendering and edge reconstruction in CT and MR data. The work highlights that while cubic-spline is often preferred for visual smoothness, it introduces artifacts (ripples) and inaccuracies in edge detection due to overshoot and sample-distance-dependent errors. The error in edge location estimation grows approximately with the third power of the sample distance, necessitating careful consideration of sampling rates relative to the point-spread function width.
