name: Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching)
head: God Rays, Light Shafts, VolumetricLightURP
body: Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching) is a real-time post-processing technique for rendering volumetric light scattering (crepuscular rays) in the Unity Universal Render Pipeline (URP) by performing per-pixel raymarching through a main light's shadow map. It approximates single in-scattering from a single directional light source, modulated by a Henyey-Greenstein phase function and estimated occlusion derived from realtime shadow sampling. Unlike slice-based volume rendering or complex shadow-map methods, it requires no preprocessing, extra scene geometry, or high fill rate, making it significantly cheaper than full volumetric ray marching. However, it is limited to a single light source and lacks full volumetric depth information, leading to artifacts when foreground objects obscure background light shafts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Screen-space position (fragment world position), camera world position, main light realtime shadow map, light position, light color/intensity, and material parameters (density, step count, max distance, scattering multiplier). Output: Accumulated volumetric light color and alpha, added additively to the screen buffer. Data Structures: Shader Constants: BaseColor (float4): Base color of the volumetric effect. Default: (1, 1, 1, 1). Density (float): Density of the volume. Default: 0.5. Range: 0 to 1. StepCount (int): Number of raymarching steps. Default: 64. Range: 16 to 128. MaxDistance (float): Maximum distance for raymarching. Default: 20. Scattering (float): Scattering multiplier for the final color. Default: 1.2. LightPos (float4): Position of the light source in world space (xyz position, w=1). Updated dynamically. LightColor (float4): Color of the light source multiplied by intensity. Updated dynamically. Vertex Shader Output: positionHCS (float4): Clip space position. positionWS (float3): World space position of the fragment. Numbered Steps: 1. Vertex Transformation: Input vertex position in object space (positionOS). Transform to clip space (positionCS) and world space (positionWS) using standard Unity vertex utilities. Pass positionWS to the fragment shader via TEXCOORD0. 2. Ray Direction Calculation: In the fragment shader, retrieve the camera world position (camPos). Calculate the ray direction by normalizing the vector from the camera to the fragment's world position: \text{rayDir} = \text{normalize}(\text{positionWS} - \text{camPos}) 3. Initialization: Initialize accumulation variable accum = 0.0. Determine the number of steps: steps = max(StepCount, 1). This prevents division by zero or invalid loop behavior if StepCount is less than 1. Calculate step size: stepSize = MaxDistance / steps. 4. Raymarching Loop: Loop i from 0 to steps - 1. Calculate distance along the ray: dist = i stepSize. Calculate sample position in world space: \text{samplePos} = \text{rayOrigin} + \text{rayDir} \times \text{dist} (Note: rayOrigin is typically the camera position or the near plane intersection, but in this specific URP post-process implementation, the ray originates from the camera and marches through the screen space volume defined by MaxDistance.) 5. Shadow Sampling: Transform samplePos to shadow coordinates: shadowCoord = TransformWorldToShadowCoord(samplePos). Sample the main light realtime shadow: shadow = MainLightRealtimeShadow(shadowCoord). This value represents the occlusion factor (1.0 if lit, 0.0 if shadowed, or intermediate values for soft shadows). 6. Phase Function Calculation: Calculate the light direction from the sample position to the light position: \text{lightDir} = \text{normalize}(\LightPos.xyz - \text{samplePos}) Calculate the cosine of the angle between the ray direction and the light direction: \cos\theta = \text{dot}(\text{rayDir}, \text{lightDir}) Compute the Henyey-Greenstein phase function with hardcoded asymmetry parameter g = 0.35: P(\theta) = \frac{1 - g^2}{(1 + g^2 - 2g \cos\theta)^{1.5}} Where g = 0.35. 7. Accumulation: Add to accum: \text{accum} += \text{shadow} \times P(\theta) \times \Density \times \text{stepSize} 8. Final Color Computation: Compute the final light amount: lightAmount = accum. Multiply LightColor.rgb by lightAmount and Scattering. Compute alpha: alpha = saturate(lightAmount). Output the result as an additive blend to the screen buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Attributes { float3 positionOS; }; struct Varyings { float4 positionHCS: SVPOSITION; float3 positionWS: TEXCOORD0; }; Varyings vert(Attributes IN) { Varyings OUT; // Standard Unity vertex transformation VertexPositionInputs pos = GetVertexPositionInputs(IN.positionOS); OUT.positionHCS = pos.positionCS; OUT.positionWS = pos.positionWS; return OUT; } uniform float4 BaseColor; uniform float Density; uniform int StepCount; uniform float MaxDistance; uniform float Scattering; uniform float4 LightPos; uniform float4 LightColor; uniform float3 camPos; // Camera world position float HenyeyGreenstein(float cosTheta, float g) { float g2 = g g; return (1.0 - g2) / pow(1.0 + g2 - 2.0 g cosTheta, 1.5); } float4 frag(Varyings IN): SVTARGET { float3 rayDir = normalize(IN.positionWS - camPos); int steps = max(StepCount, 1); float stepSize = MaxDistance / steps; float accum = 0.0; for (int i = 0; i < steps; i++) { float dist = i stepSize; float3 samplePos = camPos + rayDir dist; // Shadow sampling float4 shadowCoord = TransformWorldToShadowCoord(samplePos); float shadow = MainLightRealtimeShadow(shadowCoord); // Light direction float3 lightDir = normalize(LightPos.xyz - samplePos); float cosTheta = dot(rayDir, lightDir); // Phase function float phase = HenyeyGreenstein(cosTheta, 0.35); // Accumulation accum += shadow phase Density stepSize; } float lightAmount = accum; float3 finalColor = LightColor.rgb lightAmount Scattering; float alpha = saturate(lightAmount); return float4(finalColor, alpha); } Screen-Space God Rays is a real-time post-processing technique that approximates volumetric light scattering (crepuscular rays) by performing per-pixel additive sampling of an image light source in screen space. It simplifies the volume rendering equation to estimate single in-scattering from a single light source, modulated by an estimated occlusion factor derived from radial sampling. Unlike slice-based volume rendering or shadow-map methods, it requires no preprocessing, extra scene geometry, or high fill rate, making it significantly cheaper than volumetric ray marching. However, it is limited to single light sources and lacks full volumetric depth information, leading to artifacts when foreground objects obscure background light shafts. A post-processing technique that renders volumetric light shafts (sun shafts) by marching a view ray through a sun shadow map, accumulating in-scattered light where the ray is lit and no light where it is shadowed, modulated by ground-hugging haze density. It differs from screen-space alternatives by relying on a dedicated shadow map for occlusion rather than screen-space depth, allowing for more accurate volumetric occlusion from geometry outside the current view frustum, while trading off higher memory bandwidth for the shadow map. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels (screen resolution) and S is the number of raymarching steps (StepCount). Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, plus the memory cost of the main light's realtime shadow map. Measured Performance: In a voxel engine benchmark, enabling god rays added 2.30 ms to a 5.0 ms frame. Performance in URP depends on StepCount and shadow map resolution. Strengths: Lightweight, customizable, URP compatible, no preprocessing required, good for stylized effects. Limitations: Limited to a single directional light, no support for complex volume textures, artifacts when foreground objects obscure background light shafts due to lack of full volumetric depth. When to Use: Real-time stylized atmospheric lighting, fog beams, god rays in URP projects where performance is critical and single-light approximation is acceptable. When Not to Use: Scenes with multiple light sources, complex volumetric clouds, or when accurate occlusion from geometry outside the view frustum is required. Volumetric light shafts, commonly known as "God Rays," are a technique for rendering volumetric light scattering (fog beams, atmospheric lighting) in Unity URP using raymarching in a custom shader with main light shadow sampling. A C# controller is often used for dynamic light color, density, and quality settings. The technique is disabled by default in some engines due to performance cost. The Henyey-Greenstein phase function is commonly used to model the scattering behavior. name: Screen-Space God Rays
head: Screen-Space Radial Blur, Screen-Space Light Shafts, Radial Blur God Rays
body: Screen-Space God Rays is a real-time post-processing technique that approximates volumetric light scattering (crepuscular rays) by performing per-pixel additive sampling of an image light source in screen space. It builds on Volumetric Light Shafts (URP Raymarching) by simplifying the volume rendering equation to estimate single in-scattering from a single light source, modulated by an estimated occlusion factor derived from radial sampling. Unlike slice-based volume rendering or shadow-map methods, it requires no preprocessing, extra scene geometry, or high fill rate, making it significantly cheaper than volumetric ray marching. However, it is limited to single light sources and lacks full volumetric depth information, leading to artifacts when foreground objects obscure background light shafts. The method operates in three passes: an occlusion pre-pass, a radial blur accumulation pass, and a compositing pass. Inputs: scenetexture: The rendered scene color buffer or occlusion map. lightposscreen: The 2D screen-space coordinates of the light source (UV space [0,1] or NDC [-1,1]). density: Controls sample separation and ray spread. decay: Exponential falloff factor per sample. weight: Per-sample intensity multiplier. exposure: Final output brightness multiplier. numsamples: Number of iterations for the radial accumulation loop. Outputs: finalcolor: The final composited color with god rays added. The technique uses standard 2D textures (sampler2D) for the scene buffer and occlusion map. Uniforms are passed to the fragment shader. No complex volumetric grids or sparse structures are used. 1. Light Position Projection: Project the 3D world position of the light source into screen space. Transform the light's world position by the View-Projection matrix. Perform perspective division by w to obtain NDC coordinates. Scale and bias to the texture coordinate range [0, 1] (or [-1, 1] depending on implementation). Edge Case: If the light is behind the camera (clip w \le 0 or very small), clamp the screen position to the center of the screen (0.5, 0.5) and mark the light as not in front. 2. Occlusion Pre-Pass (Optional but Recommended): To improve occlusion accuracy, render the scene geometry as solid black and the light source as a bright shape (circle/sphere) into a separate render target. This creates a binary-like occlusion map where bright pixels indicate direct visibility of the light and black pixels indicate occlusion by geometry. This pass reduces streaking artifacts caused by surface texture variations in the main scene buffer. 3. Radial Accumulation (Fragment Shader): For each pixel in the output texture: Calculate the direction vector from the current pixel's texture coordinate (uv) to the light's screen position (light\pos). Compute the step size (delta\uv) by scaling the direction vector by the density and dividing by the number of samples. Initialize the accumulated color to zero (if using occlusion map) or the base scene color (if using direct scene buffer). Initialize the illumination decay factor to 1.0. Iterate num\samples times: Step the texture coordinate backwards along the direction vector: uv \leftarrow uv - delta\uv. Sample the texture at the new coordinate. Clamp coordinates to [0, 1] to handle boundary conditions. Multiply the sample color by the current illumination decay and the weight constant. Add the result to the accumulated color. Update the illumination decay: illumination \leftarrow illumination \times decay. The accumulation approximates the integral of in-scattered light, where the decay simulates absorption/scattering over distance. 4. Compositing: If an occlusion map was used in Step 2, add the accumulated god ray color to the original scene color using additive blending. Multiply the final color by the exposure constant. Output the result with alpha 1.0. The following is a self-contained Python-like implementation for the radial accumulation pass, assuming an occlusion map input. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegodrays(uv, lightpos, density, decay, weight, exposure, numsamples, texturesampler): # Calculate step vector from current pixel to light source deltauv = (uv - lightpos) density / numsamples currentuv = uv illumination = 1.0 color = vec3(0.0) # Initialize to zero for occlusion map; use texturesampler(uv) for direct scene buffer for i in range(numsamples): currentuv = currentuv - deltauv # Clamp to [0, 1] to handle screen boundaries samp = texturesampler(clamp(currentuv, 0.0, 1.0)) samp = samp illumination weight color = color + samp illumination = illumination decay return color exposure If using the direct scene buffer without an occlusion pre-pass, the initialization changes to color = texturesampler(uv) and the accumulation adds to this base color. NUMSAMPLES: Controls sampling density and smoothness. Typical value: 64 or 100. Higher values increase cost. density: Controls the separation between samples. Higher values decrease separation, resulting in brighter rays covering a shorter range. Typical value: 0.92. decay: Exponential falloff factor per sample. Range [0, 1]. Values close to 1.0 (e.g., 0.97) produce long, gradual rays; lower values produce short, punchy rays. Typical value: 0.96815. weight: Per-sample contribution factor. Typical value: 0.1 or 0.58. exposure: Final color multiplier. Typical value: 0.3. Light Behind Camera: If the light is behind the camera, the screen position projection may be invalid. Handle by clamping to screen center and disabling the effect or returning a default value. Off-Screen Lights: The technique only works for visible light sources. If the light moves off-screen, the rays disappear or become distorted. Depth Artifacts: Since the method lacks full volumetric depth, light shafts from background objects may appear in front of foreground objects when the light source is relatively near. This is often perceived as a lens flare effect but can break immersion. Streaking: Sampling the main scene buffer directly can cause streaks due to high-frequency surface textures. Using an occlusion pre-pass (black geometry, bright light) mitigates this. Single Light Source: The method assumes single scattering from a single light source. It does not handle multiple light sources or complex multiple scattering effects. A post-processing technique that draws light sources to a separate render target, then processes this target using a post-processing shader to create light scattering, merging it with the back buffer. Designed originally for one very strong light. Main loop: For each pixel, get texCoord. For each light, if Type == SPOTLIGHT: Calculate deltaTexCoord = (texCoord - projectedLightPos.xy) / (NUMSAMPLES Density). Initialize illuminationDecay = 1.0. Loop j from 0 to NUMSAMPLES-1: Decrease texCoord by deltaTexCoord. Sample inputTexture at modifiedPixel. Add to color: color += sample illuminationDecay Weight. Update decay: illuminationDecay = Decay. Add result to output: result += color Exposure. Pitfall: Applying this method to multiple lights resulted in a simple 'Blur' of the light source map rather than correct volumetric scattering. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the image resolution (pixels) and M is the number of samples (NUM\SAMPLES). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the temporary render targets (occlusion map, god ray buffer). Performance: Very fast. Requires only two extra render passes (occlusion pre-pass and radial blur) and a handful of texture samples per pixel. It is significantly cheaper than volumetric ray marching. Strengths: Simple to implement, low hardware requirements, no preprocessing, works with arbitrary scene complexity. Limitations: Limited to single light sources, inaccurate occlusion estimation (screen-space only), depth artifacts (background rays in front of foreground objects), fails if light is off-screen. When to Use: Real-time rendering on mobile or lower-end hardware, scenes with a dominant single light source (e.g., sun), where performance is critical and perfect physical accuracy is not required. When Not to Use: Scenes with multiple light sources, scenes requiring accurate volumetric depth interaction, or when the light source is frequently off-screen. The technique was published by Kenny Mitchell in 2007 in GPU Gems 3 as "Volumetric Light Scattering as a Post-Process". It gained widespread adoption in the gaming industry, notably in Crysis (2007), setting a standard for high-end PC games. It dominated god ray implementations for over a decade due to its speed and simplicity. The method approximates the volume rendering equation by simplifying the in-scattering term and estimating occlusion through radial sampling in screen space.
