name: Volumetric Sun Shafts (God Rays)
head: Haze volumetrics, In-scattered light shafts
body: A post-processing technique that renders volumetric light shafts (sun shafts) by marching a view ray through a sun shadow map, accumulating in-scattered light where the ray is lit and no light where it is shadowed, modulated by ground-hugging haze density. It differs from screen-space alternatives by relying on a dedicated shadow map for occlusion rather than screen-space depth, allowing for more accurate volumetric occlusion from geometry outside the current view frustum, while trading off higher memory bandwidth for the shadow map. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Depth buffer, inverse projection matrix, inverse view matrix, sun shadow map (containing lit/shadowed status), sun color, sun direction, ground plane height, and a global intensity multiplier. Outputs: A post-processing texture containing the accumulated sun shafts, composited over the scene. Data Structures: VolumetricPass Target: A render target (WebGLRenderTarget) with HalfFloatType precision, no depth buffer, sized at half the screen resolution (e.g., if screen is W \times H, target is \frac{W}{2} \times \frac{H}{2}). Shadow Map: A texture storing depth or binary lit/shadowed status for the sun light source. Parameters: STEPS: Number of march steps, set to 16. uIntensity: Global intensity multiplier, calculated as 0.07 \times \text{strength}. uGround: Height of the ground plane for density calculation, passed as a uniform. MARCHLENGTH: The last 32 units of the ray are used for marching, or 0 if the ray is shorter than 32 units. Algorithm Steps: 1. Resolution Reduction: Render the effect at half resolution to quarter the per-pixel shadow-map sampling cost, relying on the soft nature of the haze effect to hide aliasing. 2. Jittering: To hide banding artifacts in the volumetric march, jitter the start position of the ray march using interleaved gradient noise. 3. Ray Reconstruction: For each pixel, reconstruct the world position from the depth buffer using the inverse projection and view matrices. 4. Ray Definition: Compute the view ray direction \mathbf{rd} from the camera position to the reconstructed world position and its length L. 5. March Setup: Determine the march start distance as the last 32 units of the ray (or 0 if L < 32). Calculate the step length \Delta s based on 16 steps over the march length: \Delta s = \frac{\text{MARCH\LENGTH}}{\text{STEPS}} 6. Integration Loop: Loop STEPS (16) times: a. Compute sample position \mathbf{p} along the ray. b. Transform \mathbf{p} to shadow map space. c. Determine if the sample is lit by checking shadow map bounds and depth. Let S \in \{0, 1\} be the shadow factor (1 if lit, 0 if shadowed). d. Calculate ground-hugging density \rho using exponential falloff based on sample height y relative to ground level uGround: \rho = e^{-k(y - uGround)} (Note: The exact constant k is not specified in the sources.) e. Apply forward scattering phase function P(\theta), which is brighter when looking toward the sun. f. Scale the contribution by distance attenuation and density. g. Accumulate the result: Accum += S \cdot \rho \cdot P(\theta) \cdot \text{attenuation}. 7. Output: Output final color as sun color multiplied by the accumulated amount, phase, and intensity uIntensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumetricsunshafts(depthbuffer, invproj, invview, shadowmap, suncolor, sundir, uground, strength): # Parameters STEPS = 16 MARCHLENGTH = 32.0 uintensity = 0.07 strength # Output target is half resolution outwidth = depthbuffer.width // 2 outheight = depthbuffer.height // 2 output = createtexture(outwidth, outheight, type=HalfFloatType, depth=False) for y in range(outheight): for x in range(outwidth): # 1. Reconstruct world position from depth # Note: Standard reconstruction from depth buffer using invproj and invview # This step assumes a helper function to unpack depth and apply matrices worldpos = reconstructworldpos(depthbuffer, x, y, invproj, invview) # 2. Compute ray camerapos = getcameraposition() raydir = normalize(worldpos - camerapos) raylen = length(worldpos - camerapos) # 3. Determine march length marchlen = min(raylen, MARCHLENGTH) if marchlen <= 0: output[x, y] = vec3(0.0) continue steplen = marchlen / STEPS # 4. Jitter start position to hide banding # Interleaved gradient noise function jitter = interleavedgradientnoise(x, y) startoffset = jitter steplen accumulatedlight = vec3(0.0) # 5. March loop for i in range(STEPS): # Sample position t = startoffset + i steplen samplepos = camerapos + raydir t # Transform to shadow map space shadowuv = transformtoshadowspace(samplepos, shadowmapmatrix) # Check shadow # S is 1 if lit, 0 if shadowed S = sampleshadow(shadowmap, shadowuv) # Ground-hugging density # Exponential falloff based on height relative to ground heightdiff = samplepos.y - uground # Assuming a decay constant k, not specified in sources # Using a typical value for haze if k is missing, but strictly: # density = exp(-k heightdiff) # Since k is not given, we note it as a parameter density = exp(-0.5 max(0.0, heightdiff)) # Phase function (forward scattering) # Brighter when looking toward sun costheta = dot(raydir, sundir) phase = forwardscatteringphase(costheta) # Distance attenuation (simplified, exact formula not specified) attenuation = 1.0 / (t t + 1.0) accumulatedlight += S density phase attenuation steplen # 6. Output output[x, y] = suncolor accumulatedlight uintensity return output Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Banding: Banding artifacts in the volumetric march are hidden by jittering the start position using interleaved gradient noise. Short Rays: If the ray length is less than 32 units, the march length is 0, and no light is accumulated. Resolution: Running at half resolution is critical for performance; running at full resolution would significantly increase cost without proportional visual benefit due to the soft nature of the effect. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot \text{STEPS}), where W and H are the output resolution (half screen) and STEPS is 16. The cost is dominated by shadow map lookups. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the output texture (half float, 3 channels) plus the shadow map size. Performance: Runs at half resolution to reduce cost, relying on the soft nature of the haze effect. Strengths: Accurate volumetric occlusion from shadow maps, allowing shafts to be cast by geometry outside the view frustum. Limitations: Requires a dedicated shadow map and post-processing pass. Performance scales with resolution and step count. This technique is part of the volumetric rendering pipeline in a custom WebAssembly-based voxel engine, specifically implemented in src/volumetric.ts. It is designed to render atmospheric lighting effects in a browser environment. 12.8B destructible voxels rendered in the browser with Rust WASM custom engine, https://github.com/cktang88/2.5d-experiment, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Volume Rendering (GLSL)
head: Fragment Shader Ray Marching, GLSL Ray Marching Volume Rendering, GPU Ray Marching, GPU-Based Ray Marching, Ray Marching on the GPU, Ray Marching with Trilinear Interpolation, vol-fs.glsl raymarch, vol-fs2.glsl raymarch
body: Ray Marching Volume Rendering is a direct volume rendering technique that discretizes viewing rays into fixed steps to sample a 3D texture, accumulating color and opacity via front-to-back compositing within a fragment shader. It solves the problem of real-time volumetric visualization by performing the entire rendering integral in a single pass on the GPU, avoiding the memory bandwidth bottlenecks of slice-based methods like Shear-Warp. Unlike its siblings, it processes rays independently, enabling optimizations such as early ray termination, and is generally faster than Shear-Warp for equivalent visual quality. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D volume texture (density/scalar field), a transfer function (optional, for color mapping), camera position and orientation matrices, and a bounding box defining the volume extent (typically a unit cube centered at origin or [0,1]^3). Outputs: A final pixel color (vec4) with accumulated alpha. Data Structures: Volume Texture: Stored as a 3D texture (sampler3D) or a 2D texture atlas where slices are packed. If using a 2D atlas, the z-coordinate is mapped to slice index. Uniforms: uvolumesize (ivec3): Dimensions of the volume. umatrixtranslation (mat4): World-to-local transform. umatrixcameratranslation (mat4): Camera-to-world transform. uTexDim (vec3): Texture dimensions (width, height, depth). uTMK / uTMK2 (float): Transmittance multiplier constant for exponential absorption. uenablemaxvaluesampling (int): 1 for max-value sampling, 0 for standard compositing. MAXSTEPS (int): Maximum iteration count (e.g., 128, 200, 256). STEPSIZE (float): Fixed step distance (e.g., 0.01). TMMIN (float): Minimum transmittance threshold for early termination (e.g., 0.25 or 0.0). Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Read volume data from disk and estimate normals if required for shading. 2. Ray Setup: Compute ray origin in local volume space: rayOrigin = (invModel vec4(cameraPos, 1.0)).xyz. Compute ray direction in camera space: rayDircam = normalize(camrelpos.xyz). Transform ray direction to local volume space: rayDirlocal = normalize((camToLocal vec4(rayDircam, 0.0)).xyz). Alternatively, compute direction as normalize(rayOrigin - cameraPos). 3. Ray-Box Intersection: Define bounding box: boxMin = vec3(-0.5), boxMax = vec3(0.5) (or [0,1]). Compute intersection interval [tMin, tMax] using the slab method: invDir = 1.0 / (rayDir + \epsilon) t0s = (boxMin - rayOrigin) invDir t1s = (boxMax - rayOrigin) invDir tSmaller = min(t0s, t1s) tLarger = max(t0s, t1s) tMin = max(max(tSmaller.x, tSmaller.y), max(tSmaller.z, 0.0)) tMax = min(min(tLarger.x, tLarger.y), tLarger.z) If tMin >= tMax, discard the fragment (ray misses volume). Clamp tMin to 0.0. 4. Step Size Calculation: Fixed Step: Use a constant STEPSIZE (e.g., 0.01) or derive from MAXSTEPS and diagonal length: gStepSize = sqrt(3.0) / float(MAXSTEPS). Voxel-Aligned Step: Calculate dt to ensure at least one sample per voxel dimension: size = u\volume\size abs(rayDir\local) dt\vec = 1.0 / size dt = min(dt\vec.x, min(dt\vec.y, dt\vec.z)). 5. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize t = tMin, accumulatedColor = vec4(0.0), tm = 1.0 (transmittance). Loop for i from 0 to MAXSTEPS while t < tMax: a. Sample Position: pos = rayOrigin + t rayDirlocal. b. Texture Sampling: Map pos to texture coordinates (0.0 to 1.0): samplePos = pos + vec3(0.5). If using 2D atlas: Calculate zSlice = (1.0 - pos.y) (uTexDim.z - 1.0), sample two slices with texture2D, and lerp using fract(zSlice). Read density: density = texture(volumeTexture, samplePos).r. c. Color/Alpha Mapping: Map density to color: voxelcolor = texture(transferfn, vec2(density, 0.5)). Calculate alpha contribution: a = density voxelcolor.a. (Note: applies an opacity correction a{corrected} = 1.0 - (1.0 - a{val})^{dt\scale}.) d. Compositing: Standard Front-to-Back: accumulatedColor.rgb += (1.0 - accumulatedColor.a) a voxel\color.rgb accumulatedColor.a += (1.0 - accumulatedColor.a) a. Max-Value Sampling: If a > accumulatedColor.a, update accumulatedColor.rgb = voxelcolor.rgb a and accumulatedColor.a = max(a, accumulatedColor.a). Lighting (Optional): Compute light direction ld, light transmittance ltm, and add: col += (1.0 - dtm) uColor2 uLightC[k] tm ltm. e. Update Transmittance: tm = exp(-uTMK density step). f. Advance Ray: t += step. g. Early Termination: If accumulatedColor.a >= 0.95, break loop. If tm < TMMIN, break loop. If pos is outside bounds, break loop. 6. Final Output: Compute final alpha: alpha = 1.0 - tm. Return vec4(accumulatedColor.rgb / alpha, alpha). Discard if FragColor.a <= 0.001. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarch(volumetexture, transferfn, camerapos, invmodel, camtolocal, boxmin, boxmax, maxsteps, stepsize, tmmin, utmk, uenablemaxvaluesampling): # 1. Ray Setup rayorigin = (invmodel @ vec4(camerapos, 1.0)).xyz raydircam = normalize(vec3(0, 0, -1)) # Assuming camera looks down -Z, or use camrelpos raydirlocal = normalize((camtolocal @ vec4(raydircam, 0.0)).xyz) # 2. Ray-Box Intersection invdir = 1.0 / (raydirlocal + 0.0000001) # Epsilon for division by zero t0s = (boxmin - rayorigin) invdir t1s = (boxmax - rayorigin) invdir tsmaller = min(t0s, t1s) tlarger = max(t0s, t1s) tmin = max(max(tsmaller.x, tsmaller.y), max(tsmaller.z, 0.0)) tmax = min(min(tlarger.x, tlarger.y), tlarger.z) if tmin >= tmax: return None # Discard fragment tmin = max(tmin, 0.0) traveldistance = tmax - tmin step = stepsize # Or traveldistance / maxsteps # 3. Initialization accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) tm = 1.0 t = tmin # 4. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(maxsteps): if t >= tmax: break pos = rayorigin + t raydirlocal samplepos = pos + vec3(0.5) # Offset for texture coords # Sample volume density = volumetexture.sample(samplepos).r # Map to color voxelcolor = transferfn.sample(vec2(density, 0.5)) a = density voxelcolor.a # Compositing if uenablemaxvaluesampling == 1: if a > accumulatedcolor.a: accumulatedcolor.rgb = voxelcolor.rgb a accumulatedcolor.a = max(a, accumulatedcolor.a) else: accumulatedcolor.rgb += (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) a voxelcolor.rgb accumulatedcolor.a += (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) a # Update transmittance tm = exp(-utmk density step) # Advance t += step # Early Termination if accumulatedcolor.a >= 0.95: break if tm < tmmin: break # 5. Final Output alpha = 1.0 - tm if alpha <= 0.001: return None # Discard return vec4(accumulatedcolor.rgb / alpha, alpha) Parameters: MAXSTEPS: 128 (vol-fs.glsl), 200 (vol-fs2.glsl), 256. STEPSIZE: 0.01. TMMIN: 0.25 (vol-fs.glsl), 0.0 (vol-fs2.glsl). Early Ray Termination Threshold: 0.95. Sampling Rate (s): In Shear-Warp context, equivalent to virtual slices; for Ray Marching, this corresponds to MAXSTEPS or inverse step size. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: Ray direction components can be zero; handle with epsilon in invDir. Aliasing: Uniform fixed-step sampling causes aliasing artifacts if the sampling rate is too low. Visible Slices: Low sampling rates make individual slices visible; solved by increasing steps or using interpolation. Texture Coordinate Layout: Non-standard layouts (e.g., z-up in tex coords) require specific handling in sampleVolTex. Adaptive stepping based on density gradients rather than fixed intervals. Choose when volume density varies significantly and uniform sampling wastes compute. Link Marching based on density thresholds rather than fixed steps. Choose when sparse volumes benefit from skipping empty regions. Link Analytical integration over steps. Choose when exact integration over fixed intervals is required for high accuracy. Link Ray marching for light scattering in URP. Choose when rendering volumetric light effects in Unity's Universal Render Pipeline. Link Specific optimizations for cloud volumes. Choose when rendering large-scale atmospheric phenomena. Link Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D volume texture, where V is the number of voxels. Measured Performance: On a 3.8GHz Pentium 4 with GeForce FX7950 GX2, GPU Ray Marching achieved 44 fps for a 512x512x73 Knee model at 500 steps, compared to 134 fps for Shear-Warp at sampling rate 1, but Ray Marching at 400 steps (48 fps) was faster than Shear-Warp at sampling rate 10 (10 fps). Scaling: Frame rate drops linearly with increased steps or sampling rate. Strengths: Single-pass rendering, independent ray processing allows early termination and empty space skipping, higher quality than low-rate Shear-Warp. Limitations: Aliasing artifacts at low sampling rates, performance degrades with high step counts, fixed step size may oversample empty space or undersample dense regions. When to Use: Real-time visualization on standard PC hardware where simplicity and single-pass efficiency are prioritized over adaptive sampling. When Not to Use: When adaptive sampling or empty space skipping is strictly required for performance, as fixed-step marching samples uniformly along the ray. Originated in the context of GPU-based volume rendering for medical imagery, specifically as a comparison to the Shear-Warp algorithm. The method leverages the fragment shader's ability to perform parallel ray traversal, moving computational load from CPU to GPU. It was implemented to address the limitations of slice-based methods, such as visible artifacts at low sampling rates and lower frame rates for high-quality rendering. jaanonim/volume-rendering, https://github.com/jaanonim/volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, https://github.com/rbaravalle/webgl-volumetric, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) sunjianxin/rendnerwebgl, https://github.com/sunjianxin/rendnerwebgl, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU-Based Volume Rendering for Medical Imagery, https://scholarly.org/pdf/display/gpu-based-volume-rendering-for-medical-imagery, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Per-primitive Ray Sampling
head: Primitive-centric ray marching
body: Per-primitive ray sampling is a rendering strategy where each geometric primitive (specifically ellipsoids) independently updates only the ray segments it intersects, avoiding redundant parameter loads and enabling accurate Transfer Function (TF) mapping by accumulating contributions in 3D space. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Fixed Step Ray Marching and Volume Ray Casting by organizing computation around primitives rather than rays, which eliminates the need for explicit per-tile sorting required in 2D rasterization because contributions accumulate in depth order as each ray segment corresponds to a discrete depth interval. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes a set of primitives, each defined by center \mu, covariance \Sigma, support radius factor r{supp}, intensity I, and scaling factor k; a sampling step size \Delta t; a projection matrix; and a pixel grid. The output is a set of accumulated ray segments rayi for each pixel, which are subsequently traversed front-to-back for alpha blending to produce the final pixel color. Data Structures: Each primitive is defined by \mu = (\mux, \muy, \muz), covariance matrix \Sigma, support radius factor r{supp}, and intensity I. Each ray segment is a 1D array rayi for pixel i, discretized with step size \Delta t, where the j-th entry stores the accumulated intensity at depth t = j\Delta t. Steps: 1. Transform and Cull: Transform primitives by the projection matrix and process only those visible in screen space. 2. Cache Parameters: Cache ellipsoid parameters in tile-level shared memory to minimize redundant global memory accesses across pixels. 3. Determine Depth Range: For a primitive with center \mu and covariance \Sigma, determine the valid depth range. Segments within |t - \muz| \le r{supp} \cdot \sqrt{\Sigma'{zz}} are considered, where \sqrt{\Sigma'{zz}} is the standard deviation along the z-axis after projection. 4. Update Ray Segments: For each primitive, calculate the start and end indices of the affected ray segments and update them with the primitive's contribution. Formulas: Ray Parameterization: In ray space, the ray for pixel (xi, yi) is ri(t) = (xi, yi, 0) + t \cdot (0, 0, 1), where t varies along the z-axis. Sample Position: The sample position for index j is rayi[j] = \hat{V}(ri(j\Delta t)) = \hat{V}(xi, yi, j\Delta t). Primitive Contribution: The contribution of a primitive to ray segment j is: \tilde{P}(xi, yi, j \cdot \Delta t) = I \cdot \frac{\sigma(k \cdot (1 - \mathbf{d}^\top \Sigma^{-1} \mathbf{d}))}{\sigma(k)} where \mathbf{d} = [xi, yi, j\Delta t] - [\mux, \muy, \muz] is the displacement from the primitive center, k is a scaling factor, and \sigma is the sigmoid function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perprimitiveraysampling(primitives, deltat, raysegments, pixelcoords): """ primitives: List of primitives with attributes mu, Sigma, rsupp, I, k, screenxmin, screenxmax, screenymin, screenymax deltat: float, sampling step size raysegments: 2D list [H][W] of lists of floats, initialized to 0.0 pixelcoords: list of (xi, yi) tuples for each pixel """ for prim in primitives: muz = prim.mu[2] sigmazz = prim.Sigma[2, 2] rsupp = prim.rsupp I = prim.I k = prim.k Sigmainv = inverse(prim.Sigma) # Calculate depth range indices zmin = muz - rsupp sqrt(sigmazz) zmax = muz + rsupp sqrt(sigmazz) indexstart = floor(zmin / deltat) indexend = floor(zmax / deltat) # Sources do not specify the exact pixel culling loop; standard screen-space bounding box iteration is used. for y in range(prim.screenymin, prim.screenymax + 1): for x in range(prim.screenxmin, prim.screenxmax + 1): pixelid = y W + x xi, yi = pixelcoords[pixelid] for j in range(indexstart, indexend + 1): dx = xi - prim.mu[0] dy = yi - prim.mu[1] dz = (j deltat) - prim.mu[2] d = [dx, dy, dz] quadratic = dot(d, dot(Sigmainv, d)) numerator = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k (1.0 - quadratic))) denominator = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k)) contribution = I (numerator / denominator) raysegments[pixelid][j] += contribution Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in calculating d^T \Sigma^{-1} d can affect the sigmoid evaluation, especially for large displacements. Boundaries: The support radius factor r{supp} determines the cutoff; if too small, contributions are truncated, and if too large, unnecessary computations occur. Degenerate Input: If \Sigma is singular, \Sigma^{-1} is undefined, requiring a small regularization term. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of primitives and the average number of ray segments they intersect, avoiding the O(N{rays} \cdot N{steps}) complexity of naive ray marching by only processing relevant primitives for each segment. Memory Complexity: Requires storing ray segments for all pixels and caching primitive parameters in shared memory. Performance: Eliminates redundant global memory traffic by processing each primitive once and caching parameters in tile-level shared memory. Strengths: Accurate TF evaluation in 3D space, no explicit sorting required, and reduced memory traffic. Limitations: Requires efficient culling and bounding box calculation to avoid processing non-intersecting primitives, and performance may degrade with high primitive density and overlap. Per-primitive ray sampling was introduced in the context of 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering (ESVR). It addresses the overhead of naively adopting ray marching for learned primitives, where each ray step requires checking intersections and repeatedly fetching ellipsoid parameters from memory. By organizing computation around primitives, it enables real-time rendering with accurate TF mapping. ESVR: 3D Ellipsoid-based Sparse Volume Rendering via Structure-aware Primitive Learning and Per-primitive Ray Sampling, https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.05564v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Directional Derivative Diffuse Lighting
head: Density Gradient Diffuse Approximation, Inigo Quilez's directional derivatives
body: Directional Derivative Diffuse Lighting is an approximation for diffuse lighting in volumetric raymarching that estimates light scattering by comparing density at the current point and an offset point in the light direction, avoiding the need for normal calculation. It sets itself apart from standard surface raymarching normals by requiring only two density samples instead of multiple gradient estimates, making it significantly cheaper for the resource-intensive volumetric loop. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes the current 3D position p, a normalized light direction sunDirection, and a density function scene(p) that returns the scalar density at position p as inputs. It outputs a diffuse lighting factor and a linear lighting color vector to modulate the accumulated volume color. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond the density function and standard vector types. The method relies on scalar arithmetic and vector addition. Parameters: Offset Scale: 0.3 (distance along the light direction for the second sample). Ambient Color: vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75). Ambient Multiplier: 1.1. Diffuse Color: vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3). Diffuse Multiplier: 0.8. Clamp Range: [0.0, 1.0]. Steps: 1. Sample the density at the current point p. 2. Sample the density at an offset point p' located further along the light direction. 3. Calculate the diffuse factor by taking the difference between the two density samples, dividing by the offset scale, and clamping the result to [0.0, 1.0]. Formula: diffuse = clamp((scene(p) - scene(p + 0.3 sunDirection)) / 0.3, 0.0, 1.0) Interpretation: If density increases along the light path (dcurrent > doffset), the result is positive, indicating more scattering. If density decreases, the result is lower or zero, indicating less scattering. 4. Compute the linear lighting color by mixing ambient light and the calculated diffuse light. Formula: lin = vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75) 1.1 + vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3) diffuse 0.8 5. Determine the base color of the volume slice by mixing white and black based on the current density dcurrent. Formula: basecolor = mix(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), dcurrent) 6. Combine the base color with the linear lighting and the density alpha, then accumulate into the final result using the over operator. Formula: color = vec4(basecolor lin, dcurrent) Accumulation: color.rgb = color.a; res += color (1.0 - res.a);. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directionalderivativediffuselightingraymarch(origin, direction, stepsize, maxsteps, sundirection, scenefunc): """ Marches a ray through a volume applying directional derivative diffuse lighting. Args: origin (vec3): Ray origin. direction (vec3): Ray direction (normalized). stepsize (float): Constant step size for marching. maxsteps (int): Maximum number of steps to prevent infinite loops. sundirection (vec3): Normalized light direction vector. scenefunc (callable): Returns scalar density at a 3D position. Returns: vec4: Accumulated result (rgb, a). """ # Initialize accumulated result to zero (fixes bug where res was undefined/zeroed incorrectly) res = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # March along the ray for i in range(maxsteps): p = origin + direction (i stepsize) dcurrent = scenefunc(p) # Only process if density is present if dcurrent > 0.0: # Directional derivative approximation offsetscale = 0.3 poffset = p + offsetscale sundirection doffset = scenefunc(poffset) # Calculate diffuse factor diffuse = (dcurrent - doffset) / offsetscale if diffuse < 0.0: diffuse = 0.0 elif diffuse > 1.0: diffuse = 1.0 # Compute linear lighting color ambient = vec3(0.60, 0.60, 0.75) 1.1 diffuselight = vec3(1.0, 0.6, 0.3) diffuse 0.8 lin = ambient + diffuselight # Determine base color basecolor = mix(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0), vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), dcurrent) # Form slice color and apply lighting color = vec4(basecolor lin, dcurrent) color.rgb = color.a # Accumulate using over operator res.rgb += color.rgb (1.0 - res.a) res.a += color.a (1.0 - res.a) # Exit early if fully opaque if res.a >= 1.0: break return res Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Calculation Suboptimality: Standard normal calculation using getNormal requires 4-6 sample points to estimate the gradient, which is resource-intensive given the heavy volumetric loop. This method avoids that by using only 2 samples. Loop Inclusion: Unlike surface raymarching where diffuse is computed once at the surface, this calculation must be included inside the volumetric raymarching loop because density varies throughout the volume. Precision: The division by 0.3 can amplify noise if the density function is noisy. Clamping to [0.0, 1.0] prevents negative lighting contributions but may clip valid gradients if the density change is very steep. Initialization and Loop Bounds: The accumulation variable res must be explicitly initialized to vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) before the marching loop, and the loop must iterate over the ray path using the specified step size; failure to do so results in a zero output for all rays. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point, requiring exactly 2 density function evaluations per lighting calculation. This is significantly faster than gradient-based normal estimation which requires 4-6 evaluations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory, as it only stores a few scalar and vector variables. Strengths: Low computational cost, easy to implement, provides a visually plausible approximation of diffuse lighting in volumes without explicit normals. Limitations: Approximation may not capture complex scattering effects accurately. When to use: Real-time volumetric rendering where performance is critical and approximate diffuse lighting is sufficient. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring high physical accuracy, or volumes with very fine details where the fixed offset might miss significant density changes. The method is attributed to Inigo Quilez and presented in his article on directional derivatives. It was developed as an alternative to standard normal calculation in volumetric raymarching to reduce the computational cost associated with gradient estimation. Real-time dreamy Cloudscapes with Volumetric Raymarching, https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/real-time-cloudscapes-with-volumetric-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Specific Material and Geometry Rendering
head: Material Parameter Setting, DVGO Density and Color Rendering, Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering, Ray-marched Volumetric Fog, Surface and DRR Rendering Modes, Material Percentage Volume Rendering, Volumetric Heat Haze, Volumetric Geometry Rendering
body: Specific Material and Geometry Rendering is a family of techniques that define how volumetric data is mapped to optical properties (density, color, emission) and how specific geometric constraints or material compositions are handled during ray traversal. It solves the problem of translating abstract simulation data or procedural definitions into physically plausible or artistically controlled radiance contributions within the volume rendering integral. It sets itself apart from general sampling schemes by focusing on the definition of material properties [5335-material-parameter-setting.md], the handling of complex global geometries like planetary cloud shells [3480-procedural-volumetric-cloud-rendering.md], or the specific compositing of multi-material scalar fields. The family shares the fundamental volume rendering equation, where the final color C(r) along a ray r is the integral of emitted and in-scattered light attenuated by transmittance: C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigmat(t) c(t) dt where T(t) = \exp(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigmat(\tau) d\tau) is the transmittance, \sigmat is the extinction coefficient (density), and c(t) is the color/emission term [5335-material-parameter-setting.md]. Key shared mechanisms include: 1. Material Definition: Mapping raw data (scalar grids, noise fields) to \sigmat and c(t) via transfer functions, procedural noise, or neural networks [5335-material-parameter-setting.md][12839-dvgo-density-and-color-rendering.md]. 2. Geometric Constraints: Defining the spatial bounds of the volume, whether as a local box, a spherical shell, or a procedural mask [3480-procedural-volumetric-cloud-rendering.md][4248-ray-marched-volumetric-fog.md]. 3. Integration: Discretizing the integral via ray marching, accumulating radiance and transmittance step-by-step [3874-mr-voxel-volume-rendering.md][4248-ray-marched-volumetric-fog.md]. A real-time technique for rendering planetary-scale cloud layers using ray marching through 3D noise fields. It treats clouds as a global spherical shell rather than a local box, solving the problem of rendering large, physically plausible cloudscapes that conform to a planet's curvature. It distinguishes itself from grid-based methods by using procedural noise for density rather than sampled voxel data. A direct volume ray casting method that performs ray marching through a single volume region, accumulating emitted light and computing transmittance and scattering contributions from a single light source. It is distinguished by its specific implementation of Russian Roulette for early termination and its assumption of a single-volume, single-light scene structure. Simulates aerial perspective and light shafts by treating fog as a 3D volume of participating media traced via forward ray-marching from the camera to the scene. It solves the problem of rendering dynamic, light-interacting fog that absorbs and scatters light, distinguishing itself from backward ray-marching by allowing early-out optimizations when transmittance becomes negligible. Defines the optical and geometric properties of volumetric media by mapping raw data grids to physical attributes such as density, color, and emission. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the definition of these properties via explicit channel bindings and parameter sliders (Standard Volume Material) or low-level API calls (VolPack), rather than the traversal or shading algorithms themselves. DVGO (Direct Volume Gaussian Optimization) renders 3D scenes by combining a sparse voxel grid with neural networks to represent density and view-dependent color. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing novel views by decoupling geometry (density) from appearance (color). It is distinct from standard NeRF by using a voxel grid for density and a shallow MLP for color, allowing for faster training and inference while maintaining high fidelity. Definition: Surface rendering mode computes color C(s) according to the Phong equation using the volume gradient. Digitally Reconstructed Radiographs (DRRs) mode sets C(s) = (0,0,0), attenuating only the backlight by accumulated transmittance t. Maximum Intensity Projections (MIPs) output the opacity \alpha of the maximum-opacity interval along the ray. Parameter: A uniform variable tells the fragment shader which rendering mode to use. Definition: A technique for rendering volumes with mixtures of materials (e.g., bone, muscle) by creating material percentage volumes and compositing them. Steps: Assume the scalar field was sampled above Nyquist frequency or low-pass filtered. Differentiate materials by scalar value or additional composition info. Create material percentage volumes, where each is a scalar field representing one material. Associate color and opacity with each material. Obtain composite color and opacity by linearly combining the color and opacity for each material percentage volume. Use a matte volume (scalar field 0-1) to slice the volume or perform spatial set operations. Transform the volume so one axis is perpendicular to the image plane. Project plane by plane in a back-to-front manner and composite to form the final image. Definition: Produces the same result as Volumetric Geometry but adds a heat haze refraction effect. Requires V-Ray. Uses Surface channel gradient to change ray direction. Parameter: Heat Haze (hhfactor): Multiplier for refraction based on Surface channel gradient. 1 approximates normal air heat haze from temperature. 0 produces no effect. Larger values needed if using smoke/other channels as source. Only available in Volumetric Heat Haze mode. Pitfall: Heat Haze only affects camera view, not shadows cast through volume. If Heat Haze shader intersects with VRayMtl refraction, Max depth of VRayMtl may need increase. Definition: Produces the same visual result as Volumetric mode but uses procedural geometry made of multiple transparent layers. Requires V-Ray. Used for exporting deep images and render elements (normals, velocity, multi matte) not available in standard Volumetric mode. Pitfall: Approximate and Approximate+Shadows options for Scattering in Smoke color window are not supported in this mode. Cutter Geom does not work when Mode is set to Volumetric Geometry. The concept of rendering specific materials within volumes dates back to early volume visualization work. Drebin, Carpenter, and Hanrahan developed techniques for rendering volumes containing mixtures of materials, such as CT data containing bone, muscle, and flesh, by creating material percentage volumes. Modern implementations extend this to procedural generation for clouds [3480-procedural-volumetric-cloud-rendering.md] and neural representations like DVGO [12839-dvgo-density-and-color-rendering.md]. Specific rendering modes like DRRs and MIPs are standard in medical and industrial visualization contexts, while heat haze and volumetric geometry modes are specialized features in production renderers like V-Ray for 3ds Max. CISC/CMPE 454, GPU Volume Rendering, https://watkins.cs.queensu.ca/~jstewart/454/notes/44/44-gpu-volume-rendering.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) PDF Volume Visualization: Principles and Advances, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/KaufmanVolumeVisualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) FireSmoke Rendering - Phoenix for 3ds Max, https://documentation.chaos.com/space/PHX4MAX/124396558, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering
head: Nubis³, Nubis Cubed, Nubis Evolved, Volumetric Cloud Renderer, Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Real-time Volumetric Cloud Rendering
body: Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering is a real-time technique that renders planetary-scale cloud layers using ray marching through 3D noise fields, combining atmospheric lighting models with adaptive density shaping. It solves the problem of rendering large, physically plausible cloudscapes that conform to a planet's curvature, supporting cameras inside, outside, or between cloud shells. It sets itself apart from local volumetrics (like Ray-marched Volumetric Fog) by treating clouds as a global spherical shell rather than a local box, and from grid-based methods (like Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering) by using procedural noise for density rather than sampled voxel data. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position, view-projection matrix, sun direction, sun color, cloud layer parameters (base height, thickness, coverage, wind speed/direction), and noise textures (shape, detail, weather map). Outputs: In-scattered radiance, transmittance, and transmittance-weighted mean depth. Data Structures: Shape Texture: 3D texture (e.g., 128^3) containing Perlin fBm dilated by Worley noise plus Worley octaves. Tileable. Detail Texture: 3D texture (e.g., 32^3) containing Worley noise. Tileable. Weather Map: 2D texture (e.g., 512^2) storing coverage and cloud type (stratus, cumulus, cumulonimbus) per region. Framebuffers: Cloud FBO: Two color attachments (RGBA16F for radiance/transmittance, R32F for depth). Resolve FBO: Two ping-pong framebuffers (RGBA16F) for temporal history. Output FBO: Single color attachment (RGBA8) for final composite. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Setup: Convert vertex UV to ray direction based on frustum corners. Normalize ray direction in world space. Intersect ray with the spherical cloud shell defined by inner radius R{inner} and outer radius R{outer}. Let O be camera position, C be planet center (e.g., (0, -R{Earth}, 0)). oc = O - C. r{cam} = length(oc). b = dot(oc, rd). c = dot(oc, oc). h{outer} = b^2 - (c - R{outer}^2). If h{outer} < 0, no intersection. s{outer} = \sqrt{h{outer}}. t{outer\near} = -b - s{outer}. t{outer\far} = -b + s{outer}. h{inner} = b^2 - (c - R{inner}^2). If h{inner} > 0, s{inner} = \sqrt{h{inner}}, else s{inner} = 0. Determine entry tn and exit tf within the shell. 2. Density Sampling: Calculate world position P at current step. Transform P for high-res noise sampling: hiResPosition = outerProduct(P, hiResS) + outerProduct(hiResT, vec4(1.f)), where hiResT = 0.1f \times hiResNoiseTranslate and hiResS = 0.1f \times hiResNoiseScaling. Sample 4 textures from volumeHighRes at hiResPosition[0..3]. Compute hiResDensity = dot(hiResNoise, normalizeL1(hiResChannelWeights)). Apply falloff: falloff = yFalloff(P) \times xzFalloff(P). hiResDensity = falloff. Add offset: hiResDensityWithOffset = hiResDensity + hiResDensityOffset. If hiResDensityWithOffset \le 0, return 0. Sample low-res noise: loResPosition = P \times loResNoiseScaling \times 0.1f + loResNoiseTranslate. loResDensity = dot(texture(volumeLowRes, loResPosition), normalizeL1(loResChannelWeights)). Compute erosion weight: erosionWeight = pow(1.f - hiResDensity, 6) (quintic). Final density: density = hiResDensityWithOffset - erosionWeight \times loResDensityWeight \times loResDensity. Return \max(density \times densityMult \times 5.f, 0.f). 3. Lighting and Integration: For each step, calculate optical depth to the sun by taking 6 samples toward the sun direction. Compute light transmittance: lightTransmittance = \exp(\tau), where \tau is accumulated optical depth scaled by absorption. Evaluate multiple-scattering approximation (4 octaves) using attenuated extinction, contribution, and phase eccentricity. Apply phase function (e.g., two-lobe Henyey-Greenstein or Mie). Calculate in-scattered radiance analytically over the step size. Apply powder term (darkens back-lit edges) and ambient term (fades from blue at top to grey at bottom). Update transmittance: T{new} = T{old} \times \exp(-density \times stepSize). 4. Termination: Stop marching if transmittance drops below 0.5% (or log threshold -4.6). Accumulate radiance and transmittance. 5. Temporal Reprojection (Optional but common in real-time implementations): Render cloud pass at reduced resolution (e.g., 0.5x) with sub-pixel jitter (Halton sequence). Reconstruct world position from depth. Project previous frame's position using previous view-projection matrix. Blend history sample (e.g., 92% current, 8% history). Clamp history to 3x3 neighborhood to prevent ghosting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchclouds(camerapos, cameradir, sundir, suncolor, cloudparams, shapetex, detailtex, weathertex): # 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection oc = camerapos - cloudparams.planetcenter b = dot(oc, cameradir) c = dot(oc, oc) houter = bb - (c - cloudparams.router2) if houter < 0: return vec3(0.0), 1.0, 0.0 # No intersection souter = sqrt(houter) tnear = -b - souter tfar = -b + souter # Check inner shell hinner = bb - (c - cloudparams.rinner2) if hinner > 0: sinner = sqrt(hinner) tinnernear = -b - sinner tinnerfar = -b + sinner # Adjust tnear/tfar to be within shell tstart = max(tnear, tinnernear) tend = min(tfar, tinnerfar) else: tstart = tnear tend = tfar if tstart > tend: return vec3(0.0), 1.0, 0.0 # 2. Adaptive Step Size stepsize = (tend - tstart) / cloudparams.maxsteps jitter = getjitter(camerapos, cameradir) # Halton sequence based radiance = vec3(0.0) transmittance = 1.0 depthaccum = 0.0 transmittanceweighteddepth = 0.0 pos = camerapos + tstart cameradir + jitter stepsize for i in range(cloudparams.maxsteps): if transmittance < 0.005: # Early stop break # 3. Density Sampling density = sampledensity(pos, shapetex, detailtex, weathertex, cloudparams) if density > 0.0: # 4. Lighting # Optical depth to sun tau = 0.0 sunpos = pos for j in range(6): sunpos += sundir stepsize tau += sampledensity(sunpos, shapetex, detailtex, weathertex, cloudparams) stepsize lighttrans = exp(-tau cloudparams.absorptioncoeff) # Phase function cosangle = dot(normalize(cameradir), normalize(sundir)) phase = henyeygreenstein(cosangle, cloudparams.anisotropy) # Multiple scattering approximation ms = multiplescatteringapproximation(density, stepsize, cloudparams) # In-scattering inscatter = suncolor lighttrans phase ms cloudparams.sunintensity # Ambient heightratio = (length(pos - cloudparams.planetcenter) - cloudparams.rinner) / (cloudparams.router - cloudparams.rinner) ambient = mix(cloudparams.ambienttop, cloudparams.ambientbottom, heightratio) # Powder term powder = 1.0 - exp(-cloudparams.powderstrength (1.0 - cosangle)) totallight = inscatter powder + ambient cloudparams.ambientintensity # Integration radiance += totallight transmittance (1.0 - exp(-density stepsize)) transmittance = exp(-density stepsize) depthaccum += stepsize transmittanceweighteddepth += stepsize transmittance pos += cameradir stepsize meandepth = transmittanceweighteddepth / (1.0 - transmittance) if transmittance < 1.0 else 0.0 return radiance, transmittance, meandepth Parameters: shapenoisescale: Default 6.4 km. Controls cloud size. coverage: Scales weather coverage. densityThreshold: Minimum noise value for density. absorptionCoefficient: Default 1.0. scatterFactor: Forward scattering strength [0.0, 1.0]. windSpeed: Controls noise scroll speed. maxSteps: Default 128. EARLYSTOPTHRESHOLD: 1e-2f. EARLYSTOPLOGTHRESHOLD: -4.6f. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Texture History Validity: History textures must be checked for identity; reallocation or resize invalidates history. Shadow Map Basis Error: Cloud shadow maps are traced along the first directional light. Using them for non-parallel lights causes displaced shadows. Viewport Depth Mismatch: Depth reads must be offset by viewport origin to avoid tracing wrong parts of the view. Reprojection Depth Compromise: Mean cloud depth is used for reprojection; overlapping thin/far clouds cause depth ambiguity, mitigated by history clamping. Renders clouds as a spherical shell using 3D noise, combining Nubis density with Frostbite light transport. Choose for planetary-scale clouds. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) where N is number of steps and M is samples per step for lighting. Memory Complexity: O(T{shape} + T{detail} + T{weather}) for noise textures. Performance: On Mesa llvmpipe at 640x360, full-res 128 steps takes 927 ms. Half-res with temporal reprojection takes 266 ms (29% of full-res). Strengths: Physically plausible, supports arbitrary camera positions, efficient with temporal reprojection. Limitations: Approximate multiple scattering, hand-tuned sun color at low elevation, single cloud layer limit in some implementations. Originated from techniques described in "The Real-time Volumetric Cloudscapes of Horizon: Zero Dawn" (Schneider, 2015) and "Physically Based Sky, Atmosphere and Cloud Rendering in Frostbite" (Hillaire, 2016). Implemented in various open-source projects like Bevy atmosphere plugin, Depersonalizc/volumetric-clouds, and harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer. WIP: Nubis-based volumetric clouds, https://github.com/mate-h/bevy/pull/26, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Depersonalizc/volumetric-clouds, https://github.com/Depersonalizc/volumetric-clouds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer, https://github.com/harkawataryan/Volumetric-Cloud-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, https://github.com/ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Clouds from Base Shape (Nubis/Frostbite Hybrid)
head: Hillaire 2016 light, Nubis density, Planetary Cloud Layer, Spherical Shell Clouds, Volumetric Clouds as a Spherical Shell, Wrenninge multiple scattering
body: This technique renders volumetric clouds as a spherical shell surrounding a planet, using raymarching between defined inner and outer radii with density derived from 3D noise fields rather than finite 2D textures. It combines Schneider’s density model from Horizon Zero Dawn’s Nubis system with Hillaire 2016 light transport from Frostbite, allowing the cloud layer to conform to any base shape by sampling noise at 3D points in the shading frame. Unlike local volumetrics or ground fog, this method treats clouds as a planetary-scale feature, supporting multiple planets and camera positions inside, outside, or between shells. Inputs: Planet center and radius. Cloud layer inner and outer altitudes (relative to planet radius). Noise textures: 128³ Perlin-Worley shape noise and 32³ Worley detail noise. Camera position and view direction. Sun direction and intensity. Atmosphere transmittance data (required for correct lighting). Outputs: Cloud color and opacity per pixel. Transmittance and distance buffers for the camera-centered direction grid. CloudLayer Component Parameters: innerradius: Float. The inner boundary of the cloud shell. outerradius: Float. The outer boundary of the cloud shell. coverage: Float. Authored parameter controlling cloud density. density: Float. Global density multiplier. wind: Vector3. Render-space wind direction vector. noisematerial: Asset reference. Contains noise parameters. Camera-Centred Direction Grid: Dimensions: 1536 × 768 texels, centered around the base's up vector. Resolution: ~0.23° per texel. Texel Layout: cloudlight: Vector3. Cloud light contribution including air in front. transmittance: Float. Light transmittance through the cloud. frontdistance: Float. Distance to the front of the cloud shell. meandistance: Float. Mean distance of scattering events. opacity: Float. Accumulated opacity. Shadow Map: Dimensions: 512². Alignment: Aligned along the sun vector around the camera. Reach: Shadows do not extend past the map boundary (e.g., 64 km on Earth, or 4 camera altitudes). 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection: Calculate the entry and exit points of the view ray relative to the cloud shell's inner and outer radii. This logic is shared with the AtmosphereVolume component. If the ray misses the shell, the shader early-outs. 2. Layer Scaling and Lifting: Scale the cloud layer height relative to the planet's radius. Lift the layer so its bottom is at least 1.25 times the ground's maximum relief to ensure the marcher is unaware of terrain features. Example: For Earth (3.3 km relief), the layer is lifted to 4.1–6.6 km. For a 2 km planet, it is 78–208 m. 3. Density Calculation (Schneider/Nubis): Sample the 128³ Perlin-Worley shape noise at the current 3D ray position. Determine cloud cover and type based on thresholds measured directly on the noise values at a "weather scale". Apply erosion from separate noise fields if available. 4. Ray Marching: March the ray through the shell volume using a fixed step size and empty-space skipping (inherited from [771]). Note: The marcher does not account for terrain occlusion; a depth-aware march is required to fix clouds wrapping peaks. 5. Light Transport (Hillaire 2016): Sun Transmittance: Calculate sun transmittance through the atmosphere using the atmosphere's transmittance march, then through the cloud using progressive shadow samples from the 512² shadow map. Phase Function: Use a dual-lobe Henyey-Greenstein phase function for scattering. Multiple Scattering: Implement Wrenninge's multiple-scattering octaves for the cloud interior. In-Scattering: Compute lighting using a few in-scattering samples rather than a second full march. Sample the sky's light contribution from the atmosphere's multiple-scattering table. 6. Integration: Integrate scattering such that light scattering applies to the light reaching the clouds and the light they send on. Clouds are marched in the same pass as the atmosphere or ordered against it, as clouds sit inside the atmosphere. 7. Compositing: Sky Shader: Places clouds over the atmosphere's sky. Page Shader: Adds clouds in front of a fragment to its FOG buffer. The light() function reads the shadow map (one fetch) to determine cloud shadows. 8. Distance Policy: From orbit: Render the cloud layer as a texture on a sphere. From the ground: Render as a fly-through volume. The transition must be continuous and measured, not guessed. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumetricclouds(camera, planet, atmosphere, sun): # 1. Setup Grid and Shadow Map grid = createdirectiongrid(width=1536, height=768, center=planet.upvector) shadowmap = createshadowmap(size=512, direction=sun.direction, center=camera.position) # 2. Calculate Layer Bounds # Lift layer to be above terrain relief maxterrainrelief = getmaxterrainheight(planet) inneraltitude = planet.radius 1.0 + maxterrainrelief 1.25 outeraltitude = inneraltitude + cloudlayerheight # e.g., 1.5-4km for Earth # 3. March Grid Texels for block in grid.blocks2x2: # One invocation per 2x2 block marches one texel, reprojects others for texel in block: rayorigin = camera.position raydirection = getraydirection(texel, camera) # Ray-Sphere Intersection entry, exit = intersectshell(rayorigin, raydirection, planet.center, inneraltitude, outeraltitude) if entry is None: continue # Early-out if ray misses shell # Marching Variables transmittance = 1.0 cloudlight = vec3(0.0) frontdist = 0.0 meandist = 0.0 opacity = 0.0 # Step through volume stepsize = calculatestepsize(entry, exit) pos = entry while pos < exit and transmittance > 0.01: # Density Calculation noiseval = sampleshapenoise(pos, scale=weatherscale) density = calculatedensity(noiseval, coveragethresholds) if density > 0.0: # Light Transport # Sun Transmittance through Atmosphere atmtransmittance = atmosphere.gettransmittance(pos, sun.direction) # Sun Transmittance through Cloud (Progressive Shadow Samples) cloudshadow = shadowmap.sample(pos, sun.direction) # Phase Function phase = duallobehenyeygreenstein(sun.direction, raydirection) # Multiple Scattering (Wrenninge) multiscatter = getmultiplescatteringoctaves(pos) # In-Scattering Sample skylight = atmosphere.getmultiplescatteringtable(pos) # Integration Step scattering = density (atmtransmittance cloudshadow phase + skylight multiscatter) cloudlight += scattering stepsize transmittance transmittance = exp(-density stepsize) # Distance Accumulation frontdist = pos - rayorigin meandist = (meandist opacity + frontdist density stepsize) / (opacity + density stepsize) opacity += density stepsize pos += raydirection stepsize # Store Texel Data texel.cloudlight = cloudlight texel.transmittance = transmittance texel.frontdistance = frontdist texel.meandistance = meandist texel.opacity = opacity # 4. Compositing for pixel in screen: texel = grid.sample(pixel.uv) # Sky shader places clouds over atmosphere sky finalcolor = atmosphere.skycolor texel.transmittance + texel.cloudlight # Page shader adds to FOG buffer fogbuffer.add(finalcolor, texel.opacity) Noise Resolution: Shape noise 128³, Detail noise 32³. Layer Height (Earth): 1.5 to 4 km. Grid Resolution: 1536 × 768. Shadow Map: 512². Wind: Render-space vector. Terrain Occlusion: The layer is lifted, not composited. The march knows nothing of the terrain, so clouds do not wrap peaks. A depth-aware march is required to fix this. Jagged Edges: The grid's resolution (0.23° per texel) shows as jagged edges on a small planet seen whole. Shadow Reach: Shadows do not extend past the shadow map boundary (64 km on Earth, or 4 camera altitudes). Color Accuracy: Clouds take the scene's warm sun color, reddened again by the air, resulting in a pinkish-tan appearance. There is no white balance. Fixing this requires setting the scene's light to white, which is a scene change. Wind Direction: The wind is a render-space vector. On a planet, the noise drifts through the shell away from the pole. It is now aligned with the wind; the old cloud layer drifted against it. Grid Limits: The froxel grid ends at ClusterSettings::far (200 m default). Planetary clouds are kilometres out, outside the grid by two orders of magnitude. Assuming the grid covers the clouds is a mistake. Atmosphere Dependency: Clouds lit by a sun that ignores the atmosphere look wrong. The atmosphere component must be implemented first. Time and Memory Complexity: The technique inherits sampling techniques from [771]: 3D noise textures, empty-space skipping, and fixed step size. The camera-centered direction grid requires 1536 × 768 texels, with one invocation per 2×2 block. Shadow map updates are per-frame. Measured Performance: OneXFly (10 W): Current implementation cost is 39 ms when switched off, which is the only reason the frame meets the 13.9 ms budget. Direct lighting alone is at twice budget. RTX 3070 Laptop (Power-Saver): Forest5cm, steady, 300 frames: Clouds off 19.05 ms, Clouds on 21.21 ms (+2.2 ms). Earth's pole: 4.8 → 8.1 ms (sky full of clouds). Earth from 100 km: 5.2 → 11 ms. The first version read cloud shadow per fragment, costing +33 ms in the forest. The shadow map optimization removed this cost. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Conforms to any base shape; supports multiple planets; efficient lighting via few in-scattering samples and shadow maps; continuous transition between orbit and ground views. Limitations: No terrain occlusion (clouds float above peaks); jagged edges on small planets; limited shadow reach; color accuracy issues due to lack of white balance; high cost on low-power hardware. When to Use: Planetary-scale cloud rendering where clouds must follow the curvature of the planet. Real-time engines requiring efficient volumetric lighting with shadow maps. When Not to Use: Local volumetrics or ground fog (use froxel buffer instead). Scenes requiring precise terrain interaction with clouds (requires depth-aware march). Low-power hardware where the 39 ms overhead is prohibitive. Origin: The technique is based on Guerrilla's Nubis work for Horizon Zero Dawn (Schneider, SIGGRAPH 2015), which models clouds as a spherical shell over the planet. The lighting model is derived from Hillaire 2016 (Frostbite). History and Development: SIGGRAPH 2015: Schneider published "The Real-Time Volumetric Cloudscapes of Horizon Zero Dawn," establishing the spherical shell model and Nubis density. Frostbite: Hillaire 2016 introduced the energy-conserving light transport and dual-lobe Henyey-Greenstein phase function. Wrenninge: Multiple-scattering octaves were adapted for cloud interior lighting. Implementation: The technique was implemented in the opti-voxel engine (ov::Clouds component), integrated with Godot sky and page shaders, and owned by World with the atmosphere. Usage: Used in the opti-voxel engine, integrated with Godot sky and page shaders. Owned by World with the atmosphere. feat(render): volumetric clouds as a spherical shell, per planet, https://github.com/lobinuxsoft/kooch/issues/731, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric clouds from the base's shape, https://github.com/aobayama-gaming/opti-voxel/pull/145, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering
head: VolumeIntegrator::Li, Mr-Voxel Volume Integrator
body: Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting method implemented in the VolumeIntegrator::Li function that performs ray marching through a single volume region, accumulating emitted light and computing transmittance and scattering contributions from a single light source. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific implementation of Russian Roulette for early termination and its assumption of a single-volume, single-light scene structure, serving as the core integration logic within the Mr-Voxel accelerated voxel data structure. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera ray r defined by origin and direction, and a pointer to a transmittance variable T to be updated. Output: A Spectrum representing the accumulated radiance Lv along the ray. Scene Data: Access to a single volume object (volumes[0]) and a single light source (lights[0]) via the scene graph. Data Structures: The method operates within the VolumeIntegrator class. It relies on scene queries: mScene->getVolumeCount(): Returns the number of volumes (assumed to be 1). mScene->getVolumes(): Returns the array of volume objects. mScene->getLightSources(): Returns the array of light sources. volumes[0]->tau(ray, length,...): Computes optical depth (tau) for a given ray segment. volumes[0]->Lve(p): Returns emitted light at position p. volumes[0]->sigmas(p): Returns the scattering coefficient at position p. mScene->intersect(ray, &surface): Checks for surface intersections for shadow rays. Parameters: mStepSize: The nominal step size for ray marching. Russian Roulette Threshold: Transmittance value below which termination occurs (10^{-3}). Russian Roulette Probability: Probability of continuing if threshold is met (0.5). Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Sample Count: Determine the number of steps based on the ray segment length inside the volume (t1 - t0) and mStepSize. If the calculated count is 0, set it to 1. N = \max\left(1, \left\lfloor \frac{t1 - t0}{\text{mStepSize}} \right\rfloor \right) 2. Calculate Actual Step Length: Compute the precise step size \Delta t to ensure the ray exits exactly at t1. \Delta t = \frac{t1 - t0}{N} 3. Random Offset: Apply a random offset to the starting position t0 to reduce banding artifacts. The offset is uniformly distributed between 0 and \Delta t. t0' = t0 + U[0, 1) \cdot \Delta t 4. Initialize Accumulators: Set accumulated radiance Lv = 0 and transmittance Tr = 1. 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to N-1: a. Position Update: Let p{prev} be the position at the start of the step. Calculate the new position p = r(t0' + i \cdot \Delta t). b. Step Ray: Define a short ray segment from p{prev} to p with length \Delta t. c. Optical Depth: Compute the optical depth \tau{step} for this segment. The source code passes 0.5 step as the length argument to tau, implying the function might expect a radius or half-length, or it is a specific implementation detail of volumes[0]->tau. We assume standard optical depth calculation: \tau{step} = \text{volumes}[0].\text{tau}(p{prev} \to p, \Delta t, 0) d. Update Transmittance: Update the ray transmittance. Tr = Tr \cdot e^{-\tau{step}} e. Accumulate Emission: Add emitted light from the current position. Lv = Lv + \text{volumes}[0].Le(p) f. Scattering Check: Retrieve the scattering coefficient \sigmas(p) = \text{volumes}[0].\sigmas(p). If \sigmas(p) is non-zero (not black): i. Light Direction: Compute the normalized direction vector \omegaL from p to the light source position. ii. Shadow Ray: Cast a shadow ray from p in direction \omegaL. Check if it intersects a surface closer than the distance to the light. Let dL be the distance to the light. If no intersection occurs or the intersection distance t{surf} > dL, the point is unshadowed. iii. Light Transmittance: If unshadowed, compute the transmittance of light through the volume from p to the light. The source code uses mStepSize 2 as the length argument. T{light} = e^{-\text{volumes}[0].\text{tau}(\text{shadowRay}, 2 \cdot \text{mStepSize}, 0)} iv. Direct Lighting: Compute the direct lighting contribution Ld using the light's color CL and the light transmittance. Ld = T{light} \cdot CL v. Accumulate Scattering: Add the scattered light to Lv. Lv = Lv + Ld \cdot \sigmas(p) \cdot Tr g. Russian Roulette: If Tr < 10^{-3}: i. Generate a random number U[0, 1). ii. If U < 0.5, break the loop (terminate ray). iii. Otherwise, continue by scaling transmittance: Tr = Tr / 0.5. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def VolumeIntegratorLi(ray, scene, mStepSize): # Get volume and light sources (assumes single volume/light per notes) volumes = scene.getVolumes() lights = scene.getLightSources() # Determine entry (t0) and exit (t1) points of the ray within the volume # This assumes ray traversal has already determined t0 and t1 t0 = ray.entryt t1 = ray.exitt # Step 1: Calculate number of samples numsamples = int((t1 - t0) / mStepSize) if numsamples == 0: numsamples = 1 # Step 2: Calculate actual step length step = (t1 - t0) / numsamples # Step 3: Apply random offset randomoffset = random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) step tcurrent = t0 + randomoffset # Step 4: Initialize accumulators Lv = Spectrum(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) Tr = 1.0 # Step 5: Loop for i in range(numsamples): pprev = ray(tcurrent) tcurrent += step p = ray(tcurrent) # Create short ray for optical depth calculation # Note: The source code passes 0.5 step to tau, which is unusual. # We implement exactly as described in notes. stepray = Ray(pprev, p - pprev) steptau = volumes[0].tau(stepray, 0.5 step, 0) # Update transmittance Tr = Tr exp(-steptau) # Accumulate emitted light Lv = Lv + volumes[0].Le(p) # Get scattering coefficient ss = volumes[0].sigmas(p) # Check if scattering is non-zero if not ss.isblack(): # Compute light direction lightpos = lights[0].position wL = normalize(lightpos - p) # Shadow ray shadowray = Ray(p, wL) surfacehit = scene.intersect(shadowray) # Check if unshadowed disttolight = length(lightpos - p) isunshadowed = (surfacehit is None) or (surfacehit.t > disttolight) if isunshadowed: # Compute light transmittance # Note: Source code passes mStepSize 2 to tau lighttau = volumes[0].tau(shadowray, mStepSize 2, 0) lTr = exp(-lighttau) # Direct lighting contribution Ld = lTr lights[0].color # Add to accumulated radiance Lv = Lv + Ld ss Tr # Russian Roulette if Tr < 1e-3: if random.uniform(0.0, 1.0) < 0.5: break else: Tr = Tr / 0.5 return Lv Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples N per ray, where N \approx \frac{\text{Volume Length}}{\text{mStepSize}}. Each step involves volume queries and potentially a shadow ray intersection. Memory Complexity: Constant, O(1), excluding the storage of the volume data structure itself. Strengths: Simple implementation; random offset reduces banding; Russian Roulette handles long transmissive paths efficiently. Limitations: Assumes a single volume and single light source, limiting its applicability to complex scenes without modification. The specific arguments passed to tau (e.g., 0.5 step and mStepSize 2) are implementation-specific and may not generalize to other volume libraries without adaptation. When to Use: Suitable for simple volumetric scenes with a single light source where performance is prioritized over multi-light accuracy. When Not to Use: Complex scenes with multiple volumes or lights, or where high-fidelity multi-scattering is required. Mr-Voxel is a volume rendering technique developed as part of a graphics graduate thesis by C. Gibson. It combines an accelerated voxel data structure with a volume rendering library. The lighting equations are derived or loosely based on the volume rendering sections of "Physically Based Rendering, 2nd edition" by Matt Pharr. The implementation is found in the VolumeIntegrator::Li function within the Mr-Voxel repository. cgibson/Mr-Voxel, https://github.com/cgibson/Mr-Voxel, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray-marched Volumetric Fog
head: Fog Filter, Forward ray-marching fog, Full-screen volumetric fog, Volumetric Fog (CRYENGINE 3), Voxel-based Volumetric Fog
body: Ray-marched volumetric fog simulates aerial perspective and light shafts by treating fog as a 3D volume of participating media traced via forward ray-marching from the camera to the scene. It solves the problem of rendering dynamic, light-interacting fog that absorbs and scatters light, distinguishing itself from backward ray-marching by allowing early-out optimizations when transmittance becomes negligible. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position, view direction per pixel, depth buffer (for scene intersection), light position and intensity, fog density (\tau), scattering coefficient (a), and phase function parameters. Outputs: Final radiance L per pixel. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin (camera position) and direction (view vector). Depth Buffer: 2D texture mapping UV coordinates to depth values z. Light Source: Point light defined by position and intensity \Phi. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, construct a ray originating at the camera position. 2. Scene Intersection: Sample the depth buffer at the current pixel's UV coordinate to reconstruct the 3D position of the scene surface. Calculate the distance tf from the camera to this intersection point. 3. Ray Clamping: If the ray does not hit the scene (e.g., background), clamp the maximum ray distance to a predefined zfar value to prevent infinite marching. 4. Jittering (Optional but Recommended): To mitigate slice artifacts, add a pseudo-random delta step \delta to the ray's starting position or sample offsets. 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate from t=0 to t=tf with a fixed step size \Delta l. 6. In-Scattering Calculation: At each step position x, calculate the in-scattering term Li. 7. Transmittance Calculation: Calculate the transmittance T from the camera to the current step position. 8. Accumulation: Add the product of in-scattering, transmittance, and step size to the accumulated radiance. 9. Early-Out: If transmittance drops below a threshold, terminate the loop early. Formulas: The final radiance L is approximated using a Riemann sum: L = \sum{n=0}^{N} Li(x(ln), \omega) e^{-\tau ln} \Delta l Where: L: Calculated radiance. N: Total number of steps. Li(x(ln), \omega): In-scattering term at step n. e^{-\tau ln}: Transmittance from camera to distance ln. \tau: Density (extinction coefficient). ln: Distance traveled along the ray at step n. \Delta l: Ray-march step size. The in-scattering term Li for a point light is defined as: Li(x, \omega) = \frac{a \Phi}{4\pi d^2} v(x) e^{-\tau d} P(\omega, \omega') Where: a: Scattering coefficient (probability of photon scattering). \Phi: Point light intensity. d: Distance from the sample point x to the light source. v(x): Visibility of the sample point from the light source (1 if unshadowed). e^{-\tau d}: Transmittance from the light to the sample point. P(\omega, \omega'): Phase function describing scattering direction probability. Parameters: Density (\tau): Constant for uniform fog. Can be procedurally generated or sampled from textures/OpenVDB for non-uniform fog. Visibility (v(x)): Set to 1 in basic implementations; can be sampled from a light's cube shadow map for soft shadows. Phase Function (P): Uses the Schlick phase function approximation of the Henyey-Greenstein (HG) function for real-time performance, replacing the more expensive original HG function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchedvolumetricfog(camerapos, viewdir, depthbuffer, lightpos, lightintensity, fogdensity, scatteringcoeff, stepsize, zfar): # 1. Reconstruct scene intersection uv = getpixeluv() depth = depthbuffer.sample(uv) scenepos = reconstructworldposition(uv, depth) # 2. Calculate ray direction and length raydir = normalize(scenepos - camerapos) raylength = length(scenepos - camerapos) # 3. Clamp ray length if raylength > zfar: raylength = zfar # 4. Initialize accumulation accumulatedradiance = vec3(0.0) currenttransmittance = 1.0 # 5. Jitter start position to reduce slice artifacts jitter = randomfloat() stepsize # 6. March along the ray for t in range(0, int(raylength), int(stepsize)): currentpos = camerapos + raydir (t + jitter) # 7. Calculate distance to light disttolight = length(currentpos - lightpos) # 8. Calculate In-Scattering # Visibility v(x) is 1 in basic implementation visibility = 1.0 # Phase function P (Schlick approximation of HG) # Note: Exact Schlick formula parameters not provided in source, # assuming standard implementation of Schlick-HG approximation. phase = schlickhenyeygreenstein(raydir, normalize(lightpos - currentpos)) inscattering = (scatteringcoeff lightintensity / (4.0 3.14159 disttolight disttolight)) \ visibility \ exp(-fogdensity disttolight) \ phase # 9. Calculate Transmittance from camera to current step transmittance = exp(-fogdensity t) # 10. Accumulate accumulatedradiance += inscattering transmittance stepsize # 11. Early-out optimization if transmittance < 0.01: break return accumulatedradiance Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Slice Artifacts: Marching rays with the same step size starting at the same point causes samples to align on the same "slices," creating visible banding. Jittering Trade-off: Jittering reduces slice artifacts but can introduce noise, especially with larger step sizes. Infinite Marching: Rays that do not hit the scene must be clamped by zfar to prevent infinite loops. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps N per pixel (O(N)). N depends on the distance to the scene and the step size. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the accumulation, plus O(W \times H) for the depth buffer. Performance: Real-time capable on modern GPUs when using fixed step sizes and Schlick phase approximations. Performance degrades with smaller step sizes or complex visibility calculations (shadow mapping). Strengths: Simple implementation, allows early-out optimization, dynamic interaction with scene geometry and lighting. Limitations: Slice artifacts require jittering or variable step sizes; noise increases with jittering; uniform fog assumption simplifies density but limits complex volumetric structures without additional data structures. When to Use: Real-time applications requiring dynamic fog, light shafts, and aerial perspective where performance is critical. When Not to Use: Offline rendering requiring high-fidelity multi-scattering or complex non-uniform volumes without precomputed data structures. The technique is based on the principles of volume rendering and participating media, specifically the work by Toth and Umenhofer on "Real-time Volumetric Lighting in Participating Media". It has been implemented in games such as Horizon Zero Dawn, Death Stranding, and Returnal to simulate dynamic fog and light shafts. The forward ray-marching approach was chosen over backward ray-marching to facilitate early-out optimizations.
