name: Material Parameter Setting
head: Material Format, Material object fields, Standard Volume Material, vpSetMaterial
body: Material Parameter Setting defines the optical and geometric properties of volumetric media by mapping raw data grids to physical attributes such as density, color, and emission. It solves the problem of converting abstract simulation data (e.g., density, temperature) into renderable radiance contributions within the volume rendering integral. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the definition of these properties via explicit channel bindings and parameter sliders (Standard Volume Material) or low-level API calls (VolPack), rather than the traversal or shading algorithms themselves. The method operates in two primary paradigms: a high-level "Standard Volume Material" interface for direct grid binding, and a low-level "Material Format" structure for procedural or texture-driven shading. Both paradigms feed into the volume rendering integral by defining \sigmat (extinction/density) and c (color/emission). Inputs: Raw scalar/vector grids (e.g., density, temperature, labels), user-defined parameters (density multipliers, anisotropy), and optional texture descriptors. Outputs: A material state object or context configuration that defines how sample points along a ray are shaded. This structure binds named VDB grids to specific physical properties. It does not have a single C++ struct definition in the sources but is defined by its channel fields: Volume Channel: String (case-sensitive name of the VDB grid, typically 'density'). Density: Float multiplier for the volume channel. Scatter Color: RGB vector. Scatter Scale: Float multiplier for scatter intensity. Anisotropy Mode: Enum (Henyey-Greenstein or Jendersie-d’Eon). Transparency Color: RGB vector (per-wavelength attenuation). Transparency Depth: Float (cm, per-wavelength travel distance). Emission Channel: String (name of temperature grid). Emission Mode: Enum (Blackbody or Color). Defined in, this struct holds shading parameters for surface-like volumetric boundaries or procedural volumes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct Material { // Core PBR-like properties float albedo[3]; // Linear float RGB float metalness; // Float [0..1] float roughness; // Float [0..1] float F0[3]; // Linear float RGB, base reflectivity // Projection and Normal bool triplar; // True for XZ planar, False for triplanar float normalStrength; // Linear float // Texture Descriptors (-1 if unused) int albedoTex; // Texture descriptor int normalTex; // Texture descriptor int roughnessTex; // Texture descriptor int metalnessTex; // Texture descriptor int heightmapTex; // Texture descriptor (geometric displacement) int ambietTex; // Texture descriptor (ambient occlusion) }; Defined in, this is not a persistent struct but a state set via vpSetMaterial. The relevant constants are: materialnum: VPMATERIAL0 to VPMATERIAL5. property: VPAMBIENT, VPDIFFUSE, VPSPECULAR, VPSHINYNESS. surfaceside: VPEXTERIOR, VPINTERIOR, VPBOTHSIDES. Defined in, this configuration binds textures and metadata to a shader material. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct VRDFMaterialConfig { int IsLabelMap; // 1 if labelmap, 0 otherwise float P1; // Lower bound of intensity range float P99; // Upper bound of intensity range vec4 Dim; // (dimX, dimY, dimZ, 1.0f) mat4 Affine; // 4x4 affine transform mat4 InvAffine; // Inverse affine transform texture3D TFTex; // Transfer function texture texture3D VolumeTexLabels; // Label texture (fallback: BlackTex3D) texture3D VolumeTexWeights; // Weight texture (fallback: BlackTex3D or null) int HasWeights; // 1 if weights exist, 0 otherwise }; 1. Bind Volume Channel: Assign the name of the density grid to the Volume Channel field. 2. Set Density: Multiply the grid values by the Density parameter to control overall thickness. 3. Configure Scatter: Set Scatter Color and Scatter Scale to define reflection properties. 4. Select Phase Function: Choose Anisotropy Mode. Use Henyey-Greenstein (-1 to +1) for isotropic smoke or Jendersie-d’Eon for cloud droplets. 5. Configure Transparency: Set Transparency Color (darker = thicker) and Transparency Depth (in cm) to model wavelength-dependent attenuation. 6. Configure Emission (Optional): If rendering fire, bind the temperature grid to Emission Channel. Set Emission Mode to Blackbody for physical accuracy (3,000K–12,000K) or Color for artistic control. 1. Initialize Context: Create a vpContext object. 2. Set Material Properties: Call vpSetMaterial(vpc, materialnum, property, surfaceside, r, g, b). For VPSHINYNESS, set g and b to 0. 3. Define Surface Side: Use VPEXTERIOR (gradient towards viewer), VPINTERIOR (gradient away), or VPBOTHSIDES. 4. Reverse Sides (Optional): Call vpEnable(vpc, VPREVERSESURFACESIDES) to invert exterior/interior definitions. 1. Extract Dimensions: Get dimX, dimY, dimZ from d.meta.dim. 2. Determine Intensity Range: Initialize p1 = 0.0f, p99 = 1.0f. If d.tf.type == "continuous" and d.meta.intensityrange exists with length 2, set p1 = d.meta.intensityrange[0], p99 = d.meta.intensityrange[1]. 3. Compute Affine Matrices: Construct affine from d.meta.affine (4x4). Compute invAffine = affine.inverse(). 4. Select Textures: texLbl = volumeTexLabels ?? d.labelTexture ?? BlackTex3D. texW = volumeTexWeights ?? d.weightTexture ?? null. Bind VolumeTexWeights to texW or BlackTex3D. Set HasWeights = 1 if texW != null, else 0. 5. Bind Transfer Function: Bind TFTex to tfTexCurrent. Set IsLabelMap = 1 if d.tf.type == "labelmap", else 0. 6. Set Uniforms: Set P1, P99, Dim, Affine, InvAffine. Assign volumeMaterial to MeshRenderer.sharedMaterial. 1. Constructor 1 (Full): Initialize albedo, metalness, roughness, F0. Set all texture descriptors (albedoTex, etc.) to -1. Set triplar to planar (False) and normalStrength to 1.0. 2. Constructor 2 (Default F0): Initialize albedo, roughness, metalness. Call Constructor 1 with F0 = [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. Volume Rendering Integral (Context): C(r) = \int{tn}^{tf} T(t) \sigmat(t) c(t) dt Where \sigmat is derived from the Volume Channel multiplied by Density and modified by Transparency Color/Depth. Blackbody Emission (Standard Volume): Temperature T (Kelvin) maps to color C. T \approx 3,000 K \rightarrow Deep Red. T > 9,000 K \rightarrow White/Blue-White. Base Reflectivity (Material Format): For non-metal dielectrics, F0 = [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. F0: [0.04, 0.04, 0.04] for dielectrics. Anisotropy (Henyey-Greenstein): Slider range [-1, 1]. Transparency Depth: Measured in centimeters; should match real-world volume size. Material IDs: VPMATERIAL0 through VPMATERIAL5. Case Sensitivity: Volume channel names are case-sensitive. Surface Side Ambiguity: VPEXTERIOR and VPINTERIOR depend on gradient direction. Use VPREVERSESURFACESIDES if the gradient is inverted relative to the viewer. Textureless Default: Material objects default to textureless (descriptors = -1) unless explicitly bound. Labelmap Handling: In VRDF, IsLabelMap must be set correctly to switch between continuous and discrete transfer function evaluation. A specific implementation within the VRDF SDK that handles the binding of transfer functions, label maps, and weight textures to the GPU shader. It distinguishes itself by supporting label-based rendering (discrete classes) and weighted sampling. Choose this when using the VRDF SDK for scientific visualization requiring label maps or importance weighting. Time Complexity: O(1) for setting up the material state; O(N) for shading N samples along rays (dependent on the traversal method, not the material setting itself). Memory Complexity: O(1) for the material struct; O(V) for the underlying VDB grids and textures. Strengths: Standard Volume Material offers a fast path for common use cases (clouds, smoke, fire) with physically based presets. VolPack provides simple, low-level control for binary or simple scalar volumes. VRDF SDK offers flexible GPU-side transfer function handling. Limitations: Standard Volume Material's "fast path" limits procedural complexity compared to the node-based approach. VolPack is legacy and lacks modern PBR features. VRDF SDK requires manual affine matrix management. When to Use: Use Standard Volume Material for general-purpose VDB rendering. Use VolPack for legacy C-style API integration. Use VRDF SDK for custom GPU-based volume rendering pipelines with label maps. Standard Volume Material: Originated with Maxon's Cinema 4D and Redshift renderer, designed to simplify VDB volume rendering for artists. Material Format: Described in "Raymarching Distance Fields with CUDA" (2021), providing a CUDA-friendly material structure for raymarched SDFs and volumes. VolPack: Developed at Stanford University in the 1990s, providing a C library for volume rendering. VRDF SDK: An unofficial SDK by Guillaume Schneider for rendering volumetric data in Unity/Unreal, supporting label maps and transfer functions. name: Volume Material Setup
head: ApplyToMaterial, Material Initialization, Shader Parameter Binding, Volume Material Setup (Affine, Weights, Label Map), initMaterial
body: Volume Material Setup initializes the rendering state for direct volume ray casting by creating and caching a RawShaderMaterial (or equivalent shader program) configured for transparent volumetric rendering. It binds necessary textures (noise, fire profiles, transfer functions, labels, weights) and uniform parameters (affine transforms, intensity ranges) to the GPU, enabling the shader to correctly sample and composite volume data. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the binding and configuration of material resources rather than the traversal logic or the transfer function definition itself. The method constructs a material object that encapsulates all shader inputs required for volume rendering. It handles the selection of textures based on availability, computes inverse affine matrices for coordinate transformation, and sets flags to inform the shader about the data type (e.g., label map vs. continuous). Inputs: d: Data object containing metadata (d.meta), transfer function (d.tf), and optional texture references (d.labelTexture, d.weightTexture). volumeTexLabels: Optional pre-loaded 3D texture for label data. volumeTexWeights: Optional pre-loaded 3D texture for weight data. tfTexCurrent: The current transfer function texture. vs, fs: Vertex and fragment shader source code strings. Outputs: material: An initialized material object (e.g., THREE.RawShaderMaterial) ready for assignment to a mesh renderer. Uniforms Object Layout The uniforms passed to the shader are structured as follows: | Uniform Name | Type | Value/Source | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | nzw | t (Texture) | nzw.png | Noise texture for turbulence. | | fireProfile | t (Texture) | firetex.png | Fire profile texture. | | time | f (Float) | 1.0 | Time parameter for animation. | | TFTex | t (Texture) | tfTexCurrent | Transfer function texture. | | VolumeTexLabels | t (Texture) | Selected label texture | Label map texture. | | VolumeTexWeights | t (Texture) | Selected weight texture | Weight texture (or black if null). | | Affine | m4 (Matrix4) | affine | 4x4 affine transformation matrix. | | InvAffine | m4 (Matrix4) | affine.inverse | Inverse affine transformation matrix. | | Dim | v4 (Vector4) | (dimX, dimY, dimZ, 1.0) | Volume dimensions. | | P1 | f (Float) | p1 | Lower bound of intensity range. | | P99 | f (Float) | p99 | Upper bound of intensity range. | | IsLabelMap | i (Int) | 0 or 1 | Flag indicating label map usage. | | HasWeights | i (Int) | 0 or 1 | Flag indicating weight texture presence. | Texture Configuration nzw: RepeatWrapping on S and T axes; LinearFilter for mag/min. fireProfile: ClampToEdgeWrapping on S and T axes; LinearFilter for mag/min. 1. Extract Dimensions: Read dimX, dimY, dimZ from d.meta.dim. 2. Initialize Intensity Range: Set p1 = 0.0, p99 = 1.0. If d.tf.type == "continuous" and d.meta.intensityrange exists with length 2: Set p1 = d.meta.intensityrange[0]. Set p99 = d.meta.intensityrange[1]. 3. Load Noise Texture: Load nzw.png. Set wrapping to RepeatWrapping and filtering to LinearFilter. 4. Load Fire Profile Texture: Load firetex.png. Set wrapping to ClampToEdgeWrapping and filtering to LinearFilter. 5. Compute Affine Matrices: Construct affine matrix from d.meta.affine (4x4). Compute invAffine = affine.inverse(). 6. Select Label Texture: If volumeTexLabels is provided, use it. Else if d.labelTexture is provided, use it. Else, use a default black 3D texture (BlackTex3D). Bind this to VolumeTexLabels. 7. Select Weight Texture: If volumeTexWeights is provided, use it. Else if d.weightTexture is provided, use it. Else, set texW = null. If texW is not null, bind it to VolumeTexWeights and set HasWeights = 1. If texW is null, bind BlackTex3D to VolumeTexWeights and set HasWeights = 0. 8. Bind Transfer Function: Bind tfTexCurrent to TFTex. If d.tf.type == "labelmap", set IsLabelMap = 1. Else, set IsLabelMap = 0. 9. Create Material: Instantiate the material (e.g., THREE.RawShaderMaterial) with: Vertex shader vs. Fragment shader fs. Uniforms object containing all textures, matrices, vectors, and flags defined above. side: THREE.DoubleSide. blending: THREE.AdditiveBlending. transparent: true. 10. Assign Material: Assign the created material to MeshRenderer.sharedMaterial. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initmaterial(d, volumeTexLabels=None, volumeTexWeights=None, tfTexCurrent=None, vs=None, fs=None): """ Initializes and returns a RawShaderMaterial for volume rendering. """ # Step 1: Extract dimensions dimX, dimY, dimZ = d.meta.dim[0], d.meta.dim[1], d.meta.dim[2] # Step 2: Initialize intensity range p1 = 0.0 p99 = 1.0 if d.tf.type == "continuous" and hasattr(d.meta, 'intensityrange') and len(d.meta.intensityrange) == 2: p1 = d.meta.intensityrange[0] p99 = d.meta.intensityrange[1] # Step 3: Load noise texture nzw = loadtexture('nzw.png') nzw.wrapS = WRAPREPEAT nzw.wrapT = WRAPREPEAT nzw.magFilter = FILTERLINEAR nzw.minFilter = FILTERLINEAR # Step 4: Load fire profile texture fireProfile = loadtexture('firetex.png') fireProfile.wrapS = WRAPCLAMPTOEDGE fireProfile.wrapT = WRAPCLAMPTOEDGE fireProfile.magFilter = FILTERLINEAR fireProfile.minFilter = FILTERLINEAR # Step 5: Compute affine matrices affine = Matrix4(d.meta.affine) # Assuming 4x4 matrix from d.meta.affine invAffine = affine.inverse() # Step 6: Select label texture if volumeTexLabels is not None: texLbl = volumeTexLabels elif hasattr(d, 'labelTexture') and d.labelTexture is not None: texLbl = d.labelTexture else: texLbl = BlackTex3D # Default black 3D texture # Note: Binding happens in uniform setup # Step 7: Select weight texture if volumeTexWeights is not None: texW = volumeTexWeights elif hasattr(d, 'weightTexture') and d.weightTexture is not None: texW = d.weightTexture else: texW = None if texW is not None: hasWeights = 1 # Bind texW to VolumeTexWeights else: hasWeights = 0 # Bind BlackTex3D to VolumeTexWeights # Step 8: Bind Transfer Function and Flags # Bind tfTexCurrent to TFTex if d.tf.type == "labelmap": isLabelMap = 1 else: isLabelMap = 0 # Step 9: Create Uniforms Object uniforms = { 'nzw': {'type': 't', 'value': nzw}, 'fireProfile': {'type': 't', 'value': fireProfile}, 'time': {'type': 'f', 'value': 1.0}, 'TFTex': {'type': 't', 'value': tfTexCurrent}, 'VolumeTexLabels': {'type': 't', 'value': texLbl}, 'VolumeTexWeights': {'type': 't', 'value': texW if texW is not None else BlackTex3D}, 'Affine': {'type': 'm4', 'value': affine}, 'InvAffine': {'type': 'm4', 'value': invAffine}, 'Dim': {'type': 'v4', 'value': Vector4(dimX, dimY, dimZ, 1.0)}, 'P1': {'type': 'f', 'value': p1}, 'P99': {'type': 'f', 'value': p99}, 'IsLabelMap': {'type': 'i', 'value': isLabelMap}, 'HasWeights': {'type': 'i', 'value': hasWeights} } # Step 10: Instantiate Material material = RawShaderMaterial({ 'vertexShader': vs, 'fragmentShader': fs, 'uniforms': uniforms, 'side': SIDEDOUBLE, 'blending': BLENDADDITIVE, 'transparent': True }) # Step 11: Assign Material # MeshRenderer.sharedMaterial = material return material P1, P99: Floats representing the intensity range for continuous transfer functions. Default: 0.0, 1.0. IsLabelMap: Integer flag (0 or 1). 1 if d.tf.type == "labelmap". HasWeights: Integer flag (0 or 1). 1 if a weight texture is provided. time: Float, default 1.0. Missing Intensity Range: If d.meta.intensityrange is missing for a continuous TF, the range defaults to [0.0, 1.0], which may cause incorrect color mapping if the data is not normalized. Null Textures: If no label or weight texture is provided, a black 3D texture is used. The shader must handle this gracefully (e.g., treating black as zero intensity/weight). Affine Inverse: Computing the inverse affine matrix is critical for correct coordinate transformation. Singular matrices will cause errors. Texture Wrapping: Incorrect wrapping modes (e.g., RepeatWrapping for fire profile) may cause artifacts at texture boundaries. Time Complexity: O(1) for material setup, assuming texture loading is asynchronous or cached. The actual rendering cost is determined by the ray marching scheme. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the material object itself, plus the memory for the textures (which are typically loaded once and reused). Strengths: Centralizes material configuration, making it easy to switch between different rendering modes (e.g., label map vs. continuous) by changing flags. Limitations: Depends on the availability of specific textures (nzw.png, firetex.png) which may not be relevant for all volume rendering scenarios (e.g., non-fire volumes). The method is derived from implementations in WebGL-based volume rendering libraries, specifically VolumetricFire and vrdf-sdk. It reflects the pattern of initializing a RawShaderMaterial with explicit uniform bindings for textures and matrices, common in low-level graphics programming where fine-grained control over shader inputs is required. guillaume-schneider/vrdf-sdk, https://github.com/guillaume-schneider/vrdf-sdk, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) yomotsu/VolumetricFire, https://github.com/yomotsu/VolumetricFire, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: DVGO Density and Color Rendering
head: DVGO volume rendering
body: DVGO (Direct Volume Gaussian Optimization) is a method for rendering 3D scenes from images by combining a sparse voxel grid with neural networks to represent density and view-dependent color. It solves the problem of efficiently synthesizing novel views of complex scenes by decoupling the representation of geometry (density) from appearance (color). Unlike standard NeRF which uses a single MLP for both, DVGO uses a voxel grid for density and a shallow MLP for color, allowing for faster training and inference while maintaining high fidelity. It is distinct from Mr-Voxel Volume Rendering by its specific use of shifted softplus activation for density and post-activation interpolation to achieve sharp surfaces with fewer cells. Inputs: A set of N input images with known camera poses (position and orientation). A voxel grid resolution Nx \times Ny \times Nz. A feature grid V^{(f)} of size R^{C \times Nx \times Ny \times Nz} storing color features. A density grid V^{(d)} of size R^{Nx \times Ny \times Nz} storing raw density values. A shallow Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) parameterized by \Theta. Hyperparameters: shift b for softplus, number of samples n per ray. Outputs: A rendered color image for a given camera view. Data Structures: 1. Density Grid (V^{(d)}): A 3D tensor of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) storing raw scalar values \ddot{\sigma}. These values are not densities directly but inputs to the activation function. 2. Feature Grid (V^{(f)}): A 3D tensor of shape (C, Nx, Ny, Nz) storing C-dimensional feature vectors at each voxel. 3. MLP (MLP\Theta): A small neural network that takes concatenated inputs of interpolated features, positional encodings of position, and positional encodings of direction. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting: For each pixel, cast a ray r from the camera origin through the pixel center. Determine the intersection interval [tn, tf] with the volume bounds. 2. Sampling: Sample n points xi uniformly along the ray within [tn, tf]. Let \deltai be the distance between adjacent sampled points (step size). 3. Density Retrieval and Activation: Retrieve the raw density value \ddot{\sigma}i from the density grid V^{(d)} at position xi using trilinear interpolation: \ddot{\sigma}i = \text{interp}(xi, V^{(d)}) Apply the shifted softplus activation to obtain the volume density \sigmai: \sigmai = \text{softplus}(\ddot{\sigma}i) = \log(1 + \exp(\ddot{\sigma}i + b)) where b is a learnable or fixed hyperparameter shift. This ensures \sigmai \ge 0. 4. Color Feature Retrieval: Retrieve the color feature vector fi from the feature grid V^{(f)} at position xi using trilinear interpolation: fi = \text{interp}(xi, V^{(f)}) 5. Color Emission Computation: Apply positional encoding \gamma(\cdot) to the position xi and the ray direction d. Concatenate the interpolated feature fi, encoded position \gamma(xi), and encoded direction \gamma(d). Pass the concatenated vector through the shallow MLP to get the view-dependent color emission ci^{(rgb)}: ci^{(rgb)} = MLP\Theta([fi; \gamma(xi); \gamma(d)]) 6. Termination Probability: Calculate the probability \alphai that the ray terminates at sample i: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) 7. Accumulated Transmittance: Calculate the accumulated transmittance Ti from the near plane to sample i: Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) with T1 = 1. 8. Volume Rendering Quadrature: Accumulate the color contributions from all samples and add the background color c{bg} attenuated by the final transmittance: \hat{C}(r) = \sum{i=1}^{n} Ti \alphai ci^{(rgb)} + T{n+1} c{bg} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def softplus(x, b=0.0): """Shifted softplus activation.""" return np.log(1 + np.exp(x + b)) def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """ Trilinear interpolation for a 3D grid. grid: numpy array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) or (C, Nx, Ny, Nz) x, y, z: float coordinates in [0, 1] relative to grid bounds Returns: scalar or vector """ # Implementation details for trilinear interpolation are assumed standard # This is a placeholder for the actual interpolation logic pass def positionalencoding(x, mindeg, maxdeg): """ Standard positional encoding for NeRF-like methods. """ # Implementation details for positional encoding are assumed standard pass def renderray(rayorigin, raydirection, near, far, densitygrid, featuregrid, mlp, b, nsamples, cbg): """ Renders a single ray using DVGO. """ # 1. Sample points along the ray tvals = np.linspace(near, far, nsamples) points = rayorigin + tvals[:, np.newaxis] raydirection # Calculate step sizes (delta) # deltai is distance to adjacent point. For uniform sampling: delta = (far - near) / (nsamples - 1) accumulatedcolor = np.zeros(3) accumulatedtransmittance = 1.0 for i in range(nsamples): x, y, z = points[i] # 2. Retrieve density and apply activation rawdensity = trilinearinterpolate(densitygrid, x, y, z) sigma = softplus(rawdensity, b) # 3. Calculate termination probability alpha = 1.0 - np.exp(-sigma delta) # 4. Retrieve color features colorfeatures = trilinearinterpolate(featuregrid, x, y, z) # 5. Compute color emission posenc = positionalencoding(points[i], mindeg=0, maxdeg=10) direnc = positionalencoding(raydirection, mindeg=0, maxdeg=4) mlpinput = np.concatenate([colorfeatures, posenc, direnc]) coloremission = mlp(mlpinput) # 6. Accumulate weight = accumulatedtransmittance alpha accumulatedcolor += weight coloremission accumulatedtransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # 7. Add background accumulatedcolor += accumulatedtransmittance cbg return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Post-Activation Sharpness: Applying non-linear activation functions (like softplus) after trilinear interpolation (post-activation) produces sharper surfaces than pre-activation. This allows the use of fewer grid cells for surface detail. Precision: The exponential function in \alphai and Ti can suffer from underflow or overflow if \sigmai \deltai is very large or very small. Standard numerical stability techniques (e.g., log-space accumulation) should be considered, though the source notes do not specify them. Boundary Conditions: The interpolation must handle points outside the grid bounds appropriately (e.g., clamping or treating as zero density). Time Complexity: O(n \cdot N) where n is the number of samples per ray and N is the number of pixels. The MLP inference is constant time per sample relative to grid size. Memory Complexity: O(Nx Ny Nz \cdot (1 + C)) for storing the density and feature grids. This is significantly less than dense voxel grids used in traditional methods if the scene is sparse, but more than pure neural representations for simple scenes. Performance: DVGO is generally faster to train than standard NeRF because the density grid can be optimized directly and the MLP is shallow. Inference speed depends on the number of samples n and the cost of the MLP. Strengths: High-quality view-dependent rendering; efficient storage compared to dense voxel grids; sharp surfaces with fewer cells due to post-activation. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of grid resolution and hyperparameters (like b); may struggle with very large scenes without hierarchical structures. DVGO was introduced in the paper "NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance". It builds upon the principles of NeRF but introduces a hybrid representation using voxel grids for density and features. The method leverages the shifted softplus activation from Mip-NeRF to ensure non-negative densities. The key insight is that post-activation interpolation leads to sharper surfaces, reducing the need for high-resolution grids. NeRF Synthesis with Shading Guidance, https://link.springer.com/chapter/10.1007/978-981-99-9666-716, fetched 2026-10-26

name: DOSRender
head: DOS Renderer, Depth of Field Scattering, Depth-Ordered Slice Renderer, Direct Volume Rendering with Occlusion and Instance Tracking, Occlusion-Aware Slice Accumulator [S1, unofficial]
body: DOSRender is a depth-ordered, slice-based volume rendering technique that accumulates color and occlusion along a ray while simultaneously tracking semantic instance and group IDs for segmentation. It distinguishes itself from standard front-to-back ray casting by integrating precomputed occlusion samples and hierarchical group membership buffers directly into the accumulation pass, allowing for efficient occlusion-aware rendering and semantic data extraction in a single pass. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: uMvpInverseMatrix: Inverse Model-View-Projection matrix for unprojecting screen coordinates. uDepth: Current depth value for the ray. uInstanceID, uGroupID: Textures storing instance and group IDs at 2D screen positions. uIDVolume: 3D texture mapping 3D positions to instance IDs. sGroupMembership: std430 buffer mapping instance IDs to group IDs. uAccumulator: Texture storing the accumulated color, occlusion, instance ID, and group ID from previous slices. uOcclusion: Texture containing precomputed occlusion samples. uOcclusionScale: Scale factor for occlusion sample offsets. uOcclusionSamplesCount: Number of occlusion samples to average. uExtinction: Uniform float controlling the extinction coefficient multiplier. uSliceDistance: Uniform float representing the distance between slices. uColorBias, uAlphaBias, uAlphaTransfer: Parameters for transfer function biasing. Volume Color Data: Mask/data volumes and transfer functions used to sample transferSample. Outputs (Fragment Shader): oColor: vec4 containing the accumulated color and alpha. oOcclusion: float representing the remaining occlusion/transmittance. oInstanceID: uint for the current instance ID. oGroupID: uint for the current group ID. vPosition: vec2 vertex shader output representing screen position. Data Structures bGroupMembership: A std430 storage buffer (binding 0) containing uint sGroupMembership[], which maps instance IDs to group IDs. oAccColorVolume: An rgba8 image3D (binding 1), write-only, used for accumulating color across slices. Algorithm Steps 1. Initialization (Reset Pass): Reset outputs to initial values: oColor = vec4(0), oOcclusion = 1.0, oInstanceID = 0u, oGroupID = 0u. 2. Unprojection: Unproject the screen position aPosition (from vertex shader) and depth uDepth to 3D world space: vPosition3D = \frac{(uMvpInverseMatrix \times vec4(aPosition, uDepth, 1)).xyz}{w} where w is the w-component of the resulting vector. 3. Boundary Check: If any component of vPosition3D is outside the [0, 1] range, output the previous color, occlusion, instance ID, and group ID (from the accumulator or previous step) and terminate the shader execution. 4. Semantic ID Resolution: Retrieve the current instance and group IDs from 2D position textures using the screen position vPosition: glsl uint instanceID = texture(uInstanceID, vPosition).r; uint groupID = texture(uGroupID, vPosition).r; If groupID is 0 (indicating an unassigned instance): 1. Fetch a new instance ID from uIDVolume at vPosition3D. 2. Look up the new group ID from sGroupMembership using the fetched instance ID. 3. If the new group ID is non-zero, update oInstanceID and oGroupID with these new values; otherwise, retain the old IDs. 5. Volume Sampling: Sample the volume color at vPosition3D using mask/data volumes and transfer functions, applying biases: glsl vec4 transferSample = sampleVolumeColor(vPosition3D); The sampling incorporates uColorBias, uAlphaBias, and uAlphaTransfer. 6. Accumulator Retrieval: Sample the accumulator texture at the current screen position to get previous state: glsl vec4 color = texture(uAccumulator, vPosition); Let prevColor be this value. 7. Extinction and Alpha Calculation: Calculate extinction: extinction = transferSample.a \times uExtinction Calculate alpha (opacity) for the current slice: \alpha = 1.0 - \exp(-extinction \times uSliceDistance) Here, uExtinction acts as the total extinction coefficient \sigmat. 8. Occlusion Calculation: Compute occlusion attenuation by averaging precomputed occlusion samples. The samples are taken at offsets from vPosition: O = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ci \cdot e^{-\sigmat \cdot d} where Ci are the occlusion samples, \sigmat is the extinction, d is the slice distance (uSliceDistance), and N is the number of samples (uOcclusionSamplesCount). The samples are located at vPosition + occlusionSampleOffset uOcclusionScale. Update oOcclusion using this calculated value. 9. Color Blending: Calculate the color contribution: color = transferSample.rgb \times prevOcclusion \times \alpha where prevOcclusion is prevColor.a (or the stored occlusion value). Update the output color: oColor = prevColor + vec4(color \times (1.0 - prevColor.a), \alpha) Clamp the alpha component: oColor.a = \min(oColor.a, 1.0) Finally, mix the accumulated color with a white background: oColor = mix(vec4(1), vec4(color.rgb, 1), color.a). 10. Output: Write oColor, oOcclusion, oInstanceID, and oGroupID to the frame buffer or accumulator texture. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dosrenderfragment(aPosition, uDepth, uMvpInverseMatrix, vPosition, uInstanceID, uGroupID, uIDVolume, sGroupMembership, uAccumulator, uOcclusion, uOcclusionScale, uOcclusionSamplesCount, uExtinction, uSliceDistance, volumedata, transferfunction, occlusionSampleOffsets): # 1. Unproject clippos = vec4(aPosition.x, aPosition.y, uDepth, 1.0) worldposvec = mat4mulvec4(uMvpInverseMatrix, clippos) w = worldposvec.w if w == 0.0: return vec4(0.0), 1.0, 0, 0 # Fallback vPosition3D = vec3(worldposvec.x / w, worldposvec.y / w, worldposvec.z / w) # 2. Boundary Check if not (0.0 <= vPosition3D.x <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= vPosition3D.y <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= vPosition3D.z <= 1.0): prevacc = texture2d(uAccumulator, vPosition) return prevacc.rgb, prevacc.a, prevacc.b, prevacc.c # Assuming accumulator layout matches outputs # 3. Semantic ID Resolution instanceID = texture2d(uInstanceID, vPosition).r groupID = texture2d(uGroupID, vPosition).r if groupID == 0: newinstanceID = texture3d(uIDVolume, vPosition3D).r newgroupID = sGroupMembership[newinstanceID] if newgroupID != 0: instanceID = newinstanceID groupID = newgroupID # 4. Volume Sampling # Standard volume texture lookup with transfer function application transferSample = samplevolumecolor(vPosition3D, volumedata, transferfunction) # 5. Retrieve Accumulator prevColor = texture2d(uAccumulator, vPosition) prevOcclusion = prevColor.a # Assuming alpha channel stores previous occlusion/transmittance # 6. Extinction and Alpha extinction = transferSample.a uExtinction alpha = 1.0 - exp(-extinction uSliceDistance) # 7. Occlusion Calculation occlusionsum = 0.0 for i in range(uOcclusionSamplesCount): # Standard offset calculation for precomputed samples offset = occlusionSampleOffsets[i] uOcclusionScale samplepos = vPosition + offset Ci = texture2d(uOcclusion, samplepos).r occlusionsum += Ci exp(-extinction uSliceDistance) currentocclusion = occlusionsum / uOcclusionSamplesCount # 8. Color Blending colorcontribution = transferSample.rgb prevOcclusion alpha # Update color newcolor = prevColor + vec4(colorcontribution (1.0 - prevColor.a), alpha) newcolor.a = min(newcolor.a, 1.0) # Mix with white background finalcolor = mix(vec4(1.0), vec4(newcolor.rgb, 1.0), newcolor.a) # 9. Output return finalcolor, currentocclusion, instanceID, groupID Parameters steps: Number of scattering steps or depth levels. slices: Number of slices used in the rendering process. extinction: Extinction coefficient controlling light absorption/scattering intensity. aperture: Aperture size, likely controlling depth of field blur or scattering spread. samples: Number of samples used for occlusion or scattering calculations. cutDepth: Depth cutoff value, likely for clipping or limiting scattering depth. showBoundingBox: Boolean flag to render a bounding box. showAxes: Boolean flag to render coordinate axes. boundingBoxColor: RGB color array for the bounding box. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Group ID 0: A group ID of 0 indicates an unassigned instance. The shader explicitly checks for this and remaps it using the sGroupMembership buffer to prevent rendering artifacts from uninitialized group data. Out of Bounds: If the 3D position is outside the [0,1] range, the shader must correctly output the previous accumulated state to avoid discarding valid data or introducing black artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Integrates semantic segmentation (instance/group IDs) directly into the volume rendering pass, reducing the need for separate post-processing passes. Limitations: Relies on precomputed occlusion samples, which may limit dynamic occlusion scenarios. The requirement for std430 buffers and specific texture layouts may increase implementation complexity on some hardware. When to use: When semantic segmentation is required alongside volume visualization, or when occlusion-aware depth ordering is critical and can be approximated by precomputed samples. When not to use: For scenes with highly dynamic occlusion that cannot be precomputed, or when hardware does not support std430 buffers efficiently. DOSRender is described in the context of the vpt-conductor project, an unofficial implementation or toolset related to volume rendering and visualization. The technique appears to be a specialized variant of direct volume ray casting, adapted for semantic segmentation tasks by tracking instance and group IDs. UL-FRI-LGM/vpt-conductor, https://github.com/UL-FRI-LGM/vpt-conductor, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Light Transmittance Marching
head: Light Marching, Light Transmissance March, Nested Light Ray Sampling, Nested Raymarching for Light Sampling, Secondary light march, Shadow Raymarching in Volume
body: Light Transmittance Marching is a technique to compute physically accurate lighting in a volume by casting a secondary raymarch from each sample point on the primary view ray towards the light source to calculate absorbed light (transmittance). It solves the problem of volumetric occlusion, where light passing through the volume before reaching a sample point is attenuated by the medium itself. Unlike Front-to-Back Volume Rendering, which typically assumes uniform or pre-computed lighting, this method dynamically computes the light energy arriving at each sample point by accounting for the density along the path to the light. Inputs: rayOrigin: The camera position. rayDirection: The normalized direction of the primary view ray. lightDirection: The normalized direction vector from the scene to the light source (e.g., the sun). scene(pos, isLightSample): A function that returns the density at position pos. The boolean flag distinguishes between primary ray sampling and light sampling, allowing for different density evaluation strategies or optimizations. MAXSTEPS: The number of steps in the primary raymarch loop. MAXSTEPSLIGHTS: The number of steps in the nested light sampling loop. MARCHSIZE: The step size for the primary raymarch. marchSize (or stepSize): The step size for the nested light sampling loop. ABSORPTIONCOEFFICIENT: The coefficient used in Beer's Law for light absorption. Outputs: lightEnergy: The accumulated luminance for the pixel, incorporating the attenuated light contribution from each sample point along the primary ray. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables for position, density, and accumulated energy. The method relies on iterative sampling of the scene function. Parameters: MAXSTEPSLIGHTS: Set to 6 to preserve frame-rate. ABSORPTIONCOEFFICIENT: Set to 0.9. marchSize (light step): Set to 0.03. MAXSTEPS: Set to 50. MARCHSIZE (primary step): Set to 0.16. Steps: 1. Initialize the primary raymarch loop. For each step i from 0 to MAXSTEPS - 1: a. Calculate the current position p along the primary ray: p = rayOrigin + depth \cdot rayDirection where depth accumulates MARCHSIZE at each step in the primary loop. b. Sample the density at p using the primary scene function: density = scene(p, false). c. If density > 0.0: i. Initiate a nested light sampling loop to calculate light transmittance. ii. Initialize totalDensity = 0.0 and position = p. iii. For each step j from 0 to MAXSTEPSLIGHTS - 1: 1. Advance the position along the light direction: position = position + lightDirection \cdot marchSize \cdot j. 2. Sample the density at the new position using the light-specific scene function: lightSample = scene(position, true). 3. Accumulate the density: totalDensity = totalDensity + lightSample. Note: An alternative implementation accumulates density weighted by step size: totalDensity += density stepSize where stepSize = MAXLIGHTDISTANCE / NUMLIGHTSTEPS. iv. Calculate the light transmittance using Beer's Law: transmittance = e^{-ABSORPTION\COEFFICIENT \cdot totalDensity}. Note: Some implementations use exp(-totalDensity) directly if the absorption coefficient is incorporated into the density or step size. v. Multiply the primary ray's accumulated transmittance by the light transmittance: totalTransmittance = totalTransmittance \cdot transmittance. vi. Calculate the luminance contribution: luminance = density. vii. Add to the total light energy: lightEnergy = lightEnergy + totalTransmittance \cdot luminance. d. Advance the primary ray depth: depth = depth + MARCHSIZE. 2. Return lightEnergy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def lighttransmittancemarch(rayorigin, raydirection, lightdirection, scenefunc, maxsteps=50, maxstepslights=6, marchsize=0.16, lightmarchsize=0.03, absorptioncoefficient=0.9): """ Computes light energy for a single ray using nested light transmittance marching. Args: rayorigin: vec3, camera position. raydirection: vec3, normalized view ray direction. lightdirection: vec3, normalized direction to the light source. scenefunc: function(pos, islightsample) -> float, returns density. maxsteps: int, number of steps in primary raymarch. maxstepslights: int, number of steps in nested light march. marchsize: float, step size for primary raymarch. lightmarchsize: float, step size for light march. absorptioncoefficient: float, Beer's law coefficient. Returns: float, accumulated light energy. """ lightenergy = 0.0 totaltransmittance = 1.0 depth = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): p = rayorigin + depth raydirection density = scenefunc(p, False) if density > 0.0: totaldensitylight = 0.0 lightpos = p for j in range(maxstepslights): lightpos = lightpos + lightdirection lightmarchsize j lightsample = scenefunc(lightpos, True) totaldensitylight += lightsample transmittance = math.exp(-absorptioncoefficient totaldensitylight) totaltransmittance = transmittance luminance = density lightenergy += totaltransmittance luminance depth += marchsize return lightenergy Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The nested loop significantly increases algorithmic complexity. To maintain frame-rate, MAXSTEPSLIGHTS must be kept low (e.g., 6). This may require reducing the precision of the primary raymarch (e.g., reducing FBM octaves). Precision: Using a small marchSize for the light march (0.03) helps accuracy but increases the number of samples if MAXSTEPSLIGHTS is not adjusted. Boundary Conditions: The light march assumes the light source is at infinity or the direction is constant. If the light source is point-based and close, the direction lightDirection should be recalculated for each sample point, which is not covered in the basic implementation. Time Complexity: The algorithmic complexity increases due to the nested loop, requiring trade-offs like reducing primary steps or FBM octaves to preserve frame-rate. Memory Complexity: Auxiliary space is O(1), using only scalar variables for accumulation. Measured Performance: With MAXSTEPS=50 and MAXSTEPSLIGHTS=6, the method is feasible for real-time rendering on modern GPUs, provided the scene function is efficient. Strengths: Physically accurate lighting attenuation within the volume; simple to implement as a nested loop. Limitations: High computational cost due to nested sampling; assumes uniform light direction (directional light); does not account for scattering within the volume, only absorption. When to Use: When directional lighting and volumetric occlusion are required for real-time applications, and performance constraints allow for nested sampling. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Light Transmittance Marching was introduced in the context of real-time volumetric cloud rendering to address the lack of proper lighting models in early raymarching demos. It builds on the concept of Beer's Law for light absorption in participating media. name: Light-space transmittance volumes
head: Light-space transmittance, Transmittance volumes
body: Light-space transmittance volumes are a technique for computing light attenuation in participating media by pre-calculating optical depth from light sources into a 3D grid, allowing receivers to look up transmittance via interpolation. It is the volume rendering equivalent of deep shadow maps for participating media, shifting the computational burden from per-receiver ray marching to a single per-cluster grid construction. Inputs and Outputs Input: An absorbance field (voxel grid defining extinction coefficients), a set of emitter clusters (groups of light facets or the entire light source for distant receivers), and a receiver position. Output: The optical depth \tau from the emitter cluster to the receiver position, derived from the transmittance volume. Data Structures The transmittance volume is a 3D grid indexed by spatial position. For each emitter cluster, a separate grid of optical depth values is stored. The grid resolution is typically coarse relative to the scene scale (e.g., 12 \times 12 \times 16) to manage memory. The volume is implemented as a differentiable function (e.g., in JAX) of the absorbance field to ensure exact gradient computation dG/d(\text{absorbance}). Steps 1. Cluster Emission: Group light source facets into clusters. A distant receiver may treat the entire lamp as one cluster, while closer receivers may require finer clustering. 2. March and Store: For each emitter cluster, march outward through the absorbance grid from the cluster's representative origin point. Calculate the accumulated optical depth to every sample point in the grid and store these values in the cluster's transmittance volume. 3. Lookup: For a receiver at position \mathbf{p}, identify the relevant emitter cluster. Retrieve the optical depth \tau by performing trilinear interpolation on the corresponding transmittance volume at \mathbf{p}. 4. Attenuation: Compute transmittance T = e^{-\tau} for shading calculations. Formulas Optical Depth: \tau(\mathbf{p}) = \int{\mathbf{o}}^{\mathbf{p}} \sigmat(\mathbf{r}) \, d\mathbf{r}, where \mathbf{o} is the cluster origin and \sigmat is the extinction coefficient. Transmittance: T = e^{-\tau}. Parameters Grid Resolution: Coarse grids are used to limit memory (e.g., 12 \times 12 \times 16). Cluster Count: The method depends on clustering; tens of clusters are feasible, but one volume per facet is not. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Near-Field Inaccuracy: The method is an approximation twice over: it uses a single representative point for the cluster origin and interpolates \tau between samples. \tau is smooth with respect to receiver position for a fixed origin but not near the origin itself. Therefore, the near field should retain the exact ray walk. Memory Cost: Storage requires one grid of optical depths per cluster. This is efficient for tens of clusters on a coarse grid but prohibitive for one volume per facet. Clustering Dependency: Without emitter clusters, creating one volume per facet costs more than the ray walk it replaces. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computetransmittancevolume(absorbancegrid, clusterorigin, gridresolution): """ March from clusterorigin through absorbancegrid to fill a transmittance volume. Returns a 3D array of optical depths. """ volume = zeros(gridresolution) # March outward from clusterorigin to every point in the grid # Accumulate optical depth along the path for each voxel in grid: voxelpos = gridtoworld(voxel) path = rayfromto(clusterorigin, voxelpos) opticaldepth = 0.0 # Integrate absorbance along path (e.g., using Simpson's rule or simple summation) # This step replaces the per-receiver walk opticaldepth = integrateabsorbance(path, absorbancegrid) volume[voxel] = opticaldepth return volume def gettransmittance(receiverpos, clustervolume): """ Look up optical depth from the pre-computed volume using trilinear interpolation. """ voxelpos = worldtogrid(receiverpos) # Check if receiver is in near-field; if so, fall back to exact walk if isnearfield(receiverpos, clustervolume.origin): return exactraymarch(receiverpos, clustervolume.origin) tau = trilinearinterpolate(clustervolume, voxelpos) return exp(-tau) The 2D/depth-based precursor for opaque geometry, storing transmittance as a function of depth along light rays. The baseline method where each receiver marches towards the light source to calculate transmittance, which this method optimizes Parent. Time Complexity: Construction is O(N{clusters} \times N{voxels}). Lookup is O(1) per receiver via interpolation, compared to O(N{steps}) for the exact walk. Memory Complexity: O(N{clusters} \times N{voxels}) for storing optical depth grids. Performance: On a 4,096-facet lamp, 3,954 receivers, and a 12 \times 12 \times 16 grid, the graded per-call field took ~19-21 s, while uniform absorption took ~0.4 s. The exact walk cost was significantly higher, scaling with N{receivers} \times N{facets} \times (nx + ny + nz). Strengths: Eliminates per-receiver ray marching for transmittance; supports exact gradients via differentiable programming. Limitations: High memory usage for many clusters; inaccurate in the near field; requires clustering. When to Use: When the number of receivers is large and the light source can be effectively clustered; when gradients are needed. When Not to Use: When the light source has many facets requiring individual volumes; in the near field of the light. The technique is based on the concept of shadow maps (Williams 1978) and deep shadow maps (Lokovic & Veach, SIGGRAPH 2000), which compute transmittance from the light's side once into a structure indexed by position. It adapts this idea to 3D volumes for participating media. Radiation: light-space transmittance volumes for a graded medium, so each pair stops walking the absorbance grid (conditional), https://github.com/DeGrootResearchGroup/aquaflux/issues/569, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Casting with Slice-Based Sampling and Gradient Shading
head: Ray Casting (Gradient Shading Variant), psTrace
body: This method performs direct volume ray casting by sampling a 3D volume stored in a 2D texture atlas, computing surface normals via finite differences of sampled densities, and applying diffuse shading. It stops sampling when a high-density threshold is reached or the ray exits the bounding box. It is distinguished from standard ray marching by its specific use of a 2D texture atlas for 3D data storage and the explicit calculation of gradients for lighting, rather than relying solely on transmittance accumulation or pre-computed normals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D texture (volume) containing a 256x256x256 volume packed into a 16x16 grid of 16x16 slices. Camera parameters (eye position, view direction matrix). Light position (lightPos) and color (lightcolor). Output: A fragment color (glFragColor) representing the rendered pixel. Data Structures: Volume Texture: A sampler2D representing the volume. The volume is packed into a 16x16 grid of slices. Each slice is 256x256 texels. The texture coordinates are calculated as: tex256 = vec2(mod(slice,16.0), floor(slice/16.0))/16.0 + point.xy/16.0. Ray Parameters: tmin and tmax defining the intersection interval with the bounding box. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Calculate the intersection parameters tmin and tmax for the ray against the bounding box defined by boxPoint1 and boxPoint2 using intersectParams(boxPoint1, boxPoint2, eye, dir). 2. Initialization: Initialize the ray parameter t to tmin and the accumulated color color to vec3(0,0,0). 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to 1499 (1500 iterations): a. Ray Position: Calculate the current 3D point point as eye + t dir. b. Gradient Sampling: Sample the density at point and its neighbors (point +/- dt in x, y, z) using sliceSample. sliceSample performs linear interpolation between two slices (slice1 and slice2) based on rate. c. Normal Calculation: Compute the surface normal using finite differences. d. Diffuse Shading: Calculate the diffuse contribution using the computed normal and light direction. e. Termination Check: If the sampled density's red channel sample.r is greater than densitythreshold (0.3) OR t exceeds tmax, break the loop. f. Advance Ray: Increment t by dt. 4. Output: If tmin is greater than 0.0, output glFragColor = vec4(color.xyz, 1.0). Otherwise, output vec4(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0). Formulas: Normal calculation: normal = normalize(vec3(dx1.x-dx2.x, dy1.y-dy2.y, dz1.z-dz2.z)) where dx1 is sample at x+dt, dx2 is sample at x-dt, etc. Diffuse shading: color = sample cosalpha lightcolor where cosalpha = clamp(dot(normal, lightDir), 0.0, 1.0) and lightDir = normalize(lightPos - point.xyz) Parameters: dt: Step size for ray marching. Value: 0.008. densitythreshold: The red channel value threshold to stop ray marching. Value: 0.3. lightPos: Position of the light source. Value: vec3(4,4,4). lightcolor: Color of the light. Value: vec3(1,1,1). boxPoint1: Lower bound of the volume bounding box. Value: vec3(0,0,3). boxPoint2: Upper bound of the volume bounding box. Value: vec3(1,1,4). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The intersectParams function returns vec2(-1,-1) if the ray does not intersect the box, handled by checking t1t2.x > 0.0 before rendering. Precision and boundary conditions are managed by clamping slice indices and checking t > tmax to prevent out-of-bounds sampling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastslicegradient(eye, dir, volumetexture, lightpos, lightcolor): # 1. Ray-Box Intersection tmin, tmax = intersectaabb(eye, dir, vec3(0,0,3), vec3(1,1,4)) # Pitfall: intersectaabb returns vec2(-1,-1) if no intersection if tmin < 0.0: return vec4(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0) # 2. Initialization t = tmin color = vec3(0, 0, 0) # Parameters dt = 0.008 densitythreshold = 0.3 # 3. Ray Marching Loop (1500 iterations) for i in range(1500): point = eye + t dir # Sample density at point and neighbors for gradient dx1 = slicesample(volumetexture, point + vec3(dt, 0, 0)) dx2 = slicesample(volumetexture, point - vec3(dt, 0, 0)) dy1 = slicesample(volumetexture, point + vec3(0, dt, 0)) dy2 = slicesample(volumetexture, point - vec3(0, dt, 0)) dz1 = slicesample(volumetexture, point + vec3(0, 0, dt)) dz2 = slicesample(volumetexture, point - vec3(0, 0, dt)) sample = slicesample(volumetexture, point) # Normal calculation normal = normalize(vec3(dx1.x - dx2.x, dy1.y - dy2.y, dz1.z - dz2.z)) # Diffuse shading lightdir = normalize(lightpos - point) cosalpha = clamp(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0, 1.0) color = sample cosalpha lightcolor # Termination check if sample.r > densitythreshold or t > tmax: break # Advance ray t += dt # Output if tmin > 0.0: return vec4(color, 1.0) else: return vec4(0.5, 0.5, 0.5, 1.0) def intersectaabb(origin, direction, boxmin, boxmax): # Returns vec2(-1,-1) if no intersection tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < boxmin[i] or origin[i] > boxmax[i]: return (-1.0, -1.0) else: t1 = (boxmin[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (boxmax[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if tmin > tmax: return (-1.0, -1.0) if tmax < 0: return (-1.0, -1.0) return (tmin, tmax) def slicesample(texture, point): # Volume is 256x256x256 packed into 16x16 grid of 16x16 slices slicefloat = point.z sliceidx = floor(slicefloat) rate = slicefloat - sliceidx sliceidx = clamp(sliceidx, 0.0, 255.0) # Texture coordinate calculation ubase = mod(sliceidx, 16.0) / 16.0 vbase = floor(sliceidx / 16.0) / 16.0 u = ubase + point.x / 16.0 v = vbase + point.y / 16.0 # Linear interpolation between two slices based on rate val1 = texture.sample(u, v) val2 = texture.sample(u, v + 1.0/16.0) return mix(val1, val2, rate) Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of ray steps (1500 in the reference implementation). Each step involves 7 texture samples (current point + 6 neighbors) and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the ray marching state, plus the memory for the volume texture (256x256x256 packed into 256x256 2D texture). Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Simple implementation; provides basic surface-like shading via gradient estimation; efficient memory usage via texture atlas packing. Limitations: No transmittance/absorption accumulation; limited to diffuse shading; fixed step size may lead to aliasing or missed features; gradient estimation is noisy and approximate. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. This method originates from an unofficial WebGL volume rendering tutorial by tkris007. It demonstrates a practical approach to rendering 3D volumes on the web using fragment shaders and texture atlases. tkris007/webGL-volume-rendering, https://github.com/tkris007/webGL-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Sphere-Guided Volume Rendering
head: Sphere-Guided Sampling
body: Sphere-Guided Volume Rendering is a sampling strategy for neural implicit surface reconstruction that uses a trainable cloud of spheres to filter ray-marching samples. It solves the problem of inefficient sample distribution in standard volume rendering, where samples are often wasted in empty space or fail to capture thin geometry. Unlike fixed-step ray marching or methods relying on greedy optimization, this approach guides sampling by intersecting rays with a coarse surface approximation, ensuring samples are concentrated near the estimated surface. This improves sample efficiency and helps the implicit function converge to a better optimum. The method operates by first defining a coarse surface approximation using a set of spheres, then using these spheres to determine valid sampling intervals along a ray. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray p(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{v} (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{v}), a sphere cloud S = \{Si\}, and a target total sample count n. Output: A set of proposal points T along the ray. Data Structures: Sphere Cloud (S): A set of spheres Si, each defined by center \mathbf{c}i and radius ri. These are trainable parameters optimized via gradient descent. Intervals (I): A set of disjoint 1D intervals [sk, tk] representing the portions of the ray intersecting the sphere cloud. Points (T0, T): Sets of sample positions along the ray. Formulas: The probability of a ray terminating at point p(t) is defined as: w(t) = T(t) \sigma(t) where the transmittance is: T(t) = \exp \left( - \int0^t \sigma(s) ds \right) The observed color C(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) is approximated by the discretized volume rendering integral: \hat{C}(\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{v}) = \sum{i=1}^{N} Ti \alphai ci where Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) is the accumulated transmittance, and \alphai is the opacity at point pi, estimated from the density function \sigma: \alphai = 1 - \exp \left( - \int{ti}^{t{i+1}} \sigma(t) dt \right) Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize an empty set of intervals I = \emptyset. 2. For each sphere Si in the sphere cloud S: Compute the intersection of the ray p(t) with sphere Si. Add the resulting interval to I: I:= I \cup (Si \cap p(t)). 3. Find the minimal set of disjoint intervals [sk, tk] such that the union of these intervals equals I. This step merges overlapping or adjacent intersections into contiguous segments. 4. Initialize an empty set of points T0 = \emptyset. 5. For each interval k from 1 to K (where K is the number of disjoint intervals): Calculate the number of samples for this interval: nk = \lfloor n / (tk - sk) \rfloor. Generate uniformly spaced points between sk and tk and add them to T0: T0:= T0 \cup \text{linspace}(sk, tk, nk). 6. Obtain the final set of proposal points T using T0 and a sampling method of choice (e.g., importance sampling or uncertainty sampling). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphereguidedsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, spherecloud, totalsamples): """ rayorigin: 3D vector (o) raydirection: 3D vector (v) spherecloud: List of dicts, each with 'center' (3D vector) and 'radius' (float) totalsamples: Integer n Returns: List of floats (t values along the ray) """ intervals = [] # Step 1 & 2: Compute intersections for sphere in spherecloud: center = sphere['center'] radius = sphere['radius'] # Vector from ray origin to sphere center oc = rayorigin - center # Quadratic equation coefficients for ray-sphere intersection # at^2 + bt + c = 0 a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) b = 2.0 dot(oc, raydirection) c = dot(oc, oc) - radius radius discriminant = b b - 4 a c if discriminant >= 0: sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) # Ensure t1 <= t2 and t > 0 (assuming ray direction is normalized, a=1) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 # Filter for positive t values (forward ray) if t2 > 0: start = max(0.0, t1) end = t2 if start < end: intervals.append((start, end)) # Step 3: Merge intervals to find minimal disjoint set if not intervals: return [] intervals.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) mergedintervals = [] currentstart, currentend = intervals[0] for i in range(1, len(intervals)): nextstart, nextend = intervals[i] if nextstart <= currentend: # Overlapping or adjacent, merge currentend = max(currentend, nextend) else: mergedintervals.append((currentstart, currentend)) currentstart, currentend = nextstart, nextend mergedintervals.append((currentstart, currentend)) # Step 4 & 5: Distribute samples T0 = [] # Calculate total length to distribute samples proportionally totallength = sum(end - start for start, end in mergedintervals) if totallength == 0: return [] for start, end in mergedintervals: length = end - start # Proportional sample count based on interval length # Note: Source uses floor(n / (tk - sk)) which sums to less than n if not normalized. # The source algorithm 1 step 8 says: nk:= floor(n / (tk - sk)). # This implies n is distributed such that density is uniform per unit length? # Actually, looking at source: "nk:= floor(n / (tk - sk))" seems to be a typo in my interpretation # or the source implies n is a density? # Re-reading source: "calculate the number of samples nk = floor(n / (tk - sk))" # If n is total samples, this formula is dimensionally inconsistent if tk-sk is length. # However, standard interpretation of such algorithms is proportional allocation. # Let's stick strictly to the source text provided: "nk:= floor(n / (tk - sk))" # Wait, if n=100 and length=10, nk=10. If another interval has length 5, nk=20. # This would mean shorter intervals get MORE samples? That contradicts "uniformly spaced". # Let's re-read carefully: "nk:= floor(n / (tk - sk))" # If the source meant "n (tk - sk) / TotalLength", it would be proportional. # If the source literally means division, it's inverse proportional. # Given "uniformly spaced points between sk and tk", the number of points should likely scale with length. # However, the prompt says "rewrite... from plain text alone". # I must follow the source formula exactly as written in the notes: "nk:= floor(n / (tk - sk))". # This is likely a transcription error in the source notes or a specific normalization where n is not total count but a parameter. # But note 1 says "The total number of samples n to be distributed". # If I follow the formula literally: nk = floor(n / length). # I will implement the literal formula from the source notes. nk = int(totalsamples / length) if nk < 1: nk = 1 # Guard against division resulting in 0 samples for large intervals # Generate linspace # linspace(start, end, num) generates 'num' points including endpoints? # Usually in rendering, we want interior points or specific count. # Standard numpy linspace includes endpoints. # We generate nk points. step = (end - start) / (nk - 1) if nk > 1 else 0 for j in range(nk): t = start + j step T0.append(t) # Step 6: Final sampling (e.g. importance sampling) # The source says "Obtain T using T0 and the sampling method of choice". # Since no specific method is mandated in the core algorithm, we return T0 as the proposal set. # In practice, T0 might be refined. Here we return the base proposal set. return T0 Parameters: n: The total number of samples to be distributed across the sphere-ray intersections. S: The sphere cloud, acting as a coarse surface approximation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Local Minima: Spheres may get stuck in local minima during optimization, leading to poor surface approximation. Clumping: Spheres may clump together, reducing the exploration of the surface and leaving regions unsampled. Empty Intersections: If the ray does not intersect any sphere, the interval set is empty, and no samples are generated. Details inherent limitations of sphere-guided training in neural implicit surface reconstruction, specifically regarding exploration capabilities and appearance-geometry coupling. It addresses the problem where early-stage geometric estimates constrain the optimization trajectory, leading to artifacts in uncovered regions or incorrect geometry baking when combined with appearance warping. Unlike standard volume rendering which samples uniformly or via importance sampling based on density, sphere-guided methods rely on a discrete set of primitives that, once converged, may fail to recover thin structures or correct systematic errors. Time Complexity: The sampling step involves iterating over all spheres to find intersections (O(|S|)) and merging intervals (O(|S| \log |S|) due to sorting). Sample generation is linear in the number of samples. Overall, it is efficient compared to dense volumetric sampling. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the sphere cloud |S| and the number of samples n. Strengths: Improves sample efficiency by filtering out samples outside the surface region. Allows the implicit function to converge to a better optimum. Uses gradient descent to train the sphere cloud from scratch without prior initialization, unlike greedy optimization methods. Limitations: Spheres may clump or get stuck in local minima. May fail to recover thin structures if the sphere cloud is not sufficiently dense or diverse. When to use: When using base neural reconstruction methods like IDR [37], NeRF [20], or others [5, 23, 32, 36] for surface reconstruction, to improve quality. When not to use: When the surface geometry is extremely thin or complex, and the sphere approximation cannot capture it accurately. Sphere-Guided Volume Rendering was introduced in the paper "Sphere-Guided Training of Neural Implicit Surfaces". It addresses the limitations of previous methods that used greedy optimization (e.g., Neural Sparse Voxel Fields [17]) or sparse point-cloud initialization (e.g., Neural 3D Reconstruction in the Wild [31]). The method uses gradient descent to train the sphere cloud from scratch, allowing it to be trained alongside the implicit surface field. It is used in conjunction with modern systems for surface reconstruction to observe uniform improvements in quality across multiple 3D reconstruction benchmarks. name: Sphere-Guided Training Limitations
body: This article details the inherent limitations of sphere-guided training in neural implicit surface reconstruction, specifically regarding exploration capabilities and appearance-geometry coupling. It addresses the problem where early-stage geometric estimates constrain the optimization trajectory, leading to artifacts in uncovered regions or incorrect geometry baking when combined with appearance warping. Unlike standard volume rendering which samples uniformly or via importance sampling based on density, sphere-guided methods rely on a discrete set of primitives that, once converged, may fail to recover thin structures or correct systematic errors. The limitations stem from the fundamental mechanism of sphere-guided ray marching: 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection Filtering: Rays are only integrated if they intersect the current sphere cloud. Rays missing the cloud are skipped entirely. 2. Sampling Bias: The probability of sampling a region is proportional to the density of spheres in that region. Regions with many spheres receive more samples, while regions with few or no spheres receive none. 3. Early Convergence Dependency: The sphere cloud is optimized jointly with the neural network. The geometry estimated in the early iterations of training defines the initial sphere distribution, which heavily influences the subsequent optimization path. Sphere-guided methods suffer from limited exploration capabilities after the initial convergence phase. Because rays that do not intersect the sphere cloud are skipped, the method cannot recover uncovered regions, such as thin stems or sparse structures, once the sphere cloud has stabilized. This leads to incomplete reconstruction of objects with complex topology or thin features that were not well-represented in the early training stages. Systematic artifacts present in the initial geometry estimate are not corrected by the sphere guidance mechanism and may be amplified during optimization. The bias towards regions with high sphere density reinforces existing errors rather than correcting them, leading to persistent geometric inaccuracies. When combined with appearance warping methods like NeuralWarp, sphere-guided training can incorrectly bake appearance variations into the surface geometry. For instance, appearance variations on the base of objects may be misinterpreted as geometric features, leading to distorted surface reconstructions. This artifact is magnified by the sphere guidance, which reinforces the incorrect geometric interpretation. The limitations of sphere-guided training were identified in the context of "Sphere-Guided Training of Neural Implicit Surfaces". The authors observed these issues during ablation studies comparing their method against NeuS and NSVF. The reliance on coarse geometry estimated early in training was highlighted as a main limitation, particularly in scenarios involving thin structures (e.g., Ficus stems) or complex appearance variations (e.g., Materials scene). name: Ray Marching with Depth Testing
head: Manual Depth Testing, Volumetric Ray Marching
body: Ray marching with depth testing visualizes volumes by casting rays from the camera and sampling at discrete steps along each ray's path, traversing a voxel grid and applying transfer functions to map raw values to color and opacity. It solves the problem of correct occlusion between volumetric effects and solid geometry by integrating manual depth buffer comparisons into the ray marching loop. This method sets itself apart from sibling techniques like Fixed Step Ray Marching by explicitly discarding samples that lie behind opaque objects, thereby preventing visual artifacts where volume appears in front of or behind solid geometry incorrectly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera matrices (view/projection), ray origin o, ray direction d (normalized), volume textures (density, temperature), depth buffer from the geometry pass, step count N, and opacity factor o. Outputs: Final accumulated color C{acc} and opacity \alpha{acc} for the pixel. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin o and direction d. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing density and temperature values. Depth Buffer: Stores depth values zb for each pixel from the preceding geometry pass. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Derive the ray origin o and direction d from camera matrices. Calculate the intersection of the ray with the volume's bounding box to determine the entry point t{min} and exit point t{max}. 2. Step Size Calculation: Compute the step size \Delta t using the formula: \Delta t = \frac{t{max} - t{min}}{N} where N is the configurable step count. 3. Marching Loop: Iterate from t = t{min} to t{max} with increment \Delta t. For each step: a. Position Update: Calculate the current world position p(t): p(t) = o + t d where p(t) is the current position, o is the ray origin, and d is the normalized direction. b. Depth Testing: Transform the sample's world position p(t) to clip space to obtain screen depth z. Compare z against the stored depth buffer value zb with a small bias \epsilon to determine the depth weight dw: dw:= \begin{cases} 1, & \text{if } z < f(zb + \epsilon) \\ 0, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where f is the depth function mapping clip space to normalized device coordinates (typically linear or perspective division dependent on the pipeline), z is the screen depth, zb is the stored depth buffer value, and \epsilon is a small bias (e.g., 0.004) to handle precision issues. c. Sample and Weight: If dw = 0, discard the sample. If dw = 1, sample the density texture \tilde{d} and temperature at p(t). Apply the depth weight to the density: w:= \tilde{d} \cdot dw where w is the weighted density and \tilde{d} is the density value of the volume sample. d. Interpolation: Use quasi-cubic sampling to enhance interpolation quality. e. Accumulation: Update the accumulated color and opacity using alpha blending adapted from Max [13]: \alpha{acc}:= 1 - (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot (1 - \alpha{current}) C{acc}:= C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot C{current} \cdot \alpha{current} where \alpha{current} and C{current} are the opacity and color of the current voxel, derived from the weighted density w and temperature via transfer functions. f. Termination: Continue marching until the ray exits the volume (t > t{max}) or the accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} reaches a threshold (e.g., 1.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchwithdepthtesting(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, depthbuffer, stepcount, opacityfactor): # 1. Calculate bounding box intersections tmin, tmax = calculateraybboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) # 2. Calculate step size stepsize = (tmax - tmin) / stepcount # Initialize accumulation acccolor = vec3(0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # 3. Marching loop for i in range(stepcount): t = tmin + i stepsize position = rayorigin + t raydirection # Transform to clip space to get screen depth clippos = worldtoclipspace(position) z = clippos.z / clippos.w # Perspective divide for depth # Get stored depth buffer value for this pixel zb = depthbuffer.getvalueatpixel(clippos.xy) # Bias to avoid precision issues epsilon = 0.004 depthweight = 1.0 if z < zb + epsilon else 0.0 # Discard if behind opaque geometry if depthweight == 0.0: continue # Sample volume # Use quasi-cubic sampling for better interpolation density = quasicubicsample(volumetexture, position) temperature = quasicubicsample(volumetexture, position, channel='temperature') # Apply depth weight to density weighteddensity = density depthweight # Map to color and opacity via transfer functions # Note: opacityfactor is user-adjustable currentalpha = weighteddensity opacityfactor currentcolor = transferfunctiontemperaturetocolor(temperature) # Alpha blending (Max's formula) accalpha = 1.0 - (1.0 - accalpha) (1.0 - currentalpha) acccolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accalpha) currentcolor currentalpha # Early exit if fully opaque if accalpha >= 1.0: break return acccolor, accalpha def quasicubicsample(texture, uv): # Implementation from Listing 1 in R = texture.dimensions() U = uv R + 0.5 F = fract(U) U = floor(U) + F F (3.0 - 2.0 F) C = (U - vec3(0.5)) / R return texturesample(texture, C) Parameters: Step Count (N): Configurable value with options 16, 32, 64, 128, or 256. 128-256 steps provide a balance between performance and visual quality. Bias (\epsilon): A small value (e.g., 0.004) added to the depth buffer value to prevent precision issues in depth comparison. Opacity Factor: User-adjustable factor controlling the contribution of each sample to the accumulated opacity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Issues: Without a bias \epsilon, depth comparison can fail due to floating-point precision errors, causing the volume to appear incorrectly behind or in front of opaque objects. Occlusion: If depth testing is omitted, volumetric effects may render incorrectly relative to solid geometry. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps N and the number of pixels. Each pixel requires N samples in the worst case. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the volume texture and the depth buffer. The depth buffer is required from the previous pass. Performance: 128-256 steps are recommended for a balance between performance and visual quality. Strengths: Correctly handles occlusion between volumes and solid geometry, reducing artifacts. Quasi-cubic sampling improves interpolation quality over linear sampling. Limitations: Requires a pre-pass to generate the depth buffer. Precision issues can occur without proper biasing. This method is described in the context of real-time volumetric explosion special effects for games, implemented using WebGPU and WGSL shaders. It builds on classical volume ray casting techniques and alpha blending principles described by Max [13]. The specific implementation details, including manual depth testing and quasi-cubic sampling, are presented in the WSCG 2025 Proceedings.
