name: Cube-4
head: Cube-4 volume rendering architecture
body: Cube-4 is a parallel and scalable volume rendering architecture that implements a slice-parallel ray-casting algorithm with tri-linear interpolation and surface normal estimation derived from interpolated samples. It distinguishes itself from previous Cube projects by utilizing only local and fixed-bandwidth interconnections within modular rendering pipelines, avoiding complex global interconnects. Simple and local interconnections allow for easy scalability of performance. Unlike algorithms such as shear-warp, Cube-4 performs high-quality 3D interpolation and surface normal estimation without precomputations or additional data storage. It builds on Template-based Ray-Casting. Inputs and Outputs Input: A volumetric dataset of size n^3 voxels. Output: A final image projected onto the view-plane. Data Structures Volumetric Dataset: Stored in n logical memory modules, each containing n^2 words of 8 bits. Plane Buffers: FIFO buffers used to store previously fetched slices of interpolated samples to avoid repeated memory access. Two such buffers store the two previous slices of interpolated samples, delaying them by n and 2n cycles respectively. Parameters n: The dimension of the volumetric dataset (n^3 voxels). p: The number of processing elements or physical memory modules. Memory Organization To achieve conflict-free simultaneous access to a row of voxels (a beam) parallel to one of the major viewing axes, a skewed memory organization is used. 1. Logical Mapping: A skewing function maps a voxel with coordinates [z, y, x] to a logical memory module k at index i: k = (x + y + z) \mod n i = y + z \cdot n where 0 \le k, x, y, z \le n - 1. Adjacent voxels of beams in the X direction are placed in the same relative locations of adjacent memory modules (rows across the memory). 2. Physical Partitioning: A partitioning function \phi maps logical memory [k, i] to physical memory [kp, ip] for p physical memory banks, partitioning the beams in the X direction: kp = k \mod p zp = (n + \lfloor k/p \rfloor) \mod p Algorithm Steps The architecture chooses Z as the major viewing direction and beams in the X direction. 1. Ray Casting Initialization: Discrete voxel rays with a constant stepping of one in the major viewing direction (Z) are sent into the volume from each pixel on the base-plane (the face of the volumetric dataset most perpendicular to the viewing direction). 2. Slice-Parallel Traversal: The volume is traversed by processing beams along consecutive slices parallel to the base-plane (slice-parallel processing). 3. Interpolation: Two consecutive slices are required for tri-linear interpolation. The previously fetched slice is stored in a plane buffer (FIFO) to be retrieved without further access to voxel memory. 4. Gradient Estimation: A surface normal approximation for a sample point is obtained by computing the gray-level gradient. This gradient is computed using samples from three slices of interpolated samples. The two previously calculated slices of interpolated samples are stored in FIFO plane-buffers, delaying them by n and 2n cycles, respectively. 5. Shading and Classification: The computed surface normal and sample value are used to compute a color based on a local shading model and sample opacity. 6. Compositing: Shaded and classified sample values are composited along the rays into pixel values of the final image. Each slice is composited onto the intermediate results of the previous slices. 7. Final Projection: After rendering, the base-plane contains a distorted image which is warped and projected onto the view-plane. Subtopics Sub-volume Partitioning: Divides an n^3 dataset into smaller sub-volumes of resolution p, each processed by p pipelines. Chosen when hardware limits prevent full n-pipeline beams, though it introduces boundary artifacts for interpolation and gradient estimation. Beam Partitioning: Partitions beams across p < n processing elements to avoid sub-volume boundary issues. Chosen when sub-volume partitioning fails to meet memory or interpolation requirements. Performance: Cube-4 is estimated to achieve real-time performance (30 frames per second) for a 512^3 dataset with 128 pipelines running at 30 MHz. Scalability: The performance of Cube-4 grows proportionally with an increasing number of pipelines, ultimately limited only by memory speeds. It supports resolutions up to 1024^3 16-bit voxels with true real-time performance. Hardware Requirements: The slice-parallel approach operates on beams of n voxels, requiring n processing elements if not partitioned. This leads to an undesirable amount of hardware and limits the maximum size of datasets if p=n is required. Cost-Performance: The cost-performance ratio of Cube-4 is significantly better than existing solutions. Limitations: The first prototype using sub-volume partitioning revealed problems with voxel neighborhood requirements for tri-linear interpolation and gradient estimation at sub-volume boundaries. Cube-4 is the most recent approach in the Cube series of volume rendering architectures, developed by researchers at Hewlett-Packard Research Laboratories, Palo Alto, CA, including Robert S. Larson, Phil Kuekes, and Greg Snider. It was implemented on the Teramac custom computing machine. The algorithm and dataflow were simulated in C and VHDL. Cube-4 differs from previous Cube projects by using only local and fixed bandwidth interconnections. Cube-4 Implementations on the Teramac Custom Computing Machine, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh96/133-143, fetched 2026-10-26 PDF Volume Visualization and Volume Graphics, https://www3.cs.stonybrook.edu/~mueller/teaching/cse332/volvisChapter.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (book)

name: Resampling Point Shading
head: Direct Lighting on Resampling Points, Improved Resampling Point Shading, New Volume Rendering Method for Explosion Fields
body:
Resampling Point Shading is a volume rendering technique that improves shading accuracy by applying the lighting model directly to resampling points using interpolated normal vectors and opacity-weighted color interpolation, thereby avoiding Mach band artifacts and interface color confusion. It sets itself apart from its sibling Accumulative Rendering and Template-based Ray-Casting by calculating normals and lighting at the resampling point itself rather than interpolating pre-shaded vertex colors or lighting results, which preserves microstructure details and physical color consistency at media interfaces. The method modifies the standard ray casting compositing loop by introducing a specific shading calculation phase for each resampling point S along the ray. It replaces the interpolation of shaded vertex colors (Gouraud-style shading) with the interpolation of geometric and material properties, followed by a single lighting evaluation per point. Inputs: Volume dataset F with dimensions L 	imes M 	imes N. For each voxel (l, m, n): Scalar value F{l,m,n}. Material color Cm(S){l,m,n} (output of transfer function). Opacity \alpha(S){l,m,n} (output of transfer function). Ray parameters: origin, direction, step size. Lighting parameters: ambient/diffuse/specular coefficients (ka, kd, ks), light direction L(S), view direction V(S), half-vector H(S), specular exponent n. Outputs: Final pixel color C{out}. The method operates on the existing voxel grid. No new complex data structures are required beyond standard arrays for the volume data and pre-computed gradients if desired (though gradients can be computed on-the-fly). Voxel Data: 3D array of floats for scalar values. Transfer Function Output: 3D arrays for opacity (\alpha) and RGB color (Cm). Gradient Vectors: 3D array of 3-component vectors (
abla F). 1. Gradient Calculation: Calculate the gradient vector 
abla F{l,m,n} for each voxel using central differences. 
abla F{l,m,n} =  egin{bmatrix} (F{l+1,m,n} - F{l-1,m,n})/2\Delta x \ (F{l,m+1,n} - F{l,m-1,n})/2\Delta y \ (F{l,m,n+1} - F{l,m,n-1})/2\Delta z \end{bmatrix} where \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z are the voxel spacings. 2. Ray Casting Loop: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. For each resampling point S along the ray: a. Identify Surrounding Voxels: Determine the 8 voxel corners surrounding the resampling point S. Let these corners be indexed by j=1 \dots 8. b. Interpolate Normal Vector: Calculate the normal vector N(S) at the resampling point by normalizing the trilinearly interpolated gradient vectors of the 8 surrounding voxel points. N(S) = 	ext{normalize}\left( f{	ext{Trilinear}}(	ext{normalize}(
abla Fj)) ight) where f{	ext{Trilinear}} is the trilinear interpolation function. c. Interpolate Opacity and Material Color: Calculate the opacity \alpha(S) and the opacity-weighted material color 	ilde{C}m(S) at the resampling point using trilinear interpolation. \alpha(S) = f{	ext{Trilinear}}(\alphaj) 	ilde{C}m(S) = f{	ext{Trilinear}}(\alphaj Cm(S)j) where \alphaj is the opacity and Cm(S)j is the material color at vertex j. Note: The sources specify that opacity-weighted color interpolation is used to avoid interface color confusion. d. Lighting Calculation: Perform a single lighting operation using the interpolated normal N(S) and the interpolated material color 	ilde{C}m(S). 	ilde{C}S = (ka + kd (L(S) \cdot N(S))) 	ilde{C}m(S) + ks (H(S) \cdot N(S))^n where 	ilde{C}S is the shaded color at the resampling point. e. Compositing: Accumulate the shaded color 	ilde{C}S and opacity \alpha(S) into the final pixel color using the front-to-back compositing equation: C{out} = \sum{a=1}^{m} 	ilde{C}(Sa) \alpha(Sa) \prod{b=1}^{a-1} (1 - \alpha(Sb)) where 	ilde{C}(Sa) is the shaded color at resampling point Sa. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def resamplingpointshading(volumedata, transferfunction, rayorigin, raydirection, voxelsize, lightdir, viewdir, ka, kd, ks, nspecular): """ Performs volume rendering using Resampling Point Shading. Args: volumedata: 3D array of scalar values. transferfunction: Function mapping scalar value -> (color, opacity). rayorigin: 3D vector. raydirection: 3D vector. voxelsize: Scalar spacing (assumed uniform dx=dy=dz). lightdir: 3D vector (normalized). viewdir: 3D vector (normalized). ka, kd, ks: Lighting coefficients. nspecular: Specular exponent. Returns: finalcolor: 3D vector (RGB). """ # Precompute gradients for all voxels # Dimensions L, M, N L, M, N = volumedata.shape gradients = np.zeros((L, M, N, 3)) for l in range(1, L-1): for m in range(1, M-1): for n in range(1, N-1): # Central differences dx = (volumedata[l+1, m, n] - volumedata[l-1, m, n]) / (2 voxelsize) dy = (volumedata[l, m+1, n] - volumedata[l, m-1, n]) / (2 voxelsize) dz = (volumedata[l, m, n+1] - volumedata[l, m, n-1]) / (2 voxelsize) gradients[l, m, n] = [dx, dy, dz] # Normalize gradients for l in range(L): for m in range(M): for n in range(N): grad = gradients[l, m, n] norm = np.linalg.norm(grad) if norm > 1e-8: gradients[l, m, n] /= norm else: gradients[l, m, n] = [0, 0, 0] # Fallback for zero gradient # Ray casting parameters numsamples = 100 # Example, depends on ray length and step size stepsize = voxelsize # Example accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Traverse ray currentpos = rayorigin for i in range(numsamples): # Check if currentpos is within volume bounds if not isinsidevolume(currentpos, L, M, N, voxelsize): break # Get voxel coordinates l, m, n = getvoxelindices(currentpos, voxelsize) # Identify 8 surrounding voxels for trilinear interpolation # Indices for corners of the voxel containing currentpos # Assuming currentpos is inside voxel (l,m,n) # Corners are (l,m,n) to (l+1,m+1,n+1) cornerindices = [] for il in range(l, l+2): for im in range(m, m+2): for in in range(n, n+2): cornerindices.append((il, im, in)) # Trilinear interpolation weights based on fractional part of currentpos # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation requires # calculating weights wl, wm, wn based on distance to corner weights = calculatetrilinearweights(currentpos, voxelsize, l, m, n) # 1. Interpolate Normal Vector interpolatedgrad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for idx, (il, im, in) in enumerate(cornerindices): # Get gradient at corner, handle boundary conditions if necessary grad = gradients[il, im, in] # Weight by trilinear weight interpolatedgrad += grad weights[idx] # Normalize interpolated gradient to get Normal normval = np.linalg.norm(interpolatedgrad) if normval > 1e-8: NS = interpolatedgrad / normval else: NS = [0, 0, 0] # Default normal if gradient is zero # 2. Interpolate Opacity and Weighted Material Color alphasum = 0.0 weightedcolorsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for idx, (il, im, in) in enumerate(cornerindices): # Get scalar value at corner val = volumedata[il, im, in] # Apply transfer function color, alpha = transferfunction(val) # Store for interpolation # Note: We need to interpolate alpha and (alpha color) separately # But the formula says: alpha(S) = ftrilinear(alphaj) # and Cmtilde(S) = ftrilinear(alphaj Cmj) alphasum += alpha weights[idx] weightedcolorsum[0] += (alpha color[0]) weights[idx] weightedcolorsum[1] += (alpha color[1]) weights[idx] weightedcolorsum[2] += (alpha color[2]) weights[idx] alphaS = alphasum CmtildeS = weightedcolorsum # 3. Lighting Calculation # Calculate half vector H = normalize(L + V) HS = normalize(lightdir + viewdir) # Dot products LdotN = dot(lightdir, NS) HdotN = dot(HS, NS) # Blinn-Phong model # I(S) = ka Ia + kd Id (L.N) + ks Is (H.N)^n # Assuming Ia=Id=Is=1 for simplicity or incorporated into ka,kd,ks # The formula in source: CStilde = (ka + kd(L.N)) Cmtilde + ks(H.N)^n # Note: The source formula multiplies the material color by the diffuse term # and adds specular term. It does not multiply specular by material color. diffuseterm = ka + kd LdotN specularterm = ks (HdotN nspecular) # Apply to material color # CStilde = diffuseterm Cmtilde + specularterm # Note: specularterm is a scalar intensity, usually added to the color # If specularterm is meant to be white light, it's added directly. # If it's colored, it might need material color, but source formula implies scalar addition. shadedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): shadedcolor[c] = diffuseterm CmtildeS[c] + specularterm # 4. Compositing # Cout = sum( C(Sa) alpha(Sa) product(1 - alpha(Sb))) # We maintain accumulatedopacity to compute the product term contribution = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for c in range(3): contribution[c] = shadedcolor[c] alphaS # Weight by transmittance from previous steps transmittance = 1.0 - accumulatedopacity for c in range(3): accumulatedcolor[c] += contribution[c] transmittance accumulatedopacity += alphaS transmittance # Advance ray currentpos += raydirection stepsize return accumulatedcolor def isinsidevolume(pos, L, M, N, voxelsize): # Check if pos is within the bounds of the volume grid # Implementation depends on coordinate system setup return True # Placeholder def getvoxelindices(pos, voxelsize): # Convert world position to voxel indices return int(pos[0]/voxelsize), int(pos[1]/voxelsize), int(pos[2]/voxelsize) def calculatetrilinearweights(pos, voxelsize, l, m, n): # Calculate 8 weights for trilinear interpolation # This is a standard implementation detail # Returns list of 8 floats summing to 1 return [1/8] 8 # Placeholder for actual weight calculation def normalize(v): norm = np.linalg.norm(v) if norm == 0: return [0,0,0] return [x/norm for x in v] def dot(v1, v2): return sum(ab for a,b in zip(v1, v2)) Lighting Coefficients: ka, kd, ks (ambient, diffuse, specular reflection coefficients) and specular exponent n. Typical values depend on the desired material appearance; not explicitly given in sources. Voxel Spacing: \Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z. Assumed uniform in examples. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is used for normals, opacity, and weighted color. Interface Color Confusion: Interpolating color and opacity separately causes incorrect colors at interfaces (e.g., green coating at red/green interface). This is handled by using opacity-weighted color interpolation (	ilde{C}m(S) = f{	ext{Trilinear}}(\alphaj Cm(S)j)). Mach Band Phenomenon: Interpolating shaded vertex colors (Gouraud shading) causes Mach bands when normal vectors change drastically. Calculating normals at the resampling point avoids this. Microstructure Loss: Interpolating lighting results flattens curved surfaces and loses detail when viewing angles change. Calculating normals at the resampling point preserves concavity/convexity. Jaggedness: The method retains a slightly fuzzy contour line to avoid jaggedness and distortion. Zero Gradient: If the gradient vector is zero (e.g., inside a homogeneous region), normalization fails. A fallback normal (e.g., [0,0,0] or a default) should be used. Same method, emphasizing the direct application of lighting. Resampling Point Shading. Same method, emphasizing the improvements over the "current method". Resampling Point Shading. Same method, applied specifically to explosion field visualization. Resampling Point Shading. Time Complexity: The method reduces lighting calculations from 8 to 1 per resampling point, significantly improving efficiency compared to the "current method" which performs 8 lighting calculations. Interpolation operations are increased to 7 per resampling point (for color, opacity, and normal vector). Memory Complexity: No additional significant memory requirements beyond the volume data and pre-computed gradients. Measured Performance: Rendering speed improvements: 31% to 39% across various datasets (Groups A-E). Specific times on PC i3-4010U CPU, 8 GB RAM, R5 M230 GPU: Group A (4.88Mb, 1.0e4 meshes): 14.21s (Current) vs 8.93s (New). Group D (413.11Mb, 1.7e7 meshes): 227.3s (Current) vs 144.00s (New). Image Quality: Image entropy reduction: 14.15% (Group 3) and 5.68% (Group 4). Mean gradient increase: 12% (Group C), 43% (Group D), 2.6% (Group E). Image mean and standard deviation reduction for Group E: Max reductions of 28.38% and 34.88% at initial moment; average reductions of ~15% and ~5% during shockwave generation. Strengths: Avoids interface color confusion. Preserves microstructure details (concavity/convexity) under changing viewing angles. Reduces computational cost without requiring GPU acceleration or parallel computing. Produces physically consistent colors at interfaces. Limitations: Requires calculation of gradients for all voxels. Performance gain is relative to the "current method" which is already inefficient; absolute performance depends on dataset size and hardware. When to Use: Suitable for volume rendering of explosion fields and other datasets where microstructure detail and accurate interface coloring are critical, and where computational resources are limited. When Not to Use: If GPU acceleration is available and the "current method" is optimized, the relative gain may be less significant. If microstructure detail is not important, simpler methods may suffice. The method was introduced in 2024 by authors publishing in AIP Advances and Research Square as a solution to the limitations of existing volume rendering methods for explosion field visualization. The "current method" referred to in the sources involves interpolating shaded vertex colors, which leads to Mach band artifacts and interface color confusion. The new method was developed to improve shading accuracy and rendering efficiency for explosion field data, which contains complex media interfaces and microstructures. name: Ray Casting with Ray Subdividing
head: Adaptive Ray Subdivision, Ray Splitting for Perspective Rendering, Ray Subdividing
body: Ray Casting with Ray Subdividing is a technique to maintain adequate spatial sampling rates in volume rendering under perspective projection, where rays diverge as they travel deeper into the scene. It addresses the problem of undersampling distant volume slices by dynamically splitting rays when the local ray density falls below a threshold, ensuring that the footprint of each sample remains consistent with the desired resolution. Unlike fixed-step ray marching, this method adapts the integration step size based on geometric divergence rather than local data features. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A perspective camera ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, a volume dataset V, and a target sampling density or maximum footprint size in world space. Output: A color and opacity value for the pixel, computed via front-to-back compositing. Data Structures: Ray Queue: A list of active rays, where each ray stores its origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, current depth t, and accumulated color/opacity. Split Threshold: A scalar value defining the maximum allowable distance between adjacent rays at a given depth to prevent aliasing. Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel, generate an initial ray r0 from the camera center through the pixel center. Add r0 to the Ray Queue. 2. Ray Divergence Check: For each ray r in the queue, calculate the distance to its nearest neighbor rays in the screen space at the current depth t. If the distance exceeds the Split Threshold, mark r for splitting. 3. Ray Splitting: If a ray is marked for splitting, divide it into two or more sub-rays. The new origins are offset slightly in screen space, and the directions are adjusted to maintain perspective consistency. The original ray is removed from the queue, and the new sub-rays are added. 4. Ray Merging (Optional): As proposed by Kreeger et al., rays can be merged when they converge or when the sampling density exceeds the requirement, reducing computational cost. This requires tracking ray ancestry to correctly accumulate color and opacity. 5. Integration: For each ray in the queue, perform standard volume ray casting (sampling, interpolation, compositing) up to the next split/merge point or until the volume is exited. 6. Final Compositing: Combine the results from all leaf rays contributing to a pixel. Formulas: Ray Divergence Metric: Let d{screen}(ri, rj) be the Euclidean distance between the screen-space projections of rays ri and rj at depth t. Split if: d{screen}(ri, rj) > \delta{max} where \delta{max} is the maximum allowed screen-space footprint size. Parameters: \delta{max}: Typically set to the pixel size or a fraction thereof, depending on the desired anti-aliasing quality. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Splitting: If the threshold is too small, rays may split indefinitely. A maximum recursion depth or minimum ray length must be enforced. Merging Complexity: Merging rays requires careful handling of the compositing order to avoid artifacts. Not all implementations include merging; splitting is the primary mechanism. Performance: The overhead of managing the ray queue and checking divergence can be significant. Efficient spatial data structures (e.g., grids) may be needed to find nearest neighbors quickly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastingwithsubdivision(camera, volume, threshold): rayqueue = [] for pixel in pixels: ray = Ray(camera.origin, pixel.direction) rayqueue.append(ray) while rayqueue: currentrays = rayqueue.popall() nextrays = [] for ray in currentrays: # Check divergence against neighbors if isdivergent(ray, rayqueue, threshold): subrays = splitray(ray, threshold) nextrays.extend(subrays) else: # Perform integration for this ray segment color, opacity = integrateray(ray, volume) # Store result for final compositing storepixelresult(ray.pixelid, color, opacity) rayqueue = nextrays return finalimage Focuses on the dynamic adjustment of ray density based on screen-space metrics. Choose when perspective distortion causes significant sampling variation. Link Emphasizes the geometric necessity of splitting in perspective views. Choose when fixed-step methods fail to capture distant details. Link Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of splits per ray. Splits increase S in distant regions. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where D is the maximum depth of ray splitting. The ray queue grows with the number of active sub-rays. Performance: Improves image quality in distant regions compared to fixed-step ray marching. However, it is more complex to implement and may have higher overhead due to queue management. Strengths: Maintains consistent sampling density across the entire volume, reducing aliasing in perspective views. Limitations: Complex implementation; potential for high memory usage if many rays split; merging is non-trivial. When to Use: Perspective volume rendering where distant details are important and fixed-step sampling leads to aliasing. When Not to Use: Parallel projection (where rays do not diverge) or when performance is critical and some aliasing is acceptable. The concept of ray subdividing was introduced as a solution to the undersampling problem in perspective volume rendering. It is considered an equivalent approach to Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) splatting for raycasting, which handles screen-space footprint mapping. Kreeger et al. proposed improvements involving optimal splitting and merging of rays. The method is part of the broader family of image-order rendering techniques that adapt to geometric properties of the view. name: Cone Casting with Inscribed Sphere Sampling
head: Cone casting, MipNeRF Cone Sampling, Tri-MipRF Cone Casting
body: Cone casting with inscribed sphere sampling is a rendering technique that formulates a pixel as a disc on the image plane and emits a cone from the camera's projection center to sample the volume, avoiding the aliasing artifacts of distance-agnostic ray casting. Unlike sibling methods that treat pixels as points or use anisotropic Gaussian distributions for area sampling, this method uses isotropic spheres inscribed within the cone to match pre-filtered feature encodings. Inputs: Camera parameters: optical center \mathbf{o}, focal length f, pixel dimensions in world coordinates \Delta x, \Delta y. Ray direction \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p}o - \mathbf{o}, where \mathbf{p}o is the pixel center. Sampling distances ti along the ray. Model parameters: Tri-Mip encoding maps \mathcal{M}, tiny MLP weights \Theta. Scene bounds: near plane tn, far plane tf (or AABB intersections). Outputs: Final pixel color C. Data Structures: Sphere Si: Defined by center \mathbf{x}i and radius ri. Tri-Mip Encoding: Three 2D mipmap arrays representing orthogonal planes (XY, YZ, XZ). Tiny MLP: A shallow neural network mapping feature vectors to density and color. Steps: 1. Pixel Disc and Cone Definition: Calculate the pixel disc radius \tilde{r} in world coordinates: \tilde{r} = \frac{\Delta x \cdot \Delta y}{\pi} Emit a cone C from the camera projection center \mathbf{o} along the direction \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{p}o - \mathbf{o}. The apex is at \mathbf{o} and the intersection with the image plane is the disc. The central axis of the cone is defined as: \mathbf{a}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 2. Sampling Distance Selection: Determine a set of sampling distances ti by uniformly sampling between the camera's near tn and far tf planes, or the intersections of the cone's central axis with the Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the 3D space. A binary occupancy grid may be used to skip samples in empty areas and concentrate samples near surfaces. 3. Sphere Parameterization: For each distance ti, calculate the sphere center \mathbf{x}i and inscribed radius ri. The center lies on the central axis: \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}. The radius ri is calculated to ensure the sphere is inscribed within the cone: ri = \frac{\|\mathbf{x}i - \mathbf{o}\|2 \cdot f \cdot \beta}{\|\mathbf{d}\|2 \cdot \sqrt{\left(\sqrt{\|\mathbf{d}\|2^2 - f^2} - \beta\right)^2 + f^2}} where f is the focal length and \beta is a base radius parameter. 4. Featurization (Tri-Mip Encoding): Orthogonally project each sphere Si(\mathbf{x}i, ri) onto the three Tri-Mip planes (XY, YZ, XZ). Sample the corresponding mipmaps based on the sphere's occupied area to generate a feature vector \mathbf{f}i. This step leverages the isotropic pre-filtering of the Tri-Mip encoding. 5. Density and Color Prediction: Feed the feature vector \mathbf{f}i and the view direction \mathbf{d} into a tiny MLP to predict density \taui and color \mathbf{c}i: [\taui, \mathbf{c}i] = \text{MLP}(\mathbf{f}i, \mathbf{d}; \Theta) where \Theta are the MLP weights. 6. Volume Rendering Integration: Integrate the density and color of the sampled spheres using standard front-to-back volume rendering to produce the final pixel color: C = \sum{i} Ti \left(1 - \exp(-\taui (t{i+1} - ti))\right) \mathbf{c}i with Ti = \exp\left(-\sum{k < i} \tauk (t{k+1} - tk)\right) where t represents the distance between sampled spheres. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def conecastingwithinscribedspheres(o, d, pixelwidthworld, pixelheightworld, focallength, baseradius, tnear, tfar, numsamples, trimipmaps, mlpmodel): """ Renders a single pixel using cone casting with inscribed sphere sampling. Args: o: Camera optical center (list/tuple of 3 floats). d: Ray direction vector (list/tuple of 3 floats). pixelwidthworld: Width of pixel in world units. pixelheightworld: Height of pixel in world units. focallength: Camera focal length f. baseradius: Base radius parameter beta. tnear: Near plane distance. tfar: Far plane distance. numsamples: Number of spheres to sample along the cone. trimipmaps: Dictionary of 2D mipmap arrays for XY, YZ, XZ planes. mlpmodel: Function implementing the tiny MLP. Returns: finalcolor: Rendered color of the pixel. """ # 1. Calculate pixel disc radius rtilde = (pixelwidthworld pixelheightworld) / math.pi # 2. Define sampling distances tvalues = [tnear + i (tfar - tnear) / (numsamples - 1) for i in range(numsamples)] finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(numsamples): ti = tvalues[i] tnext = tvalues[i+1] if i < numsamples - 1 else tfar # 3. Sphere Center and Radius xi = [o[j] + ti d[j] for j in range(3)] distfromorigin = math.sqrt(sum((xi[j] - o[j])2 for j in range(3))) normd = math.sqrt(sum(d[j]2 for j in range(3))) # Guard against negative value inside sqrt if ||d|| < f innersqrtarg = normd2 - focallength2 if innersqrtarg < 0: innersqrtarg = 0 term = math.sqrt(innersqrtarg) - baseradius denominator = normd math.sqrt(term2 + focallength2) if denominator == 0: ri = 0.0 else: ri = (distfromorigin focallength baseradius) / denominator # 4. Featurization via Tri-Mip fxy = samplemipmap(trimipmaps['XY'], xi[0], xi[1], ri) fyz = samplemipmap(trimipmaps['YZ'], xi[1], xi[2], ri) fxz = samplemipmap(trimipmaps['XZ'], xi[0], xi[2], ri) fi = fxy + fyz + fxz # 5. Predict Density and Color taui, ci = mlpmodel(fi, d) # 6. Volume Rendering Step deltat = tnext - ti alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-taui deltat) contribution = [transmittance alpha ci[j] for j in range(3)] finalcolor = [finalcolor[j] + contribution[j] for j in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early termination if transmittance is negligible if transmittance < 1e-4: break return finalcolor def samplemipmap(mipmaparray, u, v, radius): """ Samples a 2D mipmap array at (u, v) with radius r. Selects mipmap level based on projected radius and performs bilinear interpolation. """ # Map world coordinates to normalized texture coordinates # Select appropriate mipmap level based on radius # Perform bilinear interpolation at the selected level # Return feature vector return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Placeholder for specific Tri-Mip sampling logic Parameters: baseradius (\beta): A base radius parameter controlling the scale of inscribed spheres. numsamples: Number of spheres along the cone. Not given in the sources. tiny MLP: A shallow neural network. Specific architecture (layers, activation functions) is not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Focal Length vs Ray Direction Norm: The formula for ri involves \sqrt{\|\mathbf{d}\|2^2 - f^2}. The source defines \mathbf{d} as the unnormalized vector \mathbf{p}o - \mathbf{o}, so \|\mathbf{d}\| scales with pixel size and camera intrinsics. Isotropy: The method relies on isotropic pre-filtering, which is why inscribed spheres are used instead of anisotropic multivariate Gaussians. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampled spheres per pixel. The use of a binary occupancy grid allows skipping empty space, reducing effective complexity in sparse scenes. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the Tri-Mip maps (three 2D mipmap arrays) and the tiny MLP. The Tri-Mip encoding is described as compact, requiring only three 2D maps for base levels. Strengths: Produces anti-aliased high-fidelity renderings in both close-up and distant views. Avoids the high cost of super-sampling techniques which require casting multiple rays per pixel. Limitations: Requires the specific Tri-Mip encoding structure. Incorporating pre-filtering with hash encoding is non-trivial due to hash collisions, and multivariate Gaussians are anisotropic while Tri-Mip pre-filtering is isotropic. Cone casting with inscribed sphere sampling was introduced in the Tri-MipRF paper (2023) as a rendering strategy for efficient anti-aliased neural radiance fields. It addresses the flaw in previous methods (like NeRF) that formulate pixels as single points, causing blurring in close-up views and aliasing in distant views. It differs from MipNeRF, which uses multivariate Gaussians, by using inscribed spheres to match the isotropic pre-filtering of the Tri-Mip encoding. Tri-MipRF: Tri-Mip Representation for Efficient Anti-Aliasing Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.01811, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF) Rendering
head: cone-based ray sampling
body: Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF) is a rendering technique that represents the feature aggregation of samples within a ray conical frustum in a continuous manner, enabling arbitrary supersampling of rays for novel view synthesis at multiple scales. Unlike standard ray casting which treats a pixel as an infinitesimal line, LIRF constructs each target ray by aggregating information from a cone (represented by vertices), allowing for better handling of thin structures and multi-scale synthesis. It sets itself apart from its sibling Cone Casting with Inscribed Sphere Sampling by explicitly defining a continuous implicit function over the frustum's volume to interpolate features, rather than relying solely on geometric sampling strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} of a sampled position within a conical frustum. Features of the M vertices defining the conical frustum. Image feature maps extracted from V nearby source views. Outputs: Aggregated feature for the sample at \mathbf{p} in a continuous manner. Predicted density and color for the sample. Final rendered color via volume rendering. Data Structures: Conical Frustum: Represented by M=8 vertices. The vertices are defined based on neighbor rays through neighbor pixels. Feature Maps: Extracted image feature maps with C=32 channels, sized same as the original image. Visibility Patches: Feature patches of size 7 \times 7 used to predict visibility weights. Parameters: V = 8: Number of nearby source views selected for training and testing. M = 8: Number of vertices used to represent a conical frustum. rm: Cone radius, set to the pixel width of the target image with the minimum resolution. N = 128: Number of points directly sampled on a ray. Patch size: 7 \times 7. Algorithm Steps: 1. Select Source Views: For a target view, select V=8 nearby source views. 2. Extract Features: Extract image feature maps with 32 channels from the source views, maintaining the original image dimensions. 3. Define Conical Frustum: Construct a conical frustum for the target pixel. The frustum is defined by M=8 vertices. The radius rm is determined by the pixel width of the target image at minimum resolution. 4. Sample Points: Directly sample N=128 points along the target ray. 5. Compute Visibility Weights: For each sample, match local multi-view feature patches of size 7 \times 7 from the source views to estimate visibility weights, mitigating occlusion artifacts. 6. Evaluate LIRF: For each sampled 3D position \mathbf{p} within the frustum: Input \mathbf{p} and the features of the M=8 frustum vertices into the Local Implicit Ray Function. The function outputs the aggregated feature continuously. Note: The specific mathematical formulation of the LIRF function (e.g., Eq. 5 and 6 in the source) involves scale s and relative position \Delta x. 7. Predict Radiance: Use the aggregated features to predict the density and color of the sample. 8. Volume Rendering: Render the final color of the target ray using the predicted densities and colors via standard volume rendering integration. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def LIRFRendering(targetview, sourceviews): # 1. Select V=8 nearby source views selectedviews = SelectNearbyViews(targetview, sourceviews, V=8) # 2. Extract 32-channel feature maps from selected views featuremaps = ExtractFeatures(selectedviews, channels=32) # 3. Define conical frustum vertices (M=8) # Radius rm is pixel width of target image at min resolution frustumvertices = DefineFrustumVertices(targetview, rm=pixelwidthminres) # 4. Sample N=128 points on the ray points = SamplePointsOnRay(targetview, N=128) renderedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedweight = 0.0 for point in points: # 5. Estimate visibility weights using 7x7 patches visibility = EstimateVisibility(point, featuremaps, patchsize=7) # 6. Get aggregated feature via LIRF # Input: 3D coordinate 'point' and features of 'frustumvertices' aggregatedfeature = LIRFEvaluate(point, frustumvertices, featuremaps) # 7. Predict density and color density, color = PredictRadiance(aggregatedfeature) # 8. Volume rendering step (simplified alpha compositing) # Note: Standard volume rendering equation (Eq. 1 in source) is used alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) weight = alpha exp(-sum(densitiessofar)) renderedcolor += weight color visibility accumulatedweight += weight return renderedcolor def LIRFEvaluate(point, vertices, featuremaps): """ Computes the aggregated feature for a point within the conical frustum. Uses the continuous nature of LIRF to interpolate based on relative position and scale. """ # The source mentions Eq. 5 and 6 involving scale s and relative position dx. # Specific implementation details of the MLP or interpolation function # are not fully detailed in the provided text beyond the inputs. # Assuming a standard MLP or interpolation layer takes the point # coordinates and vertex features as input to produce the aggregated feature. return InterpolateFeatures(point, vertices, featuremaps) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Occlusion: Rendering regions occluded in all input views is impossible. View Consistency: View consistency is weaker than NeRF because selected input views vary with the novel view position. Computational Cost: Rendering a pixel requires casting four rays to approximate a cone, increasing computational cost. Scale Sensitivity: Performance degrades significantly if the scale parameter or relative position components of the LIRF are removed, especially at extreme scales (\times 0.5 and \times 4). Time Complexity: Increases due to the requirement of casting four rays to approximate a cone for each pixel. Training takes approximately two days on eight V100 GPUs for 250k iterations with a batch size of 512 rays. Memory Complexity: Requires storing feature maps for V=8 source views and processing N=128 samples per ray. Performance: The full LIRF model performs better than the "single ray" variant on all scales, especially at \times 0.5 and \times 4. It outperforms IBRNet, NeuRay, and GeoNeRF in quantitative metrics (PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS) on real forward-facing scenes. Using the method's own feature extraction yields significantly better performance than using U-Net features from IBRNet. Strengths: Enables arbitrary supersampling for novel view synthesis at multiple levels of detail (anti-blurring and anti-aliasing). Better handling of thin structures compared to single-ray methods. Limitations: Cannot render fully occluded regions; weaker view consistency compared to NeRF; higher computational cost due to cone approximation. Local Implicit Ray Function (LIRF) was proposed as a novel method for generalizable radiance field representation and novel view synthesis of unseen scenes. It addresses the limitations of single-ray representations by introducing a continuous aggregation of features within a conical frustum. The method was supported by NSFC under Grant 62031023. Local Implicit Ray Function for Generalizable Radiance Field Representation, http://arxiv.org/abs/2304.12746v1, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Raycasting Phase
head: Data sampling, Ray integration, Two-Pass Raycasting with Back-Face Depth Buffering
body: The Raycasting Phase is the computational core of image-order volume rendering where optical properties are sampled along camera rays and integrated to produce pixel colors. It solves the problem of mapping discrete volumetric data to continuous screen-space pixels by performing numerical integration of the rendering equation. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its specific reliance on a two-pass geometry-based traversal strategy using back-face depth buffering to determine ray entry and exit points, as well as its sensitivity to decomposition geometry in parallel implementations. The method operates in two distinct passes to determine the integration bounds and then performs the integration. Inputs: Volumetric data grid V. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, field of view). Decomposition geometry (block structure for parallel processing). Step length parameter d. Outputs: Final pixel color C{pixel}. Intermediate fragment buffers (back-face and front-face coordinates). Data Structures: 1. Auxiliary Buffers: Two texture buffers bound to distinct texture units. One stores back-face depth/coordinates, the other stores front-face coordinates. 2. Fragment Buffer: Temporary storage for image fragments. Size constraints may require scaling down data volume if the buffer overflows (e.g., at image size 23040^3). Algorithm Steps: 1. Pass 1: Back-Face Depth Buffering Render the volume bounding box or decomposition blocks. Bind auxiliary buffers for multiple render targets (e.g., using GLARBdrawbuffers). For each fragment generated by a back-facing polygon, store its texture coordinates in the back-face buffer. Front-facing fragments are discarded or ignored in this pass. 2. Pass 2: Ray Initialization and Integration Setup Bind the two auxiliary buffers to texture units. Project a viewport-filling quadrilateral. For each pixel: Fetch back-face texture coordinates from the first buffer. If invalid (no back-face hit), discard the fragment. Otherwise, retrieve the corresponding front-face texture coordinates from the second buffer. Compute the step vector \Delta \mathbf{p} along the ray based on the predefined step length d and the distance between front and back faces. Calculate the total number of iterations N required to traverse the ray segment. 3. Integration Loop Initialize ray position \mathbf{p} at the front-face entry point. For i = 0 to N-1: Sample the volume data V(\mathbf{p}) using trilinear interpolation. Apply shading (e.g., Phong-style shader) to compute optical properties (color, opacity). Integrate the contribution into the accumulated color and opacity using a compositing scheme (e.g., front-to-back). Advance \mathbf{p} by the step vector \Delta \mathbf{p}. Note: The integration may be structured in slabs. Each slab of thickness 2d is defined by three successive samples (sf, sm, sb), with the next slab indexed by (sf, sm, sb) shifted accordingly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastingphase(volumedata, camera, steplengthd, decomposition): # Pass 1: Determine entry and exit points via back-face buffering backfacecoords = renderbackfaces(volumedata, camera, decomposition) # Pass 2: Initialize rays and integrate finalcolors = emptybuffer(camera.resolution) for pixel in camera.viewport: # Fetch back-face coordinate bfcoord = backfacecoords[pixel] if bfcoord is invalid: continue # Discard fragment # Fetch front-face coordinate ffcoord = getfrontfacecoord(pixel) # Compute ray parameters rayorigin = ffcoord raydirection = normalize(camera.direction) # Calculate step vector based on steplengthd and geometry stepvector = computestepvector(raydirection, steplengthd, ffcoord, bfcoord) # Determine number of steps numsteps = computenumsteps(rayorigin, bfcoord, stepvector) # Integration accumulatedcolor = vec3(0, 0, 0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 currentpos = rayorigin for i in range(numsteps): # Sample volume data # Trilinear interpolation is used for data sampling along the ray samplevalue = trilinearinterpolate(volumedata, currentpos) # Apply shading (Phong-style) color, opacity = applyphongshading(samplevalue, currentpos, camera) # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = Cin + (1 - Ain) Csample alphasample # Aout = Ain + (1 - Ain) alphasample weight = (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) opacity accumulatedcolor += weight color accumulatedopacity += weight # Advance position currentpos += stepvector finalcolors[pixel] = accumulatedcolor return finalcolors Parameters: d: Predefined step length. Slabs are defined with thickness 2d. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is the standard method for sampling. Shading: Phong-style shading is applied during integration. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thread Divergence: The final raycasting time is determined by the slowest thread (the one with the most integration steps). This varies significantly with view and decomposition geometry. Weak Scaling Degradation: Perspective projection causes variation in the number of samples per thread. As scale increases, each core handles a smaller portion of the frustum, increasing this variation and causing up to 20% performance degradation. Memory Overflow: Increasing image size (e.g., to 23040^3) can cause temporary fragment buffers to overflow, forcing a reduction in data size (e.g., to 19200^3). Hybrid Memory Performance: At high concurrency, hybrid-memory implementations may underperform distributed memory by 10% due to irregular block sizes (e.g., aggregated 1 \times 2 \times 3 blocks) interacting with camera direction. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays (pixels). However, parallel performance is bounded by the maximum integration steps among all threads. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the volume data size plus temporary buffers for fragments. Fragment buffer size is critical; insufficient memory forces data downsampling. Scalability: Distributed memory achieves linear scaling up to 216,000-way concurrency for the raycasting phase. Hybrid-memory implementations maintain ~80% scalability in weak scaling up to 216,000 cores but exhibit sublinear scaling in strong scaling due to irregular decomposition geometry. Performance: At 448-way concurrency with a 4608^3 dataset, the hybrid/CUDA implementation averaged 1.18s for raycasting. Strengths: No message passing is involved in the raycasting phase itself, allowing for efficient scaling in distributed memory systems. Limitations: Performance is highly sensitive to view direction relative to decomposition geometry. Perspective projection exacerbates load imbalance in weak scaling. The method originated in the context of large-scale parallel volume rendering on multi- and many-core systems. It was developed to address the challenges of scaling raycasting across distributed and hybrid memory architectures. The two-pass approach with back-face depth buffering was introduced to efficiently determine ray entry and exit points without complex ray-volume intersection algorithms, leveraging GPU rasterization capabilities. name: Pre-integration and Approximation Methods
head: Pre-integrated Volume Rendering, PIVR, Pre-integration of Transfer Function Contribution
body: Pre-integration and Approximation Methods accelerate direct volume ray casting by pre-computing the volume rendering integral for segments defined by endpoint scalar values, storing results in lookup tables to avoid on-the-fly integration of non-linear transfer functions. This approach decouples the integration of the transfer function contribution from the sampling process, allowing sampling to focus solely on volume reconstruction while solving aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency non-linear transfer functions when using standard point-sampling classification. It sets itself apart from siblings like Monte Carlo Volume Rendering and Ray Traversal and Integration Schemes by explicitly pre-computing the integral over a segment defined by endpoint scalar values and length, rather than evaluating the transfer function at discrete sample points or using stochastic sampling. All methods in this family operate on the principle that a continuous function V(\mathbf{p}) must be approximated from a discrete set of samples Vi located at grid positions \mathbf{p}i. The core mechanism involves: 1. Query Positioning: Determining the 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} where a value is needed. This may involve converting depth parameters to physical distances or warping coordinates for neural encodings. 2. Kernel/Weight Application: Computing weights wi(\mathbf{p}) based on the distance between \mathbf{p} and the sample centers \mathbf{p}i. The interpolated value is: V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i} wi(\mathbf{p}) Vi The choice of kernel (e.g., linear, cubic, inverse distance) determines the spatial extent (number of neighbors) and frequency response (aliasing vs. blurring). 3. Coordinate Transformation: Mapping world-space or camera-space coordinates to the local coordinate system of the volume data (e.g., normalized [-1, 1] or [0, 1] ranges) before interpolation. Pre-integrated Volume Rendering (PIVR) is a technique that accelerates direct volume rendering by pre-computing the volume rendering integral for all possible segment configurations and storing the results in a lookup table. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency non-linear transfer functions when using standard point-sampling classification. Unlike standard methods that apply the transfer function to individual samples, PIVR decouples the integration of the transfer function contribution from the sampling process, allowing the sampling to focus solely on volume reconstruction. It sets itself apart from siblings like Pre-integration of Transfer Function Contribution by explicitly pre-computing the integral over a segment defined by endpoint scalar values and length, rather than just integrating the transfer function parameters independently. Pre-integration of transfer function contribution is a technique that replaces on-the-fly interpolation with pre-integrated transfer function tables to perform fully-shaded semi-transparent and iso-surface volume rendering. It addresses the dichotomy between image quality and performance by pre-integrating the transfer function's contribution along ray segments, smoothing image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by mapping the pair of scalar density values at segment endpoints directly to pre-integrated color and opacity, rather than evaluating the transfer function at discrete sample points. A technique to approximate the exponential light attenuation and blending function in volume rendering with a quadratic function to allow efficient hardware implementation using Gouraud shading, while maintaining accuracy for small cell depths. Set the first coefficient a0 = 0 to simplify the blend function structure. The target exponential function is f(z) = 1 - e^{-\tau z}, where \tau is the opacity-per-unit-distance and z is the depth. The approximation is g(z) = (c0 + c1 z)(a0 + a1 z). The concept of pre-integration for volume rendering was introduced by Levoy and Whitted in 1985. The method was further developed and popularized for real-time rendering on early graphics hardware, such as the Silicon Graphics VGX and NVidia GeForce3, demonstrating performance improvements of 1-4 frames per second for 256^3 volumes. The quadratic approximation for exponential blending was proposed to facilitate hardware acceleration using Gouraud shading. Rapid Exploration of Curvilinear Grids Using Direct Volume Rendering, https://ntrs.nasa.gov/api/citations/19930015755/downloads/19930015755.pdf, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Pre-integrated Volume Rendering
head: PIVR, Pre-integration, Precomputed volume rendering integral, Preintegration Volume Rendering, Pré-integração, Engel, Kraus & Ertl 2001, Pre-integrated transfer function
body: Pre-integrated Volume Rendering (PIVR) accelerates direct volume rendering by pre-computing the volume rendering integral for a ray segment and storing the results in a lookup table for fast retrieval. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts caused by high-frequency, non-linear transfer functions when sampling sparse ray segments. Unlike standard classification which applies the transfer function to individual sample points, PIVR decouples the integration of the transfer function contribution from the sampling process, allowing the sampling to focus only on volume reconstruction while the pre-computed table handles the optical properties. It sets itself apart from Pre-integration of Transfer Function Contribution by specifically addressing the scalar field interpolation between segment endpoints to compute accurate color and opacity contributions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scalar volume data V, transfer functions for extinction density \tau(s) and color density \tilde{c}(s), ray segment length d (assumed constant per frame), and scalar values at segment endpoints sb (back) and sf (front). Outputs: Accumulated color \tilde{C} and opacity \alpha for the segment, which are composited into the final image. Data Structures: 1. Integral Table: A 1D lookup table of size 256 entries (for 8-bit scalar data). Each entry stores four 32-bit floating-point numbers: accumulated color components (\tilde{R}A, \tilde{G}A, \tilde{B}A) and accumulated opacity TA. Layout: Contiguous memory, [R, G, B, A] per entry. Values: T(s) = \int0^s \tau(s) ds and K(s) = \int0^s \tilde{c}(s) ds are pre-computed and stored. 2. Exponential Approximation Parameters: Four linear segments defined by slopes mi and intercepts bi (i=0..3) to approximate 1 - \exp(-x). Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Offline/Setup): Compute the integral functions T(s) and K(s) for all possible scalar values s \in [0, 255] using the user-supplied transfer functions \tau(s) and \tilde{c}(s). Store these values in the 256-entry 1D table. Compute the linear approximation parameters mi, bi for 1 - \exp(-x) using a brute-force minimization method for x \ge 0. 2. Ray Casting Loop (Per Ray): Iterate through the volume along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. For each segment of length d, sample the scalar field at the start (s{prev}) and end (s{curr}) of the segment. Thresholding Check: If s{max} = \max(s{prev}, s{curr}) is below a user-supplied threshold (assuming clamped transfer functions), skip the segment. 3. Segment Evaluation: Determine s{max} = \max(s{prev}, s{curr}) and s{min} = \min(s{prev}, s{curr}). Compute the difference diff = s{max} - s{min}. Compute the reciprocal invDiff = 1.0 / diff. Table Lookup: Access the integral table at indices s{max} and s{min} to retrieve T(s{max}), K(s{max}) and T(s{min}), K(s{min}). Color Computation: \Delta K = K(s{max}) - K(s{min}) \tilde{C} = d \cdot invDiff \cdot \Delta K This yields the positive raypoint light emission. Opacity Computation: x = invDiff \cdot (T(s{max}) - T(s{min})) Note that x \ge 0. Approximate the opacity using the linear segments: yi = mi \cdot x + bi \quad \text{for } i \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} \alpha = \min(y0, y1, y2, y3) This approximates 1 - \exp(-x). 4. Compositing: Combine the computed \tilde{C} and \alpha with the accumulated color and opacity from previous segments using front-to-back compositing. Formulas: The approximate opacity \alpha and emitted light intensity \tilde{C} for an interval between two raypoints with distance d and scalar values sb and sf are given by: \alpha(sf, sb, d) \approx 1 - \exp\left(\frac{d}{sb - sf} \cdot (T(sf) - T(sb))\right) \tilde{C}(sf, sb, d) \approx \frac{d}{sb - sf} \cdot (K(sb) - K(sf)) where T(s) = \int0^s \tau(s) ds and K(s) = \int0^s \tilde{c}(s) ds. Here \tau(s) is the extinction density and \tilde{c}(s) is the color density. The general volume rendering integral for opacity is: \alpha = 1 - \exp \left( - \int{li}^{lo} \lambda(V(R(l))) \times dl \right) where \lambda is the extinction coefficient function, V is the volume field, R(l) is the ray position, and li, lo are the start and end points of the segment. Parameters: Raypoint distance d: Assumed constant for all rays during a frame. Typical values tested: 0.45 and 0.9 grid units. Linear Approximation Parameters (mi, bi): Computed once via brute-force method. Specific numerical values are not provided in the sources, only that they minimize error for x \ge 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Simplified Alpha Loss: Using a simplified linear approximation for opacity (e.g., \alpha \approx \frac{d}{sb - sf} (T(sb) - T(sf))) instead of the exponential approximation results in a visible loss in contrast. Thresholding: Raypoints below a threshold should not be simply discarded if the previous point was above the threshold, as linear interpolation might exceed the threshold within the interval. However, if s{max} is below the threshold, the entire interval can be safely skipped (assuming clamped transfer functions). Discretization Artifacts: The method assumes a linear progression of scalar values between samples, which can introduce artifacts if the scalar field varies non-linearly. High-Dimensional Transfer Functions: Pre-integration is not applicable without restrictions to transfer functions of dimension greater than one due to the large memory and processing time required to build tables with at least four dimensions (for 2D TFs). Adaptive Pre-integration is a technique applied to texture slicing that pre-computes optimal step sizes for each ray based on pre-integrated emission, opacity, and second-order gradients to guarantee error bounds on ray integration. It is an adaptive approach that overcomes pre-integration artifacts by using an adaptive sampling rate based on the actual information stored in the volume and the transfer function used. It builds on Pre-integrated Volume Rendering by dynamically adjusting the discretization of the pre-integration integral rather than using a fixed slab thickness. Choose it when scalar fields vary highly non-linearly and fixed-step pre-integration artifacts are unacceptable. Direct Volume Rendering with Pre-integration renders adapted tetrahedral meshes using direct volume ray casting, accelerated by pre-integration computed in shaders. It extends pre-integrated volume rendering, which allows for faster evaluation by pre-computing all possible results from the integral and storing them in a table for lookup [Parent], to unstructured volumetric data (tetrahedral meshes). Unlike methods limited to regular grids, this approach handles the geometric complexity of unstructured grids by storing the mesh data structure in textures and using barycentric interpolation for value estimation. Choose it when rendering unstructured tetrahedral meshes requires the speedup of pre-integration. Time Complexity: The per-raypoint computation is dominated by SIMD arithmetic operations (MULPS, ADDPS, SUBPS, MINPS, RCPPS) with latencies of 4-6 cycles. The pre-computation of the lookup table is time-consuming, especially for high-dimensional transfer functions. Memory Complexity: The 1D table implementation uses 4 Kbytes (256 entries \times 4 floats \times 4 bytes), which fits in the L1 cache, avoiding cache misses associated with larger 2D tables (e.g., 512 Kbytes). Measured Performance: On a Pentium-4 2GHz, pre-integrated rendering (d=0.45, simplified alpha) took 0.158s for a 256x256 viewport, compared to 0.295s for standard classification with empty-space skipping. Pre-integration increases speed by a factor of 10 for the linear model compared to baseline. Strengths: Reduces aliasing artifacts caused by high frequencies in non-linear transfer functions. Allows for larger ray step sizes (coarser sampling) while maintaining image quality. Decouples sampling from transfer function evaluation. Limitations: Assumes linear scalar progression between samples, which can cause artifacts. Not directly applicable to high-dimensional transfer functions without restrictions. The simplified alpha approximation may reduce contrast. When to use: Suitable for interactive volume rendering on CPUs or GPUs where transfer functions are non-linear and high-frequency, and where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. When not to use: When the scalar field varies highly non-linearly within segments and adaptive sampling is not used. When rendering requires high-dimensional transfer functions without applying restrictions, as pre-integration is not applicable to TFs of dimension greater than one without significant memory and processing overhead. Pre-integrated volume rendering was introduced by Engel et al. in 2001. It was developed to overcome the problem of high Nyquist frequencies resulting from non-linear transfer functions in texture-based volume rendering. The method splits the numerical integration into two parts: one for the continuous scalar field and one for the transfer function. It was later combined with volumetric clipping and advanced lighting effects by Röttger et al.. The technique has been implemented in software systems like UltraVis and adapted for unstructured grids. name: Adaptive Pre-integration
body: Adaptive Pre-integration is a technique applied to texture slicing that pre-computes optimal step sizes for each ray based on pre-integrated emission, opacity, and second-order gradients to guarantee error bounds on ray integration. It is an adaptive approach that overcomes pre-integration artifacts by using an adaptive sampling rate based on the actual information stored in the volume and the transfer function used. It builds on Pre-integrated Volume Rendering by dynamically adjusting the discretization of the pre-integration integral rather than using a fixed slab thickness. Inputs: Volume dataset, transfer functions for opacity and color, and camera parameters. Outputs: Final color image. Data Structures: Importance volume, a floating-point texture storing the pre-computed optimal step size for each ray. Ray traversal parameters, floating-point textures storing current ray positions and accumulated opacity/color. Z-buffer, used to track ray termination. Steps: 1. Initialization: Render the bounding box of the volume in front-to-back order to provide starting locations for all rays. Initialize ray traversal parameters in floating-point textures. 2. Step Size Computation: For each ray, compute the optimal step size. This size depends on the pre-integrated emission and opacity value as well as second-order gradients. The step size is stored in the importance volume. 3. Ray Traversal: Update ray positions using the step sizes from the importance volume. 4. Pre-integration: Apply pre-integration of opacity and color transfer functions to the volume slabs defined by the entry and exit points and the distance between slices. 5. Blending (Multi-step Slicing): Internally blend the results of multiple pre-integrated slabs before writing to the framebuffer to improve image quality. 6. Termination: Rays are terminated early or when they leave the volume by setting the z-buffer for the corresponding pixels, avoiding further computation. 7. Accumulation: Resampled RGB\alpha textures are accumulated into the frame buffer using back-to-front compositing. If front-to-back compositing is used, accumulated opacities need to be stored for each pixel in the image. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Over-sampling factor: Two-times over-sampling has almost the same performance as no over-sampling due to increased cache coherency. Four-times over-sampling yields the best quality-performance tradeoff. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Artifacts: Standard pre-integration assumes a linear progression of scalar values between slices, which can introduce artifacts. Adaptive sampling mitigates this by adjusting to the actual information in the volume. Precision: Not given in the sources. Performance: Two-times over-sampling has almost the same performance as no over-sampling because of increased cache coherency. Quality: Four-times over-sampling yields the best quality-performance tradeoff using multi-step slicing. Accuracy: Guarantees error bounds on ray integration by adapting step sizes to local volume properties. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Adaptive sampling rate based on volume information and transfer function reduces artifacts from linear progression assumptions. Limitations: Requires additional rendering passes to determine if all rays have terminated. Adaptive Pre-integration was proposed by Roettger et al.. It extends the work of Engel et al. who applied pre-integration of opacity and color transfer functions to texture slicing. Roettger et al. improved image quality by internally blending results of multiple pre-integrated slabs. name: Direct Volume Rendering with Pre-integration
head: GPU-accelerated raycasting for tetrahedral meshes, PIVR, Pre-integrated Volume Rendering for Tetrahedral Meshes, Pre-integrated tetrahedral rendering
body: Direct Volume Rendering with Pre-integration renders adapted tetrahedral meshes using direct volume ray casting, accelerated by pre-integration computed in shaders. It extends pre-integrated volume rendering, which allows for faster evaluation by pre-computing all possible results from the integral and storing them in a table for lookup [Parent], to unstructured volumetric data (tetrahedral meshes). Unlike methods limited to regular grids, this approach handles the geometric complexity of unstructured grids by storing the mesh data structure in textures and using barycentric interpolation for value estimation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An adapted tetrahedral mesh defined by vertex positions, vertex scalar values, and connectivity. Camera parameters including the view vector. Transfer function parameters defining opacity \alpha and color \tilde{C}. Output: A 2D image with color and opacity per pixel. Data Structures: 1. Tetrahedral Mesh Textures: The tetrahedral mesh data structure is stored in a set of textures. These textures allow the shader to calculate the current tetrahedron and its entry/exit points for each ray integral iteration. 2. Pre-integration Table: A 3D texture storing pre-computed ray integral results. The standard table is indexed by (s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l), where s^{(f)} and s^{(b)} are the scalar values at the ray entry and exit points, and l is the thickness (distance between entry and exit). Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Table Generation): 1. Iterate over all possible combinations of entry scalar value s^{(f)}, exit scalar value s^{(b)}, and thickness l. 2. For each combination, compute the pre-integrated color \tilde{C}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) and opacity \alpha(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) using the transfer function and the volume rendering integral. 3. Store these values in the pre-integration table texture. 4. Logarithmic sampling is implemented for the thickness dimension l to handle varying scales efficiently. 2. Rendering (Ray Casting): 1. For each pixel, cast a ray through the scene. 2. Intersect the ray with the tetrahedral mesh using the texture-based mesh representation. 3. For each tetrahedron intersected by the ray segment: a. Determine the entry point and exit point of the ray within the tetrahedron. b. Estimate the scalar values s^{(f)} (at entry) and s^{(b)} (at exit) using barycentric interpolation from the vertex values of the tetrahedron. This assumes datasets with good resolution where regions of interest are highly sampled. c. Calculate the thickness l as the distance between the entry and exit points. d. Use (s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) as indices to fetch the pre-computed color \tilde{C} and opacity \alpha from the pre-integration table. e. Composite the fetched color and opacity into the ray accumulator using standard volume rendering blending equations. 4. Repeat for all intersected tetrahedra until the ray exits the volume or is fully opaque. Formulas: Barycentric Interpolation: Scalar value s at a point inside a tetrahedron is computed as s = \sum{i=1}^{4} wi si, where wi are barycentric coordinates and si are vertex scalar values. Thickness: l = \| \vec{p}{exit} - \vec{p}{entry} \|. Parameters: Logarithmic Sampling: Used for the thickness dimension l in the pre-integration table. Illustrative Effect Parameters: Various parameters (\omega, p, oo) control specific illustrative effects (see Subtopics). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Constant Gradient Artifacts: A constant gradient within each tetrahedron causes artifacts. This is noted as an issue to be solved in future work. Resolution Dependency: Barycentric interpolation for gradient estimation is sufficient only for datasets with good resolution. Occlusion: The system currently does not take occlusion by the segments into account when adapting the mesh, considering attribute errors only. An illustrative effect that highlights essential high-gradient dataset features by masking pre-integrated table entries using an approximated view-dependent gradient magnitude. It is chosen when one wants to emphasize regions of rapid scalar change without computing full gradients. It differs from full gradient enhancement by using the approximated gradient (s^{(b)} - s^{(f)})/l. Mask Calculation: m = \tilde{\omega} \cdot \left( \left| \frac{s(f) - s(b)}{l} \right| \right)^p, where \tilde{\omega} is an artificial user-defined opacity scaling factor and p is a scalar controlling gradient magnitude's effect on opacity. Masked Opacity: \alpha^{(m)}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) = 1 - e^{(m \log(1 - \alpha(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l)))}. Masked Color: \tilde{C}^{(m)}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l) = \frac{\alpha^{(m)}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l)}{\alpha(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l)} \tilde{C}(s^{(f)}, s^{(b)}, l). Implementation: The mask is applied during pre-integrated table computation, requiring no modification to the raycaster. An effect that highlights areas where the view vector and gradient vector are near orthogonal, showing contour lines of a surface, by using a pre-integrated table indexed by phi values. It is chosen for silhouette extraction. It differs from other gradient effects by indexing the table by \phi instead of scalar values. Phi Calculation: \phi = \langle \vec{n}, \vec{v} \rangle, where \vec{n} is the normalized gradient vector and \vec{v} is the view vector. Implementation: The pre-integrated table is constructed indexed by (\phi(f), \phi(b), l) instead of (s(f), s(b), l). A one-dimensional opacity transfer function \alpha(\phi) is used to highlight areas where \phi is close to 0. An illustrative effect obtained by estimating the curvature for the segment between entry and exit points to generate contour effects. It is chosen to highlight regions of high curvature change. Mask Calculation: m = \omega \cdot \left( \frac{\|\vec{n}^{(f)} - \vec{n}^{(b)}\|}{l} \right)^p, where \vec{n}^{(f)} and \vec{n}^{(b)} are normal vectors at entry and exit, l is thickness, \omega is opacity scaling factor, and p is a scalar. Implementation: The mask is applied during rendering by modifying the shader. An effect that restricts contour detection to interfaces between different materials by masking pre-integrated table entries during rendering using a windowing function and phi value. It is chosen for masked silhouettes. Mask Calculation: m = g(\|\nabla f\|) \cdot (1 - |\phi|)^p, where \nabla f is the gradient, g(\cdot) is a windowing function (usually linear clamped to [0,1]), and \phi = \langle \vec{n}, \vec{v} \rangle. Implementation: \phi is calculated in the fragment shader, and masking is applied during rendering using Equations 1 and 2. A technique that scales the entries of the pre-integrated table using a mask based on a specific value (e.g., scalar value, gradient magnitude) to create effects like banding. It is chosen for banding effects. Mask Calculation: m = ((1 + \sin(oo \pi k)) \cdot 0.5)^p, where oo is the value to mask (e.g., scalar value, gradient magnitude) and p is a scalar. Implementation: The masking is done during table computation; no modification is introduced into the rendering process. Time Complexity: Performance is primarily limited by the volume rendering stage. The method processes the adapted mesh, with performance depending on the number of tetrahedra and the complexity of illustrative effects. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the tetrahedral mesh in textures and the pre-integration table. Measured Performance: On a standard PC with an NVidia GeForce 7800 GTX (512MB) at 640x480 resolution, the direct volume renderer has a peak performance of about 800,000 tetrahedra per second. The performance change due to illustration techniques is negligible even for datasets with millions of tetrahedra. Strengths: GPU-accelerated, handles unstructured grids (tetrahedral meshes), supports various illustrative effects, negligible performance overhead for effects. Limitations: Artifacts due to constant gradient within each tetrahedron. Does not account for occlusion during mesh adaptation. Requires good resolution for accurate gradient estimation via barycentric interpolation. When to Use: When rendering unstructured volumetric data (tetrahedral meshes) with a need for fast, GPU-accelerated volume rendering and illustrative effects. When Not to Use: When high accuracy in gradient estimation is critical for low-resolution data, or when occlusion-aware mesh adaptation is required. Originating from work on pre-integrated volume rendering for regular grids [Parent], this method extends the technique to unstructured volumetric data (tetrahedral meshes). It was presented in the context of flow visualization, aiming to apply illustrative techniques to unstructured grids which had previously been limited to uniform grids. The implementation modifies a single-pass raycaster for tetrahedral meshes. name: Pre-integration of Transfer Function Contribution
head: Pre-integrated transfer function tables
body: Pre-integration of transfer function contribution is a technique that replaces on-the-fly interpolation and integration with pre-computed lookup tables to perform fully-shaded semi-transparent and iso-surface volume rendering. It addresses the dichotomy between image quality and performance by pre-integrating the transfer function's contribution along ray segments, thereby smoothing image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by mapping pairs of scalar density values directly to pre-integrated color and opacity, decoupling the integration of the transfer function from the sampling process. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset V, a color transfer function C(v), an extinction coefficient transfer function \lambda(v), and a gradient volume for shading. Output: A rendered image with reduced aliasing artifacts. Data Structures: Pre-integrated Transfer Function Table: A 2D texture or lookup table indexed by two scalar density values (e.g., vi and v{i+1}). The stored values are the pre-integrated color and opacity contributions for the segment between these two densities. Gradient Volume: Loaded into texture memory to compute gradients for shading. Note that interpolating a gradient volume without subsequent normalization is generally incorrect, though artifacts may not always be visible. Method Steps: 1. Pre-computation: Compute the analytical integration of the transfer function over the segment between two adjacent sample values. For a segment from li to lo, the resulting color C{res} and opacity \alpha are derived from the integrals: C{res} = \int{li}^{lo} C(V(R(l))) \times \exp \left( - \int{li}^l \lambda(V(R(j))) \times dj \right) \times dl \alpha = 1 - \exp \left( - \int{li}^{lo} \lambda(V(R(l))) \times dl \right) These integrals are evaluated for all relevant pairs of density values and stored in the table. 2. Ray Casting: Decompose view rays into segments of homogeneous or very similar length. 3. Lookup: For each segment, determine the scalar density values at the endpoints. Use these values to index into the pre-integrated transfer function table to retrieve the pre-computed color and opacity contribution for that segment. 4. Composition: Composite the retrieved color and opacity contributions along the ray. Note that in these approximations, color and extinction coefficient values often become absolute values rather than ratios per unit length due to the decomposition of rays into segments. 5. Shading: Load the gradient volume and compute shading. To eliminate artifacts from incorrect gradient interpolation, use a shading cube texture instead of standard texture mapping. Parameters: Table Resolution: Determined by the number of discrete density values stored. Not given in the sources. Segment Length: Should be homogeneous or very similar to ensure the validity of the pre-integrated values. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Interpolation: Interpolating a gradient volume without normalization yields incorrect results. Value Interpretation: The pre-integrated values are absolute contributions for the segment, not per-unit-length ratios. Performance: The implementation can perform fully-shaded semi-transparent and iso-surface volume rendering at 1-4 frames per second for 256^3 volumes, using an NVidia GeForce3. Hardware Limitations: Even the most recent texture mapping hardware cannot reach the performance of specialized volume rendering hardware, such as the VolumePro500 and the new VolumePro 1000, at least not when volume rendering performance is the primary metric. Strengths: Overcomes undersampling problems associated with large inter-slice distances at off-angles. Smooths image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. Limitations: Performance is inversely dependent on sampling frequency, and the sampled field behavior, when modulated by the transfer function, cannot be satisfactorily reconstructed using too low sampling frequencies. The technique was proposed by Engel et al. to smooth image imperfections caused by low sampling frequencies. It replaced earlier techniques that overcame undersampling problems by interpolating intermediate slices on-the-fly using register combiners in the fragment shader compartment.
