name: Image-based rendering integration
head: Image-Based Rendering with Impostors, Impostor rendering
body: This method integrates volume rendering into a polygonal virtual environment by treating rendered volume images as image-based primitives (impostors) within the scene. It solves the problem of combining high-fidelity volume visualization with interactive polygonal environments by offloading the computationally expensive volume rendering to a separate server, while the client handles the polygonal scene and impostor management. It sets itself apart from direct ray casting or slice-based rendering by decoupling the volume rendering computation from the display geometry, using 2D quads textured with pre-rendered volume images as the visual representation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volumetric data set, camera positions for left and right eyes (stereoscopic), head-tracker updates. Output: Stereo pair of images rendered on impostor quads within the polygonal virtual environment. Data Structures: Impostor: A geometric primitive (quad) used to represent the volume object. Texture: The rendered volume image mapped onto the impostor quad. Server State: Holds the volume data and rendering logic. Client State: Holds the polygonal environment, impostor geometry, and network communication logic. Steps: 1. Distribution: The volume rendering process is distributed to a separate server (a fast PC with sufficient memory for the volume data sets). 2. Communication: The client (implemented as a Studierstube application) communicates with the server via a Local Area Network (LAN). 3. View Request: When the user moves or the view changes, the head-tracker reports the change to the impostors on the client. The impostors update their orientation so their surface normal faces the respective eye and send a request for new volume renderings to the server for the two viewing directions (one for each eye). 4. Volume Rendering: The server receives the two viewing directions and renders the volume data for those directions. 5. Image Transmission: The server sends the rendered images back to the client. 6. Impostor Integration: The client integrates these images into the polygonal renderings of the virtual environment by mapping them as textures onto quads that act as impostors for the volume object. 7. Stereoscopic Display: Two quads act as impostors, one for each stereoscopic view. The quads are rotated around their center so their surface normal always faces the respective eye of the user. The size of the impostors does not need to be varied, as normal perspective rendering of the quads takes place afterwards. 8. Asynchronous Update: The update process happens asynchronously in a background thread to prevent the virtual environment from freezing during the rendering time (20ms to 500ms). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading import time from dataclasses import dataclass from typing import Tuple, List @dataclass class Pose: position: Tuple[float, float, float] orientation: Tuple[float, float, float] @dataclass class Image: pixels: List[List[int]] width: int height: int @dataclass class RenderRequest: volumeid: str eyeleftpose: Pose eyerightpose: Pose @dataclass class RenderResponse: imageleft: Image imageright: Image def drawquad(normal: Tuple[float, float, float], texture: Image) -> None: """Renders a quad with the given surface normal and texture mapping.""" pass def bindtexture(image: Image) -> None: """Uploads image data to GPU texture memory.""" pass class ImpostorManager: def init(self, volumeid: str, serveraddress: str): self.volumeid = volumeid self.serveraddress = serveraddress self.leftquadnormal = Pose((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1)) self.rightquadnormal = Pose((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 1)) self.lefttexture = None self.righttexture = None self.lock = threading.Lock() self.updatethread = threading.Thread(target=self.updateloop, daemon=True) self.updatethread.start() def updateloop(self): while True: # Read head-tracker for 6DoF pose lefteye, righteye = self.readheadtracker() # Update impostor orientation to face respective eyes self.leftquadnormal.orientation = self.computenormal(lefteye.position) self.rightquadnormal.orientation = self.computenormal(righteye.position) # Send request to server request = RenderRequest(self.volumeid, lefteye, righteye) response = self.sendnetworkrequest(self.serveraddress, request) # Apply textures asynchronously with self.lock: self.lefttexture = response.imageleft self.righttexture = response.imageright def readheadtracker(self) -> Tuple[Pose, Pose]: # Standard 6DoF head-tracker polling (step not detailed in sources) return Pose((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 0)), Pose((0, 0, 0), (0, 0, 0)) def computenormal(self, eyepos: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: # Returns normalized vector from quad center to eye return eyepos def sendnetworkrequest(self, address: str, req: RenderRequest) -> RenderResponse: # Standard TCP/UDP LAN socket request (step not detailed in sources) return RenderResponse(Image([], 0, 0), Image([], 0, 0)) def render(self): # Render polygonal environment pass with self.lock: if self.lefttexture: bindtexture(self.lefttexture) drawquad(self.leftquadnormal.orientation, self.lefttexture) if self.righttexture: bindtexture(self.righttexture) drawquad(self.rightquadnormal.orientation, self.righttexture) class VolumeServer: def init(self, volumedata): self.volumedata = volumedata def rendervolume(self, viewdirection: Pose) -> Image: # Software-based volume rendering (RTVR) return Image([], 0, 0) def handlerequest(self, request: RenderRequest) -> RenderResponse: imgleft = self.rendervolume(request.eyeleftpose) imgright = self.rendervolume(request.eyerightpose) return RenderResponse(imgleft, imgright) Parameters: Rendering Time: 20ms to 500ms, depending on the complexity of the volume data set and the rendering mode. Frame Rate: Up to 25fps for a resolution of 128^3 or approximately 11fps for 256^3, depending on complexity and rendering modes (e.g., surface shaded, maximum intensity projection, or non-photorealistic). Polygonal Environment Frame Rate: 60fps, independent of the volume rendering rate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Network Delay: The main problem besides the rendering rate is the network delay (lag), which results in a delayed response when manipulating the volume data. Quick Turning: The decoupling between image update and impostor display becomes visible when turning the volume object quickly, as the textures may not update fast enough to match the rapid change in viewpoint. Freezing: Without asynchronous updates, the virtual environment would freeze during the rendering time. Time Complexity: The volume rendering time varies from 20ms to 500ms per stereo pair, depending on data complexity and rendering mode. The polygonal environment continues to update at 60fps independently. Memory Complexity: The server requires enough memory to hold the volume data sets. Performance: Interactive frame (stereo pair) rates of up to 25fps for a resolution of 128^3 or approximately 11fps for 256^3. Strengths: Adds flexibility and scalability to the system by distributing volume rendering to a separate server. Allows seamless integration of volume visualization and polygonal rendering. Prevents the virtual environment from freezing during volume rendering updates. Limitations: Network delay (lag) causes delayed response when manipulating volume data. Visual artifacts may occur when turning the volume object quickly due to the asynchronous update process. When to Use: When integrating volume rendering into a polygonal virtual environment with limited client-side rendering power for volume data, and when stereoscopic visualization is required. When Not to Use: When low latency is critical and network delay is unacceptable, or when the volume data is too large for the server to handle efficiently. This method was developed by A.L. Fuhrmann et al. and presented in the paper "Distributed Software-Based Volume Visualization in a Virtual Environment" at Eurographics 2005. It builds on previous VR techniques employed in visualization settings. The system uses the Real Time Volume Rendering Library (RTVR) and the Studierstube virtual environment. It was applied to heterogeneous display settings, mixing volume rendering and polygonal rendering. name: Vector Icon Volume Rendering
head: Billboard vector icons, Vector Icon Splatting with Billboard Textures, Vector icons embedded in splat footprint, Volume Rendering with Embedded Vector Icons
body: Vector Icon Volume Rendering is a 3D raster resampling technique that integrates vector field visualization into scalar volume rendering by embedding small billboard images containing vector icons within the splat footprint of the volume rendering sheets. It solves the problem of visualizing flow direction and magnitude within a volumetric scalar field by creating an illusion of coherent flow through stochastic placement and orientation of these icons. It sets itself apart from continuous integration methods by modifying the volume integral to include rendering of tiny cylinders within a small neighborhood of each sampling point, and differs from pure vector field visualization by merging the rendering of a scalar field with that of a vector field in a single compositing pass. The method builds on the slice-based rendering principles defined in Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering. It modifies the standard volume integral to include the rendering of tiny cylinders (vector icons) within a small neighborhood of each sampling point. Inputs: 3D scalar field data (e.g., density clouds). 3D vector field data (e.g., wind velocity). Grid spacing for sheet sampling. Stochastic threshold for icon placement. Icon size limits (maximum and minimum). Color mapping parameters (e.g., altitude to color). Time step for time-varying fields. Outputs: A 2D image where the scalar volume is rendered via alpha blending, and vector flow is indicated by colored, oriented billboard icons. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing scalar values. Icon Texture Set: A set of 2D textures containing pre-rendered vector icons that move across the texture and fade in/out to simulate motion. Billboard Geometry: Implicitly defined by the splat footprint; each billboard image is oriented perpendicular to the viewing ray and parallel to the projected vector direction at the splat's center. Grid Spacing: Regular grid sampling on the current sheet. Stochastic Threshold: Heuristic determining whether a splat includes a cylinder/icon. Icon Size Scaling: Maximum size when flow is parallel to the screen plane; minimum size (dot) when flow is parallel to the viewer’s line of sight. Color Mapping: Scalar value (e.g., altitude) mapped to icon color. 1. Decompose the volume into sheets oriented parallel to the image plane. 2. Sort the sheets in back-to-front order relative to the camera for correct alpha blending compositing. 3. For each sheet, take a regular grid sampling of the vector field data. 4. Place an image reconstruction operator (splat) over each grid point. 5. Use a stochastic heuristic to determine if the current splat should include a vector icon (cylinder). 6. If included, randomly offset the icon from the splat center. 7. Orient the billboard image such that it lies perpendicular to the viewing ray and parallel to the projected vector direction at the splat's center point. 8. Scale the icon size based on the angle between the flow vector and the view direction: largest when parallel to the screen, reduced to a dot when parallel to the line of sight. 9. Render the scalar volume for the sheet using standard volume rendering techniques (texture mapping, classification, blending). 10. Add the volume integral for each pixel under both the splat and the cylinder. 11. Composite the results back-to-front. 12. For time-varying fields, produce a new rendering for each time step and animate in a movie loop. 13. Cycle through the icon texture set at rendering time, where icons move across the texture and fade in/out, to achieve the illusion of motion. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def rendervectoriconvolume(scalarvolume, vectorfield, camera, timestep, gridspacing, stochasticthreshold, maxiconsize, miniconsize): # 1. Generate sheets parallel to image plane sheets = generatesheetsparalleltoimageplane(scalarvolume.boundingbox, camera.viewdirection) # 2. Sort sheets back-to-front sheets.sort(key=lambda s: math.dist(s.center, camera.position)) framebuffer = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for sheet in sheets: # 9. Render scalar volume for sheet sheetcolor = renderscalarsheetstandard(scalarvolume, sheet, camera) # 3. Regular grid sampling on the current sheet gridpoints = sampleregulargridonsheet(sheet, gridspacing) iconlayer = [] for point in gridpoints: # 5. Stochastic heuristic if random.random() < stochasticthreshold: # 6. Random offset from center offset = (random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5)) iconpos = (point.x + offset[0], point.y + offset[1]) # 7. Orientation: perpendicular to viewing ray, parallel to projected vector flowvec = vectorfield.sample(point) projecteddir = projectvectortoscreen(flowvec, camera) billboard = createbillboard(iconpos, projecteddir, camera.viewdirection) # 8. Icon size scaling viewdir = normalize(camera.viewdirection) flownorm = normalize(flowvec) angle = math.acos(max(-1.0, min(1.0, math.dot(flownorm, viewdir)))) if abs(angle - math.pi/2) < 0.1: size = maxiconsize elif abs(angle) < 0.1 or abs(angle - math.pi) < 0.1: size = miniconsize else: size = maxiconsize math.sin(angle) billboard.size = size # 13. Texture cycling for motion illusion textureframe = gettextureframe(timestep, point, iconlayer) billboard.texture = textureframe # Color by altitude altitude = scalarvolume.sample(point) billboard.color = mapaltitudetocolor(altitude) iconlayer.append(billboard) # 10 & 11. Add volume integral and composite back-to-front sheetcolor = alphablendsplats(sheetcolor, iconlayer) framebuffer = alphablend(framebuffer, sheetcolor) return framebuffer def generatesheetsparalleltoimageplane(boundingbox, viewdirection): # Standard slice generation from parent method return [Sheet(center=boundingbox.min + i step, normal=viewdirection) for i in range(numslices)] def sampleregulargridonsheet(sheet, spacing): return [Point(x, y, sheet.center) for x in range(sheet.minx, sheet.maxx, spacing) for y in range(sheet.miny, sheet.maxy, spacing)] def projectvectortoscreen(vec, camera): # Standard projection to screen space return vec - math.dot(vec, normalize(camera.viewdirection)) normalize(camera.viewdirection) def createbillboard(position, direction, viewdirection): return {"position": position, "direction": direction, "viewdirection": viewdirection, "size": 1.0, "texture": None, "color": (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0)} def gettextureframe(timestep, point, iconlayer): # Cycle through texture set based on time and point index return iconlayer.index(point) % len(textureset) def mapaltitudetocolor(altitude): # Standard transfer function mapping return (altitude, 1.0 - altitude, 0.0, 1.0) def alphablendsplats(basecolor, splats): # Standard alpha compositing color = list(basecolor) for s in splats: color = blendtwocolors(color, s.color) return color def alphablend(a, b): return blendtwocolors(a, b) def blendtwocolors(c1, c2): return (c1[0]c1[3] + c2[0]c2[3](1-c1[3]), c1[1]c1[3] + c2[1]c2[3](1-c1[3]), c1[2]c1[3] + c2[2]c2[3](1-c1[3]), c1[3] + c2[3](1-c1[3])) def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in v)) return [x/mag for x in v] if mag > 0 else v Sparse Representation: The discrete and sparse nature of the icons can make the flow difficult to understand. This is mitigated by the texture cycling technique to create an illusion of motion. View Alignment: Icon size must be carefully scaled to avoid occlusion or invisibility when the flow is parallel to the view direction. Uses discrete billboard images to represent flow. Sets itself apart by being purely discrete and stochastic, unlike continuous vector fields. Choose when visual clarity of individual flow elements is preferred over dense field representation. Link Enhances the basic billboard method by using animated textures to simulate motion. Choose when animation is required to convey flow direction in a sparse representation. Link Integrates icons directly into the volume rendering splat footprint. Sets itself apart by merging scalar and vector rendering in a single pass per splat. Choose for tight integration of scalar context and vector direction. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient on GPU due to rasterization of billboards. Performance scales with the number of sheets and grid resolution. Strengths: Intuitive representation of flow direction; integrates well with scalar volume rendering; creates illusion of motion through animation. Limitations: Sparse representation can obscure flow; stochastic placement may lead to visual artifacts; difficult to understand flow in complex regions due to discrete nature. When to Use: Time-varying wind or fluid flow visualization where direction and magnitude are critical, and scalar context (e.g., clouds) is also needed. When Not to Use: When precise quantitative flow analysis is required, or when the flow is dense and continuous (use streamlines or pathlines instead). The technique was developed by R. Crawfis, H. Shen, and N. Max. It is described in the paper "Flow Visualization Techniques for CDF using Volume Rendering" presented at the 9th International Symposium on Flow Visualization, Heriot-Watt University, Edinburgh, 2000. The authors previously developed related techniques such as Line Bundles. The method was applied to global climate simulation data, merging white density clouds (cloudiness) with colored vector icons (wind velocity). name: Image-Based Volume Rendering
head: Image-Based Volume Rendering (IBVR) with Opacity Light Fields, Opacity Light Field Rendering
body: Image-Based Volume Rendering (IBVR) is a technique for interactively exploring arbitrarily large volumetric datasets on standard graphics hardware by decoupling the expensive volume integration from the interactive viewing phase. It solves the performance bottleneck of direct ray casting on large datasets by precomputing "ray slices" from multiple viewpoints and compositing them as opacity light fields during interaction. Unlike previous image-based methods that restricted viewpoints to a limited cone or lacked opacity for internal structure, IBVR allows unrestricted external viewpoints and arbitrary clipping surfaces to reveal interior details without re-rendering the volume. The method operates in three distinct phases: Volume Rendering (preprocessing), Key View Generation, and Interactive Viewing. It is independent of the underlying volume rendering system and dataset representation (e.g., rectilinear or irregular grids). Inputs: Volumetric dataset (scalar field). Geometric proxy surface bounding the volume (initially a bounding sphere or isosurface). Set of original viewpoints for preprocessing. User-defined parameters: number of ray slices per viewpoint, slice spacing. Outputs: Interactive 3D visualization allowing camera movement and dynamic clipping surface modification. 1. Ray Slice A Ray Slice is a 2D image where each pixel represents a partial ray projected from a specific slice location through the volume. Layout: A 2D array of RGBA values. Content: The color and opacity at each pixel correspond to the accumulated values generated by the volume integral along a viewing ray starting at the slice plane and extending through the remainder of the volumetric data towards the original viewpoint. Storage: Stored as compressed images (e.g., PNG for lossless, JPEG 2000 for lossy). 2. Geometric Proxy Surface A surface bounding the volume used to define clipping planes during interactive viewing. Layout: Standard triangle mesh or implicit surface representation. Function: Defines the boundary between the pre-rendered interior (behind the proxy relative to the camera) and the interactive exterior. The user can modify this surface (e.g., add clipping planes) to reveal internal structure. 3. Key View A composite image generated from a set of ray slices and the proxy surface for a specific viewing location. Step 1: Volume Rendering (Preprocessing) 1. Select a set of original viewpoints from which to pre-render the volume. 2. For each viewpoint, define a series of image-aligned clipping planes moving back-to-front through the volume. 3. For each clipping plane position (slice): a. Clip the volume between the clipping plane and the viewpoint. b. Render the remaining volume (from the clipping plane to the far end of the data) using a standard volume rendering algorithm with back-to-front compositing. c. Store the resulting RGBA image as a Ray Slice. Note: The number of slices per viewpoint is adjustable and dataset-dependent. Anisotropic data may require more slices along one axis. Spacing can be adapted to skip empty space or capture detail. 4. Define a Geometric Proxy Surface bounding the volume. Step 2: Key View Generation 1. Input: The set of Ray Slices, their associated viewpoint parameters, and the Geometric Proxy Surface. 2. For each desired interactive viewing location (Key View): a. Determine the intersection of the viewing rays with the Geometric Proxy Surface. b. Identify which Ray Slices are "behind" the proxy surface relative to the new viewpoint. c. Composite the relevant Ray Slices and the proxy surface to generate a Key View image. This image represents the volume intersected by the proxy surface from that specific location. Step 3: Interactive Viewing 1. Load the Key Views and the Geometric Proxy Surface into the graphics hardware. 2. Render the scene interactively: a. Render the Geometric Proxy Surface. b. Render the Key Views as Opacity Light Fields behind the proxy surface. c. Allow the user to modify the Geometric Proxy Surface (e.g., via clipping planes) to reveal interior structure. d. Because the interior structure is pre-computed in the Ray Slices/Key Views, changes to the proxy do not require volumetric re-rendering. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ibvrpipeline(volumedata, transferfunction, proxysurface, viewpoints, sliceparams): rayslices = {} for viewpoint in viewpoints: rayslices[viewpoint] = [] # Determine slice positions along the view direction viewdir = normalize(viewpoint.position - volumedata.center) numslices = sliceparams.get('numslices', 10) spacing = sliceparams.get('spacing', 1.0) slicepositions = [viewpoint.position + viewdir (i spacing) for i in range(numslices)] for pos in slicepositions: # Delegate to any arbitrary volume rendering system that computes RGBA images with back-to-front compositing for arbitrary image-aligned clipping planes. rgbaimage = rendervolumebacktofront(volumedata, transferfunction, pos, viewpoint) # Standard lossless image compression (e.g., PNG). compressedslice = compresstopng(rgbaimage) rayslices[viewpoint].append({'position': pos, 'image': compressedslice}) return rayslices def generatekeyviews(rayslices, proxysurface, keyviewpoints): keyviews = {} for kv in keyviewpoints: relevantslices = [] for vp, slices in rayslices.items(): for s in slices: # Determine if slice position is occluded by proxy surface from key viewpoint. if isbehindproxy(s['position'], kv.position, proxysurface): relevantslices.append(s) # Back-to-front alpha compositing of selected ray slices. keyviews[kv] = compositeslices(relevantslices, kv) return keyviews def renderinteractive(keyviews, proxysurface, currentcamera): # Rasterize proxy surface geometry. rasterize(proxysurface, currentcamera) # Render key view images as textured quads behind the proxy surface. for kv, image in keyviews.items(): if isinfrustum(kv.position, currentcamera): renderquad(image, kv.position, kv.orientation, currentcamera) Number of Ray Slices: User-adjustable. Dataset-dependent. Anisotropic data may need more slices along one axis. Can range from 1 to memory limits. Compression: PNG (lossless) or JPEG 2000 (lossy). Proxy Surface: Initial proxy can be a bounding sphere or isosurface. Edge Case: Sparse pre-computed ray slices may cause interpolation artifacts when the camera moves significantly between key viewpoints. Pitfall: The quality of the interactive view depends on the density of the pre-computed ray slices. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Preprocessing scales with volume size, number of viewpoints, and slices. Interactive viewing is constant relative to volume size, dependent only on key views and proxy geometry. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Scales with the number of pre-computed views and slices. Measured Performance: Tested on arbitrarily large datasets (e.g., terabyte-scale seismic data) on low-cost PC graphics hardware, achieving interactivity where direct ray casting fails. Strengths: Handles arbitrarily large datasets. Unrestricted viewpoints (unlike prior methods [22]). Allows arbitrary clipping surfaces to reveal interior structure without re-rendering. Independent of volume rendering system and dataset representation (works with irregular grids). Limitations: Requires significant preprocessing time and memory. Interactivity is limited to the pre-computed key views; significant camera movement may require interpolation or new key views. Not suitable for dynamic volumes (data changes over time) due to static preprocessing. Image-Based Volume Rendering with Opacity Light Fields was introduced by Miriah Meyer, Hanspeter Pfister, Charles Hansen, and Chris Johnson from the Scientific Computing and Imaging Institute at the University of Utah and Mitsubishi Electric Research Labs. The method was presented in a technical report (UUSCI-2005-002) in 2005. It addresses the limitations of earlier IBVR methods [4, 22] which either lacked opacity for internal views or restricted viewpoints to a limited cone. name: Key View Generation
head: Lumigraph Key View Generation
body: Key View Generation is a preprocessing step that synthesizes intermediate images (key views) from pre-computed ray slices and a geometric proxy surface. It calculates a key view for each ray slice viewpoint, where each key view represents a view of the volume bounded by the proxy surface from that specific viewpoint. Similar to lumigraph rendering, the proxy surface guides ray interpolation to generate these key views. Inputs: 1. A set of ray slices, where each slice corresponds to a specific original viewpoint. 2. A geometric proxy surface, treated as a renderable geometry. 3. Viewpoint parameters for the original viewpoints used to generate the ray slices. Outputs: A set of key views, one for each original viewpoint, stored in PNG RGBA image format. Data Structures: Ray Slices: 2D images representing the volume integration along rays from each viewpoint. Proxy Surface: A geometric surface used to bound the volume. Depth Buffer: A 2D array storing the distance from the viewpoint to the proxy surface for each pixel. Steps: 1. Proxy Rendering: For a specific original viewpoint, render the geometric proxy surface to the frame buffer. 2. Depth Query: Query the depth buffer to obtain the distance d from the viewpoint to the proxy surface for each pixel (u, v) in the key view. 3. Ray Slice Indexing: Use the depth values d to index into the ray slices, identifying the "front" and "back" ray slices that bracket the depth d. 4. Interpolation: For each pixel (u, v) in the key view: Retrieve the RGBA color values from S{front} and S{back} at the corresponding pixel coordinates. Perform linear interpolation between the two slices based on the relative depth d. Compute the final RGBA value: C{key} = w{front} \cdot C{front} + w{back} \cdot C{back} where C represents the RGBA vector, and the interpolation weights w{front} and w{back} are determined by the distance of d to the planes of S{front} and S{back}. 5. Output: Store the resulting key view as a PNG RGBA image. 6. Repeat: Repeat steps 1–5 for every original viewpoint to generate the complete set of key views. Single Ray Slice Technique: If only one ray slice is used per viewpoint, interpolation is skipped. 1. Render the proxy surface to the depth buffer. 2. For each pixel, if the depth equals the far plane distance, color the pixel black. 3. Otherwise, copy the pixel from the single ray slice. This technique removes scanning artifacts and hides surfaces external to the proxy surface. Parameters: Output Format: PNG RGBA. Interpolation Method: Linear interpolation is standard, though higher-order or nearest-neighbor interpolation could be used. Number of Ray Slices: Can be one or multiple per viewpoint, limited by memory restrictions. Pitfalls: Proxy Surface Accuracy: An inaccurate proxy surface extraction causes ghosting artifacts around the isosurface boundary. A better proxy surface allows fewer key views for smooth output images, while a coarse proxy surface requires more key views. Proxy Modification: If the proxy surface is modified (e.g., by clipping planes) to reveal interior structure, the key views must be recomputed using the new proxy geometry. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Limited by memory restrictions on the number of ray slices per viewpoint. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Interpolation errors depend on proxy surface choice and the number of key views. When to Use: Applications requiring specific viewing cones, such as surgical simulation (high accuracy), seismic data exploration (limited latitude/longitude range), or simulation data exploration (unlimited viewing freedom). When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Key View Generation is based on principles similar to lumigraph rendering, where a proxy surface guides ray interpolation to generate key views of the volume. The proxy surface is typically computed only once per volume, but can be modified to reveal interior structure. The number of key views and viewpoint locations are highly data, application, and system dependent. Image-Based Volume Rendering with Opacity Light Fields, https://publications.sci.utah.edu/publications/SCITechReports/UUSCI-2005-002.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid and Mixed Geometry
head: Hybrid ray-volume rendering
body: Hybrid and Mixed Geometry rendering addresses the problem of visualizing scenes containing both explicit polygonal geometry (e.g., surgical instruments, bounding boxes, isosurfaces) and implicit volumetric data (e.g., CT/MR scans) in a single coherent image with correct visibility and attenuation. Unlike pure volume rendering which rasterizes slices or pure ray tracing which handles only geometry, this family of methods intermixes both representations. It is distinguished from Hybrid Volume Rendering by its explicit ray-casting approach to mixing rather than slice-based or proxy-geometry rasterization, and from Hybrid Volume Rendering Scheme by focusing on the specific compositing of geometry and volume rather than a specific architectural scheme for unstructured grids. The family relies on the decomposition of the 3D volume into a set of 2D planar slices. These slices are treated as geometric primitives (typically triangles or quads) that are rasterized by the GPU. The core mechanism involves: 1. Slice Generation: The volume is intersected by a series of parallel planes. The intersection of these planes with the volume bounding box defines the polygonal shape of each slice. 2. Texture Mapping: Each slice vertex is assigned 3D texture coordinates that map to the volumetric data. The volume data is stored as a 3D texture on the GPU. 3. Rasterization and Shading: The polygons are rasterized. In the fragment shader, the 3D texture is sampled at the interpolated texture coordinates to retrieve the scalar value. 4. Classification and Blending: The scalar value is mapped to color and opacity via a transfer function. The fragments are composited using alpha blending (typically GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). 5. Sorting: The slices must be rendered in the correct depth order relative to the camera (back-to-front for standard alpha blending) to ensure correct compositing. Hybrid Ray Tracing is a method for mixing geometric and volumetric data by casting rays through the ensemble of both, drawing samples of each, and compositing them in depth-sorted order. It solves the problem of rendering scenes containing both polygonal models and volumetric data in a single pass with correct visibility and attenuation. Unlike pure volume rendering which rasterizes slices, or pure ray tracing which handles only geometry, this method simultaneously traces rays through volumetric sample arrays and polygonal databases, resampling both at equally spaced intervals to handle mixtures of geometric and volumetric data. It is distinguished from Hybrid Volume Rendering by its explicit ray-casting approach to mixing rather than slice-based or proxy-geometry rasterization. Hybrid volume rendering techniques allow polygonal geometry and volumetric data to be visualized in a single image, enabling the display of scale, grids, or other polygon-defined objects over, behind, and through volumetric data. It solves the problem of integrating explicit geometric context (such as bounding boxes, isosurfaces, or wireframes) with implicit volumetric fields. Unlike pure ray casting which treats the volume as a continuous medium, or pure polygon rendering which lacks internal structure, hybrid methods intermix both representations. It differs from Hybrid Ray Tracing by typically relying on rasterization or standard ray casting with depth-buffer integration rather than path tracing hybrids, and from Hybrid Volume Rendering Scheme by focusing on the specific compositing of geometry and volume rather than a specific architectural scheme. The Hybrid Volume Rendering Scheme is a parallel volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids that combines object-order and image-order techniques to handle complex block boundaries, dramatic cell size variations, and camera-induced load imbalances. Unlike pure image-order methods, which suffer from replicated cell loading and unequal cell distribution, or pure object-order methods, where image compositing becomes a bottleneck, this approach bounds the computation of each processing phase to adapt dynamically to the workload. Rendering occurs only inside the selected geometric object's volume. If Fire Lights are enabled, only those inside the cutter are rendered. Parameters: usegizmo (enable), gizmo (object). Invert Cutter (invgizmo): When enabled, rendering occurs only outside the render cutter. Rays not intersecting the cutter are shaded. This is distinct from a cutter with inverted geometry. Pitfall: Cutter Geom does not work in Volumetric Geometry mode. The concept of hybrid rendering, specifically blending OpenGL-rendered volumes with ray-traced non-volume objects, is implemented in software such as PyMOL via the rayvolume setting. This approach allows for features like shadows or outlines on non-volume objects while maintaining the speed of OpenGL for the volume itself, though it is limited to the current window size and does not work in headless (batch) mode. The broader field of hybrid volume rendering has evolved to handle unstructured grids and complex geometric contexts, addressing memory footprint and load imbalance issues in parallel environments. name: Hybrid Scanline A-Buffer Volume Rendering
head: Scanline A-Buffer with Volume Fragments
body: Hybrid Scanline A-Buffer Volume Rendering is a technique that integrates surface-defined geometry and procedural volume data (such as gases) into a single image by combining a fast scanline a-buffer algorithm for solids with volume rendering for translucent media. It distinguishes itself from pure ray casting by using an a-buffer to manage fragment overlap and from pure polygon rendering by explicitly handling volumetric opacity and attenuation through sorted volume fragments. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A scene containing surface-defined objects (polygons) and volume-defined objects (procedural gases/fluids); a camera view; lighting parameters. Outputs: A final 2D image with correct blending of surfaces and volumes. Data Structures: A-Buffer: A data structure associated with a scanline. For each pixel, it maintains a list of fragments. Each fragment contains coverage information (partial or full pixel coverage) and depth information (Z-depth). Volume Fragments: Sub-sections of the volume data that cover the current scanline, treated as fragments with average Z-depth values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize A-Buffer: Create an a-buffer for the current scanline. This structure contains a list for each pixel in the scanline, initialized to hold all fragments that partially or fully cover that pixel. 2. Process Surface Geometry: Render surface-defined objects into the a-buffer. These fragments are stored in the pixel lists based on their coverage and depth. 3. Process Volumes: For each volume object that intersects the current scanline: Perform volume rendering calculations for the sections of the volume covering the scanline. Generate a-buffer fragments for these separate sections of the volume. Termination Condition: Cease volume rendering for a specific pixel once full coverage of that pixel is achieved by either volume or surface-defined elements. 4. Sort Fragments: Sort the volume a-buffer fragments into the a-buffer fragment list for each pixel based on their average Z-depth values. 5. Composite: Render the final a-buffer fragment list for each pixel to produce the final color, combining the contributions of all sorted fragments. Illumination and Shadows: The system uses a physically-based low-albedo illumination and atmospheric attenuation model for gases. Volumetric shadows are combined efficiently using three-dimensional shadow tables. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridscanlineabufferrendering(scene, scanliney): # 1. Initialize A-Buffer for the scanline # Each pixel has a list of fragments abuffer = {pixelid: [] for pixelid in range(scene.width)} # 2. Render surface-defined objects for surface in scene.surfaces: if surface.intersectsscanline(scanliney): fragments = surface.getfragments(scanliney) for frag in fragments: abuffer[frag.pixelid].append(frag) # 3. Render volume-defined objects for volume in scene.volumes: if volume.intersectsscanline(scanliney): # Get sections of volume covering the scanline volumesections = volume.getsections(scanliney) for section in volumesections: # Calculate volume rendering for this section # Returns fragments with average Z-depth volumefragments = volume.rendersection(section, scanliney) for vfrag in volumefragments: # Check if pixel is already fully covered if not ispixelfullycovered(abuffer[vfrag.pixelid]): abuffer[vfrag.pixelid].append(vfrag) else: # Cease volume rendering for this pixel if fully covered pass # 4. Sort fragments by average Z-depth for each pixel for pixelid, fragments in abuffer.items(): fragments.sort(key=lambda f: f.averagezdepth) # 5. Composite final image image = {} for pixelid, fragments in abuffer.items(): # Render fragment list to produce final color # Incorporates low-albedo illumination and 3D shadow tables finalcolor = compositefragments(fragments, scene.lighting, scene.shadowtables) image[pixelid] = finalcolor return image def ispixelfullycovered(fragments): # Implementation detail: Check if coverage sum >= 1.0 or # if opaque surface fragments exist at front-most depth. # Not explicitly defined in sources, assumed standard a-buffer logic. return False # Placeholder for logic not detailed in A rendering algorithm for surface-defined objects in hybrid scenes. It creates an a-buffer for a scanline, containing a list for each pixel of all fragments that partially or fully cover the pixel. It serves as the foundation for handling the geometric components of the hybrid system. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Described as a "fast" algorithm for surface-defined objects. Strengths: Efficiently combines surface and volume rendering; uses 3D shadow tables for efficient volumetric shadowing. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: When visualizing procedural gases or fluids alongside surface-defined objects in a hybrid scene. The method was developed by David Ebert as part of a system for procedural modeling, animation, and rendering of gases, fluids, and textures. It builds upon work in solid texturing and procedural noise functions (such as Perlin’s turbulence). The approach was presented in the context of visualizing computational fluid dynamics and hybrid scenes. Procedural Modeling, Animation, and Rendering of Gases, Fluids, and Textures, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/2786953ProceduralModelingAnimationandRenderingofGasesFluidsandTextures/links/00b7d51a73e42a3c4e000000/Procedural-Modeling-Animation-and-Rendering-of-Gases-Fluids-and-Textures.pdf, fetched 2026-10-31 (unofficial) PDF Volume Rendering Methods for Computational Fluid Dynamics Visualization, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/220943451VolumeRenderingMethodsforComputationalFluidDynamicsVisualization/links/00b7d51a73e2892e23000000/Volume-Rendering-Methods-for-Computational-Fluid-Dynamics-Visualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Scanline A-buffer rendering
head: Ebert and Parent method
body: A rendering algorithm for surface-defined objects in hybrid scenes, creating an A-buffer for a scanline containing a list of all fragments that partially or fully cover each pixel. It sets itself apart by explicitly managing fragment lists per pixel to support hybrid volume rendering, unlike standard scanline renderers that discard depth information early. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scanline of pixels, geometry data for surface-defined objects. Output: An A-buffer data structure for the scanline, containing fragment lists for each pixel. Data Structures: A-buffer: An array indexed by pixel column. Each entry contains a linked list of fragments. Fragment: A data structure representing a surface patch covering part of a pixel. Fields include: zmin, zmax: Depth range of the fragment. color: Surface color/opacity. next: Pointer to the next fragment in the list. pixelcoverage: Bitmap or count of pixels covered by this fragment. Steps: 1. For each pixel in the scanline, initialize an empty fragment list in the A-buffer. 2. For each surface-defined object intersecting the scanline: a. Determine all fragments that partially or fully cover the pixel. b. For each fragment, compute its depth range (zmin, zmax) and coverage. c. Insert the fragment into the pixel's list in the A-buffer, sorted by depth (back-to-front). 3. After processing all objects, the A-buffer contains all fragments for the scanline, ready for volume rendering compositing. Formulas: Fragment coverage: C = \frac{\text{Area of intersection}}{\text{Pixel Area}} Depth sorting: Fragments are sorted such that z{i} \le z{i+1} for back-to-front rendering. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Precision: Depth values must be precise to avoid z-fighting in fragment sorting. Boundaries: Fragments covering partial pixels must be handled correctly to avoid artifacts. Degenerate input: Objects with no intersection with the scanline should be skipped. Combines this method with volume rendering for procedural gases, using Z-sorted A-buffer fragments [Parent]. Time complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels in the scanline and M is the average number of fragments per pixel. Memory complexity: O(N \cdot M) for storing fragment lists. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance degrades with high fragment density per pixel. Strengths: Explicit management of fragments allows for hybrid rendering with volume data. Limitations: High memory usage for scenes with many overlapping surfaces. When to use: Hybrid scenes with surface-defined objects and volumetric data. When not to use: Scenes with only volumetric data or simple surface rendering. Originated by Ebert and Parent in the pre-shader era, combining scanline A-buffer rendering with volume rendering to handle hybrid scenes. It was used for visualizing surface-defined objects in conjunction with procedural gases like clouds. A survey of modeling, rendering and animation of clouds in computer graphics, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-020-01953-y, fetched 2026-10-26 Volume Rendering Methods for Computational Fluid Dynamics Visualization, https://www.researchgate.net/profile/David-Ebert-4/publication/220943451VolumeRenderingMethodsforComputationalFluidDynamicsVisualization/links/00b7d51a73e2892e23000000/Volume-Rendering-Methods-for-Computational-Fluid-Dynamics-Visualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Volume Rendering Scheme
head: Scalable Hybrid Scheme, Hybrid between classical object order and image order
body: The Hybrid Volume Rendering Scheme is a parallel volume rendering algorithm for unstructured grids that combines object-order and image-order techniques to handle complex block boundaries, dramatic cell size variations, and camera-induced load imbalances. Unlike pure image-order methods, which suffer from replicated cell loading and unequal cell distribution, or pure object-order methods, where image compositing becomes a bottleneck, this approach bounds the computation of each processing phase to adapt dynamically to the workload. The algorithm operates on unstructured grids (and structured ones) by dividing work over resources such that each phase of processing is bounded in the amount of computation it can perform. The method addresses the memory footprint issues of the original 2006 Childs et al. technique by introducing the concept of partial composites. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unstructured volume data (mesh), camera parameters, transfer function, image resolution. Output: Final composited image. Data Structures: Unstructured Grid: Defined by cells and vertices. Cells vary in size and shape. Partial Composites: Intermediate image tiles stored to reduce memory footprint compared to storing full intermediate results. Processor Partitioning: Work is distributed across P processors. Steps: 1. Phase 1: Object-Order Ray Casting (Bounded): Processors perform ray casting on their local portion of the unstructured grid. To prevent load imbalance caused by large cells or camera focus, the processing of large cells is deferred. Each processor bounds the amount of computation it performs in this phase to ensure balanced workload distribution. Rays are cast through the cells owned by the processor. For each ray, the scalar values are sampled along the ray path within the cell. The sampled values are mapped to color and opacity using the transfer function. Instead of compositing into a single final image immediately, processors generate partial composites for their assigned tiles. 2. Phase 2: Image Compositing (Bounded): The partial composites from all processors are collected and composited to produce the final image. This phase handles the depth ordering and blending of the partial results. The amount of computation in this phase is also bounded to maintain balance. 3. Handling Load Imbalance: If a processor owns larger cells or the camera view focuses on a region owned by one processor, the workload would normally be unequal. The hybrid approach solves this by deferring the processing of large cells in Phase 1 and distributing the workload among processors in Phase 2. Formulas: Ray Casting: For a ray R(t) = O + tD, the color C and opacity \alpha are computed by integrating along the ray path through cell i: C = \sum{i} ci \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha = \sum{i} \alphai \prod{j < i} (1 - \alphaj) Where ci and \alphai are the color and opacity of the i-th sample, derived from the scalar value vi via the transfer function TF(vi) \rightarrow (ci, \alphai). Parameters: Number of Processors (P): Scaled up to 8,192 processors. Data Size: Operated on data sets with more than one billion cells. Partial Composite Size: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Footprint: The original 2006 technique required unnecessarily large amounts of memory to store intermediate results, affecting timing and causing crashes. The scalable hybrid scheme introduces partial composites to mitigate this. Load Imbalance: Caused by varying cell sizes or camera positions focusing on specific regions. The hybrid approach manages this by bounding computation per phase. Many-Core Architectures: The algorithm was adapted to support many-core architectures, accounting for the changed balance of computing and communication inherent in these environments. Time Complexity: The algorithm adapts its computation based on workload, performing well in all cases tested (varying camera position, data set size, transfer function, image size, and processor count). Memory Complexity: Reduced memory footprint compared to the original 2006 technique due to the use of partial composites. Scalability: Scaled up to 8,192 processors and operated on data sets with more than one billion cells. Strengths: Handles complex block boundaries, dramatic cell size variations, and camera-induced load imbalances effectively. It can operate like either an object-order or image-order technique depending on the scenario. Limitations: The original technique had high memory requirements (addressed in the scalable version). When to Use: When dealing with unstructured grids with varying cell sizes or when camera position causes load imbalance in traditional methods. When Not to Use: Not specified in the sources. The approach is based on a 2006 method by Childs et al., which was a hybrid between object-order and image-order techniques for unstructured meshes. The original work was lacking in three major respects: insufficient evaluation, high memory requirements for intermediate results, and no consideration for many-core architectures. The scalable hybrid scheme addresses these shortcomings by providing a comprehensive evaluation, introducing partial composites to reduce memory footprint, and adding support for many-core architectures. A Scalable Hybrid Scheme for Ray-Casting of Unstructured Volume Data, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2018.2833113, fetched 2026-10-24

name: Proxy Geometry and Slicing
body: Proxy Geometry and Slicing renders volumetric data by decomposing the 3D volume into a set of 2D planar slices, which are treated as explicit geometric primitives (typically triangles or quads) and rasterized by the GPU. This method solves the problem of interactive volume visualization by leveraging fixed-function rasterization and hardware alpha blending, avoiding the per-pixel ray-marching overhead of direct volume ray casting. It sets itself apart from Direct Volume Ray Casting by using explicit geometry and fixed-function blending, and from Surface Rendering Pipeline by rendering the entire volume interior rather than just isosurfaces. See Slice-based and Proxy Geometry Rendering for shared principles. Inputs: 3D volume data (stored as a 3D texture on the GPU), camera view direction, volume bounding box, slice spacing/distance. Outputs: Rasterized 2D slices composited into a 2D image. Data structures: An array of BufferGeometry objects pre-allocated to MAXSLICESCOUNT. Each geometry holds a position attribute array of 21 floats (7 vertices × 3 components) and an index array of 18 integers (6 triangles × 3 indices). Steps: 1. Bounding Box Setup: Calculate the minimum and maximum coordinates of the volume bounding box. Store the 8 corners in a corners array and create 12 Line3 edge objects connecting them. 2. Plane Generation: Create a clipping plane aligned with the camera view direction. Initialize a plane.constant value based on the camera position and view distance. 3. Slice Intersection Loop: While sliceIndex < MAXSLICESCOUNT, decrement plane.constant by window.sliceDistance. For each of the 12 edges, compute the intersection of the plane with the edge line segment. Collect valid intersection points into intersectionVertices. 4. Polygon Sorting & Triangulation: If intersectionVertices contains points, compute the centroid by summing the vertices and dividing by the count. Calculate the 2D angle of each vertex relative to the centroid using atan2(y - centroid.y, x - centroid.x). Sort the vertices by this angle. Push the centroid to the end of the sorted array to form a fan. 5. Geometry Update: Update the geometry's position attribute with the sorted vertices and centroid. Build the index array for fan triangulation. Set the draw range to the number of vertices. Mark attributes for update and compute the bounding sphere. Increment sliceIndex. 6. Texture Mapping: Each slice vertex is assigned 3D texture coordinates that map to the volumetric data. 7. Rasterization and Shading: The polygons are rasterized. In the fragment shader, the 3D texture is sampled at the interpolated texture coordinates to retrieve the scalar value. 8. Classification and Blending: The scalar value is mapped to color and opacity via a transfer function. The fragments are composited using alpha blending (typically GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). 9. Sorting: The slices must be rendered in the correct depth order relative to the camera (back-to-front for standard alpha blending) to ensure correct compositing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class BufferGeometry: def init(self): self.position = [0.0] 21 self.index = [0] 18 self.drawrange = (0, 0) def markattributesforupdate(self): pass def computeboundingsphere(self): pass class Line3: def init(self, start, end): self.start = start self.end = end class Plane: def init(self, normal, constant): self.normal = normal self.constant = constant def intersectline(self, line): # Returns intersection point or None return None class ProxyGeometrySlicer: def init(self, maxslicescount): self.maxslicescount = maxslicescount self.geometries = [BufferGeometry() for in range(maxslicescount)] self.corners = [] self.edges = [] self.sliceindex = 0 self.intersectionvertices = [] def setboundingbox(self, boxmin, boxmax): self.corners = [ boxmin, [boxmin[0], boxmin[1], boxmax[2]], [boxmin[0], boxmax[1], boxmin[2]], [boxmin[0], boxmax[1], boxmax[2]], [boxmax[0], boxmin[1], boxmin[2]], [boxmax[0], boxmin[1], boxmax[2]], [boxmax[0], boxmax[1], boxmin[2]], boxmax ] cornerpairs = [(0,1), (0,2), (0,4), (1,3), (1,5), (2,3), (2,6), (3,7), (4,5), (4,6), (5,7), (6,7)] self.edges = [Line3(self.corners[i], self.corners[j]) for i, j in cornerpairs] def updateproxygeometries(self, cameradir, viewplaneconstant, slicedistance): self.sliceindex = 0 plane = Plane(normal=cameradir, constant=viewplaneconstant) while (len(self.intersectionvertices) > 0 or self.sliceindex == 0) and self.sliceindex < self.maxslicescount: plane.constant -= slicedistance self.intersectionvertices = [] for edge in self.edges: pt = plane.intersectline(edge) if pt is not None: self.intersectionvertices.append(pt) if len(self.intersectionvertices) > 0: self.sortpolygonedges(self.intersectionvertices) self.updategeometry(self.sliceindex, self.intersectionvertices) self.sliceindex += 1 def sortpolygonedges(self, vertices): centroid = [sum(v[i] for v in vertices) / len(vertices) for i in range(3)] angles = [math.atan2(v[1] - centroid[1], v[0] - centroid[0]) for v in vertices] sortedvertices = [v for, v in sorted(zip(angles, vertices))] sortedvertices.append(centroid) vertices[:] = sortedvertices def updategeometry(self, index, vertices): self.geometries[index].position = [coord for v in vertices for coord in v] # Fan triangulation indices: (0,1,2), (0,2,3),... n = len(vertices) indices = [] for i in range(1, n - 1): indices.extend([0, i, i + 1]) self.geometries[index].index = indices + [0] (18 - len(indices)) self.geometries[index].drawrange = (0, len(vertices)) self.geometries[index].markattributesforupdate() self.geometries[index].computeboundingsphere() Parameters: MAXSLICESCOUNT (maximum number of slices supported, used to pre-allocate the geometries array). window.sliceDistance (spacing between consecutive planes). Edge cases and pitfalls: If plane.intersectLine returns undefined (degenerate intersection), the intersection is skipped. The geometries are pre-allocated with fixed sizes (7 vertices, 18 indices), so intersectionVertices.length must not exceed 7; otherwise, index bounds errors occur. Texture-Based Volume Rendering (TBVR) is a direct volume rendering technique that accelerates image-order ray casting by decomposing the 3D volume into a set of 2D planar slices. These slices are treated as geometric primitives (proxy geometry) that are rasterized by the GPU, with the volumetric data stored in 3D or 2D texture memory. Unlike View-Aligned Slicing, which dynamically computes slice geometry to maintain constant sampling distance, TBVR typically relies on fixed object-aligned slices or view-aligned slices that may vary in sampling density, trading memory efficiency and artifact susceptibility for rendering speed. Choose TBVR when maximum rendering throughput on standard graphics hardware is required and slight sampling artifacts are acceptable. View-aligned slicing is a direct volume rendering technique that decomposes a 3D volume into a series of 2D planar slices (proxy geometry) aligned with the camera's view direction. Unlike standard ray casting which samples the volume texture directly per pixel, this method generates explicit geometric primitives (triangles or quads) that are rasterized by the GPU. The primary advantage is consistent sampling distance relative to the camera, which minimizes sampling artifacts and maintains uniform slice thickness regardless of viewing angle. Choose this variant when visual fidelity and uniform sampling are prioritized over the performance cost of per-frame geometry regeneration. A raster display technique that generates several 2D slices of 3D data and combines them to produce a 3D image. It leaves gaps between the slices, forcing the user to guess about flow field conditions in those gaps. A volume rendering technique using the Volumizer library to polygonize volume data and render it in layers from back to front. The volume data is stored in a 3D texture map, and the subregion corresponding to the newly acquired slice is loaded with the new image data immediately after reconstruction. The volume data is polygonized using trilinear interpolation, then rendered in layers from back to front. A predefined blend function combines the new layer with the existing display buffer: alpha blending weights each new layer by scalar alpha and the existing buffer by 1-alpha, imparting translucency, while MIP selects the maximum of the new layer and display buffer contents regardless of alpha, used for contrast agent visualization. Not given in the sources. The technique originated from early efforts to visualize 3D data on raster display systems. Smith, Sperry, and Everton extended two-dimensional techniques by generating several two-dimensional slices and combining them to produce a three-dimensional image, marking an early application of this family. This approach leveraged the advancement of raster display systems and computer graphics techniques like ray tracing to create images that exploited higher resolution systems. Later implementations integrated real-time MRI imaging guidance, utilizing the Volumizer library and OpenGL to polygonize and render volume data in layers with alpha blending or MIP for contrast agent visualization. name: Texture-Based Volume Rendering
head: Geometry-based volume visualization, Proxy Geometry Rendering, Slice-based rendering, TBVR, Texture Based Ray Casting, Texture-based visualization
body: Texture-Based Volume Rendering (TBVR) is a direct volume rendering technique that accelerates image-order ray casting by decomposing the 3D volume into a set of 2D planar slices. These slices are treated as geometric primitives (proxy geometry) that are rasterized by the GPU, with the volumetric data stored in 3D or 2D texture memory. Unlike View-Aligned Slicing, which dynamically computes slice geometry to maintain constant sampling distance, TBVR typically relies on fixed object-aligned slices or view-aligned slices that may vary in sampling density, trading memory efficiency and artifact susceptibility for rendering speed. The method operates in three stages: Initialize, Update, and Draw. Input: Volumetric scalar field data (regular grid), transfer function (TF), camera parameters (view/projection matrices), and rendering mode (transparent/solid). Output: 2D color buffer with composited volume image. 1. Volume Texture: 3D Texture: Stores the entire volume in GPU memory. Format: GLRGBA or GLRED (for scalar data). Type: GLUNSIGNEDBYTE or GLFLOAT. Filters: GLLINEAR (trilinear interpolation). 2D Texture Stack: Stores slices as a stack of 2D textures. Requires replication along X, Y, and Z axes for object-aligned rendering, consuming 3x memory. 2. Transfer Function Texture: 1D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA color/opacity. 3. Proxy Geometry: Array of vertices defining planar polygons (quads or triangle fans) intersecting the volume bounding box. Object-Aligned: Rectangles aligned with principal axes (X, Y, Z). View-Aligned: Polygons orthogonal to the viewing direction, constructed by intersecting slicing planes with the volume bounding box. 4. Uniforms/Constants: uslices: vec3 containing texture dimensions (Dx, Dy, Dz) for coordinate normalization. uthresh: float threshold for fragment discard. ualphaScale: float multiplier for opacity. uclipPlaneX/Y/Z, uclipCubeMax/Min: Clipping parameters. 1. Initialize: Load volume data into CPU memory. Process data (e.g., compute gradients, downsample) if required. Create transfer function lookup tables (1D textures). Download volume data to GPU as 3D texture or 2D texture stack. Compile fragment shaders. 2. Update (Per Frame): Compute proxy geometry: For View-Aligned: Intersect slicing planes with the volume bounding box. Sort resulting vertices in counter-clockwise order. Construct polygon primitives (e.g., triangle fan from centroid). For Object-Aligned: Select the texture stack (X, Y, or Z) closest to the camera viewpoint. Update vertex arrays with proxy geometry vertices and their corresponding 3D texture coordinates. Texture coordinates are assigned to vertices, either on CPU or via vertex shader. Refresh textures if rendering mode or transfer function parameters change. 3. Draw: Set up rendering state: Disable lighting and culling. Enable alpha blending. For Over operator (back-to-front): Source = 1, Destination = 1 - Source Alpha. For Under operator (front-to-back): Source = 1 - Destination Alpha, Destination = 1. Disable depth testing or disable depth buffer writing if blending with opaque geometry. Bind volume texture and transfer function texture. Specify shader input parameters (matrices, uniforms). Draw slice polygons in sorted order (back-to-front for Over operator). Restore rendering state. For each fragment of a proxy polygon: 1. Interpolate Texture Coordinates: Receive interpolated 3D texture coordinates from vertex attributes. 2. Data Lookup: Sample the volume texture at the interpolated coordinates to retrieve the scalar value v. Note: If using 2D textures, bilinear interpolation is used within slices, causing artifacts at slice boundaries. 3D textures use trilinear interpolation. 3. Transfer Function Lookup: Use the scalar value v as a texture coordinate for a dependent lookup into the 1D transfer function texture to retrieve color C and opacity \alpha. 4. Illumination (Optional): Compute surface normal using central differences (finite differences) between neighboring voxels. Apply lighting model (e.g., Blinn-Phong) to modify color. 5. Compositing: The resulting color and alpha are sent to the hardware compositing stage (alpha blending). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(position, modelmatrix, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix): # Transform vertex to world space for texture coordinate calculation texposition = modelmatrix @ vec4(position, 1.0) # Camera position in world space vcam = inverse(viewmatrix)[:3, 3] glPosition = projectionmatrix @ viewmatrix @ modelmatrix @ vec4(position, 1.0) return texposition, vcam def fragmentshader(texposition, vcam, volumetexture, slicesdims, threshold, alphascale, clipcubeenabled, clipcubemax, clipcubemin, clipplanexenabled, clipplanex, clipplaneyenabled, clipplaney, clipplanezenabled, clipplanez): # Normalize texture coordinates based on volume dimensions texcoords = vec3( (texposition.x / slicesdims.x) + 0.5, (texposition.y / slicesdims.y) + 0.5, (texposition.z / slicesdims.z) + 0.5) # Sample volume data color = texture3D(volumetexture, texcoords) # Discard if below threshold if color.r < threshold: return None # Clipping logic if clipcubeenabled: if not (clipcubemin.x <= texposition.x <= clipcubemax.x and clipcubemin.y <= texposition.y <= clipcubemax.y and clipcubemin.z <= texposition.z <= clipcubemax.z): return None if clipplanexenabled and texposition.x > clipplanex: return None if clipplaneyenabled and texposition.z > clipplaney: return None if clipplanezenabled and texposition.y < clipplanez: return None # Apply alpha scale color.a = alphascale return color def shading(normal, viewdir, lightdir, Ka, Kd, Ks, shininess, lightcolour, ambientlight): halfvector = normalize(lightdir + viewdir) ambient = Ka ambientlight diffuselight = max(dot(lightdir, normal), 0.0) diffuse = Kd lightcolour diffuselight specularlight = pow(max(dot(halfvector, normal), 0.0), shininess) if diffuselight <= 0.0: specularlight = 0.0 specular = Ks lightcolour specularlight return ambient + diffuse + specular def fragmentshadersolid(texposition, vcam, volumetexture, slicesdims, threshold, alphascale, lightpos1, lightpos2): texcoords = vec3( (texposition.x / slicesdims.x) + 0.5, (texposition.y / slicesdims.y) + 0.5, (texposition.z / slicesdims.z) + 0.5) color = texture3D(volumetexture, texcoords) if color.r < threshold: return None # Compute Normal via Central Differences delta = 1.0 / 256.0 sample1 = texture3D(volumetexture, texcoords - vec3(delta, 0.0, 0.0)) sample2 = texture3D(volumetexture, texcoords + vec3(delta, 0.0, 0.0)) Nx = sample2.x - sample1.x sample1 = texture3D(volumetexture, texcoords - vec3(0.0, delta, 0.0)) sample2 = texture3D(volumetexture, texcoords + vec3(0.0, delta, 0.0)) Ny = sample2.x - sample1.x sample1 = texture3D(volumetexture, texcoords - vec3(0.0, 0.0, delta)) sample2 = texture3D(volumetexture, texcoords + vec3(0.0, 0.0, delta)) Nz = sample2.x - sample1.x normal = normalize(vec3(Nx, Ny, Nz)) L1 = normalize(lightpos1 - vec3(texposition)) L2 = normalize(lightpos2 - vec3(texposition)) V = normalize(vcam - vec3(texposition)) # Lighting constants from Ka = vec3(0.1, 0.1, 0.1) Kd = vec3(0.6, 0.6, 0.6) Ks = vec3(0.2, 0.2, 0.2) shininess = 100.0 lightcolour = vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) ambientlight = vec3(0.3, 0.3, 0.3) shade1 = shading(normal, V, L1, Ka, Kd, Ks, shininess, lightcolour, ambientlight) shade2 = shading(normal, V, L2, Ka, Kd, Ks, shininess, lightcolour, ambientlight) color.rgb = shade1 + shade2 return color PLANEINC: Increment value for plane slicing, typically initialized as 1.0 (voxel spacing). uslices: Uniform vec3 containing texture dimensions (TEXTURE\SIZE\X, TEXTURE\SIZE\Y, TEXTURE\SIZE\Z). uthresh: Uniform float threshold for discarding fragments. ualphaScale: Uniform float multiplier for fragment alpha. Lighting Constants (Phong): Ka=(0.1,0.1,0.1), Kd=(0.6,0.6,0.6), Ks=(0.2,0.2,0.2), shininess=100.0, ambientLight=(0.3,0.3,0.3), lightColour=(1.0,1.0,1.0). Precision: Trilinear interpolation in 3D textures is slightly slower than bilinear in 2D but provides better quality. Boundaries: Object-aligned slices suffer from "pop-up" artifacts when switching between texture stacks (X, Y, Z) due to changes in sampling points. Intensity Variations: As the camera moves, the sampling distance changes in object-aligned rendering, causing intensity variations. Viewing Angle: 2D texture stacks suffer from sampling artifacts when the viewing angle approaches 45 degrees relative to the slices, as the viewer sees between slice gaps. Memory: Object-aligned slices require 3x memory consumption due to data replication along principal directions. Uses fixed proxy geometry aligned with the principal axes (X, Y, Z) of the volume. Requires storing the volume as three stacks of 2D textures (replicated data), consuming 3x memory. Fast and simple to implement but suffers from memory overhead, image popping artifacts during stack swaps, and intensity variations as the camera moves. Uses proxy geometry that is orthogonal to the viewing direction. Requires 3D textures (or on-the-fly reconstruction from 2D stacks). Slower to compute geometry but more memory efficient (no replication) and provides consistent sampling distance, eliminating 45-degree viewing artifacts. A variant of object-aligned rendering where data is stored as a set of 2D texture slices. Proxy polygons are simple rectangles aligned with slices. To avoid data replication, slices can be reconstructed on the fly, incurring performance overhead. Sampling rate depends on volume resolution, which can be mitigated by adding intermediate slices and using trilinear interpolation. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of slices and the resolution of the image. Fragment shader execution is parallelized on the GPU. Memory Complexity: 3D Textures: O(N) where N is the number of voxels. 2D Textures (Object-Aligned): O(3N) due to replication along X, Y, Z axes. Measured Performance: Achieves interactive frame rates on modern GPUs by leveraging hardware texture sampling and alpha blending. 2D textures are faster than 3D textures due to simpler bilinear interpolation, but 3D textures provide better image quality. Strengths: High performance on GPUs; simple implementation; leverages standard graphics pipeline. Limitations: Artifacts at slice boundaries (2D); memory usage (2D replication); sampling artifacts at oblique angles (2D); dependency on sampling rate. When to Use: Interactive visualization where performance is critical and artifacts are acceptable or mitigated (e.g., view-aligned slices). When Not to Use: High-quality offline rendering requiring precise sampling (use ray casting); memory-constrained environments with large volumes using 2D textures. Texture-Based Volume Rendering was developed to accelerate volume rendering on graphics hardware. Early implementations used 2D textures due to hardware limitations, leading to object-aligned slicing techniques. The advent of 3D texture support in GPUs allowed for view-aligned slicing and trilinear interpolation, significantly improving image quality and eliminating viewing angle artifacts. The technique is widely used in medical imaging and scientific visualization for interactive exploration of volumetric data.
