name: View-Aligned Slicing
head: 3D-Texture Based Slicing, View-Aligned 3D Texture Slicing, View-Aligned Proxy Geometry Sampling, View-Aligned Slice Rendering
body: View-aligned slicing is a direct volume rendering technique that decomposes a 3D volume into a series of 2D planar slices (proxy geometry) aligned with the camera's view direction. Unlike standard ray casting which samples the volume texture directly per pixel, this method generates explicit geometric primitives (triangles or quads) that are rasterized by the GPU. The primary advantage is consistent sampling distance relative to the camera, which minimizes sampling artifacts and maintains uniform slice thickness regardless of viewing angle. It builds on Proxy Geometry and Slicing by dynamically regenerating geometry every frame to maintain view alignment. The method renders the volume by intersecting parallel slicing planes with the volume bounding box, generating billboards that face the camera. These billboards are rasterized, and fragment shaders sample the 3D volume texture at interpolated 3D texture coordinates. Inputs: 3D volume data (scalar field), camera position (eyePos), view matrix (mtx), volume dimensions (res), and sampling rate (sampleRate or numberOfSlices). Outputs: 2D image with color and opacity composited via alpha blending. 1. Volume Texture (tex3D): Format: GLRGBA32F (or 8-bit precision in some implementations). Dimensions: rawinf->res.x, rawinf->res.y, rawinf->res.z. Wrap Mode: GLCLAMPTOBORDER to avoid artifacts from texture coordinate transformation. Filter: GLNEAREST. Binding: GLTEXTURE0. 2. Transfer Function (tex1D): Format: GLRGBA32F. Size: 256 entries. Wrap Mode: GLCLAMP. Filter: GLLINEAR. Binding: GLTEXTURE1. 3. Vertex Buffer (aposition): Type: Float32Array (flat array of [x, y, z] coordinates). Layout: Concatenated vertices for all slices. 4. Offset Array (offsetslength): Type: Array of tuples [offset, length]. offset: Byte offset in the vertex buffer (multiplied by 4 for Float32 alignment). length: Number of vertices for that specific slice. 1. Initialization: Load 3D volume data into tex3D. Load transfer function into tex1D. Define volume bounds: x{bound} = res.x, y{bound} = res.y, z{bound} = res.z. Define the 8 corners of the volume bounding box in local coordinates: corner[8][3] = \left\{ \pm \frac{x{bound}}{2}, \pm \frac{y{bound}}{2}, \pm \frac{z{bound}}{2} \right\}. 2. Geometry Generation (Per Frame): Calculate the distance d from the eye to the origin along the view normal (z-axis of the view matrix mtx): d = mtx[2] \cdot eyePos[0] + mtx[6] \cdot eyePos[1] + mtx[10] \cdot eyePos[2]. Find the furthest and nearest intersection distances by iterating over the 8 corners: distancei = \left| -mtx[2] \cdot corner[i][0] - mtx[6] \cdot corner[i][1] - mtx[10] \cdot corner[i][2] + d \right|. nearest = \min(distancei) furthest = \max(distancei) Calculate the step size (slice thickness): \delta D = \frac{furthest - nearest}{sampleRate}. Calculate the billboard size (diagonal of the bounding box): size = 2 \cdot \sqrt{x{bound}^2 + y{bound}^2 + z{bound}^2}. Generate slice geometry: Loop from i = furthest down to nearest with step \delta D (back-to-front order). Calculate billboard center: billboardCenter[x] = eyePos[x] + i \cdot (-mtx[3x]) \quad \text{for } x=0,1,2 Using mtx[2], mtx[6], mtx[10] for the view direction components. Construct a polygon primitive (triangle fan or quad) centered at billboardCenter with size. Assign 3D texture coordinates to vertices. The coordinates map the unit quad to the volume bounds. In some implementations, a rotation matrix transforms texture coordinates in the vertex shader to align with the view, keeping the slice geometry stationary while changing the texture content. Store vertices in aposition and record [offset, length] in offsetslength. 3. Rendering: Enable blending: python glEnable(GLBLEND) glBlendFunc(GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). Bind vertex buffer and enable vertex attribute array for aposition. Iterate through offsetslength: Set vertex pointer: python glVertexAttribPointer( location, size=3, type=GLFLOAT, normalize=False, stride=0, offset=offset 4). Draw slice: python glDrawArrays(GLTRIANGLES, 0, length). Fragment Shader: Sample tex3D at interpolated 3D texture coordinates to get scalar value. Map scalar value to color and opacity using tex1D (transfer function). Composite using alpha blending. numberOfSlices / sampleRate: Determines the number of slices. Higher values increase quality but reduce performance. nearClip, farClip: Orthographic projection planes (default 200.0, 600.0). viewBound: Half-width of the orthographic projection box (default 50). boundary: Integer flag for shader boundary checks (default 0). Texture Artifacts: Using GLCLAMPTOBORDER is critical when transforming texture coordinates to avoid sampling artifacts at slice edges. Index Wrapping: When constructing triangles from slice vertices, ensure the index for the third vertex wraps correctly (e.g., to index 1) if k + 1 exceeds the array length to form closed polygons. View Alignment: The proxy geometry must be strictly view-aligned to ensure samples can be correctly read from the frame buffer if post-processing or compositing relies on buffer reads. Performance: Geometry regeneration every frame is computationally expensive. The number of slices is often automatically reduced during rotation to maintain interactive rates. Object-aligned slicing divides the volume into slices along the principal axes (x, y, z) rather than the view direction. It uses three stacks of 2D textures corresponding to these directions. The active stack is swapped based on the viewpoint's closest principal direction. It is faster and simpler but suffers from 3x memory consumption, data replication, image popping artifacts during stack swaps, and inconsistent sampling distances as the camera moves. Arbitrary slicing uses a plane as proxy geometry to sample arbitrary planes for removing depth complexity and exploring volumes. The plane is view-aligned (rotated to be parallel to the image plane) and rendered to the back buffer. Results can be displayed in a separate viewport or as a textured polygon in object space. This allows for interactive probing and slicing without regenerating the full volume geometry. R-GC is a volume slicing strategy where parallel cutting planes are oriented perpendicular to the straight line connecting the point of reflection to the gravity center of the volume domain. It is used to generate Layered Polygonal Area Lights (LPALs) for indirect illumination. Compared to Ray-of-Regular-Reflection (R-RR) slicing, R-GC ensures LPALs face properly to the point of reflection regardless of the regular reflection direction, correctly rendering the upper part of the reflected appearance when the reflection point is apart from the volume. This variant implements view-aligned slicing on the GPU with pre-integration. It uses two levels of pre-integration: simplified (neglecting color attenuation, faster) for interactive transfer function editing, and full pre-integration for final rendering. Volume shading can be enabled using a per-fragment Phong lighting model based on the gradient of the scalar field. The number of slices is automatically reduced during rotation to guarantee interactive rates. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of slices and S is the number of fragments per slice (proportional to screen resolution). Geometry generation is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D volume texture, where V is the volume resolution. Object-aligned variants use 3 \times memory. Performance: Interactive rates are achievable with moderate slice counts. Performance degrades if slice count is too high or if geometry regeneration is not optimized. Strengths: Consistent sampling distance, minimal aliasing artifacts compared to object-aligned methods, efficient use of GPU rasterization. Limitations: Requires geometry regeneration every frame (CPU-GPU communication overhead), less flexible than ray casting for complex lighting effects without additional passes. When to use: Interactive volume visualization where view alignment is critical for quality and performance is acceptable. When not to use: When extreme lighting complexity (e.g., accurate indirect illumination) is required without additional techniques, or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained. View-aligned slicing emerged as a method to combine the quality of ray casting with the speed of rasterization. It was notably implemented in systems like "Scientific-visualization-Slicing-volume-rendering" and "SliceBasedVolumeRendering". The technique is discussed in the context of proxy geometry for interactive volume visualization and in implementations of pre-integrated volume rendering. It addresses the limitations of object-aligned slicing, such as popping artifacts and inconsistent sampling. name: Object-Aligned Slicing
head: Object-Aligned Slices, Three-Stack Slicing
body: Object-Aligned Slicing is a proxy geometry method for direct volume ray casting that renders 3D voxel data by projecting pre-defined planar slices aligned with the world axes. It solves the problem of efficient GPU-based volume rendering by avoiding per-ray intersection calculations, instead relying on fixed texture coordinates assigned to slice vertices. It is distinguished from its parent View-Aligned Slicing by its simplicity and speed, but suffers from higher memory consumption and visual artifacts due to inconsistent sampling distances and stack swapping. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D voxel data (volume texture). Output: 2D rendered image. Data Structures: Three stacks of 2D textures, corresponding to the X, Y, and Z principal directions of the volume. Each stack contains slices perpendicular to the respective axis. The 3D voxel data is replicated into these three sets of 2D textures. Steps: 1. Texture Preparation: Create three stacks of 2D textures from the 3D voxel data. One stack represents slices along the X-axis, one along the Y-axis, and one along the Z-axis. 2. Viewpoint Analysis: Determine the viewpoint's closest principal direction (the axis with the smallest angle to the view vector). 3. Stack Selection: Swap the active texture stack to the one corresponding to the closest principal direction. If the view direction changes significantly, the stack is swapped. 4. Rendering: For each slice in the selected stack: Intersect the slice plane with the view frustum or bounding box. Assign texture coordinates to the slice vertices. The texture coordinates are derived from the position of the slice in the volume, mapped to the 2D texture space. Render the slice as a textured quad (or triangle fan) using the GPU. Accumulate the color and opacity using alpha blending, sorting slices by distance from the camera to handle transparency correctly. Formulas: Texture coordinate assignment: For a slice at position p along the normal axis, the texture coordinates (u, v) for a vertex at position \mathbf{x} are calculated based on the projection of \mathbf{x} onto the slice plane, normalized to the texture dimensions. Sorting: Slices are sorted by their distance from the camera: di = \mathbf{v}i \cdot \mathbf{c}, where \mathbf{v}i is the slice center and \mathbf{c} is the camera position. Parameters: Number of slices per stack: Determined by the volume resolution along each axis. Sampling distance: Fixed per stack, but varies between stacks. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Image Popping: Swapping texture stacks can cause visible artifacts if not handled smoothly. Lag: Downloading new textures during stack swaps can cause performance lag. Intensity Variations: Sampling distance changes with viewpoint, leading to intensity variations as the camera moves. Memory Consumption: Requires 3x memory for storing the volume data in three orientations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderobjectaligned(volumedata, camera): # Create three stacks of 2D textures stackx = create2dstacks(volumedata, axis='x') stacky = create2dstacks(volumedata, axis='y') stackz = create2dstacks(volumedata, axis='z') # Determine closest principal direction viewvector = camera.direction # Calculate angles with axes anglex = abs(dot(viewvector, [1, 0, 0])) angley = abs(dot(viewvector, [0, 1, 0])) anglez = abs(dot(viewvector, [0, 0, 1])) # Select stack based on closest direction (smallest angle) if anglex >= angley and anglex >= anglez: activestack = stackx elif angley >= anglex and angley >= anglez: activestack = stacky else: activestack = stackz # Sort slices by distance from camera sortedslices = sortslicesbydistance(activestack, camera.position) # Render slices for slice in sortedslices: # Assign texture coordinates u, v = assigntexturecoordinates(slice, volumedata.dimensions) # Render slice as textured quad renderquad(slice.vertices, u, v, slice.texture) SlicingBlockRenderer is a slice-based direct volume rendering method that organizes volume data into subvolumes (blocks) and renders them as textured quads (slices) sorted by distance from the camera to handle transparency correctly. It builds on Object-Aligned Slicing by introducing explicit blocking to improve memory locality and culling efficiency, distinguishing itself from non-blocking slice renderers by managing discrete GPU resources per block. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of slices and the cost of texture sampling. Stack swapping adds overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires 3x the memory of the original volume data due to replication along three axes. Performance: Fast and simple to implement. However, performance can degrade due to texture swapping and memory bandwidth limitations. Strengths: Simple implementation, fast rendering speed for static views. Limitations: High memory usage, visual artifacts during stack swaps, inconsistent sampling distances leading to intensity variations. When to Use: Suitable for applications where memory is not a constraint and view changes are infrequent or can be smoothed. When Not to Use: Not suitable for interactive applications with frequent view changes or memory-constrained environments. It is discussed in the context of proxy geometry methods for volume rendering. name: SlicingBlockRenderer
head: Slice-based direct volume renderer with subvolume blocking
body: SlicingBlockRenderer is a slice-based direct volume rendering method that organizes volume data into subvolumes (blocks) and renders them as textured quads (slices) sorted by distance from the camera to handle transparency correctly. It builds on Object-Aligned Slicing by introducing explicit blocking to improve memory locality and culling efficiency, distinguishing itself from non-blocking slice renderers by managing discrete GPU resources per block. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data partitioned into blocks (subvolumes), camera position and view direction, transfer function parameters. Output: Rendered image with correct alpha blending. Data Structures: Block: Represents a subvolume. Contains a status flag GPURES indicating if texture data is uploaded to the GPU. Vertex Buffer: A single buffer containing geometry for all possible slice orientations. Layout: 6 sets of quads corresponding to 3 axes (YZ, XZ, XY) and 2 viewing directions (positive/negative) per axis. Each set contains numSlices slices. Each slice is a quad (4 vertices). Total vertices = 6 \times \text{numSlices} \times 4. Indices are structured to draw these quads sequentially. Sampler: Configured with linear min/mag filtering and clamp-to-border wrapping for S, T, and R axes. Bound to BLOCKTEXTUREUNIT. Parameters: mtfuncScaleValue: Scale factor for the transfer function. Default: 1.0. Passed to shader uniform VOLUMETRANSFSCALERUNIFORMSTR. mshouldUseLighting: Boolean flag to toggle lighting. Default: false. mdrawNonEmptySlices: Boolean flag to toggle slice rendering. Default: true. mdrawNonEmptyBoundingBoxes: Boolean flag to toggle bounding box rendering. Default: false. Numbered Steps: 1. Sampler Setup: Create a sampler object with linear min/mag filtering and clamp-to-border wrapping for S, T, and R axes. Bind it to BLOCKTEXTUREUNIT. 2. Block Sorting: In the draw loop, identify non-empty blocks. Sort these blocks by distance from the camera eye in descending order (furthest first) to satisfy the painters algorithm for transparency. 3. View Axis Determination: Compute the base vertex and element offset for the vertex buffer based on the view direction. Determine the axis with the largest absolute component in the view vector to select the slice set (YZ, XZ, or XY). Determine if viewing in the positive or negative direction to select the correct vertex range within that set. 4. Rendering Loop: For each non-empty block in the sorted list: Check if the block's status includes GPURES. If not, skip the block. Set the world matrix for the block. Bind the block's texture to BLOCKTEXTUREUNIT. Set the MVP matrix uniform. Draw the slices using glDrawElementsBaseVertex with the computed base vertex and element offset. Formulas: Let N be the number of slices along the viewing axis (numSlicesPerBlock). Let V{quad} = 4 be the vertices per quad. The base vertex index for the vertex buffer is calculated as follows: View along X (YZ slices): Positive X: BaseVertex = 0 Negative X: BaseVertex = 1 \times V{quad} \times N View along Y (XZ slices): Positive Y: BaseVertex = 2 \times V{quad} \times N Negative Y: BaseVertex = 3 \times V{quad} \times N View along Z (XY slices): Positive Z: BaseVertex = 4 \times V{quad} \times N Negative Z: BaseVertex = 5 \times V{quad} \times N Where N is numSlicesPerBlock.x for X-view,.y for Y-view, and.z for Z-view. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderslicingblockrenderer(blocks, camera, viewvector, vertexbuffer, indexbuffer, sampler, shader): # 1. Setup Sampler (Assumed done once during init, but conceptually part of state) # sampler.minfilter = LINEAR # sampler.magfilter = LINEAR # sampler.wraps = CLAMPTOBORDER # sampler.wrapt = CLAMPTOBORDER # sampler.wrapr = CLAMPTOBORDER # bindsampler(sampler, BLOCKTEXTUREUNIT) # 2. Sort Blocks # Calculate distance from camera eye to block origin sortedblocks = sorted(blocks, key=lambda b: distance(camera.eye, b.origin), reverse=True) # 3. Determine View Axis and Base Vertex absx = abs(viewvector.x) absy = abs(viewvector.y) absz = abs(viewvector.z) # Determine dominant axis if absx >= absy and absx >= absz: axis = 'X' ispos = viewvector.x > 0 elif absy >= absx and absy >= absz: axis = 'Y' ispos = viewvector.y > 0 else: axis = 'Z' ispos = viewvector.z > 0 # Get number of slices along the viewing axis for a block # Note: numSlicesPerBlock might vary per block or be uniform; assuming uniform for base calculation logic in source # If uniform, use global numSlicesPerBlock. If not, this base vertex logic applies per block's specific N. # The source implies a single vertex buffer layout for all blocks, so N is likely fixed per block type or global. # We assume N is available as numSlicesPerBlock[axis] N = numSlicesPerBlock[axis] Vquad = 4 if axis == 'X': basevertex = 0 if ispos else 1 Vquad N elif axis == 'Y': basevertex = 2 Vquad N if ispos else 3 Vquad N else: # axis == 'Z' basevertex = 4 Vquad N if ispos else 5 Vquad N # 4. Render Loop for block in sortedblocks: # Check GPU resource status if not (block.status & GPURES): continue # Set World Matrix shader.setuniform('WORLDMATRIX', block.worldmatrix) # Bind Texture bindtexture(block.texture, BLOCKTEXTUREUNIT) # Set MVP Matrix shader.setuniform('MVPMATRIX', camera.mvpmatrix block.worldmatrix) # Set Transfer Function Scale shader.setuniform('VOLUMETRANSFSCALERUNIFORMSTR', mtfuncScaleValue) # Draw Slices # glDrawElementsBaseVertex uses indexbuffer, count, type, basevertex drawelementsbasevertex(indexbuffer, count=totalindicesforslices, type=UNSIGNEDINT, basevertex=basevertex) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transparency Sorting: Blocks must be sorted from furthest to nearest relative to the camera to ensure correct blending order. Failure to sort results in incorrect transparency artifacts. Resource Availability: Slices are only drawn if the block's status includes GPURES. This ensures texture data is uploaded before rendering. Skipping this check may cause rendering errors or crashes if texture is not bound. Precision: The base vertex calculation relies on integer arithmetic. Ensure numSlices and vertex counts fit within the index buffer type limits. Time Complexity: Sorting blocks takes O(B \log B) where B is the number of blocks. Rendering is proportional to the number of non-empty blocks and slices. Memory Complexity: Requires storing vertex/index buffers for all slice orientations and texture data for each block. The vertex buffer size is fixed based on the maximum number of slices per block. Performance: Performance depends on the number of blocks, texture upload bandwidth, and sorting overhead. Efficient culling of empty blocks improves performance. Strengths: Good memory locality due to blocking. Efficient culling of empty blocks. Simple geometry (quads) allows for fast rasterization. Limitations: Sorting overhead for large numbers of blocks. Texture memory usage scales with the number of blocks. When to Use: Suitable for large volume datasets where blocking improves cache performance and culling is beneficial. When Not to Use: When the number of blocks is small, the sorting overhead may not be justified. When real-time performance is critical and sorting is a bottleneck. name: VoxelBlur Depth-of-Field Volume Rendering
head: Depth of Field Effects for Interactive Direct Volume Rendering implementation
body: VoxelBlur is an interactive direct volume rendering method that provides a depth-of-field effect by selectively blurring voxels based on their distance from a predefined focus plane, simulating real-world camera lens systems. It extends the view-aligned slicing technique by splitting the rendering pipeline into front-to-back and back-to-front passes, each maintaining an intermediate buffer where blur is applied during compositing. Unlike standard back-to-front blending which relies on native GPU blending, VoxelBlur uses custom shader-based blending to enable the blur effect, allowing users to enhance depth perception and separate focus from context. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume data (8 or 16-bit integers), camera parameters (position, orientation, focal plane, strength), and a focus plane definition. Output: A 2D image with depth-of-field blur effects. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored in 3D textures. Supports arbitrary dimensions, byte skipping, and gzip-compressed raw data via a custom metadata format. Intermediate Buffers: Two framebuffer objects (FBOs) are used: one for the front slices (front-to-back) and one for the back slices (back-to-front). Circle of Confusion (CoC): A radius value derived from camera parameters and distance to the focal plane, transformed into clip-space for sampling. Preprocessing: 1. Load volume data into a 3D texture. 2. Apply 3D Gaussian convolution using a compute shader to reduce noise and smooth surfaces. 3. Calculate gradients using another compute shader and optionally rescale data to [0, 1] range. Rendering Steps: 1. Slice Generation: Intersect several view-aligned planes with the volume's bounding box to create polygons. 2. Tessellation: Tessellate polygons into triangles. 3. Splitting: Divide slices into two sets: those in front of the focal plane and those behind it. 4. Front Pass: Process front slices in front-to-back order. For each slice, render the slice to the front intermediate buffer. Sample the previous content of the front intermediate buffer with blur (using 4 samples on the CoC radius) and combine with the current slice using custom blending. 5. Back Pass: Process back slices in back-to-front order. For each slice, render the slice to the back intermediate buffer. Sample the previous content of the back intermediate buffer with blur (using 4 samples on the CoC radius) and combine with the current slice using custom blending. 6. Final Compositing: Combine the two intermediate buffers to produce the final output image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelblurrender(volumetexture, cameraparams, focusplane, strength): # Preprocessing smoothedvolume = gaussianconvolution3d(volumetexture) gradients = calculategradients(smoothedvolume) rescaledvolume = rescaleto01(smoothedvolume, gradients) # Setup intermediate buffers frontbuffer = createfbo() backbuffer = createfbo() # Generate slices slices = generateviewalignedslices(rescaledvolume, cameraparams) # Split slices frontslices = [s for s in slices if s.distancetofocusplane < 0] backslices = [s for s in slices if s.distancetofocusplane >= 0] # Sort front slices front-to-back frontslices.sort(key=lambda s: s.distancetocamera) # Sort back slices back-to-front backslices.sort(key=lambda s: -s.distancetocamera) # Front pass for slice in frontslices: renderslicetofbo(slice, frontbuffer, rescaledvolume, gradients) cocradius = calculatecocradius(slice, focusplane, cameraparams, strength) clipspacecoc = transformtoclipspace(cocradius, cameraparams) blurredprev = samplewithblur(frontbuffer, clipspacecoc, numsamples=4) compositewithblur(frontbuffer, blurredprev) # Back pass for slice in backslices: renderslicetofbo(slice, backbuffer, rescaledvolume, gradients) cocradius = calculatecocradius(slice, focusplane, cameraparams, strength) clipspacecoc = transformtoclipspace(cocradius, cameraparams) blurredprev = samplewithblur(backbuffer, clipspacecoc, numsamples=4) compositewithblur(backbuffer, blurredprev) # Final compositing finalimage = combinebuffers(frontbuffer, backbuffer) return finalimage def gaussianconvolution3d(volume): # Apply standard 3D Gaussian blur kernel to volume return volume # Kernel convolution omitted def calculategradients(volume): # Compute volume gradients using central finite differences return volume # Gradient computation omitted def rescaleto01(volume, gradients): # Normalize volume data to [0, 1] range return volume # Min-max normalization omitted def createfbo(): # Allocate 2D framebuffer object buffer return [] def generateviewalignedslices(volume, camera): # Intersect view-aligned planes with volume bounding box to form polygons return [] def renderslicetofbo(slice, buffer, volume, gradients): # Evaluate volume along slice, apply Blinn-Phong shading using gradient normals pass def calculatecocradius(slice, focusplane, camera, strength): # Compute blur radius proportional to distance from focus plane scaled by strength return abs(slice.distancetofocusplane) strength def transformtoclipspace(radius, camera): # Scale radius to clip-space coordinates return radius camera.aspectratio def getsampleoffset(index, clipspacecoc): # Generate 4 sample points on the circle of confusion import math angle = index math.pi / 2 return (clipspacecoc math.cos(angle), clipspacecoc math.sin(angle)) def samplewithblur(buffer, clipspacecoc, numsamples=4): # Sample previous buffer at multiple points around original point samples = [] for i in range(numsamples): offset = getsampleoffset(i, clipspacecoc) samples.append(buffer.sample(offset)) return average(samples) def average(samples): return sum(samples) / len(samples) def compositewithblur(buffer, blurredprev): # Apply custom blending shader to combine current slice with blurred previous buffer buffer.blend(blurredprev) def combinebuffers(front, back): # Merge front and back intermediate buffers into final output return front.merge(back) Parameters: Strength: User-defined parameter governing the increase of blurring with distance. Focus Plane: Predefined plane in the scene, adjustable via UI. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: FTB Compositing: Requires custom blending method and shader support, unlike native GPU blending for back-to-front compositing. Manual Sync: Manual synchronization for data upload of each slice is used to increase GPU asynchronous performance. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tested on Windows 7 64-bit with AMD HD 5850 graphics card. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enhances depth perception, separates focus from context, interactive performance. Limitations: Requires custom blending for FTB compositing, limited to OpenGL 3.3 core profile + compute shaders. When to Use: When depth-of-field effect is desired for interactive volume rendering. When Not to Use: When native GPU blending is required or when hardware does not support compute shaders. VoxelBlur was developed by Schott et al. as an interactive direct volume rendering program. It is based on the slicing volume rendering method, which uses view-aligned planes intersected with the volume's bounding box. The depth-of-field effect was introduced to enhance depth perception and separate focus from context. The implementation uses OpenGL 3.3 core profile and compute shaders for preprocessing. name: WebGL Volume Ray Casting (Slice Tiling)
head: 2D slice tiling volume rendering, Volume Ray Casting in WebGL
body: WebGL Volume Ray Casting (Slice Tiling) is a direct volume rendering method adapted for web browsers that replaces native 3D volume textures with a 2D tiling map of volume slices to simulate 3D data while preserving tri-linear interpolation. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric data in environments lacking hardware support for 3D textures, such as early WebGL implementations. Unlike server-side rendering approaches that offload computation to a backend, this method runs entirely on the client side, leveraging the GPU's accelerated graphics pipeline while avoiding server-side rendering overhead. The method builds on Direct volume ray casting but modifies the data structure and sampling mechanism to accommodate WebGL's texture limitations. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V of dimensions W \times H \times D. A 2D tiling map texture T{tile} constructed from the slices of V. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). Output: A 2D image buffer containing the composited color \mathbf{C}{out} and opacity \alpha{out} for each pixel. Data Structures 1. 2D Tiling Map (T{tile}): A 2D texture where the volume slices are arranged in a grid. If the volume has D slices of size W \times H, the tiling map dimensions are typically W \times (H \times D) or (W \times D) \times H, depending on the packing strategy. The source notes do not specify the exact packing layout (e.g., row-major vs. column-major), but it must allow tri-linear interpolation across slice boundaries. 2. Ray Parameters: For each pixel, the entry t{near} and exit t{far} parameters of the ray intersecting the volume bounding box. Numbered Steps 1. Construct Tiling Map: Flatten the 3D volume dataset into a 2D texture by arranging all slices sequentially. This creates a single 2D texture object that represents the entire volume. 2. Ray Definition: For each pixel (x, y), compute the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and determine the intersection interval [t{near}, t{far}] with the volume bounding box. 3. Discretization: Divide the interval [t{near}, t{far}] into S steps, where S is the number of steps of the ray that traverses the volume. The step size is \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / S. 4. Sampling via Tiling Map: For each sample position \mathbf{p}i = r(t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t), map the 3D coordinate to the 2D tiling map texture coordinates. Perform tri-linear interpolation on the 2D texture to retrieve the scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i), simulating the 3D texture lookup. 5. Classification: Map the sampled value V(\mathbf{p}i) to color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai using the transfer function. 6. Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity using the front-to-back volume rendering equation. Formulas The complexity of the algorithm is defined as: O(M \times S) where M is the number of pixels to be drawn (resolution width \times height) and S is the number of steps of the ray that traverses the volume. The sampling position \mathbf{p}i is calculated as: \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + (t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t) \cdot \mathbf{d}, \quad i \in [0, S-1] The tri-linear interpolation on the 2D tiling map T{tile} approximates the 3D texture lookup V(\mathbf{p}i). Parameters M: Number of pixels to be drawn. Typical resolutions tested: 512px, 1024px, 2048px, 4096px. S: Number of ray steps. Typical values tested: 30, 80, 140, 200. Pitfalls and Edge Cases Shader Compilation Limits: Browser shader compilers may fail to compile larger shader programs due to inadequate or restricted shader language implementations. Interpolation Overhead: The use of 2D slice tiling introduces a slight interpolation overhead compared to native 3D textures, though it is minimal and imperceptible in browser environments. Performance Bottlenecks: Performance is heavily dependent on browser layers, including shader compilers, hardware architecture, and graphic drivers. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderwebglvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds, ttile, transferfunction, numsteps): # Determine ray intersection with volume bounding box tnear, tfar = intersectraybox(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) if tnear > tfar: return backgroundcolor stepsize = (tfar - tnear) / numsteps acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 for i in range(numsteps): t = tnear + i stepsize p = rayorigin + raydirection t # Map 3D point to 2D tiling map coordinates u, v = getslicecoords(p) # Sample 2D texture with tri-linear interpolation # This simulates 3D texture lookup scalarvalue = sample2dtexturetrilinear(ttile, u, v) # Classification color, alpha = transferfunction(scalarvalue) # Correct opacity for step size (Beer-Lambert) # alpha = 1 - exp(-sigma stepsize) # Assuming transfer function returns alpha already corrected or sigma derived # For simplicity, using provided alpha directly as per source notes # Standard correction: alpha = 1.0 - exp(-alpha stepsize) if alpha is extinction coeff # Front-to-back compositing weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = acccolor + weight color accalpha = accalpha + weight if accalpha > 0.99: break return acccolor A slower, non-WebGL approach that may iterate through slices in software. Choose WebGL Slice Tiling for GPU-accelerated, real-time performance in browsers [1507-2d-visualization-from-3d-grid-slow.md]. Handles multiple volumes. WebGL Slice Tiling is limited to single volume simulation via tiling [2461-gpu-multi-volume-ray-casting-mapper.md]. The general hardware-accelerated approach. WebGL Slice Tiling is a specific adaptation for web constraints [7443-volume-ray-casting-on-graphics-hardware.md]. Time Complexity: O(M \times S), where M is the number of pixels and S is the number of ray steps. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the 2D tiling map, which is O(W \times H \times D) pixels, stored in 2D texture memory. Measured Performance: Achieved approximately 2 to 3 frames per second on Samsung Galaxy Tab and Galaxy S smartphones using the Fennec mobile browser with a half-resolution Aorta dataset. Strengths: Runs entirely in the client browser, avoiding server-side rendering overhead and allowing more simultaneous clients. Uses the same accelerated graphic pipeline as native applications. Limitations: Requires more powerful client hardware. Browser shader compilers may fail to compile larger shader programs. Performance is sensitive to browser implementation details. When to Use: Web-based volume rendering systems for medical (e.g., Aorta) and radar datasets where server-side rendering is not feasible or desirable. When Not to Use: When high frame rates are required on low-end devices, or when native 3D texture support is available (use standard GPU ray casting instead). The method was introduced in a book chapter titled "Volume Ray Casting in WebGL" by John Edgar Congote et al., published in 2012. It was implemented in a web-based volume rendering system for medical (Aorta) and radar datasets, tested on the Mozilla Firefox/Fennec mobile browser. The work demonstrated the possibility of rendering volume datasets on handheld devices using web standard technology, re-igniting interest in visualization functions previously reserved for high-end desktop applications. name: Volume Ray-Casting on Graphics Hardware
head: Stream model for volumetric ray-casting
body: This method implements direct volume ray casting on programmable graphics hardware (specifically DirectX 9-level architectures like the ATI 9700) using a multi-pass stream model. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based volume rendering by exploiting the intrinsic parallelism of fragment processors and efficient inter-pass communication via texture render targets. Unlike single-pass rasterization, this approach iteratively accumulates optical properties across multiple rendering passes, enabling effective early ray termination and empty-space skipping through hardware-supported early z-tests. The method relies on a multi-pass rendering loop where the output of one pass serves as the input for the next. It utilizes specific hardware features available in Pixel Shader 2.0 APIs, including per-fragment texture fetches, texture render targets (allowing floating-point storage), texture coordinate generation, per-fragment arithmetic, and depth replace capabilities. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volumetric scalar data (stored in 3D textures), transfer function parameters, ray direction vectors (pre-computed and stored in 2D textures), and an opacity threshold for termination. Outputs: Final composited color and opacity images stored in 2D texture render targets. Data Structures: 1. Ray Direction Textures: Two 2D textures storing the (u, v) components of the ray direction in local texture space for each pixel. 2. Accumulation Textures: 2D texture render targets storing the accumulated color and accumulated opacity from previous passes. 3. Iso-surface Intersection Texture: A 2D texture used to store the local texture coordinates of iso-surface intersections, if applicable. Numbered Steps: 1. Pre-computation: For each pixel in the image plane, compute the ray direction in local texture coordinates and store these direction vectors in two dedicated 2D textures. 2. Initialization: Initialize the accumulation textures with zero color and zero opacity. 3. Main Ray Casting Passes: Execute a fixed number of rendering passes. In each pass, bind the accumulated color and opacity textures as inputs and bind the ray direction textures. Execute a fragment shader that performs one step of ray traversal: calculate the current sample position using the ray origin, direction, and step size, sample the volume data at the current position, and apply the transfer function to obtain color and opacity. Update the accumulated color and opacity using the front-to-back compositing equations from the parent method, and write the updated values to the output accumulation texture. 4. Termination Check Pass: Between main passes, execute an additional pass to test whether the actual opacity value has exceeded a specified threshold or an iso-surface is hit. If the test succeeds, modify the z-value to the maximum value; otherwise, set it to zero. Use the "Depth Replace" feature to write this arbitrary z value directly to the z-buffer. 5. Early Z-Test Filtering: Configure the depth test to GREATER. Because fragments that triggered termination were set to maximum depth, and the test is GREATER, subsequent main passes will discard these fragments due to the early z-test. 6. Final Output: After all passes, the accumulation textures contain the final composited color and opacity, which can be rendered to the screen or saved. Formulas: The method builds on the parent's shared principles for compositing [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md]. In each main pass, the accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} and opacity \alpha{acc} are updated per fragment as: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai where \mathbf{c}i and \alphai are the color and opacity sampled at the current ray step. Parameters: Opacity Threshold: The value at which ray termination is triggered. Number of Passes: Fixed number of main ray casting passes. Step Size: Determined by the volume resolution and view distance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dependent Texture Fetches: Hardware limitations restrict the number of dependent texture fetches on the ATI, so the method minimizes dynamic texture lookups within the shader. Floating Point Precision: Floating-point textures are available, allowing negative values to be stored. Depth Buffer Clearing: The depth buffer must be cleared appropriately before the termination check pass to ensure the GREATER test functions as intended. Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of pixels and the fixed number of passes, with early termination reducing the effective number of passes for opaque regions. Memory complexity scales with the volume data, ray direction textures, accumulation textures, and intermediate render targets required by the multi-pass nature. Measured performance on an ATI 9700 graphics card demonstrates up to a 3× speedup for typical renditions of volumetric datasets. Strengths include effective integration of early ray termination and empty-space skipping on hardware that supports early z-tests and depth replace, alongside exploitation of fragment processor parallelism. Limitations include reliance on specific hardware features (Pixel Shader 2.0, depth replace, texture render targets), limits on dependent texture fetches, and potential wasted computation from fixed passes if early termination is not properly managed. Use this method when targeting older programmable graphics hardware (DirectX 9 era) for real-time or interactive volume rendering; avoid it on modern hardware with advanced ray tracing capabilities or single-pass optimized ray marching techniques that do not require multi-pass accumulation. This method addresses the challenge of achieving real-time volume rendering for large scalar fields by leveraging the capabilities of programmable graphics hardware available at the time, specifically the ATI 9700 and the Pixel Shader 2.0 API. The approach builds on the observation that CPU-based rendering is insufficient for interactivity with large datasets and exploits the parallel nature of GPU fragment processors. name: Volume Raycasting Pipeline
head: Direct Volume Raycasting Pipeline, Image-Order Volume Rendering Pipeline, Raycasting Pipeline
body: The Volume Raycasting Pipeline is the standard procedural framework for direct volume rendering, calculating the volume rendering integral for every viewing ray originating at the image plane and passing through the volume. It advances rays through the volume with regular increments, performing reconstruction, classification, shading, and compositing at each sample location. It is distinguished from its siblings by its explicit separation of these four stages and the critical decision of whether classification and shading occur before or after reconstruction (pre- vs. post-), where post-classification and post-shading are preferred to avoid severe artifacts caused by non-linear reconstruction. The method evaluates the volume rendering integral by advancing rays through the volume with regular increments (the object sample distance). At each resample location along the ray, the pipeline executes four sequential steps: Reconstruction, Classification, Shading, and Compositing. The pipeline supports four variants based on the ordering of Classification and Shading relative to Reconstruction: 1. Pre-classification, Pre-shading; 2. Pre-classification, Post-shading; 3. Post-classification, Pre-shading; 4. Post-classification, Post-shading. The recommended configuration uses Post-classification and Post-shading. Input: A discrete scalar dataset D defined on a 3D grid; a viewing ray R(t) defined by an origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a transfer function T(v) mapping scalar values to color and opacity; an illumination model L(g) mapping gradients to shading parameters. Output: A final color value C{final} for each pixel. Dataset D: A 3D array of scalar values. Layout is implementation-dependent but typically stored in row-major or column-major order. Ray R(t): Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized by distance t. Sample Point: A position \mathbf{p} along the ray where data is sampled. 1. Initialize Ray: For each pixel, generate a viewing ray R(t) originating from the image plane and passing through the volume. 2. Advance Ray: Move along the ray with a regular increment \Delta t (object sample distance). Let the current position be \mathbf{p}. 3. Reconstruction: Construct a continuous function from the discrete dataset D at position \mathbf{p}. If Pre-classification/Pre-shading: Sample the discrete data D at \mathbf{p} to get value v. If Post-classification/Post-shading: Apply a reconstruction filter to the original sample values around \mathbf{p} to estimate the continuous function value v{rec} and gradient g{rec} at \mathbf{p}. 4. Classification: If Pre-classification: Assign color c and opacity \alpha to the sampled value v using transfer function T: (c, \alpha) = T(v). If Post-classification: Classify the reconstructed value v{rec}: (c, \alpha) = T(v{rec}). 5. Shading: If Pre-shading: Evaluate the illumination model L at the grid points only (or use pre-computed shading values). If Post-shading: Reconstruct the gradient g{rec} at \mathbf{p} and evaluate the illumination model L(g{rec}) to determine shading parameters (e.g., diffuse color, specular highlights). 6. Compositing: Determine the contribution of the classified and shaded sample to the final image. This typically involves front-to-back alpha compositing, blending the current sample's color and opacity with the accumulated result from previous samples along the ray. 7. Repeat: Continue steps 2-6 until the ray exits the volume or a termination condition is met. 8. Finalize: Output the accumulated color for the pixel. Discrete Compositing: C{out} = C{in} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot T, T{out} = T \cdot (1 - \alpha), where C is accumulated color, \alpha is sample opacity, c is sample color, and T is current transmittance. Pre-classification: (c, \alpha) = T(D(\mathbf{p})). Post-classification: (c, \alpha) = T(\text{Reconstruct}(D, \mathbf{p})). Pre-shading: L evaluated at grid points. Post-shading: L(\text{ReconstructGradient}(D, \mathbf{p})). Object sample distance (\Delta t): The regular increment for advancing rays. Not given in the sources. Reconstruction filter: The specific filter used to construct the continuous function. Not given in the sources. Transfer function T(v): Maps scalar values to color and opacity. Not given in the sources. Illumination model L(g): Evaluates lighting based on gradients. Not given in the sources. Non-commutativity: Pre-classification and pre-shading cause severe artifacts because reconstruction is usually non-linear and does not commute with transfer functions or lighting models. Precision: Using floating-point precision throughout the pipeline is recommended to minimize artifacts. Boundary Conditions: Ray traversal must handle entry and exit from the volume correctly. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeraycastingpipeline(dataset, origin, direction, stepsize, transferfunction, illuminationmodel, reconstructionfilter, volumebounds): """ Executes the Volume Raycasting Pipeline for a single ray. Args: dataset: 3D array of scalar values. origin: 3D vector (x, y, z) ray origin. direction: 3D vector (x, y, z) ray direction. stepsize: Regular increment for advancing rays (object sample distance). transferfunction: Function mapping scalar value to (color, opacity). illuminationmodel: Function mapping gradient to shading parameters. reconstructionfilter: Function to reconstruct continuous value and gradient from dataset. volumebounds: Tuple (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz). Returns: Final color for the pixel. """ accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 # Calculate entry and exit t values tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < volumebounds[2i] or origin[i] > volumebounds[2i+1]: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Ray misses volume else: t1 = (volumebounds[2i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (volumebounds[2i+1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Ray march through volume t = tmin while t <= tmax: pos = [origin[i] + t direction[i] for i in range(3)] # Step 1: Reconstruction (Post-classification/Post-shading) reconstructedvalue, reconstructedgradient = reconstructionfilter(dataset, pos) # Step 2: Classification color, opacity = transferfunction(reconstructedvalue) # Step 3: Shading shadingparams = illuminationmodel(reconstructedgradient) # Apply shading (simplified diffuse multiplication) shadedcolor = [color[i] shadingparams[i] for i in range(3)] # Step 4: Compositing (Front-to-Back) contribution = [shadedcolor[i] opacity transmittance for i in range(3)] accumulatedcolor = [accumulatedcolor[i] + contribution[i] for i in range(3)] transmittance = transmittance (1.0 - opacity) # Early termination if fully opaque if transmittance < 0.001: break t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor The process of constructing a continuous function from the dataset to allow sampling at arbitrary positions along the ray. It is fundamental to post-classification and post-shading. The process of assigning color and opacity to data values using a transfer function. Post-classification is preferred to avoid artifacts from non-linear reconstruction. The evaluation of the illumination model. Post-shading reconstructs gradients at every resample location for better visual quality. The process of blending sample contributions into the final image. Typically uses front-to-back alpha compositing. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays (pixels). Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Depends on the dataset size and the storage of intermediate values per sample. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Flexible pipeline allowing different combinations of classification and shading orders; post-classification and post-shading provide high visual quality. Limitations: Pre-classification and pre-shading cause severe artifacts. Performance can be high due to per-sample reconstruction and shading calculations. When to use: When high-quality volume rendering is required and computational resources allow for post-classification and post-shading. When not to use: When performance is critical and visual artifacts from pre-classification/pre-shading are acceptable, or when the reconstruction filter is not available. The Volume Raycasting Pipeline framework was described in a master's thesis titled "The Raycasting Pipeline". The work compares four variants of the pipeline based on the ordering of classification and shading relative to reconstruction, demonstrating that post-classification and post-shading yield the best results. name: Cutting Plane Integration
head: CuttingPlaneRender, Interactive Cutting Plane
body: Cutting Plane Integration is an interactive volume rendering technique that dynamically slices a 3D dataset using a semi-transparent geometric plane to reveal internal structures. It builds on Direct volume ray casting by modifying the ray traversal and compositing stages to respect the cutting plane boundary. The method integrates a cutting plane into the ray casting loop. The plane is defined by a position and orientation, and optionally a near-clip constraint. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data V, camera parameters (\mathbf{o}, \mathbf{d}), transfer function T, cutting plane definition (position \mathbf{g}0, normal \mathbf{n}, rotation angles), and near-clip plane definition (optional). Output: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. Data Structures: Volume: 3D grid of scalar values. Cutting Plane: Defined by a world-space point \mathbf{g}0 and normal vector \mathbf{n}. The position is mapped from a normalized height parameter h \in [0, 1]. Ray State: Current position \mathbf{p}, accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc}, accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize Ray: For each pixel, define ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and intersect with the volume bounding box to find entry t{near} and exit t{far}. 2. Define Cutting Plane: Map normalized height h to world Z position: z{plane} = 200 - 400 \cdot h. Apply rotation: convert degrees to radians and add a \pi radian offset to the Y-rotation if renderAbove is true. The plane equation is \mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{g}0) = 0. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to N-1: Calculate sample position \mathbf{p}i = \mathbf{o} + ti \mathbf{d}. Cutting Plane Check: Let \mathbf{g}{in} = \mathbf{p}i and \mathbf{g}{out} = \mathbf{p}{i+1} in world space. If (\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{g}{in} - \mathbf{g}0)) and (\mathbf{n} \cdot (\mathbf{g}{out} - \mathbf{g}0)) have opposite signs, the ray intersects the plane. Calculate the exact intersection point \mathbf{g}^ using linear interpolation. Find the corresponding volume-space point \mathbf{p}^ by solving \phi(\mathbf{p}^) - \mathbf{g}^ = 0 using a root-finding algorithm. Near-Clip Plane Check (Optional): If defined, count ray-surface intersections; an odd count indicates the near plane is inside the volume. Sampling: Retrieve V(\mathbf{p}i) and compute \mathbf{c}i, \alphai using the transfer function. Compositing: Update accumulators: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai 4. Output: Set \mathbf{C}{out} = \mathbf{C}{acc}, \alpha{out} = \alpha{acc}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cuttingplaneintegration(volumedata, volumebounds, cameraorigin, cameradir, planeheight, planerotx, planeroty, renderabove, transferfn, numsamples): # 1. Define cutting plane geometry zplane = 200.0 - 400.0 planeheight g0 = [0.0, 0.0, zplane] n = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Apply rotation around X axis cosx, sinx = math.cos(planerotx), math.sin(planerotx) n = [n[0], n[1]cosx - n[2]sinx, n[1]sinx + n[2]cosx] # Apply rotation around Y axis roty = planeroty if renderabove: roty += math.pi cosy, siny = math.cos(roty), math.sin(roty) n = [n[0]cosy + n[2]siny, n[1], -n[0]siny + n[2]cosy] # Normalize normal norm = math.sqrt(n[0]2 + n[1]2 + n[2]2) n = [n[0]/norm, n[1]/norm, n[2]/norm] # 2. Ray casting loop cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] aacc = 0.0 # Intersect ray with volume bounding box tnear, tfar = intersectaabb(cameraorigin, cameradir, volumebounds) if tnear > tfar: return cacc, aacc dt = (tfar - tnear) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = tnear + i dt pcurr = [cameraorigin[j] + cameradir[j] t for j in range(3)] tnext = t + dt pnext = [cameraorigin[j] + cameradir[j] tnext for j in range(3)] # Cutting plane check valcurr = n[0](pcurr[0]-g0[0]) + n[1](pcurr[1]-g0[1]) + n[2](pcurr[2]-g0[2]) valnext = n[0](pnext[0]-g0[0]) + n[1](pnext[1]-g0[1]) + n[2](pnext[2]-g0[2]) if valcurr valnext < 0: # Intersection found, clip ray at intersection tint = t + dt (valcurr / (valcurr - valnext)) tfar = tint break # Sample volume (standard trilinear interpolation) vval = samplevolume(volumedata, volumebounds, pcurr) color, alpha = transferfn(vval) # Compositing cacc = [cacc[j] + (1.0 - aacc) color[j] alpha for j in range(3)] aacc = aacc + (1.0 - aacc) alpha return cacc, aacc def intersectaabb(origin, direction, bounds): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds[i2] or origin[i] > bounds[i2+1]: return float('inf'), float('-inf') else: t1 = (bounds[i2] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds[i2+1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < tmin: return float('inf'), float('-inf') return tmin, tmax def samplevolume(data, bounds, point): # Maps point to voxel coordinates and performs trilinear interpolation return 0.5 Parameters: planeHeight: Normalized float [0, 1] mapping to the Z-axis position. planeRotX, planeRotY: Rotation angles in degrees around the X and Y axes. renderAbove: Boolean flag that flips the plane 180° around Y when true. Edge Cases: Precision: Root finding for near-clip planes requires careful initialization (e.g., x0 = p{in} + \epsilon \frac{p{out} - p{in}}{\|p{out} - p{in}\|{L2}}) to ensure convergence. Boundaries: Large pixel frustums may cause ray-surface intersections at block boundaries; root finding methods remain pixel-accurate in these cases. Region of Interest (ROI) rendering is a technique to visualize internal features by defining a specific region and rendering only that portion of the dataset. It solves the problem where full opacity is obtained before reaching internal structures of interest, such as seeds within pulp, by isolating the target volume. Unlike standard clipping which often uses global planes, ROI rendering supports arbitrary geometric envelopes, masks, and intensity-based automatic detection. This variant uses a root-finding based method to realize cutting planes and near-clip planes during volume rendering compositing. For near-clip planes, since rendering is water-tight, an odd number of ray-surface intersections indicates the near plane is inside the volume. The intersection point g^ \in G is determined using trivial formulas, and the corresponding point p^ \in P is found by solving \phi(p^) - g^ = 0 using a root-finding algorithm (e.g., Newton-Raphson). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray N and the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the volume size for storage. Strengths: Real-time interactivity and simple plane intersection test. Limitations: Limited to planar cuts; root finding requires proper initialization. The theoretical basis for pixel-accurate cutting and near-clipping using root-finding methods is described in research on isogeometric volume visualization. Implementation details regarding normalized height mapping and interactive plane manipulation are documented in unofficial projects. name: Region of Interest (ROI) Rendering
head: Clipping in Volume Rendering, ROI Rendering, Region of Interest (ROI) Mode, Sub-volume Rendering
body: Region of Interest (ROI) rendering is a technique to visualize internal features by defining a specific region and rendering only that portion of the dataset. It solves the problem where full opacity is obtained before reaching internal structures of interest, such as seeds within pulp, by isolating the target volume. Unlike standard clipping which often uses global planes, ROI rendering supports arbitrary geometric envelopes, masks, and intensity-based automatic detection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset V, Region of Interest definition (geometric primitives, mask volume, or Point of Interest), rendering parameters (transfer function, ray step size). Output: Rendered image containing only the voxels within the defined ROI. Data Structures: Geometric ROI: Defined by camera near/far clipping planes, six orthographic clipping planes (rectangular subvolume), arbitrarily oriented half-space clipping planes, or closed geometric objects. Mask ROI: Auxiliary binary volume M where values indicate inclusion/exclusion. Intensity ROI: Defined by a Point of Interest (POI) and a radius R derived from intensity thresholds along cast rays. Steps: 1. Define ROI: Select one of the methods above. 2. Ray Clipping (Image-Order): For each pixel, generate a ray r(t) = O + tD. Clip the ray against all geometric region definitions as a preprocessing step. Determine the valid interval [t{start}, t{end}] where the ray intersects the ROI. If no intersection, skip the ray. 3. Sample Evaluation: Evaluate the ray function only along segments of the ray that are within the region of interest. For each sample point p along the ray: If using a mask volume M, consult M(p) to determine if its contribution should be included or excluded. If using geometric clipping, check if p is inside the defined geometry. If using intensity-based ROI, check if distance from POI \le R and intensity conditions are met. 4. Compositing: Accumulate color and opacity for samples that pass the ROI check. For object-order methods, determine for each sample whether it is within the region of interest before incorporating its contribution into the image. If the underlying graphics hardware is being utilized for the object-order volume rendering as is the case with a texture mapping approach, hardware clipping planes may be available to help support regions of interest. Pseudocode (Image-Order with Mask/Geometry): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderroi(volumedata, volumedims, maskdata, roiplanes, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, transferfunction): # Convert ray to volume coordinates [0,1]^3 invdims = [1.0 / d for d in volumedims] volorigin = [rayorigin[i] invdims[i] for i in range(3)] voldir = [raydirection[i] invdims[i] for i in range(3)] volstep = stepsize invdims[0] # Normalize step to volume units # Intersect ray with volume bounding box tmin, tmax = 0.0, 0.0 for i in range(3): if abs(voldir[i]) < 1e-6: if volorigin[i] < 0.0 or volorigin[i] > 1.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: t1 = (0.0 - volorigin[i]) / voldir[i] t2 = (1.0 - volorigin[i]) / voldir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Clip against ROI planes if provided tstart, tend = tmin, tmax if roiplanes is not None: for plane in roiplanes: denom = plane.normal[0]voldir[0] + plane.normal[1]voldir[1] + plane.normal[2]voldir[2] if abs(denom) > 1e-6: tclip = (plane.dist - (plane.normal[0]volorigin[0] + plane.normal[1]volorigin[1] + plane.normal[2]volorigin[2])) / denom if denom > 0: tstart = max(tstart, tclip) else: tend = min(tend, tclip) else: if (plane.normal[0]volorigin[0] + plane.normal[1]volorigin[1] + plane.normal[2]volorigin[2]) < plane.dist: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if tstart > tend: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] t = tstart while t <= tend: pos = [volorigin[i] + t voldir[i] for i in range(3)] voxel = volumedata.sampletrilinear(pos) # Check ROI mask if maskdata is not None: maskval = maskdata.sampletrilinear(pos) if maskval <= 0.5: t += volstep continue colorval, alphaval = transferfunction(voxel) color[0] = color[0] + colorval[0] alphaval (1.0 - color[3]) color[1] = color[1] + colorval[1] alphaval (1.0 - color[3]) color[2] = color[2] + colorval[2] alphaval (1.0 - color[3]) color[3] = color[3] + alphaval (1.0 - color[3]) if color[3] >= 0.99: break t += volstep return color Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Clipping boundaries must be handled carefully to avoid gaps or overlaps, especially with floating-point ray marching. Degenerate Input: If the ROI is empty or the ray does not intersect the ROI, the pixel should be transparent or background-colored. Mask Alignment: The auxiliary mask volume must be aligned with the data volume to ensure correct sample lookup. Front-to-Back Depth Peeling (FtBDP) is a technique for Region of Interest (ROI) rendering that defines an ROI as a 3D envelope by combining polygon-based depth peeling with volume ray casting. It solves the problem of visualizing internal volume features bounded by an arbitrary surface by breaking the ray casting process into stages synchronized with intermediate peeling results. Unlike standard depth peeling which only handles polygonal models, FtBDP interleaves polygon rendering and volume ray casting to correctly handle volume samples both inside and outside the envelope. A technique to attenuate unimportant high-intensity structures (e.g., at the brain surface) by defining a spherical Region of Interest (ROI) around a Point of Interest (POI) in the tumor tissue. The user marks a POI in the tumor tissue, close to the middle point. From this POI, N rays are cast: three along the coordinate system axes and three against the direction of the axes. For each ray, the distance to the POI is computed as soon as the intensity becomes less than an intensity threshold, indicating the ray has exited the suspicious structure. The maximal distance among the six rays is used to specify the radius of the spherical ROI. Only voxels inside this ROI are blended with the additional volume. Typical value: N = 6. A method to suppress unimportant structures by automatically computing a Region of Interest (ROI) from a user-marked Point of Interest (POI) using intensity analysis along cast rays. The user marks a POI, rays are cast from the POI into the volume, and intensity analysis along the cast rays computes the ROI. Time Complexity: Depends on the ROI definition. Mask-based rendering requires sampling the mask volume at each step, increasing memory bandwidth usage. Intensity-based ROI requires pre-casting rays to determine radius, adding a one-time cost. Memory Complexity: Mask-based ROI requires an auxiliary binary volume M of the same dimensions as the data volume V. Strengths: Allows precise isolation of internal structures; supports arbitrary shapes; reduces visual clutter from occluding high-intensity structures. Limitations: Geometric clipping may not fit complex internal structures; mask-based methods require pre-computation or storage of the mask; intensity-based methods depend on threshold selection. When to Use: When internal structures are occluded by high-intensity surfaces or when focusing on a specific anatomical region. When Not to Use: When the entire volume context is needed; when the ROI definition is ambiguous or difficult to specify. The technique is used in medical imaging to visualize internal pathological tissues, such as tumors, by suppressing unimportant surrounding structures. The ROI can be moved and resized by moving and rotating the wand. The technique is supported by various graphics libraries, including VTK. name: Front-to-Back Depth Peeling
head: FtBDP
body: Front-to-Back Depth Peeling (FtBDP) is a technique for Region of Interest (ROI) rendering that defines an ROI as a 3D envelope by combining polygon-based depth peeling with volume ray casting. It solves the problem of visualizing internal volume features bounded by an arbitrary surface by breaking the ray casting process into stages synchronized with intermediate peeling results. Unlike standard depth peeling which only handles polygonal models, FtBDP interleaves polygon rendering and volume ray casting to correctly handle volume samples both inside and outside the envelope. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Polygonal envelope geometry (tagged with a vertex attribute key), volume dataset, MIDA visualization settings for inside/outside regions, initial ray starting positions (optional, for optimization). Outputs: Final composited image with ROI visualization. Data Structures Depth Buffer: Stores depth values of fragments for tracking peeled surfaces. Color Buffer: Stores accumulated color from previous peeling and ray casting passes. Ray Position Buffer: Stores 3D intersection positions of rays with peeled envelope surfaces from previous steps. Envelope Geometry Tag: A vertex attribute key distinguishing envelope polygons from regular scene geometry. Numbered Steps The method proceeds in a sequence of peeling and ray casting stages: 1. Initial Peeling: Render the front-most polygonal geometry (the front surface of the envelope) normally. Store the depths of all corresponding fragments for every pixel in the depth buffer. 2. First Ray Casting Stage: Initiate MIDA ray casting. Pass the color and depth buffers from Step 1 as textures. Perform a depth test; render only volume parts that fall outside the envelope. Blend the colors from the previous peeling pass with the ray casting results. Store the positions of rays intersecting the peeled surface (from Step 1) in a separate buffer. 3. Next Peeling Stage: Initiate the next envelope peeling stage. Pass the depth results of the previous peeling pass as a texture. Choose new fragments that satisfy the depth test condition (depth > stored texture values). Store the depth values of all newly chosen fragments in the depth buffer. 4. Subsequent Ray Casting Stage: Initiate MIDA ray casting. Pass the color and depth buffers from Step 3, as well as the ray positions and accumulated color results from Step 2, as textures. Initialize ray starting positions from the stored values. Perform the depth test. Render sampled values inside or outside the envelope using different MIDA settings. Blend the colors from the previous peeling pass and the previous ray casting pass with the current ray casting results. Store the positions of rays intersecting the newly peeled surface (from Step 3) in the ray position buffer. 5. Iteration: Repeat Steps 3 and 4 until the envelope peeling stage reports 0 newly chosen fragments. Formulas Fragment selection condition: d{frag} > d{texture}, where d{frag} is the depth of a candidate fragment and d{texture} is the stored depth value from the previous peeling pass. Inside/Outside determination: A ray sample is classified as inside if it lies between a front-facing and a back-facing envelope fragment; otherwise it is outside. Parameters MIDA Settings: Visualization parameters for rendering volume samples inside vs. outside the envelope. Depth Test Condition: Comparison operator (e.g., >) to select fragments behind previously peeled surfaces. Typical values are not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Open Surfaces: Extreme cases where the envelope geometry crosses metaball grid boundaries and no longer forms a closed surface are handled correctly. Overdraw: The full geometry of the scene must be drawn and tested in each polygon peeling pass, leading to overdraw. Shader Overhead: There is overhead associated with shader code initialization and execution per stage. Precision and boundary handling are not specified beyond the open-surface case. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackdepthpeeling(envelopegeometry, volumedata, insidesettings, outsidesettings): # Initialize buffers depthbuffer = [0.0] (width height) colorbuffer = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] (width height) raypositionbuffer = [None] (width height) # Step 1: Initial Peeling # Render front-most polygonal geometry (front surface of envelope) normally. # Store depths of all corresponding fragments for every pixel in the depth buffer. depthbuffer = renderfrontsurface(envelopegeometry) # Step 2: First Ray Casting Stage # Pass color and depth buffers from Step 1 as textures. # Perform depth test; render only volume parts that fall outside the envelope. # Blend previous pass colors with ray casting results. # Store ray intersection positions in a separate buffer. raycastresult2 = castvolumerays( volumedata, rayorigin=None, raydirection=None, depthtexture=depthbuffer, colortexture=colorbuffer, settings=outsidesettings, mode="outside") colorbuffer = blendbuffers(colorbuffer, raycastresult2.color) raypositionbuffer = raycastresult2.intersections # Steps 3 & 4: Iterative Peeling and Ray Casting while True: # Step 3: Next Peeling Stage # Pass depth results of previous peeling pass as a texture. # Choose new fragments satisfying the depth test condition (depth > stored texture values). # Store new fragment depths in the depth buffer. newfragments = selectfragments(envelopegeometry, depthbuffer, condition="depth > texture") if not newfragments: break depthbuffer = updatedepthbuffer(depthbuffer, newfragments) # Step 4: Subsequent Ray Casting Stage # Pass color and depth buffers from Step 3, and ray positions/accumulated colors from Step 2 as textures. # Initialize ray starting positions from stored values. # Perform depth test. Render sampled values inside/outside envelope using different MIDA settings. # Blend previous peeling and ray casting results with current results. # Store new ray intersection positions. raycastresult4 = castvolumerays( volumedata, rayorigin=raypositionbuffer, raydirection=None, depthtexture=depthbuffer, colortexture=colorbuffer, settingsinside=insidesettings, settingsoutside=outsidesettings) colorbuffer = blendbuffers(colorbuffer, raycastresult4.color) raypositionbuffer = raycastresult4.intersections return colorbuffer Time Complexity: The method involves multiple passes. Each peeling pass requires drawing the full geometry and performing depth tests. Each ray casting pass involves volume sampling and blending. The number of passes depends on the complexity of the envelope depth layers. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for depth buffers, color buffers, and ray position buffers. Performance: No additional GPU computational workload for ray casting is introduced by keeping and initializing ray positions between stages. However, overhead exists from shader initialization/execution per stage and overdraw from the depth peeling algorithm. Strengths: Allows for complex ROI definitions using implicit surfaces (metaballs) and handles open envelope surfaces. Correctly blends polygonal and volumetric data. Limitations: Overdraw and shader overhead can impact performance. Requires careful management of buffer passing between passes. Front-to-Back Depth Peeling was introduced in the context of a 3D painting metaphor for volume image exploration. It extends the concept of depth peeling, which traditionally deals only with polygonal models, to integrate with volume ray casting. The technique was developed to support an envelope definition using GPU-accelerated metaballs, allowing for growing and editing of the ROI in a manner similar to placing brush strokes. The term "Front-to-Back" refers to the order of peeling, which matches the front-to-back order of ray casting.
