name: Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting
head: raycast1Layer, segment-by-segment ray casting
body: Multi-layer volume ray casting is a unified rendering framework that treats volume datasets and geometric objects (clipping geometry, embedded opaque/semi-transparent objects, editing masks, MPRs, and non-empty-space boundaries) as Volume-of-Interests (VOIs). It solves the problem of handling spatial overlaps, empty-space skipping, and multiple material-specific transfer functions in a single pass by encoding VOI interactions into a pre-generated ray-layer buffer. Unlike standard single-layer ray casting, which cannot skip empty spaces between visible samples or handle embedded objects producing multiple layers, this method explicitly stores non-overlapping ray segments per pixel. It differs from polygon-assisted ray casting and single-pass ray casters that store full 3D texture coordinates by storing only the Z-coordinate of the starting position, reducing memory usage and ensuring sampling alignment across bricks. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset partitioned into bricks, a set of VOIs (each with a priority number and material ID), and a pre-generated ray-layer buffer. Output: The final composited image color and accumulated opacity. Data Structures: Ray-Layer Buffer: A per-pixel array of ray segments. Each segment stores: rayStart: The starting Z-coordinate (depth) of the segment. rayEnd: The ending Z-coordinate of the segment. materialID: An integer identifying the material properties (e.g., transfer function) for this segment. The buffer encodes a set of non-overlapping ray segments for each pixel. Parameters: renderMpr: A boolean flag indicating whether Multi-Planar Reformation (MPR) layers should be rendered before standard ray casting for the current segment. VOI Priority: An integer assigned to each VOI. Higher priority overwrites lower priority in overlapped regions. Multiple VOIs with identical priorities are blended. Default VOI: The implicit bounding box of the volume dataset, assigned the lowest priority. Voxels excluded by all other VOIs are rendered according to this default. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Layer Buffer Generation (Pre-processing): Convert all VOI information into a ray-layer buffer. Perform depth peeling on all VOI boundaries. Organize peeled fragments into layers based on VOI priority and material ID. For each pixel, encode a set of non-overlapping ray segments, recording rayStart, rayEnd, and materialID. This step shifts computational workload to layer sorting to keep the ray-casting loop simple. 2. Multi-Layer Ray Casting Loop: For each pixel, fetch and decode the current layer information from the ray-layer buffer, including rayStart, rayEnd, and materialID. If the segment is valid, call raycast1Layer with these parameters. raycast1Layer returns a Boolean flag: true to continue to the next layer in the buffer, false to terminate the ray for the current brick. 3. Single Layer Ray Casting (raycast1Layer): Brick Boundary Check: Check if rayStart is behind the far end of the current brick. If so, return false to terminate the ray for the current brick. MPR Rendering: If renderMpr is set, render the MPR layer in the intersection of [rayStart, rayEnd] with the current brick before standard ray casting. Standard Ray Casting: Cast rays segment-by-segment within [rayStart, rayEnd] using the materialID to select the appropriate transfer function and viewing parameters. Transfer functions are stacked into a single 2D texture, with texture coordinate offsets calculated as materialID × D, where D is the size of a single transfer function. Use the ray-layer buffer to estimate gradients on layer surfaces to improve shading effects. Opacity Check: Inspect accumulated opacity to determine possible early termination. Termination Check: Check if rayEnd is behind the far end of the brick. If yes, return false (termination); otherwise, return true to continue to the next ray segment. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multilayervolumeraycasting(volumedata, raylayerbuffer, bricks, rendermprflag=False): height = len(raylayerbuffer) width = len(raylayerbuffer[0]) image = [[None] width for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 segments = raylayerbuffer[y][x] for seg in segments: raystart = seg.startz rayend = seg.endz materialid = seg.materialid # Find brick containing raystart brick = None for b in bricks: if b.startz <= raystart < b.endz: brick = b break if brick is None: continue # Call single layer caster; returns True to continue, False to terminate terminated = raycast1layer(volumedata, brick, raystart, rayend, materialid, acccolor, accopacity, rendermprflag) if terminated: break image[y][x] = acccolor return image def raycast1layer(volumedata, brick, raystart, rayend, materialid, acccolor, accopacity, rendermprflag): # Check if rayStart is behind the far end of the current brick if raystart >= brick.endz: return False # Terminate ray for current brick # Optional: Render MPR layer if flag is set if rendermprflag: # Render MPR layer in the intersection of [raystart, rayend] with the current brick # Implementation details for MPR rendering are not given in the sources. pass # Standard front-to-back compositing for the segment # See Parent for sampling, interpolation, and transfer function details # Number of samples per segment is not given in the sources. numsamples = 16 # Not given in the sources. dt = (rayend - raystart) / numsamples for i in range(numsamples): t = raystart + i dt # Sample volume value V(pi) and apply transfer function T(V) -> (ci, alphai) # Transfer function lookup uses offset: materialid D, where D is the size of a single transfer function alphai = 0.0 # Not given in the sources. colori = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Not given in the sources. # Front-to-back compositing acccolor[0] += (1.0 - accopacity) colori[0] alphai acccolor[1] += (1.0 - accopacity) colori[1] alphai acccolor[2] += (1.0 - accopacity) colori[2] alphai accopacity += (1.0 - accopacity) alphai # Inspect accumulated opacity to determine possible termination if accopacity >= 1.0: break # Check if rayEnd is behind the far end of the brick if rayend >= brick.endz: return False # Termination return True # Continue to the next ray segment Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Spaces: Single-layer ray casting cannot skip empty spaces between the first and last visible samples. Multi-layer encoding solves this by explicitly storing non-overlapping segments. Embedded Objects: Single-layer representation cannot cope with embedded objects that produce multiple layers. The ray-layer buffer explicitly handles these. Bricking Compatibility: Storing only the Z value of the starting position ensures sampling locations align across bricks, which is required for bricking. Generates the ray-layer buffer by depth-peeling VOI definitions and grouping fragments into ordered layers based on VOI priority and material ID. It differs from standard GPU-based CSG by performing stencil-like tests inside a GPU program, preserving priority and ID information. Choose this method when rendering nested, potentially self-intersecting VOIs on the GPU where standard stencil buffers fail to preserve critical priority data. Determines optimal split points along a ray to separate high-quality raycasting from lower-cost image warping. It identifies specific volumetric features for light attenuation, preserving depth cues better than simple depth-based splitting. Choose this method when rendering transparent volumes where the main visual effect occurs in the middle of a ray interval rather than at entry or exit. Time Complexity: The multi-pass depth peeling cost is nearly ignorable compared to the ray casting cost. The algorithm shifts computational workload to layer sorting to keep the ray-casting loop as simple as possible. Memory Complexity: The ray-layer buffer stores only the Z value of the starting position and material ID per segment, which is less memory-intensive than storing full 3D texture coordinates. Performance: Using a single shared ray-layer buffer for the whole volume (with bricking) is more efficient and easier to debug than using a different ray-layer buffer for each brick. Strengths: Supports interactive volume editing, cutaway views, and prioritized overlay of geometric masks, MPRs, and embedded objects. Transfer functions are stacked into a single 2D texture, with texture coordinate offsets calculated as materialID × D, where D is the size of a single transfer function. Limitations: Requires pre-generation of the ray-layer buffer, which involves depth peeling. Multi-layer volume ray casting was presented by Wei Li from Siemens Corporate Research. It integrates various volume rendering enhancements into a unified framework, including empty-space skipping, volume clipping, embedding opaque and semi-transparent objects, and volume editing through CSG operations. The method treats all these objects as VOIs, assigning priority numbers to resolve spatial overlaps. name: Ray-Layer Buffer Generation via Depth Peeling
head: VOI layer generation, peeling VOI definitions
body: This method generates the ray-layer buffer for Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting by depth-peeling Volume of Interest (VOI) definitions and grouping the resulting fragments into ordered layers based on material ID and priority. It solves the problem of correctly determining the visibility and enclosure of nested, potentially self-intersecting VOIs on the GPU, where standard stencil buffers fail to preserve the critical priority and ID information required for per-layer transfer function application. Unlike standard GPU-based Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) which uses hardware stencil buffers to count front/back fragments, this method performs similar logic inside a GPU fragment program to maintain full control over layer complexity and material assignment. Inputs: A set of VOI definitions, each associated with a unique Material ID (mtId) and a priority value. Clipping meshes (optional, used to define view frustum or user-defined boundaries). Multi-Planar Reformation (MPR) meshes (optional, representing explicit planar data). A depth-peeling renderer that outputs fragments with depth, facing (front/back), and mesh ID. Outputs: A ray-layer buffer: an array of entries per ray (pixel), where each entry contains a depth, a material ID, and potentially other metadata required for ray casting. Data Structures: insideFlag array: An array indexed by Material ID. It stores the net count of front-facing minus back-facing fragments for each VOI. rayLayerBuffer: The output structure storing the sequence of layers for each ray. Algorithm Steps: 1. Peeling: Render the scene using a depth-peeling algorithm [Eve01]. For each pass k, render only fragments with depth greater than the k-th peeled depth. 2. Inside Flag Update: For every fragment generated (even if discarded by the peeling depth test), update the insideFlag array for its associated Material ID: If the fragment is front-facing, increment insideFlag[mtId]. If the fragment is back-facing, decrement insideFlag[mtId]. This count represents the winding number or enclosure status of the fragment relative to the VOI. 3. Determine Current Material: Scan the insideFlag array to find the Material ID of the enclosing VOI with the highest priority. Let this be currentId. A VOI is considered enclosing if its insideFlag is non-zero (indicating the ray is inside the volume defined by that VOI). Priority determines which VOI takes precedence if multiple VOIs enclose the same point. 4. Layer Buffer Writing: Compare currentId with the material ID of the previous layer in the rayLayerBuffer for the current ray. If currentId differs from the previous layer's ID, write a new entry to the buffer with currentId and the current fragment's depth. Note: A back-facing fragment indicates the exit of a contributing VOI. Consequently, currentId will change (e.g., from the VOI's ID to the background or a different enclosing VOI). 5. Clipping Mesh Handling: If the fragment belongs to a clipping mesh: If front-facing: Clear all previous layers in the rayLayerBuffer for this ray (resetting the state). If back-facing: Mark layer generation as finished for this ray (no further layers are added for this ray). 6. MPR Mesh Handling: If the fragment belongs to an MPR mesh: Write the MPR layer directly to the buffer. If the MPR is inside a non-empty layer (i.e., currentId is not background), append an entry with the same depth as the MPR but using the previous material ID. This ensures the intersected layer continues after the MPR. 7. Optimization (Empty Space Merging): After generating layers, scan for empty segments between adjacent mtIdVolume layers. If the depth distance between two adjacent volume layers is shorter than a given threshold, merge them into a single layer to reduce buffer complexity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. insideFlags = {mtId: 0 for mtId in allmaterialids} rayLayerBuffer = [] # List of layers for the current ray previousLayerId = None def processfragment(fragment): global previousLayerId # 1. Update inside flags for the fragment's material ID mtId = fragment.meshid if fragment.isfrontfacing: insideFlags[mtId] += 1 else: insideFlags[mtId] -= 1 # 2. Determine current enclosing material ID # Find mtId with non-zero insideFlag and highest priority currentId = findhighestpriorityenclosingid(insideFlags) # 3. Handle Clipping Meshes if fragment.isclippingmesh: if fragment.isfrontfacing: # Clear previous layers rayLayerBuffer.clear() previousLayerId = None else: # Mark generation as finished return # Stop processing further fragments for this ray return # 4. Handle MPR Meshes if fragment.ismprmesh: # Write MPR layer addlayertobuffer(fragment.depth, fragment.mprmaterialid) # If inside a non-empty layer, append continuation entry if previousLayerId is not None and previousLayerId != backgroundid: addlayertobuffer(fragment.depth, previousLayerId) previousLayerId = fragment.mprmaterialid return # 5. Handle VOI Fragments # If currentId differs from previous layer, write new layer if currentId != previousLayerId: addlayertobuffer(fragment.depth, currentId) previousLayerId = currentId def addlayertobuffer(depth, materialid): rayLayerBuffer.append({'depth': depth, 'materialid': materialid}) def findhighestpriorityenclosingid(flags): bestid = backgroundid bestpriority = -infinity for mtId, count in flags.items(): if count != 0: # Enclosing priority = getpriority(mtId) if priority > bestpriority: bestpriority = priority bestid = mtId return bestid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Identical Depth Fragments: Standard peeling may output only one fragment when two fragments have identical depths, leading to incorrect insideFlags. This occurs when surface common points project exactly to pixel centers or when back-facing surfaces touch front-facing surfaces of the same VOI (common at bounding box corners). Hardware Depth Test Limitations: Modifying depth in a fragment program may disable hardware depth testing on some GPUs. A method to resolve ambiguity when two fragments at the same pixel have identical depths, which causes standard peeling to output only one and produce incorrect insideFlags. It encodes depth, facing, and mesh ID into a new number (similar to ray-layer buffer entry encoding) and sets it as the modified depth in the peeling fragment program. If hardware does not support depth testing with modified depth, the encoded value is written to a color channel and compared using MIN or MAX operations of the frame buffer. This issue is rare but common at corners/edges of non-empty-space bounding boxes where back-facing surfaces touch front-facing surfaces of the same VOI. Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of depth peeling passes (N) times the number of pixels, plus the cost of scanning insideFlags per fragment. The number of passes depends on the maximum number of overlapping VOIs. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for insideFlags (size proportional to number of material IDs) and the ray-layer buffer (size proportional to number of layers per ray). Strengths: Correctly handles nested, self-intersecting VOIs and preserves material priority information which hardware stencil buffers cannot. Supports clipping and MPR meshes explicitly. Limitations: Requires multiple rendering passes for depth peeling. Identical depth handling adds complexity and potential hardware compatibility issues. When to use: When rendering complex scenes with nested, overlapping volumes where material priority and correct enclosure detection are critical, and standard CSG stencil methods are insufficient. The method originates from the work on Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting on GPU, specifically the layer generation phase. It was developed to address the limitations of standard GPU-based CSG stencil buffers in the context of volume rendering, where each VOI has a priority and ID critical for layer placement. The approach builds on depth peeling techniques [Eve01] and adapts them for volume data structures. Multi-layer Volume Ray Casting on GPU, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg10/005-012, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Dual Depth Peeling
head: Bidirectional Depth Peeling, Depth Peeling Rendering Pipeline, Depth peeling loop, On-the-fly front-to-back peeling
body: Dual Depth Peeling is an order-independent transparency (OIT) technique that decomposes a scene into depth layers by rendering primitives multiple times, discarding fragments closer than the previous layer, and blending the resulting layers to assemble the final image. It improves upon standard Depth Peeling by performing simultaneous peeling in both directions—front-to-back and back-to-front—thereby reducing the total number of rendering passes required for N layers by approximately N/2. Unlike standard Depth Peeling, which processes layers sequentially, this method resolves depth ordering per pixel, making it robust against self-intersecting surfaces that often complicate depth-sorting approaches. The method executes a depth peeling loop for each frame, consisting of iterative peel and blend stages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Discrete representation of integral surfaces (e.g., triangles or quadrilaterals) with associated texture coordinates and normal vectors. Output: Final composited image with correct transparency and silhouette shading. Data Structures: 1. Color Buffer: A floating-point color buffer is used for blending to prevent banding artifacts when many surface layers are present. 2. Normal Buffer: A secondary floating-point RGBA buffer stores surface normals required for the blend stage. 3. Mask Buffer: The alpha component of the normal buffer acts as a mask to distinguish integral surface pixels from context/background pixels. 4. Depth Texture: Stores the depth information of the current surface layer, required for the depth peeling algorithm's occlusion tests. Parameters: Silhouette Color: User-specified color for fading surface edges. Lighting Model: Phong or Gooch models for diffuse color evaluation. Modulation Type: Multiplicative or additive transparency modulation. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize: Set up the floating-point color buffer, normal buffer, and depth texture. Initialize the depth peeling loop. 2. Peel Stage (Iterative): a. Depth Test: Render the primitives using a depth test that discards fragments closer than the depth stored in the depth texture from the previous iteration. For the first iteration, this is typically the near plane or a standard depth buffer. b. Shading: Perform full surface shading for the visible fragments: i. Transparency: Compute the view-dependent transparency term \alpha{view} from the fragment's normal vector. If normal-variation transparency is used, evaluate partial derivatives using dFdx and dFdy. ii. Pattern/Texture: If adaptive patterns are used, compute ls and lt using dFdx and dFdy, and evaluate the pattern equation (Equation 5 in) to obtain texture color c{tex} and texture alpha \alpha{tex}. iii. Lighting: Evaluate diffuse color c{diffuse} using the specified lighting model (Phong or Gooch). Compute specular highlight terms (c, \alpha){spec} if specified. iv. Combination: Compute the final RGBA output (c, \alpha){peel} for the peel pass. For multiplicative modulation: \alpha{final} = \alpha{view} \cdot \alpha{tex} + \alpha{specular} c{final} = c{diffuse} \cdot c{tex} + c{specular} For additive modulation: \alpha{final} = \alpha{view} + \alpha{tex} + \alpha{specular} (Note: c{final} remains c{diffuse} \cdot c{tex} + c{specular}). c. Storage: Write the final RGBA values to the color buffer. Store surface normals in the normal buffer, setting the alpha component to a mask flag indicating the pixel belongs to the integral surface. d. Depth Update: Update the depth texture with the depth values of the current layer for the next iteration. 3. Blend Stage: a. Silhouette Detection: Apply a Sobel edge detection filter to both the normal buffer and the depth buffer to determine silhouette strength. b. Masking: Use the mask flag in the normal buffer to exclude pixels that have the flag set for one of the pixels contributing to the filter, avoiding silhouette generation across surface-context and context-background boundaries. c. Silhouette Blending: Smoothly fade the surface color into the user-specified silhouette color based on the computed silhouette strength. d. Accumulation: Blend the result into the final floating-point color buffer. 4. Termination: Adaptively terminate the peeling loop if no pixels are rendered during the peel stage, determined using an occlusion query for each iteration. The total number of iterations is one greater than the number of surface layers for the current viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def dualdepthpeeling(primitives, silhouettecolor, lightingmodel, modulationtype): # Initialize buffers colorbuffer = createfloatingpointbuffer() normalbuffer = createfloatingpointbuffer() # RGBA, A is mask depthtexture = createdepthtexture() # Initial depth for first pass (e.g., near plane) currentdepth = NEARPLANE # Occlusion query for adaptive termination query = createocclusionquery() while True: # Start Occlusion Query beginocclusionquery(query) # PEEL STAGE # Render primitives with depth test against currentdepth # Discard fragments with depth < currentdepth renderprimitiveswithdepthtest(primitives, currentdepth) # Shading in Vertex/Fragment Shader # 1. Transparency alphaview = computealphaview(normal) if normalvariationtransparency: alphaview = evaluatenormalvariation(alphaview, dFdx, dFdy) # 2. Pattern/Texture if adaptivepattern: ls, lt = computepatterncoords(dFdx, dFdy) ctex, alphatex = evaluatepattern(ls, lt) else: ctex, alphatex = gettexturecoloralpha() # 3. Lighting cdiffuse = evaluatelighting(normal, position, lightingmodel) cspec, alphaspec = evaluatespecular(normal, position, viewdir) # 4. Combination if modulationtype == ADDITIVE: alphafinal = alphaview + alphatex + alphaspec else: # Multiplicative alphafinal = alphaview alphatex + alphaspec cfinal = cdiffuse ctex + cspec # Write to buffers writetocolorbuffer(cfinal, alphafinal) writetonormalbuffer(normal, maskflag=1) # Update depth texture for next iteration updatedepthtexture(currentdepth) # End Occlusion Query endocclusionquery(query) # Check if any pixels were rendered if not queryhasresults(query) or not queryispositive(query): break # Update currentdepth for next pass # In Dual Depth Peeling, this involves managing front-to-back and back-to-front # The specific logic for updating depthtexture to support bidirectional peeling # is implementation-specific but generally involves maintaining two depth textures # or a combined depth buffer that supports both directions. # For the purpose of this algorithm description, we assume the depth texture # is updated to reflect the newly peeled layer's depth boundary. currentdepth = getnextdepthboundary(depthtexture) # BLEND STAGE # Apply silhouette detection and blending applysobelfilter(normalbuffer, depthbuffer) computesilhouettestrength(sobelresults, normalbuffer.mask) blendsilhouette(colorbuffer, silhouettecolor, silhouettestrength) return colorbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Silhouette Width: Silhouettes are extracted twice (once per pair of successive depth layers), which may result in inner silhouettes of increased width. This is mitigated by using a sharp and symmetric edge detection filter. Banding Artifacts: Slight banding artifacts can appear if blending directly to the output framebuffer in the presence of many surface layers. Using a floating-point color buffer improves blending accuracy. Depth Sorting Precision: Elements at different depths within the same layer may be stored if no intermediate geometry occludes them, reducing depth-sorting precision. Integrates Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume (PVHV) analysis into the depth peeling process to cull redundant fragments, reducing the number of effective layers required for high-quality multi-view warping. Extends Dual Depth Peeling to handle volumetric data intermixed with translucent polygonal geometry by using geometry peel depths as entry/exit points for volume ray-casting. Time Complexity: Rendering speed is largely a function of surface geometry size and is dominated by the requirement to submit the surface for rendering multiple times during depth peeling. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for multiple buffers: a floating-point color buffer, a normal buffer (with mask), and a depth texture. Measured Performance: Achieves interactive frame rates exceeding 15fps on NVIDIA GTX280 for small to medium meshes of below ≈500K triangles with medium depth complexity of 10 layers or less. Strengths: Resolves depth ordering per pixel, making it robust against self-intersecting surfaces which complicate depth sorting. Reduces the number of passes by N/2 for N layers compared to standard depth peeling. Limitations: Performance degrades with larger meshes and higher depth complexity. May still store elements at different depths within the same layer if no intermediate geometry occludes them, reducing depth-sorting precision. When to Use: Suitable for interactive visualization of integral surfaces (e.g., stream surfaces, path surfaces) that may self-intersect, where correct transparency and silhouette shading are required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with very high depth complexity or extremely large meshes where the multiple render passes become prohibitive. Dual Depth Peeling was introduced as an improvement to the standard Depth Peeling algorithm to reduce the number of rendering passes required for order-independent transparency. It allows simultaneous peeling in both directions: from the camera to the background and from the background to the camera. The technique is implemented in OpenGL using GLSL shader programs, but the concepts can be ported to DirectX. It is particularly useful in illustrative rendering for integral surfaces, such as streamlines on stream surfaces, where visual clarity and correct transparency are critical. name: Effective Depth Peeling
head: DP with PVHVs, DP+PVHV, EDP (Extended Depth Peeling with PVHV), PVHV-based culling, Sampling-based backward-search algorithm
body: Effective Depth Peeling (EDP) is a visibility culling technique for multi-layer volume ray casting that integrates Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume (PVHV) analysis into the depth peeling process. It solves the problem of processing redundant, completely hidden fragments in subsequent peeling layers by implicitly identifying and culling fragments that are occluded by large-area occluders, thereby reducing the number of effective layers required for high-quality multi-view warping. Unlike standard Depth Peeling (DP) which peels one layer per pass linearly, or Umbra culling-based DP (UDP) which uses tiny pixel occluders, EDP captures important edge fragments early using wider area occluders, significantly reducing warping costs and total layer count. EDP operates by testing whether a fragment in a hidden layer lies within a PVHV defined by the occluders in the previous layer. If a fragment is inside a PVHV, it is considered fully hidden and culled; otherwise, it is retained for warping. The method uses a sampling-based backward search to approximate PVHVs without explicit edge analysis. Inputs: Z: Known-view depth texture from the previous layer (or foreground image for h=1). E: Novel-view bound radius (screen-space LCOC radius). \Delta: Depth-difference threshold for surface connectivity (default: 0.002 in normalized linear scale). |\Omega|: Number of backward-search samples (default: 14). Current layer fragments: Fragments from layer h-1 (occluders) and layer h (candidates). Outputs: Culled fragments for layer h: Only fragments not determined to be in a PVHV are passed to the next stage. Item Buffer: Stores object IDs for fragments. Used to immediately reject samples belonging to different objects during edge existence tests. Fragment Encoding: RGBA32F format, storing color, depth (z), and item index. Depth Texture (Z): Stores depth values for the occluder layer. 1. Initialization: For each fragment p in the current hidden layer h, identify its projection q onto the occluder layer h-1 (or foreground h=0). The depth of q is qz = Z(px, py). 2. LCOC Calculation: Compute the Local Cone of Confusion (LCOC) radius R in screen space based on the depth difference between p and q, and the novel-view bound E. The formula is: R = \text{ProjectToScreen}\left( \left| \frac{pz - qz}{qz} \right| E \right) where \text{ProjectToScreen} converts the physical bound to screen-space pixels. 3. Sample Generation: Generate a set of uniform random samples \Omega within a circle of radius R centered at q. The size |\Omega| is typically 14. 4. Edge Existence Test: For each sample w \in \Omega: a. Sample the depth at the offset location: wz = Z(px + wx, py + wy). b. Test if an edge exists between w and q using EdgeExists(w, q). 5. PVHV Inclusion Check: If EdgeExists(w, q) returns true, the fragment p is in a PVHV. Return true (fragment is hidden/culled). If the depth difference is small (wz \ge qz - \Delta), the sample w is on the connected surface. Bypass w (do not process as a new occluder) and continue to the next sample. If the depth difference is significant (wz < qz - \Delta), the sample may find a secondary inner occluder. Recursive Extension (CPU/Conceptual): Recursively extend the bound at w to find secondary inner occluders by calling InPVHV again. GPU Implementation: Since GPU implementations do not support recursion, use a Halton sequence for subsequent quasi-random samples to handle bound extensions naturally. Alternatively, use a conservative approximation by considering such samples as potentially in PVHVs (return true) to avoid excessive sampling. 6. Final Decision: If no samples indicate an edge or PVHV inclusion after checking all w \in \Omega, return false (fragment is fully visible/retained). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def effectivedepthpeeling(Z, E, Delta, Omegasize, ItemBuffer): """ Z: Depth texture of the occluder layer E: Novel-view bound radius Delta: Depth-difference threshold Omegasize: Number of samples ItemBuffer: Object ID buffer """ # Helper: Local Cone of Confusion radius def LCOC(pz, qz): # ProjectToScreen converts physical bound to screen pixels # Assuming normalized linear depth and screen projection logic return ProjectToScreen(abs((pz - qz) / qz) E) # Helper: Edge Existence Test def EdgeExists(w, q): # w and q are screen-space coordinates # Check if different objects if ItemBuffer[w] != ItemBuffer[q]: return True # Check depth difference wz = Z[w] qz = Z[q] if wz > (qz + Delta): return True return False # Helper: In PVHV Check def InPVHV(p, pz, conservative=False): # p is the fragment coordinate # pz is the fragment depth # q is the projection of p onto the occluder layer q = p qz = Z[q] # Calculate search radius R = LCOC(pz, qz) # Generate random samples in circle of radius R around q Omega = GetRandomSamples(R, Omegasize) for w in Omega: # Sample depth at w wz = Z[w] # Test if edge exists if EdgeExists(w, q): return True # Fragment is in PVHV # Check if on connected surface if wz >= (qz - Delta): continue # Bypass, no new occluder # Significant depth difference: potential secondary occluder if conservative: return True # Conservative approximation # Recursive extension (conceptual) # In GPU, this is handled by Halton sequence in subsequent calls # or by the caller managing the sequence if InPVHV(w, wz, conservative): return True return False # Fully hidden, no PVHV found # Main Loop for each fragment p in current layer: pz = p.depth if not InPVHV(p, pz): retainfragment(p) \Delta: Depth-difference threshold. Default: 0.002 (normalized linear scale). Trades errors for peeling efficiency. E: Novel-view bound radius. Input parameter for LCOC calculation. |\Omega|: Number of backward-search samples. Default: 14. More samples (e.g., 16) lower the chance of missing edges in complex scenes. GPU Recursion: GPU implementations do not support recursion for secondary inner occluders. A Halton sequence is used for quasi-random samples to handle bound extensions in subsequent iterations. Approximate Tests: The edge existence test is approximate. Small numbers of missing fragments may occur, but experiments show negligible error rates (e.g., 0.000014 average fraction of erroneous pixels in RU scene). Disjoint Surfaces: Few adjacent disjoint surfaces may be incorrectly considered connected. Insufficient samples may miss existing edges. A memory-optimized variant that uses a linked list structure to pack sparse valid fragments, reducing memory consumption compared to fixed-size buffers. Time Complexity: Per-layer cost is costlier than regular DP due to the PVHV culling overhead, but fewer layers are needed for similar quality. Memory Complexity: Standard EDP requires two working textures (ping-pong) for input and output layers. Packed EDP (PEDP) reduces memory by packing fragments, requiring a head texture for indexes. Performance: In the Satellites (ST) scene with E=1000mm, EDP achieves a 38.5x reduction in hidden fragments compared to Baseline DP (BDP). Speedup factors for combined DP and warping costs range from 2.3–3.4x vs BDP and 1.6–2.9x vs UDP. EDP requires only two hidden layers for high-quality DOF rendering in complex scenes, reducing effective layers by up to 2/2/3 (RU/SF/ST) for BDP and 3/2/2 for UDP. Strengths: Captures important fragments early, reduces warping cost, handles large-area occluders better than UDP. Limitations: Approximate edge tests may miss small fragments; GPU recursion limitation requires Halton sequence handling. Usage: Best for Depth-of-Field (DOF) rendering in multi-view warping applications. Effective Depth Peeling was introduced by Janghun Kim and Sungkil Lee in 2023 in the paper "Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume Rendering for Multi-View Warping". It builds on the concept of Potentially Visible Hidden-Volumes (PVHVs) and extends Depth Peeling by integrating on-the-fly fragment culling. The method is designed to improve efficiency in multi-fragment rendering and remote rendering scenarios. name: Packed Effective Depth Peeling
head: Packed EDP
body: Packed Effective Depth Peeling (PEDP) is a memory-optimized variant of Effective Depth Peeling (EDP) that reduces memory consumption by tightly packing sparse valid fragments using a linked list structure on the GPU. It solves the problem of fixed-size memory scaling in conventional Depth Peeling by removing empty pixels, causing memory consumption to scale directly with peeling efficiency. Unlike standard EDP, which retains fixed-size buffers for all potential fragment slots, PEDP dynamically allocates storage only for valid fragments, offering significant memory efficiency improvements at the cost of slightly increased warping latency due to pointer dereferencing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The set of fragments generated by the previous peeling layer h-1 (or the initial ray casting for h=0). Output: A packed linked list of fragments for layer h, stored in a node buffer, and a head texture pointing to the first node of each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Node Buffer: A dynamic array of linked list nodes. Each node consumes 16 bytes in RGBA32F format: 8 bytes: Color (RGBA32F). 4 bytes: Depth. 4 bytes: Indexed pointer to the next node (an integer index into the node buffer). 2. Head Texture: A texture of screen resolution holding 4-byte indexes to the first node of the linked list for each pixel. If a pixel has no fragments, the index is null/zero. Memory consumption: W \times H \times 4 bytes, where W and H are screen width and height. For the tested resolutions, this consumes approximately 7.9 MB. Algorithm Steps: 1. Peel Layer h: Perform the standard EDP peeling pass for layer h, generating a set of valid fragments. 2. Post-Peeling Packing: Immediately after peeling layer h, perform fragment packing to convert the sparse fragment buffer into the linked list structure. This is a per-layer process. It avoids keeping the entire layer in a fixed-size buffer. Use two working textures (input h-1 and output h) alternating in a ping-pong fashion to avoid keeping entire layers in memory. Iterate through the valid fragments generated in step 1. For each fragment, allocate a new node in the node buffer. Store the fragment's color and depth in the node. Set the node's "next" pointer to the current head of the linked list for that pixel's coordinate. Update the head texture for that pixel to point to the newly allocated node index. 3. Warping: Use the head texture and node buffer to traverse the linked lists during the warping phase. For each pixel, read the head index. Dereference the index to get the first node. Traverse the linked list using the "next" pointers until the end or a stopping condition is met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. nodebuffer = [] # List of Node objects headtexture = [0] (width height) # 4-byte indexes class Node: color: float[4] # RGBA32F depth: float nextindex: int # Index in nodebuffer def packlayerfragments(fragments, width, height): """ Pack sparse fragments into a linked list structure. fragments: List of (x, y, color, depth) tuples generated by peeling. """ # Clear head texture for this layer's new fragments # Note: In a ping-pong scheme, we might be reading from a previous head texture # but for the new layer h, we are building a fresh list. # The head texture for layer h is initialized to 0 (null). currentheadtexture = [0] (width height) # Start of new nodes in the buffer # In a real implementation, this would be an atomic counter or pre-allocated offset nextnodeindex = len(nodebuffer) for frag in fragments: x, y, color, depth = frag # Create new node node = Node() node.color = color node.depth = depth node.nextindex = currentheadtexture[y width + x] # Append to buffer nodebuffer.append(node) # Update head texture to point to this new node currentheadtexture[y width + x] = nextnodeindex nextnodeindex += 1 # Store the head texture for this layer # In a ping-pong scheme, this texture becomes the input for the next layer's warping return currentheadtexture def warplayer(headtexture, width, height): """ Traverse linked lists to warp fragments. """ for y in range(height): for x in range(width): idx = headtexture[y width + x] # Traverse the linked list while idx != 0: # Assuming 0 is null node = nodebuffer[idx] # Perform warping using node.color and node.depth #... warping logic... idx = node.nextindex Parameters and Typical Values: Node Size: 16 bytes. Head Texture Size: 4 bytes per pixel. Packing Time: For two hidden layers (L=2), packing takes 0.6–0.8 ms. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Unfriendliness: Random memory access during node traversal can be cache-unfriendly, making PEDP likely slightly slower than EDP in terms of warping speed. Dereferencing Overhead: Additional dereferencing to the first pointer in the head texture is required during warping. Memory Scaling: Memory consumption scales directly with the number of valid fragments, not the screen resolution or maximum layer count. The parent method that uses PVHVs for fragment culling. PEDP is EDP with fragment packing. EDP A depth peeling technique that renders front and back faces in separate passes. PEDP is an alternative to DDP in the context of volume ray casting. DDP The general process of generating layers. PEDP optimizes the storage of these layers. RLB Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Scales directly with the number of valid fragments and screen resolution (for the head texture). It avoids fixed-size memory scaling with the number of layers. Time: Peeling time is similar to EDP. Packing adds 0.6–0.8 ms for two hidden layers. Warping is slightly slower than EDP due to cache-unfriendly random memory access during node traversal. Measured Performance: Memory Efficiency: PEDP consumes significantly less memory than standard EDP and BDP. In the Ruins (RU) scene with E=50mm, PEDP consumes 17.7 MB compared to 316.4 MB for standard EDP, a 37.5x memory efficiency improvement over BDP. Overall memory efficiency ranges from 25.1x to 166.1x relative to BDP. Speedup: The average speedup factors of PEDP against BDP and UDP are 2.2x and 1.8x respectively for all combinations of E and scenes. Hardware: Tested on Intel Core i9-10900 2.8 GHz and NVIDIA GPU (specific model not given in notes). Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant memory reduction, making it suitable for resource-limited environments. Removes empty fragments, reducing warping workload. Limitations: Slightly slower warping than EDP due to pointer dereferencing and cache misses. Implementation complexity is higher due to linked list management on GPU. When to Use: Use PEDP when memory is a critical constraint and the scene has sparse valid fragments (high peeling efficiency). Use when the slight increase in warping latency is acceptable for the memory savings. When Not to Use: Use standard EDP if warping speed is more critical than memory usage and the scene has dense fragments. Use BDP or UDP if memory is not a constraint and simpler implementation is preferred. PEDP was introduced by Yang et al. in 2010 as part of the research on Potentially Visible Hidden-Volume Rendering (PVHVR) for Multi-View Warping. It builds on the concept of Effective Depth Peeling (EDP) by adding a fragment packing step to reduce the memory footprint of the depth peeling pipeline. The method was evaluated in the context of Depth-of-Field (DOF) rendering, where it demonstrated significant memory efficiency improvements over Baseline Depth Peeling (BDP) and Unordered Depth Peeling (UDP). name: Volume-peeling
body: Volume-peeling is a technique to correctly order translucent geometry and volumes in rasterized scenes by using geometry peel depths as entry/exit points for volume ray-casting. It extends Dual Depth Peeling to handle volumetric data intermixed with translucent polygonal geometry, ensuring that volumes are composited in the correct depth order relative to the geometry layers. It sets itself apart from standard Dual Depth Peeling by adding a specific ray-casting pass that utilizes the depth buffers generated by the geometry peeling process. Volume-peeling operates in a multi-pass pipeline that interleaves geometry peeling with volumetric ray-casting. The method requires a renderer capable of dual depth peeling and a volume mapper. Inputs: Scene containing translucent polygonal geometry and volumetric data. Renderer configuration with SetUseDepthPeelingForVolumes enabled. Ray-sampling distance and volume mapper settings. Outputs: A final composited image where translucent geometry and volumes are correctly ordered. Data Structures: Front and Back Accumulation Buffers: Separate color buffers used to accumulate fragment colors from front-to-back and back-to-front ray-casting, respectively. Depth Buffers: Updated depth values from each geometry peel pass, which define the entry and exit points for the subsequent volume ray-casting. Steps: 1. Initialization Pass: Render sections of the volume that are not enclosed within any translucent geometry. This pass initializes the front and back accumulation buffers with the colors of the volume parts visible outside the geometry. 2. Geometry Peeling Pass: Perform a dual depth peeling pass on the translucent geometry. This computes the color and depth of the front and back layers (peels) of the geometry in a single render pass. The computed colors are accumulated in separate geometry buffers, and the updated depths are stored to feed the next pair of peels. 3. Volumetric Peel Pass: Invoke the volume mapper in an additional render pass. Use the entry and exit depth points obtained from the most recent geometry peel as the boundaries for ray-casting through the volume. This renders the peels of volume contained within the current peels of geometry. 4. Simultaneous Ray-Casting: Accommodate both front and back ray-casting of the current volume peel in a single render pass. Write the fragment colors from the front ray-casting directly to the front accumulation buffer. Accumulate the fragment colors from the back ray-casting in a following pass (or buffer). 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for subsequent layers of geometry peels until all layers are processed or the maximum number of peels is reached. 6. Final Composition: Composite the front and back accumulation buffers to produce the final image. Parameters: SetUseDepthPeelingForVolumes: A boolean parameter exposed through the renderer to explicitly enable volume-peeling. It is off by default. MaxPeels: The maximum number of geometry layers to peel. Limiting this reduces the overhead of repeatedly initializing ray-casting code. Pitfalls: Overhead: There is significant overhead from repeatedly initializing ray-casting code when switching between volumetric and translucent geometry rendering passes. Performance Sensitivity: Performance is highly dependent on geometry complexity (higher complexity requires more passes) and ray-sampling distance. Degenerate Input: If the volume is entirely enclosed or entirely outside the geometry, the initialization pass handles the "outside" case, but the peeling logic must correctly handle empty depth ranges. Time Complexity: Performance depends on geometry complexity and ray-sampling distance. The time spent rendering volume peels is far greater than the time spent drawing the translucent geometry. Memory Complexity: Requires additional buffers for front and back accumulation of both geometry and volume layers, plus depth buffers for peeling. Measured Performance: Initial benchmarks suggest that the accumulated time spent peeling volumes is around 75% greater than the time required to render them without peeling. Strengths: Correctly orders translucent geometry and volumes in rasterized scenes, solving a long-standing issue in VTK. Limitations: High computational cost due to ray-casting overhead; performance degrades with high geometry complexity and large ray-sampling distances. When to Use: When correct depth ordering between translucent polygons and volumetric data is required in a rasterized rendering pipeline. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and approximate ordering is acceptable, or when the scene contains no intermixed translucent geometry and volumes. Volume-peeling was introduced as an extension to Dual Depth Peeling to address the issue of rendering translucent geometry intermixed with volumes in VTK (Visualization Toolkit). It was implemented in vtkDualDepthPeelingPass and exposed via vtkRenderer::SetUseDepthPeelingForVolumes. The technique was discussed in a Kitware blog post in June 2017 by Alvaro Sanchez and Allison Vacanti. Rendering translucent geometry intermixed with volumes, https://www.kitware.com/rendering-translucent-geometry-intermixed-with-volumes/, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Layer Separation Heuristic
head: Feature Peeling
body: The Layer Separation Heuristic determines optimal split points along a ray in multi-layer volume rendering to separate high-quality raycasting from lower-cost image warping. It solves the problem of identifying the main visual effect of light attenuation, which frequently occurs in the middle of a ray interval rather than at entry or exit. Unlike simple depth-based splitting, this heuristic identifies main visual effects along the ray, preserving depth cues and providing better visual approximation for transparent volumes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray sampled at discrete steps through the volume, where each sample provides voxel opacity \alphai and accumulated transmittance Ti. Output: A set of depth values defining layer separation points along the ray. Data Structures: The method operates on a 1D array of sample values along the ray, requiring no complex spatial data structures beyond the standard ray marching buffer. Steps: 1. Evaluate Criteria: For each sample point i along the ray, calculate a score using either the maximum opacity criterion (\alphai) or the maximum color impact criterion (Ci = \alphai \times Ti). 2. Identify Local Maxima: Find local maxima in the score sequence, where a point i is a local maximum if its score is greater than or equal to its immediate neighbors. 3. Resolve Discrete Spans: If a local maximum spans several consecutive sample points, select the median index of these points as the separation depth. 4. Select Layers: Choose the top N separation points based on their scores, with the Maximum Color Impact method generally preferred for slight visual quality advantages. Formulas: Color Impact: Ci = \alphai \cdot Ti Where: \alphai is the opacity of the voxel at sample i. Ti is the transmittance (remaining opacity along the ray segment) from the camera to sample i. Parameters: Number of Layers (N): A fixed integer determined in advance. Evaluations tested layer counts from 2 to 9. Criterion Selection: Binary choice between "Max Opacity" and "Max Color Impact". Pitfalls: Fixed Layer Count: Layers must be allocated in advance. If the heuristic is overly sensitive, it may allocate too many layers to features close to the camera, leaving distant features underrepresented. Heuristic Failure: The heuristic is fixed and cannot adapt to dynamic scene complexity; insufficient layers or poor distribution lead to visual artifacts. Depth Cues: Simple entry or exit depth choices fail to capture main light attenuation effects occurring in the middle of the ray interval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findlayerseparation(rays, numlayers, criterion="colorimpact"): """ Finds layer separation points for a batch of rays. rays: List of Ray objects, each containing a list of sample points. numlayers: Integer, number of layers to separate. criterion: String, "opacity" or "colorimpact". Returns: List of lists, where each inner list contains depth values for that ray. """ separationpoints = [] for ray in rays: points = ray.samples if not points: separationpoints.append([]) continue scores = [] for i, point in enumerate(points): alpha = point.opacity Ti = point.accumulatedtransmittance # Transmittance from camera to this point if criterion == "colorimpact": score = alpha Ti else: # maximumopacity score = alpha scores.append((score, point.depth, i)) # Find local maxima with proper boundary handling localmaxima = [] for i in range(len(scores)): ismax = True if i > 0 and scores[i][0] < scores[i-1][0]: ismax = False if i < len(scores) - 1 and scores[i][0] < scores[i+1][0]: ismax = False if ismax: localmaxima.append(scores[i]) # Resolve plateaus: if consecutive points share the max score, pick median index resolvedmaxima = [] if localmaxima: currentgroup = [localmaxima[0]] for j in range(1, len(localmaxima)): if localmaxima[j][2] == currentgroup[-1][2] + 1: currentgroup.append(localmaxima[j]) else: medianidx = currentgroup[len(currentgroup)//2][2] resolvedmaxima.append((max(currentgroup, key=lambda x: x[0])[0], next(p.depth for p in points if p.index == medianidx), medianidx)) currentgroup = [localmaxima[j]] medianidx = currentgroup[len(currentgroup)//2][2] resolvedmaxima.append((max(currentgroup, key=lambda x: x[0])[0], next(p.depth for p in points if p.index == medianidx), medianidx)) # Select top N layers based on score resolvedmaxima.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) selected = resolvedmaxima[:numlayers] depths = [m[1] for m in selected] separationpoints.append(depths) return separationpoints Groups volume elements by distance and opacity to ensure consistent shading, overcoming single-image warping limitations. Assigns high-quality raycasting to close layers and warping to distant ones, exploiting depth proximity for quality allocation. Performance: Enables multi-frame rate rendering by allowing high-quality raycasting for a subset of layers while warping the rest. Layer images can be transferred separately to the fast node as soon as completed, reducing latency. Strengths: Preserves depth cues better than single surface approaches; outperforms single layered image warps for transparent transfer functions (e.g., MANIX dataset). Limitations: Visual quality suffers if layers are not distributed well (e.g., too many close to camera); fixed number of layers limits adaptability; quality gain is less significant for opaque transfer functions revealing bones (e.g., VIX dataset). When to Use: Transparent volumes where depth cues are critical and view-dependent lighting is needed. When Not to Use: Opaque volumes with simple structures where the quality difference is negligible. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method was introduced in the context of Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering by S. Hauswiesner, D. Kalkofen, and D. Schmalstieg. It addresses the limitations of single-layer image warping by separating volume layers based on visual impact rather than uniform depth intervals. The approach was evaluated on datasets such as MANIX (head CT) and VIX (foot). Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/egpgv.egpgv10.019-026, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Layered Image Warping
head: Feature Peeling-based Layered Warping
body: Layered Image Warping is a technique for transparent volume rendering that overcomes the limitations of single-image warping by representing the inner structure of an object as multiple partial images, called layers. It solves the problem of preserving depth cues and handling view-dependent lighting in transparent volumes, which cannot be shaded correctly using a single map of normal vectors. Unlike sibling methods that use uniform or heuristic-based splitting, this method groups volume elements by distance from the camera and similar opacity to ensure consistent shading. Inputs: A volume dataset, a ray path through the volume, and a smoothing kernel for opacity. Outputs: A set of layer images, each associated with a depth value for warping. Data Structures: Layer: A 2D image buffer storing color and depth values for a specific subset of the volume. Ray Profile: A 1D array of opacity values sampled along the ray, smoothed to detect features. Algorithm Steps: 1. Smoothing: Smooth the opacity values along the ray to reduce noise. Let oi be the opacity at sample i. The smoothed opacity \hat{o}i is computed using a smoothing kernel. 2. Feature Detection: Detect local minima and maxima of the smoothed opacity \hat{o}i along the ray. 3. Layer Separation (Feature Peeling): Use the detected extrema to separate the ray into segments (layers). Noise Suppression: Suppress layers that have a total opacity of less than 10%. This threshold prevents the creation of layers from noise. Feature Preservation: Avoid separating connected, highly opaque regions, as they likely belong to the same feature. 4. Depth Value Selection: For each pixel in a layer image, determine a depth value representing the ray interval. Two methods are evaluated to locate the "main effect" of light attenuation within the layer's interval: Method A (Max Opacity): Select the point with the maximum opacity after classification within the layer's segment. Method B (Max Color Impact): Select the point with the maximum impact on color, calculated as the voxel's opacity multiplied by the remaining opacity along the ray segment. Method B is preferred for slight advantages. 5. Rendering: Render each layer independently. The depth value associated with each pixel allows for correct warping and compositing of the layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def layeredimagewarping(raysamples, smoothingkernel, minopacitythreshold=0.1): """ raysamples: list of tuples (depth, opacity, color) along the ray. smoothingkernel: function returning smoothed list of opacities. minopacitythreshold: minimum opacity for a layer to be valid (default 0.1). """ # Step 1: Smooth opacity opacities = [s[1] for s in raysamples] smoothedopacities = smoothingkernel(opacities) # Step 2: Detect local minima and maxima extremaindices = findlocalextrema(smoothedopacities) # Step 3: Separate layers using extrema layers = [] currentstart = 0 for idx in extremaindices: segment = raysamples[currentstart:idx + 1] segmentopacity = sum(s[1] for s in segment) # Noise suppression: require at least 10% opacity if segmentopacity < minopacitythreshold: currentstart = idx + 1 continue # Feature preservation: avoid splitting connected, highly opaque regions # The sources do not specify the exact heuristic for connected opaque regions. # A typical implementation would check if segmentopacity > 0.9 and merge with the next segment. # Step 4: Depth Value Selection (Method B: Max Color Impact) # Calculate transmittance (remaining opacity) before each sample in segment transmittance = 1.0 maximpact = -1.0 bestdepth = segment[0][0] for s in segment: impact = s[1] transmittance if impact > maximpact: maximpact = impact bestdepth = s[0] transmittance = (1.0 - s[1]) # Step 5: Compositing (Standard front-to-back alpha blending) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 for s in segment: c, o = s[2], s[1] color = [color[j] + c[j] o (1.0 - alpha) for j in range(3)] alpha = alpha + o (1.0 - alpha) layers.append({ 'segment': segment, 'depth': bestdepth, 'color': color }) currentstart = idx + 1 # Handle last segment if currentstart < len(raysamples): segment = raysamples[currentstart:] segmentopacity = sum(s[1] for s in segment) if segmentopacity >= minopacitythreshold: transmittance = 1.0 maximpact = -1.0 bestdepth = segment[0][0] for s in segment: impact = s[1] transmittance if impact > maximpact: maximpact = impact bestdepth = s[0] transmittance = (1.0 - s[1]) color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alpha = 0.0 for s in segment: c, o = s[2], s[1] color = [color[j] + c[j] o (1.0 - alpha) for j in range(3)] alpha = alpha + o (1.0 - alpha) layers.append({ 'segment': segment, 'depth': bestdepth, 'color': color }) return layers def findlocalextrema(values): """Returns indices of local minima and maxima.""" indices = [] for i in range(1, len(values) - 1): if (values[i] > values[i - 1] and values[i] > values[i + 1]) or \ (values[i] < values[i - 1] and values[i] < values[i + 1]): indices.append(i) return indices Parameters: Minimum Opacity Threshold: 10% (0.1). Layers with less than this opacity are suppressed to reduce noise. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noise: Without smoothing and the 10% threshold, noise can create spurious layers. Connected Opaque Regions: Highly opaque connected regions should not be split, as they belong to the same feature. Depth Selection: Using entrance or exit depth can fail to capture the main effect of light attenuation, which may occur in the middle of the ray interval. Performance: On a volumetric foot dataset (VIX), increasing the number of layers from 2 to 9 increases the average absolute pixel error (visual quality degradation) from ~0.2 to ~0.6, but also increases the framerate from ~6 fps to ~9 fps. Strengths: Provides efficient cues about the inner structure of an object and handles view-dependent lighting better than single-image warping. Limitations: Increasing layers degrades visual quality (higher pixel error). Requires deferred shading for correct view-dependent lighting. Origin: The method is based on the idea of feature peeling [MMG07] and was introduced in the context of Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering. History: It was developed to address the limitations of single image warping for transparent volumes. Usage: Used in multi-frame rate volume rendering to improve performance while maintaining visual quality. name: Distribution by Depth Layer
head: Adaptive Layer Distribution, Quality/Performance Tradeoff via Layer Count
body: Distribution by Depth Layer is a workload distribution method that assigns high-quality raycasting to the first n depth layers (representing close structures) and multi-frame rate image warping to the remaining layers. It exploits the observation that close structures contribute more to the final image than distant ones. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by using depth proximity as the primary heuristic for quality allocation, whereas Layered Image Warping focuses on the warping mechanism itself. Inputs: Volume dataset. Camera position and orientation. Target minimum frame rate (FPS{min}). Hardware configuration: a fast GPU and a slow GPU. Outputs: Final rendered image. Dynamic number of raycasted layers (n). Data Structures: Depth layers extracted from the volume dataset, ordered by distance from the camera. Parameters: n: The number of front layers to raycast. FPS{min}: The desired minimum frame rate. Steps: 1. Initial Setup: Determine the total number of layers N in the volume dataset. Initialize n to a starting value. 2. Layer Assignment: Assign layers 0 to n-1 (the closest n layers) to be rendered via raycasting on the fast GPU. Assign layers n to N-1 (the remaining back layers) to be rendered via multi-frame rate image warping on the slow GPU. 3. Rendering: Perform raycasting for the front n layers. Perform image warping for the back N-n layers. Composite the results into the final image. 4. Performance Monitoring: Measure the current frame rate FPS{curr}. 5. Adaptive Adjustment: If FPS{curr} < FPS{min}, immediately decrease n by 1. Periodically attempt to render with n+1 layers to check if improved quality is possible. 6. Repeat: Return to Step 2 for the next frame or update cycle. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distributionbydepthlayer(volume, camera, fpsmin): # Extract depth layers and sort by distance from camera (closest first) layers = sorted(volume.getdepthlayers(), key=lambda layer: layer.distancefrom(camera)) totallayers = len(layers) # Initial guess for n (number of raycasted layers) n = max(1, totallayers // 2) # Standard initialization framecount = 0 while True: # 1. Assign layers raycastlayers = layers[:n] warplayers = layers[n:] # 2. Render # Raycast close layers frontimage = raycast(raycastlayers, camera) # Warp back layers backimage = imagewarp(warplayers, camera, frontimage) # Composite finalimage = composite(frontimage, backimage) # 3. Monitor Frame Rate currentfps = 1.0 / getframetime() # 4. Adaptive Adjustment if currentfps < fpsmin: # Decrease n immediately to improve performance if n > 0: n -= 1 else: # Periodically check if higher quality is possible # Using a simple frame counter for periodicity if framecount % 30 == 0 and n + 1 <= totallayers: # Try rendering with n+1 layers testfront = raycast(layers[:n+1], camera) testback = imagewarp(layers[n+1:], camera, testfront) testfps = 1.0 / getframetime() if testfps >= fpsmin: n += 1 # Else: keep n as is yield finalimage framecount += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Input: If n=0, all layers are warped, potentially losing all high-frequency detail from close structures. If n=N, all layers are raycasted, potentially missing the performance benefit of warping. Precision: The transition between raycasting and warping at layer n may introduce visible seams if the warping accuracy is insufficient for the depth discontinuity. Boundary: The number of raycasted layers cannot exceed the total number of layers N. Extends this concept by distributing workload between GPUs to replace some image warping with raycasting for higher quality beyond strict node assignment. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of raycasted layers n. Performance (FPS) degrades linearly as n increases. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the volume dataset and intermediate buffers for raycasting and warping. Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Evaluation on a scene rotated 90 degrees showed that reconstruction error converges to the reference image as more layers are raycasted. Performance (FPS) degrades linearly as more layers are raycasted. The benefit of warping more than 6 layers vanishes. Strengths: Automatically adjusts quality/performance tradeoff based on current frame rate. Exploits the perceptual importance of close structures. Limitations: Requires two GPUs (fast and slow) for optimal implementation as described. The "vanishing benefit" after 6 layers suggests diminishing returns for high layer counts. Originated in the paper "Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering" by S. Hauswiesner, D. Kalkofen, and D. Schmalstieg (2010). The method is part of a broader framework for multi-frame rate rendering, aiming to provide the best quality for a given maximum latency by dynamically adjusting the rendering workload. name: Advanced Workload Distribution Schemes
head: Adaptive GPU Workload Distribution, Flexible Workload Distribution
body: Advanced Workload Distribution Schemes are methods that distribute rendering workload between a fast GPU (performing raycasting or image warping) and a slow GPU (performing raycasting) to improve visual quality beyond strict node assignment by replacing some image warping with raycasting. Unlike separation planes which create perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading approximation and poor adaptation to scene interest, flexible schemes adapt to focus regions, segmentations, or depth importance. The core principle is the relaxation of strict workload assignment between fast and slow nodes. When viewport resolution and sampling rate are small enough, raycasting on modern GPUs can be acceptably fast, allowing visual quality to be improved by replacing some of the image warping with raycasting. This approach requires special attention to the amount of workload shifted, as it reduces the frame rate of the fast node. The latency compensation step of the system is extended by raycasting to handle these dynamic assignments. Distribution by Quality Maps is a workload distribution method that uses a quality map to identify badly reconstructed pixels (mostly from disocclusions or undersampling during image warping) and replaces them with high-quality raycasting. Step: On the fast node: 1. Use image warping to reconstruct m layers. 2. Project the volume’s bounding geometry to the screen. 3. Iterate through the closest m layers for each pixel covered by the projection. 4. If layers are empty, raycast this pixel. Parameter: m: The number of empty layers required per pixel to classify the pixel as disoccluded. A lower m switches to raycasting more frequently. Pitfall: In layered image warping, completely empty pixels are rare, but holes in foremost layers commonly happen and disocclude content from back layers, resulting in unsatisfying reconstructions. The parameter m helps steer the quality vs. performance tradeoff. Comparison: Performance scales with frame-to-frame coherence: large viewpoint motion induces more raycasting (lower performance), while slow motion allows more warped fragments. Unlike fixed layer counts, this is user-input dependent. Origin: S. Hauswiesner, D. Kalkofen, and D. Schmalstieg, "Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering" (2010). The method addresses the limitations of traditional parallel raycasting algorithms that divide workload by separation planes in screen space or object space (sort-first or sort-last), which often lead to perceivable boundaries due to deferred shading from warped images being only an approximation to per-sample phong shading. These regions do not adapt well to what is really interesting in a scene, such as focus regions, segmentations, or magic lenses. The authors propose a more flexible workload distribution to account for the fact that features close to the current viewpoint are more important and better perceivable than distant features. name: Temporal and Procedural Techniques
body: This family encompasses techniques that generate volumetric data or manage rendering performance dynamically, rather than relying solely on static, pre-computed 3D textures. It addresses the limitations of static data in terms of memory overhead, resolution limits, and interactivity. The methods differ from standard direct volume ray casting by either computing density analytically via procedural noise functions during the ray march, applying spatial distortions to rays for focus+context, modeling deformations via inverse displacement mapping, or dynamically selecting between multi-frame rate warping and parallel raycasting based on workload complexity. The family shares the fundamental ray casting loop structure defined in Direct volume ray casting, but modifies the sampling stage or the rendering pipeline control flow. 1. Procedural Evaluation: Instead of sampling a fixed 3D texture, density V(\mathbf{p}) is computed on-the-fly using mathematical functions evaluated at the sample point \mathbf{p}. 2. Dynamic Ray Trajectories: Rays may be distorted or redirected based on lens parameters or displacement fields, requiring custom intersection logic with the volume bounding box. 3. Adaptive Rendering: The system may switch between rendering paradigms based on runtime metrics like resolution and sampling rate. Uses 3D Worley noise for density generation and light maps for scattering. Chosen for real-time animated smoke effects where memory for high-res textures is prohibitive. Applies spatially varying ray distortions for focus+context. Chosen when visualizing specific regions of interest within large datasets without occlusion. Evaluates procedural noise (FBM/Worley) directly in the fragment shader. Chosen for infinite resolution clouds and seamless animation without pre-computation. Models interactive deformations (cuts, peeling) using inverse displacement mapping. Chosen for dynamic geometric changes without mesh re-tessellation. Hybrid system switching between image-based warping and parallel raycasting. Chosen to optimize the trade-off between latency and quality based on current workload complexity. The techniques originate from the need to render complex, dynamic volumetric phenomena and interactive deformations that cannot be efficiently stored in static voxel grids. Procedural noise methods leverage the parallelism of GPUs to compute density analytically. Lens techniques extend standard projection models to support interactive exploration. Displacement mapping adapts surface modeling concepts to volume data for interactive editing. Multi-frame rate rendering addresses the performance bottlenecks of high-resolution raycasting in distributed or multi-GPU environments.
