name: Volumetric Smoke Rendering with Worley Noise and Light Maps
head: Unity Volumetric Smoke, Volumetric Smoke Rendering
body: A real-time volumetric rendering technique for smoke implemented in Unity, combining 3D Worley noise for density generation, ray marching with adaptive step sizes, and front-to-back color blending to simulate light scattering and god rays. It uses Compute Shaders for texture generation and a vertex/fragment shader pipeline for rendering. Inputs: Camera position, view direction, volume bounding box (AABB), light direction, light color, noise parameters (octaves, persistence, lacunarity, amplitude, size), and simulation parameters. Outputs: Rendered smoke image with alpha channel. Compute Shader Buffers: StructuredBuffer<float2> featurepointsbuffer2D: Buffer of 2D feature points for 2D Worley noise. RWTexture2D<float> noisetexture2D: Read-write 2D texture for storing 2D Worley noise. StructuredBuffer<float3> featurepointsbuffer3D: Buffer of 3D feature points for 3D Worley noise. RWTexture3D<float> noisetexture3D: Read-write 3D texture for storing 3D Worley noise. RWTexture2D<float> slicetexture: Read-write 2D texture for storing a slice of the 3D noise texture. RWTexture3D<float> lightdensitytexture: Read-write 3D texture for storing light density. Merged Texture: uniontexture: RenderTexture with format R8G8B8A8UNorm, dimension Tex3D, size maxsize x maxsize x maxsize (where maxsize is the maximum of worleynoisesize, lightmapresolution, and solver.densityrt dimensions). enableRandomWrite is true. MergedSample Struct: Contains four floats: noise, detail, light, mask. 1. Worley Noise Generation (Compute Shaders): Generate noise by iterating over neighboring cells to find the minimum distance to feature points. python def addworleynoise2D(id, noisetexturesizex, noisetexturesizey, cellsizex, cellsizey, featurepointsbuffer2D, noisestrength, noisetexture2D): if id.x >= noisetexturesizex or id.y >= noisetexturesizey: return cellcountx = noisetexturesizex // cellsizex cellcounty = noisetexturesizey // cellsizey texturecoordinates = (float(id.x), float(id.y)) cellcoordinates = (int(texturecoordinates[0] // cellsizex), int(texturecoordinates[1] // cellsizey)) localcoordinates = (texturecoordinates[0] / cellsizex - cellcoordinates[0], texturecoordinates[1] / cellsizey - cellcoordinates[1]) mindistance = 1.0 for offsety in range(-1, 2): for offsetx in range(-1, 2): neighbourcell = (cellcoordinates[0] + offsetx, cellcoordinates[1] + offsety) wrappedcell = (neighbourcell[0] % cellcountx, neighbourcell[1] % cellcounty) cellindex = wrappedcell[0] + wrappedcell[1] cellcountx featurepointoffset = (neighbourcell[0] + featurepointsbuffer2D[cellindex].x, neighbourcell[1] + featurepointsbuffer2D[cellindex].y) dist = distance(cellcoordinates + localcoordinates, featurepointoffset) mindistance = min(mindistance, dist) noisetexture2D[id.xy] += (1.0 - mindistance) noisestrength The 3D kernel (addworleynoise3D) follows the same logic over a 3×3×3 grid of neighboring cells. 2. Octave Generation: Loop from octave = 0 to octavecount - 1. Set worleynoisedivisionsize to (size, size, size). Call computeworleynoise3Ddetail(amplitude). Update amplitude = persistence. Update size = Mathf.CeilToInt(size / lacunarity). 3. Texture Merging: Merge textures into a single uniontexture for efficient sampling. Find kernel unitetextures. Set uniforms: unitedtexturesize, noisetexturesize, detailtexturesize, lighttexturesize, masktexturesize. Bind textures: unitedtexture, noisetexturemerge, detailtexturemerge, lighttexturemerge, masktexturemerge. Dispatch kernel with thread groups ceil(maxsize/8). 4. Ray Marching (Vertex/Fragment Shaders): Vertex shader computes world position, screen position, and camera view direction for each vertex of the rendering quad/plane. Fragment shader calculates local camera position and normalized view direction relative to the volume object. Ray-AABB intersection computes entry point (hit.x) and distance inside the box (hit.y) for the ray originating at the camera: python def RayIntersectAABB(boundsmin, boundsmax, rayorigin, raydir): invraydir = 1.0 / raydir t0 = (boundsmin - rayorigin) invraydir t1 = (boundsmax - rayorigin) invraydir tmin = min(t0, t1) tmax = max(t0, t1) dsta = max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y), tmin.z) dstb = min(tmax.x, min(tmax.y, tmax.z)) dsttobox = max(0.0, dsta) dstinsidebox = max(0.0, dstb - dsttobox) return (dsttobox, dstinsidebox) Ray start point is calculated as camera position + view direction entry distance. At each step, the merged texture is sampled to get noise, detail, and mask values. Non-united path: Calculate minimalizedobjectscale = objectscale.xyz / max(max(objectscale.x, objectscale.y), objectscale.z). Scale texCoord by minimalizedobjectscale. Sample noise from DensityTexture at scaled texCoord + 0.5. Sample detail from DensityDetailTexture at scaled texCoord + 0.5. If uselightmap, sample light from LightTexture at scaled texCoord + 0.5; else set light to 0.65f. Unscale texCoord. Sample mask from MaskTexture at original texCoord + 0.5. United path: Calculate final texCoord = fmod(texCoord + 0.5 + textureoffset / noisetexturesize + 1, 1). Sample data from UnitedTexture. Set sampledata.noise = data.r, detail = data.g, light = data.b, mask = data.a 32.0f. Process sampled values to calculate density. If density is below densitythreshold, replace with godraysstrength to allow light to pass through empty areas for god ray effects. If density is near godraysstrength threshold and light intensity is high, boost light intensity by 1.5x. Blend color using front-to-back blending: python def BlendFTB(color, newcolor): color.rgb += (1.0 - color.a) newcolor.a newcolor.rgb color.a += (1.0 - color.a) newcolor.a return color Break loop if accumulated alpha reaches 0.96. Return final surface color with alpha clamped to 1.0, and RGB channels divided by alpha. 5. Update Loop: Set useunitedtexture and uselightmap. If iteratetime, call solver.step(Time.deltaTime 1000). In FixedUpdate, set material textures and parameters. If uselightmap and counter <= 0, call computelightmap() and reset counter. If iteratezcounter <= 0, if iterateoverz, increment displaying3dslice modulo worleynoisesize.z and reset counter. densitythreshold: Threshold for density values; if density is below this, it is treated as empty/god ray area. godraysstrength: Constant density value assigned to empty areas to allow god rays to shine through. lightdecay: Exponential decay factor for light intensity over distance. densitysamplecount: Number of steps for density sampling in the ray march. lightsamplecount: Number of steps for light sampling. lightsampleperdensitysample: Ratio of light samples to density samples. lightcolor: RGB color of the light source. lightdirection: Direction vector of the light source. noisestrength: Multiplier for the Worley noise output. globallightdirection: Direction of the global light. globallightcolor: Color of the global light. godraysintensity: Intensity of the god rays effect. stepsize: Step size for light sampling. densitythreashold: Threshold for density in light sampling. octavecount: Number of octaves for Worley noise generation. Default: 5. persistance: Amplitude multiplier per octave. Default: 0.5f. lacurancy: Frequency multiplier per octave. Default: 2.0f. amplitude: Initial amplitude for Worley noise. Default: 0.075f. size: Initial resolution for Worley noise texture. Default: 16. useunitedtexture: Boolean flag to switch between merged texture sampling and individual texture sampling. Default: 0. uselightmap: Boolean flag to enable light map sampling. Default: 0. textureoffset: Vector3 parameter for noise animation offset. Calculated as (0, (-timems 0.003f worleynoisesize.y % worleynoisesize.y), 0). noisetexturesize: Vector3 parameter for Worley noise texture dimensions. lighttexturesize: Vector3 parameter for light map texture dimensions. masktexturesize: Vector3 parameter for density mask texture dimensions. objectscale: Vector4 parameter for object scaling, used to normalize texture coordinates. iteratezevery: Integer parameter controlling how often to iterate through Z slices. Default: 1. updatelightmapevery: Integer parameter controlling how often to update the light map. Default: 1. timems: Float parameter for time in milliseconds, used for animation. Range: 0 to 128. Texture Coordinate Wrapping: The united texture sampling uses fmod with +1 to handle negative coordinates and ensure wrapping within 0,1). Mask Scaling: The mask value from the united texture is scaled by 32.0f. Light Map Fallback: If uselightmap is false, the light value is hardcoded to 0.65f. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of ray marching steps (densitysamplecount) and the complexity of the Worley noise generation (number of octaves and grid size). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the 3D noise texture and light map texture. Performance: Real-time performance is achieved by using Compute Shaders for preprocessing and optimizing the ray marching loop with early exit conditions. Strengths: Efficient real-time rendering, dynamic smoke effects, support for god rays and light scattering. Limitations: Quality depends on the resolution of the noise textures and the number of ray marching steps. This technique is implemented in Unity projects for real-time volumetric smoke effects, leveraging Compute Shaders for preprocessing and a standard vertex/fragment [shader for rendering. It builds upon the principles of procedural volumetric rendering and ray marching. furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, https://github.com/furkanunsal42/VolumetricSmoke, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: GPU-accelerated ray casting with volumetric lenses
head: Magic Lens Implementation, Obstruction-free lens, Ray casting with lens distortion, Volumetric lens ray casting, obstruction-free fish-eye lens
body: A volumetric visualization technique that modifies ray paths to push away occluding geometry, creating a magnified, unobstructed view of a target region while preserving the surrounding context. It solves the problem of inspecting dense volumes where targets and occluders share similar density values, a scenario where standard density filtering fails because it removes both the target and the occluder. Unlike standard Direct Volume Ray Casting (DVR), which uses straight rays, this method distorts ray trajectories based on lens parameters to "open a hole" in the volume. The method modifies a standard DVR ray caster to incorporate a new ray definition, the lens effect, and local per-voxel Phong lighting parameters. It is implemented as a multi-pass fragment program pipeline on the GPU. Inputs: 3D texture containing volume data (density, gradient, color); camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix); lens parameters (position, size, magnification, active state); bounding box of the volumetric object. Outputs: 2D image buffer with the lens-distorted volume rendering. The implementation relies on standard GPU fragment program structures. Specific internal data structures beyond standard uniforms and texture samplers are not detailed in the sources. lensactive (boolean/int): Controls if the lens is active. lensposition (vec2): Normalized screen coordinates (0.0 to 1.0) for the lens center. lenssize (vec2): Normalized size of the lens area. lensmagnification (float): Magnification factor for the lens view. Animation parameters \alpha and \beta: Used to interpolate between straight-line classical DVR (\alpha=1, \beta=0) and the actual user-set lens values. The rendering pipeline consists of four passes for magnifier and angular lenses, with variations for feature-based and sampling-rate-based lenses. 1. Pass 1: RayDirection Calculate the ray direction for each fragment based on the viewport and lens parameters. This step determines whether a ray goes through the lens, hits a feature of interest, or calculates the distance to the lens center to achieve specific rendering effects. Feature-based lens: Adds a preliminary pass RayLensBorder before Pass 2. Sampling-rate-based lens: Replaces Pass 1 with RayStartPoints. 2. Pass 2: RayTfrontback Compute the intersections of each ray with the bounding box of the volumetric object. Store the distances from the ray start point to the front and back intersection points, denoted as t{front} and t{back}. Note: Standard OpenGL front/back face drawing cannot be used because ray directions are not always orthogonal or perspective; custom intersection calculation is required. 3. Pass 3: RayCasting Implement a ray traversal algorithm for a given step size. Access volume data (density, gradient, or color) stored in 3D textures. The ray direction from Pass 1 and the interval [t{front}, t{back}] from Pass 2 define the intersection segment. 4. Pass 4: Rendering Composite the accumulated color and opacity to produce the final image. The sources do not provide explicit pseudocode for the lens distortion formulas or the complete shader pipeline. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the standard DVR traversal with the described four-pass structure, fixing the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) intersection logic to correctly handle negative and zero ray direction components. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeraydirection(fragmentcoord, screensize, lensposition, lenssize, lensmagnification, isinsidelens): # Convert screen coordinates to normalized device coordinates ndcx = (fragmentcoord.x / screensize.x) 2.0 - 1.0 ndcy = -((fragmentcoord.y / screensize.y) 2.0 - 1.0) # Unproject to world space ray direction raydir = unprojectray(ndcx, ndcy) # If lens is active and fragment is inside lens area, distort the ray direction if isinsidelens: # Specific lens distortion formula not provided in sources # Modifies ray paths to push away occluding geometry raydir = applylensdistortion(raydir, fragmentcoord, lensposition, lenssize, lensmagnification) return raydir def computerayintersections(rayorigin, raydir, bboxmin, bboxmax): # Compute intersection of ray with axis-aligned bounding box # Returns tfront and tback # Correctly handles negative and zero direction components t1 = [(bboxmin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] if raydir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] t2 = [(bboxmax[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] if raydir[i] != 0 else float('inf') for i in range(3)] tmin = max(min(t1[0], t2[0]), min(t1[1], t2[1]), min(t1[2], t2[2])) tmax = min(max(t1[0], t2[0]), max(t1[1], t2[1]), max(t1[2], t2[2])) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: return -1.0, -1.0 # No intersection return tmin, tmax def raycast(rayorigin, raydir, tfront, tback, volumetexture, stepsize): color = vec4(0.0) alpha = 0.0 t = tfront while t < tback: samplepoint = rayorigin + t raydir density = samplevolume(volumetexture, samplepoint) # lightcolor = computephonglighting(samplepoint, density) # contribution = lightcolor (1.0 - alpha) color += contribution density alpha += density (1.0 - alpha) if alpha >= 1.0: break t += stepsize return color, alpha def render(): for each fragment: raydir = computeraydirection(fragmentcoord, screensize, lensposition, lenssize, lensmagnification, isinsidelens) rayorigin = computerayorigin(cameraparams) # tfront, tback = computerayintersections(rayorigin, raydir, bboxmin, bboxmax) if tfront > 0: finalcolor, = raycast(rayorigin, raydir, tfront, tback, volumetexture, stepsize) writetoframebuffer(finalcolor) Ray Intersection: Standard OpenGL front/back face drawing cannot be used because ray directions are not always orthogonal or perspective; custom intersection calculation is required. Animation: When activating the lens, an animation plays forward to gradually open the lens, with decreasing speed at the end to show where occluders go. When deactivating, the animation plays in reverse. Performance: Requires GPU features such as loop, early termination, and branches. Performance: Achieves 15 frames per second on a PC with 16 GB RAM and a GeForce GTX TITAN X card for volumes up to 512^3 voxels at a 1900 \times 1200 pixels screen resolution. Hardware Requirements: Requires modern GPUs with support for loops, early termination, and branches (e.g., NVIDIA GeForce 6800 or later). Strengths: Outperforms standard DVR and transfer function manipulation when occluders and targets share similar density values. User study with 8 airport security specialists showed predominantly positive Likert scale ratings for ease of use and effectiveness in both untargeted and targeted exploration. Limitations: Not suitable for carry-on baggage inspection due to strict time limits of 15 to 20 seconds; better suited for checked baggage where inspection windows extend up to 3 minutes. Scaling: Performance is dependent on GPU capabilities and volume size. Large datasets may require downsampling for smoother performance. The technique was implemented by modifying a standard DVR ray caster publicly available in the NVIDIA CUDA SDK. It was developed to address challenges in volumetric data exploration, particularly in scenarios where automatic segmentation is not optimal or where density filtering is ineffective. Baggage Inspection: Evaluated on a 283 \times 189 \times 344 voxel airport CT scan dataset to reveal objects hidden among materials of similar density. Fluid Flow Visualization: Applied to a 500^3 voxel scalar volume converted from 4595 streamlines (183K sample points) using GPU-accelerated kernel density estimation. Medical Imaging: Applied to a 512 \times 512 \times 110 voxel contrast chest CT scan to examine a tumor obscured by tissue of similar density. name: Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering (GPU Shader)
head: CloudRendererProcedural, Procedural GPU Implementation
body: This method renders volumetric clouds by evaluating density and lighting on-the-fly within a GPU fragment shader, eliminating the need for pre-computed 3D texture lookups or CPU-side ray marching. It solves the performance bottleneck of traditional volume rendering by using procedural noise (specifically Fractal Brownian Motion) to generate cloud structure and a simplified Henyey-Greenstein phase function for scattering. Unlike sibling methods that rely on fixed volumetric textures or CPU execution, this approach allows for dynamic, infinite-resolution cloud features and real-time animation via wind parameters, making it suitable for real-time engines like Unity. The method operates as a post-process or camera-attached component that intercepts the scene color and overlays procedurally generated clouds. It builds on the ray casting loop structure defined in Direct volume ray casting but replaces texture sampling with procedural noise evaluation and uses a simplified lighting model. Inputs: originalColour: The background scene color sampled from the main render texture at the current pixel UV. rayDirection: The direction vector from the camera to the pixel, derived from screen space. CameraWorldPosition: The world-space position of the camera. CloudVolumeMinBound, CloudVolumeMaxBound: Axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) defining the cloud volume in world space. SunDirection: Normalized direction vector to the sun. SunColour: RGB color of the sun. Parameters: AbsorptionCoefficient, ScatterFactor, Density Threshold, Cloud Scale, Octave Count, Wind Speed. Outputs: finalColour: The composited color of the cloud and background. The implementation passes all state via shader constants or uniforms. 1. Retrieve Background: Sample the original scene color at the current pixel coordinates: C{bg} = \text{tex2D}(\text{MainTex}, uv) 2. Initialize Ray: Set ray origin \mathbf{o} to CameraWorldPosition. Normalize the ray direction \mathbf{d} to prevent stepping errors due to large unnormalized values: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\text{input.rayDirection}) 3. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute the entry and exit distances of the ray with the cloud volume AABB using the slab method: Calculate intersection distances for each axis i \in \{x, y, z\}: t{i,entry} = \frac{\text{MinBound}i - oi}{di}, \quad t{i,exit} = \frac{\text{MaxBound}i - oi}{di} Determine global entry and exit: t{entry} = \max(t{x,entry}, t{y,entry}, t{z,entry}) t{exit} = \min(t{x,exit}, t{y,exit}, t{z,exit}) If t{entry} > t{exit}, the ray misses the volume; return C{bg}. 4. March Density and Accumulate Brightness: Initialize brightness = 0, densityTotal = 0, distanceTravelled = 0. Set step size (e.g., 20.0 units) and step limit (e.g., 64 iterations). Start ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \times t{entry}. Loop for i from 0 to stepLimit: If distanceTravelled > t{exit}, break. Advance position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{d} \times \text{stepSize}. Calculate world-scaled coordinates for noise sampling: \mathbf{p}{scaled} = \mathbf{p} \times \text{CloudScale} Procedural Density (FBM): Initialize worleyDensity = 0, amplitude = 1.0, frequency = 1.0, amplitudeTotal = 0. Loop for octave from 0 to OctaveCount - 1: Sample noise (e.g., Worley) at \mathbf{p}{scaled} \times \text{frequency}. Add to density: worleyDensity += noiseValue \times amplitude. Accumulate amplitude: amplitudeTotal += amplitude. Scale amplitude: amplitude \times= 0.5. Scale frequency: frequency \times= 2.0. Normalize density: \text{density} = \begin{cases} \frac{\text{worleyDensity}}{\text{amplitudeTotal}} & \text{if } \text{amplitudeTotal} > 0 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Lighting Calculation: Calculate sun transmittance by marching towards the sun from \mathbf{p} (see MarchLight below). Calculate camera transmittance for the current ray segment. Calculate scattering factor using Henyey-Greenstein: \text{scatter} = \frac{1 - g^2}{4\pi (1 + g^2 - 2g \cos \theta)^{3/2}} where g = \text{ScatterFactor} and \cos \theta = \text{dot}(\mathbf{d}, \text{SunDirection}). Accumulate brightness: \text{brightness} = \text{brightness} + \text{density} \times \text{sunTransmittance} \times \text{cameraTransmittance} \times \text{scatter} \times \text{stepSize} \times 0.5 Update densityTotal += density \times stepSize. Update distanceTravelled += stepSize. 5. Calculate Transmittance and Final Color: Compute cloud transmittance using Beer-Lambert law: T{cloud} = e^{-\text{densityTotal} \times \text{AbsorptionCoefficient}} Compute cloud color: C{cloud} = \text{brightness} \times \text{SunColour.rgb} Return final color with alpha: \text{return } \text{lerp}(C{bg}, C{cloud}, 1 - T{cloud}) Note: The source code uses lerp(originalColour, cloudColour, cloudColour.a) where cloudColour.a is 1 - cloudTransmittance. To calculate how much sunlight reaches the current sample point \mathbf{p}, a secondary ray march is performed towards the sun: 1. Initialize lightDensity = 0, stepSize = 20.0, stepLimit = 200. 2. Loop i from 0 to stepLimit: Advance position: \mathbf{p}{sun} = \mathbf{p} + \text{SunDirection} \times \text{stepSize}. Check if \mathbf{p}{sun} is inside the cloud volume AABB. If inside, sample noise at scaled coordinates and add to lightDensity. 3. Return transmittance: T{sun} = e^{-\text{lightDensity} \times \text{AbsorptionCoefficient}} AbsorptionCoefficient: Controls light absorption. Higher values darken clouds. ScatterFactor (g): Controls forward scattering strength. Higher values create stronger silver linings. Density Threshold: Minimum noise value to contribute to density. Higher values create gaps. Cloud Scale: World-space frequency of cloud features. Higher values result in smaller clouds. Octave Count: Number of FBM layers. Higher values increase edge detail. Wind Speed: Offsets noise coordinates over time to animate clouds. Unnormalized Ray Directions: If the ray direction is not normalized, the step size relative to the far clip plane becomes incorrect, causing the ray to step past the entire volume instantly. This prevents density gradients from being rendered. The direction must be normalized before intersection tests. Shader Loop Limits: While loops with dynamic exit conditions can cause shader compilation errors in some environments (e.g., Unity). The implementation uses a for loop with a fixed stepLimit and an internal break condition to ensure stable compilation. Unverified code. Retrieve Background bgcolor = sampletexture(maintex, uv) # 2. Initialize Ray origin = cameraworldpos direction = normalize(raydirection) # 3. Ray-Box Intersection entry, exit = rayboxintersection(origin, direction, cloudmin, cloudmax) if entry > exit: return bgcolor # 4. March Density brightness = 0.0 densitytotal = 0.0 distancetravelled = 0.0 raypos = origin + direction entry for i in range(STEPLIMIT): if distancetravelled > exit: break raypos = raypos + direction STEPSIZE distancetravelled += STEPSIZE # Procedural Density worldscaledray = raypos cloudscale # Apply wind offset to worldscaledray here if needed worleydensity = 0.0 amplitude = 1.0 frequency = 1.0 amplitudetotal = 0.0 for octave in range(octavecount): noiseval = samplenoise(worldscaledray frequency) worleydensity += noiseval amplitude amplitudetotal += amplitude amplitude = 0.5 frequency = 2.0 if amplitudetotal > 0: density = worleydensity / amplitudetotal else: density = 0.0 # Lighting suntransmittance = marchlight(raypos, cloudmin, cloudmax, sundirection, absorptioncoeff) cameratransmittance = exp(-densitytotal absorptioncoeff) scatter = henyeygreenstein(direction, sundirection, scatterfactor) brightness += density suntransmittance cameratransmittance scatter STEPSIZE 0.5 densitytotal += density STEPSIZE # 5. Final Color cloudtransmittance = exp(-densitytotal absorptioncoeff) cloudcolour = brightness suncolour.rgb alpha = 1.0 - cloudtransmittance finalcolour = lerp(bgcolor, cloudcolour, alpha) return finalcolour def rayboxintersection(origin, direction, minbound, maxbound): # Slab method with safe division for zero direction components invdir = [1.0/d if abs(d) > 1e-9 else 1e9 for d in direction] tmin = (minbound - origin) invdir tmax = (maxbound - origin) invdir entry = max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y), tmin.z) exit = min(min(tmax.x, tmax.y), tmax.z) return entry, exit def henyeygreenstein(raydir, sundir, scatterfactor): cosangle = dot(normalize(raydir), normalize(sundir)) g = scatterfactor gsq = g g numerator = 1.0 - gsq denominator = pow(1.0 + gsq - 2.0 g cosangle, 1.5) return numerator / (4.0 3.14159 denominator) def marchlight(raypos, cloudmin, cloudmax, sundir, absorptioncoeff): lightdensity = 0.0 currentpos = raypos for i in range(LIGHTSTEPLIMIT): currentpos = currentpos + sundir LIGHTSTEPSIZE # Check if inside box uvw = (currentpos - cloudmin) / (cloudmax - cloudmin) if all(0 <= uvw[i] <= 1 for i in range(3)): worldscaled = currentpos cloudscale lightdensity += samplenoise(worldscaled) LIGHTSTEPSIZE return exp(-lightdensity absorptioncoeff) def sampletexture(tex, uv): return tex[uv] # Standard texture sampling def samplenoise(p): return worleynoise(p) # Standard Worley noise evaluation def worleynoise(p): # Placeholder for standard Worley noise implementation return 0.5 def normalize(v): return v / length(v) def dot(a, b): return a.xb.x + a.yb.y + a.zb.z def length(v): return (v.x2 + v.y2 + v.z2)0.5 def lerp(a, b, t): return a + (b - a) t This variant performs the ray marching loop on the CPU rather than the GPU. It renders volumetric clouds by iterating through a defined 3D box, using noise for density and opacity parameters. It is called via renderer.RenderVolumetricClouds(boxmin, boxmax, density, noisescale, octaves, opacity) each frame. Key parameters include cloudboxmin (default -100), cloudboxmax (default 100), clouddensity, cloudnoisescale, cloudoctaves, and cloudopacity. The primary pitfall is a severe performance bottleneck due to CPU execution, which is mitigated by using 4x4 pixel striding, though this significantly reduces rendering quality. The method executes per-pixel on the GPU fragment shader. The secondary light march (MarchLight) adds a constant overhead per sample, which impacts performance at high resolutions or with high stepLimit values. The approach is optimal when viewer location changes faster than the light source or cloud geometry. This method is implemented in Unity as the CloudRendererProcedural component, attached to the main camera. The lighting model references "Physically Based Sky, Atmosphere and Cloud Rendering in frostbite" by Sebastien Hillaire (EA Frostbite) for the Henyey-Greenstein scattering function. The FBM implementation is adapted from standard techniques described by Inigo Quilez. ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, https://github.com/ldarnbr/volumetric-cloud-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) lijiemark/floating-islands-generator, https://github.com/lijiemark/floating-islands-generator, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Efficient Algorithms for Real-Time GPU Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Enhanced Geometry, https://doi.org/10.3390/sym10040125, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Displacement Mapping for Volume Rendering
head: Discontinuous Displacement Mapping, Generalized Displacement Mapping, Inverse Displacement Mapping
body: Displacement Mapping for Volume Rendering is a technique for modeling interactive deformations (cuts, peeling, deforming) on volumetric objects by applying unconventional, unorthogonal, and discontinuous displacements, avoiding mesh re-tessellation. It solves the limitation of static volumetric representations by allowing complex geometric changes without explicit surface models, building on the principles of Direct volume ray casting. Unlike surface subdivision which requires costly re-meshing for discontinuities, this method uses GPU-based volumetric rendering without mesh structures. It differs from GPU-accelerated ray casting with volumetric lenses by focusing on topological changes rather than optical refraction, and from Procedural Volumetric Cloud Rendering (GPU Shader) by explicitly separating the proxy geometry sampling from the original object evaluation via an inverse map. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A proxy scene geometry (bounding box) defining the spatial domain of the displaced object O0; a displacement function D (stored as a texture Dk); an original object representation O (e.g., scalar volume texture Oj); view parameters. Output: A rendered image of the displaced volumetric object. Data Structures: Proxy Geometry: A 3D bounding box object that defines the bounded spatial domain of the displaced object O0. If it contains volume data, it is sampled via slicing. Displacement Texture (Dk): A 3D texture storing the displacement vector field, discretized from a procedural specification, stored as 8-bit or 16-bit point numbers normalized in [0, 1] or [-1, 1]. Original Volume Texture (Oj): A 3D texture storing the scalar density or color values of the undeformed object, representing O(p). Reference Coordinate System: Let \Lambda be a common reference coordinate system shared by the object position function P and the displacement function DB, set to E^3 (3D Euclidean space). P(\lambda) maps a reference point \lambda to a point in E^3, and DB(\lambda) is the forward displacement vector function. Numbered Steps: 1. Define a common reference coordinate system \Lambda = E^3 shared by P and DB. 2. Define a proxy scene geometry (a bounding box object) to define the bounded spatial domain of the displaced object O0. 3. Render using texture-based volume rendering with view-aligned slices, sampling the proxy scene geometry with slices parallel to the view plane. 4. For each pixel in a slice, map the sampled point back to the original object space using the inverse displacement map. 5. Evaluate the original object function O(p) at the mapped point to retrieve luminance attributes. 6. Compute surface normals for lighting, using specific techniques for displaced surfaces to avoid artifacts at breaking points in discontinuous maps. Formulas: The forward displacement mapping is defined as: P0(\lambda) = P(\lambda) + DB(\lambda) where \lambda \in \Lambda, P maps reference to point in E^3, and DB is the displacement vector function. The rendering uses the inverse displacement mapping. Since \Lambda = E^3, we can simplify P(\lambda) = p and P0(\lambda) = p0. The relationship is rewritten as: p = p0 + D(p0) where: p is the point in the original object space. p0 is the point in the displaced space (sampled from the proxy). D is the inverse displacement function (often denoted DC in literature, where DC is the inverse of DB). Parameters: Reference Space \Lambda: Set to E^3 to allow displacement in any direction and magnitude. Displacement Texture Precision: 8-bit or 16-bit point numbers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderdisplacedvolume(proxyvolume, displacementtexture, originalvolume, viewmatrix, resolution): image = [] # Generate slice planes parallel to the view plane slices = generateviewalignedslices(viewmatrix, resolution) for sliceplane in slices: for u in range(sliceplane.width): for v in range(sliceplane.height): # Sample point p0 on the proxy geometry/slice p0 = sampleslicepoint(sliceplane, u, v) # Sample inverse displacement vector D(p0) d = sample3dtexture(displacementtexture, p0) # Map to original object space: p = p0 + D(p0) p = [p0[i] + d[i] for i in range(3)] # Evaluate original object O(p) density = sample3dtexture(originalvolume, p) # Compute normal for displaced surface normal = computedisplacednormal(p0, displacementtexture) # Shade and accumulate color = shade(density, normal, lightsource) image.append((u, v, color)) return image def generateviewalignedslices(viewmatrix, resolution): # Returns list of slice planes parallel to the view plane return [] def sampleslicepoint(sliceplane, u, v): # Returns 3D point p0 on the slice/proxy geometry return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def sample3dtexture(tex, point): # Trilinear interpolation of 3D texture at point return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def computedisplacednormal(p0, displacementtexture): # Finite difference approximation of normal from displacement field eps = 1e-3 dx = sample3dtexture(displacementtexture, [p0[0]+eps, p0[1], p0[2]]) - sample3dtexture(displacementtexture, [p0[0]-eps, p0[1], p0[2]]) dy = sample3dtexture(displacementtexture, [p0[0], p0[1]+eps, p0[2]]) - sample3dtexture(displacementtexture, [p0[0], p0[1]-eps, p0[2]]) dz = sample3dtexture(displacementtexture, [p0[0], p0[1], p0[2]+eps]) - sample3dtexture(displacementtexture, [p0[0], p0[1], p0[2]-eps]) tangentx = [1, 0, 0] + dx tangenty = [0, 1, 0] + dy tangentz = [0, 0, 1] + dz normal = cross(tangentx, tangenty) return normalize(normal) def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2]-a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0]-a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1]-a[1]b[0]] def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] if mag > 0 else [0, 0, 1] def shade(density, normal, lightsource): # Standard volume shading return [density, density, density] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuities: Conventional normal estimation leads to noticeable lighting artifacts on surfaces displaced in varying directions and at breaking points in a discontinuous displacement map. Correct normal calculation is required. Precision: Displacement values must be handled carefully to avoid precision loss when mapping between spaces, especially with large displacements. A rendering-time technique for adding geometric detail to volumetric simulations by shifting fluid points or surface vertices based on sampled texture maps. It solves the limitation of static volumetric meshes by allowing complex, high-frequency surface deformations without re-tessellating the underlying geometry. It distinguishes itself from standard mesh displacement by operating on volumetric data structures and supporting specialized modes like Surface-driven and Vector displacement, which handle directional consistency differently than scalar or gradient-based methods. Time Complexity: Depends on the volume rendering algorithm and the cost of texture lookups for both the proxy and displacement maps. The inverse mapping adds one extra 3D texture lookup per sample. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the proxy volume, the original volume, and the displacement texture. Strengths: Allows interactive deformation without mesh re-tessellation; supports unorthogonal and discontinuous displacements; works with implicit surfaces, level sets, and volume textures. Limitations: Requires correct normal calculation to avoid artifacts at discontinuities; proxy geometry must bound the displaced object accurately; not suitable for methods requiring explicit surface meshes. When to use: When simulating dynamic, discontinuous volumetric effects like cutting or peeling on GPU hardware without explicit mesh structures. When not to use: When high-fidelity surface continuity is required without complex normal computation, or when the displacement is purely cosmetic on a static surface. Displacement mapping is commonly used for adding surface details to an object. This method outlines a generalized notion of displacement mapping, allowing for unconventional features such as unorthogonal and discontinuous displacement. By lifting the restriction on the geometric properties of the displacement, it generates special effects including peeling, cutting, and deforming objects, which are useful for volumetric objects where the interior is represented. To address technical difficulties, it employs inverse displacement maps in 3D vector space and devises techniques including sampling displaced objects through proxy geometry and computing displaced surface normals. The approach was demonstrated on current GPU hardware, adapting slicing-based rendering strategies. name: Displacement General Setup
head: Discontinuous Displacement Mapping, Generalized Displacement Mapping, Inverse Displacement Mapping
body:
Displacement General Setup is a rendering-time technique for adding geometric detail to volumetric simulations by shifting fluid points or surface vertices based on sampled texture maps. It solves the limitation of static volumetric meshes by allowing complex, high-frequency surface deformations without re-tessellating the underlying geometry. It distinguishes itself from standard mesh displacement by operating directly on volumetric data structures and supporting specialized directional modes like Surface-driven and Vector displacement. The method applies a displacement map to a volumetric object during the rendering phase. The core logic involves sampling a texture at the location of a fluid point or surface vertex and shifting that point along a specific direction vector by a distance determined by the texture's value. Inputs: Volumetric data representing the fluid surface or volume grid. Displacement map (texture), which can be monochrome (grayscale) or colored (RGB). Parameters: displacement (boolean enable), displmul (multiplier), Type (algorithm selection), and Map (texture reference). Outputs: Rendered image with displaced geometry. Mesh preview showing the deformed surface when the Mesh Preview option is enabled. The implementation relies on the following parameters, typically stored in the renderer's material or simulation context: displacement: Boolean flag. If false, displacement is skipped. displmul: Float multiplier. Scales the final displacement magnitude. Type: Enum or string identifying the displacement algorithm. Common values are Gradient driven, Surface driven, and Vector. Map: Reference to the texture object. The renderer must support V-Ray, 3ds Max, or Phoenix texture formats. 1. Enable Check: If displacement is false, skip displacement processing. 2. Mode Detection: Determine the rendering mode. If Mode is Mesh, Ocean Mesh, or Cap Mesh, the Type parameter is ignored. In these modes, Phoenix automatically detects the map type: monochrome maps trigger Surface-driven displacement, and colored maps trigger Vector displacement. If Mode is not one of the above, use the explicit Type parameter to select the algorithm. 3. Texture Sampling: For each point P on the fluid surface or volume, sample the displacement map at P's texture coordinates to obtain T. If the map is monochrome, T is a scalar brightness value. If the map is colored, T is a 3D vector (R, G, B). 4. Direction Calculation: Determine the displacement direction vector \vec{D} based on the active algorithm. Gradient driven: Calculate the gradient of the fluid's Surface channel at P, denoted 
abla S. \vec{D} =  rac{
abla S}{\|
abla S\|}. Surface driven: Project P onto the isosurface of the fluid's Surface channel to obtain P{proj}. Calculate the surface normal \vec{N} at P{proj}. \vec{D} = \vec{N}. Vector: Use the sampled color vector from T as the direction. 5. Magnitude Calculation: If the map is monochrome, the base magnitude is T. If the map is colored, the magnitude is determined by the total intensity of the color. Let I = R + G + B. The magnitude is I. Apply the multiplier: M = 	ext{displmul} 	imes 	ext{base\magnitude}. 6. Displacement Application: Calculate the final displacement vector \vec{V} = M 	imes \vec{D} and shift the point: P{new} = P + \vec{V}. 7. Edge Case Handling: If a colored map is specified when a monochrome map is needed, the strength of the displacement is determined by the total intensity of the color. If a monochrome map is specified when a vector map is needed, the entire displacement points in a single direction. Unverified code. Enables the effect. displmul: Float. Multiplier for displacement amount. Type: Enum. Gradient driven, Surface driven, Vector. Map: Texture reference. Supports V-Ray, 3ds Max, or Phoenix formats. Mode/Type Conflict: The Type parameter is ignored in Mesh, Ocean Mesh, and Cap Mesh modes. Map Mismatch: Using a colored map in a monochrome mode results in displacement strength based on color intensity, which may be unintended. Map Mismatch: Using a monochrome map in a vector mode results in uniform direction displacement. Uses a colored vector texture to shift points, enabling asymmetric geometries like waves with convex backs and concave fronts. Choose when directional control of displacement magnitude and orientation is required. Uses a monochrome texture to shift points along the surface normal of the projected isosurface. Choose when consistent displacement direction relative to the surface is needed, avoiding the varying directions of gradient-driven methods. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Adds high-frequency detail without modifying the simulation cache; supports complex geometries via Vector displacement; integrates with existing texture workflows. Limitations: Rendering-time only (does not affect simulation physics); potential for visual artifacts if map mismatch occurs; performance impact depends on texture resolution and sampling cost. When to Use: When visual detail is needed for smoke, fire, or fluid surfaces without re-simulating or re-meshing. When Not to Use: When the displacement needs to affect the simulation physics or collision detection. Displacement mapping in volumetric rendering, specifically within the Phoenix FD context, was introduced as a method to enhance visual fidelity by shifting fluid points during rendering. The technique draws inspiration from standard geometry displacement but adapts it for volumetric data structures. It is used in Phoenix for 3ds Max to allow artists to add detail to explosions, smoke, and fire simulations interactively. name: Vector Displacement
head: Vector Texture Displacement
body: Vector Displacement is a procedural technique in volume rendering that shifts fluid or surface points based on a colored vector texture map, where the texture's RGB channels are interpreted as a 3D displacement vector. It solves the limitation of scalar displacement methods by enabling the creation of asymmetric, complex surface geometries, such as waves with convex backs and concave fronts, which scalar methods cannot produce. Unlike Surface-driven displacement, which relies on gradient fields and produces symmetrical forms, Vector Displacement allows for directional control of the displacement magnitude and orientation directly through the texture data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A colored vector texture map (RGB) containing values that can be negative or positive, interpreted according to the rendering mode. Output: A displaced volume or surface geometry where each point is shifted by the vector defined by the texture sample at that location. Data Structures: The displacement map is a 2D or 3D texture where each texel stores three floating-point or normalized integer values corresponding to the X, Y, and Z components of the displacement vector. Parameters: displ2d: Specifies the displacement technique type, set to "Vector". displmul: Specifies the displacement amount, scaling the overall magnitude of the displacement. displ2: Specifies the displacement map texture. Steps: 1. Sample Texture: For each point on the fluid volume or surface, sample the displacement map at the corresponding spatial coordinates to retrieve a color value C = (R, G, B). 2. Interpret Vector: If the rendering Mode is Mesh, Ocean Mesh, or Cap Mesh: The texture must be in V-Ray Tangent Vector format, where X and Y are 0.5-based and Z is 0.0-based. The components are interpreted as X = R - 0.5, Y = G - 0.5, and Z = B - 0.0. Gray (R=0.5, G=0.5) and black (B=0.0) result in zero displacement; brighter colors move points along positive axes; darker or negative colors move points along negative axes. If the rendering Mode is other than mesh modes: The texture is 0.0-based. The components are interpreted directly as X = R, Y = G, and Z = B. Black (0,0,0) results in no displacement; brighter colors shift points towards positive axes; negative colors shift along negative axes. 3. Scale Displacement: Apply the displacement amount controlled by the multiplier parameter displmul to the resulting vector \vec{V} = (X, Y, Z). 4. Apply Shift: Shift the point's position by the scaled vector \vec{V}{scaled}. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Mode Mismatch: If the Mode is set to Mesh, Ocean Mesh, or Cap Mesh, the texture must be in the V-Ray Tangent Vector format (X/Y 0.5-based, Z 0.0-based). Texture Format: If the Mode is not a mesh mode, the texture must be 0.0-based. Monochrome Input: If a monochrome map is passed when a vector map is required, the displacement effect points in a single direction, as the color channels are not independent. Advection Displacement is a variant of Vector Displacement that also requires a colored 0.0-based vector texture map with negative and positive values. It is functionally similar to Vector Displacement but is specifically optimized to avoid producing grainy structures in fire and smoke simulations. It is commonly combined with a Phoenix Grid Texture (with Channel set to Velocity) to produce render-time gridless advection effects. A key pitfall is that passing a monochrome map instead of a vector map causes the displacement to point in a single uniform direction. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Performance relative to other displacement methods is not given in the sources. Strengths: Capable of producing more complicated, asymmetric surfaces (e.g., convex back/concave front waves) compared to the symmetrical forms produced by Surface-driven displacement. Limitations: Requires specific texture formats depending on the rendering mode (Mesh vs. Non-Mesh), and incorrect texture format leads to erroneous displacement. Monochrome maps cannot drive directional displacement effectively. Use Cases: Ideal for simulating ocean waves, fluid surfaces with directional flow, and fire/smoke advection where grainy artifacts from scalar methods are undesirable. Vector Displacement is a feature within the Phoenix FD plugin for 3ds Max, designed to enhance the visual fidelity of fluid simulations by allowing procedural displacement during rendering. It leverages vector fields (such as velocity) to drive geometric changes, moving beyond simple scalar-based surface offsets. name: Surface Driven Displacement
head: Monochrome Texture Displacement
body: Surface Driven Displacement is a displacement technique that shifts fluid points along the normal of a specific isosurface rather than the local density gradient. It ensures that all points above or below the fluid surface are displaced in the same direction, producing results more similar to displaced solid geometry surfaces. It is distinct from Gradient-driven displacement, which uses the local density gradient for potentially varying directions, and Vector displacement, which uses a colored vector texture map. Inputs: 1. Volumetric simulation data containing a defined "Surface" channel. 2. A monochrome texture map. Outputs: 1. Displaced volumetric geometry. Data Structures: Surface Channel: Scalar field defining the fluid boundary. Exact layouts, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. Monochrome Texture: Texture where displacement magnitude is encoded in brightness at each point. Exact layouts, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. For a given point P in the fluid volume, determine its projection P{\text{proj}} onto the isosurface of the defined Surface channel. 2. Calculate the surface normal \mathbf{N} at P{\text{proj}}. 3. Sample the monochrome texture at P{\text{proj}} to obtain the displacement magnitude D, which corresponds to the texture's brightness at that location. 4. Shift the original point P along the normal \mathbf{N} by the distance D to compute the new position P': P' = P + D \cdot \mathbf{N} The sources specify shifting along the normal of the projection point rather than the gradient at the original point P. Parameters: Surface channel selection and monochrome texture mapping are required. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: This method is slower than Gradient-driven displacement because it requires finding the projection onto the isosurface and calculating the normal at that projection point. Direction Consistency: Unlike gradient-driven methods, this method ensures that points above and below the surface are displaced in the same direction relative to the surface normal, which is critical for smoke and fire simulations to maintain visual coherence. Specifies which data channel defines the fluid's surface geometry and the isosurface threshold. It relies on a specific channel's scalar values to establish the surface reference rather than computing normals from density gradients. Time Complexity: Slower than Gradient-driven displacement due to the additional computation required to find the surface projection and normal. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Surface channel data and the monochrome texture map. Strengths: Produces displacement results more similar to displaced solid geometry surfaces. It ensures consistent displacement direction for points above and below the surface, making it suitable for smoke and fire simulations. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than Gradient-driven displacement. When to use: When simulating smoke or fire where consistent surface-normal-based displacement is desired for visual realism. When not to use: When performance is critical and the directional variation of Gradient-driven displacement is acceptable or preferred. Surface Driven Displacement is a feature within Phoenix for 3ds Max, part of the V-Ray ecosystem. It is designed to handle the specific requirements of fluid simulations like smoke and fire, where standard gradient-based displacement might produce visually inconsistent results due to varying local gradients. The method relies on the concept of a "Surface Channel" to define a clear boundary for displacement operations. name: Surface Channel Definition
head: Surface Channel
body: The Surface Channel Definition specifies which data channel within a volumetric simulation defines the fluid's surface geometry for solid rendering and displacement mapping. It solves the problem of determining the boundary between the fluid and the environment by selecting a scalar field and an isosurface threshold. Unlike methods that compute normals from density gradients, this approach relies on a named simulation channel's scalar values to establish the surface reference for both standard and gradient-driven displacement. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset containing named channels (e.g., Liquid, Smoke, Temperature, Speed, Fuel, or a custom Texture map). Input: A scalar threshold value (surflevel). Input: A boolean flag for inversion (solidbelow). Output: A surface field used for mesh generation in Mesh, Ocean Mesh, Cap Mesh, and Isosurface render modes, or as the reference surface for displacement calculations. Data Structures: The specific internal data structure layout is not given in the sources. The method relies on named channels within the simulation cache. Steps: 1. Identify the selected Surface Channel (sarg) from the available simulation outputs. 2. If sarg is Texture, load the texture specified in the stex slot. In Mesh, Ocean Mesh, Cap Mesh, and Isosurface render modes, this map completely replaces loaded cache files. 3. For non-texture channels, ensure the corresponding channel output is enabled in the simulation settings (required for Speed and Fuel). 4. Evaluate the scalar value V at each voxel position \mathbf{p} from the selected channel. 5. Compare V against the Isosurface Level T. 6. Determine surface membership based on the Invert volume flag: If Invert volume is disabled: Points where V \ge T are internal/surface; points where V < T are external. If Invert volume is enabled: Points where V < T are internal/surface; points where V \ge T are external. 7. Use the resulting surface field for solid rendering or displacement mapping. Formulas: The surface boundary is defined by the isosurface condition V(\mathbf{p}) = T, where V(\mathbf{p}) is the scalar value of the selected channel at voxel position \mathbf{p}, and T is the Isosurface Level threshold. The Invert volume flag modifies the inequality for internal classification: V(\mathbf{p}) \ge T (default) or V(\mathbf{p}) < T (inverted). Parameters: Surface Channel (sarg): The identifier of the channel defining the surface. Options include: Liquid/Temperature: Defines the liquid surface. Typical ranges are 0–1 for Liquid simulations and 600–2000 for Fire/Smoke simulations. Smoke: Defines the liquid surface. Typical range is 0–1 for Fire/Smoke simulations. Speed: Defines the liquid surface. Calculated as the length of the velocity vector for each voxel. Requires the Speed channel output to be enabled. Fuel: Defines the liquid surface. Requires the Fuel channel output to be enabled. Texture: Uses a custom texture map to define the mesh surface. Requires the stex slot to specify the texture file. Isosurface Level (surflevel): The threshold value for geometry generation. Grid cells with values below this threshold are ignored. Invert Volume (solidbelow): If enabled, swaps the inside and outside definitions. By default, values above the surface level are considered internal. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Outputs: The Speed and Fuel channels will not function if their respective outputs are not explicitly enabled in the simulation settings. Texture Replacement: When using the Texture mode in Mesh, Ocean Mesh, Cap Mesh, or Isosurface modes, the selected texture map completely replaces any loaded cache files. Range Mismatch: Using default thresholds with channels that have non-standard ranges (e.g., using a 0–1 threshold for a Temperature channel in Fire/Smoke simulations which ranges 600–2000) will result in incorrect surface generation. Not given in the sources. The concept is based on the isosurface generation technique, which is unique for generating surfaces from volumetric data. While primarily used for rendering liquids, it is also applied to smoke and fire to create effects such as underwater bubbles or freezing fire. name: Dynamic Multi-Frame Rate Rendering
head: Dynamic single and multi-frame rate rendering
body: Dynamic Multi-Frame Rate Rendering is a hybrid rendering system that dynamically switches between multi-frame rate rendering (using image-based warping for low latency) and single-frame rate parallel raycasting (using all GPUs for high quality) based on current workload complexity. It solves the trade-off between the low latency of fast-node rendering and the high throughput of parallel raycasting by selecting the optimal method for the current frame's specific parameters. Unlike its siblings, which focus on procedural evaluation or specific hardware acceleration, this method focuses on runtime adaptation of the rendering paradigm itself. The method operates by periodically evaluating a decision function that predicts the performance of different rendering modes based on current scene parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current rendering parameters including sampling rate, zoom level (resolution), occlusion, dataset size, and transfer function. Outputs: A categorical decision indicating whether to use Multi-Frame Rate (MFR) rendering or Single-Frame Rate (SFR) parallel raycasting. Data Structures: Decision Function: A lookup table or mathematical model mapping input parameters (sampling rate, resolution) to predicted frame rates for both MFR and SFR modes, derived from empirical measurements. Steps: 1. Performance Data Collection: Collect performance data for the relevant parameters (sampling rate, zoom level, occlusion, dataset size, transfer function) to form a decision function. This involves measuring the frame rate of both MFR and SFR modes across the parameter space. 2. Decision Function Approximation: The full evaluation of the decision function takes approximately 2 minutes, but a good approximation can be obtained within 10 seconds. 3. Runtime Evaluation: Periodically evaluate the decision function during runtime using the current values of the input parameters. 4. Method Selection: If the volume rendering complexity exceeds a break-even point (indicated by the decision function), use multi-frame rate rendering. Otherwise, converge to single-frame rate multi-GPU raycasting to utilize all available resources and avoid image warping artifacts. 5. Re-evaluation Trigger: Recompute the performance data for the decision function if any performance-relevant parameters not input to the function change. Parameters: Sampling Rate: Ranges from 6x undersampling to 6x oversampling compared to the Nyquist rate sampling. Resolution: Measured by computing the pixel area of the bounding rectangle, serving as a measurement of the model's zoom level. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Useless GPUs in SFR: When converging to single-frame rate rendering (e.g., m=0 in the quality map approach), additional GPUs become useless as raycasting is performed entirely by the fast node. Stale Decision Function: Performance data for the decision function must be recomputed if performance-relevant parameters not input to the function change. Precision: The decision function evaluation has virtually no performance impact. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. decisionfunction = {} def evaluatedecisionfunction(samplingrate, resolution): """Queries the decision function for predicted frame rates.""" return decisionfunction.get((samplingrate, resolution), (0.0, 0.0)) def checkparamschanged(otherparams, lastparams): """Checks if performance-relevant parameters not in the function key have changed.""" return otherparams != lastparams def recomputedecisionfunction(allparams): """Rebuilds the decision function from empirical measurements.""" # Full evaluation takes ~2 minutes; a good approximation takes ~10 seconds # The exact measurement procedure is not given in the sources. pass def rendermfr(scenedata, camera): """Executes multi-frame rate rendering using image-based warping for low latency.""" # Fast node renders low-latency frame; slow nodes act as frame source # The exact warping implementation is not given in the sources. pass def rendersfrparallel(scenedata, camera): """Executes single-frame rate parallel raycasting to utilize all GPUs and avoid warping artifacts.""" # Sort-first or sort-last parallel volume raycasting # The exact parallelization strategy is not given in the sources. pass def mainloop(samplingrate, resolution, otherparams, lastparams): if checkparamschanged(otherparams, lastparams): recomputedecisionfunction(otherparams) mfrfps, sfrfps = evaluatedecisionfunction(samplingrate, resolution) method = 'MFR' if mfrfps > sfrfps else 'SFR' if method == 'MFR': rendermfr(scenedata, camera) else: rendersfrparallel(scenedata, camera) Time Complexity: The decision function evaluation has virtually no performance impact. The full evaluation of the decision function takes approximately 2 minutes, but a good approximation can be obtained within 10 seconds. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In tests with the MANIX dataset (256x256x230 voxels), multi-frame rate rendering was superior when volume rendering complexity was high, while sort-first parallel raycasting was superior when complexity was low. The performance was measured for sampling rates ranging from 6x undersampling to 6x oversampling compared to Nyquist rate sampling. Scaling: The system is designed for multi-GPU setups where a fast node handles low-latency rendering and slow nodes act as frame sources. Strengths: Provides stable frame rates and low latency to user input using multi-frame rate approach in combination with image-based rendering techniques. Avoids image warping artifacts when converging to single-frame rate rendering. Limitations: When converging to single-frame rate rendering, additional GPUs become useless as raycasting is performed entirely by the fast node. Requires periodic re-evaluation of the decision function if parameters change. When to use: Use when volume rendering complexity is high and low latency is critical. Use single-frame rate parallel raycasting when complexity is low to utilize all available resources. Dynamic Multi-Frame Rate Rendering was introduced by S. Hauswiesner, D. Kalkofen, and D. Schmalstieg in 2010. It is part of a broader effort to display transparent volumetric scenes at high frame rates and little latency to user input. The method builds on the principles of multi-frame rate rendering and parallel volume raycasting. Multi-Frame Rate Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/egpgv.egpgv10.019-026, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Time-Dependent Animation
head: Temporal Visualization, Time Animation Update, VCR-like Controls
body: Time-Dependent Animation is a technique for visualizing the temporal development of volumetric data by concatenating all time steps of a variable into a single file and playing them back with VCR-like controls. It sets itself apart from static volume rendering by treating time as a continuous dimension within the data structure, allowing for smooth playback, stepping, and speed adjustment of dynamic phenomena. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of N volumetric data sets (time steps), each with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Output: A rendered image sequence or real-time video stream representing the animation. Data Structures: The core data structure is a single concatenated file containing all time steps. To fit available memory, the data sets are pre-processed to resample them to smaller sizes. The file layout is a linear concatenation of the voxel data for each time step. For example, if each time step is 128 \times 128 \times 100 voxels, the file contains N such blocks sequentially. Parameters: animationduration: Total duration of the animation loop in seconds. dt: Time step interval in seconds. rendersettings.time: Current normalized time position in [0, 1). Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Resample all time steps to a uniform smaller size to fit into texture memory. Concatenate all time steps into a single file on disk. 2. Initialization: Load the concatenated data into GPU texture memory. Initialize rendersettings.time to 0. 3. Animation Loop: If playing is true and volumes[0].volume.timesteps > 1: Update rendersettings.time by adding dt.assecsf32() / animationduration.assecsf32(). Apply fract() to rendersettings.time to wrap it to 0, 1). Use rendersettings.time to interpolate or select the appropriate time step from the concatenated data for ray casting. 4. User Controls: Provide VCR-like controls on the interface (e.g., icon wall) to start/stop animation, single step forward/backward, set playback speed, and select specific time steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updateanimation(rendersettings, dt, animationduration, isplaying, numtimesteps): if isplaying and numtimesteps > 1: # Calculate time increment normalized to animation duration timeincrement = dt / animationduration rendersettings.time += timeincrement # Wrap time to [0, 1) rendersettings.time = rendersettings.time % 1.0 def getcurrenttimestep(rendersettings, numtimesteps): # Map normalized time [0, 1) to integer time step index timestepindex = int(rendersettings.time numtimesteps) # Handle edge case where time is exactly 1.0 (should be 0 due to modulo) if timestepindex >= numtimesteps: timestepindex = 0 return timestepindex Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory constraints: Large data sets must be resampled to fit into texture memory. Boundary conditions: Ensure time wrapping handles the transition from the last time step back to the first smoothly. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of time steps for pre-processing. Real-time rendering depends on the resolution and the efficiency of the ray casting algorithm. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the total size of all concatenated time steps. Resampling reduces this significantly. Strengths: Allows for detailed temporal analysis and comparison of dynamic phenomena. VCR-like controls provide intuitive user [interaction. Limitations: Limited by available memory for storing all time steps. Performance may degrade with high-resolution data or large numbers of time steps. This technique was demonstrated in the IEEE Visualization 2004 Contest, where the Cave software suite was used to explore volume data sets. The method was implemented using the Virvo software suite's VConv tool to merge channels and time steps into a single data file. It was tested on an nVidia 3000G graphics card with data sets such as CLOUDf at resolutions of 128 \times 128 \times 100 and 500 \times 500 \times 100 voxels. jonathonb21/volume4d-viewer, https://github.com/jonathonb21/volume4d-viewer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) IEEE Visualization 2004 Contest: User Friendly Volume Data Set Exploration in the Cave, http://web.eng.ucsd.edu/~jschulze/projects/vis04-contest/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Specific Applications and Integrators
head: X-Ray Rendering
body: This family encompasses specialized integrators and rendering modes that deviate from standard front-to-back compositing to address specific application requirements, such as projective diagnostic imaging, medical photo-realism, interactive shading approximations [15337-shading-and-occlusion-models.md], and neural scene composition [11182-compositional-rendering.md]. Unlike standard Direct Volume Ray Casting [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md], which simulates light transport via the volume rendering equation, these methods either simplify the integration (summing samples), extend it to full path tracing (Cinematic Rendering), approximate global illumination via occlusion buffers (Shading and Occlusion Models) [15337-shading-and-occlusion-models.md], or decouple object insertion in neural fields (Compositional Rendering) [11182-compositional-rendering.md]. The methods in this family build on the foundational mechanism of Direct Volume Ray Casting [19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md], including ray definition, sampling, interpolation, and transfer function mapping. However, they diverge in the Compositing (Integration) step (Step 4 of the parent's Shared principles). While standard DVR uses the front-to-back accumulation equation, specific applications modify this accumulation: Summation: Some modes simply sum interpolated scalar values, as in X-ray rendering. Path Tracing: Others trace randomized photon paths to solve the multi-dimensional rendering equation, accounting for scattering and global illumination. Layered Compositing: Some render distinct material styles into separate layers and composite them post-hoc. A base class for volumetric additive manufacturing integrators that handles projector ray sampling, time sampling, and regular versus stochastic sampling modes. It sets itself apart from sibling integrators by focusing on the temporal and geometric sampling of projector emissions rather than material compositing. Choose this method when simulating volumetric additive manufacturing processes requiring precise projector emission sampling. A physically based, real-time volume rendering technique for medical image data (CT/MRI) that solves the multi-dimensional, non-continuous rendering equation by integrating light scattered from all possible directions along a ray. It sets itself apart by tracing hundreds or thousands of photon paths per pixel to simulate complex light-matter interactions, including multiple scattering and global illumination effects like soft shadows. Choose this method when photo-realistic medical visualization with accurate lighting is required. A method for integrating newly generated 3D objects into an existing Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) scene by decoupling the rendering of the object from the background scene. It sets itself apart by performing the final alpha-blending in image space using a pre-computed scene cache, rather than accumulating the entire scene in a single ray-casting pass. Choose this method when occlusion-aware compositing of dynamic objects into static neural scenes is needed. A family that extends Direct Volume Ray Casting by modifying the compositing step to incorporate lighting, shadows, and occlusion cues, thereby enhancing depth perception and visual clarity. It sets itself apart by using simplified or image-space techniques rather than full physically-based surface/volume interaction models. Choose this method when interactive volume rendering requires enhanced depth cues without the computational cost of full global illumination. A volume picking technique that enables users to intuitively select 3D spatial positions in volumetric renderings based solely on the volume data, transfer function, and visibility perception. It sets itself apart by analyzing the derivative of accumulated opacity to detect visible structures for interaction, rather than integrating color and opacity for display. Choose this method when precise 3D spatial selection in interactive volume visualization is required. A rendering technique that maps scalar field values to auditory properties (pitch, amplitude, duration) using an auditory transfer function, generating sound via a ray-marching procedure similar to optical volume rendering. It sets itself apart by outputting auditory data instead of visual images. Choose this method for audio-visual data exploration or accessibility applications. A ray-casting method to visualize 3D power volumetric data of EME on a globe, handling non-regular grid data organized in spherical coordinates. It sets itself apart by supporting spherical coordinate systems instead of Cartesian grids. Choose this method for geospatial or spherical volumetric data visualization. A framework to synthesize all-in-focus (AiF) novel views from dual-camera image pairs (main and ultra-wide) where the main camera has consistent defocus blur due to fixed autofocus on a prominent object. It sets itself apart by explicitly handling consistent defocus blur to produce sharp, all-in-focus novel views. Choose this method when generating sharp novel views from defocused dual-camera captures is required. A method to approximate in-scattering in volume rendering using Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) and Spherical Harmonics (SH) to replace expensive double integrals with dot products and cube map lookups. It sets itself apart by using PRT/SH approximations instead of direct integration or path tracing. Choose this method when real-time in-scattering approximation is needed without full path tracing costs. A methodology for direct volume rendering that extends the standard color-opacity transfer function process by enabling the use of textures to encode additional information (e.g., fiber direction, cellular abnormalities) throughout the volume in three dimensions. It sets itself apart by integrating volumetric textures instead of just scalar values. Choose this method when rich, multi-channel volumetric data visualization is required. A volume rendering method for aurorae based on a height-based model, GPU-friendly atmosphere model, efficient ray marching with distance fields, and interactive frame rates. It sets itself apart by using a physically-based electron deposition function and spline-based footprint simulation. Choose this method for real-time, physically accurate aurora visualization. A technique that achieves results similar to traditional two-level volume rendering by rendering different styles (e.g., different transfer functions or rendering modes like MIP vs DVR) into separate layers and compositing them, rather than selecting rendering types per ray segment during integration. Step: Render each distinct material style or transfer function into a separate layer (e.g., DVR for soft tissue, DVR for bones). Composite the separate layers into a final image using a compositing function that maps the resulting layers to the view volume. Parameter: Opacity: Layers can be assigned specific opacity values during rendering or compositing (e.g., layer 1 opacity 0.4, layer 3 opacity 0.1, layer 2 opacity 0.5). Comparison: Unlike original two-level volume rendering which composites segments in the order the ray encounters materials (e.g., I = A1 B1 A2 B2), this method composites all segments of the same material separately first, then composites the intermediate results (e.g., I = A1 A2 A3 B1 B2). A complete framework for volumetric ray tracing developed by Sobierajski and Kaufman that includes global illumination effects (shadows, reflections, light interaction between volumetric/geometric objects) and volumetric rendering effects (fog, transparency). It was incorporated into VolVis, a comprehensive volume visualization system developed at Stony Brook University. A method to render features for a 3D scene representation (InstantNGP) by computing a pseudo-depth surface and sampling features locally around it, avoiding full volume rendering for computational efficiency. Step: Compute the pseudo depth of the surface as a weighted average of the depth of each sampled point in volume rendering. Compute the feature in five points around the pseudo surface point by adding small perturbations during training and inference. When optimizing the scene with CLIPNeRF, backpropagate gradients to only the rays selected by the target text label (e.g., 'apple'), rather than all rays. Parameter: Number of feature sampling points: 5 points around the pseudo surface point. Pitfall: The method is described as 'very efficient but works for training the distilled feature field', implying it may not be suitable for final inference or high-fidelity rendering compared to full volume rendering. Rendering from multiple viewpoints (offset by a fixed rotation) to enhance user perception of depth features, used for live stereoscopic display. Stereoscopic rendering required an additional 2.5ms computational cost on the NVIDIA GTX Titan Black GPU. The concept of specific integration modes originated with the distinction between "X-ray" rendering (simple summation) and "full" volume rendering (light transport simulation) in early volume visualization overviews. The "Two Level Volume Rendering" concept was formalized to handle multi-material datasets, with later variations introducing layered compositing to decouple material styles. Cinematic Rendering emerged in the medical imaging domain to provide photo-realistic, clinically accurate visualizations by incorporating global illumination via path tracing. Shading and Occlusion Models provide ambient occlusion-like cues in interactive volume rendering without the cost of full global illumination [15337-shading-and-occlusion-models.md]. Compositional Rendering decouples object and scene rendering for neural fields [11182-compositional-rendering.md]. The Sobierajski/Kaufman framework represents an early comprehensive system integrating volumetric ray tracing with geometric global illumination.
