name: ISMOS
head: Approximate Image-Space Multidirectional Occlusion Shading Model
body: ISMOS is a post-processing shading model for direct volume ray casting that simulates multidirectional lighting, shadows, and ambient occlusion within transparent volumes. It distinguishes itself from standard local illumination by providing depth cues through hard shadows and occlusion effects, while differing from deep shadow maps by computing occlusion in image space rather than via projection. The method handles opaque and transparent medium occlusion separately using full and partial occlusion techniques, blending shading from multiple layers to produce realistic results without requiring preprocessing. ISMOS operates as a decoupled post-processing pass applied to the output of a direct volume ray casting renderer. It does not modify the ray casting integration itself but enhances the resulting image with lighting information derived from the volume's geometry and opacity. Inputs: 1. Color Buffer: A floating-point texture containing the RGB color values computed by the volume ray caster. 2. Depth Texture: A floating-point texture containing depth information. The layout depends on the rendering mode: Non-transparent rendering: 1 component (depth only). Transparent object occlusion or multiple layer rendering: 4 components (depth and auxiliary data for layer management). 3. Light Parameters: Position, direction, and intensity of light sources. 4. Opacity Approximation Parameter (\beta): A scalar value stored within the color buffer (or an associated channel) used to estimate opacity at arbitrary depths. Outputs: Shaded Image: A final image with applied shadows, ambient occlusion, and directional lighting effects. Color Buffer: Stores RGB color data and the parameter \beta. The inclusion of \beta eliminates the need for a separate opacity buffer. Depth Texture: Single-component format for opaque scenes. Four-component format for transparent/multi-layer scenes. The specific content of the four components is not detailed beyond "depth texture" and "layer rendering" support, but it enables the handling of transparent object occlusion. 1. Render Volume: Perform standard direct volume ray casting to generate the initial color and depth buffers. 2. Compute Approximated Opacity: For each pixel, retrieve the approximated opacity value using the parameter \beta stored in the color buffer. This allows the model to estimate opacity at any depth z without storing a dedicated opacity texture. 3. Sample Light Directions: To simulate multidirectional lighting, generate light samples by rotating points on a disk. Define a disk with radius r, centered at (R + 0.5, 0.5, 0.0) in local sample space. Rotate the samples by an angle \phi about the y-axis (Ry(\phi)). Rotate the samples by an angle \theta about the z-axis (Rz(\theta)). 4. Calculate Occlusion: Full Occlusion: Used for opaque media. Determines if light is blocked by the volume geometry. Partial Occlusion: Used for transparent media. Accounts for the attenuation of light through transparent layers. The model distinguishes between opaque and transparent medium occlusion, handling them separately. 5. Blend Shading: Combine the occlusion shading from multiple layers (if present) and blend it with the original volume color to produce the final shaded image. The rotation of light samples is defined by the combined rotation matrix Rz(\theta) Ry(\phi): Rz(\theta) Ry(\phi) = \begin{pmatrix} \cos(\theta)\cos(\phi) & -\sin(\theta) & \cos(\theta)\sin(\phi) \\ \sin(\theta)\cos(\phi) & \cos(\theta) & \sin(\theta)\sin(\phi) \\ -\sin(\phi) & 0 & \cos(\phi) \end{pmatrix} Where: 0 \le \theta \le 2\pi 0 \le \phi \le \pi The approximated opacity is computed using the parameter \beta. The exact functional form f(\beta, z) is not provided in the sources, only that it is stored in the color buffer and used to compute opacity at any depth z. \beta: Parameter for approximated opacity. Value: Not specified in the sources. r: Radius of the disk on which light samples are placed. Value: Not specified in the sources. R: Offset added to the x-coordinate of the disk center. Value: Not specified in the sources [G: Typically R might be related to the number of samples or a scaling factor, but the source does not define it]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ismosshading(colorbuffer, depthtexture, lightsources, betaparam): """ Applies ISMOS shading to a volume rendered image. Args: colorbuffer: 2D array of floats (RGB + beta) from volume ray casting. depthtexture: 2D array of floats (1 or 4 components) from volume ray casting. lightsources: List of light source definitions (position, direction, intensity). betaparam: Scalar value for opacity approximation. Returns: shadedimage: 2D array of floats (RGB). """ height, width = colorbuffer.shape[:2] shadedimage = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) # Precompute rotation matrices for light sampling # Note: The number of samples and specific disk radius r are not defined in sources. # We assume a fixed set of angles theta and phi for demonstration. numsamples = 6 # Example value, not from source thetas = np.linspace(0, 2 np.pi, numsamples, endpoint=False) phis = np.linspace(0, np.pi, numsamples, endpoint=False) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # 1. Retrieve base color and beta basecolor = colorbuffer[y, x,:3] beta = colorbuffer[y, x, 3] # 2. Compute approximated opacity # Exact formula for opacity from beta is not provided in sources # Placeholder for opacity calculation logic opacity = computeapproximatedopacity(beta, depthtexture[y, x]) # 3. Initialize lighting contribution finalcolor = basecolor for light in lightsources: lightcontribution = np.zeros(3) # 4. Sample light directions using rotation for theta in thetas: for phi in phis: # Construct rotation matrix cost = np.cos(theta) sint = np.sin(theta) cosp = np.cos(phi) sinp = np.sin(phi) rotmatrix = np.array([ [cost cosp, -sint, cost sinp], [sint cosp, cost, sint sinp], [-sinp, 0, cosp] ]) # Define sample point on disk # Center at (R + 0.5, 0.5, 0.0) # R and r values are not specified. Using placeholders. Roffset = 0.0 # Not specified diskradius = 0.0 # Not specified # Sample on disk (simplified 2D disk in xy plane before rotation) # The source describes rotating samples on a disk. # The exact 2D coordinates on the disk are not specified. # Assuming a uniform distribution or fixed points for demonstration. samplelocal = np.array([diskradius, 0.0, 0.0]) # Rotate sample samplerotated = rotmatrix @ samplelocal # Transform to world/view space relative to light # The exact mapping from rotated sample to light direction # is not detailed. Assuming samplerotated contributes to light direction. lightdir = normalize(light.direction + samplerotated) # 5. Check occlusion # Determine if the path to the light is blocked # Full occlusion for opaque, partial for transparent isoccluded = checkocclusion(x, y, lightdir, depthtexture, opacity) if not isoccluded: lightcontribution += light.intensity light.color # 6. Blend shading # Specific blending function (e.g., additive, multiplicative) # is not detailed. Assuming simple addition for shading model. finalcolor += lightcontribution shadedimage[y, x] = finalcolor return shadedimage def computeapproximatedopacity(beta, depthvalue): """ Computes opacity using beta parameter. Note: The exact formula is not provided in the sources. """ # Placeholder implementation return beta def checkocclusion(x, y, lightdir, depthtexture, opacity): """ Checks if the pixel is occluded from the light. Uses full occlusion for opaque media and partial for transparent. Note: The specific ray marching or depth comparison logic is not detailed in the sources beyond "image-space multidirectional occlusion". """ # Placeholder for occlusion check logic return False Indirect Lighting: The model does not support indirect lighting (global illumination) because it is not interpreted within the shading model. Mitigation: The model can be extended by adding more buffers to store more precise transmittance for enclosed volumes with partially opaque objects. Transparent Layers: Handling transparent object occlusion requires a 4-component depth texture. Failure to use the correct depth texture format will result in incorrect occlusion for transparent layers. Performance: The overhead is constant for a fixed viewport size but increases with the number of light sources. Time Complexity: The performance overhead is constant for a fixed viewport size. It scales with the number of light sources, but the difference is fairly small. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for color buffer, depth texture (1 or 4 components), and the \beta parameter (stored in color buffer). No additional opacity buffer is required. Measured Performance: Hardware: Xeon CPU 2.66 GHz, NVidia GeForce GTX 295. Viewport: 580 × 580. Overhead: Full occlusion with 1 light: 13.8 ms average. Full occlusion with 2 lights: 25.6 ms average. Difference between full and partial occlusion: ~11.4 ms. Opacity approximation overhead: ~15.9 ms. FPS: Ranges from 5.1 to 23.3 depending on the method and dataset. Strengths: Provides shadow and ambient occlusion effects that supply additional depth cues compared to simple local illumination. Decoupled from the rendering pass, making it applicable to any rendering system. Does not require preprocessing. Transfer function and light position can be changed interactively. Hard shadows are almost identical to deep shadow maps. Limitations: No indirect lighting support. Performance on volume rendering itself may not be faster than highly optimized renderers, as the focus is on the shading overhead. When to Use: When depth cues from shadows and ambient occlusion are needed in direct volume rendering, and interactive light position changes are required, without the overhead of shadow map projection or preprocessing. When Not to Use: When indirect lighting (global illumination) is required. ISMOS was introduced by Y. J. and S. K. in a 2021 paper titled "Approximate Image-Space Multidirectional Occlusion Shading Model for Direct Volume Rendering". The work was supported by the Basic Research Program. The model was tested on various datasets including Engine, Teddy bear, Head, Abdomen, Carp, and Stag beetle. It was compared against deep shadow maps and image-space horizon-based ambient occlusion. name: Extinction-based Ambient Occlusion
head: AO via extinction summation, Local AO
body: Extinction-based Ambient Occlusion (AO) approximates the attenuation of diffusely reflected ambient light through local volume occlusion by summing extinction coefficients rather than tracing shadow rays. It differs from standard DVR by replacing the constant ambient term with a spatially varying occlusion factor derived from a local neighborhood integral, and from full global illumination by ignoring multi-bounce scattering and relying on a precomputed aggregate structure for speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset with extinction coefficients \tau(t) and color C{RGB}(t); ambient light intensity IA; local neighborhood definition N(s) (typically a sphere or box centered at sample point s). Output: Occluded ambient intensity I{AO}(s) and final reflected light Ei for each sample point. Data Structures: 3D Summed Area Table (SAT): A precomputed 3D array storing the cumulative sum of extinction coefficients. Let SAT[x][y][z] store the sum of \tau values in the box from (0,0,0) to (x,y,z). This allows O(1) retrieval of the sum of \tau over any axis-aligned bounding box. Weighted SAT (Optional): If the weighting function w(t) varies spatially (e.g., 1/|s-t|^2), a separate SAT for weighted extinction may be required, or the distance weighting must be applied post-aggregation if the SAT only stores raw sums. The source notes use a weighting function w{A,L} for the aggregate query, implying the SAT stores raw \tau, and weights are applied during the query or via a specific weighted aggregation strategy. Given the formula involves 1/|s-t|^2, a simple box-sum SAT is insufficient for exact integration unless the neighborhood is discretized into weighted bins or the approximation assumes constant weight over the aggregate query volume. The source states w{A,L} = r^{-2} is the inverse square of the radius of the aggregate query, suggesting a simplified approximation where the distance is approximated by the query radius. Numbered Steps: 1. Precompute SAT: Construct a 3D Summed Area Table from the volume's extinction coefficient field \tau. For each voxel (x,y,z), SAT[x][y][z] = \tau(x,y,z) + SAT[x-1][y][z] + SAT[x][y-1][z] + SAT[x][y][z-1] - SAT[x-1][y-1][z] - SAT[x-1][y][z-1] - SAT[x][y-1][z-1] + SAT[x-1][y-1][z-1]. 2. Define Neighborhood: For a sample point s, define the local neighborhood N(s). In the implementation described, this is approximated by an aggregate query volume \Omega{A,L} (e.g., a sphere or box). 3. Aggregate Extinction: Query the SAT to compute the sum of extinction coefficients \sum{\Omega{A,L}} \Delta^\tauj over the neighborhood \Omega{A,L}. 4. Compute Occlusion Factor: Calculate the local ambient occlusion intensity I{AO}(s) using the exponential attenuation model: I{AO}(s) \approx IA \cdot e^{-\int{t \in \mathbb{N}(s)} \frac{\tau(t)}{|s-t|^2} dt} The source approximates the integral \int{t \in \mathbb{N}(s)} \frac{\tau(t)}{|s-t|^2} dt using the aggregated sum. Specifically, it uses a weighting factor w{A,L} = r^{-2} (inverse square of the radius of the aggregate query) applied to the sum: \text{Exponent} = w{A,L} \cdot \sum{\Omega{A,L}} \Delta^\tauj \cdot k where k is a normal/gradient-dependent local illumination model factor. Note: The source formula (8) combines this with color and light intensity. 5. Compute Reflected Light: Calculate the final reflected light Ei for the voxel: Ei = I{A,L} \cdot e^{-w{A,L} \sum{\Omega{A,L}} \Delta^\tauj \cdot k} \cdot C{RGB} where I{A,L} is the ambient or light intensity, and C{RGB} is the voxel color. Formulas: Local AO Intensity: I{AO}(s) \approx IA \cdot e^{-\int{t \in \mathbb{N}(s)} \frac{\tau(t)}{|s-t|^2} dt}. Reflected Light: Ei = I{A,L} \cdot e^{-w{A,L} \sum{\Omega{A,L}} \Delta^\tauj \cdot k} \cdot C{RGB}. Weighting Function: w{A,L} = r^{-2}, where r is the radius of the aggregate query. Parameters: Neighborhood Size (r): The radius of the aggregate query \Omega{A,L}. Not given in the sources. Ambient Intensity (IA): Proportional to the sum of all lights. Not given in the sources. Illumination Factor (k): Normal/gradient dependent. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The exponential function can underflow if the extinction sum is large, resulting in black pixels. Clamp the exponent or use log-space arithmetic if necessary. Boundary Conditions: The SAT query must handle cases where the neighborhood extends beyond the volume bounds. Clamp the SAT query coordinates to the volume dimensions. Approximation Error: The use of a constant weight r^{-2} for the entire neighborhood introduces error, especially for large neighborhoods or non-spherical shapes. The source notes "virtually no difference in image quality" compared to individual sampling, but this is a specific trade-off. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeextinctionao(volume, sat, s, r, IA, k): """ Compute extinction-based ambient occlusion for sample point s. Args: volume: 3D array of extinction coefficients tau. sat: 3D Summed Area Table of tau. s: Sample point (x, y, z). r: Radius of the aggregate query neighborhood. IA: Ambient light intensity. k: Illumination factor. Returns: Ei: Reflected light intensity. """ # Define the bounding box of the neighborhood OmegaA,L # Assuming a spherical neighborhood approximated by a bounding box for SAT query xmin, xmax = max(0, s.x - r), min(volume.width - 1, s.x + r) ymin, ymax = max(0, s.y - r), min(volume.height - 1, s.y + r) zmin, zmax = max(0, s.z - r), min(volume.depth - 1, s.z + r) # Query SAT to get sum of tau in the box # SAT query function for 3D box sum sumtau = querysat3d(sat, xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax) # Calculate weighting factor wA,L = r^-2 # Note: If r is 0, handle division by zero. if r == 0: wAL = 0.0 else: wAL = 1.0 / (r r) # Calculate exponent exponent = wAL sumtau k # Calculate reflected light Ei # IA,L is assumed to be IA for ambient occlusion IAL = IA CRGB = volume[s.x, s.y, s.z] # Voxel color Ei = IAL math.exp(-exponent) CRGB return Ei def querysat3d(sat, xmin, ymin, zmin, xmax, ymax, zmax): """ Compute sum of elements in 3D box using SAT. """ def getval(x, y, z): # Handle boundary conditions x = max(0, min(x, sat.width - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, sat.height - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, sat.depth - 1)) return sat[x, y, z] sumbox = (getval(xmax, ymax, zmax) getval(xmin - 1, ymax, zmax) getval(xmax, ymin - 1, zmax) getval(xmax, ymax, zmin - 1) + getval(xmin - 1, ymin - 1, zmax) + getval(xmin - 1, ymax, zmin - 1) + getval(xmax, ymin - 1, zmin - 1) getval(xmin - 1, ymin - 1, zmin - 1)) return sumbox Uses a different integration strategy for volume rendering, focusing on texture-based volume accumulation. TVAM Integrator Focuses on high-fidelity global illumination and soft shadows, often using path tracing, which is more expensive than extinction-based AO. Cinematic Rendering Renders distinct material styles into separate layers and composites them post-hoc, rather than integrating lighting during ray casting. Compositional Rendering A broader category that includes extinction-based AO, cone-traced shadows, and other local illumination approximations. Shading and Occlusion Models Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point for the AO calculation after O(N) precomputation of the SAT, where N is the number of voxels. Aggregate sampling is over 45 times faster than individually sampled neighborhoods (0.22s vs 10s). Memory Complexity: O(N) for the SAT, where N is the number of voxels. Measured Performance: On the tested hardware and resolution, aggregate sampling took 0.22s compared to 10s for individual sampling, with virtually no difference in image quality. Strengths: Fast approximation of local occlusion; suitable for interactive volume rendering; simple to implement with SAT. Limitations: Approximation error due to constant weight assumption; does not account for multi-bounce scattering or complex light transport; quality depends on neighborhood size and shape approximation. When to use: When interactive performance is required and local occlusion effects are desired without the cost of full global illumination. When not to use: When physical accuracy is required, or when global illumination effects like color bleeding (beyond local approximation) are critical. Extinction-based Ambient Occlusion was introduced as a fast approximation for local illumination in volume rendering, avoiding the cost of shadow ray tracing. It builds on the concept of ambient occlusion in surface rendering but adapts it to volumes by using extinction coefficients as a proxy for opacity. The method was developed to provide a useful approximation of the effect of occlusion on diffusely reflected ambient light, which is otherwise computationally expensive to simulate with full global illumination models. name: WYSIWYP (What You See Is What You Pick)
head: Visibility-Oriented Picking, WYSIWYG picking, WYSIWYP Picking, opacity-jump picking
body: WYSIWYP is a volume picking technique that enables users to intuitively select 3D spatial positions in volumetric renderings based solely on the volume data, the transfer function, and the user's perception of visibility, without requiring pre-segmented data or metadata. It identifies the 3D position corresponding to a 2D screen click by finding the interval along the viewing ray with the largest jump in accumulated opacity. Unlike standard Direct Volume Ray Casting (DVR) which integrates color and opacity for display, WYSIWYP analyzes the derivative of accumulated opacity to detect visible structures. It is distinguished from sibling methods like the TVAM Integrator or Cinematic Rendering by its specific focus on interaction and selection rather than photorealistic shading or global illumination, and from Compositional Rendering by its single-pass, visibility-oriented criterion. Inputs: Volume scalar field data d(x). Transfer function mapping data values to source color C{src} and source opacity \alpha{src}. Camera position (eye point) and screen click coordinates. Step size h (must match DVR rendering step size for consistency). Outputs: A 3D position p representing the picked feature. Data Structures: Ray parameter s (distance along ray). Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}(s). First derivative \beta{acc}(s) = \frac{d\alpha{acc}}{ds}. Second derivative \gamma{acc}(s) = \frac{d^2\alpha{acc}}{ds^2}. Jump interval I = [i0, i{max}] and magnitude j. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def wysiwypick(cameraeye, screenclick, volumedata, transferfunction, stepsize): # 1. Ray Definition # Transform screen click to world coordinates to get ray origin and direction rayorigin = screentoworld(screenclick, cameraeye) raydirection = normalize(rayorigin - cameraeye) # Note: ray goes from eye to screen # 2. Entry Point Determination # Use a transparent bounding cube (proxy geometry) around the volume entrypoint = intersectboundingcube(rayorigin, raydirection) # 3. Ray Casting and Accumulation # Initialize accumulated opacity alphaacc = 0.0 # Store history of alphaacc for derivative calculation # We assume equidistant samples with stepsize h alphahistory = [] scurrent = 0.0 # Step through the volume until exit while True: # Current sample position in world coordinates pos = entrypoint + raydirection scurrent # Check if outside bounding box if not isinsidevolume(pos, volumedata.bounds): break # Sample data and apply transfer function dval = samplevolume(pos, volumedata) alphasrc, = transferfunction(dval) # Update accumulated opacity using front-to-back compositing # alphaacc^{n+1} = alphaacc^n + (1 - alphaacc^n) alphasrc alphaaccnew = alphaacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) alphasrc alphahistory.append(alphaaccnew) alphaacc = alphaaccnew # Advance step scurrent += stepsize # 4. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Step Size Inconsistency: If DVR uses half the step size (twice as many samples) as the picking ray, accumulated opacity varies differently, leading to incorrect picking. Plateaus: If \alpha{acc} has plateau-like regions, \gamma{acc} is constantly zero. The boundary detection is adapted to handle this by checking for transitions from negative/zero to positive for lower bounds, and zero/positive after negative for upper bounds. Noisy Data: The method does not ensure that close positions in screen space result in close 3D locations, particularly in noisy datasets. Local Illumination: The method is limited to the standard emission-absorption model and does not currently handle local illumination applied after evaluating the transfer function. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray, O(N), where N is the number of steps through the volume. Derivative calculation is also O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the history of accumulated opacity for derivative calculation. Measured Performance: In a user study with 36 test cases, WYSIWYP picked positions within one standard deviation of the mean perceived position for 89% (32 of 36) of cases. Strengths: Does not require metadata or pre-segmented data; applicable to any volumetric scalar dataset and all types of transfer functions, including "foggy" images; handles cases where threshold-based picking fails (thresholds too high/low). Limitations: Does not handle local illumination; does not guarantee spatial coherence for adjacent screen pixels in noisy data; limited to standard emission-absorption model. When to Use: When users need to pick visible structures in arbitrary volume data without metadata, or for automated slice positioning. When Not to Use: When local illumination is present, or when high spatial coherence for adjacent clicks is required in noisy data. WYSIWYP was introduced by to overcome limitations of previous picking methods that required metadata, were designed for medical data only, or provided only basic techniques like first-hit or opacity-threshold. It is based on the principle that users want to examine structures made visible by DVR and suitable transfer functions. The method was implemented in the Amira visualization software and applied to abdominal MRI scans, flow simulation vorticity fields, synthetic scalar functions, and fuel injection combustion chamber simulations. name: Hardware-Accelerated and GPU Implementations
head: GPU Volume Ray Casting, Hardware-Accelerated DVR
body: This family encompasses methods that offload the computationally intensive sampling and compositing stages of direct volume ray casting to the GPU, utilizing programmable shaders and texture hardware to achieve interactive frame rates. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based ray casting by exploiting the intrinsic parallelism of fragment processors. It differs from Shear-Warp by avoiding the final warp step and performing classification after resampling, and from Custom Hardware Units by relying on general-purpose programmable GPUs rather than dedicated ASICs. All methods in this family implement the emission-absorption optical model defined in Direct volume ray casting. The core pipeline for each pixel consists of ray generation, hardware-accelerated sampling, classification, and compositing. 1. Ray Generation: Rays are generated per-pixel, typically by computing ray parameters from camera matrices in vertex/fragment shaders or by rendering the volume's bounding box geometry to determine entry/exit points. 2. Hardware-Accelerated Sampling: Scalar volume values are sampled using the GPU's texture hardware. The volume data is stored in 3D texture memory, and the texture engine performs trilinear interpolation of the eight surrounding voxels in parallel, avoiding manual shader interpolation. 3. Fragment Shader Compositing: The ray marching loop, including classification and front-to-back compositing, is executed within the fragment shader. The standard compositing equation updates accumulated color C' and opacity \alpha': C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai 4. Early Ray Termination (ERT): Rays are terminated when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95 or 1.0) to optimize performance. Direct Volume Rendering: Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) is an image-order technique that renders 3D volumetric data directly without converting it to surface geometry. It treats the volume as a translucent gel or gas, simulating light absorption and emission as rays pass through the scalar field. Unlike indirect methods that extract intermediate geometric primitives like meshes, DVR processes the entire dataset voxel-by-voxel, preserving all internal information and allowing weak or ill-defined structures to remain visible. It is distinguished from its sibling Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering by its specific reliance on GPU-based ray casting within the fragment shader, leveraging hardware texture interpolation for sampling. GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper: The GPU Multi-Volume Ray Casting Mapper is a volume rendering technique that renders multiple volume datasets simultaneously by extending the single-volume mapper to accept multiple datasets and volume property objects, using GPU shaders for ray traversal and compositing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by compositing multiple 3D scalar fields along a single ray, using coordinate transformation matrices to align samples from different volumes to a common ray space. It builds on Hardware-Accelerated and GPU Implementations by providing the specific logic for multi-input data management and shader uniform updates required for simultaneous rendering. Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering: Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that offloads the computationally intensive sampling and compositing steps to the GPU's texture hardware and fragment shaders. It solves the performance bottleneck of software-based ray casting by utilizing 3D texture memory for trilinear interpolation and programmable shaders for front-to-back compositing. It differs from Shear-Warp by avoiding the final warp step and performing classification after resampling, and from Custom Hardware Units by relying on general-purpose programmable GPUs rather than dedicated ASICs. WebGL Multi-pass Ray-casting with 3D Geometry Intersection: This method enables interactive volume rendering of 3D volumetric datasets coexisting with 3D triangular meshes within the constraints of the WebGL API. It solves the problem of rendering hybrid scenes (volumes + geometry) on web platforms that lack native 3D texture support and often lack robust depth texture support. Unlike standard ray-casting which only samples volume data, this method integrates 3D surface occlusion and color by using a multi-pass pipeline to pre-compute depth and color information for both the volume bounding box and the 3D meshes, allowing the final ray-casting pass to correctly handle intersections and alpha blending. It is distinguished from single-pass WebGL ray-casting by its explicit handling of 3D geometry occlusion through depth buffering. Volume Ray-Casting on Graphics Hardware: This method implements direct volume ray casting on programmable graphics hardware using a multi-pass stream model. It solves the performance bottleneck of CPU-based volume rendering by exploiting the intrinsic parallelism of fragment processors and efficient inter-pass communication via texture render targets. Unlike single-pass rasterization, this approach iteratively accumulates optical properties across multiple rendering passes, enabling effective early ray termination and empty-space skipping through hardware-supported early z-tests. GPU-based Tiled Ray Casting with Depth Peeling: This method is a hardware-accelerated ray casting algorithm for volume rendering of time-varying scalar fields on unstructured tetrahedral meshes. It solves the problem of rendering non-convex meshes on GPUs by combining screen tiling for performance with depth peeling to correctly handle ray re-entry into the mesh. It sets itself apart from its sibling Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering by explicitly addressing non-convexity without convexification, and from WebGL Path Tracing Volume Rendering by using deterministic ray casting on unstructured grids rather than path tracing on regular grids. Hardware-assisted Volume Deformation: Hardware-assisted volume deformation renders non-linearly deformed volumes by integrating the deformation process directly into the fragment shader, avoiding the computational expense of pre-computing a resampled deformed volume. Unlike methods that pre-compute the deformed volume, this approach allows for dynamic deformations at interactive rates by evaluating the inverse deformation function per-pixel. It builds on Hardware-Accelerated and GPU Implementations by modifying the texture coordinate generation and sampling logic to account for spatial transformations. Hardware-Accelerated AMR Volume Rendering via Homogenization: This method renders Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data by preprocessing the hierarchy into a set of non-overlapping Cartesian grid patches, allowing standard Direct Volume Ray Casting (DVR) algorithms to be used without resampling. It differs from methods that resample AMR data to a uniform grid or render individual grids with complex boundary handling by explicitly tiling the domain with homogeneous resolution regions. GPU Based Single-Pass Raycasting: GPU Based Single-Pass Raycasting is a volume rendering technique where the volume is traversed along a single ray per pixel, implemented within the Volume Rendering Component framework. It solves the limitations of polygonal-based methods (which are limited in expressive power) and slicing techniques (which can lead to artifacts) by providing high-quality visual results. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific implementation as a single-pass fragment shader execution on modern graphics hardware, relying on hardware-accelerated 3D texture sampling for trilinear interpolation. GPU Implementation Architecture: This article describes the standard software architecture for implementing direct volume ray casting on modern GPUs using OpenGL and GLSL. It details the pipeline for generating spherical harmonic (SH) coefficient volumes and performing ray marching via fragment shaders. It distinguishes itself from generic hardware-accelerated approaches by focusing on the specific data structures (3D coefficient volumes) and rendering techniques (slice-by-slice ray marching with Monte Carlo sampling) required for advanced light-material interaction. A technique to clamp the last ray sample position to the volume or brick extents to prevent artifacts like holes in isosurfaces caused by tri-linear interpolation at brick boundaries. Clip each ray against the boundaries of the volume/brick using a method similar to Sutherland-Hodgman polygon clipping to find the intersection with the back face. Repeat the clipping process for the y- and z-axes to yield the final intersection of the ray and the back face. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def clamplastsample(pos, volextentmin, volextentmax, offset): scale = 0.0 temp = volextentmax - pos if temp.x < 0: scalex = temp.x temp = pos - volextentmin if temp.x < 0: scalex = temp.x correction = abs(scalex / offset.x) pos.x -= correction offset.x return pos Using one voxel overlap between bricks and correct last sampling points is insufficient when using pre-integration because different sampling distances occur. This is overcome by using incremental pre-integration tables as presented by Weiler et al. [WKME03]. A strategy to increase model capacity with multiple GPUs by partitioning 3D space into non-overlapping tiles, where each GPU owns a single tile's NeRF. Rendering and training avoid blending by ensuring sample intervals do not extend beyond tile boundaries. Distribute ray samples among GPUs based on the bounding box of the tiles, ensuring sample intervals do not extend beyond tile boundaries. Query sample attributes (color and density) on each respective GPU. Perform volume rendering through a global gather operation, consolidating information across all GPUs onto a single GPU to compute the final pixel color. During training forward pass, each GPU performs a global gather (broadcast) to obtain color and density from all other GPUs. Each GPU computes the loss locally and back-propagates gradients to its own parameters. No gradient communication is required. Requires synchronizing O(SK^2) data across GPUs, where K is the number of GPUs and S is the average number of samples per-ray per-GPU. Send volume planes one by one as transparent textures to the AGP (Accelerated Graphics Port) using graphic accelerators. Compose back to front. A volume rendering technique implemented by VTK that uses fixed-point arithmetic for ray casting to render volumetric data, specifically medical images. Not given in the sources. Not given in the sources. The shift from CPU-based to GPU-based volume rendering began in the early 2000s with the advent of programmable graphics pipelines (e.g., DirectX 9, OpenGL 2.0). Early implementations utilized multi-pass rendering techniques to overcome hardware limitations on dependent texture fetches and floating-point precision. The introduction of 3D texture hardware and fragment shaders allowed for single-pass ray marching, significantly improving performance and enabling interactive visualization. Recent developments focus on scaling these techniques to large datasets using multi-GPU architectures and handling complex data structures like AMR and unstructured meshes. name: Direct Volume Rendering
head: Direct Volume Rendering of regular grid data, Direct Volume Rendering via GPU-based Ray Casting, Direct Volume Visualization, Direct Volumetric Rendering, Texture-based DVR, Texture-based Direct Volume Rendering
body: Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) visualizes 3D volumetric data directly without converting it to an intermediate geometric representation, such as polygonal meshes or isosurfaces. It treats the dataset as a semi-transparent, participating medium that emits, transmits, and absorbs light, making it uniquely suited for amorphous structures like clouds, smoke, and complex internal tissue. Unlike Indirect Volume Rendering, which extracts explicit surfaces, DVR processes the entire volume data set directly, preserving all internal information and allowing weak or ill-defined structures to remain visible. The method implements the emission-absorption optical model defined in Direct volume ray casting. The core pipeline for each pixel consists of ray generation, hardware-accelerated sampling, classification, and compositing Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering. Input: A 3D scalar volume V represented as a regular grid of voxels. Each voxel stores a scalar value (typically 8–16 bits). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains an accumulated color C and opacity \alpha. 1. Volume Data: Stored in 3D texture memory on the GPU. The volume is a 3D array V{i,j,k} where values are sampled at regular grid points. 2. Transfer Function (TF): Maps scalar density values to optical properties (color C and opacity \alpha). Often implemented as a 1D texture map with hardware-supported linear interpolation. 3. Front-Face Texture (Optional): A screen-size texture encoding the entry point’s texture coordinate and depth for every pixel, used to determine ray start positions efficiently. 4. Depth Texture (Optional): Stores the depth of entry points to maintain correct depth order, particularly when cutting planes are used. 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel (i, j) in the image plane, compute the ray origin \mathbf{x} and direction \omega. The ray is defined parametrically as \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{x} + \omega \cdot t, where t is the ray parameter. The ray origin is typically the intersection of the view ray with the volume's entry surface (front face). 2. Sampling: Discretize the ray into N segments of length \Delta t. The position of the i-th sample is \mathbf{x}i = \mathbf{x} + i \cdot \Delta t \cdot \omega. Sample the scalar value di from the volume at \mathbf{x}i using trilinear interpolation of the eight surrounding voxels. Trilinear interpolation is preferred for its simplicity and hardware support. 3. Classification: Map the sampled scalar value di to color Ci and opacity \alphai using the transfer function. Color: Ci = TC(di). Opacity: The segment opacity \alphai is derived from the volume density. Using the Beer-Lambert model, the transparency of a segment is e^{-\Delta t \cdot \alpha(di)}, leading to the segment opacity approximation: \alphai = 1 - \exp(-\Delta t \cdot \alpha(di)) where \alpha(di) is the opacity density mapped from di. Note: If the sampling rate s differs from the reference rate s0, opacity must be scaled to maintain intensity: A = 1 - (1 - A0)^{s0 / s}. 4. Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity from front-to-back using alpha blending. Initialize accumulated color C'{-1} = 0 and opacity \alpha'{-1} = 0. For each sample i from 0 to N-1: C'i = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'i = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai. The final pixel color is C'{N-1} and opacity is \alpha'{N-1}. 5. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If the accumulated opacity \alpha'i exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95 or 1.0), terminate the ray marching loop early to skip obscured regions. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def directvolumerendering(volumetexture, transferfunction, rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxsamples, volumeboundsmin, volumeboundsmax): """ Renders a single ray using direct volume rendering. Args: volumetexture: 3D texture object supporting trilinear sampling. transferfunction: 1D texture mapping scalar density to (color, opacity). rayorigin: vec3, starting point of the ray. raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the ray. stepsize: float, distance between samples (Delta t). maxsamples: int, maximum number of samples to prevent infinite loops. volumeboundsmin: vec3, minimum bounds of the volume. volumeboundsmax: vec3, maximum bounds of the volume. Returns: (finalcolor: vec3, finalopacity: float) """ # Initialize accumulated color and opacity acccolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 for i in range(maxsamples): # 1. Calculate current sample position currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection (i stepsize) # 2. Check if sample is within volume bounds to avoid out-of-bounds sampling if not all(volumeboundsmin <= currentpos <= volumeboundsmax): break # 3. Sample volume density at current position # Trilinear interpolation is handled by hardware texture sampling density = volumetexture.sampletrilinear(currentpos) # 4. Classify: Map density to color and opacity # Transfer function returns (color, opacitydensity) samplecolor, opacitydensity = transferfunction.sample(density) # 5. Calculate segment opacity using Beer-Lambert law alphasegment = 1.0 - exp(-opacitydensity stepsize) # 6. Compositing: Front-to-back blending # Transmittance from previous step transmittance = 1.0 - accopacity # Contribution of current sample contribution = samplecolor alphasegment transmittance # Update accumulated values acccolor += contribution accopacity += alphasegment transmittance # 7. Early Ray Termination if accopacity >= 0.95: break return acccolor, accopacity Step Size (\Delta t): Typically set to half a voxel or 70% of the distance between adjacent voxels to satisfy sampling theory and reduce aliasing. Interpolation Scheme: Trilinear interpolation is the standard due to hardware support. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to color and opacity. Can be 1D (value-based) or 2D (value and gradient-based). Aliasing: Fixed sampling rates can cause "onion ring" artifacts. Mitigated by increasing the number of samples (reducing segment length). Opacity Scaling: When using fewer samples (larger step size), opacity must be scaled up to maintain correct visual intensity. Boundary Conditions: Rays may exit the volume before reaching maxsamples. Entry and exit points should be calculated to limit the marching range. Gradient Dependence: Gradient estimation for shading should be independent of the classification scheme to avoid artifacts. Converts volume data to an intermediate geometric representation (isosurface) before rendering. Choose when explicit surface geometry is required or when rendering speed is prioritized over internal transparency. Perturbs surface normals using a 3D texture to add high-frequency detail to DVR. Choose when visualizing multiple attributes or enhancing surface appearance without explicit mesh extraction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Limited by pixel fill rate and texture bandwidth. On mobile devices, moderate datasets (64×64×64) can achieve ~2.40 FPS. Loading new data from disk causes noticeable delay, but runtime interactions (navigation, TF changes) are typically smooth. Strengths: Preserves all data information; no preprocessing (isosurface extraction) required; handles transparent and amorphous data well. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large volumes. Sensitive to transfer function choice. Prone to aliasing artifacts if undersampled. When to Use: Rendering amorphous data (clouds, fluids), medical imaging with transparent tissues, or when full internal structure visibility is needed. When Not to Use: When explicit surface geometry is required (use Indirect Volume Rendering), or when rendering unstructured data on GPU without specialized acceleration structures. Direct Volume Rendering was introduced in the late 1980s. Tuy and Tuy (1984) presented one of the earliest techniques using ray casting for iso-surfaces. Levoy (1988) and Drebin, Carpenter, and Hanrahan (1988) provided foundational improvements for direct volume rendering, establishing the ray-casting pipeline and compositing techniques. The method has since been widely adopted in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and mobile platforms using OpenGL ES and WebGL. name: Indirect Volume Rendering
body: Indirect Volume Rendering (IVR) is a technique where volume data is converted into an intermediate traditional computer graphics representation, usually an isosurface or iso-contour, which is then rendered using standard hardware. Unlike Direct Volume Rendering, which processes the volume without generating any intermediate representation, IVR extracts an explicit geometric representation in a preprocessing step. IVR operates by converting the volumetric dataset into an intermediate representation during a preprocessing step, which is then handled by the graphics engine. The most common extraction approach, Marching Cubes, classifies each volume cell of eight neighboring voxels according to a specified iso value. Each voxel has two states (inside or outside an iso surface), yielding 2^8 = 256 possible configurations for how a surface can intersect the cube. Extracts surfaces directly from the spatial domain of the volume data. It differs from frequency domain methods by operating on voxel coordinates rather than spectral coefficients. Choose when explicit polygonal meshes are required for standard hardware rendering. See Marching Cubes. Transforms the volume data into the frequency domain (e.g., using Fourier Transform) before rendering. It differs from space domain methods by operating on spectral coefficients rather than voxel coordinates. Choose when global frequency analysis is beneficial. See Frequency Domain Rendering. Not given in the sources. name: Volumetric Normal Mapping
head: Normal vector glyphs, Volumetric bump mapping, Volumetric normal maps
body: Volumetric Normal Mapping is a technique for direct volume rendering (DVR) that introduces high-frequency visual features into 3D volume data by perturbing the surface normals of the primary volume data using a 3D texture of normal vector glyphs. It solves the problem of visualizing multiple attributes (specifically a secondary functional attribute) in 3D volume data where resolutions may differ, without requiring explicit iso-surface extraction or surface reconstruction. Unlike Direct Volume Rendering which treats data as a transparent gel, this method warps the gradients derived from the primary scalar field to simulate surface detail, distinguishing it from Indirect Volume Rendering which relies on explicit mesh extraction. Inputs and Outputs: Input 1: Primary volume data (scalar field) from which the object surface normal \vec{NO} is derived via gradients. Input 2: Tertiary attribute data (multivariate field) providing the modulation parameter \beta. Input 3: 3D Normal Map Texture containing volumetric normal vector glyphs (e.g., spherical glyphs). Output: Rendered image with perturbed shading based on the blended normal. Data Structures: 3D Normal Map Texture: An RGBA 3D texture. RGB Components: Store the normal vector \vec{NG} of the glyph at each voxel. Alpha Component: Stores the distance r from the center of the spherical glyph to its surface. Layout: The texture is repeated periodically along all axes depending on the size of the original data volume. Glyph Definition: Spherical glyphs are rasterized into the 3D normal map at random positions, and all voxels inside a spherical glyph contain a normal vector definition. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample Glyph Normal: During rendering, sample the normal vector \vec{NG} from the 3D normal map at the current fragment's location. 2. Retrieve Object Normal: Retrieve the object's original surface normal \vec{NO} derived from the gradient of the primary volume data at the current fragment. 3. Retrieve Modulation Parameter: Retrieve the tertiary attribute value \beta from the multivariate data set at the current voxel location. 4. Calculate Angle: Compute the angle \alpha between the object surface normal \vec{NO} and the glyph normal \vec{NG}: \alpha = \cos^{-1} (\vec{NO} \cdot \vec{NG}) where \vec{NO} and \vec{NG} are normalized vectors. 5. Calculate Distance: Calculate the distance d from the center of the bump (glyph) as seen from the observer/fragment: d = r \sin(\alpha) where r is the distance from the center of the spherical glyph to its surface, retrieved from the alpha component of the 3D normal map texture. 6. Evaluate Bump Size: Compare the calculated distance d with the modulation parameter \beta. 7. Apply Suppression: If d > \beta, volumetric normal mapping is denied (suppressed), and only the object surface normal contributes to shading. 8. Blend Normals: If the bump is active, calculate the final normal \vec{N} by linearly blending the object normal \vec{NO} and the glyph normal \vec{NG} weighted by \beta: \vec{N} = \vec{NO} + \beta \vec{NG} The blending is linear. 9. Shade: Use the final normal \vec{N} for illumination calculations in the fragment shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumetricnormalmapping(fragmentpos, primaryvol, tertiaryvol, normalmap): # 1. Sample Glyph Normal glyphrgba = normalmap.sample(fragmentpos) NG = normalize(glyphrgba.rgb) r = glyphrgba.a # 2. Retrieve Object Normal # Gradient calculation not given in sources dx = primaryvol.sample(fragmentpos + vec3(1,0,0)) - primaryvol.sample(fragmentpos - vec3(1,0,0)) dy = primaryvol.sample(fragmentpos + vec3(0,1,0)) - primaryvol.sample(fragmentpos - vec3(0,1,0)) dz = primaryvol.sample(fragmentpos + vec3(0,0,1)) - primaryvol.sample(fragmentpos - vec3(0,0,1)) NO = normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) # 3. Retrieve Modulation Parameter beta = tertiaryvol.sample(fragmentpos) # 4. Calculate Angle dotval = clamp(dot(NO, NG), -1.0, 1.0) alpha = acos(dotval) # 5. Calculate Distance d = r sin(alpha) # 6 & 7. Evaluate Bump Size & Apply Suppression if d > beta: Nfinal = NO else: # 8. Blend Normals Nfinal = NO + beta NG Nfinal = normalize(Nfinal) # 9. Shade # Lighting model not given in sources lightdir = normalize(vec3(0.5, 0.8, 1.0)) diffuse = max(dot(Nfinal, lightdir), 0.0) return vec3(diffuse) Parameters: \beta: A parameter from the tertiary attribute field. It controls the maximum bump size by comparing the fragment distance to the bump's center. In the teapot example, it was chosen to be constant 1.0. \vec{NO}: Object's surface normal vector. \vec{NG}: Glyph's normal vector. r: Distance from the center of the spherical glyph to its surface (stored in alpha channel). \alpha: Angle between \vec{NO} and \vec{NG}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Simple Blending Limitation: Simple blending (Eq. 1) has limited use because the size and convexity of the resulting bumps depend on where the object intersects the spherical glyphs, not just on \beta. The distance-based suppression (Eq. 2, 3) is required to control bump size effectively. Planar Assumption: Size control of the normal glyphs according to equation (2) is valid only if the surface of the primary object is almost planar with respect to the area of intersection with the spherical normal glyph. This condition is considered true for intended applications where glyphs introduce high-frequency features. Convexity: The convexity of the bumps (convex vs concave) depends on which hemisphere of the glyph the object's surface intersects with. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Visualizes multiple attributes without explicit surface reconstruction. Introduces high-frequency visual features. Works with multivariate data of different resolutions. Limitations: Limited to spherical glyphs in the described implementation. Relies on the planar surface assumption. The effect of \beta on bump size is only effective when combined with the distance-based suppression. When to use: When visualizing secondary functional attributes in 3D volume data where iso-surface extraction is undesirable or difficult due to resolution mismatches. When not to use: When precise geometric control of bump size independent of intersection location is required without the distance-based suppression mechanism. Volumetric Normal Mapping was introduced by S. Seipel in 2007. The work was presented at the Eurographics Symposium on Visualization 2007. The method addresses the challenge in medical functional imaging (e.g., PET) where multiple variables (anatomical structure and functional property) are captured at different resolutions. Unlike engineering simulations where variables share the same grid, medical imaging requires techniques to visualize these disparate attributes together. The method builds on the concept of normal mapping but extends it to 3D volumes without the need for explicit surface extraction (like Marching Cubes [LC87]), which is difficult to parameterize stably for varying iso-surface levels. name: Parallel Domain-Decomposed Ray Casting
head: MPI Ray Casting, Distributed Ray Casting
body: Parallel Domain-Decomposed Ray Casting is a parallel volume rendering technique that accelerates rendering by dividing a 3D volume dataset among multiple processing units, where each unit casts rays through its assigned subvolume independently using a front-to-back algorithm. It solves the scalability problem of direct volume ray casting for high-resolution datasets that exceed the memory of a single processor by distributing both data and computation. Unlike image-order methods (e.g., Image-order rendering) or image-space subdivision, this method uses data-space subdivision (object-space partitioning), allowing nodes to perform local ray tracing without inter-processor communication during the sampling phase. The final image is constructed by compositing the resulting partial images (subimages) in a determined depth order. The method consists of three phases: Data Distribution, Local Ray Casting, and Parallel Compositing. It builds on the core computational engine of Direct volume ray casting. Inputs: Volume data: A 3D array of scalar values (e.g., float32), shape (Z, Y, X). Transfer functions: Opacity map: 2D array, 2 rows. Row 1: scalar positions; Row 2: opacity values. Color map: 2D array, 5 rows. Row 1: scalar positions; Rows 2-4: R, G, B values. Grid dimensions: Integers px, py, pz defining the 3D grid of processes. Sampling step size: \Delta t (e.g., 0.5). Outputs: Final image: A 2D array of RGB color values (e.g., uint8). The volume is partitioned into px \times py \times pz subvolumes. For a total volume size (X{Total}, Y{Total}, Z{Total}), the segment sizes are: X{seg} = \lfloor X{Total} / px \rfloor, \quad Y{seg} = \lfloor Y{Total} / py \rfloor, \quad Z{seg} = \lfloor Z{Total} / pz \rfloor Rank k (where k = i + j \cdot px + l \cdot px py for grid indices i,j,l) receives the slice: \text{data}[l \cdot Z{seg}: (l+1) \cdot Z{seg}, \quad j \cdot Y{seg}: (j+1) \cdot Y{seg}, \quad i \cdot X{seg}: (i+1) \cdot X{seg}]. Boundary conditions apply for the last segments to cover the full extent. 1. Initialization and Distribution: Rank 0 loads the full volume and transfer functions. Rank 0 partitions the volume into chunks based on px, py, pz. Rank 0 sends each chunk along with metadata (transfer functions, grid dimensions) to the corresponding rank using point-to-point communication (e.g., MPISend). Other ranks receive their data chunk. 2. Local Ray Casting: Each rank independently executes the front-to-back ray casting algorithm on its local subvolume. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the assigned image region, a ray is defined. Sampling: The ray is sampled at intervals \Delta t. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is used to retrieve scalar values from the 8 nearest voxels in the local subvolume. Classification: The scalar value is mapped to color (Ci) and opacity (\alphai) using the transfer functions. Compositing: The front-to-back equation is applied locally: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai Ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai. Result: Each rank produces a partial image (subimage) consisting of color and opacity meshes for its portion of the image. 3. Parallel Compositing: The subimages must be composited in a strict front-to-back order determined a priori by the spatial arrangement of the subvolumes. The compositing process uses a binary-swap or tree-based reduction strategy to merge partial images. Associativity: The Porter-Duff "over" operator is associative: a \text{ over } (b \text{ over } c) = (a \text{ over } b) \text{ over } c, allowing independent segment processing. Communication: Ranks exchange their color and opacity meshes. For example, in a 2x2x2 grid, ranks with index \ge px py send their meshes to the corresponding rank < px py (where surfaceProcess = rank \% t and t = px py). Ranks < t receive meshes from deeper ranks along the Z-dimension and composite them using the associative Porter-Duff over operator. This continues until all subimages are merged into a single final image. Rank 0 gathers the final composited meshes, converts to uint8, and saves the image. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np from mpi4py import MPI def lerp(x0, x1, t): return x0 (1.0 - t) + x1 t def trilinearinterpolate(data, x, y, z): # Standard trilinear interpolation of 3D volume data ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz c000 = data[iz, iy, ix] c100 = data[iz, iy, ix+1] c010 = data[iz, iy+1, ix] c110 = data[iz, iy+1, ix+1] c001 = data[iz+1, iy, ix] c101 = data[iz+1, iy, ix+1] c011 = data[iz+1, iy+1, ix] c111 = data[iz+1, iy+1, ix+1] c00 = lerp(c000, c100, fx) c01 = lerp(c010, c110, fx) c10 = lerp(c001, c101, fx) c11 = lerp(c011, c111, fx) c0 = lerp(c00, c01, fy) c1 = lerp(c10, c11, fy) return lerp(c0, c1, fz) def interpolatetf(tftable, value): # Linear interpolation from transfer function table positions = tftable[0] values = tftable[1] idx = 0 for k in range(len(positions) - 1): if positions[k] <= value < positions[k+1]: idx = k break else: idx = len(positions) - 2 t = (value - positions[idx]) / (positions[idx+1] - positions[idx]) return lerp(values[idx], values[idx+1], t) def raycastlocal(data, opacitytf, colortf, stepsize, imagedims): height, width = imagedims colormesh = np.zeros((height, width, 3), dtype=np.float32) opacitymesh = np.zeros((height, width), dtype=np.float32) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): cacc = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], dtype=np.float32) aacc = 0.0 # Ray segment bounds within subvolume tstart, tend = 0.0, 1.0 t = tstart while t < tend: # Interpolate scalar value d from data at current ray position d = trilinearinterpolate(data, t width, t height, t) # Map to color and opacity using transfer functions alpha = interpolatetf(opacitytf, d) r = interpolatetf(colortf, d) g = interpolatetf(colortf, d) b = interpolatetf(colortf, d) ci = np.array([r, g, b], dtype=np.float32) # Front-to-back compositing cacc = cacc + (1.0 - aacc) alpha ci aacc = aacc + (1.0 - aacc) alpha if aacc >= 0.95: # Threshold cut-off break t += stepsize colormesh[y, x] = cacc opacitymesh[y, x] = aacc return colormesh, opacitymesh def parallelcompositing(colormesh, opacitymesh, rank, size, px, py, pz, comm): t = px py if rank < t: mycolor = colormesh myopacity = opacitymesh # Receive from deeper ranks along Z-dimension for c in range(1, pz): destrank = (c t) + rank if destrank < size: recvcolor, recvopacity = comm.recv(source=destrank) # Composite: mycolor is in front, recv is behind mycolor = mycolor + (1.0 - myopacity) recvcolor myopacity = myopacity + (1.0 - myopacity) recvopacity return mycolor, myopacity else: surfaceprocess = rank % t comm.send([colormesh, opacitymesh], dest=surfaceprocess) return None, None comm = MPI.COMMWORLD rank = comm.Getrank() size = comm.Getsize() if rank == 0: # Load data, TFs # Partition data into pxpypz chunks # Send chunks to other ranks pass else: # Receive chunk data, opacitytf, colortf, px, py, pz = comm.recv(source=0) colormesh, opacitymesh = raycastlocal(data, opacitytf, colortf, stepsize, imagedims) finalcolor, finalopacity = parallelcompositing(colormesh, opacitymesh, rank, size, px, py, pz, comm) if rank == 0: # Gather final images if necessary, or if rank 0 is the only surface rank # In the example, rank 0 gathers all composited meshes. pass Load Imbalance: Empty voxels (e.g., in head or vessel data) cause uneven computation loads compared to dense data (e.g., vorticity), reducing speedup. Communication Overhead: On networked workstations, communication can account for ~97% of compositing time. Compression (e.g., 4:1 ratio) can reduce this by 80%. Small Images: Small image sizes (e.g., 64x64) exhibit less speedup due to fixed overhead costs in rendering and compositing steps. Ordering: Subvolumes must be partitioned such that an unambiguous front-to-back ordering can be determined for compositing. Remote Execution: On older systems, REX was unreliable; rsh was used as a slower alternative. A variant that distributes both volume data and computation to individual processing units to render high-resolution datasets. It distinguishes itself by using data-space subdivision, which is better suited for distributed-memory environments where data can be partitioned, and composites subimages in a determined depth order using a binary-swap method. A parallel ray tracing method for tetrahedral data that distributes volume and rendering among processing nodes. It partitions the volume so each processor handles a sub-volume, then all processors accumulate interpolated values along a ray independently. Contributions are sorted with respect to visibility order before composing the final image. Its frame rate scales linearly with the number of processors. Time Complexity: The local ray casting phase is O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of samples per ray, distributed across P processors, yielding O(N \cdot M / P) for the rendering phase. The compositing phase is O(P \cdot C) where C is the cost of compositing two images, typically logarithmic in P due to binary-swap. Memory Complexity: Each node stores only its assigned subvolume, reducing memory requirements per node to V/P where V is the total volume size. Performance: On CM-5 with vorticity data, nearly linear speedup was achieved for image sizes above 64x64. On networked workstations, communication dominates compositing time. Strengths: Scalability to large datasets that do not fit in single-node memory; no inter-node communication during the computationally intensive ray casting phase. Limitations: Load imbalance due to data sparsity; communication bottleneck during compositing on slow networks. The method was developed to address the speed limitations of volume rendering on single processors. Early work by Dippe and Swensen parallelized geometric ray tracing by dividing world space. Upson argued that ray casting was difficult to parallelize due to the need for global shared memory. This method demonstrated that ray casting could be parallelized at the subvolume level on distributed systems without global shared memory. It was implemented on Sun SPARC-2 and Sun-4/260 workstations (AFITNET) and the Connection Machine CM-5. name: Parallel Volume Rendering with Local Ray Tracing and Parallel Compositing
head: Data Distributed Parallel Algorithm, Data-Distributed Parallel Ray-Traced Volume Rendering, Data-space subdivision for volume rendering, Divide-and-Conquer Parallel Volume Rendering, Divide-and-conquer ray-traced volume rendering, Parallel Volume Ray-Tracing Algorithm, Parallel Volume Rendering with Local Raytracing
body: This method is a parallel volume rendering algorithm that distributes both the volume data and the computational load across individual processing units to render high-resolution datasets that exceed the memory capacity of a single machine. It employs data-space subdivision, where the volume is partitioned into subvolumes assigned to different processors, which perform local ray tracing independently without inter-processor communication during the rendering phase. The final image is constructed by compositing the resulting subimages in a specific front-to-back order. Unlike image-space subdivision methods (e.g., Image-order rendering), this approach is designed for distributed-memory environments where data can be partitioned in memory. It builds on the associativity of the Porter and Duff 'over' compositing operator, allowing rays to be split into segments processed in parallel. Inputs: A 3D volume dataset V of size Dx \times Dy \times Dz. A viewpoint (eye position and projection parameters). Transfer functions: a color map and an opacity map. A shading model (e.g., Phong) and surface normal estimation (normalized gradient of V). A sampling rate (typically 1–2 samples per voxel). A termination threshold for accumulated opacity. n processing units (processors/nodes). Outputs: A final 2D image I of resolution W \times H. Volume Partitioning: The volume V is partitioned into n equal-sized 3D blocks (subvolumes) \tilde{V}q for 1 \le q \le n. The partitioning planes are parallel to the coordinate planes of the data. Boundary Replication: To avoid boundary artifacts during compositing, one layer of boundary grid points is replicated at each subvolume's interface so that the composited image includes the layer from the adjacent subvolume. Subimage: Each processor q generates a subimage \tilde{I}q corresponding to the contribution of \tilde{V}q. Ray Set: For each processor q, the set of rays Rq traversing its subvolume \tilde{V}q is determined. 1. Initialization: The host reads the volume data (optionally from disk) and broadcasts opacity/colormap and transformation information to the nodes. Each node receives its data-space partitioning information and its portion of the volume data \tilde{V}q. Nodes update the transfer function and transform matrices. The viewpoint coordinate is broadcast to all processors. 2. Phase 1: Local Ray Tracing (No Communication): Each processor q independently casts rays from the eye through the image plane into its assigned subvolume \tilde{V}q. For each ray \mathbf{r} \in Rq: Sample the subvolume at evenly spaced points along the ray, typically at a rate of one to two samples per voxel. At each sample point, compute color c and opacity \alpha using trilinear interpolation from the eight nearest voxels in \tilde{V}q. Apply the shading model (e.g., Phong) using the normalized gradient of the data as the surface normal. Accumulate color and opacity using the Porter and Duff 'over' operator until the subvolume is exhausted or the accumulated opacity reaches the threshold cut-off. Generate the subimage \tilde{I}q. 3. Phase 2: Parallel Compositing: The n subimages \tilde{I}1, \dots, \tilde{I}n are merged into the final image I. The merge order is determined a priori based on the unambiguous front-to-back ordering of the subvolumes. A binary-swap compositing method is used: Processors exchange and composite half-images in a tree-like structure. For example, Computer 1 keeps its left half-image and sends its right half-image to Computer 2. Computer 2 keeps its right half-image and sends its left half-image to Computer 1. Both composite the half-image they keep with the half-image they receive. This process reduces the image size for sending/compositing and keeps all processors busy. A k-D tree structure may be used to manage the compositing steps. Compression (e.g., 4-to-1 ratio) may be applied to subimages before swapping to reduce communication cost. 4. Phase 3: Image Gathering: Each node sends its portion of the final composited image back to the host for display. The compositing is based on the Porter and Duff 'over' operator, which is associative: a \text{ over } (b \text{ over } c) = (a \text{ over } b) \text{ over } c This associativity allows the ray to be broken into segments processed independently by different processors and combined later. The color C and opacity \alpha at a sample point are computed via trilinear interpolation from the eight nearest voxels vi with values di: C = \text{ColorMap}(\text{Interpolate}(d1, \dots, d8)) \alpha = \text{OpacityMap}(\text{Interpolate}(d1, \dots, d8)) The final color C{final} and opacity \alpha{final} for a ray segment are accumulated front-to-back: C{out} = C{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) C{sample} \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{sample} where (C{in}, \alpha{in}) is the accumulated value from previous samples and (C{sample}, \alpha{sample}) is the current sample. Sampling Rate: 1–2 samples per voxel. Interpolation: Trilinear. Shading: Phong lighting model. Termination: Accumulated opacity threshold cut-off. Partition Sizes: Supported 32, 64, 128, 256, and 512 nodes on CM-5. Image Resolution: Tested on 64x64 and 512x512. Load Imbalance: Data sets with many empty voxels (e.g., head, vessel) cause load imbalance, preventing linear speedup. Fixed Viewpoint Optimization: Partitioning to minimize overlap between subimages reduces merging cost but cannot be applied to animation sequences where the viewpoint changes. Communication Overhead: On networked workstations, communication dominates compositing costs (~97% of compositing time) because Ethernet bandwidth is fixed. On CM-5, communication time varied from 10% to 3% of total compositing time. Variable Network Performance: In shared environments, communication performance is difficult to characterize due to network traffic from NFS, tape backups, and other users. Boundary Artifacts: Replicating one layer of boundary grid points is required to avoid artifacts at subvolume interfaces. Unverified code. numnodes): partitioninfo = computepartitioning(volumedata, numnodes) broadcast(viewpoint, transferfunctions, partitioninfo) subvolume = extractsubvolume(volumedata, partitioninfo) subimage = localraytrace(subvolume, viewpoint, transferfunctions) synchronize() finalimage = binaryswapcompositing(subimage, partitioninfo) sendtohost(finalimage) return finalimage def localraytrace(subvolume, viewpoint, transferfunctions): width, height = getimagedimensions() subimage = createemptyimage(width, height) subvolume = replicateboundary(subvolume) for y in range(height): for x in range(width): ray = castray(viewpoint, x, y) acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 for samplepoint in ray.samplesin(subvolume): voxelvalue = trilinearinterpolate(subvolume, samplepoint) color = transferfunctions.colormap(voxelvalue) opacity = transferfunctions.opacitymap(voxelvalue) normal = normalizegradient(subvolume, samplepoint) color = applyphongshading(color, normal, viewpoint) acccolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accopacity) color accopacity = accopacity + (1.0 - accopacity) opacity if accopacity >= THRESHOLD: break subimage.setpixel(x, y, acccolor, accopacity) return subimage def getpartnernode(currentnode, step) if islefthalf(currentnode, step): sendrighthalf(currentimage, partner) receivelefthalf(partner, currentnode) currentimage = compositewithleft(receivebuffer) else: sendlefthalf(currentimage, partner) receiverighthalf(partner, currentnode) currentimage = compositewithright(receivebuffer) return currentimage def computepartitioning(volumedata, numnodes): return {"nodeid": 0, "numnodes": numnodes} def broadcast(viewpoint, transferfunctions, partitioninfo): pass def extractsubvolume(volumedata, partitioninfo): return volumedata def synchronize(): pass def sendtohost(image): pass def getimagedimensions(): return 512, 512 def createemptyimage(width, height): return [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0] for in range(height width)] def replicateboundary(subvolume): normalizegradient(subvolume, point): return (0, 0, 1) def applyphongshading(color, normal, viewpoint): return color THRESHOLD = 0.95 def getpartnernode(nodeid, step): return nodeid ^ (1 << step) def islefthalf(nodeid, step): return (nodeid >> step) % 2 == 0 def sendrighthalf(image, partner): pass def receivelefthalf(partner, sender): global receivebuffer receivebuffer = image def compositewithleft(receivebuffer): return receivebuffer def sendlefthalf(image, partner): pass def receiverighthalf(partner, sender): global receivebuffer receivebuffer = image def compositewithright(receivebuffer): return receivebuffer Time Complexity: The local ray tracing phase is O(N \cdot S) where N is the number of rays and S is the number of samples per ray, performed in parallel by n processors, yielding O(N \cdot S / n) for the rendering phase. The compositing phase involves O(\log n) steps of communication and compositing. Memory Complexity: Each node stores only its assigned subvolume \tilde{V}q, allowing the rendering of datasets larger than the memory of a single machine. Performance: On the CM-5, the algorithm demonstrated practicality with good speedup characteristics up to 512 nodes for dense data sets (vorticity). For sparse data sets (head, vessel), speedup was limited by load imbalance. On networked workstations, communication overhead was significant (~97% of compositing time) due to fixed Ethernet bandwidth. Compression (4-to-1 ratio) improved communication rates by 80%. Strengths: Suitable for distributed-memory environments; handles large datasets; no communication during the computationally intensive ray tracing phase. Limitations: Load imbalance for sparse data; communication overhead on networks with fixed bandwidth; boundary artifacts if not handled; fixed-viewpoint optimization not applicable to animations. When to use: When rendering large volume datasets on distributed-memory systems where data cannot fit in a single machine's memory. When not to use: When the dataset is small enough for a single machine; when the network bandwidth is very low and communication overhead dominates; when the viewpoint changes frequently (animation) and dynamic partitioning is not implemented. The algorithm was presented by Ma et al. in 1993. It was implemented and tested on the Connection Machine CM-5 and a network of 32 high-performance workstations (IBM RS/6000-550, HP9000/730, Sun Sparc-15/30) using PVM 3.1. The method is based on the divide-and-conquer paradigm and the associativity of the Porter and Duff 'over' operator. It was adopted by STARVolume. Tests used three data sets: 256x256x256 vorticity (CFD), 128x128x128 head (CT), and 256x256x128 vessel (MRA).
