name: GPU-based Tiled Ray Casting with Depth Peeling
head: Depth Peeling Ray Casting, GPU-based Tiled Ray Casting, GPU-based Tiled Ray Casting using Depth Peeling, Ray Casting for TVSF, Tiled Ray Casting, Tiled Ray Casting using Depth Peeling, Tiled Ray Casting with Depth Peeling
body: This method is a hardware-accelerated ray casting algorithm for volume rendering of time-varying scalar fields on unstructured tetrahedral meshes. It solves the problem of rendering non-convex meshes on GPUs by combining screen tiling for performance with depth peeling to correctly handle ray re-entry into the mesh without convexification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Unstructured tetrahedral mesh (vertices, normals, faces, tetrahedra indices, scalar values), camera parameters (eye position, view direction), and a pre-integrated Lookup Table (LUT). Output: Final color and opacity image. Data Structures: All data is stored in 2D textures (F32x4 format) to optimize GPU memory access and avoid 3D texture limitations. 1. Mesh Data Storage (144 bytes per tetrahedron): Vertices: 3 rows per tetrahedron t, indexed by (tu, tv), (tu, tv+dv), (tu, tv+2dv). RGB channels: Vertex coordinates (v{t,0..2}^{x,y,z}). Alpha channel: Fourth vertex coordinate (v{t,3}^{x,y,z}). Face Normals: 3 rows per tetrahedron t, indexed by (tu, tv), (tu, tv+dv), (tu, tv+2dv). RGB channels: Normal coordinates (n{t,0..2}^{x,y,z}). Alpha channel: Fourth normal coordinate (n{t,3}^{x,y,z}). Neighbor Data: 1 row per tetrahedron t, indexed by (tu, tv). RGB channels: Adjacency indices (a{t,0}, a{t,1}). Scalar Data: 1 row per tetrahedron t, indexed by (tu, tv+2dv). RGB channels: Gradient (gt^{x,y,z}). Alpha channel: Scalar value (st). Note: tu, tv split the tetrahedron index because GPU 2D texture indices are limited (up to 4096 per dimension). 2. Traversal Data Storage: Current Cell: Indexed by raster position. R channel: Tetrahedron index tu. G channel: Tetrahedron index tv. B channel: Intersection parameter \lambda. A channel: Scalar field value s(e + \lambda r). Color/Opacity: Indexed by raster position. RGB channels: Accumulated color. A channel: Accumulated opacity. Algorithm Steps: 1. Data Packing: Pack mesh data (vertices, normals, faces, tetrahedra) and pre-integrated tables into 2D textures. 2. Tile Partitioning: Partition the image screen into fixed-size disjoint tiles to exploit spatial and memory cache coherence. 3. Phase 1: First Intersection: Render boundary faces with Z-buffer enabled. Vertex shader sets tetrahedron index (tu, tv) at each vertex. Fragment shader computes the first intersection in Object Coordinate System (OCS) by applying inverse modeling transformation to eye (e{ocs}) and ray direction (r{ocs}). Retrieve mesh data from 2D textures. Store intersection \lambda, scalar field, and tetrahedron indices in traversal structures. 4. Phase 2: Depth Peeling Levels: Use a multi-pass approach (one layer per pass) because GPUs cannot read/write to the same texture. Render boundary faces with back-face culling ON. Fragment shader compares candidate \lambda with value stored in previous layer; if candidate \lambda \le stored \lambda, discard fragment. Apply a bias value in the comparison test to reduce numerical artifacts. This generates n layers of visible faces. The first layer is the initial set of visible faces; subsequent layers contain the next visible faces, discarding faces from previous layers. 5. Phase 3a: Ray Casting (Ping-Pong Rendering): Use a pair of traversal textures switched each pass. Render screen-aligned rectangle (or tile-aligned subregions). For each active ray, compute the next intersection along ray direction in OCS. Look for minimum \lambda (exit point) among positive denominators. Compute adjacent tetrahedron at intersection point using neighbor data. If no adjacent tetrahedron (special index), store indicating ray left mesh. Accumulate color using pre-computed color information from entry/exit points via LUT. Occlusion Test: After k ray casting passes, perform Z-update and Occlusion Test to amortize cost. Use early-z tests to avoid computation for rays that miss or have left the mesh. 6. Phase 3b: Layer Advancement: If the next depth peeling layer contains visible faces, issue a second ray casting pass using the information stored in that layer as starting points. Repeat Phase 3a and 3b until all rays leave the mesh and the following depth peeling layer does not contain visible faces. 7. Phase 4: Display: Render screen-aligned rectangle sampling the color texture generated by ray-casting pass. Formulas: Ray-Tetrahedron Intersection: \lambdai = \frac{(v - e) \cdot n{t,i}}{r \cdot n{t,i}} \quad \text{where } v = v{t,3-i} Only positive \lambdai values are considered. Entry point \lambda{in}: Maximum \lambda among values with negative denominator. Exit point \lambda{out}: Minimum \lambda among values with positive denominator. If \lambda{in} > \lambda{out}, no intersection exists. Definitions: e is eye position, r is normalized ray direction, n{t,i} is face normal, v{t,3-i} is tetrahedron vertex. Scalar Field Interpolation: s(x) = gt \cdot (x - x0) + s(x0) Where gt is the gradient of the scalar field, x0 is a reference point (e.g., a vertex), and s(x0) is the scalar value at x0. Front-to-Back Color Composition: Ck = C'{k-1} + (1 - \alpha{k-1})Ck Where Ck is the current color contribution, C'{k-1} is the accumulated color from previous steps, and \alpha{k-1} is the accumulated opacity. Parameters: Pre-integrated 3D LUT: Indexed by distances between entry and exit points (normalized using the length of the greatest edge of the mesh) and scalar field values at both points. Returns color (r,g,b) and opacity \alpha. k: Number of ray casting passes after which the Z-update and Occlusion Test is performed to amortize cost. Bias value: Used in depth peeling comparison test to reduce artifacts due to numerical calculations. Pitfalls: Non-convex meshes: Rays may exit and re-enter the mesh. Depth peeling handles this, avoiding convexification. GPU Memory Limits: 2D texture indices are limited (up to 4096 per dimension), requiring tetrahedral index splitting. MRT Limitations: Current GPUs (at time of source) do not allow writing to the frame-buffer while using Multiple Render Targets (MRTs), requiring a separate buffer for color accumulation. Branching: GPUs have limited/expensive branching, requiring fetching all vertices/normals of a tetrahedron consecutively in texture memory. Read/Write Constraints: GPUs cannot read and write to the same texture, requiring multi-pass depth peeling and ping-pong rendering for ray casting. Memory: Constrained by GPU memory available for storing mesh data in textures. Saves up to 30% memory compared to previous 3D texture layouts. Performance: Substantially faster than Weiler et al.'s technique on the same hardware. Scaling: Tiling allows variable number of intersection passes per tile, approximating minimum required passes and reducing processed fragments. Strengths: Handles general non-convex meshes without convexification; efficient 2D texture storage; exploits spatial coherence via tiling. Limitations: Limited by GPU memory (smaller datasets than CPU-based methods like HAVS); requires multiple passes for depth peeling and ray traversal. Origin: Proposed by Christian A. Pagot, Joao L. D. Comba, and Claudio T. Silva. History: Builds on the technique published at IEEE Visualization 2003 by Weiler et al. and the idea of using boundary fragments from Bunyk et al.. Usage: Implemented in C++ using DirectX 9.0 and HLSL. Tested on ATI Radeon 9700 Pro 128MB and NVIDIA GeForce 6800 GT 256MB. Used for rendering time-varying scalar fields on unstructured meshes, such as EEG brain data and procedural meshes. name: Hardware-assisted Volume Deformation
head: Deformed Volume Rendering via Inverse Deformation in Fragment Shaders, Shader-based volume warping
body: Hardware-assisted volume deformation renders deformed volumes by integrating the deformation process directly into the rendering pipeline, rather than pre-computing the deformed volume data. It solves the performance bottleneck of 3D resampling required for non-linear geometric transformations, enabling interactive visualization of dynamic deformations. Unlike methods that pre-compute the deformed volume (e.g., [LGL95]), this approach allows for dynamic deformations at interactive rates because the deformation is computed per-pixel in the fragment shader. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Undeformed volume data v stored in a 3D texture; inverse deformation function u = d^{-1}, where d maps undeformed object space to deformed object space. Output: Rendered image with deformed geometry. Data Structures: 3D Texture: Stores the scalar field of the undeformed volume v. Coordinates in this texture correspond to undeformed object space (texture space). Proxy Geometry: A series of polygons aligned with the image plane (view-aligned planes). Texture Coordinates: Assigned to each polygon fragment representing the deformed object-space coordinates. Numbered Steps: 1. Place the undeformed volume data v into a 3D texture. 2. Draw a series of polygons aligned with the image plane as proxy geometry. 3. Assign texture coordinates to each polygon representing the deformed object-space coordinates. 4. In the fragment shader, for each fragment, apply the inverse deformation function u to the deformed object-space coordinates (textCoord) to obtain undeformed object-space coordinates. 5. Sample the 3D texture using the undeformed object-space coordinates to get the scalar value. 6. Apply the transfer function to the sampled scalar value to compute the color. 7. Accumulate the color in the framebuffer using compositing operations in back-to-front order. Formulas: The deformed volume v' is defined as the composition of the undeformed volume v and the inverse deformation function u: v'(x, y, z) = (v \circ u)(x, y, z) where u = d^{-1} and d is the deformation mapping from undeformed to deformed object space. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. vec3 deformedcoords = textCoord; vec3 undeformedcoords = invDeform(deformedcoords); float scalarvalue = texture3D(texD, undeformedcoords); vec4 color = transferfunction(scalarvalue); return color; Parameters: Inverse Deformation Function (u): The mapping from deformed object space to undeformed object space. If only the forward deformation d is provided, it must be inverted using scattered data interpolation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Point sampling in the volume texture can lead to aliasing. To correctly filter the warp, the kernel radius must be determined for the spacing of the sampling in texture space, not object space. Resource Limits: Fragment programs have limited resources, making some complex deformation functions impractical to implement directly in the shader. Gradient Calculation: Shading requires the gradient of the deformed volume, which presents a hurdle for this method. A technique where volume deforming and volume rendering are incorporated into a single process. It combines Free Form Deformation (FFD) and inverse ray deformation. Unlike standard inverse deformation which samples points, this method handles different lengths of sampled intervals in polyline segments that approximate the deformed ray, often using preintegration techniques for opacity and shading. A method where the volume is subdivided by hand into logical blocks. Each block is transformed and copied to a new location, then rendered via 3D texture-mapping hardware. The resulting images are composited in back-to-front order. Gaps that develop between displaced blocks (e.g., at bending knee joints) are filled by interpolating additional boxes in these areas along the midplane of the crack. This approach enables near-interactive volume deformation. Time Complexity: Depends on the complexity of the inverse deformation function u evaluated per fragment. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the undeformed volume in 3D texture memory. Strengths: Allows for dynamic deformations at interactive rates without pre-computing the deformed volume. Limitations: Fragment program resource limits may restrict the complexity of deformation functions. Performance issues may arise due to the large number of fragments requiring deformation computation. When to use: Interactive non-linear registration, real-time volume animation, and animated deformation interaction techniques. When not to use: When the deformation function is too complex for the fragment shader's instruction limit. Applying non-linear geometric transformations to volume data is common in science and medicine for correcting imaging deformations, aligning objects, and modeling for animation. Traditionally, this required computationally expensive 3D resampling, precluding dynamic deformations. This method was introduced to leverage programmable graphics hardware for integrating spatial transformations into interactive volume visualization tools. name: Volume Rendering in 3D Slicer
head: VTK CPU Ray Casting, VTK GPU Ray Casting, VTK Multi-Volume
body: Volume rendering in 3D Slicer is a visualization technique for displaying image volumes as 3D objects directly without requiring segmentation, accomplished by specifying color and opacity for each voxel based on its image intensity. It builds on Direct volume ray casting by providing a user interface for transfer function tuning and multiple rendering backends (CPU, GPU, Multi-Volume). It distinguishes itself from general implementations by its integration with the Slicer data model, allowing for synchronized color mapping with slice views, interactive segmentation-based masking, and specific handling of medical imaging modalities (CT/MR) via presets. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A vtkMRMLVolumeNode containing scalar, RGB, or RGBA data. The volume may be associated with a segmentation mask (via the Segment Editor) to blank out regions. Output: A rendered 3D view displaying the volume with applied transfer functions, shading, and compositing. Data Structures: Transfer Functions: Defined by control points (X, O, M, S) where X is the scalar value, O is opacity, M is the mid-point, and S is sharpness. Cropping Box (ROI): A bounding box defining the region of interest. Partitions: A tuple (px, py, pz) used to split the volume into smaller chunks for GPU rendering stability. Numbered Steps: 1. Volume Preparation: If the volume is warped (affine or non-linear), the transform must be hardened on the volume data before rendering. If regions need to be hidden, a segmentation is created using Paint/Scissors effects, and the Mask volume effect fills the region with "empty" values (e.g., -1000 HU for CT air). The original volume rendering is hidden, and rendering is applied to the masked volume. 2. Backend Selection: The user selects one of three techniques in the "Rendering" section: VTK CPU Ray Casting, VTK GPU Ray Casting (default), or VTK Multi-Volume. 3. Transfer Function Application: Scalar Opacity Mapping maps scalar values to opacity and supports threshold mode with range sliders. Scalar Color Mapping maps scalar values to color but is hidden for RGB/RGBA volumes, where voxel colors are used directly. Gradient Opacity controls opacity based on the magnitude of the density gradient next to the voxel. The Shift parameter moves inner control points left/right to adjust the intensity range (e.g., shifting a 0–200 ramp to 1000–1200). 4. Sampling and Interpolation: Linear interpolation is used (default for scalar volumes) or nearest neighbor (default for labelmaps). Shading is enabled/disabled; when disabled, the output resembles an X-ray-like projection. 5. Compositing and Technique: The renderer applies one of three techniques: Composite with shading (default, standard front-to-back accumulation), Maximum Intensity Projection (brightest voxel per line), or Minimum Intensity Projection (darkest voxel per line). 6. Quality and Performance Tuning: Quality is set to Adaptive (reduces quality during interaction to maintain frame rate, optimized for CPU), Interactive speed (enforces target FPS by lowering resolution), Normal (fixed quality, default), or Maximum (oversamples for higher quality). Surface smoothing adds random noise (jitter) to raycasting lines to reduce staircase artifacts. Auto-release resources controls whether GPU memory and precomputed gradients are freed when the volume is hidden. Formulas: Compositing follows the standard front-to-back emission-absorption model defined in the parent article Direct volume ray casting. Control point interpolation uses mid-point M and sharpness S parameters to shape the transfer function ramps. Parameters: Preset: Pre-defined sets of opacity, color, and gradient transfer functions tuned for specific modalities and organs. Shift: Horizontal offset for inner transfer function control points. Quality: Adaptive, Interactive speed, Normal, Maximum. Interpolation: Linear, Nearest neighbor. Shade: Boolean (enabled/disabled). Auto-release resources: Boolean (enabled/disabled). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: TDR Error: The application crashes when rotating/zooming if the OS shuts down the app for keeping the GPU busy too long due to large volume size. Workarounds include splitting the volume into partitions, cropping/downsampling, increasing the TDR registry delay, switching to CPU rendering, or upgrading the GPU. Warped Volumes: Volumes under affine or non-linear transformations must have the transform hardened before rendering. Multi-Volume Limitations: Cropping is ignored, RGB volume rendering is unsupported, and only "Composite with shading" is allowed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getnodebyname(name):... def getactivethreedview():... volumenode = getnodebyname('skull') threedview = getactivethreedview() displaymanager = threedview.getdisplaymanagerbyclass('vtkMRMLVolumeRenderingDisplayableManager') volumemapper = displaymanager.getvolumemapper(volumenode) volumemapper.setpartitions(1, 1, 2) A rendering technique entirely realized on the CPU. It is slower than GPU options but available on all computers regardless of graphics hardware capabilities. Choose this when GPU resources are unavailable or when debugging rendering logic on hardware with limited GPU support. The default rendering technique using graphics hardware. It is typically much faster than CPU rendering and supports surface smoothing to remove staircase artifacts. Choose this for standard interactive visualization of medical volumes. A GPU-based technique that can render multiple overlapping volumes. It has significant limitations: cropping (ROI) is not supported (ignored), RGB volume rendering is not supported, and only the "Composite with shading" technique is supported. Choose this only when visualizing multiple scalar volumes simultaneously and cropping is not required. A variant where volume visualization is performed using GPU-based ray-casting on colored medical images, replacing manual transfer function tuning. The pipeline involves obtaining colored versions of monochromatic images via a color transfer pipeline and then rendering the stack. A pitfall is the appearance of unwanted dark patches in the colored volume if the reference image contains unwanted structures, which are transferred to the target. Time Complexity: Dependent on the backend. CPU rendering is predictable but slow. GPU rendering is faster but subject to TDR (Timeout Detection and Recovery) errors if the volume is too large for the GPU, causing the OS to shut down the application. Memory Complexity: GPU rendering allocates GPU memory, precomputed gradients, and space-leaping volumes. The "Auto-release resources" flag controls whether these are freed when hidden, trading memory usage for reload time. Performance: VTK GPU Ray Casting is typically much faster than CPU rendering. Quality settings like "Adaptive" or "Interactive speed" can dynamically adjust sampling to maintain frame rates. Strengths: Direct visualization without segmentation; support for multiple modalities via presets; interactive transfer function editing; synchronization with slice view color maps. Limitations: Warped volumes must be hardened before rendering; Multi-Volume backend lacks cropping and RGB support; Large volumes may cause TDR crashes on GPU. When to use: Interactive visualization of CT/MR data; when segmentation is not desired or available; when multiple overlapping volumes need to be shown (Multi-Volume). When not to use: When cropping is required with multiple volumes (Multi-Volume limitation); when RGB volume rendering is required with multiple volumes (Multi-Volume limitation); when the volume is too large for the GPU and TDR cannot be adjusted (use CPU or split partitions). Volume rendering in 3D Slicer is a visualization technique for displaying image volumes as 3D objects directly, a technique originally described as volume ray casting. The module integrates with the Slicer data model to provide presets tuned for CT and MR modalities, and synchronization with the Volumes module for consistent color mapping. The colored medical images variant extends this pipeline to include automatic colorization via deep image analogy or guided filtering, as explored in recent research. What Is Volumetric Rendering? name: GPU Based Single-Pass Raycasting
head: Single-pass raycaster, Volume Rendering Component
body: GPU Based Single-Pass Raycasting is a volume rendering technique where the volume is traversed along a single ray per pixel, implemented within the Volume Rendering Component framework. It solves the limitations of polygonal-based methods (which are limited in expressive power) and slicing techniques (which can lead to artifacts) by providing high-quality visual results. It is distinguished from its siblings by its implementation as a single-pass fragment shader execution on modern graphics hardware. It builds on Hardware-Accelerated and GPU Implementations and implements the emission-absorption optical model defined in Direct volume ray casting. The method operates within the Volume Rendering Component, separating scene graph responsibilities into data representation (VolumeData) and rendering styles (VolumeRenderStyle). The core algorithm executes a ray marching loop in the fragment shader for each pixel. Input: A 3D texture volume (voxels), camera parameters, ray generation settings (stepSize, type), acceleration settings (boundingVolumeType, traversalFunction), normal calculation settings (algorithm), and transfer functions (OpacityMap). Output: A 2D image with accumulated color and opacity per pixel. The primary data structure is the VolumeData node, which holds the volume data in its voxels field (an MFNode holding a 3D texture). Additional fields include: sliceThickness (SFVec3f): Default (1,1,1). Used to handle non-equidistant grids. dimensions (SFVec3f): Currently unused. swapped (SFBool): Helper for 16-bit volume byte swapping. Rendering settings are encapsulated in: AccelerationVolumeSettings: Contains boundingVolumeType ("boxGeometry" or "boundaryGeometry") for outer space skipping and traversalFunction ("simple" or "blockSkipping") for inner space skipping. NormalVolumeSettings: Contains algorithm ("precomputedCentralDifferences", "onlineCentralDifferences", or "onlineSobel"). RayGenerationVolumeSettings: Contains type ("simple" or "interleaved") and stepSize (e.g., 0.0039). OpacityMapVolumeStyle: Contains transferFunction (an ImageTexture) and type ("simple" or "preintegrated"). 1. Volume Loading: Load the volume data into a 3D texture. Handle byte swapping if necessary using the swapped field. Adjust sampling coordinates based on sliceThickness if the grid is non-equidistant. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel, generate a ray. The type parameter determines the generation strategy: "simple": Standard per-pixel ray generation. "interleaved": Interleaved ray generation to mitigate wood artifacts. 3. Acceleration (Outer Space Skipping): Determine the entry and exit points of the ray through the volume bounding box. The boundingVolumeType in AccelerationVolumeSettings selects between "boxGeometry" or "boundaryGeometry". 4. Acceleration (Inner Space Skipping): Traverse the volume from entry to exit. The traversalFunction in AccelerationVolumeSettings selects between "simple" or "blockSkipping". 5. Sampling and Classification: At each step along the ray, sample the 3D texture using hardware-accelerated trilinear interpolation. Apply the transfer function (defined in OpacityMapVolumeStyle) to determine color Ci and opacity \alphai. The type in OpacityMapVolumeStyle selects between "simple" or "preintegrated". 6. Normal Calculation: If lighting is enabled (ShadedVolumeStyle.lighting = TRUE), calculate surface normals. The algorithm in NormalVolumeSettings determines the method: "precomputedCentralDifferences": Fastest. "onlineCentralDifferences": Usually most appropriate. "onlineSobel": Nicest. 7. Compositing: Perform front-to-back compositing using the standard emission-absorption model: C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycast(volume, origin, direction, stepsize, boundsmin, boundsmax, transferfunction, lightingenabled=False): # Normalize direction dirlen = (direction[0]2 + direction[1]2 + direction[2]2)0.5 if dirlen == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] d = [direction[i] / dirlen for i in range(3)] # Compute entry and exit t values for AABB tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if d[i] == 0: if origin[i] < boundsmin[i] or origin[i] > boundsmax[i]: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] else: t1 = (boundsmin[i] - origin[i]) / d[i] t2 = (boundsmax[i] - origin[i]) / d[i] tenter = min(t1, t2) texit = max(t1, t2) tmin = max(tmin, tenter) tmax = min(tmax, texit) if tmin >= tmax: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax and accumulatedopacity < 0.95: # Sample position pos = [origin[i] + t d[i] for i in range(3)] # Sample volume (assume trilinear interpolation handled by volume access) value = volume.sample(pos) # Apply transfer function alpha, color = transferfunction(value, stepsize) # Lighting (if enabled) if lightingenabled: normal = volume.computenormal(pos) # Lighting model applied here # Compositing if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break accumulatedcolor[0] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha color[2] accumulatedopacity += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alpha t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor + [accumulatedopacity] stepSize: Controls the distance between samples. Example value: 0.0039. A smaller value increases quality but reduces performance. type (RayGeneration): "simple" or "interleaved". "interleaved" reduces wood artifacts. boundingVolumeType: "boxGeometry" or "boundaryGeometry". Used for outer space skipping. traversalFunction: "simple" or "blockSkipping". Used for inner space skipping to improve performance. type (OpacityMap): "simple" or "preintegrated". "preintegrated" often leads to a much better look. algorithm (NormalVolumeSettings): "precomputedCentralDifferences" (fastest), "onlineCentralDifferences" (usually most appropriate), "onlineSobel" (nicest). lighting: Boolean. If TRUE, lighting effects are calculated. Wood Artifacts: Can occur in raycasting. Mitigated by using the "interleaved" ray generation type. Non-equidistant Grids: Handled by the sliceThickness field in VolumeData, defaulting to (1,1,1). 16-bit Volume Byte Swapping: Handled by the swapped field in VolumeData. Hardware Requirements: Requires modern graphics hardware. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High visual quality compared to polygonal methods and slicing, which can be limited or artifact-prone. Limitations: Requires modern graphics hardware; current implementation is limited to one volume per scene. When to Use: When high-quality volume visualization is required and modern graphics hardware is available. When Not to Use: When hardware does not support 3D textures or fragment shaders, or when real-time performance on low-end hardware is critical. The GPU Based Single-Pass Raycasting method is implemented within the Volume Rendering Component, an X3D extension proposal. It was developed to alleviate the drawbacks of polygonal-based methods and slicing techniques. The component separates scene graph responsibilities into data representation and rendering styles, allowing for flexible configuration of rendering parameters. The implementation relies on GPU-based single-pass raycasting, traversing the volume along a single ray per pixel. instantreality 1.0 - tutorial - Volume Rendering, https://doc.instantreality.org/tutorial/volume-rendering/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: GPU Implementation Architecture
head: OpenGL/GLSL Volume Rendering Implementation
body: This article describes the standard software architecture for implementing direct volume ray casting on modern GPUs using OpenGL and GLSL. It details the pipeline for generating spherical harmonic (SH) coefficient volumes and performing ray marching via fragment shaders. It distinguishes itself from generic hardware-accelerated approaches by focusing on the specific data structures (3D coefficient volumes) and rendering techniques (slice-by-slice ray marching with Monte Carlo sampling) required for advanced light-material interaction. The implementation uses C++ with OpenGL and GLSL. The core challenge addressed is the integration of three functions (material function M, incoming light L{mi}, and outgoing light L{mi}^0) which is complex for direct SH integration. The solution approximates this integration to achieve convincing visual results. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data, material properties, lighting conditions (represented as SH coefficients), and pre-generated random sample directions. Output: Rendered image with advanced lighting interactions, specifically SH coefficient volumes for L{mi} and L{mi}^0. Data Structures: 1. 3D Coefficient Volumes: SH coefficients for L{mi} and L{mi}^0 are stored in 3D texture volumes. 2. 2D Textures: Used for uploading pre-computed data from the CPU, including normalized Cartesian vectors for Monte Carlo sampling and spherical harmonic basis functions Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) for each sample direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Generate SH Coefficient Volumes: Use Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) in conjunction with Multiple Render Targets (MRT) to generate the 3D coefficient volumes. 2. Discard Unused Coefficients: Coefficients for L{mi} can be discarded after L{mi}^0 has been computed, as they are not accessed during rendering. 3. Prepare Sampling Data (CPU Side): Generate random samples for Monte Carlo sampling on the CPU as normalized Cartesian vectors. 4. Compute Basis Functions: Compute Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) for each sample direction. 5. Upload to GPU: Upload the normalized Cartesian vectors and basis functions to the GPU as 2D textures. 6. Ray Marching (Fragment Shader): Render the volume slice by slice. 7. Cast Rays: In the fragment shader, use the uploaded random samples to cast rays. 8. Perform Integration: Execute the approximate integration of light-material interaction. 9. Finalize Contribution: After a ray terminates, multiply its contribution with the values Y{lm}(\varthetas, \phis) obtained from the second 2D texture. Formulas and Symbols: M: Material function. L{mi}: Incoming light. L{mi}^0: Outgoing light. Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi): Spherical harmonic basis functions evaluated at sample directions. The integration of M, L{mi}, and L{mi}^0 is approximated rather than computed directly due to complexity. Parameters: Samples: The number of samples affects quality. Example: 1250 samples distributed over the hemisphere. Implementation Language: C++ with OpenGL and GLSL. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Random Number Generation: The GLSL specification describes functionality for generating random numbers, but this feature was not implemented in the referenced environment. Therefore, random samples must be generated on the CPU and uploaded. Approximation: The integration technique used is not physically correct but provides convincing visual results. Direct volume rendering on GPUs that integrates rays by accumulating gradients across sequential cutting planes of the volume stored as 2D textures, bypassing GPU memory limits by paging data from CPU main memory. Definition: Stores the volume out-of-core in CPU main memory and pages it into GPU memory. Performance: Medium-sized volumes up to 512^3 can be viewed at interactive rates. Context: This approach addresses the limitation that larger volumes are restricted by GPU memory, unlike standard in-core rendering. Memory: Standard implementations are limited by GPU memory capacity. Out-of-core variants mitigate this by paging data. Performance: GPU volume rendering is fast, permitting interactive rates for medium-sized volumes (512^3). Complexity: Handling three-function SH integration is complex; the described architecture uses an approximation to maintain performance. The concepts described in this paper have been integrated into a GPU-based volume ray-caster implemented in C++ using OpenGL and GLSL. The approach builds on the effectiveness of direct volume rendering on GPUs, which is faster than ray tracing for this purpose. name: CUDA GPU Implementation
head: CUDA Raycast Backend, cvc::volren CUDA backend
body: The CUDA GPU Implementation is a direct volume ray casting method that offloads the per-ray sampling, classification, and compositing loop to the NVIDIA CUDA architecture, mirroring the semantic behavior of a reference CPU marcher while leveraging hardware acceleration for real-time performance. It sets itself apart from CPU-based ray casting by utilizing the GPU's parallel thread architecture to significantly reduce computational complexity for intersection calculation, resampling, and compositing, and differs from generic hardware-accelerated approaches by explicitly decoupling ray traversal logic from the volume data structure to allow for adaptive algorithms and custom spatial indices. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data (scalar field or SDF), transfer function (LUT), camera parameters, and rendering options (isosurface threshold, lighting model, cut planes). Output: Final 2D image (color and depth) and optional accumulated opacity. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored in device memory (texture or linear buffer). For SDF volumes, gradient computation uses de Boor splines. Transfer Function: Baked Lookup Table (LUT) stored in device memory. Spatial Index: A dynamic redundant octree (Guennebaud et al.) used for efficient neighbor sampling and adaptive traversal. Marching Cubes Tables: constant memory storage for isosurface geometry, tracked per-device to avoid cross-GPU aliasing issues. Ray Stack: A small stack stored in local memory to manage recursion for adaptive ray traversal. Parameters: Block Size: 16x16 threads per block. Ray Cap: 32 hits per ray (historically documented as unreachable due to opacity cutoff, but implemented as a hard limit for DDA collection). Isosurface Limit: Up to 8 isosurfaces/lights/cut planes per scene. Volume Limit: Exactly one volume per render in version 1. Backend Selection: backend::cpu (default), backend::cuda (demands GPU), backend::automatic (uses GPU if available, falls back silently). Math Precision: Compiled with --usefastmath. Steps: 1. Initialization: Upload volume data and LUT from host to device (H2D) for each render pass. Ensure CUDA error state is cleared before launch to prevent spurious fallbacks from previous unrelated errors. 2. Kernel Launch: Launch one CUDA thread per pixel in 16x16 blocks. 3. Ray Generation: Each thread computes ray parameters from camera matrices and determines entry/exit points via slab intersection. 4. Ray Traversal: Isosurface Path: Use Amanatides-Woo DDA to traverse cells, enumerating every crossed cell to avoid silhouette holes. General Path: Implement either constant step size or adaptive algorithm. Adaptive recursion is managed via a local memory stack. Neighbor Access: Use the dynamic redundant octree to find neighbor samples efficiently. 5. Sampling: Sample volume data using trilinear interpolation. Compute gradients using de Boor splines for SDF volumes. 6. Classification: Apply transfer functions using the baked LUT. Apply gradient ramp, density window, and cut planes. Handle NaN corners correctly by using std::min/std::max semantics (keeping NaN accumulator) rather than fminf/fmaxf (which discard NaN) for corner min/max folds. 7. Compositing: Perform front-to-back compositing on a per-cell basis. Update accumulated color C' and opacity \alpha': C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Apply Blinn-Phong lighting model if enabled. 8. Depth Latch: Store depth information for the final pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. global void raycastkernel(float volumedata, float lut, CameraParams cam, float isovalue, CutPlane cutplanes, float4 outcolor, float outdepth) { // 1. Thread Indexing int x = blockIdx.x blockDim.x + threadIdx.x; int y = blockIdx.y blockDim.y + threadIdx.y; // Check bounds if (x >= width || y >= height) return; // 2. Ray Generation Ray ray = generateray(cam, x, y); // 3. Slab Intersection float tentry, texit; if (!intersectslab(ray, volumebounds, tentry, texit)) { outcolor[y width + x] = makefloat4(0, 0, 0, 0); return; } // 4. Ray Traversal & Compositing float acccolorr = 0.0f, acccolorg = 0.0f, acccolorb = 0.0f, accalpha = 0.0f; float t = tentry; float stepsize = getstepsize(ray, tentry, texit); // Constant or adaptive // Stack for adaptive traversal (local memory) // Stack is managed implicitly by recursion or explicit local array while (t < texit) { // 5. Sampling float3 pos = ray.origin + t ray.direction; float density = samplevolumetrilinear(volumedata, pos); // Gradient computation for SDF float3 grad; if (issdf) { grad = computegradientdeboor(volumedata, pos); } else { grad = computegradienttrilinear(volumedata, pos); } // 6. Classification float alpha, colorr, colorg, colorb; // Isosurface check if (isisosurfacemode) { // Amanatides-Woo DDA ensures all crossed cells are visited // Check if cell contains isosurface using correct NaN handling if (containsisosurface(pos, isovalue)) { // Get color from LUT float4 tf = lookuplut(lut, density); alpha = tf.a; colorr = tf.r; colorg = tf.g; colorb = tf.b; // Apply lighting (Blinn-Phong) float3 lightdir = normalize(lightposition - pos); float3 viewdir = normalize(-ray.direction); float3 halfdir = normalize(lightdir + viewdir); float NdotH = max(0.0f, dot(normalize(grad), halfdir)); float specular = pow(NdotH, shininess); colorr = colorr diffuse + specular specularfactor; colorg = colorg diffuse + specular specularfactor; colorb = colorb diffuse + specular specularfactor; } else { t += stepsize; continue; } } else { // Standard DVF float4 tf = lookuplut(lut, density); alpha = tf.a; colorr = tf.r; colorg = tf.g; colorb = tf.b; // Apply gradient ramp, density window, cut planes if (applycutplanes(pos, cutplanes)) { t += stepsize; continue; } } // 7. Compositing (Front-to-Back) float weight = alpha (1.0f - accalpha); acccolorr += weight colorr; acccolorg += weight colorg; acccolorb += weight colorb; accalpha += weight; // 8. Early Ray Termination if (accalpha > 0.95f) break; // Advance t += stepsize; } // 9. Output outcolor[y width + x] = makefloat4(acccolorr, acccolorg, acccolorb, accalpha); outdepth[y width + x] = texit; // Or depth latch value } Slab-based raycasting is a CUDA GPU optimization for direct volume rendering that caches sampled voxels in shared memory as "slabs" to improve performance when volume data is accessed multiple times, such as for gradient calculation in Phong lighting. It sets itself apart from basic raycasting by trading increased shared memory overhead and reduced early ray termination granularity for cache hits on repeated voxel access. Unlike hardware texture caches, which benefit from large viewports where adjacent rays hit the same voxels, the slab cache is most efficient when the data set resolution is high compared to the viewport size. GPU-accelerated ray casting is a direct volume rendering method that offloads the per-ray sampling and integration loop to the graphics processor, enabling real-time interaction with volumetric datasets. It differs from CPU-based ray casting by leveraging the GPU's parallel architecture to significantly reduce computational complexity for intersection calculation, resampling, and compositing. As a standard image-order approach, it is embarrassingly parallel and supports numerous performance and quality enhancements. The Jittor Volume Render Cuvol Wrapper is a custom Jittor function that fuses the forward and backward passes of volume rendering into a single CUDA kernel launch sequence, managing memory aliases and gradient propagation for a sparse grid representation. It differs from standard CPU-based ray marchers by executing the core ray casting logic on the GPU via CUDA, while maintaining compatibility with Jittor's automatic differentiation engine. It builds on the CUDA GPU Implementation by providing a high-level API that handles the integration of sparse grid data structures (offsets, scaling, links) into the CUDA kernels. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Linear with respect to the number of rays (pixels) and the number of samples per ray. The GPU implementation provides significant speedups over CPU counterparts due to massive parallelism. Memory: Requires storage for the volume data, LUT, and spatial index (octree) in device memory. The octree allows for dynamic updates and control of memory footprint versus performance. Measured Performance: Hardware: NVIDIA GTX 1650. Resolution: 512x512. Results: Isosurface rendering: 160 ms (CPU) vs 65 ms (CUDA). Shaded Transfer Function + Gradient Ramp + Cut Plane: 270 ms (CPU) vs 113 ms (CUDA). Image Parity: 100% of pixels within 1 LSB with identical depth compared to CPU reference. Throughput: 16.5 Mray/s at 640x360 resolution for a single bunny model. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High performance for single-volume scenes; image-level parity with CPU reference; flexible traversal strategies (constant/adaptive); efficient neighbor access via octree. Limitations: Version 1 is limited to a single volume; limited to 8 isosurfaces/lights/cut planes; requires GPU memory for H2D uploads per render; constant memory management requires per-device tracking. When to Use: Real-time interactive volume rendering on NVIDIA hardware. Single-volume scenes with complex lighting or isosurface extraction. When image-level parity with a CPU reference is required. When Not to Use: Multi-volume scenes (v1 limitation). Non-NVIDIA hardware. Scenes requiring more than 8 isosurfaces/lights/cut planes. The CUDA GPU Implementation was developed as part of the libcvc library, specifically within the cvc::volren module, to provide a high-performance alternative to CPU-based volume rendering. It was introduced in pull request #323, which added the cvcGL VolRenNode and the volrenbunny demo. The implementation mirrors the semantic behavior of the existing CPU marcher, ensuring visual consistency while leveraging CUDA for speed. It builds on the principles of hardware-accelerated volume rendering, specifically utilizing the fragment shader-like parallelism of CUDA threads. cvcGL VolRenNode, CUDA raycast backend, and the volrenbunny demo, https://github.com/transfix/libcvc/pull/323, fetched 2026-10-25 (unofficial) Volume MLS Ray Casting, https://miriah.github.io/publications/volumemls.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Slab-based Raycasting
head: Slab-based Raycaster
body: Slab-based raycasting is a CUDA GPU optimization for direct volume rendering that caches sampled voxels in shared memory as "slabs" to improve performance when volume data is accessed multiple times, such as for gradient calculation in Phong lighting. It sets itself apart from basic raycasting by trading increased shared memory overhead and reduced early ray termination granularity for cache hits on repeated voxel access. Unlike hardware texture caches, which benefit from large viewports where adjacent rays hit the same voxels, the slab cache is most efficient when the data set resolution is high compared to the viewport size. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset (e.g., 16-bit or 8-bit), ray origin and direction per pixel, thread block configuration (bsx, bsy), slab depth (sd). Output: Rendered image with lighting (e.g., Phong) applied. Data Structures: Shared Memory Cache: A contiguous block of shared memory storing bsx \times bsy \times sd sampled voxels. Voxel Layout: The cache stores the voxel values (and potentially gradients) for the slab. The exact bit-packing depends on the data type (e.g., 16-bit integers for vmhead, 8-bit for engine). Parameters: bsx, bsy: Thread block dimensions. sd: Slab depth (number of voxels along the ray stored in the cache). sd{opt}: Optimal slab depth, which depends on the specific dataset. Algorithm Steps: 1. Block Initialization: Each thread in the block determines its ray parameters. The block calculates the spatial extent of the slab it needs to fetch. 2. Slab Fetch: The threads cooperatively fetch the volume data corresponding to the slab depth sd along their rays into the shared memory cache. This involves calculating global memory addresses for the start of the slab and fetching bsx \times bsy \times sd voxels. 3. Border Handling: Additional border voxels may be fetched to handle gradient calculations at the edges of the slab, introducing overhead. 4. Synchronization: All threads in the block synchronize (syncthreads()) to ensure the slab is fully loaded into shared memory before any thread begins processing. 5. Ray Casting Loop: Threads iterate through the slab depth sd. For each step: Read voxel value and gradient from shared memory. Compute lighting (e.g., Phong) using the gradient. Perform volume integration (compositing). Check for early ray termination. Note: Termination can only occur at the end of a complete slab, not after individual rays within the slab, reducing efficiency for solid data. 6. Next Slab: If the ray has not terminated and more volume remains, the block fetches the next slab into shared memory and repeats Step 3-5. 7. Write Output: Write the final accumulated color and opacity to global memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. shared float sharedvoxels[BSX BSY SD]; shared float sharedgradients[BSX BSY SD 3]; # Assuming 3-component gradients def slabbasedraycast(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, bsx, bsy, sd): # 1. Calculate slab bounds # Determine the range of t values for the current slab slabstartt = currentslabindex sd raystepsize slabendt = (currentslabindex + 1) sd raystepsize # 2. Fetch slab into shared memory # Each thread fetches its portion of the slab tid = threadIdx.x + threadIdx.y bsx numthreads = bsx bsy # Cooperative fetch logic # Threads iterate to fill sharedvoxels and sharedgradients for i in range(0, sd): # Calculate global memory index for the voxel at current step globalidx = getvolumeindex(rayorigin + raydirection (slabstartt + i raystepsize)) # Fetch voxel value sharedvoxels[tid sd + i] = volumedata[globalidx] # Fetch gradient for lighting (if using Phong) # Note: Gradient calculation may require neighbor fetches, handled via border logic sharedgradients[(tid sd + i) 3: (tid sd + i) 3 + 3] = computegradient(volumedata, globalidx) syncthreads() # Ensure all threads have fetched their part before next step? # Actually, usually fetch is done in parallel, then sync. # Simplified: Fetch all, then sync. syncthreads() # Ensure entire slab is in shared memory # 3. Process slab for i in range(0, sd): voxelval = sharedvoxels[tid sd + i] grad = sharedgradients[(tid sd + i) 3: (tid sd + i) 3 + 3] # Lighting calculation color = applyphonglighting(voxelval, grad) # Compositing alpha = transferfunction(voxelval) outcolor = blend(outcolor, color, alpha) outalpha = blend(outalpha, alpha) # Early termination check if outalpha >= TERMINATIONTHRESHOLD: break # 4. Increment slab index and repeat if needed currentslabindex += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhead: For basic raycasting (no lighting/gradient), caching adds 23-67% overhead because each voxel is accessed only once. Early Termination: Early ray termination is less efficient because only complete slabs can be terminated, not individual rays. This leads to performance decreases with solid/non-transparent data. Shared Memory Limits: The cache size is bsx \times bsy \times sd. For optimal configurations, this can reach 15,360 bytes, close to the 16 kB maximum on older GPUs (e.g., GTX 280), limiting occupancy to one thread block per multiprocessor. Gradient Accuracy: Gradients computed from slab data may be less exact than those from direct global memory access. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of slabs traversed. Each slab fetch is O(bsx \times bsy \times sd), and processing is O(sd). Overhead is significant for basic raycasting (23-67% slower) but beneficial for Phong lighting (12-78% faster). Memory Complexity: Shared memory usage is bsx \times bsy \times sd voxels. For vmhead, this is 15,360 bytes; for engine, up to 7,936 bytes. Measured Performance: GTX 280, vmhead (512²×294, 16-bit), Phong, 512² viewport: 67.9 fps (slab) vs 40.7 fps (basic), +78.2% speedup with bs=16\times30, sd=16. GTX 280, engine (256²×128, 8-bit), Phong, 512² viewport: 77.1 fps (slab) vs 77.6 fps (basic), -0.6% change with bs=8\times16. Scaling: Speedup decreases with increasing viewport size. Larger viewports increase hardware texture cache hit rates due to spatial locality, reducing the relative benefit of the slab cache. Strengths: Significant speedup for large, semi-transparent datasets with high resolution relative to viewport size, especially when lighting calculations require multiple voxel accesses. Limitations: Poor performance for small, solid datasets or basic raycasting due to overhead and inefficient early termination. Limited by shared memory size, potentially reducing occupancy. When to Use: Direct volume rendering of semi-transparent, high-resolution data with Phong lighting on GPUs with sufficient shared memory. When Not to Use: Basic raycasting, small solid datasets, or when early ray termination is critical for performance. Slab-based raycasting was developed as part of CUDA-based direct volume rendering techniques, specifically tested on the GeForce GTX 280. It was designed to address the inefficiency of repeated volume data access for lighting calculations (e.g., gradients for Phong shading) by leveraging shared memory. The method is particularly relevant for medical imaging applications, where data sets typically have high resolution and are semi-transparent. name: GPU-accelerated ray casting
head: CUDA Grid/Block Raycasting, CUDA Raycasting Kernel, GPU raycasting algorithm, Many-Core GPU Implementation, Standard image order approach
body: GPU-accelerated ray casting is a direct volume rendering method that offloads ray traversal and compositing to a graphics processing unit (GPU) to achieve real-time frame rates. It differs from CPU-based approaches by leveraging massive parallelism, where each thread handles a single pixel, making it an embarrassingly parallel standard image-order approach. It builds on CUDA GPU Implementation by explicitly mapping the image grid to CUDA thread blocks and utilizing hardware features like context switching to hide memory latency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric data set V, a camera view (eye point, direction), and a transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Output: A 2D image of resolution W \times H. Data Structures: Thread Block Layout: The image is treated as a 2D CUDA grid divided into thread blocks. An M \times N thread block corresponds to an M \times N pixel image tile. Memory Layout: The source volume S can be stored in array-order or Z-order. Array-order: S[i, j, k] is at memory location i + j \cdot xsize + k \cdot xsize \cdot ysize. Z-order: A 1D layout of a 2^n tree where nearby index space points are nearby in physical memory, computed via the formulation by Pascucci and Frank. Steps: 1. Ray-Bounding Box Intersection: Calculate the entry (p{in}) and exit (p{out}) points of the ray intersecting the volume bounding box. This is achieved by rendering the bounding box twice: once culling front faces and once culling back faces. 2. Thread Assignment: The CUDA runtime dynamically schedules thread blocks, assigning up to eight blocks at a time to each of the GPU’s multiprocessors. 3. Ray Marching and Compositing: Each individual CUDA thread performs raycasting for a single pixel. The thread traverses the ray from p{in} to p{out}, sampling the volume and compositing the results. 4. Resampling: Perform tri-linear interpolation to resample the volume data at the ray positions. 5. Shading: Perform resampling and compositing on the shader to reduce running time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuraycastkernel(threadid, blockid, griddims, volumetexture, transferfunction): # 1. Determine pixel coordinates from thread/block indices # Assuming a 2D grid of blocks, each block is M x N threads # This maps directly to image tiles pixelx = blockid.x blockwidth + threadid.x pixely = blockid.y blockheight + threadid.y if pixelx >= imagewidth or pixely >= imageheight: return # 2. Calculate ray origin and direction for this pixel rayorigin = geteyepoint() raydirection = getraydirection(pixelx, pixely, cameramatrix) # 3. Calculate intersection with bounding box # Render bounding box twice (front/back culling) to get pin and pout # pin, pout = calculateraybboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox) # 4. Initialize compositing variables accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) t = 0.0 stepsize = calculatestepsize(pin, pout, resolution) # 5. Ray march from pin to pout while t < distance(pin, pout): currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 6. Sample volume using tri-linear interpolation # scalarvalue = samplevolume(volumetexture, currentpos) # 7. Map scalar to color and opacity using transfer function color, opacity = applytransferfunction(scalarvalue, transferfunction) # 8. Composite (front-to-back) # alphaout = alphain + (1 - alphain) alphasample # colorout = colorin + (1 - alphain) alphasample colorsample accumulatedcolor = composite(accumulatedcolor, color, opacity) t += stepsize # 9. Write result to image buffer writepixel(pixelx, pixely, accumulatedcolor) def calculateraybboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox): # Implementation detail: Render bounding box twice # Once culling front faces to find the first hit (pin) # Once culling back faces to find the last hit (pout) # This avoids analytical intersection code in the kernel pin = renderbboxfrontculled(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox) pout = renderbboxbackculled(rayorigin, raydirection, boundingbox) return pin, pout Parameters: CUDA Version: 3.2 compiler and runtime. NVIDIA Driver: Version 270.41.19. Compute Capability: Targeted at 2.0 (Fermi-series) for additional optimizations. Shared Memory: Configured to be used as L1 cache for global memory requests. ECC Support: Enabled. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Latency: The GPU uses hardware context switches between blocks within a multiprocessor to hide memory latency. Data Size Scaling: While computational complexity for interpolation and compositing is approximately constant for the same viewpoint, processing time shows a slowly wavelike rising trend as data set size increases due to increased RAM/graphics card memory addressing time and varying computing resources. The foundational hardware-accelerated method defining the data flow between CPU-side texture preparation and GPU-side ray execution. Chosen when explicit pipeline control is needed for real-time displays like HTC Vive. Enhances visual quality by applying anisotropic shading models (Ward or Lafortune BRDFs) using precomputed covariance matrices. Chosen when surface orientation and anisotropy are critical. Supports Adaptive Mesh Refinement (AMR) data with wavelength-dependent absorption. Chosen for complex light models and higher quality compared to slicing-based approaches. Time Complexity: The computational complexity for tri-linear interpolation and compositing is approximately constant regardless of data set size increase, as the number of resampling points does not grow with data set size for the same viewpoint. Performance: In experiments with a 101 \times 101 \times 250 seismic data volume at 10 viewpoints (50 trials each, removing max/min), the GPU average time was 14.9947 ms (range [14.1886, 15.7046]), compared to a CPU average of 9486.24 ms (range [9250.04, 9737.42]). Scaling: When the data set size increased ten times (increment 10 \times 28 \times 25) at the same viewpoint, both GPU and CPU processing times showed a slowly wavelike rising trend due to increased memory addressing time and varying computing resources, despite constant computational complexity for interpolation and compositing. Strengths: Significantly faster than CPU algorithms due to lower computational complexity for intersection calculation, resampling, and compositing. It is an embarrassingly parallel standard image-order approach that supports many performance and quality enhancements. Limitations: Processing time can fluctuate based on the number of resampling points required for different viewpoints and intersections. GPU-accelerated ray casting was introduced by Röttger et al. in 2003 and Krüger and Westermann in 2003. It emerged as a standard image-order approach to overcome the limitations of earlier texture slicing methods, which suffered from visual artifacts and less flexibility. It is widely used in interactive visualization and real-time applications requiring high frame rates. name: GPU Ray Casting Pipeline
head: Basic GPU Ray Casting Pipeline, Front-to-Back GPU Ray Casting
body: The GPU Ray Casting Pipeline is the foundational hardware-accelerated method for direct volume rendering, solving the problem of efficiently integrating volumetric data into a 2D image by offloading ray traversal and compositing to the graphics processing unit. It differs from CPU-based approaches by leveraging massive parallelism to achieve real-time frame rates, which is mandatory for high-refresh-rate displays like the HTC Vive (90 Hz). It builds on GPU-accelerated ray casting by explicitly defining the data flow between CPU-side texture preparation and GPU-side ray execution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data sets (typically from CT and MRI images). Output: A final 2D image generated by the GPU. Data Structures: 1. Volume Model: The volumetric data is stored in a 3D texture on the GPU. The CPU reads the original data set and builds this model. 2. Ray Definition: Implicitly defined by the camera position and viewport geometry for each pixel. Optical and Illumination Models: Optical Model: The emission-absorption model is used to estimate the volume-rendering integral. Illumination Model: The Blinn-Phong illumination model is used to approximate the scattering of light. Algorithm Steps: 1. Data Preparation (CPU): Read the original volumetric data set. 2. Texture Upload (CPU): Build a volume model from the data and store it in a 3D texture. 3. Transfer: Pass the 3D texture to the GPU. 4. Ray Casting (GPU): Perform ray casting on the 3D texture to generate the final image. This involves casting rays from the camera through the volume and accumulating color and opacity along each ray path using front-to-back compositing. Formulas: The rendering integral is estimated using the emission-absorption model. The color C and opacity \alpha for a ray segment are accumulated. The illumination L at a sample point is calculated using the Blinn-Phong model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preparevolume(datasource): """ Reads volumetric data (e.g., CT/MRI) and creates a 3D texture. """ volumemodel = build3dtexture(datasource) return volumemodel def uploadtogpu(volumemodel): """ Passes the 3D texture to the GPU memory. """ gputexture = transfertogpu(volumemodel) return gputexture def gpuraycasting(gputexture, cameraparams): """ Performs ray casting on the 3D texture to generate the final image. Uses front-to-back compositing and Blinn-Phong illumination. """ # For each pixel in the output buffer for pixel in outputbuffer: ray = createray(cameraparams, pixel) color = vec3(0.0) alpha = 0.0 # Traverse the volume along the ray while rayinsidevolume(ray): samplepos = rayposition(ray) density = sample3dtexture(gputexture, samplepos) # Calculate illumination using Blinn-Phong model # lightcolor = blinnphonglighting(samplepos, density) # Front-to-back compositing (Emission-Absorption Model) # contribution = lightcolor (1.0 - alpha) color += contribution alpha += (1.0 - alpha) opacityfactor(density) rayadvance(ray) setpixelcolor(pixel, color) GPU-based raycasting renders volumetric datasets by casting rays from the camera through the volume on the GPU, accumulating color and opacity along each ray path. It differs from CPU-based raycasting by leveraging massive parallelism to achieve real-time frame rates, which is mandatory for high-refresh-rate displays like the HTC Vive (90 Hz). It builds on the GPU Ray Casting Pipeline by offloading the ray traversal and compositing steps to the graphics hardware. GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains (SBRT) is a direct volume rendering technique adapted for geoscientific terrain data, implemented on the GPU to enable real-time visualization. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex, layered subsurface structures by casting rays from a virtual camera through each output buffer pixel and composing sampled colors along the ray path. What sets it apart from standard raycasting is its specific adaptation to the SBRT data structure, which uses a stack-based representation of geological intervals, and its hybrid deferred strategy for normal calculation to avoid the performance bottlenecks associated with 3D convolution on sparse stack data. Not given in the sources. The basic rendering pipeline described here is intended to familiarize the reader with the different topics that appear in the rest of the thesis. The methods proposed are based on the ray casting algorithm using the front-to-back compositing scheme. The approaches presented in this thesis propose different modifications to this basic pipeline in order to obtain the desired results. Johnson [36], Visualization in Medicine by Bernhard Preim and Dirk Bartz [82], and Real-Time Volume Graphics by Klaus Engel, Markus Hadwiger, Joe M. Kniss, Christoph Rezk-Salama and Daniel Weiskopf [34], which also presents technical details for the implementation of different visualization methods. name: GPU-based Raycasting Rendering
body: GPU-based raycasting renders volumetric datasets by casting rays from the camera through the volume on the GPU, accumulating color and opacity along each ray path. It differs from CPU-based raycasting by leveraging massive parallelism to achieve real-time frame rates, which is mandatory for high-refresh-rate displays like the HTC Vive (90 Hz). It builds on the GPU Ray Casting Pipeline. Inputs: Volumetric dataset (scalar field). Camera parameters (position, orientation, projection). Transfer function (mapping scalar values to color and opacity). Optional pre-computed gradient data. Outputs: Final image (color and alpha per pixel). Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture storing scalar values. Gradient Texture: 3D RGBA texture storing pre-computed gradients, where each voxel stores gradient direction and magnitude. Transfer Function Texture: 1D or 2D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA. Steps: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the viewport, generate a ray originating from the camera position and passing through the pixel center in world space. 2. Ray-Volume Intersection: Determine the entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) distances of the ray with the volume bounding box using the slab method. If t{max} < 0 or t{min} > t{max}, the ray misses the volume or points away from it. 3. Step Size Calculation: Determine the step size along the ray based on the desired sampling density and volume resolution. 4. Sampling Loop: a. Sample the volume texture at the current ray position to get the scalar value v. b. Sample the transfer function using v to get color c and opacity \alpha. c. If pre-computed gradients are used, sample the gradient texture at the current position to get \nabla v. Otherwise, compute gradients on-the-fly using finite differences, which requires 6 extra texture fetches. d. Compositing: Update the accumulated color C{acc} and opacity A{acc} using front-to-back compositing: C{acc} = C{acc} + c \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - A{acc}) A{acc} = A{acc} + \alpha \cdot (1 - A{acc}) e. Advance the ray position by the step size. f. If A{acc} \geq 1 or the ray has exited the volume (t \geq t{max}), terminate the loop. 5. Post-Processing: Apply any final image processing (e.g., tone mapping, anti-aliasing). Parameters: Step Size: Determines sampling density. Gradient Pre-computation: Trade-off between memory usage and computational cost. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlapping Material Ranges: When transfer functions for different materials have overlapping scalar ranges, the color contribution should be set as the average of the non-transparent materials for the sample, rather than a sum. Empty-Space Skipping: Rays traversing transparent regions can be skipped to avoid unnecessary sampling. Boundary Conditions: Ensure correct handling of rays that do not intersect the volume or intersect only at the boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuraycasting(volumetex, gradienttex, tftex, camera, viewport, volumebbox, stepsize, backgroundcolor, useprecomputedgradients): image = [[list(backgroundcolor) for in range(viewport.width)] for in range(viewport.height)] for y in range(viewport.height): for x in range(viewport.width): rayorigin, raydirection = camera.generateray(x, y, viewport) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebbox) if tmax < 0 or tmin > tmax: continue acccolor = list(backgroundcolor) accalpha = 0.0 t = tmin while t < tmax and accalpha < 1.0: pos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] v = volumetex.sample(pos) c, alpha = tftex.sample(v) if useprecomputedgradients: grad = gradienttex.sample(pos) else: grad = computegradientonfly(volumetex, pos) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor[0] += c[0] weight acccolor[1] += c[1] weight acccolor[2] += c[2] weight accalpha += weight t += stepsize image[y][x] = acccolor + [accalpha] return image def rayboxintersect(origin, direction, bbox): tmin, tmax = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bbox.min[i] or origin[i] > bbox.max[i]: return -float('inf'), -float('inf') else: t1 = (bbox.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bbox.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax def computegradientonfly(tex, pos): # Standard central differences requiring 6 texture fetches dx = tex.sample([pos[0]+0.5, pos[1], pos[2]]) - tex.sample([pos[0]-0.5, pos[1], pos[2]]) dy = tex.sample([pos[0], pos[1]+0.5, pos[2]]) - tex.sample([pos[0], pos[1]-0.5, pos[2]]) dz = tex.sample([pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]+0.5]) - tex.sample([pos[0], pos[1], pos[2]-0.5]) return [dx, dy, dz] Renders the volume at a lower resolution viewport and scales the result up to the target display resolution using interpolation to reduce computational cost. It differs from full-resolution raycasting by trading spatial resolution for performance; effective because raycasting is a screen-space algorithm. Used in Unity 3D VR systems for HTC Vive to achieve real-time rendering at 90 fps, allowing comfortable movement without motion sickness. Renders function-based microstructure models directly using accelerated ray-tracing/ray-casting on the GPU, avoiding intermediate representations like BRep or voxels. Performance reaches approximately 20 frames per second on an NVidia 9600 graphics card for a 512x512 image size, independent of microstructure complexity. Rendering time remains almost identical for lattices with different densities because the complexity of the underlying mathematical function does not depend on the density of the microstructures. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the average number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: Scales with the volume dataset size, plus additional memory for pre-computed gradient textures if used. Performance: Achieves real-time frame rates (e.g., 90 fps) on modern GPUs, essential for VR applications. Function-based models achieve ~20 fps on an NVidia 9600 for 512x512 resolution. Strengths: High parallelism, real-time capability, flexible transfer functions, and effective optimization via reduced viewports or pre-computed gradients. Limitations: Pre-computed gradients increase memory usage, while reduced viewports trade spatial resolution for performance. Performance depends on step size and transfer function complexity. When to Use: Real-time visualization of volumetric data, especially in VR/AR environments or for interactive inspection. When Not to Use: When high spatial resolution is critical and performance is not a constraint, or when memory bandwidth is severely limited. GPU-based raycasting was developed to overcome the performance limitations of CPU-based raycasting for volume visualization. It is used in medical imaging for tasks such as MR bile duct examination and in VR/AR applications with head-mounted displays like the HTC Vive. The technique has also been applied to the direct rendering of function-based microstructure models for digital fabrication workflows.
