name: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains
head: Direct Volume Rendering of Stack-Based Terrains, GPU Raycasting for SBRT, SBRT Raycasting
body: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains (SBRT) is a direct volume rendering technique adapted for geoscientific terrain data, implemented on the GPU to enable real-time visualization. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex, layered subsurface structures by casting rays from a virtual camera through each output buffer pixel and composing sampled colors along the ray path. What sets it apart from standard raycasting is its specific adaptation to the SBRT data structure, which uses a stack-based representation of geological intervals, and its hybrid deferred strategy for normal calculation to avoid the performance bottlenecks associated with 3D convolution on sparse stack data. Inputs and Outputs: Input: SBRT dataset (grid dimensions grid{ancho} \times grid{alto}, maximum intervals m), camera parameters, light source position, Transfer Function (discrete lookup table), and rendering resolution. Output: Final color image buffer. Data Structures: The volumetric data is encoded into one or two GPU structures (textures or buffers). The specific layout depends on the chosen memory approach (see Subtopics). Common components include: Index Structure: Maps 2D grid coordinates to stack start positions and sizes. Interval Structure: Stores material attributes and accumulated heights for each interval. Transfer Function: Discrete lookup table mapping material values to colors. Numbered Steps: 1. Proxy Geometry Setup: Use the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of the terrain dataset as the proxy geometry for ray intersection. This maintains simplicity and fits the terrain shape. 2. Data Encoding: Encode the SBRT data into the chosen GPU structure(s) (e.g., 2D textures, 3D texture, or SSBOs). The data is organized such that the stack is extracted first, then iterated over its intervals. 3. Ray Casting Loop: For each pixel in the output buffer, cast a ray from the virtual camera. 4. Ray-Box Intersection: Intersect the ray with the bounding box to determine the entry and exit points of the ray within the terrain volume. 5. Adaptive Ray Marching: Traverse the SBRT stack along the ray to sample attributes and compose color: Empty Space: When the ray is in empty space, the step length equals the terrain cell resolution. Non-Empty Material: Once the ray collides with non-empty material, increase the sampling frequency to avoid artifacts. Stack Traversal: For each step, identify the current stack using the index structure, then iterate through its intervals to find the active material. 6. Color Composition: Map the sampled material values to colors using the discrete Transfer Function. Use front-to-back alpha blending for composition. 7. Termination: Stop the ray algorithm when the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold of 1 - \epsilon, assuming new contributions are irrelevant. 8. Deferred Normal Calculation (Hybrid Strategy): Pass 1: Render the color from the Transfer Function and store the ray-collision distance (depth) in a depth map. Pass 2: Calculate surface normals and compose the final pixel color. Obtain the 3D position of the convolution mask center by performing inverse projection from the depth map. Determine if a voxel is occupied: project the inverse projection value again; if the resulting depth is less than the camera-to-inverse-projection distance, the voxel is part of the surface. Calculate normals based on occupied neighbors in the mask. 9. Lighting: Apply the Lambertian diffuse BRDF lighting model to the final color. Formulas: Lambertian Diffuse BRDF: Ip = ia + kd (\vec{L} \cdot \vec{N}) id Where: Ip: Final intensity at point p. ia: Ambient light intensity. id: Diffuse light intensity. kd: Lambertian reflectance. \vec{L}: Vector from the object to the light source. \vec{N}: Surface normal vector at point p. Super-texels Dimensions (Approach 2): texture{ancho} = grid{ancho} \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil texture{alto} = grid{alto} \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil Where \lceil \cdot \rceil is the ceiling operator and m is the maximum number of intervals among all stacks. Rectangular Optimization (Approach 2 Variant): Minimize rec{ancho} rec{alto} subject to: rec{ancho} + rec{alto} \text{ is minimized (implied by context of minimizing area/overhead)} rec{ancho} rec{alto} \ge m rec{ancho} > 0, rec{alto} > 0 Where rec{ancho} and rec{alto} are the dimensions of the rectangular super-texel region. Parameters: \epsilon: Threshold for opacity termination. Not given in the sources. m: Maximum number of intervals among all stacks in the SBRT. SSBO Minimum Size: OpenGL implementations must support SSBOs of at least 128 MB (read/write). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Calculation Bottleneck: Using 3D convolution for normal calculation in SBRT causes a performance bottleneck because each voxel access may require locating a new stack and iterating it sequentially. The hybrid deferred strategy avoids this. Memory Waste: Approach 1 (Two 2D Textures) wastes memory because the last cells of the last row usually remain unoccupied. Precision/Boundaries: The ray intersection with the bounding box must be handled correctly to avoid sampling outside the valid data range. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersbrt(camera, lightposition, gridancho, gridalto, m, epsilon): # Pass 1: Color and Depth for y in range(gridalto): for x in range(gridancho): rayorigin = camera.getorigin() raydirection = camera.getraydirection(x, y) # Intersect with bounding box tmin, tmax = intersectaabb(rayorigin, raydirection) if tmin > tmax: continue # Ray misses terrain # Adaptive ray marching t = tmin accumulatedopacity = 0.0 color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) while t < tmax and accumulatedopacity < 1.0 - epsilon: # Determine step size if isemptyspace(rayorigin + raydirection t): step = terraincellresolution else: step = smallstepsize # Increased frequency for non-empty # Sample SBRT at current position material, height = samplesbrt(rayorigin + raydirection t, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m) # Map to color samplecolor = transferfunction[material] # Front-to-back alpha blending alpha = samplecolor[3] # Assuming RGBA color = color + samplecolor (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) t += step # Store depth for normal calculation depthmap[x, y] = t # Ray-collision distance # Store intermediate color (or final if no normals needed, but here we do deferred) # Note: The source says "obtenemos el color devuelto por la FT" in pass 1 # and "componemos el color final" in pass 2. # We store the unlit color for pass 2. finalcolorbuffer[x, y] = color # Pass 2: Normal Calculation and Final Lighting for y in range(gridalto): for x in range(gridancho): # Get depth from pass 1 depth = depthmap[x, y] # Inverse projection to get 3D position pos3d = inverseproject(camera, x, y, depth) # Calculate normal using hybrid deferred strategy # Check neighbors in a mask around pos3d normal = calculatenormalhybrid(pos3d, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m) # Get unlit color from pass 1 unlitcolor = finalcolorbuffer[x, y] # Apply Lambertian lighting L = normalize(lightposition - pos3d) N = normalize(normal) kd = 1.0 # Example reflectance ia = 0.2 # Ambient intensity id = 0.8 # Diffuse intensity diffuse = kd dot(L, N) id finalintensity = ia + diffuse # Apply lighting to color finalcolor = unlitcolor finalintensity # Write to final buffer writetooutputbuffer(x, y, finalcolor) def samplesbrt(position, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m): # Project position to grid coordinates gx, gz = projecttogrid(position) # Get stack index and size from index buffer stackstart = indexbuffer[gx, gz].R stacksize = indexbuffer[gx, gz].G # Iterate through intervals in interval buffer # Interval buffer stores [material (R), accumulatedheight (G)] currentheight = 0.0 for i in range(stacksize): intervalidx = stackstart + i material = intervalbuffer[intervalidx].R intervalheight = intervalbuffer[intervalidx].G # Check if position is within this interval # Note: The source says "comparar esta altura con G2" # Assuming G2 is the accumulated height of the current interval # and we need to check if the ray's height relative to the stack start is within this interval # This is a simplified interpretation; exact logic depends on SBRT height encoding if currentheight <= position.y < currentheight + intervalheight: return material, intervalheight currentheight += intervalheight return EMPTYMATERIAL, 0.0 def calculatenormalhybrid(pos3d, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m): # Define mask size (e.g., 3x3x3) masksize = 1 normal = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Check neighbors in the mask for dx in range(-masksize, masksize + 1): for dy in range(-masksize, masksize + 1): for dz in range(-masksize, masksize + 1): neighborpos = pos3d + (dx, dy, dz) # Check if neighbor is occupied # "Un vóxel se considera ocupado si no está ocluido por el modelo real" # "si al proyectar de nuevo el valor obtenido por la proyección inversa, # se obtiene un valor de profundidad menor que la distancia de la cámara # a la posición de la proyección inversa" # This implies checking if the neighbor's depth in the depth map is valid # and corresponds to a surface voxel # Simplified: Check if the neighbor is part of the surface if issurfacevoxel(neighborpos, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m): # Add vector to normal normal += normalize(neighborpos - pos3d) return normalize(normal) def issurfacevoxel(pos, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m): # Check if voxel is occupied and not occluded # This requires checking the SBRT data at pos material, = samplesbrt(pos, indexbuffer, intervalbuffer, gridancho, gridalto, m) if material == EMPTYMATERIAL: return False # Check occlusion: project pos again and compare depths # This is a simplified check; actual implementation requires access to depth map # and camera parameters return True # Placeholder for complex occlusion check Uses an Index Texture (grid{ancho} \times grid{alto}) storing stack start (R) and size (G), and an Interval Texture storing material (R) and accumulated height (G). Stacks are stored row-order in the Interval Texture. Sets apart: Simple indexing but wastes memory in the last row. Choose when: Memory is not a critical constraint and simplicity is preferred. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Uses a single 2D Texture with dimensions grid{ancho} \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil \times grid{alto} \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil. Regions of size \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil \times \lceil \sqrt{m} \rceil act as super-texels. Sets apart: Pseudo-indexing via regions. Choose when: m is small and square regions are efficient. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Uses a 2D Texture of dimensions (grid{ancho} m) \times grid{alto}. Intervals stored along x-axis. Sets apart: Checks spatial coherence against 3D textures. Choose when: Spatial coherence is a priority. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Uses a 3D Texture of dimensions grid{ancho} \times grid{alto} \times m. Intervals stored along z-axis. Sets apart: Standard 3D texture access. Choose when: 3D texture hardware is efficient. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Uses two Shader Storage Buffer Objects (SSBOs) for indices and intervals, using OpenGL std430 layout. Sets apart: Flexible array sizes, large memory support (128 MB min). Choose when: Large datasets or dynamic stack sizes. Link: GPU Raycasting for Stack-Based Terrains Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays (pixels) and the average stack depth. Adaptive marching reduces steps in empty space. Normal calculation is deferred and depends on output buffer size, not data size. Memory Complexity: Depends on the chosen approach. Approach 1 wastes memory in the last row. Approach 5 requires SSBOs of at least 128 MB. Measured Performance: Enables real-time rendering and visual operations such as cross-sections, material layer attenuation, and borehole visualization. Scaling: Scales with GPU hardware capabilities. Avoids CPU-GPU data transfer bottleneck. Strengths: Real-time performance, efficient memory usage with SSBOs, avoids 3D convolution bottleneck for normals. Limitations: Normal calculation is limited in number compared to gradient-based methods, though sufficient for scientific applications. Approach 1 wastes memory. When to use: Geoscientific visualization requiring real-time interaction with layered terrain data. When not: When high-fidelity, gradient-based normals are critical and performance is not a constraint. Origin: Proposed by A. Graciano, A.J. Rueda & F.R. Feito in 2017. History: Developed to address the bottleneck of data transfer between CPU and GPU in visualization systems and to enable real-time operations on SBRT data. Usage: Geoscientific applications, terrain visualization, subsurface structure visualization. name: GPU Direct Volume Rendering with Anisotropic Shading
head: CUDA DVR
body: A GPU-based direct volume ray casting algorithm that enhances visual quality by applying anisotropic shading models (Ward or Lafortune BRDFs) to volumetric data. It distinguishes itself from standard isotropic shading by precomputing and storing covariance matrices alongside gradients, allowing the reconstruction of local surface orientation and anisotropy axes on-the-fly during ray casting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D scalar field data, precomputed 3D textures for normals and covariance matrices, transfer function TF, list of light sources LS, Henyey-Greenstein phase function f{d,hg}, Ward BRDF function f{s,w}, background radiance Lb, glossiness parameter \kappaw, scaling factor \gammaw, and diffuse coefficient kd. Outputs: Final color image with accumulated radiance and opacity. Data Structures: Scalar Field: Stored in a 3D texture. Prefiltered Normals: Stored in a 3D texture, quantized to 8 bits per channel. Covariance Matrices: Stored in a 3D texture as symmetric 2x2 matrices, quantized to 8 bits per channel. Eigenvectors are not stored; they are computed during rendering to avoid interpolation inconsistencies. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Optional): If prefiltering is enabled, iterate over all voxels x. Read the symmetric 2x2 matrix C, apply Gaussian filtering, and store the result back. 2. Ray Casting Loop: For each pixel P: a. Initialize accumulated radiance L = 0 and transmittance T = 0. b. Compute the eye ray and set view direction \omega = -\text{ray.direction}. c. While the ray has not finished traversing the volume: i. Get the current ray position x. ii. Sample the symmetric 2x2 covariance matrix C and the gradient G{\sigma t} from their respective 3D textures at x. iii. Compute the surface normal N{\sigma t} = G{\sigma t} / \text{length}(G{\sigma t}). iv. Perform eigenanalysis on C to obtain eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvectors \Lambda1, \Lambda2. v. Transform eigenvectors \Lambda1, \Lambda2 to world space and normalize them using N{\sigma t} to obtain tangent vectors U and V. vi. Compute Ward anisotropy parameters uw, vw from \lambda1, \lambda2, \kappaw, \gammaw. (For Lafortune BRDF, compute corresponding parameters analogously). vii. Compute the specular coefficient ks = \text{length}(G{\sigma t}). viii. Initialize light contribution Li = 0. ix. For each light source ls \in LS: 1. Compute light direction \omega0 = \text{lightDirection}(x, ls). 2. Compute the BRDF value: f = kd f{d,hg}(\omega0, \omega) + ks f{s,w}(U, V, N{\sigma t}, uw, vw, \omega0, \omega) (\omega0 \cdot N{\sigma t}) 3. Add to light contribution: Li = Li + f \cdot \text{incomingRadianceFromLightSource}(x, ls) x. Composite the light contribution into the accumulator using the transfer function: (L, T) = \text{composite}(x, TF, L, T, Li) d. Return the final color: T \cdot Lb + L. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gpuanisotropicvolumerendering( scalarfieldtexture, normaltexture, covariancetexture, transferfunction, lightsources, kappaw, # Glossiness gammaw, # Anisotropy scaling kd # Diffuse coefficient): # Preprocessing step (optional, done once) # for x in allvoxels: # C = readsymmetric2x2matrix(covariancetexture, x) # C = filtergaussian(C) # writesymmetric2x2matrix(covariancetexture, C, x) for pixel P in screen: L = 0.0 T = 0.0 ray = computeeyeray(P) omega = -ray.direction # View direction while raycastingnotfinished(ray): x = getrayposition(ray) # Sample precomputed data C = samplesymmetric2x2matrix(covariancetexture, x) Gsigmat = samplegradient(normaltexture, x) # Compute normal Nsigmat = normalize(Gsigmat) # Eigenanalysis of covariance matrix lambda1, lambda2, Lambda1, Lambda2 = computeeigenanalysis(C) # Transform eigenvectors to world space and normalize U, V = transformtoworldspaceandnormalize(Lambda1, Lambda2, Nsigmat) # Compute Ward parameters uw, vw = computewardparameters(lambda1, lambda2, kappaw, gammaw) # Specular coefficient from gradient magnitude ks = length(Gsigmat) Li = 0.0 for ls in lightsources: omega0 = lightdirection(x, ls) # Diffuse term using Henyey-Greenstein phase function fdiffuse = kd heneygreensteinphase(omega0, omega) # Specular term using Ward BRDF # Note: The dot product (omega0. Nsigmat) is part of the BRDF evaluation in the source formula fspecular = ks wardbrdf(U, V, Nsigmat, uw, vw, omega0, omega) dot(omega0, Nsigmat) f = fdiffuse + fspecular Li += f incomingradiancefromlight(x, ls) # Composite step L, T = compositevolume(x, transferfunction, L, T, Li) return T backgroundradiance + L Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Eigenvector Interpolation: Eigenvectors must not be stored or interpolated directly. Interpolating eigenvectors leads to inconsistent results due to sign ambiguity and discontinuities. Instead, the covariance matrix components are interpolated, and eigenanalysis is performed on-the-fly. Gradient Normalization: The normal N{\sigma t} is derived from the gradient G{\sigma t}. If the gradient magnitude is zero, normalization fails. Quantization: Values are quantized to 8 bits per channel. This may introduce artifacts in high-precision requirements, though it is generally sufficient for gradient-based shading. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of ray samples and light sources. The eigenanalysis is performed per ray sample per light source, adding computational overhead compared to isotropic shading. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the scalar field, prefiltered normals, and covariance matrices. Storing the symmetric 2x2 matrix (6 values) and gradient (3 values) per voxel increases memory footprint compared to storing only the scalar field. Performance: Interactive visualization is achievable on GPU hardware. On-the-fly eigenanalysis is preferred over precomputing eigenvectors to balance memory usage and computational cost. Strengths: Provides realistic anisotropic shading effects for volumetric data, enhancing the perception of structure and orientation. Limitations: Higher memory usage due to precomputed textures. More complex than standard isotropic DVR. The method is described in "Anisotropic Ambient Volume Shading". It builds on the concept of using geometry tensors (covariance matrices) to estimate local surface orientation and anisotropy in volumetric data. The approach avoids the high cost of on-the-fly curvature estimation by prefiltering and storing the necessary tensor data. name: Jittor Volume Render Cuvol Wrapper
body: The Jittor Volume Render Cuvol Wrapper is a custom Jittor function that fuses the forward and backward passes of volume rendering into a single CUDA kernel launch sequence, managing memory aliases and gradient propagation for a sparse grid representation. It differs from standard CPU-based ray marchers by executing the core ray casting logic on the GPU via CUDA, while maintaining compatibility with Jittor's automatic differentiation engine. It builds on the CUDA GPU Implementation by providing a high-level API that handles the integration of sparse grid data structures (offsets, scaling, links) into the CUDA kernels. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A sparse grid object (containing density, SH coefficients, basis data, links, offsets, scaling), ray origins and directions (tensors), and a RenderOptions struct. Outputs: Rendered color buffer, confidence/confidence map, and optionally a log-transparency buffer if background rendering is enabled. Data Structures: RenderOptions: A struct passed to CUDA kernels containing: backgroundbrightness: float stepsize: float sigmathresh: float (density threshold for early ray termination) stopthresh: float (transparency threshold for early ray termination) nearclip: float usesphericclip: bool lastsampleopaque: bool Sparse Grid: Contains links (connectivity), offset, scaling, basisdim, basistype, basisdata, densitydata, shdata, backgroundlinks, backgrounddata. Steps: 1. Prepare Grid Offsets and Scaling: If gridcoords is true, use identity scaling. Otherwise, scale grid offsets and scaling by the number of links: gsz = \text{shape}(\text{grid}.\links)[0] \text{self}.\grid\offset = \text{grid}.\offset \times gsz - 0.5 \text{self}.\grid\scaling = \text{grid}.\scaling \times gsz Ensure gsz is treated as a Jittor array for broadcasting. 2. Initialize Log Transmit Buffer (if background is used): Create an empty buffer logtransmit with shape [rays.origins.shape[0]] and dtype matching rays.origins. Call.stopgrad() on logtransmit to prevent gradient flow through this buffer during backpropagation. 3. Launch Forward CUDA Kernel (renderraykernel): Pass grid data (density, SH, links, offset, scaling, background links/data, basis info), ray origins/directions, RenderOptions, output buffer, and logtransmit pointer (or nullptr if no background). The kernel performs ray marching, sampling the sparse grid, and compositing colors. 4. Launch Background Kernel (if background is used): Launch renderbackgroundkernel subsequently to handle background color integration using the logtransmit buffer. 5. Gradient Computation (grad): Initialize gradient buffers for density, SH, basis, and background data. Determine if gradients are needed for basis and background data based on requiresgrad flags. 6. Launch Backward CUDA Kernel (renderraybackwardkernel): Pass gradients, color cache, rays, RenderOptions, and output gradient structure. Computes gradients for density, SH, and basis data based on the forward pass results. 7. Launch Background Backward Kernel (if background is used): Launch renderbackgroundbackwardkernel to compute gradients related to background parameters. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import jittor as jt import numpy as np class VolumeRenderCuvol(jt.Function): def execute(self, grid, rays, opt, usebackground=False): # 1. Prepare grid offsets and scaling if grid.gridcoords: self.gridoffset = 0.0 self.gridscaling = 1.0 else: gsz = jt.array(np.array(grid.links.shape[0])) self.gridoffset = grid.offset gsz - 0.5 self.gridscaling = grid.scaling gsz # 2. Initialize logtransmit buffer if background is used if usebackground: self.logtransmit = jt.empty([rays.origins.shape[0]], dtype=rays.origins.dtype).stopgrad() else: self.logtransmit = None # 3. Launch forward CUDA kernel # Note: PackedVar32 is a Jittor-specific packing structure for CUDA output = jt.empty([rays.origins.shape[0], 3], dtype=rays.origins.dtype) # Kernel launch parameters blocks = (rays.origins.shape[0] + TRACERAYCUDATHREADS - 1) // TRACERAYCUDATHREADS renderraykernelblocks, TRACERAYCUDATHREADS if usebackground else None) # 4. Launch background kernel if needed if usebackground: renderbackgroundkernelblocks, TRACERAYCUDATHREADS return output def grad(self, gradoutput): # 5. Initialize gradient buffers graddensity = jt.zeroslike(self.grid.densitydata) gradsh = jt.zeroslike(self.grid.shdata) gradbasis = jt.zeroslike(self.grid.basisdata) gradbackground = jt.zeroslike(self.grid.backgrounddata) if self.grid.requiresgradbackground else None # 6. Launch backward CUDA kernel blocks = (self.rays.origins.shape[0] + TRACERAYCUDATHREADS - 1) // TRACERAYCUDATHREADS renderraybackwardkernelblocks, TRACERAYCUDATHREADS # 7. Launch background backward kernel if needed if self.usebackground: renderbackgroundbackwardkernelblocks, TRACERAYCUDATHREADS return graddensity, gradsh, gradbasis, gradbackground Parameters: opt: RenderOptions struct. Typical values for sigmathresh and stopthresh are small positive floats (e.g., 1e-4, 1e-5) to control early ray termination. stepsize depends on the desired sampling density. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use of --usefastmath in the underlying CUDA compilation may affect precision. Memory Aliases: The wrapper manages memory aliases for sparse grid data. Incorrect handling of links and offset can lead to out-of-bounds access. Background Rendering: If usebackground is true, the logtransmit buffer must be correctly initialized and passed to both forward and backward kernels. Uses slab-based traversal for efficient ray-grid intersection. Choose when the grid is dense and regular. [11383-slab-based-raycasting.md] General GPU acceleration techniques. Choose when hardware acceleration is needed but specific sparse grid optimizations are not required. [12256-gpu-accelerated-ray-casting.md] Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and samples per ray. Early ray termination (controlled by sigmathresh and stopthresh) can reduce the average number of samples. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of non-zero grid cells and rays. The sparse grid representation helps reduce memory usage compared to dense volumes. Performance: High performance on NVIDIA GPUs due to CUDA optimization. Performance scales with the number of CUDA cores and memory bandwidth. Strengths: Efficient handling of sparse data, integration with Jittor's autograd, support for background rendering. Limitations: Requires NVIDIA GPU, dependent on Jittor framework, potential precision issues with fast math. When to use: When using Jittor for differentiable volume rendering with sparse data and needing GPU acceleration. When not to use: When using other frameworks (PyTorch, TensorFlow) or when CPU-only execution is required. The Jittor Volume Render Cuvol Wrapper is part of the JNeRF project, an unofficial implementation of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) using the Jittor deep learning framework. It was developed to leverage Jittor's custom function capabilities for efficient GPU-accelerated volume rendering with automatic differentiation. The method builds on the CUDA GPU Implementation to provide a seamless integration with Jittor's computational graph. Jittor/JNeRF, https://github.com/Jittor/JNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volume Fragment Shader (Direct Ray Marching)
head: Fragment Shader Implementation, Ray-box volume rendering, Volume Rendering Shader
body: This method implements direct volume ray casting entirely within a GPU fragment shader, bypassing traditional ray-generation geometry or multi-pass accumulation buffers. It computes per-pixel ray parameters from camera matrices, performs ray-AABB intersection to determine entry and exit points, and executes the emission-absorption compositing loop directly in the fragment shader. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its reliance on hardware-accelerated texture sampling for trilinear interpolation and its specific handling of mask-based context visualization (ghosting) and intensity normalization within the shader logic itself. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D volume texture (volumeTex), 3D mask texture (maskTex), 1D lookup table (lut), 1D color transfer function (CTF), 1D gradient magnitude transfer function (GMTF), camera matrices (implicit via NDC), and UI parameters (beta, surfaceVoxelsOnly, colorGhosting, roiMin, roiMax, isoValue, quality, dithering). Outputs: Final fragment color (glFragColor). Data Structures: volumeTex: sampler3D, stores scalar volume values normalized to [0, 1]. maskTex: sampler3D, stores classification/mask data. lut: sampler1D, maps volume intensity to color/opacity. CTF: sampler1D, maps mask data to color. GMTF: sampler1D, maps gradient magnitude to shading weight. transferTex: sampler2D, used in some implementations to store 1-D LUTs as a single-row 2-D texture. Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Generation: Compute Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) from glFragCoord to ensure robustness across platforms (e.g., macOS). 2. Mask Sampling: Sample the mask texture at the current fragment's texture coordinates (glTexCoord[1].stp) to get value r. 3. Mask Classification: Sample the Color Transfer Function (CTF) using the alpha channel of r (r.a) to obtain the mask color colmask. 4. Fragment Discard: If colmask.a is 0.0, discard the fragment immediately. 5. Ray-AABB Intersection: Define the bounding box (AABB) centered at the origin with half-extents boxHalf. Compute ray direction rayDir and origin rayOrigin from camera parameters. Calculate inverse direction: invDir = 1.0 / rayDir. Compute intersection intervals for each slab: t0 = (-\text{boxHalf} - \text{rayOrigin}) \times \text{invDir} t1 = (\text{boxHalf} - \text{rayOrigin}) \times \text{invDir} Determine t{\text{min}} and t{\text{max}}: t{\text{min}} = \max(\max(t0.x, t0.y), t0.z) t{\text{max}} = \min(\min(t1.x, t1.y), t1.z) The ray intersects the box if t{\text{max}} > \max(t{\text{min}}, 0.0). 6. Volume Sampling: Sample the volume texture at the fragment's position (glTexCoord[0].stp) to get p. Extract gradient vector grad from p.rgb. Sample the Lookup Table (LUT) using p.a to get volume color colvol. Sample the Gradient Magnitude Transfer Function (GMTF) using r.a to get gradweight. 7. Compositing and Shading Logic: Case A (Full Mask): If colmask.a is 1.0: \text{color} = \text{col\vol} \times \beta + (1 - \beta) \times \text{col\mask} where \beta is a user-defined parameter modulating the influence of the volume color. Case B (Partial Mask): If colmask.a is not 1.0: Surface Voxels Only: If surfaceVoxelsOnly is true AND the gradient magnitude is small (checked via LargeGradient(grad, gradweight)): \text{color}.a = 0.0 Color Ghosting: If colorGhosting is true: \text{color} = \text{col\mask} Default Blending: Otherwise: \text{color} = \text{col\vol} \times \beta + (1 - \beta) \times \text{col\mask} 8. Final Shading: Call the shade function with color, grad, and gradweight to produce glFragColor. Intensity Normalization (Pre-processing): Before sampling, raw volume values are normalized: v{\text{norm}} = \frac{v{\text{raw}} - \text{rangeMin}}{\text{rangeMax} - \text{rangeMin}} Clamped to [0, 1]. If \text{rangeMax} - \text{rangeMin} < 10^{-6}, return 0.0 to avoid division by zero. Gamma correction is applied: v{\text{final}} = v{\text{norm}}^{\text{gamma}}. Dithering: To prevent banding artifacts, a pseudo-random hash using noiseSeed adds a random offset to the ray start position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def main(): # 1. NDC Coordinates ndc = computendc(glFragCoord) # 2. Mask Sampling r = texture3D(mask, ndc) colmask = texture1D(CTF, r.a) # 3. Discard if mask is transparent if colmask.a == 0.0: discardfragment() return # 4. Volume Sampling p = texture3D(volume, ndc) colvol = texture1D(lut, p.a) grad = p.rgb gradweight = texture1D(GMTF, r.a) # 5. Compositing Logic if colmask.a == 1.0: color = colvol beta + (1.0 - beta) colmask else: if surfacevoxelsonly and not largegradient(grad, gradweight): color.a = 0.0 elif colorghosting: color = colmask else: color = colvol beta + (1.0 - beta) colmask # 6. Final Shading glFragColor = shade(color, grad, gradweight) def computendc(fragcoord): # Robust NDC computation for macOS return vec3(fragcoord.x, fragcoord.y, 0.5) / vec3(width, height, 1.0) 2.0 - 1.0 def largegradient(grad, gradweight): # Placeholder for gradient magnitude check logic # Typically checks if gradweight exceeds a threshold return gradweight > 0.5 # Implementation detail inferred from context def shade(color, grad, gradweight): # Placeholder for lighting/shading calculation # Uses grad and gradweight to modulate color return color gradweight # Simplified shading model Parameters: beta: Float, modulates the blend between volume color and mask color. Default 1.0. surfaceVoxelsOnly: Boolean, hides interior voxels if gradient is small. colorGhosting: Boolean, displays mask color for context nodes. roiMin, roiMax: vec3, texture coordinate bounds for Region of Interest clipping, default (0,0,0) to (1,1,1). isoValue: Float, threshold for isosurface mode. quality: Float, controls step count (0.1 coarse, 1.0 fine). dithering: Float, controls random ray-start offset strength. A variant that handles colormap and inversion logic differently, specifically separating inversion application for colormap vs scalar modes. It uses integer-based fragment coordinates to determine inversion state. Definition: Uses highp usampler3D for volume and highp sampler2D for colormap. Inversion is determined by comparing comp uniform with glFragCoord. Logic: 1. Initialize invert = false. If comp.x == int(glFragCoord.x) or comp.y == int(glFragCoord.y), set invert = true. 2. Sample volume at samp. Convert red channel to float and divide by 65536.0. If samp is outside [0.0, 1.0], set value to 0.0. 3. Default color is white RGB with alpha val. 4. If usecolormap is true: Sample colormap at vec2(val, 0.5). Set color to RGB from colormap and alpha from val. 5. If invert is true AND usecolormap is false: Set color to white RGB and alpha 1.0 - val. 6. If invert is true AND usecolormap is true: Set color to white RGB and alpha 1.0. When to choose: When integer-based coordinate inversion is required for specific visualization modes or when using 16-bit integer volume data mapped to colormap. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray, which is controlled by the quality parameter. Memory Complexity: Low, as it operates per-fragment without storing large intermediate buffers, relying on GPU texture memory. Performance: Fast for small volumes or low quality settings; performance degrades with high quality (fine step count) and large volumes. Strengths: Simple implementation, leverages hardware texture sampling, supports real-time interaction via UI parameters. Limitations: Limited to direct ray casting; does not support advanced lighting or global illumination without additional shader complexity. Banding artifacts may occur without dithering. When to use: Real-time visualization of scalar volumes with simple transfer functions. When not to use: Complex lighting requirements or very large volumes requiring hierarchical traversal. This method originates from implementations in open-source visualization tools like ClearVolume-plus and VisWeb, adapting direct volume ray casting to fragment shaders. It builds on the principles of hardware-accelerated volume rendering Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering. name: Multithreaded Volume Rendering Pipeline
head: Context Switching for Data Hazards, Ray Multithreading
body: The Multithreaded Volume Rendering Pipeline is a hardware optimization technique designed to overcome data hazards in pipelined volume rendering architectures. It solves the problem where subsequent sample point addresses depend on the distance value of the current sample point, which causes pipeline stalls due to memory read delays. By processing multiple rays (threads) in a round-robin order, it maintains high pipeline utilization where sequential processing would drop below 10%. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset, camera parameters, and a ray queue structure. Output: A 2D image where each pixel's brightness is the accumulated contribution of all rays passing through it. Data Structures Ray Queue: Implemented as a shift register. Each slot in the register stores the parameters of a single ray. Slot Layout: Not given in the sources. Capacity: Up to 64 rays are processed simultaneously. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel of the final image, a ray is cast into the volume. 2. Sample Point Generation: Sample points are generated at regular intervals starting from the viewing plane (nearest to the viewer). 3. Position Calculation: The position of the sample point in the data volume is calculated. 4. Voxel Sampling: The 8 neighboring voxels are read out from volume memory. 5. Interpolation: Trilinear interpolation is performed on the 8 voxels to obtain the gray value (interpreted as opacity) of the sample point. 6. Gradient Calculation: A gradient is calculated by determining the gray value change between neighboring sample points. This gradient serves as the normal of a possible plane in the volume. 7. Shading: Using the plane normal, shading is performed to calculate how much light is reflected toward the viewer direction by diffuse and specular reflection. 8. Absorption Calculation: It is calculated how much of the reflected light intensity reaches the viewing plane due to absorption. 9. Compositing: Each contribution of a ray is accumulated to represent the brightness of the considered pixel. 10. Data Hazard Detection: The system detects that the next sample point address depends on the distance value of the current sample point, which requires reading from volume memory with a delay of 3 clock cycles plus calculation delay. 11. Context Switching: Instead of inserting no-operations (stalls), the hardware switches context to the next ray in the queue to hide the memory latency. 12. Queue Management: When a new sample point is calculated for a ray, the ray is added to the end of the ray queue (shift register). 13. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If the intensity of a ray falls below a user-defined threshold, the ray is deleted from the queue. Pseudocode The following pseudocode illustrates the round-robin processing logic within the hardware pipeline, focusing on the queue management and context switching required to hide latency. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. MAXRAYS = 64 MEMORYDELAYCYCLES = 3 class Ray: # Parameters for a single ray, stored in shift register slots # Specific fields (origin, direction, current distance, etc.) are not given in sources pass class RayQueue: def init(self, capacity): self.capacity = capacity self.rays = [None] capacity self.head = 0 self.tail = 0 self.count = 0 def isempty(self): return self.count == 0 def isfull(self): return self.count == self.capacity def enqueue(self, ray): if self.isfull(): # In a hardware shift register, the oldest ray might be dropped or overwritten # if the queue is full and a new ray needs to be processed. # The source describes it as a shift register, implying a fixed size buffer. pass self.rays[self.tail] = ray self.tail = (self.tail + 1) % self.capacity self.count += 1 def dequeue(self): if self.isempty(): return None ray = self.rays[self.head] self.head = (self.head + 1) % self.capacity self.count -= 1 return ray def peek(self): if self.isempty(): return None return self.rays[self.head] def processpipeline(rayqueue): # The hardware pipeline processes one sample point per clock cycle for the active ray # To hide the 3-cycle memory delay, we switch rays every cycle for cycle in range(numcycles): if not rayqueue.isempty(): currentray = rayqueue.peek() # Stage 1: Address Generation (Cycle 1) # Calculate position of sample point in data volume # This depends on the previous distance value, creating a hazard samplepos = calculatesampleposition(currentray) # Stage 2: Memory Read (Cycles 2-4) # Read 8 neighboring voxels. Delay is 3 clock cycles. # During these cycles, the pipeline would stall if we waited for this ray. # Instead, we switch to the next ray in the queue. voxels = readvoxels(samplepos) # Stage 3: Interpolation & Gradient (Cycle 5) # Trilinear interpolation to get opacity opacity = trilinearinterpolate(voxels) # Calculate gradient from neighboring sample points gradient = calculategradient(currentray, opacity) # Stage 4: Shading & Absorption (Cycle 6) # Calculate light reflection (diffuse/specular) lightintensity = calculateshading(gradient) # Calculate absorption absorbedintensity = calculateabsorption(lightintensity, opacity) # Stage 5: Compositing (Cycle 7) # Accumulate contribution to pixel accumulatepixel(currentray.pixelid, absorbedintensity) # Update ray state for next step currentray.updatedistance() # Check for Early Ray Termination if currentray.intensity < THRESHOLD: rayqueue.dequeue() # Remove ray from queue else: # Add ray back to end of queue for next sample point rayqueue.enqueue(currentray) # Context Switch: Move to next ray in queue for next clock cycle # The hardware automatically shifts the active ray pointer # This hides the memory latency by processing other rays pass Parameters Max Concurrent Rays: 64 rays are processed simultaneously in the round-robin queue. Memory Delay: 3 clock cycles from addressing to data out. ERT Threshold: User-defined threshold for ray intensity. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Data Hazard: Sequential processing of sample points causes pipeline stalls because the next address depends on the current distance value. Without multithreading, pipeline utilization drops to less than 10% due to the 3-cycle memory delay and address calculation delay. Queue Overflow: The source describes the queue as a shift register with a fixed capacity (64 rays). If more rays are generated than the queue can hold, older rays may be displaced or processing may stall if the queue management logic is not explicitly defined for overflow. What it is: A method that divides the volume data into spatial domains, assigning each domain to a different processor or thread group. Difference: Unlike the multithreaded pipeline which focuses on hiding latency within a single pipeline by switching rays, domain decomposition focuses on parallelizing the workload across multiple processing units by splitting the data space. When to choose: Use when the volume is large and can be effectively partitioned, and when hardware supports distributed memory or multi-core parallelism. Link: Parallel Domain-Decomposed Ray Casting What it is: The general architectural design for implementing volume rendering on GPUs, including memory hierarchies and shader models. Difference: The multithreaded pipeline is a specific optimization technique for pipelined hardware (often FPGA or custom ASIC), whereas GPU architecture is a broader framework that may use different parallelism models (SIMT). When to choose: Use when designing the overall system for a GPU, rather than optimizing a specific pipelined hardware unit. Link: GPU Implementation Architecture What it is: A specific implementation of volume rendering using NVIDIA's CUDA programming model. Difference: CUDA uses a SIMT (Single Instruction, Multiple Thread) model with warp scheduling, which is conceptually similar to multithreading but managed by the GPU driver and hardware differently than the explicit round-robin shift register described in the multithreaded pipeline. When to choose: Use when targeting NVIDIA GPUs and leveraging CUDA's high-level parallelism. Link: CUDA GPU Implementation Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: The ray queue requires storage for up to 64 rays. Measured Performance: Without multithreading, pipeline utilization drops to less than 10% due to 3-cycle memory delay and address calculation delay. With multithreading, pipeline utilization is maintained at a high level by calculating sample points for other rays instead of inserting no-operations. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Overcomes data hazards in pipelined volume rendering; maintains high pipeline utilization; hides memory latency. Limitations: Requires hardware support for context switching and a ray queue (shift register); limited to 64 concurrent rays in the described implementation. When to use: Use in hardware-accelerated volume rendering pipelines where data hazards cause significant stalls. When not: Use when the hardware does not support multithreading or when the volume data access pattern does not exhibit the described data hazard. The Multithreaded Volume Rendering Pipeline was introduced in the paper "Volume Rendering FPGA Hardware" by Lacroute et al. (1999). It was developed to address the performance bottlenecks in pipelined volume rendering hardware, specifically the data hazards caused by the dependency of sample point addresses on previous distance values. The technique is particularly relevant for FPGA-based volume rendering implementations where pipeline efficiency is critical. Volume Rendering FPGA Hardware, https://doi.org/10.5753/sbac-pad.1999.19799, fetched 2026-10-24

name: WebGL/WebGPU Browser Implementations
head: Browser-based GPU Volume Rendering
body: This family implements direct volume ray casting within web browsers using WebGL or WebGPU APIs, bypassing native desktop applications to enable interactive visualization in standard web pages. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric data without plugins by adapting GPU-accelerated ray marching to browser-specific constraints, such as the lack of 3D texture support in WebGL 1.0 or the strict memory alignment rules of WebGPU. It differs from desktop GPU implementations by prioritizing compatibility with web standards and handling browser-specific data encoding workarounds, such as packing depth into RGBA channels or using 2D texture atlases for volumetric slices. All methods in this family implement the emission-absorption optical model defined in Direct volume ray casting. The core pipeline for each pixel consists of ray generation, hardware-accelerated sampling, classification, and compositing Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering. 1. Ray Generation: Rays are generated per-pixel, typically by computing ray parameters from camera matrices in vertex/fragment shaders or by rendering the volume's bounding box geometry to determine entry/exit points Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering. 2. Hardware-Accelerated Sampling: Scalar volume values are sampled using the GPU's texture hardware. The volume data is stored in 3D texture memory, and the texture engine performs trilinear interpolation of the eight surrounding voxels in parallel, avoiding manual shader interpolation Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering. 3. Fragment Shader Compositing: The ray marching loop, including classification and front-to-back compositing, is executed within the fragment shader Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering. The standard compositing equation updates accumulated color C' and opacity \alpha': C'{i} = C'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai Ci \alpha'{i} = \alpha'{i-1} + (1 - \alpha'{i-1}) \alphai 4. Early Ray Termination (ERT): Rays are terminated when accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95 or 1.0) to optimize performance Hardware-Accelerated Volume Rendering. This method is a WebGL-based volume rendering algorithm that supports the coexistence of 3D triangular meshes and volumetric datasets by using a multi-pass rendering pipeline to handle occlusion, blending, and ray intersection with 3D geometry within WebGL constraints. It specifically addresses the lack of 3D textures and limited depth texture support in WebGL by encoding depth data into RGBA color channels and arranging volumetric slices into a 2D texture atlas. Unlike single-pass ray-casting approaches, this method explicitly separates the computation of 3D surface geometry and volume traversal into distinct passes to correctly handle transparency and occlusion between opaque meshes and semi-transparent volumes. An interactive voxel volume renderer using path tracing that runs in modern browsers via WebGL 2.0. It renders 3D scalar fields (volumes) by casting rays from the camera through the volume, accumulating color and opacity along the ray, and applying lighting/shadowing. It differs from its siblings by using a single-pass fragment shader approach with explicit ray-box intersection and Beer-Lambert integration, rather than geometry-based intersection or structured data traversal. StructuredVolumeRenderer is a reusable, graph-native WebGPU renderer for scalar, vector, and hybrid volume data, exposing facades at @luma.gl/scene/forward, /deferred, /raytrace, and /raymarch. It solves the problem of rendering structured grid data (buffers or 3D textures) in the browser by providing a fixed-step jittered ray marching implementation with front-to-back compositing. It sets itself apart from sibling WebGL implementations by leveraging the WebGPU compute/render pipeline for direct GPU execution without CPU submission, and by supporting both storage buffer and 3D texture backing with manual trilinear interpolation. The implementation of volume rendering in web browsers emerged as WebGL 1.0 and later WebGL 2.0 and WebGPU provided sufficient shader programmability and texture sampling capabilities. Early WebGL implementations faced significant limitations, particularly the absence of 3D texture support in WebGL 1.0, which necessitated workarounds such as 2D texture atlases and RGBA depth packing. The transition to WebGL 2.0 introduced 3D texture support and improved floating-point precision, enabling more direct ray casting approaches. WebGPU further advanced browser-based volume rendering by providing explicit control over memory layouts, storage buffers, and pipeline creation, allowing for more efficient handling of large datasets and complex transfer functions. These methods are primarily used in web-based medical imaging viewers, scientific data visualization dashboards, and interactive 3D web applications where native software installation is not feasible. name: WebGL Multi-pass Ray-casting with 3D Geometry Intersection
head: Five-pass ray-casting pipeline, VMesh Real-Time Rendering, WebGL volume rendering with intersected 3D geometry
body: This method enables the interactive coexistence of volumetric datasets and 3D triangular meshes in WebGL by using a multi-pass rendering pipeline to handle occlusion, blending, and ray intersection. It solves the problem of rendering opaque and transparent 3D geometry within or alongside volume data, a key requirement for medical and engineering visualizations, while adhering to WebGL constraints such as the lack of native 3D and float texture support. Unlike single-pass ray-casting approaches, this method explicitly separates the computation of depth, surface color, and volume traversal into distinct passes to correctly manage back-to-front blending and geometry intersections. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 3D triangular meshes (opaque), a volumetric dataset (represented as a 2D texture atlas), camera matrices, and transfer functions. Outputs: A final 2D image composited from volume and mesh data. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored as a 2D texture atlas where 2D slices are stacked in the Z-axis arranged in a matrix configuration on a single 2D plane. Depth Data: Since WebGL 1.0 lacks native float texture support, depth values from intermediate passes are encoded into RGBA color channels of Frame Buffer Objects (FBOs). FBOs: Multiple Frame Buffer Objects are used to store intermediate results: depth maps, surface colors, and volume coordinates. Numbered Steps: The pipeline consists of five passes (or four in the VMesh variant), executed in the following order: 1. Depth Pass (Meshes): Render the depth of all 3D meshes in the scene into an FBO. The fragment shader outputs the current depth encoded in RGBA color channels. 2. Surface Color Pass (Meshes): Render all 3D meshes into a separate FBO to store their color information. 3. Back Cube Depth Pass (Volume): Render the depth of the back side of the volume bounding box into an FBO, encoded in RGBA, using the same shader logic as Pass 1. 4. Back Coordinates Pass (Volume): Render the back faces of the volume bounding box into a separate FBO. The 3D texture coordinates are assigned as color on each vertex, so rasterization interpolates these per-vertex colors to represent volume data 3D texture coordinates. 5. Ray Traversal and Composition Pass: Render 3D objects and volume data to the screen buffer. Objects must be sorted in Z-depth order and rendered from back to front. In the fragment shader, rays are cast towards the volume. All outputs from previous passes are sampled as 2D textures. The shader performs ray marching, checks for 3D geometry intersections using depth data from Passes 1 and 3, and composites the results. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode represents the core ray-casting logic executed in the fragment shader during the final pass (Pass 5), adapted from. It assumes access to textures generated in previous passes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def unpackrgbatofloat(r, g, b, a): # Corresponds to the GLSL function in # value = r 256^3 + g 256^2 + b 256 + a # Note: The source uses bit shifting logic. # bitSh = [256^3, 256^2, 256, 1] # bitMsk = [0, 1/256, 1/256, 1/256] # The unpacking reverses the packing. # Standard packing: val = r256^3 + g256^2 + b256 + a return r (256.03) + g (256.02) + b 256.0 + a raydirection = computeraydirection(camerapos, screenpos, projectionmatrix, viewmatrix) raypos = camerapos backdepthrgba = sampletexture(depthvoltex, screenpos) backdepthfloat = unpackrgbatofloat(backdepthrgba.r, backdepthrgba.g, backdepthrgba.b, backdepthrgba.a) maxdistance = backdepthfloat stepsize = maxdistance / S accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for i from 0 to S: # Current sample position currentsamplepos = raypos + (i stepsize) raydirection # Check for 3D Geometry Intersection # Sample depth from mesh depth texture meshdepthrgba = sampletexture(depthmeshtex, screenpos) meshdepthfloat = unpackrgbatofloat(meshdepthrgba.r, meshdepthrgba.g, meshdepthrgba.b, meshdepthrgba.a) # Determine if a mesh exists at this depth closer than current ray position # Note: Depth comparison depends on coordinate system (NDC vs View Space) # If meshdepthfloat < currentdepthalongray, a mesh occludes the volume if meshexistsatdepth(meshdepthfloat, currentsamplepos): # Get mesh color meshcolor = sampletexture(colormeshtex, screenpos) # Composite mesh color with accumulated volume color # Back-to-front blending # Cout = Cvol + (1 - alphavol) Cmesh # alphaout = alphavol + (1 - alphavol) alphamesh (assuming opaque mesh, alphamesh=1) # If mesh is opaque, it blocks further volume sampling accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) meshcolor accumulatedalpha = 1.0 break # Terminate ray due to occlusion # Sample Volume Data # Use coordvoltex to get 3D texture coordinates for the current ray position # The 3D coordinates are interpolated from the back face rendering in Pass 4 # However, standard ray casting uses raypos to index into the volume atlas # The source implies using the 3D texture coordinates from the back face # to map the ray position to the volume atlas. # Interpolate sample at current raypos from volume atlas # This requires mapping raypos to the 2D atlas coordinates volumevalue = samplevolumeatlas(volumeatlastex, raypos) # Compute color and opacity using transfer function color, alpha = applytransferfunction(volumevalue) # Accumulate # Standard front-to-back compositing for volume accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha color accumulatedalpha = accumulatedalpha + (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) alpha # Early Ray Termination if accumulatedalpha >= 1.0: break # Increment ray position raypos = raypos + stepsize raydirection outputcolor = accumulatedcolor Parameters: Rendering Order: Objects (volumes and 3D opaque meshes) must be sorted in z-depth order and rendered from back to front. Blending Mode: Back-to-front blending composition is used for the ray-casting shaders in the final rendering pass. Threshold: Early ray termination occurs when accumulated opacity \alpha \ge 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lack of 3D Textures: WebGL lacks support for 3D textures, requiring the use of a 2D texture atlas workaround to sample volumetric data. Lack of Float Textures: WebGL lacks support for Float textures, requiring depth data to be encoded into RGBA color channels for storage in FBOs. Precision loss may occur during packing/unpacking. Occlusion Handling: Correctly determining if a 3D object occludes the volume requires comparing the depth of the mesh (from Pass 1) with the current ray position. This must be done at each step or at least at the entry point. Complexity: The multi-pass approach requires five rendering passes and multiple Frame Buffer Objects (FBOs), which is a downside in terms of computational overhead and memory usage. Performance: The method is designed for interactive visualization on web platforms, balancing quality with the constraints of WebGL. Strengths: Supports the coexistence of 3D triangular meshes and volumetric datasets, which is critical for medical and engineering applications. Limitations: High memory usage due to multiple FBOs; precision issues due to RGBA depth encoding; complexity of implementation due to multiple passes and sorting requirements. This method extends previous WebGL ray-casting efforts by Congote et al. [CSK 11], Mobeen et al. [MF12], and Noguera and Jiménez [NJ12] by exploring the coexistence of 3D triangular meshes along volume data within the constraints of the Web platform. It addresses challenges such as the lack of 3D and depth textures in WebGL. The VMesh variant implements a similar four-pass process using three.js for VMesh assets. Deployment of Volume Rendering Interactive Visualizations in Web Platforms With Intersected 3D Geometry, https://doi.org/10.2312/ceig.20161312, fetched 2026-10-26 VMesh: Hybrid Volume-Mesh Representation for Efficient View Synthesis, https://core.ac.uk/download/560406650.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27

name: WebGL Path Tracing Volume Rendering
head: Interactive Voxel Volume Rendering via WebGL 2.0
body: An interactive voxel volume renderer using path tracing that runs in modern browsers via WebGL 2.0. It renders 3D scalar fields by casting rays from the camera through the volume, accumulating color and opacity along the ray, and applying lighting/shadowing. It differs from standard ray casting by computing normals via central differences of opacity and applying Phong-like lighting with soft shadows, rather than relying solely on direct illumination or pre-computed lighting. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: volume: highp sampler3D containing the scalar field. volumedims: ivec3 defining the dimensions of the volume texture. transformedeye: vec3 camera position in world space. vraydir: vec3 ray direction in world space. dtscale: float step size scaling factor. lightPosition: vec3 light source position. windowLevel, windowWidth: float for window/level adjustment. rescaleSlope, rescaleIntercept: float for linear transformation of raw values. numberOfOpacitySamples, opacityMapPositions, opacityMapSamples: int, highp sampler2D, highp sampler2D for opacity transfer function. numberOfColorSamples, colorMapPositions, colorMapSamples: int, highp sampler2D, highp sampler2D for color transfer function. Output: vec4 color (RGBA) for the fragment. Data Structures Opacity/Color Maps: Stored in 2D textures. The x-coordinate represents the position (control point), and the y-coordinate represents the sample value (opacity or color intensity). The number of control points is given by numberOfOpacitySamples or numberOfColorSamples. Volume: Stored in a 3D texture (sampler3D). Algorithm Steps 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute the intersection of the ray with the volume's bounding box. \text{invDir} = \frac{1.0}{\text{dir}} t{\text{min\tmp}} = (\text{boxMin} - \text{orig}) \times \text{invDir} t{\text{max\tmp}} = (\text{boxMax} - \text{orig}) \times \text{invDir} t{\text{min}} = \min(t{\text{min\tmp}}, t{\text{max\tmp}}) t{\text{max}} = \max(t{\text{min\tmp}}, t{\text{max\tmp}}) t0 = \max(t{\text{min}.x, \max(t{\text{min}.y, t{\text{min}.z})}) t1 = \min(t{\text{max}.x, \min(t{\text{max}.y, t{\text{max}.z})}) If t0 > t1, the ray does not intersect the volume; discard the fragment. 2. Step Size Calculation: Compute the step size dt based on the volume dimensions and ray direction to ensure consistent sampling density relative to voxel size. dt{\text{vec}} = \frac{1.0}{\text{volume\dims} \times |\text{ray\dir}|} dt = dt{\text{scale}} \times \min(dt{\text{vec}.x, \min(dt{\text{vec}.y, dt{\text{vec}.z})}) Typical value for dt{\text{scale}} is not specified in the sources. 3. Ray Origin Offset: Generate a random offset to reduce aliasing. \text{seed} = \text{wang\hash}(\text{int}(gl\FragCoord.x + 1024.0 \times gl\FragCoord.y)) \text{offset} = \frac{\text{seed}}{2147483647.0} p = \text{transformed\eye} + (t0 + \text{offset} \times dt) \times \text{ray\dir} The wanghash function is defined as: python def wanghash(seed): seed = (seed ^ 61) ^ (seed >> 16) seed = 9 seed = seed ^ (seed >> 4) seed = 0x27d4eb2d seed = seed ^ (seed >> 15) return seed % 2147483647. 4. Value Rescaling: Apply linear transformation to raw volume values. \text{rescaled\value} = \text{rescaleSlope} \times \text{raw\value} + \text{rescaleIntercept}. 5. Transfer Function Application: Opacity: Find the interval [opacityMapPositions(i-1), opacityMapPositions(i)] containing the rescaled value. Interpolate between opacityMapSamples(i-1) and opacityMapSamples(i) using linear interpolation. Clamp the result multiplied by \frac{\text{value} - \text{windowFloor}}{\text{windowWidth}} to [0, 1], where \text{windowFloor} = \text{windowLevel} - \frac{\text{windowWidth}}{2.0}. Color: Similar to opacity, find the interval in colorMapPositions and interpolate between colorMapSamples(i-1) and colorMapSamples(i). 6. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize voxelColor = vec4(0.0). Loop t from t0 to t1 with step dt. Inside the loop: Sample volume value val at current position p. Get color and opacity from transfer functions applied to val. Compute valcolor = vec4(opacity color, opacity). Apply Beer-Lambert law approximation: val\color.a = 1.0 - (1.0 - val\color.a)^{dt{\text{scale}}} Update accumulated color: voxelColor.rgb += (1.0 - voxelColor.a) \times val\color.a \times val\color.rgb Update accumulated alpha: voxelColor.a += (1.0 - voxelColor.a) \times val\color.a If voxelColor.a \ge 0.95, break. Advance position: p += \text{ray\dir} \times dt. 7. Lighting Calculation: Normal Estimation: Compute voxel size: \text{voxelSize} = \frac{1.0}{\text{volume\dims}} Compute gradient using central differences of sampleVolumeOpacity (which applies opacity map to rescaled volume value): \text{gradient}.x = \frac{\text{sampleVolumeOpacity}(p + \text{vec3}(\text{voxelSize}.x, 0, 0)) - \text{sampleVolumeOpacity}(p - \text{vec3}(\text{voxelSize}.x, 0, 0))}{2.0 \times \text{voxelSize}.x} Similarly for y and z. Normalize the gradient to get voxelNormal. Diffuse: \text{lightDirection} = \text{normalize}(\text{lightPosition} - p) \text{intensity} = \max(\text{dot}(\text{voxelNormal}, \text{lightDirection}), 0.0) Specular: If \text{intensity} > 0.0: h = \text{normalize}(\text{lightDirection} + \text{transformed\eye}) \text{intSpec} = \max(\text{dot}(h, \text{voxelNormal}), 0.0) \text{spec} = \text{specular} \times \text{pow}(\text{intSpec}, \text{shininess}) With \text{shininess} = 8.0, \text{specular} = 0.5, \text{diffuse} = 0.6, \text{ambient} = 0.4. Shadow: If voxelColor.a \ge 0.20: \text{shadow} = \text{clamp}(\text{softShadow}(p) \times 2.0 + 0.1, 0.0, 1.0) Else: \text{shadow} = 1.0 Final Light Color: \text{lightColor} = \text{shadow} \times \max(\text{intensity} \times \text{diffuse} + \text{spec}, \text{ambient}) Apply lightColor to the accumulated voxelColor. 8. Soft Shadow Calculation: Sample 8 points around the voxel position p in a 3x3 grid (excluding center) with spacing \delta = \min(\text{voxelSize}.x, \min(\text{voxelSize}.y, \text{voxelSize}.z)) \times 2.0. For each point, compute: \text{pointShadow} = 1.0 - \text{traceLight}(\text{position}, \text{lightPosition}) Sum these shadows and divide by 8.0. 9. Light Tracing (Shadow Ray): Cast a ray from voxel towards light. \text{voxelToLight} = \text{light} - \text{voxel} d = \text{normalize}(\text{voxelToLight}) o = \text{voxel} - 1000.0 \times d Intersect ray with box to get box. Compute start = length(voxel - o). Sample opacity along the ray from start to box.y with step \delta = \frac{\min(\text{voxelSize}.x, \min(\text{voxelSize}.y, \text{voxelSize}.z))}{\text{samplesPerVoxel}} (where \text{samplesPerVoxel} = 1.0). Accumulate: \text{integrated} += \frac{\text{val}}{\text{samplesPerVoxel} \times 4.0} If \text{integrated} > 0.95, break. Return \text{clamp}(\text{integrated}, 0.0, 1.0). 10. SRGB Conversion: Convert linear color to SRGB. If x \le 0.0031308, return 12.92 \times x. Else return 1.055 \times x^{1/2.4} - 0.055. Pitfalls Ray-box intersection failure: If t0 > t1, the ray does not intersect the volume box. The fragment is discarded. Early termination: The ray marching loop breaks if accumulated alpha voxelColor.a \ge 0.95 to save computation. Shadow ray early termination: The light tracing loop breaks if integrated opacity \text{integrated} > 0.95. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray. The number of samples is determined by the volume dimensions, ray direction, and dtscale. Shadow calculation adds a constant overhead per lit voxel. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D volume texture and the 2D transfer function textures. Performance: Interactive performance is achieved on modern browsers via WebGL 2.0. Performance scales with resolution and volume size. Strengths: Interactive frame rates, browser-based accessibility, soft shadows for improved depth perception. Limitations: Approximate lighting (normal estimation from opacity gradients may be noisy), fixed step size (unless adaptive), limited to scalar volumes. When to use: Interactive visualization of scalar fields in web browsers. When not to use: High-fidelity offline rendering requiring accurate normal estimation from the scalar field itself, or complex volume data types (e.g., tensor fields). The method is implemented in the repository termijn/webgl-volumerendering. It demonstrates the use of WebGL 2.0 for interactive volume rendering with path tracing techniques, including lighting and shadowing, within a web browser environment. termijn/webgl-volumerendering, https://github.com/termijn/webgl-volumerendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: StructuredVolumeRenderer
head: luma.gl StructuredVolumeRenderer
body: StructuredVolumeRenderer is a reusable, graph-native GPU renderer for scalar, vector, and hybrid volume data in WebGPU environments. It consumes storage buffers or 3D textures and exposes scene renderer facades for forward, deferred, raytrace, and raymarch passes. It distinguishes itself from sibling WebGL implementations by leveraging WebGPU's storage buffer and texture binding models, manual trilinear interpolation, and fixed-step jittered ray marching with early opacity termination. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Float32 scalar buffers, WGSL-aligned float32x4 vector buffers, or matching float 3D textures. Outputs: Rendered image with premultiplied front-to-back transparency. Data Structures Scalar Source: Defined by sources.scalar.type ('buffer' or 'texture'). If 'buffer': Binding layout is read-only-storage, group 0, location 0. If 'texture': Binding layout includes viewDimension: '3d'. Vector Source: WGSL-aligned float32x4 buffers. Transforms: worldToVolumeMatrix for coordinate transformation. Camera: cameraAndSamples.xyz for ray origin derivation. Numbered Steps 1. Source Binding Setup: Determine binding type based on sources.scalar.type. If texture, set viewDimension to '3d'. 2. Offset Validation: Check if buffer offset is an integer, non-negative, and aligned to bytesPerElement. 3. Ray Generation: Compute nearWorld by unprojecting camera UV at depth 0.0. Compute farWorld by unprojecting camera UV at depth 1.0. Transform nearWorld using worldToVolumeMatrix to get rayOrigin. Transform farWorld using worldToVolumeMatrix to get rayTarget. Compute rayDirection as normalize(rayTarget - rayOrigin). 4. Ray Marching: Execute fixed-step jittered ray marching. 5. Interpolation: Perform manual eight-corner trilinear interpolation for volume values. 6. Compositing: Apply premultiplied front-to-back transparency. 7. Early Termination: Terminate ray if accumulated opacity exceeds threshold. 8. Transfer Function: Apply sequential/signed scalar transfer functions or direction/constant vector colors. Formulas Ray Origin: O = M{w2v} \cdot \text{unproject}(UV, 0.0) Ray Direction: D = \text{normalize}(M{w2v} \cdot \text{unproject}(UV, 1.0) - O) Compositing: Standard front-to-back alpha blending. Parameters Ray Samples: 72 samples per view in showcase. Boundary Handling: Second-order centered differences in interior; selectable second-order one-sided or periodic boundary handling. Glyphs: Optional 3D arrows (solid shaft-plus-cone SDFs). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Texture Binding: On adapters without float32-filterable, r32float/rgba32float textures must be bound with unfilterable-float sample type to avoid pipeline creation failure. Buffer Offset Alignment: WebGPU requires storage buffer offsets to be multiples of device.limits.minStorageBufferOffsetAlignment (commonly 256). Ray Origin: Using a single camera position for orthographic projections causes rays to converge; using near plane unprojection ensures parallel rays and correct near-plane clipping. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupbinding(sources): if sources.scalar.type == 'buffer': return { 'type': 'read-only-storage', 'group': 0, 'location': 0 } else: return { 'type': 'texture', 'group': 0, 'location': 0, 'viewDimension': '3d' } def validateoffset(binding, bytesperelement): offset = binding.offset if 'offset' in binding else 0 if not isinstance(offset, int) or offset < 0 or offset % bytesperelement != 0: raise Error('Structured volume buffer offset is not aligned to its element format.') def generateray(camerauv, worldtovolumematrix): nearworld = unproject(camerauv, 0.0) farworld = unproject(camerauv, 1.0) rayorigin = transformpoint(worldtovolumematrix, nearworld) raytarget = transformpoint(worldtovolumematrix, farworld) raydirection = normalize(raytarget - rayorigin) return rayorigin, raydirection def render(commandencoder, renderpass, structuredvolume): # Prepare and draw do not submit internally prepare(commandencoder, structuredvolume.options) draw(renderpass, structuredvolume) Uses multi-pass approach with 3D geometry intersection for ray-box intersection [6575-webgl-multi-pass-ray-casting-with-3d-geometry-intersection.md]. Choose when WebGL is required or when geometry-based intersection is preferred. Uses path tracing for more accurate lighting and scattering [8592-webgl-path-tracing-volume-rendering.md]. Choose when physically accurate lighting is needed and performance allows. Time Complexity: Fixed-step ray marching with 72 samples per view in showcase. Memory Complexity: Depends on volume resolution; 40³ showcase volume used. Performance: 30 Hz field/derivative updates without volume readback in showcase. Strengths: Reusable, graph-native, supports scalar/vector/hybrid data, manual interpolation for control. Limitations: Requires WebGPU, manual interpolation may be slower than hardware trilinear, alignment constraints. When to Use: WebGPU environments, need for reusable renderer, scalar/vector/hybrid data. When Not to Use: WebGL-only environments, need for hardware trilinear interpolation. StructuredVolumeRenderer was introduced in luma.gl PR #3104 as part of the Vector Field Lab showcase. It supports scalar, vector, and hybrid volume rendering, exposing facades for various rendering passes. The renderer is designed to be reusable and graph-native, integrating with WebGPU's command encoding and rendering pass models. feat(gpgpu): add Vector Field Lab differential operators showcase, https://github.com/visgl/luma.gl/pull/3104, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Splatch
head: Splotch
body: Splatch is a lightweight, CPU-based ray-tracing software tool designed for the fast visualization of point-like data from cosmological simulations, such as Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) outputs. It solves the problem of rendering large-scale particle datasets into realistic 3D images by optimizing ray-tracing calculations through depth-based particle ordering and analytical integration of emission and absorption along rays. Unlike general-purpose visualization packages like TIPSY or VisIVO, which are not primarily designed for ray-tracing, Splatch specifically targets the generation of ray-traced-like images that provide more realistic impressions of 3D structures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N particles, each defined by position \mathbf{p}i, peak density \rho{0,i}, spread parameter \sigmai, and emission/absorption coefficients \mathbf{E}i, \mathbf{A}i (vectors of size 3 for RGB). Camera parameters: position \mathbf{c}, look-at point \mathbf{l}, sky vector \mathbf{s}, and field-of-view angle \phi. Output: A 2D image (frame buffer) stored in a standard format (e.g., TGA, JPEG). Data Structures: Particle Data: The algorithm requires 30 bytes per particle. The exact memory layout is not specified in the sources. Frame Buffer: An array storing an RGB color triplet for every pixel of the resulting image. Initialized to black (0, 0, 0). Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Define the viewing direction \mathbf{v} = \mathbf{l} - \mathbf{c}. Determine a linear transformation matrix M that maps the camera position \mathbf{c} to the origin and aligns \mathbf{v} with the positive z-axis. Apply M to all particle positions \mathbf{p}i to obtain transformed positions \mathbf{p}'i. This simplifies subsequent operations by aligning the ray-tracing direction with the z-axis. 2. Sorting: Sort the particles in descending order of their z-coordinate in the transformed space (z'i). This ensures that particles closer to the camera (higher z) are processed first, allowing for correct front-to-back compositing. 3. Projection Setup: Apply a perspective projection using the user-defined field-of-view angle \phi. This defines the mapping from 3D world coordinates to 2D screen coordinates for each pixel. 4. Initialization: Allocate the frame buffer for the desired image resolution. Initialize all pixel values to black (0, 0, 0). 5. Rendering Loop: For each particle i in the sorted list: a. Determine the bounding box of the particle's influence on the image plane. The particle's density contribution is modeled as a Gaussian distribution: \rhoi(\mathbf{r}) = \rho{0,i} \exp(-r^2/\sigmai^2) where r is the distance from the particle center. b. The distribution is set to zero at a distance f \cdot \sigmai, where f is a compact support factor chosen such that f \cdot \sigmai \approx h (the SPH smoothing length). Rays passing further than this distance are unaffected. c. For each pixel (x,y) within the particle's footprint: i. Calculate the minimum distance d0 between the ray passing through (x,y) and the particle center in the transformed space. ii. Calculate the integral of the density along the ray: \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \rhoi(x) dx = \rho{0,i} \sigmai \exp(-d0^2/\sigmai^2) \sqrt{\pi}. iii. Update the pixel's intensity \mathbf{I} using the radiative transfer equation solution: \mathbf{I}{after} = (\mathbf{I}{before} - \mathbf{E}i/\mathbf{A}i) \exp(-\mathbf{A}i \int{-\infty}^{\infty} \rhoi(x) dx) + \mathbf{E}i/\mathbf{A}i where \mathbf{E}i and \mathbf{A}i are the emission and absorption coefficient vectors for the particle. The division and multiplication are component-wise for RGB. iv. Store the updated \mathbf{I}{after} in the frame buffer. 6. Output: Write the final frame buffer to disk in a standard format (e.g., TGA or JPEG). Pseudocode: Unverified code. imagewidth / 2.0) / (imagewidth / 2.0) ny = (y - imageheight / 2.0) / (imageheight / 2.0) rx = nx tanfovhalf ry = ny tanfovhalf rz = 1.0 r = np.array([rx, ry, rz]) runit = r / np.linalg.norm(r) # d0 is distance from ray to particle center crossprod = np.cross(posp, runit) d0 = np.linalg.norm(crossprod) # Compact support culling: skip if d0 is too large # f is typically ~3 for SPH kernels, but exact value not given if d0 > sigma 3.0: continue # Calculate integral of density along ray integralval = rho0 sigma math.exp(-(d02) / (sigma2)) math.sqrt(math.pi) # Update intensity using radiative transfer solution exponent = -Asafe integralval framebuffer[y, x] = (framebuffer[y, x] - ratio) np.exp(exponent) + ratio return framebuffer Parameters: Compact support factor f: Chosen such that f \cdot \sigmap \approx h (SPH smoothing length). Emission/Absorption ratio: Recommended to set Ep = Ap for visually appealing images. Field-of-view angle \phi: Typically set to 30 degrees. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Particle Overlap: The algorithm assumes particles do not overlap for the simple intensity update formula, but in reality, they do. The source notes that since relative intensity changes due to a single particle are small, the approximation is acceptable. Precision: The exponential decay in the Gaussian distribution can lead to underflow for large d0. The compact support factor f helps mitigate this by truncating the distribution. Division by Zero: If absorption coefficient Ap is zero, the term Ep/Ap is undefined. The sources do not specify handling for this case, so a guard should clamp or skip zero absorption. Time Complexity: CPU time T{CPU} is proportional to the number of pixels n{pixel} (T{CPU} \propto n{pixel}) and inversely proportional to the square root of the field-of-view angle \phi (T{CPU} \propto \phi^{-0.5}). Memory Complexity: The algorithm requires 30 bytes per particle. This allows rendering more than 70 million particles on a standard PC with 2 GByte of main memory. Performance: On an AMD Opteron 850 CPU (2400 MHz), rendering a frame with 1400x1050 resolution from a simulation with ~11 million gas and ~5 million star particles took ~67 seconds. Rendering a zoomed frame with 800x800 resolution from a simulation with ~5 million gas particles took ~72 seconds on the same system. Parallelization: Uses OpenMP to distribute image regions over several cores on shared memory platforms. Strengths: Fast, lightweight, handles large particle sets (millions of particles), produces realistic 3D impressions via ray-tracing. Limitations: CPU-based, not GPU-accelerated (unlike many modern splatting methods), assumes small intensity changes per particle for compositing accuracy. Splatch (Splotch) was developed by K. Dolag, C. Gheller, and S. Imboden from the Max-Planck-Institut für Astrophysik and CINECA. It was published in 2008 in the New Journal of Physics. The tool was designed to address the limitations of existing visualization packages like TIPSY and VisIVO, which were not optimized for ray-tracing-like images of particle-based cosmological simulations. It is specifically tailored for SPH data, leveraging the Gaussian-like shape of the SPH kernel.
