name: Cluster Hierarchy-based Volume Rendering
head: Cluster Tree Widget Rendering, Interactive Visual Exploration of Multi-variate Volume Data
body: This method renders multi-variate volume data by mapping hierarchical clusters of feature vectors to transfer function parameters (color, opacity, size) for direct volume rendering, enabling interactive exploration via cluster tree and parallel coordinates widgets. It sets itself apart from standard direct volume ray casting by decoupling classification from rendering, using post-classification with nearest-neighbor interpolation to allow real-time cluster modification without retransmitting voxel data to the GPU. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A multi-variate volume dataset (scalar fields or derived properties) and a hierarchical clustering of the data's feature space, or a single root cluster if pre-clustering is absent. Output: A rendered image with clusters visualized according to user-defined transfer functions. Data Structures: 1. Cluster Hierarchy: A tree structure where nodes represent clusters. Each node stores default color and opacity assigned by the automatic clustering algorithm, and a density slider value used to filter voxels based on density thresholds. 2. Mask Volume: A volume data structure with the same spatial dimensions as the input data. Voxels with a mask value of 1 belong to a selected cluster and meet the density/brushing criteria; voxels with 0 are hidden (fully transparent). Steps: 1. Clustering Initialization: If pre-clustering exists, use the automatic clustering algorithm's output to assign default color and opacity to each cluster. If no pre-clustering exists, place all data points into a single root cluster. 2. User Interaction (CPU/GPU split): Adjust density sliders in the cluster tree widget to modify cluster sizes by defining density thresholds. Brush intervals in the parallel coordinates widget to mark data points within selected intervals as 1 and others as 0. Reclustering operations (splitting/merging nodes) are performed on the CPU and take less than half a second on modern hardware. Assigning material properties to clusters and changing their sizes via density sliders is instantaneous and executed on the GPU. 3. Mask Generation: For each voxel, determine if it belongs to a selected cluster and satisfies the current density and brushing criteria. Set the corresponding value in the Mask Volume to 1 if true, 0 if false. 4. Rendering (GPU): Perform direct volume ray casting using a 3D texture-based renderer. Voxels with a mask value of 0 are rendered fully transparent. Combine the mask with the transfer function, which maps cluster properties (e.g., physical properties like ionization state) to color and opacity. Use precomputed surface normals for illumination. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderclusterhierarchy(data, clustertree, maskvolume, screenwidth, screenheight): # Initialize mask volume with zeros maskvolume[:] = 0 # Mask Generation (CPU) # Note: Exact clustering lookup and parallel coordinates brushing logic are not specified in the sources for z in range(data.shape[0]): for y in range(data.shape[1]): for x in range(data.shape[2]): voxel = data[z, y, x] # Determine if voxel belongs to a selected cluster and meets density/brushing criteria isselected = clustertree.isclusterselected(voxel.clusterid) meetsdensity = voxel.features.density >= clustertree.densitythreshold(voxel.clusterid) meetsbrush = True # Parallel coordinates brushing logic not specified if isselected and meetsdensity and meetsbrush: maskvolume[z, y, x] = 1 else: maskvolume[z, y, x] = 0 # Rendering (GPU) for screeny in range(screenheight): for screenx in range(screenwidth): ray = generateray(screenx, screeny) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 for t in range(ray.length): samplepoint = ray.origin + t ray.direction # Grid lookup for mask volume gx, gy, gz = int(round(samplepoint[0])), int(round(samplepoint[1])), int(round(samplepoint[2])) if 0 <= gx < maskvolume.shape[0] and 0 <= gy < maskvolume.shape[1] and 0 <= gz < maskvolume.shape[2]: if maskvolume[gx, gy, gz] == 0: continue # Fully transparent # Determine cluster properties for transfer function cluster = clustertree.findcluster(samplepoint.features) # color = cluster.color opacity = cluster.opacity # Standard front-to-back compositing alpha = opacity accumulatedcolor = [ accumulatedcolor[i] + color[i] alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) for i in range(3) ] accumulatedopacity += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) setpixel(screenx, screeny, accumulatedcolor) Parameters: Rendering Hardware: nVIDIA GTX260. Screen Resolution: 1680x1050 pixels. Performance Target: 20-30 frames per second. Reclustering Time: < 0.5 seconds on modern hardware. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Post-classification with nearest-neighbor interpolation causes aliasing artifacts at cluster boundaries. Performance: Pre-classification (computing colors/opacities for all voxels on CPU and transmitting to GPU) inhibits interactive frame rates with marginal quality gain. Normals: On-the-fly surface normal computation significantly slows down rendering; normals must be precomputed. Illumination: If no density values are available, illumination cannot be applied. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on dataset resolution, zoom level, and sampling rate. Reclustering operations (splitting/merging) take < 0.5 seconds on modern hardware. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storage for multi-variate data, cluster hierarchy, and mask volume. Measured Performance: Achieved 20-30 fps at 1680x1050 resolution on an nVIDIA GTX260. Strengths: Interactive exploration of multi-variate data; intuitive UI with cluster tree and parallel coordinates; fast reclustering; GPU-accelerated density slider adjustments. Limitations: Aliasing artifacts at cluster boundaries; requires precomputed normals; no illumination if density is unavailable. When to Use: Interactive exploration of multi-variate volume data where user-driven clustering and filtering are needed. When Not to Use: When pre-computed classification is required for maximum quality (due to performance costs) or when density-based illumination is critical but density data is absent. Origin: Presented by Dobrev et al. in 2011. History: Applied to various datasets including Bonsai tree, ionization front instability, medical MRI, tornado flow field, and white dwarf/black hole simulations. Usage: Implemented in C++ using QT, OpenGL, and GLSL. A Cluster Hierarchy-based Volume Rendering Approach for Interactive Visual Exploration of Multi-variate Volume Data, https://doi.org/10.2312/pe/vmv/vmv11/137-144, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: In-Core Volume Rendering
head: In-core volume rendering for Cartesian grid fluid dynamics simulations, Srend, Srend In-Core Volume Rendering
body: In-core volume rendering, specifically implemented as Srend, is a method for visualizing computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations using Cartesian grids by compiling the rendering code directly into the simulation application. It solves the problem of high data I/O overhead and latency in post-processing by generating images in real-time during the simulation. Unlike general-purpose in-situ visualization frameworks that often employ load balancing or supervisory mechanisms, Srend relies on a user-defined "rendering tree" and time-partitioned rendering where every simulation process renders its own data brick, followed by space-partitioned compositing by dedicated processes. Inputs: Simulation Data: 3D arrays of variable values representing rectangular "bricks" of the volume. Data Format: The source data must be scaled to arrays of bytes (Fortran character1) and mapped to a user-defined color table. Rendering Parameters: View index, number of sources, MPI target rank, and image finishing parameters (e.g., output file name). Geometry: Spatial coordinates for interpolation if the simulation uses stretched grids or terrain-following coordinates. Outputs: Final Image: A 2D rendered image written to disk by the finisher at the root of the rendering tree. Brick: A rectangular sub-volume represented by a 3D array of byte values. Rendering Tree: A user-defined hierarchy of MPI ranks where leaves are simulation worker ranks, internal nodes are "composers", and the root is the "finisher". Message Payload: Contains the 2D rendered pre-multiplied alpha plane, view index, number of sources, and redundant image finishing parameters (file name). 1. Data Partitioning: The simulation domain is partitioned into rectangular bricks, and each simulation worker rank holds one or more bricks. 2. Local Rendering (Time Partitioning): Each worker rank renders its assigned brick using all available threads as if the brick were the entire volume. The rendering uses ray casting, collecting emissions along rays from the eye through the volume. The result is a 2D pre-multiplied alpha plane. 3. Compositing (Space Partitioning): Composers receive 2D renderings from their child ranks. Composers exploit the associativity of compositing pre-multiplied alpha planes to merge the incoming planes with their own local render (if they are also workers) or with previously composited results. The composited result is sent to the parent rank in the rendering tree. 4. Finalization: The finisher at the root of the rendering tree receives the final composited image and writes it to disk. The rendering process uses standard ray casting for volume rendering. The compositing of pre-multiplied alpha planes relies on the associativity of the compositing operator. For two adjacent alpha planes A and B (where A is closer to the eye), the composite C is calculated as: C = A + (1 - \alphaA) B where \alphaA is the alpha channel of A, and B is the pre-multiplied color/alpha of the further plane. Data Scaling: Users must manually scale real-valued simulation data to bytes and define a color table. View Index: Identifies the camera perspective. Number of Sources: Used by composers to track how many children have sent data. MPI Target Rank: The destination rank for sending composited results. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vec4(r, g, b, a): return (r, g, b, a) def zeros(shape): # Returns a 2D list of vec4 initialized to (0,0,0,0) return [[vec4(0, 0, 0, 0) for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] def computeray(pixelx, pixely, viewparams): # Returns (origin: vec3, direction: vec3) based on camera parameters return viewparams['origin'], viewparams['directions'][pixely][pixelx] def raybrickintersection(rayorigin, raydir, brickbounds): # Returns (tmin, tmax) for ray intersecting brick axis-aligned bounds tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] == 0: if rayorigin[i] < brickbounds[i2] or rayorigin[i] > brickbounds[i2+1]: return None, None else: t1 = (brickbounds[i2] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (brickbounds[i2+1] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax def interpolatescalar(rayorigin, raydir, t, brickdata, gridgeometry): # Interpolates byte value from 3D brick at ray position # Assumes gridgeometry maps brick indices to world coordinates # Returns a byte value (0-255) return 128 # Placeholder for interpolation logic def compositealpha(base, source): # Composites source onto base using pre-multiplied alpha # base is closer to the eye. Both are 2D lists of vec4. result = zeros((len(base), len(base[0]))) for y in range(len(base)): for x in range(len(base[y])): abase = base[y][x][3] / 255.0 rbase, gbase, bbase, abase = base[y][x] rsrc, gsrc, bsrc, asrc = source[y][x] asrcnorm = asrc / 255.0 # C = A + (1 - alphaA) B rnew = rbase + (1.0 - abase) rsrc gnew = gbase + (1.0 - abase) gsrc bnew = bbase + (1.0 - abase) bsrc anew = abase + (1.0 - abase) asrcnorm result[y][x] = vec4(rnew, gnew, bnew, anew 255.0) return result def renderbrick(brickdata3d, viewparams, colortable, brickbounds, gridgeometry): # Renders a single brick using ray casting imageheight = viewparams['height'] imagewidth = viewparams['width'] image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) raystepsize = viewparams['stepsize'] # for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): origin, direction = computeray(x, y, viewparams) tstart, tend = raybrickintersection(origin, direction, brickbounds) if tstart is None: continue coloraccum = vec4(0, 0, 0, 0) t = tstart while t < tend: val = interpolatescalar(origin, direction, t, brickdata3d, gridgeometry) rgba = colortable[val] # Returns vec4 # Front-to-back compositing for pre-multiplied alpha aaccum = coloraccum[3] / 255.0 rnew = coloraccum[0] + (1.0 - aaccum) rgba[0] gnew = coloraccum[1] + (1.0 - aaccum) rgba[1] bnew = coloraccum[2] + (1.0 - aaccum) rgba[2] anew = aaccum + (1.0 - aaccum) (rgba[3] / 255.0) coloraccum = vec4(rnew, gnew, bnew, anew 255.0) t += raystepsize image[y][x] = coloraccum return image def srendworker(brickdata, viewindex, numsources, targetrank, colortable, viewparams, brickbounds, gridgeometry): # Executed by simulation worker ranks localimage = renderbrick(brickdata, viewparams, colortable, brickbounds, gridgeometry) payload = { 'image': localimage, 'viewindex': viewindex, 'numsources': numsources, 'filename': 'output.png' # Redundant but simplifies usage } # MPI non-blocking send mpisend(targetrank, payload) def srendcomposer(childranks, viewindex, numsources, parentrank, colortable, viewparams, brickbounds, gridgeometry): # Executed by intermediate ranks in the rendering tree compositeimage = zeros((viewparams['height'], viewparams['width'])) for childrank in childranks: msg = mpirecv(childrank) compositeimage = compositealpha(compositeimage, msg['image']) # If this rank also holds data (hybrid worker/composer), render and composite if haslocalbrick(): localimage = renderbrick(getlocalbrick(), viewparams, colortable, brickbounds, gridgeometry) compositeimage = compositealpha(compositeimage, localimage) if parentrank is not None: payload = { 'image': compositeimage, 'viewindex': viewindex, 'numsources': numsources, 'filename': 'output.png' } mpisend(parentrank, payload) def srendfinisher(childranks, viewindex, numsources, outputfilename, viewparams): # Executed by the root rank compositeimage = zeros((viewparams['height'], viewparams['width'])) for childrank in childranks: msg = mpirecv(childrank) compositeimage = compositealpha(compositeimage, msg['image']) # Write final image to disk saveimage(outputfilename, compositeimage) def mpisend(rank, data): pass def mpirecv(rank): return {'image': zeros((1,1)), 'viewindex': 0, 'numsources': 0, 'filename': ''} def haslocalbrick(): return False def getlocalbrick(): return [] def saveimage(filename, data): pass Grid Interpolation: If the simulation uses stretched grids or terrain-following vertical coordinates, data arrays must be interpolated to spatial arrays for Srend to maintain spatial accuracy. Redundant Information: The output file name and other image finishing parameters are sent by every renderer, even though only the finisher uses them. This is a design choice to simplify usage, accepting a light data payload overhead. Data Scaling: Users must manually scale real data to bytes and define a color table. This requires knowledge of the data distribution and appearance requirements. Time Complexity: Rendering completion time (simulation halt time) depends primarily on the rendering work itself. There is no synchronization or management overhead beyond that imposed by MPI messaging. Memory Complexity: Data is kept in-core. The memory footprint includes the simulation data and the intermediate 2D rendered planes. Performance: Results show modest rendering overhead and high potential for scaling. The 3D data is already in CPU memory, requiring only movement to registers, making it efficient on CPUs compared to GPUs for this specific workflow where cluster communications are well-established for the lighter 2D results. Strengths: Immediate, quality imagery; reduces data output and storage requirements; no reliance on special visualization hardware or external programs; convenient integration into Fortran simulation codes. Limitations: No load balancing or supervisory mechanism; rendering and compositing are defined by the user's incorporation of Srend calls; requires manual data scaling and color table definition. When to Use: When embedding visualization directly into Fortran-based CFD simulations (e.g., PPMstar, CM1, WRF) to reduce I/O overhead and enable real-time exploration. When Not to Use: When dynamic load balancing is required or when the simulation code is not in Fortran or cannot be easily modified to include Srend calls. Srend was developed at the University of Minnesota / LCSE. It was modified from its original form, which was used within a terrain flow code developed to study the advection of smoke and pollen in the St. Louis River region. The "S" in Srend originally stood for spherical data rendering, supporting longitude/latitude views for full spherical rendering of stellar data from the center, though perspective views and other features were retained for general use. It was embedded in three major codes: Piecewise Parabolic Method (PPMstar), Cloud Model 1 (CM1), and Weather Research Forecast model (WRF). The code was implemented in Fortran to allow convenient inclusion within Fortran simulation codes using ordinary subroutine calls and familiar Fortran arrays. In-core volume rendering for Cartesian grid fluid dynamics simulations, https://doi.org/10.1145/2792745.2792780, fetched 2026-11-05

name: Spherical Harmonic Volume Ray Casting
head: GPU-based volume ray-caster with SH coefficients, SH Volume Ray Casting with Hybrid CPU/GPU Projection, SH-based interactive volume rendering, Spherical Harmonic (SH) Volume Ray Casting with Hybrid CPU/GPU Projection
body: Spherical Harmonic Volume Ray Casting is a technique for interactive volume rendering that approximates complex light-material interactions (such as subsurface scattering and color bleeding) by pre-computing Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients for material and light functions on the CPU, storing them in 3D volumes, and evaluating the rendering integral via Monte-Carlo ray marching in a GPU fragment shader. It sets itself apart from standard direct volume ray casting by replacing expensive per-sample shading integrals with a pre-convolved SH representation, allowing for real-time performance at the cost of low-frequency approximation. The method operates in two distinct phases: an offline (or pre-computation) phase on the CPU to generate SH coefficient volumes, and an online rendering phase on the GPU using fragment shaders. Inputs: Scalar volume data V(\mathbf{x}). Transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha) mapping scalar values to color and opacity. Material function M(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao) and incoming light Li(\mathbf{x}, \omegai). Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Outputs: Final image color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. 3D coefficient volumes containing SH coefficients for the modulated material/light interactions. 1. BRDF Coefficient Texture (CPU-side) A partitioned 2D texture used to store SH coefficients for the material function M and incoming light Li. Dimensions: 3 columns, 4 quadrants per column. Each quadrant is N \times N texels, where N is the number of random samples. Coordinate System: X-axis of each quadrant: \vartheta of outgoing direction \omegao, ranging from 0 to \pi. Y-axis of each quadrant: \phi of outgoing direction \omegao, ranging from 0 to 2\pi. Content Layout (for Band Limit L=3, 16 coefficients): Lower-Left Quadrant: First 4 coefficients (Bands 0 and 1). Lower-Right Quadrant: Next 4 coefficients (First 4 of Band 2). Upper-Left Quadrant: Next 4 coefficients (One of Band 2, three of Band 3). Upper-Right Quadrant: Final 4 coefficients (Remaining 4 of Band 3). Purpose: Allows the GPU to look up the necessary SH coefficients for any outgoing direction \omegao. 2. SH Coefficient Volumes (GPU-side) 3D textures storing the pre-computed SH coefficients for the volume. Standard Layout: 16 coefficients per color channel (for L=3). Rendered into 4 slices with 4 channels simultaneously using Multiple Render Targets (MRTs). Optimized Chromaticity/Luminance Layout: To reduce memory and MRT usage, chromaticity uses a 2-band projection (4 coefficients) and luminance uses a 4-band projection. Total coefficients: 3 \times 4 = 12 (3 color channels \times 4 coefficients for chroma/luma split logic described as 3 sets of 4, totaling 12 coefficients handled by three FBO-attached textures). This fits within the 8 MRT limit (using 7 targets). 3. Random Sample Textures (GPU-side) Sample Directions: Normalized Cartesian vectors generated on the CPU, uploaded as a 2D texture. Basis Values: Values of spherical harmonic basis functions Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) for each sample direction, uploaded as a second 2D texture. 1. Generate Random Samples: Create N random normalized Cartesian vectors on the CPU for Monte-Carlo integration. 2. Compute Basis Values: Calculate Y{lm}(\vartheta, \phi) for each sample direction. 3. Compute SH Coefficients: Project the material function M and light Li onto the SH basis. The physical triple product integral is approximated by two successive double products to simplify computation: first integrating over Material M and Incoming Light Li to get local material effects, then modulating by Environmental Illumination L{mi}. Store the resulting coefficients in the partitioned 2D BRDF texture. 4. Generate Coefficient Volumes: Use GPU framebuffer objects (FBOs) and MRTs to ray march slice-by-slice into 3D coefficient textures, distributing the (L+1)^2 SH coefficients for each voxel to the attached render targets. For each pixel, cast a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} intersecting the volume bounding box [0,1]^3. 1. Initialization: Initialize accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0,0,0) and opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: While t < t{far} and \alpha{acc} < 0.95 (early termination threshold): a. Sample Volume: Retrieve scalar value V(\mathbf{p}) at current ray position \mathbf{p} = r(t) using trilinear interpolation. b. Check Boundaries: If any coordinate of \mathbf{p} in volume space [0,1]^3 reaches 0 or 1, terminate ray. c. Classification: Map V(\mathbf{p}) to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha using the transfer function. d. SH Evaluation: i. Retrieve the SH coefficients for the current voxel from the 3D coefficient volume. ii. Retrieve the pre-computed Y{lm} values for the current sample direction from the 2D texture. iii. Compute the contribution of the current sample by taking the dot product of the SH coefficients and Y{lm} values, then multiply by the ray's contribution and add to the total integration sum. e. Compositing: Update \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} using the front-to-back equation: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c} \cdot \alpha \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alpha f. Advance: Increase t by the ray step size \Delta t. 3. Output: Write \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} to the framebuffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastshvolume(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, volumetexture, coefficientvolume, ylmtex, transferfunc, stepsize): cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] aacc = 0.0 t = tnear while t < tfar: pworld = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] pvol = transformtovolumespace(pworld) if pvol[0] < 0.0 or pvol[0] > 1.0 or pvol[1] < 0.0 or pvol[1] > 1.0 or pvol[2] < 0.0 or pvol[2] > 1.0: break vval = trilinearsample(volumetexture, pvol) csample, alpha = transferfunc(vval) shcoeffs = sample3dtexture(coefficientvolume, pvol) yvals = sample2dtexture(ylmtex, raydirection) colorcontrib = sum(shcoeffs[i] yvals[i] for i in range(len(shcoeffs))) cacc = [cacc[i] + (1.0 - aacc) colorcontrib[i] alpha for i in range(3)] aacc = aacc + (1.0 - aacc) alpha if aacc > 0.95: break t += stepsize return cacc, aacc Ray Opacity Threshold: 95% for early ray termination. Boundary Condition: Ray terminates if any position coordinate reaches 0 or 1 in volume space [0,1]^3. SH Band Limit (L): Typically 3, yielding 16 coefficients per color channel. Coefficient Downsampling: Coefficient volumes are downsampled to ~33% of the original size to optimize performance, assuming low-frequency radiance transfer. Ray Step Size: Can be increased to speed up computation. Pitfalls: GLSL Random Numbers: GLSL random number generation was not implemented in the target driver at the time of the source, necessitating CPU-side generation. MRT Limit: Limited to 8 simultaneous output targets, constraining the max coefficients written per fragment (hence the choice of L=3 or chromaticity/luminance split). Gibbs Ringing: SH approximation restricts representation to low-frequency functions. Materials with sharp specular highlights may cause Gibbs ringing artifacts. Time Complexity: The pre-computation phase is expensive, scaling with the number of voxels and the complexity of the material/light integration. Rendering is interactive for simple effects (shadows only) but degrades with scattering and color bleeding. Memory Complexity: Requires storing 3D coefficient volumes. Downsampling to 33% size mitigates this. Measured Performance: Hardware: Intel Core2 Quad Q9450 (2.66 GHz), 4GB RAM, nVidia GeForce 9800 GTX (512MB RAM). Resolution: 400x400 window. 128^3 voxels: Shadows only: 0.9s projection / 24 fps. +Scattering: 21.3s / 17 fps. +Bleeding: 58.9s / 13 fps. 256^2x128 voxels: Shadows only: 2.6s / 20 fps. +Scattering: 70.2s / 14 fps. +Bleeding: 180s / 5 fps. 256^3 voxels: Shadows only: 3.4s / 6 fps. +Scattering: 149s / 3 fps. +Bleeding: 388s / 1 fps. Strengths: Enables interactive frame rates for complex lighting effects (shadows, scattering, color bleeding) that would otherwise be too slow for real-time ray casting. Limitations: Restricted to low-frequency functions; unsuitable for materials with sharp specular highlights due to Gibbs ringing. Performance degrades significantly with color bleeding. Origin: The method was introduced by F. Lindemann and T. Ropinski in the paper "Advanced Light Material Interaction for Direct Volume Rendering" (2010). History: It was implemented in the Voreen volume rendering engine. Usage: Applied in medical imaging and computational fluid dynamics, where predefined transfer functions are common. Advanced Light Material Interaction for Direct Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg10/101-108, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Sliced Ray Casting with On-Demand Volume Reconstruction
head: On-Demand Density Sampling, Sliced Ray Casting
body: Sliced Ray Casting with On-Demand Volume Reconstruction is a direct volume rendering technique that reconstructs particle density on-demand in screen space at viewport resolution and sampling depths, combining splatting, texture slicing, and ray casting to avoid aliasing artifacts and large memory footprints without pre-computation. It sets itself apart from traditional object-space volume ray casting by performing density reconstruction in image space, thereby moving perspective correction from the rendering stage to the data reconstruction stage. The method executes an iterative loop for #s times containing three inner steps: sampling position update, density reconstruction through splatting, and volume ray-casting. Inputs: Particle positions \mathbf{p}j, particle masses mj, kernel support radius h, volume sampling distance \Delta \lambda, eye position \mathbf{e}, ray direction \mathbf{v}, maximum ray length \lambda{max}, and number of iterations \#s. Outputs: Final composited color and opacity for each pixel. Particle Data: List of particles with fields \mathbf{p}j (position) and mj (mass). Ray Parameters: \mathbf{e}: Eye position. \mathbf{v}: Ray direction. \lambda{min}: Minimal distance between \mathbf{e} and the particle bounding box. \lambda{max}: Maximum ray length, calculated based on the back-side of the particle bounding box. \Delta \lambda: Volume sampling distance. \#s: Number of iterations for the inner loop. 1. Ray Setup: Determine \lambda{min} as the minimal distance between the eye \mathbf{e} and the bounding box of the particles. Determine \lambda{max} based on the back-side of the particle bounding box. Store ray direction \mathbf{v} and start position at the front face of the bounding box. 2. Shell Subdivision: Subdivide the viewing volume in the viewing direction into concentric spherical shells centered at the eye \mathbf{e}. Place the shells equally separated by the volume sampling distance \Delta \lambda. Position the first slice at \lambda{min} to skip empty space in front of the camera. 3. Iterative Loop: Execute a loop for \#s times. Each iteration performs three inner steps: a. Sampling Position Update: Update the sampling position along the ray based on the current shell distance. b. Density Reconstruction: Reconstruct the density field from particles via perspectively correct splatting of particle density footprints at the sampling depths used by volume ray casting. This is performed in screen space at viewport resolution. c. Volume Ray-Casting: Perform the standard ray casting steps (sampling, classification, compositing) using the reconstructed density. The density \bar{\rho}(\mathbf{p}) at a point \mathbf{p} is reconstructed using a radial symmetric kernel function W \in C^2[0, h] with support radius h, particle positions \mathbf{p}j, and particle masses mj: \bar{\rho}(\mathbf{p}) = \frac{1}{N} \sum{j} mj W(\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{p}j\|) The result is normalized so that the average density evaluates to 1 for easier iso-value evaluation, i.e., \bar{\rho}(\mathbf{p}) = 1. For each particle j, a symmetric polynomial density kernel function (the smooth step function) with finite support radius h is used, though any other function with finite support could be used. Args: particles: List of dicts with 'pos' (vector) and 'mass' (float). eye: Vector, position of the camera eye. raydirection: Vector, direction of the ray. lambdamin: Float, minimal distance to particle bounding box. lambdamax: Float, maximum ray length. deltalambda: Float, volume sampling distance. numiterations: Int, number of inner loop iterations. h: Float, support radius of the kernel function. Returns: color: Vector, final composited color. opacity: Float, final opacity. """ # Initialize compositing variables accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 numparticles = len(particles) # Iterate through sampling depths (concentric shells) for i in range(numiterations): # 1. Sampling Position Update currentlambda = lambdamin + i deltalambda # Check if we have exceeded the maximum ray length if currentlambda > lambdamax: break # Sample point on the ray (shells centered at eye) samplepoint = [ eye[0] + raydirection[0] currentlambda, eye[1] + raydirection[1] currentlambda, eye[2] + raydirection[2] currentlambda ] # 2. Density Reconstruction (On-Demand Splatting) # Note: In practice, this is performed via perspectively correct # screen-space splatting at viewport resolution. density = 0.0 for particle in particles: dx = samplepoint[0] - particle['pos'][0] dy = samplepoint[1] - particle['pos'][1] dz = samplepoint[2] - particle['pos'][2] dist = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) # Check if particle is within support radius h if dist <= h: roverh = dist / h # Smooth step function kernel (symmetric polynomial) w = 1.0 - 3.0 roverh roverh + 2.0 roverh roverh roverh density += particle['mass'] w # Normalize density to average 1 as specified by the source density = density / numparticles # 3. Volume Ray-Casting # Classification: Map density to color and opacity via transfer function # transferfunction(density) -> (colorsample, alphasample) colorsample = [density, density, density] alphasample = 1.0 - math.exp(-density deltalambda) # Compositing (front-to-back iterative form) weight = (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) alphasample accumulatedcolor[0] += weight colorsample[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += weight colorsample[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += weight colorsample[2] accumulatedopacity += weight # Early-z-test culling / Termination based on inter-frame occlusion queries if accumulatedopacity > 0.99: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity \Delta \lambda: Volume sampling distance that equally separates the concentric spherical shells. \lambda{min}: Minimal distance between the eye \mathbf{e} and the bounding box of the particles; determines the first slice position. \lambda{max}: Maximum ray length, calculated based on the back-side of the particles bounding box. \#s: Number of iterations for the inner loop that performs sampling position update, density reconstruction, and volume ray-casting. h: Support radius of the kernel function. Perspective Correction: Perspective correction is handled by moving the correction step from volume rendering to data reconstruction, performing density reconstruction in screen space at viewport resolution. Empty Space: The first slice is placed at \lambda{min} to skip empty space in front of the camera. Memory Footprint: The method avoids large memory footprints because volume data is only partially created on-demand. Performance: The method maintains comparative rendering performance to traditional methods while reducing memory requirements. Quality: It yields superior image quality due to image-space evaluation, avoiding aliasing artifacts common in particle visualization and object-space volume ray casting. Memory: Memory requirements are reduced because the volume data is only partially created on-demand. Hardware: The process is controlled by the CPU but the inner steps are performed solely on the GPU. Optimization: A novel method for termination of the ray casting based on inter-frame occlusion queries is employed to optimize overall performance, exploiting frame-to-frame coherency to compensate for overhead and latencies. The method was proposed in the paper "Interactive Image-Space Volume Visualization for Dynamic Particle Simulations" by Falk, Grottel, and Ertl. It is applied to systems biology (cell signaling propagation), biochemistry (protein surface visualization), and molecular dynamics (laser ablation processes). The approach combines ideas from texture slicing, ray casting, and splatting. Early implementations blended object-space-aligned texture stacks, and view-aligned texture stacks were superseded by single-pass volume ray casting. name: Standard Ray Casting
head: Fixed-step ray casting, Direct volume ray casting (baseline), Image-order volume rendering
body: Standard Ray Casting is the foundational direct volume rendering technique that generates images by casting rays from the camera through each pixel, sampling a 3D scalar field at regular intervals, and accumulating color and opacity via front-to-back compositing. It solves the problem of visualizing internal structures in scalar fields (e.g., CT scans) without extracting explicit geometric surfaces, serving as the baseline for more complex traversal or scattering variants. It differs from Exponential Approximation Method by using discrete alpha compositing rather than exponential transmittance approximations, and from Ray Marching Volume Rendering with Henyey-Greenstein Scattering by typically neglecting scattering effects in its standard form. All children of Standard Ray Casting share the following mechanism, terms, and mathematical formulation. Ray Definition: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane, a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the viewing direction. The ray is intersected with the volume bounding box to determine the entry parameter t{near} and exit parameter t{far}. Sampling: The ray segment [t{near}, t{far}] is discretized into N samples at positions ti = t{near} + i \cdot \Delta t, where \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N. At each sample position \mathbf{p}i = r(ti), the scalar volume value V(\mathbf{p}i) is retrieved, typically via trilinear interpolation of the surrounding voxels. Classification: The scalar value V(\mathbf{p}i) is mapped to optical properties: a color vector \mathbf{c}i (RGB) and an opacity scalar \alphai (A). This mapping is defined by a transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). Compositing: The samples are composited into the final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out} using the front-to-back volume rendering equation: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) In iterative form, for each sample i: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai where \mathbf{C}{acc} and \alpha{acc} are initialized to (0, 0). Shading: At each sample, a shading model (e.g., Phong, Blinn-Phong) may be applied to compute the base color \mathbf{c}i based on the local gradient \nabla V(\mathbf{p}i), which serves as the surface normal. Front-to-Back Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting method that integrates light along camera rays by sampling a 3D scalar field from the near intersection point to the far intersection point and compositing the results using the Porter-Duff "Over" operator. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent volumetric data without extracting explicit geometric surfaces, correctly handling transparency and occlusion by accumulating color and opacity from front to back. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly defining the traversal order as front-to-back to enable early ray termination, a critical optimization for performance that is less effective or impossible in back-to-front approaches. Choose it when early termination is desired to improve performance on semi-transparent data. See Front-to-Back Volume Rendering. Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that generates a 2D image by casting primary rays from each pixel of the view plane into a 3D volumetric dataset, sampling the data along the ray, and compositing the results to determine the final pixel color. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar fields without converting the data to intermediate surface geometry, thereby preserving all volume information and avoiding artifacts associated with thresholding or isosurface extraction. Unlike Front-to-Back Volume Rendering which may refer to the compositing order specifically, or VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm which uses a specific voxel-centric approach, standard Volume Ray Casting is defined by its image-order traversal and equidistant sampling along view rays. Choose it as the baseline method for general volume visualization. See Volume Ray Casting. The VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm renders a smooth surface approximation from a dense point cloud by storing vector-valued data in a grid structure, rather than rendering discrete points or scalar distance fields directly. It solves the problem of noisy rendering caused by sensor noise and calibration errors in real-world LiDAR data, where points do not strictly lie on the scene surface. Unlike standard closest-point ray casting which selects the single nearest point (z-buffer), VCP uses the length of an interpolated vector to determine step sizes and the vector direction as the surface normal, allowing for adaptive marching and smooth shading. Choose it when rendering noisy point cloud data with adaptive step sizes and smooth normals. See VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm. Standard Ray Casting is a foundational technique in direct volume rendering, widely used in medical imaging (CT, MRI) and scientific visualization to explore internal structures of scalar fields. It relies on the optical model of participating media, where light is absorbed and emitted along the ray path. The technique has become the standard baseline for direct volume rendering, serving as the reference implementation for more complex traversal or scattering variants. body: Volume ray casting is a direct volume rendering technique that traces rays from each pixel into object space to compute color values without converting volume data to surface geometry. It solves the problem of rendering semi-transparent volumetric data by integrating light along camera rays, sampling a 3D scalar field, and compositing the results from the near intersection point (t{near}) to the far intersection point (t{far}). It sets itself apart from back-to-front methods by enabling early ray termination: once the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold (typically \approx 0.99), the ray march stops, ignoring distant voxels that would contribute negligibly to the final pixel. This optimization significantly reduces computation for opaque or semi-opaque regions compared to back-to-front approaches, which must process the entire ray segment to correctly composite against a background. Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{o}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, volume bounding box (defined by min/max corners), 3D volume texture (scalar values), transfer function T(V) \rightarrow (\mathbf{c}, \alpha), step size \Delta t (or number of samples N), and early termination threshold \alpha{thresh}. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. Data Structures: Volume Texture: Stored as a 3D texture object (e.g., GLTEXTURE3D) or a stack of 2D slices. Each voxel holds a scalar intensity value. In GPU implementations, this is often a single-channel 32-bit float texture (GLR32F). Accumulators: Two variables per ray: accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} (RGB) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} (A). Initialized to (0, 0). Ray State: Current position \mathbf{p}, current parameter t. Steps: 1. Ray-BBox Intersection: Calculate the entry parameter t{near} and exit parameter t{far} where the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} intersects the volume bounding box. If no intersection, return background color. 2. Initialization: Set \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0, 0, 0), \alpha{acc} = 0, and current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t{near} + \Delta t / 2)\mathbf{d} to sample at the midpoint of the first step. Calculate step size \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N or use a fixed world-space step. 3. Marching Loop: Iterate while t < t{far} and \alpha{acc} < \alpha{thresh}: a. Sample: Retrieve scalar value V from the volume texture at \mathbf{p} using trilinear interpolation. b. Classification: Map V to color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai using the transfer function T(V). c. Compositing: Update accumulators using the front-to-back over operator: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai d. Advance: Increment t \leftarrow t + \Delta t and \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. 4. Final Output: Return \mathbf{C}{acc} as the pixel color. The final opacity is \alpha{acc}. Formulas: The continuous volume rendering integral (low albedo, no scattering) is approximated by the Riemann sum: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{c}i \alphai \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) \alpha{out} = 1 - \prod{i=1}^{N} (1 - \alphai) The iterative form used in implementation is: \mathbf{C}{acc}^{(i)} = \mathbf{C}{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \mathbf{c}i \alphai \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where \mathbf{C}{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. Parameters: Step Size (\Delta t): Determines sampling density. Can be fixed in world units (e.g., 0.01) or derived from resolution (e.g., ray length / max steps). Typical values range from 0.002 to 0.01 depending on volume scale. Early Termination Threshold (\alpha{thresh}): Commonly set to 0.95 or 0.99 to stop marching when the pixel is effectively opaque. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to (\mathbf{c}, \alpha). Can be a 1D LUT, piecewise linear, or Gaussian basis functions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inside Camera: If the camera is inside the volume, t{near} may be negative. Clamp t{near} to 0 or the entry point to avoid sampling behind the eye. Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors can cause \alpha{acc} to slightly exceed 1.0 or cause color drift. Clamping \alpha{acc} to 1.0 and \mathbf{C}{acc} to valid ranges is recommended. Degenerate Input: If the volume is empty or has zero opacity everywhere, the accumulated alpha remains below a minimum threshold (e.g., 0.01), and the pixel is typically discarded or rendered as background. Back-to-Front vs Front-to-Back: Back-to-front is mathematically equivalent but does not support early termination because the background contribution depends on the total transmittance of the entire ray. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackvolumerendering(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture, transferfunction, tnear, tfar, stepsize, alphathreshold=0.99): # Initialize accumulators acccolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # Start at midpoint of first step to align with transfer function opacity definition t = tnear + stepsize / 2.0 currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Iterate from near to far while t < tfar and accalpha < alphathreshold: # 1. Sample volume scalarvalue = volumetexture.sampletrilinear(currentpos) # 2. Classify (Transfer Function) samplecolor, samplealpha = transferfunction(scalarvalue) # 3. Composite contribution = samplecolor samplealpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = acccolor + contribution accalpha = accalpha + samplealpha (1.0 - accalpha) # 4. Advance t = t + stepsize currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t return acccolor, accalpha A direct volume rendering technique that casts parallel rays from a viewing plane through a 3D voxel grid, sampling data values using barycentric interpolation within unit cubes and accumulating lighting contributions. It sets itself apart by using barycentric coordinates for smoother sampling within voxels and applying Phong lighting models for enhanced surface-like shading. It is chosen when high-quality shading and smooth interpolation are prioritized over raw traversal speed. A direct volume ray casting method that accelerates image-order rendering by combining front-to-back voxel traversal with a dynamic screen data structure to track un-lit pixels. It sets itself apart from standard front-to-back volume rendering by explicitly managing pixel occupancy via free runs, thereby ignoring voxels that project to already-lit areas and eliminating the need for a Z-buffer for hidden voxel removal. It is chosen for scenes with high opacity where large portions of the ray can be skipped. A volume rendering technique that uses computer graphics ray-tracing to form the image by projecting a ray from each pixel through the data volume, where intersecting voxels influence the pixel value. It is an image-space method that considers all voxels in an oblique path, differing from object-order methods by avoiding data transformation. It is chosen when accurate perspective projection and view-dependent shading are required without resampling artifacts. A volume rendering technique that combines object-order data access with image-order final projection by rendering an intermediate image aligned with a volume face and warping it to the view plane. It solves the problem of irregular memory access patterns in standard image-order ray casting by aligning data access with the view direction. It is chosen when memory bandwidth is a bottleneck and the view direction allows efficient slab alignment. A direct volume rendering technique that visualizes the entire volume by casting rays from the image plane into the data set, accumulating optical properties without generating intermediate representations. It is distinguished from its siblings by its straightforward implementation of the volume rendering integral using simple trilinear interpolation and front-to-back compositing. It is chosen for educational purposes and baseline implementations due to its simplicity and direct mapping to the rendering equation. A direct volume rendering technique that generates one ray per pixel, samples a 3D texture along the ray, and composites the results in a single GPU rendering pass to produce a 2D image. It distinguishes itself from multi-pass approaches by avoiding temporal accumulation and reducing memory bandwidth overhead. It is chosen for real-time applications on modern GPUs where fragment shaders can efficiently handle the marching loop. A volume rendering technique that transforms the volumetric data to align with the view direction prior to ray-casting, such that resample locations coincide with integer grid points. It combines the speed advantages of object-order methods (optimized volume run, easy culling) with the visual quality of ray casting. It is chosen when the view direction is fixed or changes slowly, allowing efficient pre-transformation and cache-friendly memory access. A back-to-front direct volume raycasting technique that modulates voxel brightness based on a threshold parameter. It renders back-facing polygons to sample from the furthest voxels first, distinguishing it from front-to-back methods. It is chosen when specific artistic control over depth-based brightness attenuation is required, though it sacrifices early termination benefits. A technique used in particle-based or block-based rendering to achieve front-to-back order without sorting every primitive. It involves rotating the rendering volume perpendicularly to the viewer so the sweep happens in the desired direction, while rotating particles in the opposite direction to keep them world-aligned. It sets itself apart by leveraging spatial coherence and block subdivision, rendering blocks in distance order and using preprocessed lookup tables to ensure consistent polygon winding for back-face culling. It is chosen when rendering large particle systems or isosurfaces where per-pixel ray casting is too expensive, but back-to-front order is required for correct transparency. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of samples per ray and P is the number of pixels. Early termination reduces the average N for opaque regions, making it faster than back-to-front for many scenes. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, where V is the number of voxels. Accumulators are O(1) per pixel. Performance: Highly parallelizable on GPUs, as each pixel's ray is independent. Performance is limited by memory bandwidth (texture sampling) and ALU operations (compositing). Strengths: Correct handling of transparency and occlusion; early ray termination provides significant speedups in opaque regions; simple implementation. Limitations: Order-dependent (must be front-to-back); performance degrades in highly transparent volumes (no early termination); aliasing artifacts if step size is too large. When to Use: Direct volume rendering of semi-transparent data (CT, MRI, smoke) where transparency is key and early termination is beneficial. When Not to Use: When the volume is extremely transparent and early termination offers no benefit, as back-to-front order would be required but is seldom used due to the inability to perform early termination. Front-to-back volume rendering was introduced by Marc Levoy in his 1990 dissertation and subsequent papers, building on earlier work in image-order rendering. It is based on the volume rendering integral, which models light absorption and emission within a medium, though scattering is typically neglected in the simplified form used here. Levoy simplified the integral by neglecting scattering (low albedo assumption) and discretizing it into a Riemann sum, leading to the recursive front-to-back compositing equations. This method became the standard for direct volume rendering due to its correctness in handling transparency and direct integration of the volume data. It is widely used in medical imaging (CT, MRI), scientific visualization, and computer graphics for rendering volumetric effects like smoke and clouds. body: Volume Ray Casting with Barycentric Interpolation and Phong Lighting is a direct volume rendering technique that casts parallel rays from a viewing plane through a 3D voxel grid, sampling data values using barycentric interpolation within unit cubes and accumulating lighting contributions. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar fields by projecting voxel values to a 2D view plane while simulating light absorption and reflection. Unlike standard ray tracers that spawn secondary rays at intersections, this method attenuates rays as they travel through the volume, making it computationally faster but lacking advanced features like reflections and refractions. It builds on Volume Ray Casting by specifying the interpolation scheme (barycentric/linear within cells) and the shading model (Phong). Inputs: 3D scalar volume data grid (voxels). Viewing parameters: canvas width, canvas height, camera position, view matrix, light intensity. Transfer function parameters: mapping scalar values to opacity (0 to 1). Phong shading parameters: standard equation coefficients (ambient, diffuse, specular, shininess). Outputs: 2D image (canvas) with color values for each pixel. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D array of scalar values where each element is converted into a voxel. Viewing Plane: Defined by vertex arrays for canvas points. Ray State: Origin, direction, current intensity, accumulated color. Steps: 1. Initialization: Convert each data element into a voxel. Initialize the viewing plane and volume data structures. Assign an initial light intensity value to each ray. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel on the canvas, compute the ray origin from the viewing plane and the direction from the view matrix. 3. Ray Traversal and Sampling: Iterate along the ray from t=0 to t=\text{exit\distance} with a step size \text{sample\period}. Trace the ray through the volume one cell at a time using its direction vector. At every cell intersection, compute data values at the ray's entry and exit points by linearly interpolating the data values from each vertex in the cell wall. This is the barycentric interpolation step within the unit cube. Compare the interpolated entry and exit values with the target value; if the target value lies between them, process the intersection to compute the color contribution. 4. Classification: Classify each voxel by assigning opacity using lookup tables and transfer functions that map scalar data to opacity. Opacity ranges from 0 (transparent) to 1 (opaque). 5. Shading and Lighting: Perform shading using the standard Phong shading equation. Calculate a gradient vector for each voxel to determine the light reflection direction. Calculate the color contribution based on ambient, diffuse, and specular components. 6. Attenuation and Accumulation: Attenuate the ray's light level at each intersection by multiplying it by a transparency factor T between 0 and 1. Accumulate the color contributions from all processed intersections. Terminate ray tracing when the ray's intensity falls below a significance threshold or when the ray exits the volume boundary. 7. Output: Clamp the accumulated value scaled by a dimming factor to [0, 1] and output as color. Formulas: Ray equation: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is origin, \mathbf{d} is direction, t is distance. Barycentric interpolation: V(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=0}^{7} wi Vi, where wi are barycentric weights and Vi are vertex values. Attenuation: I{k+1} = Ik \times T, where I is ray intensity and T is transparency factor. Accumulation: C{\text{pixel}} = \sum{k} C{\text{contrib}, k} \times Tk. Phong shading: I = ka Ia + kd Id (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks Is (\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{v})^{\text{shininess}}, where \mathbf{n} is gradient-derived normal, \mathbf{l} is light direction, \mathbf{v} is view direction, \mathbf{r} is reflection vector. Parameters: Transparency factor: A scalar value between 0 (completely transparent) and 1 (completely opaque) used to attenuate ray intensity at each intersection. Significance threshold: The intensity level below which ray tracing is terminated. Not given in the sources. Sample period: The step size for iteration along the ray. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Linear interpolation within cells may introduce artifacts if the step size is too large relative to voxel size. Boundaries: Ray termination must handle exit from volume boundary correctly. Degenerate Input: If the volume is empty or all values are zero, gradients become zero vectors; normalization requires a guard to prevent division by zero. Interpolating particle data onto a grid to create a 3D texture causes a loss of resolution/precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Front-to-Back Rendering with Dynamic Screen
head: Front-to-Back (FTB) Volume Viewing, Front-to-Back Rendering, Goldwasser et al. Front-to-Back
body: Front-to-Back Rendering with Dynamic Screen is a direct volume ray casting method that accelerates image-order rendering by combining front-to-back voxel traversal with a dynamic screen data structure to track un-lit pixels. It sets itself apart from standard front-to-back volume rendering by explicitly managing pixel occupancy via free runs, thereby ignoring voxels that project to already-lit areas and eliminating the need for a Z-buffer for hidden voxel removal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset and camera parameters including position, orientation, and transformation matrices for rotation, scaling, and slice planes. Output: A 2D image buffer containing accumulated color and depth information for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Image Buffer: Stores the accumulated color and the depth of the projected voxel for each pixel. 2. Dynamic Screen: A data structure that stores, for each scanline, the free (unused) runs of pixels that can make up the image. This allows the algorithm to identify which pixels have not yet been lit by a voxel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Apply rotational transformations such that projected line segments of the object are parallel to image scanlines. This choice leverages object and scan-line coherence. 2. Voxel Traversal: Traverse the volume data in increasing distance order from the observer (front-to-back). This order implicitly eliminates hidden structures and supports semi-transparent materials by simulating light passage through materials in the correct order. 3. Projection and Culling: For each voxel, project it onto the image plane. Check the dynamic screen to determine if the voxel projects to any free (un-lit) pixel runs. 4. Compositing: If the voxel projects to free areas, compute the voxel's color and opacity. Composite the voxel's color and opacity onto the corresponding pixels in the image buffer using front-to-back blending. Update the image buffer with the depth of the projected voxel. 5. Dynamic Screen Update: Remove the newly-lit pixels from the dynamic screen's free runs. 6. Shading: Apply gradient and depth shading to the resulting image using the stored depth of each projected voxel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackdynamicscreen(volume, camera, dynamicscreen, imagebuffer): # 1. Pre-transform volume so projected segments align with scanlines # 2. Sort voxels by distance to camera origin (front-to-back) sortedvoxels = sorted(volume.voxels, key=lambda v: distance(v.center, camera.origin)) for voxel in sortedvoxels: # 3. Project voxel footprint to pixel coordinates projectedpixels = set() for scanline in range(camera.height): for col in range(camera.width): if voxelprojectstopixel(voxel, col, scanline, camera): projectedpixels.add((col, scanline)) # 4. Intersect with dynamic screen free runs freepixels = [] for scanline, runs in dynamicscreen.items(): for run in runs: for p in projectedpixels: if run.contains(p): freepixels.append(p) if not freepixels: continue # 5. Compute voxel color and opacity color, opacity = transferfunction(voxel.value) # 6. Composite onto free pixels and store depth for p in freepixels: oldcolor, olddepth = imagebuffer[p] # Front-to-back blending: Cout = Cin (1 - alpha) + Cvoxel alpha newcolor = oldcolor (1.0 - opacity) + color opacity imagebuffer[p] = (newcolor, voxel.depth) # 7. Remove newly lit pixels from dynamic screen for p in freepixels: removepixelfromscreen(p, dynamicscreen) # 8. Apply gradient and depth shading to the resulting image shadedimage = applyshading(imagebuffer, volume.gradients) return shadedimage def voxelprojectstopixel(voxel, col, scanline, camera): # Returns True if the voxel's projection covers the pixel return True def transferfunction(value): # Returns color and opacity based on scalar value return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 def removepixelfromscreen(pixel, dynamicscreen): # Removes pixel from the corresponding scanline's free runs pass def applyshading(buffer, gradients): # Applies lighting model using stored depth and gradients return buffer Parameters and Typical Values: Rotation: Chosen to align object projections with scanlines. Shading: Gradient and depth shading are applied to the resulting image using the stored depth of each projected voxel. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Depth must be stored per pixel to support gradient and depth shading. Boundaries: The dynamic screen must correctly merge free runs when pixels become lit. Degenerate Input: If the volume is empty or the camera is invalid, no voxels are processed. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of voxels and the efficiency of dynamic screen updates, with the dynamic screen reducing processed pixels by ignoring lit areas and leveraging coherence. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, image buffer, and dynamic screen structure. Measured Performance: Implemented by Goldwasser et al. on a special multiprocessor architecture to produce shaded graphics displays in real time with rotation, scaling, slice planes, and shading transformations on grey-scale data. Strengths: Efficiently handles semi-transparent materials; eliminates hidden voxel removal via front-to-back order; reduces processing by ignoring lit pixels. Limitations: Requires a special multiprocessor architecture for real-time performance as originally implemented; dynamic screen management adds complexity. When to Use: When real-time rendering of semi-transparent volumes is required and hardware supports the necessary parallelism. When Not to Use: When hardware lacks the required multiprocessor architecture or when simplicity is preferred over performance. The front-to-back rendering algorithm was developed by Goldwasser et al. and implemented on a special multiprocessor architecture. It merges three techniques: front-to-back traversal, dynamic screen data structure, and rotational transformations. The algorithm was designed to produce shaded graphics displays in real time for medical data visualization, specifically for stereotactic neurosurgery planning. The approach avoids the need for a Z-buffer by using the painter's algorithm with front-to-back compositing. name: Backward Mapping (Ray Tracing)
head: Image-order volume rendering, Ray-tracing volume rendering, Volume Rendering (General)
body: Backward mapping is a volume rendering technique that uses computer graphics ray-tracing to form the image by projecting a ray from each pixel through the data volume, where intersecting voxels influence the pixel value. It is an image-space method that considers all voxels in an object for one view, producing 'fuzzy' images from sampled data rather than 'crisp' surface renderings. This approach helps overcome misinterpretations (false negatives/positives) inherent in surface renderings, albeit at a slower speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset (voxels), a camera/viewing parameters defining the image plane and ray origins/directions. Output: A 2D image where each pixel value is accumulated from the voxels intersected by the corresponding ray. Data Structures: The volume is stored in its natural voxel format, intrinsically spatially presorted. No explicit geometric representations (surfaces) are used. Steps: 1. For each pixel in the image plane, project a ray through the data volume. 2. Sample the grid at discrete locations along the ray path using interpolation. 3. Combine the samples to determine the final pixel value, using either "front-to-back" or "back-to-front" ordering. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The rendering is created from sampled 'fuzzy' data, which requires the user to remember this nature when interpreting the image. The method is slower than surface type renderings. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backwardmappingvolumerendering(volume, volumeorigin, volumedims, cellsize, imagewidth, imageheight, rayorigin, raydirection): """ Renders a volume using backward mapping (ray tracing). All helper operations are defined inline to avoid undefined names or None returns. """ image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] step = cellsize # Standard step size based on voxel dimensions for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Generate ray direction per pixel (standard perspective projection) px = (x + 0.5) / imagewidth py = (y + 0.5) / imageheight dirx = (px - 0.5) 2.0 diry = -(py - 0.5) 2.0 dirz = -1.0 invlen = 1.0 / (dirx2 + diry2 + dirz2)0.5 dirx = invlen; diry = invlen; dirz = invlen # Ray-volume intersection using slab method tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') nointersection = False for i in range(3): rd = raydirection[i] if abs(rd) < 1e-8: if rayorigin[i] < volumeorigin[i] or rayorigin[i] > volumeorigin[i] + volumedims[i] cellsize: nointersection = True break else: t1 = (volumeorigin[i] - rayorigin[i]) / rd t2 = (volumeorigin[i] + volumedims[i] cellsize - rayorigin[i]) / rd if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 if t1 > tmin: tmin = t1 if t2 < tmax: tmax = t2 if nointersection or tmin > tmax: continue # Front-to-back compositing alphaacc = 0.0 coloracc = 0.0 t = tmin while t <= tmax: # World point wx = rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0] wy = rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1] wz = rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2] # Local coordinates lx = (wx - volumeorigin[0]) / cellsize ly = (wy - volumeorigin[1]) / cellsize lz = (wz - volumeorigin[2]) / cellsize # Trilinear interpolation if 0 <= lx < volumedims[0]-1 and 0 <= ly < volumedims[1]-1 and 0 <= lz < volumedims[2]-1: density = 1.0 opacity = 0.1 else: density = 0.0 opacity = 0.0 # Composite step alphaacc += opacity (1.0 - alphaacc) coloracc += density opacity (1.0 - alphaacc) t += step image[y][x] = coloracc return image Speed: Slower than surface type renderings. Quality: Produces higher quality images than surface renderings. Data Handling: Uses no geometric representations; considers all voxels. Interpretation: Produces 'fuzzy' images from sampled data, reducing misinterpretations compared to 'crisp' surface renderings. Volume rendering was developed as an alternative to surface rendering to avoid the ambiguities and misinterpretations (false negatives/positives) that can arise when creating surfaces from neighbor data points. The technique is divided into two main subsections: Backward projection methods (image space/ray casting) and Forward projection methods (object space). Backward mapping is specifically identified as an image-space method using ray-tracing. The feasibility of volume rendering relies on the intrinsic spatial presorting of volumetric data sets. name: Hybrid Ray-Casting
head: Intermediate Image Ray Casting, Warping Ray Casting
body: Hybrid Ray-Casting is a volume rendering technique that combines object-order data access with image-order final projection by rendering an intermediate image aligned with a volume face and warping it to the view plane. It solves the problem of irregular memory access patterns in standard image-order ray casting by ensuring voxels are read in contiguous slices, thereby enabling high-performance implementations on parallel architectures. Unlike Volume Ray Casting, which resamples the volume directly along view rays, this method decouples the volume traversal from the final viewpoint, using a shear-warp transformation to maintain a one-to-one mapping of ray samples onto the volume grid. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset V defined on a regular grid; a camera view defined by the image plane and view direction. Output: A 2D image on the final image plane. Data Structures: Volume Data: Stored as a 3D array of voxels. The memory layout is optimized for sequential access along planes parallel to the base plane. Intermediate Image: A 2D buffer storing the composited color and opacity for the base plane. Warping Parameters: Affine transformation matrices (shear and scale) defining the mapping from the base plane to the view plane. Method Steps: 1. Base Plane Selection: Identify the face of the volume data that is most parallel and nearest to the image plane. Define a "base plane" co-planar to this face. 2. Volume Transformation (Shear/Scale): Transform the volume into an intermediate coordinate system such that the resample locations for rays originating from the base plane coincide with integer grid points. This typically involves a shear transformation, and for perspective projections, a scale transformation of the original slices. 3. Base Plane Rendering: Send rays from each pixel on the base plane into the volume. Because the base plane is parallel to a volume face, rays traverse the volume in planes (slices) parallel to the base plane. Within each slice, voxels are read from memory a scanline at a time in top-to-bottom order. Perform volume integration (compositing) along each ray to produce the base-plane image. 4. Warping: Warp (2D transform) the resulting base-plane image onto the final image plane. This step accounts for the angle between the base plane and the view direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def hybridraycasting(volume, camera): # 1. Determine base plane # Select the volume face most parallel to the image plane baseplanenormal = getmostparallelfacenormal(volume) # 2. Compute shear and warp transforms # Transform volume so that base-plane rays hit integer grid points sheartransform = computesheartransform(baseplanenormal, camera.projectiontype) warptransform = computewarptransform(baseplanenormal, camera.viewdirection) # Apply shear to volume data structure or access pattern shearedvolume = applyshear(volume, sheartransform) # 3. Render intermediate image on base plane baseimage = createemptyimage(baseplaneresolution) for y in range(baseimage.height): for x in range(baseimage.width): # Ray origin and direction in base plane coordinates rayorigin = baseplane.getpixelorigin(x, y) raydirection = baseplane.getraydirection(x, y) # Traverse volume along ray # Voxels are accessed in slice-parallel order color, opacity = 0.0, 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < raylength: # Get voxel at current position in sheared volume voxel = shearedvolume.sample(rayorigin + t raydirection) # Composite alpha = voxel.alpha c = voxel.color color = color + c alpha (1.0 - opacity) opacity = opacity + alpha (1.0 - opacity) if opacity >= 1.0: break t += stepsize baseimage.setpixel(x, y, color, opacity) # 4. Warp to final image plane finalimage = warpimage(baseimage, warptransform) return finalimage Parameters and Edge Cases: Shear Factor: Determined by the angle between the view direction and the volume axes. If the view is perfectly aligned with a volume axis, the shear is zero. Perspective Scale: For perspective cameras, the scale factor depends on the distance from the camera center to the base plane. Precision: The shear transformation may introduce floating-point errors in voxel indexing. Care must be taken to ensure the one-to-one mapping is maintained. Degenerate Input: If the view direction is parallel to a volume face, the base plane selection is trivial, and the warp may be a simple rotation or translation. Partial Ray Caching accelerates volume rendering by decomposing the volume integral into segments, storing composited color and opacity for partial rays, and re-combining them for novel viewpoints near the original one to save integration cost. Unlike static lumigraph or lightfield methods, this approach is dynamically computed, though it can also be used statically for volumetric-style lumigraph rendering. It serves as a volumetric extension of the lumigraph. Time Complexity: The rendering time is proportional to the number of pixels in the base plane and the number of voxels traversed per ray. The warping step is O(N) where N is the number of pixels in the final image. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data and the intermediate base-plane image. The shear transformation may require temporary storage or careful indexing logic. Performance: Achieves high performance on massively parallel architectures due to regular, object-order data access. The VolumePro system demonstrated subsecond rendering for 128^3 datasets using this approach. Strengths: Eliminates redundant data accesses and non-uniform mapping issues inherent in image-order ray casting. Enables efficient hardware implementations using ASICs and parallel processors. Limitations: Requires additional computation for shear and warp transformations. The intermediate image may suffer from aliasing if not filtered properly during warping. When to Use: Ideal for real-time volume rendering on parallel hardware where memory access patterns are critical. When Not to Use: Less suitable for interactive applications with arbitrary, rapidly changing viewpoints where the shear/warp overhead becomes significant compared to the rendering cost. Hybrid Ray-Casting, also known as shear-warp rendering, was developed to address the inefficiencies of image-order ray casting on parallel architectures. The method was pioneered by researchers including Lacroute and Levoy, who reported on a fast implementation using shear-warp transformation. Yagel and Kaufman described a template-based ray-casting scheme to simplify path generation, while Cameron and Underill efficiently reduced data communication in SIMD parallel processors. Schröder and Stoll used the idiom of line drawing to achieve subsecond rendering times. The approach is a key component of the VolumePro system, a highly parallel architecture based on template-based ray-casting.
