name: Partial Ray Caching (Volumetric Lumigraph)
head: Intermediate Image Ray Casting, Lightfield Extension, Volumetric Lumigraph, Warping Ray Casting
body: Partial Ray Caching accelerates volume rendering by decomposing the volume integral into segments, storing composited color and opacity for partial rays, and re-combining them for novel viewpoints near the original one to save integration cost. Unlike static lumigraph or lightfield methods, this approach is dynamically computed, though it can also be used statically for volumetric-style lumigraph rendering. It serves as a volumetric extension of the lumigraph. Inputs: Volumetric dataset, initial view direction Va, target novel view direction Vb (within a limited view cone). Outputs: Rendered image for view Vb. Data Structures: 1. Slab Images: A stack of depth-layered images. Each image corresponds to a slab of the volume. 2. Partial Ray Data: Stored within the slab images, containing composited color (C) and opacity (\alpha) for each ray segment. 3. Coarse Polygonal Mesh: Computed on the fly for each layer to approximate the underlying object geometry. Steps: 1. Decomposition: Decompose the volume into slabs. 2. Initial Rendering: Render each slab into an image from the initial view direction Va, storing the partial ray integrals (composited color and opacity). 3. Mesh Generation: Compute a coarse polygonal mesh on the fly for each layer to approximate the underlying object. 4. Warping and Composition: For a novel viewpoint Vb: Map the stored slab images onto the coarse polygonal meshes. Use interpolation to obtain partial integrals at non-grid positions when combining partial rays for the new view direction Vb. Composite the billboard images (slab images) for the desired view Vb. Re-combine partial rays into complete rays for the new image. Parameters: View Cone: The method is effective for viewpoints within a specific view cone. Mueller et al. rendered warped and composited images from novel viewpoints within a 30° view cone. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gaps: Gaps may quickly emerge when the layers are kept planar when rendering from novel viewpoints. This is mitigated by computing a coarse polygonal mesh for each layer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpartialraycache(volume, initialview, targetview, viewconeangle=30.0): """ Renders a volume using partial ray caching. Args: volume: The volumetric dataset. initialview: The view direction Va used for caching. targetview: The novel view direction Vb. viewconeangle: Maximum angle deviation from initialview allowed. Returns: Rendered image for targetview. """ # Check if target view is within the valid view cone if anglebetween(initialview, targetview) > viewconeangle: raise ValueError("Target view is outside the valid view cone.") # Step 1: Decompose volume into slabs slabs = decomposevolumeintoslabs(volume) # Step 2: Render each slab from initialview, storing partial integrals # Each slab image stores composited color and opacity for partial rays slabimages = [] for slab in slabs: # Render slab from initialview # Store partial ray integrals (color C, opacity alpha) in the image img = renderslab(slab, initialview) slabimages.append(img) # Step 3: Compute coarse polygonal mesh for each layer # This prevents gaps when warping meshes = [] for i, slab in enumerate(slabs): # Approximate underlying object geometry for this slab mesh = computecoarsemesh(slab) meshes.append(mesh) # Step 4: Render for targetview by warping and composing # Initialize output image outputimage = createemptyimage() # Composite slab images for the new view for i, slabimg in enumerate(slabimages): mesh = meshes[i] # Warp the slab image onto the mesh for the targetview # Use interpolation to obtain partial integrals at non-grid positions warpedimg = warpimageontomesh(slabimg, mesh, targetview) # Composite the warped image into the output # Standard alpha compositing outputimage = composite(outputimage, warpedimg) return outputimage Performance: Saves the cost for fully integrating all rays for each new viewpoint, reducing it to the expense of compositing a few partial segments per ray, which is much lower. Hardware: Can be rendered using standard graphics hardware. Limitations: Limited to viewpoints near the original one (e.g., within a 30° view cone). Gaps may emerge if layers are kept planar. Usage: Suitable for volume rendering at great perspective distortions, such as in virtual endoscopy applications. Origin: The method falls into the domain of image-based rendering (IBR). It is a volumetric extension of the lumigraph or lightfield, albeit dynamically computed. Development: Brady et al. exploited this idea for volume rendering at great perspective distortions, such as in virtual endoscopy applications. Mueller et al. stored the rays in the form of a stack of depth-layered images and rendered these images warped and composited from novel viewpoints within a 30° view cone, using standard graphics hardware. Alternatives: An alternative method that uses a precomputed triangle mesh to achieve similar goals for iso-surface volume rendering was proposed by Chen et al.. Yagel and Shi warped complete images to nearby viewpoints, aided by a depth buffer. name: Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting
head: Basic ray-casting model, DRR Generation via Ray Casting, Digital Radiograph Synthesis, Direct Volume Rendering (Levoy's Model), Levoy Raycasting, Levoy's rendering model, Ray Casting DRR
body: Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that visualizes the entire volume by casting rays from the image plane into the data set, accumulating optical properties without generating intermediate representations. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific feed-backward traversal order and the use of Levoy’s back-lit attenuation model, which allows for early termination when accumulated opacity reaches one. Unlike Backward Mapping (Ray Tracing) which traces from light to eye, or Hybrid Ray-Casting which uses pre-integration, this method performs per-sample shading and compositing directly along the ray. Inputs: 3D volume data V with dimensions W \times H \times D, where each voxel contains a scalar value (e.g., density). Camera parameters: view direction, up vector, and image plane dimensions (width, height). Transfer functions: Tc(v) mapping scalar value v to color (R, G, B) and Ta(v) mapping scalar value v to opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Shading model parameters (e.g., light direction, ambient/diffuse coefficients). Outputs: 2D image buffer I of size W{img} \times H{img}, where each pixel contains an RGB color value. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin O (on the image plane) and direction D (normalized vector into the volume). Sample Point: Defined by position P in world space, interpolated scalar value v, and computed color C and opacity \alpha. Accumulators: C{acc}: Accumulated color (RGB), initialized to (0, 0, 0). \alpha{acc}: Accumulated opacity, initialized to 0. \tau{acc}: Accumulated transmission, initialized to 1 (where \tau = 1 - \alpha{acc}). Steps: 1. Initialization: For each pixel (x, y) in the image plane, compute the ray origin O and direction D based on camera geometry. Initialize C{acc} = (0,0,0), \alpha{acc} = 0, \tau{acc} = 1. 2. Ray Traversal: Cast the ray into the volume. Determine the entry and exit points of the ray with the volume bounding box. Optimization: Use a Digital Differential Analyzer (DDA) or Bresenham-like algorithm to step through voxels equidistantly or along voxel boundaries, rather than fixed floating-point intervals, for efficiency. 3. Sampling and Interpolation: At each step along the ray, compute the sample position P. Interpolate the volume data V at P to obtain the scalar value v. Note: The sources mention "evenly distributed points" but also "DDA/Bresenham-like" for efficiency. In implementation, DDA steps are effectively equidistant in voxel space, which approximates equidistant sampling in world space if the volume is isotropic or properly scaled. 4. Classification: Map the scalar value v to color C{sample} and opacity \alpha{sample} using the transfer functions: C{sample} = Tc(v) \alpha{sample} = Ta(v) 5. Shading: Apply the shading model to C{sample} to account for lighting based on the gradient at P and light direction. Let the shaded color be C{shaded}. 6. Compositing (Feed-Backward): Update the accumulators using the front-to-back blending equations: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{shaded} \cdot \alpha{sample} \cdot \tau{acc} \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alpha{sample} \cdot \tau{acc} \tau{acc} = 1 - \alpha{acc} 7. Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} \ge 1 (or \tau{acc} \le \epsilon for a small threshold \epsilon), terminate the ray traversal early, as subsequent samples will not contribute to the final color. 8. Final Assignment: Assign C{acc} to the pixel (x, y) in the image buffer. 9. Iteration: Repeat for all pixels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def vanhooklevoyraycasting(volume, transferfunccolor, transferfuncopacity, shadingmodel, camera, volumebounds, stepsize): """ Implements Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting. Args: volume: 3D numpy array (W, H, D) of scalar values. transferfunccolor: Function mapping scalar value -> (R, G, B). transferfuncopacity: Function mapping scalar value -> alpha in [0, 1]. shadingmodel: Function mapping (value, gradient, lightdir) -> shadedcolor. camera: Object with method getray(x, y) -> (origin, direction). volumebounds: Bounding box of the volume for ray intersection [minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz]. stepsize: Fixed physical step length along the ray. Returns: image: 2D numpy array (Himg, Wimg, 3) of RGB values. """ imgwidth = camera.width imgheight = camera.height image = np.zeros((imgheight, imgwidth, 3), dtype=np.float32) volshape = volume.shape for y in range(imgheight): for x in range(imgwidth): acccolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) accalpha = 0.0 acctau = 1.0 origin, direction = camera.getray(x, y) tmin, tmax = rayboxintersect(origin, direction, volumebounds) if tmax <= tmin: continue numsteps = int((tmax - tmin) / stepsize) for i in range(numsteps): t = tmin + i stepsize if t > tmax: break pos = origin + t direction if not isinsidevolume(pos, volumebounds): continue voxelcoords = worldtovoxel(pos, volumebounds, volshape) v = trilinearinterpolate(volume, voxelcoords, volshape) csample = transferfunccolor(v) alphasample = transferfuncopacity(v) grad = computegradient(volume, voxelcoords, volshape) cshaded = shadingmodel(v, grad, direction) contribution = cshaded alphasample acctau acccolor = acccolor + contribution accalpha = accalpha + alphasample acctau acctau = 1.0 - accalpha if accalpha >= 1.0: break image[y, x] = acccolor return image def rayboxintersect(origin, direction, bounds): tmin = -np.inf tmax = np.inf for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < bounds[i2] or origin[i] > bounds[i2+1]: return (np.inf, -np.inf) else: t1 = (bounds[i2] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (bounds[i2+1] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return (np.inf, -np.inf) return (tmin, tmax) def isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): for i in range(3): if pos[i] < bounds[i2] or pos[i] > bounds[i2+1]: return False return True def worldtovoxel(pos, bounds, volshape): normpos = (pos - bounds[0:3]) / (bounds[3:6] - bounds[0:3]) voxelcoords = normpos (np.array(volshape) - 1) return voxelcoords def trilinearinterpolate(volume, coords, shape): x, y, z = coords x = np.clip(x, 0, shape[0] - 1) y = np.clip(y, 0, shape[1] - 1) z = np.clip(z, 0, shape[2] - 1) x0, y0, z0 = np.floor([x, y, z]).astype(int) x1, y1, z1 = np.clip(x0 + 1, 0, shape[0] - 1), np.clip(y0 + 1, 0, shape[1] - 1), np.clip(z0 + 1, 0, shape[2] - 1) fx, fy, fz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 c000 = volume[x0, y0, z0] c100 = volume[x1, y0, z0] c010 = volume[x0, y1, z0] c110 = volume[x1, y1, z0] c001 = volume[x0, y0, z1] c101 = volume[x1, y0, z1] c011 = volume[x0, y1, z1] c111 = volume[x1, y1, z1] c00 = c000 (1 - fx) + c100 fx c01 = c001 (1 - fx) + c101 fx c10 = c010 (1 - fx) + c110 fx c11 = c011 (1 - fx) + c111 fx c0 = c00 (1 - fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1 - fy) + c11 fy result = c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz return result def computegradient(volume, coords, shape): x, y, z = coords dx = volume[np.clip(x+1, 0, shape[0]-1), y, z] - volume[np.clip(x-1, 0, shape[0]-1), y, z] dy = volume[x, np.clip(y+1, 0, shape[1]-1), z] - volume[x, np.clip(y-1, 0, shape[1]-1), z] dz = volume[x, y, np.clip(z+1, 0, shape[2]-1)] - volume[x, y, np.clip(z-1, 0, shape[2]-1)] return np.array([dx, dy, dz]) Subtopics: Digital Radiograph (DRR) Synthesis: A specific application of Van Hook-Levoy Ray-Casting in medical imaging, where the ray casting is used to project 3D CT data into 2D X-ray-like images. It requires strict coordinate system consistency using DICOM metadata. Feed-Forward vs. Feed-Backward: Van Hook-Levoy is a feed-backward method (ray from eye to volume), which enables early termination when opacity is 1. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of samples per ray. With DDA, S is proportional to the number of voxels intersected by the ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, plus O(1) per ray for accumulators. Performance: Naive equidistant sampling is slow. Using DDA/Bresenham-like algorithms improves traversal efficiency. GPU implementation (e.g., CUDA) can achieve real-time performance (tens to hundreds of milliseconds) compared to seconds for CPU implementations. Strengths: Visualizes the entire volume. Early termination optimization reduces computation for opaque regions. Limitations: Computationally expensive for high-resolution volumes. Requires careful handling of geometric transformations and boundary conditions to avoid artifacts. When to use: When direct visualization of internal structures is needed, and real-time performance is achievable via GPU acceleration. When not to use: When surface rendering is sufficient, or when hardware acceleration is unavailable and performance is critical. Origin: The method was published by Marc Levoy in 1988. Thomas Van Hook also explored the basic ray-casting model in 1986. History: It is one of the four main paradigms of volume rendering (along with splatting, shear-warp, and cell projection). GPU raycasting was later introduced by Kruger in 2003. Usage: Widely used in medical imaging for therapy planning and generating Digital Radiographs (DRR) from 3D CT data. 医疗影像开发实战:如何用光线投射算法快速生成DRR图像(附Python代码), https://un.csdn.net/98nhkcg5t04h, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A Parallel, Feed-Forward Volume Rendering Algorithm, https://www.cs.unc.edu/techreports/91-029.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Medical Volume Rendering Techniques, https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.07710v1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 14 Acceleration Techniques for Volume Rendering Mark W. name: Single-pass Raycasting
head: Direct Volume Rendering via Raycasting, Single Pass GPU Ray Casting, Single execution ray casting
body: Single-pass raycasting is a direct volume rendering technique that generates one ray per pixel, samples a 3D texture along the ray, and composites the results in a single GPU rendering pass to produce a 2D image. It distinguishes itself from multi-pass approaches by avoiding temporary framebuffers for intermediate ray results, thereby addressing the low efficiency of multi-pass pipelines on modern graphics hardware. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values loaded from a Uint16Array where the first three elements are dimensions (W, H, D) and the remaining elements are voxel values normalized by dividing by 4095.0. The data is stored in a THREE.Data3DTexture with format THREE.RedFormat, type THREE.FloatType, and linear filtering. Camera: Eye position and projection parameters. Lighting: Light position (often fixed at the camera position in basic implementations) and color. Parameters: Uniforms controlling rendering mode, thresholds, step size, and transfer functions. Outputs: 2D Image: A color buffer where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity from the ray traversal. The implementation relies on the following structures and uniforms: 1. Volume Texture (sampler3D volumedata): Dimensions: W \times H \times D. Coordinate space: Unit cube [0,1]^3. 2. Transfer Function Textures (sampler2D): Lookup tables for color and opacity based on density and gradient magnitude. Resolution controlled by TransferSize. 3. Ray Entry/Exit Textures (FBOs): Textures storing ray entry and exit positions for each fragment. Resolution controlled by FBOSize. 4. Uniforms: volumesize: vec3 containing the dimensions of the volume. rendermode: int (0 for First Hit, 1 for MIP). urenderthreshold: float iso-value threshold for First Hit mode. StepSize: float spatial distance between samples. MaxSamples: int limit on samples per ray. Minclip: float threshold to discard low-density samples. Apply Noise: bool toggle for stochastic ray shifting. GradDelta: vec3 offsets for gradient computation. Threshold (Shadows): float occlusion threshold for shadow rays. Quality (Shadows): int (0-100) controlling shadow ray sample count. 1. Initialization and Coordinate Transformation: Transform the camera eye position into the volume's unit cube space. The transformed eye position is calculated as: \text{transformed\eye} = \frac{\text{cameraPosition}}{\text{volume\size}} + (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) For each fragment (pixel), calculate the ray direction in unit cube space. The fragment position is normalized to [0,1]. The direction is: \vec{vray\dir} = \frac{\text{position}}{\text{volume\size}} + (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) - \text{transformed\eye} Note: In some implementations, ray entry and exit positions are pre-rendered to textures (FBOs) and looked up in the fragment shader to compute directions. 2. Ray-Box Intersection: Calculate the intersection of the view ray with the unit cube bounds [0,1]^3. If the ray does not intersect the cube (t{hit.x} > t{hit.y}), discard the fragment. Set the starting parameter t = \max(t{hit.x}, 0.0). 3. Step Size Calculation: Compute the step size dt to ensure consistent sampling relative to the grid: dt = \min \left( \frac{1}{W |vx|}, \frac{1}{H |vy|}, \frac{1}{D |vz|} \right) where \vec{v} = (vx, vy, vz) is the ray direction and W,H,D are volume dimensions. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize accumulation variables: alpha = 0.0, color = (0,0,0). Initialize previous sample point pointN0 and value valueN0 at the start position. Iterate while t < t{hit.y} and sample count < MaxSamples: a. Stochastic Shifting: If Apply Noise is true, perturb the ray position slightly to reduce banding artifacts. b. Advance Ray: Calculate next position pointN1 = pointN0 + raydir dt. c. Sample Volume: Read value valueN1 = samplevolume(pointN1). d. Minclip Check: If valueN1 < Minclip, continue to next sample (discard). e. Mode-Specific Processing: First Hit Mode (rendermode == 0): If valueN1 > urenderthreshold: Interpolate to find the exact surface position t{surf} where the value equals the threshold: t{surf} = t - dt \cdot \frac{valueN1 - u\renderthreshold}{valueN1 - valueN0} Calculate the surface normal using central differences (gradient) at the surface point. Gradient computation uses offsets defined by GradDelta. Compute lighting (diffuse/specular) using the normal and light direction. Apply transfer function to map density to color. Set final pixel color to the lit surface color and break the loop. Else: Update valueN0 = valueN1, pointN0 = pointN1, t += dt. MIP Mode (rendermode == 1): Track the maximum value encountered along the ray. Update maxval = max(maxval, valueN1). Continue to next sample. After loop, apply transfer function to maxval to determine color. f. Shadow Rays (Optional): For each sample, cast a shadow ray towards the light source. Sample until density exceeds Threshold (Shadows). Number of samples controlled by Quality (Shadows). Modulate lighting based on occlusion. 5. Transfer Function Application: Map the final scalar value (surface value for First Hit, max value for MIP) to color and opacity using the transfer function lookup tables. The transfer function allows arbitrary modulation of density and gradient magnitude lookups. Default color mapping may use the Viridis colormap. 6. Compositing: In First Hit mode, the result is the color of the first surface hit. In MIP mode, the result is the color corresponding to the maximum intensity. Standard front-to-back alpha compositing is not explicitly detailed for the final pixel in the provided code snippets for First Hit/MIP modes, as they are "single hit" or "max" projections rather than volumetric integration. The provided code for First Hit breaks on hit, and MIP takes the max, implying no alpha blending accumulation in the loop for these specific modes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def singlepassraycasting(cameraposition, volumesize, position, rendermode, urenderthreshold, minclip, applynoise, graddelta, lightposition, shininess, lightcolor, ambient, samplevolume, applytransferfunction, intersectbox): # 1. Transform eye to unit cube space transformedeye = cameraposition / volumesize + vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) # 2. Calculate ray direction in unit cube space raydir = (position / volumesize) + vec3(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) - transformedeye # 3. Intersect ray with unit cube [0,1]^3 thit = intersectbox(transformedeye, raydir) if thit[0] > thit[1]: return None # Discard tstart = max(thit[0], 0.0) # 4. Calculate step size dtvec = vec3(1.0) / (volumesize abs(raydir)) dt = min(dtvec[0], min(dtvec[1], dtvec[2])) # 5. Initialize variables alpha = 0.0 color = vec3(0.0) pointN0 = transformedeye + tstart raydir valueN0 = samplevolume(pointN0) maxval = float('-inf') # 6. Ray Marching Loop t = tstart while t < thit[1]: # Stochastic shifting if enabled if applynoise: pointN1 = pointN0 + raydir dt + vec3(random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5), random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5)) else: pointN1 = pointN0 + raydir dt valueN1 = samplevolume(pointN1) # Minclip check if valueN1 < minclip: valueN0 = valueN1 pointN0 = pointN1 t += dt continue if rendermode == 0: # First Hit if valueN1 > urenderthreshold: # Interpolate surface position linearinterpolation = (urenderthreshold - valueN0) / (valueN1 - valueN0) tsurf = t - dt linearinterpolation surfacepos = pointN0 + raydir (t - tsurf) # Calculate gradient for normal grad = computegradient(surfacepos, graddelta) normal = normalize(grad) # Lighting (single scattering model) lightdir = normalize(lightposition - surfacepos) diffuse = max(dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) specular = pow(max(dot(reflect(-lightdir, normal), -raydir), 0.0), shininess) # Transfer function tfcolor = applytransferfunction(valueN1) color = tfcolor (ambient + diffuse lightcolor + specular lightcolor) break # Exit loop on first hit else: valueN0 = valueN1 pointN0 = pointN1 elif rendermode == 1: # MIP if valueN1 > maxval: maxval = valueN1 valueN0 = valueN1 pointN0 = pointN1 t += dt # 7. Final Output if rendermode == 1: color = applytransferfunction(maxval) return vec4(color, 1.0) StepSize: Controls spatial distance between samples. Higher values reduce quality but increase speed. MaxSamples: Limits the total number of samples per ray to prevent infinite loops or excessive computation. urenderthreshold: Iso-value threshold for First Hit rendering. Only values above this trigger surface detection. Minclip: Threshold below which samples are discarded (treated as empty). FBOSize: Resolution of textures storing ray entry/exit positions. TransferSize: Resolution of transfer function lookup textures. Apply Noise: Boolean to enable stochastic ray shifting, reducing banding artifacts. GradDelta: Offsets for finite difference gradient calculation. Threshold (Shadows): Density value for shadow ray occlusion. Quality (Shadows): Number of samples for shadow ray traversal (0-100). Data Loading: Volume data is often stored in a Uint16Array with the first 3 elements as dimensions. The voxel values must be normalized by dividing by 4095.0 to fit in the [0,1] range expected by the texture. Precision: High precision (highp float) is required in shaders to avoid artifacts in ray marching and interpolation. Banding Artifacts: Regular sampling can cause banding. Stochastic ray shifting (Apply Noise) is used to mitigate this. Memory Limits: Large volumes may exceed GPU texture memory. Hierarchical grid representations or out-of-core techniques are needed for very large datasets. What it is: A raycasting method that iterates over volume primitives (voxels) and projects them onto the screen, rather than iterating over pixels [Siblings]. Difference: Single-pass is image-order (pixel-driven), while Object-Order is primitive-driven. Object-order can be more efficient for sparse data but is harder to parallelize on GPUs compared to the regular access patterns of image-order raycasting [Siblings]. When to choose: Use when the volume is sparse or when primitive-level manipulation is required. Single-pass is preferred for dense, regular grids on GPUs [Siblings]. Link: Object-Order Ray-Casting What it is: A method or parameterization technique related to controlling brightness and contrast in raycasting [Siblings]. Difference: Single-pass is a rendering pipeline strategy. RaycastBrightnessControl likely refers to a specific shading or transfer function adjustment technique applied within a raycasting framework [Siblings]. When to choose: Use when fine-tuning the visual appearance (brightness/contrast) of the raycast output is the primary goal. Link: RaycastBrightnessControl Time Complexity: O(P \cdot S), where P is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples per ray. Shadow rays add a factor of S{shadow} per sample. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume texture, where V is the number of voxels. Additional memory for FBOs and transfer functions. Performance: Single-pass solutions are more efficient than multi-pass approaches on modern GPUs because they avoid the overhead of rendering to and reading from temporary framebuffers. Strengths: High flexibility (custom shaders), real-time potential on capable hardware, accurate lighting and transfer functions. Limitations: Performance degrades with high resolution, large volumes, or complex lighting (shadow rays). Memory bound for very large volumes. When to use: Real-time visualization of moderate-sized volumes, interactive exploration, spectral DVR. When not to use: Extremely large volumes that do not fit in GPU memory without hierarchical streaming, or when offline, high-quality volume rendering is required (where path tracing or other offline methods might be better). Origin: The concept of single-pass GPU raycasting was developed to address the inefficiencies of multi-pass rendering pipelines on graphics hardware. Key Contributors: Stegmaier and colleagues extended the framework to spectral DVR using Kubelka–Munk theory. Hadwiger et al. used single-pass raycasting for implicit isosurfaces on rectilinear grids. Roettger et al. built a real-time raycaster with adaptive pre-integrated voxel classification. History: Early GPU-based solutions relied on multiple rendering passes. Single-pass techniques emerged to improve efficiency and flexibility. Usage: Used in VStudio as the primary direct volume rendering method. Extended for spectral DVR. name: Object-Order Ray-Casting
head: Data-parallel volume rendering
body: Object-order ray-casting is a volume rendering technique that transforms the volumetric data to align with the view direction prior to ray-casting, such that resample locations coincide with integer grid points. It combines the speed advantages of object-order methods (optimized volume run, easy space leaping) with the high-quality image generation of ray-casting (trilinear interpolation). Unlike image-order ray-casting, which is slow due to cache misses from irregular voxel access, or Shear-Warp, which introduces artifacts and blurring, this method maintains interactive frame rates (up to 10 fps) while preserving image quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset V of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz, a view direction, and an orthogonal projection matrix. Output: A 2D image (frame buffer) with accumulated color and opacity values for each pixel. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array of scalar values representing density or intensity. Frame Buffer: A 2D array storing accumulated color C and opacity \alpha for each pixel, initialized to (0, 0). Method Steps: 1. Transformation Decomposition: Decompose the transformation from the volume's local coordinate system to the view-aligned coordinate system into a set of affine transforms requiring shear/scale operations along orthogonal axes. 2. Resampling: Perform resampling of the volume using the decomposed affine transforms to generate regular data access to voxels. This ensures that resample locations coincide with integer grid points in the transformed space. 3. Ray-Cell Intersection and Sampling: For every cell that has to be rendered (i.e., not transparent and not hidden), load the values and gradients of the 8 vertices. Determine the rays intersecting the cell; in the transformed space, these rays are aligned with the grid axes, simplifying intersection tests. For each intersecting ray, sample colors Cs and opacities \alphas along the ray within the cell using trilinear interpolation. 4. Compositing: Update the frame buffer for the pixels corresponding to the intersected rays. The compositing follows the front-to-back accumulation model defined by Kajiya's low albedo form. Formulas: The underlying optical model is Kajiya's low albedo form: I\lambda = \int0^t C\lambda(s) \times \tau(s) \times \exp\left(-\int0^s \tau(t) \, dt\right) ds \quad (1) Where: I\lambda: Light intensity of wavelength \lambda reaching the viewpoint. C\lambda(s): Color contribution at position s. \tau(s): Extinction coefficient at position s. t: Total length of the ray through the volume. This integral is approximated using a Riemann sum with even sampling distance \Delta s. The accumulated color C{i+1} and opacity \alpha{i+1} are updated recursively in front-to-back order using the sampled color Cs and opacity \alphas at step i: C{i+1} = Ci + (1-\alphai) \alphas Cs \quad (2) \alpha{i+1} = \alphai + (1 - \alphai) \alphas \quad (3) Where: Ci, \alphai: Accumulated color and opacity before step i. Cs, \alphas: Sampled color and opacity at step i. \Delta s: Sampling distance. Parameters: Sampling Distance (\Delta s): Critical for quality vs. speed trade-off. Large \Delta s accelerates rendering but produces low-quality images. Target Performance: Up to 10 frames per second on current workstations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def objectorderraycasting(volume, viewtransform, framebuffer, deltas): # Initialize frame buffer accumulators to zero for y in range(framebuffer.height): for x in range(framebuffer.width): framebuffer[x, y].color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) framebuffer[x, y].opacity = 0.0 # Iterate over all cells in the volume for z in range(volume.depth - 1): for y in range(volume.height - 1): for x in range(volume.width - 1): cell = volume.getcell(x, y, z) if cell.istransparent(): continue if cell.ishidden(viewtransform): continue # Load 8 vertex values vertices = cell.getvertexvalues() # Ray direction in transformed space (aligned with grid axes) raydir = viewtransform.getaxisdirection() # Compute ray entry and exit points for this cell tmin, tmax = cell.computeintersection(raydir) # Step along the ray within the cell t = tmin while t < tmax: # Sample position in transformed space samplepos = cell.origin + t raydir # Trilinear interpolation of color and opacity cs, as = trilinearinterpolate(volume, samplepos, vertices) # Project to pixel coordinates px, py = viewtransform.project(samplepos) if not framebuffer.inbounds(px, py): t += deltas continue # Front-to-back compositing pixel = framebuffer[px, py] ci, ai = pixel.color, pixel.opacity # Kajiya's low albedo form approximation newalpha = ai + (1.0 - ai) as newcolor = ci + (1.0 - ai) as cs pixel.color = newcolor pixel.opacity = newalpha t += deltas def trilinearinterpolate(volume, pos, vertices): # Standard trilinear interpolation using 8 vertex values # Returns sampled color and opacity # Implementation details omitted for brevity; standard graphics operation pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sampling Distance: Large \Delta s leads to low-quality images. Cache Misses: Image-order ray-casting suffers from cache misses because every ray step loads eight samples for trilinear interpolation, which cannot be stored in memory order. Object-order ray-casting avoids this by accessing voxels a limited number of times. Hidden Volume Removal: Object-order methods traditionally struggle with skipping empty regions, especially with interactive classification. An efficient hidden volume removal technique is required to compensate for the loss of early ray termination inherent in image-order algorithms. Time Complexity: The method aims for interactive performance, targeting up to 10 fps on current workstations. In a two-pass implementation, it achieved approximately 3 fps on a 256^3 bonsai dataset. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume size and the frame buffer. Strengths: Combines speed of object-order methods (optimized volume run, easy space leaping) with high-quality image generation of ray-casting (trilinear interpolation). Avoids cache misses associated with image-order ray-casting. Avoids low sampling rates on the z-axis (1 to 1.73), pre-classification blurring, and artifacts at 45-degree viewing angles associated with Shear-Warp. Avoids blurring of small details inherent to Gaussian low-pass filters in Splatting. Limitations: Requires efficient hidden volume removal to compensate for the loss of early ray termination. Accuracy depends critically on the sampling distance \Delta s and the evaluation of sampled values. When to Use: When high-quality interactive volume rendering is required, and the hardware supports efficient 3D resampling and orthogonal projection. When Not to Use: When early ray termination is critical and hidden volume removal is not efficiently implemented, or when the view direction changes frequently and the transformation overhead is prohibitive. Object-order ray-casting was introduced as an efficient and accurate volume rendering technique to overcome the limitations of existing methods. It was developed to achieve interactive high-quality rendering (up to 10 fps) on workstations. The method builds on the idea that the projection of a parallelepipedic shape can be efficiently performed under orthogonal projection, enabling object-order traversal while maintaining ray-casting quality. It is also known as data-parallel volume rendering because operations on the volume semantically involve all voxels at once. The technique has been implemented in hardware architectures like VIRIM, which uses lookup tables for interpolation and programmable lighting/viewing parameters. name: RaycastBrightnessControl
head: RaycastColorControl
body: RaycastBrightnessControl is a back-to-front direct volume raycasting technique that modulates voxel brightness based on a threshold parameter. It renders back-facing polygons to sample from the furthest voxels first, distinguishing it from front-to-back methods. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume texture, camera position (eye.xyz), fragment position (fragment.xyz), scalar valthreshold, and step size SAMPLESTEP. Output: A 2D color buffer. Data Structures: The volume is stored in a 3D texture. The fragment shader receives interpolated screen coordinates and uniform camera data. Steps: 1. Render the volume bounding box using back-facing polygons only to ensure sampling starts at the furthest entry point relative to the camera. 2. Compute the ray direction vector \vec{d} in the fragment shader: \vec{d} = \text{eye.xyz} - \text{fragment.xyz}. 3. March along \vec{d} with a fixed step size SAMPLESTEP. 4. At each step, sample the scalar value v from the volume texture. 5. Apply valthreshold to modulate the voxel's brightness contribution. 6. Accumulate the result back-to-front and output the final color. Parameters: valthreshold: Controls the brightness of the voxels. SAMPLESTEP: Controls ray-advancement precision; smaller values improve quality but increase rendering time. Pitfalls: Requires back-facing polygon rendering; using front-facing polygons requires inverting the ray direction to fragment.xyz - eye.xyz and switching to front-to-back marching. The exact transfer function mapping v and valthreshold to brightness is not specified in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastbrightnesscontrol(eye, fragmentpos, volumetexture, valthreshold, samplestep, maxsteps): raydir = (eye[0] - fragmentpos[0], eye[1] - fragmentpos[1], eye[2] - fragmentpos[2]) length = (raydir[0]2 + raydir[1]2 + raydir[2]2)0.5 stepvec = (raydir[0]/length samplestep, raydir[1]/length samplestep, raydir[2]/length samplestep) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] currentpos = (fragmentpos[0] + stepvec[0], fragmentpos[1] + stepvec[1], fragmentpos[2] + stepvec[2]) for in range(maxsteps): if not (0.0 <= currentpos[0] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= currentpos[1] <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= currentpos[2] <= 1.0): break v = volumetexture[currentpos] brightness = v if v > valthreshold else 0.0 accumulatedcolor[0] += brightness accumulatedcolor[1] += brightness accumulatedcolor[2] += brightness currentpos = (currentpos[0] + stepvec[0], currentpos[1] + stepvec[1], currentpos[2] + stepvec[2]) return accumulatedcolor A back-to-front raycasting technique using the fragment shader volumeraycast02.fs. It uses valthreshold to control the density of the voxels. It requires back-facing polygon rendering and computes the ray direction as eye.xyz - fragment.xyz. Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray, determined by volume depth and SAMPLESTEP. Memory complexity is dominated by 3D volume texture storage. Smaller SAMPLESTEP improves quality but increases rendering time. Strengths include simple implementation for visualizing brightness variations. Limitations include the requirement for back-facing polygon rendering and the unspecified exact transfer function. The technique originated in the Visualization Library's GPU Raycast Volume Rendering guide. It is part of a suite of raycasting modes including Isosurface, MIP, and RaycastDensityControl. The implementation leverages fragment shaders for parallel volume rendering on the GPU. name: VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm
head: Vector-to-Closest-Point Ray Casting
body: The VCP Ray-Casting Algorithm renders a smooth surface approximation from a dense point cloud by storing vector-valued data in a grid structure. It solves the problem of noisy rendering caused by sensor noise and calibration errors in real-world LiDAR data, where points do not strictly lie on the scene surface. Unlike standard closest-point ray casting which selects the single nearest point (z-buffer), VCP uses the length of an interpolated vector to determine step sizes and the vector direction as the surface normal, allowing for adaptive marching and smooth shading. The method is typically implemented as a parallel GPU ray-casting kernel. Inputs and Outputs Input: A VCP grid where each cell stores either a scalar distance value (for empty blocks) or a 3D vector \vec{V} (for non-empty blocks). Input: Camera origin \mathbf{o}, viewing direction \mathbf{d}, and intersection bounds t{\text{start}}, t{\text{end}} with the volume bounding box. Input: Threshold \epsilon > 0. Output: Pixel color \mathbf{C} and surface normal \mathbf{n} at the intersection point. Data Structures The VCP grid organizes space into blocks. Each block contains: 1. Empty Block: A scalar distance d{\text{empty}} representing the distance from the block center to the nearest surface point. 2. Non-Empty Block: A 3D vector \vec{V} = (Vx, Vy, Vz) pointing from the block center to the closest surface point. Its magnitude |\vec{V}| represents the distance to the surface. Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Setup: For each pixel, define ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Compute the first and last intersection points with the object's bounding box to obtain t{\text{start}} and t{\text{end}}. 2. Marching Loop: March the ray from t{\text{start}} to t{\text{end}} using varying step sizes. Let P{\text{curr}} be the current sampling position. Determine the block containing P{\text{curr}}. Step Size Determination: If the block is empty, read the scalar distance d{\text{empty}}. If the block is non-empty, interpolate the VCP vector \vec{V} from neighboring blocks and compute its length |\vec{V}|. Let d{\text{next}} be the obtained distance value. Termination Check: If d{\text{next}} < \epsilon, assume a ray-surface intersection. Advance: If d{\text{next}} \ge \epsilon, set the step size for the next iteration to s = d{\text{next}} and advance the ray: P{\text{next}} = P{\text{curr}} + s \cdot \mathbf{d}. 3. Intersection Refinement: When d{\text{next}} < \epsilon, the exact intersection point P{\text{hit}} lies between the previous sampling point P{\text{prev}} and the current point P{\text{curr}}. Interpolate linearly to find the location where the distance is exactly \epsilon. Let d{\text{prev}} be the distance value at P{\text{prev}} and d{\text{curr}} be the value at P{\text{curr}} (which is < \epsilon). Compute interpolation factor \lambda = \frac{d{\text{prev}} - \epsilon}{d{\text{prev}} - d{\text{curr}}}. Calculate P{\text{hit}} = P{\text{prev}} + \lambda (P{\text{curr}} - P{\text{prev}}). 4. Normal Estimation: At P{\text{hit}}, the surface normal \mathbf{n} is the normalized VCP vector \vec{V} interpolated at that location, as the vector is always perpendicular to the surface. \mathbf{n} = \frac{\vec{V}}{|\vec{V}|}. 5. Lighting: Evaluate a local lighting model (e.g., Phong or Lambertian) using \mathbf{n} and the light direction to compute the pixel color. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vcpraycasting(rayorigin, raydir, vcpgrid, epsilon): # 1. Intersect ray with AABB (robust slab method) tenter, texit = -float('inf'), float('inf') for i in range(3): if raydir[i] != 0: t1 = (vcpgrid.bbox.min[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] t2 = (vcpgrid.bbox.max[i] - rayorigin[i]) / raydir[i] tenter = max(tenter, min(t1, t2)) texit = min(texit, max(t1, t2)) else: if rayorigin[i] < vcpgrid.bbox.min[i] or rayorigin[i] > vcpgrid.bbox.max[i]: return None if tenter > texit: return None # 2. Initialize marching t = tenter pprev = rayorigin + t raydir dprev = getdistanceat(vcpgrid, pprev) while t < texit: pcurr = rayorigin + t raydir dcurr = getdistanceat(vcpgrid, pcurr) # 3. Check for intersection if dcurr < epsilon: # 4. Refine intersection point if abs(dprev - dcurr) < 1e-9: phit = pcurr else: lam = (dprev - epsilon) / (dprev - dcurr) phit = pprev + lam (pcurr - pprev) # 5. Get Normal vcpvec = interpolatevcpvector(vcpgrid, phit) normlen = math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in vcpvec)) normal = (vcpvec[0]/normlen, vcpvec[1]/normlen, vcpvec[2]/normlen) # 6. Lighting (simple diffuse model) lightdir = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) lightlen = math.sqrt(sum(l2 for l in lightdir)) lightdir = (lightdir[0]/lightlen, lightdir[1]/lightlen, lightdir[2]/lightlen) diff = max(0.0, sum(nl for n,l in zip(normal, lightdir))) color = (diff, diff, diff) return color # 7. Advance stepsize = dcurr pprev = pcurr dprev = dcurr t += stepsize return None def getdistanceat(grid, point): block = grid.getblockat(point) if block.isempty: return block.scalardistance else: vec = interpolatevcpvector(grid, point) return math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in vec)) def interpolatevcpvector(grid, point): # Trilinear interpolation of vectors from 8 surrounding blocks coords = grid.worldtocell(point) ix, iy, iz = int(coords[0]), int(coords[1]), int(coords[2]) fx, fy, fz = coords[0] - ix, coords[1] - iy, coords[2] - iz # Boundary clamping helper def clamp(v, minv, maxv): return max(minv, min(v, maxv)) def getvec(x, y, z): x = clamp(x, 0, grid.width - 1) y = clamp(y, 0, grid.height - 1) z = clamp(z, 0, grid.depth - 1) return grid.getvectorat(x, y, z) v000 = getvec(ix, iy, iz) v100 = getvec(ix+1, iy, iz) v010 = getvec(ix, iy+1, iz) v110 = getvec(ix+1, iy+1, iz) v001 = getvec(ix, iy, iz+1) v101 = getvec(ix+1, iy, iz+1) v011 = getvec(ix, iy+1, iz+1) v111 = getvec(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) # Interpolate x v00 = (v100[0]-v000[0])fx + v000[0], (v100[1]-v000[1])fx + v000[1], (v100[2]-v000[2])fx + v000[2] v01 = (v110[0]-v010[0])fx + v010[0], (v110[1]-v010[1])fx + v010[1], (v110[2]-v010[2])fx + v010[2] v10 = (v101[0]-v001[0])fx + v001[0], (v101[1]-v001[1])fx + v001[1], (v101[2]-v001[2])fx + v001[2] v11 = (v111[0]-v011[0])fx + v011[0], (v111[1]-v011[1])fx + v011[1], (v111[2]-v011[2])fx + v011[2] # Interpolate y v0 = (v01[0]-v00[0])fy + v00[0], (v01[1]-v00[1])fy + v00[1], (v01[2]-v00[2])fy + v00[2] v1 = (v11[0]-v10[0])fy + v10[0], (v11[1]-v10[1])fy + v10[1], (v11[2]-v10[2])fy + v10[2] # Interpolate z return (v1[0]-v0[0])fz + v0[0], (v1[1]-v0[1])fz + v0[1], (v1[2]-v0[2])fz + v0[2] Parameters \epsilon: Threshold for surface intersection. Decreasing \epsilon allows the rendered surface to come arbitrarily close to the exact surface. Typical value: Not given in the sources. FPA is a variant used in LiDAR rendering (e.g., PCGen) to handle noise where points do not strictly lie on the surface. Instead of selecting the single closest point (standard CP ray-casting), FPA averages multiple points within a certain distance threshold near the closest point, weighting them by their inverse distance. This reduces noise in the rendered range image. It is often combined with a Ray-drop MLP to model return probability p = \text{MLP}(\theta', d, i), where \theta' is the viewing direction, d is distance, and i is intensity. The MLP has 4 layers, width 128, trained with Adam (lr 5e-3) for 10k iterations. Time Complexity: Adaptive stepping using VCP vector lengths skips empty space efficiently, reducing the number of samples compared to fixed-step ray casting. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the VCP grid, scaling with grid resolution and point cloud density. Strengths: Produces smooth surfaces from noisy point clouds; provides explicit surface normals for lighting; adaptive stepping allows efficient traversal of empty space. Limitations: Accuracy depends on the choice of \epsilon. The VCP method was introduced in the paper "Vector-to-Closest-Point Octree for Surface Ray-Casting". It addresses the limitations of standard closest-point ray casting, which is sensitive to noise and produces jagged surfaces. The method uses a VCP grid structure to store vector data, allowing for efficient ray traversal and smooth surface reconstruction. It has been applied in computer graphics for surface rendering from point clouds. name: Block-based Volume Rendering
head: Independent block rendering, Resource-independent volume rendering
body: Block-based volume rendering divides a scene into independent blocks, renders each block separately, and blends the results. It solves the problem of resource isolation in distributed or web-based rendering environments where multiple shaders cannot communicate or share intermediate state. Unlike methods that integrate all samples globally before deferred processing (e.g., MERF), this method uses segmented integration followed by inter-block blending, ensuring seamless boundaries and correct occlusion without requiring global synchronization. The method decomposes a ray traversal into two phases: intra-block rendering and inter-block compositing. It assumes a hierarchical representation of the scene with L Levels of Detail (LODs), where 2\times2 blocks are merged into one block between consecutive LODs l \in \{1, \dots, L\}. Inputs: Ray r(t) defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Scene representation: A set of K blocks intersected by the ray. Each block k contains Nk sample points. Per-sample data for block k: diffuse color \boldsymbol{c}i^k, specular feature \boldsymbol{f}i^k, and opacity \alphai^k for i=1 \dots Nk. These are retrieved from baked sparse voxel or triplane textures via an attribute query function f^{k,l}. Optional: A tiny deferred MLP \Phi^{k,l} for view-dependent effects and a proposal MLP \psi^{k,l} for sampling. Outputs: Final ray color \boldsymbol{C}(r), composed of diffuse color \boldsymbol{C}d(r) and specular feature \boldsymbol{F}(r). Data Structures: Block: A spatial partition of the volume. In hierarchical LODs, block size increases with LOD level l. Sample Point: Contains scalar opacity \alpha and vector attributes (color/feature). Algorithm Steps: 1. Intra-block Rendering: For each block k intersected by the ray, perform standard front-to-back volume rendering over its Nk samples to compute the block's aggregate properties. Calculate block diffuse color \boldsymbol{C}d^k: \boldsymbol{C}d^k = \sum{i=1}^{Nk} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^k) \right) \alphai^k \boldsymbol{c}i^k Calculate block specular feature \boldsymbol{F}^k: \boldsymbol{F}^k = \sum{i=1}^{Nk} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^k) \right) \alphai^k \boldsymbol{f}i^k Calculate block opacity \alpha^k: \alpha^k = \sum{i=1}^{Nk} \left( \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj^k) \right) \alphai^k Note: The block opacity is equivalent to the product of individual transmittances: 1 - \alpha^k = \prod{i=1}^{Nk} (1 - \alphai^k) 2. Inter-block Compositing: Depth-sort the K blocks along the ray from near to far. Blend the results of the blocks using the standard volume rendering equation, treating each block's aggregate opacity \alpha^k as a single "super-sample". Calculate final diffuse color: \boldsymbol{C}d(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \left( \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha^j) \right) \boldsymbol{C}d^k Calculate final specular feature: \boldsymbol{F}(r) = \sum{k=1}^{K} \left( \prod{j=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alpha^j) \right) \boldsymbol{F}^k The final color \boldsymbol{C}(r) combines these components, potentially applying the deferred MLP \Phi if view-dependent effects are required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blockbasedvolumerendering(ray, blocks): """ ray: object with origin, direction, and intersection range [tnear, tfar] blocks: list of Block objects intersected by the ray, sorted by distance from camera """ # Initialize accumulators for the final ray accdiffuse = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accspecular = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accopacity = 0.0 # Transmittance from previous blocks (initially 1.0, meaning no occlusion yet) transmittance = 1.0 for block in blocks: # Step 1: Intra-block rendering blockdiffuse = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] blockspecular = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] blockopacity = 0.0 blocktransmittance = 1.0 # Iterate through samples within this block for sample in block.samples: alpha = sample.opacity cdiffuse = sample.diffusecolor fspecular = sample.specularfeature # Contribution of this sample to the block's aggregates contribution = blocktransmittance alpha blockdiffuse += contribution cdiffuse blockspecular += contribution fspecular blockopacity += contribution # Update block transmittance for next sample blocktransmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Step 2: Inter-block blending # Blend the block's result into the ray using the ray's current transmittance accdiffuse += transmittance blockdiffuse accspecular += transmittance blockspecular accopacity += transmittance blockopacity # Update ray transmittance for next block transmittance = (1.0 - blockopacity) # Combine diffuse and specular components for final color finalcolor = accdiffuse + accspecular return finalcolor, accopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordering: Blocks must be strictly depth-sorted along the ray to ensure correct occlusion at inter-block edges. Lambertian Assumption: The equivalence to traditional volume rendering (where segmented integration equals global integration) holds strictly under Lambertian surface conditions where specular color is zero. Training/Rendering Consistency: To avoid discrepancies between training and inference, the same block-based pipeline must be used during training as during rendering. A specific implementation variant that emphasizes the blending mechanism across block boundaries. It ensures seamless boundaries and correct occlusion at inter-block edges, avoiding seams caused by simple averaging or incorrect depth sorting. It differs from MERF, which integrates all sample points together followed by deferred rendering, by using segmented integration (block-by-block) followed by inter-block blending. Without deferred rendering, this variant is entirely equivalent to traditional volume rendering. It supports hierarchical LODs where L is the total number of levels, and blocks are merged between consecutive LODs. Resource Independence: The primary advantage is that each block can be rendered independently by separate shaders or processes that cannot communicate, making it suitable for web-based or distributed rendering environments. Complexity: The computational complexity is linear with respect to the total number of samples N across all blocks, similar to standard volume rendering. Accuracy: Maintains 3D consistency and correct occlusion. Under Lambertian conditions, it is mathematically equivalent to global volume rendering. The method was introduced in the paper "City-on-Web: Real-Time Neural Rendering of Large-Scale Scenes on the Web". It addresses the limitations of previous neural rendering methods (like MERF) that required global integration and deferred rendering, which are difficult to implement in resource-constrained or isolated shader environments. The approach proves that segmented integration followed by alpha blending is equivalent to traditional volume rendering under Lambertian conditions, allowing for efficient, parallelizable rendering pipelines. name: Partial Segment Handling
head: Reduced Segment Length Opacity Adjustment, Segmental Replacement, Segmental Replacer Node
body: Partial Segment Handling addresses the "jerky edges" or stair-stepping artifacts that occur at volume boundaries or cutting surfaces when rays are sampled at fixed intervals, leaving an incomplete segment at the end of the ray march. It solves this by introducing a smaller final segment to fill the remaining distance to the boundary and adjusting its opacity to preserve the correct accumulated attenuation. A variant, Segmental Replacement, uses surface models to partially replace volume models to exhibit internal information while avoiding the rendering of the entire volume, facilitating real-time simulation. Inputs: Original segment length d1 (typically the fixed step size \Delta t used in the ray march). Original segment opacity \alpha1 (derived from the transfer function and extinction coefficient for length d1). Remaining distance to the volume boundary or cutting surface d2 (where 0 < d2 < d1). Optional surface model data for the replacement region. Outputs: Adjusted opacity \alpha2 for the partial segment. Rendered pixel color using either the adjusted volume segment or the surface counterpart. No specific complex data structures are required beyond the standard ray marching state. The method operates on scalar values associated with the current ray step. Segment State: Contains current position t, accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc}, and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}. Boundary Check: A boolean or distance value indicating if the next full step t + d1 exceeds the volume exit t{far} or a cutting plane. 1. Ray Marching: Perform standard front-to-back compositing for full segments of length d1 as defined in Direct volume ray casting. 2. Boundary Detection: At each step, check if the next sample position t{next} = t{current} + d1 exceeds the volume exit parameter t{far} or intersects a cutting plane. 3. Partial Segment Calculation: If a boundary is crossed: Calculate the remaining distance d2 = t{far} - t{current} (or distance to cutting plane). Sample the volume at the midpoint of the segment t{current} + d2/2. Determine the original opacity \alpha1 that would have been applied if the segment length were d1. Calculate the adjusted opacity \alpha2 for the shorter length d2 using the formula below. Composite the partial segment using \alpha2 and the color \mathbf{c} derived from the sampled data. Terminate the ray march. 4. Segmental Replacement (Variant): If using the Segmental Replacer Node strategy: Clip the volume model along vertical and horizontal planes to generate quadruple sub-parts of the original model. Identify regions where the volume model is replaced by a surface counterpart. Render the surface counterpart for the darker areas to exhibit internal information while avoiding the cost of rendering the entire volume model. The core adjustment for reduced segment length is: \alpha2 = 1 - (1 - \alpha1)^{\frac{d2}{d1}} Where: \alpha1 is the opacity of the original full segment of length d1. d1 is the original segment length (step size). d2 is the new, reduced segment length (remaining distance to boundary). \alpha2 is the adjusted opacity for the partial segment. This formula ensures that the transmission (1 - \alpha2) equals the transmission of the original segment raised to the power of the length ratio, preserving the Beer-Lambert law's exponential attenuation property for the partial distance. Segment Length (d1): Typically the fixed step size \Delta t used in the ray march. Adaptive strategies may vary d1 based on contribution. Transfer Function: Maps scalar values to extinction coefficient \sigma and color \mathbf{c}. Zero Remaining Distance: If d2 \approx 0, \alpha2 should be 0 to avoid division by zero or numerical instability in the exponent. Precision: Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient for the exponentiation, especially when d2 \ll d1. Adaptive Segments: Smaller segments are used when the contribution to the ray color is large, and longer segments when the contribution is low, to optimize for speed while yielding few artifacts. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def partialsegmenthandling(rayorigin, raydirection, tnear, tfar, stepsize, transferfunction, volumegrid, gridspacing, gridorigin): """ Renders a ray with partial segment handling at boundaries. Implements standard front-to-back compositing with opacity adjustment. """ def trilinearinterpolate(pos): # Standard trilinear interpolation gx = (pos[0] - gridorigin[0]) / gridspacing[0] gy = (pos[1] - gridorigin[1]) / gridspacing[1] gz = (pos[2] - gridorigin[2]) / gridspacing[2] gx = max(0.0, min(gx, volumegrid.shape[0] - 1.0)) gy = max(0.0, min(gy, volumegrid.shape[1] - 1.0)) gz = max(0.0, min(gz, volumegrid.shape[2] - 1.0)) x0, y0, z0 = int(gx), int(gy), int(gz) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 dx, dy, dz = gx - x0, gy - y0, gz - z0 v000 = volumegrid[x0, y0, z0] v100 = volumegrid[x1, y0, z0] v010 = volumegrid[x0, y1, z0] v110 = volumegrid[x1, y1, z0] v001 = volumegrid[x0, y0, z1] v101 = volumegrid[x1, y0, z1] v011 = volumegrid[x0, y1, z1] v111 = volumegrid[x1, y1, z1] c00 = v000 + dx (v100 - v000) c10 = v010 + dx (v110 - v010) c01 = v001 + dx (v101 - v001) c11 = v011 + dx (v111 - v011) c0 = c00 + dy (c10 - c00) c1 = c01 + dy (c11 - c01) return c0 + dz (c1 - c0) t = tnear acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 while t < tfar: tnext = t + stepsize ispartial = tnext > tfar d1 = stepsize d2 = tfar - t if ispartial else d1 tsample = t + d2 / 2.0 val = trilinearinterpolate(rayorigin + tsample raydirection) color, sigma = transferfunction(val) # Compute original opacity for full step alpha1 = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma d1) # Compute adjusted opacity for partial step using source formula alpha2 = 1.0 - math.pow((1.0 - alpha1), d2 / d1) alpha = alpha2 if ispartial else alpha1 # Front-to-back compositing weight = (1.0 - accopacity) alpha acccolor = ( acccolor[0] + weight color[0], acccolor[1] + weight color[1], acccolor[2] + weight color[2]) accopacity = accopacity + weight t = tnext if not ispartial else tfar return acccolor, accopacity A strategy where a surface model partially replaces a volume model to exhibit internal information while avoiding the rendering of the entire volume model. It is chosen when real-time simulation requires avoiding the cost of full volume rendering, and the trade-off is acceptable. An optimization where smaller segments are used when the contribution to the ray color is large, and longer segments when the contribution is low. This reduces artifacts while optimizing for speed. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples. The partial segment handling adds a constant-time check and calculation at the end of the ray march. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. No new data structures are required. Performance: The method is computationally inexpensive, adding minimal overhead to the ray march. It is suitable for real-time applications. Strengths: Eliminates jerky edges at boundaries without requiring global resampling or increased sampling density. Limitations: Only addresses artifacts at the end of the ray march. Partial Segment Handling was identified as a solution to common artifacts in volume rendering, specifically jerky edges caused by incomplete segments at volume boundaries. The technique is based on the Beer-Lambert law's exponential attenuation properties. The concept of using surface models to partially replace volume models (Segmental Replacement) was explored in hybrid rendering frameworks for real-time manipulation of volume and surface models. name: Plane-Based Sampling
head: Plan-Based Sampling Method, Plane-Based Sampling for Ray Casting
body: Plane-Based Sampling is a ray casting optimization technique that replaces per-voxel trilinear interpolation with a two-stage process: calculating ray-plane intersections and then interpolating between those intersection points using definite proportions. It solves the high computational cost of traditional Ray Casting Algorithms (RCA) by reducing the number of arithmetic operations required to determine optical properties at sampling points. Unlike standard methods that sample within every voxel individually, this method leverages the geometry of equidistant parallel planes to guarantee image density while significantly accelerating rendering speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume dataset (discrete samples), a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, and a sampling interval \Delta s. Output: The accumulated color and opacity for each pixel along the ray. Data Structures: The method relies on the geometric structure of the volume data, specifically treating it as a cluster of equidistant parallel planes. No additional complex data structures beyond the standard volume array are required. Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Cast a ray through the volume from back to front for each output image pixel. 2. Plane Identification: Identify the group of equidistant parallel planes in the volume data field that the ray travels through. 3. Intersection Calculation: Calculate the intersection points where the ray transacts with these parallel planes. 4. Proportional Interpolation: For sampling points located between adjacent intersection points, calculate their optical properties (color and opacity) using the formula of definite proportion and separated points, based on the properties of the intersection points. Formulas: The traditional RCA requires 17 additions and 16 multiplications per sampling point to locate the voxel and perform trilinear interpolation. The Plane-Based Sampling method replaces this with proportional interpolation between intersection points. If a sampling point S lies between two adjacent intersection points Ia and Ib with optical properties (\mathbf{c}a, \alphaa) and (\mathbf{c}b, \alphab), its properties are calculated as: \mathbf{c}S = \mathbf{c}a + \frac{d(S, Ia)}{d(Ia, Ib)} (\mathbf{c}b - \mathbf{c}a) \alphaS = \alphaa + \frac{d(S, Ia)}{d(Ia, Ib)} (\alphab - \alphaa) where d(\cdot, \cdot) denotes the Euclidean distance along the ray. Parameters: Sampling Interval (\Delta s): The distance between adjacent parallel planes. The method requires this distance to not far surpass the desired sampling interval to guarantee image density. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Plane Spacing: If the distance between adjacent parallel planes is significantly larger than the desired sampling interval, the method fails to guarantee image density, potentially leading to aliasing or loss of detail. Precision: The method relies on accurate intersection calculations, and standard floating-point precision issues in ray-plane intersection may apply. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def planebasedsampling(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata, planespacing, numplanes): """ rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z) raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), normalized volumedata: 3D array with bounds.min/max and interpolate(point) method planespacing: float, distance between adjacent parallel planes numplanes: int, number of parallel planes in the cluster Returns: accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity """ # Step 1: Cast ray from back to front tmin, tmax = computerayboxintersection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata) if tmin > tmax: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 frontopacity = 1.0 # Step 2 & 3: Identify parallel planes and calculate intersections # Assuming planes are aligned with the Z-axis planenormal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) intersectionpoints = [] for i in range(numplanes): planeoriginz = i planespacing planeorigin = (0.0, 0.0, planeoriginz) denom = dot(planenormal, raydirection) if abs(denom) > 1e-8: tintersect = dot(planenormal, (planeorigin - rayorigin)) / denom if tmin <= tintersect <= tmax: point = rayorigin + tintersect raydirection color, opacity = volumedata.interpolate(point) intersectionpoints.append({'t': tintersect, 'color': color, 'opacity': opacity}) # Sort intersection points from back to front (decreasing t) intersectionpoints.sort(key=lambda k: k['t'], reverse=True) # Step 4: Interpolate between intersection points for i in range(len(intersectionpoints) - 1): p1 = intersectionpoints[i] p2 = intersectionpoints[i+1] distsegment = p2['t'] - p1['t'] if distsegment <= 0: continue # Determine sampling points within this segment based on planespacing numsamples = max(1, int(distsegment / planespacing)) for j in range(numsamples): ratio = j / numsamples # Definite proportion interpolation colorsample = lerpvec3(p1['color'], p2['color'], ratio) opacitysample = lerpscalar(p1['opacity'], p2['opacity'], ratio) # Front-to-back compositing alpha = opacitysample color = colorsample accumulatedcolor = ( accumulatedcolor[0] + frontopacity color[0] alpha, accumulatedcolor[1] + frontopacity color[1] alpha, accumulatedcolor[2] + frontopacity color[2] alpha) accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + frontopacity alpha frontopacity = frontopacity (1.0 - alpha) if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def lerpvec3(a, b, t): return (a[0] + t(b[0]-a[0]), a[1] + t(b[1]-a[1]), a[2] + t(b[2]-a[2])) def lerpscalar(a, b, t): return a + t(b-a) def computerayboxintersection(origin, direction, volumedata): tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if direction[i] == 0: if origin[i] < volumedata.bounds.min[i] or origin[i] > volumedata.bounds.max[i]: return float('inf'), 0.0 else: t1 = (volumedata.bounds.min[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] t2 = (volumedata.bounds.max[i] - origin[i]) / direction[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) return tmin, tmax The baseline method that Plane-Based Sampling improves upon. It performs trilinear interpolation for every sampling point, requiring 17 additions and 16 multiplications per point. A related approach that replaces sampling points with intersection points along three groups of parallel planes along orthometric axes. However, it cannot guarantee image density when the distance between adjacent parallel planes far surpasses the sampling interval. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of arithmetic operations per sampling point compared to traditional trilinear interpolation. The traditional RCA takes 17 additions and 16 multiplications per point. The Plane-Based Sampling method is described as "faster" and improves rendering speed by over three times. The exact operation count is not given. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method does not appear to require additional large data structures beyond the volume data itself. Measured Performance: In the context of fast reconstruction of 3D biomedical models from sequential images, the method improves rendering speed by over three times compared with the conventional algorithm while maintaining image quality. Strengths: Significantly faster rendering speed; reduces computational load by using fewer intersection points and proportional division; maintains image quality. Limitations: If the distance between adjacent parallel planes is significantly larger than the desired sampling interval, the method fails to guarantee image density, potentially leading to aliasing or loss of detail. When to use: When fast reconstruction of 3D biomedical models from sequential images is required and the volume data can be effectively represented by equidistant parallel planes. When not to use: When high image density is critical and the plane spacing cannot be kept close to the sampling interval, as this leads to aliasing. The method was proposed to improve the traditional Ray Casting Algorithm (RCA) for the fast reconstruction of three-dimensional biomedical models from sequential images. It addresses the high proportion of time spent on sampling optical properties (about 39% of rendering time) in traditional RCA. The work cites Qian et al. [11] as prior art that used intersection points along three groups of parallel planes but failed to guarantee image density under certain conditions.
