name: Improved Ray Casting Volume Rendering
head: Improved light projected volume rendering, Light projected volume rendering method
body: Improved Ray Casting Volume Rendering is a direct volume rendering technique optimized for large-scale, regular 3D spatial data fields (specifically seismic data) by prioritizing rendering speed and high-frequency component preservation over physical lighting accuracy. It distinguishes itself from standard ray casting by reversing the classification and interpolation order (interpolating raw data before classification) and replacing floating-point arithmetic with fixed-point operations to accelerate trilinear interpolation. Unlike Standard Ray Casting, which classifies data first and risks filtering high-frequency color components, this method ensures the convolution operation acts on the original discrete data field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A regular 3D scalar data field V (e.g., seismic data in SEGY format), camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), a transfer function T mapping scalar values to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha, and an empty voxel marker value. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains a synthesized RGBA color value. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array of scalar values stored using fixed-point number representation for interpolation calculations to avoid time-consuming floating-point operations. Sampling Points: K equal-interval points along the ray. Parameters: K: The number of equal-interval sampling points selected along the ray for each pixel. Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Definition: For each pixel, define a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} intersecting the volume bounding box. 2. Sampling: Select K equal-interval sampling points along the ray segment within the volume. 3. Interpolation (First): For each sampling point \mathbf{p}i, perform trilinear interpolation on the original discrete 3D scalar data field V using the eight closest grid points. This yields an interpolated scalar value V{interp}. Note: This step avoids the high-frequency component loss associated with classifying discrete data before interpolation. Implementation Detail: Use fixed-point arithmetic for the interpolation weights and value accumulation to improve performance. 4. Classification (Second): Apply the transfer function T to the interpolated scalar value V{interp} to obtain the color \mathbf{c}i and opacity \alphai for the sample. \mathbf{c}i, \alphai = T(V{interp}). 5. Shading (Ignored): Explicitly ignore lighting effects and gradient calculations. The source states that for seismic data, gradient values change disorderly and lighting effects are weak, so this step is skipped to minimize computation. 6. Compositing: Synthesize the color and opacity values from front to rear using the front-to-back compositing equation. Initialize accumulated color \mathbf{C}{acc} = (0,0,0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. For each sample i from front to back: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \mathbf{c}i \cdot \alphai \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot \alphai 7. Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} approaches 1 (indicating the pixel is effectively opaque), skip the remaining voxels/samples for that ray to eliminate invalid computation. 8. Empty Voxel Skipping: Skip sampling points that fall within empty voxels (voxels with no data contribution) to accelerate rendering speed. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def improvedraycasting(volumedata, volumebounds, camera, transferfunction, K, emptyvalue): """ volumedata: 3D list/array of scalar values (fixed-point representation preferred) volumebounds: tuple (minx, maxx, miny, maxy, minz, maxz) camera: object with origin o, direction d, resolution, and getray(x, y) method transferfunction: callable scalar -> (colortuple, opacityfloat) K: int, number of sampling points per ray emptyvalue: scalar value representing empty space in volumedata """ height, width = camera.resolution # Initialize output image with RGBA tuples output = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] def intersectvolume(rayo, rayd, bounds): # Slab method to find entry (tnear) and exit (tfar) parameters tmin, tmax = 0.0, float('inf') for i in range(3): if rayd[i] == 0.0: if rayo[i] < bounds[2i] or rayo[i] > bounds[2i+1]: return None, None else: t1 = (bounds[2i] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] t2 = (bounds[2i+1] - rayo[i]) / rayd[i] tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax def isemptyvoxel(p, bounds, data, emptyval): # Check if point is within volume bounds if not (bounds[0] <= p[0] <= bounds[1] and bounds[2] <= p[1] <= bounds[3] and bounds[4] <= p[2] <= bounds[5]): return False # Map continuous coordinate to integer grid indices ix, iy, iz = int(p[0]), int(p[1]), int(p[2]) # Clamp to valid array bounds ix = max(0, min(ix, len(data)-1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, len(data[0])-1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, len(data[0][0])-1)) return data[ix][iy][iz] == emptyval for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayo, rayd = camera.getray(x, y) tnear, tfar = intersectvolume(rayo, rayd, volumebounds) if tnear is None: continue dt = (tfar - tnear) / K acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accopacity = 0.0 for k in range(K): t = tnear + k dt p = (rayo[0] + t rayd[0], rayo[1] + t rayd[1], rayo[2] + t rayd[2]) # Safety bounds check if not (volumebounds[0] <= p[0] <= volumebounds[1] and volumebounds[2] <= p[1] <= volumebounds[3] and volumebounds[4] <= p[2] <= volumebounds[5]): continue # Skip empty voxels if isemptyvoxel(p, volumebounds, volumedata, emptyvalue): continue # Step 3: Interpolate original data first (fixed-point arithmetic) vinterp = trilinearinterpolatefixedpoint(p, volumedata) # Step 4: Classify after interpolation color, opacity = transferfunction(vinterp) # Step 7: Early termination check if accopacity >= 0.99: break # Step 6: Front-to-back compositing weight = (1.0 - accopacity) opacity acccolor = (acccolor[0] + weight color[0], acccolor[1] + weight color[1], acccolor[2] + weight color[2]) accopacity = accopacity + weight output[y][x] = (acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accopacity) return output def trilinearinterpolatefixedpoint(p, volumedata): """ Performs trilinear interpolation using fixed-point arithmetic logic. p: 3D coordinate (x, y, z) volumedata: 3D array of scalars """ ix, iy, iz = int(p[0]), int(p[1]), int(p[2]) fx, fy, fz = p[0] - ix, p[1] - iy, p[2] - iz # Boundary clamping for indices ix = max(0, min(ix, len(volumedata)-1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, len(volumedata[0])-1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)) # Fetch 8 surrounding voxels v000 = volumedata[ix][iy][iz] v100 = volumedata[min(ix+1, len(volumedata)-1)][iy][iz] v010 = volumedata[ix][min(iy+1, len(volumedata[0])-1)][iz] v110 = volumedata[min(ix+1, len(volumedata)-1)][min(iy+1, len(volumedata[0])-1)][iz] v001 = volumedata[ix][iy][min(iz+1, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)] v101 = volumedata[min(ix+1, len(volumedata)-1)][iy][min(iz+1, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)] v011 = volumedata[ix][min(iy+1, len(volumedata[0])-1)][min(iz+1, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)] v111 = volumedata[min(ix+1, len(volumedata)-1)][min(iy+1, len(volumedata[0])-1)][min(iz+1, len(volumedata[0][0])-1)] # Interpolation using fixed-point math (logical structure) # In practice, weights and values are scaled integers to avoid floating-point arithmetic w000 = (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) w100 = fx(1-fy)(1-fz) w010 = (1-fx)fy(1-fz) w110 = fxfy(1-fz) w001 = (1-fx)(1-fy)fz w101 = fx(1-fy)fz w011 = (1-fx)fyfz w111 = fxfyfz return (w000v000 + w100v100 + w010v010 + w110v110 + w001v001 + w101v101 + w011v011 + w111v111) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot K) per pixel, where N is the number of pixels and K is the number of samples. The use of fixed-point arithmetic reduces the constant factor for interpolation compared to floating-point. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Strengths: Significantly faster rendering speed for large-scale seismic data due to skipped lighting calculations, fixed-point interpolation, and early termination. Preserves high-frequency color components better than standard ray casting by interpolating before classification. Limitations: Not physically accurate due to ignored lighting/shading. When to use: Ideal for real-time or near-real-time visualization of large-scale, regular 3D scalar fields (like seismic data) where interpretive clarity and speed are prioritized over photorealistic lighting. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes requiring accurate surface shading, specular highlights, or where gradient-based normal estimation is critical for visual understanding. The method was introduced in the context of 3D visualization for seismic data processing. It addresses the inherent defects of standard ray casting, specifically its heavy calculation overhead and time/space complexity which increases with data volume. Seismic data is characterized as large-scale, distributed, scattered material with different eigenvalues, no clear interfaces, and disorderly gradient directions, making traditional lighting models ineffective. The method was implemented using the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) and MFC under Microsoft Windows to display SEGY format data. Research on 3D Visualization Method of Seismic Data, https://doi.org/10.14257/ijsip.2016.9.5.39, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Multi-Pass and Compositing Techniques
head: Multi-Pass Volume Rendering, Image-Order Compositing, Two-Pass Ray Casting
body: Multi-Pass and Compositing Techniques address the computational complexity and hardware limitations of single-pass direct volume ray casting by decomposing the rendering pipeline into sequential stages. This family solves the problem of limited shader instruction counts and the lack of conditional fragment discard in early graphics hardware by isolating distinct operations—such as light attenuation, boundary detection, and ray integration—into separate rendering passes. It differs from single-pass ray marching by trading additional draw calls for the ability to reuse intermediate state stored in 2D render targets and leverage fixed-function hardware blending modes. All methods in this family build on the core loop structure defined in Image-order rendering and Direct volume ray casting. The core computational engine is split across N passes (N \ge 2), where intermediate results are persisted in 2D textures (render targets) and accessed in subsequent passes. The general mechanism involves: 1. State Persistence: Intermediate state (e.g., ray entry/exit points, accumulated light, accumulated color) is written to 2D textures after each pass and read in the next. 2. Decoupling: Distinct physical or logical operations are isolated into separate passes, such as separating light attenuation from color compositing, or boundary intersection from ray marching integration. 3. Hardware Blending: Many techniques rely on hardware-supported blending modes (e.g., 'over', 'under', additive) to accumulate values across passes, avoiding the need for complex atomic operations or conditional shader logic. 4. Geometry Proxy: Slicing or proxy geometry (e.g., slice planes, bounding box faces) is often used to drive the rendering passes, allowing the GPU rasterizer to handle ray intersection logic implicitly. Image-Order Volumetric Compositing is a volume rendering framework proposed by Marc Levoy, originally implemented on PIXEL-PLANES 5 hardware. It solves the problem of efficiently generating composite projections of volumetric data by decoupling the computation of optical properties (color and opacity) from the ray-casting process. Unlike object-order methods that traverse the volume structure, this method pre-processes the scalar data into dedicated color and opacity arrays, allowing rays to sample these pre-computed fields directly. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Two-pass and Multi-pass Techniques, by its reliance on image-order compositing where the final pixel color is derived by back-to-front blending of pre-shaded samples. Two-pass and multi-pass techniques split the direct volume ray casting workload into multiple rendering passes to isolate distinct computational stages. This family addresses hardware limitations, such as restricted shader instruction counts or the lack of conditional fragment discard, by decomposing complex operations like light attenuation, boundary detection, and ray integration into sequential steps. It differs from single-pass ray marching by trading additional draw calls for the ability to reuse intermediate state stored in 2D render targets and leverage fixed-function hardware blending modes. Compositing and Output Generation defines the final stage of direct volume ray casting, where discrete volumetric samples are aggregated into a 2D image pixel. It solves the problem of optical integration, determining how light emitted or scattered by volume elements is attenuated by absorption and combined with background light. This family is distinct from Projection and MIP Techniques because it explicitly tracks opacity and transmittance for alpha blending, preserving depth cues, whereas MIP methods discard opacity for order-independent extremum aggregation. It differs from Volume Raycasting Output Generation by focusing on the mathematical accumulation logic itself, while the sibling article covers the broader implementation pipeline including ray traversal and transfer function sampling. The concept of image-order compositing was introduced by Marc Levoy in the context of the PIXEL-PLANES 5 hardware, which allowed for efficient per-pixel processing and blending. The shift toward multi-pass techniques was driven by the architectural constraints of early graphics hardware, specifically the limited number of arithmetic instructions available in fragment shaders and the inability to easily discard fragments based on complex volume traversal logic. These methods became standard in software renderers and early GPU implementations to achieve high-quality volume rendering without requiring specialized hardware for ray tracing. Levoy, M. name: Image-Order Volumetric Compositing
head: Image-Order Compositing, Levoy's Image-Order Compositing, Levoy's Image-Order Volume Rendering
body: Image-Order Volumetric Compositing is a volume rendering framework proposed by Marc Levoy, originally implemented on the PIXEL-PLANES 5 hardware. It solves the problem of generating high-quality composite projections of volumetric data by decoupling the definition of optical properties (color and opacity) from the ray-casting integration step. Unlike methods that compute shading and compositing simultaneously in a single pass, this approach pre-processes the scalar data into separate color and opacity arrays, allowing for efficient empty space skipping and occlusion culling to achieve real-time or near real-time performance. The method operates in two distinct phases: preprocessing to generate optical property arrays, and image-order ray casting to composite the final image. Inputs and Outputs Input: A scalar data volume S, defined on a 3D grid. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains a single composite color value. Data Structures The algorithm generates two new 3D arrays from the input scalar array S: 1. Color Array (Sc): Stores the color value at each grid location. 2. Opacity Array (Ss): Stores the opacity (alpha) value at each grid location. These arrays are defined over the same grid as S. The values are determined by interpolation functions fc(x,y,z) for color and fs(x,y,z) for opacity, which are derived from Sc and Ss respectively. Preprocessing Steps 1. Gradient Computation: Compute the gradient vector \nabla S at each data sample. This is done by partially differentiating the interpolation function f(x,y,z) with respect to x, y, and z. Pitfall: If the interpolation function is not first-derivative continuous, aliasing artifacts occur due to discontinuous normal vectors. A smoother set of gradient vectors can be obtained using central differencing. 2. Color Array Generation (Sc): Perform a shading operation (e.g., Phong illumination) at each data sample in S. The normal vector for shading is the unit gradient vector derived in Step 1. The resulting color values populate Sc. 3. Opacity Array Generation (Ss): Perform surface classification on S to determine opacity. For a single iso-surface at constant value v with target opacity v{ought}: Ss(x,y,z) = \begin{cases} v{ought} & \text{if } S(x,y,z) = v \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} To reduce aliasing artifacts, Ss(x,y,z) is set to a value close to v{ought} if S(x,y,z) is close to v. To maintain a constant transition region thickness, the opacity falls off at a rate inversely proportional to the magnitude of the local gradient vector |\nabla S|. For multiple iso-surfaces, classification mappings are applied separately, and the resulting opacities are combined. Ray Casting and Compositing Steps 1. Ray Definition: Cast rays from each pixel through the volume. 2. Sampling: Sample the Sc and Ss arrays at evenly spaced locations along each ray. 3. Interpolation: Determine the color C and opacity \alpha at each sample location using the trilinear interpolation functions fc and fs. 4. Background: Add a fully opaque background to the ray. 5. Compositing: Composite the sampled values in back-to-front order to produce a single color for the pixel. The standard front-to-back or back-to-front compositing equation is applied: C{out} = C{sample} \cdot \alpha{sample} + C{accumulated} \cdot (1 - \alpha{sample}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{sample} + \alpha{accumulated} \cdot (1 - \alpha{sample}) (Note: The specific compositing order is back-to-front as stated in the source, which implies accumulating from the farthest sample to the nearest). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageordervolumetriccompositing(volumeS, resolution, numsamplesperray): """ Implements Levoy's Image-Order Volumetric Compositing. Args: volumeS: 3D array of scalar data samples. resolution: (width, height) of the output image. numsamplesperray: Number of evenly spaced samples per ray. Returns: outputimage: 2D array of RGB colors. """ # Preprocessing Phase # 1. Compute Gradient Array # Compute partial derivatives of the interpolation function f(x,y,z) # using central differencing to ensure first-derivative continuity. gradientarray = computegradient(volumeS) # 2. Generate Color Array Sc # For each voxel, compute normal = normalize(gradientarray[voxel]) # Apply Phong illumination model using normal and light direction Sc = applyshading(volumeS, gradientarray) # 3. Generate Opacity Array Ss # Define classification function for iso-surface v with opacity vought v = 0.5 # Example iso-value vought = 1.0 Ss = zeroslike(volumeS) for x, y, z in gridindices(volumeS): val = volumeS[x, y, z] gradmag = magnitude(gradientarray[x, y, z]) # Transition region logic: opacity falls off inversely proportional to gradient magnitude # Simplified: if close to v, assign opacity based on distance and gradmag if abs(val - v) < threshold: # Approximate constant transition thickness # Opacity is vought scaled by inverse gradient magnitude factor Ss[x, y, z] = vought (1.0 / (1.0 + gradmag)) else: Ss[x, y, z] = 0.0 # Ray Casting Phase outputimage = zeros((resolution[0], resolution[1], 3)) for pixelx in range(resolution[0]): for pixely in range(resolution[1]): # Define ray origin and direction for this pixel rayorigin, raydirection = getray(pixelx, pixely) # Initialize accumulated color and alpha # Add fully opaque background acccolor = backgroundcolor # e.g., (0, 0, 0) accalpha = 1.0 # Sample along ray in back-to-front order # Note: Back-to-front means starting from farthest point along ray for i in range(numsamplesperray): # Calculate sample position tfar = maxdistance tnear = 0.0 t = tfar - (i (tfar - tnear) / numsamplesperray) samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Check if sample is within volume bounds if not isinsidevolume(samplepos): continue # Interpolate color and opacity from precomputed arrays colorsample = trilinearinterpolate(Sc, samplepos) alphasample = trilinearinterpolate(Ss, samplepos) # Composite back-to-front # Cout = Csample alphasample + Cacc (1 - alphasample) # alphaout = alphasample + alphaacc (1 - alphasample) # However, standard front-to-back is more common for accumulation. # Source specifies back-to-front. # If back-to-front, we accumulate from far to near. # The formula remains the same, but the order of application changes. # Let's assume standard compositing equation applied in back-to-front order. acccolor = colorsample alphasample + acccolor (1 - alphasample) accalpha = alphasample + accalpha (1 - alphasample) # Optimization: Empty space skipping and occlusion culling # If accalpha is 1.0, break early (occlusion culling) if accalpha >= 1.0: break outputimage[pixelx, pixely] = acccolor return outputimage def computegradient(volume): # Central differencing for first-derivative continuity # Returns 3D vector field pass def applyshading(volumeS, gradientarray): # Phong illumination model # Normal = normalize(gradient) # Color = ambient + diffuse + specular pass Parameters S: Array of data samples. Sc: Array defining color at each grid location. Ss: Array defining opacity at each grid location. f(x,y,z): Interpolation function for sample value. fc(x,y,z): Interpolation function for color (transfer function). fs(x,y,z): Interpolation function for opacity (transfer function). v: Constant iso-surface value. v{ought}: Target opacity for the iso-surface. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Aliasing: Discontinuous normal vectors due to non-first-derivative continuous interpolation functions cause aliasing artifacts. Transition Region: If the opacity fall-off is not inversely proportional to the gradient magnitude, the transition region thickness will vary, leading to visual inconsistencies. Multiple Iso-surfaces: Must be handled by separately applying classification mappings and combining opacities. Performance: The system achieved real-time or near real-time performance on the PIXEL-PLANES 5 hardware. Acceleration: Uses empty space skipping and occlusion culling to accelerate rendering speed. Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Decouples shading and compositing, allowing for efficient hardware acceleration and preprocessing. Limitations: Requires significant preprocessing to generate Sc and Ss arrays. Memory usage increases due to storing these additional arrays. Origin: Proposed by Marc Levoy. Implementation: Implemented on the PIXEL-PLANES 5 hardware, which consisted of 32 independently programmable 20-MFLOPS graphics processors, 16 independently programmable renderers with 1/4 million pixel processors, a 512x512 pixel color frame buffer, and a 640 Mb/sec ring network. History: The algorithm was described in Levoy's work on image-order volumetric compositing. It was one of the early frameworks to demonstrate real-time volume rendering capabilities using specialized hardware. name: Two-pass and Multi-pass Techniques
head: Multi-pass Volume Rendering, Split-Pass Rendering
body: Two-pass and multi-pass techniques decompose the volume rendering pipeline into sequential rendering passes, using 2D textures (render targets) to persist intermediate state such as ray boundaries, light attenuation, or accumulation buffers between passes. This approach solves the limitations of early GPU hardware (e.g., lack of dynamic flow control or limited texture sampling) and optimizes performance by decoupling complex logical operations—such as ray intersection, light transport, and compositing—into specialized stages. It differs from single-pass methods by introducing a data dependency between passes, and from sibling techniques like Image-Order Volumetric Compositing by explicitly managing state persistence across distinct rasterization events rather than relying on a single integrated shader loop. All methods in this family build on the core loop structure defined in Image-order rendering and Direct volume ray casting. The core computational engine is split across N passes (N \ge 2), where intermediate results are persisted in 2D textures (render targets) and accessed in subsequent passes. The general mechanism involves: 1. State Persistence: Intermediate state (e.g., ray entry/exit points, accumulated light, accumulated color) is written to 2D textures after each pass and read in the next. 2. Decoupling: Distinct physical or logical operations are isolated into separate passes, such as separating light attenuation from color compositing, or boundary intersection from ray marching integration. 3. Hardware Blending: Many techniques rely on hardware-supported blending modes (e.g., 'over', 'under', additive) to accumulate values across passes, avoiding the need for complex atomic operations or conditional shader logic. 4. Geometry Proxy: Slicing or proxy geometry (e.g., slice planes, bounding box faces) is often used to drive the rendering passes, allowing the GPU rasterizer to handle ray intersection logic implicitly. Half-angle slicing is a two-pass per-slice rendering technique that synchronizes the slicing axis with the illumination computation to integrate volumetric lighting, including hard shadows and indirect scattering, within interactive applications. It solves the problem of computing accurate volumetric shadows without the memory overhead of pre-computed 3D shadow maps by orienting slice planes perpendicular to the half-angle vector between the eye and light directions. This orientation allows a single slice to be rendered from both the observer's and the light source's viewpoints, decoupling light transport from data volume resolution. Unlike standard view-aligned slicing, it minimizes the number of slices required to resolve lighting details such as specular highlights and avoids attenuation leakage artifacts common in 2D shadow buffer approaches. Two-pass volume rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that decouples light attenuation computation from color compositing into two distinct rasterization passes. It solves the performance bottleneck of calculating complex illumination for every pixel in real-time by pre-computing light accumulation in a dedicated light buffer during the first pass, then using this data for a fast, real-time rendering pass. It differs from standard direct volume ray casting by moving the expensive light integration step off the critical rendering path, and from single-pass methods by requiring a two-stage data dependency between the light buffer and the frame buffer. Two-Pass Ray Marching Volume Rendering is a GPU-based direct volume rendering technique that decouples the determination of ray entry and exit points from the actual volume integration (ray marching). It solves the problem of efficiently computing ray-volume intersections without requiring complex ray-triangle intersection logic in the main rendering pass by rasterizing the volume's bounding box faces into offscreen textures. Unlike single-pass raycasting, which must compute intersections within the fragment shader, this method uses hardware rasterization for boundary detection, reducing fragment shader complexity at the cost of an additional render pass and texture memory overhead. Multi-pass GPU Ray-Casting is a stream-based rendering technique that implements direct volume ray casting by splitting the ray traversal loop across multiple rendering passes, using 2D texture render targets to persist intermediate ray state. It solves the limitation of early GPU hardware (specifically Pixel Shader 2.0 era) which lacked dynamic flow control, preventing single-pass ray marchers from terminating rays early. By decoupling ray integration from termination checks, it achieves significant performance gains over unaccelerated ray casting and slice-based volume rendering (SBVR) through early ray termination and empty-space skipping. Locally Adaptive Volume Rendering (LAVR) is a two-pass technique that enhances feature visibility and reduces noise in volume rendering by dynamically adjusting fragment opacity based on the local density of contributing voxels. Unlike standard direct volume rendering which uses a fixed per-voxel opacity, LAVR decouples the classification of relevant data from the final compositing, allowing the renderer to adaptively suppress noise in sparse regions while preserving sharp borders in dense regions. It sets itself apart from siblings like Two-pass volume rendering by specifically targeting the statistical distribution of contributions per pixel rather than just splitting light transport or ray marching steps. An implementation approach for fixed-function hardware or Shader Model 2.0 limits, using additive frame-buffer blending over multiple passes with a stencil occlusion method. Shader Model 3.0 is required for the single-pass version because the number of texture samples needed exceeds the limits of Shader Model 2.0. A method to alleviate aliasing in direct rendering of binary volumes by using iterative 3D texture mapping with trilinear interpolation to generate gray level intensity data around surface boundaries. Render the binary volume using 3D texture mapping, which uses trilinear interpolation for sample points around surface boundaries, generating intensity values between 0 and 1. Iteratively repeat the process: Write each texture-mapped slice (without blending) from the frame buffer back to the texture memory as a slice of a refined volume. Iterations: Two or three iterations are normally sufficient for reasonably smooth surfaces, with higher rendering cost for more iterations. Compositing that takes place on the rendering engine. Multi-pass rendering is used. If rendering takes place on the VolumePro 1000 board, it leverages the capability of rendering multiple volumes in a single context with on-board image compositing. A technique using a combination of multiple RGBAZ value storage in the frame buffer and multi-pass rendering to yield correct transparency results with minimum performance hit. Storing more than one set of RGBAZ values is costly due to additional memory requirements and is limited by the number of values the hardware can store. Render the heterogeneous scene (containing both surface and volume objects) twice. First pass: render from the imaginary eye position. Second pass: render from the actual eye position. Combine the results of both passes to accomplish special effects such as reflection and refraction. The concept of splitting rendering tasks across multiple passes originated from the need to handle transparency and complex lighting on early graphics hardware that lacked the computational power or shader flexibility for single-pass solutions. Techniques like multi-pass multi-buffer transparency were developed to address the accumulation of round-off errors in 8-bit frame buffers. The specific application of multi-pass techniques to volume rendering, such as decoupling ray marching or light transport, emerged with the advent of programmable GPUs, allowing developers to bypass hardware limitations like the lack of dynamic flow control in Pixel Shader 2.0. These methods are widely used in medical visualization, scientific data exploration, and real-time rendering engines where performance optimization and visual fidelity trade-offs are critical. name: Half-angle slicing
head: Half angle slice axis, Halfway vector slicing, Kniss et al, Two-pass slice rendering for lighting, Volumetric lighting using half-angle slicing
body: Half-angle slicing is a two-pass per-slice rendering technique that synchronizes the slicing axis with the illumination computation to integrate volumetric lighting, including hard shadows and indirect scattering, within interactive applications. It solves the problem of computing accurate volumetric shadows without the memory overhead of pre-computed 3D shadow maps by orienting slice planes perpendicular to the half-angle vector between the eye and light directions. This orientation allows a single slice to be rendered from both the observer's and the light source's viewpoints, decoupling light transport from data volume resolution. Unlike standard view-aligned slicing, it minimizes the number of slices required to resolve lighting details such as specular highlights and avoids attenuation leakage artifacts common in 2D shadow buffer approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume dataset (scalar field), transfer function (density, color, opacity), camera position and projection, light direction (directional) or position (point), bounding box of the volume. Outputs: Final composited image in the eye buffer. Data Structures: Light Buffer: A 2D texture (render target) storing light transmissivity/attenuation. Format: 16-bit floating point per channel (e.g., R16G16B16A16Sfloat) to preserve HDR values. Resolution: 30%–50% higher than the frame buffer to mitigate shadow boundary artifacts. Initialized to 1 - \text{light intensity} (or an arbitrary image for spotlights). Eye Buffer: A 2D texture (render target) for accumulating the final composited color. Format: Same as Light Buffer. Push Constants: LightPC: lightMVP (4x4 matrix, 64 bytes), opacityCorrection (float, 4 bytes), densityMin (float, 4 bytes), densityMax (float, 4 bytes). Total: 76 bytes. EyePC: eyeMVP (4x4 matrix, 64 bytes), lightMVP (4x4 matrix, 64 bytes), opacityCorrection (float, 4 bytes), ambient (float, 4 bytes), densityMin (float, 4 bytes), densityMax (float, 4 bytes). Total: 144 bytes. Note: Vulkan guarantees only 128 bytes for push constants; this requires a driver supporting \ge 256 bytes. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute Half-Angle Vector: Calculate the normalized camera vector pointing from the camera to the object (\vec{v}) and the normalized light vector (\vec{l}) in the object's local space. \vec{v} = \text{normalize}(\text{objectPos} - \text{cameraPos}) \vec{l} = \text{normalize}(\text{lightDirection}) Compute the dot product d = \vec{l} \cdot \vec{v}. If d > 0: The half-angle vector \vec{h} is halfway between \vec{l} and \vec{v}. \vec{h} = \text{normalize}(\vec{l} + \vec{v}) If d < 0: The light is behind the volume relative to the view. The half-angle vector \vec{h} is halfway between \vec{l} and the inverted view direction (-\vec{v}). \vec{h} = \text{normalize}(\vec{l} - \vec{v}) 2. Determine Slice Bounds and Count: Project the 8 vertices of the volume's bounding box onto \vec{h} to find the minimum (min\dist) and maximum (max\dist) extents. min\dist = \min{i=0..7} (\vec{h} \cdot \text{boxVertex}i) max\dist = \max{i=0..7} (\vec{h} \cdot \text{boxVertex}i) Calculate the total length along the half-vector: L = |max\dist - min\dist|. Determine the number of slices N (e.g., default 256) and the step size: stepSize = \frac{L}{N} 3. Iterate Slices: For each slice index s from 0 to N-1: a. Generate Slice Geometry: Calculate the center of the slice plane: C = \text{origin} + \vec{h} \cdot (min\dist + s \cdot stepSize + \frac{stepSize}{2}) Intersect the slice plane with the volume bounding box to get a polygon of vertices. Sort these vertices counter-clockwise around C using the cross-product test with \vec{h}: python def comparevertices(A, B, C, normal): # Returns 1 if B is clockwise from A relative to C, else -1 if dot(normal, cross(A - C, B - C)) <= 0: return 1 else: return -1 Construct a mesh by adding a central vertex (centroid of intersection points) and connecting it to the sorted boundary vertices to form triangles. Handle winding order based on whether the view is inverted (d < 0). b. Light Pass (Light's Point of View): Render the slice geometry from the light's perspective. Shader Logic: Compute the opacity of the current sample using the transfer function. Accumulate this opacity into the Light Buffer using the "over" operator (alpha blending). Order: Render in front-to-back order with respect to the light. Result: The Light Buffer stores the transmissivity (amount of light remaining) after passing through previous slices. c. Eye Pass (Observer's Point of View): Render the same slice geometry from the camera's perspective. Shader Logic: 1. Sample the Light Buffer at the current fragment's screen coordinates to retrieve the accumulated light transmissivity T. 2. Compute the incoming light Li at the current voxel position \vec{x}: Li(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}i) = Ll \cdot T(\vec{x}l, \vec{x}) where Ll is light intensity and T is the transmissivity from the Light Buffer. 3. For multiple scattering, add an indirect component: Li(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}i) = Ll \cdot T(\vec{x}l, \vec{x}) + Ll \cdot T(\vec{x}l, \vec{x}) \cdot \text{Blur}(\theta) where \theta is a user-defined cone angle and \text{Blur} is an angle-dependent blur function. 4. Compute surface shading factor S(\vec{x}) (derived from gradient magnitude or user-defined) to weight emission and surface shading: C(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}i, \vec{\omega}o) = Le(\vec{x}) \cdot (1 - S(\vec{x})) + s(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}i, \vec{\omega}o) \cdot S(\vec{x}) where Le is emission and s is surface shading. 5. Combine with the phase function p: Li(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}i) = Ll \cdot p(\vec{x}, \vec{\omega}i, \vec{\omega}o) \cdot T(\vec{x}l, \vec{x}) + Ll \cdot T(\vec{x}l, \vec{x}) \cdot \text{Blur}(\theta) 6. Modulate the classified color by the computed light amount and composite into the Eye Buffer using the "over" operator. Order: If d > 0: Render front-to-back with respect to the observer. If d < 0: Render back-to-front with respect to the observer. 4. Final Composition: Copy the Eye Buffer to the screen. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def halfangleslicing(volumedata, camera, light, boxvertices, numslices=256): # 1. Compute half-angle vector v = normalize(camera.position - volumedata.center) l = normalize(light.direction) d = dot(l, v) h = normalize(l + v) if d > 0 else normalize(l - v) # 2. Determine slice bounds projections = [dot(h, v) for v in boxvertices] mindist, maxdist = min(projections), max(projections) L = abs(maxdist - mindist) stepsize = L / numslices # Initialize buffers lightbuffer = Texture2D(width=framewidth1.4, height=frameheight1.4, format=HDR) lightbuffer.clear(1.0 - light.intensity) eyebuffer = Texture2D(width=framewidth, height=frameheight, format=HDR) eyebuffer.clear(0.0) # 3. Iterate slices for s in range(numslices): t = mindist + s stepsize + stepsize / 2 center = volumedata.center + h t # Intersect slice plane with bounding box to get polygon vertices slicevertices = intersectplanebox(center, h, boxvertices) if len(slicevertices) < 3: continue # Sort vertices counter-clockwise around center using cross-product test centroid = sum(slicevertices) / len(slicevertices) slicevertices.sort(key=lambda p: atan2(dot(cross(p - centroid, h), cross(slicevertices[0] - centroid, h)), dot(p - centroid, h))) # Fan triangulate, handling winding order based on d < 0 indices = [] for i in range(1, len(slicevertices) - 1): if d < 0: indices.extend([0, i + 1, i]) else: indices.extend([0, i, i + 1]) mesh = Mesh(vertices=slicevertices + [centroid], indices=indices) # Light pass: render from light's POV, accumulate opacity with "over" operator render(mesh, light.viewmatrix, light.projectionmatrix) # Hardware blending accumulates alpha into lightbuffer # Eye pass: render from camera's POV render(mesh, camera.viewmatrix, camera.projectionmatrix) # Sample light buffer for transmissivity T T = sample(lightbuffer, screencoords) # Compute incoming light Li and modulate color color = modulateclassifiedcolor(T) # Composite into eyebuffer using "over" operator composite(eyebuffer, color, "over") # 4. Final composition copytoscreen(eyebuffer) Parameters: kReferenceSlices: Default number of slices (256). kLightSize: Resolution of the light buffer (512). kHDR: Buffer format (16-bit float). opacityCorrection: Scalar for adjusting opacity accumulation. densityMin, densityMax: Density range for transfer function mapping. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Attenuation Leakage: If view and light directions are perpendicular, a 2D shadow buffer approach causes blurry shadows and dark surfaces due to coarse resolution interpolation. Half-angle slicing mitigates this by decoupling light transport resolution from volume resolution, but artifacts may still appear at shadow boundaries where opacity jumps sharply. Push Constants Size: The Eye Pass push constants total 144 bytes, exceeding the Vulkan minimum guarantee of 128 bytes. Requires drivers supporting \ge 256 bytes. Single Light Source: Supports only one directional or point light source located outside the volume. Slice Spacing: To maintain consistent visual density, the slice spacing along the half-vector (ds) must be adjusted based on the angle \theta between view and light directions (dv): ds = \frac{dv}{\cos(\theta/2)} Extends half-angle slicing to approximate the angular distribution of light after multiple scattering events by convolving the particle phase function with itself, handling gradual angular spreading rather than just unscattered or diffuse light. Time Complexity: Two passes per slice. Memory Complexity: Two 2D buffers (Light and Eye) are required, significantly less than 3D shadow maps. Performance: Enables interactive frame rates for volumetric shadows. Performance is limited by the cost of generating proxy geometry and two rasterization passes per slice. Strengths: Produces hard, well-defined shadows; supports indirect lighting and multiple scattering; avoids pre-computation of shadow maps; efficient memory usage compared to 3D shadow volumes/maps. Limitations: Limited to single light sources; artifacts at shadow boundaries with sharp opacity transitions; requires high-resolution light buffers to minimize leakage; push constant size constraints on some GPUs. When to use: Interactive applications requiring dynamic volumetric shadows and translucent material rendering. When not to use: Scenes with multiple dynamic light sources or complex global illumination requiring full 3D light transport storage. Half-angle slicing was introduced by Kniss et al. in 2002. It was the first slice-based approach to synchronize rendering with illumination computation, integrating volumetric illumination models including indirect lighting and scattering within interactive applications. It builds on the concept of the half-angle vector for volume shadow computation. The technique is described in detail in "Interactive Translucent Volume Rendering and Procedural Modeling" and "Multi-Dimensional Transfer Functions for Volume Rendering". It is often cited as Kniss et al. [51] or [14] in literature. name: Multiple-Scattering Angular Distribution Estimation
head: Angular Distribution Approximation
body: A technique to approximate the angular distribution of light after multiple scattering events by convolving the particle phase function with itself, extending Half-angle slicing to handle gradual angular spreading rather than just unscattered or diffuse light. It separates the radiance into an intensity component and an angular distribution component, allowing efficient single-pass rendering of atmospheric phenomena with large forward-scattering particles. Inputs: Particle phase function P\lambda(\Omega). Extinction coefficient \beta{ex}(\vec{s}) and scattering coefficient \beta{sca}(\vec{s}) (where \beta{sca} \le \beta{ex}). Absorption coefficient \alpha\gamma(\vec{s}) (often \alpha\gamma = \beta{ex} - \beta{sca} or similar, defined by the medium's albedo properties). Light source direction \Omega{lt} and intensity Is^\lambda. Background radiance function L\lambda(\vec{s}{bg}(\vec{s}, \Omega), \Omega). Outputs: Final radiance L\lambda(\vec{s}, \Omega) for each sample point \vec{s} and view direction. Intensity buffer I\lambda(\vec{s}) storing the scalar light intensity reaching the volume. Data Structures: Pre-computed Angular Distribution Texture: A floating-point precision texture storing A^{ms}\lambda^n(\Omega) for n \in [0, N{max}]. The index n represents the number of scattering events. Light Buffer: A texture storing the scalar intensity I\lambda(\vec{s}) accumulated along the light path. Definitions: Radiance separation: L\lambda(\vec{s}, \Omega) = I\lambda(\vec{s})A\lambda(\vec{s}, \Omega). Normalization constraint: \int{4\pi} A\lambda(\vec{s}, \Omega)d\Omega = 1, \forall\vec{s}, \lambda. Boundary condition (collimated source): L\lambda(\vec{s}{bg}(\vec{s}, \Omega), \Omega) = Is^\lambda \delta(\Omega - \Omega{lt}). Pre-computation: The multiple-scattering angular distribution function A^{ms}\lambda^n(\Omega) approximates the distribution of light after n scattering events: A^{ms}\lambda^n(\Omega) = \underbrace{\delta(\Omega - \Omega{lt}) P\lambda \dots P\lambda}{n-1 \text{ times}}(\Omega) where denotes convolution over the sphere 4\pi. The maximum pre-computed scattering events is N{max} = 26. This value is chosen because the angular distribution for rain (the worst-case forward peak scenario) becomes isotropic to within 0.0001% at this point. Runtime Estimation: For a ray segment traversing from \vec{s} to \vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt}\Delta (where \vec{m} is the light direction vector and \Delta is step size), the expected number of scattering events n(\vec{s}) is estimated based on the transparency T from the light source: n(\vec{s}) = -\frac{\gamma}{\alpha\gamma \beta{ex}(\vec{s}')} \ln T(\vec{s}, \vec{s}{bg}(\vec{s}, \Omega{lt})) Note: The source text presents this formula with \gamma and \alpha\gamma \beta{ex} in the denominator, but also references Equation 22 as n(\vec{s}) = -\frac{\gamma}{\alpha\gamma \beta{ex}(\vec{s}')} \ln T. In standard radiative transfer, the mean free path is 1/\beta{ex}. The parameter \gamma likely represents a scaling factor or albedo-related term specific to the implementation. The text states "In terms of transparency from the source: n(\vec{s}) = -\frac{\gamma}{\alpha\gamma \beta{ex}(\vec{s}')} \ln T". We retain the source's notation. Intensity Update (Light Buffer Pass): The intensity I\lambda is updated along the light path. For a step from \vec{s} to \vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt}\Delta: I\lambda(\vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt}\Delta) = I\lambda(\vec{s})T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt}\Delta) + I\lambda(\vec{s})(1 - T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt}\Delta)) \frac{\beta{sca}^\lambda \Delta}{\alpha(\vec{s})} A^{ms}\lambda^{\lfloor n(\vec{s}) \rfloor + 1 + \beta{ex}^\lambda \Delta}(\Omega - \Omega{lt}) + \xi \beta{sca}^\lambda \Delta Correction/Clarification based on Eq 25 and 26 in: The source provides Eq 25 for intensity update and Eq 26 for the angular distribution term. Eq 25: I(\vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt}\Delta) = I(\vec{s})T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt}\Delta) + I(\vec{s})(1 - T(\vec{s}, \vec{s} + \vec{m}\Omega{lt}\Delta)) \frac{\beta{ex}^\lambda \Delta}{\alpha(\vec{s})} F{\lfloor n(\vec{s}) \rfloor + 1 + \beta{ex}^\lambda \Delta} Where F is the pre-computed angular distribution function sampled at the appropriate index. The term \xi in Eq 26 appears to be a noise or residual term, or potentially a typo in the source transcription for a specific scattering term. Given the context of "sum over sampling slabs", the intensity accumulation sums contributions. The index for the angular distribution texture is k = \lfloor n(\vec{s}) \rfloor + 1 + \beta{ex}^\lambda \Delta. If k > N{max}, clamp to N{max}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. """ distributions = [] # n=0: Delta function at light direction distributions.append(deltafunction(phasefunction.lightdirection)) currentdist = distributions[0] for n in range(1, numscatteringsmax + 1): # Convolve current distribution with phase function # Note: Convolution on sphere is complex; source implies iterative convolution nextdist = convolvesphere(currentdist, phasefunction) distributions.append(nextdist) currentdist = nextdist return distributions def updatelightbuffer(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, distributions, extinctioncoeffs, scatteringcoeffs, absorptioncoeffs, lightintensity, lightdirection): """ Accumulate intensity in the light buffer along the light path. Omegalt). # In the light buffer pass, we are integrating light FROM the light source. # The term (1 - T) represents the fraction of light scattered out of the beam. # The intensity contribution is proportional to the probability of scattering # in the direction of the next sample (which is along the light ray). # Source Eq 25: Inew = Iold T + Iold (1 - T) scatteringterm # Update position currentpos += lightdirection delta currentintensity = newintensity # Store currentintensity in Light Buffer at currentpos lightbuffer.set(currentpos, currentintensity) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The approximation performs best in optically thin regions and for the first few scattering events. Errors increase with the number of scattering events as the backward-directed light contribution becomes large, which the forward-peaked convolution approximation may not capture accurately. If n(\vec{s}) is large, the angular distribution becomes isotropic; clamping to N{max}=26 is sufficient for most atmospheric cases (e.g., rain). Time Complexity: Pre-computation is O(N{max} \cdot S^2) where S is the discretization of the sphere for convolution. Runtime is O(1) per sample for texture lookup and intensity update, making it efficient for single-pass rendering. Memory Complexity: Requires storing N{max} angular distribution textures. For N{max}=26, this is a fixed, small overhead. Strengths: Captures fine angularly dependent effects in the presence of large atmospheric scattering particles (forward scattering) without the cost of full path tracing. Efficient single-pass implementation. Limitations: Accuracy degrades for high scattering counts (optically thick regions) due to the neglect of backward scattering contributions in the convolution model. When to use: Atmospheric rendering with forward-scattering particles (clouds, fog, rain) where performance is critical and optical thickness is moderate. When not to use: Highly optically thick media where backward scattering dominates, or when high-fidelity multiple scattering beyond 26 events is required. Originated in the work of Riley, Ebert, Kraus, Tessendorf, and Hansen (2004) for the efficient rendering of atmospheric phenomena. It extends the half-angle slicing technique by Kniss et al. (2002) to handle multiple scattering. The method is designed for programmable graphics hardware, leveraging pre-computed textures to approximate the radiative transfer equation's angular dependence. name: Two-pass volume rendering
head: Light/Volume two-pass, Slice-based two-pass volume rendering
body: Two-pass volume rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique that separates light attenuation computation from color compositing into two distinct rasterization passes. It differs from single-pass methods by decoupling these operations into a two-stage data dependency between a dedicated light buffer and the frame buffer. The method generates proxy geometry (slice planes) along the view direction and processes them in two stages per slice. The first stage (Light Pass) accumulates light attenuation. The second stage (Eye Pass) composites color and opacity using the attenuated light from the first stage. Input: 3D volume texture (density/scalar field), 1D or 2D transfer function texture, camera matrices (eye and light view-projection), slice geometry, number of slices. Output: Final color buffer (framebuffer). Intermediate: Light buffer (2D texture storing accumulated light color and opacity). Push Constants The implementation uses two distinct push constant structures passed to vertex and fragment shaders. 1. LightPC (Light Pass): lightMVP: mat4 (Light view-projection matrix). opacityCorrection: float (Scalar multiplier for opacity). mdensityMin: float (Lower density threshold). mdensityMax: float (Upper density threshold). Total size: sizeof(LightPC). 2. EyePC (Eye Pass): eyeMVP: mat4 (Eye view-projection matrix). lightMVP: mat4 (Light view-projection matrix, reused for sampling light buffer). opacityCorrection: float. mambient: float (Ambient light intensity). mdensityMin: float. mdensityMax: float. Total size: sizeof(EyePC). Descriptor Set Bindings Volume Set: Binding 0: Volume texture (3D). Binding 1: Transfer function texture (1D or 2D). Eye Set: Binding 0: Volume texture (3D). Binding 1: Transfer function texture (1D or 2D). Binding 2: Light buffer texture (2D). Composite Set: Binding 0: Eye buffer (Frame buffer). Light Buffer Layout Resolution: Not given in the sources. Format: Typically RGBA8, storing accumulated light color and opacity. Initialization: Cleared to light color with alpha set to 0.0. 1. Generate Slice Geometry: Calculate view direction from camera. Generate slice proxy geometry spanning volume bounds. Order slices back-to-front relative to the light source. The implementation sets reverse=true to generate geometry ordered back-to-front for the "over" operator. 2. Initialize Buffers: Clear Light Buffer: Set color to light color, alpha to 0.0. Clear Eye Buffer: Set to black (0,0,0,0). 3. Iterate Slices: For each slice i from light end to eye end: a. Light Pass: Bind Light Buffer as render target. Bind Volume Set descriptors. Push LightPC constants. Draw slice geometry. Blend Mode: Premultiplied Over. Shader Logic: Sample volume, compute density, accumulate light attenuation. Write to light buffer. b. Eye Pass: Bind Eye Buffer as render target. Bind Eye Set descriptors (including Light Buffer at binding 2). Push EyePC constants. Draw slice geometry. Blend Mode: 'Under' (accumulates color and opacity front-to-back). Shader Logic: Sample volume, apply transfer function, sample light buffer for attenuation, composite color. 4. Final Composite: The Eye Buffer now contains the final composited image. Opacity Correction To maintain correct total opacity regardless of the number of slices rendered, an opacity correction scalar is applied: opacityCorrection = \frac{kReferenceSlices}{m\numSlices} Where: kReferenceSlices is a reference slice count (e.g., 256). m\numSlices is the actual number of slices rendered. Light Attenuation (Light Pass) The light pass accumulates light using premultiplied over blending. Color Compositing (Eye Pass) The eye pass composites slices front-to-back using the attenuated light from the light buffer, applying an 'under' blend to accumulate color and opacity. opacityCorrection: Scalar multiplier applied to slice opacity. Calculated as the ratio of a reference slice count to the actual slice count. mdensityMin, mdensityMax: Density thresholds passed to shaders. kLightSize: Not given in the sources. kReferenceSlices: Reference slice count for opacity correction (e.g., 256). mnumSlices: Number of slices to render (e.g., 16 to 768). mdensityScale: Scale factor for density values (e.g., 0.0 to 4.0). Upside Down Volume: Volume data uploaded from CPU stores rows top-to-bottom, causing the rendered volume to appear upside down. This is handled by a flipY function that mirrors the data along the Y axis before GPU upload. Slice Iteration Order: Slice iteration order must strictly match the front-to-back requirement from the light. The implementation fixes reverse=true unconditionally, as no modern GPU configuration requires the opposite order. Opacity Consistency: Without opacityCorrection, changing the number of slices changes the total opacity and image intensity. The correction factor ensures image intensity stays constant as slice count changes. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. kReferenceSlices = 256 def createtexture2d(width, height, format): return Texture(width, height, format) def clearrendertarget(target, color, alpha): target.clear(color=color, alpha=alpha) def generateslices(boxhalf, viewdir, numslices, reverse): return SliceProxyGeometry.generate(boxhalf, boxhalf, viewdir, numslices, reverse) def binddescriptorset(settype): # Binds the appropriate descriptor set (Volume, Eye, or Composite) pass def pushconstants(constants): # Uploads push constant data to the shader pipeline pass def drawslice(slicegeometry): # Rasterizes the slice geometry pass def setblendmode(mode): # Sets the GPU blend mode (e.g., PREMULTIPLIEDOVER, UNDER) pass lightbuffer = createtexture2d(1024, 1024, "RGBA8") eyebuffer = createtexture2d(framebufferwidth, framebufferheight, "RGBA8") volumetex = loadvolume3d(volumedata, flipy=True) tftex = loadtransferfunction(tfdata) clearrendertarget(lightbuffer, color=lightcolor, alpha=0.0) clearrendertarget(eyebuffer, color=(0, 0, 0, 0), alpha=0.0) viewdir = camera.forward() slices = generateslices( boxhalf=mboxHalf, viewdir=viewdir, numslices=mnumSlices, reverse=True # Generates back-to-front for the "over" operator) for slice in slices: # --- Light Pass --- bindrendertarget(lightbuffer) binddescriptorset("Volume") # Binding 0: Volume, Binding 1: TF pushconstants(LightPC( lightMVP=lightviewproj, opacityCorrection=kReferenceSlices / mnumSlices, mdensityMin=mdensityMin, mdensityMax=mdensityMax)) drawslice(slice) setblendmode("PREMULTIPLIEDOVER") # --- Eye Pass --- bindrendertarget(eyebuffer) binddescriptorset("Eye") # Binding 0: Volume, Binding 1: TF, Binding 2: Light Buffer pushconstants(EyePC( eyeMVP=eyeviewproj, lightMVP=lightviewproj, opacityCorrection=kReferenceSlices / mnumSlices, mambient=mambient, mdensityMin=mdensityMin, mdensityMax=mdensityMax)) drawslice(slice) setblendmode("UNDER") # Front-to-back compositing Decouples light transport (attenuation/scattering) from final compositing. Pre-computes light accumulation in a voxel grid for real-time rendering. Differs from standard ray casting by moving light integration off the critical path. Choose when complex lighting is required and can be pre-computed efficiently. Uses half-angle vectors for slice generation to optimize ray traversal. Choose when view-dependent sampling efficiency is prioritized over uniform slice distribution. Uses ray marching in two passes, potentially for adaptive resolution or different sampling strategies. Choose when adaptive sampling or multi-resolution traversal is needed. Incorporates early ray termination across multiple passes to optimize performance. Choose when large transparent or sparse volumes benefit from skipping empty space. Adapts rendering resolution or sampling density based on local volume features. Choose when detail preservation in high-frequency regions is critical. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Depends heavily on GPU blending hardware support for 'Under' and 'Over' modes. Efficient reuse of light buffer avoids recomputing attenuation. Strengths: Decouples complex light transport from compositing, allowing for more sophisticated lighting models without impacting compositing performance. Limitations: Requires two render passes per slice, increasing draw call overhead. Light buffer resolution must be sufficient to avoid artifacts. When to Use: When complex lighting is required and can be pre-computed or accumulated efficiently. When Not to Use: When memory bandwidth is a severe bottleneck (light buffer adds pressure). The technique is based on the design described in GPUGems Fig. 39-1. It is implemented in the GPUGemsVolumeRendering demo. The approach builds on the core loop structure of image-order rendering and direct volume ray casting, splitting the computational engine across two passes to persist intermediate state in 2D textures. sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, https://github.com/sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Two-Pass Lighting and Shading
head: Illumination Pass, Light/Volume two-pass, Precomputed Lighting Pass
body: Two-Pass Lighting and Shading is a volume rendering technique that decouples the computation of light transport (attenuation and scattering) from the final image compositing. It solves the performance bottleneck of calculating complex illumination for every pixel in real-time by pre-computing light accumulation in a voxel grid during a dedicated pass, then using this data for a fast, real-time rendering pass. Inputs: Volume density field (particle density \rho(s)). Extinction coefficient \sigmat (derived from density and particle area A). Light source position I and intensity L{source}. Camera parameters for the render pass. Outputs: Light Buffer: A 3D voxel grid storing pre-computed incident light values L{incident}(v) for each voxel. Frame Buffer: The final 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. 1. Voxel Grid (Light Buffer): Layout: 3D array of floating-point scalars. Size: Matches the resolution of the volume density field. Content: L{incident}(v), the total light intensity collected at voxel v from the light source, including transmission and forward scattering. 2. Volume Density Field: Layout: 3D array of density values \rho(s). Content: Particle density at each spatial location. This pass is executed only when the light source position or intensity changes. 1. Initialize Light Buffer: Create a 3D voxel grid of floating-point scalars, initialized to zero. 2. Iterate Voxels: For each voxel v inside the cloud volume: a. Trace Light Ray: Cast a ray l from voxel v towards the light source I. b. Ray Marching: Step along the ray from v to the cloud surface, covering distance D. c. Compute Transmittance: Calculate T{surface \to v} using the extinction coefficient \sigmat along the path. d. Compute Incident Light: i. Calculate direct transmission term: L{direct} = L{source} \cdot T{surface \to v}. ii. Calculate scattered contribution: Sum the light scattered from each intermediate point i along the path. Use the approximation that 50% of light scatters forward. iii. Sum terms: L{incident}(v) = L{direct} + L{scatter\term}. e. Store Result: Write L{incident}(v) to the corresponding voxel in the Light Buffer. This pass runs in real-time for every frame. 1. Initialize Frame Buffer: Clear color and opacity buffers. 2. Iterate Pixels: For each pixel in the frame buffer: a. Cast View Ray: Cast a ray s from the camera through the pixel, traversing the cloud from 0 to P. b. Ray Marching: Step along the ray with step size \Delta s. c. Accumulate Color: For each step at position s: i. Sample Light: Retrieve L{incident}(s) from the Light Buffer (Pass 1 output). ii. Compute Emission/Reflection: Determine the color contribution C(s) based on L{incident}(s) and the volume's reflective/emissive properties. iii. Compute Transmittance: Calculate T(s, s+\Delta s) using \sigmat. iv. Composite: Use front-to-back compositing with an 'under' blend to accumulate color and opacity into the frame buffer. 3. Display: Output the final frame buffer. Extinction Coefficient: \sigmat(s) = \rho(s) \cdot A Where \rho(s) is the particle density at location s, and A is the area occluded by a single particle projected on the plane perpendicular to the ray. Transmittance: T(s, s') = e^{-\int{s}^{s'} \sigmat(s'') ds''} Represents the fraction of light passing from point s to s' without being absorbed or scattered out of the ray. Incident Light (Continuous): L{incident}(v) = L{source} \cdot T{surface \to v} + \int{surface}^{v} L{scatter}(s) \cdot T{s \to v} ds The light collected at point v is the sum of: 1. Light propagated directly from the source to v, attenuated by total transmittance from the cloud surface to v. 2. Light scattered in the forward direction from intermediate points s along the ray, attenuated by transmittance from s to v. Forward Scattering Approximation: It is assumed that 50% of the scattered light is directed forward within a small solid angle (~0.0001 steradians). The remaining 50% is ignored for computational efficiency. Incident Light (Discrete Ray Marching): L{incident}(v) = L{source} \cdot T{surface \to v} + \sum{i} L{scatter}(i) \cdot T{i \to v} \cdot \Delta s Where the sum iterates over discrete steps i from the cloud surface to v, with step size \Delta s. \sigmat: Extinction coefficient. Typical values depend on the medium (e.g., water vapor density). Scattering Fraction: 0.5 (50% of light scattered forward). Solid Angle: ~0.0001 steradians for forward scattering approximation. Light Source Changes: The Light Buffer becomes invalid if the light source moves. The system must detect this and re-run Pass 1. Precision: Floating-point precision in the Light Buffer may lead to banding or noise if light values vary significantly. Boundary Conditions: The ray marching in Pass 1 must correctly identify the cloud surface to start the transmittance calculation from the correct point. Scattering Approximation: Ignoring 50% of scattered light reduces accuracy, potentially leading to darker or less realistic volumes compared to full scattering models. Time Complexity: Pass 1: O(V \cdot Nl), where V is the number of voxels and Nl is the number of steps in the light ray. Executed only on light change. Pass 2: O(P \cdot Nr), where P is the number of pixels and Nr is the number of steps in the view ray. Executed every frame. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the Light Buffer, plus O(V) for the volume density field. Performance: Significantly faster than real-time full light integration per pixel. The bottleneck is the initial light computation if the light moves frequently. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability for complex lighting; decouples lighting from view changes. Limitations: Static lighting assumption (or expensive re-computation); approximation errors in scattering; requires extra memory for the light buffer. When to Use: Real-time applications with static or slowly moving light sources (e.g., clouds, smoke). When Not to Use: Dynamic lighting with frequent changes; high-fidelity offline rendering where full scattering is required. The method is based on the principles of transmittance and scattering described by Max [12], with optimizations from Harris [13] and Tessendorf [33]. It was implemented in GPU code for real-time volumetric cloud rendering, using a pseudo-spheroid-based approach instead of a particle system. The specific implementation described in uses a CPU for the illumination pass and a GPU for the rendering pass, leveraging a pre-calculated voxel grid. Efficient Algorithms for Real-Time GPU Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Enhanced Geometry, https://doi.org/10.3390/sym10040125, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Two-Pass Ray Marching Volume Rendering
head: INTMeshVolumeRendering, Multi-pass Raycasting with OpenGL FBOs, Multi-pass raycasting - OpenGL, Two-Pass Raycasting
body: Two-Pass Ray Marching Volume Rendering is a GPU-based direct volume rendering technique that decouples the determination of ray entry and exit points from the actual volume integration (ray marching). It solves the problem of efficiently computing ray-volume intersections without requiring complex ray-triangle intersection logic in the main rendering pass by rasterizing the volume's bounding box faces into offscreen textures. Unlike single-pass raycasting, which must compute intersections within the fragment shader, this method uses hardware rasterization for boundary detection, reducing fragment shader complexity at the cost of an additional render pass and texture memory overhead. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: 3D volume dataset (scalar field), camera parameters (position, orientation, projection), volume bounding box dimensions, number of marching steps, and a transfer function mapping scalar values to RGBA. Outputs: 2D image with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: 1. Bounding Box Geometry: A cube (or box) geometry representing the volume extent. 2. Offscreen Render Targets (FBOs): Two 2D textures (FrontfaceTexture, BackfaceTexture) storing the 3D world coordinates of the ray entry and exit points for each screen pixel. Format: GLRGBA16FARB (or equivalent high-precision floating-point format like FloatType in WebGL). Dimensions: Match the screen resolution (window.innerWidth × window.innerHeight). Wrapping/Filtering: ClampToEdgeWrapping, LinearFilter. 3. Volume Data Texture: A 3D texture (volumeTex) storing the scalar field. Format: RedFormat or AlphaFormat with FloatType. Layout: If the data length does not fit a rectangular texture, it is padded with zeros to the next power-of-two or rectangular dimension. 4. Transfer Function Texture: A 1D texture (transferFuncTex) mapping scalar values to RGBA. Size: Typically 8 \times 256 pixels. Format: RGBAFormat. Content: Linear gradient where the x-axis represents the normalized scalar value and the single row stores the interpolated color and opacity. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Create an OpenGL Framebuffer Object (FBO) or WebGL WebGLRenderTarget. Generate two 2D textures (FrontfaceTexture, BackfaceTexture) attached to the FBO color attachments. Load the 3D volume data into a 3D texture. Compute dataMin and dataMax if not provided, and normalize voxel values to [0, 1]. Generate the 1D transfer function texture from user-defined control points (color and opacity stops). 2. First Pass (Boundary Rasterization): Bind the FBO. Render Back Face: Enable face culling to cull GLFRONT faces. Render the bounding box geometry. The fragment shader outputs the world position of the back-facing surface intersection for each pixel. Store this in BackfaceTexture. Render Front Face: Enable face culling to cull GLBACK faces. Render the same bounding box geometry. The fragment shader outputs the world position of the front-facing surface intersection. Store this in FrontfaceTexture. Note: The vertex shader transforms the box vertices to world space, and the fragment shader interpolates the position. Since the box is convex and viewed from outside, the front face gives the entry point and the back face gives the exit point. 3. Second Pass (Ray Marching and Compositing): Unbind the FBO (render to screen/default framebuffer). Render a fullscreen quad using a raycasting fragment shader. Shader Logic: For each pixel, sample FrontfaceTexture at the current texture coordinate to get startPos (entry point). Sample BackfaceTexture at the current texture coordinate to get endPos (exit point). Calculate the ray vector: \vec{r} = \text{endPos} - \text{startPos}. Calculate the ray length: L = \|\vec{r}\|. Calculate the step size: \Delta s = \frac{L}{\text{steps}} (or a fixed stepInc if marching in world units). Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = (0,0,0,0) and opacity A{acc} = 0. Initialize current position P = \text{startPos}. Loop for i = 0 to \text{steps}-1: Sample the volume texture at P to get scalar value v. Sample the transfer function texture at v to get color C{src} and opacity \alpha{src}. (Note: Evidence specifies sampling the TF at the volume's alpha channel: texture1D(transferFuncTex, texture3D(volumeTex,...).a)). Apply Front-to-Back Compositing: C{acc} = C{acc} + C{src} \cdot \alpha{src} \cdot (1 - A{acc}) A{acc} = A{acc} + \alpha{src} \cdot (1 - A{acc}) (Note: Some implementations use mix(dest.rgb, src.rgb, src.a) which implies C{new} = C{old}(1-\alpha) + C{src}\alpha, equivalent to the above if C{old} is background color 0). Check for Early Ray Termination (ERT): If A{acc} > 0.99 (or a threshold), break the loop. Check for Boundary Exit: If \|P - \text{startPos}\| \ge L, break the loop. Increment position: P = P + \Delta s \cdot \frac{\vec{r}}{\|\vec{r}\|}. Output C{acc} as the final fragment color. Parameters: steps: Number of marching steps per ray. Default: 50. Higher values improve quality but reduce performance. alphaCorrection: Opacity correction factor applied during compositing. Default: 0.2. resolution: Resolution of the 1D transfer function texture. Typical value: 255. dataMin / dataMax: Min/max of the volume dataset for normalization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The first pass textures must use high-precision formats (e.g., GLRGBA16FARB or FloatType) to preserve coordinate precision. Culling: Correct face culling (GLFRONT vs GLBACK) is critical to correctly determine entry and exit points. Cutting Planes: If cutting planes are used, the bounding box rasterization must be modified or additional logic added to clip the ray segment. The uenableCut uniform and plane parameters must be updated before rendering. Auto-Clear: If rendering additional elements (like cutting plane visuals) after the raycaster, renderer.autoClear must be set to false to prevent the framebuffer from being cleared between passes or elements. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertwopassvolume(camera, volumedata, transferfunction, steps=50): # Initialization rttexture = createrendertarget(screenwidth, screenheight, format=GLRGBA16FARB) volumetex = create3dtexture(volumedata, format=GLRED, type=GLFLOAT) tftex = create1dtexture(transferfunction, size=(8, 256), format=GLRGBA) # Pass 1: Boundary Rasterization bindfbo(rttexture) enablecullface(GLFRONT) renderboundingbox(side=GLBACK, output=rttexture.backfacetexture) enablecullface(GLBACK) renderboundingbox(side=GLFRONT, output=rttexture.frontfacetexture) unbindfbo() # Pass 2: Ray Marching for y in range(screenheight): for x in range(screenwidth): startpos = sample2d(rttexture.frontfacetexture, x, y) endpos = sample2d(rttexture.backfacetexture, x, y) rayvec = endpos - startpos raylen = length(rayvec) stepsize = raylen / steps acccolor = vec4(0.0) accalpha = 0.0 curpos = startpos for i in range(steps): volval = sample3d(volumetex, curpos) # Sample TF at volume alpha as per tfsample = sample1d(tftex, volval.a) srccolor = tfsample.rgb srcalpha = tfsample.a acccolor.rgb = mix(acccolor.rgb, srccolor, srcalpha) acccolor.a = mix(acccolor.a, 1.0, srcalpha) if acccolor.a > 0.99 or length(curpos - startpos) >= raylen: break curpos += stepsize normalize(rayvec) writepixel(x, y, acccolor) Specialized for light field displays, decoupling 3D ray-casting from 2D post-processing for optical distortion correction. Supports arbitrary clip regions by assembling valid clip intervals in the first pass and integrating only over remaining segments in the second pass. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of marching steps. The two-pass structure adds a constant overhead of one full-screen rasterization pass. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the two offscreen textures (entry/exit points) plus O(V) for the 3D volume texture and O(T) for the transfer function texture, where W \times H is the screen resolution, V is the volume data size, and T is the transfer function resolution. Performance: Reduces fragment shader complexity compared to single-pass raycasting by offloading intersection tests to the rasterizer. However, it incurs the cost of two render passes and texture memory bandwidth for reading/writing the intermediate textures. Strengths: Simple implementation, leverages hardware rasterization for robust boundary detection, supports early ray termination effectively. Limitations: Fixed number of steps may lead to aliasing or slow convergence; high-precision textures increase memory usage; not suitable for dynamic volumes that change every frame without careful texture management. When to Use: Static or slowly changing volumes where simplicity and robustness of boundary detection are prioritized over maximum performance or adaptive step sizes. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with very large volumes requiring adaptive step sizes or sparse data structures (consider Half-angle slicing or Multi-pass GPU Ray-Casting with Early Ray Termination for more advanced optimizations). The method originates from the work of Krüger and Westermann (2003), who introduced a two-pass GPU-based volume rendering technique using OpenGL Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) to store ray start and end positions. It is implemented in the NVIDIA CUDA SDK and WebGL implementations (e.g., INTMeshVolumeRendering in Three.js). It builds on the principles of image-order rendering and direct volume ray casting, adapting them to the constraints of GPU rasterization pipelines.
