name: Two-Pass GPU Volume Ray Casting for Light Field Displays
head: Light field display aware volume rendering, Light field rendering pipeline, Multi-projector display rendering, Two-Pass GPU Volume Ray Casting, Two-Pass Light Field Rendering, Two-pass rendering for light field displays
body: This method provides a specialized rendering pipeline for light field displays, enabling multiple freely moving naked-eye viewers to perceive virtual volumetric objects floating at fixed physical locations in the display workspace. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering by decoupling the 3D ray-casting computation from the 2D post-processing required to correct non-linear optical distortions inherent in multi-projector setups. It builds on Two-Pass Ray Marching Volume Rendering by extending the two-pass paradigm to handle multi-view light field geometry and per-projector distortion correction. The method consists of two distinct passes: a 3D rendering pass that generates per-projector views, and a 2D warping pass that corrects geometric and color distortions. Inputs: Volumetric dataset (stored in a 3D texture). Light field geometry model defining projector positions and orientations. Precomputed per-pixel lookup tables (LUTs) for distortion correction and color mapping. Outputs: Corrected images projected onto the physical light field display surface. 3D Texture: Stores the entire volumetric dataset. Trilinear texture filtering is used for resampling during ray-casting. Frame Buffer Object (FBO): Used to render per-projector views off-screen during Pass 1. Lookup Tables (LUTs): Precomputed textures stored in GPU memory. These contain per-pixel data used to warp geometry and modify colors in Pass 2. Octree (Optional): For very large datasets, the volume is decomposed into small cubical bricks organized into an octree structure maintained out-of-core. Leaves contain original data; inner nodes store filtered representations, value ranges, and optionally precomputed gradients. Pass 1: Per-Projector Volume Ray Casting 1. Initialize: For each projector in the light field display array: a. Allocate and bind an FBO texture matching the projector's resolution. b. Set the view and projection matrices based on the idealized light field geometry model for this projector. 2. Render Proxy Geometry: Render a proxy geometry (typically the volume’s bounding box) whose projection on the image plane covers all pixels emitting rays passing through the volume. 3. Ray Casting Fragment Shader: For each pixel covered by the proxy geometry: a. Ray Generation: Compute the ray origin and direction based on the projector's view and the pixel's position. b. Ray Marching: Step from sample location to sample location along the ray. c. Resampling: Fetch volume samples using trilinear texture filtering from the 3D texture. d. Compositing: Perform front-to-back compositing of sample contributions (color and opacity) using an appropriate optical model. e. Termination: Continue the loop until the volume is exited or full opacity is reached. 4. Store Result: Write the final composited color and opacity to the FBO texture for this projector. Pass 2: 2D Warping and Distortion Correction 1. Initialize: For each projector view: a. Bind the FBO texture generated in Pass 1 as a source texture. b. Set up a full-screen quad or equivalent geometry to cover the output display area. 2. Warping Fragment Shader: For each output pixel: a. Lookup: Retrieve the per-pixel lookup table data corresponding to the output pixel's position. b. Geometry Warping: Use the LUT to determine the source pixel coordinates in the Pass 1 texture, effectively warping the geometry to correct non-linear view distortions. c. Color Correction: Modify the color values using the LUT data to correct color distortions. 3. Display: Output the corrected image to the projector. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pass1volumeraycasting(projectorviews, volumetexture, lightfieldgeometry): for view in projectorviews: # Allocate and bind FBO for this projector fbotexture = allocatetexture(view.resolution) bindframebuffer(fbotexture) setviewprojection(lightfieldgeometry.getmatrix(view)) # Render proxy geometry (bounding box) to trigger fragment shader drawboundingbox() unbindframebuffer() # Store result view.pass1result = fbotexture def pass2distortioncorrection(projectorviews, distortionluts): for view in projectorviews: sourcetexture = view.pass1result luttexture = distortionluts[view.id] binddisplaytarget(view.displayarea) drawfullscreenquad() unbinddisplaytarget() def fragmentshaderpass1(rayorigin, raydirection, volumetexture): accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 step = computestepsize(raydirection, volumetexture) # Standard step calculation while t < volumetexture.maxextent and accumulatedopacity < 1.0: samplepos = rayorigin + t raydirection samplevalue = texturetrilinear(volumetexture, samplepos) color, opacity = applytransferfunction(samplevalue) alpha = opacity (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedopacity += alpha t += step return accumulatedcolor def fragmentshaderpass2(outputpixelcoord, sourcetexture, luttexture): sourceuv = lookuptablesample(luttexture, outputpixelcoord, channel="warp") colorcorrection = lookuptablesample(luttexture, outputpixelcoord, channel="color") rawcolor = texturebilinear(sourcetexture, sourceuv) correctedcolor = rawcolor colorcorrection return correctedcolor def allocatetexture(resolution): return {} # Allocates GPU texture memory def bindframebuffer(tex): pass # Sets active render target def setviewprojection(mat): pass # Updates GPU projection matrix def drawboundingbox(): pass # Triggers fragment shader for volume pixels def unbindframebuffer(): pass # Resets render target def binddisplaytarget(area): pass # Sets output display surface def drawfullscreenquad(): pass # Triggers warping shader for output pixels def texturetrilinear(tex, pos): return tex.sample(pos, filter="trilinear") # Resamples volume def applytransferfunction(val): return val.color, val.opacity # Applies optical model def computestepsize(dir, tex): return tex.resolution / max(abs(dir)) # Standard step calculation def lookuptablesample(lut, uv, channel): return lut.sample(uv, channel=channel) # Reads LUT data def texturebilinear(tex, uv): return tex.sample(uv, filter="bilinear") # Samples Pass 1 result Trilinear Texture Filtering: Used for resampling during ray-casting. Step Size: Determined by volume resolution and view distance; not explicitly defined in sources. Optical Model: Applied during compositing; specific model not detailed in sources. Large Datasets: Standard 3D textures may not fit in GPU memory. The method supports an adaptive technique using an octree decomposition into cubical bricks maintained out-of-core. Non-linear Distortions: Small non-linear view and color distortions are common in multi-projector setups and must be corrected in Pass 2. Full Opacity: The ray marching loop terminates early if full opacity is reached, which is a standard optimization but must be handled correctly to avoid artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Additional memory for FBOs and LUTs is proportional to the display resolution. For large datasets, the octree structure adds overhead but allows out-of-core processing. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables real-time volume rendering on light field displays. Separates 3D ray-casting from 2D distortion correction. Handles large datasets via octree decomposition. Limitations: Requires precomputed LUTs for distortion correction. Assumes idealized light field geometry in Pass 1. Non-linear distortions must be small enough to be corrected by 2D warping. When to Use: When rendering volumetric data on multi-projector light field displays with multiple viewers. When Not to Use: When high-precision geometric alignment is not required or when the display is not a light field type. The method was developed by Agus et al. in 2008 for the Eurographics conference. It follows the two-pass approach typical of contemporary multi-projector displays [BMY05]. The technique was designed to provide multiple freely moving naked-eye viewers with the illusion of presence of virtual volumetric objects floating at fixed physical locations in the display workspace. It is based on GPU ray-casting, which emerged as a flexible and efficient framework for real-time volume rendering. An adaptive technique based on octree decomposition was also designed to handle very large datasets. name: Volume Ray Casting and Clipping
head: Clip interval assembly and integration, Two-pass volume clipping
body: Volume Ray Casting and Clipping is a two-pass ray tracing technique for volume rendering that supports arbitrarily many overlapping clip regions with arbitrary geometry types. It solves the problem of occluding specific parts of a volume dataset using external geometry or internal clip objects. Unlike standard ray casting which integrates along the entire ray segment within the volume bounds, this method assembles a set of valid clip intervals in the first pass and integrates the volume density only over the remaining segments in the second pass. It is distinguished by its ability to handle concavities and complex intersection geometries by using surface normals to determine valid entry and exit pairs for clipping. The method operates in two logical passes, which can be combined into a single compute kernel to avoid regenerating viewing rays. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Viewing position, viewing direction, volume dataset with axis-aligned bounding box (AABB), set of active clip objects, optional depth buffer from a previous render pass. Outputs: Rendered image where volume density is integrated only outside the defined clip intervals. Data Structures: Clip Intervals (C): A set of intervals [t{start}, t{end}] representing ray parameter ranges where the volume should not be evaluated. Intersection List: A sorted list of intersection distances t and corresponding geometric normals N for all active clip objects intersected by a ray. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Generation and Volume Bounds: Generate primary viewing rays from the viewing position. Determine t{near} and t{far}, the distances from the ray's origin to the nearest and farthest intersection positions with the volume's AABB. 2. Depth Buffer Integration (Optional): If a depth buffer from a previous render pass exists, convert individual depth buffer entries to the volume coordinate system using the transformation outlined in [14] (not provided in). Transform these to ray parameter space using vector operations to obtain td. 3. Update Ray Bounds: Update the ray bounds to respect the depth buffer: t{near}:= \max(td, t{near}) t{max}:= \min(td, t{far}) These bounds remain valid for the subsequent clip interval assembly. 4. Clip Object Intersection: If the test against t{near} and t{far} yields a valid intersection, intersect the viewing ray with all active clip objects. Collect all intersection points. Let M be the total number of intersections for a ray. Sort these intersections by distance from the ray origin. 5. Interval Assembly: For each ray, determine valid clip interval pairs using the geometric normal of the surface at intersection positions to handle concavities. Let V be the normalized direction vector of the viewing ray. Let \{N{i-1}, Ni, N{i+1}, N{i+2}\} be the geometric normals at consecutive intersection indices. Let indices be 1 \leq \dots \leq i-1 < i < i+1 < i+2 \leq \dots \leq M and distances be t1 \leq \dots \leq t{i-1} \leq ti \leq t{i+1} \leq t{i+2} \leq \dots \leq tM. The variables from Equation 1 denote indices over M intersections, while the variables in Equation 2 denote distances from the origin of the viewing ray to the respective intersection position. The set of valid clip intervals L is constructed by considering the dot product V \cdot N. The source provides a partial definition for Lj based on the normal at i-1 and i+1 relative to the ray direction. The specific cases provided are: If V \cdot N{i-1} > 0: Add [t{i-1}, ti] and [t{i+1}, t{i+2}] to L. If V \cdot N{i-1} \leq 0 and i=2: Add [-\infty, t{-1}] and [ti, t{i+1}] to L. If V \cdot N{i+1} \dots (Source text cuts off): The logic implies checking normals to determine if the ray is entering or exiting the clip object, thereby identifying which segments between intersections are "inside" the clip volume and should be excluded from rendering. The final set of clip intervals C is the union of all such valid intervals L for the ray. 6. Integration (Pass 2): Integrate over the volume density with respect to the clip intervals. The rendering integral is computed only for ray segments that are not covered by the intervals in C. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Intersect ray with volume AABB tnear, tmax = intersectaabb(viewingpos, viewingdir, volumeaabbmin, volumeaabbmax) if tnear is None or tnear >= tmax: return backgroundcolor # 2. Update bounds with depth buffer if present if depthbuffer is not None: # Sources do not provide depth-to-ray-parameter transformation details td = transformdepthtorayparam(depthbuffer, viewingpos, viewingdir) tnear = max(td, tnear) tmax = min(td, tfar) if tnear >= tmax: return backgroundcolor # 3. Intersect ray with active clip objects intersections = [] # Sources do not provide arbitrary clip object intersection logic for clipobj in clipobjects: hits = intersectraywithobject(viewingpos, viewingdir, clipobj) for hit in hits: if tnear <= hit.t <= tmax: intersections.append({'t': hit.t, 'normal': hit.normal}) intersections.sort(key=lambda x: x['t']) M = len(intersections) # 4. Assemble clip intervals using geometric normals clipintervals = [] # Source uses 1-based indexing for i. We iterate 0-based windows of 4 consecutive intersections. for idx in range(3, M): nprev = intersections[idx-1]['normal'] ncurr = intersections[idx]['normal'] nnext = intersections[idx+1]['normal'] nnext2 = intersections[idx+2]['normal'] tprev = intersections[idx-1]['t'] tcurr = intersections[idx]['t'] tnext = intersections[idx+1]['t'] tnext2 = intersections[idx+2]['t'] dotprev = dot(viewingdir, nprev) dotnext = dot(viewingdir, nnext) # Case 1: V. N{i-1} > 0 if dotprev > 0: clipintervals.append([tprev, tcurr]) clipintervals.append([tnext, tnext2]) # Case 2: V. N{i-1} <= 0 and i = 2 (1-based) -> idx = 1 # This case falls outside the loop range(3, M). Handled separately below. # Handle boundary case for i=2 (idx=1) explicitly if needed if M >= 4: nprev = intersections[0]['normal'] ncurr = intersections[1]['normal'] nnext = intersections[2]['normal'] nnext2 = intersections[3]['normal'] dotprev = dot(viewingdir, nprev) if dotprev <= 0: # Source: [-\infty, t{-1}], [ti, t{i+1}] # t{-1} is undefined in source; standard practice clamps to tnear clipintervals.append([tnear, tcurr]) clipintervals.append([tnext, tnext2]) # Source cuts off after V. N{i+1}... Standard concavity logic fills remaining cases. # 5. Integrate over remaining segments segmentstorender = subtractintervals([tnear, tmax], clipintervals) color = backgroundcolor for seg in segmentstorender: # Standard volume rendering integral not detailed in color += integratevolumedensity(viewingpos, viewingdir, seg[0], seg[1], volumedata) return color def intersectaabb(origin, direction, aabbmin, aabbmax): tmin = -float('inf') tmax = float('inf') for k in range(3): if direction[k] == 0.0: if origin[k] < aabbmin[k] or origin[k] > aabbmax[k]: return None else: t1 = (aabbmin[k] - origin[k]) / direction[k] t2 = (aabbmax[k] - origin[k]) / direction[k] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None return (tmin, tmax) def subtractintervals(base, exclusions): if not exclusions: return [base] exclusions.sort() result = [] start, end = base for exstart, exend in exclusions: if exend <= start: continue if exstart >= end: break if exstart > start: result.append([start, min(exstart, end)]) start = max(start, exend) if start < end: result.append([start, end]) return result def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def intersectraywithobject(origin, direction, obj): raise NotImplementedError("Not specified in ") def transformdepthtorayparam(depthbuffer, origin, direction): raise NotImplementedError("Not specified in ") def integratevolumedensity(origin, direction, tstart, tend, volumedata): raise NotImplementedError("Not specified in ") Parameters: Clip Objects: Arbitrary geometry types. Depth Buffer: Optional. Requires transformation to volume coordinate system. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concavities: The method specifically addresses rays hitting concavities by using geometric normals to determine valid interval pairs. Incomplete Source Logic: The source text for the interval assembly logic cuts off at the condition involving N{i+1} and N{i+2}. Implementers must infer the remaining cases or consult the original paper for the complete normal-based interval selection logic. Undefined Symbols: The source uses t{-1} in a case where i=2, which is not defined in the provided equations. Time Complexity: Dominated by ray-object intersection tests. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, clip object structures, and the depth buffer if used. Strengths: Supports arbitrarily many overlapping clip regions and arbitrary geometry types. Interoperable with OpenGL rendering via depth buffer. Limitations: Requires two passes (or a complex single kernel). Logic for complex concavities is partially unspecified in the source text. When to Use: When precise clipping of volume data using complex external geometry is required. When Not to Use: When simple box clipping is sufficient, or when hardware does not support the required ray tracing primitives efficiently. The method was proposed in "Ray Traced Volume Clipping Using Multi-Hit BVH Traversal". It builds on the concept of two-pass ray marching but extends it to handle arbitrary clip geometry and depth buffer interoperability. name: Multi-pass GPU Ray-Casting with Early Ray Termination
head: Multi-pass GPU Ray Casting, Multi-pass GPU Raycaster with Early Ray Termination, Multi-pass GPU Ray-Casting with Early Ray Termination and Empty Space Skipping
body: Multi-pass GPU Ray-Casting is a stream-based rendering technique that implements direct volume ray casting by splitting the ray traversal loop across multiple rendering passes, using 2D texture render targets to persist intermediate ray state. It solves the limitation of early GPU hardware (specifically Pixel Shader 2.0 era) which lacked dynamic flow control, preventing single-pass ray marchers from terminating rays early. By decoupling ray integration from termination checks, it achieves significant performance gains over unaccelerated ray casting and slice-based volume rendering (SBVR) through early ray termination and empty-space skipping. The method relies on the shared principles of the Two-pass and Multi-pass Techniques family. It uses a sequence of passes to compute ray entry points, ray directions, and accumulated volume integration, separated by intermediate passes that enforce stopping criteria via the early Z-test. Input: 3D volume texture V, transfer function (implicit in empty-space lookup), view matrix, projection matrix. Output: 2D color/opacity texture (final image). The method requires several 2D and 3D textures. All 2D textures match the viewport resolution (e.g., 512 \times 512). 1. TMP (Entry Point Texture): Layout: 2D RGB texture. Content: Stores the 3D texture coordinates (u, v, w) of the first intersection point between the ray of sight and the front faces of the volume bounding box. Encoding: Vertex colors of the front faces are set to their 3D texture coordinates. 2. DIR (Ray Direction Texture): Layout: 2D RGBA floating-point texture. Content: RGB components: Normalized ray direction vector in local texture coordinates. Alpha component: Length of the non-normalized direction vector (ray length within the volume). Encoding: Computed by subtracting TMP coordinates from back-face texture coordinates. 3. RES (Accumulation Texture): Layout: 2D texture render target. Content: Accumulated color and opacity from previous ray-marching steps. 4. Skip Volume (Empty Space Acceleration): Layout: 3D texture. Content: Each texel stores a 2D vector (r, g) representing the minimum and maximum values of an 8 \times 8 \times 8 block of the original volume data. The volume is sampled down to 1/8 in every dimension. 5. Empty Lookup Texture: Layout: 2D texture. Content: Lookup table where Lookup(x, y) = 1 if all values between x and y in the skip-volume are 0 under the current transfer function; otherwise 0. Pass 1: Entry Point Determination 1. Set depth test to GREATER. 2. Render the front faces of the volume bounding box. 3. Issue 3D texture coordinates of each vertex as per-vertex color C{in}. 4. Write the fragment color to TMP. This stores the entry point in local texture coordinates. Pass 2: Ray Direction Determination 1. Set depth test to GREATER. 2. Render the back faces of the volume bounding box. 3. For each fragment, fetch the entry point P{entry} from TMP using the fragment's texture coordinates. 4. Let P{back} be the 3D texture coordinates of the current back-face vertex (passed as per-vertex color). 5. Compute the non-normalized direction D{raw} = P{back} - P{entry}. 6. Compute normalized direction D{norm} = \text{normalize}(D{raw}). 7. Write D{norm} to the RGB components and \|D{raw}\| to the Alpha component of DIR. Main Passes 3 to N: Ray Traversal These passes perform the actual volume integration. Let M be the number of steps per pass (typically 8). Let N be the total number of main passes required to traverse the longest ray. 1. Set depth test to GREATER. 2. Render the front faces of the volume bounding box. 3. Vertex attributes: Texture Coordinate 1: Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) (x, y) to index DIR and RES. Per-vertex Color C: 3D texture coordinates of the front face (same as Pass 1). 4. Fragment Shader Logic: Fetch entry point P{entry} = \text{tex2D}(\text{TMP}, \text{NDC}). Fetch direction D = \text{tex2D}(\text{DIR}, \text{NDC}). Fetch accumulated result R{prev} = \text{tex2D}(\text{RES}, \text{NDC}). Initialize parametric ray equation r(t) = P{entry} + t \cdot D. The parameter t is incremented by step size \Delta for M steps. For i = 0 to M-1: Compute volume coordinate V{coord} = P{entry} + (t + i \cdot \Delta) \cdot D. Sample volume: S = \text{tex3D}(V, V{coord}). Integrate using "over" compositing: R{curr} = \text{under}(S, R{prev}). Update R{prev} = R{curr}. Write R{curr} to RES. If the ray has left the volume (opacity > threshold), write opacity 1 to RES. Intermediate Passes 3 to N: Stopping Criterion Executed after every Main Pass to enable early Z-test acceleration. 1. Set depth test to GREATER. 2. Render the front faces of the volume bounding box. 3. Fragment Shader Logic: Fetch last accumulated value R{last} = \text{tex2D}(\text{RES}, \text{NDC}). Fetch direction D = \text{tex2D}(\text{DIR}, \text{NDC}). Fetch entry point P{entry} = \text{tex2D}(\text{TMP}, \text{NDC}). Compute current volume coordinate V{coord} = P{entry} + \text{Depth} \cdot D. Empty Space Check: Fetch min/max from Skip Volume: MinMax = \text{tex3D}(\text{SkipVolume}, V{coord}). Lookup emptiness: E = \text{tex2D}(\text{EmptyLookup}, MinMax). Termination Logic: If R{last}.a < 0.9999 AND E < 1 (ray not terminated and not empty): Output Depth = 0 (resume rendering). Else: Output Depth = 100 (discard subsequent fragments). Output Color = R{last} (pass through last frame's color). Formula: \text{OUT.depth} = ((R{last}.a < 0.9999) \land (E < 1)) ? 0: 100 \text{OUT.col} = R{last} M (Steps per pass): Number of ray steps performed in each main pass. Typical value: 8. Restricted by hardware shader limitations. T (Opacity Threshold): Constant threshold for early ray termination. If accumulated opacity > T, the ray is terminated. Viewport Resolution: Typically 512 \times 512. Early Z-Test Restrictions: On hardware of the era (Pixel Shader 2.0), the early Z-test is disabled if the Z-value is replaced in the shader, or if clip/texkill is used. This necessitates the separate intermediate pass. Step Size M: If M is small, many fragments outside the volume or void samples may be processed unnecessarily (up to M-1 void samples per ray). If M is large, all rays compute the same number of samples even if shorter, due to the lack of shader discard. Shader Discard: Fragment shaders cannot terminate themselves dynamically in this model; termination is enforced via the Z-buffer in the intermediate pass. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def passentrypoint(): setdepthtest(GREATER) renderfrontfacesofboundingbox() # Vertex shader sets color to 3D texture coordinates # Fragment shader writes color to TMP def passraydirection(): setdepthtest(GREATER) renderbackfacesofboundingbox() # Vertex shader sets color to 3D texture coordinates of back face # Fragment shader: # entry = tex2D(TMP, texcoord) # back = color # from vertex # dirraw = back - entry # dirnorm = normalize(dirraw) # write (dirnorm, length(dirraw)) to DIR def passraytraversal(M, delta): setdepthtest(GREATER) renderfrontfacesofboundingbox() # Vertex shader: # texcoord1 = NDC(x,y) # color = 3D texture coordinates of front face (C) # Fragment shader: # ndc = texcoord1 # entry = tex2D(TMP, ndc) # dir = tex2D(DIR, ndc).rgb # resprev = tex2D(RES, ndc) # t = currentparametrict # Incremented by delta each pass # res = resprev # for i in range(M): # volcoord = entry + (t + i delta) dir # sample = tex3D(Volume, volcoord) # res = under(sample, res) # write res to RES def passstoppingcriterion(): setdepthtest(GREATER) renderfrontfacesofboundingbox() # Vertex shader: # texcoord1 = NDC(x,y) # color = 3D texture coordinates of front face (C) # Fragment shader: # ndc = texcoord1 # lastval = tex2D(RES, ndc) # dir = tex2D(DIR, ndc).rgb # entry = tex2D(TMP, ndc) # volcoord = entry + depth dir # minmax = tex3D(SkipVolume, volcoord).rg # empty = tex2D(EmptyLookup, minmax) # if (lastval.a < 0.9999) and (empty < 1): # outdepth = 0 # else: # outdepth = 100 # outcolor = lastval # write outdepth, outcolor Uses half-angle slicing to optimize ray direction computation and texture access patterns. Half-angle slicing A simpler variant that may not include the complex acceleration passes or multi-step marching. Two-pass volume rendering Focuses on splitting the ray march itself into two passes, potentially differing in how state is managed. Two-Pass Ray Marching Volume Rendering Adapts the sampling density or pass structure based on local volume features. Locally Adaptive Volume Rendering Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M \cdot W \cdot H), where N is the number of main passes, M is steps per pass, and W \times H is viewport resolution. The number of passes N \approx K/M, where K is the max ray length in samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for TMP, DIR, RES, SkipVolume, and EmptyLookup textures. TMP, DIR, RES are W \times H. SkipVolume is 1/8 volume size. Performance: On an ATI Radeon 9800 Pro (Pixel Shader 2.0), for a 512^3 MRI Head dataset at 512 \times 512 viewport: Slice-Based Volume Rendering (SBVR): 7.1 fps. Ray Casting (RC) without acceleration: 4.8 fps. RC with Early Ray Termination (RC-\alpha): 14.4 fps. RC with Early Ray Termination and Empty-Space Skipping (RC-\beta): 23.4 fps. Other datasets (Aneurism, Foot, Engine) showed similar trends, with RC-\beta significantly outperforming SBVR and unaccelerated RC. Strengths: Reduces fragment operations for opaque structures and empty space. Provides equal sampling density along rays compared to object-order methods. Limitations: Requires multiple passes and texture lookups. Overhead from intermediate passes. M is constrained by hardware (typically 8). The method was described in a framework using the DirectX 9 SDK (Microsoft, 2002) and programmable via the Pixel Shader 2.0 API. It builds on prior work such as Cullip and Neumann (1993), Levoy (1990), and Purcell et al. (2002). The approach was developed to leverage the data-parallel nature of fragment units on recent chips (at the time) while minimizing fragment operations. It was demonstrated on hardware like the ATI Radeon 9800 Pro running Windows XP. name: Locally Adaptive Volume Rendering
head: Contribution Map Based Volume Rendering, Implementation of Locally Adaptive Volume Rendering
body: Locally Adaptive Volume Rendering (LAVR) is a two-pass technique that enhances feature visibility and reduces noise in volume rendering by dynamically adjusting fragment opacity based on the local density of contributing voxels. Unlike standard direct volume rendering which uses a fixed per-voxel opacity, LAVR decouples the classification of relevant data from the final compositing, allowing the renderer to adaptively suppress noise in sparse regions while preserving sharp borders in dense regions. It sets itself apart from siblings like Two-pass volume rendering by specifically targeting the statistical distribution of contributions per pixel rather than just splitting light transport or ray marching steps. LAVR operates as a slicing-based approach on graphics hardware using 3D textures, consisting of two distinct passes. Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset (V), a binary classification function (\delta) derived from a transfer function, and a 1D lookup texture (\alpha{lookup}). Output: A 2D color buffer with adaptively modulated opacity. 1. Contribution Map: A 2D floating-point texture (Frame Buffer Object) with dimensions matching the screen resolution (W \times H). It stores the count of relevant contributions for each pixel. 2. Alpha Lookup: A 1D texture mapping the contribution count to a final opacity value. Pass 1: Contribution Map Generation 1. Render the volume dataset using a slicing proxy (e.g., a bounding box or slice planes). 2. For each fragment, evaluate the binary classification function \delta(s) based on the scalar value s of the voxel at the fragment's position. 3. If \delta(s) = 1 (relevant contribution), add 1.0 to the pixel's color value using additive blending. If \delta(s) = 0, add 0.0. 4. The result is a 2D texture where each pixel (x, y) contains the integer count n(x, y) of relevant voxels along the ray passing through that pixel. Pass 2: Adaptive Compositing 1. Bind the Contribution Map as a 2D texture sampler. 2. Render the volume dataset again using the same slicing geometry. 3. In the fragment shader, for each fragment: a. Sample the 3D dataset to retrieve scalar values s1 and s2 at the entry and exit points of the ray segment within the current slice/proxy. b. Sample the Contribution Map at the fragment's normalized screen coordinates (xc, yc) to retrieve the total contribution count n. c. Sample the transfer function to retrieve the base color C and base opacity \alpha{base} for the scalar values. d. Calculate the final opacity \alpha{final} by sampling the \alpha{lookup} texture with the contribution count n. e. Set the fragment color to C and opacity to \alpha{final} if \alpha{base} > 0, otherwise set opacity to 0. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sample3dtexture(tex, coords): return trilinearinterpolation(tex, coords) def sample2dtexture(tex, coords): return bilinearinterpolation(tex, coords) def sample1dtexture(tex, coord): return linearinterpolation(tex, coord) def pass1fragmentshader(scalarvalue, transferfunction): # Binary classification: 1 if relevant, 0 otherwise basealpha = sample1dtexture(transferfunction, scalarvalue) if basealpha > 0.0: return (1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) else: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def pass2fragmentshader(entrycoords, exitcoords, fragcoord, fboxsize, fboysize): # Sample scalar values at entry and exit points of the ray segment scalar1 = sample3dtexture(dataset, entrycoords) scalar2 = sample3dtexture(dataset, exitcoords) # Normalize fragment coordinates to [0, 1] xc = fragcoord.x / fboxsize yc = fragcoord.y / fboysize # Retrieve total contribution count for this pixel contrib = sample2dtexture(contributionmap, (xc, yc)) # Sample transfer function for base color and opacity colorsample = sample2dtexture(transferfunction, (scalar2, scalar1)) basecolor = colorsample[:3] basealpha = colorsample[3] # Determine final opacity based on contribution count if basealpha > 0.0: finalalpha = sample1dtexture(alphalookup, contrib) else: finalalpha = 0.0 return (basecolor[0], basecolor[1], basecolor[2], finalalpha) \alpha{lookup}: A 1D texture mapping contribution counts to opacity. The shape of this curve determines the visual style (e.g., suppressing noise in low-count regions). Binary Threshold: The threshold used in Pass 1 to determine \delta(s). It is defined as \delta(s) = 1 if the transfer function's opacity \alpha{\text{TF}}(s) > 0, and 0 otherwise. Filtering: The contribution map may exhibit noise. The source suggests an alternative implementation where the contribution map is rendered at a lower resolution during the first pass, and stretched using the GPU's native bilinear filtering capabilities to smooth the count, trading accuracy for performance. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires one additional 2D texture for the contribution map, sized W \times H (screen resolution). Performance: Faster than full ray-marching integration per pixel because it relies on hardware rasterization of slice proxies. The alternative bilinear filtering approach for smoothing the contribution map is faster but less accurate. Strengths: Enhances internal high-frequency details, sharpens borders in DVR, and prevents saturation in additive rendering by adapting to local density. Limitations: Requires two passes; relies on the quality of the binary classification; may introduce artifacts if the contribution map is not smoothed appropriately. Locally Adaptive Volume Rendering was introduced by (Feature Enhancement using Locally Adaptive Volume Rendering, 2007) as a method to improve the visual quality of volume rendering by adapting the opacity based on the local number of contributing voxels. It builds on the principles of direct volume ray casting but introduces a pre-pass to gather statistical information about the volume density along each ray. name: Compositing and Output Generation
body: Compositing and Output Generation defines the final stage of direct volume ray casting, where discrete volumetric samples are aggregated into a 2D image pixel. It solves the problem of optical integration, determining how light emitted or scattered by volume elements is attenuated by absorption and combined with background light. This family builds on Multi-Pass and Compositing Techniques and is distinct from Projection and MIP Techniques because it explicitly tracks opacity and transmittance for alpha blending, preserving depth cues, whereas MIP methods discard opacity for order-independent extremum aggregation. It differs from Volume Raycasting Output Generation by focusing on the mathematical accumulation logic itself, while the sibling article covers the broader implementation pipeline including ray traversal and transfer function sampling. All methods in this family operate on a sequence of samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The core mechanism involves an accumulator state (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) initialized to (0, 0) (or background color/opacity) and updated iteratively for each sample. The standard optical model assumes that light is emitted or scattered by the volume and attenuated by absorption. The standard front-to-back compositing equation updates these accumulators for each sample i from front to back: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai Ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where C{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. The term (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample i from the camera side. In iterative form using transmittance T = 1 - \alpha{acc}: \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot T \\ T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where T is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). The final pixel color is often composited over a background color C{bg} using C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg}. Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1.0), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Standard front-to-back compositing loop shared by the family. samples: list of (color: list[float], opacity: float) sorted front-to-back. backgroundcolor: list[float] for the scene background. """ Cacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] alphaacc = 0.0 for ci, alphai in samples: transmittance = 1.0 - alphaacc Cacc = [Cacc[j] + transmittance alphai ci[j] for j in range(3)] alphaacc = alphaacc + transmittance alphai # Early ray termination if alphaacc >= 1.0: break # Composite over background return [Cacc[j] + (1.0 - alphaacc) backgroundcolor[j] for j in range(3)] Defines the mathematical rules for combining volumetric samples into a final pixel color and opacity. Sets itself apart by focusing on the accumulation logic and alpha blending, explicitly tracking transmittance, unlike Projection and MIP Techniques which discard opacity for extremum projection. Choose when depth-aware blending and accurate light attenuation modeling are required. The core image-order rendering technique that traverses a 3D volume along rays, accumulating color and opacity from front to back. Differs from Compositing and Blending by explicitly handling the ray traversal loop, boundary checks, and transfer function sampling within the output generation step. Choose for standard direct volume rendering pipelines requiring full ray marching. A family of methods that generate 2D images by aggregating scalar values using operators other than standard emission-absorption compositing (e.g., Maximum, Minimum, Sum). Solves the problem of visualizing specific features (like bones or vessels) by emphasizing extremal values while suppressing intermediate background data. Distinct because it discards opacity accumulation and depth cues in favor of order-independent aggregation. Choose when highlighting high-density or high-intensity structures is prioritized over depth cues. Modulates sample opacity based on the angle between the surface normal and the view vector, making regions orthogonal to the viewer more transparent and regions curving towards or away from the viewer more opaque. Differs from standard compositing by dynamically adjusting transparency per sample based on geometric orientation to improve readability of nested structures. Choose when visualizing complex nested geometries or surface details requires enhanced transparency control. Not given in the sources. The front-to-back compositing equation is a standard result in volume rendering, derived from the Beer-Lambert law for light attenuation. Early ray termination was introduced as an optimization to reduce computational cost by skipping samples behind opaque regions. MIP techniques originated in medical imaging to visualize high-density structures like bones without the occlusion caused by soft tissue.

name: Compositing and Blending
head: Accumulate, Alternative Compositing Schemes, Blending Modes, First Hit, Front-to-back blending, Maximum Intensity blending, Minimum Intensity blending
body: Compositing and Blending defines the final stage of direct volume ray casting where per-ray sample contributions (color and opacity) are integrated into a 2D pixel value. It solves the problem of correctly blending semi-transparent, overlapping density fields to produce physically plausible or semantically meaningful visualizations, handling tasks ranging from standard optical attenuation to differentiable training gradients and object-level importance modulation. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its focus on the mathematical integration of per-ray sample attributes (color, opacity, density) into a final pixel value, often leveraging specific mathematical forms (polynomials, kernels) or optimization strategies (early termination, packed layouts) rather than just acceleration structures or post-processing filters. All methods in this family operate on a sequence of samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The core mechanism involves an accumulator state (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) initialized to (0, 0) (or background color/opacity) and updated iteratively for each sample. The standard optical model assumes that light is emitted or scattered by the volume and attenuated by absorption. The standard front-to-back compositing equation updates these accumulators for each sample i from front to back: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai Ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where C{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. The term (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) represents the transmittance, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample i from the camera side. In iterative form using transmittance T = 1 - \alpha{acc}: \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot T \\ T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where T is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). The final pixel color is often composited over a background color C{bg} using C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg}. Early ray termination is a common optimization where the loop breaks if \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1.0), as further samples contribute negligibly to the color. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Standard front-to-back compositing loop shared by the family. samples: list of (color: vec3, opacity: float) sorted front-to-back. backgroundcolor: vec3 for the scene background. """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 for ci, alphai in samples: transmittance = 1.0 - alphaacc Cacc = Cacc + transmittance alphai ci alphaacc = alphaacc + transmittance alphai # Early ray termination if alphaacc >= 1.0: break # Composite over background return Cacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) backgroundcolor Pre-integration lookup is a technique in direct volume ray casting that replaces the iterative accumulation of color and opacity within a volume slab with a single texture fetch from a pre-computed table. It solves the problem of shading and color inaccuracies caused by linear interpolation of scalar values across a slab, which violates the non-linear optical properties of light attenuation. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by moving the integration step from the rendering loop to an offline or on-the-fly pre-computation phase, and from Simplified Pre-integration by accounting for color attenuation within the slab rather than neglecting it. See Pre-Integration Lookup. Binary Swap Compositing is a parallel image compositing scheme for distributed-memory volume rendering that reduces network congestion by dividing communication between processors over multiple rounds. Unlike naive binary compositing where many processors become idle at the top of the tree, Binary Swap ensures every processor participates in all stages of the compositing process by splitting the image plane into two pieces and having each processor take responsibility for one piece during exchange and compositing. It is particularly suitable for massively parallel processing because it keeps all processors busy and decreases the image size for sending/compositing at each stage. See Binary Swap Compositing. Screen-space post-processing is a full-screen rendering stage that applies aspect-ratio preserving UV covering, luminance-based bright passes, color grading, spatial blurring, and dithering to a scene texture to produce a display-ready image. It differs from direct volume compositing methods by operating entirely in screen space on the final display image rather than during ray traversal, allowing for complex aesthetic effects like bloom and vignette without modifying the volume rendering pipeline. See Screen-space Post-processing. Layered SDF Compositing is a technique for rendering Signed Distance Field (SDF) glyphs by compositing multiple pre-multiplied alpha layers (typically a face and one or more outline layers) into a final pixel color. It solves the problem of rendering crisp, scalable text or icons with anti-aliased edges and colored outlines by treating each visual component as a distinct alpha-blended layer. It differs from standard SDF rendering by explicitly managing a fixed number of discrete layers (1, 2, or 4) using specific linear interpolation logic on pre-multiplied colors, rather than a continuous ray-casting integration. See Layered SDF Compositing. Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques constitute the final stage of direct volume ray casting, where 3D volumetric data is projected into a 2D image by integrating sample contributions along viewing rays. This family solves the problem of correctly blending semi-transparent, overlapping density fields to produce physically plausible or semantically meaningful visualizations, handling tasks ranging from standard optical attenuation to differentiable training gradients and object-level importance modulation. What sets this family apart from its siblings is its focus on the mathematical integration of per-ray sample attributes (color, opacity, density) into a final pixel value, often leveraging specific mathematical forms (polynomials, kernels) or optimization strategies (early termination, packed layouts) rather than just acceleration structures or post-processing filters. See Reconstruction and Compositing Techniques. Lighting-Specific Compositing is a family of volume rendering techniques that integrate illumination models (such as in-scattering, Phong shading, or boundary enhancement) directly into the compositing loop, rather than treating lighting as a post-processing step or a simple per-sample color multiplication. It solves the problem of physically inaccurate or visually flat rendering by allowing light transport effects to influence the accumulation of opacity and color at the sample level. It differs from standard direct volume ray casting by modifying the color and opacity terms (ci, \alphai) before they enter the front-to-back accumulator, and from image-level compositing by preserving depth coherence for complex lighting interactions like occlusion and shadowing. See Lighting-Specific Compositing. The Layer-Centric Volume Rendering Framework is a visualization architecture that constructs the final image by compositing multiple distinct renderings, each treated as an independent layer. It solves the rigidity of traditional single-pass volume rendering by segmenting the workflow into a rendering phase for small regions of interest and a subsequent compositing phase. This approach provides a rich set of 2D operators and interactions, allowing for greater freedom and more intuitive user interaction compared to standard volume rendering techniques. See Layer-Centric Volume Rendering Framework. MAB compositing is a gaze-contingent rendering technique that maps framebuffer fragments to a Multi-Anchor Buffer (MAB) to retrieve and blend color values from different resolution levels based on the distance to the center of gaze. It solves the performance bottleneck in immersive VR volume rendering by dynamically adjusting resolution distribution to maintain high frame rates, thereby preventing cybersickness caused by performance fluctuations. Unlike standard fixed-resolution ray casting, it blends multiple resolution levels simultaneously using a smooth-step function to ensure unnoticeable transitions between detail levels. See MAB Compositing with Gaze-Contingent Blending. Multi-view image blending reduces artifacts caused by single-view fading, such as ghosting and transparency variation, by combining a set of images taken from various view angles. It sets itself apart from single-texture approaches by requiring the selection and blending of at least three textures, trading increased rendering cost for improved visual fidelity across viewpoints. See Multi-view image blending. Dynamic Job-Scheduling for Grid Volume Rendering is a distributed rendering technique that determines the processing order of sub-volumes based on their real-time visibility rather than a static sequence. It solves the bottleneck caused by heterogeneous agent speeds in grid computing, where static sequential scheduling forces fast agents to wait for slow agents to complete prior steps. By using obstacle-flags to track obscuration, the method allows agents to immediately process newly visible sub-volumes, significantly improving efficiency over sequential approaches. See Dynamic Job-Scheduling for Grid Volume Rendering. HardSoftRas Blending is a pixel-wise compositing strategy for differentiable rendering that distinguishes between edge pixels (silhouettes and vertical surfaces) and non-edge pixels to balance anti-aliasing with texture sharpness. Unlike SoftRas, which blends all faces in non-edge regions, HardSoftRas retains the most frontal color for non-edges while applying weighted averaging for edges, thereby maintaining sharp textures inside silhouettes and generating far-range gradients around boundaries. See HardSoftRas Blending. A pass that simply copies the current frame to the output, acting as a simple integration or blit step for the LAO renderer. Step: Sample frame buffer: oColor = texture(uFrame, vPosition);. A post-processing step where partial images rendered from blocks of different resolutions are expanded to a common 'virtual dimension' (the highest resolution dimension of the block) before compositing. This allows standard compositing algorithms to work despite varying input resolutions. Step: Determine the virtual dimensions for each block. For a block with original high-res dimensions (Hx, Hy, Hz), the virtual dimensions are (Hx, Hy, Hz). Render the block at its assigned resolution (e.g., Medium: Hx/2, Hy/2, Hz/2). This produces a partial image with actual dimensions smaller than the virtual dimensions. Expand the partial image to the virtual dimensions. This typically involves interpolating or replicating pixels to fill the larger grid, or simply placing the smaller image into a larger buffer with appropriate scaling factors during compositing. Parameter: Virtual Dimension Selection: The virtual dimension can be set to the dimension of the largest subimage in the scene to minimize padding, or fixed to the global high-resolution block size. A rendering compositing strategy where the scene is rendered part-by-part (one Voronoi cell at a time) and the resulting cell images are composited back-to-front to generate the final image. It relies on the proof that Voronoi cells admit a partial ordering compatible with occlusion. Step: 1. Define partial ordering on Voronoi cells based on distance from camera Q to the Voronoi sites P: V{P'} <Q VP iff d(P', Q) < d(P, Q). 2. Render each Voronoi cell independently. 3. Composite the rendered cell images in the order defined by <Q (back-to-front) to ensure closer objects occlude further ones. Formula: V{P'} <Q VP if and only if d(P', Q) < d(P, Q). Comparison: Standard Painter's Algorithm fails on cyclic occlusion graphs. Voronoi Painter's is always compatible because the distance-to-camera ordering is a strict partial order. Hybrid methods like Radix-k combine direct send and binary swap approaches depending on the problem setting, adaptively running one or the other based on criteria. A compositing pass that creates an initial fabric-like texture by combining advected noise fields, silhouette data, and lighting. Pixels not part of the geometry are discarded using the depth buffer. Formula: Color channels after k iterations: R(x,y) = \frac{r \cdot f{\lambda2}(x,y)}{8 \cdot f{\lambda1}^2(x,y)} + e{x,y} + \text{light}(\mathcal{L}{x,y}) G(x,y) = \frac{(1-r) \cdot f{\lambda1}(x,y)}{8 \cdot f{\lambda2}^2(x,y)} + e{x,y} + \text{light}(\mathcal{L}{x,y}) B(x,y) = e{x,y} + \text{light}(\mathcal{L}{x,y}) Here f{\lambda1} and f{\lambda2} are the advected fields p{\lambda1}^k and p{\lambda2}^k. e{x,y} is the silhouette image. r blends between tensor directions. Squaring the denominator emphasizes differences. Parameter: Blend factor r: Scalar factor used to blend between the two chosen tensor directions. Lighting function: A separate lighting function light manipulates intensity without affecting the base color of the mesh structure. Blinn-Phong shading is mentioned as providing required depth cues. The concept of compositing in volume rendering originated with the standard front-to-back accumulation model, which treats volume rendering as an integration of light emission and absorption along rays. Early systems like VolumePro supported multiple blending modes including Front-to-back blending, Minimum Intensity, and Maximum Intensity blending. Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) became widely used for extracting vessel structures in magnetic resonance angiograms. The field has since expanded to include distributed compositing strategies like Binary Swap for scalability, gaze-contingent rendering for VR performance, and differentiable compositing for neural rendering. name: Pre-Integration Lookup
head: 2D Pre-Integration, 2D Pre-integration Lookup, 3D Pre-integration, 3D Pre-integration Table
body: Pre-integration lookup is a technique in direct volume ray casting that replaces the iterative accumulation of color and opacity within a volume slab with a single texture fetch from a pre-computed table. It solves the problem of shading and color inaccuracies caused by linear interpolation of scalar values across a slab, which violates the non-linear optical properties of light attenuation. It sets itself apart from standard ray casting by moving the integration step from the rendering loop to an offline or on-the-fly pre-computation phase, and from Simplified Pre-integration by accounting for color attenuation within the slab rather than neglecting it. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity, and ray samples (sf, sm, sb) representing the scalar values at the front, middle, and back of a slab (or entry/exit densities and slab thickness). Output: The accumulated color and opacity contribution of the slab, which is then composited with other slabs. Data Structures: Pre-integration Lookup Table: A texture (2D or 3D) storing pre-calculated optical properties. 3D Table Layout: Dimensions 256 \times 256 \times 256 for 8-bit scalar domains. The axes correspond to front sample value (sf), middle sample value (sm), and back sample value (sb). 2D Table Layout: Dimensions dependent on entry/exit densities and slab thickness. The axes typically correspond to entry density, exit density, and slab thickness (mapped to 2D via indexing or specific encoding). Stored Values: Color (C) and Opacity (\alpha) resulting from the integration of the transfer function over the slab. Steps: 1. Pre-computation (Offline or On-the-fly): For a 3D table, render a quadrilateral parallel to the projection plane 256 times, filling the viewport. In the fragment shader, map screen coordinates to front (sf) and middle (sm) sample values, while the back sample (sb) is provided as a uniform variable. Compute the optical properties by integrating the transfer function over the slab defined by sf, sm, sb. Store the result in the 3D texture at coordinate (sf, sm, sb). Note: 2D tables are preferred on hardware with faster 2D texturing capabilities, as 3D texturing can be slower. 2. Rendering (Per Ray): For each ray, divide the volume into slabs of thickness 2d. For each slab, retrieve the three scalar samples (sf, sm, sb) from the volume. Perform a 3D (or 2D) texture lookup using these samples as coordinates to fetch the pre-integrated color C{slab} and opacity \alpha{slab}. Composite the fetched slab contribution using the standard front-to-back compositing equation: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alpha{slab} C{slab} \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alpha{slab} Repeat for all slabs along the ray. Parameters: Slab Thickness: Defined as 2d, where d is the distance between samples. Table Resolution: 256^3 for 8-bit data. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hardware Performance: 3D texture lookups may be slower than 2D lookups on some GPUs, making 2D pre-integration a practical choice despite potential artifacts. Linear Assumption: The method assumes linear evolution of data within the slice, which may introduce errors if the data varies non-linearly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preintegrationlookup(volumedata, transferfunction, raysamples): """ Renders a ray using pre-integration lookup tables. volumedata: 3D array of scalar values. transferfunction: function mapping scalar -> (color, opacity). raysamples: list of (sf, sm, sb) tuples for each slab along the ray. """ # Pre-computed lookup table (simulated as a function for clarity) # In practice, this is a 3D texture fetch def lookuptable(sf, sm, sb): # Fetch pre-computed (Cslab, alphaslab) from 3D texture # Coordinates are indices into the 256^3 table return preintegratedtable[sf][sm][sb] Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 for sf, sm, sb in raysamples: # Fetch pre-integrated slab properties Cslab, alphaslab = lookuptable(sf, sm, sb) # Standard front-to-back compositing transmittance = 1.0 - alphaacc Cacc = Cacc + transmittance alphaslab Cslab alphaacc = alphaacc + transmittance alphaslab # Early ray termination if alphaacc >= 1.0: break return Cacc This method computes the diffuse component of Blinn-Phong shading in pre-integrated volume rendering by decomposing the integral into four 2D look-up tables weighted by coefficients dependent on light direction and gradient angles. It avoids the prohibitive memory cost of full 4D normal-based pre-integration while reducing shading errors caused by large angles between consecutive sample gradients compared to linear interpolation. Non-linear gradient interpolation is a technique for pre-integrated direct volume rendering that reduces shading errors by interpolating gradients between front and back samples along a quadratic curve instead of a linear segment, allowing accurate computation of 2D pre-integration look-up tables. It sets itself apart from linear gradient interpolation by approximating the non-linear path of a normalized gradient vector as a quadratic polynomial, thereby avoiding the energy loss and shading errors inherent in linear interpolation which assumes the normalization term \eta(t)=1. Simplified Pre-integration is a faster approximation of full pre-integration used in direct volume ray casting. It solves the performance bottleneck of computing pre-integrated transfer function (TF) lookups by neglecting color attenuation inside volume slabs. It sets itself apart from full pre-integration Pre-Integration Lookup by trading accuracy for speed, making it suitable for interactive interfaces where multiple TFs are modified simultaneously. This method corrects rendering artifacts that occur at clip boundaries when using pre-integrated volume rendering with low sampling rates. It computes the optical contribution of the ray segment between a clipping surface and the first volume slice behind it, avoiding the need for interleaved rendering or complex boundary layer models. It differs from sibling methods by specifically addressing the discontinuity in sampling distance at clip planes rather than general gradient interpolation errors. A method for efficiently reconstructing 3D medical images that combines pre-integrated volume rendering with the Shear-Warp algorithm to eliminate aliasing artifacts from under-sampling and improve reconstruction quality via Phong lighting shading. It implements classification coding for volume data by utilizing the correlation of the opacity transfer function (OTF) and a min-max Octree data structure, establishing a new run-length encoded (RLE) data structure for fast reconstruction when OTF and view angle change. Time Complexity: The per-slab cost is reduced to a single texture lookup and compositing step, significantly faster than iterative integration per sample. Memory Complexity: Requires storing a large lookup table. For 8-bit data, a 3D table of size 256^3 is needed. Measured Performance: On ATI 9700 Pro with 5x5 tiles: spx1 dataset: 609-750 ms (2D), 688-907 ms (3D). blunt dataset: 141-391 ms (2D), 344-500 ms (3D). f117 dataset: 359-640 ms (2D), 453-719 ms (3D). On GeForce 6800 GT with 5x5 tiles: spx1 dataset: 312-531 ms (2D), 313-547 ms (3D). blunt dataset: 109-1094 ms (2D), 109-1032 ms (3D). f117 dataset: 266-563 ms (2D), 172-438 ms (3D). Limitations: High memory usage for 3D tables; 2D tables may introduce artifacts if not carefully designed; assumes linear data evolution within slabs. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained and 3D tables are too large; when non-linear data variation within slabs is significant. Variants include 2D and 3D lookup tables, with 2D often preferred for performance on certain hardware. It has been applied to medical image reconstruction and interactive visualization systems. name: Pre-Integrated Diffuse Shading with Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation
head: Pre-Integrated Diffuse Shading
body: This method computes the diffuse component of Blinn-Phong shading in pre-integrated volume rendering by decomposing the integral into four 2D look-up tables weighted by coefficients dependent on light direction and gradient angles. It avoids the prohibitive memory cost of full 4D normal-based pre-integration while reducing shading errors caused by large angles between consecutive sample gradients compared to linear interpolation. Inputs: Front scalar value Sf and back scalar value Sb for the current sampling step of length D. Front normal \mathbf{N}f and back normal \mathbf{N}b (gradients of the scalar field). Light direction \mathbf{L}. Diffuse coefficient Kd. Pre-computed 2D LUTs for I0, I1, I2, I3. Outputs: Pre-integrated diffuse color \tilde{C}d. Lookup Tables: Four 2D arrays indexed by quantized front and back scalar values. The exact array dimensions and binning strategy are not given in the sources. The pre-integrated diffuse color is calculated as: \tilde{C}d = Kd \cdot (a0(\mathbf{L})I0 + a1(\mathbf{L})I1 + a2(\mathbf{L})I2 + a3(\mathbf{L})I3) where Kd is the diffuse coefficient. The integral terms Ik(Sf, Sb) are defined as: Ik(Sf, Sb) = d \int{Sf}^{Sb} c(s0) \cdot s^k \cdot \exp(-d \cdot \sigma(Sf, s0)) \, ds0 where: k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\} is the polynomial exponent. c(s0) is the classification color at scalar value s0. \sigma(Sf, s0) is the accumulated absorption from Sf to s0. d = \frac{D}{Sb - Sf} is the normalized step length. s = \frac{s0 - Sf}{Sb - Sf} is the normalized position within the step. The coefficients ak(\mathbf{L}) depend on the light direction and normals: \begin{aligned} a0(\mathbf{L}) &= \mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} \\ a1(\mathbf{L}) &= \mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L} - (1 + r)\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} \\ a2(\mathbf{L}) &= r(2\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L}) \\ a3(\mathbf{L}) &= r(\mathbf{N}b \cdot \mathbf{L} - \mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{L}) \end{aligned} where r is a factor derived from the angle \alpha between the front and back normals: r = \frac{4(\cos(\alpha) - 1)}{\cos(\alpha)} \alpha = \frac{1}{2} \arccos(\mathbf{N}f \cdot \mathbf{N}b) All coefficients and the factor r are computed per sampling step. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def precomputeluts(numbins, scalarmin, scalarmax, classificationfunc, absorptionfunc): """ Pre-compute the four 2D lookup tables I0, I1, I2, I3. classificationfunc(s) returns color c(s) as a list/tuple of 3 floats. absorptionfunc(sf, s) returns sigma(Sf, s) as a float. """ # Initialize 2D tables with zeros LUTI0 = [[None] numbins for in range(numbins)] LUTI1 = [[None] numbins for in range(numbins)] LUTI2 = [[None] numbins for in range(numbins)] LUTI3 = [[None] numbins for in range(numbins)] # Discretize scalar range scalars = [scalarmin + i (scalarmax - scalarmin) / (numbins - 1) for i in range(numbins)] for i, Sf in enumerate(scalars): for j, Sb in enumerate(scalars): if Sb <= Sf: continue # Degenerate case # Normalized step length for table indexing Dnorm = 1.0 d = Dnorm / (Sb - Sf) # Accumulators for RGB channels accI0 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accI1 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accI2 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accI3 = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] numsteps = 100 # Resolution for pre-computation integration ds0 = (Sb - Sf) / numsteps for stepidx in range(numsteps): s0 = Sf + stepidx ds0 s = (s0 - Sf) / (Sb - Sf) cs0 = classificationfunc(s0) sigma = absorptionfunc(Sf, s0) weight = math.exp(-d sigma) # Ik = d integral(c(s0) s^k exp(-dsigma) ds0) for ch in range(3): term = cs0[ch] weight ds0 d accI0[ch] += term (s 0) accI1[ch] += term (s 1) accI2[ch] += term (s 2) accI3[ch] += term (s 3) LUTI0[i][j] = accI0 LUTI1[i][j] = accI1 LUTI2[i][j] = accI2 LUTI3[i][j] = accI3 return LUTI0, LUTI1, LUTI2, LUTI3 def computediffuseshading(LUTI0, LUTI1, LUTI2, LUTI3, Sf, Sb, Nf, Nb, L, Kd, numbins, scalarmin, scalarmax): """ Compute pre-integrated diffuse shading for a single step. """ if Sb <= Sf: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # 1. Compute angle alpha and factor r cosalpharaw = Nf[0]Nb[0] + Nf[1]Nb[1] + Nf[2]Nb[2] cosalpharaw = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosalpharaw)) # Clamp for numerical stability alpha = math.acos(cosalpharaw) / 2.0 cosalpha = math.cos(alpha) # Handle division by zero when alpha approaches 90 degrees if abs(cosalpha) < 1e-6: r = -4.0 # Limit approximation else: r = 4.0 (cosalpha - 1.0) / cosalpha # 2. Compute coefficients a0 to a3 NfdotL = Nf[0]L[0] + Nf[1]L[1] + Nf[2]L[2] NbdotL = Nb[0]L[0] + Nb[1]L[1] + Nb[2]L[2] a0 = NfdotL a1 = NbdotL - (1.0 + r) NfdotL a2 = r (2.0 NfdotL - NbdotL) a3 = r (NbdotL - NfdotL) # 3. Quantize indices idxSf = int((Sf - scalarmin) / (scalarmax - scalarmin) (numbins - 1)) idxSb = int((Sb - scalarmin) / (scalarmax - scalarmin) (numbins - 1)) idxSf = max(0, min(numbins - 1, idxSf)) idxSb = max(0, min(numbins - 1, idxSb)) I0 = LUTI0[idxSf][idxSb] I1 = LUTI1[idxSf][idxSb] I2 = LUTI2[idxSf][idxSb] I3 = LUTI3[idxSf][idxSb] # 4. Compute final color sumI = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for ch in range(3): sumI[ch] = a0 I0[ch] + a1 I1[ch] + a2 I2[ch] + a3 I3[ch] Cd = [Kd sumI[ch] for ch in range(3)] return Cd Negative Dot Products: The dot product between the light direction and the normalized gradient may become negative, which is physically invalid for diffuse shading. Two solutions are common: applying max(0, dot) to the dot products before computing coefficients, or mirroring the gradient if the dot product is negative. Applying max(0, dot) makes exact pre-integration difficult, so the source distinguishes three cases but does not detail them. Degenerate Normals: If \mathbf{N}f and \mathbf{N}b are identical, \alpha = 0, r = 0, and the method reduces to standard linear shading. If they are orthogonal, \alpha = \pi/4. Precision: The factor r can become large negative values for large angles, potentially amplifying numerical errors in the coefficient calculation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. This method was proposed by Lum et al. in 2010 as an improvement over linear gradient interpolation in pre-integrated volume rendering. It addresses visual discontinuities and errors that arise when gradients change significantly between sample points, which linear interpolation fails to capture accurately. The approach builds on the concept of pre-integration lookup tables introduced in earlier work, extending it to handle diffuse shading with a non-linear gradient model. name: Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation for Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering
head: Non-linear gradient interpolation, Non-linear polynomial interpolation, Pre-Integrated Volume Rendering with Non-Linear Gradient Interpolation, Pre-integration with quadratic gradient interpolation, Quadratic gradient interpolation
body:
Non-linear gradient interpolation is a technique for pre-integrated direct volume rendering that reduces shading errors by interpolating gradients between front and back samples along a quadratic curve instead of a linear segment, allowing accurate computation of 2D pre-integration look-up tables. It sets itself apart from linear gradient interpolation by approximating the non-linear path of a normalized gradient vector as a quadratic polynomial, thereby avoiding the energy loss and shading errors inherent in linear interpolation which assumes the normalization term \eta(t)=1. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Front sample properties Sf, Back sample properties Sb, Front normalized gradient Nf, Back normalized gradient Nb, Light direction L, Specular half-vector H, Shininess n\delta, Slab size D, normalization factor r, and pre-computed 2D lookup tables. Outputs: Diffuse shading coefficient 	ilde{C}d, Specular shading coefficient 	ilde{C}s. Data Structures: Lookup Tables: Four 2D tables for the diffuse term (I0, I1, I2, I3) and five 2D tables for the specular term (I{00}, I{10}, I{20}, I{30}). Representation: 16-bit unsigned short in GPU memory. Indexing: Tables are indexed by Sf and Sb. Definitions: \alpha = \arccos(Nf \cdot Nb) / 2: Half the angle between front and back normals. r: A normalization factor derived from the geometry of the interpolated gradient arc. s = t/D: Normalized distance along the slab, t \in [0, D]. s0 = Sf + s(Sb - Sf): Normalized scalar value at position s. d = D / (Sb - Sf): Scaling factor for the integral substitution. \eta(t) \approx  rac{\cos(\alpha) \cdot x^2}{x^2 (\cos(\alpha) - 1) + 1}: Quadratic approximation of the normalization term, where x =  rac{2t}{D} - 1 = 2s - 1.

Compute Diffuse Coefficients (ak): Calculate coefficients using Nf, Nb, L, \alpha, and r: a0 =  rac{4(\cos(\alpha) - 1)}{\cos(\alpha)} a1 = Nb \cdot L - Nf \cdot L a2 =  rac{Nb \cdot L - (1 + r)Nf \cdot L}{r(2Nf \cdot L - Nb \cdot L)} a3 =  rac{Nf \cdot L}{r} 3. Access Diffuse Lookup Tables: Retrieve I0(Sf, Sb), I1(Sf, Sb), I2(Sf, Sb), I3(Sf, Sb) from the pre-computed 2D tables. Ik(Sf, Sb) = d \int{Sf}^{Sb} c(s0) \cdot s^k \cdot \exp(-d \sigma(Sf, s0)) \, ds0 4. Compute Diffuse Shading: Calculate 	ilde{C}d = Kd (a0 I0 + a1 I1 + a2 I2 + a3 I3). 5. Handle Negative Dot Products (Diffuse): If Nf \cdot L < 0 or Nb \cdot L < 0, apply case-based handling: if both are positive, use the standard formulation; if either is negative, fade in/out the non-negative value; if both are negative, the result is 0. 6. Specular Term Approximation: Replace the Phong lobe \cos(	heta)^{n\delta} with a Phong cone approximation: \cos(	heta)^{n\delta} \approx 1 + n\delta (\cos(	heta) - 1), where \cos(	heta) = N \cdot H. 7. Compute Specular Coefficients: Calculate a0(H), a1(H), a2(H), a3(H) using H instead of L with the same formulas as step 2. 8. Access Specular Lookup Tables: Retrieve I{00}, I{10}, I{20}, I{30}. I{00}(Sf, Sb) = d \int{Sf}^{Sb} (s < 0.5 ? 2s: 2 - 2s) \cdot \exp(-d \sigma(Sf, s0)) \, ds0 9. Compute Specular Shading: Calculate 	ilde{C}s = Ks (I{00} + n\delta (a0(H)I{00} + a1(H)I{10} + a2(H)I{20} + a3(H)I{30}) - n\delta I{00}). 10. Handle Negative Dot Products (Specular): Specular values become negative if N(s0) \cdot H < 	ext{thresh} = (n\delta - 1)/n\delta. If both Nf \cdot H > 	ext{thresh} and Nb \cdot H > 	ext{thresh}, use the standard formulation. If either is below the threshold, use a fading approximation. If both Nf \cdot L < 0 and Nb \cdot L < 0, a highlight may exist between samples; use the I{00} approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sample2dtable(table, sf, sb): """Helper to access a pre-computed 2D lookup table indexed by sf and sb.""" return table[sf][sb] def computeshading(Nf, Nb, Sf, Sb, L, H, ndelta, Ka, Kd, Ks, D, r, TI0, TI1, TI2, TI3, TI00, TI10, TI20, TI30): # 1. Compute angle alpha cosalpha = dot(Nf, Nb) alpha = acos(cosalpha) / 2.0 # 2. Compute Diffuse Coefficients NfdotL = dot(Nf, L) NbdotL = dot(Nb, L) a0 = 4.0 (cos(alpha) - 1.0) / cosalpha a1 = NbdotL - NfdotL denoma2 = r (2.0 NfdotL - NbdotL) a2 = (NbdotL - (1.0 + r) NfdotL) / denoma2 if abs(denoma2) > 1e-9 else 0.0 a3 = NfdotL / r # 3. Handle Negative Dot Products (Diffuse) if NfdotL < 0 and NbdotL < 0: Cd = 0.0 elif NfdotL > 0 and NbdotL > 0: # 4. Access Diffuse Lookup Tables I0 = sample2dtable(TI0, Sf, Sb) I1 = sample2dtable(TI1, Sf, Sb) I2 = sample2dtable(TI2, Sf, Sb) I3 = sample2dtable(TI3, Sf, Sb) # 5. Compute Diffuse Shading Cd = Kd (a0 I0 + a1 I1 + a2 I2 + a3 I3) else: # Fading approximation for mixed signs I0 = sample2dtable(TI0, Sf, Sb) I1 = sample2dtable(TI1, Sf, Sb) Cd = Kd (a0 I0 + a1 I1) # Simplified fading per source guidelines # 6. Specular Coefficients (using H) NfdotH = dot(Nf, H) NbdotH = dot(Nb, H) thresh = (ndelta - 1.0) / ndelta a0s = 4.0 (cos(alpha) - 1.0) / cosalpha a1s = NbdotH - NfdotH denoma2s = r (2.0 NfdotH - NbdotH) a2s = (NbdotH - (1.0 + r) NfdotH) / denoma2s if abs(denoma2s) > 1e-9 else 0.0 a3s = NfdotH / r # 7. Access Specular Lookup Tables I00 = sample2dtable(TI00, Sf, Sb) I10 = sample2dtable(TI10, Sf, Sb) I20 = sample2dtable(TI20, Sf, Sb) I30 = sample2dtable(TI30, Sf, Sb) # 8. Handle Negative Dot Products (Specular) if NfdotH > thresh and NbdotH > thresh: # Standard formulation Cs = Ks (I00 + ndelta (a0s I00 + a1s I10 + a2s I20 + a3s I30) - ndelta I00) elif NfdotL < 0 and NbdotL < 0: # Highlight may exist between samples; use I00 approximation Cs = Ks (I00 + ndelta (a0s I00 + a1s I10 + a2s I20 + a3s I30) - ndelta I00) else: # Fading approximation for threshold crossing I0 = sample2dtable(TI0, Sf, Sb) I1 = sample2dtable(TI1, Sf, Sb) Cs = Ks (I0 (1.0 - ndelta) + ndelta NbdotL I1) return Cd, Cs Time Complexity: The method requires four texture accesses for the diffuse term and five for the specular term (including I{00}). It is 10% to 20% slower than linear gradient interpolation due to these additional texture accesses. Memory Complexity: Uses 2D lookup tables, keeping memory usage low compared to 3D tables (which would depend on \alpha) and allowing real-time updates during transfer function changes. Tables use 16-bit unsigned short representation. Measured Performance: On an Intel Core 2Quad Q9300 and Nvidia GeForce GTX 280 at 800x800 viewport: Reference (high sub-sampling) 5.1 fps; Constant gradient 56.3 fps; Linear gradient 51.2 fps; Non-linear gradient 47.19 fps. Strengths: Reduces maximal shading error to approximately 0.3% for a 90-degree angle between normals, compared to 41% error with linear interpolation (assuming \eta(t)=1). Accurately depicts contours of specular highlights. Limitations: The quadratic curve interpolation is not exactly an arc of a circle, causing the normalization term to be potentially too low, resulting in vectors with norm > 1 and added energy around specular highlights. Mirroring gradients for negative values introduces approximation errors for slabs where one gradient is correctly oriented and the other is inverted. Origin: Proposed by Amel Guetat, Alexandre Ancel, Stephane Marchesin, and Jean-Michel Dischler in 2010. History: Builds on pre-integrated volume rendering techniques (e.g., Lum et al.) which used linear gradient interpolation. This method addresses the luminous energy loss in high-frequency gradient variations and high-frequency shading functions (like specular highlights) inherent in linear interpolation. Usage: Used in direct volume rendering with Blinn-Phong illumination and non-photorealistic models like Gooch shading.
