name: Separable Convolution
head: Linearly separable convolution, Two-pass convolution
body: Separable convolution is a method to accelerate hologram computation by exploiting the linear separability of the lens phase function fz into independent horizontal and vertical components. It solves the performance bottleneck of point-wise integration in direct volume ray casting for holographic displays by reducing the computational complexity of the spatial convolution operation. It is distinguished from FFT-based convolution by its reliance on spatial separability rather than frequency-domain transformation, making it faster for smaller sub-hologram sizes but inapplicable when the phase function is not separable. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Target image data A (containing the square root of image intensities) and the lens phase function fz. Output: Computed hologram H. Data Structures: A: A 2D array of complex or real values representing the source image intensities. f{zx}: A 1D vector representing the horizontal component of the lens phase function. f{zy}: A 1D vector representing the vertical component of the lens phase function. H: A 2D array of the same dimensions as A, storing the resulting hologram. Prerequisites: The lens phase function fz must be linearly separable into vectors f{zx} and f{zy}. This condition holds for lens phase functions of any focal power and certain aberrations, such as horizontal astigmatism or vertical astigmatism. If fz is not linearly separable, this method cannot be applied. Formulas: The hologram H is computed by convolving the image A with the separable components sequentially: H = (A f{zx}) f{zy} where denotes the convolution operation. Parameters: Sub-hologram width: The runtime scales linearly with the sub-hologram size. Typical Performance: Calculation of a hologram with 2 million object points takes just a few milliseconds on a GPU. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Non-separable Phase Functions: If the lens phase function contains aberrations or focal properties that cannot be decomposed into independent horizontal and vertical vectors, this method fails. Spatial Variance: This method assumes the lens phase function is spatially invariant (constant over the image) to allow standard convolution. It does not support per-pixel focal control or spatially variant aberration correction. Sub-hologram Size Scaling: Unlike FFT-based convolution, the runtime of separable convolution scales linearly with the sub-hologram width. It is faster than FFT-based convolution for smaller sub-hologram sizes, but the crossover point depends on the specific hardware and implementation. Pseudocode: The implementation operates in two passes, one for each linearly separable axis. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def separableconvolution(A, fzx, fzy): """ Computes hologram H using separable convolution. Args: A: 2D array of image intensities (square root). fzx: 1D vector for horizontal phase component. fzy: 1D vector for vertical phase component. Returns: H: 2D array representing the hologram. """ # Pass 1: Convolve image A with horizontal kernel fzx # Result is stored in intermediate buffer Temp Temp = convolve2dhorizontal(A, fzx) # Pass 2: Convolve intermediate result Temp with vertical kernel fzy # Result is stored in H H = convolve2dvertical(Temp, fzy) return H def convolve2dhorizontal(Image, Kernel): """ Convolves each row of the image with the 1D horizontal kernel. """ Height, Width = Image.shape KernelLength = len(Kernel) Output = zeroslike(Image) for y in range(Height): for x in range(Width): Sum = 0 for k in range(KernelLength): # Handle boundary conditions (e.g., zero-padding or replication) # Not specified in sources; assume standard convolution boundary handling xidx = x - k + (KernelLength - 1) // 2 if 0 <= xidx < Width: Sum += Image[y, xidx] Kernel[k] Output[y, x] = Sum return Output def convolve2dvertical(Image, Kernel): """ Convolves each column of the image with the 1D vertical kernel. """ Height, Width = Image.shape KernelLength = len(Kernel) Output = zeroslike(Image) for y in range(Height): for x in range(Width): Sum = 0 for k in range(KernelLength): # Handle boundary conditions yidx = y - k + (KernelLength - 1) // 2 if 0 <= yidx < Height: Sum += Image[yidx, x] Kernel[k] Output[y, x] = Sum return Output A method to speed up hologram calculation by removing spatial variance of the lens phase function fz so it is the same for all object points, allowing substitution of point-wise integration with standard spatially invariant convolution. It computes H = A fz using the Fast Fourier Transform: H = FFT^{-1}(FFT(A) \times FFT(fz)), where \times indicates point-wise multiplication. It requires a spatially invariant lens phase function, implying focus and aberration correction is constant over the image. A key pitfall is that it does not support per-pixel focal control because the lens phase function is not spatially variant. It runs in just a few milliseconds for 2 million object points on a GPU. Unlike separable convolution, FFT convolution does not depend on sub-hologram size, whereas separable convolution scales linearly with it. Time Complexity: Scales linearly with the sub-hologram size. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the image A, the hologram H, and intermediate buffers for the two-pass convolution. Measured Performance: For a 1920x1080 hologram with 2 million object points, computation takes just a few milliseconds on a GPU. Scaling: Runtime increases linearly with sub-hologram width. Strengths: Significantly faster than point-wise integration (orders of magnitude). Faster than FFT-based convolution for smaller sub-hologram sizes. Limitations: Only applicable when the lens phase function is linearly separable. Does not support per-pixel focal control or spatially variant aberration correction. When to use: When the lens phase function is linearly separable and sub-hologram sizes are small to moderate. When not to use: When the lens phase function is not linearly separable or when per-pixel focal control is required. Separable convolution was introduced in the context of holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality by Maimone et al. in 2017. The method leverages a common simplification in image processing, applying it to hologram computation for the first time in this context. It is used in real-time holographic displays to generate holograms directly from rendered polygonal models, enabling frame rates exceeding the display refresh rate. Holographic near-eye displays for virtual and augmented reality, https://doi.org/10.1145/3072959.3073624, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Area-based Pixel Kernel
head: Area kernel, Noyau de Pixel basé sur l’aire (Area-based Pixel Kernel), Noyau d’interpolation sur l’aire des pixels
body: The Area-based Pixel Kernel is a reconstruction kernel that assigns pixel contributions proportional to the geometric area of intersection between a pixel and a thick projection line. It solves the artifact issues inherent in Dirac and B-Spline kernels, which leave unreconstructed pixels during subsampling, and linear kernels, which fail to fully exploit available data during oversampling. It is distinguished from its sibling Spatial Convolution by its specific geometric interpretation of projection thickness and its optimization via a rotation-based approximation. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Projection data p(\theta, \rho), where \theta is the angle and \rho is the radial coordinate; pixel grid coordinates (i, j); projection line thickness d\rho; pixel size \Delta p. Outputs: Reconstructed image intensity I(i, j). Data Structures: Projection Buffer: Array of values indexed by (\theta, \rho). Temporary Image I\theta: A 2D array used to store the backprojected contributions for a specific angle \theta before rotation. Result Image I: The final accumulated 2D array. Parameters: d\rho: Thickness of the projection line. \Delta p: Pixel width. \theta: Current projection angle. \rho: Radial position of the projection line. i, j: Integer pixel coordinates. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize the result image I to zero. 2. For each projection angle \theta: a. Create a temporary image I\theta of the same dimensions as I, initialized to zero. b. For each radial sample \rho in the projection p(\theta, \cdot): i. Calculate the kernel weight \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j) for every pixel (i, j) in I\theta using the formula below. ii. Add the contribution p(\theta, \rho) \times \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j) to I\theta(i, j). c. Rotate the temporary image I\theta by the angle -\theta. d. Add the rotated I\theta to the result image I. Formula: The kernel \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j) for the approximation where the projection is aligned with the axes (\phi=0) is defined as: \Lambda(\phi=0, \rho, i, j) = \begin{cases} d\rho & \text{if } [\rho - d\rho/2] = [\rho + d\rho/2] = [\rho] = i \\ \frac{d\rho + \Delta p}{2} + |\rho - i| & \text{if } [\rho - d\rho/2] < i \land [\rho + d\rho/2] = i \\ 1 & \text{if } [\rho - d\rho/2] < i \land [\rho + d\rho/2] > i \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where [\cdot] is the round function returning the nearest integer to the real parameter. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def areakernelweight(rho, drho, deltap, pixeli): """Calculates the kernel weight for a single pixel i given rho, drho, and deltap.""" def roundtoint(x): return int(math.floor(x + 0.5)) rholow = rho - drho / 2.0 rhohigh = rho + drho / 2.0 ilow = roundtoint(rholow) ihigh = roundtoint(rhohigh) imid = roundtoint(rho) if ilow == ihigh == imid == pixeli: return drho if ilow < pixeli and ihigh == pixeli: return (drho + deltap) / 2.0 + abs(rho - pixeli) if ilow < pixeli and ihigh > pixeli: return 1.0 return 0.0 def backprojectareakernel(projections, imageshape, drho, deltap): """Reconstructs an image using the Area-based Pixel Kernel approximation.""" height, width = imageshape resultimage = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for theta, rhovalues in projections: tempimage = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for rho, value in rhovalues: rholow = rho - drho / 2.0 rhohigh = rho + drho / 2.0 starti = max(0, int(math.floor(min(rholow, rhohigh) - 1))) endi = min(width, int(math.ceil(max(rholow, rhohigh) + 1))) for i in range(starti, endi): weight = areakernelweight(rho, drho, deltap, i) if weight > 0: for j in range(height): tempimage[j][i] += value weight # Rotation by -theta and accumulation. # The source does not specify the interpolation method for rotation. # Using nearest-neighbor sampling as a standard fallback. cost = math.cos(-theta) sint = math.sin(-theta) cxcenter = width / 2.0 cycenter = height / 2.0 for r in range(height): for c in range(width): dx = c - cxcenter dy = r - cycenter srcc = dx cost - dy sint + cxcenter srcr = dx sint + dy cost + cycenter srccint = int(math.floor(srcc + 0.5)) srcrint = int(math.floor(srcr + 0.5)) if 0 <= srcrint < height and 0 <= srccint < width: resultimage[r][c] += tempimage[srcrint][srccint] return resultimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Geometry: The exact calculation of the common area between a thick line and a pixel generates complex shapes requiring non-trivial decomposition into simple shapes, which is why the rotation approximation is used. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates unreconstructed pixels (holes) present in Dirac and B-Spline kernels during subsampling. Fully exploits data in oversampling scenarios, unlike linear kernels. Limitations: The rotation approximation avoids exact geometric integration, which may lead to slight inaccuracies compared to a true area calculation. The Area-based Pixel Kernel was introduced in the context of tomographic reconstruction to address the limitations of standard interpolators. It is described in the thesis "Précision et qualité en reconstruction tomographique: algorithmes et applications". Précision et qualité en reconstruction tomographique: algorithmes et applications, https://doi.org/10.70675/d2bc4875z6a5az46afz9289z2fe16b3a43f3, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Compositing
head: Composite ARGB
body: Compositing is the final step in direct volume ray casting where multiple semi-transparent sample contributions along a viewing ray are combined into a single pixel color. It solves the problem of projecting a 3D density field into a 2D image by correctly blending overlying and underlying colors using ARGB blending. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on the standard optical model of light attenuation and emission, typically implemented via front-to-back accumulation which enables early ray termination, unlike back-to-front or order-independent variants. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of samples (ci, \alphai) encountered along a ray, where ci is the sample color (RGB) and \alphai is the sample opacity (A). The samples are sorted front-to-back. Input: A background color C{bg} (default black). Output: The final pixel color C{final}. Data Structures: The method maintains an accumulator state (C{acc}, \alpha{acc}) initialized to (0, 0). C{acc}: Accumulated color, a 3-component vector (RGB). \alpha{acc}: Accumulated opacity, a scalar. Formulas: The standard front-to-back compositing equation updates the accumulators for each sample i: C{acc}^{(i)} = C{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai ci \alpha{acc}^{(i)} = \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)} + (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) \alphai where C{acc}^{(0)} = 0 and \alpha{acc}^{(0)} = 0. The term (1 - \alpha{acc}^{(i-1)}) represents the transmittance T, i.e., the fraction of light reaching sample i from the camera side. In iterative form using transmittance T = 1 - \alpha{acc}: \begin{aligned} C{final} &\leftarrow C{final} + ci \cdot \alphai \cdot T \\ T &\leftarrow T \cdot (1 - \alphai) \end{aligned} Where T is initialized to 1.0 and represents the accumulated transparency \prod (1-\alphaj). The final pixel color is composited over the background color C{bg} using: C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg}. Parameters: Early ray termination threshold: Typically 1.0 (or a value slightly less, e.g., 0.99, to avoid precision issues). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If \alpha{acc} approaches 1.0, the transmittance approaches 0. Floating-point precision errors may cause T to become slightly negative or non-zero when it should be zero, leading to minor artifacts. Clamping T to [0, 1] is recommended. Boundary: If the ray exits the volume before \alpha{acc} reaches 1.0, the remaining transmittance is applied to the background color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def compositingloop(samples, backgroundcolor): """ Standard front-to-back compositing loop. samples: list of (color: vec3, opacity: float) sorted front-to-back. backgroundcolor: vec3 for the scene background. """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 for ci, alphai in samples: transmittance = max(0.0, 1.0 - alphaacc) Cacc = Cacc + transmittance alphai ci alphaacc = min(1.0, alphaacc + transmittance alphai) # Early ray termination if alphaacc >= 1.0: break # Composite over background return Cacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) backgroundcolor Alpha compositing ray casting evaluates the volume rendering integral by marching along viewing rays and iteratively blending semi-transparent samples from the front of the ray to the back. It solves the problem of projecting a 3D density field into a 2D image without requiring binary classification, thereby eliminating false positives and false negatives. It is distinguished from its siblings by its recursive accumulation of color and opacity using the OVER operator, which enables early ray termination when the accumulated opacity reaches unity, a feature not available in back-to-front compositing. Alpha Compositing Ray Casting Ray Compositing and Accumulation is a hardware-accelerated method for aggregating color and opacity contributions into final pixel values during direct volume ray casting, specifically designed to handle sample streams that are not presented in strict ray order. Unlike software-based approaches that require sorting or random access memory for per-ray buffers, this method uses dedicated hardware structures (FIFOs and shift registers) to buffer partially accumulated values and resolve predecessor dependencies based on view direction and spatial coordinates. It is distinguished from Alpha Compositing Ray Casting by its explicit hardware implementation for non-ordered data streams, and from Raymarch Blending by its focus on fixed-function accumulation logic within the VolumePro architecture. Ray Compositing and Accumulation Average Compositing is a volume rendering technique that produces an X-ray-like image by sending a ray through the volume and compositing all found values with the same weight, taking no opacity into account. It differs from Alpha Compositing and Accumulation methods by treating every sample equally regardless of depth or transparency. Average Compositing Raymarch Blending combines a ray-marched volumetric result with an existing background scene texture using standard alpha compositing. It solves the problem of integrating semi-transparent volumetric data into a pre-rendered scene containing opaque geometry, ensuring correct occlusion where the volume interacts with the solid meshes. Unlike Alpha Compositing Ray Casting which typically handles volume-to-volume or volume-to-black blending, this method explicitly blends against a pre-existing framebuffer color. Raymarch Blending Alpha blending is a compositing technique used in direct volume ray casting to combine multiple semi-transparent contributions along a viewing ray into a final pixel color. It solves the problem of rendering translucent volumes by discretizing the continuous light transport equation, allowing for physically plausible accumulation of emitted and attenuated light. It is distinguished from simple averaging or maximum intensity projection by its use of an associative, non-commutative operator that preserves depth ordering, enabling correct compositing of independent sub-volumes or distributed rendering nodes. Alpha Blending Front-to-Back Compositing is a direct volume rendering technique that projects semi-transparent volume data to the screen by traversing viewing rays from the camera viewpoint toward the far plane, accumulating color and opacity contributions. It is distinguished from its sibling Alpha Compositing Ray Casting and Back-to-Front Compositing by its ability to exploit early ray termination, allowing the renderer to stop processing a ray once the accumulated opacity approaches 1.0, thereby significantly reducing computational cost for opaque or dense regions. Front-to-Back Compositing This method composites semi-transparent volumetric samples in an order-independent manner by employing a visibility function that represents the total transmittance between a sample and the camera. It solves the order-dependent transparency problem in direct volume rendering, enabling correct visibility composition beyond simple Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or X-ray representations. Unlike its siblings which often rely on sorting or front-to-back accumulation, this approach refactors the alpha-blending equation to avoid recursion and sorting, allowing light sources to be processed independently of the camera location. Order-Independent Volumetric Compositing via Visibility Function Definition: A projection technique that composites samples along the ray using alpha blending until the ray exits the volume or becomes fully opaque. Steps: 1. Initialize contribution = 1.0f. 2. Composite each sample: outputColor.rgb += contribution transfer.a transfer.rgb. contribution = (1 - transfer.a). Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. Early ray termination reduces the average N for opaque regions. Memory: O(1) per ray for the accumulator state. Measured Performance: Performance depends heavily on the density of the volume and the effectiveness of early ray termination. For sparse volumes, the cost is proportional to the number of occupied samples. For dense volumes, the loop may terminate early, reducing cost. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays (pixels). Parallelization is straightforward across pixels. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Physically plausible results for semi-transparent volumes; efficient early ray termination; simple implementation. Limitations: Order-dependent (requires front-to-back sorting or traversal); not suitable for order-independent transparency without modification; early ray termination can cause artifacts if not handled carefully (e.g., in distributed rendering). When to Use: Use for standard direct volume rendering where semi-transparency is required and early ray termination is beneficial. Do not use when order-independent transparency is required or when samples are not available in front-to-back order without additional buffering. Compositing in volume rendering originated from the need to combine multiple semi-transparent samples along a ray to produce a realistic 2D projection. The front-to-back approach is used in interactive volume ray tracing. The technique is fundamental to direct volume rendering and is implemented in various graphics pipelines and hardware accelerators. name: Alpha Compositing Ray Casting
head: OVER operator, OVER compositing, Porter-Duff over operator
body: Alpha compositing ray casting evaluates the volume rendering integral by marching along viewing rays and iteratively blending semi-transparent samples from the front of the ray to the back. It solves the problem of projecting a 3D density field into a 2D image without requiring binary classification, thereby eliminating false positives and false negatives. It is distinguished from its siblings by its recursive accumulation of color and opacity using the OVER operator, which enables early ray termination when the accumulated opacity reaches unity, a feature not available in back-to-front compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume grid (scalar values), a transfer function mapping scalar values to RGBA (color and opacity), a camera position (eye), a view direction, and a step size. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains an accumulated RGB color and an accumulated opacity value. Data Structures: Volume: Stored as a 3D texture or array. Values are sampled using trilinear interpolation. Transfer Function: Often stored as a 1D or 2D texture mapping input density to output RGBA. Accumulators: Per-pixel variables for accumulated color C{acc} (RGB) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} (scalar), initialized to zero. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Ray Generation: For each pixel, construct a ray origin o (eye position) and direction d (normalized view vector). 2. Intersection: Compute the entry (t{near}) and exit (t{far}) distances of the ray with the volume bounding box (typically [0,1]^3). If the ray does not intersect (t{near} > t{far}), discard the pixel. If the eye is inside the volume, clamp t{near} to 0.0 to prevent sampling behind the eye. 3. Step Size Calculation: Determine the step size \Delta t. A common approach is to divide the volume extent by the product of volume dimensions and the absolute ray direction components, taking the minimum component to ensure at least one sample per voxel dimension. Alternatively, a fixed step size can be provided. 4. Initialization: Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = (0, 0, 0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0.0. 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate from t = t{near} to t < t{far} with step \Delta t: a. Sample: Evaluate the volume value v at position p = o + t \cdot d using interpolation. b. Transfer Function: Map v to a color C{src} and opacity \alpha{src} using the transfer function. Note: Some implementations use the raw volume value directly as opacity if the transfer function's alpha channel is ignored. c. Compositing: Update the accumulators using the front-to-back OVER operator equations: \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{src} C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{src} (Note: In the color update, the (1 - \alpha{acc}) term refers to the opacity before the update in the same step, or equivalently, the transmittance from the previous step. The sources define the update as adding the source color weighted by the remaining transparency. Specifically, C{dst} \leftarrow C{dst} + (1 - \alpha{dst})C{src} where \alpha{dst} is the current accumulated opacity before adding the new sample's contribution.) d. Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (typically 0.95–0.99), break the loop. 6. Background Blending: After the loop, blend the accumulated color with a background color C{bg} (usually black or white) using the final accumulated opacity: C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg} If a white background is assumed, the final RGB is computed as RGB{out} = RGB{in} \cdot \alpha{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) \cdot 1.0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def alphacompositingraycasting(eye, raydir, volumedims, stepsize=0.01): # 1. Normalize ray direction raydir = normalize(raydir) # 2. Handle zero components to avoid division by zero safedir = vec3( 1e-10 if abs(raydir.x) < 1e-10 else raydir.x, 1e-10 if abs(raydir.y) < 1e-10 else raydir.y, 1e-10 if abs(raydir.z) < 1e-10 else raydir.z) # 3. Intersect with unit cube [0,1]^3 invdir = 1.0 / safedir tmin = (vec3(0.0) - eye) invdir tmax = (vec3(1.0) - eye) invdir tnear = max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y), tmin.z) tfar = min(min(tmax.x, tmax.y), tmax.z) # Discard if no intersection if tnear > tfar: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Clamp start to eye if inside volume tnear = max(tnear, 0.0) # 4. Initialize accumulators acccolor = vec3(0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # 5. March p = eye + tnear raydir t = tnear while t < tfar: # Sample volume val = texture(volume, p).r # Map to color/opacity # Note: Some TFs return RGBA, others use val as alpha directly tfresult = texture(transferfunction, vec2(val, 0.5)) srccolor = tfresult.rgb # Pre-multiplied RGB per srcalpha = tfresult.a # or val, depending on TF implementation # 6. Compositing (Front-to-Back) # Transmittance from previous steps transmittance = 1.0 - accalpha # Update color: Cnew = Cold + Told Csrc acccolor += transmittance srccolor # Update alpha: Anew = Aold + Told Asrc accalpha += transmittance srcalpha # 7. Early termination if accalpha >= 0.99: break # Advance p += raydir stepsize t += stepsize # 8. Blend with background (e.g., black) finalcolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accalpha) vec3(0.0) return vec4(finalcolor, accalpha) Parameters: Step Size / Resolution: Determines sampling density. Fixed step sizes are common, but adaptive steps based on density gradients can improve quality. Early Termination Threshold: Typically 0.95 to 0.99. Lower values save computation but may slightly underestimate color in transparent regions. Background Color: Usually black (0,0,0) or white (1,1,1). White background compositing is a specific variant where the alpha channel is interpreted as opacity against white. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Numerical Stability: When computing transmittance via exponential density integration (Beer's Law), adding a small epsilon (10^{-10}) to the exponent or alpha terms prevents NaNs in cumulative products. Order Dependence: The compositing operation is not commutative; samples must be processed strictly from front to back (nearest to farthest). Aliasing: Insufficient sampling along the ray leads to aliasing artifacts. The step size should satisfy the Nyquist criterion relative to the volume's highest frequency content. Back-to-Front Compositing is a volume rendering technique that determines the final pixel color by accumulating samples along a viewing ray from the far boundary (back) to the camera (front). It solves the problem of blending semi-transparent layers to produce a coherent image while enabling hardware alpha blending implementation where objects approach the viewer. Unlike its sibling Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator), which tracks accumulated opacity to enable early ray termination, back-to-front compositing does not require tracking accumulated opacity for the color calculation but consequently lacks early termination support. Subvolume Tracing renders a localized region of a volume by walking a fixed number of voxels deep along a ray and compositing the data from back to front. It differs from full volume ray casting by limiting the trace depth to a small, configurable maxDepth rather than calculating the full path through the volume cube. Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA) is a volume rendering compositing technique that modifies standard Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) to prevent high-intensity structures from being occluded by irrelevant foreground material. Unlike standard DVR, where accumulated opacity grows monotonically and causes "fog" that hides distant features, MIDA modulates previously accumulated color and opacity based on the difference between the current sample's intensity and the current maximum intensity along the ray. This allows MIDA to combine the spatial context and shading compatibility of DVR with the parameterless, high-visibility nature of Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP). Hardware Alpha Blending Compositing is a technique for direct volume ray casting that leverages the fixed-function or programmable pipeline of a GPU to perform the front-to-back (Over) or back-to-front (Under) compositing equations during rasterization[book]. It solves the problem of accumulating transmittance and color along a ray by mapping the scalar volume data to texture alpha channels and rendering proxy geometry (such as slices or splats) with specific blend factors. It differs from software-based accumulation by offloading the per-sample arithmetic to the hardware blend unit, and from Back-to-Front Compositing by relying on the GPU's depth buffer and blend state rather than explicit sorting or shader-based accumulation loops[book]. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(L) per ray, where L is the number of samples along the ray. Early ray termination reduces the average number of steps, especially in opaque regions. Memory: O(X \cdot Y) for the output image buffers (color and opacity). Performance and Scaling: Performance is heavily dependent on the density of the volume and the chosen transfer function. Highly transparent volumes require full ray traversal, while opaque volumes benefit significantly from early termination. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Produces high-quality images with smooth gradients and internal visibility. It avoids the artifacts associated with binary classification (false positives/negatives). It supports early ray termination, a significant optimization. Limitations: Computationally expensive compared to projection methods like MIP. The result is order-dependent (front-to-back), requiring careful handling of sample ordering. When to Use: Use when visualizing internal structures and textures is critical, and the volume is not extremely large or the hardware is powerful enough for ray marching. Avoid when real-time performance is required for very large datasets and internal transparency is less important than highlighting high-intensity features (use MIP instead). The method integrates samples with optical properties along viewing rays, following the volume rendering integral from light transport theory. The technique was popularized by Drebin, Carpenter, and Hu in their 1988 paper "Volume Rendering", which introduced the use of pre-multiplied color-opacity values and the OVER operator for efficient compositing. The method is modeled after optical film recorders, simulating the projection of light through a gel-like substance. The compositing rule is identical to that used by volumetric radiance fields (NeRF) and 3D Gaussian Splatting, and is implemented in differentiable rendering pipelines. name: Back-to-Front Compositing
head: Back-to-Front Alpha Blending, Back-to-Front Blending Formula, BTF Compositing
body: Back-to-front compositing is a volume rendering technique that determines the final pixel color by accumulating samples along a viewing ray from the far boundary (back) to the camera (front). It solves the problem of blending semi-transparent layers to produce a coherent image while enabling hardware alpha blending implementation where objects approach the viewer. Unlike its sibling Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator), which tracks accumulated opacity to enable early ray termination, back-to-front compositing does not require tracking accumulated opacity for the color calculation but consequently lacks early termination support. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n samples along a ray, sorted in back-to-front order (from i=0 at the far boundary to i=n-1 at the near boundary). Each sample i provides a pre-multiplied color Ci and an opacity \alphai. An initial background color C{dst} (or I0) is required. Output: The final accumulated color C{dst}. Data Structures: Sample Array: An array of structures or parallel arrays storing color (C) and opacity (\alpha) for each segment i=0 \dots n-1. Accumulators: Scalar variables for the destination/background color C{dst} and, optionally, accumulated transparency \hat{t} (if compositing over a new background is required). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set the accumulated destination color C{dst} to the background color C{bg} (or I0). If accumulated transparency is needed for subsequent compositing, initialize \hat{t} = 1.0. 2. Iteration: For each sample i from 0 to n-1 (back to front): a. Retrieve the sample color C{src} (or Ci) and opacity \alpha{src} (or \alphai). b. Update the accumulated color using the back-to-front compositing equation: C{dst} \leftarrow (1 - \alpha{src})C{dst} + C{src}. c. If accumulated transparency is being tracked, update it: \hat{t} \leftarrow \hat{t} (1 - \alpha{src}). 3. Finalization: The result is C{dst}. If accumulated transparency \hat{t} was tracked, the final opacity of the composite is 1 - \hat{t}. Formulas: The core iterative update rule for color is: C{dst} \leftarrow (1 - \alpha{src})C{dst} + C{src} Where: C{dst} is the accumulated color from samples behind the current one. \alpha{src} is the opacity of the current sample (segment i). C{src} is the pre-multiplied color of the current sample. In terms of accumulated transparency \hat{t} and accumulated color \hat{C}, the recursive formulation for n samples is: \hat{t}n = (1 - \alphan) \hat{C}n = \tilde{C}n \hat{C}i = \hat{C}{i-1}(1 - \alphai) + \tilde{C}i \hat{t}i = \hat{t}{i-1}(1 - \alphai) Where \tilde{C}i is the sample color and \alphai is the sample opacity at index i. Parameters: Alpha Scale: Opacity values \alpha are typically in the range [0, 1], where 0 is transparent and 1 is opaque. Opacity Correction: If sample spacing d{new} differs from the storage spacing d{old}, opacity must be corrected: \alpha{corrected} = 1 - (1 - \alpha{stored})^{d{new}/d{old}}. Associated colors must also be corrected: \tilde{C}{corrected} = \tilde{C}{stored} \frac{\alpha{corrected}}{\alpha{stored}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def backtofrontcompositing(samples, backgroundcolor): """ samples: list of tuples (color, opacity) sorted from back (index 0) to front (index n-1). color is pre-multiplied by opacity. backgroundcolor: tuple (r, g, b) """ acccolor = list(backgroundcolor) # Iterate from back (index 0) to front (index n-1) for samplecolor, samplealpha in samples: acccolor[0] = (1.0 - samplealpha) acccolor[0] + samplecolor[0] acccolor[1] = (1.0 - samplealpha) acccolor[1] + samplecolor[1] acccolor[2] = (1.0 - samplealpha) acccolor[2] + samplecolor[2] return acccolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ordering: Polygons must be rendered in strict back-to-front order. If rendered front-to-back or out of order, the z-buffer comparison will incorrectly reject or blend polygons, resulting in incorrect final colors because the frame buffer cannot be updated to insert a polygon in the middle of the stack. Precision: When rendering thousands of polygons with small alpha values using 8-bit per component storage, round-off errors accumulate over many polygons, resulting in gross errors in the output image. Early Termination: Back-to-front rendering does not allow for early ray termination because the accumulated opacity is not tracked/updated in the same way as front-to-back, and the final color depends on all subsequent samples. Front-to-Back Compositing is a volume rendering technique that determines the final pixel color by accumulating samples along a viewing ray from the camera (front) to the far boundary (back) using the alpha compositing "over" operator. It solves the problem of blending semi-transparent layers to produce a coherent image while enabling early ray termination, a significant performance optimization where ray traversal stops once the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold. Unlike its sibling Back-to-Front Compositing, which does not require tracking accumulated opacity for color calculation but lacks early termination, front-to-back compositing explicitly maintains accumulated opacity to drive the termination condition. Time Complexity: O(n) per ray, where n is the number of samples. All samples must be processed. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray (excluding sample storage). Performance: Back-to-front compositing is suitable for hardware implementation where objects approach the viewer. It maps directly to standard hardware alpha blending functions (e.g., GLSRCALPHA, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA). However, it is generally considered less efficient for interactive perspective ray casting compared to front-to-back because it cannot use early ray termination. Strengths: Simple hardware implementation; correct optical accumulation for semi-transparent surfaces when ordered correctly; useful if the final image needs to be composited over a new background (requires tracking accumulated transparency). Limitations: No early ray termination; sensitive to rendering order in object-order approaches; prone to precision errors with many low-opacity layers in low-bit-depth buffers. When to use: When hardware alpha blending is the primary rendering path and early termination is not critical; when compositing volumes with opaque geometry (geometry drawn before volume); when the final image must be composited over a different background. When not to use: For interactive perspective ray casting where performance is critical and early termination is desired; when sample order cannot be guaranteed. Back-to-front compositing originates from the fundamental alpha compositing equations used in computer graphics to blend semi-transparent layers. It is a numerical integration method for the absorption plus emission model using a Riemann sum approximation. The technique is widely used in volume rendering pipelines, particularly in hardware-accelerated implementations such as splatting and slice-based rendering. It is also known as "forward rendering" in the context of object-order approaches. name: Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator)
head: Front-to-Back Accumulation, Over Operator, Recursive Front-to-Back Compositing, Sorted Front-to-Back Compositing, Sorted compositing, over-operator compositing
body: Front-to-Back Compositing is a ray-casting accumulation technique that computes the final pixel color by iteratively blending semi-transparent samples along a viewing ray, starting from the camera and moving toward the background. It solves the problem of rendering volumetric data by approximating the volume rendering integral through discrete emission-absorption modeling. Unlike its sibling Back-to-Front Compositing, which requires storing only the accumulated color but prohibits early termination, this method maintains accumulated opacity to enable early ray termination. This allows the ray to stop processing once the accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold, significantly reducing computation for opaque regions. Input: A 3D volume dataset (scalar field), a transfer function mapping scalar values to color C and opacity \alpha, a viewing ray defined by origin and direction, and a background color C{bg} (typically fully opaque, \alpha=1). Output: A final pixel color C{out} and accumulated opacity \alpha{out}. The method maintains two scalar accumulators for each ray: 1. C{acc}: Accumulated color (RGB), initialized to (0, 0, 0). 2. \alpha{acc}: Accumulated opacity (scalar), initialized to 0. Note: Some formulations track transmission T{acc} = 1 - \alpha{acc}. 1. Initialization: Set C{acc} = 0, \alpha{acc} = 0 (or T{acc} = 1). 2. Ray Traversal: Iterate through sample points i = 1 \dots n along the ray from front to back. 3. Sampling: For each sample position, retrieve the scalar value from the volume and apply the transfer function to obtain the sample color Ci and sample opacity \alphai. Opacity Correction: If the sampling step size \Delta s differs from the transfer function's assumed resolution, correct the opacity to maintain physical consistency. \alpha{corrected} = 1 - (1 - \alpha{original})^{\Delta s} uses a simplified approximation or hardcoded exponent in implementations. 4. Compositing (The Over Operator): Update the accumulators using the current sample's contribution, weighted by the remaining transmission (1 - \alpha{acc}): \Delta \alphai = \alphai (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + \Delta \alphai Ci \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha{acc} + \Delta \alphai Alternatively, using transmission T{acc}: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + T{acc} \alphai Ci T{acc} \leftarrow T{acc} (1 - \alphai) 5. Early Ray Termination (Optional): If \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1 - \epsilon or 0.95), terminate the ray loop. 6. Background Blending: If the ray terminates early or completes, blend the accumulated result with the background color C{bg}: C{final} = C{acc} + (1 - \alpha{acc}) C{bg} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fronttobackcompositing(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, transferfunction, backgroundcolor, threshold=0.99): # Initialize accumulators acccolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # Ray traversal parameters stepsize = 0.01 # Example fixed step t = 0.0 maxt = length(raydirection) volumedepth # Or intersection bounds while t < maxt and accalpha < threshold: # 1. Sample position samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 2. Check bounds (simplified) if not isinsidevolume(samplepos): t += stepsize continue # 3. Retrieve scalar value and apply transfer function scalarval = volume.sample(samplepos) samplecolor, samplealpha = transferfunction(scalarval) # 4. Opacity correction for step size (if necessary) # Assuming transfer function alpha is for unit distance # Corrected alpha = 1 - (1 - alpha)^stepsize if stepsize != 1.0: samplealpha = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - samplealpha, stepsize) # 5. Compositing (Over Operator) # Weight of current sample = samplealpha (1 - accalpha) weight = samplealpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor += weight samplecolor accalpha += weight # 6. Advance ray t += stepsize # 7. Blend with background finalcolor = acccolor + (1.0 - accalpha) backgroundcolor return finalcolor, accalpha Threshold: The early termination threshold determines the trade-off between speed and accuracy. A value of 0.95–0.99 is common. Step Size: Fixed step sizes require opacity correction to prevent transparency artifacts when zooming or changing resolution. Adaptive step sizes (e.g., voxel traversal) reduce the need for correction but require complex traversal logic. Non-Premultiplied Alpha: If using non-premultiplied color values, the formula must explicitly multiply color by alpha before accumulation to prevent overflow or incorrect blending. The pseudocode above assumes Ci is the emitted color, and the weight handles the alpha blending. Associativity: The over operator is associative, allowing chunks to be composited independently before final assembly, provided they are processed in front-to-back order. IBATM is a volume rendering compositing technique that highlights specific features by modulating accumulated transparency along a viewing ray based on the difference between an incoming sample's importance and the accumulated result's importance. It generalizes Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA) by decoupling transparency modulation from color accumulation, thereby avoiding the need for complex tone-mapping of color values while allowing the final image to exist in a high dynamic range. Unlike MIDA, which modulates both color and transparency, IBATM only modulates transparency, ensuring that opacity remains bounded by 1 while color accumulates naturally. Visibility Field Computation calculates the specific contribution of each voxel to the final 2D image, accounting for its own opacity and the occlusion caused by preceding voxels along the viewing ray. It builds on Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator) by explicitly storing these per-voxel visibility weights in a data structure, enabling analysis of which parts of the volume contribute most to the image and how tissues occlude one another. The Cube-4 COM unit composes shaded volumetric samples into final pixel values using a slice-by-slice front-to-back compositing order. It solves the accumulation of color and opacity for rays traversing a volume by storing intermediate results in a base-plane buffer, enabling parallel processing across multiple rendering pipelines. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its dedicated hardware implementation on the Teramac custom computing machine, which uses specific traversal and addressing units to manage skewing and partial-beam dependencies. Merging subimages using the over compositing operator in a front-to-back order determined hierarchically by a recursive traversal of a k-D tree structure. The algorithm stores both color and accumulated opacity at each pixel to enable the over compositing operator. It traverses the k-D tree recursively, visiting the 'front' child before the 'back' child to determine the compositing order. Sibling nodes can be processed concurrently to accomplish compositing in parallel. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of samples. With early ray termination, the average case is significantly faster, especially for opaque volumes. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray for accumulators. Requires storage for the volume data and transfer function. Performance: Highly efficient on GPUs due to the iterative, branch-heavy nature of early termination, which can be managed via warp-level primitives. Strengths: Supports early ray termination, allowing for significant speedups in opaque regions. Physically plausible under the emission-absorption model. Limitations: Requires tracking accumulated opacity, increasing register pressure compared to back-to-front. Sensitive to sampling density; incorrect step sizes lead to transparency artifacts without correction. Not suitable for order-independent transparency (OIT) without sorting chunks. Front-to-back compositing is derived from the volume rendering integral, specifically the emission-absorption model described by Levoy. It is the standard compositing scheme for direct volume ray casting. The method was formalized in the context of image-order rendering to allow for efficient hardware implementation and early termination. It is distinct from back-to-front compositing, which is often preferred for texture-based rendering or hardware alpha blending without early termination. name: Importance-Based Accumulated Transparency Modulation
head: Generalized MIDA, IBATM
body: Importance-Based Accumulated Transparency Modulation (IBATM) is a volume rendering compositing technique that highlights specific features by modulating accumulated transparency along a viewing ray based on the difference between an incoming sample's importance and the accumulated result's importance. It generalizes Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA) by decoupling transparency modulation from color accumulation, thereby avoiding the need for complex tone-mapping of color values while allowing the final image to exist in a high dynamic range. Unlike MIDA, which modulates both color and transparency, IBATM only modulates transparency, ensuring that opacity remains bounded by 1 while color accumulates naturally. IBATM operates within the standard front-to-back compositing loop. It introduces a modulation factor \beta derived from an importance measure F to adjust the accumulated opacity before the standard over-operator blend. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray passing through a volume, sampled at discrete intervals. Each sample provides color c{src} and opacity \alpha{src}. State: Accumulated color c{dst} and accumulated opacity \alpha{dst}, initialized to (0, 0, 0) and 0 respectively. Parameters: F: An importance measure function applied to samples. \Delta{imp}: A function calculating the difference between two importance values. B: An assembling function mapping the difference to the range (0, 1]. Data Structures: No special data structures are required beyond standard scalar accumulators for color and opacity, and temporary variables for importance values. Algorithm Steps: For each sample i along the ray, sorted from front to back: 1. Calculate Incoming Importance: Compute fi = F(\text{sample}i). The definition of F depends on the application (e.g., scalar intensity, gradient magnitude). 2. Calculate Accumulated Importance: Compute f{acc} = F(\text{accumulated samples}). This represents the importance of the volume rendered so far along the ray. 3. Calculate Importance Difference: Compute \Delta{imp} = \Delta{imp}(fi, f{acc}). Typically, this is a subtraction, but other functions are permitted. 4. Compute Modulation Factor: Calculate \beta = B(\Delta{imp}). The function B must map the difference to the interval (0, 1]. 5. Modulate Accumulated Transparency: Update the accumulated opacity: \alpha{dst} \leftarrow \beta \cdot \alpha{dst} This step reduces the accumulated opacity if the incoming sample is deemed more important than the current accumulation. 6. Composite Color: Update the accumulated color using the standard over-operator formula with the new \alpha{dst}: c{dst} \leftarrow c{dst} + (1 - \alpha{dst}) \cdot c{src} 7. Composite Opacity: Update the accumulated opacity with the current sample's opacity: \alpha{dst} \leftarrow \alpha{dst} + (1 - \alpha{dst}) \cdot \alpha{src} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ibatmcomposite(samples, importancemeasure, importancedifffunc, assemblefunc, updateaccumulatedimportance): """ Perform Importance-Based Accumulated Transparency Modulation. Args: samples: List of tuples (color, alpha), sorted front-to-back. color is a 3-tuple (r, g, b). importancemeasure: Function f(sample) -> float. importancedifffunc: Function f(currentimp, accimp) -> float. assemblefunc: Function f(diff) -> float in (0, 1]. updateaccumulatedimportance: Function f(oldaccimp, newimp) -> float. Returns: (finalcolor, finalalpha) """ # Initialize accumulated state acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # Initialize accumulated importance. # The neutral value depends on F (e.g., 0.0 for gradient magnitude, -inf for max intensity). accimportance = 0.0 for sample in samples: csrc, asrc = sample # 1. Calculate incoming importance fi = importancemeasure(sample) # 2. Calculate accumulated importance facc = accimportance # 3. Calculate difference deltaimp = importancedifffunc(fi, facc) # 4. Compute modulation factor beta beta = assemblefunc(deltaimp) # Clamp to (0, 1] as specified by the source beta = max(1e-6, min(1.0, beta)) # 5. Modulate accumulated transparency accalpha = beta accalpha # 6. Update accumulated color acccolor = ( acccolor[0] + (1.0 - accalpha) csrc[0], acccolor[1] + (1.0 - accalpha) csrc[1], acccolor[2] + (1.0 - accalpha) csrc[2]) # 7. Update accumulated transparency accalpha = accalpha + (1.0 - accalpha) asrc # Update accumulated importance for the next step. # Aggregation strategy depends on F. accimportance = updateaccumulatedimportance(accimportance, fi) return acccolor, accalpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Dynamic Range: The resulting volume renderings are high dynamic range because color is not clamped or tone-mapped within the core algorithm. The authors adjust the high dynamic range result using brightness/contrast and a gamma curve. Color Accumulation: Unlike transparency, color can accumulate to values greater than 1. IBATM avoids modulating color to prevent the complexity of tone-mapping color channels, relying instead on the bounded nature of transparency. Importance Measure Definition: The measure F and the difference function \Delta{imp} are application-dependent. An application of IBATM where the importance measure F is the gradient magnitude of the volume data. This variant addresses the occlusion of internal lower-intensity features by external structures, which occurs when using scalar intensity as the importance measure. The modulation factor \beta is calculated as: \beta = \begin{cases} 1 - (\text{grad}i - \text{grad}{acc}) & \text{if } \text{grad}i > \text{grad}{acc} \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \text{grad}i is the gradient magnitude of the incoming sample and \text{grad}{acc} is the maximum gradient magnitude accumulated so far. This measure allows visualization of features such as cavities inside the skull that are otherwise occluded by the skull bone when using maximum intensity measures. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of samples per ray, O(N), as it adds a constant number of arithmetic operations per sample compared to standard compositing. Memory complexity is O(1) per ray, requiring only additional scalar storage for importance values. Performance: Performance is comparable to standard direct volume rendering, with minor overhead from computing the importance measure and the modulation factor. Strengths: It highlights specific features without requiring manual tuning of transfer functions, which are often sensitive and complex to design. Limitations: The output is high dynamic range, requiring additional tone-mapping steps for standard display. The quality of the result heavily depends on the choice of the importance measure F and the assembling function B. IBATM was proposed as a generalization of Maximum Intensity Difference Accumulation (MIDA) to address the limitations of transfer function manipulation in direct volume rendering. MIDA modulates both color and transparency, which can lead to color values exceeding 1 and requiring tone-mapping. IBATM separates transparency modulation from color accumulation, allowing for feature highlighting while keeping transparency bounded. The method was introduced in the paper "Fast Volumetric Data Exploration with Importance-Based Accumulated Transparency Modulation". name: Average Importance Compositing
head: AImC
body: Average Importance Compositing (AImC) is an importance-driven volume rendering technique that partially suppresses less important objects along a viewing ray rather than removing them completely, allowing sparse representation of occluding structures while preserving high-curvature areas and spatial relationships. Unlike Maximum Importance Projection (MImP), which completely removes less important objects, this method assigns a sparseness level to each object based on the fraction of its importance relative to the sum of importance of all intersected objects, ensuring that context objects remain visible but attenuated. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of segmented objects (or features) along a viewing ray r, each with an associated importance value Io. Footprint images for each object, which can be binary or grayscale. Output: A rendered pixel color and opacity, where the contribution of each object is modulated by its calculated sparseness factor So. Data Structures: Object Importance (Io): A scalar value representing the visual or semantic importance of object o. Footprint Image: A 2D image (or mask) corresponding to the projection of object o. In the basic binary approach, values are 0 or 1. In the smooth transition approach, values are in [0, 1] derived from a distance transform. Ray Intersection List: A list of objects intersected by ray r, indexed i = 1 \dots nr. Steps: 1. Cast Ray: Cast a ray r through the volume. 2. Identify Intersections: Determine the set of nr objects intersected by ray r. 3. Sum Importance: Calculate the total importance I{sum} along the ray by summing the importance values of all intersected objects: I{sum} = \sum{i=1}^{nr} Ii 4. Calculate Sparseness: For each object o intersected by the ray, calculate its sparseness factor So: So = \frac{Io}{I{sum}} 5. Evaluate Footprint Coverage: For each pixel, lookup the footprint value Fo(p) \in [0, 1] for each object. 6. Modulate Optical Properties: Combine the object's color Co and opacity \alphao with the sparseness factor So and footprint value Fo(p). The effective opacity \alpha'o and color C'o are modulated, typically as \alpha'o = \alphao \cdot So \cdot Fo(p). Color saturation can also be modulated by So to attract focus. 7. Composite: Perform standard front-to-back over-operator compositing with these modulated values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def averageimportancecompositing(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, objects, pixelu, pixelv): """ rayorigin: tuple (x, y, z) raydirection: tuple (dx, dy, dz) stepsize: float objects: list of dicts with keys: 'id': unique identifier 'importance': float Io 'footprintfunc': callable(u, v) returning [0, 1] 'color': tuple (r, g, b) 'opacity': float alphao 'bbox': tuple (minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz) pixelu, pixelv: float screen coordinates for footprint lookup Returns: list [r, g, b, alpha] """ # Step 1: Identify intersected objects and sum importance intersected = [] totalimportance = 0.0 for obj in objects: if rayintersectsaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, obj['bbox']): intersected.append(obj) totalimportance += obj['importance'] # Handle edge case: no objects or zero importance if totalimportance == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Step 2: Compute sparseness factors per object sparseness = {} for obj in intersected: sparseness[obj['id']] = obj['importance'] / totalimportance # Step 3: Ray traversal and compositing accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < 1.0 and accumulatedopacity < 1.0: # Determine which object is at current sample currentobj = None for obj in intersected: if pointinaabb(rayorigin + raydirection t, obj['bbox']): currentobj = obj break if currentobj is not None: # Get footprint value at current pixel coordinates footprintval = currentobj'footprintfunc' # Modulate opacity: alpha'o = alphao So Fo(p) so = sparseness[currentobj['id']] modulatedopacity = currentobj['opacity'] so footprintval if modulatedopacity > 1e-6: remaining = 1.0 - accumulatedopacity accumulatedcolor[0] += currentobj['color'][0] modulatedopacity remaining accumulatedcolor[1] += currentobj['color'][1] modulatedopacity remaining accumulatedcolor[2] += currentobj['color'][2] modulatedopacity remaining accumulatedopacity += modulatedopacity remaining t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor + [accumulatedopacity] def rayintersectsaabb(origin, direction, bbox): minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = bbox tmin = (minx - origin[0]) / direction[0] if direction[0] != 0 else -float('inf') tmax = (maxx - origin[0]) / direction[0] if direction[0] != 0 else float('inf') if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin tymin = (miny - origin[1]) / direction[1] if direction[1] != 0 else -float('inf') tymax = (maxy - origin[1]) / direction[1] if direction[1] != 0 else float('inf') if tymin > tymax: tymin, tymax = tymax, tymin if (tmin > tymax) or (tymin > tmax): return False if tymin > tmin: tmin = tymin if tymax < tmax: tmax = tymax tzmin = (minz - origin[2]) / direction[2] if direction[2] != 0 else -float('inf') tzmax = (maxz - origin[2]) / direction[2] if direction[2] != 0 else float('inf') if tzmin > tzmax: tzmin, tzmax = tzmax, tzmin if (tmin > tzmax) or (tzmin > tmax): return False if tzmin > tmin: tmin = tzmin return tmax >= 0 def pointinaabb(point, bbox): minx, miny, minz, maxx, maxy, maxz = bbox return minx <= point[0] <= maxx and miny <= point[1] <= maxy and minz <= point[2] <= maxz Parameters: Sparseness Factor (So): The normalized importance fraction Io / \sum Ii. Example values reported in results are 0.75, 0.5, and 0.25. Footprint Type: Binary or Grayscale (Distance Transform). Grayscale is preferred for smooth transitions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Transitions: Using binary footprints results in jaggy object boundaries and sharp transitions in visibility. Zero Importance: If the sum of importance is zero, division by zero occurs. Occlusion Artifacts: The image-space approach does not evaluate whether a suppressed context object sample is in front or behind the important object; sparseness is constant for all samples of one object along a ray, suppressing parts behind the focus object. An importance metric based on accumulated blending weights, defined as the sum of blending weights of a Gaussian across all intersecting rays (I1^i = \sum{j=1}^{K} w{ij}). This metric is particularly effective for indoor scenes with low-uncertainty Gaussians but may preserve background elements in outdoor scans if not filtered. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of intersected objects per ray nr for the importance summation and sparseness calculation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for footprint images for each object. Performance: The method is computationally more expensive than MImP due to the need to sum importance values and calculate sparseness for all objects along the ray, rather than just selecting the maximum. Strengths: Preserves spatial relationships between focus and context objects; allows high-curvature areas of occluding objects to remain visible; provides smooth transitions with grayscale footprints. Limitations: Sharp transitions with binary footprints; requires precomputed importance values and footprints; early implementations were not interactive. When to Use: When it is critical to see the spatial arrangement of multiple objects and the relative importance of occluding structures, rather than just the single most important object. Average Importance Compositing was introduced by Ivan Viola and M. Eduard Gröller in their 2004 paper "Importance-Driven Volume Rendering". It is part of a family of importance-driven rendering techniques that aim to automatically guide the viewer's attention in volume visualization. The method was implemented as a plugin in the J-Vision medical workstation and demonstrated on datasets such as the Leopard Gecko and Monster Study. It builds on the concept of importance-driven rendering, where visual cues like opacity and color saturation are modulated based on object importance. name: Visibility Field Computation
head: Visibility Contribution Calculation, Visibility Field, Voxel Visibility
body: Visibility Field Computation calculates the specific contribution of each voxel to the final 2D image, accounting for its own opacity and the occlusion caused by preceding voxels along the viewing ray. It builds on Front-to-Back Compositing (Over Operator) by explicitly storing these per-voxel visibility weights in a data structure, enabling analysis of which parts of the volume contribute most to the image and how tissues occlude one another. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D volume dataset, a transfer function mapping scalar values to color and opacity, and a camera viewpoint. Output: A visibility field V, where each voxel i has an associated visibility value vi. Data Structures Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values. Visibility Field: A 3D grid of real values (floats) with the same dimensions as the volume, storing vi. Accumulated Opacity Buffer: A per-ray temporary buffer or register holding Ai, the accumulated opacity up to voxel i. Formulas The accumulated opacity Ai at voxel i is computed using front-to-back compositing: Ai = (1 - A{i-1})ai + A{i-1} where ai is the opacity of voxel i, and A{i-1} is the accumulated opacity of the voxel immediately preceding i along the ray. The base case is A{-1} = 0. The visibility vi of voxel i is the difference between the accumulated opacity at i and the accumulated opacity at the previous voxel: vi = Ai - A{i-1} Substituting the accumulation formula, this simplifies to: vi = (1 - A{i-1})ai This value represents the fraction of the final pixel color contributed by voxel i. A fully opaque, unoccluded voxel has a visibility of 1. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevisibilityfield(volume, transferfunction, viewpoint): # Initialize visibility field with zeros visibilityfield = [0.0] volume.size # Per-ray accumulated opacity buffer rayaccumulatedopacity = [0.0] len(viewpoint.rays) # Render a series of quads parallel to the viewing plane, one for each slice for sliceidx in range(volume.depth): for rayidx, ray in enumerate(viewpoint.rays): fragment = ray.intersectslice(sliceidx) # Discard fragments that do not belong to the volume if fragment is None or not volume.contains(fragment.position): continue # Retrieve opacity from transfer function ai = transferfunction.opacity(volume[fragment.position]) Aprev = rayaccumulatedopacity[rayidx] # Compute current accumulated opacity Acurr = (1.0 - Aprev) ai + Aprev # Clamp to [0, 1] to prevent numerical drift Acurr = max(0.0, min(1.0, Acurr)) # Calculate visibility vi = Acurr - Aprev # Store visibility value at the voxel's location # Use atomic operations if multiple rays map to the same voxel visibilityfield[fragment.position] += vi # Update accumulated opacity for the next voxel along the ray rayaccumulatedopacity[rayidx] = Acurr return visibilityfield Parameters The method supports computation for up to 32 features. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Viewpoint/Transfer Function Dependence: The visibility field is strictly dependent on the viewpoint and the transfer function. It cannot be precomputed independently of these parameters. Race Conditions: In GPU implementations, multiple rays may map to the same voxel. Atomic operations are required for correctness. Precision: Visibility values are real numbers. Accumulated opacity must be clamped to [0, 1] to prevent numerical drift, though the sources do not specify a particular clamping strategy. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of voxels sampled along rays. GPU implementations achieve real-time performance. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the visibility field (same size as volume) plus temporary buffers for accumulated opacity. Strengths: Enables analysis of volume structure, occlusion relationships, and feature contribution. Useful for saliency-based visualization. Limitations: Must be recomputed for every change in viewpoint or transfer function. Not suitable for static precomputation. The concept of voxel visibility as a contribution metric originates from early volume rendering research, specifically Levoy (1988). The term "Visibility Field" and its use in saliency analysis were formalized by Luo and Dingliana (2015). The method is implemented using CUDA for ray casting and OpenGL 2.0+ for slice-based rendering. name: Cube-4 COM Unit Implementation
head: COM unit, Compositing Unit
body: The Cube-4 COM unit composes shaded volumetric samples into final pixel values using a slice-by-slice front-to-back compositing order. It solves the accumulation of color and opacity for rays traversing a volume by storing intermediate results in a base-plane buffer, enabling parallel processing across multiple rendering pipelines. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its dedicated hardware implementation on the Teramac custom computing machine, which uses specific traversal and addressing units to manage skewing and partial-beam dependencies. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Shaded samples (RGB and opacity) delivered by the SHA unit. Input: Intermediate compositing results stored in the base-plane buffer. Output: Final pixel values (RGB and opacity) written to Teramac memory. Output: Intermediate results written back to the base-plane buffer if the ray traversal is not finished. Data Structures: Base-Plane Buffer: Stores intermediate compositing results. The layout is 125 \times 25 entries per pipeline. Implemented using Teramac memory. Classification Tables: Used by the SHA unit to generate shaded samples. The tables are 32-bit wide and 256 entries deep, corresponding to the 8-bit representation of voxel values. Components: TRAVERSAL-UNIT: Tracks the current slice, beam, and partial beam indices. ADDRESSINGUNIT: Calculates the memory address in the base-plane buffer for the intermediate compositing results. COMPOSINGUNIT: Performs the front-to-back compositing operation. Algorithm Steps: 1. The TRAVERSAL-UNIT determines the current slice, beam, and partial beam indices for the incoming shaded samples. 2. The ADDRESSINGUNIT calculates the memory address in the base-plane buffer corresponding to the current sample's position. 3. The COMPOSINGUNIT retrieves the intermediate compositing result from the base-plane buffer at the addressed location. 4. The COMPOSINGUNIT composites the incoming shaded sample with the retrieved intermediate result using the front-to-back over operator. 5. Skewing and Forwarding: Due to the slice-by-slice order and skewing, values from adjacent partial beams must be forwarded to pipelines 0, 1, 2, and 4. Special handling is required when values do not originate from the same partial-beam range (cases 0, 2, 3, and 4). In these cases, intermediate results from adjacent partial beams are required. 6. The result of the compositing operation is stored back into the base-plane buffer at the addressed location. 7. If the ray traversal is finished, the final accumulated value is output to Teramac memory along with the X and Y coordinates on the base-plane. Otherwise, the intermediate result remains in the base-plane buffer for the next sample. Formulas: The front-to-back compositing over operator is applied per cycle: C{out} = C{in} + C{prev} \times (1 - A{in}) A{out} = A{in} + A{prev} \times (1 - A{in}) where C{in} and A{in} are the RGB color and opacity of the incoming shaded sample, and C{prev} and A{prev} are the RGB color and opacity of the intermediate result retrieved from the base-plane buffer. All color values are assumed to be pre-multiplied by opacity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: pipelineid: Pipeline index (0-7). shadedsample: Tuple (R, G, B, A) from SHA unit. bufferx, buffery: Coordinates in the base-plane buffer. baseplanebuffer: 3D array [pipeline][y][x] of (R, G, B, A) tuples, zero-initialized per frame. finalmemory: Output storage for completed rays. israyfinished: Boolean flag indicating ray completion. """ # 1. Retrieve intermediate result from base-plane buffer # Teramac limits memory access to one read and one write per cycle prevr, prevg, prevb, preva = baseplanebuffer[pipelineid][buffery][bufferx] # 2. Composite using front-to-back over operator newr = shadedsample[0] + prevr (1.0 - shadedsample[3]) newg = shadedsample[1] + prevg (1.0 - shadedsample[3]) newb = shadedsample[2] + prevb (1.0 - shadedsample[3]) newa = shadedsample[3] + preva (1.0 - shadedsample[3]) # 3. Handle skewing and adjacent partial beams # Hardware routing logic for skewing (forwarding adjacent partial beam results to pipelines 0, 1, 2, 4) # and special handling for cases 0, 2, 3, 4 is implemented in the addressing/forwarding unit. # 4. Check if ray is finished if israyfinished: # 5. Output final value to Teramac memory with X/Y address finalmemory.write(bufferx, buffery, newr, newg, newb, newa) else: # 6. Store intermediate result back to base-plane buffer baseplanebuffer[pipelineid][buffery][bufferx] = (newr, newg, newb, newa) Parameters: Classification Table Depth: 256 entries. Classification Table Width: 32 bits. Base-Plane Buffer Size: 125 \times 25 entries per pipeline. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Skewing: Values from adjacent partial beams must be forwarded in pipelines 0, 1, 2, and 4. Partial Beam Boundaries: Special handling is required when values do not come from the same partial-beam range (cases 0, 2, 3, and 4). Intermediate results from adjacent partial beams are required in these cases. Memory Access Limits: Teramac limits memory access to one read and one write per cycle. Initialization: The base-plane buffer must be zero-initialized at the start of each frame to prevent stale data from corrupting new ray accumulations. Performance: Achieved a frame rate of 1.5 Hz using eight parallel rendering pipelines. Frequency: Optimized from an initial 0.37 MHz to a final frequency of 0.96 MHz using multiple register stages. Hardware Cost: The complete design of eight parallel rendering pipelines uses 162,816 marketing gates. One CFB unit requires 5,578 gates, one TRI unit requires 8,557 gates, and one GRA unit requires 6,142 gates. Strengths: High parallelism through eight pipelines; optimized for the Teramac architecture. Limitations: Limited by Teramac's memory access constraints (one read/write per cycle). The Cube-4 COM unit was implemented on the Teramac custom computing machine. The COM unit is part of the Cube-4 architecture, which includes other units like the SHA (Shading), TRI (Triangle), and GRA (Gridding) units. name: Subvolume Tracing
head: Ray Marching Subvolume
body: Subvolume Tracing renders a localized region of a volume by walking a fixed number of voxels deep along a ray and compositing the data from back to front. It differs from full volume ray casting by limiting the trace depth to a small, configurable maxDepth rather than calculating the full path through the volume cube. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Object position in volume space (objPosStart), camera position in volume space (cameraPosVolSpace), maxDepth, and numLoops. Output: A final color and alpha value for the pixel. Data Structures: curColor: A 4-component vector (RGBA) initialized to transparent black (0, 0, 0, 0). curCoord: A 3D coordinate in volume space representing the current sampling position. stepCoord: A 3D vector representing the step size between samples. Parameters: maxDepth: Depth in volume space to trace. Typical value is 0.15. numLoops: Number of sampling steps. Typical value is 10 (can be 400 on high-end PCs). Algorithm Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Calculate the camera's position in volume space using a WorldToVolume matrix. 2. Boundary Calculation: Determine the front and back coordinates of the subvolume segment. frontCoord is objPosStart. backCoord is calculated as frontCoord + (normalized camera direction maxDepth). The camera direction is normalize(cameraPosVolSpace - frontCoord). 3. Step Vector Calculation: Compute the step vector: stepCoord = \frac{frontCoord - backCoord}{numLoops} 4. Initialization: Set curCoord to backCoord. 5. Aliasing Prevention: Add a per-pixel random offset to curCoord to avoid layer aliasing. The offset is stepCoord RandomFromPositionFast(objPosStart). 6. Loop: Iterate numLoops times: Sample the volume at curCoord to get intensity. Shade the intensity to get a src color/alpha pair. Composite src into curColor using alpha blending. Increment curCoord by stepCoord. 7. Return: Return curColor. Alpha Blending Formula: The blending operation combines the source color (src) and destination color (dst) as follows: res.rgb = (src.rgb \times src.a) + (dst.rgb - dst.rgb \times src.a) res.a = src.a + (dst.a - dst.a \times src.a) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def randomfrompositionfast(pos): # Standard hash-based pseudo-random function returning a value in [0, 1) x, y, z = pos n = int(math.sin(x 12.9898 + y 78.233 + z 45.164) 43758.5453) return (n - int(n)) % 1 def samplevol(coord): # The sources do not specify the volume sampling implementation return 0.0 def shadevol(intensity): # The sources do not specify the transfer function implementation return (intensity, intensity, intensity, intensity) def alphablend(dst, src): resr = (src[0] src[3]) + (dst[0] - dst[0] src[3]) resg = (src[1] src[3]) + (dst[1] - dst[1] src[3]) resb = (src[2] src[3]) + (dst[2] - dst[2] src[3]) resa = src[3] + (dst[3] - dst[3] src[3]) return (resr, resg, resb, resa) def subvolumetrace(objposstart, cameraposvolspace, maxdepth=0.15, numloops=10): if numloops <= 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) frontcoord = objposstart camdir = (cameraposvolspace[0] - frontcoord[0], cameraposvolspace[1] - frontcoord[1], cameraposvolspace[2] - frontcoord[2]) camlen = math.sqrt(camdir[0]2 + camdir[1]2 + camdir[2]2) if camlen == 0: camdir = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) else: camdir = (camdir[0]/camlen, camdir[1]/camlen, camdir[2]/camlen) backcoord = (frontcoord[0] + camdir[0] maxdepth, frontcoord[1] + camdir[1] maxdepth, frontcoord[2] + camdir[2] maxdepth) stepcoord = ((frontcoord[0] - backcoord[0]) / numloops, (frontcoord[1] - backcoord[1]) / numloops, (frontcoord[2] - backcoord[2]) / numloops) curcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) curcoord = backcoord randomoffset = randomfrompositionfast(objposstart) curcoord = (curcoord[0] + stepcoord[0] randomoffset, curcoord[1] + stepcoord[1] randomoffset, curcoord[2] + stepcoord[2] randomoffset) for in range(numloops): intensity = samplevol(curcoord) shaded = shadevol(intensity) curcolor = alphablend(curcolor, shaded) curcoord = (curcoord[0] + stepcoord[0], curcoord[1] + stepcoord[1], curcoord[2] + stepcoord[2]) return curcolor Extends subvolume tracing to render the entire volume by calculating the full path length through the volume cube. It differs by dynamically determining numLoops based on the distance through the volume rather than a fixed maxDepth. It sets maxDepth to 1.73 (\sqrt{3}), the maximum distance from a point on a unit cube to any other point. It trims front and back positions to be within the volume cube bounds. The number of loops is calculated as: distanceInVoxels = length(UnitVolumeToIntVolume(frontPos - backPos)) numLoops = min(distanceInVoxels, maxSamples) where maxSamples is typically 400 to keep within bounds. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to numLoops. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Typical settings use numLoops=10 for interactive performance, scalable to 400 on high-end PCs. Strengths: Fast rendering of local details; avoids aliasing with random offset. Limitations: Does not render the full volume; depth is fixed by maxDepth rather than volume bounds. Originating from Microsoft's Mixed Reality development documentation, this method is designed for GPU-based volume rendering in shaders. It is implemented in HLSL for vertex and pixel shaders to walk voxels and layer data back to front.
