name: MPI Defocus Rendering
head: Multiplane image defocus, Synthetic Defocus Rendering, Synthetic Defocus Rendering from MPI
body: MPI Defocus Rendering synthesizes images with realistic depth-of-field blur and lateral camera translation by compositing a precomputed Multi-Plane Image (MPI) representation. It differs from standard ray casting by operating on discrete disparity planes rather than continuous volumetric samples, allowing for efficient simulation of defocus blur via 2D image-space convolutions. This method is specifically designed for view synthesis from trained neural radiance fields (NeRFs), particularly in low-light conditions where raw sensor data is utilized. Inputs: N: Number of planes in the MPI. \mathbf{c}{mpi}^{(i)}: Color tensor for plane i (RGB, linear HDR space). \alpha{mpi}^{(i)}: Opacity tensor for plane i. i{focus}: Index of the focal plane. \Delta r: Scalar controlling the simulated aperture size (defocus strength). \Delta \mathbf{d}: 2D vector controlling lateral camera translation parallel to the image plane. Outputs: C: The final composited image. The MPI consists of N fronto-parallel RGBA planes. The planes are indexed from back to front (i = 0 to N-1). Colors are stored in linear HDR space. i{focus}: Controls the focal plane depth. \Delta r: Controls the simulated aperture size, determining defocus strength. \Delta \mathbf{d}: A 2D vector controlling camera translation parallel to the image plane. 1. Precompute MPI: Generate the MPI representation from the trained model (e.g., RawNeRF). The MPI comprises a series of fronto-parallel RGBA planes sampled linearly in disparity within a camera frustum at a central camera pose. 2. Initialize Accumulator: Set the output color accumulator C \leftarrow 0. 3. Iterate Planes: For each plane i from 0 to N-1 (back to front): a. Calculate Blur Radius: Compute the blur radius r based on the distance of the current plane from the focal plane: r = \Delta r \cdot |i - i{focus}| b. Generate Kernel: Create a blur kernel k{blur} using a circular mask of radius r centered at the origin. This is implemented as a 2D Fourier space convolution. c. Blur Color: Premultiply the plane's color by its alpha (\mathbf{c}{mpi}^{(i)} \cdot \alpha{mpi}^{(i)}) and convolve with the kernel: \mathbf{c}{blur} = \text{convolve}(\mathbf{c}{mpi}^{(i)} \cdot \alpha{mpi}^{(i)}, k{blur}) d. Blur Alpha: Convolve the plane's alpha with the kernel: \alpha{blur} = \text{convolve}(\alpha{mpi}^{(i)}, k{blur}) e. Calculate Translation Offset: Compute the translation vector \mathbf{d} for the current plane: \mathbf{d} = \Delta \mathbf{d} \cdot i f. Translate Blurred Layers: Apply continuous 2D image translation using bilinear resampling to the blurred color and alpha: \mathbf{c}{trans} = \text{translate}(\mathbf{c}{blur}, \mathbf{d}) \alpha{trans} = \text{translate}(\alpha{blur}, \mathbf{d}) g. Composite: Add the translated color to the accumulator. The transmittance is (1 - \alpha{trans}). Note that \mathbf{c}{trans} is not multiplied by \alpha{trans} here because the color was already premultiplied by alpha in step 3c. C \leftarrow \mathbf{c}{trans} + (1 - \alpha{trans}) C 4. Return Result: Output C. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mpidefocusrendering(cmpi, alphampi, ifocus, deltar, deltad): """ Synthetic defocus rendering from a Multi-Plane Image. Args: cmpi: List of N tensors (H, W, 3), colors in linear HDR space. alphampi: List of N tensors (H, W, 1), opacities. ifocus: Integer index of the focal plane. deltar: Float, simulated aperture size (defocus strength). deltad: Tuple (dx, dy), 2D vector for lateral camera translation. Returns: C: Tensor (H, W, 3), the final composited image. """ N = len(cmpi) C = zeroslike(cmpi[0]) # Initialize accumulator to 0 for i in range(N): # 1. Calculate blur radius based on distance from focal plane r = deltar abs(i - ifocus) # 2. Generate blur kernel (circular mask, radius r) # Implemented as 2D Fourier space convolution kblur = blurkernel(r) # 3. Premultiply color by alpha before blurring cpremult = cmpi[i] alphampi[i] # 4. Convolve color and alpha with kernel cblur = convolve2d(cpremult, kblur) alphablur = convolve2d(alphampi[i], kblur) # 5. Calculate translation offset for this plane d = (deltad[0] i, deltad[1] i) # 6. Translate blurred layers using bilinear resampling ctrans = translate2d(cblur, d) alphatrans = translate2d(alphablur, d) # 7. Composite: C = ctrans + (1 - alphatrans) C # Note: ctrans is already premultiplied, so no alpha multiplication here transmittance = 1.0 - alphatrans C = ctrans + transmittance C return C def blurkernel(r): """ Returns a circular mask at the origin with radius r pixels. """ # Implementation detail: 2D Fourier space convolution kernel # Not given in sources, assumed to be a standard circular box or Gaussian # normalized to sum to 1. pass def convolve2d(image, kernel): """ 2D convolution of image with kernel. """ pass def translate2d(image, offset): """ Continuous 2D image translation using bilinear resampling. offset: (dx, dy) """ pass Premultiplication: The color must be premultiplied by alpha before blurring. If alpha is not applied to the translated color component (\mathbf{c}{trans}) during accumulation, it is because the premultiplication in the blur step already accounts for it. Failing to premultiply will result in incorrect color bleeding at alpha boundaries. Indexing: MPI planes are indexed from back to front (i=0 is back). Color Space: Colors must be in linear HDR space during processing. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W \cdot K^2), where N is the number of planes, H \times W is the image resolution, and K is the blur kernel size (proportional to \Delta r). The convolution and translation are performed per plane. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot H \cdot W). The MPI requires storing N planes of color and alpha. Strengths: Efficient simulation of defocus blur and lateral translation without per-pixel ray marching. Suitable for high dynamic range (HDR) raw image synthesis. Limitations: Relies on the quality of the precomputed MPI. Discrete plane representation may introduce artifacts if disparity sampling is insufficient. Defocus blur is approximated via 2D convolution, which assumes thin-lens optics and may not capture complex lens aberrations. When to use: When synthetic defocus and camera translation are required for view synthesis from a NeRF, especially in low-light scenarios using raw data. When not to use: When high-fidelity volumetric rendering with continuous depth is required, or when lens effects beyond simple defocus are needed. MPI Defocus Rendering was introduced in the context of "NeRF in the Dark," a method for high dynamic range view synthesis from noisy raw images. The approach leverages the efficiency of Multi-Plane Images (MPIs) to avoid the computational cost of full volumetric ray casting for defocus effects. It builds on prior work addressing synthetic defocus [2, 45, 51] (cited in) but adapts it for raw sensor data and HDR rendering. The method was developed to handle the challenges of low-light photography, where Bayer masking and raw domain processing are necessary to mitigate noise artifacts. NeRF in the Dark: High Dynamic Range View Synthesis from Noisy Raw Images, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01571, fetched 2026-10-26

name: View-Dependent Transparency
head: Angle-Based Transparency, Image fading with incidence angle, Incidence angle fading
body: View-Dependent Transparency (VDT) is a compositing technique that modulates sample opacity based on the geometric relationship between the surface normal and the viewer's direction, rather than relying solely on intrinsic material properties. It solves the problem of visual clutter in integral surface rendering by making regions orthogonal to the viewer more transparent and regions curving towards or away from the viewer more opaque, thereby improving the readability of nested structures and silhouettes. It differs from standard Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) by introducing view-dependent opacity modulation to enhance shape perception, and from billboard-based fading which suffers from ghosting artifacts when moving around complex objects. The method operates on the output of the ray casting loop, specifically modifying the opacity \alphai of each sample before or during the compositing step. Two primary variants are defined: Angle-Based Transparency and Normal-Variation Transparency. Inputs: Surface normal vector \mathbf{n} at the sample point. Normalized view vector \mathbf{v} from the camera to the sample point. Pixel coordinates (i, j) for image-space derivatives. Parameter \gamma \in [0, 1] for Normal-Variation Transparency. User-adjustable transparency range [\alpha{min}, \alpha{max}]. Outputs: Modified view-dependent opacity \alpha{view} or final opacity \alpha. No specific complex data structures are required beyond the standard sample attributes (ci, \alphai, \mathbf{n}i, \mathbf{v}i). The normal \mathbf{n} must be available in the same coordinate space as \mathbf{v} (typically view space or world space, provided they are consistent). This method computes transparency based on the incidence angle between the surface normal and the view vector. 1. Compute the dot product of the surface normal \mathbf{n} and the normalized view vector \mathbf{v}: d = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} 2. Apply the arccosine function to the dot product result to obtain the angle \theta \in [0, \pi]: \theta = \arccos(d) 3. Scale the result by 2/\pi to normalize the transparency to the range [0, 1]: \alpha{view} = \frac{2}{\pi} \arccos(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}) Interpretation: Regions where the surface is orthogonal to the viewer (\mathbf{n} \perp \mathbf{v}, dot product \approx 0) yield \alpha{view} \approx 1 (transparent in the context of the source's description of "more transparent", though the formula yields 1. Note: The source states "regions orthogonal to the viewer become more transparent... \alpha{view} varies the transparency". In standard alpha blending, \alpha=1 is opaque. However, the source text says "decreases the transparency as the object silhouette is approached". At the silhouette, \mathbf{n} \perp \mathbf{v}, so \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} = 0, \arccos(0) = \pi/2, \alpha{view} = 1. The source says "surface regions orthogonal to the viewer become more transparent". This implies \alpha{view} might be used as a transparency factor T or the formula is inverted in implementation, OR the source defines \alpha{view} as the transparency (inverse of opacity). Let's re-read carefully: "choosing the view-dependent transparency \alpha{view}:= \frac{2}{\pi} \arccos(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v})... surface regions orthogonal to the viewer become more transparent". If \alpha{view} is transparency, then \alpha{view}=1 is fully transparent. If it is opacity, \alpha{view}=1 is fully opaque. The source calls it "transparency \alpha{view}". Later it says "decreases the transparency as the object silhouette is approached". At silhouette, \alpha{view}=1. If 1 is transparency, transparency is high. This contradicts "decreases transparency". Let's look at the other end. Front-facing: \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{v}, dot=1, \arccos(1)=0, \alpha{view}=0. Back-facing: \mathbf{n} = -\mathbf{v}, dot=-1, \arccos(-1)=\pi, \alpha{view}=2. The range is [0, 2]. The source says "regions orthogonal... become more transparent". If \alpha{view} is opacity, 0 is transparent, 1 is opaque. Front-facing (0) is transparent. Silhouette (1) is opaque. This matches "decreases transparency as silhouette is approached" (Transparency goes from High to Low). So \alpha{view} is Opacity. The text "choosing the view-dependent transparency \alpha{view}" uses the word transparency loosely to mean the alpha channel value. We will treat \alpha{view} as the opacity contribution derived from the angle. This method approximates local surface curvature perpendicular to the viewer using image-space partial derivatives. 1. Retrieve the surface normal \mathbf{n}(i,j) at pixel (i,j) and extract its z-component nz (assuming view space where z is the view direction). 2. Compute the partial derivatives of nz with respect to pixel coordinates i and j: \frac{\partial nz}{\partial i}, \quad \frac{\partial nz}{\partial j} 3. Calculate the base view-dependent term \alpha{view}: \alpha{view} = \left( \left(\frac{\partial nz}{\partial i}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{\partial nz}{\partial j}\right)^2 \right)^{\gamma/2} Note: The source states \alpha{view} is not necessarily limited to the unit interval and must be clamped before applying the exponent \gamma if the exponentiation is part of the clamping logic, or simply that the base value must be handled. The formula shows the exponent \gamma/2 applied to the sum of squares. The pitfall says "must be clamped before \gamma is applied". This implies the base B = (\dots)^2 might need clamping or normalization, or the result of the square root before exponentiation. Given the formula structure, we compute the magnitude of the gradient, then raise to \gamma/2. 4. Constrain the final opacity \alpha to the user-adjustable interval [\alpha{min}, \alpha{max}]: \alpha = (1 - \alpha{view}) \cdot \alpha{min} + \alpha{view} \cdot \alpha{max} Note: This linear interpolation assumes \alpha{view} is normalized to [0,1]. If \alpha{view} exceeds 1, it should be clamped to 1 before this step. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def anglebasedvdt(n: vec3, v: vec3) -> float: """ Computes view-dependent opacity using the angle between normal and view vector. n: Surface normal (normalized). v: View vector (normalized). Returns: Opacity alphaview in [0, 1] (clamped). """ dotproduct = dot(n, v) # Clamp dot product to [-1, 1] to handle floating point errors dotproduct = clamp(dotproduct, -1.0, 1.0) angle = acos(dotproduct) alphaview = (2.0 / PI) angle return clamp(alphaview, 0.0, 1.0) def normalvariationvdt(ni: vec3, nj: vec3, gamma: float, alphamin: float, alphamax: float) -> float: """ Computes view-dependent opacity using image-space normal derivatives. ni: Normal at pixel (i, j). nj: Normal at pixel (i+1, j) or (i, j+1) depending on derivative direction. Note: In a real shader, these are interpolated neighbors. Here we assume ni is n(i,j) and we need derivatives. For the sake of self-contained pseudocode, we assume access to partial derivatives dnzdi and dnzdj. """ # Extract z-components nzi = ni.z # We need the derivatives. In a real implementation, these are computed # from neighboring normals in the framebuffer. # dnzdi = n(i+1,j).z - n(i,j).z # dnzdj = n(i,j+1).z - n(i,j).z # For this function signature, we assume these are passed or computed externally. # To make it self-contained, we define a helper or assume inputs are derivatives. # Let's assume inputs are the derivatives directly for clarity of the formula. pass def normalvariationvdtfromderivatives(dnzdi: float, dnzdj: float, gamma: float, alphamin: float, alphamax: float) -> float: """ Computes view-dependent opacity using pre-computed normal derivatives. """ # Compute magnitude of gradient gradsq = (dnzdi 2) + (dnzdj 2) # The source says alphaview is not limited to unit interval and must be clamped # before gamma is applied. This phrasing is slightly ambiguous. # Formula: alphaview = (gradsq)^(gamma/2). # If gradsq is large, alphaview is large. # We clamp alphaview to [0, 1] before the final interpolation. alphaview = gradsq (gamma / 2.0) alphaview = clamp(alphaview, 0.0, 1.0) # Interpolate to user-defined range alpha = (1.0 - alphaview) alphamin + alphaview alphamax return alpha def compositingwithvdt(samples, backgroundcolor, vdtmethod, gamma=1.0, alphamin=0.1, alphamax=0.9): """ Standard front-to-back compositing with View-Dependent Transparency. samples: list of (color: vec3, opacity: float, normal: vec3, viewvector: vec3, pixelcoords: (i,j)) """ Cacc = vec3(0.0) alphaacc = 0.0 # Pre-compute view vector for all samples if not provided per sample # Assuming samples contain normal and we compute view vector from camera pos and sample pos for sample in samples: ci = sample.color alpharaw = sample.opacity n = sample.normal v = sample.viewvector i, j = sample.pixelcoords # Compute VDT opacity if vdtmethod == "angle": alphavdt = anglebasedvdt(n, v) elif vdtmethod == "normalvariation": # In a real rasterizer, derivatives are available. # Here we simulate the call. # We need neighbors. This pseudocode assumes a simplified access. # For a complete implementation, this requires a post-process or # specific ray-casting buffer layout. # We will assume a helper getnormalderivatives(i, j) exists. dnzdi, dnzdj = getnormalderivatives(i, j) alphavdt = normalvariationvdtfromderivatives(dnzdi, dnzdj, gamma, alphamin, alphamax) else: alphavdt = alpharaw # Fallback # Combine raw opacity and VDT opacity? # The source implies VDT replaces or modulates the transparency. # "modulates opacity based on the angle" # Usually: alphafinal = alpharaw alphavdt or alphafinal = alphavdt. # The source for Angle-Based says "choosing the view-dependent transparency alphaview". # It does not explicitly say multiply. It says "varies the transparency". # In IRIS (S3), it is used for integral surfaces where the surface itself has the opacity. # So alphafinal = alphavdt is likely the intended use for iso-surfaces. # For volumes, it might be a modulation. # Given "modulates opacity", we use multiplication to be safe, or replacement if it's the primary opacity source. # Let's use multiplication as it is a "variation technique". alphai = alpharaw alphavdt transmittance = 1.0 - alphaacc Cacc = Cacc + transmittance alphai ci alphaacc = alphaacc + transmittance alphai if alphaacc >= 1.0: break return Cacc + (1.0 - alphaacc) backgroundcolor Ghosting and Transparency Variation Artifacts: When using billboard-based fading (a related technique), moving the camera causes ghosting (duplicated features) and transparency variation artifacts because blending two half-faded textures is not equivalent to a single opaque texture. Flat Surface Opacity: In Angle-Based Transparency, large, almost flat parts of the integral surface result in high opacity (if facing the viewer) or low opacity (if orthogonal), which can obscure layers below if the curvature radius is large. Unbounded Values: In Normal-Variation Transparency, \alpha{view} is not necessarily limited to the unit interval and must be clamped before the final interpolation step. Derivative Calculation: Normal-Variation Transparency requires accurate image-space partial derivatives of the normal's z-component, which can be noisy or inaccurate at low resolutions. A transparency variation technique that approximates local surface curvature perpendicular to the viewer using image-space partial derivatives of the normal's z-component, making the surface more opaque where it curves away and more transparent when oriented perpendicular to the viewer. It is chosen when the goal is to emphasize surface details like creases and small features, or when viewing nested structures (e.g., flow tubes) where curvature indicates depth. It differs from Angle-Based Transparency by providing stronger opacity gradients at silhouettes and being less dependent on the global view direction, allowing curved features to be identified even when viewed frontally. Time Complexity: Angle-Based Transparency is O(1) per sample, requiring only a dot product and arccosine. Normal-Variation Transparency requires computing image-space derivatives, which adds overhead for neighbor lookups and derivative calculations, potentially requiring a post-processing pass or specific buffer layouts. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory for Angle-Based. Normal-Variation requires storing normals and potentially neighbor normals or derivative buffers. Performance: Angle-Based is very cheap. Normal-Variation is also cheap but depends on derivative accuracy. Billboard fading is 2-3 times slower than single texture fetches and requires blending multiple textures. Strengths: Improves readability of complex shapes and nested structures; highlights silhouettes and curvature. Limitations: Can obscure layers below if surfaces are large and flat (Angle-Based); prone to ghosting artifacts if implemented via billboards (S1); requires accurate normals. When to use: When visualizing integral surfaces or volumes where shape perception and layer separation are critical. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical and derivative computation is too expensive, or when the geometry is highly fragmented (billboard artifacts). View-Dependent Transparency was introduced to improve the readability of volumetric and integral surface visualizations. Bruckner and Gröller (2007) cited it as a composition strategy for direct volume rendering to enhance shape perception. The specific Angle-Based and Normal-Variation formulas were proposed in the context of the IRIS (Illustrative Rendering for Integral Surfaces) system, which aimed to provide cheap, effective transparency variation for large surfaces. Earlier work by Jakobsen (2000) discussed fading billboards based on incidence angle, noting the associated artifacts. name: Energy Region Compositing
head: Energy Compositing
body: Energy Region Compositing is a volume rendering technique that composites multiple energy volumes within a specific region of interest defined by a magnitude volume. It renders a volume using multiple energy volumes, blending colors based on normalized intensities above a threshold. It differs from standard composite rendering by using a separate magnitude volume to define visibility and applying a threshold to energy intensity before compositing. Inputs and Outputs: viewmatrix: A 3x3 or 4x4 matrix containing view vectors. Indices 0:3 are the U vector, 4:7 are the V vector, and 8:11 are the View vector. volume: The main magnitude volume object with attributes dimx, dimy, dimz and a method getmaximum(). imagesize: Integer width and height of the output image (assumed square). image: Output array of size imagesize imagesize 4 (RGBA). energyvolumes: Dictionary mapping integer energy IDs to Volume objects. magnitudeVolume: A separate volume object used to define the region of interest. interactivemode: Boolean flag determining step size. Data Structures: colorDictionary: Maps energy IDs to RGB colors. Colors are generated from permutations of [1, 0, 0.5, 1] taken 3 at a time. voxelcords: 3D coordinates calculated per ray step. Parameters: step: Loop step size. Set to 20 if interactivemode is true, otherwise 1. Note: Source snippets show conflicting values (2 or 10), but the primary definition states 20. threshold: Energy intensity threshold. Set to 0.3 (30%). Formulas: Ray extent diagonal: \text{diagonal} = \lfloor \sqrt{3} \times \max(\text{dim}x, \text{dim}y, \text{dim}z) / 2 \rfloor + 1 Voxel coordinates: \text{voxel\cords} = \mathbf{u} \times (i - \text{image\center}) + \mathbf{v} \times (j - \text{image\center}) + \mathbf{view} \times k + \text{volume\center} Composite color update: \text{current\r} = \text{color\a} \times \text{color\voxel}[0] + (1 - \text{color\a}) \times \text{initial\r} (Same for g and b) Steps: 1. Initialize image to zeros. 2. Generate colorDictionary: Generate permutations of [1, 0, 0.5, 1] taken 3 at a time. Map each energy ID in energyvolumes to a unique permutation. Set ID 0 to [0, 0, 0]. 3. Extract vectors from viewmatrix: \mathbf{u} = \text{view\matrix}[0:3]. \mathbf{v} = \text{view\matrix}[4:7]. \mathbf{view} = \text{view\matrix}[8:11]. 4. Calculate centers: \text{image\center} = \text{image\size} / 2. \text{volume\center} = [\text{volume.dim\x}/2, \text{volume.dim\y}/2, \text{volume.dim\z}/2]. 5. Calculate diagonal using the formula above. 6. Set step: 20 if interactivemode else 1. 7. Loop over pixel coordinates (i, j) with step size. 8. Initialize initialr, initialg, initialb to 0. 9. Loop along ray depth k from diagonal down to -diagonal. 10. Compute voxelcords using the formula above. 11. Sample magnitudeVolume at voxelcords to get g. 12. If g \neq 0: Set colorvoxel to the output of a transfer function evaluated at g (e.g., tfunc.getcolor(g)); otherwise, set colorvoxel to [0, 0, 0]. 13. Sample the main volume at voxelcords. If value > 0: Iterate through all energyvolumes. For each energy, get intensitymax (from volume) and energyintensity (interpolated at voxelcords). If energyintensity / intensitymax > 0.3: Update colorvoxel: \text{color\voxel} = \text{color\voxel} \times (1 - \text{ratio}) + \text{colorDictionary}[key] \times \text{ratio} where \text{ratio} = \text{energy\intensity} / \text{intensity\max}. 14. Calculate colora as the maximum component of colorvoxel. 15. Update accumulated color: \text{current\r} = \text{color\a} \times \text{color\voxel}[0] + (1 - \text{color\a}) \times \text{initial\r} (Same for g and b) \text{initial\r}, \text{initial\g}, \text{initial\b} = \text{current\r}, \text{current\g}, \text{current\b} 16. After ray loop, clamp and convert final colors to 8-bit integers: \text{red} = \lfloor \text{current\r} \times 255 \rfloor \text{ if } < 255 \text{ else } 255 (Same for g, b) 17. Assign RGBA values to image at index (j \times \text{image\size} + i) \times 4. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np from itertools import permutations def getvoxelInterpolated(volume, x, y, z): # Standard trilinear interpolation or nearest neighbor lookup return 0.0 def renderenergyregioncompositing(viewmatrix, volume, imagesize, image, energyvolumes, magnitudeVolume, interactivemode): # Clear image image.fill(0) # Generate color dictionary perm = np.asarray(list(permutations([1, 0, 0.5, 1], 3))) ids = list(energyvolumes.keys()) colorDictionary = {0: [0, 0, 0]} for i in range(len(ids)): colorDictionary[ids[i]] = perm[i] # Extract vectors uvector = viewmatrix[0:3].reshape(-1, 1) vvector = viewmatrix[4:7].reshape(-1, 1) viewvector = viewmatrix[8:11].reshape(-1, 1) # Centers imagecenter = imagesize / 2 volumecenter = np.asarray([volume.dimx / 2, volume.dimy / 2, volume.dimz / 2]).reshape(-1, 1) # Diagonal diagonal = np.sqrt(3) np.max([volume.dimx, volume.dimy, volume.dimz]) / 2 diagonal = int(math.floor(diagonal)) + 1 # Step size (sources show conflicting values: 2, 10, or 20; using 20 per primary definition) step = 20 if interactivemode else 1 for i in range(0, imagesize, step): for j in range(0, imagesize, step): initialr, initialg, initialb = 0, 0, 0 for k in range(diagonal, -diagonal, -1): # Compute voxel coordinates voxelcords = (np.dot(uvector, i - imagecenter) + np.dot(vvector, j - imagecenter) + np.dot(viewvector, k) + volumecenter) # Sample magnitude volume g = getvoxelInterpolated(magnitudeVolume, voxelcords[0], voxelcords[1], voxelcords[2]) # Initialize colorvoxel per voxel colorvoxel = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) if g != 0: # Transfer function not defined in source; applies magnitude to color colorvoxel = transferfunction(g) # Sample main volume value = getvoxelInterpolated(volume, voxelcords[0], voxelcords[1], voxelcords[2]) if value > 0: for key, energyvol in energyvolumes.items(): intensitymax = energyvol.getmaximum() if intensitymax > 0: energyintensity = getvoxelInterpolated(energyvol, voxelcords[0], voxelcords[1], voxelcords[2]) ratio = energyintensity / intensitymax if ratio > 0.3: colorvoxel = np.add(np.multiply(colorvoxel, 1 - ratio), np.multiply(colorDictionary[key], ratio)) colora = np.max(colorvoxel) currentr = colora colorvoxel[0] + (1 - colora) initialr currentg = colora colorvoxel[1] + (1 - colora) initialg currentb = colora colorvoxel[2] + (1 - colora) initialb initialr, initialg, initialb = currentr, currentg, currentb # Clamp and convert red = math.floor(currentr 255) if currentr < 255 else 255 green = math.floor(currentg 255) if currentg < 255 else 255 blue = math.floor(currentb 255) if currentb < 255 else 255 alpha = math.floor(np.max(colorvoxel) 255) if np.max(colorvoxel) < 255 else 255 # Assign to image idx = (j imagesize + i) 4 image[idx] = red image[idx + 1] = green image[idx + 2] = blue image[idx + 3] = alpha Time Complexity: O(\text{image\size}^2 \times \text{diagonal} \times N), where N is the number of energy volumes. Memory Complexity: O(\text{image\size}^2) for the output image, plus storage for all volume data. Performance: Uses a large step size (20) in interactive mode to speed up rendering. Strengths: Allows visualization of specific energy types within a defined region of interest. Limitations: Relies on a separate magnitude volume for region definition; thresholding is fixed at 30%. name: Multi-Mode Volume Ray Casting
head: Custom Volume Ray Casting with Shading and Multiple Modes, MyVolumeRayCastCompositeFunction
body: Multi-Mode Volume Ray Casting is a custom implementation of direct volume ray casting that extends the standard compositing approach to support three distinct rendering modes: Full (standard compositing with shading), Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP), and XRay (average intensity projection). Unlike standard compositing which relies on pre-multiplied alpha blending, this method explicitly calculates shaded color contributions and blends them with the background using a specific accumulation formula, while also supporting nearest-neighbor interpolation and Phong shading. It is designed for scalar volume data and is implemented as a custom ray cast function within the VTK framework. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume dataset. The implementation supports only VTKUNSIGNEDCHAR (8-bit) and VTKUNSIGNEDSHORT (16-bit) data types. Input: Rendering parameters including ray start position, ray increment, number of steps, and transfer functions (scalar-to-color and scalar-to-opacity). Input: Shading tables for diffuse and specular components (Red, Green, Blue channels) and encoded normals. Output: Final pixel color (R, G, B) and accumulated opacity \alpha. Data Structures: The method operates on two primary information structures passed to the ray casting function: 1. vtkVolumeRayCastDynamicInfo: Contains per-ray runtime data. NumberOfStepsToTake (int): Total steps to iterate. TransformedStart (float[3]): Ray origin in voxel space. TransformedIncrement (float[3): Step vector in voxel space. Color (float[4]): Output color (R, G, B, \alpha). NumberOfStepsTaken (int): Actual steps executed (for early termination). 2. vtkVolumeRayCastStaticInfo: Contains per-volume static data. ScalarDataPointer (void): Pointer to the raw voxel data. ScalarDataType (enum): Data type identifier. RedDiffuseShadingTable, GreenDiffuseShadingTable, BlueDiffuseShadingTable (float): Lookup tables for diffuse shading. RedSpecularShadingTable, GreenSpecularShadingTable, BlueSpecularShadingTable (float): Lookup tables for specular shading. EncodedNormals (unsigned short): Pre-computed normal vectors. DataIncrement (int[3]): Strides for x, y, z dimensions to calculate linear memory offset. Volume (vtkVolume): Reference to the volume object containing transfer functions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Retrieve dataptr from staticInfo->ScalarDataPointer. Retrieve numsteps, raystart, and rayincrement from dynamicInfo. Retrieve transfer functions ScalarToOpacityTF and ScalarToColorTF from staticInfo->Volume. Retrieve xinc, yinc, zinc from staticInfo->DataIncrement. Initialize ray position in voxel space: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{ray\start}. Initialize accumulators: CR = CG = CB = 0.0, \alpha{acc} = 0.0. Initialize MIP variables: \alpha{max} = 0.0, V{max} = 0.0. Initialize global maximum scalar value V{global\max} = 0.0. 2. Ray Loop: Iterate for i from 0 to num\steps - 1: Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} \ge 1.0, break the loop. Voxel Coordinate Calculation: Round the current ray position to the nearest integer to get voxel coordinates: vx = \text{round}(px), \quad vy = \text{round}(py), \quad vz = \text{round}(pz) Data Access: Calculate linear offset: \text{offset} = vz \cdot \text{zinc} + vy \cdot \text{yinc} + vx \cdot \text{xinc} Retrieve scalar value: V = \text{data\ptr}[\text{offset}]. Global Maximum Update: If V > V{global\max}, set V{global\max} = V. Mode-Specific Processing: Let \mathbf{c}{raw} = (r, g, b) be the color from ScalarToColorTF[V] and \alpha be the opacity from ScalarToOpacityTF[V]. Mode MIP (currentRenderMode == 0): If V > V{max}: V{max} = V \mathbf{c}{raw} = \text{ScalarToColorTF}[V] Set \alpha{acc} = 1.0 - \alpha. (Note: The source sets accumulators to the new color multiplied by opacity, but effectively MIP replaces the accumulated color with the max intensity's color when a new max is found, and forces opacity to ensure the final pixel reflects this max). Specifically: CR = \alpha \cdot r, \quad CG = \alpha \cdot g, \quad CB = \alpha \cdot b \alpha{acc} = 1.0 - \alpha Mode XRay (currentRenderMode == 1): Accumulate scalar values into all color channels: CR \leftarrow CR + V CG \leftarrow CG + V CB \leftarrow CB + V Mode Full (currentRenderMode == 2): Lookup \mathbf{c}{raw} = (r, g, b) from ScalarToColorTF[V]. Compute shaded values (assuming shading tables are applied to r, g, b based on normals, resulting in shaded r, g, b): r{shaded} = \alpha \cdot r, \quad g{shaded} = \alpha \cdot g, \quad b{shaded} = \alpha \cdot b Accumulate color using the specific blending formula: CR \leftarrow r{shaded} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{acc}) + CR CG \leftarrow g{shaded} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{acc}) + CG CB \leftarrow b{shaded} \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{acc}) + CB Accumulate opacity: \alpha{acc} \leftarrow \alpha \cdot (1.0 - \alpha{acc}) + \alpha{acc} Ray Advancement: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{ray\increment} 3. Finalization: Cap all accumulated color intensities CR, CG, CB at 1.0. Write final color (CR, CG, CB) and opacity \alpha{acc} to dynamicInfo->Color. Write number of steps taken to dynamicInfo->NumberOfStepsTaken. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def castray(dataptr, scalardatatype, dynamicinfo, staticinfo, currentrendermode): # 1. Initialization numsteps = dynamicinfo.NumberOfStepsToTake raystart = dynamicinfo.TransformedStart rayincrement = dynamicinfo.TransformedIncrement xinc, yinc, zinc = staticinfo.DataIncrement scalartocolortf = staticinfo.Volume.ScalarToColorTF scalartoopacitytf = staticinfo.Volume.ScalarToOpacityTF # Accumulators accumr = 0.0 accumg = 0.0 accumb = 0.0 accumalpha = 0.0 # MIP variables maxval = 0.0 maxcolorr = 0.0 maxcolorg = 0.0 maxcolorb = 0.0 # Global max for XRay normalization (assumed available globally or passed) globalmaxval = getglobalmax() # Ray position posx = raystart[0] posy = raystart[1] posz = raystart[2] # 2. Loop stepstaken = 0 for i in range(numsteps): # Early termination if accumalpha >= 1.0: break # Voxel coordinates (nearest neighbor) voxelx = round(posx) voxely = round(posy) voxelz = round(posz) # Data access offset = voxelz zinc + voxely yinc + voxelx xinc scalarval = dataptr[offset] # Update global max if scalarval > globalmaxval: setglobalmax(scalarval) # Get transfer function values # Note: In the source, ScalarToColorTF returns RGB, ScalarToOpacityTF returns Alpha colorrgb = scalartocolortf(scalarval) rraw, graw, braw = colorrgb alpha = scalartoopacitytf(scalarval) # Mode processing if currentrendermode == 0: # MIP if scalarval > maxval: maxval = scalarval maxcolorr = rraw maxcolorg = graw maxcolorb = braw accumalpha = 1.0 - alpha accumr = alpha rraw accumg = alpha graw accumb = alpha braw elif currentrendermode == 1: # XRay accumr += scalarval accumg += scalarval accumb += scalarval elif currentrendermode == 2: # Full # Apply shading (simplified: source implies shading tables modify r,g,b) # Assuming rraw, graw, braw are already shaded or shading is a lookup rshaded = alpha rraw gshaded = alpha graw bshaded = alpha braw accumr = rshaded (1.0 - accumalpha) + accumr accumg = gshaded (1.0 - accumalpha) + accumg accumb = bshaded (1.0 - accumalpha) + accumb accumalpha = alpha (1.0 - accumalpha) + accumalpha # Advance ray posx += rayincrement[0] posy += rayincrement[1] posz += rayincrement[2] stepstaken += 1 # 3. Finalization # Cap colors accumr = min(accumr, 1.0) accumg = min(accumg, 1.0) accumb = min(accumb, 1.0) # For XRay, normalize by global max (implied by "normalization" note, though not explicitly in loop) if currentrendermode == 1 and globalmaxval > 0: accumr /= globalmaxval accumg /= globalmaxval accumb /= globalmaxval accumalpha = 1.0 # XRay typically opaque? Source doesn't specify alpha for XRay output, but sets accumalpha=0 initially. # Standard XRay is often just color. We leave alpha as accumulated or set to 1.0 if required by caller. # Source sets accumalpha=0 initially and never updates it in XRay mode. dynamicinfo.Color[0] = accumr dynamicinfo.Color[1] = accumg dynamicinfo.Color[2] = accumb dynamicinfo.Color[3] = accumalpha dynamicinfo.NumberOfStepsTaken = stepstaken Parameters: currentRenderMode: Integer constant. 0 for MIP, 1 for XRay, 2 for Full. Default is 2 (Full). globalMaximumScalarValue: Static float used to normalize XRay mode output. Initialized to 0.0, updated during ray casting to the maximum scalar value encountered in the dataset. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Type Support: Only VTKUNSIGNEDCHAR and VTKUNSIGNEDSHORT are supported. Other types trigger a warning and do not render. Early Termination: The loop breaks if accumopacity >= 1.0. This is a standard optimization but must be handled correctly in MIP mode where opacity might not accumulate traditionally. XRay Normalization: The source mentions globalMaximumScalarValue is used to normalize XRay output, but the pseudocode in the source does not explicitly show the division step inside the loop or at the end, only that it is initialized and updated. The implementer must ensure normalization occurs to keep values in [0,1]. Shading Tables: The source mentions shading tables but the pseudocode simplifies shading to opacity color. In a full implementation, the shading tables (diffuse/specular) must be applied to the raw color values before accumulation in Full mode. The base method using front-to-back compositing without multiple modes. A sibling technique often used in MIP mode, focusing on the highest intensity along the ray. Techniques used in Full mode to enhance depth perception. Time Complexity: O(N) per ray, where N is the number of steps. Early termination can reduce this in opaque regions. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it only stores accumulators and current position. The volume data is accessed directly. Performance: Depends heavily on the volume size and transfer function evaluation cost. Nearest-neighbor interpolation is faster than trilinear but may produce aliasing artifacts. Strengths: Supports multiple rendering modes in a single pass; explicit shading control; early termination. Limitations: Limited to integer data types; nearest-neighbor interpolation may cause jagged edges; XRay normalization requires global data pass. This method is a custom implementation of volume ray casting, originally developed as part of the VTK (Visualization Toolkit) examples. It extends the vtkVolumeRayCastCompositeFunction to provide additional flexibility in rendering modes and shading. It is documented in unofficial VTK examples and tutorials. TotteKarlsson/vtkExamples, https://github.com/TotteKarlsson/vtkExamples, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray casting with on-the-fly region growing
head: On-the-fly region growing ray casting
body: This method extends standard direct volume ray casting by integrating a local region growing algorithm during ray traversal to eliminate artifacts caused by contrast inhomogeneities, such as isolated "particle-like" regions in medical imaging. Unlike standard ray casting which may render these artifacts as part of the surface, or undersampling which loses local features, this approach filters small isolated noise while preserving large structural boundaries like endocardial walls. It is specifically designed for 3-D navigation in cardiac MSCT data where contrast distribution is non-uniform. The method operates within the standard direct volume ray casting framework [Parent]. For each pixel, a ray is cast into the volume. The algorithm modifies the standard detection and refinement steps by inserting a region growing stage whenever an object is detected via thresholding. Inputs: Volume data V (scalar field, e.g., Hounsfield Units). Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}). Contrast Threshold CT (scalar, typical range 40–120 HU). Size Threshold ST (scalar, typical range 1000–1500 voxels). Volume bounding box. Outputs: Final pixel color and opacity. Surface point coordinates for shading. Stack: A LIFO structure used to store voxel coordinates (x, y, z) and their values during region growing. Visited Set: A boolean grid or hash set marking voxels already processed in the current region growing instance to prevent cycles and redundant processing. Region Counter: An integer tracking the number of voxels in the current growing region. 1. Ray Casting Initialization: For each pixel, define ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Intersect with volume bounding box to get t{near} and t{far} [Parent]. 2. Rough Detection Loop: Iterate along the ray from t{near} to t{far} with a step size \Delta t sufficient to avoid missing surfaces. At sample position \mathbf{p}i, retrieve voxel value V(\mathbf{p}i) [Parent]. Check if V(\mathbf{p}i) < CT. If V(\mathbf{p}i) \ge CT, continue to next sample. If V(\mathbf{p}i) < CT, a potential object is detected. Proceed to Region Growing. 3. Region Growing: Initialize Stack with \mathbf{p}i. Initialize Visited set with \mathbf{p}i. Initialize RegionSize = 0. While Stack is not empty: Pop voxel \mathbf{v} from Stack. Increment RegionSize. If RegionSize \ge ST, stop growing. The region is considered "relevant" (e.g., a wall). Break loop. For each neighbor \mathbf{n} of \mathbf{v} (6-connected or 26-connected, not specified but implied by "neighborhood"): If \mathbf{n} is within volume bounds and not in Visited: Retrieve V(\mathbf{n}). If V(\mathbf{n}) < CT: Add \mathbf{n} to Visited. Push \mathbf{n} to Stack. 4. Decision and Continuation: If RegionSize < ST: The detected region is an artifact. Mark these voxels as "ignored" for this ray (or simply continue the ray casting loop from the point after the artifact, omitting the artifact's contribution to the surface detection). The text states "omit it, and continue the ray-casting process using the rough detection scheme." This implies the ray traversal continues past the artifact cluster. If RegionSize \ge ST: The region is relevant. The first detected voxel \mathbf{p}i is assumed to be on the surface. Stop ray traversal for this pixel. Proceed to Refinement. 5. Refinement: Perform 3-D linear interpolation in the neighborhood of the surface point \mathbf{p}i using the eight surrounding voxels. Search for the local gradient maximum to determine precise surface orientation. Compute shading based on the surface normal [Parent, S1]. Composite the result using the standard front-to-back equation [Parent]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastwithregiongrowing(volume, cameraorigin, cameradirection, CT, ST): """ Casts a ray and applies on-the-fly region growing to filter artifacts. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel values. cameraorigin: (x, y, z) tuple. cameradirection: (dx, dy, dz) tuple. CT: Contrast Threshold (float). ST: Size Threshold (int). Returns: color: (r, g, b) tuple. alpha: float. surfacepoint: (x, y, z) tuple or None. """ # 1. Ray-Bounding Box Intersection (Standard) tnear, tfar = intersectraybbox(cameraorigin, cameradirection, volume.bbox) # 2. Rough Detection and Region Growing t = tnear step = getstepsize(volume.resolution) # Small enough to avoid missing surfaces while t <= tfar: p = cameraorigin + t cameradirection voxelval = interpolatevolume(volume, p) if voxelval < CT: # Object detected, launch region growing regionsize, isrelevant = performregiongrowing(volume, p, CT, ST) if isrelevant: # Relevant region found (e.g., wall) surfacepoint = p break else: # Artifact detected, skip this region and continue ray # Note: The algorithm continues the loop, effectively skipping the artifact # The exact skipping mechanism (how far to jump) is not specified, # but logically it must advance past the artifact cluster. # For implementation, we might need to track the max extent of the artifact. # Here we assume the loop continues to the next sample, # but in practice, one might skip ahead. # Based on "continue the ray-casting process", we just proceed. pass t += step if surfacepoint is not None: # 3. Refinement # Perform 3-D linear interpolation in neighborhood of surfacepoint # Search for local gradient maximum normal = computegradientmax(volume, surfacepoint) color = computeshading(volume, surfacepoint, normal) alpha = 1.0 # Assuming opaque surface for navigation context return color, alpha, surfacepoint else: # No relevant surface found, return background or transparent return (0, 0, 0), 0.0, None def performregiongrowing(volume, seedpoint, CT, ST): """ Grows a region from seedpoint. Returns (size, isrelevant). """ stack = [seedpoint] visited = {seedpoint} regionsize = 0 while stack: current = stack.pop() regionsize += 1 if regionsize >= ST: return regionsize, True neighbors = getneighbors(current, volume.bbox) for n in neighbors: if n not in visited: val = interpolatevolume(volume, n) if val < CT: visited.add(n) stack.append(n) return regionsize, False Contrast Threshold (CT): The Hounsfield Unit value below which voxels are considered part of the object or artifact. Typical range: 40 to 120 HU. Size Threshold (ST): The maximum number of voxels allowed for a "particle-like" region to be considered an artifact. If the region size is smaller than ST, it is filtered out. Typical range: 1000 to 1500 voxels. CT Too High: If CT is set too high, occluding regions become too large and may connect to the actual walls (e.g., endocardial walls). This causes them to lose their "particle-like" isolated nature, making them indistinguishable from relevant structures and thus harder to filter as artifacts. Computational Cost: The region growing stage increases computational requirements. On a 2-GHz CPU with 1-GB memory, the average time for ventricle exploration is 3 seconds with ST=1500, which is twice the time required without region growing. The computation time increases with ST. No Pre-segmentation: The method does not require pre-segmentation, which is an advantage for flexibility but a disadvantage for performance. Time Complexity: The base ray casting is O(N) per pixel where N is the number of samples. The region growing adds overhead proportional to the size of the detected regions. In the worst case, if many large regions are detected, the complexity increases significantly. The source notes that computation time is twice that of standard ray casting. Memory Complexity: Requires additional memory for the Stack and Visited set during region growing. The size is proportional to the largest artifact region detected along the ray. Performance: Tested on cardiac MSCT data (512x512 matrix, ~200 slices, voxel size 0.33-0.4 mm³). Average 100-150 eliminated regions per view. Strengths: Eliminates artifacts due to contrast inhomogeneities without pre-segmentation; improves visibility of walls (e.g., endocardial walls, coronary sinus); preserves local surface features better than undersampling. Limitations: Increased computational cost (2x slower); sensitive to parameter selection (CT and ST trade-off); requires interactive parameter tuning for optimal results. When to Use: 3-D navigation in medical volumes with non-uniform contrast (e.g., cardiac MSCT) where small isolated artifacts obscure important structures. When Not to Use: Real-time applications requiring high frame rates where the 2x overhead is unacceptable; volumes with uniform contrast where artifacts are not an issue. The method was proposed by J.L. Coatrieux, K. Rioual, C. Göksu, E. Unanua, and P. Haigron from the Laboratoire Traitement du Signal et de l’Image, INSERM U642, Université de Rennes 1. It was published in 2005 in the IEEE Transactions on Information Technology in Biomedicine. The work was motivated by the need for pre-operative planning in Cardiac Resynchronisation Therapy, specifically for 3-D navigation into heart cavities using multislice X-Ray Computed Tomography (MSCT) data. The algorithm builds on the general framework of ray casting with rough detection and linear interpolation refinement. Ray casting with "on-the-fly" region growing: 3-D navigation into cardiac MSCT volume., https://doi.org/10.1109/TITB.2005.864373, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Implicit Volumetric Rendering for RNR-Map
head: GSN-style rendering, RNR-Map rendering
body: Implicit Volumetric Rendering for RNR-Map is a technique used in the RNR-Map decoder to compute pixel colors by integrating occupancy and appearance along rays, modified from GSN to render individual pixels efficiently without upsampling. It differs from its parent Direct volume ray casting by using a neural decoder to map latent features to optical properties and by targeting sparse pixel rendering for navigation tasks rather than full-image synthesis. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Query pose \mathbf{p} (camera position and orientation). Camera intrinsics. RNR-Map m, a tensor of size 128 \times 128 \times 32. Ray \mathbf{r} defined by pixel coordinates (h, w). Outputs: Rendered color c(\mathbf{r}, m) for the ray. Data Structures: RNR-Map (m): A 3D tensor with dimensions 128 \times 128 \times 32. Spatial dimensions (128 \times 128) represent a 32\text{m} \times 32\text{m} area. Each grid cell represents a physical region of 25\text{cm} \times 25\text{cm}. The depth dimension (32) is the feature dimension D. Latent Code (q): A vector of size D=32 retrieved from m via bilinear interpolation. Steps: 1. Ray Definition: Given query pose \mathbf{p} and camera intrinsics, determine the 3D position corresponding to pixel (h, w). Define a ray \mathbf{r}(u) passing through this pixel, where u is the distance from the camera center along the ray. 2. Sampling: Sample 3D points along the ray segment [un, uf] (near and far clipping planes). 3. Feature Retrieval: For each sampled 3D point, calculate its position in the RNR-Map coordinate system. Retrieve the corresponding latent feature q from the map m using bilinear interpolation, as map positions have continuous values. 4. Local Coordinate Transformation: Compute the local pose \mathbf{p}' (relative pose in a grid) for the sampled point. Determine the view direction \mathbf{d}. 5. Decoding: Pass \mathbf{p}', \mathbf{d}, and q into the decoder network. The latent code q modulates a linear layer. The decoder outputs occupancy \sigma and appearance \mathbf{a} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for the sampled point. 6. Integration: Calculate the rendered color c(\mathbf{r}, m) by integrating the product of transmittance, occupancy, and appearance along the ray. Formulas: The rendered color is computed as: c(\mathbf{r},m) = \int{un}^{uf} Tr(u) \sigma(\mathbf{r}(u),q)\mathbf{a}(\mathbf{r}(u), \mathbf{d}, q) du where transmittance Tr(u) is defined as: Tr(u) = \mathrm{exp} \left( -\int{un}^{u} \sigma(\mathbf{r}(u'), q) du' \right) Here, \mathbf{r} is the ray, m is the map, u is the distance along the ray, un and uf are near and far clipping planes, \sigma is occupancy, and \mathbf{a} is appearance. Parameters: Image resolution: 128 \times 128 pixels. RNR-Map tensor size: 128 \times 128 \times 32. Grid cell physical size: 25\text{cm} \times 25\text{cm}. Pitfalls: Unobserved regions are rendered as empty space. Small objects and texture details are often ignored. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderrnrmap(rayorigin, raydirection, cameraintrinsics, querypose, rnrmap): """ Renders a single ray using the RNR-Map implicit volumetric rendering method. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera center. raydirection: 3D vector, viewing direction for pixel (h, w). cameraintrinsics: Camera matrix parameters. querypose: Pose of the query camera. rnrmap: Tensor of shape (128, 128, 32). Returns: color: 3D vector, rendered color. """ # 1. Define ray segment [un, uf] # Intersection with volume bounding box to find un and uf un, uf = intersectraybbox(rayorigin, raydirection) # 2. Sample points along the ray # Number of samples N is not explicitly given, but integration is required # We assume a discrete approximation with N samples N = 64 # Placeholder for implementation detail not in source usamples = linspace(un, uf, N) coloraccum = 0.0 transmittanceaccum = 1.0 for i, u in enumerate(usamples): # 3. Calculate 3D point on ray point3d = rayorigin + u raydirection # 4. Calculate map position and retrieve latent code q # Map position calculation depends on coordinate system alignment # Assuming a standard transformation from world to map grid mappos = worldtomapgrid(point3d) # Bilinear interpolation to get q from rnrmap q = bilinearinterpolate(rnrmap, mappos) # 5. Compute local pose p' and view direction d # Local pose is relative pose in a grid pprime = computelocalpose(point3d, querypose) d = raydirection # View direction # 6. Decode occupancy and appearance # Decoder network structure adopted from GSN # q modulates a linear layer sigma, appearance = decodernetwork(pprime, d, q) # 7. Integrate # Transmittance calculation # Note: In discrete form, we update transmittance based on previous sigma # Tr(u) = exp(-integral from un to u of sigma) # We approximate the integral incrementally # Calculate transmittance at current sample # Tr(ui) = Tr(u{i-1}) exp(-sigmai deltau) # However, the formula defines Tr(u) as the integral up to u # Standard front-to-back compositing uses accumulated transmittance # deltau is step size deltau = (uf - un) / N # Update transmittance for the current segment # Ti = exp(-integral{un}^{ui} sigma) # We can maintain an accumulated integral of sigma # Or use the standard discrete approximation: # alphai = 1 - exp(-sigmai deltau) # Ti = product{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - alphaj) # Using the explicit integral form from source: # c(r) = integral Tr(u) sigma(u) a(u) du # Discrete approximation: # color += Tcurrent sigma appearance deltau # Calculate current transmittance T(u) # T(u) = exp(-sum{j=0}^{i-1} sigmaj deltau) # We need to track the accumulated sigma integral if i == 0: accumulatedsigmaintegral = 0.0 else: accumulatedsigmaintegral += sigma deltau Tu = exp(-accumulatedsigmaintegral) # Add contribution coloraccum += Tu sigma appearance deltau # Update accumulated transmittance for next step if needed for alpha # But here we integrate directly return coloraccum Note: The pseudocode above implements the integral equation directly. It renders individual pixels efficiently without upsampling, suitable for sparse pixel calculation in navigation tasks. Choose RNR-Map for image-based localization and navigation where computational efficiency for specific pixels is prioritized over full-image quality. RNR-Map (Link placeholder). name: Specific Data Formats and Integrators
body: This family categorizes direct volume ray casting methods by their specific data storage formats (e.g., 3D textures, fixed-point grids) and the integrators used to process them. It distinguishes between GPU-native texture-based ray marching and CPU-optimized fixed-point arithmetic, addressing performance bottlenecks in memory bandwidth and computational precision for large-scale datasets. All methods in this family adhere to the core mechanism of Direct volume ray casting: defining rays, sampling volume data, classifying via transfer functions, and compositing using front-to-back integration. The divergence lies in the data representation (texture vs. grid) and the arithmetic precision (floating-point vs. fixed-point) used during sampling and accumulation. This method renders volumetric data by storing the voxel space in a GPU 3D texture (sampler3D) and performing raycasting directly in the fragment shader. It replaces 2D texture atlases with a single 3D volume texture, enabling larger XYZ volumes and sharing the in-memory representation with path-tracing and isosurface modes. Unlike meshing methods that require building and uploading geometry, it avoids the overhead of many draw calls by rendering a single screen-covering quad. It requires WebGL2 for Data3DTexture support. Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that replaces standard floating-point arithmetic with fixed-point operations for interpolation and accumulation to improve computational efficiency. It is specifically implemented in the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) via the vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper class. Unlike general-purpose ray casting which may rely on hardware floating-point units, this method optimizes performance by intercepting decimal parts and using integer-based arithmetic, making it particularly suitable for large-scale volumetric datasets such as seismic or medical images where memory bandwidth and CPU cycles are constrained. It builds on the standard front-to-back compositing algorithm but introduces optimizations like MinMaxVolume generation to skip empty voxels. Definition: Solves transport for multiple rays in parallel on CPU by iterating over rays and calling the single-ray solver for each. Step: Loop ray from 0 to numrays - 1. Calculate offset = ray numsamples. Call solveoneray with sigma + offset, source + offset, numsamples, ds, and initialintensity[ray]. Store result in output[ray]. Layout: Input arrays sigma, source, initialintensity are row-major [ray][sample]. Output array output is [ray]. The use of 3D textures for ray marching became standard with the advent of programmable GPUs and WebGL2, allowing direct access to volumetric data without intermediate geometry. Fixed-point ray casting was developed to address performance limitations in CPU-based rendering engines like VTK, particularly for large medical and seismic datasets where floating-point precision was not strictly necessary for visual fidelity but consumed significant resources. wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, https://github.com/wyh1309/hpcfoundationaldemos, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Raymarching with 3D Volume Texture
head: 3D Texture Raycasting, 3D texture raymarching, Ray tracing through 3D mesh, RayMarchedAtlasVolume, Wolfenstein-style 3D raycasting
body: This method performs direct volume ray casting by representing the voxel space as a sampler3D texture and executing the ray marching loop within the fragment shader. It replaces previous texture atlas approaches, allowing for larger XYZ volumes, simpler edge handling, and a unified in-memory representation shared with path tracing and isosurface modes. Unlike meshing methods, it avoids the overhead of generating and uploading geometry via a single draw call. Inputs: Volume Data: A 3D texture (volumeTexture) containing voxel intensities. Lookup Table: A 2D texture (gLutTexture) mapping intensity to color/alpha. Camera/Scene: Ray origin, direction, near/far clip planes, and volume scale. Parameters: BREAKSTEPS, maxSteps, gNChannels, volumeScale, SLICES. Outputs: Fragment Color: The final composited color and alpha for each pixel. CPU-side Data Buffer Layout: The volume data is stored in a 1D array representing a 3D grid with 4 channels. The layout is defined as: \text{data}[i + ix \cdot 4 + iy \cdot 4 \cdot sx + iz \cdot 4 \cdot sx \cdot sy] Where: i is the channel index (0–3). ix, iy, iz are the voxel coordinates. sx, sy are the width and height of the volume. The data is normalized to 8-bit precision (0–255) before upload. GPU-side Textures: 1. volumeTexture: A Data3DTexture (WebGL2 required). Holds the 8-bit voxel intensities. 2. gLutTexture: A DataTexture of size 256 \times 4. It contains a combined Lookup Table (LUT) for up to 4 active channels, mapping intensity to RGBA. 1. CPU Data Preparation: Iterate through all active channels (0 to gNChannels - 1). For each voxel (ix, iy, iz), normalize the raw intensity to 0–255 and store it in the buffer at the calculated offset. Masking (if enabled): If a mask channel is specified and maskAlpha < 1.0, iterate through the volume again. For each voxel, determine maskVal (1.0 if mask intensity > 0, else maskAlpha) and multiply the existing intensity value by maskVal. Upload the buffer to the volumeTexture. 2. Vertex Shader (Setup): Render a single quad covering the screen. Pass ray origin and direction (eyed) to the fragment shader. 3. Fragment Shader (Ray Marching): Calculate Step Count: Compute the scaled steps based on the ray length and volume scale: \text{scaledSteps} = \text{BREAK\STEPS} \times \left\| \frac{\text{eye\d.xyz}}{\text{volumeScale}} \right\| Clamp Steps: Clamp the step count to the valid range: \text{csteps} = \text{clamp}(\text{scaledSteps}, 1.0, \text{maxSteps}) Calculate Inverse Step Size: \text{invstep} = \frac{\text{tfar} - \text{tnear}}{\text{csteps}} Where tfar and tnear are the far and near clip distances. Ray Dithering: Compute a random offset to reduce banding: r = \text{rand}(\text{eye\d.xy}) Note: The original implementation disabled dithering for single-slice volumes (SLICES == 1.0) to prevent Moiré patterns, but the current implementation unconditionally applies dithering. Marching Loop: For k = 0 to \text{csteps} - 1: 1. Compute current ray position: \text{pos} = \text{origin} + (\text{tnear} + k \cdot \text{invstep} + r \cdot \text{invstep}) \cdot \text{direction} 2. Sample the volume texture: \text{intensity} = \text{sampler3D}(\text{volumeTexture}, \text{pos}) 3. Reconstruct Color/Alpha: Use the sampled intensity and gNChannels to index into gLutTexture and retrieve the RGBA value. 4. Composite: Perform front-to-back alpha blending using the retrieved RGBA and the accumulated result. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. uniform sampler3D volumeTexture; uniform sampler2D gLutTexture; uniform int gNChannels; uniform float BREAKSTEPS; uniform vec3 volumeScale; uniform float maxSteps; uniform float tnear; uniform float tfar; uniform vec3 eyed; uniform vec3 origin; vec4 rayMarch() { // 1. Calculate Step Count float scaledSteps = BREAKSTEPS length(eyed / volumeScale); float csteps = clamp(scaledSteps, 1.0, maxSteps); // 2. Calculate Inverse Step Size float invstep = (tfar - tnear) / csteps; // 3. Ray Dithering // Note: Current implementation unconditionally uses rand. // Original code used: float r = (SLICES == 1.0) ? 0.0: rand(eyed.xy); float r = rand(eyed.xy); vec4 accColor = vec4(0.0); float accAlpha = 0.0; // 4. Marching Loop for (int k = 0; k < int(csteps); k++) { float t = tnear + (float(k) + r) invstep; vec3 pos = origin + t eyed; // 5. Sample Volume // Assuming pos is normalized to [0,1] for texture sampling float intensity = texture(volumeTexture, pos).r; // 6. Reconstruct Color/Alpha from LUT // The LUT is 256x4. We map intensity (0-255) to the row. // gNChannels selects the channel offset or specific LUT entry. // Simplified LUT lookup: vec4 lutEntry = texture(gLutTexture, vec2((intensity / 255.0) 255.0, float(gNChannels) / 4.0)); // 7. Front-to-Back Compositing float alpha = lutEntry.a; vec4 color = lutEntry; accColor = accColor + color (1.0 - accAlpha); accAlpha = accAlpha + alpha (1.0 - accAlpha); if (accAlpha >= 1.0) { break; } } return accColor; } BREAKSTEPS: Base number of steps. Typical values depend on volume resolution and desired quality. volumeScale: Uniform vec3 scaling the volume dimensions for step calculation. maxSteps: Upper limit for the number of steps. gNChannels: Uniform integer specifying the number of active channels (up to 4). SLICES: Constant float indicating the number of slices (depth) in the volume. WebGL1 Compatibility: The method requires Data3DTexture and sampler3D, which are WebGL2 features. It will fail on WebGL1 fallback paths. Single-Slice Moiré: Random ray dithering causes Moiré patterns in single-slice volumes. The original code disabled dithering for SLICES==1.0, but the new code unconditionally applies dithering, potentially reintroducing this artifact. Masking Semantics: Masking is applied by scaling per-voxel intensity before LUT lookup. This affects alpha and color, not just RGB, and is applied up to 4 times (once per channel). Performance: When masking is enabled, the CPU traverses the full 3D volume twice per active channel (once for intensity, once for mask), which is costly for large volumes. Uses fixed-point arithmetic instead of floating-point for sampling and accumulation. Chosen when hardware lacks robust FP32 support or for deterministic results. Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting Uses 2D texture atlases to represent volume slices. Chosen for WebGL1 compatibility or when 3D textures are not supported. Texture Atlas Raymarching Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of steps per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot C), where V is the volume voxel count and C is the number of channels (up to 4). Measured Performance: Rendered 128x128x128 or 256x256x256 voxels in 12.4ms. Strengths: Avoids overhead of many draw calls and VBO management. Allows larger XYZ volumes compared to texture atlases. Simplifies edge handling compared to atlas methods. Shares memory representation with path tracing and isosurface modes. Limitations: Requires WebGL2. Limited to 4 channels. Cannot "pre-fuse" channels on the GPU as it does not write to 3D textures. Turning channels on/off requires rebuilding the 3D texture. 8-bit precision limits dynamic range. When to Use: When WebGL2 is available, large volumes are needed, and a unified memory representation with other rendering modes (path tracing) is desired. When Not to Use: On WebGL1-only hardware, or when more than 4 channels are required. This method was introduced by toloudis in Pull Request #370 for AllenCell/vole-core, dated January 30, 2026. It evolved from earlier techniques that represented voxel space in a 3D texture for Wolfenstein-style 3D raycasting. The primary motivation was to simplify the in-memory representation by sharing the 3D texture with path tracing and isosurface modes, and to overcome the limitations of texture atlases (such as edge issues and fusion overhead). name: Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting
head: vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper
body: Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting is a direct volume rendering technique that replaces standard floating-point arithmetic with fixed-point arithmetic for interpolation and accumulation to improve computational efficiency. Implemented primarily via VTK's vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper, it is designed to handle large volumetric datasets, such as seismic or medical images, by optimizing the ray casting loop through early termination and empty voxel skipping. It distinguishes itself from floating-point counterparts by trading some precision for speed, specifically avoiding time-consuming floating-point operations and decimal interception during the resampling phase. Inputs: Volume Data: A structured 3D grid stored in vtkImageData. The scalar data is typically a 1-component array (e.g., int16, uint16, float32). For seismic data, this may originate from SEG-Y format, which consists of a 3200-byte header string, a 400-byte binary header, and trace headers, though the mapper expects preprocessed vtkImageData. Transfer Functions: Color Transfer Function (vtkColorTransferFunction): Maps scalar values to RGB colors. Opacity Transfer Function (vtkPiecewiseFunction): Maps scalar values to opacity \alpha. Gradient Transfer Function (Optional): Maps gradient magnitude to opacity/weight for edge enhancement. Volume Properties: Shading coefficients (ambient, diffuse, specular), interpolation type, and light position. Camera/View: View frustum and clipping planes. Outputs: Image Buffer: A 2D RGBA image rendered to the screen or off-screen buffer. The core data structure is vtkImageData, which defines: Dimensions: (Z, Y, X), derived from the input volume. Spacing: (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), derived from pixel spacing and slice thickness. Origin: (0, 0, 0) or patient coordinates. Scalars: The raw voxel values. The mapper internally may generate a MinMaxVolume (precomputed min/max values for sub-volumes) to optimize ray casting by skipping empty regions. The rendering process follows the standard direct volume ray casting pipeline, modified for fixed-point arithmetic: 1. Initialization: Instantiate vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper and set the input vtkImageData. Configure vtkVolumeProperty with transfer functions and shading parameters. 2. Ray Generation: For each pixel in the output image, generate a ray from the camera origin through the pixel center into the volume. 3. Sampling: Determine sample positions along the ray. The sample distance ds is typically set to the pixel diagonal divided by a factor (e.g., 5) or a fixed value like 1.0. Fixed-Point Interpolation: Unlike standard ray casting which uses floating-point interpolation, this method uses fixed-point arithmetic for interpolation. Sampling points are often non-integers; linear interpolation is preferred over nearest-neighbor to avoid obvious edges, despite higher computational cost. The fixed-point implementation intercepts decimal parts to accelerate arithmetic. 4. Classification: Retrieve the scalar value s at the interpolated sample position. Map s to color C and opacity \alpha using the transfer functions. If gradient-based shading is enabled, compute the gradient magnitude and adjust opacity/weight. 5. Compositing (Front-to-Back): Initialize accumulated color C{acc} = (0,0,0,0) and accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} = 0. For each sample i along the ray: Calculate the contribution of the current sample: C{acc} = C{acc} + Ci \cdot \alphai \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) \alpha{acc} = \alpha{acc} + \alphai \cdot (1 - \alpha{acc}) Early Termination: If \alpha{acc} approaches 1 (e.g., > 0.99), the pixel is effectively opaque. Skip the remaining voxels along the ray to eliminate invalid computation. 6. Empty Voxel Skipping: Use the precomputed MinMaxVolume or boundary checks to skip over empty elements (voxels with no contribution). 7. Shading: If ShadeOn() is enabled, calculate lighting effects (diffuse/specular) based on the gradient of the volume data at the sample point. Note that classification data is used after interpolation to filter high-frequency color components. 8. Output: Write the final C{acc} to the pixel buffer. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fixedpointvolumeraycast(volumedata, camera, transferfunctions, properties): """ Simulates the core fixed-point volume ray casting loop. Note: Actual VTK implementation uses hardware-specific fixed-point optimizations. """ # 1. Setup width, height = camera.imagewidth, camera.imageheight outputimage = zeros((height, width, 4)) # Precomputed min/max for optimization (from MinMaxVolume) minmaxvolume = computeminmaxvolume(volumedata) # Sample distance pixeldiagonal = sqrt(volumedata.spacing[0]2 + volumedata.spacing[1]2) sampledistance = pixeldiagonal / 5.0 # Typical value from # 2. Ray Loop for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin = camera.getorigin() raydirection = camera.getraydirection(x, y) # Normalize direction raydirection = normalize(raydirection) # Intersect ray with volume bounding box tmin, tmax = intersectboundingbox(rayorigin, raydirection, volumedata.bounds) if tmax < tmin: outputimage[y, x] = (0, 0, 0, 0) continue # Initialize compositing acccolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # 3. Sample Loop t = tmin while t < tmax: # Get sample position pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Check if pos is inside volume if not isinsidevolume(pos, volumedata): t += sampledistance continue # Fixed-point interpolation: Sample scalar value # In VTK, this uses fixed-point arithmetic to avoid float overhead scalarval = interpolatefixedpoint(pos, volumedata) # Classification color, alpha = transferfunctions.map(scalarval) # Shading (if enabled) if properties.shadeon: gradient = computegradient(pos, volumedata) # Apply lighting model (diffuse/specular) # Note: VTK applies classification after interpolation pass # Front-to-back compositing # Cacc = Cacc + C alpha (1 - alphaacc) # alphaacc = alphaacc + alpha (1 - alphaacc) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = acccolor + color weight accalpha = accalpha + weight # Early termination if accalpha >= 0.99: break t += sampledistance outputimage[y, x] = (acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accalpha) return outputimage Interpolation Type: Linear is preferred to avoid edge artifacts, despite higher cost. Sample Distance: Often set to pixeldiagonal / 5.0 or 1.0. Shading Coefficients: Ambient: 0.2 Diffuse: 0.9 Specular: 0.2 Specular Power: 10 Opacity Points (Example): (120, 0.0), (250, 1.0), (520, 1.0), (650, 0.0). Color Points (Example): (120, 0.999, 0.384, 0.384), (250, 1.0, 1.0, 0.705), (520, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0), (650, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Precision: Fixed-point arithmetic may introduce quantization errors compared to floating-point. Interpolation Artifacts: Nearest-neighbor interpolation causes obvious edges; linear is required for smooth results. Z-Spacing Calculation: If DICOM slices are not contiguous or ordered, calculating Z-spacing as abs(SliceLocation[i] - SliceLocation[i+1]) may yield incorrect depth. Memory Usage: Large 3D datasets (e.g., seismic) can consume significant resources. Memory-mapped files are recommended for efficient I/O. Empty Voxels: Failure to skip empty voxels leads to wasted computation. The MinMaxVolume optimization is critical for performance. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of samples per ray. Early termination reduces S for opaque regions. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, plus O(V/8) or similar for the MinMaxVolume optimization structure. Performance: Offers a balance between performance and accuracy. Fixed-point arithmetic improves operation efficiency by avoiding time-consuming floating-point operations. It is considered more efficient than standard OpenGL-based implementations in some aspects. Strengths: High image quality, efficient handling of large datasets via fixed-point math and early termination, good support for medical and seismic data formats. Limitations: Fixed-point precision limits dynamic range compared to floating-point. Requires preprocessed vtkImageData. Not suitable for unstructured grids without conversion. When to Use: When rendering large, structured volumetric datasets (seismic, medical) where performance is critical and fixed-point precision is sufficient. When Not to Use: When high dynamic range or extreme precision is required, or when working with unstructured data. Fixed-Point Volume Ray Casting was developed as part of the Visualization Toolkit (VTK) library, specifically within the vtkFixedPointVolumeRayCastMapper class. It was designed to address the computational demands of 3D seismic data visualization, which involves large datasets in SEG-Y format. The method leverages the fact that many volume rendering operations (interpolation, accumulation) can be approximated with fixed-point arithmetic to gain speed, particularly on hardware where floating-point units were historically less efficient or when integer arithmetic was preferred for throughput. It is widely used in seismic exploration and medical imaging visualization systems.
