Assumes Lambertian surfaces and isotropic, homogeneous media. """ # Constants from segment definition fval = mediaprops.scatteringcoeff mediaprops.phasefunction(segment.direction) Trval = geometry.transmittance(x, segment.furthestpoint) Lval = geometry.radianceat(segment.furthestpoint) # Geometry term integrals and derivatives (Fl, gradFl, hessFl) # These require 3x3 matrix operations for 3D form factors Fl = geometry.integrategeometryterm(x, segment) gradFl = geometry.gradientgeometryterm(x, segment) hessFl = geometry.hessiangeometryterm(x, segment) # Simplified derivatives for homogeneous media (L, f constant) # Lj approx L f (Tr Fl) # gradLj approx L f (Tr gradFl + gradTr Fl) # hessLj approx L f (Tr hessFl + gradTr gradFl + gradFl gradTr + hessTr Fl) gradTr = geometry.gradienttransmittance(x, segment.furthestpoint) hessTr = geometry.hessiantransmittance(x, segment.furthestpoint) Lj = Lval fval Trval Fl gradLj = Lval fval (Trval gradFl + gradTr Fl) hessLj = Lval fval ( Trval hessFl + outerproduct(gradTr, gradFl) + outerproduct(gradFl, gradTr) + hessTr Fl) return Lj, gradLj, hessLj def computecachepointderivatives(x, mediaprops, geometry, numangularsamples=64, numraysteps=16): """ Computes L, gradL, hessL at point x using stratified sampling and proxy triangulation. """ totalL = 0.0 totalgradL = Vector3(0, 0, 0) totalhessL = Matrix3(0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0) # Stratified sampling in sphere/circle strata = stratifiedsamplesphere(numangularsamples, numraysteps) for stratum in strata: # Build proxy triangle/trapezoid from angular samples and ray march steps segment = buildsegment(stratum, x) # Compute contribution Lj, gradLj, hessLj = computesegmentradiancederivatives(x, segment, mediaprops, geometry) # Accumulate (pdf is handled by stratification weights, assumed 1 for uniform stratification here) totalL += Lj totalgradL += gradLj totalhessL += hessLj return totalL, totalgradL, totalhessL def getvalidradius(L, hessL, epsilon): """ Computes the principal radii of the valid region ellipsoid. Returns the minimum radius (most restrictive) for isotropic caching. """ eigenvalues = hessL.eigenvalues() # 3D formula: Ri = sqrt(15 L epsilon / (5 |lambdai|)) # Using the smallest eigenvalue magnitude for the smallest radius (isotropic case) minabseigenvalue = min(abs(e) for e in eigenvalues) if minabseigenvalue == 0: return float('inf') R = math.sqrt((15 L epsilon) / (5 minabseigenvalue)) return R def rendervolumetricradiancecaching(cameraray, cachesingle, cachemulti, epsilon, stepsize): """ Renders a single ray using the radiance cache. """ # Ray march along the camera ray t = 0.0 while t < raylength(cameraray): x = cameraray.origin + t cameraray.direction stepsize t += stepsize # Query single scattering cache Lsingle = interpolatefromcache(x, cachesingle, epsilon) # Query multiple scattering cache Lmulti = interpolatefromcache(x, cachemulti, epsilon) # If no valid points, compute and add to cache if Lsingle is None: L, gradL, hessL = computecachepointderivatives(x, mediaprops, geometry) R = getvalidradius(L, hessL, epsilon) cachesingle.insert(x, L, gradL, hessL, R) Lsingle = L if Lmulti is None: L, gradL, hessL = computecachepointderivatives(x, mediaprops, geometry, ismultiplescattering=True) R = getvalidradius(L, hessL, epsilon) cachemulti.insert(x, L, gradL, hessL, R) Lmulti = L if Lsingle is not None and Lmulti is not None: return Lsingle + Lmulti return 0.0 def interpolatefromcache(x, octree, epsilon): """ Interpolates radiance from valid cache points in the octree. """ # Find all cache points whose valid radius includes x validpoints = octree.queryradius(x, epsilon) if not validpoints: return None numerator = 0.0 denominator = 0.0 for point in validpoints: dist = distance(x, point.position) d = 1.0 - dist / point.radius if d < 0: continue w = 3 d d - 2 d d d Lpred = point.L + dot(point.gradL, x - point.position) numerator += Lpred w denominator += w if denominator == 0: return None return numerator / denominator \varepsilon: Tolerance value controlling error in radiance caching. Typical value: 1.5 	imes 10^{-4} for the Patio scene. Ray marching step size: Uniform step size of 0.1 used in 3D results unless stated otherwise. Samples per pixel: 16 samples per pixel used in 3D results unless stated otherwise. Angular samples: The accuracy of the subdivision relies on dense sampling of the angular domain. Specific numbers vary, but 256 angular samples were used for reference gradient computation in 2D validation. Occlusion Ignorance: Ignoring visibility derivatives leads to poor cache distribution and imprecise extrapolation during reconstruction, failing to represent high-frequency shadows and rapid radiance changes. Occlusion-unaware methods fail to estimate gradients in complex shadows and tend to concentrate cache points near reflecting geometry, requiring radius-clamping heuristics to mitigate oversampling. Penumbra Regions: Occlusion-unaware gradients ignore light effects in penumbra regions, causing extrapolation failures and visible artifacts on shadow patterns. Sampling Rate Limits: The sampling rate limits the amount of radiance changes that can be recovered, especially for fine details like small light sources not computed using Next Event Estimation (NEE). Multiple Scattering Variance: Multiple scattering is limited to the second bounce to reduce excessive variance when computing reference derivatives with finite differences. Isotropic Cost: Using isotropic points with the smallest principal axis of the Hessian is the most costly scenario compared to previous work because it requires more points. Time: The method reduces computation time by up to 30% compared to previous work (Jarosz et al. [2008]) while providing improved results. In the 'Statues' scene, it took 154 minutes with ~19k cache points, compared to 155 minutes for Jarosz et al. [2008] with similar point counts. In the Patio scene, anisotropic points reduced total computation time by 30% compared to isotropic points at the same error tolerance. Memory: Memory usage is proportional to the number of cache points. The occlusion-aware method requires significantly fewer points than occlusion-unaware methods for comparable results (e.g., 3k vs 35k in the Strips scene). Statues Scene: ~19k cache points, 16k samples/cache, 154 minutes. Patio Scene: Anisotropic cache: 21k points, 81 minutes (cache gen) + 13 min (render) = 94 min total. Isotropic cache: 32k points, 122 min (cache gen) + 13 min (render) = 135 min total. Jarosz et al. [2008]: 36k points, 124 min (cache gen) + 12 min (render) = 136 min total. Strips Scene: Occlusion-unaware required 35k points; occlusion-aware required 3k points. 2D Overlapping Shadows: Anisotropic technique reduced cache size by 32% (~13k points) compared to isotropic points at the same error threshold. 2D Square Light: Anisotropic cache reduced the number of cache points by up to 20% compared to isotropic cache at the same error threshold. Strengths: Correctly captures complex radiance changes and high-frequency shadows by placing more points near shadow boundaries. Does not rely on radius-clamping heuristics. Interpolates in linear space, where the Hessian-based metric more accurately predicts error. Limitations: Isotropic caching is costly. Sampling rate limits recovery of fine details from small light sources. Multiple scattering is limited to two bounces to control variance. Use for scenes with complex occlusions, shadows, and penumbra regions in participating media. Use when high-frequency shadow details are critical and first-order gradient methods fail. Use when computational efficiency is important and anisotropic caching can be employed. Avoid if the scene has very small light sources that are not handled by NEE, as sampling rate limits may cause artifacts. Avoid if multiple scattering beyond two bounces is required without significant variance reduction techniques. Graph. 37, 2. The method is based on previous work by Jarosz et al. [2008], which this work extends with occlusion-aware second-order derivatives. Previous methods ignored occlusion/visibility changes or relied only on first-order derivatives, leading to suboptimal cache distributions in scenes with occluders. This method derives a 2D theory of light transport in participating media to validate the approach before generalizing to 3D. The method is used in ACM Transactions on Graphics, Vol. 37, No. 2, Article 20, February 2018. name: Light Cache Rendering Pipeline
head: GPU Volume Ray-Caster with Light Cache, Illumination Cache Volume Rendering, TBRayMarcher, TBRayMarcher Plugin
body: The Light Cache Rendering Pipeline is a direct volume ray-casting technique that pre-computes lighting distributions inside a volume and stores them in an illumination cache, drastically improving rendering performance. Unlike standard ray-marching which recalculates illumination per frame, this method exploits the assumption of isotropic light scattering to separate volume density evaluation from lighting computation, allowing for fast updates when only light positions change. It sets itself apart from siblings like Radiance Caching by using aggregate queries on a 3D Summed Area Table (SAT) for speed, yielding results similar in quality to dense sampling but much faster. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset V (voxel values), Transfer Function TF, Light sources L, Camera parameters. Output: Rendered image pixels. Intermediate Data Structures: Volume Texture V: 3D texture storing volume data. Normalized to 8-bit precision to fit within texture constraints. Light Cache Texture T: 3D texture containing summation terms for Ambient Occlusion (AO)/color bleeding and directional shadows in different channels. SAT Texture S: 3D Summed Area Table texture constructed from the transfer-function-applied volume texture. Data Structures and Layout: Volume Texture V: Stores the scalar field values. For large datasets, chunked into sub-volumes (e.g., max 2048 voxels per dimension in DX11/DX12). Light Cache Texture T: Stores pre-computed attenuation factors. One channel (or set of channels) for AO/color bleeding, others for directional shadows per light source. SAT Texture S: Stores cumulative sums of extinction coefficients to enable O(1) neighborhood queries. Algorithm Steps: 1. Check for Changes: Determine if the Transfer Function (TF) or light positions (L) have changed relative to the volume dataset. 2. Update Light Cache (if TF changed): a. Apply TF to volume V and store result to texture T. b. Compute SAT from texture T using recursive doubling with ping-pong textures S and T. Store SAT to S. c. Compute AO/Color Bleeding: For each voxel in S, sample shells from S, sum weighted shells, and store the sum to texture T. This computes the aggregate extinction over a neighborhood \Omega. 3. Update Directional Shadows (if L or TF changed): a. For each light source L: b. For each voxel in S, query cuboids towards light source L, sum weighted cuboids, and store sum to texture T. 4. Ray-Casting Pass: a. For each pixel on screen: b. Compute entry and exit points for volume V. c. Compute ray R from entry and exit points. d. For each sample position P along ray R: i. Lookup volume V and apply TF. ii. Lookup texture T (Light Cache). iii. Evaluate illumination model using the cached terms. iv. Add contribution to pixel. Formulas: The attenuation factor \tauL for a light source L is computed as e^{-\int \tau(t) dt}, where \tau(t) is the extinction coefficient. In the discretized setup, this involves the sum of extinction coefficients \sum{\Omega} \Delta t \tauj over a voxel neighborhood \Omega. The SAT allows efficient computation of these sums via aggregate queries. Parameters: Rendering Backend: DirectX 11 is required for best performance; DirectX 12 has unresolved issues, and Vulkan does not work. Data Precision: Voxel data is normalized to 8-bit precision. Max Texture Extent: 2048 voxels per dimension in DX11/DX12. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Chunking Artifacts: Large datasets must be chunked due to texture size limits. This causes incorrect lighting at chunk borders because each chunk is illuminated independently, making borders incorrectly bright. VRAM Limits: Crashes can occur well below the 2048 voxel limit due to VRAM fragmentation and available memory. TF Changes: If the Transfer Function changes, the entire light cache (SAT and shadow factors) must be recomputed. Light Position Changes: If only light positions change, only directional shadow factors need recomputation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lightcacherenderingpipeline(volumeV, transferfunction, lightsources, camera): """ Main rendering pipeline for Light Cache Volume Rendering. """ # Check if TF or lights changed tfchanged = checktfchange() lightschanged = checklightschange() if tfchanged: # Apply TF to volume V and store result to texture T textureT = applytransferfunction(volumeV, transferfunction) # Compute SAT from texture T # Using recursive doubling with ping-pong textures S, T textureS = computesat(textureT) # Compute Ambient Occlusion / Color Bleeding factors for voxel in textureS: # Sample shells from S shells = sampleshells(textureS, voxel) # Sum up weighted shells aofactor = sumweighted(shells) # Store sum to texture T (AO channel) textureT.setao(voxel, aofactor) if lightschanged or tfchanged: # Compute Directional Shadow factors for light in lightsources: for voxel in textureS: # Query cuboids towards light source L cuboids = querycuboids(textureS, voxel, light) # Sum up weighted cuboids shadowfactor = sumweighted(cuboids) # Store sum to texture T (Shadow channel for light) textureT.setshadow(voxel, light, shadowfactor) # Ray Casting Pass image = createemptyimage() for pixel in image: # Compute entry and exit point for volume V entry, exit = computeraybounds(pixel, camera, volumeV) # Compute ray R ray = createray(entry, exit) accumulatedcolor = 0 for samplepos in ray.samples(): # Lookup volume V and apply transfer function density = lookupvolume(volumeV, samplepos) tfvalue = applytransferfunctionvalue(density, transferfunction) # Lookup texture T (Light Cache) aofactor = lookuplightcacheao(textureT, samplepos) shadowfactors = lookuplightcacheshadows(textureT, samplepos, lightsources) # Evaluate illumination model # Note: Specific illumination model formula not detailed in sources, # but uses cached terms. Assuming standard volumetric shading: # I = tfvalue aofactor product(shadowfactors) lightintensity illumination = evaluateillumination(tfvalue, aofactor, shadowfactors, lightsources) # Add contribution to pixel accumulatedcolor += illumination image[pixel] = accumulatedcolor return image Photon Map Caching for Volumes is a global illumination (GI) acceleration technique designed for slow-moving or evolving volumetric scenes, such as cumulus clouds. It addresses the high computational cost of calculating light bounces inside participating media by pre-computing and caching photon maps. Unlike standard ray-marching which recalculates illumination per frame, this method caches indirect lighting data, significantly speeding up rendering when the scene geometry and lighting remain static. Time Complexity: The pre-computation of the SAT is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. The AO/shadow factor computation is also efficient due to aggregate queries. The ray-casting pass is O(P \cdot S) where P is pixels and S is samples per ray, but lighting evaluation is O(1) due to cache lookup. Memory Complexity: Requires storing Volume Texture V, Light Cache Texture T, and SAT Texture S. Memory usage scales with volume resolution and number of light sources. Measured Performance: Aggregate sampling is over 45 times faster than individual neighborhood sampling (0.22s vs 10s) with virtually no difference in image quality. Strengths: Drastic performance improvement for static or slowly changing lighting scenarios; efficient updates for light position changes. Limitations: Requires isotropic scattering assumption; chunking artifacts at borders; VRAM limitations; backend dependency (DX11 best). When to Use: Static or slowly evolving volumetric scenes with isotropic scattering, where lighting changes are limited to light position or TF updates. When Not to Use: Scenes with anisotropic scattering, highly dynamic lighting, or very large datasets that cannot be chunked without unacceptable artifacts. The method is based on an implementation by Sundén and Ropinski. It is implemented in the TBRayMarcher Plugin for Unreal Engine. The technique relies on the assumption that volume material scatters light isotropically, allowing the lighting distribution inside the volume to be pre-computed and stored in an illumination cache. This approach was developed to address the high computational cost of calculating light bounces inside participating media. name: Photon Map Caching for Volumes
body: Photon Map Caching for Volumes is a global illumination (GI) acceleration technique designed for slow-moving or evolving volumetric scenes, such as cumulus clouds. It addresses the high computational cost of calculating light bounces inside participating media by pre-computing and caching photon maps. Unlike standard ray-marching which recalculates illumination per frame, this method caches indirect lighting data, significantly speeding up rendering when the scene geometry and lighting remain static. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric scene definition (density, scattering properties), a static or slowly evolving geometry, and a fixed lighting configuration. Output: A cached photon map data structure storing photon positions, directions, and flux values within the volume, used to approximate indirect illumination during rendering. Data Structures: The photon map is typically stored as a spatial data structure (e.g., a k-d tree or grid) containing photons. Each photon entry includes: Position (x, y, z) Direction (\theta, \phi) Flux (energy) A pointer or index to the next photon in the spatial structure for efficient nearest-neighbor search. Steps: 1. Photon Emission: Photons are emitted from light sources into the volume. 2. Photon Tracing: Photons are traced through the volume, undergoing absorption and scattering events based on the volume's optical properties. 3. Storage: When a photon interacts with the volume (e.g., scatters), its state (position, direction, flux) is stored in the photon map cache. 4. Rendering: During the rendering pass, the cached photon map is queried to estimate the indirect illumination at sample points within the volume, replacing expensive real-time GI calculations. Parameters: Number of Photons: Determines the accuracy of the indirect illumination estimate. Higher counts improve quality but increase memory and pre-computation time. [Not given in the sources.] Search Radius: The radius within which neighboring photons are searched to estimate density/illumination. [Not given in the sources.] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lighting Changes: If the lighting configuration changes, the cached photon maps become invalid and must be regenerated. High Transparency: For highly transparent volumes viewed with high gamma settings, stochastic transparency may discard many low-opacity samples, potentially reducing the effectiveness of the cache. Irradiance Reconstruction is a variant technique that calculates diffuse indirect illumination of visible surface points by sampling the radiance of the nearest voxels in an imperfect volume. It differs from standard photon mapping by operating on voxel-based radiance data rather than discrete photons. It is chosen when the scene contains inaccuracies like missing voxels, as the low-frequency nature of diffuse indirect illumination masks these imperfections while providing substantial performance gains. To avoid bias from self-intersections, the surface point p is displaced half a voxel along the normal n to position p', and a more accurate radiance distribution is recomputed from neighboring voxels. A key pitfall is that voxels behind the surface do not contribute to the computation. Time Complexity: Pre-computation time is proportional to the number of photons traced and the complexity of the volume. Rendering time is reduced as GI calculations are replaced by cache lookups. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is proportional to the number of photons stored in the cache. Performance: Significant speedup for slow-moving volumes like cumulus clouds. Performance gains are substantial due to the approximation of indirect illumination. Strengths: Efficient for static or slowly changing scenes; reduces per-frame GI cost. Limitations: Requires regeneration if lighting changes; less effective for highly transparent volumes with high gamma settings due to sample discarding. When to Use: Slow-moving/evolving volumes with static lighting. When Not to Use: Dynamic lighting scenarios or highly transparent volumes where stochastic transparency discards samples. Photon Map Caching for Volumes is discussed in the context of rendering slow-moving volumes such as cumulus clouds. It is presented as a method to cache photon maps to speed up the rendering of light bounces inside the volume. The technique is part of a broader set of tips for volume rendering in Houdini. name: Indirect Illumination Modeling via Baking
head: Baking-based Occlusion for Indirect Lighting, Irradiance Volume Baking, SH Occlusion Caching
body: This method models indirect illumination in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by precomputing occlusion information and storing it in Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients within 3D volumes. It solves the difficulty of calculating occlusion in 3DGS, which uses differentiable forward mapping splatting rather than ray marching. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like the Light Cache Rendering Pipeline by explicitly baking geometric occlusion into SH coefficients to approximate indirect lighting, inspired by real-time rendering techniques such as Irradiance Volumes and Light Probes. Inputs: Optimized 3D Gaussians \mathcal{G} (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity, color). A 3D grid space where occlusion volumes are placed. A distance threshold \tau for binary occlusion determination. Outputs: Occlusion Volumes \mathcal{V}{occl}, where each volume vi^{occl} contains SH coefficients fi^o representing the occlusion function O(\theta, \phi). (Optional) Illumination Volumes \mathcal{V}{illu} containing SH coefficients for environment illumination. Data Structures: Occlusion Volume vi^{occl}: A 3D grid cell. Field coeffs: Array of SH coefficients fi^o (dimension depends on SH order, typically L=2 or 3 for real-time, though exact order is "Not given in the sources" beyond the general SH architecture mention). These coefficients represent the occlusion function O(\theta, \phi). Steps: 1. Placement: Regularly place occlusion volumes \mathcal{V}{occl} in the 3D space surrounding the scene geometry. 2. Depth Rendering: For each volume vi^{occl}, perform six forward mapping splatting passes to render a depth cubemap \{\hat{D}p^i\}{p=1}^6, where p indexes the six faces of the cubemap. 3. Binary Conversion: Convert the depth cubemap \{\hat{D}p^i\} into a binary occlusion cubemap \{\hat{O}p^i\} using the distance threshold \tau. Let d be the depth value at a pixel in the cubemap. \hat{O}p^i(x,y) = 1 if d < \tau, else 0 (or vice versa depending on definition; the source implies "occlusion" is cached, so likely 1 for occluded/hidden, but the formula 1-m suggests m is occlusion factor. The source states "convert... into binary occlusion cubemap", implying a threshold test). 4. SH Convolution: Numerically calculate the convolution of the binary occlusion cubemap with SH basis functions Y{lm} to obtain the SH coefficients fi^o for the volume. The occlusion function O(\omega) is approximated as: O(\omega) \approx \sum{l=0}^{L} \sum{m=-l}^{l} fi^o(l,m) Y{lm}(\omega) The coefficients fi^o(l,m) are derived from the integral of the occlusion cubemap against the basis functions. 5. Illumination Caching (Optional): Similarly, cache environment illumination into illumination volumes \mathcal{V}{illu} using SH coefficients derived from captured environment cubemaps \{\hat{I}p^i\}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakeocclusionvolumes(gaussians, gridspacing, threshold): """ Precompute occlusion SH coefficients for a 3D grid of volumes. """ occlusionvolumes = [] # 1. Place volumes in 3D space # Assuming a regular grid covering the scene bounding box gridpoints = generate3dgrid(gridspacing) for point in gridpoints: voccl = {} # 2. Render depth cubemap for this volume center # Perform 6 forward mapping splatting passes depthcubemap = [] for faceindex in range(6): # Define camera orientation for the cubemap face campos = point camforward = getcubemapfacedirection(faceindex) camup = getupvector(camforward) # Render depth using 3DGS forward mapping # This projects 3D Gaussians onto the 2D plane of the cubemap face depthmap = renderdepthgaussiansplatting( gaussians=gaussians, cameraposition=campos, cameraforward=camforward, cameraup=camup) depthcubemap.append(depthmap) # 3. Convert depth cubemap to binary occlusion cubemap occlusioncubemap = [] for depthmap in depthcubemap: # Binary thresholding # 1 if occluded (depth < threshold), 0 otherwise # Note: Exact binary logic (1 for occluded vs 1 for visible) # depends on how O(theta, phi) is defined in the final shading. # Source says "binary occlusion cubemap". binarymap = (depthmap < threshold).astype(float) occlusioncubemap.append(binarymap) # 4. Calculate SH coefficients from occlusion cubemap # Convolve the cubemap with SH basis functions shcoeffs = computeshcoefficientsfromcubemap(occlusioncubemap) voccl['coeffs'] = shcoeffs occlusionvolumes.append(voccl) return occlusionvolumes def computeshcoefficientsfromcubemap(cubemapfaces): """ Compute SH coefficients by integrating the cubemap values against SH basis functions. """ # Initialize coefficients array for desired SH order L # Number of coefficients = (L+1)^2 numcoeffs = (3 + 1)2 # Assuming L=2 or 3, exact L not specified coeffs = np.zeros(numcoeffs) # Integrate over the sphere using the 6 cubemap faces for face in cubemapfaces: # Iterate over pixels in the face for y in range(face.height): for x in range(face.width): # Get direction vector for this pixel omega = getdirectionfromcubemappixel(face, x, y) # Get value from occlusion cubemap val = face[y, x] # Add to SH coefficients # flm = integral( f(omega) Ylm(omega) domega) # Discrete approximation for l in range(3): # Assuming L=2 or 3 for m in range(-l, l+1): idx = getshindex(l, m) ylm = sphericalharmonic(l, m, omega) coeffs[idx] += val ylm # Normalize by solid angle of each pixel (approximate) # Not given in sources, but required for correct SH projection solidangle = 4 np.pi / (6 face.width face.height) coeffs = solidangle return coeffs Parameters: Distance Threshold \tau: Manually set threshold to determine occlusion from depth. Value: "Not given in the sources." Grid Spacing: Determines the density of occlusion volumes. Value: "Not given in the sources." Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The conversion from depth to binary occlusion is sensitive to the threshold \tau. Boundaries: The method relies on forward mapping splatting, which may have artifacts at volume boundaries if not handled carefully. Degenerate Input: If the scene geometry is sparse, the depth cubemap may have large gaps, leading to inaccurate occlusion estimates. A sibling method that uses a light cache rendering pipeline. It differs by focusing on the rendering pipeline structure rather than explicit SH baking of occlusion. Choose when a full pipeline integration is preferred over explicit volume caching. Light Cache Rendering Pipeline Time Complexity: Precomputation involves Nv \times 6 rendering passes, where Nv is the number of occlusion volumes. Each pass is O(Ng) where Ng is the number of Gaussians. SH convolution is O(Np) where Np is the number of pixels in the cubemap. Memory Complexity: O(Nv \times C), where C is the number of SH coefficients per volume. Measured Performance: "Not given in the sources." Strengths: Efficient online calculation of indirect illumination by leveraging precomputed SH coefficients. Limitations: Requires precomputation step; accuracy depends on grid density and threshold. When to Use: When indirect illumination is needed in 3DGS and real-time performance is critical, and precomputation is acceptable. When Not to Use: For dynamic scenes where geometry changes frequently, as precomputation would need to be repeated. The method is inspired by the "Indirect Lighting Cache" used in real-time rendering. It draws inspiration from precomputation techniques in the video game industry, such as Irradiance Volume in Blender, Lightmass Volume in Unreal, and Light Probes in Unity. It was introduced in the GS-IR (3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering) framework. name: Extinction-based Shading and Illumination
head: Extinction-based shading, SAT-based illumination
body: Extinction-based Shading and Illumination is a GPU-accelerated technique that computes ambient occlusion, color bleeding, and directional soft shadows in direct volume ray casting by aggregating exponential extinction coefficients using a 3D Summed Area Table (SAT). Unlike traditional ray-marching shadowing or opacity-based occlusion methods, it approximates spherical and conical neighborhoods with axis-aligned cuboid shells, enabling distance-weighted aggregation in constant time per sample. It sets itself apart from siblings like Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading by providing global illumination effects (occlusion, bleeding) rather than just local surface reflection, and from Extinction-based Shadow and Scattering Approximation by unifying these effects into a single SAT-based framework with specific cuboid-shell approximation strategies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume dataset V, Transfer Function (TF) mapping scalar values to extinction coefficient \tau and base color C{base}, light source positions (static or dynamic), camera parameters. Outputs: Final image with modulated colors Ci at each sample point. Data Structures: 1. Extinction SAT Texture: A 3D texture storing the prefix sums of extinction coefficients \tau. 2. Light Cache Texture: A 3D ping-pong texture that becomes a light cache during rendering, storing precomputed illumination factors (AO, color bleeding, static shadows). Numbered Steps: 1. Construct Extinction SAT: Compute extinction coefficient \tau(\mathbf{p}) for each voxel based on the TF. Build the 3D SAT using a recursive doubling technique with a logarithmic number of passes. Simultaneously build the Color Bleeding SAT (storing vector \tau{C{RGB}}) in the same texture pass. 2. Compute Ambient Occlusion (AO) and Color Bleeding: Approximate the spherical neighborhood \OmegaA using a series of cuboid shells Shi. Query the SAT for each shell to get the aggregate sum of extinction coefficients SAT(Shi). Accumulate AO values iteratively: \tau{Sh0} = SAT(Sh0) \cdot r{Sh0}^{-2} \tau{Sh{i+1}} = \tau{Shi} + (SAT(Sh{i+1}) - SAT(Shi)) \cdot r{Sh{i+1}}^{-2} where r{Shi} is the radius of shell i. Store the result in the Light Cache Texture. This step is independent of light position and only requires recomputation when the TF changes. 3. Compute Directional Soft Shadows (if dynamic): For each voxel and light source, define a cone \Psi towards the light. Determine the primary cone axis as the coordinate axis with the smallest angle to the vector towards the light source. Define two secondary axes from the remaining four possibilities to form two axis-aligned planes. Approximate the cone \Psi with a series of cuboids placed along these two planes. Query the Extinction SAT for these cuboids to compute attenuation. Weight the sum using wL = V^{-1}, where V is the aggregate query size. Store in Light Cache if static; otherwise compute per frame. 4. Rendering (Ray Casting Loop): For each sample point \mathbf{p}i along the ray: Retrieve base color C{base} and opacity \alpha from TF. Retrieve precomputed AO/Color Bleeding from Light Cache. If dynamic shadows, query Extinction SAT for the cone \Psi to get shadow attenuation. Compute lighting term L(\mathbf{p}i) using Eq. 8 below. Compute final color Ci = C{base} \cdot L(\mathbf{p}i). Formula: The reflected light Ei for a voxel due to a light source (ambient or directional) is: Ei = I{A,L} \cdot e^{-w{A,L} \sum{\Omega{A,L}} \Delta^{\tauj} \cdot k} \cdot C{RGB} Where: I{A,L}: Ambient or light source intensity. w{A,L}: Weighting function. wA = r^{-2} for AO, wL = V^{-1} for shadows. \sum{\Omega{A,L}} \Delta^{\tauj}: Sum of extinction coefficients over the query region (obtained via SAT). k: Local illumination factor (e.g., gradient-based normal). C{RGB}: Color vector (for color bleeding) or base color. Parameters: Number of Shells: As few as 3 shells are sufficient for AO. Increase if radius of \OmegaA exceeds 10% of dataset radius. Cone Sampling: User-defined sampling frequency and growth rate on the primary axis. SAT Resolution: Can be lower than volume resolution. Pitfalls: TF Dependency: The SAT must be updated whenever the Transfer Function changes because extinction coefficients are TF-dependent. Light Count: Rendering time increases linearly with the number of light sources, as extinction must be estimated for each. Precision: Cuboid approximation of cones may introduce artifacts if the cone is highly oblique relative to axes; handled by choosing the primary axis with the smallest angle. Approximates spherical occlusion using cuboid shells and inverse-square weighting. Sets it apart by caching AO independently of light position, incurring zero rendering cost. Choose when global shading without light dependency is needed. Ambient Occlusion Stores RGB vectors in the SAT alongside extinction. Sets it apart by computing color bleeding simultaneously with the extinction SAT at no extra computation cost. Choose when inter-reflection color transfer is required. Color Bleeding via SH Projection Uses cuboid approximation of light cones. Sets it apart by caching static shadow factors once and querying dynamic shadows per frame. Choose for soft shadows with static or dynamic lights. Next Event Estimation for Emissive Volumes Time Complexity: SAT construction requires O(\log N) passes per dimension. Rendering cost is zero for cached AO/color bleeding and a single texture lookup for static shadows per sample; dynamic shadows require per-frame SAT queries proportional to the number of cuboid samples. Memory Complexity: Requires two auxiliary 3D textures (SAT and Light Cache). Performance: Head (128x256x256, SAT 192^3, 15 shells): 111fps (AO only), 143fps (dynamic). Engine (256x256x128, SAT 64^3, 50 cone samples): 57fps (AO only), 130fps (dynamic). Cornell Box (256^3, SAT 256^3, 5 shells, 60 cone samples, static): 133fps (AO only), 161fps (static). Pelvis (512x512x461, SAT 64^3, 5 shells, 50 cone samples, dynamic): 15fps (AO only), 26fps (dynamic). Strengths: Interactive frame rates for global illumination effects; decouples lighting from view changes (AO); efficient constant-time neighborhood queries. Limitations: Memory intensive for high-resolution SATs; requires SAT rebuild on TF change; performance degrades with many light sources. Developed by Schlegel et al. in 2011 [SMP11], this technique builds on earlier SAT-based ambient occlusion work by Desgranges and Engel [DE07]. It was introduced to provide interactive global illumination in volume ray casting by leveraging the order-independent summation property of extinction coefficients. It is used in scientific visualization and medical imaging where realistic lighting enhances depth perception. name: Extinction-based Shadow and Scattering Approximation
head: Cone approximation via SAT, Extinction SAT queries
body: A technique to approximate directional shadows and light scattering by computing the extinction of light intensity for voxels using a 3D Summed Area Table (SAT), avoiding the propagation of illumination from outside the volume. It differs from half-angle slicing [14] by handling any light type and multiple sources, and from Ropinski et al.'s method by computing voxel extinction rather than propagating external illumination. Inputs: Scalar volume V, transfer function TF, light source positions \mathbf{L}j, cone angle \Psi, sampling frequency f, growth rate g, weighting function h. Outputs: Light cache texture containing shadow and ambient occlusion (AO)/color bleeding terms. Data Structures: 1. Extinction SAT: 3D texture of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Each voxel stores the cumulative sum of extinction coefficients \sigmat along the three axes. 2. Light Cache Texture: 3D texture storing precomputed shadow and AO terms per voxel. Steps: 1. Construct Extinction SAT: Compute the 3D SAT of the extinction coefficient field \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). For a volume of size N, construction time is O(N). 2. Determine Primary Axis: For each light source, identify the coordinate axis with the smallest angle to the light direction vector. This axis defines the primary sampling direction for the shadow cone. 3. Sample Primary Axis: Define sampling points along the primary axis using the user-defined sampling frequency f and growth rate g. The growth rate controls the change of frequency over distance, allowing coarser sampling further away. 4. Derive Cuboid Queries: For each sample point, project the query cone (defined by angle \Psi) onto the primary-secondary axis planes. Derive axis-aligned cuboids that cover this cone projection. 5. Compute Extinction via SAT: Perform SAT lookups to sum extinction coefficients for the derived cuboids. Apply the weighting function h to weight cuboids differently to adjust shadow strength. 6. Store in Light Cache: Store the computed shadow and AO/color bleeding terms in the light cache texture to avoid duplicate queries during raycasting. 7. Raycasting Application: During the raycasting pass, apply illumination terms using one additional texture lookup per sample from the light cache. Parameters: Cone angle \Psi: Typical values 1.0 to 5.0 degrees. Sampling frequency: A few dozen lookups per cone and voxel are sufficient. Growth rate: Adjusts sampling density based on distance. Weighting function h: Strengthens or weakens shadow effect. Pitfalls: Using very few cone samples (e.g., 12) results in clearly visible cuboid artifacts. SAT resolution can be a fraction of the volume dataset size without exposing conspicuous artifacts, but too low resolution causes blurred shadows. An algorithm to compute approximate shadows for volumetric rendering by baking axis-aligned light extinction into textures and interpolating, avoiding full shadow raycasts per voxel or raymarch step. It computes axis-aligned extinction via cumulative products of extinction along each axis, writing each axis to a different texture concurrently. It collapses these into two interpolated directional extinction values to reduce bandwidth cost during raymarching. Precomputation cost is <1ms across tested scenarios. Time Complexity: SAT construction is O(N) where N is the number of voxels. Shadow computation per frame is O(M \cdot K) where M is the number of voxels and K is the number of cone samples. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Extinction SAT and Light Cache textures, both O(N). Performance: SAT construction for 256^3 volume takes 0.311s; for 64^3 it takes 0.029s. AO/color bleeding computation for 256^3 texture with 3 shells takes 0.0307s, compared to 3.0818s for explicit sampling of radius 7. Shadow computation for 64^3 texture with 50 samples takes 0.0079s/frame. Strengths: Fast, flexible, handles any light type and multiple sources, handles light sources within or on the border of the dataset without additional effort. Interactive performance is maintained even with dynamic transfer functions. Limitations: Approximation artifacts if cone samples are too few. Requires recomputation of SAT and AO terms when transfer function or light source position changes. Originated in GPU volume ray-casting for interactive rendering with dynamic transfer functions and light sources. It was developed to provide realistic looking images with improved depth and occlusion effects at interactive frame rates. Extinction-based Shading and Illumination in GPU Volume Ray-Casting, https://www.ifi.uzh.ch/dam/jcr:ffffffff-9e7f-2af5-ffff-ffffcf9259bb/FastShadows.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Ignis: Eulerian Fluid Simulation and Rendering at VR Frame Rates, https://doi.org/10.1145/3610542.3626120, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Image Plane Sweep Volume Illumination
head: Image Plane Sweep, Sundén et al
body: Image Plane Sweep Volume Illumination is a GPU-based volume ray-casting technique that reduces illumination computation complexity by exploiting the plane sweep paradigm. It enables interactive frame rates while supporting advanced effects such as scattering and shadowing. Unlike standard ray casting which casts viewing rays directly from the viewpoint, this method computes illumination for a screen-space line first, then casts viewing rays line by line. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Scalar volume data V, light direction \mathbf{l}, view direction \mathbf{v}, camera parameters, and transfer functions for color C{base} and opacity \alpha. Output: Final composited image with volumetric illumination (shadows and scattering). Data Structures: Illumination Buffer: A 2D buffer storing precomputed illumination values for each screen-space line segment. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing the scalar field V. Steps: 1. Project Light Direction: Project the light direction vector \mathbf{l} onto the image plane to determine the sweep direction. 2. Line-Sweep Illumination Computation: Perform a line-sweep computation in image space along the projected light direction. This step calculates illumination information (such as shadowing and scattering contributions) for each screen-space line. The optical model considers either single scattering with a single light direction, or multiple scattering resulting from a rather high albedo. To capture high-frequency shadows and diffuse scattering simultaneously, these two formulations are combined. 3. Viewing Ray Casting: Once illumination information for a line is computed, cast viewing rays from the image plane line by line. 4. Shading Modification: Modify the shading of the samples using the ray casting algorithm based on the precomputed line lighting. The base color C{base} and opacity \alpha are computed as per standard direct volume ray casting, and the final color is modulated by the precomputed illumination term. The opacity \alpha is derived solely from the transfer function and is generally not modified by the shading model, preserving the physical interpretation of density. The shading model affects only the color channel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imageplanesweepvolumeillumination(volume, lightdir, viewdir, camera): # Step 1: Project light direction onto the image plane sweepdir = normalize(lightdir - dot(lightdir, viewdir) viewdir) # Step 2: Line-sweep illumination computation in image space width, height = camera.resolution illuminationbuffer = [[0.0] width for in range(height)] # Group pixels into lines aligned with sweepdir lines = grouppixelsbyline(sweepdir, width, height) for line in lines: # Compute illumination for the line (shadows, scattering) # Sources do not specify the exact integration formula for line illumination [Comment] lineillum = computelineillumination(line, volume, lightdir, camera) for i, pixel in enumerate(line): illuminationbuffer[pixel.y][pixel.x] = lineillum[i] # Step 3 & 4: Cast viewing rays line by line and apply shading image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(height)] for line in lines: for pixel in line: rayorigin = camera.origin raydir = normalize(pixel.position - rayorigin) acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for sample in marchvolume(rayorigin, raydir, volume): val = volume.sample(sample.position) basecolor, alpha = transferfunction(val) lightterm = illuminationbuffer[pixel.y][pixel.x] shadedcolor = [c lightterm for c in basecolor] weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = [acccolor[i] + shadedcolor[i] weight for i in range(3)] accalpha += weight image[pixel.y][pixel.x] = acccolor return image def grouppixelsbyline(sweepdir, width, height): # Standard rasterization: assign each pixel to a line index based on sweepdir lines = {} for y in range(height): for x in range(width): lineidx = x sweepdir.y - y sweepdir.x if lineidx not in lines: lines[lineidx] = [] lines[lineidx].append((x, y)) return list(lines.values()) def computelineillumination(line, volume, lightdir, camera): # Sources do not specify the exact integration formula for line illumination [Comment] return [1.0] len(line) def transferfunction(val): # Standard transfer function mapping scalar value to color and opacity return [0.5, 0.5, 0.5], 0.1 def marchvolume(origin, direction, volume): # Standard volume marching along ray return [(origin[i] + j direction[i]) for j in range(10) for i in range(3)] Parameters: Sweep Resolution: Not given in the sources. Scattering Model: Combines single scattering and multiple scattering approximations. Lighting Model: Typically uses Phong illumination or simplified intensity models as per the parent article. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: If the light direction is parallel to the image plane, the sweep direction may become degenerate. Computes illumination assuming a single light direction and single scattering events. Sets it apart by capturing high-frequency shadowing effects. Choose when direct lighting and sharp shadows are the primary visual requirement. See Direct volume ray casting. Computes illumination assuming multiple scattering events, typically triggered by high albedo volumes. Sets it apart by capturing diffuse scattering effects. Choose when volumetric haze or fog-like appearance is desired. See Direct volume ray casting. Time Complexity: Reduces illumination computation complexity compared to standard ray casting by leveraging the plane sweep paradigm. Memory Complexity: Requires additional storage for the illumination buffer. Measured Performance: Achieves interactive frame rates. Strengths: Supports scattering and shadowing interactively; combines high-frequency shadows with diffuse scattering. Limitations: Limited to specific lighting configurations (single light direction for single scattering). When to Use: When interactive performance is required for volumes with complex lighting effects like shadows and scattering. When Not to Use: When global illumination with multiple lights is required without approximation. Image Plane Sweep Volume Illumination was proposed by Sundén et al.. It is based on a reformulation of the optical model to integrate advanced illumination effects into GPU-based volume ray-casters. The method was developed to address the computational cost of volumetric lighting in real-time applications. Interactive Volume Rendering with Volumetric Illumination, https://doi.org/10.2312/conf/eg2012/stars/053-074, fetched 2026-10-26 Enhanced perception in volume visualization, https://doi.org/10.5821/dissertation-2117-94929, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Kaufman's Shaded Volume Rendering
head: Kaufman's Method, Shaded Volume Visualization
body: Kaufman's Shaded Volume Rendering is a direct volume ray casting technique designed to produce informative, rather than physically accurate, representations of volumetric data for scientific and engineering interpretation. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading by explicitly decoupling the shading model from physical realism, allowing users to modify shading parameters to highlight specific features through a simplified intensity model that incorporates solid texture maps. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A 3D scalar field (volume data), a view ray direction \mathbf{u}, light source positions and intensities, ambient light parameters, and transfer functions for color and opacity. Outputs: A final pixel color and accumulated opacity. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array S of scalar values. Solid Texture Map: A 3D array M mapping spatial coordinates to texture values. Transfer Functions: Td(\lambda, S, M): Color transfer function mapping scalar value and texture to RGB intensity. O(s): Opacity transfer function mapping scalar value to opacity. Lighting Parameters: Ka(\lambda): Ambient coefficient. Ia: Ambient intensity. K(\lambda): Base diffuse coefficient. Ij: Intensity of the j-th light source. \mathbf{L}j: Vector to the j-th light source. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Casting: Cast a ray for each pixel in the image plane. 2. Cell Traversal: Step through each cell along the ray. For each cell, step through the ray segment within the cell. 3. Sample Evaluation: At each stepping point \mathbf{p}, retrieve the scalar value s = S(\mathbf{p}) from the volume data and the texture value m = M(\mathbf{p}) from the solid texture map. 4. Normal Approximation: Compute the normal approximation \mathbf{N} using the local gradient of the scalar field at \mathbf{p}. 5. Lighting Computation: Calculate the perceived intensity I(\lambda) at the sample point using the simplified shading equation: I(\lambda) = Ka(\lambda)Ia + Kd(\lambda, S, M) \frac{(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}j)Ij}{|\mathbf{N}||\mathbf{L}j|} Where the diffuse coefficient Kd is defined as: Kd(\lambda, S, M) = K(\lambda) Td(\lambda, S(\mathbf{p}), M(\mathbf{p})) The term \frac{(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}j)Ij}{|\mathbf{N}||\mathbf{L}j|} represents the normalized diffuse lighting contribution from the j-th light source. 6. Accumulation: Accumulate the color and opacity along the ray using the intensity integral approximation. For a step of size du at distance d: I(\mathbf{u}) = \frac{w}{d} \rho(d) O(s) [Ka(\lambda)Ia + Kd(\lambda, S, M)(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}j)Ij] + (1 - \rho(d)bc(\mathbf{u})) du Where \rho(d) is atmospheric attenuation, bc is background color, w is a weight factor, and du is the step size. 7. Termination: Repeat steps 2-6 until the ray exits the volume or the accumulated opacity reaches unity. 8. Storage: Store the final accumulated color and opacity for the pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def kaufmanshadedvolumerendering(volumedata, texturemap, viewrayorigin, viewraydirection, lightsources, ambientintensity, ambientcoeff, colortransferfunc, opacitytransferfunc, basediffusecoeff, stepsize, maxdistance, bounds): accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < maxdistance: pos = viewrayorigin + viewraydirection t if not isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): break s = samplescalar(volumedata, pos, bounds) m = sampletexture(texturemap, pos, bounds) alphasample = opacitytransferfunc(s) if alphasample <= 0.0: t += stepsize continue normal = computegradientnormal(volumedata, pos, bounds) normal = normalize(normal) ambientlight = ambientcoeff ambientintensity diffusecoefficient = basediffusecoeff colortransferfunc(None, s, m) diffuselight = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for light in lightsources: lightdir = normalize(light['position'] - pos) dotproduct = dot(normal, lightdir) if dotproduct > 0: diffuselight += diffusecoefficient dotproduct light['intensity'] perceivedintensity = ambientlight + diffuselight rhod = 1.0 w = stepsize d = max(t, 1e-6) bc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] contribution = (w / d) rhod alphasample perceivedintensity + (1 - rhod bc) stepsize accumulatedcolor += contribution accumulatedopacity += alphasample (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): return bounds[0] <= pos[0] <= bounds[1] and bounds[2] <= pos[1] <= bounds[3] and bounds[4] <= pos[2] <= bounds[5] # Standard boundary check def samplescalar(volumedata, pos, bounds): ix, iy, iz = int(pos[0]), int(pos[1]), int(pos[2]) # Standard nearest-neighbor sampling; trilinear is standard if not isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): return 0.0 return volumedata[ix, iy, iz] def sampletexture(texturemap, pos, bounds): ix, iy, iz = int(pos[0]), int(pos[1]), int(pos[2]) # Standard nearest-neighbor sampling; trilinear is standard if not isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): return 0.0 return texturemap[ix, iy, iz] def computegradientnormal(volumedata, pos, bounds): dx = volumedata[int(pos[0])+1, int(pos[1]), int(pos[2])] - volumedata[int(pos[0])-1, int(pos[1]), int(pos[2])] # Standard finite difference dy = volumedata[int(pos[0]), int(pos[1])+1, int(pos[2])] - volumedata[int(pos[0]), int(pos[1])-1, int(pos[2])] # Standard finite difference dz = volumedata[int(pos[0]), int(pos[1]), int(pos[2])+1] - volumedata[int(pos[0]), int(pos[1]), int(pos[2])-1] # Standard finite difference return [dx, dy, dz] def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def normalize(v): mag = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 if mag == 0: return [0,0,0] return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] Parameters: Color Transfer Function: Defined for red, green, and blue; maps scalar value to intensity. Opacity Transfer Function: Defines opacity as a function of scalar value. Solid Texture Map: A 3D map M used to modulate the diffuse coefficient. Light Sources: Position and intensity Ij. Ambient Coefficient Ka and Intensity Ia: Control the ambient lighting component. Base Diffuse Coefficient K: Scales the diffuse lighting. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transfer Function Selection: The selection of desired transfer functions is noted as very difficult. Gradient Approximation: The normal \mathbf{N} is approximated by the local gradient. This can be noisy in low-resolution data. Physical Accuracy: The method is not physically accurate; it is designed for interpretability. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray and the number of light sources. O(N \cdot L) where N is the number of samples and L is the number of light sources. Memory Complexity: O(V) for storing the volume data and texture map, where V is the volume of the data. Strengths: Allows user modification of shading parameters to highlight features; provides informative representation for scientists/engineers. Limitations: Not physically accurate; selection of transfer functions is difficult; relies on gradient-based normals which can be noisy. When to Use: When the goal is to create an informative visualization for scientific analysis rather than a photorealistic image. Kaufman's Shaded Volume Rendering was introduced by Arie Kaufman in the context of volume visualization principles. The method is part of the broader field of volume visualization, aiming to provide tools for scientists and engineers to interpret volumetric data. The specific shading equation and accumulation method are detailed in Kaufman's work on volume visualization. PDF Volume Visualization: Principles and Advances, https://courses.cs.duke.edu/spring03/cps296.8/papers/KaufmanVolumeVisualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Color Bleeding via SH Projection
head: Chromaticity Effects, Diffuse Shadowed Radiance Transfer
body: This method computes indirect illumination (color bleeding) in direct volume rendering by projecting the accumulated radiance along random rays onto Spherical Harmonics (SH) basis functions. It solves the problem of capturing chromaticity effects—where the color of the medium changes as light travels through it—which simpler shading models ignore. Unlike sibling methods that rely solely on local gradient estimation or absorption-only models, this approach evaluates the full volume rendering integral to capture how the medium's color influences the scattered light. The method extends the standard direct volume ray casting loop by adding a pre-computation or offline phase to estimate the indirect lighting term, which is then used during the final rendering pass. Input: Scalar volume data V, transfer functions for base color C{base} and opacity \alpha, optional material function M, and SH order L. Output: SH coefficients representing the indirect illumination field. SH Coefficients: An array storing coefficients c{lm} for the spherical harmonics basis functions Y{lm} at each spatial location. Ray Data: Accumulated color L{mi} and direction \omegai for each sampled ray. 1. Ray Casting: For each voxel or sample point \mathbf{x}, cast N rays in random directions \omegai based on a modified adaptive sampling scheme. 2. Volume Integration: For each ray \omegai, evaluate the front-to-back compositing volume rendering integral to obtain the accumulated color L{mi}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai). This integral models the color and intensity changes (chromaticity) as the ray travels through the medium. The integration uses the base color C{base} and opacity \alpha derived from the transfer functions. Optionally, the material function M can be included in the integration. 3. SH Projection: After completing the raycasting for the current sample, perform the SH projection. For each ray i with direction \omegai (defined by angles \varthetas, \phis) and accumulated color L{mi}, update the total sum of the SH projection. The accumulated color channel values are used as weights for the SH basis functions Y{lm}(\varthetas, \phis). The update rule for the SH coefficients c{lm} at location \mathbf{x} is: c{lm}(\mathbf{x}) \leftarrow c{lm}(\mathbf{x}) + L{mi}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai) \cdot Y{lm}(\varthetas, \phis) Note: The weighting with the clamped cosine term (depending on the angle between \nabla \tau and the light vector) is omitted because the modified sampling approach already incorporates similar behavior. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computecolorbleedingsh(volume, transferfunctions, numrays, shorder): """ Computes SH coefficients for color bleeding via volume ray casting. """ import math import random def sampleuniformsphere(): u = random.random() v = random.random() theta = 2.0 math.pi u phi = math.acos(2.0 v - 1.0) return (math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta), math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta), math.cos(phi)) def cartesiantospherical(v): theta = math.atan2(v[1], v[0]) r = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) phi = math.acos(v[2] / r) return theta, phi def evaluatesh(l, m, theta, phi): # Standard spherical harmonic basis function Ylm evaluation # Implementation relies on associated Legendre polynomials return math.sqrt((2 l + 1) / (4 math.pi)) (math.cos(m theta) if m >= 0 else math.sin(-m theta)) numvoxels = volume.shape[0] volume.shape[1] volume.shape[2] shcoeffs = [[0.0] ((shorder + 1)2) for in range(numvoxels)] for xidx in range(numvoxels): localshsum = [0.0] ((shorder + 1)2) currentpos = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) stepsize = 1.0 for in range(numrays): omegai = sampleuniformsphere() Lmi = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 while transmittance > 1e-6: vval = volume[currentpos] alpha = transferfunctions.opacity(vval) color = transferfunctions.color(vval) contribution = transmittance alpha color Lmi = [Lmi[j] + contribution[j] for j in range(3)] transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) currentpos = tuple(p + omegai[d] stepsize for d, p in enumerate(currentpos)) theta, phi = cartesiantospherical(omegai) for l in range(shorder + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): idx = l (l + 1) + (m + l) ylm = evaluatesh(l, m, theta, phi) localshsum[idx] += Lmi[0] ylm shcoeffs[xidx] = localshsum return shcoeffs Number of Rays (N): Not given in the sources. SH Order (L): Not given in the sources. Step Size: Not given in the sources. Material Function Exchange: If the material function M is evaluated during ray marching, it is baked into the SH coefficients. Changing M requires re-performing the SH projection. To allow interactive exchange, neglect M during ray marching and use transfer function color, provided the new material has a similar hue. Cosine Weighting: Do not apply a clamped cosine weighting based on the angle between the gradient and light vector, as the modified sampling scheme already accounts for this. Chromaticity: Unlike methods that only consider absorption (e.g., Ritschel [Rit07]), this method captures chromaticity effects by evaluating the full volume rendering integral. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Captures chromaticity effects (color changes through the medium) which gradient-based shading misses. Provides better depth separation compared to conventional gradient-based shading. Limitations: High memory usage for storing SH coefficients. Non-interactive if material functions are baked into the SH projection. Computationally expensive due to multiple ray casts per voxel. When to Use: When accurate color bleeding and chromaticity effects are required, and interactive material editing is not needed or can be handled by using transfer function colors only. When Not to Use: When real-time interactive material changes are required and the performance cost of re-computing SH is prohibitive, or when memory is constrained. This method was introduced by Lindemann and Ropinski in 2010. It is an extension of diffuse shadowed radiance transfer, adapted for volume rendering. It differs from Ritschel's approach [Rit07] by considering the full volume rendering integral rather than just absorption, thereby capturing chromaticity effects. The method is part of the broader effort to improve lighting and shading in direct volume rendering beyond simple Phong models. Advanced Light Material Interaction for Direct Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/vg/vg10/101-108, fetched 2026-10-26

name: On-the-fly pre-shading
head: Pre-shading with 3D Texturing, VanGelder and Kim pre-shading
body:
On-the-fly pre-shading is a fast technique that pre-shades a volume on the fly and then slices and composites an RGB volume to obtain an image with shading effects. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Illumination Caching by computing shading dynamically during the slicing process rather than caching it in a separate data structure, and from Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Shading by deferring the accumulation of shading into a pre-shaded RGB texture space before compositing. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scalar volume dataset V, transfer functions for color C{base} and opacity \alpha, and lighting parameters (\mathbf{l}, ka, kd, ks, n). Output: A shaded RGB image. Data Structures: 1. Scalar Volume: 3D array of scalar values. 2. Pre-shaded RGB Volume: A 3D texture where each voxel stores the shaded color C{shaded}. The opacity is typically stored separately or integrated during compositing. 3. Ray/Plane Parameters: View direction, camera position, and slice spacing. Steps: 1. Gradient Estimation: For each voxel \mathbf{p}i in the volume, estimate the normal \mathbf{n}i using central finite differences: 
abla V(\mathbf{p}i) \approx \left(  rac{V(\mathbf{p}i + \Delta x) - V(\mathbf{p}i - \Delta x)}{2\Delta x},  rac{V(\mathbf{p}i + \Delta y) - V(\mathbf{p}i - \Delta y)}{2\Delta y},  rac{V(\mathbf}i + \Delta z) - V(\mathbf{p}i - \Delta z)}{2\Delta z} ight) \mathbf{n}i =  rac{
abla V(\mathbf{p}i)}{\|
abla V(\mathbf{p}i)\|} Handle zero-gradient voxels by assigning a default normal (e.g., (0,0,1)) to avoid division by zero. 2. Shading Computation: Compute the lighting term L(\mathbf{p}i) using the Phong model: L(\mathbf{p}i) = ka + kd (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks (\mathbf{r}i \cdot \mathbf{v})^n Where \mathbf{r}i = 2(\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l})\mathbf{n}i - \mathbf{l}. 3. Pre-shading: Map the scalar value to base color C{base} and compute the shaded color: C{shaded}(\mathbf{p}i) = C{base}(V(\mathbf{p}i)) \cdot L(\mathbf{p}i) Store C{shaded} in the pre-shaded RGB volume. 4. Slicing and Compositing: Render the pre-shaded RGB volume using 3D texturing. Slices are taken at arbitrary small distances to avoid popping. The RGB values are accumulated using front-to-back alpha compositing. The opacity \alpha is derived from the transfer function and accumulated separately or integrated with the color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ontheflypreshading(volume, transferfunc, lightdir, viewdir, ambient, diffuse, specular, shininess): # Step 1 & 2: Pre-shade the volume shadedvolume = empty3dtexture(volume.dimensions) for p in volume.voxels: # Estimate normal grad = finitedifferencegradient(volume, p) if norm(grad) == 0: normal = (0, 0, 1) # Default normal else: normal = normalize(grad) # Compute lighting r = 2 dot(normal, lightdir) normal - lightdir lighting = ambient + diffuse dot(normal, lightdir) + specular pow(dot(r, viewdir), shininess) # Map to color and shade basecolor = transferfunc.color(volume[p]) shadedcolor = basecolor lighting shadedvolume[p] = shadedcolor # Step 3: Slice and composite image = emptyimage() for ray in raysfromcamera(): accumulatedcolor = (0, 0, 0) accumulatedalpha = 0 for t in ray.samples: # Interpolate from pre-shaded volume cshaded = shadedvolume.interpolate(ray.positionat(t)) alpha = transferfunc.opacity(volume[ray.positionat(t)]) # Front-to-back compositing weight = alpha exp(-accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += cshaded weight accumulatedalpha += alpha weight image[ray.pixel] = accumulatedcolor return image Time Complexity: O(N) for pre-shading, where N is the number of voxels. Slicing is O(R \cdot S), where R is rays and S is samples. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the pre-shaded RGB volume. Performance: Fast due to one-pass shading and efficient 3D texture interpolation. Avoids multiple passes through rasterization hardware. Strengths: High performance, no popping artifacts with small slice distances. Limitations: Requires additional memory for the pre-shaded volume. Shading is static per voxel, not dynamic per sample along the ray. On-the-fly pre-shading was introduced by VanGelder and Kim. It was developed as a fast alternative to multi-pass methods like those by Meißner et al. which suffered from performance loss. It leverages 3D texture hardware interpolation. name: Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Illumination
head: Phong Illumination
body:
Direct Volume Rendering with Phong Illumination is a shading technique that combines Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) with the Phong reflection model to produce photo-realistic images with strong depth cues and a plastic appearance. It distinguishes itself from non-photorealistic methods like Tone or Contour Rendering by calculating ambient, diffuse, and specular light intensities at each sample point, thereby revealing internal structures through surface-like highlights. Unlike siblings such as Pre-integrated Volume Rendering, which focuses on integration accuracy, or Next Event Estimation for Emissive Volumes, which uses explicit light sampling, this method relies on local gradient-based approximations of surface normals to modulate the base color derived from transfer functions. The method extends the standard DVR pipeline by inserting a shading step between sample classification and compositing. It operates on a scalar volume field V and produces a 2D image. Input: Scalar volume data V, transfer functions mapping scalar values to color \mathbf{c} and opacity \alpha, camera parameters (view direction \mathbf{v}), light source parameters (direction \mathbf{l}, color \mathbf{c}p), and rendering parameters (sampling distance, Phong coefficients). Output: Image plane pixels with color values \mathbf{C}{out}. Volume Data: A 3D grid of scalar values V(x,y,z). Sample Point: Contains interpolated scalar value, gradient 
abla V, base color \mathbf{c}{base}, opacity \alpha, and shaded color \mathbf{c}{shaded}. Ray State: Accumulated ray color \mathbf{C}^{in} and ray opacity \alpha^{in}. 1. Ray Casting and Sampling: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Place sample points xi evenly along the ray at a fixed Sampling Distance. Interpolate the scalar value V(xi) and the gradient 
abla V(xi) from the neighboring voxels. 2. Classification: Map the scalar value V(xi) to a base color \mathbf{c}{base} and opacity \alpha(xi) using 1D transfer functions. The opacity \alpha(xi) is determined solely by the transfer function and is not modified by the shading model. 3. Gradient Estimation: Estimate the surface normal \mathbf{n}i at xi by normalizing the gradient 
abla V(xi). The gradient can be estimated using: Central Differences: Fast but lower quality. 4D Linear Regression: Higher quality, lower approximation error, but computationally expensive. The normal is calculated as: \mathbf{n}i =  rac{
abla V(xi)}{\|
abla V(xi)\|} 4. Phong Shading: Calculate the shaded color \mathbf{c}{shaded}(xi) by modulating the base color \mathbf{c}{base} with the Phong illumination model, including depth cueing. The opacity remains \alpha(xi). The Phong term combines ambient, diffuse, and specular components. The highlight direction \mathbf{h} is approximated as: \mathbf{h} =  rac{\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}}{\|\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}\|} where \mathbf{v} is the normalized view direction and \mathbf{l} is the normalized light direction. The final color component \lambda \in \{r, g, b\} is computed as: C{\lambda}(xi) =  rac{C^p{\lambda} ka^{\lambda} +  rac{kd^{\lambda} (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{l}) + ks^{\lambda} (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{h})^n}{k1 + k2 d(xi)}}{d^{\lambda}} Where: C^p{\lambda}: Color of the directional light source. ka^{\lambda}, kd^{\lambda}, ks^{\lambda}: Ambient, diffuse, and specular reflection coefficients. n: Shininess exponent for the specular highlight. k1, k2: Constants for linear depth cueing. d(xi): Perpendicular distance from the image plane to the sample point xi. d^{\lambda}: A normalization factor or distance attenuation term (exact definition of d^{\lambda} in the denominator is not explicitly defined in the source beyond being a distance-related term, often implying a global attenuation or normalization). Note: The source formula places the depth cueing denominator inside the bracketed lighting term, divided by a final d^{\lambda}. 5. Compositing: Blend the sample points along the ray in Front-to-Back (FTB) order. Update the accumulated ray color \mathbf{C}^{out} and opacity \alpha^{out} using the following equations for each sample point xi: C^{out}{\lambda}(ui) = C^{in}{\lambda}(ui) + (1 - \alpha^{in}(ui)) \cdot C{\lambda}(xi) \cdot \alpha(xi) \alpha^{out}(ui) = \alpha^{in}(ui) + (1 - \alpha^{in}(ui)) \cdot \alpha(xi) Where ui is the current ray, C^{in} and \alpha^{in} are the values before blending the current sample, and C^{out} and \alpha^{out} are the values after blending. Args: volume: 3D array of scalar values V(x,y,z). transferfunction: Function mapping scalar value to (color, opacity). camera: Object containing view direction v and ray generation logic. light: Object containing direction l and color cp. params: Dictionary containing: samplingdistance: float ka: float (ambient coefficient) kd: float (diffuse coefficient) ks: float (specular coefficient) n: float (shininess exponent) k1: float (depth cueing constant 1) k2: float (depth cueing constant 2) gradientmethod: 'centraldiff' or 'linearregression' Returns: Image array. """ imagewidth, imageheight = camera.resolution image = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): ray = camera.castray(x, y) raycolor = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) rayopacity = 0.0 # Sample along the ray t = 0.0 while t < ray.maxdistance and rayopacity < 1.0: samplepos = ray.origin + t ray.direction # 1. Classification # Interpolate scalar value V from volume vval = interpolatevolume(volume, samplepos) # Map to base color and opacity basecolor, alpha = transferfunction(vval) # 2. Gradient Estimation # Estimate gradient at samplepos if params.gradientmethod == 'centraldiff': grad = estimategradientcentraldiff(volume, samplepos) else: grad = estimategradientlinearregression(volume, samplepos) # Normalize gradient to get normal gradnorm = np.linalg.norm(grad) if gradnorm > 1e-6: normal = grad / gradnorm else: normal = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # 3. Phong Shading # Calculate lighting components # l is normalized light direction # v is normalized view direction (from sample to camera) # Note: ray.direction is from camera to sample, so view vector is -ray.direction viewdir = -ray.direction viewdir = viewdir / np.linalg.norm(viewdir) lightdir = light.direction lightdir = lightdir / np.linalg.norm(lightdir) # Highlight direction H = (V + L) / |V + L| hvec = viewdir + lightdir hnorm = np.linalg.norm(hvec) if hnorm > 1e-6: h = hvec / hnorm else: h = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Dot products nl = np.dot(normal, lightdir) nh = np.dot(normal, h) # Depth cueing # d(xi) is perpendicular distance from image plane # Assuming camera at origin looking down Z, or using ray parameter t # Source defines d(xi) as perpendicular distance from image plane. # In standard ray casting, if image plane is at t=0, d(xi) = t. depthdist = t # Phong formula with depth cueing # Clambda(xi) = ( Cplambda ka + (kd (NL) + ks (NH)^n) / (k1 + k2 d(xi))) / dlambda # Note: The source formula has dlambda in the denominator outside the bracket. # Assuming dlambda is a global attenuation or 1.0 if not specified. # We will assume dlambda = 1.0 for standard implementation unless specified. ambientterm = params.ka diffuseterm = params.kd nl specularterm = params.ks (nh params.n) depthfactor = params.k1 + params.k2 depthdist # Avoid division by zero if depthfactor < 1e-6: depthfactor = 1e-6 lighting = (diffuseterm + specularterm) / depthfactor # Combine with ambient and light color # Cp is light color shadedcolor = np.zeros(3) for c in range(3): # Cplambda is light color component lightcolorc = light.color[c] # dlambda is not explicitly defined, assuming 1.0 or normalized dlambda = 1.0 shadedcolor[c] = (lightcolorc params.ka + lighting) / dlambda # 4. Compositing (Front-to-Back) # Cout = Cin + (1 - alphain) Csample alphasample # alphaout = alphain + (1 - alphain) alphasample alphasample = alpha if alphasample > 0: transmittance = 1.0 - rayopacity raycolor += transmittance shadedcolor alphasample rayopacity += transmittance alphasample t += params.samplingdistance image[y, x] = raycolor return image def estimategradientcentraldiff(volume, pos): """Estimate gradient using central differences.""" # Implementation depends on volume coordinate system # Returns vector (dx, dy, dz) pass def estimategradientlinearregression(volume, pos): """Estimate gradient using 4D linear regression.""" # Implementation involves fitting a plane to local neighborhood # Returns vector (dx, dy, dz) pass Sampling Distance: Defines the even spacing between sample points. Smaller distances increase quality but cost more time. ka, kd, ks: Ambient, diffuse, and specular coefficients. Typical values depend on the material appearance desired (e.g., plastic-like). n: Shininess exponent. Higher values produce sharper specular highlights. k1, k2: Depth cueing constants. k1 is the base factor, k2 scales the distance attenuation. Gradient Quality: The quality of the Phong result is heavily dependent on the gradient estimation. Central differences are fast but low quality; 4D linear regression is higher quality but expensive. Performance: The method is very expensive in time and calculation because it requires gradient precalculation for every sample point and costly vector-based light intensity calculations. Opacity Invariance: The shading model does not modify opacity. If the transfer function produces high opacity, the depth cues may be obscured by the solid appearance. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the number of samples per ray. The constant factor is high due to gradient estimation and vector math per sample. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, plus O(1) per ray for accumulation. Performance: Significantly slower than non-photorealistic methods (Tone, Contour) or simple DVR due to gradient computation and Phong lighting calculations. Strengths: Produces the most photo-realistic image quality among implemented methods, providing good depth effect and plastic appearance. Limitations: Computationally expensive; sensitive to gradient noise; does not account for global illumination effects like shadows or inter-reflections. When to use: When photo-realism and depth perception are prioritized over performance. When not to use: When real-time performance is required or when the data is noisy (gradient estimation fails). The method was implemented as part of a volume visualization system described in "Implementation of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering" (2005) by Thurner et al.. It builds upon the standard DVR pipeline introduced by [4] (likely Levoy, 1988) and integrates the Phong Illumination model [5] (likely Phong, 1975) to enhance visual realism. The approach was compared against MIP, LMIP, Tone Rendering, and Contour Rendering within the same framework.
