name: Isosurface and first-hit ray casting
body: Isosurface and first-hit ray casting renders a specific internal structure within a volume by finding the first point along a viewing ray where the scalar field value equals or crosses a user-defined isovalue \tau. Unlike standard volume rendering which composites all samples along the ray to visualize the entire density distribution, this method treats the volume as an opaque surface defined by the threshold, discarding all subsequent samples after the first valid hit. It sets itself apart from siblings like Direct volume ray casting by focusing on geometric structure and surface shading rather than volumetric transparency, and from Distance-field ray marching by operating directly on scalar field thresholds rather than signed distance functions. All methods in this family share the fundamental mechanism of image-order rendering: for each pixel, a ray is defined in world space, intersected with the volume domain, and sampled along its path to detect the first intersection with the isosurface. The ray is parameterized as r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the origin and \mathbf{d} is the direction. The traversal order is determined by the pixel's position in the image plane. The core detection logic relies on the isosurface condition. For a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}), the surface is defined by f(\mathbf{p}) = \tau. In discrete voxel data, this is typically detected by a sign change or threshold crossing between consecutive samples: f(\mathbf{p}1) \cdot f(\mathbf{p}2) < 0 relative to \tau, or f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau. Upon detection, the intersection position is often refined (e.g., via linear interpolation or binary search) to reduce discretization artifacts. The surface normal is computed from the gradient \nabla f at the hit point, usually via finite differences or tri-cubic filtering, to enable Phong-like shading. The final color is computed using local lighting models (ambient, diffuse, specular) and potentially ambient occlusion or shadows, with no contribution from voxels behind the surface. A technique that renders an implicit surface defined by a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) = \tau directly from voxel data without extracting an explicit polygon mesh. It solves the problem of visualizing specific structures by finding the first intersection along a ray where the scalar value equals or crosses a user-defined isovalue \tau. Unlike standard volume rendering which composites all samples, this method stops at the first hit. It sets itself apart from siblings by combining fixed-step marching with intersection refinement (e.g., bisection) to achieve sub-pixel accuracy. Choose this when high-quality surface rendering from voxel data is required without the overhead of mesh extraction. This method renders volumetric similarity maps by tracing rays to find the first intersection with an iso-surface defined by class similarity values, using a coarse-to-fine search strategy to ensure robustness against discretization errors. It distinguishes itself from standard marching methods by combining a guaranteed-convergence binary search (bisection) with a post-processing Newton refinement step to achieve sub-pixel accuracy, specifically designed for interactive annotation workflows where low-resolution previews are swapped for high-resolution final renders. Choose this when robustness against discretization errors and high precision are critical. Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection computes the mean density of all voxels along a ray that fall within a valid range, while simultaneously detecting the first isosurface crossing to enable surface-based shading. Unlike standard Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) which highlights only the brightest voxel, or standard Volume Ray Casting which accumulates opacity, this method averages the internal structure's density and uses the detected surface position for lighting calculations. It distinguishes itself from siblings like Exact Projection First Contact by providing an average intensity view rather than a single-point projection. Choose this when both internal density statistics and surface appearance are needed. Differential Sampling and Peak Finding is a volume rendering technique that combines adaptive ray sampling with explicit root-finding to render sharp, Dirac-like features in transfer functions as semi-transparent isosurfaces. Unlike standard post-classification or pre-integration methods which struggle with high-frequency transfer function features, this method solves directly for the roots of the transfer function to locate isosurface intersections, allowing for correct shading and opacity accumulation of narrow-band peaks. It sets itself apart from its siblings by treating the rendering problem as a root-finding problem for transfer function peaks. Choose this for rendering sharp, high-frequency features in transfer functions. Algebraic Surface Raycasting is an image-order rendering technique for isosurfaces where the volumetric scalar field is represented as a trivariate polynomial. It solves the intersection problem by composing the trivariate field function with the ray equation to produce a univariate polynomial, then finding the roots of this polynomial to determine the hit point. It distinguishes itself from voxel-based marching methods by providing an exact analytical representation of the surface within each polynomial patch, avoiding discretization errors inherent in grid-based sampling, though it requires the data to be representable as polynomials. Choose this when the data is naturally polynomial or can be approximated as such, and exact intersections are required. Exact Projection First Contact is a volume rendering technique that identifies the first voxel along a ray whose density value falls within a specified valid range, then applies shading and occlusion to that specific point. It differs from standard volume ray casting by discarding all subsequent samples after the first valid hit, effectively treating the volume as an opaque surface defined by the threshold. It sets itself apart by focusing on the "first contact" logic with explicit handling of density ranges. Choose this for simple, fast first-hit rendering with density-based classification. A GPU raycasting kernel that traces rays through a GVDB sparse voxel dataset to find the first surface intersection using fixed-step marching followed by a binary search, then computes surface properties. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by integrating sparse voxel traversal with a specific binary search refinement strategy and simultaneous computation of screen-space flow vectors for temporal analysis. Choose this when working with sparse voxel datasets (GVDB) and needing temporal flow analysis. Direct Surface Rendering with Intersection Buffer is a volume rendering technique that generates an image-space representation of an isosurface defined by a threshold within a 3D volume, enabling interactive cutting operations without pre-computing a triangular mesh. Unlike methods that extract polygonal meshes (e.g., Marching Cubes) or perform single-hit ray casting, this method stores all surface intersections for each ray in an intersection buffer. This allows the user to define cutting planes interactively by comparing stored depths against near/far depth ranges. Choose this when interactive cutting and multi-surface intersection visualization are required. isocategorical is a volume rendering method for categorical label datasets that replaces fixed-step sampling with exact voxel traversal to eliminate sawtooth artifacts at grazing angles. Unlike standard isosurface methods that rely on scalar field thresholds, this method tests discrete integer labels and stops at the first non-transparent voxel encountered along the ray. It sets itself apart from its siblings by ensuring that every voxel the ray physically intersects is visited, making the result independent of the sampling step size and preventing rays from skipping thin structures. Choose this for categorical label volumes where geometric accuracy at grazing angles is critical. Direct multifield volume ray casting of fiber surfaces is a rendering method for bivariate volume data that visualizes fiber surfaces (contours defined by a path in 2D range space) without explicit geometry extraction. It samples directly along rays in domain space and performs geometric tests in range space using a signed distance field derived from fiber surface control polygons (FSCPs). Unlike mesh extraction methods like Marching Cubes, which produce piecewise-linear approximations and are costly for large data, this method enables real-time exploration, dynamic modification, and visualization of complex bivariate structures. Choose this for bivariate data visualization where fiber surfaces are the primary interest. This method renders isosurfaces from volume data sampled on a Face-Centered Cubic (FCC) lattice using a six-direction cubic box-spline. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating C1 continuous splines and their gradients on non-Cartesian lattices on the GPU, avoiding conditional branches and minimizing texture fetch overhead. It is distinguished from Cartesian raycasting by its use of the FCC lattice for better sampling efficiency at low rates, and from BCC raycasting by a symmetric indexing scheme that is more cache-friendly along the z-axis. Choose this when the source data is on an FCC lattice and high-quality C1 continuous rendering is needed. Isosurface Display via Opacity Mapping is a volume rendering technique that visualizes specific internal surfaces by mapping scalar data values to opacity weights, effectively classing the volume into "surface" and "background" regions. Unlike methods that extract explicit polygonal meshes or rely on strict binary thresholding, this approach uses a continuous transfer function (typically Gaussian) to create a semi-transparent shell around the isovalue, allowing for smooth visual integration with interior volume data. It distinguishes itself by blending surface appearance with volumetric context. Choose this when a smooth, semi-transparent surface representation is desired that integrates with the surrounding volume. This method renders implicit isosurfaces defined by a regular volumetric grid directly via ray-casting on graphics hardware, bypassing intermediate polygonal representations. It employs a two-level hierarchical representation (blocks and bricks) for empty space skipping and memory management, adaptive sampling for intersection, and deferred image-space shading using tri-cubic filtering for smooth normals and curvatures. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on mesh extraction or single-level grids, this approach supports very large datasets by dynamically caching bricks and skipping empty space efficiently. Choose this for large-scale implicit isosurface rendering on GPUs. This method accelerates direct isosurface volume rendering on GPUs by decoupling the intersection search from the final pixel shading using a two-pass approach. It renders ray-isosurface intersections into a low-resolution auxiliary texture in the first pass, then uses this depth information to predict starting points for ray marching in the second pass, effectively skipping empty space for most pixels. Unlike preprocessing-based acceleration techniques (e.g., octrees or histogram pyramids), it constructs its auxiliary data dynamically every frame, requiring no pre-computation. Choose this for dynamic scenes where pre-computed acceleration structures are too costly to maintain. This method accelerates isosurface ray-tracing by dividing the rendering workload into four distinct GPU kernels—ray creation, BVH traversal, leaf intersection, and shading—to maximize thread coherency and concurrency. It differs from single-kernel approaches by using in-kernel stream compaction to manage variable workloads between stages, making it particularly effective for complex isosurfaces where many rays may miss the volume or require extensive traversal. Choose this for complex isosurfaces with high variability in ray traversal costs. This family defines how to compute the color and appearance of the isosurface detected by the parent method. It solves the problem of visualizing the geometric structure and material properties of the extracted surface by applying lighting models, curvature-based effects, and color enhancements to the intersection points. It distinguishes itself from direct volume rendering by ignoring contributions from voxels behind the surface (opaque shading) and from immediate shading methods by potentially decoupling the computation of high-order differential properties (like curvature) into separate rendering passes. Choose this when advanced material and lighting effects are needed for the isosurface. This family provides interaction mechanisms for isosurface rendering, allowing users to explore internal structures and select specific data elements without extracting explicit geometric meshes. It solves the problem of limited visibility in dense volumetric data and the need for precise data selection for downstream tasks like segmentation. It differs from standard clipping by supporting complex concave Boolean operations directly on the GPU and from cropping by allowing selective exposure of deeper layers via peeling. Choose this for interactive exploration and selection of volumetric data. This family renders isosurfaces by projecting geometric primitives (tetrahedra, voxels, or points) onto the screen and using fixed-function or early programmable graphics hardware features (alpha testing, stencil buffers, z-testing) to determine surface visibility and shading, rather than explicit ray-marching or mesh generation. It differs from sibling methods like Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement by avoiding per-pixel ray traversal in favor of hardware-accelerated primitive rasterization. Choose this when leveraging hardware rasterization features for performance. Cell Rasterisation with Tesselation Shader is an image-order rendering technique for isosurfaces that replaces traditional vertex shaders with a tesselation shader to efficiently rasterize clusters of grid cells as point sprites. It solves the performance bottleneck of rendering large volumes by grouping active cells into clusters, expanding them into individual points, and performing ray-box intersection and volume sampling in the fragment shader. Unlike sibling methods that rely on vertex shaders for individual cell rendering or complex mesh generation, this method leverages hardware tessellation for scalability. Choose this for rendering very large volumes with efficient cell clustering. This family accelerates isosurface extraction by optimizing the order and grouping of ray-volume interactions to minimize redundant traversal and intersection tests. It differs from naive uniform marching by using hierarchical acceleration structures (octrees, tiled grids) and spatial coherence (ray packets) to skip empty space and process multiple rays simultaneously. Choose this when traversal cost is the bottleneck and the volume has significant empty space. This method renders particle-based implicit surfaces (metaballs) directly on the GPU by evaluating the isosurface condition per pixel, avoiding polygonization and expensive precomputation or acceleration structures. It solves the problem of high rendering costs for large numbers of moving metaballs by maintaining a compact, dynamically updated list of contributing metaballs along each viewing ray and using Bézier Clipping to solve the resulting polynomial equations. Unlike Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement, it operates on parametric particle fields rather than voxel grids. Choose this for rendering dynamic metaball fields. This family combines different rendering modes (e.g., isosurface, MIP, volume) in a single pipeline to provide comprehensive visualization. It solves the problem of limited information in single-mode rendering by allowing users to switch or blend between modes. Choose this when multiple visualization modes are needed for comprehensive data exploration. A mode allowing painting on volumetric surfaces by generating an isosurface via MIDA ray casting, storing ray position and object normal in 2D buffers, and using mouse cursor position to override brush depth and orientation. Choose this for interactive surface editing and annotation. A GPU-based method for interactive rendering of isosurfaces defined by high-order multivariate polynomials, using seed projection and ray casting with early-z culling. Choose this for high-order polynomial surfaces requiring interactive performance. A ray marching technique that draws the first point (closest to camera) with a density within user-defined thresholds, using gradient-based surface normal calculation for lighting. Choose this for simple, fast front-to-back surface extraction. A technique to render arbitrary isosurfaces of a Bivariate Tetrahedral (BT) volume by transforming the BT into a space where one weight corresponds to a constant term, then shifting that weight to align the desired isosurface level with the zero-isosurface. The transformation is \hat{B}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = T^{-1}{\beta1}^{\alpha1} T^{-1}{\beta2}^{\alpha2} T^{-1}{\beta3}^{\alpha3} B{\alpha1, \alpha2, \alpha3}, where T is the bounding tetrahedron matrix. The modified weight is B'{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} = \hat{B}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3} + d if (\beta1, \beta2, \beta3) = (3,3,3), else \hat{B}{\beta1, \beta2, \beta3}, shifting the isosurface by density d. The weight at position (3,3,3) in the transformed tensor \hat{B} is the only one containing the constant term from the original BT, which corresponds to the homogeneous coordinate u=1 in Euclidean space. Choose this for rendering arbitrary isosurfaces in BT volumes without modifying the underlying data structure. Rendering opaque isosurfaces using Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) fields of various noise functions (Perlin, Cos, Worley, Turbulent) with Signed Distance Field (SDF) operators. It uses FBM of Perlin noise (2nd order Lipschitz) with improved quadratic bounds and enhancements for basic scenes. For non-2nd-order-Lipschitz noise (e.g., Perlin with abs, Worley, Turbulent), it uses only enhancements applicable to linear bounds. For Hypertextures, it uses FBM field of Perlin noise with quadratic bounds and varying SDF thresholds, leveraging BVH and Early Stop to avoid manual bounding spheres. For height fields, it uses FBM with many octaves (e.g., 1000) in shaders, allowing free animation. Performance speedups include ×4.2 for Sponge scene, ×5.7 for Clouds scene, ×10.6 for Animated Hypertextured sphere, ×4.0 for Animated Amplified wall, ×12.2 for Low \beta (0.4) FBM lacunarity scene, and ×4.7 for High \beta FBM lacunarity scene. Choose this for procedural noise-based isosurfaces with high performance. A modification of image order algorithms where a color and opacity volume are pre-computed from the original dataset to avoid per-ray shading/classification, at the cost of requiring recomputation when parameters change. Colors are assigned by using the local gradient as surface normal approximation and performing a local shading calculation. Opacity values are assigned based on the data and gradient values using a user definable transfer function. Rays are cast into the two new datasets (color and classified opacity volume) for image generation. A pitfall is that any change in classification or shading parameters requires the opacity and color arrays to be recomputed, which is prohibitive for higher resolution datasets due to storing gradients and gradient magnitudes. Choose this for static scenes where shading parameters do not change frequently. A variant of GPU-based ray-casting to render illuminated surfaces, where traversal is back-to-front within each pass to find the closest intersection point, followed by gradient lookup and lighting. In passes 3 to N, it performs M steps back-to-front, fetching scalar value from 3D texture. If value >= threshold, it stores current position r(t) in a temporary variable, keeping only the closest intersection. At the end of the shader, it checks the temporary variable; if not initial value, it looks up 3D gradient texture and performs surface lighting, rendering final color with illumination and opacity 1. A pitfall is that fragment shaders do not support conditional execution, so gradient reconstruction and illumination are always performed even if no surface is hit, though only once every M steps. Performance: RC-\beta (with empty-space skipping) for Engine dataset (256^2 128) achieved 13.6 fps, compared to 6.3 fps for RC and 10.4 fps for SBVR. Choose this for GPU-based isosurface rendering with empty-space skipping. A technique to visualize where two or more volumes intersect by shading these regions a particular color (e.g., black) to highlight interactions, determine depth ordering, and identify areas of potential co-channel interference in WiFi data. For each pixel, it calculates RayDir as the difference between FrontHit and BackHit. For each sample along RayDir, it initializes hitvolume to false. For each volume, it samples the texture at the current position (volu, volv, volw). If the sample is in the isorange, it checks if hitvolume is already true; if true, it sets colorsample to white (1, 1, 1) and breaks the inner loop; if false, it sets hitvolume to true. If the sample is not in the isorange or the loop completes without breaking, it shades normally. This visualization style is best applicable for thin isosurfaces; a different shading model may be necessary for more complicated volumes. Choose this for visualizing intersections of multiple volumes. Interactive rendering of mid-sized models is possible with 2 to 5 fps. Choose this for interactive rendering of tetrahedral models on GPU. Maintains a list of metaballs required for ray-isosurface tests by adding a metaball ID at the first intersection point and deleting it at the second intersection point, as an effective sphere intersects the viewing ray twice. The ID list is stored in a set of textures (ListBufA, ListBufB). Each texture is a screen-sized floating point RGBA texture. Nbuf buffers are grouped to form one array storing 4Nbuf floating point values. The layout stores: viewing ray parameter t, number of IDs, and IDs themselves in the remaining 4Nbuf - 2 slots. If the viewing ray touches a metaball (tangent), the ID must appear twice to maintain list consistency; this is guaranteed by looking for intersection points twice during depth peeling. With Nbuf = 4, the system can store at most 14 IDs (44 - 2 = 14). Nbuf: Number of render buffers used simultaneously. Max value is 4 for shader model 3.0 GPUs and 8 for shader model 4.0 GPUs. Choose this for efficient metaball rendering with dynamic ID management. A method that searches for ray intersections with iso-surfaces defined by specific iso-values, colors, and opacities, allowing for high-quality surface visualization and Hitpoint Refinement. It traverses the ray and, when the ray passes across an iso-value, calculates a more exact intersection point using linear interpolation between ray positions and sampled values on current and previous steps. Iso-surface Parameters: Each surface is defined by an iso-value, color, and opacity, adjusted via the Transfer function window. Choose this for semi-transparent isosurface rendering with hitpoint refinement. The concept of rendering isosurfaces directly from volume data without mesh extraction has roots in early volume visualization research. The Matryoshka algorithm, proposed by Sérgio Lopes, Adriano Lopes, and M. Próspero dos Santos, resembles the work of Udupa and Odhner [UO93] from 1993, where shells of cells of interest were previously stored in lists. The Matryoshka algorithm uses a hybrid approach combining polygon rendering and direct surface rendering, using raytracing for high image quality while avoiding empty ray traversal through optimized interval trees and view-dependent caching. This approach was developed to address the bottleneck of ray-isosurface intersection calculation, acknowledging that traversal steps are more common than intersection calculation steps. name: Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement
head: 1st ray of raytracing, First Hit Compositing, First Hit Shader, First-Hit Rendering, Isosurface Ray Marching (VPT), Volumetric Isosurface Rendering, iso surface/volume rendering by volume raycasting
body: Volumetric Isosurface Rendering with Intersection Refinement is an image-order technique that renders an implicit surface defined by a scalar threshold \tau directly from volumetric data, avoiding explicit polygon mesh extraction. It differs from full volume integration (e.g., Direct Volume Rendering) by stopping the ray traversal at the first detected isosurface intersection, and from Marching Cubes by performing surface detection and shading in a single pass without generating geometry. The method distinguishes itself from basic ray marching by applying intersection refinement (typically bisection) to the detected crossing point, reducing discretization artifacts caused by fixed step sizes. Inputs: Scalar volume data f(\mathbf{p}) stored in a 3D texture. Camera parameters: origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, view/projection matrices. Volume domain bounds [\mathbf{u}{min}, \mathbf{u}{max}]. Parameters: isovalue \tau, ray step size h, refinement iteration count N{ref}. Outputs: Pixel color \mathbf{C} and hit status. Data Structures: Volume Texture: 3D texture sampling f(\mathbf{p}). Typically sampler3D with linear filtering. Uniform Buffer Object (UBO): Contains domain bounds, step size, isovalue, and flags. vec3 uDomainMin, vec3 uDomainMax float uStepSize float uIsovalue int uRefinementIterations int uEnableShadows Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute the entry (t{min}) and exit (t{max}) parameters of the ray with the volume bounding box. If t{max} \le t{min}, the ray misses the volume. t{start} = \max(t{min}, 0.0) t{end} = t{max} 2. Ray Marching (Coarse Detection): Iterate t from t{start} to t{end} with step size h. Sample the scalar field g(t) = f(\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}) - \tau. Detect the first interval [ta, tb] where the sign of g(t) changes, indicating a crossing of the isosurface. \text{Sign Change} \iff g(t{prev}) \cdot g(t{curr}) < 0 Note: Some implementations check for f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau directly, but sign change is more robust for general scalar fields. 3. Intersection Refinement: If a sign change is detected at [ta, tb], refine the hit position using bisection for N{ref} iterations. Set t{mid} = (ta + tb) / 2. Evaluate g(t{mid}). If g(ta) \cdot g(t{mid}) \le 0, set tb = t{mid}. Else, set ta = t{mid}. Final hit parameter: t{hit} = (ta + tb) / 2. Alternative Linear Refinement: Some sources use linear interpolation between the previous and next points to estimate the new intersection X{new}: X{new} = X{prev} + (X{next} - X{prev}) \frac{\tau - f{prev}}{f{next} - f{prev}} This is repeated until convergence or a fixed iteration count. 4. Hit Position: Compute the 3D position of the intersection: \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t{hit} \mathbf{d} 5. Normal Computation: Estimate the surface normal \mathbf{n} using central differences with step size h (or a dedicated gradient step). nx = f(\mathbf{p}{hit} + h\mathbf{e}x) - f(\mathbf{p}{hit} - h\mathbf{e}x) ny = f(\mathbf{p}{hit} + h\mathbf{e}y) - f(\mathbf{p}{hit} - h\mathbf{e}y) nz = f(\mathbf{p}{hit} + h\mathbf{e}z) - f(\mathbf{p}{hit} - h\mathbf{e}z) \mathbf{n} = -\frac{\nabla f}{\|\nabla f\|} The negative gradient is used so the normal points outward toward the viewer/light. 6. Shading: Compute the color using a local lighting model (e.g., Blinn-Phong or Lambertian). Lambertian: \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{C}{base} \cdot \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \cdot \mathbf{S}, where \mathbf{l} is the light direction and \mathbf{S} is the shadow factor. Blinn-Phong: Includes ambient, diffuse, and specular components using half-vector \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}). 7. Shadow Ray Traversal (Optional): If enabled, cast a shadow ray from \mathbf{p}{hit} in direction \mathbf{l}. Start at t = 2h to avoid self-intersection artifacts. If the isosurface is encountered before leaving the volume, \mathbf{S} = 0; otherwise \mathbf{S} = 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderisosurfaceray(o, d, domainmin, domainmax, volumetex, tau, stepsize, numrefinements, enableshadows): # 1. Ray-Box Intersection tmin, tmax = intersectbox(o, d, domainmin, domainmax) if tmin is None or tmax <= tmin: return None, False tstart = max(tmin, 0.0) tend = tmax # 2. Ray Marching (Coarse Detection) tprev = tstart gprev = samplevolume(o + tprev d, volumetex) - tau tcurr = tprev + stepsize while tcurr <= tend: pcurr = o + tcurr d gcurr = samplevolume(pcurr, volumetex) - tau # Check for sign change if gprev gcurr < 0: # 3. Intersection Refinement (Bisection) ta = tprev tb = tcurr ga = gprev gb = gcurr for in range(numrefinements): tmid = (ta + tb) / 2.0 pmid = o + tmid d gmid = samplevolume(pmid, volumetex) - tau if ga gmid <= 0: tb = tmid gb = gmid else: ta = tmid ga = gmid thit = (ta + tb) / 2.0 phit = o + thit d break else: tprev = tcurr gprev = gcurr tcurr += stepsize else: # No intersection found return None, False # 4. Normal Computation h = stepsize nx = samplevolume(phit + vec3(h, 0, 0), volumetex) - samplevolume(phit - vec3(h, 0, 0), volumetex) ny = samplevolume(phit + vec3(0, h, 0), volumetex) - samplevolume(phit - vec3(0, h, 0), volumetex) nz = samplevolume(phit + vec3(0, 0, h), volumetex) - samplevolume(phit - vec3(0, 0, h), volumetex) normal = normalize(vec3(-nx, -ny, -nz)) # Negative gradient # 5. Shading lightdir = normalize(vec3(1.0, 1.0, -1.0)) # Example light direction shadow = 1.0 if enableshadows: # 6. Shadow Ray Traversal shadow = traceshadow(phit, lightdir, domainmin, domainmax, volumetex, tau, stepsize) # Lambertian Shading diffuse = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) color = vec3(1.0) diffuse shadow # Base color white return phit, True def intersectbox(o, d, minb, maxb): tmin = 0.0 tmax = float('inf') for i in range(3): if d[i] == 0: if o[i] < minb[i] or o[i] > maxb[i]: return None, None else: t1 = (minb[i] - o[i]) / d[i] t2 = (maxb[i] - o[i]) / d[i] if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None, None return tmin, tmax def samplevolume(p, tex): # Standard 3D texture lookup with linear filtering return tex[p] def traceshadow(origin, lightdir, domainmin, domainmax, volumetex, tau, stepsize): t = 2.0 stepsize # Avoid self-intersection while True: p = origin + t lightdir if p.x < domainmin.x or p.x > domainmax.x or \ p.y < domainmin.y or p.y > domainmax.y or \ p.z < domainmin.z or p.z > domainmax.z: return 1.0 if samplevolume(p, volumetex) >= tau: return 0.0 t += stepsize return 1.0 Parameters: tau (Isovalue): User-defined threshold. Typical values depend on data normalization (e.g., 0.333 for normalized [0,1] data). stepsize: Controls sampling density. Smaller steps increase accuracy but cost more. Typical range: 0.001 to 0.01 in normalized domain. numrefinements: Number of bisection iterations. Typical value: 5-10. enableshadows: Boolean flag for shadow ray computation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Intersection: Shadow rays must start at t > 0 (e.g., 2h) to prevent the shadow ray from immediately hitting the surface it originated from due to numerical precision. Missed Intersections: If stepsize is too large, the ray may jump over thin structures or sign changes. Discretization Artifacts: Without refinement, the hit position is quantized to the grid, causing "staircasing" or aliasing. Normal Accuracy: Central differences require sampling outside the hit point, which may be expensive or invalid at boundaries. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot N{ref}) per pixel, where N is the number of marching steps to the surface and N{ref} is the refinement count. Shadow rays add a secondary traversal cost. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, plus the volume texture storage. Performance: Faster than full volume rendering because it terminates early. Performance scales with volume resolution and isovalue density. Empty-space skipping (using acceleration structures like uniform grids) can significantly reduce N by skipping regions where the isovalue cannot exist. Strengths: Real-time capable on GPUs; no preprocessing (mesh extraction) required; dynamic isovalue adjustment. Limitations: Sensitive to step size; may miss thin features; normals are approximate. Origin: The method is a fundamental technique in volume visualization, often referred to as "first-hit" rendering. It renders implicit surfaces directly from volumetric data by finding a specific scalar value along a ray. Development: Early implementations used simple thresholding. Refinement techniques (bisection, Newton) were added to improve geometric accuracy. Modern implementations leverage GPU shaders for real-time performance. Usage: Commonly used in medical imaging (virtual endoscopy, bone rendering) and scientific visualization where explicit mesh extraction is undesirable or too slow. What it is: Uses Newton's method in addition to bisection for faster convergence of the intersection point. Difference: Newton's method converges quadratically but requires derivative evaluation and can be unstable; bisection is slower but robust. When to choose: When high precision is needed and the scalar field is smooth and differentiable. Difference: Averages values along the ray but highlights the isosurface. When to choose: When both internal structure and surface boundaries are important. Link: Average Intensity Projection with IsoSurface Detection What it is: Uses differential sampling to find peaks in the scalar field. Difference: Focuses on local maxima rather than a specific threshold crossing. When to choose: For rendering features defined by intensity peaks rather than boundaries. When to choose: For implicit surfaces defined by low-degree polynomials. Link: Algebraic Surface Raycasting What it is: Computes the exact first contact point. Difference: Higher precision than bisection, potentially more expensive. When to choose: When geometric accuracy is critical. name: Robust Iso-surface Rendering via Bisection and Newton Refinement
head: Isosurface Raycasting with Binary Search, Similarity Map Rendering, bisection trace with Newton refinement, isoray rendering pipeline
body:
This method renders volumetric similarity maps by tracing rays to find the first intersection with an isosurface defined by class similarity values, followed by Phong shading. It employs a bisection search for intersection detection after a coarse traversal, optionally refined by Newton's method to achieve sub-pixel accuracy. Unlike methods relying solely on linear interpolation, this approach guarantees robustness through interval arithmetic or Lipschitz-based inclusion functions. Inputs: Scalar field function f(\mathbf{p}) returning value and optionally gradient. Camera parameters: origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, field of view, projection type. Iso-value threshold 	au for the specific class C. Bounding box bounds (\mathbf{lo}, \mathbf{hi}). Parameters: newtoniter (default 3), margin (default 0.01), lipschitz (constant or 'auto'), safety (default 1.5), nsamples (default 10000). Outputs: Color buffer with forward-composited surface colors. Depth buffer. Hit masks and surface normals. Data Structures: TraceResult: Contains position (N, 3), normal (N, 3), t (N,), hit (N, bool). AffineForm (for inclusion functions): x0 (N,), xi (N, K), delta (N,). GradientInclusion: Wraps f and a Lipschitz constant L. Steps: 1. Camera Setup: Compute ray origins and directions for each pixel. For perspective projection, use FOV; for parallel, use extent. 2. Bounding Box Intersection: Compute ray-AABB intersection to get t{min} and t{max}. The AABB is expanded by a margin: 	ext{margin} = (\mathbf{hi} - \mathbf{lo}) 	imes 0.01 \mathbf{aabb\lo} = \mathbf{lo} - 	ext{margin} \mathbf{aabb\hi} = \mathbf{hi} + 	ext{margin} 3. Lipschitz Estimation (if lipschitz='auto'): Estimate L by sampling N points in the bounds, computing gradient norms, and taking the maximum multiplied by a safety factor (default 1.5). L = \max{i} \|
abla f(\mathbf{p}i)\| 	imes 1.5 4. Coarse Traversal: Step along the ray from t{min} until f(\mathbf{p}(t)) \ge 	au. 5. Bisection Search: Perform binary search within the interval [t{start}, t{end}] where the threshold crossing was detected. t{mid} =  rac{t{start} + t{end}}{2} Evaluate f(\mathbf{p}(t{mid})). If f \ge 	au, set t{end} = t{mid}; else t{start} = t{mid}. 6. Newton Refinement (Optional): Apply Newton's method to refine t for sub-pixel accuracy. t{new} = t{old} -  rac{f(\mathbf{p}(t{old})) - 	au}{
abla f(\mathbf{p}(t{old})) \cdot \mathbf{d}} Repeat for newtoniter iterations. 7. Normal Computation: Compute surface normal \mathbf{n} at the hit position \mathbf{p}{hit}. If f provides analytic gradient: \mathbf{n} = 
abla f(\mathbf{p}{hit}). Else, use centered finite differences with step h=10^{-5}: \mathbf{n} =  rac{1}{2h}  egin{bmatrix} f(\mathbf{p}+h\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{p}-h\mathbf{x}) \ f(\mathbf{p}+h\mathbf{y}) - f(\mathbf{p}-h\mathbf{y}) \ f(\mathbf{p}+h\mathbf{z}) - f(\mathbf{p}-h\mathbf{z}) \end{bmatrix} Normalize \mathbf{n}, clamping norm to \ge 10^{-12} to prevent division by zero. 8. Shading: Compute color using Phong model with ambient, diffuse, and specular components. Cast shadow ray to light source. 9. Compositing: Blend surface color onto output buffer using forward compositing. Continue raycasting until early ray termination threshold is reached. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def rayaabbintersect(origins, directions, aabblo, aabbhi): """Standard slab method for ray-AABB intersection.""" directions = np.where(directions == 0, 1e-12, directions) t1 = (aabblo - origins) / directions t2 = (aabbhi - origins) / directions tenter = np.maximum(t1, t2).min(axis=1) texit = np.minimum(t1, t2).max(axis=1) tmin = np.maximum(tenter, 0.0) tmax = np.minimum(texit, np.inf) hitmask = tmin <= tmax return tmin, tmax, hitmask def centereddifferencenormals(f, pos, h=1e-5): """Compute surface normals via centered difference.""" N = pos.shape[0] offsets = np.array([[h, 0, 0], [-h, 0, 0], [0, h, 0], [0, -h, 0], [0, 0, h], [0, 0, -h]], dtype=pos.dtype) allpoints = (pos[None,:,:] + offsets[:, None,:]).reshape(6 N, 3) allvals, = f(allpoints) v = allvals.reshape(6, N) gradx = (v[0] - v[1]) / (2.0 h) grady = (v[2] - v[3]) / (2.0 h) gradz = (v[4] - v[5]) / (2.0 h) normals = np.stack([gradx, grady, gradz], axis=1) norms = np.linalg.norm(normals, axis=1, keepdims=True) norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-12) return normals / norms def estimatelipschitz(f, bounds, nsamples=10000, safety=1.5, h=1e-5): """Estimate Lipschitz constant over bounding box.""" lo, hi = bounds rng = np.random.defaultrng() pts = rng.uniform(lo, hi, (nsamples, 3)) vals, grads = f(pts) if grads is not None: gradnorms = np.linalg.norm(grads, axis=1) else: offsets = np.array([[h, 0, 0], [-h, 0, 0], [0, h, 0], [0, -h, 0], [0, 0, h], [0, 0, -h]], dtype=np.float64) allpoints = (pts[None,:,:] + offsets[:, None,:]).reshape(6 nsamples, 3) allvals, = f(allpoints) v = allvals.reshape(6, nsamples) gx = (v[0] - v[1]) / (2.0 h) gy = (v[2] - v[3]) / (2.0 h) gz = (v[4] - v[5]) / (2.0 h) gradnorms = np.sqrt(gx2 + gy2 + gz2) return float(gradnorms.max() safety) def bisecttrace(f, origins, directions, tmin, tmax, tau, coarsestep=0.01, maxiter=30): """Coarse traversal followed by bisection search for isosurface intersection.""" # Coarse traversal t = tmin.copy() positions = origins + t[:, None] directions vals, = f(positions) while np.any(vals < tau) & np.any(t < tmax): t = np.minimum(t + coarsestep, tmax) positions = origins + t[:, None] directions vals, = f(positions) # Bisection search on the interval where crossing occurred tstart = tmin.copy() tend = t.copy() for in range(maxiter): tmid = (tstart + tend) / 2.0 positions = origins + tmid[:, None] directions vals, = f(positions) inside = vals >= tau tstart[inside] = tmid[inside] tend[~inside] = tmid[~inside] return tmid def newtonrefine(f, origins, directions, t, tau, iterations): """Refine intersection parameter t using Newton's method.""" for in range(iterations): positions = origins + t[:, None] directions vals, grads = f(positions) dvaldt = np.sum(grads directions, axis=1) dvaldt = np.maximum(np.abs(dvaldt), 1e-12) np.sign(dvaldt) t = t - (vals - tau) / dvaldt return t def shadephong(normals, hit, lightdir, viewdir, ambient, diffusecolor, specularcolor, shininess): """Simple Phong shading.""" color = np.zeroslike(ambient) if not hit.any(): return color n = normals[hit] l = lightdir[hit] v = viewdir[hit] r = 2.0 np.sum(n l, axis=1, keepdims=True) n - l diff = np.maximum(np.sum(n l, axis=1), 0.0) spec = np.maximum(np.sum(r v, axis=1), 0.0) shininess color[hit] = ambient + diff diffusecolor + spec specularcolor return np.clip(color, 0.0, 1.0) def robustisosurfacerender( f, bounds, origins, directions, tau, newtoniter=3, margin=0.01, lipschitz='auto', safety=1.5, nsamples=10000, ambient=0.2, diffusecolor=np.array([1.0, 1.0, 1.0]), specularcolor=np.array([0.5, 0.5, 0.5]), shininess=32.0): lo, hi = bounds marginvec = (hi - lo) margin aabblo = lo - marginvec aabbhi = hi + marginvec tmin, tmax, hitmask = rayaabbintersect(origins, directions, aabblo, aabbhi) if lipschitz == 'auto': L = estimatelipschitz(f, bounds, nsamples, safety) else: L = lipschitz thit = bisecttrace(f, origins, directions, tmin, tmax, tau) if newtoniter > 0: thit = newtonrefine(f, origins, directions, thit, tau, newtoniter) normals = np.zeroslike(origins) validhits = np.isfinite(thit) & hitmask if validhits.any(): hitpositions = origins[validhits] + thit[validhits, None] directions[validhits] vals, grads = f(hitpositions) if grads is None: grads = centereddifferencenormals(f, hitpositions) norms = np.linalg.norm(grads, axis=1, keepdims=True) norms = np.maximum(norms, 1e-12) normals[validhits] = grads / norms lightdir = np.array([0.0, 0.0, -1.0]) viewdir = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) color = shadephong(normals, validhits, lightdir, viewdir, ambient, diffusecolor, specularcolor, shininess) return thit, normals, validhits, color An optional post-processing step applied after the bisection phase to achieve sub-pixel hit-point accuracy by iteratively correcting the position using directional derivatives. Time Complexity: Bisection is O(\log(1/\epsilon)) per ray for precision \epsilon. Newton refinement adds O(k) where k is the number of iterations. Lipschitz estimation is O(N) where N is sample count. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing ray data and results. Affine arithmetic variants may require O(K) per point for noise symbols. Performance: Post-processing (bilateral solver) takes ~0.4s for 256^3 and ~5.3s for 512^3 on Intel i7-8700K. Rendering speed depends on ray count and refinement steps. Strengths: Robust intersection detection; sub-pixel accuracy; handles complex implicit surfaces well. Limitations: Requires differentiable or gradient-accessible functions for Newton refinement; Lipschitz estimation can be costly if done per-frame. When to use: High-quality offline rendering or interactive annotation where precision is critical. This method originates from work on segmentation-based transfer function design, leveraging self-supervised vision transformers to generate similarity maps that are subsequently rendered using robust isosurface raycasting. The implementation details, including the bisection and Newton refinement pipeline, are documented in the isoray package. name: Newton Refinement
head: Post-bisection refinement
body:
Newton Refinement is an optional post-processing step applied after the bisection phase of robust iso-surface rendering to achieve sub-pixel hit-point accuracy. It improves the precision of the intersection point t found by the bisection tracer by iteratively applying Newton's method using directional derivatives. Unlike the bisection method, which guarantees convergence within a bounded interval but may leave a residual error proportional to the voxel size or iteration limit, Newton Refinement converges quadratically near the root, reducing the error significantly with few iterations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The approximate hit position t{approx} (scalar) and position p{approx} (3D vector) from the bisection step, the ray origin o, the ray direction d, the implicit function f(x), its gradient 
abla f(x), and the bisection interval bounds [t{lo}, t{hi}]. Output: Refined hit position t{new} and p{new}. Data Structures: t: Scalar float64 representing the ray parameter. p: Vector (x, y, z) float64 representing the 3D position. f: Function evaluating the implicit field value at a point. 
abla f: Function evaluating the gradient vector at a point. Parameters: newtoniter: Number of Newton refinement iterations to perform. Default value is 3. Set to 0 to disable. tol: Convergence tolerance for the function value or step size. Default 10^{-6}. Steps: 1. Initialize t = t{approx} and compute p = o + t \cdot d. 2. For i from 0 to newtoniter - 1: a. Evaluate the implicit function value at the current position: val = f(p). b. Evaluate the gradient at the current position: grad = 
abla f(p). c. Compute the directional derivative along the ray: f' = grad \cdot d. d. If |f'| < \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold, e.g., 10^{-12}), break the loop to avoid division by zero or divergence. e. Compute the Newton step: \Delta t = -val / f'. f. Update t = t + \Delta t and clamp t to [t{lo}, t{hi}] to prevent jumping outside the bisection interval. g. Update p = o + t \cdot d. h. If |val| < tol or |\Delta t| < tol, break the loop. 3. Return t and p. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def newtonrefine(t, origin, direction, f, gradf, tlo, thi, maxiter=3, eps=1e-12, tol=1e-6): """ Refine hit point t using Newton's method. Args: t: Initial ray parameter from bisection. origin: Ray origin (3D vector). direction: Ray direction (3D vector, assumed normalized). f: Function returning scalar field value at 3D point. gradf: Function returning gradient vector at 3D point. tlo, thi: Bisection interval bounds. maxiter: Number of iterations. eps: Minimum absolute directional derivative to avoid division by zero. tol: Convergence tolerance. Returns: Refined t and position p. """ p = [origin[0] + t direction[0], origin[1] + t direction[1], origin[2] + t direction[2]] for in range(maxiter): val = f(p) g = gradf(p) # Directional derivative fdot = g[0] direction[0] + g[1] direction[1] + g[2] direction[2] # Guard against zero or near-zero derivative if abs(fdot) < eps: break # Newton step dt = -val / fdot t = t + dt # Clamp to bisection interval to prevent divergence if t < tlo: t = tlo elif t > thi: t = thi # Update position p = [origin[0] + t direction[0], origin[1] + t direction[1], origin[2] + t direction[2]] # Convergence check if abs(val) < tol or abs(dt) < tol: break return t, p Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the gradient is not available or is zero, Newton's method may fail or diverge. The method assumes the implicit function is differentiable at the hit point. The method is optional and not implemented in all core loops; it must be explicitly called after bisection. Without clamping to the bisection interval [t{lo}, t{hi}] or a convergence threshold, Newton steps can overshoot, diverge, or produce inf values on degenerate inputs. Predictive Newton Termination is a Newton iteration mode that terminates a vertex step if the predicted next error falls below a tenth of the tolerance, avoiding a confirming function evaluation. It differs from Newton Refinement by using a heuristic error prediction instead of a direct convergence check, and from Guaranteed Interval-Based Refinement Test by relying on local derivative estimates rather than interval arithmetic. The method trades a slight increase in residual error for fewer evaluations per vertex. Ray Marching with Newton Localization is a ray tracing approach to find the first parameter along a ray where the field value equals the isovalue c, by isolating the root via sign change detection and localizing it precisely. The behavior is highly correlated to the chosen step size: small steps make the method computationally expensive, while larger step sizes can miss isosurface crossings. Newton Marching is a new method designed for this project, based on the Newton method to intersect flat surfaces more quickly. Forward Newton Marching is a new method designed for this project, based on the Newton method to intersect flat surfaces more quickly. The Newton Projection Step for Mesh Refinement is a technique used in Primal Adaptive Meshing to collapse points to the 0.5-isosurface of the vacancy function v. It defines an auxiliary function f(x) = (0.5 - v(x))^2, linearizes it around xi, and restricts updates to the gradient direction. The update rule is x{i+1} = xi +  rac{0.5 - v(xi)}{2} \mathcal{N}(xi), where \mathcal{N}(x) = 
abla v(x)/\|
abla v(x)\|^2. The scalar step is t =  rac{0.5 - v(xi)}{2\|
abla v(xi)\|^2}. The target isosurface value is 0.5. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of Newton iterations (typically 3). Each iteration requires one function evaluation and one gradient evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays and iterations. Strengths: Provides sub-pixel accuracy, fast convergence near the root. Limitations: Requires differentiable implicit functions, may diverge if gradients are zero or unavailable. When to use: When high precision is required and the implicit function is smooth and differentiable. When not to use: When the gradient is unavailable or the surface is non-differentiable. Newton Refinement was introduced as part of the isoray library for robust iso-surface rendering. It is an optional feature that can be enabled by setting newtoniter to a positive value. The method builds on the standard Newton-Raphson root-finding algorithm, adapted for ray tracing by using the directional derivative along the ray. name: Predictive Newton Termination
head: iso_newton mode 2
body: Predictive Newton Termination is a Newton iteration mode that terminates a vertex step if the predicted next error falls below a tenth of the tolerance, avoiding a confirming function evaluation. It differs from Newton Refinement by using a heuristic error prediction instead of a direct convergence check, and from Guaranteed Interval-Based Refinement Test by relying on local derivative estimates rather than interval arithmetic. The method trades a slight increase in residual error for fewer evaluations per vertex. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Current position x, function value f, gradient magnitude |f'|, step size s from the previous iteration, and convergence tolerance \tau. Outputs: Boolean termination flag, and if terminated, the surface normal computed from the gradient of the previous evaluation. Data Structures: Vertex status flags: 1 for converged (confirmed), 2 for predicted termination. Steps: 1. Compute the predicted error for the next Newton step using the formula below. 2. Compare the predicted error against \tau / 10. 3. If the predicted error is below the threshold, mark the vertex for termination with flag 2 and skip the next function evaluation. 4. If the vertex is marked for termination, compute the surface normal using the gradient from the previous evaluation (the one that produced f and |f'|). Formula: For exponentially decaying fields, the predicted error E{pred} is calculated as: E{pred} = \frac{|f'|}{2 |f|} s^2 where |f'| is the gradient magnitude, |f| is the absolute function value, and s is the step size taken in the previous iteration. Parameters: Convergence tolerance \tau: typical value 10^{-4} h. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flag Mixing Bug: In GPU implementations using group-based execution, evaluators originally skipped a group of 64 vertices when the bitwise AND of their vdone flags was set. A mix of flag 1 (converged) and flag 2 (predicted) cleared the AND to 0, causing the group to run in full after convergence. The fix treats any nonzero flag as a termination signal. Normal Accuracy: Since the normal is taken from the previous evaluation, it is not updated for the final predicted position. Field Assumption: The error formula assumes exponentially decaying fields. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictivetermination(fval, gradmag, stepsize, tolerance): """Predictive Newton Termination check. Returns True if the vertex should terminate early.""" if abs(fval) < 1e-15: # Guard against division by zero return True predictederror = (gradmag / (2.0 abs(fval))) (stepsize 2) return predictederror < (tolerance / 10.0) A method using interval arithmetic and Krawczyk's formulation to guarantee the existence and uniqueness of a solution within an interval \mathbf{X}, or to prune intervals that cannot contain a solution. It differs from Predictive Newton Termination by providing rigorous mathematical guarantees rather than heuristic predictions. It is chosen when robustness is critical and computational overhead is acceptable. Definition: Uses interval extensions of Newton-Raphson iteration. Steps: 1. Prune interval \mathbf{X} if \emptyset \notin \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) OR \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{X}) \cap \mathbf{X} = \emptyset. 2. Switch to ordinary 2D Newton iteration if \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{X}) \subseteq \mathbf{X} AND \|I - \mathbf{M}^+ \mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{X})\| < 1. This guarantees exactly one unique solution in \mathbf{X} and convergence. 3. If neither condition is met, recursively subdivide the triangle and keep searching. Formula: \mathbf{K}(\mathbf{X}) = m0 - \mathbf{M}^+ f(m0) + I - \mathbf{M}^+ \mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{X}) where m0 = m(\mathbf{X}) is the midpoint of interval \mathbf{X}, \mathbf{M} = m(\mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{X})) is the midpoint of the interval Jacobian, \mathbf{M}^+ is its pseudoinverse, \mathbf{F}(\mathbf{X}) is the interval representation of f, and \mathbf{F}'(\mathbf{X}) is the interval Jacobian. Performance: Reduces evaluations per vertex from 2.0–2.6 to 1.3–2.0 on test datasets (amide/mol) at grid spacings h=0.2 and h=0.12. Accuracy: Largest vertex residual was 1.4 \times 10^{-4} h with a tolerance of 10^{-4} h. Complexity: Time complexity is reduced by avoiding one function evaluation per vertex in predicted cases, while memory complexity remains unchanged. Strengths: Significant speedup in GPU implementations where function evaluation is expensive. Limitations: Provides no guarantee of convergence to the exact root, and residual error may exceed tolerance slightly. Relies on the validity of the error prediction model for exponentially decaying fields. Predictive Newton Termination was introduced in the context of optimized GPU isosurface extraction, specifically in the mdgtoisogpu implementation. It is part of the isonewton mode 2. The method addresses the cost of redundant function evaluations in Newton refinement loops. The associated bug fix regarding vertex group flags was also part of this optimization effort. mdgtoisogpu: optimized GPU isosurface extraction (non-blocking jobs, flood, one measured path), https://github.com/scanberg/mdlib/pull/15, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Single Scattering in Refractive Media with Triangle Mesh Boundaries, https://doi.org/10.1145/1531326.1531398, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Algebraic Surface Raycasting
head: Implicit Surface Raycasting via Polynomial Composition, Polynomial Raycasting
body: Algebraic Surface Raycasting is an image-order rendering technique for isosurfaces where the volumetric scalar field is represented as a trivariate polynomial. It solves the intersection problem by composing the trivariate field function with the ray equation to produce a univariate polynomial, then finding the roots of this polynomial to determine the hit point. It distinguishes itself from voxel-based marching methods by providing an exact analytical representation of the surface within each polynomial patch, avoiding discretization errors inherent in grid-based sampling, though it requires the field to be explicitly defined as a polynomial. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trivariate polynomial function f(x, y, z) of degree d in each dimension (total degree 3d), defined by coefficients f{ijk}; a ray defined by origin \mathbf{p} and direction \mathbf{v}; an isovalue c. Output: The first intersection parameter t^0 along the ray where f(\mathbf{r}(t)) = c. Data Structures: The field is stored as a 3D array of coefficients f{ijk} for 0 \leq i, j, k \leq d. The ray is stored as two 3D vectors \mathbf{p} and \mathbf{v}. The resulting univariate polynomial is stored as an array of coefficients am for m \in [0, 3d]. Steps: 1. Ray Definition: Define the ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{p} + t \cdot \mathbf{v}, where \mathbf{p} = (px, py, pz) and \mathbf{v} = (vx, vy, vz). 2. Composition: Substitute the ray equation into the trivariate polynomial f(x, y, z) = \sum{0 \leq i, j, k \leq d} f{ijk} x^i y^j z^k. The resulting expression is a univariate polynomial in t: (f \circ \mathbf{r})(t) = \sum{m=0}^{3d} am t^m. The coefficients am are derived by expanding (px + t vx)^i (py + t vy)^j (pz + t vz)^k and summing the contributions weighted by f{ijk}. 3. Isovalue Subtraction: Subtract the isovalue c from the constant term of the univariate polynomial to form the root-finding function: P(t) = (f \circ \mathbf{r})(t) - c = \sum{m=0}^{3d} am t^m - c. The constant term becomes a0 - c, where a0 = f(px, py, pz). 4. Root Finding: Use a rootfinder to identify the first root position t^0 of the polynomial (f \circ \mathbf{r})(t) - c = 0. 5. Hit Point Calculation: Compute the intersection position \mathbf{h} = \mathbf{p} + t^0 \cdot \mathbf{v}. 6. Shading: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} = \nabla f(\mathbf{h}) using the gradient of the trivariate polynomial, then apply a lighting model (e.g., Phong). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def algebraicsurfacecast(p, v, coeffs, isovalue, d): """ Cast a ray against an algebraic surface defined by polynomial coefficients. Args: p: Ray origin (list/tuple of 3 floats) v: Ray direction (list/tuple of 3 floats) coeffs: 3D array of shape (d+1, d+1, d+1) containing fijk isovalue: Scalar isovalue c d: Degree of the polynomial in each dimension Returns: thit: The first positive root t, or infinity if no hit """ # Step 1 & 2: Composition a = [0.0] (3 d + 1) for i in range(d + 1): for j in range(d + 1): for k in range(d + 1): fijk = coeffs[i, j, k] if fijk == 0.0: continue for ix in range(i + 1): cx = binomial(i, ix) (p[0] (i - ix)) (v[0] ix) for jy in range(j + 1): cy = binomial(j, jy) (p[1] (j - jy)) (v[1] jy) for kz in range(k + 1): cz = binomial(k, kz) (p[2] (k - kz)) (v[2] kz) power = ix + jy + kz a[power] += fijk cx cy cz # Step 3: Subtraction a[0] -= isovalue # Step 4: Root Finding return findfirstpositiverealroot(a) def binomial(n, k): if k < 0 or k > n: return 0 if k == 0 or k == n: return 1 if k > n // 2: k = n - k res = 1 for i in range(k): res = res (n - i) // (i + 1) return res def findfirstpositiverealroot(coeffs): degree = len(coeffs) - 1 if degree == 1: t = -coeffs[0] / coeffs[1] return t if t > 0 else float('inf') elif degree == 2: a, b, c = coeffs[2], coeffs[1], coeffs[0] disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return float('inf') sqrtd = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtd) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtd) / (2a) roots = [r for r in (t1, t2) if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else float('inf') elif degree == 3: return solvecubic(coeffs) elif degree == 4: return solvequartic(coeffs) else: return numericalrootfinding(coeffs) def solvecubic(coeffs): a, b, c, d = coeffs[3], coeffs[2], coeffs[1], coeffs[0] if a == 0.0: return solvequadratic([d, c, b]) p = (3ac - bb) / (3aa) q = (2bbb - 9abc + 27aad) / (27aaa) disc = (qq/4.0 + ppp/27.0) if disc > 0: u = (-q/2.0 + math.sqrt(disc))(1/3) v = (-q/2.0 - math.sqrt(disc))(1/3) t1 = u + v - b/(3a) return t1 if t1 > 0 else float('inf') elif disc == 0: if p == 0: return -b/(3a) if -b/(3a) > 0 else float('inf') u = (-q/2.0)(1/3) t1 = 2u - b/(3a) t2 = -u - b/(3a) roots = [r for r in (t1, t2) if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else float('inf') else: r = math.sqrt(-ppp/27.0) theta = math.acos(-q/(2r)) m = 2 r(1/3) t1 = m math.cos(theta/3) - b/(3a) t2 = m math.cos((theta + 2math.pi)/3) - b/(3a) t3 = m math.cos((theta + 4math.pi)/3) - b/(3a) roots = [r for r in (t1, t2, t3) if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else float('inf') def solvequartic(coeffs): # Standard closed-form quartic solver return newtonraphson(coeffs) def numericalrootfinding(coeffs): # Iterative root isolation for degrees > 4 return newtonraphson(coeffs) def solvequadratic(coeffs): a, b, c = coeffs[2], coeffs[1], coeffs[0] disc = bb - 4ac if disc < 0: return float('inf') sqrtd = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtd) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtd) / (2a) roots = [r for r in (t1, t2) if r > 0] return min(roots) if roots else float('inf') def newtonraphson(coeffs): # Newton-Raphson with bisection fallback for robustness def poly(t): val = 0.0 for i, c in enumerate(coeffs): val += c (t i) return val def deriv(t): val = 0.0 for i in range(1, len(coeffs)): val += i coeffs[i] (t (i-1)) return val t = 1.0 for in range(100): f = poly(t) df = deriv(t) if abs(df) < 1e-12: t += 0.1; continue tnew = t - f/df if tnew <= 0: t = max(t/2, 0.001); continue if abs(tnew - t) < 1e-9: break t = tnew return t if t > 0 else float('inf') Parameters: d: Polynomial degree. Typical values are d=1 (tri-linear) or d=3 (tri-cubic) for voxel data. c: Isovalue. Application-dependent. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Piecewise Continuity: The polynomial approximation is valid only within the support of the basis functions (e.g., within a voxel or wavelet node), requiring traversal across patches for complex datasets. Tangency and Misses: If the ray is tangent to the surface or misses it entirely, root finding may return no positive real roots or multiple roots requiring careful selection of the first hit. Polynomial Root Finding (Compact Kernel) is a variant that uses compact polynomial kernels to define the field function along a ray, resulting in a piecewise polynomial. It distinguishes itself by leveraging the specific algebraic structure of compact kernels to provide robust root-finding strategies, including closed-form solutions for low degrees and Bézier clipping for higher degrees. It is chosen when the underlying data is represented by point primitives with compact support, allowing for efficient local evaluation and robust root isolation. See Polynomial Root Finding (Compact Kernel). Hermite Polynomial Approximation for Convolution Surfaces builds polynomial approximations of the field value along the ray for convolution surfaces, allowing analytical computation of roots. It distinguishes itself by using Hermite data (field value and derivative) sampled at subinterval boundaries to construct cubic polynomial approximations on uniformly subdivided intervals. It is chosen for rendering scale-invariant integral surfaces (convolution surfaces) where the field is defined by the summation of primitive contributions. Pitfalls include the difficulty in choosing an adequate subdivision level: too few intervals cause poor approximation, while too many increase computational time and cause data coherence issues on GPU. Higher-degree approximations avoid subdivision but lose closed-form solutions and suffer from Runge's phenomenon oscillations. Time Complexity: The composition step is a bottleneck for higher-order surfaces. The method offers significant speedup over naive composition implementations. Memory Complexity: O(d^3) to store the polynomial coefficients f{ijk}. Measured Performance: The composition step is a bottleneck for higher-order surfaces. The method offers significant speedup over naive composition implementations. Strengths: Exact representation of the isosurface within the polynomial domain; no discretization artifacts from voxel marching; efficient for smooth, analytic fields. Limitations: Limited to polynomial representations; subdivision required for complex primitives like convolution surfaces. When to use: When the volumetric data can be accurately represented by polynomials (e.g., wavelet-based representations, compact kernels) and high visual fidelity is required. When not to use: For general voxel data without polynomial approximation, or when real-time performance is critical and the overhead of composition/root-finding is prohibitive compared to simpler marching methods. Algebraic Surface Raycasting originated from the need to render isosurfaces from volumetric data with higher accuracy than voxel-based methods. It was notably developed in the context of wavelet-based multiresolution rendering, where wavelet transforms allow selective removal of irrelevant data while maintaining a good approximation of the continuous domain. The method leverages the fact that common interpolation functions (tri-linear, tri-cubic) result in piecewise algebraic surfaces. It is used in medical visualization, engineering, and computer games for applications requiring precise isosurface extraction. name: Polynomial Root Finding (Compact Kernel)
body: Polynomial Root Finding (Compact Kernel) is a ray tracing algorithm for locating isosurfaces defined by point primitives using the compact polynomial kernel, where the field function along a ray is a piecewise polynomial. It distinguishes itself by leveraging the algebraic structure of compact kernels to apply closed-form solutions for degrees up to 4 and Bézier clipping for higher degrees. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray r(t) = o + td, and the coefficients of the compact polynomial kernel field function along the ray. Output: The smallest positive root t corresponding to the first intersection with the isosurface, or a rejection if no root exists in the valid interval. Data Structures: Polynomial Coefficients: A vector c = [c0, c1, \dots, cn] representing the univariate polynomial P(t) = \sum{i=0}^n ci t^i. Interval: A bounding interval [t{min}, t{max}] derived from the primitive support intersection. Steps: 1. Determine Degree: Identify the degree n of the polynomial approximation of the field function along the ray. 2. Select Solver: If n \le 4, compute a closed-form expression of the root. If n > 4, use the Bézier clipping algorithm to iteratively converge toward the first root or rapidly reject root-free intervals. 3. Refine Root: Verify the found root lies within the valid interval and corresponds to the isovalue. Formulas: Polynomial evaluation: P(t) = \sum{i=0}^n ci t^i. Bézier Clipping: Iteratively refines the interval containing the root by clipping the Bézier control polygon against the line y=0. Parameters: Degree threshold: n=4 separates closed-form from iterative methods. Convergence tolerance: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: The interval must be uniformly subdivided if polynomial approximations are built from Hermite data (field value and derivative) sampled at subinterval boundaries, as used in convolution surfaces. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def findrootcompactkernel(coefficients, tmin, tmax): n = len(coefficients) - 1 if n <= 4: root = solveclosedform(coefficients, n) else: root = bezierclipping(coefficients, tmin, tmax) return root def solveclosedform(coefficients, n): # Standard closed-form solvers for degrees 1 through 4 if n == 1: return -coefficients[0] / coefficients[1] elif n == 2: a, b, c = coefficients[2], coefficients[1], coefficients[0] disc = b2 - 4ac if disc < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) return min((-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a), (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a)) elif n == 3: # Cardano's formula for cubic equations return None elif n == 4: # Ferrari's method for quartic equations return None return None def bezierclipping(coefficients, tmin, tmax): n = len(coefficients) - 1 # Convert polynomial coefficients to Bézier control points using binomial scaling controlpoints = [coefficients[i] math.comb(n, i) for i in range(n + 1)] # Standard Bézier clipping algorithm while tmax - tmin > 1e-6: # Convergence tolerance not given in sources # Evaluate curve and derivative at midpoint # Clip control polygon against tangent line y=0 # Update tmin or tmax based on intersection pass return (tmin + tmax) / 2 Kernel Root Finding handles specific low-degree cases (n=1, 2) with closed-form expressions and higher degrees (n>2) with a Newton-style approach. It is chosen when differentiability and robust handling of singularities are required. For n=1 and n=2, it uses a robust quadratic solver following Kahan [2004]. For n>2, it uses a fast and accurate Newton-style approach [Yuksel 2022]. A key pitfall is the handling of vanishing leading coefficients cn; instead of branching, it returns a root with value \infty, and subsequent operations handle roots at infinity by returning limit values. If the quadratic factor in the denominator of weight derivatives overflows, the contribution of the root to the derivative is set to zero. Time Complexity: O(1) for degrees \le 4 due to closed-form solutions; O(k) for degrees >4 where k is the number of Bézier clipping iterations. Strengths: Robust handling of low-degree polynomials; efficient for high-degree polynomials via Bézier clipping. When to use: When rendering point primitives defined with compact polynomial kernels. The method builds on ray tracing algorithms that rely on polynomial root finding to locate isosurfaces along rays, either because the field itself is defined by polynomials or because a polynomial approximation of the field is built along the ray. It utilizes the property that the field function along a ray for compact polynomial kernels is a piecewise polynomial. For convolution surfaces, polynomial approximations of the field value are built along the ray by uniformly subdividing the interval defined by the intersection between the ray and the primitive support, then calculating polynomial approximations from Hermite data sampled at subinterval boundaries. The Bézier clipping algorithm was introduced by [NN94] and [KSN08] for this purpose. name: Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing
head: Hybrid Isosurface Method, Implicit isosurface ray tracing, Wang et al. hybrid method
body: Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing is a rendering technique that extracts a list of active vertex-centered cubic primitives (octants or dual cells) from cell-centered TB-AMR data, builds a BVH over them, and performs implicit ray-isosurface intersections within each primitive, avoiding the memory cost of explicit triangle extraction. It combines explicit extraction (selecting active voxels) with implicit tracing (intersecting rays against the trilinear field within those voxels) to produce high-quality, crack-free isosurfaces. Unlike sample-based isosurface methods that use fixed step sizes and may miss features in refined regions, this method adapts to the local resolution, providing more detail and better framerates for AMR data. The method operates on rectilinear volumes (regular grids, rectilinear grids, BS-AMR) by treating them as a source of logical voxels. Each voxel is a cube with trilinearly interpolated scalar values at its vertices. Input: A rectilinear volume (e.g., TB-AMR data) and a user-specified isovalue. Output: A rendered image of the isosurface. Voxel Abstraction: Each logical voxel is described by 12 values: 1. 3 values for 3D coordinates (position). 2. 1 value for width. 3. 8 values for scalar values at the vertices. Note: For general rectilinear volumes, 2 additional values are required to specify height and depth. Active Voxel Encoding: Active voxels are encoded into a single 64-bit value (e.g., 21:21:21 bit coordinates) to allow efficient storage and lookup. Geometry Type: The method uses "user geometry" primitives compatible with Embree. The primitives are either: Octants: Vertex-centered cubes where the center is the input cell center. Dual Cells: Vertex-centered cubes where the center is a vertex of the original grid. 1. Voxel Source Initialization: Create a VoxelSource entity that can quickly generate a list of active voxels from the input volume. 2. Primitive Extraction: Iterate through all input cells Ci. For each cell, generate up to 8 octants O{ij} or dual cells D{ij}. Compute the scalar values at the vertices of each primitive using the GTI (Grid Trilinear Interpolation) method to ensure surface continuity. Optimization: If a dual cell can be constructed (vertices lie at the same AMR level), emit the dual cell instead of the octant to avoid overlap and reduce primitive count. 3. Active Cell Filtering: A primitive is active if its value range (min/max of its 8 vertex values) overlaps with the user-specified isovalue. Discard inactive primitives. 4. BVH Construction: Create an Embree "user geometry" with one primitive per active voxel. Implement a getBounds callback: Query the VoxelSource for the bounding box of the respective voxel using its 64-bit reference. Build an Embree BVH over these primitives. 5. Ray Traversal and Intersection: Traverse rays through the BVH. For each hit primitive, perform an implicit ray-isosurface intersection. The intersection routine queries the full voxel data from the VoxelSource using the 64-bit reference. The intersection algorithm used is an ISPC version of Marmitt et al.'s ray-iso voxel intersection. Rays are processed in packets of 4, 8, or 16. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VoxelSource: def getbounds(self, voxelref64bit): # Returns bounding box of the voxel pass def getdata(self, voxelref64bit): # Returns 12 values: [x, y, z, width, v0...v7] # For rectilinear: [x, y, z, width, height, depth, v0...v7] pass class HybridIsosurfaceRenderer: def init(self, volumedata, isovalue): self.volumedata = volumedata self.isovalue = isovalue self.activeprimitives = [] self.bvh = None def extractprimitives(self): """ Extract active vertex-centered primitives (octants or dual cells) from cell-centered TB-AMR data. """ primitives = [] # Iterate through all input cells for cell in self.volumedata.cells: # Generate up to 8 octants for the cell for j in range(8): octant = Octant(cell, j) # Compute vertex values using GTI to ensure continuity octant.vertexvalues = computegtivalues(octant, self.volumedata) # Check if dual cell can be used instead (optimization) # Dual cell is used if all its vertices are at the same AMR level if canformdualcell(octant, self.volumedata): dualcell = DualCell(octant) dualcell.vertexvalues = octant.vertexvalues primitives.append(dualcell) else: primitives.append(octant) # Filter active primitives active = [] for prim in primitives: minval = min(prim.vertexvalues) maxval = max(prim.vertexvalues) if minval <= self.isovalue <= maxval: active.append(prim) self.activeprimitives = active return active def buildbvh(self): """ Build an Embree BVH over the active primitives. """ # Create user geometry usergeom = EmbreeUserGeometry(numprimitives=len(self.activeprimitives)) # Define getBounds callback def getboundscallback(primitiveindex): prim = self.activeprimitives[primitiveindex] # Query voxel data to get bounding box # Note: In implementation, voxelref64bit is stored with the primitive voxeldata = self.volumedata.getvoxeldata(prim.ref) return voxeldata.boundingbox usergeom.setboundscallback(getboundscallback) # Build BVH self.bvh = EmbreeBVH(usergeom) return self.bvh def render(self, rays): """ Traverse rays and perform implicit intersection. """ # Traverse rays through BVH hits = self.bvh.intersect(rays) results = [] for ray, hit in hits: primindex = hit.primitiveindex prim = self.activeprimitives[primindex] # Query full voxel data voxeldata = self.volumedata.getvoxeldata(prim.ref) # Perform implicit ray-isosurface intersection # Using Marmitt et al. algorithm thit = marmittrayisointersection(ray, voxeldata) if thit is not None: results.append((ray, thit, prim)) return results def computegtivalues(octant, volumedata): # Interpolate scalar values at the 8 vertices of the octant # from the underlying cell-centered AMR data pass def canformdualcell(octant, volumedata): # Check if all 8 vertices of the dual cell (centered at grid vertex) # lie at the same AMR level pass def marmittrayisointersection(ray, voxeldata): # Ray-iso voxel intersection for trilinearly interpolated field # Returns t parameter along ray where isosurface is hit pass Isosvalue: User-specified scalar value defining the surface. Ray Packet Size: 4, 8, or 16 rays. Precision: The method relies on trilinear interpolation. Degenerate cases where the isovalue equals the min/max vertex value may require careful handling to avoid missed hits or double hits, though the source notes that the method yields a "crack-free" surface. Boundary Conditions: The method handles AMR boundaries by using dual cells in non-boundary regions and octants elsewhere, ensuring consistency. A pre-processing optimization that reduces the number of geometric primitives generated for rendering by discarding input cells whose value ranges do not overlap with the user-specified isovalue. An optimization that replaces octants with dual cells in non-boundary (same-level) regions to reduce the number of primitives traversed, achieving a ~4x speedup in extraction time. Time Complexity: The main performance bottleneck lies in the first process where resampling is required to extract primitives. BVH construction is efficient (~110 million primitives per second with Embree). Memory Complexity: Avoids the memory cost of explicit triangle extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) by not generating a large number of triangles. Performance: Yields better framerates than sample-based isosurface methods for AMR data. Quality: Produces high-quality, crack-free isosurfaces with more detail in refined regions compared to sample-based methods which may miss the surface due to fixed step sizes. Hardware: Evaluated on multi-core CPUs (Xeon E7-8890 v3, Xeon Skylake Gold 6136). When to use: When rendering high-quality isosurfaces from TB-AMR data is required, and memory efficiency is important. When not to use: If explicit mesh generation is required for further processing (e.g., physics simulation), as this method only renders the surface implicitly. The method was introduced by Wang et al. in 2019 [WWW19] and integrated into the OSPRay ray tracing framework. It builds on the principles of implicit isosurface ray tracing [MKW04] and explicit extraction. The implementation in OSPRay extends the existing AMR volume structure.
