name: Ray Traversal and Coherency
body: This family accelerates isosurface extraction by optimizing the order and grouping of ray-volume interactions to minimize redundant traversal and intersection tests. It differs from naive uniform marching by using hierarchical acceleration structures (octrees, tiled grids) and spatial coherence (ray packets) to skip empty space and process multiple rays simultaneously. The family shares the core mechanism of Isosurface and first-hit ray casting: constructing a ray per pixel and finding the first point where f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau or a sign change occurs. Upon detection, the intersection is refined (e.g., linear interpolation) and shaded using \nabla f. The key distinction is the traversal strategy: instead of marching voxel-by-voxel, rays are accelerated by hierarchical culling using min-max bounds in octrees or tiled grids to skip sub-volumes where \tau \notin [\min, \max], coherence exploitation by grouping rays into packets to traverse the acceleration structure together, and list-based restriction by pre-computing a short, front-to-back list of candidate blocks or pixels for each ray. A technique using a min-max octree of macro-cells (n^3 cells, n \in [3,10]) to accelerate iso-surface extraction. It sets itself apart by projecting trimmed macro-cells to the screen and casting local rays only at uncolored pixels, avoiding empty space traversal. Choose it when interactive threshold adjustment is needed without dedicated acceleration hardware, and when macro-cell culling effectively skips empty space. A two-phase method combining object-order traversal with restricted ray casting on multi-core processors. It sets itself apart by decoupling candidate block identification from ray casting execution, using dynamic task allocation to solve load-balancing and memory hierarchy overhead problems. Choose it when rendering on multi-core CPUs and static screen partitioning causes uneven workloads. A two-phase algorithm for rendering isosurfaces on multi-core processors using a BONO tree for hierarchical culling and list-based restriction. It sets itself apart by maintaining a short, front-to-back ordered list of candidate blocks per pixel, achieving coherence and efficiency without SIMD instruction-level parallelism dependencies. Choose it when high-resolution rendering is needed on multi-core CPUs without relying on dedicated hardware or surface fitting techniques. A method for interactive isosurface extraction from large volumetric datasets stored in octrees. It sets itself apart by grouping neighboring rays into 2x2 packets to exploit spatial coherence during traversal and intersection, dynamically switching to coarser levels of detail (LOD). Choose it when rendering large volumes on commodity CPUs where spatial coherence can be maintained via ray packets and multiresolution structures. A ray traversal method that extracts iso-surfaces by recording the first scalar intensity encountered along a viewing ray. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or Accumulate compositing by its immediate termination upon the first hit. Choose it when isolating high-density or specific threshold structures without contribution from deeper volumes is required. The "First Depth" or "First Intensity" traversal strategy was introduced by Tuy and Tuy in 1984 to extract isosurfaces. This approach contrasts with accumulation-based methods (like Levoy’s 1988 compositing) by stopping at the first surface hit. Modern implementations leverage octrees and ray coherence to make this interactive on large datasets. name: Cell-Based First-Hit Ray Casting
body: Cell-based first-hit ray casting is a volume rendering technique that accelerates iso-surface extraction by dividing the volume into cubic sub-volumes called macro-cells. It solves the performance bottleneck of conventional ray casting by avoiding empty space traversal and reducing the average ray path length to only a few steps per pixel. It sets itself apart from its siblings by using a min-max octree to cull macro-cells and projecting only those containing iso-surface portions to the screen, where local rays are cast. Unlike Hybrid Strategy for Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing or Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing, it does not rely on dedicated acceleration hardware or surface fitting techniques that lack interactive threshold adjustment. Inputs: Volume data V with dimensions Dx \times Dy \times Dz. One or more iso-value thresholds \tau. Camera parameters (eye position, view direction, projection matrix). Macro-cell dimension parameter n (typically 4–10). Outputs: Color image buffer C of resolution W \times H. A per-pixel hit flag to prevent re-rendering pixels that have already found an intersection. Data Structures: 1. Min-Max Octree: Each node stores minval and maxval representing the minimum and maximum data values in the sub-volume it covers. Leaf nodes represent macro-cells. A macro-cell consists of n^3 data cells (defined by (n+1)^3 voxel grid points). 2. Ray History Buffer: Stores cells encountered along the last ray and a flag indicating if an iso-surface portion is contained there. This exploits inter-ray coherency to skip intersection tests for rays visiting the same cells. 3. Pixel Hit Flags: Boolean array of size W \times H. If the flag for a pixel is true, no more local rays are cast at this pixel. Algorithm Steps: 1. Build Min-Max Octree: Recursively subdivide the volume. For each node, compute minval and maxval of the contained data. Leaf nodes correspond to macro-cells of size n \times n \times n cells. 2. Traverse Octree in Viewing Order: Start at the root. For a current node, check if any threshold \tau satisfies: \text{min\val} \le \tau \le \text{max\val}. If the condition fails, cull the entire subtree. If the condition passes, sort the 8 child nodes based on the viewing vector to ensure correct front-to-back processing order. This is done using a representative ray direction that intersects all sub-volumes. Recursively process children. 3. Process Leaf Nodes (Macro-Cells): When a leaf node (macro-cell) is reached, it contains potential iso-surface portions. Trimming: Trim the macro-cell to the smallest cuboid containing the portions of the iso-surfaces. Projection: Project the trimmed macro-cell onto the screen plane. Rasterization: Rasterize the projection to identify all pixels (x, y) covered by the macro-cell. 4. Cast Local Rays: For each covered pixel (x, y): If the pixel hit flag is true, skip this pixel. Construct a local ray originating from the camera eye, passing through (x, y), and clipped to the entry and exit points of the macro-cell. Early Scanline Termination (Optional Optimization): If the pixel is likely to not find an intersection, skip the ray cast to save time. Voxel Traversal: Use a fast voxel traversal algorithm (e.g., Amanatides and Woo) to iterate through cells pierced by the local ray within the macro-cell. Boundary Check: For each cell, determine if it is a "boundary cell" (contains data values both above and below \tau). Intersection Test: If a boundary cell is found, perform a ray-surface intersection test. Fast Intersection Method: Divide the ray segment through the cell into two equal parts. Evaluate density at endpoints. If signs differ, linearly interpolate the intersection point. Exact Intersection Method (Alternative): Invert trilinear interpolation to find exact intersection points. Shading: If an intersection is found: Calculate the gradient \nabla f at the intersection point using trilinear interpolation of the gradient components. Compute color using shading model (e.g., Phong). Assign color to C[y][x]. Set the pixel hit flag to true. Coherency Check: Use the Ray History Buffer to skip intersection tests if the current ray visits the same cells as the previous ray and the buffer indicates no surface was found. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cellbasedfirsthitraycasting(volume, thresholds, camera, n, width, height): # 1. Build Min-Max Octree (standard recursive subdivision) octree = buildoctree(volume, n) # 2. Initialize Output Structures colorbuffer = [[None] width for in range(height)] hitflags = [[False] width for in range(height)] rayhistorybuffer = {} # Maps cellid -> hassurface (bool) # 3. Traverse Octree traversenode(octree, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height) return colorbuffer def buildoctree(volume, n): # Standard recursive subdivision into cubic blocks # Returns tree nodes with.minval,.maxval,.children,.isleaf,.bounds pass # Implementation details omitted as standard def traversenode(node, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height): # Culling: Check if any threshold is within node's min/max range cull = True for tau in thresholds: if node.minval <= tau <= node.maxval: cull = False break if cull: return # If leaf node (macro-cell) if node.isleaf: processmacrocell(node, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height) return # Internal node: Sort children by viewing order # Use representative ray direction to determine order children = sorted(node.children, key=lambda child: dotproduct(vectorsub(child.center, camera.eye), camera.direction)) for child in children: traversenode(child, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height) def processmacrocell(node, camera, thresholds, colorbuffer, hitflags, rayhistorybuffer, n, width, height): # 1. Trim macro-cell to smallest cuboid containing iso-surfaces trimmedcuboid = computetrimmedcuboid(node.bounds, thresholds) # 2. Project trimmed cuboid to screen screenrect = projectcuboidtoscreen(trimmedcuboid, camera) # 3. Rasterize and cast local rays for y in range(screenrect.ymin, screenrect.ymax): for x in range(screenrect.xmin, screenrect.xmax): # Skip if pixel already hit if hitflags[y][x]: continue # Construct local ray clipped to macro-cell ray = createlocalray(camera, x, y, node.bounds) # 4. Voxel Traversal within macro-cell (Amanatides & Woo) cells = amanatideswootraversal(ray, node.bounds, n) intersectionfound = False for cell in cells: # Check coherency cellid = getcellid(cell, node.bounds) if cellid in rayhistorybuffer and not rayhistorybuffer[cellid]: continue # Skip intersection test based on history # Check if boundary cell if isboundarycell(cell, thresholds): # Perform intersection test hitpoint, hitnormal = fastraysurfaceintersection(ray, cell, thresholds) if hitpoint is not None: # Shading gradient = trilineargradient(cell, hitpoint) color = phongshading(hitpoint, hitnormal, gradient, camera) # Update output colorbuffer[y][x] = color hitflags[y][x] = True intersectionfound = True # Update history buffer for this cell rayhistorybuffer[cellid] = True break # First hit wins if not intersectionfound: # Mark cells visited in this ray as 'no surface' for coherency for cell in cells: cellid = getcellid(cell, node.bounds) if cellid not in rayhistorybuffer: rayhistorybuffer[cellid] = False def fastraysurfaceintersection(ray, cell, thresholds): # Fast intersection method: divide segment into two, check signs, interpolate p1 = ray.origin + ray.direction cell.entryt p2 = ray.origin + ray.direction cell.exitt d1 = trilinearsample(p1) d2 = trilinearsample(p2) for tau in thresholds: if (d1 - tau) (d2 - tau) < 0: # Linear interpolation t = cell.entryt + (tau - d1) / (d2 - d1) (cell.exitt - cell.entryt) hitpoint = ray.origin + ray.direction t hitnormal = trilineargradient(cell, hitpoint) return hitpoint, hitnormal return None, None def dotproduct(a, b): return a.xb.x + a.yb.y + a.zb.z def vectorsub(a, b): return (a.x-b.x, a.y-b.y, a.z-b.z) def computetrimmedcuboid(bounds, thresholds): return bounds # Exact cuboid logic def projectcuboidtoscreen(cuboid, camera): return {'ymin':0, 'ymax':1, 'xmin':0, 'xmax':1} # Standard projection def createlocalray(camera, x, y, bounds): return {'origin': camera.eye, 'direction': camera.direction, 'entryt': 0.0, 'exitt': 1.0} # Ray clipping def amanatideswootraversal(ray, bounds, n): return [{'entryt': 0.0, 'exitt': 1.0, 'coords': (0,0,0)}] # Standard traversal def getcellid(cell, bounds): return str(cell.coords) def isboundarycell(cell, thresholds): return True # Standard boundary check def trilinearsample(point): return 0.5 # Standard interpolation def trilineargradient(cell, point): return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Standard gradient def phongshading(point, normal, gradient, camera): return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Standard shading Parameters: n: Macro-cell dimension. Typical values: 3–10. Thresholds: Iso-values. Example: 0 HU (soft tissue) to 1100 HU (stent). Image Resolution: 512x512 in reported experiments. Pitfalls: Macro-cell Size: Small n increases octree traversal and projection overhead, splits rays into more segments, and increases expensive ray initialization steps for rays traveling along iso-surfaces without intersecting. Large n reduces early termination effectiveness because small critical regions are less likely to be detected. Viewing Order: Ray segments must be processed in correct viewing order to ensure the first intersection determines the final pixel color. Failure to sort child nodes by viewing vector causes visibility artifacts. Distance Coding: Not used because it would require recomputation for each new iso-value. Soft Tissue Occlusion: When low thresholds hide the surface of interest (e.g., soft tissue hiding a stent), conventional ray casting may be faster because ray-surface distances are short. Cell-based method suffers as almost all macro-cells must be processed and "peep holes" delay termination. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of macro-cells intersecting the iso-surface and the local ray path length. Significantly faster than conventional ray casting when higher thresholds hide soft tissue and reduce macro-cell processing. Measured Performance: Virtual angioscopy (stented aorta): Average frame time 1.291s vs 2.119s for conventional. 450 HU threshold (bones/stent): 1.953s vs 8.563s (4.38x speedup). 1100 HU threshold (stent only): 0.609s vs 12.781s (20.98x speedup). Ray Path Reduction: Reduces average steps per pixel from ~35.5 (conventional) to ~15.6 (cell-based), and further to ~3.9 with optimizations (trimming, early termination). Strengths: Short average ray path lengths; cache-coherent access (each macro-cell processed once); supports interactive threshold adjustment; no dedicated hardware required. Limitations: Performance degrades when low thresholds cause extensive macro-cell processing due to fine-structured tissue ("peep holes"); small macro-cells increase overhead; large macro-cells reduce culling efficiency. When to Use: Fast perspective iso-surfacing, virtual endoscopy, interactive threshold adjustment. When Not to Use: Low-resolution previews (use conventional ray casting or progressive rendering); scenarios with very low thresholds where soft tissue occludes the surface of interest. Origin: Proposed by André Neubauer, Lukas Mroz, H. Hauser, and R. Wegenkittl in 2002. Development: Developed as part of the AlVis project for visualization of high-resolution industrial CT data (aluminum foam) and tested for virtual angioscopy (stent placement assessment). Comparison: Contrasted with Surface Fitting techniques (e.g., Hietala et al.) which require dedicated hardware and lack interactive threshold adjustment. Contrasted with exact ray-surface intersection methods (Lin et al., Parker et al.) which are more accurate but computationally expensive; this method uses a faster, slightly less accurate approximation. name: Hybrid Strategy for Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing
head: Novel Hybrid Strategy, Object-order projection with restricted ray tracing
body: This method enables interactive isosurface rendering on multi-core processors by combining object-order traversal with restricted ray casting. It solves the load-balancing and memory hierarchy overhead problems inherent in static screen partitioning by dynamically allocating ray casting tasks to threads while maintaining spatial locality. Unlike sibling methods that may use static grids or purely image-order traversal, this approach explicitly decouples the identification of candidate data blocks from the ray casting execution, using a two-phase process to restrict the search space to a small, front-to-back list of blocks per pixel. The method operates in two distinct phases: an object-order identification phase and an image-order restricted ray casting phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset V partitioned into 3D tiles (data blocks). A viewing frustum defined by the camera position and orientation. An isosurface threshold \tau. Output: A rendered image where each pixel contains the color of the first isosurface intersection. Data Structures: 1. 3D-Tiled Dataset: The volume is divided into fixed-size 3D blocks. 2. Candidate Lists: For each pixel (or packet of pixels), a list of data blocks that are both visible and intersect the isosurface (\min(block) \le \tau \le \max(block)), ordered front-to-back relative to the viewpoint. Numbered Steps: 1. Phase I: Object-Order Identification 1. Partition the image screen into initial groups (e.g., packets of adjacent pixels). 2. Traverse the 3D-tiled dataset using the compact indexing structure. 3. Project the 3D blocks from object space onto the image space to determine visibility. 4. For each pixel/packet, identify blocks that intersect the isosurface. 5. Sort these blocks in front-to-back order relative to the viewpoint. 6. Store the resulting limited-size lists of candidate blocks for each pixel. 2. Phase II: Restricted Ray Casting 1. Dynamically allocate groups of ray casting tasks (pixels/packets) to available processor cores. This dynamic allocation ensures load balancing while preserving spatial locality by assigning adjacent pixels to the same thread when possible. 2. For each assigned pixel, retrieve its ordered list of candidate blocks. 3. Cast the primary ray through the candidate blocks in order. 4. Within each block, perform the standard isosurface ray casting (marching or traversal) to find the first intersection point where f(\mathbf{p}) \ge \tau. 5. Refine the intersection and shade the pixel. 6. If an intersection is found, terminate ray casting for that pixel; otherwise, continue to the next block in the list. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import threading def getray(camera, pixel): return camera.project(pixel) def renderpixel(pixel, color): image[pixel] = color def raycastblock(ray, block, threshold): # Standard isosurface traversal within a single block # Returns intersection point or None return None class TaskQueue: def init(self, tasks): self.tasks = list(tasks) self.lock = threading.Lock() def pop(self): with self.lock: if self.tasks: return self.tasks.pop() return None def worker(queue, candidatelists, threshold, image): while True: pixel = queue.pop() if pixel is None: break blocks = candidatelists[pixel] ray = getray(camera, pixel) hit = False for block in blocks: intersection = raycastblock(ray, block, threshold) if intersection is not None: renderpixel(pixel, intersection.color) hit = True break if not hit: renderpixel(pixel, backgroundcolor) def hybridisosurfacerendering(volumeblocks, camera, threshold, numthreads, image, backgroundcolor): # Phase I: Object-Order Identification candidatelists = {} pixels = [(x, y) for x in range(camera.width) for y in range(camera.height)] for pixel in pixels: ray = getray(camera, pixel) visibleblocks = [] for block in volumeblocks: if block.isvisible(ray) and block.intersectsisosurface(threshold): visibleblocks.append(block) visibleblocks.sort(key=lambda b: b.distancefromviewpoint(ray.origin)) candidatelists[pixel] = visibleblocks # Phase II: Restricted Ray Casting with Dynamic Allocation taskqueue = TaskQueue(pixels) threads = [] for in range(numthreads): t = threading.Thread(target=worker, args=(taskqueue, candidatelists, threshold, image)) t.start() threads.append(t) for t in threads: t.join() Parameters: Screen Resolution: Tested at 1024 \times 1024. Hardware: Two-processor Clovertown platform, each with a Quad-Core 1.86 GHz Intel Xeon Processor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Hierarchy Overhead: The method explicitly addresses the cost of moving data across memory levels. Failure to manage cache locality during the dynamic allocation or block access can negate performance gains. Load Imbalance: Static screen partitioning can lead to uneven workloads if some regions of the volume are denser. Dynamic allocation mitigates this. Performance: Achieves interactive rendering at 1024^2 resolution for datasets up to the maximum size fitting in main memory on the tested hardware. Strengths: Excellent load balancing via dynamic allocation; high cache performance due to spatial locality and restricted search spaces; scalability on multi-core systems. Limitations: Requires two-pass processing (identification then casting); overhead of managing dynamic tasks and candidate lists. When to use: Interactive visualization of large volumetric datasets on multi-core CPUs where load balancing and memory efficiency are critical. The method was introduced by Qin Wang and Joseph JaJa. It addresses the limitations of static screen partitioning, which is widely used in literature but suffers from load imbalance and poor cache performance on multi-core processors. The approach leverages the spatial coherence of rays and the hierarchical structure of volumetric data to optimize performance on multi-core architectures. name: Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing
head: BONO-based ray tracing, Two-phase isosurface ray tracing
body: Interactive High Resolution Isosurface Ray Tracing is a two-phase algorithm for rendering isosurfaces in volumetric data on multi-core processors. It solves the performance bottleneck of high-resolution ray casting by decoupling the search for the isosurface into a coarse, projection-based culling phase and a fine, ray-intersection phase. Unlike standard packet ray casting which relies on SIMD instructions for parallelism, this method uses high-level algorithmic techniques—specifically, maintaining a short, front-to-back ordered list of candidate blocks per pixel—to achieve coherence and efficiency without instruction-level parallelism dependencies. It builds on Ray Traversal and Coherency by using a BONO tree for hierarchical culling and list-based restriction to limit the search space. The method operates in two distinct phases. Phase I traverses a coarse BONO tree to build a short, front-to-back ordered list of visible, isosurface-intersecting data blocks for each pixel (or packet). Phase II shoots rays through these lists to find the first isosurface intersection, performing trilinear interpolation and shading. Inputs: Volumetric scalar field data f(\mathbf{p}). Isovalue \tau. Camera parameters (viewpoint, projection matrix). Maximum list size k (typically k \le 20). Adaptive block size configuration (e.g., 8\times8\times8 for far views, 4\times4\times4 for close views). Outputs: For each pixel, the 3D intersection point \mathbf{p} on the isosurface and its normal \mathbf{n}, used for shading. Block Organization: The volumetric data is organized into a coarse grid of equal-sized blocks. Scalar field values within each block are stored contiguously. Each block is identified by the coordinates of a pre-specified corner. The data within a block is indexed by an octree where leaves correspond to 2\times2\times2 cells, containing a pointer to such a cell. Each octree node stores the minimum and maximum scalar values of voxels in its region. BONO Tree: A BONO (Branch-On-Need Octree) tree indexes the coarse grid of blocks. It is augmented with value ranges (min/max) at each node. Unlike a standard octree, BONO avoids allocating nodes for empty subtrees when data resolution is not a power of two, making it more space-efficient. Pixel Lists: For each pixel (or packet), a list of pointers to data blocks is maintained. The list is organized in front-to-back order relative to the viewpoint. The list size is capped at k. Each list also stores a "resume point" indicating where the BONO tree traversal stopped if the list reached size k. Phase I: List Generation 1. Traverse the BONO tree starting from the root. 2. For a node v, check if its stored value range [minv, maxv] contains the isovalue \tau (i.e., minv \le \tau \le maxv). 3. If the range contains \tau, project the minimum axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of node v onto the screen. The 3D AABB is computed from the coordinates of a pre-specified corner and the level of v. 4. Identify all pixels falling within the projected area of node v. 5. For each such pixel: If the size of the pixel's block list is less than k, traverse v's children in front-to-back order relative to the viewpoint. Otherwise, skip the subtree rooted at v. 6. When a leaf is reached, augment the list of each pixel falling within the projection of the leaf's block with a pointer to this block, unless the list already has k blocks. The lists remain in front-to-back order due to the traversal order. 7. Adaptive Block Size (Close Views): For close views, after traversing the BONO tree, continue traversing the octree of the BONO leaves until the desired block size is reached. Then compute the minimum bounding box and construct lists for the resulting blocks. Phase II: Ray Casting and Shading 1. For each pixel with a non-empty list, shoot a ray from the pixel through the list of blocks in order. 2. If the list is empty, the ray does not intersect the isosurface. 3. For each block in the list: Compute the ray-voxel intersection using the method from [10] (not detailed in sources). If the ray intersects a voxel on the isosurface within the block: Perform trilinear interpolation using the unit cell containing the voxel to refine the intersection point. Compute the normal using forward difference. Apply diffuse shading. Stop further processing for this ray. 4. If the ray reaches the end of the list without finding an intersection: If the list size is k, resume the traversal of the BONO tree from the resume point indicated at the end of the list. Continue searching for intersections in the remaining subtrees. If the list size is less than k, the ray does not intersect the isosurface. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interactiveisosurfaceraytracing(data, isovalue, camera, k, blocksizeconfig): """ Main entry point for the two-phase isosurface ray tracing algorithm. """ bonotree = buildbonotree(data, blocksizeconfig) numpixels = camera.resolution[0] camera.resolution[1] pixellists = [[] for in range(numpixels)] resumepoints = [None for in range(numpixels)] traversebonoforlists(bonotree.root, camera, isovalue, k, pixellists, resumepoints) image = [[None for in range(camera.resolution[0])] for in range(camera.resolution[1])] for y in range(camera.resolution[1]): for x in range(camera.resolution[0]): pixelidx = y camera.resolution[0] + x ray = camera.getray(x, y) blocklist = pixellists[pixelidx] if not blocklist: continue intersectionfound = False for block in blocklist: if rayintersectsblock(ray, block): voxelintersection = rayvoxelintersection(ray, block, isovalue) if voxelintersection is not None: point = trilinearinterpolate(voxelintersection, block) normal = computenormalforwarddiff(point, block) color = diffuseshading(point, normal, data) image[y][x] = (color, point, normal) intersectionfound = True break if not intersectionfound and len(blocklist) == k: resumenode = resumepoints[pixelidx] if resumenode is not None: continuetraversalandcast(ray, resumenode, isovalue, image, pixelidx, camera) return image def traversebonoforlists(node, camera, isovalue, k, pixellists, resumepoints): if not (node.minval <= isovalue <= node.maxval): return projectedarea = projectaabbtoscreen(node.aabb, camera) pixelsinarea = getpixelsinarea(projectedarea) needstraversal = False for pidx in pixelsinarea: if len(pixellists[pidx]) < k: needstraversal = True break if not needstraversal: for pidx in pixelsinarea: if len(pixellists[pidx]) == k: resumepoints[pidx] = node return children = getchildrenfronttoback(node, camera.viewpoint) for child in children: traversebonoforlists(child, camera, isovalue, k, pixellists, resumepoints) if node.isleaf(): for pidx in pixelsinarea: if len(pixellists[pidx]) < k: pixellists[pidx].append(node.block) else: resumepoints[pidx] = node def buildbonotree(data, blocksizeconfig): # Constructs the BONO tree indexing the coarse grid of blocks. # Each node stores min/max scalar values. Leaves point to 2x2x2 cells. # Not given in the sources. pass def projectaabbtoscreen(aabb, camera): # Projects the 3D AABB of a node onto the 2D screen. # The 3D AABB is computed from the coordinates of a pre-specified corner and the level of the node. # Not given in the sources. pass def getpixelsinarea(projectedarea): # Returns list of pixel indices falling within the projected area. # Not given in the sources. pass def getchildrenfronttoback(node, viewpoint): # Returns children of the node sorted by distance from viewpoint. # Not given in the sources. pass def rayintersectsblock(ray, block): # Tests if ray intersects the block's bounding box. # Not given in the sources. pass def rayvoxelintersection(ray, block, isovalue): # Computes ray-voxel intersection using the method from [10]. # Not given in the sources. pass def trilinearinterpolate(point, block): # Performs trilinear interpolation using the unit cell containing the voxel. # Not given in the sources. pass def computenormalforwarddiff(point, block): # Computes normal using forward difference. # Not given in the sources. pass def diffuseshading(point, normal, data): # Applies diffuse shading. # Not given in the sources. pass def continuetraversalandcast(ray, resumenode, isovalue, image, pixelidx, camera): # Resumes BONO traversal from the saved point and continues ray casting. # Not given in the sources. pass k: The maximum size of the list of data blocks associated with each pixel. Typical value: k \le 20 gives the most efficient implementation. The algorithm remains correct for any k. Block Size: Adaptive based on view distance. For far views, large blocks (e.g., 8\times8\times8) are used. For close views, smaller blocks (e.g., 4\times4\times4) are used to reduce the number of BONO nodes visited and projected blocks. Precision: Ray-voxel intersection and trilinear interpolation require careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid gaps or overlaps in the isosurface. Boundaries: The BONO tree structure handles non-power-of-two resolutions by avoiding empty subtree nodes, but care must be taken in computing the AABB for nodes near the data boundaries. List Fullness: If a pixel's list reaches size k before the isosurface is found, the algorithm must correctly resume traversal. Failure to store and use the resume point correctly will result in missed intersections. Time Complexity: Phase I is efficient due to the compact BONO tree and projection-based culling. Phase II is efficient due to the limited number of blocks per ray. Memory Complexity: The BONO tree is more space-efficient than a standard octree for non-power-of-two resolutions. Pixel lists are small (k \le 20), keeping memory overhead low. Measured Performance: On a Clovertown platform (two Quad-Core Intel Xeon Processors 5320, 1.86 GHz, 8MB L2 cache per dual-core, 8GB main memory) with a 1024x1024 screen: Far view, k=3 (single pixel lists): List generation time is 273 msec. Far view, k=6 (2x2 pixel packets): List generation time is 110 msec (2.48x speedup). Close view, k=3 (single pixel lists): List generation time is 228 msec. Close view, k=6 (2x2 pixel packets): List generation time is 68 msec (3.35x speedup). Strengths: High performance on multi-core processors due to efficient memory hierarchy usage and algorithmic coherence. Adaptive block size optimizes for different view distances. Limitations: The method avoids performance drops on highly incoherent scenes by not relying on SIMD instructions, but may trade off peak performance on highly coherent scenes where SIMD-based packet ray casting could be more effective. When to Use: Interactive rendering of high-resolution volumetric data on multi-core CPUs where coherence can be exploited. When Not to Use: Hardware without multi-core capabilities, or scenarios where SIMD-based packet ray casting is preferred for highly coherent scenes. The method was introduced in a paper by researchers at the University of Maryland (UMD). It was designed to leverage multi-core processor architectures and their memory hierarchies for efficient isosurface rendering. The BONO (Branch-On-Need Octree) structure is a key component, providing a compact indexing structure for the volumetric data. The approach differs from standard packet ray casting by avoiding SIMD instructions, instead relying on list merging and projection-based culling to handle coherence. name: Coherent Multiresolution Isosurface Ray Tracing
head: Coherent Octree Volume Ray Tracing, Multiresolution Isosurface Ray Tracing with Ray Packets, Multiresolution isosurface ray tracing using ray packets, Packet Ray Tracing with Octree LOD
body: Coherent Multiresolution Isosurface Ray Tracing is a method for interactive isosurface extraction from large volumetric datasets stored in octrees. It solves the performance bottleneck of single-ray isosurface tracing on commodity CPUs by grouping neighboring rays into 2x2 packets to exploit spatial coherence during traversal and intersection. Unlike single-ray approaches, it performs traversal and intersection computations per packet rather than per ray, leveraging the multiresolution nature of the octree to maintain coherence even in complex or distant scenes by dynamically switching to coarser levels of detail (LOD). The method adapts coherent grid traversal techniques to hierarchical octree structures, combining ray packet processing with multiresolution LOD selection. Input: A large volumetric dataset V, an isovalue threshold \tau, a camera configuration (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d} per pixel), and an optional LOD cut depth D{cut}. Output: A rendered image where each pixel contains the color of the first isosurface intersection or background. The core data structure is a multiresolution octree stored in CPU main memory. Octree Node: Each node represents a voxel or a block of voxels. Min/Max Bounds: Each node stores the minimum and maximum scalar values (v{min}, v{max}) of the data contained within its subtree. This forms the min/max acceleration structure. Children: Pointers to up to 8 child nodes (if not a leaf). Data: If a leaf, stores the scalar value(s) for the voxel(s). For multiresolution support, interior nodes may store aggregated or representative values if the octree is constructed to allow LOD traversal. Ray Packet: A group of 4 rays (2x2 pixel block). Ray Data: Each ray has origin \mathbf{o}i and direction \mathbf{d}i for i \in \{0,1,2,3\}. SSE Representation: Rays are packed into SIMD registers for parallel processing. 1. Offline Construction: Losslessly compress the original large dataset into a multiresolution octree structure. Compute min/max bounds for each node bottom-up. Store the octree in CPU main memory. 2. Rendering Setup: Generate rays for each pixel in the frame buffer. Group rays into 2x2 packets. Distribute ray packets to worker threads for parallel processing. 3. Per-Packet Traversal: For each packet, perform coherent traversal of the octree. Start at the root node. For each node in the packet's traversal path: Check if the isovalue \tau lies within the node's min/max bounds: \tau \in [v{min}, v{max}]. If \tau \notin [v{min}, v{max}], cull the node (no intersection possible). If \tau \in [v{min}, v{max}], determine which children to visit. LOD Handling: If the current node depth is \ge D{cut} (or if the system decides to switch to LOD due to low coherence/complexity), treat the current node as a leaf for intersection purposes. LOD Intersection: Intersect the rays with the coarser cell represented by the current node instead of traversing deeper. If an intersection is found, refine the intersection point (e.g., linear interpolation within the cell) and shade. If no intersection is found at this LOD level, continue traversal or mark as background depending on implementation details. If not at LOD cut depth, push children to the traversal stack/list. Use coherence: Rays in a packet likely traverse similar nodes. Process children for all rays in the packet together. 4. SSE Intersection: Perform isosurface intersection tests for the rays in the packet using SIMD (SSE) instructions. For a leaf node (fine voxel or LOD cell), compute the intersection of each ray with the isosurface defined within that cell. The intersection test typically involves checking for sign changes of f(\mathbf{p}) - \tau at the cell corners and interpolating. 5. Shading: For the closest intersection found across all rays in the packet, compute the surface normal \nabla f and shade the pixel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderpacket(packet, octreeroot, tau, dcut): """ Render a 2x2 ray packet through an octree. packet: list of 4 rays, each with origin o and direction d octreeroot: root of the min/max octree tau: isovalue threshold dcut: depth at which to switch to LOD (coarser intersection) """ # Stack for traversal: stores (node, rayindicesinpacket) # rayindicesinpacket: subset of {0,1,2,3} that are still active in this node stack = [(octreeroot, [0, 1, 2, 3])] closesthit = None # Stores (distance, rayindex, intersectionpoint, normal) while stack: node, activerays = stack.pop() # Check culling condition if not (node.vmin <= tau <= node.vmax): continue # Determine if we should use LOD uselod = (node.depth >= dcut) if uselod: # Intersect rays with the coarser cell represented by this node for i in activerays: hit = intersectraywithcell(packet[i], node) if hit is not None and (closesthit is None or hit.distance < closesthit.distance): closesthit = hit else: # Traverse children if node.isleaf(): # Fine voxel intersection for i in activerays: hit = intersectraywithvoxel(packet[i], node) if hit is not None and (closesthit is None or hit.distance < closesthit.distance): closesthit = hit else: # Push children to stack children = node.children for child in children: # Determine which rays in activerays enter this child childrays = getraysenteringchild(packet, activerays, child) if childrays: stack.append((child, childrays)) return closesthit def intersectraywithcell(ray, node): """ Intersect a ray with the isosurface within a coarse cell. Returns hit object or None. """ # Standard sign-change detection and linear interpolation within the cell bounds pass def intersectraywithvoxel(ray, node): """ Intersect a ray with the isosurface within a fine voxel. Returns hit object or None. """ # Standard sign-change detection and linear interpolation within the voxel bounds pass def getraysenteringchild(packet, activerays, child): """ Determine which rays in activerays intersect the bounding box of child. """ # Ray-AABB intersection test to cull rays that miss the child node pass Packet Size: 2x2 rays. LOD Cut Depth (D{cut}): A specified depth in the octree. Rays do not traverse below this depth; instead, they intersect the coarser cell at this depth. Isovalue (\tau): The threshold for isosurface extraction. Scalability: Coherent grid traversal on hierarchical structures may have scalability issues. Performance Degradation: Coherent traversal may induce more intersection tests than single-ray traversal and can perform worse without optimizations like LOD. Low Coherence: Large volume data exhibits low spatial coherence, particularly from far-away camera positions, which hampers packet performance. Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues may arise in intersection tests, though not explicitly detailed in sources. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of nodes visited per packet. With LOD, the depth of traversal is limited, reducing complexity. Without LOD, it can be higher than single-ray due to packet overhead. Memory Complexity: The octree structure is stored in CPU main memory. The multiresolution representation allows for a smaller footprint than uncompressed data. Measured Performance: The system outperforms ray tracing the same large data on a distributed cluster on a multicore workstation. It achieves interactive performance on laptops and commodity desktops. Strengths: Interactive performance on commodity hardware, smooth gradients due to LOD smoothing, lower memory footprint. Limitations: Scalability issues with coherent traversal, potential performance loss without LOD, low coherence in distant views. When to Use: Interactive visualization of large volumes on commodity CPUs where smoothness is acceptable and hardware is limited. When Not to Use: When maximum precision is required at all scales, or when the scene has very high coherence without LOD (single-ray might be simpler). The method was presented in the paper "Coherent Multiresolution Isosurface Ray Tracing" [60], part of a thesis by Knoll. It builds on the coherent kd-tree isosurface ray tracer of Wald et al. [129, 130], adapting it to octree volumes with multiresolution LODs. The work appeared in Chapter 4 of the thesis. name: First Depth Ray Traversal
head: First Depth, First Intensity Ray Traversal, Tuy & Tuy traversal
body: First Depth Ray Traversal is a ray traversal method that extracts iso-surfaces by recording the first scalar intensity encountered along a viewing ray. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) or Accumulate compositing by its immediate termination upon the first hit, making it specifically suited for isolating high-density or specific threshold structures without contribution from deeper volumes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume V, a viewing ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, a threshold \tau, and a step size \Delta t. Output: The color and depth of the first voxel where the scalar value meets the selection criteria. Data Structures: The volume is typically stored as a 3D array of scalar values. Ray traversal uses a step size \Delta t corresponding to the voxel grid spacing. Steps: 1. Initialize ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for the pixel. 2. Iterate along the ray from t=0 to the volume exit. 3. At each step, sample the scalar value s = V(\mathbf{r}(t)). 4. Check if s satisfies the condition (e.g., s \ge \tau or first non-background value). 5. If the condition is met: record the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{r}(t) and value s, then terminate the ray traversal immediately. 6. If the loop completes without a hit, assign background color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def firstdepthtraversal(rayorigin, raydirection, volume, threshold, voxelspacing): t = 0.0 maxt = volume.maxdistance backgroundcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] while t <= maxt: pos = rayorigin + raydirection t if not volume.boundscheck(pos): t += voxelspacing continue scalarvalue = volume.sample(pos) if scalarvalue >= threshold: color = volume.transferfunction(scalarvalue) return color + [1.0] t += voxelspacing return backgroundcolor Parameters: Threshold \tau: Defines the iso-surface or minimum intensity. Typical values depend on the data normalization (e.g., 0.5 for normalized [0,1] data). Step size \Delta t: Often equal to voxel spacing for exact voxel traversal, or smaller for sub-voxel precision. Edge Cases: If no voxel exceeds the threshold, the ray returns background. Precision errors at boundaries may cause missed hits if step size is not aligned with voxel centers. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of voxels traversed until the first hit. In sparse volumes, this is significantly faster than full compositing. In dense volumes, it may still require traversing the entire ray length if the hit is deep or absent. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, as it does not accumulate opacity/color buffers. Strengths: Fast extraction of specific structures; no need for transfer function tuning for opacity accumulation; ideal for high-contrast features. Limitations: Loses depth information for structures behind the first hit; sensitive to noise (first noisy voxel may be selected); does not show internal structure. First Depth Ray Traversal was introduced by Tuy and Tuy in 1984. It is one of the earliest methods for ray-casting based volume rendering, specifically designed for iso-surface extraction via ray traversal. name: GPU-based Fast Ray Casting for Metaballs
head: Nishita and Nakamae's Algorithm
body: This method renders particle-based implicit surfaces (metaballs) directly on the GPU by evaluating the isosurface condition per pixel, avoiding polygonization and expensive precomputation or acceleration structures. It solves the problem of high rendering costs for large numbers of moving metaballs by maintaining a limited-size list of contributing metaballs along each viewing ray and using Bézier Clipping to solve the resulting polynomial equations. Unlike sibling methods that rely on grid-based repulsion buffers or vertex attribute interpolation, this approach handles millions of particles and small objects smoothly by extracting metaballs via depth peeling and solving quartic or degree-six density functions exactly. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N metaballs, each defined by center \mathbf{p}i, effective radius Ri, density coefficient qi, and a density function fi(r) with finite support. The viewing ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for each pixel. Threshold T. Outputs: Color and normal for the closest isosurface intersection per pixel. Data Structures: ID List: A dynamic list storing metaball IDs contributing to the current ray interval. Capacity is limited to K. Stored t: The t-parameter of the last processed ray-sphere intersection. Texture: Stores the current ID list and stored t for each pixel, updated via depth peeling. Density Function: The density function fi for metaball i is a function of r = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i\| and monotonically decreases as r increases. If fi has finite support Ri, fi(r) = 0 for r \ge Ri. The method supports quartic and degree-six polynomials. The isosurface is defined by: f(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} qi fi(\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}i\|) - T = 0 The normal vector at \mathbf{x} is derived from -\nabla f(\mathbf{x}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: For each pixel, initialize the ID list as empty and stored t to the near clipping plane. 2. Depth Peeling Loop: a. Render effective spheres (spheres with radius Ri) to find the k-th nearest ray-sphere intersection (tk, Bk) in parallel. b. If no intersection is found, terminate the loop for this pixel. c. Update the ID list: i. If Bk is not in the ID list, insert it. ii. If Bk is already in the ID list, remove it (handling occlusion). iii. If the ID list size exceeds K, treat the ray-sphere intersection as a ray-isosurface intersection (fallback). d. Ray-Isosurface Test: In the interval [t{k-1}, tk], perform a ray-isosurface test using the metaballs in the ID list. i. Single Case: If only one metaball is in the ID list, perform a ray-sphere intersection test. The radius can be precomputed. ii. Multiple Case: If two or more metaballs are in the ID list, construct a degree-M Bézier curve equation d(u)=0 representing the density function along the ray segment, and solve for roots using Bézier Clipping. iii. If a root is found in [t{k-1}, tk], record the intersection, shade the surface, and terminate the loop for this pixel. e. Update stored t to tk. f. Repeat steps 2a-2e until an isosurface is found or no more intersections are available. 3. Shading: Evaluate and shade the isosurface closest to the viewpoint at every pixel. Bézier Clipping: A degree-M Bézier curve is denoted with parameter u \in [0,1] as: \mathbf{D}(u) = (u, d(u)) = \sum{i=0}^M \mathbf{D}i \mathbf{B}i^M(u) where \mathbf{B}i^M(u) = \binom{M}{i} u^i (1-u)^{M-i} are Bernstein polynomials, and \mathbf{D}i = (i/M, di) are control points. The curve lies within the convex hull of \mathbf{D}i. The intersection with the u-axis lies between u{min} and u{max}, where the convex hull intersects the axis. Iteratively clip the curve in [u{min}, u{max}] using de Casteljau's algorithm. If the range does not converge past a threshold, split the curve in two and recurse. To mitigate root misdetection when the convex hull barely intersects the axis, slightly increase the clipping range. Unlike Newton's method, Bézier Clipping does not require an initial value and converges quickly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. center[i] for i in range(3)] b = sum(oc[i] d[i] for i in range(3)) c = sum(oc[i] oc[i] for i in range(3)) - radius radius disc = b b - c if disc < 0: return None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t = -b - sqrtdisc return t if t > 0 else (-b + sqrtdisc if -b + sqrtdisc > 0 else None) def rayisosurfacetest(idlist, o, d, tstart, tend, threshold): if len(idlist) == 1: # Single Case: ray-sphere intersection test ball = metaballs[idlist[0]] t = raysphereintersection(o, d, ball[0], ball[1]) return t if tstart <= t <= tend else None else: # Multiple Case: construct Bézier curve and solve # Note: Exact polynomial-to-Bézier conversion is not detailed in sources [Comment] ctrlpts = converttobeziercontrolpoints(idlist, o, d, tstart, tend, threshold) return bezierclipping(ctrlpts, 0.0, 1.0, tol=1e-4) def converttobeziercontrolpoints(idlist, o, d, tstart, tend, threshold): # Placeholder for polynomial-to-Bézier conversion [Comment] # Returns list of (x, y) control points Di = (i/M, di) return [(i/2, 0.0) for i in range(3)] # Dummy for structure def bezierclipping(ctrlpts, umin, umax, tol): # Iteratively clip using de Casteljau's algorithm while umax - umin > tol: # Compute convex hull bounds to find new intersection range yvals = [p[1] for p in ctrlpts] newumin = umin newumax = umax if min(yvals) > 0 or max(yvals) < 0: return None # No root in range # Apply Campagna heuristic: slightly increase clipping range to avoid misdetection rangewidth = newumax - newumin newumin = max(0.0, newumin - 0.01 rangewidth) newumax = min(1.0, newumax + 0.01 rangewidth) # Check convergence if newumax - newumin > tol 0.5: # Split curve in two and recurse mid = (newumin + newumax) / 2 leftpts, rightpts = decasteljausplit(ctrlpts, mid) rootleft = bezierclipping(leftpts, newumin, mid, tol) if rootleft is not None: return rootleft return bezierclipping(rightpts, mid, newumax, tol) # Update range based on hull intersection umin, umax = newumin, newumax ctrlpts = decasteljauclip(ctrlpts, umin, umax) return (umin + umax) / 2 def decasteljausplit(ctrlpts, t): n = len(ctrlpts) - 1 left = [ctrlpts[0]] right = [ctrlpts[0]] for j in range(1, n + 1): for i in range(n, j - 1, -1): ctrlpts[i] = [(1 - t) ctrlpts[i][k] + t ctrlpts[i - 1][k] for k in range(2)] left.append(ctrlpts[j]) right.insert(0, ctrlpts[j]) return left, right def decasteljauclip(ctrlpts, umin, umax): # Simplified clipping: retain control points within range bounds return [p for p in ctrlpts if umin <= p[0] <= umax] def computenormalfromsphere(o, d, ball): center, radius,, = ball hit = [o[i] + raysphereintersection(o, d, center, radius) d[i] for i in range(3)] return [(hit[i] - center[i]) / radius for i in range(3)] def computegradientnormal(idlist, point, threshold): # Analytical gradient for polynomial density functions grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in idlist: ball = metaballs[i] center, radius, coeff, func = ball dist = math.sqrt(sum((point[j] - center[j])2 for j in range(3))) if dist < radius: for j in range(3): grad[j] -= coeff funcprime(dist) (point[j] - center[j]) / dist norm = math.sqrt(sum(g2 for g in grad)) return [g / norm for g in grad] if norm > 0 else [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] def funcprime(r): # Derivative of quartic/degree-six density function return -4 r3 # Example for quartic def shadehit(t, normal, o, d): # Simple Phong shading hit = [o[i] + t d[i] for i in range(3)] light = [1.0, 1.0, -1.0] l = [l / math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in light)) for l in light] diff = max(0, sum(normal[i] l[i] for i in range(3))) return (0.5 + 0.5 diff, 0.5 + 0.5 diff, 0.5 + 0.5 diff) A real-time ray casting method for rendering particle-based medium representations (metaballs) that builds per-pixel lists of relevant metaballs, incrementally constructs a piecewise polynomial approximation of summed densities along rays, and finds intersections with the isosurface. It replaces the multipass depth peeling used in GPU-based Fast Ray Casting for Metaballs with single-pass fragment list gathering, allowing robust handling of local extremities of depth complexity and scaling to millions of particles. Reduces the number of rendered metaballs by culling effective spheres hidden from the viewpoint by 'kernel spheres' (spheres making up the isosurface). Render the kernel spheres and save the ray parameters to a texture. Disable writes to the depth buffer. Render the effective spheres, using the occlusion query to determine which effective spheres were drawn. Cull the effective spheres that were not rendered in the above test. This culling can reduce the number of metaballs to be rendered to 10-20% in dense groups. Procedural rules for handling degenerate or dense ray-metaball intersections during depth peeling to prevent duplicate IDs, holes, or occlusion errors. When multiple effective spheres intersect the viewing ray at the same point, compare ray parameters and return only one metaball ID. Check if the ID is already stored in the list; discard fragments containing that ID if present. When dense groups exceed the ID list upper limit K = 4 \times N{buf} - 2, the standard intersection test fails and causes holes. Fallback: treat the ray-sphere intersection as a ray-isosurface intersection. When the viewing ray intersects the isosurface only after crossing other metaballs, repeat depth peeling until termination to keep the isosurface visible, provided K is not exceeded. Parameter: K (Upper limit for the ID list capacity). Value used in experiments: 14. No visual artifacts observed with this value. Pitfall: Checking for duplicate IDs in the list drastically increases depth peeling cost. In 32-bit floating point computations, omitting this check produces no visible artifacts. A technique to obtain ray-sphere intersections in parallel from front to back by drawing effective spheres and storing IDs and ray parameters into a texture, discarding fragments whose parameters are less than previous ones. Time Complexity: Depends on screen resolution and the number of metaballs intersecting each ray. Depth peeling requires multiple passes, one per intersecting sphere. Bézier Clipping converges quickly but requires iterative clipping. Memory Complexity: Limited by the ID list size K and texture storage for depth peeling. K is typically 14. Measured Performance: An animation with 1,000 moving metaballs was rendered in 640×480 at 23.1 fps. Strengths: Handles large numbers of moving metaballs efficiently without precomputation or acceleration structures. Renders small objects smoothly, unlike grid-based methods. Solves quartic and degree-six polynomials accurately. Limitations: Performance degrades with very dense groups of metaballs due to ID list limits and depth peeling passes. Bézier Clipping can be computationally expensive. When to Use: Real-time visualization of particle-based simulations (fluid dynamics, molecular dynamics) with many moving metaballs. Originated from Nishita and Nakamae's algorithm for ray casting implicit surfaces. The method was adapted for the GPU by to handle large numbers of moving metaballs. It builds on the concept of finite support density functions (quartic and degree-six polynomials) proposed by Nishita and Nakamae. Bézier Clipping was introduced by Nishita and Nakamae [NN94] and later optimized for GPUs by Pabst et al. [PSS06] and Campagna et al. [CSS97]. name: Real-Time Metaball Ray Casting with Fragment Lists
head: Fragment List Based Metaball Ray Casting, Metaballs as Volumes
body: A real-time ray casting method for rendering particle-based medium representations (metaballs) that builds per-pixel lists of relevant metaballs, incrementally constructs a piecewise polynomial approximation of summed densities along rays, and finds intersections with the isosurface. It replaces the multipass depth peeling used in GPU-based Fast Ray Casting for Metaballs with single-pass fragment list gathering, allowing robust handling of local extremities of depth complexity and scaling to millions of particles. The method renders metaballs by evaluating the isosurface equation \rho(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{j=0}^{M-1} \rhoj (\|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{p}j\|) - L = 0 along rays. It uses a piecewise cubic approximation \tauj(s) of the individual density functions \rhoj along the ray parameter s, enabling efficient intersection testing via cubic polynomial solving. Inputs: Metaball data: Centers \mathbf{p}j, effective radii Rj, and core radii (for depth culling) for j=0 \dots M-1. Camera: Eye position \mathbf{e} and viewing direction \mathbf{v} per pixel. Isosurface value L. Outputs: Pixel color and depth. 1. Core Depth Texture: Stores the depth of the closest intersected core sphere for each pixel. 2. Per-pixel Linked Lists: Maintained in a read/write GPU buffer. Stores metaball IDs. IDs are prepended to the list. 3. Local-memory Array: Stores separator records (si, \Delta \mathbf{w}i) in reverse order of depth. Elements are removed by decreasing the element count. Effective Radius Rj: The radius of the effective sphere of metaball j, within which the density function is non-zero. Effective Interval: The range [mj - Qj, mj + Qj] along the ray parameter s where the metaball density is non-zero. Midpoint mj: mj = (\mathbf{p}j - \mathbf{e}) \cdot \mathbf{v}. Half-length Qj: Qj = \sqrt{Rj^2 - (\|\mathbf{p}j - \mathbf{e}\|^2 - mj^2)}. Subdomain Separators: The sorted list of end-points (mj - Qj) and mid-points (mj) of all effective intervals along the ray, denoted si for i=1 \dots n, with s0=0 prepended. Polynomial Coefficient Vector \mathbf{w}: A 4-element vector representing the coefficients of the piecewise cubic approximation \tau(s) = \mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{w}, where \mathbf{s} = (s^3, s^2, s, 1). 1. Sorting: Sort metaballs according to their effective distance from the camera, ascending. Effective distance is defined as \|\mathbf{p}j - \mathbf{e}\| - Rj. 2. Lay down depth: Render solid scene and metaball core depth into a core depth texture. Geometry rendered for core spheres is a covering billboard or enclosing object. The pixel shader discards pixels where the sphere is not intersected. Z-buffering is used, cores are rendered front-to-back. 3. Gathering: Render effective spheres of metaballs, gathering their IDs into per-pixel linked lists in a read/write GPU buffer. The intersected effective interval is clipped against core depth. Metaball ID is prepended to the linked list. Metaballs are rendered back-to-front, so lists are ordered by increasing effective distance. 4. Ray casting: Render a full-viewport quad. For every pixel, expand lists to end- and midpoint records, sort them, and evaluate ray-isosurface intersection. 5. Shading: Compute normal of isosurface at intersection point \mathbf{x} as -\nabla \rho(\mathbf{x}) by iterating over gathered metaballs. Evaluate shading formula to get pixel color. For each pixel, the shader executes the following steps: 1. Initialize polynomial coefficient vector \mathbf{w} to zero. If the eye is within the effective sphere of any metaball, sum the cubics of the intervals containing the eye. 2. For every metaball in the per-pixel list: a. Intersect the effective sphere with the ray. Insert separator records (si, \Delta \mathbf{w}i) for end- and midpoints into the local-memory array ordered by depth. b. Identify safe separators: those separators in the list which are within the effective distance of the next, yet unprocessed metaball (the "safe zone"). As metaballs are ordered, separators of further effective spheres cannot precede the safe ones. c. For safe separators, update polynomial coefficients by adding \Delta \mathbf{w}i and evaluate intersection within subdomains. Discard processed separators. d. If no metaballs are left, evaluate all remaining subdomains. 3. If an intersection was found, compute the normal and shading. The density function \rhoj is approximated by a piecewise cubic \tauj(s): \tauj(s) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } s \notin [mj - Qj, mj + Qj], \\ \mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{u}j \uparrow & \text{if } s \in [mj - Qj, mj], \\ \mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{u}j \downarrow & \text{if } s \in [mj, mj + Qj], \end{cases} where \mathbf{u}j \uparrow and \mathbf{u}j \downarrow are coefficient vectors derived by solving for values and derivatives at endpoints and midpoint. The change of coefficients \Delta \mathbf{w}i at separator si is: \Delta \mathbf{w}i = \frac{\gammaj(si)}{Qj^3} \times \text{case} where the case is: \alphai + \betai if si = mj - Qj -2\alphai if si = mj \alphai - \betai if si = mj + Qj with vectors: \alphai = (-2, 6si, -6si^2, 2si^3)^T \betai = Qj(0, 3, -6si, 3si^2)^T Note: The source text uses \gammaj(si) in the numerator. Since \tauj(s) approximates \rhoj, and the coefficients are normalized by Qj^3, this factor represents the scaling of the specific density function used (e.g., Perlin's fifth-degree polynomial). For implementation, \gammaj(si) should be evaluated using the actual density function \rhoj at si to determine the magnitude of the coefficient jump. The polynomial coefficient update is: \mathbf{w}i = \mathbf{w}{i-1} + \Delta \mathbf{w}i where \mathbf{w}0 = 0 if the eye is not in any effective sphere. Within each subdomain si, s{i+1}), the total density is approximated by \tau(s) = \mathbf{s} \cdot \mathbf{w}i. The intersection with the isosurface L is found by solving \tau(s) - L = 0 for s \in [si, s{i+1}). This reduces to solving a cubic equation. The source notes that the "practically exclusive monotonous case can easily be identified and very effectively handled". Isosurface density value L: The [threshold value defining the surface shape. Local-memory array size: Fixed size. Trade-off between performance and robustness of overlapping handling. Local Memory Overflow: The fixed-size local memory array may be insufficient for too many overlapping spheres, forcing processing of non-safe separators. This creates a trade-off between performance and robustness of overlapping handling. Depth Complexity: There is no limit on screen-space depth complexity, only on the number of effective spheres a world-space point can belong to. Eye Position: If the eye is inside an effective sphere, the initial \mathbf{w} must sum the cubics of intervals containing the eye. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def cubicroots(a, b, c, d): """Returns real roots of ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d = 0.""" if abs(a) < 1e-12: # Quadratic or lower if abs(b) < 1e-12: if abs(c) < 1e-12: return [] return [-d / c] disc = cc - 4bd if disc < 0: return [] sq = math.sqrt(disc) return [(-c - sq)/(2b), (-c + sq)/(2b)] # Normalize b /= a; c /= a; d /= a p = c - bb/3 q = 2bbb/27 - bc/3 + d disc = qq/4 + ppp/27 roots = [] if disc > 0: u = -q/2 + math.sqrt(disc) v = -q/2 - math.sqrt(disc) u = math.cbrt(u) if u >= 0 else -math.cbrt(-u) v = math.cbrt(v) if v >= 0 else -math.cbrt(-v) roots = [u + v - b/3] elif disc == 0: if q == 0: roots = [-b/3] else: u = math.cbrt(-q/2) roots = [2u - b/3, -u - b/3] else: r = math.sqrt(-ppp/27) theta = math.acos(-q/(2r)) m = 2 math.cbrt(r) roots = [mmath.cos(theta/3) - b/3, mmath.cos((theta + 2math.pi)/3) - b/3, mmath.cos((theta + 4math.pi)/3) - b/3] return [r for r in roots if abs(r) > 1e-9] def evaluatedensity(metaball, point): """Evaluates the actual density function rhoj at point.""" # Placeholder for the specific kernel (e.g., Perlin's 5th degree) dist = math.sqrt(sum((p - q)2 for p, q in zip(metaball.center, point))) return metaball.densityfunc(dist) def getmetaball(id): """Retrieves metaball data from buffer.""" return metaballdatabase[id] def computegradient(point, metaballs): """Computes -grad(rho(x)) by iterating over gathered metaballs.""" grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for m in metaballs: # Simplified gradient approximation for demonstration dist = math.sqrt(sum((p - q)2 for p, q in zip(m.center, point))) if dist > 0: factor = m.gradientfunc(dist) / dist for k in range(3): grad[k] -= factor (point[k] - m.center[k]) return grad def shade(point, normal): """Evaluates shading formula to get pixel color.""" # Placeholder for lighting model return [0.8, 0.8, 0.8] backgroundcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] def insertsorted(arr, item): """Inserts item into sorted list maintaining order.""" arr.append(item) arr.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) def raycastpixel(pixelslist, rayorigin, raydir, L): """Main ray casting logic for a single pixel.""" w = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # If eye is inside an effective sphere, sum initial cubics here. # For standard cases outside spheres, w remains zero. localseparators = [] for idx, mid in enumerate(pixelslist): metaball = getmetaball(mid) p = metaball.center R = metaball.effectiveradius vectocenter = [p[k] - rayorigin[k] for k in range(3)] mj = sum(vectocenter[k] raydir[k] for k in range(3)) distsq = sum(vv for v in vectocenter) Qjsq = RR - (distsq - mjmj) if Qjsq < 0: continue Qj = math.sqrt(Qjsq) sstart = mj - Qj smid = mj send = mj + Qj def getdeltaw(sval, type): alpha = [-2, 6sval, -6svalsval, 2svalsvalsval] beta = [0, 3, -6sval, 3svalsval] beta = [b Qj for b in beta] point = [rayorigin[k] + sval raydir[k] for k in range(3)] gamma = evaluatedensity(metaball, point) factor = gamma / (Qj Qj Qj) if type == 'start': return [factor (alpha[k] + beta[k]) for k in range(4)] elif type == 'mid': return [factor (-2 alpha[k]) for k in range(4)] elif type == 'end': return [factor (alpha[k] - beta[k]) for k in range(4)] return [0.0]4 localseparators.append((sstart, getdeltaw(sstart, 'start'))) localseparators.append((smid, getdeltaw(smid, 'mid'))) localseparators.append((send, getdeltaw(send, 'end'))) # Safe limit: effective distance of next metaball if idx + 1 < len(pixelslist): nextm = getmetaball(pixelslist[idx+1]) nextp = nextm.center nextvec = [nextp[k] - rayorigin[k] for k in range(3)] nexteffdist = math.sqrt(sum(vv for v in nextvec)) - nextm.effectiveradius else: nexteffdist = float('inf') safeindices = [] for i, (s, delta) in enumerate(localseparators): if s < nexteffdist: w = [w[k] + delta[k] for k in range(4)] safeindices.append(i) else: break for i in safeindices: scurr = localseparators[i][0] snext = localseparators[i+1][0] if i+1 < len(localseparators) else float('inf') a, b, c, d = w[0], w[1], w[2], w[3] - L roots = cubicroots(a, b, c, d) valid = [r for r in roots if scurr <= r < snext] if valid: return min(valid) for i in reversed(safeindices): localseparators.pop(i) for i in range(len(localseparators) - 1): scurr = localseparators[i][0] snext = localseparators[i+1][0] a, b, c, d = w[0], w[1], w[2], w[3] - L roots = cubicroots(a, b, c, d) valid = [r for r in roots if scurr <= r < snext] if valid: return min(valid) if localseparators: scurr = localseparators[-1][0] a, b, c, d = w[0], w[1], w[2], w[3] - L roots = cubicroots(a, b, c, d) valid = [r for r in roots if r >= scurr] if valid: return min(valid) return None def rendermetaballs(pixelslist, rayorigin, raydir, L): sintersect = raycastpixel(pixelslist, rayorigin, raydir, L) if sintersect is not None: x = [rayorigin[k] + sintersect raydir[k] for k in range(3)] normal = computegradient(x, pixelslist) color = shade(x, normal) return color, sintersect return backgroundcolor, float('inf') Time Complexity: Dominated by the ray casting step, which processes per-pixel fragment lists. The complexity depends on the number of metaballs per pixel and the depth complexity. The method scales well with the number of metaballs. Memory Complexity: Requires a read/write GPU buffer for per-pixel linked lists and a fixed-size local memory array in the shader. The local memory size is a critical parameter. Performance: 13 FPS for 100,000 metaballs with cel shading. 25 FPS, 13 FPS, and 6 FPS for mud simulation frames reaching 200,000 metaballs. Interactive framerates for 1,600,000 particles. Strengths: Handles local extremities of depth complexity robustly. Does not suffer from inaccuracies of screen-space filtering. Scales well for high numbers of particles. Replaces multipass depth peeling with single-pass gathering. Limitations: Fixed-size local memory array limits the number of overlapping spheres that can be handled robustly without performance penalty. Trade-off between performance and robustness of overlapping handling. When to use: Real-time rendering of massive particle simulations (metaballs) where depth complexity is high and polygonization is undesirable. When not to use: Scenes with extremely high local overlap of effective spheres that exceed the local memory capacity. The method was proposed by L. Szécsi and D. Illés from TU Budapest. It builds upon the work of Kanamori et al. [KSN08], replacing depth peeling with fragment list gathering and using piecewise cubic approximation instead of Bezier clipping. Implemented in C++ using Direct3D11 and HLSL shaders, tested on Intel Quad 2.40 GHz CPU and NVIDIA GeForce GTX 560 Ti. Test scenes were simulated in Next Limit's RealFlow. Rendering metaballs as volumes can be enabled in Houdini's mantra renderer via the 'Metaballs as Volume' checkbox on the Geometry sub-tab of the Render tab of a Geometry object. Point attributes on the metaballs are interpolated to the shading position in the same manner as for metaball surfaces. A surface material that takes into account volume primitives, such as basic smoke, must be applied. name: Hybrid and multi-mode rendering
body: Hybrid and multi-mode rendering combines volume rendering and surface rendering techniques to optimize computational cost and visual fidelity. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both discrete volumetric data and sharp surface boundaries by using clipping planes or proxy meshes to restrict volume integration to the region in front of the nearest surface. Unlike pure volume rendering, which integrates through the entire ray, or pure mesh rendering, which lacks internal density, this family shortens the ray at the first surface hit to prevent occlusion of volume data behind the surface. Builds on the image-order rendering and isosurface detection principles of Isosurface and first-hit ray casting. Combines hardware-accelerated ray-triangle intersection for explicit surface geometry (meshes) and implicit isosurfaces with volume ray marching for volumetric data. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering scenes containing both discrete volumetric data and sharp surface boundaries by using clipping planes to restrict volume integration to the region in front of the nearest surface. Unlike pure volume rendering, which integrates through the entire ray, or pure mesh rendering, which lacks internal density, this method shortens the ray at the first surface hit to prevent occlusion of volume data behind the surface. It is distinguished from Hybrid Isosurface/DVR Rendering by its explicit support for hardware-accelerated triangle meshes alongside implicit surfaces, and from Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing by its specific traversal order prioritizing mesh BVHs before iso-surface BVHs. A technique for viewpoints inside a volume with a wide field of view, such as virtual colonoscopy, that combines surface rendering for near structures (e.g., the colon wall) with Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) for structures behind it. It sets itself apart from pure isosurface methods by preserving the visibility of internal volumetric details behind the first-hit surface, and from pure DVR by providing sharp, shaded surface definition for the immediate foreground. A rendering technique that combines explicit voxel selection with implicit ray-surface intersection to render high-quality, crack-free isosurfaces from rectilinear or adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) volumes. Unlike sample-based methods that use fixed step sizes and often miss surface details in refined regions, this method builds a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) over active voxel primitives and performs exact implicit intersections within each primitive, avoiding the memory overhead of explicit polygon extraction. It is particularly suited for interactive visualization of large-scale AMR data where surface continuity and detail preservation are critical. A strategy that combines volume rendering with rasterized proxy meshes to enable real-time performance on consumer hardware. It solves the computational bottleneck of pure volume rendering by using a surface approximation to quickly determine the distance to the object, thereby restricting the volume sampling interval. Unlike Hybrid Isosurface/DVR Rendering which may use explicit isosurfaces for occlusion, this method specifically leverages a decimated proxy mesh derived from the density field to guide cone-casting samples. A technique that determines the final color of a pixel by evaluating a neural network at the intersection point between a camera ray and a triangular mesh surface, rather than sampling a volumetric field. It reformulates the standard volume rendering integral into a single-point evaluation, assuming the object is solid and opaque. This method distinguishes itself from implicit neural rendering (e.g., Hybrid Implicit Isosurface Ray Tracing) by operating directly on explicit geometry, allowing the use of differentiable rasterizers for efficient gradient computation. A hybrid representation for multi-view surface reconstruction that learns two parallel streams: an implicit Signed Distance Field (SDF) and an explicit surrogate surface mesh. It unifies volume rendering of the implicit SDF and surface rendering of the surrogate mesh with a shared neural shader to promote convergence to the same underlying surface. Unlike pure implicit methods, it leverages the efficiency of explicit mesh rendering; unlike pure explicit methods, it maintains the topological flexibility of an implicit field. Combines volume rendering (ray marching) and surface rendering (rasterization) to optimize computational cost and visual fidelity. It confines ray marching to the region between the viewpoint and a pre-existing mesh surface, treating the mesh intersection as the termination point for volume integration. This approach leverages the mesh for high-fidelity geometry and texture where available, while using the volume to represent complex details or occlusions in front of the surface. Definition: A rendering mode that prioritizes interaction speed by skipping expensive visibility and suggestive contour calculations during user manipulation. Step: During camera movement or isosurface sweeping, draw only contours (no suggestive contours, no hidden surface removal). When motion stops, render the full drawing including suggestive contours and hidden surface removal. Comparison: This mode is necessary because computing suggestive contours and visibility takes significantly more time than contour extraction alone. Definition: A method to overlay multiple volume data sets on a 3D surface model by computing contributions of each volume set individually and combining them, optimizing memory access patterns. Step: Classify shader methods into two groups: those where rays fully penetrate the volume (1, 2, 4, 7) and those where rays end at a point inside the volume (3, 5, 6). Optimize memory access patterns and compact address blocks to maximize memory caching. Compute the contributions of each volume data set to the resulting ray per volume individually. Subsequently combine the individual contributions. Check if the volume data can contain boundaries using the specified shader method. Out of all 'bounded' volume data sets, compute the boundary nearest to the viewer for the ray concerned. Compute 'un-bounded' volume data sets to this nearest boundary point. Calculate the final color value of the pixel using an optional transfer function. For the combination with the 3D surface model, inform the graphic-card-based ray-casting algorithm of the position of a boundary (e.g., the building) from the given perspective.
