name: Distance-field ray marching
head: Sphere tracing, SDF ray marching, Distance field rendering
body: Distance-field ray marching is an image-order rendering technique that finds surface intersections by iteratively stepping along a ray using a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to determine the step size, allowing for approximate intersection detection without explicit mesh geometry. It solves the problem of rendering complex, continuous implicit surfaces by leveraging the mathematical guarantee that no geometry exists within the distance value returned by the SDF. Unlike Direct volume ray casting which integrates density, or Isosurface and first-hit ray casting which may use analytic intersections, this method relies on the Lipschitz property of the distance field to ensure safe, non-penetrating steps. The method operates on the principle that a Signed Distance Function f(\mathbf{p}) provides a lower bound on the distance to the nearest surface. For any point \mathbf{p} in space, f(\mathbf{p}) returns the shortest Euclidean distance to the implicit surface, with a sign indicating position: f(\mathbf{p}) < 0 inside, f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 on the surface, and f(\mathbf{p}) > 0 outside. The core algorithm, known as sphere tracing, proceeds as follows for each pixel: 1. Ray Definition: A ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. 2. Initialization: The accumulated distance t is initialized to 0 (or a near-plane value). 3. Marching Loop: Evaluate the scene SDF at the current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to get the distance d = f(\mathbf{p}). Termination Check: If d < \epsilon (a small convergence threshold, e.g., 0.001), the ray has hit the surface. If t > t{max} (maximum ray distance), the ray has escaped. Step: Advance the ray by the distance value: t \leftarrow t + d. This step size is guaranteed not to penetrate the surface because the SDF satisfies the Lipschitz condition with constant 1. 4. Shading: Upon hit, compute surface properties (normal, color) and lighting. The scene SDF is typically composed of primitives using Boolean operations: union is min(d1, d2), intersection is max(d1, d2), and subtraction is max(-d1, d2). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} to the local space of the primitive via M^{-1}\mathbf{p} before evaluation. Evaluates the integral of a 3D Gaussian mixture along camera rays to resolve spatial overlap and self-attenuation, operating on a continuous probabilistic density field rather than a discrete SDF. Renders 2D heightmap terrains by stepping along the ray until the ray's height drops below the terrain surface defined by the heightmap value at the ray's xz position. Provides analytical building blocks for distance-field ray marching by defining the signed Euclidean distance from any point in 3D space to the surface of a geometric primitive. Allows raymarched SDF objects to correctly occlude and be occluded by standard mesh-based geometry by querying the scene's depth buffer to determine the distance to the nearest mesh surface. Extends sphere tracing by explicitly writing the computed surface hit point's depth to the hardware depth buffer (SVDepth) to ensure correct occlusion ordering with rasterized geometry. Extends distance-field ray marching by continuing the ray path after a surface intersection to simulate specular reflections, effectively transitioning from raycasting to raytracing. Computes the color of surface points identified by distance-field ray marching by estimating surface normals and applying reflectance models to determine how light interacts with the geometry. Approximates the Space Distance Field (SDF) using a deep neural network and renders images by marching rays along the estimated distance field, trading computational speed for geometric flexibility. Generates point clouds or render images by sampling points near or on the zero-level set of a Signed Distance Function (SDF), focusing on extracting geometric representations. A parallelization technique that maintains a dynamic mask of unfinished rays to prevent wasted computation on rays that have already converged or escaped. Addresses the problem of applying spatial transformations (rigid body motion, scaling, deformation) to Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDFs) during ray marching. Adapts distance-field ray marching to simulate LiDAR sensor data by detecting surface intersections and projecting them onto a framebuffer as a sparse point cloud. A real-time WebGL2 renderer that generates an infinite procedural synthwave city using signed-distance fields (SDFs) within a single fullscreen fragment shader, requiring no meshes, textures, or scene graph. A single-function ray integrator that resolves a complete ray by compositing terrain, water, sky, cloud volume, and aerial perspective, handling the sequential evaluation of distinct environmental layers. Computes the surface normal at a point on a Signed Distance Field (SDF) by numerically approximating the gradient of the distance function f using finite differences and normalizing the result. Prevents moiré artifacts and jagged edges caused by high-frequency noise octaves or fine geometric details aliasing against the pixel grid, often integrating frequency-aware logic directly into the procedural evaluation. Simulates light transport through participating media, such as clouds, smoke, fog, and planetary atmospheres, by integrating density and scattering properties along view rays. Encompasses techniques to reduce the computational cost of distance-field ray marching and sparse volume rendering, primarily by minimizing the number of expensive Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluations or traversal steps. Renders scenes defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by casting rays from a camera, marching them to surface intersections, and shading the hit points using the Blinn-Phong lighting model. Renders dynamic, complex scenes by streaming object definitions from the CPU to the GPU in structured buffers, allowing for per-pixel evaluation of multiple objects without hardcoding the scene geometry in the shader. Provides the mechanism to evaluate the distance from a query point to the nearest surface in a scene, serving as the fundamental query primitive for distance-field ray marching. Renders particle-based data (such as Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics fluid simulations) by treating the volume as a continuous scalar field composed of additive weighted radial basis functions (RBFs), specifically Gaussians. A geometric method for rendering implicit surfaces by iteratively stepping along a ray using the distance to the nearest surface as the step size. Not given in the sources. An algorithm for transforming a Signed Distance Bound (SDB) into a polygon mesh by combining sphere tracing (ray marching) with traditional polygonization techniques like Marching Cubes. An alternative focus+context visualization used when WebGL2 image2D/atomicuint support is unavailable (e.g., SwiftShader, sandboxed environments). It modulates the per-sample alpha of a ray-march shader using a focus sphere kernel. Initialize sphere center to mesh bounding box center: sphereCenter = ((bbox.min + bbox.max) 0.5). Initialize sphere radius to 25% of the smallest bounding box dimension: initialRadius = min(bboxSize.x, bboxSize.y, bboxSize.z) 0.25. Set uniforms: uSphereCenter = sphereCenter, uSphereRadius = initialRadius, uFocusMode = 1. On pointer down (button 0), set dragging=true, record lastX/lastY, and capture pointer. On pointer move while dragging, calculate dx/dy from lastX/lastY. Compute worldPerPixel = (sphereRadius / canvas.clientHeight) 2.0. Extract camera right/up vectors. Update sphereCenter: sphereCenter += right (dx worldPerPixel) + up (-dy worldPerPixel). Update uSphereCenter uniform. On pointer up, set dragging=false and release pointer capture. On dispose, remove event listeners and set uFocusMode = 0. The focus mask is computed as focusT = clamp(distance(p, sphereCenter) / sphereRadius, 0, 1); focusMask = pow(focusT, 4.0); perSampleAlpha = focusMask. A method to ray trace Blinn soft objects with constant radius by applying sphere-tracing after performing a mapping that allows computing a signed distance approximation to the density field. A pipeline for rendering mega-scale periodic shell-lattice structures that combines hybrid implicit lattice and mesh shell representations, using an augmented tracing distance query to avoid costly SDF calculations. Leverages lattice periodicity for efficiency by employing a local tracing distance query within a single cell. Pre-compute near-far bounds for each ray by counting the minimum and maximum distances of ray-to-mesh intersections. Sample 64 coarse points along the ray. Adopt a progressive up-sampling strategy to guide the sampling of 64 fine points, yielding 128 samples for each ray. Distillation loss: Supervised with output from the teacher model (NeuS) for queried color and SDF value. Background supervision: Binary cross-entropy loss using foreground masks for unbounded backgrounds. Batch size: 512 rays. Optimizer: Adam with initial learning rate 0.0005 and cosine annealing scheduler with 5000 warm-up steps. Hardware: Single Nvidia RTX3090-24G GPU. Training time: Approximately 16 hours for each model. Model Architecture: Geometry Code lg(x) (dim 32), Texture Code lt(x) (dim 32), Sign Distance h(x) (dim 1). Interpolated Items include lt(x) (dim 32), gradient of SDF |\text{grad}x s| (dim 256), s (dim 256), \gamma (dim 256), h(x) (dim 1), d (dim 160), \gamma (dim 32). Geometry Decoder outputs (256, 256, 256). Radiance Decoder outputs (3). Calculate the back plate position first. Calculate the front plate position. Perform the marching algorithm along the ray from the observer's point of view through the cube, potentially starting this in the same shader as the front plate calculation to avoid launching the process twice. Update the controller and view matrix based on the old one, applying rescaling if necessary. Draw the frame around the volume and generate the color maps. A raymarching debug overlay that color-codes each pixel based on the number of sphere tracing iterations required to reach the surface, visualized with a Turbo/Viridis colormap. Map step count 1–12 to cobalt/emerald colors. Map step count 13–30 to cyan/yellow colors. Map step count 31–64 to orange/magenta colors, typically occurring at grazing silhouettes. Render a chain of 5 translucent Marching Spheres along a demonstration ray converging toward the target geometry. Distance-field ray marching, often referred to as sphere tracing, was popularized by John C. Hart in 1992 with his paper "Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces". The method gained significant traction in the demoscene and real-time graphics community in the early 2000s, particularly through the work of Inigo Quilez, who detailed distance estimators and procedural modeling techniques. It has since become a standard technique for rendering implicit surfaces, fractals, and procedural geometry in shaders and real-time applications. name: FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration
head: High-level view algorithm of how step size is computed during the FBM loop, Procedural FBM Sphere Tracing
body: This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by computing valid Sphere Distance Bounds (SDB) and adaptive step sizes using a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) derived from the FBM structure itself. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM sum at every step, this approach progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and larger step sizes. It builds on Sphere Tracing and Step Rules by replacing explicit spatial acceleration structures with a procedural hierarchy that reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. The algorithm integrates the FBM summation loop with the sphere tracing step computation. Instead of evaluating all n octaves to get a single distance value, it computes the FBM value F, the derivative along the ray dF, and a valid step size incrementally. It uses a bounding volume BVH representing the maximum possible contribution of the remaining uncomputed octaves to decide whether to compute a step size and whether to terminate the octave loop early. Inputs: p: Current 3D position in space. n: Total number of octaves in the FBM sum. v: Threshold function (hypertexture), typically approximated by its 1st order affine Taylor polynomial. u: Normalized ray direction vector. k: Early Stop threshold parameter (integer). \lambda{noise}, \gamma{noise}: Lipschitz constants for the base noise function (e.g., Perlin noise [Per85] or Worley noise [Wor96]). Outputs: F: The final FBM value at the hit point or current position. step: The computed step size to advance the ray. Data Structures: F: Scalar accumulator for the FBM sum. dF: Scalar accumulator for the directional derivative along the ray. step: Scalar accumulator for the total step size. BVH: Scalar bounding volume representing the upper bound of the remaining FBM contribution. inclFuncParams: Tuple (BVH, \lambda, dF, \gamma) passed to the intersection function. Parameters: n: Typical value 20 (as used in Sponge scene tests). k: Typical values tested: 0, 1, 2, 3. \epsilon: Convergence threshold for surface hit (from parent algorithm). t{max}: Maximum ray distance (from parent algorithm). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize F \leftarrow 0, dF \leftarrow 0, step \leftarrow 0. Set global Lipschitz constants \lambda \leftarrow \lambda{noise} \times n and \gamma \leftarrow \gamma{noise} \times n. 2. Octave Loop: Iterate i from 1 to n: a. Accumulate Octave: Add the current octave value to the sum: F \leftarrow F + oi(p), where oi(p) is the i-th octave of the noise function evaluated at p. b. Accumulate Derivative: Add the derivative of the current octave along the ray direction: dF \leftarrow dF + (u \cdot o'i(p)), where o'i(p) is the gradient of the octave. c. Compute Bounding Volume: Calculate the bounding volume for the remaining octaves: BVH \leftarrow F + s(i+1, n), where s(i+1, n) is the sum of the absolute maximum bounds of the remaining octaves from i+1 to n. d. Determine Step Computation: Determine if a step size needs to be computed: compStep \leftarrow (i == n) OR (BVH - v(0) < 0). This condition is true if it is the last octave or if the bounding volume indicates the ray is outside the threshold region (empty space). e. Compute Step Size: If compStep is true: i. Adaptive Lipschitz: Replace global constants with local values for the current partial sum: \lambda \leftarrow \lambda{noise} \times i, \gamma \leftarrow \gamma{noise} \times i. ii. Prepare Parameters: Set inclFuncParams \leftarrow (BVH, \lambda, dF, \gamma). iii. Intersect: Compute the current step size increment: curr\step \leftarrow intersect(inclFuncParams, v). The intersect function solves for the distance t such that the inclusion function (based on BVH, \lambda, dF, \gamma) intersects the threshold v. iv. Update Step: step \leftarrow step + curr\step. v. Sub-stepping Guard: If Sub-stepping is enabled, enforce minimum step: step \leftarrow \max(step, curr\step). f. Sub-stepping (Optional): If Sub-stepping is enabled: i. Move ray position: p \leftarrow p + u \cdot curr\step. ii. Update sum: F \leftarrow v(curr\step). iii. Update threshold: v \leftarrow v at curr\step. iv. Update derivative: dF \leftarrow dF + \gamma \cdot curr\step. v. Clamp derivative: dF \leftarrow \max(dF, \lambda). g. Early Stop + k: Decrement k \leftarrow k - 1. If k < 0, break the loop. 3. Return: Return F and step. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbmspheretracingstep(p, n, vfunc, u, k, lambdanoise, gammanoise, noisefunc): """ Compute FBM value and step size using BVH acceleration. Args: p: Current 3D position (vec3) n: Number of octaves (int) vfunc: Threshold function (callable, approximated by 1st order Taylor) u: Ray direction (vec3, normalized) k: Early stop threshold (int) lambdanoise: Lipschitz constant for base noise gammanoise: Second Lipschitz constant for base noise noisefunc: Base noise function (e.g., Perlin) Returns: F: Final FBM value (float) step: Computed step size (float) """ F = 0.0 dF = 0.0 step = 0.0 # Global Lipschitz constants for the full FBM sum lam = lambdanoise n gam = gammanoise n for i in range(1, n + 1): # Evaluate current octave oi = noisefunc(p, octave=i) oigrad = noisefuncgradient(p, octave=i) # Accumulate FBM sum and derivative F += oi dF += dot(u, oigrad) # Compute Bounding Volume for remaining octaves # s(i+1, n) is the sum of absolute bounds of remaining octaves. # Not given in the sources. Implementer must derive based on specific FBM definition. sremaining = 0.0 BVH = F + sremaining # Determine if step size computation is required compStep = (i == n) or (BVH - vfunc(0) < 0) if compStep: # Adaptive Lipschitz: use local constants for current partial sum lam = lambdanoise i gam = gammanoise i # Prepare inclusion function parameters inclFuncParams = (BVH, lam, dF, gam) # Compute current step size # intersect solves for t where inclusion function intersects v(t) # Not given in the sources. Implementer must derive based on the specific inclusion function. currstep = 0.0 # Update total step size step += currstep # Sub-stepping guard (optional) # step = max(step, currstep) # Commented out if SS is on, as per source # Sub-stepping related updates # Move along ray p = p + u currstep # Update sum and threshold F = vfunc(currstep) # vfunc = vfuncatstep(vfunc, currstep) # Update threshold function state # Not given in the sources. Implementer must derive based on specific threshold function. # Update derivative dF += gam currstep dF = max(dF, lam) # If Improved Quadratic (not detailed in source, assumed part of inclFuncParams) pass # Early Stop + k k -= 1 if k < 0: break return F, step Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thread Divergence: The Early Stop feature causes thread divergence within a warp, as different rays may exit the octave loop at different iterations. However, rays from the same warp are spatially coherent, so divergence is typically limited to a single octave. GPU Memory Usage: The method avoids O(n) per-thread data storage required by dynamic re-ordering methods [WH96], making it more suitable for fast GPU implementation. Threshold Approximation: The threshold function v(p) is approximated by its 1st order (affine) Taylor polynomial. Higher order approximations were not implemented as they showed no noticeable error improvement. Noise Parameters: The algorithm requires \lambda{noise} and \gamma{noise} for arbitrary noise functions. Default values depend on the specific noise implementation (e.g., Perlin with or without abs()). This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by treating the cascaded sum of octaves as a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and empty space skipping. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. It builds on FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration by replacing the explicit spatial tree with a procedural hierarchy derived from the FBM structure itself. Time Complexity: The average cost per step is reduced from O(N) to O(k), where k is the number of octaves computed before early termination or bounding volume check. Memory Complexity: O(1) per thread, avoiding the O(n) storage required by dynamic re-ordering methods. Measured Performance: Tested on an Nvidia RTX 4080 Ti at 1024×1024 resolution on a "Sponge" scene (20-octave Perlin noise FBM): Ray Marching (Early Stop): Reduced average octaves from 49,596.3 to 24,252.6 (close view) and 56,577.8 to 10,347.0 (far view). Time reduced from 770.0ms to 399.8ms (1.9x speedup) and 843.0ms to 178.4ms (4.7x speedup). Sphere Tracing (Adaptive Lipschitz): Reduced average steps from 428.1 to 331.7 (close view) and 223.7 to 154.5 (far view). Time reduced from 110.2ms to 87.1ms (1.3x speedup) and 42.4ms to 28.3ms (1.5x speedup). Sphere Tracing (Sub-stepping): Further reduced time from 87.1ms to 72.5ms (1.2x speedup over Adaptive Lipschitz) in close view, and 28.3ms to 22.0ms (1.3x speedup) in far view. Sphere Tracing (Early Stop + k=1): Reduced time from 72.5ms to 65.0ms (1.1x speedup) in close view, and 22.7ms to 16.7ms (1.4x speedup) in far view. Strengths: Significant performance gains in scenes with large empty spaces or intricate details where FBM evaluation is costly. Low memory overhead makes it GPU-friendly. Limitations: Step sizes may be slightly smaller than those from dynamic re-ordering methods [WH96], but the overhead is much lower. Thread divergence from Early Stop is minimal due to spatial coherence. When to Use: Rendering procedural volumetric noise (FBM) where evaluation cost is high and empty space skipping is beneficial. When Not to Use: Scenes where FBM evaluation is cheap or where dynamic re-ordering's slightly better step sizes are critical and memory is not a constraint. The method was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". It was implemented in GLSL fragment shaders and tested on high-end GPUs. The approach leverages the mathematical properties of FBM to create an implicit BVH, avoiding the need for external acceleration structures. It addresses the computational bottleneck of evaluating high-octave FBM noise in sphere tracing, particularly in large, detailed scenes. name: FBM Sphere Tracing with Implicit BVH
head: Dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchy for FBM, Progressive evaluation of octaves
body: This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by treating the cascaded sum of octaves as a dynamic, implicit Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH). It progressively evaluates octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold, allowing for early termination and empty space skipping. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness. It builds on FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration by replacing the explicit spatial tree with a procedural hierarchy derived from the FBM structure itself. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. FBM parameters: octave count N, amplitude Ai and frequency Fi for each octave i \in [0, N-1]. Base noise function n(\mathbf{p}) with range [-1, 1]. Isosurface threshold v (typically 0). Outputs: Distance to the nearest surface intersection or empty space indicator. Accumulated density (for volume rendering). Data Structures: No explicit tree nodes are stored; the hierarchy is implicit in the loop order of octave evaluation. Variables: val (current accumulated FBM value) and rem (remaining maximum possible contribution of uncomputed octaves). Algorithm: The core optimization occurs within the FBM evaluation loop. Instead of computing all N octaves, the algorithm maintains a bound on the maximum possible value the remaining octaves can add. If the current value plus this maximum bound cannot reach the threshold v, the point is guaranteed to be outside the object (assuming the object exists where f(\mathbf{p}) > v), and the loop terminates early. 1. Initialize val = 0. 2. Initialize rem = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} Ai. This represents the worst-case contribution if all remaining noise samples were at their maximum positive value (1). 3. Iterate through octaves i from 0 to N-1: a. Compute noise sample ni = n(\mathbf{p} \cdot Fi). b. Update val: val = val + Ai \cdot ni. c. Update rem: rem = rem - Ai. Since the base noise is bounded in [-1, 1], removing Ai correctly bounds the maximum possible contribution of all remaining unprocessed octaves. d. Early Termination Check: If val + rem < v, terminate the loop immediately. The point is outside the object. 4. If the loop completes, val is the full FBM value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fbmwithimplicitbvh(p, octaves, threshold): """ Computes FBM with early termination based on implicit BVH bounds. Args: p: 3D point position. octaves: List of tuples (amplitude, frequency) for each octave. threshold: The isosurface threshold (typically 0). Returns: The FBM value if fully computed, or the partial value if early terminated. Note: The caller must handle the 'early terminated' state to skip ray marching steps. """ val = 0.0 # Initialize rem as the sum of all amplitudes (worst-case potential of all octaves) rem = sum(a for a, f in octaves) for i, (amplitude, frequency) in enumerate(octaves): # Evaluate base noise at scaled position. # Standard 3D noise function bounded in [-1, 1]. noiseval = noise(p frequency) # Add current octave contribution val += amplitude noiseval # Update remaining bound: remove current amplitude from potential max # The remaining octaves can contribute at most their sum of amplitudes rem -= amplitude # Check if it's impossible to reach the threshold # If val + rem < threshold, even if all remaining noise samples are 1, # the total will be below the threshold. if val + rem < threshold: return val, True # True indicates early termination return val, False # False indicates full computation Parameters: Threshold v: The density threshold defining the object boundary. Default is 0. Object exists where f(\mathbf{p}) > v. Octave count N: The number of noise layers. Higher counts increase complexity and the Lipschitz constant. Amplitude Ai: Typically decreases with octave index (e.g., Ai = A0 \cdot \text{lacunarity}^{-i}). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The accumulation of val and rem must be done with sufficient precision to avoid false positives in the early termination check, especially when rem is small. Noise Range: The method assumes the base noise function is strictly bounded in [-1, 1]. Gradient Calculation: For sphere tracing step sizes, gradients are still required. If early termination occurs, the gradient is undefined or incomplete. The algorithm must ensure that sphere tracing steps are only taken when the full FBM (or a sufficiently accurate approximation) is available, or use the partial value with caution. This method accelerates the ray marching of implicit surfaces defined by a sum of bounded functions Fn(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^n fi(\mathbf{p}) by exploiting the known value ranges of individual terms. It constructs an implicit hierarchy where partial sums serve as bounding volumes for the final sum, allowing early termination when the potential range of the total function excludes the isosurface threshold. It differs from explicit BVH approaches by computing bounds on-the-fly from pre-sorted function ranges rather than traversing a spatial tree structure. A technique to render hypertextures by modulating a smooth main shape function with FBM noise, while preserving the ability to use the implicit BVH and gradient-based sphere tracing optimizations. It defines a smooth base shape function S(\mathbf{p}) (e.g., a sphere or plane) and computes the FBM noise N(\mathbf{p}). Unlike naive hypertexture rendering which might require full evaluation of complex modulated functions, this method keeps the structure compatible with the progressive octave evaluation and gradient-based stepping. Time Complexity: Reduces average evaluation cost per step in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves needed to prove emptiness. In dense regions, the cost remains O(N) as all octaves must be evaluated. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory is required, as no explicit tree structure is stored. The hierarchy is implicit in the evaluation order. Measured Performance: Speedups up to 12-fold on opaque or constant semi-transparent scenes compared to classical sphere tracing, and up to 2-fold on non-constant density volumetric scenes. Gains of up to \times 1.8 are attributed specifically to the progressive octave evaluation. Strengths: Real-time performance on large, detailed scenes; no precomputation or storage overhead; compatible with animated content due to proceduralism. Limitations: Effectiveness depends on the distribution of the noise; if the object is dense and fills most of the scene, early termination opportunities are reduced. The method assumes the base noise is bounded in [-1, 1]. Originating from the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes", this method addresses the high rendering cost of procedural 3D noise in real-time applications. Precomputing volumes is storage-prohibitive for large open worlds and prevents animation. The method leverages the structure of FBM, treating cascaded sums as nested bounding volumes to enable efficient empty space skipping. It is part of a broader effort to accelerate sphere tracing for general Signed Distance Functions (SDF) by combining progressive evaluation with Lipschitz-based stepping. name: Implicit BVH for Sum of Bounded Functions
head: Procedural Bounding Volume Hierarchy
body: This method accelerates the ray marching of implicit surfaces defined by a sum of bounded functions Fn(\mathbf{p}) = \sum{i=1}^n fi(\mathbf{p}) by exploiting the known value ranges of individual terms. It constructs an implicit hierarchy where partial sums serve as bounding volumes for the final sum, allowing early termination when the potential range of the total function excludes the isosurface threshold. It differs from explicit BVH approaches by computing bounds on-the-fly from pre-sorted function ranges rather than traversing a spatial tree structure. Inputs: A set of n scalar functions fi: \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}, where each fi is bounded within [-\Delta{fi}, \Delta{fi}]. A target threshold value v (typically 0 for isosurfaces). A ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} for ray marching. Outputs: The intersection distance t along the ray, or a failure indicator if no intersection exists within the marching bounds. Data Structures: Precomputed Range Sum Array: An array S of size n+1 where S[k] = s(k, n) = \sum{m=k}^{n} \Delta{fm} for k \in [1, n+1], with S[n+1] = 0. Sorted Functions: The functions fi must be sorted such that \Delta{f1} \geq \Delta{f2} \geq \dots \geq \Delta{fn}. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute \Delta{fi} for all i. Sort fi in descending order of \Delta{fi}. Compute the suffix sums s(i+1, n) for all i \in [1, n]. 2. Ray Marching Initialization: Start at t=0 (or ray origin offset). 3. Iteration: For each marching step: a. Evaluate the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Initialize partial sum F{current} = 0 and current index i=1. c. Early Termination Check Loop: While i \leq n: i. Evaluate fi(\mathbf{p}) and update F{current} \leftarrow F{current} + fi(\mathbf{p}). ii. Compute the inclusion interval for the final sum Fn based on the current partial sum: Fn = F{current} \pm s(i+1, n). iii. Check if the threshold v lies outside this interval. If v < F{current} - s(i+1, n) or v > F{current} + s(i+1, n), then no root exists for Fn at this \mathbf{p} in the current direction. Terminate the ray march (return failure). iv. Increment i. d. If the loop completes, Fn(\mathbf{p}) = F{current} is the exact function value. e. Check if |Fn(\mathbf{p}) - v| < \epsilon (convergence). If yes, return t. f. Compute step size h (e.g., using Lipschitz constants if available, or fixed step) and advance t \leftarrow t + h. Formulas: Inclusion Function for Intermediate Sum: F{i+1} = Fi(\mathbf{p}) \pm \Delta{f{i+1}} \quad (4) where \Deltaf is the bound such that f \in [-\Deltaf, \Deltaf]. Sum of Ranges: s(i, j) = \sum{m=i}^{j} \Delta{fm} \quad \text{for } j \geq i. Inclusion Function for Final Sum from Partial Sum: Fn = Fi(\mathbf{p}) \pm s(i+1, n) \quad (6). Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence tolerance for ray marching. Not given in the sources. Step size strategy: Not given in the sources (depends on Lipschitz continuity assumptions in later sections). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unsorted Functions: If functions are not sorted by descending \Delta{fi}, the early termination guarantee is weakened or invalid, potentially leading to incorrect skips or missed intersections. Invalid Bounds: If \Delta{fi} is not a tight bound, the inclusion interval becomes loose, reducing the effectiveness of early termination but maintaining correctness. Lipschitz Continuity: This method assumes only boundedness. If the derivative is not Lipschitz continuous, standard sphere tracing step sizes may be invalid, requiring alternative marching strategies. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchsumofboundedfunctions(rayorigin, raydirection, functions, deltas, threshold, maxsteps, stepsizefunc): """ functions: list of callable fi(p) deltas: list of float Deltafi, sorted descending threshold: float v """ n = len(functions) # Precompute suffix sums s(i+1, n) # s[k] corresponds to s(k+1, n) for k in 0..n-1 # s[n] = 0 suffixsums = [0.0] (n + 1) currentsum = 0.0 for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): currentsum += deltas[i] suffixsums[i] = currentsum t = 0.0 for step in range(maxsteps): p = rayorigin + t raydirection partialsum = 0.0 earlystop = False for i in range(n): partialsum += functionsi # Inclusion interval for final sum Fn based on partial sum F{i+1} # Fn = partialsum +/- s(i+1, n) # Note: suffixsums[i] is s(i+1, n) because i is 0-indexed # i=0 -> suffixsums[0] = s(1, n) # i=1 -> suffixsums[1] = s(2, n) lowerbound = partialsum - suffixsums[i] upperbound = partialsum + suffixsums[i] if threshold < lowerbound or threshold > upperbound: earlystop = True break if earlystop: return None # No intersection # If loop completes, partialsum is the exact Fn(p) if abs(partialsum - threshold) < 1e-6: return t # Advance ray t += stepsizefunc(partialsum, deltas) # Implementation depends on Lipschitz info return None # Max steps reached Uses derivative bounds to compute safe step sizes. Chosen when functions are differentiable and Lipschitz constants are known. Link: Lipschitz Sphere Tracing. Uses explicit spatial subdivision. Chosen for sparse scenes or when functions have complex spatial locality not captured by range bounds. Link: Octree BVH. Time Complexity: O(n) per ray marching step in the worst case (evaluating all functions). Best case is O(1) if early termination occurs at the first function. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store precomputed range sums and function references. Strengths: No spatial data structure construction overhead; efficient for functions with rapidly decaying ranges (e.g., FBM octaves). Limitations: Requires prior knowledge of tight bounds \Delta{fi}; sorting overhead; less effective if bounds are loose or functions have similar ranges. When to Use: When the implicit function is a sum of many bounded terms with known, decreasing ranges (e.g., procedural noise). When Not to Use: When functions are not bounded or bounds are unknown; when spatial coherence is high and explicit BVH is more efficient. Originated in the context of fast sphere tracing for procedural volumetric noise. The method was introduced to exploit the hierarchical nature of FBM (Fractional Brownian Motion) noise, where higher-frequency octaves have smaller amplitudes, allowing them to be treated as bounding volumes for lower-frequency sums. It is used in real-time rendering of procedural landscapes and materials. name: Raymarching with Depth Buffer Occlusion
head: Depth-buffered Raymarching, Raymarching with Mesh Interaction, Z-Buffer Occlusion
body: Raymarching with Depth Buffer Occlusion is a technique that allows raymarched Signed Distance Field (SDF) objects to correctly occlude and be occluded by standard mesh-based geometry in a scene. It solves the problem where raymarched objects typically float on top of all other geometry because the raymarching loop ignores the depth of existing meshes. By sampling the scene's depth buffer to determine the distance to the nearest mesh surface, the raymarcher can terminate early if it passes that distance, ensuring proper layering. The method integrates the scene's depth buffer into the sphere tracing loop defined in Distance-field ray marching. It requires access to the camera's view matrix, inverse view matrix, and the rendered depth texture. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} (camera position in world space). Ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized direction in world space). Depth buffer texture \mathcal{D} (e.g., CameraDepthTexture). View matrix V and Inverse View Matrix V^{-1}. SDF function f(\mathbf{p}). Outputs: Final color C for the pixel, blending the raymarched SDF result with the background mesh color. 1. Depth Buffer: A 2D texture storing depth values, accessed via CameraDepthTexture. The values are typically non-linear and must be converted to linear eyespace depth. 2. Vertex Shader Output: A structure containing the world-space ray direction, normalized in the Z-axis. 1. Ray Direction Normalization (Vertex Shader): The ray direction \mathbf{r}d is computed in eyespace (view space). In eyespace, z < 0 is forward. To calculate the true distance from the depth buffer, the ray direction is normalized such that its Z-component magnitude is 1.0. Let \mathbf{r}n be the Z-normalized ray direction in eyespace: \mathbf{r}n = \frac{\mathbf{r}d}{|rd.z|} The absolute value |rd.z| is used to prevent flipping the ray direction if rd.z is negative. Transform \mathbf{r}n from eyespace to worldspace using the inverse view matrix V^{-1}: \mathbf{r}{world} = V^{-1} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{r}n \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} (Treating \mathbf{r}n as a direction vector, the w-component is 0). 2. Depth Sampling (Fragment Shader): Sample the depth buffer at the current pixel's UV coordinates to get the non-linear depth value d{nl}. Convert this to linear eyespace depth d{eye}. Calculate the true Euclidean distance s from the camera origin to the mesh surface along the ray. Using similar triangles, the ratio of the true distance |r| to the eyespace depth d{eye} is equal to the ratio of the length of the Z-normalized ray |\mathbf{r}n| to 1: s = d{eye} \times |\mathbf{r}n| where |\mathbf{r}n| = \sqrt{r{n,x}^2 + r{n,y}^2 + r{n,z}^2}. 3. Raymarching Loop: Perform standard sphere tracing starting from the camera origin \mathbf{o} with direction \mathbf{r}{world}. For each step i: Current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{r}{world}. Evaluate SDF: dist = f(\mathbf{p}). Occlusion Check: If the accumulated distance t \ge s, the ray has passed the mesh surface. Terminate the loop and return a transparent color to allow the mesh to show through. Surface Hit Check: If dist < \epsilon (convergence threshold), the ray hit the SDF surface. Compute shading and return the color. Step: Advance t \leftarrow t + dist. Max Steps: If i exceeds a maximum step count, terminate. 4. Blending: The final pixel color is a blend of the background mesh color and the raymarched SDF color. If the raymarcher returns transparent (due to occlusion), the background mesh color is used. If it returns an opaque SDF color, it is composited over the background. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(vertexpos, invviewmatrix): # Ray direction in eyespace (view space) rdeyespace = normalize(vertexpos) # Normalize Z-component magnitude to 1.0 to prevent flip rneyespace = rdeyespace / abs(rdeyespace.z) # Transform to worldspace (direction vector, w=0) rayworld = invviewmatrix @ vec4(rneyespace, 0.0) return rayworld.xyz def fragmentshader(uv, roworld, rdworld, rayworld, depthtexture, colortexture, nearplane): # Sample depth buffer depthnl = depthtexture.sample(uv).r # Convert to linear eyespace depth (standard projection math) deptheye = 1.0 / (depthnl (1.0 - nearplane) + nearplane) # Calculate true distance to mesh surface scalefactor = length(rayworld) s = deptheye scalefactor # Sample background mesh color bgcolor = colortexture.sample(uv).rgb # Raymarch loop t = 0.0 maxsteps = 64 hitcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for i in range(maxsteps): if t >= s: break p = roworld + t rdworld dist = f(p) # Scene SDF evaluation if dist < 0.001: normal = computesdfnormal(f, p) hitcolor = vec4(shadesurface(p, normal), 1.0) break t += dist # Alpha blend with background finalcolor = bgcolor (1.0 - hitcolor.a) + hitcolor.rgb hitcolor.a return finalcolor Max Steps: Typically 64. Convergence Threshold (\epsilon): Typically 0.001. Near Plane: Standard camera parameter. Depth Texture: Platform-specific sampler (e.g., CameraDepthTexture). Ray Direction Flip: In eyespace, z < 0 is forward. Dividing the ray direction by rd.z without taking the absolute value will flip the ray direction if rd.z is negative, causing the raymarched scene to appear inverted. Depth Precision: The depth buffer may have limited precision. Using linear conversion is crucial to convert non-linear depth values to linear distances for accurate comparison. Near Plane Clipping: The depth buffer only contains information for pixels within the view frustum and beyond the near plane. Transparency: If the mesh in the depth buffer is transparent, the depth value may not represent the true front-most surface. This method assumes the depth buffer contains the front-most opaque geometry. This variant addresses the occlusion of scale-invariant integral surfaces (like skeleton-based sphere-cones) in the depth buffer. It computes a scaling factor for the radii of sphere-cone primitives to guarantee correct occlusion. The worst-case configuration for this scaling is two segment primitives aligned with the viewing direction -\mathbf{v}, both having radius \tau at point q. Due to surface scale invariance, the scaling factor is computed numerically for a unit radius case, representing the distance from q to the isosurface in direction \mathbf{v}. This worst-case configuration is independent of the actual skeleton layout, requiring no additional skeleton processing. This variant extends the Holistic UOI pipeline to support 3D object intersections and LOD management by using multipass rendering instead of single-pass. Each scene SDF component is defined as an independent virtual scene equation and rendered in a separate pass. A custom floating-point depth buffer stores the minimum distance values from previous passes. During subsequent passes, the depth buffer acts as another SDF component, and an additional check terminates the raymarch if the traveled distance is smaller than the stored depth buffer value. This solves the original single-pass limitation where occlusion algorithms could not handle intersections between SDF components. Time Complexity: Adds O(1) overhead per pixel for depth sampling and distance calculation. The raymarching loop may terminate earlier, potentially reducing the number of SDF evaluations if the mesh is closer than the SDF surface. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the depth buffer texture, which is typically already present in the rendering pipeline. Performance: The method is efficient as it leverages existing hardware depth buffers. The primary cost is the additional arithmetic for depth conversion and the early exit check. Strengths: Enables seamless integration of raymarched SDF objects with traditional mesh-based geometry, allowing for correct occlusion and interaction. Limitations: Only works with opaque mesh geometry in the depth buffer. Transparent meshes or SDF objects rendered after the depth pass may not occlude correctly. Requires access to the depth buffer, which may not be available in all rendering contexts (e.g., deferred rendering without depth pre-pass). The technique was popularized by Adrian Booth in a blog post detailing the implementation of raymarched distance fields in Unity. It addresses a common issue in hybrid rendering pipelines where raymarched objects fail to interact with rasterized geometry. The method relies on standard graphics API features (depth buffers, view matrices) and does not require specialized hardware beyond standard GPU capabilities. name: SDF Depth Buffer Integration
head: Depth Writing with Hit Detection, Raymarching with Depth Buffer Output, Sphere Tracing for Depth Output, Sphere Tracing with Depth Buffer Output
body: SDF Depth Buffer Integration is a technique that extends sphere tracing by explicitly writing the computed surface hit point's depth to the hardware depth buffer (SVDepth). This allows ray-marched SDF geometry to participate in standard depth testing, ensuring correct occlusion between sphere-traced objects and rasterized geometry. Without this integration, the depth buffer records the depth of the proxy mesh face (e.g., a bounding cube) rather than the actual ray-marched surface, leading to incorrect occlusion where rasterized objects behind the SDF surface appear in front, or vice versa. It builds on Distance-field ray marching. The method operates in the fragment shader, extending the standard sphere tracing loop to output both color and depth. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Vertex shader output struct v2f containing clip-space position, object-space local position (ray origin), and object-space view direction (ray direction). Output: SVTARGET (color) and SVDepth (depth value). Data Structures: The vertex-to-fragment struct v2f layout is: position (SVPOSITION): Clip-space vertex position. localPosition (TEXCOORD0): Object-space vertex position, used as the ray origin. viewDirection (TEXCOORD1): Object-space vector from camera to vertex, un-normalized. Parameters: MAXSTEPS: Maximum ray march iterations. Typical value: 32. THICKNESS: SDF value threshold for hit detection. Typical value: 0.001. NORMALEPSILON: Offset for finite difference normal estimation. Typical value: 0.01. Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Setup: Calculate localPosition as the vertex position in object space. Calculate viewDirection as vertex - objectSpaceCameraPos in object space. Calculate position using UnityObjectToClipPos(vertex). 2. Fragment Shader Initialization: Extract pos from localPosition. Normalize viewDirection to get dir. Initialize progress (accumulated distance) to 0. Initialize hitsurface flag to false. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate up to MAXSTEPS. Calculate sample point: samplePoint = pos + dir progress. Evaluate SDF: distance = scene(samplePoint). Hit Check: If distance < THICKNESS, set hitsurface = true and break. Step: Advance ray: progress = progress + distance. 4. Miss Handling: If !hitsurface, execute discard. This prevents writing to SVTARGET or SVDepth and avoids driver differences associated with clip(-1). 5. Color Calculation: Compute surface color using samplePoint (normal estimation, lighting) and write to SVTARGET. 6. Depth Calculation: Transform samplePoint to clip space: tracedClipPos = UnityObjectToClipPos(float4(samplePoint, 1.0)). Compute NDC depth: depth = tracedClipPos.z / tracedClipPos.w. Write depth to SVDepth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vert(vertex, worldtoobject, worldspacecamerapos): # Clip-space position for rasterization position = modelviewprojectionmatrix float4(vertex, 1.0) # Ray origin in object space localposition = vertex # Ray direction in object space (un-normalized to preserve interpolation precision) objectspacecamerapos = worldtoobject float4(worldspacecamerapos, 1.0) viewdirection = vertex - objectspacecamerapos return v2f(position, localposition, viewdirection) def frag(i): pos = i.localPosition dir = normalize(i.viewdirection) progress = 0.0 samplepoint = vec3(0.0) hitsurface = False for in range(MAXSTEPS): samplepoint = pos + dir progress distance = scene(samplepoint) if distance < THICKNESS: hitsurface = True break progress += distance if not hitsurface: return # discard pixel # Compute surface color via normal estimation and diffuse lighting color = rendersurface(samplepoint) # Transform hit point to clip space tracedclippos = modelviewprojectionmatrix float4(samplepoint, 1.0) # Perspective divide for NDC depth depth = tracedclippos.z / tracedclippos.w return color, depth Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Proxy Mesh Depth: Without explicit depth output, the GPU records the proxy mesh depth, causing incorrect occlusion. Early-Z Optimization: Writing SVDepth disables the GPU's early-Z optimization for affected pixels because the hardware cannot know the depth before the fragment shader runs. Discard vs Clip: Using clip(-1) can cause issues with depth buffering or sorting; discard is preferred. Unnormalized View Direction: The view direction is stored un-normalized in TEXCOORD1 to avoid precision loss in interpolation, but must be normalized in the fragment shader. Render Queue: The shader should use Queue=Geometry+1 to render after standard opaque geometry, ensuring rasterized meshes write depth first. DisableBatching=True is required as batching breaks the object-to-world transform used for ray setup. IgnoreProjector=True avoids projector interference. A pixel shader technique to extract the near and far depth values of active cells for ray marching. It uses alpha blending to simultaneously store the smallest depth in the RGB channels and the largest depth in the Alpha channel. The view space Z component (input.projPos.w) is output to the Red channel for the smallest depth and to the Alpha channel for the largest depth. The hardware's output merger keeps the smallest value for color components (RGB) and the largest value for the alpha component when blending, allowing extraction of both near and far depths in a single pass. Clips the ray segment to the viewport boundaries to avoid accessing out-of-bounds depth buffer texels. Viewport bounds are defined as xMax=csZBufferSize.x-0.5, xMin=0.5, yMax=csZBufferSize.y-0.5, yMin=0.5. Alpha for Y clipping is calculated as (P1.y - ((P1.y > yMax) ? yMax: yMin)) / (P1.y - P0.y) if P1.y is out of bounds. Alpha for X clipping is calculated similarly, taking the maximum alpha. Endpoints are interpolated to the clipped position: P1 = lerp(P1, P0, alpha), k1 = lerp(k1, k0, alpha), Q1 = lerp(Q1, Q0, alpha). P0 is assumed to be in the viewport, and P1-P0 is never zero when clipping is required, avoiding division by zero. Integration of KRS ray-casting into incrementally rendered scenes using the depth buffer. The depth buffer is used for early termination of rays. Depth is output from the ray casting shader if necessary, e.g., for transparent geometry rendering or deferred shading. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of ray march steps (MAXSTEPS) per pixel. Memory Complexity: Constant per pixel for the depth buffer write. Performance: Writing SVDepth disables early-Z optimization, which can impact performance on fill-rate limited hardware. Strengths: Ensures correct occlusion between SDF geometry and rasterized geometry. Limitations: Disables early-Z; requires careful render queue management (Geometry+1). When to Use: When SDF geometry needs to occlude or be occluded by rasterized geometry. When Not to Use: When SDF geometry is rendered last and does not need to interact with depth from other geometry, or when early-Z performance is critical and occlusion is not required. The method was introduced in Tutorial 045 of the Ronja Tutorials series, extending previous sphere tracing tutorials (043, 044) to address the depth buffer problem. It is implemented in Unity using HLSL/CG. The technique is part of the broader field of signed distance field rendering and ray marching. name: Deferred SDF Rendering
head: Deferred Signed Distance Field rendering, SDF G-buffer pre-pass
body: Deferred SDF Rendering is a technique that decouples Signed Distance Field (SDF) geometry generation from lighting calculations by rendering SDFs to a G-buffer during a pre-pass. This approach allows SDF geometry to participate in standard deferred post-processing effects such as screen-space reflections, ambient occlusion, and bloom, while reducing shader cost and register pressure compared to integrated forward rendering. It differs from integrated SDF rendering by sacrificing high-quality, SDF-specific reflections and shadows in exchange for compatibility with the existing deferred lighting pipeline. The method renders SDFs using a full-screen triangle pass during the G-buffer pre-pass, utilizing a modified standard shader. The core challenge is generating correct ray directions for ray marching and outputting depth values that correctly sort against existing polygonal geometry in the depth buffer. Inputs: Vertex position (v.vertex) and texture coordinates (v.texcoord) from the full-screen triangle. Camera parameters: WorldSpaceCameraPos (eye position), InverseViewProjectionMatrix (inverse of V \times P), UNITYMATRIXVP (view-projection matrix). SDF field definition (implicit in the shader logic, e.g., sphere, box). Outputs: G-buffer data (albedo, normal, roughness, etc., as defined by the modified standard shader). Depth value (outDepth) written to the depth buffer. Vertex Input: Standard vertex structure containing position and UVs. Vertex Output: Structure containing clip-space position (pos) and texture coordinates (tex). Ray Data: eye: float3 world-space camera position. worldPos: float3 world-space position on the far plane (derived from UVs). worldDir: float3 normalized ray direction. 1. Vertex Shader (Pass-through): The vertex shader passes the input vertex position and texture coordinates to the fragment shader without modification. o.pos = v.vertex o.tex = v.texcoord 2. Fragment Shader: Ray Origin and Direction: Calculate the ray origin as the world-space camera position. eye = \text{WorldSpaceCameraPos} Transform the screen-space texture coordinates (ranging from [0, 1]) to clip-space coordinates (ranging from [-1, 1]), setting z=1.0 (far plane) and w=1.0. Note that the y-component must be flipped to match the coordinate system convention. clipPos = (2.0 \cdot i.tex.xy - 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) clipPos.y = -clipPos.y Transform the clip-space position to world space using the inverse view-projection matrix, then perspective divide to obtain the world position on the far plane. worldPos = \text{InverseViewProjectionMatrix} \times clipPos worldPos.xyz = \frac{worldPos.xyz}{worldPos.w} Compute the ray direction by normalizing the vector from the eye to the world position. worldDir = \text{normalize}(worldPos.xyz - eye) 3. Ray Marching: Perform standard SDF ray marching using eye and worldDir to find the hit position (hitPos) on the SDF surface. (Implementation details of the SDF field and marching loop are assumed to be provided by the specific SDF shader logic). 4. Depth Output: To ensure the SDF geometry correctly occludes other geometry and is occluded by it, project the hitPos to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC) using the view-projection matrix and output the depth. clipPos = UNITY\MATRIX\VP \times (hitPos, 1.0) outDepth = \frac{clipPos.z}{clipPos.w} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. struct VertexOutputDeferred { float4 pos: SVPOSITION; float2 tex: TEXCOORD0; }; VertexOutputDeferred vertSDFDeferred(float4 v.vertex: POSITION, float2 v.texcoord: TEXCOORD0) { VertexOutputDeferred o; o.pos = v.vertex; o.tex = v.texcoord; return o; } float4 fragSDFDeferred(VertexOutputDeferred i): SVTARGET { // 1. Calculate Ray Origin float3 eye = WorldSpaceCameraPos; // 2. Calculate Ray Direction // Map UV [0,1] to Clip Space [-1,1], set z=1 (far plane), flip Y float4 clipPos = float4(i.tex.xy 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0, 1.0); clipPos.y = -clipPos.y; // Transform to World Space float4 worldPos = mul(InverseViewProjectionMatrix, clipPos); worldPos.xyz = worldPos.xyz / worldPos.w; // Normalize direction float3 worldDir = normalize(worldPos.xyz - eye); // 3. Ray Marching (Placeholder for specific SDF logic) // float hitDist = RayMarchSDF(eye, worldDir); // float3 hitPos = eye + worldDir hitDist; // For the purpose of depth output, assume hitPos is calculated: float3 hitPos =...; // Result of SDF ray march // 4. Output Depth // Project hitPos to NDC float4 clipHitPos = mul(UNITYMATRIXVP, float4(hitPos, 1.0)); float outDepth = clipHitPos.z / clipHitPos.w; // Write depth to SVDepth (or equivalent depth target) // Note: In Unity's deferred pre-pass, depth is often handled automatically // if SVDEPTH is used, or via a separate depth pass. // The source explicitly calculates outDepth for this purpose. // Output G-buffer data (Albedo, Normal, etc.) //... return float4(0, 0, 0, 1); // Placeholder for G-buffer output } Far Plane: The ray direction calculation assumes a far plane depth of 1.0 in clip space. If the camera's far plane is significantly different, the ray direction accuracy may degrade for distant objects, though normalization mitigates this for direction. Coordinate System: The y-flip in clip space is critical. Failure to flip y results in inverted ray directions, causing SDFs to render incorrectly or not at all. Depth Precision: Writing depth for ray-marched surfaces requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially for thin SDF features or very close/far distances. Lighting Quality: Decoupling lighting from SDF rendering prevents the production of high-quality reflections and shadows specific to the SDF geometry. Shadow Cost: Rendering SDFs into shadowmaps is possible but significantly increases shadow cost and may not be supported by all deferred pipelines without custom modifications. Material Control: Using the standard material system applies settings (roughness, emissive) uniformly to all SDFs rendered with that material, lacking fine-grained control per SDF instance. Time Complexity: The pre-pass adds a full-screen triangle draw call. The fragment shader cost is dominated by the SDF ray marching loops and branches. However, by decoupling lighting, the lighting calculation itself is not repeated per SDF pixel in the main lighting pass, potentially reducing overall register pressure and shader complexity. Memory Complexity: Requires standard G-buffer storage. No additional memory for SDF-specific lighting data is needed in the deferred pipeline. Strengths: Integrates SDFs into existing deferred post-processing effects (SSR, SSAO, Bloom). Reduces shader register pressure by separating geometry generation from lighting. Correctly sorts SDFs against polygonal geometry via depth buffer integration. Limitations: Lacks high-quality, SDF-specific reflections and shadows. Shadow map rendering for SDFs is expensive and non-trivial. Limited material control granularity when using standard shaders. When to Use: When SDFs are used for environmental geometry or effects that benefit from screen-space post-processing, and high-fidelity SDF-specific lighting (like accurate SDF shadows) is not required. When Not to Use: When high-quality reflections or shadows on SDF geometry are critical, or when fine-grained material control per SDF instance is needed. This technique was demonstrated by the author of "Interplay of Light" in December 2017, using Unity 2017.2. It was developed as an experiment to integrate SDFs into an actual rendering engine context, leveraging Unity's material system and deferred rendering pipeline. The SDF implementations referenced were based on external posts (not detailed in the source), and the approach was described as a "fun exercise" and "hacky" but functional for integrating SDFs with post-processing effects. name: Depth Buffering Setup
head: Depth State Setup, Depth Write Configuration
body: This method configures the graphics pipeline state to ensure that ray-marched surfaces in a Signed Distance Field (SDF) volume rendering pass correctly participate in the depth buffer. By writing the correct depth value to SVDepth, the rendered volume occludes other geometry behind it and is itself occluded by geometry in front of it, solving the problem of incorrect depth ordering in hybrid rendering pipelines. It differs from sibling methods like Deferred SDF Rendering by focusing specifically on the depth state configuration required for immediate occlusion culling during the volume pass, rather than deferring the entire lighting computation. The setup involves configuring the depth stencil state before the volume rendering draw call. This ensures that the depth buffer, potentially populated by a previous pass of opaque objects, is used for both reading (occlusion) and writing (depth update). Inputs: Current render target and depth stencil view. Desired depth comparison function (typically Less). Flag to enable depth writes. Outputs: Configured graphics pipeline state object (or equivalent API state). Data Structures: No specific data structures are created by this setup step itself. It modifies the pipeline state. However, it relies on the existence of a depth buffer (e.g., SVDepth target) populated by previous passes. Steps: 1. Enable Depth Testing: Set the depth test function to Less. This ensures that a fragment is only written if its depth value is strictly less than the current value in the depth buffer. 2. Enable Depth Writing: Set the depth write mask to enabled. This allows the ray-marched surface's computed depth to update the depth buffer, occluding subsequent geometry. 3. Configure Depth Stencil State: Apply the depth test and write settings to the current render pass or pipeline state. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def setupdepthbuffering(): # Step 1: Set depth comparison function to Less # This matches the standard behavior for opaque surfaces depthstate = DepthStencilState( depthcomparefunction=CompareFunction.Less, depthwriteenabled=True, stencilfront=StencilOpState.default(), stencilback=StencilOpState.default(), mask=0xFF, writemask=0xFF) # Step 2: Apply depth state to the pipeline or render pass # In a typical API, this might be part of a RenderPipelineDescriptor pipelinedescriptor.depthstencil = depthstate # Note: The depth buffer itself must be cleared or populated # by previous passes (e.g., opaque geometry pass) before this. # Ensure the depth buffer is bound to the render target. Parameters: depthcomparefunction: Less. depthwriteenabled: True. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Depth buffer precision (16-bit vs 24-bit vs 32-bit) can affect the accuracy of occlusion, especially for large scenes or thin geometry. Use 24-bit or 32-bit depth buffers for high-precision requirements. Ordering: If the volume rendering pass is not ordered correctly relative to opaque geometry, occlusion will be incorrect. Typically, opaque geometry is rendered first, followed by the volume pass. Clamping: Ensure that the depth values written by the ray marcher are within the valid range [0, 1] (or [-1, 1] depending on the API) to avoid undefined behavior. This variant emphasizes the reuse of the depth buffer from a previous pass (e.g., opaque objects and background) to occlude volume portions behind objects. It involves rendering all objects and background into a floating-point pbuffer, computing diffuse surface color in a vertex program, and outputting final color in a fragment program using standard shadow maps and light data structures. The depth buffer from this pass is then reused during the volume rendering pass to ensure that portions of the volume occluded by an object do not contribute to the final image. Time Complexity: O(1) for state setup. The actual occlusion check is performed per-fragment during the volume rendering pass, adding negligible overhead to the ray marching computation. Memory Complexity: O(1) for state setup. No additional memory is allocated by this step. Performance: Improves performance by culling volume fragments that are occluded by opaque geometry, reducing the number of ray marching steps required. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective for occlusion culling, integrates well with standard rendering pipelines. Limitations: Requires correct ordering of rendering passes. Does not handle transparent geometry or complex lighting interactions directly. The concept of using depth buffers for occlusion in volume rendering is well-established. The specific integration of depth buffering with SDF ray marching is discussed in the context of lighting models for participating media, where the depth buffer from a previous pass of opaque objects is reused to occlude volume portions. The use of Less depth comparison and enabled depth writes is a standard practice in graphics programming, as seen in various implementations. statusfailed/wgpu-voxel-terrain, https://github.com/statusfailed/wgpu-voxel-terrain, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) A lighting model for general participating media, https://doi.org/10.1145/1053427.1053446, fetched 2026-11-02

name: Depth Buffer Integration for Occlusion
head: Objects and Shadows Rendering, Occlusion Culling via Depth Buffer, UDP (Umbra DP), Umbra DP
body: Depth Buffer Integration for Occlusion is a pixel-based culling technique used within hybrid Extended Depth Peeling (EDP) schemes to handle deeper volume layers. It reuses the depth buffer from a preliminary object rendering pass to discard volume fragments that lie behind opaque geometry. Unlike Extended Depth Peeling, which uses wider area occluders for higher accuracy at greater computational cost, this method treats a single back-projected pixel as the occluder, offering a lighter-weight alternative for deep layers where visibility gains from complex culling diminish. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene containing opaque objects and a participating medium; a pre-computed depth buffer from an object rendering pass. Output: A volume rendering result where fragments occluded by opaque objects are discarded. Data Structures: Depth Buffer: A floating-point buffer storing the depth values of opaque surfaces. LightImage: A mipmap pyramid structure used for blurring light data, though primarily associated with shadow computation in the setup pass. Steps: 1. Object Rendering Pass: Render all opaque objects and the background into a floating-point pixel buffer (pbuffer). 2. Color Computation: Use a vertex program to compute the diffuse surface color of the objects. To prevent clamping artifacts during subsequent texture lookups, store this computed color value in a texture coordinate rather than the standard color output. 3. Shadow and Final Color: Use a fragment program to output the final color for the objects. This involves applying a standard shadow map for object self-shadows and using a light data structure to compute projected shadows cast by the objects onto the participating medium. 4. Depth Buffer Capture: The depth buffer generated in Step 1 is preserved and reused. 5. Volume Rendering with Occlusion: During the volume rendering pass (specifically for deeper layers in a hybrid EDP scheme), compare the depth of each volume fragment against the stored depth buffer. 6. Culling: If a volume fragment's depth is greater than the depth stored in the buffer (indicating it is behind an opaque object), discard the fragment. The technique considers the back-projected pixel extent as the occluder, culling fragments in its umbrae. Parameters and Edge Cases: Hybrid Scheme: This method is typically applied only to deeper layers (e.g., layer index h > 2) in a hybrid scheme, while Extended Depth Peeling (EDP) handles the frontmost layers (h \le 2). Propagation: The culling effect from earlier layers propagates to deeper layers, making this simple technique effective even if less precise than EDP. Precision: The use of a floating-point pbuffer ensures accurate depth storage for the comparison. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthbufferintegrationocclusion(volumefragments, objectdepthbuffer): """ Discards volume fragments that are occluded by opaque objects. Args: volumefragments: List of volume fragment objects, each having a 'depth' attribute. objectdepthbuffer: 2D array or texture containing depth values of opaque objects. Returns: List of volume fragments that are not occluded. """ visiblefragments = [] for frag in volumefragments: # Get the depth of the opaque object at the fragment's screen position # Note: Exact sampling method depends on the specific renderer implementation occluderdepth = sampledepthbuffer(objectdepthbuffer, frag.screenposition) # If the volume fragment is behind the opaque object, discard it # Standard depth test: fragment is visible if fragdepth < occluderdepth # Assuming standard OpenGL/DirectX depth buffer conventions where smaller is closer if frag.depth < occluderdepth: visiblefragments.append(frag) return visiblefragments Uses wider area occluders for higher culling efficiency in frontmost layers but is more computationally expensive. Choose EDP for h \le 2 where fragment reduction is most critical for warping. Extended Depth Peeling Unaware of scene information and inefficient compared to both EDP and UDP. Generally not recommended for modern hybrid schemes. Basic Depth Peeling Time Complexity: Low overhead per fragment compared to EDP, as it involves a simple depth comparison per pixel. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the depth buffer from the object pass. Performance: EDP reduces hidden fragments significantly more than UDP (up to 38.5× vs BDP, and 3.4× more than UDP on average in the first hidden layer). However, UDP adds non-trivial overhead for visibility tests in deeper layers where gains are smaller. Strengths: Simple to implement; effective when combined with EDP for front layers; reduces unnecessary shading for deep volume parts behind objects. Limitations: Less effective than EDP at reducing fragments due to the "tiny pixel" occluder assumption; may leave some fragments near object edges that EDP would catch. When to use: For deeper volume layers (h > 2) in a hybrid rendering pipeline where the marginal benefit of EDP does not justify its cost. The technique is rooted in the work of Lee et al. (2010) on "Umbra culling"-based Depth Peeling (UDP). It was integrated into hybrid schemes by Kim and Lee (2023) to optimize multi-view warping by handling deep layers efficiently after front layers are processed by EDP. The concept of reusing depth buffers for volume occlusion was also explored in earlier lighting models for participating media, such as those by Jensen et al. (2005), which utilized depth buffers to occlude volume portions behind objects.
