name: Lighting and Shading Models
body:
Lighting and Shading Models compute the color of surface points identified by distance-field ray marching by estimating surface normals and applying reflectance models to determine how light interacts with the geometry. This family solves the problem of shading ray-marched geometry without explicit mesh topology, distinguishing itself from Distance Color Blending by calculating geometric lighting contributions (diffuse/specular) rather than relying solely on distance-based color mapping, and from Ray-marched Shadows by focusing on local reflectance properties rather than global occlusion calculations. All methods in this family operate on a surface point \mathbf{p} and its associated geometric data, primarily the surface normal \mathbf{n}. The normal is typically derived from the Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) using the gradient: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{p})\|} where 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) is estimated via finite differences, such as solving a linear system based on values at vertices of a tetrahedron, or via back-propagation. The core shading computation generally follows this structure: 1. Geometric Setup: Determine the view direction \mathbf{v} (from \mathbf{p} to camera) and light direction \mathbf{l} (from \mathbf{p} to light source). 2. Occlusion/Ambient Occlusion: Calculate shadow factors or ambient occlusion values to determine how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from the environment or specific lights. 3. Reflectance Model: Compute the diffuse and specular components based on the angle between \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, and the reflection vector \mathbf{r}. 4. Color Accumulation: Combine the base material color with the lighting contributions, often modulated by depth cueing or atmospheric effects. Enhances depth perception by blending sampled voxel colors with a background color based on distance from the viewer. It solves the foreground/background distinction problem in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear transparency falloff that dims distant objects and shifts their hue, simulating atmospheric haze or aerial perspective. Unlike standard lighting models that compute surface reflectance, this method operates on the accumulated color along the ray, modulating it with depth. Choose it when foreground/background distinction is needed in dense volumetric data without explicit mesh topology. Determines if a surface point is occluded from a light source by performing a sphere trace from the point towards the light. Unlike rasterization-based shadow maps, this method computes occlusion directly from the Signed Distance Function (SDF) of the scene, producing alias-free hard shadows with a single additional traversal per light. It sets itself apart from Soft Shadow Ray Marching by returning a binary occlusion result rather than a continuous penumbra factor, and from Shadow Casting Algorithm by marching from surface points toward lights rather than projecting light through a volumetric dataset. Choose it for alias-free hard shadows directly from SDFs, avoiding rasterization shadow maps. Approximates the darkening of crevices and contact points by sampling the signed distance function (SDF) along the surface normal. It detects occlusion by comparing the actual distance to nearby geometry against the expected distance if the surface were isolated; a smaller actual distance indicates an obstacle is closer, reducing the ambient light contribution. Unlike screen-space methods or shadow maps, this technique requires no separate rendering pass, relying solely on the scene's distance function sampled differently. It is computationally cheaper than full ray-marched shadows but provides a local approximation of global illumination effects. Choose it for computationally cheaper local approximation of global illumination without separate rendering passes. Extends standard distance-field ray marching by iteratively casting new rays upon surface intersection to simulate specular reflections. It solves the problem of rendering mirror-like or glossy surfaces in implicit geometry by continuing the ray path after a hit, rather than terminating at the first surface. It sets itself apart from Distance Color Blending by handling geometric specular bounces rather than volumetric color blending, and from Screen-Space Reflections by operating in 3D space via Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) rather than 2D screen-space depth buffers. Choose it for mirror-like or glossy surfaces in implicit geometry, operating in 3D space rather than screen-space. Renders iridescent surfaces by modulating a cosine-based palette function with a perturbed surface normal, simulating thin-film interference colors, while combining this base color with multi-component specular highlights and directional shadowing. It differs from standard diffuse or simple specular models by generating color variation through geometric perturbation rather than wavelength-dependent physics, and it differs from physically accurate thin-film models by using a computationally cheaper, artistic approximation driven by position and normal noise. Choose it for artistic thin-film interference simulation via geometric perturbation rather than wavelength-dependent physics. Computes eight distinct visualization layers simultaneously in a single forward pass, returning them as a tuple of tensors. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Distance Color Blending or Ray-marched Shadows by decoupling geometric, photometric, and stylistic attributes into parallel outputs rather than combining them into a single RGB image, allowing for flexible post-processing or neural network ingestion. Choose it when decoupling geometric, photometric, and stylistic attributes into parallel outputs is required for post-processing or neural ingestion. Approximates complex lighting environments and specular reflections by decomposing incident radiance into a sum of Spherical Gaussians, which are then rendered as discrete point lights or integrated into a microfacet BRDF model. It solves the problem of efficient relighting in scenes with spatially variant lighting, such as Neural Radiance Fields (NeRFs), by avoiding the high computational cost of full spherical harmonic integration. Unlike Diffuse Lighting Models which ignore view-dependent effects, SG Shading explicitly models specular highlights and view-dependent reflectance. Choose it for efficient relighting in scenes with spatially variant lighting like NeRFs, avoiding full spherical harmonic integration. A family of techniques used in distance-field ray marching to suppress banding and layering artifacts caused by low step counts or discrete sampling intervals. Unlike standard fixed-step marching which produces visible intensity bands, these methods introduce controlled randomness to the sampling process—either by perturbing the ray's UV coordinates based on hit distance, offsetting the initial depth using a blue noise texture, or jittering the step size itself. This breaks up coherent aliasing patterns while maintaining the sharpness of volumetric features like god rays. Choose it to break up coherent aliasing patterns from low step counts while maintaining sharp volumetric features. Provide a mechanism for users to define arbitrary illumination logic for volume rendering, bypassing standard predefined lighting equations. They solve the problem of rigid lighting constraints by allowing per-voxel or per-surface-point computation of color based on user-defined material properties, geometric data, and environmental factors. What sets this family apart from its siblings is the architectural approach to integration: some methods inject custom logic via API callbacks into a rendering pipeline, while others implement self-contained mathematical models or procedural rules directly within the shading step. Choose it when rigid lighting constraints must be bypassed via API callbacks or self-contained mathematical models. A real-time shading technique for procedural neon city scenes that computes diffuse, specular, ambient occlusion, metallic reflection, and emissive contributions per pixel. It distinguishes itself by integrating a metalness-driven specular model and a Fresnel-weighted metallic reflection term tailored for high-contrast, emissive aesthetics. Choose it for high-contrast, emissive aesthetics with metalness-driven specular and Fresnel-weighted reflections. Calculate the illumination of surfaces by simulating the scattering of light, providing the primary visual cue for surface orientation and shape in ray-marched and rasterized rendering. This family distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Reflections or Iridescent Material with Perturbation by focusing exclusively on non-specular, non-directional reflectance, often serving as the base layer for more complex shading. Choose it as the base layer for non-specular, non-directional reflectance in ray-marched or rasterized rendering. Renders scenes defined by implicit surfaces (Signed Distance Fields) by casting rays from a camera, iteratively marching them to a surface, and shading the hit point using the Blinn-Phong reflectance model. It differs from analytical ray tracing by using iterative distance estimation to handle complex, non-analytic geometry, and it differs from pure SDF rendering by applying a specific local lighting approximation (Blinn-Phong) rather than global illumination or complex material models. Choose it for applying a specific local lighting approximation (Blinn-Phong) to complex, non-analytic geometry via iterative distance estimation. Write a material ID, the distance, and the local coordinate p into global variables whenever an object's distance is smaller than the stored distance. At the end of the rendering process, evaluate the material to get color, roughness, etc., and perform shading. A modern approach offloading meshing and AO to compute shaders to achieve smooth, high-fidelity AO that avoids the rigid look of per-vertex discrete levels. Voxel chunk data is held in a 3D texture, and a compute shader evaluates the local density field within a small spherical kernel (e.g., a 3 	imes 3 	imes 3 or 5 	imes 5 	imes 5 window) around each surface point. If the procedural generation pipeline generates a distance field rather than raw block binaries, short-range cone tracing through the local SDF provides smooth, realistic contact shadows baked directly into the output mesh buffers during the surface extraction pass (such as Marching Cubes or Surface Nets). Kernel window sizes for local density field evaluation are typically 3 	imes 3 	imes 3 or 5 	imes 5 	imes 5. name: Distance Color Blending
head: Depth-Cued Colors, Exponential fog, Intensity Depth-Cuing, Aerial perspective, Chroma-depth, Pseudo chroma-depth
body: Distance Color Blending is a shading technique that enhances depth perception in volume rendering by dimming distant voxels and shifting their color toward a background hue, simulating aerial perspective. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear color and intensity falloff based on the sample's distance from the camera. Unlike simple intensity depth-cuing which only reduces brightness, this method modulates the color spectrum (typically adding blue) to exploit the human visual tendency for cool colors to recede. It is distinct from Ambient Occlusion via SDF as it relies on view-dependent distance rather than local geometric curvature, and from Multi-Layer Shading / OmniShader by being a per-sample color modulation rather than a complex multi-pass lighting integration. Inputs: cv: Original voxel color (RGB) at the current sample point. cb: Background color (RGB), typically a shade of blue or gray. dv: Fractional distance of the sample through the volume, normalized to [0, 1]. k{ds}: Magnitude of the blending effect (default 1.0). k{de}: Rate of application (exponent) for the depth falloff (default 0.5). Outputs: cd: Final depth-cued color (RGB). Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond the standard ray-marching state (current position, accumulated color, step size). The fractional depth dv is maintained as a scalar accumulator. Steps: 1. Calculate Fractional Depth: Determine the total length of the ray segment traversing the volume (L{total}) and the current distance traveled from the camera origin (L{current}). Compute dv = L{current} / L{total}. If the total length is zero, set dv = 0. 2. Compute Blending Factor: Calculate the blending weight B using the exponential power function: B = k{ds} \cdot dv^{k{de}} Clamp B to the range [0, 1] to prevent overflow or negative values due to precision errors. 3. Blend Colors: Interpolate between the original voxel color cv and the background color cb using B: cd = (1 - B) cv + B cb 4. Output: Use cd as the color contribution for the current sample in the volume integration loop. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distancecolorblending(cv, cb, dv, kds=1.0, kde=0.5): """ Applies distance color blending to a voxel color. Args: cv: vec3, original voxel color. cb: vec3, background color (e.g., blue or gray). dv: float, fractional distance through volume [0.0, 1.0]. kds: float, magnitude of blending effect. kde: float, exponent for depth falloff. Returns: vec3, the depth-cued color. """ # Calculate blending factor B = kds dv ^ kde # Clamp dv to [0, 1] to handle edge cases where ray extends slightly beyond bounds dvclamped = max(0.0, min(1.0, dv)) # Compute B B = kds (dvclamped kde) # Clamp B to [0, 1] B = max(0.0, min(1.0, B)) # Blend colors: cd = (1 - B) cv + B cb cd = (1.0 - B) cv + B cb return cd Parameters: k{ds}: Controls the size of the color blending effect. Typical value: 1.0. k{de}: Controls the rate of application of color blending. Typical value: 0.5. cb: Background color. If cb is a shade of gray (a, a, a), only intensity depth-cuing (dimming) occurs. If cb is blue-shifted (a, b, c with c > a, b), it introduces a cool shift in distant regions. Example: cb = (0, 0, 0.15). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hard Transfer Functions: This technique avoids the information loss associated with hard transfer functions by modulating existing colors rather than masking them. Precision: Ensure dv is correctly normalized. If the ray does not fully traverse the volume (e.g., clipped by near/far planes), dv should reflect the fraction of the visible segment or the absolute distance relative to a global max depth, depending on implementation. Color Perception: Using a non-gray background color significantly alters the perceived depth. A blue background simulates atmospheric haze, while a gray background only simulates fog density. Exponential Depth Cueing is a shading technique that simulates atmospheric fog to enhance depth perception in volume rendering by dimming distant voxels. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear transparency falloff based on normalized depth. Unlike linear cueing, it uses an exponential function to control how rapidly objects recede into darkness, allowing for more natural aerial perspective effects. See Exponential Depth Cueing. A technique to simulate atmospheric attenuation as depth cuing, blending colors of distant objects with the background color to indicate distance. The blending factor s is calculated as: s = \frac{1 + \text{depth} \times z}{1 + z{\max}} where depth is the attenuation parameter, z is the z-value of the fragment, and z{\max} is the maximal z-value in the scene. The final color intensity I is modified to: sI + (1 - s)I{bg} where I is the original intensity and I{bg} is the background color intensity. This method is simpler but less perceptually accurate than exponential variants for large depth ranges. A color modification technique based on the eye's lens refracting colored light at different angles to enhance depth perception in angiography images. It assigns reddish tones to closer objects and blueish tones to further ones, leveraging the chromatic aberration of the human eye. Time and Memory Complexity: The time complexity of the blending calculation is O(1) per sample, as it involves only basic arithmetic operations (power, multiplication, addition). The memory complexity is O(1) as no additional buffers are required beyond the standard ray-marching state. Measured Performance: Performance is independent of the number of light sources and geometry complexity, depending only on the resolution of the input image or the number of volume samples. It is highly efficient and suitable for real-time rendering. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Enhances depth perception significantly with minimal computational cost; avoids the "flat" look of un-cued volumes. Limitations: It is an empirical approximation and does not simulate true physical light scattering (participating media). The effect is view-dependent and may not accurately represent the physical density of the volume. When to Use: Use when depth perception is critical and computational resources are limited, or when a stylized "aerial perspective" look is desired. When Not to Use: Do not use when physically accurate light transport (e.g., volumetric shadows, scattering) is required, as this method only modulates color and intensity. Distance Color Blending is an extension of intensity depth-cuing, a technique documented by Segal and Akeley in the specification of the first version of OpenGL. It was adapted for volume rendering by Interrante et al. to enhance the perception of depth in medical and scientific visualization. The method relies on the artistic principle of aerial perspective, where distant objects appear cooler and less saturated, a technique used by painters for centuries. It is commonly used in medical imaging (e.g., OCT, CT) to distinguish overlapping structures. name: Exponential Depth Cueing
head: Fog Depth Cueing
body: Exponential Depth Cueing is a shading technique that simulates atmospheric fog to enhance depth perception in volume rendering by dimming distant voxels. It solves the problem of foreground/background distinction in dense volumetric data by applying a non-linear transparency falloff based on normalized depth. Unlike linear cueing, it uses an exponential function to control how rapidly objects recede into darkness, allowing for more natural aerial perspective effects. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: frontfactor (fog transparency at the front plane), density (fog density parameter), and depth (normalized distance of the voxel from the viewer). Outputs: A transparency factor T used to modulate the voxel's color components. Data Structures: The method relies on scalar parameters and a single computed transparency value. No complex data structures are required beyond the standard volume rendering context. Steps: 1. Enable depth cueing in the rendering context. 2. Set the depth cueing parameters (frontfactor and density). 3. For each voxel or sample point along the ray: a. Determine the normalized depth value (0 at front, 1 at back). b. Calculate T using the formula below. c. Multiply the voxel's color components by T. Formula: The fog transparency T is calculated as: T = \text{front\factor} \times \exp(-\text{density} \times \text{depth}) where T is fog transparency, depth is 0 at the front plane and 1 at the back plane, and each voxel color component is multiplied by T during rendering. Parameters: frontfactor: Transparency of the fog at the front plane. Must be positive. Usually < 1.0. Larger values brighten the foreground. density: Controls the fog density, determining how rapidly objects recede into darkness. depth: Normalized depth value, where 0 is at the front plane of the viewing volume and 1 is at the back plane. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Parameter Constraints: frontfactor must be positive. Boundaries: depth must be strictly normalized between 0 and 1 as defined by the viewing volume planes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def exponentialdepthcueing(frontfactor: float, density: float, depth: float) -> float: """Calculate fog transparency for exponential depth cueing.""" return frontfactor math.exp(-density depth) def applycueingtovoxel(color: tuple, frontfactor: float, density: float, depth: float) -> tuple: """Multiply each voxel color component by the fog transparency.""" T = exponentialdepthcueing(frontfactor, density, depth) return (color[0] T, color[1] T, color[2] T) An efficient ray marching algorithm designed to accurately generate spatial-temporal points for deformable tissue reconstruction, balancing rendering speed and reconstruction quality. It outperforms the Depth-Cueing method in PSNR (33.374 vs 31.325) and SSIM (0.907 vs 0.897) on the EndoNeRF dataset, while maintaining competitive inference speed (1.73 fps vs 1.95 fps). The Depth-Cueing method suffers from suboptimal performance due to reliance on noisy and incomplete stereo depth data and is inapplicable for temporal interpolation due to the absence of stereo depth in certain contexts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Comparative data for the "Depth-Cueing" method on the EndoNeRF dataset shows a test speed of 1.95 fps, PSNR of 31.325, SSIM of 0.897, and LPIPS of 0.132. Strengths: Introduces black "fog" to make distant voxels appear darker than close ones, aiding foreground/background distinction. Limitations: Relies on noisy and incomplete stereo depth data, and is inapplicable for temporal interpolation due to the absence of stereo depth in certain contexts. When to Use: When distinguishing foreground objects from background objects in volumetric data. When Not to Use: In dynamic scenes requiring temporal interpolation or when stereo depth data is noisy/incomplete. Exponential Depth Cueing was introduced as part of the VolPack volume rendering library. It is designed to introduce black "fog" to make distant voxels appear darker than close ones, thereby aiding in the distinction of foreground objects from background objects. The technique is implemented via specific API calls (vpEnable and vpSetDepthCueing) within the VolPack context. name: Linear Depth Cueing
head: Atmospheric Attenuation Depth Cuing, Color attenuation, Depth-based Attenuation, depth cuing
body: Linear Depth Cueing is a technique to simulate atmospheric attenuation, blending the colors of distant objects with a background color to indicate distance and enhance depth perception. It differs from Exponential Depth Cueing by using a linear interpolation factor based on depth rather than an exponential decay function. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Original color intensity I, background color intensity I{bg}, current fragment depth z, maximum scene depth z{\max}, and a depth cueing parameter depth. Outputs: Modified color intensity I'. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard scalar values for depth and color components. The implementation relies on computing a scalar blending factor s. Steps: 1. Determine the maximum depth z{\max} for the scene. 2. For each fragment at depth z, calculate the blending factor s using the linear formula: s = \frac{1 + \text{depth} \times z}{1 + z{\max}} 3. Compute the final color intensity I' by blending the original intensity I with the background intensity I{bg} using s: I' = sI + (1 - s)I{bg} Parameters: depth: A non-zero argument specifying whether depth cuing is used. If zero, attenuation is not applied. Typical values observed in examples include 0.3. z{\max}: The maximal z-value in the scene, computed by the rendering code. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If depth is zero, the blending factor s becomes \frac{1}{1 + z{\max}}, which may not result in the expected "no cueing" behavior if the formula is applied blindly without a conditional check. The source implies a conditional: "if depth is non-zero then... sets [formula]". Precision issues may arise if z{\max} is very large or very small relative to z and depth. The method assumes z and z{\max} are in the same coordinate system. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lineardepthcueing(I, Ibg, z, zmax, depthparam): """ Applies linear depth cueing to a color intensity. Args: I: Original color intensity (scalar or vector). Ibg: Background color intensity. z: Current fragment depth. zmax: Maximum depth in the scene. depthparam: Depth cueing strength parameter. Returns: Modified color intensity. """ # If depthparam is zero, no cueing is applied if depthparam == 0: return I # Calculate blending factor s s = (1 + depthparam z) / (1 + zmax) # Blend original intensity with background intensity Iprime = s I + (1 - s) Ibg return Iprime Uses an exponential function for non-linear depth progression, offering different visual characteristics than linear blending. See Exponential Depth Cueing. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment for the color blending calculation. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for storing z{\max} and the blending factor. Strengths: Simple to implement; effectively simulates atmospheric haze or fog to enhance depth perception. Limitations: Linear progression may not accurately model real-world atmospheric scattering, which is often exponential. Performance impact is negligible. When to use: When a simple, computationally inexpensive method is needed to enhance depth perception in volume or surface rendering. When not to use: When high-fidelity atmospheric scattering is required, or when the scene depth range is extremely large, making linear interpolation less perceptually accurate. Linear Depth Cueing was introduced in the context of computing and displaying isosurfaces in R, specifically for visualizing elevation data such as the Maunga Whau volcano. It is also discussed in the context of dense geometric flow visualization, where it is combined with desaturation and darkening techniques to enhance depth perception in vector field data. name: Ray-marched Shadows
head: Hard Shadow Casting, Hard Shadow Ray Marching, Hard Shadows, Hard Shadows via Sphere Tracing, SDF Shadow Ray Marching, SDF Shadows
body: Ray-marched shadows determine if a surface point is occluded from a light source by performing a sphere trace from the point towards the light. Unlike rasterization-based shadow maps, this method computes occlusion directly from the Signed Distance Function (SDF) of the scene, producing alias-free hard shadows with a single additional traversal per light. It sets itself apart from Soft Shadow Ray Marching by returning a binary occlusion result rather than a continuous penumbra factor, and from Shadow Casting Algorithm by marching from surface points toward lights rather than projecting light through a volumetric dataset. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface point \mathbf{x} (from primary ray march), scene SDF f(\mathbf{p}), light position \mathbf{l} (or direction for directional lights), maximum traversal distance D, and self-shadowing offset t{min}. Output: Shadow factor kd \in \{0, 1\}, where 0 indicates the point is in shadow and 1 indicates it is fully lit. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond the SDF evaluation function and standard scalar/vector types. The algorithm maintains two scalar variables: current distance along the ray t and the minimum distance to geometry d at the current sample point. Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: Define the shadow ray origin \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{r}{Ld} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{x}). Initialize traversal distance t = t{min} and distance to surface d = 0. 2. Sphere Traversal Loop: While t < D: a. Evaluate the scene SDF at the current ray position \mathbf{r}S(t) = \mathbf{x} + t \mathbf{r}{Ld} to get d = f(\mathbf{r}S(t)). b. Occlusion Check: If d < \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold, e.g., 10^{-3}), the ray has intersected geometry. Return 0 (in shadow). c. Advance: Update t \leftarrow t + d. 3. Completion: If the loop finishes without intersection (i.e., t \ge D), return 1 (not in shadow). Formulas: The shadow ray is defined as: \mathbf{r}S(t) = \mathbf{x} + t \mathbf{r}{Ld} where \mathbf{x} is the surface point, t is the distance along the ray, and \mathbf{r}{Ld} is the unit vector towards the light source. Parameters: t{min}: Initial traversal distance. Must be > \epsilon to prevent self-shadowing. Typical values depend on the SDF's precision but are often around 0.01 to 0.1. D: Maximum ray traversal distance. For point lights, this is the distance to the light source. For directional lights, it is an arbitrary large value sufficient to cover the scene. \epsilon: Intersection threshold. Typical value 10^{-3} or 10^{-4}. MAX\MARCH\STEPS: Maximum number of iterations to prevent infinite loops in degenerate cases. Typical value 255. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computehardshadow(x, lightpos, scenesdf, tmin, maxdist, epsilon=1e-3): """ Computes hard shadow for point x relative to lightpos using SDF scenesdf. Args: x: vec3, surface point. lightpos: vec3, position of the light source. scenesdf: function, returns signed distance at a point. tmin: float, initial offset to prevent self-shadowing. maxdist: float, maximum distance to march (distance to light or large value). epsilon: float, intersection threshold. Returns: float: 1.0 if lit, 0.0 if in shadow. """ # Calculate light direction lightdir = normalize(lightpos - x) # Initialize traversal t = tmin d = 0.0 # Safety counter to prevent infinite loops steps = 0 maxsteps = 255 while t < maxdist and steps < maxsteps: # Evaluate SDF at current ray position # rS(t) = x + t lightdir currentpos = x + lightdir t d = scenesdf(currentpos) # Check for intersection if d < epsilon: return 0.0 # In shadow # Advance along the ray by the distance to the nearest surface # Clamp step to prevent zero/negative steps from precision errors t += max(d, 1e-4) steps += 1 return 1.0 # Not in shadow Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: If t{min} is 0, the initial sample point is \mathbf{x} itself. Since f(\mathbf{x}) \approx 0 for a point on the surface, d < \epsilon triggers immediately, incorrectly marking the point as in shadow. The solution is to set t{min} > \epsilon. Alternatively, the ray origin can be offset by the normal: \mathbf{x} + \mathbf{n} \cdot \text{offset}. Precision: Floating-point precision errors in SDF evaluation can cause jittering shadows near the surface. Using a slightly larger t{min} or normal offset mitigates this. Directional Lights: For directional lights, D must be large enough to encompass the entire scene. If D is too small, objects behind the light source (relative to the camera) may incorrectly appear lit if the ray terminates before reaching "infinity". Soft Shadow Ray Marching computes a continuous shadow factor (0.0 to 1.0) by accumulating the ratio of the distance to intervening geometry relative to the distance traveled along the ray. Unlike hard shadows, it simulates the penumbra of an area light by tracking the minimum "cone ratio" or occlusion factor. It sets itself apart from Shadow Casting Algorithm by providing smooth, alias-free penumbrae without requiring separate shadow map passes. See Soft Shadow Ray Marching. The Shadow Casting Algorithm projects light through a volumetric dataset to compute occlusion, enabling the simultaneous rendering of embedded geometric polygons and volumetric data. It treats illumination as a projection through space, allowing textures and shadows to be handled as extensions of the same resampling pipeline. See Shadow Casting Algorithm. This method calculates self-shadowing for volumetric clouds by performing an additional ray march towards the light source at each sample point to compute transmittance. It is a direct, image-order technique that avoids the precision limitations of shadow maps and the approximation errors of transmittance function mapping. See Volume Cloud Self-Shadowing via Ray Marching. A technique to fix artifacts where pixels were wrongly shadowed due to depth-buffer ray tracing. Depth-buffer ray tracing caused "phantom wedges" because the depth buffer only stores the nearest surface, resulting in 16% of traceable pixels being wrongly shadowed. Removal of this specific depth-buffer trace is required to fix these artifacts. A shadow computation technique where a shadow ray is cast for each sample towards the light source. The shadow ray is sampled until occluding matter with density above a specified threshold is encountered. The quality of the shadow is controlled by a slider (0-100) determining the number of samples taken during traversal. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of surface points (pixels) and M is the average number of steps per shadow ray. M depends on scene complexity and D. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, as no shadow maps or buffers are required. Performance: Hard shadows are straightforward to implement with SDFs compared to rasterization, requiring only one additional sphere trace per light source per pixel. Strengths: Alias-free shadows, no resolution dependence (unlike shadow maps), easy integration with SDF scenes, supports soft shadows with minimal modification. Limitations: Sensitive to t{min} and \epsilon settings to avoid self-shadowing and precision artifacts. When to use: Ideal for SDF-based rendering, real-time demos, or scenes with simple geometry where alias-free shadows are critical. Not suitable for highly complex scenes with many lights where performance is paramount. Ray-marched shadows originated with the development of Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering. Charles Bloom popularized the technique in his 2013 blog post "Raymarching Distance Fields," noting that shadows are "fairly easy to implement" by simply checking if the path to the light is obstructed. The specific algorithm for hard shadows (Algorithm 3.2) is attributed to Inigo Quilez. It is used in volume visualization for self-shadowing and in game engines like Minecraft (via shaders like Iris/Hearthlight) to replace depth-buffer shadows. name: Soft Shadow Ray Marching
head: Global Shading with Soft Shadows, MIP shadow, Penumbra Approximation, Quilez soft shadows, Soft Shadow Casting via Raymarching
body: Soft Shadow Ray Marching computes a continuous shadow factor (0.0 to 1.0) for a surface point by ray marching towards a light source and accumulating the ratio of the distance to intervening geometry relative to the distance traveled. Unlike hard shadow ray marching, which returns a binary occlusion result, this method simulates the penumbra of an area light by tracking the minimum "cone ratio" or occlusion factor along the ray. It sets itself apart from Shadow Casting Algorithm by providing smooth, alias-free penumbrae without requiring separate shadow map passes or low-pass filtering. Inputs: p: The 3D surface point being shaded. lightPos: The 3D position of the light source. map(p): The Signed Distance Function (SDF) of the scene, returning the distance to the nearest surface. k: The softness/sharpness coefficient (dimensionless). maxDist: The maximum distance to march (typically the distance to the light or a fixed limit). minDist: The minimum starting distance (to prevent self-intersection). Outputs: shadowFactor: A float in [0.0, 1.0], where 1.0 is fully lit and 0.0 is fully shadowed. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Calculate the light direction vector: \vec{d} = \text{normalize}(\text{lightPos} - p). Initialize the shadow factor: res = 1.0. Initialize the traversal distance: t = \text{minDist}. A typical value for minDist is 0.01 to avoid self-intersection artifacts. Determine the maximum march distance: maxDist = \min(\text{length}(\text{lightPos} - p), \text{fixed\limit}). Some implementations use a fixed limit (e.g., 30.0 or 60.0) regardless of light position to bound performance. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate for a fixed number of steps (e.g., 32 to 64) or until t \ge maxDist. Evaluate the SDF at the current sample point: h = \text{map}(p + t \cdot \vec{d}). Hard Occlusion Check: If h < \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold like 0.001), the ray has hit an object; return 0.0. Soft Shadow Update: Update the shadow factor by taking the minimum of the current value and the ratio of the distance to the surface (h) to the distance traveled (t), scaled by k: res = \min(res, k \cdot \frac{h}{t}) This ratio tracks the minimum clearance relative to distance, creating a penumbra region. Step Advancement: Advance the ray by the distance to the nearest surface. To prevent overshooting small features or moving too fast, the step size is often clamped: t = t + \text{clamp}(h, \text{step\min}, \text{step\max}) Typical clamping range is [0.02, 0.25], though some implementations use [0.03, 0.8]. 3. Termination: If the loop completes without hitting an object, return the clamped result: \text{clamp}(res, 0.0, 1.0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softshadowraymarch(p, lightpos, mapfunc, k=16.0, maxsteps=32): """ Computes soft shadow factor for point p towards lightpos. Args: p: vec3, surface point lightpos: vec3, light position mapfunc: function(vec3) -> float, SDF of the scene k: float, softness coefficient (default 16.0) maxsteps: int, maximum number of march steps Returns: float, shadow factor in [0.0, 1.0] """ # 1. Initialization lightdir = normalize(lightpos - p) res = 1.0 t = 0.01 # minDist to avoid self-intersection # Calculate max distance: distance to light or a fixed limit disttolight = length(lightpos - p) maxdist = min(disttolight, 30.0) # 30.0 is a common fixed limit # 2. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(maxsteps): if t >= maxdist: break # Sample SDF h = mapfunc(p + t lightdir) # Hard occlusion check if h < 0.001: return 0.0 # Soft shadow update: track minimum cone ratio # Formula: res = min(res, k h / t) res = min(res, k h / t) # Advance ray, clamping step size to prevent overshooting step = clamp(h, 0.02, 0.25) t += step # 3. Return clamped result return clamp(res, 0.0, 1.0) Parameters and Typical Values: k (Softness/Sharpness): Controls the width of the penumbra. Higher values produce sharper shadows (narrower penumbra), lower values produce softer shadows (wider penumbra). Typical values range from 4.0 to 32.0. minDist (Start Offset): Prevents the ray from starting inside the surface. Typical value: 0.01. maxDist (Max March): Limits the shadow ray length. Can be the distance to the light or a fixed constant (e.g., 30.0 or 60.0). Step Clamp: Limits the maximum step size to ensure fine geometry is not skipped. Typical range: [0.02, 0.25], though some implementations use [0.03, 0.8]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: If the ray starts exactly at the surface point (t=0), the SDF query returns 0, causing immediate false occlusion. A small minDist offset is required. Linear Drop-off Artifacts: Using a linear denominator for the distance ratio (e.g., h/t) can cause severe shadow artifacts when light sources are very close to objects, as the ratio changes rapidly. Some implementations use a logarithmic denominator (\log(t \cdot w + 1)) to mitigate this. Precision: If h is very small but not below the threshold, the ratio h/t becomes small, correctly darkening the shadow. However, floating-point precision issues near the surface can cause flickering if the step size is not clamped. Calculates soft shadow visibility (0.0 to 1.0) towards a directional light (e.g., the sun) by marching along the light direction, using a dithered rotation of the light vector per pixel to create a penumbra that averages out with supersampling. It sets itself apart from standard soft shadow ray marching by normalizing the penumbra calculation by t \cdot \text{sunY} rather than distance alone, preventing false heavy shadows on flat ground where clearance is proportional to distance. Choose this variant when rendering directional lights over large, flat surfaces where standard distance-based penumbrae would incorrectly darken the ground plane. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of ray march steps. Typically fixed between 32 and 64 steps per shadow ray. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory buffers are required; it uses the same SDF queries as the primary ray march. Performance: Soft shadows are "almost free" compared to hard shadows in SDF ray marching because they require no additional ray casts or texture lookups, only a few extra arithmetic operations per step. Strengths: Produces smooth, alias-free penumbrae. Works with dynamic geometry without requiring shadow map recomputation. Integrates seamlessly with existing SDF ray marching pipelines. Limitations: Approximates area lights; the softness is controlled by a single scalar k rather than a true light radius, which may not match physical accuracy for all light sizes. Performance is linear with the number of lights; multiple lights require multiple shadow ray marches. Can suffer from artifacts if the light is very close to the surface due to the linear ratio assumption. The technique was popularized by Inigo Quilez, who described it as a way to obtain soft shadows with a penumbra region using distance fields by inspecting the distance d from the ray to surrounding geometry and the traversal distance t. The method leverages the global geometric information provided by SDFs to approximate the visibility of an area light without the overhead of shadow maps or multiple ray samples. name: Soft Shadow Visibility with Dithered Penumbra
head: Dithered Penumbra Shadow Visibility
body: Calculates soft shadow visibility (0..1) towards the sun by marching along the sun direction. It sets itself apart from standard soft shadow ray marching by normalizing the penumbra calculation by t \cdot \text{sunY} rather than distance alone, preventing false heavy shadows on flat ground where clearance is proportional to distance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Height field function heightAtExtended(x, z), sun direction vector \vec{S} = (dx, dy, dz), pixel coordinates (ox, oz), camera origin oy, and parameters shadowMaxDistance, shadowSoftness, shadowMinStep, shadowSteps. Output: A single float value in [0, 1] representing shadow visibility. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond the height field access function. The algorithm maintains scalar state variables for the ray march. Parameters: shadowMaxDistance: Maximum distance to check for shadows. shadowSoftness: Parameter controlling shadow softness. shadowMinStep: Minimum step size for shadow ray marching. shadowSteps: Number of shadow ray march iterations. softness: Derived parameter, calculated as 6 \times \text{shadowSoftness} + 2. sunY: Vertical component of the sun direction, clamped to \ge 0.12. Steps: 1. Initialize ray distance t = 0, clearance h = 0, and visibility V = 1. 2. Loop i from 0 to shadowSteps - 1: a. Calculate distance-based step: d{\text{step}} = t \times 0.15. b. Calculate gap-based step: g{\text{step}} = h > 0 \ ? \ h \times 0.5 \: \ \text{shadowMinStep}. c. Determine step size: \Delta t = \min(d{\text{step}}, g{\text{step}}). d. Advance ray: t \leftarrow t + \max(\Delta t, \text{shadowMinStep}). e. If t > \text{shadowMaxDistance}, break loop. f. Calculate new clearance: h = oy + dy \times t - \text{heightAtExtended}(ox + dx \times t, oz + dz \times t). g. If h < 0 (terrain hit): i. Return \text{clamp01}(V \times \max(0, 1 + h / (\text{shadowMinStep} \times 1.5))). h. Calculate visibility ratio: R = (\text{softness} \times h) / (t \times \text{sunY}). i. Update visibility: V = \min(V, R). 3. Return \text{clamp01}(V). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def softshadowvisibility(ox, oz, oy, dx, dy, dz, shadowmaxdistance, shadowsoftness, shadowminstep, shadowsteps, heightatextended): # Derived parameters softness = 6 shadowsoftness + 2 suny = max(dy, 0.12) t = 0.0 h = 0.0 visibility = 1.0 for in range(shadowsteps): # Step size calculation distancestep = t 0.15 gapstep = h 0.5 if h > 0 else shadowminstep step = min(distancestep, gapstep) # Advance ray t += max(step, shadowminstep) # Boundary check if t > shadowmaxdistance: break # Calculate clearance hx = ox + dx t hz = oz + dz t terrainheight = heightatextended(hx, hz) h = oy + dy t - terrainheight # Terrain hit detection if h < 0: # Clamp visibility contribution from the hit contribution = max(0.0, 1.0 + h / (shadowminstep 1.5)) return max(0.0, min(1.0, visibility contribution)) # Visibility update # Formula: visibility = min(visibility, (softness h) / (t sunY)) ratio = (softness h) / (t suny) visibility = min(visibility, ratio) return max(0.0, min(1.0, visibility)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Flat Ground: Using a simple clearance/distance ratio fails on flat ground because clearance is proportional to distance, causing false heavy shadows. Normalizing by t \cdot \text{sunY} ensures flat ground is fully lit. Ridge Shoulders: Without gap limiting, the shadow ray can skip over ridge shoulders, creating hard stair-step shadow edges aligned with the heightfield grid. Sun Direction: The sun's vertical component (sunY) must be clamped to a minimum value (0.12) to prevent division by zero or extreme values when the sun is near the horizon. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is shadowSteps. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Performance: In the source implementation (M-series Mac, 6 workers, 1536² heightfield), rendering time scales with resolution. For 1920×1080 high quality, 18.7M rays were processed in 34.0 seconds. Generation is a fixed cost and does not scale with image size. Strengths: Efficient soft shadow calculation without expensive supersampling or kernel sampling. Handles flat terrain correctly. Limitations: Fixed number of steps may not adapt to complex terrain features at varying distances. This method is part of a procedural terrain rendering pipeline described in the theme1 repository by mingderwang. It is designed for real-time or near-real-time rendering of large-scale terrain with volumetric clouds and water, leveraging distance-proportional ray marching for terrain intersection. theme1, https://github.com/mingderwang/theme1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Shadow Casting Algorithm
head: cast shadows algorithm
body: The Shadow Casting Algorithm projects light through a volumetric dataset to compute occlusion, enabling the simultaneous rendering of embedded geometric polygons and volumetric data. It treats illumination as a projection through space, allowing textures and shadows to be handled as extensions of the same resampling pipeline. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volumetric data, embedded geometric polygons, and a light source definition. Output: An array of total voxel colors representing the final illumination after shadowing. Data Structures: Voxel Array: A 3D grid storing initial light strengths or opacities. Polygon Data: Geometric definitions of embedded surfaces, often scan-converted into the volume space. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the 2D profile geometry or polygon data into the array of initial light strengths. Assign all voxels in the volumetric data a slightly non-zero opacity if simulating effects like dust-filled rooms. 2. Resampling (Shadow Calculation): Perform shadow calculation by projecting light through the dataset. The standard implementation involves three successive resampling steps to map the light field onto the volume. 3. Optimization: Reorganize the order of operations to eliminate one resampling step, yielding crisper shadows. 4. Attenuation: Apply tri-linear interpolation during 3D scan-conversion to resample 3D data. 5. Final Computation: Compute the array of total voxel colors. Pitfalls: Excessive Blurring: Frequent tri-linear interpolation for resampling 3D data causes excessive blurring during 3D scan-conversion, resulting in softer polygonal edges than desired. A better filter would reduce this blurring. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """Interpolate value at fractional coordinates (x, y, z) in a 3D grid.""" ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz ix, iy, iz = max(0, min(ix, len(grid)-2)), max(0, min(iy, len(grid[0])-2)), max(0, min(iz, len(grid[0][0])-2)) v000 = grid[ix][iy][iz] v100 = grid[ix+1][iy][iz] v010 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz] v110 = grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz] v001 = grid[ix][iy][iz+1] v101 = grid[ix+1][iy][iz+1] v011 = grid[ix][iy+1][iz+1] v111 = grid[ix+1][iy+1][iz+1] lerp = lambda a, b, t: a + t (b - a) c00 = lerp(v000, v100, fx) c10 = lerp(v010, v110, fx) c01 = lerp(v001, v101, fx) c11 = lerp(v011, v111, fx) c0 = lerp(c00, c10, fy) c1 = lerp(c01, c11, fy) return lerp(c0, c1, fz) def shadowcastingalgorithm(voxelgrid, polygons, lightsource): """Standard implementation with three successive resampling steps.""" dims = (len(voxelgrid), len(voxelgrid[0]), len(voxelgrid[0][0])) lightarray = [[[0.0] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] # Initialization: load polygon geometry into initial light strengths # Standard polygon scan-conversion fills intersected voxels with intensity for poly in polygons: # poly.scanconvert(dims) would return voxel coordinates here pass # Assign slightly non-zero opacity to voxels for dust/beam effects opacitygrid = [[[1e-4] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] # Step 1: Resample based on volume density resampled1 = [[[0.0] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] for i in range(dims[0]): for j in range(dims[1]): for k in range(dims[2]): resampled1[i][j][k] = trilinearinterpolate(lightarray, i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5) opacitygrid[i][j][k] # Step 2: Resample based on polygon occlusion resampled2 = [[[0.0] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] for i in range(dims[0]): for j in range(dims[1]): for k in range(dims[2]): resampled2[i][j][k] = trilinearinterpolate(resampled1, i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5) # Step 3: Final resampling to map to output space totalvoxelcolors = [[[0.0] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] for i in range(dims[0]): for j in range(dims[1]): for k in range(dims[2]): totalvoxelcolors[i][j][k] = trilinearinterpolate(resampled2, i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5) return totalvoxelcolors def optimizedshadowcasting(voxelgrid, polygons, lightsource): """Reorganized order to eliminate one resampling step.""" dims = (len(voxelgrid), len(voxelgrid[0]), len(voxelgrid[0][0])) lightarray = [[[0.0] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] for poly in polygons: # poly.scanconvert(dims) would return voxel coordinates here pass opacitygrid = [[[1e-4] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] # Optimized sequence combines or reorders steps to skip one resampling totalvoxelcolors = [[[0.0] dims[2] for in range(dims[1])] for in range(dims[0])] for i in range(dims[0]): for j in range(dims[1]): for k in range(dims[2]): val = trilinearinterpolate(lightarray, i + 0.5, j + 0.5, k + 0.5) totalvoxelcolors[i][j][k] = val opacitygrid[i][j][k] return totalvoxelcolors Texture projection maps 2D textures onto geometric and volumetric data by projecting textures through space onto surfaces. It solves the difficulty of wrapping textures around volumetrically defined objects, where the defining surfaces are not explicitly known, by projecting through space rather than relying on surface parameterization. It differs from direct surface wrapping by treating the texture as a light-like projection, allowing it to be handled as a straightforward extension of the shadow casting algorithm. A strategy to render geometric objects defined by extrusion of 2D profiles using the shadow casting algorithm to simulate volumetric light shafts. The profile is loaded into the array of initial light strengths, and all voxels in the volumetric data are assigned a slightly non-zero opacity to obtain the effect of sculpted shafts of light passing through a dust-filled room. If the beam is assumed to pass through the volumetric data without attenuation, it can be rendered without a separate shadow pass and without the accompanying 3D representation. A comparison algorithm consisting of a simple ray marcher that uses shadow maps for visibility queries. The shadow map used for visibility tests is laid out in 8 × 8 blocks such that the texels in each block are scanned in Z-order curve for cache coherence optimization. Time Complexity: Adding shadows roughly doubles the time required to compute the array of total voxel colors. However, it does not affect the time required to generate each frame in a rotation sequence when lighting and data are fixed, the observer moves, and specular highlights are absent. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The addition of textures increases image generation time by roughly 50%, depending on the number and size of textured polygons. Strengths: Produces images free from aliasing artifacts and handles mixtures of geometric and volumetric data efficiently. Limitations: The standard implementation suffers from blurring due to tri-linear interpolation. Computational expense can be high for complex polygonal data, potentially requiring hierarchical data structures or unified data structures for both geometric and volumetric data to speed up processing. The Shadow Casting Algorithm was developed in the context of rendering mixtures of geometric and volumetric data, particularly for applications such as radiation treatment planning. It addresses the challenge of visualizing how light (or radiation beams) interacts with both explicit geometric structures and implicit volumetric data simultaneously. The work acknowledges contributions from the Computer Science and Radiation Oncology departments, utilizing CT scans and electron density maps for validation. name: Texture Projection
head: Texture Projection for Volumetric Objects
body: Texture projection maps 2D textures onto geometric and volumetric data by projecting them through space onto encountered surfaces. It solves the difficulty of wrapping textures around volumetrically defined objects, which requires knowing where their defining surfaces lie. Implemented as a straightforward extension of the shadow-casting algorithm, it avoids explicit surface parameterization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A volumetric dataset, a geometric dataset (e.g., polygonal meshes), and a 2D texture image. Outputs: A rendered image where textures are mapped onto the surfaces encountered by the projection rays. Data Structures: The method treats the texture as a spatial field projected along specific directions and does not define new complex data structures beyond those used in the base hybrid ray tracer. Steps: 1. Extend the Shadow-Casting Algorithm: Adapt the existing shadow-casting logic to handle texture data alongside occlusion data. 2. Project Textures Through Space: Cast rays or define projection vectors that traverse the volumetric and geometric data. 3. Map Textures onto Surfaces: As the projection encounters surfaces (either from the volumetric dataset or embedded polygons), sample and map the texture onto these surfaces. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Spectral Mismatch: Geometric, volumetric, and texture data exhibit different spectra, requiring care when mixing them to avoid visual artifacts. Surface Definition Difficulty: Wrapping textures around volumetrically defined objects is difficult because it requires knowing where their defining surfaces lie; texture projection avoids this by projecting through space rather than wrapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def textureprojection(volumetricdata, geometricdata, textureimage, projectiondirections, width, height): """Projects textures onto volumetric and geometric surfaces via spatial projection.""" renderedimage = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): rayorigin = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) raydir = normalize((x - width/2, y - height/2, -1.0)) texaccum = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) texweight = 0.0 t = 0.0 while t < maxdistance: point = addvectors(rayorigin, scalevector(raydir, t)) hitvol = volumetricdata.contains(point) hitpoly = geometricdata.intersects(point) if hitvol or hitpoly: if hitvol: uv = projectpointtotexture(point, projectiondirections) else: uv = getpolygonuv(point, hitpoly) sample = sampletexture(textureimage, uv) texaccum = addcolors(texaccum, sample) texweight += 1.0 t += stepsize if texweight > 0: finaltex = scalecolor(texaccum, 1.0 / texweight) else: finaltex = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) renderedimage[y][x] = finaltex return renderedimage def normalize(v): l = (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) def addvectors(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def scalevector(v, s): return (v[0]s, v[1]s, v[2]s) def addcolors(c1, c2): return (c1[0]+c2[0], c1[1]+c2[1], c1[2]+c2[2]) def scalecolor(c, s): return (c[0]s, c[1]s, c[2]s) def projectpointtotexture(point, directions): return tuple(max(0.0, min(1.0, dot(point, d))) for d in directions) def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def volumetricdata.contains(point): return True # Standard volume lookup def geometricdata.intersects(point): return None # Standard ray-polygon intersection def sampletexture(tex, uv): return (uv[0], uv[1], 0.5) # Standard bilinear sampling def getpolygonuv(point, polygon): return (0.0, 0.0) # Standard UV mapping Maps 2D textures onto 3D surfaces by applying planar mapping in three perpendicular planes (XY, XZ, YZ) and interpolating results based on surface normal alignment. It solves texture stretching on complex, non-planar surfaces such as spheres or organic shapes. Unlike planar projection which uses only two coordinates, triplanar mapping uses three orthogonal projections weighted by the surface normal to ensure seamless coverage regardless of orientation. Choose it when rendering organic shapes or spheres where planar projection causes distortion. See Triplanar Texture Projection. Complexity: Described as a straightforward extension of the shadow-casting algorithm. Specific time and memory complexity are not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids the hard problem of determining defining surfaces for volumetric objects, making it easier to apply textures to complex volumetric data. Limitations: Requires care when mixing geometric, volumetric, and texture data due to spectral mismatch. Performance: Specific performance metrics are not given in the sources. Texture projection was introduced in the context of interactive visualization of 3D medical data and rendering mixtures of geometric and volumetric data. The approach is similar to methods described by Feibush [1980] and builds upon the hybrid ray tracer detailed in the technical report [Levoy 1988c]. A comprehensive survey of texture mapping algorithms was published by Heckbert [1986]. name: Triplanar Texture Projection
head: Round Cube Mapping, Trianplanar Texture Projection, Triplanar Mapping, Triplanar Texture Mapping
body: Triplanar texture projection is a technique for mapping 2D textures onto 3D surfaces by applying planar mapping in three perpendicular planes (XY, XZ, YZ) and interpolating the results based on surface normal alignment. It solves the problem of texture stretching that occurs with simple planar projection on complex, non-planar surfaces such as spheres or organic shapes. Unlike Planar Projection Texture Mapping, which uses only two coordinates, triplanar mapping uses three orthogonal projections weighted by the surface normal to ensure seamless coverage regardless of surface orientation. Inputs: p: A 3D position vector (px, py, pz) in world or object space. n: A 3D surface normal vector (nx, ny, nz) at position p. tex: A 2D texture sampler. k: A hardness parameter (scalar), typically k \ge 1. Outputs: color: The resulting RGB color sampled from the texture. Data Structures: The texture tex is a standard 2D array of color values. The position p and normal n are 3D vectors. Steps: 1. Compute Absolute Normal Components: Calculate the absolute values of the normal components: |nx|, |ny|, |nz|. 2. Apply Hardness: Raise the absolute normal components to the power of k to control the sharpness of the blending. Let wx = |nx|^k, wy = |ny|^k, wz = |nz|^k. 3. Sample Textures for Each Plane: XY Plane: Sample the texture using coordinates (px, py). This corresponds to the projection along the Z-axis. Weight: wz. XZ Plane: Sample the texture using coordinates (px, pz). This corresponds to the projection along the Y-axis. Weight: wy. YZ Plane: Sample the texture using coordinates (py, pz). This corresponds to the projection along the X-axis. 4. Weighted Summation: Compute the weighted sum of the three samples: \text{color} = wx \cdot \text{sample}(py, pz) + wy \cdot \text{sample}(px, pz) + wz \cdot \text{sample}(px, py) 5. Normalization: Divide the weighted sum by the sum of the weights to normalize the result: \text{color} = \frac{wx \cdot \text{sample}(py, pz) + wy \cdot \text{sample}(px, pz) + wz \cdot \text{sample}(px, py)}{wx + wy + wz} If wx + wy + wz = 0 (degenerate normal), return a default color or the sample from the dominant axis. Formula: The general formula for weighted triplanar mapping is: \text{texture}{\text{triplanar}}(p, n, k) = \frac{|nx|^k \text{sample}(py, pz) + |ny|^k \text{sample}(px, pz) + |nz|^k \text{sample}(px, py)}{|nx|^k + |ny|^k + |nz|^k} where \text{sample}(u, v) is the texture sampling function. For linear weighting (k=1): \text{texture}{\text{triplanar}}(p, n) = \frac{|nx| \text{sample}(py, pz) + |ny| \text{sample}(px, pz) + |nz| \text{sample}(px, py)}{|nx| + |ny| + |nz|} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def triplanartextureprojection(p: Vec3, n: Vec3, tex: Sampler2D, k: float = 1.0) -> Vec3: # sample(u, v) is a standard 2D texture lookup function # 1. Compute absolute normal components absn = abs(n) # 2. Apply hardness parameter weights = pow(absn, k) # 3. Sum of weights for normalization weightsum = weights.x + weights.y + weights.z # Handle degenerate case where normal is zero vector if weightsum == 0.0: return sample(p.x, p.y) # Fallback to XY plane # 4. Sample textures for each plane # XY plane: projected along Z, uses px, py, weighted by |nz|^k samplexy = sample(p.x, p.y) # XZ plane: projected along Y, uses px, pz, weighted by |ny|^k samplexz = sample(p.x, p.z) # YZ plane: projected along X, uses py, pz, weighted by |nx|^k sampleyz = sample(p.y, p.z) # 5. Weighted sum color = (weights.x sampleyz + weights.y samplexz + weights.z samplexy) # 6. Normalize return color / weightsum Parameters: k: Hardness parameter. Controls how sharply the texture blends between planes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Normal: If the normal vector is (0,0,0), the denominator becomes zero. Memory Bandwidth: Triplanar mapping requires three texture lookups per shading point. Heightmap Sampling: It is not suitable for sampling heightmaps in the distance function (map function) during ray marching because the texture lookups happen at every step, causing high memory bandwidth overhead. This variant addresses the issue of hard edges between voxel faces in voxel-based rendering. Instead of using the axis-aligned normal of the voxel face, it computes a smooth normal by drawing a line from the voxel center to the ray intersection point. This centroid normal is then used for the triplanar weighting. This results in a soft transition between texture patches on different faces of a voxel, avoiding the visible seams present in standard AABB texturing. A simpler technique that maps a 2D texture to a 3D point using only two of the three coordinates (e.g., px, pz for the XZ plane). It is suitable for planar surfaces like floors but causes stretching on complex surfaces. It serves as the basis for triplanar mapping by extending the concept to three axes. Time Complexity: O(1) per shading point, but with a constant factor of 3 texture lookups and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory. Performance: Significantly slower than planar or biplanar mapping due to three texture samples per pixel/ray step. Strengths: Eliminates texture stretching on arbitrary surfaces; seamless blending between axes; no need for UV unwrapping. Limitations: High memory bandwidth usage; not suitable for heightmap sampling in distance functions; potential for texture aliasing if not filtered properly. When to Use: Shading complex organic or curved surfaces where UV mapping is difficult or impossible. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and surfaces are planar; when sampling heightmaps in the ray marching loop. Triplanar mapping, also known as round cube mapping, was introduced as a solution to the limitations of planar projection mapping in raymarching engines. It allows for procedural texture application on distance fields without explicit UV coordinates. The technique is widely used in real-time rendering and voxel-based graphics to provide consistent texturing across complex geometries. name: Volume Cloud Self-Shadowing via Ray Marching
head: Self-Shadowing via Ray Marching, Transmittance-based Self-Shadowing
body: This method computes volumetric self-shadowing by performing an additional ray march towards the light source at each sample point along the primary view ray to calculate transmittance. It is distinct from shadow mapping techniques (like Beer's Shadow Map or Transmittance Function Mapping) because it avoids precision limits associated with texture resolution, offering richer detail at the cost of higher computational overhead. Inputs: Primary ray sample point position P in the volume. Volume density/opacity function \sigma(x) or discrete opacity \alpha. Light direction L. Number of shadow ray steps Ns. Outputs: Transmittance T from P to the light, representing the self-shadow factor. Data Structures: No complex structures required. Standard scalar variables for position, step size, and accumulated transmittance. Steps: 1. Initialize accumulated transmittance T = 1.0. 2. Determine step size \Delta d. The total distance to the light is often approximated or bounded. For cloud rendering, a fixed small number of steps is typical. 3. Loop i from 0 to Ns - 1: a. Calculate current position: Pi = P + i \cdot \Delta d \cdot L. b. Sample the volume density \sigma(Pi) or opacity \alphai at Pi. c. Update transmittance: T = T \cdot (1 - \alphai) or T = T \cdot e^{-\sigma(Pi) \Delta d}. 4. Return T as the shadow factor. Parameters: Ns: Number of shadow ray march steps. Typical value is ~6 steps on PC/Console. Pitfalls: Insufficient steps cause noise. Too short steps cause brightness artifacts (under-shading). Too long steps cause noise (aliasing). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeselfshadow(pos, lightdir, densityfunc, numsteps): """ Computes self-shadow transmittance via ray marching. Args: pos: Current 3D position in the volume. lightdir: Normalized direction vector to the light source. densityfunc: Function returning density/opacity at a 3D position. numsteps: Integer number of steps to take towards the light. Returns: float: Transmittance value between 0 and 1. """ # Estimate step size. # Note: The exact distance to the light is not always needed if # we assume the volume is bounded or the light is at infinity. # A common approach is to march a fixed distance or use the # remaining distance to the volume boundary. # For simplicity, assuming a fixed step size or normalized march. # If light is directional (infinity), we march a fixed distance D. # If point light, D is distance to light. # Here we assume a normalized march over a conceptual distance D. # Let's assume D is passed or derived from context. # If not given, we assume the loop covers the relevant local neighborhood. # Guard against zero steps if numsteps <= 0: return 1.0 # Determine step size. # In many cloud shaders, the "distance" is abstracted. # We assume a uniform step size stepsize is defined by the caller # or derived from the primary ray's step size. # For this generic implementation, we assume a normalized step size of 1.0 # per step for the sake of the formula, scaled by a global marchdistance. # However, standard practice implies a fixed count. # Let's assume stepsize is provided or calculated as totaldist / numsteps. # Since totaldist is not in inputs, we assume the caller handles the # spatial scaling, and this function just accumulates opacity. # Alternative interpretation: The ray marches a fixed physical distance. # Let's assume stepsize is an input or global constant. # To be self-contained, we will assume a unit step size for the loop, # and the caller is responsible for the physical distance scaling. transmittance = 1.0 stepsize = 1.0 # Placeholder for physical distance per step for i in range(numsteps): # Current sample position samplepos = pos + lightdir (i stepsize) # Sample density/opacity # densityfunc returns either density (sigma) or opacity (alpha) # We assume it returns opacity alpha for direct multiplication alpha = densityfunc(samplepos) # Accumulate transmittance # T = T (1 - alpha) transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early exit if fully shadowed if transmittance <= 0.0: return 0.0 return transmittance This variant computes self-shadow visibility by sampling points along the direction from a surface point to the light to make the process differentiable for joint optimization of geometry and light. It calculates visibility fv(wi; x) using the formula fv(wi; x) = 1 - \sum{j=1}^{N} \alphaj \prod{k=1}^{j-1} (1 - \alphak), where \alphaj is the discrete opacity at sample j. This allows online computation for optimizing object geometry and light position simultaneously. Limited Secondary Ray Sampling is an optimization strategy for computing volumetric self-shadowing in distance-field ray marching. It reduces the computational cost of secondary ray traces by limiting their maximum travel distance and adaptively reducing the number of samples based on primary ray depth and local density. Unlike global shadowing methods, it restricts self-shadowing to a local neighborhood, trading long-range accuracy for performance. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of shadow steps Ns. Since a secondary ray is marched for every primary sample, the cost is O(Np \cdot Ns), where Np is the number of primary samples. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per sample. Performance: Significantly more expensive than shadow mapping or Transmittance Function Mapping (TFM). TFM with 7 Fourier coefficients is roughly equivalent to Ray Marching with 1-2 steps in efficiency. Strengths: High detail, no shadow map aliasing, accurate volumetric attenuation. Limitations: High computational cost, sensitive to step count (noise vs. brightness artifacts). When to use: When visual fidelity of self-shadowing is critical and hardware budget allows, or when shadow map precision is insufficient. When not to use: When performance is paramount or for projecting shadows onto other objects (shadow mapping is preferred). The method originates from real-time volumetric cloud rendering techniques, notably discussed in industry implementations such as those in Unreal Engine 4 and other high-fidelity cloud systems. It is often contrasted with Beer's Shadow Map and Transmittance Function Mapping (TFM) in technical articles detailing cloud rendering pipelines. 体积云效果的实现，游戏世界的云合雾集, https://leihuo.163.com/institution/news/20230719/384231099592.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) PIR: Photometric Inverse Rendering with Shading Cues Modeling and Surface Reflectance Regularization, https://doi.org/10.1109/3dv66043.2025.00055, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Limited Secondary Ray Sampling
head: Limited Secondary Light Sampling, Secondary Ray Optimization
body: Limited Secondary Ray Sampling is an optimization strategy for computing volumetric self-shadowing in distance-field ray marching. It reduces computational cost by limiting the maximum travel distance of secondary rays and adaptively reducing sample counts based on primary ray depth and local density. Unlike global shadowing methods, it restricts self-shadowing to a local neighborhood, trading long-range accuracy for performance. The method augments standard primary ray marching (view direction) with secondary ray marching (light direction) to estimate transmittance and lighting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Primary ray origin, direction, accumulated density along the primary ray, light direction, and density field access function. Output: Shadowed radiance contribution for the current primary sample. Data Structures: Primary Ray State: Accumulated density \taup, current position P, step size hp. Secondary Ray State: Accumulated density \taus, current position Q, step size hs. Parameters: D{max}: Maximum secondary ray distance. Typical value: 1000 meters. N{sec}: Number of secondary samples. Adaptive based on primary distance and density. \tau{thresh}: Primary ray termination threshold. When \taup \ge \tau{thresh}, the cloud is treated as fully opaque. Algorithm Steps: 1. Primary Ray Marching: March along the view direction. At each primary sample point Pi, if accumulated density \taup \ge \tau{thresh}, terminate the primary ray and treat the point as fully opaque. 2. Adaptive Sampling: Calculate N{sec}. Reduce N{sec} logarithmically as the primary sample distance from the camera increases, which is effective with minimal quality impact. Reduce N{sec} for primary samples with low density \rho(Pi), as transparency tolerates lower lighting accuracy. 3. Secondary Ray Marching: Initialize the secondary ray at Pi towards the light direction L. Limit the maximum travel distance to D{max} to reduce computational cost. Use a linear scale for the sample distribution along the secondary ray. 4. Weighting & Accumulation: For each secondary step, sample the density, accumulate optical depth \taus, and apply a linear importance weight to fade out distant samples. This avoids hard margins in the lighting calculation. 5. Lighting Calculation: Compute transmittance T = e^{-\taus}. Combine the weighted transmittance with the primary ray color to produce the final shadowed radiance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def limitedsecondaryraysampling(primaryorigin, primarydir, lightdir, densityfield, Dmax=1000.0, tauthresh=5.0, basesecondarysamples=16, primarystep=1.0): """ Perform primary ray march with adaptive secondary light sampling. """ primarypos = primaryorigin primarydir = normalize(primarydir) lightdir = normalize(lightdir) taup = 0.0 # Standard lighting constants lightcolor = vec3(1.0) basecolor = vec3(0.0) while taup < tauthresh: # Sample density at current primary position rhop = densityfield.sample(primarypos) # Adaptive secondary sample count distfromcam = length(primarypos - primaryorigin) # Logarithmic reduction with distance from camera distfactor = max(1.0, log(distfromcam + 1.0)) # Linear reduction with low density densityfactor = max(0.1, rhop / 10.0) numsecondary = max(1, int(basesecondarysamples / (distfactor densityfactor))) # Secondary ray march towards light secondarypos = primarypos taus = 0.0 weightedtransmittance = 0.0 weightsum = 0.0 # Linear scale for sample distribution step = Dmax / numsecondary for i in range(numsecondary): secondarypos += lightdir step # Check max distance limit distfromprimary = length(secondarypos - primarypos) if distfromprimary > Dmax: break # Sample density at current position rhos = densityfield.sample(secondarypos) # Accumulate optical depth taus += rhos step # Linear importance weighting to fade out distant samples # Avoids hard margins in lighting calculation w = max(0.0, 1.0 - (distfromprimary / Dmax)) # Compute transmittance transmittance = exp(-taus) # Accumulate weighted contribution weightedtransmittance += w transmittance weightsum += w # Normalize weighted light by sum of weights shadowfactor = weightedtransmittance / weightsum if weightsum > 0 else 1.0 # Combine with primary ray color color = basecolor + shadowfactor lightcolor # Advance primary ray taup += rhop primarystep primarypos += primarydir primarystep yield color # Terminate when accumulated density reaches threshold return vec3(0.0) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hard Margins: Failing to fade out secondary samples causes visible artifacts at the edge of the shadow volume. Precision: Accumulated density can overflow if step sizes are too large or not clamped. Boundary: Secondary rays may exit the volume prematurely; ensure the density field returns zero outside bounds. A specific implementation mode in Unreal Engine's Volumetric Cloud system that uses secondary ray marching for shadowing. It produces sharp, colored shadows but is limited in trace distance due to sample constraints. It is more expensive than Beer Shadow Maps but supports ground-to-sky-to-space transitions and provides volumetric self-shadow color. The cost is driven by the Shadow View Sample Count Scale parameter on the Volumetric Cloud component. A key pitfall is the limited distance shadows can be traced. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Significantly faster than full secondary ray marching due to distance and sample count limits. On console platforms (Xbox One, PS4), Beer Shadow Maps are often recommended over Ray Marched shadows due to cost, though Ray Marched provides better quality. Strengths: Local self-shadowing is accurate and colored; performance is manageable for real-time. Limitations: Shadows do not extend beyond D{max} (e.g., 1000m); long-range shadows require alternative methods like Beer Shadow Maps. The method originates from practical implementations of efficient volumetric clouds in real-time rendering, particularly in community-driven discussions on density thresholds and secondary ray limits, and is formally documented in Unreal Engine's Volumetric Cloud system. It addresses the high cost of secondary ray marching for self-shadowing by introducing locality and adaptivity.
