name: Ambient Occlusion via SDF
head: AO Ray Marching, Alex Evans AO, Cheap Ambient Occlusion, Normal-direction AO, Proximity-based Occlusion, Ray Marched Ambient Occlusion, Real Ambient Occlusion, SDF AO
body: Ambient Occlusion via SDF approximates the darkening of crevices and contact points by sampling the signed distance function (SDF) along the surface normal. It detects occlusion by comparing the actual distance to nearby geometry against the expected distance if the surface were isolated; a smaller actual distance indicates an obstacle is closer, reducing the ambient light contribution. Unlike screen-space methods or shadow maps, this technique requires no separate rendering pass, relying solely on the scene's distance function sampled differently. It is computationally cheaper than full ray-marched shadows but provides a local approximation of global illumination effects. Inputs: p: The 3D position of the surface point being shaded. n: The normalized surface normal at p. scene(p): The scene SDF function returning the distance to the nearest surface. Outputs: ao: A scalar value in [0, 1], where 0 is fully occluded (black) and 1 is fully lit. Data Structures: No complex structures. Standard floating-point variables. Parameters: numsteps: Number of samples along the normal. Typical values: 5, 20. stepdist: Base step size. Typical values: 0.015, 0.08, or derived via linear interpolation. decay: Exponential decay factor for sample weights. Typical values: 0.6, 0.7. multiplier: Scaling factor applied to the accumulated occlusion before clamping. Typical values: 1.4, 2.0. power: Exponent applied to the final AO term to amplify contrast. Typical value: 40. Algorithm: The method casts a ray from p along n in discrete steps. At each step i, it evaluates the SDF at position pi = p + n \cdot di. The occlusion is determined by the difference between the step distance di and the SDF value hi = \text{scene}(pi). If hi < di, another surface is closer than the empty space expected, indicating occlusion. There are three common variations in implementation found in the sources: 1. Linear Step with Exponential Decay (Alex Evans style): Samples at fixed intervals with decaying weights. 2. Squared Difference with Inverse Distance Weighting: Uses a squared difference term divided by the step index to penalize closer obstacles more heavily while reducing influence of distant samples. 3. Sum Ratio: Sums the SDF values and divides by the expected sum if no occlusion existed. Pseudocode (Linear Step with Exponential Decay): This variant is preferred for its stability and widespread use in real-time raymarching. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ambientocclusionlinear(p, n, numsteps=5, basestep=0.08, decay=0.7, multiplier=2.0): """ Computes ambient occlusion by sampling the SDF along the normal. Args: p: vec3, surface position. n: vec3, surface normal (normalized). numsteps: int, number of samples (typically 5). basestep: float, base distance increment (typically 0.08). decay: float, weight decay per step (typically 0.7). multiplier: float, scaling factor for occlusion intensity (typically 2.0). Returns: float: Ambient occlusion factor in [0, 1]. """ occ = 0.0 weight = 1.0 for i in range(1, numsteps + 1): dist = basestep i d = scene(p + n dist) occ += (dist - d) weight weight = decay return max(0.0, min(1.0, 1.0 - multiplier occ)) Pseudocode (Squared Difference Variant): Used in some tutorials for a different falloff characteristic. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ambientocclusionsquared(p, n, stepdist=0.015, stepnbr=20): """ Computes AO using squared difference and inverse step weighting. """ occlusion = 1.0 currentstep = stepnbr while currentstep > 0: dist = currentstep stepdist sdfval = scene(p + n dist) contribution = (dist - sdfval) 2 / currentstep occlusion -= contribution currentstep -= 1 return max(0.0, min(1.0, occlusion)) Pseudocode (Sum Ratio Variant): Provides a normalized ratio of sampled distances to expected empty space. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ambientocclusionsumratio(p, n, aosteps=5, aostepsize=0.1): """ Computes AO by summing SDF values and dividing by the expected unoccluded sum. """ totalsteps = aosteps sumdist = 0.0 for i in range(totalsteps): samplepos = p + n (i + 1) aostepsize sumdist += scene(samplepos) expectedsum = totalsteps aostepsize return max(0.0, min(1.0, sumdist / expectedsum)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distant Artifacts: If the total travel distance is too long, distant geometry may contribute to the occlusion term, creating incorrect darkening in open areas. Precision: High-precision SDFs require highp float precision to avoid flickering. Normal Accuracy: The method assumes n is accurate; SDF normals are typically computed via finite differences. A variant that estimates AO based on the number of raymarching steps required to hit a surface during the primary ray march, rather than a separate normal-based pass. Mechanism: During the standard sphere-tracing loop, if the surface is hit at step index i out of a maximum Steps, the AO coefficient is calculated as 1 - \frac{i}{\text{Steps}-1}. Pros: Zero additional SDF evaluations; leverages existing raymarch data. Cons: Tightly coupled with raymarch resolution; the "Real Ambient Occlusion" normal-sampling method is generally more reliable. Estimates AO by sampling the SDF at multiple points distributed on a sphere around the surface point, providing a more isotropic occlusion estimate than normal-only sampling. Mechanism: Samples are placed using a golden-ratio-based spherical distribution to ensure uniform density. N: Number of samples (aoSamples). R: Kernel radius (aoKernelSize). For i from 0 to N-1: py = 1 - \frac{i}{N} \cdot 2 r = \sqrt{1 - py^2} \theta = \phi \cdot i, where \phi = \pi(3 - \sqrt{5}) px = \cos(\theta) \cdot r pz = \sin(\theta) \cdot r Sample position: \text{hitPos} + (px, py, pz) \cdot R Accumulate: \text{ao} += \text{saturate}(\frac{\text{SDF}}{R}) Final AO: 1 - (1 - \frac{\sum \text{saturate}(\text{SDF}/R)}{N \cdot 0.5})^2 Parameters: aoSamples typically 8 (range 0-32); aoKernelSize typically 0.075 (range 0.0-0.25). Pros: Better handles occlusion from sides, not just above/below the normal. Cons: More expensive (N SDF calls per pixel vs 5-20 for normal AO). Decreases the luminosity of ambient light in creases and crevices to simulate occlusion based on object proximity, using the distance field itself rather than Screen Space Ambient Occlusion (SSAO). Mechanism: Samples equally spaced points perpendicular to the surface and calculates the weighted sum of deltas of surface distances with distance field distances to approximate how occluded that surface is from surrounding geometry. Pros: More accurate than SSAO for implicit surfaces. Cons: Requires perpendicular sampling directions, increasing computational cost compared to single-normal sampling. Time Complexity: O(k), where k is the number of AO samples (typically 5-20). It adds a constant overhead to the shading cost per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1). No separate shadow maps or AO passes are required, as the same distance function is sampled differently. Performance: Significantly faster than screen-space ambient occlusion (SSAO) or ray-marched shadows because it avoids large kernel samples or secondary ray tracing through the entire scene. Strengths: Resolution-independent (unlike SSAO). Works well with procedural SDFs and fractals. Uses fixed decay (0.7) and multiplier (1.4 or 2.0) in standard implementations. Limitations: Approximate: Only considers the local neighborhood along the normal (or sphere). Can produce artifacts if the total travel distance is too long, as distant surfaces may incorrectly contribute to the occlusion term. Dependent on normal quality; SDF normals are computed via finite differences. The technique is rooted in the early days of real-time raymarching in WebGL and GLSL. Alex Evans popularized the "cheap ambient occlusion" method using normal-direction SDF sampling in his 2012 GDC talk "Real-Time Ray Tracing" and subsequent demos. The squared-difference variant is often cited in educational tutorials explaining the geometric intuition of AO via SDFs. name: Spherical Ambient Occlusion
head: Hemisphere AO, Spherical Sampling AO
body: Spherical Ambient Occlusion estimates ambient occlusion by sampling the Signed Distance Field (SDF) at points distributed uniformly on a sphere around the surface point, then combining these samples to compute an occlusion factor. It differs from its parent, Ambient Occlusion via SDF, which typically compares the SDF value along a single normal direction against an unoccluded expectation, by using a multi-directional spherical probe to capture occlusion from all sides. Inputs: hitPos: The 3D position on the surface where shading is computed. normal: The surface normal at hitPos (used to define the local coordinate system for the sphere, though the specific rotation logic is implicit in the sample generation relative to the normal). aoSamples: Number of spherical samples (integer). aoKernelSize: Radius of the AO sampling sphere (float). Outputs: ao: The final ambient occlusion factor in the range [0, 1], where 0 is fully occluded (dark) and 1 is fully open (bright). Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar values and simple 3D vectors. Parameters: aoSamples: Number of samples. Typical value: 8. Range: 0–32. aoKernelSize: Sampling radius. Typical value: 0.075. Range: 0.0–0.25. Algorithm: The method generates sample points on a unit sphere using a golden-ratio-based spiral distribution to ensure uniform density and avoid clustering at the poles. It then scales these points by aoKernelSize, samples the SDF, and aggregates the results. 1. Initialize ao = 0.0. 2. Define constants: \phi = \pi (3 - \sqrt{5}). N = \text{aoSamples}. 3. Loop i from 0 to N - 1: a. Calculate spherical coordinates for the i-th sample: py = 1 - \frac{i}{N} \cdot 2. r = \sqrt{1 - py^2}. \theta = \phi \cdot i. px = \cos(\theta) \cdot r. pz = \sin(\theta) \cdot r. b. Construct the sample direction vector \mathbf{p} = (px, py, pz). c. Transform \mathbf{p} to world/local space aligned with the surface normal. Note: The source code implies \mathbf{p} is in a local coordinate system where the Y-axis is the normal. In implementation, this requires constructing a basis from the normal. d. Calculate the sample position: \mathbf{samplePos} = \text{hitPos} + \mathbf{p} \cdot \text{aoKernelSize}. e. Sample the SDF: d = \text{SDF}(\mathbf{samplePos}). f. Accumulate the occlusion contribution: s = \text{saturate}(d / \text{aoKernelSize}). \text{ao} += s. 4. Normalize the accumulated value: \text{ao} = \text{ao} / (N \cdot 0.5). 5. Apply a non-linear transfer function to enhance contrast: \text{ao} = 1.0 - (1.0 - \text{ao})^2. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalambientocclusion(hitpos, normal, aosamples, aokernelsize): if aosamples == 0: return 1.0 phi = 3.141592653589793 (3.0 - (5.0 0.5)) aoacc = 0.0 # Construct a local coordinate system from the normal # Assuming normal is normalized # Create two tangent vectors orthogonal to normal # A simple robust method: if abs(normal.y) < 0.9999: up = Vector3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) else: up = Vector3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) tangent1 = normalize(cross(normal, up)) tangent2 = cross(normal, tangent1) for i in range(aosamples): # Calculate spherical coordinates py = 1.0 - (i / aosamples) 2.0 r = (1.0 - py py) 0.5 theta = phi i px = cos(theta) r pz = sin(theta) r # Construct sample vector in local space (Y is normal) sampledir = tangent1 px + Vector3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) py + tangent2 pz # Sample position samplepos = hitpos + sampledir aokernelsize # Sample SDF sdfval = samplesdf(samplepos) # Accumulate # saturate(x) = clamp(x, 0.0, 1.0) s = clamp(sdfval / aokernelsize, 0.0, 1.0) aoacc += s # Normalize ao = aoacc / (aosamples 0.5) # Non-linear transfer ao = 1.0 - (1.0 - ao) 2.0 return ao Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Samples: If aoSamples is 0, the loop does not run, and the result should be 1.0 (fully open) to avoid division by zero or undefined behavior. Precision: The calculation of r = \sqrt{1 - py^2} can suffer from precision issues if py is very close to \pm 1. However, with uniform distribution, this is rare. Boundary Conditions: If the sampling sphere extends outside the valid SDF domain, the SDF sampling function must handle out-of-bounds queries gracefully (e.g., by returning a large positive value or clamping). Normal Alignment: The sample distribution assumes the Y-axis of the local coordinate system aligns with the surface normal. Incorrect basis construction will lead to incorrect occlusion estimates. A shading technique that probes nearby directions to darken points enclosed by material, providing 3-D depth cues for crevices and folds. It probes 12 nearby directions at each isosurface point and darkens points based on the probe results. The parameter aoradius specifies the radius in cells for probing nearby directions. A key characteristic is that the AO effect only darkens points; it does not brighten them, and the output values stay within [0, 1]. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples (aoSamples). Each sample requires one SDF query. Memory Complexity: O(1), as it only stores a few scalar values and vectors. Performance: With a typical sample count of 8, the method is relatively fast. Increasing the sample count linearly increases the cost. Strengths: Provides a good balance between performance and visual quality. The golden-ratio distribution ensures uniform sampling with few samples. Limitations: The fixed kernel size may not adapt well to varying feature scales. It does not account for self-shadowing from distant geometry, only local occlusion. When to Use: Suitable for real-time rendering where performance is critical but some ambient occlusion is desired. When Not to Use: When high-quality, global occlusion is required, or when the scene has large-scale occluding structures. Spherical Ambient Occlusion is a technique used in real-time graphics, particularly in Unity-based projects, to add depth and detail to surfaces defined by Signed Distance Fields. It builds on the general concept of ambient occlusion by using a spherical sampling pattern to estimate how much of the hemisphere around a surface point is occluded by nearby geometry. samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity, https://github.com/samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) feat(immersive): pre-integrated transfer function (single-field renderscene), https://github.com/ManuelBehrendt/Mera.jl/pull/269, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Layer Shading / OmniShader
head: OmniShader
body: Multi-Layer Shading (OmniShader) computes eight distinct visualization layers simultaneously in a single forward pass, returning them as a tuple of tensors. It decouples geometric, photometric, and stylistic attributes into parallel outputs rather than combining them into a single RGB image, allowing for flexible post-processing or neural network ingestion. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes ray directions, surface coordinates, surface normals, surface distances, pixel frames, camera orientation, a cyclic colormap, a degree parameter, and a decay factor as inputs. It outputs a tuple of eight tensors: (lambertianlayer, distancelayer, proximitylayer, vignettelayer, normallayer, laplacianlayer, tangentlayer, spinlayer). Data Structures: The implementation relies on tensor operations, such as cyclic shifting. A key internal structure is cycliccmap, a colormap tensor that is cyclically shifted by 65 positions on axis -2: self.cycliccmap = self.cycliccmap.roll(65, -2). Parameters: decayfactor: A float, default 0.01, used in the distance shading calculation. degree: An integer parameter used in tangent and spin shading calculations. Steps: 1. Compute Surface Normals: Estimate the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the intersection point \mathbf{p} using the gradient of the Signed Distance Function (SDF) f. This is done by solving a linear system derived from finite differences at the vertices of a regular tetrahedron centered at 0, or via back-propagation. 2. Compute Surface Laplacian: Estimate the Laplacian \Delta f at \mathbf{p} using the same tetrahedral samples used for the normal. The formula is: (\Delta f)(p) \approx \frac{6}{\epsilon^2} \left( f(p) - \frac{1}{4}\sum{i=0}^3f(p+\epsilon vi) \right) where \epsilon is a small constant and vi are the tetrahedron vertices. 3. Prepare Camera Orientation: Compute the conjugate of the camera orientation quaternion: cameraorientationconj = cameraorientation.conjugate()[..., None, None,:]. 4. Compute Lambertian Layer: Apply the Lambertian shader to ray directions and surface normals. 5. Compute Distance Layer: Apply the distance shader to pixel coordinates, surface coordinates, and the decayfactor. 6. Compute Proximity Layer: Apply the proximity shader to surface distances. 7. Compute Vignette Layer: Apply the vignette shader to ray directions and pixel frames. 8. Compute Normal Layer: Apply the normal shader to surface normals. The normals \mathbf{n}=(x,y,z) are typically mapped to RGB using absolute values: (\lvert x \rvert, \lvert y \rvert, \lvert z \rvert). 9. Compute Laplacian Layer: Apply the Laplacian shader to the computed surface Laplacian values, normalizing them between 0 and 1 and applying gamma correction. 10. Compute Tangent Layer: Apply the tangent shader using cameraorientationconj, ray directions, surface normals, the shifted cycliccmap, and degree. 11. Compute Spin Layer: Apply the spin shader using cameraorientationconj, surface normals, the shifted cycliccmap, and degree. 12. Return: Return the tuple of all eight layers. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multilayershading(raydirections, surfacenormals, surfacecoords, surfacedistances, pixelframes, cameraorientation, cycliccmap, degree, decayfactor, surfacelaplacian, pxcoords): # 1. Prepare camera orientation conjugate cameraorientationconj = cameraorientation.conjugate()[..., None, None,:] # 2. Shift cyclic colormap shiftedcmap = cycliccmap.roll(65, -2) # 3. Compute layers (exact shading formulas not provided in sources) lambertianlayer = raydirections surfacenormals distancelayer = pxcoords surfacecoords decayfactor proximitylayer = surfacedistances vignettelayer = raydirections pixelframes normallayer = surfacenormals.abs() laplacianlayer = surfacelaplacian.clamp(0, 1) tangentlayer = cameraorientationconj raydirections surfacenormals shiftedcmap[degree] spinlayer = cameraorientationconj surfacenormals shiftedcmap[degree] # 4. Return all layers as a tuple return (lambertianlayer, distancelayer, proximitylayer, vignettelayer, normallayer, laplacianlayer, tangentlayer, spinlayer) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The Laplacian and Normal calculations rely on finite differences with a small constant \epsilon. Boundary Conditions: The distance and proximity shaders may behave unpredictably at the exact start or end of the ray march if not clamped. Quaternion Conjugate: Incorrect handling of quaternion conjugation can lead to misaligned tangent and spin layers. This variant involves a check within the forward pass to determine if the shading model is a "two-stage renderer". It verifies if the optimization configuration opt.arch.shading.model is set to either "MLPFeaTwoStage22" or "MLPFeaTwoStage13". If true, specific optimization flags are set. Time and Memory Complexity: The method performs a single forward pass to compute all eight layers, which is computationally efficient compared to running eight separate render passes. However, it requires memory to store eight output tensors simultaneously. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High efficiency due to single-pass computation; flexible output for downstream tasks (e.g., neural networks, post-processing). Limitations: Requires all input data (normals, Laplacian, etc.) to be available or computed in the same pass, which may increase intermediate memory usage. When to Use: Use when you need multiple visualization attributes (normals, depth, curvature, etc.) for the same scene geometry without the overhead of multiple render passes. The method originates from a ray marching visualization toolkit that implements various ray marching techniques. It is used in contexts requiring detailed geometric and photometric analysis of ray-marched scenes, such as in neural rendering pipelines or advanced visualization tools. kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF, https://github.com/Nemo1999/Joint-TensoRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Dither
head: UV Dithering, Distance-based UV Perturbation
body: Ray Marching Dither is a technique to reduce banding artifacts in ray marching by perturbing the UV coordinates based on the ray distance. It sets itself apart from Ray Marching Jittering by applying perturbation to the UV coordinates rather than the step size, and from Distance Color Blending by focusing on geometric sampling stability rather than color interpolation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current UV coordinates (uv), ray distance (t), dithering strength factor (cfDither), and a pseudo-random number generator function (rand). Output: Perturbed UV coordinates. Data Structures: uv: vec2 representing the current UV coordinate. t: float representing the ray distance (hit distance). cfDither: float parameter controlling dithering intensity. Steps: 1. Calculate the dither amount based on the squared ray distance and the strength factor: \text{dither} = t^2 \cdot c\fDither 2. Generate two random values using the rand function with specific offsets derived from the original UV coordinates: rx = \text{rand}(uv + \text{vec2}(0.12, 0.32)) ry = \text{rand}(uv + \text{vec2}(0.42, 0.52)) 3. Perturb the UV coordinates by adding the random value scaled by the dither amount, then subtracting half the dither amount to center the perturbation: uv.x += rx \cdot \text{dither} - \frac{\text{dither}}{2.0} uv.y += ry \cdot \text{dither} - \frac{\text{dither}}{2.0} 4. Reconstruct the ray origin and direction from the perturbed UVs to continue the ray march. Parameters: cfDither: Dithering strength factor. Typical value: 0.001. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchingdither(uv, t, cfDither, randfunc): """ Perturbs UV coordinates based on ray distance to reduce banding. Args: uv (vec2): Current UV coordinates. t (float): Ray distance (hit distance). cfDither (float): Dithering strength factor (e.g., 0.001). randfunc (function): Pseudo-random number generator taking a vec2 input. Returns: vec2: Perturbed UV coordinates. """ # Step 1: Calculate dither amount dither = t t cfDither # Step 2: Generate random values with specific offsets # Offsets are hardcoded as per source implementation offsetx = vec2(0.12, 0.32) offsety = vec2(0.42, 0.52) rx = randfunc(uv + offsetx) ry = randfunc(uv + offsety) # Step 3: Perturb UVs # Add random component scaled by dither, then subtract half dither to center uv.x += rx dither - dither / 2.0 uv.y += ry dither - dither / 2.0 # Step 4: Return perturbed UVs # Note: Reconstructing ray origin/direction from UVs is handled by the caller # using the standard camera ray generation formula. return uv Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For very large t, t^2 may cause floating-point precision issues or overflow. Boundary Conditions: If uv is near texture boundaries, perturbation might sample outside valid ranges. Determinism: The rand function must be deterministic for the same input uv to avoid flickering if not intended. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel per step, as it involves simple arithmetic and a random function call. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional data structures required. Strengths: Simple to implement, effective at reducing visible banding artifacts in ray marching. Limitations: May introduce slight blurring or noise if the dither strength is too high. Not suitable for all types of artifacts (e.g., step-size related aliasing is better handled by Ray Marching Jittering). When to Use: When banding artifacts are visible due to fixed step sizes or quantization in UV space. When Not to Use: When high precision is required without any perturbation, or when step-size aliasing is the primary issue. Originated from practical implementations in WebGL ray marching, as seen in the WebGL-RayMarch repository. It is a technique used to improve the visual quality of ray-marched scenes by mitigating banding. nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, https://github.com/nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Blue Noise Dithering
head: Blue Noise Ray Offset, Temporal Blue Noise Dithering
body: Blue Noise Dithering is a technique to reduce visible banding artifacts in volumetric ray marching by introducing a random offset to the ray step start position, derived from a blue noise texture, allowing for larger step sizes without quality loss. It sets itself apart from Ray Marching Jittering by using a structured blue noise pattern rather than uniform or white noise, which minimizes clumping and produces a less perceptible error pattern, and from its parent Ray Marching Dither by specifically targeting the initialization offset of the ray march loop to enable significant performance gains through increased step sizes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: uBlueNoise: A 2D sampler texture containing a pre-generated blue noise pattern. frame: The current frame index (integer). rayOrigin: The starting position of the ray (vec3). rayDir: The direction of the ray (vec3). MARCHSIZE / STEPSIZE: The distance advanced per raymarching step. Note: uses MARCHSIZE while uses STEPSIZE; they represent the same parameter. NUMSTEPS: The maximum number of raymarching iterations. Outputs: The result of the raymarching loop, typically a color or density value. Data Structures: Blue Noise Texture: A 2D texture (typically 1024x1024 or similar power-of-two resolution) where the red channel contains values in the range 0, 1). Parameters: Typical Values: NUMSTEPS: Reduced from 250 to 50 in optimized implementations. STEPSIZE: Increased from 0.05 to 0.5 in optimized implementations. Performance Impact: This configuration reduces total iterations from 5000 to 100 while maintaining similar output quality. Temporal Shift: The frame-dependent shift uses frame % 32 and divides by sqrt(0.5). Numbered Steps: 1. Sample Blue Noise: Sample the blue noise texture at normalized fragment coordinates. The coordinates are calculated as glFragCoord.xy / 1024.0. Extract the red channel value. 2. Calculate Temporal Offset: Add a frame-dependent shift to the sampled blue noise value to ensure temporal variation. The shift is calculated as float(frame % 32) / sqrt(0.5). 3. Compute Final Offset: Apply the fract function to the sum of the blue noise value and the temporal shift to keep the result in the range [0, 1). This value serves as the [dithering offset. 4. Initialize Ray Distance: Calculate the initial ray march distance t by multiplying the STEPSIZE (or MARCHSIZE) by the computed offset. 5. Execute Ray Marching Loop: Iterate NUMSTEPS times. In each iteration, calculate the sample position using rayOrigin + rayDir t. Advance t by STEPSIZE (or MARCHSIZE) in subsequent steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bluenoisedithering(rayOrigin, rayDir, uBlueNoise, frame, STEPSIZE, NUMSTEPS): # Step 1: Sample blue noise texture # Coordinates normalized to 0, 1) assuming 1024x1024 texture uv = glFragCoord.xy / 1024.0 blueNoise = texture2D(uBlueNoise, uv).r # Step 2 & 3: Calculate temporal offset and apply fract # Temporal shift ensures the pattern changes every frame temporalShift = float(frame % 32) / sqrt(0.5) offset = fract(blueNoise + temporalShift) # Step 4: Initialize ray distance t = STEPSIZE offset # Step 5: Execute ray marching loop for i in range(NUMSTEPS): # Calculate sample position samplePos = rayOrigin + rayDir t # Perform shading/sampling logic here (e.g., density accumulation) #... # Advance ray distance t += STEPSIZE return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Noticeable Pattern: The dithering pattern can be noticeable in single frames if only spatial noise is used. This is mitigated by adding the temporal component based on the frame count. Banding Artifacts: Visible banding occurs if the step size is increased without dithering. The blue noise offset resolves this by distributing the sampling error. Precision: The use of fract ensures the offset remains bounded, preventing the ray from starting outside the intended volume or causing negative distances if not handled correctly. Uses only the spatial blue noise texture without temporal variation. Suitable for static scenes or when frame coherence is not required. [Link Adds a frame-dependent shift to the blue noise value. Recommended for animated scenes to prevent static pattern visibility. Link Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps. The dithering calculation is O(1) per pixel. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the dithering offset calculation, plus the memory cost of the blue noise texture (typically small, e.g., 1024x1024x4 bytes). Measured Performance: In the cited implementation, reducing iterations from 5000 to 100 (by increasing step size from 0.05 to 0.5 and steps from 250 to 50) resulted in a significant performance improvement while maintaining similar output quality. Strengths: Allows for larger step sizes, reducing the number of samples needed per ray. Reduces visible banding artifacts effectively. Limitations: The dithering pattern may be visible in single frames without temporal variation. Requires a pre-generated blue noise texture. When to Use: When ray marching volumetric effects (clouds, fog, light shafts) and performance is a concern, and banding artifacts are visible with standard step sizes. When Not to Use: When high-quality single-frame stills are required without temporal averaging, or when the blue noise texture is not available. Blue Noise Dithering in the context of volumetric ray marching was popularized by Maxime Heckel in his blog posts on real-time volumetric rendering. The technique leverages the properties of blue noise, which has a power spectrum that is concentrated at higher frequencies, making it less visible to the human eye compared to white or pink noise. This allows for the introduction of random offsets that disrupt regular sampling patterns without introducing noticeable noise artifacts. Real-time dreamy Cloudscapes with Volumetric Raymarching, https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/real-time-cloudscapes-with-volumetric-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) On Shaping Light: Real-Time Volumetric Lighting with Post-Processing..., https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/shaping-light-volumetric-lighting-with-post-processing-and-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching Jittering
head: Dithering Offset, Jittered Ray Marching, Randomized Step Size Ray Marching
body: Ray Marching Jittering is a technique to reduce aliasing artifacts, specifically banding, in volume rendering by introducing random variation to the ray marching step size. It solves the problem of clearly defined intensity bands caused by fixed step sizes in participating media. Unlike fixed stepping, which causes banding, jittering removes these artifacts while keeping features like god rays sharp and focused. Inputs: stepSize: The fixed base step size for ray marching. dithering: A scalar parameter controlling the magnitude of jitter (typically > 0.0). vtexcoord: The texture coordinate or ray origin parameter used for hashing. tMin: The starting distance along the ray. Outputs: tStart: The perturbed starting distance for the ray march. Data Structures: The method requires only scalar parameters and a deterministic hash function. Steps: 1. Calculate a jitter offset based on the texture coordinate and dithering strength. 2. Determine the start time for the ray march by adding the jitter offset to the minimum distance. 3. March the ray using a step size that varies randomly between 0.5 \times \text{stepSize} and 1.5 \times \text{stepSize}. Formulas: The jitter offset is calculated as: \text{jitter} = \begin{cases} \text{hash}(\text{v\tex\coord}) \times \text{stepSize} \times \text{dithering} & \text{if } \text{dithering} > 0.0 \\ 0.0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The start time is: t{\text{Start}} = t{\text{Min}} + \text{jitter} The step size for each march is a random value s such that: s \in [0.5 \times \text{stepSize}, 1.5 \times \text{stepSize}] Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deterministichash(v): # Standard deterministic hash returning a float in [0.0, 1.0) h = 0 for c in v: h = (h 31 + int(c 1000)) & 0xFFFFFFFF return (h & 0x7FFFFFFF) / 0x7FFFFFFF def calculatejitteredstart(tmin, stepsize, dithering, vtexcoord): """Calculate the jittered start position for ray marching.""" if dithering > 0.0: hashvalue = deterministichash(vtexcoord) jitter = hashvalue stepsize dithering tstart = tmin + jitter else: tstart = tmin return tstart def marchwithjitteredstep(stepsize, vtexcoord, tstart): """Perform a single ray march step with jittered size.""" hashvalue = deterministichash(vtexcoord) stepvariation = 0.5 + 1.0 hashvalue # Range [0.5, 1.5] currentstep = stepsize stepvariation return tstart + currentstep Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fixed step sizes introduce aliasing in the form of clearly defined bands of intensity in the volume region. Without dithering, adapting step sizes for performance can cause juddering. A rendering technique using dithering without temporal accumulation (TAA) to break up slicing artifacts from undersampling, ensuring stability in VR where HMD movement causes smearing in TAA. It adapts the raymarch step size based on varying performance conditions to maintain frame targets. Adapted step counts can vary by a factor of 4; without dithering, this causes juddering, but with dithering, the image remains stable with only small noise. In tested scenarios (Smoke Rings, Dust Devil, Wall of Fire), raymarch stage times were 3.69ms, 4.77ms, and 3.82ms respectively. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In VR scenarios using an NVIDIA RTX 3080 and Valve Index HMD at 2016 x 2240 x 2 resolution, raymarch stage times were 3.69ms (Smoke Rings), 4.77ms (Dust Devil), and 3.82ms (Wall of Fire). Total frame times were around 9.6-9.7ms. Scaling: Adaptive dithering allows step counts to vary by a factor of 4 to meet frame targets without visual artifacts like juddering. Strengths and Limitations: Removes banding while keeping god rays sharp and focused. Provides temporally stable images in VR without the smearing artifacts associated with TAA. Introduces a small amount of noise. When to use it and when not: Use when rendering volumes with fixed step sizes that exhibit banding artifacts, especially in VR where TAA is problematic. Originating from techniques to handle aliasing in ray marching through participating media, jittering was identified as a solution to banding in underwater scene rendering. Adaptive dithering was later developed for real-time volumetric lighting in VR to avoid TAA smearing. xwghua/clearvolume-plus, https://github.com/xwghua/clearvolume-plus, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) CS348b Final Project - Rendering Underwater Scenes, http://www.graphics.stanford.edu/courses/cs348b-competition/cs348b-04/underwater/index.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Ignis: Eulerian Fluid Simulation and Rendering at VR Frame Rates, https://doi.org/10.1145/3610542.3626120, fetched 2026-10-30

name: Custom Shading Models
head: Custom Shading Routines, Per-voxel Shading Callbacks
body:
Custom Shading Models provide a framework for defining arbitrary illumination calculations within volume rendering and ray-marching pipelines, allowing developers to replace standard analytic lighting with user-defined logic. This family enables the implementation of specialized effects such as physically based microfacet reflections, directional occlusion, and color-space-specific glow, which are not covered by generic diffuse or specular models. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Distance Color Blending by operating on explicit geometric data (normals, positions) rather than raw scalar field values, and from Ambient Occlusion via SDF by allowing full directional light integration rather than just ambient darkening. All methods in this family operate on a surface point \mathbf{p} and its associated geometric data, primarily the surface normal \mathbf{n}. The normal is typically derived from the Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) using the gradient: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{p})\|} where 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) is estimated via finite differences, such as solving a linear system based on values at vertices of a tetrahedron, or via back-propagation. The core shading computation generally follows this structure: 1. Geometric Setup: Determine the view direction \mathbf{v} (from \mathbf{p} to camera) and light direction \mathbf{l} (from \mathbf{p} to light source). 2. Occlusion/Ambient Occlusion: Calculate shadow factors or ambient occlusion values to determine how much light reaches \mathbf{p} from the environment or specific lights. 3. Reflectance Model: Compute the diffuse and specular components based on the angle between \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, and the reflection vector \mathbf{r}. 4. Color Accumulation: Combine the base material color with the lighting contributions, often modulated by depth cueing or atmospheric effects. The GGX Microfacet BRDF is a specular reflection model that approximates surface roughness using the Gaussian distribution of microfacet normals (GGX) combined with the Schlick Fresnel approximation and a Smith geometry function. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Blinn-Phong with Metallic Reflections, by providing physically plausible energy conservation and accurate specular highlights for rough surfaces, whereas Blinn-Phong is an empirical approximation. It serves as the standard for high-quality specular shading in real-time engines and voxel renderers. This method applies lighting (diffuse, specular, and ambient) to a face color based on the surface normal and light direction. It is designed for SDF-based rendering where the "face" represents a discretized surface element. It differs from general volume shading by operating directly on the extracted face geometry's color and alpha, using a simplified analytic lighting model rather than full ray-marched integration. A custom shading model for ray-marched signed distance fields that extends the classic Blinn-Phong approximation with environment reflections and emissive contributions to simulate urban night scenes. It distinguishes itself from standard Blinn-Phong by modulating specular intensity, power, and reflection weight based on a material's metallic property, and from GGX microfacet models by using a simplified Schlick-like Fresnel term rather than a full microfacet distribution. Multidirectional Occlusion Shading (M-DOS) is a direct volume rendering technique that simulates directional light scattering to produce realistic soft-shadowing and depth cues. Unlike the original MS-DOS model, which constrains the light direction to the viewing direction and uses symmetric disc-shaped Gaussian kernels, M-DOS allows arbitrary light positioning within the hemisphere defined by the view vector by using elliptical footprints derived from a tilted cone. It achieves this through incremental convolution of an opacity buffer, requiring no precomputation and maintaining interactive frame rates. HQS1R is a high-quality point cloud rendering method that reduces aliasing by blending overlapping points together, similar to mipmapping. It is a simplified, compute-based implementation of the blending algorithm from [BHZK05], designed to be faster than aliased GLPOINTS results while providing anti-aliasing. Unlike surface splatting [ZPVG01], it blends overlapping points without considering oriented disks with variable radii. It sets itself apart from the Single-Atomic High-Quality Variant (HQS1x) by using a robust overflow protection mechanism that prevents artifacts when more than 255 points contribute to a pixel. This method performs volume raycasting illumination in the YUV color space to decouple luminance from chrominance, allowing for independent control of brightness and color. It differs from standard RGB shading by computing lighting effects (such as specular highlights and glow) primarily on the luminance channel, while interpolating color channels based on a technique-derived factor. This approach is particularly useful for capturing indirect illumination independently of the transfer function. Tangent Space Shading is a gradient-less lighting technique that approximates the diffuse lighting component of the Phong shading model without computing explicit gradients for every texel. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GGX Microfacet BRDF and Light Evaluation for SDF Faces by its reliance on rendering artifacts (double-pass texture coordinate offsets) rather than geometric derivatives to simulate surface orientation. Voxel-Specific Shading Pipelines are a family of rendering techniques designed to compute illumination for data stored in discrete 3D grids (voxels). Unlike continuous surface shading which operates on smooth Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or triangle meshes, these methods operate on the discrete topology of voxel cells, handling both surface-like boundaries and volumetric density. The family encompasses approaches ranging from per-voxel geometric shading with hard shadows to CPU-based palette index manipulation and dedicated volumetric ray-marching shaders for fluid simulations. Definition: A procedural surface shader for roads that differentiates between asphalt, curb/shoulder, and terrain based on lateral distance to the road centerline, including emissive lane markings. Steps: 1. Calculate d = p.x - 	ext{roadX}(p.z) and ad = |d|. 2. If ad < 	ext{ROAD\HALF\WIDTH}: set albedo to dark gray, metal to 0.35, emissive to 0.0. Calculate lane lines using smoothstep for edge lines, center line, and dashed separators. Add emissive cyan color for lines. 3. Else if ad < 	ext{ROAD\HALF\WIDTH} + 	ext{SHOULDER}: set albedo to dark gray, metal to 0.1, emissive to magenta strip at road edge. 4. Else: set albedo to very dark, metal to 0.0, emissive to 0.0. Parameters: Asphalt metal: 0.35 (wet-look). Lane line color: 	ext{vec3}(0.15, 1.0, 1.1) 	imes 1.3. Edge line offset: 	ext{ROAD\HALF\WIDTH} - 0.3. Center line offset: 0.18. Dashed line frequency: p.z 	imes 0.18. Steps: 1. Divide each triangle into four subtriangles by splitting each edge in the middle. 2. Apply either Gouraud or Phong shading algorithm to the sub-triangles. 3. This process can be iterated several times. The smooth argument specifies one plus the number of times to divide the triangles. Parameters: smooth: integer specifying one plus the number of subdivision iterations. smooth=1 means no subdivision. Pitfalls: Using too high a level of smooth can cause rendering quality to deteriorate due to artifacts from polygon filling, exacerbated on devices using anti-aliasing. The concept of custom shading in volume rendering originated with early libraries like VolPack, which introduced the vpSetCallback mechanism allowing users to define per-voxel shading routines instead of relying on fixed lookup tables. This allowed for arbitrary color transfer functions and lighting models but noted potential performance degradation. Modern implementations have expanded this to include physically based rendering (PBR) models like GGX, specialized techniques for point clouds like HQS1R, and color-space specific methods like YUV shading. The family also encompasses discrete voxel-specific pipelines [17027-voxel-specific-shading-pipelines.md] and procedural surface shaders for specific domains like road rendering. name: GGX Microfacet BRDF
head: GGX BRDF, GGX Microfacet BRDF Model, GGX Microfacet Model, GGX Microfacet Specular Model, GGX Shading, Walter et al. Specular
body: The GGX Microfacet BRDF models specular reflection by assuming the surface consists of microscopic facets with normals distributed according to the Generalized Trowbridge-Reiss (GGX) distribution. It sets itself apart from simpler models like Blinn-Phong by providing physically plausible energy conservation and accurate long-tail specular highlights for rough surfaces. It builds on Custom Shading Models by replacing the empirical specular term with a rigorous microfacet formulation. Inputs: Surface normal \mathbf{n} (unit vector). View direction \mathbf{v} (unit vector, from surface to camera). Light direction \mathbf{l} (unit vector, from surface to light). Roughness \rho (scalar, typically [0, 1]). Diffuse albedo Kd (RGB vector). Specular albedo Ks (RGB vector, often derived from F0 for metals). Outputs: Diffuse radiance contribution Ld. Specular radiance contribution Ls. Total reflected radiance L = Ld + Ls. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The computation relies on scalar and vector arithmetic. Parameters: \rho: Roughness. Typical values range from 0.0 (smooth) to 1.0 (rough). In some implementations, \rho is squared to get \alpha. Kd: Diffuse albedo. Ks: Specular albedo at normal incidence (F0 for dielectrics, measured for metals). Steps: 1. Compute Half Vector: Calculate the half-vector \mathbf{h} between \mathbf{v} and \mathbf{l}. \mathbf{h} = \frac{\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}}{\|\mathbf{v} + \mathbf{l}\|} If \mathbf{v} \approx -\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{h} is undefined; use \mathbf{n} or a default reflection vector. 2. Compute Dot Products: \muv = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}, 0.0) \mul = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0.0) \muh = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h}, 0.0) \mu{lh} = \mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{h} = \max(\mathbf{l} \cdot \mathbf{h}, 0.0) 3. Compute Alpha: \alpha = \rho^2 4. Compute Normal Distribution Function (D): The GGX distribution describes the probability density of microfacet normals. D(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{h}) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi \left( (\alpha^2 - 1)\muh^2 + 1 \right)^2} Add a small epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}) to the denominator to prevent division by zero when \muh=1 and \alpha=1. 5. Compute Geometry Function (G): Two common variants exist. Variant A (Smith Geometry, Unreal/Filament style): k = \frac{(\rho + 1)^2}{8} G1(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \alpha) = \frac{\muv}{\muv(1 - k) + k} G2(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) = G1(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \alpha) \cdot G1(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, \alpha) Variant B (Unreal Engine / NRRF style): S(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) = \mul \sqrt{\alpha^2 + \muv^2(1 - \alpha^2)} G2(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) = \frac{1}{2(S(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) + S(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}, \mathbf{v}))} 6. Compute Fresnel Function (F): The Schlick approximation is standard. F(Ks, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}) = Ks + (F{90}(Ks) - Ks)(1 - \mu{lh})^5 Where F{90}(Ks) is the reflectance at grazing angles. F{90}(Ks) = \min\left(\frac{\text{lum}(Ks)}{0.04}, 1.0\right) \text{lum}(C) = 0.213 Cr + 0.715 Cg + 0.072 Cb For simple dielectrics with constant F0: F(F0, \mu{lh}) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - \mu{lh})^5 7. Compute Specular BRDF: fs(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) = \frac{D(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{h}) G2(\alpha, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) F(Ks, \mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l})}{4 \muv \mul} Add epsilon to 4 \muv \mul to prevent division by zero. 8. Compute Diffuse BRDF: fd(Kd) = \frac{Kd}{\pi} 9. Combine: fr(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) = fd(Kd) + fs(\mathbf{v}, \mathbf{l}) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ggxmicrofacetbrdf(n, v, l, roughness, kd, ks): # 1. Half vector h = normalize(v + l) # 2. Dot products nv = max(dot(n, v), 0.0) nl = max(dot(n, l), 0.0) nh = max(dot(n, h), 0.0) lh = max(dot(l, h), 0.0) # 3. Alpha alpha = roughness roughness alpha2 = alpha alpha # 4. D (GGX) denom = (alpha2 - 1.0) (nh nh) + 1.0 D = alpha2 / (PI denom denom + 1e-6) # 5. G (Smith Geometry - Variant A) k = ((roughness + 1.0) 2) / 8.0 g1v = nv / (nv (1.0 - k) + k + 1e-6) g1l = nl / (nl (1.0 - k) + k + 1e-6) G = g1v g1l # 5. G (Smith Geometry - Variant B, alternative) # sv = nl sqrt(alpha2 + nv nv (1.0 - alpha2)) # sl = nv sqrt(alpha2 + nl nl (1.0 - alpha2)) # G = 1.0 / (2.0 (sv + sl) + 1e-6) # 6. F (Schlick) lumks = 0.213 ks.r + 0.715 ks.g + 0.072 ks.b f90 = min(lumks / 0.04, 1.0) F = ks + (f90 - ks) ((1.0 - lh) 5) # 7. Specular BRDF specular = (D G F) / (4.0 nv nl + 1e-6) # 8. Diffuse BRDF diffuse = kd / PI # 9. Total return diffuse + specular This method defines a surface reflectance function R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) that combines a specular microfacet term with a diffuse Lambertian term, incorporating specific simplifications from the Filament and Unreal Engine renderers. It sets itself apart from the parent GGX Microfacet BRDF by using a specific analytical form for the geometry function G and embedding the incoming cosine term (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i) directly into the specular denominator structure to simplify integration in neural radiance field contexts. A method to ensure energy conservation for rough metals by compensating for energy lost in single-scattering GGX specular lobes, using a precomputed directional albedo table. It uses a precomputed 32x32 directional albedo table E(\mu, \alpha), where \mu is cosine and \alpha is roughness. This ensures white rough metal reflects ~100% at every roughness, correcting the energy loss inherent in single-scattering approximations. Models perfectly smooth surfaces where outgoing radiance is not scattered but mirrors the incident trajectory across the surface normal. The BRDF is defined as f{r,m} = \frac{\delta(\cos \thetai - \cos \thetar)}{\cos \thetai} \delta(\phii - (\phir \pm \pi)) where \delta is the Dirac delta function, \thetai, \thetar are incident and reflected polar angles, and \phii, \phir are azimuthal angles. The pitfall is that the Dirac delta function yields zero for any non-zero parameter mismatch, meaning no light is reflected if the geometric reflection conditions are not perfectly satisfied. Time Complexity: O(1) per shading point. The computation involves a few trigonometric-like operations (dot products, powers) and is significantly more expensive than Blinn-Phong but cheaper than full path tracing. Memory Complexity: O(1). No large tables are required for the base model, though multi-scattering variants may require a small lookup table (e.g., 32x32). Performance: On modern GPUs, this is highly efficient. The Schlick Fresnel and GGX D/G functions are cheap to evaluate. Strengths: Physically plausible appearance, handles a wide range of roughnesses, energy conserving (with proper Fresnel), widely supported in rendering engines. Limitations: Single-scattering approximation loses energy for very rough metals (addressed by multi-scattering variants). Does not account for subsurface scattering or complex thin-film effects without extensions. When to use: General-purpose physically based rendering (PBR) for rough surfaces. When not to use: Perfect mirrors (use Specular Reflection), subsurface scattering, or when computational budget is extremely tight and visual fidelity is secondary (use Blinn-Phong). The GGX microfacet model was introduced by Walter et al. in "Microfacet Models for Refraction through Rough Surfaces" (2007). It replaced the Beckmann distribution with the GGX (Generalized Trowbridge-Reiss) distribution, which provides a better fit for the long tails of specular highlights observed in real-world materials. The model is widely used in modern real-time and offline renderers, including Unreal Engine and Filament. name: Microfacet BRDF with Simplified GGX and Schlick Fresnel
head: NeRV BRDF, Walter et al. BRDF with Filament/Unreal simplifications
body: This method defines a surface reflectance function R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) that combines a specular microfacet term with a diffuse Lambertian term, incorporating specific simplifications from the Filament and Unreal Engine renderers. It sets itself apart from the parent GGX Microfacet BRDF by using a specific analytical form for the geometry function G and embedding the incoming cosine term (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i) directly into the specular denominator structure to simplify integration in neural radiance field contexts. Inputs: \mathbf{x}: 3D surface location. \boldsymbol{\omega}i: Incoming light direction (unit vector). \boldsymbol{\omega}o: Outgoing view direction (unit vector). \mathbf{n}: Surface normal at \mathbf{x} (unit vector). \gamma: Roughness parameter (scalar, \gamma > 0). \mathbf{a}: Diffuse albedo (scalar or RGB vector). F0: Fresnel reflectance at normal incidence (scalar, typically 0.04 for dielectrics). Outputs: R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o): Reflectance value (scalar or RGB vector matching \mathbf{a}). Data Structures: Vectors \mathbf{n}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \mathbf{h} are 3D unit vectors. Scalars \gamma, \rho, k, F0, \mathbf{a} are floats. Steps: 1. Compute the half-vector \mathbf{h}: \mathbf{h} = \frac{\boldsymbol{\omega}o + \boldsymbol{\omega}i}{\|\boldsymbol{\omega}o + \boldsymbol{\omega}i\|} 2. Compute intermediate roughness parameters: \rho = \gamma^2 k = \frac{\gamma^4}{2} 3. Compute the Normal Distribution Function (NDF) D(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{n}, \gamma): D(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{n}, \gamma) = \frac{\rho^2}{\pi \left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^2 (\rho^2 - 1) + 1 \right)^2} 4. Compute the Fresnel term F(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{h}) using Schlick's approximation: F(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{h}) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - (\boldsymbol{\omega}i \cdot \mathbf{h}))^5 5. Compute the Geometry function G(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \gamma): G(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \gamma) = \frac{(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o)(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i)}{\left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o)(1-k) + k \right) \left( (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i)(1-k) + k \right)} 6. Compute the specular reflectance component. Note the denominator includes (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o): R{spec} = \frac{D(\mathbf{h}, \mathbf{n}, \gamma) F(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{h}) G(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o, \gamma)}{4(\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o)} 7. Compute the diffuse reflectance component. Note the inclusion of the cosine term (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i): R{diff} = (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i)(1 - F(\boldsymbol{\omega}i, \mathbf{h})) \left(\frac{\mathbf{a}}{\pi}\right) 8. Sum components: R(\mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\omega}i, \boldsymbol{\omega}o) = R{spec} + R{diff} Pitfalls: The definition of R includes the multiplication by the Lambert cosine term (\mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i) in the diffuse part and implicitly in the geometry term structure, which simplifies equations in the main paper but means the geometric term G and diffuse term are structured differently than standard separable forms. Ensure \mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}o and \mathbf{n} \cdot \boldsymbol{\omega}i are non-negative (front-facing surfaces) to avoid division by zero or negative energy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def microfacetbrdfsimplifiedggxschlick(n, wi, wo, gamma, a, F0): # 1. Half vector h = wi + wo hlen = sqrt(dot(h, h)) if hlen < 1e-6: return 0.0 # Degenerate case h = h / hlen # 2. Parameters rho = gamma gamma k = (gamma 4) / 2.0 # 3. NDF D nh = dot(n, h) nh2 = nh nh denomd = (nh2 (rho rho - 1.0) + 1.0) D = (rho rho) / (pi denomd denomd) # 4. Fresnel F widoth = dot(wi, h) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) ((1.0 - widoth) 5) # 5. Geometry G no = dot(n, wo) ni = dot(n, wi) # Avoid division by zero if no < 1e-6 or ni < 1e-6: return 0.0 gnum = no ni gdenom1 = no (1.0 - k) + k gdenom2 = ni (1.0 - k) + k G = gnum / (gdenom1 gdenom2) # 6. Specular term # Note: Standard microfacet BRDF divides by 4 (n. wo) # The source formula explicitly shows this denominator. spec = (D F G) / (4.0 no) # 7. Diffuse term # Includes (n. wi) factor as per source definition diff = ni (1.0 - F) (a / pi) # 8. Total return spec + diff The Modified Disney Principled BRDF is a simplified surface reflectance model derived from the Disney Principled BRDF, tailored for use in the Absorption-Based Scene Diffusion Factorization (ABSDF) framework. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating complex microfacet reflections by reducing the original model's complexity while retaining its core appearance capabilities for metals and plastics. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Microfacet BRDF with Simplified GGX and Schlick Fresnel, by explicitly adopting a Lambertian diffuse term, omitting sheen and clearcoat lobes, and assuming double-sided surfaces to facilitate analytical factorization. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per shading point. Requires several dot products, a square root, and basic arithmetic. Memory: O(1) auxiliary storage for intermediate vectors and scalars. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Computationally efficient due to simplified analytical forms for D, F, and G. The specific geometry term G simplifies integration in neural rendering contexts. Limitations: The simplified geometry term may not preserve energy conservation as strictly as more complex Smith geometry functions in extreme grazing angles. The assumption of F0 = 0.04 limits accuracy for conductors/metals unless modified. When to use: Use when implementing neural radiance field relighting (e.g., NeRV) or when a fast, dielectric-focused microfacet model is needed. Do not use for high-fidelity metallic rendering without modifying F0 and the geometry term. This BRDF parameterization is used in the NeRV (Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields) method for relighting and view synthesis. It builds on the standard microfacet BRDF described by Walter et al. and incorporates simplifications from the Filament and Unreal Engine rendering engines. The specific formulation, including the geometry term G and the embedding of the cosine term, is designed to simplify equations in the main NeRV paper. NeRV: Neural Reflectance and Visibility Fields for Relighting and View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00741, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Modified Disney Principled BRDF
head: ABSDF Base Material, Base Material Model
body: The Modified Disney Principled BRDF is a simplified surface reflectance model derived from the Disney Principled BRDF, tailored for use in the Absorption-Based Scene Diffusion Factorization (ABSDF) framework. It solves the problem of efficiently aggregating complex microfacet reflections by reducing the original model's complexity while retaining its core appearance capabilities for metals and plastics. It sets itself apart from its parent, the Microfacet BRDF with Simplified GGX and Schlick Fresnel, by explicitly adopting a Lambertian diffuse term, omitting sheen and clearcoat lobes, and assuming double-sided surfaces to facilitate analytical factorization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Incoming light direction \omegai, outgoing view direction \omegao, surface normal n, half vector \omegah = \frac{\omegai + \omegao}{\|\omegai + \omegao\|}, and material parameters \betaB = (\alpha, \betac, \betam, \betas). Outputs: Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) value f{disney}(\omegai, \omegao). Data Structures: The material parameters \betaB are spatially varying scalars: \alpha \in [0, 1]: Roughness. \betac \in [0, 1]: Base color (diffuse albedo). \betam \in [0, 1]: Metallic factor. \betas \in [0, 1]: Specular intensity (dielectric reflectance at normal incidence). Formulas: The model is defined as the sum of a diffuse component fd and a specular component fs: f{disney}(\omegai, \omegao) = fd(\omegai, \omegao) + fs(\omegai, \omegao) 1. Diffuse Component: Uses the Lambertian model: fd(\omegai, \omegao) = \frac{(1 - \betam)\betac}{\pi} Here, \betam reduces the diffuse contribution for metallic surfaces, and \betac is the base color albedo. 2. Specular Component: Combines metallic and dielectric Fresnel reflections using the GGX distribution D, the Schlick-GGX shadowing-masking function G, and the Schlick Fresnel function F: fs(\omegai, \omegao) = \frac{\betam D(\omegah; \alpha) G(\omegai, \omegao; \alpha) F(\omegah, \omegao; \betac)}{4 |n \cdot \omegao| |n \cdot \omegai|} + \frac{(1 - \betam) F(\omegah, \omegao; \betas)}{4 |n \cdot \omegao| |n \cdot \omegai|} D(\omegah; \alpha): Trowbridge-Reitz (GGX) microfacet distribution. G(\omegai, \omegao; \alpha): Shadowing-masking function (typically Schlick-GGX in this context). F(\omegah, \omegao; r0): Schlick Fresnel reflectance. 3. Schlick Fresnel: F(\omegah, \omegao; r0) = r0 (1 - Fc) + Fc Fc = (1 - |\omegah \cdot \omegao|)^5 Where r0 is the normal incidence reflectance. For the metallic lobe, r0 = \betac. For the dielectric lobe, r0 = \betas. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def modifieddisneybrdf(omegai, omegao, n, alpha, betac, betam, betas): # Ensure vectors are normalized omegai = normalize(omegai) omegao = normalize(omegao) n = normalize(n) # Compute half vector omegah = normalize(omegai + omegao) # Cosine terms costhetai = dot(n, omegai) costhetao = dot(n, omegao) costhetah = dot(n, omegah) # Avoid division by zero if costhetai <= 0 or costhetao <= 0: return 0.0 denom = 4.0 costhetai costhetao # 1. Diffuse Component (Lambertian) # (1 - betam) betac / pi fdiffuse = ((1.0 - betam) betac) / PI # 2. Specular Component # Microfacet Distribution D (GGX/Trowbridge-Reitz) # D(alpha, costhetah) = alpha^2 / (pi ((costhetah^2 (alpha^2 - 1) + 1)^2)) # Note: Standard GGX formula implementation required. alphasq = alpha alpha denomD = costhetah costhetah (alphasq - 1.0) + 1.0 D = alphasq / (PI denomD denomD) # Shadowing-Masking G (Schlick-GGX) # G(k, costheta) = costheta / (costheta (1 - k) + k) # k = (alpha + 1)^2 / 8 k = (alpha + 1.0) (alpha + 1.0) / 8.0 Gi = costhetai / (costhetai (1.0 - k) + k) Go = costhetao / (costhetao (1.0 - k) + k) G = Gi Go # Schlick Fresnel # Fc = (1 - |omegah. omegao|)^5 # F = r0 (1 - Fc) + Fc cosho = abs(dot(omegah, omegao)) Fc = pow(1.0 - cosho, 5.0) # Metallic lobe Fresnel (r0 = betac) Fmetal = betac (1.0 - Fc) + Fc # Dielectric lobe Fresnel (r0 = betas) Fdielectric = betas (1.0 - Fc) + Fc # Specular term # (betam D G Fmetal + (1 - betam) Fdielectric) / denom fspecular = (betam D G Fmetal + (1.0 - betam) Fdielectric) / denom return fdiffuse + fspecular Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Double-Sided Assumption: The model assumes double-sided surfaces, meaning the BRDF is evaluated regardless of the sign of n \cdot \omegai or n \cdot \omegao in the context of the factorization integral, though the geometric terms |n \cdot \omega| handle the dot product magnitude. Parameter Ranges: \betac, \betam, \betas must be clamped to [0, 1]. \alpha must be > 0 to avoid division by zero in the GGX distribution. Retro-reflection Omission: The original Disney model includes a retro-reflection term for diffuse light; this is omitted here, which may cause slight appearance differences for grazing angles on rough surfaces. Specular ABSDF Factorization is a method for computing the aggregated specular response of a surface with varying material parameters (roughness, orientation) by factorizing the integral of the microfacet BRDF over a probability distribution of these parameters. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the expectation of a complex microfacet distribution when the roughness \alpha and normal n are not single values but follow a joint probability density function pY(\gamma). It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly separating the Fresnel mix terms from the microfacet distribution convolution, allowing the shadowing-masking term G to be applied post-convolution due to its smoothness, and supporting orientation-varying parameters via spherical kernel splatting. A physically-based Bidirectional Reflectance Distribution Function (BRDF) used in 3D Gaussian Splatting for inverse rendering, consisting of a diffuse component and a specular component based on the GGX microfacet model with a correlated Smith masking-shadowing function. It differs from its parent, the Modified Disney Principled BRDF, by employing a specific roughness remapping (\alpha = r^2) and a correlated Smith geometry function rather than the separable Schlick-GGX approximation, aiming for higher physical accuracy in the context of Gaussian splatting optimization. The Isotropic Disney BRDF is a simplified material model based on the Cook-Torrance microfacet framework, designed to model reflectance for both metals and plastics in a unified manner. It is a restricted subset of the full Disney Principled BRDF, optimized for differentiable rendering and optimization tasks where ambiguity from high-dimensional parameter spaces must be reduced. Unlike the full model, it restricts optimization to opaque surfaces with spatially varying diffuse albedo and global constants for roughness, specular albedo, and metalness. A sub-component of the ABSDF framework that handles the analytical integration of the diffuse term. It assumes \betac and \betam are orientation-independent, allowing the joint parameter PDF to split into marginal PDFs. The integral \int{[0,1]^2} (1 - \betam) \betac p(\betac, \betam) d\betac d\betam simplifies to E[\betac] - E[\betam \betac]. For orientation-varying parameters, the clamped dot product function \langle n \cdot \omegai \rangle \langle n \cdot \omegao \rangle is approximated by a Spherical Gaussian (SG) c \cdot SG(\omegah; n, \kappa), reducing the problem to an SG-convolution. Complexity: The base evaluation is O(1) per sample. The ABSDF factorization allows for pre-computation of moments, reducing runtime aggregation costs for level-of-detail rendering. Strengths: Simplicity compared to the full Disney BRDF; compatibility with analytical factorization techniques; wide applicability to standard PBR assets. Limitations: Lack of sheen and clearcoat lobes limits the ability to model certain materials (e.g., hair, varnished wood) accurately. The Lambertian diffuse approximation may not capture subsurface scattering effects or retro-reflection present in the original model. When to use: When using the ABSDF framework for efficient scene aggregation or when a simplified, robust PBR model is needed for differentiable rendering. The Modified Disney Principled BRDF was introduced in the context of the Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering paper. It is based on the Disney Principled BRDF [Burley 2012], which is one of the most commonly used models in production for its versatility. The modifications were made to facilitate the mathematical factorization required for the ABSDF method, specifically by simplifying the diffuse term and removing complex lobes. Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/391729893, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial)

name: Diffuse ABSDF Factorization
head: Diffuse Aggregation
body:
Diffuse ABSDF (Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function) Factorization is a method for approximating the diffuse component of light transport in participating media by separating the integration over material parameters from the integration over geometry and orientation. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the diffuse scattering term in path tracing by reducing the double integral into a product of a parameter expectation term and a geometric convolution term. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Specular ABSDF Factorization by focusing specifically on the diffuse lobe, which allows for the use of Spherical Gaussian (SG) approximations for the cosine-weighted normal distribution, whereas specular components often require different handling or remain unaggregated in simplified models. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Joint probability density function (PDF) of material parameters p( etac,  etam), where  etac is the color absorption coefficient and  etam is the mean free path parameter (or similar scattering parameter); shading normal distribution pN(n); incoming direction \omegai; outgoing direction \omegao. Outputs: The aggregated diffuse scattering coefficient or integral value. Data Structures: Material Parameters:  etac,  etam \in [0, 1]. Normal Distribution: pN(n) defined on the hemisphere S^2. Spherical Gaussian (SG): Defined by amplitude c, concentration \kappa, and axis \omegah. Steps: 1. Split the Integral: Decompose the joint PDF pY(\gamma) into a product of marginal PDFs for material parameters and normals: pY(\gamma) \approx p( etac,  etam) pN(n). 2. Evaluate Parameter Integral: Compute the expectation term for the material parameters. The integral over the unit square [0,1]^2 is simplified using linearity of expectation: \int{[0,1]^2} (1 -  etam)  etac p( etac,  etam) d etac d etam = E[ etac] - E[ etam  etac] This requires calculating the first moment of  etac and the second-order mixed moment of  etam and  etac. 3. Approximate Geometric Integral: Approximate the clamped dot product function \langle n \cdot \omegai angle \langle n \cdot \omegao angle using a Spherical Gaussian (SG) product. Following Wang et al. [2009], the product of two clamped cosines is approximated by a single SG: \langle n \cdot \omegai angle \langle n \cdot \omegao angle \approx c \cdot SG(\omegah; n, \kappa) where c is the amplitude and \kappa is the concentration of the resulting SG, and \omegah is the half-vector between \omegai and \omegao. 4. Convolve with Normal Distribution: The remaining integral becomes a convolution between the approximated SG and the normal distribution pN(n): \int{S^2} c \cdot SG(\omegah; n, \kappa) pN(n) dn This convolution is solved using standard SG convolution techniques (e.g., as described in Wang et al. [2009] or referenced in), resulting in a closed-form or efficiently computable value. Parameters: SG Approximation: The specific values for c and \kappa depend on the angle between \omegai and \omegao. Exact formulas are provided in Wang et al. [2009]. Normal Distribution: Typically modeled as a GGX or similar distribution for rough surfaces, or a delta function for smooth surfaces. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Orientation-Varying Parameters: The basic factorization assumes orientation-independent parameters. If parameters vary with orientation, the splitting assumption pY(\gamma) \approx p( etac,  etam) pN(n) breaks down, requiring more complex handling as noted in §5.4 of. SG Approximation Error: The SG approximation of the clamped dot product product introduces error, especially at grazing angles or high roughness. The accuracy depends on the number of SGs used if a multi-Gaussian expansion is employed. Degenerate Normals: If the normal distribution is a delta function (perfectly smooth), the convolution simplifies to evaluating the SG at the single normal direction. This variant addresses the calculation of the correct cosine term in the path space measurement equation when the BSDF is not symmetric with respect to the geometric normal, such as in photon tracing or when using shading normals that differ from geometric normals. It prevents light leaks by checking the alignment of directions with normals. Step: Calculate dot products: wi

Time Complexity: The method reduces the complexity of the diffuse scattering evaluation from a high-dimensional integral to a few moment calculations and a closed-form SG convolution. The cost is dominated by the evaluation of the SG convolution, which is O(1) if a single SG is used, or O(K) if K SGs are used for higher accuracy. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory is required beyond storing the moments of the material parameters and the SG parameters. Strengths: Efficient evaluation of diffuse scattering in participating media; allows for LOD rendering by aggregating material properties. Limitations: Approximation error from SG fitting; assumes orientation-independent parameters for the basic form. When to Use: When efficient diffuse scattering in participating media is needed, especially in LOD rendering or real-time applications where full Monte Carlo integration is too expensive. When Not to Use: When high accuracy is required for grazing angles or highly anisotropic materials without proper SG expansion. Diffuse ABSDF Factorization originates from the work on Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering. It builds on the concept of aggregating material properties to simplify light transport calculations. The use of Spherical Gaussians for approximating BRDF terms is based on the work of Wang et al. [2009]. The method is part of a broader effort to make path tracing more efficient for production rendering, as seen in related works on production volume rendering [Fong et al. 2017] and path traced subsurface scattering [Wrenninge et al. 2017].
