name: Specular ABSDF Factorization
head: Specular Aggregation
body: Specular ABSDF Factorization computes the aggregated specular response of a surface with spatially varying material parameters by factorizing the integral of the microfacet BRDF over a joint probability distribution of those parameters. It solves the problem of efficiently evaluating the expectation of a complex microfacet distribution when the surface normal n and roughness \alpha follow a probability density function pY(\gamma) rather than taking single values. It sets itself apart from its siblings by explicitly separating the Fresnel mix terms from the microfacet distribution convolution, applying the shadowing-masking term G post-convolution due to its smoothness, and supporting orientation-varying parameters via spherical kernel splatting. The method computes the aggregated specular term by substituting the specular BRDF fs into the Aggregated BSDF (ABSDF) integral and expanding it into terms involving the Fresnel mix R and the microfacet distribution D. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The probability density function pY(\gamma) of material parameters \gamma = (n, \alpha, \betac, \betam, \betas), where n is the normal, \alpha is the roughness, and \beta terms are Fresnel coefficients. Output: The aggregated specular radiance contribution. Data Structures: SGGX Mixture: The surface Normal Distribution Function (NDF) pN(n) is represented as a mixture of k SGGX lobes: pN(n) = \sum{i=1}^k wi D{i,sggx}(n), where weights wi are positive and sum to 1. Precomputed Tables: Moments of the microfacet distribution M5(\alpha) and convolved distributions D{conv} are stored in lookup tables. Steps: 1. Substitution and Expansion: Substitute fs(\omegai, \omegao; \gamma) into the ABSDF integral (Eq. 7) and expand into terms involving R (Fresnel mix) and D (microfacet distribution): \int{\Gamma} fs(\omegai, \omegao; \gamma) \langle n \cdot \omegai \rangle \langle n \cdot \omegao \rangle pY(\gamma) d\gamma = \frac{1}{4} \int{\Gamma} (1 - Fc) R D pY(\gamma) d\gamma + Fc \int{\Gamma} R D pY(\gamma) d\gamma where R = \betam \betac + (1 - \betam)\betas and D = D(\omegah; n, \alpha) G(\omegai, \omegao; n, \alpha) 1(n \cdot \omegao) 1(n \cdot \omegai). 2. Splitting the PDF: Split the joint PDF pY(\gamma) into independent components for the Fresnel coefficients and the geometric parameters: pY(\gamma) \approx p{Y1}(\betac, \betam, \betas) p{Y2}(n, \alpha). 3. Evaluate Parameter Integral: Evaluate the integral over the Fresnel parameters \Gamma1 as moments: \int{\Gamma1} R p{Y1}(\gamma) d\gamma = E[\betam \betac] + E[\betas] - E[\betam \betas]. 4. Evaluate Microfacet Integral: Evaluate the integral over the geometric parameters \Gamma2 using precomputed tables. The convolution of the SGGX mixture with an isotropic spherical distribution g(\omega; n) is approximated by a roughened SGGX: \int{S^2} g(\omega; n) D{sggx}(n; R, \alpha) dn \approx D{sggx}(\omega; R, \alpha + \Delta) where R stays fixed but \alpha gains additional values. 5. Final Expression: Multiply the shadowing-masking term G to each lobe post-convolution, as it is very smooth: \int{\Gamma2} D p{Y2}(\gamma) d\gamma \approx \sum{i=1}^{2} \sum{j=1}^{k} wi m{ij} D{conv}(\omegah){ij} S{ij}(\omegai, \omegao) G{ij}(\omegai, \omegao) where S{ij} = S(\omegai, \omegao; \alpha{ij}) and G{ij} is the shadowing-masking term. Parameters: Spherical Domain Partition Size: Coarse partitioning such as 3 \times 3 is sufficient for orientation-varying parameters because angular frequency decreases as the scale of aggregation becomes larger. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The approximation of the convolution as a roughened SGGX relies on the validity of the eigenbasis parameterization. Boundaries: The Heaviside step functions 1(n \cdot \omegao) and 1(n \cdot \omegai) must be handled correctly to ensure clamped dot products. This method approximates the aggregated microfacet distribution \hat{D}{mic} of a scene or material asset by modeling the statistical spread of roughness values \alpha and fitting a two-lobed weighted sum to the expected distribution. It solves the problem of representing heterogeneous roughness distributions in a compact, analytically tractable form suitable for real-time rendering, avoiding the invalid range errors of Gaussian approximations by using a Beta distribution for the underlying roughness density. It sets itself apart from its parent by providing the specific statistical fitting mechanism for the microfacet term, and from simple single-lobe approximations by guaranteeing higher accuracy and never being worse than simple averaged roughness fits. Choose it when rendering scenes with significant roughness variation where single-lobed approximations fail to capture the statistical spread. The final expression for the specular component involves multiplying the shadowing-masking term G to each lobe post-convolution. The expression consists of contributions from all convolved NDF lobes, where each term is multiplied by its scaling factor to account for the specific roughness and orientation. This is an extension of the factorization to handle orientation-varying material parameters by computing directional moments weighted by a spherical kernel. It allows the model to capture view-dependent appearance changes due to orientation-varying material parameters. Steps: 1. For a direction \omega, weight each surface sample by a spherical function s(Tx \omega) as a kernel. 2. Compute directional moments E\omega[\beta] and E\omega[\beta \beta'] by integrating over the surface area A: E\omega[\beta] = \frac{\intA \betax s(Tx \omega) dx}{\intA s(Tx \omega) dx}, \quad E\omega[\beta \beta'] = \frac{\intA \betax \beta'x s(Tx \omega) dx}{\intA s(Tx \omega) dx} where Tx is the local transform at x. 3. For the specular component, set the kernel s(\omega) to the microfacet distribution. For the diffuse component, set the kernel s(\omega) to the Spherical Gaussian (SG) from Eq. 14. 4. Query the directional moments at \omegah when evaluating the specular and diffuse components. 5. During precomputation, splat each surface sample to the spherical partition. Time Complexity: The method reduces the complexity of aggregating microfacet distributions by precomputing moments and convolutions, allowing for efficient runtime evaluation using lookup tables. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for precomputed tables of moments and convolved distributions, as well as the spherical partition for orientation-varying parameters. Strengths: Efficiently handles material variation and orientation changes without requiring per-pixel integration of complex microfacet distributions. Limitations: The accuracy depends on the approximation of the convolution as a roughened SGGX and the coarse partitioning of the spherical domain. Specular ABSDF Factorization was introduced in the paper "Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering" by Yang Zhou, Tao Huang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Pradeep Sen, and Ling-Qi Yan. The method builds on previous work in microfacet theory and aggregation, such as the SGGX distribution [Heitz et al. 2015] and the aggregation of roughness distributions [Xu et al. 2013]. name: Aggregated Microfacet Distribution Approximation
head: Beta Distribution Fitting, Roughness Aggregation
body: This method approximates the aggregated microfacet distribution \hat{D}{mic} of a scene or material asset by modeling the statistical spread of roughness values \alpha and fitting a two-lobed weighted sum to the expected distribution. It solves the problem of representing heterogeneous roughness distributions in a compact, analytically tractable form suitable for real-time rendering, avoiding the invalid range errors of Gaussian approximations by using a Beta distribution for the underlying roughness density. It sets itself apart from its parent, Specular ABSDF Factorization, by providing the specific statistical fitting mechanism for the microfacet term, and from simple single-lobe approximations by guaranteeing higher accuracy and never being worse than simple averaged roughness fits. Inputs: The marginal density function of roughness pA(\alpha), modeled as a Beta distribution B(\alpha; a, b) with shape parameters a and b. The base microfacet distribution function D{mic}(\omegah; \alpha) (e.g., GGX). Outputs: A mapping M2(a, b) that returns the weights m1, m2 and roughness parameters \alpha1, \alpha2 for the two-lobed approximation. Data Structures: A 2D lookup table storing the precomputed mapping (m1, \alpha1, \alpha2) for discrete values of a and b. Steps: 1. Model the roughness distribution pA(\alpha) using a Beta distribution B(\alpha; a, b). 2. Define the aggregated microfacet distribution as the expectation of the microfacet distribution over the roughness distribution: \hat{D}{mic}(\omegah) = \int0^1 D{mic}(\omegah; \alpha) pA(\alpha) d\alpha This integral represents a weighted average of infinite microfacet lobes with different possible \alpha values. 3. Approximate \hat{D}{mic}(\omegah) by a weighted average of two lobes: \hat{D}{mic}(\omegah) \approx m1 D{mic}(\omegah; \alpha1) + m2 D{mic}(\omegah; \alpha2) where m1 + m2 = 1. 4. Perform a nonlinear least-square fit to find the best mapping (m1, \alpha1, \alpha2) = M2(a, b) given the shape parameters a and b of the Beta distribution. 5. Store the mapping M2(a, b) in a 2D lookup table for runtime retrieval. Parameters: a, b: Shape parameters of the Beta distribution for roughness. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using a Gaussian distribution for pA(\alpha) is invalid because it does not respect the [0, 1] bounds of \alpha, potentially leading to invalid range errors. A truncated Gaussian can be restricted to the valid range but requires a more tedious fitting process. This method models the aggregated microfacet roughness distribution pA(\alpha) using a Beta distribution B(\alpha; a, b) to estimate the statistical spread of roughness values \alpha from asset data. It sets itself apart from Gaussian approximations because the Beta distribution is naturally bounded within the valid [0, 1] range of \alpha, preventing invalid range errors. Choose this method when the roughness distribution is strictly bounded and requires a statistically accurate representation. See Aggregated Microfacet Distribution via Beta Distribution. The Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF) is a method for efficient scene appearance aggregation for Level-of-Detail (LoD) rendering. It sets itself apart from explicit geometry rendering by precomputing aggregated visibility and material properties, allowing the renderer to avoid tracing explicit geometry and shadow rays. Choose this method when rendering scenes with high geometric complexity and instancing where explicit geometry tracing is too costly. See Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF). The Horizon Principled BRDF is a bidirectional reflectance distribution function used in the Horizon rendering engine. It sets itself apart from general aggregation functions by fixing specific parameter values (such as \gamma=2 for the main lobe and \gamma=1 for clear coat) and implementing a specific diffuse Fresnel variation to correct edge darkening. Choose this method when using the Horizon rendering engine or requiring a Disney-compatible principled shading approach. See Horizon Principled BRDF. A method to fit aggregated microfacet distributions using a 2-lobe weighted sum. It sets itself apart from single-lobe fits with simple averaged roughness by being overall more accurate and guaranteed to be never worse. Choose this method when balancing computational cost and accuracy for microfacet approximation. Time and Memory Complexity: Precomputation involves a nonlinear least-square fit, which is performed offline. Runtime cost is dominated by a 2D table lookup for the mapping M2(a, b) and the evaluation of two microfacet lobes, which is constant time relative to the number of roughness samples. Memory usage is determined by the resolution of the 2D lookup table storing M2(a, b). Measured Performance: The 2-lobe fit is validated against ground-truth aggregated microfacet distributions and is shown to be more accurate than single-lobe fits with simple averaged roughness. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: It accurately captures the statistical spread of roughness in heterogeneous materials without the boundary errors of Gaussian approximations. It provides a guaranteed improvement over simple single-lobe approximations. Limitations: It requires offline precomputation of the fitting table. The accuracy depends on the expressiveness of the Beta distribution to model the true roughness density pA(\alpha). When to Use: Not given in the sources. The method originates from research on efficient scene appearance aggregation for Level-of-Detail rendering. It addresses the need to represent the far-field appearance of scene aggregates by integrating light transport over positions, allowing for the avoidance of explicit geometry tracing. The use of the Beta distribution for roughness modeling and the 2-lobe approximation for the microfacet term are specific contributions to this framework. name: Aggregated Microfacet Distribution via Beta Distribution
head: Beta Distribution Microfacet Roughness
body: This method models the aggregated microfacet roughness distribution pA(\alpha) using a Beta distribution B(\alpha; a, b) to estimate the statistical spread of roughness values \alpha from asset data. It is chosen over Gaussian approximations because the Beta distribution is naturally bounded within the valid [0, 1] range of \alpha, preventing the invalid range errors that occur when Gaussian tails exceed these bounds. Inputs: A set of roughness maps or a statistical summary (mean \mu and variance \sigma^2) of the roughness values \alpha from the input assets. Outputs: Shape parameters a and b for the Beta distribution, and the resulting probability density function pA(\alpha). Data Structures: The method operates on scalar values. The roughness \alpha is a float in [0, 1]. The parameters a and b are positive floats. Steps: 1. Compute the mean \mu and variance \sigma^2 of the roughness values \alpha from the input data. 2. Calculate the shape parameter a using the formula: a = -\frac{\mu (\sigma^2 + \mu^2 - \mu)}{\sigma^2}. 3. Calculate the shape parameter b using the formula: b = \frac{(\sigma^2 + \mu^2 - \mu)(\mu - 1)}{\sigma^2}. 4. Define the aggregated distribution as the Beta distribution with these parameters: pA(\alpha) = B(\alpha; a, b). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fitbetadistribution(meanmu, variancesigma2): """ Estimates Beta distribution shape parameters a and b from mean and variance. Args: meanmu (float): The mean roughness value. variancesigma2 (float): The variance of the roughness values. Returns: tuple: (a, b) shape parameters for the Beta distribution. """ # Calculate the common term (sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu) term = variancesigma2 + meanmu2 - meanmu # Calculate shape parameter a # Source formula: a = -mu (sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu) / sigma^2 a = -meanmu term / variancesigma2 # Calculate shape parameter b # Source formula: b = (sigma^2 + mu^2 - mu) (mu - 1) / sigma^2 b = term (meanmu - 1) / variancesigma2 return a, b Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Range Validity: Unlike Gaussian distributions, the Beta distribution naturally respects the [0, 1] range of \alpha. This avoids the pitfall where a Gaussian fit for roughness maps might assign non-zero probability to invalid roughness values outside [0, 1]. Parameter Constraints: The shape parameters a and b must be positive for a valid Beta distribution. The source formulas are derived from the moments of the Beta distribution. If the input \mu and \sigma^2 do not correspond to a valid Beta distribution (e.g., variance is too large for the given mean), the resulting a or b may be negative or zero, leading to undefined behavior. The source notes that this fitting is performed on actual assets, implying the data is well-behaved. Truncated Gaussian Alternative: A truncated Gaussian could be restricted to the valid range and may produce similar quality, but the fitting process is more tedious. This variant involves fitting roughness maps from assets to beta distributions to estimate the distribution of alpha (roughness). It is preferred over Gaussian distributions because Gaussians can exceed the valid [0, 1] range of alpha, whereas beta distributions are bounded. Truncated Gaussians could be restricted to the valid range and may produce similar quality, but the fitting process is more tedious. Time and Memory Complexity: The fitting process involves constant-time arithmetic operations given the mean and variance. The complexity is O(1) per asset or map summary. Storing the parameters a and b requires minimal memory (two floats). Measured Performance: The source validates the approach by estimating pA(\alpha) from roughness maps used for actual assets. The fits are described as "reasonably accurate" and adapt to different modes of real data. The method is compared to ground-truth aggregated microfacet distributions and simple averaged roughness, showing that the fits are "overall more accurate and guaranteed to be never worse than the simple fits". Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Naturally bounded to [0, 1], avoiding invalid roughness values. More accurate than simple averaged roughness. Limitations: Requires accurate estimation of mean and variance. The source does not provide specific hardware performance metrics or resolution scaling data. When to Use: Use this method when aggregating microfacet distributions for level-of-detail rendering or when approximating the roughness distribution from asset data, especially when the roughness values are bounded in [0, 1] and a Gaussian approximation would risk exceeding these bounds. This method appears in the 2022 Computer Graphics Forum paper "Advances in Neural Rendering" by Tretschk et al., which uses a Beta distribution to represent the roughness distribution pA(\alpha). It builds on the Aggregated Microfacet Distribution Approximation [10880-aggregated-microfacet-distribution-approximation.md]. name: Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF)
head: ABSDF-based method, Scene Appearance Aggregation for LoD Rendering
body: The Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF) is a method for efficient scene appearance aggregation for Level-of-Detail (LoD) rendering, designed to handle scenes with high geometric complexity and instancing. It defines a 4D function of incident and outgoing directions that describes the far-field appearance of a scene aggregate by integrating the 8D light transport function over positions, effectively capturing the aggregated appearance of all surfaces within a volume. Unlike explicit geometry rendering, ABSDF precomputes aggregated visibility and material properties, allowing the renderer to avoid tracing explicit geometry and shadow rays, thereby reducing the sample count required for convergence. It builds on Aggregated Microfacet Distribution Approximation by providing a closed-form factorization that supports all-frequency and view-dependent effects. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene composed of multiple aggregated objects and instances, defined by their geometry, materials (modeled via Disney Principled BRDF with GGX microfacets), and spatial layout. Output: A rendered image at a specified LoD resolution (e.g., 64^3, 128^3, 256^3, 512^3) with precomputed aggregated data structures. Data Structures: The method relies on a voxel grid representation of the scene. Each voxel stores aggregated data derived from the surfaces within it. 1. Aggregated Interior Visibility (AIV): A high-dimensional data structure representing visibility within the volume. It is compressed using Compact Principal Component Analysis (CPCA). 2. Aggregated Boundary Visibility (ABV): A data structure representing visibility at the boundaries of the voxel, used to compute partial occlusion between different instances. 3. NDF Lobes: The material appearance is approximated using up to 4 surface Normal Distribution Function (NDF) lobes in the "maximum" configuration. Parameters: LoD Resolution: The spatial subdivision resolution (e.g., 64^3, 128^3). NDF Lobes: Number of lobes for material approximation (up to 4). Truncation Thresholds: Coefficient truncation for AIV and ABV data (e.g., 1%, 10%). CPCA Representatives: Number of representatives kept for CPCA compression (1 or more). Steps: 1. Spatial Subdivision: Subdivide the scene into voxels at a resolution suitable for the pixel footprint, ensuring each voxel satisfies the far-field assumption. 2. Precomputation: For each voxel, integrate the product of base material, foreshortening factors, and bidirectional visibility over the underlying surfaces to compute the ABSDF. Compute Aggregated Interior Visibility (AIV) and Aggregated Boundary Visibility (ABV). Apply CPCA to compress the high-dimensional AIV data. Apply coefficient truncation to AIV and ABV data to reduce memory footprint. Use a truncated ellipsoid primitive to approximate the voxel shape, improving the preservation of local correlation compared to a cubic primitive. 3. Instance Selection: For scenes with multiple aggregated objects and instancing, each instance selects its LoD level based on its screen-space projection size. 4. Rendering: Trace rays through the voxel grid. For each voxel hit, evaluate the ABSDF to determine the outgoing radiance. The ABSDF factorization allows for efficient evaluation and sampling. Use ABV to compute partial occlusion between different instances, treating them as uncorrelated. Use precomputed AIV to determine visibility, avoiding the tracing of shadow rays. Perform splitting to allocate more samples for lighting (e.g., Next Event Estimation) since the representation is already anti-aliased. Formulas: The ABSDF \hat{f}(\omegai, \omegao) is defined by integrating the product of base material, foreshortening factors, and bidirectional visibility over the underlying surfaces. The normalization term uses the projected area |A|{\omegao} for simplicity, though the visible projected area |Av(\omegao)| could also be used as it cancels out in accumulation equations. The symmetry property of the ABSDF is: |A|{\omegao} \hat{f}(\omegai, \omegao) = |A|{\omegai} \hat{f}(\omegao, \omegai) where |A|{\omegao} is the projected area of the voxel in the direction \omegao. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Independence Assumptions: Eq. 6 assumes independence between visibility and material in a single voxel, which can lead to artifacts, especially at coarse scales. Eq. 25 assumes independence between visibility along two directions, which can lead to incorrect occlusion when the camera and light source are collocated. Angular Resolution: At the coarsest scale, the multi-lobe NDF may not have sufficient angular resolution to resolve all highlights, resulting in a slightly darker look. Truncation Errors: Hard shadows may have small imperfections due to visibility coefficient truncation and compression. 1% truncation results in visible inaccuracy, while 10% truncation introduces barely recognizable error. CPCA Compression: Using only 1 CPCA representative reduces CPCA to simple vector quantization and approximates per-cluster subspaces poorly. Memory Complexity: The memory footprint is largely independent of the original scene complexity, providing asymptotic benefits for larger scenes. It requires more memory than HybridLoD and NonExp mainly due to high-dimensional aggregated visibility data even after compression. The memory cost is agnostic to whether the original scene contains instanced geometry. Performance: The method is comparable to the PT (Path Tracing) baseline in terms of rendering speed, whereas HybridLoD and NonExp are significantly slower, likely due to the complexity of nested ray marching or sampling. The method avoids spending a large number of samples to trace explicit geometry, allowing for more samples to be allocated for lighting. Quality: The method achieves superior quality compared to existing methods (HybridLoD, NonExp) and DAP on various scenes, as shown by lower RMSE in comparisons. Scaling: The memory footprint scales quadratically with respect to LoD resolution. If a model only occupies a small portion of the rendered image, a coarser LoD level with much smaller memory is needed. When to Use: Suitable for large, complex scenes with high geometric complexity and instancing, where explicit rendering is infeasible due to memory constraints. When Not to Use: Not suitable for small scenes where explicit representation is more efficient. Currently limited to direct illumination; supporting global illumination would require modeling multiple scattering between scene parts. The Aggregated Bidirectional Scattering Distribution Function (ABSDF) method was presented in the paper "Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering" by Yang Zhou, Tao Huang, Ravi Ramamoorthi, Pradeep Sen, and Ling-Qi Yan, published in October 2024. The method addresses the challenge of rendering large, complex scenes with high geometric detail by aggregating the appearance of surfaces within a volume into a compact representation. It builds upon previous work in appearance aggregation and LoD rendering, aiming to provide a scalable solution for physically based rendering of massive scenes. Efficient Scene Appearance Aggregation for Level-of-Detail Rendering, https://core.ac.uk/works/391729893, fetched 2026-11-01 (unofficial)

name: Horizon Principled BRDF
head: Disney Principled BRDF variant, Horizon PBR
body: The Horizon Principled BRDF is a bidirectional reflectance distribution function used in the Horizon rendering engine, designed to be compatible with Disney's principled shading approach. It solves the problem of providing a physically plausible, energy-conserving shading model that supports a wide range of material types (dielectric, metallic, clear coat, sheen) through a unified set of normalized parameters. It sets itself apart from its parent, Aggregated Microfacet Distribution Approximation, by fixing specific parameter values (such as \gamma=2 for the main lobe and \gamma=1 for clear coat) and implementing a specific diffuse Fresnel variation to correct edge darkening, rather than using a general aggregation function. The Horizon BRDF computes the total reflected radiance fr(l, v) as the sum of a diffuse component fd and a specular component fs: fr(l, v) = fd + fs where l is the incoming light vector, v is the outgoing view vector, and n is the surface normal vector. The method requires the following inputs and parameters, all normalized between 0 and 1 unless specified: albedo: Surface color at the point. roughness: Controls microfacet alignment. 0 is smooth, 1 is rough. F0: Base reflectivity constant for the material. anisotropic: Controls anisotropy. 0 is isotropic, 1 is highly anisotropic. Subsurface: Blends diffuse with a Hanrahan-Krueger inspired subsurface BRDF. 0 is no subsurface, 1 is full blending. Metallic: 0 is dielectric, 1 is metallic. Specular: Intensity of specular light. 0 is low, 1 is high. Specular Tint: Interpolates specular color between achromatic (white, 0) and base color (1). Sheen: Intensity of edge reflections. 0 is low, 1 is high. Sheen Tint: Tint for sheen reflections. Clear Coat: Intensity of the second specular lobe. 0 is none, 1 is full. Clear Coat Gloss: Smoothness of the clear coat lobe. 0 is matte, 1 is satin. absorption coefficient (\alpha), distance (l), concentration (c): Used for translucent materials via Beer-Lambert law. The method operates on standard 3D vectors for l, v, n, h, x, y. The halfway vector h is computed as: h = \frac{l + v}{|l + v|} The diffuse component uses a modified Lambertian model with a Fresnel factor to prevent edge darkening. 1. Calculate the base Lambertian diffuse: f{Lambert} = \frac{albedo}{\pi} 2. Calculate the diffuse Fresnel factor FD{90}: FD{90} = 0.5 + 2(h \cdot v)^{roughness} 3. Compute the final diffuse term: fd = f{Lambert} \left[1 + (FD{90} - 1)(1 - (l \cdot n))^5\right] \left[1 + (FD{90} - 1)(1 - (n \cdot v))^5\right] This factor accounts for the portion of light reflected vs. refracted based on viewing angle, reducing incident reflectance by half at sharp angles for smooth surfaces and increasing response for rough surfaces. The specular component follows the Cook-Torrance microfacet model: fs = \frac{D(h) F(h, v) G(l, h, v)}{4(l \cdot n)(n \cdot v)} where D is the Normal Distribution Function (NDF), F is the Fresnel coefficient, and G is the Geometry Shadowing Function. Uses the Schlick approximation: F{Schlick}(F0, h, v) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - (h \cdot v))^5 Horizon uses the Generalized Trowbridge-Reiss (GTR) distribution with fixed \gamma values. Main Lobe (\gamma = 2): Equivalent to GGX. Used for the base material. D{GGX} = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi \left[1 + (\alpha^2 - 1)(h \cdot n)^2\right]^2} where \alpha = roughness^2. Clear Coat Lobe (\gamma = 1): Used for the clear coat layer. This lobe is always isotropic and non-metallic. Due to a singularity at \gamma=1, the limit form is used: D{GTR1} = \frac{\alpha^2 - 1}{2\pi \log(\alpha^2) \left[1 + (\alpha^2 - 1)(h \cdot n)^2\right]} Anisotropic Main Lobe: If anisotropic > 0, the main lobe uses an anisotropic GTR form: D{GTR2, anisotropic} = \frac{1}{\pi \alphax \alphay \left[\frac{(h \cdot x)^2}{\alphax^2} + \frac{(h \cdot y)^2}{\alphay^2} + (h \cdot n)^2\right]^2} where x and y are tangent and binormal vectors. The anisotropic roughness parameters are: \alphax = \frac{roughness^2}{ar}, \quad \alphay = roughness^2 \cdot ar The aspect ratio ar is derived from the anisotropic parameter: ar = \sqrt{1 - 0.9 \cdot anisotropic} The factor 0.9 limits the aspect ratio to 10:1. Uses the separable Smith GGX function. Isotropic: G{GGX} = \frac{1}{(l \cdot h) + \sqrt{\alpha^2 + (l \cdot h)^2 - \alpha^2(l \cdot h)^2}} Anisotropic: G{GGX, anisotropic} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2} \sqrt{(l \cdot h)^2 + \alphax^2(l \cdot x)^2 + \alphay^2(l \cdot y)^2 + (l \cdot h)^2}} Subsurface Blending: The Subsurface parameter blends the calculated fd with a Hanrahan-Krueger inspired subsurface BRDF. This is not a substitute for full subsurface transport; it does not bleed light into shadows or through the surface. Beer-Lambert Law: For translucent materials (glass, liquids), light absorption is modeled independently: \frac{I1}{I0} = e^{-\alpha l c} where I0 is incident intensity, I1 is transmitted intensity, \alpha is the absorption coefficient, l is the distance light travels, and c is the concentration of absorbing elements. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def dot(a, b): return sum(x y for x, y in zip(a, b)) def horizonprincipledbrdf(l, v, n, albedo, roughness, F0, anisotropic, metallic, specular, speculartint, sheen, sheentint, clearcoat, clearcoatgloss, subsurface, tangentx, tangenty, absorptioncoeff, distance, concentration): # 1. Precompute vectors h = [l[i] + v[i] for i in range(3)] hlen = math.sqrt(dot(h, h)) h = [x / hlen for x in h] costhetal = dot(l, n) costhetav = dot(v, n) costhetah = dot(h, n) costhetahv = dot(h, v) # 2. Compute Diffuse Component flambert = [x / math.pi for x in albedo] fd90 = 0.5 + 2.0 (costhetahv roughness) terml = 1.0 + (fd90 - 1.0) ((1.0 - costhetal) 5) termv = 1.0 + (fd90 - 1.0) ((1.0 - costhetav) 5) fd = [x terml termv for x in flambert] # 3. Compute Specular Component (Main Lobe) alpha = roughness 2 if anisotropic > 0: ar = math.sqrt(1.0 - 0.9 anisotropic) alphax = alpha / ar alphay = alpha ar denomndf = costhetah 2 + (dot(h, tangentx) 2) / (alphax 2) + (dot(h, tangenty) 2) / (alphay 2) Dmain = 1.0 / (math.pi alphax alphay (denomndf 2)) gdenomsq = 2.0 (costhetah 2) + (alphax 2 dot(l, tangentx) 2) + (alphay 2 dot(l, tangenty) 2) Gmain = 1.0 / (math.sqrt(2.0) math.sqrt(gdenomsq)) else: denomndf = 1.0 + (alpha - 1.0) (costhetah 2) Dmain = alpha / (math.pi (denomndf 2)) gdenom = costhetah + math.sqrt(alpha 2 + (costhetah 2) - (alpha 2 (costhetah 2))) Gmain = 1.0 / gdenom Fmain = F0 + (1.0 - F0) ((1.0 - costhetahv) 5) specdenom = 4.0 costhetal costhetav if specdenom < 1e-8: fsmain = 0.0 else: fsmain = (Dmain Fmain Gmain) / specdenom # 4. Compute Clear Coat Specular Component (Isotropic, gamma=1) ccalpha = clearcoatgloss 2 alphasq = ccalpha 2 denomndfcc = 1.0 + (alphasq - 1.0) (costhetah 2) logalphasq = math.log(alphasq) if abs(logalphasq) < 1e-8: Dcc = 1.0 / math.pi else: Dcc = (alphasq - 1.0) / (2.0 math.pi logalphasq denomndfcc) Fcc = F0 + (1.0 - F0) ((1.0 - costhetahv) 5) gdenomcc = costhetah + math.sqrt(ccalpha 2 + (costhetah 2) - (ccalpha 2 (costhetah 2))) Gcc = 1.0 / gdenomcc fscc = (Dcc Fcc Gcc) / specdenom if specdenom > 1e-8 else 0.0 fs = fsmain + clearcoat fscc # 5. Subsurface Blending # The Hanrahan-Krueger formula is not provided in the sources. # A linear blend with a placeholder subsurface term would be: fd = lerp(fd, fsubsurface, subsurface) # fdfinal = fd # 6. Sheen # The Sheen BRDF formula is not provided in the sources. fsheen = 0.0 # 7. Total fr = [fd[i] + fs + fsheen for i in range(3)] # 8. Translucency (Beer-Lambert) # Applied to transmitted light: Itransmitted = Iincident exp(-absorptioncoeff distance concentration) return fr Singularity at \gamma=1: The GTR NDF has a singularity at \gamma=1. The source specifies using the limit form D{GTR1} for the clear coat lobe. Edge Darkening: Standard Lambertian diffuse is darker at grazing angles. The Horizon model addresses this with the FD{90} Fresnel variation. Subsurface Limitations: The subsurface blending parameter does not perform full subsurface transport; it does not bleed light into shadows or through the surface. Clear Coat Constraints: The clear coat lobe is always isotropic and non-metallic, regardless of the main lobe's settings. Not given in the sources. The Horizon Principled BRDF was introduced in the Horizon rendering engine. It is inspired by Disney's "principled" shading approach, adhering to its usability and interactivity principles. The engine is used for visualizing large medical imaging datasets, such as fiber tracking algorithms generating millions of streamlines, and translucent materials like glass and liquids. The BRDF was published in a preprint in 2023. Horizon, closing the gap between cinematic visualization and medical imaging, https://doi.org/10.1101/2023.07.11.23292519, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Phys3DGS BRDF Function
head: Phys3DGS BRDF
body: A physically-based BRDF function used in 3D Gaussian Splatting for inverse rendering, consisting of a diffuse and a specular component. It differs from its parent, Modified Disney Principled BRDF, by employing a specific roughness remapping (\alpha = r^2) and a correlated Smith masking-shadowing function rather than a separable approximation. Inputs: \omegai: Incident light direction. \omegao: Outgoing view direction. \bm{n}: Surface normal. \bm{a}: Base color (diffuse albedo). m: Metallic value (scalar). r: Roughness parameter (scalar). Outputs: f(\omegao, \omegai): Reflected radiance factor. Steps: 1. Compute Roughness Remapping: \alpha = r^2. 2. Compute Half Vector: \bm{h} = (\omegai + \omegao) / \|\omegai + \omegao\|. 3. Compute Fresnel Term (F): F0 = 0.04(1 - m) + \bm{a}m. Then F(\bm{h}, \bm{n}) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - \bm{h} \cdot \bm{n})^5. 4. Compute Normal Distribution Function (D): D(\alpha, \bm{h}, \bm{n}) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi ((\bm{h} \cdot \bm{n})^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1)^2}. 5. Compute Masking-Shadowing Function (G): G{\lambda}(\alpha, \bm{n} \cdot \omegai) = \frac{1}{2(\sqrt{1 + \alpha(1 - (\bm{n} \cdot \omegai)^2)/(\bm{n} \cdot \omegai)^2} - 1)}. G(\alpha, \bm{n}, \omegai, \omegao) = \frac{1}{1 + G{\lambda}(\alpha, \bm{n} \cdot \omegai) + G{\lambda}(\alpha, \bm{n} \cdot \omegao)}. 6. Compute Final BRDF: f(\omegao, \omegai) = \frac{1-m}{\pi}\bm{a} + \frac{DFG}{4(\omegai \cdot \bm{n})(\omegao \cdot \bm{n})}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phys3dgsbrdf(omegai, omegao, n, a, m, r): # 1. Roughness remapping alpha = r r # 2. Half vector h = normalize(omegai + omegao) # 3. Fresnel F0 = 0.04 (1 - m) + a m costhetah = dot(h, n) F = F0 + (1 - F0) (1 - costhetah)5 # 4. Normal Distribution Function (GGX) costhetahsq = costhetah costhetah denomD = costhetahsq (alpha alpha - 1) + 1 D = (alpha alpha) / (pi denomD denomD) # 5. Masking-Shadowing Function (Correlated Smith) def lambdaggx(alpha, costheta): # costheta is n. omega if costheta == 0: return 0.0 term = 1 + (alpha (1 - costheta costheta)) / (costheta costheta) term = max(term, 0.0) return 1.0 / (2.0 (sqrt(term) - 1.0)) costhetai = dot(n, omegai) costhetao = dot(n, omegao) lambdai = lambdaggx(alpha, costhetai) lambdao = lambdaggx(alpha, costhetao) G = 1.0 / (1.0 + lambdai + lambdao) # 6. Final BRDF denomspec = 4.0 costhetai costhetao if denomspec == 0: return 0.0 specular = (D F G) / denomspec diffuse = ((1 - m) / pi) a return diffuse + specular Parameters: m (metallic): Optimized during training. Regularizer weight \lambda{smooth} is 0.02. r (roughness): Optimized during training. Regularizer weight \lambda{smooth} is 0.02. \bm{a} (base color): Optimized during training. Regularizer weight is 0.06. Edge Cases: Grazing Angles: If \bm{n} \cdot \omegai or \bm{n} \cdot \omegao approaches 0, the specular denominator approaches 0. Zero Half Vector: If \omegai = -\omegao, the half vector is undefined. Precision in Lambda: The term inside the square root for G{\lambda} must be non-negative; numerical errors at grazing angles require a max(term, 0.0) guard. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Standard vector operations are O(1) per evaluation. Strengths and Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. The Phys3DGS BRDF function was introduced in "Phys3DGS: Physically-based 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering" (ECCV 2024 Submission #12158). It provides a differentiable, physically-based material model within the 3D Gaussian Splatting framework for inverse rendering. name: Isotropic Disney BRDF
head: Cook-Torrance based Disney BRDF, Disney BRDF Material Model, Simplified Disney BRDF
body: The Isotropic Disney BRDF is a simplified material model based on the Cook-Torrance microfacet framework, designed to model reflectance for both metals and plastics in a unified manner. It is a restricted subset of the full Disney Principled BRDF, optimized for differentiable rendering and optimization tasks where ambiguity from high-dimensional parameter spaces must be reduced. Unlike the full model, it restricts optimization to opaque surfaces with spatially varying diffuse albedo and global constants for roughness, specular albedo, and metalness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface position \mathbf{x}, incoming light direction \omegai, outgoing view direction \omegao, normal \mathbf{n}. Parameters: a(\mathbf{x}) \in [0, 1]^3: Diffuse albedo, spatially varying. s \in [0, 1]: Specular albedo, global constant. \beta \in [0, 1]: Surface roughness, global constant. m \in [0, 1]: Metalness, global constant. Output: Reflected radiance Lr(\omegao). Data Structures: The model assumes a single material instance per surface or texture-mapped parameters. The albedo a is stored as a 3-channel texture or array indexed by \mathbf{x}. The parameters s, \beta, m are scalar constants or global uniforms. Formulas: The BRDF fr(\omegai, \omegao) is composed of a diffuse term and a specular term, blended by the metalness parameter m: fr(\omegai, \omegao) = (1 - m) f{diff} + m f{spec} The diffuse term uses a simplified Lambertian model modulated by the diffuse albedo: f{diff} = \frac{a(\mathbf{x})}{\pi} The specular term follows the Cook-Torrance model: f{spec} = \frac{D(\mathbf{h}) F(\omegai, \mathbf{h}) G(\omegai, \omegao, \mathbf{h})}{4 (\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai) (\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegao)} Where: \mathbf{h} = \frac{\omegai + \omegao}{\|\omegai + \omegao\|} is the half-vector. D(\mathbf{h}) is the Normal Distribution Function (NDF). The sources cite the Disney BRDF but do not provide the explicit NDF formula (e.g., GGX or Beckmann) in the provided text. Standard Disney implementations typically use a GGX distribution: D(\mathbf{h}) = \frac{\alpha^2}{\pi ((\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h})^2 (\alpha^2 - 1) + 1)^2}, where \alpha is derived from roughness \beta. F(\omegai, \mathbf{h}) is the Fresnel term. The sources do not specify the exact Fresnel equation (e.g., Schlick approximation). Typically F(\omegai, \mathbf{h}) = F0 + (1 - F0)(1 - \omegai \cdot \mathbf{h})^5, where F0 is the specular albedo s for dielectrics and interpolated for metals. G(\omegai, \omegao, \mathbf{h}) is the geometry function. The sources do not specify the exact geometry function (e.g., Schlick-GGX). Typically G(\omegai, \omegao, \mathbf{h}) = G{Schlick}(\omegai, \mathbf{n}, \alpha) G{Schlick}(\omegao, \mathbf{n}, \alpha). Steps: 1. Retrieve diffuse albedo a(\mathbf{x}) from the spatial texture at point \mathbf{x}. 2. Compute the half-vector \mathbf{h} from \omegai and \omegao. 3. Evaluate the NDF D(\mathbf{h}) using roughness \beta. 4. Evaluate the Fresnel term F(\omegai, \mathbf{h}) using specular albedo s and metalness m. 5. Evaluate the geometry term G(\omegai, \omegao, \mathbf{h}) using roughness \beta. 6. Compute the specular BRDF value f{spec} using the Cook-Torrance formula. 7. Compute the diffuse BRDF value f{diff} using a(\mathbf{x}). 8. Blend the terms: fr = (1 - m) f{diff} + m f{spec}. 9. Multiply fr by the incident radiance Li(\omegai) and integrate over the hemisphere (typically via Monte Carlo sampling). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def isotropicdisneybrdf(x, omegai, omegao, n, atexture, s, beta, m): # 1. Retrieve diffuse albedo a = atexture.sample(x) # Spatially varying # 2. Compute half vector h = normalize(omegai + omegao) # 3. Evaluate NDF D(h) # Note: Exact NDF formula not provided in sources # Assuming standard GGX implementation alpha = beta # Or mapped from beta nh = dot(n, h) if nh <= 0: return 0.0 denom = (nh nh) (alpha alpha - 1) + 1 D = (alpha alpha) / (pi denom denom) # 4. Evaluate Fresnel F(omegai, h) # Note: Exact Fresnel formula not provided in sources # Assuming Schlick approximation # F0 depends on metalness m and specular albedo s F0 = mix(vec3(s), a, m) # Interpolate between specular albedo and diffuse albedo F = F0 + (1 - F0) pow(1 - dot(omegai, h), 5) # 5. Evaluate Geometry G(omegai, omegao, h) # Note: Exact Geometry formula not provided in sources # Assuming Schlick-GGX def schlickggx(v, n, alpha): nv = dot(v, n) if nv <= 0: return 0.0 r = alpha + (1 - alpha) nv nv return nv / (nv (1 - r) + r) G = schlickggx(omegai, n, alpha) schlickggx(omegao, n, alpha) # 6. Compute specular term noi = dot(n, omegai) noo = dot(n, omegao) if noi <= 0 or noo <= 0: return 0.0 fspec = (D F G) / (4 noi noo) # 7. Compute diffuse term fdiff = a / pi # 8. Blend fr = (1 - m) fdiff + m fspec return fr Parameters: a(\mathbf{x}): Diffuse albedo, range [0, 1]^3. s: Specular albedo, range [0, 1]. \beta: Roughness, range [0, 1]. m: Metalness, range [0, 1]. Edge Cases: If \mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai \le 0 or \mathbf{n} \cdot \omegao \le 0, the BRDF is zero (backface or grazing). Precision issues may arise when \beta is very small (mirror-like) or very large (rough). A method for factorizing the specular component of the BRDF, used in conjunction with this model for differentiable rendering [10872-specular-absdf-factorization.md]. A physically-based BRDF function for 3D Gaussian Splatting, offering an alternative shading model [11071-phys3dgs-brdf-function.md]. Complexity: The evaluation is O(1) per sample, but the cost depends on the complexity of the NDF, Fresnel, and Geometry functions, which are not fully specified in the sources. Performance: The model is described as "simplified" and "robust to roughness variations" compared to more complex basis-based methods. It is used in Monte Carlo shading, requiring N samples for convergence. Strengths: Unified framework for metals and plastics; intuitive parameters; reduced ambiguity in optimization by restricting to opaque surfaces. Limitations: Simplified; does not include all features of the full Disney Principled BRDF (e.g., clearcoat, sheen); assumes isotropy. When to use: When optimizing material parameters for opaque surfaces in differentiable rendering pipelines. The Isotropic Disney BRDF is based on the Cook-Torrance model. It is derived from the Disney Principled BRDF, which is widely adopted in movies and games for its versatile appearance and intuitive controls. The specific simplified version used here is employed in differentiable rendering contexts, such as DIB-R++ and texture-space differentiable rendering, to facilitate learning and optimization of lighting and material parameters. DIB-R++: Learning to Predict Lighting and Material with a Hybrid Differentiable Renderer, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2111.00140, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Material and Lighting Reconstruction for Complex Indoor Scenes with Texture-space Differentiable Rendering, https://doi.org/10.2312/sr.20211292, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Simplified Disney BRDF with SG Distribution
head: Isotropic specular BRDF
body: This method approximates the specular component of the Isotropic Disney BRDF using a single Spherical Gaussian (SG) distribution to enable closed-form integration with distant illumination. It sets itself apart from standard microfacet models by replacing the complex GGX distribution and Schlick-Fresnel terms with a parameterized SG, allowing the entire specular response to be represented as a single analytic function for efficient relighting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Surface point x, surface normal n, view direction \omegao, incident light direction \omegai, roughness parameter \lambda, and monochrome specular color \mu. Outputs: Specular reflectance fs(\omegao, \omegai; x) represented as an SG. Data Structures: The specular distribution is represented by a single Spherical Gaussian: G(h; \xi, \lambda, \mu) Where: h: The half-vector, defined as h = \frac{\omegao + \omegai}{\|\omegao + \omegai\|2}. \xi: The lobe axis (direction). \lambda: The sharpness/width parameter. \mu: The amplitude/color vector. Steps: 1. Assumption of Isotropy and Monochrome: The method assumes the specular lobe is isotropic, meaning the lobe axis \xi aligns with the surface normal n (\xi = n). It also assumes monochrome specular reflection, meaning the three components of the color vector \mu are identical. 2. Spherical Warping of Distribution: To evaluate the BRDF at point x for a specific view direction \omegao, the distribution D must be spherically warped. The original distribution D(h) = G(h; n, \lambda, \mu) is transformed into a view-dependent distribution Dx(h): Dx(h) = G\left(h; n, \frac{\lambda}{4h \cdot \omegao}, \mu\right) Here, the sharpness parameter is adjusted by the factor \frac{1}{4h \cdot \omegao}. 3. Approximation of Fresnel/Shadowing Term: The term M, which accounts for Fresnel and shadowing effects in the Cook-Torrance model, is approximated as a constant value Mx at location x. This constant is evaluated at the mirror reflection direction: Mx(\omegao, \omegai) \approx M(\omegao, 2(\omegao \cdot n)n - \omegai) Note: The source text contains a typo in the mirror direction formula in equation (7), listing -\omegao instead of -\omegai. Standard reflection geometry dictates the incident direction is reflected, so the second argument is the reflection of \omegai about n. 4. Combining into Final SG Representation: The specular BRDF fs is constructed by combining the warped distribution Dx and the constant approximation Mx. The amplitude \mu is scaled by Mx: fs(\omegao, \omegai; x) = G\left(h; n, \frac{\lambda}{4h \cdot \omegao}, Mx \mu\right) This results in a single SG that represents the specular reflectance. Pitfalls: Isotropic Assumption: The alignment of \xi with n assumes no anisotropic roughness. If anisotropy is present, this model fails. Monochrome Assumption: The constraint that \mu components are identical prevents modeling colored specular highlights (e.g., gold or copper metals) unless the color is handled separately or the assumption is relaxed. Approximation Error: Approximating M as a constant ignores the angular variation of Fresnel and shadowing, which may introduce errors at grazing angles or for high-index materials. This variant details the specific mathematical transformation required to evaluate the BRDF in the context of distant illumination. It involves warping the distribution D to depend on the view direction \omegao and approximating the Fresnel/shadowing term M as a constant Mx evaluated at the mirror direction. This allows the specular term to remain a single SG, facilitating closed-form integration with the SG representation of distant lighting. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for BRDF evaluation, as it involves evaluating a single SG. The overall rendering cost is dominated by the closed-form integration of the product of SGs (lighting, BRDF, and cosine term). Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storing only the parameters \lambda and \mu for the specular term, plus the SG parameters for the environment map and diffuse albedo. Strengths: Enables efficient inverse rendering and relighting by allowing all terms in the rendering equation (lighting, BRDF, cosine) to be represented as SGs and integrated in closed form. Limitations: Cannot model anisotropic materials or colored specular highlights due to the isotropic and monochrome assumptions. Accuracy depends on the validity of the constant approximation for M. This method originates from the PhySG paper, which proposes inverse rendering with Spherical Gaussians for physics-based material editing and relighting. It simplifies the Disney Principled BRDF by using a single SG to represent the specular distribution, enabling efficient analytical integration with distant illumination. PhySG: Inverse Rendering with Spherical Gaussians for Physics-based Material Editing and Relighting, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00541, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Light Evaluation for SDF Faces
body: This method applies diffuse, specular, and ambient lighting to a face color based on a surface normal and light direction. It operates directly on discretized face geometry data rather than integrating light along a ray. Inputs: faceColor: A float4 containing the base RGB color and alpha (\alpha) of the surface face. n: The surface normal vector (\mathbf{n}), typically derived from the SDF gradient. LightAngle: A scalar defining the light direction via sine and cosine parameters. Diffuse: A scalar diffuse intensity factor. Ambient: A scalar ambient intensity factor. Outputs: color: A float4 representing the final lit color and alpha. Data Structures: The normal \mathbf{n} is a normalized 3D vector. The light direction \mathbf{l} is constructed from LightAngle. Steps: 1. Normal Adjustment: Set the z-component of the normal to its absolute value: nz = |nz|. 2. Light Direction Construction: Construct the light direction vector \mathbf{l} from the sine and cosine of LightAngle, then normalize it. 3. Specular Addition: Compute the base color clamped to zero, add the specular contribution scaled by the face alpha: \mathbf{c} = \max(\text{faceColor.rgb}, 0) + \text{GetSpecular}(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}) \times \text{faceColor.a}. 4. Diffuse Modulation: Multiply the color by the factor (1 - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \times \Diffuse): \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} \times (1 - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \times \Diffuse). 5. Ambient/Height Modulation: Multiply the color by a linear interpolation between Ambient and 1 controlled by the squared z-component of the normal: \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c} \times \text{lerp}(\Ambient, 1, nz^2). 6. Output Assembly: Set the final color to \text{float4}(\mathbf{c}, \text{faceColor.a}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def evaluatelightface(facecolor, normal, lightangle, diffuse, ambient): # 1. Normal adjustment: n.z = abs(n.z) n = [normal[0], normal[1], abs(normal[2])] # 2. Light direction: normalize light vector from sin/cos of LightAngle sinval = math.sin(lightangle) cosval = math.cos(lightangle) lightdir = [cosval, sinval, 0.0] mag = math.sqrt(lightdir[0]2 + lightdir[1]2 + lightdir[2]2) lightdir = [lightdir[i] / mag for i in range(3)] # 3. Specular addition: col = max(faceColor.rgb, 0) + GetSpecular(n, light) faceColor.a # GetSpecular implementation not provided in sources # Standard Blinn-Phong specular calculation specular = computespecular(n, lightdir) basergb = [max(facecolor[i], 0.0) for i in range(3)] litcolor = [basergb[i] + specular[i] facecolor[3] for i in range(3)] # 4. Diffuse modulation: col = (1 - dot(n, light) Diffuse) dotnl = n[0]lightdir[0] + n[1]lightdir[1] + n[2]lightdir[2] litcolor = [litcolor[i] (1.0 - dotnl diffuse) for i in range(3)] # 5. Ambient/Height modulation: col = lerp(Ambient, 1, n.z n.z) heightfactor = n[2] n[2] ambientblend = ambient + (1.0 - ambient) heightfactor finalcolor = [litcolor[i] ambientblend for i in range(3)] # 6. Output assembly: color = float4(col, faceColor.a) return [finalcolor[0], finalcolor[1], finalcolor[2], facecolor[3]] def computespecular(n, l): # Standard Blinn-Phong specular calculation halfvec = [l[i] + n[i] for i in range(3)] hmag = math.sqrt(halfvec[0]2 + halfvec[1]2 + halfvec[2]2) halfvec = [halfvec[i] / hmag for i in range(3)] dotnh = max(halfvec[0]n[0] + halfvec[1]n[1] + halfvec[2]n[2], 0.0) specval = dotnh 32 return [specval, specval, specval] This variant integrates lighting directly into the SDF gradient evaluation loop. It calculates the gradient at the current ray-marched position to determine the normal dynamically, rather than relying on pre-computed normals. Steps: Calculate the gradient at the current position: \mathbf{g} = \nabla f(\mathbf{p}). Calculate the magnitude: m = \|\mathbf{g}\|. Normalize to get the normal: \mathbf{n} = \mathbf{g} / m. Calculate lighting using the color, normal, light direction, and view direction: \text{col.rgb} = \text{calculateLighting}(\text{col.rgb}, \mathbf{n}, \text{getLightDirection}(-\text{ray.direction}), -\text{ray.direction}, 0.15). Set alpha to 1.0 and break the marching loop: \text{col.a} = 1.0; \text{break}. Parameters: MinGradient is the minimum gradient magnitude threshold required to consider a voxel as a surface for lighting calculation. MinVal is the minimum density value threshold for surface detection. MaxVal is the maximum density value threshold for surface detection. Pitfalls: If the gradient magnitude is zero or very small, division by zero occurs during normalization. The code assumes gradMag > MinGradient before normalizing, implying a check or clamp is handled elsewhere or MinGradient prevents zero division. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. This method originates from implementations in Unity-based SDF renderers, specifically the unity-nanovdb-renderer and UnityVolumeRendering projects. andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, https://github.com/andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GitHub - mlavik1/UnityVolumeRendering: Volume rendering, implemented in..., https://github.com/mlavik1/UnityVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Blinn-Phong with Metallic Reflections
head: Neon City Lighting, Wet Asphalt Shader
body: A custom shading model for ray-marched signed distance fields that extends the classic Blinn-Phong approximation with environment reflections and emissive contributions to simulate urban night scenes. It distinguishes itself from standard Blinn-Phong by modulating specular intensity, power, and reflection weight based on a material's metallic property, and from GGX microfacet models by using a simplified Schlick-like Fresnel term rather than a full microfacet distribution. Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p} in world space. Ray direction \mathbf{rd} (from camera to \mathbf{p}, normalized). Material structure sf containing albedo (base color), metal (float in [0, 1]), and emissive (self-illuminated color). Scene functions: calcNormal(p), softShadow(p, l, radius), calcAO(p, n), skyColor(r). Outputs: Final color vec3. Data Structures: The material structure sf is determined by a material ID derived from the SDF evaluation (e.g., via hashing cell coordinates). Steps: 1. Calculate normal \mathbf{n} = \text{calcNormal}(\mathbf{p}). 2. Determine surface properties (sf.albedo, sf.metal, sf.emissive) based on material ID. 3. Define light direction \mathbf{l} = \text{normalize}(\text{vec3}(-0.5, 0.8, -0.25)) and light color \mathbf{c}L = \text{vec3}(0.5, 0.65, 1.0). 4. Calculate diffuse factor d = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}, 0.0). 5. Calculate shadow factor s = \text{softShadow}(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \cdot 0.03, \mathbf{l}, 12.0). 6. Apply shadow to diffuse: d \leftarrow d \cdot s. 7. Calculate half-vector \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{rd}). 8. Calculate specular intensity \text{spec} = \text{pow}(\max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h}, 0.0), \text{mix}(32.0, 140.0, \text{sf.metal})) \cdot s. 9. Calculate ambient occlusion \text{ao} = \text{calcAO}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{n}). 10. Calculate base color \mathbf{c}{\text{base}} = \text{sf.albedo} \cdot (\text{ambient} \cdot \text{ao}) + \text{sf.albedo} \cdot \mathbf{c}L \cdot d + \mathbf{c}L \cdot \text{spec} \cdot \text{mix}(0.4, 2.0, \text{sf.metal}). 11. Calculate Fresnel term F = \text{pow}(1.0 - \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot (-\mathbf{rd}), 0.0), 5.0). 12. Calculate reflected color \mathbf{c}{\text{refl}} = \text{skyColor}(\text{reflect}(\mathbf{rd}, \mathbf{n})). 13. Add reflection contribution: \mathbf{c}{\text{base}} \leftarrow \mathbf{c}{\text{base}} + \mathbf{c}{\text{refl}} \cdot \text{mix}(0.03, 0.6, \text{sf.metal}) \cdot (0.25 + 0.75 \cdot F) \cdot \text{ao}. 14. Add emissive contribution: \mathbf{c}{\text{final}} = \mathbf{c}{\text{base}} + \text{sf.emissive}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mix(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) def reflect(I, N): return I - 2.0 dot(I, N) N def blinnphongmetallic(p, rd, sf, ambient=0.16): n = calcNormal(p) l = normalize(vec3(-0.5, 0.8, -0.25)) cL = vec3(0.5, 0.65, 1.0) d = max(dot(n, l), 0.0) s = softShadow(p + n 0.03, l, 12.0) d = d s h = normalize(l - rd) spec = pow(max(dot(n, h), 0.0), mix(32.0, 140.0, sf.metal)) s ao = calcAO(p, n) cbase = sf.albedo (ambient ao) + sf.albedo cL d + cL spec mix(0.4, 2.0, sf.metal) F = pow(1.0 - max(dot(n, -rd), 0.0), 5.0) crefl = skyColor(reflect(rd, n)) cbase = cbase + crefl mix(0.03, 0.6, sf.metal) (0.25 + 0.75 F) ao cfinal = cbase + sf.emissive return cfinal Parameters: Light Direction: \text{vec3}(-0.5, 0.8, -0.25) Light Color: \text{vec3}(0.5, 0.65, 1.0) Ambient Intensity: 0.16 Specular Power: Interpolated between 32.0 (non-metal) and 140.0 (metal) Specular Intensity Multiplier: Interpolated between 0.4 (non-metal) and 2.0 (metal) Fresnel Power: 5.0 Reflection Intensity: Interpolated between 0.03 (non-metal) and 0.6 (metal) Fresnel Reflection Weight: 0.25 + 0.75 \cdot F Edge Cases: If \mathbf{n} is zero (degenerate SDF), the normal must be clamped or defaulted to \text{vec3}(0,1,0) to avoid division by zero in normalization. Time complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Not given in the sources. The model is defined in the referenced codebase as a lighting model combining Blinn-Phong diffuse/specular, metallic environment reflections weighted by a Schlick-like Fresnel term, and emissive contributions for neon effects. name: Multidirectional Occlusion Shading
head: Elliptical Kernel Convolution, M-DOS, Multidirectional OS, Multidirectional Occlusion Model
body: Multidirectional Occlusion Shading (M-DOS) is a direct volume rendering technique that simulates directional light scattering to produce realistic soft-shadowing and depth cues. Unlike the original MS-DOS model, which constrains the light direction to the viewing direction and uses symmetric disc-shaped Gaussian kernels, M-DOS allows arbitrary light positioning within the hemisphere defined by the view vector by using elliptical footprints derived from a tilted cone. It achieves this through incremental convolution of an opacity buffer, requiring no precomputation and maintaining interactive frame rates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Volume dataset, camera parameters (view direction \mathbf{v}), light source parameters (position or direction \mathbf{l}), aperture angle \theta, tilt angle \alpha. Outputs: Final rendered image with shading effects. Data Structures: Opacity Buffer (Oi): A 2D texture storing the accumulated opacity for slice i, initialized to zero. Color Buffer (Ci): A 2D texture storing the accumulated color for slice i. Kernel Texture (G\epsilon): A 128 \times 128 texture storing the elliptical weighting function. Parameters: \theta (theta): Aperture angle of the conical phase function. \alpha (alpha): Tilt angle of the conical phase function, determining the light direction relative to the view. R: Distance from the scattering point to the slice plane, derived from the geometric setup. Geometric Setup: The method approximates light transport using a tilted cone-shaped phase function \Phi{\theta,\alpha}. The axis of the cone is parallel to the light direction \mathbf{l}. The intersection of this cone with the viewing plane (slice plane) forms an ellipse \epsilon. The ellipse is defined by its major axis A and minor axis B. 1. Calculate Ellipse Axes: The distances a1 and a2 from the center O to the edges of the ellipse along the major axis are: a1 = R \frac{\sin(\pi/2 - \theta)}{\sin(\pi/2 + \theta - \alpha)} a2 = R \frac{\sin(\pi/2 + \theta)}{\sin(\pi/2 - \theta - \alpha)} The major axis A is: A = \frac{a1 + a2}{2} The distance from the center O to the ellipse center C is: kOCk = \frac{|a2 - a1|}{2} The minor axis B is calculated using a modified radius R' and modified distance d': B = \sqrt{R'^2 - kOCk^2 + d'^2} where R' and d' are derived from the geometric intersection analysis involving the circle \kappa intersecting at C. 2. Define Weighting Function: The weighting function WL(x,y) at position (x,y) relative to the ellipse center is defined implicitly by k: WL(x, y) = 1 - k where k is the solution to the quadratic equation: \frac{(x - (1-k)kOCk)^2}{A^2} + \frac{y^2}{B^2} = k^2 The point O represents the projection of the light vector and has the highest incident energy. 3. Kernel Alignment: The kernel G\epsilon is aligned with the light direction by rotating it so its major axis aligns with the 2D projection of the light vector \mathbf{L'} on the viewing plane: \frac{\mathbf{L'}}{k\mathbf{L'}k} = \frac{\mathbf{OC}}{kOCk} The kernel is stored in a texture and updated whenever lighting parameters change. Algorithm Steps: The rendering proceeds slice-by-slice in front-to-back order. For each slice i: 1. Compute Modulation Factor: Calculate the visibility \lambdai for the current slice using the previous slice's opacity buffer O{i-1} and the elliptical kernel G\epsilon: \lambdai = \frac{1}{1 + G\epsilon O{i-1}} where denotes convolution. 2. Update Opacity Buffer: Convolve the previous opacity buffer with the kernel and add the current slice's opacity \alphai: Oi = G\epsilon O{i-1} + \alphai 3. Modulate Color: Multiply the current slice's color contribution ci by the modulation factor \lambdai: c'i = ci \cdot \lambdai 4. Composite: Propagate the modified color c'i and the current opacity \alphai to the next composite step using traditional alpha-blending with the over operator. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def multidirectionalocclusionshading(volumeslices, viewportwidth, viewportheight, theta, alpha, lightdir): # Initialize buffers Oprev = [[0.0] viewportwidth for in range(viewportheight)] Cprev = [[0.0] viewportwidth for in range(viewportheight)] # Generate elliptical kernel Gepsilon # R is derived from slice distance; compute a1, a2, A, B, kOCk # Solve implicit quadratic for WL(x,y) to fill kernel texture Gepsilon = generateellipticalkernel(theta, alpha, R, viewportwidth, viewportheight) # Rotate kernel to align major axis with 2D projection of lightdir Gepsilon = rotatekernel(Gepsilon, lightdir) for slice in volumeslices: # 1. Get current slice opacity and color alphai = min(1.0, max(0.0, slice.opacity)) ci = slice.color # 2. Calculate modulation factor lambdai blurredopacity = convolve2d(Oprev, Gepsilon) lambdai = [1.0 / (1.0 + rowval) for rowval in blurredopacity] # 3. Update opacity buffer for next slice Onext = [[blurredopacity[r][c] + alphai for c in range(viewportwidth)] for r in range(viewportheight)] # 4. Modulate color cmodulated = [[ci[r][c] lambdai[r][c] for c in range(viewportwidth)] for r in range(viewportheight)] # 5. Composite using over operator Cnext = [[(cmodulated[r][c] alphai) + (Cprev[r][c] (1.0 - alphai)) for c in range(viewportwidth)] for r in range(viewportheight)] # Update buffers for next iteration Oprev = Onext Cprev = Cnext return Cprev def zeroslike(shape): return [[0.0] shape[1] for in range(shape[0])] def convolve2d(buffer, kernel): # Standard 2D convolution with boundary clamping h, w = len(buffer), len(buffer[0]) kh, kw = len(kernel), len(kernel[0]) result = [[0.0] w for in range(h)] padh, padw = kh // 2, kw // 2 for r in range(h): for c in range(w): acc = 0.0 for kr in range(kh): for kc in range(kw): br, bc = r + kr - padh, c + kc - padw if 0 <= br < h and 0 <= bc < w: acc += buffer[br][bc] kernel[kr][kc] result[r][c] = acc return result def generateellipticalkernel(theta, alpha, R, width, height): # Compute a1, a2, A, B, kOCk from formulas # Solve WL(x,y) = 1 - k for each pixel relative to ellipse center # Scale and rotate to fit texture bounding box pass # Implementation follows standard implicit surface rasterization def rotatekernel(kernel, lightdir): # Apply 2D rotation matrix to align major axis with light projection pass # Standard matrix rotation applied to kernel coordinates Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Geometry: The tilt angle \alpha must be limited to 0, \pi/2 - \theta) to prevent the cone-section from degenerating into hyperbolas or parabolas. Precision Loss: Massive downscaling of the coordinate system to fit the kernel into the texture bounding box may lead to a loss of precision. Light Direction: The method assumes the light source is within the hemisphere defined by the view vector; traversal reversal for opposite hemisphere lights is a potential extension but not part of the core method. Kernel Updates: The kernel G\epsilon is only recomputed when tilt, aperture, light direction, or slice distance changes, which may cause artifacts if parameters change rapidly without triggering an update. Time Complexity: The method performs an incremental convolution per slice. The convolution cost depends on the kernel size, which is fixed at 128 \times 128 in the source. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for two render targets (intermediate image and occlusion buffer) per slice and one kernel texture (128 \times 128). Performance: Performs at interactive frame-rates with negligible performance penalty compared to state-of-the-art models. No precomputation is required. Strengths: Allows arbitrary light positioning within the view hemisphere; gradient-free (suitable for noisy data like ultrasound); no precomputation or additional data storage compared to shadow maps or light volumes. Limitations: Precision loss due to kernel scaling; limited to the hemisphere defined by the view vector without traversal reversal; artifacts may occur if the light direction changes rapidly without kernel updates. Origin: Developed by Veronika Šoltészová, Daniel Patel, Stefan Bruckner, and Ivan Viola. Paper: "A Multidirectional Occlusion [Shading Model for Direct Volume Rendering" (2010). Development: Extends the original MS-DOS model by Mathias Schott et al. (2009), which constrained light to the viewing direction and used symmetric disc-shaped Gaussian kernels. M-DOS removes this constraint using elliptical footprints derived from a tilted cone. Usage: Implemented as a plugin to VolumeShop using C++ and OpenGL/GLSL. Used to visualize CT datasets (gecko, carp, human foot, human hand, human thorax) and 3D cardiac ultrasound. User studies showed high preference for directional lighting over headlamp or raycasting for depth cues.
