name: Single-Atomic High-Quality Robust Variant (HQS1R)
head: Compute-based blending, High-Quality Shader, High-Quality Shader with Single Atomic Reduction, Robust high-quality shading with overflow protection
body: HQS1R is a high-quality point cloud rendering method that reduces aliasing by blending overlapping points together, similar to mipmapping. It is a simplified, compute-based implementation of the blending algorithm from [BHZK05], designed to be faster than aliased GLPOINTS results while providing anti-aliasing. Unlike surface splatting [ZPVG01], it blends overlapping points without considering oriented disks with variable radii. It sets itself apart from the Single-Atomic High-Quality Variant (HQS1x) by using a robust overflow protection mechanism that prevents artifacts when more than 255 points contribute to a pixel. HQS1R operates on a set of points, each with a position and color. It computes the average color of overlapping points within a depth range using a single 64-bit atomic operation per point in the fast path, with overflow protection via fallback buffers. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of points, each defined by a 3D position \mathbf{p} and a color \mathbf{c} = (r, g, b). Output: A framebuffer containing the average color for each pixel, resolved from the main buffer and fallback buffers. Data Structures: The method uses a custom 64-bit integer layout to pack color and count data. 1. Main Buffer (ssRGBA): A 64-bit integer per pixel. Bits 0-15: Count (Alpha/Counter). Bits 16-31: Blue component (b). Bits 32-47: Green component (g). Bits 48-63: Red component (r). Format: 16-16-16-16 bit pattern. 2. Fallback Buffers: Two 64-bit integer buffers per pixel, used when the main buffer count exceeds 255. fallback[2 pixelID + 0]: Stores Red (bits 32-63) and Green (bits 0-31). fallback[2 pixelID + 1]: Stores Blue (bits 32-63) and Alpha/Count (bits 0-31). Format: 16-16-16-16 bit pattern. Numbered Steps: 1. Depth Map Pass (Required for high-quality variations): Compute a depth map over all points, resulting in a total of two geometry passes and one screen pass. 2. Screen Pass (Render Pass): For each point: a. Transform the point position to screen space and determine the pixel ID (pixelID) it covers. b. Encode the point's color (r, g, b) and a count of 1 into a 64-bit integer rgba: \text{rgba} = (r \ll 48) \mid (g \ll 32) \mid (b \ll 16) \mid 1 where r, g, b are 16-bit unsigned integers. c. Perform an atomic addition of rgba to the main framebuffer buffer ssRGBA at pixelID, storing the previous value in old: \text{old} = \text{atomicAdd}(\text{ssRGBA}[\text{pixelID}], \text{rgba}) d. Extract the lower 16 bits of old to get the previous count: \text{count} = \text{old} \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} e. Check if count >= 255. If true, an overflow condition is detected. f. If count == 255 (indicating this is the first thread to overflow for this pixel): i. Atomically exchange the main buffer value to 0 to reset it: \text{atomicExchange}(\text{ssRGBA}[\text{pixelID}], 0) ii. Extract the previous color components from old and accumulate them into local variables r, g, b, and set a=1: r += (\text{old} \gg 48) \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} g += (\text{old} \gg 32) \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} b += (\text{old} \gg 16) \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} a = 1 iii. Add 255 to a to account for the points already counted in the buffer before the reset: a += 255 g. If overflow was detected (count >= 255): i. Encode the accumulated color (r, g) and accumulated alpha/count (b, a) into two 64-bit integers: \text{rg} = (r \ll 32) \mid g \text{ba} = (b \ll 32) \mid a ii. Write the accumulated values to the two separate fallback buffers using atomicAdd. Indices are fallback[2 pixelID + 0] for rg and fallback[2 pixelID + 1] for ba: \text{atomicAdd}(\text{fallback}[2 \times \text{pixelID} + 0], \text{rg}) \text{atomicAdd}(\text{fallback}[2 \times \text{pixelID} + 1], \text{ba}) 3. Resolve Pass: Combine the results from the main buffer and fallback buffers to compute the final average color for each pixel. a. For each pixel, read ssRGBA, fallback[2 pixelID + 0], and fallback[2 pixelID + 1]. b. Extract the total count and color components from all buffers. c. Normalize the accumulated color by dividing by the total count to get the average color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def atomicAdd(arr, idx, val): arr[idx] += val return arr[idx] - val def atomicExchange(arr, idx, val): old = arr[idx] arr[idx] = val return old OVERFLOWTHRESHOLD = 255 def renderpoint(position, color): # 1. Transform point to screen space # Not given in the sources. pos = position pixelid = 0 # 2. Encode color and count into 64-bit integer r = int(color[0] 65535.0) g = int(color[1] 65535.0) b = int(color[2] 65535.0) rgba = (r << 48) | (g << 32) | (b << 16) | 1 # 3. Atomic addition to main buffer old = atomicAdd(ssRGBA, pixelid, rgba) # 4. Extract previous count count = old & 0xFFFF # 5. Check for overflow if count >= OVERFLOWTHRESHOLD: a = 1 # 6. If this is the first thread to overflow (count == 255) if count == OVERFLOWTHRESHOLD: # Reset main buffer atomicExchange(ssRGBA, pixelid, 0) # Accumulate previous values from 'old' r += (old >> 48) & 0xFFFF g += (old >> 32) & 0xFFFF b += (old >> 16) & 0xFFFF a += OVERFLOWTHRESHOLD # 7. Encode accumulated values for fallback buffers rg = (r << 32) | g ba = (b << 32) | a # 8. Write to fallback buffers atomicAdd(fallback, 2 pixelid + 0, rg) atomicAdd(fallback, 2 pixelid + 1, ba) Parameters: Overflow Threshold: 255. If the counter reaches exactly 255, the current pixel's buffer is reset to zero and data is moved to fallback buffers. Bit Pattern: 16 bits for Red, 16 bits for Green, 16 bits for Blue, 16 bits for Counter (Alpha/Count). Total 64 bits. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overflow: If more than 1023 points contribute to a pixel, the naive 18-18-18-10 bit pattern (used in HQS1×) overflows. The 16-16-16-16 pattern handles up to 255 points in the main buffer before falling back, with a safety margin of 65,536 - 256 counts. Simultaneous Accesses: The unused 2^{16} - 256 counts serve as a safety margin for potentially several thousand simultaneously executing threads to detect the overflow. If more or significantly fewer than 65k simultaneous accesses to a pixel are expected, the bit pattern may be changed accordingly. A variant of HQS that reduces atomic operations by encoding RGB channels and counter into a single 64-bit integer. It uses a 18-18-18-10 bit pattern, where the 10-bit counter allows correct computation of the sum of up to 1023 points per pixel. However, this naive approach is prone to overflow artifacts when more than 1023 points contribute to a pixel's average color value, leading to strongly noticeable rendering artifacts in larger scenes. HQS1R is robust against these overflow artifacts compared to HQS1×, with negligible overhead. Time Complexity: The method requires two geometry passes and one screen pass for high-quality variations. The render pass performs a single atomic operation per point in the fast path, reducing memory bandwidth usage compared to the standard HQS. Memory Complexity: Uses a 64-bit integer per pixel for the main buffer and two 64-bit integers per pixel for fallback buffers. Performance: Achieves higher frame rates than aliased GLPOINTS results while providing anti-aliasing. The robust variant, HQS1R, shows negligible overhead compared to the unstable HQS1× version. Strengths: Reduces aliasing, robust against overflow artifacts, efficient memory access pattern. Limitations: Requires fallback buffers for overflow handling, which increases memory usage. When to use: Point cloud rendering where anti-aliasing is desired and performance is critical. When not to use: Scenes with extremely high point density per pixel where fallback buffers might become a bottleneck. HQS1R was introduced in the paper "Rendering Point Clouds with Compute Shaders and Vertex Order Optimization". It is a compute-based implementation of the blending algorithm from [BHZK05]. The method was developed to address the limitations of traditional GLPOINTS rendering, such as aliasing and performance issues, by leveraging compute shaders for parallel processing. The HQS1R variant was specifically designed to handle overflow conditions robustly, ensuring high-quality rendering even in dense point clouds. Rendering Point Clouds with Compute Shaders and Vertex Order Optimization, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.14345, fetched 2026-10-26

name: YUV Color Space Shading with Glow
body: This method performs volume raycasting illumination in the YUV color space to decouple luminance from chrominance. It differs from standard RGB shading by computing lighting effects primarily on the luminance channel, while interpolating color channels based on a technique-derived factor. Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p} and normal \mathbf{n} (derived from SDF gradient). View direction \mathbf{v} and light direction \mathbf{l}. Base color values \mathbf{C}1, \mathbf{C}2 in YUV space. Interpolation factor \alpha derived from the technique's output. Glow mapping function G(\cdot) and additional texture fetch for glow. Outputs: Final shaded color \mathbf{C}{final} in YUV space. Data Structures: YUV Color Vector: \mathbf{C} = [Y, U, V]^T. Glow Texture: 2D or 3D texture storing glow intensity. Steps: 1. Geometric Setup: Compute normal \mathbf{n}, view vector \mathbf{v}, and light vector \mathbf{l}. 2. Luminance Calculation: Calculate the luminance component Y as the minimum of two values, Y1 and Y2: Y = \min(Y1, Y2) 3. Color Interpolation: Interpolate the chrominance components (U, V) between two color states \mathbf{C}1 and \mathbf{C}2 using the factor \alpha: \mathbf{C}{interp} = (1 - \alpha) \mathbf{C}1 + \alpha \mathbf{C}2 4. Specular Highlight (Optional): Add specular highlights to the luminance channel. 5. Volumetric Glow: Realize volumetric glow by exploiting an additional texture fetch and a glow mapping function: \mathbf{C}{final} = \mathbf{C}{interp} + [G(\text{GlowTexture}(\mathbf{p})), 0, 0]^T This allows indirect illumination to be captured independently of the transfer function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def yuvshadingwithglow(p, n, v, l, C1yuv, C2yuv, alpha, glowtexture, glowfunc): # Step 1: Geometric Setup # n, v, l are assumed normalized # Step 2: Luminance Calculation Y1 = C1yuv[0] Y2 = C2yuv[0] Y = min(Y1, Y2) # Step 3: Color Interpolation U = (1.0 - alpha) C1yuv[1] + alpha C2yuv[1] V = (1.0 - alpha) C1yuv[2] + alpha C2yuv[2] # Step 4: Specular Highlights h = (v[0] + l[0], v[1] + l[1], v[2] + l[2]) hlen = math.sqrt(h[0]2 + h[1]2 + h[2]2) h = (h[0]/hlen, h[1]/hlen, h[2]/hlen) spec = math.pow(max(n[0]h[0] + n[1]h[1] + n[2]h[2], 0.0), 32.0) Y += spec # Step 5: Volumetric Glow glowintensity = glowtexture.fetch(p) glowcontribution = glowfunc(glowintensity) Y += glowcontribution return [Y, U, V] Parameters: \alpha: Interpolation factor derived from the technique's output. Edge Cases: Precision: YUV conversion and interpolation may introduce precision errors. Converts RGB images to YUV color space and back using JPEG standard conversion matrices. Definition: Linear transformation using fixed 3x3 matrices. Parameters: RGBTOYUV: Matrix [[0.299, 0.587, 0.114], [-0.168736, -0.331264, 0.5], [0.5, -0.418688, -0.081312]]. YUVTORGB: Matrix [[1.0, 0.0, 1.402], [1.0, -0.34414, -0.71414], [1.0, 1.772, 0.0]]. YUVOFFSET: Array [0, 128.0, 128.0] reshaped to (1,1,-1), added to YUV output. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for YUV color vectors and glow texture. Strengths: Decouples luminance and chrominance. Can capture indirect illumination independently of the transfer function. Limitations: Requires conversion steps if input/output is RGB. Glow implementation adds texture fetch overhead. Originated in Timo Ropinski's work on advanced illumination techniques for GPU-based volume raycasting. The method leverages the YUV color space to simplify lighting calculations and enhance visual effects like glow. The RGB to YUV conversion matrices are based on JPEG standards. GPU-Based Volume Ray-Casting with Advanced Illumination, https://www.uni-ulm.de/fileadmin/websiteuniulm/iui.inst.100/institut/Papers/viscom/2008/advancedillumination.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) weiyithu/NerfingMVS, https://github.com/weiyithu/NerfingMVS, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Tangent Space Shading
head: vzTangentSpaceShader, vzTMTangentSpaceShader
body: Tangent Space Shading is a gradient-less lighting technique that approximates the diffuse lighting component of the Phong shading model without computing explicit gradients for every texel. It is distinguished from sibling methods like GGX Microfacet BRDF and Light Evaluation for SDF Faces by its reliance on rendering artifacts (double-pass texture coordinate offsets) rather than geometric derivatives to simulate surface orientation. Inputs: Volume data (voxels). Light direction vector \mathbf{l}. View direction (implicit via camera). Outputs: Rendered image with diffuse shading approximation. Data Structures: Volume texture (bricked or continuous). Two render passes with modified texture coordinates. Steps: 1. First Pass: Draw the volume slice using standard texture coordinates. 2. Second Pass: Draw the volume slice again using slightly offset texture coordinates. 3. Gradient Approximation: The difference between the two passes effectively computes the component of the gradient along the light vector. This difference is used to modulate the diffuse lighting intensity. 4. Lighting Model: Apply an approximation of the diffuse component of the Phong shading model using the computed gradient component. Parameters: Light direction: User-adjustable. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bricking Artifacts: The technique produces visible seams for bricked shapes along the borders of the bricks. Incorrect Lighting: The shader does not generate physically correct lighting; it creates a visual effect via a system-dependent technique. Recommendation: Use Voxel Shading Pipeline (specifically vzTMGradientShader) for correct volumetric lighting if bricking artifacts are a concern. Performance: Efficient as it avoids per-texel gradient computation. Quality: Provides higher image quality and better depth cues than unshaded rendering, but lacks physical accuracy. Limitations: Not suitable for applications requiring correct volumetric lighting or where bricking seams are unacceptable. Tangent Space Shading was introduced by Brian Cabral in SIGGRAPH 1997. It was implemented in the SGI OpenGL Volumizer library as vzTangentSpaceShader.

name: Voxel-Specific Shading Pipelines
head: Voxel Lighting, Voxel Shading
body: Voxel-Specific Shading Pipelines are a family of rendering techniques designed to compute illumination for data stored in discrete 3D grids (voxels). Unlike continuous surface shading which operates on smooth Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or triangle meshes, these methods operate on the discrete topology of voxel cells, handling both surface-like boundaries and volumetric density. The family encompasses approaches ranging from per-voxel geometric shading with hard shadows to CPU-based palette index manipulation and dedicated volumetric ray-marching shaders for fluid simulations. All methods in this family operate on a voxel grid structure where data is indexed by integer coordinates (x, y, z). The core distinction from continuous shading is the handling of geometry and lighting: 1. Discrete Coordinates: Positions are often rounded or mapped to voxel cells. For surface shading, the "surface" is defined by the boundary between occupied and empty voxels, or by an isosurface threshold within the grid. 2. Neighbor Dependence: Lighting calculations frequently depend on the occupancy or value of immediate neighboring voxels to determine occlusion, shading factors, or gradients, rather than casting long-distance rays for every light sample (except in explicit ray-marching variants). 3. Data Types: Inputs include block types, palette indices, or continuous scalar/vector fields (e.g., temperature, velocity) stored in the voxel cells. A per-voxel lighting model that combines Lambertian diffuse, rim lighting, and GGX-like specular terms with hard shadows. It differs by operating on discrete voxel coordinates, rounding hit positions, and using secondary ray occlusion checks for shadows. Choose this for high-quality, physically-inspired shading of voxel-based geometry. A CPU-based algorithm that simulates directional sunlight by modifying voxel palette indices based on neighbor occupancy. It differs by using simple integer arithmetic and clamping to tone groups, avoiding complex geometric calculations. Choose this for performance-critical voxel engines where visual fidelity is secondary to speed. A dedicated pipeline for volumetric data (fire, smoke) that reads scalar/vector fields from grids like Phoenix FD or V-Ray Volume Grids. It differs by providing UI-driven controls for emission, scattering, and displacement, handling volumetric opacity accumulation rather than surface reflection. Choose this for simulating and rendering volumetric effects. The concept of shading voxel data emerged with the rise of voxel-based games and simulation tools. Early implementations, such as those in voxel engines, relied on simple neighbor checks to simulate lighting via palette manipulation to save CPU cycles. As GPU capabilities increased, more complex pipelines were developed to apply standard BRDFs (like GGX) to voxel surfaces, treating the voxel grid as a discrete mesh. Concurrently, 3D simulation software (e.g., Maya with Phoenix FD, V-Ray) developed specialized shaders to handle the volumetric nature of fluid and fire data, which standard surface materials could not render. name: Voxel Shading Pipeline
head: Block Shading, Shading and Lighting, Voxel Lighting
body: The Voxel Shading Pipeline computes the final color of a voxel hit during ray marching by combining albedo sampling, Lambertian diffuse lighting, rim lighting, and specular integration. It distinguishes itself from continuous shading by operating on discrete voxel coordinates and neighbor-dependent lighting calculations, specifically using hard shadow rays and per-voxel specular highlights rather than smooth surface approximations. It serves as the foundational lighting model for voxel-specific rendering, upon which more complex effects like refraction or global illumination are built. Inputs: hitPosition: World-space position of the ray-voxel intersection. hitCell: Integer coordinates (x, y, z) of the hit voxel. hitFaceNormal: Normal vector of the hit voxel face. rayDir: Camera ray direction. sunVec: World-space sun direction. time: Current simulation time (for sun rotation). tLimit, maxSteps: Parameters for shadow ray tracing. Outputs: finalColor: The computed RGB color of the pixel. Data Structures: TraceResult: Struct containing hit (bool), t (float, distance), cell (ivec3), normal (vec3). BLOCKEMISSIVE: Integer constant identifying emissive block types. Steps: 1. Intersection Validation: If the ray hits a voxel (tr.hit is true): If tr.t <= 0.0, set hitPosition = camPos. Else, set hitPosition = camPos + rayDir (tr.t + 1e-5). Extract hitCell = tr.cell and hitFaceNormal = tr.normal. 2. Vector Normalization: N = \text{normalize}(\text{hitFaceNormal}) L = \text{normalize}(\text{sunVec}(time \times \text{SUN\ROT\SPEED})) V = \text{normalize}(\text{rayDir}) 3. Local Coordinate Calculation: Compute local position within the voxel: \text{local} = \text{hitPosition} - \text{vec3}(\text{float}(\text{hitCell}.x), \text{float}(\text{hitCell}.y), \text{float}(\text{hitCell}.z)) Apply fracturing for texture sampling: \text{localPos} = \text{fract}(\text{local}) 4. Albedo and Environment Sampling: Sample block albedo: albedo = sampleBlockAlbedoTexmanual(hitCell, localPos, hitFaceNormal). Compute absorption color: absorpColor = absorp(...). Compute sky color: If atmosphere enabled: sky = 1.0 - exp(-atmosphere(...)) Else: sky = absorpColor 5. Lighting Components: Diffuse: nDotL = \max(0.0, N \cdot L) \text{lambert} = nDotL Rim Lighting: \text{rim} = \text{pow}(1.0 - \max(0.0, N \cdot V), 2.2) \times 0.12 Constants: lightColor = vec3(1.0, 0.96, 0.85) ambient = vec3(0.12, 0.14, 0.18) 6. Shadow Casting: Initialize shadow = 1.0. If shadows enabled: Trace voxel from hitPosition + N 0.01 in direction L. If sh.hit is true, shadow = 0.0. 7. Direct and Indirect Light: directLight = lightColor lambert indirectLight = 0.25 albedo Emissive Handling: If block type is BLOCKEMISSIVE: emission = getEmissiveColor(hitCell) getEmissiveIntensity(hitCell) indirectLight += 0.35 emission directLight += emission 0.5 8. Final Color Composition: diffAlbedo = albedo absorpColor Base lit color: \text{lit} = (\text{shadow} \times \text{directLight} + \text{ambient}) \times \text{diffAlbedo} + (\text{indirectLight} \times \text{absorpColor}) + \text{rim} \times 0.6 \times \text{absorpColor} 9. Specular Integration (Microfacet/GGX-like): Parameters: roughness = 0.54, F0 = 0.14. Compute half vector: H = \text{normalize}(L - V) Compute dot products: dotLH = \max(0.0, L \cdot H) dotNH = \max(0.0, N \cdot H) dotNL = \max(0.0, N \cdot L) Compute D (Normal Distribution): \alpha = \text{roughness}^2 \alphaSqr = \alpha^2 \text{denom} = dotNH^2 \times (\alphaSqr - 1.0) + 1.0 D = \frac{\alphaSqr}{\pi \times \text{denom}^2 + 1e-6} Compute F (Fresnel): F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) \times \text{pow}(1.0 - dotLH, 5.0) Compute Geometry/Approximation term: k = 0.5 \times \alpha k2 = k^2 \text{specularTerm} = \frac{dotNL \times D \times F}{\max(1e-6, dotLH^2 \times (1.0 - k2)) + k2} Add to lit: \text{lit} += \text{shadow} \times \text{specularTerm} \times \text{absorpColor} \times \text{lit} Apply shadow modifier to final lit: \text{lit} = \max(0.7, \text{shadow}) 10. Tone Mapping: finalColor = 1.0 - exp(-2.0 lit) 11. Miss Case: If no hit, finalColor = sky. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelshadingpipeline(hit, campos, raydir, time, sunrotspeed, tlimit, maxsteps): if not hit: return computeskycolor(raydir) # 1. Intersection Position if hit.t <= 0.0: hitposition = campos else: hitposition = campos + raydir (hit.t + 1e-5) hitcell = hit.cell hitnormal = hit.normal # 2. Vectors N = normalize(hitnormal) L = normalize(sunvec(time sunrotspeed)) V = normalize(raydir) # 3. Local Coords local = hitposition - vec3(float(hitcell.x), float(hitcell.y), float(hitcell.z)) localpos = fract(local) # 4. Sampling blocktype = getblocktype(hitcell) albedo = sampleblockalbedo(hitcell, localpos, hitnormal) absorpcolor = computeabsorption(hitcell, campos, L) # Sky if atmosphereenabled: sky = 1.0 - exp(-computeatmosphere(raydir, campos, L)) else: sky = absorpcolor # 5. Lighting Basics ndotl = max(0.0, dot(N, L)) rim = pow(1.0 - max(0.0, dot(N, V)), 2.2) 0.12 lightcolor = vec3(1.0, 0.96, 0.85) ambient = vec3(0.12, 0.14, 0.18) # 6. Shadows shadow = 1.0 if shadowsenabled: sh = tracevoxel(hitposition + N 0.01, L, tlimit, maxsteps) if sh.hit: shadow = 0.0 # 7. Direct/Indirect directlight = lightcolor ndotl indirectlight = 0.25 albedo if blocktype == BLOCKEMISSIVE: emission = getemissivecolor(hitcell) getemissiveintensity(hitcell) indirectlight += 0.35 emission directlight += emission 0.5 # 8. Composition diffalbedo = albedo absorpcolor lit = (shadow directlight + ambient) diffalbedo + (indirectlight absorpcolor) + rim 0.6 absorpcolor # 9. Specular roughness = 0.54 F0 = 0.14 alpha = roughness roughness alphasqr = alpha alpha H = normalize(L - V) dotLH = max(0.0, dot(L, H)) dotNH = max(0.0, dot(N, H)) dotNL = max(0.0, dot(N, L)) denom = dotNH dotNH (alphasqr - 1.0) + 1.0 D = alphasqr / (PI denom denom + 1e-6) F = F0 + (1.0 - F0) pow(1.0 - dotLH, 5.0) k = 0.5 alpha k2 = k k specterm = (dotNL D F) / (max(1e-6, dotLH dotLH (1.0 - k2)) + k2) lit += shadow specterm absorpcolor lit lit = max(0.7, shadow) # 10. Tone Mapping finalcolor = 1.0 - exp(-2.0 lit) return finalcolor This method extends the basic pipeline by adding shadow ray casting, Phong-like specular highlights, and recursive or discrete refraction bounces. It is distinguished by its support for recursive light transport through semi-transparent volumes and specific handling of voxel-space coordinate offsets for shadow and refraction ray origins. A lighting optimization that computes illumination per voxel block rather than per pixel, then applies per-pixel modifiers to retain shading detail. It calculates base lighting values for an entire voxel block and applies per-pixel adjustments to prevent uniform shading and maintain surface variation. Time Complexity: Dominated by the shadow ray trace, which requires an additional voxel traversal per lit pixel. The specular calculation involves several trigonometric and power operations per pixel. Memory Complexity: Low; requires only the voxel grid and albedo textures. No large buffers for global illumination are needed. Strengths: Fast enough for interactive frame rates on simple scenes; hard shadows and per-voxel speculars provide strong visual cues for voxel structure. Limitations: Hard shadows can appear aliased; no indirect lighting bounce (except simple emissive contribution); specular highlights are discrete per voxel, which may look blocky at high resolutions. When to use: Real-time voxel games where performance is critical and stylized, blocky lighting is acceptable. When not to use: Photorealistic rendering requiring soft shadows or global illumination. The method originates from early interactive voxel world shaders, specifically those implementing ray-marched voxel rendering with basic lighting models. It was developed to provide visually distinct lighting for voxel-based environments without the computational cost of full path tracing. The specific implementation details, such as the GGX-like specular approximation and tone mapping, were popularized in community-driven GLSL shader repositories.
