name: Shading with Shadows, Specular, and Refraction
head: Voxel Shading with Shadows, Specular, and Refraction
body: This method computes the final color of a hit voxel by combining diffuse and specular lighting from multiple light sources, handling shadow casting to occlude lights, and managing refraction through volumetric structures. It extends the basic voxel shading pipeline by adding shadow ray casting, Phong-like specular highlights, and recursive or discrete refraction bounces. It is distinguished from simpler shading models by its support for recursive light transport through semi-transparent volumes and its specific handling of voxel-space coordinate offsets for shadow and refraction ray origins. Inputs: renderingattributes: Contains lightcount, array of light sources (each with diffuse and specular color), ambientcolour, and flags for shadow/refraction enablement. hit: The hit point structure from the ray marcher, containing hitpos (world position), hitscale (log2 of voxel size or similar scale factor), and hitt (distance along ray). shadingattributes: Contains normal (surface normal at hit point), colour (RGBA color sampled from voxel, where a is alpha), refractiveindex (material refractive index). eyeray: The primary ray, containing direction (view direction). tree: The volume data structure for ray casting. stack: Auxiliary stack for recursive ray casting. recursions: Current recursion depth counter. Outputs: out: A vec4 representing the final computed color (RGB + alpha, though alpha handling in output is implicit in the accumulation logic). The method relies on structures defined in the parent Voxel Shading Pipeline and the ray marcher. Key fields include: hit.hitscale: Used to compute geometric offsets. MAXSCALE is a constant defining the maximum scale (smallest voxel). HALFSQRT2 is a constant \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}. shadingattributes.colour.a: Alpha value of the hit voxel. refractionmode: Enum indicating CONTINUOUS or DISCRETE refraction. refractiondiscretestepsmax: Maximum number of steps for discrete refraction. refractiondiscretestep: Step size for discrete refraction. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def shade(renderingattributes, eyeray, hit, stack, tree, refractiveindex, recursions): # 1. Normalize normal normal = normalize(shadingattributes.normal) # 2. Initialize output and view direction out = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) viewdir = eyeray.direction # 3. Iterate over lights for i in range(renderingattributes.lightcount): light = renderingattributes.lights[i] lightdir = normalize(light.position - hit.hitpos) # Assuming point light; adjust for directional lightdistance = exp2f(23.0) # Large number representing infinity attenuation = 1.0 # 4. Shadow Ray Casting if shadowsenabled and dot(lightdir, normal) < 0.0: # Cast shadow ray shadowrayorigin = hit.hitpos + (-lightdir) (HALFSQRT2 exp2f(hit.hitscale - MAXSCALE)) shadowray = Ray(shadowrayorigin, -lightdir) shadowhit = raycast(tree, shadowray, stack) # If shadow ray hits something closer than the light, skip this light if shadowhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE and shadowhit.hitt < lightdistance: continue # 5. Diffuse Contribution diffusefactor = attenuation max(0.0, dot(normal, -lightdir)) diffusecolour = shadingattributes.colour.rgb light.diffuse out += vec4(diffusefactor diffusecolour, 0.0) # 6. Specular Contribution if dot(normal, lightdir) < 0.0: reflection = reflect(lightdir, normal) specularfactor = pow(max(0.0, dot(reflection, viewdir)), 32.0) out += vec4(specularfactor (shadingattributes.colour.rgb light.specular), 0.0) # 7. Refraction Handling if refractionenabled and shadingattributes.colour.a < 1.0: oneminusalpha = 1.0 - shadingattributes.colour.a out = shadingattributes.colour.a # Modulate existing color by alpha # Determine surface normal for refraction (reverse if entering) refractnormal = normal if dot(normal, eyeray.direction) > 0.0: refractnormal = -normal # Calculate refraction ray eta = refractiveindex / shadingattributes.refractiveindex refractdir = refract(eyeray.direction, refractnormal, eta) refractrayorigin = hit.hitpos + refractdir (HALFSQRT2 exp2f(hit.hitscale - MAXSCALE)) refractray = Ray(refractrayorigin, refractdir) if refractionmode != CONTINUOUS: # Discrete Refraction currentrefractiveindex = shadingattributes.refractiveindex discreterayorigin = refractrayorigin + refractdir (HALFSQRT2 exp2f(hit.hitscale - MAXSCALE)) discreteray = Ray(discreterayorigin, -refractdir) # Note: direction negated in source logic refractedtimes = 0 for step in range(refractiondiscretestepsmax): refractionhit = raycast(tree, discreteray, stack) # Check for exit or invalid hit minfloat = exp2f(-MAXSCALE) if refractionhit.hitscale == MAXSCALE or refractionhit.hitt <= minfloat: break # Look up attachment (voxel data) refractionattachment = lookupattachment(tree, refractionhit) if refractionattachment.refractiveindex != currentrefractiveindex: refractedtimes += 1 eta = currentrefractiveindex / refractionattachment.refractiveindex # Update normal refnormal = normalize(refractionhit.normal) if dot(refnormal, refractdir) > 0.0: refnormal = -refnormal # Update refraction direction refractdir = refract(refractdir, refnormal, eta) discreteray.direction = -refractdir # Negate as per source logic currentrefractiveindex = refractionattachment.refractiveindex # Advance discrete ray discreteray.origin += refractdir refractiondiscretestep else: # Continuous Refraction (Recursive) if refractionhit.hitscale >= MAXSCALE: # Hit background or empty space out += vec4(oneminusalpha renderingattributes.ambientcolour, 0.0) else: # Hit another voxel refractionattachment = lookupattachment(tree, refractionhit) # Update normal refnormal = normalize(refractionhit.normal) if dot(refnormal, refractdir) > 0.0: refnormal = -refnormal # Calculate new refraction direction eta = refractionattachment.refractiveindex / refractiveindex refractdir = refract(refractdir, refnormal, eta) # Set new origin refractrayorigin = refractionhit.hitpos + refractdir (HALFSQRT2 exp2f(refractionhit.hitscale - MAXSCALE)) refractray = Ray(refractrayorigin, refractdir) # Recursive call if refractionhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE: recursiveresult = shade(renderingattributes, refractray, refractionhit, stack, tree, refractionattachment.refractiveindex, recursions + 1) out += recursiveresult return out MAXSCALE: Constant defining the smallest voxel scale. exp2f(MAXSCALE) is the minimum voxel size. HALFSQRT2: Constant \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} \approx 0.7071. 32.0f: Exponent for specular highlight (Shininess). exp2f(23): Approximation for infinity in shadow ray distance checks. refractiondiscretestepsmax: Number of steps for discrete refraction. Not given in sources. refractiondiscretestep: Step size for discrete refraction. Not given in sources. Precision: The use of exp2f for scale calculations requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially for very small or large scales. Boundary Conditions: The check shadowhit.hitscale < MAXSCALE ensures that only valid voxel hits are considered for occlusion. Hits at MAXSCALE (empty space) are ignored. Normal Orientation: The normal must be reversed if the dot product with the view/refraction direction is positive, indicating the ray is exiting the surface. Recursion Depth: The method supports recursive bounces up to a template parameter. Deep recursion can lead to performance issues or stack overflow. Discrete Refraction Logic: The source code negates the direction in discrete refraction (discreterefractionray.direction = -refractionray.direction). This appears to be a specific implementation detail that may need verification against the intended physics. Time Complexity: O(L \cdot (1 + R)), where L is the number of lights and R is the number of refraction bounces. Each light requires a shadow ray cast. Refraction adds recursive ray casts. Memory Complexity: O(R) for the recursion stack, where R is the maximum refraction depth. Not given in the sources. Performance scales linearly with the number of lights and refraction depth. High refraction depths can significantly impact performance. Strengths: Supports complex lighting effects including shadows, specular highlights, and refraction. Handles semi-transparent volumes. Limitations: Recursive refraction can be computationally expensive. Discrete refraction logic is complex and may not accurately model continuous refraction. Use when realistic lighting with shadows and refraction is required for volumetric data. Avoid for real-time applications with strict performance constraints and high refraction depths. This method is part of the catchouli/VolumeRender project. It extends basic voxel shading to include more advanced lighting effects. catchouli/VolumeRender, https://github.com/catchouli/VolumeRender, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Fast Shading for Voxel Engines
body: Fast Shading for Voxel Engines is a CPU-based lighting algorithm designed for voxel engines that assumes vertical sun rays. It modifies voxel palette indices to simulate lighting by checking immediate neighbors, operating on palettes where indices are grouped into dark-to-light gradients (e.g., 1-32, 33-64). It is faster but less visually detailed than its sibling Voxel Shading Pipeline, using fewer neighbor checks than more complex models. Inputs: A 3D voxel grid of dimensions xsize \times ysize \times zsize, where each voxel stores a palette index. Outputs: The same voxel grid with modified palette indices representing shaded lighting. Data Structures: The voxel grid is indexed by integer coordinates (x, y, z). Each voxel contains a single integer representing a palette index. The palette is structured such that indices 1 to 32 represent the first tone group, 33 to 64 the second, and so on. Parameters: xsize, ysize, zsize: The dimensions of the voxel grid. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate through every voxel in the grid, excluding the boundary layers to avoid out-of-bounds checks. The loops run for x from 1 to xsize-2, y from 1 to ysize-2, and z from 1 to zsize-2. 2. Retrieve the current voxel's palette index: v = \text{get\voxel\pal}(x, y, z). 3. If v = 0 (empty), skip to the next voxel. 4. Calculate the lower bound (color margin) for the current tone group: m = \lfloor \frac{v-1}{32} \rfloor \times 32 + 1 5. Initialize a shading offset d = 0. 6. Check neighbors to determine occlusion/shading based on the assumption of vertical sun rays: If the voxel at (x, y+1, z) is occupied (v{top} \neq 0), subtract 3 from the potential brightness (add 3 to offset d). If any of the voxels at (x+1, y+1, z), (x-1, y+1, z), (x+1, y+1, z+1), or (x+1, y+1, z-1) are occupied, subtract 2 from the potential brightness (add 2 to offset d). If any of the voxels at (x+1, y, z+1), (x-1, y, z-1), (x+1, y, z-1), or (x-1, y, z+1) are occupied, subtract 1 from the potential brightness (add 1 to offset d). Note: The source specifies specific neighbor coordinates for each weight. The logic implies that higher y neighbors (above) have a stronger shading effect, consistent with vertical sun rays being blocked by overhead geometry. 7. Calculate the new index: v{new} = v - d. 8. Clamp the new index to the lower bound of its tone group: \text{if } v{new} < m, \text{ then } v{new} = m 9. Write the modified voxel index back: \text{set\voxel\pal}(x, y, z, v{new}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastshadevoxels(grid, xsize, ysize, zsize): for x in range(1, xsize - 1): for y in range(1, ysize - 1): for z in range(1, zsize - 1): v = grid[x, y, z] # Skip empty voxels if v == 0: continue # Calculate tone group lower bound colormargin = ((v - 1) // 32) 32 + 1 shadingoffset = 0 # Check neighbors for shading # Weight 3: Directly above if grid[x, y + 1, z] != 0: shadingoffset += 3 # Weight 2: Upper neighbors (diagonal and cardinal in Y+ plane) if (grid[x + 1, y + 1, z] != 0 or grid[x - 1, y + 1, z] != 0 or grid[x + 1, y + 1, z + 1] != 0 or grid[x + 1, y + 1, z - 1] != 0): shadingoffset += 2 # Weight 1: Side neighbors (diagonal in Y plane) if (grid[x + 1, y, z + 1] != 0 or grid[x - 1, y, z - 1] != 0 or grid[x + 1, y, z - 1] != 0 or grid[x - 1, y, z + 1] != 0): shadingoffset += 1 # Apply shading newv = v - shadingoffset # Clamp to tone group lower bound if newv < colormargin: newv = colormargin grid[x, y, z] = newv fastshade1 is a fast shading algorithm for voxel engines that assumes vertical sun rays. It modifies voxel palette indices to simulate lighting, working with palettes where indices 1-32, 33-64, etc., represent dark-to-light gradients. It is faster but less visually detailed than its sibling fastshade2, using fewer neighbor checks. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, as it iterates through the grid once. The constant factor is low due to simple integer arithmetic and neighbor lookups. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, operating in-place on the voxel grid. Performance: Designed for CPU-only rendering engines. It is significantly faster than ray-marching or complex normal-based shading because it avoids floating-point lighting calculations and long-distance ray casts. Strengths: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time CPU rendering in voxel engines. Simple to implement. Limitations: Visual quality is limited by the discrete palette steps and the simplified lighting model (vertical sun rays only). It does not support dynamic light sources or complex material properties. The shading is static relative to the voxel structure. Fast Shading for Voxel Engines was developed as part of the DOOMMY voxel engine, a voxel-based game engine that uses only CPU for rendering and Lua for scripting. The engine was created by jabberx in 2012. The method is designed to provide basic lighting effects in a resource-constrained environment without GPU acceleration. jabberx/doommy, https://github.com/jabberx/doommy, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: fast_shade1
body: fastshade1 is a fast shading algorithm for voxel engines that assumes vertical sun rays. It modifies voxel palette indices to simulate lighting, working with palettes where indices 1-32, 33-64, etc., represent dark-to-light gradients. It is faster but less visually detailed than its sibling fastshade2, using fewer neighbor checks. Inputs and outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid of dimensions xsize \times ysize \times zsize, where each voxel stores a palette index (integer). Index 0 represents empty space. Output: The same voxel grid with modified palette indices to reflect shading. Data structures: Voxel grid: A 3D array or linear buffer indexed by (x, y, z). Palette index: An integer value. The shading logic relies on the grouping of indices into tone groups of size 32. Parameters: xsize, ysize, zsize: The dimensions of the current level in voxels. Steps: 1. Iterate through the voxel grid. The loops run from 1 to xsize-2, 1 to ysize-2, and 1 to zsize-2. This boundary exclusion avoids checking neighbors outside the chunk boundaries for the current processing scope. 2. Retrieve the current voxel's palette index: v = \text{get\voxel\pal}(x, y, z). 3. Calculate the lower bound (color margin) for the current tone group: \text{color\margin} = \lfloor \frac{v-1}{32} \rfloor \times 32 + 1 where \lfloor \cdot \rfloor is the floor function. 4. If v \neq 0 (the voxel is occupied), calculate the shading adjustment by checking specific neighbors: Subtract 3 if the voxel at (x, y+1, z) is occupied (non-zero). Subtract 2 if the voxel at (x+1, y+1, z) is occupied. Subtract 1 if the voxel at (x+1, y, z+1) is occupied OR if the voxel at (x-1, y, z-1) is occupied. Let d be the sum of these subtractions. 5. Update the voxel index: v{\text{new}} = v - d. 6. Clamp the result to the tone group lower bound: if v{\text{new}} < \text{color\margin}, set v{\text{new}} = \text{color\margin}. 7. Write the modified voxel index back: \text{set\voxel\pal}(x, y, z, v{\text{new}}). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastshade1(grid, xsize, ysize, zsize): for x in range(1, xsize - 1): for y in range(1, ysize - 1): for z in range(1, zsize - 1): voxel = grid[x, y, z] # Skip empty voxels if voxel == 0: continue # Calculate tone group lower bound colormargin = ((voxel - 1) // 32) 32 + 1 # Calculate shading discount based on neighbors discount = 0 # Check (x, y+1, z): subtract 3 if occupied if grid[x, y + 1, z] != 0: discount += 3 # Check (x+1, y+1, z): subtract 2 if occupied if grid[x + 1, y + 1, z] != 0: discount += 2 # Check (x+1, y, z+1) OR (x-1, y, z-1): subtract 1 if either occupied if grid[x + 1, y, z + 1] != 0 or grid[x - 1, y, z - 1] != 0: discount += 1 # Apply shading newvoxel = voxel - discount # Clamp to tone group lower bound if newvoxel < colormargin: newvoxel = colormargin grid[x, y, z] = newvoxel Edge cases and pitfalls: The voxel index must not drop below the lower bound of its tone group (\text{color\margin}). If v{\text{new}} < \text{color\margin}, clamp it to \text{color\margin}. The iteration bounds exclude the outermost layer of voxels (0 and size-1). This implies the algorithm processes interior voxels of a chunk, likely assuming boundary voxels are handled separately or are static. The algorithm assumes a specific palette structure where brightness is grouped in blocks of 32. Gathers the light intensity of the 26 neighbors surrounding a specific voxel within a chunk to determine local lighting conditions for smoothing calculations. Time and memory complexity: Time complexity: O(N), where N is the number of voxels processed. Each voxel requires a constant number of neighbor checks (up to 4 specific neighbors) and arithmetic operations. Memory complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as it modifies the grid in place. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths and limitations: Strengths: Fast execution due to minimal neighbor checks and simple arithmetic. Suitable for CPU-only rendering engines. Limitations: Less visually detailed than fastshade2. Assumes vertical sun rays, limiting directional lighting flexibility. When to use it and when not: Use when performance is critical and vertical lighting is sufficient. Do not use when complex directional lighting or higher visual fidelity is required. Origin: The algorithm originates from the DOOMMY voxel engine, an unofficial voxel-based game engine that uses only CPU for rendering and Lua for scripting. Author: jabberx. Date: 2012. History and development: The algorithm is part of the DOOMMY engine's shading system, designed to provide basic lighting effects efficiently on CPU hardware. Where it is used: DOOMMY voxel engine. jabberx/doommy, https://github.com/jabberx/doommy, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Neighborhood Light Gathering
body: Voxel Neighborhood Light Gathering computes local lighting conditions for a target voxel by sampling the light intensity of its 26 immediate neighbors within a voxel chunk. It solves discontinuous lighting at chunk boundaries and provides smoothed shading for voxel engines by aggregating neighbor data. It differs from its parent fastshade1 by explicitly handling inter-chunk neighbor lookups and boundary conditions. Inputs: voxel: The target ChunkVoxel for which lighting is calculated. chunk: The voxel chunk containing the target voxel, providing access to neighbor chunks and local coordinate mapping. Outputs: neighborhood: An array of size NEIGHBORCOUNT (26) containing the light intensity (Option<u8>) of each neighbor. Data Structures: neighborhood: An array of length 26. Each element stores the light intensity of a neighbor. If a neighbor is inaccessible or invalid, the value is None or a default max intensity. IVec3: A 3D integer vector type representing voxel coordinates (x, y, z). IVec2: A 2D integer vector type used for mapping coordinates across chunk boundaries. Parameters: NEIGHBORCOUNT: usize = 26. Calculated as (3 \times 3 \times 3) - 1, representing all voxels in a 3 \times 3 \times 3 cube centered on the target voxel, excluding the center itself. MAXNATURALINTENSITY: A constant representing the maximum possible natural light intensity, used as a fallback for out-of-bounds or missing neighbors. Steps: 1. Initialize a mutable array neighborhood of size NEIGHBORCOUNT with default values (None). 2. Retrieve the base chunk's light and kind storage using getlight and getkind. 3. Convert the input voxel (ChunkVoxel) to an IVec3 base coordinate, denoted as basevoxel. 4. Iterate through neighbor offsets using three nested loops: y from -1 to 1, z from -1 to 1, x from -1 to 1. 5. Construct a direction vector dir = IVec3::new(x, y, z). 6. If dir is the zero vector (0, 0, 0), skip to the next iteration. 7. Calculate the neighbor voxel coordinate: sidevoxel = basevoxel + dir. 8. Determine if sidevoxel is within the current chunk's horizontal bounds. The source specifies checking if y == 0 for horizontal bounds, which implies a specific coordinate system orientation where the Y-axis is vertical and X/Z are horizontal. If out of bounds horizontally: Calculate the neighbor chunk using chunk.neighbor(dir). Calculate the local voxel coordinate in that chunk using chunk::overlapvoxel(voxel, IVec2::new(dir.x, dir.z)). Retrieve light and kind data from the neighbor chunk. If the neighbor chunk does not exist or light/kind data is unavailable, set intensity to MAXNATURALINTENSITY. Otherwise, apply the same opaque/zero check used for internal voxels to determine the final intensity. If within bounds: Retrieve light and kind data from the current chunk's storage. Apply the opaque/zero check to determine the intensity. 9. Store the calculated intensity (Option<u8>) into the neighborhood array at the current index i and increment i. 10. After iterating through all 26 neighbors, return the populated neighborhood array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from typing import List, Optional, Tuple IVec3 = Tuple[int, int, int] IVec2 = Tuple[int, int] def gatherneighborhoodlight(voxel: 'ChunkVoxel', chunk: 'VoxelChunk') -> List[Optional[int]]: NEIGHBORCOUNT = 26 MAXNATURALINTENSITY = 255 # Value not specified in sources neighborhood: List[Optional[int]] = [None] NEIGHBORCOUNT i = 0 basevoxel: IVec3 = voxel.toivec3() lightstorage = chunk.getlight() kindstorage = chunk.getkind() for y in range(-1, 2): for z in range(-1, 2): for x in range(-1, 2): if x == 0 and y == 0 and z == 0: continue dir: IVec3 = (x, y, z) sidevoxel: IVec3 = (basevoxel[0] + dir[0], basevoxel[1] + dir[1], basevoxel[2] + dir[2]) intensity: Optional[int] = None # Check horizontal bounds condition from source if sidevoxel[1] == 0: # y == 0 check per source notes neighborchunk = chunk.neighbor(dir) if neighborchunk is None: intensity = MAXNATURALINTENSITY else: localcoord: IVec2 = (dir[0], dir[2]) nlight = neighborchunk.getlight() nkind = neighborchunk.getkind() if nlight is None or nkind is None: intensity = MAXNATURALINTENSITY else: # Opaque/zero check logic not detailed in sources intensity = nlight if nkind > 0 else 0 else: clight = lightstorage.get(sidevoxel) ckind = kindstorage.get(sidevoxel) if clight is None or ckind is None: intensity = MAXNATURALINTENSITY else: # Opaque/zero check logic not detailed in sources intensity = clight if ckind > 0 else 0 neighborhood[i] = intensity i += 1 return neighborhood Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Chunk Boundaries: The method must correctly handle neighbors that lie in adjacent chunks using chunk.neighbor(dir) and chunk::overlapvoxel. Missing Neighbors: If a neighbor chunk does not exist or light/kind data is unavailable, the intensity defaults to MAXNATURALINTENSITY. Coordinate System: The source's mention of y == 0 for horizontal bounds is specific to the engine's coordinate system. Opaque/Zero Check: The exact logic for the opaque/zero check is not detailed in the source. Implementers should define it based on their voxel kind definitions. Time Complexity: O(1) per voxel, as it always checks a fixed number of 26 neighbors. Memory Complexity: O(1) per voxel, requiring storage for 26 neighbor intensities. Strengths: Simple to implement, fast, handles chunk boundaries explicitly. Limitations: Limited to local lighting effects, may not capture global lighting phenomena like shadows or reflections accurately. Voxel Neighborhood Light Gathering is part of the "projekto" project by afonsolage. It is designed for voxel engines that use chunk-based data structures and require efficient, local lighting calculations. The method builds on the assumptions of fastshade1 but extends it to handle inter-chunk lighting more robustly. projekto, https://github.com/afonsolage/projekto, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Shader Volumetric Ray Marching
head: Phoenix Volumetric Rendering, V-Ray Volume Grid Shading
body: Voxel Shader Volumetric Ray Marching is a shading method for Fire/Smoke simulations and meshes that reads voxel grid data from a Phoenix Simulator or V-Ray Volume Grid to handle volumetric shading, as standard Maya materials cannot shade volumetrics directly. It distinguishes itself from its siblings by providing specific rollouts for Fire, Smoke Color, and Smoke Opacity, and by supporting both pure volumetric ray marching and "Render as Geometry" procedural geometry modes. Unlike Voxel Shading Pipeline which may rely on discrete neighbor dependence for lighting, this method explicitly traces camera and shadow rays through the grid with configurable step sizes and sampling filters. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Voxel grid data (Temperature, Smoke, Speed, Fuel, Velocity, etc.), camera position/direction, light sources, and shader parameters (Step %, Sampler Type, Surface Channel, etc.). Outputs: Colored pixel values, optionally with Render Elements (Normals, Velocity, Z-Depth, Material ID) if "Render as Geometry" is enabled. Data Structures: The method operates on a 3D voxel grid indexed by integer coordinates (x, y, z). Each cell contains scalar or vector fields (e.g., Temperature, Smoke density, Velocity vector). The grid is accessed via ray marching, where continuous ray positions are mapped to grid cells. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, cast a primary camera ray into the scene. 2. Cutter Check (Optional): If rendUseGizmo is enabled, check if the ray intersects the render cutter geometry. If rendInvGizmo is enabled, shade rays that do not intersect the cutter. If the ray is outside the allowed volume, return background color. 3. Ray Marching Loop: a. Determine step size: step = \text{cell\size} \times (\text{Step \%} / 100). b. If Step % > 100, cells are skipped, causing artifacts. c. Advance ray by step along its direction. d. Sample the voxel grid at the current ray position. The sampling method depends on Sampler Type: Box: No blending; return value of the single cell containing the ray. Linear: Linear blending between adjacent voxels. Spherical: Weight-based sampling for smoothest look. e. Accumulate optical depth and color based on the sampled values (Smoke, Temperature, etc.) and the current lighting state. f. Repeat until the ray exits the grid or reaches a maximum distance. 4. Shadow Ray Marching (Lighting): a. For each light source, cast a shadow ray from the current shading point to the light. b. Determine shadow step size: shadow\step = \text{cell\size} \times (\text{Shadow Step \%} / 100). c. March along the shadow ray, accumulating opacity. Higher Shadow Step % speeds up rendering, especially for dome/area lights. 5. Surface Shading (If applicable): a. If "Render as Geometry" (geommode) is enabled, the volume is converted to procedural geometry (transparent layers). b. Otherwise, if a Surface Channel (sarg) is defined, compute the isosurface using rendSurfLevelx/t/s/v/f. c. Apply displacement based on rendDispltSurf type (Gradient driven, Surface driven, Vector, or Advection). d. Compute normals and lighting for the surface. 6. Heat Haze (Optional): If rendHeatHaze > 0, perturb the ray direction based on the gradient of the Surface Channel. 7. Motion Blur (Optional): a. If volMoblurMethod is "Ray-traced", sample the velocity at multiple time steps along the ray. b. If "Grid-based", use a pre-pass to generate streaks. c. If rendVelTexture is set, use the texture's RGB values (Y/Z flipped to Blue/Green) as velocity vectors to stretch the simulation content. d. Apply mbmult multiplier to blur strength. 8. Border Fade: If the ray is within borderFade distance of the grid boundary, fade the opacity to transparent to prevent sharp edges. 9. Compositing: Combine fire and smoke colors/opacities. Fire opacity mode (emIgnoreAlpha) determines if fire uses smoke opacity, is fully visible (additive blending), or uses own opacity. Formulas: Step Size: s = C \cdot \frac{P}{100}, where C is cell size, P is Step %. Velocity Texture Mapping: vy = -Tb, vz = -Tg, where Tb, Tg are Blue and Green texture components. Heat Haze Perturbation: \vec{d}{new} = \vec{d}{old} + k \cdot \nabla S, where k is rendHeatHaze value, S is Surface channel. Parameters with Typical Values: Step % (rendstep): Recommended \ge 90\%. Shadow Step % (rendshadstep): Typically higher than Step %. Isosurface Level (rendSurfLevel): Default 0.5. Heat Haze (rendHeatHaze): 1 approximates normal heat haze. Sampler Type: Box (fastest), Linear (20-30% faster than Spherical), Spherical (smoothest). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Step % > 100: Causes cell skipping and artifacts. Step % < 90%: Required for render curves or texture maps to capture details smaller than a voxel, but increases render time. Render as Geometry: Slows down rendering significantly. Grid-based Motion Blur: Requires pre-pass, uses more memory, and only affects Volumetric/Volumetric Geometry/Volumetric Heat Haze modes. Velocity Texture: Y/Z components are flipped (Blue/Green channels). Fire Opacity: "Fully Visible" mode uses additive blending and is not suitable for fire+smoke mix. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelshadervolumetricraymarching(rayorigin, raydirection, grid, params): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 grid: VoxelGrid (access methods: getscalar(x,y,z), getvector(x,y,z)) params: dict containing all shader parameters """ cellsize = grid.cellsize steppct = params['rendstep'] shadowsteppct = params['rendshadstep'] borderfadedist = params['borderFade'] samplertype = params['sampler'] surfacechannel = params['sarg'] isosurfacelevel = params['rendSurfLevelx'] # Simplified for one channel heathazestrength = params['rendHeatHaze'] velocitytexture = params['rendVelTexture'] motionblurmethod = params['volMoblurMethod'] mbmult = params['mbmult'] usecutter = params['rendUseGizmo'] invertcutter = params['rendInvGizmo'] cuttergizmo = params['cuttergizmo'] # Geometric object renderasgeometry = params['geommode'] fireopacitymode = params['emIgnoreAlpha'] smokecolorsource = params['difSource'] fireemissionsource = params['emSource'] # Initialize accumulators accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 currentpos = rayorigin currentdir = raydirection # Check cutter if usecutter: if invertcutter: if rayintersectsgizmo(rayorigin, raydirection, cuttergizmo): return vec3(0.0) # Ray intersects cutter, so it's outside (inverted) else: if not rayintersectsgizmo(rayorigin, raydirection, cuttergizmo): return vec3(0.0) # Ray does not intersect cutter, so it's outside # Determine step size stepsize = cellsize (steppct / 100.0) if steppct > 100: # Artifacts may appear, but we proceed as per source pass # Main ray march while currentpos is inside grid: # Check border fade disttoboundary = distancetogridboundary(currentpos, grid) if disttoboundary < borderfadedist: fadefactor = disttoboundary / borderfadedist # Apply fade to accumulated color/opacity? Source says content becomes transparent. # We'll apply it to the final contribution. pass # Sample grid if samplertype == 'Box': voxelvalue = grid.getscalaratposition(currentpos) elif samplertype == 'Linear': voxelvalue = grid.getlinearinterpolatedscalar(currentpos) elif samplertype == 'Spherical': voxelvalue = grid.getsphericalweightedscalar(currentpos) # Heat Haze if heathazestrength > 0: surfacegradient = grid.getgradientofsurfacechannel(currentpos, surfacechannel) currentdir = normalize(currentdir + heathazestrength surfacegradient) # Accumulate color and opacity # Simplified accumulation logic smokedensity = grid.getscalar('Smoke', currentpos) temperature = grid.getscalar('Temperature', currentpos) # Smoke Color smokecolor = computesmokecolor(smokedensity, temperature, smokecolorsource, params) # Fire Emission firecolor = computefireemission(temperature, fireemissionsource, params) # Shadow Ray Marching shadowopacity = 0.0 shadowstepsize = cellsize (shadowsteppct / 100.0) shadowpos = currentpos shadowdir = normalize(lightposition - currentpos) while shadowpos is inside grid and shadowopacity < 1.0: shadowpos += shadowstepsize shadowdir shadowopacity += grid.getscalar('Smoke', shadowpos) shadowstepsize # Combine contribution = (smokecolor (1.0 - shadowopacity) + firecolor) smokedensity stepsize accumulatedcolor += contribution (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity += smokedensity stepsize # Advance currentpos += stepsize currentdir # Apply border fade to final result if needed #... # Fire Opacity Mode if fireopacitymode == 'Fully Visible': # Additive blending, no alpha return accumulatedcolor elif fireopacitymode == 'Use Smoke Opacity': return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity else: # Use Own Opacity return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity def computesmokecolor(smokedensity, temperature, source, params): if source == 'Constant Color': return params['difSimpleColor'] elif source == 'Temperature': return remaptemperaturetocolor(temperature, params['difScattering']) elif source == 'Smoke': return remapsmoketocolor(smokedensity, params['difScattering']) elif source == 'Texture': return params['difTexture'].sample(params['texcoords']) elif source == 'RGB': return grid.getvector('RGB', params['texcoords']) elif source == 'Fuel': return remapfueltocolor(grid.getscalar('Fuel', params['texcoords']), params['difScattering']) else: return vec3(0.0) def computefireemission(temperature, source, params): if source == 'Temperature': return remaptemperaturetofirecolor(temperature) elif source == 'Smoke': return remapsmoketofirecolor(grid.getscalar('Smoke', params['texcoords'])) elif source == 'Speed': return remapspeedtofirecolor(grid.getscalar('Speed', params['texcoords'])) elif source == 'Fuel': return remapfueltofirecolor(grid.getscalar('Fuel', params['texcoords'])) elif source == 'Texture': return params['emTexture'].sample(params['texcoords']) elif source == 'RGB': return grid.getvector('RGB', params['texcoords']) else: return vec3(0.0) def rayintersectsgizmo(origin, direction, gizmo): # Placeholder for geometric intersection test # Standard ray-triangle or ray-bounding box intersection return False Smoke Color Mapping determines the diffuse color of the smoke volume. It requires external light to become visible if GI is enabled. The Based on (difSource) parameter specifies the source channel: Constant Color (default), Temperature, Smoke, Speed, Texture, RGB, or Fuel. If Based on is not Texture, the color can be modulated by a texture map (difModulate). The Scattering (difScattering) parameter controls light ray scattering, with options for Ray-traced (GI only, slowest, most realistic), Disabled (uses Diffuse Multiplier for brightness), and Approximate. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of ray steps, which is inversely proportional to Step % and Shadow Step %. Shadow rays add additional cost, especially with many lights. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the voxel grid and any additional textures (Velocity, Displacement). Grid-based motion blur requires a pre-pass and more memory. Measured Performance: Box sampler is fastest. Linear is 20-30% faster than Spherical. Spherical is smoothest but slowest. "Render as Geometry" slows down rendering significantly. Grid-based motion blur is slower than Ray-traced due to pre-pass. Scaling: Performance degrades with higher resolution grids and lower step percentages. Strengths: Supports complex volumetric shading, motion blur, displacement, and render elements (via Render as Geometry). Limitations: "Render as Geometry" is slow. Grid-based motion blur requires more memory. Step % < 90% increases render time. When to Use: For Fire/Smoke simulations where volumetric shading is required and standard materials cannot be used. When Not to Use: When performance is critical and visual quality of sampling is less important (use Box sampler). When deep images or render elements are not needed (avoid Render as Geometry). The Voxel Shader is part of the Phoenix FD plugin for Maya, developed by Chaos Group. It was created to address the limitation that Maya materials cannot shade volumetrics directly, providing specific rollouts for Fire, Smoke Color, and Smoke Opacity. It supports rendering from Phoenix Simulator data and V-Ray Volume Grids. Voxel Shader - Phoenix for Maya, https://documentation.chaos.com/space/PHX4MAYA/125768009, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Diffuse Lighting Models
body: Diffuse lighting models calculate surface illumination by simulating light scattering, providing the primary visual cue for surface orientation and shape in ray-marched and rasterized rendering. This family distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Distance Color Blending and Specular and Reflective Shading by focusing exclusively on non-specular reflectance, often serving as the base layer for more complex shading. All methods in this family operate on a surface point \mathbf{p} and its associated geometric data, primarily the surface normal \mathbf{n}, as detailed in Lighting and Shading Models. Applies the Phong reflection model to SDF surfaces, distinguishing itself from Lambertian Lighting in SDF by including specular highlights and from Blinn-Phong Shading in Volume Rendering by using the exact reflected light vector rather than the half-vector approximation. Choose it when a shinier appearance with precise specular reflections is required. Calculates pure diffuse illumination by clamping the dot product of the normal and light direction to zero, focusing solely on the diffuse component unlike Phong Shading with SDF Normals or Blinn-Phong Shading in Volume Rendering which include specular highlights. Choose it for physically plausible, matte shading that reveals surface curvature. Applies the Blinn-Phong model to volume data, using the half-vector approximation for specular highlights which is computationally cheaper than calculating the reflection vector, and differs from Lambertian Lighting in SDF by including specular and ambient components. Choose it for efficient glossy surface simulation in volume rendering. Computes lighting colors at mesh vertices and linearly interpolates them across facets, solving the faceted appearance of polygonal approximations by creating continuous color gradients, unlike Phong shading which interpolates normals. Choose it for performance-critical rasterized rendering of curved surfaces. A shading model assuming uniform lighting where light surrounds an object equally in all directions. glShadeModel(GLFLAT) Flat shading diminishes the three dimensionality of the scene. The concept of flat shading was formalized in early graphics APIs like OpenGL, which provided glShadeModel(GLFLAT) to specify uniform lighting across primitives. Gouraud shading, also known as smooth shading, was introduced to provide subtle color changes across surfaces by interpolating vertex colors, assuming light comes from a particular direction. These models are foundational in visualizing data, such as in Fire Dynamics Simulation tools like Smokeview. Smokeview (Version 6) A Tool for Visualizing Fire Dynamics Simulation Data Volume II: Technical Reference Guide, https://doi.org/10.6028/nist.sp.1017-2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Phong Shading with SDF Normals
head: Phong Shading using SDF Gradients, normal vector interpolation shading
body:
Phong Shading with SDF Normals is a lighting model for ray-marched Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) that applies the Phong reflection model using surface normals estimated from the SDF gradient. Unlike Lambertian Lighting in SDF, which computes only diffuse illumination, this method includes specular highlights, providing a shinier appearance. It differs from Blinn-Phong Shading in Volume Rendering by using the exact reflection vector \mathbf{r} rather than the half-vector, and from Gouraud Shading by computing lighting per-fragment using interpolated or gradient-derived normals rather than interpolating pre-computed vertex colors. Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p} (position in world space). SDF function f(\mathbf{x}). Light positions \mathbf{l}j and intensities \vec{i}j (RGB vectors) for j=1 \dots N. Material properties: diffuse coefficient \vec{k}d (RGB), specular coefficient \vec{k}s (RGB), shininess \alpha (scalar). Camera position \mathbf{c}. Outputs: Final color \vec{C} (RGB vector). Data Structures: Vectors are 3D floats. Dot products yield scalars. Element-wise multiplication (\odot) applies to RGB vectors. Steps: 1. Compute Normal: Estimate the surface normal \hat{\mathbf{n}} at \mathbf{p} using the SDF gradient 
abla f(\mathbf{p}). As per the parent Diffuse Lighting Models, this is typically done via finite differences: \hat{\mathbf{n}} =  rac{
abla f(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla f(\mathbf{p})\|} Ensure 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) is not zero to avoid division by zero; if zero, use a default normal (e.g., \mathbf{0} or \mathbf{1}) or skip lighting. 2. Compute Directions: View direction: \hat{\mathbf{v}} =  rac{\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}}{\|\mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p}\|}. For each light j: Light direction: \hat{\mathbf{l}}j =  rac{\mathbf{l}j - \mathbf{p}}{\|\mathbf{l}j - \mathbf{p}\|}. Reflection direction: \hat{\mathbf{r}}j = 2(\hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{l}}j)\hat{\mathbf{n}} - \hat{\mathbf{l}}j. 3. Accumulate Lighting: Initialize total color \vec{C} = \vec{0}. For each light j: Compute diffuse term: Dj = \max(0, \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{l}}j). Compute specular term: Sj = \max(0, \hat{\mathbf{r}}j \cdot \hat{\mathbf{v}})^\alpha. If either dot product is negative, the term is clipped to zero. Compute contribution: \vec{C}j = (Dj \odot \vec{k}s \odot \vec{i}j) + (Sj \odot \vec{k}d \odot \vec{i}j). Note: The source formula assigns \vec{k}s to the diffuse dot product and \vec{k}d to the specular dot product, which is non-standard (typically \vec{k}d is diffuse, \vec{k}s is specular). However, the source explicitly states: "contribute a term (\hat{L} \cdot \hat{N})(\vec{k}s \odot \vec{i}) + (\hat{R} \cdot \hat{V})^\alpha (\vec{k}d \odot \vec{i})". We follow the source's explicit formula. \vec{C} \leftarrow \vec{C} + \vec{C}j. 4. Return Color: Return \vec{C}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def phongshadingsdf(p, sdffunc, lights, material, camerapos): # 1. Compute Normal eps = 1e-4 grad = vec3( sdffunc(p + vec3(eps, 0, 0)) - sdffunc(p - vec3(eps, 0, 0)), sdffunc(p + vec3(0, eps, 0)) - sdffunc(p - vec3(0, eps, 0)), sdffunc(p + vec3(0, 0, eps)) - sdffunc(p - vec3(0, 0, eps))) / (2 eps) nhat = normalize(grad) # 2. View Direction vhat = normalize(camerapos - p) color = vec3(0.0) for light in lights: # 3. Light Directions lhat = normalize(light.position - p) rhat = reflect(-lhat, nhat) # reflect(vector, normal) computes 2(N.L)N - L # 4. Dot Products nl = dot(nhat, lhat) rv = dot(rhat, vhat) # Clip negative values nl = max(nl, 0.0) rv = max(rv, 0.0) # 5. Phong Contribution (per source formula) # Note: Source swaps ks and kd roles compared to standard convention diffuseterm = nl (material.ks light.intensity) specularterm = pow(rv, material.alpha) (material.kd light.intensity) color += diffuseterm + specularterm return color Parameters: \vec{k}s: Specular reflection coefficient (RGB vector). \vec{k}d: Diffuse reflection coefficient (RGB vector). \alpha: Shininess exponent (scalar). \vec{i}: Light intensity (RGB vector). Edge Cases: Zero Gradient: If 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) \approx \mathbf{0}, the normal is undefined. Return ambient color or black. Negative Dot Products: Terms with negative dot products are ignored (clipped to zero). Applies directional diffuse and specular lighting to SDF text using estimated normals and configurable light angles. It builds on this method by computing lighting contributions per fragment based on the Phong reflection model. Time Complexity: O(N) per fragment, where N is the number of lights. Each light requires gradient estimation (constant time, 6 SDF queries for finite differences) and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per fragment. Performance: Computationally more expensive than Lambertian shading due to specular calculations and multiple light loops. Gradient estimation adds overhead compared to analytic normals. Strengths: Provides realistic specular highlights for SDF surfaces; simple to implement. Limitations: Normal estimation via finite differences can be noisy or inaccurate for complex SDFs; performance scales linearly with light count. When to use: When specular highlights are desired for SDF-rendered objects and performance allows for multiple light evaluations. When not to use: For real-time applications with many lights where performance is critical, or when analytic normals are available. Phong shading was originally developed by Bui Tuong Phong for polygonal meshes, computing interpolated normals across facets. In the context of SDFs, it adapts this concept by deriving normals from the SDF gradient. The specific formula provided in appears in a university project writeup (COS 426 Final Project) and may not reflect standard textbook definitions, particularly regarding the assignment of \vec{k}s and \vec{k}d to diffuse and specular terms respectively. Computing and Displaying Isosurfaces in R, https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v028.i01, fetched 2026-10-27 PDF COS 426 Final Project Writeup Raymarching with Signed Distance Fields, https://jbaum98.github.io/cos426finalproject/writeup.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Phong Lighting
head: SDF Directional Lighting, TextMeshPro Lighting
body: SDF Phong Lighting applies directional diffuse and specular lighting to Signed Distance Field (SDF) text using estimated surface normals and a configurable light angle. It builds on Phong Shading with SDF Normals by computing lighting contributions per fragment based on the Phong reflection model, using normals derived from the SDF gradient. Inputs and Outputs: Input: SDF value d, surface normal \mathbf{n}, base color C{base}, and lighting parameters. Output: Final fragment color C{final}. Data Structures: Lighting Parameters: A configuration struct containing: LightAngle (float): Light direction in radians (default 3.1416). SpecularColor (vec3): Specular highlight color (default 1,1,1). SpecularPower (float): Specular intensity multiplier (default 2.0). Reflectivity (float): Specular shininess exponent (default 10). Diffuse (float): Diffuse lighting factor (default 0.5). Ambient (float): Ambient lighting factor (default 0.5). Steps: 1. Compute Light Direction: Derive the normalized light direction vector \mathbf{l} from LightAngle. \mathbf{l} = (\cos(\text{\LightAngle}), \sin(\text{\LightAngle}), 0) 2. Compute Specular Term: Calculate the specular contribution using the Phong specular model. \text{spec} = \text{pow}(\max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}), \text{\Reflectivity}) 3. Scale Specular: Multiply the specular term by SpecularColor and SpecularPower. C{spec} = \text{\SpecularColor} \times \text{spec} \times \text{\SpecularPower} 4. Compute Diffuse Term: Calculate the diffuse attenuation using a subtraction-based model. C{diff} = 1 - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \times \text{\Diffuse} 5. Compute Ambient Term: Apply an ambient term that varies based on the normal's Z-component. C{amb} = \text{lerp}(\text{\Ambient}, 1, \mathbf{n}z^2) 6. Combine: Multiply the base color by the diffuse and ambient terms, then add the specular term. C{final} = C{base} \times C{diff} \times C{amb} + C{spec} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x, self.y, self.z = x, y, z def dot(self, other): return self.x other.x + self.y other.y + self.z other.z def scale(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + (b - a) t def sdfphonglighting(n: Vec3, basecolor: Vec3, lightangle: float, specularcolor: Vec3, specularpower: float, reflectivity: float, diffuse: float, ambient: float) -> Vec3: # 1. Compute light direction from angle l = Vec3(math.cos(lightangle), math.sin(lightangle), 0.0) # 2. Compute specular term dotnl = max(0.0, n.dot(l)) spec = pow(dotnl, reflectivity) specularterm = specularcolor.scale(spec specularpower) # 3. Compute diffuse term diffusefactor = 1.0 - (dotnl diffuse) # 4. Compute ambient term ambientfactor = lerp(ambient, 1.0, n.z n.z) # 5. Combine finalcolor = basecolor.scale(diffusefactor ambientfactor).add(specularterm) return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Degeneracy: If \nabla d is zero, normalization fails. Negative Diffuse: The formula 1 - (\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}) \times \text{\Diffuse} can produce negative lighting if \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l} is large and \text{\Diffuse} > 1. Light Angle Interpretation: The source uses LightAngle as a single float, implying a 2D direction. Adds a colored glow around the text by computing a falloff function based on the signed distance and applying it to a glow color. Parameters include GlowColor (default 0,1,0,0.5), GlowOffset (default 0), GlowInner (default 0.05), GlowOuter (default 0.05), and GlowPower (default 0.75). Implementation calls GetGlowColor(sd, scale) and adds the result to the face color: faceColor.rgb += glowColor.rgb glowColor.a. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(1) per fragment, involving trigonometric functions, dot products, and power operations. Memory: O(1) auxiliary storage for parameters and intermediate vectors. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Simple to implement; provides visual depth to SDF text; configurable via scalar parameters. Limitations: Diffuse model is non-standard (subtraction-based); light direction is limited to a 2D angle in the source implementation; no shadowing is included. When to Use: Use for 2D text rendering or simple volumes where a single directional light is sufficient. When Not to Use: Do not use for physically based rendering or scenes requiring multiple lights, shadows, or complex material interactions. Not given in the sources. andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, https://github.com/andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Per-Fragment Phong Lighting with Gradient Normals
head: Gradient-based Phong Shading, Phong Lighting with Gradient Normals, Phong Shading with Gradient Normals
body: Per-fragment Phong Lighting with Gradient Normals is a volume rendering shading technique that enhances the visual perception of internal structures by applying Phong or Gouraud shading models to voxels based on normals derived from the scalar field's gradient. It distinguishes itself from standard threshold-based shading by providing a "realistic" 3D view through dynamic lighting calculations that interact with the volume's internal density variations, rather than relying solely on surface boundaries. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (density values), a transfer function defining opacity/color, a light vector, and rendering parameters (threshold, interpolation mode, highlight toggle). Output: A 2D image where each fragment's color is modulated by the Phong lighting model. Data Structures: Scalar Field: A 3D grid of density values. The sources indicate 12-bit precision (range 0–4095). Light Vector: A 3D vector (Lx, Ly, Lz) that moves with the view vector. Normal Vector: A 3D vector (Nx, Ny, Nz) calculated per fragment. Steps: 1. Ray Marching: Perform standard volume ray marching to sample the scalar field along the ray. 2. Gradient Calculation: For each sample point (fragment) along the ray, calculate the normal vector \mathbf{N} by computing the gradient of the scalar field \phi at that point. The gradient is computed using finite differences. The specific interpolation method (nearest neighbor or trilinear) affects the accuracy of the density values used in this calculation. Formula: \mathbf{N} = \nabla \phi = \left( \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial \phi}{\partial z} \right). Normalize \mathbf{N} to unit length. 3. Threshold Check: Determine if the current sample's density value \phi is above the user-defined threshold value T. If \phi < T, shading is not applied (or the fragment is treated as background/transparent depending on the transfer function's opacity at that density). If \phi \ge T, proceed to lighting calculation. 4. Lighting Calculation: Calculate the shading color using the Phong or Gouraud model. Let \mathbf{V} be the view vector (from fragment to camera). Let \mathbf{L} be the light vector. Let \mathbf{R} be the reflection vector: \mathbf{R} = 2(\mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L})\mathbf{N} - \mathbf{L} (standard Phong reflection). The diffuse component is proportional to \max(0, \mathbf{N} \cdot \mathbf{L}). The specular component is proportional to \max(0, \mathbf{R} \cdot \mathbf{V})^{\text{shininess}}. The final color is a combination of ambient, diffuse, and specular terms, modulated by the base color from the transfer function. 5. Interpolation: When calculating the gradient or shading colors, use either nearest neighbor or trilinear interpolation for the density values. Trilinear interpolation provides smoother gradients but may blur sharp features; nearest neighbor preserves sharpness but may introduce artifacts. 6. Highlights: If the "Shading with Highlights" option is enabled, include the specular term in the calculation. Parameters: Threshold Value (T): Selects the density region for shading. Range: 0 to 4095. Typical values: ~400 for skin, ~1700 for bones, 3200 for teeth. Light Vector: Moves with the view vector. Interpolation Mode: Nearest neighbor or trilinear. Highlight Toggle: Boolean to enable/disable specular highlights. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def perfragmentphonggradientnormal(scalarfield, rayorigin, raydirection, threshold, interpolationmode, enablehighlights): # Initialize accumulated color and opacity accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Ray marching loop (simplified) for t in range(0, maxdistance, stepsize): pos = rayorigin + t raydirection density = samplescalarfield(scalarfield, pos, interpolationmode) # Threshold check if density < threshold: continue # Calculate normal from gradient gradx = computegradientx(scalarfield, pos, interpolationmode) grady = computegradienty(scalarfield, pos, interpolationmode) gradz = computegradientz(scalarfield, pos, interpolationmode) normal = normalize((gradx, grady, gradz)) # View and Light vectors viewvector = normalize(-raydirection) # Assuming camera at origin looking down -Z or similar lightvector = getlightvector(viewvector) # Light moves with view # Phong Lighting Model # Diffuse diff = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightvector)) # Specular (if enabled) spec = 0.0 if enablehighlights: reflection = reflect(lightvector, normal) spec = pow(max(0.0, dot(reflection, viewvector)), shininess) # Combine lighting shadingfactor = ambient + diffusescale diff + specularscale spec # Get base color from transfer function basecolor = transferfunctioncolor(density) baseopacity = transferfunctionopacity(density) # Apply shading to color shadedcolor = basecolor shadingfactor # Alpha compositing (front-to-back) alpha = baseopacity stepsize densityscale # Simplified opacity model accumulatedcolor = accumulatedcolor + shadedcolor alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) accumulatedopacity = accumulatedopacity + alpha (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) if accumulatedopacity > 0.99: break return accumulatedcolor def samplescalarfield(field, pos, mode): if mode == 'nearest': return field[nearestvoxel(pos)] elif mode == 'trilinear': return trilinearinterpolate(field, pos) else: raise ValueError("Unknown interpolation mode") def computegradientx(field, pos, mode): # Finite difference approximation # Note: Exact implementation depends on grid spacing and boundary handling # Assuming uniform grid spacing of 1.0 for simplicity valright = samplescalarfield(field, pos + (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), mode) valleft = samplescalarfield(field, pos - (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), mode) return (valright - valleft) / 2.0 def computegradienty(field, pos, mode): valup = samplescalarfield(field, pos + (0.0, 1.0, 0.0), mode) valdown = samplescalarfield(field, pos - (0.0, 1.0, 0.0), mode) return (valup - valdown) / 2.0 def computegradientz(field, pos, mode): valfront = samplescalarfield(field, pos + (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), mode) valback = samplescalarfield(field, pos - (0.0, 0.0, 1.0), mode) return (valfront - valback) / 2.0 def reflect(light, normal): # R = 2(N.L)N - L dotnl = dot(normal, light) return (2.0 dotnl normal) - light Diffuse Lighting for Volume Ray Casting illuminates a volume by calculating normals for every voxel using finite differences of the scalar field, then applying a diffuse lighting model. It provides geometric cues that allow standard diffuse lighting models to interact with the volume's internal structure. This method extends per-fragment Phong lighting by applying two alpha-modulation techniques to enhance the visual perception of volume boundaries: boundary enhancement via absorption approximation and facing subtraction for silhouette definition. It distinguishes itself from standard gradient-based Phong shading by explicitly modifying the fragment alpha based on the gradient magnitude and the view direction relative to the surface normal. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples along all rays. The gradient calculation adds a constant factor (typically 6-8 extra samples for central differences) per fragment. Memory Complexity: O(V) where V is the volume of the scalar field, required to store the density values. Performance: The method is interactive when combined with efficient ray marching and transfer function pre-integration, as noted in the evaluation of the dual-domain interface. The choice of interpolation (nearest vs. trilinear) affects both quality and speed. Strengths: Provides a realistic 3D impression by leveraging internal density gradients, not just surfaces. Allows selective shading of specific tissue types via thresholding. Limitations: Can only visualize one tissue type at a time if using a single threshold, unlike full volume rendering which assigns opacity to all tissues. Gradient noise can lead to noisy normals if the scalar field is not smooth. When to use: When a realistic, shaded appearance of specific internal structures (e.g., bones, skin) is desired, and the user wants to control which density ranges are illuminated. When not to use: When simultaneous visualization of multiple tissue types with varying opacities is required (use full Volume Rendering instead). This method originates from early volume visualization applications, specifically the "VOLUME RENDERING Application" by Thomas Lidy (2001-2002). It was designed to provide a "realistic" view of medical datasets (human skin, bones, teeth) by applying Phong/Gouraud shading to density gradients. It was later referenced in the context of flexible transfer function design tools, where it served as a shading option for volume exploration. The technique relies on the principle that the gradient of a scalar field approximates the surface normal, even for implicit surfaces defined by the field. name: Diffuse Lighting for Volume Ray Casting
head: Gradient Normal Lighting, Gradient-based Lighting in MRT Raycasting
body: Diffuse Lighting for Volume Ray Casting illuminates a volume by calculating normals for every voxel using finite differences of the scalar field, then applying a diffuse lighting model. It provides geometric cues that allow standard diffuse lighting models to interact with the volume's internal structure. The method operates during the ray casting loop at the shading stage for each sampled voxel. It requires access to the scalar field values of the current sample and its immediate neighbors along the three principal axes. Inputs: scalar: The scalar value V(x, y, z) at the current ray position tr. tr: The current 3D texture coordinate (ray position) in the volume. voxelJump: A uniform vector (dx, dy, dz) representing the distance between adjacent voxels. lightDir: A uniform vector representing the direction to the light source in eye space. diffColor: A uniform vector representing the diffuse color of the light. samp: The current sample color (RGB) derived from the transfer function. Outputs: Updated samp color, modulated by the diffuse lighting contribution. The method operates directly on the volume texture without requiring additional data structures. 1. Sample the current voxel's scalar value scalar. 2. Calculate the gradient vector (normal) by subtracting the current scalar from its neighbors in the X, Y, and Z directions using finite differences. 3. Normalize the gradient vector to get the surface normal. 4. Calculate the diffuse contribution using the dot product of the light direction and the normal, clamped to 0. 5. Multiply the sample's color by the diffuse contribution and the light color. Let V(x, y, z) be the scalar value at position (x, y, z). Let dx, dy, dz be the voxel jumps. The gradient components are calculated as: nx = V(x+dx, y, z) - V(x, y, z) ny = V(x, y+dy, z) - V(x, y, z) nz = V(x, y, z-dz) - V(x, y, z) The normal vector N is: N = \text{normalize}(nx, ny, nz) The diffuse factor D is: D = \max(\text{dot}(L, N), 0.0) The final output color C{out} (RGB part of the sample) is: C{out} = C{in} \times D \times C{light} Where C{in} is the original sample color and C{light} is diffColor. lightDir: Uniform vector for the light direction in eye space. diffColor: Uniform vector for the diffuse color of the light. voxelJump: Uniform vector representing the distance between voxels, used to offset sampling positions for finite differences. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the logic described in the source. It assumes a standard volume texture lookup function. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatediffuselighting(sampcolor, tr, scalar, lightdir, diffcolor, voxeljump): # 1. Calculate Gradient Components using Finite Differences # X-axis: forward difference valright = samplevolume(tr + vec3(voxeljump.x, 0.0, 0.0)) nx = valright - scalar # Y-axis: forward difference valup = samplevolume(tr + vec3(0.0, voxeljump.y, 0.0)) ny = valup - scalar # Z-axis: backward difference (as per source code) valback = samplevolume(tr + vec3(0.0, 0.0, -voxeljump.z)) nz = valback - scalar # 2. Normalize the Gradient to get the Normal normal = normalize(vec3(nx, ny, nz)) # 3. Calculate Diffuse Factor diffusefactor = max(dot(lightdir, normal), 0.0) # 4. Modulate Sample Color illuminatedcolor = sampcolor diffusefactor diffcolor return illuminatedcolor def samplevolume(coord): # Standard volume texture lookup returning scalar value V at coord pass # Implementation depends on specific texture API Transparent Transfer Functions: The technique was tested only with opaque transfer functions. When used with transparent transfer functions, the rendering yields incoherent visual effects. Time Complexity: The method adds three additional texture lookups and basic vector operations per shaded voxel. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the volume texture and standard uniforms. Performance: Fetching data from neighbor voxels and performing extra calculations increases rendering cost, potentially impacting performance. Strengths: Simple to implement; works with any scalar field; provides immediate visual improvement in depth perception and shape definition. Limitations: Incoherent results with transparent transfer functions; sensitive to scalar field noise. This technique is described in the context of comparing GPU-based volume ray casting implementations across Fragment Shader, Compute Shader, OpenCL, and CUDA. It is presented as a standard method for adding illumination to volume rendering by leveraging the gradient of the scalar field as a proxy for surface normals. name: Phong Shading with Boundary Enhancement and Facing Subtraction
head: Boundary-enhanced volume shading, Gradient-based Phong shading
body: This method extends per-fragment Phong lighting by applying two alpha-modulation techniques to enhance the visual perception of volume boundaries: boundary enhancement via absorption approximation and facing subtraction for silhouette definition. It distinguishes itself from standard gradient-based Phong shading by explicitly modifying the fragment alpha based on the gradient magnitude and the view direction relative to the surface normal. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar field (stored as a 3D texture tex3D) containing precomputed gradient components (gx, gy, gz) and magnitude (||g||). A 1D transfer function texture (tex1D) maps scalar values to color and alpha. Output: A fragment color and alpha value. Data Structures: The source code references specific uniform structures for lighting and rendering parameters: lightt: Contains coefficients kd (diffuse), ks (specular), ka (ambient). renderingt (or myRender): Contains integer flags boundary and facing. If >0, the respective effect is enabled. Numbered Steps: 1. Gradient Extraction: Sample the 3D texture at the current fragment's position to retrieve the gradient vector components (gx, gy, gz) and the precomputed magnitude ||g||. 2. Normal Computation: Normalize the gradient vector to obtain the surface normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{n} = \frac{(gx, gy, gz)}{||(gx, gy, gz)||} 3. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the normal \mathbf{n} into view space using the model-view matrix. The vertex shader computes the eye vector \mathbf{E} and light vector \mathbf{L} in view space and passes them as varyings. 4. Lighting Calculation: Compute the diffuse term D using the dot product of the normal \mathbf{n} and the light direction \mathbf{L}: D = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{L}, 0) Compute the reflection vector \mathbf{r}: \mathbf{r} = \text{reflect}(-\mathbf{L}, \mathbf{n}) Compute the specular term S using a specular exponent of 512: S = \max(\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}, 0)^{512} Compute the ambient term A by sampling the 1D transfer function at the scalar value: A = \text{TF}(t) Combine terms to get the initial color contribution: C = ks S + kd D + ka A 5. Boundary Enhancement: If the boundary flag is enabled, modify the fragment alpha \alpha using an absorption approximation based on the gradient magnitude: \alpha' = \alpha (1 - e^{-||g||}) This step enhances the visibility of boundaries where the gradient magnitude is high. 6. Facing Subtraction: If the facing flag is enabled, further modify the alpha by subtracting the facing component relative to the view vector \mathbf{V} (or eye vector \mathbf{E}). The source code uses ndotv, defined as \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}: \alpha'' = \alpha' (1 - |\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}|) This reduces alpha for surfaces facing the viewer, enhancing silhouette definition. Note: The formula in the notes uses absolute value |\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}|, while the code snippet uses 1-ndotv. Given the context of "facing subtraction" for silhouettes, the absolute value ensures symmetry for both front and back faces, or it assumes a specific winding. The code snippet 1-ndotv implies a non-absolute dot product, which would only affect front-facing fragments if \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} > 0. However, the formula explicitly states |\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}|. We follow the formula's explicit definition for the general case, but note the code implementation may vary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(vertexpos, modelviewmatrix): # Compute eye vector in view space vertexviewpos = modelviewmatrix vertexpos eyevector = normalize(-vertexviewpos.xyz) # Light direction is fixed in this implementation (0,0,-1) lightvector = vec3(0, 0, -1) return eyevector, lightvector def fragmentshader(gradienttex, tftex, scalarvalue, normal, eyevector, lightvector, boundaryflag, facingflag): # 1. Lighting Terms # Diffuse diffuseterm = max(dot(normal, lightvector), 0.0) # Specular reflection = reflect(-lightvector, normal) specularterm = pow(max(dot(reflection, normal), 0.0), 512.0) # Ambient / Transfer Function tfsample = texture1D(tftex, scalarvalue) ambientterm = tfsample # Initial Color and Alpha # Assuming uniform coefficients kd, ks, ka are passed color = ks specularterm + kd diffuseterm + ka ambientterm alpha = tfsample.a # 2. Boundary Enhancement # Gradient magnitude is assumed to be passed or computed from gradient vector # In the source, magnitude is extracted from the 3D texture gradientmagnitude =... # Extracted from tex3D if boundaryflag > 0: alpha = alpha (1.0 - exp(-gradientmagnitude)) # 3. Facing Subtraction # ndotv is n. v ndotv = dot(normal, eyevector) if facingflag > 0: # Formula specifies absolute value, code snippet does not. # Using absolute value as per formula description for silhouette enhancement. alpha = alpha (1.0 - abs(ndotv)) return color, alpha Parameters: kd, ks, ka: Diffuse, specular, and ambient lighting coefficients. boundary: Integer flag. If >0, boundary enhancement is enabled. facing: Integer flag. If >0, facing subtraction is enabled. Specular exponent: Fixed at 512.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Gradient: If the gradient magnitude is zero, the normal is undefined. The source does not specify a fallback, but numerically, normalization of a zero vector results in NaN/Inf. A guard against zero-length gradients is required. Facing Subtraction Sign: The discrepancy between the formula (|\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v}|) and the code snippet (1-ndotv) must be resolved. The formula suggests handling both front and back faces, while the code only affects front-facing fragments (where \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{v} > 0). Implementers should choose based on whether back-face silhouettes are desired. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment, assuming constant-time texture lookups and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per fragment, plus the storage for the 3D gradient texture and 1D transfer function texture. Strengths: Enhances the perception of internal structures and boundaries in volume data without requiring explicit surface extraction. The high specular exponent (512) creates sharp highlights, emphasizing surface-like qualities. Limitations: Relies on precomputed gradients, increasing memory bandwidth and storage requirements. The facing subtraction can make volumes appear hollow or less dense if over-applied. The fixed specular exponent may not be suitable for all material appearances. When to use: When visualizing complex internal structures where boundary definition is critical, and explicit surface extraction is too expensive or unnecessary. When not to use: When real-time performance is constrained by memory bandwidth, or when a more physically accurate lighting model is required. This method originates from a GitHub repository for scientific visualization, specifically focusing on slicing and volume rendering techniques. It is an implementation detail found in educational or prototype code rather than a peer-reviewed algorithm. The technique combines standard Phong shading with specific alpha modulation strategies to improve the visual clarity of volume data. extrovert7986/Scientific-visualization-Slicing-volume-rendering, https://github.com/extrovert7986/Scientific-visualization-Slicing-volume-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)
