name: Flipped Reflection Ray Masking
head: Flipped Reflection Rays
body: Flipped Reflection Ray Masking is a regularization method for few-shot novel view synthesis that generates additional training rays from input viewing directions and estimated surface normals, casting them toward the identical target pixels as the original rays. It filters out ineffective rays based on the angle between the viewing direction and the normal to stabilize training and reduce floating artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Original input ray directions (\mathbf{d}{in}), estimated surface normal vectors (\mathbf{n}), and a threshold angle parameter (\tau). Outputs: A filtered set of flipped reflection rays (\mathbf{d}{flip}) used for training supervision. Data Structures: The method operates on standard 3D vector arrays for ray directions and surface normals. Steps: 1. Derive the flipped reflection rays from the original input ray directions and the estimated surface normals. 2. Cast the derived rays toward the identical target pixels as the original input rays. 3. Compute \theta, the angle between the input viewing direction \mathbf{d}{in} and the surface normal vector \mathbf{n} at each pixel. 4. If \theta > \tau, discard the corresponding flipped reflection ray; otherwise, retain it for training supervision. Formulas: The flipped reflection direction is computed as: \mathbf{d}{flip} = 2(\mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n})\mathbf{n} - \mathbf{d}{in} where \mathbf{d}{in} is the original viewing direction and \mathbf{n} is the surface normal. The angle \theta is calculated as: \theta = \arccos\left( \frac{\mathbf{d}{in} \cdot \mathbf{n}}{\|\mathbf{d}{in}\| \|\mathbf{n}\|} \right) The term "flipped" refers to the reflected ray having an opposite direction relative to the camera, effectively pointing from the object surface back toward the camera's general hemisphere. Parameters: \tau (tau): Threshold angle in degrees for ray masking. The optimal value is 90^\circ. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def computeflippedreflectionmasking(inputraydirs, surfacenormals, thresholddegrees=90.0): """ Computes flipped reflection rays and masks ineffective ones based on the angle between the input viewing direction and the surface normal. Args: inputraydirs (np.ndarray): Array of shape (N, 3) representing input ray directions. surfacenormals (np.ndarray): Array of shape (N, 3) representing estimated surface normals. thresholddegrees (float): The threshold angle tau in degrees. Default 90.0. Returns: np.ndarray: Array of shape (N, 3) containing the flipped reflection rays. Pixels where the ray was masked are set to zero vectors. """ # Normalize input vectors for accurate angle calculation din = inputraydirs / np.linalg.norm(inputraydirs, axis=1, keepdims=True) n = surfacenormals / np.linalg.norm(surfacenormals, axis=1, keepdims=True) # Step 1: Compute the flipped reflection direction dotproduct = np.sum(din n, axis=1) dflip = 2.0 dotproduct[:, np.newaxis] n - din # Step 2: Compute the angle theta between input direction and normal costheta = np.clip(dotproduct, -1.0, 1.0) thetadegrees = np.degrees(np.arccos(costheta)) # Step 3: Apply masking # If theta > tau, discard the ray; otherwise, retain it mask = thetadegrees <= thresholddegrees dflipmasked = np.where(mask[:, np.newaxis], dflip, 0.0) return dflipmasked Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Normals: If surface normals are zero vectors or poorly estimated (common in early training phases), the angle calculation becomes unstable. The masking strategy effectively filters these invalid additional rays at the initial training phase, leading to high-quality supervision and stabilizing training. Precision: Ensure dot products are clipped to [-1, 1] before arccos to avoid numerical domain errors. A complementary loss function used with flipped rays to reduce floating artifacts based on uncertainty. Ensures consistency between bottleneck features of original and flipped rays. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method adds a parallel branch of ray supervision without increasing the number of ray march steps. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Requires storing additional ray directions and normals for the flipped rays during training. Performance: On the Realistic Synthetic 360° dataset, the 90^\circ masking strategy yields the highest PSNR (19.55), SSIM (0.767), and lowest LPIPS (0.180) and Average Error (0.101) among masking variants. Strengths: Stabilizes training in few-shot scenarios by filtering invalid rays at the initial phase and reducing floating artifacts. Limitations: Using too strict a threshold (e.g., \tau = 30^\circ or 60^\circ) degrades quality by filtering too many rays, reducing supervision. Using no masking yields inferior results due to noise from ineffective rays. When to use: Few-shot novel view synthesis where surface normal estimation is available or learnable. When not to use: Dense-view scenarios where standard supervision is sufficient, or when normal estimation is unreliable. Flipped Reflection Ray Masking was introduced in the FlipNeRF paper in 2023. It is built upon MixNeRF, leveraging a mixture model framework. The method addresses the limited input views in novel view synthesis by using flipped reflection rays as effective additional training resources. It is particularly relevant for few-shot learning where accurate depth and normal estimation are critical. FlipNeRF: Flipped Reflection Rays for Few-shot Novel View Synthesis, https://doi.org/10.1109/iccv51070.2023.02092, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Iridescent Material with Perturbation
head: Iridescent Material (Cosine Palette), Iridescent Material with Specular and Shadow
body: This method generates an iridescent appearance on ray-marched surfaces by mapping a perturbed surface normal to a color via a cosine palette function, simulating thin-film interference colors. It combines this base iridescent layer with a multi-component specular highlight and a directional shadow term. It differs from Ray Marching with Reflections by using a procedural color palette driven by normal perturbation rather than recursive ray tracing for color, and from Spherical Gaussian Shading by using a fixed cosine palette rather than analytically approximated lobes for the base color. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin (rayOrigin), ray direction (rayDirection), surface position (pos), surface normal (nor), light position (lightPos), and a gamma exponent (GAMMA, typically 2.2). Outputs: A linear RGB color vector (color) before gamma correction, or a screen-space RGB vector after correction. Data Structures: vec3: 3-component floating-point vector (x, y, z). float: 32-bit floating-point scalar. pal parameters: Vectors a, b, c, d of type vec3. Formulas: 1. Cosine Palette: pal(t, a, b, c, d) = a + b \cdot \cos(2\pi (c \cdot t + d)) Where t is a scalar input, and a, b, c, d are vec3 parameters. The code approximates 2\pi as 6.28318. 2. Spectrum Function: spectrum(n) = pal(n, \mathbf{0.5}, \mathbf{0.5}, \mathbf{1.0}, \mathbf{d}) Where \mathbf{0.5} and \mathbf{1.0} are vec3 vectors with all components equal to the scalar value, and \mathbf{d} = (0.0, 0.33, 0.67). 3. Gamma Correction: \text{linearToScreen}(C) = C^{1/\text{GAMMA}} Where C is a vec3 and the power operation is component-wise. Parameters: GAMMA: Gamma correction exponent. Typical value: 2.2. Perturbation scale: 0.05 (multiplier for perturb). Perturbation frequency: 10.0 (multiplier for pos in sin). Base layer intensity multiplier: 2.0 (multiplier for the dot product input to spectrum). Specular modulation frequency: 20.0. Specular modulation phase offset: -3.0. Specular power: 32.0. Specular base weight: 0.1. Secondary specular additive constant: 0.3. Secondary specular power: 8.0. Secondary specular weight: 0.1. Shadow dome direction: (0, 1, 0). Shadow slope: 0.5. Shadow bias: 1.2. Shadow power: 3.0. Steps: 1. Calculate Reflection Vector: Compute the reflection vector of the ray direction against the surface normal: \text{reflection} = \text{reflect}(\text{rayDirection}, \text{nor}). 2. Calculate Perturbation: Compute a perturbation vector based on the surface position: \text{perturb} = \sin(\text{pos} \times 10.0). 3. Calculate Base Iridescent Color: a. Compute the dot product between the perturbed normal and the eye direction (normalized vector from surface to ray origin): \text{dotVal} = \text{dot}(\text{nor} + \text{perturb} \times 0.05, \text{eyeDirection}) \times 2.0 b. Map this value to color using the spectrum function: \text{color} = \text{spectrum}(\text{dotVal}). 4. Calculate Specular Highlights: a. Compute the primary specular term: i. Clamp the dot product of the reflection vector and light direction to [0, 1]: s = \text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\text{reflection}, \text{lightDirection}), 0.0, 1.0) ii. Modulate with a sine wave and raise to a power: \text{specular} = \text{pow}((\sin(s \times 20.0 - 3.0) \times 0.5 + 0.5) + 0.1, 32.0) \times s iii. Scale by 0.1: \text{specular} = \text{specular} \times 0.1 b. Add a secondary specular component: i. Compute a new clamped dot product (same as step 4.a.i): s2 = \text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\text{reflection}, \text{lightDirection}), 0.0, 1.0) ii. Add offset, raise to power, and scale: \text{secondary} = \text{pow}(s2 + 0.3, 8.0) \times 0.1 iii. Add to specular: \text{specular} = \text{specular} + \text{secondary}. 5. Calculate Shadow: a. Define dome direction as \text{dome} = (0, 1, 0). b. Compute shadow factor: \text{shadow} = \text{pow}(\text{clamp}(\text{dot}(\text{nor}, \text{dome}) \times 0.5 + 1.2, 0.0, 1.0), 3.0). 6. Combine Colors: \text{color} = \text{color} \times \text{shadow} + \text{specular}. 7. Gamma Correction: Convert linear RGB to screen space: \text{color} = \text{linearToScreen}(\text{color}). The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import Tuple def vec3add(a: Tuple[float, float, float], b: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1], a[2] + b[2]) def vec3sub(a: Tuple[float, float, float], b: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (a[0] - b[0], a[1] - b[1], a[2] - b[2]) def vec3mulscalar(v: Tuple[float, float, float], s: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (v[0] s, v[1] s, v[2] s) def vec3dot(a: Tuple[float, float, float], b: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> float: return a[0] b[0] + a[1] b[1] + a[2] b[2] def vec3normalize(v: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: s = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0] / s, v[1] / s, v[2] / s) def vec3sin(v: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (math.sin(v[0]), math.sin(v[1]), math.sin(v[2])) def vec3clamp(v: Tuple[float, float, float], lo: float, hi: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: return (max(lo, min(hi, v[0])), max(lo, min(hi, v[1])), max(lo, min(hi, v[2]))) def vec3reflect(I: Tuple[float, float, float], N: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: dotval = vec3dot(I, N) return (I[0] - 2 dotval N[0], I[1] - 2 dotval N[1], I[2] - 2 dotval N[2]) def pal(t: float, a: Tuple[float, float, float], b: Tuple[float, float, float], c: Tuple[float, float, float], d: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """Cosine palette function.""" arg = (c[0]t + d[0], c[1]t + d[1], c[2]t + d[2]) cosarg = (math.cos(6.28318 arg[0]), math.cos(6.28318 arg[1]), math.cos(6.28318 arg[2])) return (a[0] + b[0]cosarg[0], a[1] + b[1]cosarg[1], a[2] + b[2]cosarg[2]) def spectrum(n: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """Spectrum function using specific palette parameters.""" a = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) b = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) c = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) d = (0.0, 0.33, 0.67) return pal(n, a, b, c, d) def gamma(color: Tuple[float, float, float], g: float) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """Apply gamma correction component-wise.""" return (color[0]g, color[1]g, color[2]g) def lineartoscreen(linearrgb: Tuple[float, float, float], gammaval: float = 2.2) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """Convert linear RGB to screen space.""" return gamma(linearrgb, 1.0 / gammaval) def iridescentmaterial(rayorigin: Tuple[float, float, float], raydirection: Tuple[float, float, float], pos: Tuple[float, float, float], nor: Tuple[float, float, float], lightpos: Tuple[float, float, float], gammaval: float = 2.2) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: """ Calculate iridescent shading with perturbation, specular, and shadow. """ eyedirection = vec3normalize(vec3sub(rayorigin, pos)) lightdirection = vec3normalize(vec3sub(lightpos, pos)) reflection = vec3reflect(raydirection, nor) perturb = vec3sin(vec3mulscalar(pos, 10.0)) perturbednor = vec3add(nor, vec3mulscalar(perturb, 0.05)) dotval = vec3dot(perturbednor, eyedirection) 2.0 color = spectrum(dotval) dotreflight = vec3dot(reflection, lightdirection) s = vec3clamp(dotreflight, 0.0, 1.0) sinterm = math.sin(s 20.0 - 3.0) modulated = sinterm 0.5 + 0.5 modulated += 0.1 specular = (modulated 32.0) s specular = 0.1 s2 = vec3clamp(dotreflight, 0.0, 1.0) secondary = ((s2 + 0.3) 8.0) 0.1 specular += secondary dome = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) dotnordome = vec3dot(nor, dome) shadowarg = dotnordome 0.5 + 1.2 shadowclamped = vec3clamp(shadowarg, 0.0, 1.0) shadow = shadowclamped 3.0 color = (color[0] shadow + specular, color[1] shadow + specular, color[2] shadow + specular) color = lineartoscreen(color, gammaval) return color A technique for rendering iridescence in thin films (soap bubbles, oil films) using Airy summation for s/p polarization over multiple wavelengths. It samples 9 wavelengths to compute the interference pattern and applies the model over a dielectric or metal base. For metal bases, it derives the complex Index of Refraction (IOR) from F0 and edge tint using Gulbrandsen's inversion. A key pitfall is handling thin films at zero thickness as a special case to avoid numerical instability or incorrect reflection. A technique to blend Blinn-Phong lighting with iridescent lighting to create tinted iridescent objects. It calculates a Blinn-Phong specular term (power) multiplied by a tint color to get baseColor. It calculates the standard iridescent color (color shadow + specular). It then blends the two using mix(baseColor, color, mixBaseAndIridescent). The parameter mixBaseAndIridescent controls the blend factor, typically in range [0,1]. Time Complexity: Constant number of trigonometric, power, and vector operations per surface hit. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Very fast, suitable for real-time ray marching. Strengths: Produces vibrant, procedural iridescent colors without complex physics simulation; easy to tune via palette parameters. Limitations: Physically approximate; the "cosine palette" is an artistic approximation of thin-film interference, not a rigorous physical model. When to use: When a stylized, colorful iridescent effect is desired for ray-marched objects (e.g., crystals, soap bubbles) and physical accuracy is not required. When not to use: When physically accurate thin-film interference is required (use Thin-Film Interference via Airy Summation instead). The method originates from community-driven shader art, specifically popularized by Thomas Hooper's "Crystals" shader and discussed in tutorials on ray marching with Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). It leverages the "cosine palette" technique, a common tool in Shadertoy programming for generating smooth, periodic color gradients. The specific combination of perturbation, specular, and shadow terms was detailed in a tutorial by Varun (Show HN: Iridescent crystal with raymarching and signed distance fields). Show HN: Iridescent crystal with raymarching and signed distance fields, https://varun.ca/ray-march-sdf/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Add volumetric rendering, advanced materials, and imager effects, https://github.com/MihrimatriX/photon-engine/pull/3, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Gaussian Shading
head: SG Shading, SG-Based Rendering, Shading Rendering of Spherical Gaussians, Specular BRDF Approximation
body: Spherical Gaussian (SG) Shading is a technique that approximates direct illumination and specular BRDFs using a mixture of Spherical Gaussian basis functions to enable fast, analytic integration and automatic differentiation. It distinguishes itself from Monte Carlo (MC) integration by being less expensive and more robust to roughness variations, though it sacrifices high-frequency detail accuracy. It is primarily used in differentiable rendering and inverse rendering pipelines where lighting and material parameters must be optimized jointly. The method operates on a surface point \mathbf{p} with normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{v}, and incident light direction \mathbf{l}. It approximates the rendering equation by representing both the incident radiance and the BRDF lobes as sums of Spherical Gaussians. 1. Spherical Gaussian (SG) Kernel: Defined by four parameters: \omega \in S^2 (input direction), \xi \in S^2 (axis/center), \lambda \in \mathbb{R}^+ (sharpness), and \mu \in \mathbb{R}^{3+} (amplitude/HDR RGB color). 2. Lighting Representation: A mixture of K SGs representing the environment map or spatially variant lights, with parameters \gamma = \{ \xi{lk}, \lambda{lk}, \mu{lk} \}{k=1}^K. Typical K is 128 for fitting HDR environment maps. 3. Volumetric SG (VSG) Layout: Stored as an 8-channel tensor \mathcal{L} \in \mathbb{R}^{8 \times X \times Y \times Z}. Each voxel contains opacity \alpha \in [0, 1], HDR RGB intensity c \in \mathbb{R}^3, lobe axis \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3, and sharpness \sigma \in \mathbb{R}^+. The Spherical Gaussian function is defined as: G(\omega; \xi, \lambda, \mu) = \mu e^{\lambda(\xi \cdot \omega - 1)} Cosine foreshortening is approximated by a single SG: |\mathbf{n} \cdot \omegai| \approx Gc(\omegai; \mathbf{n}, 2.133, 1.17) The specular lobe of the BRDF is fitted to a single monochromatic SG, denoted fr^{(SG)}, forming a sum of diffuse and specular lobes. The final pixel color S^{(SG)} is computed by integrating the product of the BRDF, incident radiance, and cosine term: S^{(SG)}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{n}, \omegao; \theta, \gamma) = \int{S^2} fr^{(SG)}(\mathbf{x}, \omegai, \omegao; \theta) Li^{(SG)}(\omegai; \gamma) Gc(\omegai) d\omegai where Li^{(SG)} is the incident radiance represented by K SGs. Alternatively, each SG can be rendered as 5 point lights (1 center + 4 sampled around). For k point lights with intensity \mathbf{I}i, the shading is: \mathbf{S}{SG}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=1}^k \frac{\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r}) \cdot \mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r})}{|\mathbf{N}(\mathbf{r})| |\mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r})|} \cdot \frac{\mathbf{I}i}{\gamma \cdot \mathbf{Dis}i(\mathbf{r})^2} where \mathbf{L}i(\mathbf{r}) is the direction from light to point, \mathbf{Dis}i(\mathbf{r}) is the distance, and \gamma is a hyperparameter controlling luminance. For VSG, incident radiance R(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{l}, \mathcal{L}) at point \mathbf{p} in direction \mathbf{l} is calculated via alpha compositing along N equi-spaced points: R(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{l}, \mathcal{L}) = \left( \prod{i=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphai) \right) \sum{k=1}^{N} \alphak G(-\mathbf{l}; ck, \muk, \sigmak) The total image for ray \mathbf{r} combines diffuse, specular, and SG shading: I(\mathbf{r}) = Id(\mathbf{r}) + Is(\mathbf{r}) + V(\mathbf{r})\mathcal{R}(\mathbf{r})S{SG}(\mathbf{r}) where V is shadow visibility and \mathcal{R} is reflectance. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalgaussianshading(surfacepoint, normal, viewdir, lightingparams, method="pointlight"): """ Compute shading using Spherical Gaussians. Args: surfacepoint: 3D position p. normal: Surface normal n. viewdir: View direction v. lightingparams: Dictionary containing 'K', 'SGs' (list of dicts with 'xi', 'lambda', 'mu'), or 'VSGvolume' for volumetric method. method: 'analytic' for direct integration, 'pointlight' for 5-light approximation. Returns: Color C. """ if method == "pointlight": totalshading = np.zeros(3) gamma = lightingparams.get('gamma', 1.0) for sg in lightingparams['SGs']: lights = generatepointlightsfromsg(sg['xi']) for lightdir, lightintensity in lights: ldir = normalize(lightdir) dist = 1.0 cosine = max(dot(normal, ldir), 0.0) attenuation = lightintensity / (gamma dist2) totalshading += cosine attenuation return totalshading elif method == "analytic": cosinesg = {'xi': normal, 'lambda': 2.133, 'mu': 1.17} specularsg = fitspecularsg(normal, viewdir, roughness=0.1, metalness=0.5) color = np.zeros(3) for sg in lightingparams['SGs']: # The analytic integral of the product of SGs on a sphere is not provided in the sources. # Standard closed-form integration applies. color += integratesgproduct(cosinesg, specularsg, sg) return color def sphericalgaussian(direction, axis, sharpness, amplitude): """Evaluate a single Spherical Gaussian: G(w; xi, lambda, mu) = mu exp(lambda (xi. w - 1)).""" return amplitude exp(sharpness (dot(axis, direction) - 1.0)) def generatepointlightsfromsg(centeraxis): """Generate 5 light directions around the SG center axis.""" lights = [(centeraxis, 1.0)] for i in range(4): offset = orthogonalvector(centeraxis) lights.append((normalize(centeraxis + 0.5 offset), 0.5)) return lights def fitspecularsg(normal, viewdir, roughness, metalness): """Fit a single monochromatic SG to the specular lobe of the BRDF.""" halfvec = normalize(normal + viewdir) sharpness = 2.0 / (roughness2 + 1e-6) return {'xi': halfvec, 'lambda': sharpness, 'mu': 1.0} def integratesgproduct(sg1, sg2, sg3): # The analytic integral of the product of SGs on a sphere is not provided in the sources. # Standard closed-form integration applies. return np.zeros(3) K: Number of SGs. Typical value is 128 for fitting HDR environment maps. \gamma: Hyperparameter for luminance control in point-light approximation. \beta: Surface roughness. SG shading is robust to variations in \beta. \sigma: VSG sharpness. If \sigma \gg 1, VSG reduces to RGB\alpha. High Frequency Loss: SGs smooth out high-frequency details and sharp corners. They are not precise enough for real-time scenarios requiring high fidelity without a very large number of coefficients. HDR Lighting: If the environment is HDR, SGs should be placed far from the scene to assume distant lighting. VSG Degeneracy: If \sigma \gg 1 in VSG, the representation loses directional lighting capability and becomes a standard RGB\alpha volume. Coefficient Count: Accurate reconstruction may require significantly more coefficients than dense pixel maps (e.g., 896 SGs vs 98,304 pixels for an HDR map). A specific application of SG shading within Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) for relighting. It combines diffuse (Id), specular (Is), and SG shading (S{SG}) modulated by shadow visibility (V) and reflectance (\mathcal{R}). It allows for material editing and scene relighting by optimizing SG parameters. A voxel-based representation for 3D spatially-varying lighting where each voxel acts as a light source parameterized by SG lobes. It captures view-dependent effects and directional lighting in 3D space, unlike standard RGB\alpha volumes. It is calculated via alpha compositing along rays. Assumes full light source visibility, ignoring self-occlusions and assuming all light sources in the upper hemisphere above any surface are fully visible. It accelerates rendering by representing environment lighting and scene BRDFs as mixtures of spherical Gaussians, enabling the hemispherical integral of incoming light multiplied by the BRDF to be computed in closed form. Assuming full light source visibility is unable to simulate effects such as cast shadows due to occlusion of light sources by scene geometry, though it works well for mostly convex objects. Time Complexity: Faster than Monte Carlo (MC) integration because it uses analytic integration of SG products. The cost scales linearly with the number of SGs K. Memory Complexity: Compact. Requires significantly fewer parameters than dense environment maps (e.g., 896 parameters for K=128 SGs vs 98,304 for a dense HDR map). VSG adds spatial storage overhead (8 \times X \times Y \times Z). Performance: Robust to roughness variations. MC is better for mirror-like objects (low roughness) where high frequencies are preserved, but SG is more efficient for moderate-to-high roughness. Limitations: Loses high-frequency details. Not suitable for real-time rendering if high precision is required without large K. When to Use: Differentiable rendering, inverse rendering, optimization of lighting/materials, and scenes with moderate roughness. When Not to Use: Real-time rendering requiring high-fidelity specular highlights with sharp features, or scenes with very low roughness (mirrors) where MC is superior. Spherical Gaussian shading was introduced as a compact approximation for direct illumination in differentiable rendering frameworks, specifically within the DIB-R++ pipeline. It builds on the mathematical properties of Spherical Gaussians to allow analytic integration of the rendering equation, facilitating gradient-based optimization of lighting and materials. It has been applied in various contexts including intrinsic decomposition, relighting in NeRFs, and 3D inverse rendering with spatially varying lighting. name: Neon Raymarcher Shading Model
head: Milestone 2 shading, Procedural Neon Shading
body: The Neon Raymarcher Shading Model is a real-time shading technique for procedural neon city scenes that computes diffuse, specular, ambient occlusion, metallic reflection, and emissive contributions per pixel. It uses a fixed-step shadow ray and a metallic Fresnel weighting scheme tailored to the compressed distance field geometry of the scene. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Surface point \mathbf{p}, surface normal \mathbf{n}, view direction \mathbf{rd} (from \mathbf{p} to camera), light direction \mathbf{lightDir} (from \mathbf{p} to light), material properties: albedo \mathbf{c}{albedo}, metalness m \in [0,1], emissive color \mathbf{c}{emissive}, and light color \mathbf{c}{light}. Outputs: Final pixel color \mathbf{c}{final}. Data Structures: The material state sf contains: albedo: vec3 metal: float (0.0 to 1.0) emissive: vec3. Steps: 1. Geometric Setup: Calculate the half-vector \mathbf{h} between the view direction \mathbf{rd} and light direction \mathbf{lightDir}: \mathbf{h} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{lightDir} - \mathbf{rd}) Calculate the dot products for diffuse, specular, and Fresnel terms: d{diff} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{lightDir}, 0.0) d{spec} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{h}, 0.0) d{fresnel\dot} = \max(\mathbf{n} \cdot (-\mathbf{rd}), 0.0). 2. Shadow Calculation: Compute the shadow factor S by casting a shadow ray from an origin offset along the normal to prevent self-shadowing artifacts: \mathbf{p}{shadow} = \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{n} \times 0.03 The shadow function returns a value in [0, 1] indicating occlusion, using a fixed maximum distance of 12.0 units: S = \text{Shadow}(\mathbf{p}{shadow}, \mathbf{lightDir}, 12.0) The effective diffuse lighting is modulated by this shadow: L{diff} = d{diff} \times S. 3. Ambient Occlusion Calculation: Compute the ambient occlusion factor A using the function calcAO(p, n). 4. Specular Reflection: Calculate the specular contribution using a power exponent mixed based on metalness: C{spec} = \text{pow}(d{spec}, \text{mix}(32.0, 140.0, m)) \times S. 5. Metallic Reflection: Calculate the Fresnel factor F using a power of 5.0: F = \text{pow}(1.0 - d{fresnel\dot}, 5.0) Get the sky color \mathbf{c}{sky} by reflecting the view direction \mathbf{rd} about the normal \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{r} = \text{reflect}(\mathbf{rd}, \mathbf{n}) \mathbf{c}{sky} = \text{skyColor}(\mathbf{r}) Calculate the metallic reflection intensity I{metal}: I{metal} = \text{mix}(0.03, 0.6, m) \times (0.25 + 0.75 \times F) The metallic reflection contribution is: C{metal} = \mathbf{c}{sky} \times I{metal} \times A. 6. Color Accumulation: Combine the components. The base color is the albedo modulated by ambient light and AO, plus the diffuse light contribution. The specular and metallic reflections are added. Finally, the emissive color is added: \mathbf{c}{final} = \mathbf{c}{albedo} \times (\text{ambient} \times A) + \mathbf{c}{albedo} \times \mathbf{c}{light} \times L{diff} + \mathbf{c}{light} \times C{spec} \times \text{mix}(0.4, 2.0, m) + C{metal} + \mathbf{c}{emissive}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def neonraymarchershading(p, n, rd, lightDir, lightCol, sf, ambient): # 1. Geometric Setup halfVec = normalize(lightDir - rd) diffdot = max(dot(n, lightDir), 0.0) specdot = max(dot(n, halfVec), 0.0) fresneldot = max(dot(n, -rd), 0.0) # 2. Shadow Calculation # Offset normal to prevent self-shadowing pshadow = p + n 0.03 # Source does not provide implementation for shadowray def shadowray(origin, dir, maxdist): # Standard distance-field shadow raymarcher omitted by source return 1.0 shadow = shadowray(pshadow, lightDir, 12.0) diffterm = diffdot shadow # 3. Ambient Occlusion # Source does not provide implementation for calcao def calcao(point, normal): # Standard hemisphere visibility estimation omitted by source return 1.0 ao = calcao(p, n) # 4. Specular Reflection speccontrib = pow(specdot, mix(32.0, 140.0, sf.metal)) shadow # 5. Metallic Reflection fresnel = pow(1.0 - fresneldot, 5.0) r = reflect(rd, n) # Source does not provide implementation for skycolorfunction def skycolorfunction(reflecteddir): # Environment map lookup omitted by source return vec3(0.0) skycolor = skycolorfunction(r) metalbase = mix(0.03, 0.6, sf.metal) metalgrazingboost = 0.25 + 0.75 fresnel metalcontrib = skycolor metalbase metalgrazingboost ao # 6. Color Accumulation basecolor = sf.albedo (ambient ao) + sf.albedo lightCol diffterm color = basecolor + lightCol speccontrib mix(0.4, 2.0, sf.metal) + metalcontrib color += sf.emissive return color Parameters: Shadow ray origin offset: 0.03 units along \mathbf{n}. Shadow ray max distance: 12.0 units. Specular exponent range: 32.0 (non-metal) to 140.0 (metal). Specular intensity range: 0.4 (non-metal) to 2.0 (metal). Fresnel power: 5.0. Metallic reflection base intensity: 0.03 (non-metal) to 0.6 (metal). Metallic reflection grazing boost: 0.25 (normal) to 0.75 (grazing). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-Shadowing: The normal offset of 0.03 is critical to prevent the shadow ray from intersecting the surface itself, which causes dark artifacts. Sky Color: The skyColor function is an external dependency not defined in the shading model; it must be implemented to return appropriate environment colors for the reflection. Time Complexity: The shading cost is dominated by the shadowray and calcao functions, which involve additional distance field evaluations. The core shading formula is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, storing only intermediate vectors and scalars. Strengths: Real-time performance on modern hardware due to a simplified shading model tailored for the neon city aesthetic. Limitations: The shadow ray is cast in a fixed direction with a fixed max distance, which may not accurately represent complex lighting scenarios. The ambient occlusion approximation may lack detail compared to screen-space or baked solutions. When to use: Ideal for real-time rendering of stylized, neon-lit urban environments where performance is critical. When not to use: Not suitable for physically accurate rendering or scenes requiring complex dynamic lighting. The Neon Raymarcher Shading Model is implemented in the "neon-raymarcher" project by PIGJET, a real-time raymarched demo of a procedural neon city. It is designed to complement the specific distance field geometry of the scene, which includes compressed building distances and a ground plane. PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, https://github.com/PIGJET/neon-raymarcher, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Surface Point Sampling for SDFs
head: Forplane Rendering Procedure, Sphere Tracing Surface Sampling
body: Surface Point Sampling for SDFs generates training data or rendering samples by querying a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to locate points near the implicit surface, rather than sampling uniformly throughout the volume. It solves the problem of inefficient volumetric coverage, where most uniform samples fall in empty space or deep inside geometry, providing critical gradient information for the signed distance field values off the zero-level set. It differs from uniform volume sampling by focusing density on the surface transition region, and from pure surface sampling by providing gradient information for the signed distance field (SDF) values off the zero-level set. The method encompasses several strategies for generating points near the SDF surface, primarily categorized by their application in training (Neural Geometric Level of Detail) or rendering (Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction). Inputs: Bounding volume B (typically [-1, 1]^3). SDF function f(\mathbf{p}). Ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Indicator grid Go (in deformable tissue context). Static and dynamic fields \{V^s{3d}, V^d{3d}\}4. Tiny MLP \theta. Outputs: Point set P distributed around the surface. Expected color \hat{C} and depth \hat{D}. Point: Coordinates (x, y, z) and optionally time \tau. Feature Vector: v(x, y, z, \tau) initialized to 1, updated via interpolation. Encoded Features: Concatenation of coordinate-time encoding b(x, y, z, \tau) and interpolated features v(x, y, z, \tau). This variant, used in Neural Geometric Level of Detail (NGLOD), generates surface points for training implicit shapes. 1. Uniform Initialization: Sample points uniformly distributed in the bounding volume B = [-1, 1]^3. 2. Ray Casting: Choose random points on a sphere to form a ray direction \mathbf{d}. Define ray r(t). 3. Sphere Tracing: Test if the ray hits the surface using sphere tracing (as defined in Distance-field ray marching). Evaluate d = f(\mathbf{p}) at current position. Advance t \leftarrow t + d. Terminate if d < \epsilon (hit) or t > t{max} (miss). 4. Collection: Continue sampling rays until enough rays hit the surface. The hit points constitute the surface samples. 5. Near-Surface Perturbation (Optional): To improve training convergence, perturb surface samples with Gaussian noise \sigma = 0.01 to generate near-surface points. This variant, used in Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction, samples points along a ray filtered by an indicator grid to focus on the surface region. 1. Uniform Ray Sampling: Uniformly sample points Pu along the ray r(t). 2. Indicator Filtering: Pass Pu through the indicator grid Go to obtain sample points P distributed around the surface. 3. Feature Interpolation: For each point P(x, y, z, \tau) in P: Initialize feature vector v(x, y, z, \tau) = 1. Iterate over 4 levels of static and dynamic fields \{V^s{3d}, V^d{3d}\}4 and dimension pairs (xy, xz, x\tau, yz, y\tau, z\tau). For each grid G and dimension pair ij, perform bi-linear interpolation B(G, i, j). Update v via element-wise multiplication: v \leftarrow v \odot B(G, i, j). 4. Encoding and Prediction: Concatenate coordinate-time encoding b(x, y, z, \tau) with features v(x, y, z, \tau). Pass through tiny MLP \theta to predict color ci and density \sigmai. 5. Volume Rendering: Render expected color \hat{C} and depth \hat{D} by integrating radiance and density along the ray: \hat{C} = \int{tn}^{tf} w(t) \cdot c(r(t), d) \, dt \hat{D} = \int{tn}^{tf} w(t) \cdot t \, dt w(t) = \exp\left(-\int{tn}^{t} \sigma(r(s)) \, ds\right) \sigma(r(t)) Return \hat{C}, \hat{D}. This variant extracts a point cloud from a Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) by projecting random points onto the shape surface S. It does not guarantee uniform sampling over S. 1. Uniform Sampling: Sample a point p uniformly from the bounding box B: p \sim U[B]. 2. Direction Sampling: For each p, sample nv directions vi uniformly from the unit sphere S^2: V(p) = \{vi(p) \sim U[S^2]\}{i=1}^{nv}. 3. Visibility Avoidance: Compose these directions to estimate the best direction vb^(p) to avoid visibility \xi(p, v) = 0. 4. Projection: Compute the surface point q(p, vb^(p)) using the PDDF depth and direction. The condition for q being on S is \xi(p, v) = 1 and q(p, v) = p + d(p, v)v. 5. Iterative Refinement: Repeat the process NH times, starting from the newly found point q (i.e., p \leftarrow q), to improve accuracy for depths far from S. Precision Thresholds: Sphere tracing requires a small convergence threshold \epsilon (e.g., 0.001) to terminate without infinite loops. Lipschitz Guarantee: The step size t \leftarrow t + d is guaranteed not to penetrate the surface because the SDF satisfies the Lipschitz condition with constant 1. Depth Accuracy: PDDF sampling accuracy degrades far from the surface, necessitating iterative refinement to converge to the true boundary. Visibility Checks: Directions yielding \xi(p, v) = 0 (occluded or invalid) must be filtered to avoid sampling inside geometry or invalid regions. Unverified code. Returns a list of 3D points on the surface. """ surfacepoints = [] halfbox = boundingboxsize / 2.0 for in range(numrays): # 1. Choose random point on sphere for ray direction theta = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) phi = math.acos(random.uniform(-1, 1)) # Ray direction d = [ math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta), math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta), math.cos(phi) ] # 2. Ray origin: random point in bounding box o = [ random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox), random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox), random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox) ] # 3. Sphere Tracing t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): p = [o[i] + t d[i] for i in range(3)] dist = sdffunction(p) if dist < epsilon: surfacepoints.append(p) break if t > boundingboxsize 2: break t += dist return surfacepoints Unverified code. """ points = [] halfbox = boundingboxsize / 2.0 for in range(10000): # 1. Uniform sample in bounding box p = [ random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox), random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox), random.uniform(-halfbox, halfbox) ] currentp = p for in range(nh): # 2. Sample nv directions bestv = None bestdist = float('inf') for in range(nv): # Uniform direction on sphere theta = random.uniform(0, 2 math.pi) phi = math.acos(random.uniform(-1, 1)) v = [ math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta), math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta), math.cos(phi) ] # 3. Estimate best direction to avoid visibility issues # Note: Exact PDDF query API not specified in sources depth = pddffunction(currentp, v) if depth is not None and depth > 0: q = [currentp[i] + depth v[i] for i in range(3)] # Check if q is on surface (xi=1) if pddffunction.isonsurface(q): currentp = q break points.append(currentp) return points Near-Surface Point Sampling generates training data points in the immediate vicinity of a mesh surface by perturbing existing surface samples with Gaussian noise. It solves the problem of insufficient volumetric coverage near the geometry boundary, which is critical for training neural implicit representations to converge on the correct surface location. It differs from uniform volume sampling by focusing density on the surface transition region, and from pure surface sampling by providing gradient information for the signed distance field (SDF) values off the zero-level set. This method estimates the full parameter set (position, normal, tangent vectors, and scales) for a surfel representation starting from a triangle mesh. It solves the problem of defining local tangent frames and anisotropic kernel shapes for point clouds sampled from meshes, where positions and normals are known but geometric extent is not. It differs from sibling methods by deriving tangent scales from the local point cloud neighborhood structure rather than mesh connectivity or fixed heuristics, offering two variants: isotropic scaling for performance and anisotropic scaling for quality. SDF-guided Sampling is a surface-aware sampling strategy that uses a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to estimate ray-surface intersections, followed by fine-grained sampling around the intersection point to accelerate rendering and emphasize the relationship between surface and radiance fields. It differs from standard NeRF sampling by reducing the number of required sampling points through early surface localization, and from pure mesh-based methods by retaining the flexibility of implicit field evaluation without requiring explicit mesh vertex interpolation. Bidirectional Projective Sampling is a boundary sampling method for physics-based differentiable rendering that generates seed rays from both sensors and emitters to initialize a guiding structure, addressing inefficiencies when scenes contain small-area lights at a distance. It improves upon Zhang et al.'s projective sampling by incorporating rays emitted directly from small-area emitters into the seed ray set during the projection operation, ensuring all successfully projected rays contribute to the guiding structure regardless of emitter size. Unlike previous methods that rely solely on sensor-spawned rays, which have a near-zero probability of intersecting small-area emitters, this method guarantees intersection by explicitly sampling from the emitter, thereby maximizing contribution to the boundary integral. This method extracts a differentiable surface point from volume rendering samples by linearly interpolating SDF zero-crossings, enabling the enforcement of multi-view feature consistency constraints. It differs from sibling methods by relying on the hierarchical sampling density near the surface to approximate the zero-crossing with a single secant step, rather than recursive root-finding or mesh-based parameterization. Definition: The incorporation of projection points derived from gradient information into the power diagram computation to accurately capture the underlying surface, particularly in regions with complex topology or fine details. Steps: Projection points are especially valuable for reconstructing thin structures, sharp edges, and regions with high curvature variation that might otherwise be inadequately captured by discrete SDF sampling points alone. Comparison: The baseline method using only sampling points without projections exhibits substantial topological defects and missing features, whereas the projection-enhanced approach preserves topological integrity. Definition: Constructs a SurfaceInteraction3f structure from a ray and intersection time, computing normal, frame, and other interaction properties without SDF autodiff support. Steps: Set si.t = t, si.p = ray(t), si.shframe.n = normalize(gradient(si.p)), initialize sh frame, set si.n = si.shframe.n, si.wi = tolocal(-ray.d), si.wavelengths = ray.wavelengths, si.dpdu = shframe.s, si.dpdv = shframe.t. Definition: A method to extract a point cloud (PC) from a Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) by projecting random points onto the shape surface S. It does not guarantee uniform sampling over S. Steps: Sample a point p uniformly from the bounding box B: p ~ U[B]. For each p, sample nv directions vi uniformly from the unit sphere S^2: V(p) = {vi(p) ~ U[S^2]}{i=1}^{nv}. Compose these directions to estimate the best direction vb(p) (as in §V-A2 and §V-A3, but without optimization) to avoid visibility ξ(p, v) = 0. Compute the surface point q(p, vb(p)) using the PDDF depth and direction. The condition for q being on S is ξ(p, v) = 1 and q(p, v) = p + d(p, v)v. Repeat the process NH times, starting from the newly found point q (i.e., p <- q), to improve accuracy for depths far from S. Parameters: nv: Number of directions sampled per point. Typical value: 128. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of rays and steps in sphere tracing. Sphere tracing is O(N \cdot S) where N is the number of rays and S is the average number of steps to convergence. Indicator grid sampling adds overhead for grid lookups and MLP inference. Memory Complexity: Low for sphere tracing (only storing points). Indicator grid sampling requires storing the indicator grid and field levels. Strengths: Efficiently targets the surface region, reducing wasted samples in empty space. Provides necessary gradients for training implicit fields. Limitations: Sphere tracing can be slow for complex SDFs with many steps. Explicit PDDF sampling does not guarantee uniform distribution. When to Use: Training neural implicit representations (NGLOD), rendering dynamic deformable tissues, extracting point clouds from PDDFs. The method is used in Neural Geometric Level of Detail (NGLOD) to generate surface and near-surface training points. It was further developed in Efficient Deformable Tissue Reconstruction using indicator grids for dynamic scenes. Explicit sampling methods were introduced for Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDF) to extract point clouds. Power diagram enhancements with projection points were proposed for adaptive isosurface extraction. name: Near-Surface Point Sampling
head: DeepSDF sampling, Non-Uniform Surface Sampling
body: Near-Surface Point Sampling generates a non-uniform distribution of query points for training implicit surface representations, specifically Signed Distance Fields (SDFs). It solves the problem of insufficient training data density near the object boundary, which is critical for accurate surface reconstruction. It sets itself apart from uniform volume sampling by concentrating samples in the immediate vicinity of the mesh, and from pure surface sampling by including a controlled noise perturbation to regularize the gradient field. Inputs: A watertight mesh M with correct face normals. Number of points N (default 500,000). Standard deviation for noise \sigma (default 0.01). Bounding radius R (default 1.0, unit sphere). Outputs: A set of N 3D points P = \{p1, \dots, pN\}. Corresponding SDF values D = \{d1, \dots, dN\} and signs S = \{s1, \dots, sN\}. Data Structures: Surface Point Cloud: A set of points on the mesh surface, typically stored in a kd-tree for nearest-neighbor queries. Training Batch: A list of tuples (pi, di, si). Steps: 1. Mesh Normalization: Transform the mesh M so that it fits inside a unit sphere centered at the origin. This ensures consistent scale for the noise perturbation and bounding volume. 2. Surface Sampling: Generate a set of points P{surf} uniformly distributed on the surface of M. The number of surface points is determined by the desired split ratio. According to the DeepSDF paper, a 2:2:1 split is used for surface, near, and uniform samples, meaning N{surf} = N{near} = \frac{2}{5}N and N{uniform} = \frac{1}{5}N. 3. Near-Surface Perturbation: For each point p \in P{surf}, generate a perturbed point p' by adding Gaussian noise: p' = p + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma^2 I) where \sigma = 0.01. These points form the set P{near}. 4. Uniform Volume Sampling: Generate N{uniform} points uniformly distributed within the bounding sphere of radius R. These points form the set P{uniform}. 5. SDF Calculation: For all points in P{near} \cup P{uniform}, calculate the SDF value and sign: Value: Find the closest point q on the surface point cloud using a kd-tree. The distance is d = \|p' - q\|. Sign: Determine if the point is inside or outside the surface. Normal Method: Compute the dot product of the vector (p' - q) and the normal nq at q. If (p' - q) \cdot nq < 0, the point is inside (negative sign). Depth Method: Project the point into the camera frame of each scan. If the point's depth is greater than the depth buffer value for any camera, it is outside (positive sign). 6. Validation: Check the fraction of points inside the shape (negative SDF). If this fraction is less than minsize (default 0), throw an exception. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def nearsurfacepointsampling(mesh, N=500000, sigma=0.01, R=1.0, minsize=0.0): # 1. Normalize mesh to unit sphere mesh = normalizetounitsphere(mesh) # 2. Determine counts based on 2:2:1 split Nsurf = int(2/5 N) Nnear = int(2/5 N) Nuniform = N - Nsurf - Nnear # 3. Generate surface points Psurf = samplemeshsurface(mesh, Nsurf) # 4. Generate near-surface points via perturbation noise = np.random.normal(0, sigma, (Nnear, 3)) Pnear = Psurf[:Nnear] + noise # 5. Generate uniform volume points Puniform = sampleuniforminsphere(R, Nuniform) # 6. Combine all points Pall = np.vstack([Pnear, Puniform]) # 7. Calculate SDF values and signs # Assuming getsurfacepointcloud returns a kd-tree and normals pointclouddata = getsurfacepointcloud(mesh, surfacepointmethod='sample') kdtree = pointclouddata.kdtree normals = pointclouddata.normals D = np.zeros(N) S = np.zeros(N) for i, p in enumerate(Pall): # Find closest point on surface dist, idx = kdtree.query(p) q = kdtree.data[idx] n = normals[idx] D[i] = dist # Determine sign using normal method vec = p - q if np.dot(vec, n) < 0: S[i] = -1.0 # Inside else: S[i] = 1.0 # Outside # 8. Validate minsize fractioninside = np.sum(S == -1.0) / N if fractioninside < minsize: raise Exception(f"Too few points inside shape: {fractioninside} < {minsize}") return Pall, D, S Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-watertight meshes: The sampling method requires watertight meshes with correct face normals. Non-watertight meshes may produce incorrect surface point clouds. Sign Ambiguity: The normal method can produce "bubble" artifacts in concave regions or near holes. The depth method is more robust but less accurate. Precision: The noise \sigma is small relative to the unit sphere scale. Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient for the perturbation. Projects grid voxels onto the isosurface using the gradient. It differs by using a single-step projection based on unit-length gradients, whereas Near-Surface Point Sampling uses random Gaussian perturbation of existing surface points. Samples visibility discontinuities (silhouettes). It differs by targeting the geometric condition where the surface normal is perpendicular to the view vector, rather than perturbing surface points. Mixes uniform volume, uniform surface, and perturbed surface samples. It differs by using area-weighted triangle selection and explicit mixing strategies, whereas Near-Surface Point Sampling is a specific perturbation technique often used within such frameworks. Visualizes velocity fields near contour surfaces. It builds on Near-Surface Point Sampling by using distance-field estimation to restrict particle placement to a band around the isosurface. Generates points on mesh triangles for NeRF training. It differs by focusing on uniform spatial distribution over mesh geometry for training data generation, rather than foot-point projection or edge-based sampling. Time Complexity: Dominated by the kd-tree query for SDF calculation, which is O(N \log M) where M is the number of surface points in the cloud. Memory Complexity: O(M) to store the surface point cloud and kd-tree. Performance: Training is performed on NVIDIA Tesla V100 GPUs using PyTorch with a batch size of 512. Strengths: Provides high-density samples near the surface, which improves the accuracy of the learned SDF. Limitations: Requires a watertight mesh and correct normals for the sampling method. The sign determination can be ambiguous in complex geometries. The method was proposed in the DeepSDF paper. It is used in neural implicit surface reconstruction to provide training data that emphasizes the surface boundary. The implementation is available in the meshtosdf repository. name: Distance Field Foot Point Generation
head: Foot point extraction, Point Engine for Distance Fields (hgridf), Point generation from DFV, hgridf point generation
body:
A method to generate surface points (foot points) from a clamped, signed distance field volume (DFV) by projecting grid voxels onto the isosurface along the gradient direction. It differs from general scalar field foot point estimation by relying on the specific property that the gradient of a distance field is unit length, allowing for a single-step projection without iterative refinement. It builds on Near-Surface Point Sampling. Inputs: A hierarchical grid of distance field values (hgridf) representing a signed distance field volume (DFV). Outputs: A set of 3D points lying on the isosurface (typically d=0) and their corresponding gradient vectors, stored for rendering. Data Structures: HGridf Cell: Contains a flag indicating if the cell is "dirty" (needs regeneration) or "clean" (cached). Vertex Array: Stores generated foot points pf and gradients \mathbf{g}. Display List: Cached rendering primitive generated from the vertex array. Algorithm Steps: 1. Iterate through all cells in the hierarchical grid. 2. Skip cells that are empty. 3. For each non-empty cell: a. If the cell is "dirty": i. Traverse all voxels within the cell. ii. For each voxel at position p with distance value d: 1. Check if d \in [0, \sqrt{3}). If not, skip this voxel. 2. Compute the gradient \mathbf{g}{raw} using central differences on the distance field values surrounding p. 3. Normalize the gradient: \mathbf{g} =  rac{\mathbf{g}{raw}}{\|\mathbf{g}{raw}\|}. 4. Calculate the foot point position: pf = p - d \mathbf{g}. 5. Store pf and \mathbf{g} in the vertex array. iii. Generate a display list from the vertex array. iv. Mark the cell as "clean". b. If the cell is "clean": i. Render the associated display list. 4. Move to the next cell. Formulas: Foot Point Calculation: pf = p - d \mathbf{g} Where: pf: The foot point (closest point on the isosurface). p: The position of the current voxel in the grid. d: The signed distance value at voxel p. \mathbf{g}: The normalized gradient vector of the distance field at p. Gradient Normalization: \mathbf{g} =  rac{
abla d}{\|
abla d\|} Where 
abla d is the gradient computed via central differences. Parameters: Interval Threshold: \sqrt{3}. The interval [0, \sqrt{3}) is used to select voxels. This value ensures that all voxels on the positive side of the isosurface are included if they belong to cells intersected by the isosurface, preventing holes in the generated point cloud. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Medial Surface: The gradient \mathbf{g} is undefined at points belonging to the medial surface (where there is an equal shortest distance to two or more surface points). The method assumes \mathbf{g} is well-defined. Gradient Accuracy: Central differences do not yield an exact unit gradient for non-trivial distance fields. Normalization is required to correct this. Holes: Using an interval smaller than [0, \sqrt{3}) may cause holes to appear in the rendered surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computecentralgradient(grid, p): """Compute gradient at p using central differences.""" dx = (grid[p.x + 1, p.y, p.z] - grid[p.x - 1, p.y, p.z]) / 2.0 dy = (grid[p.x, p.y + 1, p.z] - grid[p.x, p.y - 1, p.z]) / 2.0 dz = (grid[p.x, p.y, p.z + 1] - grid[p.x, p.y, p.z - 1]) / 2.0 return (dx, dy, dz) def vectorlength(v): """Compute Euclidean norm of a 3D vector.""" return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) def createdisplaylist(vertexarray): """Cache vertex array for rendering.""" return list(vertexarray) def renderdisplaylist(displaylist): """Render cached points.""" for pt, grad in displaylist: # Render point at pt (implementation-specific) pass def generatefootpoints(hgridf): """ Generates foot points for a distance field volume using hgridf. """ for cell in hgridf.cells: if cell.isempty: continue if cell.isdirty: vertexarray = [] for voxel in cell.voxels: p = voxel.position d = voxel.distancevalue # Check interval [0, sqrt(3)) if d < 0 or d >= math.sqrt(3): continue # Compute gradient using central differences graw = computecentralgradient(hgridf.grid, p) # Normalize gradient gnorm = vectorlength(graw) if gnorm == 0: continue # Avoid division by zero; gradient undefined at medial surface g = (graw[0] / gnorm, graw[1] / gnorm, graw[2] / gnorm) # Calculate foot point pf = (p.x - d g[0], p.y - d g[1], p.z - d g[2]) vertexarray.append((pf, g)) # Generate display list from vertex array cell.displaylist = createdisplaylist(vertexarray) cell.isdirty = False cell.isclean = True if cell.isclean: renderdisplaylist(cell.displaylist) An algorithm to detect the medial axis (MA) of a general implicit surface by analyzing characteristic lines (normals) and detecting changes in foot points, providing subgrid accuracy without thinning or post-processing. It differs from its parent Distance Field Foot Point Generation by not just generating surface points, but by identifying the locus of centers of maximal inscribed spheres (the medial axis) to compute the Local Feature Size (LFS) field. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The cost is dominated by gradient computation and normalization for voxels in the 0, \sqrt{3}) band. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Caching via display lists reduces repeated computation for static scenes. Performance: Extremely fast for distance fields compared to iterative methods or Marching Cubes, as it requires only a single projection step per voxel. Strengths: Simple implementation; no iterative convergence required; suitable for interactive applications where latency is critical. Limitations: Only applicable to [signed distance fields (DFVs); fails or produces artifacts at the medial surface where the gradient is undefined. When to use: When rendering isosurfaces from pre-computed distance fields in interactive applications. When not to use: For general scalar fields (requires iterative refinement or Marching Cubes) or when medial axis accuracy is required without post-processing. The method originates from the work on hardware-accelerated point rendering of isosurfaces, specifically within the context of the "point engine for synthetic volume". It leverages the mathematical properties of signed distance fields to simplify surface point generation. The approach was detailed in the paper "Hardware Accelerated Point Rendering of Isosurfaces". It is part of a broader family of near-surface point sampling techniques used in volume rendering. name: Medial Axis Detection via Foot Point Method
head: Foot Point Method for Medial Axis
body: This method detects the medial axis (MA) of a general implicit surface by analyzing characteristic lines (normals) and detecting changes in foot points, providing subgrid accuracy without thinning or post-processing. It differs from its parent Distance Field Foot Point Generation by not just generating surface points, but by identifying the locus of centers of maximal inscribed spheres (the medial axis) to compute the Local Feature Size (LFS) field. Inputs: Implicit surface function F(\mathbf{x}) = 0. Grid of query points \mathcal{Q}. Outputs: Set of medial axis points \mathcal{M}. Local Feature Size (LFS) field \lambda(\mathbf{x}) at grid nodes bounding the isosurface. Data Structures: Medial Axis Set \mathcal{M}: A list of 3D points \mathbf{m} \in \mathbb{R}^3. LFS Field \lambda: A scalar field defined on grid nodes \mathbf{x}g that bound the isosurface. Parameters: Threshold angle \alpha: Defined by \cos(\alpha) = 0.9. Steps: 1. Grid Processing: Iterate over each grid point \mathbf{q} \in \mathcal{Q}. 2. Find Foot Point \mathbf{p}: Compute the nearest point \mathbf{p} on the surface F(\mathbf{x})=0 to \mathbf{q} using gradient descent. The segment \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}} is perpendicular to the surface and forms part of a characteristic line. 3. Find Far Point \mathbf{q}^: Extend the characteristic line from \mathbf{p} through \mathbf{q} (away from the surface) to find the point \mathbf{q}^ that intersects the far face of the current voxel. 4. Find Far Foot Point \mathbf{p}^: Compute the foot point \mathbf{p}^ on the surface corresponding to \mathbf{q}^ using gradient descent. 5. Check MA Crossing: Calculate the angle \theta between the vector \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}} and \overline{\mathbf{p}^\mathbf{q}^}. Specifically, check the angle between the segments \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}} and \overline{\mathbf{p}^\mathbf{q}^}. If the angle between the line segments \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{q}} and \overline{\mathbf{p}^\mathbf{q}^} is greater than \alpha (i.e., \cos(\theta) < 0.9), the segment \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^} crosses the medial axis. 6. Estimate MA Position: If a crossing is detected, estimate the position of the medial axis point \mathbf{m} along the segment \overline{\mathbf{p}\mathbf{p}^} using a first-order (tangent plane) approximation to the surface at \mathbf{p}^. 7. Construct LFS Field: After processing all grid points, construct the LFS field \lambda(\mathbf{x}). For each grid node \mathbf{x}g bounding the isosurface, set \lambda(\mathbf{x}g) to the distance to the closest medial axis point \mathbf{m} \in \mathcal{M}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def findfootpointgradientdescent(q, F, gradF, maxiter=100, tol=1e-6): """ Finds the nearest point p on the surface F(x)=0 to query point q. Uses gradient descent. """ p = q.copy() for in range(maxiter): fval = F(p) if abs(fval) < tol: break g = gradF(p) normg = np.linalg.norm(g) if normg < 1e-10: break # Step along normal direction to approach surface step = fval / normg p = p - step g return p def detectmedialaxis(gridpoints, F, gradF, voxelsize): """ Detects medial axis points and constructs LFS field. """ medialaxispoints = [] cosalpha = 0.9 threshold = cosalpha # Note: In practice, gridpoints should be those bounding the isosurface # or a dense grid covering the volume of interest. for q in gridpoints: # Step 2: Find foot point p for q p = findfootpointgradientdescent(q, F, gradF) # Step 3: Find q along characteristic intersecting far face of voxel # Characteristic direction is from p to q (or q to p, but we go away from p) # Vector pq vecpq = q - p # Normalize normpq = np.linalg.norm(vecpq) if normpq < 1e-10: continue dirchar = vecpq / normpq # Find intersection with far face of voxel containing q # Assuming axis-aligned voxel grid with size voxelsize # This requires determining which face is the "far" face relative to p # For simplicity, we extend by one voxel length in the direction of the characteristic # A robust implementation would compute exact ray-box intersection qstar = q + dirchar voxelsize # Step 4: Find foot point p for q pstar = findfootpointgradientdescent(qstar, F, gradF) # Step 5: Check angle between pq and pq # Vector pq vecpstarqstar = qstar - pstar normpstarqstar = np.linalg.norm(vecpstarqstar) if normpstarqstar < 1e-10: continue dirpstarqstar = vecpstarqstar / normpstarqstar # Cosine of angle between the two characteristic directions # Note: The text says "angle between line segments pq and pq" # This usually implies the angle between the vectors originating from the surface # or the vectors along the characteristics. costheta = np.dot(dirchar, dirpstarqstar) if costheta < threshold: # Step 6: Estimate MA position along p-p # Using first-order tangent plane approximation at p # The MA point m is the intersection of the normal at p and the normal at p? # Or intersection of the characteristic lines? # The text says "position of the MA along pp can be found by using a # first-order (tangent plane) approximation to the surface at the point p" # This implies projecting p onto the tangent plane at p? # Or finding the intersection of the line pp with the tangent plane at p? # Let's assume the latter: Intersection of line segment pp with tangent plane at p # Tangent plane at p: normal is gradF(p) nstar = gradF(pstar) normnstar = np.linalg.norm(nstar) if normnstar < 1e-10: continue nstar = nstar / normnstar # Line segment pp: P(t) = p + t (pstar - p), t in [0, 1] # Plane: (x - pstar). nstar = 0 # (p + t(pstar - p) - pstar). nstar = 0 # (p - pstar + t(pstar - p)). nstar = 0 # (p - pstar). nstar + t (pstar - p). nstar = 0 # t = - (p - pstar). nstar / (pstar - p). nstar # t = (pstar - p). nstar / (pstar - p). nstar = 1? # This would mean the intersection is at p. That doesn't seem right for MA detection. # Re-reading: "first-order (tangent plane) approximation to the surface at point p" # The medial axis is the locus of centers of spheres tangent to the surface. # The center of such a sphere lies on the normal. # The MA point m is the intersection of the normal at p and the normal at p? # If we approximate the surface locally as planes, the intersection of the two normals # gives the center of the circle tangent to both planes. # Normal at p np = gradF(p) normnp = np.linalg.norm(np) if normnp < 1e-10: continue np = np / normnp # Intersection of line p + tnp and line pstar + snstar # This is a standard line-line intersection in 3D. # If lines are skew, we find the closest points. # However, for small distances, they might intersect. # Let's find the point m on the segment pp that is closest to the intersection of normals? # The text says "position of the MA along pp". # Let's assume the MA point is the intersection of the normal at p and the tangent plane at p? # No, the MA is equidistant. # Let's stick to the most literal interpretation of "first-order approximation at p" # to find the position along pp. # Perhaps it means: The MA point m is the projection of p onto the tangent plane at p? # Or the projection of p onto the tangent plane at p? # Given the ambiguity, a common approach in such foot-point methods is: # m = p + t (pstar - p) # where t is determined by the geometry of the normals. # Let's use the intersection of the normal at p with the tangent plane at p. # Line: L(t) = p + t np # Plane: (x - pstar). nstar = 0 # (p + tnp - pstar). nstar = 0 # t = (pstar - p). nstar / (np. nstar) denom = np.dot(np, nstar) if abs(denom) < 1e-10: continue t = np.dot(pstar - p, nstar) / denom # Clamp t to [0, 1] to stay on segment pp t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) m = p + t (pstar - p) medialaxispoints.append(m) # Step 7: Construct LFS field # For each grid node bounding the isosurface, find distance to closest m in medialaxispoints # This is a separate pass. return medialaxispoints def computelfsfield(gridnodes, medialaxispoints): """ Computes the LFS field lambda(x) for grid nodes bounding the isosurface. """ lfsfield = {} for x in gridnodes: mindist = float('inf') for m in medialaxispoints: dist = np.linalg.norm(x - m) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist lfsfield[x] = mindist return lfsfield Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Descent Failure: If the gradient is zero or the surface is not smooth, findfootpointgradientdescent may fail or converge to a local minimum. Ensure the implicit function is differentiable and use a robust solver with fallbacks. Voxel Intersection: Determining the "far face" of the voxel for \mathbf{q}^ requires precise ray-box intersection logic. Use a standard ray-box intersection algorithm (e.g., slab method) to find the exact exit point of the ray from the voxel containing \mathbf{q}. Degenerate Normals: If the normal at \mathbf{p} or \mathbf{p}^ is near-zero, the tangent plane approximation is invalid. Check for small norms before division. Singular Points: The method detects the MA proper, not the singular points where the MA terminates (e.g., vertices of a polyhedron). The sizing field construction generates a scalar field h(\mathbf{x}) that controls particle distribution density to ensure \varepsilon-sampling and smooth triangle gradation for isosurface meshing. It differs from raw geometric sampling by enforcing a \delta-Lipschitz continuity constraint on the field, preventing abrupt changes in triangle size that would degrade mesh quality. This method builds on the medial axis detection provided by Medial Axis Detection via Foot Point Method by utilizing the resulting local feature size to initialize the field. Time Complexity: Dominated by the gradient descent for foot point computation for each grid point and each \mathbf{q}^. If N is the number of grid points, and K is the average number of iterations for gradient descent, the complexity is O(N \cdot K). The LFS field construction is O(N{nodes} \cdot |\mathcal{M}|), which can be optimized with spatial indexing (e.g., k-d tree) to O(N{nodes} \log |\mathcal{M}|). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store grid points and intermediate results, plus O(|\mathcal{M}|) for the medial axis points. Strengths: Subgrid accuracy, no thinning or post-processing required, robust to free parameters. Limitations: Relies on accurate gradient computation and foot point finding. May miss singular points of the MA. When to Use: When high-quality meshing is required and the LFS field is needed for adaptive sampling. When Not to Use: If the surface is not smooth or gradients are unreliable. The method was developed as part of work on topology, accuracy, and quality of isosurface meshes using dynamic particles. It builds on the foot point method described in [17] (not cited in the provided sources, but referenced in). The specific paper is "Topology, Accuracy, and Quality of Isosurface Meshes Using Dynamic Particles". name: Sizing Field Construction
body: The sizing field construction generates a scalar field h(\mathbf{x}) that controls particle distribution density to ensure \varepsilon-sampling and smooth triangle gradation for isosurface meshing. It differs from raw geometric sampling by enforcing a \delta-Lipschitz continuity constraint on the field, preventing abrupt changes in triangle size that would degrade mesh quality. This method builds on the medial axis detection provided by Medial Axis Detection via Foot Point Method by utilizing the resulting local feature size to initialize the field. Inputs: Implicit surface function F(\mathbf{x}) and its Hessian matrix \mathbf{H}F. Local feature size field \lambda(\mathbf{x}) derived from the medial axis detection. Sampling parameter \varepsilon. Gradient limit parameter \delta. Time step \Delta t for the iterative update. Convergence threshold \tau (default 10^{-5}). Outputs: Discrete sizing field h{ijk} defined on a 3D grid lattice. Data Structures: Grid: 3D array of floats h[Nx][Ny][Nz]. Hessian: 3×3 symmetric matrix per grid node for curvature calculation. LFS Field: 3D array of floats lambda[Nx][Ny][Nz]. Steps: 1. Compute Maximum Curvature: For each grid node \mathbf{x}{ijk} in the narrow band around the isosurface, compute the maximum curvature \kappa{max}(\mathbf{x}) from the Hessian of F. The radius of curvature is r(\mathbf{x}) = 1/|\kappa{max}(\mathbf{x})|. 2. Initialize Field: Compute the initial sizing field h0(\mathbf{x}) using Equation (1): h0(\mathbf{x}) = C \min(\lambda(\mathbf{x}), 1/|\kappa{max}(\mathbf{x})|) where C = 2\varepsilon. 3. Iterative Gradient Limiting: Update the field iteratively to enforce the \delta-Lipschitz condition using Equation (2): h{ijk}^{n+1} = h{ijk}^n + \Delta t \cdot \min(0, \delta - \Delta{ijk}^+) where \Delta{ijk}^+ is the discrete gradient magnitude defined in Equation (3). 4. Convergence Check: Repeat Step 3 until the maximum relative change in h across all nodes is less than \tau. Formulas: Initial Field (Eq. 1): h0(\mathbf{x}) = C \min(\lambda(\mathbf{x}), 1/|\kappa{max}(\mathbf{x})|) \lambda(\mathbf{x}): Local feature size at \mathbf{x}. \kappa{max}(\mathbf{x}): Maximum principal curvature at \mathbf{x}. C: Constant, defined as 2\varepsilon. Update Rule (Eq. 2): h{ijk}^{n+1} = h{ijk}^n + \Delta t \cdot \min(0, \delta - \Delta{ijk}^+) \Delta t: Time step for the discrete operator. \delta: Maximum allowed gradient magnitude. Gradient Magnitude (Eq. 3): \Delta{ijk}^+ = \sqrt{ \max(Dx^+ h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \min(Dx^- h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \max(Dy^+ h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \min(Dy^- h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \max(Dz^+ h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 + \min(Dz^- h{ijk}^n, 0)^2 } Dx^+, Dx^-: Forward and backward difference operators in the x-direction. Dy^+, Dy^-: Forward and backward difference operators in the y-direction. Dz^+, Dz^-: Forward and backward difference operators in the z-direction. Parameters: \varepsilon: Sampling parameter. Controls the sampling density relative to the local feature size. Literature suggests \varepsilon = 0.5 as a loose upper bound. \delta: Gradient limit. Controls the smoothness of triangle size transition. \delta < \varepsilon generally produces well-shaped triangles. \Delta t: Time step. Not explicitly defined in sources, but required for the iterative solver. \tau: Convergence threshold. Default 10^{-5}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Curvature: If \kappa{max}(\mathbf{x}) = 0, the radius of curvature is infinite, but the \min function with \lambda(\mathbf{x}) bounds the field. Boundary Conditions: The method operates on a narrow band around the isosurface, so grid nodes outside this band are not processed. Convergence: The iterative process must converge; if \Delta t is too large, the update may oscillate or diverge. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computemaxcurvature(H): """Compute maximum principal curvature from 3x3 Hessian matrix.""" v = [1.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(50): Hv = [H[0][0]v[0] + H[0][1]v[1] + H[0][2]v[2], H[1][0]v[0] + H[1][1]v[1] + H[1][2]v[2], H[2][0]v[0] + H[2][1]v[1] + H[2][2]v[2]] norm = math.sqrt(Hv[0]2 + Hv[1]2 + Hv[2]2) if norm == 0: return 0.0 v = [Hv[0]/norm, Hv[1]/norm, Hv[2]/norm] Hv = [H[0][0]v[0] + H[0][1]v[1] + H[0][2]v[2], H[1][0]v[0] + H[1][1]v[1] + H[1][2]v[2], H[2][0]v[0] + H[2][1]v[1] + H[2][2]v[2]] return Hv[0]v[0] + Hv[1]v[1] + Hv[2]v[2] def computesizingfield(lambdafield, hessianfield, epsilon, delta, dt, tolerance=1e-5): C = 2 epsilon Nx, Ny, Nz = lambdafield.shape h = [[[0.0]Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] # Step 1 & 2: Initialize field for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): for k in range(Nz): kappamax = computemaxcurvature(hessianfield[i][j][k]) radiuscurv = 1.0 / abs(kappamax) if abs(kappamax) > 1e-10 else float('inf') h[i][j][k] = C min(lambdafield[i][j][k], radiuscurv) # Step 3 & 4: Iterative gradient limiting while True: maxrelchange = 0.0 hnew = [[[0.0]Nz for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)] for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): for k in range(Nz): # Forward differences dxp = h[i+1][j][k] - h[i][j][k] if i < Nx-1 else 0.0 dyp = h[i][j+1][k] - h[i][j][k] if j < Ny-1 else 0.0 dzp = h[i][j][k+1] - h[i][j][k] if k < Nz-1 else 0.0 # Backward differences dxm = h[i][j][k] - h[i-1][j][k] if i > 0 else 0.0 dym = h[i][j][k] - h[i][j-1][k] if j > 0 else 0.0 dzm = h[i][j][k] - h[i][j][k-1] if k > 0 else 0.0 # Gradient magnitude gradmag = math.sqrt(max(dxp, 0.0)2 + min(dxm, 0.0)2 + max(dyp, 0.0)2 + min(dym, 0.0)2 + max(dzp, 0.0)2 + min(dzm, 0.0)2) # Update rule update = dt min(0.0, delta - gradmag) hnew[i][j][k] = h[i][j][k] + update # Convergence tracking currentval = h[i][j][k] relchange = abs(update / currentval) if abs(currentval) > 1e-10 else abs(update) if relchange > maxrelchange: maxrelchange = relchange # Swap buffers for i in range(Nx): for j in range(Ny): for k in range(Nz): h[i][j][k] = hnew[i][j][k] if maxrelchange < tolerance: break return h Provides the \lambda(\mathbf{x}) field used in the initialization. LFS Estimation. Computes \kappa{max} from the Hessian of F. Curvature Computation. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Smaller values of \varepsilon produce more geometrically accurate meshes, while smaller values of \delta generate more regular triangulations; smaller values of either parameter inherently increase the overall number of triangles. Strengths: Ensures \varepsilon-sampling and smooth triangle gradation. The \delta-Lipschitz property prevents poor-quality triangles. Limitations: Requires computation of the Hessian and local feature size. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. The sizing field construction was introduced in the context of dynamic particle systems for isosurface meshing. It builds upon the work of Persson on \delta-Lipschitz fields. The method is designed to adapt particle distribution to local geometric features, ensuring both accuracy and mesh quality. Topology, Accuracy, and Quality of Isosurface Meshes Using Dynamic Particles, https://doi.org/10.1109/tvcg.2007.70604, fetched 2026-10-30
