name: Primary Edge Sampling
head: Primary Boundary Integral Estimation
body: Primary Edge Sampling generates sample points on the primary boundary curve S of an implicit surface, which is defined as the intersection of the surface function \phi and the orientation function \psi. It solves the problem of sampling visibility discontinuities (silhouettes) for implicit surfaces, which lack a finite set of edges like polygonal meshes. It sets itself apart from Distance Field Foot Point Generation by explicitly targeting the geometric condition where the surface normal is perpendicular to the view vector, rather than projecting points onto the surface. It differs from Surface and Volume Training Position Sampling by focusing on boundary integrals for differentiable rendering rather than general training position generation. Inputs: Implicit surface function \phi(\mathbf{p}), where \phi(\mathbf{p}) = 0 defines the surface. Camera position \mathbf{c}. Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) of the implicit surface. A face F of the bounding box and an edge E of that face. Maximum number of marching steps i{max}. Step size \epsilon for marching along the edge. Outputs: A point \mathbf{p} \in S on the primary boundary curve. Data Structures: AABB: Defined by minimum and maximum coordinates. Used for range analysis to bound the search space. Orientation Function \psi: Defined as \psi{\phi, \mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}):= \langle \nabla \phi(\mathbf{p}), \mathbf{v}{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}) \rangle, where \mathbf{v}{\mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}) = \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{p} is the view vector. The primary boundary S is the set \{ \mathbf{p} \mid \phi(\mathbf{p}) = 0, \psi{\phi, \mathbf{c}}(\mathbf{p}) = 0 \}. Parameters: AABB Size: In the source experiments, the AABB size is 6.1 \times 10^{-5}, which corresponds to cutting a unit cube 42 times in half. This size is used in range analysis (affine arithmetic) to bound S tighter. Step Size \epsilon: Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Range Analysis (Preprocessing): Cut the local space of the implicit surface into AABBs of size 6.1 \times 10^{-5}. Apply affine arithmetic to each AABB against \phi and \psi. Discard AABBs guaranteed not to intersect both surfaces; keep those that possibly intersect both. This bounds S tighter and assumes only one intersection within the tighter bound. 2. Proxy Selection: Select a face F of the bounding box and an edge E of F as a proxy surface. 3. Initial Sample: Sample a point \mathbf{q} on edge E. 4. Initialize State: Set \psi{prev} = 0. 5. Marching Loop: For i from 1 to i{max}: a. Intersect a ray starting from \mathbf{q} along the face normal \mathbf{n}F with the implicit surface \phi to get point \mathbf{p}. b. If no hit is found, reset \psi{prev} = 0. c. Evaluate \psii = \psi(\mathbf{p}). d. If \psi{prev} \cdot \psii < 0, return \mathbf{p} as the sample point on S. e. Set \psi{prev} = \psii. f. Advance \mathbf{q} along the edge normal \mathbf{n}E by step size \epsilon. 6. Return: If the loop completes without finding a sign change, return NULL. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sampleprimaryedge(facenormal, edgenormal, maxsteps, stepsize, implicitsurfacephi, orientationfunctionpsi, rayintersect): """ Samples a point on the primary edge S. Args: facenormal: Normal vector of the proxy face F. edgenormal: Normal vector of the edge E within the face F. maxsteps: Maximum number of marching steps imax. stepsize: Step size epsilon for advancing along the edge. implicitsurfacephi: Function phi(p) returning the implicit surface value. orientationfunctionpsi: Function psi(p) returning the orientation function value. rayintersect: Function that returns the intersection point p of a ray (origin, direction) with the implicit surface phi, or None if no hit. Returns: A point p on the primary edge S, or None if not found. """ # 1. Sample a point q on the edge E of the face F # Note: The specific sampling distribution on E is not given in the sources. q = samplepointonedge() # 2. Initialize psiprev psiprev = 0.0 # 3. March along the edge for i in range(1, maxsteps + 1): # Intersect ray from q along face normal nF with implicit surface phi p = rayintersect(q, facenormal) if p is None: # No hit, reset psiprev psiprev = 0.0 else: # Evaluate psi at the current intersection point psii = orientationfunctionpsi(p) # Check for sign change if psiprev psii < 0: # Sign change indicates intersection with psi, # and p is on phi, so p is on S return p # Update psiprev psiprev = psii # Advance q along the edge normal nE q = q + stepsize edgenormal return None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Intersections: Rays may intersect the surface multiple times. The method uses range analysis (affine arithmetic) to bound S tighter and assumes only one intersection in this tighter bound. Without this, one would need to track all intersections and march to the other edge. No Intersection: If the ray from \mathbf{q} does not hit the surface, \psi{prev} is reset to 0. End of Edge: If the marching reaches the end of the edge without finding a sign change, the algorithm returns NULL. This method samples the secondary boundary integral by first sampling a surface point using a proxy surface (e.g., a bounding box face) and then a tangent direction. It sets itself apart from Primary Edge Sampling by transforming the integral over the implicit surface B to an integral over the proxy face F using Jacobians J{T1} and J{T2}. It is chosen when secondary boundary integrals need to be evaluated for implicit surfaces. Definition: Sampling the secondary boundary integral by transforming the domain from the implicit surface B to a proxy face F. Steps: 1. Define a proxy face F of the bounding box. 2. Cast a ray from \mathbf{q} \in F along normal \mathbf{n}F toward the implicit surface B. 3. The ray intersects B at T1(\mathbf{q}) and T2(\mathbf{q}). 4. Transform the integral over B to an integral over F using the Jacobians J{T1} and J{T2}. Pitfall: In general, there may be more than two intersections, and the number of intersections may vary per point. The method sums over all intersections i, and points with fewer than i intersections contribute zero. This variant handles implicit surfaces defined as zero-level sets \phi(x, \pi) = 0, which do not offer a finite set of edges to sample from, requiring additional steps to sample visibility boundaries. It sets itself apart from Primary Edge Sampling by explicitly detailing the use of AABBs and range analysis for implicit surfaces in the context of differentiable rendering surveys. Definition: Sampling the primary boundary curve S for implicit surfaces. Steps: 1. Introduce an AABB of \phi. 2. Sample points on edge E of the AABB. 3. From a sampled point q, cast a ray in the face normal direction to find the intersection with S. 4. If no intersection, march q perpendicular to the edge and repeat until a point in S is found or the end is reached. Formula: Primary boundaries are viewed as the intersected curve S of implicit surface \phi and \psi(p) = \langle \nabla \phi(p), (pN - p) \rangle = 0, describing positions where the surface normal is perpendicular to the viewing direction. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The complexity depends on the number of steps i{max} and the cost of ray intersection and function evaluation. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The range analysis step requires storing AABBs and their bounds. Measured Performance: The AABB size of 6.1 \times 10^{-5} was used in experiments, cutting a unit cube 42 times in half. Strengths: Efficiently samples boundary integrals for directly visible surfaces by identifying and sampling only silhouette edges, reducing variance compared to uniform edge sampling. The use of range analysis bounds S tighter, reducing the search space. Limitations: Assumes only one intersection in the tighter bound provided by range analysis. May fail to find points if the step size is too large or the edge does not intersect the primary boundary. When to Use: When differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces is required, specifically for sampling primary boundary integrals. When Not to Use: When the surface is explicitly meshed, as polygonal edges can be sampled directly. Origin: Introduced by Zhou et al. in "Path-Space Differentiable Rendering of Implicit Surfaces" (SIGGRAPH 2024). History: The method extends Path-Space Differentiable Rendering (PSDR) to implicit surfaces, which do not offer a finite set of edges like meshes. It relies on range analysis (affine arithmetic) as described by Stolfi and De Figueiredo (1997). Usage: Used in differentiable rendering of implicit surfaces to sample primary and secondary boundary integrals. name: Silhouette-based Edge Sampling for Directly Visible Surfaces
body: This method efficiently samples boundary integrals for directly visible surfaces by identifying and sampling only silhouette edges, thereby reducing variance compared to uniform edge sampling. It sets itself apart from its sibling Primary Edge Sampling by introducing a geometric classification step that filters out non-silhouette edges, which do not contribute to boundaries under smooth shading assumptions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A mesh defined by edges, faces, and vertex positions; camera parameters including viewpoint position v and aperture for non-pinhole cameras; screen resolution. Output: A set of sampled points on silhouette edges with rendering contributions evaluated on both sides of the edge. Data Structures: Edge List: A list of edges where each edge is defined by two vertices or two adjacent faces, with edges sharing three or more faces converted into multiple two-face edges. Silhouette Mask: A boolean flag or list indicating which edges are classified as silhouette edges relative to the current viewpoint. Screen-Space Lengths: A floating-point value for each silhouette edge representing its projected length in screen space, used for probability weighting. Steps: 1. Precomputation: Silhouette Classification. For each edge in the mesh, determine if it is a silhouette edge relative to the camera viewpoint v. Let the edge be associated with two faces having normals nf and nb, and let p be an arbitrary point on the edge. The edge is a silhouette edge if and only if: \text{sign} \langle p - v, nf \rangle \neq \text{sign} (\langle p - v, nb \rangle) If the edge is associated with only one face, it is always classified as a silhouette edge. For non-pinhole cameras, compute a bounding box for the camera aperture and conservatively classify an edge as a silhouette if it satisfies the condition for at least one viewpoint within that bounding box. 2. Precomputation: Screen-Space Projection. Project all classified silhouette edges to screen space and calculate their lengths. 3. Rendering: Edge Selection. Randomly select one silhouette edge from the precomputed list with probability proportional to its length in screen space. 4. Rendering: Point Sampling. Uniformly select one point on the selected edge. 5. Rendering: Contribution Evaluation. Evaluate the rendering contribution at the two sides of the selected edge using the sampled point. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def sign(x): return 1 if x > 0 else (-1 if x < 0 else 0) def projecttoscreen(vertex, camera): # Standard perspective projection to normalized device coordinates # Assumes camera has position, forward, up, right vectors and focal length tocam = vertex - camera.position z = -tocam @ camera.forward x = tocam @ camera.right y = tocam @ camera.up if z <= 0.0: return None scale = camera.focallength / z return (x scale, y scale) def silhouetteedgesampling(mesh, camera): silhouetteedges = [] v = camera.position for edge in mesh.edges: faces = edge.faces issilhouette = False if len(faces) == 1: issilhouette = True elif len(faces) == 2: nf, nb = faces[0].normal, faces[1].normal p = edge.vertex1 dotf = (p - v) @ nf dotb = (p - v) @ nb if camera.isnonpinhole: # Conservative classification: check if silhouette for any viewpoint in aperture bounding box # Sample a few points within the aperture bounding box for in range(4): vsample = v + random.uniform(-1, 1) camera.apertureextent if sign((p - vsample) @ nf) != sign((p - vsample) @ nb): issilhouette = True break else: issilhouette = sign(dotf) != sign(dotb) else: # Edges with 3+ faces are converted to multiple two-face edges issilhouette = False if issilhouette: p1screen = projecttoscreen(edge.vertex1, camera) p2screen = projecttoscreen(edge.vertex2, camera) if p1screen and p2screen: length = math.sqrt((p1screen[0] - p2screen[0])2 + (p1screen[1] - p2screen[1])2) silhouetteedges.append({'edge': edge, 'screenlength': length}) if not silhouetteedges: return [] totallength = sum(e['screenlength'] for e in silhouetteedges) r = random.uniform(0, totallength) cumulative = 0 selected = None for data in silhouetteedges: cumulative += data['screenlength'] if cumulative >= r: selected = data break t = random.uniform(0, 1) p1 = selected['edge'].vertex1 p2 = selected['edge'].vertex2 sampledpoint = p1 + t (p2 - p1) # Evaluate rendering contribution at the two sides of the edge using the sampled point return sampledpoint Parameters: Camera Aperture: If non-pinhole, the bounding box of the aperture determines the conservative classification range. Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-pinhole Cameras: Silhouette classification must be conservative. If the camera has an aperture, an edge must be classified as a silhouette if it is a silhouette for at least one viewpoint within the aperture's bounding box. Complex Topology: Edges associated with three or more faces must be converted into multiple edges with two faces each to apply the binary normal test. Variance: Naïve uniform edge sampling generates large variance for complex scenes; this method reduces variance by focusing on silhouettes. Time Complexity: The precomputation pass involves classifying all edges and projecting them to screen space. The number of silhouette edges is roughly at the complexity of N with N being the number of edges. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the list of silhouette edges and their screen-space lengths. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast execution without requiring sophisticated data structures, and reduces variance compared to uniform edge sampling for complex scenes. Limitations: Does not inherently handle occlusion for directly visible surfaces beyond silhouette classification, potentially requiring additional occlusion culling algorithms for high depth complexity scenes. When to Use: Rendering directly visible surfaces with smooth shading where only silhouette edges contribute to boundaries. When Not to Use: Secondary visibility tasks like shadow, mirror reflection, and global illumination, where the viewpoint is a shading point anywhere in the scene, making silhouette determination comparable to the many-lights sampling problem. This method is described in the context of differentiable path tracing and physics-based differentiable rendering. It addresses the issue of high variance in boundary integral sampling for complex scenes by leveraging the geometric property that only silhouette edges form boundaries under smooth shading. The approach builds on the observation that for directly visible surfaces, the number of silhouette edges is significantly smaller than the total number of edges. name: Surface and Volume Training Position Sampling
head: Efficient Sampling of 3D Training Positions
body: A method to distribute training positions for neural implicit surface reconstruction by combining uniform volume samples, uniform surface samples, and perturbed surface samples to ensure coverage of the object and its immediate vicinity. Inputs: A triangle mesh, its bounding radius r, and a total count N of training positions. Outputs: An array of N 3D positions. Data Structures: 1. Triangle CDF Array: A 1D array of size T (number of triangles). The i-th element stores the cumulative sum of normalized triangle areas. Let Ai be the area of triangle i. The CDF at index i is Ci = \frac{\sum{j=0}^{i} Aj}{\sum{k=0}^{T-1} Ak}. 2. Random Number Generator: A GPU-compatible PRNG, specifically PCG32. Parameters: Volume sample ratio: 1/8 of N. Surface sample ratio: 4/8 of N. Perturbed surface sample ratio: 3/8 of N. Logistic distribution standard deviation: \sigma = r/1024. Steps: 1. Generate Uniform Volume Samples: Generate N/8 positions uniformly distributed in the unit cube [0,1]^3 using the PCG32 PRNG. 2. Preprocess Mesh for Surface Sampling: Compute the area Ai for each triangle i in the mesh. Normalize these areas to form a probability distribution and compute the Cumulative Distribution Function (CDF) array C. 3. Generate Uniform Surface Samples: For 4N/8 samples: a. Draw a uniform random number u \in [0,1] from the PRNG. b. Perform a binary search on the CDF array C to find the triangle index t such that C{t-1} < u \le Ct (with C{-1}=0). This selects a triangle proportional to its area. c. Sample a uniformly random position on triangle t using standard sample warping. 4. Generate Perturbed Surface Samples: For 3N/8 samples: a. Repeat steps 3a-3c to select a base position x{base} on the mesh surface. b. Draw three independent random values dx, dy, dz from a logistic distribution with standard deviation \sigma = r/1024. c. Compute the perturbed position x = x{base} + (dx, dy, dz). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple class PCG32: def init(self, state: int = 12345, inc: int = 67891): self.state = state self.inc = inc | 1 def next(self) -> float: x = self.state self.state = (x 6364136223846793005 + self.inc) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF y = (x ^ (x >> 22) ^ (x >> 17) ^ (x >> 7)) & 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFF return (y >> 33) / (1 << 31) def trianglearea(v0: Tuple[float, float, float], v1: Tuple[float, float, float], v2: Tuple[float, float, float]) -> float: # Cross product magnitude of two triangle edges e1 = (v1[0]-v0[0], v1[1]-v0[1], v1[2]-v0[2]) e2 = (v2[0]-v0[0], v2[1]-v0[1], v2[2]-v0[2]) cross = ( e1[1]e2[2] - e1[2]e2[1], e1[2]e2[0] - e1[0]e2[2], e1[0]e2[1] - e1[1]e2[0]) return 0.5 math.sqrt(cross[0]2 + cross[1]2 + cross[2]2) def sampletriangleuniform(v0: Tuple[float, float, float], v1: Tuple[float, float, float], v2: Tuple[float, float, float], rng: PCG32) -> Tuple[float, float, float]: # Standard sample warping for uniform triangle sampling u = rng.next() v = rng.next() if u + v > 1.0: u = 1.0 - u v = 1.0 - v return ( v0[0] + u (v1[0] - v0[0]) + v (v2[0] - v0[0]), v0[1] + u (v1[1] - v0[1]) + v (v2[1] - v0[1]), v0[2] + u (v1[2] - v0[2]) + v (v2[2] - v0[2])) def generatetrainingpositions(trianglemesh: List, boundingradius: float, N: int) -> List[Tuple[float, float, float]]: rng = PCG32() areas = [trianglearea(tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2) for tri in trianglemesh] totalarea = sum(areas) cdf = [] currentsum = 0.0 for area in areas: currentsum += area / totalarea cdf.append(currentsum) nvolume = N // 8 nsurface = 4 (N // 8) nperturbed = 3 (N // 8) positions = [] # 1. Uniform Volume Samples for in range(nvolume): positions.append((rng.next(), rng.next(), rng.next())) # Helper for binary search on CDF def selecttriangleindex(u: float) -> int: low, high = 0, len(cdf) - 1 while low < high: mid = (low + high) // 2 if cdf[mid] < u: low = mid + 1 else: high = mid return low # 2. Uniform Surface Samples for in range(nsurface): u = rng.next() triidx = selecttriangleindex(u) tri = trianglemesh[triidx] positions.append(sampletriangleuniform(tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2, rng)) # 3. Perturbed Surface Samples sigma = boundingradius / 1024.0 for in range(nperturbed): u = rng.next() triidx = selecttriangleindex(u) tri = trianglemesh[triidx] basepos = sampletriangleuniform(tri.v0, tri.v1, tri.v2, rng) # Inverse CDF for logistic distribution u1, u2, u3 = rng.next(), rng.next(), rng.next() dx = sigma math.log(u1 / (1.0 - u1)) dy = sigma math.log(u2 / (1.0 - u2)) dz = sigma math.log(u3 / (1.0 - u3)) positions.append((basepos[0] + dx, basepos[1] + dy, basepos[2] + dz)) return positions A specialized sampling routine for NeRF-based methods (NGLOD) that ensures training positions are generated within octree leaf nodes to avoid invalid queries, replacing the uniform unit cube sampling. It works by rejection sampling a uniformly random leaf node from the array of all octree nodes, then generating a uniform random position within the voxel of the selected leaf node. A key pitfall is that perturbed surface samples might fall outside the octree leaf nodes; this is handled by using the small perturbation standard deviation (r/1024), which is small enough to almost never leave the octree, so the surface sampling routine does not need modification. Not given in the sources. Originated in the "Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding" paper by Mueller et al.. name: Spot Noise (Motion Blurred Particles near Contour Surfaces)
head: Motion blurred particles
body:
Spot noise visualizes 3D velocity fields in a thickened region around a contour surface by rendering motion-blurred ellipsoidal particles, allowing for interactive rotation and animation using standard hardware graphics pipelines. Unlike methods that represent tangential flows on surfaces (such as stream surfaces) or require surface parameterization, this technique operates on contour surfaces of scalar functions that are generally unrelated to the velocity vectors, meaning the flow is not necessarily tangent to the surface. It builds on Near-Surface Point Sampling by using distance-field estimation to restrict particle placement to a specific band around the isosurface. Inputs: A 3D vector field V(x,y,z) defined on a rectilinear lattice. A scalar function f(x,y,z) defined on the same rectilinear lattice. A contour value C defining the surface f(x,y,z) = C. A distance parameter D defining the thickness of the region around the contour. A particle count N per marked cell. A particle radius r. A fading constant k. Outputs: A rendered image containing semi-transparent, motion-blurred ellipsoidal particles overlaid on the contour surface. 1. Lattice Grid: Stores values for f(x,y,z) and the precomputed magnitude of its gradient |
abla f(x,y,z)| at each vertex. |
abla f| is computed via finite differences of neighboring vertex values of f. 2. Cell Marking Array: A boolean flag for each lattice cell indicating if it intersects the region d(x,y,z) < D. A cell is marked if at least one of its vertices is within distance D of the contour surface. 3. Particle Linked List: Stores active particles. Each node contains: Position (x,y,z). Velocity (Vx, Vy, Vz). Age a. Status (active/deleted). D: The maximum distance from the contour surface for particle existence. Must be larger than the lattice cell size for the marking procedure to work efficiently. N: The number of particles randomly inserted in each marked cell. r: The radius of the particle. k: Constant used in the fading calculation. 1. Precompute Gradient Magnitude: For each lattice vertex, approximate the gradient 
abla f using finite differences of neighboring vertex values of f. Store the magnitude |
abla f(x,y,z)|. 2. Mark Cells: Identify all lattice vertices within distance D of the contour surface f(x,y,z)=C. Mark all lattice cells that have at least one marked vertex. Update these markings whenever the user changes C or D. 3. Initialize Particles: For each marked cell, randomly insert N particles within the cell boundaries. Add these particles to the linked list with initial age a=0. 4. Time Step Update (for each frame/animation step): Integration: Move each particle in the linked list using second-order Runge-Kutta integration. Sample velocity V at the particle's current position by trilinearly interpolating from the eight surrounding lattice vertices of the vector field. Boundary Check: If a particle moves into an unmarked cell or out of the data volume, schedule it for deletion. Replenishment: Check that all marked cells still contain N particles. Add new particles or delete excess particles to maintain the count N in each marked cell. 5. Rendering: Render the opaque contour surface first. Render the particles as semi-transparent objects after the opaque objects, combining them with the contour surface in the z-buffer. Particles are all the same color and do not require sorting. To determine if a particle at (x,y,z) is within the valid region, estimate the distance d(x,y,z) from the contour surface f(x,y,z)=C using Levoy's technique: 1. Trilinearly interpolate the scalar value f(x,y,z) from the eight surrounding lattice vertices. 2. Trilinearly interpolate the gradient magnitude |
abla f(x,y,z)| from the eight surrounding lattice vertices. 3. The distance is approximated by: d(x,y,z) =  rac{|f(x,y,z) - C|}{|
abla f(x,y,z)|} (Note: The source text states the quantities are trilinearly interpolated but the specific equation formula was garbled in the provided notes; this is the standard Levoy distance estimation formula implied by the context of using f and |
abla f|.) A particle is rendered only if d(x,y,z) < D. Particles are drawn as blurred ellipses stretched in the direction of motion. A single blurred disk texture is mapped to a 3D rectangle defined by four vertices. Rectangle Vertices: The vertices of the rectangle are located at: P + S + T, \quad P + S - T, \quad P - S - T, \quad P - S + T Where: P is the particle's position vector relative to the viewpoint. V is the particle's velocity vector. r is the particle radius. S and T are orthogonal vectors defining the ellipse axes: S = r  rac{V 	imes P}{|V 	imes P|} T =  rac{V}{|V|} r -  rac{S 	imes P}{|S 	imes P|} 	imes r \quad 	ext{(Corrected interpretation of garbled source)} Source Text: T = V + r -  rac{S 	imes P}{|S 	imes P|}. Interpretation: The source text for T is garbled ("T = V + r -..."). However, it states T is along the velocity direction, and the second term ensures the particle shrinks to a small round dot of radius r when velocity approaches zero or is oriented near the viewing direction. A robust implementation normalizes V for direction and scales by r. The term  rac{S 	imes P}{|S 	imes P|} suggests a correction for perspective or alignment. Given the garbled nature, the core logic is: S is perpendicular to both velocity and view direction (width), and T is primarily along velocity (length) but adjusted to prevent degenerate shapes. Particle Size Factor (b): The size of the particle is proportional to a factor b = s(d), where: s(d) = 1 for small d (close to surface). s(d) decreases continuously to 0 when d reaches D. To handle birth fading, the actual size factor is: b = \min(s(d), k \cdot a) Where a is the age of the particle and k is a constant. This ensures new particles fade in at birth and old particles fade out as they are deleted. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def trilinearinterpolate(grid, x, y, z): """ Interpolate value from 8 surrounding lattice vertices. grid: 3D array of values. x, y, z: float coordinates in lattice space. Returns: interpolated float value. """ # Implementation details omitted for brevity; standard trilinear interpolation pass def computegradientmagnitude(gridf, x, y, z): """ Compute |grad f| using finite differences. """ # Finite difference approximation pass def getparticlesizefactor(d, D, age, k): """ Calculate size factor b. s(d) decreases from 1 to 0 as d goes from 0 to D. """ # Linear fade for s(d) as per description sd = max(0.0, 1.0 - d / D) return min(sd, k age) def renderspotnoise(particles, viewpoint, contoursurface, vectorfield, scalarfield, C, D, N, r, k): """ Main rendering loop for a single frame/time step. """ # 1. Update Particle Positions (Physics) newparticles = [] particlestodelete = [] for particle in particles: # Second-order Runge-Kutta integration # k1 = V(particle.pos) # k2 = V(particle.pos + 0.5 dt k1) # particle.pos += dt k2 # particle.vel = V(particle.pos) # particle.age += dt # Boundary Check # Estimate distance d from contour fval = trilinearinterpolate(scalarfield, particle.pos) gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(scalarfield, particle.pos) if gradmag == 0: d = 1e9 # Avoid division by zero else: d = abs(fval - C) / gradmag # Check if in marked region (simplified: check distance and volume bounds) # In a full implementation, check if particle is in a marked cell if d >= D or not involume(particle.pos): particlestodelete.append(particle) else: newparticles.append(particle) # Remove deleted particles for p in particlestodelete: particles.remove(p) # 2. Replenish Particles # Ensure N particles per marked cell # This requires tracking particles per cell or re-scanning marked cells # For simplicity, we assume a global replenishment strategy or cell-based list # The source says: "check that all marked cells still have N particles" # Implementation would involve a grid of particle lists or spatial hash # 3. Render # Draw opaque contour surface first drawcontoursurface(contoursurface) # Draw particles for particle in newparticles: # Calculate shape vectors S and T # P is position relative to viewpoint P = particle.pos - viewpoint.pos V = particle.vel # Handle degenerate cases (V=0 or V parallel to P) if norm(V) < 1e-6 or norm(cross(V, P)) < 1e-6: # Draw as small dot drawdisk(particle.pos, r) else: S = r normalize(cross(V, P)) # T calculation from source: T = V + r - (S x P) / |S x P| # This source formula is garbled. # Logical interpretation: T is along V, scaled by r, with correction Vnorm = normalize(V) # Correction term to shrink when aligned with view correction = cross(S, P) if norm(correction) > 1e-6: correction = normalize(correction) else: correction = Vnorm # Fallback # Reconstructing T based on "T is along velocity direction" # and "shrinks to small round dot" # A common approach for motion blur is T = r Vnorm # The source's specific garbled formula likely intended: # T = r Vnorm - (some term) # Given the ambiguity, we use a standard motion blur vector T = r Vnorm # Define rectangle vertices v1 = particle.pos + S + T v2 = particle.pos + S - T v3 = particle.pos - S - T v4 = particle.pos - S + T # Calculate size factor fval = trilinearinterpolate(scalarfield, particle.pos) gradmag = computegradientmagnitude(scalarfield, particle.pos) d = abs(fval - C) / gradmag if gradmag > 0 else 1e9 b = getparticlesizefactor(d, D, particle.age, k) drawblurredrectangle(v1, v2, v3, v4, b) Time Complexity: Particle movement: O(N{total}) per time step, where N{total} is the total number of particles. Distance estimation: O(1) per particle (trilinear interpolation). Replenishment: Depends on implementation, but checking marked cells and particle counts is O(N{cells}) or O(N{total}) depending on spatial indexing. Memory Complexity: O(N{total}) for the particle linked list. O(N{cells}) for the cell marking array. O(V) for the lattice grids (V is number of lattice vertices). Performance: The method uses hardware rendering for interactive speed, allowing real-time rotation and animation. On SGI workstations (Elanm graphics, Onyxm workstation), it achieved real-time rotation and particle motion on small data sets and interactive performance on large data sets. The use of a single blurred disk texture mapped to a 3D rectangle is efficient for hardware rasterization. Strengths: Interactive performance. Does not require surface parameterization. Handles non-tangential flows naturally. Simple compositing (no sorting required for same-color particles). Limitations: Particles may overlap and obscure each other (though less so than static icons). Requires a thickened region around the surface, which can be memory intensive if D is large. Garbled formulas in the original source for T and the distance equation require careful implementation interpretation. Origin: The method was proposed by Nelson Max, Roger Crawfis, Charles Grant, and Lawrence from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. History: It was presented as one of four techniques for visualizing vector fields only near surfaces, aiming to overcome the overlap and occlusion issues of traditional 3D vector icons. The method builds on earlier work by Levoy for distance estimation and van Wijk for motion-blurred particles, but adapts them for contour surfaces rather than stream surfaces. Usage: Implemented in C++ using SGI's Invent2 for the user interface. It was used to visualize airflow through a HEPA filter and tornado velocity data sets. Visualizing 3D velocity fields near contour surfaces. Revision 1, https://digital.library.unt.edu/ark:/67531/metadc1395286/?q=vector field volume rendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Surface Sampling for NeRF Rendering
head: Random point sampling on mesh triangles for NeRF input
body: Generates random points on the surface of a 3D object (specifically on triangles) to be used as input for a neural network reflectance model. It differs from its siblings by focusing on uniform spatial distribution over mesh geometry for training data generation, rather than foot-point projection or edge-based sampling. Inputs: A mesh defined by vertices and triangular faces. Outputs: A list of 3D points on the surface. Data Structures: vertices: Array of shape (N, 3), where N is the number of vertices. faces: Array of shape (M, 3), where M is the number of triangles. Each row contains indices into vertices. Steps: 1. For each face in the surface, extract vertices v1, v2, v3. 2. Generate two random numbers a and b between 0 and 1. 3. If a + b > 1, swap them: a, b = 1 - a, 1 - b. 4. Calculate c = 1 - a - b. 5. Compute the point as a convex combination of the vertices: point = a \cdot v1 + b \cdot v2 + c \cdot v3. 6. Append the point to the list. 7. Repeat for the specified number of samples per face. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def samplesurfacepoints(vertices, faces, samplesperface): """ Generate random points uniformly distributed on the surface of a mesh. Args: vertices: np.ndarray of shape (N, 3) faces: np.ndarray of shape (M, 3) with vertex indices samplesperface: int, number of points to sample per triangle Returns: np.ndarray of shape (M samplesperface, 3) """ allpoints = [] for face in faces: v1 = vertices[face[0]] v2 = vertices[face[1]] v3 = vertices[face[2]] for in range(samplesperface): # Generate two random numbers between 0 and 1 a = np.random.rand() b = np.random.rand() # Ensure uniform distribution over the triangle if a + b > 1: a = 1 - a b = 1 - b c = 1 - a - b # Convex combination point = a v1 + b v2 + c v3 allpoints.append(point) return np.array(allpoints) Parameters: samplesperface: Number of points to generate per triangle. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating point errors in random number generation are negligible for typical mesh scales. Boundaries: The method assumes valid triangle geometry (non-degenerate faces). Degenerate triangles (zero area) will produce points along a line or point, which may bias the distribution if not filtered. Creates a training dataset by sampling points on surfaces, computing their colors via ray tracing, and encoding view/light directions as spherical coordinates (theta, phi). It differs from the base method by adding directional encoding for view and light vectors, enabling the neural network to learn view-dependent reflectance. Choose this when training a NeRF-based reflectance model that requires explicit angular encoding of illumination and viewing geometry. Steps: 1. For each visible surface, sample 20 points. 2. For each point, compute the color using raytracer.calculatecoloratpoint. 3. Compute camera difference vector cam\diff = camera\position - point. 4. Calculate \theta{cam}: \theta{cam} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(cam\diff[1], cam\diff[0])). 5. Calculate \phi{cam}: \phi{cam} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(cam\diff[2], \sqrt{cam\diff[0]^2 + cam\diff[1]^2})). 6. Compute light difference vector light\diff = light.position - point. 7. Calculate \theta{light}: \theta{light} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(light\diff[1], light\diff[0])). 8. Calculate \phi{light}: \phi{light} = \text{degrees}(\arctan2(light\diff[2], \sqrt{light\diff[0]^2 + light\diff[1]^2})). 9. Append the point, view directions [\theta{cam}, \phi{cam}], light directions [\theta{light}, \phi{light}], and color to their respective lists. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def encodesphericaldirections(point, cameraposition, lightposition): """ Encode view and light directions as spherical coordinates (theta, phi). Args: point: np.ndarray of shape (3,) cameraposition: np.ndarray of shape (3,) lightposition: np.ndarray of shape (3,) Returns: tuple: (viewdirs, lightdirs) where each is np.ndarray of shape (2,) """ # Camera direction camdiff = cameraposition - point thetacam = np.degrees(np.arctan2(camdiff[1], camdiff[0])) phicam = np.degrees(np.arctan2(camdiff[2], np.sqrt(camdiff[0]2 + camdiff[1]2))) viewdirs = np.array([thetacam, phicam]) # Light direction lightdiff = lightposition - point thetalight = np.degrees(np.arctan2(lightdiff[1], lightdiff[0])) philight = np.degrees(np.arctan2(lightdiff[2], np.sqrt(lightdiff[0]2 + lightdiff[1]2))) lightdirs = np.array([thetalight, philight]) return viewdirs, lightdirs Time and memory complexity: Linear in the number of triangles and samples per triangle. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with mesh complexity. Strengths: Simple, uniform sampling over mesh surfaces. Limitations: Does not account for surface curvature or importance; may require many samples for high-frequency details. When to use: When generating training data for reflectance models where uniform spatial coverage is sufficient. When not: When importance sampling or adaptive sampling is required. Origin: Unofficial implementation in the NeRF-Renderer repository. History and development: Used in the context of training neural reflectance fields by providing surface points with associated view and light directions. Where it is used: In research and experimental implementations of NeRF-based reflectance rendering. matthxie/NeRF-Renderer, https://github.com/matthxie/NeRF-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NeRF-Based Reflectance Rendering
head: ObjectReflectanceNeRF Rendering
body: NeRF-Based Reflectance Rendering is a technique that modifies the base color of a 3D object's surface by applying a neural network reflectance model. It operates on points sampled from visible surfaces to account for view-dependent and light-dependent color variations. It differs from standard NeRF rendering by focusing on surface-level reflectance modification rather than volumetric density and color estimation, building on Surface Sampling for NeRF Rendering. Inputs: cameraposition: 3D vector. lightposition: 3D vector. object3d: 3D object containing visible surfaces (triangles) with vertices and normals. resolution: Tuple (height, width). f: Focal length (implicit in projection formula). Outputs: buffer: Image of shape (height, width, 3) containing modified colors. Data Structures: Surface: Contains vertices (N, 3), normals (N, 3), and faces. ObjectReflectanceNeRF: A neural network model. Steps: 1. Initialize buffer of shape (height, width, 3) with zeros. 2. Identify visible surfaces from object3d relative to cameraposition. 3. For each visible surface: a. Sample 80 points on the surface. b. Compute view directions: viewdirs = cameraposition - points. Normalize along the last axis. c. Compute light directions: lightdirs = lightposition - points. Normalize along the last axis. d. Interpolate normals. Note: A common pitfall is interpolating by taking the mean of all surface normals and tiling, which ignores local geometry variation. e. Convert points, normals, viewdirs, and basecolors to PyTorch tensors. f. Pass tensors through the ObjectReflectanceNeRF model (or ReflectanceNeRF) within a torch.nograd() block to get modifiedcolors. g. Project each point to image coordinates: d = point - camera\position x = \text{int}(f \cdot d[0] / d[2] + width / 2) y = \text{int}(f \cdot d[1] / d[2] + height / 2) h. If 0 \le x < width and 0 \le y < height, set buffer[y, x] = modifiedcolor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def renderreflectancenerf(model, object3d, cameraposition, lightposition, resolution, f): height, width = resolution buffer = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) # Get visible surfaces and sample points # Note: Actual surface sampling logic depends on VectorObject implementation pointslist = [] viewdirslist = [] lightdirslist = [] basecolorslist = [] for surface in object3d.visiblesurfaces(cameraposition): # Sample 80 points on the surface points = samplepointsonsurface(surface, numsamples=80) # Compute directions viewdirs = cameraposition - points viewdirs = viewdirs / np.linalg.norm(viewdirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) lightdirs = lightposition - points lightdirs = lightdirs / np.linalg.norm(lightdirs, axis=-1, keepdims=True) # Interpolate normals # Pitfall: Avoid simple mean tiling normals = interpolatenormals(surface, points) # Get base colors (e.g., from vertex colors or texture) basecolors = getbasecolors(surface, points) pointslist.append(points) viewdirslist.append(viewdirs) lightdirslist.append(lightdirs) basecolorslist.append(basecolors) if not pointslist: return buffer # Concatenate all points allpoints = np.concatenate(pointslist) allviewdirs = np.concatenate(viewdirslist) alllightdirs = np.concatenate(lightdirslist) allbasecolors = np.concatenate(basecolorslist) # Convert to tensors positions = torch.FloatTensor(allpoints) viewdirs = torch.FloatTensor(allviewdirs) lightdirs = torch.FloatTensor(alllightdirs) basecolors = torch.FloatTensor(allbasecolors) # Render with torch.nograd(): modifiedcolors = model(positions, viewdirs, lightdirs, basecolors) modifiedcolors = modifiedcolors.numpy() # Project and fill buffer d = allpoints - cameraposition xs = (f d[:, 0] / d[:, 2] + width / 2).astype(int) ys = (f d[:, 1] / d[:, 2] + height / 2).astype(int) for i in range(len(allpoints)): x, y = xs[i], ys[i] if 0 <= x < width and 0 <= y < height: buffer[y, x] = modifiedcolors[i] return buffer A variant that separates geometric/lighting feature encoding from color modification using a two-branch MLP architecture. It decouples spatial/lighting feature extraction from color modulation, allowing the base color to only affect the final color modifier stage rather than the initial feature encoding. Layout: Encoder input is (N, 9) [position(3), viewdir(3), lightdir(3)]. Encoder output is (N, 256). Color network input is (N, 259) [encoderoutput(256), basecolor(3)]. Color network output is (N, 3). Step: Concatenate encoder output (256D) with base color (3D) to form a 259D vector. Return the Sigmoid output directly as the modified color. Parameter: hiddendim: Number of neurons per hidden layer. Default is 256. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is dominated by the neural network inference for each sampled point. With 80 points per surface and potentially many surfaces, this can be computationally expensive compared to simple shading. Memory usage is proportional to the number of sampled points and the size of the render buffer. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Captures complex view-dependent and light-dependent reflectance properties. Limitations: Interpolation of normals by taking the mean of all surface normals and tiling ignores local geometry variation, leading to artifacts. When to use: When accurate reflectance modeling is required for synthetic data generation or specific material rendering. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical or when simple shading suffices. Originated from the NeRF-Renderer project by matthxie. It extends the concept of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) to specifically model reflectance on surfaces rather than volumetric properties. NeRF-Renderer, https://github.com/matthxie/NeRF-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Surfel Parameterization from Mesh Sampling
head: Point Cloud Surfel Estimation, Surfel Parameterization
body:
Surfel parameterization from mesh sampling is a method to estimate surfel parameters (tangent vectors and scales) for a point cloud sampled from a triangle mesh, where point positions and face normals are obtained directly from sampling, and remaining parameters are estimated from the local neighborhood structure. It builds on Surface Point Sampling for SDFs by providing the geometric basis for rendering sampled points as splats. It differs from Near-Surface Point Sampling and SDF-guided Sampling by focusing on the estimation of local tangent frames and anisotropic scales from the discrete point cloud neighborhood rather than generating the points themselves. It differs from Bidirectional Projective Sampling by using local PCA or isotropic heuristics for frame alignment rather than projective geometry from multiple views. Inputs: A triangle mesh. Outputs: A point cloud where each point has a position, a face normal, two tangent vectors, and two scale parameters (defining the surfel kernel). Data Structures: Point Cloud: A list of points. Each point i stores: pos: 3D position vector \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. normal: 3D face normal vector \mathbf{n}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit length). tangent1: 3D tangent vector \mathbf{t}{i,1} \in \mathbb{R}^3. tangent2: 3D tangent vector \mathbf{t}{i,2} \in \mathbb{R}^3. scale1: Scalar scale s{i,1} \in \mathbb{R}^+. scale2: Scalar scale s{i,2} \in \mathbb{R}^+. Spatial Acceleration Structure: A spatial index (e.g., KD-tree, octree) built on the sampled points to enable efficient nearest-neighbor queries. The sources note that the same structure is used for optimization initialization and splitting criteria. Steps: 1. Sample Points and Normals: Sample points from the triangle mesh. For each sample, record the 3D position \mathbf{p}i and the face normal \mathbf{n}i. This is done directly from the sampling procedure. 2. Estimate Tangent Vectors and Scales: For each point \mathbf{p}i, estimate the tangent frame and scales using one of two strategies: Isotropic Scaling or Anisotropic Scaling. Strategy A: Isotropic Scaling 1. Construct Tangent Vectors: Create an orthonormal basis for the tangent plane using the normal \mathbf{n}i. A standard orthonormal frame construction is used. Let \mathbf{n}i = (nx, ny, nz). If |nz| < 0.9, choose \mathbf{a} = (0, 0, 1). Else, choose \mathbf{a} = (1, 0, 0). \mathbf{t}{i,1} = 	ext{normalize}(\mathbf{a} - (\mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{n}i)\mathbf{n}i). \mathbf{t}{i,2} = \mathbf{n}i 	imes \mathbf{t}{i,1}. 2. Estimate Scale: Calculate the mean distance to orientation-aware nearest neighbors. Query the spatial acceleration structure for the k nearest neighbors of \mathbf{p}i (where k is a small constant, e.g., 10-20). Filter neighbors to ensure their normals are "orientation-aware" (compatible with \mathbf{n}i, typically \mathbf{n}j \cdot \mathbf{n}i > 0 or similar threshold). Compute distances dj = ||\mathbf{p}j - \mathbf{p}i|| for compatible neighbors. Set s{i,1} = s{i,2} = 	ext{mean}(dj). Strategy B: Anisotropic Scaling 1. Identify Compatible Neighbors: Query the spatial acceleration structure for the k nearest neighbors of \mathbf{p}i. Filter these neighbors to keep only those with compatible normal orientation (e.g., \mathbf{n}j \cdot \mathbf{n}i > 	au, where 	au is a threshold like 0.5 or 0.9). 2. Project to Tangent Plane: For each compatible neighbor \mathbf{p}j, compute the vector \mathbf{v}j = \mathbf{p}j - \mathbf{p}i. Project \mathbf{v}j onto the tangent plane defined by \mathbf{n}i: \mathbf{v}{j, 	ext{proj}} = \mathbf{v}j - (\mathbf{v}j \cdot \mathbf{n}i)\mathbf{n}i 3. 2D PCA: Construct a local 2D coordinate system for the tangent plane. Let \mathbf{u}1 be an arbitrary unit vector orthogonal to \mathbf{n}i (e.g., via cross product with a world up vector, then orthogonalized). Let \mathbf{u}2 = \mathbf{n}i 	imes \mathbf{u}1. For each projected vector \mathbf{v}{j, 	ext{proj}}, compute coordinates (xj, yj): xj = \mathbf{v}{j, 	ext{proj}} \cdot \mathbf{u}1 yj = \mathbf{v}{j, 	ext{proj}} \cdot \mathbf{u}2 Compute the 2 	imes 2 covariance matrix C of the points (xj, yj): C =  egin{bmatrix} 	ext{Var}(x) & 	ext{Cov}(x,y) \ 	ext{Cov}(x,y) & 	ext{Var}(y) \end{bmatrix} Where 	ext{Var}(x) =  rac{1}{N} \sum (xj -  ar{x})^2, etc., and N is the number of compatible neighbors. 4. Eigendecomposition: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and eigenvectors \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2 of C. Assume \lambda1 \ge \lambda2 \ge 0. The eigenvectors \mathbf{e}1 = (e{1x}, e{1y}) and \mathbf{e}2 = (e{2x}, e{2y}) define the principal directions in the local 2D tangent space. 5. Define Tangent Vectors and Scales: The tangent vectors in 3D are: \mathbf{t}{i,1} = e{1x}\mathbf{u}1 + e{1y}\mathbf{u}2 \mathbf{t}{i,2} = e{2x}\mathbf{u}1 + e{2y}\mathbf{u}2 The scales are derived from the eigenvalues. Typically, the scale is proportional to the square root of the eigenvalue (representing the standard deviation of the point distribution along that axis): s{i,1} = \alpha \sqrt{\lambda1} s{i,2} = \alpha \sqrt{\lambda2} Where \alpha is a scaling factor (e.g., 1.0 or a constant related to the kernel width). The sources state eigenvalues determine anisotropic scales. Parameters: k: Number of nearest neighbors for PCA/isotropic estimation. Not given in the sources. 	au: Normal compatibility threshold. Not given in the sources. \alpha: Scale multiplier for eigenvalues. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sharp Edges: Isotropic scaling can produce minor visual artifacts at sharp geometric edges where an isotropic kernel does not conform well to the local surface curvature. Degenerate Neighbors: If fewer than 3 compatible neighbors are found for PCA, the covariance matrix is singular. A fallback to isotropic scaling or a default scale is required. Computational Cost: Anisotropic scaling has higher computational overhead and memory consumption due to the eigendecomposition and neighbor filtering. A method to compute curvatures (Gaussian and Mean) and local differential geometry for a visible oriented point (p, v) using only the directional distance field d(p, v) and its derivatives with respect to p. It constructs a local coordinate system at the surface point q = p + d(p, v)v by choosing two tangent vectors tx, ty \in Tq(S) such that ||t\alpha||2 = 1 and tx^T ty = 0. In practice, this is done by sampling Gaussian vectors and extracting an orthogonal tangent basis. The surface is reparameterized near q0 via S(x, y) = q0 + x tx + y ty + fS(x, y)n0, where x and y control position on the tangent plane, or equivalently p(u) = p0 + x tx + y ty where u = (x, y). The first-order derivatives of the surface at u=0 are \partiali S|{u=0} = ti + (
ablap d(p, v0) ti) v0, where i \in \{x, y\}. The metric tensor (first fundamental form) is g{ij} = \partiali S^T \partialj S = \delta{ij} + ci cj + ci v0^T tj + cj v0^T ti, where ck = 
ablap d tk. In theory, since 
ablap d is parallel to normal n and orthogonal to tangents, cx = cy = 0, so g{ij} = \delta{ij}. In practice, use the theoretical value g = I2. The shape tensor (second fundamental form) is \Pi{ij} = (tj^T Hp[d] ti) n0^T v0, where Hp[d] is the Hessian of d with respect to p at u=0, and n0 is the surface normal at q0. Gaussian curvature is CK = \det(\Pi) / \det(g) and Mean curvature is CH = 	ext{tr}(\Pi g^{-1}). Time Complexity: Isotropic scaling is O(k) per point for neighbor query and mean calculation, where k is the number of neighbors. Anisotropic scaling is O(k \log N) or O(k) depending on the spatial structure, plus O(1) for 2D PCA (constant size matrix), but with a higher constant factor due to eigendecomposition and projection. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the point cloud and spatial structure, where N is the number of points. Anisotropic scaling requires storing neighbor indices and temporary projection arrays. Performance: The isotropic variant is computationally efficient and available as a drop-in replacement when performance is critical. The anisotropic variant is used for quality in experiments but incurs higher overhead. Strengths: Anisotropic scaling eliminates edge artifacts observed with isotropic kernels by adapting the kernel shape to the local point distribution. Limitations: Isotropic scaling produces artifacts at sharp edges. Anisotropic scaling is slower and uses more memory. The method originates from the 3DSS (3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering) paper. It is used in inverse rendering pipelines to prepare point clouds for splatting-based rendering and relighting. The local differential geometry computation is described in the context of Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3594225, fetched 2026-10-29

name: SDF-guided Sampling
head: Shao et al. SDF-guided Sampling, Surface-guided Sampling Strategy
body: SDF-guided Sampling is a surface-aware sampling strategy that uses a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to estimate ray-surface intersections, followed by fine-grained sampling around the intersection point to accelerate rendering and emphasize the relationship between surface and radiance fields. It differs from standard NeRF sampling by reducing the number of required sampling points through early surface localization, and from pure mesh-based methods by retaining the flexibility of implicit field evaluation without requiring explicit mesh vertex interpolation. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Depth bounds [tn, tf] defining the integration interval along the ray. Surface field function s(x), which outputs a scalar value for any point x. Parameters: Ns: Number of uniform sampling points for initial coarse sampling. Nr: Number of sampling points for fine-grained sampling around the surface. \delta: Interval size for fine-grained sampling around the intersection. Threshold T = 0.5 for determining intersection. Outputs: A set of sample points concentrated around the estimated surface intersection, used to evaluate the radiance field. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required beyond the ray parameters and the implicit field function s(x); the method relies on querying the field at discrete points. Steps: 1. Coarse Uniform Sampling: Generate Ns points uniformly distributed along the ray within the depth bounds [tn, tf]. The i-th point xi is calculated as: xi = o + ti d where ti are uniformly spaced values in [tn, tf]. 2. Intersection Estimation: Query the surface field value s(xi) for each coarse sample point. Identify the first intersection position t{int} by finding the smallest ti such that the surface field value exceeds the threshold: t{int} = \min \{ ti \mid s(o + ti d) \ge 0.5 \}. 3. Fine-Grained Sampling: Perform fine-grained sampling around the intersection in an interval of \delta with Nr sampling points to consider the radiance field surrounding the real surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linspace(start, stop, num): """Generate num evenly spaced values over [start, stop].""" step = (stop - start) / (num - 1) if num > 1 else 0 return [start + i step for i in range(num)] def sdfguidedsampling(o, d, tn, tf, sfield, Ns, Nr, delta, threshold=0.5): """ Perform SDF-guided sampling along a ray. Args: o: Ray origin (3D vector) d: Ray direction (3D vector, assumed normalized) tn: Near depth bound (float) tf: Far depth bound (float) sfield: Function that returns surface field value s(x) for point x Ns: Number of coarse sampling points Nr: Number of fine sampling points delta: Interval size for fine sampling around intersection threshold: Threshold for surface intersection detection (default 0.5) Returns: List of sample points (3D vectors) concentrated around the surface """ # Assumes standard vector addition and scalar multiplication # Step 1: Coarse uniform sampling tcoarse = linspace(tn, tf, Ns) pointscoarse = [o + t d for t in tcoarse] # Step 2: Find first intersection tint = None for i in range(Ns): ti = tcoarse[i] xi = pointscoarse[i] sval = sfield(xi) if sval >= threshold: tint = ti break if tint is None: return [] # Step 3: Fine-grained sampling around intersection tfine = linspace(tint - delta, tint + delta, Nr) pointsfine = [o + t d for t in tfine] return pointsfine Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Intersection: If the ray does not intersect the surface within [tn, tf] (i.e., no s(xi) \ge 0.5), the method yields no fine samples. Threshold Sensitivity: The threshold of 0.5 is specific to the DoubleField formulation. Other SDF representations might use 0.0 (zero-level set). The implementer must ensure the threshold matches the normalization of the provided SDF field. Discrete Sampling: The intersection detection relies on discrete coarse samples. If the surface is thin or the coarse sampling is too sparse, the intersection might be missed or inaccurately located. Time Complexity: Dominated by Ns queries to the SDF field for coarse sampling, plus Nr queries for fine sampling, totaling Ns + Nr field evaluations. Memory Complexity: Auxiliary memory scales linearly with the number of sample points, O(Ns + Nr), as it only stores the generated coordinates. Performance: Reported to be much faster than standard NeRF sampling due to fewer sampling points needed for integration. Strengths: Accelerates rendering by focusing samples on the surface; emphasizes the relationship between surface and radiance fields, facilitating training and fine-tuning. Limitations: Requires a well-defined SDF field; performance depends on the accuracy of the SDF; may fail if the surface is not well-represented by the SDF threshold. When to Use: When a high-quality SDF is available and rendering speed is a priority, particularly for human reconstruction and rendering where surface detail is critical. The method was proposed by Shao et al. in the context of the DoubleField network, which bridges neural surface and radiance fields for high-fidelity human reconstruction and rendering. It was introduced to accelerate the rendering process and strengthen the learned relationship between the surface and radiance fields. The approach is part of a broader trend of using implicit representations (SDFs) to guide sampling in neural rendering, as noted in recent surveys of learning-based 3D representations. Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26 DoubleField: Bridging the Neural Surface and Radiance Fields for High-fidelity Human Reconstruction and Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01541, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Bidirectional Projective Sampling
head: Bidirectional projection, Projective sampling with emitter-emitted seed rays
body: Bidirectional Projective Sampling is a boundary sampling method for physics-based differentiable rendering that generates seed rays from both sensors and emitters to initialize a guiding structure, addressing inefficiencies when scenes contain small-area lights at a distance. It improves upon Zhang et al.'s projective sampling by incorporating rays emitted directly from small-area emitters into the seed ray set during the projection operation, ensuring all successfully projected rays contribute to the guiding structure regardless of emitter size. Unlike previous methods that rely solely on sensor-spawned rays, which have a near-zero probability of intersecting small-area emitters, this method guarantees intersection by explicitly sampling from the emitter, thereby maximizing contribution to the boundary integral. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Scene geometry (triangular meshes), emitter definitions (triangular meshes with intensity/distance properties), sensor/camera parameters, differentiating geometry (the shape being optimized or differentiated), and a target number of seed rays N. Outputs: An initialized guiding structure containing contributions to the boundary integral, ready for importance sampling. Data Structures: Guiding Structure: A data structure storing accumulated contributions from projected rays to support importance sampling of path segments. Seed Rays: Defined by origin \mathbf{o}, direction \boldsymbol{\omega}, and source type ('sensor' or 'emitter'). Origins remain fixed during projection; directions are determined by the projection result. Formulas: The method estimates the local formulation of the boundary integral derivative: \frac{\partial I}{\partial \pi} = \int{\partial \mathcal{A}} \int{S^2} Li(\mathbf{x}b, \boldsymbol{\omega}) Wi(\mathbf{x}b, \boldsymbol{\omega}) \sin \phi \left(\frac{\partial \pi \mathbf{x}b}{\partial \pi} \cdot \mathbf{n}b\right) d\boldsymbol{\omega} dl(\mathbf{x}b) + \int{\mathcal{A}} \int{S^1} Li(\mathbf{x}b, \phi) Wi(\mathbf{x}b, \phi) \kappa(\phi) \left(\frac{\partial \pi \mathbf{x}b}{\partial \pi} \cdot \mathbf{n}b\right) d\phi dA(\mathbf{x}b) Where: \pi: Geometric parameters being differentiated. \mathcal{A}: The differentiating geometry surface. \partial \mathcal{A}: The boundary of the differentiating geometry. \mathbf{x}b: A point on the boundary. \boldsymbol{\omega}: Direction in S^2. Li: Incident radiance. Wi: Weight function. \phi: Angle. \mathbf{n}b: Normal at \mathbf{x}b. \kappa(\phi): Curvature-related term. Parameters: Ray Split Ratio: 30% of seed rays are emitted by emitters, 70% are spawned from the sensor. Inverse Rendering Remeshing Interval: Geometry is intermittently remeshed every 20 iterations. Inverse Rendering Sample Doubling Interval: The number of samples per pixel is doubled every 200 iterations. Numbered Steps: 1. Assign Rays to Emitters: Determine the number of rays each emitter must generate based on its intensity and distance from the differentiating shape. Closer and stronger emitters receive more rays. 2. Sample Emitter Points: For each emitter ray, sample a triangle on the emitter proportional to its area, then uniformly sample a point within that triangle to serve as the starting point (origin) for the seed ray. 3. Sample Geometry Points: Determine the endpoint of the seed ray by selecting a triangle on the shape being differentiated based on its area and uniformly sampling a point within that triangle. 4. Generate Emitter Rays: Create seed rays connecting the sampled emitter point to the sampled geometry point. 5. Generate Sensor Rays: Generate seed rays from the sensor side. These rays must directly hit the background plane without intersecting any other geometries as the first ray segment. 6. Combine Rays: Combine the emitter-emitted rays and sensor-spawned rays. Use the specified split ratio (30% emitter, 70% sensor). 7. Reflect Sensor Rays: For sensor rays that hit the background plane, reflect them. These reflected rays affect the geometry being differentiated as the second ray segment. 8. Project Rays: Project the adjusted seed rays onto the geometric boundaries. Use JUMP and WALK strategies for triangular meshes to ensure tangency. Origins remain fixed; directions are determined by the projection results. Filter contributions: Only projected rays that intersect the scene emitter (small-area light) are kept to contribute to the guiding structure. For emitter-emitted rays, all successfully projected rays contribute. 9. Initialize Guiding Structure: Compute the locations of the projected rays within the guiding structure and evaluate their contributions using the integrand in eq. (7) to initialize the guiding structure. 10. Importance Sampling: Perform importance sampling of path segments from the initialized guiding structure, complete the segments into full paths, and evaluate their contributions to the boundary integral. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Parameterization Artifacts: Current state-of-the-art boundary sampling methods parameterize the 3D boundary sample space with the first dimension representing mesh edges and the remaining two dimensions representing unit directions. This 1D edge parameterization breaks the continuous connectivity of silhouette edges, causing sparse and high-frequency features in the guiding structure despite the underlying sample space being intrinsically smooth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import random import math class Ray: def init(self, origin, direction, source): self.origin = origin self.direction = direction self.source = source # 'sensor' or 'emitter' def bidirectionalprojectivesampling(sceneemitters, differentiatinggeometry, camera, numseedrays): # Step 1: Assign rays to emitters based on intensity and distance emitterweights = {} totalweight = 0.0 for emitter in sceneemitters: dist = min(math.sqrt(sum((emitter.center[i] - v[i])2 for i in range(3))) for v in differentiatinggeometry.vertices) weight = emitter.intensity / (dist dist) emitterweights[emitter] = weight totalweight += weight targetemitterrays = int(numseedrays 0.3) emitterassignments = {} remaining = targetemitterrays for emitter, weight in emitterweights.items(): count = int(targetemitterrays (weight / totalweight)) emitterassignments[emitter] = count remaining -= count for i, emitter in enumerate(emitterweights.keys()): if remaining > 0: emitterassignments[emitter] += 1 remaining -= 1 emitterrays = [] # Steps 2, 3, 4: Generate emitter-emitted seed rays for emitter, count in emitterassignments.items(): for in range(count): emittertriangle = sampletrianglebyarea(emitter.triangles) origin = uniformsampletriangle(emittertriangle) geotriangle = sampletrianglebyarea(differentiatinggeometry.triangles) endpoint = uniformsampletriangle(geotriangle) direction = normalize(endpoint - origin) emitterrays.append(Ray(origin, direction, 'emitter')) # Step 5: Generate sensor-spawned seed rays sensorraycount = int(numseedrays 0.7) sensorrays = [] for in range(sensorraycount): ray = generateprimaryrayfromcamera(camera) if ray.intersectsbackgroundplane() and not ray.intersectsgeometry(differentiatinggeometry): sensorrays.append(ray) # Step 6: Combine rays allseedrays = emitterrays + sensorrays # Step 7: Reflect sensor rays that hit background for i, ray in enumerate(allseedrays): if ray.source == 'sensor' and ray.intersectsbackgroundplane(): allseedrays[i] = reflectray(ray, backgroundplane) # Step 8: Project rays onto geometric boundaries guidingstructure = {} for ray in allseedrays: # Project using JUMP and WALK strategies for tangency projectedray = projectrayontoboundary(ray, differentiatinggeometry) # Filter contributions: Only projected rays that intersect the scene emitter are kept # For emitter-emitted rays, all successfully projected rays contribute if ray.source == 'emitter' or projectedray.intersectsemitter(sceneemitters): # Step 9: Compute location and evaluate contribution contribution = evaluateboundaryintegralcontribution(projectedray, differentiatinggeometry) guidingstructure[projectedray.location] = contribution # Step 10: Importance sampling is performed later using the structure return guidingstructure def sampletrianglebyarea(triangles): areas = [computetrianglearea(t) for t in triangles] totalarea = sum(areas) r = random.uniform(0, totalarea) cumulative = 0.0 for t, area in zip(triangles, areas): cumulative += area if r <= cumulative: return t return triangles[-1] def uniformsampletriangle(triangle): u, v = random.uniform(0, 1), random.uniform(0, 1) if u + v > 1: u = 1 - u v = 1 - v return triangle.v0 + u (triangle.v1 - triangle.v0) + v (triangle.v2 - triangle.v0) def computetrianglearea(triangle): return 0.5 length(cross(triangle.v1 - triangle.v0, triangle.v2 - triangle.v0)) def projectrayontoboundary(ray, geometry): # JUMP and WALK strategies for triangular meshes to ensure tangency # Source does not specify implementation details. pass def evaluateboundaryintegralcontribution(projectedray, geometry): # Evaluates contribution using the integrand from the boundary integral formula # Source does not specify implementation details. pass def generateprimaryrayfromcamera(camera): # Standard camera ray generation pass def reflectray(ray, plane): # Standard reflection calculation pass def normalize(v): return [x / math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) for x in v] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def length(v): return math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in v)) Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: The method achieves lower variance gradients in the forward differentiable rendering process and better geometry reconstruction quality in the inverse-rendering results compared to state-of-the-art projective-sampling-based methods. Hardware: Experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA RTX 3090 graphics card. Intersection Queries: Performed using OptiX. Scaling: The number of samples per pixel is doubled every 200 iterations during optimization. Strengths: Improves efficiency in scenes with small-area emitters (e.g., mobile phone flashlights) by ensuring rays intersect the emitter, which previous methods struggled with. Limitations: The underlying guiding structures for triangle meshes can still suffer from sparse and high-frequency features due to the 1D edge parameterization of the boundary sample space. When to Use: Use for differentiable rendering of geometry with small-area lights to improve guiding structure quality for importance sampling. When Not to Use: Not explicitly stated, but less beneficial for scenes with large-area emitters where sensor rays are sufficient. Origin: The method was proposed as an augmentation of previous projective-sampling-based boundary-sampling methods, specifically improving upon Zhang et al.'s method. History: It was developed to address the inefficiency of previous methods in scenes with small-area emitters, where the probability of sensor-spawned rays intersecting the emitter approaches zero as the emitter size approaches a point light. Usage: Implemented on the cudaadrgb backend from Mitsuba 3 using the Dr. Jit framework for forward/reverse-mode AD and GPU kernel compilation. Bidirectional projective sampling for physics-based differentiable rendering, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.vrih.2025.05.001, fetched 2026-10-27

name: Explicit Sampling for Point Cloud Extraction
head: PC extraction from DDF, SI3DR evaluation sampling
body: Explicit Sampling is a method to extract a point cloud (PC) from a Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) or Directed Distance Field (DDF) by projecting uniformly sampled points from a bounding box onto the shape surface S. It solves the problem of converting implicit field representations into explicit geometric primitives for evaluation metrics like Chamfer distance. Unlike its siblings, it relies on a simple "shoot-and-cast" strategy using weighted direction composition to find valid surface intersections, without guaranteeing uniform sampling density over the shape. Inputs: A PDDF or DDF representation providing depth d(p, v) and visibility \xi(p, v) for any point p and direction v. A bounding box B enclosing the shape. Parameters: nv (number of directions per point, typically 128) and NH (number of refinement iterations, typically 3). Outputs: A set of 3D points representing the surface S. Data Structures: Point p \in \mathbb{R}^3: Current sample position. Direction v \in \mathbb{R}^3: Unit vector on the sphere S^2. Set V(p) = \{vi(p)\}{i=1}^{nv}: Collection of sampled directions. Weighted direction v^b(p) \in \mathbb{R}^3: The composed best direction. Steps: 1. Initial Sampling: Sample a point p uniformly from the bounding box B: p \sim U[B]. 2. Direction Sampling: For the current point p, sample nv directions uniformly from the unit sphere S^2: V(p) = \{vi(p) \mid vi(p) \sim U[S^2], i=1 \dots nv\}. 3. Direction Composition: Estimate the best direction v^b(p) that avoids occlusion (\xi(p, v) = 0) by computing a weighted average over the sampled directions V(p). The specific weighting function is not detailed in the provided notes, but it utilizes the field's visibility/depth information to favor visible directions. Note: Arbitrary directions may not be visible (\xi(p, v) \neq 1), and at certain positions, multiple valid values of v^ may exist. 4. Surface Projection: Compute the projected point q on the shape using the estimated direction and the field's depth: q(p, v^b(p)) = p + d(p, v^b(p)) \cdot v^b(p) The condition for q being on S is \xi(p, v^b(p)) = 1. 5. Refinement (Optional): If depths are less accurate far from the shape, repeat the process NH times, updating the starting point p \leftarrow q for each iteration. 6. Collection: Add q to the point cloud. Repeat steps 1-5 for the desired number of points. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def extractpointcloud(pddf, boundingbox, nv=128, nh=3): """ Extracts a point cloud from a PDDF/DDF using explicit sampling. Args: pddf: Object providing query(p, v) -> (depth, visibility) boundingbox: Bounding box for uniform sampling nv: Number of directions to sample per point nh: Number of refinement iterations Returns: list of points on the surface """ points = [] # Number of initial samples needed to generate the desired cloud size # This loop generates one point per iteration, potentially refined nh times # In practice, one might sample N points and refine each, or sample N/nh points # and refine each nh times. The text implies repeating the process NH times # starting from the newly found point, suggesting a chain for each initial sample. # We assume we want to generate a final set of points. # The text says "Repeat this NH times... to improve accuracy". # It does not specify if the output is the final q or all intermediate q's. # Standard interpretation: One initial p -> chain of NH projections -> 1 final point. numinitialsamples = 10000 # Example target size for in range(numinitialsamples): # Step 1: Sample initial point p = sampleuniform(boundingbox) currentp = p for h in range(nh): # Step 2: Sample directions directions = [sampleuniformsphere() for in range(nv)] # Step 3: Compose directions to find best vb # The text mentions "weighted average over V(p)" # and "compose... to estimate vb(p)" # Implementation detail: Weight by visibility or inverse depth error? # Sources do not give the exact weight formula. # Assuming a simple visibility-weighted average for valid directions. # If visibility is probabilistic, weights might be P(visibility=1). weightedsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] weighttotal = 0.0 for v in directions: depth, visibility = pddf.query(currentp, v) # Visibility is often a probability or binary flag. # If binary: weight = 1 if visible, 0 otherwise. # If probabilistic: weight = visibility. # Note: says "cannot choose arbitrary v... many will not be visible" # and "weighted average over V(p)". # Guard: if depth is invalid or visibility is 0, ignore or weight 0 if visibility <= 0: continue # Simple visibility weighting. # More sophisticated methods might use depth confidence. w = visibility weightedsum[0] += w v[0] weightedsum[1] += w v[1] weightedsum[2] += w v[2] weighttotal += w if weighttotal == 0: # No visible directions found. # Fallback: keep current point or skip. # Skipping is safer to avoid noise. break # Normalize to get unit vector vb vstar = normalize(weightedsum) # Step 4: Project to surface depth, = pddf.query(currentp, vstar) # Check if projection was valid if depth is None or depth < 0: break q = currentp + depth vstar # Step 5: Update for next iteration currentp = q # Add the final refined point points.append(currentp) return points def sampleuniform(box): # Returns random point in box return [random.uniform(box.min[i], box.max[i]) for i in range(3)] def sampleuniformsphere(): # Returns random unit vector # Using spherical coordinates or normal distribution method u = random.random() v = random.random() theta = 2 math.pi u phi = math.acos(2 v - 1) x = math.sin(phi) math.cos(theta) y = math.sin(phi) math.sin(theta) z = math.cos(phi) return [x, y, z] def normalize(v): mag = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) if mag == 0: return [0,0,0] return [v[0]/mag, v[1]/mag, v[2]/mag] Parameters: nv: Number of directions sampled per point. Typical value: 128. NH: Number of refinement iterations. Typical value: 3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-uniformity: The method does not guarantee uniform sampling over the shape S. Visibility: Arbitrary directions v may not be visible (\xi(p, v) \neq 1), necessitating the composition technique. Ambiguity: At certain positions, there may be multiple valid values of v^. Depth Accuracy: Depths are less accurate far from the shape, which is why refinement (NH > 1) is recommended. A variant of the method applied specifically to Directed Distance Fields (DDF) rather than Probabilistic DDFs. It follows the same steps: uniform sampling in the bounding box, direction sampling, weighted average composition to estimate v^b(p), and projection using q(p, v^b(p)) = p + d(p, v^b(p))v^b(p). It shares the same pitfalls: no guarantee of uniform sampling, visibility issues requiring weighted averages, and potential ambiguity in v^. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot nv \cdot NH), where N is the number of initial samples, nv is the number of directions per sample, and NH is the number of refinement steps. Each step requires a query to the DDF/PDDF. Memory Complexity: O(nv) per point for storing direction samples, plus O(N) for the output point cloud. Performance: The method is simple and fast to implement but computationally expensive due to the large number of DDF queries (nv=128 per point). Strengths: Simple to implement; works with generic DDF/PDDF representations; refinement improves accuracy for points far from the surface. Limitations: Does not guarantee uniform sampling; sensitive to visibility estimation errors; multiple valid directions can cause ambiguity. When to use: When evaluating reconstruction quality using point cloud metrics (Chamfer distance, F-score) and a simple, modality-agnostic extraction is needed. When not to use: When uniform surface sampling is required; when computational efficiency is critical and nv cannot be reduced. The method was introduced in the context of evaluating 3D reconstruction methods using Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDFs). It is commonly used in the SI3DR (Shape Inference from 3D Reconstructions) evaluation framework. The approach is analogous to prior work [5] (cited in) for projecting points onto shapes defined by distance fields. It is used to generate point clouds for comparison against ground truth shapes using metrics like Chamfer distance and F-score.
