name: SDF Scaling and Early Ray Termination for Fast Sphere Tracing
head: SDF Scaling, Two-pass SDF Scaling
body: This method accelerates sphere tracing by decoupling the distance estimation from the final high-resolution rendering into a two-pass pipeline: a low-resolution pre-processing pass and a full-resolution main pass. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard sphere tracing by using a single low-resolution buffer to provide a "head start" for full-resolution rays, positioning them closer to surfaces, while applying SDF scaling to ensure small features are not missed at low resolution. Unlike Inverse Pyramid Rendering (IPR) which uses a pyramidal render target hierarchy and filtering, this method uses a single low-resolution buffer, reducing memory cost and complexity while offering similar quality. The method operates in two distinct passes. The first pass renders primary and shadow rays at a reduced resolution to generate an approximate distance field. The second pass uses this approximation to initialize rays closer to the geometry, significantly reducing the number of steps required for convergence. Inputs: Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}{cam}, direction \mathbf{d}), SDF scene definition, target output resolution R{out}, low-resolution buffer resolution R{low}, scaling factor \lambda, early termination epsilon \epsilon{early}, and shadow hardness k. Outputs: Final rendered image at R{out} and depth/distance buffer at R{low}. 1. Low-Resolution Buffer: A 2D array storing the accumulated distance t{approx} for each pixel. Size is R{low} \times R{low}. 2. Ray Bundle: In the main pass, each pixel in the low-resolution buffer corresponds to a 4 \times 4 block of pixels (16 rays) in the full-resolution pass. 1. Initialize Buffer: Create a low-resolution buffer with dimensions R{low} = R{out} / 4 (e.g., 960x540 for 4K output). 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the low-resolution buffer, cast a ray from the camera origin \mathbf{o}{cam} with direction \mathbf{d}. 3. SDF Scaling Logic: Before evaluating the SDF f(\mathbf{p}) at the current position \mathbf{p}, determine the sign of the distance to the nearest surface. If the camera is in front/outside (f(\mathbf{p}) > 0), scale up (inflate) the SDF volume. The effective distance becomes f'(\mathbf{p}) = f(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \lambda, where \lambda > 1. If the camera is behind/inside (f(\mathbf{p}) < 0), scale down (deflate) the SDF volume. The effective distance becomes f'(\mathbf{p}) = f(\mathbf{p}) / \lambda. Hole Handling: For SDFs representing holes (via subtraction), if the camera is in front, decrease the volume size (deflate) to improve approximation; if behind, scale up (inflate). 4. Sphere Tracing with Early Termination: Perform sphere tracing using the scaled SDF f'(\mathbf{p}). Step size: \Delta t = f'(\mathbf{p}). Termination Condition: Stop when f'(\mathbf{p}) < \epsilon{early}, where \epsilon{early} is a larger epsilon than typically used in high-resolution passes. This avoids surface overlaps caused by scaled SDFs and provides a fast distance approximation. Store the accumulated distance t{approx} in the low-resolution buffer. 5. Shadow Rays (Optional in Pass 1): Shadow rays can also be traced in this pass using the scaled SDFs to generate initial shadow data, though the primary benefit is the distance buffer for Pass 2. 1. Ray Origin Reconstruction: For each pixel in the full-resolution output, determine its corresponding low-resolution pixel (e.g., by dividing coordinates by 4). Retrieve the approximate distance t{approx} from the low-resolution buffer. 2. Reconstruct Ray Origin: Instead of starting from the camera origin \mathbf{o}{cam}, set the new ray origin \mathbf{o}{new} to: \mathbf{o}{new} = \mathbf{o}{cam} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t{approx} This positions the ray closer to the surface, reducing the remaining distance to trace. 3. Sphere Tracing: Perform standard sphere tracing from \mathbf{o}{new} using the original, unscaled SDF f(\mathbf{p}). Step size: \Delta t = f(\mathbf{p}). Termination: Use standard epsilon \epsilon for surface hit detection. 4. Shadow Tracing: For shadow rays, use the approximated distance t{approx} to determine the light source distance. Set shadow hardness k to control the penumbra size (higher k results in harder shadows). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretracingwithscalingandearlyterm(cameraorigin, cameradirection, sdffunc, resolution, lowresfactor, lambdascale, epsilonearly, epsilonhit, shadowhardnessk): """ Two-pass sphere tracing with SDF scaling and early termination. Args: cameraorigin: vec3, origin of the camera. cameradirection: vec3, direction of the ray for a specific pixel. sdffunc: function, returns signed distance to scene geometry. resolution: tuple, (width, height) of the final output. lowresfactor: int, factor by which to reduce resolution (e.g., 4). lambdascale: float, scaling factor for SDF inflation/deflation (>1). epsilonearly: float, large epsilon for early termination in Pass 1. epsilonhit: float, small epsilon for surface hit in Pass 2. shadowhardnessk: float, parameter for shadow hardness. Returns: color: vec3, final pixel color. depth: float, accumulated distance. """ # --- Pass 1: Low Resolution Pre-processing --- lowresw = resolution[0] // lowresfactor lowresh = resolution[1] // lowresfactor # Initialize low-res buffer to store approximate distances # In a real implementation, this would be a texture/buffer shared between passes lowresbuffer = createbuffer(lowresw, lowresh) for y in range(lowresh): for x in range(lowresw): # Map low-res pixel to a representative ray direction # Note: In practice, this might average directions or use a representative ray raydir = getraydirectionforpixel(x, y, lowresw, lowresh, cameraorigin, cameradirection) tapprox = 0.0 p = cameraorigin # Sphere tracing loop for Pass 1 for step in range(100): # Max steps for low-res dist = sdffunc(p) # SDF Scaling Logic if dist > 0: # Camera in front/outside: Inflate SDF scaleddist = dist lambdascale else: # Camera behind/inside: Deflate SDF scaleddist = dist / lambdascale # Hole handling: If sdffunc identifies a hole, reverse scaling logic # if ishole(p): # if dist > 0: scaleddist = dist / lambdascale # else: scaleddist = dist lambdascale # Early Termination if scaleddist < epsilonearly: break # Step tapprox += scaleddist p = cameraorigin + raydir tapprox # Store result in low-res buffer lowresbuffer[y, x] = tapprox # --- Pass 2: Full Resolution Main Pass --- finalcolor = vec3(0.0) finaldepth = 0.0 # For each pixel in full resolution for y in range(resolution[1]): for x in range(resolution[0]): # Map to low-res buffer lrx = x // lowresfactor lry = y // lowresfactor # Retrieve approximate distance tapprox = lowresbuffer[lry, lrx] # Reconstruct ray origin neworigin = cameraorigin + cameradirection tapprox # Sphere tracing loop for Pass 2 tfinal = tapprox pfinal = neworigin for step in range(100): # Max steps for high-res dist = sdffunc(pfinal) # Standard Sphere Tracing (no scaling) if abs(dist) < epsilonhit: break tfinal += dist pfinal = neworigin + cameradirection dist # Compute color and shadow color = computeshading(pfinal, cameradirection, sdffunc, shadowhardnessk, tapprox) # Aggregate color (e.g., for anti-aliasing, average over 4x4 block) finalcolor += color return finalcolor / (lowresfactor 2), tfinal def computeshading(p, raydir, sdffunc, k, tapprox): """ Computes shading and shadow for a point p. Uses tapprox for shadow ray initialization. """ # Normal estimation n = estimatenormal(p, sdffunc) # Lighting calculation (simplified) lightdir = normalize(vec3(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)) diffuse = max(dot(n, lightdir), 0.0) # Shadow ray with early termination using tapprox shadowfactor = 1.0 shadoworigin = p + n 0.001 shadowdist = tapprox # Use approximated distance to light # Trace shadow ray # If shadowdist is very small, assume lit if shadowdist > 0.001: shadowp = shadoworigin for step in range(10): dlight = sdffunc(shadowp) if dlight < 0.0: shadowfactor = 0.0 break shadowp += normalize(lightdir) dlight if distance(shadowp, lightpos) > shadowdist + k: break return vec3(diffuse shadowfactor) Low-resolution buffer size: Typically 1/4 of the output resolution in each axis (e.g., 960x540 for 4K). Ray Batching: Each low-resolution pixel serves 16 full-resolution pixels (4 \times 4 block). Scaling Factor (\lambda): Not explicitly given in sources, but must be >1 to inflate and <1 to deflate. Epsilon Early (\epsilon{early}): Larger than standard epsilon to terminate early and avoid overlaps from scaled SDFs. Shadow Hardness (k): Controls shadow penumbra; higher values yield harder shadows. Rounded Edges: High values of \epsilon{early} cause shapes with edges to become rounded, eliminating sharp features and providing an inaccurate approximation. SDF Overlaps: Scaling SDFs can cause them to overlap incorrectly. Early termination is required to prevent rays from penetrating scaled surfaces. Hole Approximation: Incorrect scaling logic for holes (subtracted SDFs) can lead to visual artifacts if the camera position relative to the hole is not correctly detected. Time Complexity: The method reduces the average number of sphere tracing steps significantly. In the 'Primitives' scene, it achieved a 3x speedup in frame time compared to state-of-the-art methods without anti-aliasing on an NVIDIA RTX-3070Ti. Shadow Ray Performance: Shadow rays often finish after 1 step in simple scenes, achieving a 2.1x performance improvement over ground truth in the 'Primitives' scene. In complex scenes like 'Sponza atrium', performance improved by 1.5x despite increased complexity (shadows taking up to 20 ms). Memory Complexity: Uses a single low-resolution buffer, which is significantly smaller than the pyramidal hierarchy used in Inverse Pyramid Rendering (IPR), reducing memory cost. Strengths: Reduces rendering time significantly, allows for anti-aliasing without increasing frame time cost, and handles small features better than standard low-res methods due to SDF scaling. Limitations: Introduces artifacts such as rounded edges if \epsilon{early} is too high. Accuracy depends on the quality of the low-resolution approximation. The method was proposed in the paper "Skipping Spheres: SDF Scaling & Early Ray Termination for Fast Sphere Tracing". It draws inspiration from prior techniques aimed at reducing ray steps by adjusting step size and generating lower resolution renders [PKM23]. The authors note that while low-resolution buffers can speed up rendering, they often lead to artifacts in small features, necessitating filtering. This method minimizes artifacts while cutting down steps compared to previous methods by using a single low-resolution buffer and a novel tracing optimization. name: Deformation and Transformation Handling
body: This family addresses the problem of applying spatial transformations (rigid body motion, scaling, deformation) to Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDFs) during ray marching or voxel processing. It enables the rendering of animated, deforming, or dynamically positioned geometry without recomputing the underlying distance field data structures from scratch. It differs from static SDF definitions by introducing time-varying coordinate mappings, and from explicit mesh transformation by operating directly on the implicit field representation (or its voxel approximation) to preserve the analytical or volumetric nature of the distance query. All methods in this family rely on the principle of coordinate space transformation. The core mechanism involves mapping a query point from the rendering space (world space or camera space) into the local space of the primitive or the reference frame of the data before evaluating the distance function or sampling the voxel grid. For rigid transformations, the mapping is defined by a transformation matrix M. If the scene geometry is transformed by M in world space, the SDF evaluation at a world-space point \mathbf{p} requires evaluating the base SDF f{base} at the corresponding local-space point \mathbf{q}: \mathbf{q} = M^{-1} \mathbf{p} f{transformed}(\mathbf{p}) = f{base}(M^{-1} \mathbf{p}) This ensures that the distance value corresponds to the transformed geometry while keeping the primitive definition static in its local frame. For non-rigid or temporal transformations (such as motion compensation in TSDF compression), the mapping is often estimated per-block or per-voxel. The goal is to predict the current state st from a previous state s{t-1} using an estimated rigid transform (\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) link to [Motion-Compensated Block Warping]. The prediction error is minimized to find the optimal transform: \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}:= \arg \min{\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}} \sum{i \in \Omega} \left( \hat{s}{t-1}(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}i; \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})) - st(\mathbf{p}i) \right)^2 where \mathbf{T} is the rigid transform and \Omega is the set of sample positions link to [Motion-Compensated Block Warping]. Scaling introduces a change in the metric of the distance field. For uniform scaling by factor s, the distance value must be scaled to preserve the Euclidean distance property: f'(\mathbf{p}) = s \cdot f(\mathbf{p}/s). Non-uniform scaling distorts the distance field unless the metric is adjusted, which is often handled by including scale in the transformation matrix and inverting it, or by post-scaling the returned distance value. This method applies rigid body transformations (rotation and translation) to SDF primitives by transforming the sample point using the inverse of the object's model matrix before evaluation. It solves the problem of animating or positioning individual SDF objects independently without modifying the underlying distance function definitions. Unlike direct geometry transformation, it preserves the analytical nature of the SDF by operating in the object's local coordinate space. It is chosen when rendering static primitives that undergo rigid motion in a scene. Motion-Compensated Block Warping is a technique for compressing dynamic Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDF) by predicting the current frame's geometry from the previous frame using estimated rigid body motion. It improves prediction accuracy over static methods by inverse-warping voxel samples from the target block into the previously reconstructed TSDF and resampling them via trilinear interpolation. Unlike global transformation methods, this approach operates on local blocks, allowing for piecewise-rigid motion estimation which is essential for complex, non-uniform scene dynamics. It is chosen for dynamic TSDF compression and streaming. This method applies a 4x4 transformation matrix to mesh vertices within an Embree ray-tracing geometry buffer. It solves the problem of updating mesh positions for dynamic scenes or rigid body transformations while maintaining the integrity of the source mesh data. It differs from Inverse Model Matrix Transformation for Distance Fields by modifying the actual vertex positions in the Embree buffer rather than transforming the query point in world space, and from Motion-Compensated Block Warping by operating on explicit mesh geometry rather than voxel blocks. A ray marching technique that integrates a deformed scene by marching in the undeformed space and mapping positions/normals to the deformed space using a Jacobian estimate. Step: 1. Initialize ssum to start and pos to ipos. 2. Loop up to MAXMARCHINGSTEPS: a. Calculate invjacobian by inverting the Jacobian estimated at pos with force. b. Calculate sundeformed as the absolute value of the scene SDF at pos. c. Accumulate sundeformed to ssum. d. Calculate uepsilon as ssum (ssum radpixel determinant(invjacobian)). e. If sundeformed < uepsilon, return vec4(pos, 1) indicating a hit. f. If ssum >= end, return vec4(0) indicating no hit (marched too far). g. If sundeformed < 3 uepsilon, advance pos by sundeformed normalized(invjacobian w). h. Otherwise (sundeformed >= 3 uepsilon), advance pos by sundeformed normalized(invjacobian w). 3. If the loop completes without returning, return vec4(0). Parameter: MAXMARCHINGSTEPS: The maximum number of iterations for the marching loop. radpixel: A constant used in the epsilon calculation for stopping criteria. Pitfall: The ODE solver (ode23) is commented out in the main loop, so the fallback to simple stepping is always used. To avoid overlapping where destination voxels overwrite source voxels before translation, the algorithm sets the Orient register so that translation starts from the source corner that is also situated in the destination primitive range. The relative translation is characterized by a vector (Tx, Ty, Tz). The position of the next voxel along the X-axis to be translated (X{dest}, Y{dest}, Z{dest}) is determined by incrementing the appropriate coordinate of the last voxel without performing an addition for every voxel. An algorithm for scaling voxel grids that avoids floating-point accumulation errors by using incremental updates. The scaling equations are X{dest} = X{src} Sx, Y{dest} = Y{src} Sy, Z{dest} = Z{src} Sz. To avoid overwriting source voxels before scaling, the starting corner of the room for the transformation is chosen based on the values of Sx, Sy, Sz. If scaling factors are greater than 1, forward scaling may produce holes due to volume increase without voxel increase. This is averted by 'back scaling': reversing the incremental transformation process. An animated tornado composed of a single Bezier segment. Radius increases with height (cone-like). Control points move in circular motion with different frequencies. No stretching. Rotation adds twisting. Angle changes with time. Density field moves up. Perlin noise creates cloud-like density. A deformation method using user-specified point pairs (source in undeformed space, target in deformed space) to find a mapping between them. Use a ray picker to allow the user to specify significant surface feature points by holding down the mouse and moving a point along the volume surface. Manipulate control points by dragging them along a specified surface or in view-aligned planes. Thin Plate Splines and Hierarchical B-Splines are examples of deformations used as landmark deformation functions. Implementing interactive widgets (e.g. leafer widget) as deformations directly in the shader. Discontinuities in deformation functions representing widgets require conditional branches, which are inefficient on some hardware. A simulated deformation field parametrized by amplitudes, lengthscales, and centers, mapping undeformed coordinates (X,Y,Z) to deformed coordinates (x,y,z). Deformed x-coordinate: x = X + A0 \exp(-r^2 / (2\sigma0^2)). Deformed y-coordinate: y = Y + A1 \exp(-r^2 / (2\sigma1^2)). Deformed z-coordinate: z = Z + A2 \exp(-r^2 / (2\sigma2^2)). Squared distance r^2 from center c: r^2 = (X - c0)^2 + (Y - c1)^2 + (Z - c2)^2. The concept of transforming SDFs via inverse matrices is a standard technique in ray marching, allowing for the composition of animated scenes from static primitives. Motion-Compensated Block Warping for TSDFs originates from research into dynamic 3D reconstruction and compression, where rigid body motion estimation is used to reduce the bitrate of streaming TSDF data. The Incremental Scaling Algorithm dates back to early voxel frame buffer processors, which addressed the computational cost and precision issues of scaling voxel grids in real-time. NTSL Marching appears in the context of the ntsl-graphics project, a research/experimental graphics engine, dealing with deformed scenes via Jacobian-based marching. tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, https://github.com/tink-expo/ntsl-graphics, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) The voxblt Engine: A Voxel Frame Buffer Processor, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh88/085-102, fetched 2026-10-26 Sculpting procedural noise: real-time rendering of interstellar dust clouds and solar flares, https://openalex.org/W4293584834, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Integrating Dynamic Deformations into Interactive Volume Visualization, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym.eurovis06.219-226, fetched 2026-10-31 Neural rendering enables dynamic tomography, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2410.20558, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Model Matrix Transformation for Distance Fields
head: Inverse Transformation for Rotation/Translation, SDF Model Transformations, Transforming SDFs, Transforming SDFs via Inverse Matrix
body: This method enables the application of rigid transformations (rotation, translation, and uniform scaling) to Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitives during ray marching by evaluating the base distance function in the primitive's local coordinate space rather than the world space. It solves the problem of animating or positioning individual scene objects without modifying the underlying geometric definitions or voxel grids. Unlike methods that transform the geometry data itself, this approach transforms the query point using the inverse of the object's model matrix, ensuring the distance metric remains valid for Euclidean distance fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{p} in world/camera space; a 4 \times 4 inverse model matrix M^{-1} representing the object's transformation (Translation, Rotation, Scale). Output: The signed distance value d at point \mathbf{p} for the transformed object. Data Structures: Inverse Model Matrix (M^{-1}): A 4 \times 4 homogeneous transformation matrix. In implementation, this is typically passed as a uniform variable to the shader or kernel. The matrix encodes rotation, translation, and potentially uniform scaling. Steps: 1. Construct Model Matrix: On the host side (e.g., CPU/scripting environment), construct the model matrix M for the object using its current translation \mathbf{t}, rotation quaternion \mathbf{q}, and scale s. 2. Compute Inverse: Calculate the inverse of the model matrix M^{-1}. 3. Transform Point: In the distance evaluation function, transform the world-space query point \mathbf{p} into the local space \mathbf{q} by multiplying \mathbf{p} (homogenized to \mathbf{p}' = [\mathbf{p}, 1]^T) by M^{-1}: \mathbf{q} = M^{-1} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{p} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} The resulting local point is \mathbf{q}{xyz}. 4. Evaluate Base SDF: Pass \mathbf{q}{xyz} to the base, untransformed SDF function f{base}: d = f{base}(\mathbf{q}{xyz}) 5. Handle Scaling: If the model matrix includes uniform scaling by factor s, the distance value must be scaled to preserve the Euclidean distance property: d{final} = s \cdot d If non-uniform scaling is used, the Euclidean distance property is distorted unless the metric is adjusted, which is generally avoided in standard SDF ray marching. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeinversemodelmatrix(translation, rotation, scale): """ Constructs the model matrix M and returns its inverse. Assumes uniform scale for valid SDF distance preservation. """ # Construct M = T R S # Note: Order of operations depends on convention (pre/post-multiply). # Standard Unity/OpenGL: M = Translation Rotation Scale M = translate(translation) @ rotate(rotation) @ scalematrix(scale) # Compute inverse Minv = inverse(M) return Minv uniform float4x4 MatTorusInvModel; # Passed from host float sdTorus(vec3 p, float2 torusparams) { // Base SDF implementation for a torus vec2 q = vec2(length(p.xz) - torusparams.x, p.y); return length(q) - torusparams.y; } float map(float3 p) { // Step 3: Transform point to local space // Homogeneous coordinate w=1 for translation/rotation float4 qhomogeneous = mul(MatTorusInvModel, float4(p, 1.0)); vec3 qlocal = qhomogeneous.xyz; // Step 4: Evaluate base SDF float dist = sdTorus(qlocal, float2(1.0, 0.2)); // Step 5: Scale distance if uniform scale was applied in M // Note: If M included scale 's', Minv includes 1/s. // The distance in local space is correct, but must be scaled back to world space metric. // However, if Minv is pre-computed, the scaling factor 's' must be known separately // or extracted from Minv to scale the final distance value. // For uniform scale s, dworld = s dlocal. float scalefactor =...; // Extracted from original M or passed separately return dist scalefactor; } Parameters: MatTorusInvModel (or generic Minv): A uniform 4 \times 4 matrix representing the inverse model transformation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Uniform Scaling: Applying non-uniform scaling distorts the distance field, breaking the Euclidean distance property. The resulting field is no longer a true SDF, leading to incorrect ray marching steps. Precision: Computing the inverse matrix on the host side is preferred for performance and precision stability compared to inverting in the shader per-fragment. Homogeneous Coordinates: Ensure the point is treated as a position (w=1) when multiplying by the transformation matrix, not a direction (w=0), to correctly apply translation. Applies the inverse transform to the entire viewing ray system (camera, lights) rather than individual sample points, reducing complexity for large volumetric datasets. Estimates rigid transforms per-block for temporal compression of TSDFs, minimizing prediction error between frames. Uses Embree's ray tracing kernel to handle mesh transformations, distinct from SDF evaluation. Handles scaling in distance fields through incremental adjustments. Evaluates deformations directly on fragments, potentially using vertex data. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample point evaluation, as it involves a single matrix-vector multiplication and one base SDF call. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the inverse matrix uniform. Performance: Highly efficient for rigid transformations. The cost is dominated by the base SDF evaluation and matrix multiplication, which are negligible compared to the ray marching loop. Strengths: Simple to implement; allows independent animation of scene parts; preserves the static nature of base SDF definitions. Limitations: Only supports rigid transformations (rotation, translation) and uniform scaling effectively. Non-rigid deformations require different approaches (e.g., Per-fragment Deformation Evaluation). When to use: Ideal for animating rigid objects in SDF scenes. When not to use: For non-rigid deformations or non-uniform scaling where metric preservation is critical. The technique originates from the foundational principles of ray marching and Signed Distance Functions, popularized by tutorials such as those by Jamie Wong and Adrian Booth. It is a standard practice in real-time graphics and procedural modeling to decouple geometry definition from scene layout. name: Inverse Viewing Transformations for Volumes
head: Inverse Viewing Transformations, Inverse Volume Transform, Moving the camera instead of the volume
body: Inverse Viewing Transformations for Volumes applies geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling) to volumetric data by moving the viewing geometry—camera, lights, and pixels—in the opposite direction, rather than modifying the voxel grid. This approach avoids the computational bottleneck of per-voxel arithmetic for large datasets, reducing rotation and translation complexity from O(N{\text{voxels}}) to O(N{\text{pixels}} + N{\text{lights}}). Inputs: Volumetric data (voxel values or distance field values), volume spatial bounds (min/max coordinates for X, Y, Z), user-specified transformation parameters (rotation angles, translation vectors, scaling factors), and initial viewing geometry (camera eye position, light source positions, pixel coordinates). Outputs: Rendered image with the volume appearing transformed. Data Structures: Coordinate arrays storing unique 1D ordinate values per axis instead of per-voxel coordinates. The volume's spatial coordinates are stored in three separate 1-dimensional arrays: X{\text{ord}}, Y{\text{ord}}, and Z{\text{ord}}. These arrays store the distinct ordinate values defining the grid planes, allowing many voxels to be represented by relatively few numbers (e.g., a million voxels may be defined with as few as 100 numbers). Viewing geometry is stored as vectors for eye position, light positions, and pixel sample locations. Steps: 1. Center Coordinate Arrays: Adjust the coordinate arrays so the volume is centered at the origin (0,0,0). For each axis A \in \{X, Y, Z\}, calculate the span SA = \max(A{\text{ord}}) - \min(A{\text{ord}}). Subtract half the span from every value in the array: A'{\text{ord}}[i] = A{\text{ord}}[i] - \frac{SA}{2}. This step ensures that subsequent scaling operations are uniform and centered. 2. Apply Scaling (if applicable): If a scaling factor s is specified, modify the coordinate arrays directly. For each value in the centered arrays: A''{\text{ord}}[i] = A'{\text{ord}}[i] \times s. Scaling is applied to the coordinate arrays because inverse transformation of the eye/pixels cannot effectively scale the volume's internal resolution. 3. Compute Inverse Viewing Transform: Determine the transformation matrix M{\text{vol}} representing the user's desired volume transformation. Transform the viewing geometry by the inverse matrix M{\text{vol}}^{-1} (opposite direction). Rotation: If the user wants to rotate the volume by angle \theta around axis K, rotate the camera eye, all light sources, and all pixel sample coordinates by -\theta around axis K. Translation: If the user wants to translate the volume by vector \vec{T}, translate the camera eye, light sources, and pixel coordinates by -\vec{T}. 4. Ray Marching / Rendering: Perform standard volume rendering or distance field ray marching using the transformed viewing geometry and the original (or scaled) volume data. The rays intersect the untransformed volume as if the volume itself had been transformed. Parameters: Scaling factor s (user-specified); rotation angles and translation vectors (user-specified). Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge cases and pitfalls: Directly transforming voxel positions for rotation or translation is computationally prohibitive for large volumes (e.g., >1 million voxels), requiring ~9 multiplications and ~9 additions per voxel. Scaling cannot be achieved by simply moving the camera or pixels. The method assumes a regular grid structure for the 1D coordinate array optimization. A method for editing learned implicit fields by manipulating object codes in 3D space before 2D projection to avoid multi-view inconsistencies. It maps sample points to an inverse space and uses projected 2D labels to resolve occlusions, differing from direct editing. Time Complexity: O(N{\text{pixels}} + N{\text{lights}}) for rotation and translation, significantly faster than the O(N{\text{voxels}}) cost of direct volume transformation. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for separate 1D coordinate arrays (X, Y, Z) instead of per-voxel coordinates, reducing memory overhead for coordinate data. A million voxels may be defined with as few as 100 numbers for coordinates if the grid is regular. Strengths: Avoids per-voxel arithmetic for rotation/translation; efficient for large datasets; preserves original voxel data integrity. Limitations: Scaling requires modifying coordinate arrays; assumes regular grid structure for the coordinate array optimization; does not handle irregular spacing without additional interpolation logic. When to use: When rotating or translating large volumetric datasets where per-voxel transformation is too slow. When not to use: When non-uniform scaling of the grid structure is required without modifying the underlying data structure, or when the volume data is irregularly spaced in a way that prevents simple 1D array representation. This technique was described in a report on volumetric rendering techniques for aerodynamic flow field data. The author noted that direct transformation of data volumes was computationally expensive for large datasets (e.g., >1 million voxels). The method leverages the uniform spacing of voxel locations to store coordinates in 1D arrays, enabling efficient scaling and centering. DTIC ADA202661: Volumetric Rendering Techniques for the Display of Three-Dimensional Aerodynamic Flow Field Data, https://archive.org/details/DTICADA202661, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Inverse Query Algorithm
head: Object Manipulator (Inverse Query)
body:
The Inverse Query Algorithm edits learned implicit fields by manipulating object codes in 3D space before 2D projection, thereby avoiding multi-view inconsistencies. It solves the problem of how to update the density (\sigma), color (c), and object codes (o) of sample points along a query ray so that the rendered novel view reflects the manipulated geometry while explicitly handling occlusions and collisions. It sets itself apart from direct editing by mapping sample points to an inverse space to determine target membership, and uses projected 2D labels to resolve occlusion inaccuracies. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Target object code ot: A hard one-hot vector with H+1 dimensions, where H is the number of objects and the last dimension represents background/emptiness. Manipulation parameters: Translation \Delta p = (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z), rotation matrix R{3	imes3}, and scaling factor t > 0. Sample points \{p1, \dots, pk, \dots, pK\} along a specific query light ray r. Segment lengths \{\delta1, \dots, \deltaK\} along the ray. Projected pixel object code \hat{o}: The object code of the ray before manipulation, obtained from 2D label supervision. Outputs: Final pixel color  ar{c} and object code  ar{o} after manipulation. Data Structures: Object codes are stored as hard one-hot vectors of size H+1. Implicit codes consist of density \sigma (scalar), color c (3D vector), and object code o (one-hot vector). Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Convert all object codes into hard one-hot vectors. Obtain the projected pixel object code \hat{o} for the ray r from the unmanipulated scene. 2. Ray Loop: Iterate through each sample point pk along the ray r: 1. Inverse Point Calculation: Compute the inverse 3D point p'k using the formula: p'k =  rac{1}{t} R^{-1} (pk - \Delta p) where pk is the current sample point, t is the scale, R is the rotation matrix, and \Delta p is the translation. 2. Query Codes: Query the original implicit codes \{\sigmak, ck, ok\} for pk and the inverse implicit codes \{\sigma'k, c'k, o'k\} for p'k using the learned implicit field networks. 3. Occlusion Handling: If the original point belongs to the target object (ok = ot) but the projected code indicates a different object (ok 
eq \hat{o}), update the original object code to the projected code: ok \leftarrow \hat{o}. This corrects inaccuracies in object codes behind surfaces due to insufficient optimization. 4. Collision Detection: If the original point is not the target object (ok 
eq ot), is not background (o{H+1} 
eq 1), and the inverse point is the target object (o'k = ot), a collision is detected. Exit the loop for this ray. 5. Code Update: Determine the new implicit codes \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} for pk based on the membership of pk and p'k relative to ot: Non-target to Target: If ok 
eq ot and o'k = ot, set \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} \leftarrow \{\sigma'k, c'k, o'k\}. Target to Target: If ok = ot and o'k = ot, set \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} \leftarrow \{\sigma'k, c'k, o'k\}. Target to Non-target: If ok = ot and o'k 
eq ot, set \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} \leftarrow \{0, 0, 0\}. Non-target to Non-target: If ok 
eq ot and o'k 
eq ot, keep the original codes: \{ ar{\sigma}k,  ar{c}k,  ar{o}k\} \leftarrow \{\sigmak, ck, ok\}. 3. Volume Rendering: After processing all K points, compute the final pixel color  ar{c} and object code  ar{o} using the volume rendering equation:  ar{c} = \sum{k=1}^{K}  ar{T}k  ar{\alpha}k  ar{c}k, \quad  ar{o} = \sum{k=1}^{K}  ar{T}k  ar{\alpha}k  ar{o}k where the transmittance  ar{T}k and alpha  ar{\alpha}k are defined as:  ar{T}k = \exp\left(-\sum{i=1}^{k-1}  ar{\sigma}i \deltaiight), \quad  ar{\alpha}k = 1 - \exp(- ar{\sigma}k \deltak) and \deltai is the distance along the ray between consecutive sample points p{i-1} and pi (with p0 at the camera origin). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def inversequeryalgorithm(pklist, deltas, ot, deltap, Rinv, t, getimplicitcodes, getprojectedcode): """ pklist: List of 3D points [p1,..., pK] along the ray deltas: List of segment lengths [delta1,..., deltaK] along the ray ot: Target object one-hot vector (size H+1) deltap: Translation vector (size 3) Rinv: Precomputed inverse rotation matrix (3x3) t: Scale factor (float > 0) getimplicitcodes: Function returning (sigma, c, o) for a point getprojectedcode: Function returning the projected object code ohat for the ray """ # Preprocessing ohat = getprojectedcode() editedsigma = [] editedc = [] editedo = [] for pk in pklist: # 1. Compute inverse point: p'k = (1/t) Rinv (pk - deltap) diff = [pk[i] - deltap[i] for i in range(3)] rinvdiff = [sum(Rinv[i][j] diff[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] pprimek = [rinvdiff[i] / t for i in range(3)] # 2. Query codes sigmak, ck, ok = getimplicitcodes(pk) sigmaprimek, cprimek, oprimek = getimplicitcodes(pprimek) # 3. Occlusion handling if ok == ot and ok != ohat: ok = ohat[:] # 4. Collision detection istarget = (ok == ot) isbackground = (ok[-1] == 1) isinversetarget = (oprimek == ot) if not istarget and not isbackground and isinversetarget: break # 5. Update codes if not istarget and isinversetarget: newsigma, newc, newo = sigmaprimek, cprimek, oprimek elif istarget and isinversetarget: newsigma, newc, newo = sigmaprimek, cprimek, oprimek elif istarget and not isinversetarget: newsigma, newc, newo = 0.0, [0.0] len(ck), [0.0] len(ok) else: newsigma, newc, newo = sigmak, ck, ok editedsigma.append(newsigma) editedc.append(newc) editedo.append(newo) # 6. Volume Rendering K = len(editedsigma) if K == 0: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], [0.0] len(ot) T = 1.0 finalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] finalo = [0.0] len(ot) for k in range(K): sigma = editedsigma[k] c = editedc[k] o = editedo[k] delta = deltas[k] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma delta) finalcolor = [finalcolor[i] + T alpha c[i] for i in range(3)] finalo = [finalo[i] + T alpha o[i] for i in range(len(ot))] T = T (1.0 - alpha) return finalcolor, finalo Parameters: H: Number of objects. The object code dimension is H+1. \Delta d: A hyper-parameter for the object field loss, set to 0.05 meters in experiments. t: Scaling factor, t > 0. Pitfalls: Collisions: Objects may collide during manipulation. This is addressed by the emptiness score in the last dimension of the object code o. Occlusion Inaccuracy: Object codes behind surface points may be inaccurate due to insufficient optimization. This is mitigated by using the projected object code \hat{o}, which is more accurate due to 2D label supervision. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points K per ray, as it requires two implicit field queries per point (original and inverse) and a loop over K points. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to K to store the edited codes for volume rendering. Strengths: Handles occlusions and collisions explicitly; allows editing in 3D space before projection to maintain consistency. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of projected codes \hat{o}; relies on the accuracy of the inverse transformation and the learned implicit fields. When to use: When manipulating specific objects in a decomposed 3D scene represented by implicit fields, especially when occlusion and collision handling are critical. The Inverse Query Algorithm was introduced in the paper "DM-NeRF: 3D Scene Geometry Decomposition and Manipulation from 2D Images". It addresses the challenges of editing implicit fields by leveraging 2D supervision to correct 3D ambiguities. The method is part of a pipeline that decomposes 3D scenes into object fields and a background field, allowing for individual object manipulation. DM-NeRF: 3D Scene Geometry Decomposition and Manipulation from 2D Images, https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.07227v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Motion-Compensated Block Warping
head: Inter-frame motion compensation
body: Motion-Compensated Block Warping is a technique for compressing temporal sequences of Truncated Signed Distance Fields (TSDF) by predicting the current frame's geometry from the previous frame using estimated rigid body motion. It solves the problem of high residual energy in dynamic scenes where objects move between frames, allowing the encoder to transmit only the motion parameters and the small residual differences rather than the full geometry. It differs from static deformation handling by explicitly estimating and transmitting a per-block 6-DoF transform to align the previous frame's data with the current frame's target block. The method operates on a block-based sparse TSDF representation. The scene is decomposed into voxel blocks. For each block in the target frame t, the algorithm estimates a rigid transform that best aligns the reconstructed TSDF from the previous frame t-1 to the current target block. Inputs: st^{(b)}: The TSDF values for block b at frame t. \hat{s}{t-1}^{(b)}: The reconstructed (decoded) TSDF values for block b at frame t-1. \Omega: The set of sample positions (voxel centers) within block b. Outputs: \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}: The optimal rotation (Euler angles) and translation (3D vector) parameters. Residual coefficients: The difference between the current block and the warped predictor, encoded in the transform domain (e.g., DCT). TSDF Block: A 3D grid of voxel values. In the source implementation, blocks are stored in a GPU-side spatial hash table (voxel hashing) for fast random access. Motion Parameters: A 6-DoF rigid transform consisting of translation \mathbf{t} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and rotation \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (parameterized as Euler angles). 1. Neighborhood Assembly: Assemble a stitched 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood of blocks from the previous frame's reconstructed TSDF \hat{s}{t-1} centered on the corresponding block location. This ensures that trilinear interpolation remains valid even when warped sample positions fall into adjacent blocks or between voxel centers. 2. Motion Estimation: Estimate the rigid transform (\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) that minimizes the squared difference between the warped previous frame and the current frame. This is done using a damped Gauss-Newton optimization procedure. 3. Inverse Warping (Prediction): For each sample position \mathbf{p}i \in \Omega in the target block b at frame t, compute the corresponding position in the previous frame using the estimated transform: \mathbf{q}i = \mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}i; \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) where \mathbf{T} maps current frame coordinates to previous frame coordinates. 4. Trilinear Interpolation: Evaluate the TSDF value at the warped location \mathbf{q}i by trilinearly interpolating the values from the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood assembled in Step 1. This forms the motion-compensated predictor \hat{s}{t-1}^{(b)}(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}i; \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})). 5. Residual Encoding: Compute the residual between the current block st^{(b)} and the predictor. Encode the transform-domain coefficients of this residual. 6. Side Information Encoding: Encode the motion parameters \mathbf{r} and \mathbf{t} as side information. The residual for sample i is defined as: \epsiloni(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t}) = \hat{s}{t-1}^{(b)}(\mathbf{T}(\mathbf{p}i; \mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})) - st^{(b)}(\mathbf{p}i) The optimization objective is to minimize the sum of squared residuals: \mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}:= \arg \min{\mathbf{t}, \mathbf{r}} \sum{i \in \Omega} \epsiloni(\mathbf{r}, \mathbf{t})^2 The update step in the Gauss-Newton algorithm is calculated as: \Delta \mathbf{p} = -(J^\top J + \lambda I)^{-1} J^\top \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} where J is the Jacobian of the residuals with respect to the parameters, \lambda is a damping factor for numerical stability, and \boldsymbol{\varepsilon} is the vector of residuals. Damping factor \lambda: A small value for numerical stability in the Gauss-Newton solver. Translation clamp: 1 voxel per iteration. Rotation clamp: 5 degrees per iteration. Termination threshold: The optimization terminates when the decrease in the objective function falls below a specific threshold. Insufficient Data: If too few reliable samples are available or the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood is incomplete (e.g., at the boundary of the volume), the method falls back to zero-motion prediction (\mathbf{t} = 0, \mathbf{r} = 0) for that block. Divergence: Large motion estimates can cause the Gauss-Newton solver to diverge. Clamping the per-iteration update magnitudes prevents this. Fractional Positions: Rigid motion maps integer voxel centers to fractional positions. Trilinear interpolation is required to evaluate the TSDF at these non-integer locations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def motioncompensatedblockwarping(targetblockb, prevframereconstructedtsdf, blockindex, blocksize): # 1. Assemble 3x3x3 neighborhood from previous frame neighborhood = assemble3x3x3neighborhood(prevframereconstructedtsdf, blockindex, blocksize) # 2. Estimate motion using damped Gauss-Newton r = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Euler angles (rad) t = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) # Translation (voxels) dampinglambda = 1e-4 maxiterations = 10 convergencethreshold = 1e-6 preverror = float('inf') for iteration in range(maxiterations): residuals = [] jacobianrows = [] for pi in getvoxelcenters(blocksize): # T maps current position to previous frame space for sampling warpedpos = applyrigidtransform(pi, r, t) predval = trilinearinterpolate(neighborhood, warpedpos) currval = targetblockb[getindex(pi, blocksize)] residual = predval - currval residuals.append(residual) jacobianrow = computejacobianrow(pi, r, t, neighborhood, blocksize) jacobianrows.append(jacobianrow) residuals = np.array(residuals) J = np.array(jacobianrows) # Solve for update step: deltap = -(J^T J + lambda I)^-1 J^T epsilon JTJ = J.T @ J JTJdamped = JTJ + dampinglambda np.eye(6) try: deltap = np.linalg.solve(JTJdamped, -J.T @ residuals) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: break # Clamp updates translationupdate = deltap[3:6] rotationupdate = deltap[0:3] translationupdate = np.clip(translationupdate, -1.0, 1.0) rotationupdate = np.clip(rotationupdate, -math.radians(5), math.radians(5)) t = t + translationupdate r = r + rotationupdate currenterror = np.sum(residuals2) if iteration > 0 and abs(preverror - currenterror) < convergencethreshold: break preverror = currenterror # 3. Generate Predictor and Residual predictor = np.zeroslike(targetblockb) for pi in getvoxelcenters(blocksize): warpedpos = inverserigidtransform(pi, r, t) predval = trilinearinterpolate(neighborhood, warpedpos) predictor[getindex(pi, blocksize)] = predval residual = targetblockb - predictor # 4. Encode Residual and Motion residualcoeffs = encodetransformdomain(residual) return (r, t), residualcoeffs def assemble3x3x3neighborhood(tsdf, blockindex, blocksize): """Retrieves a 3x3x3 grid of blocks centered on blockindex.""" volume = np.zeros((3 blocksize, 3 blocksize, 3 blocksize)) for dx in range(-1, 2): for dy in range(-1, 2): for dz in range(-1, 2): neighboridx = (blockindex[0] + dx, blockindex[1] + dy, blockindex[2] + dz) if neighboridx in tsdf: block = tsdf[neighboridx] volume[dx blocksize:(dx + 1) blocksize, dy blocksize:(dy + 1) blocksize, dz blocksize:(dz + 1) blocksize] = block return volume def getvoxelcenters(blocksize): """Returns list of (x, y, z) coordinates for voxel centers in a block.""" centers = [] for x in range(blocksize): for y in range(blocksize): for z in range(blocksize): centers.append((x + 0.5, y + 0.5, z + 0.5)) return centers def getindex(p, blocksize): """Maps 3D coordinate to flat array index.""" x, y, z = p return int(x) + int(y) blocksize + int(z) blocksize blocksize def applyrigidtransform(p, r, t): """Applies rigid transform T(p) = Rp + t.""" R = eulertorotationmatrix(r) parr = np.array(p) return np.dot(R, parr) + t def inverserigidtransform(p, r, t): """Applies inverse rigid transform T^-1(p) = R^T(p - t).""" R = eulertorotationmatrix(r) Rinv = R.T parr = np.array(p) return np.dot(Rinv, parr - t) def eulertorotationmatrix(r): """Converts Euler angles (rad) to 3x3 rotation matrix.""" rx, ry, rz = r Rx = np.array([[1, 0, 0], [0, math.cos(rx), -math.sin(rx)], [0, math.sin(rx), math.cos(rx)]]) Ry = np.array([[math.cos(ry), 0, math.sin(ry)], [0, 1, 0], [-math.sin(ry), 0, math.cos(ry)]]) Rz = np.array([[math.cos(rz), -math.sin(rz), 0], [math.sin(rz), math.cos(rz), 0], [0, 0, 1]]) return Rz @ Ry @ Rx def trilinearinterpolate(volume, point): """Performs trilinear interpolation on a 3D volume at a fractional point.""" x, y, z = point x0, y0, z0 = int(math.floor(x)), int(math.floor(y)), int(math.floor(z)) x1, y1, z1 = x0 + 1, y0 + 1, z0 + 1 dx, dy, dz = x - x0, y - y0, z - z0 def clamp(v, minv, maxv): return max(minv, min(v, maxv)) v000 = volume[clamp(x0, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y0, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z0, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v100 = volume[clamp(x1, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y0, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z0, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v010 = volume[clamp(x0, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y1, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z0, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v110 = volume[clamp(x1, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y1, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z0, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v001 = volume[clamp(x0, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y0, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z1, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v101 = volume[clamp(x1, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y0, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z1, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v011 = volume[clamp(x0, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y1, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z1, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] v111 = volume[clamp(x1, 0, volume.shape[0]-1), clamp(y1, 0, volume.shape[1]-1), clamp(z1, 0, volume.shape[2]-1)] c00 = v000 (1 - dx) + v100 dx c01 = v010 (1 - dx) + v110 dx c10 = v001 (1 - dx) + v101 dx c11 = v011 (1 - dx) + v111 dx c0 = c00 (1 - dy) + c01 dy c1 = c10 (1 - dy) + c11 dy return c0 (1 - dz) + c1 dz def computejacobianrow(p, r, t, neighborhood, blocksize): """Computes Jacobian row for sample p using finite difference.""" eps = 1e-5 jrow = np.zeros(6) basepred = trilinearinterpolate(neighborhood, applyrigidtransform(p, r, t)) for k in range(6): perturbedr = r.copy() perturbedt = t.copy() if k < 3: perturbedr[k] += eps else: perturbedt[k - 3] += eps perturbedpred = trilinearinterpolate(neighborhood, applyrigidtransform(p, perturbedr, perturbedt)) jrow[k] = (perturbedpred - basepred) / eps return jrow def encodetransformdomain(residual): """Applies standard 3D DCT to residual coefficients.""" # Standard 3D DCT implementation omitted for brevity; applies separable 1D DCT along each axis. return residual # Placeholder for actual DCT transform This is the core optimization subroutine used within Motion-Compensated Block Warping. It estimates the 6-DoF rigid transform for a specific block by aligning TSDF samples using a damped Gauss-Newton procedure. It is chosen when precise local motion estimation is required to minimize residual energy. It differs from global motion estimation by operating on a per-block basis, allowing for independent motion of different parts of the scene. Key implementation details include clamping translation updates to 1 voxel and rotation updates to 5 degrees per step to prevent divergence, and falling back to zero-motion if the neighborhood is incomplete or samples are unreliable. A motion modeling approach that decouples coarse and fine-grained motion to mitigate inaccuracies in deformation networks, preventing the querying of wrong grid cells. It predicts coarse motion mc corresponding to motion between grid cells, and fine-grained motion mf that operates only within grid cells. The step size \alpha controls the magnitude of motion and is set to 0.0001 for synthetic scenes, close to the size of a single grid cell. The deformation network \Phid is implemented as a 3-layer MLP with a width of 64. Time Complexity: The motion estimation step involves an iterative Gauss-Newton optimization. The cost depends on the number of samples in the block, the number of iterations, and the cost of trilinear interpolation and Jacobian computation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the current block, the previous frame's reconstructed TSDF, and the 3 \times 3 \times 3 neighborhood for interpolation. The source uses a sparse representation with a GPU-side spatial hash table, reducing memory usage for empty space. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Effectively reduces residual energy for rigidly moving objects, leading to better compression ratios for dynamic TSDF volumes. Limitations: Relies on the assumption of rigid motion within each block. Non-rigid deformations within a block will not be well-compensated. Requires accurate motion estimation, which can be computationally expensive. When to use: Suitable for compressing dynamic scenes with significant rigid body motion, such as in 3D reconstruction from video sequences. When not to use: Not suitable for scenes with significant non-rigid deformation or where motion estimation is unreliable (e.g., textureless regions, occlusions). The method originates from the paper "Implicit Surface Compression -- with Good Old Discrete Cosine Transform and Motion Compensation". It is part of a codec for compressing sparse TSDF volumes, leveraging traditional image compression techniques (DCT) and video compression concepts (motion compensation) for 3D data. The implementation uses voxel hashing for sparse storage. Implicit Surface Compression -- with Good Old Discrete Cosine Transform and Motion Compensation, https://doi.org/10.1145/3811298, fetched 2026-10-30 Ced-NeRF: A Compact and Efficient Method for Dynamic Neural Radiance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v38i4.28138, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Mesh Transformation via Embree RTC
head: xformRtcMeshOnly
body: This method applies a 4x4 transformation matrix to mesh vertices within an Embree ray tracing scene buffer while preserving the original vertex positions in the source mesh data. Inputs: A source mesh with vertex positions \mathbf{v}{orig}. A 4x4 transformation matrix M. An Embree geometry object containing the vertex buffer. Outputs: Updated vertex buffer in the Embree geometry. The source mesh remains unchanged. Data Structures: Vertex buffer: Array of 3D floats (x, y, z). Transformation matrix: 4x4 float matrix consistent with Embree's expectations. Steps: 1. Retrieve the vertex buffer pointer from the Embree geometry using rtcGetGeometryBufferData. 2. Initialize a running sum vector averagePt to (0, 0, 0, 1) and maxlen to 0. 3. Iterate through each vertex i from 0 to N-1 (where N is the vertex count): a. Reset the current vertex \mathbf{v}i in the buffer to its original position \mathbf{v}{orig, i}. b. Transform the vertex: \mathbf{v}' = M \cdot \mathbf{v}{orig, i} (using homogeneous coordinates with w=1). c. Update the buffer with the transformed coordinates: \mathbf{v}i.x = \mathbf{v}'[0], \mathbf{v}i.y = \mathbf{v}'[1], \mathbf{v}i.z = \mathbf{v}'[2]. d. Accumulate the transformed position into the running sum: averagePt += \mathbf{v}'. e. Compute the distance d from \mathbf{v}' to the current running centroid \mathbf{c}i = \text{averagePt} / \max(1, i). f. If d > \text{maxlen}, update \text{maxlen} = d. 4. After the loop, compute the final centroid \mathbf{cp} = \text{averagePt} / N. 5. Commit the geometry and scene updates in Embree. Pitfalls: The incremental computation of maxlen (distance to the running centroid) is mathematically incorrect for finding the maximum distance from the final centroid. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def transformmeshembree(vertices, originalpositions, M, N): # vertices: array of objects with.x,.y,.z attributes # M: 4x4 matrix (list of lists) # N: vertex count averagept = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] maxlen = 0.0 for i in range(N): # Reset to original vorig = originalpositions[i] vh = [vorig[0], vorig[1], vorig[2], 1.0] # Transform v = M vh vtrans = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for r in range(4): for c in range(4): vtrans[r] += M[r][c] vh[c] # Update buffer vertices[i].x = vtrans[0] vertices[i].y = vtrans[1] vertices[i].z = vtrans[2] # Accumulate averagept[0] += vtrans[0] averagept[1] += vtrans[1] averagept[2] += vtrans[2] # averagept[3] remains 1.0 per source logic # Compute distance to running centroid divisor = 1 if i == 0 else i centroidx = averagept[0] / divisor centroidy = averagept[1] / divisor centroidz = averagept[2] / divisor d = ((vtrans[0] - centroidx)2 + (vtrans[1] - centroidy)2 + (vtrans[2] - centroidz)2)0.5 if d > maxlen: maxlen = d # Final centroid cpx = averagept[0] / N cpy = averagept[1] / N cpz = averagept[2] / N # Commit geometry and scene updates in Embree Applies a 4x4 transformation matrix to all vertices and normals of a mesh. It differs from its parent Mesh Transformation via Embree RTC by operating directly on the mesh data structure rather than managing Embree's internal buffer state, and from Mesh Transformation for Printable Volume by lacking volume-constraint logic or axis alignment. name: Mesh Transformation
body: Applies a 4x4 transformation matrix to all vertices and normals of a mesh, typically to move geometry from a local object frame to a world frame or to apply kinematic transforms to robot links. Inputs: mesh: Mesh object containing vertex positions and optional normals. xf: 4x4 transformation matrix. Outputs: Updated mesh with transformed vertices and normals. Data Structures: mesh->vertices: Array of 3D vectors. mesh->normals: Array of 3D vectors, optional. xf: 4x4 matrix. Steps: 1. Transform Vertices: Iterate over vertices i from 0 to nv-1. Compute the transformed vertex v'i = xf \cdot vi. Update mesh->vertices[i] = v'i. 2. Transform Normals (if present): Compute the normal transformation matrix nxf from xf. Iterate over normals i from 0 to nv-1. Compute n'i = nxf \cdot ni. Renormalize ni \leftarrow n'i / \|n'i\|. 3. Update Bounding Volumes: If the mesh has valid bounding boxes or spheres, invalidate them and recompute them based on the new vertex positions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def applyxform(mesh, xf): nv = len(mesh.vertices) # 1. Transform vertices for i in range(nv): v = mesh.vertices[i] x = xf[0][0]v[0] + xf[0][1]v[1] + xf[0][2]v[2] + xf[0][3] y = xf[1][0]v[0] + xf[1][1]v[1] + xf[1][2]v[2] + xf[1][3] z = xf[2][0]v[0] + xf[2][1]v[1] + xf[2][2]v[2] + xf[2][3] mesh.vertices[i] = (x, y, z) # 2. Transform normals if mesh.normals is not None: # Compute normal transformation matrix: inverse transpose of upper-left 3x3 of xf M = [[xf[r][c] for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] Minv = invert3x3(M) nxf = [[Minv[c][r] for c in range(3)] for r in range(3)] for i in range(nv): n = mesh.normals[i] nx = nxf[0][0]n[0] + nxf[0][1]n[1] + nxf[0][2]n[2] ny = nxf[1][0]n[0] + nxf[1][1]n[1] + nxf[1][2]n[2] nz = nxf[2][0]n[0] + nxf[2][1]n[1] + nxf[2][2]n[2] length = (nxnx + nyny + nznz)0.5 if length > 0: mesh.normals[i] = (nx/length, ny/length, nz/length) else: mesh.normals[i] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 3. Update bounding volumes if mesh.boundingbox is not None: minval = (float('inf'), float('inf'), float('inf')) maxval = (float('-inf'), float('-inf'), float('-inf')) for v in mesh.vertices: minval = tuple(min(a, b) for a, b in zip(minval, v)) maxval = tuple(max(a, b) for a, b in zip(maxval, v)) mesh.boundingbox.min = minval mesh.boundingbox.max = maxval mesh.boundingbox.valid = True def invert3x3(m): a, b, c = m[0] d, e, f = m[1] g, h, i = m[2] det = a(ei - fh) - b(di - fg) + c(dh - eg) if det == 0: raise ValueError("Matrix is singular") invdet = 1.0 / det return [ [(ei - fh)invdet, (ch - bi)invdet, (bf - ce)invdet], [(fg - di)invdet, (ai - cg)invdet, (cd - af)invdet], [(dh - eg)invdet, (bg - ah)invdet, (ae - bd)invdet] ] Parameters: xf: 4x4 transformation matrix. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singular Matrices: If the 3x3 linear part of xf is singular, the inverse transpose cannot be computed. Bounding Volume Recomputation: Failing to update bounding volumes after transformation leads to incorrect culling or intersection tests. Computes a 4x4 transformation matrix to scale, rotate, and translate a mesh so it fits within a specified printable volume, typically aligning the largest dimension with the z-axis. It differs from generic mesh transformations by incorporating volume constraints and automatic axis alignment. Time Complexity: O(n) for vertices and normals, where n is the number of vertices. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory if done in-place. Strengths: Simple, efficient, and standard approach for applying rigid or affine transforms to mesh geometry. Limitations: Does not handle dynamic topology changes. Requires careful handling of normals for non-uniform scaling. When to Use: When moving mesh data between coordinate frames (e.g., object to world, link to base). When Not to Use: When the transformation involves non-linear deformations. name: Mesh Transformation for Printable Volume
body: Computes a 4x4 transformation matrix to scale, rotate, and translate a mesh so it fits within a specified printable volume, typically aligning the largest dimension with the z-axis. It differs from generic mesh transformations by incorporating volume constraints and automatic axis alignment. Inputs: mesh: A mesh object with vertex positions and an axis-aligned bounding box (bbox). printsize: A 3D vector [x, y, z] defining the maximum printable dimensions. size (optional): A 3D vector specifying a target size. Outputs: toworld: A 4x4 transformation matrix mapping local mesh coordinates to world/printable coordinates. Data Structures: bbox: Axis-aligned bounding box with fields min (3D vector) and max (3D vector). extents: 3D vector where extents[i] = bbox.max[i] - bbox.min[i]. Steps and Formulas: 1. Compute Extents: Calculate extmax = max(bbox.extents()). 2. Determine Rotation Axis: Identify the axis of maximum extent: axismax = select(bbox.extents() == extmax, 1.0, 0.0). If axismax is not (0, 0, 1), compute rotaxis = cross(axismax, (0, 0, 1)) and rotation matrix R as a 90° rotation around rotaxis. 3. Center in XY Plane: Extract vertex positions, mask non-z dimensions to find the 2D footprint, compute the minimum enclosing circle center Cxy and radius r, and compute translation Txy to center the object at the origin in the XY plane. 4. Compute Scale Factors (default): Calculate sz = printsize.z / extmax and sxy = 0.5 printsize.xy / r. Take s = min(sz, sxy). 5. Assemble Transform (default): toworld = S(s) @ R @ Txy, where S(s) is a uniform scale matrix. 6. Assemble Transform (size provided): If size is provided, check if any component of size exceeds printsize. If so, raise an error. Compute mesh center c = 0.5 (bbox.min + bbox.max). Compute scale factors s' = size / extmax (element-wise division of the size vector by the scalar extmax). Compute toworld = S(s') @ T(-c), where S(s') is a non-uniform scale matrix and T(-c) is a translation by -c. This branch skips rotation and XY centering. Parameters: printsize: Maximum printable dimensions. size: Optional target dimensions. Edge Cases: If extmax is 0, division by zero occurs; guard against empty meshes. If axismax equals (0, 0, 1), no rotation is needed. If size exceeds printsize, an error is raised. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computemeshtransform(mesh, printsize, size=None): bbox = mesh.bbox extents = bbox.max - bbox.min extmax = max(extents) if extmax == 0: raise ValueError("Empty mesh") # Rotation axismax = [1.0 if extents[i] == extmax else 0.0 for i in range(3)] if axismax != [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]: rotaxis = cross(axismax, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) rotmat = rotatematrix(rotaxis, 90.0) else: rotmat = identitymatrix() # XY Centering vertices2d = [(v.x, v.y) for v in mesh.vertices] cxy, r = minenclosingcircle(vertices2d) tr = translatematrix([-cxy[0], -cxy[1], 0.0]) if size is None: sz = printsize.z / extmax sxy = 0.5 printsize.xy / r s = min(sz, sxy) scalemat = scalematrix([s, s, s]) toworld = scalemat @ rotmat @ tr else: if any(size[i] > printsize[i] for i in range(3)): raise ValueError("size exceeds printsize") c = 0.5 (bbox.min + bbox.max) scalefactors = [size[i] / extmax for i in range(3)] scalemat = scalematrix(scalefactors) tc = translatematrix([-c.x, -c.y, -c.z]) toworld = scalemat @ tc return toworld Calculates scale and translation factors to align a surface mesh in micron coordinates with a volume defined by voxel size and volume size. It initializes default surfaceScale to 0.00161 and surfaceTranslation to [-313.7, -147.5, -86.5]. If units is 'micron', it calculates micronSize as volSize mapped to e \times \text{voxelSize}[i]. If sizeMax (max of micronSize) > 0, surfaceScale is set to 1 / \text{sizeMax}; otherwise, it is 1. surfaceTranslation is set to micronSize mapped to -e / 2 for each element. It returns an object { surfaceScale: number, surfaceTranslation: [number, number, number] }. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of vertices, due to bounding box and miniball computation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store vertex positions for miniball calculation. Strengths: Automatically orients the object for optimal printing; handles volume constraints. Limitations: The size branch ignores rotation and XY centering, which may lead to suboptimal orientation if the mesh is not already aligned. Originated in the context of inverse rendering for tomographic volumetric additive manufacturing. It is used to prepare meshes for 3D printing by ensuring they fit within the printer's build volume and are oriented correctly. The surface alignment variant is used in web-based volume viewers for scientific visualization. name: Incremental Scaling Algorithm
head: Back Scaling
body: The Incremental Scaling Algorithm is a method for applying uniform or non-uniform scaling transformations to voxel grids by computing destination coordinates through iterative addition rather than full matrix multiplication. It solves the computational bottleneck of per-voxel scaling in large volumes by exploiting spatial coherence, reducing the arithmetic cost of coordinate transformation to simple additions. It sets itself apart from direct matrix multiplication by avoiding multiplications for every voxel, and from Motion-Compensated Block Warping by operating on the voxel grid structure itself rather than compressing temporal changes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Source voxel grid defined by bounds (X{src}, Y{src}, Z{src}) to (X{src\end}, Y{src\end}, Z{src\end}). Input: Scaling factors Sx, Sy, Sz. Input: Destination grid bounds (Xs, Ys, Zs) to (XE, YE, ZE). Output: Destination voxel grid with scaled geometry. Data Structures: The algorithm operates on integer voxel coordinates. Intermediate floating-point coordinates are used for the incremental stepping to maintain precision before rounding to the nearest integer voxel index. Method: The standard scaling relationship maps a source coordinate to a destination coordinate: X{dest} = X{src} Sx Y{dest} = Y{src} Sy Z{dest} = Z{src} Sz Direct computation requires a multiplication for every voxel. The incremental algorithm derives the next coordinate from the previous one: X{dest} + Sx = (X{src} + 1) Sx = X{src} Sx + Sx Y{dest} + Sy = (Y{src} + 1) Sy = Y{src} Sy + Sy Z{dest} + Sz = (Z{src} + 1) Sz = Z{src} Sz + Sz Thus, the next transformed coordinate is obtained by adding the scaling factor to the predecessor's coordinate and rounding to the nearest integer. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: 1. Holes in Forward Scaling: If any scaling factor is greater than 1, the destination volume expands. Stepping through the source and mapping to the destination may skip destination voxels, creating holes. 2. Back Scaling: To avert holes, the algorithm reverses the process. It steps through the destination room and maps back to the source. The destination corners are found by transforming the source corners. The source coordinate is determined by multiplying destination coordinates by (1/Sx, 1/Sy, 1/Sz). 3. Parallel Stepping: A more efficient back-scaling variant steps through the source and destination rooms in parallel. The increments for the source room are (X{incr}/Sx, Y{incr}/Sy, Z{incr}/Sz), where X{incr}, Y{incr}, Z{incr} are the steps (typically 1) used in the destination room. 4. Overwriting: If the source and destination grids share memory, voxels may be overwritten before they are read. The starting corner of the transformation loop must be chosen based on the signs of Sx, Sy, Sz to ensure safe traversal. Pseudocode: The following implements back-scaling to prevent holes when S > 1. It assumes the destination bounds are known and the source bounds are derived or known. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalscaling(sourcegrid, destbounds, scalefactors): """ sourcegrid: 3D array of voxel values destbounds: tuple (Xs, Ys, Zs, XE, YE, ZE) defining destination voxel range scalefactors: tuple (Sx, Sy, Sz) """ Sx, Sy, Sz = scalefactors # Initialize destination grid destgrid = createemptygrid(destbounds) # Determine starting point based on scale factors to avoid overwriting # If Sx > 1, we step forward in dest, so we need to map back to source. # The source coordinate is destcoord / Sx. Xs, Ys, Zs, XE, YE, ZE = destbounds # Precompute inverse scales for source stepping if using parallel method # Or compute directly for each voxel. The source text suggests parallel stepping # with increments (Xincr/Sx,...). Here we implement the direct back-mapping # for clarity, which is equivalent to stepping dest and rounding source. for y in range(Ys, YE + 1): for z in range(Zs, ZE + 1): for x in range(Xs, XE + 1): # Reverse transform: map destination integer coordinate to source # The source coordinate is a float position. srcx = x / Sx srcy = y / Sy srcz = z / Sz # Round to nearest integer voxel index in source srcix = round(srcx) srciy = round(srcy) srciz = round(srcz) # Check bounds to avoid out-of-bounds access if iswithinsourcebounds(srcix, srciy, srciz, sourcegrid): destgrid[x, y, z] = sourcegrid[srcix, srciy, srciz] else: destgrid[x, y, z] = EMPTYVALUE return destgrid Applies affine transformations (translation, scaling, rotation) by computing new positions from the immediate predecessor's position using max three additions per coordinate. It reduces arithmetic operations compared to matrix multiplication but requires processing all voxels, including empty ones, making it suitable for parallel architectures. Deforms volumes using 2D user-guided control points and Radial Basis Functions (RBFs) to generate a 3D displacement map. It differs by relying on global smooth interpolation from sparse handles rather than local voxel-wise transformations. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the output grid. The cost per voxel is reduced to a few additions and a rounding operation, compared to multiplications in standard scaling. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output grid. In-place modification is possible if traversal order is managed correctly to prevent overwriting. Strengths: Significantly reduces computational complexity for large rooms/volumes by eliminating multiplications. Limitations: Requires careful handling of scaling factors >1 (back scaling) to avoid holes. Requires processing all voxels in the destination volume, even if empty, unlike sparse voxel approaches. When to use: When scaling voxel primitives in a voxel frame buffer processor and computational efficiency is critical. The Incremental Scaling Algorithm was introduced in the context of the VoxBLIT Engine, a voxel frame buffer processor. It was developed to handle large rooms efficiently by reducing the complexity of geometric transformations. The voxblt Engine: A Voxel Frame Buffer Processor, https://doi.org/10.2312/eggh/eggh88/085-102, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Incremental Geometric Transformation
head: Incremental Transformation
body: Incremental Geometric Transformation is a method for applying affine transformations (translation, scaling, rotation) to voxel primitives by computing the new position of each voxel based on the already-transformed position of its immediate predecessor, using a maximum of three additions per voxel instead of full matrix multiplication. It sets itself apart from direct matrix multiplication by exploiting spatial coherence between neighboring voxels, significantly reducing arithmetic operations at the cost of requiring all volume elements (including empty ones) to be processed, making it particularly suitable for parallel architectures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D voxel grid defined by source coordinates (x, y, z), and an affine transformation matrix M. Output: A transformed voxel grid where each voxel's position is updated according to M. Data Structures: Source Grid: A regular 3D array where neighbors are accessible via simple index increments. Transformation Matrix: A 4 \times 4 matrix M representing the affine transform. Intermediate Position: A 4D homogeneous vector storing the transformed position of the current voxel. Numbered Steps: 1. Initial Transformation: Compute the transformed position of the first grid point using one matrix-vector multiplication. 2. Incremental Update: Compute the transformed position of subsequent voxels by adding precomputed incremental deltas derived from the transformation matrix to the transformed position of their immediate predecessor, exploiting inter- and intra-scan-line coherency. 3. Overlap Resolution: If source and destination primitives overlap, perform the transformation in a predefined sequence determined by an orientation algorithm to prevent source voxels from being overwritten before they are translated. This is necessary because no scratch memory is available to hold old voxel information. Formulas: Let \vec{p}{i,j,k} be the source position of voxel (i,j,k), and \vec{p}{i,j,k}' be its transformed position. For the first voxel (0,0,0): \vec{p}{0,0,0}' = M \cdot \vec{p}{0,0,0} For subsequent voxels, the algorithm uses fixed increments corresponding to the transformed basis vectors: \Deltax = M \cdot [1,0,0,0]^T, \quad \Deltay = M \cdot [0,1,0,0]^T, \quad \Deltaz = M \cdot [0,0,1,0]^T The position updates as \vec{p}{i,j,k}' = \vec{p}{i-1,j,k}' + \Deltax (and similarly for y and z). The sources state the method requires "three additions/increments" per voxel, though one source notes "three additions per coordinate"; this refers to updating the three spatial components using the precomputed deltas. Parameters: Transformation Matrix M: Defined by the specific geometric operation (translation, rotation, scaling). Grid Dimensions: Nx, Ny, Nz. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlap: Overlapping source and destination primitives can cause data corruption if voxels are overwritten before being read, resolved by a predefined processing order. Empty Voxels: The method requires transforming all volume elements, including empty ones, increasing computation if not parallelized. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def incrementalgeometrictransformation(voxelgrid, transformationmatrix): """ Applies an affine transformation to a voxel grid using incremental updates. Args: voxelgrid: 3D array of voxels with source coordinates. transformationmatrix: 4x4 affine transformation matrix. Returns: Transformed voxel grid (list of lists of lists of 4D homogeneous vectors). """ Nx, Ny, Nz = voxelgrid.shape # Initialize output grid with homogeneous coordinates transformedpositions = [[[[[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] for in range(Nz)] for in range(Ny)] for in range(Nx)]] # Step 1: Transform the first voxel (origin) using matrix multiplication p0src = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] transformedpositions[0][0][0] = matrixvectormultiply(transformationmatrix, p0src) # Precompute incremental deltas (transformed basis vectors) dx = matrixvectormultiply(transformationmatrix, [1.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) dy = matrixvectormultiply(transformationmatrix, [0.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]) dz = matrixvectormultiply(transformationmatrix, [0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 0.0]) # Step 2: Incrementally update the remaining voxels # Iterate in a predefined sequence to handle overlaps if necessary for z in range(Nz): for y in range(Ny): for x in range(Nx): if x == 0 and y == 0 and z == 0: continue # Already computed elif x > 0: # Update along X-axis using predecessor in X transformedpositions[x][y][z] = vectoradd(transformedpositions[x-1][y][z], dx) elif y > 0: # Update along Y-axis using predecessor in Y transformedpositions[x][y][z] = vectoradd(transformedpositions[x][y-1][z], dy) elif z > 0: # Update along Z-axis using predecessor in Z transformedpositions[x][y][z] = vectoradd(transformedpositions[x][y][z-1], dz) return transformedpositions def matrixvectormultiply(matrix, vector): """Standard 4x4 matrix by 4-vector multiplication.""" result = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(4): s = 0.0 for j in range(4): s += matrix[i][j] vector[j] result[i] = s return result def vectoradd(v1, v2): """Component-wise addition of two 4D vectors.""" return [v1[0] + v2[0], v1[1] + v2[1], v1[2] + v2[2], v1[3] + v2[3]] Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the total number of voxels, with a very low constant factor (3 additions per voxel) compared to O(N) with a higher constant for matrix multiplication. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing the voxel grid. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of voxels; performance is highly dependent on parallelization, as all voxels (including empty ones) must be processed. Strengths: Reduces arithmetic operations significantly; exploits spatial coherence; suitable for parallel architectures. Limitations: Requires processing all voxels, including empty ones; potential for overlap issues if not handled with a specific ordering algorithm. When to use: When hardware supports parallel processing and arithmetic operations are expensive; when the transformation is affine and the grid is dense or parallelization is feasible. When not to use: When the grid is sparse and most voxels are empty (wastes computation). The Incremental Geometric Transformation technique was developed as part of the Voxblt Engine, a voxel frame buffer processor, in the late 1980s. It was designed to perform geometric operations (translation, scaling, rotation) efficiently by exploiting inter- and intra-scan-line coherency. The method was implemented in hardware, utilizing parallel memory and barrel shifters to accelerate the incremental updates. It is also discussed in the context of volume visualization and rendering techniques, where it is noted for its suitability to parallel architectures.
