name: Face Normal Computation
head: Face Normal Accumulation for Smooth Normals, Face Normal Calculation, computeFaceNormal, getShadingFaceNormal
body: Face Normal Computation determines the geometric orientation of a polygonal face (typically a triangle) to provide shading information for ray-marched distance fields or rasterized meshes. It solves the problem of deriving a consistent surface normal from discrete vertex positions when an explicit normal attribute is unavailable. Unlike Vertex Normal Averaging for Shading, which computes smooth per-vertex normals by aggregating face normals, this method yields the flat normal for a single face. Inputs: Vertex positions: v0, v1, v2 \in \mathbb{R}^3, representing the three corners of the triangle face. Ray direction d and hit axis information for the axis-aligned heuristic. Outputs: Face normal: n \in \mathbb{R}^3, a unit vector perpendicular to the triangle plane. Data Structures: Vertex array: A contiguous buffer or list of 3D vectors. Face index array: Indices pointing to vertices in the vertex array. Steps: 1. Extract Vertices: Retrieve the 3D coordinates v0, v1, v2 for the current face using the face index array. 2. Compute Edge Vectors: Calculate two edge vectors originating from the same vertex (e.g., v0): e1 = v1 - v0 e2 = v2 - v0 3. Cross Product: Compute the unnormalized normal vector n{raw} using the cross product of the edge vectors: n{raw} = e1 \times e2 This vector is perpendicular to the triangle plane. 4. Normalization: Normalize n{raw} to obtain the unit face normal n: n = \frac{n{raw}}{\|n{raw}\|} Special handling is required for degenerate triangles where \|n{raw}\| is near zero. Alternative: Axis-Aligned Heuristic (Ray-Marching Specific) In voxel-based or signed distance field (SDF) ray-marching implementations, if the hit location is known to be on a specific axis-aligned face, the normal can be derived directly from the ray direction components to ensure it points back toward the ray origin. If the hit is on the X-axis face: n = (\text{select}(-1, 1, dx < 0.0), 0, 0) If the hit is on the Y-axis face: n = (0, \text{select}(-1, 1, dy < 0.0), 0) If the hit is on the Z-axis face: n = (0, 0, \text{select}(-1, 1, dz < 0.0)) Here, \text{select}(a, b, c) returns b if condition c is true, else a. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def select(a, b, condition): """Returns b if condition is true, else a.""" return b if condition else a def computefacenormal(v0, v1, v2): """ Computes the geometric face normal for a triangle defined by v0, v1, v2. Returns a normalized 3D vector. """ # Step 1: Compute edge vectors e1 = (v1[0] - v0[0], v1[1] - v0[1], v1[2] - v0[2]) e2 = (v2[0] - v0[0], v2[1] - v0[1], v2[2] - v0[2]) # Step 2: Cross product e1 x e2 nx = e1[1] e2[2] - e1[2] e2[1] ny = e1[2] e2[0] - e1[0] e2[2] nz = e1[0] e2[1] - e1[1] e2[0] # Step 3: Handle degenerate cases magsq = nx nx + ny ny + nz nz # Threshold for degenerate triangle (zero area) if magsq < 1e-20: # Return a default up vector for degenerate faces return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Step 4: Normalize mag = math.sqrt(magsq) return (nx / mag, ny / mag, nz / mag) def computefacenormalaxisheuristic(raydirection, axis): """ Computes face normal based on ray direction for axis-aligned hits. axis: 0 for X, 1 for Y, 2 for Z. Returns normal pointing back toward the ray origin. """ dx, dy, dz = raydirection if axis == 0: return (select(-1.0, 1.0, dx < 0.0), 0.0, 0.0) elif axis == 1: return (0.0, select(-1.0, 1.0, dy < 0.0), 0.0) elif axis == 2: return (0.0, 0.0, select(-1.0, 1.0, dz < 0.0)) else: raise ValueError("Axis must be 0, 1, or 2") Parameters: Degeneracy Threshold: 10^{-20} is used to detect zero-length normals. Default Normal: [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] is used as a fallback for degenerate triangles. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Triangles: If vertices are collinear or identical, the cross product is zero. Normalizing a zero vector causes division by zero. The method must check the squared magnitude against a small epsilon and substitute a default vector. Winding Order: The direction of the normal depends on the order of v0, v1, v2. Precision: For very small or very large coordinates, floating-point precision errors in the cross product may affect the normal's accuracy. Computes a smooth shading normal for a polygonal face by averaging the pre-computed vertex normals of its three corners and normalizing the result. It serves as the shading-based alternative to geometric face normal computation. This approach reduces visible faceting on rendered isosurfaces compared to flat shading. A technique to ensure accuracy of the mesh distance field sign by using a weighted sum of normals on incident faces. It addresses the breakdown of face normals near edges or vertices when generating the sign of a distance field. Interpolates face normals to pixel space using fragment attributes and identity weights. Computes pixel positions in world coordinates from the depth buffer and camera intrinsics/extrinsics. Calculates direction vectors from each pixel to the camera and normalizes them. Computes the dot product between pixel normals and directions to camera. Time Complexity: O(1) per face. The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (subtractions, multiplications, one square root). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. No additional data structures are required beyond the input vertex positions. Strengths: Simple to implement; does not require pre-computed normal attributes; geometrically exact for the triangle geometry. Limitations: Produces flat shading (faceted appearance) if used directly for per-vertex shading without averaging; sensitive to vertex winding order; degenerate triangles require special handling. When to use: When only vertex positions are available and flat shading is acceptable, or as a precursor to vertex normal averaging. When not to use: When smooth shading is required without post-processing (use Vertex Normal Averaging for Shading or Gradient-Based Surface Normal Estimation); when the mesh has significant degenerate geometry and robust fallbacks are not implemented. Face normal computation is a fundamental technique in computer graphics, originating from the basic principles of polygonal mesh rendering. The geometric method using the cross product of edge vectors is standard in rasterization and ray tracing pipelines. The axis-aligned heuristic appears in specialized voxel-based or SDF ray-marching implementations. The method is widely used in real-time rendering engines and offline renderers as a fallback or primary method for shading when explicit normals are absent. mstampfli/voxelG, https://github.com/mstampfli/voxelG, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) seung-lab/zmesh, https://github.com/seung-lab/zmesh, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, https://github.com/leonzheng2/INF584-HighResolutionSparseVoxelDAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) prateekchandan/Advanced-CG-High-Resolution-Sparse-Voxel-DAGs, https://github.com/prateekchandan/Advanced-CG-High-Resolution-Sparse-Voxel-DAGs, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, https://github.com/dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) elyssov/prometheus-engine, https://github.com/elyssov/prometheus-engine, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) PDF Generating Signed Distance Fields from Triangle Meshes using Vulkan..., https://williamwhitehouse.dev/assets/projects/2023/sdf-gen/gen-sdf-from-meshes-using-vulkan-compute-report.pdf, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) GAP-LAB-CUHK-SZ/gaustudio, https://github.com/GAP-LAB-CUHK-SZ/gaustudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Vertex Normal Averaging for Shading
head: Face Normal Computation (shading-based), Shading Normal Computation, Surface Normal Averaging for Shading
body: Vertex Normal Averaging for Shading computes smooth surface normals for a mesh by averaging the geometric normals of all adjacent triangles sharing a vertex, then normalizing the result. It solves the faceting artifact inherent in flat shading by providing interpolated normals for Gouraud or Phong shading. Unlike its sibling Face Normal Computation, which computes a single normal per face, this method produces per-vertex normals that vary across the surface, enabling smooth lighting transitions. Inputs: A list of triangles, where each triangle is defined by three vertex indices. Each triangle must have a precomputed geometric face normal. Outputs: A list of vertex normals, one for each unique vertex in the mesh. Data Structures: 1. Vertex Accumulator: A list or array of structures, one per vertex. Each structure contains: normal: A 3D vector (Vector3) initialized to (0, 0, 0). faceCount: An integer initialized to 0. 2. Triangle List: An array of triangles. Each triangle stores indices to its three vertices and its precomputed face normal vector. Steps: 1. Initialization: Create the vertex accumulator list with size equal to the number of unique vertices. Set all normal vectors to zero and all faceCount integers to zero. 2. Accumulation: Iterate through every triangle in the mesh. For each triangle with face normal \mathbf{n}f and vertex indices i0, i1, i2: Add \mathbf{n}f to accumulator[i0].normal. Add \mathbf{n}f to accumulator[i1].normal. Add \mathbf{n}f to accumulator[i2].normal. Increment accumulator[i0].faceCount by 1. Increment accumulator[i1].faceCount by 1. Increment accumulator[i2].faceCount by 1. 3. Normalization: Iterate through every vertex in the mesh. For each vertex v: Let \mathbf{S} be accumulator[v].normal and C be accumulator[v].faceCount. If C > 0, compute the averaged normal \mathbf{n}v = \frac{\mathbf{S}}{C}. Normalize \mathbf{n}v to unit length: \mathbf{n}v \leftarrow \frac{\mathbf{n}v}{\|\mathbf{n}v\|}. Store \mathbf{n}v as the final vertex normal. 4. Usage: Pass the computed vertex normals to the rendering pipeline for shading calculations. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computevertexnormals(triangles, numvertices): # Step 1: Initialization # Each vertex has an accumulated normal vector and a count of adjacent faces accumulators = [] for i in range(numvertices): accumulators.append({ 'normal': Vector3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 'faceCount': 0 }) # Step 2: Accumulation for triangle in triangles: # triangle.normal is the precomputed geometric face normal # triangle.v0, triangle.v1, triangle.v2 are vertex indices n = triangle.normal accumulators[triangle.v0]['normal'] += n accumulators[triangle.v0]['faceCount'] += 1 accumulators[triangle.v1]['normal'] += n accumulators[triangle.v1]['faceCount'] += 1 accumulators[triangle.v2]['normal'] += n accumulators[triangle.v2]['faceCount'] += 1 # Step 3: Normalization vertexnormals = [] for i in range(numvertices): acc = accumulators[i] if acc['faceCount'] > 0: # Average the accumulated normals avgnormal = acc['normal'] / acc['faceCount'] # Normalize to unit length finalnormal = normalize(avgnormal) else: # Fallback for isolated vertices or degenerate cases finalnormal = Vector3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) # Default up vector vertexnormals.append(finalnormal) return vertexnormals Parameters: Weighting: The basic method uses equal weighting for all adjacent faces. Sources do not specify area-weighted or angle-weighted variants. Edge Cases: If a vertex is not shared by any triangle (isolated), faceCount remains 0. The implementation must handle division by zero. Pitfalls: Unindexed Meshes: If the mesh is stored as an unindexed, unordered list of vertices ("big mash of vertexes"), determining adjacency requires iterating through all triangles for each vertex, which is O(N \cdot M) where N is vertices and M is triangles. An index buffer or hash map is required for efficiency. Performance: Computing and storing vertex normals increases memory usage and pre-processing time compared to flat shading. Initialization: Failure to reset accumulators to zero before a new computation leads to incorrect results. Time Complexity: O(F + V), where F is the number of faces and V is the number of vertices. One pass over faces for accumulation, one pass over vertices for normalization. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the accumulator structures. Strengths: Produces smooth shading on curved surfaces; simple to implement; standard technique for mesh rendering. Limitations: Does not account for surface curvature or area; sharp edges appear smooth unless hard edges are explicitly marked (not covered in sources); requires precomputed face normals. When to use: When smooth shading is desired for a mesh with known topology. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained, or when flat shading is sufficient for the visual style. The technique is described in the context of R's rgl package for rendering isosurfaces, where it is used to reduce faceting artifacts by passing averaged normals to the underlying rendering function. It is also widely discussed in the context of Marching Cubes algorithms for generating meshes from voxel data, where it is essential for smooth visualization of the resulting surface. The method is a standard practice in computer graphics for Gouraud shading. name: Normal Regularization
head: spatial interpolation of normals
body: Normal Regularization is a technique to alleviate numerical instability (jitter) of surface normals near the Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) zero-level set, specifically at cusps where the function is not first-order differentiable. It solves the problem of unreliable gradients leading to inaccurate surface reconstruction in differentiable volume rendering by replacing naively sampled normals with interpolated normals from the neighborhood. It builds on SDF Normal Estimation via Finite Differences and is distinguished from siblings like Lambertian Shading with Gradient Normals and Gradient-Based Surface Normal Estimation by its specific focus on stabilizing gradients for UDF-based open surface reconstruction during volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of points p(ti) along a ray, the UDF \Psi(\cdot), its derivative \Psi'(\cdot) which returns gradients, and a neighborhood size parameter K. Output: A regularized normal vector \mathbf{n}(p(ti)) at the query point. Data Structures: Point Sequence: An ordered list of 3D points p(ti) sampled along the ray, where ti is the distance along the ray. Gradient Buffer: Stores \Psi'(p(t{i-k})) for k \in [1, K]. Parameters: K: Number of neighboring points used for interpolation. Typical values are not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Robust Structure Rendering
head: R1-R5
body: Robust Structure Rendering is a methodology for visualizing structures with consistently well-defined boundaries and rapid density changes normal to the boundary, such as bone in CT scans. It addresses the problem of digitization effects and numerical instability in normal estimation by retaining the original scene for scene-space normal estimation while preparing the structure itself via combinations of interpolation, grey transforms, and filtering. It is distinguished from frail structure rendering by its reliance on the original scene's density gradients for normals, assuming the structure satisfies specific robustness conditions. Inputs: A digital scene (volume data) containing a structure of interest; a classification of the structure as "robust". Outputs: A rendered image with reduced digitization artifacts and stable surface normals. Data Structures: The method operates on a 3D voxel grid. The scene data consists of scalar intensity values. Intermediate structures may be represented as binary masks (segmented) or grey-level volumes (filtered/interpolated). Definitions of Operators: The following operators are used in the method sequences: Ir: Trilinear scene interpolation. I{lr}: Bilinear-cubic scene interpolation. Ib: Shape-based binary scene interpolation using city block distance. I\gamma: Shape-based binary scene interpolation using a more accurate approximation to Euclidean distance. Sb: Segmentation using thresholding. Bs: Surface detection in binary scenes with integer coordinate for boundary faces. B': Surface detection using a threshold in grey scenes. F: Filtering operation. G: Grey transform. L: Linear interpolation/smoothing. C: Classification. Algorithm Steps: 1. Scene Retention: Retain the original unmodified scene data. This scene is used exclusively for normal estimation, leveraging the fact that robust structures satisfy the condition that scene density changes most rapidly normal to the boundary. 2. Structure Preparation: Prepare the structure representation to minimize digitization effects. This involves applying a sequence of operators from the set \{Ir, I{lr}, Ib, I\gamma, Sb, Bs, B', F, G, L, C\} to create a smoothed or interpolated representation of the structure. 3. Rendering: Render the prepared structure using the normals estimated from the original scene. Method Variants (R1-R5): The source defines five specific sequences for robust structure rendering. The following are the reconstructed sequences based on the provided expressions: R1: R1(B, Ib Sb) Uses binary segmentation (Sb) followed by shape-based interpolation (Ib). R2: R2(B', I\gamma) Uses grey-level surface detection (B') followed by Euclidean distance interpolation (I\gamma). R3: R3(Ir, C, Ir) Uses trilinear interpolation (Ir) and classification (C). R4: R4(B', L, I\gamma) Uses grey-level surface detection (B'), linear interpolation/smoothing (L), and Euclidean distance interpolation (I\gamma). This is cited as the best method for robust structures, with quality comparable to high-quality grey-volume rendering. R5: R5(B, F, Ib Sb, I\gamma) An improvement over R4. It combines binary segmentation (B), filtering (F), shape-based interpolation (Ib Sb), and Euclidean interpolation (I\gamma). It reduces "slicing artifacts" and better defines sutures. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Thin Parts: Aspects of bony structures, such as thin parts, may be closer to being frail than robust. In these cases, the assumption that scene-space normals are reliable may fail. Digitization Effects: Without the preparation step (interpolation/filtering), the discrete nature of the voxel grid causes jagged boundaries and noisy normals. Frail Structure Rendering is the counterpart to robust rendering for structures that do not satisfy the robust conditions (e.g., bone in MR images). Unlike robust rendering, it cannot rely on the original scene for normal estimation because scene-space normals are unreliable. It requires careful scene preparation (using operators F, Go, Gs) to create a scene suitable for normal estimation, in addition to preparing the structure. Example sequences include F1 through F6, such as F1(R1(B', Ir, I')) and F6(R6(B, Sb Fs G, Bs I's Sb, Fs G, B, I's Sb)). Strengths: Retains the original scene for normal estimation, ensuring accurate gradient direction where the structure is robust. Structure preparation minimizes digitization artifacts. R4 provides quality comparable to high-quality grey-volume rendering. R5 further reduces slicing artifacts. Limitations: Only applicable to "robust" structures. Fails for "frail" structures (e.g., MR bone) where density gradients are not reliable for normal estimation. Performance: Not explicitly quantified in terms of FLOPS or memory in the sources. The complexity depends on the specific sequence of interpolation and filtering operators chosen. The classification of structures into "robust" and "frail" was introduced to systematize the discussion of imaging transforms for visualizing surfaces and volumes. The methods were demonstrated on a talar bone from a normal human volunteer in an MR scene with a domain of 256 \times 256 \times 62 and voxel size 0.7 \text{ mm} \times 0.7 \text{ mm} \times 1.5 \text{ mm}. The work emphasizes the importance of carefully selecting imaging transforms to handle digitization effects and normal estimation stability. name: Gradient-Based Surface Normal Estimation

body: Gradient-Based Surface Normal Estimation computes surface normals for a volumetric representation by evaluating the spatial gradient of a local density field (which resembles a signed distance field) and normalizing the resulting vector. Unlike methods that rely on explicit mesh normals or complex depth-peeling techniques, this approach derives geometry directly from the voxelized volume data, ensuring high resolution and coherence with the underlying voxel grid. It is primarily used in solid voxelization pipelines and particle system simulations where on-the-fly normal computation is preferred over storing explicit normal textures. Inputs: A 3D volume grid V of density values. The grid dimensions are typically W \times H \times D (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 100 or 512^3). A query point p (integer voxel coordinates (x, y, z)) or a continuous position for ray marching. Outputs: A surface normal vector \mathbf{N} at the query point. Optionally, an encoded RGB texture where normals are stored as 8-bit unsigned integers. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D array of floating-point or integer density values. In GPU implementations, this may be packed into bitmasks or 32-bit integers for efficient lookup. Normal Texture (Precomputed Path): A 2D texture of size W \times H (flattened from 3D slices) with format GLRGB and type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. The memory layout is interleaved RGB: index 3 \times (v \times \text{width} + u) + 0 is Red, +1 is Green, +2 is Blue. Algorithm Steps: 1. Gradient Estimation: Compute the gradient \mathbf{G} = (Gx, Gy, Gz) using central finite differences. For a voxel at integer coordinates (x, y, z): Gx = \frac{V(x+1, y, z) - V(x-1, y, z)}{2} Gy = \frac{V(x, y+1, z) - V(x, y-1, z)}{2} Gz = \frac{V(x, y, z+1) - V(x, y, z-1)}{2} 2. Normalization: Normalize the gradient vector to obtain the surface normal \mathbf{N}. The normal points in the direction of the negative gradient (outward from the surface): \mathbf{N} = -\frac{\mathbf{G}}{\|\mathbf{G}\|} = \left( -\frac{Gx}{\sqrt{Gx^2 + Gy^2 + Gz^2}}, -\frac{Gy}{\sqrt{Gx^2 + Gy^2 + Gz^2}}, -\frac{Gz}{\sqrt{Gx^2 + Gy^2 + Gz^2}} \right) 3. Encoding (Optional Precomputation): Map the normalized components Nx, Ny, Nz \in [-1, 1] to 8-bit unsigned integers CR, CG, CB \in [0, 255] for storage in a texture: CR = 255 \cdot (Nx + 1) \cdot 0.5 CG = 255 \cdot (Ny + 1) \cdot 0.5 CB = 255 \cdot (Nz + 1) \cdot 0.5 4. On-the-Fly Evaluation (Alternative): For ray marching or particle queries, skip precomputation. Sample the density field at the query point p and its neighbors to compute \mathbf{G} and \mathbf{N} directly in the shader or kernel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computegradientnormal(volume, x, y, z, width, height, depth): """ Computes the surface normal at voxel (x, y, z) using central finite differences. volume: 3D list or array of density values. x, y, z: Integer coordinates within the volume bounds. width, height, depth: Dimensions of the volume. Returns: Normalized normal vector (nx, ny, nz). """ # Helper to safely fetch voxel value with boundary clamping def getvoxel(ix, iy, iz): # Clamp coordinates to valid range [0, dim-1] ix = max(0, min(ix, width - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, height - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, depth - 1)) return volume[ix][iy][iz] # 1. Compute central differences # Note: Sources use division by 2 for central difference step size gx = (getvoxel(x + 1, y, z) - getvoxel(x - 1, y, z)) / 2.0 gy = (getvoxel(x, y + 1, z) - getvoxel(x, y - 1, z)) / 2.0 gz = (getvoxel(x, y, z + 1) - getvoxel(x, y, z - 1)) / 2.0 # 2. Compute magnitude magnitude = math.sqrt(gx gx + gy gy + gz gz) # 3. Handle zero gradient (constant region) to avoid division by zero if magnitude < 1e-9: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Or a default normal, e.g., (0,0,-1) # 4. Normalize and negate (gradient points inward, normal points outward) nx = -gx / magnitude ny = -gy / magnitude nz = -gz / magnitude return (nx, ny, nz) def encodenormaltorgb(nx, ny, nz): """ Encodes a normalized normal vector into 8-bit RGB values [0, 255]. """ r = int(255 (nx + 1.0) 0.5) g = int(255 (ny + 1.0) 0.5) b = int(255 (nz + 1.0) 0.5) return (max(0, min(255, r)), max(0, min(255, g)), max(0, min(255, b))) Parameters: Kernel Size: The density estimation kernel size is typically 2^3 (8 voxels) for fast computation, which provides acceptable quality for normal estimation. Voxel Resolution: Common resolutions include 256 \times 256 \times 100 for precomputed textures and 512^3 for particle system simulations. Epsilon (Continuous Sampling): If using continuous coordinates for ray marching, a fixed epsilon (e.g., 0.0001) may be used for finite differences, though direct gradient sampling calls are preferred to reduce numerical instability. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Conditions: Voxels at the boundaries (e.g., x=0 or x=255) request out-of-bounds neighbors. The implementation must clamp coordinates or replicate boundary values, which can cause gradient inaccuracies at the edges. Zero Gradient: In constant regions (empty space or solid interior), the gradient magnitude is zero, leading to division by zero and NaN/Inf normals. A guard check for \|\mathbf{G}\| \approx 0 is required. Precision Loss: Using a fixed epsilon for continuous sampling that is not aligned with the volume sampling frequency can cause precision loss or aliasing. Hardware Limits: On older DX10 hardware, 32-bit integer lookup textures are not supported, requiring bitwise arithmetic or breaking integers into 16-bit parts, which increases lookup counts. It differs from standard gradient estimation by introducing explicit control over edge rounding and thickness, making it suitable for stylized or physically plausible beveled geometry in ray marching. It builds on SDF Normal Estimation via Finite Differences. It differs from standard Signed Distance Field (SDF) normal estimation by operating on a directed, modulated field that encodes visibility and orientation information, allowing normals to be derived directly from the field's spatial derivatives without explicit mesh reconstruction. This method estimates surface normals for shading by computing 2D spatial gradients from a rendered depth image (distance from the view plane to the surface). It enables post-processing illumination without recomputing the volume rendering. Unlike 3D gradient estimation which operates on volumetric data, this approach operates on the 2D image plane, making it computationally cheaper but susceptible to artifacts when depth values represent disjoint volumetric regions. Gradient-Based Diffuse Shading computes the diffuse lighting intensity for a voxel by estimating the local surface normal via finite differences and applying a dot product with a light direction vector. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering by explicitly deriving surface geometry from the density gradient to simulate diffuse reflection, rather than relying solely on opacity or color transfer functions. Estimates mesh vertex normals by computing the negative gradient of the occupancy output with respect to the vertex positions. The process involves converting vertices to a PyTorch tensor, passing them through a differentiable model to get occupancy logits, summing the output, and calling backward to extract the gradient, which is then normalized as the normal. Computes specular highlights by finding the volume surface intersection via ray marching, estimating the surface normal via finite differences of the volume texture, and applying a Blinn-Phong shading model. The ray marcher samples the volume until a threshold is crossed, then computes the normal using central finite differences at the intersection point to calculate the specular intensity. Time Complexity: O(1) per query for precomputed textures (texture lookup). O(1) per query for on-the-fly evaluation (constant number of volume samples, typically 6-8). Memory Complexity: O(W \times H \times D) for the volume grid. O(W \times H) for the precomputed normal texture (if used). Measured Performance: In a particle system collision response test with a 512^3 voxelgrid, computation times were 0.32 ms for 256^2 particles, 1.0 ms for 512^2 particles, and 4.0 ms for 1024^2 particles. Strengths: Does not rely on mesh normals, providing high-resolution normals coherent with the voxelized volume. Faster to compute than larger-support distance fields or depth peeling. Simple to implement and efficient for dynamic scenes. Limitations: Accuracy degrades at boundaries due to clamping. Sensitive to noise in the density field. Zero-gradient regions produce undefined normals. When to Use: High-resolution voxelized scenes, particle systems, dynamic solid voxelization where mesh normals are unavailable or too coarse. When Not to Use: When explicit, smooth mesh normals are required, or when the volume data is extremely noisy without smoothing. The method originates from single-pass GPU solid voxelization techniques, notably presented in "Single-pass GPU Solid Voxelization and Applications". It was developed to provide efficient, high-resolution surface normals for dynamic scenes without relying on traditional mesh-based normal data. The approach leverages the fact that a local density field, computed via a small kernel, resembles a signed distance field, allowing gradients to serve as accurate normal estimates. It has been applied in particle system collision detection, solid voxelization of dynamic scenes, and various volume rendering shading pipelines. name: SDF Bevel Generation
head: Distance Field Bevel, SDF Surface Normal Estimation
body: SDF Bevel Generation estimates 3D surface normals for lighting by sampling a Signed Distance Function (SDF) height field at four cardinal offsets, computing finite differences, and applying bevel shaping parameters. It differs from standard gradient estimation by introducing explicit control over edge rounding and thickness, making it suitable for stylized or physically plausible beveled geometry in ray marching. It builds on SDF Normal Estimation via Finite Differences. Input: SDF texture or volume, UV coordinates, texture dimensions (textureWidth, textureHeight), and bevel parameters (Bevel, BevelOffset, BevelWidth, BevelRoundness, BevelClamp, GradientScale, BevelAmount). Output: Surface normal vector n. SDF Sample Array h: A vector of 4 floats storing the sampled SDF values at the cardinal offsets. h.x: SDF at uv - delta.xz h.y: SDF at uv + delta.xz h.z: SDF at uv - delta.zy h.w: SDF at uv + delta.zy Bevel (float, default 0.5): Enables bevel generation when > 0. BevelOffset (float, default 0): Shifts the sampled height field values. BevelWidth (float, default 0): Controls bevel thickness, clamped to min 0.01. BevelRoundness (float, default 0): Controls edge rounding via sine interpolation. BevelClamp (float, default 0): Clamps bevel height to prevent over-extrusion artifacts. GradientScale (float): Scaling factor for the final gradient magnitude. BevelAmount (float): Multiplier for gradient scaling. 1. Compute Delta: Calculate the step size in texture space: \delta = (1.0/\text{textureWidth}, 1.0/\text{textureHeight}, 0.0). 2. Sample SDF: Sample the SDF at four cardinal offsets relative to the current UV uv: hx = \text{SampleSDF}(uv - \delta.xz), hy = \text{SampleSDF}(uv + \delta.xz), hz = \text{SampleSDF}(uv - \delta.zy), hw = \text{SampleSDF}(uv + \delta.zy). Store in array h = [hx, hy, hz, hw]. 3. Apply Offset: Add BevelOffset to all values in h. 4. Normalize Width: Divide all values in h by \max(0.01, \text{BevelWidth}). 5. Apply Roundness: If BevelRoundness > 0, apply sine interpolation to smooth edges: hi = \text{lerp}(hi, \sin(hi \cdot \pi/2), \text{BevelRoundness}) for each i \in \{x, y, z, w\}. 6. Clamp: Clamp the values in h using BevelClamp to prevent over-extrusion. 7. Scale Gradient: Scale the height differences by \text{BevelAmount} \times \text{BevelWidth} \times \text{GradientScale} \times -2.0. 8. Compute Tangents: Calculate two tangent vectors va and vb from the finite differences: va = \text{normalize}(-1, 0, hy - hx), vb = \text{normalize}(0, 1, hw - hz). 9. Compute Normal: Calculate the cross product of va and vb, then apply a flip factor f based on face orientation: n = (va \times vb) \cdot f, where f = (1, 1, -1) for front faces and f = (1, 1, 1) for back faces. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def normalize(v): l = math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) return (v[0]/l, v[1]/l, v[2]/l) if l > 1e-8 else (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + (b - a) t def clamp(v, mn, mx): return max(mn, min(mx, v)) def cross(a, b): return (a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]) def sdfbevelgeneration(uv, texturewidth, textureheight, sdfsample, params, isfront): beveloffset = params.get('BevelOffset', 0.0) bevelwidth = params.get('BevelWidth', 0.0) bevelroundness = params.get('BevelRoundness', 0.0) bevelclamp = params.get('BevelClamp', 0.0) gradientscale = params.get('GradientScale', 1.0) bevelamount = params.get('BevelAmount', 1.0) deltax = 1.0 / texturewidth deltay = 1.0 / textureheight hx = sdfsample(uv[0] - deltax, uv[1]) hy = sdfsample(uv[0] + deltax, uv[1]) hz = sdfsample(uv[0], uv[1] - deltay) hw = sdfsample(uv[0], uv[1] + deltay) h = [hx, hy, hz, hw] h = [val + beveloffset for val in h] effectivewidth = max(0.01, bevelwidth) h = [val / effectivewidth for val in h] if bevelroundness > 0: h = [lerp(val, math.sin(val math.pi / 2.0), bevelroundness) for val in h] if bevelclamp > 0: h = [clamp(val, -bevelclamp, bevelclamp) for val in h] scalefactor = bevelamount bevelwidth gradientscale -2.0 h = [val scalefactor for val in h] dydx = h[1] - h[0] dydy = h[3] - h[2] va = normalize((-1.0, 0.0, dydx)) vb = normalize((0.0, 1.0, dydy)) f = (1.0, 1.0, -1.0) if isfront else (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) crossprod = cross(va, vb) normal = (crossprod[0]f[0], crossprod[1]f[1], crossprod[2]f[2]) return normal Zero Width: BevelWidth is clamped to a minimum of 0.01 to prevent division by zero. Backface Orientation: The normal must be flipped for backfaces to ensure correct lighting orientation. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise with very small BevelWidth values, mitigated by the clamping. Degenerate Input: If the SDF is constant, the gradient will be zero, resulting in an undefined normal. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it involves a fixed number of texture samples and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Provides explicit control over edge appearance (bevel width and roundness), which is useful for stylized rendering. Limitations: Relies on texture sampling, which may introduce aliasing if the texture resolution is low. The quality depends on the accuracy of the SDF texture. When to Use: When stylized beveled edges are desired in ray-marched SDF rendering. When Not to Use: When high-precision, smooth normals are required without stylization, or when the SDF is not available as a texture. It differs from standard Signed Distance Field (SDF) normal estimation by operating on a directed, modulated field that encodes visibility and orientation information, allowing normals to be derived directly from the field's spatial derivatives without explicit mesh reconstruction. The MDF function d(p, v), typically implemented as a neural network or analytical function. Outputs: Surface normal vector n(p, v) \in \mathbb{R}^3. In practice, this is often a neural network (e.g., SIREN) taking (p, v) as input. Steps: 1. Evaluate the gradient of the distance function with respect to the query point p: 
ablap d(p, v) This is computed using automatic differentiation if d is a neural network, or finite differences if d is a discrete field. 2. Normalize the gradient to obtain the unit normal: n(p, v) =  rac{
ablap d(p, v)^T}{\|
ablap d(p, v)\|} Note: The transpose notation T in the source indicates that the gradient is treated as a row vector in the derivation, but the result is a column vector normal. In implementation, this is simply the normalized gradient vector. 3. Ensure the normal points away from the surface. The property n(p, v)^T v < 0 must hold. If the computed normal does not satisfy this orientation constraint relative to v, flip the sign: 	ext{if } n(p, v)^T v \ge 0: \quad n(p, v) = -n(p, v) Special Case: Unoriented Distance Field (UDF) If the field is an Unoriented Distance Field (UDF), where v^(p) is the optimal closest point direction, the gradient simplifies significantly: 
ablap 	ext{UDF}(p) = n(p, v^(p))^T Furthermore, due to the directed Eikonal property, the gradient is equal to the negative transpose of the optimal direction: 
ablap 	ext{UDF}(p) = -v^(p)^T Thus, for a UDF, the normal is simply: n(p) = -
ablap 	ext{UDF}(p) provided \|

Precision: Near the surface, the gradient norm should be close to 1. Deviations indicate approximation errors in the MDF. This enables local field-based geometric analysis without explicit mesh reconstruction. Formulas: Gaussian curvature: CK = \det(	ext{II}) / \det(g), where 	ext{II} is the second fundamental form and g is the first fundamental form (metric tensor) derived from the DDF Hessian \mathcal{H}p[d]. Mean curvature: CH = 	ext{tr}(	ext{II} g^{-1}), computed using the shape tensor derived from the DDF derivatives. Implementation: Derivatives of d with respect to p are computed using auto-differentiation. When to choose: When geometric smoothness or curvature-based shading is required directly from the implicit field, avoiding mesh extraction. A theoretical derivation showing that the gradient of the UDF at point p is equal to the negative transpose of the optimal direction v^(p), under the assumption that v^(p) is not multivalued. Formula: 
ablap 	ext{UDF}(p) = n(p, v^(p))^T derived from the S/UDF Eikonal equation and the definition of surface normals. Pitfall: The derivation holds only when v^(p) is not multivalued, i.e., p is not on the medial surface S or the medial surface of S. Time Complexity: O(1) per query point, dominated by the evaluation of the gradient via automatic differentiation or finite differences. Memory Complexity: Depends on the MDF storage. For neural networks, it is the size of the network weights. For discrete fields, it is the grid size. Strengths: No explicit mesh reconstruction required; differentiable; works directly with the field representation. Limitations: Accuracy depends on the quality of the MDF approximation; undefined at medial surfaces or multivalued regions. When to use: When normals are needed for shading or visibility in ray marching or differentiable rendering pipelines using implicit fields. When not to use: When high-precision curvature or normal information is required at medial surfaces or complex topologies where the field is ambiguous. Originated in the context of Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDF) and Modulated Distance Fields for 3D reconstruction and rendering. The method leverages the property that the gradient of a distance field points in the direction of the surface normal, extended to directed and modulated fields. It is used in single-image 3D reconstruction and view-consistent rendering pipelines. name: 2D Gradient Estimation for Shading
head: Depth Image Gradient Shading, Normal Map Calculation, Post-processing Normal Estimation from Depth
body: This method estimates surface normals for shading by computing 2D spatial gradients from a rendered depth image representing the distance from the view plane to the surface. It enables post-processing illumination without recomputing the volume rendering. Unlike 3D gradient estimation which operates on volumetric data, this approach operates on the 2D image plane, making it computationally cheaper but susceptible to artifacts when depth values represent disjoint volumetric regions. Inputs: A depth image Z where each pixel (xp, yp) stores the distance from the camera view plane to the nearest surface intersection. Outputs: A normal map where each pixel stores a unit normal vector \mathbf{n}. Data Structures: Z: 2D array of floating-point values representing depth. \mathbf{n}: 2D array of 3D vectors (nx, ny, nz). Parameters: \Delta x, \Delta y: Step sizes for the central difference approximation. Typically equal to the pixel spacing in the x and y directions, respectively. Larger values can be used to smooth the resulting normals. Algorithm: 1. For each pixel (xp, yp) in the depth image Z: a. Compute the partial derivative with respect to x using central differences: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial x} \simeq \frac{Z(xp + \Delta x, yp) - Z(xp - \Delta x, yp)}{2 \Delta x} b. Compute the partial derivative with respect to y using central differences: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial y} \simeq \frac{Z(xp, yp + \Delta y) - Z(xp, yp - \Delta y)}{2 \Delta y} c. Set the partial derivative with respect to z to 1: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial z} \simeq 1 d. Construct the gradient vector \mathbf{g} = \left( \frac{\partial Z}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial Z}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial Z}{\partial z} \right). e. Normalize \mathbf{g} to produce the unit normal vector \mathbf{n}: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{g}}{\|\mathbf{g}\|} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computenormalmap(depthimage, dx=1, dy=1): """ Computes surface normals from a depth image using 2D central differences. Args: depthimage: 2D list or array of floats, Z[y, x]. dx: Step size in x direction in pixels (default 1). dy: Step size in y direction in pixels (default 1). Returns: normalmap: 2D list of tuples (nx, ny, nz). """ height = len(depthimage) width = len(depthimage[0]) normalmap = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for y in range(height): for x in range(width): # Central difference for x xleft = max(0, x - dx) xright = min(width - 1, x + dx) dzdx = (depthimage[y][xright] - depthimage[y][xleft]) / (2.0 dx) # Central difference for y yup = max(0, y - dy) ydown = min(height - 1, y + dy) dzdy = (depthimage[ydown][x] - depthimage[yup][x]) / (2.0 dy) # dz/dz is always 1 dzdz = 1.0 # Gradient vector gx, gy, gz = dzdx, dzdy, dzdz # Normalize length = math.sqrt(gxgx + gygy + gzgz) if length > 0: normalmap[y][x] = (gx / length, gy / length, gz / length) else: normalmap[y][x] = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) return normalmap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disjoint Regions: Normals computed from depth values may represent disjoint regions in the volume, leading to blurring of sharp features on object edges. Boundary Conditions: The sources do not specify boundary handling. Implementers must clamp coordinates or use one-sided differences at image edges. Step Size Selection: Care must be taken when selecting \Delta x and \Delta y. Refines standard estimation by restricting normal computation to pixels within the same continuous curvature region, preventing blurring across disjoint boundaries. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Allows post-processing shading without recomputing the volume render. Limitations: Prone to artifacts at object boundaries and occlusions due to the assumption of local depth continuity. When to use: When a depth image is already available and high-fidelity edge preservation is not critical, or when used as a base for more advanced techniques like curvature-constrained estimation. This technique is described in the context of volume rendering and surface illumination models, specifically for capturing ambient, diffuse, and specular lighting. It is presented as an alternative to 3D finite difference gradient estimation, leveraging the depth buffer generated during rendering. The problem of disjoint regions causing edge blurring is noted, with references to prior work such as [Yagel92a] for curvature-constrained approaches. name: Curvature-Constrained 2D Gradient Estimation
head: Curvature-Constrained Normal Estimation
body: Curvature-Constrained 2D Gradient Estimation refines standard 2D gradient estimation by restricting normal computation to pixels within the same continuous curvature region, preventing the blurring of sharp features across disjoint object boundaries. Unlike standard 2D gradient estimation, which computes normals from depth values that may represent disjoint regions in the volume, this method ensures that edges remain sharp by avoiding the blending of gradients across discontinuities. It builds on 2D Gradient Estimation for Shading by adding a context-aware filtering step before gradient calculation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A depth image Z (distance from view plane to surface), where Z(x, y) is the depth at pixel coordinates (x, y). Output: A normal vector \vec{n} = (nx, ny, nz) for each pixel. Data Structures: Depth image Z: A 2D array of floating-point values representing depth. Neighborhood Np: A user-defined set of pixel offsets relative to the target pixel p. Steps: 1. Locate Continuous Curvature Regions: Identify pixels that belong to the same continuous curvature region. Two pixels are considered to be in the same "context" if their depth values and the first derivative of the depth at these locations do not greatly differ. 2. Select Valid Neighbors: For a target pixel p, select only those pixels within the user-defined neighborhood Np that belong to the same context as p. 3. Estimate Gradient Components: Compute the gradient components using only the selected valid neighbors. If standard central differences cannot be used due to context mismatch, use off-centered differences (forward or backward). Forward difference for x-component: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial x} \simeq \frac{Z(xp + \Delta x, yp) - Z(xp, yp)}{\Delta x} Backward difference for x-component: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial x} \simeq \frac{Z(xp, yp) - Z(xp - \Delta x, yp)}{\Delta x} Forward difference for y-component: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial y} \simeq \frac{Z(xp, yp + \Delta y) - Z(xp, yp)}{\Delta y} Backward difference for y-component: \frac{\partial Z}{\partial y} \simeq \frac{Z(xp, yp) - Z(xp, yp - \Delta y)}{\Delta y} 4. Compute Normal: Normalize the resulting gradient vector to obtain the surface normal. Parameters: \Delta x, \Delta y: Step sizes for finite differences. These may be reduced to improve accuracy within the curvature region. Neighborhood size: User-defined radius for context checking. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Disjoint boundaries: Standard central differences may blend across object edges if not constrained by curvature context. Derivative discontinuities: The first derivative of depth may vary significantly across edges, requiring careful context definition. A method to provide more accurate normal estimations by detecting image discontinuities and restricting gradient estimation to pixels within the same 'context' as the target pixel. Two pixels are in the same context if their depth values and the first derivative of the depth at these locations do not greatly differ. This ensures that sharp object edges and slope changes are not smoothed out, unlike standard gradient shading which might blend across discontinuities. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity: Depends on the neighborhood size and context checking overhead. Generally faster than 3D gradient estimation. Memory complexity: Requires storage for the depth image and potentially intermediate derivative values for context checking. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales with the size of the neighborhood and the complexity of the depth image. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Prevents blurring of sharp features, maintains edge sharpness, allows quick lighting changes without recomputing depth. Limitations: Less accurate than 3D gradient estimation, requires careful tuning of context parameters. When to Use: Use when sharp object edges must be preserved and 3D gradient estimation is too expensive. When Not to Use: Do not use when high accuracy is required and 3D gradient estimation is feasible. Curvature-Constrained 2D Gradient Estimation was developed to address the issue of normal blurring across disjoint regions in volume rendering. It builds on earlier work in 2D gradient estimation and context-sensitive normal estimation. The method is particularly useful in applications where sharp features must be preserved without the computational cost of 3D gradient estimation. name: Explicit Surface Normal Estimation via Ray Sampling
head: Explicit Normal Estimation, Explicit Surface Normal Estimation, NeRF Normal Estimation via Adjacent Rays, Ray-based Normal Estimation
body: This method estimates surface normals for volume rendering by evaluating the depth of a ray and two adjacent rays to construct a local surface plane. It solves the problem of inaccurate or noisy normals derived from finite differences on discrete depth maps by using continuous ray evaluation. Unlike 2D Gradient Estimation for Shading, which computes gradients from a pre-rendered depth image using pixel indices, this method operates directly on the learned geometric model during ray casting, ensuring normals are consistent with the underlying implicit surface representation. Inputs: A primary training ray r with origin o and direction \mathbf{d}. A learned neural radiance field (or similar implicit surface model) capable of returning depth d(\cdot) for any given ray. Access to neighboring rays in the image grid. Outputs: A unit surface normal vector \mathbf{n}(r, r{n1}, r{n2}) at the surface point of ray r. Data Structures: Ray representation: Tuple or struct containing origin o \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction \mathbf{d} \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized). Depth value: Scalar d \in \mathbb{R}^+. 3D Point: Vector ps \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Select Adjacent Rays: For the current ray r, identify two adjacent rays r{n1} and r{n2} from the four immediate neighboring pixels in the image grid. To prevent unstable normal calculation, ensure that one neighbor is adjacent along the X-axis and the other along the Y-axis. 2. Evaluate Depths: Query the model for the estimated depth values d(r), d(r{n1}), and d(r{n2}). 3. Compute 3D Surface Points: Convert the depth values into 3D coordinates using the ray origins and directions: ps(r) = o + \mathbf{d}(r) d(r) ps(r{n1}) = o{n1} + \mathbf{d}(r{n1}) d(r{n1}) ps(r{n2}) = o{n2} + \mathbf{d}(r{n2}) d(r{n2}) 4. Compute Unnormalized Normal: Calculate the cross product of the vectors formed by the three surface points: \hat{\mathbf{n}}(r, r{n1}, r{n2}) = (ps(r{n1}) - ps(r)) \times (ps(r{n2}) - ps(r)) 5. Normalize: Normalize the resulting vector to obtain the unit normal: \mathbf{n}(r, r{n1}, r{n2}) = \frac{\hat{\mathbf{n}}(r, r{n1}, r{n2})}{\|\hat{\mathbf{n}}(r, r{n1}, r{n2})\|} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def estimatenormal(rayr, rayn1, rayn2, depthmodel): """ Estimates surface normal using explicit ray sampling. Args: rayr: Ray object with origin o and direction d for the primary ray. rayn1: Ray object for the first adjacent neighbor (X-axis). rayn2: Ray object for the second adjacent neighbor (Y-axis). depthmodel: Function that takes a ray and returns depth d. Returns: nhat: Normalized surface normal vector. """ # Step 2: Evaluate depths dr = depthmodel(rayr) dn1 = depthmodel(rayn1) dn2 = depthmodel(rayn2) # Step 3: Convert depth to 3D surface points # ps(r) = o + d(r) d pr = rayr.o + rayr.d dr pn1 = rayn1.o + rayn1.d dn1 pn2 = rayn2.o + rayn2.d dn2 # Step 4: Compute unnormalized normal via cross product # nhat = (pn1 - pr) x (pn2 - pr) vec1 = pn1 - pr vec2 = pn2 - pr nhatunnorm = np.cross(vec1, vec2) # Step 5: Normalize norm = np.linalg.norm(nhatunnorm) if norm < 1e-8: # Fallback for degenerate cases (e.g., collinear points) # Return a default normal or handle error; source does not specify fallback. return np.array([0.0, 0.0, 1.0]) nhat = nhatunnorm / norm return nhat Parameters: Neighbor selection: Random selection from the 4 immediate neighbors, constrained to one X-adjacent and one Y-adjacent pixel. Bundle Adjustment: A preprocessing step may be applied to RPC models to improve camera accuracy before normal estimation. Learned Camera Adjustment: A per-image shift parameter qj on the XY-axis may be used to adjust camera accuracy during training. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Unstable Calculation: Selecting two neighbors along the same axis (e.g., both X-adjacent) can lead to unstable normal calculations. The method explicitly requires one X and one Y neighbor. Degenerate Geometry: If the three points are collinear, the cross product is zero. The pseudocode includes a guard for this. Precision: The accuracy depends on the precision of the depth estimation and the camera parameters. Bundle adjustment and learned camera adjustments are used to mitigate camera inaccuracies. Aligns the explicitly estimated normals with the gravity axis to enforce local planarity on flat surfaces. It is chosen when rendering satellite imagery or scenes with strong planar structures to reduce geometric noise. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it requires evaluating the model for exactly three rays (the primary and two neighbors). Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray for storing the three depth values and points. Strengths: Provides normals that are consistent with the learned geometry without relying on discrete pixel gradients. It captures local surface orientation directly from the implicit field. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than finite difference methods on depth maps because it requires multiple forward passes through the neural network per ray. It is sensitive to depth estimation errors and camera calibration inaccuracies. When to use: When high-quality geometric regularization is needed for training NeRFs, particularly in satellite imagery or structured environments where planarity constraints are beneficial. When not to use: When real-time inference speed is critical and the overhead of multiple ray evaluations is prohibitive, or when the depth map is already available and sufficient for shading purposes. The method was introduced in the context of "SatGeo-NeRF," a NeRF model for satellite imagery that incorporates geometric regularization. It builds on the foundational NeRF rendering equations and adapts them to handle the specific challenges of satellite data, such as camera inaccuracies and the need for planar surface consistency. The approach was influenced by the need to align estimated normals with the gravity axis for better geometric regularization. name: Gravity-Aligned Planarity Regularization
head: GAP Regularization, SatGeo-NeRF Planarity Loss
body: Gravity-Aligned Planarity Regularization is a geometric regularization technique for volume rendering that aligns depth-inferred surface normals with the gravity axis to enforce local planarity. It solves the problem of geometric artifacts and non-planar noise on flat surfaces (e.g., ground planes in satellite imagery) by coupling adjacent rays through a shared surface approximation, thereby facilitating cross-ray gradient flow. Unlike standard NeRF training which treats rays independently, this method imposes area-based geometric constraints. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A set of rays R, where each ray r is defined by origin o and direction d. The rays are associated with a camera model (e.g., RPC models with Bundle Adjustment and learned camera adjustments). Outputs: A scalar planarity loss value L{planar} used for backpropagation. Data Structures Ray: Defined by origin o and direction d. Surface Point: 3D coordinate ps(r). Normal: Unit vector \hat{n}. Parameters Gravity Axis (g): In UTM coordinate systems, the ground lies in the XY-plane, so the Z-axis approximates the inverse gravity vector. Value: g = (0, 0, 1)^T. Regularization Weight (\lambda{planar}): Empirically chosen weight for the planarity loss. Value: 0.1. Activation Epoch: The regularizer is enabled at epoch three of training, once a coarse scene representation is learned. Steps 1. Select Neighbors: For each ray r, select two random adjacent rays, r{n1} and r{n2}, from the four immediate neighboring pixels. To prevent unstable normal calculation, ensure one neighbor is sampled from each of the two adjacent pixels in the X- and Y-axes. 2. Estimate Depths: Evaluate all three rays (r, r{n1}, r{n2}) to determine their estimated depth values d(r) using the volume rendering equation (Eq. 4 in). 3. Compute Surface Points: Convert the depth values into 3D surface points by following each ray along its direction: ps(r) = r(d(r)) = o + d(r)d This is performed for r, r{n1}, and r{n2}. 4. Estimate Surface Normal: Approximate the local surface plane normal \hat{n}(r, r{n1}, r{n2}) using the cross product of the vectors formed by the three surface points: \hat{n}(r, r{n1}, r{n2}) = (ps(r{n1}) - ps(r)) \times (ps(r{n2}) - ps(r)) Normalize the resulting vector to ensure unit length, denoted as n(r, r{n1}, r{n2}). 5. Compute Loss: Calculate the planarity loss by summing the squared L2 distance between the gravity axis g and the estimated surface normals over all rays R: L{planar}(R) = \sum{r \in R} \| g - n(r, r{n1}, r{n2}) \|^2 The total loss contribution is \lambda{planar} L{planar}(R). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gravityalignedplanarityregularization(rays, depthestimator, gravityaxis=(0, 0, 1)): """ Computes the Gravity-Aligned Planarity Regularization loss. Args: rays: List of Ray objects, each having origin 'o' and direction 'd'. Each ray must have a method to find adjacent rays. depthestimator: Function that takes a ray and returns estimated depth d(r). gravityaxis: 3D vector representing the gravity prior. Default is (0, 0, 1). Returns: scalar: The planarity loss value. """ totalloss = 0.0 for ray in rays: # Step 1: Select two random adjacent rays from immediate neighbors # Constraint: One neighbor from X-axis adjacent pixels, one from Y-axis adjacent pixels neighborrays = ray.getimmediateneighbors() # Filter neighbors to ensure spatial diversity (X and Y axis coverage) # Implementation detail: Select rn1 and rn2 such that they are not collinear # with ray in a way that creates degenerate triangles, and cover X/Y axes. rn1, rn2 = selectdiverseneighbors(neighborrays) # Step 2: Estimate depths for all three rays dr = depthestimator(ray) drn1 = depthestimator(rn1) drn2 = depthestimator(rn2) # Step 3: Compute 3D surface points # ps(r) = o + d(r) d psr = ray.o + dr ray.d psrn1 = rn1.o + drn1 rn1.d psrn2 = rn2.o + drn2 rn2.d # Step 4: Estimate surface normal via cross product # Vector 1: from r to rn1 vec1 = psrn1 - psr # Vector 2: from r to rn2 vec2 = psrn2 - psr # Cross product normalunnormalized = crossproduct(vec1, vec2) # Normalize to unit length normal = normalize(normalunnormalized) # Step 5: Compute squared L2 distance to gravity axis # || g - n ||^2 diff = gravityaxis - normal lossterm = dotproduct(diff, diff) totalloss += lossterm return totalloss def selectdiverseneighbors(neighbors): """ Selects two neighbors from the immediate neighbors list. Ensures one is from X-adjacent pixels and one from Y-adjacent pixels. """ # Implementation depends on specific ray indexing/grid structure. # The source mandates: "sample one neighbor from each of the two # adjacent pixels in X- and Y-axis". # This function should return two rays satisfying this constraint. # If not enough neighbors exist, handle edge case (e.g., return None or skip). raise NotImplementedError("Specific neighbor selection logic depends on ray grid topology.") Edge Cases and Pitfalls Degenerate Planes: If the three surface points are collinear, the cross product yields a zero vector. Normalization of a zero vector is undefined. The source notes that selecting neighbors from distinct X and Y axes helps prevent unstable calculations. Camera Accuracy: The accuracy of the surface points depends on the camera model. The method assumes Bundle Adjustment preprocessing and learned camera adjustments (XY-axis shifts per image) are applied to improve accuracy. Training Timing: Enabling this regularizer too early (before a coarse scene representation is learned) may hinder convergence. It is explicitly enabled at epoch three. Time Complexity: Adds overhead proportional to the number of rays |R| due to the evaluation of two additional rays per primary ray and the cross-product calculation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing depth values for adjacent rays temporarily during the loss computation. No persistent large data structures are introduced beyond the standard NeRF representation. Strengths: Effectively mitigates overfitting-induced geometric artifacts on flat surfaces (e.g., ground in satellite imagery). Couples adjacent rays to facilitate cross-ray gradient flow, unlike independent ray training. Limitations: Specific to scenes with a known gravity axis (e.g., satellite imagery in UTM coordinates). Not applicable to arbitrary indoor or non-terrestrial scenes without a defined gravity prior. Performance: On the DFC2019 satellite reconstruction benchmark, SatGeo-NeRF (using this regularizer) improved Mean Altitude Error by 14.0% and 11.4% relative to baselines like EO-NeRF and EO-GS. Gravity-Aligned Planarity Regularization was introduced in the SatGeo-NeRF paper. It is designed specifically for geometrically regularized NeRFs for satellite imagery. The method leverages the known alignment of scene content in the UTM coordinate system, where the ground is in the XY-plane and the Z-axis approximates the inverse gravity vector. It is one of three model-agnostic regularizers proposed in SatGeo-NeRF, alongside Granularity Regularization and Depth-Supervised Regularization. name: Gradient-Based Diffuse Shading
head: Smooth gradient shading using interpolation
body: Gradient-Based Diffuse Shading computes the diffuse lighting intensity for a voxel by estimating the local surface normal via finite differences and applying a dot product with a light direction vector. It sets itself apart from standard volume rendering by explicitly deriving surface geometry from the density gradient to simulate diffuse reflection, rather than relying solely on opacity or color transfer functions. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D voxel grid (CT scan data) with dimensions height, width, depth. A current voxel position (x, y, z) and its density value currentVoxel. The previous voxel's density prevVoxel and position prevRay (for interpolation). A light source position defined by lightSourceX, LIGHTSOURCEY, and LIGHTSOURCEZ. A boolean flag isGradientInterpolation. Output: A scalar diffuse lighting value in the range [0, 1]. Data Structures The voxel data is accessed via a 3D array or linearized memory layout. BONEVALUE: A threshold constant representing the density value of bone or the surface boundary. Steps 1. Estimate Surface Normal: Compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} at (x, y, z) using a finite difference method on the local density field. The specific implementation is encapsulated in getSurfaceNormal(view, x, y, z, height, width, depth). 2. Light Source Position: Define the light source position \mathbf{L}{pos}: Lx = \text{lightSourceX} (controlled by a user slider). Ly = \text{ctScan.getCT\z\axis()} / 4. Lz = \text{ctScan.getCT\x\axis()}. 3. Light Direction: Calculate the light direction vector \mathbf{l} from the intersection point \mathbf{I} to the light source: \mathbf{l} = \mathbf{L}{pos} - \mathbf{I} Normalize \mathbf{l} and \mathbf{n}: \hat{\mathbf{l}} = \frac{\mathbf{l}}{\|\mathbf{l}\|}, \quad \hat{\mathbf{n}} = \frac{\mathbf{n}}{\|\mathbf{n}\|} 4. Gradient Interpolation (Optional): If isGradientInterpolation is true, currentVoxel \neq BONEVALUE, and z > 0: Find the exact intersection z-coordinate z{exact} via linear interpolation between prevVoxel and currentVoxel along prevRay: z{exact} = \text{linearInterpolationPosition}(\text{BONE\VALUE}, \text{prevVoxel}, \text{currentVoxel}, \text{prevRay}, z) Recalculate the surface normal \mathbf{n}' and intersection point \mathbf{I}' at z{exact}. Update \mathbf{l} using \mathbf{I}' and re-normalize. 5. Compute Diffuse Intensity: Calculate the diffuse lighting value D: D = \max(0, \hat{\mathbf{n}} \cdot \hat{\mathbf{l}}) Return D. Parameters lightSourceX: X-axis position of the light source, controlled by a slider. isGradientInterpolation: Boolean flag enabling smooth gradient shading via sub-voxel intersection estimation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls If currentVoxel equals BONEVALUE, gradient interpolation is skipped. If z \le 0, gradient interpolation is skipped. The normal estimation getSurfaceNormal must handle boundary conditions where neighbors are out of bounds. The light source position depends on the CT scan's axis definitions, which may vary between datasets. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gradientbaseddiffuseshading(view, x, y, z, height, width, depth, currentVoxel, prevVoxel, prevRay, lightSourceX, isGradientInterpolation, BONEVALUE): # Step 1: Estimate surface normal surfaceNormal = getSurfaceNormal(view, x, y, z, height, width, depth) # Step 2: Define light source position # ctScan.getCTzaxis() and ctScan.getCTxaxis() are assumed to be # methods returning the respective axis dimensions or offsets. lightSourceY = ctScan.getCTzaxis() / 4 lightSourceZ = ctScan.getCTxaxis() lightSourceXpos = lightSourceX # Intersection point I (initially the current voxel position) intersectionX = x intersectionY = y intersectionZ = z # Step 3 & 4: Gradient Interpolation if enabled if isGradientInterpolation and currentVoxel != BONEVALUE and z > 0: # Find exact intersection z via linear interpolation exactZ = linearInterpolationPosition(BONEVALUE, prevVoxel, currentVoxel, prevRay, z) # Recalculate surface normal and intersection at exactZ # Note: The exact X, Y coordinates for the new intersection are not specified # in the source, so we assume they are derived from the ray path at exactZ. # This is a gap filled with. intersectionZ = exactZ intersectionX, intersectionY = getRayIntersectionXY(prevRay, exactZ) surfaceNormal = getSurfaceNormal(view, intersectionX, intersectionY, intersectionZ, height, width, depth) # Step 3: Compute light direction lightDirectionX = lightSourceXpos - intersectionX lightDirectionY = lightSourceY - intersectionY lightDirectionZ = lightSourceZ - intersectionZ # Normalize light direction lightLength = sqrt(lightDirectionX2 + lightDirectionY2 + lightDirectionZ2) if lightLength == 0: return 0.0 lightDirX = lightDirectionX / lightLength lightDirY = lightDirectionY / lightLength lightDirZ = lightDirectionZ / lightLength # Normalize surface normal normalLength = sqrt(surfaceNormal.x2 + surfaceNormal.y2 + surfaceNormal.z2) if normalLength == 0: return 0.0 normalX = surfaceNormal.x / normalLength normalY = surfaceNormal.y / normalLength normalZ = surfaceNormal.z / normalLength # Step 5: Compute diffuse intensity dotProduct = normalX lightDirX + normalY lightDirY + normalZ lightDirZ diffuse = max(0.0, dotProduct) return diffuse Binary Gradient Shading is a technique for computing diffuse or specular lighting on binary voxel models by approximating surface normals using 6-connected (face-adjacent) neighbors. name: Binary Gradient Shading
body: Binary Gradient Shading is a technique for computing diffuse or specular lighting on binary voxel models by approximating surface normals using 6-connected (face-adjacent) neighbors. It sets itself apart from general gradient shading by restricting normal estimation to binary data, allowing for a compact 5-bit encoding of the 26 possible normal directions and enabling hardware-accelerated lookup table (LUT) based lighting calculations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A binary voxel dataset (pre-image) where surface voxels are marked (value 1) and background voxels are 0. Output: A rendered image with lighting intensity, where surface normals are encoded in a secondary framebuffer. Data Structures: Surface Normal Encoding: Each surface voxel's normal is stored in a single byte (8 bits). Bits 0-4 (5 bits): Encode the surface normal vector. There are exactly 26 possible normal directions derived from the 6-connected neighborhood. Bits 5-7 (3 bits): Store an approximation of the surface depth coordinate. This allows the lighting model to include depth cueing alongside reflection. Lookup Table (LUT): A hardware output lookup table mapping the 26 encoded normal values (plus potentially depth variations) to final light intensity values. Algorithm Steps: 1. Identify Surface Voxels: Determine which voxels in the binary dataset are surface voxels (value 1) and have at least one background neighbor (value 0). 2. Estimate Normal Vector: For each surface voxel, examine its 6-connected (face-adjacent) neighbors. Initialize a normal vector \mathbf{n} = (0, 0, 0). For each of the 6 neighbors: If the neighbor has value 0 (background), add a component to \mathbf{n} in the direction opposite to the neighbor's position relative to the center voxel. Specifically, if the neighbor is at offset (dx, dy, dz) where dx, dy, dz \in \{-1, 0, 1\} and only one is non-zero, add (-dx, -dy, -dz) to \mathbf{n}. The resulting vector \mathbf{n} points outward from the surface. Note that the magnitude is not normalized; the direction is determined by the sum of contributions from background neighbors. 3. Encode Normal: Map the resulting direction to one of the 26 possible discrete normal values. Assign the corresponding 5-bit code to the normal field of the output byte. 4. Encode Depth: Calculate or retrieve the depth coordinate (e.g., distance along the ray or z-coordinate) for the surface voxel. Pack the 3 most significant bits of this depth approximation into the remaining 3 bits of the output byte. 5. Store Normal: Write the 8-bit encoded value (5-bit normal + 3-bit depth) to the second framebuffer. 6. Compute Lighting: Define a lighting function L(\mathbf{n}, \mathbf{l}) that computes light intensity based on the surface normal \mathbf{n} and the incident light direction \mathbf{l}, including diffuse/specular terms and depth cueing. Pre-compute L for all 26 possible normal values (and potentially depth variations) for the current light direction and lighting model. Load these computed intensity values into a hardware output lookup table. 7. Render: For each pixel, retrieve the encoded normal/depth byte from the second framebuffer and use it as an index into the LUT to fetch the final light intensity. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computebinarygradientnormal(voxel, neighbors6): """ Computes the unnormalized normal vector for a surface voxel by examining its 6-connected neighbors. Args: voxel: The center voxel (assumed to be 1). neighbors6: List of 6 neighbor values and their offsets. Each element is (value, offsetx, offsety, offsetz). Returns: A tuple (nx, ny, nz) representing the unnormalized normal vector. """ nx, ny, nz = 0, 0, 0 for val, dx, dy, dz in neighbors6: if val == 0: # Background neighbor # Add component in the opposite direction nx -= dx ny -= dy nz -= dz return (nx, ny, nz) def encodenormalanddepth(normalvec, depthapprox): """ Encodes the normal vector and depth into a single byte. Args: normalvec: Tuple (nx, ny, nz) from computebinarygradientnormal. depthapprox: Approximate depth coordinate (e.g., 8-bit value). Returns: An 8-bit integer: [3 bits depth][5 bits normal index]. """ # Map normal vector to one of 26 discrete indices # This requires a predefined mapping or hashing of the 26 possible # (nx, ny, nz) directions to indices 0-25. normalindex = mapnormaltoindex(normalvec) # Extract top 3 bits of depth depthbits = (depthapprox >> 5) & 0x07 # Pack: bits 7-5 are depth, bits 4-0 are normal encodedbyte = (depthbits << 5) | normalindex return encodedbyte def setuplightinglut(lightdirection, lightingmodel): """ Pre-computes light intensity for all 26 normal directions. Args: lightdirection: Unit vector (lx, ly, lz). lightingmodel: Function or parameters for diffuse/specular reflection. Returns: A list of 26 float values representing intensity for each normal index. """ lut = [] for i in range(26): normalvec = indextonormalvector(i) # Compute intensity based on normal and light direction intensity = lightingmodel.computeintensity(normalvec, lightdirection) lut.append(intensity) return lut def renderbinarygradientshading(voxeldata, lightdirection, lightingmodel): """ Main rendering pipeline for Binary Gradient Shading. """ # Step 1-5: Compute normals and encode them secondframebuffer = [] for voxel in voxeldata: if issurfacevoxel(voxel): neighbors = get6connectedneighbors(voxel) normalvec = computebinarygradientnormal(voxel, neighbors) depth = getdepth(voxel) encoded = encodenormalanddepth(normalvec, depth) secondframebuffer.append(encoded) else: secondframebuffer.append(0) # Background # Step 6: Setup LUT lut = setuplightinglut(lightdirection, lightingmodel) # Step 7: Render using LUT finalimage = [] for encoded in secondframebuffer: normalindex = encoded & 0x1F # Extract 5-bit normal intensity = lut[normalindex] finalimage.append(intensity) return finalimage Parameters: Normal Encoding: 5 bits. Depth Encoding: 3 bits. Total Bits per Normal: 8 bits (1 byte). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Light Direction Changes: Changing the light direction or lighting model (e.g., surface reflection coefficients) requires regenerating the lookup table entries. It does not allow for per-pixel recalculation of the dot product, which is a limitation compared to general gradient shading. Normal Ambiguity: The method relies on 6-connected neighbors. Corner or edge cases where multiple neighbors are background may result in unnormalized vectors that still map to one of the 26 discrete directions. The mapping must be consistent. Depth Precision: Only 3 bits are available for depth, which may lead to coarse depth cueing. Time Complexity: Normal computation is O(1) per surface voxel (constant number of neighbors). Lighting lookup is O(1) per pixel. Total time is linear in the number of surface voxels/pixels. Memory Complexity: Requires a secondary framebuffer of size equal to the image resolution, storing 1 byte per pixel. The LUT is small (26 entries). Performance: Fast due to hardware LUT usage. Avoids per-pixel floating-point dot products. Strengths: Efficient for binary data; simple hardware implementation; supports depth cueing. Limitations: Limited to 26 normal directions; lighting changes require LUT regeneration; coarse depth precision. When to Use: Binary voxel models where performance is critical and lighting changes are infrequent. When Not to Use: Continuous scalar fields, dynamic lighting, or when high-quality smooth shading is required. Binary Gradient Shading was introduced in the context of hardware support for binary voxel models. It is described in the paper "Hardware Support for the Display and Manipulation of Binary Voxel Models". The method leverages the discrete nature of binary data to simplify normal estimation and lighting calculation, making it suitable for early hardware implementations with limited floating-point capabilities. name: Principal Curvature Direction Estimation
head: Discrete Curvature Estimation (Monga et al.), Monga's algorithm
body: A method to compute principal curvature directions in 3D scalar fields faster than extremal value quadratic forms, by computing an orthonormal basis for the gradient and solving for the angle theta. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Lambertian Shading with Gradient Normals by providing directional curvature information rather than just surface orientation, and from Discrete Gaussian Curvature Estimation by offering continuous directional vectors rather than topological classification. Inputs: Scalar field F(x, y, z). Gradient vector G = \nabla F = (g0, g1, g2)^T. Hessian matrix D^2 F (second derivatives of F). Outputs: Principal curvature directions in the plane orthogonal to G. Angle \theta defining the direction within that plane. Data Structures: Gradient vector G: 3 floats. Scalar \gamma: 1 float. Orthonormal matrix P: 3x3 floats. Angle \theta: 1 float. Steps: 1. Compute the gradient magnitude components: \gamma = \sqrt{g0^2 + g1^2} \|G\| = \sqrt{g0^2 + g1^2 + g2^2} 2. Handle degenerate cases: If \gamma = 0, the matrix construction fails. Use a standard basis instead. If \|G\| = 0, the point is a critical point; curvature is undefined. 3. Construct the orthonormal basis vectors h and f in the plane orthogonal to G: h = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{g1}{\gamma} \\ -\frac{g0}{\gamma} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix} f = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{g2 \cdot g0}{\gamma \cdot \|G\|} \\ \frac{g2 \cdot g1}{\gamma \cdot \|G\|} \\ \frac{\gamma}{\|G\|} \end{pmatrix} The first column of P is G/\|G\|. The matrix P rotates the first basis vector into the direction of G. 4. Express any vector v in the orthogonal complement of G as: v = h \cdot \cos \theta + f \cdot \sin \theta 5. Solve for \theta using the derivative of the curvature \kappav with respect to \theta vanishing: \tan 2\theta = \frac{2 \cdot h'(D^2 F)f}{h'(D^2 F)h - f'(D^2 F)f} where h'(D^2 F)h denotes the second derivative of the scalar field F in the direction of the basis vectors. 6. Resolve orientation flips during path line tracing using a heuristic with a globally defined reference field (e.g., cylindrical) to align directions consistently. Pitfalls: If \gamma = 0, the matrix construction fails; use a standard basis instead. At umbilical points (locally flat/spherical surfaces), the denominator vanishes. Handle by increasing the filter width of the differentiation operator. The algorithm only solves for \theta in (-\pi/2, +\pi/2), causing curvature directions to flip 180 degrees along field lines, preventing consistent orientation for tracing. This method classifies vertices on a triangular mesh as elliptic (local extrema) or hyperbolic (saddle/blending regions) by evaluating the sign of the discrete Gaussian curvature. It distinguishes itself from continuous curvature estimation by providing a robust Boolean classification based on the angular defect, which is computationally cheaper and less sensitive to noise than second-derivative approximations. It builds on Principal Curvature Direction Estimation by offering a topological classification rather than directional magnitude. Time Complexity: Faster than extremal value quadratic forms. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Considerably faster method for computing principal directions in three-dimensional scalar fields. Limitations: Only solves for \theta \in (-\pi/2, +\pi/2), resulting in curvature fields that are not oriented consistently. Curvature directions might flip about 180 degrees along a particular field line. Tracing these fields in a globally consistent way becomes impossible without a heuristic. Monga et al. derived this method for computing principal directions in three-dimensional scalar fields. It is used in interactive volume illustration and surface hatching.
