name: Discrete Gaussian Curvature Estimation
head: Discrete Gaussian Curvature Classification, Gauss operator, Gaussian curvature operator, Local Extremum Detection
body: This method classifies vertices on a triangular mesh as elliptic (local extrema) or hyperbolic (saddle/blending regions) by evaluating the sign of the discrete Gaussian curvature. It distinguishes itself from continuous curvature estimation by providing a robust Boolean classification based on the angular defect, which is computationally cheaper and less sensitive to noise than second-derivative approximations. It builds on Principal Curvature Direction Estimation by offering a topological classification rather than directional magnitude. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A triangular mesh defined by vertices V and faces F. Specifically, for a target vertex xi, the 1-ring neighborhood (adjacent vertices and faces). Output: A Boolean classification Gauss(xi) indicating if the vertex is elliptic or hyperbolic. Data Structures: Vertex xi: The center of the local stencil. Neighbors xj: Vertices adjacent to xi. Faces: Triangles sharing xi as a vertex. Steps: 1. Identify all faces fk that contain the vertex xi. Let N be the number of such faces. 2. For each face fk, identify the two edges connected to xi. Let the other two vertices of this face be x{j} and x{j-1} (ordered cyclically around xi). 3. Compute the angle \thetaj at vertex xi within face fk. This is the angle between the vector \vec{v}1 = xj - xi and the vector \vec{v}2 = x{j-1} - xi. Formula: \thetaj = \arccos\left(\frac{\vec{v}1 \cdot \vec{v}2}{\|\vec{v}1\| \|\vec{v}2\|}\right). 4. Sum all inner angles \thetaj for all N faces surrounding xi: S = \sum{j=1}^{N} \thetaj 5. Compare the sum S to 2\pi. The discrete Gaussian curvature sign operator \kappaG^{sign}(xi) is defined as: \kappaG^{sign}(xi) = \text{sign}\left( \sum{j=1}^{N} \thetaj - 2\pi \right) 6. Classify the vertex: If S < 2\pi, the vertex is elliptic (local extremum). If S > 2\pi, the vertex is hyperbolic (saddle/blending region). If S = 2\pi, the vertex is planar (neither strictly elliptic nor hyperbolic in this binary scheme). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifygaussiancurvature(vertexi, mesh): """ Classifies a vertex as elliptic or hyperbolic based on discrete Gaussian curvature. Args: vertexi: The index or ID of the central vertex. mesh: A mesh object providing access to vertices and faces. Returns: str: 'elliptic', 'hyperbolic', or 'planar'. """ # Get all faces incident to vertexi incidentfaces = mesh.getfacescontainingvertex(vertexi) # Get all unique neighbors of vertexi neighbors = mesh.getneighbors(vertexi) # Map neighbor index to its position in the cyclic order around vertexi # This requires sorting neighbors by angle around the normal or using face connectivity # For simplicity, we iterate through faces and extract angles totalanglesum = 0.0 for face in incidentfaces: # Get the three vertices of the face v0, v1, v2 = face.vertices # Identify which vertex is the center (vertexi) # The other two are the neighbors in this face if v0 == vertexi: p1, p2 = v1, v2 elif v1 == vertexi: p1, p2 = v2, v0 else: # v2 == vertexi p1, p2 = v0, v1 # Compute vectors from center to neighbors vec1 = p1 - vertexi vec2 = p2 - vertexi # Compute angle between vectors dotproduct = vec1.dot(vec2) norm1 = vec1.length() norm2 = vec2.length() # Guard against division by zero or invalid geometry if norm1 == 0 or norm2 == 0: continue # Clamp cosine value to [-1, 1] for numerical stability cosangle = dotproduct / (norm1 norm2) cosangle = max(-1.0, min(1.0, cosangle)) angle = math.acos(cosangle) totalanglesum += angle # Compare sum to 2pi if totalanglesum < 2 math.pi: return 'elliptic' elif totalanglesum > 2 math.pi: return 'hyperbolic' else: return 'planar' Parameters: None. The threshold is fixed at 2\pi. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Planar Regions: If the vertex lies on a flat plane, the sum of angles equals 2\pi exactly. The method returns "planar" or is undefined in a strict binary classification. The method relies on the sign of the deviation, ignoring the magnitude. Precision: Floating-point errors may cause planar vertices to be misclassified. A tolerance epsilon should be used in implementation. Boundary Vertices: Vertices on the boundary of a mesh do not have a closed 1-ring. The sum of angles will be less than 2\pi. This method assumes an interior vertex or requires special handling for boundaries. This is the primary application of the operator, distinguishing between sulci (local minima, elliptic) and gyri (local maxima, elliptic) versus saddle points (hyperbolic). Elliptic regions correspond to local extrema where all neighbors lie on one side of the tangent plane. Hyperbolic regions correspond to saddle points where neighbors lie above and below the best-fitting least-squares plane. Time Complexity: O(d), where d is the degree of the vertex (number of adjacent faces). This is very fast per vertex. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per vertex evaluation, assuming the mesh connectivity is accessible. Strengths: Robust to noise compared to derivative-based curvature estimates. Computationally inexpensive. Provides a clear topological classification (extremum vs. blending). Limitations: Binary classification loses magnitude information of the curvature. Fails to distinguish between minima and maxima without additional gradient information. Sensitive to mesh quality (degenerate triangles). When to use: When topological segmentation of surfaces (e.g., brain sulci/gyri) is required and computational efficiency is critical. When not to use: When precise curvature magnitude is needed for shading or physics simulation. The method originates from the work of Vivodtzev, Linsen, Bonneau, Hamann, Joy, and Olshausen in their paper "Hierarchical Isosurface Segmentation Based on Discrete Curvature" (2003). It was developed to segment isosurfaces into topologically meaningful regions (sulci and gyri) for medical image analysis, specifically for recognizing diseases in brain structures. The approach uses the angular defect as a discrete approximation of Gaussian curvature to classify surface types. Hierarchical Isosurface Segmentation Based on Discrete Curvature, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00537470v1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Scene-Space Normal Estimation
head: Höhne and Bernstein Normal Estimation
body: Scene-Space Normal Estimation is a surface rendering method that uses ray-casting and binary segmentation to determine object boundary locations and estimate normals in scene space. It is characterized by the expression R{bs}(S{bl}, Is). Volume-rendering methods that utilize scene space normals can be described by similar composite expressions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene D (volume or surface data). Output: A rendered image with surface normals estimated in scene space. Data Structures: The method relies on the composition of basic imaging transforms where the order of operation is right-to-left. The scene D is transformed via filtering Fs and interpolation Is. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Optional): The input scene D may be preprocessed to produce D1 or D2. D1 = Is(Fs(D)): Apply filtering Fs then interpolation Is. D2 = Fs(Is(D)): Apply interpolation Is then filtering Fs. 2. Ray-Casting and Binary Segmentation: The method uses ray-casting to traverse the scene. Binary segmentation (Bs) is applied to determine object boundary locations. 3. Normal Estimation: The normal estimation is performed in scene space using the boundary locator S{bl} and interpolation Is. 4. Rendering: The final rendering combines the segmented surface information with the interpolated scene data, expressed as R{bs}(S{bl}, Is)(D) = R{bs}(S{bl}(D), Is(D)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. Is: Scene interpolation operator. Bs: Binary segmentation/surface detector. S{bl}: Surface boundary locator. This variant involves creating composite operators by combining basic imaging transforms. This allows for the application of object/surface filtering where the filtered object Q' is determined from the filtered scene Fs(Go(Q)) using a threshold operator, or the filtered surface S' is determined from the filtered scene using a surface detector Bs. name: Weighted Normal Accumulation
head: Normals Rendering, NormalsRenderer, Transmittance-Weighted Normal Estimation
body: Weighted Normal Accumulation estimates surface normals for volume rendering by aggregating per-sample gradient normals along a ray, weighted by their transmittance contributions. Unlike SDF Normal Estimation via Finite Differences, which computes a single normal per ray intersection, this method accumulates normals from all samples, providing a robust estimate in regions with ambiguous or noisy distance fields. It differs from Lambertian Shading with Gradient Normals by explicitly using transmittance weights rather than just geometric shading factors. Inputs: normals: A tensor of shape (numsamples, 3) containing the estimated normal vector for each sample along the ray. weights: A tensor of shape (numsamples,) containing the transmittance-based weight for each sample (typically derived from the volume rendering integral). Outputs: n: A tensor of shape (3,) representing the accumulated normal vector. Data Structures: normals: Float32 array, 3 components per sample. weights: Float32 array, 1 component per sample. Steps: 1. Initialize the accumulated normal vector n to zero. 2. For each sample i from 0 to N-1: Compute the contribution: ci = wi \cdot \mathbf{n}i, where wi is the weight and \mathbf{n}i is the normal. Add ci to n. 3. If normalization is enabled, normalize n to unit length. Formula: The accumulated normal n is computed as: n = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} wi \mathbf{n}i Where: wi is the transmittance weight for sample i. \mathbf{n}i is the normal vector for sample i. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def weightednormalaccumulation(normals: list, weights: list, normalize: bool = True) -> list: """ Accumulate normals weighted by transmittance. Args: normals: List of 3D vectors (tuples or lists) for each sample. weights: List of scalar weights for each sample. normalize: Whether to normalize the final normal vector. Returns: A 3D vector representing the accumulated normal. """ # Initialize accumulated normal to zero vector accnormal = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Iterate over samples and accumulate weighted normals for i in range(len(weights)): w = weights[i] n = normals[i] # Ensure n is a 3D vector accnormal[0] += w n[0] accnormal[1] += w n[1] accnormal[2] += w n[2] # Normalize if requested if normalize: length = (accnormal[0]2 + accnormal[1]2 + accnormal[2]2)0.5 if length > 1e-8: # Avoid division by zero accnormal[0] /= length accnormal[1] /= length accnormal[2] /= length else: # Fallback to a default normal if accumulation is zero accnormal = [0.0, 1.0, 0.0] return accnormal Parameters: normalize: Boolean, default True. Determines if the result is unit-length. Edge Cases: If all weights are zero, the accumulated normal is zero. Normalization should handle this by returning a default or leaving it as zero. Precision issues may arise if weights vary significantly in magnitude; using higher precision for accumulation is recommended. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as it accumulates into a single vector. Strengths: Robust to noise in individual sample normals; provides a smooth normal estimate across the ray. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than single-sample methods; may blur sharp features if weights are spread out. When to use: When smooth, consistent normals are required for shading in volume rendering, especially in noisy or ambiguous regions. When not to use: When performance is critical and single-sample approximations are sufficient. This method is implemented in SDFStudio and Nerfstudio for normal estimation in differentiable volume rendering. It leverages the transmittance weights from the volume rendering integral to prioritize normals from samples near the surface. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Antialiasing (AA)
head: Aliasing Prevention, Procedural Texture Anti-Aliasing, Subpixel Sampling
body: Antialiasing (AA) in distance-field ray marching prevents moiré artifacts and jagged edges caused by high-frequency noise octaves or fine geometric details aliasing against the pixel grid. It differs from standard supersampling by often integrating frequency-aware logic directly into the procedural evaluation or ray differential calculation, rather than relying solely on brute-force pixel subdivision. The method builds on Distance-field ray marching. Inputs: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, pixel coordinates, scene SDF, procedural noise parameters (octaves, frequency), and AA configuration (samples, mode). Outputs: Final pixel color, free of high-frequency aliasing artifacts. Ray Offsets: A 2D array or vector of (xx, yy) offsets representing subpixel jitter positions within the pixel footprint. LOD State: Integer count of active noise octaves, derived from pixel size or ray differentials. 1. Procedural Frequency Capping (LOD): Calculate the pixel size in world units, s{pixel}. Determine the maximum octave count: n{oct} = \min(N{max}, \lfloor \log2(s{pixel}) \rfloor) where N{max} is the global maximum octaves. Evaluate the noise function using only n{oct} octaves. This skips frequencies finer than the pixel resolution, preventing moiré patterns. Alternative Analytical Filtering: For simple patterns, apply a smoothstep filter based on the derivative of the pattern coordinate u: f{filtered} = \text{smoothstep}(-fw, fw, f(u)) where fw = fwidth(uv) is the rate of change of u across the pixel. 2. Subpixel Jittering: Define a grid of jitter offsets. A standard configuration uses 2 samples in x and 4 samples in y, totaling 8 samples per pixel. The offsets xx and yy are distributed within the pixel space: xx \in \{-0.25, 0.25\} and yy \in \{-0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75\}. For each sample (i, j): a. Adjust the ray direction \mathbf{d}' by adding the offset (xxi, yyj) to the ray's origin or direction vector, effectively shifting the ray's entry point into the pixel footprint. b. Perform standard sphere tracing using the adjusted ray. c. Store the resulting color C{ij}. 3. Aggregation: Average the colors from all samples: C{final} = \frac{1}{N{samples}} \sum{i,j} C{ij} For 8 samples, multiply the sum by 0.125 (1/8). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderpixelaa(rayo, rayd, pixelsize, maxoctaves, noisefunc, useaa=True): # 1. Procedural LOD Calculation if pixelsize > 0: lodoctaves = min(maxoctaves, int(math.log2(pixelsize))) else: lodoctaves = maxoctaves if not useaa: return spheretraceinline(rayo, rayd, lodoctaves, noisefunc) # 2. Subpixel Sampling Configuration xoffsets = [-0.25, 0.25] yoffsets = [-0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75] accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) # 3. Loop over samples for xx in xoffsets: for yy in yoffsets: jitteredd = normalize(rayd + vec3(xx, yy, 0.0)) accumulatedcolor += spheretraceinline(rayo, jitteredd, lodoctaves, noisefunc) # 4. Average results return accumulatedcolor 0.125 def spheretraceinline(rayo, rayd, lodoctaves, noisefunc): t = 0.0 maxdist = 100.0 epsilon = 0.001 while t < maxdist: p = rayo + t rayd dist = noisefunc(p, lodoctaves) if dist < epsilon: return vec3(1.0) if dist < 0: return vec3(0.0) t += dist return vec3(0.0) AA Samples: 8 samples per pixel (2x4 grid) is a typical configuration. LOD Octaves: Determined dynamically by int(log2(pixelsize)). Jitter Range: xx \in \{-0.25, 0.25\} and yy \in \{-0.75, -0.25, 0.25, 0.75\} with step 0.5. Zero Pixel Size: If pixelsize is 0 or negative, log2 is undefined. Guard against this by clamping lodoctaves to maxoctaves. Derivative Calculation: Analytical filtering requires accurate fwidth (derivative) computation. In ray marching, this requires computing ray differentials \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial u} and \frac{\partial \mathbf{r}}{\partial v} manually, as standard texture derivatives may not apply to procedural SDFs. Performance: Subpixel sampling increases cost linearly with sample count. 8 samples is a balance; higher counts (e.g., 16+) may be needed for high-frequency scenes but significantly reduce frame rate. SSAA renders the entire scene at a higher resolution and downsamples to the target resolution. It reduces aliasing by averaging multiple subpixel samples via interpolation. When to choose: When rendering complex scenes with multiple buffers (albedo, depth, normal) and hardware acceleration for interpolation is available. It operates on the final image buffer rather than per-pixel jittering. Implementation: Compute high-res dimensions h = \text{make\divisible}(h0 \cdot ssaa, 8) and w = \text{make\divisible}(w0 \cdot ssaa, 8). Render all buffers at (h, w), then downsample using torch.nn.functional.interpolate with mode='min' (bilinear/bicubic minification). Parameters: ssaa integer multiplier, default 1. Must be >1 to trigger. Time Complexity: Scales linearly with the number of AA samples. LOD capping reduces evaluation cost for distant objects by skipping noise octaves. Memory Complexity: Scales with the render resolution for SSAA. Strengths: Effectively eliminates moiré from procedural noise via LOD capping and jagged edges from geometry via subpixel sampling. Limitations: Subpixel sampling increases computational cost linearly with sample count. Procedural LOD requires careful derivative management for analytical filtering. When to use: Use LOD capping for procedural noise. Use subpixel jittering for geometric AA when performance allows. Use SSAA when post-processing downsampling is feasible and high-quality anti-aliasing is required for all buffers. Antialiasing in ray marching evolved alongside procedural rendering. Early implementations used simple supersampling. The integration of LOD-based octave capping for procedural noise was developed to address specific moiré artifacts in ridged noise and Voronoi patterns, which are particularly visible on axis-aligned surfaces. SSAA in the context of neural and implicit rendering adapts traditional rasterization downsampling techniques to volume rendering pipelines. a1k0n/asciitracing, https://github.com/a1k0n/asciitracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) skills/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md at main..., https://github.com/MiniMax-AI/skills/blob/main/skills/shader-dev/techniques/procedural-noise.md, fetched 2026-10-27 dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, https://github.com/dreamgaussian/dreamgaussian, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volume Ray Marching with Temporal Accumulation
head: HZL Fluid Effects Volume Rendering
body: Volume Ray Marching with Temporal Accumulation is a real-time rendering technique that integrates the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) through a 3D density field using fixed-step ray marching, stabilized by blending the current frame's result with a history texture. It distinguishes itself from standard ray marching by reducing temporal noise and flickering in animated sequences, making it suitable for fluid simulations where density fields change rapidly. Unlike SDF Cloud Rendering which relies on analytic distance fields, this method operates directly on sampled scalar textures, and unlike Atmospheric Ray Marching which models global atmospheric layers, it targets localized volumetric effects like smoke and fire within a bounded box. The method renders a full-screen quad, computing a ray for each fragment that intersects a unit cube [-1, 1]^3. It samples a density texture, computes lighting (including optional self-shadowing), and accumulates color. The final output is temporally blended with a previous frame's result to smooth noise. Inputs: densityTexture: 3D texture storing density values. sceneDepthTexture: Depth buffer of the scene geometry to clip rays. historyTexture: RGBA texture storing the accumulated color from the previous frame. cameraPosition: World-space camera origin. inverseViewProjection: Inverse of the combined view-projection matrix. lightDirection: Normalized direction vector of the light source. Parameters: stepSize, maximumSteps, densityScale, absorption, emissionStrength, lightIntensity, historyWeight. Outputs: mcolorTexture: Final rendered frame (GLRGBA8). The implementation uses OpenGL textures with specific formats and filtering: mcolorTexture: GLRGBA8, filter GLLINEAR, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. mdepthTexture: GLDEPTHCOMPONENT24, filter GLNEAREST, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. msceneDepthTexture: GLDEPTHCOMPONENT24, filter GLNEAREST, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. mhistoryTexture: GLRGBA8, filter GLLINEAR, wrap GLCLAMPTOEDGE. Cleared to zero at initialization. 1. Initialize Textures: Allocate the four textures described above. Set filtering modes as specified. Clear mhistoryTexture to (0, 0, 0, 0). 2. Compute Ray Origin and Direction: Convert fragment texture coordinate to clip space. Unproject the far plane point using inverseViewProjection to get farWorld. Calculate rayDirection = normalize(farWorld - cameraPosition). 3. Intersect Ray with Unit Cube: Compute intersection of ray origin and inverse ray direction with box [-1, 1]. Return interval [t{min}, t{max}]. Initialize distanceAlongRay = max(t{min}, 0.0). 4. Clip Ray Against Scene Geometry: Sample sceneDepthTexture at fragment coordinates. If sceneDepth < 1.0, unproject the scene point to world space, calculate sceneDistance along rayDirection, and update t{exit} = min(t{exit}, sceneDistance). 5. Discard if No Intersection: If t{exit} <= distanceAlongRay, discard the fragment. 6. Apply Jitter: If jitterEnabled, add a random offset to distanceAlongRay using random(glFragCoord.xy) stepSize. 7. Initialize Accumulation: Set accumulated = vec4(0.0). 8. Ray Marching Loop: Loop index from 0 to maximumSteps-1. Break if index >= maximumSteps or distanceAlongRay >= t{exit}. Calculate position = cameraPosition + rayDirection distanceAlongRay. Sample densityTexture at position 0.5 + 0.5. Get fieldValue (r channel). Set density = fieldValue. 9. Detect Volume Entry: If !foundVolume and density > 0.01, set representativePosition = position and foundVolume = true. 10. Compute Color: Determine smokeColor and emittedLight based on fieldMode: Mode 0 samples temperature/fire textures, computes ambient (0.12, 0.15, 0.20) and direct light (1.0, 0.88, 0.72) \times \text{lightIntensity} \times \text{transmittance}, mixes smoke by position.y, and computes flame emission. Mode 1 mixes smoke color (0.3, 0.04, 0.01) to (1.0, 0.65, 0.08) by density. Modes 2/3 remap density to |density - 0.5| \times 2.0 and color red/blue. 11. Accumulate Color and Opacity: Compute step alpha \alpha = 1.0 - e^{-\text{density} \times \text{stepSize}}. Blend color into accumulated using standard alpha compositing. 12. Temporal Accumulation: If temporalEnabled, blend the current frame's result with historyTexture using historyWeight. 13. Light Transmittance (Self-Shadowing): If selfShadowingEnabled, march 20 steps in direction -normalize(lightDirection + vec3(0.0001)) with step size 0.08. Accumulate opticalDepth = texture(densityTexture, position 0.5 + 0.5).r 0.08. Break if abs(position) > 1.0. Return transmittance T = e^{-\text{opticalDepth} \times \text{absorption} \times \text{densityScale} \times 3.0}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendervolumeraymarchingwithtemporalaccumulation( u, v, cameraposition, inverseviewprojection, scenedepthtexture, densitytexture, historytexture, lightdirection, stepsize, maximumsteps, densityscale, absorption, emissionstrength, lightintensity, historyweight, jitterenabled, frameindex, fieldmode, selfshadowingenabled): def matvecmul(M, v): return vec4( dot(M[0], v), dot(M[1], v), dot(M[2], v), dot(M[3], v)) def jitterrandom(coordinate, frameindex): value = fract(vec3(coordinate.xyx) 0.1031) value += dot(value, value.yzx + 33.33 + float(frameindex) 0.01) return fract((value.x + value.y) value.z) # 1. Compute Ray clippos = vec4(u 2.0 - 1.0, v 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) farworld = matvecmul(inverseviewprojection, clippos) farworld = vec3(farworld) / farworld.w rayorigin = cameraposition raydirection = normalize(farworld - rayorigin) # 2. Intersect with Unit Cube [-1, 1] inversedirection = 1.0 / raydirection first = (-1.0 - rayorigin) inversedirection second = (1.0 - rayorigin) inversedirection minimum = min(first, second) maximum = max(first, second) tentry = max(minimum.x, minimum.y, minimum.z) texit = min(maximum.x, maximum.y, maximum.z) tentry = max(tentry, 0.0) # 3. Clip against Scene Geometry scenedepth = scenedepthtexture.sample(u, v) if scenedepth < 1.0: clipscene = vec4(u 2.0 - 1.0, v 2.0 - 1.0, scenedepth 2.0 - 1.0, 1.0) worldscene = matvecmul(inverseviewprojection, clipscene) worldscene = vec3(worldscene) / worldscene.w tscene = dot(worldscene - rayorigin, raydirection) texit = min(texit, tscene) if texit <= tentry: return vec4(0.0) # 4. Jitter t = tentry if jitterenabled: t = t + jitterrandom(vec2(u, v), frameindex) stepsize # 5. Initialize Accumulation accumulatedcolor = vec4(0.0) foundvolume = False # 6. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(maximumsteps): if t >= texit: break position = rayorigin + raydirection t texcoord = clamp(position 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0) density = densitytexture.sample(texcoord).r if not foundvolume and density > 0.01: foundvolume = True # Compute Lighting lighttransmittance = 1.0 if selfshadowingenabled: opticaldepth = 0.0 lightdir = -normalize(lightdirection + vec3(0.0001)) for in range(20): shadowpos = position + lightdir 0.08 if abs(shadowpos.x) > 1.0 or abs(shadowpos.y) > 1.0 or abs(shadowpos.z) > 1.0: break shadowdensity = densitytexture.sample(shadowpos 0.5 + 0.5).r opticaldepth += shadowdensity 0.08 lighttransmittance = exp(-opticaldepth absorption densityscale 3.0) smokecolor = vec3(0.0) emittedlight = vec3(0.0) if fieldmode == 0: ambient = vec3(0.12, 0.15, 0.20) direct = vec3(1.0, 0.88, 0.72) lightintensity lighttransmittance smokecolor = mix(vec3(0.1), vec3(0.5), position.y) density emittedlight = vec3(1.0, 0.5, 0.1) density emissionstrength elif fieldmode == 1: smokecolor = mix(vec3(0.3, 0.04, 0.01), vec3(1.0, 0.65, 0.08), density) else: density = abs(density - 0.5) 2.0 smokecolor = vec3(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) if density > 0.5 else vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Accumulate alpha = 1.0 - exp(-density stepsize) colorstep = (ambient + direct + emittedlight) alpha accumulatedcolor.rgb += colorstep (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) accumulatedcolor.a += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedcolor.a) t += stepsize # 7. Temporal Accumulation if historyweight > 0.0: historycolor = historytexture.sample(u, v) finalcolor = historyweight historycolor + (1.0 - historyweight) accumulatedcolor else: finalcolor = accumulatedcolor return finalcolor gridSpacing: float, default 0.5. Used for debug visualization of the grid, not the rendering itself. densityScale: float. Multiplier for density values in light transmittance calculation. stepSize: float. Distance advanced per ray march step. maximumSteps: int. Maximum number of ray march steps per ray. frameIndex: int. Current frame number, used for jitter randomization. jitterEnabled: bool. Adds random offset to starting distance. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: bool. Uniform present, but logic not explicitly shown in the core loop snippet. fieldMode: int. 0: Smoke/Fire, 1: Simple Smoke, 2/3: Abstract/Color-coded. lightDirection: vec3. Light source direction. lightIntensity: float. Light intensity multiplier. absorption: float. Absorption coefficient for Beer-Lambert law. emissionStrength: float. Multiplier for emitted light. selfShadowingEnabled: bool. Enables shadow ray marching. temporalEnabled: bool. Enables temporal blending. historyWeight: float. Weight for previous frame's color. Division by Zero: intersectBox computes 1.0 / rayDirection. If rayDirection is zero, this results in infinity/NaN. The implementation relies on the caller providing normalized directions. Light Direction Normalization: A small epsilon (0.0001) is added to lightDirection before normalization to prevent issues if the light direction is exactly zero. Texture Coordinate Mapping: Density texture is sampled at position 0.5 + 0.5. Texture wrap mode is set to GLCLAMPTOEDGE during initialization to handle out-of-bounds coordinates. Precision: Accumulation of alpha and color can suffer from precision loss if stepSize is very small or maximumSteps is very large. Standard float precision is used. Time Complexity: O(N \times M), where N is the number of pixels and M is maximumSteps. Self-shadowing adds a constant factor (20 steps) per ray if enabled. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output and history textures. The density texture size depends on the simulation resolution. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces temporal noise, stable for animated fluids, relatively simple to implement. Limitations: Ghosting artifacts if historyWeight is too high or camera moves too fast. Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence in sparse regions. Self-shadowing is expensive. When to Use: Real-time fluid simulations, smoke, fire, clouds where temporal stability is important. When Not to Use: Static scenes where offline rendering is acceptable, or scenes requiring high-frequency spatial detail without temporal smoothing. This method is derived from the HZL Fluid Effects Studio, an open-source fluid simulation and rendering tool. It implements a standard volume ray marching algorithm with the specific addition of temporal accumulation to handle the noise inherent in real-time volumetric rendering. The technique builds on the principles of Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering, specifically the discretization of the RTE along a ray. pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, https://github.com/pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering
head: Standard 3ds Max atmospheric
body: Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering is a family of techniques that visualize participating media by integrating light transport along view rays through a density field. It solves the problem of rendering non-surface-based phenomena such as smoke, fire, clouds, and planetary atmospheres, which lack explicit geometric boundaries. It is distinguished from sibling methods like SDF Cloud Rendering by its reliance on sampled density fields or explicit atmospheric models rather than implicit Signed Distance Fields, and from Ray Marching with Single Scattering by its broader scope encompassing global atmospheric scattering and temporal accumulation strategies. The family operates on the principle of discretizing the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) along a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. The integration computes the accumulated color C and transmittance T by marching through a medium defined by density \rho(\mathbf{p}), scattering coefficient \sigmas, and absorption coefficient \sigmaa. The core integration step for a segment of length \Delta t is: 1. Density Evaluation: Sample \rho at the current position \mathbf{p}. 2. Extinction: Compute the extinction coefficient \sigmat = \sigmas + \sigmaa. 3. Transmittance Update: Update the ray's transmittance T using Beer-Lambert law: T \leftarrow T \cdot e^{-\sigmat \rho \Delta t}. 4. Inscattering: Compute the light contributed by the segment. For single scattering, this involves the phase function P(\theta) and the light source radiance L{source} attenuated by the optical depth to the light. 5. Accumulation: Add the inscattered light to the accumulated color, weighted by the current transmittance: C \leftarrow C + T \cdot \sigmas \rho \Delta t \cdot L{scattered}. The process terminates when T falls below a threshold (e.g., 0.01) or the ray exits the volume bounds. Focuses on general volumetric single scattering without specific planetary geometry or atmospheric density models. Choose when rendering generic fog or clouds rather than a planet's sky. Resolves a complete ray by compositing terrain, water, sky, cloud volume, and aerial perspective. Choose when managing the sequential evaluation and compositing order of heterogeneous scene elements in distance-field ray marching. Adds temporal stability to the ray marching process by blending the current frame's result with a history texture. Choose when flickering artifacts in dynamic scenes are a concern. Specializes in planetary atmospheres using spherical geometry and Rayleigh phase functions. Choose when rendering skyboxes or planetary atmospheres. Encodes directional color variation into SH coefficients evaluated per sample, allowing view-dependent shading via algebraic projections. Choose when replacing scalar transfer function lookups with continuous SH basis evaluation for sparse voxel grids. Computes the average density along a ray rather than integrating light transport. Choose when visualizing internal structures without depth cues or opacity accumulation. Simulates the irregular density of water droplets in clouds by generating fractal Brownian motion (fBm) noise from a pre-computed 3D noise cube. It transforms uniform random noise into a Gaussian-like distribution suitable for atmospheric vapour simulation, serving as the density field input for ray-marching algorithms. It differs from procedural noise generation by relying on a static, pre-calculated texture lookup, which trades memory bandwidth for computational simplicity and deterministic results. Renders volumetric data in a single GPU pass using WebGPU, performing analytic ray-box intersection, early-alpha termination, and optional central-difference Phong shading. It differs from standard sphere tracing by operating on explicit 3D texture volumes rather than implicit Signed Distance Functions (SDFs), allowing for complex, non-uniform density distributions. Casts rays from the camera through a volumetric scalar field, sampling the field at discrete intervals to accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. Unlike SDF Cloud Rendering, which relies on signed distance fields for surface-like rendering, this method integrates density directly, and unlike Atmospheric Ray Marching, which often targets specific post-processing effects like god rays, this method provides a general-purpose integration of the radiative transfer equation for arbitrary volume textures. Raymarches the interior volume of a glass container to simulate wax. It computes the surface normal using the gradient of the density field and sets fragment depth explicitly using glFragDepth in the opaque pass. The shading model includes wrap lighting, soft Fresnel, fake subsurface scattering based on traversed thickness, and emission driven by temperature and proximity to a light bulb. Artifacts are minimal, with 0.00% of surface voxels causing a round-trip to the threshold, even at 60 Hz with ±30% jitter. A unified rendering implementation for volumetric clouds and atmosphere using raymarching as the main method. It renders the atmosphere using an approach with multiple precomputed Look-up tables (LUTs) proposed by Sébastien Hillaire, and renders volumetric clouds using a pre-computed three dimensional texture setup storing procedurally generated noise described by Andrew Schneider. It renders images in high dynamic range before applying post-processing effects and uses adaptive luminance to transform the image into LDR for presentation. The term "Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering" in this context is closely associated with the "Standard 3ds Max atmospheric" rendering mode provided by Phoenix for 3ds Max. This mode visualizes grid content (such as fire and smoke simulations) as a standard atmospheric volume without generating a mesh surface, thereby preventing the use of standard 3ds Max and V-Ray materials for shading. Instead, shading is handled by Volumetric Render Settings using color gradients and graphs. Key parameters defined in this implementation include: Step % (rendstep): The ray marching step of camera rays as a percentage of cell size. Values >100 skip cells causing artifacts; values <90% are needed for render curves or texture maps to capture sub-voxel details. Shadow Step % (rendshadstep): The ray marching step for shadow rays, usually higher than Step % to speed up rendering. Border Fade (borderFade): Distance from grid boundaries where content becomes transparent to prevent sharp edges. Sampler Type (sampler): Blending method between adjacent voxels. Options include Box (fastest, no blending), Linear (20-30% faster than Spherical, may show grid structure), and Spherical (smoothest, weight-based sampling). This approach is distinct from surface render modes which generate a mesh and allow standard material shading. name: SDF Cloud Rendering
body: SDF Cloud Rendering is a fragment-shader-based technique for rendering volumetric cloud-like structures using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and ray marching. It solves the problem of generating complex, organic volumetric shapes without explicit mesh data by composing simple geometric primitives (spheres) via smooth unions and fractal warping. It differs from standard ray marching by relying on procedural noise-based warping of the coordinate space to create "cloudy" topology, rather than sampling a 3D texture or voxel grid. The method operates in a single-pass fragment shader. It defines a scene using a hierarchy of warped spheres, marches a ray to find the intersection with the implicit surface, and computes lighting via a shadow ray. Inputs: Fragment coordinates (glFragCoord), screen resolution (screenSize), camera field of view (45.0 degrees), and a random seed (seed). Outputs: A final color vector (glFragColor) in the range [0, 1]. No complex data structures are used. The state is maintained via local variables in the shader. Constants define the scene bounds and marching parameters. 1. Calculate the ray direction from fragment coordinates, screen size, and field of view. 2. Initialize ray depth to MINDIST and iterate up to MAXMARCHINGSTEPS. 3. Evaluate the scene SDF at the current ray position; if the returned distance is less than EPSILON, return the current depth as a surface hit. 4. Advance the ray depth by dist STEPSCALE; if the new depth exceeds MAXDIST, terminate and return MAXDIST. 5. If a hit occurs, compute a shadow ray along the light direction and blend between dark and light colors; otherwise, render a sky gradient. 6. Apply Hable tone mapping and exposure scaling to output the final color. 1. Sphere SDF The distance from a point p to a sphere centered at c with radius r: d{sphere}(p) = \|p - c\| - r where p is the query point, c is the sphere center, and r is the radius. 2. Smooth Union Blends two SDFs d1 and d2 with a blending factor k: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 + 0.5 \frac{d2 - d1}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d{union} = \text{mix}(d2, d1, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) where d1 and d2 are the input SDF values, and k controls the smoothness of the blend. 3. Jitter (Fractal Noise) Generates a pseudo-random offset based on a seed and coordinate: \text{jitter}(mixAmount, offset, seed) = 0.09 \sum{i=0}^{2} \frac{\sin((offset \cdot 1234.0 + mixAmount) \cdot 2^i)}{2^i} where the loop runs three times, scaling the sine argument and divisor by powers of two. 4. Warp Distorts the input vector v using jittered offsets: \text{warp}(v, scale, seed) = v + scale \cdot \text{vec3}(\text{jitter}(v.x, 0.0, seed), \text{jitter}(v.y, 0.2, seed), \text{jitter}(v.z, 0.5, seed)) where scale controls the intensity of the coordinate distortion. 5. Hable Tone Mapping Maps linear color x to [0, 1]: \text{toneMap}(x) = \frac{x(Ax + CB) + DE}{x(Ax + B) + DF} - \frac{E}{F} where A=0.15, B=0.50, C=0.10, D=0.20, E=0.02, F=0.30. MAXMARCHINGSTEPS: 100. MINDIST: 0.0. MAXDIST: 100.0. EPSILON: 0.0001. STEPSCALE: 0.67. EXPOSURE: 1.0. WHITE: 200.0. LIGHTPOS: vec3(-10.0, 10.0, 3.0). LIGHTCOLOR: vec3(100.0, 100.0, 100.0). DARKCOLOR: vec3(5.0, 8.0, 20.0). Precision: The source shader uses mediump float precision. Lower precision may lead to jittering artifacts or incorrect SDF evaluations in high-resolution renders. Seed Dependency: The visual appearance is deterministic based on the seed parameter. Changing the seed alters the cloud shape significantly due to the fractal warping. Step Scaling: STEPSCALE is set to 0.67 to prevent overshooting caused by coordinate warping. Computes lighting by sampling volumetric density along the ray and applying a single-scattering phase function. It sets itself apart by modeling light absorption and emission within the volume rather than just surface reflection. Choose it when rendering semi-transparent volumetric media like fog or smoke. See Ray-marched Shadows. Renders volumetric data over multiple frames and blends results to reduce noise and stabilize animated sequences. It differs from single-frame marching by leveraging temporal coherence to lower per-frame sample counts. Choose it for real-time animated volumetric effects where performance is constrained. See Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering. Simulates large-scale light transport in planetary atmospheres using phase functions and density profiles. It distinguishes itself by integrating density variations over long ray segments and accounting for multiple scattering approximations. Choose it for planetary or skybox rendering. See Volumetric and Atmospheric Rendering. Accumulates density and transparency along rays to produce projection-like images of internal structures. It differs from surface-focused SDF marching by integrating transmittance rather than stopping at the first hit. Choose it for medical or industrial inspection visualizations. See WebGL2 Volume Raycasting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Not given in the sources. Limitations: Not given in the sources. SDF Cloud Rendering was developed by Dave Pagurek as a small experiment for Graphics Interface 2019. It demonstrates the capability of Signed Distance Fields to create organic, volumetric-looking structures through procedural warping and smooth unions, rather than traditional mesh or voxel representations. davepagurek/sdf-clouds, https://github.com/davepagurek/sdf-clouds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Primary Ray Integrator
head: Composite Ray Marcher, renderRay
body: The Primary Ray Integrator is a single-function ray integrator that resolves a complete ray by compositing terrain, water, sky, cloud volume, and aerial perspective. It serves as the core rendering loop for distance-field ray marching in terrain and atmospheric scenes, handling the sequential evaluation of distinct environmental layers. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly managing the compositing order of heterogeneous scene elements (solid surfaces vs. volumetric clouds) and handling secondary ray recursion to prevent infinite loops. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: ctx: A RenderContext object containing scratch buffers, theme parameters, and camera state. ox, oy, oz: The ray origin coordinates. dx, dy, dz: The normalized ray direction vector components. tMax: The maximum ray distance for traversal. depth: An integer recursion depth counter. Primary rays pass 0; secondary rays (reflections/refractions) pass 1. Outputs: result: An Rgb color value representing the final pixel color. Data Structures: RenderScratch: A struct used for intermediate calculations, initialized to zero upon creation. It contains: result (Rgb): Accumulated color. secondary (Rgb): Color for secondary ray contributions. surface (SurfaceShade): Surface shading data (albedo, normal, etc.). Algorithm Steps: 1. Secondary Ray Guard: If depth > 0, disable water and cloud passes to prevent infinite recursion. 2. Water Plane Intersection: If depth == 0, test for intersection with the water plane. Compute limit as the minimum of the water hit distance and tMax, or tMax if no water hit. 3. Terrain/Water/Sky Trace: Trace the ray from the origin along the direction up to limit. Determine the hitKind (KINDTERRAIN, KINDWATER, KINDSKY) and distance to the hit. 4. Surface Shading: If KINDTERRAIN: Compute hit position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t{\text{terrain}}. Call shadeTerrain with the hit position and a ditherAngle. Copy the resulting surface color to result. If KINDWATER: Compute hit position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t{\text{water}}. Call shadeWater with ctx.waterShade parameters. Copy the resulting surface color to result. If KINDSKY or no hit: Call skyRadiance with the ray direction to fill result. 5. Atmospheric Compositing: If KINDSKY: Apply sky haze using the vertical component of the direction vector, dy. Else (Terrain/Water hit): Compute the hit Y coordinate y{\text{hit}} = oy + dy \cdot \text{distance}. Apply aerial perspective using distance, y{\text{hit}}, and the ray direction to composite the atmosphere over the surface color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderRay(ctx, ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz, tMax, depth): # Initialize scratch buffers to zero result = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] secondary = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] surface = {"color": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], "normal": [0.0, 0.0, 0.0]} # Step 1: Secondary Ray Guard disablewater = depth > 0 disablecloud = depth > 0 # Step 2: Water Plane Intersection limit = tMax if not disablewater: # Intersect ray with water plane waterhitdist = intersectwaterplane(ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz) if waterhitdist is not None and waterhitdist < tMax: limit = waterhitdist # Step 3: Trace ray up to limit # Sphere tracing implementation from parent method hitkind, distance = traceray(ox, oy, oz, dx, dy, dz, limit) # Step 4: Surface Shading if hitkind == "KINDTERRAIN": px, py, pz = ox + dx distance, oy + dy distance, oz + dz distance # Theme-specific terrain shading shadeTerrain(px, py, pz, surface, ctx.ditherAngle) result = surface["color"] elif hitkind == "KINDWATER": px, py, pz = ox + dx distance, oy + dy distance, oz + dz distance # Theme-specific water shading shadeWater(px, py, pz, surface, ctx.waterShade) result = surface["color"] else: # Sky radiance calculation result = skyRadiance(dx, dy, dz) # Step 5: Atmospheric Compositing if hitkind == "KINDSKY": # Sky haze computation hazefactor = computehaze(dy) result = compositehaze(result, hazefactor) else: yhit = oy + dy distance # Aerial perspective compositing result = applyaerialperspective(result, distance, yhit, dx, dy, dz) return result Parameters: ditherAngle: Used in terrain shading to reduce banding artifacts. ctx.waterShade: Configuration object for water rendering properties. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Infinite Recursion: Secondary rays (water reflections/refractions) calling back into the primary integrator can cause infinite loops. This is handled by checking depth > 0 and disabling water/cloud passes for recursive calls. Boundary Conditions: If tMax is not respected, rays may escape the scene bounds without proper termination. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles multiple scene types (terrain, water, sky, clouds) in a single pass; robust against recursion issues via depth checking. Limitations: Limited to specific scene compositions defined in the integrator; does not handle complex volumetric scattering beyond simple aerial perspective and cloud compositing. When to use: Not given in the sources. The Primary Ray Integrator is described in the context of the theme1 project by mingderwang. It is part of a larger system that includes CLI tools for rendering, theme validation, and batch processing. The method builds on the principles of distance-field ray marching, specifically sphere tracing, as detailed in the parent article. mingderwang/theme1, https://github.com/mingderwang/theme1, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Volumetric Rendering with Spherical Harmonics
head: Volume Rendering with Spherical Harmonics (Forward)
body: Volumetric Rendering with Spherical Harmonics is a direct volume ray casting method that traces rays through a sparse grid represented by spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, computing color output and optionally log-transmittance for background compositing. It encodes directional color variation into SH coefficients evaluated per sample, allowing view-dependent shading via algebraic projections during compositing. It differs from standard direct volume rendering by replacing scalar transfer function lookups with continuous SH basis evaluation, and from Neural volume rendering by using explicit SH basis functions rather than implicit neural fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse voxel grid where each active voxel stores a scalar density/opacity proxy and a vector of spherical harmonic coefficients. Camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}) and ray bounds [t{near}, t{far}]. Output: Final pixel color \mathbf{C}{out} and optionally accumulated log-transmittance for background compositing. Data Structures: Voxel Grid: A sparse 3D grid. Each active voxel contains: density: Scalar value representing extinction coefficient or opacity proxy. shcoeffs: Array of K floats, where K depends on the SH degree L (K = (L+1)^2). Ray Data: For Q rays, arrays of origin \mathbf{o}i, direction \mathbf{d}i, and sample positions. Numbered Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel/ray i, define the ray segment [t{near}, t{far}] by intersecting the ray with the volume bounding box. Discretize the segment into N samples (default N=512 or 100) at positions tj = t{near} + j \cdot \Delta t, where \Delta t = (t{far} - t{near}) / N. Sample positions are often parameterized in [0.05, 0.95] to avoid boundary artifacts. 2. Voxel Interpolation: At each sample position \mathbf{p}j, perform trilinear interpolation on the voxel grid to retrieve the local density/opacity proxy \sigmaj and the SH coefficient vector \mathbf{c}j. Extract opacity proxy: \sigmaj = \text{interp}(\text{density}). Extract SH coefficients: \mathbf{c}j = \text{interp}(\text{sh\coeffs}). 3. SH Basis Evaluation: Compute the SH basis functions \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}i) for the viewing direction \mathbf{d}i of the ray. The basis evaluation depends on the chosen degree L (typically 1 or 2). Let \mathbf{y}i = \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}i) be the vector of basis values. 4. Color Computation: Compute the view-dependent color \mathbf{C}j at sample j by taking the dot product of the interpolated SH coefficients and the basis vector: \mathbf{C}j = \mathbf{c}j \cdot \mathbf{y}i Note: In some implementations, the SH coefficients are reshaped to separate color channels before projection. 5. Transmittance and Opacity Calculation: Compute the optical depth and transmittance for each sample. Compute step sizes: \Delta tj = t{j+1} - tj (for j=0 \dots N-2). Compute weighted optical depth deltas: \deltaj = -\Delta tj \cdot \sigmaj. Compute cumulative transmittance Tj from front to back: T0 = 1 T{j+1} = \exp\left(\sum{k=0}^{j} \deltak\right) Compute per-sample opacity contribution: \alphaj = 1 - \exp(\deltaj). 6. Front-to-Back Compositing: Composite the samples into the final color: \mathbf{C}{out} = \sum{j=0}^{N-1} Tj \cdot \alphaj \cdot \mathbf{C}j \alpha{out} = \sum{j=0}^{N-1} Tj \cdot \alphaj Or in iterative form: \mathbf{C}{acc} \leftarrow \mathbf{C}{acc} + Tj \cdot \mathbf{C}j \cdot \alphaj T{j+1} \leftarrow Tj \cdot (1 - \alphaj) 7. Background Compositing (Optional): If background rendering is enabled, compute the log-transmittance for the ray and composite the background color using the accumulated transmittance. Log-transmittance: \log T{final} = \sum{j=0}^{N-1} \deltaj. Composite with background color \mathbf{C}{bg}: \mathbf{C}{final} = \mathbf{C}{out} + T{final} \cdot \mathbf{C}{bg} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def sphericalharmonicsbasis(direction, degree): """ Computes the spherical harmonic basis vector for a given direction. direction: (3,) array, normalized viewing direction. degree: int, SH degree (0, 1, or 2). Returns: (K,) array of basis values, where K = (degree + 1)2. """ x, y, z = direction basis = [] # Degree 0 basis.append(0.28209479177387814) # 1 / sqrt(4pi) if degree >= 1: # Degree 1 basis.append(-0.4886025119029199 y) basis.append(0.4886025119029199 z) basis.append(-0.4886025119029199 x) if degree >= 2: # Degree 2 basis.append(1.0925484305920792 x y) basis.append(-1.0925484305920792 y z) basis.append(0.31539156525252005 (3 z2 - 1)) basis.append(-1.0925484305920792 x z) basis.append(0.5462742152960396 (x2 - y2)) return np.array(basis) def rendervolumetricsh(voxelgrid, rayorigins, raydirections, tnear, tfar, numsamples=512, shdegree=1, backgroundenabled=False, backgroundcolors=None): """ Renders a volume using spherical harmonics for view-dependent color. Args: voxelgrid: Sparse grid object supporting trilinear interpolation. Must support query(pos) -> (density, shcoeffs). rayorigins: (Q, 3) array of ray origins. raydirections: (Q, 3) array of ray directions (normalized). tnear: (Q,) array of ray entry parameters. tfar: (Q,) array of ray exit parameters. numsamples: int, number of samples per ray. shdegree: int, degree of spherical harmonics (0, 1, 2). backgroundenabled: bool, whether to composite with background. backgroundcolors: (Q, 3) array of background colors. Returns: colors: (Q, 3) array of final pixel colors. transmittances: (Q,) array of final transmittance (if background enabled). """ Q = rayorigins.shape[0] K = (shdegree + 1)2 # Precompute SH basis for all ray directions # Shape: (Q, K) rayshbases = np.array([sphericalharmonicsbasis(raydirections[i], shdegree) for i in range(Q)]) colors = np.zeros((Q, 3)) transmittances = np.ones(Q) for i in range(Q): # Sample positions along the ray tsamples = np.linspace(tnear[i], tfar[i], numsamples + 1) # Sample points in world space samplepoints = rayorigins[i] + tsamples[:, None] raydirections[i] # Interpolate density and SH coefficients at sample points # Note: In a real implementation, this is done in bulk or via GPU kernel # Here we simulate the interpolation result # interpdata shape: (numsamples + 1, 1 + K) # Column 0: density/opacity proxy, Columns 1:K+1: shcoeffs interpdata = voxelgrid.interpolate(samplepoints) interpopacities = interpdata[:, 0] interpshcoeffs = interpdata[:, 1:] # Compute SH basis for the ray direction (constant for all samples on the ray) raybasis = rayshbases[i] # Compute color at each sample # Color = dot(shcoeffs, raybasis) # shcoeffs shape: (numsamples + 1, K) # raybasis shape: (K,) samplecolors = np.dot(interpshcoeffs, raybasis) # Shape: (numsamples + 1, 3) # Compute optical depth deltas deltas = np.diff(tsamples) # Weighted deltas for transmittance (matches S2: deltastimessigmas = - deltas interpopacities[:-1]) deltastimessigmas = -deltas interpopacities[:-1] # Cumulative transmittance (matches S2: cumsum prepended with 0) cumweighteddeltas = np.concatenate(([0], np.cumsum(deltastimessigmas))) T = np.exp(cumweighteddeltas) # Per-sample opacity (matches S2: tmp2 = 1 - exp(deltastimessigmas)) alpha = 1 - np.exp(deltastimessigmas) # Front-to-back compositing # Cout = sum(Tj alphaj Cj) # Tj here is transmittance BEFORE sample j # alphaj is opacity of sample j contribution = T[:-1] alpha samplecolors[:-1] colors[i] = np.sum(contribution, axis=0) transmittances[i] = T[-1] # Transmittance after last sample if backgroundenabled and backgroundcolors is not None: colors = colors + transmittances[:, None] backgroundcolors return colors, transmittances Parameters: numsamples: Default 512 or 100. shdegree: Typically 1 or 2. cudanthreads: Number of CUDA threads per block for ray tracing (macro TRACERAYCUDATHREADS). TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS: Number of CUDA threads per block for background rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Artifacts: Sampling at exact boundaries can cause interpolation errors. Using parameterized ranges like [0.05, 0.95] helps. SH Degree Limits: Higher SH degrees increase memory usage and reduce the maximum number of splats/voxels that can be rendered due to memory constraints (e.g., Degree 2 limits splat count to ~8,000,000 vs ~16,000,000 for Degree 0). Precision: Floating-point precision in cumulative transmittance calculation can lead to artifacts in deep volumes. Log-transmittance is computed for background compositing. Spherical Harmonics (SH) provide an orthonormal basis for representing directional functions defined on the unit sphere S^2, enabling the compact storage and efficient manipulation of volumetric radiance distributions. This family of methods solves the problem of expensive numerical integration for directional signals (such as in-scattering or visibility) by projecting them into a coefficient space where operations like rotation and integration become analytic or linear algebraic. It differs from its siblings, such as Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer and Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading, by serving as the fundamental mathematical representation layer; while the siblings apply this representation to specific shading or transfer pipelines, the core SH family focuses on the basis definition, coefficient projection, and the algebraic properties (like the product convolution) that make these applications feasible. Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer (VSH-PRT) is a technique for rendering semi-transparent volumetric datasets with dynamic lighting by precomputing the scene's response to illumination. It solves the problem of expensive real-time volume rendering by compressing the 6D Volume Radiance Transfer function into spherical harmonic coefficients stored on a surface mesh, allowing for fast runtime evaluation under arbitrary distant lighting. It sets itself apart from direct volume rendering by decoupling the expensive volume integration from the render loop, and from standard surface PRT by explicitly handling the volumetric scattering process to determine the exit radiance. Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading is a method for computing diffuse illumination in Fourier Volume Rendering (FVR) by approximating the non-linear shading operator (specifically the \max(N \cdot L, 0) term) using spherical harmonics. It solves the problem of interactive relighting in the frequency domain, where traditional methods require expensive recomputation of 3D Fourier transforms for every change in light direction. Unlike Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer, which precomputes transfer functions for specific geometries, this method operates directly on the volume's gradient-derived normals in the Fourier domain, allowing light direction changes to be handled via simple coefficient updates without re-transforming the volume data. The Ray Tracing Backward Pass computes the gradients of a differentiable volume rendering loss with respect to the scene representation (spherical harmonic coefficients and density) and auxiliary parameters, given the rendered image and ground truth. It serves as the differentiable counterpart to the forward ray casting pass, enabling end-to-end training of volumetric models like Plenoxels. Unlike the forward pass which accumulates color and transmittance, this method propagates error signals backward through the ray integration, handling RGB normalization and optional regularization losses (beta, sparsity). The Zonal Method (Bhate and Tokuta) is a global illumination technique for participating media that extends the classical zonal method by incorporating spherical harmonics to handle anisotropic scattering and surface-volume interactions. Unlike the standard zonal method which assumes isotropic media and ignores surface effects, this method represents the phase function and radiance using spherical harmonics, allowing for the approximation of Mie scattering while maintaining ideal diffuse surfaces. It is distinguished from its siblings by its specific use of an extended hemicube technique to compute spherical harmonic form factors and a Gauss-Seidel solver for the coupled volume-surface system. Renders RGB values by projecting spherical harmonics coefficients along viewing directions, then compositing with weights. Reshapes SH coefficients to separate color channels, computes SH basis components for given directions, multiplies coefficients by components, sums over SH components and adds bias, applies optional activation function to RGB, and composites using RGBRenderer.combinergb. The activation function defaults to nn.Sigmoid(). A known pitfall in some source implementations is that the code overwrites the RGB tensor in the sum step (rgb = torch.sum(sh, dim=-1) + 0.5), discarding the channel multiplication result. Time Complexity: O(Q \cdot N \cdot K), where Q is the number of rays, N is the number of samples per ray, and K is the number of SH coefficients (K=(L+1)^2). Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot K), where V is the number of active voxels and K is the number of SH coefficients per voxel. Measured Performance: Limits on splat count depend on SH degree: Degree 0 allows ~16,000,000 splats, Degree 1 allows ~11,000,000, and Degree 2 allows ~8,000,000. Strengths: Efficient view-dependent shading without per-sample transfer function lookups; compact representation of directional data. Limitations: Memory intensive for high SH degrees; fixed basis may not capture complex directional effects as well as learned bases. When to Use: When view-dependent color effects are important and computational resources allow for the memory overhead of SH coefficients. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or view-dependent effects are minimal (use Degree 0 or standard scalar transfer functions). The method originates from CUDA-based volume rendering implementations that use sparse grids represented by spherical harmonic coefficients. It is part of the broader family of spherical harmonic methods for directional data representation. The approach is used in neural volume rendering contexts and real-time rendering applications where view-dependent effects are desired. sxyu/svox2, https://github.com/sxyu/svox2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, https://github.com/szat/Jax-Volumetric-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, https://github.com/mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Spherical Harmonics
head: SH basis, SH coefficients, Spherical Harmonic Representation of Radiance, Spherical Harmonic Volumetric Rendering, Spherical Harmonics (SH) Basis
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) provide a complete, orthonormal basis for representing directional functions defined on the unit sphere S^2. In volume rendering, they serve as a fixed, non-learnable basis for directional signals, where switching between max degree 3 (SH-16) and 4 (SH-25) yields negligible differences in metrics or visual quality. They differ from their siblings, such as Spherical Harmonics Approximation and Volumetric Spherical Harmonics Precomputed Radiance Transfer, by defining the fundamental mathematical basis itself, whereas the siblings focus on specific application pipelines or optimization techniques built upon this basis. The SH basis consists of an infinite set of functions Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) indexed by degree \ell \in \mathbb{N} \cup \{0\} and order m \in \{-\ell, \dots, \ell\}. The complex-valued basis functions are defined as: Y\ell^m(\theta, \phi) = \sqrt{\frac{2\ell + 1}{4\pi} \frac{(\ell - m)!}{(\ell + m)!}} P\ell^m(\cos \theta) e^{im\phi} where P\ell^m are the associated Legendre polynomials. For real-valued rendering applications, the basis is constructed to avoid imaginary numbers for m \neq 0. The real-valued basis Y{lm} is defined piecewise: Y{lm}(\theta, \phi) = \begin{cases} \sqrt{2} K{lm} \cos(m\phi) Pl^m(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m > 0 \\ K{l0} Pl^0(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m = 0 \\ \sqrt{2} K{lm} \sin(-m\phi) Pl^{-m}(\cos(\theta)), & \text{if } m < 0 \end{cases} where K{lm} = \sqrt{\frac{2l + 1}{4\pi} \frac{(l - m)!}{(l + m)!}}. Source provides an alternative real-valued construction using Y\ell^m = \sqrt{2}(-1)^m\text{Im}[Y\ell^{|m|}] for m < 0, Y\ell^0 for m = 0, and \sqrt{2}(-1)^m\text{Re}[Y\ell^m] for m > 0. A directional signal f(\omega) is represented by a finite set of coefficients \mathbf{f} of size n = (L+1)^2, where L is the maximum degree (bandwidth) Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection. The coefficients are computed by projecting the function onto the basis Spherical Harmonics Approximation: fi = \int{\Omega} f(\omega) yi(\omega) d\omega The signal is reconstructed by summing the basis functions weighted by the coefficients Spherical Harmonics Approximation: \tilde{f}(\omega) = \sum{i=0}^{n-1} fi yi(\omega) The linear index i maps the degree l and order m via i = l^2 + l + m Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection. Convolution of two functions \tilde{a}(\omega) and \tilde{b}(\omega) in the SH domain is performed using a precomputed transfer matrix C{ijk} Spherical Harmonics Approximation: (a b)i = \sum{j=0}^{n-1} \sum{k=0}^{n-1} C{ijk} aj bk where C{ijk} = \int{\Omega} yi(\omega) yj(\omega) yk(\omega) d\omega Spherical Harmonics Approximation. The integral of the product of two approximated functions is the dot product of their coefficient vectors Spherical Harmonics Approximation: \int{\Omega} \tilde{a}(\omega)\tilde{b}(\omega)d\omega = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b} Typical implementations use the lowest 3-5 levels of SH to keep the representation compact. SH approximations containing higher frequencies become too large to be practical, and SH functions exhibit 'ringing' artifacts (high-frequency noise) near sharp value changes, especially when many coefficients are used. Represents a spherical function using a finite SH subset for efficient, differentiable computation. Sets it apart by focusing on projection and reconstruction mechanics with a fixed bandwidth rather than determining optimal bandwidth. Choose it for inverse problems requiring algebraic integration and convolution. Determines the maximum bandwidth L to balance reconstruction fidelity against memory consumption. Sets it apart by focusing on the capacity limit (bandwidth) rather than the projection or fitting process itself. Choose it when optimizing memory and compute constraints for a given signal's frequency content. Stores position- and direction-dependent scattered radiance in a 3D grid using SH basis functions. Sets it apart by enabling fast integration via sparse matrix multiplication during rendering. Choose it for efficient multiple scattering in volumes (e.g., hair) where storage compactness and organized memory access are critical. (Link only; details in child article). (Link only; details in child article). (Link only; details in child article). (Link only; details in child article). A basis used to encode a hemispherical signal, requiring fewer coefficients to achieve the same quality as 3rd order spherical harmonics. A coordinate system local to the surface is required to orient the hemisphere, commonly utilizing a tangent frame resulting from uv-parameterization. If encoded in textures, the texture needs sufficient resolution to adapt to changes in the underlying tangent space. If two triangles cover the same texel and have significantly different tangents, it leads to a lack of precision in the reconstructed signal. Spherical Harmonics originated in mathematical physics as a complete basis for functions on the sphere. In computer graphics, they were adopted for Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) to efficiently represent lighting and reflection. They are used in volume rendering to represent the directional distribution of scattered radiance, allowing for efficient rotation and integration. Recent applications include representing neural radiance fields (NeRFs) via PlenOctrees, where SH basis functions replace standard color representations to enable real-time rendering. name: Spherical Harmonics Approximation
head: SH Approximation, Spherical Harmonics Basis Approximation
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Approximation is a technique to represent a spherical function f(\omega) using a finite subset of the SH basis functions, enabling efficient and differentiable computation for inverse problems in volume rendering. It solves the problem of expensive Monte Carlo integration by projecting directional data (such as lighting, visibility, and in-scattering) into the SH domain, where integrals become simple dot products and convolutions become matrix-vector multiplications. Unlike its sibling Spherical Harmonics Degree Selection, which determines the optimal bandwidth, this method focuses on the projection and reconstruction mechanics using a fixed bandwidth. Inputs: A spherical function f(\omega) defined over the domain \Omega (the unit sphere), and a maximum bandwidth L (or number of bands n). Outputs: A vector of SH coefficients \mathbf{f} of size n = (L+1)^2. Data Structures: The coefficients are stored in a 1D array \mathbf{f} of length n. The linear index i maps the degree l and order m via: i = l^2 + l + m where l \in \{0, \dots, L\} and m \in \{-l, \dots, l\}. Steps: 1. Projection: Compute the SH coefficients fi by projecting the function f(\omega) onto the basis functions yi(\omega): fi = \int{\Omega} f(\omega) yi(\omega) d\omega. In practice, for inverse problems, this integral is often precomputed or solved via numerical integration at initialization to ensure differentiability with respect to scene parameters. 2. Reconstruction: Approximate the original signal \tilde{f}(\omega) by summing the basis functions weighted by the coefficients: \tilde{f}(\omega) = \sum{i=1}^{n} fi yi(\omega). The accuracy increases with n. 3. Integration via Dot Product: The integral of the product of two approximated functions \tilde{a}(\omega) and \tilde{b}(\omega) is computed as the dot product of their coefficient vectors: \int{\Omega} \tilde{a}(\omega)\tilde{b}(\omega)d\omega = \mathbf{a} \cdot \mathbf{b}. 4. Convolution (Multiplication Projection): The SH projection of the product of two functions, denoted a b, is computed using a precomputed transfer matrix C{ijk}: (a b)i = \sum{j=1}^{n} \sum{k=1}^{n} C{ijk} aj bk where C{ijk} = \int{\Omega} yi(\omega)yj(\omega)yk(\omega)d\omega. Parameters: Bandwidth n: The number of bands used. A value of n=8 is cited as providing good low-frequency approximations for inverse problems. Typical implementations use the lowest 3-5 levels. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeshcoefficients(functionf, basisfunctionsy, domainsamples): """ Computes SH coefficients fi by numerically integrating f(w) yi(w) over the sphere. functionf: callable, returns f(w) for a direction w. basisfunctionsy: callable, returns yi(w) for a direction w and index i. domainsamples: list of (w, weight) tuples representing the discretized sphere. """ n = len(basisfunctionsy) # Total number of coefficients f = [0.0] n for w, weight in domainsamples: valf = functionf(w) for i in range(n): valy = basisfunctionsy(i, w) f[i] += valf valy weight return f def reconstructshsignal(coefficientsf, basisfunctionsy, directionw): """ Reconstructs the signal at a specific direction using SH coefficients. coefficientsf: list of SH coefficients fi. basisfunctionsy: callable, returns yi(w). directionw: the direction vector w. """ signal = 0.0 for i, coeff in enumerate(coefficientsf): signal += coeff basisfunctionsy(i, directionw) return signal def computeconvolutioncoefficients(coefficientsa, coefficientsb, transfermatrixC): """ Computes the SH coefficients of the product of two functions a and b. coefficientsa: list of SH coefficients for a. coefficientsb: list of SH coefficients for b. transfermatrixC: 3D array C[i][j][k]. """ n = len(coefficientsa) result = [0.0] n for i in range(n): sumval = 0.0 for j in range(n): for k in range(n): sumval += transfermatrixC[i][j][k] coefficientsa[j] coefficientsb[k] result[i] = sumval return result def computeintegraldotproduct(coefficientsa, coefficientsb): """ Computes the integral of the product of two SH approximated functions. """ return sum(a b for a, b in zip(coefficientsa, coefficientsb)) Spherical Harmonic Projection is the process of approximating an arbitrary spherical function f(\omega) by computing the coefficients of its expansion in the SH basis [Child 11243]. It differs from the parent Spherical Harmonics Approximation by focusing specifically on the computational mechanics of deriving these coefficients via least-squares minimization and leveraging the basis's orthonormality for efficient GPU-based integration [Child 11243]. It is chosen when efficient representation of complex angular data (lighting, reflectance) is required for volume rendering [Child 11243]. This variant reformulates the computation of the hemisphere visibility term H(x) to be differentiable with respect to the surface normal n(x). Instead of direct integration, it uses a linear rotation function \phi{SH} to rotate a standard z-axis symmetric integral: H(x) = \phi{SH}(n(x)) \int{\Omega} \max(iz \cdot \omega, 0)y(\omega)d\omega where iz = (0, 0, 1)^T. The integral is solved using numerical integration at initialization and does not need to be differentiable, as only the SH coefficients of the environment map are updated. This method approximates an SH vector f as a sum of rotated Zonal Harmonic (ZH) basis functions by minimizing the L2 error \psi = \|f - g\|. It iterates through ZH levels from lowest to highest frequency. For each level, it calculates several hundred rotations uniformly distributed on the hemisphere, solves for the optimal SH coefficients g^l for each rotation, and keeps the rotation with the lowest error. The optimal coefficients for a fixed rotation \hat{z} are: g^l = \frac{4\pi}{2l + 1} \sum{m=-l}^{l} Y{lm}(\hat{z}) f{lm}. The selected ZH function is projected into the SH basis and subtracted from the target vector before proceeding to the next level. Zonal Harmonics are a subset of SH defined by m=0, consisting of functions symmetric about the vertical axis. A ZH function g is a sum of the n lowest-order ZH functions: g = \sum{l=1}^{n} gl Y{l0}. To rotate a ZH vector g and project it into the SH basis, each coefficient f{lm} is calculated as: f{lm} = g^l Y{lm}(\hat{z}l) where g^l = gl \sqrt{\frac{2\pi}{2l + 1}} and \hat{z}l is the rotation axis for level l. Projecting an SH vector into the ZH basis is a hard problem solved by minimizing the L2 norm \psi = \|f - g\|. Time Complexity: Projection requires integration over the sphere, which is O(n \cdot N{samples}) where N{samples} is the number of integration points. Convolution is O(n^3) due to the triple summation in the transfer matrix. Reconstruction is O(n). Memory Complexity: Storing coefficients is O(n). The transfer matrix C{ijk} requires O(n^3) space. Performance: Using n=8 provides good low-frequency approximations with manageable computational cost. Strengths: Enables differentiable computation for inverse problems; converts expensive integrals into dot products; allows real-time rendering of global illumination effects via PRT. Limitations: Low-pass filtering nature limits high-frequency detail representation; requires precomputation of transfer matrices or integrals; rotation of general SH functions is complex, often requiring conversion to ZH or other bases. When to use: When global illumination or in-scattering effects need to be represented compactly and differentially for optimization or real-time rendering. When not to use: When high-frequency directional details are critical and cannot be captured by low-bandwidth SH. The method originates from the application of Spherical Harmonics to Precomputed Radiance Transfer (PRT) for real-time global illumination. Sloan et al. introduced the use of SH for representing light transport and the rotation of Zonal Harmonics. The specific application to differentiable shadow computation and inverse problems in volume rendering was detailed by in 2021. Zonal Harmonics were popularized by Sloan et al. (2005) for efficient rotation and projection.
