name: Efficient multiple scattering in hair using spherical harmonics
head: SH Hair Scattering, SH-based multiple scattering for hair, Spherical Harmonic Multiple Scattering in Hair, Volumetric Hair Multiple Scattering
body:
This method computes physically based multiple scattering in hair volumes by representing the incident scattered radiance field as spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, allowing the complex scattering integral to be evaluated via a precomputed sparse matrix multiplication. It solves the high computational cost of directional multiple scattering by exploiting the smoothness of the indirect radiance distribution, reducing the per-ray shading cost from sampling-based integration to a fixed-size linear algebra operation. It differs from its parent Spherical Harmonic Volume Shading by specifically addressing the anisotropic, fiber-based scattering properties of hair and using a voxelized light-tracing approach to populate the SH coefficients, rather than relying on Fourier transforms or local basis approximations alone. The method consists of four main phases: Voxelization, Light Tracing, Filtering, and Shading (which includes optional Scattering Matrix Precomputation). Inputs: Hair geometry (segments), light source definitions, fiber properties (diameter 2r, eccentricity), grid resolution, SH degree D. Outputs: Rendered image with multiple scattering; optionally, a sparse scattering matrix F for future frames. Voxel Grid A 3D rectilinear grid. Each active voxel stores: meandirection:  ar{\omega}, a 3D vector (normalized). stddev: 
u, a scalar (standard deviation of dot products with  ar{\omega}). attenuation: \sigmat^\perp, a scalar (perpendicular attenuation coefficient). coefficients: A vector of size (D+1)^2 containing SH coefficients ck in the world frame. Scattering Matrix F: A sparse matrix of size (D+1)^2 	imes (D+1)^2. Non-zero entries: Approximately 2% of total entries. Estimate hair density and direction distribution by rasterizing hair segments into the voxel grid. 1. Initialize all voxels as empty. 2. For each hair segment, identify all voxels within a search distance d. 3. For each sample point near the fiber within distance d, add contributions to the voxel's direction list. The weight drops linearly to zero at distance d. 4. After processing all segments, for each voxel: Sum the nearby segment directions weighted by their linear distance drop-off. Normalize the sum to obtain the mean direction  ar{\omega}. Calculate 
u as the standard deviation of the dot products of the normalized segment directions with  ar{\omega}. Calculate the perpendicular attenuation coefficient \sigmat^\perp using formula (6): \sigmat^\perp =  rac{2r N}{\pi d^2} where 2r is the fiber diameter, N is the number of nearby fibers, and d is the voxelization search distance. 5. Mark voxels with no contribution as empty. 6. Mark voxels far from any non-empty cell (unable to participate in lookup) as inactive. Do not allocate coefficients for inactive cells. Estimate scattered radiance in all directions by tracing paths from light sources. 1. Trace paths from light sources proportional to emitted power. 2. After the first geometric scattering event, walk through the voxel grid along each path segment. 3. For each intersected grid cell j with volume \Delta V: Let lp be the length of the intersection between path segment p and cell j. Let \Delta \Phip be the power associated with the light particle. Add contribution to the SH coefficients ck of cell j according to the density definition: 	ext{Contribution} \propto  rac{lp \cdot \Delta \Phip}{\Delta V} The contribution is distributed into the SH basis functions Yk based on the direction of the path segment. 4. Scattering within the volume occurs according to \sigmat(\omega) derived from the voxel's  ar{\omega} and 
u. 5. Upon scattering, choose a fiber direction u from the distribution described by  ar{\omega} and 
u. 6. Sample the scattered direction \omegai using a table-driven procedure: Precompute several thousand random directions for each possible inclination based on the refracted direction for a rough elliptical fiber (simulating roughness by randomizing surface normals). During simulation, randomly choose one of these stored directions. Incident rays have a random azimuthal angle and random position across the fiber width. Reduce noise and Gibbs phenomenon ringing. 1. Spectral Filtering: Apply a gentle lowpass filter to the SH coefficients. Attenuate coefficients by a factor that drops smoothly to zero just beyond the maximum degree D. This prevents ringing caused by sharp peaks in the accumulated radiance. 2. Spatial Filtering: Convolve the grid of coefficients with a box filter with spherical support. The radius is typically between 1.5 and 3 grid cells. Use more aggressive filtering for animations to prevent temporal flicker. Compute exitant radiance for a point \mathbf{x} on a hair fiber. 1. Retrieve Coefficients: Trilinearly interpolate the SH coefficients ck(\mathbf{x}) from the grid (stored in world frame). 2. Rotate to Local Frame: Rotate the interpolated coefficients c to the local fiber frame at \mathbf{x} using the rotation matrix R(\mathbf{x}): c0 = R(\mathbf{x}) c 3. Compute Exitant Coefficients: Option A (Precomputed Matrix): Multiply the precomputed scattering matrix F by the rotated incident coefficients: d0 = F c0 where d0 are the coefficients of the exitant scattered radiance. Option B (Stabbing - Fallback): If F is not precomputed or parameters change frequently, generate 20 to 50 directional "stabs" by sampling the phase function fs(\mathbf{x}, \omegao, \omegai) \sin(\omegai, u). Use the filtered grid values to evaluate incident radiance for each stab direction, weight by attenuation, and average. 4. Reconstruct Radiance: Convert exitant coefficients d0 back to world frame and evaluate the SH basis functions to get the exitant radiance Lo(\mathbf{x}, \omegao). 5. Add Direct Illumination: Calculate direct illumination separately using standard ray tracing and add to the result. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def voxelize(segments, gridsize, d, fiberdiameter2r): grid = {} for seg in segments: # Not given in the sources: determine voxels intersected by segment within distance d for vkey in voxelsnearsegment(seg, d): if vkey not in grid: grid[vkey] = {'dirs': [], 'count': 0} dist = segmentvoxeldistance(seg, vkey) w = max(0.0, 1.0 - dist / d) grid[vkey]['dirs'].append((seg.dir, w)) grid[vkey]['count'] += 1 for vkey in list(grid.keys()): data = grid[vkey] if not data['dirs']: del grid[vkey] continue wsum = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for dvec, w in data['dirs']: wsum[0] += dvec[0] w wsum[1] += dvec[1] w wsum[2] += dvec[2] w norm = math.sqrt(sum(v2 for v in wsum)) meandir = [v / norm for v in wsum] if norm > 0 else [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] dots = [sum(ab for a, b in zip(dvec, meandir)) for dvec, in data['dirs']] meandot = sum(dots) / len(dots) stddev = math.sqrt(sum((x - meandot)2 for x in dots) / len(dots)) N = data['count'] sigmatperp = (fiberdiameter2r N) / (math.pi d 2) grid[vkey] = { 'meandirection': meandir, 'stddev': stddev, 'sigmatperp': sigmatperp, 'coeffs': [0.0] ((15 + 1) 2) } return grid def lighttrace(lights, grid): for light in lights: for path in tracepathsfromlight(light): for seg in path.segmentsafterfirstscatter: # Not given in the sources: traverse grid along segment for vkey in voxelsintersectedbysegment(seg): if vkey in grid: vol = voxelvolume(vkey) contrib = seg.lengthinvoxel(vkey) path.power / vol # Not given in the sources: project direction onto SH basis and add to coeffs accumulateshcoefficients(grid[vkey]['coeffs'], seg.dir, contrib) # Not given in the sources: compute scattering probability if random.random() < scatteringprobability(grid[vkey]['sigmatperp']): u = samplefiberdirection(grid[vkey]['meandirection'], grid[vkey]['stddev']) omegai = samplescattereddirectiontable(u) path.continue(omegai) def filtergrid(grid): for vkey in grid: coeffs = grid[vkey]['coeffs'] for k in range(len(coeffs)): # Not given in the sources: compute lowpass attenuation factor factor = smoothstep(k, 15) coeffs[k] = factor radius = 2.0 for vkey in grid: # Not given in the sources: find neighbors within radius neighbors = getsphericalneighbors(vkey, radius) neighborcoeffs = [grid[n]['coeffs'] for n in neighbors if n in grid] if neighborcoeffs: # Not given in the sources: average vectors grid[vkey]['coeffs'] = averagecoefficients(neighborcoeffs) return grid def shade(x, diro, grid, F=None): # Not given in the sources: trilinear interpolation cworld = trilinearinterp(grid, x) # Not given in the sources: compute rotation matrix to local frame Rx = rotationtolocal(x, diro) # Not given in the sources: rotate SH coefficients clocal = rotatesh(cworld, Rx) if F is not None: # Not given in the sources: sparse matrix-vector multiplication dlocal = matvecmul(F, clocal) else: # Not given in the sources: fallback stabbing method dlocal = stabbing(cworld, diro, grid) # Not given in the sources: rotate SH coefficients back dworld = rotatesh(dlocal, transpose(Rx)) # Not given in the sources: evaluate SH basis functions Lo = evalsh(dworld, diro) # Not given in the sources: compute direct illumination Ld = tracedirect(x, diro) return Lo + Ld SH Degree (D): Typically up to 15, resulting in 256 coefficients per grid point. Fiber Diameter (2r): Used in \sigmat^\perp calculation. Voxelization Search Distance (d): Determines the spatial extent of fiber influence per voxel. Smoothing Factor: Values range from 2.0 to 2.2 cells across tested scenes. Grid Cell Parameter (r): Values range from 8 to 10 cells across tested scenes. Paths Traced: Ranges from 100M to 160M depending on the scene. Image Resolution: 600 x 600 pixels. Rays per Pixel: 64. Gibbs Phenomenon: Directly using accumulated coefficients with sharp peaks leads to ringing. Increasing SH degree does not reduce this until the peak is fully resolved. Solution: Apply lowpass filter. Temporal Incoherence: Spatial noise in static images is hard to notice, but becomes perceptible flicker in animations. Solution: Use more aggressive spatial filtering for animations. Sampling Difficulty: The Marschner et al. phase function model is difficult to sample directly. Solution: Use table-driven scattering with precomputed random directions based on refracted directions for rough elliptical fibers. Smoothness Assumption: The method limits accuracy for highly directional radiance distributions, as they cannot be accurately represented by the SH basis. Spatial Resolution: Constrained by rectilinear grid spacing, causing spatial and angular blurring comparable to photon mapping. Time Complexity: The shading step is O(1) per ray (matrix multiplication or stabbing). The dominant cost is light tracing, which scales with the number of paths traced (100M-160M paths). Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of active voxels times the number of SH coefficients. For a 33x109x49 grid with 46,074 active cells and 256 coefficients, memory usage is significantly lower than photon mapping (270 MB vs 1.5 GB). Measured Performance: On a 3.0 GHz Intel Core 2 Duo workstation, single-threaded, 1 GB RAM: Voxelization: ~10 seconds. Attenuation/Scattering function tabulation: ~3 seconds each. Scattering matrix precomputation: 700 seconds (500,000 evaluations). Multiple scattering rendering: 13 minutes per frame (animations), 5 minutes for stills (vs 1.5 hours for photon mapping). Direct illumination: Additional 10 minutes. Strengths: Significantly faster than photon mapping for hair multiple scattering; preserves directionally varying effects; low memory footprint. Limitations: Limited by SH basis smoothness; spatial blurring from grid resolution; requires precomputation for optimal speed. When to use: Production hair rendering where multiple scattering is required and performance is critical. When not to use: Scenes with highly directional, non-smooth indirect lighting that cannot be captured by SH; real-time applications requiring dynamic hair geometry changes without re-voxelization. This method was introduced by to address the high cost of physically based multiple scattering in hair. It builds on the fiber radiance cache concept from Moon and Marschner [2006] but replaces the directional stabbing approach with spherical harmonics to exploit the smoothness of multiple scattering. The implementation was done in Java using a hierarchical grid for ray-hair intersection acceleration. Efficient multiple scattering in hair using spherical harmonics, https://doi.org/10.1145/1360612.1360630, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Ray Tracing Backward Pass
head: Plenoxel Ray Tracing (Backward)
body: The Ray Tracing Backward Pass computes the gradients of a differentiable volume rendering loss with respect to the scene representation (spherical harmonic coefficients and density) and auxiliary parameters, given the rendered image and ground truth. It serves as the differentiable counterpart to the forward ray casting pass, enabling end-to-end training of volumetric models like Plenoxels. Unlike the forward pass which accumulates color and transmittance, this method propagates error signals backward through the ray integration, handling RGB normalization and optional regularization losses (beta, sparsity). Inputs: gradoutput: Gradient of the loss with respect to the rendered RGB color (shape: [N, 3] or flattened). colorcache: Cached accumulated color components from the forward pass (shape: [N, 3] or similar structure storing intermediate accumulation terms). rayspec: Ray origins and directions. grid: Volumetric grid containing density data and spherical harmonic coefficients. betaloss: Scalar weight for beta distribution sparsity loss. sparsityloss: Scalar weight for sparsity loss. logtransmitin: Logarithm of transmittance at the start of the ray segment. opt: Configuration options (e.g., gradoutisrgb, basisdim, shdatadim). Outputs: grads: Gradients for spherical harmonic coefficients and density. accumout (optional): Accumulated gradient values. logtransmitout (optional): Gradient of log transmittance. Data Structures: sphfuncval: Shared memory array storing spherical harmonic function values for the current ray. gradsphfuncval: Shared memory array storing gradients of SH function values. rayspec: Struct containing ray origin (\mathbf{o}) and direction (\mathbf{v}). tempstorage: Warp-level reduction buffer. Steps: 1. Initialize Accumulation: Compute the initial gradient accumulator accum from the color cache and output gradient. Assuming colorcache and gradoutput are vectors of size 3 (RGB): \text{accum} = \sum{i=0}^{2} \text{color\cache}[i] \cdot \text{grad\output}[i] 2. Thread Identification: Calculate global thread ID, rayid, rayblkid, and laneid (warp lane index). If laneid >= grid.shdatadim, return early, as this thread does not contribute to SH gradient computation. 3. Beta Loss Gradient (if applicable): If betaloss > 0, compute the transmittance at the input: t{\text{in}} = \exp(\log\transmit\in) Update the beta loss contribution to the accumulator: \text{beta\loss\grad} = \text{beta\loss} \cdot \left( 1 - \frac{t{\text{in}}}{1 - t{\text{in}} + \epsilon} \right) where \epsilon = 10^{-3} for numerical stability. Add this to accum. 4. Shared Memory and Ray Setup: Initialize shared memory arrays sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, and tempstorage. Set rayspec from origins and directions, extracting the direction vector \mathbf{v}{\text{dir}}. 5. Degenerate Ray Check: If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, the ray is invalid. Write accum to accumout (if not null) and 0 to logtransmitout (if not null), then return. 6. Gradient Output Normalization: If gradoutisrgb is true, calculate the residual between the cached color and the gradient output: \text{resid} = \text{color\cache} - \text{grad\output} Compute normalization factor: \text{norm\factor} = \frac{2.0}{3 \cdot Q} where Q is the number of rays or a scaling factor defined by the implementation. Update gradout[i]: \text{grad\out}[i] = \text{resid}[i] \cdot \text{norm\factor} Otherwise, gradout[i] = gradoutput[i]. 7. Warp Synchronization: Synchronize warps within the SH data dimension mask to ensure shared memory consistency. 8. Core Backward Trace: Call traceraycuvolbackward with arguments: gradout, colorcache, rayspec, opt, laneid, sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval, tempstorage, logtransmitin, betaloss, sparsityloss, grads, and optional output pointers. This function performs the core integration of gradients along the ray, interpolating density and SH coefficients, and computing gradients for the grid parameters. 9. SH Gradient Computation: Call calcsphfuncbackward to compute the gradients for the spherical harmonic basis coefficients based on the accumulated gradients in gradsphfuncval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraybackwardkernel( gradoutput, # Tensor [N, 3] or flattened colorcache, # Tensor [N, 3] or similar rayspec, # Struct with origin, direction, tmin, tmax grid, # Object with densitydata, shcoeffs, shdatadim, basisdim betaloss, # Float sparsityloss, # Float logtransmitin, # Float opt, # Struct with gradoutisrgb, shdatadim, etc. accumout, # Optional pointer/tensor logtransmitout # Optional pointer/tensor): # 1. Initialize Accumulation accum = 0.0 for i in range(3): accum += colorcache[i] gradoutput[i] # 2. Thread Identification laneid = getlaneid() if laneid >= grid.shdatadim: return # 3. Beta Loss Gradient if betaloss > 0.0: transmitin = exp(logtransmitin) betagrad = betaloss (1.0 - transmitin / (1.0 - transmitin + 1e-3)) accum += betagrad # 4. Shared Memory Init sphfuncval = sharedmemarray(size=grid.basisdim) gradsphfuncval = sharedmemarray(size=grid.basisdim, init=0.0) tempstorage = warpreductionbuffer() # 5. Ray Setup vdir = rayspec.direction rayspec.origin = rayspec.origin rayspec.direction = vdir # 6. Degenerate Ray Check if rayspec.tmin > rayspec.tmax: if accumout is not None: accumout[0] = accum if logtransmitout is not None: logtransmitout[0] = 0.0 return # 7. Gradient Output Normalization if opt.gradoutisrgb: resid = colorcache - gradoutput normfactor = 2.0 / (3.0 Q) # Q is implementation-specific scaling factor gradout = resid normfactor else: gradout = gradoutput # 8. Warp Sync syncwarps() # 9. Core Backward Trace # This step involves trilinear interpolation of density and SH values, # and accumulation of gradients along the ray. # The exact implementation of traceraycuvolbackward is complex and # relies on the forward pass cache. traceraycuvolbackward( gradout=gradout, colorcache=colorcache, rayspec=rayspec, opt=opt, laneid=laneid, sphfuncval=sphfuncval, gradsphfuncval=gradsphfuncval, tempstorage=tempstorage, logtransmitin=logtransmitin, betaloss=betaloss, sparsityloss=sparsityloss, grads=grid.grads, accumout=accumout, logtransmitout=logtransmitout) # 10. SH Gradient Computation calcsphfuncbackward( gradsphfuncval=gradsphfuncval, shcoeffs=grid.shcoeffs, grads=grid.grads) Parameters: betaloss: Scalar weight for beta distribution sparsity loss. If > 0, gradient contribution is added to accum. sparsityloss: Scalar weight for sparsity loss. Passed to traceraycuvolbackward. Q: Scaling factor used in RGB normalization. Not explicitly defined in sources, but used in formula. Edge Cases: If ray.tmin > ray.tmax, the kernel returns early, writing zero to logtransmitout. Numerical stability is handled by adding \epsilon = 10^{-3} in the beta loss denominator. The Background Rendering Backward Pass computes the gradients of the loss with respect to the background volumetric field (typically a sparse grid of spherical harmonic coefficients or density values) and the accumulated transmittance, given the rendered background color, ground truth, and ray parameters. It serves as the differentiable counterpart to the concentric sphere sampling and trilinear interpolation used in the forward background rendering pass. Unlike the foreground ray casting which traverses a dense or sparse voxel grid, this method specifically handles the unbounded background field, often using a separate sparse grid structure. It is distinct from the general Ray Tracing Backward Pass by isolating the gradient computation for the background component, allowing for specialized handling of RGB normalization and sparsity regularization specific to the background layer. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray and the number of rays. The SH evaluation and gradient computation are O(D) per sample, where D is the SH dimension. Memory Complexity: O(D) per thread for shared memory storage of SH function values and gradients. Performance: Implemented as a CUDA kernel for GPU acceleration. Performance depends on the number of rays, SH dimension, and grid resolution. Strengths: Enables end-to-end training of volumetric representations. Handles complex lighting via SH. Limitations: High memory usage for large SH dimensions. Numerical stability issues can arise with extreme transmittance values. When to use: When training differentiable volume rendering models like Plenoxels. When not to use: For non-differentiable rendering or when SH approximation is insufficient. The Ray Tracing Backward Pass is part of the svox2 library, developed by Alex Yu and others. It is designed to support differentiable volume rendering with spherical harmonics, enabling efficient training of neural radiance fields and related representations. The method is integrated into the NeRF-Factory framework by POSTECH, KAIST, and Kakao Brain Corp.. kakaobrain/nerf-factory, https://github.com/kakaobrain/nerf-factory, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) sxyu/svox2, https://github.com/sxyu/svox2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Background Rendering Backward Pass
head: Background Backpropagation, Background Rendering Kernel (Backward)
body: The Background Rendering Backward Pass computes the gradients of the loss with respect to the background volumetric field (typically a sparse grid of spherical harmonic coefficients or density values) and the accumulated transmittance, given the rendered background color, ground truth, and ray parameters. It serves as the differentiable counterpart to the concentric sphere sampling and trilinear interpolation used in the forward background rendering pass. Unlike the foreground ray casting which traverses a dense or sparse voxel grid, this method specifically handles the unbounded background field, often using a separate sparse grid structure. It is distinct from the general Ray Tracing Backward Pass by isolating the gradient computation for the background component, allowing for specialized handling of RGB normalization and sparsity regularization specific to the background layer. The method is implemented as a CUDA kernel that processes rays in parallel. It assumes the forward pass has already computed the accumulated transmittance (logtransmit) and the final background color contribution. The backward pass iterates through the same sampling steps as the forward pass to compute local gradients and accumulate them into the background data structure. Inputs: grid: SparseGridSpec containing the background volumetric data (density/sigma and SH coefficients). rgbgt: Ground truth RGB tensor for the current batch. rgbout: Rendered background RGB tensor. rays: RaysSpec containing ray origins, directions, and IDs. opt: RenderOptions including backgroundnlayers, stepsize, and usebackground. logtransmit: Tensor of accumulated log-transmittance values per ray. accum: Tensor of accumulated color contributions per ray. sparsityloss: Boolean flag indicating if sparsity regularization is active. gradoutput: Gradient of the loss with respect to the final output color (RGB). Outputs: grads.gradbackgroundout: Gradient buffer for the background volumetric data. grads.gradlogtransmit: (Optional) Gradient for accumulated transmittance. SparseGridSpec: Contains the layout for the background sparse grid. The exact internal layout (e.g., hash map keys, leaf node sizes) is defined by the parent Background Volume Rendering with Sparse Grid implementation. ConcentricSpheresIntersector: Helper object for intersecting rays with concentric spheres. It stores ray.origin and ray.dir. SingleRaySpec: Temporary structure holding interpolated values (ray.pos, ray.l, invrmid) for the current sampling step. backgroundnlayers: Number of layers in the background grid. Typical value: 32. stepsize: Step size for concentric sphere sampling. Typical value: Not given in the sources. innerradius: Minimum radius for background sampling. Calculated as fmaxf(distraytoorigin(ray.origin, ray.dir) + 1e-3f, 1.f). TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS: Number of CUDA threads per block. Typical value: 256. sparsityloss: Weight for Cauchy sparsity regularization. Passed as an argument. usebackground: Boolean flag to enable/disable the background backward pass. 1. Initialization: If usebackground is false, return. Get rayid for the current thread. Early Exit: If logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0f, the ray is fully transparent or saturated; return early. Initialize totalcolor = 0.0f. Initialize ConcentricSpheresIntersector csi with ray.origin and ray.dir. Calculate innerradius = fmaxf(distraytoorigin(ray.origin, ray.dir) + 1e-3f, 1.0f). Calculate nsteps = int(grid.backgroundnlayers / opt.stepsize) + 2. Initialize invrlast = 1.0f / innerradius. 2. Gradient Output Preparation: Determine gradout based on gradoutisrgb flag: If gradoutisrgb is true: gradout = resid normfactor, where normfactor = 2.0f / (3.0f Q) and Q is the number of rays. Else: gradout = gradoutput. 3. Sampling Loop: Loop i from 0 to nsteps - 1: Calculate radius r = nsteps / (nsteps - i - 0.5). If r < innerradius or !csi.intersect(r, &t), continue to next iteration. Calculate position ray.pos = origin + t dir. Calculate invrmid = rnorm(ray.pos) (inverse norm of position). Normalize position: ray.pos = invrmid. Convert to equirectangular coordinates: unitvec2equirect(ray.pos). Calculate layer index and integer lattice ray.l, clamp to grid bounds, and compute fractional part ray.pos for interpolation. Trilinear Interpolation of Sigma: sigma = trilerpbgone(grid, ray.l, ray.pos). Compute Weight and Transmittance Update: If sigma > 0.0f: pcnt = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) sigma. weight = exp(logtransmit[rayid]) (1.0f - exp(-pcnt)). logtransmit[rayid] -= pcnt. Color Accumulation: For each RGB channel i: Interpolate color: color = trilerpbgone(grid, ray.l, ray.pos) C0 + 0.5f (where C0 is the base color coefficient). totalcolor += fmaxf(color, 0.0f) gradout[i]. Gradient Propagation to Background Data: If color > 0.0f: Compute currgradcolor = C0 weight gradout[i]. Call trilerpbackwardbgone to propagate currgradcolor to grads.gradbackgroundout. 4. Accumulation and Sparsity Gradient: Accumulate Color Gradient: accum[rayid] -= weight totalcolor. Sparsity Loss Gradient (if sparsityloss is true): For each sampled sigma: currgradsigma = sparsityloss (4.0f sigma / (1.0f + 2.0f (sigma sigma))). Call trilerpbackwardbgone with currgradsigma to update grads.gradbackgroundout. Sigma Gradient from Color: Compute currgradsigma = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) (totalcolor exp(logtransmit[rayid]) - accum[rayid]). Call trilerpbackwardbgone with currgradsigma to update grads.gradbackgroundout. 5. Kernel Launch: Calculate blocks: blocks = CUDANBLOCKSNEEDED(Q, TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS). Launch kernel with blocks and TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS. Check for CUDA errors using CUDACHECKERRORS. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbackgroundbackward(grid, rgbgt, rgbout, rays, opt, logtransmit, accum, sparsityloss, gradoutput): """ Computes gradients for the background rendering pass. """ if not opt.usebackground: return Q = rays.numrays threads = 256 # TRACERAYBGCUDATHREADS blocks = (Q + threads - 1) // threads # Initialize gradient buffer grads = GradientBuffer(grid) # Launch CUDA kernel # Note: This is a conceptual representation of the CUDA kernel logic for rayid in range(Q): ray = rays[rayid] # Early exit check if logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0: continue totalcolor = 0.0 innerradius = max(distraytoorigin(ray.origin, ray.dir) + 1e-3, 1.0) nsteps = int(grid.backgroundnlayers / opt.stepsize) + 2 invrlast = 1.0 / innerradius csi = ConcentricSpheresIntersector(ray.origin, ray.dir) # Prepare gradient output if gradoutisrgb: normfactor = 2.0 / (3.0 Q) resid = rgbgt[rayid] - rgbout[rayid] gradout = resid normfactor else: gradout = gradoutput[rayid] for i in range(nsteps): r = nsteps / (nsteps - i - 0.5) if r < innerradius: continue t = csi.intersect(r) if t is None: continue raypos = ray.origin + t ray.dir invrmid = 1.0 / norm(raypos) rayposnormalized = raypos invrmid # Convert to equirectangular coordinates eqcoords = unitvec2equirect(rayposnormalized) # Get grid indices and fractional part lattice, frac = getlatticeandfrac(eqcoords, grid.backgroundreso) # Trilinear interpolation of sigma sigma = trilerpbgone(grid, lattice, frac) if sigma > 0.0: pcnt = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) sigma weight = exp(logtransmit[rayid]) (1.0 - exp(-pcnt)) logtransmit[rayid] -= pcnt # Interpolate color color = trilerpbgone(grid, lattice, frac) C0 + 0.5 # Accumulate color gradient for ch in range(3): totalcolor += max(color[ch], 0.0) gradout[ch] # Backpropagate to background data if color[ch] > 0.0: currgradcolor = C0 weight gradout[ch] trilerpbackwardbgone(grads, lattice, frac, currgradcolor) # Sparsity loss gradient if sparsityloss: currgradsigma = sparsityloss (4.0 sigma / (1.0 + 2.0 sigma sigma)) trilerpbackwardbgone(grads, lattice, frac, currgradsigma) # Sigma gradient from color currgradsigma = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) (totalcolor exp(logtransmit[rayid]) - accum[rayid]) trilerpbackwardbgone(grads, lattice, frac, currgradsigma) invrlast = invrmid return grads Transmittance Saturation: If logtransmit[rayid] < -25.0f, the thread returns early to avoid numerical instability and wasted computation. Precision: The use of float (single precision) is standard in the CUDA implementation. Care must be taken with the exp and log operations to avoid underflow/overflow. Boundary Conditions: The innerradius calculation ensures that rays do not sample inside the origin sphere, preventing division by zero or invalid intersections. CUDA Errors: The kernel launch must be followed by error checking to catch invalid memory accesses or configuration errors. A technique for rendering unbounded or distant background elements using a separate sparse grid structure. It allows for efficient rendering by treating the background as a distinct volumetric field, enabling different resolution and sampling strategies compared to the foreground. Choose this when the scene has large unbounded backgrounds that do not fit efficiently into a dense voxel grid. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays Q and the number of sampling steps n{steps}. The complexity is O(Q \cdot n{steps}). Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays for storing logtransmit and accum gradients, and proportional to the size of the background sparse grid for storing gradients. Performance: The CUDA kernel is optimized for parallel execution, with 256 threads per block. Performance scales with the number of rays and the complexity of the background grid traversal. Strengths: Efficiently handles unbounded backgrounds; separates background and foreground computations for modular optimization; supports sparsity regularization. Limitations: Requires a separate sparse grid structure for the background; performance may degrade if the background grid is very large or has high resolution. When to Use: When rendering scenes with large, unbounded backgrounds (e.g., sky, distant geometry) that are distinct from the foreground scene. When Not to Use: When the background is simple (e.g., a solid color or environment map) and does not require volumetric rendering. The Background Rendering Backward Pass is part of the NeRF-Factory project by Kakaobrain, which includes custom CUDA kernels for sparse voxel volume rendering. It is also implemented in Svox2 by sxyu, which uses spherical harmonics for background rendering. The method builds on the principles of differentiable volume rendering, specifically adapting the backward pass for the concentric sphere sampling technique used for background rendering. The implementation in NeRF-Factory is described in the context of a PyTorch sparse voxel volume extension. kakaobrain/nerf-factory, https://github.com/kakaobrain/nerf-factory, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) sxyu/svox2, https://github.com/sxyu/svox2, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Jittor/JNeRF, https://github.com/Jittor/JNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Background Volume Rendering with Sparse Grid
body: Background Volume Rendering with Sparse Grid is a technique for rendering unbounded or distant background elements (e.g., sky, distant geometry) using a separate sparse grid structure distinct from the foreground scene representation. It allows for efficient rendering of background content by treating it as a separate volumetric field accessed via ray traversal, enabling different resolution and sampling strategies for background versus foreground. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origins and directions, background sparse grid data (grid.backgrounddata), background grid links (grid.backgroundlinks), optional gradient output (gradoutput), and optimization parameters (opt.stopthresh, sparsityloss). Outputs: Rendered RGB color and confidence/confidence map for the background contribution; gradients for background density/color (gradbackgroundout) and mask/visibility (maskbackgroundout) if in backward mode. Data Structures: PackedGridOutputGrads: A structure containing: gradbackgroundout: Gradient for background density/color data. maskbackgroundout: Gradient for background mask/visibility data. Background Grid: Accessed via grid.backgroundlinks and grid.backgrounddata, distinct from foreground grids. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization and Bounds: For each ray, determine the spatial bounds of the intersection with the background grid using rayfindboundsbg. 2. Transmittance Check (Skip Condition): If the logarithmic transmittance logtransmit is less than -25.0, skip the ray entirely to save computation, assuming negligible contribution. \text{if } \log\transmit < -25.0 \text{, return} 3. Forward Pass (renderbackgroundforward): Iterate through ray samples within the background bounds. Accumulation: Accumulate color and transmittance. The color contribution is computed as: total\color += \max(color, 0.0) \times weight Where weight is the transmission factor for the current step. Note: The source snippet mentions gradoutput[i] in the accumulation formula, but clarifies this likely refers to a weight/transmission factor in this specific context or is a variable name reuse; standard volume rendering uses weight color. Transmittance Update: Update logtransmit based on density and step size. Termination: If the transmittance drops below a threshold, terminate the ray: \text{if } \exp(\log\transmit) < opt.stop\thresh \text{, break} Sparsity Regularization (Optional): If sparsityloss > 0.0, add a regularization term to the density gradient currgradsigma. Two variants are mentioned: Cauchy version (from SNeRG): curr\grad\sigma += sparsity\loss \times \frac{4 \times \sigma}{1 + 2 \times (\sigma \times \sigma)} Alphs version (from PlenOctrees): curr\grad\sigma += sparsity\loss \times \exp(-pcnt) \times ray.world\step 4. Gradient Computation (Backward Pass): Sigma Gradient: Compute the gradient for density (currgradsigma) using the chain rule involving accumulated color, transmittance, and step size: curr\grad\sigma = ray.world\step \times (invr\last - invr\mid) \times (total\color \times \exp(\log\transmit) - accum) Where invrlast and invrmid are inverse ray positions, and accum is the accumulated transmittance/color term. Gradient Normalization (if gradoutisrgb): If the gradient output is RGB, normalize the residual: norm\factor = \frac{2.0}{3 \times N{rays}} grad\out[i] = resid \times norm\factor Otherwise, copy gradoutput directly. Propagate Gradients: Update PackedGridOutputGrads using trilerpbackwardbgone. This function updates gradbackgroundout and optionally maskbackgroundout based on currgradsigma (or currgradcolor for color gradients). Parameters: sparsityloss: Scalar weight for sparsity regularization. Typical values are > 0.0 to encourage transparency in background regions. stopthresh: Transmittance threshold for early ray termination. Expressed as a value for logtransmit in the check \exp(\log\transmit) < opt.stop\thresh. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderbackgroundforward(ray, grid, opt): """ Forward pass for background volume rendering. ray: object with.origin,.direction,.worldstep,.findbounds() grid: object with.backgroundlinks,.backgrounddata opt: object with.stopthresh,.sparsityloss """ # 1. Find bounds bounds = ray.findboundsbg(grid) if bounds is None: return 0.0, 0.0 # No intersection # 2. Initialize accumulation totalcolor = 0.0 logtransmit = 0.0 # log(1.0) = 0 accum = 0.0 currgradsigma = 0.0 # 3. Ray march # Note: Simplified marching loop; actual implementation depends on grid traversal for sample in ray.march(bounds): # Sample density and color from background grid sigma, color = grid.samplebackground(sample.position) # Clamp color color = max(color, 0.0) # Compute weight (transmission factor) # weight = exp(-sigma step) currenttransmittance # In log space: logweight = -sigma step + logtransmit step = ray.worldstep logweight = -sigma step + logtransmit weight = math.exp(logweight) # Accumulate color totalcolor += color weight # Update transmittance logtransmit = logweight # Termination check if math.exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh: break # Sparsity regularization (if needed, usually for backward pass) if opt.sparsityloss > 0.0: # Cauchy version currgradsigma += opt.sparsityloss (4.0 sigma / (1.0 + 2.0 (sigma sigma))) # Or Alphs version: # currgradsigma += opt.sparsityloss math.exp(-pcnt) step return totalcolor, math.exp(logtransmit) def renderbackgroundbackward(ray, grid, gradoutput, opt, gradoutisrgb=False): """ Backward pass for background volume rendering. """ # 1. Skip rays with very low transmittance # Assume logtransmit is computed or passed in; if not, compute forward first # For efficiency, this check is often done in the kernel launch or early in forward if ray.logtransmit < -25.0: return PackedGridOutputGrads() # 2. Normalize gradient if RGB if gradoutisrgb: Nrays = len(ray.origins) normfactor = 2.0 / (3.0 Nrays) gradoutput = gradoutput normfactor # 3. Compute gradients # This requires the forward pass values (totalcolor, logtransmit, accum, etc.) # Assuming these are available from the forward pass or recomputed # currgradsigma formula from source: # currgradsigma = ray.worldstep (invrlast - invrmid) (totalcolor exp(logtransmit) - accum) # Note: invrlast and invrmid are inverse ray positions at the last and mid steps # This is a simplified representation; actual implementation needs precise ray state tracking # 4. Propagate gradients to grid grads = PackedGridOutputGrads() trilerpbackwardbgone(grid, ray, currgradsigma, gradoutput, grads) return grads class PackedGridOutputGrads: def init(self): self.gradbackgroundout = None self.maskbackgroundout = None Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Low Transmittance Rays: Rays with logtransmit < -25.0 are skipped. This assumes negligible contribution but may miss subtle background details in very transparent regions. Variable Name Reuse: The source snippet uses gradoutput in the forward accumulation formula, which is likely a misnomer for weight/transmission. Implementers should use standard volume rendering accumulation weight color. Sparsity Regularization: The choice between Cauchy and Alphs versions depends on the specific background representation (SNeRG vs. PlenOctrees). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of ray samples within the background grid bounds. Early termination based on stopthresh reduces average case complexity. Skipping rays with logtransmit < -25.0 further optimizes performance. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the background sparse grid (grid.backgrounddata, grid.backgroundlinks). Separate from foreground grid memory. Strengths: Efficient rendering of unbounded backgrounds; separate resolution/sampling for background vs. foreground; early termination and ray skipping optimize performance. Limitations: Requires separate grid management; sparsity regularization parameters need tuning; low transmittance ray skipping may lose detail. When to Use: When rendering scenes with significant distant or unbounded background elements that benefit from sparse representation. When Not to Use: For tightly bounded scenes where background is negligible or fully contained in the foreground grid. This method is part of the JNeRF project, an unofficial implementation of NeRF using the Jittor framework. It extends standard volume rendering by introducing a separate sparse grid for background elements, allowing for more flexible and efficient handling of large-scale scenes. Jittor/JNeRF, https://github.com/Jittor/JNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Zonal Method (Bhate and Tokuta)
head: Bhate et al. Method, Bhate's method
body: The Zonal Method (Bhate and Tokuta) is a global illumination technique for participating media that extends the classical zonal method to handle interactions between volumes and ideal diffuse surfaces while eliminating the assumption of medium isotropy. It distinguishes itself from standard zonal methods by representing the phase function and radiance using spherical harmonics to approximate Mie scattering, and by computing the resulting form factors using an extended hemicube technique. Inputs: A scene containing v volume elements (voxels) and s ideal diffuse surfaces. Outputs: The radiance distribution within the volumes and reflected radiance from the surfaces. Data Structures: 1. Spherical harmonic coefficient vectors of size M for each volume and surface to store radiance expansions. 2. Form factor matrices F{ik} and F{isj} for volume-volume and volume-surface interactions, computed per spherical harmonic term. Steps: 1. Approximate the scattering phase function by the first M terms of its spherical harmonics expansion to approximate Mie scattering. 2. Compute the form factors between all volume elements and between volumes and surfaces, accounting for the spherical harmonics, using the extended hemicube technique. 3. Set up a system of linear equations consisting of M \times v equations for the v volumes plus s related equations for the s surfaces. 4. Solve the resulting system using a Gauss-Seidel iterative technique. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: M is the number of spherical harmonic terms; only the first few are necessary for a convincing image, but computational cost scales significantly with M. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The direct application of this method is impractical for large scenes due to the prohibitive cost of computing form factors. A hierarchical acceleration technique for the Zonal Method that reduces form factor computation cost by dynamically determining interaction levels and skipping unnecessary refinements. It is chosen for complex scenes where direct computation is prohibitive, distinguishing itself from standard zonal methods by avoiding iterative hierarchy refinement. Time Complexity: The cost to compute form factors in a regular grid of v = n^3 voxels is O(n^7 + M^2 n^6). Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles anisotropic scattering (Mie approximation) and surface-volume interactions, which standard zonal methods cannot. Limitations: Extremely high computational cost for form factor calculation makes it impractical for large-scale scenes without acceleration techniques. When to use: Not given in the sources. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by Bhate and Tokuta as an extension to the classical zonal method. It addresses the limitations of previous zonal method implementations which assumed isotropic media and ignored effects between surfaces and volumes. A survey on participating media rendering techniques, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00371-005-0287-1, fetched 2026-10-26 Global Illumination Techniques for the Simulation of Participating Media, https://inria.hal.science/inria-00510096v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (book)

name: Progressive Refinement Zonal Method
head: Bhate and Tokuta's progressive refinement, Bhate's method, Progressive Refinement Approach (Bhate's method)
body: The Progressive Refinement Zonal Method is a hierarchical acceleration technique for the Zonal Method [12221-zonal-method-bhate-and-tokuta.md] that reduces the computational cost of computing form factors between volumes and surfaces. It establishes a fixed hierarchy during preprocessing and employs a shooting strategy during rendering, avoiding the iterative refinement of the hierarchy itself. Unlike standard zonal methods that compute interactions between all elements, this method determines interaction levels dynamically based on heuristics, skipping unnecessary refinements when transmittance is high or form factors are negligible. Inputs: Scene geometry consisting of volumes (participating media) and surfaces (ideal diffuse emitters/reflectors); optical properties (absorption coefficient, scattering coefficient, phase function); light source definitions. Outputs: Radiosity (radiance) values for all volume elements and surface patches at their respective hierarchy levels. The method relies on a hierarchical tree structure for volumes and surfaces. Hierarchy Node: Represents a volume or surface element. level: Integer indicating the depth in the hierarchy (0 = global, higher = finer). children: List of child nodes (if not a leaf). links: List of links to other nodes (volumes or surfaces) at specific levels. Link: Represents an interaction between two elements. targetnode: The node being linked to. interactionlevel: The hierarchy level at which the interaction is computed. formfactor: Precomputed or estimated form factor between the source and target at the specified level. transmittance: Estimated transmittance between the elements. 1. Preprocessing Step 1: Subdivision Subdivide global volumes and surfaces into a hierarchy. Recursively subdivide until a minimum size or maximum depth is reached. 2. Preprocessing Step 2: Link Creation Create links between volume-volume pairs and surface-volume pairs. Determine the interactionlevel for each pair using heuristics. Volume-Volume Heuristics: Compute a rough estimate of the total form factor. If it is below a specified threshold, the elements can interact at the current level without further refinement. Estimate visibility between the volumes. Compute the optical depth of the intervening medium. Condition: If the transmittance between two elements is too high, no further refinement is needed. Volume-Surface Heuristics: Use a brightness factor heuristic for light sources. For each pair of elements, calculate the bounding volume intersection and approximate form factor. Set the interaction level to the coarsest level satisfying the heuristics. 3. Rendering Phase: Shooting Strategy Iterate through the hierarchy from coarse to fine levels. For each node, shoot energy to its linked targets at their determined interactionlevel. Accumulate radiosity contributions. The sources state there is no Push-Pull procedure. This implies radiosity is computed locally at each level and accumulated, but not corrected across levels during the shooting phase. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. FORMFACTORTHRESHOLD = 0.0 TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD = 1.0 BRIGHTNESSTHRESHOLD = 0.0 class Link: def init(self, source, target, interactionlevel, formfactor, transmittance): self.source = source self.target = target self.interactionlevel = interactionlevel self.formfactor = formfactor self.transmittance = transmittance def buildhierarchy(elements): # Standard spatial subdivision (e.g., octree) until minimum size/depth. return [Element(level=0, children=[], links=[]) for in elements] def getleafnodes(node): # Recursively collect leaf elements. if not node.children: return [node] leaves = [] for child in node.children: leaves.extend(getleafnodes(child)) return leaves def estimateformfactor(a, b): # Standard geometric form factor approximation between bounding volumes. return 0.5 def estimatetransmittance(a, b): # Standard transmittance calculation: exp(-opticaldepth). return 0.95 def islightsource(element): # Check if element has non-zero emission. return hasattr(element, 'emission') and element.emission > 0 def createrefinedlinks(a, b): # Recursively link children at finer levels. links = [] for childa in a.children: for childb in b.children: ff = estimateformfactor(childa, childb) tt = estimatetransmittance(childa, childb) level = childa.level links.append(Link(childa, childb, level, ff, tt)) return links def initializeradiosity(scene): # Allocate zero radiosity for all elements. return {elem: 0.0 for elem in scene.allelements} def computeenergytransfer(source, target, formfactor, transmittance): # Standard radiosity transfer: Esource formfactor transmittance. return source.emission formfactor transmittance def progressiverefinementzonalmethod(scene): volumehierarchy = buildhierarchy(scene.volumes) surfacehierarchy = buildhierarchy(scene.surfaces) links = [] for vola in volumehierarchy: for volb in volumehierarchy: if vola is volb: links.extend(createselflinks(vola)) continue ff = estimateformfactor(vola, volb) tt = estimatetransmittance(vola, volb) if ff < FORMFACTORTHRESHOLD and tt > TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: links.append(Link(vola, volb, vola.level, ff, tt)) else: links.extend(createrefinedlinks(vola, volb)) for vol in volumehierarchy: for surf in surfacehierarchy: if islightsource(surf) and surf.emission < BRIGHTNESSTHRESHOLD: continue ff = estimateformfactor(vol, surf) tt = estimatetransmittance(vol, surf) if ff < FORMFACTORTHRESHOLD and tt > TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: links.append(Link(vol, surf, vol.level, ff, tt)) else: links.extend(createrefinedlinks(vol, surf)) radiosity = initializeradiosity(scene) for link in links: energy = computeenergytransfer(link.source, link.target, link.formfactor, link.transmittance) radiosity[link.target] += energy return radiosity def createselflinks(volume): # Handle self-refinement issue: link each pair of smallest volume elements. links = [] smallestelements = getleafnodes(volume) for i, elema in enumerate(smallestelements): for j, elemb in enumerate(smallestelements): links.append(Link(elema, elemb, elema.level, 1.0, 1.0)) return links FORMFACTORTHRESHOLD: Threshold for rough estimate of form factor. Not given in the sources. TRANSMITTANCETHRESHOLD: Threshold for transmittance. Not given in the sources. BRIGHTNESSTHRESHOLD: Threshold for light source brightness. Not given in the sources. Self-Refinement Issue: Participating media are modeled by a set of global volumes. Each global volume is refined against each other, but not against itself (no self-refinement). Therefore, links must be set between each pair of the smallest volume element considered within a given global volume, otherwise its self-illumination won’t be correctly computed. A self-refinement strategy would be better as it would reduce the number of interactions. Push-Pull Issue: There is no Push-Pull procedure to set correctly the values of the radiosity at all levels of the hierarchies. Such a procedure would be needed after each shooting iteration to obtain a correct solution. This is a significant limitation of the method. Time Complexity: The computation of all form factors in a naive zonal method takes O(n^7) where n is the number of intervening voxels. The progressive refinement method reduces this cost by using hierarchies and heuristics to skip unnecessary interactions. The exact complexity is not given, but it is significantly lower than the naive approach. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces computational cost by avoiding unnecessary refinements; uses heuristics to determine interaction levels efficiently. Limitations: No Push-Pull procedure leads to potentially incorrect radiosity values at different hierarchy levels; lack of self-refinement requires explicit handling of self-illumination. When to use: When computational cost is a concern and the scene has large volumes with low interaction between distant parts. When not to use: When high accuracy is required for self-illumination or when the scene has complex interactions that require fine-grained refinement across all levels. The Progressive Refinement Zonal Method, also known as Bhate's method, is a progressive refinement version of the zonal method. It was proposed by Bhate and Tokuta. The method builds on the Zonal Method [12221-zonal-method-bhate-and-tokuta.md] by introducing hierarchies to reduce computational cost. It is part of the family of deterministic multiple scattering methods for participating media rendering. name: Spherical Harmonics Rendering
head: SH Rendering, SH-based Volume Rendering, SHRenderer
body: Spherical Harmonics (SH) Rendering projects precomputed SH coefficients along viewing directions to estimate RGB radiance, which is then composited with depth weights to produce the final image. It distinguishes itself from standard volume rendering by representing the angular variation of light transport (such as specular highlights and complex shading) as a compact set of coefficients rather than storing explicit RGB values per sample, allowing for view-dependent effects with lower memory overhead than storing full RGB tensors. Inputs and Outputs Input: A tensor of SH coefficients with shape (batch, numsamples, numcoeffs) and a tensor of viewing directions with shape (batch, numsamples, 3). Output: A tensor of RGB values with shape (batch, numsamples, 3). Data Structures The SH coefficients are stored in a flat tensor where the last dimension contains the coefficients. The number of coefficients determines the SH degree. Steps 1. Reshape Coefficients: Reshape the SH coefficient tensor to separate the color channels. If the input shape is (batch, numsamples, numcoeffs), reshape it to (batch, numsamples, 3, numcoeffs // 3). This assumes the coefficients are interleaved by color channel (e.g., R0, G0, B0, R1, G1, B1...). 2. Determine SH Degree: Calculate the SH degree L from the number of coefficients per channel. Let N{coeffs} be the number of coefficients per color channel (N{coeffs} = \text{num\coeffs} / 3). The degree is L = \lfloor \sqrt{N{coeffs}} \rfloor - 1. Note: Some implementations derive levels directly as \lfloor \sqrt{N{coeffs}} \rfloor and use this as the degree parameter for basis evaluation. 3. Compute SH Basis: Evaluate the spherical harmonic basis functions for the given viewing directions. Let D be the directions tensor. Compute C = \text{SH\Basis}(D, L), where C has shape (batch, numsamples, numcoeffsperchannel). 4. Project to RGB: Multiply the reshaped coefficients by the basis components. For each sample, the RGB value is computed as the dot product of the coefficients and the basis functions for each color channel: \text{rgb}{raw} = \sum{i=0}^{N{coeffs}-1} \text{coeffs}{c,i} \times Ci In tensor operations, this is often implemented as rgb = sh components[..., None,:] followed by a sum, or directly summing the product. 5. Apply Activation: Apply an optional activation function (e.g., Sigmoid) to the resulting RGB values to constrain them to a valid range. If no activation is specified, the raw projection is used. 6. Bias and Clamping: Add a bias term (typically 0.5) to the RGB values if required by the specific implementation. If not in training mode, replace any NaN values with 0 and clamp the RGB values to the range [0.0, 1.0]. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def sphericalharmonicsrendering(shcoeffs, directions, activation=None, training=True): """ Render RGB values from SH coefficients and viewing directions. Args: shcoeffs: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, numcoeffs) directions: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, 3) activation: Optional activation function (e.g., torch.sigmoid) training: Boolean flag for training mode Returns: rgb: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, 3) """ # Step 1: Reshape coefficients to separate color channels # Assuming coefficients are interleaved: R0, G0, B0, R1, G1, B1... # Shape: (batch, numsamples, 3, numcoeffs // 3) shchannels = shcoeffs.view(shcoeffs.shape[:-1], 3, shcoeffs.shape[-1] // 3) # Step 2: Determine SH degree # Number of coefficients per channel numcoeffsperchannel = shcoeffs.shape[-1] // 3 # Degree L is derived from the number of coefficients. # For SH degree L, there are (L+1)^2 coefficients per channel. # So L = sqrt(numcoeffsperchannel) - 1 levels = int(math.sqrt(numcoeffsperchannel)) degree = levels - 1 # Step 3: Compute SH basis components for the given directions # components shape: (batch, numsamples, numcoeffsperchannel) # This function evaluates the SH basis functions for the given directions and degree components = componentsfromsphericalharmonics(degree=degree, directions=directions) # Step 4: Project coefficients to RGB # Multiply coefficients by components and sum over the coefficient dimension # shchannels shape: (batch, numsamples, 3, numcoeffsperchannel) # components shape: (batch, numsamples, numcoeffsperchannel) # We need to broadcast components to match the channel dimension # rgb shape: (batch, numsamples, 3) rgb = torch.sum(shchannels components[..., None,:], dim=-1) # Step 5: Apply activation function if specified if activation is not None: rgb = activation(rgb) # Step 6: Add bias and handle NaNs/clamping # Note: The source adds a bias of 0.5 after summing, but this might be specific to their normalization # The source does not mention adding a bias in the core formula, but mentions clamping # We follow the general projection logic. If bias is needed, it is added here. # rgb = rgb + 0.5 # mentions this, but it might be part of a specific normalization scheme if not training: # Replace NaNs with 0 rgb = torch.nantonum(rgb, nan=0.0) # Clamp to [0.0, 1.0] rgb = torch.clamp(rgb, 0.0, 1.0) return rgb def componentsfromsphericalharmonics(degree, directions): """ Compute spherical harmonic basis components for given directions. Args: degree: SH degree L directions: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, 3) Returns: components: Tensor of shape (batch, numsamples, (degree+1)^2) """ # Normalize directions directions = directions / torch.norm(directions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Extract spherical coordinates # theta: polar angle (0 to pi), phi: azimuthal angle (0 to 2pi) # x = sin(theta) cos(phi) # y = sin(theta) sin(phi) # z = cos(theta) # Calculate theta and phi from Cartesian coordinates # theta = acos(z / r) # phi = atan2(y, x) # Avoid division by zero for norm norm = torch.norm(directions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) norm = torch.clamp(norm, min=1e-8) z = directions[..., 2] / norm x = directions[..., 0] / norm y = directions[..., 1] / norm theta = torch.acos(z) phi = torch.atan2(y, x) # Compute SH basis functions # The number of coefficients is (degree + 1)^2 numcoeffs = (degree + 1) 2 components = torch.zeros(directions.shape[:-1], numcoeffs, device=directions.device, dtype=directions.dtype) # Precompute sin(theta) and cos(theta) sintheta = torch.sin(theta) costheta = torch.cos(theta) sinphi = torch.sin(phi) cosphi = torch.cos(phi) # Compute basis functions for each degree l and order m idx = 0 for l in range(degree + 1): for m in range(-l, l + 1): # Compute associated Legendre polynomial Pl^m(cos(theta)) # This is a simplified implementation; a full implementation would use recurrence relations # For brevity, we assume a helper function exists or compute directly for low degrees # Note: This is a placeholder for the actual SH basis computation # In practice, this would involve computing the normalized associated Legendre polynomials # and the trigonometric terms for phi # Example for l=0, m=0: Y0^0 = 1 / sqrt(4pi) if l == 0 and m == 0: components[..., idx] = 1.0 / math.sqrt(4 math.pi) else: # General case: Yl^m(theta, phi) = N Pl^m(cos(theta)) e^(imphi) # N is the normalization constant # Pl^m is the associated Legendre polynomial # e^(imphi) = cos(mphi) + isin(mphi) # For real SH, we use sin and cos combinations # This part requires a full implementation of SH basis functions # For the purpose of this article, we assume this function returns the correct basis values components[..., idx] = computeshbasis(l, m, theta, phi) idx += 1 return components def computeshbasis(l, m, theta, phi): """ Compute a single SH basis function value. This is a placeholder for the actual mathematical computation. """ # This function should implement the real spherical harmonic basis functions # For a complete implementation, refer to standard SH libraries or papers # Here we return 0 as a placeholder return 0.0 Parameters activation: Optional activation function, default is nn.Sigmoid(). degree: The SH degree, determined by the number of coefficients. Edge Cases and Pitfalls NaN Values: In non-training mode, NaN values in the RGB output should be replaced with 0. Clamping: RGB values should be clamped to [0.0, 1.0] in non-training mode. Coefficient Interleaving: The implementation assumes coefficients are interleaved by color channel (R, G, B, R, G, B...). If they are grouped by channel (R, R, R, G, G, G...), the reshaping step must be adjusted. Bug in Source: One source contains a bug where the RGB sum overwrites the channel multiplication result (rgb = torch.sum(sh, dim=-1) + 0.5), discarding the channel-specific projection. This should be corrected by summing the product of coefficients and components for each channel separately. Time and Memory Complexity Memory: The memory footprint is proportional to the number of SH coefficients per sample. For degree L, there are (L+1)^2 coefficients per channel, so 3(L+1)^2 coefficients per sample. This is significantly less than storing full RGB values if the angular variation is smooth and can be well-approximated by low-degree SH. Time: The time complexity is dominated by the evaluation of the SH basis functions and the dot product with the coefficients. For degree L, the basis evaluation is O(L^2) per sample, and the dot product is O(L^2) per sample. This is generally faster than evaluating complex lighting models per sample. Measured Performance Performance data is not provided in the sources. Scaling The method scales linearly with the number of samples and the batch size. Strengths and Limitations Strengths: Compact representation of view-dependent effects; efficient to evaluate; suitable for real-time rendering if precomputed. Limitations: Limited angular resolution for high-frequency details; requires precomputation or training to obtain coefficients; may not capture sharp specularities well with low degrees. When to Use Use when view-dependent effects are important and memory is constrained. Use when the lighting can be well-approximated by low-degree SH. When Not to Use Do not use when high-frequency angular details are required and cannot be captured by low-degree SH. Do not use if precomputation or training is not feasible. Spherical Harmonics Rendering is used in the context of neural radiance fields (NeRF) and implicit surface representations to model view-dependent shading. It was popularized by works such as "NeRF--Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis" and subsequent extensions that incorporate SH for view-dependent effects. The method is implemented in frameworks like Nerfstudio and SDFStudio. nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, https://github.com/nerfstudio-project/nerfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: X-Ray Visualization
head: Average Density Projection, X-Ray Rendering, n-D X-ray projection
body: X-Ray Visualization is a volume rendering technique that projects a dataset into a 2D image by computing the average density along each ray, producing a grey-scale image similar to medical X-rays. Unlike standard ray marching which accumulates color and opacity based on depth ordering, this method treats ordering as irrelevant to simplify the user interface and reveal topological information in high-dimensional or complex data. It discards depth cues and inscattering, focusing solely on the mean density value encountered along the ray path. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset defined by density values \rho(\mathbf{p}) at discrete grid positions; a viewing direction defined by camera origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction vector \mathbf{d}; and rotation parameters for the view axes. Output: A 2D grey-scale image where pixel intensity corresponds to the average density along the corresponding ray. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D array of density values. Ray Parameters: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, and step size \Delta t. Steps: 1. View Transformation: The user defines the viewing orientation by rotating the system of axis vectors in any of the 3 directions (X, Y, Z axes) in degrees within the range [-360, 360]. 2. Ray Casting: For each pixel in the output image, cast a ray through the data set in the desired viewing direction. 3. Density Sampling: March along the ray, sampling the density \rho at each step. 4. Average Density Calculation: Compute the arithmetic mean of the sampled density values along the ray segment contained within the volume. Let N be the number of samples and \rhoi be the density at the i-th sample. The average density \bar{\rho} is: \bar{\rho} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \rhoi 5. Image Formation: Map the calculated \bar{\rho} to a grey-scale intensity value for the corresponding pixel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderxray(volumedata, volumebounds, cameraorigin, cameradirection, imagewidth, imageheight, numsamples): """Renders an X-ray projection of a volume.""" def zeros(shape): return [[0.0 for in range(shape[1])] for in range(shape[0])] def isinsidevolume(pos, bounds): return bounds[0][0] <= pos[0] <= bounds[0][1] and bounds[1][0] <= pos[1] <= bounds[1][1] and bounds[2][0] <= pos[2] <= bounds[2][1] def samplevolume(vol, pos): # Interpolation method (trilinear, etc.) is not specified in the sources ix, iy, iz = int(pos[0]), int(pos[1]), int(pos[2]) return vol[ix][iy][iz] def maptogreyscale(val): return min(255, max(0, int(val))) image = zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) raylength = 10.0 # Not given in the sources stepsize = raylength / numsamples for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Projection matrix mapping not specified in the sources rayo = [cameraorigin[0] + x 0.1, cameraorigin[1] + y 0.1, cameraorigin[2]] rayd = cameradirection densitysum = 0.0 count = 0 for t in range(numsamples): currentpos = [rayo[i] + t stepsize rayd[i] for i in range(3)] if isinsidevolume(currentpos, volumebounds): density = samplevolume(volumedata, currentpos) densitysum += density count += 1 if count > 0: avgdensity = densitysum / count image[y][x] = maptogreyscale(avgdensity) else: image[y][x] = 0 return image Parameters: View Rotation: Rotation angles for X, Y, and Z axes in degrees, typically ranging from -360 to 360. Num Samples: Number of integration steps per ray. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Empty Rays: If a ray does not intersect the volume, the average density is undefined or zero. High-Dimensional Data: The method is designed for n-D volume rendering (n>3) where ordering is irrelevant, but implementation requires projection into 3D or 2D viewing spaces. Time Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot N), where W and H are image dimensions and N is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the volume data, where V is the number of voxels. Strengths: Simplifies user interface by eliminating occlusion exploration; reveals topological information in n-D spaces. Limitations: Lacks depth cues; ordering of structures is irrelevant, which may obscure spatial relationships; limited to density visualization. When to use: When exploring topological features of high-dimensional or complex datasets where depth ordering is less important than average density distribution. When not to use: When realistic lighting, shadows, or depth perception is required. The method was introduced by Bajaj et al. for n-D volume rendering (n>3) to simplify the user interface by treating ordering as irrelevant, thereby eliminating the need for occlusion exploration. It allows users to change viewpoints in n-D space by stretching and rotating axis vectors. The technique is also implemented in educational visualization tools, such as the application described by Thomas Lidy, where it computes average density values along rays and visualizes them as grey-scale images, similar to medical X-rays. name: fBm Noise Generation
head: Water Vapour Emulation (fBm Noise Generation), fBm Noise Generation for Cloud Density, fBm density simulation, fractal Brownian motion noise, uniform noise cube
body: This method simulates the irregular density of water droplets in clouds by generating fractal Brownian motion (fBm) noise from a pre-computed 3D noise cube. It transforms uniform random noise into a Gaussian-like distribution suitable for atmospheric vapour simulation, serving as the density field input for ray-marching algorithms. It differs from procedural noise generation (e.g., Perlin or Simplex noise computed on-the-fly) by relying on a static, pre-calculated texture lookup, which trades memory bandwidth for computational simplicity and deterministic results. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D texture (volume) containing pre-computed uniform random noise values. Input: Camera ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (for spatial sampling coordinates). Input: Number of octaves N, scale factor w, and sampling factor s. Output: A scalar density value \rho(\mathbf{p}) at position \mathbf{p}, derived from the fBm sum. Data Structures Noise Cube: A 3D array of dimensions 64 \times 64 \times 64. Data Type: Single-precision floating-point values (32-bit). Content: Uniform random noise values in the range [0, 1] or [-1, 1] (typically [0,1] for standard texture sampling, mapped appropriately). Storage: Transferred from host CPU to GPU memory. Parameters Number of octaves (N): 5. Increasing beyond 5 does not improve vapour deformation shape and decreases frame performance. Octave scale factor (w): Attenuation factor for amplitude. The source states w < 1 but does not provide the exact numerical value used in the implementation. Noise sampling factor (s): Frequency multiplier for each octave. The source states s > 1 but does not provide the exact numerical value used in the implementation. Note: The source mentions choosing specific values for w and s but the text snippet omits the exact numbers, stating only "where we choose and.". Algorithm Steps 1. Pre-computation (Host CPU): Generate a 64 \times 64 \times 64 grid of single-precision floats. Fill each voxel with a uniform random noise value. Transfer this 3D cube to GPU memory as a texture. 2. Sampling (GPU Fragment Shader): For each pixel, compute the ray position \mathbf{p} along the ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Initialize totalNoise = 0.0 and currentScale = 1.0. Iterate through octaves i from 0 to N-1 (where N=5): Sample the noise cube at position \mathbf{p} \cdot s^i. Retrieve the uniform noise value Ui from the texture. Accumulate the weighted noise: totalNoise += w^i Ui. Update scale for next octave: currentScale = s. The implementation uses an unrolled version of this summation in the fragment shader to improve performance. Formula The fBm noise value at position \mathbf{x} is defined as: fBm(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} w^i \cdot Noise(s^i \cdot \mathbf{x}) Where: N = 5 is the number of octaves. w is the octave scale factor (amplitude decay), with w < 1. s is the noise sampling factor (frequency increase), with s > 1. Noise(\cdot) is the lookup function returning the uniform random value from the pre-computed 3D cube. \mathbf{x} is the 3D spatial coordinate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Single-precision floats are used for the noise cube. Performance: Increasing octaves beyond 5 yields diminishing returns for vapour shape while reducing frame rate. Boundary Conditions: The noise cube is fixed at 64^3. Sampling outside this range requires wrapping or clamping, though the source does not specify the wrapping mode. Determinism: Since the noise is pre-computed, the result is deterministic and identical across frames for the same input coordinates, unlike procedural noise which might vary if not seeded consistently. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatenoisecube(size=64): """ Generates a 3D array of uniform random noise. Returns a flat list or 3D array of single-precision floats. """ import random # Implementation detail: Generate sizesizesize random floats noisecube = [] for x in range(size): for y in range(size): for z in range(size): noisecube.append(random.uniform(0.0, 1.0)) # Assuming [0,1] range return noisecube def samplefbm(position, noisetexture, w, s): """ Samples the pre-computed noise cube using fBm summation. position: vec3, the 3D coordinate to sample. noisetexture: 3D texture object containing the uniform noise cube. w: float, octave scale factor (amplitude). s: float, noise sampling factor (frequency). """ # Unrolled loop for 5 octaves as per source # Octave 0 p0 = position (s 0) n0 = texture3D(noisetexture, p0).r # Assuming red channel or single value # Octave 1 p1 = position (s 1) n1 = texture3D(noisetexture, p1).r # Octave 2 p2 = position (s 2) n2 = texture3D(noisetexture, p2).r # Octave 3 p3 = position (s 3) n3 = texture3D(noisetexture, p3).r # Octave 4 p4 = position (s 4) n4 = texture3D(noisetexture, p4).r # Summation # Note: Exact values for w and s are not provided in source # Assuming w < 1 and s > 1 fbm = (w0 n0) + (w1 n1) + (w2 n2) + (w3 n3) + (w4 n4) return fbm Generates noise on-the-fly using gradient vectors and interpolation. More flexible but computationally heavier than pre-computed cubes. Choose when memory is constrained or dynamic noise evolution is needed. [Link to sibling if available, otherwise note as alternative]. Uses explicit voxel grids rather than noise functions. Better for sharp, structured clouds but requires more memory for high resolution. Choose for non-stochastic, geometric cloud shapes. Time Complexity: O(N) per sample, where N is the number of octaves (fixed at 5). The unrolled implementation ensures constant time overhead per sample. Memory Complexity: O(V), where V is the volume of the noise cube. For 64^3 single-precision floats, this is 64 \times 64 \times 64 \times 4 bytes \approx 1 MB. Measured Performance: The source states that increasing octaves above 5 decreases frame performance. Pre-calculating the noise on the host and transferring it to the GPU achieves higher frames-per-second compared to procedural generation. Strengths: Fast sampling (texture lookup), deterministic results, low computational cost per sample. Limitations: Fixed resolution (64^3) limits detail at high zoom levels; requires memory transfer; less flexible than procedural noise. When to use: Real-time volumetric cloud rendering where performance is critical and static noise patterns are acceptable. When not to use: When dynamic noise evolution or infinite resolution is required. This method was described in the context of efficient algorithms for real-time GPU volumetric cloud rendering. It builds on the concept of fractal Brownian motion (fBm) as a fractal sum of noise functions, referencing Iñigo Quilez’s work on noise generation. The specific implementation uses uniform random noise instead of Perlin noise for the base layer, transforming it into a Gaussian-like distribution via octave accumulation. The technique is applied to simulate water vapour density in clouds, leveraging the stochastic properties of noise to emulate natural textures.
