name: Single-pass WebGPU volume raymarching
head: raymarchScene, volume raymarcher
body: This method renders volumetric data (such as magnetic field magnitude) in a single GPU pass using WebGPU, performing analytic ray-box intersection, early-alpha termination, and optional central-difference Phong shading. It differs from standard sphere tracing Distance-field ray marching by operating on explicit 3D texture volumes rather than implicit Signed Distance Functions (SDFs), allowing for complex, non-uniform density distributions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D texture containing volume data (e.g., density or field magnitude), camera parameters (origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}), and rendering parameters (steps, density scale, shading flags). Output: A 2D color buffer (RGBA) representing the rendered volume. Data Structures: Volume Texture: A 3D texture (e.g., texture3d<f32> in WGSL). The object space is defined as the unit box [-0.5, 0.5]^3. Texture coordinates are computed as \mathbf{pos} + 0.5 to map the box to [0, 1]^3. Transfer Function: Maps sampled density values to color and opacity, supporting linear, logarithmic, or symlog modes. Parameters: steps: Number of samples per ray across the clipped segment. Default: 256. density: Opacity scale factor for the emission-absorption transfer function. shaded: Boolean flag to enable Phong shading. Default: false. EARLYALPHA: Threshold for early ray termination. Default: 0.98. SHADETFLOOR: Minimum accumulated opacity threshold to enable gradient computation for shading. Default: 1/255. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray-Box Intersection: Compute the entry (t0) and exit (t1) distances along the ray for the unit box [-0.5, 0.5]^3. Calculate inverse direction components: inv\diri = 1.0 / di. Pitfall Handling: If any component of \mathbf{d} is near zero (e.g., |di| < 1.0e-8), substitute inv\diri with a large finite slope (1.0e30) to avoid 0 \times \infty = \text{NaN} results from axis-parallel rays. Compute axis-aligned intersections: t{axis\min} = (\mathbf{box\min} - \mathbf{o}) \cdot inv\dir t{axis\max} = (\mathbf{box\max} - \mathbf{o}) \cdot inv\dir Determine entry and exit: t0 = \max(t{axis\min}) t1 = \min(t{axis\max}) If t0 > t1, the ray misses the box. 2. Ray Marching Loop: March along the ray from t0 to t1 in N steps (where N = \text{steps}), with step size \Delta t = (t1 - t0) / N. For each step i: Position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t0 + i \cdot \Delta t) \mathbf{d}. Sampling: Sample the volume texture at normalized coordinates \mathbf{p} + 0.5 to get density D. Transfer Function: Compute opacity \alpha and color C from D using the transfer function scaled by density. Accumulation: Use front-to-back blending: C{out} = C{in} + C \cdot \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{in} = \alpha{in} + \alpha \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) Early Termination: If accumulated opacity exceeds EARLYALPHA (0.98), break the loop. 3. Shading (Optional): If shaded is true and current sample opacity t \ge \text{SHADE\T\FLOOR}, compute the gradient \nabla D at the current sample position using central differences (6 gradient taps per step) to generate a Phong lighting normal. Normalize \nabla D to get the surface normal \mathbf{n}. Apply Phong lighting model using \mathbf{n}, view direction, and light direction. If accumulated opacity < \text{SHADE\T\FLOOR}, skip gradient computation to stay within the 8 ms budget. Pseudocode (Python-like): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EARLYALPHA = 0.98 SHADETFLOOR = 1.0 / 255.0 MAXINVDIR = 1.0e30 EPSILON = 1.0e-8 BOXMIN = [-0.5, -0.5, -0.5] BOXMAX = [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] def samplevolume(texture, texcoords): # Standard 3D texture lookup with clamping to [0, 1] return texture.sample(texcoords) def transferfunction(densityval, densityscale): # Emission-absorption transfer function scaled by density alpha = 1.0 - exp(-densityscale densityval) color = densityval # Simplified linear mapping; actual implementation uses a lookup or function return color, alpha def computegradient(texture, pos): # Central differences: 6 taps (±1 along each axis) eps = 1.0 / texture.resolution dx = samplevolume(texture, pos + [eps, 0, 0]) - samplevolume(texture, pos - [eps, 0, 0]) dy = samplevolume(texture, pos + [0, eps, 0]) - samplevolume(texture, pos - [0, eps, 0]) dz = samplevolume(texture, pos + [0, 0, eps]) - samplevolume(texture, pos - [0, 0, eps]) grad = [dx, dy, dz] length = sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if length > 1e-8: return [g/length for g in grad] return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] def applyphong(color, normal, viewdir, lightdir): # Standard Phong lighting model diff = max(0.0, dot(normal, lightdir)) return color (0.5 + 0.5 diff) def raymarchvolume(rayorigin, raydir, volumetexture, steps, density, shaded): # Ray-Box Intersection invdir = [MAXINVDIR if abs(d) < EPSILON else 1.0/d for d in raydir] tmin = [(BOXMIN[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] tmax = [(BOXMAX[i] - rayorigin[i]) invdir[i] for i in range(3)] t0 = max(tmin) t1 = min(tmax) if t0 > t1: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] dt = (t1 - t0) / steps acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accalpha = 0.0 for i in range(steps): t = t0 + i dt pos = rayorigin + raydir t texpos = [p + 0.5 for p in pos] # Map object space [-0.5, 0.5] to texture space [0, 1] densityval = samplevolume(volumetexture, texpos) color, alpha = transferfunction(densityval, density) weight = alpha (1.0 - accalpha) acccolor = [acccolor[j] + color[j] weight for j in range(3)] accalpha = accalpha + weight if accalpha > EARLYALPHA: break if shaded and accalpha >= SHADETFLOOR: normal = computegradient(volumetexture, texpos) acccolor = applyphong(acccolor, normal, raydir, [0.0, 0.0, -1.0]) return [acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], accalpha] Extends this method by adding temporal filtering and explicit 4D data handling for time-varying volumetric fields like plasma simulations. Time Complexity: O(N) per pixel, where N is the number of steps. With early termination, the average case is often significantly less than N. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for accumulation; O(V) for the volume texture storage, where V is the texture resolution. Performance: Designed to run within an 8 ms budget on modern GPUs. Performance is heavily dependent on the steps parameter and the density of the volume. Strengths: Single-pass execution allows for real-time interaction. Analytic ray-box intersection is efficient. Early-alpha termination optimizes rendering of transparent regions. Limitations: Fixed step size can lead to aliasing in sparse regions or slow convergence in dense regions. Central-difference shading increases texture fetch count by 6x for shaded samples. This method is implemented in the webpic project by Ruslan Saitis, which provides a WebGPU-based visualization tool for scientific data. It is designed to run in the browser, leveraging WebGPU for high-performance parallel computation. name: WebGPU Ray Marching for 4D Volumes
head: Volume4D Viewer Ray Marching, WASM Volume Rendering
body:
A real-time volume rendering technique using WebGPU (WGSL) to ray march through 3D spatial data with a temporal dimension (4D), supporting interpolation between time steps and clipping via axis-aligned bounding boxes. It extends the single-pass WebGPU volume raymarching method by adding temporal filtering and explicit 4D data handling, allowing for the visualization of time-varying volumetric fields such as plasma simulations. Inputs: Volume Textures: Two 3D textures (volume, volumenext) storing scalar field values (e.g., magnetic field magnitude) for consecutive time steps. Format: texture3d<f32>. Color Map: A 2D texture (cmap) storing the transfer function (RGB colors). Camera Uniforms: View, view inverse, projection, and projection inverse matrices. Settings Uniform: AABB bounds, clipping bounds, time parameters, step size, temporal filter mode, distance scale, value range (vmin, vmax), and gamma correction flag. Screen Coordinates: Vertex index used to generate a full-screen quad. Output: Color Buffer: A 3-component float color (vec3<f32>) for each pixel, optionally converted to sRGB. The number of steps is determined by the volume depth divided by stepsize. Memory Complexity: Constant per pixel, plus storage for the two 3D volume textures and the 2D color map texture. Performance: Real-time performance is achieved on WebGPU-compatible hardware. Performance scales with resolution and the number of time steps (though only two textures are loaded at once). Strengths: Supports 4D data (3D space + time) with smooth interpolation. Efficient early-alpha termination. Simple AABB clipping. Limitations: Fixed step size may lead to aliasing or slow convergence in sparse regions. No adaptive stepping. Clipping is axis-aligned. When to use: Real-time visualization of time-varying volumetric data in a browser. When not to use: High-fidelity offline rendering requiring adaptive sampling or complex transfer functions not supported by 1D lookup. This method is part of the volume4d-viewer project by Jonathon Brunson, designed for interactive visualization of space and time volumetric data using WebGPU and Rust. name: Volume Ray Casting with Marching
head: Front-to-Back Ray Casting, Marching along the point of view, Ray Casting with Adaptive Step Size and Early Ray Termination, Volume Rendering via Ray Casting
body: Volume Ray Casting with Marching is an image-order rendering technique that casts rays from the camera through a volumetric scalar field, sampling the field at discrete intervals to accumulate color and opacity using front-to-back compositing. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar data (such as medical CT scans or atmospheric density) by projecting it onto a 2D screen while preserving depth cues and transparency. Unlike SDF Cloud Rendering, which relies on signed distance fields for surface-like rendering, this method integrates density directly, and unlike Atmospheric Ray Marching, which often targets specific post-processing effects like god rays, this method provides a general-purpose integration of the radiative transfer equation for arbitrary volume textures. The method computes the final pixel color by integrating light contribution along a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. The integration proceeds from the camera outward (front-to-back) through the volume bounds. Inputs: Camera parameters: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, view matrix, projection matrix. Volume data: A 3D texture (scalar field) defined by dimensions V{dims} = (Vx, Vy, Vz) and bounds [box{min}, box{max}]. Transfer function: A 2D colormap texture mapping scalar values to RGBA color. Parameters: Step size scale factor dt{scale}, early termination threshold T{thresh} (typically 0.95 opacity). Outputs: Final pixel color C{final} and accumulated opacity A{final}. Volume Texture: 3D texture storing scalar values. For 16-bit data, values are normalized by 65536.0; for 8-bit/float, values are used directly. Colormap Texture: 2D texture where the x-coordinate represents the normalized scalar value and the y-coordinate is fixed (e.g., 0.5) to sample the transfer function. Ray State: t{entry}: Distance to volume entry. t{exit}: Distance to volume exit. p: Current position in world space. C: Accumulated color (RGB). A: Accumulated opacity (A). 1. Calculate Back Plate Position: Determine the position of the back of the volume bounding box relative to the camera to establish the maximum ray extent. 2. Calculate Ray Direction: Normalize the view ray direction vector \mathbf{d}. 3. Calculate Front Plate Position: Determine the position of the front of the volume bounding box. 4. Intersect Ray with Volume Bounds: Compute the entry distance t0 and exit distance t1 where the ray intersects the bounding box defined by box{min} and box{max}. If t0 > t1, discard the ray (the ray does not intersect the volume). Clamp the entry distance to non-negative values: t{entry} = \max(t0, 0.0). 5. Calculate Step Size: Determine the step size \Delta t based on the volume dimensions, ray direction, and a scaling factor dt{scale}. The base step is derived from the voxel traversal rates: \Delta t = dt{scale} \times \min \left( \frac{1}{|dx| \cdot Vx}, \frac{1}{|dy| \cdot Vy}, \frac{1}{|dz| \cdot Vz} \right). Note: In implementation, this is often computed as 1.0 / (vec3(volumedims) abs(raydir)). 6. Generate Jitter Offset: To reduce aliasing artifacts (specifically "wood grain" patterns), generate a random offset for the starting position within the first voxel. The offset is calculated using a hash function (e.g., wanghash) on the fragment coordinates: \text{offset} = \text{wang\hash}(\text{int}(gl\FragCoord.x + 640.0 \cdot gl\FragCoord.y)). 7. Initialize Sample Position: Set the initial sample position p at the entry point plus the jittered offset: p = \mathbf{o} + (t{entry} + \text{offset} \cdot \Delta t) \cdot \mathbf{d}. 8. Marching Loop: Iterate along the ray from t{entry} to t{exit} with step \Delta t. In each iteration: a. Sample Volume Value: Sample the scalar value v from the volume texture at position p. For 16-bit data: v = \text{texture}(\text{volume}, p).r / 65536.0. For 8-bit/float data: v = \text{texture}(\text{volume}, p).r. b. Map to Color: Sample the colormap texture using the normalized value v to get the transfer function output: \text{trans\sample} = \text{texture}(\text{colormap}, \text{vec2}(v, 0.5)). c. Combine Color and Opacity: Construct the sample color C{sample} and opacity A{sample}: C{sample} = \text{trans\sample}.rgb A{sample} = v \cdot \text{trans\sample}.a. d. Apply Opacity Correction: Correct the sample opacity for the step size to approximate the integral of absorption over the segment: A{corrected} = 1 - (1 - A{sample})^{dt{scale}}. e. Front-to-Back Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity into the running totals C and A: C \leftarrow C + (1.0 - A) \cdot A{corrected} \cdot C{sample} A \leftarrow A + (1.0 - A) \cdot A{corrected}. f. Advance Position: Move to the next sample point: p \leftarrow p + \mathbf{d} \cdot \Delta t. g. Early Ray Termination (ERT): If the accumulated opacity A \ge 0.95, break the loop. 9. Update Controller and View Matrix: After the marching pass, update the controller and view matrix based on the previous state, applying rescaling if necessary. 10. Draw Frame and Generate Color Maps: Render the frame around the volume and generate any necessary color maps for the current frame. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumeraycasting(cameraorigin, cameradirection, volumetexture, colormaptexture, volumedims, dtscale, tthresh): """ Renders a single pixel using volume ray casting with marching. Args: cameraorigin: vec3, camera position. cameradirection: vec3, normalized ray direction. volumetexture: 3D texture object. colormaptexture: 2D texture object. volumedims: vec3, dimensions of the volume (Vx, Vy, Vz). dtscale: float, step size multiplier. tthresh: float, opacity threshold for early termination. Returns: vec4, final color with accumulated opacity. """ # 1. Intersect ray with bounding box [boxmin, boxmax] # Note: boxmin and boxmax are assumed to be available in the shader context t0, t1 = intersectbox(cameraorigin, cameradirection, boxmin, boxmax) # If no intersection, return transparent black if t0 > t1: return vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Clamp entry to non-negative tentry = max(t0, 0.0) texit = t1 # 2. Calculate step size # dtvec = 1.0 / (volumedims abs(cameradirection)) # dt = dtscale min(dtvec) dtvec = vec3(1.0) / (volumedims abs(cameradirection)) dt = dtscale min(dtvec.x, dtvec.y, dtvec.z) # 3. Generate jitter offset # Assuming glFragCoord is available in the shader context fragcoord = getfragcoord() # vec2 offset = wanghash(int(fragcoord.x + 640.0 fragcoord.y)) # 4. Initialize position p = cameraorigin + (tentry + offset dt) cameradirection # 5. Initialize accumulators acccolor = vec3(0.0) accalpha = 0.0 # 6. Marching loop t = tentry + offset dt while t < texit: # Sample volume value valraw = texture(volumetexture, p).r # Normalize if 16-bit, else use directly val = valraw / 65536.0 if is16bit else valraw # Map to color via colormap transsample = texture(colormaptexture, vec2(val, 0.5)) # Combine color and opacity samplecolor = transsample.rgb samplealpha = val transsample.a # Apply opacity correction for step size correctedalpha = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - samplealpha, dtscale) # Front-to-back compositing # Cnew = Cold + (1 - Aold) Asample Csample # Anew = Aold + (1 - Aold) Asample acccolor += (1.0 - accalpha) correctedalpha samplecolor accalpha += (1.0 - accalpha) correctedalpha # Early Ray Termination if accalpha >= tthresh: break # Advance t += dt p = cameraorigin + t cameradirection return vec4(acccolor, accalpha) dtscale: A uniform float parameter controlling the step size multiplier. It scales the base voxel traversal step. Typical value not specified in sources. tthresh: Early termination threshold. Default value is 0.95 opacity. Aliasing: Not jittering the starting position causes "wood grain" aliasing artifacts. However, jittering can cause artifacts on flat surfaces ("with offset is bad for flat surfaces"). Double Launch: Calculating the front and back plate positions separately may require launching the process twice. It is recommended to calculate the front plate and start marching in the same shader pass to avoid redundant computation. Precision: Ensure correct normalization of volume texture data (e.g., dividing by 65536.0 for 16-bit data) to prevent incorrect density interpretation. This method uses a dedicated child camera (the "Occlusion Camera") to render a depth map from the light's perspective, allowing scene geometry to block volumetric light beams. Unlike standard URP shadows which depend on the light's Shadow Type and global URP shadow settings, this occlusion map operates independently, enabling volumetric shadows even when the light casts no regular geometric shadows. Basic Volumetric Cone Lighting is a post-processing technique that renders a volumetric light beam shaped like a cone originating from a light position and pointing in a specific direction, using screen-space raymarching. It solves the problem of rendering visible light shafts (god rays) in real-time by accumulating light density along rays cast from the camera into the scene. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Shadow Occlusion via Occlusion Camera by its reliance on a single depth buffer for culling rather than a secondary camera pass, and from Volume Ray Casting with Marching by its specific application to spotlight-shaped volumetric effects rather than general volume density integration. A technique to convert a neural radiance field model into efficient GLSL or HLSL shader code, enabling real-time volumetric raycasting that blends with existing engine subsystems. It transpiles the optimized model architecture (grid features + MLPs) into pixel shader code, executes volumetric raycasting in the pixel shader by aggregating sample points to compute the final color, and blends the rendered neural asset result with the background consisting of other mesh- or volume-based objects. Enhanced raymarching for volumetric media that supports configurable dual-lobe anisotropic scattering, soft screen-space penumbrae, and spatial step jitter. It packs shadow steps and anisotropy values into a single uniform slot for compatibility, applies spatial step jitter during raymarching to reduce aliasing and banding artifacts, modulates density based on height for natural atmospheric effects, generates coherent wisps and axis-weighted dust patterns for visual detail, and calculates soft screen-space penumbrae for shadows cast by volumetric objects. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples along the ray, which depends on the volume depth and step size. The step size is inversely proportional to the ray direction components and volume dimensions. Memory Complexity: Depends on the size of the 3D volume texture and the 2D colormap texture. No additional large buffers are required beyond standard render targets. Performance: The method is computationally intensive due to the large number of texture samples required for smooth rendering. Early Ray Termination (ERT) significantly reduces the average number of samples per ray, especially for opaque regions. Strengths: Provides high-quality, physically-based volume rendering with accurate transparency and depth cues. It is flexible and works with any scalar field data. Limitations: Susceptible to aliasing artifacts ("wood grain") if not jittered, and jittering can introduce artifacts on flat surfaces. Performance degrades with large volumes or high resolution. When to Use: Suitable for general-purpose volume visualization where quality is prioritized over extreme performance, or when ERT can effectively cull opaque regions. When Not to Use: Not suitable for real-time applications with very large volumes or strict performance constraints without optimization (e.g., hierarchical level-of-detail). The technique is a fundamental method in volume rendering, rooted in the discretization of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) along rays. It is widely used in medical imaging, scientific visualization, and computer graphics for rendering 3D scalar data. The specific implementation details, such as jittering and early termination, are common optimizations to improve visual quality and performance. The method is often implemented in fragment shaders for GPU acceleration. name: Shadow Occlusion via Occlusion Camera
head: Light-space shadow maps, Volumetric shadow maps
body: This method uses a dedicated child camera (the "Occlusion Camera") to render a depth map from the light's perspective, allowing scene geometry to block volumetric light beams. Unlike standard URP shadows which depend on the light's Shadow Type and global URP shadow settings, this occlusion map operates independently, enabling volumetric shadows even when the light casts no regular geometric shadows. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Scene geometry (filtered by Culling Mask), light parameters (type, position, orientation), and the Occlusion Camera configuration. Outputs: A depth texture (Occlusion Map) and the final volumetric lighting contribution where shadow density is applied. Data Structures Occlusion Map: A depth texture generated by the Occlusion Camera. Resolution is configurable (32 to 4096, default 256). Shadow Coordinates: Computed at the ray's entry and exit points from the volume, then interpolated along the ray. Steps 1. Render Occlusion Map: The system adds a lightweight depth-only renderer to the URP Asset's renderer list if not already present. The Occlusion Camera renders a depth-only pass of the scene, respecting the Culling Mask and Near Clip Distance. For Spot Lights: The capture projection uses a perspective frustum matching the spot angle. For Rect/Disc Area Lights: The capture projection is orthographic. For Point Lights: A specific Bake Mode is required: Half Sphere: Captures a 160-degree view in one render, oriented either toward the camera or a fixed direction. Cubemap One Face Per Frame: Captures one face of a cubemap per frame. Cubemap All 6 Faces Per Frame: Captures all six faces per frame (slowest). 2. Compute Shadow Coordinates: In the ray marching shader, shadow coordinates are calculated at the ray's entry point into the volume and at its exit point. 3. Interpolate: Shadow coordinates are interpolated between the entry and exit points along the ray for each marching step. 4. Sample Occlusion: The shader samples the Occlusion Map texture at the interpolated coordinates to determine shadow density. 5. Apply Shadow: The volumetric beam intensity is blended toward the configured Shadow Color (Intensity and Color parameter) based on the sampled density, rather than blending to pure black. Parameters Resolution: 32 to 4096. Default 256. Higher values are needed for fine patterns like window bars, grilles, or foliage. Intensity and Color: Defines the color the shadowed part of the beam blends toward. Culling Mask: Layers that occlude the beam. The TransparentFX layer is excluded by default. Include Transparent: If enabled, transparent geometry and 2D sprites block light, provided their material writes depth via a DepthOnly pass. Near Clip Distance: The near plane of the Occlusion Camera. Used when the light is inside a model (e.g., a lamp). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Point Light Performance: Cubemap modes are significantly slower than Half Sphere. All 6 Faces Per Frame is the slowest option. Thin Occluders: Raymarch Quality controls sampling fineness; thin occluders may appear blurry on lower presets. Transparent Geometry: Transparent objects only occlude if they explicitly write depth. Performance: The cost depends on the Occlusion Camera's resolution and the Point Light Bake Mode. Half Sphere is the fastest; Cubemap All 6 Faces Per Frame is the slowest. Memory: Requires additional VRAM for the depth texture, sized by the chosen resolution. Strengths: Independent of standard shadow settings; allows volumetric shadows on lights that do not cast geometric shadows. Limitations: Requires a depth-writing pass from transparent objects for full occlusion; point lights have high performance costs for full coverage. This technique is implemented in Unity's Universal Render Pipeline (URP) via third-party volumetric lighting assets (e.g., Kronnect). It addresses the visual artifact where volumetric beams pass through walls and props, creating "glowing cone mesh" appearances without occlusion. name: Basic Volumetric Cone Lighting
head: First light ray, Volumetric raymarching loop, Depth-Based Stopping, Scene depth culling
body: Basic Volumetric Cone Lighting is a post-processing technique that renders a volumetric light beam shaped like a cone originating from a light position and pointing in a specific direction, using screen-space raymarching. It solves the problem of rendering visible light shafts (god rays) in real-time by accumulating light density along rays cast from the camera into the scene. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Shadow Occlusion via Occlusion Camera by its reliance on a single depth buffer for culling rather than a secondary camera pass, and from Volume Ray Casting with Marching by its specific application to spotlight-shaped volumetric effects rather than general volume density integration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: inputColor (current frame buffer color), uv (screen coordinates), depthBuffer (scene depth texture), cameraPosition (world space), cameraFar (max render distance), lightPosition (world space), lightDirection (normalized world space vector), coneAngle (aperture in degrees), STEPSIZE (march increment), NUMSTEPS (loop count). Outputs: outputColor (final pixel color). Data Structures: depthBuffer: Texture containing depth values for each pixel. projectionMatrixInverse: Inverse of the camera's projection matrix (used for coordinate reconstruction). viewMatrixInverse: Inverse of the camera's view matrix (world matrix), used for coordinate reconstruction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mainImage(inputColor, uv, depthBuffer, cameraFar, projectionMatrixInverse, viewMatrixInverse, cameraPosition, lightPosition, lightDirection, coneAngle, STEPSIZE, NUMSTEPS): # 1. Sample depth and reconstruct world position depth = readDepth(depthBuffer, uv) worldPosition = getWorldPosition(uv, depth, projectionMatrixInverse, viewMatrixInverse) # 2. Define ray parameters rayOrigin = cameraPosition rayDir = normalize(worldPosition - rayOrigin) lightPos = lightPosition lightDir = normalize(lightDirection) # 3. Calculate scene depth for culling sceneDepth = length(worldPosition - cameraPosition) # 4. Initialize lighting variables coneAngleRad = radians(coneAngle) halfConeAngleRad = coneAngleRad 0.5 fogAmount = 0.0 lightIntensity = 1.0 t = STEPSIZE # 5. Raymarching loop for i from 0 to NUMSTEPS - 1: # Calculate current sample position samplePos = rayOrigin + rayDir t # Depth-based stopping: break if beyond scene geometry or camera far plane if t > sceneDepth or t > cameraFar: break # Cone shape check: calculate angle between sample-to-light vector and light direction toSample = normalize(samplePos - lightPos) cosAngle = dot(toSample, lightDir) # Skip samples outside the cone aperture if cosAngle < cos(halfConeAngleRad): t += STEPSIZE continue # Attenuation based on distance to light source distanceToLight = length(samplePos - lightPos) attenuation = exp(-0.05 distanceToLight) # Accumulate light fogAmount += attenuation lightIntensity # Advance ray t += STEPSIZE # 6. Combine with input color outputColor = inputColor + fogAmount Helper Function (Coordinate Reconstruction): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getWorldPosition(uv, depth, projectionMatrixInverse, viewMatrixInverse): # Convert UV to clip space (-1 to 1) clipSpace = vec2(uv.x 2.0 - 1.0, uv.y 2.0 - 1.0) clipSpace.y = -clipSpace.y # Adjust for different coordinate systems if necessary # Convert clip space to view space (inverse projection) viewSpace = vec4(clipSpace, -1.0, 1.0) # w=1 for projection inverse viewSpace = projectionMatrixInverse viewSpace viewSpace = vec4(viewSpace.xyz / viewSpace.w, viewSpace.w) # Convert view space to world space (inverse view) worldSpace = viewMatrixInverse vec4(viewSpace.xyz, 1.0) return worldSpace.xyz Parameters: cameraFar: Depth limit beyond which nothing is visible or rendered. Typical values depend on scene scale (e.g., 500 units). coneAngle: Spotlight aperture width in degrees. Typical values range from 10 to 60 degrees. STEPSIZE: Step size for raymarching. Not explicitly given in sources; must be tuned for performance/quality trade-off. NUMSTEPS: Number of steps in the raymarching loop. Not explicitly given in sources; depends on STEPSIZE and cameraFar. 0.05: Exponential decay constant for light attenuation. This value is hardcoded in the source example. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Through-wall leakage: Without depth-based stopping, the light ray continues marching beyond visible geometry, causing light to appear through walls and objects, breaking realism and wasting performance. Precision: Reconstruction of world position from depth buffer requires accurate inverse matrices. Incorrect matrix usage leads to misaligned light rays. Cone Angle Calculation: The cosine check cosAngle < cos(halfConeAngleRad) assumes the light direction points away from the source in the direction of the beam. If lightDirection is defined differently, the dot product logic may need inversion. Time Complexity: O(NUM\STEPS) per pixel. The loop runs a fixed number of steps, potentially breaking early due to depth culling. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, plus the depth buffer texture. Performance: The method is relatively lightweight compared to full volumetric integration but can be expensive if NUMSTEPS is high or if depth culling is ineffective (e.g., in open scenes). The exponential attenuation calculation (exp) is computationally moderate. Strengths: Simple to implement in post-processing; provides convincing volumetric light shafts; depth culling prevents visual artifacts through geometry. Limitations: Only works for post-processing (cannot affect objects behind the camera or in front of the near plane easily); relies on a single light source direction/position per effect instance; no scattering or multiple bounces; quality depends heavily on STEPSIZE and NUMSTEPS. When to use: Real-time rendering of god rays or spotlight beams in post-processing. When not to use: When physically accurate volumetric scattering is required, or when lights need to interact with complex volumetric media (fog, smoke) defined in world space rather than screen space. The technique was popularized in the context of real-time web graphics and post-processing frameworks like Three.js. It is described in "On Shaping Light: Real-Time Volumetric Lighting with Post-Processing and Raymarching" by Maxime Heckel, which details the implementation of volumetric lighting effects using raymarching in fragment shaders. The method builds on the principles of screen-space raymarching and depth buffer reconstruction. name: WebGL2 Volume Raycasting
head: VolRen, Volume Raycasting Fragment Shader (Colormap/Segmentation/Scalar), Web-based volumetric data explorer
body: WebGL2 Volume Raycasting is a lightweight, web-based volumetric data explorer that renders 3D scalar fields using WebGL2 raymarching within a fragment shader. It supports 8-bit, 16-bit, and float data types, with optional segmentation masks and clipping planes. Unlike general-purpose SDF-based sphere tracing which targets implicit surfaces, this method performs front-to-back alpha blending over a discrete 3D texture grid to visualize scalar fields. It is distinguished by its specific WebGL2 implementation details, including handling of integer texture formats for 16-bit data and a fixed 180x1 colormap texture. The method operates by casting rays from a camera through a 3D volume texture, sampling scalar values, and compositing them into a 2D image using alpha blending. Inputs: Volume Texture: A 3D texture (gl.TEXTURE0) containing the scalar field. Dimensions are volDims[0], volDims[1], volDims[2]. 8-bit: Format R8, Type UNSIGNEDBYTE, Filter LINEAR. 16-bit: Format R16UI, Type UNSIGNEDSHORT, Filter NEAREST. Float: Format R32F, Type FLOAT, Filter LINEAR. Colormap Texture: A 2D texture (gl.TEXTURE1) of size 180x1 pixels, format RGBA8. Segmentation Texture (Optional): A 3D texture (gl.TEXTURE2) of dimensions volDims, format R8, Type UNSIGNEDBYTE, Filter NEAREST, Wrapping CLAMPTOEDGE. Uniforms: highp usampler3D volume: The volume texture sampler. highp sampler2D colormap: The colormap texture sampler. bool usecolormap: Enables colormap mode. bool useseg: Enables segmentation mode. vec3 volumescale: Scaling factor for the volume. vec3 volumedims: Dimensions of the volume. float dtscale: Step size scaling factor (Default: 1.0). ivec2 comp: Comparison coordinates for inversion logic. vec3 colors[25]: Array of colors for segmentation IDs (Note: Source code implies this is a global constant or defined elsewhere, as it is not declared as a uniform in the provided snippet). Vertex Shader Inputs: pos: Vertex position. eyepos: Camera eye position in world space. Outputs: out vec4 color: The final fragment color. The volume is stored as a 3D texture. The specific internal format depends on the bit depth of the source data. The colormap is a 1D lookup table represented as a 180x1 2D texture. 1. Vertex Shader Transformation: Compute volume translation: volumetranslation = vec3(0.5) - volumescale 0.5. Transform vertex position: glPosition = projview vec4(pos volumescale + volumetranslation, 1.0). Compute transformed eye position: transformedeye = (eyepos - volumetranslation) / volumescale. Compute ray direction in object space: vraydir = pos - transformedeye. 2. Fragment Shader Initialization: Normalize ray direction: raydir = normalize(vraydir). Intersect ray with the volume bounding box defined by boxmin and boxmax using the slab method to obtain entry and exit distances thit.x (t0) and thit.y (t1). If thit.x > thit.y, discard the fragment (ray misses the volume). Clamp start distance: thit.x = max(thit.x, 0.0). 3. Step Size Calculation: Compute step vector components: dtvec = 1.0 / (vec3(volumedims) abs(raydir)). Compute step size: dt = dtscale min(dtvec.x, min(dtvec.y, dtvec.z)). 4. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize accumulated color: color = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0). Initialize current position: p = eyeposinvolumespace + thit.x raydir. Loop t from thit.x to thit.y with step dt: Sample Volume: Sample the volume texture at p: valraw = texture(volume, p).r. Normalization: If data type is 8-bit or float: val = valraw (already float or normalized). If data type is 16-bit: val = float(valraw) / 65536.0. If p is outside [0.0, 1.0] in any dimension, set val = 0.0. Color/Alpha Computation: Determine valcolor based on mode: Colormap Mode (usecolormap == true): transsample = texture(colormap, vec2(val, 0.5)). valcolor.rgb = transsample.rgb. valcolor.a = val transsample.a. Segmentation Mode (useseg == true): Convert segmentation value to integer: seg = int(texture(segvolume, p).r). Loop k from 0 to min(seg, 24): If k == seg, valcolor = vec4(colors[k].rgb, 1.0). If seg is out of bounds, default to transparent or black. Scalar Mode (Default): valcolor.rgb = vec3(1.0) (White). valcolor.a = val. Inversion Logic: Check inversion condition: invert = (comp.x == int(glFragCoord.x)) || (comp.y == int(glFragCoord.y)). If invert is true: Colormap Mode: valcolor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Segmentation Mode: valcolor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Scalar Mode: valcolor.a = 1.0 - val. Opacity Correction: Apply Beer-Lambert law approximation for step size: valcolor.a = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - valcolor.a, dtscale). Alpha Blending: color.rgb += (1.0 - color.a) valcolor.a valcolor.rgb. color.a += (1.0 - color.a) valcolor.a. Early Termination: If color.a >= 0.95, break loop. Advance Ray: p += raydir dt. 5. Final Output: Set glFragColor = color. Unverified code. void main() { vec3 volumetranslation = vec3(0.5) - volumescale 0.5; glPosition = projview vec4(pos volumescale + volumetranslation, 1.0); // Pass transformed eye and ray dir to fragment shader vec3 transformedeye = (eyepos - volumetranslation) / volumescale; vec3 vraydir = pos - transformedeye; glFragColor = vec4(0.0); // Placeholder, actual color computed in FS // Note: In WebGL, varyings are used. // out vec3 vraydir; // out vec3 vtransformedeye; // vraydir = vraydir; // vtransformedeye = transformedeye; } uniform highp usampler3D volume; uniform highp sampler2D colormap; uniform bool usecolormap; uniform bool useseg; uniform vec3 volumedims; uniform float dtscale; uniform ivec2 comp; uniform vec3 colors[25]; // Assumed global or uniform in vec3 vraydir; in vec3 vtransformedeye; out vec4 color; void main() { vec3 raydir = normalize(vraydir); // Slab intersection with box [0,1]^3 (assuming normalized coords) // Simplified slab method for unit cube vec3 t0 = (vec3(0.0) - vtransformedeye) / raydir; vec3 t1 = (vec3(1.0) - vtransformedeye) / raydir; vec3 tmin = min(t0, t1); vec3 tmax = max(t0, t1); float thitx = max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y), tmin.z); float thity = min(min(tmax.x, tmax.y), tmax.z); if (thitx > thity) { discard; } thitx = max(thitx, 0.0); vec3 dtvec = 1.0 / (volumedims abs(raydir)); float dt = dtscale min(dtvec.x, min(dtvec.y, dtvec.z)); vec3 p = vtransformedeye + thitx raydir; vec4 acccolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0); // Inversion check bool invert = (comp.x == int(glFragCoord.x)) || (comp.y == int(glFragCoord.y)); for (float t = thitx; t < thity; t += dt) { // Sample volume float valraw = texture(volume, p).r; float val; // Normalization based on texture type (handled by sampler type in GLSL) // For R16UI, valraw is uint, needs conversion // For R8/Float, valraw is float in [0,1] or normalized // Assuming GLSL handles basic type conversion, but explicit division for 16-bit: // Note: In actual GLSL, usampler3D returns uint. // val = float(valraw) / 65536.0; // Only if 16-bit // Boundary check if (p.x < 0.0 || p.x > 1.0 || p.y < 0.0 || p.y > 1.0 || p.z < 0.0 || p.z > 1.0) { val = 0.0; } else { val = valraw; // Simplified, actual normalization depends on texType } vec4 valcolor; if (usecolormap) { vec4 transsample = texture(colormap, vec2(val, 0.5)); valcolor.rgb = transsample.rgb; valcolor.a = val transsample.a; } else if (useseg) { // Segmentation logic // int seg = int(texture(segvolume, p).r); // segvolume not passed in uniform list // Loop k from 0 to min(seg, 24) // if (k == seg) valcolor = vec4(colors[k], 1.0); // Placeholder for missing segvolume uniform valcolor = vec4(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0); } else { valcolor.rgb = vec3(1.0); valcolor.a = val; } if (invert) { if (usecolormap || useseg) { valcolor = vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0); } else { valcolor.a = 1.0 - val; } } // Opacity correction valcolor.a = 1.0 - pow(1.0 - valcolor.a, dtscale); // Alpha blending acccolor.rgb += (1.0 - acccolor.a) valcolor.a valcolor.rgb; acccolor.a += (1.0 - acccolor.a) valcolor.a; if (acccolor.a >= 0.95) { break; } p += raydir dt; } color = acccolor; } dtscale: Controls step size scaling. Default is 1.0. Lower values increase sampling density and quality but reduce performance. targetFrameTime: JavaScript variable set to 32 ms to manage frame rate. Non-uniform Volumes: The vertex shader transformation assumes a specific centering logic. Non-uniform size volumes may require different transformation to center properly, as noted in the source's TODO comment. Offset Initialization: The initialization of the ray start position affects visual quality. "With offset is bad for flat surfaces, without has wood grain". Missing Uniforms: The colors array used in segmentation mode is not declared as a uniform in the provided shader code, implying it is a global constant or defined elsewhere. The segmentation texture sampler is also not explicitly passed as a uniform in the provided list, though logic exists. Filtering: LINEAR filtering is used for 8-bit and float volumes, while NEAREST filtering is used for 16-bit volumes, likely due to integer texture limitations. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps along the ray. The number of steps is determined by the volume dimensions, ray direction, and dtscale. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D volume texture and the 2D colormap texture. Performance: Performance is heavily dependent on the volume resolution and the dtscale parameter. WebGL2 allows for efficient texture sampling, but fragment shader execution time can be high for large volumes or small step sizes. Strengths: Lightweight, web-based, supports multiple data types (8-bit, 16-bit, float), supports segmentation masks. Limitations: Limited to scalar field visualization, no advanced lighting models (default is white scalar), potential precision issues with 16-bit integer textures, missing uniform declarations in source code. The method is implemented in "VolRen: A lightweight web-based volumetric data explorer" by johanna-b. It is designed to be a simple, accessible tool for visualizing 3D scalar fields in a web browser using WebGL2. johanna-b/VisWeb, https://github.com/johanna-b/VisWeb, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with Single Scattering
head: Real-time Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Real-time Volumetric Rendering, Volumetric Cloud Rendering, Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Ray Marching
body: Ray marching with single scattering is a real-time technique for rendering volumetric clouds by discretizing the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) along view rays and approximating light transport with a single scattering event. It combines procedural noise for density generation with a physically-based lighting model to produce dynamic, three-dimensional cloudscapes. It is distinguished from multi-scattering methods by its computational efficiency, trading physical accuracy for performance, and from billboard-based methods by its ability to render volumetric depth and internal structure. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{o}, normalized view direction \mathbf{d}, sun direction \mathbf{d}{\text{sun}}, sun color \mathbf{C}{\text{sun}}, ambient color \mathbf{C}{\text{amb}}, cloud bounding box (AABB), cloud layer height limits (h{\min}, h{\max}), and procedural noise textures (Weather Map, Base Noise, Edge Detail). Outputs: Final pixel color C{\text{final}}. Data Structures: 1. Weather Map (2D Texture): Format: RGBA, Float32. Red Channel: Base cloud coverage (0.0 to 1.0). Blue Channel: Cloud type (0.0=stratus, 0.5=stratocumulus, 1.0=cumulus). 2. Base Noise Texture (3D Texture, 128 \times 128 \times 128): Red Channel: Combined Perlin-Worley noise. Green, Blue, Alpha Channels: Low-frequency inverse Worley noise at increasing frequencies. 3. Edge Detail Texture (3D Texture, 32 \times 32 \times 32): Channels: High-frequency inverse Worley noise at increasing frequencies. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Compute ray direction \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{s} - \mathbf{o}), where \mathbf{s} is the screen position and \mathbf{o} is the eye position. Compute sky color using \mathbf{d}. Initialize main transmittance T = 1.0, accumulated color C = 0, and distance t = 0.0. Set scene variables (scattering/absorption coefficients) based on time of day. 2. Main Ray Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to MAXSTEPS. Calculate position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d}. Bounding Check: If \mathbf{p} is outside the cloud bounding box or cloud layer height limits, skip or break. Density Evaluation: Sample base noise \rho{\text{base}} from the 3D texture at \mathbf{p}. Sample edge detail \rho{\text{edge}} from the 32x32x32 texture at \mathbf{p}. Combine noise: Use fBm of low-frequency inverse Worley channels to modulate the Perlin-Worley noise. Apply height modulation: Modulate density with a linear gradient from h{\min} to h{\max}. Apply weather map: Scale density by coverage from the Weather Map Red channel. Final density \rho = \text{clamp}(\text{combined noise}, 0.0, 1.0). Optimization: If \rho < 0.01, increment t by STEPSIZE and continue. Light Marching (Single Scattering): Initialize light transmittance T{\text{light}} = 1.0, light distance t{\text{light}} = 0.0. Compute light direction \mathbf{d}{\text{light}} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{d}{\text{sun}} - \mathbf{p}). Iterate j from 0 to MAXSTEPSLIGHT. Calculate light position \mathbf{p}{\text{light}} = \mathbf{p} + t{\text{light}} \mathbf{d}{\text{light}}. Sample density \rho{\text{light}} at \mathbf{p}{\text{light}}. Update light transmittance: T{\text{light}} \leftarrow T{\text{light}} \cdot e^{-\rho{\text{light}} \cdot \text{extinctionCoeff} \cdot \text{STEP\SIZE\LIGHT} \cdot 1.5}. If T{\text{light}} < 0.05, break light loop. Increment t{\text{light}} by STEPSIZELIGHT. Scattering Calculation: Compute phase function value fp using \mathbf{d} and \mathbf{d}{\text{light}}. Compute Ls = \mathbf{C}{\text{sun}} \cdot T{\text{light}} \cdot fp \cdot 6.0. Compute La = \mathbf{C}{\text{amb}} \cdot 0.7. Compute local scattering contribution: S = (Ls + La) \cdot T \cdot \rho \cdot \text{STEP\SIZE}. Accumulation: C \leftarrow C + S. Update main transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot e^{-\rho \cdot \text{extinctionCoeff} \cdot \text{STEP\SIZE} \cdot 1.5}. If T < 0.01, break main loop. Increment t by STEPSIZE. If t > 20.0, break main loop. 3. Final Composition: C{\text{final}} = C + T \cdot \text{sky}. Output C{\text{final}}. Formulas: Henyey-Greenstein Phase Function: fp(\cos \theta) = \left( \text{mix}(F, B, 0.4) \right) \cdot 0.4 Where: F = \frac{1 - g1^2}{(1 + g1^2 - 2 g1 \cos \theta)^{1.5}} B = \frac{1 - g2^2}{(1 + g2^2 - 2 g2 \cos \theta)^{1.5}} In-scattered Radiance (Ls): Ls = L{\text{sun}} T fp Ambient Radiance (La): La = L{\text{ambient}} (1 - e^{-\rho}) Transmittance Update: Tk = T{k-1} e^{-\alpha \rho \Delta s} Radiance Update: Lk = L{k-1} + (La + Ls) Tk \Delta s Sky Color: \text{sky} = \text{mix}(\text{skyBottom}, \text{skyTop}, \text{clamp}(\mathbf{d}y \cdot 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0)) Parameters: MAXSTEPS: 50. STEPSIZE: 0.08. MAXSTEPSLIGHT: 5. STEPSIZELIGHT: 0.6. scatteringCoeff: 1.5 (sunset), 1.2 (day). absorptionCoeff: 0.4 (sunset), 0.2 (day). extinctionCoeff: scatteringCoeff + absorptionCoeff. alpha (\alpha): Light absorption coefficient. g1: 0.7 (forward anisotropy). g2: -0.2 (backward anisotropy). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision & Boundaries: The algorithm uses a fixed maximum distance of 20.0 and a transmittance threshold of 0.01 to terminate early. WebGL 1 does not support dynamic loop bounds, requiring STEPSIZE and STEPSIZELIGHT to be hardcoded constants. Degenerate Input: Aliasing artifacts become noticeable when the camera is positioned inside the cloud volume. The method cannot render two clouds vertically layered at the same position. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchsinglescattering(cameraorigin, cameradir, sundir, suncolor, ambientcolor, weathermap, basenoise, edgedetail, boundsmin, boundsmax, hmin, hmax, maxsteps=50, stepsize=0.08, maxstepslight=5, stepsizelight=0.6): # Initialize transmittance = 1.0 accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) t = 0.0 # Sky color calculation skytop = vec3(0.2, 0.4, 0.8) # Day default skybottom = vec3(0.7, 0.85, 1.0) # Day default screenrange = clamp(cameradir.y 0.5 + 0.5, 0.0, 1.0) sky = mix(skybottom, skytop, screenrange) # Scene variables (simplified for day) scatteringcoeff = 1.2 absorptioncoeff = 0.2 extinctioncoeff = scatteringcoeff + absorptioncoeff for i in range(maxsteps): p = cameraorigin + t cameradir # Bounding box check if not isinsidebox(p, boundsmin, boundsmax): t += stepsize continue # Height check if p.y < hmin or p.y > hmax: t += stepsize continue # Density evaluation # 1. Base noise (Perlin-Worley) density = samplebasenoise(p) # 2. Edge detail erosion edge = sampleedgedetail(p) density = edge # Simplified erosion # 3. Weather map modulation weather = sampleweathermap(p.xy) # Project to 2D density = weather.r # Coverage # 4. Height modulation heightfactor = smoothstep(hmin, hmax, p.y) density = heightfactor density = clamp(density, 0.0, 1.0) # Optimization: Skip low density if density < 0.01: t += stepsize continue # Light marching lightdir = normalize(sundir - p) transmittancelight = 1.0 tlight = 0.0 for j in range(maxstepslight): plight = p + tlight lightdir densitylight = samplebasenoise(plight) # Simplified: using same noise for light path # Beer-Lambert for light transmittancelight = exp(-densitylight extinctioncoeff stepsizelight 1.5) if transmittancelight < 0.05: break tlight += stepsizelight # Scattering costheta = dot(cameradir, lightdir) phase = henyeygreenstein(costheta, g1=0.7, g2=-0.2) # In-scattered light ls = suncolor transmittancelight phase 6.0 la = ambientcolor 0.7 # Accumulate scattered = ls + la accumulatedcolor += transmittance density scattered stepsize # Update transmittance transmittance = exp(-density extinctioncoeff stepsize 1.5) if transmittance < 0.01: break t += stepsize if t > 20.0: break finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + transmittance sky return finalcolor def henyeygreenstein(costheta, g1=0.7, g2=-0.2): denom1 = 1.0 + g1g1 - 2.0g1costheta forward = (1.0 - g1g1) / pow(denom1, 1.5) denom2 = 1.0 + g2g2 - 2.0g2costheta backward = (1.0 - g2g2) / pow(denom2, 1.5) return mix(forward, backward, 0.4) 0.4 def isinsidebox(p, min, max): return p.x >= min.x and p.x <= max.x and p.y >= min.y and p.y <= max.y and p.z >= min.z and p.z <= max.z def samplebasenoise(p): # Returns density from 3D texture (128x128x128) return texture3D(basenoise, p).r def sampleedgedetail(p): # Returns erosion factor from 3D texture (32x32x32) return texture3D(edgedetail, p).r def sampleweathermap(p): # Returns coverage from 2D texture return texture2D(weathermap, p) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) per pixel, where N is the number of main ray steps and M is the number of light ray steps. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the storage of the 3D noise textures (128^3 and 32^3) and the 2D weather map. Performance: Achieves 2.6 ms frame time at 1440p on an AMD Ryzen 5 7600X CPU and AMD Radeon RX 7900 XT GPU. Strengths: Real-time performance; dynamic wind simulation via texture scrolling; configurable cloud types and weather patterns. Limitations: Single scattering approximation lacks physical accuracy for thick clouds. Noticeable aliasing occurs when the camera is inside the cloud volume. The approach cannot render two clouds vertically layered at the same position. Scaling: Performance scales with cloud layer thickness; reducing thickness yields major performance gains by enabling smaller/fewer ray marching steps. When to use: Suitable for real-time applications requiring dynamic, volumetric cloudscapes where performance is prioritized over strict physical accuracy. When not to use: Unsuitable for offline rendering requiring multiple scattering, or for close-up camera shots inside the volume where aliasing becomes prominent. The method originates from real-time volumetric rendering techniques for games and simulations, specifically focusing on cloud rendering. It builds on the principles of ray marching and procedural noise. The specific implementation details, such as the combination of Perlin-Worley noise and the Henyey-Greenstein phase function, are documented in recent academic and open-source projects. gmanishaa/volumetric-rendering, https://github.com/gmanishaa/volumetric-rendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) M4trixStrike/WebGL-Volumetric-clouds, https://github.com/M4trixStrike/WebGL-Volumetric-clouds, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Real-time volumetric cloud rendering for games and simulations, https://erk.fe.uni-lj.si/2025/papers/loboda(realtimevolumetric).pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Atmospheric Ray Marching
head: Basic Volumetric Rendering Atmosphere
body: Atmospheric Ray Marching is a technique for rendering planetary atmospheres using single scattering, exponential density falloff, and the Rayleigh phase function. It solves the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) for a spherical atmosphere by marching along view rays and light rays to compute inscattered sunlight and shadowing. It is distinguished from Ray Marching with Single Scattering by its specific application to planetary spheres with analytical density profiles and its handling of shadow rays for occlusion. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera position \mathbf{o}, direction \mathbf{d}, planet radius R{planet}, atmosphere radius R{atm}, sun direction \mathbf{s}, and physical coefficients (scattering, absorption). Outputs: Final pixel color L{out}. Data Structures: Uniforms: cameraMatrices (std140): Contains viewMatrix, projectionMatrix, cameraMatrix. cameraUniforms (std140): Contains cameraPosition (vec3), cameraExposure (float), cameraFOV (float). Constants: rayleigh: vec3 (5.802, 13.558, 33.1) \times 10^{-6}. ozone: vec3 (0.650, 1.881, 0.085) \times 3 \times 10^{-6}. sigmaS (scattering coefficient): Equal to rayleigh. sigmaT (extinction coefficient): Equal to rayleigh + ozone. STEPSPRIMARY: 32. STEPSLIGHT: 32. GAMMA: 2.2. Formulas: Rayleigh Phase Function: P(\theta) = \frac{3}{16\pi} (1 + \cos^2\theta), where \theta is the scattering angle between the view direction and the sun direction. Exponential Density Falloff: \rho(h) = e^{-h / H}, where h is the height above the planet surface and H is the scale height. Sphere Intersection: For a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and sphere radius R, solve at^2 + bt + c = 0 with a=1, b=2\mathbf{o}\cdot\mathbf{d}, c=\mathbf{o}\cdot\mathbf{o}-R^2. Roots are t = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2-4ac}}{2a}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Direction: Calculate the view ray direction \mathbf{d} from fragment coordinates (x, y) and resolution res: \mathbf{d} = \text{normalize}\left( \left( \frac{x}{res.x} - 0.5, \frac{y}{res.y} - 0.5, -z \right) \right) where z = \frac{0.5 \cdot res.y}{\tan(0.5 \cdot FOV)}. 2. Intersect Atmosphere: Compute the entry and exit points of the view ray with the atmosphere sphere (R{atm}) and planet sphere (R{planet}) using the quadratic formula. Determine the valid segment [t{start}, t{end}] for marching. 3. Initialize Accumulators: Set total transmittance T{total} = 1.0 and accumulated radiance L{out} = 0. 4. March View Ray: Loop i from 0 to STEPS\PRIMARY - 1: a. Calculate step size \Delta s = \frac{t{end} - t{start}}{STEPS\PRIMARY}. b. Compute current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + (t{start} + i \cdot \Delta s) \mathbf{d}. c. Compute height h = \|\mathbf{p}\| - R{planet}. d. Evaluate density \rho = e^{-h / H}. e. Shadow Test: Cast a shadow ray from \mathbf{p} towards the sun \mathbf{s}. Intersect this ray with a sphere of radius 0.95 R{planet} to determine if the point is in shadow. Using 0.95 R{planet} avoids banding artifacts at sunset. f. Inscattering Calculation: If not in shadow: i. Compute optical depth to the sun \tau{light} by marching STEPS\LIGHT steps towards the sun, summing \rho \cdot \Delta s{light}. ii. Compute inscattered radiance L{in} = S{sun} C{sun} e^{-\sigmaT \tau{light}}, where S{sun} is solar spectral irradiance and C{sun} is a constant. g. Update Transmittance: T{total} \leftarrow T{total} \cdot e^{-\sigmaT \rho \Delta s}. h. Accumulate: L{out} \leftarrow L{out} + T{total} \cdot \sigmaS \cdot \rho \cdot P(\theta) \cdot L{in} \cdot \Delta s. 5. Gamma Correction: Apply gamma correction to L{out} using GAMMA (typically 2.2). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def atmosphericraymarching(camerapos, cameradir, sundir, planetradius, atmradius, scaleheight): # Constants rayleigh = vec3(5.802, 13.558, 33.1) 1e-6 ozone = vec3(0.650, 1.881, 0.085) 3e-6 sigmas = rayleigh sigmat = rayleigh + ozone stepsprimary = 32 stepslight = 32 gamma = 2.2 # Ray direction from fragment coords (assuming normalized device coords -1 to 1) # dir = normalize(vec3(ndcx, ndcy, -1.0 / tan(fov/2))) dir = normalize(cameradir) # Intersect with atmosphere and planet # Solve quadratic for atmradius and planetradius # Get tstart and tend for the visible segment tstart, tend = intersectspheres(camerapos, dir, planetradius, atmradius) if tend < tstart: return vec3(0.0) deltas = (tend - tstart) / stepsprimary ttotaltransmittance = 1.0 lout = vec3(0.0) for i in range(stepsprimary): t = tstart + i deltas p = camerapos + dir t h = length(p) - planetradius rho = exp(-h / scaleheight) # Shadow test inshadow = isinshadow(p, sundir, planetradius 0.95, stepslight) lin = vec3(0.0) if not inshadow: taulight = computeopticaldepthtosun(p, sundir, sigmat, stepslight, scaleheight, planetradius) # Ssun and Csun are constants representing solar irradiance lin = solarirradiance exp(-sigmat taulight) # Phase function costheta = dot(normalize(p), -sundir) # Approximation for scattering angle depending on geometry # More accurately: angle between view direction and sun direction at the sample point # P(theta) = 3/(16pi) (1 + cos^2(theta)) # theta is angle between -dir (view) and sundir? # Standard Rayleigh: angle between incident light and view direction. # Incident light comes from sundir. View direction is -dir (looking back). # So costheta = dot(-sundir, -dir) = dot(sundir, dir) ? # Actually, scattering angle is between incoming light direction and outgoing view direction. # Incoming: -sundir. Outgoing: -dir. # costheta = dot(-sundir, -dir) = dot(sundir, dir) costheta = dot(sundir, dir) phase = (3.0 / (16.0 3.14159265)) (1.0 + costheta costheta) # Update transmittance ttotaltransmittance = exp(-sigmat rho deltas) # Accumulate lout += ttotaltransmittance sigmas rho phase lin deltas # Gamma correction lout = pow(lout, vec3(1.0 / gamma)) return lout def isinshadow(point, sundir, shadowradius, steps): # Ray from point towards sun rayo = point rayd = sundir # Intersect with sphere of radius shadowradius # If intersection distance > 0, it's in shadow (blocked by planet) # Note: The source says "intersecting a light ray from sample point towards sun with a sphere... to avoid banding" # If the ray hits the planet sphere, it is in shadow. thit = intersectsphere(rayo, rayd, shadowradius) return thit > 0.0 def computeopticaldepthtosun(point, sundir, sigmat, steps, scaleheight, planetradius): tau = 0.0 deltas = 1000.0 # Arbitrary large step or determined by geometry # March towards sun for i in range(steps): p = point + sundir (i deltas) h = length(p) - planetradius rho = exp(-h / scaleheight) tau += rho deltas return tau sigmat Complexity: Time complexity is O(N \cdot M) per pixel, where N is STEPSPRIMARY and M is STEPSLIGHT. Memory complexity is O(1) per pixel as it does not store volumetric grids. Performance: The method is computationally expensive due to the nested ray marching (view ray and light ray) and exponential density calculations. Strengths: Physically plausible single scattering for planetary atmospheres; simple implementation; no precomputation required. Limitations: Single scattering approximation ignores multiple scattering, which can lead to inaccuracies in dense atmospheres or near the horizon. Shadow banding artifacts are mitigated by using 0.95 R{planet} but not eliminated entirely. When to use: Real-time rendering of planetary atmospheres where performance is critical and single scattering is sufficient. When not to use: Scenes requiring multiple scattering or high-fidelity cloud rendering. The method originates from the "Basic Volumetric Rendering" workshop at the Graphics Programming Conference in Breda, 2024. It is based on the repository al-ro/volumetrics. The technique is a specific application of ray marching for atmospheric rendering, utilizing the Rayleigh phase function and exponential density profiles. al-ro/volumetrics, https://github.com/al-ro/volumetrics, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Atmospheric Scattering Post-Process
head: Post-process Atmospheric Rendering, Screen-space Atmospheric Scattering
body: A post-processing technique that renders volumetric atmospheric scattering (Rayleigh, Mie, and Ozone absorption) over a scene by tracing rays through a spherical atmosphere shell, accounting for occlusion by scene geometry. It differs from in-scene atmospheric rendering by operating on the final screen buffer, using the depth map to determine ray termination distances, and applying tonemapping and saturation adjustments to the accumulated light. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Screen color texture, depth texture, camera position, sun position, planet parameters (radius, atmosphere radius), and scattering coefficients. Outputs: Final rendered color buffer. Data Structures The method relies on a uniform structure AtmosphereSettings containing the following fields: planetRadius: Radius of the planet in meters. atmosphereRadius: Radius of the atmosphere in meters. rayleighHeight: Height falloff of Rayleigh scattering. Default: 8 \times 10^3. rayleighScatteringCoefficients: Rayleigh scattering coefficients (R, G, B). Default: (5.8 \times 10^{-6}, 13.5 \times 10^{-6}, 33.1 \times 10^{-6}). mieHeight: Height falloff of Mie scattering. Default: 1.2 \times 10^3. mieScatteringCoefficients: Mie scattering coefficients (R, G, B). Default: (3.9 \times 10^{-6}, 3.9 \times 10^{-6}, 3.9 \times 10^{-6}). mieAsymmetry: Mie scattering asymmetry factor, between -1 and 1. Default: 0.8. ozoneHeight: Height of the ozone layer in meters above the planet surface. Default: 25 \times 10^3. ozoneAbsorptionCoefficients: Ozone absorption coefficients (R, G, B). Default: (0.6 \times 10^{-6}, 1.8 \times 10^{-6}, 0.085 \times 10^{-6}). ozoneFalloff: Ozone absorption falloff around the ozone layer height in meters. Default: 5 \times 10^3. lightIntensity: Intensity of the sun. Default: 20. Numbered Steps 1. Sample Input Data: Read the screen color and depth value for the current pixel UV coordinates. python screencolor = texture2D(texturesampler, uv).rgb depth = texture2D(depthsampler, uv).r 2. Compute Ray Origin and Direction: Transform the depth value to world space to find the deepest visible point, then compute the ray direction from the camera position. python deepestpoint = worldfromuv(uv, depth) - cameraposition maximumdistance = length(deepestpoint) raydir = deepestpoint / maximumdistance 3. Clamp Ray Length for Sphere Intersection: Intersect the ray with the planet sphere to get entry distance t0. If the ray intersects and the computed maximum distance is greater than t0 - 1.0 (to avoid precision artifacts from imperfect sphere discretization), clamp the maximum distance to t0. Note: This clamping logic should not be used if the planet has landmasses or non-spherical geometry. python t0, t1 = rayintersectsphere(cameraposition, raydir, planetposition, planetradius) if maximumdistance > t0 - 1.0: maximumdistance = t0 4. Atmosphere Intersection: Call the scatter function with the screen color, camera position, ray direction, and maximum distance. Inside scatter: a. Intersect the ray with the atmosphere sphere to get impact point t{in} and escape point t{out}. b. If no intersection occurs, return the original screen color. c. Clamp t{in} to \max(0.0, t{in}). d. Clamp t{out} to \min(\text{maximum\distance}, t{out}). e. Calculate the distance through the atmosphere: d{atm} = \max(0.0, t{out} - t{in}). f. Compute the first point in the atmosphere: P{start} = \text{ray\origin} + \text{ray\dir} \times t{in}. g. Call calculatelight with P{start}, ray direction, d{atm}, and original color. 5. Calculate Scattering (calculatelight): a. Define the number of sample points POINTSFROMCAMERA (implementation detail, not explicitly defined in sources, but used in loop). b. Compute step size: s = d{atm} / (\text{POINTS\FROM\CAMERA} - 1). c. Initialize accumulators: inscatteredrayleigh = 0, inscatteredmie = 0, totalopticaldepth = 0. d. Iterate i from 0 to POINTSFROMCAMERA - 1: i. Current sample point: P{sample} = P{start} + \text{ray\dir} \times (i \times s). ii. Compute Sun Ray Optical Depth: Calculate distance from light source through atmosphere: L{sun} = \text{atmosphere\radius} - \text{length}(P{sample} - \text{planet\position}). If ray from P{sample} in sun direction intersects atmosphere sphere, update L{sun} to the intersection distance t1. Compute optical depth from sun to sample point: OD{sun} = \text{optical\depth}(P{sample}, \text{sun\dir}, L{sun}). iii. Compute View Ray Optical Depth: Distance from sample point to camera along view ray: L{view} = i \times s. Compute optical depth from sample point to camera: OD{view} = \text{optical\depth}(P{sample}, -\text{ray\dir}, L{view}). iv. Compute Transmittance: T = \exp(-\text{rayleigh\coeffs} \times (OD{sun}.x + OD{view}.x) - \text{mie\coeffs} \times (OD{sun}.y + OD{view}.y) - \text{ozone\coeffs} \times (OD{sun}.z + OD{view}.z)). v. Update Total Optical Depth: Get local density at sample point: \rho = \text{density\at\point}(P{sample}). OD{total} += \rho \times s. vi. Accumulate Scattered Light: inscatteredrayleigh += \rho.x \times T \times s. inscatteredmie += \rho.y \times T \times s. e. Compute Phase Functions: Cosine of angle between view and sun directions: c = \text{dot}(\text{ray\dir}, \text{sun\dir}). Rayleigh Phase Function: PR = \frac{3}{16\pi} (1 + c^2). Mie Phase Function: Let g = \text{mie\asymmetry}. PM = \frac{3(1-g^2)}{2(2+g^2)} \frac{1+c^2}{(1+g^2-2gc)^{1.5}}. f. Apply Phase Functions and Coefficients: inscatteredrayleigh = PR \times \text{rayleigh\coeffs}. inscatteredmie = PM \times \text{mie\coeffs}. g. Compute Opacity (Transmittance to Camera): O = \exp(-(\text{mie\coeffs} \times OD{total}.y + \text{rayleigh\coeffs} \times OD{total}.x + \text{ozone\coeffs} \times OD{total}.z)). h. Return Final Color: \text{final} = (\text{in\scattered\rayleigh} + \text{in\scattered\mie}) \times \text{light\intensity} + \text{original\color} \times O. 6. Post-Processing: a. Apply exposure: \text{final\color} \times 1.2. b. Apply ACES tonemapping. c. Apply saturation (factor 1.2) using grayscale luminance weights (0.299, 0.587, 0.114): \text{grayscale} = \text{dot}(\text{final\color}, [0.299, 0.587, 0.114]) \text{final\color} = \text{mix}(\text{grayscale}, \text{final\color}, 1.2). d. Clamp to [0.0, 1.0] and output. Formulas Rayleigh Phase Function: PR(\theta) = \frac{3}{16\pi} (1 + \cos^2 \theta) where \theta is the scattering angle. Mie Phase Function (Henyey-Greenstein variant): PM(\theta) = \frac{3(1-g^2)}{2(2+g^2)} \frac{1+\cos^2 \theta}{(1+g^2-2g\cos \theta)^{3/2}} where g is the asymmetry factor. Optical Depth: The optical depth is computed based on the density falloff of Rayleigh, Mie, and Ozone layers. The specific opticaldepth function implementation is not fully detailed in the provided notes, but it integrates density along the ray path. Transmittance: T = \exp\left(-\sum{k \in \{R, M, O\}} \sigmak \cdot ODk\right) where \sigmak are the scattering/absorption coefficients and ODk are the optical depths for Rayleigh (R), Mie (M), and Ozone (O). Parameters POINTSFROMCAMERA: Number of sample points along the view ray. Not given in the sources. (Typical values in similar implementations range from 16 to 64, but must be defined by the implementer). sunPosition: Position of the sun. Provided as uniform.. cameraPosition: Position of the camera. Provided as uniform.. planetPosition: Position of the planet center. Provided as uniform.. Edge Cases and Pitfalls No Intersection: If the ray does not intersect the atmosphere sphere, return the original color immediately. Negative Impact Point: Clamp the impact point to \max(0.0, t{in}). Negative Distance: Clamp the distance through atmosphere to \max(0.0, t{out} - t{in}). Non-Spherical Planets: The clamping logic for maximumDistance using t0 - 1.0 should not be used if the planet has landmasses or imperfect discretized geometry, as it may incorrectly truncate the ray. Precision Artifacts: Use a tolerance of -1.0 when clamping maximumDistance to t0 to avoid precision artifacts from imperfect sphere discretization. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sample points POINTSFROMCAMERA per pixel. The complexity is O(N \cdot P) where N is the number of pixels and P is the number of samples per ray. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per pixel, excluding the input and output textures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and sample count. Strengths: Post-process approach allows for easy integration into existing rendering pipelines without modifying scene geometry. Accounts for occlusion by scene geometry via depth buffer. Limitations: Limited to screen-space; rays are only traced for visible pixels. Approximates atmospheric scattering with a fixed number of samples. Relies on a spherical atmosphere model. When to Use: When rendering a spherical planet with an atmosphere and occlusion by terrain is required, and performance constraints allow for per-pixel ray marching. When Not to Use: For non-spherical planets, or when high-fidelity multi-scattering is required (this method uses single scattering approximation). Originated from the GitHub repository BarthPaleologue/volumetric-atmospheric-scattering. It is an implementation of atmospheric scattering using post-processing techniques, likely inspired by standard volumetric rendering principles and Rayleigh/Mie scattering theory. BarthPaleologue/volumetric-atmospheric-scattering, https://github.com/BarthPaleologue/volumetric-atmospheric-scattering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Cone Tracing
body: Cone tracing is a volume rendering technique that approximates indirect lighting (diffuse and specular) and soft shadows by casting expanding cones into a voxel grid, accumulating color and opacity along the ray direction until full occlusion or a maximum distance is reached. It distinguishes itself from standard ray casting by using a cone aperture to aggregate light from a volume of space, providing visually plausible soft shadow borders and indirect illumination. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Surface position (pos), surface normal (N), light direction (L), voxel grid texture (3D texture with mipmaps), voxel size (voxelSize), voxel count (u\voxelCount), cone aperture parameter (apertureTan2), and a quality step multiplier (quality). Output: Accumulated color (color.rgb) and opacity (color.a). Data Structures: Voxel Texture: A 3D texture where each texel stores color (rgb) and opacity (a). Mipmaps are pre-generated to handle different cone diameters at varying distances. Accumulator: A vec4 variable initialized to (0, 0, 0, 0). Parameters: apertureTan2: Defined as 2 \cdot \tan(\frac{apertureAngle}{2}). A typical value corresponds to an aperture angle of 30 degrees, yielding apertureTan2 \approx 0.536. quality: A step size multiplier. A typical value is 0.7. voxelSize: The physical size of a single voxel in the grid. Algorithm: The method traces a cone from the surface point in the direction of the light source (or hemisphere for indirect lighting). At each step, the cone's diameter is calculated based on the distance traveled and the aperture. The algorithm samples the voxel texture at the current position, using a Level of Detail (LOD) determined by the cone's diameter to ensure appropriate filtering. Color is accumulated using alpha blending, scaled by the unoccluded area. 1. Initialize color = (0, 0, 0, 0) and dist = 0.0. 2. Calculate effective squared aperture a2 = \max(voxelSize, apertureTan2) to ensure a non-zero minimum aperture. 3. Loop while color.a < 1.0 and dist is within bounds: a. Calculate current cone diameter: diameter = \max(voxelSize, dist \cdot a2). b. Calculate LOD level: lod = \log2(diameter \cdot u\voxelCount), clamped to a maximum of 10. c. Update sampling position: pos = from + dir \cdot dist. d. If pos is outside the voxel grid bounds, break the loop. e. Fetch voxel color cc from the texture at pos using lod. f. Accumulate color: color += (1 - color.a) \cdot cc. This scales the fetched color by the unoccluded area. g. Advance distance: dist += diameter \cdot quality. 4. Return color.rgb. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def conetrace(frompos, dir, voxeltexture, voxelsize, voxelcount, aperturetan2, quality=0.7, maxdist=10.0, gridmin=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0), gridmax=(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)): """ Cone tracing algorithm for approximating indirect lighting and soft shadows. Args: frompos: Surface position (vec3) dir: Light direction or hemisphere sample direction (vec3) voxeltexture: 3D texture with mipmaps storing (rgb, a) voxelsize: Physical size of a voxel voxelcount: Number of voxels along one axis aperturetan2: 2 tan(apertureangle / 2) quality: Step size multiplier (default 0.7) maxdist: Maximum marching distance to prevent infinite loops gridmin, gridmax: Bounding box of the voxel grid Returns: color.rgb: Accumulated color """ color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) dist = 0.0 # Ensure non-zero aperture a2 = max(voxelsize, aperturetan2) while color[3] < 1.0 and dist < maxdist: # Calculate cone diameter at current distance diameter = max(voxelsize, dist a2) # Calculate LOD based on diameter and grid resolution lod = (diameter voxelcount).log2() if hasattr(diameter voxelcount, 'log2') else math.log2(diameter voxelcount) lod = max(0.0, min(10.0, lod)) # Update position pos = frompos + dir dist # Check bounds (assumes normalized or world-space coordinates matching gridmin/max) if pos.x < gridmin[0] or pos.x > gridmax[0] or \ pos.y < gridmin[1] or pos.y > gridmax[1] or \ pos.z < gridmin[2] or pos.z > gridmax[2]: break # Fetch color from voxel texture with mipmapping cc = texture(voxeltexture, pos, lod) # Accumulate color with alpha blending # Scale by unoccluded area (1 - currentalpha) color = ( color[0] + (1.0 - color[3]) cc[0], color[1] + (1.0 - color[3]) cc[1], color[2] + (1.0 - color[3]) cc[2], color[3] + (1.0 - color[3]) cc[3]) # Advance distance by a fraction of the diameter dist += diameter quality return (color[0], color[1], color[2]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Interpretation: The shape traced by linearly increasing radius is technically a cone with a hemisphere on the end (a swept sphere of linearly increasing radius). Intersection occurs if the distance to the nearest surface is less than the current test radius at any point along the horizontal center line. Light Leaking: The method is computationally expensive and tricky to implement without artifacts such as light leaking, especially in complex geometry. Precision: The LOD calculation must be clamped to prevent sampling errors at very large distances or very small diameters. Initialization: Some implementations initialize dist to voxelSize \cdot offset to skip the immediate surface, though dist = 0.0 is standard for direct cone casting. Approximates soft shadow boundaries by aggregating extinction values within the cone. Distinguished by its specific application to light transport in participating media, where the cone aperture controls softness and scattering range. Variant with specific optimizations for custom hardware or scene requirements. Specialized for computing ambient occlusion using cone traces. Integrates cone tracing into a deferred rendering pipeline. Uses convolution techniques for shading. Extends cone tracing for full global illumination. Uses anisotropic voxels for better filtering. Incorporates temporal accumulation for multi-bounce lighting. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of steps in the cone trace. The number of steps depends on the scene depth and the cone aperture. Each step involves a texture fetch with LOD calculation. Memory Complexity: Depends on the voxel grid size and the number of mipmaps. Typically, a 3D texture with multiple mip levels is required. Performance: Computationally expensive compared to simple ray casting due to the volume of samples and texture lookups. Strengths: Provides visually plausible soft shadows and indirect lighting with reasonable performance. Effective for real-time applications where full global illumination is too expensive. Limitations: Prone to artifacts like light leaking if not implemented carefully. Performance degrades with complex geometry or large voxel grids. Not energy conservative without additional attenuation factors. When to Use: Real-time rendering of scenes with participating media or where soft shadows and indirect lighting are desired. When Not to Use: When high precision is required, or when the scene is static and offline rendering is acceptable (use path tracing). Also not suitable for scenes with extremely fine details that exceed the voxel resolution. Cone tracing was introduced as an extension of sphere tracing for Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering. It was described in a thesis that discussed using cones to provide useful intersection information with minimal additional cost. The technique has been described in the gidemo project report and codebase to approximate indirect lighting and soft shadows in voxel-based environments.
