name: SDF Ray Marching with Eikonal Correction
head: Eikonal-corrected ray marching, distance field ray marching with step correction
body: This method marches a ray through a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to find surface intersections while applying a correction factor to counteract distance elongation along non-cardinal directions caused by the Eikonal equation. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by explicitly scaling step sizes based on ray direction to prevent overshooting and jitter. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (normalized). SDF field SDF(x, y, z). Maximum ray march steps N{max} (typical value: 128, range 8–512). Hit threshold distance \epsilon (implicit in hitThreshold()). Progress multiplier k (16.0 for ray origin march, 32.0 for shadow march). Eikonal correction factor C{eikonal}, computed from ray direction D. Outputs: Hit distance t. Hit status flag. Data Structures: The SDF is stored as a 3D texture or voxel grid, accessed via world-space coordinates mapped to texture coordinates. No additional complex data structures are required beyond standard ray parameters and SDF lookup. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize current ray distance t = 0.0 and progress accumulator res = 1.0. 2. Loop up to N{max} iterations: a. Calculate current world position: P = O + D \cdot t. b. Check bounds: If P is out of the SDF volume, return 0.0. c. Sample SDF: d = SDF(P). d. Check hit: If d \le \epsilon, set hit position to P, set res = 0.0, and return 1.0. e. Apply Eikonal correction: Clamp d to a minimum positive value (0.0001), then multiply by the correction factor: d{corrected} = \max(d, 0.0001) \cdot C{eikonal}. f. Update progress: res = \min(res, k \cdot d{corrected} / t). g. Advance ray: t = t + d{corrected}. 3. Return 1.0 if the loop finishes without hitting. Formula: The core step advancement formula is: t{new} = t{old} + \max(d, 0.0001) \cdot C{eikonal} where d is the raw SDF value at the current position, and C{eikonal} is the correction factor derived from the ray direction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarcheikonalcorrected(origin, direction, sdfsample, maxsteps=128, k=16.0, hitthreshold=0.001): t = 0.0 res = 1.0 eikonalfix = calceikonalcorrection(direction) for in range(maxsteps): currentpos = origin + direction t if not iswithinsdfbounds(currentpos): return 0.0 dist = sdfsample(currentpos) if dist <= hitthreshold: return 1.0 correcteddist = max(dist, 0.0001) eikonalfix if t > 0: res = min(res, k correcteddist / t) t += correcteddist return 1.0 def calceikonalcorrection(direction): # Standard geometric correction for non-cardinal ray directions # Returns a scalar multiplier >= 1.0 based on direction alignment with grid axes. return 1.0 def iswithinsdfbounds(pos): # Standard AABB boundary check return True Parameters: maxsteps: 128 (typical), range 8–512. k: 16.0 for ray origin march, 32.0 for shadow march. eikonalfix: Calculated by calcEikonalCorrection(dir). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Distance Elongation: The Eikonal equation causes distance values to be larger than the true Euclidean distance along non-cardinal directions, leading to larger step sizes than necessary. The eikonalfix factor corrects this. Zero Distance: If dist is 0 or negative, it is clamped to 0.0001 to prevent zero-step stalls. Out of Bounds: Rays leaving the SDF volume must be handled explicitly to avoid sampling errors. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of ray march steps (up to maxsteps). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, plus the SDF texture storage. Performance: The correction factor calculation adds minimal overhead; the main cost is SDF sampling. The correction improves accuracy for non-cardinal rays but may increase step counts if the correction factor is large. Strengths: Improves accuracy of ray marching in SDFs, especially for rays not aligned with grid axes. Limitations: Requires a method to calculate the Eikonal correction factor, which is not detailed in the source. When to use: When high accuracy is required in SDF ray marching, particularly for non-axis-aligned rays. When not to use: If performance is critical and approximate results are acceptable, or if rays are always aligned with cardinal directions. This method is part of the implementation of signed distance fields in Unity, as described in an unofficial GitHub repository by samuelbigos. It addresses a known issue in SDF rendering where the Eikonal equation introduces directional bias in the distance values, which is corrected during ray marching to ensure accurate surface intersection detection. samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity, https://github.com/samuelbigos/signeddistancefieldsinunity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray Marching with SDFs and Soft Accumulation
head: Jellyfish Ray Marching with Soft Accumulation, Soft Accumulation for Thin Geometry
body: A rendering technique for hair-thin geometry (such as jellyfish tentacles) that prevents flickering by replacing hard surface intersection with soft accumulation. Instead of stopping at the first hit, each ray march step adds a contribution based on the distance to the surface, fading in smoothly via an exponential falloff. This sets it apart from standard SDF ray marching, which typically terminates on hard intersection, and from Aggressive Ray Marching with SDF, which focuses on step size optimization rather than anti-aliasing thin strands. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin ro, ray direction d, time t, phase offset \phi, scene parameters (bell radius, tentacle length, school count), and SDF functions for the bell (sdBell), tentacles (sdTentacles), and arms (sdArms). Outputs: Final color col for the pixel. Data Structures: Ray State: travel (float, accumulated distance), trans (float, transparency, initialized to 1.0), rad (vec3, accumulated radial color), strands (float, accumulated strand contribution). Scene Constants: MARCHSTEPS (120), TENTLEN (3.0), ARMLEN (1.5), SCHOOL (5), GLOW, HOT (lighting intensity parameters). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchsdfsoftaccumulation(ro, d, t, ph): # Camera/ray setup (from evidence) ro = vec3(0.0, 0.10 + 0.16 sin(t 0.08), 5.60) ro.xz = rot(0.07 sin(t 0.11)) ro.xz uv = (2.0 glFragCoord.xy - uresolution) / uresolution.y d = normalize(fw 1.85 + rt uv.x + upv uv.y) col = vec3(0.0) for i in range(SCHOOL): # Compute centre with sinusoidal drift centre = computecentresinusoidaldrift(i, t, ph) # Transform ray origin relative to center o = (ro - centre) / data.w # Apply tilt rotations o.xy = rot(tilt.x) o.xy o.zy = rot(tilt.y) o.zy # Ray-sphere intersection for marching bounds bo = o - vec3(0.0, -1.4, 0.0) b = dot(bo, d) disc = b b - dot(bo, bo) + 2.7 2.7 tmax = -b + sqrt(disc) # Initialize marching state pc = pulse(t 0.42 + ph 0.37) travel = max(-b - sq, 0.0) + dither # sq and dither not defined in sources trans = 1.0 strands = 0.0 rad = vec3(0.0) for s in range(MARCHSTEPS): if travel > tmax or trans < 0.05: break p = o + d travel # SDF evaluation db = sdBell(p, pc, t, ph) dt = sdTentacles(p, pc, t, ph) da = sdArms(p, t, ph) # Step size stride = clamp(min(db, min(dt, da)) 0.70, 0.010, 0.18) # Soft accumulation for strands taper = 1.0 - smoothstep(0.55, 1.05, -p.y / TENTLEN) strands += exp(-max(dt, 0.0) 95.0) stride 8.5 taper strands += exp(-max(da, 0.0) 45.0) stride 3.0 # Bell surface shading if db < 0.012: # Compute normal via finite differences n = bellNormal(p, pc, t, ph) # Uses e = vec2(0.0035, 0.0) fres = pow(1.0 - abs(dot(n, -d)), 2.4) lam = 0.35 + 0.65 abs(dot(n, normalize(vec3(-0.35, 1.0, 0.45)))) ribs = pow(0.5 + 0.5 cos(16.0 atan(p.z, p.x)), 14.0) op = 0.075 + 0.42 fres + ribs 0.12 rad += trans op (GLOW (0.75 + 1.15 lam) + HOT (fres 1.30 + ribs 0.60)) trans = 1.0 - op stride = 0.026 # Force small step for bell surface detail travel += stride # Apply fog fog = exp(-0.055 max(length(ro - centre) - 3.0, 0.0)) col += (rad + GLOW strands 0.16 + HOT strands strands 0.006) fog # Post-processing col = vec3(1.0) - exp(-col 1.85) col = max(col - vec3(0.0175, 0.0160, 0.0060), vec3(0.0)) output = pow(col, vec3(1.0 / 2.2)) return output def pulse(x): x = fract(x) if x < 0.28: return smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, x / 0.28) else: return 1.0 - smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, (x - 0.28) / 0.72) Formulas: Per-step soft contribution: e^{-95\,d}, where d is the distance to the tentacle surface. Pulse function (swim cycle): pulse(x) = \text{fract}(x); if x < 0.28 return \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.0, x / 0.28); else return 1.0 - \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.0, (x - 0.28) / 0.72). Tone mapping and black point: col = \text{vec3}(1.0) - \exp(-col \cdot 1.85); col = \max(col - \text{vec3}(0.0175, 0.0160, 0.0060), \text{vec3}(0.0)); \text{output} = \text{pow}(col, \text{vec3}(1.0 / 2.2)). Pitfalls: Hard intersection of thin geometry causes flickering as strands slip between sample points. Hair-thin tentacles and arms alias severely across frames if rendered with hard SDF hits. Soft accumulation solves these issues by fading contributions in smoothly based on distance to the SDF surface, multiplied by stride and a taper factor that fades near the base. Renders a swarm of butterflies by combining SDFs for individual anatomical parts with ray marching in a transformed local coordinate space to handle dynamic wing flapping and orientation. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by using a non-rigid "un-bend" transform to animate wings and a specific stability clamping strategy for step sizes, building on the soft accumulation techniques of Ray Marching with SDFs and Soft Accumulation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of march steps per ray (O(MARCH\STEPS)) and the number of objects in the school (O(SCHOOL)). Memory Complexity: Constant per ray, storing only a few floating-point accumulators. Performance: Roughly one minute of rendering per 10 seconds of output on integrated graphics. Single frames are near-instant, allowing for rapid iteration. Strengths: Eliminates flickering and aliasing artifacts common in rendering hair-thin geometry with hard SDF intersections. Provides smooth, fluid motion for dynamic thin structures. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of exponential falloff constants (e.g., 95.0 for tentacles) to balance visibility and performance. The soft accumulation approach may result in slightly lower contrast or "ghosting" if not properly attenuated by transparency. When to Use: Ideal for rendering thin, strand-like geometry (hair, tentacles, grass) where traditional hard intersection causes temporal instability. When Not to Use: Not suitable for solid, opaque objects where precise surface definition is required without transparency artifacts. Originating from the manim-glsl-jellyfish project by el-bakkali, this technique was developed to render a school of jellyfish using signed distance functions for the bell, tentacles, and arms. It addresses the specific challenge of animating thin, dynamic structures without the visual artifacts associated with discrete ray marching steps. The method is implemented in GLSL shaders and integrated with the Manim animation engine for timeline control. el-bakkali/manim-glsl-jellyfish, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-jellyfish, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Butterfly Ray Marching with SDFs
head: Butterfly SDF Ray Marching, Swarm SDF Rendering
body: Butterfly Ray Marching with SDFs renders a swarm of butterflies by combining Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for individual anatomical parts (body, wings, antennae) with ray marching in a transformed local coordinate space to handle dynamic wing flapping and orientation. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by using a non-rigid "un-bend" transform to animate wings and a specific stability clamping strategy for step sizes, building on the soft accumulation techniques of Ray Marching with SDFs and Soft Accumulation. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d in world space. Time t and phase offset. Swarm data array SWARM containing position and velocity vectors for each butterfly. Parameters: MARCHSTEPS (maximum iterations per butterfly) and SWARMSIZE (number of butterflies). Outputs: Final pixel color C{out}. Data Structures: SWARM[i]: A 4-component vector storing the base position and velocity/orientation data for butterfly i. mapButterfly(p, t, phase): Returns a 2-component vector h where h.x is the signed distance and h.y is the material ID (0 for wings, 1 for body). Step-by-Step Method: 1. Local Space Transformation: For each butterfly i in the swarm: Retrieve velocity vector v and base position from SWARM[i]. Determine the forward vector. If |v{xy}| < 10^{-4}, derive forward from the cross product of the dorsal axis and (1, 0, 0) to avoid singularity. Construct a basis matrix from the velocity vector and a dorsal axis (interpolated between world up and camera direction). Apply a roll rotation to the basis. Transform the world ray origin o and direction d into the butterfly's local space by applying the basis and dividing the origin by a scale factor. 2. Sphere Intersection: Compute the intersection of the transformed ray with a unit sphere bounding the butterfly: b = \text{dot}(o{local}, d{local}) disc = b^2 - \text{dot}(o{local}, o{local}) + 1.45^2 If disc < 0, skip this butterfly. Calculate t{max} = -b + \sqrt{disc}. If t{max} \le 0, skip. 3. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize travel = \max(-b - \sqrt{disc}, 0) + \text{dither}. Iterate k from 0 to MARCHSTEPS: If travel > t{max}, break. Compute point p = o{local} + d{local} \cdot travel. Evaluate h = \text{mapButterfly}(p, t, \text{phase}). If h.x < 0.0022, a hit is found. Set hit = travel, hp = p, mat = h.y, and break. Advance step: travel \leftarrow travel + \text{clamp}(h.x \cdot 0.62, 0.0035, 0.22) Note: The step size is clamped because the un-bend transform is not rigid. 4. SDF Evaluation (mapButterfly): Body SDF: Clamp z to [-0.38, 0.30]. Compute normalized height u. Calculate radius r using a base term, a Gaussian bump for the thorax, and an offset. Return distance to cylinder surface defined by x, y \cdot 1.12, z - z{offset}. Antenna SDF: Take absolute x. Clamp normalized z to [0, 1]. Compute cubic Bezier-like control point c. Return distance to line segment with radius interpolating between 0.0045 and 0.014 based on u. Wing SDF: Compute wing distance. Combine: Body SDF = \min(\text{Body}, \text{Antenna}). If \text{Wing} < \text{Body}, return (\text{Wing}, 0). Else, return (\text{Body}, 1). 5. Normal Calculation: Compute normal n using central differences on mapButterfly with \epsilon = 0.0018. 6. Shading: Wings (Material 0): Transform hit point to wing space. Calculate outline and base color. Lambertian lighting: L = 0.22 + 0.78 \max(\text{dot}(n, \text{sun}), 0). Subsurface scattering approximation: S = \text{base} \cdot \max(-\text{dot}(n, \text{sun}), 0) \cdot \max(\text{dot}(rd, \text{sun}), 0)^{2.2} \cdot 6.0. Rim lighting: R = \text{mix}(\text{SUNCOL}, \text{AMBER\BRIGHT}, 0.55) \cdot \text{pow}(1.0 - \text{abs}(\text{dot}(n, -d)), 3.0) \cdot 0.24. Specular: Spec = \text{SUNCOL} \cdot \text{pow}(\max(\text{dot}(\text{reflect}(-\text{sun}, n), -d), 0), 28.0) \cdot 0.14. Final: shade = \text{base} \cdot (L + 0.18) + S + \text{base} \cdot \text{through} \cdot 0.60 + R + Spec. Body (Material 1): Lambertian lighting: L = 0.25 + 0.75 \max(\text{dot}(n, \text{sun}), 0). Fuzz factor: F = 0.5 + 0.5 \sin(hp.z \cdot 180.0) \sin(hp.x \cdot 150.0). Final: shade = \text{vec3}(0.070, 0.042, 0.032) \cdot L \cdot (0.8 + 0.3 F) + \text{SUNCOL} \cdot \text{pow}(1.0 - \text{abs}(\text{dot}(n, -d)), 2.5) \cdot 0.55. 7. Compositing: Calculate distance dist = |ro - origin|. Haze factor: H = \exp(-0.055 \cdot \max(dist - 2.0, 0.0)). col = \text{mix}(\text{background}(rd, uv), shade, H). Apply tonemapping and gamma correction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def butterflyraymarch(ro, rd, t, phase, swarmdata, marchsteps): """ ro: Ray origin (vec3) rd: Ray direction (vec3) t: Time (float) phase: Phase offset (float) swarmdata: List of butterfly data (vec4) marchsteps: Max iterations (int) """ finalcolor = vec3(0.0) for i in range(len(swarmdata)): data = swarmdata[i] pos = data.xyz vel = data.w # Packed velocity/orientation data # 1. Local Space Transformation forward = normalize(vel.xy) if length(vel.xy) > 1e-4 else cross(vec3(0,1,0), vec3(1,0,0)) # Pitfall handling dorsal = mix(vec3(0,1,0), normalize(ro - pos), 0.5) # Dorsal axis mixed between up and camera direction basis = constructbasis(forward, dorsal) # Standard orthonormal basis construction olocal = transformpoint(basis, ro - pos) / scale # Divide origin by scale dlocal = transformvector(basis, rd) # 2. Sphere Intersection b = dot(olocal, dlocal) disc = b b - dot(olocal, olocal) + 1.45 1.45 if disc < 0.0: continue sq = sqrt(disc) tmax = -b + sq if tmax <= 0.0: continue travel = max(-b - sq, 0.0) + dither() # Dither initialization hitt = -1.0 hitplocal = vec3(0.0) hitmat = 0.0 # 3. Ray Marching for k in range(marchsteps): if travel > tmax: break plocal = olocal + dlocal travel h = mapbutterfly(plocal, t, phase) if h.x < 0.0022: hitt = travel hitplocal = plocal hitmat = h.y break step = clamp(h.x 0.62, 0.0035, 0.22) # Stability clamp for non-rigid transform travel += step if hitt < 0.0: continue # 4. Normal Calculation n = butterflynormal(hitplocal, t, phase) # Central differences with epsilon 0.0018 # 5. Shading shade = vec3(0.0) if hitmat < 0.5: # Wing shading v = towingspace(vec3(abs(hitplocal.x), hitplocal.y, hitplocal.z), t, phase) w = vec2(v.x, v.z) outline = wingoutline(w) basecol = wingcolour(w, outline, hash11(i + 5.0) 0.35) lambert = 0.22 + 0.78 max(dot(n, sun), 0.0) through = max(-dot(n, sun), 0.0) back = pow(max(dot(rd, sun), 0.0), 2.2) rim = pow(1.0 - abs(dot(n, -rd)), 3.0) shade = basecol (lambert + 0.18) shade += basecol through back 6.0 shade += basecol through 0.60 shade += mix(suncol, amberbright, 0.55) rim 0.24 shade += suncol pow(max(dot(reflect(-sun, n), -rd), 0.0), 28.0) 0.14 else: # Body shading lambert = 0.25 + 0.75 max(dot(n, sun), 0.0) fuzz = 0.5 + 0.5 sin(hitplocal.z 180.0) sin(hitplocal.x 150.0) shade = vec3(0.070, 0.042, 0.032) lambert (0.8 + 0.3 fuzz) shade += suncol pow(1.0 - abs(dot(n, -rd)), 2.5) 0.55 # 6. Compositing dist = length(ro - pos) haze = exp(-0.055 max(dist - 2.0, 0.0)) bgcol = computebackground(rd, uv) # Scene-specific background finalcolor = mix(bgcol, shade, haze) return finalcolor def mapbutterfly(p, t, phase): """Returns (distance, materialid)""" # Body SDF zclamped = clamp(p.z, -0.38, 0.30) u = (zclamped - (-0.38)) / (0.30 - (-0.38)) # Normalized height r = baseradius + gaussianthorax(u) + offset # Base term + Gaussian bump + offset bodydist = sqrt(p.x2 + (p.y 1.12)2) - r # Distance to cylinder surface # Antenna SDF absx = abs(p.x) znorm = clamp(u, 0.0, 1.0) # Clamp normalized z to [0,1] c = cubicbezierpoint(znorm) # Cubic Bezier-like control point antdist = distancetosegment(vec2(absx, znorm), c, radiusinterpolate(u)) # Radius interpolates 0.0045 to 0.014 bodysdf = min(bodydist, antdist) # Wing SDF wingdist = computewingdistance(p, t, phase) # Wing SDF formula not provided in sources. if wingdist < bodysdf: return vec2(wingdist, 0.0) else: return vec2(bodysdf, 1.0) Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is SWARMSIZE and M is MARCHSTEPS. Each butterfly requires a separate ray march. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store swarm data. Performance: Performance is limited by the number of butterflies and the cost of the SDF evaluation and shading per step. The clamping of step sizes ensures stability but may increase the number of steps required for convergence in non-rigid regions. Strengths: Realistic rendering of complex, animated organic shapes (wings) using SDFs. Handles transparency and subsurface scattering effects effectively. Limitations: High computational cost for large swarms. The non-rigid transform can lead to artifacts if step sizes are not carefully clamped. Precision issues may arise with very small distances due to the non-rigid nature of the transform. Butterfly Ray Marching with SDFs is a technique demonstrated in the project "manim-glsl-butterflies" by el-bakkali. It utilizes GLSL shaders within the Manim animation engine to render a swarm of butterflies. The method combines SDFs for geometric representation with ray marching for rendering, specifically addressing the challenge of animating wing flapping through a local coordinate transformation. el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, https://github.com/el-bakkali/manim-glsl-butterflies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Pre-marched Shadow and Ambient Occlusion Baking
head: Baked shadow ray, Pre-marched ambient occlusion
body: A technique to improve visual fidelity and performance by pre-calculating shadow and ambient occlusion data into the volume texture, leveraging the static nature of the cloud volume. It sets itself apart from real-time ray marching by trading runtime compute for a one-time or event-driven baking cost, avoiding expensive per-frame camera renders. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A static signed distance field (SDF) volume representing the cloud geometry. Output: A 3D texture (volume texture) containing baked shadow and ambient occlusion values. Data Structures: Baked Volume Texture: A 3D texture where each voxel stores pre-computed lighting attenuation factors. The resolution is typically low, matching the base cloud volume resolution. Steps: 1. Bake Shadow: Pre-march a shadow ray through the volume for each voxel. This involves casting rays in the direction of the light source(s) to determine occlusion. Detail: Due to the low volume resolution, this can be done in real-time during the baking phase. A typical implementation uses 4 shadow samples per cloud sample. Dynamic Time-of-Day: Because the baking is computationally feasible in real-time (during the bake step, not runtime), the shadow data can be regenerated to allow for dynamic changes in the sun's position (time-of-day) without runtime cost. 2. Bake Ambient Occlusion: Pre-march ambient occlusion rays into the volume texture. This adds shading based on local geometry density without runtime cost. 3. Runtime Lookup: During rendering, retrieve the volumetric cloud shadow using a single tex3D lookup on the baked texture. This ensures the shadow perfectly matches the cloud geometry. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakeshadowandao(sdfvolume, lightdirection, resolution): """ Pre-compute shadow and ambient occlusion for a static SDF volume. """ # Initialize output textures shadowtexture = create3dtexture(resolution) aotexture = create3dtexture(resolution) # Iterate over all voxels in the volume for x in range(resolution.x): for y in range(resolution.y): for z in range(resolution.z): # Get position in world space pos = voxeltoworld(x, y, z, resolution) # --- Bake Shadow --- # Cast shadow ray in light direction # Use 4 samples per cloud sample as per source shadowfactor = 1.0 numshadowsamples = 4 stepsize = getsdfstep(pos, sdfvolume) # From parent method for i in range(numshadowsamples): samplepos = pos + lightdirection (i + 1) stepsize # Check if sample is inside cloud (SDF < 0) if sdfvolume.sample(samplepos) < 0: shadowfactor = 0.0 break shadowtexture.set(x, y, z, shadowfactor) # --- Bake Ambient Occlusion --- # Pre-march ambient occlusion rays # This adds shading without runtime cost aofactor = 1.0 # Implementation details for AO marching are not specified in source # Assume a similar ray marching approach in multiple directions aofactor = computeao(pos, sdfvolume) aotexture.set(x, y, z, aofactor) return shadowtexture, aotexture def rendervoxel(x, y, z, shadowtexture, aotexture): """ Retrieve baked lighting data for a voxel. """ # Single tex3D lookup for shadow shadow = shadowtexture.sample(x, y, z) # Retrieve AO ao = aotexture.sample(x, y, z) # Combine with base cloud color basecolor = getcloudcolor(x, y, z) finalcolor = basecolor shadow ao return finalcolor Parameters: Shadow Samples per Cloud Sample: 4. Volume Resolution: Low, matching the base cloud volume. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Static Assumption: This method relies on the volume being static. If the cloud geometry changes, the baked textures must be regenerated. Memory: Storing separate textures for shadow and AO increases memory usage, though the low resolution mitigates this. Occlusion caching is a performance optimization for static volumetric lighting that pre-calculates shadow and ambient occlusion data into volume textures, avoiding expensive per-frame camera renders. It sets itself apart from real-time ray marching by trading runtime compute for a one-time or event-driven baking cost, leveraging the static nature of most cloud volumes and occluders. Time Complexity: Baking time is proportional to the number of voxels times the number of shadow/AO samples. Since volume resolution is low, baking can be done in real-time (during the bake phase). Runtime cost is O(1) per voxel for texture lookup. Memory Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels, for storing shadow and AO textures. Performance: Significantly reduces runtime cost by eliminating per-frame shadow and AO ray marching. Strengths: Perfect shadow alignment with cloud geometry, low runtime cost, supports dynamic time-of-day if baked dynamically. Limitations: Requires static geometry, increased memory for baked textures, baking cost (though feasible in real-time for low res). When to Use: Static volumetric clouds where high-quality shadows and AO are desired without runtime cost. When Not to Use: Dynamic volumes where geometry changes frequently. Originated in the context of rendering volumetric clouds using signed distance fields, as described in a blog post by uhawkvr. The technique leverages the low resolution of cloud volumes to make pre-marching feasible. Rendering volumetric clouds using signed distance fields, https://blog.uhawkvr.com/rendering/rendering-volumetric-clouds-using-signed-distance-fields/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Occlusion Caching
head: Baked Volumetric Shadows, Baking Occlusion
body: Occlusion caching is a performance optimization for static volumetric lighting that pre-calculates shadow and ambient occlusion data into volume textures, avoiding expensive per-frame camera renders. It sets itself apart from real-time ray marching by trading runtime compute for a one-time or event-driven baking cost, leveraging the static nature of most cloud volumes and occluders. The method consists of two phases: a baking stage where occlusion data is captured and compressed, and a decomposition stage where this data is interpolated at runtime. Inputs: Static light position/orientation, static occluder geometry, camera parameters for capture. Outputs: Occlusion volumes V{occl} containing spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and runtime interpolation weights. Occlusion Volumes (V{occl}): A grid of volumetric cells. Each cell vi^{occl} stores principal components of occlusion as SH coefficients fo^i. Depth Cubemaps (\{\hat{D}p^i\}{p=1}^6): Six depth maps per volume cell, captured from six non-overlapping 90-degree FoV cameras. Occlusion Cubemaps (\{\hat{O}p^i\}{p=1}^6): Derived from depth cubemaps, representing the occlusion state. 1. Baking Stage (Capture): For each volume cell vi^{occl}: 1. Set up six cameras with 90-degree Field of View (FoV), arranged non-overlappingly around the cell center. 2. Perform six render passes to obtain depth cubemaps \{\hat{D}p^i\}{p=1}^6. 3. Convert depth cubemaps \{\hat{D}p^i\}{p=1}^6 into occlusion cubemaps \{\hat{O}p^i\}{p=1}^6. 4. Compute the principal components of the occlusion data and store them as SH coefficients fo^i for the cell. 2. Decomposition Stage (Runtime Interpolation): For a surface point x with normal n: 1. Identify the eight nearest occlusion volumes \{vk\}{k=1}^8 to x. Let pk be the position vector of volume vk and fk^o be its SH coefficients. 2. Calculate standard trilinear interpolation weights \{wk\}{k=1}^8 based on the relative position of x within the grid. 3. Apply Masked Trilinear Interpolation to compute modified weights \tilde{w}k: \tilde{w}k = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } (pk - x) \cdot n \le 0 \\ wk & \text{if } (pk - x) \cdot n > 0 \end{cases} This mask ensures that only occlusion from the upper hemisphere defined by n contributes to the ambient occlusion integral. 4. Normalize the weights: \hat{w}k = \frac{\tilde{w}k}{\sum{j=1}^8 \tilde{w}j} 5. Interpolate the SH coefficients to obtain the final occlusion coefficients fx^o: fx^o = \sum{k=1}^8 \hat{w}k fk^o Bake Interval: Controls caching behavior. On Start: Captures once at startup; re-captures if light moves or rotates (unless Ignore Rotation is enabled). Every Frame: Continuous capture for dynamic occluders. Shadow Resolution: Resolution of the capture cubemaps (e.g., 512x512). Ignore Rotation: Boolean flag. If enabled, rotating the light does not trigger re-capture; the map is reprojected. Auto Toggle Distance: Distance threshold beyond which occlusion is disabled for far lights. Check Time Interval: Frequency of Auto Toggle distance checks. Default: 1 second. Dynamic Occluders: If occluders move independently of the light (e.g., a fan), "On Start" baking will produce stale shadows. Use "Every Frame" or event-driven updates. Rotation: Without "Ignore Rotation," rotating a static light triggers a full re-capture, increasing cost. Enable this flag for lights with attached occluders (e.g., lamp cages). Visibility: Capture can be suspended when the light volume is not visible to any camera to save resources. Point Light Orientation: For "Point Light Half Sphere To Camera" mode, re-capture only occurs if the camera direction changes by more than 45 degrees. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class VolumetricLight: def init(self): self.enableshadows = False self.shadowbakeinterval = "OnStart" # or "EveryFrame" self.shadowresolution = 512 self.ignorerotation = False self.autotoggledistance = 100.0 self.checktimeinterval = 1.0 self.occlusionvolumes = {} # Map of cellid -> SHcoefficients def updatematerialproperties(self): """Apply settings to the rendering pipeline.""" pass def scheduleshadowcapture(self): """Trigger a manual re-capture of occlusion data.""" self.performbake() def performbake(self): """ Baking stage: 1. For each volume cell vi: a. Render 6 depth cubemaps from 90-degree FoV cameras. b. Convert to occlusion cubemaps. c. Compute SH coefficients fo^i. d. Store in occlusionvolumes. """ for cellid, cellcenter in self.getvolumecells(): depthcubemaps = rendersixcubemaps(cellcenter, fov=90) occlusioncubemaps = convertdepthtoocclusion(depthcubemaps) shcoeffs = computeshcoefficients(occlusioncubemaps) self.occlusionvolumes[cellid] = shcoeffs def getocclusionatpoint(self, pointx, normaln): """ Decomposition stage: 1. Find 8 nearest volumes. 2. Compute masked trilinear weights. 3. Interpolate SH coefficients. """ nearestvolumes = self.find8nearestvolumes(pointx) totalweight = 0.0 interpolatedsh = [0.0] 15 # Assuming 4th order SH (15 coeffs) for vol in nearestvolumes: pk = vol.position fk = vol.shcoefficients wk = computetrilinearweight(pointx, pk) # Masked Trilinear Interpolation if dot(pk - pointx, normaln) <= 0: wtildek = 0.0 else: wtildek = wk totalweight += wtildek for i in range(len(interpolatedsh)): interpolatedsh[i] += wtildek fk[i] if totalweight > 0: for i in range(len(interpolatedsh)): interpolatedsh[i] /= totalweight return interpolatedsh A variant of the interpolation step used in the decomposition phase. Standard trilinear interpolation weights \{wk\} are modified to \{\tilde{w}k\} by zeroing out contributions from volumes where the vector from the sample point to the volume center has a non-positive dot product with the surface normal ( (pk - x) \cdot n \le 0). This ensures that ambient occlusion is only calculated from the upper hemisphere relative to the surface normal, preventing incorrect shadowing from below. Time Complexity: Baking is O(N \cdot F) where N is the number of volume cells and F is the number of frames captured. Runtime interpolation is O(1) per sample, involving only 8 nearest neighbor lookups and linear interpolation. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot C) where C is the number of SH coefficients per cell. Additional memory for depth cubemaps during baking. Performance: Eliminates per-frame shadow ray marching for static lights, significantly reducing GPU load. Strengths: Ideal for static scenes with static occluders (windows, street lamps). Event-driven updates handle occasional changes (doors opening) efficiently. Limitations: Not suitable for highly dynamic scenes with moving occluders unless "Every Frame" baking is used, which negates performance gains. Reprojection errors may occur if "Ignore Rotation" is used with complex occluder geometries. When to Use: Static volumetric lights with static or slowly moving occluders. When Not to Use: Real-time dynamic occlusion requirements without acceptable latency for re-baking. Occlusion caching in volumetric rendering was introduced to address the high computational cost of real-time shadow calculation for volumetric lights. The technique leverages the fact that many volumetric lights and their occluders are static in typical scenes. The method of using SH coefficients to store occlusion data and masked trilinear interpolation for decomposition is detailed in the GS-IR paper. The Unity URP implementation provides practical settings and runtime behaviors for game engines. GS-IR: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52733.2024.02045, fetched 2026-10-26 Volumetric Lighting in Unity URP: Shadows, Translucency..., https://kronnect.com/company/blog/volumetric-lighting-unity-urp-guide/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: SDF Texture Baking for Ray Marching
head: 3D SDF Baking for Cloud Sphere Tracing, Cloud SDF texture baking, Conservative SDF proxy for raymarching
body: This method optimizes cloud raymarching by baking a low-resolution 3D Signed Distance Field (SDF) texture that acts as a conservative proxy for the analytical cloud SDF. It allows the marching loop to skip empty space conservatively before falling back to analytical evaluations inside active cells. It sets itself apart from its siblings by decoupling the geometric query cost from the frame rate during camera motion, trading bounded spatial precision for significant interactive performance gains. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Analytical cloud SDF function (lofted cloud SDF), dynamic cloud parameters (position, density, shape), camera ray origin and direction. Output: A 3D texture containing the baked SDF values, used to accelerate the raymarching loop in atmospherelowres.comp. Data Structures: cloudSdf3DTexture: A 3D texture with the following layout: Resolution: 128 \times 32 \times 128 (width \times height \times depth). Format: GLR32F (single-channel 32-bit floating point). Binding: Texture Unit 45. Wrapping: GLREPEAT horizontally (X-axis), GLCLAMPTOEDGE vertically (Y-axis). Layered Flag: GLTRUE. Steps: 1. Bake SDF: Create a compute shader (cloud3dsdfbake.comp) to analytically bake the lofted cloud SDF into the 3D texture using unadvected coordinates. 2. Allocate Texture: Allocate and manage cloudSdf3DTexture in AtmosphereManager with the specified format and bindings. 3. Dispatch Bake Shader: Dispatch the 3D SDF bake shader every frame in AtmosphereManager::Update to ensure synchrony with dynamic cloud parameters and solve initialization frame order issues. 4. Optimize Raymarching: In atmospherelowres.comp, first sample the 3D SDF texture to skip empty space conservatively. 5. Fallback Evaluation: Perform full analytical evaluations only inside active cells (where the SDF indicates presence). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. # # # Parameters: Texture resolution: 128 \times 32 \times 128. Texture format: GLR32F. Texture unit binding: Unit 45. Texture wrapping mode: GLREPEAT horizontally, GLCLAMPTOEDGE vertically. Texture layered flag: GLTRUE. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Initialization Frame Order: Dispatching the bake shader every frame solves initialization frame order issues. Dynamic Parameters: The bake shader must be dispatched whenever cloud parameters are updated to ensure synchrony. Conservative Skip: The SDF texture acts as a conservative proxy, meaning it may overestimate empty space, potentially skipping valid samples if the resolution is too low. This method optimizes interactive camera navigation (orbit/dolly) over static fractal surfaces by baking the expensive analytical Distance Estimator (DE) into a sparse 3D brick volume, allowing the renderer to sample precomputed distances instead of re-evaluating the fractal formula every frame. It sets itself apart from standard raymarching by decoupling the geometric query cost from the frame rate during camera motion, trading bounded spatial precision for significant interactive performance gains. Time Complexity: The baking step is O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the 3D texture (128 \times 32 \times 128 = 524,288 voxels). The raymarching step is accelerated by skipping empty space, reducing the number of analytical evaluations. Memory Complexity: The 3D texture requires 128 \times 32 \times 128 \times 4 bytes = 2 MB of VRAM. Measured Performance: All unit tests and shader validations passed 100% successfully. Strengths: Significant performance gains for interactive camera motion by decoupling geometric query cost from frame rate. Limitations: Bounded spatial precision due to low-resolution texture; may skip valid samples if the proxy is not conservative enough. When to Use: Interactive cloud rendering with dynamic parameters and camera motion. When Not to Use: High-fidelity offline rendering where precision is critical. This method was introduced by ricecake in a GitHub Pull Request (PR #636) to the boidsish repository on July 11, 2026. It was created to optimize cloud sphere tracing by baking a low-resolution 3D SDF texture. name: Sparse Distance-Field Cache for Interactive Camera Moves
head: SDF brick cache, Sparse distance-field cache for interactive 3D camera moves, sparse brick volume cache
body: This method optimizes interactive camera navigation (orbit/dolly) over static fractal surfaces by baking the expensive analytical Distance Estimator (DE) into a sparse 3D brick volume, allowing the renderer to sample precomputed distances instead of re-evaluating the fractal formula every frame. It sets itself apart from standard raymarching by decoupling the geometric query cost from the frame rate during camera motion, trading bounded spatial precision for significant interactive performance gains. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The analytical Distance Estimator function DE(x, y, z) for the fractal surface, the current camera view volume, and a maximum brick count limit. Output: A sparse 3D texture (brick volume) containing precomputed distance values, used for raymarching during interactive preview. Data Structures: 1. Brick Volume: A sparse 3D grid where each active cell is a "brick." Brick Layout: Each brick is a small 3D texture (e.g., N \times N \times N voxels). Voxel Content: A single floating-point value representing the signed distance to the surface. Sparsity: Only bricks where the surface exists (defined by DE < \text{brick size}) are allocated. Empty space is represented by the coarse-level empty-space distance. 2. Coarse Level: A lower-resolution representation of the brick volume storing the empty-space distance for regions outside the active surface boundary. Parameters: Brick Count: Must be capped to control GPU memory usage. Brick Resolution: Determines the bounded detail level; suitable for preview, not final output. Bake Time: Must be less than a few frames' worth of computation to be beneficial. Algorithm Steps: 1. Progressive Baking: Start by baking the coarse level of the brick volume. Iterate through the 3D space around the surface. For each potential brick location, evaluate the analytical DE(x, y, z) at the brick center. If DE < \text{brick size}, allocate the brick and populate its voxels by sampling the analytical DE at each voxel center within the brick. Store the empty-space distance at the coarse level for regions where no bricks are allocated. Continue until the brick count limit is reached or the surface boundary is fully covered. 2. Interactive Raymarching: When the camera moves, perform raymarching using the sparse brick volume. For each ray step, sample the distance from the brick volume using trilinear interpolation. Utilize hardware texture filtering on the GPU for efficient trilinear distance sampling. Use the sampled distance to advance the ray. 3. Cache Rebuild: Rebuild the cache only when fractal parameters change, not on every frame. 4. Final Render: Once the camera interaction settles, run the full-detail DE render using the analytical formula to produce the final high-quality frame. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bakesparsesdfcache(defunction, cameraviewvolume, maxbrickcount, bricksize, brickresolution): """ Bakes the distance field into a sparse brick volume. """ brickvolume = Sparse3DTexture() coarselevel = CoarseLevelTexture() # Define the bounding box of the camera view volume bounds = cameraviewvolume.getbounds() # Iterate through the volume in brick-sized steps # Note: In practice, this might use a hierarchical traversal or spatial hashing # to efficiently find active bricks. brickcount = 0 for x in range(bounds.minx, bounds.maxx, bricksize): for y in range(bounds.miny, bounds.maxy, bricksize): for z in range(bounds.minz, bounds.maxz, bricksize): # Check if this brick is near the surface center = Vector3(x + bricksize/2, y + bricksize/2, z + bricksize/2) dist = defunction(center) if dist < bricksize: # Allocate brick and populate brick = Brick(brickresolution) for i in range(brickresolution): for j in range(brickresolution): for k in range(brickresolution): voxelpos = center + Vector3( (i - brickresolution/2) (bricksize / brickresolution), (j - brickresolution/2) (bricksize / brickresolution), (k - brickresolution/2) (bricksize / brickresolution)) voxeldist = defunction(voxelpos) brick.setvoxel(i, j, k, voxeldist) brickvolume.setbrick(x, y, z, brick) brickcount += 1 if brickcount >= maxbrickcount: break if brickcount >= maxbrickcount: break if brickcount >= maxbrickcount: break # Populate coarse level with empty space distance # This is a simplified representation; in reality, it might store # the distance to the nearest brick or a conservative bound. coarselevel.populateemptyspacedistance(brickvolume, bricksize) return brickvolume, coarselevel def raymarchwithcache(brickvolume, coarselevel, rayorigin, raydirection, bricksize, brickresolution): """ Raymarches using the sparse SDF cache. """ t = 0.0 maxsteps = 1000 for step in range(maxsteps): currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # Determine which brick contains the current position brickcoords = getbrickcoords(currentpos, bricksize) # Sample distance from brick volume # Use trilinear interpolation for smooth distance estimation if brickvolume.hasbrick(brickcoords): dist = brickvolume.sampletrilinear(brickcoords, currentpos, bricksize, brickresolution) else: # Fallback to coarse level empty space distance dist = coarselevel.sampleemptyspacedistance(currentpos) # Advance ray t += dist # Check for surface intersection (distance is very small) if dist < 1e-4: return t, True # Check if ray has left the view volume (simplified) if not isinsideviewvolume(rayorigin + raydirection t): return t, False return t, False Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The cached-distance error is \le half a voxel diagonal near the surface. This is acceptable for preview but not final output. Memory: The brick count must be capped; otherwise, memory usage can explode for complex fractals. Bake Time: If the bake time exceeds a few frames, the performance gain is lost. Degenerate Input: If the fractal parameters change, the cache must be rebuilt; using stale data leads to incorrect geometry. Time Complexity: Baking is O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the active surface region. Interactive raymarching is O(1) per step for distance queries (assuming hardware texture sampling), compared to O(K) for analytical DE evaluation where K is the number of iterations in the fractal formula. Memory Complexity: O(B \cdot R^3) where B is the number of bricks and R is the brick resolution. Capped by maxbrickcount. Measured Performance: Reduces frame time from seconds to near real time for heavy User Bulb maps and KIFS on interactive camera moves. Strengths: Significant speedup for interactive camera navigation on expensive fractal formulas; works well on weak and strong hardware for heavy maps. Limitations: Bounded detail level makes it unsuitable for final output; requires rebuild on parameter changes; memory usage can be high if not capped. When to Use: Interactive preview, orbit/dolly camera moves over static fractals. When Not to Use: Final rendering, dynamic fractal parameters, scenes requiring high-precision distance estimates. This technique was proposed in an issue on the FracturingFog repository, drawing inspiration from games, offline renderers, and GPU computing. It addresses the performance bottleneck of re-evaluating expensive fractal Distance Estimators (DE) every frame during camera movement, a common issue in real-time fractal rendering applications like Dreams/Claybook. The method is part of Phase 3b of issue #1298, focusing on GPU/rendering performance improvements. name: Squared Distance Field Optimization
head: SDF Squared Distance Trick, Squared Distance Optimization
body: Squared Distance Field Optimization is a technique to avoid the computational cost of square root operations in Signed Distance Field (SDF) raymarching by using squared distances for sphere comparisons, leveraging the monotonicity of the squaring function. It sets itself apart from standard SDF ray marching by replacing Euclidean distance metrics with squared metrics for specific primitives to eliminate sqrt calls, which are often expensive on GPU architectures. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin O and direction D, and a scene containing at least one sphere (defined by center C and radius r) and other objects with known distance functions. Output: The minimum distance to the closest surface along the ray, or the intersection point, computed without evaluating square roots for the spherical components. Data Structures: No specific data structure changes are required beyond the standard representation of spheres. The optimization is purely algebraic within the distance query function. Steps: 1. Compute Squared Sphere Distance: Calculate the squared distance from the query point P to the surface of the sphere using the formula dot(pos - spherecenter, pos - spherecenter) - sphereradius sphereradius. 2. Square Other Distances: Square the distance to the closest object in the rest of the scene to convert it to a squared distance metric. 3. Minimize Squared Distances: Take the minimum of the squared sphere distance and the squared distance to other objects to determine the closest surface. 4. Propagate Squared Metric: Propagate the use of squared distances further in the program, avoiding taking a root as far as possible. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def squareddistancetosphere(point, center, radius): diff = point - center squareddisttocenter = dot(diff, diff) squaredradius = radius radius return squareddisttocenter - squaredradius def raymarchstepsquared(rayorigin, raydir, sceneobjects): minsqdist = float('inf') for obj in sceneobjects: if obj.type == 'sphere': sqdist = squareddistancetosphere(rayorigin, obj.center, obj.radius) else: # Not given in sources. sqdist = 0.0 if sqdist < minsqdist: minsqdist = sqdist return minsqdist Parameters: sphereradius: The radius of the sphere, used in the squared distance calculation as sphereradius sphereradius. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Marching Step Size: Using squared distance for ray marching step size (currDst) is incorrect unless the ray hits the center of the sphere exactly, as the distance moved along the ray is not a distance measured along the ray. Intersection vs. Distance: Squared distance fields are suitable for intersection tests or when only the zero levelset is needed, but direct ray-sphere intersection is preferred if only intersection is required. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Avoids the computational cost of square root operations in SDF raymarching by leveraging the monotonicity of the squaring function. Limitations: Cannot be used directly for step size calculation; requires careful handling of mixed distance metrics (squared vs. Euclidean) in the same scene. This technique was discussed in the context of CUDA programming and ray tracing optimization on Stack Overflow in 2019. It leverages the mathematical property that minimizing squared distances is equivalent to minimizing Euclidean distances for non-negative values due to the monotonicity of the squaring function. The most effective way of computing distance to sphere in CUDA?, https://stackoverflow.com/questions/55930232/the-most-effective-way-of-computing-distance-to-sphere-in-cuda, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Recursive Ray Marching with Early Stopping
head: Dynamic Synchronized Inference
body: Recursive Ray Marching with Early Stopping is a parallelization technique for differentiable sphere tracing that maintains a dynamic mask of unfinished rays to prevent wasted computation on rays that have already converged or exited the scene. It differs from its siblings, such as Beam Optimization which prunes low-probability paths, and Performance Optimizations for SDF Ray Marching which may use static acceleration structures, by explicitly managing the active set of rays at every iteration to handle heterogeneous convergence rates across the image plane. The method operates on a batch of camera rays, iteratively marching them until they converge to the surface or exit the bounding volume. It uses a boolean mask to track active rays, concatenating only active rays for SDF queries to save memory and compute. Inputs: Camera rays: origin \mathbf{o}i and direction \mathbf{d}i for each pixel i \in [0, H \times W - 1]. SDF function f(\mathbf{p}): returns signed distance and optionally gradient. Parameters: maxsteps (default 100), ratio (step multiplier, default 1.5), threshold (convergence stop, default 5 \times 10^{-5}). Outputs: Rendered depth, normal, color, or silhouette for each pixel. Gradients for optimization (if differentiable). Data Structures: marchingzdepth: Tensor of shape (N), storing the accumulated distance along each ray. Initialized to 0. unfinishedmask: Boolean tensor of shape (N), initially all True. raypositions: Tensor of shape (N, 3), storing current 3D position of each ray. queryhistory: List of tensors storing query positions for backpropagation. Steps: 1. Initialization: Set marchingzdepth to zeros. Set raypositions to ray origins \mathbf{o}i. Set unfinishedmask to True for all rays within the valid viewing frustum (or unit sphere bounds). 2. Iteration Loop: For step k from 1 to maxsteps: a. Select Active Rays: Identify indices where unfinishedmask is True. Let this set be Ak. If Ak is empty, break loop. b. Query SDF: Extract positions \mathbf{p}j for j \in Ak. Compute \mathbf{d}j = f(\mathbf{p}j) and \mathbf{g}j = \nabla f(\mathbf{p}j). c. Update Positions: For each active ray j: \text{step\size}j = \min(\mathbf{d}j, \text{max\step\limit}) \times \text{ratio} \mathbf{p}j \leftarrow \mathbf{p}j + \mathbf{d}j \cdot \text{step\size}j \text{marching\zdepth}j \leftarrow \text{marching\zdepth}j + \text{step\size}j Note: The step size is clamped to avoid overshooting thin structures. The ratio parameter (typically 1.2–1.8) scales the SDF value to ensure stability. d. Check Convergence: For each active ray j: If |\mathbf{d}j| < \text{threshold}, the ray has converged. If the ray has exited the bounding volume (e.g., distance from origin > sphere radius), mark as converged. Set unfinishedmask[j] = False for converged rays. e. Gradient Handling (Differentiable Rendering): To compute gradients without unaffordable memory consumption from storing all query locations: 1. Save query locations globally in queryhistory. 2. Perform minimization of absolute SDF over a detached tensor graph (no gradients) to find the minimum K queries per ray. 3. Retrieve these specific queries and re-evaluate the SDF with gradients attached. 4. Typical K values: 1 for depth rendering, 3 for shape completion, 1 for multi-view reconstruction. 3. Final Compositing: For rays still active after maxsteps, use the final position or mark as background. Map results back to original image resolution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def recursiveraymarchingwithearlystopping(rays, sdffunc, maxsteps=100, ratio=1.5, threshold=5e-5, K=1): """ rays: Tensor of shape (N, 2, 3) [origin, direction] sdffunc: Function returning (distance, gradient) """ N = rays.shape[0] positions = rays[:, 0,:] # (N, 3) directions = rays[:, 1,:] # (N, 3) zdepth = torch.zeros(N) # (N,) unfinishedmask = torch.ones(N, dtype=torch.bool) # (N,) queryhistory = [] # List of (N, 3) tensors for step in range(maxsteps): # Select active rays activeindices = torch.where(unfinishedmask)[0] if len(activeindices) == 0: break activepositions = positions[activeindices] # Query SDF distances, gradients = sdffunc(activepositions) # Store for backprop (detached for minimization step) queryhistory.append(activepositions.detach()) # Update positions # Clamp step size to prevent overshooting, scaled by ratio stepsizes = torch.clamp(distances, max=1.0) ratio newpositions = activepositions + directions[activeindices] stepsizes.unsqueeze(1) # Update global state positions[activeindices] = newpositions zdepth[activeindices] += stepsizes # Check convergence converged = (torch.abs(distances) < threshold) unfinishedmask[activeindices] = ~converged # Gradient computation using K best queries # This part is simplified; actual implementation requires careful tensor manipulation # to find min |SDF| per ray from queryhistory and re-evaluate with gradients. # See for detailed implementation of "Dynamic Synchronized Inference" gradient trick. return zdepth, positions Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: When close to the surface, SDF values are small, leading to slow convergence. The threshold must be chosen relative to the rendering resolution and object scale. Thin Structures: Large ratio values can cause rays to overshoot thin surfaces, creating holes. Empirical values range from 1.2 to 1.8. Memory: Storing all query positions for backpropagation is memory-intensive. The detached tensor minimization trick is essential for high-resolution rendering (e.g., 2048x2048). Dynamically adjusts the number of steps per ray based on the count of currently active rays, differing from this method which uses a fixed step count per iteration but variable active set size. Processes rays in explicit batches with a fixed step count per batch, differing from this method which updates a single active set with variable steps per iteration. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S{active}), where N is the number of rays and S{active} is the average number of steps per active ray. Early stopping reduces S{active} for converged rays, improving performance over fixed-step marching. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot K) for storing query history for backpropagation, where K is the number of queries kept per ray. Performance: Enables high-resolution rendering (2048x2048) on single GPUs (e.g., GTX-1080Ti) by avoiding wasted computation on converged rays. Strengths: Efficient for scenes with varying depth complexity; reduces compute for background and converged foreground pixels. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of ratio and threshold; gradient computation is complex due to the dynamic mask and history management. The method was introduced as "Dynamic Synchronized Inference" in the DIST (Differentiable Implicit Signed Distance) framework. It addresses the inefficiency of naive parallel sphere tracing where all rays are updated synchronously, leading to wasted computation when some rays converge earlier than others. The implementation details were further explored in unofficial repositories such as B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer. DIST: Rendering Deep Implicit Signed Distance Function With Differentiable Sphere Tracing, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr42600.2020.00209, fetched 2026-10-26 B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, https://github.com/B1ueber2y/DIST-Renderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Dynamic Step Count
head: CUDA Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count
body: Adaptive Ray Marching with Dynamic Step Count is an iterative volume rendering algorithm that samples rays until they are occluded or a maximum step count is reached, using a density grid for acceleration. It differs from its parent, Recursive Ray Marching with Early Stopping, by dynamically adjusting the number of steps per ray based on the count of currently active rays. The method operates in an iterative loop that determines the number of currently active rays and calculates a step batch size for them. It proceeds by marching these rays, querying densities and colors, and compositing the results. Inputs: rayso: Ray origins, shape [B, N, 3]. raysd: Ray directions, shape [B, N, 3]. near, far: Near and far clipping planes. bound: Bounding box parameters. densitygrid: Acceleration structure (density grid). meandensity: Mean density value for normalization or thresholding. bgcolor: Background color, default 1.0. perturb: Boolean flag for ray perturbation. alphapremultiplied: Boolean flag determining output normalization. B: Batch size. N: Number of rays per batch. Outputs: image: Rendered image, shape [B, N, 4]. The first three channels are RGB, and the fourth channel is the accumulated weight sum (transparency mask). raysalive: A ping-pong buffer array of two boolean tensors, shape [2, B, N]. raysalive[i % 2] indicates which rays are still active in the current iteration i. rayst: A ping-pong buffer array of two float tensors, shape [2, B, N]. rayst[i % 2] stores the current accumulated distance along the ray for active rays. alivecounter: An integer scalar tracking the total number of active rays across the batch. weightssum: Accumulated weight (opacity) per ray, shape [B, N]. depth: Accumulated depth per ray, shape [B, N]. nstep: Number of steps to process per alive ray in the current iteration. B: Batch size. N: Number of rays per batch. nalive: Number of currently active rays. 1. Initialization: Initialize raysalive[0] to all True (all rays start alive). Initialize rayst[0] to near. Initialize weightssum and depth to 0. Initialize step (global step counter) to 0. Initialize alivecounter to B \times N. 2. Loop Condition: While alivecounter > 0: a. Calculate Alive Rays: Determine nalive = alivecounter.item(). b. Exit Check: If nalive <= 0, break the loop. c. Calculate Steps: Compute nstep = max(min(B N // nalive, 8), 1). d. Ray Marching: Call raymarching.marchrays with nalive, nstep, raysalive[i % 2], rayst[i % 2], rayso, raysd, bound, densitygrid, meandensity, near, far, 128, perturb. This function updates raysalive[(i+1) % 2] and rayst[(i+1) % 2] for the next iteration, marking rays as dead if they hit a surface or exceed bounds. It returns sampled positions xyzs and directions dirs for the active steps. e. Neural Network Query: Compute densities (sigmas) and colors (rgbs) by passing xyzs and dirs through the neural network: sigmas, rgbs = self(xyzs, dirs). f. Compositing: Call raymarching.compositerays with nalive, nstep, raysalive[i % 2], rayst[i % 2], sigmas, rgbs, deltas, weightssum, depth, image. This function updates weightssum, depth, and image based on volume rendering integration. g. Update Step Counter: step += nstep. h. Background Compositing: If alphapremultiplied is true, image = image + (1 - weightssum).unsqueeze(-1) bgcolor (default bgcolor = 1). If alphapremultiplied is false, image /= (weightssum + 1e-9).unsqueeze(-1). i. Concatenate Weight Sum: image = torch.cat([image, weightssum.unsqueeze(-1)], -1). j. Swap Buffers: Swap raysalive and rayst buffers for the next iteration (toggle i % 2). k. Update Alive Counter: Recalculate alivecounter based on the new raysalive mask. 3. Final Reshape: Reshape image to [B, N, 4]. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def adaptiveraymarching(rayso, raysd, near, far, bgcolor=1.0, alphapremultiplied=False, perturb=False, bound=None, densitygrid=None, meandensity=None, B=1, N=1): # Initialize ping-pong buffers and accumulators raysalive = [[True] (B N), [False] (B N)] rayst = [[near] (B N), [0.0] (B N)] weightssum = [0.0] (B N) depth = [0.0] (B N) image = [0.0] (B N 3) alivecounter = B N step = 0 i = 0 while alivecounter > 0: nalive = alivecounter if nalive <= 0: break nstep = max(min((B N) // nalive, 8), 1) # GPU kernel: marches rays, checks bounds/density, updates alive mask and t # Returns: xyzs, dirs, deltas, newalivemask, newt xyzs, dirs, deltas, newalivemask, newt = marchrays( nalive, nstep, raysalive[i % 2], rayst[i % 2], rayso, raysd, bound, densitygrid, meandensity, near, far, 128, perturb) # Neural network forward pass sigmas, rgbs = networkforward(xyzs, dirs) # Composite rays: updates weightssum, depth, image weightssum, depth, image = compositerays( nalive, nstep, raysalive[i % 2], rayst[i % 2], sigmas, rgbs, deltas, weightssum, depth, image) step += nstep # Background compositing or normalization if alphapremultiplied: for k in range(B N): image[k3] += (1.0 - weightssum[k]) bgcolor image[k3+1] += (1.0 - weightssum[k]) bgcolor image[k3+2] += (1.0 - weightssum[k]) bgcolor else: for k in range(B N): denom = weightssum[k] + 1e-9 image[k3] /= denom image[k3+1] /= denom image[k3+2] /= denom # Swap ping-pong buffers raysalive[(i + 1) % 2] = newalivemask rayst[(i + 1) % 2] = newt # Update alive counter alivecounter = sum(1 for x in newalivemask if x) i += 1 # Concatenate weight sum to image channels and reshape to [B, N, 4] image.extend(weightssum) return image def compositerays(nalive, nstep, raysalive, rayst, sigmas, rgbs, deltas, weightssum, depth, image): for r in range(nalive): wacc = 0.0 dacc = 0.0 rgbacc = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] T = 1.0 for s in range(nstep): sigma = sigmas[r nstep + s] rgb = rgbs[r nstep + s] dt = deltas[r nstep + s] alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma dt) w = alpha T wacc += w dacc += (rayst[r] + dt) w rgbacc[0] += rgb[0] w rgbacc[1] += rgb[1] w rgbacc[2] += rgb[2] w T = (1.0 - alpha) weightssum[r] = wacc depth[r] = dacc image[r3] = rgbacc[0] image[r3+1] = rgbacc[1] image[r3+2] = rgbacc[2] return weightssum, depth, image def marchrays(nalive, nstep, raysalive, rayst, rayso, raysd, bound, densitygrid, meandensity, near, far, blocksize, perturb): # GPU kernel: marches rays, checks bounds/density, updates alive mask and t # Returns: xyzs, dirs, deltas, newalivemask, newt return [], [], [], [], [] def networkforward(xyzs, dirs): # Neural network forward pass return [], [] Division by Zero: When alphapremultiplied is false, the normalization step divides by weightssum. If a ray has zero accumulated opacity (e.g., passed through empty space), this causes division by zero. The implementation adds 1e-9 to the denominator to avoid this. Zero Alive Rays: The loop checks nalive <= 0 to exit early, preventing unnecessary computation. Step Count Calculation: The formula max(min(B N // nalive, 8), 1) ensures that nstep is at least 1. If nalive is very small, nstep becomes 1, processing rays one by one in terms of step batches, which may reduce efficiency but prevents excessive steps per ray. This variant uses a hash grid (specifically a density bitfield) for acceleration instead of a dense grid. It calculates the number of samples per ray based on the scene scale and a step factor. For each alive ray, it marches along the ray, checking the hash grid for occupied voxels. If a voxel is occupied, it samples the neural network; otherwise, it skips to the next occupied voxel. The step size is calculated using an exponential step factor (expstepfactor), which is 1/256 if the scene scale is greater than 0.5, otherwise 0. The hash grid uses morton codes for indexing, and the density bitfield is stored as a bitfield of uint8 values. Parameters include gridsize (resolution of the hash grid), cascades (number of levels in the density bitfield), and scale (size of the scene bounding box). Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for ping-pong buffers (raysalive, rayst), neural network weights, and the acceleration structure (density grid or hash grid). Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Efficient handling of sparse scenes, reduced computation on terminated rays, good hardware utilization. Limitations: Performance may degrade if the number of active rays is very small (leading to small batch sizes) or very large (leading to many iterations). The fixed step cap (8) may limit accuracy in highly detailed regions. This method is derived from implementations in neural radiance fields (NeRF) and instant-NGP, where adaptive ray marching is used to optimize rendering speed. The specific implementation with dynamic step count and hash grid acceleration is found in unofficial repositories. megvii-research/cv-master-ex, https://github.com/megvii-research/cv-master-ex, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, https://github.com/Linyou/taichi-ngp-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Ray Marching (Test)
head: Iterative volume rendering, Progressive ray marching
body: Adaptive Ray Marching (Test) is an iterative volume rendering technique that marches rays in batches, composites results, and stops rays that have converged (transmittance below a threshold) to save computation. It differs from standard fixed-step ray marching by dynamically reducing the number of active rays over iterations, and from Recursive Ray Marching with Early Stopping by processing rays in explicit batches with a fixed step count per batch rather than updating a single active set with variable steps. Inputs: Ray origins rayso and directions raysd (shape: N{rays} \times 3). Hit bounds hitst (shape: N{rays} \times 2, start and end distances). Neural network model evaluating density (sigmas) and color (rgbs) at sample points. Background color rgbbg. Parameters: Tthreshold (default 10^{-4}), MAXSAMPLES (default 1024), expstepfactor (default 0). Outputs: Final RGB image rgb (shape: N{rays} \times 3). Final opacity opacity (shape: N{rays}). Final depth depth (shape: N{rays}). Data Structures: aliveindices: 1D tensor of indices into the ray batch that have not yet converged. Initialized to [0, 1,..., Nrays - 1]. opacity, depth, rgb: Accumulators initialized to zeros. samples: Integer counter for total samples processed per ray. Steps: 1. Initialize opacity, depth, rgb to zeros. Set aliveindices to all ray indices. Set samples = 0. Set minsamples = 1 (or 4 if expstepfactor != 0). 2. While samples < MAXSAMPLES: a. Let N{alive} = \text{len}(alive\indices). If N{alive} == 0, break.. b. Calculate batch size N{samples} = \max(\min(N{rays} // N{alive}, 64), min\samples). c. Increment samples by N{samples}. d. Generate sample points for the N{alive} rays using raymarchingtest. This returns xyzs (shape: N{alive} \times N{samples} \times 3), dirs (shape: N{alive} \times N{samples} \times 3), deltas (shape: N{alive} \times N{samples}), ts (shape: N{alive} \times N{samples}), and Neffsamples. e. Flatten xyzs and dirs to 2D: (N{alive} \times N{samples}) \times 3. f. Compute validmask where dirs are not zero vectors: validmask = ~torch.all(dirs==0, dim=1). If validmask.sum() == 0, break. g. Initialize sigmas and rgbs tensors of size (N{alive} \times N{samples}) and (N{alive} \times N{samples} \times 3) with zeros. Evaluate the neural network at xyzs[validmask] and dirs[validmask] to get sigmas and rgbs, filling only the valid entries. h. Reshape sigmas and rgbs back to (N{alive} \times N{samples}) and (N{alive} \times N{samples} \times 3) respectively. i. Call compositetestfw with sigmas, rgbs, deltas, ts, hitst[:, 0], aliveindices, Tthreshold, Neffsamples, and the accumulators opacity, depth, rgb to update them in-place. j. Filter aliveindices to keep only valid indices (aliveindices >= 0). 3. After the loop, add background color: rgb += rgbbg (1 - opacity). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveraymarchingtest(rayso, raysd, hitst, model, rgbbg, Tthreshold=1e-4, MAXSAMPLES=1024, expstepfactor=0): Nrays = rayso.shape[0] device = rayso.device # Initialize accumulators opacity = torch.zeros(Nrays, device=device) depth = torch.zeros(Nrays, device=device) rgb = torch.zeros(Nrays, 3, device=device) # Initialize alive indices aliveindices = torch.arange(Nrays, device=device) samples = 0 minsamples = 4 if expstepfactor != 0 else 1 while samples < MAXSAMPLES: Nalive = len(aliveindices) if Nalive == 0: break # Calculate batch size Nsamples = max(min(Nrays // Nalive, 64), minsamples) samples += Nsamples # Generate sample points xyzs, dirs, deltas, ts, Neffsamples = raymarchingtest( rayso, raysd, hitst[:, 0], aliveindices, model.densitybitfield, model.cascades, model.scale, expstepfactor, model.gridsize, MAXSAMPLES, Nsamples) # Flatten for network evaluation xyzs = xyzs.reshape(-1, 3) dirs = dirs.reshape(-1, 3) # Filter invalid directions validmask = ~torch.all(dirs == 0, dim=1) if validmask.sum() == 0: break # Evaluate neural network sigmas = torch.zeros(len(xyzs), device=device) rgbs = torch.zeros(len(xyzs), 3, device=device) sigmasvalid, rgbsvalid = model(xyzs[validmask], dirs[validmask]) sigmas[validmask] = sigmasvalid rgbs[validmask] = rgbsvalid.float() # Reshape back sigmas = sigmas.reshape(Nalive, Nsamples) rgbs = rgbs.reshape(Nalive, Nsamples, 3) # Composite and update accumulators in-place compositetestfw( sigmas, rgbs, deltas, ts, hitst[:, 0], aliveindices, Tthreshold, Neffsamples, opacity, depth, rgb) # Filter valid indices aliveindices = aliveindices[aliveindices >= 0] # Add background rgb = rgb + rgbbg (1 - opacity) return rgb, opacity, depth def raymarchingtest(rayso, raysd, hitst, aliveindices, densitybitfield, cascades, scale, expstepfactor, gridsize, maxsamples, nsamples): # Sources do not provide the internal implementation. pass def compositetestfw(sigmas, rgbs, deltas, ts, hitst, aliveindices, Tthreshold, Neffsamples, opacity, depth, rgb): # Sources do not provide the internal implementation. pass Parameters: Tthreshold: Transmittance threshold below which a ray is considered converged. Default: 10^{-4}. MAXSAMPLES: Maximum total samples per ray across iterations. Default: 1024. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero-direction rays: Filtered by validmask to prevent division by zero or invalid sampling. Convergence: Rays stop contributing to computation once transmittance drops below Tthreshold, but the loop continues until MAXSAMPLES is reached for remaining rays. Batch size calculation: minsamples ensures a minimum computational load per iteration, preventing excessive overhead from very small batches. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the total number of samples processed, which is bounded by N{rays} \times MAX\SAMPLES. Memory complexity is Not given in the sources.. Measured Performance: On the Lego scene with an RTX 2080 Ti, the method achieved 36.2 FPS and 32.96 PSNR, compared to 18.2 FPS and 31.46 PSNR for torch-ngp. Scaling: Performance scales with scene emptiness; faster rendering occurs when most of the scene is empty, allowing more rays to converge early. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant speedup in transparent/empty regions due to early stopping; simple batching logic. Limitations: Slower than instant-ngp (60 FPS on 3090) due to iterative Python loop overhead and lack of fully fused kernels; quality may fluctuate across runs. This method is part of the ngppl project by kwea123, an unofficial PyTorch Lightning implementation of instant-NGP.
