name: Block Culling
head: RT+Cull
body: Block culling is an optimization technique for volume rendering that reduces the time required to reach content values inside RGBA volumes by skipping blocks that do not contribute to the visible result. It is particularly effective when sparsity in the volume data results from runtime parameters, such as a narrower allowed density range, rather than inherent data sparsity. Unlike Beam Optimization which focuses on ray coherence, or Bounding Shape Optimization which uses geometric bounds, block culling operates on the hierarchical block structure to prune traversal paths based on content relevance. Block culling integrates with hardware ray tracing (RT) to evaluate whether a block contains relevant content before performing expensive ray marching or traversal steps. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical volume data structure (e.g., bricks or blocks), a user-defined content range (density/opacity thresholds), and ray intersection data. Output: A rendered image with reduced computation time by skipping irrelevant blocks. Data Structures: The method relies on the existing block hierarchy. Each block typically stores metadata indicating its content range (min/max density or opacity). If this metadata is not explicitly stored, it must be computed or approximated. Steps: 1. Ray-Block Intersection: Determine if a ray intersects a block in the hierarchy. 2. Content Range Check: Compare the block's stored content range against the user-requested content range. 3. Culling Decision: If the block's content range does not overlap with the user-requested range, the block is culled (skipped). If there is an overlap, the block is processed (traversed or ray-marched). 4. Traversal/Rendering: Proceed with standard ray tracing or block walking for non-culled blocks. Parameters: User-requested content range: The density/opacity interval of interest. Typical values depend on the application (e.g., [0.1, 0.9] for visible structures). Block content range: Precomputed min/max values for each block. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Culling Benefit: If the user-requested content range is greater than or equal to the actual content range of the volume, block culling provides no significant performance gain. Performance Regression: The method does not cause significant performance regression when it cannot impact performance (i.e., when no blocks are culled). Sparse Content: If the volume is inherently too sparse, block culling may not be as effective as block walking, and the overhead of checking ranges might outweigh benefits if not optimized. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def blockculling(ray, blockhierarchy, usercontentrange): """ ray: Ray origin and direction blockhierarchy: Root block of the volume hierarchy usercontentrange: Tuple (mindensity, maxdensity) """ if blockhierarchy is None: return None # Check if ray intersects block if not rayintersectsblock(ray, blockhierarchy.bounds): return None # Check if block contains relevant content if not rangesoverlap(blockhierarchy.contentrange, usercontentrange): return None # Cull this block # If leaf block, perform ray marching or shading if blockhierarchy.isleaf: return raymarchblock(ray, blockhierarchy.data, usercontentrange) # Recurse into children results = [] for child in blockhierarchy.children: result = blockculling(ray, child, usercontentrange) if result is not None: results.append(result) return compositeresults(results) def rangesoverlap(rangea, rangeb): return rangea.min <= rangeb.max and rangeb.min <= rangea.max Edit culling is a technique used during the construction of Signed Distance Field (SDF) bricks to reduce the number of edits evaluated per brick, thereby reducing construction latency. It determines which edits affect a sub-brick based on the principle that a sub-brick is entirely encapsulated by its parent, ensuring that no edit affecting the child is missed while culling those that do not. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the hierarchical relationship between parent and child bricks to minimize redundant distance evaluations during the critical construction phase. Block walking with culling combines block walking and block culling algorithms to reduce the time to reach content values inside RGBA volumes. In block traversal mode, 'RT+Walk+Cull' achieved 5.543ms on Fish (a) and 6.945ms on Fish (c). In blend mode, 'RT+Walk+Cull' achieved 107.725ms on Fish (a) and 11.892ms on Fish (c). The combination results in the best performance on average compared to using either technique alone or standard ray tracing. Time and Memory Complexity: Time: Reduces rendering time by skipping irrelevant blocks. Performance gains are most significant when sparsity results from runtime parameters. Memory: Requires storing content range metadata for each block. No additional significant memory overhead is noted. Measured Performance: Block Traversal Mode: Fish (c): RT+Cull achieved 4.823ms vs 7.375ms for RT. Fish (a): RT+Cull achieved 9.740ms vs 9.745ms for RT. Chip (d): RT+Cull achieved 2.309ms vs 2.310ms for RT. Rock (e): RT+Cull achieved 7.949ms vs 7.949ms for RT. Blend Mode: Fish (c): RT+Cull achieved 8.079ms vs 10.798ms for RT. Fish (a): RT+Cull achieved 113.780ms vs 113.983ms for RT. Chip (d): RT+Cull achieved 15.132ms vs 15.098ms for RT. Scaling: Performance gains are consistent across different datasets (Fish, Chip, Rock) when sparsity is present. No significant performance regression when no blocks are culled. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Effective for runtime-adjustable density ranges; no significant penalty when ineffective. Limitations: Less effective when content is inherently too sparse (block walking may be better); requires precomputed content ranges. When to Use: Use when sparsity is due to runtime parameters (e.g., narrow density ranges) rather than inherent data sparsity. Use in conjunction with block walking for optimal performance. When Not to Use: Avoid when the user-requested content range covers the entire actual content range, as no culling benefit is realized. Avoid when content is inherently too sparse, as block walking may be more effective. Block culling was introduced in the context of sparse volume rendering using hardware ray tracing. It was developed to address the performance challenges of rendering large, sparse RGBA volumes by leveraging the hierarchical block structure to skip irrelevant data. The technique is part of a broader set of optimizations including block walking and beam optimization. name: Edit Culling
body: Edit culling is a technique used during the construction of Signed Distance Field (SDF) bricks to reduce the number of edits evaluated per brick, thereby reducing construction latency. It determines which edits affect a sub-brick based on the principle that a sub-brick is entirely encapsulated by its parent, ensuring that no edit affecting the child is missed while culling those that do not. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by focusing on the hierarchical relationship between parent and child bricks to minimize redundant distance evaluations during the critical construction phase. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A parent brick's index buffer (list of active edits), the edit definitions (including smooth blending dependencies), and the brick geometry (size and midpoint). Output: A new index buffer for the sub-brick containing indices of edits that affect the sub-brick, guaranteed to be unique and in ascending order. Data Structures: Bitfield: A 32-element array of 32-bit unsigned integers (uint32[32]), totaling 1024 bits. This supports a maximum of 1024 edits. Index Buffer: A list of integers representing the indices of the set bits in the bitfield. Dependency Buffer: A structure mapping smooth edits to their required dependencies. Parameters: Max Edits: 1024. Brick Size: The physical size of the brick volume. Steps: 1. Initialize a 1024-bit bitfield (32 uint32 words) to all zeros. 2. Iterate through each edit index i present in the parent brick's index buffer: a. Evaluate the edit's distance function at the midpoint of the sub-brick, denoted as d{mid}. b. Compare d{mid} to the brick size S. c. If d{mid} > S, the edit is culled; do not set its bit. d. If d{mid} \le S, set the i-th bit in the bitfield to 1. e. If the edit is smooth, retrieve its dependencies from the dependency buffer and set the corresponding bits for each dependency in the bitfield to 1. 3. Construct the index buffer: a. Perform a prefix sum (scan) on the bitfield to determine the position of each set bit. b. Write the indices of the set bits to the global index buffer in ascending order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def editculling(parentindexbuffer, edits, brickmidpoint, bricksize, maxedits=1024): # Initialize bitfield: 32 uint32s bitfield = [0] 32 # Helper to set bit i def setbit(i): wordidx = i // 32 bitidx = i % 32 bitfield[wordidx] |= (1 << bitidx) # Helper to get bit i def getbit(i): wordidx = i // 32 bitidx = i % 32 return (bitfield[wordidx] >> bitidx) & 1 # Step 2: Evaluate edits for editidx in parentindexbuffer: edit = edits[editidx] # Evaluate distance at midpoint dist = edit.distancefunction(brickmidpoint) # Culling condition: if distance > brick size, cull if dist > bricksize: continue # Set bit for this edit setbit(editidx) # Handle smooth blending dependencies if edit.issmooth: for depidx in edit.dependencies: setbit(depidx) # Step 3: Construct index buffer indexbuffer = [] for i in range(maxedits): if getbit(i): indexbuffer.append(i) return indexbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Approximation Error: The method relies on evaluating the distance at the midpoint. This is an approximation; precise signed distance function intersection calculation would be more accurate but is more expensive. Smooth Blending Overhead: High edit counts with smooth blending significantly increase the number of edits per brick because dependencies are added, increasing the index buffer size. Bounding Sphere Limitation: The source notes that bounding spheres are used for intersection detection in some contexts, which can result in more edits being evaluated than necessary. However, the primary algorithm described uses midpoint evaluation against brick size. Time Complexity: The algorithm iterates through the parent's index buffer and performs constant-time bit operations. The prefix sum is linear in the number of edits (1024). It significantly reduces the total amount of work compared to evaluating all edits. Memory Complexity: Requires a fixed 1024-bit bitfield per brick during construction and an index buffer for the output. The index buffer size varies; in optimal cases (e.g., Fractal scene), it references less than 10 edits, but in worst cases (e.g., Drops scene with 1024 edits and smooth blending), it can be much larger. Performance: In the "Drops" scene at a brick size of 0.0625, enabling edit culling increased construction performance by a factor of 32, reducing construction times to less than 100 milliseconds, whereas without it, construction took multiple seconds. Strengths: Dramatically reduces construction latency for scenes with many edits; ensures correct geometry by maintaining sorted, unique indices; leverages hierarchical encapsulation. Limitations: The midpoint evaluation is an approximation and may cull edits that actually intersect the brick (false negatives) or keep edits that don't (false positives, though the condition d{mid} > S is conservative for culling). Smooth blending increases memory overhead. When to Use: When constructing SDF bricks hierarchically and the number of edits is large (up to 1024). Particularly effective when sparsity results from runtime parameters or when construction latency is critical. When Not to Use: When precise intersection is required and the cost of midpoint approximation is unacceptable, or when the number of edits is very small (overhead may not be justified). Edit culling was introduced in the context of real-time rendering and construction of Signed Distance Fields, specifically within hierarchical brick-based representations. It addresses the bottleneck of evaluating hundreds of edits per brick during construction, which is critical for interactive applications. The technique was developed to make real-time reconstruction of SDF geometry feasible, as construction without it was too slow for interactive use. Real-time Rendering and Construction of Signed Distance Fields, https://jambuttenshaw.github.io/devportfolio/Dissertation.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Bounding Shape Optimization
head: Bounding Shape Culling
body: Bounding Shape Optimization accelerates volumetric rendering by skipping density evaluations in empty space using pre-defined bounding shapes. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space by restricting ray marching to regions where density is non-zero. Unlike Beam Optimization which optimizes for caustic beams, or Block Culling which uses grid-based culling, this method generalizes the concept of space-leaping by allowing arbitrary closed geometry (e.g., spheres, cylinders) to define the volume extent. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D, density field \rho(x), and a bounding shape definition B. Output: Rendered color and opacity for the ray. Data Structures: The bounding shape B is defined by its geometric parameters. For a sphere, this is the center C and radius R. For other shapes, the intersection function must be defined. The density field is sampled only within the bounds of B. Steps: 1. Define Boundaries: Identify the region where density is non-zero. This is modeled as a bounding shape B. The closer B is to the actual density field, the fewer "useless" steps are performed. 2. Compute Intersections: Use a surface rendering technique to find the intersection points of the ray (O, D) with the bounding shape B. This yields the entry point t{in} and exit point t{out} along the ray. 3. Ray Marching: Perform classical volumetric rendering only for samples located between t{in} and t{out}. 4. Step Size Adaptation (Optional): To improve performance, step sizes can increase as the ray progresses through the medium, as imprecisions have less impact further along the ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderraywithboundingshape(rayorigin, raydirection, densityfield, boundingshape): # Step 1 & 2: Find intersection with bounding shape # For a sphere with center C and radius R: # oc = rayorigin - C # a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) # b = 2.0 dot(oc, raydirection) # c = dot(oc, oc) - R R # discriminant = b b - 4 a c # If no intersection, return background color if discriminant < 0: return backgroundcolor sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) tenter = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) texit = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 a) # If the ray starts inside, adjust tenter if tenter < 0: tenter = 0.0 texit = texit # Keep exit as is, or recalculate if needed # Step 3 & 4: Volumetric rendering inside bounds color = vec3(0.0) opacity = 0.0 t = tenter stepsize = initialstepsize while t < texit and opacity < 1.0: # Sample density at current position pos = rayorigin + raydirection t density = densityfield.sample(pos) # Accumulate color and opacity # Standard volume integration (e.g., front-to-back) attenuation = exp(-density stepsize) color += (1.0 - opacity) density stepsize lightcolor opacity += (1.0 - opacity) (1.0 - attenuation) # Adaptive step size: increase step size as we go deeper # This is a heuristic; specific formula not provided in sources stepsize = stepsize 1.1 t += stepsize return color Parameters: Bounding Shape Choice: The type of geometry used (e.g., Sphere, Cylinder, Box). Sphere Marching is selected in the reference implementation for its simplicity and efficiency. Container Definition Fineness: Finer container definitions (tighter bounds) improve volume render efficiency by reducing the number of samples taken in empty space. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ray Origin Inside: If the ray origin is inside the bounding shape, t{enter} must be clamped to 0 or the negative root must be ignored to avoid backward marching. Tightness: Loose bounding shapes result in unnecessary density evaluations. The optimization gain is directly proportional to how tightly the shape fits the non-zero density region. Intersection Precision: Floating-point errors in intersection calculation can cause rays to miss the volume or march slightly outside it, leading to artifacts or wasted computation. Convex Polyhedron Bounding is a space-leaping technique for direct volume rendering that accelerates ray traversal by enclosing objects within a convex polyhedron. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space by allowing rays to skip large volumes of non-data voxels. Unlike Bounding Shape Optimization which generalizes the concept, this method specifically constructs a convex hull around the object, and differs from Bounding Volume Extrusion by using a general polyhedron rather than a prism tailored for caustic beams. Container-based Ray Marching uses closed geometry as a bounding container to ray march only where there actually is density, improving efficiency. It restricts ray marching to regions where density exists, using closed geometry as a bounding container. Finer container definitions improve volume render efficiency compared to coarse or non-existent containers. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of density evaluations from O(N) (where N is the total ray length in steps) to O(N{inside}), where N{inside} is the number of steps within the bounding shape. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the bounding shape parameters and the density field. No additional large data structures are needed beyond the shape definition. Strengths: Significant performance boost in scenes with mostly empty density fields. Simple to implement for basic shapes like spheres and boxes. Limitations: Requires pre-defining or computing the bounding shape. If the density field is dense or irregularly shaped, the bounding shape may not provide significant culling benefits. Does not handle dynamic deformation of the density field automatically without updating the bounds. When to Use: Ideal for procedural noise fields, interstellar dust, or solar flares where large portions of the volume are empty. When Not to Use: When the density field fills the entire volume or when the bounding shape computation cost outweighs the savings from culling. Bounding Shape Optimization was introduced in the context of real-time rendering of interstellar dust clouds and solar flares. The method leverages the hypothesis that such density fields are mostly empty, allowing for significant performance gains by skipping empty space. It is also discussed in the context of production volume rendering, where closed geometry containers are used to optimize ray marching efficiency. name: Convex Polyhedron Bounding
head: PARC (Polygon assisted ray casting)
body: Convex Polyhedron Bounding is a space-leaping technique for direct volume rendering that accelerates ray traversal by enclosing objects within a convex polyhedron. It solves the problem of inefficiently stepping through empty space by allowing rays to skip large volumes of non-data voxels. Unlike its sibling Bounding Shape Optimization which generalizes the concept, this method specifically constructs a convex hull around the object, and differs from Bounding Volume Extrusion by using a general polyhedron rather than a prism tailored for caustic beams. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset containing one or few distinct objects; the geometric definition of the object's surface or voxel extent. Output: A convex polyhedron (defined by a set of planes or vertices) that tightly encloses the object, used to cull empty space during ray marching. Data Structures: The polyhedron is typically represented by its defining planes. Each plane i is defined by a normal vector \mathbf{n}i and a distance di from the origin, such that a point \mathbf{p} is inside if \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{p} + di \ge 0 for all i. Alternatively, it may be stored as a list of vertices and faces. The exact layout is not specified in the sources. Steps: 1. Object Identification: Identify the voxels belonging to the object(s) in the volume. 2. Polyhedron Construction: Compute a convex polyhedron that encloses all identified object voxels. The sources do not specify the algorithm for this construction (e.g., QuickHull, Graham scan). 3. Ray Traversal Setup: For each ray, determine the entry and exit points of the ray with respect to the convex polyhedron. 4. Space Leaping: If the ray does not intersect the polyhedron, skip the ray entirely. If it intersects, traverse only the segment within the polyhedron using standard volume rendering techniques. 5. Fallback: For volumes with many objects, the method suggests using bounding boxes instead, implying convex polyhedra are best for few, complex objects. Parameters: Number of Objects: The method is recommended for volumes with "few objects". Precision: The method is distinct from "Adaptive ray traversal" which uses low-precision fast traversal for empty space and high-precision for vicinity voxels. Convex polyhedron bounding is a geometric culling step, not a precision-adaptive step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Multiple Objects: If the volume contains many objects, the convex hull may become too large or complex, reducing efficiency. The sources recommend bounding boxes for such cases. Construction Cost: The cost of computing the convex hull must be amortized over many rays. Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convexpolyhedronbounding(volumedata, objectmask): # 1. Identify object voxels objectvoxels = getvoxelcenters(objectmask) # 2. Build convex polyhedron # Note: Specific algorithm for convex hull construction is not provided in sources polyhedron = computeconvexhull(objectvoxels) # 3. For each ray for ray in rays: # 4. Intersect ray with polyhedron tmin, tmax = rayintersectpolyhedron(ray, polyhedron) if tmin == None: # Ray misses the object entirely, skip continue # 5. March ray within the bounding volume rendersegment(ray, tmin, tmax, volumedata) Computes tight convex hulls for caustic beams using 6-triangle hulls, superior to planar prism approximations for warped beams. Represents the bound as a reduced set of half-spaces for efficient distance queries, clustering orientations to minimize plane count. Decomposes point sets into a union of tighter convex volumes via recursive cutting planes, better for concave shapes than a single hull. Time Complexity: Construction of the convex hull is O(N \log N) for N vertices, but the specific complexity is not given in the sources. Ray intersection with a convex polyhedron is linear in the number of faces. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of faces/vertices in the polyhedron. Not given in the sources. Performance: Effective for volumes with few objects. For many objects, bounding boxes are preferred. Strengths: Tighter bounds than axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) for rotated or irregular objects, reducing empty space traversal. Limitations: Higher computational cost to construct and intersect than AABBs. Not suitable for scenes with many small objects. The method was introduced in the context of Direct Volume Rendering Techniques, specifically as part of the PARC (Polygon assisted ray casting) approach. It is designed for space-leaping in volumes with few objects. name: Bounding Volume Extrusion
head: 6-triangle convex hull method for caustic beams, Tight Bounding Volume Computation
body: Bounding Volume Extrusion is a technique to compute tight convex hull bounding volumes for caustic beams, enabling efficient rasterization of inscattered light while minimizing fill-rate overhead. Unlike the standard bounding prism method, which approximates bilinear beam sides with planar prisms and suffers from poor accuracy on strongly warped or focused beams, this method constructs a 6-triangle convex hull that tightly encloses the beam geometry. Inputs: Caustic beam defined by a base triangle vertices v0, v1, v2 and corresponding beam direction vectors d0, d1, d2 at each vertex. Scene geometry for occlusion testing. View frustum parameters. Outputs: A set of 6 triangles forming the bounding volume of the caustic beam. Data Structures: Beam Space Coordinate System: A local coordinate system is established for each beam: Origin: Coincides with vertex v0 of the base triangle. Y-axis: Aligned with the normal of the base triangle. Direction Vectors: The beam direction vectors di are scaled such that their y-coordinate is exactly 1.0. Area Function Coefficients: Three coefficients for the second-order area function A(y), precomputed during beam generation. Steps: 1. Coordinate Transformation: Transform the beam vertices and direction vectors into the local beam space defined above. 2. Precompute Area Function: Calculate the coefficients for the cross-sectional area function A(y). In this coordinate system, the area of the parallel cross-section of the beam is a second-order expression over the local y-coordinate. A(y) = c2 y^2 + c1 y + c0 where c0, c1, c2 are the precomputed coefficients. This allows evaluation of the cross-section with a single dot product later. 3. Determine Extrusion Length: Compute the maximum possible length by intersecting beam edges with the view frustum. Refine the length by intersecting beam edges with surrounding scene geometry using approximate ray tracing (Szirmay-Kalos et al. [2005]) within the geometry shader. Apply energy approximation for divergent beams: if the beam is divergent, limit the extrusion length to the distance where the contribution becomes negligible, maximizing extrusion only up to that point. 4. Generate Bounding Volume (6-Triangle Method): For each of the three edges of the base triangle, identify the corresponding vertex on the top triangle (the end of the extrusion). Construct a plane for each edge containing the base edge and the opposite top vertex, such that the entire beam lies in the negative half-space of the plane (touching plane). Simplify the computation: Instead of intersecting full prisms, take the triangle formed by one base edge and one top vertex directly as one side of the bounding volume. Select one such triangle for each of the three base edges, resulting in 3 side triangles. The base and top triangles form the remaining 2 faces. The 6th is likely the top triangle or a specific hull face. The text says "bounding volume is defined by six triangles". 5. Watertightness Check: Check if multiple consistent triangulations exist for any edge (i.e., the beam side is close to planar). If multiple candidates exist, revert to the bounding prism method to ensure a watertight volume. If no ambiguity exists, emit the 6 triangles from the geometry shader. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeboundingvolume(basevertices, beamdirections, scenegeometry, viewfrustum): """ Computes the 6-triangle convex hull bounding volume for a caustic beam. Args: basevertices: List of 3 vec3s [v0, v1, v2] beamdirections: List of 3 vec3s [d0, d1, d2] scenegeometry: Data structure for approximate ray tracing viewfrustum: View frustum planes Returns: List of 6 triangles (each triangle is 3 vec3s) or None if fallback is needed """ # Step 1: Coordinate Transformation # Origin at v0, y-axis is triangle normal v0, v1, v2 = basevertices d0, d1, d2 = beamdirections trianglenormal = normalize(cross(v1 - v0, v2 - v0)) # Scale directions so y-coordinate is 1 # dscaled.y = 1 => dscaled = d / (d. normal) # Note: If d. normal is 0 or negative, beam is parallel or backward, handle as edge case scalefactors = [dot(d, trianglenormal) for d in [d0, d1, d2]] # Check for degenerate directions if any(sf <= 0 for sf in scalefactors): return fallbackprismmethod(basevertices, beamdirections) scaleddirections = [d / sf for d, sf in zip([d0, d1, d2], scalefactors)] # Step 2: Precompute Area Function Coefficients # A(y) = c2y^2 + c1y + c0 # Exact coefficient calculation from bilinear patch area is not detailed in sources c0, c1, c2 = 0.0, 0.0, 0.0 # Step 3: Determine Extrusion Length # Max length from view frustum # Exact frustum intersection algorithm is not detailed in sources maxlengthfrustum = 100.0 # Refine with scene geometry using approximate ray tracing (Szirmay-Kalos et al. [2005]) # Exact ray tracing implementation is not detailed in sources maxlengthscene = 50.0 # Energy approximation for divergent beams # Exact energy threshold function is not detailed in sources energylimitlength = 10.0 # Combine lengths extrusionlength = min(maxlengthfrustum, maxlengthscene, energylimitlength) # Calculate top vertices topvertices = [v + d extrusionlength for v, d in zip(basevertices, scaleddirections)] v0top, v1top, v2top = topvertices # Step 4: Generate Bounding Volume (6-Triangle Method) # Construct side triangles: each edge of base + opposite top vertex tri1 = [v0, v1, v2top] tri2 = [v1, v2, v0top] tri3 = [v2, v0, v1top] # Base and Top triangles tribase = [v0, v1, v2] tritop = [v0top, v1top, v2top] # Step 5: Watertightness Check # Check if multiple consistent triangulations exist for any edge # Exact ambiguity check algorithm is not detailed in sources if isambiguoustriangulation(tri1, tri2, tri3, basevertices, topvertices): return fallbackprismmethod(basevertices, beamdirections) # The source specifies the volume is defined by six triangles, selected for each edge independently return [tri1, tri2, tri3, tribase, tritop, tritop] def fallbackprismmethod(basevertices, beamdirections): # Revert to Ernst et al. [2005] bounding prism method # Exact implementation is not detailed in sources return [] def isambiguoustriangulation(tri1, tri2, tri3, base, top): # Check if any side is close to planar, leading to multiple consistent triangulations # Exact implementation is not detailed in sources return False Time Complexity: The method adds overhead to the geometry shader for extrusion length calculation (ray tracing) and triangle selection. The precomputation of area coefficients is done during beam generation. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory; coefficients are stored per beam. Performance: Significantly reduces fill-rate compared to the bounding prism method, especially for strongly warped or focused beams where the prism method yields a poor approximation. Strengths: Tighter convex hull approximation than prisms; efficient rasterization; handles dynamic scenes without precomputation. Limitations: Numerical instability can lead to non-watertight volumes if multiple triangulations are consistent; requires fallback to less efficient prism method in such cases. Approximate ray tracing may miss thin occluders. Origin: Proposed by Liktor et al. in "Real-time volume caustics with adaptive beam tracing" (2011). History: Builds on earlier caustic beam tracing methods. The bounding prism method by Ernst et al. [2005] was the prior standard for bounding caustic beams. Usage: Used in real-time volume caustics rendering to accumulate inscattered light efficiently. name: Implicit Convex Hulls
head: Convex Hull Bounding Volumes, Simplified Convex Hulls
body: Implicit Convex Hulls provide a compact, convex bounding volume for the point set generated by Sphere Carving, enabling efficient distance queries for ray marching. Unlike Bounding Volume Extrusion which uses axis-aligned or oriented boxes, or Approximate Convex Decomposition which partitions space into multiple non-convex or convex parts, this method represents the bound as a single convex polyhedron defined by a reduced set of half-spaces. It solves the problem of expensive distance evaluation against a high-resolution convex hull by clustering half-space orientations to preserve the bounding property with significantly fewer planes. Inputs: S: The final sphere set from Sphere Carving. P: The point set generated by S. H: The full set of half-spaces \{\Pii\} defining the convex hull H(P). Each half-space \Pii is characterized by a normal vector ni and a distance offset, implicitly defined by the supporting planes of the hull. m: The target number of half-spaces for the simplified volume (typical value: 20). Outputs: He: The reduced set of half-spaces defining the simplified bounding volume \mathcal{B}. d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}): The distance function from a query point \mathbf{p} to the bounding volume. Data Structures: Half-space \Pii: Defined by normal vector \mathbf{n}i (unit length) and scalar di such that \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{x} + di \le 0 for all \mathbf{x} \in H. Cluster centers: Vectors in the space of half-space orientations. Steps: 1. Extract Orientations: Collect the normal vectors \{\mathbf{n}i\} from the full set of half-spaces H defining the convex hull of P. 2. Cluster Orientations: Apply a k-means clustering algorithm to the set of vectors \{\mathbf{n}i\} with k=m. The algorithm partitions the normals into m clusters based on their angular similarity. 3. Determine Cluster Representatives: For each cluster, compute the cluster center (mean vector) or select the representative normal. Let the set of representative normals be \{\mathbf{c}j\}{j=1}^m. 4. Project to Existing Half-Spaces: For each cluster representative \mathbf{c}j, find the existing half-space \Pi{k} in H whose normal \mathbf{n}k is most similar to \mathbf{c}j (e.g., maximum dot product). This step ensures the reduced set He consists of actual supporting planes from the original hull, preserving the convex bounding property. 5. Construct Reduced Set: Form He from the selected half-spaces. The bounding volume is \mathcal{B} = \bigcap{\Pi \in He} \Pi. 6. Distance Evaluation: For a query point \mathbf{p}, compute the distance to \mathcal{B}: d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) = \max{\Pii \in He} (\mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{p} + di) If d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) > \varepsilon (where \varepsilon is the sphere carving threshold or a small epsilon), the signed distance field value is \tilde{f} = d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}). Otherwise, \tilde{f} = f(\mathbf{p}), where f is the underlying SDF. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesimplifiedconvexhull(halfspaces, m): """ halfspaces: List of tuples (n, d) representing n.x + n.y + n.z + d <= 0 m: Number of clusters (e.g., 20) Returns: List of (n, d) for the simplified hull """ # Step 1: Extract normals normals = [hs[0] for hs in halfspaces] # Step 2: K-means clustering on normals # Initialize centroids randomly or using k-means++ centroids = initializecentroids(normals, m) for iteration in range(maxiterations): # Assign each normal to nearest centroid assignments = [[] for in range(m)] for i, n in enumerate(normals): # Find index of closest centroid bestidx = argmin([dot(n, c) for c in centroids]) # Maximize dot product for unit vectors assignments[bestidx].append(i) # Update centroids newcentroids = [] for clusterindices in assignments: if not clusterindices: newcentroids.append(centroids[0]) # Handle empty cluster else: # Mean of normals in cluster meann = sum(normals[i] for i in clusterindices) / len(clusterindices) newcentroids.append(normalize(meann)) # Check convergence if all(allclose(c, nc) for c, nc in zip(centroids, newcentroids)): break centroids = newcentroids # Step 3 & 4: Project cluster centers to existing half-spaces simplifiedhalfspaces = [] for centroid in centroids: # Find the half-space with normal most aligned with centroid bestscore = -infinity besths = None for hs in halfspaces: score = dot(centroid, hs[0]) if score > bestscore: bestscore = score besths = hs simplifiedhalfspaces.append(besths) return simplifiedhalfspaces def distancetosimplifiedhull(p, simplifiedhalfspaces): """ p: Query point (x, y, z) simplifiedhalfspaces: List of (n, d) Returns: Distance to the convex hull """ maxdist = -infinity for n, d in simplifiedhalfspaces: # Distance from point to plane n.x + d = 0 is (n.p + d) / |n| # Since n is unit, distance is n.p + d dist = dot(n, p) + d if dist > maxdist: maxdist = dist return maxdist Edge Cases: Empty Clusters: If a cluster has no normals assigned, the centroid remains undefined. A guard is needed to re-initialize or assign a default normal. Degenerate Input: If P is collinear or coplanar, the convex hull may be degenerate. The half-space extraction must handle this, potentially resulting in fewer than expected unique normals. Precision: Floating-point errors in dot products during clustering and projection can lead to slight violations of the bounding property. Using a small epsilon in the distance check mitigates visual artifacts. A bounding volume B constructed as the geometric convex hull H(P) of the point set P generated by Sphere Carving. It is represented as an intersection of oriented half-spaces. This is the base representation before simplification. It guarantees the bounding property but is computationally expensive for distance evaluation due to the large number of half-spaces required for high fidelity. Time Complexity: Construction: O(N \cdot m \cdot I), where N is the number of half-spaces in the full hull, m is the target number of clusters, and I is the number of k-means iterations. Distance Query: O(m), as it requires computing the distance to each of the m half-spaces and taking the maximum. Memory Complexity: O(m) to store the simplified half-spaces, compared to O(N) for the full hull. Measured Performance: Using m \approx 20 half-spaces yields a shape almost equivalent to the full resolution (e.g., 768 half-spaces) but with significantly more efficient distance evaluation. The cost of distance evaluation should remain negligible compared to the cost of the underlying SDF function f. Strengths: Compact representation. Preserves convex bounding property. Fast distance queries suitable for real-time ray marching. Limitations: Approximation error increases as m decreases. Construction requires clustering, which adds preprocessing overhead. When to Use: When a tight, convex bound is needed for acceleration in ray marching, and the underlying SDF is expensive to evaluate. When memory bandwidth is a constraint. When Not to Use: When exact bounding is required. When the scene is highly non-convex and a single convex hull is too loose. The method originates from the Sphere Carving algorithm, which produces a final sphere set S and an associated point set P. The convex hull of P bounds the object and can be exploited to build efficient bounding volumes. The approach of simplifying the half-space set via clustering was introduced to address the computational intensity of evaluating distance against a high-resolution convex hull. name: Approximate Convex Decomposition
head: Plane Cutting Decomposition, Recursive Convex Decomposition
body: Approximate Convex Decomposition (ACD) is a post-processing method that decomposes a point set P (generated by Sphere Carving) into a union of tighter convex bounding volumes by recursively cutting the set with planes. Unlike a single convex hull, which can be loose for concave shapes, ACD creates a union of simpler convex shapes that conform more closely to the object's surface. It sets itself apart from siblings like Bounding Volume Extrusion and Implicit Convex Hulls by explicitly using a cutting-plane strategy inspired by mesh decomposition to minimize the total volume of the resulting hulls. Inputs: Point set P: A dense set of points close to the object surface, generated by Sphere Carving. Sphere set S: The set of spheres used in the preceding Sphere Carving step. V0: The volume of the initial bounding volume. ni: Number of iterations used in Sphere Carving (determines point cloud density). Outputs: A set of convex polyhedra (or ellipsoids) whose union bounds the object \mathcal{O}. Data Structures: P: List of 3D points. S: List of spheres (center, radius). \Pi: Cutting plane defined by normal \mathbf{n} and distance d from origin, or implicitly by the infinite sphere S\infty. Steps: 1. Sampling: Sample a set of candidate cutting planes \{\Pii\} (typically hundreds) from the space surrounding the point set P. 2. Selection: For each candidate plane \Pii, split P into two disjoint subsets \mathcal{L} (left) and \mathcal{R} (right) based on the signed distance d(\Pii, \mathbf{p}): \mathcal{L} = \{\mathbf{p} \in P, d(\Pii, \mathbf{p}) < 0\} \mathcal{R} = \{\mathbf{p} \in P, d(\Pii, \mathbf{p}) \geq 0\} Compute the score \sigma(P, \Pii) as the sum of the volumes of the convex hulls of these subsets: \sigma(P, \Pii) = V(H(\mathcal{L})) + V(H(\mathcal{R})) where V is the volume function and H is the convex hull operator. Select the plane \Pi that minimizes this score: \Pi = \arg \mini \sigma(P, \Pii) 3. Bounding Maintenance (Infinite Sphere): To ensure the resulting hulls bound the object, the cutting plane \Pi is treated as an infinite sphere S\infty added to the sphere set S. The convex hull created by trilaterating the extended sphere set \mathcal{S} \cup S\infty bounds the intersection of the object and the plane: H(\widetilde{T}(\mathcal{S} \cup S\infty)) \supset \mathcal{O} \cap \Pi where \widetilde{T} denotes the trilateration operation. 4. Finite Sphere Replacement: Replace S\infty with a large finite sphere tangent to \Pi. Radius: Set to the size of V0 (the initial volume). Center: Located on the line perpendicular to \Pi passing through the centroid of the subset (\mathcal{L} or \mathcal{R}). This replacement maintains the bounding guarantee and allows reuse of Sphere Carving intersection calculations. 5. Recursion: Recursively apply steps 2-4 to subsets \mathcal{L} and \mathcal{R} until a user-defined number of convex parts is reached or a stopping criterion is met. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def approximateconvexdecomposition(P, S, V0, maxparts): """ Recursively decomposes point set P into convex hulls. P: list of 3D points S: list of spheres (tuples of center, radius) V0: initial volume size (scalar) maxparts: target number of convex parts """ if len(P) == 0: return [] # Base case: if we reached the desired number of parts or P is small enough # Note: The exact stopping condition for recursion depth vs part count # is not fully specified in sources, but maxparts is the user-defined limit. # We assume a helper function getconvexhullvolume exists. if len(P) < 4 or countcurrentparts() >= maxparts: # Return the convex hull of the current subset # The bounding sphere logic is handled during the split return [computehull(P, S, V0)] # 1. Sample candidate planes candidateplanes = sampleplanes(P, count=100) # "hundreds" bestplane = None minscore = infinity # 2. Evaluate scores for plane in candidateplanes: # Split P L = [p for p in P if signeddistance(plane, p) < 0] R = [p for p in P if signeddistance(plane, p) >= 0] if not L or not R: continue # Compute score: sum of volumes of convex hulls # Note: Computing exact convex hull volume can be expensive. # Sources mention this step is the bottleneck. volL = computeconvexhullvolume(L) volR = computeconvexhullvolume(R) score = volL + volR if score < minscore: minscore = score bestplane = plane bestL = L bestR = R if bestplane is None: return [computehull(P, S, V0)] # 3. Create bounding volumes for L and R # Treat bestplane as infinite sphere Sinf # Replace with large finite sphere tangent to plane # Center for L's sphere centroidL = computecentroid(bestL) sphereL = createlargesphere(bestplane, centroidL, V0) # Center for R's sphere centroidR = computecentroid(bestR) sphereR = createlargesphere(bestplane, centroidR, V0) # 4. Recurse # Pass the new sphere sets to maintain bounding property # SL = S + {sphereL} # SR = S + {sphereR} # Note: The source implies S is extended with the cutting plane sphere. # In recursion, we must pass the relevant sphere context. hullsL = approximateconvexdecomposition(bestL, S + [sphereL], V0, maxparts) hullsR = approximateconvexdecomposition(bestR, S + [sphereR], V0, maxparts) return hullsL + hullsR def createlargesphere(plane, centroid, V0): """ Creates a large finite sphere tangent to the plane, centered on the perpendicular line through the centroid. """ # Radius is size of V0 radius = V0 # Normal of the plane n = plane.normal # Center is centroid projected onto the plane? # Source says: "center located on a line perpendicular to the plane # and passing through the centroid". # And "tangent to Pi". # Distance from centroid to plane is d. # The sphere is tangent to the plane. # If centroid is on one side, the center is shifted by radius along the normal. dist = signeddistance(plane, centroid) # If centroid is on the negative side (dist < 0), normal points to positive. # To be tangent and contain the centroid-side volume, the center must be # shifted away from the plane by radius. # Actually, the sphere bounds the hull. The hull is on one side of the plane. # The sphere must cover that side. # If the plane is the boundary, the sphere center is at distance 'radius' # from the plane, on the side of the subset. if dist < 0: center = centroid - n (radius - abs(dist)) # Adjust to be tangent # Simpler: Center is at distance 'radius' from plane along normal. # If subset is on negative side, center is at planenormal (-radius) + planepoint? # Let's use the explicit geometric construction: # Plane equation: n. x + d = 0. # Center C satisfies: n. C + d = -radius (if normal points out) or similar. # Source: "center located on a line perpendicular to the plane and passing through the centroid" # This implies the x,y (in plane coords) are same as centroid. # Only the depth changes. # Let's assume standard plane representation (n, d) where n is unit normal. # Distance from centroid to plane is dist. # We want a sphere of radius R tangent to plane. # The center is at distance R from the plane. # The centroid is inside the hull bounded by the sphere. # So the center is shifted from the centroid by (R - dist) along the normal? # If dist is negative, centroid is 'below' plane. Center should be 'below' plane by R. # So centerz = planez - R. # Centroidz = planez + dist. # Shift = centerz - centroidz = -R - dist. shift = -radius - dist center = centroid + n shift else: shift = radius - dist center = centroid + n shift return (center, radius) def computeconvexhullvolume(points): # Implementation of 3D convex hull volume calculation # Not provided in sources pass def computecentroid(points): return sum(points) / len(points) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The cutting plane selection requires multiple convex hull computations, which is computationally expensive and can be sensitive to numerical precision in volume calculations. Boundaries: Simply taking the convex hull of split point sets \mathcal{L} and \mathcal{R} is not sufficient to guarantee the bounding property (\mathcal{O} \not\subset H(\mathcal{L}) \cup H(\mathcal{R})). The sphere intersection logic is mandatory. Degenerate Input: If the point set P is not dense enough (too few iterations ni in Sphere Carving), the decomposition may not accurately capture the shape, leading to loose bounds. Time Complexity: The cutting plane selection step is the bottleneck, requiring multiple convex hull computations for hundreds of candidate planes. The decomposition process usually takes a few seconds to complete. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of points in P and the number of convex parts generated. The sphere set S grows with each recursive step if not managed carefully, though the implementation reuses calculations. Measured Performance: For models like "House" (17 iterations, 4 parts), decomposition took 2.7 seconds. For "Amphora" (7 iterations, 29 parts), it took 49.9 seconds. Strengths: Produces tighter bounding volumes than a single convex hull, leveraging the detailed information in the point set P. Maintains the bounding guarantee. Limitations: Slow due to the exhaustive search for the optimal cutting plane. The method draws inspiration from mesh decomposition and could be replaced with more efficient methods. When to use: When tighter bounds are needed for ray marching acceleration and the object has significant concavity. Suitable for real-time applications if the pre-processing time is acceptable. Approximate Convex Decomposition in this context is a post-processing step for the Sphere Carving algorithm. It draws inspiration from approximate convex decomposition methods typically applied to meshes, specifically citing [Thul et al. 2018]. The method was introduced in the paper "Sphere Carving: Bounding Volumes for Signed Distance Fields". name: Dynamic SDF Ray Marching with Structured Buffers
head: Procedural Geometry Ray Marching, SDF Ray Marching with Dynamic Object Buffers, SDF Ray Marching with GPU Buffers
body: This method renders dynamic, complex scenes by streaming object definitions from the CPU to the GPU in structured buffers, allowing for per-pixel evaluation of multiple objects without hardcoding the scene geometry in the shader. Unlike static SDF implementations where the scene is hardcoded in GLSL, this approach enables dynamic worlds with many moving characters and objects by replacing CPU-side ray termination logic with a GPU-side buffer of object structs that return a composite type (distance, color, ID) from the distance function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A subset of scene objects (culled from the full scene), passed as a structured buffer on the GPU. Each element defines the object's type, position, rotation, scale, and average color. Output: For each pixel, the final color and depth, derived from the closest object hit by the ray. Data Structures: 1. Render Input Buffer (GPU Structured Buffer): Layout: Array of ObjectDefinition structs. ObjectDefinition fields: id: Integer identifier (inferred from buffer index during search). type: Enum or integer indicating the SDF primitive type (e.g., sphere, box). position: float3 (world space position). rotation: float3 or quat (orientation). scale: float3 (uniform or non-uniform scaling). color: float3 (average/base color). 2. Distance Function Return Struct: Layout: struct { float distance; float3 color; int id; }. distance: The local signed distance to the object's surface. color: The color associated with the hit object. id: The ID of the object in the input buffer that produced this distance. Numbered Steps: 1. Culling: Cull the scene into a manageable subset of objects visible in the view frustum. Ray-marching performs automatic partial occlusion culling, and frustum/occlusion culling are partly automatic. 2. Buffer Preparation: Pass the subset of objects into a render input buffer on the CPU. Create a typed buffer (e.g., C-style struct) where each element defines the object's function type, position, rotation, scale, and average color. 3. Upload: Transfer the buffer to the GPU if it is not already present. 4. Ray Marching Loop (Per Pixel): Initialize ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. For each iteration k: Buffer Search: Perform a per-step search through the input buffer to evaluate which item is closest to the current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Transform Application: Apply transforms to either the rays (inverting figure rotations before GPU upload) or the distance functions (moving function origin for position changes, adjusting side lengths for scale changes). The simplest approach is to modify the rays before passing them to the core distance function. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF for each object. The distance function returns a complex type (struct) containing the local distance, local color, and an ID tied to the input buffer element. ID Inference: The ID is inferred from the loop counter of the buffer search, as the mapping function loops through the input buffer to find the closest figure. Color Determination: Determine the color from the average color of the buffer element corresponding to the ID, or procedurally (e.g., mapping iteration count to a palette weighted towards the stored average). Step Size: Use the minimum distance found across all objects in the buffer as the step size for the next iteration. Termination: If the minimum distance < \epsilon (convergence threshold), the ray has hit the closest object. Terminate the loop. 5. Shading: Pass the output color directly to the screen or into lighting code based on the collision point and the returned ID/color. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def vec3sub(a, b): return [a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]] def vec3len(v): return math.sqrt(v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2) class ObjectDefinition: def init(self, objid, objtype, position, rotation, scale, color): self.id = objid self.type = objtype self.position = position self.rotation = rotation self.scale = scale self.color = color class SDFResult: def init(self, distance, color, objid): self.distance = distance self.color = color self.id = objid def sdfsphere(p, center, radius): return vec3len(vec3sub(p, center)) - radius def evaluateobjectsdf(p, obj): # Transform point to local object space # Rotation transformation omitted; apply inverse rotation matrix to localp localp = [(p[i] - obj.position[i]) / obj.scale[i] for i in range(3)] dist = float('inf') if obj.type == 0: # Sphere dist = sdfsphere(localp, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0], 1.0) elif obj.type == 1: # Box d = [abs(localp[0]) - 1.0, abs(localp[1]) - 1.0, abs(localp[2]) - 1.0] dist = max(d[0], max(d[1], d[2])) return SDFResult(distance=dist, color=obj.color, objid=obj.id) def raymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, objects, maxsteps=64, epsilon=0.001, maxdist=100.0): t = 0.0 hitcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(maxsteps): currentpos = [rayorigin[i] + t raydirection[i] for i in range(3)] minresult = SDFResult(distance=float('inf'), color=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0], objid=-1) for i in range(len(objects)): obj = objects[i] result = evaluateobjectsdf(currentpos, obj) if result.distance < minresult.distance: minresult = result if minresult.distance < epsilon: hitcolor = minresult.color break elif t > maxdist: break t += minresult.distance return hitcolor Parameters: Transform Strategy: Either transform rays (requires inverting rotations on CPU) or transform distance functions (adjust origin for position, side lengths for scale). Color Generation: Can use average color from buffer element or procedural color weighted towards stored average. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Performance: The method requires a per-step search through the input buffer for every ray iteration, which can be computationally expensive compared to static scenes. Precision: Transforming points to local space for SDF evaluation requires careful handling of rotation and scale to avoid precision issues, especially with large scenes or extreme scales. Buffer Size: The number of objects in the buffer directly impacts performance. Culling is essential to keep the buffer size manageable. Defines the basic building blocks (spheres, boxes, etc.) used in the buffer. SDF Primitive Definitions Details on how to apply rotation and scale to objects in the buffer. Deformation and Transformation Handling Techniques to reduce the cost of the per-step buffer search. Acceleration and Optimization Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) per pixel, where N is the number of objects in the buffer and M is the number of ray-marching steps. This is significantly slower than static SDF rendering where N is effectively constant or hardcoded. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the structured buffer on the GPU. Not given in the sources. Strengths: Dynamic scenes, easy to add/remove objects, no need to recompile shaders for scene changes. Not given in the sources. Limitations: Performance degrades linearly with the number of objects. Not suitable for very large numbers of objects without additional acceleration structures (e.g., BVH, which is not covered in the basic structured buffer approach). Not given in the sources. When to Use: Real-time rendering of dynamic scenes with a moderate number of objects where procedural geometry is desired. Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Scenes with thousands of objects, or where maximum performance is critical and the scene is static. Not given in the sources. This method was described in the context of implementing Signed Distance Field (SDF) ray marching for dynamic worlds, specifically addressing how to stream objects to the GPU and handle multiple colors without hardcoding the scene in GLSL. It is used in procedural geometry engines and real-time SDF rendering, such as in the Claybook engine. The approach leverages GPU structured buffers (or equivalent typed buffers in HLSL/GLSL) to pass complex object data to the shader, allowing the distance function to return a composite type including distance, color, and ID. name: Sphere Tracing and Step Rules
head: Ray Marching, Distance Field Ray Marching
body: Sphere tracing is a geometric method for rendering implicit surfaces by iteratively stepping along a ray using the distance to the nearest surface as the step size. It solves the problem of rendering complex, continuous geometry without explicit polygonal meshes by leveraging the mathematical guarantee that the Signed Distance Function (SDF) provides a lower bound on the distance to the nearest surface. It differs from its siblings, such as FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration and Coarse-to-Fine Sphere Tracing, by relying on the exact Lipschitz property of the SDF for step sizing rather than hierarchical acceleration structures or multi-resolution sampling strategies. The method operates on the principle that a Signed Distance Function f(\mathbf{p}) provides a lower bound on the distance to the nearest surface. For any point \mathbf{p} in space, f(\mathbf{p}) returns the shortest Euclidean distance to the implicit surface, with a sign indicating position: f(\mathbf{p}) < 0 inside, f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 on the surface, and f(\mathbf{p}) > 0 outside. The core algorithm, known as sphere tracing, proceeds as follows for each pixel: 1. Ray Definition: A ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} is defined, where \mathbf{o} is the camera origin and \mathbf{d} is the normalized direction vector. 2. Initialization: The accumulated distance t is initialized to 0 (or a near-plane value). 3. Marching Loop: Evaluate the scene SDF at the current ray position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to get the distance d = f(\mathbf{p}). Termination Check: If d < \epsilon (a small convergence threshold, e.g., 0.001), the ray has hit the surface. If t > t{max} (maximum ray distance), the ray has escaped. Step: Advance the ray by the distance value: t \leftarrow t + d. This step size is guaranteed not to penetrate the surface because the SDF satisfies the Lipschitz condition with constant 1. 4. Shading: Upon hit, compute surface properties (normal, color) and lighting. Scene composition is typically achieved by combining primitive SDFs using Boolean operations: Union is \min(d1, d2), Intersection is \max(d1, d2), and Subtraction is \max(-d1, d2). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} to the local space of the primitive via M^{-1}\mathbf{p} before evaluation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, maxsteps, maxdistance, epsilon): """ Core sphere tracing algorithm. Args: rayorigin: Camera origin (vec3) raydirection: Normalized ray direction (vec3) sdf: Signed Distance Function callable sdf(p) maxsteps: Maximum number of iterations maxdistance: Maximum ray travel distance epsilon: Convergence threshold for surface hit Returns: hitdistance: Distance along ray to surface, or None hitpoint: 3D position of hit, or None """ t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdistance: break p = rayorigin + t raydirection d = sdf(p) if d < epsilon: return t, p t += d return None, None This method accelerates the sphere tracing of isosurfaces defined by Fractal Brownian Motion (FBM) noise by computing valid Sphere Distance Bounds (SDB) and adaptive step sizes using a dynamic Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) derived from the FBM structure itself. It reduces the average evaluation cost in empty space from O(N) to O(k), where k \ll N is the number of octaves required to prove emptiness, by progressively evaluating octaves while bounding the remaining potential contribution to determine if the total function value can exceed the isosurface threshold. Unlike naive sphere tracing which evaluates the full FBM at every step, this approach supports features like Adaptive Lipschitz constants, Sub-stepping, Early Stop+k, and Quadratic Taylor inclusion functions. This method extends standard sphere tracing to render scenes composed of primitive shapes, character segments (letters), and arcs using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex geometric text and decorative arcs alongside standard diffuse geometry by treating them as distinct hit types with specialized distance queries and normal estimation. Unlike standard sphere tracing which typically handles uniform primitives, this approach integrates a composite SDF evaluation that prioritizes character and arc geometry when the ray is near a surrounding bounding box, and employs variance-based adaptive sampling to converge path-traced lighting. Non-Linear Sphere Tracing (NLST) is a rendering method for directly visualizing deformed Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) without converting them to explicit meshes. It solves the incompatibility between standard sphere tracing and non-linear deformation techniques (such as Linear Blend Skinning or Free-Form Deformations), which invalidate the Euclidean distance metric required for safe stepping. Unlike meshing approaches like Marching Cubes, NLST maintains infinite resolution and sharp features, and unlike methods requiring inverse deformations, it works with general forward deformation functions by integrating the ray path as a curve in object space. This family defines the logic for determining the distance \Delta t to advance a ray along its direction \mathbf{d} and the conditions under which the marching loop terminates. It solves the problem of balancing rendering accuracy (avoiding missed geometry or aliasing) against computational cost (minimizing samples in empty space). It is distinguished from Sphere Tracing by relaxing the strict Lipschitz safety constraint (\Delta t \le f(\mathbf{p})) in favor of heuristic, error-based, or geometric bounds that allow larger steps in safe regions, and from Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by dynamically varying \Delta t per sample rather than using a global constant. Coarse-to-fine sphere tracing is an acceleration strategy for rendering deep implicit signed distance functions (SDFs) that reduces computational cost by initializing ray marching at a lower resolution and progressively refining it. It differs from standard single-resolution sphere tracing by leveraging the spatial coherence of nearby rays; since neighboring rays often traverse similar paths, information from coarse passes allows fine-resolution rays to start closer to the surface, significantly reducing the number of SDF evaluations required for convergence. Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit is a deferred rendering technique that extends standard sphere tracing by tracking two distinct hit points per pixel: a primary surface hit (the nearest geometric intersection) and a represent hit (a proxy for the surface at the pixel's radius). This dual-pass approach is designed to handle transparency and aliasing artifacts at object edges by evaluating visibility and occlusion from both points and selecting the ray with greater visual impact (higher alpha). It differs from standard sphere tracing by explicitly maintaining a "represent" state to capture edge information that would otherwise be missed by a single convergence check. Bidirectional sphere tracing is a robust surface extraction technique that mitigates the convergence failures of standard sphere tracing when rays miss surface edges or intersect surfaces non-orthogonally. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which relies on a single forward march that may stall or overshoot, this method uses forward and backward traces to narrow the candidate range of the surface position, then refines the zero-level set using additional solvers. It is distinct from FBM Sphere Tracing with BVH Acceleration and Coarse-to-Fine Sphere Tracing by replacing the iterative step-size heuristic with a bounded search interval derived from two opposing traces. Relaxed sphere tracing is an acceleration technique for distance-field ray marching that increases the step size beyond the conservative SDF value to reduce iteration counts. It scales the step by a relaxation factor \omega, reverting to the standard safe step if the new sample indicates the ray has jumped over the surface (i.e., the unbounding spheres of consecutive steps are disjoint). It is distinguished from Enhanced Sphere Tracing by its simpler geometric assumption; while relaxed tracing uses a fixed scalar multiplier, enhanced tracing computes an optimal tangential step size for planar surfaces, offering superior convergence at the cost of higher per-step complexity. Cloud Tracing with Pseudo-Spheroids renders volumetric clouds by tracing rays through a set of implicit surfaces (pseudo-spheroids) and sampling noise only within those volumes. It differs from general sphere tracing by explicitly managing a list of intersected cloud primitives, sorting them by depth, and using a distance-based Level of Detail (LOD) to vary step size, optimizing the trade-off between visual fidelity and computational cost. An optimization to eliminate unnecessary distance computations for collections of objects by using the triangle inequality to bound the distance to an object based on previous evaluations and ray traversal. An optimization using the triangle inequality to reduce unnecessary distance evaluations, particularly effective for large assortments of objects. If all primitives (e.g., 14 Bezier curves) are nearly equidistant from the eye, the triangle inequality does not significantly reduce unnecessary distance evaluations until sphere tracing has traversed much of each ray. For 9 spheres/plane, triangle inequality reduced execution time from 2:53 to 1:19 (46% relative time). For the zeno logo, triangle inequality reduced execution time from 26:29 to 19:23 (73% relative time). When combined with convexity, triangle inequality enhances ordinary sphere tracing by 60%. Slice raybundle for current chunk: curraybundle = raybundle[chunkstart: chunkstart + self.chunksize]. Call parent forward method: curcolor = super().forward(sampler, implicitfn, curraybundle). Append color to list: chunkcolors.append(curcolor). Concatenate all chunk colors along dimension 0: color = torch.cat(chunkcolors, dim=0). Return concatenated color. chunksize: maximum number of rays processed in a single forward pass. The term "sphere tracing" and the geometric method for antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces were introduced in [Kay & Kajiya, 1986]. The method was presented as a geometric alternative to standard ray tracing, particularly suited for implicit surfaces defined by distance fields. It gained prominence for its ability to handle complex geometric modeling operations and its inherent support for antialiasing through symbolic prefiltering. name: Quadric Tracing
body:
Quadric tracing is a method to accelerate sphere tracing by precomputing an augmented distance field using quadric surfaces (second-degree algebraic surfaces) to bound or unbound scene geometry, reducing the number of Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluations. It solves the slowdown of sphere tracing near surfaces and with increasing scene complexity, where function evaluation time and convergence slow drastically. Unlike relaxed sphere tracing (which uses a scalar to determine step size and reverts if too large) or enhanced sphere tracing (which uses previous two radii to approximate planar surfaces), quadric tracing uses precomputed geometric bounds to accelerate convergence. It stops when the computed distance value dips below a threshold, switching to enhanced sphere tracing for final convergence. Inputs: A 3D grid of precomputed quadric parameters and SDF values; a ray defined by origin p0 and direction v (|v|2 = 1). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray. Data Structures: The accelerator data structure is a regular 3D grid. Each cell stores: Quadric of Revolution: 96 bits (3 floats). Defined relative to the grid point pc. The axis of revolution direction n \in \mathbb{R}^3 (|n|2 = 1) is multiplied by 2 + k to store the quadric parameters. The scalar parameter k \in [-1, 1] encodes the shape (eccentricity and curvature). SDF Value: 32 bits (1 float). A signed distance function value d stored for the cell. Total: 128 bits per cell. Preprocessing: For every cell in parallel on the GPU, starting from the quadric origin pc: 1. Shoot rays in N uniformly sampled directions vi (i = 1, \dots, N). 2. Sphere trace each ray pc + t vi until the surface or the bounding box is reached. 3. For each ray-surface intersection (xi, yi, zi):= pc + ti vi, compute the unique ki \in [-1, 1] value defining the quadric of revolution touching the surface at that point. Operate in the 2D plane defined by vi and normal n. Let q = (qx, qy) \in \mathbb{R}^2 be the rotated projection where n is the y-axis. Solve for k using the quadratic equation: qx^2 k^2 + (2 \operatorname{sgn}(qy) qy^2 - qy) k - qy^2 = 0 Select the smaller solution for ki. 4. To obtain the unbounding quadric within the cell, we need the narrowest candidate unbounding quadric region from all rays; therefore, k:= \min \{ki \mid i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\}. 5. Store the axis direction n (normalized gradient -

abla f(p)|) scaled by 2+k, and the SDF value. Rendering: 1. For each evaluation point along the ray, query the closest grid cell to get k, n, and d. 2. Intersect the ray with the precomputed quadric to accelerate tracing convergence. 3. If the quadric intersection yields a valid step that does not skip the surface, take it. Otherwise, fall back to standard sphere tracing or enhanced sphere tracing. 4. Stop when the distance value dips below a threshold. Conic Section Definitions: The quadric is a revolution of a conic section. The conic section coefficients A, B, C are functions of k: A(k) = k^2, \quad B(k) = 2(k - 1/2), \quad C(k) = -k These define the implicit equation in the 2D plane (y-axis is axis of revolution): A \cdot x^2 + B \cdot y^2 + C \cdot y = 0 \quad (1) The polar parametrization of the conic section is s(t) = [\cos(t) \cdot r(t), \sin(t) \cdot r(t)]^T, where: r(t) =  rac{-C \cdot \sin(t)}{A \cdot \cos^2(t) + B \cdot \sin^2(t)} The interval L(k) restricts the parameter t to avoid unwanted hyperbola branches: L(k) =  egin{cases}  rac{\pi}{2}, & 	ext{if } A(k) \cdot B(k) \geq 0 \ \arctan\left(\sqrt{ rac{-A}{B}}ight), & 	ext{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (k \in [-1, 1]) \quad (2) The implicit equation of the unbounding quadric of revolution in 3D (z-axis is axis of revolution) is: A \cdot (x^2 + y^2) + B \cdot z^2 + C \cdot z = 0 \quad (3) Ray-Quadric Intersection: Given ray p0 + t \cdot v (p0 = (x0, y0, z0), v = (vx, vy, vz)), substitute into (3) to solve at^2 + bt + c = 0: a = A \cdot vx^2 + A \cdot vy^2 + B \cdot vz^2 b = 2A \cdot x0 vx + 2A \cdot y0 vy + 2B \cdot z0 vz + C vz c = A \cdot (x0^2 + y0^2) + B \cdot z0^2 + C \cdot z0 Let roots be t1 \leq t2. If no real roots, I:= [-\infty, +\infty]. If 0 
eq |k| < 1/2 (hyperbolas), omit the unwanted branch: I:=  egin{cases} [-\infty, t2] & 	ext{if } (z0 + t1 vz) \cdot k < 0 \ [t1, +\infty] & 	ext{if } (z0 + t2 vz) \cdot k < 0 \end{cases} If none of the conditions apply, I remains as previously defined. Selecting Intersection t: Evaluate the following conditional assignments in order to find the first valid intersection t \geq 0: 1. t:= t2 if t1 = -\infty 2. t:= t1 if 0 < t2 < +\infty 3. t:= \infty if t1 < 0 4. t:= 0 if otherwise Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def intersectquadric(p0, v, A, B, C, k): # Quadratic coefficients for ray p0 + tv against A(x^2+y^2) + Bz^2 + Cz = 0 a = A (v.x2 + v.y2) + B v.z2 b = 2 A (p0.x v.x + p0.y v.y) + 2 B p0.z v.z + C v.z c = A (p0.x2 + p0.y2) + B p0.z2 + C p0.z # Solve quadratic equation if abs(a) < 1e-9: if abs(b) < 1e-9: return float('inf') t1 = -c / b t2 = float('inf') else: disc = b2 - 4 a c if disc < 0: t1 = float('-inf') t2 = float('inf') else: sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(disc) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 # Omit unwanted hyperbola branch if |k| < 0.5 and k != 0 if abs(k) < 0.5 and k != 0: z1 = p0.z + t1 v.z z2 = p0.z + t2 v.z if z1 k < 0: t1 = float('-inf') if z2 k < 0: t2 = float('inf') # Select first valid intersection t >= 0 per source assignment order t = float('inf') if t1 == float('-inf'): t = t2 elif 0 < t2 < float('inf'): t = t1 elif t1 < 0: t = float('inf') else: t = 0 return t def quadrictrace(p0, v, grid, maxsteps=100, threshold=1e-4): """ Quadric tracing algorithm. grid.query(p) returns a cell struct with.A,.B,.C,.k,.d (SDF value). """ p = p0 for in range(maxsteps): cell = grid.query(p) d = cell.d if d < threshold: return p # Query quadric parameters for current cell A, B, C, k = cell.A, cell.B, cell.C, cell.k # Compute acceleration step from quadric intersection tq = intersectquadric(p, v, A, B, C, k) # Take quadric step if valid and does not skip the surface, else fall back to SDF step if tq > 0 and tq <= d: t = tq else: t = d p = p + t v return p # Non-convergence or max steps reached Combines regular or improved quadratic Taylor bounds with enhancements: Sub-stepping, ES+1, and Adaptive computation of \gamma{Fn}. Using k > 1 was never found to be faster when using quadratic bounds. On the Sponge scene with all enhancements, Linear bounds have 362.3 avg steps, 3815.0 avg octaves, 65.0 ms time. Regular Quad has 70.0 avg steps, 651.1 avg octaves, 16.3 ms time, offering a 	imes 4.0 speedup vs Linear and 	imes 6.7 speedup vs naive. On Sponge (far) scene, Linear (far) has 147.8 avg steps, 749.6 avg octaves, 16.7 ms time. Regular Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.8 ms time (	imes 1.7 vs Linear, 	imes 4.1 vs naive). Improved Quad has 55.8 avg steps, 300.6 avg octaves, 9.7 ms time (	imes 1.7 vs Linear, 	imes 4.2 vs naive). With enhancements, quadratic bounds provide massive performance gains over linear bounds with same enhancements (	imes 4.0 and 	imes 1.7 speedups on test scenes) and 	imes 6.7 and 	imes 4.1 speedups over the naive method. Quadric tracing offers a 20% to 100% speedup in rendering static scenes. It amortizes the slowdown caused by the complexity of the geometry. The method takes much larger steps along the ray, often skipping several grid cells without skipping ray-surface intersections. However, sometimes the quadric does not contain the whole cell it is assigned to, so the acceleration is zero or negligible for some positions. About 20% of expensive signed distance function evaluations are saved. Quadric tracing was introduced to accelerate sphere tracing for implicit surfaces defined by signed distance functions (SDFs). Most implicit surface representations require conversion to a triangle list for efficient, real-time visualization, but distance-based representations allow sphere tracing to enable raytracing for the whole scene within milliseconds using the GPU. The representation supports set operations such as union, intersection, subtraction, and real-time offsets, allowing any CSG tree to be constructed from a large set of primitives. However, function evaluation time and convergence slow drastically with scene complexity. The method generalizes the unbounding sphere and separating plane approach to unbounding quadrics for any SDF. It is applicable to light visibility computation such as soft shadows, ambient occlusion, and global illumination, as well as room impulse response estimation and deep learning based implicit signed distance functions.
