name: Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing
head: Enhanced Sphere Tracing - Over Relaxation, Over-Relaxation Raymarching, Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing with Screen-Space Intersection Selection, Over-relaxation sphere tracing with screen-space selection, Over-relaxation-based sphere tracing, Over-relaxed sphere tracing, Sphere tracing with over-relaxation
body: Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing accelerates the standard sphere tracing algorithm by stepping further than the conservative signed distance bound allows, controlled by a relaxation parameter \omega \in 1, 2). It reduces the number of Signed Distance Function ([SDF) evaluations by 20–40% in typical 3D renders. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which guarantees no surface penetration per step, this method risks overshooting the surface; it detects this via an overlap test between consecutive unbounding spheres and falls back to standard sphere tracing if an intersection is missed. It also incorporates screen-space error metrics to select the best shading point when the ray grazes an object or exceeds the maximum iteration count, reducing artifacts compared to simply using the last evaluated point. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized ray direction \mathbf{d}, SDF function f(\mathbf{p}), relaxation parameter \omega (typically 1.2), maximum iterations N{max} (e.g., 80), maximum distance t{max}, minimum distance t{min}, pixel radius r{pixel} (radius of a pixel at t=1), convergence threshold \epsilon (e.g., 0.001), and a boolean forceHit. Outputs: The distance t to the surface, or a sentinel value (e.g., \infty) if no valid intersection is found within constraints. Data Structures: The algorithm maintains scalar state variables for the current ray distance t, the best candidate distance candidatet, the best candidate screen-space error candidateerror, the previous step's radius previousRadius, and the current step length stepLength. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set t = t{min}. Set candidatet = t{min} and candidateerror = \infty. Set previousRadius = 0. Determine the sign of the starting position relative to the surface: functionSign = +1 if f(\mathbf{o}) \ge 0, else -1. This handles rays starting inside the object. 2. Marching Loop: Iterate i from 0 to N{max} - 1: Evaluate SDF: Compute position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and evaluate d = f(\mathbf{p}). Hit Detection: If |d| < \epsilon, the ray has converged to the surface; return t. Calculate Radius: Compute signedRadius = functionSign \cdot d and radius = |d|. Overshoot Detection (SOR Fail): Check if the current over-relaxed step would skip over the surface. This occurs if \omega > 1 AND the sum of the current radius and the previous radius is less than the previous step length: \text{sorFail} = (\omega > 1) \land (\text{radius} + \text{previousRadius} < \text{stepLength}). This condition ensures that the unbounding spheres of the current and previous steps do not overlap, implying the ray segment between them might contain a surface. Handle Failure or Advance: If sorFail is true: Retreat the ray to the position before the over-relaxed step. The fallback position is calculated as: \mathbf{p}{fallback} = \mathbf{p}{prev} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \delta{i-1} \cdot (1 - \omega) where \delta{i-1} is the step size of the previous iteration. In terms of distance t, this effectively resets the step size to the standard SDF value by making the next step negative, backing the ray up to a safe point. The implementation achieves this by updating stepLength as stepLength = (1 - omega) and setting \omega = 1. Do not update candidatet or candidateerror for this failed step. If sorFail is false: Calculate the new step length: stepLength = signedRadius \cdot \omega. Update previousRadius = radius. Calculate screen-space error: error = radius / t. Division by zero is avoided if t{min} > 0. Update Best Candidate: If error < candidateerror, update candidatet = t and candidateerror = error. Early Termination: If error < r{pixel} (sub-pixel accuracy) or t > t{max}, break the loop. Advance Ray: t \leftarrow t + \text{stepLength}. 3. Result Selection: After the loop, if forceHit is false AND (t > t{max} OR candidateerror > r{pixel}), return \infty (no hit). Otherwise, return candidatet. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def overrelaxationspheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, maxiterations, tmin, tmax, pixelradius, omega=1.2, forcehit=False, epsilon=1e-3): """ Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing with screen-space intersection selection. Args: rayorigin: Camera origin (vec3) raydirection: Normalized ray direction (vec3) sdf: Signed Distance Function callable sdf(p) maxiterations: Maximum number of iterations (e.g., 80) tmin: Minimum ray distance tmax: Maximum ray distance pixelradius: Radius of a pixel at t=1 (sub-pixel threshold) omega: Relaxation parameter in 1, 2). Default 1.2. forcehit: If True, return candidatet even if error > pixelradius. epsilon: Convergence threshold for surface hit. Returns: hitdistance: Distance along ray to surface, or float('inf') if no hit. """ t = tmin candidateerror = float('inf') candidatet = tmin previousradius = 0.0 steplength = 0.0 # Determine sign based on starting position fo = sdf(rayorigin) functionsign = -1.0 if fo < 0 else 1.0 for in range(maxiterations): # Evaluate SDF at current position p = rayorigin + t raydirection signedradius = functionsign sdf(p) radius = abs(signedradius) # Hit detection if radius < epsilon: return t # Check for over-relaxation failure (overshoot) # Condition: omega > 1 AND spheres do not overlap sorfail = (omega > 1) and ((radius + previousradius) < steplength) if sorfail: # Fallback to standard sphere tracing # Retreat and disable over-relaxation steplength = (1.0 - omega) omega = 1.0 else: # Calculate step length using over-relaxation steplength = signedradius omega previousradius = radius # Calculate screen-space error error = radius / t if t > 0 else float('inf') # Update best candidate if error < candidateerror: candidatet = t candidateerror = error # Early termination if sub-pixel accuracy reached or max distance exceeded if error < pixelradius or t > tmax: break # Advance ray t += steplength # Final result selection if not forcehit and (t > tmax or candidateerror > pixelradius): return float('inf') return candidatet Parameters: \omega: Relaxation parameter. Range [1, 2). Typical value is 1.2 for a balance of performance and quality. Values up to 1.6 are used in some implementations. A value of 1.0 is standard sphere tracing. N{max}: Maximum iterations. Typical value 80. r{pixel}: Pixel radius at t=1. Used for early termination and candidate selection. \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Standard value \approx 0.001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overshooting: If \omega is too large, the ray may skip over surfaces. The overlap test detects this, but frequent failures degrade performance. Non-Lipschitz SDFs: Numeric or user-defined distance estimators (e.g., User Bulb) may not satisfy the Lipschitz condition, making the overlap test unreliable. In such cases, fall back to \omega=1 or tune \omega carefully. Grazing Rays: Rays grazing an object's edge may terminate in mid-air. The screen-space error metric selects the point with the smallest unbounding sphere radius, as measured in screen-space, reducing "aura" artifacts. Self-Intersection: Secondary rays may self-intersect. A dynamic \epsilon offset (e.g., 2 \cdot |f(p)|) is recommended for secondary rays. Branch Divergence: Checking if the fallback sphere overlaps the current sphere to avoid re-tracing adds branching, which can reduce GPU performance. A variant for conformally transformed [Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRSs) that uses binary search on unbounding spheres instead of distance values. It is an extreme form of over-relaxation tailored for geometries where the world-space sphere center differs from the query point [10174-binary-sphere-tracing.md]. Predicts step size by assuming local planarity, using historical SDF values to allow larger steps than standard over-relaxation while reducing overshoot corrections [13706-accelerating-sphere-tracing.md]. Performance: Reduces the number of SDF evaluations (steps) by 20–40% in 3D renders compared to standard sphere tracing. Measured Performance: In a city scene (1280x720, NVIDIA GTX Titan), rendering time dropped from 20.409 ms (48.998 Hz) to 16.829 ms (59.421 Hz). In a jewel scene, it dropped from 3.472 ms (288.018 Hz) to 2.978 ms (335.744 Hz). Path tracing integration also showed improvements (101.934 ms vs 118.302 ms for one sample). Scaling: Performance gains are consistent across hardware. Strengths: Faster convergence, fewer iterations, better handling of grazing rays via screen-space selection. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \omega; larger \omega causes earlier fallback to standard tracing. Non-Lipschitz SDFs may require disabling over-relaxation. The method was introduced by Keinert et al. in 2014 in the paper "Enhanced Sphere Tracing". It builds on the principle of over-relaxation from numerical analysis to accelerate the convergence of sphere tracing. It is widely used in real-time ray marching, including in tools like User Bulb and KIFS. name: Binary Sphere Tracing
head: Speculative sphere tracing with overrelaxation
body: Binary sphere tracing is a trial-and-error search algorithm designed to find unbounding spheres for conformally transformed Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRSs). It serves as an extreme variant of over-relaxation sphere tracing, specifically tailored for geometries where the center of the world-space sphere is not necessarily at the original world-space point. Unlike direct sphere tracing, which relies on distance functions, binary sphere tracing only requires a binary intersection test with a sphere, relaxing the requirement that kernel geometries be defined by explicit distance functions. It is distinguished by its binary decision process: it either advances the ray by the full diameter of a confirmed unbounding sphere or reduces the probe radius, effectively acting as a numerical root-finding method employing binary search. Inputs: Ray origin \tau, ray direction \omega, initial probe radius s = 1, error threshold \epsilon, bonus factor \xi{bonus}, penalty factor \xi{penalty}. Outputs: Intersection point \tau. Data Structures: State is maintained in scalar variables \tau and s, along with a boolean result from the intersection test. The algorithm iteratively refines the probe sphere until it converges on an intersection or the probe radius falls below \epsilon. The probing sphere does not need to be centered at the last known free ray position; it only needs to touch it. 1. Initialize the probe radius s \leftarrow 1. 2. While s > \epsilon: a. Construct a probe sphere centered at c = \tau + \omega s with radius s. b. Evaluate ISUNBOUNDING(c, s). This function returns true if the probe sphere is an unbounding sphere (i.e., it does not intersect the geometry). c. If ISUNBOUNDING is true: i. Advance the ray origin by the sphere's diameter: \tau \leftarrow \tau + \omega (2s). ii. Increase the probe radius for the next iteration to traverse empty areas faster: s \leftarrow s \cdot \xi{bonus}. d. If ISUNBOUNDING is false: i. Reduce the probe radius: s \leftarrow s \cdot \xi{penalty}. ii. Keep \tau unchanged to re-evaluate a smaller probe at the same location. 3. Return \tau as the intersection point. Parameters: \xi{bonus}: Factor to increase probe radius upon success. Typical value: 2.0. \xi{penalty}: Factor to decrease probe radius upon failure. Typical value: 0.3. \epsilon: Error threshold for termination. Must be set much lower than in regular sphere tracing to avoid artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def binarytrace(rayorigin: Vector3, raydirection: Vector3, epsilon: float, xibonus: float = 2.0, xipenalty: float = 0.3) -> Vector3: """ Binary sphere tracing for conformally transformed KRSs. Args: rayorigin: Starting point of the ray (tau). raydirection: Normalized direction of the ray (omega). epsilon: Convergence threshold for probe radius. xibonus: Multiplier for probe radius on success. xipenalty: Multiplier for probe radius on failure. Returns: The estimated intersection point. """ s = 1.0 # Initial probe radius while s > epsilon: # Probe sphere center touches the current ray position # Center is at tau + omega s probecenter = rayorigin + raydirection s # Check if the probe sphere is unbounding (does not intersect geometry) if isunbounding(probecenter, s): # Success: Advance ray by diameter (2s) rayorigin = rayorigin + raydirection (2.0 s) # Increase probe radius for faster traversal of empty space s = s xibonus else: # Failure: Probe intersects geometry # Reduce probe radius to refine search s = s xipenalty return rayorigin def isunbounding(center: Vector3, radius: float) -> bool: """ Binary intersection test for the conformally transformed KRS geometry. Returns True if the sphere centered at center with radius does not intersect the geometry (is an unbounding sphere). The sources do not provide the implementation for this helper. """ raise NotImplementedError Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuities: Binary tracing produces visual discontinuities where unbounding sphere decisions diverge between adjacent pixels. Iteration Count: It requires approximately twice as many iterations as direct sphere tracing due to suboptimal unbounding spheres and rejected probes. Termination: The error threshold \epsilon must be significantly lower than in standard sphere tracing to prevent artifacts caused by the binary search nature. Geometry Constraints: This method is necessary for non-symmetric KRSs where conformal transformation moves the sphere center away from the original world-space point. Time Complexity: Rendering times scale linearly with the number of expansion levels in the KRS model, despite exponential geometry expansion. Performance: On an nVidia GeForce Titan X at 1920 × 1200 resolution, direct sphere tracing of linear KRS geometries maintained 15 FPS up to 28 expansion levels (approximately 0.5 billion toroidal primitives). Binary sphere tracing performed poorly in comparison, achieving only 14 expansion levels at 15 FPS. Strengths: It enables the rendering of conformally transformed geometries that do not have explicit distance functions, relying only on binary intersection tests. It can exploit coherence by performing initial steps at lower resolution. Limitations: Higher iteration count compared to direct sphere tracing. Performance is heavily dependent on camera view, with significantly shorter frame times in scenes with large empty zones. Binary sphere tracing was introduced in the context of Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRSs). It is described as an extreme version of sphere tracing with over-relaxation [KSK14], removing the option to revert to classical sphere tracing near surfaces or to accept unbounding spheres larger than speculated. These restrictions are necessary to admit conformally transformed geometry where the sphere center is displaced. The method is part of a pipeline where task buffers are processed, and free distance/index are updated upon task completion. name: Accelerating Sphere Tracing
head: Planar Assumption Sphere Tracing, Predictive Sphere Tracing
body: Accelerating Sphere Tracing is a ray marching step rule that predicts the next step distance by assuming the object surface is locally planar near the current ray position. This allows for larger, more aggressive steps than standard Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing while reducing the frequency of overshoot corrections. It builds on Over-relaxation Sphere Tracing by incorporating historical SDF values to refine step prediction. Inputs: Ray origin p0, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), SDF function f(\cdot), safety factor \omega \in (0, 1), termination threshold \epsilon. Outputs: Intersection point p{hit}, number of steps. Data Structures: Current position pn \in \mathbb{R}^3. Previous position p{n-1} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Current SDF value rn = f(pn) \in \mathbb{R}. Previous SDF value r{n-1} = f(p{n-1}) \in \mathbb{R}. Previous step distance dn = \|pn - p{n-1}\| \in \mathbb{R}. Steps: 1. Initialize ray parameters and set p0 as the ray origin. 2. For each step n starting from 0: evaluate rn = f(pn). 3. If rn is below the threshold \epsilon, terminate as the intersection is found. 4. If n = 0, calculate the initial step distance d1 = r0 using standard sphere tracing to establish history. For n > 0, retrieve the previous SDF value r{n-1} and previous step distance dn. 5. Calculate the predicted radius r{n+1} using the planar assumption formula: r{n+1} = \frac{dn - r{n-1} + rn}{dn + r{n-1} + rn}. 6. Calculate the next step distance d{n+1} = rn + \omega r{n+1}. 7. Move the ray to p{n+1} = pn + d{n+1} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 8. Check for overshoot by evaluating r{n+1}' = f(p{n+1}). If r{n+1}' + rn < d{n+1}, the ray has jumped over the object. 9. If overshoot is detected, retreat by \omega r{n+1}: p{n+1} \leftarrow p{n+1} - \omega r{n+1} \cdot \mathbf{d}. Then proceed with standard sphere tracing logic for the remaining distance, meaning the next step distance will be set to f(p{n+1}). 10. Update history: p{n-1} \leftarrow pn, pn \leftarrow p{n+1}, r{n-1} \leftarrow rn, rn \leftarrow f(p{n+1}), dn \leftarrow d{n+1}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def acceleratingspheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, omega, epsilon): pcurr = rayorigin rcurr = sdf(pcurr) # Handle first step to initialize history dprev = rcurr pprev = pcurr rprev = rcurr pnext = pcurr + dprev raydirection rnext = sdf(pnext) # Update history after first standard step pprev = pcurr rprev = rcurr dprev = dprev pcurr = pnext rcurr = rnext while rcurr >= epsilon: # Calculate predicted radius based on planar assumption numerator = dprev - rprev + rcurr denominator = dprev + rprev + rcurr if denominator == 0: rpred = 0.0 else: rpred = numerator / denominator # Calculate next step distance dnext = rcurr + omega rpred # Move ray pnext = pcurr + dnext raydirection rnext = sdf(pnext) # Check for overshoot if rnext + rcurr < dnext: # Overshoot detected: retreat by omega rpred pnext = pnext - omega rpred raydirection rnext = sdf(pnext) # Proceed with standard sphere tracing logic for next step dnext = rnext # Update history pprev = pcurr rprev = rcurr dprev = dnext pcurr = pnext rcurr = rnext return pcurr Parameters: \omega: Safety factor multiplier applied to the predicted additional distance to prevent overshooting into concave geometry. Value range: (0, 1). Pitfalls: Concave Geometry: The planar assumption may cause the predicted step to land inside the object if the surface is concave. The safety factor \omega \in (0, 1) is applied to r{n+1} to reduce the step size and maintain a margin, preventing deep penetration. Overshoot Correction: If overshoot is detected, the ray retreats by \omega r{n+1} and proceeds with standard sphere tracing logic. Initial Steps: The formula requires r{n-1} and dn, so the first step cannot use this formula directly. A standard sphere tracing step is typically used to initialize history. Performance: Rendering time is approximately 0.8 times that of conventional Relaxation Sphere Tracing. Strengths: Allows more aggressive stepping than standard over-relaxation, reducing the number of steps and overshoot corrections. Limitations: Relies on the planar assumption, which may be inaccurate for highly curved or concave surfaces, requiring the safety factor \omega. Origin: The method was proposed in 2018 as an improvement over Enhanced Sphere Tracing and Relaxation Sphere Tracing. Development: It aims to make ray marching steps bolder by using historical SDF values to predict the next step size based on a planar surface assumption. 要約Accelerating Sphere Tracing～より良いレイマーチングに向けて Part2～, https://qiita.com/Hirai0827/items/e05e13f343357d648b1b, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Step Size and Termination Rules
head: Ray Marching Parameters and Compositing
body: Step Size and Termination Rules define the control flow logic for ray-marching loops, determining how far a ray advances per iteration (\Delta t) and when the loop halts. This family solves the trade-off between computational efficiency (skipping empty space) and visual fidelity (avoiding missed geometry or aliasing). It sets itself apart from specific implementations like Sphere Tracing or Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by providing the general framework for adaptive stepping, early termination, and safety constraints applicable to both Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and volumetric density fields. All methods in this family operate on a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized by accumulated distance t. The core loop evaluates a scene function (SDF, density field, or volume texture) at the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to determine the next step size \Delta t and check for termination. Termination Conditions: 1. Surface Hit: The ray has intersected the target geometry. For SDFs, this is typically |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon or f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0. For volumes, this may be a density threshold or opacity accumulation. 2. Escape/Miss: The ray has traveled beyond a maximum distance t{max} or exceeded a maximum iteration count N{max}. 3. Early Termination (Volumes): Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1 - \epsilon), or accumulated transmission falls below a minimum threshold, allowing the ray to stop early as further contributions are negligible. Step Size Determination: The step size \Delta t is computed based on the local scene properties: SDF-based: \Delta t is often derived from the SDF value f(\mathbf{p}), potentially scaled by a relaxation factor or Lipschitz constant \lambda. Volume-based: \Delta t may be fixed, adaptive based on density gradients, or constrained by minimum/maximum bounds to prevent aliasing or excessive computation. Safety: Steps must be chosen to ensure the ray does not penetrate the surface or skip over significant volumetric features, often requiring conservative clamping. Pseudocode Structure: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchloop(rayorigin, raydirection, scenefunc, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon): """ Generic ray marching loop with adaptive step size and termination. Args: rayorigin (vec3): The starting point of the ray. raydirection (vec3): The normalized direction of the ray. scenefunc (function): A function evaluating the scene (SDF or density) at point p. maxdist (float): The maximum distance the ray can travel. maxsteps (int): The maximum number of iterations allowed. epsilon (float): The convergence threshold for hit detection. Returns: tuple: (hit: bool, distance: float) """ t = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): # Check for escape if t > maxdist: return False, t # Calculate current position p = rayorigin + raydirection t # Evaluate scene function val = scenefunc(p) # Termination: Hit if ishit(val, epsilon): return True, t # Termination: Early Exit (Volume specific) if isearlyexit(val, t): return False, t # Or handle partial contribution # Step Size Calculation step = computestepsize(val, t, i) # Safety Clamp step = max(step, minstep) step = min(step, maxstep) t += step # Max steps reached return False, t Standard Constant Step Ray Marching uses a predefined constant step size \Delta t, simplifying implementation but requiring careful tuning to avoid aliasing or missed details. It differs from Sphere Tracing by ignoring local geometry constraints for performance, and from SDF Ray Marching with Grid Lookup by not using interpolation for precise intersection detection. Sphere Tracing uses the SDF value at the current position as a safe lower bound for the distance to the nearest surface, allowing the ray to "jump" forward by that exact distance. This guarantees that the ray never overshoots or penetrates the surface, provided the function satisfies the Lipschitz condition. It is distinguished from its siblings by its adaptive step sizing which significantly reduces the number of function evaluations required to converge on a surface. Step Size Optimization encompasses techniques that dynamically determine the distance \Delta t to advance a ray, replacing fixed-step methods to balance computational cost and visual fidelity. It differs from Sphere Tracing in that while sphere tracing strictly uses the SDF value as a lower bound for the step (often with a relaxation factor), step size optimization includes broader strategies like error estimation, gap limiting, and integration-based adaptive stepping that may not rely solely on the geometric distance bound. Termination criteria define the conditions under which a ray-marching loop halts, ensuring the algorithm returns a valid intersection point or correctly identifies a miss without infinite iteration. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sphere Tracing by focusing on the general control flow logic applicable to both Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and volumetric density fields, rather than the specific geometric step-size constraints of sphere tracing or the fixed-step simplicity of constant marching. Definition: Dynamic adjustment of the minimum step size based on distance from camera and accumulated density to reduce samples in less important areas. Mechanism: Inside the cloud (distanceField \le 0), increase minStepSize by STEPINSCREASEOVERDENSITY multiplied by the current sampleDensity. After advancing the ray, increase minStepSize by STEPINCREASEOVERDISTANCE multiplied by the stepSize used. Parameters: STEPINSCREASEOVERDENSITY: Constant controlling how much minStepSize increases per unit of sampleDensity. STEPINCREASEOVERDISTANCE: Constant controlling how much minStepSize increases per unit of stepSize (distance traveled). Comparison: Increases step size further from camera (less detail needed) and behind dense areas (less light contribution), unlike fixed step sizes. Definition: Cone step mapping and relaxed cone step mapping are space leaping acceleration techniques used in ray marching. Definition: A fix for volumetric cloud rendering where sphere tracing takes overly aggressive step sizes, skipping cloud boundaries and leaving circular/scalloped density artifacts. Mechanism: Clamp the pre-computed 2D organic cell SDF in cloudweatherbake.comp to a conservative maximum of 30000.0 uWorldScale. Reduce the sphere tracing step size multiplier from 0.8 to 0.4 in atmospherelowres.comp to make the empty space skipping strictly conservative. Clamp the empty space skipping step size to a maximum of 2000.0 worldScale to prevent overly aggressive jumps that bypass cloud details or boundaries. Parameters: SDF Max Clamp: 30000.0 uWorldScale. Step Size Multiplier: 0.4 (reduced from 0.8). Step Size Max Clamp: 2000.0 worldScale. Pitfall: In empty regions of the weather map, the organic cell SDF returned uncapped values (up to 1e14), causing bilinear filtering to interpolate extremely large values near cloud edges. The empty-space skipping sphere tracing loop used an aggressive step multiplier of 0.8 with no upper bound, resulting in rays jumping past the actual cloud surface. The concept of step size and termination is fundamental to all ray-marching techniques. Early implementations often used fixed steps due to simplicity, but this led to aliasing and missed geometry in complex scenes. The introduction of Sphere Tracing by John Hart provided a mathematically safe adaptive step size based on SDFs. Subsequent developments, such as those in volumetric cloud rendering, introduced adaptive minimum step sizes to optimize performance in large, sparse volumes. Specific implementations, like the conservative step sizing fixes for volumetric clouds, highlight the ongoing need to balance aggressive space-leaping with visual fidelity. steubengineer/imaginaryVolumes, https://github.com/steubengineer/imaginaryVolumes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Volumetric Cloud Rendering - Jack Tollenaar, https://www.jacktollenaar.top/articles/clouds.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) What is Ray Marching? name: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching
head: Constant Step Distance Sampling, Constant step ray marching, March Calculation
body: Standard Constant Step Ray Marching is an iterative root-finding technique for determining the intersection of a ray with an implicit surface or evaluating volumetric fields by stepping along the ray at fixed intervals. It solves the problem of rendering implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or scalar fields without requiring analytical intersection solutions or polygonal mesh rasterization. Unlike Sphere Tracing, which dynamically adjusts step size based on the local SDF value to guarantee no overshooting, this method uses a predefined constant step size \Delta t, simplifying implementation but requiring careful tuning to avoid aliasing or missed details. It differs from Step Size Optimization by ignoring local geometry constraints for performance, and from SDF Ray Marching with Grid Lookup by not using interpolation for precise intersection detection. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized ray direction \mathbf{d}, fixed step size \Delta t, maximum travel distance t{max}, maximum iteration count N{max}, and convergence threshold \epsilon. Outputs: Intersection distance t{hit} (or null if missed), and optionally the hit position \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Ray State: A scalar t representing accumulated distance, initialized to t{min} (near clipping plane). Scene Function: A function f(\mathbf{p}) that returns a scalar value. For SDFs, f(\mathbf{p}) is the signed distance to the nearest surface; for boolean volumes, it may return a boolean or density. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set accumulated distance t \leftarrow t{min} and step counter k \leftarrow 0. 2. Position Calculation: Compute the current sample point \mathbf{p}k = \mathbf{o} + t \mathbf{d}. 3. Sampling: Evaluate the scene function at \mathbf{p}k to get value v = f(\mathbf{p}k). 4. Termination Check: If v \le 0 (for SDFs) or v indicates a hit (e.g., density threshold), the ray has intersected the surface. Return t as the intersection distance. If t > t{max} or k \ge N{max}, the ray has escaped or exceeded resources. Return null/miss. 5. Step Advancement: Advance the ray by the constant step size: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. 6. Increment: Increment step counter k \leftarrow k + 1. 7. Loop: Repeat from Step 2. Formulas: The ray position at step k is defined as: \mathbf{r}(k) = \mathbf{o} + k \Delta t \mathbf{d} where \mathbf{o} is the ray origin, \mathbf{d} is the unit ray direction, \Delta t is the predefined constant step size, and k \in \{0, 1, 2,...\} is the step number. For SDFs, the intersection is detected when: f(\mathbf{r}(k)) \le 0 Parameters with Typical Values: \Delta t: Fixed step size. Typical values range from 0.001 to 0.1 depending on scene scale and desired precision. t{max}: Maximum ray distance. Typical values: 10.0 to 100.0. N{max}: Maximum iterations. Typical values: 50 to 255. \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Typical value: 0.001. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overshooting: If \Delta t is too large relative to the scene's high-frequency details, the ray may jump over thin objects or surfaces, resulting in missed intersections. Aliasing: Large \Delta t can cause jagged edges or "staircasing" artifacts on curved surfaces. Performance: Unlike Sphere Tracing, constant step marching does not adapt to empty space, leading to unnecessary samples in large voids. Precision: For SDFs, checking f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0 may return a point slightly inside the surface. Midpoint approximation (t - 0.5 \Delta t) can improve accuracy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def standardconstantstepraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, stepsize, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon): """ Performs standard constant step ray marching. Args: rayorigin (vec3): The starting point of the ray. raydirection (vec3): The normalized direction of the ray. stepsize (float): The fixed distance to advance per iteration (Delta t). maxdist (float): The maximum distance the ray can travel. maxsteps (int): The maximum number of iterations allowed. epsilon (float): The threshold for considering a hit (for SDFs, <= 0 is hit). Returns: float or None: The distance to the intersection, or None if no hit is found. """ t = 0.0 # Accumulated distance k = 0 # Step counter # scenesdf(p) evaluates the scene's signed distance or density field at point p def scenesdf(p): # Implementation depends on scene definition (e.g., SDF primitives, volume grid) pass while k < maxsteps: # 1. Calculate current position currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 2. Evaluate scene function value = scenesdf(currentpos) # 3. Check for intersection if value <= epsilon: # Hit detected # Optional: Refine position using midpoint approximation hitdistance = t - 0.5 stepsize return hitdistance # 4. Check for escape if t > maxdist: return None # 5. Advance ray by constant step t += stepsize # 6. Increment step counter k += 1 # Max steps reached without hit return None An optimization for sampling within the volume to determine the entry point into solid matter more accurately. It mitigates the inefficiency of constant step marching in large empty spaces by first taking large steps to find the approximate boundary, then switching to smaller constant steps to pinpoint the entry. A modification of Evans' method using a ray equation for sampling, allowing for constant step marching along the normal to compute ambient occlusion. It samples along the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the hit point \mathbf{x} using the ray equation \mathbf{r}n(k) = \mathbf{x} + k \Delta t \mathbf{n}. The occlusion is calculated as AO = 1 - \frac{1}{2} \sum{k=1}^{k{max}} \frac{1}{k} (k \Delta t - f(\mathbf{r}n(k))). Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of steps taken. Since \Delta t is constant, N \approx t{max} / \Delta t. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, as only the current position and accumulated distance need to be stored. Performance: Faster to implement and compute per step than adaptive methods because it avoids branching based on SDF values for step size calculation. However, it is less efficient in terms of total samples for scenes with large empty regions, as it samples uniformly regardless of distance to geometry. Strengths: Simple implementation, predictable memory usage, no risk of infinite loops due to oscillating step sizes (if N{max} is enforced). Limitations: Prone to overshooting thin geometry if \Delta t is too large; requires manual tuning of \Delta t for different scene scales; less accurate than Sphere Tracing for SDFs. When to Use: Suitable for simple scenes, volumetric rendering where uniform sampling is acceptable, or when hardware constraints favor fixed-step loops over dynamic branching. When Not to Use: When rendering complex SDF scenes with high-frequency details or large empty spaces, where adaptive stepping (Sphere Tracing) is preferred. Standard Constant Step Ray Marching originated as a fundamental technique for rendering implicit surfaces before the widespread adoption of Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for adaptive stepping. It is closely related to early ray tracing methods for implicit curves and surfaces, such as those described by Taubin. The method is often contrasted with "Sphere Tracing" (Hart 1995), which uses the SDF value as the step size to guarantee convergence. name: Iteration-Based Coloring
head: Iteration count, Step count coloring [S1, unofficial]
body: Iteration-Based Coloring is a rendering technique where the final pixel color is determined by the number of raymarching steps taken before the ray terminates (either by hitting a surface or reaching a maximum step count). It visualizes the computational intensity of the raymarch, highlighting regions where the ray traveled further or required more sampling iterations. Unlike standard shading which relies on material properties and lighting, this method maps algorithmic performance metrics directly to visual output. Inputs: Ray origin and direction for each pixel. Implicit surface function or voxel data structure. Maximum step count limit (N{max}). Fixed step size (\Delta t). Outputs: Pixel color value. Data Structures: Step counter: An integer tracking the number of iterations performed for the current ray. Termination flag: Boolean indicating if the ray has hit a surface or exceeded N{max}. Steps: 1. Initialize the ray for the current pixel using the camera parameters. 2. Initialize step counter k = 0. 3. While k < N{max} and ray is not terminated: a. Evaluate the distance to the nearest surface (or check voxel occupancy) at the current ray position. b. Advance the ray along its direction by the step size \Delta t. c. Increment k. 4. Determine the color based on the final value of k. Formulas: The color intensity C is mapped linearly to the step count k. A common normalization maps k to the range [0, 255]: C = \left\lfloor \frac{k}{N{max}} \times 255 \right\rfloor Where: k is the number of steps taken. N{max} is the maximum allowed steps. Parameters: N{max}: The maximum number of steps. A typical value cited is 64. \Delta t: The fixed step size. Typically set to 1.0 for standard constant step marching. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Termination: Rays that never hit a surface (e.g., background) will always result in N{max} steps, returning the maximum intensity value. Precision: Floating-point accumulation errors may cause the ray to overshoot or undershoot the surface slightly, requiring a small epsilon threshold for hit detection. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: rayorigin: vec3, origin of the ray. raydirection: vec3, normalized direction of the ray. surfacefunction: callable, returns distance to surface at a point. maxsteps: int, maximum number of raymarching iterations. stepsize: float, fixed distance to advance per step. Returns: int: Step count taken before termination. """ currentpos = rayorigin stepcount = 0 for i in range(maxsteps): dist = surfacefunction(currentpos) if dist < 1e-4: return stepcount currentpos = currentpos + raydirection stepsize stepcount += 1 return stepcount A variant that visualizes geometric depth by mapping the z-coordinate of the first surface hit to grayscale intensity, rather than computational step count. It differs from its parent by encoding spatial distance instead of algorithmic intensity. Time Complexity: O(N \times S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of steps per ray. The complexity is dominated by the raymarching loop. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as only the step count and current position need to be stored. Performance: Visualizes computational intensity, making it useful for debugging raymarchers or creating abstract visual effects. It does not provide physically accurate shading. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides immediate feedback on raymarch efficiency and surface proximity. Limitations: Does not convey material properties or lighting. The technique was described in a 2013 blog post on raymarching distance fields, where it was presented as a simple way to "spice up" black and white renders by visualizing where the most intensive portions of the image are. name: Depth Rendering
body: Depth Rendering is a visualization technique that maps ray traversal metrics to grayscale intensity, providing a direct representation of distance or computational depth. The source implementation computes intensity from the number of traversal steps, while the accompanying documentation describes an alternative mapping using the hit position's z-coordinate. Inputs: tree: Voxel data structure containing spatial bounds tree->min[2] and tree->max[2] along the depth axis, and side length tree->gridlength. rc: Render context providing pixel dimension rc.ny (assumed square) and ray generation rc.getRayForPixel(x, y) returning origin o and direction d. texturearray: Output buffer of size ny ny 4 (RGBA), where each pixel occupies 4 unsigned chars. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin o (vec3) and direction d (vec3, typically normalized). Voxel Grid: Uniform grid spanning [0, gridlength) in each axis. Parameters: gridlength: Side length of the voxel grid, used for normalization. factor: Normalized intensity value in range [0, 1]. Algorithm: 1. Initialize OpenMP threads equal to the number of CPU processors. 2. Parallelize the outer pixel loop over y. 3. For each pixel (x, y): a. Compute index = y (ny 4) + x 4. b. Initialize ray traverser with tree, o, and d. c. Traverse the tree: i. While not terminated: If leaf node has data, break loop. Else, call t.step(). d. Get hit position pos = t.getCurrentPosition(). e. Compute intensity from step count: factor = \frac{stepcount}{\log2(gridlength)} (Note: The source notes describe an alternative position-based factor factor = \frac{|pos[2]|}{|tree->max[2]| - |tree->min[2]|}, but the executable code uses step count.) f. Compute grayscale color: val = 255 \times (1 - factor) g. Write to texturearray: texturearray[index] = val texturearray[index+1] = val texturearray[index+2] = val texturearray[index+3] = 1 (Alpha) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderdepth(tree, rc, texturearray): ny = rc.ny gridlength = tree.gridlength log2size = math.log2(gridlength) if gridlength > 0 else 1.0 for y in range(ny): partindex = y (ny 4) for x in range(ny): index = partindex + x 4 ray = rc.getRayForPixel(x, y) o, d = ray.origin, ray.direction stepcount = 0 hit = False # DDA initialization for uniform grid if d[0] == 0: tmaxx = float('inf') else: tmaxx = ((0 if d[0] > 0 else gridlength) - o[0]) / d[0] if d[1] == 0: tmaxy = float('inf') else: tmaxy = ((0 if d[1] > 0 else gridlength) - o[1]) / d[1] if d[2] == 0: tmaxz = float('inf') else: tmaxz = ((0 if d[2] > 0 else gridlength) - o[2]) / d[2] stepx = 1 if d[0] > 0 else -1 stepy = 1 if d[1] > 0 else -1 stepz = 1 if d[2] > 0 else -1 tdeltax = abs(1.0 / d[0]) if d[0] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltay = abs(1.0 / d[1]) if d[1] != 0 else float('inf') tdeltaz = abs(1.0 / d[2]) if d[2] != 0 else float('inf') curx = int(o[0]) if 0 <= o[0] < gridlength else -1 cury = int(o[1]) if 0 <= o[1] < gridlength else -1 curz = int(o[2]) if 0 <= o[2] < gridlength else -1 # Traverse until bounds exceeded or hit found while stepcount < gridlength 3 + 100: if 0 <= curx < gridlength and 0 <= cury < gridlength and 0 <= curz < gridlength: hit = True break if tmaxx < tmaxy: if tmaxx < tmaxz: curx += stepx tmaxx += tdeltax else: curz += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz else: if tmaxy < tmaxz: cury += stepy tmaxy += tdeltay else: curz += stepz tmaxz += tdeltaz stepcount += 1 # Compute intensity from step count factor = stepcount / log2size factor = max(0.0, min(1.0, factor)) val = int(255 (1.0 - factor)) texturearray[index] = val texturearray[index+1] = val texturearray[index+2] = val texturearray[index+3] = 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If gridlength == 0, log2size is clamped to 1.0 to prevent NaN/Inf. Termination: If the ray escapes the tree without hitting a surface, the loop terminates when bounds are exceeded. The code sets alpha to 1 regardless of hit status. Coordinate System: The notes' formula uses abs(pos[2]), implying depth is the Z-axis. Standard graphics APIs often use Y or -Z for depth. A variant that normalizes the logarithmic distance traveled by the ray to the range [0, 1], where brighter pixels indicate further travel distance. It calculates distance d = |pi - p0|, computes \log(d), and normalizes it. This helps visualize depth over large ranges where linear mapping would compress distant details. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of pixels and S is the average number of steps per ray. Parallelized with OpenMP. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the output texture array. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides immediate visual feedback on object proximity. Limitations: Does not account for surface orientation or lighting; linear mapping may not be perceptually uniform. Originated in early voxel rendering implementations for CPU-based raycasting, specifically in the cpuvoxelraycaster project by Forceflow. name: Depth Shading
head: Depth-Only Shading
body: Depth shading is a 2D discrete shading technique that computes pixel intensity solely from the depth coordinate of the closest surface voxel, without considering surface orientation. It differs from gradient-based methods by ignoring normals, resulting in a simple inverse-depth mapping where closer features appear brighter and distant features appear darker. Inputs: 1. A depth shaded pre-image: a 2D array (Z-buffer) where each pixel (x, y) stores the distance to the closest non-empty surface voxel along the viewing ray. 2. (Optional) A second framebuffer containing the pre-image data for storage. Outputs: 1. A 2D intensity image where pixel brightness is determined by the stored depth value. Data Structures: Z-buffer: A 2D array of size W \times H (image resolution). Each element stores a scalar depth value z. In the context of the original binary voxel implementation, this represents the distance to the first non-zero byte encountered during ray casting. Steps: 1. Ray Casting / Data Traversal: Execute the underlying ray casting algorithm (e.g., sphere tracing or voxel traversal) to identify surface voxels. 2. Depth Storage: For each pixel (x, y), store the distance to the closest non-empty voxel found along the viewing ray into the Z-buffer at index (x, y). If no surface is hit, the value may remain undefined or a maximum depth, depending on the traversal implementation. 3. Intensity Calculation: Compute the output intensity I(x, y) for each pixel based on its depth value z = D(x, y). The intensity is inversely proportional to the depth: I(x, y) \propto \frac{1}{z} In the specific hardware implementation described by, this relationship is discretized. The depth coordinate is mapped to one of 128 possible values. A lookup table (LUT) is populated with intensity values calculated as a function of these 128 depth levels. 4. Lookup: Apply the LUT to the Z-buffer values to generate the final shaded image. Pitfalls: Loss of Detail: Because surface orientation (normals) is not considered, surface discontinuities and object boundaries are lost. Ambiguity: Without normal information, the shading cannot distinguish between concave and convex features or lighting effects like specular highlights. Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the shading step itself, assuming the Z-buffer is already populated. The dominant cost is the preceding ray casting/traversal step. Performance: Very fast shading stage; suitable for real-time display if the depth buffer is available. Strengths: Simple to implement; requires minimal additional computation after depth acquisition; effective for highlighting proximity to the viewer. Limitations: Lacks geometric detail due to the absence of normal vectors; produces flat, silhouette-like shading. Depth shading was introduced in the context of hardware support for binary voxel models. It is described as a "depth shaded pre-image" technique, serving as a foundational step before more complex shading methods like binary gradient shading. It is categorized under 2D discrete shading techniques in volume visualization literature. name: Step Size Selection
head: Constant Step Ray Marching, Constant step marching, Fixed-step volume rendering, Ray Marching with Fixed Step Count, Simple ray marching, Step Size Determination, Step Size Heuristic, Volumetric Raymarching with Constant Step
body: Step Size Selection determines the distance between consecutive samples (\Delta t) along a ray during volume rendering, balancing rendering speed against the accuracy of the Riemann sum approximation of the light transport integral. Unlike adaptive methods that vary step size based on local density or geometry, this method employs a fixed or heuristically derived constant step count, simplifying implementation but risking aliasing if the step is too large for the scene's frequency content. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Entry distance t{min} and exit distance t{max} of the volume bounding box. Camera Field of View (FOV) in radians. Image resolution (width W, height H). Volume dataset (3D texture or implicit function). Parameters: NumSteps (fixed iteration count) or STEPSIZE (fixed distance). Outputs: Accumulated color and opacity (transmittance) for the pixel. Ray State: A vector \mathbf{p} representing the current position along the ray. Accumulator: A scalar or vector (e.g., result) storing the accumulated color/opacity. Step Vector: A precomputed vector \mathbf{s} representing the displacement per step. 1. Ray Initialization: Determine the ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. For screen-space rendering, transform screen coordinates to world space using the inverse Model-View-Projection matrix. 2. Step Size Determination: Calculate the step size \Delta t. This can be: Fixed by a user-defined constant STEPSIZE. Derived from a fixed NumSteps over the total ray length L = t{max} - t{min}. Heuristically estimated based on the projected pixel size at t{min}. 3. Iteration Loop: For i from 0 to N-1 (where N is NumSteps): a. Sample: Evaluate the volume density \sigma at the current position \mathbf{p}. b. Composite: Update the accumulator using front-to-back compositing: C{out} = C{in} + (1 - C{in}) \cdot \sigma \cdot \Delta t (Note: Specific implementations may normalize \sigma by N or scale it, e.g., multiplying by 4.0, depending on data range.) c. Advance: Update position \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + \mathbf{d} \cdot \Delta t. d. Boundary Check: Verify if \mathbf{p} remains within the volume bounds (e.g., unit cube [-1, 1]). If outside, add zero contribution and continue the loop. 4. Termination: Return the accumulated color. If early termination is used, stop if accumulated opacity reaches 1.0. Projected Pixel Width Heuristic: \text{projPixWidth} = 2 \cdot \tan\left(\frac{\text{fov}}{2}\right) \cdot t{min} Where \text{fov} is in radians and t{min} is the distance to the volume entry. Fixed Step from Count: \Delta t = \frac{t{max} - t{min}}{\text{NumSteps}} Sphere Hit Test (for implicit volumes): \text{distance}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{C}) < R Where \mathbf{C} is the sphere center and R is the radius. NumSteps: Fixed number of samples per ray. Typical value: 64. STEPSIZE: Fixed distance units per step. Typical value: 0.01. fov: Field of view angle. Typically in degrees in code, converted to radians for trigonometric functions. tmin: Distance to volume entry. Centre, Radius: Sphere geometry parameters. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatedensity(pos): # Evaluates volume density at pos pass def stepsizeselection(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, numsteps): # 1. Calculate step size based on fixed count totaldistance = tmax - tmin stepsize = totaldistance / numsteps # 2. Initialize state currentpos = rayorigin + raydirection tmin accumulatedcolor = 0.0 accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # 3. Iterate for i in range(numsteps): # Boundary check: unit cube [-1, 1] using strict inequality inside = (-1.0 < currentpos.x < 1.0) and \ (-1.0 < currentpos.y < 1.0) and \ (-1.0 < currentpos.z < 1.0) if inside and accumulatedopacity < 1.0: # Map to [0, 1] for texture sampling texcoord = (currentpos + 1.0) 0.5 # Sample density, scale by 4.0, normalize by numsteps density = evaluatedensity(texcoord) samplecontribution = density 4.0 / numsteps # Front-to-back compositing accumulatedcolor += (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) samplecontribution accumulatedopacity += samplecontribution # Advance ray currentpos += raydirection stepsize return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity Aliasing/Filtering: If STEPSIZE is too large, small frequency features (clouds, smoke) are missed, causing a filtering issue. Shadow Misses: Large step sizes may skip over small solid objects casting shadows on the volume, missing shadow effects. Boundary Exclusion: Strict inequality checks (e.g., < 1.0) may exclude points exactly at the boundary, affecting the last few samples. Data Scaling: Texture sampling assumes specific data ranges (e.g., [0,1]); incorrect scaling (e.g., missing the 4.0 factor in some implementations) leads to incorrect density values. This method normalizes the volume dataset's physical dimensions to a unit cube to ensure consistent sampling density regardless of resolution or aspect ratio. It computes a base step size from the maximum volume dimension and an optional axis-wise scaling factor. Choose this when rendering arbitrary voxel grids that need uniform visual density across different aspect ratios. This method scales the step size based on the viewing angle relative to the volume, using a cone angle parameter to balance speed and quality in atmospheric clouds. It varies the step count dynamically based on geometry orientation, unlike standard constant step marching. Choose this for horizon views where more steps are needed compared to top-down views. A Monte Carlo importance sampling technique that constructs a PDF matching the exponential transmittance component to cancel it analytically. It treats the integration domain as trapezoidal segments defined by the bounding box corners, allowing direct sampling of free path length. Choose this when avoiding fixed-step iteration errors in complex light transport is required. A scheme where the step size \tau grows exponentially with distance t along the ray: \tau:= t/256, clamped to [\text{diag}/1024, \text{size} \times \text{diag}/1024]. This allows computation cost to grow logarithmically with scene diameter while maintaining quality. Choose this for large scenes where uniform sampling would be prohibitively expensive, accepting a variable number of steps. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the fixed number of steps per ray. Total time is proportional to pixel count \times N. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, excluding the volume texture storage. Performance: Fast and predictable, as it avoids branching for adaptive decisions or complex distance queries. However, it may waste samples in empty regions or undersample dense regions compared to adaptive methods. Strengths: Simple implementation, no complex data structures, predictable memory usage. Limitations: Prone to aliasing if step size is not carefully chosen relative to scene scale and pixel size; inefficient for large empty spaces. When to Use: Uniform media, simple volumes, or when implementation simplicity is prioritized over optimal sampling efficiency. When Not to Use: Complex scenes with high-frequency details requiring adaptive sampling, or very large scenes where exponential or sparse stepping is needed. Originating from early volumetric rendering techniques, constant step ray marching was popularized in tutorials and real-time graphics for its simplicity. It is a core component of many volume rendering pipelines, often serving as the baseline before introducing adaptive or sparse techniques. The method is widely used in real-time applications like procedural terrain and cloud rendering, where fixed-step approximations provide sufficient visual quality with low computational overhead. name: Raycasting Step Size & Aspect Ratio Normalization
head: Aspect Ratio Normalized Ray Marching, Fixed-Step Ray Marching Setup, Normalized Step Size Calculation
body: This method establishes a uniform step size for volume rendering by normalizing the volume dataset's physical dimensions to a unit cube, ensuring consistent sampling density regardless of resolution or aspect ratio. It computes a base step size from the maximum volume dimension and an optional axis-wise scaling factor to map arbitrary voxel grids into normalized space. Inputs: Volume dimensions: W (width), H (height), D (depth) in voxels. Optional aspect ratios: \mathbf{a} = (ax, ay, az) defining relative scaling of axes. Step scale multiplier: s{scale}. Outputs: Normalized step size: \Delta. Scaling factor: \mathbf{f} (used to map volume to unit cube). Data Structures: dimensions: Tuple of three integers (W, H, D). aspectRatios: Tuple of three floats (ax, ay, az). stepScale: Single float. Numbered Steps: 1. Calculate Max Dimension: Determine the largest dimension of the volume. M = \max(W, H, D) 2. Compute Base Step Size: Calculate the inverse of the maximum dimension. \Delta{base} = \frac{1}{M} 3. Handle Aspect Ratios: If aspect ratios are provided to handle non-cubic volumes explicitly: Clamp aspect ratios to a minimum of \mathbf{0}. Compute the scaling factor \mathbf{f} to map the volume into a unit cube coordinate system: \mathbf{f} = \frac{\mathbf{1}}{\left(\mathbf{1} \cdot M\right) / (\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{a})} Where \mathbf{1} = (1,1,1), \mathbf{d} = (W,H,D), and \mathbf{a} = (ax, ay, az). Vector operations are component-wise. The source computes per-axis step size as 1.0 / (di \cdot (M/di)), which algebraically simplifies to 1/M, confirming the step size remains uniform while the scaling factor adjusts the spatial mapping. 4. Apply Step Scale: Multiply the base step size by the user-defined scale factor, clamped to a minimum of 0.1. \Delta = \max(\Delta{base} \cdot s{scale}, 0.1) 5. Pass to Shader: Upload \Delta (and \mathbf{f} if used) as uniform variables to the ray marching shader. Parameters: stepScale: Multiplier for the base step size during ray marching. Clamped to a minimum of 0.1. aspectRatios: Vector defining the relative scaling of volume axes. Clamped to a minimum of \mathbf{0}. fovy: Vertical field of view in radians (used in the Projection Factor variant). pixelTolerance: Desired pixel tolerance for step sizing (used in the Projection Factor variant). screenDivisor: Resolution divisor, default 1.0 or 8.0 for min-depth pass (used in the Projection Factor variant). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Dimensions: If any dimension is 0, the calculation would divide by zero; a guard clause returns a default step size of 1.0. Zero Aspect Ratios: Clamping to 0 is specified in the source, but zero values in the denominator of the scale factor calculation will produce infinite scaling unless the renderer's coordinate mapping logic handles it. Precision: Using float for step size is standard in shaders; host-side calculations should match shader precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computestepsizeandscale(width, height, depth, aspectratios=None, stepscale=1.0): """ Computes the normalized step size and scaling factor for volume ray marching. Args: width (int): Volume width in voxels. height (int): Volume height in voxels. depth (int): Volume depth in voxels. aspectratios (tuple): Optional (ax, ay, az). Defaults to (1, 1, 1). stepscale (float): Multiplier for the base step size. Returns: tuple: (stepsize, scalefactor) """ # 1. Calculate max dimension maxdim = max(width, height, depth) if maxdim == 0: return 1.0, (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Guard against division by zero # 2. Base step size basestep = 1.0 / maxdim # 3. Aspect ratio handling if aspectratios is None: aspectratios = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Clamp aspect ratios to minimum 0 ax, ay, az = max(aspectratios[0], 0.0), max(aspectratios[1], 0.0), max(aspectratios[2], 0.0) dimensions = (float(width), float(height), float(depth)) # Compute scale factor: vec3(1) / ((vec3(1) maxSize) / (dimensions aspectRatios)) # Component-wise division scalex = 1.0 / ((1.0 maxdim) / (dimensions[0] ax)) scaley = 1.0 / ((1.0 maxdim) / (dimensions[1] ay)) scalez = 1.0 / ((1.0 maxdim) / (dimensions[2] az)) scalefactor = (scalex, scaley, scalez) # 4. Apply step scale and clamp to min 0.1 finalstep = max(basestep stepscale, 0.1) return finalstep, scalefactor Uniform Ray Marching generates 3D sample positions along rays within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a fixed spacing between samples. It serves as a fallback strategy for environments lacking adaptive libraries or as a debug mode that treats an atlas texture as the full volume without brick traversal. It replaces coarse sampling to avoid aliasing artifacts, such as concentric "sampling rings," caused by steep gradients near inner radius cuts. Calculates a scaling factor for ray marching step sizes based on camera FOV and pixel tolerance to ensure consistent visual quality across resolutions. The formula is F = \frac{1}{2 \tan(\frac{\theta}{2})} \cdot \frac{Wy}{\text{pixelTolerance}} where \theta is vertical FOV, Wy is screen height, and pixelTolerance is in pixels. Parameters include fovy (vertical FOV in radians), pixelTolerance (desired pixel tolerance), and screenDivisor (resolution divisor, default 1.0 or 8.0 for min-depth pass). Time Complexity: O(1) for step size calculation. Ray marching traversal is O(N) where N is the step count. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the step size and scale factor variables. Performance: Provides consistent rendering speed as step count is predictable. Strengths: Simple to implement; ensures consistent sampling density across different volume resolutions. Limitations: Does not adapt to local detail. When to Use: When consistent sampling density is critical or when hardware/software constraints prevent adaptive stepping. This method is derived from practical implementations in open-source volume rendering projects, specifically qt-viewer-pro and VolumeRendering. It addresses the common problem of visual artifacts that arise when ray marching through volumes with varying aspect ratios or resolutions using naive fixed steps. A related variant calculates step scaling based on camera FOV and pixel tolerance to maintain visual quality across resolutions. wpop/qt-viewer-pro, https://github.com/wpop/qt-viewer-pro, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, https://github.com/jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) RvanderLaan/SVDAG-Compression, https://github.com/RvanderLaan/SVDAG-Compression, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Uniform Ray Marching
head: Fixed-Step Ray Marching Setup, Normalized Step Size Calculation, Parallel Ray Sampling (Fallback), Ray-to-Sample Generation, Simple ray marching (debug view), Uniform Ray Marching for Visualization
body: Uniform Ray Marching is a sampling strategy that generates 3D sample positions along rays within an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) using a fixed spacing between consecutive samples. It serves as a debug rendering mode for direct atlas sampling without brick traversal, a PyTorch-native fallback for environments lacking custom CUDA extensions, and a dense uniform sampler for Line-of-Sight (LOS) integral visualization. It sets itself apart from adaptive methods like NeRF Ray Marching Optimizations by using constant intervals rather than density-based acceleration, and from Oversampled 3D Ray March by not enforcing strict slab ownership at LOD boundaries. Inputs: rayso: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray origins. raysd: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing ray directions. aabbmin, aabbmax: Vectors defining the AABB boundaries. renderstepsize: Scalar float defining the fixed distance between sample points. rmaxrsun: Optional float specifying an outer sphere radius in solar radii (R{sun}) for clipping. atlasSize: Scalar for volume texture normalization (used in debug/atlas mode). numSteps: Integer specifying the number of steps (alternative input to renderstepsize). Outputs: samplepositions: Tensor of 3D coordinates along the rays. ts: Tensor of segment start times (depths). te: Tensor of segment end times (depths). rayidx: Tensor mapping samples to original rays. valid: Boolean mask indicating rays with valid intersections. Data Structures: Rays are typically stored as (N, 6) arrays where the first 3 columns are origins and the last 3 are directions. Depth values are masked with MAXDEPTH (constant 10000.0) to mark invalid entries before sorting and trimming. Steps: 1. Ray Preparation: Extract origins and directions. Normalize directions and compute inverse directions if using slab-based intersection. 2. AABB Intersection: Compute near (tmin) and far (tmax) intersection distances for each ray against the AABB. Filter rays where tmin < tmax. Initialize a valid mask ok = (tmax > tmin). 3. Optional Sphere Clipping: If rmaxrsun is provided, clip the ray interval to an outer sphere. Calculate coefficients for the quadratic equation |o + t d|^2 = (r{max}/scale)^2: A = \sum (rays\d^2) B = 2.0 \sum (rays\o \cdot rays\d) C = \sum (rays\o^2) - \rho^2 where \rho = r{max\rsun} / aabb\scale. Solve for intersection times t{in} and t{out} using the quadratic formula. Handle numerical safety by clamping A to 10^{-20} and the discriminant disc = B^2 - 4AC to 0.0. Update interval bounds: t{min} = \max(t{min}, t{in}) and t{max} = \min(t{max}, t{out}). Update valid mask: ok = ok & hit. 4. Step Size Calculation: Determine the step size and number of steps. If using renderstepsize: Calculate steps per ray as \lceil (t{max} - t{min}) / render\step\size \rceil, clamped to a minimum of 1. If using numSteps: Calculate stepSize = rayLength / numSteps. 5. Sample Generation: Generate uniform sample points along the valid intervals. Method A (Edge-based): Create linearly spaced points u in [0, 1]. Compute edge coordinates edges = t{min} + (t{max} - t{min}) \cdot u. Flatten to get start times ts and end times te. Method B (Offset-based): Generate delta offsets scaled by MARCHSIZE (or renderstepsize). Add deterministic noise (0.5) or uniform noise [0.01, 0.99] if required. Compute sampled depths and sort them. 6. Position Computation: Compute 3D positions as pos = ori + t \cdot dir. For atlas debugging: Compute UV coordinates as atlasUV = (pos / normalizedSize) + 0.5. 7. Post-Processing: Identify invalid depths by comparing against mindepth and maxdepth. Mask invalid depths with MAXDEPTH and sort them to the end. Trim outputs to nummaxsteps (maximum valid steps per ray). Construct rayidx mapping each sample to its source ray. Pseudocode: Unverified code. AABB Intersection # Handle zero direction components to avoid division by zero invdir = torch.where(raysd.abs() > 1e-8, 1.0 / raysd, 0.0) t1 = (aabbmin - rayso) invdir t2 = (aabbmax - rayso) invdir tmin = torch.maximum(t1, t2).min(dim=1).values tmax = torch.minimum(t1, t2).max(dim=1).values validmask = tmax > tmin tmin = tmin.maskedfill(~validmask, 0.0) tmax = tmax.maskedfill(~validmask, 0.0) # 2. Optional Sphere Clipping if rmaxrsun is not None: rho = rmaxrsun / aabbscale A = (raysd raysd).sum(dim=1) B = 2.0 (rayso raysd).sum(dim=1) C = (rayso rayso).sum(dim=1) - rho rho A = torch.maximum(A, torch.tensor(1e-20)) disc = BB - 4.0AC disc = torch.maximum(disc, torch.tensor(0.0)) sqrtdisc = torch.sqrt(disc) tin = (-B - sqrtdisc) / (2.0 A) tout = (-B + sqrtdisc) / (2.0 A) tmin = torch.maximum(tmin, tin) tmax = torch.minimum(tmax, tout) hitsphere = (disc >= 0) & (tmax > tmin) validmask = validmask & hitsphere # 3. Step Size and Count raylengths = tmax - tmin nsteps = torch.ceil(raylengths / renderstepsize).long() nsteps = torch.maximum(nsteps, torch.oneslike(nsteps)) maxsteps = nsteps.max().item() idx = torch.arange(maxsteps, device=rayso.device).unsqueeze(0) nstepsexp = nsteps.unsqueeze(1) stepmask = idx < nstepsexp ts = tmin.unsqueeze(1) + idx.float() renderstepsize ts = ts.maskedfill(~stepmask, 0.0) te = ts + renderstepsize te = torch.minimum(te, tmax.unsqueeze(1)) tsflat = ts[stepmask] teflat = te[stepmask] rayindices = torch.arange(N, device=rayso.device).repeatinterleave(nsteps) # 4. Compute Positions dirsnorm = raysd / raysd.norm(dim=1, keepdim=True) oriflat = rayso[rayindices] dirflat = dirsnorm[rayindices] positions = oriflat + tsflat.unsqueeze(1) dirflat return positions, tsflat, teflat, rayindices, validmask Parameters: numSteps: Typically 512. MAXDEPTH: Constant 10000.0 used to mark invalid depths. EARLYEXITALPHA: Threshold for breaking the march loop in composition. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Depths: Depths outside the AABB or sphere are masked with MAXDEPTH and sorted to the end to allow trimming to the maximum valid steps per ray. Numerical Stability: The discriminant in sphere intersection must be clamped to 0.0 to avoid NaNs from negative values due to precision errors. Zero Direction Components: Division by zero in inverse direction calculation must be guarded, typically by clamping the denominator or using a safe division function. Enforces strict slab ownership and corrected exit-face probing to resolve LOD boundary discontinuities. Choose when visual artifacts from empty-space skipping are present. Replaces fixed intervals with adaptive step sizes (exponential stepping, empty space skipping). Choose for performance optimization in NeRFs. Samples only within intersected voxels with probabilities proportional to distance. Choose for sparse voxel fields with variable intersection counts. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot S), where N is the number of rays and S is the number of steps per ray. The calculation is highly parallelizable as each ray's samples are independent. Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot S) to store sample positions, depths, and indices. Strengths: Simple to implement, deterministic (with fixed noise), no dependency on custom CUDA extensions (PyTorch-native fallback). When to use: Debugging, visualization, LOS integral rendering where aliasing artifacts from coarse sampling must be avoided, or as a baseline fallback. When not to use: Large-scale NeRF training where performance is critical, or sparse voxel grids where traversal acceleration is preferred. name: Oversampled 3D Ray March
head: slab tiling fix
body: Oversampled 3D Ray March is a sampling strategy for distance-field ray marching that resolves discontinuities at Level-of-Detail (LOD) boundaries by ensuring every fine sample owns the slab it represents as its midpoint, clipped to the brick's segment. It solves the problem of unprobed material at chunk exit faces caused by previous empty-space skip logic, which led to zero contribution and visual artifacts. It sets itself apart from standard uniform marching by enforcing strict slab ownership and corrected exit-face probing, and from NeRF Ray Marching Optimizations by focusing on geometric tiling correctness rather than density-based acceleration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin O, ray direction D, brick segment bounds [0, len] along the ray, and LOD interface boundaries. Output: A sequence of sample positions and associated density/color values that tile exactly across LOD boundaries without gaps. Data Structures: Sample Point: A 3D vector (x, y, z) representing the position in world space. Slab: Defined by the interval [t{start}, t{end}] along the ray parameter t. Steps: 1. Calculate Ray Segment: Determine the intersection of the ray with the current brick's AABB to find the entry t{entry} and exit t{exit} parameters. The segment length is len = t{exit} - t{entry}. 2. Determine Sample Count: Calculate the number of fine samples N required based on the desired spatial resolution or step size s. N = \lceil len / s \rceil. 3. Compute Slab Thickness: The thickness of each slab is \Delta t = len / N. 4. Assign Slab Ownership: For each sample index i from 0 to N-1: The slab for sample i is defined by the interval [t{entry} + i \cdot \Delta t, t{entry} + (i+1) \cdot \Delta t]. The sample position Pi is the midpoint of this slab: Pi = O + D \cdot (t{entry} + (i + 0.5) \cdot \Delta t) This midpoint is clipped to the brick's segment to ensure it lies within [t{entry}, t{exit}]. 5. Correct Empty-Space Skip Probing: When skipping empty space, the probe must extend one stride past each cube's exit face. This ensures that material in the last sub-stride is probed, preventing the cube from contributing zero and eliminating discontinuities at exit faces. If using a stride S{stride}, the probe position is P{probe} = P{current} + D \cdot S{stride}. The next iteration starts from this probe position, ensuring coverage of the boundary region. Parameters: Step size s: Determined by the LOD level and brick size. Not given in the sources. Stride for empty-space skip: The previous implementation strode 1.9 level voxels, which was incorrect. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: LOD Interfaces: Slab thicknesses must tile [0, len] exactly at LOD interfaces to avoid gaps or overlaps. Exit Face Discontinuities: Failing to probe past the exit face leaves material unprobed, causing zero contribution and visual discontinuities. Precision: Ensure floating-point precision is sufficient to handle small slab thicknesses at high LODs. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def oversampledraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, brickentryt, brickexitt, stepsize): """ Performs oversampled 3D ray marching with correct slab tiling and exit-face probing. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray (normalized). brickentryt: float, t parameter where ray enters the brick. brickexitt: float, t parameter where ray exits the brick. stepsize: float, desired distance between sample midpoints. Returns: list of 3D vectors, sample positions. """ length = brickexitt - brickentryt if length <= 0: return [] numsamples = math.ceil(length / stepsize) slabthickness = length / numsamples samples = [] for i in range(numsamples): tmid = brickentryt + (i + 0.5) slabthickness tclipped = max(brickentryt, min(tmid, brickexitt)) samplepos = rayorigin + raydirection tclipped samples.append(samplepos) return samples def correctemptyspaceskip(rayorigin, raydirection, currentt, stride): """ Calculates the next probe position for empty-space skipping, ensuring one stride past the exit face is probed. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, origin of the ray. raydirection: 3D vector, direction of the ray. currentt: float, current t parameter. stride: float, distance to skip. Returns: float, next t parameter. """ nextt = currentt + stride return nextt A raymarching loop that uses stable, uniform linear marching between bounding bounds to eliminate artifacts like spots, missing clouds, noise, and banding, replacing unstable backing-up/bifurcated stepping loops. It corrects empty space skipping using a robust positive-step bifurcated step size logic to handle coordinate jumping and infinite loops. Choose this when rendering low-resolution volumes where unstable stepping causes visible artifacts. It is a variant focused on stability in low-resolution contexts, whereas Oversampled 3D Ray March focuses on LOD tiling correctness. Measured Performance: CPU replica worst-case two-cube split error: -3.99% to +0.68%. Browser A/B (HOA heart, pinned L4, 64 chunks, WebGPU): whole-image TV -2.7% x / -2.2% y. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Eliminates discontinuities at LOD boundaries and exit faces; ensures exact tiling of slabs. Limitations: Requires careful calculation of slab thickness and midpoint positioning; may increase sample count slightly. When to Use: Use when rendering multi-LOD volumes where discontinuities at chunk boundaries are visible. Use when empty-space skipping causes artifacts due to unprobed material at exit faces. When Not to Use: Not needed for single-level rendering, which takes an exact path and is bit-identical to previous methods. Not needed if high-resolution rendering does not exhibit LOD-related artifacts. Originated in the context of streamed multi-LOD rendering fixes, specifically addressing ray-march ringing and slab tiling issues in the Niivue project. It was developed to correct errors in empty-space skip logic that caused material to be unprobed at chunk exit faces. The method was implemented and tested on both CPU and WebGPU backends, with measured improvements in visual consistency. feat(niivue): streamed multi-LOD rendering fixes, LOD compensation, budget plans, and block inspection, https://github.com/niivue/mono/pull/138, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Optimize cloud rendering with eroded Voronoi weather maps and stable linear raymarching, https://github.com/ricecake/boidsish/pull/679, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)
