name: NeRF Ray Marching Optimizations
head: Accelerated NeRF Ray Marching, Occupancy Grids for Empty Space Skipping
body: A set of three techniques to optimize NeRF ray marching performance with imperceptible error: exponential stepping, empty space skipping, and sample compaction. It builds on Uniform Ray Marching by replacing fixed uniform intervals with adaptive step sizes and skipping empty regions via multiscale occupancy grids. Inputs: Ray origin o, ray direction d, scene bounding box size s (largest axis), NeRF model f{\theta}, current training step count. Outputs: Sample positions along the ray, transmittance, accumulated color. Data Structures: 1. Occupancy Grids: A cascade of K grids. Each grid has resolution 128^3. Cells are laid out in Morton (z-curve) order. Each cell stores occupancy as a single bit. 2. Density Grids: A second set of K grids with the same layout, storing full-precision floating-point density values. Parameters: Fixed step size for unit cube scenes: \Delta t = \sqrt{3}/1024. Transmittance stopping threshold: 10^{-4}. Number of grids K: 1 for synthetic NeRF scenes; K \in [1, 5] for larger real-world scenes. Grid resolution: 128^3. Update frequency: Every 16 training iterations. Density decay factor: 0.95. Occupancy threshold t: 0.01 \cdot 1024/\sqrt{3}. Number of candidate cells M: K \cdot 128^3 for first 256 steps; K \cdot 128^3 / 2 for subsequent steps. Steps: 1. Step Size Selection: If the scene is bounded to the unit cube [0,1]^3, set \Delta t = \sqrt{3}/1024. Otherwise, set \Delta t = t/256, where t is the current distance along the ray. Clamp \Delta t to [-\frac{\sqrt{3}}{1024} \cdot s, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{1024} \cdot s], where s is the size of the largest axis of the scene's bounding box. 2. Grid Query: For a sample position x, determine which grid to query. Among the grids covering x, select the finest one with cell side-length larger than the current step size \Delta t. The domain for grid k is [-2^{k-1}+0.5, 2^{k-1}+0.5]^3, centered around (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). 3. Empty Space Skipping: Query the occupancy bit of the cell containing x in the selected grid. If the bit is low (0), skip the sample. 4. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize transmittance T = 1.0. While T > 10^{-4}: Calculate next sample position x = o + t \cdot d. Check occupancy. If occupied, query NeRF model f{\theta}(x) to get density \sigma and color C. Update transmittance: T \leftarrow T \cdot \exp(-\sigma \cdot \Delta t). Accumulate color: C{out} \leftarrow C{out} + T \cdot (1 - \exp(-\sigma \cdot \Delta t)) \cdot C. Update distance: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. Recalculate \Delta t based on new t if using exponential stepping. 5. Grid Update (Every 16 iterations): Decay density values in all cells by a factor of 0.95. Sample M candidate cells: If training step < 256: Sample M = K \cdot 128^3 cells uniformly without repetition. If training step \ge 256: Set M = K \cdot 128^3 / 2. Partition into two sets: First M/2 cells sampled uniformly among all cells. Remaining M/2 cells sampled via rejection sampling restricted to currently occupied cells. For each candidate cell, set its density value to \max(\text{current}, \text{NeRF density at random location in cell}). Update occupancy bits by thresholding density with t = 0.01 \cdot 1024/\sqrt{3}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def morton3d(x, y, z): code = 0 for i in range(7): code |= (x & (1 << i)) << (2 i) code |= (y & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 1) code |= (z & (1 << i)) << (2 i + 2) return code def mortondecode3d(code, bits=7): x, y, z = 0, 0, 0 for i in range(bits): x |= (code & (1 << (3 i))) << i y |= (code & (1 << (3 i + 1))) << i z |= (code & (1 << (3 i + 2))) << i return x, y, z def samplepointincell(grididx, cellidx, resolution=128): x, y, z = mortondecode3d(cellidx) k = grididx + 1 minval = -2(k-1) + 0.5 width = 2k cellsize = width / resolution return (minval + x cellsize + random.random() cellsize, minval + y cellsize + random.random() cellsize, minval + z cellsize + random.random() cellsize) def queryoccupancygrid(x, grids, stepsize): bestk = -1 for kidx in range(len(grids) - 1, -1, -1): k = kidx + 1 minval = -2(k-1) + 0.5 width = 2k if not (minval <= x[0] <= minval + width and minval <= x[1] <= minval + width and minval <= x[2] <= minval + width): continue cellside = width / 128.0 if cellside > stepsize: bestk = kidx break if bestk == -1: return 0 k = bestk + 1 minval = -2(k-1) + 0.5 width = 2k cellside = width / 128.0 u = int((x[0] - minval) / cellside) v = int((x[1] - minval) / cellside) w = int((x[2] - minval) / cellside) u = max(0, min(127, u)) v = max(0, min(127, v)) w = max(0, min(127, w)) idx = morton3d(u, v, w) return grids[bestk][idx] def updategrids(grids, densitygrids, step, kcount, nerfmodel): if step % 16 != 0: return for i in range(kcount): for j in range(len(densitygrids[i])): densitygrids[i][j] = 0.95 if step < 256: M = kcount 1283 selectedindices = random.sample(range(1283), M) else: M = kcount 1283 // 2 selectedindices = random.sample(range(1283), M // 2) occupiedindices = [i for grid in grids for i, bit in enumerate(grid) if bit == 1] occupiedset = set(occupiedindices) for in range(M // 2): while True: cand = random.randint(0, 1283 - 1) if cand in occupiedset: selectedindices.append(cand) break threshold = 0.01 1024 / math.sqrt(3) for idx in selectedindices: grididx = idx // (1283) cellidx = idx % (1283) point = samplepointincell(grididx, cellidx) sigma, = nerfmodel(point) densitygrids[grididx][cellidx] = max(densitygrids[grididx][cellidx], sigma) grids[grididx][cellidx] = 1 if densitygrids[grididx][cellidx] > threshold else 0 def nerfraymarching(o, d, s, nerfmodel, grids, densitygrids, step): t = 0.0 T = 1.0 Cout = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] if s <= 1.0: deltat = math.sqrt(3) / 1024.0 else: deltat = math.sqrt(3) / 1024.0 s while T > 1e-4: x = (o[0] + t d[0], o[1] + t d[1], o[2] + t d[2]) occ = queryoccupancygrid(x, grids, deltat) if occ == 1: sigma, C = nerfmodel(x) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-sigma deltat) T = T math.exp(-sigma deltat) Cout[0] += T alpha C[0] Cout[1] += T alpha C[1] Cout[2] += T alpha C[2] t += deltat if s > 1.0: deltat = t / 256.0 maxdeltat = math.sqrt(3) / 1024.0 s deltat = max(0.0, min(maxdeltat, deltat)) return Cout Time Complexity: Computation cost grows only logarithmically in scene diameter due to exponential step size growth. Memory Complexity: K \times 128^3 bits for occupancy grids and K \times 128^3 floats for density grids. Performance: One order of magnitude faster than using triangle BVH for rayshape intersections on RTX 3090 GPU. Strengths: Imperceptible error, significant speedup for large scenes. Limitations: Requires maintaining and updating grids, which adds complexity. Originated in "Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding" by Müller et al. (2022). Used in Instant-NGP for fast NeRF training and rendering. name: Voxel-Aware Masked Ray Sampling
head: Hierarchical Sampling for Sparse Feature Volume, Inside-Voxel Sampling, NSVF Hierarchical Ray Sampling with Voxel-Aware Masking, NSVF parallel ray sampling, NSVF voxel intersection sampling, Ray-Voxel Intersection Sampling
body: Voxel-Aware Masked Ray Sampling is a ray sampling strategy for sparse voxel fields that ensures all sampling points lie strictly within intersected voxels, preventing invalid "air" samples common in unconstrained hierarchical sampling. It handles variable numbers of voxel intersections per ray by padding and masking tensors, supporting hierarchical sampling ratios where coarse and fine passes are constrained to valid sparse regions. Unlike standard NeRF which uses uniform or stratified sampling along the entire ray, this method restricts integration to occupied sparse voxels, offering significant memory and compute savings for sparse scenes. Inputs: Ray origins and directions for a batch of rays. Sparse voxel grid structure (defining voxel bounds and IDs). Parameters: chunksize (default 4096), maxhits (default 60), raymarchingstepsize (default 0.01), finenumsampleratio (default 0), inversedistancecoarsesampling (default 'none'), backgrounddepth (default 5.0), fixednumsamples (default 0). Outputs: sampleddists: Tensor of shape (numrays, maxsteps) containing distances from camera origin for each sample point. sampledidx: Tensor of shape (numrays, maxsteps) containing voxel IDs for each sample point. sampledmasks: Boolean tensor indicating valid samples. Rendered colors, depths, and other attributes after compositing. Data Structures: 1. Intersection Outputs Dictionary: mindepth: Tensor of shape (numrays,), distance to voxel entry. maxdepth: Tensor of shape (numrays,), distance to voxel exit. intersectedvoxelidx: Tensor of shape (numrays, maxhits), voxel IDs. probs: Tensor of shape (numrays, maxhits), sampling probabilities. steps: Tensor of shape (numrays,), number of samples per ray. 2. All Results Dictionary (Post-processing): missed: Tensor of shape (fullsize,), boolean mask for rays hitting no voxels. colors: Tensor of shape (fullsize, 3). depths: Tensor of shape (fullsize,). normal: Tensor of shape (fullsize, 3) (optional). voxeldepth: Tensor of shape (fullsize,) (optional). voxeledges: Tensor of shape (fullsize, 3) (optional). featn2: Tensor of shape (fullsize,) (optional). Steps: 1. Ray-Voxel Intersection Sampling: Identify pairs P = \{(r, v)\} where ray r intersects voxel v. For each ray, determine the entry (mindepth) and exit (maxdepth) distances in world space, and the corresponding voxel indices. Calculate sampling probabilities probs proportional to the distance within each voxel: \text{dists}i = \max(0, \text{max\depth}i - \text{min\depth}i) Mask out invalid voxels (where ptsidx == -1) by setting their dists to 0. \text{probs}i = \frac{\text{dists}i}{\sumj \text{dists}j} Determine the number of steps steps for each ray. If fixednumsamples > 0, steps is constant. Otherwise: \text{steps} = \frac{\sumi \text{dists}i}{\text{raymarching\stepsize}} If finenumsampleratio > 0 (hierarchical fine pass), update steps: \text{steps} = (\text{intersected\voxel\idx} \neq -1).sum(-1).float() \times \text{fine\num\sample\ratio} 2. Inside-Voxel Sampling: For each intersected voxel v and ray r, sample points. Convert world-space distance dw to sparse-space distance ds using the ray-voxel exit positions: ds = dw - (dw^{(r,v)} - ds^{(r,v)}) where dw^{(r,v)} is the world-space distance of the ray-voxel exit, and ds^{(r,v)} is the sparse-space distance of the same exit point. Perform uniform coarse sampling and importance sampling in the sparse space to generate Nc coarse and Ni importance samples. 3. Parallel Processing and Padding: If the total number of rays fullsize exceeds chunksize (4096), split rays into chunks. Process each chunk independently. Find maxlen, the maximum number of steps across all chunks. Pad outputs: sampledidx: Fill masked/invalid positions with -1. sampleddepth: Fill masked/invalid positions with MAXDEPTH. sampleddists: Fill masked/invalid positions with 0.0. Concatenate chunks and truncate to maxlen. 4. Masking and Truncation: Identify rays that hit the maximum depth boundary: \text{sampled\masks} = (\text{sampled\depth} == \text{MAX\DEPTH}) Calculate the maximum valid steps across all rays: \text{num\max\steps} = \maxi (\sim \text{sampled\masks}i).sum() Truncate tensors to nummaxsteps: \text{sampled\dists} = \text{sampled\dists}[:,: \text{num\max\steps}] \text{sampled\idx} = \text{sampled\idx}[:,: \text{num\max\steps}] 5. Compositing and Background Handling: Render colors and depths. Identify missed rays (those with no valid voxel intersections). \text{missed} = \text{fill\in}((\text{fullsize},), \text{hits}, \text{all\results}['\text{missed}'], 1.0) Fill missed rays with background values: \text{colors} = \text{fill\in}((\text{fullsize}, 3), \text{hits}, \text{all\results}['\text{colors}'], 0.0) \text{depths} = \text{fill\in}((\text{fullsize},), \text{hits}, \text{all\results}['\text{depths}'], 0.0) Add background contribution: \text{colors} += \text{missed.unsqueeze}(-1) \times \text{bg\color} \text{depths} += \text{missed} \times \text{BG\DEPTH} where bgcolor is derived from allresults['colors'] and BGDEPTH is self.field.bgcolor.depth. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def voxelawaremaskedraysampling(rays, voxelgrid, args): """ rays: (numrays, 3) origins, (numrays, 3) directions voxelgrid: Sparse voxel structure args: Configuration object """ fullsize = rays.shape[0] chunksize = args.chunksize if hasattr(args, 'chunksize') else 4096 maxhits = args.maxhits if hasattr(args, 'maxhits') else 60 raymarchingstepsize = args.raymarchingstepsize if hasattr(args, 'raymarchingstepsize') else 0.01 finenumsampleratio = args.finenumsampleratio if hasattr(args, 'finenumsampleratio') else 0.0 fixednumsamples = args.fixednumsamples if hasattr(args, 'fixednumsamples') else 0 bgdepth = args.backgrounddepth if hasattr(args, 'backgrounddepth') else 5.0 # 1. Ray-Voxel Intersection # Returns: mindepth, maxdepth, intersectedvoxelidx, probs, steps # Note: Implementation details of ray-voxel intersection depend on voxelgrid structure. # We assume a function that returns these tensors. mindepth, maxdepth, intersectedvoxelidx, probs, steps = rayvoxelintersection(rays, voxelgrid, maxhits) # 2. Calculate Steps # Mask invalid voxels (idx == -1) validmask = intersectedvoxelidx != -1 dists = (maxdepth - mindepth).maskedfill(~validmask, 0.0) # Normalize probabilities distssum = dists.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) probs = dists / distssum.maskedfill(distssum == 0, 1.0) # Avoid div by zero # Determine number of samples per ray if fixednumsamples > 0: steps = torch.full((fullsize,), fixednumsamples, dtype=torch.float32, device=rays.device) else: steps = dists.sum(dim=-1) / raymarchingstepsize # Hierarchical fine pass adjustment if finenumsampleratio > 0: validcount = validmask.sum(dim=-1).float() steps = validcount finenumsampleratio # 3. Inside-Voxel Sampling # Sample points within voxels # Returns: sampleddists, sampledidx, sampledmasks sampleddists, sampledidx, sampledmasks = insidevoxelsampling( rays, mindepth, maxdepth, intersectedvoxelidx, probs, steps, args) # 4. Parallel Processing (if needed) # If fullsize > chunksize, split and pad if fullsize > chunksize: chunks = [] for i in range(0, fullsize, chunksize): chunkrays = rays[i:i+chunksize] # Re-run intersection and sampling for chunk #... (simplified for brevity, assuming same logic) # Pad results to uniform length #... chunks.append(chunkresults) sampleddists, sampledidx, sampledmasks = padandconcatchunks(chunks) else: # Pad to uniform shape if rays have different step counts maxsteps = sampleddists.shape[1] sampleddists = padtensor(sampleddists, maxsteps, padvalue=0.0) sampledidx = padtensor(sampledidx, maxsteps, padvalue=-1) sampledmasks = padtensor(sampledmasks, maxsteps, padvalue=False) # 5. Truncation # Find max valid steps nummaxsteps = (~sampledmasks).sum(dim=-1).max().item() sampleddists = sampleddists[:,:nummaxsteps] sampledidx = sampledidx[:,:nummaxsteps] # 6. Compositing # Render colors and depths colors, depths = rendervolume(sampleddists, sampledidx, rays, voxelgrid) # Handle missed rays missed = (sampledidx[:, 0] == -1) # Simplified check # Fill missed rays colors = fillin(colors, ~missed, 0.0) depths = fillin(depths, ~missed, 0.0) # Add background bgcolor = getbgcolor() # From field colors += missed.unsqueeze(-1) bgcolor depths += missed bgdepth return colors, depths, sampleddists, sampledidx def insidevoxelsampling(rays, mindepth, maxdepth, intersectedvoxelidx, probs, steps, args): """ Samples points inside voxels using distance conversion. """ # Generate sample indices based on steps # For each ray, generate 'steps' number of samples # Use probs for importance sampling if needed # Initialize tensors numrays = rays.shape[0] maxsteps = steps.max().int().item() sampleddists = torch.zeros((numrays, maxsteps), device=rays.device) sampledidx = torch.full((numrays, maxsteps), -1, dtype=torch.long, device=rays.device) sampledmasks = torch.zeros((numrays, maxsteps), dtype=torch.bool, device=rays.device) for i in range(numrays): nsamples = int(steps[i].item()) if nsamples == 0: continue # Get voxel indices for this ray voxelindices = intersectedvoxelidx[i] validvoxels = voxelindices != -1 validvoxelindices = voxelindices[validvoxels] # Get distances for valid voxels dmin = mindepth[i][validvoxels] dmax = maxdepth[i][validvoxels] # Sample points # Uniform or importance sampling within each voxel #... # Distance conversion # ds = dw - (dwout - dsout) #... # Fill sampleddists and sampledidx #... return sampleddists, sampledidx, sampledmasks def padtensor(tensor, maxlen, padvalue): """ Pads tensor to maxlen along dim 1. """ currentlen = tensor.shape[1] if currentlen < maxlen: padding = torch.full((tensor.shape[0], maxlen - currentlen), padvalue, device=tensor.device) if tensor.dtype == torch.bool: padding = padding.bool() tensor = torch.cat([tensor, padding], dim=1) return tensor def fillin(tensor, mask, fillvalue): """ Fills values where mask is False with fillvalue. """ tensor = tensor.clone() tensor[~mask] = fillvalue return tensor def getbgcolor(): # Placeholder for background color retrieval return torch.tensor([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) A rendering pipeline that dynamically allocates voxels only where objects and surfaces exist, restricting ray marching and volume integration to occupied regions. It performs ray-voxel intersection tests to identify sparse voxels traversed by camera rays, samples points within them, and applies volume rendering. Pitfalls include reduced throughput in high-complexity or noisy scenarios. Operating frequencies are typically 5 Hz for tracking and 2 Hz for optimization on synthetic datasets. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of intersected voxels per ray and the number of samples per voxel. Parallel processing with chunking (default 4096 rays) helps manage memory and latency. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of rays and the maximum number of voxel intersections (maxhits, default 60) plus samples per intersection. Padding ensures uniform tensor shapes. Performance: On a single NVIDIA RTX 3090, per-frame tracking takes ~150-200 ms and joint frame/map optimization takes 450-550 ms. Typical operating frequencies are 5 Hz for tracking and 2 Hz for optimization on the Replica dataset. Strengths: Efficient for sparse scenes by ignoring empty space. Prevents invalid sampling outside voxels, which is crucial for sparse feature volumes. Limitations: Performance degrades in highly complex or noisy scenes. Requires careful handling of variable intersection counts via padding and masking. Originating from the NSVF (Neural Sparse Voxel Fields) framework, this method was developed to address the inefficiency of dense volume rendering in sparse environments. It builds on the concept of sparse voxel grids, where only occupied regions are stored and processed. The hierarchical sampling strategy ensures that sampling points remain within valid voxels, avoiding the "air" sampling issues of unconstrained methods. It is used in neural implicit reconstruction and rendering pipelines, particularly for dynamic scenes and SLAM systems. facebookresearch/NSVF, https://github.com/facebookresearch/NSVF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) MonoNeuralFusion: Online Monocular Neural 3D Reconstruction with Geometric Priors, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2209.15153, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Vox-Fusion: Dense Tracking and Mapping with Voxel-based Neural Implicit Representation, https://doi.org/10.1109/ismar55827.2022.00066, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Adaptive Step Size Calculation
head: Cone-angle based step size, Step Size Calculation, Step Size Determination, Step Size Heuristic
body: Adaptive Step Size Calculation determines the distance between samples during ray marching by varying the step size based on the ray's position and a cone angle parameter. It differs from standard constant step ray marching by dynamically adjusting the step size rather than using a fixed value. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Current ray time t, cone angle \alpha, minimum step size dt{min}, maximum step size dt{max}. Output: Step size dt. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute the raw step size by multiplying the current ray time by the cone angle. 2. Clamp the result to the range [dt{min}, dt{max}]. Formula: The step size is calculated as: dt = \text{clamp}(t \cdot \alpha, dt{min}, dt{max}) Where: t: Current ray time. \alpha: Cone angle for volume rendering. dt{min}: Minimum step size. dt{max}: Maximum step size. Parameters: dt{min}: Not given in the sources. dt{max}: Not given in the sources. \alpha: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculateadaptivestepsize(t: float, coneangle: float, dtmin: float, dtmax: float) -> float: """ Calculate adaptive step size based on cone angle heuristic. Args: t: Current ray time/distance. coneangle: Cone angle for volume rendering. dtmin: Minimum step size. dtmax: Maximum step size. Returns: Clamped step size. """ rawstep = t coneangle stepsize = max(dtmin, min(dtmax, rawstep)) return stepsize Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If t=0, the step size becomes 0, which may cause infinite loops or degenerate behavior. A guard should ensure t > 0 or use a minimum step size. Precision issues may arise if t \cdot \alpha is very small or very large relative to floating-point limits. Renders volumetric clouds by adaptively selecting the number of ray march steps based on the viewing angle and using cone sampling to approximate light transport within the volume. It balances rendering performance and visual quality by using fewer steps for top-down views and more steps for horizon views. It differs from standard constant step ray marching by varying the step count dynamically and from sibling methods by using a fixed kernel of 6 offset vectors rotated towards the light source for density estimation along the light path. Choose it when rendering volumetric clouds where viewing angle significantly impacts visual quality and performance. Performs volume rendering by combining adaptive ray marching with temporal accumulation to reduce noise and flickering in animated scenes. It builds on Adaptive Step Size Calculation by using density thresholds to vary step size, and extends standard ray marching by reprojection of the previous frame's color and alpha into the current frame's screen space. It is distinct from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count and Cone Sampling by relying on spatial reprojection rather than cone-based filtering for temporal stability. Choose it when rendering animated volumetric scenes requiring temporal stability and noise reduction. Time and Memory Complexity: The calculation is O(1) in time and memory, as it involves simple arithmetic operations on scalar values. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. name: Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count and Cone Sampling
head: Adaptive Step Count with Cone Sampling
body: This method renders volumetric clouds by adaptively selecting the number of ray march steps based on the viewing angle and using cone sampling to approximate light transport within the volume. It balances rendering performance and visual quality by using fewer steps for top-down views and more steps for horizon views, while cone sampling mitigates artifacts from single-sample lighting. It differs from standard constant step ray marching by varying the step count dynamically and from sibling methods by using a fixed kernel of 6 offset vectors rotated towards the light source for density estimation along the light path. Inputs: Ray origin O and direction D (normalized). Ray segment bounds t{start} and t{end} in world space. Pixel identifier (integer) for jittering. Time variable T for wind animation. Light direction L (normalized). Earth center position C{earth}. Parameters: baseDensityFactor, jitterfactor, eccentricity, silverintensity, silverspread, brightness. Outputs: Accumulated color C{out} (RGB). Accumulated density \alpha{accum} (scalar, clamped to 1.0). The method uses a fixed kernel of 6 offset vectors defined in local space and rotated to align with the light direction. Kernel Offsets (Local): 1. (0.1, 0.25, -0.15) 2. (0.2, 0.5, 0.2) 3. (-0.2, 0.1, -0.1) 4. (-0.05, 0.75, 0.05) 5. (-0.1, 1.0, 0.0) 6. (0.0, 3.0, 0.0) 1. Calculate Adaptive Step Count: Compute the dot product of the ray direction D and the world up vector U = (0, 1, 0). Calculate the number of steps N{steps} using linear interpolation between 35 and 60 steps based on the viewing angle. Top-down views (d \approx 1) use 35 steps; horizon views (d \approx 0) use 60 steps. d = \text{dot}(D, U) N{steps} = \lfloor \text{mix}(35.0, 60.0, 1.0 - d) \rfloor 2. Initialize Variables: Compute the step size \Delta t = (t{end} - t{start}) / N{steps}. Initialize transmittance T{trans} = 1.0 and accumulated density \alpha{accum} = 0.0. Initialize output color C{out} = (0, 0, 0). 3. Construct Light Rotation Matrix (TBN): Find the axis with the largest absolute component in L, denoted V{max}. Compute Z{comp} = \text{cross}(L, V{max}) and X{comp} = \text{cross}(Z{comp}, L). Form the rotation matrix M{sun} with columns X{comp}, L, and Z{comp}. M{sun} = \begin{bmatrix} X{comp} & L & Z{comp} \end{bmatrix} 4. Precompute Cone Sampling Offsets: Transform the 6 local kernel offsets K{local}[i] into world space aligned with the light: K{world}[i] = M{sun} \times K{local}[i] for i \in [0, 5]. 5. Ray Marching Loop: Iterate j from 0 to N{steps} - 1. a. Calculate Sample Position: Compute current t = t{start} + j \cdot \Delta t. Generate a jitter offset using pixelID and t to select an index modulo 16, then retrieve jitterLocation. Update position P: P = O + t \cdot (D + (\text{jitterLocation}.x, (\text{jitterLocation}.x + \text{jitterLocation}.y) \cdot \text{jitterfactor}, \text{jitterLocation}.y)) b. Sample Density: Transform P to relative atmospheric coordinates and divide by 8.0 to control noise frequency. Skew the sample point using wind direction and time T. Calculate relative height h from P and C{earth}. Sample low-frequency density: \rho{base} = \text{SampleLowFreq}(P{skewed}, P, h, C{earth}) \cdot \text{baseDensityFactor}. If \rho{base} > 0.0, erode with high-frequency noise: \rho{high} = \text{ErodeCloud}(\rho{base} \cdot 1.4, D, P{skewed}, h). Update accumulated density: \alpha{accum} \leftarrow \alpha{accum} + \rho{high} \cdot 0.5. Check for early termination: if \alpha{accum} \ge 1.0, set \alpha{accum} = 1.0 and break the loop. c. Cone Sampling for Lighting: Initialize densityAlongLight = 0.0. Loop i from 0 to 5. Calculate light sample position: P{light} = P + \Delta t \cdot K{world}[i] \cdot i. Sample density at P{light}. If density > 0.0, erode with high-frequency noise and add to densityAlongLight. d. Compute Light Energy and Update Color: Calculate total light energy using GetLightEnergy with parameters: relative height h, densityAlongLight, \rho{base}, Henyey-Greenstein phase function value p(\theta) with eccentricity eccentricity, cosine of the angle between light and view direction, step size \Delta t, and brightness multiplier brightness. Update transmittance and color: T{trans} = \text{mix}(T{trans}, E{light}, 1.0 - \alpha{accum}) C{out} \leftarrow C{out} + T{trans} Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchadaptivecone(rayorigin, raydir, tstart, tend, pixelid, time, lightdir, earthcenter, params): # 1. Adaptive step count dotval = dot(raydir, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)) maxsteps = floor(mix(35.0, 60.0, 1.0 - dotval)) stepsize = (tend - tstart) / maxsteps # 2. Initialize transmittance = 1.0 accumdensity = 0.0 returncolor = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 3. TBN matrix for light maxcompidx = argmax(abs(lightdir)) maxcompunit = vec3([1.0 if i == maxcompidx else 0.0 for i in range(3)]) zcomp = cross(lightdir, maxcompunit) xcomp = cross(zcomp, lightdir) sunrotmatrix = mat3(xcomp, lightdir, zcomp) # 4. Precompute cone offsets localoffsets = [ vec3(0.1, 0.25, -0.15), vec3(0.2, 0.5, 0.2), vec3(-0.2, 0.1, -0.1), vec3(-0.05, 0.75, 0.05), vec3(-0.1, 1.0, 0.0), vec3(0.0, 3.0, 0.0) ] noisekernel = [sunrotmatrix @ k for k in localoffsets] # 5. Marching loop for step in range(maxsteps): t = tstart + step stepsize # Jitter jitteridx = hash(pixelid, t) % 16 jitterloc = getjitter(jitteridx) # Standard lookup/pseudo-random retrieval jitteroffset = vec3(jitterloc.x, (jitterloc.x + jitterloc.y) params.jitterfactor, jitterloc.y) pos = rayorigin + t (raydir + jitteroffset) # Density sampling relcoords = transformtoatmosphere(pos) / 8.0 skewedpoint = skewwithwind(relcoords, time) relheight = computerelativeheight(pos, earthcenter) basedensity = samplelowfrequency(skewedpoint, pos, relheight, earthcenter) params.baseDensityFactor if basedensity > 0.0: highfreqdensity = erodecloudwithhighfrequency(basedensity 1.4, raydir, skewedpoint, relheight) accumdensity += highfreqdensity 0.5 if accumdensity >= 1.0: accumdensity = 1.0 break # Cone sampling densityalonglight = 0.0 for i in range(6): lightpos = pos + stepsize noisekernel[i] float(i) lightbase = samplelowfrequency(lightpos, lightpos, relheight, earthcenter) if lightbase > 0.0: lighthigh = erodecloudwithhighfrequency(lightbase 1.4, raydir, lightpos, relheight) densityalonglight += lighthigh # Light energy & update cosangle = dot(raydir, lightdir) hgvalue = heneygreenstein(cosangle, params.eccentricity, params.silverintensity, params.silverspread) totallightenergy = getlightenergy(relheight, densityalonglight, basedensity, hgvalue, cosangle, stepsize, params.brightness) transmittance = mix(transmittance, totallightenergy, 1.0 - accumdensity) returncolor += transmittance return returncolor baseDensityFactor: Controls cloud density center intensity. Default: 0.380. jitterfactor: Multiplier for jitter offset in Y component. Default: 1.180. eccentricity: Henyey-Greenstein scattering parameter. Default: 0.6. silverintensity: Parameter for modified Henyey-Greenstein function. Default: 0.7. silverspread: Parameter for modified Henyey-Greenstein function. Default: 0.1. brightness: Lighting brightness multiplier. Default: 5.0. Precision: The mixing of transmittance and light energy requires careful handling of floating-point precision to avoid banding, especially at low densities. Boundaries: The ray segment bounds t{start} and t{end} must correctly clip against the volume boundaries (e.g., sphere intersection with atmosphere). Degenerate Input: If the ray direction is parallel to the world up vector, the dot product is 1 or -1. The formula handles d \approx 1 (top-down) well. If d is negative (viewing from below), the mix parameter 1.0-d exceeds 1, potentially exceeding 60 steps. The source specifies "horizon views" for d near 0, implying the method is optimized for viewing from above or the horizon. Kernel Alignment: The TBN matrix construction assumes L is not parallel to the chosen maxComp axis. If L is parallel, the cross product becomes zero. A fallback axis selection is not explicitly detailed in the source but is a standard implementation requirement. Time Complexity: O(N{steps} \cdot K), where N{steps} is the adaptive step count (35-60) and K=6 is the number of cone samples. The complexity is linear with respect to the number of steps and constant with respect to the scene size (assuming texture lookups are O(1)). Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per pixel, excluding the noise texture/sampler state. Specific performance metrics (FPS, resolution) are not provided in the sources. The method scales well with resolution as it is a per-pixel operation. The adaptive step count reduces computational load for top-down views, providing a performance benefit in scenes with significant vertical viewing angles. Strengths: Reduces artifacts from single-sample lighting via cone sampling. Adaptive steps optimize performance based on viewing angle. Limitations: Fixed kernel size (6 samples) may not capture complex light transport in very dense volumes. The method relies on procedural noise, which may lack the detail of texture-based approaches. Use for real-time volumetric cloud rendering where performance is critical and visual quality needs to be maintained across varying camera angles. Not suitable for offline rendering where higher fidelity light transport (e.g., multiple scattering) is required. Not suitable for scenes with dynamic light sources that change rapidly, as the TBN matrix must be recomputed per ray. The method is derived from the implementation in the open-source project "realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes" by erickTornero. The technique combines adaptive step sizing, which is common in ray marching to optimize performance, with cone sampling, a technique used to approximate the integration of light through a volume by sampling along a cone aligned with the light direction. The method is used in real-time graphics applications, specifically for rendering atmospheric clouds in games or simulations. erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, https://github.com/erickTornero/realtime-volumetric-cloudscapes, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Ray Marching with Temporal Reprojection
head: HZL Fluid Effects Studio volume renderer, field mode shading
body: This method performs volume rendering by combining adaptive ray marching with temporal accumulation to reduce noise and flickering in animated scenes. It builds on Adaptive Step Size Calculation by using density thresholds to vary step size, and extends standard ray marching by reprojection of the previous frame's color and alpha into the current frame's screen space. It is distinct from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Count and Cone Sampling by relying on spatial reprojection rather than cone-based filtering for temporal stability. Inputs: Ray origin and direction. Volume density field (accessed via ray marching). stepSize: Base step length for ray marching through the volume. densityScale: Scaling factor applied to density in the opacity calculation. absorption: Absorption coefficient multiplier used in the opacity exponent. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: Boolean flag that doubles the step size (multiplies by 4.0) when density falls below 0.004. historyTexture: Previous frame's accumulated color and alpha buffer. historyWeight: Base weight for temporal history blending, modulated by alpha difference. emittedLight: Emissive contribution per unit step. smokeColor: Base color of the volume. fieldMode: Integer switch (0-7) controlling the smoke color mapping logic via conditional branches. Outputs: Final accumulated color (accumulated.rgb) and alpha (accumulated.a). Data Structures: accumulated: A vector or struct holding rgb (float3) and a (float). Initialized to zero. history: Sampled from historyTexture at reprojected UV coordinates. Holds rgb and a. representativePosition: World or view space position of the current ray step, used for reprojection. Parameters: stepSize: Base step length. densityScale: Scaling factor. absorption: Absorption multiplier. adaptiveSteppingEnabled: Boolean. historyWeight: Base blend weight. emissionStrength: Multiplier for emitted light (used in emittedLight calculation). fieldMode: Integer (0-7). Steps: 1. Initialize accumulated.rgb and accumulated.a to zero. 2. Loop through ray steps: a. Compute currentStep. If adaptiveSteppingEnabled is true and current density < 0.004, set currentStep = stepSize 4.0. Otherwise, currentStep = stepSize. b. Calculate opacity: opacity = 1.0 - \exp(-density \cdot densityScale \cdot currentStep \cdot absorption \cdot 4.0). c. Update accumulated color: accumulated.rgb \leftarrow accumulated.rgb + (1.0 - accumulated.a) \cdot (opacity \cdot smokeColor + emittedLight \cdot currentStep). d. Update accumulated alpha: accumulated.a \leftarrow accumulated.a + (1.0 - accumulated.a) \cdot opacity. e. If accumulated.a > 0.985, break the loop. f. Increment distanceAlongRay by currentStep. 3. If accumulated.a < 0.002, discard the fragment (do not write to color buffer). 4. If temporalEnabled is true and foundVolume is true: a. Project representativePosition to previous clip space. b. Compute UV coordinates from previous clip space. c. Clamp UV to [0.0, 1.0]. d. Sample historyTexture at clamped UV to get history. e. Compute responsiveWeight: responsiveWeight = historyWeight \cdot (1.0 - |history.a - accumulated.a|). f. Blend: accumulated = mix(accumulated, history, clamp(responsiveWeight, 0.0, 0.95)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptiveraymarchingwithtemporalreprojection(rayorigin, raydirection, volumesampler, historytexture, camerastate, params): # Initialize accumulation accumulatedrgb = vec3(0.0) accumulateda = 0.0 # Parameters stepsize = params.stepSize densityscale = params.densityScale absorption = params.absorption adaptiveenabled = params.adaptiveSteppingEnabled historyweight = params.historyWeight emittedlight = params.emittedLight smokecolor = params.smokeColor fieldmode = params.fieldMode # Temporal reprojection state temporalenabled = params.temporalEnabled foundvolume = False # Ray marching loop distancealongray = 0.0 while True: # Get density at current position rayposition = rayorigin + raydirection distancealongray density = volumesampler.sample(rayposition) # Adaptive step size if adaptiveenabled and density < 0.004: currentstep = stepsize 4.0 else: currentstep = stepsize # Opacity calculation opacity = 1.0 - exp(-density densityscale currentstep absorption 4.0) # Color accumulation accumulatedrgb += (1.0 - accumulateda) (opacity smokecolor + emittedlight currentstep) # Alpha accumulation accumulateda += (1.0 - accumulateda) opacity # Termination if accumulateda > 0.985: foundvolume = True break distancealongray += currentstep # Max step limit not given in sources; implementation requires a loop bound or distance threshold. # Discard transparent fragments if accumulateda < 0.002: return None # Temporal reprojection if temporalenabled and foundvolume: # Project representative position to previous frame's clip space prevclippos = camerastate.previousviewprojection @ rayposition # Compute UV if prevclippos.w > 0.0: prevuv = vec2(prevclippos.x / prevclippos.w, prevclippos.y / prevclippos.w) prevuv = vec2(clamp(prevuv.x, 0.0, 1.0), clamp(prevuv.y, 0.0, 1.0)) # Sample history history = historytexture.sample(prevuv) # Responsive weight responsiveweight = historyweight (1.0 - abs(history.a - accumulateda)) # Blend blendfactor = clamp(responsiveweight, 0.0, 0.95) accumulatedrgb = mix(accumulatedrgb, history.rgb, blendfactor) accumulateda = mix(accumulateda, history.a, blendfactor) return vec4(accumulatedrgb, accumulateda) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Temporal Reprojection Bounds: If the previous frame projection has w <= 0.0, the UV calculation is invalid. Clamp UV to [0.0, 1.0] to avoid sampling outside bounds. Ghosting: Mitigated by scaling historyWeight with (1.0 - abs(history.a - accumulated.a)) and clamping the blend factor to [0.0, 0.95]. Transparent Pixels: Fragments with final opacity below 0.002 are discarded to avoid rendering transparent pixels. Field Mode: The fieldMode parameter (0-7) controls smoke color mapping logic via conditional branches, but the specific logic is not detailed in the sources. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces temporal noise and flickering through reprojection. Adaptive stepping reduces steps in low-density regions. Limitations: Ghosting is mitigated by alpha-difference weighting and blend clamping. Requires valid previous frame projection. When to Use: Not given in the sources. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. This method is associated with the HZL Fluid Effects Studio volume renderer, as implemented in the pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio repository. It combines adaptive ray marching with temporal accumulation techniques. HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, https://github.com/pvasbob/HZL-fluidEffectsStudio, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Predictive Adaptive SDF Ray Marching
head: Raytracer 30
body: Predictive Adaptive SDF Ray Marching is a ray marching algorithm for Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) that determines step size using a linear prediction based on the previous two distance estimates, scaled by a reduction factor to prevent overshooting. It differs from standard constant step methods by adapting to local geometry curvature and from other adaptive methods by relying on temporal continuity of distance estimates rather than cone sampling or external data structures for step prediction. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray r (origin O, direction D), SDF function SDF(P), maximum step count stepcount, reduction factor STEPSIZEREDUCTION (typically 0.87). Output: A vec2 containing the hit distance t and the final step size used. Data Structures: Variables: t: Current ray distance along the ray (float). ft: SDF value at current position t (float). pft: Previous SDF value ft from the prior iteration (float). dt: Calculated step size for the current iteration (float). nft: New SDF value at the predicted position (float). Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0. 2. Evaluate the SDF at the ray origin: ft = SDF(RAY(r, t)). 3. Initialize previous distance pft = 0. 4. Initialize step size dt = 0. 5. Loop for i from 0 to stepcount: a. Calculate the predicted step size dt using the formula: dt = ft \times \left(1 - \text{STEP\SIZE\REDUCTION} \times \frac{pft - ft - dt}{pft - ft + dt}\right) b. Evaluate the SDF at the new position: nft = SDF(RAY(r, t + dt)). c. Check for overshooting or invalid step: If dt < ft + nft: Update ft = nft. Update t = t + dt. Else: Reduce step size to the current distance estimate: dt = ft. Update t = t + dt. Re-evaluate SDF at the new position: ft = SDF(RAY(r, t)). d. Update pft for the next iteration: pft = ft (Note: The source implies pft tracks the previous ft; in the loop, pft should be updated to the ft value before it was potentially updated in step c, or effectively the ft from the start of the iteration. Based on the formula structure pft - ft, pft is the SDF value from the previous step's end, and ft is the current step's start. The source code logic suggests pft is the ft from the previous iteration. Let's trace: Start: ft0. Iter 1: pft=0, ft=ft0. Calc dt. Get nft. If valid, ft \leftarrow nft, t \leftarrow t+dt. Next iter: pft should be old ft. The source says "pft = 0" init. It does not explicitly show pft update in the loop text, but logically pft must be the ft from the previous iteration. We will assume pft is updated to the ft value at the end of the successful step or the re-evaluated ft). Correction based on standard predictive algorithms and source context: The variable pft represents the SDF value at the position of the previous step. In the first iteration, it is 0. After a step, pft becomes the ft of that step. 6. Return vec2(t, dt). Parameters: STEPSIZEREDUCTION: A constant float value of 0.87. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero: The denominator pft - ft + dt could be zero if pft + dt = ft. This requires a guard or epsilon check. Overshooting: The condition dt < ft + nft handles cases where the linear prediction would jump past the surface or into a region where the distance estimate is invalid. If this condition fails, the step is clamped to ft. Initial Step: The first step uses pft=0, which may result in a large initial step if ft is large, potentially skipping small features. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def predictiveadaptivesdfraymarching(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunc, stepcount=100, reductionfactor=0.87): t = 0.0 ft = sdffunc(rayorigin + raydirection t) pft = 0.0 dt = 0.0 for i in range(stepcount): # Calculate predicted step size # Guard against division by zero denominator = pft - ft + dt if abs(denominator) < 1e-6: dt = ft else: dt = ft (1.0 - reductionfactor (pft - ft - dt) / denominator) # Evaluate SDF at predicted position nft = sdffunc(rayorigin + raydirection (t + dt)) # Check for overshooting if dt < ft + nft: # Valid step pft = ft ft = nft t += dt else: # Overshoot or invalid, clamp step to current distance estimate dt = ft t += dt ft = sdffunc(rayorigin + raydirection t) pft = ft # Update pft for next iteration as the current ft return t, dt Time and Memory Complexity: Time: O(N) where N is the number of steps, which is typically fewer than constant step marching for smooth surfaces due to adaptive sizing, but more expensive per step due to the prediction calculation. Memory: O(1) auxiliary memory. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Adapts to local geometry, potentially reducing step count for smooth surfaces. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that distance estimates change linearly, which may fail for highly curved or complex geometries. The reduction factor is hardcoded. When to Use: Use for smooth SDFs where step size adaptation improves performance. Not suitable for highly discontinuous or noisy SDFs. The method originates from the "Interactive-SDF-Renderer" project by Csabix, presented as an unofficial implementation. It is also known as "Raytracer 30". name: Dynamic SDF Ray Marching with Adaptive Step Skipping
head: Ray Advancing Kernel, SDF Marching
body: A GPU-based ray marching technique for Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) that advances ray origins by predicted distances, skips empty space using an octree, handles floor reflections, and tracks shadow visibility metrics for soft shadows. Unlike standard SDF marching which uses fminf(distance, maxstep), this method uses a predicted distance from previous steps (prevdistances) to determine step size and visibility, allowing for adaptive skipping of empty space via the octree. Inputs and Outputs: The kernel operates on device buffers. positions: Vector3f array of current ray origins. distances: float array of raw distance field values retrieved at the current position. payloads: SdfPayload array containing ray state (alive, dir, nsteps, idx). prevdistances: float array storing the distance estimate from the previous step for each ray. totaldistances: float array accumulating total distance traveled (used for visibility metrics). minvisibility: float array tracking minimum visibility values. octreenodes: Optional reference to a TriangleOctree structure for spatial acceleration. floory: Float constant defining the floor plane height. distancescale: Float multiplier for distance scaling. zerooffset: Float offset subtracted from raw distance. maximumdistance: Float threshold for ray termination. k: Constant factor for visibility calculation (value not specified in sources). Data Structures: SdfPayload: alive: bool (or equivalent flag) indicating if the ray is active. dir: Vector3f ray direction. nsteps: uint32t or int step counter. idx: uint32t thread/element index. Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate thread index i. If i >= nelements, terminate. 2. Check payloads[i].alive. If false, return. 3. Retrieve raw distance draw = distances[i]. Compute adjusted distance: distance = (draw - zerooffset) distancescale. 4. Advance position: pos = positions[i] + distance payloads[i].dir. 5. Octree Skip: If octreenodes exists and pos is not contained in the octree (!TriangleOctree::contains(octreenodes, pos)): Calculate intersection distance octreedistance = TriangleOctree::rayintersect(octreenodes, pos, payloads[i].dir). Add epsilon to prevent self-intersection: octreedistance += 1e-6f. Update distance and position: distance += octreedistance, pos += octreedistance payloads[i].dir. 6. Floor Reflection: If pos.y() < floory and payloads[i].dir.y() < 0.0f: Calculate floor intersection: floordist = -(pos.y() - floory) / payloads[i].dir.y(). Update distance and position: distance += floordist, pos += floordist payloads[i].dir. Terminate ray: payloads[i].alive = false. 7. Update position buffer: positions[i] = pos. 8. Visibility Metric Update: If totaldistances is not null and distance > 0.0f: Calculate intermediate values: y = \frac{distance^2}{2 \cdot prev\distances[i]} d = \sqrt{distance^2 - y^2} Calculate total distance so far: totaldistance = totaldistances[i]. Update minimum visibility: min\visibility[i] = \min(min\visibility[i], \frac{k \cdot d}{\max(0.0, total\distance - y)}) Update history: prevdistances[i] = distance, totaldistances[i] += distance. 9. Survival Check: Determine if ray should continue: Condition: stayalive = (distance > maximumdistance) && (fabsf(distance / 2) > 3 maximumdistance). If not stayalive, set payloads[i].alive = false and return. 10. AABB Containment: If !aabb.contains(pos), set payloads[i].alive = false and return. 11. Increment step counter: payloads[i].nsteps++. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def advanceposkernelsdf(positions, distances, payloads, prevdistances, totaldistances, minvisibility, octreenodes, floory, distancescale, zerooffset, maximumdistance, k, aabb, nelements): i = getthreadindex() if i >= nelements: return payload = payloads[i] if not payload.alive: return # Step 3: Retrieve and scale distance rawdist = distances[i] distance = (rawdist - zerooffset) distancescale # Step 4: Advance position pos = positions[i] + distance payload.dir # Step 5: Octree skip if octreenodes is not None and not triangleoctreecontains(octreenodes, pos): octreedistance = triangleoctreerayintersect(octreenodes, pos, payload.dir) octreedistance += 1e-6f # Epsilon to prevent self-intersection distance += octreedistance pos += octreedistance payload.dir # Step 6: Floor reflection if pos.y < floory and payload.dir.y < 0.0f: floordist = -(pos.y - floory) / payload.dir.y distance += floordist pos += floordist payload.dir payload.alive = False # Step 7: Update position positions[i] = pos # Step 8: Visibility metrics if totaldistances is not None and distance > 0.0f: prevd = prevdistances[i] # Avoid division by zero if prevd is 0, though logic implies prevd > 0 for valid history if prevd > 0.0f: y = (distance distance) / (2.0f prevd) dval = sqrt(max(0.0f, distance distance - y y)) totaldist = totaldistances[i] denom = max(0.0f, totaldist - y) if denom > 0.0f: visibilityval = (k dval) / denom minvisibility[i] = min(minvisibility[i], visibilityval) prevdistances[i] = distance totaldistances[i] += distance # Step 9: Survival check # Note: The source condition "distance > maximumdistance && fabsf(distance / 2) > 3maximumdistance" # implies the ray must be far from the surface AND the step size must be large relative to the threshold. # If distance <= maximumdistance, the ray is killed (stayalive = False). stayalive = (distance > maximumdistance) and (abs(distance / 2.0f) > 3.0f maximumdistance) if not stayalive: payload.alive = False return # Step 10: AABB containment if not aabbcontains(aabb, pos): payload.alive = False return # Step 11: Increment steps payload.nsteps += 1 Parameters: MARCHITER: Constant set to 10000 (likely max iterations in testbed context). zerooffset: Float offset subtracted from raw distance. distancescale: Float multiplier applied to distance. maximumdistance: Float threshold for ray termination. k: Constant for visibility calculation (value not specified in sources). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Self-intersection: When skipping octree nodes, a small epsilon 1e-6f is added to the intersection distance to handle precision issues. Floor Termination: If the ray hits the floor (pos.y() < floory and moving downwards), the ray is marked as dead immediately after calculating the intersection. Division by Zero: In the visibility formula, prevdistances[i] and totaldistance - y are used as denominators. The source code uses fmaxf(0.0f,...) for the latter, but explicit checks for zero prevdistances are recommended to prevent NaN propagation. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays and steps, but adaptive skipping via octree reduces the number of SDF evaluations in empty space. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for prevdistances, totaldistances, and minvisibility buffers in addition to standard ray buffers. Strengths: Adaptive step size based on previous estimates allows for larger steps in empty space. Octree integration enables efficient skipping of large empty volumes. Visibility metrics support soft shadow calculation. Limitations: Requires maintaining history buffers (prevdistances). Floor reflection logic is hardcoded and may not generalize to all scenes. The survival condition distance > maximumdistance kills rays that are close to surfaces, which might be undesirable for high-precision surface rendering if maximumdistance is set too high. When to use: Scenes with large empty spaces where octree acceleration is effective, and soft shadow visibility metrics are required. When not to use: Scenes without a defined floor plane, or where high-precision surface proximity requires smaller, more frequent steps than the adaptive predictor allows. Originating from the Dynamic-NGPs project, this method is part of a pipeline for training and rendering dynamic neural graphics primitives. It is used in the rendering phase (render.py) to generate frames from trained models, incorporating spatial acceleration and shadow visibility tracking. jaeyeol816/Dynamic-NGPs, https://github.com/jaeyeol816/Dynamic-NGPs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Dartmouth Distance Sampling
head: PDF for Sampling, Probability Density Function (PDF) for Sampling, Segment-based Distance Sampling
body: Dartmouth Distance Sampling is a Monte Carlo importance sampling technique for volume rendering that constructs a probability density function (PDF) matching the exponential transmittance component of the light transport integral to cancel it analytically. It differs from standard ray marching by treating the integration domain as a series of trapezoidal segments defined by the projected corners of the bounding box, allowing for direct sampling of the free path length rather than fixed or adaptive step iteration. Inputs and Outputs Input: Camera ray origin O, direction D, three sorted projected corner distances along the ray t{C,1}, t{C,2}, t{C,3}, extinction coefficient \sigmat, and the distance from a sample point x towards the light source dm(x). Output: A sampled distance x along the ray, drawn from the constructed PDF. Data Structures The method partitions the ray into three segments based on the projected box corners: [0, t{C,1}], [t{C,1}, t{C,2}], and [t{C,2}, t{C,3}]. Each segment i stores a precomputed integral weight \mathcal{I}i representing the accumulated transmittance over that interval. Formulas The PDF is constructed by combining the probability of selecting a segment with the conditional probability of selecting a distance within that segment. 1. Segment Selection Probability: The probability of selecting segment i is proportional to the radiance scattered within that segment relative to the total maximum unoccluded radiance: P(x \in [t{C,i-1}, t{C,i}]) = \frac{\mathcal{I}i}{\text{total}} Where \mathcal{I}i = \int{t{C,i-1}}^{t{C,i}} e^{-\sigmat(x + dm(x))} dx. 2. Conditional Distance Probability: Given segment i is selected, the probability density for distance x is the transmittance at x normalized by the segment integral: P(x | x \in [t{C,i-1}, t{C,i}]) = \frac{T'(x)}{\mathcal{I}i} = \frac{e^{-\sigmat(x + dm(x))}}{\mathcal{I}i} Where T'(x) is the transmittance at x. 3. Final PDF: The assembled PDF for a point x relative to the projected corners is: \text{PDF}(x) = \begin{cases} \frac{\mathcal{I}1}{\text{total}} \cdot \frac{T'(x)}{\mathcal{I}1} & x < t{C,1} \\ \frac{\mathcal{I}2}{\text{total}} \cdot \frac{T'(x)}{\mathcal{I}2} & t{C,1} < x < t{C,2} \\ \frac{\mathcal{I}3}{\text{total}} \cdot \frac{T'(x)}{\mathcal{I}3} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} The source notation uses \mathcal{I}'i and \mathcal{I}'i(x) interchangeably for the transmittance term, which simplifies to T'(x). Steps 1. Project Corners: Compute the intersection distances of the ray with the bounding box geometry to obtain sorted values t{C,1}, t{C,2}, t{C,3}. 2. Compute Integrals: Calculate \mathcal{I}i for each segment by integrating the exponential transmittance function over the segment bounds. 3. Select Segment: Generate a uniform random number to select segment i with probability \mathcal{I}i / \text{total}. 4. Sample Distance: Within the selected segment, sample the exact continuous distance x using the conditional PDF P(x | \text{segment } i). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def dartmouthdistancesampling(rayorigin, raydir, boxmin, boxmax, sigmat, lightdir): # 1. Project box corners onto the ray (slab method) tmin = (boxmin - rayorigin) / raydir tmax = (boxmax - rayorigin) / raydir tenter = max(min(tmin), min(tmax)) texit = min(max(tmin), max(tmax)) # Source defines three projected corners; we use entry, exit, and a third boundary tC = sorted([tenter, texit, texit + 1.0]) # 2. Precompute segment integrals Ii segments = [(0.0, tC[0]), (tC[0], tC[1]), (tC[1], tC[2])] I = [] # Assuming collimated light, dm(x) is linear: dm(x) = ax + b a = lightdir.dot(raydir) b = (rayorigin - lightorigin).dot(lightdir) k = sigmat (1.0 + a) for start, end in segments: if abs(k) < 1e-9: Ival = (end - start) math.exp(-sigmat b) else: Ival = (math.exp(-k start - sigmat b) - math.exp(-k end - sigmat b)) / k I.append(Ival) totalI = sum(I) # 3. Select segment based on probability Ii / totalI r = random.random() cumulative = 0.0 segmentidx = 0 for i, val in enumerate(I): cumulative += val / totalI if r < cumulative: segmentidx = i break start, end = segments[segmentidx] # 4. Sample x within the segment using the conditional PDF # Inversion sampling for exponential distribution over [start, end] u = random.random() if abs(k) < 1e-9: x = start + u (end - start) else: x = -math.log(math.exp(-k start) - u (math.exp(-k start) - math.exp(-k end))) / k return x Edge Cases and Pitfalls Geometry Mismatch: The method fails when the exit point along the camera ray is much closer than the distance from the origin towards the light source. Non-Constant Distance: It deviates in cases where the distance to the box boundary is not constant (i.e., d{E,S} \neq d{E,E}). Discontinuities: The presence of box corners creates a function that is not smooth, with clear differences in the rate of change around the distance of the projected corners. A variant that explicitly discretizes the ray into segments corresponding to geometric features before applying the PDF. It sets itself apart by prioritizing geometric alignment over continuous distribution fitting, and should be chosen when scene boundaries dominate variance. Emphasizes the construction of the probability density function to match the integrand's exponential term. It differs by focusing on analytical cancellation of the transmittance decay, and is preferred when homogeneous media or collimated lighting are present. Complexity: Requires computing segment integrals, which for heterogeneous media is handled by subdividing the space and multiplying transmittance evaluations at runtime rather than costly precomputation. Strengths: Cancels the exponential transmittance term analytically, reducing variance in Monte Carlo integration. Limitations: Fails or deviates significantly when the light source geometry does not align with the camera ray's exit point or when boundary distances are not constant. The PDF is not necessarily monotonically decreasing. When to use: Homogeneous media with simple light geometries where the exponential term dominates the variance. Dartmouth Distance Sampling was introduced in the paper "Collimated Whole Volume Light Scattering in Homogeneous Finite Media". It is part of an optimized Monte Carlo integration strategy for volume rendering that connects light rays along the camera ray to reduce redundant computations. name: SDF Ray Marching with Grid Lookup
head: Camera ray intersection via ray marching, Intersect kernel, camera ray marching
body: A GPU-based ray marching algorithm that samples a 3D Signed Distance Function (SDF) grid to find the first intersection point of a ray with the zero-level set (surface). It sets itself apart from Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by using linear interpolation to evaluate the SDF at arbitrary points within the grid bounds, allowing for precise intersection detection without fixed step constraints. Inputs and Outputs: grid: 3D tensor of float SDF values, shape (gridresx, gridresy, gridresz). origins: 2D tensor of float ray origins, shape (N, 3). directions: 2D tensor of float ray directions, shape (N, 3). originimagedistances: 1D tensor of float distances from camera origin to image plane, shape (N,). pixeldistances: 1D tensor of float distances from camera origin to pixel locations, shape (N,). boundingboxmin: 3D vector defining the minimum corner of the SDF grid's axis-aligned bounding box. boundingboxmax: 3D vector defining the maximum corner of the SDF grid's axis-aligned bounding box. gridresx, gridresy, gridresz: Integer resolutions of the SDF grid along each axis. maxsteps: Integer maximum number of marching steps per ray (default: 1000). voxelposition: 2D tensor of float, shape (N, 3), storing the voxel coordinates of the intersection. intersectionpos: 2D tensor of float, shape (N, 3), storing the 3D world coordinates of the intersection. gottenresult: 1D tensor of int, shape (N,), flag indicating if an intersection was found (1) or not (0). Data Structures: The SDF grid is stored as a contiguous 3D array. Ray parameters are stored in parallel arrays for batch processing. Steps: 1. Initialize depth = 0, firsttime = true, gottenresult = 0 for each ray. 2. Loop for maxsteps: a. Calculate current point: reachedpointx = origins[i] + depth directions[i] (and y, z). b. Call ValueAt to get SDF distance at reachedpoint. c. Check for exit: If distance == -1, set voxelposition and intersectionpos to -1, set gottenresult = 1, and break. d. Check for intersection: If distance < pixeldistances[pixelindex] / originimagedistances[pixelindex] depth AND distance is truthy (non-zero), record intersection. Set voxelposition to floor of current point (clamped to gridres - 1). Set intersectionpos to current point. Set gottenresult = 1 and break. e. Increment depth. ValueAt (Trilinear Interpolation): 1. Compute fractional coordinates tx, ty, tz relative to the grid cell containing the point. 2. Interpolate along X to get c01, c23, c45, c67. 3. Interpolate along Y to get c0, c1. 4. Interpolate along Z for final result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def valueat(grid, point, gridres, boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax): # Map world point to grid coordinates gridx = (point[0] - boundingboxmin[0]) / (boundingboxmax[0] - boundingboxmin[0]) (gridres[0] - 1) gridy = (point[1] - boundingboxmin[1]) / (boundingboxmax[1] - boundingboxmin[1]) (gridres[1] - 1) gridz = (point[2] - boundingboxmin[2]) / (boundingboxmax[2] - boundingboxmin[2]) (gridres[2] - 1) # Check bounds if not (0 <= gridx < gridres[0] and 0 <= gridy < gridres[1] and 0 <= gridz < gridres[2]): return -1.0 # Get integer and fractional parts ix = int(gridx) iy = int(gridy) iz = int(gridz) fx = gridx - ix fy = gridy - iy fz = gridz - iz # Clamp indices ix = max(0, min(ix, gridres[0] - 1)) iy = max(0, min(iy, gridres[1] - 1)) iz = max(0, min(iz, gridres[2] - 1)) # Trilinear interpolation c000 = grid[ix][iy][iz] c100 = grid[min(ix + 1, gridres[0] - 1)][iy][iz] c010 = grid[ix][min(iy + 1, gridres[1] - 1)][iz] c110 = grid[min(ix + 1, gridres[0] - 1)][min(iy + 1, gridres[1] - 1)][iz] c001 = grid[ix][iy][min(iz + 1, gridres[2] - 1)] c101 = grid[min(ix + 1, gridres[0] - 1)][iy][min(iz + 1, gridres[2] - 1)] c011 = grid[ix][min(iy + 1, gridres[1] - 1)][min(iz + 1, gridres[2] - 1)] c111 = grid[min(ix + 1, gridres[0] - 1)][min(iy + 1, gridres[1] - 1)][min(iz + 1, gridres[2] - 1)] # Interpolate along X c01 = c000 (1 - fx) + c100 fx c23 = c010 (1 - fx) + c110 fx c45 = c001 (1 - fx) + c101 fx c67 = c011 (1 - fx) + c111 fx # Interpolate along Y c0 = c01 (1 - fy) + c23 fy c1 = c45 (1 - fy) + c67 fy # Interpolate along Z return c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz def raymarchingwithgridlookup(grid, origins, directions, originimagedistances, pixeldistances, gridres, boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax, maxsteps=1000): N = len(origins) voxelposition = [[-1.0, -1.0, -1.0] for in range(N)] intersectionpos = [[-1.0, -1.0, -1.0] for in range(N)] gottenresult = [0] N for i in range(N): depth = 0.0 gottenresult[i] = 0 for step in range(maxsteps): # Calculate current point reachedpoint = [ origins[i][0] + depth directions[i][0], origins[i][1] + depth directions[i][1], origins[i][2] + depth directions[i][2] ] # Get SDF distance distance = valueat(grid, reachedpoint, gridres, boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax) # Check for exit if distance == -1.0: voxelposition[i] = [-1.0, -1.0, -1.0] intersectionpos[i] = [-1.0, -1.0, -1.0] gottenresult[i] = 1 break # Check for intersection threshold = (pixeldistances[i] / originimagedistances[i]) depth if distance < threshold and distance != 0.0: # Record intersection floorpoint = [float(int(p)) for p in reachedpoint] clampedpoint = [ max(0.0, min(floorpoint[0], gridres[0] - 1)), max(0.0, min(floorpoint[1], gridres[1] - 1)), max(0.0, min(floorpoint[2], gridres[2] - 1)) ] voxelposition[i] = clampedpoint intersectionpos[i] = reachedpoint gottenresult[i] = 1 break depth += 1.0 return voxelposition, intersectionpos, gottenresult This method extends SDF ray marching to handle hierarchical voxel grids with varying resolutions. It solves the problem of evaluating the Signed Distance Function (SDF) at arbitrary points near boundaries between different resolution levels, where standard tri-linear interpolation is invalid. It sets itself apart from its parent by replacing the uniform interpolation kernel with a local polynomial fit derived from a linear system, ensuring continuity across resolution boundaries. name: Raycasting with Irregular Grid Interpolation
head: Adaptive Grid Raycasting, TSDF Zero-Level Set Extraction
body: This method extends SDF ray marching to handle hierarchical voxel grids with varying resolutions. It solves the problem of evaluating the Signed Distance Function (SDF) at arbitrary points near boundaries between different resolution levels, where standard tri-linear interpolation is invalid. It sets itself apart from its parent by replacing the uniform interpolation kernel with a local polynomial fit derived from a linear system, ensuring continuity across resolution boundaries. Inputs: Camera pose (R, t) and intrinsic calibration K. Hierarchical TSDF grid composed of voxel blocks with potentially different resolutions. Pre-computed depth range map: for each pixel, the minimum and maximum depth values derived from projecting the bounding boxes of observed voxel blocks into the image. Outputs: A map of 3D points and surface normals (and optionally surface colors) corresponding to the zero-level set F(X) = 0. Data Structures: Depth Range Map: A 2D array mapping pixel coordinates (u, v) to a depth interval [d{min}, d{max}]. Voxel Block: Internal grid data layout and storage format are not given in the sources. Algorithm: 1. Pre-computation: Project the bounding boxes of all observed voxel blocks into the image plane. For each pixel, determine the plausible depth range [d{min}, d{max}] by filling these projections with appropriate minimum and maximum depth values. 2. Ray Casting Loop: For each pixel (u, v), construct the ray origin and direction from the camera model (R, t, K). Initialize the ray step range using the pre-computed [d{min}, d{max}] for this pixel. Perform ray marching steps along the line of sight to find the point X where F(X) = 0. 3. SDF Evaluation F(X): At each ray marching step, evaluate the SDF at the current 3D point X = (X, Y, Z) by identifying the 8 surrounding grid points (corners of the voxel cube containing X). Check if any two of these 8 surrounding grid points reside in different resolution levels (i.e., different voxel blocks). If all 8 points reside in the same resolution level, use standard tri-linear interpolation by accumulating values from the 8 surrounding grid points weighted by linear interpolation coefficients. If points span different resolutions, use the irregular interpolation function defined below. 4. Irregular Grid Interpolation: When the 8 surrounding points span different resolutions, solve for the interpolating function coefficients. The function is defined as: F(X, Y, Z) = a1 XYZ + a2 XY + a3 YZ + a4 XZ + a5 X + a6 Y + a7 Z + a8 Each of the 8 surrounding grid points (Xi, Yi, Zi) with known SDF values F(Xi, Yi, Zi) provides one equation. This results in the linear system: \mathbf{A} \begin{pmatrix} a1 \\ \vdots \\ a8 \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} F(X1, Y1, Z1) \\ \vdots \\ F(X8, Y8, Z8) \end{pmatrix} The matrix \mathbf{A} is constructed such that row i is: [Xi Yi Zi, \ Xi Yi, \ Yi Zi, \ Xi Zi, \ Xi, \ Yi, \ Zi, \ 1] To solve this system efficiently: a. Arbitrarily shift the coordinate system of the points such that the first point becomes the origin (X1 = 0). b. This trivially solves for a8 (the constant term). c. Solve the remaining inhomogeneous 7 \times 7 system for a1, \dots, a7 using Gaussian elimination. d. Evaluate F(X, Y, Z) using the solved coefficients. 5. Termination: The exact termination tolerance and maximum step count are not given in the sources. The method iterates along the line of sight within the pre-computed depth range to find the zero-level set. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trilinearinterpolate(points8, values8, query): # Assumes points8 form a unit cube with points8[0] as the minimum corner x0, y0, z0 = points8[0] fx = query[0] - x0 fy = query[1] - y0 fz = query[2] - z0 w000 = (1-fx)(1-fy)(1-fz) w100 = fx(1-fy)(1-fz) w010 = (1-fx)fy(1-fz) w110 = fxfy(1-fz) w001 = (1-fx)(1-fy)fz w101 = fx(1-fy)fz w011 = (1-fx)fyfz w111 = fxfyfz return (w000values8[0] + w100values8[1] + w010values8[2] + w110values8[3] + w001values8[4] + w101values8[5] + w011values8[6] + w111values8[7]) def gaussianelimination(A, b): # Solves Ax = b for square A using Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting n = len(A) M = [A[i][:] + [b[i]] for i in range(n)] for i in range(n): maxrow = i for k in range(i+1, n): if abs(M[k][i]) > abs(M[maxrow][i]): maxrow = k M[i], M[maxrow] = M[maxrow], M[i] pivot = M[i][i] if abs(pivot) < 1e-12: continue for k in range(i+1, n): factor = M[k][i] / pivot for j in range(i, n+1): M[k][j] -= factor M[i][j] x = [0.0] n for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): x[i] = M[i][n] for j in range(i+1, n): x[i] -= M[i][j] x[j] x[i] /= M[i][i] return x def evaluatesdfirregular(points8, values8, querypoint): # Shift coordinates so the first point is at the origin origin = points8[0] shiftedpoints = [(p[0]-origin[0], p[1]-origin[1], p[2]-origin[2]) for p in points8] shiftedquery = (querypoint[0]-origin[0], querypoint[1]-origin[1], querypoint[2]-origin[2]) # a8 is the value at the origin (first point) a8 = values8[0] # Build 7x7 system for a1..a7 using points 1..7 (indices 1 to 7) A = [] b = [] for i in range(1, 8): x, y, z = shiftedpoints[i] row = [xyz, xy, yz, xz, x, y, z] A.append(row) b.append(values8[i] -
