name: Ray Marching
head: Ray Marching Step, SDF-based Ray Stepping, Signed Distance Field stepping, jittered ray marching
body: Ray marching is an iterative technique for finding intersections with solid geometry or evaluating volumetric fields by stepping along a ray and testing for intersections. It is used when the surface function is not easy to solve analytically or when rendering non-uniform volumetrics, implicit functions, fractals, and parametric surfaces where intersection is not known ahead of time. Unlike classical ray tracing which seeks exact intersections directly, ray marching works iteratively, moving the ray through space in steps until a surface is found, a maximum distance is exceeded, or enough samples are collected for volume integration. It sets itself apart from its parent Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by encompassing a broader family of methods, including adaptive stepping via Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and fixed-step approaches for volume rendering, whereas the parent specifically refers to the fixed-stride mitigation of root-finding drawbacks. Inputs: Ray origin ro and direction rd (normalized). Scene representation: A function scene(p) that returns a value at point p. This value is either a Signed Distance Function (SDF) for surface rendering or a density/opacity field for volume rendering. Parameters: u{maxDis}: Maximum ray distance (far plane). u{eps}: Hit threshold (surface proximity). u{maxSteps}: Maximum number of iterations. min\step\len, max\step\len: Bounds for step size. Outputs: For surface rendering: Hit position, surface normal, and final color. For volume rendering: Accumulated color and opacity. No complex data structures are required for the core algorithm itself, as it relies on procedural evaluation. For acceleration (space leaping), preprocessed safety distances or grids may be used. For volume rendering, the scene is often represented as a neural network or a 3D texture grid. The general iterative process is as follows: 1. Ray Generation: Compute ray origin ro and direction rd for the current pixel. 2. Initialization: Set total distance traveled t = 0 and current position p = ro. 3. Iteration Loop: Repeat for i = 0 to u{maxSteps}: a. Query Scene: Evaluate the scene function at the current position: dist = scene(p). If using SDF: dist is the distance to the nearest surface. If using Volume: dist is the density or transmittance contribution at p. b. Termination Check: If dist < u{eps} (for SDF) or sufficient samples accumulated (for Volume), break loop. If t + dist \ge u{maxDis}, break loop (missed geometry/background). c. Advance Ray: Sphere Tracing (Adaptive): Advance by the SDF value: t \leftarrow t + dist. This is safe because no geometry exists within distance dist. Fixed Step: Advance by a constant \Delta t: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. d. Update Position: p \leftarrow ro + t \cdot rd. 4. Post-Processing: If hit (t < u{maxDis}): Compute lighting (diffuse, specular, ambient) using normals derived from numerical differentiation of the SDF. If miss: Output clear/background color. For Volume: Accumulate color and opacity using the volume rendering equation. The following pseudocode implements the standard sphere tracing variant, which is the most common form of ray marching for implicit surfaces. It uses explicit vector operations to remain valid Python. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def raymarch(ro, rd, scenefunc, maxsteps, maxdist, epsilon): """ Iteratively march a ray to find intersection with implicit surface defined by scenefunc. Args: ro: list[float], ray origin [x, y, z] rd: list[float], normalized ray direction [x, y, z] scenefunc: function, returns SDF value (distance to nearest surface) for a point maxsteps: int, maximum number of iterations maxdist: float, maximum distance to search epsilon: float, threshold for hit detection Returns: float: total distance traveled if hit, maxdist if missed """ t = 0.0 # total distance travelled for in range(maxsteps): # Calculate current position p = [ro[0] + t rd[0], ro[1] + t rd[1], ro[2] + t rd[2]] # Query scene distance dist = scenefunc(p) # Check for hit or max distance if dist < epsilon: return t + dist if t + dist > maxdist: return maxdist # Advance ray by the distance to the nearest surface (Sphere Tracing) # This is safe because no geometry exists inside the sphere of radius dist t += dist return maxdist def computenormal(scenefunc, p, h=0.001): """ Compute surface normal via numerical differentiation of SDF. """ dx = scenefunc([p[0] + h, p[1], p[2]]) - scenefunc([p[0] - h, p[1], p[2]]) dy = scenefunc([p[0], p[1] + h, p[2]]) - scenefunc([p[0], p[1] - h, p[2]]) dz = scenefunc([p[0], p[1], p[2] + h]) - scenefunc([p[0], p[1], p[2] - h]) length = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) if length == 0.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] return [dx/length, dy/length, dz/length] Sphere Tracing Update: p{n+1} = pn + d(pn)\hat{d}, where pn is current position, d(pn) is SDF value, \hat{d} is ray direction. Sphere SDF: distance = \|p\| - r. Cube SDF: distance = \max(|p.x| - s, |p.y| - s, |p.z| - s), where s is half-size. Union SDF: distance = \min(distance1, distance2). Jensen's Inequality Bias (Volume): Assuming constant extinction leads to bias: \exp(\mathbb{E}[-\tau]) \le \mathbb{E}[\exp(-\tau)]. u{eps}: Hit threshold. Typical value: 0.001. min\step\len, max\step\len: Bounds for step size. Overestimation: Sphere tracing requires the SDF to be conservative (never overestimate true distance). If the distance function is optimistic, the ray can step past geometry and miss it. Precision: Insufficient precision can lead to "holes" or incorrect intersections. Volume Bias: Fixed-step ray marching for volumes ignores true heterogeneity, leading to bias characterized by Jensen's inequality. Performance at Low Samples: Ray marching performs poorly at lower sample counts for volume rendering compared to distance sampling. Accumulates color and opacity per step along the ray rather than stopping at the first hit. Sets itself apart by supporting translucent and participating media. Choose it when rendering fog, clouds, or neural radiance fields. Determines the increment \Delta t or adaptive jump distance at each iteration. Sets itself apart by focusing on the trade-off between sampling density and computational cost. Choose it when optimizing convergence or avoiding aliasing in volumetric integration. Combines adaptive SDF stepping with spatial acceleration structures like 3D textures or sparse grids. Sets itself apart by replacing procedural evaluation with fast texture lookups. Choose it when rendering large, precomputed distance fields or voxel-based scenes. Complexity: High computational complexity due to many iterations required per pixel. Performance: On an RTX 8000 GPU at 1024 spp, ray marching on a room scene took 11.0 \pm 0.5 ms. On a GTX 980 Ti at 256 spp, it took 10.3 \pm 0.2 ms. Scaling: Scalability to large explicit scenes is poor unless acceleration structures (BVH, grids) are used for distance queries. Strengths: Natural for procedural geometry, compact scene representation, easy integration of global illumination and soft shadows. Limitations: Inefficient for explicit triangle meshes without SDF conversion; poor convergence at low sample counts for volumes. When to Use: Rendering implicit surfaces, fractals, volumetrics, and parametric surfaces where analytical intersection is difficult. Ray marching was first encountered by the author in the context of per-pixel displacement mapping techniques, specifically relief mapping of non-height-field surface details. It is a technique similar to traditional ray tracing but relies on iterative stepping rather than direct intersection solving. It is widely used in real-time differentiable volume rendering (e.g., NeRF) and procedural graphics/shaders (e.g., ShaderToy). name: Sphere Tracing
head: Hart's Sphere Tracing, SDF Sphere Tracing, SDF Tracing
body: Sphere Tracing is an iterative ray-marching algorithm for rendering implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or Lipschitz continuous implicit functions. It solves the problem of finding the intersection between a camera ray and a complex, analytically defined geometry without explicit polygonal meshes. Unlike standard ray marching which uses fixed steps, Sphere Tracing uses the SDF value at the current position as a safe lower bound for the distance to the nearest surface, allowing the ray to "jump" forward by that exact distance. This guarantees that the ray never overshoots or penetrates the surface, provided the function satisfies the Lipschitz condition. It is distinguished from its siblings, such as Standard Constant Step Ray Marching, by its adaptive step sizing which significantly reduces the number of function evaluations required to converge on a surface. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized ray direction \mathbf{d}, scene function f(\mathbf{p}) returning the signed distance to the nearest surface, maximum traversal distance t{max}, maximum iteration count N{max}, and convergence threshold \epsilon. Output: Intersection distance t{hit} (or boolean hit status) and optionally the intersection point \mathbf{p}{hit} = \mathbf{o} + t{hit}\mathbf{d}. Data Structures: The method maintains a scalar accumulator t for the total distance traveled along the ray. No complex data structures are required for the core algorithm, though acceleration structures (like bounding spheres or grids) may be used to optimize the evaluation of f(\mathbf{p}). Mathematical Foundation: The core safety guarantee relies on the Lipschitz condition. A function f is Lipschitz continuous with constant \lambda if |f(\mathbf{x}) - f(\mathbf{y})| \le \lambda \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\| for all \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}. For a general Lipschitz function, the safe step size is s = \frac{|f(\mathbf{x})|}{\lambda}. If f is a true Signed Distance Function (SDF), then \lambda = 1 and the step size is exactly f(\mathbf{x}). The value f(\mathbf{x}) represents the radius of an "unbounding sphere" centered at \mathbf{x} that is guaranteed not to contain any part of the surface. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize accumulated distance t = 0.0 (or a small epsilon to avoid starting exactly on the surface if f(\mathbf{o})=0). 2. Loop for i from 0 to N{max}: a. Calculate current position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Evaluate the scene function: d = f(\mathbf{p}). c. Termination Check (Hit): If |d| < \epsilon (or d < \epsilon for unsigned distance fields), the surface has been hit. Return t as the intersection distance. Note: Some implementations check d < \epsilon assuming positive distances outside, while others check absolute value for signed fields. d. Termination Check (Miss): If t > t{max}, the ray has escaped the scene. Return failure/no hit. e. Step Update: Advance the ray by the distance value: t \leftarrow t + d. Safety Note: In practice, d is often clamped to a minimum step size to prevent infinite loops in flat regions or numerical instability. 3. If the loop completes without hitting the surface, return failure/no hit. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, scenesdf, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon): """ Performs sphere tracing to find the intersection of a ray with an SDF surface. Args: rayorigin (vec3): The starting point of the ray. raydirection (vec3): The normalized direction of the ray. scenesdf (function): A function f(p) returning the signed distance to the nearest surface. maxdist (float): The maximum distance the ray can travel. maxsteps (int): The maximum number of iterations allowed. epsilon (float): The convergence threshold for hit detection. Returns: tuple: (hit: bool, distance: float) """ t = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): # Check if ray has exceeded maximum distance if t > maxdist: return False, t # Calculate current position on the ray p = rayorigin + raydirection t # Evaluate the Signed Distance Function at the current position dist = scenesdf(p) # Check for surface hit # Using absolute value for signed distance fields, or just dist < epsilon for unsigned if abs(dist) < epsilon: return True, t # Advance the ray by the distance to the surface # This is the core "sphere tracing" step: the ray moves by the radius of the # unbounding sphere, guaranteeing no surface is skipped. t += dist # Max steps reached without hitting surface return False, t Parameters and Typical Values: \epsilon (Convergence Threshold): Typically 0.001 to 0.0001. Some implementations use a relative threshold like 0.001 \times t. N{max} (Max Steps): Typically 10 to 128 for simple scenes, up to 1024 for complex or deep volumes. t{max} (Max Distance): Scene-dependent, often 100.0 or determined by the camera's far plane. Minimum Step Size: Often clamped to a small value (e.g., 0.0001) to prevent stagnation in flat areas or numerical errors. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lipschitz Violation: If the scene function is not Lipschitz continuous with constant \lambda=1 (i.e., it is not a true SDF), the step size d may be larger than the actual distance to the surface, causing the ray to overshoot and miss the intersection. Flat Surfaces: When the ray grazes a surface or moves parallel to a flat region, the SDF value remains large, leading to large steps that may skip over the surface if the surface is not perfectly planar or if numerical precision issues arise. Inside the Surface: If the ray starts inside the object (f(\mathbf{p}) < 0), the step size becomes negative, moving the ray backward. The algorithm must handle this, often by checking for sign changes or using absolute values for step sizing in specific variants. Precision: Floating-point precision errors can cause the ray to oscillate near the surface or fail to converge within \epsilon. Using a relative epsilon or a minimum step size helps mitigate this. The Zeno implementation is a specific software architecture for sphere tracing that prioritizes ease of extension for new implicit surfaces over raw shading performance. It solves the problem of rapidly prototyping mathematical implicit surfaces by allowing new primitives to be added by defining only a signed distance bound, while avoiding the manual derivation of surface normals. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing implementations by replacing the explicit normal function with a fixed six-sample numerical gradient approximation, accepting the minor performance cost as negligible compared to ray intersection overhead. Cone intersection is an antialiasing technique for sphere tracing that represents a pixel as a viewing cone rather than a point ray, allowing symbolic prefiltering to eliminate aliasing artifacts at grazing angles. It differs from standard sphere tracing by detecting intersections with an "inner cover" surface and computing the fractional coverage of the pixel by the implicit surface, whereas siblings like Segment Tracing or Quadric Tracing focus on varying step sizes or bounding volumes without necessarily computing area-based coverage fractions. Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm that computes local Lipschitz bounds on candidate segments to determine adaptive step sizes, reducing the number of field function queries compared to global Lipschitz bound methods like Sphere Tracing. It works for a particular class of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces, leveraging the composition of distance functions and kernel functions to compute directional Lipschitz bounds. Unlike Sphere Tracing, which uses a global bound that limits step size efficiency, Segment Tracing allows larger, safer steps by adapting to the local gradient and field values. Enhanced Sphere Tracing is a family of ray-marching optimizations that accelerate convergence toward implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by taking steps larger than the strict Lipschitz bound or by predicting optimal step sizes based on local surface geometry. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard sphere tracing, which becomes prohibitively slow when rays graze surfaces at shallow angles or when the surface is locally planar. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which uses the queried distance value as the step size, enhanced variants either over-relax the step size by a constant factor or infer the next step size from the previous two distance queries to approximate the surface as locally flat. Uniform Sphere Tracing is a volume rendering technique that uses ray marching along a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to detect volume boundaries and applies Beer's Law for optical depth integration under a uniform density assumption. It solves the problem of rendering participating media with constant optical properties by stepping through the volume, accumulating absorption and scattering, and blending the result with the background. It is distinguished from its parent Sphere Tracing by its specific application to uniform density volume rendering and its reliance on fixed or clamped step sizes for the marching phase, while using SDF evaluation primarily for surface detection rather than purely adaptive step sizing for optical integration. Synchronized-tracing is a tile-based rendering pipeline for implicit volumes (blobtrees) that synchronizes threads within a subfrustum to allow coherent field evaluation, using sparse bottom-up tree traversal to prune the blobtree on-the-fly. It is designed for interactive modeling scenarios where no preprocessing is required when primitive parameters are updated. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by introducing a synchronization mechanism via a low-resolution A-buffer to manage thread coherence within workgroups, and by using compact, smooth CSG operators to compute tight bounding volumes for approximate signed distance fields. Relaxed sphere tracing is a ray marching technique that accelerates the convergence of standard sphere tracing by scaling the conservative step size by a relaxation factor, allowing the ray to traverse empty space more quickly. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard sphere tracing in large empty volumes by reducing the number of iterations required to reach a surface, while maintaining safety by reverting to the standard step size if the unbounding spheres of consecutive steps become disjoint. It is distinguished from Standard Constant Step Ray Marching by its adaptive, distance-field-driven step sizing, and from Enhanced Sphere Tracing by its simpler geometric fallback logic which may result in smaller steps near complex geometry. Cone-Traced Supersampling (CTSS) is an efficient spatial antialiasing solution for Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering that performs supersampling along the traced ray near surfaces with partial visibility. It identifies object contours by evaluating cone intersections within a pixel's view frustum, avoiding the need for casting additional rays per pixel or offline prefiltering. Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER) extends CTSS to locate and resolve complex pixels with geometric edges in relatively flat regions that are otherwise undetected by cone intersections. Unlike conventional supersampling, CTSS minimizes shading computations, and unlike post-processing filters, it avoids undesirable blurriness and ghosting. Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) are a procedural modeling technique for generating complex, fractal-like geometries using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and reflection transformations. It solves the problem of evaluating global distance functions for recursive structures without recursion, enabling real-time sphere tracing on parallel hardware like GPUs. Unlike standard Iterated Function Systems (IFS) which require recursive traversal and cause divergent control flow, KRS uses a fixed operation count logarithmic time algorithm, allowing efficient parallelization. An algorithm using the chessboard metric (or Manhattan metric) for distance computation, potentially resulting in more efficiently computed distances and ray intersection. Left as further research. An optimization that decreases the number of calculations made in each march by enclosing several objects into one bounding sphere. Objects should be bound in an adaptive way, enclosing objects depending on how they are grouped per frame, approximating the sphere definition for increased performance rather than computing it exactly. Performance gain increases as the number of objects inside the sphere increases, with a gain occurring when >3 objects are enclosed (e.g., 25% FPS increase at 10 enclosed objects). Performance decreases if <4 objects are enclosed. Bounding Spheres can work together with Orthogonal Culling by culling bounding spheres instead of single objects, decreasing the number of orthogonal projections made. Implemented and tested in the GLSL shader. Integrates ray marching with distance-based empty space leaping for complex scenes, using coarse SDFs to compute large skips in low-density regions before switching to fine-grained tracing near features. Balances speed and accuracy in multi-material volumes. A set of optimization nodes embedded directly in hierarchical construction trees to reduce the computational cost of field function evaluation while preserving Lipschitz or conservative properties. Avoids external accompanying data structures such as octrees by embedding acceleration nodes directly in the construction tree. Uses proxy and continuous level of detail nodes to reduce the overall evaluation cost. Applies a normal warping technique to enhance surface details with negligible computational overhead. Speeds up signed distance field evaluation by up to three orders of magnitude compared to standard evaluation. Applies to both ray-surface intersection computation in sphere tracing applications and polygonization algorithms. A method for visualizing surfaces encoded by harmonic functions (including angle-valued functions and those with singularities) by using conservative Harnack bounds on the growth of harmonic functions to determine step sizes, avoiding numerical issues common to generic root finding methods. Uses conservative Harnack bounds on the growth of harmonic functions to determine the step size for each iteration, ensuring the step does not cross a level set boundary. Performs pointwise evaluation of the harmonic function at the current position to check for convergence to the target level set. Unlike sphere tracing which uses distance bounds, Harnack tracing uses bounds on the growth of harmonic functions; it avoids numerical issues common to generic root finding methods and can visualize surfaces directly from point clouds or polygon soup without linear solves or mesh extraction. A method for fully real-time deformable SDF-based worlds, using a global dense SDF with mip levels for acceleration. Constructs a global SDF, builds 5 mip levels where each level encodes distance values twice as great as the previous, uses sphere-tracing sampling coarser mip levels to travel greater distances conservatively, and ascends/descends mip levels based on sampled distance magnitude. Modification: Apply pre-defined 'brushes' to the world SDF. Only nearby affected areas are re-evaluated due to brush locality. Uses a global SDF volume of resolution 1024x1024x512 with five mip levels. The volume is dense (empty and non-empty regions stored alike). Compact data structures (like SVOs) are incompatible with this modification method because surface-intersecting voxel counts are not static, requiring slow insertions and indirection tables. Dense volumes allow direct spatial indexing. Used in Claybook (Aaltonen, 2018). Time Complexity: The number of iterations depends on the distance to the surface and the local geometry. In empty space, steps are large, leading to O(1) or very few iterations. Near the surface, steps become small, leading to O(\log(1/\epsilon)) iterations for convergence. Worst-case scenarios occur when rays graze surfaces or pass close to parallel surfaces, requiring many small steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for the core algorithm. Memory usage depends on the storage of the SDF (implicit function evaluation vs. voxel grid) and any acceleration structures. Measured Performance: Performance varies significantly by scene complexity. In simple scenes with few primitives, sphere tracing is very fast. In complex scenes with many primitives, the cost of evaluating the SDF for each step becomes dominant. Bounding sphere optimizations can increase FPS by 25% when >3 objects are enclosed. Strengths: No preprocessing required for implicit surfaces; perfect geometry representation; easy to combine primitives using CSG operations; adaptive step size reduces evaluations in empty space. Limitations: Requires the scene to be representable as an SDF or Lipschitz function; can be slow for complex scenes with many primitives if no acceleration structure is used; sensitive to the Lipschitz constant; may require many iterations near flat or grazing surfaces. When to Use: Ideal for rendering procedural geometry, fractals, and smooth CSG combinations where explicit mesh generation is undesirable or too costly. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes with explicit polygonal meshes unless converted to SDFs; may be inefficient for highly detailed, non-procedural geometry without acceleration structures. Sphere Tracing was introduced by John Hart in 1996 in the paper "Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces". It was developed as a method to render implicit surfaces defined by distance functions without the need for explicit polygonal meshes or complex intersection algorithms. The method leverages the geometric property of distance functions to provide safe stepping distances, ensuring accurate and antialiased rendering of complex implicit shapes. It has since become a fundamental technique in procedural rendering, real-time graphics, and neural rendering. Variants and optimizations, such as relaxed sphere tracing and enhanced sphere tracing, have been developed to address performance bottlenecks in specific scenarios. name: Zeno Implementation
head: Zeno, Zeno Implementation for Implicit Surfaces
body:
The Zeno implementation is a software architecture for sphere tracing that prioritizes ease of extension for new implicit surfaces over raw shading performance. It solves the problem of rapidly prototyping mathematical implicit surfaces by allowing new primitives to be added by defining only a signed distance bound, while avoiding the manual derivation of surface normals. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing implementations by replacing the explicit normal function with a fixed six-sample numerical gradient approximation, accepting the minor performance cost as negligible compared to ray intersection overhead. The method implements sphere tracing within the Zeno rendering system. It requires the user to provide a signed distance function for ray intersection. Shading is handled via a numerical gradient approximation rather than an analytical normal function. Input: A signed distance bound function d(\mathbf{p}) that returns the distance from a point \mathbf{p} to the implicit surface. Output: A rendered image of the implicit surface. No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard ray and point representations; the core data is the distance bound function d(\mathbf{p}). 1. Define Distance Bound: Implement the function d(\mathbf{p}) for the implicit surface. This function must return the signed distance from any point \mathbf{p} to the surface. 2. Ray Marching: Perform sphere tracing along the ray. At each step, evaluate d(\mathbf{p}) to determine the step size. If d(\mathbf{p}) > \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small threshold), advance the ray position \mathbf{p} by d(\mathbf{p}). If d(\mathbf{p}) \le \epsilon, the surface has been hit. 3. Gradient Approximation: To compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} at the hit point \mathbf{p}, use a six-sample numerical gradient approximation of the distance bound gradient 
abla d(\mathbf{p}). The normal is calculated as \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla d(\mathbf{p})}{\|
abla d(\mathbf{p})\|}. The gradient 
abla d(\mathbf{p}) is approximated using central finite differences across six samples along the coordinate axes. 4. Shading: Use the computed normal \mathbf{n} for standard shading calculations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def zenospheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, distanceboundfunc, epsilon=1e-4): """ Implements sphere tracing for the Zeno system. Args: rayorigin: list of 3 floats, origin of the ray. raydirection: list of 3 floats, direction of the ray (normalized). distanceboundfunc: callable, returns float distance for a 3D point. epsilon: float, threshold for surface hit detection. Returns: hitpoint: list of 3 floats, point of intersection, or None if no hit. normal: list of 3 floats, surface normal at hit point, or None if no hit. """ t = 0.0 maxsteps = 1000 # p = add(rayorigin, scale(raydirection, t)) for in range(maxsteps): d = distanceboundfunc(p) # Check for surface hit if d <= epsilon: normal = computenumericalgradientnormal(distanceboundfunc, p) return p, normal # Advance ray t += d p = add(rayorigin, scale(raydirection, t)) return None, None def computenumericalgradientnormal(distanceboundfunc, p, h=1e-4): """ Computes the surface normal using a six-sample numerical gradient approximation. Args: distanceboundfunc: callable, returns float distance for a 3D point. p: list of 3 floats, point at which to compute gradient. h: float, step size for finite differences. Returns: normal: list of 3 floats, normalized gradient. """ # Central differences along x, y, z axes pxp = add(p, scale([h, 0.0, 0.0], 1.0)) pxm = add(p, scale([-h, 0.0, 0.0], 1.0)) pyp = add(p, scale([0.0, h, 0.0], 1.0)) pym = add(p, scale([0.0, -h, 0.0], 1.0)) pzp = add(p, scale([0.0, 0.0, h], 1.0)) pzm = add(p, scale([0.0, 0.0, -h], 1.0)) gx = (distanceboundfunc(pxp) - distanceboundfunc(pxm)) / (2.0 h) gy = (distanceboundfunc(pyp) - distanceboundfunc(pym)) / (2.0 h) gz = (distanceboundfunc(pzp) - distanceboundfunc(pzm)) / (2.0 h) length = sqrt(gxgx + gygy + gzgz) if length == 0.0: return [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # return [gx / length, gy / length, gz / length] def add(a, b): return [a[0] + b[0], a[1] + b[1], a[2] + b[2]] def scale(v, s): return [v[0] s, v[1] s, v[2] s] def sqrt(x): return x 0.5 Epsilon: Threshold for surface hit detection. Not given in the sources. Gradient Step Size (h): Step size for numerical gradient. Not given in the sources. CSG and Blending: The negative part of the signed distance bound is only necessary for constructive solid geometry (CSG) and blending operations. It is not needed for visualizing functions that are zero-valued inside the implicit surface. Performance: The numerical gradient approximation is less efficient than an analytical normal function, but its impact on rendering performance is negligible because most time is spent on ray intersection. Time Complexity: Dominated by ray intersection steps. The numerical gradient adds a constant overhead of 6 distance function evaluations per shading point. Memory Complexity: Low, as no complex data structures are required. Strengths: Simplicity of implementation for new implicit surfaces; ease of incorporating new primitives by defining only a distance bound. Limitations: Slightly slower shading due to numerical gradient; less precise normals compared to analytical methods. When to Use: Visualization of mathematical tasks and investigation of new implicit surfaces where rapid prototyping is more important than maximum rendering speed. When Not to Use: Production rendering where performance is critical and analytical normals are available. The Zeno implementation was developed as part of the Zeno rendering system, which implemented sphere tracing for antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces. It was used for visualization of mathematical tasks, such as the animated short "Air on the Dirac Strings" (Sandin et al., 1993), which involved a homotopy removing a 720° twist from a ribbon using interpolated quaternion rotations. The system demonstrated that sphere tracing simplifies the implementation of implicit surface ray tracers while running at speeds comparable to other implicit surface rendering algorithms. name: Cone Intersection
head: Cone Tracing, Antialiased Ray Intersection, Cone Tracing with Covers, Cone-object intersection
body: Cone intersection is an antialiasing technique for sphere tracing that represents a pixel as a viewing cone rather than a point ray, allowing symbolic prefiltering to eliminate aliasing artifacts at grazing angles. It differs from standard sphere tracing by detecting intersections with an "inner cover" surface and computing the fractional coverage of the pixel by the implicit surface, whereas siblings like Segment Tracing or Quadric Tracing focus on varying step sizes or bounding volumes without necessarily computing area-based coverage fractions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A signed distance function (SDF) f(x) defining the implicit surface, a ray origin o and direction d, and camera parameters (field of view \theta, resolution Nh, Nv). Output: A final pixel color and opacity, computed by compositing shading values from representative samples along the ray. Data Structures: Ray State: Current position x, accumulated opacity \alpha{acc}, accumulated color c{acc}. Sample List: A bounded list (max 4 samples) storing representative points (xi), their distances ti, their pixel radii r{p,i}, and their coverage fractions \alphai. Parameters: rp: Pixel radius. Defined as half the diameter of a pixel. \theta: Field of view angle. Nh, Nv: Horizontal and vertical resolution. Step-by-Step Method: 1. Calculate Pixel Radius: Determine the radius of the pixel rp at the current traversal distance t. The sources provide an approximation using the maximum resolution dimension: rp(t) = t \cdot \frac{2 \tan(\theta/2)}{\max(Nh, Nv)} Note that rp grows linearly with distance t. 2. Define Inner Cover: Construct the inner cover surface f{inner}(x) by offsetting the SDF by the pixel radius: f{inner}(x) = f(x) + rp Sphere tracing is performed on this inner cover surface instead of the original surface f(x). 3. Ray Traversal (Sphere Tracing): Iterate along the ray starting from t=0. At each step, evaluate f(x) at the current point x. Step Size: The step size S{next} is determined by the radius of the unbounding sphere, defined as the sum of the pixel radius and the SDF value: S{next} = rp + f(x). (Note: describes a comparable traversal step that may take the ray through the surface). Update Position: x \leftarrow x + S{next} \cdot d. Convergence Test: If f(x) \le 0 (or a small epsilon), the ray has intersected the original surface. Terminate traversal for this ray. 4. Identify Representative Samples: During traversal, track unbounding spheres (spheres of radius rp + f(x) centered at x) that fall within the cone bounds. A cone intersection is indicated if the ray intersects the inner cover, which corresponds to the condition f(x) \le rp. The "representative" point for a cone intersection is the center of the smallest unbounding sphere (with respect to pixel size) among those inside the cone. This point is the location along the ray section closest to the surface. Keep track of up to four such representative points to maintain performance. 5. Calculate Coverage Fraction (\alpha): For each representative point x, calculate the fraction of the pixel covered by the surface. Assuming local planarity, the surface intersects the cone's cross-section (a disk of radius rp) with a straight edge at signed distance f(x) from the center. The coverage fraction \alpha is given by the formula derived by Thompson (1990): \alpha = \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{\pi} \left( \frac{f(x)}{rp} \sqrt{1 - \left(\frac{f(x)}{rp}\right)^2} + \arcsin\left(\frac{f(x)}{rp}\right) \right) If f(x) > rp, \alpha = 0. If f(x) < -rp, \alpha = 1. This \alpha represents the opacity of the surface at this intersection. 6. Shading and Compositing: Shade the representative point x to get color c{shade} and alpha \alpha{shade} (if the surface has material properties). Accumulate the coverage \alpha as opacity. Composite the colors using the Porter-Duff "over" operator: c{out} = c{in} + c{shade} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{shade} \cdot (1 - \alpha{in}) For intersection edges involving multiple surfaces, keep track of all SDFs whose unbounding spheres fit within the cone bounds. Use the SDFs of each intersecting surface to provide proportions for combining their shading properties. 7. Final Output: The final pixel color is the accumulated color after processing all representative samples and the background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def coneintersectionraytrace(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, fov, resolution): """ Performs cone intersection ray tracing for a single pixel. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) tuple raydirection: (x, y, z) tuple (normalized) sdf: function f(x, y, z) returning signed distance fov: field of view in radians resolution: (width, height) tuple Returns: (finalcolor, finalalpha) """ nh, nv = resolution maxres = max(nh, nv) t = 0.0 maxsteps = 100 accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 # List to store representative samples: (t, fval, rp, shadecolor, shadealpha) # Limit to 4 samples for performance samples = [] for step in range(maxsteps): x = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) rp = t (2.0 math.tan(fov / 2.0)) / maxres fval = sdf(x[0], x[1], x[2]) if fval <= 0.0: shadecolor, shadealpha = shadesurface(x, sdf) newr = accumulatedcolor[0] + shadecolor[0] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newg = accumulatedcolor[1] + shadecolor[1] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newb = accumulatedcolor[2] + shadecolor[2] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newa = accumulatedalpha + shadealpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor = (newr, newg, newb) accumulatedalpha = newa break if fval <= rp: shadecolor, shadealpha = shadesurface(x, sdf) samples.append((t, fval, rp, shadecolor, shadealpha)) stepsize = rp + fval if stepsize <= 1e-6: stepsize = 1e-6 t += stepsize if t > 1000.0: break # Composite samples back-to-front for i in range(len(samples) - 1, -1, -1): ts, fs, rps, shadecolor, shadealpha = samples[i] ratio = fs / rps ratio = max(-1.0, min(1.0, ratio)) if ratio >= 1.0: alphacov = 0.0 elif ratio <= -1.0: alphacov = 1.0 else: term1 = ratio math.sqrt(1.0 - ratio ratio) term2 = math.asin(ratio) alphacov = 0.5 + (1.0 / math.pi) (term1 + term2) effectivealpha = alphacov shadealpha newr = accumulatedcolor[0] + shadecolor[0] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newg = accumulatedcolor[1] + shadecolor[1] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newb = accumulatedcolor[2] + shadecolor[2] (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) newa = accumulatedalpha + effectivealpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor = (newr, newg, newb) accumulatedalpha = newa return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedalpha def shadesurface(point, sdf): """ Computes surface normal via finite differences and returns a simple diffuse color. Actual shading logic is application-specific. """ eps = 1e-4 dx = sdf(point[0]+eps, point[1], point[2]) - sdf(point[0]-eps, point[1], point[2]) dy = sdf(point[0], point[1]+eps, point[2]) - sdf(point[0], point[1]-eps, point[2]) dz = sdf(point[0], point[1], point[2]+eps) - sdf(point[0], point[1], point[2]-eps) normal = (dx, dy, dz) lenn = math.sqrt(normal[0]2 + normal[1]2 + normal[2]2) if lenn > 0: normal = (normal[0]/lenn, normal[1]/lenn, normal[2]/lenn) else: normal = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) lightdir = (1.0, 1.0, -1.0) lenl = math.sqrt(lightdir[0]2 + lightdir[1]2 + lightdir[2]2) lightdir = (lightdir[0]/lenl, lightdir[1]/lenl, lightdir[2]/lenl) diff = max(0.0, normal[0]lightdir[0] + normal[1]lightdir[1] + normal[2]lightdir[2]) color = (diff, diff, diff) alpha = 1.0 return color, alpha Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Premature Shrinking: If the SDF is expensive or approximated by a bound, the unbounding sphere radius may shrink below the pixel radius prematurely, leading to incorrect cone intersections. Distance Approximation: If the SDF is inaccurate, use the first-order approximation d(x) \approx f(x) / \|\nabla f(x)\| for distance estimation, which is asymptotic to geometric distance. Representative Point Off-Surface: The representative sample is off the implicit surface. A usable surface normal must be defined by assuming continuity in the gradient of the distance function. Performance: Tracking sample lists becomes expensive at higher resolutions, causing frame rates to drop significantly. Ellipsoid Scaling: For non-uniformly scaled objects (e.g., ellipsoids), signed distance bounds may return underestimated distances (as low as 1% of actual distance), affecting cone intersection accuracy. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of steps, but the number of steps depends on the accuracy of the distance estimate. Halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Memory Complexity: Low, but requires storing a list of representative samples (limited to 4) per pixel. Performance: Achieves around 60 fps for 512x512 resolution, but drops considerably for larger resolutions due to the cost of tracking sample lists. Sphere tracing rendered a complex scene in 12:47 at 256x256 resolution. Strengths: Eliminates aliasing artifacts from point sampling, especially at silhouette edges and grazing angles. Can also prefilter texture aliasing. Limitations: Does not antialias edges projected from the camera perspective onto the object itself (maintains interactive frame rates). Convergence is entirely linear, unlike interval analysis which has a quadratically convergent refinement stage. Cone intersection was introduced as an antialiasing method by Amanatides (1984) for computing intersections of cones with spheres, planes, and polygons. Hart and DeFanti (1991) extended this to implicit surfaces using sphere tracing and the concept of "covers" (offset surfaces). The technique is implemented in the zeno rendering system. name: Segment Tracing
body: Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm that computes local Lipschitz bounds on candidate segments to determine adaptive step sizes, reducing the number of field function queries compared to global Lipschitz bound methods like Sphere Tracing. It works for a particular class of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces, leveraging the composition of distance functions and kernel functions to compute directional Lipschitz bounds. Unlike Sphere Tracing, which uses a global bound that limits step size efficiency, Segment Tracing allows larger, safer steps by adapting to the local gradient and field values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray \delta(t), a hierarchical skeletal implicit surface model where primitives and operators support local Lipschitz bound queries, an initial candidate step distance \varepsilon0, an amplification factor \kappa, and a threshold \mu. Output: The intersection parameter t along the ray, or the domain exit parameter. Data Structures: The method requires the implicit model to implement specific queries for each primitive and operator node: 1. Field function evaluation f(p). 2. Local Lipschitz bound over a segment \lambda(e), where e is a segment of the ray. 3. Local Lipschitz bound over a sphere \lambda(S) (used in some implementations for tighter bounds). Numbered Steps: 1. Compute the intersection between the ray and the domain [t-, t+] = \Delta \cap \Omega, and initialize t = t-. 2. Set the initial candidate stepping distance \varepsilon0. 3. While t < t+: 1. Compute the field function value f(t) at the current position. 2. If |f(t)| < \mu, an intersection has occurred; terminate and return t. 3. Define the candidate segment e(t, \varepsiloni) = [\delta(t), \delta(t + \varepsiloni)]. 4. Compute the local directional Lipschitz bound \lambda(e(t, \varepsiloni)) for the candidate segment. This step leverages the fact that primitives are defined as a composition of a distance function and a kernel function. 5. Evaluate f(pi^) (where pi^ is the current point) and compute the safe stepping increment s(t, \varepsiloni) using the formula: s(t, \varepsiloni) = \min \left( \frac{|f(t)|}{\lambda(e(t, \varepsiloni))}, \varepsiloni \right) where s is the effective stepping distance, f(t) is the field function value, \lambda(e) is the local Lipschitz bound on segment e, and \varepsiloni is the candidate distance. 6. Update the position: t \leftarrow t + s(t, \varepsiloni). 7. Compute the next candidate stepping distance \varepsilon{i+1} = \kappa \cdot s(t, \varepsiloni), where \kappa is the geometric amplification factor. Parameters: \mu: The threshold value from which an intersection is considered to have occurred (|f(t)| < \mu). \varepsilon0: The initial candidate step distance. Its value has little impact on performance; if too large, the initial Lipschitz bound is large, leading to small subsequent steps. \kappa: The geometric amplification factor for the next candidate step. Typical value is \kappa \approx 2. Must be > 1. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: If \varepsilon0 is too large, the computed Lipschitz bound \lambda(e(t0, \varepsilon0)) is large (upper bound), causing the next candidate distance \varepsilon1 to be small. If \varepsilon0 \to \infty, \lambda(e) becomes the global bound. If the computation of local bounds is too complex or computationally intensive for a given operator or primitive, the algorithm automatically reverts to the standard Sphere Tracing framework locally. The method works only for a particular class of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces and is not directly applicable to a wide range of volumes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def segmenttracing(rayorigin, raydirection, domainmin, domainmax, fieldfunction, locallipschitzsegment, epsilon0, kappa, mu): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 (normalized) domainmin: float (tmin) domainmax: float (tmax) fieldfunction: function(p) -> float locallipschitzsegment: function(t, epsilon) -> float epsilon0: float kappa: float (> 1) mu: float """ t = domainmin epsilon = epsilon0 while t < domainmax: # Evaluate field function at current position p = rayorigin + t raydirection fval = fieldfunction(p) # Check for intersection if abs(fval) < mu: return t # Compute local Lipschitz bound for candidate segment [t, t + epsilon] lambdabound = locallipschitzsegment(t, epsilon) # Compute safe stepping increment if lambdabound == 0: step = epsilon else: step = min(abs(fval) / lambdabound, epsilon) # Clamp step to domain boundary to prevent overshoot and fix boundary precision step = min(step, domainmax - t) # Update position t = t + step # Amplify candidate step for next iteration epsilon = kappa step return domainmax # No intersection within domain The parent method using a global Lipschitz bound. Choose when simplicity is preferred and local bound computation is not feasible. [1674-sphere-tracing.md] Uses cone intersection tests for tighter bounds. Choose when higher precision is needed for complex primitives. [1553-cone-intersection.md] Uses quadric approximations for step size. Choose for quadric-based implicit surfaces. Choose for a simple speedup over standard Sphere Tracing without local bound computation. [3805-over-relaxation-sphere-tracing.md] Reduces queries by a factor of 1.2. Choose for a minor improvement over Sphere Tracing. [3811-enhanced-sphere-tracing.md] Uses non-linear transformations. Choose for specific non-linear field representations. Memory Complexity: Does not require accelerating data structures such as voxel grids or octrees for storing the local Lipschitz bound. Measured Performance: Reduces field function queries by up to three orders of magnitude compared to Sphere Tracing, resulting in accelerations of up to \times 10, despite the extra computational cost of Lipschitz bound queries. Scaling: Performance gains are most significant for hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces where local bounds can be computed efficiently. Strengths: Significantly reduces the number of field function queries; no need for precomputed acceleration structures; adapts to local gradient variations. Limitations: Requires primitives and operators to implement complex local Lipschitz bound queries; not directly applicable to a wide range of volumes; overhead from bound computation can negate benefits if not optimized. When to use: When rendering hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces and field function evaluation is expensive. When not to use: When the implicit model does not support local Lipschitz bound queries, or when the overhead of computing these bounds exceeds the savings from fewer field evaluations. The method leverages the structure of hierarchical skeletal implicit surfaces, where primitives are defined as a composition of a distance function and a kernel function, allowing for the computation of local directional Lipschitz bounds. name: Enhanced Sphere Tracing
head: Aggressive Marching, Aggressive Ray Marching, Aggressive Sphere Tracing, Bálint and Valasek method, Over-relaxed sphere tracing, Sphere tracing with over-relaxation
body: Enhanced Sphere Tracing is a family of ray-marching optimizations that accelerate convergence toward implicit surfaces defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) by taking steps larger than the strict Lipschitz bound or by predicting optimal step sizes based on local surface geometry. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard sphere tracing, which becomes prohibitively slow when rays graze surfaces at shallow angles or when the surface is locally planar. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which uses the queried distance value as the step size, enhanced variants either over-relax the step size by a constant factor or infer the next step size from the previous two distance queries to approximate the surface as locally flat. The term "Enhanced Sphere Tracing" refers to two distinct but related algorithmic strategies: Aggressive/Over-relaxed Marching (accelerating convergence via scalar multiplication) and Geometric Enhancement (predicting step size via historical data). Both require a conservative SDF (one that never overstates the distance to the surface) to ensure robustness. Input: Ray origin p \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray direction v \in \mathbb{R}^3 (normalized, |v|=1), SDF query function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, maximum iteration count i{max}, convergence threshold \epsilon, and method-specific parameters (\alpha, \omega, or \sigma). Output: Distance t \in [0, +\infty) traveled along the ray to the surface, or a failure state if i{max} is exceeded. History State: Stores the SDF values from the previous two steps (r{i-1}, ri) and the step size taken to reach the current step (di). Accumulator: Total distance traveled t. This variant multiplies the safe step size by a factor \alpha > 1 (or \omega > 1) to accelerate convergence, particularly for grazing rays. It requires a safety check to prevent skipping the surface if the SDF is non-conservative or the geometry is too thin. Parameters: \alpha: Aggressive multiplier. Default 1.5. Range 1.2–1.8. \omega: Over-relaxation factor. Value 1.6. \sigma: Overstepping factor in [0, 1]. Typical value \approx 1.2. \lambda: Global Lipschitz bound of the SDF. Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0, r{prev} = 0, r{curr} = 0. 2. Loop while t < b (max distance) and iterations < i{max}: 3. Query SDF: d = f(p + t \cdot v). 4. Calculate safe step: s = |d| / \lambda. 5. Calculate over-step: o = (1 + \sigma) \cdot s. 6. Safety Check: If the over-step o causes the new sphere to not overlap with the previous safe sphere (i.e., the step is too large relative to the local geometry or d is negative/inside), revert to standard sphere tracing step s. Alternative Implementation (Keinert et al.): Calculate over-relaxed step step = \omega \cdot |d|. If step > |d| (overshoots safe radius), retreat to t + |d| (back to safe boundary). 7. Update position: t \leftarrow t + step. 8. Update history: r{prev} \leftarrow r{curr}, r{curr} \leftarrow d. 9. Check convergence: If |d| < \epsilon, break and return t. This variant assumes the surface is locally flat and calculates the optimal step size using the radii of the two previous unbounding spheres. It is more expensive per step than aggressive marching but converges faster on smooth surfaces. Parameters: \omega: Relaxation parameter for locally concave regions. Range \omega \in (0, 1]. Typical range (0.7, 1]. Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0, r{i-1} = 0, ri = 0, r{i+1} = \infty, di = 0. 2. Loop for i from 0 while i < i{max} and r{i+1} is not too small: 3. Calculate Step Size: Compute di using the geometric formula derived from similar triangles: di = ri + \omega \cdot ri \cdot \frac{di - r{i-1} + ri}{di + r{i-1} - ri} Note: In the first iteration, r{i-1}=0, di=0. The formula simplifies or requires a fallback to standard step size ri for the very first step if division by zero occurs. 4. Step: Advance ray: t \leftarrow t + di. 5. Query: Evaluate SDF at new position: r{i+1} = f(p + t \cdot v). 6. Safety Check (Fallback): If the spheres are disjoint (di > ri + r{i+1}), the step was too large and may have missed the surface. Reset step to conservative size: di \leftarrow ri. Re-evaluate SDF at the corrected position: r{i+1} = f(p + (t{old} + di) \cdot v). Update t to reflect the corrected step. 7. Update History: Shift values: r{i-1} \leftarrow ri, ri \leftarrow r{i+1}. 8. Convergence: If |r{i+1}| < \epsilon, break and return t. Thin Geometry: Aggressive marching (\alpha > 1) can cause the ray to trespass two surfaces in a single step if the geometry is super thin, leaving the ray front end outside the shape and causing infinite marching or small holes. Non-Conservative SDFs: Over-relaxation is unsound if the SDF overstates the distance (is not 1-Lipschitz or conservative). It may skip surfaces entirely. Non-Smooth Surfaces: On fractals or non-smooth surfaces (e.g., Mandelbulb), the geometric enhancement provides only marginal improvement over basic sphere tracing, as the "locally flat" assumption fails. Grazing Incidence: Standard sphere tracing is slow when the angle \theta between the ray and surface normal is small. Enhanced methods mitigate this, but aggressive marching requires careful tuning of \alpha to avoid instability. The Parallel Sphere Carving Algorithm is a method for automatically computing tight bounding volumes for objects defined by a conservative signed distance field (SDF). It solves the problem of accelerating implicit surface queries (such as sphere tracing or polygonization) by generating a lightweight bounding proxy function fe that avoids expensive SDF evaluations outside the object. Unlike sphere tracing, which discards empty segments along a ray to find an intersection, Sphere Carving discards empty volumes (spheres) in space to find a bounding volume of the surface. It is agnostic of the function representation, requiring only a conservative SDF query, and provides strict bounding guarantees that neural or interval-arithmetic methods may lack. A technique where you march a small distance further outside the Minimum Distance Sphere (MDS) edge to decrease the number of times marched, increasing performance. March to the edge of the MDS, then march a small distance further outside. Compare the original MDS with the new MDS; if they overlap, continue marching further. If the two MDSs do not overlap, step back to the edge of the first MDS and continue normally. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF queries significantly compared to standard sphere tracing. For grazing angles, the minimum number of steps k decreases from k{std} to k{enh}. Formula for aggressive marching convergence: k > k{min} = \frac{\log \epsilon - \log d}{\log |1 - \alpha \sin \theta|}. Example: For d=1.0, \epsilon=5 \times 10^{-5}, \theta=10^\circ, steps decrease from 52 (conventional) to 33 (aggressive \alpha=1.5). Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storing only a few scalar values (t, r{i-1}, ri, di) per ray. Performance: Aggressive marching with \sigma \approx 1.2 reduces field function queries by a factor of 1.2 and speeds up computation by the same factor. Geometric enhancement (Bálint & Valasek) outperforms relaxed sphere tracing by up to 1.5 times on smooth surfaces and up to 50% better than Hart and Keinert et al.'s variant in error-decrease velocity. On non-smooth surfaces (Mandelbulb), it performs slightly better than basic tracing but is on par with relaxed tracing within error margins. Strengths: Faster convergence on planar/smooth surfaces; stabilizes training in neural rendering by allowing sampling behind the surface; prevents geometry vanishing at grazing angles under non-uniform scaling. Limitations: Risk of missing thin geometry; requires conservative SDFs; higher computational cost per step for geometric enhancement due to formula evaluation. Enhanced Sphere Tracing originated from the need to accelerate real-time rendering of implicit surfaces. The "Relaxed Sphere Tracing" variant was introduced by Keinert et al. in 2014, proposing over-relaxation to accelerate convergence. The "Enhanced Sphere Tracing" variant, specifically the geometric approach using historical step data, was proposed by Bálint and Valasek in 2018, optimizing for locally planar surfaces. The aggressive marching strategy was also independently applied in differentiable neural rendering contexts to stabilize training and speed up forward propagation. name: Parallel Sphere Carving Algorithm
body: The Parallel Sphere Carving Algorithm is a method for automatically computing tight bounding volumes for objects defined by a conservative signed distance field (SDF). It solves the problem of accelerating implicit surface queries (such as sphere tracing or polygonization) by generating a lightweight bounding proxy function fe that avoids expensive SDF evaluations outside the object. Unlike sphere tracing, which discards empty segments along a ray to find an intersection, Sphere Carving discards empty volumes (spheres) in space to find a bounding volume of the surface. It is agnostic of the function representation, requiring only a conservative SDF query, and provides strict bounding guarantees that neural or interval-arithmetic methods may lack. The algorithm iteratively carves an initial large bounding volume V0 using spheres defined by the SDF, extracting intersection points to compute a bounding volume. The process is parallelized into four kernels per iteration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A conservative signed distance field function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, where |f(p)| \le d(p, \partial \mathcal{O}). An initial large bounding volume V0 (typically an icosphere). A distance threshold \tau (typical value: 0.1). Outputs: A set of empty spheres S and a point set P whose convex hull bounds the object surface \partial \mathcal{O}. Data Structures: S: Array of empty spheres (center and radius). P: Array of 3D points. P': Temporary array of intermediate intersection points. pairs: Array of sphere index pairs (a, b). All arrays are pre-allocated with sufficient memory. Parallel updates to arrays require one atomic counter per array. The Empty Sphere Criterion: For any point p, the sphere S(p, |f(p)|) does not intersect the object's surface \partial \mathcal{O}: \forall \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \ S(\mathbf{p}, |f(\mathbf{p})|) \cap \partial \mathcal{O} = \emptyset Here, f is a conservative SDF where |f(p)| \le d(p, \partial O). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Sample points P on the surface of V0. Create initial sphere set S0 = \{ \text{sphere}(p, |f(p)|) \mid p \in P \}. Verify coverage: for an icosphere, ensure every triangle \Delta(a,b,c) is contained in the union of spheres at its vertices: \Delta(a,b,c) \subset S(a) \cup S(b) \cup S(c). If not, increase subdivision. 2. Iteration Loop: While \max{p \in P} f(p) > \tau: Kernel 1 (Gather Pairs): Identify intersecting sphere pairs. Kernel 2 (Compute Intersections): Calculate 3-sphere intersections (trilateration) for triplets. Kernel 3 (Filter Points): Discard points inside the current sphere set. Kernel 4 (Augment Spheres): Add new spheres based on filtered points. 3. Termination: The loop ends when \max(f(P)) \le \tau. The result is the final sphere set S and point set P. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math from typing import List, Tuple, Callable def parallelspherecarving(f: Callable, V0, tau: float) -> Tuple[List, List]: # Initialization: sample points on V0 surface P = samplesurface(V0) # Create initial sphere set S0 = { sphere(p, |f(p)|) | p in P } S = [(p, abs(f(p))) for p in P] # Verify coverage: for an icosphere, ensure every triangle is covered by vertex spheres if not isicospherecovered(V0, S): raise ValueError("Initial coverage constraint not met") while P and max(f(p) for p in P) > tau: pairs = [] # Kernel 1: Gather intersecting sphere pairs for a in range(len(S)): for b in range(a + 1, len(S)): if spheresintersect(S[a], S[b]): pairs.append((a, b)) Pprime = [] # Kernel 2: Compute intersection points for triplets (trilateration) for (a, b) in pairs: for c in range(b + 1, len(S)): pts = intersectthreespheres(S[a], S[b], S[c]) Pprime.extend(pts) Pnew = [] # Kernel 3: Filter points inside the volume for p in Pprime: isinside = False for s in S: # Discard if distance to center < radius, accounting for precision if math.dist(p, s[0]) < s[1]: isinside = True break if not isinside: Pnew.append(p) # Kernel 4: Augment sphere set for p in Pnew: if f(p) > tau: S.append((p, abs(f(p)))) P = Pnew return S, P def samplesurface(V0): # Returns vertices of the recursively subdivided icosahedron V0 return V0.vertices def isicospherecovered(V0, S): # Checks if every triangle of V0 is contained in the union of spheres at its vertices for tri in V0.triangles: a, b, c = tri Sa, Sb, Sc = S[a], S[b], S[c] if not triangleinsphereunion(a, b, c, Sa, Sb, Sc): return False return True def triangleinsphereunion(a, b, c, Sa, Sb, Sc): # Standard geometric coverage test # Checks if triangle vertices and centroid are within the union of spheres centers = [Sa[0], Sb[0], Sc[0]] radii = [Sa[1], Sb[1], Sc[1]] points = [a, b, c, ((a[0]+b[0]+c[0])/3, (a[1]+b[1]+c[1])/3, (a[2]+b[2]+c[2])/3)] return all(any(math.dist(p, ctr) <= rad for ctr, rad in zip(centers, radii)) for p in points) def spheresintersect(s1, s2): c1, r1 = s1 c2, r2 = s2 return math.dist(c1, c2) <= r1 + r2 def intersectthreespheres(s1, s2, s3): c1, r1 = s1 c2, r2 = s2 c3, r3 = s3 d = math.dist(c1, c2) if d > r1 + r2 or d < abs(r1 - r2): return [] # Trilateration formulas from Appendix A.2 x = (r12 - r22 + d2) / (2 d) ysq = r12 - x2 if ysq < 0: return [] y = math.sqrt(ysq) # Basis vectors ex = ((c2[0]-c1[0])/d, (c2[1]-c1[1])/d, (c2[2]-c1[2])/d) # ey perpendicular to ex and in plane of c1,c2,c3 v = (c3[0]-c1[0], c3[1]-c1[1], c3[2]-c1[2]) dotvex = v[0]ex[0] + v[1]ex[1] + v[2]ex[2] ey = (v[0]-dotvexex[0], v[1]-dotvexex[1], v[2]-dotvexex[2]) eylen = math.sqrt(ey[0]2 + ey[1]2 + ey[2]2) if eylen < 1e-9: return [] # Spheres are collinear ey = (ey[0]/eylen, ey[1]/eylen, ey[2]/eylen) ez = (ex[1]ey[2]-ex[2]ey[1], ex[2]ey[0]-ex[0]ey[2], ex[0]ey[1]-ex[1]ey[0]) # Solve for z using third sphere offset = (xex[0] + yey[0] + c1[0] - c3[0], xex[1] + yey[1] + c1[1] - c3[1], xex[2] + yey[2] + c1[2] - c3[2]) zsq = r32 - (offset[0]2 + offset[1]2 + offset[2]2) if zsq < 0: return [] z = math.sqrt(zsq) # Return points in original frame p1 = (c1[0] + xex[0] + yey[0] + zez[0], c1[1] + xex[1] + yey[1] + zez[1], c1[2] + xex[2] + yey[2] + zez[2]) p2 = (c1[0] + xex[0] + yey[0] - zez[0], c1[1] + xex[1] + yey[1] - zez[1], c1[2] + xex[2] + yey[2] - zez[2]) return [p1, p2] Parameters: \tau: Distance threshold for stopping. Typical value: 0.1. V0: Initial volume. Size: Usually two orders of magnitude larger than the object. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Conservative SDFs: Underestimating distance causes slow convergence and high computational cost due to O(n^3) intersection calculations and many spheres. Overestimated SDFs: Break the bounding guarantee. The algorithm progresses, but the result is not guaranteed to bound the object. Initialization Coverage: The initial sphere set S0 must cover the entire surface of V0. For an icosphere, this is checked per triangle. Precision: Filtering points inside the sphere set volume accounts for floating-point precision by discarding a point if its distance to any sphere center is less than the sphere radius. A strategy for initializing the Sphere Carving algorithm using a recursively subdivided icosahedron (icosphere) as the initial bounding volume V0. It is chosen because sampling is straightforward (using vertices) and the coverage constraint can be checked per triangle \Delta(a,b,c) using only the spheres at its vertices. If the triangle is not contained in the union of the spheres at its vertices, the subdivision level is increased. Time Complexity: The complexity of the sphere intersection routine is O(n^3), where n is the number of spheres, due to evaluating every possible triplet of sphere intersections. Memory Complexity: Compact representation. The bounding volume is stored as a set of convex polyhedra or ellipsoids, which is more memory-efficient than external acceleration structures like grids or octrees. Performance: Requires a small number of field function queries (#f), from a few thousand for complex objects to less than one hundred for an exact SDF. The algorithm typically converges in less than 20 iterations. Strengths: Agnostic of function representation; provides strict bounding guarantees; terminates in seconds; no training time required. Limitations: Computationally intensive for overly conservative SDFs (underestimated distances), which require more iterations and spheres. Overly conservative functions may require a larger initial volume or denser sampling. Sphere Carving was introduced by Hugo Schott, Theo Thonat, Thibaud Lambert, Eric Guérin, and Axel Paris. It is designed to accelerate queries in sphere tracing, polygonization, and simulation by generating a bounding proxy signed distance function fe. The method draws inspiration from techniques that carve space using empty spheres, similar to how sphere tracing discards empty segments. It is particularly useful for procedurally defined implicit surfaces such as exact or Lipschitz functions, BlobTrees, or neural representations. name: Uniform Sphere Tracing
head: Ray Marching for Volumes, Rustgpu Sphere Tracing Implementation, Uniform Density Volume Rendering, Volume Rendering with Ray Marching (Uniform Sphere)
body: Uniform Sphere Tracing is a volume rendering technique that uses ray marching along a Signed Distance Field (SDF) to detect volume boundaries and applies Beer's Law for optical depth integration under a uniform density assumption. It solves the problem of rendering participating media with constant optical properties by stepping through the volume, accumulating absorption and scattering, and blending the result with the background. It is distinguished from its parent Sphere Tracing by its specific application to uniform density volume rendering and its reliance on fixed or clamped step sizes for the marching phase, while using SDF evaluation primarily for surface detection rather than purely adaptive step sizing for optical integration. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D (normalized), SDF function f(P), maximum iterations N{max}, minimum step size d{min}, maximum step size d{max}, cutoff threshold d{cut}, absorption coefficient \sigmaa, volume scatter color C{vol}, background color C{bg}. Outputs: Final pixel color C{final}, boolean hit flag, final position, iteration count. Data Structures: Sphere Class (for bounding/intersection): center: vec3 (e.g., [0, 0, -4]) radius: float (e.g., 1.0) sigmaa: float (e.g., 0.1) scatter: vec3 (e.g., [0.8, 0.1, 0.5]) intersect: Method returning intersection distances t0, t1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Initialization: For each pixel, compute ray origin O and direction D. 2. Bounding Intersection: Check if the ray intersects the volume's bounding object (e.g., a sphere). If no intersection, return C{bg}. If intersection exists, calculate entry point P1 = O + D \cdot t0 and exit point P2 = O + D \cdot t1. Calculate total distance through volume L = t1 - t0 (assuming normalized D). 3. Ray Marching Loop: Initialize itercount = 0, hitsdf = false, currentpos = O, priord = \infty, terminated = false, and distance = 0.0001. While itercount < N{max}: Update currentpos = O + \text{distance} \cdot D. Evaluate SDF: s = f(\text{current\pos}). Check termination: If s \le d{cut}, set hitsdf = true and break loop. Determine step increment: d{step} = \text{clamp}(s, d{min}, d{max}). Update distance += d{step}. Increment itercount. 4. Optical Integration (Beer's Law): Calculate transmittance T through the volume based on the straight-line distance L. Formula: T = e^{-L \cdot \sigmaa}. 5. Color Blending: Calculate final color: C{final} = T \cdot C{bg} + (1 - T) \cdot C{vol}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def uniformspheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunc, sphereobj, minstep=0.0001, maxstep=0.001, cutoff=0.05, itermax=1000): # 1. Bounding Intersection t0, t1 = sphereobj.intersect(rayorigin, raydirection) if not t0: return sphereobj.backgroundcolor, False, rayorigin, 0, 0.0 # Distance through volume (straight line for uniform density) distancethroughvolume = t1 - t0 # 2. Ray Marching for SDF Hit Detection itercount = 0 hitsdf = False currentpos = rayorigin priord = float('inf') terminated = False distance = 0.0001 while itercount < itermax: currentpos = rayorigin + distance raydirection increment = sdffunc(currentpos, itercount, priord) # Check termination before advancing to prevent overshoot if increment <= cutoff: hitsdf = True break # Clamp step size and advance clampedincrement = max(minstep, min(increment, maxstep)) distance += clampedincrement priord = increment itercount += 1 # 3. Optical Integration sigmaa = sphereobj.sigmaa transmittance = math.exp(-distancethroughvolume sigmaa) # 4. Color Blending backgroundcolor = sphereobj.backgroundcolor volumecolor = sphereobj.scatter finalcolor = transmittance backgroundcolor + (1.0 - transmittance) volumecolor return finalcolor, hitsdf, currentpos, itercount, distance Parameters: minstep: Minimum allowed step increment. Typical: 0.0001. maxstep: Maximum allowed step increment. Typical: 0.001 for clamped ray marching, or larger for pure sphere tracing. cutoff: Threshold below which the surface is considered hit. Typical: 0.05. itermax: Maximum number of iterations. sigmaa: Absorption coefficient. Typical: 0.1. scatter: Volume scatter color. Typical: [0.8, 0.1, 0.5]. backgroundcolor: Background color. Typical: [0.572, 0.772, 0.921]. Pitfalls: SDF Scaling: Scaling the input position vector to the SDF closure (e.g., v 10.0) without adjusting the step size or SDF output accordingly breaks the sphere tracing property, causing the ray to overshoot collisions. The SDF distance does not scale linearly with the ray step in a way that preserves the tracing logic when the position is scaled but the step is not adjusted. Step Clamping: Using very small maxstep values effectively turns sphere tracing into uniform ray marching, losing the benefit of large steps in empty space. Spectral tracking is a volume rendering technique that efficiently handles per-wavelength optical properties by decomposing the medium's scattering and absorption coefficients into spectral components, using a single majorant density to drive the sampling process for all wavelengths simultaneously. Unlike naive delta tracking which handles each wavelength separately, spectral tracking invokes the tracker only once for all wavelengths, computing a spectrally resolved collision weight at each collision to counteract the discrepancy between the single sampling distribution and the true per-wavelength free-path distribution. This reduces the number of tracker invocations and leverages vectorized operations, making it particularly effective for spectrally heterogeneous media. Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing is a robust sphere tracing method that automatically scales step sizes based on data from previous iterations, using a scalar hyperparameter similar to the learning rate of gradient descent methods. It sets itself apart from its parent Uniform Sphere Tracing by replacing fixed or heuristic step rules with an adaptive scaling mechanism that reduces the frequency of invalid, over-relaxed step sizes, thereby minimizing the need for robustness-preserving fallback steps. Compared to Spectral Tracking, it exhibits a smaller effect on performance from its step-scale hyperparameters and performs up to par with or outperforms the most efficient concurrent methods depending on iteration count limits. A technique to reduce visual discontinuities (jagged edges/artifacts) between adjacent rays by allowing a tolerance error in the intersection condition that scales with screen-space distance from the origin. Unlike standard sphere tracing which requires f(p)=0, this method accepts a larger error for rays further away (in screen space), reducing step count and discontinuities without affecting visual quality. The update rule becomes p{i+1} = pi + d \cdot (f(pi) - \text{err}(\|pi - o\|2)), where \text{err}(\|pi - o\|2) is an error function based on the screen-space distance from the ray origin o to the current point pi. This allows for coarser intersection checks at a distance, mitigating the "wavy" artifacts caused by non-continuous step sizes between neighboring pixels. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance depends on maxstep and SDF evaluation cost. Memory Complexity: O(1) per ray, as it only stores current position, distance, and iteration count. Performance: Small maxstep values result in more iterations but stable convergence, while larger values reduce iteration count but risk overshooting if the SDF is improperly scaled. Strengths: Simple to implement, robust for convex shapes, efficient for uniform density volumes. Limitations: Struggles with non-convex shapes without additional logic. Sensitive to SDF scaling errors. Discontinuities between adjacent rays can cause visual artifacts if not handled. When to use: Rendering simple volumetric effects like fog, smoke, or clouds with uniform density. When not to use: Rendering complex, non-uniform, or highly heterogeneous media where delta tracking or spectral tracking is more appropriate. Uniform Sphere Tracing for volumes combines SDF-based ray marching for boundary detection with uniform density optical depth integration. The specific implementation details, such as the Rust-based closure-based SDF evaluator and step clamping, are documented in community resources. The volume rendering aspect, including Beer's Law application and sphere object structure, is detailed in tutorials on volume rendering. The technique has been adapted to reduce visual discontinuities by relaxing intersection conditions based on screen-space distance.
