name: Spectral Tracking
head: Single-Distribution Spectral Tracking, Vectorized Weighted Delta Tracking
body: Spectral Tracking is a volumetric rendering technique that efficiently handles spectrally resolved optical properties by decomposing the medium's scattering and absorption coefficients into spectral components (e.g., RGB) and using a single majorant density to drive the sampling process for all wavelengths simultaneously. Unlike naive delta tracking, which invokes the tracker separately for each wavelength, spectral tracking invokes the tracker only once, computing a spectrally resolved collision weight at each step to counteract the discrepancy between the single sampling distribution and the true per-wavelength free-path distribution. It differs from its parent, Uniform Sphere Tracing, by replacing the scalar transmittance accumulation with a vectorized throughput update that accounts for spectral variance, and from its sibling, Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing, by explicitly managing spectral weights rather than relaxing the majorant bound. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A Volume Scene Definition (vsdf) containing the density volume, emission volume, and a global scattering ratio (scatter); a ray (ray) with origin o and direction d; a maximum travel distance (maxdistance); and a random number generator state (rng). Output: A pair containing the total path length traveled and a spectral throughput vector (f) representing the accumulated contribution. Data Structures: vec3f: A 3-component vector representing spectral values (Red, Green, Blue). sigmat, sigmas, sigmaa, sigman: Spectral vectors for total extinction, scattering, absorption, and null (non-interaction) coefficients. Pt, Ps, Pn, Pa: Scalar probabilities for total, scattering, null, and absorption events, derived from the spectral coefficients and the majorant. wD (or contrib): A spectral vector used to track the weight correction factor. In the implementation, this is updated element-wise. Parameters: majorantdensity: The upper bound on the total extinction coefficient across all wavelengths and space. Typically set to maxdensity. imaxdensity: The inverse of the majorant density (1 / \text{majorant\density}). scatter: A scalar representing the albedo or scattering ratio of the medium. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Retrieve maxdensity from the volume object (densityvol->maxvoxel object->densitymult). Set majorantdensity = maxdensity and imaxdensity = 1.0 / majorantdensity. Initialize pathlength = 0.0. Initialize spectral throughput vectors: tr = vec3f(1.0) (transmittance) and f = vec3f(1.0) (final contribution/throughput). Calculate initial scattering coefficient vector: sigmas = vsdf.scatter maxdensity. Calculate scattering probability: Ps = sigmas imaxdensity. Initialize spectral weight vector wD to ones, though the specific implementation handles weights via the contrib vector logic below. The theoretical formulation initializes wD \leftarrow (1, \dots, 1)^{N\lambda}. 2. Loop: Generate a uniform random number \zeta \in 0, 1) using rng. Compute tentative distance: t = -\ln(1 - \zeta) / \text{majorant\density}. Update pathlength += t. (Note: Source uses pathlength -= log(1 - rand1f(rng)) imaxdensity, which is mathematically equivalent to adding -\ln(\dots)/\text{majorant}). Termination Check: If pathlength >= maxdistance, break the loop. Calculate current position: \mathbf{x} = \text{ray}.o + \text{path\length} \times \text{ray}.d. Evaluate total extinction coefficient at \mathbf{x}: \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) = \text{vec3f}(\text{eval\vpt\density}(vsdf, \mathbf{x})). Calculate null (non-interaction) coefficient: \sigman(\mathbf{x}) = \text{majorant\density} - \sigmat(\mathbf{x}). Calculate [absorption coefficient: \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}) = \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) - \sigmas. (The implementation assumes a homogeneous scattering ratio vsdf.scatter applied to the local total extinction or uses a pre-computed constant sigmas. Based on code, sigmas is constant, but sigmat varies. This implies the albedo varies spectrally via sigmat while the scattering ratio is fixed, or sigmas is derived differently. The code sigmaa = sigmat - sigmas implies sigmas is the scattering part of the majorant, which is constant. This is a specific implementation detail.) Calculate Pt(\mathbf{x}) = \sigmat(\mathbf{x}) \times \text{imax\density}. Calculate Pn(\mathbf{x}) = \sigman(\mathbf{x}) \times \text{imax\density}. Calculate Pa(\mathbf{x}) = 1.0 - Ps - Pn(\mathbf{x}). (Note: Ps is constant from initialization). Generate a random number \xi \in 0, 1). Absorption: If \xi < Pa(\mathbf{x}) (specifically max(Pa) > rand1f(rng) in to handle vector max, though theoretically it compares against the scalar probability derived from the spectral weight or max component): Calculate contribution weight: \text{contrib} = \sigmaa(\mathbf{x}) / (\text{majorant\density} \times Pa(\mathbf{x})). Normalize: \text{contrib} /= \max(\text{contrib}). Set event type to EVENTABSORB. Return { pathlength, tr contrib }. Scattering: Else if \xi < Pa(\mathbf{x}) + Pt(\mathbf{x}) (implemented as else if (max(Pt) > rand1f(rng)) in, which is a simplification or specific variant where scattering is checked against total probability minus null/absorption logic, or specifically max(Pt) implies checking if scattering is the dominant event relative to a threshold. The standard spectral tracking checks \xi < Pa + Pt. The implementation uses max(Pt) > rand1f(rng). This suggests a specific branching logic. We follow for implementation): Calculate contribution weight: \text{contrib} = \sigmas / (\text{majorant\density} \times Ps). Normalize: \text{contrib} /= \max(\text{contrib}). Set event type to EVENTSCATTER. Return { pathlength, tr contrib }. Null (Non-Interaction): Else: Calculate contribution weight: \text{contrib} = \sigman(\mathbf{x}). Normalize: \text{contrib} /= \max(\text{contrib}). Update throughput: f \leftarrow f \times \text{contrib}. (Note: The implementation does not explicitly update tr with [exponential attenuation in the null branch in the provided snippet, but tr is updated at the start of the loop iteration tr = exp(-sigmatpathlength)? No, the snippet shows tr = exp(-sigmatpathlength) inside the loop. This formula is suspicious for delta tracking where transmittance is handled by the weight. However, we must transcribe the source faithfully. The source includes tr = exp(-sigmatpathlength). This is likely a bug in the referenced implementation or a specific variant, but we record it as written.) If the loop completes without returning (i.e., max distance reached), return { maxdistance, f }. Pseudocode (based on): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import random def evalspectraltracking(vsdf, maxdistance, rng, ray): object = vsdf.object densityvol = object.densityvol maxdensity = densityvol.maxvoxel object.densitymult majorantdensity = maxdensity imaxdensity = 1.0 / maxdensity pathlength = 0.0 tr = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] f = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] # sigmas is assumed constant based on vsdf.scatter in this implementation sigmas = [vsdf.scatter maxdensity, vsdf.scatter maxdensity, vsdf.scatter maxdensity] Ps = [s imaxdensity for s in sigmas] while True: # Sample path length randval = random.random() pathlength -= math.log(1.0 - randval) imaxdensity if pathlength >= maxdistance: break currentpos = (ray.o[0] + pathlength ray.d[0], ray.o[1] + pathlength ray.d[1], ray.o[2] + pathlength ray.d[2]) # Evaluate spectral extinction sigmat = [evalvptdensity(vsdf, currentpos)[0], evalvptdensity(vsdf, currentpos)[1], evalvptdensity(vsdf, currentpos)[2]] # Calculate coefficients sigman = [majorantdensity - s for s in sigmat] sigmaa = [sigmat[i] - sigmas[i] for i in range(3)] # Calculate probabilities Pt = [s imaxdensity for s in sigmat] Pn = [s imaxdensity for s in sigman] Pa = [1.0 - Ps[i] - Pn[i] for i in range(3)] # Update transmittance (Note: This line appears in source, # though standard DT handles transmittance via weights. # Included here as per source.) tr = [tr[i] math.exp(-sigmat[i] pathlength) for i in range(3)] contrib = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Event selection # Note: Source uses max(Pa) and max(Pt) for comparison. # This implies checking against the maximum component of the spectral vector. if max(Pa) > random.random(): # Absorption contrib = [sigmaa[i] / (majorantdensity Pa[i]) for i in range(3)] maxc = max(contrib) contrib = [c / maxc for c in contrib] vsdf.event = "EVENTABSORB" vsdf.density = sigmat return { pathlength, [tr[i] contrib[i] for i in range(3)] } elif max(Pt) > random.random(): # Scattering contrib = [sigmas[i] / (majorantdensity Ps[i]) for i in range(3)] maxc = max(contrib) contrib = [c / maxc for c in contrib] vsdf.event = "EVENTSCATTER" vsdf.density = sigmat return { pathlength, [tr[i] contrib[i] for i in range(3)] } else: # Null event contrib = sigman maxc = max(contrib) contrib = [c / maxc for c in contrib] f = [f[i] contrib[i] for i in range(3)] return { maxdistance, f } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Variance Growth: If the spectral weights wD deviate significantly from 1 (e.g., when P\lambda \ll |\mu\lambda / \bar{\mu}|), the throughput can grow geometrically, leading to high variance. Implementation Discrepancy: The implementation in contains a transmittance update tr = exp(-sigmatpathlength) which is non-standard for Delta Tracking (where transmittance is usually implicit in the weight or handled via the majorant sampling). This may lead to incorrect results if not accounted for, as noted by the issue reporter. Constant Scattering: The implementation assumes sigmas is constant (vsdf.scatter maxdensity), which may not hold for heterogeneous media with varying albedo. Unidirectional Spectral Tracking is a variant that employs specific unidirectional event selection logic to simplify throughput update and termination conditions for single-bounce or specific path configurations [14101-unidirectional-spectral-tracking.md]. It relies on a mean-based majorant rather than a per-voxel maximum, differing from the parent Spectral Tracking which uses a global or per-voxel maximum majorant [14101-unidirectional-spectral-tracking.md]. This variant combines spectral tracking with decomposition tracking to further reduce variance and render time in heterogeneous volumes, particularly for subsurface scattering. By using approximate minimum and maximum values over the entire medium (found via random sampling in a pre-pass) for control and free-path-sampling coefficients, it achieves a 2.70× reduction in LTUV over delta tracking, with decomposition tracking providing an additional 2.05× reduction. In the translucent dragon scene, this combination reduced total render time by 22% and yielded 1.65× lower RMSE compared to delta tracking. The performance gain is attributed to different path distributions and lower throughputs allowing Russian roulette to terminate paths earlier. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of steps along the ray. Each step involves evaluating the density volume and performing vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space per ray, excluding the storage for the volume data itself. Performance: Spectral tracking reduces the number of tracker invocations compared to naive delta tracking by handling all wavelengths in a single pass. In the translucent dragon scene, spectral tracking reduced LTUV by 2.70× over delta tracking. Combined with decomposition tracking, it reduced render time by 22%. Strengths: Efficient handling of spectrally resolved properties; reduced variance compared to naive per-wavelength delta tracking; suitable for heterogeneous volumes. Limitations: Variance can increase if the majorant bound is loose or if spectral weights deviate significantly from 1. The implementation in has noted correctness issues regarding transmittance calculation. Spectral Tracking was introduced by Kutz et al. in the paper "Spectral and Decomposition Tracking for Rendering Heterogeneous Volumes". It was implemented in the Yocto/GL project by RickyMexx as evalspectraltracking. The method addresses the inefficiency of handling spectrally resolved collision coefficients by invoking the tracker separately for each wavelength, instead using a single distribution for all wavelengths and reweighting. name: Unidirectional Spectral Tracking
body: Unidirectional Spectral Tracking is a spectral volume rendering technique that samples absorption, scattering, and null events using a majorant density to drive the sampling process, returning the path length and spectral contribution while handling Russian roulette implicitly via event selection. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a Voxelized Path Tracing Density field (vsdf); a maximum voxel density maxdensity; a maximum ray distance maxdistance; a random number generator rng. Output: A pair containing the total pathlength traveled and the spectral throughput (radiance contribution). Data Structures: vsdf: A data structure providing density evaluation. It returns a vector of total density and a scalar scatter ratio (albedo) at a given position. rng: A random number generator capable of producing uniform floating-point numbers in 0, 1). Parameters: maxdensity: The maximum voxel density of the volume multiplied by an object density multiplier (\rho{max} = \text{voxel\max} \times \text{density\mult}). imaxdensity: The inverse of maxdensity (1.0 / \text{max\density}). majorantdensity: The majorant used for [distance sampling. In this implementation, it is the mean of the scatter product with maxdensity: \bar{\sigma}M = \text{mean}(\text{vsdf.scatter} \times \text{max\density}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize pathlength to 0.0, transmittance \mathbf{T} to \vec{1}, and throughput \mathbf{f} to \vec{1}. 2. Loop indefinitely: a. Sample Path Length: If majorantdensity is 0.0, set pathlength to -\text{FLT\MAX}. Otherwise, sample u1 \sim \mathcal{U}[0,1) and compute: \text{path\length} \leftarrow \text{path\length} - \frac{\ln(1 - u1)}{\text{majorant\density}} b. Termination: If pathlength \ge maxdistance, break the loop. c. Position: Calculate current position: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \text{path\length} \times \mathbf{d} d. Evaluate Cross-sections: Evaluate the VPT density at \mathbf{p} to get total density vector \boldsymbol{\sigma}t and scatter ratio s: \boldsymbol{\sigma}t = \text{eval\vpt\density}(\text{vsdf}, \mathbf{p}) s = \text{vsdf.scatter} Compute component cross-sections: \boldsymbol{\sigma}s = \boldsymbol{\sigma}t \times s \boldsymbol{\sigma}a = \boldsymbol{\sigma}t \times (\vec{1} - s) \boldsymbol{\sigma}n = \text{max\density} \times \vec{1} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}t e. Update Transmittance: \mathbf{T} \leftarrow \mathbf{T} \times (\vec{1} - \boldsymbol{\sigma}t \times \text{imax\density}) f. Event Selection: Determine the event type e and the corresponding coefficient \mue. Sample e \in \{\text{EVENT\NULL}, \text{EVENT\SCATTER}, \text{EVENT\ABSORB}\} proportionally to the norms of \boldsymbol{\sigma}n, \boldsymbol{\sigma}s, and \boldsymbol{\sigma}a. If e = \text{EVENT\NULL}, \mue = \boldsymbol{\sigma}n. If e = \text{EVENT\SCATTER}, \mue = s (scalar, applied to throughput). If e = \text{EVENT\ABSORB}, \mue = \vec{1} - s (scalar, applied to throughput). g. Null Event: If e = \text{EVENT\NULL}, continue to the next iteration (loop back to step 2a). h. Update Throughput: \mathbf{f} \leftarrow \mathbf{f} \times \mue p = \mathbf{f} i. Return: Return the pair (pathlength, f / mean(p)). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def unidirectionalspectraltracking(rayo, rayd, vsdf, maxdensity, maxdistance, rng): imaxdensity = 1.0 / maxdensity # majorantdensity is precomputed as the mean of scatter product with maxdensity majorantdensity = maxdensity vsdf.scatter pathlength = 0.0 transmittance = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] throughput = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] while True: if majorantdensity == 0.0: pathlength = -float('inf') else: u1 = rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0) pathlength -= math.log(1.0 - u1) / majorantdensity if pathlength >= maxdistance: break currentpos = [rayo[i] + pathlength rayd[i] for i in range(3)] sigmat = evalvptdensity(vsdf, currentpos) scatterratio = vsdf.scatter sigmas = [sigmat[i] scatterratio for i in range(3)] sigmaa = [sigmat[i] (1.0 - scatterratio) for i in range(3)] sigman = [maxdensity - sigmat[i] for i in range(3)] transmittance = [transmittance[i] (1.0 - sigmat[i] imaxdensity) for i in range(3)] # Standard spectral event selection proportional to coefficient norms normn = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in sigman)) norms = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in sigmas)) norma = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in sigmaa)) totalnorm = normn + norms + norma if totalnorm == 0: e = "EVENTNULL" else: u2 = rng.uniform(0.0, 1.0) if u2 < normn / totalnorm: e = "EVENTNULL" elif u2 < (normn + norms) / totalnorm: e = "EVENTSCATTER" else: e = "EVENTABSORB" if e == "EVENTNULL": mue = sigman elif e == "EVENTSCATTER": mue = scatterratio else: mue = 1.0 - scatterratio if e == "EVENTNULL": continue # Element-wise multiplication: if mue is scalar, broadcast; if vec, element-wise if isinstance(mue, (int, float)): throughput = [throughput[i] mue for i in range(3)] else: throughput = [throughput[i] mue[i] for i in range(3)] p = throughput[:] meanp = sum(p) / 3.0 if meanp == 0.0: return pathlength, [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] return pathlength, [x / meanp for x in throughput] def evalvptdensity(vsdf, pos): # Standard VPT density lookup returning a vec3 return vsdf.densityat(pos) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Majorant: If majorantdensity is 0.0, the distance sampling formula involves division by zero. The implementation must handle this by setting pathlength to -\text{FLT\MAX} (or a sufficiently large value) to effectively terminate or skip the step. name: Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing
head: Automatic Step Size Relaxation in Sphere Tracing
body:
Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing is a robust sphere tracing method that automatically scales step sizes based on data from previous iterations, using a scalar hyperparameter similar to the learning rate of gradient descent methods. It sets itself apart from its parent Uniform Sphere Tracing by replacing fixed step rules with an adaptive scaling mechanism that reduces the frequency of invalid, over-relaxed step sizes, thereby minimizing the need for robustness-preserving fallback steps. Compared to Spectral Tracking, it exhibits a smaller effect on performance from its step-scale hyperparameters and performs up to par with or outperforms the most efficient concurrent methods depending on iteration count limits. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluator F(x). Scalar hyperparameter \alpha (step size scaling factor). Maximum iteration count N{max}. Surface threshold \epsilon (convergence tolerance). Outputs: Intersection point x{hit} or null if no intersection is found within N{max} iterations. Data Structures: Current position xt \in \mathbb{R}^3. Previous distance value d{prev} = F(x{t-1}). Current distance value d{curr} = F(xt). Step size st \in \mathbb{R}. Algorithm: 1. Initialize x0 = o. 2. Evaluate d0 = F(x0). 3. Set initial step size s0 = d0. If d0 \le \epsilon, return x0. 4. For t = 0 to N{max} - 1: a. Move along the ray: x{next} = xt + st \cdot d. b. Evaluate distance: d{next} = F(x{next}). c. Check convergence: If d{next} \le \epsilon, return x{next}. d. Calculate adaptive step size for next iteration: The exact mathematical update rule is not given in the sources. The method scales the step size based on data from previous iterations using the scalar hyperparameter \alpha. e. Update state: xt \leftarrow x{next}, d{prev} \leftarrow d{next}. 5. Return null (failure). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def autorelaxedspheretracing(o, d, F, alpha, Nmax, eps): x = o dprev = F(x) if dprev <= eps: return x s = dprev # Standard initial step size for t in range(Nmax): xnext = x + s d dnext = F(xnext) if dnext <= eps: return xnext # Exact step size update formula not given in sources; scales step based on previous iteration data using hyperparameter alpha x = xnext dprev = dnext return None # Failure to converge within Nmax Parameters: \alpha: Scalar hyperparameter controlling step size scaling, used similarly to the learning rate in gradient descent. Typical values are not given in the sources. \epsilon: Surface threshold. Not given in the sources. N{max}: Maximum iteration count. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Over-relaxed step sizes: The method can generate invalid step sizes if \alpha is too large, causing the ray to jump over the surface. However, it generates significantly fewer of these compared to concurrent variants, reducing the need for fallback steps. Precision: Standard floating-point precision issues apply to SDF evaluation and ray marching. Degenerate Input: If F(x) is not a valid SDF (i.e., |
abla F| 
eq 1), the step size relaxation may fail to converge or produce incorrect results. A triggering strategy for Signed Distance Functions (SDF) that uses the Eikonal equation property to accelerate finding the zero-level set point x. It initializes an arbitrary point x0 in the implicit field of SDF F and updates the point using the rule x{t+1} = xt - \eta F(xt) 
abla{xt} F, where \eta \le 1 is the step size. This accelerates standard SGD when far from the surface and provides damping to prevent penetration when close. It is distinct from Auto-Relaxed Sphere Tracing as it is a gradient-based optimization scheme rather than a ray-marching step size adaptation, though both leverage SDF properties. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of iterations required to converge. Measured Performance: Outperforms or performs up to par with the most efficient concurrent sphere tracing methods, depending on iteration count limits. It has a smaller effect on performance from its step-scale hyperparameters than concurrent variants. Strengths: Robustness against invalid step sizes; reduced need for fallback logic; efficient convergence for both procedural and discrete SDFs. Limitations: Requires tuning of \alpha; performance is sensitive to the choice of \alpha in complex scenes, though less so than other adaptive methods. When to use: When robustness is critical and fallback steps are expensive; when working with SDFs where standard sphere tracing might overshoot or undershoot. When not to use: When strict determinism without hyperparameter tuning is required; when the SDF does not satisfy the Eikonal equation. The method was proposed by Róbert Bán and Gábor Valasek in May 2023. The concept of using SDF properties for acceleration is also related to sphere tracing-based triggering strategies described in later works on deep implicit surface networks. name: Synchronized-tracing
head: Synchronized Tracing of Primitive-based Implicit Volumes
body: Synchronized-tracing is a tile-based rendering pipeline for implicit volumes (blobtrees) that synchronizes threads within a subfrustum to allow coherent field evaluation, using sparse bottom-up tree traversal to prune the blobtree on-the-fly. It is designed for interactive modeling scenarios where no preprocessing is required when primitive parameters are updated. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by introducing a synchronization mechanism via a low-resolution A-buffer to manage thread coherence within workgroups, and by using compact, smooth CSG operators to compute tight bounding volumes for approximate signed distance fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A blobtree representing implicit surfaces/volumes, consisting of thousands of primitives. The blobtree is defined by primitive parameters that may be updated dynamically. Output: Rendered image of the implicit surface/volume. Data Structures: Blobtree: A hierarchical structure of implicit primitives combined using CSG operators. Low-resolution A-buffer: Stores the primitives of interest for a given screen tile. This structure is used to synchronize threads within a subfrustum. Tight Bounding Volume: Computed for all primitives of the blobtree. Parameters: Lipschitz Bound: For approximate signed distance fields, the Lipschitz bound should be close to 1. Tile Dimensions: Not given in the sources. Subfrustum Size: Not given in the sources. Steps: 1. Compute Tight Bounding Volume: For all primitives of the blobtree, compute a tight augmented bounding volume (or volume of interest) using compact, smooth CSG operators extended from standard bounded operators. This is particularly relevant when using approximate signed distance fields where the Lipschitz bound is close to 1. 2. Tile-based Processing: Divide the screen into tiles. For each tile, identify the primitives of interest and store them in the low-resolution A-buffer. 3. Synchronization: Use the low-resolution A-buffer during ray processing to synchronize threads within a subfrustum. This synchronization allows for coherent field evaluation within workgroups. 4. Sparse Bottom-up Tree Traversal: Perform a sparse bottom-up tree traversal on the blobtree to prune it on-the-fly. This step decorrelates field evaluation complexity from the full blobtree size. 5. Ray Processing: Execute ray processing using the sphere tracing algorithm. The sphere tracing algorithm uses the signed distance field values to determine step sizes [Parent]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Relaxed Sphere Tracing
head: Keinert et al. sphere tracing
body: Relaxed sphere tracing is a sphere tracing variant that scales up the signed distance function estimate (SDFE) value to take larger steps, thereby improving rendering performance. It reverts to the basic conservative step size if the unbounding spheres of two consecutive steps are disjoint, ensuring that no surface intersections are skipped. It is distinguished from its sibling Enhanced Sphere Tracing by its simpler geometric approximation; while relaxed tracing uses a fixed relaxation factor, enhanced tracing optimally approximates planar surfaces by ensuring consecutive unbounding spheres are tangential, resulting in decisively better error-decrease velocity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray direction \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{R}^3 with |\mathbf{v}|=1, Signed Distance Function Estimate f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, relaxation parameter \omega, maximum iteration count i{max}, and a minimum distance threshold for termination. Output: Distance t \in 0, \infty) traveled along the ray to the surface. Data Structures: Scalar variables: t (current distance), ri ([SDF value at previous step), r{i+1} (SDF value at current step), di (step size), i (iteration counter). Parameters: \omega: Relaxation parameter. A typical example value is 0.6, yielding a step size factor of 1.6. The sources do not specify a general optimal range, but it must be positive. i{max}: Maximum number of iterations to prevent infinite loops in empty space. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0, i = 0, ri = 0, r{i+1} = \infty. 2. Loop while i < i{max} and r{i+1} is not "too small" (indicating the surface has not been reached or passed): a. Calculate the relaxed step size: di = ri + \omega \cdot ri = ri(1 + \omega). b. Sample the SDF at the new position: r{i+1} = f(\mathbf{p} + (t + di)\mathbf{v}). c. Safety Check: If the unbounding spheres of the previous step (radius ri) and the current step (radius r{i+1}) are disjoint, the step di was too large and might have skipped the surface. The condition for disjointness is di > ri + r{i+1}. d. If disjoint (di > ri + r{i+1}): i. Revert to the conservative step size: di = ri. ii. Re-sample the SDF at the corrected position: r{i+1} = f(\mathbf{p} + (t + di)\mathbf{v}). e. Update distance and state: t = t + di, ri = r{i+1}. f. Increment iteration: i = i + 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def relaxedspheretracing(p, v, f, omega, imax, mindist): t = 0.0 i = 0 rprev = 0.0 rcurr = float('inf') while i < imax and rcurr > mindist: # Step 1: Calculate relaxed step size d = rprev (1.0 + omega) # Step 2: Sample SDF at new position rcurr = f(p + (t + d) v) # Step 3: Safety check for disjoint unbounding spheres # If the step size d is greater than the sum of the radii, # the spheres are disjoint and the surface might be skipped. if d > rprev + rcurr: # Revert to conservative step size d = rprev # Re-sample rcurr = f(p + (t + d) v) # Step 4: Update state t = t + d rprev = rcurr i = i + 1 return t Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The check di > ri + r{i+1} relies on floating-point arithmetic. In degenerate cases where the surface is extremely close, precision errors might cause unnecessary fallbacks or missed detections. Termination: The algorithm terminates when r{i+1} becomes "too small." The exact threshold is not specified in the sources, but it typically corresponds to a value near machine epsilon or a predefined resolution limit. Lipschitz Constant: The SDF f is assumed to have a Lipschitz constant \text{Lip } f \le 1. This property ensures that the distance function does not change faster than the Euclidean distance, which is fundamental to the correctness of sphere tracing. Transformation for Boundary Inspection: An alternative formulation by Bálint and Valasek incorporates a transformation into the SDF to prevent overstepping the nonzero boundary without explicit branching. Let \alpha = \frac{\sqrt{2}}{p \cdot \text{width}^2 \cdot \text{Cheigh} \cdot t^2} (where p, \text{width}, \text{Cheigh}, and t are scene-specific parameters). One can inspect g(t) = f(\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v}) - \alpha t. The modified SDF is: F(t) = \frac{f(\mathbf{p} + t\mathbf{v})}{1 + \alpha - \alpha t} This transformation efficiently offsets the surface by a value that increases with distance, allowing the use of standard sphere tracing logic on F(t) without special termination conditions. Performance: Relaxed sphere tracing offers a performance increase over basic sphere tracing by taking larger steps in empty space or far from surfaces. However, it is decisively worse than Enhanced Sphere Tracing in terms of error-decrease velocity across all iteration counts. Enhanced tracing outperforms relaxed tracing on every iteration count because its optimal approximation of smooth surfaces allows for longer steps and fewer execution branches caused by fallbacks. Complexity: Time complexity is O(k) where k is the number of iterations, similar to basic sphere tracing, but with a potentially smaller k due to larger steps. Memory complexity is O(1) as it only stores a few scalar values per ray. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides a good balance between speed and safety compared to basic sphere tracing. Limitations: The fixed relaxation factor \omega is not adaptive. In regions with high curvature or complex geometry, the fallback mechanism may trigger frequently, reducing the performance benefit. It is less efficient than enhanced sphere tracing. Relaxed sphere tracing was introduced by Keinert et al. [KSK14] as a faster algorithm via relaxation of the original sphere tracing method. It was later used in the Claybook project to implement a real-time simulation-based computer game. The method was analyzed and compared against basic and enhanced sphere tracing by Csaba Bálint and Gábor Valasek in their 2018 paper "Accelerating Sphere Tracing". The authors noted that while Keinert's method scales up the conservative step size, it requires a check for disjoint unbounding spheres to maintain correctness. It solves the performance bottleneck of standard sphere tracing in large empty volumes by allowing the step size to grow as the ray travels further from the origin, while retaining the safety checks of relaxed sphere tracing to prevent skipping intersections. It is distinguished from basic sphere tracing by its adaptive step growth and from standard relaxed sphere tracing by the explicit addition of a growing minimum step component. The method advances a ray along a parameter t using a Signed Distance Function (SDF) to determine step sizes. It maintains a minimum step size msp that increases linearly with each iteration, ensuring that steps do not shrink below a growing threshold. It also implements a backward correction mechanism to handle cases where the distance estimate drops significantly, which can occur with glassy artifacts or rapid changes in geometry. name: Cone-Traced Supersampling
head: Cone-Traced Supersampling With Subpixel Edge Reconstruction, Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER)
body: Cone-Traced Supersampling (CTSS) is an efficient spatial antialiasing solution for Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering that performs supersampling along the traced ray near surfaces with partial visibility. It identifies object contours by evaluating cone intersections within a pixel's view frustum, avoiding the need for casting additional rays per pixel or offline prefiltering. Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER) extends CTSS to locate and resolve complex pixels with geometric edges in relatively flat regions that are otherwise undetected by cone intersections. Unlike conventional supersampling, CTSS minimizes shading computations, and unlike post-processing filters, it avoids undesirable blurriness and ghosting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray traced through an SDF volume, the pixel's view frustum geometry, and the SDF function S(\mathbf{p}). Output: A final pixel color with reduced aliasing artifacts. Data Structures: Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized as \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Cone: Defined by the ray direction \mathbf{d}, the apex at the ray origin or current marching position, and an angular radius \theta derived from the pixel's solid angle. Visibility State: A boolean or float indicating if the ray has hit a surface or escaped. Steps: 1. Cone Intersection Evaluation: Construct a cone representing the pixel's view frustum at the current ray marching position and evaluate if it intersects the SDF surface to identify surfaces with partial visibility (object contours). 2. Contour Detection: Mark the pixel as containing a contour if the cone intersects the surface; otherwise, classify it as flat or fully inside/outside. 3. Supersampling along the Ray: For pixels identified as contours, perform supersampling along the traced ray near the surface intersection. 4. Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER): Detect complex pixels with geometric edges in relatively flat regions that were not identified by the cone intersection step and resolve them. 5. Specialized Sampling Strategy: Apply a sampling strategy that minimizes the number of shading computations during supersampling. 6. Correlation and Aggregation: Correlate sample visibility to aggregate the samples for the final pixel color. Formulas: Ray march: \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Surface hit condition: S(\mathbf{p}) < \epsilon. Visibility aggregation: V{\text{final}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum{i=1}^{N} Vi. Parameters: maxsteps: Maximum number of ray marching steps. Typical value: 100. epsilon: Surface proximity threshold. Typical value: 10^{-3}. pixelfrustum.angleradius: Angular radius of the pixel's view frustum. Derived from camera FOV and resolution. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Complex Pixels in Flat Regions: Geometric edges in relatively flat regions are otherwise undetected by cone intersections and require SER. Precision: SDF evaluation near the surface requires high precision to avoid artifacts. Boundaries: Handling pixels at the edge of the screen or near the camera origin may require special frustum construction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Step 2: Cone Intersection Evaluation # Construct cone at hitpoint with direction raydirection and angular radius derived from pixelfrustum # Not given in the sources. coneangle = pixelfrustum.angleradius coneaxis = raydirection # Evaluate if cone intersects SDF surface # Not given in the sources. iscontour = evaluateconeintersection(hitpoint, coneaxis, coneangle, sdffunction) # Step 3 & 5: Supersampling and Specialized Sampling Strategy if iscontour: samples = [] # Specialized sampling strategy to minimize shading computations # Not given in the sources. offsets = [0.0, 0.1, -0.1] for offset in offsets: samplepos = hitpoint + raydirection offset sampledist = sdffunction(samplepos) visibility = 1.0 if sampledist >= 0.0 else 0.0 samples.append(visibility) # Step 6: Correlation and Aggregation # Not given in the sources. finalvisibility = sum(samples) / len(samples) return shade(hitpoint, finalvisibility) # Step 4: Subpixel Edge Reconstruction (SER) for flat regions else: # Check for complex edges not detected by cone intersection # Not given in the sources. if evaluatesercondition(hitpoint, sdffunction, pixelfrustum): edgesamples = performser(hitpoint, sdffunction, pixelfrustum) finalvisibility = sum(edgesamples) / len(edgesamples) return shade(hitpoint, finalvisibility) else: return shade(hitpoint, 1.0) def evaluateconeintersection(apex, axis, angle, sdf): # Evaluate SDF at cone boundary points to check for intersection # Not given in the sources. return False def evaluatesercondition(point, sdf, frustum): # Check for edges in flat regions # Not given in the sources. return False def performser(point, sdf, frustum): # Measured Performance: Delivers comparable antialiasing quality at significantly lower computational cost than conventional supersampling. Strengths: Provides efficient spatial antialiasing without additional rays per pixel, offline prefiltering, or post-processing blurriness and ghosting. Limitations: Requires cone intersection evaluation, which may be complex to implement, and relies on SER for flat regions with edges. When to Use: Real-time SDF rendering where antialiasing is required without significant performance loss. When Not to Use: Scenes with no complex edges or when post-processing filters are acceptable and performance is not a concern. Cone-Traced Supersampling (CTSS) was introduced as an efficient and robust spatial antialiasing solution for SDF rendering. It naturally complements the sphere tracing algorithm and can be easily implemented in existing real-time SDF renderers. The technique was proposed to address the limitations of conventional supersampling and post-processing filters. name: Kernel-Reflection Sequences
body: Kernel-Reflection Sequences (KRS) are a procedural modeling technique for generating complex, fractal-like geometries using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) and reflection transformations. It solves the problem of evaluating global distance functions for recursive structures without recursion, enabling real-time sphere tracing on parallel hardware like GPUs. Unlike standard Iterated Function Systems (IFS) which require recursive traversal and cause divergent control flow, KRS uses a fixed operation count logarithmic time algorithm, allowing efficient parallelization. Inputs: A world-space point \mathbf{x}w. A KRS defined by two finite sequences: kernel sets K0, \dots, Kn where each Ki is defined by a distance function ki(\mathbf{x}), and reflection operators \mathcal{R}0, \dots, \mathcal{R}{n-1}. Each \mathcal{R}i corresponds to a reflection plane defined by \mathbf{u}i \cdot \mathbf{x} - wi = 0, where \mathbf{u}i is the unit normal and wi is the distance from the origin. Outputs: The signed distance d from \mathbf{x}w to the KRS geometry. Data Structures: The KRS is stored as two arrays of length n+1 and n respectively: kernels containing functions or data structures for k0, \dots, kn, and reflections containing structures for \mathcal{R}0, \dots, \mathcal{R}{n-1} where each structure holds the plane normal \mathbf{u}i and plane offset wi. Algorithm: 1. Initialize \mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathbf{x}w. 2. Initialize distance d \leftarrow kn(\mathbf{x}) (distance to the top-level kernel). 3. Loop for i from n-1 down to 0:. 4. If \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{u}i - wi > 0 (point is behind the mirror), transform \mathbf{x} \leftarrow \mathcal{R}i \mathbf{x}. 5. Update d \leftarrow \min(d, ki(\mathbf{x})). 6. Return d. The recursive definition of expansion level geometries Li is: L{i+1} = K{i+1} \cup Li \cup \mathcal{R}i Li, with base case L0 = K0. The distance function l{i+1}(\mathbf{x}) for the KRS is computed iteratively using the reflection plane equation \mathbf{u}i \cdot \mathbf{x} - wi = 0. If \mathbf{u}i \cdot \mathbf{x} - wi \leq 0, then l{i+1}(\mathbf{x}) = \min(k{i+1}(\mathbf{x}), li(\mathbf{x})). If \mathbf{u}i \cdot \mathbf{x} - wi > 0, then l{i+1}(\mathbf{x}) = \min(k{i+1}(\mathbf{x}), li(\mathcal{R}i(\mathbf{x}))). This can be evaluated in a single pass from the top level down to the base level without recursion. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distancetokrs(xw, kernels, reflections): """ Computes the distance from xw to the KRS. Args: xw: World space point (vector). kernels: List of distance functions [k0,..., kn]. reflections: List of reflection plane definitions [(u0, w0),..., (u{n-1}, w{n-1})]. Returns: d: Distance to the KRS geometry. """ n = len(kernels) - 1 x = xw # Initialize distance to the top-level kernel Kn d = kernelsn # Iterate from level n-1 down to 0 for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): ui, wi = reflections[i] # Check if point is behind the mirror plane if dot(ui, x) - wi > 0: # Transform point to the reflected space dist = dot(ui, x) - wi x = x - 2.0 dist ui # Update distance with the current level's kernel d = min(d, kernelsi) return d Parameters: Sphere tracing termination threshold: Inversely proportional to camera depth, set to assure that the final unbounding sphere projected onto the viewport is smaller than a pixel. A higher threshold makes kernel geometries appear thicker. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intersection with Mirror Plane: If a previous level geometry Ai is not entirely on the negative side of the mirror plane but intersects it, the formula still applies. This is equivalent to discarding the part of the geometry on the positive side, providing an underestimation for the distance to the mirrored geometry, which remains suitable for sphere tracing. Lipschitz Constant: Standard KRS transformations have a Lipschitz constant of unity. The method can handle any Lipschitz transformation by sacrificing performance. A technique to combine multiple KRSs to produce natural disorder and hide symmetry by taking the union of their geometries. It maintains the free distance along the ray for all KRS components, always choosing the minimal one, and advancing the ray with the radius of the unbounding sphere of the respective component. The search ends when the step size for the minimal component meets the error threshold. Performance does not depend on the number of KRS components, but rather on the number of sphere tracing steps required, with a slight overhead of maintaining a small sorted index of free distances for minimum selection. The error threshold is inversely proportional to camera depth and set to assure that the final unbounding sphere projected onto the viewport is smaller than a pixel. Higher threshold levels make kernel geometries appear thicker and cause distant geometries to merge into smoother formations, losing sub-pixel details. Time Complexity: Logarithmic time with respect to the number of levels n, due to the fixed operation count per level and non-recursive evaluation. Memory Complexity: Independent of the number of levels, requiring only a few registers of read-write memory for the iterative evaluation. Performance: Efficient for GPU sphere tracing due to the lack of recursion and divergent control flow. Performance depends on the number of sphere tracing steps required, not the number of KRS components in the union case. Strengths: Real-time rendering capability, continuous level-of-detail, automatic minification filtering, and suitability for parallel hardware. Limitations: Symmetry may be visible if only a single KRS is used, requiring multiple KRSs or other techniques to hide symmetry. Higher thresholds can cause distant geometries to merge, losing sub-pixel details. Kernel-Reflection Sequences were proposed in a paper titled "Kernel-Reflection Sequences" (2016). The approach is inspired by Iterated Function Systems (IFS) but modifies them to allow for real-time rendering without concessions in visible detail. It was developed to model natural phenomena in uncompromising detail and extents without obvious clues of symmetry. The method extends sphere tracing to conformally transformed geometries and includes a GPU load balancing scheme. name: Analytical and Differentiable Methods
head: Differentiable Sphere Tracing, Analytical SDF Rendering
body: Analytical and Differentiable Methods extend sphere tracing to support inverse graphics and real-time analytical rendering by ensuring the entire rendering pipeline is differentiable with respect to scene parameters or by evaluating Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) analytically without discretization. Unlike standard sphere tracing which produces non-differentiable outputs or requires precomputed grids, these methods enable gradient-based optimization of neural implicit representations or compile CSG trees into optimized shaders for real-time analytical evaluation. This sets them apart from Uniform Sphere Tracing by prioritizing gradient flow or analytical precision over uniform sampling, and from Differentiable Sphere Tracing by encompassing a broader class of techniques including non-neural analytical shading. The implementation depends on the specific variant (Differentiable vs. Analytical), but the core differentiable pipeline described in follows these steps. Inputs: Ray origin o and direction d. Neural SDF parameters \Theta (weights/biases of MLP S(x; \Theta)). Appearance parameters \Phi (diffuse albedo MLP weights), \{ \xik, \lambdak, \muk \}{k=1}^M (environment map Spherical Gaussian coefficients), \{\lambda, \mu\} (specular BRDF parameters). Outputs: Rendered color C for the ray. Gradients \frac{\partial C}{\partial \Theta}, \frac{\partial C}{\partial \Phi}, etc., for backpropagation. Data Structures: Neural Network MLP for S(x; \Theta) and a(x; \Phi). Spherical Gaussian (SG) coefficients for environment map. Steps: 1. Sphere Tracing: Find the intersection point x between the ray r(t) = o + td and the surface S(x; \Theta) = 0 using sphere tracing. Let t be the accumulated distance. At each step, evaluate S(x; \Theta) where x = o + td. Update t \leftarrow t + S(x; \Theta). Terminate when S(x; \Theta) < \epsilon or max steps reached. 2. Normal Computation: Compute the surface normal n at x via automatic differentiation of the SDF: n = \nablax S(x; \Theta) In practice, this is computed using the framework's autodiff engine (e.g., PyTorch torch.autograd.grad) on the MLP output with respect to input coordinates x. 3. Albedo Computation: Compute the diffuse albedo a(x; \Phi) at x using the appearance MLP: a = a(x; \Phi) 4. Rendering Equation Evaluation: Compute the color C by evaluating the rendering equation in closed form using the Spherical Gaussian (SG) approximation: C = \int{\Omega} Li(\omega) \cdot fr(\omega, d) \cdot (\omega \cdot n)^+ d\omega Approximated as a sum of SGs: C \approx \sum{k=1}^M \xik \cdot \frac{(\lambdak (\omegak \cdot n) + \muk)^+}{\lambdak + 1} \cdot f{specular}(d, n, \omegak) + a \cdot f{diffuse} Where Li is the environment map represented by SGs \xik, \lambdak, \muk, \omegak. fr is the BRDF, split into diffuse (proportional to a) and specular (parameters \{\lambda, \mu\}). The key differentiability comes from the closed-form integration of SGs, which is differentiable w.r.t. n, \xik, \lambdak, \muk, a, and \{\lambda, \mu\}. Parameters: \epsilon: Termination threshold. Not given in the sources. M: Number of SGs for environment map. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-differentiable steps: Standard sphere tracing involves discrete steps and comparisons, which are non-differentiable. notes that their pipeline is fully differentiable because the output color is differentiable w.r.t. the parameters, but the ray marching itself must be handled carefully. The sources do not specify how the discrete nature of sphere tracing is made differentiable (e.g., via straight-through estimator or continuous relaxation). [G: In practice, gradients are often propagated through the final hit point x assuming the hit is stable, or using techniques like differentiable ray marching that relax the step size. This detail is not explicitly covered in the provided sources.] Precision: Automatic differentiation of the SDF requires the MLP to be smooth. Discontinuities in the SDF (e.g., from CSG operations in analytical variants) can break differentiability. Differentiable Sphere Tracing (DIST) is a rendering algorithm for implicit SDFs represented by neural networks, enabling efficient forward and backward passes for inverse graphics optimization. It solves the problem of non-differentiable or computationally prohibitive ray marching in neural implicit representations by optimizing the rendering pipeline for GPU efficiency. It sets itself apart from naive sphere tracing by using a coarse-to-fine approach and aggressive ray marching to save computation, and from standard differentiable renderers by providing a specific gradient approximation that reduces memory consumption while maintaining training performance. Choose this when performing inverse graphics with neural SDFs. Link: Differentiable Sphere Tracing. An approach that avoids discretization by sphere-tracing analytical SDFs at render time, using offline compilation of CSG trees into optimized shaders. It sets itself apart by compiling CSG trees into a large set of shaders, each correctly rendering a portion of the scene with minimum SDF evaluations per ray. Choose this for real-time rendering of complex CSG geometries where offline compilation is acceptable. Pitfall: Not suited for real-time modification because continuously recompiling shaders at runtime is not feasible or effective for GPU hardware. Presented by Aeva (2022). A technique using analytical derivatives of noise to compute fast normals and slopes, which helps speed up the raymarching process by adjusting step size based on slope. It sets itself apart by leveraging the Lipschitz constant of noise functions to dynamically adjust step size (smaller steps for steeper slopes). Choose this for raymarching noise-based terrains or fractals where normal computation is a bottleneck. Used in the 'Rainforest' Shadertoy example (2016) for raymarching a signed distance field of a tree-populated terrain. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of sphere tracing steps. Differentiable methods may incur overhead from automatic differentiation. Analytical methods have high offline compilation cost but potentially lower runtime cost due to optimized shader sets. Memory Complexity: Neural SDFs require storing MLP weights. Analytical CSG requires storing compiled shaders. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables gradient-based optimization; avoids discretization artifacts; speeds up raymarching via slope-aware step sizes. Limitations: Analytical CSG is not suitable for real-time modification; Differentiable sphere tracing requires careful handling of non-differentiable steps. When to use: Inverse graphics with neural SDFs; Real-time analytical CSG rendering; Performance-critical noise-based raymarching. When not to use: When real-time modification of analytical CSG is required; When gradients are not needed and simplicity is preferred. Differentiable Sphere Tracing: Originated with PhySG (2021), which introduced a fully differentiable pipeline for inverse rendering with spherical Gaussians and neural SDFs. Analytical SDF Rendering: Presented by Aeva (2022), focusing on real-time rendering of CSG trees without discretization. Analytical Derivatives for Normals: Used in Shadertoy examples (2016), such as 'Rainforest', to optimize raymarching of noise-based SDFs. name: Differentiable Sphere Tracing
head: Differentiable Sphere Tracing Renderer, DIST
body: Differentiable Sphere Tracing (DIST) is a rendering algorithm for implicit Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) represented by neural networks, enabling efficient forward and backward passes for inverse graphics optimization. It solves the problem of non-differentiable or computationally prohibitive ray marching in neural implicit representations by optimizing the rendering pipeline for GPU efficiency. It sets itself apart from naive sphere tracing by using a coarse-to-fine approach and aggressive ray marching to save computation, and from standard differentiable renderers by providing a specific gradient approximation that reduces memory consumption while maintaining training performance. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A neural network f representing the SDF f: \mathbb{R}^3 \rightarrow \mathbb{R}, camera parameters (intrinsic matrix K, extrinsic rotation R, position c), image dimensions (H, W), and rendering parameters (max iterations, convergence threshold, bounding volume). Outputs: Rendered image (RGB), depth, surface normals, opacity, and gradients with respect to SDF parameters and camera pose. Data Structures: Ray Positions: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) storing the current 3D position of each ray. Ray Directions: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) storing normalized ray vectors. Foreground Masks: Boolean tensor of shape (H, W, 1) indicating which pixels have not yet converged or exited the bounding volume. SDF Values: Tensor of shape (H, W, 1) storing the signed distance at current positions. Parameters: numiterations: Maximum number of ray marching steps. Typical value: 2000. convergencethreshold: Distance threshold below which a ray is considered to have hit the surface. Typical value: 10^{-3}. boundingradius: Optional radius for spherical bounding volume. If provided, rays are clamped to this radius. marchstep: Integer, number of marching steps per ray (in some implementations). Default: 50. buffersize: Integer, size of the marching buffer. Default: 5. raymarchingratio: Float, ratio for ray marching bounds. Default: 1.5. maxsampledist: Float, maximum sampling distance. Default: 0.2. threshold: Float, SDF threshold for surface detection. Default: 5 \times 10^{-5}. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize iteration counter n=0, accumulated distance d^{(0)}=0, and current position p^{(0)} = c (camera center). Initialize intrinsic camera matrix K and its inverse K{inv}. Generate a 2D homogeneous grid map for image dimensions (H, W) and project it to camera space using K{inv} to create homocalib (shape 3, H \times W). Compute camera rays by rotating the calibrated homogeneous coordinates with the rotation matrix R: rays = R^T \times \text{homo\calib}, then normalize the vectors. Initialize foregroundmasks to True for all finite ray positions: foregroundmasks = torch.all(torch.isfinite(raypositions), dim=-1, keepdim=True). If boundingradius is set, compute intersection with sphere: a = \sum (\text{ray\directions} \cdot \text{ray\directions}) b = 2 \sum (\text{ray\directions} \cdot \text{ray\positions}) c = \sum (\text{ray\positions} \cdot \text{ray\positions}) - \text{bounding\radius}^2 d = b^2 - 4ac t = \frac{-b - \sqrt{d}}{2a} Update positions if hit: raypositions = torch.where(bounded, raypositions + raydirections t, raypositions) where bounded = d >= 0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: Loop numiterations times: Query the SDF value b^{(n)} = f(p^{(n)}) at the current position using the neural network. Check convergence: converged = torch.abs(signeddistances) < convergencethreshold. Update ray position: If iteration i > 0: raypositions = torch.where(foregroundmasks & ~converged, raypositions + raydirections signeddistances, raypositions). If i == 0: raypositions = torch.where(foregroundmasks, raypositions + raydirections signeddistances, raypositions). Note: The step size is the signed distance value itself. If boundingradius is set, update foreground masks: bounded = torch.norm(raypositions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) < boundingradius; foregroundmasks = foregroundmasks & bounded. Break loop if all rays are either out of foreground or converged: if torch.all(~foregroundmasks | converged): break. 3. Gradient Computation (Backward Pass): Detach ray positions and enable grad: raypositions = raypositions.detach(); raypositions.requiresgrad(True). Compute gradient of SDF w.r.t. positions: gradpositions, = torch.autograd.grad(outputs=signeddistances, inputs=raypositions, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(signeddistances), retaingraph=True). Compute dot products: g{out\dir} = \sum (\text{grad\outputs} \cdot \text{ray\directions}) g{pos\dir} = \sum (\text{grad\positions} \cdot \text{ray\directions}) Compute output gradient: gradoutputs = -goutdir / gposdir. Zero gradients for unconverged points: gradoutputs = torch.where(converged, gradoutputs, torch.zeroslike(gradoutputs)). Compute gradients w.r.t. SDF parameters: gradparameters = torch.autograd.grad(outputs=signeddistances, inputs=parameters, gradoutputs=gradoutputs, retaingraph=True). Return gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def differentiablespheretracing(sdfnetwork, cameraintrinsics, cameraextrinsics, imageheight, imagewidth, numiterations=2000, convergencethreshold=1e-3, boundingradius=None): """ Performs differentiable sphere tracing for a neural SDF. Args: sdfnetwork: Neural network representing the SDF. cameraintrinsics: 3x3 intrinsic matrix K. cameraextrinsics: 3x3 rotation matrix R and 3x1 translation vector t. imageheight: H imagewidth: W numiterations: Max marching steps. convergencethreshold: SDF threshold for convergence. boundingradius: Optional spherical bounding radius. Returns: renderedimage, depth, normals, gradients """ # 1. Initialize Camera Rays # Create homogeneous grid (3, H, W) y, x = torch.meshgrid(torch.arange(imageheight), torch.arange(imagewidth), indexing='ij') homogrid = torch.stack([x, y, torch.oneslike(x)], dim=0).float() # Shape: (3, H, W) # Project to camera space: Kinv @ homogrid Kinv = torch.inverse(cameraintrinsics) homocalib = torch.matmul(Kinv, homogrid.view(3, -1)) # Shape: (3, HW) # Rotate to world space: R^T @ homocalib R = cameraextrinsics[:3,:3] rays = torch.matmul(R.t(), homocalib) # Shape: (3, HW) rays = rays / torch.norm(rays, dim=0, keepdim=True) # Normalize rays = rays.view(3, imageheight, imagewidth).permute(1, 2, 0) # Shape: (H, W, 3) # Camera position campos = -torch.matmul(R.t(), cameraextrinsics[:3, 3:4]).squeeze() # Shape: (3,) # Initialize Ray Positions raypositions = campos.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0).repeat(imageheight, imagewidth, 1) # Shape: (H, W, 3) raydirections = rays # Initialize Masks foregroundmasks = torch.ones((imageheight, imagewidth, 1), dtype=torch.bool, device=raypositions.device) # Handle Bounding Radius if boundingradius is not None: # Compute intersection with sphere a = torch.sum(raydirections raydirections, dim=-1, keepdim=True) b = 2 torch.sum(raydirections raypositions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) c = torch.sum(raypositions raypositions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) - boundingradius 2 d = b 2 - 4 a c # Clamp d to avoid NaNs d = torch.clamp(d, min=0.0) t = (-b - torch.sqrt(d)) / (2 a) bounded = d >= 0 raypositions = torch.where(bounded, raypositions + raydirections t, raypositions) foregroundmasks = foregroundmasks & bounded.unsqueeze(-1) # 2. Ray Marching Loop for i in range(numiterations): # Query SDF # Reshape positions for network input if necessary (e.g., batch dim) posflat = raypositions.view(-1, 3) sdfvalues = sdfnetwork(posflat).view(imageheight, imagewidth, 1) # Check Convergence converged = torch.abs(sdfvalues) < convergencethreshold # Update Positions # Only march if foreground and not converged marchmask = foregroundmasks.squeeze(-1) & ~converged.squeeze(-1) if i == 0: # First step: march all foreground rays updatemask = foregroundmasks.squeeze(-1) else: updatemask = marchmask # Avoid division by zero or invalid steps stepsize = torch.where(updatemask, sdfvalues, torch.zeroslike(sdfvalues)) raypositions = torch.where(updatemask.unsqueeze(-1), raypositions + raydirections stepsize, raypositions) # Update Foreground Masks if boundingradius is not None: distfromorigin = torch.norm(raypositions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) bounded = distfromorigin < boundingradius foregroundmasks = foregroundmasks & bounded # Check if all rays are done if torch.all(~foregroundmasks.squeeze(-1) | converged.squeeze(-1)): break # 3. Backward Pass (Gradient Computation) # Detach positions to break the computational graph from the forward pass raypositionsdetached = raypositions.detach() raypositionsdetached.requiresgrad(True) # Re-query SDF for gradient computation posflatdetached = raypositionsdetached.view(-1, 3) sdfvaluesdetached = sdfnetwork(posflatdetached).view(imageheight, imagewidth, 1) # Compute gradient of SDF w.r.t. positions gradoutputs = torch.oneslike(sdfvaluesdetached) gradpositions, = torch.autograd.grad( outputs=sdfvaluesdetached, inputs=raypositionsdetached, gradoutputs=gradoutputs, retaingraph=True, creategraph=True) # Compute dot products for chain rule approximation gradoutputsdotdirections = torch.sum(gradoutputs raydirections, dim=-1, keepdim=True) gradpositionsdotdirections = torch.sum(gradpositions raydirections, dim=-1, keepdim=True) # Avoid division by zero gradpositionsdotdirections = torch.clamp(gradpositionsdotdirections, min=1e-6, max=1e6) # Compute output gradient gradoutputs = -gradoutputsdotdirections / gradpositionsdotdirections # Zero gradients for unconverged points gradoutputs = torch.where(converged, gradoutputs, torch.zeroslike(gradoutputs)) # Compute gradients w.r.t. SDF parameters # Note: In practice, this is done by calling backward() on the loss or using torch.autograd.grad on the network parameters # Here we simulate the gradient flow to the network weights # The actual implementation would pass gradoutputs back to the network # For the purpose of this pseudocode, we assume the network parameters are accessible # and we compute their gradients. # Return results # Depth is the accumulated distance along the ray # Depth = ||raypositions - campos|| depth = torch.norm(raypositions - campos.unsqueeze(0).unsqueeze(0), dim=-1) # Normals are the normalized gradient of the SDF normals = gradpositions / (torch.norm(gradpositions, dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-12) return raypositions, sdfvalues, normals, depth, gradoutputs The Instant-NSR-PL Forward Pass renders scenes by marching rays through a neural Signed Distance Function (SDF) and accumulating color, normals, depth, and opacity along each ray. It computes the composite RGB image, surface normals, depth, and opacity by querying a geometry network for SDF values and gradients, computing opacity from the SDF and ray direction, and accumulating results along the ray. Differentiable Silhouette Rendering is a technique to render binary silhouettes of 3D shapes represented by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) in a way that allows gradient back-propagation to scene parameters. It solves the non-differentiability of standard binary silhouette detection (e.g., ray termination at infinity) by computing a "soft" silhouette value based on the minimum absolute SDF encountered along a ray. It sets itself apart from its parent Differentiable Sphere Tracing by focusing specifically on the silhouette supervision signal rather than full photometric or geometric rendering, and from siblings like Instant-NSR-PL Forward Pass by relying on the minimum absolute distance query rather than normal-based edge detection. The SDF Direct Diffuse Integrator is a differentiable rendering method that computes direct illumination for scenes defined by Signed Distance Functions (SDFs). It extends standard path tracing by incorporating a boundary integral term evaluated at grazing points, enabling accurate gradient computation for thin surfaces and silhouettes. Unlike standard differentiable sphere tracing, it explicitly handles visibility discontinuities at object boundaries using a relaxed boundary formulation. Recovers a complete 3D shape from a single depth image by optimizing a latent code through a differentiable renderer, requiring no additional training of the shape generator. It sets itself apart from its sibling DeepSDF by replacing fixed-distance sampling with adaptive sampling via differentiable sphere tracing, which better captures boundaries and thin structures. It differs from Differentiable Sphere Tracing by explicitly combining a Directional Distance Function (DDF) for ray intersection with a Signed Distance Function (SDF) for loss computation, avoiding standard sphere tracing iterations. Predicts 3D shape from multiple color images by minimizing cross-view photometric consistency loss without requiring segmentation masks. It differs from encoder-based methods like PMO by using random initialization and an implicit representation, making it robust to initialization noise and camera focal length changes. This method optimizes an initial camera pose toward a ground truth pose by minimizing gradients computed from 2D depth and binary silhouette observations using a differentiable SDF renderer. It is distinct from sibling methods like Instant-NSR-PL Forward Pass which may optimize shape parameters, by focusing specifically on pose recovery given a fixed shape. It differs from Differentiable Silhouette Rendering by explicitly combining silhouette cross-entropy with a scale-invariant depth loss. A method using a reparameterization function T for Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) that strictly satisfies the boundary requirement \partial\pi T(\omegab, \pi) = \partial\pi \omegab. It constructs a 3D vector field \mathbf{V}: \mathbf{V}(x, \pi):= -\frac{\partialx \phi(x, \pi0)}{\phi(x, \pi) \|\partialx \phi(x, \pi0)\|2}, where x \in \mathbb{R}^3 is any point, and \pi0 is the value of \pi in the current scene (detached version). The evaluation distance function t is constructed by reusing samples from sphere tracing: t:= \frac{\sum{i=1}^N w^{(i)} ti}{\sum{i=1}^N w^{(i)}}, where ti are intermediate distances and w^{(i)} is a weighting function. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity is proportional to the number of pixels, the number of iterations, and the cost of the neural network forward pass per iteration. Memory complexity is dominated by storing the ray positions, directions, and intermediate SDF values for all pixels, as well as the computational graph for back-propagation. Measured Performance: DIST is designed to run efficiently on commodity GPUs with affordable memory consumption. It uses a coarse-to-fine approach and aggressive ray marching to save computation compared to naive sphere tracing. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Fully differentiable, supports inverse graphics optimization, handles complex geometry via neural SDFs, efficient on GPUs. Limitations: Prohibitive for naive sphere tracing due to recursive computational graphs; requires careful tuning of convergence thresholds and bounding volumes. Division by zero in gradient calculation must be handled by clamping. When to Use: Use for inverse graphics problems involving neural implicit representations, such as 3D shape prediction from 2D images. Use when differentiable rendering of SDFs is required for optimization. When Not to Use: Do not use for explicit mesh rendering or voxel-based rendering where other methods are more efficient. Do not use if high precision is required for very thin structures without adaptive sampling. Differentiable Sphere Tracing (DIST) was proposed by Liu et al. in 2020. It bridges the gap between inverse graphics methods and deep learning-based implicit signed distance functions. The method optimizes both the forward and backward passes of the rendering layer to make it run efficiently with affordable memory consumption on a commodity graphics card. It enables geometric reasoning with strong generalization capability, allowing high-quality 3D shape prediction by performing iterative optimization with various 2D supervisions. The method has been implemented in PyTorch and used for single-view and multi-view inverse optimization.
