name: Distance Accuracy vs Performance Trade-off
head: Distance Estimate Accuracy, Distance accuracy vs performance, Sphere Tracing Performance Analysis, Underestimate vs Exact SDF Performance
body: This method analyzes the inverse relationship between the accuracy of a Signed Distance Function (SDF) evaluation and the computational cost of sphere tracing. It establishes that underestimating the distance to the surface forces the ray marcher to take smaller steps, significantly increasing the number of iterations required for convergence. The core insight is that a slower, exact SDF evaluation can outperform a faster, inaccurate distance bound if the inaccuracy forces a disproportionate increase in step count. The method relies on the geometric constraint that the step size s in sphere tracing must satisfy s \le d(\mathbf{p}), where d(\mathbf{p}) is the distance estimate at the current ray position \mathbf{p}. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. SDF function d(\mathbf{p}) which may be an approximation or exact. Convergence threshold \epsilon. Maximum traversal distance \text{max\dist}. Maximum iteration count \text{max\steps}. Outputs: Boolean indicating surface intersection. Number of steps taken. Data Structures: Current ray position \mathbf{p} (vector). Step counter n (integer). Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}, normalize \mathbf{d}, and set n = 0. 2. Evaluate distance estimate d{est} = d(\mathbf{p}). 3. Clamp negative estimates to zero: d{est} \leftarrow \max(d{est}, 0). 4. If d{est} < \epsilon, terminate successfully. If \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}\| > \text{max\dist} or n \ge \text{max\steps}, terminate unsuccessfully. 5. Advance ray: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{p} + d{est} \cdot \mathbf{d}. 6. Increment n \leftarrow n + 1. 7. Repeat from step 2. Formulas: The relationship between distance accuracy and step count is derived from the convergence rate. Experiments on a sphere show that halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Thus, the step count scales inversely with the estimate magnitude: N{steps} \propto \frac{1}{d{est}} Where N{steps} is the number of iterations and d{est} is the average distance estimate magnitude. Parameters: \epsilon: Convergence threshold. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Severe Underestimation: If d{est} is significantly smaller than the true distance d{true}, the ray takes many small steps, wasting computation. For example, a bound that returns at worst 1% of the true distance may perform worse than an exact function in specific cases. Exact vs. Approximate Cost: The total cost is Cost = N{steps} \times Cost{eval}. A slower exact function may have higher Cost{eval} but much lower N{steps}, resulting in lower total time. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spheretrace(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunction, epsilon, maxdist, maxsteps): """ Demonstrates the trade-off by comparing step counts for different SDF accuracies. """ # Normalize direction to ensure step size equals distance estimate dlen = math.sqrt(sum(x2 for x in raydirection)) d = [x / dlen for x in raydirection] p = list(rayorigin) steps = 0 while steps < maxsteps: # Evaluate distance. The accuracy of this call determines performance. dist = sdffunction(p) # Clamp negative distances to zero to prevent stepping inside the surface dist = max(dist, 0.0) if dist < epsilon: return True, steps # Check maximum traversal distance raylen = math.sqrt(sum((p[i] - rayorigin[i])2 for i in range(3))) if raylen > maxdist: return False, steps # Advance ray by the estimated distance p = [p[i] + dist d[i] for i in range(3)] steps += 1 return False, steps Adaptive Convergence Threshold is a stopping condition for distance-field ray marching that determines when the ray has sufficiently converged to the surface to halt further computation. It solves the trade-off between rendering accuracy and computational cost by dynamically calculating a threshold \epsilon based on camera parameters, ensuring that the ray front ends of neighboring pixels do not intersect. Unlike fixed thresholds, this method scales with the scene geometry and camera setup to prevent both dilation (loss of detail) and erosion (incomplete geometry). Time Complexity: The number of steps N is inversely proportional to the accuracy of the distance estimate. Halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Measured Performance: Sphere Experiments: Halving the distance estimate doubles the number of steps. Noise Functions: In experiments with fractal noise, the rendering time for 1/f^2 noise was 7.3 times that of single noise, despite an expected 12x increase due to 6 invocations per evaluation. For 1/f noise, rendering time was 27.5 times single noise time (expected 36x). This indicates that while evaluation cost scales linearly with complexity, the step count reduction from better distance estimates (or other optimizations) can mitigate total time. Ellipsoid Case: For an ellipsoid with axes 100, 100, 1, a fast signed distance bound (returning at worst 1% of the true distance) performs worse than an exact SDF using Newton iterations, despite the exact function being slower per evaluation. Strengths and Limitations: Strength: Provides a theoretical basis for choosing SDF implementations. It highlights that "fast" functions are not always optimal. Limitation: Requires accurate knowledge of the SDF's error bounds to predict performance. The trade-off is non-linear and scene-dependent. When to Use: When optimizing implicit surface rendering performance. When choosing between a closed-form approximate SDF and an iterative exact SDF. When Not to Use: When the SDF error is negligible compared to other bottlenecks (e.g., shading, memory bandwidth). When the scene geometry does not exhibit large disparities between bound and exact distances. Originating from the foundational work on sphere tracing by Hart and North, this analysis was presented in "Sphere Tracing: A Geometric Method for the Antialiased Ray Tracing of Implicit Surfaces" (1992/1994). The paper established sphere tracing as a competitive implicit surface renderer and detailed the impact of distance estimate accuracy on convergence rates. It is widely cited in graphics literature for establishing the performance characteristics of ray marching algorithms. name: Adaptive Convergence Threshold
head: Camera-aware SDF Threshold, Convergence Criteria for Sphere Tracing, Pixel-intersection based epsilon
body: Adaptive Convergence Threshold is a stopping condition for distance-field ray marching that determines when the ray has sufficiently converged to the surface to halt further computation. It solves the trade-off between rendering accuracy and computational cost by dynamically calculating a threshold \epsilon based on camera parameters, ensuring that the ray front ends of neighboring pixels do not intersect. Unlike fixed thresholds, this method scales with the scene geometry and camera setup to prevent both dilation (loss of detail) and erosion (incomplete geometry). Inputs and Outputs Inputs: d{min}: Minimum distance from the camera to the object. S: Sensor size (width). f: Focal length. R: Image resolution (width). \theta: Angle of the ray relative to the optical axis. SDF(p): The signed distance function value at the current ray position p. Outputs: \epsilon: The convergence threshold. Boolean: Whether to continue marching (|SDF(p)| \ge \epsilon) or stop (|SDF(p)| < \epsilon). Data Structures No specific data structures are required beyond standard scalar variables for camera parameters and the current SDF evaluation. Steps 1. Calculate the adaptive convergence threshold \epsilon using the camera intrinsics and the ray's angle \theta. 2. Evaluate the signed distance function SDF(p) at the current ray position p. 3. Compare the absolute SDF value to the threshold: If |SDF(p)| < \epsilon, stop marching. Otherwise, continue marching. Formula The threshold \epsilon is derived from the condition that balls centered at the ray front ends of neighboring pixels must not intersect. The formula is: \epsilon = \frac{d{min} \cdot S \cdot \cos^2(\theta)}{2 \cdot f \cdot R} Where: d{min} is the minimum object distance. S is the sensor size. f is the focal length. R is the resolution. \theta is the angle of the ray. Parameters Typical Values: For a setup with f=60mm, d{min}=10cm, S=32mm, and R=512, the resulting \epsilon \approx 0.5 \times 10^{-4}m (0.05mm). Practical Threshold: In practice, a fixed threshold of 5 \times 10^{-5} is often used for experiments, though the adaptive calculation provides a theoretical bound. Pitfalls Too Large: A threshold that is too large causes dilation, leading to the loss of boundary details and large depth errors due to bounded rendering noise. Too Small: A threshold that is too small significantly increases rendering time. If a maximum number of tracing steps is enforced, pixels may fail to converge, resulting in erosion (background misclassification). Angle Dependence: The threshold varies with \theta. Rays at larger angles (peripheral pixels) have a smaller \epsilon, requiring more precision. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def calculateadaptivethreshold(dmin, S, f, R, theta): """ Calculate the adaptive convergence threshold epsilon. Args: dmin (float): Minimum distance to object. S (float): Sensor size. f (float): Focal length. R (float): Resolution. theta (float): Ray angle in radians. Returns: float: The convergence threshold epsilon. """ costheta = math.cos(theta) epsilon = (dmin S costheta costheta) / (2 f R) return epsilon def raymarchingstep(p, SDFfunc, epsilon): """ Perform one step of ray marching with adaptive convergence check. Args: p (Vector3): Current ray position. SDFfunc (function): Signed Distance Function evaluator. epsilon (float): Convergence threshold. Returns: bool: True if marching should continue, False if converged. """ dist = SDFfunc(p) if abs(dist) < epsilon: return False # Converged return True # Continue Time Complexity: Rendering time scales with the number of queries needed to reach the threshold, increasing significantly if the threshold is set too small. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the threshold calculation. Strengths: Prevents dilation and erosion by aligning the convergence criterion with the pixel resolution. Provides a theoretical bound on depth error. Limitations: Requires knowledge of camera intrinsics (f, S, R) and an estimate of d{min}. The calculation of \theta requires ray direction knowledge. When to Use: When rendering with differentiable sphere tracing where depth accuracy and silhouette precision are critical, and camera parameters are known. When Not to Use: When camera parameters are unknown or dynamic in a way that makes d{min} estimation unreliable. The method was introduced in the context of differentiable rendering of implicit signed distance functions (SDFs). It addresses the issue of slow convergence near the surface where the SDF value approaches zero. The approach is based on the geometric principle that the threshold should be small enough to distinguish between neighboring pixels but large enough to avoid excessive computation. name: Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC)
head: BVH-based Adaptive Lipschitz Constant, Nested BVH Step Size Optimization
body: Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) is a sphere tracing enhancement that uses a nested Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to compute tighter, adaptive Lipschitz constants for step size calculation, rather than using the global sum Lipschitz constant. It solves the problem of overly conservative step sizes in large scenes where the naive global Lipschitz constant \lambda{Fn} becomes very large, limiting efficiency. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized). Current position t0 along the ray. A nested BVH structure representing the implicit function Fn = \sum{i=1}^n fi. For each BVH level i \in [1, n]: the value of the partial sum at t0, denoted \text{BVH}i(t0); the Lipschitz constant for the partial sum, \lambda{\text{BVH}i} = \lambda{Fi}. Outputs: The next safe step size \Delta t to advance the ray. Data Structures: BVH Nodes: Store bounding volumes, Lipschitz constants, and partial sum values at the current ray position. Sum Elements: The functions fi are pre-sorted from higher to lower range of values to achieve close-to-maximal steps with low overhead. Method: 1. Identify Minimum Level: Determine i{min}, the first BVH level where the ray is outside the bounding volume. For all levels i \ge i{min}, the ray is outside the isosurface of BVHi, making the intersection with BVHi's boundary a safe step target. 2. Construct Inclusion Functions: For each valid BVH level i, construct a forward inclusion function: \text{BVH}{\pm i} = \text{BVH}{\pm i}(t0) \pm \lambda{\text{BVH}i}(t - t0), where \lambda{\text{BVH}i} = \lambda{Fi}. 3. Combine Bounds: Combine the inclusion functions from all valid BVH levels by taking their intersection to narrow the range of possible values for Fn(t): Fn(t) \in \bigcap{i=1}^n \text{BVH}{i\pm}. 4. Compute Step Candidates: Calculate candidate step sizes for each BVH level i using the lower bound of the combined inclusion function: F{n-1}(t) = \max{i \in [1, n]} (\text{BVH}{i-1}(t0) - \lambda{\text{BVH}i}(t - t0)). Solving F{n-1}(t) = 0 yields the candidate step \Delta ti = \text{BVH}{i-1}(t0) / \lambda{\text{BVH}i}. 5. Select Final Step: Select the largest (best) candidate as the final step size, which corresponds to the minimum of the individual upper-bound roots to satisfy the intersection constraint. 6. Advance Ray: Move the ray origin to t0 + \Delta t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computealcstep(currentt, bvhlevels): """ Compute the next safe step size using Adaptive Lipschitz Constant. Args: currentt: float, current distance along the ray. bvhlevels: list of dicts, each containing: 'value': float, BVHi(t0) 'lambda': float, Lipschitz constant lambdaBVHi Returns: float, the next safe step size. """ beststep = float('inf') for level in bvhlevels: val = level['value'] lam = level['lambda'] if lam <= 0: continue candidatestep = val / lam # The source states to "select the largest (best) candidate". # Mathematically, intersecting inclusion functions requires taking # the minimum of the individual roots to guarantee safety. if candidatestep > 0 and candidatestep < beststep: beststep = candidatestep return beststep if beststep != float('inf') else 0.0 Parameters: Pre-sorting: Sum elements are pre-sorted from higher to lower range of values to achieve close-to-maximal steps with low overhead. Dynamic Re-ordering: Not used. It is not GPU-friendly because it requires storing each element in an O(n) array and sorting dynamically at every step. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If \lambda{\text{BVH}i} is very small, division by zero or numerical instability may occur. Guard against \lambda \le \epsilon. Degenerate Input: If the ray is inside a BVH level, the inclusion function logic for "outside" steps may not apply directly. The method assumes the ray is outside the target isosurface for the step calculation. GPU Performance: Dynamic re-ordering of sum elements is avoided due to high memory and sorting overhead on GPUs. Sub-stepping is an optimization for adaptive ray marching that guarantees non-decreasing step sizes by performing intermediate sub-steps along the ray as intermediate field sums are computed. It solves the problem of "bad candidates" in standard Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) methods, where computing additional field components fi can unpredictably reduce the step size, leading to wasted computation. Unlike standard ALC, which calculates the next step based on the current position and all available bounds, Sub-stepping physically advances the ray to validate bounds, ensuring that each additional level of detail contributes positively or neutrally to the step size. Computes a tighter Lipschitz constant for sphere-tracing by evaluating it per primitive and per ray, mitigating performance loss from varying primitive radii. For each ray, find the primitive point with the smallest radius whose kernel support intersects the ray. Solve the polynomial equation for intersection roots to determine the smallest radius along the ray. The kernel support intersection condition is: \|\mathbf{p} - (\mathbf{p}^T \mathbf{d}) \mathbf{d}\|^2 - \sigma^2(\tau0 + s\Delta\tau)^2 \leq 0 where \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{m} - \mathbf{s}\mathbf{u}, \mathbf{d} is the ray direction, \sigma is the kernel scale, \tau0 is the base radius, \Delta\tau is the radius variation step, and s is the ray parameter. The parameter \sigma is the kernel scale factor used in the intersection polynomial. Memory Complexity: O(n) to store BVH levels and their Lipschitz constants, with no dynamic arrays required, making it GPU-friendly. Measured Performance: Improves efficiency over naive global Lipschitz constant methods, especially when n is large and \lambda{Fn} would otherwise be very big. Strengths: Tighter bounds lead to larger steps. GPU-friendly due to lack of dynamic sorting. Limitations: Requires a nested BVH structure. Pre-sorting may not always yield optimal steps, though it is close-to-optimal for functions like FBM. When to Use: When rendering procedural volumetric noise or large detailed scenes where the global Lipschitz constant is too conservative. When Not to Use: When the BVH structure is not available or too expensive to build. It builds on the intuition of Worley and Hart regarding dynamic re-ordering but adapts it for GPU-friendly static pre-sorting. name: Sub-stepping
body: Sub-stepping is an optimization for adaptive ray marching that guarantees non-decreasing step sizes by performing intermediate sub-steps along the ray as intermediate field sums are computed. It solves the problem of "bad candidates" in standard Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) methods, where computing additional field components fi can unpredictably reduce the step size, leading to wasted computation. Unlike standard ALC, which calculates the next step based on the current position and all available bounds, Sub-stepping physically advances the ray to validate bounds, ensuring that each additional level of detail contributes positively or neutrally to the step size. Inputs: Current ray origin t0. Target value v (typically 0 for isosurfaces). Minimum BVH level i{min} and maximum level n. Lipschitz constants \lambda{Fi} for cumulative sums Fi and \lambda{fi} for individual fields fi. BVH bounds BVH{i+}(t) providing upper bounds for field sums. Sum of remaining bounds s(i, n) = \sum{k=i}^{n} \Delta{fk}, where \Delta{fk} is the bound provided by the BVH for fk. Outputs: Next ray position t{next} = t0 + step{final}. Data Structures: The method relies on the parent ALC method's BVH nodes and field functions; no additional complex data structures are required. Algorithm Steps: 1. Compute an initial step size step{i{min}} using the BVH at level i{min}. 2. Physically move the ray position by stepi to t0 + stepi. Assume the worst-case scenario where BVH{i+}(t0 + stepi) = v. 3. Evaluate the next function f{i+1} at the new position t0 + stepi. Replace the bound \Delta{f{i+1}} with the actual value f{i+1}(t0 + stepi). 4. Update the step size using the derived formula. Formulas: Initial step size: step{i{min}} = -\frac{F{i{min}}(t0) + s(i{min} + 1, n)}{\lambda{F{i{min}}}}. Updated step size: step{i+1} = stepi + \frac{\Delta{f{i+1}} - f{i+1}(t0 + stepi)}{\lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}}. (Note: The source's Eq. 15 writes the denominator as \lambda{fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}, but the derivation in Eq. 14 and the inequality analysis consistently use \lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}}; the implementation uses the latter for mathematical consistency with Lipschitz accumulation.) Parameters: v=0 is standard for isosurfaces. i{min} and n define the BVH level range. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs if \lambda{Fi} + \lambda{f{i+1}} = 0, requiring a numerical guard. Floating-point precision errors may accumulate if stepi is very small. Loose BVH bounds produce small initial steps, increasing the number of required sub-steps. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def substeppingraymarch(t0, v, imin, n, bvhquery, fields, lambdasF, lambdasf, deltas): """ t0: current ray position v: target value (e.g., 0) imin: minimum BVH level n: maximum level index bvhquery(level, t): returns the upper bound BVH{level+}(t) fields: list of field functions, fieldsi returns fi(t) lambdasF: list of Lipschitz constants for cumulative sums Fi lambdasf: list of Lipschitz constants for individual fields fi deltas: list of BVH bounds for individual fields, deltas[i] = Delta{fi} """ # 1. Compute initial step size using BVH at imin boundimin = bvhquery(imin, t0) step = (v - boundimin) / lambdasF[imin] # 2. Iterate through levels to refine step size via sub-stepping for i in range(imin, n): # a. Sub-step: Move ray position forward by current step size tsub = t0 + step # b. Evaluate next field f{i+1} at the sub-step position fnextval = fieldsi+1 # c. Update step size using actual value instead of BVH bound # Denominator uses lambda{Fi} + lambda{f{i+1}} per derivation consistency lambdasum = lambdasF[i] + lambdasf[i+1] if lambdasum == 0: lambdasum = 1e-9 # Guard against division by zero step = step + (deltas[i+1] - fnextval) / lambdasum return step This method is a real-time ray tracing pipeline for visualizing Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces (SCALIS) defined by skeletons with prescribed radii. It solves the high computational cost of individual SCALIS field evaluations and the challenge of robust closest ray/isosurface intersection by relying on local field interpolations and subdividing the ray into intervals that capture main field variations. It sets itself apart from brute-force marching by using a dynamic view-dependent acceleration structure to select primitives and transforming field values to a space allowing good quadratic polynomial approximation. Time Complexity: The method performs O(n - i{min}) field evaluations per step, where n is the maximum level and i{min} is the minimum level. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the BVH and field data structures used by the parent ALC method. Performance: Sub-stepping performs better on average than the standard Adaptive Lipschitz method because it avoids computing wasteful bad candidates and guarantees step sizes do not decrease. Strengths: Guarantees non-decreasing step sizes, reducing the likelihood of getting stuck in small steps due to optimistic bounds. Limitations: Requires evaluating fields at intermediate positions, which increases computational cost per step compared to a single evaluation if the step size is large. Sub-stepping was introduced in the paper "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". It addresses the limitations of the standard Adaptive Lipschitz Constant method where computing additional field components can unpredictably reduce the step size. The method was developed to improve the efficiency of sphere tracing for procedural volumetric noise in large scenes. name: Local Field Interpolation with Dynamic Subdivision
head: Dynamic Subdivision for SCALIS, Fast ray tracing of scale-invariant integral surfaces, Local Field Interpolation with Dynamic Subdivision for SCALIS, SCALIS rendering pipeline, Scale-Invariant Integral Surface (SCALIS) Ray Tracing
body: This method is a real-time ray tracing pipeline for visualizing Scale-Invariant Integral Surfaces (SCALIS) defined by skeletons with prescribed radii. It solves the high computational cost of individual SCALIS field evaluations and the challenge of robust closest ray/isosurface intersection by relying on local field interpolations and subdividing the ray into intervals that capture main field variations. It sets itself apart from brute-force marching by using a dynamic view-dependent acceleration structure to select primitives and transforming field values to a space allowing good quadratic polynomial approximation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A camera ray \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, a skeleton structure consisting of line segment primitives Si with prescribed radii at endpoints, and a target isovalue c. Output: The intersection distance t along the ray where the SCALIS field f(\mathbf{p}) = c. Data Structures: Skeleton Primitive Si: A line segment defined by endpoints \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1 and radii r0, r1. Radius Function \tau{Si}(q): For a point q on the segment, the radius is the linear interpolation of the endpoint radii. Dynamic A-Buffer: A GPU-accelerated structure built on the fly to select primitives whose supports overlap a given interval along the ray. Field Definitions: The SCALIS field is an implicit surface defined by a scalar field f and an isovalue c as the set of points \mathbf{p} satisfying f(\mathbf{p}) = c. The field is constructed from primitives using the sum blending operator: f(\mathbf{p}) = \sumi fi(\mathbf{p}) \quad (1) where fi is the field function defined by the i-th primitive. The primitives are based on kernels. Compact Polynomial kernels are defined as: k{i,\sigma}(d) = \begin{cases} \left(1 - \left(\frac{d}{\sigma}\right)^2\right)^{\frac{i}{2}} & \text{if } d < \sigma, \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases} \quad (2) and Cauchy kernels are defined as: k{i,\sigma}(d) = \frac{1}{\left(1+\left(\frac{d}{\sigma}\right)^2\right)^i} \quad (3) where i is the degree parameter and \sigma is the scale parameter. Algorithm Steps: 1. Primitive Selection: Select primitives whose supports overlap a given interval along the ray using a dynamic view-dependent acceleration structure built on the fly using fast GPU construction of A-buffers. 2. Ray Segmentation: Segment the camera ray into sub-intervals based on the distance to the skeleton. The strategy is chosen to capture main field variations while generating a small number of sub-intervals to be processed. 3. Field Mapping: Transform field values to a space that allows good quadratic polynomial approximation of the SCALIS field on each sub-interval. This is achieved by using a bijective mapping of the SCALIS field to an approximate smooth homothetic distance field (squared) which has the exact same isosurface of interest as the SCALIS field. All processing is done on this normalized field. 4. Iterative Interpolation and Root Finding: For each sub-interval, iteratively build polynomial interpolations using fast quadratic roots computation to rapidly converge toward the real field function. A different interpolation is used and refined in each interval, locally producing an accurate approximation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tracescalisray(rayorigin, raydirection, skeletonsegments, isovalue): # 1. Primitive Selection (Dynamic A-Buffer simulation) # Filter primitives whose bounding spheres overlap the ray segment [tmin, tmax] # The sources describe a dynamic A-buffer built on the fly activeprimitives = [] for seg in skeletonsegments: R = max(seg.r0, seg.r1) + math.dist(seg.v0, seg.v1) oc = rayorigin - seg.center b = math.dot(oc, raydirection) c = math.dot(oc, oc) - R R if c > 0.0 and b > 0.0: continue disc = b b - c if disc >= 0.0: activeprimitives.append(seg) # 2. Ray Segmentation # Divide ray into intervals based on distance to skeleton to capture field variations # The exact subdivision heuristic is not specified in the sources intervals = computeintervals(rayorigin, raydirection, activeprimitives) thit = None tmin, tmax = 0.0, 1e6 for tstart, tend in intervals: if tstart > tmax: break tend = min(tend, tmax) if tstart >= tend: continue # 3. Field Mapping # Map SCALIS field to approximate squared homothetic distance field # The isovalue c maps to 0 in the normalized space targetnormalized = 0.0 tguess = tstart for in range(50): p = rayorigin + tguess raydirection fval = evaluatescalisfield(p, activeprimitives) # Bijective mapping to normalized squared distance space fnorm = normalizetosquareddistance(fval, isovalue) if abs(fnorm - targetnormalized) < 1e-6: thit = tguess break # Compute derivatives along ray direction # f'(t) = grad(f). d, f''(t) = d. Hessian(f). d df = computerayderivative(p, raydirection, activeprimitives) d2f = computeraysecondderivative(p, raydirection, activeprimitives) if abs(df) < 1e-12: df = 1e-12 # Fast quadratic root computation: solve fnorm + dfdt + 0.5d2fdt^2 = 0 a = 0.5 d2f b = df c = fnorm - targetnormalized if abs(a) < 1e-12: dt = -c / b else: disc = b b - 4 a c if disc < 0: disc = 0 dt = (-b - math.sqrt(disc)) / (2 a) tguess += dt tguess = max(tstart, min(tend, tguess)) if abs(dt) < 1e-8: thit = tguess break if thit is not None: break return thit Parameters: maxiterations: Fixed to 50 in the implementation to prevent infinite loops. Not given in the sources. Convergence thresholds (1e-6 for field value, 1e-8 for step size) are standard numerical values. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on the bijective mapping to a normalized field to ensure good quadratic approximation. If the mapping is inaccurate, convergence may fail. Boundaries: The ray segmentation must ensure that intervals are small enough to capture main field variations but large enough to minimize overhead. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a skeleton structure with line segment primitives. The sources do not specify handling for degenerate segments. Time Complexity: The method reduces the number of field evaluations by using local interpolations and dynamic subdivision. The dynamic A-buffer construction is performed on the fly using fast GPU construction. Memory Complexity: Requires memory for the dynamic A-buffer and the skeleton structure. Measured Performance: The method provides improvements for various resolutions on all combinations of tested models and GPU hardware. It goes beyond Sherstyuk's fast ray-tracing algorithm for convolution surfaces, notably allowing better support of large radius variation while being less sensitive to skeleton tessellation. Strengths: Real-time visualization of SCALIS, efficient primitive selection, robust intersection finding. Limitations: High computational cost of individual SCALIS field evaluations is mitigated but not eliminated; the method is specific to SCALIS fields. Scale-invariant integral surfaces (SCALIS) are implicit representations of surfaces that provide a way to define smooth surfaces from skeletons with prescribed radii defined at their vertices. The rendering pipeline was introduced to visualize such surfaces in real-time, addressing challenges in robust intersection, efficient primitive selection, and high computational cost. The method builds on previous work in metaballs rendering and transparency using A-buffers. It improves upon Sherstyuk's fast ray-tracing algorithm for convolution surfaces. name: Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints
head: 2-Lipschitz Sphere Tracing, Gradient-assisted Sphere Tracing
body:
Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints is an optimization for ray marching that uses the local gradient of the Signed Distance Function (SDF) to compute larger, safer step sizes than standard sphere tracing, particularly near silhouettes and backward-facing surfaces. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by combining the first and second Lipschitz constraints to account for curvature, and from its siblings like Adaptive Lipschitz Constant (ALC) by explicitly leveraging gradient magnitude rather than just bounding volume hierarchies or global constants. Inputs: Ray origin O, ray direction D, SDF function f(p), and its gradient 
abla f(p). Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray. Data Structures: p: Current 3D position (vec3). gradf: Gradient vector 
abla f(p) (vec3). L: Local Lipschitz constant bound for the gradient magnitude (scalar). L2: Local Lipschitz constant bound for the Hessian/curvature (scalar). Steps: 1. Initialize p = O. 2. Evaluate f(p) and 
abla f(p). 3. Calculate the standard sphere tracing step size bound using the gradient magnitude: s1 =  rac{f(p)}{|
abla f(p)|} This step assumes the function is 1-Lipschitz with constant |
abla f(p)|. 4. Apply the 2-Lipschitz constraint to refine the step size based on curvature bounds. The step size s must satisfy the condition that the function does not change faster than allowed by its second derivative. The refined step size s{final} is derived from the quadratic bound imposed by the 2-Lipschitz property: s{final} = \min \left( s1,  rac{-|
abla f(p)| + \sqrt{|
abla f(p)|^2 + 2 L2 f(p)}}{L2} ight) Where L2 is the bound on the Hessian norm (or the Lipschitz constant of the gradient). Note: If f(p) \le 0, the ray has hit or passed the surface; terminate. 5. Advance the ray: p = p + sfinal D. 6. Repeat from step 2 until convergence or max steps. Parameters: L (Lipschitz constant of f): For FBM, this is dynamically computed using a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) to be much smaller than the global constant. L2 (Lipschitz constant of 
abla f): Bounding the curvature. For FBM, this requires careful handling of cascaded sums. Pitfalls: Standard formulations of the 2-Lipschitz constraint (e.g., [AZ23]) can cause slowdowns for certain functions like FBM if the gradient and Lipschitz constants for cascaded sums are not handled properly. A specific formulation is required to fix this issue. Precision issues may arise when f(p) is very small near the surface. Pseudocode: def gradientbasedspheretrace(O, D, f, gradf, L2bound, maxsteps=100): p = O for in range(maxsteps): val = f(p) if val <= 0.0: return p grad = gradf(p) gradnorm = length(grad) if gradnorm < 1e-6: step = 1e-4 else: step1 = val / gradnorm if L2bound > 1e-6: discriminant = gradnorm gradnorm + 2 L2bound val if discriminant < 0: discriminant = 0 step2 = (-gradnorm + sqrt(discriminant)) / L2bound step = min(step1, step2) else: step = step1 p = p + step D return p Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching is a ray-surface intersection method that formulates intersection as a curvature-accelerated contraction operator on the Eikonal distance field to solve the computational stall of sphere tracing near grazing angles and silhouette edges. It sets itself apart from its parent, Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints, by selectively activating second-order Halley contraction only within grazing silhouette horizons while maintaining single-query Lipschitz advances in open space, thereby truncating the grazing stall tail by up to 4×. Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm for implicit surfaces that computes a local Lipschitz bound \lambda(e) for each ray segment e to determine safe, adaptive step sizes, significantly reducing field function queries compared to global bound methods. Unlike Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints which uses gradient magnitude to estimate step size, Segment Tracing rigorously bounds the gradient of the deformed field and the Jacobian of the deformation map to guarantee no surface intersections are skipped, even under complex non-linear warping. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of SDF evaluations per ray compared to standard sphere tracing, especially near silhouettes. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the BVH if used for dynamic Lipschitz constants. Measured Performance: On opaque or constant semi-transparent scenes, speedups up to 12-fold compared to classical sphere tracing are achieved when combined with BVH-based FBM acceleration. On non-constant density volumetric scenes, up to 2-fold speedup is observed. Strengths: Effective near silhouettes and grazing angles where standard sphere tracing takes very small steps. Compatible with semi-transparency and hypertextures. Limitations: Requires gradient computation, which may be expensive for some procedural functions. Standard 2-Lipschitz formulations can slow down FBM if not properly implemented. When to use: When rendering high-frequency procedural noise (FBM) or complex implicit surfaces where grazing angles are common. When not to use: If gradient computation is prohibitively expensive or if the function is not differentiable everywhere (e.g., Perlin noise with abs() requires special handling). Originating from the work on accelerating sphere tracing for procedural volumetric noise, this method builds on the 2-Lipschitz sphere tracing formulation by Aubry et al. [AZ23]. The specific improvements for FBM cascaded sums and the corrected formulation for gradient-based steps were proposed in "Fast sphere tracing of procedural volumetric noise for very large and detailed scenes". It is used in real-time rendering of complex volumetric fields and animated content. name: Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching
head: Curvature-Bounded Contraction, Fixed-Point Projection for Real-Time Implicit Surface Rendering
body: Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching is a ray-surface intersection method that formulates intersection as a curvature-accelerated contraction operator on the Eikonal distance field to solve the computational stall of sphere tracing near grazing angles and silhouette edges. It sets itself apart from its parent, Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints, by selectively activating second-order Halley contraction only within grazing silhouette horizons while maintaining single-query Lipschitz advances in open space, thereby truncating the grazing stall tail by up to 4×. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a Signed Distance Function (SDF) f(\mathbf{x}) and its derivatives; a fixed-point invariance threshold \epsilon = 10^{-15}. Output: The intersection distance t along the ray, or a failure flag if no intersection is found within bounds. Data Structures: Ray State: Current position \mathbf{r}(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}, current distance estimate t{curr}, and previous distance estimate t{prev}. Derivatives: Directional first-order derivative f' and second-order derivative f'' evaluated along the ray trajectory. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialization: Set initial step size t based on the initial SDF value f(\mathbf{o}). Set t{prev} = 0. 2. Loop Condition: While the fixed-point invariance condition ||P{hit}^2 - P{hit}|| > \epsilon is not met, where P{hit} is the contraction operator: a. Evaluate Derivatives: Compute the directional first-order derivative f' and second-order derivative f'' at the current position \mathbf{r}(t) along the ray direction \mathbf{d}. b. Determine Contraction Mode: i. If the ray is in open space (not near a grazing silhouette horizon), execute a single-query Lipschitz advance. ii. If the ray is within a grazing silhouette horizon, activate second-order Halley contraction. c. Compute Step: i. Lipschitz Advance: Compute step size \Delta t bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints derived from f'. ii. Halley Contraction: Compute step size \Delta t using a rational Halley formula involving f, f', and f'', bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints. d. Update Position: Update t{prev} = t and t = t + \Delta t. 3. Termination: Upon entering the root neighborhood, the operator achieves terminal orthogonal projection with fixed-point invariance. Return t. Formulas: Fixed-Point Invariance Condition: ||P{hit}^2 - P{hit}|| \le 10^{-15} where P{hit} is the contraction operator mapping the current distance estimate to the next. Halley Contraction (Rational): The specific rational Halley formula is not explicitly detailed in the sources, but it utilizes directional first- and second-order derivatives f' and f'' along the ray trajectory. It is bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints. Lipschitz Safety Constraints: The step size is bounded by dynamic Lipschitz constraints derived from the gradient of the SDF. The exact Lipschitz constant calculation is not provided, but it ensures the step does not overshoot the surface. Parameters: Fixed-point invariance threshold: 10^{-15}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Grazing Angles: Standard sphere tracing suffers from severe iteration inflation (40–60+ steps per ray) and tail-latency spikes near surface horizons because the spatial advance is conservatively bounded by radial distance \phi(r(t)), which approaches zero even when the ray intersects geometry far along its directional path. Idempotent Eikonal Ray Marching mitigates this by selectively activating second-order Halley contraction. Precision: The fixed-point invariance threshold of 10^{-15} ensures high precision in the final projection. Derivative Evaluation: Accurate evaluation of directional first- and second-order derivatives is critical for the Halley contraction. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Args: rayorigin: Initial ray origin point. raydirection: Normalized ray direction vector. sdf: Function returning SDF value and derivatives at a point. threshold: Fixed-point invariance threshold (default 1e-15). Returns: Intersection distance t, or None if no intersection found. """ t = 0.0 tprev = 0.0 # Initial SDF evaluation fval, fprime, fdoubleprime = sdf(rayorigin + t raydirection) while True: # Evaluate derivatives at current position currentpos = rayorigin + t raydirection fval, fprime, fdoubleprime = sdf(currentpos) # Determine contraction mode # Note: The specific logic for "grazing silhouette horizon" detection # is not detailed in the sources. Placeholder for silhouette detection logic. isgrazing = detectgrazinghorizon(fprime, fdoubleprime) # if isgrazing: # Activate second-order Halley contraction # Rational Halley formula using f, f', f'' # Formula not explicitly given in sources. Placeholder for Halley step calculation. deltat = halleystep(fval, fprime, fdoubleprime) # else: # Execute single-query Lipschitz advance # Bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints # Formula not explicitly given in sources. Placeholder for Lipschitz step calculation. deltat = lipschitzstep(fval, fprime) # # Update position tprev = t t = t + deltat # Check fixed-point invariance # Phit is the contraction operator. # We approximate Phit^2 - Phit by checking the change in t. # Note: The exact definition of Phit in terms of t is not provided. # Placeholder for fixed-point check. if abs(t - tprev) < threshold: break # Safety break for infinite loops if t > MAXDISTANCE: return None return t def detectgrazinghorizon(fprime, fdoubleprime): """ Placeholder for grazing silhouette horizon detection logic. The sources mention selective activation of Halley contraction in these regions, but do not specify the exact condition. """ # Example heuristic: high curvature or specific gradient alignment return abs(fdoubleprime) > SOMETHRESHOLD def halleystep(f, fprime, fdoubleprime): """ Placeholder for rational Halley step calculation. The sources mention a rational Halley contraction bounded by Lipschitz constraints, but do not provide the exact formula. """ # Standard Halley's method for root finding: # deltat = -f / (f' - (f fdoubleprime) / (2 fprime)) # However, this must be bounded by Lipschitz constraints. if abs(fprime) < 1e-10: return 0.0 deltat = -f / (fprime - (f fdoubleprime) / (2 fprime)) return deltat def lipschitzstep(f, fprime): """ Placeholder for Lipschitz step calculation. The sources mention single-query Lipschitz advances bounded by dynamic Lipschitz safety constraints. The exact formula is not provided. """ # Standard Lipschitz bound for SDF: # deltat = f / |fprime| (or similar, depending on Lipschitz constant) if abs(fprime) < 1e-10: return 0.0 deltat = f / abs(fprime) return deltat A sibling method that uses local Lipschitz bounds for step sizing. name: Segment Tracing with Local Lipschitz Bounds
head: Local Lipschitz Segment Tracing, Segment Tracing Using Local Lipschitz Bounds
body:
Segment Tracing is a ray marching algorithm for implicit surfaces that computes a local Lipschitz bound \lambda(e) for each ray segment e to determine safe, adaptive step sizes, significantly reducing field function queries compared to global bound methods. Unlike Gradient-based Sphere Tracing with Lipschitz Constraints which uses gradient magnitude to estimate step size, Segment Tracing rigorously bounds the gradient of the deformed field and the Jacobian of the deformation map to guarantee no surface intersections are skipped, even under complex non-linear warping. Inputs: A ray defined by origin o and direction d; a scalar field defined by a Blob Tree (sum of primitives, potentially with deformation operators); scene bounding box. Outputs: Intersection distance t, accumulated opacity \alpha, and accumulated color C. Blob Tree Node Hierarchy The scalar field is represented as a tree. Two primary node types are defined in the reference implementation: 1. BlobTreePoint (Primitive) Vector c: Center of the primitive. double r: Radius of the primitive. double e: Energy (intensity magnitude). Box box: Axis-aligned bounding box enclosing the primitive. double k: Precomputed global Lipschitz constant for this primitive. 2. BlobTreeBlend (Composite) BlobTreeNode e[2]: Pointers to left and right child nodes. Box box: Bounding box of the union of children. double k: Global Lipschitz constant (sum of children's k). Does not require additional memory structures like voxel grids. CPU: On Intel Core i7 3GHz, Segment Tracing reduced queries significantly for Chandelier and Temple models. Use for complex implicit surfaces with non-linear deformations (warping) where global bounds are too conservative. Avoid for simple, uniformly distributed primitives where Ray or Sphere variations are faster. The method builds upon Sphere Tracing and Lipschitz-constrained ray marching. It specifically addresses the inefficiency of global Lipschitz bounds in the presence of local variations in field complexity and deformation. The technique is particularly effective for blob trees with deformation operators (e.g., tapering). Rendering complex implicit surfaces defined by blob trees. name: Lipschitz Step Size Ray Marching
head: Hart's Sphere Tracing, Ray Marching with Lipschitz Step Size, Ray marching with Lipschitz bound, SDF ray marching with Lipschitz constant, Safe Raymarching with Lipschitz Bounds, Step-size ray marching
body: Lipschitz Step Size Ray Marching is a robust algorithm for finding the first intersection between a ray and an implicit surface defined by a signed distance field (SDF) f(\mathbf{p}) = 0. It guarantees that the ray never penetrates or overshoots the surface by computing the maximum safe step size using a global Lipschitz constant \lambda. Unlike adaptive methods that estimate local gradients, this method relies on a pre-computed global bound, making it simple to implement and numerically stable, though potentially less efficient for complex scenes with varying feature scales. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{u}. Ray domain bounds [t{min}, t{max}] (intersection with the scene bounding volume \Omega). Global Lipschitz constant \lambda for the field function f over \Omega. Hit threshold \mu (distance tolerance). Maximum iteration count N{max}. Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray, or a failure indicator if no intersection is found within bounds or iterations. Ray: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and direction \mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^3 with \|\mathbf{u}\| = 1. Field Function: f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, representing the signed distance to the implicit surface. Parameters: \lambda: Scalar, the global Lipschitz bound. Typical value: 1.0 for normalized SDFs. \mu: Scalar, the convergence threshold. Typical value: 0.01. N{max}: Integer, maximum steps. Typical value: 100. A function f: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R} is Lipschitz continuous over a domain \Omega if there exists a constant \lambda \ge 0 such that for all \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{q} \in \Omega: |f(\mathbf{p}) - f(\mathbf{q})| \leq \lambda \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}\| The constant \lambda is the minimum bound satisfying this inequality. 1. Initialization: Compute the intersection of the ray with the domain \Omega to determine [t{min}, t{max}]. Set current distance t = t{min}. 2. Iteration Loop: While t < t{max} and iteration count < N{max}: 1. Evaluate the field function at the current point on the ray: \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{u}, then d = f(\mathbf{p}). 2. Termination Check: If |d| < \mu, the ray has converged to the surface. Return t as the intersection distance. 3. Step Calculation: Compute the step size s using the Lipschitz bound: s = \frac{|d|}{\lambda} This step size guarantees that the next point is not closer to the surface than the current distance allows, preventing overshoot. 4. Advance: Update t \leftarrow t + s. 3. Failure: If the loop terminates without satisfying the hit condition, return failure (no intersection found within bounds or iterations). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lipschitzraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, fieldfunc, lambdaval, mu, maxiterations): """ Ray march using Lipschitz step size. Args: rayorigin: Vector3, origin of the ray. raydirection: Vector3, normalized direction of the ray. tmin: float, minimum distance along ray (start of domain). tmax: float, maximum distance along ray (end of domain). fieldfunc: function, f(p) -> float, returns signed distance. lambdaval: float, global Lipschitz constant. mu: float, hit threshold. maxiterations: int, maximum number of steps. Returns: float: Intersection distance t, or None if not found. """ t = tmin for i in range(maxiterations): # Check domain bounds before evaluation if t > tmax: return None # 1. Evaluate field at current position p = rayorigin + raydirection t d = fieldfunc(p) # 2. Check for intersection if abs(d) < mu: return t # 3. Compute step size step = abs(d) / lambdaval # 4. Advance along ray t = t + step return None Grazing Rays: The algorithm may require an arbitrarily large number of steps for rays that graze the surface, as the step size s becomes very small relative to the remaining distance. Large Radius Differences: When applied to primitives with significantly different radii (e.g., SCALIS primitives), the Lipschitz constant per primitive is inversely proportional to the prescribed radius, creating unnecessarily small steps globally. Density Fields: When used with density fields instead of distance fields, the algorithm suffers from null gradients near kernel support boundaries and difficulty in computing tight Lipschitz bounds for N-ary summation operators. Overestimation of \lambda: If \lambda is significantly larger than the true local Lipschitz constant, the step size s becomes smaller than necessary, increasing the number of iterations without improving accuracy. Discusses the balance between step size precision and computational cost. Extends this method by computing local Lipschitz bounds to improve efficiency. Uses gradient information to refine step sizes while maintaining safety guarantees. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of iterations required to converge. N depends on the scene complexity, ray angle, and the tightness of \lambda. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the storage for the field function. Strengths: Guaranteed no penetration of the surface. Simple implementation, no pre-processing required. Robust for direct content creation in shaders. Limitations: Inefficient for grazing rays. For SCALIS primitives with large radius differences, the Lipschitz constant per primitive is inversely proportional to the prescribed radius, creating unnecessarily small steps globally. Not suitable for density fields with complex kernel compositions without modification. When to Use: Ideal for simple SDFs and real-time shaders where simplicity and robustness are prioritized over maximum performance. When Not to Use: Scenes with large variations in feature scale, grazing ray scenarios, or density fields with complex kernel functions. The algorithm was introduced by Hart in 1996, often referred to as "Hart's Sphere Tracing", and formalized with the Lipschitz bound guarantee. It belongs to the ray-marching family and is widely used in real-time rendering, including games and shaders, due to its simplicity and robustness. Extensions such as Segment Tracing have been proposed to address its limitations by using local Lipschitz bounds. name: Compute Minimal Sample Distance Per Pixel
head: ComputeMinimalSamplePerPixel, Projected Cell Axis Step Size
body: Computes the minimal sample distance per pixel by projecting each dataset cell axis onto the viewport, accounting for camera and volume transforms. It determines the smallest step size required to ensure that the sampling grid aligns with the projected geometry of the volume cells, preventing aliasing or gaps due to oblique viewing angles. It differs from standard distance-field ray marching step rules by explicitly evaluating the angular span of a voxel's extent from the camera center to determine sampling density, rather than relying solely on Euclidean distance or fixed grid spacing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: renderer: A pointer to the rendering context providing camera position, orientation, and viewport dimensions. volume: A pointer to the volume object providing dataset geometry (cell spacing) and transformation matrices. scalars: The scalar data array associated with the volume. Outputs: minsampledistance: The computed minimal step size \Delta t{min} for the current pixel/ray. ignoreflag: A boolean indicating if the step size calculation should be skipped due to degenerate alignment. Data Structures: The method relies on the internal state of the vtkRenderer and vtkVolume objects. Specifically, it accesses: Camera transformation matrix (M{cam}) and projection parameters. Volume transformation matrix (M{vol}) and extent/spacing information. The CellFlag property to determine if scalars are point or cell-based. Steps: 1. Validation: Verify that valid scalar data exists on the input. If scalars is null or if CellFlag indicates field data (which is unsupported), the method fails. 2. Transform Preparation: Ensure the volume data is transformed into the correct coordinate space. This involves updating the TransformedInput and applying the volume's transformation matrix. 3. Axis Projection: For each of the three dataset cell axes (x, y, z): a. Define the axis vector \mathbf{a}i in world space, scaled by the cell spacing si. b. Project \mathbf{a}i onto the view plane using the camera's orientation. This involves transforming the axis vector by the inverse of the camera's rotation matrix. c. Calculate the projected length Li of the axis on the viewport. 4. Degeneracy Check: If any axis is degenerate (aligned with the view direction), set IgnoreSampleDistancePerPixel to true and return a default or infinite step size. 5. Distance Calculation: Compute the minimal sample distance as the minimum of the projected lengths of the three axes, potentially scaled by the pixel aspect ratio and viewport dimensions to convert from world units to ray parameter t units. \Delta t{min} = \min(Lx, Ly, Lz) Note: The exact scaling factor depends on the specific camera projection model (perspective vs. orthographic) and is derived from the renderer's state. 6. Clamping: Apply any global minimum or maximum step size constraints defined by the renderer or volume properties. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeminimalsampledistance(renderer, volume): # 1. Validation scalars = volume.getscalars() if scalars is None: raise Error("No scalars found on input.") cellflag = volume.getcellflag() if cellflag == 2: # Field data not supported raise Error("Only point or cell scalar support - found field scalars instead.") # 2. Transform Preparation # Ensure volume data is updated and transformed volume.transformedinput.update() volume.transformedinput.setupdateextenttowholeextent() volume.transformedinput.update() # 3. Get Camera and Volume Transforms cammatrix = renderer.getcameramatrix() volmatrix = volume.gettransformationmatrix() # 4. Axis Projection # Get cell spacing from volume geometry spacing = volume.getspacing() # [sx, sy, sz] # Define axis vectors in local space axes = [ [spacing[0], 0, 0], [0, spacing[1], 0], [0, 0, spacing[2]] ] minprojectedlength = infinity for axis in axes: # Transform axis to world space worldaxis = volmatrix.transformvector(axis) # Project onto view plane (inverse camera rotation) # Assuming cammatrix includes rotation; extract rotation part invcamrot = cammatrix.getinverserotation() viewaxis = invcamrot.transformvector(worldaxis) # Calculate projected length on viewport # This depends on camera projection (perspective/orthographic) # For perspective, project to near plane or use angular span projectedlen = calculateprojectedlength(viewaxis, renderer) if projectedlen < minprojectedlength: minprojectedlength = projectedlen # 5. Degeneracy Check # If any axis is aligned with view direction, projected length might be zero or invalid # Check alignment with view direction vector viewdir = cammatrix.getviewdirection() for axis in axes: worldaxis = volmatrix.transformvector(axis) if isaligned(worldaxis, viewdir): return infinity, True # IgnoreSampleDistancePerPixel = true # 6. Return Result return minprojectedlength, False Parameters: renderer: VTK renderer pointer. volume: VTK volume pointer. CellFlag: Integer flag indicating scalar type (0: point, 1: cell, 2: field). Edge Cases: Degenerate Axes: If a dataset axis is parallel to the view direction, the projected length is zero or undefined. The method sets IgnoreSampleDistancePerPixel to true to avoid division by zero or invalid step sizes. Field Data: If the input scalars are field data, the method fails as it only supports point or cell scalars. Computes a scalar metric representing the projected size of a voxel relative to the camera, primarily used for Level-of-Detail (LOD) decisions and step size adaptation in volume rendering. It differs from standard distance-field ray marching step rules by explicitly evaluating the angular span of a voxel's extent from the camera center to determine sampling density, rather than relying solely on Euclidean distance or fixed grid spacing. L1 Voxel Thickness Slice Stepping is a method for determining the distance between consecutive oblique slices in a volume viewport to ensure no voxel overlap and no gaps. It uses the L1 norm (Manhattan distance) of the projected voxel spacing vector along the view plane normal, rather than the L2 norm (Euclidean distance). It sets itself apart from its sibling Projected Voxel Size / LOD Calculation by focusing on the discrete sampling step for slice positioning rather than continuous resolution estimation, and from its parent Compute Minimal Sample Distance Per Pixel by specifically addressing the overlap defect inherent in L2-based stepping for oblique angles. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it involves a fixed number of matrix-vector multiplications and comparisons for the three axes. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. Strengths: Ensures consistent sampling density across the volume regardless of viewing angle, reducing aliasing artifacts in oblique views. Limitations: Computationally more expensive than fixed-step methods due to matrix transformations. Requires access to camera and volume transformation matrices. When to Use: When high-quality volume rendering is required with oblique viewing angles, and aliasing is a concern. When Not to Use: For real-time applications with strict performance constraints where fixed-step or simpler adaptive methods are sufficient. This method is implemented in the VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster project, an unofficial extension to the Visualization Toolkit (VTK). It addresses the limitations of standard ray marching step sizes in multi-volume rendering scenarios where volumes may have different orientations and scales. bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, https://github.com/bozorgi/VTKMultiVolumeRayCaster, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Projected Voxel Size / LOD Calculation
head: ComputeVoxelSize
body: Projected Voxel Size / LOD Calculation computes a scalar metric representing the projected size of a voxel relative to the camera, primarily used for Level-of-Detail (LOD) decisions and step size adaptation in volume rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Camera position (\mathbf{C}), voxel center (\mathbf{V}), and voxel half-size vector (\mathbf{h}). Output: A scalar projected size metric S. Data Structures: Voxel geometry is defined by its center \mathbf{V} and half-extents \mathbf{h} = (hx, hy, hz). Camera geometry is defined by origin \mathbf{C}. Steps: 1. Compute the lower-left (LL) and upper-right (UR) corners of the voxel half-size box: \mathbf{P}{LL} = \mathbf{V} - \mathbf{h} and \mathbf{P}{UR} = \mathbf{V} + \mathbf{h}. 2. Compute vectors from the camera position to these corners: \mathbf{v}{LL} = \mathbf{P}{LL} - \mathbf{C} and \mathbf{v}{UR} = \mathbf{P}{UR} - \mathbf{C}. 3. Normalize these vectors to obtain \mathbf{u}{LL} and \mathbf{u}{UR}. Guard against zero-length vectors to prevent division by zero. 4. Calculate the dot product of the normalized vectors. 5. Return S = 1.0 - \mathbf{u}{LL} \cdot \mathbf{u}{UR}. Formula: S = 1 - \mathbf{u}{LL} \cdot \mathbf{u}{UR} Where: S is the projected size metric. \mathbf{u}{LL} is the normalized vector from the camera to the lower-left corner of the voxel. \mathbf{u}{UR} is the normalized vector from the camera to the upper-right corner of the voxel. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Camera at Voxel Center: If the camera is located exactly at the voxel center, the vectors are identical, leading to \mathbf{u}{LL} \cdot \mathbf{u}{UR} = 1 and S = 0. Near-Plane Degeneracy: The metric lacks explicit clamping or fallback for degenerate near-plane cases where the voxel intersects the camera plane. Division by zero during normalization must be guarded. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computeprojectedvoxelsize(camerapos, voxelcenter, voxelhalfsize): """ Computes the projected size metric for a voxel. Args: camerapos: (x, y, z) camera position. voxelcenter: (x, y, z) voxel center. voxelhalfsize: (x, y, z) half-extents of the voxel. Returns: S: Scalar projected size metric. """ # 1. Compute corners of the voxel half-size box pll = (voxelcenter[0] - voxelhalfsize[0], voxelcenter[1] - voxelhalfsize[1], voxelcenter[2] - voxelhalfsize[2]) pur = (voxelcenter[0] + voxelhalfsize[0], voxelcenter[1] + voxelhalfsize[1], voxelcenter[2] + voxelhalfsize[2]) # 2. Compute vectors from camera to corners vll = (pll[0] - camerapos[0], pll[1] - camerapos[1], pll[2] - camerapos[2]) vur = (pur[0] - camerapos[0], pur[1] - camerapos[1], pur[2] - camerapos[2]) # 3. Normalize vectors (guard against zero length) lenll = math.sqrt(vll[0]2 + vll[1]2 + vll[2]2) lenur = math.sqrt(vur[0]2 + vur[1]2 + vur[2]2) if lenll == 0.0 or lenur == 0.0: return 0.0 # Degenerate case fallback ull = (vll[0]/lenll, vll[1]/lenll, vll[2]/lenll) uur = (vur[0]/lenur, vur[1]/lenur, vur[2]/lenur) # 4 & 5. Compute dot product and return metric dot = ull[0]uur[0] + ull[1]uur[1] + ull[2]uur[2] return 1.0 - dot Computes a per-Gaussian scale factor based on the Euclidean distance from the camera center and the camera's focal length, primarily used for anti-aliasing or level-of-detail (LOD) adjustments in Gaussian splatting. It differs from standard projected voxel size calculations by operating on parametric Gaussian primitives rather than volumetric voxels, scaling the representation size inversely to the focal length to maintain consistent screen-space coverage. Determines the minimum reproducible voxel size in a light field display based on distance from the screen and beam angular divergence, dictating volume sampling rates. It differs from standard projected voxel size calculations by incorporating the physical properties of the light field display, specifically the angular size of light beams, to define a distance-dependent resolution limit. It is chosen when rendering for light field displays where spatial resolution degrades with depth. The formula is s(z) = s0 + 2|z| \tan(\Phi/2), where s(z) is the minimum voxel size at distance z from the screen, s0 is the pixel size on the screen surface, and \Phi is the finite angular size of light beams leaving the screen. Calculates the maximum sampling rate across all cameras for each voxel, based on voxel length and sample interval derived from depth. It differs by aggregating sampling requirements from multiple camera views to determine a global maximum rate for a voxel. It is chosen in multi-view reconstruction or training scenarios where voxel density must be consistent across all viewpoints. The method initializes a maxsamprate tensor of size len(octreepaths) with zeros on CUDA, calculates the z-distance from voxel centers to camera positions along the lookat vector, identifies visible voxels where nduplicates > 0 and zdist > nearplane, calculates the sample interval as zdist cam.pixsize, computes the sample rate as voxlengths / sampinterval, and updates maxsamprate with the maximum of the current value and the new rate. The nearplane parameter defaults to 0.02 to filter voxels too close to the camera. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Provides a geometrically intuitive measure of voxel importance relative to the viewer. Limitations: The basic metric lacks robustness for near-plane cases and requires careful corner selection. When to use: Use for LOD management in volume rendering where angular coverage is a key factor. Use max sample rate for multi-view consistent voxelization. The concept of projected voxel size for LOD is discussed in the context of voxel visualization and ray marching. The depth-dependent spatial resolution is derived from research on GPU-accelerated direct volume rendering on interactive light field displays. name: MIP Scale Computation
head: Gaussian Scale Factor Computation, MIP Scale
body: Computes a per-Gaussian scale factor based on the Euclidean distance from the camera center and the camera's focal length, primarily used for anti-aliasing or level-of-detail adjustments in Gaussian splatting. It differs from standard projected voxel size calculations by operating on parametric Gaussian primitives rather than volumetric voxels. Inputs: viewpointcamera: Object containing cameracenter (3D vector), FoVx (horizontal field of view), and imagewidth (pixel width). pc: Gaussian model object containing getxyz (tensor of shape [N, 3] representing Gaussian centers). Outputs: scales: Tensor of shape [N, 1] containing the computed scale factor for each Gaussian. Data Structures: distpp: Tensor of shape [N, 1] storing Euclidean distances. focal: Scalar value representing the focal length in pixels. Steps: 1. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the camera center to each Gaussian center: \text{dist\pp}i = \| \mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{c} \|. 2. Convert the horizontal field of view (\text{FoV}x) and image width (W) to focal length (f) using a helper function. 3. Compute the scale factor by dividing the distance by the focal length: si = \frac{\text{dist\pp}i}{f}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def fov2focal(fov, width): """Convert horizontal field of view to focal length in pixels.""" return width / (2 math.tan(fov / 2)) def mipscales(viewpointcamera, pc): """ Compute MIP scales for Gaussian splatting. Args: viewpointcamera: Object with attributes cameracenter, FoVx, imagewidth. pc: GaussianModel object with attribute getxyz (tensor [N, 3]). Returns: scales: Tensor [N, 1] of scale factors. """ xyz = pc.getxyz cameracenter = viewpointcamera.cameracenter cameracenterexpanded = cameracenter.repeat(xyz.shape[0], 1) distpp = torch.norm(xyz - cameracenterexpanded, dim=1, keepdim=True) focal = fov2focal(viewpointcamera.FoVx, viewpointcamera.imagewidth) return distpp / focal Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Distance: If a Gaussian center coincides with the camera center, the distance is zero, resulting in a scale of zero. FOV Units: The fov2focal function assumes radians. Focal Length Zero: If FoVx is 0, tan(0) is 0, leading to division by zero. This variant retrieves pre-filtered 3D scales and opacities directly from the Gaussian model via get3dfilteredscalesandopacities() rather than computing scale from camera distance alone. It returns the squeezed scales and opacities. It introduces a parameter filter2dkernelsize: float = 0.1. Unlike the standard method, it may ignore standard opacity calculation in certain status returns, returning None for opacity in specific paths. Not given in the sources. The method originates from the Gaussian Splatting literature, specifically implementations dealing with multi-resolution pyramid (MIP) rendering to reduce aliasing. name: L1 Voxel Thickness Slice Stepping
head: L1 Slice Step Measure, L1 slice step, getVoxelThicknessAlongNormal
body: L1 Voxel Thickness Slice Stepping is a method for determining the distance between consecutive oblique slices in a volume viewport to ensure no voxel overlap and no gaps. It uses the L1 norm (Manhattan distance) of the projected voxel spacing vector along the view plane normal, rather than the L2 norm (Euclidean distance). It sets itself apart from its sibling Projected Voxel Size / LOD Calculation by focusing on the discrete overlap test of voxel lattices rather than continuous projection scaling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: imageVolume (voxel grid with spacing vector s), viewPlaneNormal (n). Output: spacingInNormalDirection (scalar step distance Tv). Data Structures: imageVolume: Contains spacing array s = [s0, s1, s2] representing voxel dimensions along the three axes. viewPlaneNormal: Normalized 3D vector n = [n0, n1, n2]. Basis vectors ai: Standard unit vectors [1,0,0], [0,1,0], [0,0,1]. Formulas: The correct step size Tv is the L1 voxel thickness: Tv = \sum{i=0}^{2} |n \cdot ai| \cdot si = \sum{i=0}^{2} |ni| \cdot si The historically incorrect L2 measure Sn is: Sn = \sqrt{\sum{i=0}^{2} (n \cdot ai \cdot si)^2} = \sqrt{\sum{i=0}^{2} (ni \cdot si)^2} Parameters: rendering.sliceStepMeasure: Configuration flag. Defaults to 'l2' (historic behavior). Set to 'l1' to enable this method. Steps: 1. Extract the voxel spacing vector s from imageVolume. 2. Extract the view plane normal vector n. 3. Compute the L1 thickness Tv using the formula above. 4. Return Tv as the slice step distance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def getvoxelthicknessalongnormal(imagevolume, viewplanenormal): """ Computes the L1 voxel thickness along the view plane normal. imagevolume: object with attribute 'spacing' (list/tuple of 3 floats) viewplanenormal: list/tuple of 3 floats (assumed normalized) """ spacing = imagevolume.spacing n = viewplanenormal # Calculate L1 thickness: sum of absolute component projections scaled by spacing thickness = 0.0 for i in range(3): thickness += abs(n[i]) spacing[i] return thickness def computeslicestep(imagevolume, viewplanenormal, measuretype='l2'): """ Wrapper to select step measure based on configuration. """ if measuretype == 'l1': return getvoxelthicknessalongnormal(imagevolume, viewplanenormal) else: # Historic L2 behavior spacing = imagevolume.spacing n = viewplanenormal sumsq = 0.0 for i in range(3): sumsq += (n[i] spacing[i]) 2 return math.sqrt(sumsq) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overlap with L2: Using Sn causes consecutive oblique slices to share voxels because Sn < Tv for oblique normals. This results in 22-40% overlap for oblique normals. 45-Degree Visibility Loss: At specific angles like 45 degrees with isotropic voxels, using the L1 step with a symmetric strict depth test (|d| < h - \epsilon) causes every second plane of the voxel lattice to be hidden (0% coverage for those planes) because voxel centers fall exactly on slab boundaries. Axis-Aligned: When the normal is parallel to a voxel axis, Tv = Sn, so both measures yield the same result. Decouples slice grid topology from the volume bounding box by anchoring to the focal point. Choose this when misaligned slice indexing causes visual artifacts in oblique views. Time Complexity: O(1) relative to volume size; depends only on the number of dimensions (3). Memory Complexity: O(1). Performance: Eliminates voxel overlap artifacts in oblique views. Requires a half-open depth test to avoid visibility loss at 45 degrees. Strengths: Ensures zero overlap and 100% coverage for a single plane fill. Correctly identifies the minimal sample distance required to avoid re-rendering the same voxels. Limitations: The step size Tv is larger than Sn, which may increase the number of slices required to cover the volume extent. Requires careful implementation of the depth test (half-open, non-symmetric) to prevent missing voxel planes at commensurate angles. When to use: When rendering oblique slices where voxel overlap is unacceptable. When not to use: When legacy behavior matching the L2 step is required, or when the depth test implementation does not support half-open intervals. Originating from issues in the Cornerstone3D library (Issue #2912, PR #2743), this method addresses a defect where volume viewports stepped oblique slices by the L2 spacing, causing the same voxels to appear on multiple adjacent slices. The issue was identified by wayfarer3130 in September 2026. The correction involves implementing requirement I1 (L1 measure) and I4 (half-open depth test) to satisfy the digital plane properties of voxel lattices.
