name: Time-Aware Adaptive Step Size
head: Ray Step Size Steering, Ray step size adaptation, Use Case 1
body: Time-Aware Adaptive Step Size is a technique for controlling rendering frame rate by dynamically adjusting the ray step size based on a predicted rendering time. It solves the problem of maintaining a target frame rate during interactive exploration, particularly when scene complexity changes due to camera movement or transfer function adjustments. It sets itself apart from reactive methods like OLP and PID controllers by predicting rendering time proactively before rendering each frame, thereby avoiding the one-frame lag inherent in reactive approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Camera path, transfer function \kappa, total duration T, target rendering time t{target}, reference step size \delta{ref}, time prediction model ENTIRE, and the volume dataset. Outputs: Adapted step size \delta{adapt} for each frame, which is used by the renderer. Data Structures: Time Prediction Model (ENTIRE): A learned model that takes volume, pose, and transfer function as input and outputs predicted time t{pred}. Impact Function (G(\cdot)): A function modeling the relative impact of ray step size on rendering time, determined experimentally by sampling rendering times of different volumes/poses and normalizing with respect to \delta{ref}. Inverse Impact Function (G^{-1}(\cdot)): The inverse of G, used to calculate the required step size adjustment. Parameters: \delta{ref}: Reference ray step size used for normalization and as the starting point for adaptation. t{pred}: The predicted rendering time for the current frame, obtained from the ENTIRE model. t{target}: The target rendering time for the frame (e.g., 25 ms for 40 FPS). G(\cdot): Function modeling relative impact of step size on time. Numbered Steps: 1. Start a timer for the total duration T. 2. While the current timer value is less than T: a. Get the current camera pose from the path at the current timer value. b. Get the current transfer function \kappa at the current timer value. c. Predict the rendering time t{pred} using the ENTIRE model with the volume, current pose, and current transfer function. d. Calculate the adapted step size \delta{adapt} using the formula: \delta{adapt} = \delta{ref} G^{-1}\left(\frac{t{target}}{t{pred}}\right) e. Render the volume using the adapted step size \delta{adapt}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def timeawareadaptivestepsize(path, transferfunction, totalduration, ttarget, deltaref, Ginv, entiremodel, volume): """ Steers ray step size based on predicted rendering time. Args: path: Function returning camera pose given time. transferfunction: Function returning transfer function given time. totalduration: Total duration T of the animation/path. ttarget: Target rendering time (e.g., 25 ms). deltaref: Reference ray step size. Ginv: Inverse of the impact function G. entiremodel: The ENTIRE time prediction model. volume: The volume dataset. """ currenttime = 0.0 while currenttime < totalduration: # Get current camera pose and transfer function pose = path(currenttime) tf = transferfunction(currenttime) # Predict rendering time using the ENTIRE model # ENTIRE prediction time is less than 0.3 ms tpred = entiremodel(volume, pose, tf) # Calculate adapted step size # Formula: deltaadapt = deltaref Ginv(ttarget / tpred) ratio = ttarget / tpred deltaadapt = deltaref Ginv(ratio) # Render the volume with the adapted step size # renderer(volume, pose, tf, deltaadapt) # [Implementation of renderer is not provided in sources] # Advance time (step size in time domain, not ray step size) # The source implies a loop over time, but doesn't specify the time step. # We assume a small time increment dt for the loop. dt = 0.016 # Example: 60 FPS time step, adjust as needed currenttime += dt Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dramatic Time Changes: OLP and PID controllers struggle with dramatic rendering time changes induced by transfer function adjustments, whereas ENTIRE maintains stable predictions. Manual Tuning: PID controllers require careful manual tuning of proportional, integral, and derivative settings, which differ across volumes, renderers, and hardware. Time-Aware Adaptive Step Size avoids this by using a learned model. Reactive Lag: Reactive methods (OLP, PID) suffer from a one-frame lag because they adjust based on past frames. Time-Aware Adaptive Step Size predicts proactively, avoiding this lag. Misprediction: ENTIRE may occasionally produce fluctuations due to misprediction (e.g., frames 49 and 126 in experiments). Time Complexity: The time prediction using ENTIRE is less than 0.3 ms. The overall frame time is dominated by the rendering step, which is adjusted to meet t{target}. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: In experiments with the CUDA raycaster and Nyx dataset, ENTIRE achieved more stable frame rates compared to OLP and PID controllers, especially during dramatic rendering time changes. The target rendering time was 25 ms (40 FPS). Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Proactive prediction avoids one-frame lag; no manual tuning required; stable frame rates during dramatic changes; high PSNR values with imperceptible degradation in image quality. Limitations: Requires training a learned model (ENTIRE); may have occasional fluctuations due to misprediction; fundamentally different cost profile compared to reactive methods. When to use: Interactive volume exploration where maintaining a target frame rate is essential, especially when transfer functions or camera poses change significantly. When not to use: When a learned model cannot be trained or is unavailable; when strict real-time guarantees are needed without any potential for misprediction-induced fluctuations. Origin: The method is part of the ENTIRE (Learning-based Volume Rendering Time Prediction) framework. History and Development: The method was evaluated in the context of the ENTIRE paper, which compares it against OLP and PID controllers for load balancing and frame rate control. Where it is used: Interactive volume visualization, particularly for exploring volumes with dynamic transfer functions and camera paths. ENTIRE: Learning-based Volume Rendering Time Prediction, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2501.12119, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Termination Criteria
head: Ray Marching Stop Conditions, Loop Break Conditions
body: Termination criteria define the conditions under which a ray-marching loop halts, ensuring the algorithm returns a valid intersection point or correctly identifies a miss without infinite iteration. It solves the problem of premature termination (missing thin geometry), self-intersection artifacts (due to insufficient epsilon), and excessive computation (tracing through empty space or deep into volumes). It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Sphere Tracing by focusing on the general control flow logic applicable to both Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and volumetric density fields, rather than the specific geometric step-size constraints of sphere tracing or the fixed-step simplicity of constant marching. All methods in this family operate on a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized by accumulated distance t. The core loop evaluates a scene function (SDF, density field, or volume texture) at the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to determine the next step size \Delta t and check for termination. Termination Conditions: 1. Surface Hit: The ray has intersected the target geometry. For SDFs, this is typically |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon or f(\mathbf{p}) \le 0. For volumes, this may be a density threshold or opacity accumulation. 2. Escape/Miss: The ray has traveled beyond a maximum distance t{max} or exceeded a maximum iteration count N{max}. 3. Early Termination (Volumes): Accumulated opacity \alpha{acc} exceeds a threshold (e.g., 1 - \epsilon), or accumulated transmission falls below a minimum threshold, allowing the ray to stop early as further contributions are negligible. Step Size Determination: The step size \Delta t is computed based on the local scene properties: SDF-based: \Delta t is often derived from the SDF value f(\mathbf{p}), potentially scaled by a relaxation factor or Lipschitz constant \lambda. Volume-based: \Delta t may be fixed, adaptive based on density gradients, or constrained by minimum/maximum bounds to prevent aliasing or excessive computation. Safety: Steps must be chosen to ensure the ray does not penetrate the surface or skip over significant volumetric features, often requiring conservative clamping. Pseudocode Structure: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchloop(rayorigin, raydirection, scenefunc, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon): t = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return False, t p = rayorigin + raydirection t val = scenefunc(p) # Termination: Hit if ishit(val, epsilon): return True, t # Termination: Early Exit (Volume specific) if isearlyexit(val, t): return False, t # Or handle partial contribution # Step Size Calculation step = computestepsize(val, t, i) # Safety Clamp step = max(step, minstep) step = min(step, maxstep) t += step return False, t Sphere Tracing Termination and Clipping defines the conditions under which a ray-marching loop halts, ensuring the algorithm returns a valid intersection point or correctly identifies a miss without infinite iteration. It solves the problem of premature termination (missing thin geometry), self-intersection artifacts (due to insufficient epsilon), and excessive computation (tracing through empty space or deep into volumes). It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Early Termination by focusing specifically on the geometric constraints of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and the numerical stability of the step-size logic, rather than volumetric opacity accumulation. See Sphere Tracing Termination and Clipping. Ray marching with early termination is a control flow strategy applied to the iterative ray marching loop to halt computation once the ray has interacted with the target scene or exceeded computational limits. It solves the problem of unnecessary processing by breaking the loop when a surface intersection is detected or when the ray has traveled beyond a defined maximum distance. Unlike methods that strictly iterate a fixed number of steps regardless of scene content, this approach dynamically adapts the loop duration based on geometric or volumetric feedback, significantly improving performance for sparse or bounded scenes. See Ray Marching with Early Termination. Definition: An optimization to stop ray marching when the accumulated transmission falls below a small threshold, saving computation in dense volumes. Parameter: Threshold: A small value (e.g., 10^{-3} or 0.001) representing the minimum transmission. Below this, the contribution to the final color is considered negligible. Pitfall: Simply stopping and ignoring the remaining volume contribution is statistically incorrect and introduces bias. It is acceptable for visual rendering but not for high-precision scientific simulation (e.g., thermonuclear engineering). The concept of early termination in ray marching emerged alongside the practical implementation of volume rendering and SDF-based rendering in real-time graphics. As ray marching became a standard technique for rendering implicit surfaces and volumetric data, the computational cost of iterating through empty space or fully opaque regions became a bottleneck. The specific threshold-based early exit for volumes was discussed in community-driven educational resources, highlighting the trade-off between rendering speed and physical accuracy. The geometric termination criteria for sphere tracing, including oscillation detection and grazing resolution, were developed to address numerical instability and visual artifacts like "auras" and self-intersections in SDF rendering. name: Sphere Tracing Termination and Clipping
head: Sphere Tracing Stopping Criteria, Sphere Tracing Termination Conditions
body: Sphere Tracing Termination and Clipping defines the conditions under which a ray-marching loop halts, ensuring the algorithm returns a valid intersection point or correctly identifies a miss without infinite iteration. It solves the problem of premature termination (missing thin geometry), self-intersection artifacts (due to insufficient epsilon), and excessive computation (tracing through empty space or deep into volumes). It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Ray Marching with Early Termination by focusing specifically on the geometric constraints of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) and the numerical stability of the step-size logic, rather than volumetric opacity accumulation. The method operates on a ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and normalized direction \mathbf{d}, parameterized by accumulated distance t. The core loop evaluates a scene function f(\mathbf{p}) (the SDF) at the current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to determine the next step size \Delta t and check for termination. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), scene function f(\mathbf{p}), maximum distance t{max}, maximum iterations N{max}, stopping distance threshold \delta, oscillation threshold factor (typically 6), and far plane clipping depth D{clip}. Outputs: Boolean indicating hit/miss, and the final distance t or intersection point \mathbf{p}. State: Current distance t, current position \mathbf{p}, previous distance d{bk-1} (for oscillation check), minimum screen-space distance d{min} (for grazing detection). Constants: \delta = 0.0003, N{max} = 200, D{clip} = 5. 1. Initialization: Set t = 0.0, d{bk-1} = \infty, d{min} = \infty. 2. Iteration Loop: For i from 0 to N{max}: a. Far Plane Clip: If t > D{clip}, terminate as miss. b. Position Evaluation: Compute \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. c. SDF Query: Compute d = f(\mathbf{p}). d. Grazing/Screen-Space Tracking: If d < d{min}, update d{min} = d. e. Termination: Surface Hit: If |d| < \delta, terminate as hit. f. Termination: Oscillation: If |d - d{bk-1}| < 6\delta, terminate as miss (oscillation detected). g. Step Size Calculation: Compute \Delta t = d (standard sphere tracing) or \Delta t = (1+\sigma)d/\lambda (overstepping). h. Update State: Set d{bk-1} = d. i. Advance: t = t + \Delta t. 3. Post-Loop Grazing Resolution: If the loop terminated due to N{max} or far plane without a hit, check if d{min} \le \text{pixel\radius}/2. If true, return the position corresponding to d{min} as the intersection point to eliminate "aura" artifacts. Otherwise, return miss. Stopping Distance: |f(\mathbf{p})| < \delta. Oscillation Check: |d{bk} - d{bk-1}| < 6\delta. Screen-Space Termination: Terminate if screen-space distance \le \frac{1}{2} \times \text{pixel\distance}. Cone Tracing Error Threshold (Adaptive): \hat{\epsilon}(\hat{s}) = \hat{s} \hat{r}p, where \hat{s} is the distance along the ray in undeformed space and \hat{r}p is the radius of one pixel in undeformed space. Pixel Radius in Undeformed Space: \hat{r}p = s rp JD^{-1}, where s is the distance in deformed space, rp is the pixel radius in deformed space, and JD^{-1} is the inverse Jacobian determinant. \delta = 0.0003. N{max} = 200. D{clip} = 5. Oscillation factor: 6. Precision: If \delta is too large, the surface appears to "swim" depending on the view direction. Self-Intersection: Secondary rays (refraction/reflection) may immediately satisfy |f(\mathbf{p})| < \epsilon at the origin. This is mitigated by using a dynamic epsilon \epsilon{dynamic} = 2\max(\epsilon{min}, |f(\mathbf{p})|). Grazing Rays: Standard termination may leave rays ending in empty space near the surface, creating an "aura" artifact. Screen-space tracking resolves this by selecting the closest approach point. Oscillation: In noisy or discontinuous SDFs, the step size may oscillate, causing the ray to jitter. The oscillation check prevents infinite loops in these degenerate cases. Unverified code. """ t = 0.0 dprev = float('inf') dmin = float('inf') # Store positions for grazing resolution posatdmin = rayorigin for i in range(maxiterations): # 1. Far Plane Clipping if t > farplaneclip: return False, t, None # 2. Evaluate SDF p = rayorigin + raydirection t d = scenefunc(p) # 3. Track minimum distance for grazing resolution if d < dmin: dmin = d posatdmin = p # 4. Termination: Surface Hit if abs(d) < stoppingdist: return True, t, p # 5. Termination: Oscillation Detection # Check if the step size is oscillating significantly if abs(d - dprev) < 6 stoppingdist: return False, t, None # 6. Update previous distance dprev = d # 7. Step Size Calculation (Standard Sphere Tracing) # In practice, d is the distance to the surface, so we step by d # Note: For SDFs, d should be positive for empty space. # If d < 0, the ray is inside the object. step = d # Safety clamp to prevent infinite loops from precision errors if step < 1e-6: step = 1e-6 t += step # 8. Post-Loop: Screen-Space Grazing Resolution # If we didn't hit, check if we grazed the surface # Terminate if screen-space distance is less than half pixel distance if pixelradius > 0 and dmin <= pixelradius / 2.0: return True, t, posatdmin return False, t, None A constant-time heuristic to detect non-collision within a working interval, avoiding expensive root-finding. It provides immediate non-collision detection and a conservative starting point, unlike Bracketed Newton Bisection which searches for monotonic intervals. Computes a local offset dynamically at each intersection point (\epsilon{dynamic} = 2\max(\epsilon{min}, |f(\mathbf{p})|)) to prevent self-intersection in secondary rays. It adapts to local signed distance bounds, unlike global constant epsilon. Accelerates sphere tracing through convex objects by avoiding internal steps when the ray origin is inside the object. It relies on bounding volume geometry rather than per-step gradient computations. A post-processing step to smooth discontinuities in f(\mathbf{p}) and reduce visual artifacts in procedural texturing. It trades slight geometric error for reduced screen-space discontinuities. Tracks the 'grazing point' (where ray direction is tangent to surface normal) during sphere tracing. It explicitly identifies and refines grazing contacts, which standard termination rules often miss. A binary filtering technique that discards ray samples where the gradient magnitude is below a threshold tg. It ensures only significant surface samples contribute, unlike geometric bounds. Determines an adaptive error threshold \hat{\epsilon}(\hat{s}) = \hat{s} \hat{r}p based on ray distance and pixel footprint. It ensures rays terminate when the pixel cone intersects the surface, preventing "swimming" artifacts if the threshold is too high. A rendering mode that traverses voxels and sums values until opaque (early termination) or non-zero (blending). High voxel access costs can negate performance gains from block walking. Recursively subdivides intervals, using local Lipschitz bounds \lambda(e) to shrink intervals asymmetrically (ea = a + |f(a)|/\lambda(e), eb = b - |f(b)|/\lambda(e)). It reduces field function queries compared to standard bisection. Eliminates "aura" artifacts by using the point of closest screen-space approach as the intersection if the ray does not strictly intersect. It terminates when screen-space distance \le half pixel distance. Clips upward-tracing rays to the top of a particle pile to prevent walking through empty cells. It uses a 64-thread compute pass to find the highest particle center and clips rays to the slab under it plus the largest radius. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of iterations, bounded by N{max}. Oscillation and far-plane checks provide O(1) early exits. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory for state variables (t, d, d{min}). Measured Performance: With \delta=0.0003 and N{max}=200, the method is efficient for primary rays. Far-plane clipping at depth 5 reduces unnecessary computation in large scenes. Strengths: Robust against infinite loops via oscillation detection; handles grazing rays via screen-space selection; prevents self-intersection via dynamic epsilon. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \delta to avoid swimming artifacts; oscillation detection may terminate valid rays in highly noisy SDFs; screen-space resolution requires tracking additional state. When to Use: Primary ray tracing for SDFs; scenes with potential grazing angles; secondary rays requiring self-intersection prevention. When Not to Use: Volumetric rendering requiring opacity accumulation (use Ray Marching with Early Termination); scenes with extreme SDF discontinuities where oscillation detection might fail. The method originates from the foundational sphere tracing algorithm by John C. Hart (1996), which established the use of SDF values as step sizes. The specific termination criteria, including oscillation detection and far-plane clipping, were detailed in the "Neural Geometric Level of Detail" paper by Laine et al. (2021). The concept of cone tracing for adaptive error thresholds was introduced by McGuire (2013) in the context of deformed SDFs. name: Affine Arithmetic Early Skip Test
head: Early exit Sphere Marching (ESM) condition, Underestimation test
body: The Affine Arithmetic Early Skip Test is a constant-time heuristic used in distance-field ray marching to detect if a ray does not collide with an object within a specific working interval, thereby avoiding expensive root-finding operations. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Bracketed Newton Bisection (BNB) by providing immediate non-collision detection and a conservative starting point for subsequent searches, rather than searching for monotonic intervals of derivatives. The method approximates the high-degree polynomial representation of the Signed Distance Field (SDF) as a quadratic equation to determine intersection existence. It relies on affine arithmetic principles to bound the uncertainty of the polynomial coefficients over a normalized working interval. Inputs: Polynomial coefficients cc0, \dots, cc9 derived from the SDF expansion. Ray entry point and direction (implicitly handled via the normalized parameter t). Boolean flag indicating if the ray starts inside the volume. Outputs: Boolean skip: True if the ray is guaranteed not to intersect the object within the working interval. tstart: A candidate starting parameter for the subsequent root-finding search (if skip is False). The method operates on an array of scalar coefficients cci and floating-point values. 1. Factorization: Factorize the standard polynomial PN(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}t) into the form at^2 + bt + c = 0. The coefficients b and c are constant, while a is a function of t: b = cc1 c = cc0 a(t) = cc9 t^7 + cc8 t^6 + \dots + cc3 t + cc2 2. Define Working Interval: Assume a normalized working range of [0, 1] for the ray segment within the current node, where t=0 is the entry and t=1 is the exit. 3. Compute Underestimated Coefficient a: Calculate a conservative lower bound for a(t) over t \in [0, 1] using affine arithmetic underestimation. If the ray starts outside the object (standard case), compute a{under} as: a{under} = cc2 + \sum{i=3}^{9} cci \epsiloni where \epsiloni is defined as: \epsiloni = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } cci > 0 \\ 1 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} If the ray starts inside the volume, swap the condition of \epsiloni (i.e., \epsiloni = 1 if cci > 0, else 0) to adapt the underestimation process for finding intersections from the inside. 4. Solve Quadratic: Solve the quadratic equation a{under} t^2 + b t + c = 0 for t. Calculate the discriminant \Delta = b^2 - 4 a{under} c. If \Delta < 0, there are no real roots for the underestimated polynomial. 5. Skip Decision: If the underestimated polynomial has no roots within the working interval [0, 1] (either \Delta < 0 or roots are outside [0, 1]), then the original polynomial has no roots in this interval. Return skip = True. If roots exist, return skip = False. 6. Starting Point Selection: If skip is False, identify the roots of the underestimated quadratic. Select the smaller positive root within the working interval as tstart. This value serves as a better starting point for the subsequent root-finding search using the original high-degree polynomial. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def affinearithmeticearlyskip(cc, insidevolume=False): """ Performs the Affine Arithmetic Early Skip Test. Args: cc: List of coefficients [cc0, cc1,..., cc9]. insidevolume: Boolean, True if ray starts inside the volume. Returns: skip: Boolean, True if no intersection is possible in [0, 1]. tstart: Float, candidate starting t for further search, or None. """ # Step 1: Extract constant coefficients b and c b = cc[1] c = cc[0] # Step 3: Compute underestimated coefficient a # Base term is cc2 aunder = cc[2] # Summation for i from 3 to 9 for i in range(3, 10): cci = cc[i] # Determine epsiloni based on sign of cci if insidevolume: # Swap condition for inside volume epsiloni = 1 if cci > 0 else 0 else: # Standard condition for outside volume epsiloni = 0 if cci > 0 else 1 aunder += cci epsiloni # Step 4: Solve quadratic aunder t^2 + b t + c = 0 discriminant = b b - 4 aunder c if discriminant < 0: # No real roots for underestimated polynomial return True, None sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) # Calculate roots # Avoid division by zero if aunder is 0, though typically aunder != 0 in valid SDF contexts if abs(aunder) < 1e-9: # Linear case: bt + c = 0 if abs(b) > 1e-9: tlinear = -c / b roots = [tlinear] else: roots = [] else: t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 aunder) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 aunder) roots = [t1, t2] # Step 5 & 6: Check roots within [0, 1] and select start point validroots = [t for t in roots if 0 <= t <= 1] if not validroots: # No roots in working interval -> Skip return True, None else: # Roots exist -> Cannot skip # Use the smaller root as starting point tstart = min(validroots) return False, tstart Precision: The method relies on floating-point arithmetic. If a{under} is very close to zero, the quadratic formula may suffer from cancellation errors. A fallback to linear solving is recommended if |a{under}| is negligible. Conservatism: The underestimation is conservative. If the underestimated polynomial has roots, the original polynomial might still not have roots (false positive for intersection). However, if the underestimated polynomial has no roots, the original definitely has none (true negative for collision). Inside Volume: The logic for \epsiloni must be correctly swapped when the ray origin is inside the volume; failure to do so results in an incorrect bound. Time Complexity: O(1). The test involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (summing 7 terms and solving a quadratic) regardless of the polynomial degree or scene complexity. Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is allocated beyond local variables. Strengths: Provides constant-time detection for non-collisions, which is significantly faster than iterative root-finding methods like BNB when the ray misses the object. It also provides a heuristic starting point for the actual solver, potentially reducing the number of iterations required. Limitations: It is an approximation. It cannot find the exact intersection point, only determine existence or provide a starting guess. It is specific to the polynomial representation of the SDF. When to use: Use as a pre-check before invoking expensive root-finding algorithms (like BNB) in sphere tracing or analytic intersection solvers for high-order SDF approximations. The method was proposed in the context of rendering piecewise approximations of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) using analytic intersections, specifically to address the lack of early skip strategies in methods like Bracketed Newton Bisection (BNB). BNB searches monotonic intervals of derivatives, which can be computationally expensive and does not offer early exit for non-collisions. The Affine Arithmetic Early Skip Test was introduced to provide a constant-time alternative for detecting non-collisions and improving the convergence of subsequent root-finding steps. name: Dynamic Epsilon for Self-Intersection Prevention
head: Dynamic offset, Dynamic ε for self-intersection prevention
body: Dynamic epsilon is a method for preventing self-intersection artifacts in secondary rays (such as refraction or reflection) within sphere tracing by computing a local offset dynamically at each intersection point, rather than using a global constant. It solves the problem where global epsilon values are inappropriate for sphere tracing because intersection distances from the surface exhibit large variations, particularly when screen-space termination metrics are used. Unlike siblings that may use fixed offsets or affine arithmetic, this method adapts the offset magnitude to the local signed distance bound, ensuring robustness against precision issues near the surface while maintaining performance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The intersection point p obtained from sphere tracing, the signed distance function value f(p) at that point, and a global minimal offset constant \epsilon{min}. Output: A dynamic offset value \epsilon{dynamic} and the new ray origin for the secondary ray. Data Structures: No specific complex data structures are required beyond standard floating-point variables for the point p, the scalar distance f(p), and the constants. Parameters: \epsilon{min}: A global minimal offset value. It must be chosen carefully; if too small, it causes numerical problems (when f(p) \approx 0) and poor performance (slow acceleration away from the surface). If too large, it may introduce visible artifacts. The sources do not provide a specific numerical value, but note that manually choosing \epsilon{min} is easier and more robust than choosing a global epsilon that works for all distances. Formulas: The dynamic epsilon is calculated as: \epsilon{dynamic} = 2 \cdot \max(\epsilon{min}, |f(p)|) This ensures that \epsilon{dynamic} \ge 2 \cdot \epsilon{min}, which obviates numerical problems associated with f(p) \approx 0. Steps: 1. At each intersection point p obtained from sphere tracing, compute the signed distance bound f(p). 2. Calculate \epsilon{dynamic} using the formula \epsilon{dynamic} = 2 \cdot \max(\epsilon{min}, |f(p)|). If |f(p)| \ge \epsilon{min}, then \epsilon{dynamic} = 2 \cdot |f(p)|. If |f(p)| \le \epsilon{min}, then \epsilon{dynamic} = 2 \cdot \epsilon{min}. 3. Offset the new ray origin for the secondary ray by \epsilon{dynamic} along the surface normal at p (or along the ray direction, though the normal is preferred for refraction to avoid grazing issues). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computedynamicepsilonoffset(p, fp, epsilonmin, normal): """ Computes the new ray origin for a secondary ray to prevent self-intersection. Args: p: The intersection point from sphere tracing. fp: The signed distance function value at p. epsilonmin: The global minimal offset constant. normal: The surface normal at p. Returns: neworigin: The offset ray origin for the secondary ray. """ # Calculate dynamic epsilon based on the absolute signed distance # Formula: epsilondynamic = 2 max(epsilonmin, abs(fp)) absfp = abs(fp) epsilondynamic = 2.0 max(epsilonmin, absfp) # Offset the ray origin along the normal # Note: The sources specify offsetting along the normal. # In some contexts, offsetting along the ray direction is mentioned, # but normal offset is standard for refraction to prevent grazing self-intersection. neworigin = p + epsilondynamic normal return neworigin Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Issues: If f(p) is very close to zero, a global epsilon might be too small, causing self-intersection. The dynamic method ensures \epsilon{dynamic} \ge 2 \cdot \epsilon{min}, avoiding this. Performance Degradation: If \epsilon{min} is too small, the sphere tracing for the secondary ray must spend many iterations accelerating away from the surface, degrading performance. Screen-Space Termination: Standard origin offsetting is insufficient for sphere tracing because the intersection point can be far from the surface, especially when using epsilon-based termination. Dynamic epsilon accommodates these large variations. Uses affine arithmetic to skip steps where the ray cannot intersect the object. Choose when performance is critical and the scene has simple primitives. Accelerates intersection tests for convex objects enclosed in convex bounding volumes. Choose when rendering scenes with many convex primitives. Reduces discontinuity artifacts in sphere tracing using fixed-point iteration. Choose when procedural texturing causes visual artifacts at intersection boundaries. Detects grazing points to improve intersection accuracy. Choose when rendering scenes with thin geometry or grazing angles. Uses gradient magnitude to adjust step sizes. Choose when the signed distance function has varying smoothness. Time Complexity: The computation of \epsilon{dynamic} is negligible because f(p) is already known after tracing to the surface. The offset operation is a simple vector addition and scalar multiplication. Memory Complexity: Constant space, requiring only a few additional floating-point variables. Measured Performance: The sources do not provide specific benchmark numbers. However, it is noted that manually choosing \epsilon{min} is more robust than a global epsilon, and the cost of computing \epsilon{dynamic} is negligible. Scaling: The method scales well as it does not depend on the number of iterations or scene complexity, only on the local properties at the intersection point. Strengths: Adapts to local surface distance, preventing self-intersection artifacts even with large variations in intersection distances. Robust against precision issues near the surface. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \epsilon{min}. If \epsilon{min} is too small, performance may degrade due to slow acceleration away from the surface. When to Use: Use when rendering secondary rays (refraction/reflection) in sphere tracing, especially with screen-space termination metrics. When Not to Use: Not necessary for primary rays or when using a different intersection method that does not suffer from self-intersection issues. Dynamic epsilon was introduced in the paper "Enhanced Sphere Tracing" by. The paper presents several performance and quality enhancements to classical sphere tracing, including this method for dynamically preventing self-intersections upon converting signed distance bounds. The method addresses the limitations of global epsilon values in the context of sphere tracing, where intersection distances can vary significantly. The work is part of a broader effort to improve the robustness and performance of sphere tracing in real-time and non-real-time rendering contexts. name: Convex Object Optimization
head: Convex Shape Optimization for Internal Origins, Convex bounding volume optimization, Internal Ray Optimization, Inverse ray tracing for convex objects
body: Convex Object Optimization is a technique for accelerating sphere tracing through convex objects represented by a signed distance field (SDF) enclosed by a convex bounding volume. It solves the problem of inefficient ray marching when the ray origin lies inside the object, where standard sphere tracing requires many small steps to traverse the interior. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by avoiding internal steps entirely for internal origins, and from gradient-based optimizations by relying only on the bounding volume geometry rather than per-step gradient computations. The method assumes the object is enclosed by a convex bounding volume (e.g., a sphere, box, or convex polyhedron) for which ray intersection can be computed efficiently. It categorizes the ray origin o relative to the bounding volume and the object surface into three cases. Inputs: Ray origin o, ray direction d (normalized), object SDF function f(p), bounding volume geometry B. Outputs: Intersection distance t along the ray, or null if no intersection. Bounding Volume B: A convex shape supporting an analytic ray intersection test. For a sphere, this is defined by center c and radius r. For other convex shapes, an intersection function intersect(ray, B) returning the smallest positive t is required. SDF f(p): A function returning the signed distance to the object surface. f(p) < 0 indicates inside, f(p) > 0 outside. 1. Detect Case: Determine the position of the ray origin o relative to the bounding volume B and the object f. Compute tb = \text{intersect}(Ray(o, d), B). If tb is null, the ray does not intersect the bounding volume; return null. Check if o is inside the object: inside\obj = (f(o) < 0). Check if o is inside the bounding volume: inside\bound = (tb < 0 \text{ or } o \text{ is inside } B). Note: Standard ray intersection returns positive t for forward direction. If the origin is inside, the intersection with the boundary in the forward direction is positive, but the origin is geometrically inside. A robust check is: if f(o) < 0, the origin is inside the object. If f(o) \ge 0, check if o is inside B using a point-in-convex-volume test. The three cases are: Case 1: Origin outside bounding volume (o \notin B). Case 2: Origin inside bounding volume but outside object (o \in B and f(o) \ge 0). Case 3: Origin inside bounding volume and inside object (o \in B and f(o) < 0). 2. Handle Case 1 (Origin outside bounding volume): The ray enters the bounding volume at tb. Set new origin o' = o + tb \cdot d. Perform standard sphere tracing starting from o' using f(p). Return the result. 3. Handle Case 2 (Origin inside bounding volume, outside object): The ray is already inside the bounding volume but outside the object. Perform standard sphere tracing starting from o using f(p). Return the result. 4. Handle Case 3 (Origin inside bounding volume and inside object): This is the optimization case. Tracing forward through the interior is costly. Find the intersection of the ray with the bounding volume in the forward direction. Let this distance be t{exit\bound}. t{exit\bound} = \text{intersect}(Ray(o, d), B). Compute the point on the bounding volume boundary: p{bound} = o + t{exit\bound} \cdot d. Perform sphere tracing in the inverse ray direction starting from p{bound}. Inverse ray: origin p{bound}, direction -d. Trace using f(p) until an intersection is found. Let the distance along the inverse ray be t{inv}. The intersection point in world space is p{hit} = p{bound} - t{inv} \cdot d. The intersection distance for the original ray is t = t{exit\bound} - t{inv}. Return t. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def convexoptimizedspheretrace(o, d, f, B): """ o: vec3, ray origin d: vec3, normalized ray direction f: function, signed distance field B: object, convex bounding volume with intersect(ray) method """ # Step 1: Check if ray intersects bounding volume at all tb = B.intersect(Ray(o, d)) if tb is None: return None # Step 2: Determine if origin is inside the object insideobj = f(o) < 0 # Step 3: Determine if origin is inside the bounding volume # Point-in-convex-volume test insidebound = B.containspoint(o) # Case 1: Origin outside bounding volume if not insidebound: # Advance to bounding volume entry oprime = o + tb d # Standard sphere trace from entry point return spheretrace(oprime, d, f) # Case 2: Origin inside bounding volume, outside object if not insideobj: # Standard sphere trace from origin return spheretrace(o, d, f) # Case 3: Origin inside bounding volume and inside object # Find exit point from bounding volume texitbound = B.intersect(Ray(o, d)) pbound = o + texitbound d # Trace backwards from boundary # Inverse ray: origin pbound, direction -d tinv = spheretrace(pbound, -d, f) if tinv is None: return None # Calculate original intersection distance # The hit point is pbound - tinv d # Original ray: o + t d = pbound - tinv d # o + t d = (o + texitbound d) - tinv d # t d = (texitbound - tinv) d # t = texitbound - tinv t = texitbound - tinv return t def spheretrace(o, d, f): """ Standard sphere tracing loop. """ maxsteps = 1000 maxdist = 100.0 t = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): p = o + t d dist = f(p) if dist < 1e-4: # Hit threshold return t if t > maxdist: return None t += dist return None Hit Threshold: 10^{-4} is typical for sphere tracing. Max Steps: Not given in the sources. A value of 1000 is standard for sphere tracing. Max Distance: Not given in the sources. Scene-dependent. Precision: When t{exit\bound} \approx t{inv}, the result t may suffer from cancellation errors. However, since t{inv} is the distance from the boundary to the surface, and the origin is inside, t{inv} is generally small compared to t{exit\bound} unless the origin is very close to the boundary. Degenerate Bounding Volume: If the bounding volume is not strictly convex, the intersection test may fail or return incorrect results. Origin on Boundary: If f(o) \approx 0, the case classification may be unstable. Treat as outside object (Case 2) if f(o) \ge 0. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of iterations for internal origins from O(D) where D is the diameter of the object, to O(1) for the bounding volume intersection plus O(d{exit}) where d{exit} is the distance from the boundary to the surface. This is significantly faster for large objects. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for the bounding volume intersection. Measured Performance: In a test scene with 3 spheres, a ground plane, and a dodecahedron with a bounding sphere, using two reflection bounces and eight refraction bounces, the convex optimization provided a speedup of around 10% (2.73 ms with optimization vs. 3.03 ms without). Strengths: Avoids costly marching through the interior of the object. Avoids the often costly computation of the gradient per iteration step, which is not feasible in real-time applications. Limitations: Requires a convex bounding volume that supports efficient ray intersection. Not applicable to non-convex objects without decomposition. The optimization was proposed by Hart et al. [Har96] for sphere tracing convex objects. However, many of the original optimizations involved the often costly computation of the gradient per iteration step, which is not feasible in real-time applications. The specific implementation described here, which uses inverse ray tracing from a bounding volume, is presented in the context of Enhanced Sphere Tracing. name: Discontinuity Reduction via Fixed-Point Iteration
head: Discontinuity smoothing, Fixed-point iteration smoothing, Fixed-point smoothing
body: Discontinuity reduction via fixed-point iteration is a post-processing step applied to intersection points retrieved by sphere tracing to smooth out discontinuities in the signed distance function f(p) and reduce artifacts in procedural texturing. It sets itself apart from its siblings by trading a slight increase in average geometric error for significantly reduced visual discontinuities across the screen-space domain, whereas Affine Arithmetic Early Skip Test focuses on skipping empty space and Dynamic Epsilon for Self-Intersection Prevention focuses on preventing self-intersection artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: The method takes an initial intersection point p0 obtained from sphere tracing, the ray direction d, the ray origin o, the SDF function f, and a screen-space error function \text{err}(\cdot) as inputs. It outputs a smoothed intersection point p{final} that satisfies the fixed-point condition. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required. The method operates on scalar and vector variables: pi represents the current point estimate (vec3), d is the ray direction (vec3, normalized), o is the ray origin (vec3), f(p) is the SDF value at point p (float), and \text{err}(r) is the screen-space error threshold based on distance from origin (float). Parameters: The number of iterations N is typically 3, which is sufficient to eliminate artifacts. Some visualizations use 5 iterations. The screen-space error function \text{err}(r) defines the target error tolerance based on the distance from the ray origin, and its exact implementation depends on the screen-space criterion used (e.g., pixel radius). Algorithm Steps: 1. Obtain the initial intersection point p0 from the sphere tracing loop. 2. For i from 0 to N-1: a. Calculate the current distance from the ray origin: ri = \|pi - o\|2. b. Evaluate the SDF at the current point: vali = f(pi). c. Calculate the target error: targeti = \text{err}(ri). d. Update the point using the fixed-point iteration formula: p{i+1} = pi + d \cdot (vali - targeti). 3. Return pN as the smoothed intersection point. Formula: The core update rule is derived from seeking a point p such that f(p) = \text{err}\left(\|p - o\|2\right). The iterative update moves the point along the ray direction d by the difference between the current SDF value and the target screen-space error: p{i+1} = pi + d \cdot (f(pi) - \text{err}(\|pi - o\|2)) \quad (3) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def discontinuityreduction(p0, d, o, f, errfunc, numiterations=3): """ Smooths an intersection point obtained from sphere tracing. Args: p0: Initial intersection point (vec3) from sphere tracing. d: Ray direction (vec3), assumed normalized. o: Ray origin (vec3). f: Signed Distance Function (callable taking vec3, returning float). errfunc: Screen-space error function (callable taking distance float, returning float). numiterations: Number of smoothing iterations (int). Returns: Smoothed intersection point (vec3). """ p = p0 for i in range(numiterations): # Calculate distance from ray origin distfromorigin = length(p - o) # Evaluate SDF at current point sdfval = f(p) # Get target error from screen-space criterion targeterror = errfunc(distfromorigin) # Update point along ray direction # p{i+1} = pi + d (f(pi) - err(||pi - o||2)) p = p + d (sdfval - targeterror) return p Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The average value of f(p) may increase after applying this technique, resulting in greater overall geometric error. However, this is a deliberate trade-off to achieve significantly reduced discontinuities and better visual quality. The method assumes the fixed-point iteration converges, and with typical parameters (3-5 iterations), it effectively smooths discontinuities caused by limited sphere tracing iterations and constant/screen-space thresholds. The update moves strictly along the ray direction d, so if the true intersection is significantly off-axis, this method may not correct it fully, but it is designed to smooth discontinuities along the ray path. Uses affine arithmetic to skip empty space efficiently. Choose when performance in empty regions is critical. Prevents self-intersection artifacts in secondary rays. Choose when rendering reflections/refractions from SDF surfaces. Accelerates tracing through convex objects using bounding volumes. Choose when rendering scenes with many convex SDF objects. Detects grazing intersections to improve normal accuracy. Choose when surface normals are critical for shading. The time complexity is O(N), where N is the number of smoothing iterations, and each iteration requires one SDF evaluation and one error function evaluation. The memory complexity is O(1), as it only stores the current point and a few scalars. The method adds a low, fixed cost to the rendering pipeline. In the source experiments, it was used to improve visual quality without significantly impacting frame rates, especially when combined with other optimizations like convex object optimization which provided a ~10% speedup in a path tracer. It significantly reduces visual artifacts in procedural texturing caused by discontinuities in intersection distance and traveled distance. It allows for satisfying images even with reduced precision and a low number of sphere tracing iterations. However, it increases the average geometric error of the intersection point. It is a post-processing step and does not improve the accuracy of the sphere tracing itself, only the visual smoothness of the result. It should be used when rendering procedural textures or when visual smoothness is more important than strict geometric accuracy, especially with limited iteration counts. It should not be used when strict geometric accuracy is required, or when the SDF is not continuous/smooth enough for the fixed-point iteration to converge effectively. The method was introduced in. It addresses the issue that limited sphere tracing iterations and constant or screen-space based termination criteria lead to discontinuities in the intersection points' distance from the surface and the distance traveled along the ray. These discontinuities cause unpleasant artifacts, particularly with procedural texturing. The technique employs a fixed-point iteration scheme to smooth out these discontinuities in the SDF f(p). name: Ray Intersection with Grazing Point Detection
body: A ray intersection method that performs sphere tracing to find the primary intersection while simultaneously tracking the 'grazing point' (the point on the surface where the ray direction is tangent to the surface normal, indicated by a zero directional derivative). It returns the intersection time, validity, grazing point status, and the grazing point position. It sets itself apart from standard sphere tracing by explicitly identifying and refining grazing contacts, which are often missed or poorly resolved by standard termination rules. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ray ray (origin o, direction d, maxt maxt), a Signed Distance Field (SDF) evaluator self.at(p), and a directional derivative evaluator self.dirderiv(p, d). Output: Intersection time t, validity flag isvalid, grazing point position grz, and grazing time grzt. Data Structures: ray: Struct containing o (Point3f), d (Vector3f, normalized), maxt (float). self: Object providing at(p) returning float SDF, and dirderiv(p, d) returning float directional derivative. Parameters: ITXREFINE: Half-width of the interval for final intersection refinement. Value from utils.ITXREFINE. ITXEPS: Minimum signed distance threshold for valid intersection/grazing candidate. Value from utils.ITXEPS. SDFEPS: Threshold for absolute SDF value to confirm grazing point lies on surface. Value from utils.SDFEPS. SDFDERIVEPS: Threshold for absolute directional derivative to confirm tangency. Value from utils.SDFDERIVEPS. NUMGRZ: Maximum iterations for grazing point refinement. Value from utils.NUMGRZ. GRZMODE: String, either 'secant' or 'bisection', determining the refinement method for grazing points. Steps: 1. Initialization: Copy input ray parameters. Set t = 0. Set flags: noitx = True (no intersection found), inrange = True (ray within bounds), posdir = True (directional derivative positive). Set grzt = 0 (grazing time). Set minsdf = 1 (minimum SDF encountered for grazing candidates). Check bounding box intersection: If ray origin is inside the bounding box, set t = 0; otherwise, set t = mint + RAYEPS (where mint is the entry time into the bounding box). Clamp ray.maxt to the bounding box max intersection time. 2. Sphere Tracing Loop: Enter a loop continuing while noitx is True AND inrange is True. Suspend gradients during this loop. Evaluate point p = ray(t). Evaluate signed distance d = self.at(p). Evaluate directional derivative dir = self.dirderiv(p, ray.d). Identify Grazing Candidates: Create mask: idx = (~posdir) & (dir > 0) & (d < minsdf) & (d > ITXEPS). This identifies points where the ray was previously moving away (~posdir), is now moving towards the surface (dir > 0), has a smaller SDF than previous candidates (d < minsdf), and is not too close to the surface (d > ITXEPS). Update grzt and minsdf for indices satisfying idx. Advance Ray: t += d. Update posdir = (dir > 0). Update noitx = (d > ITXEPS). Update inrange = self.inrange(p) & (t < ray.maxt). 3. Grazing Point Refinement: After the loop, call self.getgrz(ray, grzt - minsdf, grzt + minsdf) to refine the grazing point position. The getgrz method uses either secant or bisection iteration to find the root of the directional derivative within the interval. Verification: Verify the grazing point grz is valid if: abs(self.at(grz)) < SDFEPS, abs(self.dirderiv(grz, ray.d)) < SDFDERIVEPS, and self.at(grz) > ITXEPS. 4. Intersection Refinement and Finalization: Determine ray validity: isvalid = (~noitx) & inrange. If isvalid is False, set t = infinity. If isvalid is True, refine the intersection time using self.refineintersect(ray, t - ITXREFINE, t + ITXREFINE). The refineintersect method uses bisection iteration to find the root of the SDF within the interval. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rayintersectgrz(ray, sdfeval, dirderiveval, utils): """ Ray intersection with grazing point detection. Args: ray: Ray object with o, d, maxt. sdfeval: Function self.at(p) returning SDF. dirderiveval: Function self.dirderiv(p, d) returning directional derivative. utils: Object containing ITXREFINE, ITXEPS, SDFEPS, SDFDERIVEPS, NUMGRZ, GRZMODE, RAYEPS. Returns: t: Intersection time. isvalid: Boolean indicating valid intersection. grz: Grazing point position. grzvalid: Boolean indicating valid grazing point. """ t = 0.0 noitx = True inrangeflag = True posdir = True grzt = 0.0 minsdf = 1.0 # Check bounding box intersection if isinsideboundingbox(ray.o): t = 0.0 else: t = mint + utils.RAYEPS ray.maxt = min(ray.maxt, maxtbox) # Suspend gradients during loop with suspendgrad(): while noitx and inrangeflag: p = ray.o + ray.d t d = sdfeval(p) dir = dirderiveval(p, ray.d) # Identify potential grazing points if (not posdir) and (dir > 0) and (d < minsdf) and (d > utils.ITXEPS): grzt = t minsdf = d # Advance ray t += d posdir = (dir > 0) noitx = (d > utils.ITXEPS) inrangeflag = checkinrange(p) and (t < ray.maxt) # Refine grazing point grz = getgrz(ray, grzt - minsdf, grzt + minsdf, sdfeval, dirderiveval, utils) # Verify grazing point grzvalid = (abs(sdfeval(grz)) < utils.SDFEPS) and \ (abs(dirderiveval(grz, ray.d)) < utils.SDFDERIVEPS) and \ (sdfeval(grz) > utils.ITXEPS) # Determine ray validity isvalid = (not noitx) and inrangeflag if not isvalid: t = float('inf') else: # Refine intersection t = refineintersect(ray, t - utils.ITXREFINE, t + utils.ITXREFINE, sdfeval, utils) return t, isvalid, grz, grzvalid def getgrz(ray, tmin, tmax, sdfeval, dirderiveval, utils): """Refine grazing point using secant or bisection method.""" if utils.GRZMODE == 'secant': return getgrzsecant(ray, tmin, tmax, sdfeval, dirderiveval, utils) elif utils.GRZMODE == 'bisection': return getgrzbisection(ray, tmin, tmax, sdfeval, dirderiveval, utils) else: raise ValueError(f"Unsupported GRZMODE: {utils.GRZMODE}") def getgrzsecant(ray, tmin, tmax, sdfeval, dirderiveval, utils): """Secant method for finding the grazing point.""" d = ray.d L = ray(tmin) R = ray(tmax) cnt = 0 with suspendgrad(): while cnt < utils.NUMGRZ: dL = dirderiveval(L, d) dR = dirderiveval(R, d) if abs(dR - dL) < 1e-12: break M = R - dR (R - L) / (dR - dL) dM = dirderiveval(M, d) if dM < 0: L = M if dM > 0: R = M cnt += 1 return L def getgrzbisection(ray, tmin, tmax, sdfeval, dirderiveval, utils): """Bisection method for finding the grazing point.""" d = ray.d L = ray(tmin) R = ray(tmax) cnt = 0 with suspendgrad(): while cnt < utils.NUMGRZ: M = (L + R) / 2 dM = dirderiveval(M, d) if dM < 0: L = M if dM > 0: R = M cnt += 1 return L def refineintersect(ray, tmin, tmax, sdfeval, utils): """Bisection method for refining the intersection point.""" if utils.NUMREFINE == 0: return (tmin + tmax) / 2 L = tmin R = tmax cnt = 0 with suspendgrad(): while cnt < utils.NUMREFINE: dL = sdfeval(ray(L)) dR = sdfeval(ray(R)) M = (L + R) / 2 dM = sdfeval(ray(M)) if dM > 0: L = M if dM < 0: R = M cnt += 1 return (L + R) / 2 def isinsideboundingbox(p): # Placeholder for bounding box check implementation return True def checkinrange(p): # Placeholder for in-range check implementation return True def suspendgrad(): # Placeholder for gradient suspension context manager class DummyContext: def enter(self): return self def exit(self, args): pass return DummyContext() A method for selecting an appropriate intersection point when sphere tracing fails to converge (e.g., maximum iterations exceeded), particularly when a ray grazes an object's edge. It selects the point along the ray with the smallest unbounding sphere radius, as measured in screen-space. It terminates the ray early if the unbounding sphere radius is smaller than one half the size of a pixel. Parameters include pixelRadius (radius of a pixel at t = 1) and forceHit (boolean enforcing the use of the candidatet value as the result). It uses an over-relaxation sphere tracing step length calculation with a fallback to bisection-like refinement if the step length decreases significantly. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. omega = 1.2 t = tmin candidateerror = float('inf') candidatet = tmin previousRadius = 0.0 stepLength = 0.0 functionSign = -1 if f(o) < 0 else 1.0 for i in range(MAXITERATIONS): signedRadius = functionSign f(d t + o) radius = abs(signedRadius) sorFail = omega > 1 and (radius + previousRadius) < stepLength if sorFail: stepLength -= omega stepLength omega = 1.0 else: stepLength = signedRadius omega previousRadius = radius error = radius / t if not sorFail and error < candidateerror: candidatet = t candidateerror = error if not sorFail and (error < pixelRadius or t > tmax): break t += stepLength if (t > tmax or candidateerror > pixelRadius) and not forceHit: return float('inf') return candidatet Time Complexity: The main loop runs until intersection or max iterations. The grazing point refinement adds a constant number of iterations (NUMGRZ) per ray. The intersection refinement adds NUMREFINE iterations. Overall, it is comparable to standard sphere tracing but with a small constant overhead for grazing detection and refinement. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per ray, storing a few scalar values and flags. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales linearly with the number of rays. The constant overhead of grazing detection may become more significant for scenes with many grazing rays. Strengths: Explicitly handles grazing contacts, which are often missed or poorly resolved by standard sphere tracing. Provides a fallback grazing point even if the primary intersection is not found. Limitations: Requires evaluation of the directional derivative, which may be more expensive than the SDF itself. The coarse sphere-traced grazing time grzt is insufficiently accurate and requires root-finding refinement. Implementation of the relaxation technique combined with this method can yield diminished rendering performance due to diverging threads. When to use: When accurate handling of grazing contacts is important, such as in high-quality rendering or when dealing with complex geometry where rays frequently skim surfaces. When not to use: When performance is critical and grazing contacts are rare or can be ignored. When the directional derivative is not available or expensive to compute. Originated from the implementation in zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary. The method is designed to handle the challenges of sphere tracing near object boundaries, particularly grazing contacts. The screen-space aware intersection point selection variant is described in "Enhanced Sphere Tracing". zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, https://github.com/zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Enhanced Sphere Tracing, https://kev.town/raymarching-toolkit/media/enhancedspheretracing.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gradient Magnitude Windowing
body: Gradient Magnitude Windowing is a binary windowing function used to determine if a ray sample's gradient magnitude satisfies requirements for further rendering, specifically for contour rendering where high gradient magnitude indicates an object surface. It solves the problem of isolating object surfaces by ensuring only samples exceeding a gradient magnitude threshold contribute to the rendering process. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The gradient vector \mathbf{g} at the current ray sample position, and the scalar threshold parameter tg. Output: A binary weight w(|\mathbf{g}|) indicating whether the sample satisfies the rendering requirements. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the scalar threshold tg and the computed gradient magnitude |\mathbf{g}|. Steps: 1. Compute the gradient magnitude |\mathbf{g}| from the gradient vector \mathbf{g} at the current sample point. 2. Compare |\mathbf{g}| against the threshold tg. 3. Apply the windowing function w(|\mathbf{g}|): If |\mathbf{g}| > tg, set w(|\mathbf{g}|) = 1. If |\mathbf{g}| < tg, set w(|\mathbf{g}|) = 0. Formulas: The windowing function is defined as: w(|\mathbf{g}|) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } |\mathbf{g}| > tg \\ 0 & \text{if } |\mathbf{g}| < tg \end{cases} Where: |\mathbf{g}| is the magnitude of the gradient vector. tg is the gradient magnitude threshold. Parameters: tg: The gradient magnitude threshold. No typical value is given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The binary nature of the window means small fluctuations in gradient estimation near tg can cause flickering or discontinuous artifacts. Boundary: The case |\mathbf{g}| = tg is not explicitly defined in the source equations. Gradient Estimation: The quality of this method depends heavily on the gradient estimation method; 4D linear regression produces better results than central differences, which affects the reliability of |\mathbf{g}|. Args: magnitude (float): The gradient magnitude |g|. threshold (float): The gradient magnitude threshold tg. Returns: float: 1.0 if |g| > tg, 0.0 if |g| < tg. """ if magnitude > threshold: return 1.0 elif magnitude < threshold: return 0.0 else: # Equality case |g| = tg is not defined in the source # Defaulting to 0.0 for safety, but implementation may vary return 0.0 Contour Rendering Shading is a view-dependent shading technique that highlights object surfaces by weighting ray samples based on the alignment between the view vector and the surface gradient. It solves the problem of visualizing distinct structural boundaries in volume data where conventional opacity transfer functions fail. Unlike standard shading methods that rely on lighting models, it produces a non-photorealistic line-art effect maximized when the view direction is tangent to the surface. Choose it when rendering contour-based visualizations or when structural boundaries need emphasis over photorealism. Time and memory complexity: Not given in the sources. It is used to filter ray samples based on their gradient magnitudes, specifically for contour rendering where high gradient magnitude indicates an object surface. name: Contour Rendering Shading
head: Gradient-based Contour Shading, View-dependent Contour Shading
body: Contour Rendering Shading is a view-dependent shading technique that highlights object surfaces by weighting ray samples based on the alignment between the view vector and the surface gradient. It solves the problem of visualizing distinct structural boundaries (contours) in volume data, particularly where conventional opacity transfer functions fail to separate structures with different density ranges, such as internal organs or cavities. Unlike standard shading methods that rely on lighting models, this method produces a non-photorealistic line-art effect where intensity is maximized when the view direction is tangent to the surface (gradient perpendicular to view). Inputs: Ray sample position P. Normalized view vector V (from camera to sample). Gradient vector G = \nabla f(P) at position P, where f is the scalar volume field. Gradient magnitude |g| = \|G\|. Windowing function w(|g|) output from the parent method Gradient Magnitude Windowing. Exponent parameter n. Outputs: Contour intensity Ic. (Optional) Opacity \alphac for compositing. Data Structures: Vectors V and G are 3D floating-point vectors. Scalar Ic is a single floating-point value. Steps: 1. Normalize Vectors: Ensure V and G are unit vectors. If G is zero, the contour intensity is zero. \hat{V} = \frac{V}{\|V\|}, \quad \hat{G} = \frac{G}{\|G\|} 2. Calculate Dot Product: Compute the dot product \kappa between the normalized view vector and the normalized gradient vector. \kappa = \hat{V} \cdot \hat{G} \kappa = 1 implies the view vector is aligned with the gradient (looking directly at the surface normal). \kappa \approx 0 implies the view vector is perpendicular to the gradient (tangent to the surface), indicating a contour edge. 3. Calculate Contour Weight: Compute the view-dependent weight s(\kappa) using the exponent n. s(\kappa) = (1 - \kappa)^n This term assigns high weights to samples where \kappa \approx 0 (contours) and low weights where \kappa \approx 1. 4. Combine with Windowing: Multiply the contour weight by the gradient magnitude windowing function w(|g|) from the parent method to produce the final intensity. Ic = w(|g|) \cdot s(\kappa) w(|g|) ensures that only samples with significant gradient magnitudes (likely on a surface) contribute. 5. Assign Opacity (Optional): The intensity Ic can be used directly as the opacity \alpha for the ray sample during compositing, ensuring contour lines are more opaque than non-contour regions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def contourshading(V, G, wgradientmagnitude, n): """ Calculate contour intensity for a ray sample. Args: V: Normalized view vector (3D float). G: Gradient vector at sample point (3D float). wgradientmagnitude: Output from Gradient Magnitude Windowing function. n: Exponent controlling contour thickness. Returns: Ic: Contour intensity. """ # Step 1: Normalize gradient if non-zero if G[0] == 0 and G[1] == 0 and G[2] == 0: return 0.0 magG = (G[0]2 + G[1]2 + G[2]2) 0.5 Ghat = (G[0] / magG, G[1] / magG, G[2] / magG) # V is assumed normalized per source requirements # Step 2: Calculate dot product kappa kappa = V[0] Ghat[0] + V[1] Ghat[1] + V[2] Ghat[2] # Step 3: Calculate contour weight # Source defines s(kappa) = (1 - kappa)^n. # Clamp base to non-negative to prevent complex results for fractional n base = max(0.0, 1.0 - kappa) skappa = base n # Step 4: Combine with windowing Ic = wgradientmagnitude skappa return Ic Parameters: n: Exponent controlling contour line thickness/sharpness. Higher n results in thinner, sharper contours. Typical Value: For 12-bit gradient quantization, n \approx 4 is recommended to avoid artifacts from quantization errors. No other typical value is given. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normalization: Vectors V and G must be normalized before calculating \kappa to ensure \kappa is in the expected range and the dot product accurately reflects the angle. Zero Gradient: If G = 0, the gradient direction is undefined and the intensity is zero. Voxels with zero gradient magnitude are typically skipped by the windowing function. Quantization Artifacts: With low-bit gradient quantization (e.g., 12-bit), high values of n amplify quantization errors near contours, causing bright/dark artifacts. Use n \approx 4 for 12-bit data. View Dependence: The term (1 - \kappa)^n is view-dependent, making pre-computation or standard empty-space skipping techniques (which rely on static voxel properties) infeasible. A specific application of contour rendering shading for visualizing object contours in medical CT scans, such as internal organs (human body, vertebrae with screws) and cavities (bronchia, frontal sinuses). It allows simultaneous visualization of structures with different density ranges where conventional transfer functions are difficult to tune. It uses the formula g(|\nabla(P)|) = 0 to skip voxels with no gradient, but due to view dependence, efficient skipping is challenging. It employs an exponent n (typically around 4 for 12-bit quantization) to control contour sharpness. Time Complexity: The shading calculation is O(1) per sample. However, because the contour weight s(\kappa) is view-dependent, conventional empty-space skipping techniques (which rely on static gradient magnitude thresholds) are infeasible, potentially increasing the number of samples processed. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per sample. Performance: Rendering times depend on the compositing strategy. Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) based contour rendering is faster than blending because it allows more efficient skipping of black voxels and simpler compositing. Example performance on a 256^2 \times 225 head scan: 85ms for MIP, 150ms for blending. Strengths: Effective for visualizing boundaries and contours in complex, multi-density volumes (e.g., medical images) where standard opacity transfer functions fail. Limitations: View-dependent nature prevents static optimization of voxel skipping. Sensitive to gradient quantization errors if n is too high. When to Use: When the goal is to highlight object boundaries and contours in non-photorealistic rendering, especially for medical imaging with mixed density structures. When Not to Use: When photorealistic lighting is required, or when performance is critical and the volume has large empty regions that could be skipped using static methods (since view-dependence prevents this). Contour rendering shading was introduced as part of non-photorealistic volume rendering techniques to address the limitations of conventional transfer functions in visualizing specific structural features like contours. It builds on the concept of using gradient magnitude to identify surfaces and adds view-dependence to distinguish between front-facing surfaces and silhouette contours. The method was developed in the context of fast visualization of object contours, particularly for medical imaging applications such as CT scans of internal organs and cavities. The specific formulation with the exponent n and the combination with gradient windowing is detailed in research from the mid-2000s. Implementation of Importance-Driven Volume Rendering, https://www.cg.tuwien.ac.at/research/publications/2005/Thurner-2005-IVR/Thurner-2005-IVR-paper.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Fast Visualization of Object Contours by Non-Photorealistic Volume Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1111/1467-8659.00538, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Early Ray Marching Termination (Threshold)
head: Threshold-based Termination, Transmission Threshold Stopping
body: Early Ray Marching Termination (Threshold) is an optimization technique that halts the ray marching loop when the accumulated transmission falls below a user-defined small value, thereby skipping the computation of negligible volume contributions. It is primarily used to accelerate rendering in dense volumes or to implement "picking" interactions in volume visualization systems by identifying the first location where opacity exceeds a threshold. Unlike standard constant step marching, which samples until exit or hit, this method trades statistical accuracy for performance by discarding the "long tail" of the volume's contribution. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), volume density field \rho(\mathbf{p}), transfer function mapping density to absorption coefficient \sigmaa and color \mathbf{c}, threshold \tau (typically 10^{-3} or 0.001). Output: Final pixel color \mathbf{C} (if used for rendering) or 3D position \mathbf{p}{hit} (if used for picking). Data Structures: Accumulated transmission T \leftarrow 1.0. Accumulated color \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{0}. Current ray distance t \leftarrow 0.0 [Parent]. Step size \Delta t determined by parent step rules (e.g., SDF distance or fixed step) [Parent]. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize T = 1.0, \mathbf{C} = \mathbf{0}, t = 0.0. 2. While t < t{max} and T > \tau: a. Evaluate position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. b. Sample density \rho = \rho(\mathbf{p}). c. Compute absorption coefficient \sigmaa = \sigmaa(\rho) and color \mathbf{c} = \mathbf{c}(\rho). d. Compute optical thickness \Delta \tau{opt} = \sigmaa \Delta t. e. Compute local opacity contribution: 1 - e^{-\Delta \tau{opt}}. f. Update accumulated color: \mathbf{C} \leftarrow \mathbf{C} + \mathbf{c} \cdot T \cdot (1 - e^{-\Delta \tau{opt}}). g. Update accumulated transmission: T \leftarrow T \cdot e^{-\Delta \tau{opt}}. h. Advance ray: t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. 3. If loop terminated due to T \le \tau: For rendering: Return \mathbf{C} (ignoring remaining volume). For picking: Return \mathbf{p} at the step where T dropped below \tau (or 1-T exceeded 1-\tau). 4. If loop terminated due to t \ge t{max}: Return \mathbf{C} (fully transmitted background or black). Formulas: Transmission update: T{new} = T{old} \cdot e^{-\sigmaa \Delta t}. Threshold condition: Stop if T < \tau. Picking condition: Stop if 1 - T > 1 - \tau (i.e., accumulated opacity exceeds threshold). Parameters: \tau: Threshold value. Common value is 10^{-3} (0.001). In picking, it may be set to 0 for "first-hit" or a higher value to ignore transparent regions. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Bias: Stopping early introduces statistical bias because the remaining volume contribution is discarded. This is acceptable for visual rendering but invalid for high-precision scientific simulation (e.g., neutron transport). Zero Threshold: Setting \tau = 0 results in "first-hit" behavior. In foggy or noisy volumes, this may return positions in the background surrounding features rather than the feature itself. High Threshold: A non-zero threshold may cause the ray to miss relatively transparent but visible regions, causing the ray to exit the dataset without picking the intended feature. Precision: Ensure \tau is small enough to preserve visual fidelity but large enough to provide performance gains. Values like 10^{-3} imply 0.1\% remaining transmission. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def earlyterminationmarch(rayorigin, raydir, volumesampler, threshold=1e-3, maxsteps=1000, stepsize=0.01): """ Ray march with early termination based on accumulated transmission threshold. Args: rayorigin: (x, y, z) origin of the ray. raydir: (x, y, z) normalized direction vector. volumesampler: Function that returns (density, color) at a 3D position. threshold: Transmission threshold to stop early (default 1e-3). maxsteps: Maximum number of iterations to prevent infinite loops. stepsize: Distance to advance per step. Returns: finalcolor: (r, g, b) accumulated color. hitposition: (x, y, z) position where threshold was crossed, or None. Limitations: Introduces visual bias by discarding the volume tail; not suitable for physically accurate scientific simulation; threshold selection is critical and non-trivial. When not to use: High-precision scientific simulation (e.g., thermonuclear engineering) where statistical accuracy is required; scenes with large transparent regions where thresholding might miss features.
