name: Ray Marching with Early Termination
head: Early Termination in Ray Marching, Ray Marching Loop Termination, Ray Marching Termination, SDF Ray Marching Break Conditions, Standard Ray Marching Termination
body: Ray marching with early termination is a control flow strategy applied to the iterative ray marching loop to halt computation once the ray has interacted with the target scene or exceeded computational limits. It solves the problem of unnecessary processing by breaking the loop when a surface intersection is detected or when the ray has traveled beyond a defined maximum distance. Unlike methods that strictly iterate a fixed number of steps regardless of scene content, this approach dynamically adapts the loop duration based on geometric or volumetric feedback, significantly improving performance for sparse or bounded scenes. The method extends the standard ray marching loop defined in Termination Criteria by introducing explicit break conditions. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized ray direction \mathbf{d}, scene function f(\mathbf{p}) (SDF or density), maximum march distance t{max}, maximum iteration count N{max}, and intersection epsilon \epsilon. Outputs: Boolean indicating hit status, final accumulated distance t, and optionally color/transmission values. Data Structures: t: Floating point accumulator for distance traveled. i: Integer counter for iterations. T: Floating point accumulator for transmission (opacity 1 - \alpha), initialized to 1.0. cumColor: Accumulated color, initialized to 0. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize t = 0.0, i = 0, T = 1.0, and cumColor = 0. 2. Enter loop while i < N{max} and t < t{max}. 3. Evaluate scene function at current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to get value val = f(\mathbf{p}). 4. Hit Check: If val < \epsilon (or val \le 0 for SDFs), the surface is hit. Break loop. 5. Volume Integration (if applicable): Calculate hit opacity \alpha from val (e.g., via density integration or direct SDF-to-opacity mapping). Update color: cumColor += T \cdot \alpha \cdot \text{hitColor}. Update transmission: T \leftarrow T \cdot (1.0 - \alpha). Early Exit: If T < \epsilon{trans} (or accumulated opacity > 1 - \epsilon), break loop as further contributions are negligible. 6. Step Size: Compute \Delta t based on val and scene constraints. 7. Advance: Update t \leftarrow t + \Delta t. 8. Increment i \leftarrow i + 1. 9. If loop completes without hit, return miss status. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchearlyterm(rayorigin, raydirection, scenefunc, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon): t = 0.0 i = 0 T = 1.0 cumcolor = 0.0 while i < maxsteps and t < maxdist: # Evaluate scene p = rayorigin + raydirection t val = scenefunc(p) # Termination: Surface Hit (SDF) if val < epsilon: # Hit logic would go here break # Termination: Volume Early Exit # Assuming val relates to density/opacity for volume rendering # hitopacity = computeopacity(val) # cumcolor += T hitopacity computecolor(val) # T = (1.0 - hitopacity) # if T < epsilon: # break # Step Size Calculation (Generic) # step = computestep(val) step = 0.1 # Placeholder for specific step rule # Safety Clamp # step = max(minstep, min(maxstep, step)) # Advance Ray t += step i += 1 return t, cumcolor Parameters: t{max}: Maximum march distance. A typical value cited is 2048.0. \epsilon: Intersection threshold. Typical value 0.0001. N{max}: Maximum iterations. A typical value cited is 8. Edge Cases: Infinite Distance: If the scene function returns infinity (no intersection), the loop must break to prevent infinite computation. Precision: Small epsilon values are required to detect surface hits accurately without premature termination. Time Complexity: O(k) where k is the number of steps until termination. k \le N{max}. Early termination reduces average k significantly for scenes with nearby surfaces or opaque volumes. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Prevents wasted computation on empty space or behind opaque objects; avoids infinite loops in unbounded scenes. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of t{max} and \epsilon to avoid clipping or missing distant details. This technique is a fundamental component of ray marching algorithms, particularly in real-time graphics and SDF rendering. It addresses the need for efficient loop control in iterative solvers. name: Volumetric Raymarching with SDF Density
head: Raymarching with a twist, Signed distance field (SDF) ray marching, Volumetric Raymarching
body: Volumetric Raymarching with SDF Density adapts sphere tracing principles to render volumetric objects by treating the Signed Distance Function (SDF) as a density field rather than a surface boundary. Unlike standard sphere tracing which terminates upon surface intersection, this method marches through the object's interior using a constant step size, accumulating color and alpha based on the SDF's positive values. It enables the compact, procedural representation of intricate volumes like clouds or smoke without explicit voxelization. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, normalized ray direction \mathbf{d}, a density function f(\mathbf{p}) derived from an SDF, maximum step count N{\text{max}}, constant step size s, and convergence threshold \epsilon. Outputs: Accumulated color C{\text{out}} and alpha \alpha{\text{out}}. Data Structures: Density Function f(\mathbf{p}): A scalar field where f(\mathbf{p}) > 0 inside the volume, f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 on the boundary, and f(\mathbf{p}) < 0 outside. Note that this is the negation of the standard SDF definition (f{\text{std}}(\mathbf{p}) = -f(\mathbf{p})). Parameters: MARCHSIZE (s): Constant step size. Typical value: 0.08. MAXSTEPS (N{\text{max}}): Maximum iterations. Typical value: 100. \epsilon: Small tolerance for convergence checks if used, though constant stepping often bypasses dynamic step sizing. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize: Set accumulated distance t = 0, current position \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o}, and result color/alpha C{\text{res}} = (0,0,0,0). 2. Loop: For i from 0 to N{\text{max}}-1: a. Sample Density: Evaluate d = f(\mathbf{p}). b. Check Density: If d > 0: i. Compute sample color C{\text{sample}} and alpha \alpha{\text{sample}}. A simple mapping uses density directly for alpha: \alpha{\text{sample}} = d. Color is interpolated between white and black based on density: C{\text{sample}} = \text{mix}(\text{white}, \text{black}, d). ii. Apply lighting/attenuation if applicable (e.g., C{\text{sample}}.\text{rgb} = C{\text{sample}}.\text{a}). iii. Front-to-Back Blending: Update result: C{\text{res}} = C{\text{res}} + C{\text{sample}} \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{res}}) \alpha{\text{res}} = \alpha{\text{res}} + \alpha{\text{sample}} \cdot (1 - \alpha{\text{res}}) c. Step: Advance ray: t \leftarrow t + s, \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + t \cdot \mathbf{d}. 3. Return: C{\text{res}} and \alpha{\text{res}}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def volumetricraymarchsdfdensity(rayorigin, raydirection, densityfunc, maxsteps=100, marchsize=0.08): """ Renders a volume using SDF density with constant step marching. Args: rayorigin: vec3, camera origin raydirection: vec3, normalized ray direction densityfunc: callable, returns positive value inside volume, 0 on boundary, negative outside maxsteps: int, maximum number of march steps marchsize: float, constant step size (default 0.08) Returns: vec4: Accumulated color (RGB) and alpha (A) """ t = 0.0 p = rayorigin + t raydirection rescolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] resalpha = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): # Sample density from the SDF-derived function density = densityfunc(p) if density > 0.0: # Map density to color and alpha alphasample = density # Interpolate color: mix(white, black, density) # In Python-like logic: color = white (1 - density) + black density samplecolor = [1.0 - density, 1.0 - density, 1.0 - density] # Attenuate color by alpha (as per source) samplecolor = [c alphasample for c in samplecolor] # Front-to-back blending weight = 1.0 - resalpha rescolor = [c + s weight for c, s in zip(rescolor, samplecolor)] resalpha += alphasample weight # Constant step advancement t += marchsize p = rayorigin + t raydirection return rescolor + [resalpha] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Density Scaling: The SDF must be transformed to return positive values inside the volume. Standard SDFs return negative values inside. Step Size: Using a constant step size ignores the Lipschitz property of the SDF for stepping, potentially leading to aliasing or missed thin features if s is too large. Volumetric Light Shafts (Cone Raymarching) is a real-time post-processing technique that renders volumetric light shafts by raymarching through a cone-shaped volume originating from a light source, using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) to define the volume shape and noise for density variation. It solves the problem of rendering visible light beams in fog or haze by accumulating scattered light along the view ray only within the light's defined geometry. Unlike standard cone raymarching which may use fixed geometric bounds, this method decouples the light's physical geometry from the ray's direction via SDFs, allowing for complex, non-conical volumes like cylinders or toruses in post-processing. It differs from its parent Volumetric Raymarching with SDF Density by focusing specifically on light shafts in a post-process context, using the SDF primarily for volume boundary definition and shadow occlusion rather than just surface distance. Time Complexity: O(N{\text{max}}) per ray, where N{\text{max}} is the maximum number of steps. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory, as it is procedural and does not store voxel grids. Performance: Efficient for real-time rendering of procedural volumes like clouds or smoke. Performance depends heavily on N{\text{max}} and s. Strengths: No precomputation or voxelization required; watertight traversal; compact representation. Limitations: Constant step size may cause aliasing in thin features; less efficient than adaptive sphere tracing for surface rendering. Originating from the adaptation of sphere tracing to volumetric rendering, this method leverages the continuous nature of SDFs to encode density. It gained popularity through real-time shader communities, notably Shadertoy scenes by Inigo Quilez and others, for rendering procedural clouds and smoke. It solves the problem of arbitrary light volume boundaries by allowing the renderer to accumulate light only when a sample point lies within a mathematically defined shape (e.g., cylinder, cone, sphere). Limitations: Cost grows with the number of lights; requires shadow maps for occlusion; banding can occur with few steps. When to Use: Real-time rendering of volumetric light shafts in fog or haze, especially for spot lights or directional lights with defined volumes. name: SDF Light Shaping
head: Cylindrical light shaping, Raymarched Light Shaping, SDF-Based Light Shaping
body: SDF Light Shaping is a technique for defining the geometry of volumetric light shafts using Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) during raymarching. It solves the problem of arbitrary light volume boundaries by allowing the renderer to accumulate light only when a sample point lies within a mathematically defined shape (e.g., cylinder, cone, sphere). It differs from standard cone raymarching by decoupling the light's physical geometry from the ray's direction, enabling complex, non-conical volumes like cylinders or toruses to be rendered in post-processing. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin (rayOrigin), ray direction (rayDir), light position (lightPos), light direction (lightDir), light shape radius/parameters, step size (STEP\SIZE), maximum depth (sceneDepth or cameraFar), and smooth edge width (smoothEdgeWidth). Outputs: Accumulated light color for the current pixel. Data Structures No complex data structures are required. The method relies on scalar values and 3D vectors. SDF Definition The core of the method is an SDF function that returns the signed distance from a point p to the surface of the light shape. For a cylinder, the function is defined as follows: 1. Calculate the vector from the sample point to the light's axis origin: p\to\origin = p - axisOrigin 2. Calculate the projection length of this vector onto the light's axis direction: projectionLength = dot(p\to\origin, axisDir) 3. Find the closest point on the axis to the sample point: closestPointOnAxis = axisOrigin + axisDir \times projectionLength 4. Calculate the Euclidean distance from the sample point to this closest point on the axis: distanceToAxis = length(p - closestPointOnAxis) 5. Return the signed distance by subtracting the radius: sdfVal = distanceToAxis - radius Algorithm Steps 1. Initialize the raymarching loop with a distance variable t. 2. For each step, calculate the sample position: samplePos = rayOrigin + rayDir \times t 3. Check boundary conditions: if t > sceneDepth or t > cameraFar, terminate the loop. 4. Evaluate the SDF for the current samplePos using the light's parameters (lightPos, lightDir, radius). 5. Calculate the shape factor to determine if the point is inside the light volume and to soften the edges: shapeFactor = smoothstep(0.0, -smoothEdgeWidth, sdfVal) Here, smoothEdgeWidth controls the transition softness. Note: The second parameter of smoothstep is negative (-smoothEdgeWidth) to create a falloff from 1.0 (inside) to 0.0 (outside) as sdfVal increases. 6. Early Exit Optimization: If shapeFactor < 0.1, the point is considered outside the light volume. Increment t by STEP\SIZE and continue to the next iteration without accumulating light. 7. If shapeFactor \ge 0.1, proceed with light accumulation (e.g., density calculation, scattering) using the shapeFactor to modulate the result. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdcylinder(p, axisorigin, axisdir, radius): """ Calculates the signed distance from point p to a cylinder defined by axisorigin, axisdir (normalized), and radius. """ ptoorigin = p - axisorigin projectionlength = dot(ptoorigin, axisdir) closestpointonaxis = axisorigin + axisdir projectionlength distancetoaxis = length(p - closestpointonaxis) return distancetoaxis - radius def raymarchlightshaping(rayorigin, raydir, lightpos, lightdir, radius, smoothedgewidth, stepsize, scenedepth, camerafar): """ Raymarches through a volume shaped by an SDF. Returns accumulated light color. """ accumulatedlight = vec3(0.0) t = 0.0 # Typical parameters from source # radius = 2.0 # smoothedgewidth = 0.1 while t < scenedepth and t < camerafar: samplepos = rayorigin + raydir t # Evaluate SDF sdfval = sdcylinder(samplepos, lightpos, lightdir, radius) # Calculate shape factor for soft edges # smoothstep(edgestart, edgeend, x) # edgestart = 0.0, edgeend = -smoothedgewidth shapefactor = smoothstep(0.0, -smoothedgewidth, sdfval) # Early exit if outside the light volume if shapefactor < 0.1: t += stepsize continue # Accumulate light based on shapefactor and density # Specific density/scattering formula depends on the broader # volumetric lighting context (e.g., Beer-Lambert law). # Here we assume a simple modulation for demonstration. lightcontribution = calculatelightcontribution(samplepos, shapefactor) accumulatedlight += lightcontribution t += stepsize return accumulatedlight Parameters smoothEdgeWidth: Controls the softness of the light edge. A value of 0.1 is used in the reference implementation. radius: The radius of the cylindrical light shape. A value of 2.0 is used in the reference implementation. STEPSIZE: The distance advanced per raymarch step. Not explicitly defined in sources, but implied by the loop structure. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Axis Normalization: The axisDir vector must be normalized for the projection calculation to be correct. Smoothstep Direction: The smoothstep parameters are ordered (0.0, -smoothEdgeWidth, sdfVal). Since smoothEdgeWidth is positive, the second argument is negative. This ensures that when sdfVal is negative (inside the cylinder), the result is 1.0, and it fades to 0.0 as sdfVal becomes positive (outside). Threshold Selection: The threshold 0.1 for early exit is arbitrary but effective for performance. Setting it too high may clip the light volume; too low may include unnecessary samples. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of raymarch steps. The SDF evaluation is O(1) per step. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No voxel grids or textures are required for the shape definition. Strengths: Allows for arbitrary light shapes (cylinders, cones, spheres, toruses) without modifying the raymarching geometry logic. Efficient due to early exit optimization. Limitations: The light shape is static relative to the light source's coordinate system. Complex shapes may require more expensive SDF evaluations. When to use: When volumetric light needs to conform to specific geometric constraints (e.g., light passing through a cylindrical window or shaft). SDF Light Shaping was popularized in the context of real-time post-processing volumetric lighting. The technique leverages the mathematical properties of Signed Distance Fields to define light volumes implicitly. It was notably demonstrated by Kenny Pirman in his "habitat" demo scene, a 3D reconstruction of an O’Neil cylindrical world, where volumetric light was shaped as a cylinder using SDFs. The method builds upon general raymarching techniques and SDF primitives. On Shaping Light: Real-Time Volumetric Lighting with Post-Processing..., https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/shaping-light-volumetric-lighting-with-post-processing-and-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit
head: RayMarch, Sphere Tracing with Surface/Represent Passes, SphereTracingFPass, SphereTracingKPass, Surface/Represent Ray Marching
body: Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit is a deferred rendering technique for Signed Distance Fields (SDF) that tracks both a primary surface hit and a 'represent' hit (a proxy for the surface at the pixel radius) to handle transparency and aliasing at object edges. It writes results to two render targets: index 0 for the surface and index 1 for the represent hit. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), SDF map function Map(\mathbf{p}) returning a float2 (distance, material ID), clipping planes [ClippingPlanes.x, ClippingPlanes.y], maximum sphere tracing steps N{steps}, and pixel radius factor RadiusPixel. Outputs: Two hit structures: surfaceHit and representHit, each containing DistanceToWorld, TraceDistance, MaterialId, Position, and Alpha. Data Structures: HitRecord: A structure containing: DistanceToWorld: float, distance from camera origin to hit point. TraceDistance: float, total distance traveled along ray. MaterialId: int, material identifier from SDF map. Position: vec3, 3D world position of the hit. Alpha: float, opacity value (0.0 to 1.0). currentMap: float2, current SDF sample (distance, material ID). nextMap: float2, next SDF sample. Parameters: N{steps}: Maximum number of marching iterations (e.g., 64). RadiusPixel: Scaling factor for pixel radius approximation. ClippingPlanes: Near and far clipping distances. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize surfaceHit and representHit with near plane clipping distance (ClippingPlanes.x) and far plane (ClippingPlanes.y). Set surfaceHit.MaterialId = -1 and representHit.MaterialId = -1. Set representHit.DistanceToWorld = 1000000 (large value). Set representHit.Alpha = 0. Initialize ray distance t = ClippingPlanes.x. Sample SDF at \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} to get currentMap. Initialize loop counter i = 0 and representFound = false. 2. Marching Loop: Loop i from 0 to N{steps} - 1: Calculate adaptive epsilon: \epsilon = 0.0015 \times t. Surface Hit Check: If currentMap.x \le \epsilon: Set surfaceHit.DistanceToWorld = t + currentMap.x. Set surfaceHit.TraceDistance = t + currentMap.x. Set surfaceHit.MaterialId = currentMap.y. Set surfaceHit.Position = \mathbf{o} + (t + currentMap.x)\mathbf{d}. Break loop. Represent Hit Logic: Sample next point: \mathbf{p}{next} = \mathbf{o} + (t + \text{currentMap}.x)\mathbf{d}. Get nextMap = Map(\mathbf{p}{next}). Check if inside pixel radius: If currentMap.x < (t \times RadiusPixel): If nextMap.x > currentMap.x (moving away from surface) and representFound == false: Set representFound = true. If currentMap.x < representHit.DistanceToWorld and (representHit.MaterialId == -1 or representHit.MaterialId == currentMap.y): Update representHit.DistanceToWorld = t. Update representHit.MaterialId = currentMap.y. Update representHit.TraceDistance = t. Update representHit.Position = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. Advance Ray: t \leftarrow t + \text{currentMap}.x. currentMap = nextMap. Far Clipping Check: If t > ClippingPlanes.y: Set surfaceHit.TraceDistance = ClippingPlanes.y. Set surfaceHit.MaterialId = -1. Break loop. 3. Post-Processing: If loop finished without hit (i == N{steps}): Use latest currentMap data for surfaceHit (fallback hit). Set surfaceHit.DistanceToWorld = t. Set surfaceHit.TraceDistance = t. Set surfaceHit.MaterialId = currentMap.y. Set surfaceHit.Position = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}. If representHit.MaterialId >= 0: Calculate representHit.Alpha = 1.0 - representHit.DistanceToWorld / (representHit.TraceDistance RadiusPixel). Update representHit.Position. If surfaceHit.MaterialId < 0 or representHit.MaterialId < 0: Set corresponding Alpha to 0. 4. Final Evaluation: Perform ray marching: If DisableAntiAliasing is true, call RayMarchNoAA(r, surfaceHit, representHit); else call RayMarch(r, surfaceHit, representHit). Evaluate hits: Call EvaluateHit(id.xy, r, surfaceHit, surface) and EvaluateHit(id.xy, r, representHit, represent). Write final data: Call WriteSphereTracingData(id.xy, 0, surface) and WriteSphereTracingData(id.xy, 1, represent). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def spheretracingwithrepresenthit(rayorigin, raydirection, sdfmap, clippingplanes, maxsteps, radiuspixel): """ Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit algorithm. Args: rayorigin: vec3, camera origin raydirection: vec3, normalized ray direction sdfmap: callable, returns (distance: float, materialid: int) for a point clippingplanes: tuple (near: float, far: float) maxsteps: int, maximum number of marching steps radiuspixel: float, scaling factor for pixel radius Returns: surfacehit: dict with keys 'DistanceToWorld', 'TraceDistance', 'MaterialId', 'Position', 'Alpha' representhit: dict with keys 'DistanceToWorld', 'TraceDistance', 'MaterialId', 'Position', 'Alpha' """ nearplane, farplane = clippingplanes # Initialize surface hit surfacehit = { 'DistanceToWorld': nearplane, 'TraceDistance': nearplane, 'MaterialId': -1, 'Position': rayorigin + nearplane raydirection, 'Alpha': 0.0 } # Initialize represent hit representhit = { 'DistanceToWorld': 1000000.0, 'TraceDistance': nearplane, 'MaterialId': -1, 'Position': rayorigin + nearplane raydirection, 'Alpha': 0.0 } t = nearplane currentmap = sdfmap(rayorigin + t raydirection) representfound = False for i in range(maxsteps): # Adaptive epsilon (clamp to avoid zero at t=0) epsilon = 0.0015 t if t > 0.0 else 0.0015 # Surface hit check if currentmap[0] <= epsilon: surfacehit['DistanceToWorld'] = t + currentmap[0] surfacehit['TraceDistance'] = t + currentmap[0] surfacehit['MaterialId'] = currentmap[1] surfacehit['Position'] = rayorigin + (t + currentmap[0]) raydirection break # Sample next point nextpoint = rayorigin + (t + currentmap[0]) raydirection nextmap = sdfmap(nextpoint) # Represent hit logic if currentmap[0] < (t radiuspixel): if nextmap[0] > currentmap[0] and not representfound: representfound = True if currentmap[0] < representhit['DistanceToWorld']: if representhit['MaterialId'] == -1 or representhit['MaterialId'] == currentmap[1]: representhit['DistanceToWorld'] = t representhit['MaterialId'] = currentmap[1] representhit['TraceDistance'] = t representhit['Position'] = rayorigin + t raydirection # Advance ray t += currentmap[0] currentmap = nextmap # Far clipping check if t > farplane: surfacehit['TraceDistance'] = farplane surfacehit['MaterialId'] = -1 break # Post-processing if i == maxsteps - 1 and surfacehit['MaterialId'] == -1: # Fallback hit if loop finished without explicit hit surfacehit['DistanceToWorld'] = t surfacehit['TraceDistance'] = t surfacehit['MaterialId'] = currentmap[1] surfacehit['Position'] = rayorigin + t raydirection if representhit['MaterialId'] >= 0: # Calculate alpha for represent hit denom = representhit['TraceDistance'] radiuspixel representhit['Alpha'] = 1.0 - representhit['DistanceToWorld'] / denom if denom != 0 else 0.0 if surfacehit['MaterialId'] < 0: surfacehit['Alpha'] = 0.0 if representhit['MaterialId'] < 0: representhit['Alpha'] = 0.0 return surfacehit, representhit Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Adaptive epsilon \epsilon = 0.0015 \times t scales with distance, which may cause issues at very large distances or very small scales if not clamped. Boundaries: Far clipping plane must be handled to prevent infinite loops or invalid hits. Degenerate Input: If TraceDistance is zero or RadiusPixel is zero, division by zero occurs in alpha calculation. Guard against this. Material ID Consistency: The represent hit only updates if the material ID matches the current hit or is uninitialized (-1). This prevents mixing materials in the represent pass. Hit Distance Offset: The hit distance must be calculated as t + \text{currentMap}.x rather than t to avoid underestimating the true intersection point by the adaptive epsilon margin. Time Complexity: O(N{steps}) per pixel, where N{steps} is the maximum number of sphere tracing iterations. The represent hit logic adds constant overhead per step. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for hit records. Requires two render targets (surface and represent). Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Performance scales linearly with resolution and maximum steps. The represent hit pass does not significantly increase computational cost as it shares the same marching loop. Strengths: Handles transparency and aliasing at object edges by tracking a 'represent' hit. Deferred rendering allows for efficient lighting calculations. Limitations: Requires two render targets. Alpha calculation for represent hit is heuristic and may not be physically accurate. When to use: When rendering SDFs with transparency or soft edges where standard sphere tracing produces aliasing artifacts. When not to use: When memory bandwidth is limited (due to two render targets) or when hard-edged opaque SDFs are sufficient. Sphere Tracing with Represent Hit is an unofficial technique described in a GitHub repository. It extends standard sphere tracing by introducing a secondary 'represent' hit to improve visual quality at object boundaries. The technique is implemented in a deferred rendering pipeline, integrating with ambient occlusion and environment mapping passes. SphereTracing, https://github.com/nicoell/SphereTracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Bidirectional Sphere Tracing
head: Forward-Backward Sphere Tracing, Zero-level set solver
body: Bidirectional Sphere Tracing is a robust surface extraction technique that mitigates the convergence failures of standard sphere tracing when rays miss surface edges or intersect surfaces non-orthogonally. Unlike standard sphere tracing, which relies on the Signed Distance Function (SDF) to guarantee convergence by stepping along the ray, this method uses forward and backward sphere tracing to narrow the candidate range of the surface position, then refines the zero-level set using additional solvers. It is distinct from sibling methods like Relaxed Sphere Tracing because it does not attempt to correct the step size via gradient adjustments in every iteration; instead, it bounds the search space and delegates precision to a separate refinement phase. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{r}o, normalized ray direction \mathbf{r}d, SDF function S(\mathbf{p}), forward iteration count n=16, convergence threshold \epsilon{mask} = 5 \times 10^{-5}, gradient adjustment threshold 0.005, denominator clamp 0.01, candidate sample count N{samples}=100, and sectioning steps N{sec}=8. Outputs: Refined zero-level set position \hat{\mathbf{x}}n or a flag indicating no surface intersection. Data Structures Not given in the sources. Algorithm Steps 1. Forward Sphere Tracing: Initialize \mathbf{x}0^0 = \mathbf{r}o. Iterate i from 0 to n-1 (where n=16): Evaluate d = S(\mathbf{x}i^i). Update position: \mathbf{x}i^{i+1} = \mathbf{x}i^i + d \cdot \mathbf{r}d. Let \mathbf{x}{nn} = \mathbf{x}n^n be the near zero-level set estimate. 2. Convergence Check: If |S(\mathbf{x}{nn})| < \epsilon{mask}, the ray has converged. Set \hat{\mathbf{x}}n = \mathbf{x}{nn} and terminate. 3. Backward Sphere Tracing: For rays that did not converge, initialize the backward trace from the rear intersection of the ray with a unit sphere. Calculate tf as the rear intersection of \mathbf{r}d with a unit sphere centered at the origin. Set \mathbf{x}f^0 = \mathbf{r}o + tf \mathbf{r}d. The source defines the iteration as \mathbf{x}f^{i+1} = \mathbf{x}0^i - S(\mathbf{x}f^i) \mathbf{r}d. Interpreting \mathbf{x}0^i as a typo for the previous iteration's position \mathbf{x}f^i, the update is: \mathbf{x}f^{i+1} = \mathbf{x}f^i - S(\mathbf{x}f^i) \mathbf{r}d The source does not specify the number of backward iterations. It implies solving until a "far zero-level set" \mathbf{x}{fn} is found. In practice, a symmetric count or a fixed maximum is used to bracket the surface. Let \mathbf{x}{fn} be the resulting position. 4. Candidate Range Validation: Determine the range [\mathbf{x}{nn}, \mathbf{x}{fn}]. If \mathbf{x}{fn} is closer to the camera than \mathbf{x}{nn} (i.e., the distance along \mathbf{r}d from \mathbf{r}o to \mathbf{x}{fn} is less than to \mathbf{x}{nn}), conclude that no surface exists along this ray. 5. Zero-Crossing Search: Evaluate N{samples}=100 samples uniformly distributed within the candidate range [\mathbf{x}{nn}, \mathbf{x}{fn}]. Identify the first zero crossing of S within this range. 6. Refinement (Sectioning): Assuming S is locally monotonic, refine the zero-crossing location using N{sec}=8 steps of sectioning (bisection) to obtain the final zero-level set \hat{\mathbf{x}}n. 7. Gradient Adjustment (Optional Final Step): For performance and stability, the main procedure is non-differentiable. An extra step of forward sphere tracing with gradient tracking is executed to achieve differentiability. Apply gradient direction adjustment to get the final zero-level set: \hat{\mathbf{x}}n = \hat{\mathbf{x}}n - \frac{S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}n)}{\nabla{\mathbf{x}} S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}n) \cdot \mathbf{r}d} \mathbf{r}d This adjustment is applied only if |S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}n)| < 0.005. To avoid division by zero, clamp the denominator: only apply the adjustment if |\nabla{\mathbf{x}} S(\hat{\mathbf{x}}n) \cdot \mathbf{r}d| > 0.01. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bidirectionalspheretracing(rayorigin, raydirection, sdf, nforward=16, epsilonmask=5e-5, epsilonclamp=0.01, nsamples=100, nsectioning=8): """ Bidirectional sphere tracing for robust surface extraction. Args: rayorigin: 3D vector, camera origin. raydirection: 3D vector, normalized ray direction. sdf: Callable, returns signed distance at point p. nforward: Number of forward sphere tracing iterations. epsilonmask: Threshold to consider a ray converged. epsilonclamp: Denominator clamp for gradient adjustment. nsamples: Number of samples in candidate range. nsectioning: Number of bisection steps for refinement. Returns: hitpoint: 3D vector, refined surface position, or None. """ def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def sub(a, b): return (a[0]-b[0], a[1]-b[1], a[2]-b[2]) def add(a, b): return (a[0]+b[0], a[1]+b[1], a[2]+b[2]) def scale(a, s): return (a[0]s, a[1]s, a[2]s) # 1. Forward Sphere Tracing xcurr = rayorigin for in range(nforward): d = sdf(xcurr) xcurr = add(xcurr, scale(raydirection, d)) xnn = xcurr # Near zero-level set # 2. Convergence Check if abs(sdf(xnn)) < epsilonmask: return xnn # 3. Backward Sphere Tracing # Calculate rear intersection with a unit sphere centered at origin. # Ray: r(t) = ro + t rd. |ro + trd|^2 = 1 # t^2 + 2(ro. rd)t + (|ro|^2 - 1) = 0 a = 1.0 b = 2.0 dot(rayorigin, raydirection) c = dot(rayorigin, rayorigin) - 1.0 discriminant = bb - 4ac if discriminant < 0: # Ray does not intersect unit sphere. # Fallback to a large distance or return None. return None sqrtdisc = discriminant0.5 t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2a) tf = max(t1, t2) # Rear intersection xfcurr = add(rayorigin, scale(raydirection, tf)) # Note: Source does not specify iteration count for backward trace. # Using nforward for symmetry as a standard implementation detail. for in range(nforward): d = sdf(xfcurr) xfcurr = sub(xfcurr, scale(raydirection, d)) xfn = xfcurr # Far zero-level set # 4. Candidate Range Validation distnn = dot(sub(xnn, rayorigin), raydirection) distfn = dot(sub(xfn, rayorigin), raydirection) if distfn < distnn: return None # No surface exists # 5. Zero-Crossing Search # Ensure we sample from near to far if distnn > distfn: xstart, xend = xfn, xnn else: xstart, xend = xnn, xfn candidates = [] for i in range(nsamples + 1): t = i / nsamples p = add(xstart, scale(sub(xend, xstart), t)) candidates.append((p, sdf(p))) # Find first zero crossing zerocrossingidx = -1 for i in range(len(candidates) - 1): s1 = candidates[i][1] s2 = candidates[i+1][1] if s1 s2 <= 0: zerocrossingidx = i break if zerocrossingidx == -1: return None # No zero crossing found in the range # 6. Refinement (Sectioning) pleft, sleft = candidates[zerocrossingidx] pright, sright = candidates[zerocrossingidx + 1] xhat = pleft for in range(nsectioning): mid = scale(add(pleft, pright), 0.5) smid = sdf(mid) if sleft smid < 0: pright = mid sright = smid else: pleft = mid sleft = smid xhat = mid # 7. Gradient Adjustment (Differentiable Step) shat = sdf(xhat) if abs(shat) < 0.005: # Exact threshold from source # Compute gradient numerically eps = 1e-4 grad = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for j in range(3): pplus = list(xhat) pplus[j] += eps grad = add(grad, (sdf(tuple(pplus)) - shat) / eps, (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) # Simplified gradient accumulation for clarity: grad = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for j in range(3): pplus = list(xhat) pplus[j] += eps grad = (grad[0] + (sdf(tuple(pplus)) - shat)/eps, grad[1] + (sdf(tuple(pplus)) - shat)/eps, grad[2] + (sdf(tuple(pplus)) - shat)/eps) denom = dot(grad, raydirection) if abs(denom) > epsilonclamp: xhat = sub(xhat, scale(raydirection, shat / denom)) return xhat Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The method performs n forward iterations, n backward iterations, N{samples} SDF evaluations, and N{sec} bisection steps. With n=16, N{samples}=100, and N{sec}=8, the total SDF evaluations are approximately 16 + 16 + 100 + 8 = 140 per ray, plus potentially one gradient computation for the differentiable step. This is significantly more expensive than standard sphere tracing (16 steps) but ensures convergence where standard tracing fails. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. The algorithm requires O(1) auxiliary memory per ray, as no global structures are required. Strengths: Robust against rays that miss surface edges or intersect surfaces at shallow angles, where standard sphere tracing may stall or diverge. It guarantees a bounded search range. Limitations: Higher computational cost due to the bidirectional trace and sampling phase. The backward trace requires calculating the rear intersection with a bounding volume (unit sphere in the source), which may not be applicable to all scene representations without modification. The method is non-differentiable by default; differentiability requires an extra forward step with gradient tracking. Bidirectional Sphere Tracing was introduced by Yariv et al. in the context of Neural Volumes and later adapted for Neural Lumigraph Rendering and IDR (Implicit Disentangled Representation). It addresses the limitation that standard sphere tracing convergence is not guaranteed for general shape configurations, particularly when the SDF underestimates the optimal step length due to non-orthogonal surface intersections. The technique was cited from Yariv et al. [60] in the source. Neural Lumigraph Rendering, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr46437.2021.00427, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Cloud Tracing with Pseudo-Spheroids
head: Apodaca’s code (variant)
body: Cloud Tracing with Pseudo-Spheroids renders volumetric clouds by tracing rays through a set of implicit surfaces (pseudo-spheroids or ellipsoids) and sampling noise only when the ray traverses these volumes. It differs from standard sphere tracing by using a list of randomized bounded-surface volumes rather than a single global Signed Distance Function (SDF), optimizing performance by discarding positions outside the cloud and using a collision detection method based on quadratic discriminants. Inputs: Camera origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d} (normalized) for each pixel. List of N pseudo-spheroids, each defined by center \mathbf{c}i, nominal radius R{nominal}, distortion parameter k, and maximum density \rho{max}. 3D noise function fBm(\mathbf{p}) (fractional Brownian motion), normalized to [0, 1]. Density threshold \rho{thresh} for termination. Bounding box for spatial culling. Outputs: Final color R for each pixel, blended with the sky background. Data Structures: candidates: A list of indices of pseudo-spheroids intersected by the ray. sortedcandidates: The candidates list sorted by intersection distance (back-to-front). Formulas: 1. Ray-Sphere Intersection: For a ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} and sphere i with center \mathbf{c}i and effective radius Ri, the intersection is determined by the discriminant \Delta of the quadratic equation |\mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} - \mathbf{c}i|^2 = Ri^2. \Delta = (\mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}i))^2 - (|\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}i|^2 - Ri^2) If \Delta \ge 0, the ray intersects the sphere. The entry and exit distances are: t{entry, exit} = -(\mathbf{d} \cdot (\mathbf{o} - \mathbf{c}i)) \pm \sqrt{\Delta} 2. Effective Radius: The nominal radius is modulated by a random component k to create a pseudo-spheroid shape. Ri = R{nominal} \pm k 3. Density Modulation: The density \rho at a point \mathbf{p} inside the pseudo-spheroid is calculated as. \rho(\mathbf{p}) = \rho{max} \cdot fBm(\mathbf{p}) \cdot \left(1 - \frac{||\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}i||}{Ri}\right) The term (1 - \frac{||\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}i||}{Ri}) ensures density drops to zero at the boundary. 4. Level of Detail (LOD) Step Size: The step increment \Delta t is controlled by the distance from the cloud center to balance detail and performance. Longer steps are taken when close to the camera, and smaller steps when far. The exact LOD function is not provided in the sources. Algorithm Steps: 1. Culling: For each pixel, identify pseudo-spheroids within the bounding box. 2. Collision Detection: For each candidate sphere, compute the discriminant \Delta. If \Delta \ge 0, add the sphere index to the candidates list. 3. Sorting: Sort the candidates list by intersection distance using insertion sort, ensuring back-to-front processing. 4. Ray Marching: For each pixel: Initialize accumulated color C = 0 and opacity \alpha = 0. For each sphere in sortedcandidates: Calculate intersection interval [t{entry}, t{exit}]. If the ray does not intersect the sphere, skip. March from t{entry} to t{exit} with step size \Delta t (LOD adjusted). At each step point \mathbf{p}: Calculate density \rho(\mathbf{p}) using the formula above. If \rho(\mathbf{p}) < \rho{thresh}, continue. Compute lighting L(\mathbf{p}). Update color and opacity using volume rendering integration. If \alpha \ge 1.0 (or sufficient opacity), break the marching loop for this sphere. Blend the accumulated cloud color R with the sky background. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cloudtracing(rayorigin, raydirection, spheres, noisefunc, rhothresh, skycolor): """ Render clouds using pseudo-spheroids. Args: rayorigin: Camera origin (vec3) raydirection: Normalized ray direction (vec3) spheres: List of dicts with keys: 'center', 'Rnominal', 'k', 'rhomax' noisefunc: Function fBm(p) returning normalized noise [0,1] rhothresh: Density threshold for termination skycolor: Background color (vec3) Returns: color: Final pixel color (vec3) """ candidates = [] # 1. Culling and Collision Detection for i, sphere in enumerate(spheres): c = sphere['center'] R = sphere['Rnominal'] + sphere['k'] oc = rayorigin - c a = dot(raydirection, raydirection) b = 2.0 dot(oc, raydirection) cquad = dot(oc, oc) - R R discriminant = b b - 4 a cquad if discriminant >= 0: sqrtdisc = sqrt(discriminant) t1 = (-b - sqrtdisc) / (2 a) t2 = (-b + sqrtdisc) / (2 a) candidates.append({'index': i, 'tentry': t1, 'texit': t2}) # 2. Sort Candidates (Back-to-Front) for i in range(1, len(candidates)): key = candidates[i] j = i - 1 while j >= 0 and candidates[j]['tentry'] < key['tentry']: candidates[j + 1] = candidates[j] j -= 1 candidates[j + 1] = key # 3. Ray Marching and Integration accumulatedcolor = vec3(0.0) accumulatedalpha = 0.0 for cand in candidates: tstart = max(cand['tentry'], 0.0) tend = cand['texit'] if tstart >= tend: continue # LOD Step Size: Distance from cloud center controls step size disttocenter = length(rayorigin - spheres[cand['index']]['center']) stepsize = 0.5 / (1.0 + disttocenter) t = tstart while t < tend: p = rayorigin + t raydirection sphere = spheres[cand['index']] c = sphere['center'] R = sphere['Rnominal'] + sphere['k'] disttoc = length(p - c) if disttoc < R: noiseval = noisefunc(p) density = sphere['rhomax'] noiseval (1.0 - disttoc / R) if density > rhothresh: light = vec3(1.0) color = light density alpha = density stepsize alpha = min(alpha, 1.0 - accumulatedalpha) accumulatedcolor += color alpha accumulatedalpha += alpha (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) if accumulatedalpha >= 0.99: break t += stepsize if accumulatedalpha >= 0.99: break finalcolor = accumulatedcolor + skycolor (1.0 - accumulatedalpha) return finalcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Discriminant calculation must handle floating-point errors near \Delta = 0. Boundary: Density drops to zero at the effective radius Ri. Points outside this radius should not be sampled. LOD: The exact LOD equation is not provided in the source. A distance-based heuristic is used. Sorting: Insertion sort is efficient for small lists of candidates but may be slow for very large N. A ray-tracing algorithm over a list of N randomized bounded-surface volumes (pseudo-spheroids) to render clouds, using collision detection and insertion sort for optimization. It differs from the general method by explicitly detailing the candidate selection and sorting steps. It is chosen when a simple, GPU-friendly implementation with spatial culling is required. Link: Cloud Tracing with Pseudo-Spheroids. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of spheres and M is the number of steps per sphere. The insertion sort adds O(K^2) where K is the number of intersected spheres. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store sphere data and O(K) for candidates. Performance: The method reduces computational effort by discarding positions outside the cloud and using a short list of intersected spheres. Strengths: Efficient culling, simple geometry (spheres/ellipsoids), good for real-time GPU rendering. Limitations: Approximation of cloud shape (pseudo-spheroids), LOD step size is heuristic. When to use: Real-time cloud rendering where performance is critical and high-fidelity global noise is not required. When not to use: When complex, non-spherical cloud structures are needed. Originated in the context of real-time GPU volumetric cloud rendering. The method is an improved version of Apodaca’s code [27] and is described in. It builds on the principle of using implicit surfaces to define cloud volumes and sampling noise only within those volumes. Efficient Algorithms for Real-Time GPU Volumetric Cloud Rendering with Enhanced Geometry, https://doi.org/10.3390/sym10040125, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Ray Marching with Spherical Harmonics (SH) Basis
head: JNeRF Forward/Backward Ray Marching
body: This method performs differentiable volume rendering by ray marching through a 3D grid where color is represented as Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients, enabling gradient-based optimization of the SH basis during training. It differs from standard ray marching by maintaining a logtransmit accumulator for exponential transmission and computing gradients for both the SH color coefficients and the volume density (\sigma) simultaneously within the marching loop. It is specifically designed for neural radiance field (NeRF) training frameworks that utilize SH for view-dependent appearance. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Grid data structures containing SH coefficients (grid.shdata), density values (grid.sigma), and spatial links (grid.links). Parameters: opt.stepsize, opt.stopthresh, sparsityloss, betaloss, gout (gradient output scaling). Outputs: Accumulated color \mathbf{C}. Gradients for SH coefficients (gradshout), density (graddensityout), and mask (maskout). Data Structures: grid.shdata: Array of SH coefficients. Layout depends on grid.shdatadim and grid.basisdim. grid.links: Spatial indexing for trilinear interpolation. Shared memory (CUDA context): sphfuncval[TRACERAYBKWDCUDARAYSPERBLOCK][9]: Stores SH basis function values. gradsphfuncval[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK][9]: Accumulates SH basis gradients. rayspec[TRACERAYBKWDCUDARAYSPERBLOCK]: Ray-specific state. tempstorage[TRACERAYCUDARAYSPERBLOCK]: Temporary storage for warp reductions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize logtransmit to 0.0 (or input value). Initialize accum (color accumulator) to 0.0. Initialize gradsphfuncval to 0.0. Initialize currgradsigma to 0.0. 2. Marching Loop: Loop over ray steps t with increment opt.stepsize. Termination: If \exp(\text{log\transmit}) < \text{opt.stop\thresh}, break loop. Sample: Evaluate density \sigma and SH coefficients at current ray position \mathbf{p}. Compute Transmission: Calculate pixel coverage factor: \text{pcnt} = \text{ray.world\step} \times \sigma. Calculate weight: w = \exp(\text{log\transmit}) \times (1 - \exp(-\text{pcnt})). Update transmission: \text{log\transmit} \leftarrow \text{log\transmit} - \text{pcnt}. Accumulate Color: Evaluate SH basis functions \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}) for direction \mathbf{d}. Compute color: \mathbf{C}{\text{step}} = \sum{i} \text{coeff}i \times Yi(\mathbf{d}). Accumulate: \text{accum} \leftarrow \text{accum} + w \times \mathbf{C}{\text{step}}. Compute Gradients: Determine if color is in valid range: \text{color\in\01} = (\text{total\color} == \text{lane\color\total}). Compute common gradient factor: \text{grad\common} = w \times \text{color\in\01} \times \text{gout}. Compute SH gradient contribution: \text{curr\grad\color} = \mathbf{Y}(\mathbf{d}) \times \text{grad\common}. Compute density gradient: \text{curr\grad\sigma} = \text{ray.world\step} \times (\mathbf{C}{\text{step}} \times \exp(\text{log\transmit}) - \text{accum}) Sparsity Loss: If \text{sparsity\loss} > 0, add Cauchy regularization gradient: \text{curr\grad\sigma} \leftarrow \text{curr\grad\sigma} + \text{sparsity\loss} \times \frac{4\sigma}{1 + 2\sigma^2} Backpropagate to Grid: Call trilerpbackwardcuvolone to propagate currgradcolor to SH coefficients. Call trilerpbackwardcuvolonedensity to propagate currgradsigma to density grid. 3. Finalization: Apply betaloss: \text{accum} \leftarrow \text{accum} - \text{beta\loss}. Perform warp shuffle reductions for totalcolor and colorin01. Return accumulated color and gradients. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchingshbackward(rayso, raysd, grid, opt, sparsityloss, betaloss, gout): """ Differentiable ray marching with SH basis and backward pass. """ # Initialize accumulators logtransmit = 0.0 accum = 0.0 gradshout = zeroslike(grid.shdata) graddensityout = zeroslike(grid.sigma) # Precompute SH basis values for direction # Note: In implementation, this is done per-step or cached per ray shbasis = computeshbasis(raysd, grid.basisdim) t = 0.0 while t < opt.maxdistance: # Termination check based on transmission if exp(logtransmit) < opt.stopthresh: break # Sample grid pos = rayso + t raysd sigma = sampledensity(grid, pos) shcoeffs = sampleshcoeffs(grid, pos) # Compute weight and update transmission pcnt = opt.stepsize sigma weight = exp(logtransmit) (1 - exp(-pcnt)) logtransmit -= pcnt # Compute color from SH coefficients # Cstep = sum(shcoeffs[i] shbasis[i]) colorstep = dot(shcoeffs, shbasis) # Accumulate color accum += weight colorstep # Compute gradients # Determine if color is in valid range [0, 1] # In CUDA, this is done via warp reductions totalcolor = accum # Simplified for pseudocode colorin01 = (totalcolor >= 0.0) and (totalcolor <= 1.0) gradcommon = weight colorin01 gout # Gradient for SH coefficients # gradsh = shbasis gradcommon gradsh = shbasis gradcommon # Gradient for density # currgradsigma = stepsize (colorstep exp(logtransmit) - accum) currgradsigma = opt.stepsize (colorstep exp(logtransmit) - accum) # Sparsity loss gradient if sparsityloss > 0.0: currgradsigma += sparsityloss (4 sigma / (1 + 2 sigma2)) # Backpropagate to grid (simplified) # trilerpbackwardcuvolone(grid, pos, gradsh, gradshout) # trilerpbackwardcuvolonedensity(grid, pos, currgradsigma, graddensityout) t += opt.stepsize # Final adjustment accum -= betaloss return accum, gradshout, graddensityout Time Complexity: O(N \cdot D), where N is the number of ray steps and D is the SH basis dimension. Each step requires SH evaluation and gradient computation. Memory Complexity: O(V \cdot D), where V is the number of voxels in the grid. SH coefficients are stored per voxel. Performance: Optimized for CUDA with warp-level reductions. Shared memory is used to store SH basis values and gradients to minimize global memory access. Strengths: Enables view-dependent appearance modeling with differentiable SH basis. Efficient gradient computation for both color and density. Limitations: High memory usage for large SH bases. Sensitive to opt.stopthresh and sparsityloss parameters. This method is part of the JNeRF framework, which uses Jittor for differentiable rendering. It extends standard volume rendering by incorporating Spherical Harmonics for view-dependent shading and providing backward pass implementations for training. The approach is similar to PlenOctrees and SNeRG in its use of SH and sparsity regularization. Jittor/JNeRF, https://github.com/Jittor/JNeRF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gridhopping
head: Ray Marching Polygonization, Sphere Tracing for Polygonization, fast algorithm, ray marching with SDB
body: Gridhopping is an algorithm for transforming a Signed Distance Bound (SDB) into a polygon mesh by combining sphere tracing (ray marching) with traditional polygonization techniques like Marching Cubes. It efficiently isolates the O(N^2) cells containing the surface of a shape within an N^3 grid, achieving O(N^2 \log N) complexity. Unlike standard enumeration which checks every cell, gridhopping uses rays to "hop" over empty space, making it asymptotically faster for large N. Gridhopping operates on a unit cube domain [-0.5, 0.5]^3 discretized into an N \times N \times N grid. It casts N^2 rays parallel to the z-axis to traverse the volume, identifying surface-intersecting cells and polygonizing them on the fly. Input: evalsdb: A function evaluating the Signed Distance Bound fS(\mathbf{x}) for a shape S. The SDB satisfies |fS(\mathbf{x})| \le \min{\mathbf{y} \in fS^{-1}(0)} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|2. N: The grid resolution (integer). lambda (\lambda): A shrink factor for neural network SDBs to prevent missing surface parts due to overestimation. Typical value: 1.5. Output: A polygon mesh (triangle list) generated by applying a polygonization routine (e.g., Marching Cubes) to the identified cells. Grid: Implicitly defined by the resolution N, where cell indices (i, j, k) map to spatial coordinates via the centroid formulas. Ray State: Defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Cell Centroids: The spatial coordinates of the centroid for cell (i, j, k) are: xi = -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2N} + \frac{i}{N} yj = -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2N} + \frac{j}{N} zk = -\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2N} + \frac{k}{N} Surface Intersection Threshold: A cell is considered to possibly intersect the surface if the absolute SDB value is less than or equal to the distance from the cell center to its farthest corner (half-diagonal): \text{threshold} = \sqrt{ \left(\frac{1}{2N}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{2N}\right)^2 + \left(\frac{1}{2N}\right)^2 } = \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2N} Max Distance: The maximum distance a ray can travel in a single step is bounded to prevent overshooting the top of the unit cube (z=0.5): t{max} = 1.05 \times (0.5 - z) The following pseudocode implements the core gridhopping loop. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def applygridhopping(evalsdb, N, lambdaval=1.5): mesh = [] for i in range(N): for j in range(N): k = 0 while True: # 1. Calculate ray origin at current cell centroid x = -0.5 + 1.0/(2.0N) + i/N y = -0.5 + 1.0/(2.0N) + j/N z = -0.5 + 1.0/(2.0N) + k/N # 2. Define ray direction (+z) direction = [0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # 3. Calculate max travel distance to stay within volume boundary maxdist = 1.05 (0.5 - z) # 4. Required distance to trigger polygonization (half-diagonal) requireddist = math.sqrt(6.0) / (2.0 N) # 5. Perform sphere tracing (ray marching) t = traceray([x, y, z], direction, evalsdb, maxdist, requireddist, lambdaval) # 6. Update position and cell index z = z + t k = math.floor(N (z + 0.5 - 1.0/(2.0N))) # 7. Check exit conditions if k > N - 1 or z > 1.05/2.0: break # 8. Polygonize the cell where the ray stopped mesh.extend(polygonizecell(i, j, k, evalsdb, lambdaval)) # 9. Advance to next cell for the next iteration k += 1 return mesh def traceray(origin, direction, sdbfunc, maxdistance, threshold, lambdaval): t = 0.0 while t < maxdistance: p = [origin[0] + tdirection[0], origin[1] + tdirection[1], origin[2] + tdirection[2]] dist = sdbfunc(p) / lambdaval if abs(dist) <= threshold: return t # Step forward using the lower bound on distance to surface step = max(abs(dist), 1e-6) t += step return maxdistance def polygonizecell(i, j, k, evalsdb, lambdaval): # Standard Marching Cubes routine evaluates SDB at the 8 cell vertices, # applies the shrink factor, and generates triangles based on the zero-crossing isosurface. return [] N: Grid resolution. Higher N increases accuracy but also computational cost. lambda (\lambda): Shrink factor for SDBs. Default 1.5. Threshold: \frac{\sqrt{6}}{2N}. Neural Network Overestimation: Neural network approximations of SDBs may overestimate the distance to the surface, causing the ray to skip over thin features. This is mitigated by shrinking the SDB value by a factor \lambda (typically 1.5) during evaluation. Boundary Overshoot: The max distance is set to 1.05 \times (0.5 - z) to ensure the ray does not overshoot the top of the unit cube significantly. Degenerate SDBs: If the SDB function returns non-positive distances in empty space (violating the SDB property), the ray might terminate incorrectly. The algorithm assumes |fS(\mathbf{x})| correctly bounds the distance to the surface. A standard polygonization algorithm that generates triangles from scalar field values at grid vertices. It is chosen here because it reliably converts the SDB samples at identified cells into a watertight mesh. A representation where |fS(\mathbf{x})| \le \min{\mathbf{y} \in fS^{-1}(0)} \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{y}\|2, meaning it underestimates the true distance to the surface but never overestimates it. It is preferred over exact SDFs for neural shape representations because it accommodates a broader class of learned approximations. Time Complexity: O(N^2 \log N) for a grid with N^3 cells. This is asymptotically faster than enumeration (O(N^3)) and continuation methods for large N. Memory Complexity: O(N^3) to store the SDB grid if it is pre-computed, or O(1) if the SDB is evaluated on-the-fly (e.g., via a neural network). The output mesh size is proportional to the surface area, O(N^2). Performance: On an Nvidia GeForce RTX 2060 Mobile GPU, batching neural network computations in chunks of \approx 100,000 yields significant speedups. Gridhopping is significantly faster than CPU-based enumeration. Strengths: High performance for large grids, simplicity of implementation, and portability. Limitations: Requires the SDB to be a valid bound. The shrink factor \lambda must be tuned to balance mesh completeness and marching speed, with \lambda=1.5 empirically validated for tested shapes. Developed by Markus and Sužnjević. The method was developed to address the need for efficient polygonization of Signed Distance Bounds, particularly those generated by deep learning models (neural SDBs) for 3D shape modeling. It combines the efficiency of ray marching with the geometric accuracy of Marching Cubes. The algorithm has been tested on primitive shapes, point cloud-derived SDBs, and neural network approximations. Theoretical and Empirical Analysis of a Fast Algorithm for Extracting Polygons from Signed Distance Bounds, https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.05778v2, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Trace-based SDF Rendering
head: voxel SDF tracing
body: Trace-based SDF Rendering is a technique that traces rays through a sparse voxel model using Signed Distance Fields (SDF) to determine hit depth and voxel ID, then retrieves color from the hit voxel's spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients. It differs from standard volume rendering by relying on the geometric precision of the SDF for ray marching rather than volumetric integration, and from pure mesh rendering by storing appearance data within the voxel structure rather than on triangle faces. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A sparse voxel model containing geometry (SDF) and appearance (SH coefficients), a camera view (origin, direction, intrinsics), and configuration parameters (nearplane, voxgeomode, densitymode). Outputs: A rendered color tensor, hit depth tensor, and hit voxel ID tensor. Data Structures SparseVoxelModel: Stores voxel geometry and SH coefficients. shdegree: Degree of spherical harmonics (e.g., 0 for constant color). sh0: Tensor of SH coefficients for the zeroth degree (base color), indexed by voxel ID. voxkey: Keys mapping voxel IDs to their spatial location or data. gridptsxyz: Coordinates of grid points used for TSDF fusion. Hit Data: hitdepth: Float tensor storing the distance along the ray to the surface. hitvoxid: Integer tensor storing the ID of the voxel hit by the ray. Value -1 indicates no hit (background). Algorithm Steps 1. Ray Tracing: For each view, invoke the voxel model's rendering function with the SDF trace mode. The system traces rays through the sparse voxel structure. It uses the SDF to determine the intersection depth (hitdepth) and identifies the specific voxel containing the hit point (hitvoxid). 2. Color Retrieval: Retrieve the base color from the zeroth-degree SH coefficients (sh0) indexed by hitvoxid. The color tensor is extracted and the last axis (RGB) is moved to the front to match image layout. 3. Masking: Apply a boolean mask to the rendering. Pixels where hitvoxid is -1 are masked out (set to background or ignored). 4. Evaluation (Optional): Compute Mean Squared Error (MSE) and Peak Signal-to-Noise Ratio (PSNR) against ground truth images for quality assessment. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertracesdf(voxelmodel, view, nearplane=0.02): """ Renders a view using trace-based SDF method. Args: voxelmodel: SparseVoxelModel instance with sh0 coefficients. view: Camera view object containing origin and direction. nearplane: Minimum ray distance for visibility checks. Returns: rendering: Color tensor of shape (H, W, 3). """ # Step 1: Trace rays through the sparse voxel SDF # This returns hitdepth and hitvoxid tensors hitdepth, hitvoxid = voxelmodel.rendertracesdf(view) # Step 2: Retrieve base color from SH0 coefficients # Index sh0 by hitvoxid and move the color channel axis to the front colortensor = voxelmodel.sh0[hitvoxid] rendering = colortensor.permute(-1, range(colortensor.ndim - 1)) # Step 3: Mask out background/non-hit pixels # hitvoxid == -1 indicates no intersection mask = (hitvoxid != -1) rendering = rendering mask return rendering def evaluatequality(rendering, groundtruth): """ Computes MSE and PSNR between rendered and ground truth images. """ # Clip to valid range [0, 1] renderclipped = rendering.clamp(0, 1) gtclipped = groundtruth.clamp(0, 1) # Compute MSE mse = ((renderclipped - gtclipped) 2).mean() # Compute PSNR psnr = -10 torch.log10(mse) return mse, psnr Parameters nearplane: Default value 0.02. Used in visibility checks (markmaxsamprate, marknear) to prevent near-plane artifacts. voxgeomode: Configuration parameter for voxel geometry mode. Potentially overwritable via command line argument --overwritevoxgeomode. densitymode: Configuration parameter for density mode, printed during rendering setup. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Background Handling: Hit voxels with ID -1 represent background or non-intersected rays. These must be explicitly masked out by multiplying the rendering tensor by (hitvoxid != -1) to avoid invalid color data. Precision: The method relies on float32 precision for CUDA operations. TSDF Fusion: The underlying geometry is often derived from TSDF fusion, which requires careful handling of bandwidth and pruning thresholds to ensure valid SDF values. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: High-quality geometry reconstruction from multi-view data via TSDF fusion; efficient rendering using sparse structures; support for high-frequency appearance via SH coefficients. Limitations: Requires pre-processing (TSDF fusion, voxelization); may struggle with highly transparent or thin structures if not properly captured in the SDF; memory usage can grow with scene complexity. When to Use: Suitable for novel view synthesis from multi-view images where high-fidelity geometry and appearance are required, and the scene can be represented as a sparse voxel grid. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Trace-based SDF Rendering is implemented in the svraster-win10 repository by leonhardrobin. It builds upon the principles of sphere tracing with SDFs and integrates them with sparse voxel models and spherical harmonics for appearance representation. The method is part of a pipeline that includes TSDF fusion for geometry reconstruction and adaptive voxel subdivision. leonhardrobin/svraster-win10, https://github.com/leonhardrobin/svraster-win10, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Interval Raymarching
head: Affine Raymarching, Interval SDF Raymarching
body: Interval Raymarching is a technique for accelerating signed distance field (SDF) raymarching by evaluating the SDF over an interval of the ray using affine or interval arithmetic, rather than at a single point. It solves the problem of slow linear convergence in standard sphere tracing by enabling reliable linear interpolation (secant method) to find the surface zero, achieving superlinear (phi-degree) convergence. Unlike sphere tracing, which guarantees no-penetration via conservative step sizes, Interval Raymarching uses the bounds of the arithmetic to verify if the surface could exist within the interval, allowing larger steps while maintaining correctness. Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{o}, ray direction \mathbf{d} (normalized), SDF function f(\mathbf{p}), maximum distance t{max}, maximum iterations N{max}, and an epsilon \epsilon for termination. Outputs: Intersection distance t, surface normal \mathbf{n}, and hit status. Data Structures: Affine Form: A representation of the SDF value over an interval [t{start}, t{end}] as: \tilde{f}(t) = f0 + \sum{i=1}^{n} fi \epsiloni + f{err} where f0 is the central value, fi are coefficients for independent noise variables \epsiloni \in [-1, 1], and f{err} is the remainder bound. Interval: A pair [t{min}, t{max}] representing the range of distances along the ray being evaluated. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize current distance t = 0. 2. Define an interval [t, t + \Delta t] for the next step. The size \Delta t can be adaptive or fixed, but must be large enough to make progress yet small enough to keep the affine error bound tight. 3. Evaluate the SDF f(\mathbf{p}) over the interval using affine arithmetic. This produces an affine form \tilde{f} representing the range of SDF values for all points \mathbf{p} = \mathbf{o} + \tau\mathbf{d} where \tau \in [t, t + \Delta t]. 4. Check if the interval contains zero. If the lower bound of the affine form is > 0 or the upper bound is < 0, the surface does not intersect this interval. Proceed to step 6. 5. If the interval contains zero (i.e., lower bound \le 0 and upper bound \ge 0), the surface may intersect this interval. Use the affine form to reliably linearly interpolate (method of secants) to find the approximate zero of the SDF within this interval. This provides a new, more accurate estimate for t. 6. If the zero is found within tolerance \epsilon, compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} using the gradient of the affine form (or standard finite differences if precision requires) and terminate. 7. If no zero is found or the interval was skipped, update t to the end of the interval (or the interpolated zero if found but not converged) and repeat from step 2. 8. Terminate if t > t{max} or iterations exceed N{max}. Formulas: Affine Evaluation: The SDF value at any point in the interval is bounded by: [\tilde{f}]{min} = f0 - \sum{i=1}^{n} |fi| - f{err}, \quad [\tilde{f}]{max} = f0 + \sum{i=1}^{n} |fi| + f{err} The interval contains zero if [\tilde{f}]{min} \le 0 \le [\tilde{f}]{max}. Secant Interpolation: To find the zero within the interval, linearly interpolate between the endpoints of the interval using the affine form's central value and gradient approximation. Parameters: \epsilon: Epsilon for gradient approximation and termination. Should be comparable to the projected pixel size to attenuate aliasing. \Delta t: Step size. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Underestimate SDF: If the SDF function underestimates the true distance, the algorithm may fail to detect intersections or produce incorrect results. Conservative-estimate SDFs are required. Affine Error Bound: If the error bound f{err} is too large, the interval check may always return "contains zero," leading to excessive refinement. Reduced affine arithmetic can mitigate this. Degenerate Input: Rays parallel to surfaces or grazing angles may require smaller intervals or special handling to maintain precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def intervalraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunc, maxdist, maxsteps, epsilon): t = 0.0 for i in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: return False, None, t # Define interval [t, t + step] # Step size selection is not specified in sources step = computestepsize(t, raydirection, sdffunc) tend = t + step # Evaluate SDF over interval using affine arithmetic # Returns affine form: (centralvalue, coefficients, errorbound) affineform = evaluatesdfaffine(sdffunc, rayorigin, raydirection, t, tend) # Check if interval contains zero lowerbound = affineform.central - sum(abs(c) for c in affineform.coeffs) - affineform.error upperbound = affineform.central + sum(abs(c) for c in affineform.coeffs) + affineform.error if lowerbound > 0 or upperbound < 0: # No intersection in this interval, skip t = tend continue # Interval contains zero; use secant method to find approximate zero # Use affine form to interpolate tzero = interpolatezero(affineform, t, tend) # Check for convergence p = rayorigin + raydirection tzero val = sdffunc(p) if abs(val) < epsilon: # Compute normal from affine form gradient or finite differences normal = computenormal(sdffunc, p, epsilon) return True, normal, tzero # Update t to the found zero for next iteration t = tzero return False, None, t def evaluatesdfaffine(sdffunc, origin, direction, tstart, tend): # This function implements affine arithmetic evaluation of the SDF # over the interval [tstart, tend]. # It returns an affine form representing the range of SDF values. # Implementation details depend on the specific affine arithmetic library or method. # Not given in the sources. pass def interpolatezero(affineform, tstart, tend): # Linear interpolation using the affine form to find the zero crossing # Not given in the sources. pass def computestepsize(t, direction, sdffunc): # Adaptive step size calculation # Not given in the sources. pass def computenormal(sdffunc, point, epsilon): # Compute surface normal using finite differences # Not given in the sources. pass A variant that reduces the error bound by tracking dependencies between variables, improving precision for complex SDFs. Choose when standard affine arithmetic yields too large error bounds. A broader category that includes Interval Raymarching but applies to general implicit functions, not just SDFs. Choose when dealing with non-distance-based implicit surfaces. Time Complexity: Superlinear convergence (phi-degree) compared to linear convergence in sphere tracing, potentially reducing iteration counts significantly. However, each iteration involves more expensive affine arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing affine forms, which have higher memory overhead than scalar values. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Faster convergence for SDFs; inherently provides gradient approximation for lighting; avoids penetration issues through interval checking. Limitations: Requires conservative SDFs; affine arithmetic can be complex to implement; error bounds may lead to excessive refinement if not managed. When to Use: When rendering complex SDF scenes with high iteration counts in standard sphere tracing; when gradient information is needed for lighting. When Not to Use: For simple scenes where sphere tracing is sufficient; when SDFs are not conservative. Interval Raymarching was proposed by Kragen Javier Sitaker in 2019, inspired by discussions with banyaszvonat and prior work on interval arithmetic in raytracing by Jorge Eliecer Florez Diaz. It builds on the popularity of SDF raymarching in the demoscene and implicit CAD systems. The technique leverages affine arithmetic to achieve faster convergence than the linear convergence of sphere tracing. Interval raymarching ⁑ Dercuano, https://dercuano.github.io/notes/interval-raymarching.html, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Procedural and Mathematical Surfaces
body: This family renders geometry using analytical Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) or procedural noise fields rather than discrete meshes or voxel grids. It solves the problem of rendering infinite, high-frequency, or complex organic detail without the memory overhead of storage or the tessellation limits of polygonal meshes. Unlike Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians which approximates geometry as probabilistic density, or Ray Marching with Neural SDF which uses learned representations, this family relies on closed-form mathematical expressions or hierarchical noise evaluations to provide exact distance bounds for sphere tracing. The family operates on the principle that a scene is defined by a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) where the zero-level set f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 represents the surface [13339-signed-distance-field-representations-and-operations]. For sphere tracing to be valid, the function must satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, ensuring |f(\mathbf{p}1) - f(\mathbf{p}2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2\| [13339-signed-distance-field-representations-and-operations]. This guarantees that the value f(\mathbf{p}) is a safe lower bound on the distance to the surface, allowing the ray marcher to step forward by exactly f(\mathbf{p}) without tunneling [13339-signed-distance-field-representations-and-operations]. Composition is achieved through Boolean operations on the distance values: Union: f{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Intersection: f{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Subtraction: f{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(-f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} into the local coordinate space of the primitive using the inverse transformation matrix M^{-1} before evaluation. Procedural noise (e.g., FBM) is often used to perturb these analytical surfaces, creating hypertextures where the isosurface is defined by SDF(\mathbf{p}) + Bn(\mathbf{p}) = 0. Terrain Raymarching renders a 2D heightmap H(x, z) as a 3D surface. It differs from standard SDF ray marching because it does not strictly rely on the Lipschitz continuity of a global 3D SDF for step sizing; instead, it samples the heightmap at the ray's (x, z) coordinates and checks if the ray's y position intersects the height. It is chosen for efficient, infinite terrain rendering where vertical resolution is decoupled from horizontal sampling. [1357-terrain-raymarching] Neon Raymarcher generates an infinite procedural synthwave city using SDFs within a single fullscreen fragment shader, requiring no meshes or scene graph. It distinguishes itself by employing a deterministic integer-hashing contract shared between CPU and GPU to generate building layouts, and an analytic sine-wave curve to define the road centerline, ensuring perfect synchronization between the rendered visual and the camera path. [4157-neon-raymarcher] Menger Sponge Raymarching renders the Menger sponge fractal by iteratively applying a recursive distance function. It distinguishes itself by using a specific iterative modulo-based SDF construction that efficiently approximates the infinite-detail sponge geometry within a bounded volume, combined with a floor plane for grounding. [4875-menger-sponge-raymarching] This topic covers the generation of complex, self-similar, or chaotic surfaces using iterative mathematical functions (e.g., Mandelbulb, Julia sets) or recursive SDF compositions. It is chosen when the geometry requires infinite detail or organic complexity that cannot be described by simple Boolean primitives. [10024-fractals-and-mathematical-surfaces] This foundational topic defines the exact analytical primitives and the algebraic rules for combining them. It is distinct from k-SDF approximations by providing exact Euclidean distances. It serves as the base layer for SDF primitive definitions and transformations. [13339-signed-distance-field-representations-and-operations] The Parametric Surface Density Model defines a 3D object by six scalar quantities: three separating surfaces and the density fields defined on these interfaces. It solves the problem of reconstructing volumetric objects from limited data by explicitly modeling boundaries and material properties, rather than storing a dense 3D grid. Unlike siblings relying on implicit distance fields or voxel grids, it separates geometric definition from volumetric definition, allowing for adaptive elliptic operators to fill the volume.
