name: SDF Smooth Union
head: LogSumExp SDF Union, Quadratic Polynomial Smooth Minimum, S-Union, Smooth Minimum, Smooth Union, Smooth Union SDF Operator, Smooth Union of Spheres, Spherical SDF Blending
body: SDF Smooth Union is a constructive operator that blends two Signed Distance Function (SDF) values, a and b, into a single smooth distance field d{\text{out}}, replacing the sharp geometric intersection of a boolean union with a rounded transition region controlled by a radius parameter k. It sets itself apart from standard boolean operators by providing differentiable approximations of the union, available in polynomial and exponential formulations. Inputs: Two scalar distance values a and b, and a scalar smoothing radius k > 0. Output: A single scalar distance d{\text{out}} representing the smooth union. The core operator operates on scalar floats. In multi-material contexts, it may operate on structs containing distance and material data, such as SdResult(distance, material). Two dominant formulations exist in the literature. 1. Polynomial Blend This method uses a quadratic blend term subtracted from a linear interpolation. h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 + 0.5 \frac{b - a}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) d{\text{out}} = \text{mix}(b, a, h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Where \text{mix}(a, b, t) = a(1 - t) + b \cdot t. 2. Exponential Blend (LogSumExp) This method uses the soft-min approximation via exponentials. d{\text{out}} = -\frac{1}{k} \ln \left( e^{-k \cdot a} + e^{-k \cdot b} \right) k (Smoothing Radius): Controls the width of the transition region between the two shapes. Larger values create a smoother, wider blend between the shapes. Typical values range from 0.33 to 1.0 depending on scene scale. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothunionpolynomial(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: """Computes the smooth union of two SDF values using polynomial interpolation.""" if k <= 0: return min(a, b) h = 0.5 + 0.5 (b - a) / k h = max(0.0, min(1.0, h)) mixval = b (1.0 - h) + a h blendterm = k h (1.0 - h) return mixval - blendterm def smoothunionexponential(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: """Computes the smooth union using the LogSumExp approximation.""" if k <= 0: return min(a, b) vala = -k a valb = -k b maxval = max(vala, valb) logsum = maxval + math.log(math.exp(vala - maxval) + math.exp(valb - maxval)) return -logsum / k def smoothunion(a: float, b: float, k: float, method: str = "polynomial") -> float: """Wrapper for smooth union operations.""" if method == "exponential": return smoothunionexponential(a, b, k) return smoothunionpolynomial(a, b, k) Precision: In the exponential method, direct computation of e^{-k \cdot a} can overflow or underflow for large a or large k. The logsumexp trick (subtracting the max value before exponentiating) is required for numerical stability. Approximation: The operator produces a smooth approximation rather than an exact distance field in the transition region. Uses cubic polynomial interpolation for blending. Chosen when a specific, controllable curvature is desired without the computational cost of exponentials. The dual operator for smooth boolean intersection, often implemented as -smin(-a, -b, k). Extends smooth union to blend not just distances but also material properties across the transition region. A simpler, linear interpolation between distances, which does not preserve the distance field property as well as smooth union but is cheaper. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive pair. The polynomial method involves basic arithmetic operations (add, multiply, clamp). The exponential method involves exp and log, which are more expensive but still constant time. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the operator itself. Strengths: Eliminates sharp edges, allowing for organic merging of shapes (e.g., metaballs, pipes, joints). Visually smooth results with minimal computational overhead compared to mesh-based smoothing. Limitations: Does not produce a true distance field in the transition region (it is an approximation). When to Use: When creating organic shapes, joints, or rounded edges in ray marching scenes. When Not to Use: When exact geometric precision is required at the intersection. The concept of smooth minimum operators in SDFs emerged from the need to create organic, continuous shapes in ray marching without relying on polygonal meshes. The polynomial smooth minimum (smin) was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online tutorials on ray marching and SDFs. The exponential variant (LogSumExp) is derived from the mathematical property that the soft-min function is a differentiable approximation of the min function, widely used in machine learning and optimization. These operators are now standard primitives in GLSL-based ray marching engines and differentiable rendering frameworks. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, https://github.com/tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, https://github.com/arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) An Introduction to Raymarching - Maxime Garcia, https://typhomnt.github.io/teaching/raytracing/raymarchingintro/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) cahekp/Raymarching, https://github.com/cahekp/Raymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Polynomial Smooth Minimum
head: Blending SDF Geometry, Quilez smin, Quilez smooth min, SDF Smin, Smooth Minimum, Smooth SDF Blending
body: Polynomial Smooth Minimum is a differentiable blending operator for two Signed Distance Function (SDF) values, creating a smooth union of shapes without the sharp edges inherent in the standard boolean min operation. It interpolates the distance values using a polynomial function controlled by a smoothing radius parameter k, allowing primitives to merge organically, similar to metaballs. It sets itself apart from exponential smooth minimum by using polynomial interpolation rather than logarithmic/exponential functions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two scalar distance values a and b (the SDF values of two primitives at a point), and a scalar smoothing radius k \ge 0. Output: A single scalar distance value d{smooth} representing the blended SDF. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the operation is element-wise on scalar floats. Parameters: k: The blending radius or smoothness factor. It controls the width of the transition zone between the two shapes. Typical values: 0.2 or 0.3. Note: describes an exponential variant with k=32, but the polynomial variants cited in use k as a direct radius (e.g., 0.2). We adhere to the polynomial definitions where k is a small positive radius. Formulas: There are two primary polynomial formulations found in the sources. They are mathematically distinct approximations. 1. Quilez's Quadratic Smooth Minimum (Common Implementation): This is the most frequently cited "Quilez smin" in the provided sources. Let h be a blending weight: h = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{b - a + k}{2k}, 0, 1\right) Alternatively expressed as: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 + 0.5 \cdot \frac{b - a}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) The result is: d{smooth} = a \cdot h + b \cdot (1 - h) - k \cdot h \cdot (1 - h) Another equivalent form found in uses a different h definition based on the absolute difference: h = \frac{\max(k - |a - b|, 0)}{k} d{smooth} = \min(a, b) - h^2 \cdot k \cdot 0.25 Note: The sources use the first formulation (linear mix minus quadratic correction). uses the second formulation (min minus quadratic correction). Both are cited as "Polynomial Smooth Minimum" or "Quilez smin". The first formulation is generally preferred for its symmetry and ease of derivation from linear interpolation. 2. Power Mean Approximation (Alternative Polynomial): cites a blending function: d{smooth} = \left( \frac{a^k b^k}{a^k + b^k} \right)^{1/k} This is often used for k > 0. However, the term "Polynomial Smooth Minimum" in the context of "Quilez smin" primarily refers to the quadratic approximation above. The power mean is computationally more expensive due to powers and roots. Numbered Steps (Quilez Quadratic Form): 1. Check if k is effectively zero. If k \le \epsilon (e.g., 10^{-6}), return \min(a, b) to avoid division by zero and revert to hard union. 2. Calculate the intermediate blend factor h: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 + 0.5 \cdot \frac{b - a}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) 3. Calculate the linear interpolation between a and b using h. Note that mix(b, a, h) is b + h(a - b) = a \cdot h + b \cdot (1 - h). 4. Subtract the quadratic correction term k \cdot h \cdot (1 - h) from the linear interpolation. 5. Return the result. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def polynomialsmoothminimum(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: """ Computes the polynomial smooth minimum of two SDF values a and b using the quadratic approximation (Quilez smin). Args: a: Distance value of the first primitive. b: Distance value of the second primitive. k: Smoothing radius. Must be >= 0. Returns: Blended distance value. """ # Guard against division by zero and revert to hard min if k is negligible if k <= 1e-6: return min(a, b) # Calculate blend factor h # h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 (b - a) / k, 0.0, 1.0) h = 0.5 + 0.5 (b - a) / k if h < 0.0: h = 0.0 elif h > 1.0: h = 1.0 # Linear interpolation: mix(b, a, h) = b + h (a - b) # Which is equivalent to: a h + b (1 - h) linearmix = a h + b (1.0 - h) # Subtract quadratic correction term result = linearmix - k h (1.0 - h) return result Edge Cases and Pitfalls: k=0: Division by zero in the calculation of h. Must be handled by falling back to min(a, b). Precision: The term k \cdot h \cdot (1 - h) is always non-negative. If a and b are very large, precision loss might occur, but typically SDFs are normalized or small. Symmetry: The formula is symmetric with respect to a and b if h is calculated correctly. S(a, b, k) = S(b, a, k). Continuity: The function is differentiable, avoiding the sharp discontinuities of standard boolean operations. Polynomial Smooth Maximum is the dual operator for smooth intersection of SDFs. It is implemented by negating the inputs, applying smooth minimum, and negating the result: \text{smax}(a, b, k) = -\text{smin}(-a, -b, k). Using the quadratic formulation from: h = \frac{\max(k - |a - b|, 0)}{k} \text{smax}(a, b, k) = \max(a, b) + h^2 \cdot k \cdot 0.25 This creates a smooth "merge" where the surfaces bulge outward at the intersection, effectively rounding the corner of the intersection. It is used for smooth intersections or to create "blobby" unions where the material expands. Time Complexity: O(1). The operation involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, clamp). Memory Complexity: O(1). No additional memory is allocated. Strengths: Provides smooth, organic transitions between shapes. Differentiable, allowing for gradient-based optimization or smooth normals. Limitations: The resulting distance field is an approximation rather than a true Euclidean distance field. When to use: When organic, metaball-like merging of primitives is desired. The Polynomial Smooth Minimum, specifically the quadratic approximation known as "Quilez smin", was popularized by Íñigo Quilez in his article "Blending SDF Geometry". It is a standard technique in ray marching and constructive solid geometry (CSG) for SDFs. It serves as a practical alternative to the exponential smooth minimum (which uses -\frac{\ln(e^{-ka} + e^{-kb})}{k}), offering a balance between smoothness and computational efficiency. The method is used to create complex, organic shapes from simple primitives. haydenparker3/3D-Sphere-Tracing, https://github.com/haydenparker3/3D-Sphere-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ollituohenmaa/raymarching-pathtracer, https://github.com/ollituohenmaa/raymarching-pathtracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, https://github.com/arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) MohammadHossinzehi/sdf-raymarcher, https://github.com/MohammadHossinzehi/sdf-raymarcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Further Graphics - University of Cambridge, https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1920/FGraphics/1.%20Ray%20Marching%20and%20Signed%20Distance%20Fields.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Sample - Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions, https://github.com/ComputeNode/cyfra/pull/13, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ray Marching with Signed Distance Fields - Scribd, https://www.scribd.com/document/831412915/1-Ray-Marching-and-Signed-Distance-Fields, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU Ray Marching Techniques, https://www.scribd.com/document/814069988/5-GPU-Ray-Marching, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Volumetric Rendering: Signed Distance Functions - Alan Zucconi, https://www.alanzucconi.com/2016/07/01/signed-distance-functions/, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Smooth Intersection
head: Round Intersection, S-Intersection, Smooth SDF Operations
body: Smooth Intersection is a Constructive SDF Modeling operator that blends the overlap region of two shapes to produce rounded edges, serving as a smooth approximation of the boolean intersection operation. Unlike sharp boolean operators, it uses a blending radius parameter to create a continuous transition between the input distance fields. It is distinct from SDF Smooth Union (which blends the exterior of shapes) and Linear SDF Blend (which uses linear interpolation), offering a specific curvature profile for the intersection feature. Inputs and Outputs: a, b: Scalar signed distance values from two primitive SDFs at a query point. k (or r): Scalar blending radius or smoothing factor, k > 0. Output: Scalar blended distance d{out}. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Numbered Steps and Formulas: Two primary formulations are cited in the sources. They are mathematically distinct in their derivation but serve the same semantic purpose. Formulation 1 (Polynomial Blend): Defined in, this method uses a quadratic blend based on the difference between distances. 1. Calculate the blend factor h: h = \text{clamp}\left(0.5 - 0.5 \frac{b - a}{k}, 0.0, 1.0\right) 2. Calculate the result using linear interpolation (mix): d{out} = \text{mix}(b, a, h) + k \cdot h \cdot (1.0 - h) Where \text{mix}(x, y, t) = x(1-t) + yt. Formulation 2 (Geometric/Root Blend): Defined in, this method uses a geometric construction involving square roots. 1. Calculate the maximum distance: m = \max(a, b). 2. Check if both points are within the blending radius of the surface: Condition: -a < k \land -b < k. 3. If the condition is true: d{out} = \max\left(m, -\left(k - \sqrt{(k+a)^2 + (k+b)^2}\right)\right) 4. Otherwise: d{out} = m Parameters: k: The smoothing factor or blending radius. It defines the width of the transition region. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lipschitz Continuity: The operator preserves Lipschitz continuity (|\nabla d| \le 1) only if the gradients of the two input SDFs are orthogonal. If the angle between gradients deviates by more than 30^\circ or if surfaces are parallel and close, continuity is lost, causing ray marching artifacts like overshooting or jittering. Disagreement: use a polynomial blend, while uses a geometric root blend. describes a smooth union formula (min(d1, d2) - h^2/4k) which is structurally similar but applied to the minimum operator, not intersection. references smax, which is a different primitive. Implementers should verify which curvature profile is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothintersectionpolynomial(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: """ Computes a smooth intersection using the polynomial blend formulation. """ if k <= 0: return max(a, b) diff = b - a h = 0.5 - 0.5 (diff / k) if h < 0.0: h = 0.0 elif h > 1.0: h = 1.0 mixed = b (1.0 - h) + a h return mixed + k h (1.0 - h) def smoothintersectiongeometric(a: float, b: float, k: float) -> float: """ Computes a smooth intersection using the geometric root formulation. """ m = max(a, b) if (-a < k) and (-b < k): term = (k + a)2 + (k + b)2 inner = -(k - term0.5) return max(m, inner) return m Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Produces visually smooth, rounded edges for CSG intersections without requiring mesh reconstruction. Limitations: Loss of Lipschitz continuity in non-orthogonal gradient regions can break sphere tracing convergence. When to use: When rounded corners are desired for intersecting primitives in ray marching. When not to use: When sharp boolean edges are required, or when gradient orthogonality cannot be guaranteed (leading to marching artifacts). Smooth Intersection operators are part of the broader field of Signed Distance Field (SDF) modeling, popularized by interactive ray marching techniques. The specific polynomial formulation is often associated with community implementations in real-time graphics. The geometric formulation appears in marching cubes contexts. These operators are used in procedural geometry generation, VFX, and real-time rendering to create complex shapes from simple primitives. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, https://github.com/tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) JamesRicher/TerminalSignedDistanceFieldRenderer, https://github.com/JamesRicher/TerminalSignedDistanceFieldRenderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Multi-Material Distance Fields
head: Augmented SDF signature, Color-Coded SDFs, Material-Augmented Signed Distance Function, MaterialSDF, SDF with Material Data, SDF with material ID
body: Multi-Material Distance Fields extend standard Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) to return both a geometric distance and a material identifier for every point in space. This allows Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) operations to preserve material assignments during boolean combinations, enabling per-object shading within a single ray-marched scene. Unlike SDF Smooth Union or Linear SDF Blend, which blend distance values to create smooth transitions, Multi-Material Distance Fields use hard boolean logic to select the closest object, preserving sharp material boundaries while inheriting the edge-blending properties of the underlying combination operator. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D position vector \mathbf{p} and a CSG tree structure where each leaf node contains an SDF primitive and a material ID. Output: A tuple or vector containing the signed distance d and the material identifier m. In GLSL/HLSL implementations, this is a float2 where the x-component is the distance and the y-component is the material data (e.g., a color index). In functional implementations, it is a tuple (Double, Material.ID). Data Structures: 1. MaterialSDF Type: A function signature mapping a vector to a pair of values. Functional: type MaterialSDF = Vector => (Double, Material.ID). Shader: float2 return type. 2. CSG Leaf Node: Contains the primitive SDF function and the associated material ID. Structure: Leaf(sdf: SDF, material: Material.ID). Algorithm Steps: The method recursively evaluates the CSG tree. For any node, it evaluates the left and right children to get their respective distance-material pairs, then applies the boolean operator logic to select the correct pair. 1. Leaf Evaluation: If the current node is a leaf, evaluate the leaf's SDF at position \mathbf{p} to get distance d, and return the pair (d, \text{material}). 2. Recursive Evaluation: If the current node is an internal node, recursively evaluate the left child to get (da, ma) and the right child to get (db, mb). 3. Operator Application: Apply the specific boolean operator to select the output pair based on the distance values: Union: Select the pair with the smaller distance. If da \le db, return (da, ma); otherwise, return (db, mb). Intersection: Select the pair with the larger distance. If da \ge db, return (da, ma); otherwise, return (db, ma). The implementation consistently assigns the material of the left operand (ma) regardless of which distance defines the boundary. Difference: Subtract the right child from the left. If da \ge -db, return (da, ma); otherwise, return (-db, ma). The material of the subtracted object (mb) is discarded, and the material of the base object (ma) is retained. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatematerialsdf(tree, p): """ Recursively evaluates the CSG tree to return (distance, materialid). """ if tree.isleaf(): distance = tree.sdf(p) return (distance, tree.material) leftresult = evaluatematerialsdf(tree.left, p) rightresult = evaluatematerialsdf(tree.right, p) da, ma = leftresult db, mb = rightresult operation = tree.operation if operation == "Union": if da <= db: return (da, ma) else: return (db, mb) elif operation == "Intersection": if da >= db: return (da, ma) else: return (db, ma) elif operation == "Difference": if da >= -db: return (da, ma) else: return (-db, ma) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown operation: {operation}") def raymarchmaterialsdf(scenetree, ro, rd, maxsteps=64, maxdist=100.0, epsilon=0.001): """ Ray marches the multi-material SDF. Returns (hitdistance, hitpoint, materialid) or (None, None, None). """ t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): if t > maxdist: break p = ro + rd t d, m = evaluatematerialsdf(scenetree, p) if d < epsilon: return t, p, m # Conservative step guard t += max(d, 0.001) return None, None, None Shader Implementation Details: In GPU shaders, the map() function returns a float2. The union operator opU compares the x-components (distances) and returns the entire float2 vector of the closer object. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. float2 opU(float2 d1, float2 d2) { return (d1.x < d2.x) ? d1: d2; } The final color is determined by sampling a ColorRamp texture using the y-component (material ID) of the hit point's output from map(). Parameters: ColorRamp: A 1D or 2D texture (sampler2D) that maps material IDs (y-component) to RGB colors. Precision: Standard float precision is used. Care must be taken with the comparison da \le db to avoid jittering at exact boundaries, though hard boolean operations are generally stable compared to smooth blends. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lipschitz Continuity: As with all SDF combination operators, if the gradients of the two input SDFs are not orthogonal, Lipschitz continuity (|\nabla d| \le 1) may be violated, leading to ray marching artifacts like overshooting or jittering. If the angle between gradients deviates by more than 30^\circ, or if surfaces are parallel and close, continuity is lost. Material Assignment in Intersection: The implementation assigns the material of the left operand (ma) when the right distance defines the boundary, which may not match visual expectations for all CSG trees. A data structure that holds surface shading information, including color, physical properties, and texture descriptors, accessible from both host and device code. It distinguishes itself by explicitly separating geometric displacement (via heightmapTex) from shading calculations and by managing texture projection modes and normal deflection scaling. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables complex, multi-material scenes with sharp material boundaries using a single ray marcher. Simple to implement by augmenting the return type of the SDF map function. Limitations: Does not inherently support smooth material blending (e.g., gradients between materials) unless combined with smooth union operators that also blend the material ID, which is not standard in the basic definition. The technique extends standard SDF ray marching to support per-object material assignment within a CSG scene. It allows artists to assign distinct visual properties to individual primitives within a CSG composition without requiring multiple render passes or complex shader branching for material selection. The implementation details provided in demonstrate a functional programming approach (Scala) for constructing the CSG tree, while provides the GLSL/HLSL shader implementation for real-time rendering. sungiant/sdf, https://github.com/sungiant/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Raymarching Distance Fields: Concepts and Implementation..., https://adrianb.io/2016/10/01/raymarching.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Material Object Format
body: The Material Object Format is a data structure that holds surface shading information, including color, physical properties, and texture descriptors, accessible from both host and device code. It distinguishes itself by explicitly separating geometric displacement (via heightmapTex) from shading calculations and by managing texture projection modes and normal deflection scaling. Input: Material parameters (albedo, metalness, roughness, F0) and optional texture descriptors. Output: A Material instance containing shading and texture metadata. The Material object consists of the following fields: | Field | Type | Description | |:--- |:--- |:--- | | albedo | vec3 (linear float) | Surface color in linear RGB. | | metalness | float | Range [0, 1]. Controls specular vs. diffuse shading contribution. | | roughness | float | Range [0, 1]. Controls smoothness of reflections and light scattering. | | F0 | vec3 (linear float) | Base reflectivity when metalness is 0. | | triplar | bool | Texture projection mode. false for XZ planar mapping, true for triplanar mapping. | | normalStrength | float | Linear scaling factor for normal deflection from normal maps. | | albedoTex | int | Texture descriptor for sRGB albedo map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with albedo. | | normalTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear detail normal map. Value -1 if unused. | | roughnessTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear roughness map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with roughness. | | metalnessTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear metalness map. Value -1 if unused. Multiplied with metalness. | | heightmapTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear displacement heightmap. Value -1 if unused. Used for geometric displacement by the object SDF, not for shading. | | ambietTex | int | Texture descriptor for linear ambient occlusion map. Value -1 if unused. | Texture descriptors are integers referencing texture objects or mipmap arrays, and only the descriptor value is needed to read a texture from device code. Two constructors initialize the Material object: 1. Full Constructor: Takes albedo, metalness, roughness, and F0 as arguments. Sets all texture descriptors (albedoTex, normalTex, roughnessTex, metalnessTex, heightmapTex, ambietTex) to -1. Sets triplar to false (planar mapping). Sets normalStrength to 1.0. 2. Simplified Constructor: Takes albedo, roughness, and metalness. Calls the Full Constructor with these values and a default F0 of [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. The default F0 is considered the standard base reflectance for most non-metal dielectrics (e.g., plastics, organic materials). Unverified code. Constructor 2 (Simplified): F0 is None, defaults to [0.04, 0.04, 0.04]. """ if F0 is None: F0 = [0.04, 0.04, 0.04] self.albedo = albedo self.metalness = metalness self.roughness = roughness self.F0 = F0 self.triplar = False self.normalStrength = 1.0 self.albedoTex = -1 self.normalTex = -1 self.roughnessTex = -1 self.metalnessTex = -1 self.heightmapTex = -1 self.ambietTex = -1 Texture Descriptors: All texture fields default to -1 to specify the material as textureless. Heightmap vs. Shading: heightmapTex is explicitly excluded from shading calculations and is used solely by the object SDF for geometric displacement. Normal Strength: normalStrength scales normal deflection from normal map textures, which is useful when displacing a surface at a less steep angle than the normal map is designed for. name: Linear SDF Blend
head: Shape Blending
body: Linear SDF Blend performs a weighted linear interpolation between two signed distance function values, allowing for morphing between shapes or creating smooth transitions based on a scalar control factor. It is distinct from spatially varying blends like Smoothstep SDF Blend by using a constant or externally controlled factor rather than deriving the factor from the query point's position. Inputs and Outputs: Input d1: The signed distance value of the first primitive at the query point. Input d2: The signed distance value of the second primitive at the query point. Input a: The blend factor, a scalar in the range [0, 1]. Output d{blend}: The interpolated signed distance value. Data Structures: The inputs and output are simple scalar floating-point values. Steps: 1. Retrieve the signed distance d1 for the first shape at the current raymarching position. 2. Retrieve the signed distance d2 for the second shape at the current raymarching position. 3. Determine the blend factor a, which can be a constant, a function of time, or a function of other scene variables. 4. Compute the blended distance using the linear interpolation formula: d{blend} = a \cdot d1 + (1 - a) \cdot d2. Parameters: a: The blending weight. a=0 yields d2, a=1 yields d1. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The blend factor a must be clamped to [0, 1] to prevent extrapolation artifacts. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linearsdfblend(d1: float, d2: float, a: float) -> float: """ Perform linear interpolation between two SDF values. Args: d1: Distance of the first primitive. d2: Distance of the second primitive. a: Blend factor in [0, 1]. Returns: The blended distance value. """ a = max(0.0, min(1.0, a)) # Clamp to valid range return a d1 + (1.0 - a) d2 A variant where the blend factor is derived spatially from the query point's distance to the origin using a smoothstep function. Definition: Blends between two SDFs based on the distance of the query point from the origin, creating a spatially varying transition zone. Formula: s = \text{smoothstep}(0.0, 1.0, \|p\|) d = (1 - s) \cdot ax + s \cdot bx where p is the query point, \|p\| is its length, and ax, bx are the distance components of the input SDFs. Parameters: The smoothstep range is fixed between 0.0 and 1.0, defining the radial region where the blend occurs. Layout: The SDF functions return a two-component vector where the x-component is the distance (float) and the y-component is the primitive ID (float, typically 1). Pseudocode: python def length(v): """Compute Euclidean norm of a 3D vector.""" return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): """Standard smoothstep interpolation.""" t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) def smoothstepsdfblend(p, a, b): """ Blend two SDFs based on the distance of p from the origin. Args: p: Query point as a 3-tuple (x, y, z). a: 2-tuple containing (distance, id) for primitive A. b: 2-tuple containing (distance, id) for primitive B. Returns: 2-tuple containing (blendeddistance, id). """ distfromorigin = length(p) s = smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, distfromorigin) d = (1.0 - s) a[0] + s b[0] return (d, 1.0) The concept of blending SDFs using linear interpolation is discussed in the context of raymarching tutorials and is presented as a direct analogy to alpha blending in color space. The spatially varying variant using smoothstep is documented in raymarching tutorials. name: Smooth SDF Composition
head: Signed Distance Function (SDF) Scene Composition, Smooth Min SDF, Smooth Union of SDFs
body: Smooth SDF Composition blends multiple primitive Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) into a single continuous field using a smooth minimum operator, avoiding the sharp creases produced by standard constructive SDF modeling. Unlike the nearest-surface control of Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination), this method creates a transitional volume between objects, enabling organic merging effects in ray marching. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two or more scalar SDF values (d1, d2, \dots) evaluated at a point p, and a blending factor k \ge 0. Output: A single blended distance value d{smooth}. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the scalar values returned by individual primitive SDF evaluators (e.g., sdfTorus, sdfBox as defined in). Steps: 1. Evaluate the individual SDF for each primitive at the query point p. For example, calculate d{torus} and d{box}. 2. Select a blending factor k. A typical value is 0.5 for moderate blending. 3. Compute the smooth minimum of the distances using the formula: d{smooth} = -\frac{1}{k} \ln(e^{-k d1} + e^{-k d2}) This formula approximates the minimum while maintaining C^1 continuity. 4. Return d{smooth} as the distance to the nearest object in the blended scene. Parameters: k: Blending factor. Controls the width of the transition zone. Larger k approaches the hard minimum; smaller k creates a smoother, wider blend. Typical value: 0.5. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If k=0, the formula involves division by zero. In practice, if k is very small, the result approaches the arithmetic mean or requires a fallback to the standard minimum. Precision issues may arise if d1 and d2 differ significantly in magnitude, causing one exponential term to dominate and underflow/overflow. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def smoothmin(d1: float, d2: float, k: float) -> float: if k == 0.0: return min(d1, d2) # Clamp to prevent exp() overflow for large positive distances kd1 = -k max(d1, -100.0) kd2 = -k max(d2, -100.0) exp1 = math.exp(kd1) exp2 = math.exp(kd2) return -1.0 / k math.log(exp1 + exp2) def evaluatescenesdf(primitives, k): if not primitives: return float('inf') currentdist = primitives[0]() for i in range(1, len(primitives)): nextdist = primitives[i]() currentdist = smoothmin(currentdist, nextdist, k) return currentdist Computes the minimum signed distance from a point to any primitive in the scene, effectively performing a union operation. It differs from Smooth SDF Composition by aggregating multiple distinct primitives into a single scene-level distance field rather than composing a single smooth blend of shapes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables organic, fluid merging of shapes without sharp edges. Limitations: The smooth transition zone can obscure the true boundary of objects, potentially causing ray marching artifacts if the step size is not adjusted for the gradient changes in the blend region. name: Scene SDF Evaluation
head: SDF Scene Composition, Signed Distance Function (SDF) Scene Composition
body: Scene SDF Evaluation computes the minimum signed distance from a query point to any primitive in a scene, effectively performing a union operation. Inputs: A scene structure containing lists of primitives (e.g., spheres, cuboids). A query point P. Transformations mapping local primitive coordinates to world space. Outputs: A scalar value representing the signed distance from P to the nearest surface in the scene. Data Structures: Scene: Contains arrays for primitive types and integer counts. spheres: Array of sphere primitives. Each sphere has a center C and radius R. cuboids: Array of cuboid primitives. Each cuboid has a center C, orientation Q, and half-extents H. spherecount: Integer count of spheres. cuboidcount: Integer count of cuboids. ComposedSDF (Variant): A container holding a list of SDF objects and a corresponding stack of transformation matrices (one per SDF). Steps: 1. Initialize mindist to MAXSIGNEDDISTANCE (10000.0). 2. Iterate through all spheres (0 to scene.spherecount): transform P into the local coordinate system of the current sphere, evaluate the sphere's SDF, and update mindist = min(mindist, d{sphere}). 3. Iterate through all cuboids (0 to scene.cuboidcount): transform P into the local coordinate system of the current cuboid using its orientation Q and center C, evaluate the cuboid's SDF, and update mindist = min(mindist, d{cuboid}). 4. Return mindist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatescenesdf(scene, point): """ Computes the minimum signed distance from point to any primitive in the scene. """ # Initialize with MAXSIGNEDDISTANCE mindist = 10000.0 # Evaluate all spheres for i in range(scene.spherecount): sphere = scene.spheres[i] # Transform point to sphere's local space localpoint = point - sphere.center # Evaluate sphere SDF: distance to center minus radius dist = (localpoint.x2 + localpoint.y2 + localpoint.z2)0.5 - sphere.radius if dist < mindist: mindist = dist # Evaluate all cuboids for i in range(scene.cuboidcount): cuboid = scene.cuboids[i] # Transform point to cuboid's local space translated = point - cuboid.center localpoint = cuboid.orientation.inverse() translated # Evaluate cuboid SDF: max(|x|-wx, |y|-wy, |z|-wz) abslocal = (abs(localpoint.x), abs(localpoint.y), abs(localpoint.z)) dist = max(abslocal[0] - cuboid.halfextents.x, abslocal[1] - cuboid.halfextents.y, abslocal[2] - cuboid.halfextents.z) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist return mindist Parameters: MAXSIGNEDDISTANCE: Default 10000.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If objects overlap or share faces, artifacts may occur in determining interior-ness. A variant that combines multiple SDFs into a single queryable SDF by passing a list of SDFs and a stack of transforms (one per SDF) to a constructor. Pitfall: Objects should not overlap or share faces, otherwise there will be artifacts in the SDF query in determining interior-ness. Not given in the sources. name: SDF Intersection
head: CSG Intersection, Constructive SDF Modeling, Intersection of SDFs, Min/Max Combination, SDF Boolean Operations, SDF Composition, SDF Intersection via Max, SDF Max
body: SDF Intersection is a boolean operation that computes the region common to two or more Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitives by returning the maximum distance value at any sampling point. It effectively requires the ray to be inside both shapes simultaneously, allowing for the construction of complex geometries akin to Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG). Unlike the union operation (min), which combines shapes into a single volume, intersection creates sharp, non-smooth corners where the surfaces meet. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Two SDF functions, S1(p) and S2(p), and a query point p in 3D space. Output: A single scalar value representing the signed distance to the intersection of the two shapes. Data Structures: No specific data structures are required beyond the scalar values returned by the primitive SDF evaluations. The operation is point-wise and stateless. Steps: 1. Evaluate the signed distance of the first shape at point p: d1 = S1(p). 2. Evaluate the signed distance of the second shape at point p: d2 = S2(p). 3. Return the maximum of the two distances: d{intersect} = \max(d1, d2). Formulas: The intersection of two SDFs A and B at point p is defined as: S{intersect}(p) = \max(SA(p), SB(p)) For a point to be inside the resulting intersection volume, it must satisfy SA(p) \le 0 AND SB(p) \le 0. Parameters: None. The operation is deterministic based on the input SDFs. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-smooth derivatives: Standard max produces non-smooth intersections with discontinuous derivatives at the boundary where SA(p) = SB(p). Precision: Near the intersection boundary, floating-point precision errors can cause jitter if the step size in ray marching is not sufficiently small. Degenerate input: If one SDF is always greater than the other in the region of interest, the result is simply the boundary of the "inner" shape. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfintersection(p, sdfa, sdfb): """ Computes the intersection of two SDFs at point p. Args: p: vec3, the query point in 3D space. sdfa: function, returns signed distance for shape A. sdfb: function, returns signed distance for shape B. Returns: float, the signed distance to the intersection of A and B. """ da = sdfa(p) db = sdfb(p) return max(da, db) Uses smooth minimum/maximum functions (e.g., smin) to approximate intersections with continuous derivatives, avoiding the sharp corners of standard max. Choose when visual smoothness is prioritized over exact geometric intersection. Smooth SDF Composition The parent method that combines primitives using min (union). Intersection is a sibling operation used within scene evaluation to carve out holes or combine shapes. Scene SDF Evaluation Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation, requiring two primitive SDF evaluations and one max operation. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional memory required. Performance: Extremely fast per-ray cost. High per-ray evaluation counts are inherent to ray marching and depend on scene complexity, ray direction, step size strategy, and surface proximity, rather than the intersection operation itself. Strengths: Exact watertight surfaces; no mesh topology errors; trivial to implement; supports arbitrary combinations of primitives. Limitations: Discontinuous derivatives lead to non-smooth normals; does not support smooth blending by default. When to use: When exact boolean intersection is required and sharp edges are acceptable or desired. When not to use: When smooth transitions between shapes are needed (use Smooth SDF Composition). The concept of using min and max operators for SDF boolean operations was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his writings on raymarching and procedural geometry. The technique allows for the creation of complex CSG-like models using simple mathematical functions, avoiding the need for mesh-based boolean operations which suffer from robustness issues. It is a fundamental building block in procedural raymarching scenes, enabling the creation of intricate patterns and fractals. name: Pyroclastic Sphere Primitive
body: The Pyroclastic Sphere Primitive is a procedural signed distance field (SDF) primitive that generates organic, cloud-like volumes by displacing a base sphere's surface with procedural noise. It solves the problem of creating complex, non-convex volumetric shapes with overhangs and disconnected density regions from a simple analytical base. It distinguishes itself from standard SDF primitives by adding a noise term to the distance function, and from pure noise fields by maintaining a coherent spherical topology that can be smoothed via antialiasing. It builds on SDF Primitive Definitions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: World position \mathbf{p}, sphere center \mathbf{c}, radius r, noise function m(\cdot), noise amplitude A, gamma correction \gamma, 2D displacement flag d{2D}, voxel size \mathbf{v}, base density \rho0. Output: Sampled density value \rho(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: The primitive requires access to a procedural noise evaluator (e.g., FBM) and the following parameters: radius (r): Scalar float. wsCenter (\mathbf{c}): 3D vector. amplitude (A): Scalar float. gamma (\gamma): Scalar float. displace2D (d{2D}): Boolean. density (\rho0): Scalar float. Steps: 1. Transform to Local Space: Compute the local position \mathbf{p}{local} relative to the sphere center, normalized by the radius: \mathbf{p}{local} = \frac{\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}}{r} 2. Determine Noise Sample Point: Determine the point \mathbf{p}{noise} used for noise evaluation. If 2D displacement is enabled, project \mathbf{p}{local} onto the unit sphere surface; otherwise, use \mathbf{p}{local} directly: \mathbf{p}{noise} = \begin{cases} \frac{\mathbf{p}{local}}{\|\mathbf{p}{local}\|} & \text{if } d{2D} \\ \mathbf{p}{local} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 3. Evaluate Noise: Evaluate the procedural noise function m(\mathbf{p}{noise}) (typically Fractal Brownian Motion). Apply gamma correction and scale by amplitude: n = A \cdot \gamma(m(\mathbf{p}{noise})) Note: The source code applies gamma to the raw noise output before scaling. 4. Compute Base Distance: Calculate the signed distance of the point from the sphere surface in local space: d{sphere} = \|\mathbf{p}{local}\| - 1.0 5. Compute Filter Width: Determine the antialiasing threshold width based on the world-space voxel size \mathbf{v}: w{filter} = \|\mathbf{v}\| w{threshold} = \frac{w{filter} \cdot 0.5}{r} 6. Compute Pyroclastic Value: Combine the sphere distance and noise. The source code uses fit (equivalent to smoothstep) to blend between 1.0 and 0.0 based on the difference between the sphere distance and the noise displacement, centered at 0 with width w{threshold}: v{pyro} = \text{smoothstep}(-w{threshold}, w{threshold}, d{sphere} - n) Note: The formula in the text uses \max(r - \|\mathbf{p}/r\| + |m(\mathbf{p})|, 0), but the implementation code uses sphereFunc - fractalFunc inside a smoothstep. The code is the authoritative implementation detail for the "pyroclastic" look described in section 2.5.4. 7. Output Density: Scale the pyroclastic value by the base density: \rho(\mathbf{p}) = \rho0 \cdot v{pyro} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pyroclasticspheresample(pworld, center, radius, noisefunc, amplitude, gamma, displace2d, voxelsize, basedensity): # 1. Transform to local space localp = (pworld - center) / radius # 2. Determine noise sample point if displace2d: # Project onto unit sphere surface normlocal = length(localp) if normlocal < 1e-6: noisep = localp # Fallback for origin, though unlikely in volume else: noisep = localp / normlocal else: noisep = localp # 3. Evaluate noise with gamma and amplitude rawnoise = noisefunc(noisep) gammanoise = rawnoise gamma # Assuming gamma is exponent noiseval = amplitude gammanoise # 4. Compute sphere distance spheredist = length(localp) - 1.0 # 5. Compute filter width voxellen = length(voxelsize) thresholdwidth = (voxellen 0.5) / radius # 6. Compute pyroclastic value using smoothstep # smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x) # Here edge0 = -thresholdwidth, edge1 = thresholdwidth, x = spheredist - noiseval pyrovalue = smoothstep(-thresholdwidth, thresholdwidth, spheredist - noiseval) # 7. Output density return basedensity pyrovalue def smoothstep(edge0, edge1, x): t = max(0.0, min(1.0, (x - edge0) / (edge1 - edge0))) return t t (3.0 - 2.0 t) Parameters: radius: Radius of the base sphere. amplitude: Scaling factor for the noise displacement. gamma: Exponent for gamma correction applied to the noise function output. displace2D: Boolean flag. If true, noise is evaluated on the sphere surface normal, preventing overhangs. If false, 3D displacement allows disconnected density regions. density: Base density multiplier. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Overhangs: If displace2D is false, high noise amplitude can cause the density to disconnect from the main body, creating floating artifacts. This is intentional for the "pyroclastic" look but may be undesirable for solid objects. Origin Singularity: When \mathbf{p}{local} is near zero, normalization for 2D displacement is unstable. Clamp or handle the zero vector case explicitly. Precision: The subtraction d{sphere} - n can suffer from cancellation errors if the noise amplitude is large relative to the sphere distance. Defines an implicit surface by displacing the radius of a base sphere using animated procedural noise. It distinguishes itself by combining low-frequency "breathing" with high-frequency fBM, whereas the Pyroclastic Sphere focuses on the specific antialiased density blending and 2D/3D displacement modes for volumetric overhangs. Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, dominated by the noise function evaluation (typically O(N) where N is the number of octaves in FBM). Memory Complexity: O(1) for parameters. The noise function may require temporary memory for intermediate octave evaluations. Strengths: Generates complex, organic shapes from simple parameters. The 2D displacement mode provides a smooth, solid look, while 3D displacement allows for complex, disconnected cloud structures. Antialiasing is handled via the smoothstep threshold. Limitations: The noise displacement can create non-manifold or disconnected density regions if not constrained. Performance depends heavily on the complexity of the underlying noise function. When to use: Ideal for volumetric clouds, smoke, or organic blobs where a spherical base is appropriate but surface detail is needed. When not to use: For hard-surface modeling or when strict manifold geometry is required without post-processing. The Pyroclastic Sphere Primitive was introduced in the context of production volume rendering, specifically within the framework of solid noise primitives. It is described in "Production Volume Rendering". The technique leverages the concept of using noise as a displacement field on a distance function, a common practice in procedural modeling and texturing (e.g., Ebert et al.). The specific "pyroclastic" naming and the implementation details regarding 2D vs 3D displacement for controlling overhangs are detailed in the source material. name: Deforming SDF Sphere with Noise
head: Animated Noise SDF Sphere, Animated SDF Displacement, SDF Sphere with Noise Displacement, Signed Distance Field (SDF) Sphere with Noise Displacement
body: This method defines an implicit surface by displacing the radius of a base sphere using animated procedural noise, creating a time-varying organic shape. It distinguishes itself from static SDF primitives by combining a low-frequency sinusoidal "breathing" modulation with high-frequency fractal Brownian motion (fBM) and sinusoidal products to generate complex surface topology. Inputs: \mathbf{p}: The 3D point in world space to evaluate. t: The global animation time (gtime). sphereradius: The base radius R of the sphere. noiseamplitude: The scaling factor A{noise} for the displacement magnitude. Outputs: d(\mathbf{p}): The signed distance from \mathbf{p} to the deformed surface. No auxiliary data structures are required; the method relies on scalar arithmetic and vector operations. sphereradius (R): Base radius of the sphere. noiseamplitude (A{noise}): Scaling factor for displacement magnitude. gtime (t): Global time variable, advancing per frame. The signed distance is calculated as: d(\mathbf{p}) = \|\mathbf{p}\| - (r(t) + D(\mathbf{p}, t)) Where: 1. Base Radius r(t): r(t) = R + A{breath} \sin(\omega{breath} t) With A{breath} = 0.25 and \omega{breath} = 2.0. 2. Sinusoidal Displacement D{sin}: D{sin} = \sin(16 x + \phi) \sin(16 y + \phi) \sin(16 z + \phi) Where \phi = 6.0 t. 3. fBM Displacement D{fbm}: D{fbm} = \text{fBM}(2\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{v}(t)) Where \mathbf{v}(t) = (t, 0.7t, 1.3t). 4. Total Displacement D: D = A{noise} \left( 0.6 D{sin} + 0.8 (D{fbm} - 0.5) \right) The term (D{fbm} - 0.5) centers the fBM output, assuming it ranges in [0, 1]. 1. Calculate the time-varying base radius r using the sine wave modulation. 2. Calculate the phase offset \phi for the sinusoidal component. 3. Compute the sinusoidal displacement D{sin} by multiplying three sine waves modulated by the point coordinates and phase. 4. Compute the fBM displacement D{fbm} by evaluating the noise function at a scaled and time-shifted position. 5. Combine the sinusoidal and fBM components into a total displacement D, weighted by noiseamplitude. 6. Return the signed distance as the Euclidean norm of \mathbf{p} minus the sum of the displaced radius r and displacement D. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math class Vec3: def init(self, x, y, z): self.x = x self.y = y self.z = z def mul(self, s): return Vec3(self.x s, self.y s, self.z s) def add(self, other): return Vec3(self.x + other.x, self.y + other.y, self.z + other.z) def norm(self): return math.sqrt(self.x2 + self.y2 + self.z2) def hash3d(v): # Standard deterministic hash for value noise h = int(v.x 127.1 + v.y 311.7 + v.z 74.7) h = (h << 13) ^ h return 1.0 - 2.0 ((h (h h 15731 + 789221) + 1376312589) & 0x7fffffff) / 0x7fffffff def valuenoise(p): # Trilinear interpolation of surrounding hash values ix, iy, iz = int(math.floor(p.x)), int(math.floor(p.y)), int(math.floor(p.z)) fx, fy, fz = p.x - ix, p.y - iy, p.z - iz fx, fy, fz = fxfx(3-2fx), fyfy(3-2fy), fzfz(3-2fz) def lerp(a, b, t): return a + t (b - a) n00 = lerp(hash3d(Vec3(ix, iy, iz)), hash3d(Vec3(ix+1, iy, iz)), fx) n10 = lerp(hash3d(Vec3(ix, iy+1, iz)), hash3d(Vec3(ix+1, iy+1, iz)), fx) n01 = lerp(hash3d(Vec3(ix, iy, iz+1)), hash3d(Vec3(ix+1, iy, iz+1)), fx) n11 = lerp(hash3d(Vec3(ix, iy+1, iz+1)), hash3d(Vec3(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1)), fx) return lerp(lerp(n00, n10, fy), lerp(n01, n11, fy), fz) def fractalbrownianmotion(p, octaves=4): # Layered value noise with decreasing amplitude and frequency val = 0.0 amp = 1.0 freq = 1.0 for in range(octaves): val += amp valuenoise(p freq) amp = 0.5 freq = 2.0 return val def signeddistance(p, gtime, sphereradius, noiseamplitude): # 1. Base radius breathes over time r = sphereradius + 0.25 math.sin(gtime 2.0) # 2. Phase for sinusoidal displacement phase = gtime 6.0 # 3. Sinusoidal displacement component sindisp = math.sin(16.0 p.x + phase) math.sin(16.0 p.y + phase) math.sin(16.0 p.z + phase) # 4. Total displacement displacement = noiseamplitude (0.6 sindisp + 0.8 (fbm - 0.5)) # 6. Final SDF return p.norm() - (r + displacement) def spheretrace(orig, dir, maxsteps=128, minstep=0.01, sphereradius=1.5, noiseamplitude=1.0, gtime=0.0): pos = Vec3(orig.x, orig.y, orig.z) for in range(maxsteps): d = signeddistance(pos, gtime, sphereradius, noiseamplitude) if d < 0.0: return True step = max(d 0.1, minstep) pos = Vec3(pos.x + dir.x step, pos.y + dir.y step, pos.z + dir.z step) return False fBM Range: The formula assumes fractalbrownianmotion returns values in [0, 1]; if the implementation returns [-1, 1], the centering term (D{fbm} - 0.5) will shift the displacement bias. name: Offset Surface Evaluation
head: Distance to Offset Surfaces, Global offset, Local offset, Point-to-set distance
body: Offset Surface Evaluation computes the distance from a query point to a surface generated by offsetting a skeleton geometry by a fixed distance. It defines smooth, thickened representations of curves, surfaces, or meshes for implicit modeling and ray marching. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on a global point-to-set distance search (global offset) rather than a local parametric displacement, which avoids the interior self-intersections and high-degree algebraic artifacts common in local offset methods. The method evaluates the distance to an offset surface by finding the closest point on the underlying skeleton geometry. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point \mathbf{p}, skeleton geometry S (e.g., a space curve or surface), constant offset distance c. Output: Signed distance d(\mathbf{p}) to the offset surface. Data Structures: Skeleton representation: Parametric form \mathbf{s}(t) for curves or \mathbf{s}(u,v) for surfaces, or a mesh vertex list with normals. Distance metric: Euclidean distance. Steps: 1. Search Skeleton: Search the entire set S for the closest point \mathbf{s}^ to \mathbf{p}. 2. Solve for Curves: For a parametric curve \mathbf{s}(t), find the point where the tangent is perpendicular to the vector pointing to \mathbf{p} by solving (\mathbf{s}(t) - \mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{s}'(t) = 0. This can be converted to a degree-5 Bernstein polynomial and solved via convex hull bounding. 3. Search for Meshes: For meshes, iterate over vertices or primitives to find the minimum distance. 4. Compute Distance: Calculate the Euclidean distance d{\text{raw}} = \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{s}^\|. 5. Apply Offset: The signed distance to the offset surface is d(\mathbf{p}) = d{\text{raw}} - c. Parameters: c: Constant offset distance applied to the skeleton. Typical values are not given in the sources. Pitfalls: Interior Surfaces: Global offsets avoid interior surfaces, whereas local offsets can cause gradient discontinuities or result in high-degree algebraic representations. Mesh Self-Intersection: When offsetting a mesh by moving vertices along normals, self-intersections are not handled automatically. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def offsetsurfacedistance(p, skeletonprimitives, c): """ Computes distance from point p to the offset surface of a skeleton by distance c. skeletonprimitives: list of objects with a closestpoint(p) method. c: float, constant offset distance. """ mindistsq = float('inf') for prim in skeletonprimitives: # Primitive-specific closest point search (curve parameter solve or triangle test) pt = prim.closestpoint(p) distsq = (p[0] - pt[0])2 + (p[1] - pt[1])2 + (p[2] - pt[2])2 if distsq < mindistsq: mindistsq = distsq rawdist = mindistsq0.5 return rawdist - c Creates an offset surface from a mesh by moving vertices along their computed normals by a given distance. It is a local offset method, distinct from the global point-to-set distance approach. It is chosen for mesh-based modeling where normals are available. It does not handle self-intersections, as vertices are moved independently along their original normals. Definition: Parametric displacement of mesh vertices. Steps: 1. Ensure normals are computed: mesh->neednormals(). 2. Iterate over all vertices i from 0 to nv-1. 3. Update vertex position: mesh->vertices[i] += amount mesh->normals[i]. 4. Invalidate bounding box and bounding sphere flags. Parameters: amount: distance to offset along normals. Pitfalls: Does not handle self-intersections; vertices are moved independently along their original normals. Time Complexity: Depends on the skeleton search. For a mesh, it is O(N) where N is the number of primitives, unless accelerated by a BVH or grid. For parametric curves, it involves solving polynomial equations, which is constant time but potentially expensive per evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the skeleton geometry. Strengths: Global offsets avoid interior surfaces and are more desirable for ray-tracing and CSG operations. They provide smooth, continuous distance fields. Limitations: Local offsets can cause gradient discontinuities. Mesh-based local offsets do not handle self-intersections. When to use: When a smooth, thickened representation of a curve or surface is needed for ray marching or implicit modeling. When not to use: When the skeleton has high curvature leading to self-intersections, or when performance is critical and the skeleton is a large mesh without acceleration structures. The concept of offset surfaces is rooted in computer-aided geometric design (CAGD) and implicit surface rendering. Global offsets are defined geometrically by the implicit equation d(\mathbf{p}) = 0, where d(\mathbf{p}) is the point-to-set distance to a closed skeleton geometry S. When d is constant, the surface fleshes out the skeleton. The formulation of point-to-set distance reduces the search space for closest point determination to primitives such as parametric surfaces. Global offsets are usually defined as geometric implicit surfaces, whereas local offsets are usually defined parametrically. Global offsets are considered more desirable [Hoffman, 1989] as they avoid interior surfaces which can cause problems in ray-tracing and CSG [van Wijk, 1984]. The offset of an algebraic implicit surface is algebraic, though of higher degree in general. name: Boolean Operations on Distance Fields
head: Boolean Operations on SDFs, SDF Boolean Operations, SDF Boolean Operators, SDF Boolean Union, SDF Min, Boolean Union on Distance Fields
body: Boolean operations on Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) are Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) primitives that combine the scalar fields of two or more shapes to create complex geometries. By applying component-wise minimum or maximum functions to the distance values, these operations define the union, intersection, and difference of volumes. Unlike Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) which may focus on specific blending or hierarchical structures, this method provides the fundamental algebraic operators for exact CSG composition, ensuring the resulting field remains a valid SDF (satisfying the Lipschitz condition) for use in sphere tracing. The method evaluates two SDFs, f1(\mathbf{p}) and f2(\mathbf{p}), at a query point \mathbf{p} and combines their scalar outputs. The result is a new SDF f{result}(\mathbf{p}) representing the combined shape. Inputs: Two SDF functions f1, f2: \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}, and a query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: A scalar distance value d{result} \in \mathbb{R}. Optionally, a material ID or normal vector may be returned alongside the distance. The core data structure is the scalar distance value. When tracking material identity (e.g., for shading different primitives differently), the SDF evaluation returns a pair: vec2 or struct { distance: float, materialid: int }. The distance component (.x) is used for ray marching. The material ID component (.y) is used for shading logic. Let d1 = f1(\mathbf{p}) and d2 = f2(\mathbf{p}). 1. Union: The volume occupied by either shape. The distance is the minimum of the two, as the surface is defined by the closest boundary. d{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(d1, d2) 2. Intersection: The volume occupied by both shapes. The distance is the maximum of the two, as the surface is defined by the farthest boundary that still keeps the point inside both volumes. d{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(d1, d2) 3. Subtraction (Difference): The volume of the first shape minus the second. The second shape's distance is negated (inverting its inside/outside status) before taking the maximum. d{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(d1, -d2) Note: Some sources define subtraction as A - B using \max(dA, -dB), while others describe it as removing object 1 from object 2 using \max(-d1, d2). The standard CSG interpretation A \setminus B uses \max(dA, -dB). The following implementation handles both scalar distance and material ID tracking, consistent with and. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatesdfunion(p, sdf1, sdf2): """ Computes the union of two SDFs. Returns (distance, materialid). """ d1, id1 = sdf1(p) d2, id2 = sdf2(p) if d1 < d2: return d1, id1 else: return d2, id2 def evaluatesdfintersection(p, sdf1, sdf2): """ Computes the intersection of two SDFs. Returns (distance, materialid). """ d1, id1 = sdf1(p) d2, id2 = sdf2(p) if d1 > d2: return d1, id1 else: return d2, id2 def evaluatesdfsubtraction(p, sdf1, sdf2): """ Computes the difference (subtraction) of two SDFs: sdf1 - sdf2. Returns (distance, materialid). """ d1, id1 = sdf1(p) d2, id2 = sdf2(p) # Negate the distance of the subtracted object negd2 = -d2 if d1 > negd2: return d1, id1 else: return negd2, id2 def scenesdf(p, primitives): """ Combines multiple primitives using union. primitives: list of (sdffunc, materialid) """ # Initialize with a large distance (empty space) # and a background material ID (e.g., 0) currentdist = float('inf') currentid = 0 for sdffunc, matid in primitives: d, = sdffunc(p) # Union operation: take the minimum distance if d < currentdist: currentdist = d currentid = matid return currentdist, currentid Operation Type: Enum or string indicating 'union', 'intersection', or 'difference'. Smoothness (Optional): Standard boolean operations produce sharp edges. Smooth variants (e.g., Smooth Union) use a blending parameter k to interpolate between min/max, but this breaks the exact SDF property (Lipschitz constant 1) and is not a strict boolean operation. Lipschitz Condition: The min/max of 1-Lipschitz functions is also 1-Lipschitz, preserving the validity of sphere tracing. Normals: The normal at the surface is the gradient of the resulting SDF. For boolean operations, the normal is simply the normal of the primitive that determined the minimum/maximum distance. If d{union} = d1, then \mathbf{n} = \nabla f1(\mathbf{p}). If d{union} = d2, then \mathbf{n} = \nabla f2(\mathbf{p}). Degenerate Intersection: If two shapes touch exactly, the distance is 0. The normal may be undefined or ambiguous if the gradients are opposite. In practice, sphere tracing handles this by stopping at the surface. Precision: When d1 \approx d2, floating-point precision errors may cause flickering or incorrect normal selection. Using a small epsilon for comparison can help, but strict equality is rare in continuous space. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive pair. For N primitives combined via union, the complexity is O(N) per ray step, as each primitive must be evaluated to find the minimum distance. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory per operation. No additional data structures are required beyond the primitive definitions. Performance: The operations are extremely fast, consisting of basic arithmetic comparisons. They are highly parallelizable on GPUs. Strengths: Exact CSG representation; no tessellation required; infinite resolution; easy to animate and transform. Limitations: Sharp edges only (without smooth blending); complex scenes with many primitives can be slow due to O(N) evaluation per step; no support for non-manifold geometry or holes that require topological changes beyond CSG. Boolean operations on SDFs were popularized by Inigo Quilez in his articles on distance functions and raymarching. The technique leverages the mathematical properties of distance fields to allow constructive solid geometry without explicit mesh representation. It is a cornerstone of procedural raymarching, enabling the creation of complex scenes from simple primitives like spheres, boxes, and tori. The method is widely used in real-time graphics, demoscene productions, and educational raymarching tutorials. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, https://github.com/Leesan-haruki/FunctionRenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, https://github.com/nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChadMcKinney/Dirac-Sea-Engine, https://github.com/ChadMcKinney/Dirac-Sea-Engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) 6 – Raymarching: Floor + Union of Rounded Box and Sphere, http://www.geeks3d.com/20130524/building-worlds-with-distance-functions-in-glsl-raymarching-glslhacker-tutorial-opengl/6/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Skipping Spheres: SDF Scaling & Early Ray Termination for Fast Sphere..., https://diglib.eg.org/items/7f21e58c-639e-4359-bf94-414738612006, fetched 2026-10-27 PDF Further Graphics - name: Implicit Surface Representation
head: Grid-based SDF, Tricubic SDF, Zero-level set surface
body: This method represents an implicit surface as a grid-based Signed Distance Function (SDF) using tricubic interpolation to ensure continuous surface normals. It defines the surface geometry as the zero-level set of a scalar field f{implicit}(\mathbf{p}). It is distinguished from analytical primitives by its reliance on discrete grid storage and higher-order interpolation, which provides C^1 continuity for shading, whereas analytical methods (like Standard Solid Primitives) are typically only C^0 or discontinuous at boundaries. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D grid of scalar values representing the signed distance to the surface at grid vertices. Output: A continuous scalar field f{implicit}(\mathbf{p}) and its gradient \nabla f{implicit}(\mathbf{p}) for any query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3. Data Structures The core data structure is a 3D array (grid) of floating-point values. Let G be a grid of size Nx \times Ny \times Nz. Each cell (i, j, k) stores the distance value d{i,j,k} at the corresponding vertex. The grid spacing (resolution) is uniform, denoted by \Delta. Formulas The implicit surface S{implicit} is defined as the set of points where the function evaluates to zero: S{implicit} = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{pmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^3 \mid f{implicit}(x, y, z) = 0 \right\} To evaluate f{implicit}(\mathbf{p}) and its normal \mathbf{n} = \nabla f{implicit}(\mathbf{p}) at an arbitrary point \mathbf{p}, tricubic interpolation is performed. Let \mathbf{p} lie within a grid cell defined by vertices \mathbf{v}{ijk} for i,j,k \in \{0,1\}. The value is computed by applying 1D cubic Hermite interpolation along each axis. Parameters Grid Resolution: Determines the spatial frequency of the SDF. Higher resolution increases accuracy but memory cost. Interpolation Order: Tricubic (order 3) is specified to ensure continuous normals. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatetricubicsdf(grid, p, spacing): """ Evaluates the implicit surface function and its gradient at point p using tricubic interpolation on a uniform grid. Args: grid: 3D numpy array of shape (Nx, Ny, Nz) containing distance values. p: 3D vector (x, y, z) of the query point. spacing: float, the uniform distance between grid vertices. Returns: value: float, the signed distance f(p). normal: 3D vector, the gradient df/dp (surface normal). """ # 1. Map world point to grid coordinates # Assume grid origin is at (0,0,0) for simplicity; adjust if offset exists. gx = p[0] / spacing gy = p[1] / spacing gz = p[2] / spacing # 2. Find the base cell indices (floor) ix = int(floor(gx)) iy = int(floor(gy)) iz = int(floor(gz)) # 3. Calculate local fractional coordinates within the cell [0, 1] tx = gx - ix ty = gy - iy tz = gz - iz # 4. Retrieve the 8 corner values and their gradients (if stored) # Note: Standard SDF grids store only values. To get continuous normals # via tricubic interpolation, one typically needs the gradients at vertices # or computes them from the values. The source cites diffsdf which # implies a specific implementation. Here we assume a standard tricubic # interpolation that requires vertex values and potentially vertex gradients. # If only values are stored, bicubic/tricubic interpolation of values alone # does not guarantee C1 continuity of the gradient unless the grid is # constructed specifically (e.g., via gradient descent optimization). # We assume the grid stores values and we compute the field value. # Retrieve 8 corner values # Handle boundary checks def getval(i, j, k): if 0 <= i < grid.shape[0] and 0 <= j < grid.shape[1] and 0 <= k < grid.shape[2]: return grid[i, j, k] return 0.0 # Default to 0 or infinity for out-of-bounds; implementation dependent. v000 = getval(ix, iy, iz) v100 = getval(ix+1, iy, iz) v010 = getval(ix, iy+1, iz) v110 = getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz) v001 = getval(ix, iy, iz+1) v101 = getval(ix+1, iy, iz+1) v011 = getval(ix, iy+1, iz+1) v111 = getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) # 5. Perform Tricubic Interpolation # First, interpolate along X for each YZ plane # Cubic Hermite kernel for value and derivative? # Standard tricubic interpolation of values only yields C0 continuity. # To achieve C1 (continuous normals) as stated in, the underlying # data usually includes vertex gradients or the grid is optimized such that # the interpolated field is smooth. # Without explicit vertex gradients in the grid structure description, # we assume a standard tricubic blend of values. # Interpolate along X v00 = cubichermite(v000, v100, tx) v01 = cubichermite(v010, v110, tx) v10 = cubichermite(v001, v101, tx) v11 = cubichermite(v011, v111, tx) # Interpolate along Y v0 = cubichermite(v00, v10, ty) v1 = cubichermite(v01, v11, ty) # Interpolate along Z value = cubichermite(v0, v1, tz) # 6. Compute Normal (Gradient) # The normal is the gradient of the interpolated field. # If only values are stored, the gradient is approximated by finite differences # or requires storing vertex gradients. implies continuous normals, # suggesting the method in diffsdf handles this. # A robust implementation would compute the gradient of the tricubic basis functions. # For brevity and based on "grid-based SDF with tricubic interpolation", # we note that the gradient is derived from the same interpolation weights. # Specific gradient computation depends on whether vertex gradients are stored. # If not, finite difference of the interpolated value is a common fallback, # though it breaks the C1 guarantee of the interpolation itself. # We assume the standard approach: compute gradient of the tricubic polynomial. normal = computetricubicgradient(grid, ix, iy, iz, tx, ty, tz, spacing) return value, normal def cubichermite(p0, p1, t): """Standard cubic Hermite interpolation for values only (C0).""" # This is insufficient for C1 normals. # True tricubic for C1 requires derivatives. # Given the constraint of "grid-based SDF", we assume the grid allows # for smooth evaluation. return (2ttt - 3tt + 1)p0 + (ttt - 2tt + t)p1 # Placeholder for derivative info Note: The pseudocode above highlights the ambiguity. Achieving continuous normals with only vertex values requires the interpolation function itself to be C^1, which standard tricubic interpolation of values is not (it is C^0). Precision: Floating-point errors in interpolation can cause artifacts near the zero-level set. Memory: O(Nx Ny Nz) for the grid storage. Time: Evaluation is O(1) per query point, involving a fixed number of arithmetic operations for interpolation. Strengths: Continuous surface normals enable smooth shading and differentiable rendering without explicit mesh extraction. Limitations: Memory usage scales with volume rather than surface area. High resolution is needed for fine details. This representation is used in differentiable rendering pipelines, specifically in the implementation based on the cudaadrgb backend of Mitsuba 3. name: Standard Solid Primitives
head: Analytical SDF Primitives, Closed-Form SDFs, Natural Quadrics (subset)
body: Standard Solid Primitives provide exact, closed-form Signed Distance Functions (SDFs) for canonical geometric shapes, enabling efficient distance-field ray marching without explicit mesh tessellation. Unlike Distance to Natural Quadrics which focuses on the algebraic derivation of quadric surfaces, this family emphasizes the practical implementation of exact distance bounds for spheres, boxes, tori, and their combinations, guaranteeing that sphere tracing steps do not overshoot surfaces. The family operates on the principle that a scene is defined by a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) where the zero-level set f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 represents the surface. For sphere tracing to be valid, the function must satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, ensuring |f(\mathbf{p}1) - f(\mathbf{p}2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2\|. This guarantees that the value f(\mathbf{p}) is a safe lower bound on the distance to the surface, allowing the ray marcher to step forward by exactly f(\mathbf{p}) without tunneling. Composition is achieved through Boolean operations on the distance values: Union: f{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Intersection: f{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Subtraction: f{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(-f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} into the local coordinate space of the primitive using the inverse transformation matrix M^{-1} before evaluation. Procedural noise (e.g., FBM) is often used to perturb these analytical surfaces, creating hypertextures where the isosurface is defined by SDF(\mathbf{p}) + Bn(\mathbf{p}) = 0. Provides exact distance bounds for a wide variety of canonical shapes (spheres, boxes, tori) and their combinations, guaranteeing that ray marching steps do not overshoot surfaces. Provides exact SDFs for standard solid modeling primitives, including planes, spheres, cylinders, cones, and tori, operating in standard Euclidean space. [Cylindrical SDF Primitives]: A technique for rendering implicit geometry defined by SDFs using ray marching, specifically for cap cylinder shapes, often involving nested cylinder calculations for complex lighting or structural details. The use of analytical SDFs for ray marching was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his 2009 article "Distance Functions". Prior to this, distance fields were often approximated or limited to simple spheres. The formalization of exact SDFs for boxes, tori, and cones allowed for the creation of complex CSG models in real-time shaders. The concept of using Lp norms or Generalized Distance Functions (GDF) to approximate more complex shapes like icosahedrons was later explored to extend the primitive library.
