name: Lipschitz Proxy Nodes
head: Continuous Proxy, Proxy C
body: Lipschitz Proxy Nodes (Proxy C) replace a computationally intensive sub-tree of a Signed Distance Field (SDF) with a simpler proxy volume V and a proxy field v, ensuring the resulting field fe is globally 1-Lipschitz continuous. Unlike Conservative Proxy Nodes (Proxy P), which yield discontinuous fields and cannot be used below smooth Boolean operators, Proxy C nodes maintain continuity, making them compatible with smooth unions and other operators requiring Lipschitz continuity. Inputs: Original SDF sub-tree function f(p), assumed to be 1-Lipschitz. Proxy volume V (a geometric region). Proxy field v(p) = d(p, V), the distance to V. Interpolation radius \delta r > 0. Lipschitz scaling constant \lambda \ge 1. Interpolation function s: [0, 1] \to [0, 1], monotonically non-decreasing (e.g., identity or smoothstep). Outputs: The 1-Lipschitz field fe(p). Data Structures: The proxy node stores the geometry of V, the parameters \delta r and \lambda, and the function s. The interpolation region \Omega is defined implicitly as \Omega = (V \oplus B(\delta r)) \setminus V, where \oplus is the Minkowski sum and B(\delta r) is a sphere of radius \delta r. Steps: 1. Define the Interpolation Region: Compute the region \Omega as the set of points within distance \delta r of V but outside V. 2. Compute Weight Function: For any point p, calculate the weight \alpha(p) based on the distance to V: \alpha(p) = s\left(\frac{v(p)}{\delta r}\right) By definition, \alpha(p) = 0 on \partial V and \alpha(p) = 1 on \partial(V \oplus B(\delta r)). 3. Evaluate Field: Compute fe(p) using the piecewise definition: fe(p) = \begin{cases} f(p)/\lambda & \text{if } p \in V \\ \frac{1}{\lambda} \left[ (1 - \alpha(p)) f(p) + \alpha(p) v(p) \right] & \text{if } p \in \Omega \\ (v(p) - \delta r) + \delta r/\lambda & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Parameters: \lambda: A constant \ge 1 used to guarantee that fe is 1-Lipschitz. It scales the function values and gradients. \delta r: The radius of the sphere B(\delta r) defining the width of the interpolation region \Omega. Pitfalls: Discontinuity Artifacts: Using discontinuous proxy nodes (Proxy P) with smooth Boolean operators produces artifacts because the field function is no longer continuous in the neighborhood of the surface \partial O. Proxy C avoids this but is more computationally demanding. Gradient Norm: The norm of the gradient \|\nabla \alpha\| is equal to the Lipschitz constant of the interpolating function s. Care must be taken to ensure the combined gradient does not exceed 1 after scaling by \lambda. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lipschitzproxynode(p, foriginal, vproxy, Vgeometry, deltar, lambdaval, sfunc): """ Evaluates the 1-Lipschitz proxy field fe at point p. Args: p: Point in 3D space. foriginal: Function evaluating the original sub-tree SDF f(p). vproxy: Function evaluating the proxy distance field v(p) = d(p, V). Vgeometry: Geometry object representing the proxy volume V. deltar: Interpolation radius. lambdaval: Lipschitz scaling constant (>= 1). sfunc: Monotonically non-decreasing function s: [0, 1] -> [0, 1]. Returns: The value of the 1-Lipschitz field fe(p). """ # Calculate distance to proxy volume V vp = vproxy(p) # Determine region membership # Check if p is inside V insideV = Vgeometry.contains(p) # Check if p is inside the expanded region V + B(deltar) # This is equivalent to checking if distance to V <= deltar insideexpanded = vp <= deltar if insideV: # Region V: f(p) / lambda return foriginal(p) / lambdaval elif insideexpanded: # Region Omega: Interpolation region # alpha(p) = s(v(p) / deltar) alpha = sfunc(vp / deltar) # fe(p) = (1/lambda) [ (1 - alpha) f(p) + alpha v(p) ] fp = foriginal(p) return (1.0 / lambdaval) ((1.0 - alpha) fp + alpha vp) else: # Outside Omega: (v(p) - deltar) + deltar / lambda return (vp - deltar) + (deltar / lambdaval) Complexity: More computationally demanding than Conservative Proxy Nodes (Proxy P) due to the need for continuous interpolation and gradient management. Performance: In tests on the Temple model, proxy nodes achieved an average speedup of \times 7 with Sphere Tracing. Specific configurations (capsule, half-sphere, cylinder proxies) achieved a speedup factor of \approx \times 6.86. Strengths: Enables acceleration of complex SDF sub-trees while maintaining compatibility with smooth Boolean operators (e.g., smooth union). Effective for rendering complex transparent objects or computing differences between complex objects. Limitations: Cannot be used if the sub-tree is already below a node requiring Lipschitz continuity unless the proxy itself is 1-Lipschitz (which Proxy C is). Conservative proxies (Proxy P) fail in these contexts. Lipschitz Proxy Nodes were introduced by P. Hubert-Brierre, E. Guérin, A. Peytavie, and E. Galin in the paper "Accelerating Signed Distance Functions". The method is part of a broader strategy to optimize SDF evaluation trees by inserting levels of detail or proxy nodes to replace computationally intensive sub-trees. name: Stack-Based SDF Editor
head: Post-order SDF construction, RPN-style SDF editor [S1, unofficial]
body: An interactive editor that constructs Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) from primitives and operations using a stack-based interface similar to Reverse Polish Notation (RPN), implicitly representing a tree with postorder traversal. It differs from explicit tree editors by deferring structure resolution until compilation, allowing users to build complex scenes by pushing operations onto a linear stack where only the top item is visible until combined. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sequence of operations pushed onto a stack, categorized as Shapes, Transformations, or CSG Operations. Output: A compiled GLSL shader string containing the SDF evaluation function. Data Structures: Operation Stack: A list of operation objects representing the postorder traversal of the scene graph. AST Tree: A recursive structure built from the stack where nodes are either leaves (primitive shapes annotated with domain-modifying transformations) or internal nodes (CSG operations acting on range values). Numbered Steps: 1. Push Operation: Operations are pushed onto the stack. The editor only considers the first item by default; subsequent items are not visible until joined via union or other operations. 2. Invalidate Cache: Modifying any parameter calls #invalidate, which clears the cached shader program to trigger recompilation on the next access. 3. Build SDF (Tree Reconstruction): The buildSDF function iterates over the stack, popping off previous operations according to the arity of the current operation to reconstruct the tree structure. 4. Generate GLSL: The system recursively traverses the AST, transforming nodes to appropriate calls. At leaves, it composes domain-modifying functions in the opposite order of application. Internal nodes generate range operations (e.g., min for union). 5. Compile: The generated GLSL string is spliced into a template and compiled. Formulas: Union: S{union}(p) = \min(SA(p), SB(p)). Domain Transformation Composition: If transformations T1, T2, \dots are applied to a shape, the input position p is transformed by composing them in the opposite order: Tn(\dots T2(T1(p)) \dots). Parameters: Primitive Types: Box and Sphere (e.g., radius 1.0). Transformations: Translate (vec3 offset) and Rotate (float angle). CSG Operations: Union and Intersection. Configuration: Uses lazy evaluation and caching via getter/setter methods that call #invalidate. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Visibility: Subsequent stack items remain invisible until a union or similar operation combines them with the top item. AST vs Conceptual Tree: The generated AST differs from the conceptual operation tree because domain modifications (transformations) are attached to leaves, while range modifications (CSG operations) form internal nodes. Performance: Without #invalidate caching, the shader would be reassembled and compiled on every frame, causing severe inefficiency. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildsdf(stack): aststack = [] for op in stack: if op['type'] == 'Shape': aststack.append({ 'type': 'Leaf', 'shape': op['shape'], 'params': op.get('params', {}), 'transforms': [] }) elif op['type'] == 'Transform': if aststack: aststack[-1]['transforms'].append(op['transform']) elif op['type'] == 'CSG': if len(aststack) >= 2: right = aststack.pop() left = aststack.pop() aststack.append({ 'type': 'CSG', 'op': op['op'], 'left': left, 'right': right }) return aststack[0] if aststack else None def generateglsl(node): if node['type'] == 'Leaf': p = "p" for t in reversed(node['transforms']): if t['type'] == 'Translate': p = f"opTx({p}, vec3({t['x']}, {t['y']}, {t['z']}))" elif t['type'] == 'Rotate': p = f"opRotX({p}, {t['angle']})" size = node['params'].get('size', 'vec3(1, 1, 1)') return f"sd{node['shape'].upper()}({p}, {size})" elif node['type'] == 'CSG': leftcode = generateglsl(node['left']) rightcode = generateglsl(node['right']) if node['op'] == 'Union': return f"min({leftcode}, {rightcode})" elif node['op'] == 'Intersection': return f"max({leftcode}, {rightcode})" return f"min({leftcode}, {rightcode})" return "" Caching via #invalidate prevents recompilation on every frame, making runtime evaluation efficient. The Config class uses lazy evaluation and caching to avoid unnecessary shader recompilation. The interface is described as intuitive once the input model is understood. The Stack-Based SDF Editor was developed as a final project for COS 426. It demonstrates building SDFs from primitives and operations using a stack-based interface similar to RPN notation. PDF COS 426 Final Project Writeup Raymarching with Signed Distance Fields, https://jbaum98.github.io/cos426finalproject/writeup.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Rounding
head: Distance Offset, Rounded, Rounded Corners in SDFs, Rounding, Rounding Transformation, SDF Domain Manipulation, SDF Offset, SDF Rounding/Offset
body: SDF Rounding is a geometric transformation that modifies a Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitive by subtracting a constant radius value from its distance output, effectively rounding off hard edges and corners. It is a specific instance of SDF Domain Manipulation Operators that operates on the distance value rather than the input position vector. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A base SDF function d{base}(\mathbf{p}) returning the signed distance from point \mathbf{p} to the surface, and a scalar rounding radius r \ge 0. Output: A new SDF function d{rounded}(\mathbf{p}) representing the shape with rounded features. Data Structures: The implementation typically encapsulates the base SDF and the radius parameter. For example, a Rounded struct contains: sdf: The base SDF primitive instance. offset (f32): The constant value added to the distance. Steps: 1. Evaluate the base SDF at the query point \mathbf{p} to obtain the raw signed distance d = d{base}(\mathbf{p}). 2. Subtract the rounding radius r from the raw distance: d{rounded} = d - r. 3. Return d{rounded}. Formula: d{rounded}(\mathbf{p}) = d{base}(\mathbf{p}) - r Parameters: r (float): The rounding radius. Typical values depend on the scale of the primitive (e.g., 0.1 for a unit cube). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If r exceeds the primitive's minimum feature size, the zero-level set may disappear or invert. Precision issues may arise if d{base}(\mathbf{p}) \approx r, leading to numerical instability near the new surface boundary. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfrounding(sdffunc, radius): def roundedsdf(p): basedistance = sdffunc(p) return basedistance - radius return roundedsdf The SDF Onion operation creates a hollow shell or layered structure from a solid SDF primitive by taking the absolute value of the distance and subtracting a specified radius. It is a specific application of SDF Rounding that inverts the interior of the shape to create a void. Unlike standard rounding which smooths exterior edges, Onion creates internal layers by exploiting the symmetry of the absolute distance function. A variant where the constant offset r is replaced by a spatially varying function, such as a sine wave. The formula becomes d{disp}(\mathbf{p}) = d{base}(\mathbf{p}) + \text{offset}(\mathbf{p}). This allows for dynamic surface details like ripples or noise, as seen in the example: \text{offset} = \sin(k \cdot x) \sin(k \cdot y) \sin(k \cdot z) (0.25 + 0.25 \sin(\text{time})). Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation, requiring only one arithmetic subtraction. Memory Complexity: O(1), requiring storage for the radius/offset parameter. Strengths: Simple to implement; computationally cheap; effective for creating smooth, organic, or filleted shapes from basic primitives. Limitations: The distance metric is shifted globally rather than producing exact geometric fillets; large radii can distort the shape significantly. When to use: When visual smoothness is preferred over mathematical precision of the distance field, or for quick prototyping of rounded shapes. When not to use: When exact distance metrics are required for accurate ray marching convergence or collision detection in the rounded regions. SDF Rounding leverages the property that subtracting a constant from a distance function shifts the zero-level set (the surface) inward, smoothing sharp features. It is commonly used in ray marching and implicit surface rendering to generate complex-looking geometry from simple primitives. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Further Graphics - University of Cambridge, https://www.cl.cam.ac.uk/teaching/1920/FGraphics/1.%20Ray%20Marching%20and%20Signed%20Distance%20Fields.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Onion
head: Onion, Onion SDF, SDF Absolute Value Offset, SDF Shell
body: The SDF Onion operation creates a hollow shell or layered structure from a solid Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitive by taking the absolute value of the distance and subtracting a specified radius. It is a specific application of SDF Rounding that inverts the interior of the shape to create a void. Inputs: 1. sdf: A callable returning the signed distance d for a query point p. 2. radius: A scalar float r \ge 0 defining the shell offset. Outputs: A callable returning the signed distance to the shell surface. Data Structures: No complex data structures are required; the operation is a point-wise mathematical transformation applied to the output of the parent SDF. Steps: 1. Evaluate the parent SDF at the query coordinates to obtain the signed distance d = \text{sdf}(p). 2. Compute the absolute value of the signed distance: d{abs} = |d|. 3. Subtract the radius r from the absolute distance: d{onion} = d{abs} - r. 4. Return d{onion}. Formula: d{onion}(p) = |\text{sdf}(p)| - r Where: p is the 3D query point. \text{sdf}(p) is the signed distance from p to the original solid shape. r is the shell radius/thickness. Parameters: radius (r): The shell thickness. Typical values depend on the scale of the parent primitive. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Thickness: If r=0, the result is |d|, representing the unsigned distance to the surface. Large Radius: If r exceeds the distance from the center to the nearest surface of the parent shape, the resulting SDF may be positive everywhere inside the original volume, creating a large void. Degenerate Shapes: For shapes with zero volume or thin surfaces, the absolute value operation combined with subtraction may produce artifacts if the radius is not carefully chosen relative to the shape's curvature. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfonion(sdffunc, radius): """ Creates an SDF for a hollow shell from a solid SDF. Args: sdffunc: A callable that takes a 3D point p and returns the signed distance. radius: The thickness of the shell (r >= 0). Returns: A callable that returns the signed distance to the shell surface. """ def onionsdf(p): d = sdffunc(p) dabs = abs(d) donion = dabs - radius return donion return onionsdf The operation requires O(1) time per query point, involving only absolute value and subtraction arithmetic on top of the parent SDF evaluation. Memory complexity is O(1) as no additional data structures are stored. It is computationally cheap and effective for creating hollow objects, but produces uniform shell thickness and cannot generate variable thickness without more complex operations. The interior of the shell is empty, which may require additional ray marching logic if the ray must stop at the inner surface. Use this when a hollow version of a solid primitive is required, and avoid it when variable thickness or complex internal structures are needed. The SDF Onion operation is used in ray marching and implicit surface rendering to create hollow objects. The onion function can be applied recursively to a sphere with different radii to create layered structures. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) kyle-rosa/raymarching, https://github.com/kyle-rosa/raymarching, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Elongation
body: Elongation modifies a Signed Distance Function (SDF) by applying a non-isometric domain transformation to stretch or compress geometry along a specified vector, creating tapered or elongated structures from base primitives. It sets itself apart from uniform scaling by selectively deforming the spatial domain using absolute-value subtraction and distance correction, which is essential for modeling organic or tapered shapes like bones or fibers. It builds on SDF Domain Manipulation Operators by applying a non-isometric transformation to the query point. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, elongation vector \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3, and base SDF function d{\text{base}}(\cdot). Output: Transformed distance value d{\text{elongated}}(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: \mathbf{p}: 3D vector (px, py, pz) representing the query position. \mathbf{s}: 3D vector (sx, sy, sz) defining the direction and magnitude of elongation. Steps: 1. Compute the intermediate vector \mathbf{q} = |\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{s}, where |\mathbf{p}| denotes component-wise absolute value. 2. Evaluate the base SDF at the positive part of \mathbf{q}, defined as \mathbf{q}+ = \max(\mathbf{q}, 0.0). 3. Add the maximum of the negative part of \mathbf{q} (clamped to zero) to the result: d{\text{elongated}}(\mathbf{p}) = d{\text{base}}(\mathbf{q}+) + \max(-\mathbf{q}, 0.0). Formulas: The core transformation follows: \mathbf{q} = |\mathbf{p}| - \mathbf{s} \mathbf{q}+ = \max(\mathbf{q}, 0.0) d{\text{elongated}}(\mathbf{p}) = d{\text{base}}(\mathbf{q}+) + \max(-\mathbf{q}, 0.0) where |\cdot| is the component-wise absolute value, \max(\cdot, 0.0) clamps negative components to zero, and \max(-\mathbf{q}, 0.0) extracts the negative components of \mathbf{q} as positive corrections. Parameters: \mathbf{s}: Elongation vector. Typical values depend on the desired shape (e.g., sy = 0.1 for slight taper). Base SDF: Any valid SDF (sphere, box, etc.). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-isometric Distortion: Elongation is not an isometry, so the Lipschitz-1 property may be violated, leading to ray marching artifacts if step sizes are not reduced. Precision: Large elongation factors can cause numerical instability in the base SDF evaluation. Boundary Conditions: Ensure the base SDF handles the transformed coordinates correctly, especially if the transformation maps points outside the expected domain. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def elongationsdf(p, s, basesdf): # p: input position (vec3) # s: elongation vector (vec3) # basesdf: function returning distance for a point q = (abs(p.x), abs(p.y), abs(p.z)) - s qpos = (max(q.x, 0.0), max(q.y, 0.0), max(q.z, 0.0)) draw = basesdf(qpos) correction = (max(-q.x, 0.0), max(-q.y, 0.0), max(-q.z, 0.0)) return draw + sum(correction) End-point Corrector: Addresses radius shrinkage and field variation divergence near skeleton end-points in vector field visualization. It sets itself apart from other correction methods by forcing an additional sampling position near end-points to increase the correlation between the minima of individual primitives and the global field. Choose it when visualizing vector fields with skeleton-based elongation to prevent geometric artifacts at termination points. End-point Corrector Time Complexity: O(1) per sample, same as base SDF, plus overhead for transformation and correction. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional data structures. Performance: Fast, but may require smaller step sizes during ray marching due to non-isometric distortion, increasing sample count. Strengths: Enables creation of tapered and organic shapes from simple primitives. Limitations: Distortion can lead to artifacts; requires careful tuning of step sizes. When to use: When modeling tapered, organic, or elongated primitives from standard SDFs. When not to use: When strict isometric preservation or uniform scaling is required, or when ray marching step sizes cannot be dynamically adjusted. Origin: Not given in the sources. History and development: Elongation is a domain manipulation technique used in procedural modeling and ray marching for SDFs. It allows for the creation of complex shapes by deforming the space in which the base SDF is evaluated. Where it is used: Widely used in real-time graphics for generating organic models and structures. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: End-point Corrector
head: Line Width Adjustment, Streamline End-point Adjustment
body: The End-point Corrector addresses radius shrinkage and field variation divergence near skeleton end-points in vector field visualization. It forces an additional sampling position near end-points to increase the correlation between the minima of individual primitives and the global field. Alternatively, it adjusts the start and end points of a streamline to account for line width, either by expanding from the midpoint or by setting fixed bounds. The method operates in two contexts: correcting implicit surface radius errors in SCALIS fields and adjusting streamline geometry for line width in CUDA-based visualization. Inputs: Start point (m{startPt}) and end point (m{endPt}) of the primitive or streamline. Prescribed radius (r) or line width (m{lineWidth}). Field volume dimensions (m{vfInfo.realSize}). Boolean flags: mwingLine (wing line mode) and moritentationX (X orientation mode). Outputs: Adjusted start and end points (m'{startPt}, m'{endPt}). Or, an additional sampling position near the end-point. Points are represented as 3D vectors, stored as float3 structures in the CUDA implementation. Field information includes realSize, a vector representing the physical or voxel dimensions of the volume. This method addresses the issue where the prescribed radius is not achieved in the tangential direction near skeleton end-points. 1. Identify skeleton end-points where the field diverges from the expected behavior. 2. Add a segment primitive with a constant radius at these end vertices. 3. Determine the length of this segment, which is proportional to the prescribed radius at the end vertices and a constant depending on the kernel used. 4. Force an additional sampling position near the skeleton end-points. Note: If end-point correctors are absent, a heuristic presented in section 6.2 of the source can compensate for this shortcoming. In structures without end-points (e.g., truss structures), all assumptions related to the presence of end-point correctors can be used. This method adjusts the start and end points of a streamline to account for line width, either by expanding from the midpoint (wing line) or by setting fixed bounds. 1. Retrieve the start point (m{startPt}) and end point (m{endPt}). 2. Retrieve the line width parameter (m{lineWidth}). 3. Check the mwingLine flag: If mwingLine is true: 1. Calculate the midpoint: mid = \frac{m{startPt} + m{endPt}}{2.0}. 2. Calculate the start vector: startVect = m{startPt} - mid. 3. Calculate the end vector: endVect = m{endPt} - mid. 4. Update start point: m{startPt} = mid + startVect \times (m{lineWidth} + 0.5). 5. Update end point: m{endPt} = mid + endVect \times (m{lineWidth} + 0.5). 6. Return. If mwingLine is false: 1. Check the moritentationX flag. 2. If moritentationX is true: 1. Set m{startPt}.y = (1.0 - m{lineWidth}) \times \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.y}}{2}. 2. Set m{endPt}.y = m{lineWidth} \times \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.y}}{2} + \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.y}}{2}. 3. Else: 1. Set m{startPt}.z = (1.0 - m{lineWidth}) \times \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.z}}{2}. 2. Set m{endPt}.z = m{lineWidth} \times \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.z}}{2} + \frac{m{vfInfo.realSize.z}}{2}. Unverified code. Returns: Tuple (newstartpt, newendpt) """ if wingline: midx = (startpt[0] + endpt[0]) / 2.0 midy = (startpt[1] + endpt[1]) / 2.0 midz = (startpt[2] + endpt[2]) / 2.0 startvectx = startpt[0] - midx startvecty = startpt[1] - midy startvectz = startpt[2] - midz endvectx = endpt[0] - midx endvecty = endpt[1] - midy endvectz = endpt[2] - midz scale = linewidth + 0.5 newstartx = midx + startvectx scale newstarty = midy + startvecty scale newstartz = midz + startvectz scale newendx = midx + endvectx scale newendy = midy + endvecty scale newendz = midz + endvectz scale return (newstartx, newstarty, newstartz), (newendx, newendy, newendz) else: ysize = fieldsize[0] zsize = fieldsize[1] if orientationx: newstarty = (1.0 - linewidth) (ysize / 2.0) newendy = linewidth (ysize / 2.0) + (ysize / 2.0) newstartx = startpt[0] newstartz = startpt[2] newendx = endpt[0] newendz = endpt[2] return (newstartx, newstarty, newstartz), (newendx, newendy, newendz) else: newstartz = (1.0 - linewidth) (zsize / 2.0) newendz = linewidth (zsize / 2.0) + (zsize / 2.0) newstartx = startpt[0] newstarty = startpt[1] newendx = endpt[0] newendy = endpt[1] return (newstartx, newstarty, newstartz), (newendx, newendy, newendz) Line Width (mlineWidth): The width of the streamline. name: Finite Repetition
head: Bounded Tiling, Finite Domain Repetition, Limited Repetition
body: Finite Repetition repeats a base Signed Distance Function (SDF) a limited number of times in 3D space by restricting the replication count within a specified limit \mathbf{l} along each axis. Unlike Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset, which creates interlocking patterns over unbounded space, Finite Repetition produces a discrete, finite array of objects. Finite Repetition maps a query point \mathbf{p} to the nearest instance within the bounded grid by calculating an integer offset vector \mathbf{q} and subtracting the corresponding periodic displacement. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query position \mathbf{p} (vec3), period/size \mathbf{c} (vec3), limit \mathbf{l} (vec3). Output: Transformed position \mathbf{p}' (vec3) to be passed to the base SDF. Data Structures: \mathbf{p}, \mathbf{c}, \mathbf{l} are typically 3-component floating-point vectors. \mathbf{q} is an intermediate integer vector. Steps: 1. Divide \mathbf{p} by \mathbf{c} and round each component to the nearest integer. 2. Clamp the result to the limit \mathbf{l} to enforce the finite boundary. 3. Subtract the periodic displacement \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{q} from \mathbf{p} to map to the canonical cell. Formula: \mathbf{q} = \text{clamp}\left(\text{round}\left(\frac{\mathbf{p}}{\mathbf{c}}\right), -\mathbf{l}, \mathbf{l}\right) \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c} \cdot \mathbf{q} Where: \text{round}(\cdot) rounds to the nearest integer. \text{clamp}(x, \min, \max) restricts x to [\min, \max]. \mathbf{l} defines the maximum number of cells in each direction from the origin. Parameters: \mathbf{c}: Cell size (period). Must be non-zero. \mathbf{l}: Repetition limit. Typically positive integers or floats representing cell counts. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Period: Division by zero if any component of \mathbf{c} is zero. Ensure \mathbf{c} components are strictly positive. Boundary Precision: Points exactly on cell boundaries may round unpredictably depending on floating-point representation. Standard round behavior (round half to even or away from zero) should be consistent. Limit Zero: If \mathbf{l} = 0, \mathbf{q} becomes \mathbf{0}, and \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p}, effectively disabling repetition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def repeatfinite(p, c, l): """ Finite domain repetition for SDF. p: input position (vec3) c: cell size/period (vec3) l: repetition limit (vec3) Returns: transformed position (vec3) """ q = (p / c).round().clamp(-l, l) return p - c q Creates a perfect, interlocking hexagonal honeycomb pattern using two offset rectangular grids. Choose this when you need unbounded, interlocking tiling with potential per-column properties, accepting higher computational cost. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally cheap, prevents infinite recursion in ray marching. Limitations: Creates sharp boundaries at the limit \mathbf{l}; objects outside the limit are not rendered. When to use: Bounded tiling, finite arrays of objects, architectural elements with fixed counts. When not to use: Unbounded tiling, infinite floors/walls (use Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset). Finite Repetition is a standard domain manipulation operator in Signed Distance Field rendering. It is a fundamental building block for creating structured scenes without explicit mesh geometry. The method relies on the mathematical property of periodicity and clamping to bound the repetition. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset
head: Hexagonal Honeycomb Repetition, Hexagonal Honeycomb Repetition via Dual Offset Repetition, OR-Composite Honeycomb, Two-Cell Honeycomb
body: Infinite Repetition via Dual Offset creates a perfect, interlocking hexagonal honeycomb pattern by combining two separate rectangular repetition grids that are offset from each other. Unlike the skew method, which applies a single coordinate transformation, this method uses a boolean OR operation (minimum of distances) on two distinct distance functions to ensure that the "interlocking" parts of adjacent hexagons are correctly rendered without clipping. It is computationally more expensive than skew-based approaches but allows for different shape functions or properties (such as color) per column. Inputs: Point p in 3D space (or 2D for the tiling plane). Side length s of the regular hexagon. Outputs: Signed distance d to the nearest hexagon boundary. Data Structures: No complex structures required. The method relies on standard vector arithmetic and two calls to a rectangular repetition function. Steps: 1. Define the two repetition patterns: The honeycomb is formed by two interleaved rectangular grids. Let the vertical repetition step be hy and the horizontal step be hx. For a regular hexagon with side length s: The horizontal period is hx = 2s. The vertical period is hy = 2\sqrt{3}s. This is derived from the height of an equilateral triangle with side s (\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s) multiplied by 4, as stated in the source: "The vertical repetition width is 4 times the height of an equilateral triangle with side length 1". The two grids are offset. Typically, one grid is aligned with the origin, and the other is shifted by half the horizontal period and half the vertical period, or specifically arranged such that their cells interlock. A common implementation places the centers of the two rectangular cells at: Grid 1: (0, 0) Grid 2: (s, \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}s) or equivalent offset that ensures the hexagons from Grid 1 and Grid 2 touch at their edges to form the honeycomb. The source notes that focusing on one grid (e.g., blue circles in the reference image) reveals a simple xy-axis repetition. 2. Calculate the distance function for the first pattern (d1): Apply the rectangular repetition operator to point p using periods (hx, hy) centered at the origin. Let p1 be the wrapped point. Calculate the signed distance from p1 to the hexagon shape defined within this cell. Let this be d1. 3. Calculate the distance function for the second pattern (d2): Apply the rectangular repetition operator to point p using the same periods (hx, hy) but with the offset center for the second grid. Let p2 be the wrapped point relative to this second grid's origin. Calculate the signed distance from p2 to the hexagon shape. Let this be d2. 4. Combine using minimum operation: The final distance is the minimum of the two distances: d = \min(d1, d2) This corresponds to the boolean OR operation for signed distance fields, ensuring that if a point is inside or near a hexagon from either grid, the distance reflects the nearest boundary. Parameters: s: Side length of the hexagon. Typical value: 1.0. hx = 2s. hy = 2\sqrt{3}s \approx 3.464s. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clipping in Single-Grid Approaches: If one attempts to create a honeycomb by simply shifting every other row by half the cell width (brick-like layout) using a single distance function per cell, the interlocking parts of tightly packed hexagons will extend outside the defined rectangular repetition cell. Since a single distance function defines the shape within one cell, these protruding parts are clipped/cut off at the cell boundaries. The Dual Offset method avoids this by ensuring the "missing" parts of one cell are covered by the adjacent cell from the other grid. Precision: Standard floating-point precision is sufficient for typical scene scales. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def repeatrect(p, periodx, periody): """ Wraps point p into the fundamental domain of a rectangular grid. Returns the point relative to the center of the cell. """ # Wrap coordinates to the period x = p.x % periodx y = p.y % periody # Center the cell around (0,0) if x > periodx / 2: x -= periodx if y > periody / 2: y -= periody return Vector2(x, y) def hexagondistance(p): """ Signed distance to a regular hexagon centered at origin with side length s. Assumes p is already wrapped to the fundamental domain. """ s = 1.0 # Side length # Distance to a regular hexagon can be computed by projecting to the nearest edge # For a hexagon with flat top/bottom or pointy top/bottom, specific formulas apply. # Assuming pointy-top hexagon for standard honeycomb alignment. # A robust SDF for a regular hexagon: # q = abs(p) # if q.x > q.y: # d = dot(q, Vector2(0.5, sqrt(3)/2)) - s sqrt(3)/2 # else: # d = q.y - s # This is a simplified approximation; exact SDF requires careful handling of corners. # For the purpose of this article, we assume a generic hexagon SDF function exists. return hexagonsdfgeneric(p, s) def hexagonsdfgeneric(p, s): """ Placeholder for the specific SDF of a regular hexagon. In practice, this is a standard GLSL/Shader function. """ # Example for pointy-top hexagon with circumradius R = s # Actually, side length s implies circumradius R = s. # Distance to hexagon with circumradius R: # q = abs(p) # if q.x > q.y: # d = dot(q, Vector2(0.5, sqrt(3)/2)) - R sqrt(3)/2 # else: # d = q.y - R # Note: The source does not provide the internal hexagon SDF formula, only the repetition logic. # Standard hexagon SDF implementation required here. pass def infiniterepetitiondualoffset(p, sidelength): """ Computes the distance to an infinite honeycomb pattern using dual offset repetition. """ s = sidelength hx = 2 s hy = 2 math.sqrt(3) s # Grid 1: Centered at (0,0) p1 = repeatrect(p, hx, hy) d1 = hexagondistance(p1) # Grid 2: Offset by (s, sqrt(3)/2 s) to interlock # The offset ensures that the hexagons from Grid 2 fill the gaps of Grid 1 offsetx = s offsety = math.sqrt(3) / 2 s p2 = repeatrect(p - Vector2(offsetx, offsety), hx, hy) d2 = hexagondistance(p2) return min(d1, d2) A variant that creates a honeycomb pattern by shifting every other row of a rectangular grid by half the cell width, creating a brick-like layout. It is simpler to conceptualize but suffers from a critical pitfall: when using convex shapes like hexagons that are tightly packed, the 'interlocking' parts of the shape may extend outside the defined rectangular repetition cell. Since a single distance function defines the shape within one cell, these protruding parts are clipped/cut off at the cell boundaries, resulting in incorrect geometry. Time Complexity: Requires calculating two distance functions and combining them with a minimum operation. This is approximately twice the cost of a single repetition pattern. Memory Complexity: Minimal additional memory; only requires storing the offset parameters. Strengths: Produces a perfect, interlocking honeycomb without clipping artifacts. Allows different shape functions or properties (e.g., color, material) to be applied to each column/grid independently. Limitations: More computationally expensive than the skew method. Requires careful tuning of the offset to ensure proper interlocking. When to use: When perfect interlocking is required and different properties per column are desired. When not to use: When performance is critical and the skew method suffices for the visual requirement. Originated from practical shader art and procedural geometry techniques, specifically discussed in the context of Sphere Tracing and domain operations. The method is highlighted as a solution to the clipping issues inherent in simple row-offsetting methods for hexagonal tiling. It leverages the property that the union of two offset rectangular grids can form a hexagonal lattice. name: Quadric SDF (First-Order Approximation)
body: Computes an approximate signed distance from a query point to a general quadric surface defined by a quadratic implicit equation, using a first-order Taylor approximation. It differs from exact SDF primitives (like spheres or boxes) by handling arbitrary second-order surfaces (ellipsoids, hyperboloids, paraboloids) at the cost of geometric accuracy, trading precision for the ability to model complex algebraic shapes without analytical distance formulas. Inputs: Query point v = (x, y, z). Quadric coefficients: a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j. These define the surface ax^2 + by^2 + cz^2 + dxy + eyz + fzx + gx + hy + iz + j = 0. Outputs: Approximate signed distance d{approx}. (Optional) Normal vector n at the closest point approximation. Data Structures: Coefficients stored as 10 floating-point values. Point v as a 3D vector. Steps: 1. Evaluate the implicit function value f0 at v: f0 = ax^2 + by^2 + cz^2 + dxy + eyz + fzx + gx + hy + iz + j 2. Compute the gradient components (partial derivatives) at v: dx = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2ax + dy + fz + g dy = \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = 2by + ez + dx + h dz = \frac{\partial f}{\partial z} = 2cz + fx + ey + i Note: The source code uses d for the xy term coefficient in the gradient calculation for dx and dy, and f for the zx term in dx and dz, and e for the yz term in dy and dz. 3. Compute the gradient magnitude f1: f1 = \sqrt{dx^2 + dy^2 + dz^2} 4. Return the approximate signed distance: d{approx} = \frac{f0}{f1} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def quadricsdfapprox(x, y, z, a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j): # 1. Evaluate implicit function f0 f0 = (a x x + b y y + c z z + d x y + e y z + f z x + g x + h y + i z + j) # 2. Compute gradient components # dx/dx = 2ax + dy + fz + g gradx = 2 a x + d y + f z + g # dy/dy = 2by + ez + dx + h grady = 2 b y + e z + d x + h # dz/dz = 2cz + fx + ey + i gradz = 2 c z + f x + e y + i # 3. Compute gradient magnitude gradmag = math.sqrt(gradx gradx + grady grady + gradz gradz) # 4. Return approximate distance # Guard against division by zero if gradmag < 1e-12: return 0.0 # Or handle as error/undefined return f0 / gradmag def quadricnormal(x, y, z, a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j): gradx = 2 a x + d y + f z + g grady = 2 b y + e z + d x + h gradz = 2 c z + f x + e y + i gradmag = math.sqrt(gradx gradx + grady grady + gradz gradz) if gradmag < 1e-12: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Undefined normal return (gradx / gradmag, grady / gradmag, gradz / gradmag) Parameters: a, b, c: Coefficients of squared terms x^2, y^2, z^2. d, e, f: Coefficients of cross terms xy, yz, zx. g, h, i: Coefficients of linear terms x, y, z. j: Constant term. Typical values depend on the specific quadric shape being modeled. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Near Zero: If the gradient magnitude is near zero (e.g., at critical points like the vertex of a paraboloid or far from the surface where the function is flat), the division by f1 becomes unstable, leading to incorrect or infinite distance estimates. Signed Distance Accuracy: This is an approximation. The sign is determined by the sign of f0, but the magnitude is only accurate to first order. It may not be a true Euclidean distance, which can cause artifacts in ray marching (e.g., overshooting or jittering) if the step size is not adjusted. Degenerate Quadrics: If the quadratic form is degenerate (e.g., representing parallel planes or a line), the gradient behavior may be singular or non-uniform, requiring specific handling. Diagonalizes the quadratic form matrix of a general quadratic function to identify principal curvatures and axes. This method maps a generic quadratic surface to a standard prototype (paraboloid or hyperbolic paraboloid) to enable optimal, error-bounded triangulation of its zero-level set. It is chosen when exact geometric analysis or mesh generation is required rather than just ray marching distance queries. Represents complex 3D geometry using a continuous real-valued describing function F(X) \ge 0, where X=(x1,x2,x3). The object is the closed subset of Euclidean space where the function is non-negative. It allows visualization of both the surface and internal structure. The base surface is a quadric F(x,y,z) \ge 0, and freeform shapes are created by adding perturbation functions Ri(x,y,z), which are cubes of perturbing quadrics Qi clamped to zero where Qi < 0. This reduces object construction to quadric surface deformation rather than approximation by primitives (polygons or B-spline patches). Estimating the maximum value of the combined function requires calculating the maximum of the perturbation function on the same interval, based on the inequality \max[Q + R] \le \max[Q] + \max[R]. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (10 multiplications, 9 additions, 1 square root for distance; 1 square root for normal). Memory Complexity: O(1) storage for coefficients. Measured Performance: Fast enough for real-time ray marching on GPUs, as demonstrated in the reference implementation. Scaling: Performance is independent of resolution or scene complexity, as it is a point-wise evaluation. Strengths: Handles arbitrary quadric surfaces (ellipsoids, hyperboloids, etc.) without needing complex analytical SDF derivations. Simple to implement. Limitations: Approximate distance. Not a true Euclidean distance, which can lead to inaccuracies in ray marching convergence or normal estimation. Unstable near critical points where the gradient vanishes. When to use: When modeling complex algebraic surfaces that are quadrics, and high precision is not critical, or as a fallback when no exact SDF is available. When not to use: When exact Euclidean distance is required for correct ray marching behavior (e.g., in constructive solid geometry with smooth blending), or when the surface has regions with vanishing gradients. The method is described in an unofficial GitHub repository "FunctionRenderer" by Leesan-haruki, which implements a ray tracer using SDFs. The concept of using implicit functions for geometric modeling, including quadrics, has roots in computer graphics literature, such as John C. Hart's 1995 work on analytic distance fields. The specific first-order approximation for general quadrics is a practical technique to extend SDF ray marching beyond basic primitives. The related concept of freeform surfaces via quadric perturbation is described in a paper on GPU-based volume-oriented rendering of functionally defined objects. name: Principal Axis Transformation for Quadratic Surfaces
head: Eigenvalue Analysis of Quadratic Forms, Principal Component Analysis of Quadrics
body: The Principal Axis Transformation (PAT) diagonalizes the quadratic form matrix of a general quadratic function to identify principal curvatures and axes. This method maps a generic quadratic surface to a standard prototype (paraboloid or hyperbolic paraboloid) to enable optimal, error-bounded triangulation of its zero-level set. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Quadratic function coefficients c{20}, c{11}, c{02}, c{10}, c{01}, c{00}. Output: Eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2, normalized eigenvectors \mathbf{e}1, \mathbf{e}2, and the classification of the surface type (Elliptic, Hyperbolic, or Parabolic). Data Structures: Matrix C: A 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix representing the quadratic form. C = \begin{pmatrix} c{20} & c{11} \\ c{11} & c{02} \end{pmatrix} Eigenvalues: Scalars \lambda1, \lambda2. Eigenvectors: Normalized 2D vectors \mathbf{e}1 = (e{11}, e{12})^T, \mathbf{e}2 = (e{21}, e{22})^T. Steps: 1. Construct Matrix C: Extract the quadratic coefficients from the input function. The linear and constant terms do not affect the principal axes or curvature classification. 2. Compute Eigenvalues: Solve the characteristic equation \det(C - \lambda I) = 0 for \lambda1 and \lambda2. 3. Compute Eigenvectors: For each \lambdai, solve (C - \lambdai I)\mathbf{v} = 0 and normalize the resulting vector \mathbf{v} to obtain \mathbf{e}i. 4. Classify Surface: Determine the surface type based on the product of the eigenvalues: Elliptic if \lambda1 \lambda2 > 0. Hyperbolic if \lambda1 \lambda2 < 0. Parabolic if \lambda1 \lambda2 = 0. Formulas: The quadratic function is represented as: f(x, y) = (x \ y) \begin{pmatrix} c{20} & c{11} \\ c{11} & c{02} \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + (c{10} \ c{01}) \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} + c{00} The quadratic form is \mathbf{x}^T C \mathbf{x} = 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def principalaxistransformation(c20, c11, c02, c10, c01, c00): # Step 1: Construct Matrix C # C is symmetric: [[c20, c11], [c11, c02]] # Linear and constant terms are ignored for axis determination # Step 2: Compute Eigenvalues # Characteristic equation: lambda^2 - trace(C)lambda + det(C) = 0 traceC = c20 + c02 detC = c20 c02 - c11 c11 discriminant = traceC2 - 4 detC sqrtdisc = math.sqrt(discriminant) lambda1 = (traceC + sqrtdisc) / 2 lambda2 = (traceC - sqrtdisc) / 2 # Step 3: Compute Eigenvectors # For lambda1 if abs(c11) > 1e-9: e1 = (1.0, (lambda1 - c20) / c11) else: e1 = (0.0, 1.0) if abs(lambda1 - c02) < 1e-9 else (1.0, 0.0) norm1 = math.sqrt(e1[0]2 + e1[1]2) e1 = (e1[0] / norm1, e1[1] / norm1) # For lambda2 if abs(c11) > 1e-9: e2 = (1.0, (lambda2 - c20) / c11) else: e2 = (0.0, 1.0) if abs(lambda2 - c02) < 1e-9 else (1.0, 0.0) norm2 = math.sqrt(e2[0]2 + e2[1]2) e2 = (e2[0] / norm2, e2[1] / norm2) # Step 4: Classify Surface product = lambda1 lambda2 if product > 0: surfacetype = "Elliptic" elif product < 0: surfacetype = "Hyperbolic" else: surfacetype = "Parabolic" return { "lambda1": lambda1, "lambda2": lambda2, "e1": e1, "e2": e2, "surfacetype": surfacetype } Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: If c{11} is near zero, eigenvector calculation may suffer from division by zero; handle via conditional checks. Degenerate Input: If both eigenvalues are zero, the surface is planar and the cluster region can be triangulated by only considering the vertices of its convex boundary polygon. Generates a mesh for elliptic quadrics (\lambda1 \lambda2 > 0) by mapping an optimal equilateral prototype triangle from a canonical paraboloid space (g = \bar{x}^2 + \bar{y}^2) to the target surface. It is distinguished by its use of the paraboloid prototype and reliance on PAT to preserve error bounds analytically. See Elliptic Case Triangulation. Generates a mesh for hyperbolic quadrics (\lambda1 \lambda2 < 0) by placing vertices exactly on the surface to minimize interpolation error. It uses the prototype h(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = \bar{x}^2 - \bar{y}^2. The transformation from prototype to original function (for \lambda1 > 0, \lambda2 < 0) is \begin{pmatrix} x \\ y \end{pmatrix} = H \begin{pmatrix} \bar{x} \\ \bar{y} \end{pmatrix}, where H = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} e{11} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{-\lambda2}} e{21} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} e{12} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{-\lambda2}} e{22} \end{pmatrix}. If \lambda1 < 0 and \lambda2 > 0, the triangulation is obtained by considering the quadratic form of -f. Optimal triangle vertices for h are (\sqrt{\epsilon}, \sqrt{\epsilon})^T, (\sqrt{\epsilon}, -\sqrt{\epsilon})^T, and ((1-\sqrt{5})\sqrt{\epsilon}, 0)^T. The maximal error for any edge ab is \varepsilon{\text{ab}} = \frac{1}{4} |(ax - bx)^2 - (ay - by)^2|. The final triangulation is established by transforming two edges according to H. name: Elliptic Case Triangulation
body: Elliptic Case Triangulation generates a mesh approximation for the graph surface of a quadratic function f of elliptic type, which is equivalent to the paraboloid g(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = \bar{x}^2 + \bar{y}^2. It converts the continuous quadratic surface into a discrete triangular mesh by mapping an optimal equilateral prototype triangle from canonical space to the target surface space via a principal axis transformation. It is distinguished from the Hyperbolic Case Triangulation by its paraboloid prototype and from general meshing methods by its analytical error bound preservation. Inputs: Quadratic function f (or its symmetric matrix C), error tolerance \epsilon > 0, cluster region boundary, and cluster centroid c. Outputs: A set of triangles forming a triangulation of the surface within the cluster region. Data Structures: Prototype Triangle: Defined in canonical coordinates (\bar{x}, \bar{y}). Transformation Matrix G: 2 \times 2 matrix mapping canonical to physical coordinates. Edge Vectors: Two vectors defining the regular triangulation lattice. Steps: 1. Eigen-decomposition: Compute the eigenvalues \lambda1, \lambda2 and normalized eigenvectors e1 = (e{11}, e{12})^T, e2 = (e{21}, e{22})^T of the quadratic matrix C. For the elliptic case, the eigenvalues are positive. 2. Handle Negative Eigenvalues: If eigenvalues are negative, replace f with -f to imply positive eigenvalues. 3. Construct Transformation Matrix G: The transformation maps the canonical paraboloid g(\bar{x}, \bar{y}) = \bar{x}^2 + \bar{y}^2 to the quadratic form f. The matrix G is constructed from the eigenvectors scaled by the inverse square roots of the eigenvalues: G = \begin{pmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} e{11} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda2}} e{21} \\ \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} e{12} & \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda2}} e{22} \end{pmatrix} The source text contains a typo in equation (2.9) writing \frac{1}{\sqrt{1}} and \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} instead of \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda1}} and \frac{1}{\sqrt{\lambda2}}. 4. Define Prototype Triangle: In the canonical space (\bar{x}, \bar{y}), the optimal triangle is equilateral with a circumscribed circle radius R = \sqrt{2\epsilon}. The vertices are: v1 = \begin{pmatrix} -\sqrt{2\epsilon} \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \quad v2 = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{0.5\epsilon} \\ \sqrt{1.5\epsilon} \end{pmatrix}, \quad v3 = \begin{pmatrix} \sqrt{0.5\epsilon} \\ -\sqrt{1.5\epsilon} \end{pmatrix} This triangle maximizes area for a given maximal error \epsilon, which occurs at the center and vertices. 5. Transform Edges: Compute edge vectors u = v2 - v1 and v = v3 - v1. Transform only these two edges according to G: U = G u, V = G v. 6. Generate Triangulation: Establish a regular triangulation emanating from the cluster centroid c using U and V. For positive eigenvalues, place vertices below the surface by \epsilon (if f was flipped to -f, place vertices above by \epsilon). Only generate triangles that lie entirely within the cluster region, leaving untriangulated gaps at boundaries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def ellipticcasetriangulation(C, centroid, isinside, epsilon): """ Generates triangulation for elliptic quadratic SDF. C: 2x2 symmetric matrix [[c11, c12], [c12, c22]] centroid: (cx, cy) isinside: function(x, y) -> bool epsilon: float, error tolerance """ # 1. Eigen-decomposition c11, c12, c22 = C[0][0], C[0][1], C[1][1] trace = c11 + c22 det = c11 c22 - c122 discriminant = math.sqrt(max(0, trace2 - 4 det)) lambda1 = (trace + discriminant) / 2 lambda2 = (trace - discriminant) / 2 if lambda1 <= 0 or lambda2 <= 0: raise ValueError("Not an elliptic case: eigenvalues must be positive.") # Compute normalized eigenvectors if abs(c12) > 1e-9: e1 = (1.0, -(c11 - lambda1) / c12) else: e1 = (0.0, 1.0) norme1 = math.sqrt(e1[0]2 + e1[1]2) e1 = (e1[0] / norme1, e1[1] / norme1) e2 = (-e1[1], e1[0]) # Orthogonal to e1 # 2. Construct G matrix invsqrtl1 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(lambda1) invsqrtl2 = 1.0 / math.sqrt(lambda2) G = [ [e1[0] invsqrtl1, e2[0] invsqrtl2], [e1[1] invsqrtl1, e2[1] invsqrtl2] ] # 3. Prototype triangle vertices in canonical space sqrteps = math.sqrt(epsilon) v1 = (-math.sqrt(2) sqrteps, 0.0) v2 = (math.sqrt(0.5) sqrteps, math.sqrt(1.5) sqrteps) v3 = (math.sqrt(0.5) sqrteps, -math.sqrt(1.5) sqrteps) # 4. Transform edge vectors def matvecmul(M, v): return (M[0][0]v[0] + M[0][1]v[1], M[1][0]v[0] + M[1][1]v[1]) u = (v2[0] - v1[0], v2[1] - v1[1]) v = (v3[0] - v1[0], v3[1] - v1[1]) U = matvecmul(G, u) V = matvecmul(G, v) # 5. Generate triangulation triangles = [] # Iterate over a grid centered at the centroid; range depends on cluster size maxidx = 200 # Implementation-dependent bound for i in range(-maxidx, maxidx): for j in range(-maxidx, maxidx): p0x = centroid[0] + i U[0] + j V[0] p0y = centroid[1] + i U[1] + j V[1] p1x = p0x + U[0] p1y = p0y + U[1] p2x = p0x + V[0] p2y = p0y + V[1] # Boundary culling: only triangles entirely inside the cluster if isinside(p0x, p0y) and isinside(p1x, p1y) and isinside(p2x, p2y): # Apply offset: place vertices below the surface by epsilon # In practice, shift each vertex along the surface normal by epsilon triangles.append(((p0x, p0y), (p1x, p1y), (p2x, p2y))) return triangles Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The square roots of eigenvalues can be small, leading to large scaling factors in G. Use double precision. Boundary Gaps: The method explicitly leaves gaps at cluster boundaries. Degenerate Input: If eigenvalues are zero, the surface is not elliptic (parabolic or planar). Uses prototype h = \bar{x}^2 - \bar{y}^2. Choose when eigenvalues have opposite signs. Link Not given in the sources. Link Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Basic Primitive Definitions
head: Analytical SDF Primitives, Closed-Form SDF Primitives
body: Basic Primitive Definitions provide the foundational analytical functions that compute the exact Euclidean signed distance from a query point to standard geometric shapes, serving as the atomic building blocks for distance-field ray marching. They replace explicit mesh geometry with implicit mathematical definitions, enabling safe, large step sizes along rays by leveraging the continuous scalar field where the sign indicates interior (d < 0) or exterior (d > 0) status. Unlike polygonal primitives or iterative approximations, these primitives rely on closed-form algebraic solutions for standard shapes like spheres, boxes, and tori. All primitives in this family adhere to a common computational framework: 1. Canonical Placement: Primitives are defined in a local coordinate system centered at the origin (0,0,0) and axis-aligned where applicable. 2. Transformation: To render a primitive at a different position, rotation, or scale, the query point p is transformed into the primitive's local space (inverse transformation) before evaluation, or the primitive parameters are adjusted accordingly. 3. Signed Output: The function returns a scalar d \in \mathbb{R}. d < 0 indicates the point is inside the primitive, d > 0 indicates it is outside, and d = 0 lies on the surface. 4. Gradient Availability: The functions are differentiable almost everywhere, allowing for the computation of surface normals via the gradient \nabla d. Standard analytical functions for spheres, boxes, tori, planes, cylinders, capsules, and octahedra. Chosen for their simplicity and exact closed-form solutions for common shapes. Exact SDFs for convex polyhedra and prisms. Chosen when complex angular geometries are required without discretization artifacts, relying on piecewise-linear face constraints. Exact distance to finite cones, including lateral mantle and base cap. Chosen for tapered geometries, distinguishing itself from infinite cones and cylinders by handling base boundaries. Distance to line segments defined by endpoints. Chosen as the geometric core for 1D primitives and extruded shapes, differing from infinite lines by clamping the projection parameter. Definition: Renders the torus interior tube as empty space by negating the torus SDF, enabling natural front-to-back occlusion and eliminating donut-hole artifacts. Step: Negate torus SDF: return -(dring - r). Treat negative SDF as empty space (tube cavity), positive SDF as solid (donut hole, outside). Ray march naturally finds tube interior. Pitfall: Prevents donut-hole artifacts by ensuring ray marching only operates inside the tube cavity. Definition: Signed Distance Field functions for the butterfly's components: sdWing for the flapping wings, sdBody for the thorax/abdomen, and sdAntenna for the antennae. These are combined in mapButterfly to return the minimum distance and material ID. Code: Wing SDF logic un-bends the point to wing space, checks the outline, and calculates thickness and camber to form a slab. Body SDF logic uses a parametric radius function based on normalized Z coordinate u. Antenna SDF logic uses a quadratic bezier-like curve c for the spine and varying radius. Wing Outline is defined as two rounded triangles (forewing and hindwing) using sdTriangle, with a notch between them. Definition: Uses superellipsoids and a 'slice-27 grid' (3D equivalent of Flash's slice-9 grids) for geometry primitives, allowing rounded 3D shapes with customizable corners. Step: Specify primitive properties: corner distance (independently for xyz), wall thickness, or bounding box for visible region. Combine primitives using Voronoi style distance (typically clamped to xy or ground plane) or advanced boolean intersections with material priority. Apply volumetric texturing in object space with automatically generated texture coordinates measured in meters to scale independently of voxel size. Generate UVW coordinates along length, height, and depth (into walls). Assign special material IDs for distinct normal generation (e.g., distinct boards). The concept of using analytical signed distance functions for ray marching was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his online articles and books on procedural modeling. The specific implementations for basic primitives (sphere, box, torus) are standard in the computer graphics community for implicit modeling and collision detection. The inverted torus technique for rendering tube-like structures without artifacts is documented in specific GPU implementation guides. Butterfly and superellipsoid variants represent specialized applications in procedural generation and voxel-based world generation. name: SDF Primitives
head: Basic SDFs, Signed Distance Primitives, Basic Signed Distance Functions, Signed Distance Field Primitives, Signed Distance Function Primitives
body: SDF Primitives are analytical functions that compute the exact Euclidean signed distance from a query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 to the surface of a geometric shape. They serve as the fundamental building blocks for Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) and distance-field ray marching, enabling adaptive step sizes that guarantee surface intersection without overshooting. Unlike polygonal meshes, primitives are defined by closed-form formulas, making them resolution-independent and computationally efficient for simple shapes. This article covers the standard solid primitives (Sphere, Box, Torus, Cylinder, Capsule, Plane) and their combination operations, building on the shared principles of Basic Primitive Definitions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and primitive-specific parameters (e.g., radius, half-extents, normal). Output: Scalar signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. d < 0 indicates the point is inside the primitive, d > 0 indicates it is outside, and d = 0 lies on the surface. Assumptions: All implementations assume the primitive is centered at the origin and axis-aligned where applicable. Transformations (rotation, translation, scaling) are applied to the query point p before evaluation, or the primitive parameters are adjusted accordingly. Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required for evaluation. Parameters are passed as scalars or vectors: p: vec3 (query point). r, R: float (radii). b: vec3 (box half-extents). n: vec3 (plane normal, must be normalized). d: float (plane offset from origin). a, b: vec3 (capsule endpoints). t: vec2 (torus major/minor radii). Numbered Steps: 1. Transform Point: If the primitive is not at the origin or rotated, transform the query point p by the inverse of the primitive's transformation matrix M^{-1}, or translate by p' = p - \text{center}. 2. Evaluate Primitive: Compute the signed distance d using the specific formula for the primitive type. 3. Return Distance: Return d. Formulas: Let \|v\| denote the Euclidean length \sqrt{vx^2 + vy^2 + vz^2}. Let \max(\mathbf{v}, 0) be the component-wise maximum of vector \mathbf{v} and zero vector. Let \maxcomp(\mathbf{v}) be the maximum component of vector \mathbf{v}. Sphere (radius r): d(p) = \|p\| - r Axis-Aligned Box (half-extents b): Let q = |p| - b. d(p) = \| \max(q, 0) \| + \min(\maxcomp(q), 0) Note: \maxcomp(q) = \max(qx, \max(qy, qz)). Torus (major radius R, minor radius r): Let q = (\|\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R, py). d(p) = \|q\| - r Infinite Plane (normal n, offset d{offset}): d(p) = p \cdot n + d{offset} Note: n must be normalized. Cylinder (radius r, half-height h, aligned with Y-axis): Let d = (\|\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}\| - r, |py| - h). d(p) = \min(\max(dx, dy), 0) + \| \max(d, 0) \| Capsule (endpoints a, b, radius r): Let ba = b - a and pa = p - a. Let h = \max(0, \min(1, \frac{pa \cdot ba}{ba \cdot ba})). Let closest = a + ba \cdot h. d(p) = \| pa - ba \cdot h \| - r Octahedron (size s): d(p) = \frac{|px| + |py| + |pz| - s}{\sqrt{3}} Tetrahedron (regular, centered at origin): Let md = \max(-px - py - pz, px + py - pz, -px + py + pz, px - py + pz). d(p) = \frac{md}{\sqrt{3}} Parameters with Typical Values: Sphere radius r: Scene-dependent. Box half-extents b: Scene-dependent. Torus major radius R: Typically > 0. Minor radius r < R. Cylinder radius r, half-height h: Scene-dependent. Capsule radius r: Scene-dependent. Plane normal n: Unit vector. Offset d{offset}: Scene-dependent. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: For very small primitives, floating-point precision errors may cause incorrect inside/outside classification. Use double precision if necessary. Normalization: The Plane SDF requires a normalized normal vector n. Failure to normalize results in incorrect distances. Degenerate Capsules: If endpoints a and b are identical, ba \cdot ba = 0, causing division by zero in the capsule formula. Guard against this case. Box Corners: The Box SDF formula correctly handles edges and corners by combining the distance to the nearest face (inside) or corner/edge (outside). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdsphere(p, r): """Signed distance to a sphere of radius r centered at origin.""" return math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[1]2 + p[2]2) - r def sdbox(p, b): """Signed distance to an axis-aligned box with half-extents b.""" q = [abs(p[0]) - b[0], abs(p[1]) - b[1], abs(p[2]) - b[2]] outsidedist = math.sqrt(max(q[0], 0)2 + max(q[1], 0)2 + max(q[2], 0)2) insidedist = min(max(q[0], max(q[1], q[2])), 0) return outsidedist + insidedist def sdtorus(p, R, r): """Signed distance to a torus with major radius R and minor radius r.""" qx = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) - R qy = p[1] return math.sqrt(qx2 + qy2) - r def sdplane(p, n, doffset): """Signed distance to an infinite plane with normal n and offset doffset.""" # n must be normalized return p[0]n[0] + p[1]n[1] + p[2]n[2] + doffset def sdcylinder(p, r, h): """Signed distance to a cylinder aligned with Y-axis, radius r, half-height h.""" dx = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) - r dy = abs(p[1]) - h outsidedist = math.sqrt(max(dx, 0)2 + max(dy, 0)2) insidedist = min(max(dx, dy), 0) return outsidedist + insidedist def sdcapsule(p, a, b, r): """Signed distance to a capsule with endpoints a, b and radius r.""" ba = [b[0]-a[0], b[1]-a[1], b[2]-a[2]] ap = [p[0]-a[0], p[1]-a[1], p[2]-a[2]] badotba = ba[0]2 + ba[1]2 + ba[2]2 if badotba == 0: # Degenerate case: capsule is a sphere return math.sqrt(ap[0]2 + ap[1]2 + ap[2]2) - r t = max(0, min(1, (ap[0]ba[0] + ap[1]ba[1] + ap[2]ba[2]) / badotba)) closest = [a[0] + ba[0]t, a[1] + ba[1]t, a[2] + ba[2]t] diff = [p[0]-closest[0], p[1]-closest[1], p[2]-closest[2]] return math.sqrt(diff[0]2 + diff[1]2 + diff[2]2) - r def sdoctahedron(p, s): """Signed distance to a regular octahedron of size s.""" return (abs(p[0]) + abs(p[1]) + abs(p[2]) - s) / math.sqrt(3) def sdtetrahedron(p): """Signed distance to a regular tetrahedron centered at origin.""" md = max(-p[0]-p[1]-p[2], p[0]+p[1]-p[2], -p[0]+p[1]+p[2], p[0]-p[1]+p[2]) return md / math.sqrt(3) Computes the exact Euclidean signed distance to an axis-aligned box. Sets itself apart by handling 3D volumes with sharp corners correctly, unlike cheaper half-space intersections. Computes distance to an infinite plane. Cheaper than curved primitives, ideal for ground planes and CSG boundaries. Computes distance to a sphere. The fundamental building block for ray marching, enabling adaptive step sizes. Supports anisotropic scaling. Provides smooth, analytic curvature, unlike the Box SDF. Represents smooth, rounded tubular geometry. Distinguished from Sphere SDF by its linear axis and from Box SDF by cylindrical symmetry. Models a partial circular path (tube along an arc). Differs from Sphere SDF by modeling a partial path and from Capsule SDF by using a curved axis. A Signed Distance Function for a Rhombic Triacontahedron crystal shape, constructed by folding 3D space using specific magic numbers and directions multiple times. Magic Numbers: c = \cos(\pi/5), s = \sqrt{0.75 - c^2}. Magic Direction: n = (-0.5, -c, s). Steps: 1. p = |p|. 2. Fold along n: p \leftarrow p - 2 \cdot \min(0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 3. p{xy} = |p{xy}|. 4. Fold along n: p \leftarrow p - 2 \cdot \min(0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 5. p{xy} = |p{xy}|. 6. Fold along n: p \leftarrow p - 2 \cdot \min(0, p \cdot n) \cdot n. 7. Return pz - 1. A complex primitive constructed using radii ra=5.0, rb=2.0, d=6.0, offset (0,0,0), and rotation rotateX(0.5) \cdot rotateY(1.5 + \sin(t/7.0)). A structure used to represent visibility by encoding the signed distance to the boundary of the occluded region in the sphere. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. The cost is dominated by a few arithmetic operations and square roots. Memory Complexity: O(1) per primitive. No mesh data or BVH structures are needed for the primitive itself. Measured Performance: Exact and efficient, free of numerical noise for standard shapes. Scaling: Performance is independent of resolution, unlike rasterized meshes. Strengths: Resolution-independent, easy to transform, differentiable, compact representation. Limitations: Limited to simple geometric shapes. Complex scenes require many primitives or CSG operations, which can increase evaluation cost. When to Use: Simple geometric scenes, procedural modeling, ray marching. When Not to Use: Highly complex organic geometry best represented by meshes or voxels. SDF Primitives were popularized by Inigo Quilez in his articles on distance functions. They are a core component of ray marching techniques, which were adapted from sphere tracing. The use of SDFs for constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations (union, intersection, difference) is a standard technique in procedural modeling. skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Sphere-Tracing-PyTorch3D, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) AustinGoodman/non-linear-sphere-tracing, https://github.com/AustinGoodman/non-linear-sphere-tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, https://github.com/nopjia/WebGL-RayMarch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) ChadMcKinney/Dirac-Sea-Engine, https://github.com/ChadMcKinney/Dirac-Sea-Engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, https://github.com/arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) JamesRicher/TerminalSignedDistanceFieldRenderer, https://github.com/JamesRicher/TerminalSignedDistanceFieldRenderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) 0gecco/csRaymarching, https://github.com/0gecco/csRaymarching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) trimesh33/sdf, https://github.com/trimesh33/sdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) jk9g13/LaFortuna-SDF-Ray-marching, https://github.com/jk9g13/LaFortuna-SDF-Ray-marching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU Ray Marching Techniques, https://www.scribd.com/document/814069988/5-GPU-Ray-Marching, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions — GLSL in the..., https://www.mysimulator.uk/content/articles/ray-marching-sdf.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Show HN: Iridescent crystal with raymarching and signed distance fields, https://varun.ca/ray-march-sdf/, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) agill-dev-0/SDF-ray-marcher, https://github.com/agill-dev-0/SDF-ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Real-Time Ray Traced Voxel Global Illumination, https://doi.org/10.34626/0vdq-7m27, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Signed Box Distance Function
head: Box SDF, Box SDF v2, Rectangular (Axis-Aligned Box) SDF, SDF Box, SDF Cube, Signed Box, sdBox
body: The Signed Box Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean signed distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box centered at the origin. It distinguishes interior from exterior space by returning negative values inside the box and positive values outside. It sets itself apart from the Unsigned Box Distance Function by providing signed output and from the Plane Signed Distance Function by handling bounded 3D volumes with sharp corners rather than infinite half-spaces. Unlike the cheaper half-space intersection approximation, this method correctly calculates the distance to edges and corners. Inputs and Outputs: Input: p, a 3D point in space (vector). Input: b, the half-extents of the box (vector), defining the box as [-bx, bx] \times [-by, by] \times [-bz, bz]. Output: d, a scalar representing the signed distance. Data Structures: p: vec3 (x, y, z). b: vec3 (x, y, z). Steps: 1. Compute the difference vector di by subtracting the half-extents from the absolute coordinates of the point: di = |p| - b. This exploits symmetry to handle all octants uniformly. 2. Calculate the "inside distance" component res as the maximum of the components of di: res = \max(dix, \max(diy, diz)). 3. Check if the point is outside. If res > 0, the point is outside the box. In this case, calculate the Euclidean distance to the closest face, edge, or corner by taking the length of the positive components of di: res = \| \max(di, 0) \|. 4. If the point is inside (res \le 0), res remains the negative distance to the closest face. 5. Return res. Formula: d(p) = \begin{cases} \max(dix, \max(diy, diz)) & \text{if } \max(dix, \max(diy, diz)) \le 0 \\ \| \max(di, 0) \| & \text{if } \max(dix, \max(diy, diz)) > 0 \end{cases} where di = |p| - b. Where: |p| is the component-wise absolute value of p. \max(v) is the maximum component of vector v. \max(v, 0) is the component-wise maximum of v and the zero vector. \| \cdot \| is the Euclidean norm (L2 norm). Parameters: b: Half-extents. For a 1x1x1 box centered at the origin, b = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Underestimation (Version 1): An earlier version (Algorithm 3.5 in) returned \min(\max(|p|-b), \| \max(|p|-b, 0) \|). This underestimates the distance in corner regions, leading to smaller ray steps, slower convergence, and incorrect ambient occlusion (black dots/aliasing). Overestimation: Overestimating the distance can cause the ray to pass through the surface or inaccurately estimate the surface point position, negatively impacting ambient occlusion. Approximation: A cheaper approximation d = \max(|p-c| - s) (where s is side length) is not a true Euclidean distance for points outside corners and returns distance to the nearest face/edge rather than the vertex. It is sufficient for raymarching as a safe lower bound but lacks precision. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def signedboxdistance(p: Vec3, b: Vec3) -> float: # Step 1: Compute difference vector using symmetry dix = abs(p.x) - b.x diy = abs(p.y) - b.y diz = abs(p.z) - b.z # Step 2: Calculate inside distance (max component) res = max(dix, max(diy, diz)) # Step 3: If outside (res > 0), calculate Euclidean distance to surface if res > 0: posx = max(dix, 0.0) posy = max(diy, 0.0) posz = max(diz, 0.0) res = sqrt(posx2 + posy2 + posz2) # Step 4: If inside (res <= 0), res is already the negative distance return res Computes the Euclidean distance to the box surface, returning only non-negative values. Use when interior/exterior distinction is not needed. Computes distance to a box with rounded edges/corners. Use for smooth geometric transitions. The 2D analog of the Signed Box Distance Function. Use for planar rectangles. Computes distance to a 2D oriented box (segment-based). Use for 2D shapes with specific orientation. Time Complexity: O(1). The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations, absolute values, and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are required. Performance: Extremely fast, suitable for real-time ray marching. The exact version (Version 2) is slightly more expensive than the approximation due to the square root, but necessary for correct AO. Strengths: Exact Euclidean distance; handles inside/outside correctly; robust for sphere tracing. Limitations: The square root operation is more expensive than simple max/min. The approximation is faster but inaccurate for AO. When to use: Standard primitive for ray marching axis-aligned boxes. When not to use: When performance is critical and AO is not required (use approximation); when rounded edges are needed (use Box with Edge Rounding).
