name: Unsigned Box Distance Function
head: Unsigned Box, udBox
body: The Unsigned Box Distance Function computes the Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of an axis-aligned box centered at the origin, returning only non-negative values regardless of whether the point lies inside or outside the volume. Unlike its sibling, the Signed Box Distance Function, which distinguishes interior from exterior space, this method treats the box as a solid boundary where internal points are measured by their distance to the nearest face. Inputs and outputs: Input: p (vec3), the query point in 3D space. Input: b (vec3), the half-extents of the box along the X, Y, and Z axes. The box is centered at (0,0,0) and spans [-bx, bx] \times [-by, by] \times [-bz, bz]. Output: d (float), the unsigned Euclidean distance from p to the box surface. Data structures: No complex data structures are required. The function operates on standard 3D vectors. Formula: The distance is calculated using the following formula: d = \|\max(|p| - b, 0)\| Where: |p| denotes the component-wise absolute value of vector p, i.e., (|px|, |py|, |pz|). \max(v, 0) denotes the component-wise maximum of vector v and the scalar 0, i.e., (\max(vx, 0), \max(vy, 0), \max(vz, 0)). \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm (length) of the resulting vector. Step-by-step derivation: 1. Compute the absolute coordinates of the point: q = |p|. 2. Subtract the box half-extents: r = q - b. 3. Clamp negative values to zero: s = \max(r, 0). This step effectively ignores the interior of the box, treating any negative distance (interior) as zero distance to the surface. 4. Compute the Euclidean length of the remaining vector: d = \sqrt{sx^2 + sy^2 + sz^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def udBox(px, py, pz, bx, by, bz): """ Computes the unsigned distance from point p to an axis-aligned box centered at the origin with half-extents b. Args: px, py, pz: Query point coordinates bx, by, bz: Box half-extents Returns: Non-negative Euclidean distance to the box surface. """ # Step 1: Component-wise absolute value of p absx = abs(px) absy = abs(py) absz = abs(pz) # Step 2: Subtract half-extents diffx = absx - bx diffy = absy - by diffz = absz - bz # Step 3: Component-wise max with 0 (clamp negatives to zero) clampedx = max(diffx, 0.0) clampedy = max(diffy, 0.0) clampedz = max(diffz, 0.0) # Step 4: Euclidean norm (length) distance = (clampedx2 + clampedy2 + clampedz2)0.5 return distance Parameters and typical values: b: Must be positive. If any component is zero, the box degenerates into a plane, line, or point. p: Any real-valued 3D coordinate. Edge cases and pitfalls: Inside the box: If the point is strictly inside the box, the intermediate diff vector will have negative components. The clamping step sets these to 0. If the point is inside, the distance returned is the distance to the nearest face (if only one component is negative) or 0 (if the point is strictly inside all boundaries, though the formula \max(|p|-b, 0) yields a vector of zeros only if |p| \le b component-wise, resulting in distance 0). The formula provided returns 0 if the point is inside the box volume because \max(|pi| - bi, 0) = 0 for all i, leading to a zero vector and thus distance 0. Precision: Near the box edges and corners, the function is continuous but not differentiable. Floating-point precision issues may arise when |pi| \approx bi. Degenerate input: If b contains negative values, the geometric interpretation is invalid. Evaluates the signed distance from a point to an axis-aligned cuboid, handling both outside and inside distances. It transforms the point using the cuboid's 4x4 matrix, calculates distances to faces, and combines outside and inside distance components. The cuboid struct layout is: transform (Mat4, 64 bytes), dimensions (Vec3, 12 bytes), padding (u32, 4 bytes), totaling 80 bytes with 16-byte alignment. Construction uses Cuboid::new(dimensions).translate(v).rotate(v). Time complexity: O(1). The calculation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations (absolute value, subtraction, comparison, square root). Memory complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are allocated. Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation, suitable for real-time ray marching and collision detection where interior/exterior distinction is not required. Limitations: Does not provide information about whether the point is inside or outside the volume. Not suitable for operations requiring signed distance properties (e.g., smooth unions, boolean operations with SDFs). The Unsigned Box Distance Function is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering, often used in GLSL-based ray marchers. It is part of the collection of SDF primitives popularized by the glsl-sdf-primitives library. While the signed variant is more common in constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations, the unsigned variant is useful for simple boundary checks or when the interior is treated as empty space. marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, https://github.com/unfinishedprogram/ray-marcher, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Box with Edge Rounding SDF
head: Rounded Box SDF, SDF Primitive: Box with Edge Rounding, sdBoxRounded
body: Computes the signed distance to an axis-aligned box with rounded edges and corners, defined by half-extents b and edge radius e. It extends the basic box distance by replacing sharp corners with spherical fillets, allowing for smooth geometric transitions in ray marching. It differs from the Unsigned Box Distance Function by providing signed interior/exterior information and from the Rectangle Signed Distance Function by supporting 3D volumes with uniform edge rounding rather than planar rectangles. Inputs: p: Query point (vec3). b: Half-extents of the box (vec3). e: Edge/corner rounding radius (float). Outputs: Signed distance value (float). Negative inside, positive outside, zero on surface. Data Structures: Standard 3D vector types for p and b. Scalar float for e. Steps: 1. Compute d = |p| - b. 2. Compute q = \max(d, 0). 3. Compute m = \max(dx, \max(dy, dz)). 4. Return \|q\| + \min(m, 0) - e. Formula: The signed distance is calculated by projecting the query point onto the box's exterior, measuring the distance to the closest face/edge/corner, and subtracting the rounding radius. \text{sd} = \| \max(|p| - b, 0) \| + \min(\max(|p| - b)x, \max(|p| - b)y, \max(|p| - b)z) - e where | \cdot | is component-wise absolute value, \max(\cdot) applies the maximum operator to each component or across components, \| \cdot \| is the Euclidean length, and e is the rounding radius. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdboxrounded(p, b, e): # p: vec3, b: vec3, e: float d = abs(p) - b q = max(d, 0.0) m = max(d.x, max(d.y, d.z)) return length(q) + min(m, 0.0) - e Parameters: e: Edge radius. Must satisfy 0 \le e \le \min(bx, by, bz). Edge Cases: e = 0: Reduces to the standard Signed Box Distance Function. e = \min(b): The box becomes a sphere with radius \min(b) if bx=by=bz, or a capsule-like shape otherwise. Precision issues near the boundaries between face, edge, and corner regions. Signed distance to a 2D rounded box with corner radius r. Formula: \text{box2d}(p, b - r) - r. Implementation: pub fn roundedbox2d(p: Vec2, b: Vec2, r: f32) -> f32 { box2d(p, b - Vec2::splat(r)) - r }. Time Complexity: O(1) per query. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Smooth geometry, efficient ray marching, no need for mesh tessellation. Limitations: Rounding radius must be uniform. When to use: When smooth, rounded boxes are required in ray marching. When not to use: When sharp corners are needed (use standard box) or when non-uniform rounding is required. name: Rectangle Signed Distance Function
head: 2D Rectangle SDF, sdRect
body: Computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the boundary of an axis-aligned rectangle centered at the origin. It is the 2D analog of the Signed Box Distance Function. Inputs: p: Query point in 2D space. hsize: Half-extents of the rectangle along the x and y axes. Outputs: d: Signed distance. Data Structures: Tuples or lists of two floating-point numbers for p and hsize. Steps: 1. Calculate the displacement vector dv from the rectangle's boundary: dvx = |px| - hsizex, \quad dvy = |py| - hsizey where |px| and |py| apply the absolute value component-wise. 2. Calculate the exterior distance using the positive components of dv: outsideDistance = \sqrt{\max(dvx, 0)^2 + \max(dvy, 0)^2} where \max(dv, 0) applies the maximum operator to each component with 0, and \|\cdot\| is the Euclidean length. 3. Calculate the interior distance using the closest edge: insideDistance = \min(\max(dvx, dvy), 0) This captures the distance to the closest edge when the point is inside the rectangle. 4. Return the sum: d = outsideDistance + insideDistance Formula: d = \|\max(dv, 0)\| + \min(\max(dvx, dvy), 0) where dv = |p| - hsize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdRect(p, hsize): dvx = abs(p[0]) - hsize[0] dvy = abs(p[1]) - hsize[1] posx = dvx if dvx > 0.0 else 0.0 posy = dvy if dvy > 0.0 else 0.0 outsidedist = (posx2 + posy2)0.5 insidedist = min(max(dvx, dvy), 0.0) return outsidedist + insidedist Parameters: hsize: Typical values depend on scene scale. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Precision: Near the boundary, floating-point precision may cause jitter. Clamping or epsilon checks are often used in ray marching loops to prevent infinite loops or z-fighting. Degenerate Input: If hsize contains zero or negative values, the geometry is invalid or degenerate. Not given in the sources. A 3D extension for a cube centered at the origin with width, height, and length equal to 2.0 (half-extents of 1.0). Definition: d = \|\max(d, 0)\| + \min(\max(dx, \max(dy, dz)), 0) where d = |p| - (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). Code: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cubeSDF(p): dx = abs(p[0]) - 1.0 dy = abs(p[1]) - 1.0 dz = abs(p[2]) - 1.0 posx = dx if dx > 0.0 else 0.0 posy = dy if dy > 0.0 else 0.0 posz = dz if dz > 0.0 else 0.0 outsidedist = (posx2 + posy2 + posz2)0.5 insidedist = min(max(dx, max(dy, dz)), 0.0) return outsidedist + insidedist Not given in the sources. name: Oriented Box2D SDF
head: Oriented Box SDF, Rotated Box2D SDF
body: Computes the signed Euclidean distance from a 2D point to a line segment of arbitrary length and thickness, effectively representing a 2D box with rounded corners oriented along the segment axis. It differs from the Unsigned Box Distance Function by providing signed output and from the Signed Box Distance Function by operating in 2D with a specific segment-based orientation rather than a general 3D axis-aligned or oriented box. It serves as a primitive for constructing 2D shapes in ray marching or implicit modeling. Inputs: Point p \in \mathbb{R}^2. Segment endpoints a, b \in \mathbb{R}^2. Full thickness th \in \mathbb{R} (width of the box perpendicular to the segment). Outputs: Signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. Data Structures: Vectors are 2D floats. No complex packing required. Steps: 1. Calculate segment length l = \|b - a\|. 2. Edge Case: If l \le 10^{-6}, the segment is degenerate. Return the distance to a circle centered at a with radius th \cdot 0.5. d = \text{circle}(p - a, th \cdot 0.5) Where \text{circle}(v, r) = \|v\| - r. 3. Calculate unit direction vector d{vec} = (b - a) / l. 4. Calculate center of segment c = (a + b) \cdot 0.5. 5. Calculate vector from center to point q = p - c. 6. Rotate q into the local frame aligned with d{vec}. The local x-axis aligns with the segment, and the y-axis is perpendicular. local.x = d{vec}.x \cdot q.x + d{vec}.y \cdot q.y local.y = -d{vec}.y \cdot q.x + d{vec}.y \cdot q.y Note: The source specifies local.y = -d.y q.x + d.x q.y. This is a 90-degree rotation. 7. Calculate half-extents h = (l \cdot 0.5, th \cdot 0.5). 8. Compute the 2D box distance using the box2d function: d = \text{box2d}(local, h) Where \text{box2d}(v, h) = \|\max(v, 0)\| + \min(\max(vx, vy), 0). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def orientedbox2dsdf(p, a, b, th): # Step 1: Segment length diff = b - a l = length(diff) # Step 2: Degenerate case if l <= 1e-6: return length(p - a) - (th 0.5) # Step 3: Direction dvec = diff / l # Step 4 & 5: Center and relative vector center = (a + b) 0.5 q = p - center # Step 6: Rotate into local frame # local.x is projection onto segment direction # local.y is projection onto perpendicular direction localx = dvec.x q.x + dvec.y q.y localy = -dvec.y q.x + dvec.x q.y # Step 7: Half extents hx = l 0.5 hy = th 0.5 # Step 8: Box distance # max(v, 0) applies max component-wise dx = max(localx, 0.0) dy = max(localy, 0.0) dist = length([dx, dy]) # min(max(vx, vy), 0) mincomponent = min(max(localx, localy), 0.0) return dist + mincomponent Parameters: th: Typical values depend on scene scale. Must be positive. 1e-6: Threshold for degenerate segment detection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Segment: If a \approx b, the direction vector is undefined. The method falls back to a circle. Precision: Division by small l causes instability. The threshold 10^{-6} mitigates this. Thickness: If th is zero, the shape becomes a line segment. The distance function still works but represents a 1D object in 2D space. A variant representing a glass panel with variable thickness and surface perturbations. It constructs an SDF by deforming an axis-aligned box SDF using elevation profiles f and g for the front and back faces. The thickness t(\mathbf{x}) is defined as t + f(\mathbf{x}x, \mathbf{x}y) for \mathbf{x}z > 0 and t + g(\mathbf{x}x, \mathbf{x}y) otherwise, where f and g are differentiable functions (e.g., procedural noise). This allows modeling hand-blown glass with bubbles and surface irregularities. However, replacing t with t(\mathbf{x}) in the standard box SDF definition creates a discontinuity around xz = 0 and inaccurate distance evaluation near the center plane. Time Complexity: O(1). Constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Efficient primitive for 2D ray marching; handles arbitrary orientation and thickness; robust to degenerate inputs. Limitations: Only applicable in 2D; assumes uniform thickness along the segment; not suitable for complex 3D box orientations directly (requires 3D extension). When to use: When rendering 2D shapes with rounded corners defined by a central spine or segment. When not to use: For 3D boxes or non-uniform thickness profiles. The Oriented Box2D SDF is derived from computational geometry libraries for signed distance functions, specifically documented in the sdf-math-rs repository. It is used in procedural generation and ray marching of 2D implicit surfaces. The underlying box distance formula \|\max(\mathbf{q}, 0)\| + \min(\max(\mathbf{q}x, \mathbf{q}y), 0) is a standard definition for 2D box SDFs, often attributed to Inigo Quilez. name: Plane Signed Distance Function
head: Plane SDF, Plane distance, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Plane, Signed Plane, sdPlane
body: The Plane Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to an infinite plane defined by a normal vector and an offset. It serves as a fundamental building block in constructive solid geometry (CSG) and ray marching, providing a differentiable, closed-form distance metric that is computationally cheaper than curved primitives. Unlike the Sphere SDF which measures radial deviation, the Plane SDF measures linear deviation along a single axis, making it ideal for defining ground planes, clipping boundaries, or combining with other primitives via min/max operators. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and plane definition parameters. Output: A scalar d \in \mathbb{R} representing the signed distance. d < 0 indicates the point is on the side opposite to the normal (inside/negative half-space), d > 0 indicates the point is on the normal side (outside/positive half-space), and d = 0 lies on the plane. Data Structures: The plane is defined by two common parameterizations, both requiring a unit normal vector: 1. Normal-Offset Form: A unit normal vector \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a scalar offset h \in \mathbb{R}. The plane equation is \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{n} + h = 0. 2. Point-Normal Form: A unit normal vector \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a point \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^3 lying on the plane. The offset is derived as h = -\mathbf{r} \cdot \mathbf{n}. Formulas: The signed distance d is calculated as the projection of the vector from the plane to the point onto the normal. Using Normal-Offset form: d = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + h Using Point-Normal form: d = (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{r}) \cdot \mathbf{n} Note: Some sources define the offset sign differently. Hart defines f(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x} \cdot \mathbf{n} - h, where h is the distance from the origin along \mathbf{n}. This is equivalent to the offset form if h{\text{offset}} = -h{\text{Hart}}. The implementation below uses the standard GLSL convention where d = \mathbf{p} \cdot \mathbf{n} + h. Parameters: \mathbf{n}: Unit normal vector. Must be normalized (\|\mathbf{n}\| = 1). h: Offset from the origin. \mathbf{r}: A point on the plane (alternative to h). Pitfalls: Normalization: The normal vector \mathbf{n} must be normalized. If \mathbf{n} is not unit length, the result is scaled by \|\mathbf{n}\|, producing incorrect distances. Sign Convention: The sign of the distance depends on the direction of \mathbf{n}. Ensure consistency with the rest of the scene's SDF composition (e.g., CSG unions/intersections). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdplane(p, n, h): """Computes the signed distance from point p to a plane defined by unit normal n and offset h.""" return p[0] n[0] + p[1] n[1] + p[2] n[2] + h def sdplanefrompoint(p, n, r): """Computes the signed distance from point p to a plane defined by unit normal n and point r on the plane.""" return (p[0] - r[0]) n[0] + (p[1] - r[1]) n[1] + (p[2] - r[2]) n[2] def raymarchplane(o, d, n, h, maxt=100.0, eps=1e-4): """Ray marches along direction d from origin o using the plane SDF.""" t = 0.0 # Initialize step distance for in range(100): # Fixed iteration limit p = (o[0] + d[0] t, o[1] + d[1] t, o[2] + d[2] t) dist = sdplane(p, n, h) if abs(dist) < eps: # Convergence check return t, p if t + dist > maxt: # Boundary check return maxt, None t += dist # Advance ray return t, None Extends the basic SDF by explicitly exposing the distance parameter and shortest distance vector calculation to support iterative constraint solving in dual contouring algorithms. Time Complexity: O(1). Requires 3 multiplications and 2 additions (dot product + offset). Memory Complexity: O(1). Stores only the normal vector (3 floats) and offset (1 float), or normal and point (6 floats). Strengths: Exact, differentiable, and extremely fast. Ideal for infinite boundaries and ground planes. Limitations: Represents only infinite planes. Cannot model finite planar patches (like triangles) without additional logic (e.g., bounding box checks or combining with other primitives). When to use: Defining ground planes, clipping volumes, or as a component in CSG operations. When not to use: When a finite planar surface is required (use Triangle SDF or mesh-based methods). The Plane SDF is one of the basic primitives in the repertoire of analytic distance functions used in ray marching. It appears in foundational works on implicit surfaces and sphere tracing. Hart cites it as a standard primitive for defining ground planes in ray marching scenes. The GLSL implementation sdPlane provides the normal-offset formulation commonly used in real-time graphics. The formulation is consistent with the geometric definition of distance from a point to a hyperplane in Euclidean space. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, https://github.com/zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GPU Ray Marching of Distance Fields, https://www2.compute.dtu.dk/pubdb/edoc/imm6392.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, http://graphics.cs.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/zeno.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Plane Representation for Dual Contouring
head: Plane Class for Dual Contouring, Plane Constraint Representation, Plane Representation
body: The Plane Representation for Dual Contouring is a geometric data structure used to define linear constraints for locating feature points in dual contouring algorithms. It represents a plane via a unit normal vector and a scalar distance from the origin, enabling efficient signed distance queries. It differs from the parent Plane Signed Distance Function by explicitly exposing the distance parameter and shortest distance vector calculation as part of its interface for iterative constraint solving. Inputs and Outputs Input: A point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and an unnormalized normal vector \mathbf{n}{\text{in}} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for construction; a query point \mathbf{q} \in \mathbb{R}^3 for distance evaluation. Output: A signed distance scalar and a shortest distance vector for a given query point. Data Structures The representation consists of a single class or struct with two fields: normal: A Vector3 representing the unit normal \mathbf{n}, guaranteed to be normalized (\|\mathbf{n}\| = 1). distance: A float representing the scalar d in the plane equation \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Numbered Steps 1. Construction from Point and Normal: a. Normalize the input normal: \mathbf{n} = \frac{\mathbf{n}{\text{in}}}{\|\mathbf{n}{\text{in}}\|}. b. Calculate the distance parameter using the dot product: d = -\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p}. c. Store \mathbf{n} and d in the structure. 2. Signed Distance Query: a. Compute the signed distance: d{\text{signed}} = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{q} + d. b. Return d{\text{signed}}. 3. Shortest Distance Vector: a. Compute the signed distance d{\text{signed}} using Step 2. b. Compute the vector from the point to the plane: \mathbf{v} = d{\text{signed}} \cdot \mathbf{n}. c. Return \mathbf{v}. Formulas Plane Equation: \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{x} + d = 0. Distance Parameter: d = -\mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{p}. Signed Distance: D(\mathbf{q}) = \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{q} + d. Shortest Vector: \mathbf{v} = D(\mathbf{q}) \mathbf{n}. Parameters Normalization: The normal vector must be normalized before storing. Iterative Solving Context: In dual contouring, these planes are used to iteratively move a feature point. A typical step size factor is ~0.7 along the resultant average vector to stabilize convergence. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Zero Normal: Not given in the sources. Precision: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Plane: def init(self, point: Vector3, normal: Vector3): self.normal = normal.normalize() self.distance = -self.normal.dot(point) def signeddistance(self, point: Vector3) -> float: return self.normal.dot(point) + self.distance def shortestdistancevector(self, point: Vector3) -> Vector3: dist = self.signeddistance(point) return self.normal dist Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. name: Sphere Signed Distance Function
head: Sphere SDF, SDF Sphere, Sphere SDF Primitive, SDF Sphere Primitive, Signed Distance Function Sphere, Signed Distance Field (SDF) Sphere
body: The Sphere Signed Distance Function (SDF) computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point in 3D space to the surface of a sphere, returning a negative value if the point is inside and a positive value if outside. It serves as the fundamental building block for distance-field ray marching, enabling adaptive step sizes that guarantee surface intersection without overshooting when the step size equals the computed distance. It is the 3D analog of the Circle SDF. Input: A query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, a sphere center c \in \mathbb{R}^3, and a sphere radius r \in \mathbb{R}{\ge 0}. Optionally, a transformation matrix M if the sphere is defined in a local coordinate system. Output: A scalar signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. d < 0: Point is inside the sphere. d = 0: Point is on the surface. d > 0: Point is outside the sphere. The sphere is defined by a center vector and a scalar radius. In Rust implementations, the sphere is packed into a struct with a 4x4 transform matrix (64 bytes), a radius (4 bytes), and padding (12 bytes), totaling 80 bytes aligned to 16 bytes. Sphere Struct (Rust/Layout) transform: Mat4 (64 bytes). radius: f32 (4 bytes). padding: [u32; 3] (12 bytes). Total Size: 80 bytes, #[repr(C, align(16))]. In CPU or shader implementations, the center c and radius r are passed as function arguments or uniform variables. The signed distance d(p) from a point p to a sphere with center c and radius r is: d(p) = \| p - c \| - r Where \| \cdot \| denotes the Euclidean norm (L2 norm). If the point p is given in a local coordinate system and the sphere is defined by a transformation matrix M (where M transforms local space to world space), the point is first transformed: p{world} = M \cdot \begin{bmatrix} px \\ py \\ pz \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Then the distance is computed using p{world} and the sphere's world-space center and radius. Note that if M includes non-uniform scaling, the resulting function is no longer a true Euclidean SDF. Center (c): The 3D coordinates of the sphere's center. In learnable models (e.g., NeRFs), this is a trainable parameter. Radius (r): The radius of the sphere. Default is often 1.0 or 0.5 in examples. In learnable models, this is also a trainable parameter. Transformation Matrix (M): A 4x4 matrix used to position, rotate, and scale the sphere in world space. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def spheresdf(p: tuple, center: tuple, radius: float) -> float: """Computes the signed distance from point p to a sphere defined by center and radius.""" dx = p[0] - center[0] dy = p[1] - center[1] dz = p[2] - center[2] disttocenter = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) return disttocenter - radius def spheresdftransformed(p: tuple, transformmatrix: list, centerlocal: tuple, radius: float) -> float: """Computes SDF for a sphere defined in local space, transformed by a 4x4 matrix.""" px, py, pz = p w = 1.0 M = transformmatrix wx = M[0][0]px + M[1][0]py + M[2][0]pz + M[3][0]w wy = M[0][1]px + M[1][1]py + M[2][1]pz + M[3][1]w wz = M[0][2]px + M[1][2]py + M[2][2]pz + M[3][2]w cx = M[0][0]centerlocal[0] + M[1][0]centerlocal[1] + M[2][0]centerlocal[2] + M[3][0]w cy = M[0][1]centerlocal[0] + M[1][1]centerlocal[1] + M[2][1]centerlocal[2] + M[3][1]w cz = M[0][2]centerlocal[0] + M[1][2]centerlocal[1] + M[2][2]centerlocal[2] + M[3][2]w dx = wx - cx dy = wy - cy dz = wz - cz disttocenter = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) return disttocenter - radius def spheretrace(origin: tuple, direction: tuple, center: tuple, radius: float, maxsteps: int = 100, maxdist: float = 100.0, eps: float = 1e-4) -> float: """ Marches a ray using the Sphere SDF to find the closest surface intersection. Returns the distance along the ray, or float('inf') if no intersection is found. """ t = 0.0 for in range(maxsteps): p = (origin[0] + tdirection[0], origin[1] + tdirection[1], origin[2] + tdirection[2]) d = spheresdf(p, center, radius) if d < eps: return t if t > maxdist: return float('inf') t += max(d, eps) return float('inf') Precision: Near the surface (d \approx 0), floating-point precision errors can cause jitter in normal estimation or ray marching termination. Using a small epsilon threshold for termination is standard. Non-Uniform Scaling: If the transformation matrix M includes non-uniform scaling, the resulting function is no longer a true Euclidean SDF. The distance values will be distorted, leading to incorrect step sizes in ray marching. Zero Radius: A sphere with radius 0 is a point. The SDF returns the distance to the center point. This is valid but may cause infinite loops in ray marching if not handled (the ray might never "hit" a point unless it passes exactly through it). Definition Order: In some scripting languages (e.g., Fennel/Lua), the SDF function must be defined before the object constructor that uses it, due to top-down definition order. The Circle SDF computes the signed distance from a 2D query point to the perimeter of a circle. It is the 2D analog of the Sphere SDF. It returns negative values inside, positive outside, and zero on the boundary. It is used when rendering 2D scenes or cross-sections of 3D volumes. A Distance Estimator is a function that computes the minimum distance from a query point to any object in a scene, often returning the distance along with the identifier or color of the closest object. It initializes the minimum distance to a maximum draw distance (e.g., 1000) and iterates through scene primitives, updating the minimum if a closer object is found. This avoids recomputing color lookups for the endpoint later. While the Sphere SDF returns the distance to a single sphere, a Distance Estimator aggregates multiple SDFs (including the Sphere SDF) to find the global minimum. Time Complexity: O(1) per evaluation. It involves a constant number of arithmetic operations (subtractions, multiplications, one square root). Memory Complexity: O(1) if parameters are passed as arguments. O(1) if stored in a struct (80 bytes on GPU as per). Performance: Extremely fast. The square root operation is the most expensive part, but modern GPUs have dedicated hardware for length() or sqrt(). Strengths: Exactness: Provides the exact Euclidean distance, unlike grid-based SDFs which are approximations. Adaptive Stepping: Enables sphere tracing, where the ray step size is equal to the distance to the surface, guaranteeing no surface is missed and minimizing the number of evaluations. Normal Estimation: The gradient of the SDF provides the surface normal, which can be computed analytically or via finite differences. Limitations: No Non-Uniform Scaling: As noted, non-uniform scaling breaks the SDF property. Single Primitive: Only represents a sphere. Complex scenes require combining multiple SDFs using Boolean operations (Union, Intersection). When to Use: Ideal for ray marching simple geometric shapes, procedural modeling, and collision detection where exact distances are required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for highly complex, organic shapes where grid-based SDFs or mesh-based ray tracing are more appropriate. The Sphere SDF is one of the most basic and fundamental Signed Distance Functions, originating from the field of geometric modeling and ray marching. Inigo Quilez compiled a comprehensive list of distance functions for various primitives. The mathematical basis for sphere tracing using SDFs was established by T. A. Nylander in "Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces" (1999). It is used in neural implicit representations (e.g., NeRFs) as a learnable primitive. name: Circle Signed Distance Function
head: 2D Circle SDF, 2D Sphere SDF, Circle SDF, sdCircle
body: The Circle Signed Distance Function computes the signed distance from a 2D query point to the perimeter of a circle centered at the origin. It returns a negative value inside the circle, a positive value outside, and zero on the boundary. It serves as the 2D analog of the Sphere Signed Distance Function. Inputs: p: A 2D query point, represented as a vector (px, py). r: The radius of the circle, a scalar. Outputs: d: The signed distance from p to the circle boundary. Data Structures: Not given in the sources. Formula: The signed distance is calculated as the Euclidean norm of the query point minus the radius: d = \|p\| - r where \|p\| = \sqrt{px^2 + py^2}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdcircle(p: tuple, r: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance from point p to a circle of radius r centered at origin. Args: p: Tuple (x, y) representing the 2D query point. r: Float representing the radius of the circle. Returns: Float representing the signed distance. Negative if inside, positive if outside. """ return (p[0] 2 + p[1] 2) 0.5 - r Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sign Interpretation: A negative result indicates the point is inside the circle, zero indicates it is on the boundary, and a positive result indicates it is outside. Zero Radius: If r=0, the function returns the distance to the origin. This is mathematically valid but may cause degenerate behavior in ray marching if not handled. Negative Radius: The radius r should be non-negative. If a negative radius is passed, the sign of the distance will be inverted relative to the geometric expectation. Off-Center Circles: For circles not centered at the origin, the query point must be translated by the circle's center vector before evaluation. Time Complexity: O(1). Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Extremely fast evaluation; analytically exact distance. Limitations: Only applies to circles centered at the origin. When to use: Ideal for 2D ray marching and procedural texture generation. The Circle SDF is the 2D analog of the Sphere Signed Distance Function. Its implementation relies on the standard definition of Euclidean distance. erbenpeter/sdf, https://github.com/erbenpeter/sdf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ellipsoid Signed Distance Function
head: Ellipsoid SDF
body: Computes the signed distance from a 3D point to an ellipsoid defined by semi-axes radii, or to a 2D disk (a degenerate ellipsoid with one radius set to zero) for handling non-watertight surfaces like walls. It distinguishes itself from the Sphere Signed Distance Function by supporting anisotropic scaling, and from the Signed Box Distance Function by providing smooth, analytic curvature. Two variants exist: a fast approximation and a more accurate iterative-free formula. Inputs: Point p \in \mathbb{R}^3 in local ellipsoid coordinates. Radii vector r = (rx, ry, rz) \in \mathbb{R}^3{>0} (or rz=0 for a disk). Outputs: Signed distance d. Positive outside, negative inside. Data Structures: Vectors p, r are standard 3D floats. Steps: 1. Normalize the point by dividing by radii: p' = p / r. 2. Compute k1 = \|p'\|. 3. Compute k2 = \|p / (r \cdot r)\| (where r \cdot r is component-wise squaring). 4. Calculate distance: d = \frac{k1(k1 - 1.0)}{k2}. Parameters: rx, ry, rz: Semi-axes lengths. Typical values depend on scene scale. For a 2D disk, set rz = 0 and use the SDDF variant described in Background. Edge Cases: If ri = 0, the division is undefined. Use the 2D disk SDDF formulation instead. If k2 \approx 0 (point at origin), distance is 0. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ellipsoidsdf(p: Vec3, r: Vec3) -> float: # p: point in local space # r: semi-axes (rx, ry, rz) # Component-wise division pdivr = p / r # k1 = length(p / r) k1 = length(pdivr) # Component-wise squared radii rsq = r r # k2 = length(p / (r r)) pdivrsq = p / rsq k2 = length(pdivrsq) # Avoid division by zero if point is at origin if k2 == 0.0: return 0.0 # Formula: k1 (k1 - 1.0) / k2 d = k1 (k1 - 1.0) / k2 return d Alternative Approximation: A faster variant uses the minimum radius: d{approx} = (k1 - 1.0) \cdot \min(rx, ry, rz) This variant is noted as less robust than the iterative-free formula. A special case where rx=ry=rz. Use when isotropy is required. Use for axis-aligned rectangular volumes. The ellipsoid SDF is smoother but computationally heavier. Use for linear extrusions. The ellipsoid SDF is a single blob, not a line segment. Time Complexity: O(1) with a few multiplications, divisions, and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Analytic, differentiable, handles anisotropy. The accurate formula is exact for the ellipsoid shape. Limitations: The accurate formula can be numerically unstable if k2 is very small. The approximation is not a true SDF (gradient magnitude \neq 1). When to use: When anisotropic shapes are needed and analytical gradients are required for ray marching or optimization. The ellipsoid SDF is derived from the geometric property that an ellipsoid is a scaled sphere. The accurate formula d = \frac{k1(k1 - 1.0)}{k2} is attributed to Inigo Quilez. It is widely used in ray marching for soft shadows and reflections. The 2D disk variant is used in recent neural rendering approaches to handle non-watertight objects like curtains or walls by setting one radius to zero, resulting in a Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF). name: Capsule Signed Distance Function
head: 3D Capsule SDF, Capsule Rendering via Distance Check, Capsule SDF, Capsule3D SDF, Signed Capsule, sdCapsule
body: The Capsule Signed Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point in 3D space to the surface of a capsule, defined as a line segment with a constant radius. It represents smooth, rounded tubular geometry for ray marching and volume rendering without polygonal approximation. It is distinguished from the Sphere SDF by its linear axis and from the Box SDF by its cylindrical symmetry and hemispherical ends. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3, capsule endpoints a, b \in \mathbb{R}^3, radius r \in \mathbb{R}^+. Output: Signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}, where d < 0 indicates inside, d > 0 outside, and d = 0 on the surface. Data Structures: The evaluation requires only scalar and vector variables; no auxiliary data structures are needed. Parameters: p: The query point in 3D space. a, b: The start and end points of the capsule's central axis. Note that defines a and b as 2D vectors extended to 3D with a zero z-component. r: The radius of the capsule. Typical values depend on scene scale; hardcodes r=0.12. Algorithm: The capsule is the Minkowski sum of a line segment \overline{ab} and a sphere of radius r. The distance is the distance from p to the segment \overline{ab}, minus r. 1. Compute the vector representing the capsule axis: ba = b - a. 2. Compute the vector from the start point to the query point: pa = p - a. 3. Compute the squared length of the axis: len\sq = ba \cdot ba. 4. Handle degenerate case: If len\sq < \epsilon (where \epsilon is a small positive number, e.g., 10^{-12}), the capsule collapses to a sphere centered at a. Return length(pa) - r. 5. Compute the projection parameter h of pa onto ba, clamped to [0, 1]: h = \text{clamp}\left( \frac{pa \cdot ba}{len\sq}, 0.0, 1.0 \right). This h identifies the closest point on the infinite line passing through a and b that lies within the segment. 6. Compute the closest point on the segment: closest = a + ba \cdot h. 7. Compute the vector from the closest point to p: diff = p - closest = pa - ba \cdot h. 8. Return the distance: d = length(diff) - r. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdcapsule(p: Vec3, a: Vec3, b: Vec3, r: float) -> float: ba = b - a pa = p - a lensq = dot(ba, ba) # Guard for degenerate segment per if lensq < 1e-12: return length(pa) - r h = clamp(dot(pa, ba) / lensq, 0.0, 1.0) closest = a + ba h diff = p - closest return length(diff) - r Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Segment: If a = b, the division by len\sq causes NaN. A guard check for len\sq < \epsilon is required. Precision: For very long capsules, len\sq may overflow if not using double precision, though standard float32 handles typical scene scales. Axis Alignment: The formula is general for any orientation. A specialized version where the capsule is aligned with a coordinate axis (e.g., Y-axis) exists. A specialized version where the capsule is aligned with a coordinate axis (e.g., Y-axis). It sets itself apart from the general form by simplifying the projection step to a single coordinate clamp. Choose it when rendering static, axis-aligned tubes. See Axis-Aligned Capsule SDF. The 2D equivalent, computing distance to a line segment with rounded ends in a plane. It sets itself apart from the 3D version by operating in two dimensions for sprite-based or 2D volumetric effects. Choose it for 2D ray marching or procedural 2D geometry. See 2D Capsule SDF. Time Complexity: O(1). The calculation involves a constant number of vector operations (subtraction, dot product, length). Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are allocated. Performance: The primitive evaluation is extremely fast, making it suitable for real-time ray marching and volume rendering. Strengths: Exact distance, smooth normals (derivable via finite differences or analytical gradient), supports arbitrary orientation and position. Limitations: Cannot represent non-uniform thickness (tapered capsules require more complex functions). The Capsule SDF is a standard primitive in Signed Distance Field rendering, implemented in GLSL and Rust. It is widely used in ray marching demos, procedural geometry generation, and collision detection in real-time graphics. The mathematical formulation relies on the property that the distance to a capsule is the distance to its central segment minus the radius. name: Arc Signed Distance Function
head: SDF Arc, sdArc
body: Computes the signed distance from a 3D point to a tube of radius arctuberadius running along a circular arc defined by a center, orientation, aperture, and radii ra and rb. It differs from the Sphere Signed Distance Function by modeling a partial circular path rather than a closed surface, and from the Capsule Signed Distance Function by using a curved (circular) axis instead of a linear segment. Inputs: Point p = (px, py, pz); Arc parameters: arccenter (C), arctuberadius (rt), orientationangle (\theta), apertureangle (\alpha), ra (Ra), rb (Rb). Precomputed constants: scacos (\cos \theta), scasin (\sin \theta), scbcos (\cos(\alpha/2)), scbsin (\sin(\alpha/2)). A global depth value is used for the z-coordinate of the arc plane. Outputs: Signed distance d. Data Structures: The Arc struct contains: vec3 arccenter: Center of the arc in 3D space. float arctuberadius: Radius of the tube. float orientationangle: Rotation of the arc plane around the Z-axis (degrees). float apertureangle: Total angular span of the arc (degrees). float scacos, float scasin: Precomputed \cos(\theta) and \sin(\theta). float scbcos, float scbsin: Precomputed \cos(\alpha/2) and \sin(\alpha/2). float ra: Radius of the circle defining the arc path. float rb: Radius of an inner circle (default 0.0f). Steps: 1. Construct position vector in the arc's local XY plane: pos = (px, py, \text{depth}). 2. Translate by arc center: pos \leftarrow pos - C. 3. Rotate by orientation angle \theta: x = posx \cos \theta - posy \sin \theta y = posx \sin \theta + posy \cos \theta posx = x, \quad posy = y 4. Symmetrize X: posx \leftarrow |posx|. 5. Compute intermediate value k: k = \begin{cases} posx \sin(\alpha/2) + posy \cos(\alpha/2) & \text{if } \cos(\alpha/2) posx > \sin(\alpha/2) posy \\ \sqrt{posx^2 + posy^2} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} 6. Compute project distance: d{proj} = \sqrt{posx^2 + posy^2 + Ra^2 - 2 Ra k} - Rb 7. Compute final distance: d = \sqrt{d{proj}^2 + pz^2} - rt Pitfalls: Angles must be converted from degrees to radians (\times \pi/180) before computing sine/cosine. The depth parameter is a global constant for the arc's Z-plane, not derived from pz. Precision issues may arise if Ra \approx 0 or if the point is far from the arc. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdarc(p: Vec3, arc: Arc, depth: float) -> float: # 1. Construct position vector pos = Vec3(p.x, p.y, depth) # 2. Translate by arc center pos = pos - arc.arccenter # 3. Rotate by orientation angle x = pos.x arc.scacos - pos.y arc.scasin y = pos.x arc.scasin + pos.y arc.scacos pos.x = x pos.y = y # 4. Take absolute value of x pos.x = abs(pos.x) # 5. Compute intermediate value k if arc.scbcos pos.x > arc.scbsin pos.y: k = pos.x arc.scbsin + pos.y arc.scbcos else: k = length(pos.x, pos.y) # 6. Compute project distance # Note: pos.length() in 2D is sqrt(pos.x^2 + pos.y^2) distsq = pos.x pos.x + pos.y pos.y projectdistance = sqrt(distsq + arc.ra arc.ra - 2.0 arc.ra k) - arc.rb # 7. Compute final distance return sqrt(projectdistance projectdistance + p.z p.z) - arc.arctuberadius Computes the exact arc length l(a, \rho0) for a quadratic Gaussian Splatting primitive using the integral l(a, \rho0) = \int \sqrt{1 + (2at)^2} dt. The solution is l(a, \rho0) = \frac{u\sqrt{1+u^2} + \ln(u + \sqrt{1+u^2})}{4a} where u = 2at. This is used for high-quality surface reconstruction but is not part of the standard SDF distance calculation. Time Complexity: O(1) per point. Requires several trigonometric precomputations and basic arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) for the Arc struct. Strengths: Efficiently models curved tubular structures without voxelization. Limitations: Limited to specific circular arc geometries; requires precomputed trigonometric values. When to use: When rendering curved tubes or rings defined by a center, orientation, and aperture. When not: For linear tubes (use Capsule Signed Distance Function) or closed spheres (use Sphere Signed Distance Function). The Arc SDF is defined in the SDF-Sphere-Tracing repository by AlerianEmperor. It utilizes fast trigonometric approximations and SSE optimizations for performance. The geodesic arc length formula is derived in "Quadratic Gaussian Splatting" for second-order geometric primitives. name: Polyhedral Primitives
head: Polyhedral SDFs, Polyhedron Signed Distance Functions
body: Polyhedral primitives compute the exact Euclidean signed distance from a query point to the surface of convex polyhedra, enabling precise ray marching and collision detection for shapes with flat faces and sharp edges. They are distinguished from smooth primitives (like spheres) by their piecewise-linear geometry and from implicit surfaces by their reliance on symmetry folding or explicit face/edge projections to resolve the distance analytically. All primitives in this family adhere to a common computational framework: 1. Canonical Placement: Primitives are defined in a local coordinate system centered at the origin (0,0,0) and axis-aligned where applicable. 2. Transformation: To render a primitive at a different position, rotation, or scale, the query point p is transformed into the primitive's local space (inverse transformation) before evaluation, or the primitive parameters are adjusted accordingly. 3. body: Computes the exact signed distance from a query point to the surface of a regular octahedron centered at the origin. It solves the geometric query required for ray marching or collision detection involving octahedral primitives. It is distinguished from other polyhedral SDFs by its reliance on coordinate permutation to handle the octahedron's symmetry, reducing the problem to a single face evaluation. Inputs: p \in \mathbb{R}^3: The query point in local space. s \in \mathbb{R}: The size parameter. In the source implementation, this represents the distance from the center to the vertices along the axes (the "radius" of the octahedron). Outputs: d \in \mathbb{R}: The signed distance. Negative inside, positive outside, zero on the surface. Data Structures: Standard 3D vector p = (px, py, pz). Steps: 1. Symmetry Reduction: Compute p' = |p| = (|px|, |py|, |pz|). This folds the space into the first octant, exploiting the octahedron's symmetry. 2. Central Region Check: Calculate m = p'x + p'y + p'z - s. If 3 \cdot p'x < m, the point is closest to the face normal to the x-axis. Set q = p'. Else if 3 \cdot p'y < m, the point is closest to the face normal to the y-axis. Set q = (p'y, p'z, p'x) (permutation). Else if 3 \cdot p'z < m, the point is closest to the face normal to the z-axis. Set q = (p'z, p'x, p'y) (permutation). Else, the point is in the central region (closest to the origin relative to the face planes). Return d = m \cdot \tan(\pi/6). Note: \tan(\pi/6) \approx 0.57735027. 3. Face Distance Calculation: For the selected q = (qx, qy, qz): Calculate k = \text{clamp}(0.5 \cdot (qz - qy + s), 0, s). The distance to the face is the Euclidean norm of the vector from the query point to the closest point on the face plane within the face bounds: d = \sqrt{qx^2 + (qy - s + k)^2 + (qz - k)^2} Return d. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdoctahedron(p: list[float], s: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance to an octahedron of size s. p: [x, y, z] s: size (distance from center to vertex) """ # Step 1: Symmetry reduction px, py, pz = abs(p[0]), abs(p[1]), abs(p[2]) # Step 2: Central region check m = px + py + pz - s # Determine closest face via permutation # Note: The conditions 3p < m identify which coordinate is the "smallest" relative to the sum, # effectively identifying the closest face normal direction in the folded space. if 3.0 px < m: qx, qy, qz = px, py, pz elif 3.0 py < m: qx, qy, qz = py, pz, px elif 3.0 pz < m: qx, qy, qz = pz, px, py else: # Central region: closest to origin return m math.tan(math.pi / 6.0) # Step 3: Face distance # k is the projection onto the edge direction to find the closest point on the face k = max(0.0, min(s, 0.5 (qz - qy + s))) # Vector from q to the closest point on the face dx = qx dy = qy - s + k dz = qz - k return math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) Parameters: s: Typical values depend on scene scale. Must be positive. Edge Cases: s=0: The octahedron is a point. The function returns |px| + |py| + |pz| (L1 norm) if not in central region logic, but the central region logic dominates near origin. Specifically, if p=0, m=-s, returns -s \tan(\pi/6). Precision: The permutation logic relies on strict inequalities. Points exactly on the boundaries between regions (e.g., 3px = m) are handled by the elif chain, ensuring continuity. Computes the signed distance to an equilateral triangle with inscribed radius r. It transforms the query point into a canonical orientation, reflects it if necessary to handle symmetry, clamps to the triangle bounds, and returns the distance. It is chosen when 2D triangular primitives are needed in SDF workflows. Based on Inigo Quilez's exact function. Steps: 1. k = \sqrt{3.0}. 2. Transform p: px = |px| - r, py = py + r/k. 3. Limitations: Only applies to regular octahedra. Irregular octahedra require decomposition or approximation. name: Cone Signed Distance Function
head: Cone SDF, sdCone, Signed Cone, Signed Capped Cone, Exact Cone SDF, Signed Distance Function (SDF) for Cone
body: The Cone Signed Distance Function computes the exact Euclidean distance from a query point to the surface of a cone, defined by a base radius and height, with a sign indicating whether the point lies inside or outside the volume. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering or querying conical primitives in ray marching and implicit surface modeling without approximation errors associated with polygonal meshes. It is distinguished from the Segment Signed Distance Function by its continuous lateral surface and from Polyhedral Primitives by its smooth, non-polyhedral geometry. The method evaluates the distance to a cone aligned with the Y-axis. Two primary implementations exist in the literature: an "exact" geometric projection method that handles the base cap and side slope separately, and a simplified dot-product method often used for infinite or specific capped variants where the base cap is handled implicitly or the cone is defined by a slope vector. Input: Query point p \in \mathbb{R}^3. Parameters: Base radius r, height h. Output: Signed distance d \in \mathbb{R}. No complex data structures are required. The computation operates on scalar values and 2D/3D vectors. This implementation, derived from Inigo Quilez's work and implemented in Rust, computes the distance to the side slope and the base cap independently, then combines them. 1. Canonical Projection: Project the 3D point p into a 2D cross-section q in the plane containing the cone's axis (Y-axis) and the radial distance. q = (\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}, py) Let qx = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} and qy = py. 2. Define Geometry: Define the tip and base vertices in this 2D space. Tip: t = (0, 0) Base: b = (r, -h) Vector along the side slope: ba = b - t = (r, -h) 3. Distance to Side Slope: Compute the distance from q to the line segment connecting the tip and the base edge. Vector from tip to query: d1 = q - t = q Squared length of side slope: m2 = \|ba\|^2 = r^2 + h^2 Projection parameter u (clamped to segment): u = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{d1 \cdot ba}{m2}, 0, 1\right) Closest point on segment: c{side} = t + ba \cdot u Side distance: dist{side} = \|q - c{side}\| 4. Distance to Base Cap: Compute the distance from q to the base disk. Clamp the radial component of q to the base radius to find the closest point on the infinite plane of the base, then check if it's within the disk. Closest point on base plane within radius: c{cap} = (\text{clamp}(qx, 0, r), -h) Vector from q to this point: d3 = q - c{cap} Cap distance: dist{cap} = \|d3\| 5. Combine Distances: The unsigned distance is the minimum of the side and cap distances. dist = \min(dist{side}, dist{cap}) 6. Inside Test: Determine if the point is inside the cone. A point is inside if it is below the apex (qy \le 0), above the base (qy \ge -h), and radially within the cone's slope. The slope condition is derived from the line equation passing through (0,0) and (r, -h): x \cdot (-h) - y \cdot r = 0 \Rightarrow x \cdot h + y \cdot r = 0 (checking sign). inside = (qy \le 0) \land (qy \ge -h) \land (qx \cdot h + qy \cdot r \le 0) Note: The condition qx \cdot h + qy \cdot r \le 0 ensures the point is on the "inner" side of the slope line relative to the axis. 7. Return Signed Distance: d = \begin{cases} -dist & \text{if } inside \\ dist & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Some implementations use a normalized vector c to define the cone's orientation and slope, often treating it as an infinite cone or handling caps differently. 1. Projection: q = (\|p{xz}\|, py). 2. Vector Definition: Let c be a normalized 2D vector (cx, cz) representing the cone's axis and slope. For a cone opening along -Y, c might be defined relative to the geometry. 3. Distance Calculation: d1 = -py - cz d2 = \max(q \cdot c{xy}, py) d = \| \max((d1, d2), 0) \| + \min(\max(d1, d2), 0) Note: Sources and show variations. uses sdCone with a normalized vector c. uses a different algebraic form involving projections. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sdcone(p: tuple, r: float, h: float) -> float: """ Computes the signed distance to a capped cone. Cone apex at (0,0,0), base center at (0, -h, 0), base radius r. Axis aligned with Y. """ # 1. Project to 2D cross-section qx = math.sqrt(p[0]2 + p[2]2) qy = p[1] # 2. Define 2D points # Tip at (0, 0), Base edge at (r, -h) tipx, tipy = 0.0, 0.0 basex, basey = r, -h # 3. Distance to side slope segment # Vector ba from tip to base bax = basex - tipx bay = basey - tipy m2 = bax2 + bay2 # Vector d1 from tip to q d1x = qx - tipx d1y = qy - tipy # Projection u u = (d1x bax + d1y bay) / m2 u = max(0.0, min(1.0, u)) # Closest point on segment closestx = tipx + u bax closesty = tipy + u bay distside = math.sqrt((qx - closestx)2 + (qy - closesty)2) # 4. Distance to base cap # Clamp qx to [0, r] to find closest point on the base disk clampedqx = max(0.0, min(r, qx)) capclosestx = clampedqx capclosesty = basey distcap = math.sqrt((qx - capclosestx)2 + (qy - capclosesty)2) # 5. Minimum unsigned distance dist = min(distside, distcap) # 6. Inside test # Inside if: below apex (qy <= 0), above base (qy >= -h), # and inside the slope (qx h + qy r <= 0) inside = (qy <= 0.0) and (qy >= -h) and ((qx h + qy r) <= 0.0) # 7. Return signed distance if inside: return -dist else: return dist r: Base radius. Typical values depend on scene scale. h: Height of the cone. Degenerate Cone: If r=0 or h=0, the cone degenerates to a line segment or a disk. The formula may produce NaNs or incorrect distances if not guarded. handles r=0 implicitly via the clamp, but h=0 results in a flat disk where the "side" distance logic might fail if not careful with division by zero in m2 if r=h=0. Precision: The inside test relies on floating-point comparisons. Points very close to the surface may oscillate between inside and outside due to precision errors. It is often safer to use a small epsilon for the inside test boundary checks in ray marching to avoid z-fighting or incorrect shading. Axis Alignment: The standard implementation assumes the cone is aligned with the Y-axis. For arbitrary orientations, the point p must be transformed into the cone's local space using the inverse of the cone's transformation matrix before evaluation [Parent]. Time Complexity: O(1). The computation involves a fixed number of arithmetic operations, square roots, and comparisons. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures are needed. Strengths: Exact distance calculation allows for large step sizes in ray marching, improving performance. Smooth gradients (except at the base edge and apex) allow for accurate normal computation. Limitations: The function is not differentiable at the base edge (where the side slope meets the base cap) and at the apex. This can cause artifacts in normal-based shading or physics if not handled. When to use: When rendering conical objects with high precision is required, or when using the SDF for collision detection where exact boundaries matter. When not to use: If the cone is part of a complex mesh where polygonal approximation is sufficient and faster, or if the cone is extremely long and thin, where precision issues might arise. The exact signed distance function for a cone was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his article on distance functions. It is a fundamental primitive in the family of SDFs used for ray marching. The geometric derivation relies on projecting the 3D point onto the 2D plane containing the cone's axis and computing the distance to the line segment representing the cone's profile. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, https://github.com/tdhooper/glsl-marching-cubes, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, https://github.com/bhubbard/sdf-math-rs, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Sphere tracing: a geometric method for the antialiased ray tracing of implicit surfaces, http://graphics.cs.illinois.edu/sites/default/files/zeno.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Segment Signed Distance Function
head: Segment SDF, sdSegment, Distance to line segment
body: The Segment Signed Distance Function computes the Euclidean distance from a query point to a finite line segment defined by two endpoints. It solves the problem of determining proximity to 1D geometric primitives in 3D space, serving as the foundational building block for more complex shapes like capsules and tubes. It differs from infinite line distance functions by clamping the projection parameter to the segment bounds, ensuring the result is zero if the point lies on the segment and correctly handling points projecting outside the endpoints. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point p (vector), segment endpoints a and b (vectors). Output: Scalar signed distance d. Note: While the parent family defines signed distance with negative values inside, a line segment has zero volume. Standard implementations return the non-negative Euclidean distance. For signed operations (e.g., in CSG), the sign is often determined by an external orientation or treated as unsigned distance. Data Structures: Vectors p, a, b of dimension N (typically 2 or 3). Scalar intermediate values for projection parameter t or h. Steps: 1. Compute the segment vector: ab = b - a. 2. Compute the vector from the start point to the query point: ap = p - a. 3. Compute the squared length of the segment: len\sq = ab \cdot ab. 4. Handle degenerate segments: If len\sq is near zero (e.g., < 10^{-12}), the segment is a point. The closest point is a (or b). Return \|p - a\|. 5. Compute the projection parameter t (or h) of p onto the line defined by ab: t = \frac{ap \cdot ab}{len\sq} 6. Clamp t to the segment bounds [0, 1]: t{clamped} = \text{clamp}(t, 0.0, 1.0) 7. Compute the closest point on the segment: closest = a + ab \cdot t{clamped} 8. Return the Euclidean distance: d = \| p - closest \| Alternative Formula (Normalized): Some implementations normalize the direction vector first: 1. v = \frac{b - a}{\|b - a\|} 2. l = \text{clamp}(v \cdot (p - a), 0, \|b - a\|) 3. d = \| p - a - l \cdot v \| Parameters: p: Query point. a, b: Segment endpoints. Epsilon for degenerate check: Typically 10^{-12} or 10^{-8} depending on precision requirements. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Segment: If a = b, the denominator in step 4 becomes zero. Division by zero must be avoided by checking len\sq against a small epsilon. Precision: In floating-point arithmetic, checking for exact equality with zero is unsafe. Use epsilon comparisons for degenerate checks. Signedness: As a 1D object in 3D space, it has no interior. The "signed" aspect is often implicit or handled by the caller (e.g., in CSG operations) rather than the primitive itself returning negative values for "inside". Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdsegment(p, a, b): """ Computes the Euclidean distance from point p to the segment [a, b]. Args: p: Vector-like object with subtraction, dot product, and length. a: Start point of the segment. b: End point of the segment. Returns: float: Distance from p to the closest point on the segment. """ # 1. Segment vector ab = b - a # 2. Vector from start to query point ap = p - a # 3. Squared length of segment lensq = ab.dot(ab) # 4. Handle degenerate segment (point) if lensq < 1e-12: return p.length() # Distance from p to a (since a == b) # 5. Projection parameter t = ap.dot(ab) / lensq # 6. Clamp to segment bounds t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) # 7. Closest point closest = a + ab t # 8. Distance return (p - closest).length() Checks if a query point Q lies on the line segment between endpoints Pi and Pj. It calculates the distances d1 = \|Pi - Q\|, d2 = \|Pj - Q\|, and d3 = \|Pi - Pj\|. If d3 + \epsilon < d1 + d2, the point is not on the segment (triangle inequality violation due to floating point error or actual deviation); otherwise, it is considered on the segment. Uses an epsilon of 10^{-8}. Computes the closest point on a line segment [v0, v1] to a query point p. The result is guaranteed to lie on the closed segment by clamping the interpolation parameter t to [0, 1]. Supports generic vector types with arithmetic and dot product support. Computes the signed distance to a 2D capsule (stadium shape) defined by endpoints a and b and radius r. The formula is simply the segment distance minus the radius: d = \text{segment}(p, a, b) - r. Negative values indicate the point is inside the capsule. Time Complexity: O(1). Involves a constant number of vector subtractions, dot products, and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures required. Strengths: Extremely fast, numerically stable (with epsilon checks), and differentiable almost everywhere (gradient is the normalized vector from closest point to p, except at endpoints and the midpoint of degenerate cases). Limitations: Not signed in the traditional volumetric sense (no interior). Requires epsilon handling for degenerate cases. When to use: Ray marching for thin objects, collision detection, proximity queries. When not to use: When a true volumetric interior is required (use Cylinder or Capsule instead). The segment distance function is a fundamental primitive in Signed Distance Field (SDF) rendering, popularized by Inigo Quilez's online articles on distance functions. It is widely used in real-time graphics for rendering thin structures like wires, hair, and tubes without explicit mesh geometry. The algorithm is derived from basic vector projection geometry. name: Line Segment Distance
head: Point-to-Line Distance Calculation, Segment SDF, sdSegment
body: Computes the Euclidean distance from a query point p to a line segment defined by endpoints l0 and l1. It differs from infinite line distance by checking projection bounds before computing the final distance, ensuring the result correctly handles points outside the segment endpoints. This method is used as a signed distance field (SDF) primitive in ray marching. Inputs: p: Query point (vec3). l0: Segment start point (vec3). l1: Segment end point (vec3). Outputs: dist: Euclidean distance (float). Data Structures: None required; scalar/vector operations only. Steps: 1. Compute vector v = l1 - l0. 2. Compute vector w = p - l0. 3. Compute dot product c1 = dot(v, w). 4. If c1 <= 0.0, the closest point is l0. Return length(p - l0). 5. Compute dot product c2 = dot(v, v). 6. If c2 <= c1, the closest point is l1. Return length(p - l1). 7. Compute projection parameter b = c1 / c2. 8. Compute projection point pb = l0 + b v. 9. Return length(p - pb). Formulas: v = l1 - l0 w = p - l0 c1 = v · w c2 = v · v b = c1 / c2 pb = l0 + b v dist = ||p - pb|| Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def linesegmentdistance(p, l0, l1): v = l1 - l0 w = p - l0 c1 = dot(v, w) if c1 <= 0.0: return length(p - l0) c2 = dot(v, v) if c2 <= c1: return length(p - l1) b = c1 / c2 pb = l0 + b v return length(p - pb) Parameters: None. Edge Cases: Degenerate Segment: If l0 == l1, c2 is 0. Division by zero occurs in step 7. Guard against this by checking c2 < epsilon and returning length(p - l0) if true. Precision: Near-boundary cases may suffer from floating-point inaccuracies. Use a small epsilon for comparisons if high precision is required. Computes the distance from a point to an infinite line defined by two points. It differs from segment distance by omitting endpoint clamping, making it suitable for directional constraints or unbounded ray approximations. Choose it when the query geometry extends infinitely in both directions rather than being bounded by endpoints. Time Complexity: O(1). Fixed number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Fast, numerically stable for non-degenerate segments, easy to implement. Limitations: Degenerate segments (zero length) cause division by zero. Not suitable for infinite lines. When to use: SDF primitives for ray marching, collision detection with thin objects. name: Point-to-Line Distance
head: DistToLineSq, Distance to Line Squared, Point-to-Line Vector
body: Computes the vector from a point to the closest point on an infinite line, or the squared Euclidean distance to that line. It serves as the geometric core for Line Segment Distance, which clamps this result to segment bounds. Unlike segment distance, this method assumes an infinite extent, making it suitable for directional constraints or unbounded ray approximations. Inputs: p: The query point (3D vector). o: A point on the line (origin, 3D vector). d: The direction vector of the line (3D vector). Outputs: qp: The vector from the closest point on the line to p (3D vector). distSq: The squared Euclidean distance (scalar). Data Structures: Standard 3D floating-point vectors. No complex packing required. Steps: 1. Compute the projection scale factor scalefactor representing the position along the direction vector d closest to p: \text{scale\factor} = \frac{\mathbf{op} \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}} where \mathbf{op} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}. 2. Compute the closest point q on the line: \mathbf{q} = \mathbf{o} + \text{scale\factor} \times \mathbf{d}. 3. Compute the residual vector qp from the closest point to the query point: \mathbf{qp} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}. 4. Compute the squared distance: \text{distSq} = \|\mathbf{qp}\|^2. Formula: The squared distance is computed via orthogonal projection subtraction: \text{distSq} = \| (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}) - \frac{(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}) \cdot \mathbf{d}}{\mathbf{d} \cdot \mathbf{d}} \mathbf{d} \|^2 where \mathbf{op} = \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pointtolinedistance(p, o, d): # Vector from line origin to point op = p - o # Dot products dotopd = dot(op, d) dotdd = dot(d, d) # Guard against zero-length direction vector if dotdd == 0.0: # Direction is zero; closest point is the origin itself qp = p - o distsq = dot(qp, qp) return qp, distsq # Projection scale factor scalefactor = dotopd / dotdd # Closest point on the infinite line q = o + scalefactor d # Vector from closest point to original point qp = p - q # Squared Euclidean distance distsq = dot(qp, qp) return qp, distsq Parameters: d must be non-zero. If d is zero, the line is undefined. Implementation should handle dot(d, d) == 0 to avoid division by zero. Edge Cases: Zero Direction: If \mathbf{d} = \mathbf{0}, the line collapses to a single point \mathbf{o}. The distance is \|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{o}\|. Precision: For very long lines or small distances, floating-point cancellation may occur in \mathbf{p} - \mathbf{q}. Using the projection formula directly on the normalized direction may improve stability if \mathbf{d} is normalized beforehand. Time Complexity: O(1) constant time. Requires a few dot products and vector additions. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space. Strengths: Extremely fast; no branching required if direction is guaranteed non-zero. Limitations: Does not account for segment endpoints. Using this for a segment without clamping yields incorrect distances near the ends. This method is a fundamental linear algebra operation used in computer graphics, physics engines, and geometric modeling. wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, https://github.com/wanmeihuali/taichi3dgaussiansplatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Real-time BC6H compression on GPU, https://github.com/knarkowicz/GPURealTimeBC6H, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Higher Order Algebraic Signed Distance Fields
head: HOASDFs
body: Higher Order Algebraic Signed Distance Fields (HOASDFs) generalize traditional signed distance fields by approximating the distance function over a larger area using local Taylor approximations or least squares fit polynomials. Inputs: A set of sample points with associated distance values and, optionally, partial derivatives for Hermite interpolation. Outputs: A query function D(\mathbf{x}) that returns the signed distance and potentially geometric properties such as surface normals at any point \mathbf{x}. Data Structures: The field stores coefficients for polynomial approximations. Taylor Fields: Store the value and partial derivatives up to order n at each sample point. Least Squares Fields: Store coefficients of a polynomial fitted to a local neighborhood of samples. Steps: 1. Formulation: Formulate the sampling and reconstruction process as a function approximation problem combining local Taylor approximations. 2. Accuracy Characterization: Derive the error bound for arbitrary sampling topologies and interpolation schemes by noting that the error bound of a combination of Taylor approximations is closed under convex barycentric combination. 3. Extension to Least Squares: Extend the framework to least squares fit polynomial fields. 4. Implementation: For regular grids, utilize GPU filtering to implement highly efficient queries on both Taylor and least squares fields. 5. Hermite Interpolation: Store partial derivatives directly in the field data and use Hermite interpolation for queries, trading query time for higher accuracy. 6. Conversion: Convert traditional zero order signed distance fields to higher order representations using a general framework. 7. Optimization: Decrease filtering footprint size via simplicial interpolation schemes to balance performance and storage. Formulas: The Taylor expansion of the distance function D around a sample point \mathbf{s} up to order n is: D(\mathbf{x}) \approx D(\mathbf{s}) + \nabla D(\mathbf{s}) \cdot (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{s}) + \frac{1}{2} (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{s})^T \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{s}) (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{s}) + \dots where \nabla D(\mathbf{s}) is the gradient and \mathbf{H}(\mathbf{s}) is the Hessian matrix at \mathbf{s}. The final query result is computed as a convex barycentric combination of these local expansions. Parameters: Order (n): The degree of the Taylor approximations or polynomial fields used to represent the distance function. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Higher order expansions amplify floating-point errors near the surface; clamping or fallback to zero-order queries may be required. Boundaries: Sampling irregularities at domain edges break barycentric weight computation; padding or boundary-aware interpolation is needed. Degenerate Input: Collinear or coplanar sample points produce singular barycentric systems; fallback to inverse-distance weighting or grid-aligned queries is required. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def queryhoasdf(x, samples, order): # samples: list of dicts with keys 'pos', 'val', 'grad', 'hess' weights = computebarycentricweights(x, samples) result = 0.0 for i, s in enumerate(samples): delta = [x[j] - s['pos'][j] for j in range(3)] polyval = s['val'] if order >= 1: polyval += sum(s['grad'][j] delta[j] for j in range(3)) if order >= 2: polyval += 0.5 sum(s['hess'][j][k] delta[j] delta[k] for j in range(3) for k in range(3)) result += weights[i] polyval return result def computebarycentricweights(x, samples): # Compute barycentric coordinates for a simplex (4 points in 3D) # Fallback to inverse-distance weighting if topology is not a simplex if len(samples) == 4: p0, p1, p2, p3 = [s['pos'] for s in samples] v0 = [p1[j]-p0[j] for j in range(3)] v1 = [p2[j]-p0[j] for j in range(3)] v2 = [p3[j]-p0[j] for j in range(3)] d00 = sum(v0[j]v0[j] for j in range(3)) d01 = sum(v0[j]v1[j] for j in range(3)) d02 = sum(v0[j]v2[j] for j in range(3)) d11 = sum(v1[j]v1[j] for j in range(3)) d12 = sum(v1[j]v2[j] for j in range(3)) d22 = sum(v2[j]v2[j] for j in range(3)) denom = d00 d11 - d01 d01 w1 = (d11 d02 - d01 d12) / denom w2 = (d00 d12 - d01 d02) / denom w3 = 1.0 - w1 - w2 w0 = 1.0 - w1 - w2 - w3 return [w0, w1, w2, w3] else: dists = [sum((x[j] - s['pos'][j])2 for j in range(3)) for s in samples] invdists = [1.0 / (d + 1e-8) for d in dists] total = sum(invdists) return [w / total for w in invdists] Use local Taylor expansions. Sets apart by leveraging derivative data for higher accuracy. Choose when query accuracy is prioritized over raw speed. Link Fit polynomials to local neighborhoods. Sets apart by smoothing noise across samples. Choose when robustness to sampling irregularities is needed. Link Stores partial derivatives directly. Sets apart by enabling exact gradient reconstruction at sample points. Choose when surface normals or precise geometric properties are required. Performance: GPU filtering can be utilized for efficient queries on regular grids. Accuracy: Higher order fields provide better accuracy and can infer geometric properties like normals. Storage: Techniques decrease filtering footprint size to balance performance and storage, improving quality without increasing footprint. When to use: When higher accuracy is needed without increasing sampling density, or when geometric properties like normals are required. When not to use: When query performance is critical and lower accuracy is acceptable. Proposed by Gábor Valasek and Róbert Bán in January 2022.
