name: Smooth Blending and CSG Operations
head: Smooth Minimum, SDF Boolean Operations, Constructive Solid Geometry with SDFs
body: This family covers the construction of complex geometry from primitives using Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) operations (union, intersection, subtraction) and the smoothing of these operations to create organic transitions. It solves the problem of creating non-polygonal, continuous surfaces from analytical distance functions. It is distinguished from SDF Domain Manipulation Operators by focusing on boolean composition rather than spatial transformation, and from Basic Primitive Definitions by combining multiple primitives into a single field. The core mechanism relies on the property that the signed distance field (SDF) of a union of shapes is the minimum of their individual SDFs, and the intersection is the maximum. Union: The SDF for the union of two shapes S1 and S2 is: S{union}(\mathbf{x}) = \min(S1(\mathbf{x}), S2(\mathbf{x})) Intersection: The SDF for the intersection of two shapes S1 and S2 is: S{intersect}(\mathbf{x}) = \max(S1(\mathbf{x}), S2(\mathbf{x})) Subtraction: Subtracting shape S2 from S1 is equivalent to intersecting S1 with the inverse of S2 (where the sign is flipped): S{subtraction}(\mathbf{x}) = \max(S1(\mathbf{x}), -S2(\mathbf{x})) These operations allow for the construction of arbitrary complex geometries from a list of primitive edits. A function used to blend primitive shapes over a fixed radius, allowing for smoothed addition and subtraction in CSG operations. Definition The standard smooth minimum function has an infinite range, reaching zero at infinity. However, for real-time applications like the game Dreams, a modified formula is used that blends over a fixed radius. Formula The specific formula is not provided in the sources. Parameter Blend radius: A specified radius over which shapes blend. This replaces the infinite range of the standard smooth minimum. Usage Used in Dreams for creating intuitive sculpting tools for user-generated content, allowing edits to be union-ed or subtracted with smooth transitions. This topic covers the historical context and general application of SDF operations. History Inigo Quilez produced the first results recognizable as modern SDF in 2007, demonstrating techniques for efficient soft shadows, smooth blending, and domain repetition. This topic details the implementation of complex composite structures, specifically using bubbles on a panel. Definition The SDF for bubbles is defined as the union of N ellipsoids. Since ellipsoid SDFs lack a simple closed form, a lower bound of the signed distance field is used. Each bubble i has position \mathbf{x}i, semi-axis lengths \mathbf{r}i, and orientation angles \thetai in the \{X, Z\} plane and \phii in the \{Y, Z\} plane. Formula The full bubble field SDF is the union of all N individual distance functions: S{bubbles}(\mathbf{x}) = \bigcup{i=1}^N Bi(\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i, \mathbf{r}i, \thetai, \phii) where the union operator \bigcup is defined by \bigcup(S1, S2) = \min(S1, S2). The bubbles are subtracted from the displaced panel using the intersection operator \bigcap, defined by \bigcap(S1, S2) = \max(S1, -S2). The final distance function is: S{final} = \bigcap(S{panel}, S{bubbles}) Layout To manage a high number of bubbles efficiently, a regular voxel grid is defined inside the panel. Each voxel contains a maximum of one bubble to prevent overlapping. This allows S{bubbles} to be interpreted as a single SDF and traversed using a fast voxel traversal algorithm. Signed Distance Fields have a natural affinity for Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG), where solid 3D shapes can be constructed through unions and subtractions between primitive shapes. In 2007, Inigo Quilez demonstrated techniques for smooth blending and domain repetition, marking the emergence of modern SDF techniques. In the game Dreams, SDFs are used to create simple and intuitive sculpting tools for user-generated content. Objects, called 'Things', are constructed from lists of 'edits' (primitive shapes described by analytical SDFs). Edits are applied in a linear list, supporting binary union, subtraction, and smoothed operations. name: SDF Transformations and Operations
head: SDF Boolean and Transform Operations, Smooth Blending and Domain Repetition
body: This method defines the mathematical operations for modifying Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) via geometric transformations, Boolean combinations, and spatial repetitions. It solves the problem of constructing complex procedural geometry from simple primitives without explicit mesh data. What sets it apart is the ability to maintain the distance field property (Euclidean distance to the surface) through min/max blending and coordinate manipulation, enabling efficient ray marching of intricate scenes. Inputs: A 3D point \mathbf{p}, primitive SDF functions di(\mathbf{p}), transformation matrices or functions T(\mathbf{p}), and blending parameters \alpha. Outputs: A scalar distance value d(\mathbf{p}). Point: 3D vector \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z). Transformation: 3 \times 3 rotation matrix R and translation vector \mathbf{t}, or a composed function T(\mathbf{p}). Blending parameter: Scalar \alpha > 0 (softness). 1. Basic Boolean Operations Combine two SDFs d1(\mathbf{p}) and d2(\mathbf{p}): Union: d{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(d1(\mathbf{p}), d2(\mathbf{p})) Intersection: d{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(d1(\mathbf{p}), d2(\mathbf{p})) Subtraction: d{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(d1(\mathbf{p}), -d2(\mathbf{p})) 2. Smooth Blending (Soft Union/Intersection) Approximates smooth transitions between shapes using the \min\alpha operator: \min\alpha(a, b) = \frac{a + b - \sqrt{(a - b)^2 + \alpha^2}}{2} Smooth Union: d{soft\union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min\alpha(d1(\mathbf{p}), d2(\mathbf{p})) Smooth Intersection: d{soft\intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max\alpha(d1(\mathbf{p}), d2(\mathbf{p})) where \max\alpha(a, b) = \frac{a + b + \sqrt{(a - b)^2 + \alpha^2}}{2} Parameter \alpha: Controls softness. Smaller values approximate hard Boolean operations. Typical values: 0.01 to 0.5. 3. Geometric Transformations To transform a primitive, modify the query point \mathbf{p} before evaluating the SDF: Translation: d(\mathbf{p}) = d{prim}(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{t}) Rotation: d(\mathbf{p}) = d{prim}(R^T (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{t})) Scaling: d(\mathbf{p}) = d{prim}(\mathbf{s}^{-1} (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{t})) / \min(|\mathbf{s}|) Note: Scaling distorts the distance field. The distance must be divided by the scale factor to maintain correct metric properties. Uniform scaling is preferred to avoid anisotropic distortion. 4. Domain Repetition (Tiling) Repeats a primitive pattern infinitely in space by mapping the query point into a local cell: \mathbf{p}{local} = \mathbf{p} - \text{round}(\mathbf{p} / \text{period}) \times \text{period} Implementation: Use modulo arithmetic or floor functions to wrap coordinates. Pitfall: Discontinuities at tile boundaries can cause artifacts if not handled carefully. The round function ensures symmetry around the origin of each tile. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothmin(a, b, alpha): """Smooth union approximation.""" h = clamp(0.5 + 0.5 (b - a) / alpha, 0.0, 1.0) return lerp(b, a, h) - alpha h (1.0 - h) def transformpoint(p, rotationmatrix, translation, scale): """Apply inverse transform to point for SDF evaluation.""" # Translate p = p - translation # Rotate (inverse rotation is transpose for orthogonal matrices) p = dot(rotationmatrix, p) # Scale (divide by scale factor) p = p / scale return p def sdfwithtransforms(p, primitivesdf, rotation, translation, scale): """Evaluate SDF with geometric transformations.""" ptransformed = transformpoint(p, rotation, translation, scale) return primitivesdf(ptransformed) / abs(scale) def domainrepetition(p, period, primitivesdf): """Repeat primitive pattern in 3D space.""" pmod = p - floor(p / period + 0.5) period return primitivesdf(pmod) Hard Boolean operations using min/max. Basic shapes (sphere, box, etc.). This article. Time Complexity: O(1) per primitive evaluation. Total time scales linearly with the number of primitives in the scene. Memory Complexity: O(1) storage. No volumetric grid required. Strengths: Infinite resolution, compact representation, efficient for complex scenes with many instances. Limitations: No internal details (hollow objects are tricky), scaling distorts distance field, smooth blending introduces approximation error. When to use: Procedural geometry, soft shadows, ambient occlusion approximation, infinite tiling. When not to use: Need for exact internal geometry, non-uniform scaling with high precision requirements. Inigo Quilez produced the first results recognizable as modern SDF in 2007, demonstrating techniques for efficient soft shadows, smooth blending, and domain repetition. This work built upon earlier concepts by Alex Evans (2006) and Keenan Crane (2005), focusing on constraining fields to be Euclidean distances for efficient ray marching. name: SDF Transformation
head: SDF Transforms, Transformed SDF, Transforming SDFs, SDF Affine Transformation, SDF Model Transformations, SDF Inverse Transformation, SDF Spatial Transformations, Rigid Body Transformation of SDFs, Inverse Transformation for Rotation/Translation
body: SDF Transformation is a technique for applying geometric transformations (rotation, translation, scaling, and deformation) to Signed Distance Field primitives by manipulating the query point coordinates before evaluating the base distance function. It solves the problem of positioning and animating implicit surfaces in world space without modifying the underlying primitive definition, preserving the mathematical integrity of the distance field for ray marching. Unlike Uniform Scaling of SDFs, which handles exact distance compensation for uniform factors, or Lipschitz Transformation Bounds, which derives safety bounds for non-linear deformations, standard SDF Transformation relies on the inverse mapping of isometries (which preserve distance) or explicit scaling factors. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{x} in world space, a transformation T (defined by parameters such as rotation matrix R, translation vector \mathbf{t}, or scale factor s), and a base SDF function f(\mathbf{p}). Output: The signed distance d from \mathbf{x} to the transformed surface, and optionally the surface normal. Data Structures: Transformation Matrix: A 4 \times 4 homogeneous matrix M representing the local-to-world transform. For rigid bodies, this is composed of rotation R and translation \mathbf{t}. For scaling, it may be diagonal. Point: A 3D vector \mathbf{x} or homogeneous 4D vector \mathbf{x}h = (\mathbf{x}, 1). Steps: 1. Compute Inverse Transform: Determine the inverse of the transformation T^{-1} (or M^{-1}) that maps world coordinates back to the primitive's local space. For translation by \mathbf{t}: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} - \mathbf{t}. For rotation by angle \theta around an axis: Use the transpose of the rotation matrix, which corresponds to rotation by -\theta. Note: GLSL/WebGL lacks built-in matrix inversion; use the property R^{-1} = R^T. For uniform scale s: \mathbf{x}' = \mathbf{x} / s. For combined affine transform M = T \cdot R \cdot S: Compute M^{-1}. 2. Transform Query Point: Apply T^{-1} to the world query point \mathbf{x} to obtain the local point \mathbf{p}{local}. \mathbf{p}{local} = T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) 3. Evaluate Base SDF: Query the base distance function with the transformed point. d{local} = f(\mathbf{p}{local}) 4. Adjust Distance (Non-Isometries Only): If the transformation is not an isometry (e.g., scaling or non-uniform deformation), scale the returned distance to preserve metric correctness. For uniform scale s: d = s \cdot d{local}. For isometries (rotation, translation): d = d{local}. 5. Compute Normal (Optional): If normals are required, evaluate the gradient in local space and transform it back to world space using the inverse transpose of the linear part of the transformation. \mathbf{n}{world} = (M^{-1})^T \cdot \mathbf{n}{local} (Note: For pure rotation, the inverse transpose is the rotation matrix itself. For scaling, normals must be renormalized if anisotropic scaling is used, though standard SDF ray marching often assumes isotropic or rigid transforms for normal accuracy). Formulas: General Transformed Surface: f(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) = 0. Isometry Distance Preservation: d(\mathbf{x}, I \circ f^{-1}(0)) = d(I^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), f^{-1}(0)). Uniform Scale Distance: d(\mathbf{x}, S(f^{-1}(0))) = s \cdot d(S^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), f^{-1}(0)) where S^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) = \mathbf{x}/s. Parameters: orientation: Quaternion or rotation matrix specifying rotation. translation: 3-element vector specifying translation. origin: Center point for transformation (default often (0,0,0) or (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) depending on implementation). iGlobalTime: Animation time variable (e.g., in Shadertoy). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def transformsdf(querypoint, transformmatrix, basesdf, scalefactor=None): """ Evaluates an SDF with a geometric transformation applied. Args: querypoint: np.ndarray (3,), the point in world space to query. transformmatrix: np.ndarray (4, 4), the local-to-world transformation matrix. basesdf: callable, the untransformed signed distance function. scalefactor: float, optional. Required if transformmatrix includes non-uniform or uniform scaling to correct distance magnitude. If None, assumes isometry (rotation/translation). Returns: float: The signed distance to the transformed surface. """ # 1. Compute inverse transformation # Inverse of a 4x4 matrix. For pure rotation, use transpose. # For affine M = T R S, Minv = Sinv Rinv Tinv invtransform = np.linalg.inv(transformmatrix) # 2. Transform query point to local space # Treat point as homogeneous coordinate (x, y, z, 1) localpointhomogeneous = np.append(querypoint, 1.0) localpointhomogeneous = invtransform @ localpointhomogeneous # Extract xyz localpoint = localpointhomogeneous[:3] # 3. Evaluate base SDF distancelocal = basesdf(localpoint) # 4. Adjust distance for non-isometries if scalefactor is not None: # For uniform scaling, multiply distance by scale factor # For non-uniform, this simple scalar multiplication is an approximation # and may require Lipschitz bounds distanceworld = scalefactor distancelocal else: # Isometry (rotation/translation) preserves distance distanceworld = distancelocal return distanceworld def rotateyinverse(point, angle): """ Applies the inverse of a Y-axis rotation. Inverse of rotation by theta is rotation by -theta. """ c = np.cos(-angle) s = np.sin(-angle) # Rotation matrix around Y: # [ c 0 s ] # [ 0 1 0 ] # [-s 0 c ] x = point[0] c + point[2] s y = point[1] z = -point[0] s + point[2] c return np.array([x, y, z]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Matrix Inversion: In GLSL/WebGL, inverse() may not be available or efficient. For rotation matrices, use the transpose (negative angle). Non-Uniform Scaling: Simple scalar multiplication of the distance is incorrect for non-uniform scaling. It requires conservative bounds or Lipschitz constants to avoid overestimation. Deformation: Non-linear deformations (twist, bend) break local linearity, potentially affecting normal estimation and step size accuracy in ray marching. Tiling: Infinite tiling requires the position to be in the positive quadrant or handled via modulo arithmetic carefully to avoid discontinuities. Computes distances to implicitly defined surfaces after applying spatial transformations by adjusting the Lipschitz constant of the inverse transformation. It differs from Uniform Scaling of SDFs by handling non-uniform and non-linear deformations via the Jacobian norm, and from Spatial and nD transforms by explicitly deriving the Lipschitz constant required for safety rather than just applying the inverse transform. Computes the scalar value d = f(\mathbf{x}) for an implicit surface at query points \mathbf{x}, where d represents the signed distance or density. It solves the problem of determining whether a point lies inside, outside, or on the contour of a volume, which is fundamental for ray marching and isosurface extraction. It differs from Batched SDF Inference by operating on arbitrary single points rather than fixed neural network batches, and from DeepSDF Neural Network by using explicit analytical or grid-based storage rather than learned latent codes. Uniform scaling of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) is a technique to transform an implicit surface by a uniform factor while preserving the correctness of the distance value for ray marching. It solves the problem that scaling is not a rigid body transformation and distorts distances; without correction, the ray marching algorithm may overestimate the distance to the surface, causing the object to disappear. Unlike Non-Uniform Scaling of SDFs, which requires conservative bounds to avoid overestimation, uniform scaling allows for an exact compensation of distance distortion. Spatial and nD transforms apply geometric transformations to Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitives by inverse-transforming the query point rather than the geometry itself. This approach allows for the rotation, translation, scaling, and permutation of SDF models within the distance function evaluation. It sets itself apart from direct geometry manipulation by maintaining the mathematical integrity of the distance field while enabling complex hierarchical or per-node transformations, particularly in multidimensional data structures. A technique to create a 'blob effect' by perturbing the position \mathbf{p} with trigonometric functions before querying the SDF. This is noted as 'cheating' because it breaks the strict mathematical properties of the SDF. Step: Perturb coordinates using sine/cosine functions. Example: p[0] += 0.02 cos(8 p[1] + 3 p[2]), p[1] += 0.02 sin(6 p[2] + 7 p[0]), p[2] += 0.02 cos(8 p[0] + 9 p[0]). Time Complexity: O(1) per query, assuming the transformation matrix inversion is precomputed or cached. The cost is dominated by the base SDF evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) for storing transformation parameters (matrix, vector). Performance: Extremely fast for rigid body transformations (rotation/translation) as they involve only matrix-vector multiplication. Scaling adds a single multiplication. Strengths: Enables complex scene composition, animation, and hierarchical modeling without modifying primitive code. Preserves SDF properties for isometries. Limitations: Non-isometric transformations (scaling, deformation) require careful distance correction to avoid ray marching artifacts (e.g., missing surfaces or incorrect normals). Non-linear deformations can break the Lipschitz condition, leading to inaccurate step sizes in sphere tracing. When to Use: Ideal for rigid body animation, camera-relative effects, and simple scaling. Use Lipschitz Transformation Bounds for complex non-linear deformations where distance accuracy is critical. The technique of transforming SDFs by applying the inverse transformation to the query point was popularized by Inigo Quilez in his articles on raymarching. It is based on the mathematical property that implicit surfaces can be transformed by modifying their domain. Hart's work on GPU Ray Marching further formalized the distinction between isometries (which preserve distance) and non-isometries (which require scaling compensation). name: Lipschitz Transformation Bounds
head: Distances to Transformed Objects, SDF Transformation with Lipschitz Bounds, Transformed implicit surfaces
body: Lipschitz Transformation Bounds compute distances to implicitly defined surfaces after applying spatial transformations by adjusting the Lipschitz constant of the inverse transformation. It differs from Uniform Scaling of SDFs by handling non-uniform and non-linear deformations via the Jacobian norm, and from Spatial and nD transforms by explicitly deriving the Lipschitz constant required for safety rather than just applying the inverse transform. Inputs: A transformation function T(\mathbf{x}) and its inverse T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}), a base SDF function d(\mathbf{x}) for the untransformed primitive, and a ray origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}. Outputs: A safe step size \Delta t for ray marching and the transformed distance value. Data Structures: Standard vector and matrix types for coordinates and transformation parameters. Method: The distance to a transformed implicit surface defined by f(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x})) = 0 is not simply d(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x})). The Lipschitz constant of the composition is no greater than the product of the component Lipschitz constants, requiring adjustment by the Lipschitz constant of the inverse transformation T^{-1}. 1. Identify Transformation Type: Determine if T is an isometry, uniform scale, linear deformation, taper, or twist. 2. Compute Lipschitz Constant (L): Calculate the Lipschitz constant of T^{-1}, representing the maximum stretching factor of the inverse transformation. Isometry: If T preserves distances (rotation, translation, reflection), L = 1. The distance is exact: d(T^{-1}(\mathbf{0})) = d(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) - T^{-1}(\mathbf{0})). Uniform Scale: If T(\mathbf{x}) = s\mathbf{x}, the inverse scales by 1/s. The Lipschitz constant is L = 1/s. The distance is scaled: d(s T^{-1}(\mathbf{0})) = \frac{1}{s} d(T^{-1}(\mathbf{x}) - T^{-1}(\mathbf{0})). Linear Deformation: For a linear matrix M, L is found by the power method, which iteratively finds the largest eigenvalue of a matrix. Taper: Defined as \text{taper}(\mathbf{x}) = (s(z)x, s(z)y, z). The Lipschitz constant is determined by the tightest tapering: Lip{taper} = \min \frac{1}{s(z)} over the domain. Twist: Defined by rotation angle \theta(z). Twisting is not Lipschitz over unbounded domains; it must be constrained to a domain like a unit cylinder along the twisting axis. The bound is Lip{twist} = \sqrt{4 + \frac{\theta^2}{4}}. 3. Calculate Safe Step: The maximum safe step size \Delta t is computed by dividing the queried distance by L. 4. March: Advance the ray by \Delta t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def computelipschitzbound(transformtype, params): """Returns the Lipschitz constant L for the inverse transformation.""" if transformtype == 'isometry': return 1.0 elif transformtype == 'uniformscale': return 1.0 / params['scale'] elif transformtype == 'lineardeformation': # Power method to find largest singular value of Minv M = params['Minv'] v = [1.0, 1.0, 1.0] for in range(20): vnew = [sum(M[i][j] v[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] vnew2 = [sum(M[j][i] vnew[j] for j in range(3)) for i in range(3)] norm = math.sqrt(sum(xx for x in vnew2)) v = [x / norm for x in vnew2] return math.sqrt(sum(vnew2[i] v[i] for i in range(3))) elif transformtype == 'taper': # L = min(1/s(z)) over the domain, typically precomputed or via interval analysis return params['mininversescale'] elif transformtype == 'twist': theta = params['maxangle'] return math.sqrt(4.0 + (theta theta) / 4.0) else: raise ValueError("Unsupported transformation type") def raymarchstep(rayorigin, raydirection, sdffunc, transformtype, params): """Performs one step of ray marching using Lipschitz bounds.""" # Apply inverse transformation to current point if transformtype == 'uniformscale': p = [rayorigin[i] / params['scale'] for i in range(3)] elif transformtype == 'twist': theta = params['maxangle'] p = [ rayorigin[0] math.cos(theta) - rayorigin[2] math.sin(theta), rayorigin[1] / 2.0, rayorigin[0] math.sin(theta) + rayorigin[2] math.cos(theta) ] else: p = list(rayorigin) dist = sdffunc(p) L = computelipschitzbound(transformtype, params) step = abs(dist) / L return [rayorigin[i] + raydirection[i] step for i in range(3)], step Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Twisting on Unbounded Domains: Twisting is not Lipschitz over infinite space. It must be constrained to a bounded domain (e.g., a unit cylinder) to define a valid L. Precision: The Lipschitz constant is an upper bound. Using a loose bound results in smaller steps (slower convergence) but safety. Using a bound that is too tight causes tunneling. Non-Linear Taper: The Lipschitz constant for tapering depends on the derivative \alpha'(z). It must be computed per interval or via interval analysis. Warped-Space SDF Ray Marching renders scenes with regularly spaced geometry (e.g., urban environments) by defining the scene in a sheared coordinate space ("road space") where buildings are axis-aligned. It differs from standard Euclidean ray marching by applying a safety factor (Lipschitz bound) to the computed distances to compensate for the non-Euclidean metric introduced by the spatial transformation, preventing the ray from tunneling through walls. Choose it when rendering structured environments with consistent geometry spacing. A method to compute the bound of the norm of the Jacobian for a tapering transformation to determine the Lipschitz bound. For a tapering transformation \omega^{-1}(\mathbf{p}) = (\alpha(z)x, \alpha(z)y, z), the Jacobian matrix is: \mathbf{J}{\omega^{-1}} = \begin{pmatrix} \alpha & 0 & \beta \\ 0 & \alpha & 0 \\ \beta & 0 & 1 \end{pmatrix} where \beta = \alpha'. The Euclidean norm (Lipschitz bound) is: \|\mathbf{J}{\omega^-}\| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\sqrt{\alpha^2 + 2\beta^2 + 1 + (1 + \alpha)\sqrt{\alpha^2 - 2\alpha + 4\beta^2 + 1}} For a given input interval, this norm can be obtained by developing the equation or by interval analysis. Non-uniform spatial distortion is applied by modifying space as a function of position. An example of a twist deformation in GLSL is: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. float fScene(vec3 pt) { pt.y -= 1; float t = (pt.y + 2.5) sin(time); return sdCube(vec3( pt.x cos(t) - pt.z sin(t), pt.y / 2, pt.x sin(t) + pt.z cos(t)), vec3(1)); } This applies a rotation that varies with the y-coordinate, effectively twisting the cube. Time Complexity: O(1) per step for isometry and uniform scale. O(k) for linear deformation (power method iterations). O(1) for taper/twist if precomputed or simple analytic bounds are used. Memory Complexity: O(1). Strengths: Guarantees no tunneling for transformed primitives. Simple to implement for common transforms. Limitations: The bound is a worst-case estimate, which can lead to smaller step sizes than necessary, increasing the number of samples. Non-linear transforms require careful evaluation of the Lipschitz constant over the ray segment. When to Use: When rendering transformed SDF primitives (rotated, scaled, sheared, twisted) in ray marching. When Not to Use: For simple translations/rotations where the bound is 1, standard SDF evaluation is sufficient. For highly complex non-linear deformations where computing the Jacobian norm is expensive, other methods might be preferred. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. The method computes distances to implicitly defined surfaces after applying spatial transformations by adjusting the Lipschitz constant of the inverse transformation. Later work extended this to segment tracing using local Lipschitz bounds. Practical GLSL implementations of these deformations are provided in lecture notes. name: Warped-Space SDF Ray Marching
head: Road-space SDF, Sheared SDF
body: Warped-Space SDF Ray Marching is a technique for rendering scenes with regularly spaced geometry (such as urban environments) by defining the scene in a sheared coordinate space ("road space") where buildings are axis-aligned, simplifying distance field computation. It differs from standard Euclidean ray marching by applying a safety factor to the computed distances to compensate for the non-Euclidean metric introduced by the spatial transformation, preventing the ray from tunneling through walls. Inputs: Ray query point p{world} in world space. Scene definition: A set of buildings, each defined by a center c and half-extents h in road space. Road geometry function roadX(z), which returns the lateral offset of the road center at longitudinal position z. Ground plane height y{ground}. Safety factor \alpha = 0.8. Outputs: Marched distance d{out} and material ID. Data Structures: Buildings are stored in a grid or hash map indexed by longitudinal cell. Each building entry contains: center: vec3 (cx, cy, cz) in road space. halfExt: vec3 (hx, hy, hz) in road space. materialID: integer. Steps: 1. Transform to Road Space: For a given world point p, compute its road space coordinate q: q = (px - roadX(pz), py, pz) This transformation shears the world such that the road runs along the z-axis in road space. 2. Cell Identification: Determine the longitudinal cell index for the current z-coordinate: baseCz = \lfloor qz / BLOCK\DEPTH \rfloor where BLOCK\DEPTH is the grid cell size in the z-direction. 3. Neighbor Iteration: Iterate over 2 sides, NROWS rows, and 3 z-neighbors (dz \in \{-1, 0, 1\}). 4. Distance Computation: For each present building, compute the signed distance to the axis-aligned box: d{box} = sdBox(q - b.center, b.halfExt). 5. Take Minimum: Track the minimum distance found across all buildings as best. 6. Apply Safety Factor: Multiply best by 0.8. 7. Ground Comparison: Compare best with the ground plane distance; return the smaller distance and corresponding material ID. Formulas: Coordinate transformation: q = (px - roadX(pz), py, pz). Warped distance: d{warped} = d{box}(q - b.center, b.halfExt) \times 0.8. Parameters: \alpha = 0.8: Safety factor. Chosen because |roadX'| \le \sim 0.52, so the compression factor peaks at \sim 1.13. Since 0.8 < 1/1.13, this ensures a valid Lipschitz lower bound, preventing tunneling. BLOCK\DEPTH: Grid cell size in z. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tunneling: Because the warped space is not Euclidean, the box distance is compressed by |\nabla qx| = \sqrt{1 + roadX'(z)^2}. Without the 0.8 factor, the marcher could step too far and pass through walls. Degenerate Input: If roadX'(z) is large, the compression factor increases. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. from math import floor, abs, max, inf GROUNDMATERIALID = 0 def raymarchwarped(pworld, roadXfunc, buildingsgrid, BLOCKDEPTH, yground, alpha=0.8): """ Performs a single distance query in warped space. pworld: tuple/list of 3 floats (x, y, z) in world space. roadXfunc: callable returning lateral offset for a given z. buildingsgrid: dict mapping cellz -> list of building dicts. BLOCKDEPTH: float, longitudinal cell size. yground: float, ground plane height. alpha: float, safety factor (default 0.8). Returns: (distance, materialid) """ # 1. Transform world point to road space pz = pworld[2] roadoffset = roadXfunc(pz) q = (pworld[0] - roadoffset, pworld[1], pz) # 2. Determine longitudinal cell index basecz = int(floor(q[2] / BLOCKDEPTH)) bestdist = inf bestmatid = -1 # 3. Iterate over 3 z-neighbors (dz=-1 to 1) # Source iterates over 2 sides, NROWS rows, and 3 z-neighbors; # here we iterate over buildings in the relevant cells. for dz in [-1, 0, 1]: cellz = basecz + dz cellbuildings = buildingsgrid.get(cellz, []) for b in cellbuildings: # 4. Compute box distance in road space v = (q[0] - b.center[0], q[1] - b.center[1], q[2] - b.center[2]) dx = abs(v[0]) - b.halfExt[0] dy = abs(v[1]) - b.halfExt[1] dzbox = abs(v[2]) - b.halfExt[2] # Standard AABB SDF dbox = max(dx, max(dy, dzbox)) # 5. Take minimum distance if dbox < bestdist: bestdist = dbox bestmatid = b.materialid # 6. Apply safety factor bestdist = alpha # 7. Compare with ground plane distance dground = pworld[1] - yground if dground < bestdist: return dground, GROUNDMATERIALID else: return bestdist, bestmatid Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of buildings in the current and adjacent longitudinal cells. Typically small due to spatial partitioning. Memory Complexity: O(B) where B is the total number of buildings, stored in a grid/hash structure. Strengths: Simplifies building placement and SDF computation by aligning geometry with the coordinate axes in road space. Efficient for dense, regular urban layouts. Limitations: Only suitable for scenes with a dominant directional structure (e.g., roads). Requires careful tuning of the safety factor based on the maximum shear rate. Not suitable for arbitrary curved paths without complex roadX(z) definitions. When to use: Urban environments, highways, or any scene with a strong linear or gently curving central axis. When not to use: Scenes with no dominant direction, or where high precision is required without the overhead of dynamic safety factor calculation. The technique is described in the context of a WebGL raymarcher implementation, specifically for rendering urban environments efficiently. It leverages the concept of Lipschitz transformation bounds to ensure valid distance queries in non-Euclidean spaces. name: Implicit Surface Field Function Evaluation
head: Field Function Evaluation, Implicit Function Evaluation
body: Implicit Surface Field Function Evaluation computes the scalar value d = f(\mathbf{x}) for an implicit surface at query points \mathbf{x}, where d represents the signed distance or density. It solves the problem of determining whether a point lies inside, outside, or on the contour of a volume, which is fundamental for ray marching and isosurface extraction. It differs from Batched SDF Inference by operating on arbitrary single points rather than fixed neural network batches, and from DeepSDF Neural Network by using explicit analytical or grid-based storage rather than learned latent codes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point coordinates (x0, y0, z0), step size dz, number of points num\points. Output: Array of scalar density/distance values densities. Data Structures: Isosurface: Interface class containing the field function implementation. densities: Array of floats of size num\points. Steps: 1. If the implicit surface has an associated transformation matrix T, compute the inverse transformation T^{-1}. 2. Transform the query point \mathbf{x}{world} = (x0, y0, z0) by T^{-1} to obtain the local coordinate \mathbf{x}{local} = (xt, yt, zt). If no transformation is applied, T^{-1} is the identity, so \mathbf{x}{local} = \mathbf{x}{world}. 3. Evaluate the primitive field function f(\mathbf{x}{local}) to get the signed distance d. 4. Store d in the output array. 5. Increment the query point along the +z axis: z0 \leftarrow z0 + dz. 6. Repeat steps 2–5 for num\points. Formulas: For a sphere of radius R centered at the origin: f(x,y,z) = x^2 + y^2 + z^2 - R^2 d < 0: Point is inside the volume. d > 0: Point is outside the volume. d = 0: Point is on the contour. Parameters: dz: Delta step size along the +z axis for batch evaluation. num\points: Number of points to evaluate in the batch. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatefieldfunction(x0, y0, z0, dz, numpoints, radius, inversetransformmatrix): """ Evaluates the implicit field function for a sphere along the +z axis. Args: x0, y0, z0: Starting coordinates of the query point. dz: Step size along the z-axis. numpoints: Number of points to evaluate. radius: Radius of the sphere. inversetransformmatrix: 4x4 matrix representing T^-1. Returns: densities: List of float values representing the field function output. """ densities = [] sqrrad = radius radius for i in range(numpoints): # Step 1: Transform query point to local space # Homogeneous coordinate transformation (4x4 matrix) xlocal = inversetransformmatrix[0][0] x0 + inversetransformmatrix[0][1] y0 + inversetransformmatrix[0][2] z0 + inversetransformmatrix[0][3] ylocal = inversetransformmatrix[1][0] x0 + inversetransformmatrix[1][1] y0 + inversetransformmatrix[1][2] z0 + inversetransformmatrix[1][3] zlocal = inversetransformmatrix[2][0] x0 + inversetransformmatrix[2][1] y0 + inversetransformmatrix[2][2] z0 + inversetransformmatrix[2][3] # Step 2: Evaluate sphere field function sqrdist = xlocal xlocal + ylocal ylocal + zlocal zlocal d = sqrdist - sqrrad # Step 3: Store result densities.append(d) # Step 4: Increment z for next point z0 = z0 + dz return densities Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point errors may cause d to be slightly non-zero for points exactly on the contour. Boundaries: The bounding box of the implicit surface must be computed and reported to optimize culling, as it is not always trivial to derive from the field function alone. Implements runtime evaluation of an SDF defined on a 3D voxel grid, supporting configurable interpolation orders. Choose this when using grid-based storage rather than analytical primitives. Time Complexity: O(num\points) per evaluation, assuming constant-time primitive evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space for analytical primitives; O(V) for grid-based implementations where V is the number of voxels. Strengths: Compact and precise representation of volumes; efficient for simple primitives. Limitations: Difficult to determine bounding boxes for complex implicit functions; limited to specific geometric shapes or grid-based approximations. When to use: Simple analytical shapes or pre-computed voxel grids. When not to use: Complex, non-analytical surfaces requiring neural network inference or high-resolution grid storage. Implicit surfaces were introduced as a compact and precise way to describe volumes in 3D space, avoiding the need for explicit polygonal approximations. The concept is foundational for contouring algorithms like Marching Cubes and Dual Contouring. The specific implementation details described here, including the Isosurface interface and batch evaluation along the +z axis, are documented in an unofficial source by Zukkers. name: SDF Evaluation Implementation
head: SDF Evaluation and Gradient, SDF Handler Implementation, SDF Query Handler, SDF Value and Gradient Evaluation
body:
This method implements the runtime evaluation of Signed Distance Function (SDF) values and their spatial gradients for procedural or grid-based implicit surfaces. It solves the problem of efficiently querying the distance field d = f(\mathbf{p}) and its derivative 
abla f(\mathbf{p}) during ray marching or mesh extraction. It differs from Implicit Surface Field Function Evaluation by providing concrete data structures (voxel grids) and interpolation strategies (linear vs. cubic) required for differentiable rendering and robust boundary handling. The implementation supports two primary data sources: analytical primitives (via a query handler) and pre-computed voxel grids. The core logic involves loading the data, defining an evaluation interface, and computing values/derivatives based on the selected interpolation mode. Inputs: SDF data source: A file path (.sdf,.npy,.vol) or a named primitive identifier. Interpolation mode: String 'linear' or 'cubic' (controlled by utils.SDFMODE). Query point: 3D coordinate \mathbf{p} = (x, y, z). Outputs: Scalar distance value d \in \mathbb{R}. Gradient vector 
abla d = ( rac{\partial d}{\partial x},  rac{\partial d}{\partial y},  rac{\partial d}{\partial z}). 1. Voxel Grid (mi.TensorXf / mi.Texture3f): Shape: (res, res, res, 1), where res is the resolution read from the file header. Storage: Float values representing distance at voxel centers. Acceleration: Disabled (useaccel=False) to allow direct access to raw tensor data for interpolation. 2. SDF Query Handler (SDFQueryHandler): Stores the SDF name and validates it against a registry using isvalidsdfname(name). Contains a lambda function sdffunc that maps glm::vec3 to the underlying evaluation routine sdf::evaluate(name, glmp). 1. Initialization: If using a named primitive, instantiate SDFQueryHandler with the name. Validate the name; if invalid, raise std::runtimeerror("unknown SDF '...'"). If using a grid file (.sdf,.npy,.vol): Parse the first element as resolution res. Load the remaining grid data. Create a tensor mi.TensorXf with shape (res, res, res, 1). Wrap in mi.Texture3f with useaccel=False. 2. Value Evaluation at Point \mathbf{p}: Let mode be utils.SDFMODE. If mode is 'linear': Perform trilinear interpolation on the voxel grid at \mathbf{p}. Return the interpolated scalar value d. If mode is 'cubic': Perform tricubic interpolation on the voxel grid at \mathbf{p}. Return the interpolated scalar value d. If using SDFQueryHandler (primitives): Call sdf::evaluate(name, p). 3. Gradient Evaluation at Point \mathbf{p}: Let mode be utils.SDFMODE. If mode is 'linear': Compute central finite differences with step size \epsilon = 10^{-5}. 
abla d \approx \left(  rac{d(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \hat{x}) - d(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \hat{x})}{2\epsilon},  rac{d(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \hat{y}) - d(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \hat{y})}{2\epsilon},  rac{d(\mathbf{p} + \epsilon \hat{z}) - d(\mathbf{p} - \epsilon \hat{z})}{2\epsilon} ight). If mode is 'cubic': Retrieve the pre-computed gradient from the cubic interpolation routine. Return 
abla d directly from self.grid.evalcubicgrad(p)[1][0]. 4. Normal Computation (Optional): To compute the surface normal \mathbf{n} at query point \mathbf{q}: Evaluate 
abla d at \mathbf{q}. Normalize: \mathbf{n} =  rac{
abla d}{\|
abla d\|}. For directional derivative along direction \mathbf{d}: Compute \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{d}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np import glm class SDFEvaluator: def init(self, datasource, mode='linear', epsilon=1e-5): """ Initialize SDF evaluator.:param datasource: Path to grid file or SDF name string.:param mode: 'linear' or 'cubic'.:param epsilon: Step size for finite differences if mode is 'linear'. """ self.mode = mode self.epsilon = epsilon self.grid = None self.sdffunc = None # Check if datasource is a name (primitive) or path (grid) if isvalidsdfname(datasource): self.sdfname = datasource # Define lambda for primitive evaluation # Converts glm::vec3 to internal format and calls sdf::evaluate self.sdffunc = lambda p: sdfevaluateprimitive(self.sdfname, p) else: # Load grid data self.grid = loadsdfgrid(datasource) # grid is mi.TensorXf with shape (res, res, res, 1) # Wrapped in mi.Texture3f with useaccel=False def evaluatevalue(self, p): """ Evaluate SDF value at point p.:param p: numpy array or glm::vec3 of shape (3,):return: float distance value """ if self.sdffunc is not None: return self.sdffunc(p) if self.mode == 'linear': return self.grid.eval(p)[0] elif self.mode == 'cubic': return self.grid.evalcubic(p)[0] else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown mode: {self.mode}") def evaluategradient(self, p): """ Evaluate SDF gradient at point p.:param p: numpy array or glm::vec3 of shape (3,):return: numpy array of shape (3,) representing gradient """ if self.sdffunc is not None: # For primitives, gradient might be analytical or finite-diff # Assuming analytical if available, else fallback to finite diff # Note: Source does not specify primitive gradient method explicitly, # so we assume finite difference for consistency with linear mode if needed, # or analytical if the primitive supports it. # Based on, cubic uses pre-computed, linear uses finite diff. # We apply finite diff for linear mode primitives if no analytical grad exists. # For simplicity, assuming primitive evaluation returns value only here, # so we use finite diff for gradient if sdffunc is used. pass if self.mode == 'linear': # Central finite differences dx = (self.evaluatevalue(p + np.array([self.epsilon, 0, 0])) - self.evaluatevalue(p - np.array([self.epsilon, 0, 0]))) / (2 self.epsilon) dy = (self.evaluatevalue(p + np.array([0, self.epsilon, 0])) - self.evaluatevalue(p - np.array([0, self.epsilon, 0]))) / (2 self.epsilon) dz = (self.evaluatevalue(p + np.array([0, 0, self.epsilon])) - self.evaluatevalue(p - np.array([0, 0, self.epsilon]))) / (2 self.epsilon) return np.array([dx, dy, dz]) elif self.mode == 'cubic': # Retrieve pre-computed gradient return self.grid.evalcubicgrad(p)[1][0] else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown mode: {self.mode}") def querynormal(self, q): """ Compute normal at point q.:param q: Point in 3D space:return: Normalized gradient vector """ grad = self.evaluategradient(q) norm = np.linalg.norm(grad) if norm == 0: return np.array([0, 0, 0]) # Degenerate case return grad / norm def querydirectionalderivative(self, q, direction): """ Compute directional derivative.:param q: Point in 3D space:param direction: Direction vector (assumed normalized):return: Scalar directional derivative """ grad = self.evaluategradient(q) return np.dot(grad, direction) utils.SDFMODE: String, 'linear' or 'cubic'. 'cubic' provides smoother geometry and is theoretically more robust but is significantly slower. epsilon: Float, default 10^{-5}. Step size for finite difference gradient calculation in linear mode. Precision: Linear interpolation with finite differences is sensitive to the choice of \epsilon. Too small leads to numerical noise; too large leads to approximation error. Boundaries: Grid-based evaluation requires handling points outside the voxel bounds. The sources do not specify boundary conditions (e.g., clamp, wrap, or error), so implementation must define this behavior. Degenerate Input: If the gradient magnitude is zero, the normal is undefined. The pseudocode returns a zero vector. Memory: Cubic interpolation requires storing additional derivative data or computing it on the fly, increasing memory bandwidth usage. Evaluates SDF values for multiple spatial samples simultaneously to manage memory constraints during inference. It differs from single-sample evaluation by processing batches and from training methods by focusing solely on forward evaluation without gradient accumulation. Classifies SDF samples into positive, negative, and valid near-zero categories using a relaxation threshold scaled to voxel size. It solves ambiguous SDF magnitudes during ray marching by identifying samples near the zero-level set. It differs from Batched SDF Inference by focusing on validation rather than generation, and from Eikonal SDF Refinement by using a simple threshold check. Optimizes a neural implicit SDF to reconstruct 3D surfaces from point clouds by enforcing the Eikonal equation (\|
abla d\| = 1). Unlike density-based methods like NeRF, it predicts signed distance values for explicit surface extraction. It differs from SDF Optimization via Finite Differences by using automatic differentiation for exact gradients. A neural network architecture taking a latent code and 3D coordinates as input to output SDF values. Implemented as an MLP with skip connections and Tanh activation, it predicts distances by concatenating shape-specific latent codes with coordinates. Optimizes SDF values and learnable weights to minimize geometric difference between extracted and target meshes. It differs from standard evaluation by treating SDF values as learnable parameters and using finite difference gradients for optimization. It builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation. Computes the SDF for the Mandelbulb fractal using iterative derivative-based estimation in polar coordinates. It differs from standard primitives by approximating distance to non-algebraic surfaces and builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation. Optimizes voxelized SDF and material volumes (albedo, roughness, metallic) by minimizing L1 difference between rendered and reference images. It differs from pure geometry optimization by jointly updating material grids and from neural SDF methods by using explicit grid-based representations with periodic upsampling. It builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation for the forward pass. A conservative SDF variant that accelerates queries by embedding a bounding volume. It solves performance bottlenecks for points far from the surface by returning the distance to the bounding volume instead. Computes approximate SDF textures efficiently using a multi-pass sweep approach, propagating distance information from surface primitives. It trades geometric precision for speed and texture-based storage, intended for use in Sphere Tracing. A memory-efficient method to extract boundaries between multiple materials by storing the blended Extended Signed Distance Function (ESDF) in a Z-buffer. It updates the Z-buffer for each material where the current entry is greater than the current ESDF, simultaneously storing the material index. The material index m(x, y) at pixel (x, y) is determined by m(x, y) = \arg \minm \{sm(x, y)\}, where sm is the ESDF for material m. Time Complexity: Linear in the number of samples for batched evaluation. Cubic interpolation is significantly slower than linear interpolation due to higher-order derivative calculations. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the voxel grid size res^3 for grid-based SDFs. Cubic interpolation may require additional memory for gradient storage or computation. Performance: Cubic interpolation provides smoother geometry and is theoretically more robust but is much slower than linear interpolation. Strengths: Supports both analytical primitives and grid-based data. Provides differentiable gradients for optimization. Limitations: Grid-based methods are memory-intensive for high resolutions. Linear interpolation with finite differences can be noisy. When to Use: Use linear mode for performance-critical applications or real-time rendering. Use cubic mode for high-quality offline rendering or when smooth geometry is critical. The method originates from differentiable rendering frameworks that support SDFs, such as the work by Wang et al. (2024) on "A Simple Approach to Differentiable Rendering of SDFs". It builds on earlier work in mesh extraction from segmented volumes, such as the non-manifold mesh extraction by Bertram et al. (2005), and practical implementations in open-source repositories like subgrid-marching and relaxed-boundary. hbaktash/subgrid-marching, https://github.com/hbaktash/subgrid-marching, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, https://github.com/zichenwang01/relaxed-boundary, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Non-manifold Mesh Extraction from Time-varying Segmented Volumes used for Modeling a Human Heart, https://doi.org/10.2312/vissym/eurovis05/199-206, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Batched SDF Inference
head: Batched SDF Evaluation
body: Batched SDF Inference evaluates Signed Distance Function (SDF) values for a large set of spatial samples in batches to manage memory constraints during inference. It differs from single-sample evaluation by processing multiple points simultaneously, and from training methods by focusing solely on forward evaluation without gradient accumulation for optimization. Inputs: A list of 3D query points \mathbf{p}i. An SDF model or function capable of decoding/evaluating distance values. maxbatch: Integer maximum batch size for inference, default 32^3 = 32768. Outputs: An array of SDF values d(\mathbf{p}i) corresponding to each input point. Data Structures: samples: A 2D array or tensor of shape (N, 4), where N is the total number of samples. Columns 0-2 store the coordinates (x, y, z), and column 3 stores the computed SDF value. Steps: 1. Disable automatic differentiation (gradients) for the inference process to save memory and computation. 2. Determine the total number of samples N. 3. Initialize a head pointer h = 0. 4. While h < N: a. Calculate the end of the current batch: e = \min(h + \text{max\batch}, N). b. Extract the subset of samples from index h to e-1. c. Decode or evaluate the SDF for this subset. d. Store the resulting SDF values in column 3 of the samples array for indices h to e-1. e. Increment h by \text{max\batch}. 5. Return the SDF values from column 3 of the samples array. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def batchedsdfinference(samples, sdfmodel, maxbatch=323): """ Evaluates SDF values for a large set of samples in batches. Args: samples: Array of shape (N, 3) containing query points (x, y, z). sdfmodel: Object or function with a method to evaluate SDF values. maxbatch: Integer maximum batch size. Default 32768. Returns: Array of SDF values of shape (N,). """ # Disable gradients for memory efficiency with torch.nograd(): numsamples = samples.shape[0] head = 0 sdfvalues = np.empty(numsamples) while head < numsamples: # Determine batch end end = min(head + maxbatch, numsamples) # Extract subset batchpoints = samples[head:end] # Decode SDF for subset # Implementation detail: sdfmodel.evaluate(batchpoints) batchsdfs = sdfmodel.evaluate(batchpoints) # Store in column 3 (mapped to 1D array for return) sdfvalues[head:end] = batchsdfs # Increment head head += maxbatch return sdfvalues Parameters: maxbatch: Integer maximum batch size for inference. Default value is 32^3. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If maxbatch is larger than the total number of samples, the loop runs once. Precision issues may arise if the SDF model involves floating-point operations on very large coordinate sets; however, standard batched inference does not inherently introduce more precision errors than single-pass evaluation. Memory limits are the primary driver for batching; if maxbatch is too large, out-of-memory errors may occur depending on the hardware. A compute shader kernel that calculates the SDF value for each voxel in a grid. It serves as the atomic evaluation step within batched inference pipelines. Evaluates SDFs for volumetric structures across multiple joint configurations and query points simultaneously, enabling efficient batched inference for robotic kinematics. Provides real-time inspection of SDF properties at specific 3D coordinates, outputting the signed distance value, analytical gradient, and hit classification. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of samples, with a constant factor dependent on the SDF evaluation cost per point. Memory Complexity: O(\text{max\batch}) for the active batch, plus O(N) to store the final results. This is significantly lower than evaluating all N points in a single forward pass if N \gg \text{max\batch}. Strengths: Manages memory constraints for large-scale point cloud or voxel grid evaluations. Limitations: Introduces slight overhead from loop management compared to a single vectorized operation if memory permits. When to use: When evaluating SDFs for millions of points (e.g., voxel grids, dense point clouds) where GPU memory is limited. When not to use: For small numbers of points where the overhead of batching is unnecessary. Batched SDF Inference is a practical implementation technique used in distance-field ray marching and procedural surface rendering pipelines. It is commonly found in unofficial implementations of SDF-based renderers, such as the DIST-Renderer, where large-scale evaluation is required for training or inference. name: SDF Value Computation
head: IsoVal.compute
body: SDF Value Computation is a compute shader kernel that calculates the Signed Distance Function (SDF) value for each voxel in a grid. It transforms grid coordinates to world space, evaluates the SDF function, and stores the result. It serves as the atomic evaluation step within batched inference pipelines. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A linearized 3D grid of voxel indices (IDs), a 4 \times 4 transformation matrix ShapeToWorld mapping local shape coordinates to world space, and the shape's intrinsic size SHAPESIZE. Output: A 1D array or texture IsoVals storing the computed SDF value for each voxel. Data Structures: IsoVals: A 1D array storing SDF values, indexed by a linearized 3D coordinate ID. ShapeToWorld: A 4 \times 4 matrix. SHAPESIZE: A scalar defining the scale or extent of the primitive shape. Steps: 1. Grid Coordinate Retrieval: For each voxel, determine its 3D grid coordinates from its linear ID. 2. Local Position Calculation: Convert the grid coordinates into a local surface position using a helper GetPosSurface(id). 3. World Space Transformation: Transform the local position \mathbf{p}{local} to world space \mathbf{p}{world} using the transformation matrix: \mathbf{p}{world} = \mathbf{M}{shape\to\world} \cdot \mathbf{p}{local} where \mathbf{M}{shape\to\world} is ShapeToWorld. 4. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF function F(\mathbf{p}) at the world position. The function depends on the specific primitive shape defined by SHAPESIZE. d = \text{SDF}(\mathbf{p}{world}, \text{SHAPE\SIZE}) 5. Storage: Store the computed distance d in the output array IsoVals at the index corresponding to the voxel ID. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdfvalue(voxelid, shapetoworldmatrix, shapesize, griddims, gridorigin): # Step 1 & 2: Get local position from grid ID using GetPosSurface(id) # Standard linear ID to 3D coordinate conversion for a regular grid x = (voxelid % griddims[0]) / griddims[0] y = ((voxelid // griddims[0]) % griddims[1]) / griddims[1] z = (voxelid // (griddims[0] griddims[1])) / griddims[2] localpos = (x, y, z) # Step 3: Transform to world space using ShapeToWorld worldposx = shapetoworldmatrix[0][0] localpos[0] + shapetoworldmatrix[0][1] localpos[1] + shapetoworldmatrix[0][2] localpos[2] + shapetoworldmatrix[0][3] worldposy = shapetoworldmatrix[1][0] localpos[0] + shapetoworldmatrix[1][1] localpos[1] + shapetoworldmatrix[1][2] localpos[2] + shapetoworldmatrix[1][3] worldposz = shapetoworldmatrix[2][0] localpos[0] + shapetoworldmatrix[2][1] localpos[1] + shapetoworldmatrix[2][2] localpos[2] + shapetoworldmatrix[2][3] worldpos = (worldposx, worldposy, worldposz) # Step 4: Evaluate SDF function at the world position with SHAPESIZE # The specific primitive function depends on the shape type and uses shapesize as a parameter. # Common implementations: sphere (length(point) - size), box (length(max(abs(point) - size, 0.0)) - size) sdfvalue = evaluatesdfprimitive(worldpos, shapesize) # Step 5: Store result in IsoVals at index voxelid return sdfvalue def evaluatesdfprimitive(point, size): # Shape-specific SDF evaluation. Sources do not specify the exact primitive function. raise NotImplementedError("Specific SDF primitive function not defined in source.") Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in the transformation matrix multiplication can cause slight inaccuracies in the distance value, potentially affecting marching convergence. Boundary Conditions: The definition of GetPosSurface must correctly handle grid boundaries to avoid out-of-bounds access or incorrect coordinate mapping. Shape Definition: The SDF evaluation must be consistent with the SHAPESIZE interpretation (e.g., radius vs. half-extent). Calculates SDF and RGB for 3D points relative to a single camera view, solving geometric and photometric consistency. It differs by incorporating view-dependent color and depth comparison, whereas this method is view-agnostic and geometry-only. Not given in the sources. name: Per-Frame SDF Computation
body: Per-Frame SDF Computation calculates the Signed Distance Function (SDF) and RGB color for a set of 3D points by projecting them into a single camera view. It solves the problem of assigning geometric and photometric consistency to 3D points relative to a specific training view by comparing projected depths against a pre-computed depth map. It differs from multi-view fusion methods by operating on a single viewpoint at a time, serving as the atomic unit for subsequent TSDF fusion or colorization. Inputs: points: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D point coordinates in world space. fullprojtransform: Tensor of shape (4, 4) representing the combined projection and view transformation matrix. depthmap: Tensor of shape (H, W) containing the depth values for the current view. rgbmap: Tensor of shape (H, W, 3) containing the RGB color values for the current view. Outputs: sdf: Tensor of shape (N, 1) containing the signed distance values. rgb: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the sampled RGB colors. mask: Boolean tensor of shape (N, 1) indicating valid projections. Data Structures: Points, depth, and RGB maps are stored as floating-point tensors. Steps: 1. Homogenization: Append a column of ones to points to create homogeneous coordinates of shape (N, 4). 2. Projection: Multiply the homogeneous points by fullprojtransform to obtain clip-space coordinates. p{clip} = P{world} \times M{proj} Where P{world} is the (N, 4) homogeneous point matrix and M{proj} is the (4, 4) transformation matrix. 3. Perspective Division: Extract the z-coordinate (z{clip}) and divide the x and y coordinates by z{clip} to compute normalized device coordinates (NDC). x{ndc} = \frac{x{clip}}{z{clip}}, \quad y{ndc} = \frac{y{clip}}{z{clip}} 4. Masking: Create a boolean mask where -1 \le x{ndc} \le 1, -1 \le y{ndc} \le 1, and z{clip} > 0. Points failing any condition are invalid. 5. Depth Sampling: Sample the depthmap at (x{ndc}, y{ndc}) using bilinear interpolation with border padding, then reshape to (N, 1). 6. Color Sampling: Sample the rgbmap at (x{ndc}, y{ndc}) using bilinear interpolation with border padding, then reshape to (N, 3). 7. SDF Calculation: Compute the SDF as the difference between the sampled depth and the projected z-coordinate. sdf = d{sampled} - z{clip} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdfperframe(points, fullprojtransform, depthmap, rgbmap): # points: (N, 3), fullprojtransform: (4, 4), depthmap: (H, W), rgbmap: (H, W, 3) N = len(points) H, W = len(depthmap), len(depthmap[0]) # 1. Homogenize pointshomo = [[p[0], p[1], p[2], 1.0] for p in points] # 2. Project to clip space pointsclip = [[sum(pointshomo[i][k] fullprojtransform[k][j] for k in range(4)) for j in range(4)] for i in range(N)] xclip = [p[0] for p in pointsclip] yclip = [p[1] for p in pointsclip] zclip = [p[2] for p in pointsclip] # 3. Perspective division eps = 1e-7 xndc = [x / (z + eps) for x, z in zip(xclip, zclip)] yndc = [y / (z + eps) for y, z in zip(yclip, zclip)] # 4. Create projection mask mask = [(x >= -1.0 and x <= 1.0 and y >= -1.0 and y <= 1.0 and z > 0) for x, y, z in zip(xndc, yndc, zclip)] # 5 & 6. Sample depth and RGB (bilinear with border padding) def bilinearsample(mapdata, u, v): u0, u1 = max(0, min(int(u), W-2)), max(0, min(int(u)+1, W-1)) v0, v1 = max(0, min(int(v), H-2)), max(0, min(int(v)+1, H-1)) fu, fv = u - int(u), v - int(v) wa, wb, wc, wd = (1-fu)(1-fv), (1-fu)fv, fu(1-fv), fufv if len(mapdata[0][0]) == 3: return [wamapdata[v0][u0][c] + wbmapdata[v0][u1][c] + wcmapdata[v1][u0][c] + wdmapdata[v1][u1][c] for c in range(3)] return wamapdata[v0][u0] + wbmapdata[v0][u1] + wcmapdata[v1][u0] + wdmapdata[v1][u1] depthsampled = [] rgbsampled = [] for i in range(N): u = (xndc[i] + 1.0) / 2.0 (W - 1) v = (yndc[i] + 1.0) / 2.0 (H - 1) depthsampled.append(bilinearsample(depthmap, u, v)) rgbsampled.append(bilinearsample(rgbmap, u, v)) # 7. Compute SDF sdf = [d - z for d, z in zip(depthsampled, zclip)] return sdf, rgbsampled, mask Parameters: paddingmode: 'border' is used to handle out-of-bounds coordinates. aligncorners: False is used for standard grid sampling. Edge Cases: Division by Zero: If z{clip} \le 0, the point is behind the camera or on the near plane, and these points are masked out. Out of Bounds: Points projecting outside [-1, 1] in NDC space are masked out, and border padding ensures sampling does not return NaN or extreme values for slightly out-of-bounds points. Point Colorization via Projective SDF assigns RGB colors to a set of 3D points by projecting them into training views, filtering based on alpha confidence and projective depth consistency, and sampling the closest valid color from the rendered reference frames. It differs from standard nearest-neighbor colorization by enforcing geometric consistency through a projective SDF metric, ensuring that sampled colors correspond to the visible surface rather than occluded geometry or background. Unbounded TSDF Fusion extends Per-Frame SDF Computation by fusing SDF values from multiple frames in contracted space with adaptive truncation, then uncontracting the space. If an inverse contraction transform is provided, points outside the unit sphere (||samples|| > 1) are identified. The base truncation sdf\trunc is set to 5 \times voxel\size. For points outside the unit sphere, truncation is scaled by 1/(2-||x||). If no inverse contraction is provided, sdf\trunc remains a constant 5 \times voxel\size. TSDFs are initialized to -1, RGBs to 0, and weights to 1. The algorithm iterates through a viewpointstack, calling computesdfperframe for each view. The SDF is flattened, and the mask is updated to include points where SDF > -sdf\trunc. SDF is normalized by sdf\trunc, clamped to [-1, 1], and the mask is applied. TSDF and RGB are updated using a weighted average: new = (old \times w + val) / (w + 1). Weights are updated: w{new} = w{old} + 1. If inverse contraction is provided, samples are uncontracted before returning. Time Complexity: O(N) per frame, where N is the number of points, dominated by matrix multiplication and bilinear sampling. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing intermediate tensors (clip coordinates, NDC, masks, sampled values). Strengths: Efficiently computes geometric consistency for a single view and integrates seamlessly with multi-view fusion pipelines. Limitations: Only considers one view at a time and does not handle occlusions from other views within the single-frame computation (this is handled in the fusion step). When to use: When initializing or updating SDF fields for a specific training view. When not to use: When multi-view consistency is required immediately without fusion. Per-Frame SDF Computation is part of the 2D Gaussian Splatting pipeline, specifically used in the context of post-processing or refining 3D points using depth information from training views. It originates from the work on 2D Gaussian Splatting by Inria's GRAPHDECO research group. hbb1/2d-gaussian-splatting, https://github.com/hbb1/2d-gaussian-splatting, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Point Colorization via Projective SDF
head: Projective SDF Colorization, Projective SDF Filtering & Color Sampling
body: Point Colorization via Projective SDF assigns RGB colors to a set of 3D points by projecting them into training views, filtering based on alpha confidence and projective depth consistency, and sampling the closest valid color from the rendered reference frames. It differs from standard nearest-neighbor colorization by enforcing geometric consistency through a projective Signed Distance Field (SDF) metric, ensuring that sampled colors correspond to the visible surface rather than occluded geometry or background. Inputs: pts: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D point coordinates in world space. voxelmodel: A sparse voxel representation capable of rendering color, depth, and alpha. camlst: List of training camera objects, each providing position, lookat, project, and render methods. args.alphathres: Scalar threshold for alpha filtering (e.g., 0.5). args.usemean: Boolean flag to select mean depth (True) or median depth (False) from the renderer. Outputs: closestcolor: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing the assigned RGB color for each point. closestdist: Tensor of shape (N) containing the minimum projective SDF distance for each point. Data Structures: closestcolor: Initialized to [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] for all points. closestdist: Initialized to +\infty for all points. validptsidx: Indices of points currently considered valid, initially all points projected within the image bounds. Parameters: mode='bilinear': Interpolation mode for gridsample. aligncorners=False: Coordinate alignment setting for gridsample to prevent edge bias. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Set closestcolor to 0.5 for all N points. Set closestdist to +\infty for all N points. 2. Iterate over Training Cameras: For each camera cam in camlst: a. Render Reference Frame: Call renderpkg = voxelmodel.render(cam, colormode="sh0", outputdepth=True, outputT=True). Extract framecolor from renderpkg['color']. Select framedepth: if args.usemean is true, use renderpkg['rawdepth'][[0]] (mean); otherwise, use renderpkg['rawdepth'][[2]] (median). Compute framealpha = 1 - renderpkg['rawT']. Get image dimensions H, W from framedepth.shape[-2:]. b. Project Points: Compute projected UV coordinates: ptsuv = cam.project(pts). Filter points outside the image bounds [-1, 1]: filteridx = torch.where((ptsuv.abs() <= 1).all(-1))[0]. Update valid indices and points: validptsidx = filteridx. validpts = pts[filteridx]. ptsuv = ptsuv[filteridx]. If validpts is empty, skip to the next camera. c. Alpha Filtering: Sample alpha at projected UVs using bilinear interpolation: \text{pts\frame\alpha} = \text{grid\sample}(\text{frame\alpha}.view(1,1,H,W), \text{pts\uv}.view(1,1,-1,2), \text{mode}='bilinear', \text{align\corners}=False).flatten(). Filter points with alpha below threshold: filteridx = torch.where(ptsframealpha > args.alphathres)[0]. Update valid arrays: validptsidx = validptsidx[filteridx]. validpts = validpts[filteridx]. ptsuv = ptsuv[filteridx]. If validpts is empty, skip to the next camera. d. Compute Projective SDF Distance: Sample frame depth at projected UVs: \text{pts\frame\depth} = \text{grid\sample}(\text{frame\depth}.view(1,1,H,W), \text{pts\uv}.view(1,1,-1,2), \text{mode}='bilinear', \text{align\corners}=False).flatten(). Compute camera-space depth for each point: \text{pts\depth} = (\text{valid\pts} - \text{cam.position}) \cdot \text{cam.lookat}. Compute absolute projective distance: \text{pts\dist} = |\text{pts\frame\depth} - \text{pts\depth}|. e. Update Closest Color: Identify points with smaller distance than current best: filteridx = torch.where(ptsdist < closestdist[validptsidx])[0]. Update valid indices for this iteration: validptsidx = validptsidx[filteridx]. ptsuv = ptsuv[filteridx]. ptsdist = ptsdist[filteridx]. validpts = validpts[filteridx]. If validpts is empty, continue to next camera. Sample color at filtered UVs: \text{pts\color} = \text{grid\sample}(\text{frame\color}.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0), \text{pts\uv}.view(1,1,-1,2), \text{mode}='bilinear', \text{align\corners}=False).squeeze().T. Update global closest arrays: closestdist[validptsidx] = ptsdist. closestcolor[validptsidx] = ptscolor. 3. Return: Return closestcolor and closestdist. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def pointcolorizationviaprojectivesdf(pts, voxelmodel, camlst, args): """ Args: pts: (N, 3) tensor of 3D points voxelmodel: SparseVoxelModel with render method camlst: List of camera objects args: Object with alphathres, usemean Returns: closestcolor: (N, 3) tensor closestdist: (N,) tensor """ N = pts.shape[0] closestcolor = torch.full((N, 3), 0.5, dtype=torch.float32, device=pts.device) closestdist = torch.full((N,), float('inf'), dtype=torch.float32, device=pts.device) for cam in camlst: # 1. Render reference frame renderpkg = voxelmodel.render(cam, colormode="sh0", outputdepth=True, outputT=True) framecolor = renderpkg['color'] if args.usemean: framedepth = renderpkg['rawdepth'][[0]] else: framedepth = renderpkg['rawdepth'][[2]] framealpha = 1 - renderpkg['rawT'] H, W = framedepth.shape[-2:] # 2. Project points ptsuv = cam.project(pts) # Filter points outside image bounds [-1, 1] validmask = (ptsuv.abs() <= 1).all(dim=-1) validindices = torch.where(validmask)[0] if validindices.numel() == 0: continue validpts = pts[validindices] ptsuvvalid = ptsuv[validindices] # 3. Alpha filtering ptsframealpha = F.gridsample( framealpha.view(1, 1, H, W), ptsuvvalid.view(1, 1, -1, 2), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).flatten() alphamask = ptsframealpha > args.alphathres validindices = validindices[alphamask] validpts = validpts[alphamask] ptsuvvalid = ptsuvvalid[alphamask] if validindices.numel() == 0: continue # 4. Compute Projective SDF ptsframedepth = F.gridsample( framedepth.view(1, 1, H, W), ptsuvvalid.view(1, 1, -1, 2), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).flatten() # Camera space depth: dot product of point offset and look-at vector ptsdepth = (validpts - cam.position) @ cam.lookat # Absolute distance ptsdist = (ptsframedepth - ptsdepth).abs() # 5. Update closest currentclosest = closestdist[validindices] updatemask = ptsdist < currentclosest updateindices = validindices[updatemask] updateptsuv = ptsuvvalid[updatemask] updateptsdist = ptsdist[updatemask] if updateindices.numel() == 0: continue # Sample color (permute to (C, H, W) for gridsample) ptscolor = F.gridsample( framecolor.permute(2, 0, 1).unsqueeze(0), updateptsuv.view(1, 1, -1, 2), mode='bilinear', aligncorners=False).squeeze().T # Update global arrays closestdist[updateindices] = updateptsdist closestcolor[updateindices] = ptscolor return closestcolor, closestdist Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundaries: Points projected exactly to the image edge may suffer from interpolation bias if aligncorners=True; the method uses aligncorners=False to mitigate this. Degenerate Input: If no training views cover a point (all projections outside bounds or low alpha), the point retains the initial color [0.5, 0.5, 0.5] and distance \infty. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot C), where N is the number of points and C is the number of training cameras. Each camera requires rendering and grid sampling operations proportional to N. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing closestcolor and closestdist. Strengths: Robust to occlusion by using projective depth consistency; leverages existing sparse voxel rendering infrastructure. Limitations: Requires access to training views and their depth/alpha outputs; performance scales linearly with the number of cameras. This method is part of the SVaR (Sparse Voxel Rasterization) pipeline for 3D reconstruction and colorization. It builds on Per-Frame SDF Computation to assign colors to points derived from adaptive sparse voxels. The approach was introduced in the context of efficient mesh extraction and colorization from sparse voxel representations. leonhardrobin/svraster-win10, https://github.com/leonhardrobin/svraster-win10, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)
