name: Batched SDF Query with Joint Configuration
body: This method evaluates Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for volumetric structures across multiple joint configurations and query points simultaneously, enabling efficient batched inference for robotic kinematics. It differs from single-configuration queries by integrating Forward Kinematics (FK) chains to support automatic differentiation with respect to joint angles, facilitating gradient-based optimization tasks like collision avoidance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: points tensor of shape (N, d) representing N geometric points in d dimensions (typically 2 or 3). Input: jointconfiguration tensor of shape (B, J) representing B batched configurations, each with J joint angles. Input: rangeperdim tensor of shape (d, 2) specifying the minimum and maximum range for each dimension. Input: computegrad boolean flag; if False, gradient computation is skipped for performance. Output: sdfval tensor of shape (B, N) containing signed distance values. Output: sdfgrad tensor of shape (B, N, d) containing gradients with respect to points, or None if computegrad is False. Data Structures: The implementation relies on a custom PyTorch Function subclass (e.g., ObjectFrameSDF) to manage the forward pass and backward pass for autograd. The backward pass specifically computes \frac{\partial \text{sdf\val}}{\partial \text{points}} using the saved SDF gradient from the forward pass. Steps: 1. Validation: Check if query points lie within the specified rangeperdim using a helper function isinside. This function returns a boolean tensor indicating membership. \text{is\inside}(\mathbf{P}, \mathbf{R}) = \bigwedge{i=0}^{d-1} (R{i,0} \le P{:,i} \le R{i,1}) Where \mathbf{P} is the points tensor and \mathbf{R} is the range tensor. 2. Configuration Application: Apply the current joint configuration to the SDF object. This transforms the query points into the object's local frame via Forward Kinematics. 3. SDF Evaluation: Evaluate the SDF value at the transformed points. If computegrad is True, also compute the gradient of the SDF with respect to the points in the object frame. 4. Gradient Accumulation (Backward): If computegrad is True, the backward pass computes the gradient of the loss with respect to the input points: \frac{\partial \text{loss}}{\partial \mathbf{P}{\text{obj}}} = \frac{\partial \text{loss}}{\partial \text{sdf\val}} \otimes \text{sdf\grad} Where \otimes denotes element-wise multiplication broadcasted appropriately. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def isinside(points: torch.Tensor, rangeperdim: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor: """ Check if points are within the specified range per dimension.:param points: Tensor of shape (N, d):param rangeperdim: Tensor of shape (d, 2) with [min, max] for each dim:return: Boolean tensor of shape (N,) """ return torch.all((rangeperdim[:, 0] <= points) & (points <= rangeperdim[:, 1]), dim=-1) class BatchedSDFQuery: def init(self, sdfobject, computegrad=True): self.sdfobject = sdfobject self.computegrad = computegrad def query(self, points: torch.Tensor, jointconfig: torch.Tensor, rangeperdim: torch.Tensor) -> tuple: """ Query SDF for batched joint configurations.:param points: Tensor of shape (N, d):param jointconfig: Tensor of shape (B, J):param rangeperdim: Tensor of shape (d, 2):return: sdfval (B, N), sdfgrad (B, N, d) or None """ # Validate points are within range # Note: In practice, this might be used for culling or assertion # isinside(points, rangeperdim) # Set joint configuration in the SDF object # This step internally handles Forward Kinematics to transform points self.sdfobject.setjointconfiguration(jointconfig) # Query the SDF # The underlying C++/CUDA kernel or PyTorch Function handles the batched evaluation sdfval, sdfgrad = self.sdfobject(points, computegrad=self.computegrad) return sdfval, sdfgrad def exampleusage(): # Setup device = torch.device('cuda') d = 3 N = 200 numconfigs = 1000 # Base joint configuration thbase = torch.tensor([0.0, -math.pi / 4.0, 0.0, math.pi / 2.0, 0.0, math.pi / 4.0, 0.0], device=device) # Perturbations for batch thperturbation = torch.randn(numconfigs - 1, 7, device=device) 0.1 th = torch.cat((thbase.view(1, -1), thperturbation + thbase)) # Query points y = 0.02 queryrange = torch.tensor([[-1, 0.5], [y, y], [-0.2, 0.8]], device=device) # Generate coordinates (simulated helper) # coords, pts = getcoordinatesandpointsingrid(0.01, queryrange, device) # For this example, assume pts is generated pts = torch.rand(N, d, device=device) (queryrange[:, 1] - queryrange[:, 0]) + queryrange[:, 0] # Initialize SDF object (mock) # s = CachedSDF(...) # Query without gradients # sdfval, sdfgrad = s(pts, th, computegrad=False) # Query with gradients for optimization th.requiresgrad = True # sdfval, sdfgrad = s(pts, th, computegrad=True) # loss = sdfval.sum() # loss.backward() # print(th.grad) # Contains d(sdfval)/d(th) Parameters: computegrad: Boolean. Default True. If False, skips gradient computation, improving performance. points: Input tensor of shape (N, d). rangeperdim: Input tensor of shape (d, 2). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure joint configurations are normalized or handled correctly if angles wrap around (e.g., -\pi to \pi). Boundaries: Points outside rangeperdim may yield undefined or incorrect SDF values if not pre-filtered. Degenerate Input: Empty point sets or zero-sized batches should be handled gracefully by the underlying batched kernel. Computes SDF values for a single configuration. Use when batch processing is not required. Returns both SDF values and gradients for a single configuration. Use when gradients are needed but batched joint configurations are not. Time and Memory Complexity: Time complexity scales linearly with the number of points N and the number of batched configurations B. Memory complexity is dominated by the storage of B \times N SDF values and gradients. Measured Performance: On an RTX 4070 with an 8-link Kuka robot: Single configuration with 100K points: 3.1 ms. 1000 configurations x 10K points: 198 ms. 5000 configurations x 10K points: 997 ms. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: High throughput for batched queries; supports autograd for optimization. Limitations: Performance degrades with very large batch sizes if memory is constrained; requires GPU acceleration for optimal performance. When to Use: Use for trajectory optimization, collision avoidance, and any scenario requiring gradient-based optimization over joint configurations. When Not to Use: Avoid for single-point queries where overhead of batching is not justified. This method originates from the pytorchvolumetric library by the University of Michigan ARM Lab. It is designed to integrate volumetric SDF representations with robotic kinematics, enabling efficient collision checking and optimization in high-dimensional configuration spaces. name: SDF Value and Gradient Query
head: Live Cursor Measurement Caliper, ObjectFrameSDF query, Step Ruler Caliper, measureSdfRayCaliper
body:
SDF Value and Gradient Query is a method for inspecting Signed Distance Field (SDF) properties at specific 3D coordinates in real-time, typically for debugging, calibration, or precise spatial interaction. It outputs the signed distance d(\mathbf{p}), the analytical normal 
abla d(\mathbf{p}), and hit classification for a given point \mathbf{p}. It differs from SDF Value Computation by focusing on interactive, single-point or sparse inspection rather than bulk volume evaluation, and from Batched SDF Query with Joint Configuration by handling static object frames rather than articulated joint hierarchies. The method supports two primary implementation patterns: interactive ray-casting inspection (caliper) and programmatic object-frame queries. Inputs: A 3D point \mathbf{p} in world or object coordinates; a boolean flag computegrad (default True). Outputs: Signed distance d(\mathbf{p}) \in \mathbb{R}. Gradient/Normal 
abla d(\mathbf{p}) \in \mathbb{R}^3. Hit classification (e.g., COURSE SURFACE, GLASS MARBLE, ABYSS, SKY RAY). Raycasting Scene: A spatial acceleration structure (e.g., o3d.t.geometry.RaycastingScene) storing triangle meshes. Query Points: A tensor or array of shape (N, 3) or (B, N, 3) for batched queries. 1. Point Acquisition: Interactive: Cast a ray from the camera through the mouse cursor to intersect the scene. Determine the 3D world point \mathbf{p}. Programmatic: Generate query points using a grid resolution and query range, or accept user-defined coordinates. 2. Distance and Gradient Computation: Query the SDF representation at \mathbf{p}. If computegrad is True, compute the gradient. For mesh-based SDFs, the gradient is derived from the vector from the query point to the closest point on the surface: \mathbf{g} = \mathbf{p}{closest} - \mathbf{p} 
abla d(\mathbf{p}) =  rac{\mathbf{g}}{\|\mathbf{g}\|} \quad 	ext{if } \|\mathbf{g}\| > 0 If computegrad is False, skip gradient calculation to improve speed. 3. Verification and Classification: Verify the normal magnitude: \|
abla d(\mathbf{p})\| \approx 1.000. Classify the hit target based on material properties or depth (e.g., COURSE SURFACE, ABYSS). Apply a free-space probe offset (e.g., +1m) if required for visualization. 4. Performance Analysis (Optional): Compare optimized marching steps against legacy steps to calculate percentage reduction in steps, often utilizing bounds and \kappa-March optimizations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def querysdfvalueandgradient(mesh, point, computegrad=True): """ Queries the SDF value and gradient for a single point. Args: mesh: A triangle mesh object supporting raycasting or closest point queries. point: A numpy array or tensor of shape (3,) representing [x, y, z]. computegrad: Boolean flag. If False, gradient computation is skipped. Returns: distance: Float, the signed distance. gradient: Numpy array of shape (3,), the normalized gradient/normal. hitinfo: String or enum, classification of the hit target. """ # 1. Find closest point on the mesh surface # Implementation depends on the backend (e.g., Open3D, custom BVH) # Assuming a generic closestpoint query that returns the closest surface point closestpoint = mesh.getclosestpoint(point) # 2. name: Cached SDF
head: CachedSDF, Voxel Grid SDF
body:
Cached SDF accelerates Signed Distance Field queries by storing quantized distance values in a voxel grid, falling back to a ground truth SDF for points outside the cache. It differs from standard SDF primitives by trading far-field precision for significant memory savings and query speed, using Int8 quantization to compress the field. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A ground truth SDF function S{gt}(p), a voxel grid resolution VOXEL (or resolution), a bounding box defined by range\per\dim with padding, and an out-of-bounds strategy. Output: A voxel grid storing quantized signed distances, and a query function returning (d, 
abla d) for any point p. Data Structures: The core structure is a 3D voxel grid of type Int8 (8-bit signed integer). Grid Dimensions: W 	imes H 	imes D, where dimensions are derived from the object's bounding box divided by VOXEL. Chunking: In some implementations, the grid is divided into chunks of size CHUNK 	imes CHUNK 	imes CHUNK (e.g., 32^3) for memory management. Padding: A border of PAD voxels (e.g., 2) surrounds the active region to handle boundary conditions. Quantization Formula: The signed distance d at a voxel center is quantized to an 8-bit integer v using the scale factor SDF\SCALE: v = 	ext{clamp}\left( 	ext{round}\left(  rac{d}{VOXEL} 	imes SDF\SCALE ight), -128, 127 ight) Decoding back to distance: d{decoded} =  rac{v}{SDF\SCALE} 	imes VOXEL Typical parameters include VOXEL = 0.25 meters, SDF\SCALE = 32, and SDF\MAX = 127. Query Algorithm: 1. Transform: Convert query point p from world frame to object frame using the inverse transformation matrix. 2. Grid Lookup: Determine if p lies within the cached voxel grid bounds. If inside: Perform trilinear interpolation of the 8 neighboring Int8 values to get a floating-point distance d{cached}. Compute the gradient 
abla d via finite differences of the interpolated values or by querying the ground truth SDF at the same point if gradient accuracy is critical. If outside: Apply the outofboundsstrategy. Default strategy: Compare p against the object's bounding box. If outside, return a conservative under-approximation or a large constant distance. Alternative strategy (LOOKUPGTSDF): Query the ground truth SDF S{gt}(p) directly. 3. Return: Return (d, 
abla d). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np class CachedSDF: def init(self, sdfgt, voxelsize=0.25, scale=32, padding=2): self.sdfgt = sdfgt self.voxelsize = voxelsize self.scale = scale self.padding = padding self.grid = None self.boundsmin = None self.boundsmax = None def build(self, boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax): """Build the voxel grid from the ground truth SDF.""" # Calculate grid dimensions dims = np.ceil((boundingboxmax - boundingboxmin) / self.voxelsize).astype(int) # Add padding dimspadded = dims + 2 self.padding self.grid = np.zeros(dimspadded, dtype=np.int8) # Define bounds for the active region (excluding padding) self.boundsmin = boundingboxmin self.boundsmax = boundingboxmax # Iterate over voxels and populate for x in range(dimspadded[0]): for y in range(dimspadded[1]): for z in range(dimspadded[2]): # Convert voxel index to world coordinate # Assuming origin at boundingboxmin - padding voxelsize pworld = boundingboxmin + (np.array([x, y, z]) - self.padding) self.voxelsize # Transform to object frame (simplified: assume identity for object frame) pobj = pworld # Query ground truth SDF d = self.sdfgt(pobj) # Quantize # Formula: round(d / VOXEL SDFSCALE), clamped to [-128, 127] val = int(round(d / self.voxelsize self.scale)) val = np.clip(val, -128, 127) self.grid[x, y, z] = val def query(self, pworld): """Query the cached SDF for a point in world coordinates.""" # Transform to object frame pobj = pworld # Placeholder for actual transformation matrix application # Check if inside grid bounds # Calculate voxel coordinates # pobj corresponds to index: (pobj - boundsmin) / voxelsize + padding # We need to check if this index is within [0, dimspadded) # Simplified bounds check if not self.isinsidegrid(pobj): # Out-of-bounds strategy # Default: under-approximate or use GT # For this implementation, we fallback to GT if outside d, grad = self.sdfgt(pobj) return d, grad # Interpolate from grid dcached = self.trilinearinterpolate(pobj) # Gradient approximation (finite difference) eps = self.voxelsize 0.1 dx = self.trilinearinterpolate(pobj + np.array([eps, 0, 0])) - dcached dy = self.trilinearinterpolate(pobj + np.array([0, eps, 0])) - dcached dz = self.trilinearinterpolate(pobj + np.array([0, 0, eps])) - dcached grad = np.array([dx, dy, dz]) / eps return dcached, grad def isinsidegrid(self, pobj): # Check if pobj is within the padded grid bounds # This requires knowing the exact mapping from world to grid indices # For brevity, assuming a helper exists that maps pobj to (i,j,k) # and checks 0 <= i,j,k < grid.shape return True # Placeholder for actual bounds check logic def trilinearinterpolate(self, pobj): # Convert pobj to floating point voxel coordinates # i = (pobj - boundsmin) / voxelsize + padding # Sample 8 neighbors and interpolate # Return decoded distance: val / scale voxelsize return 0.0 # Placeholder for actual interpolation logic Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss: Distances beyond \pm 4 voxels from the surface are saturated to SDF\MAX (127) or -128, losing precision for far-field queries. Out-of-Bounds: The default bounding box comparison for out-of-bounds points always under-approximates the SDF value, which may be insufficient for collision detection requiring strict guarantees. Truncation: Using a Truncated SDF (TSDF) variant reduces grid size significantly (e.g., 150x smaller) by only storing values within truncationdistance of the surface, but out-of-bounds points return the truncation value. A variant where truncationdistance creates a smaller voxel grid covering only the near-surface region. Out-of-bounds points return the truncation value. Choose when memory is constrained and far-field accuracy is not needed. The underlying analytic or high-resolution SDF used to populate the cache and handle out-of-bounds queries. Choose when exact precision is required for complex shapes. Time Complexity: Query time is O(1) for in-bounds points (trilinear interpolation) and O(1) for out-of-bounds if using bounding box check, or O(N) if falling back to ground truth SDF. Memory Complexity: O(W 	imes H 	imes D) bytes, where W,H,D are grid dimensions. Int8 quantization reduces memory by 8x compared to float32. Performance: Dramatically faster than using the ground truth SDF for out-of-bounds queries. Strengths: Low memory footprint, fast query times, suitable for real-time applications. Limitations: Loss of precision for far-field queries, under-approximation for out-of-bounds points with default strategy. Cached SDF was introduced as a method to optimize SDF queries in volumetric representations, particularly in robotics and simulation contexts where frequent distance queries are needed. It leverages the spatial coherence of SDFs to store values in a voxel grid, reducing the computational cost of evaluating complex implicit surfaces. sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, https://github.com/sh1ftmaker/voxel-wars, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) GitHub - UM-ARM-Lab/pytorchvolumetric: Volumetric structures such as..., https://github.com/UM-ARM-Lab/pytorchvolumetric, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: SDF Validity Check with Relaxation
body: This method classifies Signed Distance Field (SDF) samples into positive, negative, and valid near-zero categories by applying a relaxation threshold scaled to the voxel size. It solves the problem of ambiguous SDF magnitudes during ray marching by explicitly identifying samples near the zero-level set. It differs from Batched SDF Inference by focusing on post-evaluation validation rather than generation, and from Eikonal SDF Refinement by using a simple threshold check rather than solving the Eikonal equation for gradient correction. Inputs: sdfvalues: Array of SDF values for a batch of samples. voxelsize: The spatial size of the voxel grid cell. relaxation: A dimensionless constant factor defining the validity threshold. Outputs: validmask: Boolean array indicating which samples are within the valid relaxation band. positivemask: Boolean array for samples with SDF > threshold. negativemask: Boolean array for samples with SDF < -threshold. Data Structures: sdfvalues: 1D or N-dimensional array of floats. validmask, positivemask, negativemask: Boolean arrays of the same shape as sdfvalues. Parameters: relaxation: Default value is 1.5. Steps: 1. Calculate the relaxation threshold: T = \text{voxel\size} \times \text{relaxation}. 2. Identify positive samples: those where \text{sdf} > T. 3. Identify negative samples: those where -\text{sdf} > T (equivalent to \text{sdf} < -T). 4. Identify valid samples: those where |\text{sdf}| \le T. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def checkvalid(sdfvalues, voxelsize, relaxation=1.5): """ Classify SDF samples based on relaxation threshold. Args: sdfvalues: Array of SDF values. voxelsize: Size of one voxel in world units. relaxation: Threshold factor (default 1.5). Returns: validmask: Samples near zero (|sdf| <= threshold). positivemask: Samples far positive (sdf > threshold). negativemask: Samples far negative (sdf < -threshold). """ # Calculate threshold threshold = voxelsize relaxation # Identify positive samples: SDF value > voxelsize relaxation positivemask = sdfvalues > threshold # Identify negative samples: -SDF value > voxelsize relaxation # Equivalent to sdfvalues < -threshold negativemask = -sdfvalues > threshold # Identify valid samples: absolute SDF value <= voxelsize relaxation validmask = abs(sdfvalues) <= threshold return validmask, positivemask, negativemask Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If voxelsize is zero, the threshold becomes zero, potentially misclassifying all non-zero values as invalid. Guard against division by zero or invalid grid configurations. Precision issues near the threshold boundary may cause flickering if the SDF value oscillates around T. Consider using a small epsilon for floating-point comparisons if stability is required. Corrects inaccurate SDF values near the zero-level set by solving the Eikonal equation |\nabla \phi| = 1 over neighboring voxels. It sets itself apart by using an analytical solution to ensure the gradient magnitude is exactly 1, rather than just smoothing values. It builds on this method. Not given in the sources. name: Eikonal SDF Refinement
head: Eikonal Distance Field Solver, Fast Marching SDF Correction
body: Eikonal SDF Refinement corrects inaccurate Signed Distance Field (SDF) values near the zero-level set by solving the Eikonal equation |\nabla \phi| = 1 using a fast-marching style approach over neighboring voxels. It differs from simple relaxation methods by computing an analytical Eikonal solution in 3D and 2D planes to enforce the exact gradient magnitude constraint. It builds on SDF Validity Check with Relaxation. Inputs: A 3D grid of SDF values \phi and grid spacing g. Outputs: Updated SDF values \phi' where the Eikonal constraint is satisfied. Data Structures: phi: 3D array of floats, indexed by (x, y, z). g: Scalar float representing the distance between adjacent voxel centers. Parameters: g: Grid spacing, calculated as g = sdfRadius 2.0 / sdfTexSizeX. Steps: 1. Iterate over every voxel (x, y, z) in the grid. 2. Compute distances to immediate neighbors along the X, Y, and Z axes using neighborMin, which returns min(abs(a), abs(b)) where a and b are the SDF values at kernel + delta and kernel - delta for that axis. 3. Pass the three neighbor distances to eikonal3d. If it returns true, use the result as the candidate distance e. Otherwise, fallback to 2D combinations (eikonal2d for XY, XZ, and YZ planes) and take the minimum valid result. 4. If the computed Eikonal distance e is less than the current voxel value current and current > g, update current = e. Formulas: 3D Eikonal Solution: Given neighbor distances u1, u2, u3 and grid spacing g: e = \frac{1}{n} \left( \sum{i=1}^{n} ui + \sqrt{ \left(\sum{i=1}^{n} ui\right)^2 - n \left( \sum{i=1}^{n} ui^2 - g^2 \right) } \right) where n=3. Returns false if the discriminant d = \left(\sum ui\right)^2 - n \left( \sum ui^2 - g^2 \right) < 0. 2D Eikonal Solution: Given two neighbor distances h, v and grid spacing g: If |h - v| \ge g: e = \min(h, v) + g Else: e = \frac{1}{2} \left( (h+v) + \sqrt{(h+v)^2 - 2(h^2 + v^2 - g^2)} \right). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def eikonal2d(h, v, g): if abs(h - v) >= g: return min(h, v) + g sumhv = h + v sumsq = h2 + v2 discriminant = sumhv2 - 2 (sumsq - g2) if discriminant < 0: return None return 0.5 (sumhv + math.sqrt(discriminant)) def eikonal3d(u, g): n = 3 sumu = sum(u) sumusq = sum(val2 for val in u) discriminant = sumu2 - n (sumusq - g2) if discriminant < 0: return None, False e = (1.0 / n) (sumu + math.sqrt(discriminant)) return e, True def neighbormin(phi, x, y, z, axis): if axis == 0: n1, n2 = phi[x+1, y, z], phi[x-1, y, z] elif axis == 1: n1, n2 = phi[x, y+1, z], phi[x, y-1, z] else: n1, n2 = phi[x, y, z+1], phi[x, y, z-1] return min(abs(n1), abs(n2)) def refinesdf(phi, g): height, width, depth = phi.shape for x in range(1, width - 1): for y in range(1, height - 1): for z in range(1, depth - 1): current = phi[x, y, z] if current <= g: continue u = [ neighbormin(phi, x, y, z, 0), neighbormin(phi, x, y, z, 1), neighbormin(phi, x, y, z, 2) ] beste = current e3d, valid3d = eikonal3d(u, g) if valid3d: beste = min(beste, e3d) else: candidates = [] exy = eikonal2d(u[0], u[1], g) if exy is not None: candidates.append(exy) exz = eikonal2d(u[0], u[2], g) if exz is not None: candidates.append(exz) eyz = eikonal2d(u[1], u[2], g) if eyz is not None: candidates.append(eyz) if candidates: beste = min(beste, min(candidates)) if beste < current: phi[x, y, z] = beste Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The 3D Eikonal solver returns false if the discriminant d < 0, forcing a fallback to 2D planes. This handles degenerate cases where the gradient direction does not align with a single axis or plane. Boundary conditions: The pseudocode assumes interior voxels and requires padding or clamping for grid edges. Precision: The square root and discriminant calculations require floating-point stability. name: SDF Training with Eikonal Loss
head: Implicit Geometric Regularization, Implicit neural representations with Eikonal regularization, Neural SDF Training with Eikonal Regularization, SDF Surface Training with Eikonal Loss, Training of Deep Implicit Surface Networks (SDF MLP)
body:
This method trains a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) to predict a Signed Distance Function (SDF) directly from raw 3D point cloud data by enforcing the Eikonal equation, which requires the gradient magnitude of the SDF to be unity everywhere. Unlike methods that require pre-computed 3D supervision (such as occupancy grids or pre-computed SDFs) or explicit regularization on the zero-level set, this approach relies on implicit geometric regularization to produce high-fidelity surfaces with smooth topology. It sets itself apart from standard SDF evaluation implementations by introducing a specific loss term that penalizes deviations of the gradient norm from 1, thereby ensuring the learned function behaves as a true distance field rather than an arbitrary implicit function. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point cloud P = \{pi\} with associated normals N = \{ni\} (optional) and a bounding box \Omega defining the training volume. Output: An MLP parameterized by 	heta that approximates the signed distance function \phi(x; 	heta). Data Structures: MLP Architecture: A feed-forward neural network. Common configurations include depth D and width W (e.g., D6-W60). The network uses a non-linear differentiable activation function applied entrywise, typically Softplus. Point Cloud Data: Tensors of shape (N, 3) for vertices and (N, 3) for normals. Optimizer State: Parameters for Adam optimizer (learning rate, weight decay). Numbered Steps: 1. Data Preprocessing: Load the point cloud vertices. Center the point cloud by subtracting the mean: P{centered} = P - 	ext{mean}(P). Normalize the 3D space to a bounding box, typically [-1, 1]^3. 2. Pretraining (Optional but Recommended): Sample random points uniformly within the bounding box \Omega. Pretrain the SDF using a "sphere loss" or similar initialization loss to ensure the network starts with a plausible distance field structure. This involves minimizing the distance of points to a unit sphere or similar prior. 3. Sampling: Surface Points: Sample a batch of points xs from the input point cloud P. Eikonal Points: Sample a batch of points xe uniformly from the bounding box \Omega. These points cover the volume, including free space and inside the object, to enforce the gradient constraint globally. 4. Forward Pass & Gradient Computation: Query the MLP for distances and gradients at the sampled points. For surface points xs: Compute distance ds = \phi(xs; 	heta). For eikonal points xe: Compute distance de = \phi(xe; 	heta) and gradient 
abla \phi(xe; 	heta) using automatic differentiation. Note: Ensure requiresgrad=True is set for input points before computing gradients to enable backpropagation. 5. Loss Computation: The total loss \mathcal{L} is a weighted sum of the following terms: Point Cloud Loss (\mathcal{L}{data}): Encourages the SDF to be zero at the observed points. \mathcal{L}{data} =  rac{1}{Ns} \sum{i=1}^{Ns} |\phi(x{s,i}; 	heta)| If normals are available, an additional alignment term can be added: \lambda3 |1 - \langle 
abla{x} \phi(x), n(x) angle|. Eikonal Loss (\mathcal{L}{eikonal}): Enforces the unit gradient magnitude constraint |
abla \phi(x)| = 1. \mathcal{L}{eikonal} =  rac{1}{Ne} \sum{j=1}^{Ne} \left( \|
abla \phi(x{e,j}; 	heta)\|2 - 1 ight)^2 Some implementations use the absolute difference |\|
abla \phi\|2 - 1|. Interior/Free-Space Regularization (Optional): Penalizes points inside the object or in free space to prevent flat regions or spurious outliers. \mathcal{L}{inter} = \mathbb{E}{x \in \Omega} \left[ \exp(- eta0 |de|) ight] Where  eta0 is typically set to 100 (or 1e2). This term is often weighted by interweight. Total Loss: \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}{data} + \lambda{eik} \mathcal{L}{eikonal} + \lambda{inter} \mathcal{L}{inter} Typical values: \lambda{eik} \in [0.01, 0.02], \lambda{inter} varies by config. 6. Optimization: Perform backpropagation: optimizer.zerograd(), loss.backward(), optimizer.step(). Use the Adam optimizer with a learning rate starting at 1e-3 and weight decay 1e-4. Apply a learning rate scheduler (e.g., LambdaLR) decaying every 20 epochs by a factor of 10. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn class NeuralSDF(nn.Module): def init(self, hiddendim=64, numlayers=6): super().init() layers = [] layers.append(nn.Linear(3, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.Softplus()) for in range(numlayers - 1): layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, hiddendim)) layers.append(nn.Softplus()) layers.append(nn.Linear(hiddendim, 1)) self.network = nn.Sequential(layers) def forward(self, x): return self.network(x) def computeeikonalloss(gradient): """ Computes the Eikonal loss: mean squared error of gradient norm from 1. Args: gradient: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing spatial gradients. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ gradnorm = torch.norm(gradient, dim=1, keepdim=True) # Shape (N, 1) return torch.mean((gradnorm - 1.0) 2) def trainsdf(model, pointcloud, bounds, config): """ Trains the SDF model using Eikonal regularization. """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3, weightdecay=1e-4) scheduler = torch.optim.lrscheduler.LambdaLR(optimizer, lrlambda=lambda epoch: 0.1 (epoch // 20)) # Pretraining phase (optional) #... (implement sphere loss pretraining)... for epoch in range(config.numepochs): # 1. Sample points # Surface points from point cloud surfacepoints = samplerandompoints(pointcloud, config.batchsize) # Eikonal points uniformly in bounding box eikonalpoints = samplerandompointsuniform(bounds, config.batchsize) # Ensure gradients are tracked surfacepoints.requiresgrad(True) eikonalpoints.requiresgrad(True) # 2. Forward pass # Surface distances surfacedist = model(surfacepoints).squeeze(-1) # Eikonal distances and gradients eikonaldist = model(eikonalpoints).squeeze(-1) # Compute gradients using autograd gradients = torch.autograd.grad( eikonaldist, eikonalpoints, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(eikonaldist), creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] # 3. Compute Losses # Point cloud loss (L1 distance to 0) lossdata = torch.mean(torch.abs(surfacedist)) # Eikonal loss losseikonal = computeeikonalloss(gradients) # Interior/Free-space regularization (optional) # Penalize points close to zero in the volume to avoid flat regions # Using exp(-beta |dist|) where beta=100 beta = 100.0 lossinter = torch.mean(torch.exp(-beta torch.abs(eikonaldist))) # Total loss totalloss = (lossdata + config.eikonalweight losseikonal + config.interweight lossinter) # 4. Backpropagate optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() scheduler.step() Parameters: eikonalweight: Weight for the gradient magnitude regularization term. Typical value: 0.01 to 0.02. interweight: Weight for the interior/free-space regularization term. batchsize: Number of points sampled per optimization step. bounds: Spatial limits for sampling random eikonal points, typically [-1, 1]^3. learningrate: Initial learning rate for Adam, typically 1e-3. activation: Non-linear activation function, typically Softplus. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Non-Uniqueness: The solution to the Eikonal equation vanishing on a point set is not unique. The method relies on implicit regularization to find a plausible SDF rather than any arbitrary solution. Approximation Quality: The zero-level isosurface only approximates the ground-truth mesh; quality depends on MLP capacity (depth/width). Gradient Computation: requiresgrad=True must be set for input points before computing gradients to enable backpropagation. Precision: Using absolute difference vs. squared difference in Eikonal loss can affect stability; squared difference is more common in literature, while absolute difference is used in some implementations. Compresses a large SDF network into a smaller MLP by minimizing output discrepancy, transferring geometric knowledge from a teacher to a student network. Combines explicit ellipsoidal priors with neural residuals to learn a Signed Directional Distance Function, handling occlusions and avoiding iterative sphere tracing. Defines training for an SDF baseline using Instant-NGP architecture, explicitly including a sign loss for free-space samples to enforce positive SDF values outside the surface. Optimizes an SDF using a multi-resolution tetrahedral grid, combining L1 regression, Eikonal regularization, and weight normalization for efficient mesh extraction. Defines auxiliary loss terms (beyond primary Eikonal) to enforce geometric priors, surface alignment, and smoothness, suppressing free surfaces in unobserved volumes. (No details provided in sources). A network that captures geometric bias between volume rendering and point modeling, trained on high-fidelity points to enhance detail representation. It filters points with predicted variance below a threshold \epsilon to create a set Ps, then optimizes a bias MLP fb using L1 loss against ideal SDF values (assumed 0) on these points: L{bias} =  rac{1}{D{Ps}} \sum |f\epsilon(xP) - (f(xP) + fb(xP))|. Trains a network to predict Unsigned Distance Function (UDF) values and gradients, projecting query points onto the implicit surface via gradient descent and minimizing Chamfer distance. It moves samples x{sample} to the surface using x{moved} = x{sample} -  rac{
abla 	ext{UDF}(x{sample})}{\|
abla 	ext{UDF}(x{sample})\|} \cdot 	ext{UDF}(x{sample}). A critical pitfall is ensuring samples.requiresgrad = True before gradient computation. Represents geometry as a surface S = \{x \mid F(x) = 0\} and transforms it to a volumetric model by computing pseudo-density \sigmai = \Psi(F(xi)) using a Laplace cumulative distribution function parameterized by an optimizable scale  eta. Unlike volumetric radiance fields, it restricts the network to predict density based only on spatial coordinates, allowing color to depend on view direction. A baseline method that trains an MLP to regress a pre-computed approximated SDF using L1 loss, serving as a fidelity comparison. It approximates the SDF locally using s(x) = n^{T} (x - y^) where y^ is the closest point on the surface. This method results in fewer details compared to Eikonal regularization because it approximates the SDF nearby the surface rather than strictly on it. The goal is to regress a feed-forward network to approximate the SDF induced by a surface, preferred over occupancy learning because SDFs are more immediately useful for graphics operations like CSG and distance queries. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of MLP evaluations per batch and the number of epochs. Inference time for a D6-W60 MLP is approximately 20.8 seconds for mesh extraction (Marching Cubes) on a single object. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the MLP size (parameters) and the batch size of points stored in memory during training. Performance: Produces state-of-the-art implicit neural representations with higher fidelity and detail compared to regression-based methods or those requiring 3D supervision. Strengths: Works directly from raw point clouds without pre-computed 3D supervision; enforces smooth, plausible zero-level sets through implicit regularization; differentiable end-to-end. Limitations: Approximation quality is limited by MLP capacity; the solution to the Eikonal equation is not unique, relying on SGD to find a good local minimum; requires careful tuning of regularization weights (\lambda{eik}). When to Use: When high-fidelity surface reconstruction from point clouds is required without access to ground-truth SDFs or occupancy grids. When Not to Use: When real-time inference is critical and MLP evaluation is too slow, or when the input data is extremely noisy and requires explicit topological constraints beyond implicit regularization. The method was introduced by Amos Gropp et al. in 2020 in the paper "Implicit Geometric Regularization for Learning Shapes". It addresses the limitation of previous implicit neural representations that required 3D supervision (pre-computed SDFs or occupancy grids). The key insight is that minimizing the deviation of the gradient norm from 1 (the Eikonal equation) acts as an implicit geometric regularizer, favoring smooth and natural zero-level set surfaces even when trained only on raw point cloud data. It has been widely adopted in subsequent works such as VolSDF and various neural surface rendering pipelines. name: MLP Distillation
head: Knowledge Distillation for SDF, SDF Distillation
body: MLP Distillation compresses a large Signed Distance Function (SDF) network into a smaller MLP by minimizing the output discrepancy between the two networks at sampled points. The teacher network f uses 256 hidden channels, while the student network f{\text{small}} uses 16 hidden channels. The method transfers geometric knowledge from the teacher to the student over a fixed number of iterations before replacing the teacher for subsequent finetuning. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A pre-trained large SDF network f (teacher) with 256 hidden channels, a randomly initialized small SDF network f{\text{small}} (student) with 16 hidden channels, and a set of training rays \mathbf{r} sampled from the training dataset. Output: The updated weights of the distilled small SDF network f{\text{small}}. Data Structures: Teacher Network f: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 256 hidden units. Student Network f{\text{small}}: Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 16 hidden units. Sampled Points \mathbf{x}i: 3D coordinates along the training rays. Parameters: Distillation Iterations: 5,000 iterations. Loss Function: L1 loss. Gradient Handling: Stop gradient applied to teacher outputs. Algorithm: 1. Sampling: For each of the 5,000 distillation iterations, sample a batch of random rays \mathbf{r} from the training set. 2. Point Evaluation: For each ray, evaluate the teacher network f and the student network f{\text{small}} at the sampled points \mathbf{x}i along the ray. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the distillation loss \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} using the L1 norm of the difference between the teacher's and student's SDF outputs. A stop gradient operation is applied to the teacher's output to prevent it from updating during this phase. \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}}(\mathbf{r}):= \sum{i=0}^{N-1} |f(\mathbf{x}i) - f{\text{small}}(\mathbf{x}i)| where N is the number of sampled points per ray. 4. Optimization: Update the weights of f{\text{small}} by minimizing \mathcal{L}{\text{dist}} using gradient descent. 5. Replacement: After 5,000 iterations, discard the original teacher network f and replace it with the distilled network f{\text{small}} for subsequent finetuning stages. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mlpdistillation(teachermodel, studentmodel, trainingrays, iterations=5000): # teachermodel: MLP with 256 channels # studentmodel: MLP with 16 channels for iteration in range(iterations): # 1. Sample random rays from the training set raysbatch = sampletrainingrays(trainingrays) # 2. Extract 3D coordinates xi along the rays points = raysbatch.points # 3. Evaluate teacher network with stop gradient teacheroutputs = teachermodel.forward(points, stopgradient=True) # 4. Evaluate student network studentoutputs = studentmodel.forward(points) # 5. Compute L1 loss: Ldist(r) = sum{i=0}^{N-1} |f(xi) - fsmall(xi)| loss = sum(abs(teacheroutputs - studentoutputs)) # 6. Update student weights via gradient descent gradients = computegradients(loss, studentmodel.parameters()) studentmodel.updateweights(gradients) # 7. Discard original teacher and switch to distilled counterpart for finetuning return studentmodel Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Ensure the student network is initialized with appropriate weights to avoid vanishing gradients during the initial distillation steps. Boundaries: The method assumes the sampled points \mathbf{x}i are within the domain where the teacher model provides meaningful SDF values. Degenerate Input: If the training rays do not cover the scene uniformly, the distilled model may inherit biases from the teacher's sampling distribution. Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic method for converting trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models between heterogeneous architectures, including MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, and hash tables. It solves the problem of architectural incompatibility by constructing a unified two-level view of volume representations and performing distillation progressively from shallower to deeper levels. Unlike methods that distill only between identical architectures, PVD enables any-to-any conversion while maintaining teacher performance, leveraging a block-wise training strategy to accelerate the process significantly. Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) Training is a method for learning implicit surface representations from oriented point clouds by supervising a neural network to output a probability distribution over depths rather than a single scalar value. It solves the problem of representing discontinuous directed distance fields (DDFs) with a continuous (C^1) network, enabling accurate modeling of surface occlusions and visibility transitions. It distinguishes itself from standard SDF training by explicitly modeling depth as a discrete mixture of delta functions and enforcing view consistency inequalities to ensure geometric coherence across different viewing directions. Time Complexity: The distillation process requires 5,000 iterations of forward and backward passes through both networks. Memory Complexity: The student network uses significantly less memory than the teacher (16 channels vs. 256 channels). Measured Performance: The method enables the use of a small 16-channel MLP for inference while maintaining the geometric accuracy of a 256-channel MLP. Strengths: Significant reduction in model size and inference latency; preserves high-quality geometry learned by the teacher. Limitations: Requires a pre-trained large teacher model; distillation quality depends on the coverage of sampled points. When to Use: When real-time rendering is required but the initial training used a large, slow network. When Not to Use: When the teacher model is not available or when the scene geometry is too complex for a small MLP to capture even with distillation. MLP Distillation was introduced in the context of HybridNeRF, an efficient neural rendering method that combines volumetric and surface-based approaches. The method addresses the challenge of complex backgrounds and the high cost of separate NeRF background models. By distilling a large SDF into a smaller one, it enables real-time rendering without doubling inference costs. The approach builds on SDF Training with Eikonal Loss, using the large network to learn accurate scene geometry before compression. name: Progressive Volume Distillation
head: PVD
body: Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) is a systematic method for converting trained Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) models between heterogeneous architectures, including MLPs, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, and hash tables. It solves the problem of architectural incompatibility by constructing a unified two-level view of volume representations and performing distillation progressively from shallower to deeper levels. Unlike methods that distill only between identical architectures, PVD enables any-to-any conversion while maintaining teacher performance, leveraging a block-wise training strategy to accelerate the process significantly. Inputs and Outputs Input: A trained teacher model \phi^ (of any architecture: Hash, VM, MLP, or Tensor) and a target student architecture (different from or same as the teacher). Output: A trained student model \phis that approximates the teacher's radiance field. Data Structures and Unified View PVD maps all NeRF architectures to a unified two-level view consisting of a feature extraction stage \phi1^ and a decoding stage \phi2^. The teacher model is split into two cascaded modules: \phi^(x, d) = \phi2^(\phi1^(x, d)) where x is the 3D coordinate and d is the view direction. The split depends on the architecture: 1. Hybrid Representations: \phi1^ is the explicit part (e.g., hash table lookup, tensor grid access) and \phi2^ is the implicit part (e.g., MLP decoder). 2. Purely Implicit (MLP): The network is split by depth. \phi1^ comprises the first K layers, and \phi2^ comprises the remaining layers. Default K=4. 3. Purely Explicit (Plenoxels): \phi2^ is set to an identity function, as the explicit grid directly outputs density and color. Loss Functions The total loss L combines volume-aligned loss, density loss, color loss, RGB loss, and regularization: L = \omega1 L{v2} + \omega2 L{\sigma 2} + \omega3 L{c 2} + \omega4 L{rgb 2} + \omega5 L{reg} where \|\cdot\|^2 denotes the squared L2 norm. 1. Volume-Aligned Loss (L{v2}): Aligns the intermediate feature outputs of the teacher and student. L{v2} = \| \phi{1t}^(x, d) - \phi{1s}^(x, d) \|^2 where \phi{1t}^ and \phi{1s}^ are the outputs of the first stage for the teacher and student, respectively. 2. Density Loss (L{\sigma 2}): Matches the density \sigma after clipping to a constrained range [a, b] to ensure numerical stability. L{\sigma 2} = \| \min(\max(\sigmat, a), b) - \min(\max(\sigmas, a), b) \|^2 where \sigmat and \sigmas are the teacher and student densities. The range [a, b] limits values that are physically consistent (transparent or opaque) but numerically unstable. 3. Color Loss (L{c 2}): Matches the color outputs. L{c 2} = \| ct - cs \|^2 where ct and cs are the color outputs. 4. RGB Loss (L{rgb 2}): Matches the final rendered RGB values. L{rgb 2} = \| \text{RGB}t - \text{RGB}s \|^2 5. Regularization (L{reg}): Applied only to specific explicit or hybrid students. For Plenoxels and VM-decomposition: Add L1 sparsity loss and Total Variation (TV) regularization loss. For other architectures: Not applied (or zero). Parameters Loss Weights: \omega1 = 2 \times 10^{-3} (volume-aligned), \omega2 = 2 \times 10^{-3} (density), \omega3 = 2 \times 10^{-3} (color), \omega4 = 1 (RGB). \omega5 is not explicitly given in the sources. Density Range [a, b]: Specific values for a and b are not given in the sources, but the clipping function \min(\max(\sigma, a), b) is mandatory. Optimization: Adam Optimizer with initial learning rate 0.02. Batch Size: 4096 rays. Total Steps: 20,000 steps. Algorithm: Block-wise Distillation To accelerate training, PVD uses a block-wise strategy that progressively unfreezes deeper stages of the student network, leveraging the volume-aligned loss to stabilize early training. 1. Stage 1 (Steps 1–3,000): Forward pass only through the student's first stage \phi{1s}^ to compute L{v2} and L{\sigma 2} (using teacher's \phi{1t}^ and \sigmat). Backpropagate gradients to update \phi{1s}^. Note: The teacher's \phi{1t}^ is frozen and used as a reference. 2. Stage 2 (Steps 3,001–8,000): Forward pass through student's \phi{1s}^ and \phi{2s}^ to compute intermediate outputs. Compute L{v2}, L{\sigma 2}, L{c 2}, and L{reg} (if applicable). Backpropagate gradients to update \phi{1s}^ and \phi{2s}^. 3. Stage 3 (Steps 8,001–20,000): Forward pass through the full student network \phis^ to compute final rendered RGB. Compute full loss L including L{rgb 2}. Backpropagate gradients to update all student parameters. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressivevolumedistillation(teachermodel, studentmodel, numsteps=20000, batchsize=4096, lr=0.02, a=0.0, b=10.0): # Loss weights from wv2, ws2, wc2, wrgb = 2e-3, 2e-3, 2e-3, 1.0 wreg = 1.0 # Not given in sources optimizer = Optimizer(studentmodel.parameters(), lr=lr) for step in range(1, numsteps + 1): rays = samplerays(batchsize) # Teacher forward pass (frozen) with torch.nograd(): tfeat = teachermodel.phi1(rays.x, rays.d) tsigma = getdensity(tfeat) tcolor = getcolor(tfeat, rays.d) trgb = renderray(teachermodel, rays) # Student forward pass Stage 1 sfeat = studentmodel.phi1(rays.x, rays.d) ssigma = getdensity(sfeat) scolor = getcolor(sfeat, rays.d) # Losses lossv2 = mse(sfeat, tfeat) losss2 = mse(clip(tsigma, a, b), clip(ssigma, a, b)) lossc2 = mse(scolor, tcolor) if step <= 3000: loss = wv2 lossv2 + ws2 losss2 optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() elif step <= 8000: lossreg = regularizationloss(studentmodel) if studentmodel.isexplicit else 0.0 loss = wv2 lossv2 + ws2 losss2 + wc2 lossc2 + wreg lossreg optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() else: srgb = renderray(studentmodel, rays) lossrgb = mse(srgb, trgb) lossreg = regularizationloss(studentmodel) if studentmodel.isexplicit else 0.0 loss = wv2 lossv2 + ws2 losss2 + wc2 lossc2 + wrgb lossrgb + wreg lossreg optimizer.zerograd() loss.backward() optimizer.step() def mse(a, b): return sum((x - y)2 for x, y in zip(a, b)) / len(a) def clip(x, lo, hi): return max(lo, min(hi, x)) def samplerays(n): return [(randompoint(), randomdirection()) for in range(n)] def getdensity(feat): return feat # Simplified for pseudocode def getcolor(feat, d): return feat # Simplified for pseudocode def renderray(model, rays): return [integrateray(model, r) for r in rays] def regularizationloss(model): return l1norm(model.weights) + tvnorm(model.weights) class Optimizer: def init(self, params, lr): self.params = params; self.lr = lr def zerograd(self): [p.grad.zero() for p in self.params] def step(self): [p.data -= self.lr p.grad for p in self.params] Edge Cases and Pitfalls Numerical Instability: Optimizing density \sigma directly is unstable. Clipping \sigma to [a, b] is required. Gradient Saturation: Applying density loss on \exp(-\sigmai \deltai) is inefficient due to gradient saturation and high computational cost of exponentials during block-wise implementation. Architecture Split: For purely explicit models (Plenoxels), \phi2^ is identity, so no MLP decoding occurs. A method for mutual conversion between different NeRF architectures (implicit, explicit, hybrid) using a unified two-level view and active learning strategies to accelerate distillation and improve synthesis quality. Time Complexity: Distillation is significantly faster than training from scratch. An MLP-based NeRF distilled from a hashtable-based Instant-NGP model takes 1.5 hours compared to 25 hours for training from scratch. Speedup Factor: 10x to 20x faster than training the original NeRF from scratch. Memory Complexity: Depends on the student architecture. The method itself does not add significant memory overhead beyond storing the teacher and student models. Performance: Maintains teacher performance levels. Conversions between Hash, VM, MLP, and Tensors maintain performance comparable to the teacher model and training from scratch. Strengths: Enables any-to-any conversion; accelerates training; improves synthesis quality via density clipping and volume-aligned loss. Limitations: Requires a trained teacher model; performance depends on the quality of the teacher. Hardware: Experiments performed on a single NVIDIA V100 GPU. Progressive Volume Distillation was proposed in the paper "One Is All: Bridging the Gap between Neural Radiance Fields Architectures with Progressive Volume Distillation". It addresses the diversity of NeRF architectures (MLP, sparse tensors, low-rank tensors, hash tables) which have different trade-offs in training speed, rendering speed, and geometric manipulability. Prior methods focused on distilling between models of the same architecture, whereas PVD provides a systematic framework for heterogeneous conversion. The method was validated on NeRF-Synthetic, LLFF, and TanksAndTemples datasets. One Is All: Bridging the Gap between Neural Radiance Fields Architectures with Progressive Volume Distillation, https://doi.org/10.1609/aaai.v37i1.25135, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning
head: PVD-AL
body: Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning (PVD-AL) is a method for mutual conversion between different Neural Radiance Field (NeRF) architectures (implicit, explicit, and hybrid). It accelerates distillation and improves synthesis quality by splitting the teacher and student models into cascaded modules and applying active learning strategies to select important camera poses, rays, and sample points. It sets itself apart from standard distillation by using a block-wise training schedule that spares networks from forwarding the entire network and rendering RGB outputs in early phases, and by dynamically selecting hard examples across three levels of granularity. Inputs: Teacher model \phi^t (architecture can be MLP, hybrid, or Plenoxels). Student model \phi^s (target architecture). Training dataset containing camera poses and rays. Hyperparameters: \omega1, \dots, \omega5 (loss weights), K (split point for MLP layers), N{sp} (number of important sample points). Outputs: Distilled student model \phi^s. The method operates on three levels of active learning sets, updated per epoch: 1. TCP (Important Camera Poses): A set of camera poses identified as difficult for the student. 2. TSR (Important Sample Rays): A set of rays identified as difficult. 3. TSP (Important Sample Points): A set of 3D points along rays identified as difficult, selected based on weight metrics. The core mechanism splits any model \phi^ into a cascade of two modules: \phi^(x, d) = \phi^2(\phi^1(x, d)) For MLP NeRF: \phi^1 consists of the first K layers; \phi^2 consists of the remaining layers. For Hybrid Representations: \phi^1 is the explicit part (e.g., voxel grid); \phi^2 is the implicit part (e.g., MLP). For Plenoxels (Purely Explicit): \phi^1 is the full grid; \phi^2 is the identity function. The total loss L is a weighted sum of five terms: L = \omega1 L{v2} + \omega2 L{\sigma 2} + \omega3 L{c 2} + \omega4 L{\text{rgb} 2} + \omega5 L{\text{reg}} 1. Volume-aligned loss (L{v2}): Aligns the outputs of the first module \phi1 between teacher and student: L{v2} = || \phi{1t}(x, d) - \phi{1s}(x, d) ||2^2 where \phi{1t} and \phi{1s} are the outputs of the first module for the teacher and student, respectively. 2. Density loss (L{\sigma 2}): Mean-squared error (MSE) between teacher and student density \sigma. 3. Color loss (L{c 2}): MSE between teacher and student color c. 4. RGB loss (L{\text{rgb} 2}): MSE between rendered RGB images. 5. Regularization (L{\text{reg}}): Depends on the student model; for Plenoxels and VM-decomposition, it includes L1 sparsity loss and Total Variation (TV) regularization. 1. Initialization: Initialize TCP, TSR, and TSP sets. 2. Epoch Loop: For each training epoch: a. Pose Selection: Generate random poses and select important poses from TCP to form trainposes. b. Ray Sampling: Sample rays from trainposes to form allbatchrays. c. Batch Processing: For each batch of rays: i. Ray Selection: Generate random rays and select important rays from TSR to form trainrays. ii. Point Sampling: Sample points from trainrays to form traindata. iii. Forward Pass: Forward traindata through both teacher (teamodel) and student (stumodel) to get outputs teaout and stuout. iv. Point Selection (Active Learning): Extract weight metrics PW from teaout and stuout (specifically density/color weights). Sort points by PW to get indices sortedPW. Select the top N{sp} points as TSP: TSP = sortedPW[:Nsp]. v. Loss Calculation: Calculate L{\sigma 2} and L{c 2} using only the points in TSP. Calculate L{v2} using all points in traindata. Calculate L{\text{rgb} 2} and L{\text{reg}} as appropriate. vi. Backpropagation: Update student model parameters using total loss L. 3. Update Active Sets: Update TCP, TSR, and TSP based on training progress (details of update logic not fully specified in source, but implied by "continually analyze"). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainpvdal(teamodel, stumodel, traindataset, hyperparams): """ teamodel: Teacher NeRF model stumodel: Student NeRF model traindataset: Dataset containing camera poses and rays hyperparams: Dictionary containing omega weights, K, Nsp, numepochs """ # Initialize active learning sets TCP = set() # Important Camera Poses TSR = set() # Important Sample Rays TSP = set() # Important Sample Points # Split models based on architecture # For MLP: teamodel1 = teamodel[:K], teamodel2 = teamodel[K:] # For Hybrid: teamodel1 = explicitpart, teamodel2 = implicitpart # For Plenoxels: teamodel1 = fullgrid, teamodel2 = identity for epoch in range(hyperparams.numepochs): # 1. Active Learning: Camera Poses # Generate random poses randomposes = [traindataset.getpose(i) for i in range(hyperparams.numposes)] # Select important poses from TCP selectedtcpposes = random.sample(list(TCP), min(10, len(TCP))) trainposes = randomposes + selectedtcpposes # 2. Sample Rays allbatchrays = [traindataset.sampleraysfrompose(p) for p in trainposes] for batchrays in allbatchrays: # 3. Active Learning: Rays # Generate random rays randomrays = [traindataset.sampleray() for in range(len(batchrays))] # Select important rays from TSR selectedtsrrays = random.sample(list(TSR), min(10, len(TSR))) trainrays = randomrays + selectedtsrrays # 4. Sample Points traindata = [traindataset.samplepointsonray(r) for r in trainrays] # 5. Forward Pass teaout = teamodel(traindata) stuout = stumodel(traindata) # 6. Active Learning: Points (TSP) # Extract weights (e.g., density or color magnitude) teaweights = [abs(o.density) for o in teaout] stuweights = [abs(o.density) for o in stuout] combinedweights = [t + s for t, s in zip(teaweights, stuweights)] # Sort points by weight (descending) sortedindices = sorted(range(len(combinedweights)), key=lambda i: combinedweights[i], reverse=True) # Select top Nsp points TSPindices = sortedindices[:hyperparams.Nsp] # 7. Loss Calculation # Volume-aligned loss on all points Lv2 = sum((t.phi1 - s.phi1)2 for t, s in zip(teaout, stuout)) / len(teaout) # Density and Color losses on TSP only teaouttsp = [teaout[i] for i in TSPindices] stuouttsp = [stuout[i] for i in TSPindices] Lsigma2 = sum((t.density - s.density)2 for t, s in zip(teaouttsp, stuouttsp)) / len(teaouttsp) Lc2 = sum((t.color - s.color)2 for t, s in zip(teaouttsp, stuouttsp)) / len(teaouttsp) # RGB and Regularization losses # Note: RGB loss requires rendering full images, which is skipped in early block-wise phases # For simplicity, assuming standard rendering for these losses Lrgb2 = computergbloss(teamodel, stumodel, trainrays) Lreg = computeregularization(stumodel) # Total Loss L = (hyperparams.omega1 Lv2 + hyperparams.omega2 Lsigma2 + hyperparams.omega3 Lc2 + hyperparams.omega4 Lrgb2 + hyperparams.omega5 Lreg) # 8. Backpropagation stumodel.zerograd() L.backward() stumodel.step() # 9. Update Active Sets (Simplified) # Add current difficult poses/rays/points to sets TCP.update(trainposes) TSR.update(trainrays) TSP.update(TSPindices) def computergbloss(teamodel, stumodel, rays): """Renders RGB images for teacher and student and computes MSE.""" # Implementation depends on renderer; returns scalar MSE pass def computeregularization(model): """Computes L1 sparsity and TV regularization based on student architecture.""" # Implementation depends on student model type pass Numerical Instability in Density Loss: The density loss L{\sigma 2} is hard to optimize directly because density reflects light transmittance, leading to numerical instability when \sigma is very high or very low (completely transparent or opaque). Mitigation: This is handled by: 1. Density Range Constraint: Clipping the density values. 2. Volume-Aligned Loss: Using L{v2} to stabilize training by aligning intermediate representations rather than just final outputs. 3. Block-wise Distillation: In early training phases, only forward stage 1 (\phi1) to spare networks from forwarding the entire network and rendering RGB outputs, which significantly accelerates the distillation process. Time: The block-wise strategy accelerates distillation by sparing networks from forwarding the entire network and rendering RGB outputs in early phases. Active learning reduces the number of samples needed to grasp complex concepts compared to traditional supervised learning. Memory: Memory usage depends on the student architecture (MLP, sparse tensor, etc.) and the size of the active learning sets (TCP, TSR, TSP). Strengths: Enables mutual conversion between different NeRF architectures (implicit, explicit, hybrid). Significantly improves synthesis quality and accelerates training compared to standard distillation. Three-level active learning (poses, rays, points) efficiently transfers knowledge by focusing on difficult examples. Limitations: Density loss optimization remains challenging without the specific mitigations (clipping, volume-aligned loss). Use when converting between different NeRF architectures (e.g., MLP to Plenoxels) and needing high-quality results with faster training. Use when computational resources are limited and active learning can reduce the number of required training samples. PVD-AL was introduced in the paper "Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning for Efficient NeRF Architecture Conversion". It builds upon the Progressive Volume Distillation (PVD) method [Parent], which allows any-to-any conversions between NeRF architectures by distilling progressively on different levels of volume representations [Parent]. The method addresses the inefficiency of traditional distillation by introducing active learning strategies and a block-wise training schedule. It leverages the observation that different parts of a NeRF model correspond to different learning objectives, allowing for modular distillation. Progressive Volume Distillation with Active Learning for Efficient NeRF Architecture Conversion, https://doi.org/10.1007/s11263-026-02815-1, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) Training
head: DDF Learning and Loss Functions, PDDF Optimization, Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF), View Consistency Inequality
body:
Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) Training is a method for learning implicit surface representations from oriented point clouds by supervising a neural network to output a probability distribution over depths rather than a single scalar value. It solves the problem of representing discontinuous directed distance fields (DDFs) with a continuous (C^1) network, enabling accurate modeling of surface occlusions and visibility transitions. It distinguishes itself from standard SDF training by explicitly modeling depth as a discrete mixture of delta functions and enforcing view consistency inequalities to ensure geometric coherence across different viewing directions. Inputs and Outputs: The network takes an oriented point 	au = (p, v) as input, where p \in B is a 3D position and v \in S^2 is a viewing direction. The network predicts a visibility scalar \xib(p, v) \in [0, 1] and a probabilistic depth distribution P{p,v}(d). The distribution is a mixture of K Dirac delta functions: P{p,v}(d) = \sum{i=1}^K wi(p, v) \delta(d - di(p, v)) where wi are mixture weights (\sum wi = 1) and di are delta locations. The final predicted depth is d{i^} where i^ = \arg\maxi wi. Data Structures: The network outputs K+1 values per oriented point: \xib (visibility prediction), di (depth component i for i=1 \dots K), and wi (weight component i for i=1 \dots K). The weights are constrained such that \sum{i=1}^K wi = 1. Numbered Steps: 1. Data Extraction: Generate six types of samples (p, v) from the mesh to train the network: (U) Uniform: Random (p, v) within the bounding volume and sphere. (A) At-surface: Samples where ground truth visibility \xi(p, v) = 1. (B) Bounding: Samples where p \in \partial B (boundary of bounding volume) and v points interior. (S) Surface: Samples where p \in S (on the surface) and v is uniformly distributed on the sphere U[S^2]. (T) Tangent: Samples where v lies in the tangent space of the surface point q(p, v) \in S. (O) Offset: Samples where p is offset from (T) samples along the surface normal n(p, v) by a small value. 2. View Consistency Inequality Enforcement: Ensure that if a surface point q1 is visible from 	au1 = (p1, v1) (i.e., q1 = p1 + d(	au1)v1 \in S) and q1 also lies on the ray from 	au2 = (p2, v2) (i.e., \exists t > 0 such that p2 + t v2 = q1), then: (i) \xi(	au2) = 1 (the point is visible from 	au2) and (ii) d(	au2) \le ||p2 - q1||2 = t (the depth from 	au2 is no greater than the distance to the known surface point). 3. Loss Computation: Compute the following loss terms per oriented point: Minimum Distance Loss: Trains the highest probability depth component i^ = \arg\maxj wj: \mathcal{L}d = \xi |d{b i^} - d|. Visibility Loss: Binary cross-entropy between ground truth \xi and prediction \xib: \mathcal{L}\xi = 	ext{BCE}(\xi, \xib). First-Order Normals Loss: Matches surface normals derived from 
ablap d{b i^} to ground truth normals n: \mathcal{L}n = -\xi |n^T n{b i^}(p, v)|. Directed Eikonal Regularization: Applied to visibility and each delta component di: \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} = \gamma{	ext{E},d} \sum{i=1}^K \xi [
ablai \widehat{d}i v + 1]^2 + \gamma{	ext{E},\xi} [
abla\xi \widehat{\xi} v]^2. Weight Field Regularization: Encourages low entropy (preventing unnecessary switching of i^) and transition at discontinuities: \mathcal{L}W = \gammaV \mathcal{L}V + \gammaT \mathcal{L}T. 4. Optimization: Minimize the total loss \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}d + \mathcal{L}\xi + \mathcal{L}n + \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} + \mathcal{L}W using gradient descent. Parameters: K: Number of Dirac delta components. Typical value is K=2 to represent discontinuities without sacrificing efficiency. \gamma{	ext{E},d}, \gamma{	ext{E},\xi}: Eikonal regularization weights. \gammaV, \gammaT: Weight field regularization weights. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuities: Standard DDFs are discontinuous at surface collisions and occlusions. PDDF handles this by allowing the weight field w(p, v) to smoothly transition from one index i^ to another j at discontinuities, causing the selected delta component d{i^} to jump to dj, creating the desired discontinuity in d while keeping the network C^1. Precision: The use of \arg\max for i^ introduces a non-differentiable step. The smooth transition of weights ensures that the distribution is differentiable, but the final depth selection is discrete. The loss functions are designed to train the components such that the correct component has the highest weight. The PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss (\mathcal{L}S) is the primary training objective for Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields, designed to supervise the network's prediction of visibility, surface normals, and a mixture of depth components. It solves the problem of learning accurate implicit surface representations from oriented point clouds by combining geometric consistency, visibility prediction, and regularization of the probabilistic weight fields. It distinguishes itself from standard SDF training by explicitly modeling depth as a discrete mixture of delta functions (PDDF) and enforcing transitions between these components at surface discontinuities via a dedicated weight transition loss. Time Complexity: Rendering is a single forward pass per pixel, independent of mesh complexity. Training requires generating samples and computing gradients for all loss terms. Memory Complexity: The network stores weights for K depth components and visibility. For K=2, this is minimal overhead over a standard DDF. Strengths: Handles discontinuities (occlusions, self-occlusions) naturally via the probabilistic mixture. View consistency is enforced. Efficient rendering. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of weight field regularization to prevent unnecessary switching of i^. The discrete selection of i^ is non-differentiable, though the underlying distribution is smooth. When to use: When learning implicit surfaces from oriented point clouds or meshes where occlusions and visibility changes are significant. When not to use: For simple, convex, or non-occluding shapes where a standard SDF or DDF suffices. Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields were introduced to address the limitations of standard Directed Distance Fields (DDFs) in representing discontinuous fields with continuous neural networks. The method builds on the properties of DDFs, specifically the View Consistency Inequality, which ensures geometric coherence across viewing directions. The key innovation is the modification of the depth field d to output a probability distribution over depths, allowing a C^1 network to represent discontinuous fields. This approach is particularly useful for differentiable rendering and shape reconstruction from oriented point clouds. Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations, https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2025.3594225, fetched 2026-10-29
