name: PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss
head: PDDF loss
body:
The PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss (\mathcal{L}S) is the training objective for Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDF), a method that represents 3D shapes using a probabilistic distribution over directed distance components. It solves the problem of training neural networks to predict depth, visibility, and surface normals from oriented point data by combining a minimum distance loss, visibility and normal matching, Directed Eikonal regularization, and weight field regularizations. It sets itself apart from standard SDF training by explicitly modeling the uncertainty and switching between multiple delta components via a probabilistic weight field, rather than predicting a single deterministic distance value. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Oriented points (p, v) where p is position and v is view direction. Ground truth data includes visibility \xi, surface normal n, and depth d. Predictions from the network are visibility \hat{\xi}, depth components \hat{d}i, and weights wi for i \in \{1, \dots, K\}. Outputs: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}S. Data Structures: K: Number of delta components. Sources specify K=2. i^: The maximum likelihood index, defined as i^ = \arg \maxj wj. \hat{d}{b{i^}}: The depth component corresponding to the maximum likelihood index. n{b{i^}}(p, v): The surface normal derived from the gradient of the predicted depth at the maximum likelihood index, 
ablap \hat{d}{b{i^}}. Formulas: The total loss is a weighted sum of five components: \mathcal{L}S = \gammad \mathcal{L}d + \gamma\xi \mathcal{L}\xi + \gamman \mathcal{L}n + \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} + \mathcal{L}W \quad (2) 1. Minimum Distance Loss (\mathcal{L}d): Trains the highest probability depth component to match the ground truth depth. \mathcal{L}d = \xi | \hat{d}{b{i^}} - d | where \xi is the ground truth visibility. 2. Visibility Objective (\mathcal{L}\xi): Binary cross-entropy between predicted visibility \hat{\xi} and ground truth visibility \xib (denoted as \xi in the loss formula context, but \xib in the definition). \mathcal{L}\xi = 	ext{BCE}(\hat{\xi}, \xib) 3. Normals Loss (\mathcal{L}n): Matches the predicted surface normal (derived from 
ablap \hat{d}{b{i^}}) to the ground truth normal n. \mathcal{L}n = -\xi | n^T n{b{i^}}(p, v) | 4. Directed Eikonal Regularization (\mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}}): Applied to the visibility and each delta component of depth, analogous to SDF work. \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} = \gamma{	ext{E},d} \sumi \xi \left[ 
ablai \hat{d}i v + 1 ight]^2 + \gamma{	ext{E},\xi} [
abla\xi \hat{\xi} v]^2 where 
ablai denotes the gradient with respect to the i-th component. 5. Weight Field Regularization (\mathcal{L}W): Encourages low entropy outputs and controlled transitions. \mathcal{L}W = \gammaV \mathcal{L}V + \gammaT \mathcal{L}T Weight Variance Loss (\mathcal{L}V): Encourages low entropy PDDF outputs to prevent i^ from switching unnecessarily. \mathcal{L}V = \sumi wi Weight Transition Loss (\mathcal{L}T): Encourages the maximum likelihood delta component to change i^ when a discontinuity is required. \mathcal{L}T = \max(0, \varepsilonT - |
ablap w{1n}|)^2 where \varepsilonT is a hyper-parameter controlling the desired transition speed. Parameters: \gammad, \gamma\xi, \gamman, \gammaV, \gammaT, \gamma{	ext{E},d}, \gamma{	ext{E},\xi}: Weighting hyper-parameters for each loss term. Values not given in the sources. \varepsilonT: Hyper-parameter for transition speed. Value not given in the sources. K=2: The number of delta components. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pddfshapefittingloss(p, v, dgt, ngt, xigt, xibgt, dpred, xipred, wpred, gammad, gammaxi, gamman, gammaV, gammaT, gammaEd, gammaExi, epsilonT): """ Computes the PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss. Args: p: Position tensor. v: View direction tensor. dgt: Ground truth depth tensor. ngt: Ground truth normal tensor. xigt: Ground truth visibility tensor. xibgt: Ground truth visibility tensor for BCE (xib in source). dpred: Predicted depth components tensor [K,...]. xipred: Predicted visibility tensor. wpred: Predicted weights tensor [K,...]. gammad, gammaxi, gamman, gammaV, gammaT, gammaEd, gammaExi: Loss weights. epsilonT: Transition speed hyper-parameter. Returns: Total loss scalar. """ # Find maximum likelihood index i # wpred shape: [K,...] # argmax returns indices along dim 0 istar = torch.argmax(wpred, dim=0) # Gather the depth component corresponding to i # dpred shape: [K,...] # We need to index dpred with istar. # Assuming standard broadcasting or gather implementation: # dbistar = dpred[istar,...] # Note: In a real implementation, gather or advanced indexing is used. # Here we assume a helper or direct indexing if shapes align. # For simplicity in pseudocode, we assume dpred[istar] retrieves the correct component. dbistar = dpred[istar] # Compute predicted normal from gradient of dbistar w.r.t p # nbistar = gradient(dbistar, p) # Note: Source says nbi(p,v) via gradp dbi. # We assume a function computegradient that returns the gradient vector. nbistar = computegradient(dbistar, p) # 1. Minimum Distance Loss Ld # Ld = xi | dbi - d | # xi is ground truth visibility (xigt) Ld = xigt torch.abs(dbistar - dgt) # 2. Visibility Objective Lxi # Lxi = BCE(xi, xib) # xi is prediction (xipred), xib is ground truth (xibgt) Lxi = binarycrossentropy(xipred, xibgt) # 3. Normals Loss Ln # Ln = -xi | n^T nbi | # n is ground truth normal (ngt) # xi is ground truth visibility (xigt) dotproduct = torch.sum(ngt nbistar, dim=-1) Ln = -xigt torch.abs(dotproduct) # 4. Directed Eikonal Regularization LDE # LDE = gammaEd sumi [ xi (gradi(di). v + 1)^2 ] + gammaExi [ xi (gradxi(xi). v)^2 ] # Note: Source formula has xi inside the sum for d and outside for xi? # Source: gammaE,d Σi ξ [∇i d̂i v + 1]^2 + γE,ξ [∇ξ ξ̂ v]^2 # It seems xi (ground truth visibility) is used as a mask for the depth term. LDEd = torch.zeroslike(Ld) for i in range(K): graddi = computegradient(dpred[i], p) term = torch.sum(graddi v, dim=-1) + 1 LDEd += xigt (term 2) LDEd = gammaEd LDEd gradxi = computegradient(xipred, p) termxi = torch.sum(gradxi v, dim=-1) LDExi = gammaExi (termxi 2) LDE = LDEd + LDExi # 5. Weight Field Regularization LW # LV = sumi wi LV = torch.sum(wpred, dim=0) # LT = max(0, epsilonT - |gradp w1n|)^2 # Note: Source says "using w1 alone is sufficient". # w1n likely refers to the gradient of w1 along the normal direction n? # Or gradient of w1? Source: |∇p w1n|. # Given "w1n" and context of "transition speed", it might be the gradient of w1. # However, "w1n" is ambiguous. Let's assume it means the gradient of w1 with respect to p. # But wait, "w1n" could mean w1 projected on n? # Source text: "LT = max(0, εT − |∇pw1n|) 2". # In many contexts, subscript n denotes normal component. # But ∇p is spatial gradient. # Let's assume it is the magnitude of the spatial gradient of w1. # If it meant normal component, it would likely be (∇p w1. n). # Given the ambiguity, we compute the magnitude of the gradient of w1. # Note: LT is only applied to S and T data. We assume a mask is applied later or inputs are filtered. gradw1 = computegradient(wpred[0], p) maggradw1 = torch.norm(gradw1, dim=-1) LT = torch.clamp(epsilonT - maggradw1, min=0) 2 LW = gammaV LV + gammaT LT # Total Loss LS = gammad Ld + gammaxi Lxi + gamman Ln + LDE + LW return LS Edge Cases and Pitfalls: \mathcal{L}T is only applied to oriented points that are surface (S) and tangent (T) data, where a discontinuity is desired. Applying it to other data types (e.g., occluded points) is incorrect. The index i^ is determined by the maximum weight wj. If weights are equal, the behavior is not specified. Precision issues may arise in gradient computation for \mathcal{L}{	ext{DE}} and \mathcal{L}T if the network outputs are not smooth. The Conditional Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (CPDDF) is a generative method that encodes 3D shapes into a latent vector and decodes it into a depth field for efficient rendering. It builds on PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss by conditioning the probabilistic distance field on a learned latent representation zs rather than a fixed parameterization. This allows for the generation of diverse shapes from a Gaussian prior while maintaining the rendering efficiency of directed distance fields. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Encourages low entropy outputs to prevent unnecessary switching of the maximum likelihood component, while allowing transitions at discontinuities. Uses directed Eikonal regularization for better surface alignment. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of hyper-parameters (\gamma values, \varepsilonT). The transition loss \mathcal{L}T is only applicable to specific data types (S and T). When to use: When training PDDF models for ray-based shape representations where probabilistic depth prediction is beneficial. When not to use: When a deterministic SDF is sufficient and probabilistic modeling adds unnecessary complexity. The PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss was introduced in the paper "Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations". It is part of the broader development of Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDF) for representing 3D shapes. The method builds on prior work in SDF training and directed distance fields. name: Conditional Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (CPDDF)
head: CPDDF decoder, Conditional Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (CPDDF) with Shape VAE, Shape VAE
body: The Conditional Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (CPDDF) is a generative method that encodes 3D shapes into a latent vector and decodes it into a depth field for efficient rendering. It builds on PDDF Shape-Fitting Loss by conditioning the probabilistic distance field on a learned latent representation zs rather than a fixed parameterization. This allows for the generation of diverse shapes from a Gaussian prior while maintaining the rendering efficiency of directed distance fields. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A point cloud P with associated normals N (size 1024 points). Output: A latent shape vector zs (dimension d{zs}) and, via the decoder, a depth value d(p, v | zs) for a query point p and view direction v. Data Structures: 1. PointNet Encoder Output: A vector of size 2 d{zs}. 2. Latent Vector zs: A vector of size d{zs}. 3. Posterior Parameters: Mean \mu and diagonal log-variance \Sigma, each of size d{zs}. Architecture Details: 1. PointNet Encoder: Consists of four Conv1D-BatchNorm-ReLU blocks with channel sizes 64, 64, 128, and 1024, followed by global max pooling. The pooled output passes through an MLP with two hidden layers of size 512 (Linear-BatchNorm-ReLU, dropout 0.1). The final output size is 2 d{zs}. 2. Variational Posterior Networks: Two separate networks compute the parameters for the approximate posterior q(zs | P, N) = \mathcal{N}(zs | \mu(P, N), \Sigma(P, N)). Each network is structured as Linear-ReLU-Linear with layer dimensions equal to d{zs}. The first network takes the first half of the PointNet output to compute \mu, and the second takes the second half to compute \Sigma. 3. CPDDF Decoder: An eight-layer modulated SIREN network. The layer sizes are 512, 512, 512, 512, 256, 256, 256, 256. It takes the latent vector zs and spatial/view inputs to compute the depth field. Training Objective: The model is trained using a \beta-VAE loss: \mathcal{E}{\text{VAE}} = \mathcal{E}S + \beta \mathcal{L}{\text{KL}} where \mathcal{L}{\text{KL}} is the KL divergence between the approximate posterior and a standard Gaussian prior \mathcal{N}(0, I), and \mathcal{E}S is the reconstruction likelihood loss. The total loss includes weighted terms for depth, normals, and other constraints: \mathcal{L}{\text{total}} = \gammad \mathcal{L}d + \gamma\xi \mathcal{L}\xi + \gamman \mathcal{L}n + \gammaV \mathcal{L}V + \gamma{E,d} \mathcal{L}{E,d} + \gamma{E,\xi} \mathcal{L}{E,\xi} + \gamma{V,\xi} \mathcal{L}{V,\xi} + \gammaT \mathcal{L}T. Parameters: d{zs} (latent dimension): 400. \beta (KL weight): 0.05. Loss weights: \gammad=5, \gamma\xi=10, \gamman=10, \gammaV=1, \gamma{E,d}=0.1, \gamma{E,\xi}=0.1, \gamma{V,\xi}=0.1, \gammaT=0.1. Optimizer: Adam (lr=10^{-4}, \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.999). Training iterations: 100,000. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.nn.functional as F class PointNetEncoder(nn.Module): def init(self, dimzs): super().init() # Four Conv1D-BatchNorm-ReLU blocks self.conv1 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(4, 64, 1), nn.BatchNorm1d(64), nn.ReLU()) # 4 inputs: 3 coords + 1 normal? Source says point cloud with normals. Standard PointNet uses 3 coords + 1 normal = 4 channels. self.conv2 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(64, 64, 1), nn.BatchNorm1d(64), nn.ReLU()) self.conv3 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(64, 128, 1), nn.BatchNorm1d(128), nn.ReLU()) self.conv4 = nn.Sequential(nn.Conv1d(128, 1024, 1), nn.BatchNorm1d(1024), nn.ReLU()) # MLP with two hidden layers of size 512 self.mlp = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(1024, 512), nn.BatchNorm1d(512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Dropout(0.1), nn.Linear(512, 512), nn.BatchNorm1d(512), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(512, 2 dimzs)) def forward(self, x): # x shape: (B, 4, 1024) x = self.conv1(x) x = self.conv2(x) x = self.conv3(x) x = self.conv4(x) # Global max pooling x = torch.max(x, 2, keepdim=True)[0] x = x.view(x.size(0), -1) return self.mlp(x) class PosteriorNetwork(nn.Module): def init(self, dimzs): super().init() self.net = nn.Sequential( nn.Linear(dimzs, dimzs), nn.ReLU(), nn.Linear(dimzs, dimzs)) def forward(self, x): return self.net(x) class CPDDFDecoder(nn.Module): def init(self, dimzs): super().init() # Eight layers: 512, 512, 512, 512, 256, 256, 256, 256 # Using modulated SIREN. For implementation, we assume a standard MLP structure # with sine activations as per SIREN [41], modulated by zs. # Note: Exact SIREN modulation implementation details are not fully specified in # beyond "modulated SIREN approach [41]". We use a placeholder for the SIREN layer logic. self.layers = nn.ModuleList() sizes = [512, 512, 512, 512, 256, 256, 256, 256] indim = dimzs # Assuming zs is concatenated or modulates the first layer input # Simplified structure for demonstration of dimensions # In practice, SIREN layers use sin activation and frequency modulation currentdim = dimzs for size in sizes: self.layers.append(SIRENLayer(currentdim, size)) # SIRENLayer is a standard SIREN layer with sine activation currentdim = size def forward(self, zs, query): # query: (B, 3) or (B, 4) depending on view direction inclusion x = zs # Initial modulation or concatenation logic from [41] for layer in self.layers: x = layer(x) return x class SIRENLayer(nn.Module): def init(self, infeatures, outfeatures, w0=30.0): super().init() self.linear = nn.Linear(infeatures, outfeatures) self.w0 = w0 self.initweights() def initweights(self): with torch.nograd(): self.linear.weight.uniform(-1 / self.linear.infeatures, 1 / self.linear.infeatures) def forward(self, x): return torch.sin(self.linear(x) self.w0) def computevaeloss(mu, logvar, beta=0.05): # KL divergence between N(mu, exp(logvar)) and N(0, I) klloss = -0.5 torch.sum(1 + logvar - mu.pow(2) - logvar.exp()) return klloss beta def trainstep(pointcloud, normals, encoder, posteriormu, posteriorlogvar, decoder, optimizer): # pointcloud: (B, 1024, 3), normals: (B, 1024, 3) # Combine to (B, 4, 1024) x = torch.cat([pointcloud, normals], dim=2).permute(0, 2, 1) # Encode encoderout = encoder(x) # (B, 2dimzs) # Split for posterior mu = posteriormu(encoderout[:,:encoderout.size(1)//2]) logvar = posteriorlogvar(encoderout[:, encoderout.size(1)//2:]) # Reparameterization std = torch.exp(0.5 logvar) eps = torch.randnlike(std) zs = mu + eps std # Decode (example: compute depth for a set of query points) # queries: (B, N, 3) # depth = decoder(zs, queries) # Compute losses (simplified) kl = computevaeloss(mu, logvar) reconloss = 0 # Placeholder for ES calculation totalloss = reconloss + kl optimizer.zerograd() totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() return totalloss.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The PointNet encoder requires exactly 1024 points with normals. Input point clouds must be upsampled or downsampled to this size. The posterior networks split the encoder output evenly; incorrect splitting will break the independence assumption of the mean and variance networks. The modulated SIREN decoder requires careful initialization of frequencies (typically w0=30) to avoid high-frequency artifacts, as per standard SIREN practice. Time Complexity: Training requires 100K iterations with a minibatch size of 32 shapes. Each shape uses 1.2K points (for A/U categories) or 300 points (for S/B/T/O categories). Memory Complexity: The latent vector size is 400. The encoder output is 800. The decoder has 8 layers with up to 512 units. Strengths: Enables efficient rendering of diverse shapes via latent sampling. The directed distance field allows for fast depth estimation. Limitations: Limited to single categories of ShapeNet (e.g., cars). Requires point cloud input with normals. The CPDDF method was introduced in "Representing 3D Shapes with Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields" (CVPR 2022). It extends the Probabilistic Directed Distance Field (PDDF) framework by incorporating a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) structure to learn a latent space of shapes. The method uses a PointNet encoder and a modulated SIREN decoder. Representing 3D Shapes with Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields, https://doi.org/10.1109/cvpr52688.2022.01874, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SDDF with Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals
head: Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF), Scene-level SDDF
body: This method learns a scene-level Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF) by combining an explicit ellipsoidal prior with an implicit neural residual network. It solves the problem of reconstructing complex 3D environments from sensor data (LiDAR or RGB-D depth) while maintaining differentiability for novel view synthesis and avoiding the iterative sphere tracing required by standard SDFs. Unlike its siblings, it explicitly models occlusions via ellipsoids to handle discontinuities, while the neural network recovers fine details, satisfying the directional Eikonal constraint by construction. Inputs: A set of sensor measurements \{Tt, Zt\}{t=1}^T, where Tt \in SE(3) is the sensor pose and Zt contains viewing directions vi \in S^2 and range measurements r{t,i} \in \mathbb{R}{>0}. Query inputs: a 3D position p \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction v \in S^2. Outputs: The predicted SDDF value \hat{f}(p, v), representing the signed distance to the observed surface along direction v from position p. Data Structures: 1. Ellipsoid Prior: A set of M learnable ellipsoids. Each ellipsoid j is defined by parameters \thetaj (center, orientation, scale). The total number of ellipsoids M is typically 128 (256 for Gibson Allensville). 2. Latent Feature Network (L): A neural network that maps the intersection point and viewing direction to a latent feature vector z \in \mathbb{R}^m. 3. Residual Decoder (R): A neural network that takes the latent feature z and outputs the residual prediction \deltaf(p, v). Definitions: SDDF Definition: For a query (p, v), the SDDF f^(p, v) is the signed distance to the first intersection of the ray p + dv with the occupied space boundary \partial O. The sign is positive if p is in free space and negative if p is inside the occupied space. The function is continuous when entering occupied space from free space, but discontinuous when leaving occupied space (inside-out). This discontinuity is handled by assuming sensors remain in free space, observing the scene from outside-in. Directional Eikonal Constraint: The gradient of the SDDF with respect to position p in the direction v must have unit magnitude: \nablap f(p, v) \cdot v = 1. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Ellipsoids: Initialize the M ellipsoids to approximate the coarse shape of the scene. Do not use K-means++ initialization alone, as it causes excessive ellipsoids for planar surfaces and larger errors. Use a method that provides a balanced initial coverage. 2. Compute Ellipsoid Prior f(p, v): For a query (p, v), compute the distance to the nearest ellipsoid surface along v. Let dj(p, v) be the distance from p to the surface of ellipsoid j along direction v. The prior f(p, v) is the minimum of these distances, considering the sign based on whether p is inside or outside the ellipsoid. Note: The exact closed-form solution for dj(p, v) involves solving a quartic equation for the intersection of a ray and an ellipsoid. The sources state that gradients are derived in closed-form to accelerate training, but do not provide the explicit quartic solver code. 3. Find Intersection Point: Identify the ellipsoid j^ that provides the minimum distance f(p, v). Compute the intersection point p{\text{int}} = p + f(p, v)v to pass to the latent network. 4. Construct Latent Feature z: Pass p{\text{int}} and v through the Latent Feature Network L to obtain z = L(p{\text{int}}, v). The network is designed such that the resulting residual satisfies the directional Eikonal constraint. 5. Predict Residual \deltaf(p, v): Pass z through the Residual Decoder R to obtain the residual: \deltaf(p, v) = R(z). 6. Compute Final SDDF: Combine the prior and the residual: \hat{f}(p, v) = f(p, v) + \deltaf(p, v) Training: Loss Function: Minimize the difference between \hat{f}(p, v) and the ground truth SDDF derived from sensor measurements. Negative Sample Augmentation: Include negative SDDF samples (points inside the object) in the training data. Without this, ellipsoids regress into the interior of objects, leading to missing ray intersections and wrong ellipsoid selection. Embedding: Use polynomial embedding for the neural networks. Fourier embedding is inferior due to the need for scene-specific spatial frequency tuning. Fourier embedding formula (for ablation comparison): \mathbf{m} = [\sin(2\pi\mathbf{B}{\text{p}}\mathbf{p}), \cos(2\pi\mathbf{B}{\text{p}}\mathbf{p}), \sin(2\pi\mathbf{B}{\text{v}}\mathbf{v}), \cos(2\pi\mathbf{B}{\text{v}}\mathbf{v})] where \mathbf{B}p, \mathbf{B}v \in \mathbb{R}^{25 \times 3} are random Fourier features sampled from \mathcal{N}(0, 1). Parameters: Number of ellipsoids M: 128 (default), 256 for Gibson Allensville. RGB-D Downsampling: 20× for most datasets, 5× for Replica Hotel, to match LiDAR ray density. Fourier Feature Dimensions: 25 (for ablation). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuity: The SDDF is discontinuous when a ray leaves the occupied space from inside out. This is handled by assuming sensors remain in free space. Too Few Ellipsoids: Prevents accurate approximation of object shapes. Too Many Ellipsoids: Causes the model to learn spurious occlusions between ellipsoids and moves redundant ellipsoids out of the scene during testing. Missing Negative Samples: Causes ellipsoids to regress into object interiors, leading to missing ray intersections. K-means++ Initialization: Causes larger errors due to excessive ellipsoids for planar surfaces. The explicit geometric representation using learnable ellipsoids to approximate coarse shapes and handle occlusions. It provides an analytic, differentiable prior that satisfies the directional Eikonal equation by construction. Time Complexity: Inference is a single forward pass through the ellipsoid prior and the neural network, making it faster than iterative sphere tracing methods. It is 1.5× faster than SDF-Instant-NGP sphere tracing and 4× faster than Nerfacto. Memory Complexity: Low GPU memory usage. On Replica-Hotel, max training GPU memory is 3.3 GB, significantly lower than RaDe-GS (18.7 GB) and Nerfacto (4.7 GB). Performance: On Replica-Hotel (Intel 14900K CPU, NVIDIA RTX-3090 GPU), training time is 100 minutes, inference time is 69 ms/frame, and the model has 2.7M parameters. Strengths: Single-query differentiable novel view synthesis. Handles occlusions explicitly. Low memory footprint. Robust to varying viewing distances due to Eikonal constraint satisfaction. Works with LiDAR and depth-only data. Limitations: Slower inference than highly optimized Gaussian Splatting methods like RaDe-GS (69 ms vs 7 ms). Requires careful tuning of the number of ellipsoids. Sensitive to initialization. When to Use: When geometric reconstruction accuracy with low memory usage is required, and differentiable depth rendering is needed without RGB supervision. When Not to Use: Avoid when maximum inference speed is required (use RaDe-GS) or when photometric rendering with RGB supervision is the primary goal (use Nerfacto). The method was introduced in "Learning Scene-Level Signed Directional Distance Function With Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals". It addresses the limitations of previous SDDF formulations: object-level SDDF ignores objects behind the viewing position, and PDDF lacks sign information and has discontinuities. This method defines a scene-level SDDF that is continuous when entering occupied space and retains sign information, enabling accurate scene reconstruction from sensor data. Learning Scene-Level Signed Directional Distance Function With Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals., https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2026.3688658, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Ellipsoid SDDF Prior
head: Ellipsoid Signed Directional Distance Function, Single Ellipsoid SDDF, Ellipsoid-based Prior Network, Prior network P
body: The Ellipsoid SDDF Prior is an explicit geometric representation that approximates the coarse shape of an environment using a set of M learnable ellipsoids. It serves as the foundational prior for a Signed Directional Distance Function (SDDF), handling occlusions explicitly and providing a closed-form analytical solution for the distance field. It differs from implicit neural fields by offering an analytic, differentiable geometric prior that satisfies the directional Eikonal equation by construction, leaving fine details to be recovered by a subsequent neural residual network. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Ray origin \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3, ray direction \mathbf{v} \in \mathbb{S}^2 (unit vector), and ellipsoid parameters: center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^3, rotation matrix \mathbf{R} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}, and radii vector \mathbf{r} \in \mathbb{R}^3+. Outputs: SDDF value f(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}; \mathcal{E}), intersection indicator i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}), and sign indicator s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}). Data Structures: Ellipsoid Parameters: \mathbf{c}: Center position. \mathbf{R}: Rotation matrix. Parameterized via Lie algebra: \mathbf{T} = \mathbf{T}0 \exp(\xi^\wedge), where \mathbf{T}0 is a fixed initial pose, \xi = (\boldsymbol{\rho}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) \in \mathbb{R}^6 is learnable, \boldsymbol{\rho} is translation, \boldsymbol{\theta} maps to rotation via skew-symmetric matrix \xi^\wedge and matrix exponential. \mathbf{r}: Radii vector. Parameterized as \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{r}0 \exp(\mathbf{s}), where \mathbf{r}0 \in \mathbb{R}^3+ is fixed initialization and \mathbf{s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is learnable. This ensures \mathbf{r} remains positive. \mathbf{Q}0 = \text{diag}(\mathbf{r}). Formulas and Definitions: 1. Local Frame Transformation: Transform world-space coordinates to the ellipsoid's local frame: \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{R}^\top (\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}) \mathbf{v}' = \mathbf{R}^\top \mathbf{v} \mathbf{w}' = \mathbf{p}' \times \mathbf{v}' \mathbf{Q}1 = \det(\mathbf{Q}0) \mathbf{Q}0^{-1} 2. Intersection Indicator: Determines if the ray intersects the ellipsoid. i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{v}'^\top \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}' - \mathbf{w}'^\top \mathbf{Q}0^2 \mathbf{w}' If i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0, the ray does not intersect the ellipsoid. 3. Sign Indicator: Determines if the point is inside or outside the ellipsoid. s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) = \mathbf{p}'^\top \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{p}' - \det(\mathbf{Q}0)^2 s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0 means \mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{E} (inside); s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) > 0 means \mathbf{p} \notin \mathcal{E} (outside). This form is used for better numerical stability than \mathbf{p}'^\top \mathbf{Q}0^{-2} \mathbf{p}' - 1. 4. Validity Function: Handles cases where the ellipsoid is behind the ray. \beta = \max(i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}), 0) + \epsilon, \quad \epsilon > 0 v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) = -\frac{\det(\mathbf{Q}0)\sqrt{\beta} + \mathbf{p}'^\top \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'}{\mathbf{v}'^\top \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'} s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0 indicates the ellipsoid is behind the view ray. 5. SDDF Prior Value: f(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}; \mathcal{E}) = \begin{cases} -\frac{\det(\mathbf{Q}0)\sqrt{\beta} + \mathbf{p}'^\top \mathbf{Q}1^\top \mathbf{v}'}{\mathbf{v}'^\top \mathbf{Q}1^\top \mathbf{v}'}, & v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) \geq 0 \\ \infty, & v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0 \end{cases} When i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0 (no intersection) and valid, this simplifies to the distance to a virtual plane: -\frac{\mathbf{p}'^\top \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'}{\mathbf{v}'^\top \mathbf{Q}1^2 \mathbf{v}'}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def ellipsoidsddfprior(p, v, c, R, r): # Helper definitions for self-contained execution def diag(vec): return [[vec[0], 0, 0], [0, vec[1], 0], [0, 0, vec[2]]] def det3x3(M): return M[0][0](M[1][1]M[2][2] - M[1][2]M[2][1]) - M[0][1](M[1][0]M[2][2] - M[1][2]M[2][0]) + M[0][2](M[1][0]M[2][1] - M[1][1]M[2][0]) def invdiag(M): return [[1.0/M[0][0], 0, 0], [0, 1.0/M[1][1], 0], [0, 0, 1.0/M[2][2]]] def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def dot(a, b): return a[0]b[0] + a[1]b[1] + a[2]b[2] def matvec(M, v): return [M[0][0]v[0] + M[0][1]v[1] + M[0][2]v[2], M[1][0]v[0] + M[1][1]v[1] + M[1][2]v[2], M[2][0]v[0] + M[2][1]v[1] + M[2][2]v[2]] def matmul(A, B): return [[A[0][0]B[0][0]+A[0][1]B[1][0]+A[0][2]B[2][0], A[0][0]B[0][1]+A[0][1]B[1][1]+A[0][2]B[2][1], A[0][0]B[0][2]+A[0][1]B[1][2]+A[0][2]B[2][2]], [A[1][0]B[0][0]+A[1][1]B[1][0]+A[1][2]B[2][0], A[1][0]B[0][1]+A[1][1]B[1][1]+A[1][2]B[2][1], A[1][0]B[0][2]+A[1][1]B[1][2]+A[1][2]B[2][2]], [A[2][0]B[0][0]+A[2][1]B[1][0]+A[2][2]B[2][0], A[2][0]B[0][1]+A[2][1]B[1][1]+A[2][2]B[2][1], A[2][0]B[0][2]+A[2][1]B[1][2]+A[2][2]B[2][2]]] # 1. Compute Q0 and Q1 Q0 = diag(r) detQ0 = det3x3(Q0) Q1 = matmul([[detQ0, 0, 0], [0, detQ0, 0], [0, 0, detQ0]], invdiag(Q0)) Q1sq = matmul(Q1, Q1) Q0sq = matmul(Q0, Q0) # 2. Transform to local frame pprime = matvec(R, [p[0]-c[0], p[1]-c[1], p[2]-c[2]]) vprime = matvec(R, v) wprime = cross(pprime, vprime) # 3. Compute Intersection Indicator vQ1sqv = dot(vprime, matvec(Q1sq, vprime)) wQ0sqw = dot(wprime, matvec(Q0sq, wprime)) i = vQ1sqv - wQ0sqw # 4. Compute Sign Indicator pQ1sqp = dot(pprime, matvec(Q1sq, pprime)) s = pQ1sqp - detQ02 # 5. Compute Validity and SDDF epsilon = 1e-8 beta = max(i, 0.0) + epsilon denomvalid = dot(vprime, matvec(Q1sq, vprime)) numvalid = detQ0 (beta 0.5) + dot(pprime, matvec(Q1sq, vprime)) if denomvalid == 0: vval = 0.0 else: vval = -(numvalid / denomvalid) s if vval < 0: return float('inf'), i, s denomsddf = denomvalid numsddf = detQ0 (beta 0.5) + dot(pprime, matvec(Q1, vprime)) if denomsddf == 0: fval = float('inf') else: fval = -numsddf / denomsddf return fval, i, s Parameters: M: Number of ellipsoids. Defines the capacity of the explicit prior. Typical value not specified. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: No Intersection: If i(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) < 0, the SDDF is \infty. This must be handled to avoid numerical issues. Ellipsoid Behind Ray: If s(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) > 0 (point outside) and the ellipsoid is behind the ray, the standard formula yields a negative value, but the true SDDF should be \infty. The validity function v(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) detects this and returns \infty. Numerical Stability: A small \epsilon > 0 is added to \beta in the square root term to ensure stable backward propagation. Predicts a correction term \deltaf(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) to refine the coarse geometric prior. It differs from standard MLPs by using a linear transformation of degree-2 monomial embeddings of the intersection point and local direction, inspired by the polynomial nature of the ellipsoid SDDF. Choose this when fine geometric details must be recovered while preserving the Eikonal constraint. See Residual Network for SDDF Correction. Computes the SDDF for a union of M ellipsoids by aggregating individual properties via min/max operations. It differs from single-ellipsoid evaluation by prioritizing intersected ellipsoids and handling scene-level occlusions. Choose this for multi-object scenes where O(M) per-ray scaling is acceptable. See Fusing Multiple Ellipsoid SDDFs. Manually implements gradient computation for the ellipsoidal SDDF prior to optimize GPU memory and speed, replacing automatic differentiation. It differs from standard autograd by explicitly deriving chain-rule gradients for intermediate scalar variables in the local frame. Choose this when training large-scale scenes with strict memory constraints. See Custom Backward Propagation for Ellipsoidal SDDF Prior. Complexity: The prior network computation is O(M) per ray due to the min/max operations over M ellipsoids. Strengths: Provides a closed-form, differentiable geometric prior that satisfies the directional Eikonal equation by construction. Handles occlusions explicitly. Compatible with unsigned DDF by setting one axis radius to 0 (forming a 2D disk) for non-watertight objects. Limitations: The prior network alone provides only a coarse approximation; fine details require the residual network. Numerical stability requires careful handling of the validity function and \epsilon. When to use: When a coarse, analytic geometric prior is needed for scene-level SDDF reconstruction, especially for differentiable rendering or SLAM where Eikonal constraints are beneficial. The method originates from the paper "Learning Scene-Level Signed Directional Distance Function With Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals". It addresses the challenge of learning a continuous, implicit representation of scene-level SDDFs, which are sensitive to both position and direction. The approach builds on the definition of SDDF as a function measuring signed distance from a point to an occupied space along a viewing direction, extending object-level SDDFs to scene-level representations. Learning Scene-Level Signed Directional Distance Function With Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals., https://doi.org/10.1109/tpami.2026.3688658, fetched 2026-10-26

name: SDF-Instant-NGP Training
head: SDDF Training, SDF baseline training
body:
This method defines the training procedure for a Signed Distance Function (SDF) baseline network, specifically referred to as SDF-Instant-NGP in the source literature. It is distinguished from its parent method, SDF Training with Eikonal Loss, by the explicit inclusion of a sign loss term applied to free-space samples to enforce positive SDF values outside the surface, and by the specific hyperparameter configuration (batch size, learning rate, epochs) used for the SDF baseline in the RaDe-GS context. Inputs: A set of near-surface samples \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}} with corresponding distance labels yi \in \mathbb{R}. A set of free-space positions \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}. A differentiable SDF model f(\mathbf{x}; 	heta). Outputs: Trained network parameters 	heta that minimize the combined loss function. The training data consists of two sets of 3D points: \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}} containing near-surface points with distance labels yi \in \mathbb{R}, and \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}} containing free-space positions that provide only sign supervision. 1. Sample Generation: Generate two types of training samples: SDF samples \mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}} with distance labels yi, and free space positions \mathbf{x}j \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}. 2. Forward Pass: For each batch of samples, compute the predicted SDF values f(\mathbf{x}) and their gradients 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) with respect to the input coordinates using automatic differentiation. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the three components of the loss function: SDF loss (l{	ext{SDF}}) for near-surface samples, sign loss (l{	ext{sign}}) for free-space samples, and Eikonal loss (l{	ext{eik}}) for all samples. 4. Optimization: Update the network parameters using the Adam optimizer to minimize the total loss. 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 2-4 for 300 epochs. The total loss is the sum of three terms: l{	ext{SDF}} =  rac{1}{\|\mathcal{X}{	ext{near}}\|} \sum{\mathbf{x}i \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}}} |f(\mathbf{x}i) - yi| \quad (63) l{	ext{sign}} =  rac{1}{\|\mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}\|} \sum{\mathbf{x}j \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}} \exp(-\lambda f(\mathbf{x}j)) \quad (64) l{	ext{eik}} =  rac{1}{\|\mathcal{X}{	ext{near}}\| + \|\mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}\|} \sum{\mathbf{x}k \in \mathcal{X}{	ext{near}} \cup \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}} \| |
abla f(\mathbf{x}k)| - 1 \| \quad (65) Where: \|\mathcal{X}{	ext{near}}\| and \|\mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}\| are the number of samples in each set. f(\mathbf{x}) is the SDF model output. yi is the ground truth distance label. 
abla f(\mathbf{x}) is the gradient of the SDF with respect to the input position. \lambda is a parameter for the sign loss. Not given in the sources. Batch size: 60. Optimizer: Adam. Learning rate: 0.0001. Epochs: 300. \lambda: Value not specified in the source section. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn import torch.optim as optim def computesdfloss(prednear, labelsnear): return torch.mean(torch.abs(prednear - labelsnear)) def computesignloss(predfree, lambdaparam): return torch.mean(torch.exp(-lambdaparam predfree)) def computeeikonalloss(prednear, inputsnear, predfree, inputsfree): gradnear = torch.autograd.grad( prednear, inputsnear, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(prednear), creategraph=False, retaingraph=True, onlyinputs=True)[0] gradfree = torch.autograd.grad( predfree, inputsfree, gradoutputs=torch.oneslike(predfree), creategraph=False, retaingraph=False, onlyinputs=True)[0] gradnormnear = torch.norm(gradnear, dim=1, keepdim=True) gradnormfree = torch.norm(gradfree, dim=1, keepdim=True) return torch.mean(torch.abs(gradnormnear - 1.0)) + torch.mean(torch.abs(gradnormfree - 1.0)) def trainsdfbaseline(model, nearsamples, nearlabels, freesamples, lambdaparam, batchsize=60, lr=0.0001, epochs=300): optimizer = optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=lr) for epoch in range(epochs): nearindices = torch.randperm(nearsamples.size(0)) freeindices = torch.randperm(freesamples.size(0)) for i in range(0, nearsamples.size(0), batchsize): nearidx = nearindices[i:i+batchsize] xnear = nearsamples[nearidx] ynear = nearlabels[nearidx] freeidx = freeindices[i:i+batchsize] xfree = freesamples[freeidx] optimizer.zerograd() prednear = model(xnear) predfree = model(xfree) losssdf = computesdfloss(prednear, ynear) losssign = computesignloss(predfree, lambdaparam) losseik = computeeikonalloss(prednear, xnear, predfree, xfree) totalloss = losssdf + losssign + losseik totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() The source does not specify the value of \lambda, the sampling strategy for \mathcal{X}{	ext{free}}, or how to handle precision issues and degenerate inputs. What it is: A method that uses spherical priors or constraints to regularize the SDF. Difference: Focuses on geometric priors rather than just point-wise supervision. When to choose: When scene geometry can be approximated by spheres or when spherical priors improve convergence. Link: Sphere Loss What it is: A technique where a smaller network is trained to mimic a larger, pre-trained SDF network. Difference: Focuses on model compression and inference speed rather than initial training from scratch. When to choose: When deployment constraints require a smaller model. Link: MLP Distillation What it is: The primary method in the source paper, which uses ellipsoidal priors and neural residuals to learn a Signed Directional Distance Function. Difference: This is the advanced method; SDF-Instant-NGP is the baseline used for comparison. When to choose: For higher accuracy and robustness, especially in complex scenes. Link: SDDF with Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals The method trains for 300 epochs. The source does not report time or memory complexity, measured performance metrics, specific limitations, or usage guidelines for this baseline. The method is described in the paper "Learning Scene-Level Signed Directional Distance Function With Ellipsoidal Priors and Neural Residuals". It is presented as a baseline (SDF-Instant-NGP) for the proposed SDDF method in the RaDe-GS framework. It is used for training a standard SDF network to serve as a comparison point for the more advanced SDDF method. name: TetraSDF Training Procedure
head: SDF neural network training, TetraSDF optimization
body: TetraSDF Training Procedure optimizes a neural network to represent a signed distance field (SDF) using a multi-resolution tetrahedral grid, combining L1 regression, Eikonal regularization, and weight normalization constraints. It differs from standard MLP-based SDF training by utilizing a tetrahedral grid structure for spatial representation, which allows for efficient multi-resolution handling and specific mesh extraction via sub-polygonization. Inputs and Outputs Input: A dataset of 3D points with ground truth SDF values, typically sampled from a mesh (e.g., Stanford 3D scanning models). Output: A trained TetraSDF neural network model capable of evaluating SDF values and gradients at arbitrary 3D coordinates. Data Structures TetraSDF Network: A neural network defined by numlayers, numhidden, levels, rmin, rmax, and T. numlayers: Number of hidden layers (default 4). numhidden: Number of hidden units per layer (default 12). levels: Multi-resolution levels (default 4). rmin, rmax: Resolution bounds for the tetrahedral grid, dependent on the chosen resolution preset (small, medium, large). T: A parameter related to the tetrahedral grid structure (default 21). useA: Boolean flag for using a preconditioner (default True). StanfordDataset: A custom dataset class that provides point-cloud samples and ground truth SDF labels. DataLoader: A standard iterator that shuffles data and yields batches of size BATCHSIZE. Parameters BATCHSIZE: 1000. lr (Adam learning rate): 1 \times 10^{-3}. eikonalweight: 5 \times 10^{-3}. EPOCH: 10. Tmax (for scheduler): EPOCH \times \frac{\text{len(training\data)}}{BATCH\SIZE}. Resolution presets: small: r{min}=2, r{max}=32. medium: r{min}=4, r{max}=64. large: r{min}=8, r{max}=128. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Set random seeds for Python, NumPy, and PyTorch. Create the TetraSDF network instance with specified hyperparameters. Load the training dataset (StanfordDataset) and create a DataLoader with BATCHSIZE=1000 and shuffle=True. Initialize the Adam optimizer with lr=1e-3. Initialize the CosineAnnealingLR scheduler with Tmax calculated as above. Define the L1 Loss criterion (nn.L1Loss). 2. Epoch Loop: Iterate for EPOCH times (default 10). Resampling: If epoch == 0, call traindataloader.dataset.resample() to resample the dataset. 3. Batch Loop: Iterate through each batch in traindataloader. Data Loading: Retrieve inputs (points) and labels (ground truth SDF) from the batch and move them to the GPU. Gradient Zeroing: Reset accumulated gradients to zero. Forward Pass: Compute predicted SDF values: predsdf = net.sdf(inputs)[:, 0]. L1 Loss Calculation: Compute L{L1} = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^N | \hat{y}i - yi | where \hat{y}i is predsdf and yi is labels. Eikonal Loss Calculation: Set points = inputs.detach().clone().requiresgrad(True). Compute the gradient of the SDF output with respect to the input points: J = torch.autograd.grad(net.sdf(points).sum(), points, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0]. Compute the Eikonal loss: L{eik} = \mathbb{E} [ (\| \nabla \phi(\mathbf{x}) \|2 - 1)^2 ] using eik = (J.norm(p=2, dim=1) - 1.0).pow(2).mean(). Weight Norm Loss Calculation: Compute L{wn} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{i=1}^M \mathbb{E} [ (1 - \| \mathbf{W}i \|2)^2 ] where \mathbf{W}i are the layer weights in net.fc. Total Loss: Sum the losses: loss = L1Loss + eikonalweight Leik + Lwn. Backward Pass: Compute gradients of the total loss with respect to all network parameters. Optimizer Step: Update network parameters using the Adam algorithm. Scheduler Step: Update the learning rate using cosine annealing. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn from torch.utils.data import DataLoader def l1loss(pred, target): return torch.mean(torch.abs(pred - target)) def weightnormloss(fclayer): total = 0.0 count = 0 for param in fclayer.parameters(): if param.dim() > 1: # Compute L2 norm per output neuron (row-wise for shape (out, in)) rownorms = torch.norm(param, p=2, dim=1) total += torch.mean((1.0 - rownorms) 2) count += 1 return total / count if count > 0 else 0.0 def adamstep(params, grads, state, lr, beta1=0.9, beta2=0.999, eps=1e-8): for p, g in zip(params, grads): if p.grad is None: continue g = g.data state[p] = state.get(p, {'m': 0.0, 'v': 0.0}) m, v = state[p]['m'], state[p]['v'] state[p]['m'] = beta1 m + (1 - beta1) g state[p]['v'] = beta2 v + (1 - beta2) g 2 mhat = state[p]['m'] / (1 - beta1 (state[p].get('step', 0) + 1)) vhat = state[p]['v'] / (1 - beta2 (state[p].get('step', 0) + 1)) p.data -= lr mhat / (torch.sqrt(vhat) + eps) state[p]['step'] = state[p].get('step', 0) + 1 def cosineannealingstep(optimizer, epoch, Tmax, lrmin=0): lr = lrmin + (1 - optimizer.paramgroups[0]['lr']) (1 + math.cos(math.pi epoch / Tmax)) / 2 for group in optimizer.paramgroups: group['lr'] = lr BATCHSIZE = 1000 EPOCH = 10 eikonalweight = 5e-3 for epoch in range(EPOCH): runningloss = 0.0 runningl1loss = 0.0 if epoch == 0: traindataloader.dataset.resample() for i, data in enumerate(traindataloader, 0): inputs, labels = data inputs = inputs.cuda() labels = labels.cuda() optimizer.zerograd() predsdf = net.sdf(inputs)[:, 0] l1lossval = l1loss(predsdf, labels) points = inputs.detach().clone().requiresgrad(True) J = torch.autograd.grad(net.sdf(points).sum(), points, creategraph=True, retaingraph=True)[0] eik = (J.norm(p=2, dim=1) - 1.0).pow(2).mean() wnlossval = weightnormloss(net.fc) loss = l1lossval + eikonalweight eik + wnlossval loss.backward() adamstep(net.parameters(), net.parameters(), optimizer.statedict(), lr=1e-3) cosineannealingstep(optimizer, epoch, Tmax) runningloss += loss.item() runningl1loss += l1lossval.item() Edge Cases and Pitfalls Sharp Slopes: Without the Eikonal loss, the estimated SDF values develop sharp slopes. This is mitigated by adding L{eik} with a weight of 5 \times 10^{-3}. Precision: The use of detach().clone().requiresgrad(True) is critical for computing the Eikonal loss correctly without interfering with the main gradient flow for the L1 loss. When to use: When training a TetraSDF model for 3D shape representation. TetraSDF was developed by NAVER Corp. and released as an open-source project. name: Regularization and Gradient Losses
head: SDF Regularization, Gradient Constraints, Surface Consistency Losses
body:
This family defines auxiliary loss terms used during the training of neural Signed Distance Field (SDF) networks to enforce geometric priors, improve surface smoothness, and prevent artifacts in regions lacking direct supervision. Unlike the primary Eikonal loss which enforces unit gradient magnitude everywhere, these terms target specific geometric properties such as surface alignment between different field representations, local smoothness of the distance function, and the suppression of "free surfaces" in unobserved volumes. They are typically combined with photometric or depth supervision to stabilize the optimization of implicit surfaces. All methods in this family operate on the output of a neural network f(\mathbf{x}) that predicts the SDF value s at a query point \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3. The core mechanism involves computing a scalar loss \mathcal{L} based on the predicted SDF values s(\mathbf{x}) or their spatial gradients 
abla s(\mathbf{x}), and backpropagating this loss to update the network weights. Common characteristics include: 1. Query Points: Losses are computed over a set of sampled points \mathcal{Q}, which may include points on the surface (where s \approx 0), points in free space (s > 0), or points inside the object (s < 0). 2. Gradient Dependence: Many terms rely on the gradient of the SDF, 
abla s(\mathbf{x}), either explicitly (e.g., smoothness between adjacent gradients) or implicitly (e.g., enforcing magnitude via Eikonal, though Eikonal is covered in the parent article). 3. Regularization Goal: The objective is not to fit observed data directly but to constrain the solution space to be geometrically plausible (smooth, compact, consistent). 4. Weighting: Each loss term is typically multiplied by a hyperparameter \lambda to balance its influence against other losses (e.g., photometric loss, Eikonal loss). Enforces geometric consistency between a primary SDF network and a secondary Directional Distance Field (DDF) network. It ensures that points predicted by the DDF to lie on the surface actually correspond to the zero-level set of the SDF. This is particularly useful when training multi-representation models to resolve depth ambiguities. It differs from standard SDF supervision by comparing two learned representations rather than a network against ground truth. See Surface SDF Loss for implementation details. Regularizes the reconstructed surface by penalizing the difference between gradients of the SDF at adjacent sampled points. This encourages geometric smoothness and reduces high-frequency noise in the predicted distance field. It is computed by comparing the gradient 
abla d\Omega(\mathbf{p}) at a point \mathbf{p} with the gradient at a perturbed point \mathbf{p} + \varepsilon. The loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}s =  rac{1}{N{sm}} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{X}} \| 
abla d\Omega(\mathbf{p}) - 
abla d\Omega(\mathbf{p} + \varepsilon) \|2 where \mathcal{X} is the set of sampled points, N{sm} is the number of points used for computing the loss, d\Omega is the SDF output, and \varepsilon is a small perturbation vector. This term is applied to the geometry MLP parameters. A variant used in sparse-view reconstruction pipelines (e.g., SDFStudio) that applies SDF supervision only to a subset of points extracted from sparse input data. The process involves: 1. Extracting sparse points and weights from the input batch. 2. Filtering points to keep only those inside the unit sphere (norm < 1.0). 3. Evaluating the SDF network at these filtered points. 4. Computing the loss as the mean of the absolute SDF values weighted by the input weights. In the specific implementation cited, the loss is multiplied by a factor of 0.0, effectively disabling it or serving as a placeholder for future tuning. This suggests that in some configurations, sparse point supervision is optional or handled differently. Designed to prevent the generation of "uncontrollable free surfaces" behind visible surfaces in sparse-view neural surface reconstruction. It penalizes points that are close to the zero-level set in unobserved regions, encouraging the SDF values to be large (far from zero) in free space behind the visible geometry. The loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}{sparse} =  rac{1}{\|\mathbb{Q}\|} \sum{q \in \mathbb{Q}} \exp(-	au |s(q)|) where \mathbb{Q} is the set of sampled points, s(q) is the predicted SDF value, and 	au is a temperature parameter controlling the penalty strength. By minimizing this term, the network is encouraged to make |s(q)| large for points q behind visible surfaces, thus pushing the zero-level set away from these ambiguous regions. A complementary regularization term used in SparseNeuS to further suppress free surfaces. It directly penalizes points located behind visible surfaces by encouraging their absolute SDF values to be large. The term is defined as: \mathcal{L}{rescale} = |s(q)| \cdot 	au where |s(q)| is the absolute SDF value of a sampled point q behind the visible surface, and 	au is a hyperparameter. This linear penalty works in conjunction with the exponential sparseness term to ensure compact geometry. Regularization of neural SDFs has become critical as implicit representations are applied to sparse-view and unstructured data where photometric supervision is insufficient. The Eikonal loss [12] (covered in the parent article) established the baseline for enforcing unit gradients. Subsequent works introduced specialized terms to handle specific failure modes: Smoothness: Early neural surface reconstruction methods noted that raw SDF predictions can be noisy, leading to jagged meshes. Gradient-based smoothness losses were introduced to enforce local continuity. Multi-Representation Consistency: As models like MonoSDF and others began using directional distances to resolve depth ambiguities, losses enforcing consistency between different field representations (SDF vs. DDF) became necessary. Sparse View Artifacts: In sparse-view settings (e.g., SparseNeuS), the lack of supervision behind visible surfaces leads to "flying artifacts" or free surfaces. Sparseness regularization and rescaling terms were proposed to penalize zero-crossings in these unobserved regions, ensuring the reconstructed geometry is compact and well-defined. autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Ray-Distance Volume Rendering for Neural Scene Reconstruction, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72630-922, fetched 2026-10-26 SparseNeuS: Fast Generalizable Neural Surface Reconstruction from Sparse Views, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-313, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Surface SDF Loss
head: SDF Supervision Loss, Ground Truth SDF Loss
body: The Surface SDF Loss is a supervised regularization term that constrains a neural network's predicted Signed Distance Field (SDF) values to match ground truth SDF data. It solves the problem of ensuring geometric accuracy by minimizing the discrepancy between predicted signed distances and known surface locations. Unlike the parent Eikonal loss which enforces gradient magnitude constraints, this loss directly supervises the scalar field values. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of query points \mathcal{Q}, the neural network's predicted SDF values s(\mathbf{x}) for \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{Q}, and ground truth SDF values s{GT}(\mathbf{x}) for the same points. Output: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}s. Data Structures: Points \mathbf{x} are typically sampled from the object surface, free space, or interior. s{GT} is pre-computed or retrieved from a ground truth source (e.g., rendered from meshes using tools like Trimesh). Steps: 1. Evaluate the neural network fs(\mathbf{x}) to obtain predicted SDF values s for all query points \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{Q}. 2. Retrieve corresponding ground truth SDF values s{GT} for each \mathbf{x}. 3. Compute the absolute difference between predicted and ground truth values for each point. 4. Calculate the mean of these absolute differences over the entire set \mathcal{Q}. Formula: \mathcal{L}s(s) = \|s - s{GT}\|1 = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{Q}|} \sum{\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{Q}} |s(\mathbf{x}) - s{GT}(\mathbf{x})| Where: s is the predicted SDF value. s{GT} is the ground truth SDF value. \|\cdot\|1 denotes the L1 norm (mean absolute error in this context). Parameters: Weighting factor \lambdas: Multiplies \mathcal{L}s in the total loss function. Typical values are not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ground Truth Availability: Requires access to accurate ground truth SDFs, which may need to be generated via ray marching against mesh representations. Sampling Density: The loss depends on the distribution of query points \mathcal{Q}. Insufficient sampling near the surface may lead to poor convergence. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesurfacesdfloss(predictedsdf: Tensor, groundtruthsdf: Tensor) -> Tensor: """ Computes the L1 loss between predicted SDF values and ground truth SDF values. Args: predictedsdf: Tensor of shape (N,) containing predicted SDF values s. groundtruthsdf: Tensor of shape (N,) containing ground truth SDF values sGT. Returns: Scalar Tensor representing the mean absolute error. """ # Compute element-wise absolute difference absdiff = torch.abs(predictedsdf - groundtruthsdf) # Compute mean over all query points loss = torch.mean(absdiff) return loss A variant applied to Directional Distance Field (DDF) models rather than the SDF model itself. It constrains DDF predictions to be consistent with SDF surface predictions. It computes points using DDF predictions (\mathbf{p} + d\mathbf{r}) for point-direction pairs (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{r}) pointing to the surface, and minimizes the L1 norm of the SDF value at these points: \mathcal{L}{ts}(d) = \|fs(\mathbf{p} + d\mathbf{r})\|1. This ensures the DDF-derived point lies close to the SDF zero-level set. It is applied only to the DDF model, not the SDF model. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of query points |\mathcal{Q}|, as it involves a single pass of subtraction, absolute value, and mean calculation. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to |\mathcal{Q}| to store predicted and ground truth values. Strengths: Directly enforces geometric accuracy against known ground truth. Simple to implement and differentiate. Limitations: Requires ground truth SDF data, which may not always be available. Does not enforce smoothness or gradient constraints (handled by Eikonal loss). When to use: When ground truth SDFs are available and geometric fidelity is prioritized over gradient consistency. When not to use: When ground truth is unavailable or when only gradient-based regularization is desired. The Surface SDF Loss is introduced in the context of the FIRe (Fast Inverse Rendering Using Directional and Signed Distance Functions) framework. It is used to supervise the SDF network to predict signed distances consistent with ground truth SDFs generated from rendered rays using Trimesh. The approach is part of a broader family of regularization and gradient losses for implicit surface representations. autonomousvision/sdfstudio, https://github.com/autonomousvision/sdfstudio, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) FIRe: Fast Inverse Rendering Using Directional and Signed Distance Functions, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qj0ymDlRYZs, fetched 2026-10-30

name: SDF Loss
head: L1 SDF Loss, Signed Distance Field Loss
body: SDF Loss is a regression loss function used to supervise neural networks predicting Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) by minimizing the L1 distance between predicted signed distances and ground truth SDF values. It is distinguished from occupancy-based losses (e.g., Occupancy Networks) by directly optimizing geometric accuracy rather than binary classification, though it is often combined with sign supervision for stability in meta-learning contexts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Predicted signed distance s and ground truth signed distance s{GT} at sampled points. Output: Scalar loss value \mathcal{L}s. Data Structures: s: Scalar tensor of predicted distances. s{GT}: Scalar tensor of ground truth distances. Formula: The SDF Loss is defined as the L1 norm of the difference between the predicted and ground truth signed distances: \mathcal{L}s(s) = \|s - s{GT}\|1 Parameters: None inherent to the loss definition. Weights may be applied if combined with other losses (see Subtopics). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdfloss(predictedsdf: Tensor, groundtruthsdf: Tensor) -> Tensor: """ Computes the L1 loss between predicted and ground truth SDF values. Args: predictedsdf: Tensor of predicted signed distances. groundtruthsdf: Tensor of ground truth signed distances. Returns: Scalar tensor representing the mean L1 loss. """ # Calculate absolute difference diff = abs(predictedsdf - groundtruthsdf) # Return mean over all elements return diff.mean() Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Clamping Instability: Clamping L1 loss values during gradient-based meta-learning can lead to unstable training. Precision: Ensure ground truth SDFs are computed accurately (e.g., via ray marching against meshes) to avoid supervising with noisy targets. A multitask loss function designed for stable training of MetaSDF in 3D. It addresses instability caused by clamping L1 loss in inner-loop meta-learning by tracking both SDF values and occupancy (the sign of the SDF). The network predicts two values: the distance to the surface and the sign of the distance function (inside or outside). The loss combines the L1 SDF loss with a binary cross-entropy sign loss, weighted using the uncertainty loss weighting scheme described by Kendall et al. [43]. This strategy effectively combines the loss terms of DeepSDF (L1 SDF) and Occupancy Networks (sign/occupancy). It is critical for stable training in MetaSDF, whereas DeepSDF profits little from this combination. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of sampled points, as it involves a single pass of absolute difference and mean calculation. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the difference tensor before reduction. Strengths: Directly optimizes geometric accuracy; simple to implement; robust to outliers compared to L2 loss. Limitations: Can be unstable in meta-learning if not combined with sign supervision or uncertainty weighting. When to use: When precise geometric reconstruction is required and ground truth SDFs are available. When not to use: When training is unstable due to meta-learning inner loops without sign supervision. The SDF Loss was introduced in the context of inverse rendering and SDF modeling, specifically in the FIRe (Fast Inverse Rendering Using Directional and Signed Distance Functions) framework. It is based on the principle of supervising neural networks to predict signed distances close to ground truth SDFs. The composite variant was developed for MetaSDF to enable stable meta-learning of SDFs by incorporating occupancy information. FIRe: Fast Inverse Rendering Using Directional and Signed Distance Functions, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qj0ymDlRYZs, fetched 2026-10-30 MetaSDF: Meta-learning Signed Distance Functions, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2006.09662, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Off-surface Point Loss
head: Off-surface Loss
body: The off-surface point loss is a regularization term used in training Signed Distance Field (SDF) networks to enforce that the predicted distance values are positive and large for points located far outside the target geometry. It complements the surface SDF loss by penalizing the network for predicting negative or small positive values in the exterior region, thereby preventing the SDF from collapsing or becoming ambiguous in empty space. It is distinct from the SDF Loss which primarily targets points on or near the surface. The method operates in the canonical space of the target mesh (e.g., SMPL). It involves sampling points in the exterior volume and applying an exponential penalty based on the network's output. Inputs: f{\sigmaf}(\mathbf{x}): The SDF network function parameterized by \sigmaf, returning the signed distance at point \mathbf{x}. \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{off}}: A set of sampled points in canonical space. |P|: The number of points in \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{off}}. Outputs: \mathcal{L}O: The scalar off-surface point loss value. Data Structures: \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{off}}: A set of 3D coordinates. In the source implementation, |P| = 1024. Points are sampled such that their Euclidean distance to the canonical mesh surface is greater than 20cm. Steps: 1. Sample 1024 points \hat{\mathbf{x}} in canonical space such that the distance from \hat{\mathbf{x}} to the canonical mesh surface is > 20cm. Let this set be \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{off}}. 2. For each point \hat{\mathbf{x}} \in \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{off}}, evaluate the SDF network f{\sigmaf}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}). 3. Compute the loss using the formula: \mathcal{L}O = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{\hat{\mathbf{x}} \in \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{off}}} \exp \left( -100 \cdot f{\sigmaf}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \right) where the coefficient 100 (written as 1e^2 in the source) scales the penalty. Parameters: Number of points |P|: 1024. Distance threshold for sampling: > 20cm. Exponential coefficient: 100 (1e^2). Weight \lambdaO: 100 (used in total loss combination, though the formula itself contains the internal coefficient). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If the network predicts negative values for off-surface points, the exponent becomes positive, leading to an exponentially large loss, which can cause training instability if not balanced. The threshold of 20cm is specific to the scale of the SMPL mesh; scaling the mesh or changing the domain requires re-evaluating this threshold. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def offsurfacepointloss(sdfnetwork, pointsoff, numpoints=1024): """ Computes the off-surface point loss. Args: sdfnetwork: Function fsigmaf(x) returning SDF value. pointsoff: Array of shape (numpoints, 3) containing points > 20cm from the mesh surface in canonical space. numpoints: Number of points (default 1024). Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # Evaluate SDF at all off-surface points # Shape: (numpoints,) sdfvalues = sdfnetwork(pointsoff) # Compute exponential penalty # Coefficient is 100 (1e2) as per source # exp(-100 f(x)) penalties = torch.exp(-100.0 sdfvalues) # Average over all points loss = torch.mean(penalties) return loss The inside point loss is a variant that regularizes points located inside the mesh. It samples 1024 points in canonical space that are inside the mesh and whose distance to the surface is greater than 1cm. The loss is defined as: \mathcal{L}I = \frac{1}{|P|} \sum{\hat{\mathbf{x}} \in \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{in}}} \text{sigmoid} \left( 5000 \cdot f{\sigmaf}(\hat{\mathbf{x}}) \right) where \hat{\mathbf{X}}{\text{in}} is the set of inside points, and the coefficient is 5000 (5e^3). This encourages the SDF to be negative inside the volume. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of sampled points |P|. Each point requires one forward pass through the SDF network. Memory Complexity: Linear with respect to |P| to store the sampled points and intermediate SDF values. Strengths: Effectively pushes the SDF values positive in the exterior, preventing "floating" artifacts or incorrect zero-level sets far from the surface. Limitations: The choice of sampling distance (20cm) and coefficient (100) is heuristic and tied to the specific mesh scale (SMPL). It does not enforce the Eikonal equation (gradient magnitude = 1), which is handled by separate regularization. The off-surface point loss was introduced in the ARAH (Animatable Volume Rendering of Articulated Human SDFs) method. It is part of a set of regularization losses including Eikonal loss, inside point loss, and skinning loss, designed to train robust SDF representations for articulated human bodies. name: SDF Smoothness Loss
head: Gradient Penalty Loss, SDF Gradient Regularization, Smooth Loss (Ls)
body:
SDF Smoothness Loss regularizes the reconstructed surface by penalizing the difference between the spatial gradients of the Signed Distance Function (SDF) at adjacent sampled points, thereby encouraging geometric smoothness and reducing high-frequency artifacts in the predicted field. It differs from the Eikonal loss, which enforces the gradient magnitude to be unity, by instead enforcing consistency between local gradient directions and magnitudes across small spatial perturbations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of sampled points \mathcal{X}, the SDF network d\Omega(\cdot), and a small perturbation vector \varepsilon. Output: A scalar loss value \mathcal{L}s. Data Structures: \mathcal{X}: A set of N{sm} 3D points \mathbf{p}. \varepsilon: A small perturbation vector (magnitude not specified in). Steps: 1. For each point \mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{X}, compute the SDF value s = d\Omega(\mathbf{p}). 2. Compute the spatial gradient of the SDF at \mathbf{p}: 
abla d\Omega(\mathbf{p}). This is typically obtained via automatic differentiation of the network output with respect to the input coordinates. 3. Compute the perturbed point \mathbf{p}' = \mathbf{p} + \varepsilon. 4. Compute the SDF value s' = d\Omega(\mathbf{p}'). 5. Compute the spatial gradient of the SDF at \mathbf{p}': 
abla d\Omega(\mathbf{p} + \varepsilon). 6. Compute the Euclidean distance between the two gradients. 7. Average these distances over all points in \mathcal{X}. Formula: The smooth loss \mathcal{L}s is defined as: \mathcal{L}s =  rac{1}{N{sm}} \sum{\mathbf{p} \in \mathcal{X}} \left\| 
abla d\Omega(\mathbf{p}) - 
abla d\Omega(\mathbf{p} + \varepsilon) ight\|2 Where: N{sm} is the number of points used to compute the smooth loss. \mathbf{p} is a query point in the set \mathcal{X}. d\Omega(\mathbf{p}) is the SDF output produced by the geometry MLP for point \mathbf{p}. \varepsilon is a small perturbation applied to the point. 
abla d\Omega(\cdot) denotes the gradient of the SDF with respect to the spatial coordinates. Parameters: \varepsilon: Small perturbation. Value not given in. N{sm}: Number of points. Not given in. Weighting factor \lambdas: Not explicitly defined in, but standard practice applies a weight to balance with other losses. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesdfsmoothnessloss(network, points, epsilon): """ Computes the SDF Smoothness Loss. Args: network: Neural network predicting SDF values. points: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing query points p. epsilon: Tensor of shape (3,) or (N, 3) containing perturbation vector. Returns: Scalar loss value. """ # Compute gradients at original points points.requiresgrad(True) sdforiginal = network(points) gradoriginal = torch.autograd.grad( sdforiginal.sum(), points, creategraph=True)[0] # Compute gradients at perturbed points pointsperturbed = points + epsilon pointsperturbed.requiresgrad(True) sdfperturbed = network(pointsperturbed) gradperturbed = torch.autograd.grad( sdfperturbed.sum(), pointsperturbed, creategraph=True)[0] # Compute L2 norm of the difference diff = gradoriginal - gradperturbed loss = torch.mean(torch.norm(diff, dim=1)) return loss A variant for discrete SDF fields (e.g., on tetrahedral grids) that uses normal smoothing via gradient alignment and K-nearest neighbor weighted averaging. It computes the gradient of the SDF within a tetrahedron as a linear function of SDF values at vertices and spatial gradients of interpolation weights. Smoothed SDF values are computed using a weighted average of K-nearest sites, where neighbors are found once per up-sampling step via KD-trees. The regularization loss aligns the gradient of the SDF with the gradient of the smoothed SDF. It also employs a total variation loss on tetrahedral mesh edges. Formula: The regularization loss component is: \mathcal{L}{reg} = 0.5 \sumt \left( 1 -  rac{
abla s{df,t} \cdot 
abla s{df,t}^{smooth}}{\|
abla s{df,t}\| \|
abla s{df,t}^{smooth}\|} ight)^2 Where 
abla s{df,t} is the gradient in tetrahedron t, and 
abla s{df,t}^{smooth} is the gradient of the smoothed SDF. Parameters: w{reg}: Weight factor for regularization loss. w{tv}: Weight factor for total variation loss. Time Complexity: Requires two forward passes and two gradient computations per point (original and perturbed), making it roughly twice the cost of a single gradient evaluation. Memory Complexity: Requires storing gradients for both the original and perturbed points during the backward pass. Strengths: Directly penalizes geometric irregularities and high-frequency noise in the SDF field, leading to smoother surfaces. Limitations: Depends on the choice of perturbation \varepsilon; if \varepsilon is too large, it may not capture local smoothness; if too small, it may be sensitive to numerical noise. Not given in is the optimal range for \varepsilon. When to use: When the reconstructed surface exhibits jaggedness or high-frequency artifacts despite Eikonal regularization. The SDF Smoothness Loss was introduced in the context of ray-distance volume rendering for neural scene reconstruction. It addresses potential depth ambiguities and surface irregularities by encouraging the SDF gradients to be consistent over small spatial distances.
