name: PatchNet
head: Patch-Based Generalizable Deep Implicit 3D Shape Representations
body: PatchNet represents a 3D object as a collection of learnable surface patches, where each patch models the geometry within a specific radius from its center using a neural implicit function. It solves the problem of generalizable surface reconstruction by treating patch latent codes and extrinsic parameters (position, orientation, radius) as free variables optimized directly during training (auto-decoding), rather than regressing them from an encoder. This approach allows for controllable deformation and generalization across object categories, outperforming global implicit representations like DeepSDF and structured approaches like DSIF, particularly when training data is limited. Inputs: A watertight mesh (for training) or point samples with truncated signed distance field (SDF) values (for test-time optimization). Outputs: A blended SDF field gi(x) representing the object surface, from which meshes can be extracted via Marching Cubes. Patch Extrinsic Parameters (e{i,p}) Each patch p of object i is defined by 7 parameters e{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}^7: Radius r{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}: The spherical radius of the patch. Center c{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The 3D position of the patch center. Orientation \phi{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Euler angles defining the rotation of the patch's canonical frame. Patch Latent Code (z{i,p}) z{i,p} \in \mathbb{R}^{128}: A vector describing the intrinsic geometry of the patch surface. Network Weights (\theta) Parameters of the fully-connected neural network that maps (z, x) to SDF values. 1. Preprocessing: Center the input mesh and fit it tightly into the unit sphere. Sample points mostly close to the surface and compute their truncated signed distance to the object surface, truncating at 0.1. 2. Latent Codes: Initialize all patch latent codes z{i,p} to zero. 3. Positions: Initialize patch centers c{i,p} using greedy farthest point sampling of the object's surface point samples. 4. Radii: Set each patch radius r{i,p} to the minimum value such that every surface point sample is covered by its closest patch. 5. Orientation: Align the z-axis of the patch coordinate system with the surface normal at the closest point to the patch center. The network f(x, z, \theta) takes a query point x \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a latent code z \in \mathbb{R}^{128} as input and outputs a scalar SDF value. Structure: Eight weight-normalized fully-connected layers with 128 output dimensions and ReLU activations. Concatenation: The latent code z and query point x are concatenated to the input of the fifth layer. Output: The last layer outputs a single scalar, passed through a \tanh activation to bound the SDF value. Training minimizes the total loss L over network weights \theta, patch latent codes \{zi\}, and extrinsics \{ei\} for all objects i: \arg\min{\theta, \{zi\}, \{ei\}} \sumi L(zi, ei, \theta) The total loss is defined as: L(zi, ei, \theta) = L{recon}(zi, ei, \theta) + L{ext}(ei) + L{reg}(zi) 1. Reconstruction Loss (L{recon}) Minimizes the difference between predicted and ground truth SDF values for points within each patch's bounds: L{recon}(zi, ei, \theta) = \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} \frac{1}{|S(e{i,p})|} \sum{x \in S(e{i,p})} |f(x, z{i,p}, \theta) - s(x)| Where: NP = 30 is the number of patches. S(e{i,p}) is the set of normalized point samples within the bounds of patch p. s(x) is the ground truth truncated SDF value. 2. Extrinsic Loss (L{ext}) Guides the placement and orientation of patches: L{ext}(ei) = L{sur}(ei) + L{cov}(ei) + L{rot}(ei) + L{scl}(ei) + L{var}(ei) Surface Loss (L{sur}): Ensures patches stay close to the surface: L{sur}(ei) = \omega{sur} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} \max\left( \frac{1}{|Oi|} \sum{x \in Oi} \|c{i,p} - x\|^2, t \right) Where Oi is the set of surface points of object i, and t = 0.06 is a threshold. Coverage Loss (L{cov}): Encourages uncovered surface points Ui to be covered by at least one patch: L{cov}(ei) = \omega{cov} \cdot \frac{1}{|Ui|} \sum{x \in Ui} \frac{w{i,p,x}}{\sum{p} w{i,p,x}} (\|c{i,p} - x\|^2 - r{i,p}) Where w{i,p,x} = \exp\left(-0.5 \cdot \left(\frac{\|c{i,p} - x\|^2 - r{i,p}}{\sigma}\right)^2\right) with \sigma = 0.05. Rotation Loss (L{rot}): Aligns patch orientation with surface normals: L{rot}(ei) = \omega{rot} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} (1 - \langle \phi{i,p} \cdot [0,0,1]^T, n{i,p} \rangle)^2 Where n{i,p} is the surface normal at o{i,p} = \arg\min{x \in Oi} \|x - c{i,p}\|^2. Scale Loss (L{scl}): Encourages small patch radii to prevent overlap: L{scl}(ei) = \omega{scl} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} r{i,p}^2 Variance Loss (L{var}): Encourages similar patch sizes: L{var}(ei) = \omega{var} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} (r{i,p} - mi)^2 Where mi is the mean patch radius of object i. 3. Regularization (L{reg}) L2 regularizer on latent codes assuming a Gaussian prior: L{reg}(zi) = \omega{reg} \cdot \frac{1}{NP} \sum{p=0}^{NP-1} \|z{i,p}\|^2 For a new object given point samples and SDF values, optimize for patch latent codes and extrinsics using the same initialization, while keeping network weights \theta fixed. Use for surface reconstruction and generalizable 3D shape representation when training data is limited or when cross-dataset generalization is required. Avoid if the object geometry requires highly variable patch sizes that cannot be captured by the regularization. PatchNet was introduced by Tretschk et al. in the paper "PatchNets: Patch-Based Generalizable Deep Implicit 3D Shape Representations". The method builds upon DeepSDF by introducing a patch-based representation with learnable extrinsics. It was developed to address the limitations of global implicit representations and structured implicit functions, particularly in terms of generalization and handling articulated deformations. It was compared against concurrent work such as Deep Structured Implicit Functions (DSIF). name: Deep Medial Field (DMF) Network Architecture
head: DMF Network
body:
The Deep Medial Field (DMF) Network is a neural implicit surface representation that extends the DeepSDF architecture by predicting the medial field in addition to the signed distance field (SDF) and its gradient. While DeepSDF outputs only the SDF value \Phi(x), DMF predicts two medial field components M^+(x) and M^-(x), the SDF \Phi(x), and the SDF gradient 
abla\Phi(x). This extension allows for the efficient computation of medial field ambient occlusion (MFAO) and provides information about local shape thickness. It is distinct from Vox2SDF which uses voxel grids, and builds on the DeepSDF Neural Network by adding specific heads to handle the discontinuous nature of the medial field. Inputs: A 3D point x \in \mathbb{R}^3. Outputs: Four values: 1. M^+(x) \in \mathbb{R}: Medial field value for the outside of the shape (x \in O^+). 2. M^-(x) \in \mathbb{R}: Medial field value for the inside of the shape (x \in O^-). 3. \Phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}: Signed distance value. 4. 
abla\Phi(x) \in \mathbb{R}^3: Gradient of the SDF. Data Structures: The network consists of a shared fully connected backbone (MLP) and four separate fully connected heads. Shared Backbone: An MLP with 6 hidden layers. It takes the transformed input coordinates and outputs a shared feature vector. Heads: Four separate MLPs, each with 2 hidden layers. Each hidden layer contains 64 neurons. The output layer is linear. Head 1: Outputs M^+(x). Head 2: Outputs M^-(x). Head 3: Outputs \Phi(x). Head 4: Outputs 
abla\Phi(x). Parameters: Random Fourier Features (RFF): 64 bands are used to transform input coordinates. Weighting Constant (\alpha): Set to 10^{-3}. Activation: The backbone and heads use the same activation functions as the core MLP in [Gropp et al. 2020] (typically GeLU or ReLU with geometric initialization, though specific activation names are not explicitly detailed in the provided text, the structure is defined by the layer counts). Algorithm: 1. Input Transformation: Transform the input coordinate x into Random Fourier Features (RFF). Let fi be the i-th Fourier feature band. 2. Feature Weighting: Weight each Fourier feature fi by wi = \alpha ||fi||, where ||fi|| is the frequency of the i-th band and \alpha = 10^{-3}. This weighting preserves the network's bias towards spherical topology. 3. Concatenation: Concatenate the weighted Fourier features with the original un-transformed coordinates x. 4. Shared Encoding: Pass the concatenated vector through the shared backbone MLP (6 hidden layers) to obtain a shared feature vector h. 5. Head Decoding: Pass h through each of the four separate heads to obtain the outputs: M^+(x) M^-(x) \Phi(x) 
abla\Phi(x) 6. Medial Field Combination: Compute the final medial field M(x) using the sign of \Phi(x) to handle the discontinuity at the surface \partial O: M(x) =  egin{cases} M^+(x) & 	ext{if } \Phi(x) > 0 \ M^-(x) & 	ext{if } \Phi(x) < 0 \end{cases} This formulation allows the network to model the discontinuity of the medial field at the surface, which ordinary Lipschitz MLPs cannot approximate directly. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def randomfourierfeatures(x, numbands=64, alpha=1e-3): """ Transforms input coordinates x into weighted Random Fourier Features. x: numpy array of shape (3,) Returns: concatenated weighted RFF and original x """ # Generate random frequencies B and biases b for RFF # Note: In practice, B and b are fixed random matrices/vectors # B shape: (numbands, 3) # b shape: (numbands,) # For implementation completeness, we assume these are pre-defined or generated once. # Here we simulate the generation for a single call, but in a real network, # these weights are fixed parameters. B = np.random.randn(numbands, 3) b = np.random.uniform(0, 2 np.pi, numbands) # Compute raw Fourier features # z = B @ x + b z = np.dot(B, x) + b # Compute frequencies (norms of rows in B) freqs = np.linalg.norm(B, axis=1) # Weight features # wi = alpha ||fi|| # The features are sin(z) and cos(z). The weighting applies to the feature values. # The source says "Features are weighted by wi = alpha ||fi||". # Usually, RFF features are sqrt(2/B) cos(z + b). # The weighting here seems to scale the features by the frequency. # Let's assume the features are the sin/cos components. # Feature vector F = [cos(z), sin(z)] Fcos = np.cos(z) Fsin = np.sin(z) # Weighting # The source implies weighting the Fourier features themselves. # wi = alpha freqs[i] # We apply this weight to the feature components. weightedcos = Fcos (alpha freqs) weightedsin = Fsin (alpha freqs) # Concatenate weighted features with original coordinates # Note: The source says "Weighted features are concatenated with original coordinates". # It does not specify if the unweighted features are also included. # Given "Input coordinates are transformed into Random Fourier Features... Features are weighted... Weighted features are concatenated", # it implies only the weighted RFFs are used alongside x. weightedfeatures = np.concatenate([weightedcos, weightedsin]) inputvector = np.concatenate([weightedfeatures, x]) return inputvector def sharedbackbone(inputvector): """ Shared FC Backbone MLP with 6 hidden layers. Assumes standard geometric initialization and activation from Gropp et al. 2020. """ # Placeholder for the actual MLP implementation # The source specifies 6 hidden layers. # We assume a standard MLP structure. # Since the exact activation and initialization are referenced from Gropp et al. 2020, # and not fully detailed here, we note this as a dependency. # For the purpose of this self-contained pseudocode, we define a generic MLP. # In a real implementation, one would use the specific initialization from Gropp et al. pass def headmlp(sharedfeature, numhidden=64): """ Two-layer MLP head with 64 neurons per hidden layer. """ # Placeholder for the head MLP pass def predict(x): """ Full DMF Network prediction. """ # 1. Input coordinates are transformed into Random Fourier Features (64 bands) # 2. Features are weighted by wi = alpha ||fi|| # 3. Weighted features are concatenated with original coordinates inputvec = randomfourierfeatures(x, numbands=64, alpha=1e-3) # 4. Input passes through shared backbone MLP (6 hidden layers) sharedfeat = sharedbackbone(inputvec) # 5. Shared feature vector is passed to 4 separate heads # Head 1: M+(x) Mplus = headmlp(sharedfeat, numhidden=64) # Head 2: M-(x) Mminus = headmlp(sharedfeat, numhidden=64) # Head 3: Phi(x) Phi = headmlp(sharedfeat, numhidden=64) # Head 4: Gradient Phi(x) GradPhi = headmlp(sharedfeat, numhidden=64) # 6. Heads output M+(x), M-(x), Phi(x), GradPhi(x) # Combine M+ and M- based on sign of Phi if Phi > 0: M = Mplus else: M = Mminus return M, Phi, GradPhi Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Discontinuity: The medial field has a discontinuity at the surface \partial O. Ordinary MLPs are Lipschitz and cannot approximate this discontinuity directly. The solution is to predict M^+ and M^- separately for the outside and inside, then combine them based on the sign of \Phi(x). Fourier Feature Weighting: The weighting constant \alpha must be small (10^{-3}) to preserve the network's bias towards spherical topology. Time and Memory Complexity: The complexity is dominated by the shared backbone MLP and the four heads. The backbone has 6 hidden layers, and each head has 2 hidden layers with 64 neurons. The input dimension is 3 + 2 	imes 64 = 131. The output dimension is 1 + 1 + 1 + 3 = 6. Memory: The number of parameters depends on the layer widths. The backbone width is not explicitly given, but the heads have 64 neurons. The backbone likely has a similar width. Time: Inference is fast as it involves only forward passes through small MLPs. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Provides medial field information for ambient occlusion approximation (MFAO) and local shape thickness. Handles the discontinuity of the medial field effectively. Limitations: Requires predicting additional outputs (M^+, M^-) which increases model size and training complexity compared to standard DeepSDF. When to Use: Use when medial field information is needed for applications like ambient occlusion or shape analysis. Not needed if only SDF is required. The Deep Medial Field Network was introduced by Daniel Rebain, Ke Li, Vincent Sitzmann, Soroosh Yazdani, Kwang Moo Yi, and Andrea Tagliasacchi in the paper "Deep Medial Fields". It builds upon the DeepSDF architecture [Gropp et al. 2020] and Random Fourier Features [Tancik et al. 2020]. The method was developed to provide an efficient alternative for approximating ambient occlusion using the medial field. Deep Medial Fields, https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.03804v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: LocalMap SDF Network Inference
head: LocalMap Decoder, LocalMap SDF Network
body: The LocalMap SDF Network Inference method is a neural network architecture that encodes 3D spatial coordinates into feature vectors and decodes them into Signed Distance Field (SDF) values and inverse sigma (isigma) values for density estimation. It is a specific implementation within the LocalMap framework, distinguishing itself from general-purpose implicit surface networks by its dual-output design for simultaneous geometry and density prediction. It builds on the DeepSDF Neural Network concept but specializes in the decoding stage for local map representations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D position vector \mathbf{xyz} = (x, y, z). Output: A tensor containing two scalar values: the SDF value and the raw inverse sigma value. Data Structures: The decoder output is a tensor with shape (N, 2) for N points, where the last dimension is split into two channels: Channel 0: SDF value. Channel 1: Raw inverse sigma value (before activation). Parameters: kdecoderimplementation: Integer flag (0 or 1) selecting the decoder backend. 0: Custom PyTorch Linear stack. 1: TCNN (Tiny CUDA Neural Network) FullyFusedMLP. kbceisigma: Scaling factor applied to the softplus output of the inverse sigma. encodingtype: Enum or string specifying the positional encoding scheme used by pencodingmap. normalized: Boolean flag indicating if input coordinates are normalized before encoding. Steps: 1. Position Encoding: Encode the input position \mathbf{xyz} using the encoding map. \mathbf{xyz\feat} = \text{encoding}(\mathbf{xyz}, \text{encoding\type}, \text{normalized}) 2. Feature Decoding: Pass the encoded features \mathbf{xyz\feat} through the selected decoder. If kdecoderimplementation == 0: \mathbf{output} = \text{decoder}(\mathbf{xyz\feat}) If kdecoderimplementation == 1: \mathbf{output} = \text{p\decoder\tcnn}(\mathbf{xyz\feat}) 3. Split Output: Split the decoder output tensor along the last dimension into two parts: SDF and raw isigma. [\text{sdf}, \text{raw\isigma}] = \text{split}(\mathbf{output}, \{1, 1\}, \text{dim}=-1) 4. Inverse Sigma Activation: Apply the softplus function to the raw isigma and scale it. \text{isigma} = 1 + \text{softplus}(\text{raw\isigma}, \beta=100) \times \text{k\bce\isigma} The final output tensor is [\text{sdf}, \text{isigma}]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def localmapsdfinference(xyz, encodingmap, decoder, decodertcnn, kdecoderimplementation, kbceisigma, encodingtype, normalized): """ Perform SDF and isigma inference for a batch of 3D points. Args: xyz: Tensor of shape (N, 3) containing 3D coordinates. encodingmap: Object with method 'encoding(xyz, encodingtype, normalized)'. decoder: PyTorch module for custom Linear stack (used if kdecoderimplementation == 0). decodertcnn: TCNN FullyFusedMLP module (used if kdecoderimplementation == 1). kdecoderimplementation: Integer (0 or 1) selecting the decoder backend. kbceisigma: Float scaling factor for inverse sigma. encodingtype: String or enum for encoding scheme. normalized: Boolean for coordinate normalization. Returns: sdf: Tensor of shape (N, 1) with SDF values. isigma: Tensor of shape (N, 1) with scaled inverse sigma values. """ # Step 1: Encode input position xyzfeat = encodingmap.encoding(xyz, encodingtype, normalized) # Step 2: Pass through decoder if kdecoderimplementation == 0: output = decoder(xyzfeat) elif kdecoderimplementation == 1: output = decodertcnn(xyzfeat) else: raise ValueError("kdecoderimplementation must be 0 or 1") # Step 3: Split output into SDF and raw isigma # Assuming output shape is (N, 2) sdf, rawisigma = torch.split(output, 1, dim=-1) # Step 4: Apply softplus and scaling to isigma # Softplus with beta=100 isigma = 1.0 + F.softplus(rawisigma, beta=100) kbceisigma return sdf, isigma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Decoder Selection: Ensure kdecoderimplementation matches the available backend. Using TCNN requires TCNN to be compiled and linked. Softplus Stability: The beta parameter in softplus is fixed at 100. This is a steep approximation of the max function, which may cause gradient issues if not handled carefully during training, though inference is stable. Input Normalization: The normalized flag must be consistent with how the encoding map was configured during training/inference setup. Converts voxel grids to SDFs using a different architectural approach, focusing on grid-based representations rather than local map feature encoding [4047-vox2sdf.md]. The training procedure for the parent DeepSDF architecture, which provides the latent code generation and optimization strategy [4738-deepsdf-training-loop.md]. An alternative neural network architecture for implicit surfaces, using medial axis representations [19789-deep-medial-field-dmf-network-architecture.md]. Time Complexity: Depends on the encoder and decoder depth. TCNN implementation (k=1) is generally faster on GPU due to fused operations. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only stores the decoder weights and encoding map parameters. No large voxel grids or point clouds are stored in the network itself. Strengths: Efficient evaluation of SDF and density at arbitrary points; supports two backend implementations for flexibility. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of kbceisigma and encoding parameters; TCNN dependency adds compilation complexity. When to use: When integrating SDF and density prediction into a LocalMap-based rendering pipeline. When not to use: When a pure voxel-based or point-cloud-based SDF representation is preferred. The LocalMap SDF Network Inference method is part of the GS-SDF project by hku-mars, which combines Gaussian Splatting with Signed Distance Fields. It was developed to provide a differentiable way to represent geometry and density for novel view synthesis and editing tasks. The method leverages the LocalMap framework for efficient feature encoding and decoding. hku-mars/GS-SDF, https://github.com/hku-mars/GS-SDF, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: SDF Optimization via Finite Differences
head: Finite Difference SDF Optimization, Mesh-Difference SDF Training
body: This method optimizes the values of a Signed Distance Field (SDF) and associated learnable weights to minimize the geometric difference between an extracted mesh and a target reference mesh. It differs from standard SDF evaluation by treating SDF values as learnable parameters updated via gradient descent, using finite difference gradients for the SDF rather than analytical derivatives. It builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation. Inputs: Target mesh geometry (reference). Initial SDF grid values. Initial learnable weights: \beta (size N \times 12), \alpha (size N \times 8), \gamma (size N), where N is the number of cubes. Outputs: Optimized SDF values. Optimized weights \beta, \alpha, \gamma. Data Structures: sdf: Vector of SDF values, size N{sdf}. beta: Matrix, size N \times 12, RowMajor. alpha: Matrix, size N \times 8, RowMajor. gamma: Vector, size N. Parameters: eps: Finite difference step size, 10^{-4}. clamprange: SDF value bounds, [-1.0, 1.0]. maxupdates: Number of SDF values to update per iteration, \min(100, N{sdf}). Steps: 1. Initialization: Set \beta, \alpha, \gamma to zero. Add noise: \beta{i,j} \leftarrow \beta{i,j} + \text{noise}() \times 0.1, \alpha{i,j} \leftarrow \alpha{i,j} + \text{noise}() \times 0.1, \gammai \leftarrow \gammai + \text{noise}() \times 0.1 for all i, j. 2. Gradient Computation: Loop i from 0 to maxupdates - 1: a. Store sdf[i] as sdforig. b. Perturb: sdf[i] += eps. c. Extract mesh meshplus using current SDF and weights. d. Compute loss lossplus between meshplus and target. e. Perturb: sdf[i] -= 2 eps (resulting in sdforig - eps). f. Extract mesh meshminus. g. Compute loss lossminus. h. Reset: sdf[i] += eps (restoring sdforig). i. Compute gradient: sdfgrad[i] = (lossplus - lossminus) / (2 eps). 3. Optimization Step: Apply gradient step: optimizer.step(sdf, sdfgrad). 4. Clamping: Clamp all SDF values to [-1.0, 1.0]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def optimizesdffinitedifference(sdf, beta, alpha, gamma, targetmesh, eps=1e-4, clampmin=-1.0, clampmax=1.0, maxupdates=100, numiterations=1000, learningrate=1e-3): """ Optimizes SDF values and weights using finite difference gradients. """ Nsdf = len(sdf) # Initialization beta[:] = 0.0 alpha[:] = 0.0 gamma[:] = 0.0 # Add noise beta += np.random.randn(beta.shape) 0.1 alpha += np.random.randn(alpha.shape) 0.1 gamma += np.random.randn(gamma.shape) 0.1 for iteration in range(numiterations): sdfgrad = np.zeroslike(sdf) limit = min(maxupdates, Nsdf) # Loop i from 0 to min(100, sdf.size())-1 for i in range(limit): sdforig = sdf[i] # Perturb sdf[i] += eps sdf[i] = sdforig + eps # Extract meshplus using current SDF and weights meshplus = None # Implementation not specified in sources lossplus = 0.0 # Compute loss between meshplus and target # Perturb sdf[i] -= 2eps sdf[i] = sdforig - eps meshminus = None # Extract meshminus lossminus = 0.0 # Compute lossminus # Reset sdf[i] += eps sdf[i] = sdforig # Compute gradient sdfgrad[i] = (lossplus - lossminus) / (2 eps) # Apply gradient step sdf -= learningrate sdfgrad # Clamp SDF values to [-1.0, 1.0] np.clip(sdf, clampmin, clampmax, out=sdf) return sdf, beta, alpha, gamma Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The finite difference step eps must be small enough to approximate the derivative but large enough to avoid numerical noise in mesh extraction and loss computation. Boundaries: SDF values are clamped to [-1.0, 1.0], which may affect gradients near the boundaries. Degenerate Input: If the target mesh is empty or invalid, the loss computation may fail. Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization reconstructs unknown meshes by optimizing a randomly initialized Signed Distance Field (SDF) to minimize geometric differences against a reference mesh using multiview mask and depth losses. It builds on SDF Optimization via Finite Differences by treating the SDF values as learnable parameters updated via gradient descent rather than fixed analytical functions. Time Complexity: Each gradient computation for one SDF value requires two mesh extractions and two loss computations. With maxupdates = 100, this is O(100 \cdot (M{extract} + L{compute})) per iteration, where M{extract} is mesh extraction cost and L{compute} is loss computation cost. Memory Complexity: Stores SDF, beta, alpha, gamma, and temporary meshes for perturbation. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Updating only 100 SDF values per iteration allows for faster convergence or larger grids, but may slow down global convergence. Strengths: Does not require analytical gradients for the SDF or mesh extraction, making it applicable to complex implicit surface definitions. Limitations: Computationally expensive due to repeated mesh extractions. Gradient noise may affect stability. When to use: When analytical gradients are unavailable or too complex to derive, and the SDF representation is flexible enough to be optimized directly. When not to use: When real-time performance is critical, or when the SDF is defined by simple primitives with known analytical gradients. This method is associated with the FlexiCubes framework, which uses a learnable SDF representation for mesh optimization. The approach of optimizing SDF values directly via finite differences is a technique used in neural implicit surface reconstruction and mesh optimization pipelines. ddiakopoulos/flexicubescpp, https://github.com/ddiakopoulos/flexicubescpp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization
head: nvdiffrec-style optimization
body: Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization reconstructs unknown 3D meshes by optimizing a randomly initialized Signed Distance Field (SDF) to minimize geometric differences against a reference mesh using multi-view images. It solves the problem of recovering geometry from sparse or noisy observations by treating mesh vertices or SDF values as differentiable parameters updated via gradient descent. It sets itself apart from its siblings by directly optimizing the SDF field values (and optionally learnable weights) to minimize multiview mask and depth losses, relying on automatic or analytical gradients for the SDF evaluation rather than finite differences. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view images or masks of the target object, camera poses, and a randomly initialized SDF field. Outputs: An optimized SDF field and/or mesh geometry that minimizes the difference between the rendered view and the target reference data. Data Structures: SDF Field: A scalar field S defined on a domain. In tetrahedral implementations, each vertex vi has an SDF value Si \in \mathbb{R} and a deformation value \Delta vi \in \mathbb{R}^3. Mesh Representation: The surface is extracted from the SDF (e.g., via DMTet) to compute rendering losses. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the SDF field randomly. If using DMTet, initialize vertices with base positions and zero deformations. 2. Rendering: Render the current mesh/SDF from the given camera poses to obtain rendered masks M'. 3. Loss Calculation: Compute the loss between the rendered output and the ground truth (reference mesh/masks). Mask Loss: Calculate the L1 norm between the ground truth mask M and the rendered mask M': L{mask} = \frac{|M - M'|}{2} Depth Loss: Minimize depth differences against the reference mesh. Regularization: Optionally add a developability regularizer (L{dev}) to encourage fabricability from panels. Add Implicit Geometric Regularization (IGR) as an eikonal loss to constrain the gradient magnitude of the SDF field f\theta to be close to 1: L{eikonal} = E{v0 \in V0} (||\nabla f\theta (v0)||^2 - 1)^2 4. Optimization: Update the SDF values and/or vertex deformations using gradient descent to minimize the total loss. 5. Progressive Encoding (Optional): If using neural representations, employ progressive position encoding to alleviate high-frequency noise while retaining details. The encoding frequency is gradually increased after training reaches a certain stage. Parameters: Regularization Weights: Initially set low to avoid hindering convergence; incrementally increased if artifacts appear. L1 Regularizer on Flexible Weights: Generally low impact for single shape, but stabilizes generative pipelines. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. for iteration in range(numiterations): # 1. Update mesh geometry: vi' = vi + deltavi currentvertices = vertexdeformations + basevertices # Surface extraction (e.g., DMTet) converts SDF and vertices to explicit mesh meshvertices, meshfaces = extractsurface(currentvertices, sdfvalues) # 2. Render current mesh to get masks renderedmasks = projectandrasterize(meshvertices, meshfaces, cameraposes) # 3. Compute Losses # Mask Loss: L1 norm between ground truth and rendered mask lossmask = torch.mean(torch.abs(groundtruthmasks - renderedmasks)) / 2.0 # Eikonal Regularization: Constrain gradient magnitude of SDF to 1 # Compute SDF gradients via automatic differentiation sdfgradients = computesdfgradients(sdfvalues, currentvertices) losseikonal = torch.mean((torch.norm(sdfgradients, dim=-1)2 - 1)2) # Developability Regularizer (optional) lossdev = computedevelopabilityloss(meshvertices, meshfaces) # Total Loss totalloss = lossmask + lambdaeikonal losseikonal + lambdadev lossdev # 4. Backpropagate and Update totalloss.backward() # Update SDF values sdfvalues = sdfvalues - learningrate sdfvalues.grad # Update vertex deformations vertexdeformations = vertexdeformations - learningrate vertexdeformations.grad # Clear gradients sdfvalues.grad.zero() vertexdeformations.grad.zero() # Progressive Position Encoding Update if iteration in encodingschedule: increaseencodingfrequency() This method is a gradient-based optimization technique for recovering mesh geometry from multi-view images by optimizing vertex positions. It solves the problem of slow convergence and loss of sharp features (silhouettes, thin structures) in inverse rendering, which occurs when standard Laplacian smoothing dilutes sparse silhouette gradients. It sets itself apart from its parent Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization by replacing the Laplacian postfilter with an edge-aware cross-bilateral filter that preserves values on silhouettes, enabling faster convergence on models with thin structures or many silhouettes. This variant approximates non-deformed initial mesh geometry with a set of spheres to compute visibility. The mesh is deformed by translating and rotating these spheres, allowing inverse problems to supervise sphere parameters and update geometry. To determine the initial position and radius of each sphere, it minimizes the total volume occupied by the sphere set outside the mesh (sphere outside volume) along with a term encouraging the sphere set to cover the mesh surface, optimized using gradient descent. It connects sphere centers as an embedded graph to drive mesh deformation, where each sphere is connected to its K-nearest vertices on the template. Mesh deformation is parameterized by the rotation and translation of each sphere, which are optimized using rendering loss during inverse problems. This variant defines object geometry as a Signed Distance Field (SDF) on a tetrahedral mesh T. Each vertex vi has an SDF value Si \in \mathbb{R} and a deformation value \Delta vi \in \mathbb{R}^3. The mesh is updated as vi' = vi + \Delta vi. It supervises the optimization using rendered masks derived from projecting the object according to camera poses. It uses progressive position encoding to alleviate high-frequency noise while retaining details, gradually increasing the encoding frequency after training reaches a certain stage. It adds Implicit Geometric Regularization (IGR) as an eikonal loss to constrain the gradient magnitude of the SDF field f\theta to be close to 1: L{eikonal} = E{v0 \in V0} (||\nabla f\theta (v0)||^2 - 1)^2. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of optimization iterations and the cost of rendering/gradient computation per iteration. Gradient descent requires multiple forward and backward passes per step. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the resolution of the SDF grid or the number of vertices in the tetrahedral mesh, plus the memory for storing gradients and intermediate rendering buffers. Strengths: Can recover detailed geometry from sparse views; differentiable nature allows end-to-end optimization with other neural components; eikonal regularization helps maintain smooth, well-defined surfaces. Limitations: Sensitive to initialization; prone to local minima; high-frequency noise can be introduced without proper regularization (e.g., eikonal loss or progressive encoding); computationally expensive due to repeated rendering and gradient computation. When to Use: When reconstructing geometry from multi-view images where explicit mesh topology is unknown or difficult to match; when integrating mesh optimization into differentiable rendering pipelines. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical; when the target geometry is extremely complex with thin structures that require specialized filtering (see Inverse Mesh Recovery with Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering). Gradient-based mesh optimization for SDFs has been developed in the context of differentiable rendering and inverse graphics. The FlexiCubes method popularized optimizing SDF values and learnable weights to minimize geometric differences against reference meshes. The DMTet approach combines tetrahedral meshes with SDFs and eikonal regularization for robust surface reconstruction. Sphere fitting variants offer an alternative parameterization for deformation and visibility computation in inverse problems. name: Inverse Mesh Recovery with Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering
head: Edge-aware cross-bilateral filter for mesh recovery, Spatiotemporal optimizer for inverse recovery
body: This method is a gradient-based optimization technique for recovering mesh geometry from multi-view images by optimizing vertex positions. It solves the problem of slow convergence and loss of sharp features (silhouettes, thin structures) in inverse rendering, which occurs when standard Laplacian smoothing dilutes sparse silhouette gradients. It sets itself apart from its parent Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization by replacing the Laplacian postfilter with an edge-aware cross-bilateral filter that preserves values on silhouettes, enabling faster convergence on models with thin structures or many silhouettes. The method follows the Large Steps framework, but replaces the postfilter on the intermediate variable mt with a mesh cross-bilateral filter. The optimization minimizes the geometric difference between the rendered views of the current mesh and the reference multi-view images. Inputs: Reference multi-view images (depth/mask or photometric data). Initial mesh geometry (typically a sphere). Hyperparameters: learning rate \alpha, Adam momentum \beta1, \beta2, regularization \lambda, bilateral filter range parameters \sigma\phi, \sigmad. Outputs: Optimized mesh vertex positions. Data Structures: Mesh: Defined by vertex positions V \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N} and connectivity. Vertex Normals: \hat{n} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times N}, computed from mesh geometry. Gradient Vectors: h \in \mathbb{R}^N (scalar field to be filtered, e.g., displacement or loss gradient). Laplacian Matrix: L \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}, the standard cotangent Laplacian. Parameters: \alpha (learning rate): 1 \times 10^{-2} for cube, 3 \times 10^{-2} for dragon. \beta1, \beta2 (Adam momentum): 0.9, 0.99. \lambda (regularization weight): 19. \sigma\phi (photometric range parameter): 0.4. \sigmad (spatial distance parameter): 0.5. N{samples}: 16 samples per pixel for forward rendering, 1 sample per pixel for gradient. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the mesh as a sphere with approximately 10,000 vertices. 2. Iteration Loop: For each optimization step t: a. Rendering: Render all views using the current mesh. Use 16 samples per pixel for the forward pass and 1 sample per pixel for the gradient computation. b. Loss Computation: Compute the loss using the L1 norm between the rendered output and the reference. c. Gradient Update: Compute the gradient of the loss with respect to the mesh parameters. Update the vertex positions using the UniformAdam optimizer with parameters \beta1=0.9, \beta2=0.99 and learning rate \alpha. d. Prefiltering: Apply a Laplacian prefilter to the gradient/parameter update. This step is crucial for diffusing silhouette gradients. e. Postfiltering (Cross-Bilateral Filter): Apply the mesh cross-bilateral filter to the intermediate variable mt (the update or state being filtered). This replaces the Laplacian smoothing used in Large Steps. i. Sample N=32 directions si \in S^2 on the unit sphere using the Sobol sequence. ii. Compute diagonal data matrices Wi and partition of unity matrices \Phii for each direction si. iii. Construct the matrix M by concatenating vectors Wi h and Wi \mathbf{1}. iv. Solve the linear system (I + \lambda L) X = M for X. v. Compute the filtered result \tilde{h} using component-wise operations on X. f. Optional Postfilter on vt: In ablation studies, applying a bilateral filter on the intermediate variable vt (along with UniformAdam infinity norm) was found to perform well, though it may cause small cracks on sharp edges. g. Learning Rate Schedule: Apply an exponential learning rate scheduler that reduces the learning rate to a factor of 0.6 at the end of the optimization. 3. Upsampling (Conditional): For models with thin structures (e.g., dragon), upsample the mesh at specific iterations (10, 30, 60) by remeshing to reduce the average edge length by a factor of 2. Models with sharp edges but no thin structures (e.g., cube) do not require remeshing. Cross-Bilateral Filter Formula: The filtered vector \tilde{h} is computed as: \tilde{h} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N \Phi(\hat{n}, si) (I + \lambda L)^{-1} W(\hat{n}, si) h}{\sum{i=1}^N \Phi(\hat{n}, si) (I + \lambda L)^{-1} W(\hat{n}, si) \mathbf{1}} where: h is the vector to be filtered. \mathbf{1} is the vector of ones. Wi = W(\hat{n}, si) is the diagonal data matrix with elements \exp(\hat{n} \cdot si / \sigmad). \Phii = \Phi(\hat{n}, si) is the diagonal partition of unity matrix with elements \exp(\hat{n} \cdot si / \sigma\phi). L is the Laplacian matrix. \lambda is the regularization parameter. N=32 is the number of sampled directions. Efficient Implementation: To avoid N separate matrix solves, concatenate the vectors Wi h and Wi \mathbf{1} into a single matrix M \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 2N}: M = \left[ \begin{array}{c|c} W1 h & W1 \mathbf{1} \\ \vdots & \vdots \\ WN h & WN \mathbf{1} \end{array} \right] Compute X = (I + \lambda L)^{-1} M using a single matrix solve (e.g., Cholesky decomposition). The final \tilde{h} is obtained by component-wise division of the first N columns of X by the second N columns, weighted by \Phii. Pitfalls: Laplacian preconditioning smooths gradients at silhouettes, causing them to be diluted. This is problematic for models with thin structures and many silhouettes (e.g., dragon), as vertices near but not on silhouettes receive no silhouette gradients, and Laplacian smoothing dilutes the values on the silhouette vertices. Using a bilateral filter on vt can cause small cracks in the edges due to aggressive updates, although it provides comparable convergence to the proposed method on cubes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch def computecrossbilateralfilter(h, normals, L, lambdareg, sigmaphi, sigmad, numdirections=32): """ Compute the mesh cross-bilateral filter efficiently using a single matrix solve. Args: h: Tensor (V,) - vector to be filtered (mt) normals: Tensor (V, 3) - vertex normals L: Tensor (V, V) - Laplacian matrix lambdareg: float - regularization parameter sigmaphi: float - photometric range parameter sigmad: float - spatial distance parameter numdirections: int - number of Sobol directions (default 32) Returns: htilde: Tensor (V,) - filtered vector """ V = h.shape[0] # 1. Sample directions on unit sphere using Sobol sequence sobol = torch.quasirandom.SobolEngine(3, scramble=True) raw = sobol.draw(numdirections) directions = raw 2 - 1 # Map to [-1, 1] directions = directions / (torch.norm(directions, dim=1, keepdim=True) + 1e-8) # Normalize # 2. Compute weights for each direction # normals: (V, 3), directions: (numdirections, 3) -> dots: (V, numdirections) dots = torch.matmul(normals, directions.T) # Wi diagonal elements: exp(nhat. si / sigmad) W = torch.exp(dots / sigmad) # Phii diagonal elements: exp(nhat. si / sigmaphi) Phi = torch.exp(dots / sigmaphi) # 3. Construct matrix M = [W1 h... WN h | W1 1... WN 1] # Wh: (V, numdirections) where col i = W[:, i] h Wh = h.unsqueeze(1) W # W1: (V, numdirections) where col i = W[:, i] W1 = W M = torch.cat([Wh, W1], dim=1) # 4. Solve (I + lambda L) X = M using Cholesky A = torch.eye(V, device=h.device) + lambdareg L try: Lchol = torch.linalg.cholesky(A) X = torch.linalg.chosolve((Lchol, True), M) except RuntimeError: X = torch.linalg.solve(A, M) # 5. Compute htilde = sum(Phii X[:, i]) / sum(Phii X[:, N+i]) numerator = torch.sum(Phi X[:,:numdirections], dim=1) denominator = torch.sum(Phi X[:, numdirections:], dim=1) denominator = torch.clamp(denominator, min=1e-8) return numerator / denominator def optimizemesh(vertices, normals, L, views, alpha, beta1, beta2, lambdareg, sigmaphi, sigmad, maxiters, upsampleiters=None): """ Main optimization loop for inverse mesh recovery. """ optimizer = torch.optim.Adam([vertices], lr=alpha, betas=(beta1, beta2)) scheduler = torch.optim.lrscheduler.ExponentialLR(optimizer, gamma=0.6(1/maxiters)) for t in range(maxiters): # Render all views using current mesh # loss = computeloss(vertices, views) # L1 norm # Backpropagate & Update with UniformAdam optimizer.zerograd() # loss.backward() # grad = vertices.grad # optimizer.step() # Prefilter (Laplacian) # gradprefiltered = torch.linalg.solve(torch.eye(V) + lambdareg L, grad) # Postfilter (Cross-Bilateral) on the update mt mt = computecrossbilateralfilter( gradprefiltered, normals, L, lambdareg, sigmaphi, sigmad) vertices.data += mt # Optional Postfilter on vt (ablation) # if usevtfilter: # vt = computecrossbilateralfilter(vt, normals, L, lambdareg, sigmaphi, sigmad) # Upsampling (Conditional) if upsampleiters and t in upsampleiters: # mesh.remesh(edgelengthfactor=0.5) pass scheduler.step() return vertices This is the core filtering mechanism used in the method. It replaces the postfilter on mt with a cross-bilateral filter using vertex normals \hat{n} for the data term. It samples N=32 directions si \in S^2 on the unit sphere using the Sobol sequence. It computes the filter efficiently by concatenating vectors W(\hat{n}, si)h and W(\hat{n}, si)\mathbf{1} into matrix M = [W(\hat{n}, s1)h \dots W(\hat{n}, sN)h \mid W(\hat{n}, s1)\mathbf{1} \dots W(\hat{n}, sN)\mathbf{1}], then computing (I + \lambda L)^{-1} M using a single matrix solve. The filtered result is \tilde{h} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^N \Phi(\hat{n}, si) (I+\lambda L)^{-1} W(\hat{n}, si) h}{\sum{i=1}^N \Phi(\hat{n}, si) (I+\lambda L)^{-1} W(\hat{n}, si) \mathbf{1}}. The diagonal elements of Wi are computed using the von Mises-Fisher kernel \exp(\hat{n} \cdot si / \sigmad), and \Phii using \exp(\hat{n} \cdot si / \sigma\phi). Time Complexity: The cross-bilateral filter requires solving a linear system (I + \lambda L)^{-1} M. The overhead over Large Steps (which uses Laplacian smoothing) is minor (<10%). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the Laplacian matrix L and the matrix M of size N \times 2K. Performance: On an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3080 GPU, the method converges faster than Large Steps on models with thin structures and many silhouettes (e.g., dragon). Strengths: Preserves sharp edges and silhouettes better than Laplacian smoothing. Faster convergence on thin structures. Low overhead. Limitations: Introduces two new hyperparameters (\sigma\phi, \sigmad) that require tuning. Assumes spatial coherence in parameters. Bilateral filtering on vt can cause small cracks on sharp edges. When to use: When recovering meshes with thin structures, many silhouettes, or sharp edges where Laplacian smoothing dilutes gradients. When not to use: When parameters lack obvious spatial coherence. The method was introduced in the paper "Spatiotemporal Bilateral Gradient Filtering for Inverse Rendering". It builds on the Large Steps framework, which uses Laplacian smoothing and an infinity norm as filters. The authors found that Laplacian preconditioning smooths gradients at silhouettes, causing them to be diluted, which is problematic for models with thin structures. The proposed method replaces the postfilter with a mesh cross-bilateral filter, inspired by the generalized bilateral filter from Solomon et al. [2014]. The implementation uses PyTorch [Paszke et al. 2019] and Mitsuba 3 [Jakob et al. 2022]. name: Mandelbulb SDF Evaluation
head: Fractal SDF, Mandelbulb, Mandelbulb Distance Estimator, Mandelbulb Fractal SDF, Mandelbulb distance function, sdMandelbulb
body: The Mandelbulb SDF Evaluation computes the signed distance from a 3D point to the boundary of the Mandelbulb fractal using an iterative derivative-based estimation. It differs from standard primitives by using polar coordinate transformations and derivative tracking to approximate the distance to a non-algebraic surface. It builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation. The method uses the distance estimation technique for iterated function systems, where the distance is approximated by the radius of the current point scaled by the logarithm of its magnitude and divided by the accumulated derivative of the iteration function. Input: point (vec3): The 3D query point in world space. center (vec3): The center of the Mandelbulb. scale (float): Global scaling factor applied to the input point offset and the final returned distance. power (float): Exponent for the fractal mapping that controls the geometric complexity and shape of the Mandelbulb. maxiterations (int): Maximum number of fractal iterations performed per point evaluation. bailout (float): Maximum radius threshold to break iteration early and prevent numerical overflow. Output: distance (float): The estimated signed distance from point to the Mandelbulb surface. No persistent data structures are required. Temporary variables include: z (vec3): Current position in the transformed space. dr (float): Accumulated derivative of the iteration function with respect to the initial position. r (float): Magnitude (radius) of z. theta, phi (float): Spherical angles. 1. Initialization: Translate and scale the input point: z = \frac{\text{point} - \text{center}}{\text{scale}}. Initialize derivative: dr = 1.0. Initialize radius: r = 0.0. 2. Iteration Loop: For i from 0 to maxiterations - 1: Calculate current radius: r = \|z\|. Bailout Check: If r > \text{bailout}, break the loop. Convert to spherical coordinates: \theta = \arccos\left(\frac{zz}{r}\right). \phi = \operatorname{atan2}(zy, zx). Update derivative: dr = r^{\text{power} - 1} \cdot \text{power} \cdot dr + 1.0. Calculate radial power: zr = r^{\text{power}}. Scale angles: \theta \leftarrow \theta \cdot \text{power}. \phi \leftarrow \phi \cdot \text{power}. Transform back to Cartesian coordinates: z \leftarrow zr \cdot (\sin\theta\cos\phi, \sin\theta\sin\phi, \cos\theta) + \frac{\text{point} - \text{center}}{\text{scale}}. 3. Distance Calculation: Calculate distance: d = \frac{0.5 \cdot \ln(r) \cdot r}{dr}. Scale the result: d = d \cdot \text{scale}. Return d. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdMandelbulb(point: vec3, center: vec3, scale: float, power: float, maxiterations: int, bailout: float) -> float: # 1. Initialize z = (point - center) / scale dr = 1.0 r = 0.0 # 2. Iterate for i in range(maxiterations): r = length(z) if r > bailout: break # Guard against division by zero in acos if r < 1e-6: break # Spherical coordinates theta = acos(z.z / r) phi = atan2(z.y, z.x) # Update derivative dr = pow(r, power - 1.0) power dr + 1.0 # Radial power zr = pow(r, power) # Scale angles theta = theta power phi = phi power # Transform back to Cartesian and add constant offset z.x = zr sin(theta) cos(phi) z.y = zr sin(theta) sin(phi) z.z = zr cos(theta) z = z + (point - center) / scale # 3. Distance Estimator if r < 1e-6: return 0.0 distance = 0.5 log(r) r / dr distance = distance scale return distance power: 8.0 is the classic Mandelbulb exponent. maxiterations: Defined as an integer. One implementation fixes it at 6. Not given in the sources. bailout: 2.0 is standard for escape radius. scale: Depends on the desired size of the object in the scene. Division by Zero: If r=0 (the point is exactly at the origin of the iteration space), \arccos(zz/r) is undefined. Guard against r < \epsilon. Precision: Floating point precision issues can cause jitter in the distance estimate for points very close to the surface, especially with high power values. Inside the Fractal: The distance estimator d = \frac{0.5 \ln(r) r}{dr} is valid for points outside the fractal (where r \to \infty). For points inside, the distance is not well-defined by this formula, and ray marching may fail or require a different estimator. Time Complexity: O(I), where I is the number of iterations. Each iteration involves trigonometric functions and vector operations. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary memory is required. Performance: The Mandelbulb SDF is computationally expensive per evaluation due to the trigonometric functions (sin, cos, atan2, acos) and power calculations. It is significantly slower than primitive SDFs but allows for infinitely detailed geometry. Strengths: Generates complex, organic-looking fractal geometry with a single function. No mesh storage required. Limitations: High computational cost. The distance estimate is an approximation and may not be perfectly tight, potentially leading to slightly larger step sizes in ray marching or visual artifacts if the derivative is inaccurate. name: SDF and Material Optimization Pipeline
head: SDF training loop, relaxed boundary optimization
body: This method optimizes a voxelized signed distance field (SDF) and associated material volumes (albedo, roughness, metallic) by minimizing the L1 difference between rendered images and reference images. It differs from pure geometry optimization by jointly updating material grids, and from neural SDF methods by using explicit grid-based representations with periodic upsampling. It builds on SDF Evaluation Implementation for the forward rendering pass. Inputs: Scene definition containing geometry and initial material volumes. Reference images rendered from multiple sensor viewpoints. Configuration parameters: sdfres, sphereradius, lr, batchsize, spp, sppgrad, laplacianweight, lrdecay, upsample epochs, lrdownsample epochs, checkpoint interval. Outputs: Optimized SDF grid stored as.npy. Optimized material grids (albedo, roughness, metallic) stored as.npy and.vol. Loss curves and intermediate optimization videos. Data Structures: SDF Grid: 3D tensor of shape (res, res, res) representing the signed distance field. Initialized as a sphere. Material Grids: 3D tensors for basecolor (albedo), roughness, and metallic. Resampled to match sdfres. Optimizer State: Adam optimizer state for the SDF grid and material grids. Checkpoint Format: 1D array where the first element is the resolution res, followed by the flattened grid values grid.flatten(). Parameters: lr: Base learning rate for Adam. lralbedoscale, lrroughnessscale, lrmetallicscale: Multipliers for material learning rates relative to lr. laplacianweight: Weight for the Laplacian regularization term. lrdecay: Factor by which lr is divided during upsample/lrdownsample epochs. batchsize: Number of sensor images processed per epoch. sdfres: Target resolution for SDF and material volumes. spp, sppgrad: Samples per pixel for rendering and gradient estimation. Steps: 1. Initialization: Load the scene and sensors. Render reference images using a non-differentiable integrator. Initialize the SDF as a SphereSDF with resolution sdfres and radius sphereradius. Enable gradients on the SDF grid tensor. Traverse scene parameters to identify material volumes (basecolor, reflectance, roughness, metallic). If material volumes exist, upsample their resolution to sdfres using upsampleto and update the scene parameters. Configure the Adam optimizer with base learning rate lr. Add the SDF grid to the optimizer. If materials are enabled, add their grids to the optimizer and set per-parameter learning rates: lralbedo = lr lralbedoscale lrroughness = lr lrroughnessscale lrmetallic = lr lrmetallicscale. 2. Optimization Loop: Calculate steps per epoch: steps = ceil(numsensor / batchsize). For each epoch: Calculate number of indices: numindices = min(batchsize, numsensor). Generate indices: indices = [(j steps + epoch % steps) % numsensor for j in range(numindices)]. Shuffle indices. Initialize losssum = 0. For each index i in indices: Render image using the SDF integrator with spp, sppgrad, and seed epoch numsensor + i. Compute L1 loss: loss = l1loss(image, refimages[i]) / batchsize. Accumulate loss: losssum += loss. Backpropagate: dr.backward(loss). Compute regularization loss: regloss = laplacianweight laplacianloss(sdf.grid.tensor()). Backpropagate regularization: dr.backward(regloss). Update parameters: optimizer.step(). Redistance the SDF grid: grid = redistance(optimizer['grid'], method='fastsweep'). Convert grid to 4D tensor: grid = atleast4d(TensorXf(grid)). Update optimizer grid: optimizer['grid'] = grid. Update scene parameters with optimizer state. If epoch in upsample list: Decay learning rate: lr /= lrdecay. Update optimizer learning rates for grid and materials. Upsample SDF: upsamplesdf. Upsample materials: upsamplegrid (only if resolution != 256). If epoch in lrdownsample list: Decay learning rate: lr /= lrdecay. Update optimizer learning rates for grid and materials. If epoch % checkpoint == 0: Save checkpoint: flatten grid, prepend resolution, save as [resolution] + grid.tolist() to.npy. Repeat for materials if enabled. 3. Finalization: Save final SDF and material grids in [resolution] + grid.tolist() format to.npy. Write material grids to.vol files via mi.VolumeGrid. Generate optimization video (24 FPS) from optdir. Plot L1 loss over epochs and save as loss.pdf, loss.png, loss.npy. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import os import numpy as np import drjit as dr def geth2sensors(numtheta, numphi, resx, resy, radius, height): return [type('Sensor', (), {'id': i})() for i in range(numtheta numphi)] class SphereSDF: def init(self, res, radius): self.grid = dr.zeros((res, res, res), dtype=dr.float32) coords = np.mgrid[-1:1:res1j, -1:1:res1j, -1:1:res1j] dist = np.sqrt(np.sum(coords2, axis=0)) self.grid[:] = (dist - radius) 2.0 def tensor(self): return self.grid class Adam: def init(self, lr): self.lr = lr self.state = {} def setitem(self, key, val): self.state[key] = val def setlearningrate(self, mapping): for k, v in mapping.items(): self.state[k] = v def step(self): for k, v in self.state.items(): v[:] -= self.lr dr.grad(v) def upsampleto(tensor, targetres): return dr.interpolate(tensor, targetres) def upsamplesdf(sdf, grid): sdf.grid[:] = upsampleto(grid, sdf.grid.shape[0]) def upsamplegrid(tensor): return upsampleto(tensor, tensor.shape[0] 2) def redistance(grid, method): return dr.abs(grid) dr.sign(grid) def atleast4d(tensor): return dr.reshape(tensor, (1, tensor.shape)) def TensorXf(tensor): return tensor def laplacianloss(grid): kernel = np.zeros((3,3,3)) kernel[1,1,1] = -6 kernel[1,1,0] = kernel[1,1,2] = kernel[1,0,1] = kernel[1,2,1] = kernel[0,1,1] = kernel[2,1,1] = 1 return dr.sum(dr.convolve(grid, kernel)2) def l1loss(a, b): return dr.sum(dr.abs(a - b)) def savecheckpoint(expdir, epoch, sdf, sceneparams, data = [res] + grid.flatten().tolist() np.save(os.path.join(sdfdir, f"sdf-{epoch}.npy"), data) if optalbedo: data = [res] + sceneparams[albedoname].flatten().tolist() np.save(os.path.join(sdfdir, f"albedo-{epoch}.npy"), data) if optroughness: data = [res] + sceneparams[roughnessname].flatten().tolist() np.save(os.path.join(sdfdir, f"roughness-{epoch}.npy"), data) if optmetallic: data = [res] + sceneparams[metallicname].flatten().tolist() np.save(os.path.join(sdfdir, f"metallic-{epoch}.npy"), data) def savefinal(expdir, sdf, sceneparams, optalbedo, optroughness, optmetallic, albedoname, roughnessname, metallicname): sdfdir = os.path.join(expdir, "params") os.makedirs(sdfdir, existok=True) grid = sdf.grid.tensor() res = grid.shape[0] data = [res] + grid.flatten().tolist() np.save(os.path.join(sdfdir, "sdf-final.npy"), data) if optalbedo: data = [res] + sceneparams[albedoname].flatten().tolist() np.save(os.path.join(sdfdir, "albedo-final.npy"), data) if optroughness: data = [res] + sceneparams[roughnessname].flatten().tolist() np.save(os.path.join(sdfdir, "roughness-final.npy"), data) if optmetallic: data = [res] + sceneparams[metallicname].flatten().tolist() np.save(os.path.join(sdfdir, "metallic-final.npy"), data) def generatevideos(optdir): pass def plotloss(losses, expdir): pass def optimizesdfandmaterials(expconfig, renderconfig, diffconfig, scenepath, outdir): expdir = os.path.join(outdir, expconfig["expname"]) os.makedirs(expdir, existok=True) scene = mi.loadfile(scenepath, HIDEENV=renderconfig["hideenv"]) sensors = geth2sensors( numsensortheta=expconfig["numsensortheta"], numsensorphi=expconfig["numsensorphi"], resx=renderconfig["resx"], resy=renderconfig["resy"], radius=1.3, height=0.4) numsensor = len(sensors) refdir = os.path.join(expdir, "ref") os.makedirs(refdir, existok=True) refintegrator = mi.loaddict({"type": renderconfig["refintegrator"]}) refimages = [] with dr.suspendgrad(): for i in range(numsensor): refimage = refintegrator.render(scene=scene, sdf=SphereSDF(1, 1), sensor=sensors[i], spp=renderconfig["refspp"]) refimages.append(refimage) sdf = SphereSDF(res=expconfig["sdfres"], radius=expconfig["sphereradius"]) dr.enablegrad(sdf.grid.tensor()) params = mi.traverse(scene) optalbedo = 'main-bsdf.basecolor.volume.data' in params or 'main-bsdf.reflectance.volume.data' in params optroughness = 'main-bsdf.roughness.volume.data' in params optmetallic = 'main-bsdf.metallic.volume.data' in params sceneparams = params if optalbedo: albedoname = 'main-bsdf.basecolor.volume.data' if 'main-bsdf.basecolor.volume.data' in params else 'main-bsdf.reflectance.volume.data' sceneparams[albedoname] = upsampleto(sceneparams[albedoname], expconfig["sdfres"]) sceneparams.update() if optroughness: roughnessname = 'main-bsdf.roughness.volume.data' sceneparams[roughnessname] = upsampleto(sceneparams[roughnessname], expconfig["sdfres"]) sceneparams.update() if optmetallic: metallicname = 'main-bsdf.metallic.volume.data' sceneparams[metallicname] = upsampleto(sceneparams[metallicname], expconfig["sdfres"]) sceneparams.update() optimizer = Adam(lr=expconfig["lr"]) optimizer['grid'] = sdf.grid.tensor() if optalbedo: optimizer[albedoname] = sceneparams[albedoname] optimizer.setlearningrate({albedoname: expconfig["lr"] expconfig["lralbedoscale"]}) if optroughness: optimizer[roughnessname] = sceneparams[roughnessname] optimizer.setlearningrate({roughnessname: expconfig["lr"] expconfig["lrroughnessscale"]}) if optmetallic: optimizer[metallicname] = sceneparams[metallicname] optimizer.setlearningrate({metallicname: expconfig["lr"] expconfig["lrmetallicscale"]}) sdfintegrator = mi.loaddict({"type": renderconfig["sdfintegrator"]}) steps = int(np.ceil(numsensor / expconfig["batchsize"])) losses = [] lr = expconfig["lr"] for epoch in range(expconfig["numepoch"]): losssum = dr.Float(0) numindices = min(expconfig["batchsize"], numsensor) indices = [(j steps + epoch % steps) % numsensor for j in range(numindices)] np.random.shuffle(indices) for i in indices: seed = epoch numsensor + i image = sdfintegrator.render( scene=scene, sdf=sdf, sensor=sensors[i], spp=renderconfig["spp"], sppgrad=renderconfig["sppgrad"], seed=seed, params=sceneparams) loss = l1loss(image, refimages[i]) / expconfig["batchsize"] losssum += loss dr.backward(loss) regloss = expconfig["laplacianweight"] laplacianloss(sdf.grid.tensor()) losssum += regloss dr.backward(regloss) optimizer.step() grid = redistance(optimizer['grid'], method='fastsweep') grid = atleast4d(TensorXf(grid)) optimizer['grid'] = grid sdfparams.update(optimizer) sceneparams.update(optimizer) if epoch in expconfig["upsample"]: lr /= expconfig["lrdecay"] optimizer.setlearningrate({'grid': lr}) if optalbedo: optimizer.setlearningrate({albedoname: lr expconfig["lralbedoscale"]}) if optroughness: optimizer.setlearningrate({roughnessname: lr expconfig["lrroughnessscale"]}) if optmetallic: optimizer.setlearningrate({metallicname: lr expconfig["lrmetallicscale"]}) upsamplesdf(sdf, optimizer['grid']) if expconfig["sdfres"] != 256: if optalbedo: sceneparams[albedoname] = upsamplegrid(sceneparams[albedoname]) if optroughness: sceneparams[roughnessname] = upsamplegrid(sceneparams[roughnessname]) if optmetallic: sceneparams[metallicname] = upsamplegrid(sceneparams[metallicname]) sceneparams.update() if epoch in expconfig["lrdownsample"]: lr /= expconfig["lrdecay"] optimizer.setlearningrate({'grid': lr}) if optalbedo: optimizer.setlearningrate({albedoname: lr expconfig["lralbedoscale"]}) if optroughness: optimizer.setlearningrate({roughnessname: lr expconfig["lrroughnessscale"]}) if optmetallic: optimizer.setlearningrate({metallicname: lr expconfig["lrmetallicscale"]}) if epoch % expconfig["checkpoint"] == 0: savecheckpoint(expdir, epoch, sdf, sceneparams, optalbedo, optroughness, Precision and boundary conditions are not explicitly detailed in the sources. Time Complexity: Dominated by rendering per epoch. Each epoch processes batchsize images. Total epochs is numepoch. Rendering cost depends on spp, sppgrad, and scene complexity. Memory Complexity: Proportional to sdfres^3 for the SDF grid and material grids. Strengths: Jointly optimizes geometry and materials. Uses explicit grids for easy manipulation and upsampling. Limitations: Resolution is fixed until upsample epochs. Upsampling materials is skipped at resolution == 256 to prevent artifacts. Learning rate decay is critical for convergence. When to use: When reference images are available and both geometry and material properties need to be recovered. When not to use: When no reference images are available or when neural representations are preferred for higher resolution without upsampling. name: Augmented SDF
head: Conservative SDF Construction from Bounding Volume, tilde f
body: Augmented SDF is a conservative variant of a signed distance field (SDF) that accelerates field queries by embedding a bounding volume derived from the object's geometry. It solves the performance bottleneck of expensive SDF evaluations for points far from the surface by returning the distance to the bounding volume instead. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The original SDF function f(\mathbf{p}) and a point set P generated by Sphere Carving. Output: The augmented SDF function \tilde{f}(\mathbf{p}). Data Structures: Bounding Volume \mathcal{B}: A geometric representation of the object's extent constructed as the convex hull H(P) of P, or a union of convex polyhedra or ellipsoids derived from P. The memory footprint is compact and embedded directly in the function definition, avoiding external acceleration structures like grids or octrees. Parameters: \varepsilon (epsilon): A small positive constant ensuring the 0-level set of \tilde{f} matches f. Typical value: 0.01. Steps: 1. Bounding Volume Construction: Compute the geometric convex hull H(P) of the point set P generated by Sphere Carving. This hull is guaranteed to contain the object O (O \subset H(P)). 2. Query Optimization: For a query point \mathbf{p}, compute the distance to the bounding volume \mathcal{B}, denoted d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}). 3. Conditional Evaluation: If d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) > \varepsilon, return d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}); otherwise, return f(\mathbf{p}). Formula: The conservative SDF is defined as: \tilde{f}(\mathbf{p}) = \begin{cases} d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) & \text{if } d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) > \varepsilon \\ f(\mathbf{p}) & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} Where: \mathbf{p} is the query point. \mathcal{B} is the bounding volume. d(\mathbf{p}, \mathcal{B}) is the distance from \mathbf{p} to \mathcal{B}. f(\mathbf{p}) is the original SDF value. \varepsilon is the threshold constant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def augmentedsdf(p, f, B, epsilon=0.01): """Compute the augmented SDF value for point p.""" disttobound = convexhulldistance(p, B) if disttobound > epsilon: return disttobound return f(p) def convexhulldistance(p, B): """Compute distance from p to convex hull B defined by vertices and faces.""" mindist = float('inf') for face in B.faces: # Distance to the plane of the face d = pointtoplanedistance(p, face) if d < mindist: mindist = d return mindist def pointtoplanedistance(p, face): """Distance from point p to the plane defined by face normal and a vertex.""" normal = face.normal v = face.vertex return abs(dot(p - v, normal)) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: GPU Memory Access Patterns: In per-pixel cost comparison visualizations (e.g., Sphere Tracing), artifacts may appear due to GPU memory access pattern inconsistencies when branching between the bounding volume check and the original SDF evaluation. Conservativeness: The bounding volume must strictly contain the object; the convex hull H(P) satisfies O \subset H(P) when P is derived correctly from Sphere Carving. Generates the point set P and empty spheres S used to construct the bounding volume. It iteratively carves space to find surface points. Chosen when a conservative geometric bound is needed for a given SDF. Sphere Carving Computes the geometric convex hull H(P) from point set P. Sets it apart by guaranteeing O \subset H(P) for conservative bounds. Chosen when a tight, memory-efficient proxy is required. Convex Hull Time Complexity: The query time is O(1) for points outside the bounding volume (distance to \mathcal{B}), and O(T) for points inside, where T is the cost of the original SDF f. Memory Complexity: Compact. The bounding volume is embedded in the function definition, avoiding the memory overhead of external acceleration structures like grids or octrees. Performance: In tests with ~1 million queries in a box surrounding the object, \tilde{f} performs 3.3 to 4.9 times faster on average than the base field f. In Sphere Tracing scenarios, using a convex bound can provide up to a 50% speedup. Strengths: Fast queries for points far from the surface; compact memory footprint; compatible with other acceleration techniques like Sphere Tracing or Segment Tracing. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of the point set P via Sphere Carving; potential artifacts in GPU visualizations due to memory access patterns. When to use: When the SDF evaluation is expensive and many queries occur outside the immediate vicinity of the surface. When not to use: When the object is highly non-convex and the bounding volume becomes too loose, reducing the effectiveness of the early-out check. Augmented SDF was introduced in the context of Sphere Carving, a method for constructing bounding volumes for SDFs. The technique leverages the property that the convex hull of points generated by Sphere Carving contains the object, allowing for a conservative approximation of the distance field. It is used in applications such as sphere tracing, polygonization, and simulation to accelerate field queries. name: Sweep-based SDF Generation
head: Approximate Distance Field computation, Marching Parabolas, SDF Generation via Sweep Passes
body: Sweep-based SDF Generation is an algorithm to compute an approximate Signed Distance Field (SDF) texture efficiently without brute-force per-pixel distance calculation. It is intended for use in Sphere Tracing. The method sets itself apart from exact analytical SDF evaluations by using a multi-pass sweep approach that propagates distance information from rendered surface primitives through the volume, trading geometric precision for computational speed and texture-based storage. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D or 3D texture containing initial distance values, typically resulting from an initial sweep along the X-axis or direct rasterization of surfaces. Output: A quantized Signed Distance Field texture where each texel stores an approximate distance value. Data Structures: Texture Storage: The SDF is stored in a quantized format to avoid floating-point storage requirements. Common formats include UNORMR8 (range 0–255) or SNORMR8 (range -127 to 127). Shared Memory: A local memory buffer (sharedMem) used within a compute shader workgroup to store a segment of the row being processed. Intermediate Textures: If the quantization factor requires high precision during intermediate calculations, intermediate result textures may require twice the bits of the input storage to prevent overflow during parabolic addition. Parameters: EDFRANGE: The maximum quantizable distance. For UNORMR8, this is 255; for SNORMR8, this is 127. QUANITZATIONFACTOR: A rescaling factor used to convert floating-point distances to integer storage. LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX: The local workgroup size, typically 256 due to mobile device constraints. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initial Rasterization (2D Context): Render surfaces into the distance field texture. In 2D, this is done by drawing lines a couple of pixels wide to get accurate subpixel distances for the immediate vicinity of surfaces. 2. X-Axis Sweep: The input texture is assumed to have already been swept in the X direction. 3. Y-Axis Sweep: Perform a sweep along the Y axis using an extension compute shader. 4. Synchronization: Insert a memory barrier to ensure synchronization between passes. 5. Z-Axis Sweep: Perform a sweep along the Z axis. 6. Completion: The SDF generation is complete. Row Processing Logic (The Sweep Pass): The core computation occurs when processing a single row (or column) of the texture. The algorithm processes a row by: 1. Loading the input value for the current invocation. 2. Quantizing the value: out = uint(input QUANITZATIONFACTOR). Values greater than EDFRANGE EDFRANGE indicate "infinity". 3. Storing the quantized value to sharedMem[rowInvocationID]. 4. Synchronizing all threads in the workgroup (BARRIER()). 5. Iterating over a range of offsets i from -EDFRANGE to EDFRANGE (excluding 0 for optimization). 6. For each offset, calculating the wrap-around coordinate and the distance between the current invocation and the neighbor. 7. Updating the local minimum using the parabolic distance approximation. Formula: The distance update rule for each neighbor in the sweep is: \text{newDist} = \min(\text{currentDist}, \text{sharedMem}[\text{newCoordinate}] + \text{distanceBetween}^2) Where: \text{currentDist} is the current minimum distance found for the invocation. \text{sharedMem}[\text{newCoordinate}] is the quantized distance value stored in shared memory at the neighbor's position. \text{distanceBetween} = \text{rowInvocationID} - \text{newCoordinate}. \text{newCoordinate} = \text{coordinateWrapAround}(\text{rowInvocationID} + i), which is typically x % ROWLENGTH. Post-Processing: After the loop, the final result is de-quantized: \text{result} = \text{float}(\text{out}) \times \text{QUANITZATIONFACTOR\RCP} Where QUANITZATIONFACTORRCP is the reciprocal of the quantization factor. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. EDFRANGE = 255 # For UNORMR8 QUANITZATIONFACTOR = 255.0 QUANITZATIONFACTORRCP = 1.0 / QUANITZATIONFACTOR LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX = 256 inputval = texelFetch(inputtex, localid).r out = uint(inputval QUANITZATIONFACTOR) sharedMem[localid] = out barrier() for i in range(-EDFRANGE, EDFRANGE + 1): if i == 0: continue # Calculate neighbor coordinate with wrap-around newcoord = (localid + i) % rowlength # Calculate distance between current invocation and neighbor distancebetween = localid - newcoord # Parabolic distance approximation update # sharedMem[newcoord] contains the quantized distance from the neighbor candidate = sharedMem[newcoord] + (distancebetween distancebetween) if candidate < out: out = candidate result = float(out) QUANITZATIONFACTORRCP texelStore(outputtex, localid, result) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Row Length vs. Workgroup Size: If the row length exceeds LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX, sharedMem must be pre-loaded with LOCALWORKGROUPSIZEX + 2EDFRANGE samples to handle wrap-around and range access. Overflow: Intermediate result textures require twice the bits of the input storage to prevent overflow during the parabolic addition (\text{distanceBetween}^2). Infinity Handling: Values exceeding EDFRANGE EDFRANGE after quantization should be treated as infinity to avoid incorrect minimums. Time Complexity: The non-optimal version (without prefix-sum/scan) has a complexity proportional to O(\text{EDF\RANGE}) per pixel per sweep pass. Performance: On a 320GB/s GDDR5 desktop GPU, the performance bound is around 6ms for SDF computation. The non-optimal algorithm is expected to take between 500-1000ms assuming 2TB/s shared memory speed and EDFRANGE=255. Memory Complexity: Requires shared memory proportional to the workgroup size plus a halo for the sweep range. Intermediate textures may require double the bit-depth of the final output. Strengths: Efficient generation of approximate SDFs for sphere tracing; avoids expensive per-pixel analytical distance calculations; suitable for real-time rendering on GPUs. Limitations: The result is an approximation, not an exact Euclidean distance field; accuracy depends on EDFRANGE and the initial rasterization quality; performance degrades with larger EDFRANGE in the non-optimized version. When to use: When an approximate SDF is sufficient for sphere tracing and performance is critical, especially on mobile or constrained hardware. When not to use: When exact Euclidean distances are required for collision detection or precise ray marching. The method is described in the context of adding an "Approximate Distance Field computation extension" to the Irrlicht engine. It builds upon the "Marching Parabolas" technique, which is analogous to blur functions in shared memory. The concept of rendering surfaces to get accurate subpixel distances and then sweeping to propagate them was discussed in the context of fast pixelshader 2D raytracing. The non-optimal version can be optimized using prefix-sum/scan algorithms or warp-level primitives like NVshuffle.
