name: Quadratic Bezier Tube Deformation
head: Bezier Curve Deformation, Quadratic Bezier Tube
body: Quadratic Bezier Tube Deformation maps points from an arbitrary spline tube defined by quadratic Bezier segments to a canonical vertical cylinder, enabling the use of pre-defined density fields [10061-spline-tube-to-cylinder-mapping.md]. It solves the inverse parameterization problem in volumetric rendering by providing a robust Signed Distance Function (SDF) to the curve, which yields the curvilinear abscissa required for texture coordinate calculation. It is distinguished from cubic spline approaches by its computational simplicity in finding the closest point and curvilinear abscissa, though it imposes stricter constraints on segment concatenation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point P in world space; a ray origin and direction for bounding box culling; a list of quadratic Bezier segments defining the curve. Each segment i is defined by three control points Ai, Bi, Ci. Output: The deformed coordinates (u, v, w) in the canonical cylinder space, where u and v are angular/radial coordinates and w is the curvilinear abscissa (normalized height) [10061-spline-tube-to-cylinder-mapping.md]. Data Structures: Bezier Segment: Defined by three 3D vectors A, B, C. A: Start point (t=0). B: Control point (pulls the curve). C: End point (t=1). Segment List: An ordered array of segments. For concatenation, the start of segment i+1 must equal the end of segment i (A{i+1} = Ci). Formulas: The quadratic Bezier curve for a segment is defined as: Q(t) = (1-t)^2 A + 2(1-t)t B + t^2 C, \quad t \in [0, 1] The segment starts at A when t=0, finishes at C when t=1, and is pulled toward B in between. The tangent at t=0 is parallel to vector \vec{AB} = B - A, and the tangent at t=1 is parallel to vector \vec{BC} = C - B. To find the deformation, we must find the closest point on the curve to P. This is achieved by computing the SDF to the quadratic Bezier segment. The SDF implementation (based on Quilez 2013) returns both the distance and the parameter t of the closest point, which corresponds to the curvilinear abscissa. Steps: 1. Initialize: Set mindist to infinity and bestt to 0. 2. Iterate Segments: For each segment i in the curve: a. Optimization (Ray Casting): Perform a ray-casting test against the bounding box of segment i relative to the ray origin. If the ray does not intersect the bounding box, skip this segment. Cache this result per pixel to avoid re-evaluation during ray marching. b. SDF Evaluation: Compute the SDF from point P to the quadratic Bezier segment i. Let the result be di and the closest point parameter be ti. c. Update Minimum: If di < \text{min\dist}, set \text{min\dist} = di and \text{best\t} = ti. 3. Map to Cylinder: Using the best t found, map the point to the canonical cylinder [10061-spline-tube-to-cylinder-mapping.md]. The height w is normalized based on the total length of the curve or the segment's contribution. The radial and angular coordinates are derived from the vector from the closest point on the curve to P [10061-spline-tube-to-cylinder-mapping.md]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def quadraticbeziersdf(P, A, B, C): """Computes SDF to a quadratic Bezier segment. Returns (distance, t). """ def Q(t): u = 1.0 - t return ((uu)A[0] + 2.0utB[0] + ttC[0], (uu)A[1] + 2.0utB[1] + ttC[1], (uu)A[2] + 2.0utB[2] + ttC[2]) def dQ(t): u = 1.0 - t return (2.0u(B[0]-A[0]) + 2.0t(C[0]-B[0]), 2.0u(B[1]-A[1]) + 2.0t(C[1]-B[1]), 2.0u(B[2]-A[2]) + 2.0t(C[2]-B[2])) t = 0.5 for in range(10): diff = (P[0]-Q(t)[0], P[1]-Q(t)[1], P[2]-Q(t)[2]) dot = diff[0]dQ(t)[0] + diff[1]dQ(t)[1] + diff[2]dQ(t)[2] if abs(dot) < 1e-6: break ddot = dQ(t)[0]2 + dQ(t)[1]2 + dQ(t)[2]2 + \ diff[0]2.0(C[0]-2.0B[0]+A[0]) + diff[1]2.0(C[1]-2.0B[1]+A[1]) + diff[2]2.0(C[2]-2.0B[2]+A[2]) if abs(ddot) < 1e-12: break t -= dot / ddot t = max(0.0, min(1.0, t)) dist = math.sqrt((P[0]-Q(t)[0])2 + (P[1]-Q(t)[1])2 + (P[2]-Q(t)[2])2) return dist, t def getboundingbox(A, B, C): """Computes axis-aligned bounding box for quadratic Bezier segment. """ denomx = A[0] - 2.0B[0] + C[0] textx = max(0.0, min(1.0, (A[0]-B[0])/denomx)) if denomx != 0 else 0.0 denomy = A[1] - 2.0B[1] + C[1] texty = max(0.0, min(1.0, (A[1]-B[1])/denomy)) if denomy != 0 else 0.0 denomz = A[2] - 2.0B[2] + C[2] textz = max(0.0, min(1.0, (A[2]-B[2])/denomz)) if denomz != 0 else 0.0 mins = [min(A[0], B[0], C[0]), min(A[1], B[1], C[1]), min(A[2], B[2], C[2])] maxs = [max(A[0], B[0], C[0]), max(A[1], B[1], C[1]), max(A[2], B[2], C[2])] for text in [textx, texty, textz]: if 0.0 < text < 1.0: u = 1.0 - text ext = (uu)A[0] + 2.0utextB[0] + texttextC[0] exty = (uu)A[1] + 2.0utextB[1] + texttextC[1] extz = (uu)A[2] + 2.0utextB[2] + texttextC[2] mins[0] = min(mins[0], ext); mins[1] = min(mins[1], exty); mins[2] = min(mins[2], extz) maxs[0] = max(maxs[0], ext); maxs[1] = max(maxs[1], exty); maxs[2] = max(maxs[2], extz) return mins, maxs def rayintersectsbbox(rayorigin, raydirection, mins, maxs): """Checks if ray intersects AABB using slab method. Returns True. """ eps = 1e-8 tmin = (mins[0] - rayorigin[0]) / max(abs(raydirection[0]), eps) tmax = (maxs[0] - rayorigin[0]) / max(abs(raydirection[0]), eps) if tmin > tmax: tmin, tmax = tmax, tmin tymin = (mins[1] - rayorigin[1]) / max(abs(raydirection[1]), eps) tymax = (maxs[1] - rayorigin[1]) / max(abs(raydirection[1]), eps) if tymin > tymax: tymin, tymax = tymax, tymin if (tmin > tymax) or (tymin > tmax): return False if tymin > tmin: tmin = tymin if tymax < tmax: tmax = tymax tzmin = (mins[2] - rayorigin[2]) / max(abs(raydirection[2]), eps) tzmax = (maxs[2] - rayorigin[2]) / max(abs(raydirection[2]), eps) if tzmin > tzmax: tzmin, tzmax = tzmax, tzmin if (tmin > tzmax) or (tzmin > tmax): return False if tzmin > tmin: tmin = tzmin return tmax >= 0.0 def deformpoint(P, rayorigin, raydirection, segments, pixelcache): """Deforms point P to cylinder coordinates using quadratic Bezier segments.""" mindist = float('inf') bestt = 0.0 bestseg = None cachekey = (rayorigin[0], rayorigin[1], rayorigin[2], raydirection[0], raydirection[1], raydirection[2]) for i, seg in enumerate(segments): A, B, C = seg if cachekey in pixelcache: if not pixelcache[cachekey].get(i, True): continue bboxmins, bboxmaxs = getboundingbox(A, B, C) intersects = rayintersectsbbox(rayorigin, raydirection, bboxmins, bboxmaxs) if cachekey not in pixelcache: pixelcache[cachekey] = {} pixelcache[cachekey][i] = intersects if not intersects: continue dist, t = quadraticbeziersdf(P, A, B, C) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist bestt = t bestseg = seg A, B, C = bestseg invt = 1.0 - bestt closestpoint = ((invtinvt)A[0] + 2.0invtbesttB[0] + besttbesttC[0], (invtinvt)A[1] + 2.0invtbesttB[1] + besttbesttC[1], (invtinvt)A[2] + 2.0invtbesttB[2] + besttbesttC[2]) vec = (P[0]-closestpoint[0], P[1]-closestpoint[1], P[2]-closestpoint[2]) u = math.atan2(vec[1], vec[0]) v = math.sqrt(vec[0]2 + vec[2]2) w = bestt return u, v, w Parameters: Ray Casting Cache: Enabled per pixel. Bounding Box Check: Used for early rejection. Note: The source indicates that a complex bounding box calculation was removed in favor of simpler ray-casting because the former was slower on average. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concatenation: Quadratic Bezier segments are difficult to concatenate smoothly. Only one control point (B) is "free" per segment. A is fixed by the previous segment's C. B must be constrained to ensure derivative continuity. Modifying one segment affects all subsequent segments. Performance: The SDF evaluation scales linearly with the number of segments. Without bounding box/ray-casting optimization, this is expensive. The ray-caching optimization is critical for performance in volumetric rendering. SDF Availability: The method relies on the availability of an SDF for quadratic Bezier segments that returns the curvilinear abscissa. This is a key reason for choosing quadratic over cubic splines. Uses open uniform B-splines instead of Bezier curves. It constructs a lattice of curves in world space to avoid inverse parameterization issues, allowing flexible shape manipulation on the CPU. Choose this when smooth, global deformation of complex volumes (like fire) is needed and CPU-side evaluation is acceptable. Time Complexity: Linear O(N) with respect to the number of Bezier segments, where N is the number of segments. With ray-casting optimization, the constant factor is significantly reduced, often evaluating only a small subset of segments per ray step. Memory Complexity: Low. Requires storing control points for the segments and a small cache per pixel for bounding box intersection results. Strengths: Computationally simpler than cubic splines for finding the closest point and curvilinear abscissa. Robust SDF implementation available. Limitations: Difficult to concatenate segments smoothly. Modifications to one segment propagate to all subsequent segments. Bounding box calculation overhead can negate benefits if not optimized (ray-casting is preferred). When to Use: When a simple, robust deformation is needed for procedural volumes and the curve structure is relatively static or simple. When Not to Use: When high-degree smoothness across many segments is required, or when the curve topology changes frequently. The technique was developed for the real-time rendering of interstellar dust clouds and solar flares. Quadratic Bezier curves were chosen over cubic splines because solving for the closest point and curvilinear abscissa is computationally simpler, and a suitable SDF implementation returning the curvilinear abscissa was available (Quilez 2013). The method was implemented in a renderer using Sphere Marching for bounding box detection. A reference implementation for bounding box computation by Quilez (2020) was tested but found to be slower than simple ray-casting, leading to its removal. name: Curve-based Volumetric Free-Form Deformation
head: Volumetric Free-Form Deformation
body: Curve-based Volumetric Free-Form Deformation (VFFD) is a technique for manipulating the macro shape and flow of a volumetric unit volume (specifically procedural fire) using an open uniform B-spline curve. It solves the problem of real-time macro-level interactivity and deformation by constructing a lattice of curves around a central spline, allowing flexible shape manipulation while maintaining texture coordinates for rendering. Unlike direct deformation methods that require solving inverse parameterization on the GPU, VFFD evaluates the deformation on the CPU to build a world-space lattice, which the graphics hardware then implicitly evaluates via texture coordinate interpolation. Inputs: Control points Pi for the center spline, where i = 0 \dots n-1 and n is the number of control points. Fire radius r, defining the cross-section size. Lattice resolution c, determining the number of samples along the curve. B-spline degree p (typically 2 or 3 for uniform B-splines). Outputs: A lattice in world space consisting of c sections, where each section is defined by four corner curves. Texture coordinates assigned to lattice vertices to map back to the unit fire volume. Data Structures: Control Points: Array of 3D vectors Pi. Knot Vector: Values ti defining the B-spline domain. Corner Curves: Four sets of control points defining the cross-section at each lattice section. Lattice Vertices: Points in world space with associated texture coordinates (x, y, z). Formulas: The center curve C(t) is defined by the open uniform B-spline: C(t) = \sum{i=0}^{n-1} N{i, \text{degree}}(t) \cdot Pi \quad (6) where N{i,p}(t) is the B-spline basis function of degree p. The knot values ti for an open uniform B-spline are defined as: ti = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } i \leq \text{degree} \\ i - \text{degree} & \text{if } \text{degree} < i < n \\ n - \text{degree} & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (3) The basis functions are computed recursively: N{i,0}(t) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } ti \leq t < t{i+1} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \quad (4) N{i,p}(t) = \frac{t{i+p+1} - t}{t{i+p} - ti} N{i,p-1}(t) + \frac{t - ti}{t{i+p+1} - t{i+1}} N{i+1,p-1}(t) \quad (5) Steps: 1. Sample Center Curve Properties: For each control point Pi, determine the parameter t at which that control point has the most influence. For a uniform B-spline, this is t = \frac{i}{n-1} for i = 0 \dots n-1. 2. Compute Normal and Velocity: At each sampled t, compute the velocity vector \vec{V}i (tangent) and normal vector \vec{N}i of the center curve C(t). 3. Define Cross-Section Plane: For each control point Pi, define a square in the plane spanned by \vec{N}i and \vec{V}i, centered at Pi. 4. Set Cross-Section Size: The edge length of the square is 2r, where r is the fire radius. 5. Align Squares: Align all n squares along their respective central curve normals \vec{N}i to reduce twisting. 6. Generate Corner Curves: Generate four additional curves by placing control points on the corners of these squares. These four curves form the boundaries of the lattice sections. 7. Sample Lattice Sections: Sample the center curve parameter t uniformly c times (where c is the lattice resolution) to obtain c values of t in the domain [0, 1]. 8. Evaluate Corner Positions: For each of the c sampled t values, evaluate the four corner curves using Equation (6) to obtain c sets of correlated positions on the four corner curves. These positions define the vertices of the lattice sections. 9. Assign Texture Coordinates: Assign each lattice vertex a texture coordinate \text{tex}i = (x, \frac{i}{c-1}, z), where x and z are 1 or -1 depending on which corner curve the vertex belongs to, and i is the index of the lattice section (0 \dots c-1). 10. Render Lattice: Divide the lattice into a finite set of cubes and render only the required triangles within these cubes to minimize pixel shader coverage and ensure every section is rendered. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computebsplinebasis(t, knots, degree): """ Computes the B-spline basis functions N{i,p}(t) for a given t. knots: list of knot values ti degree: integer degree p Returns: list of basis function values N{i, degree}(t) """ n = len(knots) - 1 # Number of control points basis = [0.0] n # Initialize degree 0 basis functions N = [0.0] n for i in range(n): if knots[i] <= t < knots[i+1]: N[i] = 1.0 else: N[i] = 0.0 # Compute higher degree basis functions for p in range(1, degree + 1): for i in range(n - p + 1): leftnum = knots[i+p] - t leftden = knots[i+p] - knots[i] left = (leftnum / leftden) N[i] if leftden != 0 else 0.0 rightnum = t - knots[i] rightden = knots[i+p+1] - knots[i+1] right = (rightnum / rightden) N[i+1] if rightden != 0 else 0.0 basis[i] = left + right # Update N for next iteration for i in range(n - p + 1): N[i] = basis[i] return basis def curvebasedvffd(controlpoints, radius, latticeresolution, degree): """ Constructs the VFFD lattice. controlpoints: list of 3D vectors Pi radius: float r latticeresolution: int c degree: int p Returns: list of lattice sections, each section is a list of 4 corner points """ n = len(controlpoints) # 1. Compute knot vector for open uniform B-spline knots = [] for i in range(n + degree + 1): if i <= degree: knots.append(0.0) elif i < n: knots.append(i - degree) else: knots.append(n - degree) # Normalize knots to [0, 1] domain for sampling # Note: The paper uses t in [0,1] for sampling, but knot values are used in basis function evaluation. # The sampling t values are linearly spaced in [0,1]. # The basis function evaluation uses the actual knot vector. # 2. Sample center curve properties at t = i / (n-1) # Note: The paper states t = i / (n-1) for i = 0... n-1. # This is an approximation for the "most affected" parameter. samplest = [i / (n - 1) for i in range(n)] # 3. Compute normal and velocity for each sample # This requires differentiating the B-spline curve C(t). # C'(t) is the velocity vector. # Normal is computed from C'(t) and C''(t) or a fixed up vector. # For implementation, we assume a function computetangentandnormal(t, controlpoints, knots, degree) exists. normals = [] velocities = [] for t in samplest: tangent = computetangent(t, controlpoints, knots, degree) normal = computenormal(tangent, controlpoints, knots, degree) normals.append(normal) velocities.append(tangent) # 4. Define corner control points for each section # For each control point Pi, we have a normal Ni and velocity Vi. # We define a square in the plane defined by Ni and Vi, centered at Pi. # Edge length is 2r. # The four corners are: # C1 = Pi + r Ni + r Vinormalized # C2 = Pi - r Ni + r Vinormalized # C3 = Pi - r Ni - r Vinormalized # C4 = Pi + r Ni - r Vinormalized # Note: Vi must be normalized for this to work correctly as a square. cornercontrolpoints = [] for i in range(n): P = controlpoints[i] N = normals[i] V = velocities[i] Vnorm = normalize(V) # Define the four corners of the square cross-section c1 = P + radius N + radius Vnorm c2 = P - radius N + radius Vnorm c3 = P - radius N - radius Vnorm c4 = P + radius N - radius Vnorm cornercontrolpoints.append([c1, c2, c3, c4]) # 5. Sample lattice sections # Sample t uniformly c times in [0, 1] latticetvalues = [i / (latticeresolution - 1) for i in range(latticeresolution)] latticesections = [] for t in latticetvalues: sectioncorners = [] for corneridx in range(4): # Evaluate the corner curve at t # The corner curve is defined by the control points in cornercontrolpoints # We need to compute the B-spline for each corner curve. # Since the corner control points are fixed for each i, we evaluate the B-spline # using the same knot vector and degree. # Get basis functions for this t basis = computebsplinebasis(t, knots, degree) # Evaluate the corner curve cornerpoint = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for i in range(n): cp = cornercontrolpoints[i][corneridx] cornerpoint[0] += basis[i] cp[0] cornerpoint[1] += basis[i] cp[1] cornerpoint[2] += basis[i] cp[2] sectioncorners.append(cornerpoint) latticesections.append(sectioncorners) return latticesections Parameters: n: Number of control points. r: Radius of the fire, defining the cross-section size. c: Resolution of the lattice, determining the number of samples along the curve. p: Degree of the B-spline. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Inverse Parameterization: The pixel shader operates on deformed world space P' to return texture space P, but the deformation function D(P) defines P' from P. This cannot be solved analytically on the GPU. The method avoids this by evaluating D(P) on the CPU to build the lattice. Pixel Coverage: The shader can only render to locations occupied by triangle fragments. The final pixel coverage is not known a priori. The method solves this by dividing the lattice into cubes and rendering only required triangles. Discontinuities: Linear interpolation on the lattice creates discontinuities in the first derivative of the curve on the borders of each lattice section. Refining the lattice resolution approximates the continuous deformation. Precision: The knot vector construction and basis function evaluation must handle edge cases where denominators are zero (e.g., t{i+p} - ti = 0). Time Complexity: The lattice construction is O(c \cdot n), where c is the lattice resolution and n is the number of control points. Rendering is O(c) triangles. Memory Complexity: O(c \cdot n) for storing the lattice vertices and control points. Performance: The performance impact of additional lattice sections is relatively small, allowing over-estimation of resolution. Strengths: Real-time macro-level interactivity, flexible shape manipulation, avoids inverse parameterization on GPU. Limitations: Discontinuities in the first derivative at lattice section borders, limited to fixed number of points without loss of detail (cannot deform entire volume with noise in real time). When to Use: When real-time deformation of volumetric fire or similar volumes is required, and macro-level control is needed. When Not to Use: When high-frequency micro-details need to be deformed in real time, or when smooth first-derivative continuity across lattice sections is critical without high resolution. Curve-based Volumetric Free-Form Deformation was introduced by Alfred R. Fuller, Hari Krishnan, Karim Mahrous, Bernd Hamann, and Kenneth I. Joy from the University of California, Davis, in 2007. It was developed as part of a system for generating procedural volumetric fire in real time, combining curve-based deformation with hardware-accelerated volumetric rendering and procedural noise. The method builds on earlier work in curve-based fire design and particle simulation. Real-time procedural volumetric fire, https://doi.org/10.1145/1230100.1230131, fetched 2026-11-05 PDF Real-time Procedural Volumetric Fire - UC Davis, https://web.cs.ucdavis.edu/~hamann/FullerKrishnanMahrousHamannJoyFirePaperForI3D2007AsSubmitted11012006.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Torus Signed Distance Function
head: Link SDF, Link Shape SDF, Signed Torus, sdTorus
body: Computes the signed distance from a query point to the surface of a torus centered at the origin and aligned with the Y-axis. It provides the primitive distance query required for distance-field ray marching and constructive solid geometry (CSG) operations. It is distinguished from sibling primitives like the Cylinder Signed Distance Function by its closed-loop topology and from Distance to Superquadrics by its specific algebraic form for a torus. Inputs: p = (px, py, pz): Query point in 3D space. R: Major radius (distance from the torus center to the tube centerline). r: Minor radius (radius of the tube cross-section). Outputs: d: Signed distance. Positive outside the torus, negative inside, zero on the surface. Data Structures: None required; scalar computation. Steps: 1. Compute the radial distance of the point's projection onto the XZ plane from the origin: \rho = \sqrt{px^2 + pz^2}. 2. Construct a 2D vector q = (qx, qy) representing the offset from the torus centerline: qx = \rho - R, qy = py. 3. Compute the Euclidean distance from q to the origin and subtract the minor radius: d = \sqrt{qx^2 + qy^2} - r. Formula: d = \sqrt{(\sqrt{px^2 + pz^2} - R)^2 + py^2} - r Parameters: R > 0: Major radius. r > 0: Minor radius. Constraint: r < R yields a standard ring torus; r = R yields a horn torus; r > R yields a self-intersecting spindle torus. Edge Cases: Origin: If p=(0,0,0), \rho=0, q=(-R, 0), d = R - r. Precision: Near the surface or when \rho \approx R, standard floating-point precision is sufficient. Self-intersection: For spindle tori (r > R), the SDF remains mathematically valid but defines a complex nested inside region. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdtorus(p: tuple, R: float, r: float) -> float: """ Computes signed distance to a torus centered at origin, aligned with Y-axis. p: (px, py, pz) R: Major radius r: Minor radius """ px, py, pz = p # Radial distance in the XZ plane rho = (px2 + pz2)0.5 # 2D vector from the torus centerline to the point qx = rho - R qy = py # Signed distance: distance to centerline minus tube radius return (qx2 + qy2)0.5 - r A variation that includes a length parameter for non-circular cross-sections or deformed tori, sometimes referred to as a link shape. Use when modeling chain links or specific mechanical parts. Link SDF. A torus where r > R. The SDF formula remains the same, but the topology changes to a self-intersecting shape. Use for specific organic or abstract shapes. Spindle Torus. Time Complexity: O(1). Requires two square roots and basic arithmetic. Memory Complexity: O(1). No auxiliary data structures. Strengths: Exact analytic solution; no iterative approximation; robust for ray marching. Limitations: Only applies to perfect tori. Cannot model tori with varying cross-sections or twists without deformation. When to use: When rendering or ray marching perfect toroidal shapes. When not to use: For complex toroidal structures with varying thickness or non-circular cross-sections. The SDF for a torus is a standard primitive in signed distance function libraries, popularized by tools like the glsl-sdf-primitives repository. It is a fundamental building block for CSG operations involving toroidal shapes. skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, https://github.com/skmhrk1209/Torch-Sphere-Tracer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, https://github.com/marklundin/glsl-sdf-primitives, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Infinite Tiling with Modulo
head: Infinite Crystal Grid SDF, Infinite Tiling via Modulo, Modulo SDF, Modulo Tiling, Repeat function, Tiling SDFs, Tiling via Modulo
body: Infinite Tiling with Modulo is a technique for rendering infinite repeating patterns by using the modulo operator to fold space, allowing a single primitive SDF to be tiled infinitely. It sets itself apart from explicit mesh instances by computing the scene geometry implicitly at essentially zero extra cost per instance, enabling ray-marched fractal renderers like Mandelbulbs and Menger sponges. Unlike Constructive SDF Modeling (Min Combination) which combines distinct primitives, this method duplicates a single primitive's domain across all space. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray position p (vec3), tile period/size c (float). Output: Transformed position q (vec3) suitable for SDF evaluation. Data Structures: None required beyond standard vector types. Steps: 1. Apply the modulo operation to the sampling point p using the period c. 2. Center the result within the tile. The standard implementation centers the tile around the origin by subtracting half the period. 3. Evaluate the base SDF using the transformed coordinate q. Formulas: The core transformation is defined as: q = \text{mod}(p, c) - \frac{c}{2} Where: p is the world-space ray position. c is the period or size of the tile. \text{mod}(a, b) is the floating-point modulo operation. q is the folded coordinate. Parameters: c (Tile Size): The period of the modulo operation. Lower values make objects appear closer; higher values make them further apart. Offset: Some implementations add an offset before modulo to center the tile differently, e.g., mod(p + offset, c) - offset. A common offset is 1.5 for a period of 3.0 to center a tile at the origin. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def repeat(p: Vector3, c: float) -> Vector3: """ Tiles space infinitely by folding the sampling point p using modulo. Args: p: The world-space position to tile. c: The period (size) of the tile. Returns: The folded position q. """ # Apply modulo to fold space into the range 0, c) # Then shift by -c/2 to center the tile around the origin in range [-c/2, c/2) q = mod(p, c) - 0.5 c return q def sdftiled(p: Vector3, c: float, basesdffunc) -> float: """ Evaluates an SDF with infinite tiling. Args: p: World-space position. c: Tile period. basesdffunc: Function that computes the SDF for a single tile centered at origin. Returns: Signed distance to the nearest tiled surface. """ q = repeat(p, c) return basesdffunc(q) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision errors in mod can cause artifacts at tile boundaries if not handled carefully, though standard [GLSL/HLSL mod is generally sufficient for visual ray marching. Symmetry: The standard mod(p, c) - c/2 assumes the base SDF is symmetric around the origin. If the base SDF is not symmetric, the tiles will appear shifted or distorted. Negative Coordinates: The standard repeat function works correctly for negative coordinates due to the properties of modulo and the centering shift. However, some simplified explanations assume positive quadrants. A variant of Infinite Tiling which produces a finite number of repetitions of a shape. It takes an additional vector \vec{l} as input, where \vec{l} is the corner of the box used to limit the number of repetitions of the shape. This allows for controlled tiling within a specific volume rather than infinite space. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray step, as it adds only a few arithmetic operations (modulo, subtraction) before the base SDF evaluation. Memory Complexity: O(1), no additional data structures are required. Performance: Enables rendering of scenes with effectively infinite geometry at real-time frame rates, provided the base SDF is efficient. Strengths: Extremely low memory footprint; ideal for fractals and procedural environments. Limitations: All tiles are identical copies; cannot vary geometry per tile without additional logic (e.g., coordinate-dependent transformations). The technique is fundamental to ray marching with SDFs, popularized by demoscene artists and researchers like Inigo Quilez. It leverages the mathematical property of periodicity to create complex structures like Menger sponges and Mandelbulbs from simple primitives. arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, https://github.com/arguskern/lumina-graphics-lab, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Painting with Math: A Gentle Study of Raymarching, https://blog.maximeheckel.com/posts/painting-with-math-a-gentle-study-of-raymarching/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Ray Marching and Signed Distance Functions: Sphere Tracing..., https://www.mysimulator.uk/articles/ray-marching/, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) PDF COS 426 Final Project Writeup Raymarching with Signed Distance Fields, https://jbaum98.github.io/cos426finalproject/writeup.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Distance Field Representations and Sampling
head: Distance Field Sampling, Distance Field Traversal
body: This family defines the mechanisms for querying scalar fields that represent implicit surfaces or volumetric data via distance metrics, enabling ray marching and spatial queries. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods by focusing on the sampling interface and data structures required to evaluate these fields efficiently, rather than the geometric primitives themselves. While SDF Primitive Definitions provides the analytical building blocks, this family addresses how those blocks are stored (textures, grids, neural networks) and accessed (bounded lookups, probabilistic outputs, haptic constraints) in a rendering or simulation pipeline. The family operates on the principle that a scene is defined by a scalar field f(\mathbf{p}) where the zero-level set f(\mathbf{p}) = 0 represents the surface. For sphere tracing to be valid, the function must satisfy the Lipschitz condition with constant 1, ensuring |f(\mathbf{p}1) - f(\mathbf{p}2)| \le \|\mathbf{p}1 - \mathbf{p}2\|. This guarantees that the value f(\mathbf{p}) is a safe lower bound on the distance to the surface, allowing the ray marcher to step forward by exactly f(\mathbf{p}) without tunneling. Composition is achieved through Boolean operations on the distance values: Union: f{union}(\mathbf{p}) = \min(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Intersection: f{intersect}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Subtraction: f{sub}(\mathbf{p}) = \max(-f1(\mathbf{p}), f2(\mathbf{p})). Transformations are applied by mapping the query point \mathbf{p} into the local coordinate space of the primitive using the inverse transformation matrix M^{-1} before evaluation. Procedural noise (e.g., FBM) is often used to perturb these analytical surfaces, creating hypertextures where the isosurface is defined by SDF(\mathbf{p}) + Bn(\mathbf{p}) = 0. Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching is a technique for rendering implicit surfaces defined by a 3D distance texture, specifically addressing the problem of invalid distance values at the texture boundaries. It employs two nested bounding boxes (an inner "red" box and an outer "green" box) to distinguish between valid texture data and a boundary shell where samples may be unreliable. Unlike standard texture lookups that might return erroneous distances near edges, this method returns the distance to the outer boundary for points in the invalid shell, ensuring the ray marcher steps safely without tunneling into undefined data. It enables the inclusion of pre-computed distance textures (e.g., the Stanford Bunny) into scenes using standard SDF composition operators. See Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching. Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDFs) are a variant of Directed Distance Fields (DDFs) designed to differentiably model the inherent discontinuities in the underlying field, specifically surface and occlusion discontinuities. While standard DDFs output a single scalar depth value, PDDFs modify the formulation so that the network outputs probability distributions over rays rather than a single value, allowing a C^1 continuous neural network to represent the discontinuous field of a DDF. This enables efficient differentiable rendering and geometry extraction without the training instability caused by hard discontinuities. See Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDFs). This method provides haptic rendering for sparse, oriented point cloud data by constructing a 3D signed distance field (SDF) on a regular grid using embedded "packing spheres". It solves the problem of generating stable collision forces from incomplete geometric data where traditional mesh-based or dense implicit function methods fail due to sparsity. Unlike sibling methods that rely on dense sampling or explicit surface reconstruction, this technique uses the local normal direction to define minimum-volume spheres that approximate the object's interior, allowing a proxy to be constrained to the zero-iso-surface via gradient descent. See Sparse Point Set Haptic Rendering via Distance Field. Definition: A trait-based abstraction for sampling distance fields defined in terms of specific Distance metrics. It allows samplers to abstract sampling across multiple different Distance metrics. Implementation: If S implements ScalarSource, Sampler implements Sample<Signed>. The sample method calls self.source.samplescalar(p). If S implements VectorSource, Sampler implements Sample<Directed>. The sample method calls self.source.samplevector(p). If S implements HermiteSource, Sampler implements samplenormal method which calls self.source.samplenormal(p). Layout: The Sampler struct contains a reference to the source (&'a S). It implements the Sample<D> trait for Signed and Directed distance types based on the source implementing ScalarSource or VectorSource. Definition: A traversal method where ray marching is performed through distance fields. Naive storage of one distance value per voxel is impractical for large grids due to memory and bandwidth costs. Optimization: Memory costs are reduced by lowering field resolution to 1:4 scale (one distance value per 64 voxels), combined with occupancy masks. Masks are queried whenever sampled distance values are zero. Performance: Pre-processing takes 10x more GPU time than XBrickMap. Traversal is not considerably shorter than space partitioning methods (~8% difference). Definition: Space skipping traversal using tiled 256³ 8-directional distance fields at 1:4 resolution, combined with 4³ occupancy bitmasks. It creates 8 separate manhattan fields, each considering only voxels ahead of the associated ray octant direction. Distances are only propagated across rows of opposing axis directions with respect to the octant. Layout: Memory cost is 8 bytes per 4³ voxel plus 1 bit per 1³ voxel. Performance: Compared to traditional distance fields, it lowers the overall number of iterations by ~20-25% and increases throughput for incoherent rays by ~30-50%. On Sponza 2k, OctantDF achieves 129.0 Mrays/s for primary rays and 84.9 Mrays/s for primary + 1 diffuse bounce. Definition: A ray function that computes the distance along the ray until a specific scalar value \sigma is encountered. Useful to emphasize depth where specific tissue is located. Definition: A 2.5D indicator \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}] combining UV coordinates and signed distance to resolve ambiguity for points perpendicular to the mesh surface. Calculation: Calculate signed distance \bar{d}: project point x onto mesh surface at x0, obtain direction \tilde{r} = x - x0, get surface normal \tilde{n} at x0, and compute \bar{d} = \text{sign}(\tilde{r} \cdot \tilde{n}) \|\tilde{r}\|2. Formula: Define signed height: \tilde{h} = [u, v, \bar{d}], where [u, v] is the 2D coordinate on the UV map and \bar{d} is the signed distance. Distance fields have been a cornerstone of implicit surface representation since the introduction of Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) for ray marching. The specific techniques detailed in this family, such as bounded texture sampling and probabilistic outputs, emerged from the need to handle discrete data structures (textures, point clouds) and differentiable rendering pipelines in modern graphics. The use of distance fields for haptic feedback dates back to early virtual reality research, where stable collision detection was required for real-time force feedback. The integration of distance fields into neural rendering (PDDFs) and avatar synthesis (Signed Height Indicators) represents a more recent development, leveraging the differentiability of neural networks to overcome the discontinuities inherent in traditional geometric representations. https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, https://github.com/swiftcoder/isosurface, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dubiousconst282/VoxelRT, https://github.com/dubiousconst282/VoxelRT, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) PDF CS 519: Scientific Visualization - University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign, https://courses.grainger.illinois.edu/cs519/fa2017/Lecture%2012%20-%20Volume%20Visualization.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) UVA: Towards Unified Volumetric Avatar for View Synthesis, Pose rendering, Geometry and Texture Editing, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2304.06969, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching
head: 3D Texture Distance Function with Boundary Shell, Distance function for a cube sized 3D texture
body: Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching is a technique for rendering implicit surfaces defined by a 3D distance texture, specifically addressing the problem of invalid distance values at the texture boundaries. It employs two nested bounding boxes (an inner "red" box and an outer "green" box) to distinguish between valid texture data and a boundary shell where samples may be unreliable. Unlike standard texture lookups that might return erroneous distances near edges, this method returns the distance to the outer boundary for points in the invalid shell, ensuring the ray marcher steps safely without tunneling into undefined data. It enables the inclusion of pre-computed distance textures (e.g., the Stanford Bunny) into scenes using standard SDF composition operators. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A query point \mathbf{x} in world space, a 3D distance texture texture, and parameters textureBoundary and textureShell. Output: A signed distance value res representing the distance to the implicit surface or the texture boundary. Data Structures: 3D Distance Texture: A voxel grid storing distance values. In the reference implementation, dimensions are 192 \times 192 \times 192. textureBoundary: A vector defining the half-dimensions of the inner valid region. Value: (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). textureShell: A vector defining the thickness of the boundary region where data is considered invalid. Value: (0.05, 0.05, 0.05). Algorithm Steps: 1. Calculate Distance to Inner Valid Region Boundary: Compute the distance from \mathbf{x} to the inner valid region box, offset by the shell thickness. This assumes \mathbf{x} is outside the valid region initially. \mathbf{di} = |\mathbf{x}| - \text{textureBoundary} + \text{textureShell} 2. Compute Outer Distance (Fallback): Calculate the norm of the adjusted distance vector. This value is used if the point is outside the valid texture space or in the invalid shell. res = \| \max(\mathbf{di}, 0) \| Note: The source notation \|\cdot\| denotes the Euclidean norm. The formula clamps \mathbf{di} directly to avoid inflating the distance with an extra shell offset. 3. Check Valid Region: Determine if \mathbf{x} is inside the inner valid region by checking the components of \mathbf{di}. c = \max(d{ix}, \max(d{iy}, d{iz})) 4. Lookup if Inside: If c < 0, the point is inside the valid region. Adjust coordinates to align with texture space: \mathbf{x}{adj} = \mathbf{x} + \text{textureBoundary} Perform texture lookup: res = \text{lookupTexture}(\text{texture}, \mathbf{x}{adj}) 5. Return Result: Return res. If the point was outside the valid region (or in the shell), res holds the distance to the boundary calculated in Step 2. If inside, it holds the texture value. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bounded3ddistancetextureraymarching(x, texture, textureboundary, textureshell): """ Computes the signed distance for a point x using a bounded 3D distance texture. Args: x (vec3): Query point in world space. texture (3D array): The distance field texture. textureboundary (vec3): Half-dimensions of the inner valid region. Default: (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). textureshell (vec3): Thickness of the invalid boundary shell. Default: (0.05, 0.05, 0.05). Returns: float: Signed distance to the surface or boundary. """ # Step 1: Calculate distance to the inner valid region boundary, offset by shell di = abs(x) - textureboundary + textureshell # Step 2: Compute fallback distance (distance to the outer boundary of the valid region) # max(di, 0) ensures we only consider positive distances (clamps negatives to 0) # The norm ||...|| is computed as the Euclidean norm of the resulting vector adjusteddi = max(di, 0.0) res = (adjusteddi.x2 + adjusteddi.y2 + adjusteddi.z2)0.5 # Step 3: Check if point is inside the inner valid region # c is the maximum component of di. If c < 0, all components are negative, meaning inside. c = max(di.x, max(di.y, di.z)) # Step 4: If inside, perform texture lookup if c < 0: # Adjust coordinates to map to texture space [0,1] xadj = x + textureboundary # Standard 3D texture lookup (e.g., trilinear interpolation) res = texture[xadj] # Step 5: Return result return res Parameters and Typical Values: textureBoundary: (0.5, 0.5, 0.5). textureShell: (0.05, 0.05, 0.05). Texture Dimensions: 192 \times 192 \times 192 with an inner valid region of 128 \times 128 \times 128. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Invalid Boundary Data: Texture samples in the region between the inner valid region and the outer texture edge (the "green box" boundary) may contain invalid distance values. The algorithm remedies this by returning the distance to the outer boundary (red box) for these points, preventing the ray marcher from entering invalid data. Scale Mismatch: The distance returned by the texture lookup must be in accordance with the scale of the scene. If not, an appropriate bound must be applied. Normal Estimation: When estimating normals (e.g., using Algorithm 3.1 from the source), the epsilon value must be adjusted to account for the voxel spacing in the texture. If the value is too small, the representation may appear "grainy". Mesh Holes: For accurate distance field generation from meshes (like the Stanford Bunny), holes in the mesh must be closed before conversion to a 3D texture. A variant that returns a constant step size \Delta t for points outside the texture volume to mitigate AO artifacts caused by the bounding shell. Time Complexity: O(1) per query, involving basic vector arithmetic and one texture lookup. Memory Complexity: Depends on the 3D texture size. For a 192^3 texture, this is significant compared to procedural SDFs. Strengths: Allows the use of pre-computed distance fields from meshes (e.g., Stanford Bunny) in ray marching scenes. Handles boundary conditions robustly to prevent tunneling. Limitations: Requires storing the 3D texture, which consumes more memory than procedural SDFs. The textureShell parameter is heuristic and determined by trial and error, potentially varying between textures. When to Use: When rendering complex, pre-computed distance fields from meshes where procedural SDFs are insufficient or impractical. When Not to Use: When memory is constrained or when the scene geometry is simple enough for analytical SDFs. This method originates from research on GPU ray marching for ambient occlusion and distance fields. It was developed to integrate pre-computed 3D distance textures (such as the Stanford Bunny) into ray marching pipelines, addressing the specific challenge of invalid distance values at the texture boundaries. The technique is described in the context of the GEL (GEometry and Linear algebra) framework. name: Ambient Occlusion Specific Distance Function
head: Distance function for a cube sized 3D texture (AO variant), Distance function for a cube sized 3D texture. Version for ambient occlusion
body: This method is a specialized distance function for a cube-sized 3D texture designed to mitigate artifacts in ambient occlusion (AO) calculations caused by the texture's bounding shell. While the standard distance function returns the distance to the outer boundary for points outside the texture volume, this variant returns a constant step size \Delta t. This prevents the bounding "red box" from contributing to the occlusion result, which otherwise causes visible artifacts on surfaces like the bunny's face. It is used in conjunction with Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching but modifies the boundary handling logic specifically for AO shading. Inputs: Query point x (vec3). 3D texture containing signed distance values. Constant \Delta t (float), passed from the ambient occlusion algorithm to determine the sample point along the ray equation. Parameters: textureBoundary = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5), textureShell = (0.05, 0.05, 0.05). Outputs: Distance value res (float). Data Structures: The 3D texture is cube-sized. textureBoundary defines the half-width of the valid region center. textureShell defines the boundary offset value. Steps: 1. Compute the absolute value of the query point: |x|. 2. Calculate the distance vector di from the inner valid region box: di = |x| - \text{textureBoundary} + \text{textureShell} This computes component-wise distances to the inner box faces. 3. Determine if the point x is inside the inner valid region (the "green box" area) by computing: c = \max(d{ix}, \max(d{iy}, d{iz})) 4. If c < 0, the point is inside the inner valid region: Adjust the coordinates to map back to the texture space: x = x + \text{textureBoundary}. Lookup the distance value from the 3D texture: res = lookupTexture(texture, x). 5. If c \ge 0 (point is outside the inner valid region): Return the constant \Delta t: res = \Delta t. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def distancefunctionao(x, texture, deltat): textureboundary = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) textureshell = (0.05, 0.05, 0.05) absx = (abs(x[0]), abs(x[1]), abs(x[2])) di = ( absx[0] - textureboundary[0] + textureshell[0], absx[1] - textureboundary[1] + textureshell[1], absx[2] - textureboundary[2] + textureshell[2]) c = max(di[0], max(di[1], di[2])) if c < 0: adjustedx = (x[0] + textureboundary[0], x[1] + textureboundary[1], x[2] + textureboundary[2]) res = lookuptexture(texture, adjustedx) else: res = deltat return res def lookuptexture(texture, coords): # Standard 3D texture sampling with coordinate clamping x, y, z = coords x = max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) y = max(0.0, min(1.0, y)) z = max(0.0, min(1.0, z)) return texture[int(x)][int(y)][int(z)] Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Using the standard distance function (Algorithm 4.1) for ambient occlusion causes the bounding red box to contribute to the occlusion result, leading to artifacts on the bunny's face. The mesh must be closed (holes filled) before conversion to a 3D distance texture to ensure correct representation. Not given in the sources. This method originates from work on GPU ray marching for ambient occlusion using the GEL (GEometry and Linear algebra) framework. It addresses specific artifacts observed when rendering the Stanford Bunny mesh, where the standard distance function caused incorrect occlusion near the texture boundaries. The approach modifies the distance function f(x) used in the ambient occlusion algorithm (Algorithm 3.4) to use f{BA}(x) instead of fB(x), while keeping the sphere tracing algorithm unchanged. name: Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDFs)
head: Probabilistic DDF
body: Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields (PDDFs) are a variant of Directed Distance Fields (DDFs) designed to differentiably model the inherent discontinuities in the underlying field, specifically surface and occlusion discontinuities. While standard DDFs output a single scalar depth value, PDDFs modify the formulation so that the network outputs probability distributions over rays rather than a single value, allowing a C^1 continuous neural network to represent the discontinuous field of a DDF. This enables efficient differentiable rendering and geometry extraction without the training instability caused by hard discontinuities. Inputs and Outputs Input: A query point \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^3 and a viewing direction \mathbf{v} \in S^2. Output: A probability density function P{\mathbf{p},\mathbf{v}}(d) over depths d \ge 0, from which a final depth d^ and visibility \xi(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) are derived. Data Structures The network output is a density field representing a mixture of Dirac delta functions. For a fixed number of components K, the output consists of: 1. Mixture Weights: A vector \mathbf{w} = [w1, w2, \dots, wK] where wi \ge 0 and \sum{i=1}^K wi = 1. 2. Delta Locations: A vector \mathbf{d} = [d1, d2, \dots, dK] where di \ge 0. Parameters K: The number of mixture components in the Dirac delta mixture. The typical value used in the source literature is K=2. Algorithm The PDDF is evaluated as follows: 1. Network Forward Pass: Given input (\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}), the neural network outputs the mixture weights \mathbf{w} and delta locations \mathbf{d}. 2. Probability Density Definition: The probability density over depth is defined as: P{\mathbf{p},\mathbf{v}}(d) = \sum{i=1}^K wi \delta(d - di) where \delta(\cdot) is the Dirac delta function. 3. Depth Selection: The output depth d^ is determined by selecting the delta component with the highest weight: i^ = \operatorname{arg\,max}{i} wi d^ = d{i^}. 4. Visibility: The visibility field \xi(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) is handled separately and remains unchanged from the standard DDF formulation. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def evaluatepddf(network, p, v, K=2): """ Evaluates a Probabilistic Directed Distance Field. Args: network: A neural network function that takes (p, v) and returns weights w and depths d. p: Query point (3D vector). v: Viewing direction (3D vector). K: Number of mixture components (default 2). Returns: dstar: The selected output depth. w: The full weight vector (for analysis/gradient flow). d: The full depth vector (for analysis/gradient flow). """ # 1. Network Forward Pass # The network outputs K weights and K depths. # Weights must sum to 1. Depths are non-negative. w, d = network(p, v) # 2. Depth Selection # Find the index of the maximum weight istar = argmax(w) # 3. Output Depth dstar = d[istar] return dstar, w, d Edge Cases and Pitfalls Discontinuous Output Depth: Discontinuities in the output depth d^ occur when the dominant weight w{i^} switches from one delta location di to another dj which may be arbitrarily far apart. Smooth Transition Handling: To handle the discontinuity in d^ while maintaining a C^1 network, the weight field \mathbf{w}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{v}) is allowed to smoothly transition between indices at surface or occlusion discontinuities. This ensures the network remains differentiable even though the final selected depth d^ is discontinuous. Weight Normalization: The weights wi must strictly sum to 1. In implementation, this is typically enforced via a Softmax layer at the network output. What it is: A method using bounded 3D distance textures for ray marching. Difference: Uses explicit texture lookups for distance bounds rather than neural network outputs. When to choose: When hardware acceleration for texture sampling is preferred over neural inference. Link: Bounded 3D Distance Texture Ray Marching What it is: Haptic rendering using distance fields derived from sparse point sets. Difference: Focuses on haptic feedback and point-set based geometry rather than differentiable neural shape representation. When to choose: For haptic simulation tasks with sparse data. Link: Sparse Point Set Haptic Rendering via Distance Field Time Complexity: O(K) per pixel for the forward pass, where K is the number of mixture components. With K=2, this is constant time relative to scene complexity, dominated by the neural network inference cost. Memory Complexity: O(K) per query point for storing weights and depths. Strengths: Enables differentiable rendering of shapes with complex topology and occlusions by smoothing the training signal via probability distributions. Allows extraction of classical unsigned distance fields and higher-order geometry (normals, curvatures) via network derivatives. Limitations: The output depth d^ is still discontinuous, which can cause artifacts in rendering if not handled carefully during the final selection step. The method relies on neural network capacity to learn the weight transitions. When to use: When training neural implicit representations for 3D shapes, single-image 3D reconstruction, or generative modeling where differentiability is crucial. When not to use: When non-differentiable, hard-cutoff distance fields are sufficient and neural network overhead is prohibitive. Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields were introduced to address the difficulty of training differentiable neural networks with standard DDFs, which are inherently discontinuous functions of position and view direction. The method was proposed in the paper "Representing 3D Shapes with Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields" (CVPR 2022) and further detailed in "Probabilistic Directed Distance Fields for Ray-Based Shape Representations" (TPAMI 2025). It is applied to single-shape fitting, unpaired 3D-aware generative image modeling, and single-image 3D reconstruction tasks. name: Sparse Point Set Haptic Rendering via Distance Field
head: Augmented Point Set Rendering, Distance Field based Haptic Rendering of Scattered Oriented Points
body:
This method provides haptic rendering for sparse, oriented point cloud data by constructing a 3D signed distance field (SDF) on a regular grid using embedded "packing spheres". It solves the problem of generating stable collision forces from incomplete geometric data where traditional mesh-based or dense implicit function methods fail due to sparsity. Unlike sibling methods that rely on dense sampling or explicit surface reconstruction, this technique uses the local normal direction to define minimum-volume spheres that approximate the object's interior, allowing a proxy to be constrained to the zero-iso-surface via gradient descent. Input: An augmented point set s(P, n) consisting of N points Pi and their corresponding outward-facing unit normals ni. Output: A 3D grid of distance values \phi(x, y, z) representing the signed distance to the object surface, and a haptic force feedback loop. 1. Augmented Point Set: A list of tuples (Pi, ni) where Pi \in \mathbb{R}^3 and ni \in \mathbb{R}^3 with \|ni\|=1. 2. 3D Grid: A regular 3D grid of voxels. The grid dimensions are chosen to fit the haptic device's interaction space (e.g., 300 	imes 300 	imes 300 for a 4-inch cube). Each node stores a scalar distance value and a classification (inside/outside/boundary). For each point Pi in the augmented point set, compute the minimum radius ri of a sphere centered along the inward normal direction -ni that contains at least one other point Pj on its boundary. 1. For every other point Pj (j 
eq i), calculate the vector a{ij} = Pj - Pi. 2. Calculate the angle 	heta{ij} between a{ij} and the inward normal -ni. 3. If 	heta{ij} < \pi/2 (i.e., -ni \cdot a{ij} > 0), the point Pj lies in the forward hemisphere of the normal. Compute the radius r{ij} and center c{ij} of the unique sphere passing through Pi and Pj with normal ni at Pi: r{ij} =  rac{1}{2} |a{ij}| \sec(	heta{ij}) c{ij} = Pi - r{ij} ni 4. The packing radius ri for point Pi is the minimum of all valid r{ij}: ri = \min{j 
eq i, 	heta{ij} < \pi/2} r{ij} The center ci is the c{ij} corresponding to the minimizing j. Map each point Pi to the nearest grid node. The grid nodes containing mapped points are marked as "inside" or "boundary" depending on their neighborhood status. Compute the signed distance field \phi on the grid using an iterative erosion process. 1. Initialize all grid nodes. Nodes not mapped to any point are initially considered "outside". 2. Set the distance value of all "outside" nodes to 1. 3. Identify "boundary" nodes as those inside nodes that have at least one outside neighbor. 4. Perform iterative erosion using a structuring element B of unit radius to erode the set of inside nodes S: Level 0: Set the distance value of current boundary nodes to 0. Relabel these nodes as "outside". Level k: Identify new boundary nodes (inside nodes with at least one outside neighbor). Set their distance values to -(k-1) (or decreasing integer values: -1, -2, \dots). Relabel them as "outside". 5. Repeat until no inside nodes remain. Note: The sources describe this as an erosion process where distance values decrease into the object. The zero-level set represents the surface. At each haptic update cycle (targeting >1 kHz, i.e., <1 ms per update): 1. Let Xh be the position of the Haptic Interface Point (HIP) and Xp be the position of the haptic proxy. 2. Compute the distance \phi(Xp) at the proxy location by trilinear interpolation of the distance field values at the 8 nearest grid nodes. 3. If \phi(Xp) > 0, the proxy is outside the object. No collision occurs. Set Xp = Xh and no force is generated. If \phi(Xp) < 0, the proxy is inside the object (collision detected). 1. Minimize the objective function \Psi(Xp) to find the new proxy position Xp^{(k+1)} from current position Xp^{(k)}: \Psi(Xp) =  rac{1}{2} \|Xp - Xh\|^2 +  rac{\lambda}{2} |\phi(Xp)|^2 2. The gradient of the objective function is: 
abla \Psi(Xp) = (Xp - Xh) + \lambda \phi(Xp) 
abla \phi(Xp) 3. Update the proxy position using gradient descent: Xp^{(k+1)} = Xp^{(k)} -  eta \phi(Xp^{(k)}) 
abla \phi(Xp^{(k)}) - \gamma (Xp^{(k)} - Xh) where  eta = \gamma \lambda, and \gamma is a step size parameter. 4. The term (Xp - Xh) pulls the proxy toward the HIP, while \phi(Xp) 
abla \phi(Xp) pushes the proxy toward the zero-iso-surface (the object boundary). 5. Compute the reaction force f using Hooke's Law: f = -k (Xh - Xp) where k is the stiffness constant and (Xh - Xp) is the penetration depth vector. Unverified code. Args: points: List of N points Pi (3D coordinates). normals: List of N outward unit normals ni. Returns: radii: List of minimum radii ri. centers: List of sphere centers ci. Args: gridshape: Tuple (D, H, W) of the 3D grid. points: List of points Pi. normals: List of normals ni. packingcenters: List of sphere centers ci. packingradii: List of sphere radii ri. Returns: distfield: 3D numpy array of distance values. """ # This is a conceptual implementation of the erosion boundary detection # In practice, this involves convolution or neighbor checks. # We return a list of coordinates. boundarynodes = [] # Iterate over all inside nodes insideindices = np.where(insidemask) for i, j, k in zip(insideindices): # Check 6-connected neighbors neighbors = [ (i+1, j, k), (i-1, j, k), (i, j+1, k), (i, j-1, k), (i, j, k+1), (i, j, k-1) ] isboundary = False for ni, nj, nk in neighbors: # Check bounds if 0 <= ni < distfield.shape[0] and \ 0 <= nj < distfield.shape[1] and \ 0 <= nk < distfield.shape[2]: if not insidemask[ni, nj, nk]: isboundary = True break else: # Out of bounds is considered outside isboundary = True break if isboundary: boundarynodes.append((i, j, k)) return boundarynodes def hapticupdate(HIP, distfield, gridspacing, kstiffness, gamma, lambdaparam): """ Performs one step of haptic rendering. Args: HIP: 3D position of the Haptic Interface Point (Xh). distfield: The precomputed 3D distance field. gridspacing: Physical size of one voxel. kstiffness: Hooke's constant k. gamma: Step size parameter. lambdaparam: Weighting parameter lambda. Returns: proxypos: New proxy position (Xp). force: Reaction force vector. """ Xh = HIP # Initial proxy position can be HIP or previous proxy position Xp = Xh # Compute distance at proxy phi = trilinearinterpolate(Xp, distfield, gridspacing) if phi > 0: # Outside object proxypos = Xh force = np.array([0.0, 0.0, 0.0]) return proxypos, force # Inside object: Minimize objective function # Xp^(k+1) = Xp^(k) - beta phi gradphi - gamma (Xp - Xh) # beta = gamma lambda beta = gamma lambdaparam # Compute gradient of distance field at Xp gradphi = computegradient(Xp, distfield, gridspacing) # Gradient descent iteration (usually 1-2 iterations are sufficient for stability) # The source implies a single update step per haptic cycle or a few iterations. # We perform one update step here. displacement = Xp - Xh forceterm = -gamma displacement surfaceterm = -beta phi gradphi Xpnew = Xp + forceterm + surfaceterm # Compute reaction force penetrationdepth = Xh - Xpnew force = -kstiffness penetrationdepth return Xpnew, force def trilinearinterpolate(point, distfield, gridspacing): """ Trilinear interpolation of the distance field at a given point. """ # Convert world coordinates to grid indices # This is a placeholder for the actual interpolation logic pass def computegradient(point, distfield, gridspacing): """ Computes the gradient of the distance field using finite differences. """ # This is a placeholder for the actual gradient calculation pass Grid Resolution: The grid size must fit the haptic device's interaction space. Example: 300 	imes 300 	imes 300 for a 4-inch cube. Stiffness Constant (k): Hooke's constant for the reaction force. Step Size (\gamma): Parameter in the gradient descent update rule. Weighting (\lambda): Parameter balancing proxy-HIP distance and surface constraint. Sparse Sampling Leakage: If the input point set is not dense enough, the embedded packing spheres may leak out of the actual object boundary, causing incorrect distance field values, particularly near corners or concave regions. Optimization of Distance Field Computation: It is not necessary to compute the distance field for all inside grid nodes. The proxy rarely sinks more than 3-4 voxel lengths into the object. Calculating distances only up to 5 or 6 nodes inside the bounding surface is sufficient for stable haptic feedback. Time Complexity: Pre-computation of the distance field is O(N \cdot M) where N is the number of points and M is the number of grid nodes, dominated by the erosion process. Haptic update is O(1) per frame (trilinear interpolation and gradient descent). Memory Complexity: O(D \cdot H \cdot W) for the 3D grid storage. Measured Performance: Force calculation takes 0.02 ms on a CORE 2 QUAD CPU @ 2.66GHz with 2GB RAM, well below the 1 ms requirement for smooth haptic rendering (1 kHz update rate). Pre-computation times vary by dataset size: 3,725 points (grid 186 	imes 173 	imes 87): 38.09 seconds for 824,463 inside nodes. 5,153 points (grid 126 	imes 187 	imes 72): 26.25 seconds for 304,072 internal nodes. 3,751 points: 110.82 seconds for 1,129,209 inside points. 3,756 points (water hydrant): 30.86 seconds for 586,222 points. Strengths: Optimized for sparse data sets; provides stable haptic feedback; allows combined hapto-visual rendering. Limitations: Sensitive to point density (leakage); pre-computation can be slow for large grids; limited to regular grid structures. When to use: When rendering haptic feedback for sparse, oriented point clouds where mesh reconstruction is difficult or unnecessary. When not to use: For dense point clouds (other methods may be more efficient) or when high-fidelity visual rendering of complex surfaces is required without haptics. Origin: Proposed in 2013 by researchers publishing in the International Journal of Computer Applications. History: The method addresses limitations of dense point cloud methods (like Leeper et al.'s implicit function) and point proxy methods by using a spherical volume proxy defined by a distance field. It builds on the concept of "augmented point sets" (points with normals) similar to point shells. Usage: Used for haptic rendering of scattered oriented point cloud data and visual rendering of the zero iso-surface for combined hapto-visual experience. name: SDF Transformations
head: SDF Composition, SDF Modifiers
body: SDF Transformations modify the spatial domain of a Signed Distance Field (SDF) primitive by applying geometric operations to the query point \mathbf{p} before evaluation, enabling complex procedural geometry such as repetition, deformation, and dynamic animation without mesh processing. Unlike static primitives, this method allows for the composition of infinite or dynamically varying scenes with extremely low memory footprint, as the scene is defined by functions rather than data structures. It sets itself apart from SDF Primitive Definitions by focusing on the manipulation of the input coordinate space rather than the analytical distance formula itself. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Query point \mathbf{p} (typically in world space), primitive parameters (e.g., spacing, twist angle), and optionally time t for dynamic operators. Output: Transformed point \mathbf{p}' used to evaluate the base SDF, or the final distance value d = SDF{base}(\mathbf{p}'). Data Structures: No persistent data structures are required. The transformation is computed on-the-fly per ray march step. For dynamic operators, a Holistic Scene Dynamics (HSD) function may store parameters per object instance. Steps: 1. Identify Transformation Type: Determine if the operation is static (repetition, deformation) or dynamic (time-varying affine transformation). 2. Apply Coordinate Mapping: Transform the query point \mathbf{p} into the local or transformed space \mathbf{p}' using the specific transformation function T(\mathbf{p}). For Repetition (Tiling): Apply modular arithmetic to create a periodic grid. For Deformation: Apply a non-linear function to the coordinates. For Dynamic Operators: Calculate a transformation matrix or vector based on the HSD function, time t, and object ID, then apply it to the ray position. 3. Evaluate Base SDF: Compute the distance d using the base primitive's SDF function with the transformed point: d = SDF{base}(\mathbf{p}'). 4. Return Distance: Return d to the ray marching loop. Formulas: Repetition (Tiling): \mathbf{p}' = \text{mod}(\mathbf{p}, \mathbf{s}) - \frac{\mathbf{s}}{2} Where \mathbf{s} is the spacing vector (e.g., vec3(1.0)). Deformation (Twist): \mathbf{p}' = \text{twist}(\mathbf{p}) Where twist is a custom function, typically rotating the x and y coordinates based on the z height. Dynamic Transformation: The position on the ray is transformed at each iteration. If M(t, \mathbf{p}) is the dynamic transformation matrix derived from the HSD function: \mathbf{p}' = M(t, \mathbf{p}) \cdot \mathbf{p} The HSD function is defined as f{HSD}: D \times t \rightarrow V, where D is object input data, t is simulation time, and V is the dynamics variation (e.g., transformation matrix). Parameters: Spacing (\mathbf{s}): Vector defining the tile size. Typical value: vec3(1.0) for unit cubes. Twist Angle: Scalar defining rotation per unit height. Typical value: PI for a full twist. Time (t): Float for dynamic animations. Updates per frame. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Lipschitz Condition: Transformations must preserve the Lipschitz constant of 1 to ensure the distance value remains a safe lower bound for sphere tracing. Non-linear deformations like twisting can violate this if not carefully implemented, potentially causing tunneling. Boundary Precision: In repetition, the mod operation can introduce precision errors at tile boundaries. Using spacing/2 offset helps center the tiles. Dynamic Grid Calculation: In Dynamic Operators, the grid cell vector must be calculated independently from the Instancing operator to ensure the transformation is applied correctly before instancing logic. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sdftransformations(p, primitivefunc, transformtype, params): """ Applies SDF transformations to a query point. Args: p: vec3, query point in world space. primitivefunc: function, base SDF function (e.g., sphere, box). transformtype: str, 'repetition', 'deformation', or 'dynamic'. params: dict, transformation parameters. Returns: float, signed distance to the transformed surface. """ pprime = p if transformtype == 'repetition': spacing = params.get('spacing', vec3(1.0)) # Apply tiling transformation pprime = mod(p, spacing) - spacing / 2.0 elif transformtype == 'deformation': twistangle = params.get('twistangle', 0.0) # Apply twist deformation # Example: rotate x,y based on z z = p.z angle = z twistangle c = cos(angle) s = sin(angle) x = p.x y = p.y pprime = vec3(x c - y s, x s + y c, z) elif transformtype == 'dynamic': # Dynamic Operators require additional processing # 1. Calculate grid cell vector independently gridcell = calculategridcell(p, params.get('gridsize', 1.0)) # 2. Apply HSD function to get transformation # HSD: fHSD(D, t) -> V time = params.get('time', 0.0) objectid = params.get('objectid', 0) transformationmatrix = hsdfunction(gridcell, time, objectid) # 3. Apply transformation to ray position # Note: In a full ray marcher, this happens per step. # Here we assume p is the current step position. pprime = transformationmatrix p # Evaluate base primitive with transformed point distance = primitivefunc(pprime) return distance def calculategridcell(p, gridsize): """Helper to calculate grid cell for dynamic operators.""" return floor(p / gridsize) def hsdfunction(gridcell, time, objectid): """ Placeholder for Holistic Scene Dynamics Function. Returns a transformation matrix based on noise or time. """ # Example: Simple translation based on time and noise noiseval = noise(gridcell + time) translation = vec3(noiseval, 0.0, 0.0) # Return identity matrix with translation return mat4(1.0) + translationmatrix(translation) An extension to the Global operators collection that applies unique affine transformations and material animations to 3D objects using the Holistic Scene Dynamics (HSD) function. Unlike original Global operators which used the Instancing operator's output (grid cell vector) as input, Dynamic Operators calculate the grid cell vector independently and transform the ray before applying the Instancing operator. This allows for dynamic variations per 3D object, such as wind effects on grass or flying objects, by applying an additional transformation to the position on the ray from the camera to the SDF component at each iteration of the ray marching algorithm. Time Complexity: O(1) per ray march step, as transformations are simple arithmetic or matrix operations. Memory Complexity: O(1), as no scene data structures are stored; only shader code and parameters. Performance: Extremely efficient for complex procedural landscapes with hundreds of blended primitives, consuming effectively zero scene memory beyond the framebuffer. Strengths: Infinite detail, low memory usage, natural integration with volumetrics, and ability to create complex geometry from simple functions. Limitations: Transformations must preserve the Lipschitz condition to avoid tunneling; complex deformations may require smaller step sizes or adaptive marching. Dynamic operators add overhead for HSD function evaluation and grid cell calculation. SDF Transformations are a core technique in procedural ray marching, popularized by shaders like those in "A Ray Marching Primer" and tutorials by Tektite. The concept of using mod for repetition and coordinate manipulation for deformation is standard in GLSL shader programming. Dynamic Operators were introduced in the context of the Holistic UOI rendering pipeline to address the need for dynamic, unlimited object instancing with unique variations. ray marching vs ray tracing, https://tutorials.tektite.studio/ray-marching/ray-marching-vs-ray-tracing/, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Real-time visualization of Dynamic Unlimited Objects Instancing, https://doi.org/10.24132/csrn.2018.2802.4, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Global Distance Query via Local-Global Blending
head: Local-Global Blending SDF
body: This method constructs a global signed distance field (SDF) FG that retains the sharp geometric features of a local patch-based representation FL while enabling valid distance queries across the entire bounding domain. It solves the problem where local representations are accurate near the surface but fail or become unstable far away, and standard learned global fields smooth out sharp corners. It differs from pure local methods by providing a global query capability and from pure global methods by preserving high-frequency local details through a blending region. Inputs and Outputs Input: A local SDF FL(\mathbf{x}) defined near the surface S, and a global SDF FO(\mathbf{x}) defined over the entire domain. Output: A blended global SDF FG(\mathbf{x}). Data Structures The method operates on scalar fields. The global field FO is implemented as a vanilla 8-layered Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP) with 512 neurons per layer, equipped with positional encoding. The local field FL is typically a patch-based representation. Parameters \delta1 = 0.001: Inner boundary of the blending region. \delta2 = 0.03: Outer boundary of the blending region. Domain D = [-1, 1]^3: The bounding box of the shape. Steps 1. Define three regions based on the absolute value of the local distance |FL(\mathbf{x})|: Region R1 = \{ \mathbf{x} \mid |FL(\mathbf{x})| < \delta1 \} Region R2 = \{ \mathbf{x} \mid \delta1 \le |FL(\mathbf{x})| \le \delta2 \} Region R3 = D \setminus (R1 \cup R2) 2. For a query point \mathbf{x}, determine which region it falls into. 3. If \mathbf{x} \in R1, return FL(\mathbf{x}). 4. If \mathbf{x} \in R3, return FO(\mathbf{x}). 5. If \mathbf{x} \in R2, compute the blended value FG(\mathbf{x}) using weights derived from the normalized distance parameter s(\mathbf{x}). Formulas The normalized distance parameter s(\mathbf{x}) maps |FL(\mathbf{x})| \in [\delta1, \delta2] to [0, 1]: s(\mathbf{x}) = \frac{|FL(\mathbf{x})| - \delta1}{\delta2 - \delta1} The weight functions use the smoothstep function h(s) = 3s^2 - 2s^3: w0(s) = 1 - h(s) w1(s) = h(s) The blended field in R2 is: FG(\mathbf{x}) = w0(s(\mathbf{x})) FL(\mathbf{x}) + w1(s(\mathbf{x})) FO(\mathbf{x}) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def smoothstep(s): """Standard smoothstep function.""" return 3 s s - 2 s s s def globaldistancequery(x, FL, FO, delta1=0.001, delta2=0.03): """ Compute the blended global SDF value at point x. Args: x: Query point (vector). FL: Function returning local SDF value. FO: Function returning global SDF value. delta1: Inner blending boundary. delta2: Outer blending boundary. Returns: Blended SDF value. """ # Evaluate local distance valL = FL(x) absvalL = abs(valL) # Region R1: Use local field directly if absvalL < delta1: return valL # Region R3: Use global field directly if absvalL > delta2: return FO(x) # Region R2: Blend # Normalize distance to [0, 1] s = (absvalL - delta1) / (delta2 - delta1) # Compute weights using smoothstep h = smoothstep(s) w0 = 1.0 - h w1 = h # Evaluate global field valO = FO(x) # Linear blend return w0 valL + w1 valO Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: The transition in R2 is C^1 continuous due to smoothstep, but the derivative of the absolute value function at FL(\mathbf{x})=0 is discontinuous. However, since R1 uses FL directly and R2 starts at \delta1 > 0, the discontinuity at zero is handled by the exclusive boundary of R1. Boundary Definition: The regions are defined by the magnitude of FL. If FL is not a true distance field (violating Lipschitz condition), the blending may not preserve the exact geometry as intended. Domain: The method assumes the domain D is bounded, typically [-1, 1]^3 for CAD models. Defines the basic analytical shapes (spheres, boxes) used to construct FL or FO. SDF Primitive Definitions Discusses how FL and FO are stored and sampled (e.g., neural networks, grids). Distance Field Representations and Sampling Describes how to apply transformations to the primitives before blending. SDF Transformations Time Complexity: O(1) per query, dominated by the evaluation of FL and FO. If FO is an 8-layer MLP, this involves several matrix multiplications and activations. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of FL (patch-based) and FO (MLP weights). The MLP has 8 \times 512 \times 512 weights (plus biases), which is significant but manageable. Strengths: Retains sharp features (corners, edges) that are lost in standard global neural SDFs, while providing a valid distance field for the entire domain, enabling operations like offsetting and boolean operations globally. Limitations: Requires both a local and a global representation. The blending region R2 introduces a transition zone where the geometry is an approximation. When to use: When high-fidelity local details are required alongside global scene queries (e.g., collision detection, ray marching across the whole object). When not to use: If only local rendering is needed, or if memory is extremely constrained and storing both fields is prohibitive. This method was introduced in the context of CAD model representation, specifically to address the need for global signed distance functions in CAD applications. Standard patch-based representations are accurate near the surface but do not support global queries. Learned global fields (like those using MLPs) smooth out sharp features. The blending strategy allows the retention of sharp features from the local representation while leveraging the global coverage of the learned field. The global field FO is obtained following the strategy by Lin et al. [2024], using positional encoding as introduced by Mildenhall et al. [2020] and Tancik et al. [2020b].
