name: SDF Text Rendering
head: TMP_SDF-Mobile Overlay
body: SDF Text Rendering is a mobile-optimized technique for rendering text using Signed Distance Fields (SDFs) by sampling a pre-computed font atlas in screen space. It solves the problem of rendering crisp, scalable text with outlines and gradients on constrained hardware by omitting complex 3D effects like bevels, bump mapping, and environment mapping found in full desktop SDF shaders. It differs from its sibling RayMarchedHeading by operating on 2D texture samples rather than performing 3D raymarching through an extruded volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 2D font atlas texture (MainTex) containing the SDF values in the alpha channel, vertex positions, UV coordinates, and UI parameters (scale, bias, outline width, colors). Output: A final color half4 c for each pixel, including face color, outline color, and alpha. Data Structures: The vertex shader outputs a pixelt struct with the following layout: vertex: SVPOSITION (Clip space position). faceColor: COLOR (RGBA). outlineColor: COLOR1 (RGBA). texcoord0: TEXCOORD0 (Texture UV for atlas sampling; Mask UV for clipping). param: TEXCOORD1 (Packed half4: x = Scale, y = BiasIn, z = BiasOut, w = BiasFace). mask: TEXCOORD2 (Position in clip space xy; Softness factors zw). Parameters: GradientScale (float, default 5): Scales the distance field gradient for the font atlas. WeightNormal (float, default 0): Base weight value for normal text style. WeightBold (float, default 0.5): Base weight value for bold text style. FaceDilate (Range -1 to 1, default 0): Dilates the face color region. OutlineWidth (Range 0 to 1, default 0): Thickness of the outline. OutlineSoftness (Range 0 to 1, default 0): Softness applied to both sides of the outline. PerspectiveFilter (Range 0 to 1, default 0.875): Factor for perspective correction of the distance field scale. Sharpness (Range -1 to 1, default 0): Adjusts the sharpness of the distance field sampling. ClipRect (vector, default -32767,-32767,32767,32767): Clipping rectangle for UI masking. MaskSoftnessX/Y (float, default 0): Softness factors for the clipping mask. Steps: 1. Compute Pixel Size: Calculate the pixel size in world space from the clip position and projection matrix. \text{pixelSize}w = vPosition.w \text{pixelSize} = \frac{\text{pixelSize}w}{\begin{bmatrix} \text{ScaleX} \\ \text{ScaleY} \end{bmatrix} \cdot \left| \begin{bmatrix} P{00} & P{01} \\ P{10} & P{11} \end{bmatrix} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} \text{ScreenParams}x \\ \text{ScreenParams}y \end{bmatrix} \right|} Where P is the projection matrix UNITYMATRIXP and ScreenParams is the screen resolution. 2. Compute Base Scale: Derive the base scale factor from the pixel size. scale = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{pixelSize}x^2 + \text{pixelSize}y^2}} 3. Apply Perspective Filter: If the projection is orthographic (UNITYMATRIXP[3][3] == 0), lerp between the absolute scale and a view-direction dependent scale using PerspectiveFilter to prevent distortion. Otherwise, use the computed scale directly. 4. Compute Weight and Dilate: Calculate the text weight based on normal/bold states and apply face dilation. weight = \frac{\text{lerp}(\WeightNormal, \WeightBold, bold)}{4.0} weight = (weight + \FaceDilate) \cdot \ScaleRatioA \cdot 0.5 5. Compute Bias and Outline: Determine the bias values for the face and outline regions, adjusting for softness. scale = \frac{scale}{1 + (\OutlineSoftness \cdot \ScaleRatioA \cdot scale)} bias = (0.5 - weight) \cdot scale - 0.5 outline = \OutlineWidth \cdot \ScaleRatioA \cdot 0.5 \cdot scale 6. Pack Parameters: Pack the computed values into the param output for the fragment shader. param.x = scale param.y = bias - outline param.z = bias + outline param.w = bias 7. Sample Distance Field: In the fragment shader, sample the alpha channel of the font atlas. d = \text{tex2D}(\MainTex, input.texcoord0.xy).a \cdot input.param.x 8. Compute Face Color: Determine the face color based on the distance value and the face bias. c = input.faceColor \cdot \text{saturate}(d - input.param.w) 9. Apply Outline: If outline is enabled, blend between the outline color and face color based on the distance relative to the outline bias. c = \text{lerp}(input.outlineColor, c, \text{saturate}(d - input.param.z)) \cdot \text{saturate}(d - input.param.y) 10. Apply Clipping Mask: Softly clip the text using the ClipRect and mask softness. m = \text{saturate}((\ClipRect.zw - \ClipRect.xy - |input.mask.xy|) \cdot input.mask.zw) c = m.x \cdot m.y Pseudocode: Unverified code. It differs from its sibling RayMarchedHeading by performing actual 3D raymarching through an extruded SDF rather than marching 2D blur taps along a smear line. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel, as it involves a single texture sample and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the shader state; O(N) for the font atlas texture where N is the number of characters. Measured Performance: Optimized for mobile devices by omitting bevel, bump, environment mapping, and glow options. Strengths: High performance, crisp text at any scale, supports outlines and gradients. Limitations: Limited to 2D rendering; no true 3D depth effects like bevels or lighting interactions with 3D geometry. When to use: UI text rendering on mobile or low-power devices where performance is critical. When not to use: When 3D text effects, bevels, or integration with 3D lighting are required. SDF Text Rendering is a method popularized by Unity's TextMeshPro asset, specifically the mobile-optimized variant TMPSDF-Mobile. It leverages the properties of Signed Distance Fields to render text efficiently on GPUs. The technique is widely used in mobile game UIs and applications requiring scalable, high-quality text. name: True Raymarched Text Reveal
head: Raymarched SDF Heading, Text load-in v2, true raymarching
body: True Raymarched Text Reveal is a technique that renders text animations by converting DOM glyphs into a 3D Signed Distance Field (SDF), marching rays through it, and revealing the text using smooth-min metaballs and SDF-gradient lighting. It differs from its sibling RayMarchedHeading by performing actual 3D raymarching through an extruded SDF rather than marching 2D blur taps along a smear line. Inputs: DOM heading glyphs at measured positions, scene parameters (MAXSTEPS, SURFACEDIST, smooth-min k, front softness). Outputs: A rendered image of the text reveal, eventually crossfading to the selectable DOM heading. Data Structures: SDF Texture: A 3D texture representing the extruded SDF of the text. Ray State: Per-pixel ray origin and direction. Steps: 1. SDF Generation: Rasterize DOM heading glyphs at their measured positions on a 2D grid. Convert the rasterized glyphs into a real Signed Distance Field (SDF) using an exact Euclidean distance transform. The implementation uses the Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher algorithm with tiny-sdf style seeding to handle sub-pixel edges. Extrude the 2D SDF into 3D space to create a volumetric representation of the text. 2. Ray Setup: Set the ray origin and per-pixel ray direction. Use CSS pixels as world units. This ensures that a ray passing through pixel coordinate q in the viewport hits the text plane exactly at q, keeping the WebGL rendering aligned with the DOM layout. 3. Raymarching: March rays through the 3D SDF. In each step, evaluate the SDF distance d at the current ray position. Advance the ray by distance d. Repeat up to MAXSTEPS iterations. Terminate if the distance d is within SURFACEDIST (indicating a hit) or if MAXSTEPS is reached. 4. Reveal Logic: The text is revealed via a smooth-max intersection with a sweeping half-space. Metaball droplets are placed on the front of the reveal sweep. These droplets melt into the emerging glyphs using a polynomial smooth-min function controlled by the parameter smooth-min k. The front softness parameter controls the softness of the reveal sweep. 5. Shading: Compute normals at hit points using the SDF gradient. The implementation uses Inigo Quilez's getNormal method. Calculate lighting as ambient (based on normal.y) plus diffuse lighting. Apply a Beer's-law exponential depth fade to the lighting. 6. Handoff: As the animation progress settles, the shader converges onto analytically antialiased flat glyphs. Crossfade from the raymarched shader to the selectable DOM heading. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchtextreveal(pixelcoord, rayorigin, raydirection, sdftexture, params): """ Renders a single pixel of the raymarched text reveal. Args: pixelcoord: (x, y) CSS pixel coordinates. rayorigin: vec3 origin of the ray. raydirection: vec3 direction of the ray. sdftexture: 3D texture containing the extruded SDF of the text. params: Object containing MAXSTEPS, SURFACEDIST, smoothmink, frontsoftness, progress. Returns: vec3: Final color of the pixel. """ currentpos = rayorigin color = vec3(0.0) hit = False # Raymarching loop for i in range(params.MAXSTEPS): # Evaluate SDF at current position # Note: sdftexture lookup returns distance to nearest surface dist = sdftexture.sample(currentpos) # Check for surface hit if dist < params.SURFACEDIST: hit = True break # Advance ray currentpos += raydirection dist if hit: # Compute normal using SDF gradient (Inigo Quilez's method) # This requires sampling the SDF at small offsets around currentpos normal = computesdfgradient(currentpos, sdftexture) # Lighting calculation ambient = normal.y 0.5 + 0.5 # Simple ambient based on normal.y diffuse = computediffuselighting(normal, params.lightangle) # Beer's law exponential depth fade depth = length(currentpos - rayorigin) fade = exp(-params.depthfadefactor depth) color = (ambient + diffuse) fade # Reveal logic (simplified representation) # The actual reveal is a smooth-max intersection with a sweeping half-space # and metaball droplets melting into glyphs via polynomial smooth-min. # This affects whether the hit is considered "visible" in the final composite. revealfactor = computerevealfactor(currentpos, params.progress, params.frontsoftness, params.smoothmink) color = revealfactor else: # Background color or transparency color = vec3(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) return color def computesdfgradient(pos, sdftexture): """ Computes the gradient of the SDF at pos using central differences. """ eps = 0.001 dx = sdftexture.sample(pos + vec3(eps, 0, 0)) - sdftexture.sample(pos - vec3(eps, 0, 0)) dy = sdftexture.sample(pos + vec3(0, eps, 0)) - sdftexture.sample(pos - vec3(0, eps, 0)) dz = sdftexture.sample(pos + vec3(0, 0, eps)) - sdftexture.sample(pos - vec3(0, 0, eps)) return normalize(vec3(dx, dy, dz)) def computerevealfactor(pos, progress, frontsoftness, smoothmink): """ Computes the visibility factor based on the reveal animation. This involves a smooth-max intersection with a sweeping half-space and polynomial smooth-min with metaball droplets. """ # Placeholder for the complex reveal logic described in # The exact polynomial smooth-min formula and half-space sweep parameters # are not fully detailed in the source notes. # Assuming a simple progress-based mask for implementation completeness. # In practice, this would use smoothmin(pos, halfspace, k) and droplet interactions. return smoothstep(0.0, 1.0, progress) Parameters: MAXSTEPS: Maximum number of raymarch steps allowed per ray. SURFACEDIST: Distance threshold below which a ray is considered to have hit the surface. smooth-min k: Smoothness parameter controlling the blending of the polynomial smooth-min function. front softness: Controls the softness of the reveal sweep. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Sub-pixel edges require careful handling during SDF generation (Felzenszwalb–Huttenlocher with tiny-sdf seeding) to avoid aliasing artifacts. Alignment: Using CSS pixels as world units is critical to keep WebGL and DOM aligned; deviation causes misalignment. Performance: Raymarching is computationally expensive; MAXSTEPS must be tuned to balance quality and performance. The parent method that generates the 3D SDF from text. True Raymarched Text Reveal builds on this by adding the raymarching and reveal logic. See SDF Text Rendering. The previous attempt which used 2D blur taps along a smear line. It is not true raymarching and lacks the 3D SDF volume and metaball interactions. See RayMarchedHeading. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to MAXSTEPS per pixel. The SDF generation is done offline or on the CPU/GPU once per frame if dynamic. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the 3D SDF texture. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Strengths: True 3D raymarching allows for complex lighting, shadows, and interactions (metaballs) that 2D techniques cannot achieve. The alignment with DOM ensures crisp final output. Limitations: Computationally intensive compared to 2D techniques. Requires careful tuning of parameters to avoid artifacts. When to use: When high-quality, animated 3D text reveals are needed and performance allows for raymarching. When not to use: When performance is critical and 2D effects are sufficient. The technique was developed by milesroxas and added to the Suits & Sandals website as part of an immersive demo section. It is built from the techniques described in Maxime Heckel's "Painting with Math: A Gentle Study of Raymarching". It serves as an improved approach to the previous "RayMarchedHeading" attempt, which was not true raymarching. Add true-raymarching text reveal section to immersive demo, https://github.com/milesroxas/sas-site/pull/5, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Infinite Floor Projection
head: testFloor
body: Infinite Floor Projection is a technique for rendering an infinite, textured planar surface (typically a floor) by projecting screen coordinates into world space using perspective division, then applying player rotation and a checkerboard pattern. It differs from standard texture mapping by calculating world-space coordinates directly per pixel using perspective division, allowing for seamless infinite tiling without UV wrapping artifacts. It builds on Procedural and Mathematical Surfaces by explicitly deriving the world coordinate increments from the view frustum geometry rather than relying on pre-projected screen coordinates. Inputs: Screen dimensions: SCRWIDTH, SCRHEIGHT. Player state: player.lookAngle (rotation in radians), player.x, player.y, player.z (position). Constants: moveVertical scaling factor (16.0), look angle multiplier (6.2, approximating 2\pi). Outputs: Pixel colors (e.g., red or blue for a checkerboard pattern). Data Structures: No complex data structures; state is held in scalar variables and simple loops. Steps: 1. Calculate Look Angle Offset: Compute lookAngle as -player.lookAngle 6.2. Clamp this value to the range [0, SCRHEIGHT]. 2. Calculate Vertical Scale: Compute moveVertical as player.z / 16.0. If moveVertical is zero, clamp it to 0.0001 to prevent division by zero. 3. Iterate Screen Rows: Loop y from yStart to yEnd (typically the visible screen height). 4. Iterate Screen Columns: Loop x from -SCRWIDTHHALF to SCRWIDTHHALF. 5. Compute Depth Proxy: Calculate z = y + lookAngle. Clamp z to 0.0001 if it is less than or equal to zero to prevent division by zero. 6. Project to World Space: Calculate intermediate world coordinates fx and fy: fx = \frac{x}{z} \times moveVertical fy = \frac{200}{z} \times moveVertical. 7. Apply Player Rotation: Rotate the world coordinates by the player's look angle: rx = fx \times \sin(\text{angle}) - fy \times \cos(\text{angle}) + \frac{\text{player.y}}{60.0} ry = fx \times \cos(\text{angle}) + fy \times \sin(\text{angle}) - \frac{\text{player.x}}{60.0}. 8. Mirror Coordinates: To handle negative coordinates for tiling, mirror them: If rx < 0, set rx = -rx + 1. If ry < 0, set ry = -ry + 1.. 9. Cull Invalid Tiles: If rx <= 0 or ry <= 0 or rx >= 5 or ry >= 5, skip drawing (or draw background). 10. Determine Pattern: Draw red if rx % 2 == ry % 2, else draw blue. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderinfinitefloor(player, scrwidth, scrheight): # Constants LOOKANGLEMULTIPLIER = 6.2 MOVEVERTICALSCALE = 16.0 MINZ = 0.0001 MINMOVEVERTICAL = 0.0001 FLOOROFFSETX = 60.0 FLOOROFFSETY = 60.0 TILELIMIT = 5 # 1. Calculate Look Angle Offset lookangle = -player.lookAngle LOOKANGLEMULTIPLIER lookangle = clamp(lookangle, 0, scrheight) # 2. Calculate Vertical Scale movevertical = player.z / MOVEVERTICALSCALE if movevertical == 0: movevertical = MINMOVEVERTICAL # 3 & 4. Iterate Screen Pixels for y in range(ystart, yend): for x in range(-scrwidth // 2, scrwidth // 2): # 5. Compute Depth Proxy z = y + lookangle if z <= 0: z = MINZ # 6. Project to World Space fx = (x / z) movevertical fy = (200 / z) movevertical # 7. Apply Player Rotation rx = fx sin(player.lookAngle) - fy cos(player.lookAngle) + (player.y / FLOOROFFSETY) ry = fx cos(player.lookAngle) + fy sin(player.lookAngle) - (player.x / FLOOROFFSETX) # 8. Mirror Coordinates if rx < 0: rx = -rx + 1 if ry < 0: ry = -ry + 1 # 9. Cull Invalid Tiles if rx <= 0 or ry <= 0 or rx >= TILELIMIT or ry >= TILELIMIT: continue # 10. Determine Pattern if (rx % 2) == (ry % 2): drawpixel(x + scrwidth // 2, y, color=RED) else: drawpixel(x + scrwidth // 2, y, color=BLUE) Parameters: moveVertical scaling factor: 16.0. Look angle multiplier: 6.2 (approximates 2\pi). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: z and moveVertical are clamped to small positive values (0.0001) to prevent division by zero errors. Coordinate Wrapping: The mirroring step (rx = -rx + 1) handles negative world coordinates to create a seamless tiling effect without explicit modulo operations on negative numbers. Tiling Limit: The culling step (rx >= 5, ry >= 5) limits the visible tiles, likely for performance or to define a finite visible area in this specific implementation. Floor Rendering via Ray Casting is a technique for rendering an infinite textured floor by casting rays from the camera plane through screen pixels to the world grid, interpolating world coordinates (x, y) based on the distance from the camera to the screen row. It differs from standard texture mapping by calculating world-space coordinates directly per pixel using perspective division, allowing for seamless infinite tiling without UV wrapping artifacts. It builds on Infinite Floor Projection by explicitly deriving the world coordinate increments from the view frustum geometry rather than relying on pre-projected screen coordinates. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of pixels rendered, as each pixel is processed in a nested loop. Memory Complexity: O(1), as no large data structures are required. Strengths: Simple to implement; no UV mapping or texture coordinates needed; seamless infinite tiling. Limitations: The specific implementation uses a fixed tile limit (5x5), which may not represent a truly infinite floor in all contexts; the perspective projection is approximated using screen coordinates and depth proxies rather than full 3D ray casting. When to Use: Simple 2D/3D hybrid rendering where performance is critical and complex geometry is not required. When Not to Use: When accurate perspective projection or complex floor interactions (e.g., slopes, holes) are needed. The technique originates from the Voxel1993 project, a voxel engine implementation. It is used in simple voxel-based rendering engines to provide a textured ground plane without the overhead of full 3D geometry or texture mapping. name: Floor Rendering via Ray Casting
head: DDA Floor Casting, Raycast Floor Projection
body: Floor Rendering via Ray Casting is a technique for rendering an infinite textured floor by casting rays from the camera plane through screen pixels to the world grid, interpolating world coordinates (x, y) based on the distance from the camera to the screen row. It differs from standard texture mapping by calculating world-space coordinates directly per pixel using perspective division, allowing for seamless infinite tiling without UV wrapping artifacts. It builds on Infinite Floor Projection by explicitly deriving the world coordinate increments from the view frustum geometry rather than relying on pre-projected screen coordinates. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Screen dimensions (SCREEN\WIDTH, SCREEN\HEIGHT), horizon line (HORIZON), player position in world/grid space (playerX, playerY), player orientation vector (dirX, dirY), and camera plane vector (planeX, planeY). Outputs: A pixel buffer where each pixel (x, y) below the horizon is colored based on the floor grid cell (cellX, cellY) intersected by the ray. Data Structures: normalizedLeft: A 2D vector (normalizedLeftX, normalizedLeftY) representing the normalized direction to the left edge of the view frustum at the near plane. normalizedRight: A 2D vector (normalizedRightX, normalizednormalizedRightY) representing the normalized direction to the right edge of the view frustum at the near plane. floorXStart, floorYStart: Floating-point accumulators for the current world grid coordinates at the left edge of the current screen row. floorXDirInc, floorYDirInc: Floating-point increments for advancing the world grid coordinates across one screen pixel horizontally. Steps: 1. Calculate Frustum Edge Vectors: Compute the unnormalized direction vectors for the left and right edges of the view frustum at the near plane. The near plane is implicitly defined by the camera plane geometry. \begin{aligned} nearPlaneX1 &= dirX - planeX \\ nearPlaneY1 &= dirY - planeY \\ nearPlaneX2 &= dirX + planeX \\ nearPlaneY2 &= dirY + planeY \end{aligned} Normalize these vectors to unit length: \begin{aligned} normalizedLeftX &= \frac{nearPlaneX1}{\sqrt{nearPlaneX1^2 + nearPlaneY1^2}} \\ normalizedLeftY &= \frac{nearPlaneY1}{\sqrt{nearPlaneX1^2 + nearPlaneY1^2}} \\ normalizedRightX &= \frac{nearPlaneX2}{\sqrt{nearPlaneX2^2 + nearPlaneY2^2}} \\ normalizedRightY &= \frac{nearPlaneY2}{\sqrt{nearPlaneX2^2 + nearPlaneY2^2}} \end{aligned} 2. Iterate Screen Rows: Loop through screen rows y from the bottom of the screen (SCREEN\HEIGHT) up to the horizon (HORIZON). The floor is rendered for y > HORIZON. 3. Calculate Distance and Increments: For each row y, calculate the perspective distance factor yDistance and the horizontal world coordinate increments per pixel. yDistance = \frac{HORIZON}{y - HORIZON} \begin{aligned} floorXDirInc &= yDistance \times \frac{normalizedRightX - normalizedLeftX}{SCREEN\WIDTH} \\ floorYDirInc &= yDistance \times \frac{normalizedRightY - normalizedLeftY}{SCREEN\WIDTH} \end{aligned} Note: yDistance represents the distance from the camera to the floor plane at row y. In the source implementation, HORIZON is equated to PLAYER\HEIGHT (camera height). 4. Initialize Row Start Coordinates: Calculate the starting world grid coordinates for the left edge of the current row. This is the player's grid position plus the offset to the left edge of the view frustum scaled by the distance. \begin{aligned} floorXStart &= worldToGrid(playerX) + yDistance \times normalizedLeftX \\ floorYStart &= worldToGrid(playerY) + yDistance \times normalizedLeftY \end{aligned} Note: worldToGrid converts world coordinates to grid indices. If the grid size is 1.0, this may be an identity or scaling function. 5. Iterate Screen Columns: For each column x from 0 to SCREEN\WIDTH - 1: a. Determine the grid cell indices: \begin{aligned} cellX &= \lfloor |floorXStart| \rfloor \\ cellY &= \lfloor |floorYStart| \rfloor \end{aligned} b. Update the start coordinates for the next pixel in the row: \begin{aligned} floorXStart &+= floorXDirInc \\ floorYStart &+= floorYDirInc \end{aligned} c. Render the pixel using cellX and cellY. For example, a checkerboard pattern can be applied: \text{if } ((cellX + cellY) \pmod 2) \neq 0 \text{ then color} = (0, 0, 255, 255) \text{ else color} = (255, 255, 255, 255) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderfloor(SCREENWIDTH, SCREENHEIGHT, HORIZON, playerX, playerY, dirX, dirY, planeX, planeY, worldToGrid): """ Renders the floor for a single frame. Assumes dirX, dirY, planeX, planeY are already normalized or consistent with the camera setup. """ # 1. In the source implementation, this is equated to HORIZON. HORIZON: The y-coordinate on the screen corresponding to the camera height (vanishing line). Floor rendering occurs for screen y values from SCREEN\HEIGHT down to HORIZON + 1. SCREEN\HEIGHT: The total height of the canvas in pixels. The bottom pixel is at y = SCREEN\HEIGHT. SCREEN\WIDTH: The total width of the canvas in pixels. Used to calculate ray increment and floor step increments. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Wall/Floor Sync: The floor rendering may appear 'out of sync' with wall rendering, where floor tiles appear to slide or change color near walls as the player moves. This is attributed to a discrepancy between the distance used for wall height calculation (from DDA) and the distance used for floor interpolation (yDistance), although these are described as 'two different types of distances'. Horizon Division: The formula for yDistance involves division by (y - HORIZON). If y approaches HORIZON, the distance approaches infinity, potentially causing floating-point overflow or extreme coordinate values. The loop condition y > HORIZON prevents division by zero but requires handling large coordinates near the horizon. Grid Coordinate Sign: The use of Math.abs before Math.floor implies that the floor grid is symmetric around the origin or that the sign of the world coordinate is ignored for cell indexing. Time Complexity: O(W \times H), where W is screen width and H is screen height (specifically H - HORIZON). Each pixel requires a constant number of arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary space, excluding the output buffer. Strengths: Simple to implement; provides infinite floor tiling without UV mapping; consistent with ray-cast wall rendering. Limitations: Potential visual artifacts near walls due to distance calculation mismatch; no perspective-correct texture filtering (nearest-neighbor sampling implied by integer cell indexing); performance is linear with screen resolution. When to use: Simple 2.5D raycasting engines (e.g., Wolfenstein 3D style) where performance is critical and high-fidelity texture mapping is not required. When not to use: When perspective-correct texture mapping, mipmapping, or complex floor materials are needed. This technique is described in the context of implementing a raycaster with both wall and floor rendering. It is presented as a method to solve the problem of rendering an infinite floor in a raycasting engine, where the floor coordinates are interpolated based on the distance from the camera. The source notes that the basic idea uses PLAYER\HEIGHT (position of camera) and the formula PLAYER\HEIGHT / (y - HORIZON) to interpolate floor coordinates. name: Parametric Surface Density Model
head: 3D object model with six parameters
body: The Parametric Surface Density Model is a 3D object representation defined by six scalar quantities: three separating surfaces and the density fields defined on these interfaces. It solves the problem of reconstructing a 3D volumetric field from density fields defined on these interfaces. The method separates the geometric definition (the surfaces) from the volumetric definition (the densities), using an adaptive elliptic operator to fill the volume. Inputs: Data defining three planar curves that generate the separating surfaces. A set of example deformations for PCA-based surface deformation. Outputs: A 3D volumetric representation defined by the three separating surfaces and the interpolated density fields. Data Structures: Separating Surfaces: Represented by their planar generators (curves) rotated around an axis. Exact field layouts and bit packing are not given in the sources. Density Fields: Scalar fields \rhoi(\mathbf{p}) defined on the surface Si. Volumetric Field: A 3D scalar field V(\mathbf{p}) reconstructed from the surface densities. Steps: 1. Define Separating Surfaces: Construct three separating surfaces S1, S2, S3 by rotating three planar curves around an axis. 2. Define Surface Densities: Assign a density field \rhoi to each surface Si. 3. Reconstruct Volumetric Field: Fill the 3D volume with a scalar field based on the surface densities using an adaptive elliptic operator. Let V(\mathbf{p}) be the reconstructed field. The operator solves a partial differential equation (PDE) such that V(\mathbf{p}) matches \rhoi on Si and is smooth elsewhere. 4. Iterative Refinement: For tomographic reconstruction, iterate a 1D approach across slices, adding a smoothing term between slices to ensure consistency. Formulas: Surface generation: Si is generated by rotating a planar curve around an axis. Field matching: V(\mathbf{p}) = \rhoi(\mathbf{p}) for \mathbf{p} \in Si. Not given in the sources. Parameters: Number of separating surfaces: 3. Number of density fields: 3. Axis of rotation: Not specified in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Curves: If the planar curves do not generate valid closed surfaces, the separation of space may be ill-defined. Precision: The adaptive elliptic operator requires careful numerical implementation to maintain stability near boundaries. This variant addresses the deformation of the separating surfaces (the planar generators) using Principal Component Analysis (PCA). It is chosen when the object's shape varies across a set of examples and a compact basis of deformations is needed. Definition: Deformation is characterized by finding an optimal basis of deformations obtained via PCA on a set of examples. Steps: 1. Construct a random example set where realizations are obtained by integrating the solution of a linear stochastic differential equation. 2. Apply PCA to the set of example deformations to obtain a basis. 3. Search for an optimal basis from the PCA results to characterize surface deformation. When to choose: Use this when the object exhibits natural variations in shape that can be modeled as stochastic processes, allowing for efficient representation and generation of new shapes. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. The iterative reconstruction and PDE solving steps likely dominate, depending on the resolution of the adaptive elliptic operator. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of parameters defining the planar curves and the density fields, plus the storage for the reconstructed 3D volume if explicitly stored. Strengths: Explicitly models boundaries and internal properties; allows for adaptive smoothing; supports iterative 1D reconstruction with smoothing between slices. Limitations: Requires defining three specific surfaces; complex to implement the adaptive elliptic operator; limited to objects that can be separated by three rotating planar curves. When to use: Ideal for reconstructing 3D objects from limited tomographic data where the object can be approximated by three distinct regions separated by smooth surfaces. The Parametric Surface Density Model was proposed in the context of tomographic reconstruction from a small number of views. The work, authored by an unnamed researcher (thesis/report), focuses on defining a 3D object model characterized by six quantities: three separating surfaces and density fields on these interfaces. The primary difficulty addressed was filling a 3D field from the density fields on the interfaces, leading to the proposal of an adaptive elliptic operator. The model also incorporates deformation via PCA on stochastic examples, allowing for the characterization of surface variations. name: Neural and Implicit Representations
body: Neural and Implicit Representations render scenes by evaluating continuous scalar fields—parameterized as neural networks, Gaussian mixtures, or radial basis functions—along camera rays to compute geometry and appearance Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians, Ray Marching with Neural SDF, RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing, and MetaNLR++. This family replaces analytical primitives or explicit meshes with learned or weighted fields, enabling high-fidelity rendering of complex structures through ray marching or path tracing. Unlike Raymarching with Depth Buffer Occlusion and Acceleration and Optimization, which rely on explicit depth buffers, voxel grids, or BVH acceleration, this family evaluates continuous implicit functions directly along rays, trading computational overhead for geometric continuity and data-driven reconstruction. Evaluates a continuous Gaussian mixture field along camera rays to compute accurate volumetric integrals, explicitly handling primitive overlap and self-attenuation Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians. It serves as a ground-truth baseline to analyze approximations in standard rasterization-based 3D Gaussian Splatting, such as ignoring spatial overlap and using approximate projected shapes Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians. Unlike rasterization, it performs adaptive sampling along rays to resolve the exact order and contribution of overlapping Gaussians, ensuring precision governed by sample count rather than rasterization artifacts Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians. Choose when exact volumetric integration of Gaussian primitives is required. Approximates the Signed Distance Field using a deep neural network and renders images by marching rays along the estimated distance field Ray Marching with Neural SDF. It differs from traditional SDF rendering by replacing the analytical distance function with a learned implicit representation, allowing for the reconstruction of complex geometries from data rather than explicit modeling Ray Marching with Neural SDF. Choose when data-driven surface reconstruction from a neural network is preferred over analytical primitives. Renders volumetric data represented as particles by modeling the scene as a continuous scalar field composed of additive weighted radial basis functions (RBFs), specifically Gaussians RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing. It solves the visual clutter and pathological performance issues associated with BVH-based ray tracing of overlapping splatted particles by treating the volume as a single unified field rather than discrete geometric proxies RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing. Unlike splatting, it allows for adjustable smoothing via kernel parameters and supports full path tracing through Delta Tracking RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing. Choose when unbiased path tracing of particle-based volumes is required. Combines a neural implicit shape representation (SDF) with 2D CNN-based image feature extraction, aggregation, and re-projection for novel view synthesis MetaNLR++. It solves slow training and rendering times of previous neural lumigraph methods by leveraging meta-learning to specialize initializations, enabling high-quality convergence in minutes and real-time rendering MetaNLR++. Unlike volumetric methods, it renders explicit surfaces via sphere tracing, and uses deep feature blending to inpaint geometry errors and avoid artifacts from imperfect shape reconstruction MetaNLR++. Choose when fast, high-quality novel view synthesis with explicit surface rendering is needed. A neural mesh-based implicit field method that disentangles geometry and texture codes for editing. Step: Pre-compute near-far bounds for each ray by counting the minimum and maximum distances of ray-to-mesh intersections. Sample 64 coarse points along the ray. Adopt a progressive up-sampling strategy to guide the sampling of 64 fine points, yielding 128 samples for each ray. Formula: Distillation loss: Supervised with output from the teacher model (NeuS) for queried color and SDF value. Formula referenced as Eq.(4) in Sec 3.2. Background supervision: Binary cross-entropy loss using foreground masks for unbounded backgrounds. Parameter: Batch size: 512 rays. Optimizer: Adam with initial learning rate 0.0005 and cosine annealing scheduler with 5000 warm-up steps. Hardware: Single Nvidia RTX3090-24G GPU. Training time: Approximately 16 hours for each model. Layout: Model Architecture: Geometry Code lg(x) (dim 32), Texture Code lt(x) (dim 32), Sign Distance h(x) (dim 1). Interpolated Items include lt(x) (dim 32), gradient of SDF |\nablax s| (dim 256), s (dim 256), \gamma (dim 256), h(x) (dim 1), d (dim 160), \gamma (dim 32). Geometry Decoder outputs (256, 256, 256). Radiance Decoder outputs (3). A rendering architecture that combines an implicit function (scene representation), a sampling scheme (raymarching), and a renderer to produce images from ray bundles Implicit Function Rendering Pipeline. Choose when a modular pipeline separating implicit representation, sampling, and rendering is desired. The concept of implicit surfaces dates back to constructive solid geometry, but neural implicit representations emerged with the advent of deep learning. NeuMesh builds on distillation from the NeuS teacher model to optimize disentangled geometry and texture codes. MetaNLR++ leverages meta-learning with the Reptile algorithm to accelerate convergence on new scenes MetaNLR++. RBF-based methods integrate radial basis functions into unbiased path tracing frameworks for particle volumes RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing. name: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians
head: 3D Gaussian Ray Marching, Gaussian Volume Integration
body: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians is a volume rendering method that evaluates the continuous Gaussian mixture field along camera rays to compute accurate volumetric integrals, explicitly handling primitive overlap and self-attenuation. It serves as a ground-truth baseline to analyze the approximations inherent in standard rasterization-based 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), such as ignoring spatial overlap and using approximate projected shapes. Unlike 3DGS, which relies on screen-space sorting and alpha blending, this method performs adaptive sampling along rays to resolve the exact order and contribution of overlapping Gaussians, ensuring precision governed by sample count rather than rasterization artifacts. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of N 3D Gaussians, each defined by a mean position \boldsymbol{\mu}i, a covariance matrix \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), an opacity \alphai, and a color/density value. Input: Camera ray r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d} for each pixel. Output: Final pixel color C and accumulated opacity A. Data Structures The method reuses the standard 3DGS data structures: Tensors: Arrays storing positions (\mathbb{R}^3), scales (\mathbb{R}^3), rotations (\mathbb{R}^4, quaternions), opacities (\mathbb{R}), and colors (\mathbb{R}^3 or SH coefficients). Bounding Volumes: Axis-aligned bounding boxes (AABBs) or other bounding primitives are used to cull Gaussians that do not intersect the ray's bounding frustum or tile. Algorithm Steps 1. Culling: For each ray, identify the subset of Gaussians whose bounding volumes intersect the ray's path within the near/far clipping planes. 2. Adaptive Sampling: Determine sample points along the ray. Unlike fixed-step marching, adaptive sampling increases density in regions where the Gaussian mixture field changes rapidly (e.g., near Gaussian centers or boundaries) to accurately resolve overlap. 3. Field Evaluation: At each sample point tk, evaluate the Gaussian mixture. The density \sigma(tk) and color c(tk) are computed by aggregating contributions from all active Gaussians i: \sigma(tk) = \sum{i \in \text{active}} \alphai \cdot \mathcal{N}(r(tk); \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{\Sigma}i) c(tk) = \frac{\sum{i \in \text{active}} \alphai \cdot \mathcal{N}(r(tk); \boldsymbol{\mu}i, \mathbf{\Sigma}i) \cdot ci}{\sigma(tk) + \epsilon} where \mathcal{N} is the Gaussian probability density function, and \epsilon is a small constant to prevent division by zero. 4. Integration: Perform volumetric integration using the evaluated density and color. The standard volume rendering integral is discretized: C = \sum{k} Tk \cdot (1 - e^{-\sigma(tk) \Delta tk}) \cdot c(tk) T{k+1} = Tk \cdot e^{-\sigma(tk) \Delta tk} where \Delta tk is the step size, Tk is the transmittance at step k, and T0 = 1. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the color and opacity for the final pixel. Parameters Sample Count: The number of samples per ray. Higher counts improve accuracy but increase computational cost. Adaptive Threshold: The tolerance for step size adjustment based on field gradient. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision: Floating-point precision errors can accumulate during long ray marches or when evaluating very small Gaussian contributions. Boundary Handling: Gaussians truncated at their support radius may cause artifacts if the ray passes near the boundary without sufficient sampling. Performance: Naive evaluation of all Gaussians per sample is O(N \cdot M) where M is sample count, requiring efficient spatial indexing (e.g., BVH or grid). Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raymarchgaussians(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, maxsamples=1000): """ Ray-marches through a set of 3D Gaussians. gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: center: (x, y, z) cov3d: 3x3 covariance matrix opacity: float color: (r, g, b) """ # 1. Culling: Filter gaussians intersecting the ray's bounding box # Implementation detail: Use AABB intersection test activegaussians = [g for g in gaussians if intersectsray(g.bbox, rayorigin, raydirection)] if not activegaussians: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), 0.0 # 2. Adaptive Sampling: Generate sample points # Implementation detail: Determine tmin and tmax from bounding boxes # Generate adaptive t values based on Gaussian density gradients tsamples = generateadaptivesamples(rayorigin, raydirection, activegaussians, maxsamples) accumulatedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] accumulatedopacity = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 for i in range(len(tsamples) - 1): tstart = tsamples[i] tend = tsamples[i+1] tmid = (tstart + tend) / 2.0 deltat = tend - tstart # 3. Field Evaluation at midpoint density = 0.0 weightedcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] point = rayorigin + raydirection tmid for g in activegaussians: # Evaluate Gaussian PDF at point # Use Mahalanobis distance: d2 = (p - mu)^T Sigma^-1 (p - mu) distsq = mahalanobissquared(point, g.center, g.cov3d) # Truncate if outside support radius if distsq > g.supportradiussq: continue pdf = gaussianpdf(distsq, g.cov3d) contribution = g.opacity pdf density += contribution weightedcolor[0] += contribution g.color[0] weightedcolor[1] += contribution g.color[1] weightedcolor[2] += contribution g.color[2] if density < 1e-6: continue # Normalize color color = [c / density for c in weightedcolor] # 4. Integration # Alpha = 1 - exp(-density deltat) alpha = 1.0 - math.exp(-density deltat) accumulatedcolor[0] += transmittance alpha color[0] accumulatedcolor[1] += transmittance alpha color[1] accumulatedcolor[2] += transmittance alpha color[2] accumulatedopacity += transmittance alpha transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) if transmittance < 1e-4: break return accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm is a volumetric rendering method for 3D Gaussians that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral using an extinction-based model. It distinguishes itself from splatting-based approaches by performing adaptive binning and analytical integration along rays, ensuring that overlapping Gaussians are resolved with precision governed by sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Unlike raytracing solutions for Gaussians, this method explicitly accounts for primitive overlap in the integration process. This method represents the view-dependent color (radiance) of a 3D Gaussian primitive as a function of the viewing direction using spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. It solves the problem of storing directional color variation (such as highlights and reflections) compactly without requiring per-ray neural network queries. Unlike simple point colors or view-independent RGB values, this model captures specular effects and directional shading. It is distinct from its siblings in the tree: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians uses this representation for color evaluation during rasterization, whereas OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm and Physics-based Gaussian Simulation do not inherently rely on this specific view-dependent color encoding. Physics-based Gaussian Simulation integrates continuum mechanics or particle dynamics directly into 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), treating each Gaussian kernel as a discrete physical particle with volume. This approach creates a unified simulation-to-rendering pipeline where the geometric representation serves as the simulation mesh, enabling physically accurate dynamics, real-time interaction, and editing of high-fidelity virtual content. Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes static appearance, these methods decouple or tightly couple physical state (position, velocity, deformation) from radiometric properties to support dynamic scenes. Weighted Blending is a sort-free, image-order rendering technique for 3D Gaussians that resolves the hidden-surface problem by computing a weighted average of all ray-Gaussian intersection depths. Unlike NeRF-style methods that sort intersections and use closer Gaussians to attenuate further ones, this method blends all intersections simultaneously without sorting, extending Order Independent Transparency (OIT) principles to 3D opaque surfaces. The Two-Stage Optimization Pipeline is a post-processing refinement method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that decouples geometric alignment from material/lighting optimization to improve reconstruction quality and enable relighting. It addresses the limitations of coarse geometry from initial regressors and accumulated pose errors by first correcting camera poses and refining geometry, then locking geometry to optimize material and lighting parameters using pre-computed visibility. It differs from standard 3DGS by introducing explicit normal vectors and a visibility pre-computation step, and from pose-free methods like CF3DGS by using a dedicated pose correction stage. A ray marching-based renderer that follows the 3DGS model of opacity, reusing the data structures (tensors with weights, positions, scales, and rotations), activation functions, and learning rates of 3DGS. Differs from OTS Marcher in the model of opacity/extinction used, but shares the same ray marching pipeline structure (per-primitive pass, tiling, sorting, per-pixel kernel). A custom ray tracing solution for physically accurate volumetric integration of 3D Gaussians, potentially including scattering. Uses icosahedrons to bound Gaussians. Proposed an alternative kernel function to increase compactness. A proposal by Sun et al. to accelerate the ray tracing of pretrained 3D Gaussians using stochastic subsampling. Does not offer a backward pass. Reaches frame rates about 3× below 3DGS. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M) for naive evaluation, where N is the number of Gaussians and M is the number of samples per ray. With spatial acceleration structures (BVH/Grid), this can be reduced to O(K \cdot M) where K is the number of active Gaussians per ray. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store Gaussian parameters. Performance: Significantly slower than rasterization-based 3DGS due to the per-ray evaluation and lack of GPU-friendly parallelism in early implementations. Stochastic subsampling can improve speed but still trails 3DGS by ~3×. Strengths: Accurately handles overlapping Gaussians and self-attenuation, providing a ground-truth reference for 3DGS approximations. Limitations: High computational cost makes real-time rendering challenging without significant optimization or hardware acceleration. The method was introduced to systematically analyze the approximations made in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), specifically regarding spatial overlap and sorting. It was developed as part of the work "Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?". The study demonstrated that while 3DGS approximations have negligible impact on still images with many Gaussians, accurate ray-marching is essential for understanding the underlying volumetric physics and for applications requiring high fidelity. Subsequent works like Condor and GRay have explored ray-tracing variants for performance and physical accuracy. name: OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm
head: Adaptive Binning Ray Marching, OTS Marcher, OTS Marching, Ray Marching (OTS scheme)
body: The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm is a volumetric rendering method for 3D Gaussians that evaluates the full Gaussian mixture to accurately handle primitive overlap and compute the volumetric integral using an extinction-based model. It distinguishes itself from splatting-based approaches by performing adaptive binning and analytical integration along rays, ensuring that overlapping Gaussians are resolved with precision governed by sample count rather than relying on rasterization approximations. Unlike raytracing solutions for Gaussians, this method explicitly accounts for primitive overlap in the integration process. The algorithm performs adaptive sampling along each viewing ray to resolve Gaussian overlap. It iterates over the Gaussian mixture twice: first to establish bin borders adapted to the Gaussian data, and second to perform analytical integration into bins of variable extent. The bins are then blended together following the volume integral equation. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussians defined by position, scale, rotation, and color; a viewing ray defined by origin \mathbf{o} and direction \mathbf{d}; a maximum ray depth or opacity threshold. Outputs: The final pixel color I(\mathbf{x}) and accumulated transmittance. Density Section Buffer: A fixed-size buffer storing sections. Each section is defined by: start: The start parameter t along the ray. end: The end parameter t along the ray. density: The sampling density for this section. Bin: A segment of the ray defined by start and end t values, storing integrated color and extinction. 1. Adaptive Binning Initialization: Create a fixed-size density section buffer. Iterate over all Gaussians to fill the buffer. For each Gaussian, compute its intersection interval with the ray. Define the start and end of the sampling section using the Gaussian's position \pm 3 standard deviations along the ray direction. Compute the density such that a pre-defined number of bins fit within the space defined by start and end. 2. Section Merging: Add the new section to the density section buffer. Combine existing and new sections to ensure they are ordered and non-overlapping. If sections overlap, the section with the higher sampling density takes precedence in the overlap area. Combining two sections can result in up to three new sections. Sections that fall outside the buffer capacity are deferred to the next batch. 3. Bin Creation: Traverse the merged sections to create bins. The size of each bin is inversely proportional to the density of the section it belongs to. 4. Blending Integral Computation (Batching): Divide the work into batches of bins (e.g., 128 bins per batch). Initialize the first batch at t=0. Subsequent batches start at the end-border of the last bin of the previous batch. Iterate over the Gaussian mixture again to compute integrals for each bin in the current batch. For each bin, compute 4 values: Red, Green, Blue, and integrated extinction (opacity). Colors are multiplied by the per-Gaussian integrated extinction. Stop when all Gaussians are processed or accumulated opacity reaches a high threshold. 5. Blending: Blend the bin evaluations together using the following equation: I(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{i=0}^{\infty} \gammai \prod{j=0}^{i-1} e^{-\rhoj} + cb \prod{j=0}^{\infty} e^{-\rhoj} Where: \gammai is the color contribution of bin i. \rhoj is the integrated extinction (opacity) of bin j. The term \prod{j=0}^{i-1} e^{-\rhoj} is the transmittance factor, cached between iterations to avoid redundant computation. cb is the background color. 6. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients manually using a front-to-back strategy. Two variants exist: Attached: Considers the numerical integration procedure and border positions in the gradient calculation. Detached: Assumes the numerical method can be ignored, keeping sampling and border positions constant with respect to differentiation. The detached variant performs significantly better. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def otsmarchingraymarch(rayorigin, raydirection, gaussians, backgroundcolor, maxsectionsbuffer, binsperbatch=128, opacitythreshold=0.99, binspergaussian=10): """ Renders a single ray using the OTS Marching Algorithm. """ # 1. Adaptive Binning Initialization sections = [] for g in gaussians: # Compute intersection interval along ray using position +/- 3 standard deviations tstart = g.position - 3.0 g.scale tend = g.position + 3.0 g.scale if tstart > tend: tstart, tend = tend, tstart # Compute density such that a pre-defined number of bins fit in the space length = tend - tstart density = binspergaussian / length if length > 0 else 0.0 newsection = Section(start=tstart, end=tend, density=density) sections = mergesections(sections, newsection, maxsectionsbuffer) # 2. Bin Creation bins = createbins(sections) # 3. Blending Integral Computation (Batching) totalcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 for batchstart in range(0, len(bins), binsperbatch): batchend = min(batchstart + binsperbatch, len(bins)) currentbatchbins = bins[batchstart:batchend] for bin in currentbatchbins: bincolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] binextinction = 0.0 # Iterate over Gaussians again to compute integrals for each bin for g in gaussians: # Check overlap and compute analytical integral if g.overlapssegment(bin.start, bin.end): c, e = g.integrateoversegment(bin.start, bin.end) bincolor[0] += c[0] bincolor[1] += c[1] bincolor[2] += c[2] binextinction += e # Front-to-back blending matching Eq. 3 transmittancefactor = exp(-binextinction) totalcolor[0] += bincolor[0] transmittance totalcolor[1] += bincolor[1] transmittance totalcolor[2] += bincolor[2] transmittance transmittance = transmittancefactor # Check accumulated opacity threshold if 1.0 - transmittance >= opacitythreshold: break if 1.0 - transmittance >= opacitythreshold: break # Add background totalcolor[0] += backgroundcolor[0] transmittance totalcolor[1] += backgroundcolor[1] transmittance totalcolor[2] += backgroundcolor[2] transmittance return totalcolor, transmittance def mergesections(existing, newsec, maxsize): """ Combines newsec with existing sections ensuring order and no overlap. Higher density wins in overlap. Combining 2 sections creates up to 3 new sections. """ merged = existing + [newsec] merged.sort(key=lambda s: s.start) result = [] for sec in merged: if not result: result.append(sec) continue last = result[-1] if sec.start < last.end: # Overlap exists if sec.density >= last.density: # Higher density wins: extend last section, discard lower density part last.end = max(last.end, sec.end) else: # Lower density wins in overlap: split last section last.end = sec.start result.append(sec) else: result.append(sec) # Defer excess sections to next batch if buffer full if len(result) > maxsize: result = result[:maxsize] return result def createbins(sections): """ Traverse sections to create bins. Bin size is inversely proportional to density. """ bins = [] for sec in sections: if sec.density <= 0: continue binwidth = 1.0 / sec.density t = sec.start while t < sec.end: binend = min(t + binwidth, sec.end) bins.append(Bin(start=t, end=binend)) t = binend return bins class Section: def init(self, start, end, density): self.start = start self.end = end self.density = density class Bin: def init(self, start, end): self.start = start self.end = end Batch Size: Typically 128 bins per batch. Activation Function: Softplus with \beta = 2 is used instead of sigmoid to allow Gaussians to become fully opaque. Standard Deviation Factor: 3 standard deviations are used to define the start and end of sampling sections. Buffer Overflow: Sections that fall out of the fixed-size density section buffer are deferred to the next batch. Opacity Convergence: Using a constant opacity initialization can prevent convergence for large Gaussian counts. A power function fitting opacity to the number of Gaussians is recommended for initialization. Gradient Choice: The attached gradient variant is computationally more expensive and performs worse than the detached variant. Performance: The algorithm is considerably slower than splatting, typically between one and two orders of magnitude slower, depending on the scene. Accuracy: It provides accurate resolution of Gaussian overlap and precise perspective projection, serving as a testbed to examine the importance of these factors in 3DGS. Complexity: The algorithm requires iterating over the Gaussian mixture twice per batch (once for binning, once for integration), leading to higher computational cost compared to single-pass splatting. Strengths: Accurate volumetric rendering, handles overlap correctly, accounts for primitive overlap in integration unlike some raytracing solutions. Limitations: Low performance compared to splatting; implementation complexity is higher. The OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm was introduced in the paper "Does 3D Gaussian Splatting Need Accurate Volumetric Rendering?". It was developed as part of an implementation to study the impact of approximations like spatial overlap and sorting in 3D Gaussian Splatting. The implementation builds on the original 3DGS code base to enable meaningful comparisons. name: View-dependent color with Spherical Harmonics
head: Rendering with Spherical Harmonics, SH Color Representation, SH Render, SH to RGB, Spherical Harmonic Colour Model, Spherical Harmonic Evaluation, Spherical Harmonics Color Evaluation, Spherical Harmonics for View-Dependent Color
body: This method represents the view-dependent color (radiance) of a 3D Gaussian primitive as a function of the viewing direction using spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients. It solves the problem of storing directional color variation (such as highlights and reflections) compactly without requiring per-ray neural network queries. Unlike simple point colors or view-independent RGB values, this model captures specular effects and directional shading. It is distinct from its siblings in the tree: Ray-marching on 3D Gaussians uses this representation for color evaluation during rasterization, whereas OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm and Physics-based Gaussian Simulation do not inherently rely on this specific view-dependent color encoding. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians. For each Gaussian i: Position \mathbf{p}i. Camera parameters (position \mathbf{c}, orientation). SH coefficients \mathbf{k}i (see Data structures). Maximum SH degree L=3. Outputs: For each Gaussian projected onto the image plane, an RGB color value \mathbf{C}i corresponding to the viewing direction. Data structures: Each Gaussian stores 48 SH coefficients in a contiguous array of 32-bit floats. The layout is organized by color channel, with 16 coefficients per channel (Red, Green, Blue). Indices 0–2: Degree 0 (DC) coefficients for R, G, B. Indices 3–47: Higher-order coefficients for R, G, B. Specifically, the coefficients are stored in increasing order of degree and order. The first 3 elements are the DC color (f{dc\0..2}), and the next 45 elements are the rest coefficients (f{rest\0..f{rest\44}). Constants: The following normalization constants are used: SH\C0 = 0.28209479177387814 SH\C1 = 0.4886025119029199 SH\C2\0 = 1.0925484305920792 SH\C2\1 = -0.3153915652525201 SH\C2\2 = 0.5462742152960396 SH\C2\3 = -0.3153915652525201 SH\C2\4 = 0.1084622861184793 SH\C3\0 = -0.5900435899266435 SH\C3\1 = 2.890611442640554 SH\C3\2 = -0.4576460222995229 SH\C3\3 = 0.3731763325901154 SH\C3\4 = -0.4576460222995229 SH\C3\5 = 1.445305721320277 SH\C3\6 = -0.5900435899266435 Numbered Steps: 1. Compute Viewing Direction: For a given Gaussian with mean position \mathbf{p} and camera center \mathbf{c}, compute the normalized viewing direction vector \mathbf{d} = \frac{\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}}{\|\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{c}\|}. Let \mathbf{d} = (x, y, z). 2. Evaluate Spherical Harmonics: Compute the color Cc(\mathbf{d}) for each color channel c \in \{R, G, B\} using the stored coefficients \mathbf{k}c and the direction \mathbf{d}. The basis functions Yl^m(\mathbf{d}) are fixed polynomials of x, y, z. The evaluation follows the formula: \begin{aligned} Cc(\mathbf{d}) = \max\Big(0, \quad & SH\C0 \cdot k{0,c} \\ & - SH\C1 \cdot y \cdot k{1,c} + SH\C1 \cdot z \cdot k{2,c} - SH\C1 \cdot x \cdot k{3,c} \\ & + SH\C2\0 \cdot xy \cdot k{4,c} - SH\C2\1 \cdot yz \cdot k{5,c} + SH\C2\2 \cdot (2z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{6,c} \\ & - SH\C2\3 \cdot xz \cdot k{7,c} + SH\C2\4 \cdot (x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{8,c} \\ & - SH\C3\0 \cdot y(3x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{9,c} + SH\C3\1 \cdot xyz \cdot k{10,c} \\ & - SH\C3\2 \cdot y(4z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{11,c} + SH\C3\3 \cdot z(2z^2 - 3x^2 - 3y^2) \cdot k{12,c} \\ & - SH\C3\4 \cdot x(4z^2 - x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{13,c} + SH\C3\5 \cdot z(x^2 - y^2) \cdot k{14,c} \\ & - SH\C3\6 \cdot x(x^2 - 3y^2) \cdot k{15,c} \quad + 0.5 \Big) \end{aligned} Where k{i,c} are the coefficients for channel c at index i in the coefficient array. Note: The source provides the explicit polynomial expansion. The term +0.5 is a bias added before the ReLU activation to handle negative SH values, as colors must be non-negative. The \max(0, \dots) operation acts as a ReLU. 3. Composite: Use the computed RGB color \mathbf{C}i in the front-to-back compositing rule for the Gaussian splat. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math SHC0 = 0.28209479177387814 SHC1 = 0.4886025119029199 SHC20 = 1.0925484305920792 SHC21 = -0.3153915652525201 SHC22 = 0.5462742152960396 SHC23 = -0.3153915652525201 SHC24 = 0.1084622861184793 SHC30 = -0.5900435899266435 SHC31 = 2.890611442640554 SHC32 = -0.4576460222995229 SHC33 = 0.3731763325901154 SHC34 = -0.4576460222995229 SHC35 = 1.445305721320277 SHC36 = -0.5900435899266435 def evalshdegree0(k0): """Evaluate degree 0 (DC) component.""" return SHC0 k0 def evalshdegree1(k1, k2, k3, x, y, z): """Evaluate degree 1 components.""" return -SHC1 y k1 + SHC1 z k2 - SHC1 x k3 def evalshdegree2(k4, k5, k6, k7, k8, x, y, z): """Evaluate degree 2 components.""" xx = x x yy = y y zz = z z return (SHC20 x y k4 SHC21 y z k5 + SHC22 (2 zz - xx - yy) k6 SHC23 x z k7 + SHC24 (xx - yy) k8) def evalshdegree3(k9, k10, k11, k12, k13, k14, k15, x, y, z): """Evaluate degree 3 components.""" xx = x x yy = y y zz = z z return (-SHC30 y (3 xx - yy) k9 + SHC31 x y z k10 SHC32 y (4 zz - xx - yy) k11 + SHC33 z (2 zz - 3 xx - 3 yy) k12 SHC34 x (4 zz - xx - yy) k13 + SHC35 z (xx - yy) k14 SHC36 x (xx - 3 yy) k15) def shtorgb(shcoeffs, viewdir): """ Convert SH coefficients to RGB color for a given view direction. Args: shcoeffs: List or array of 48 floats. Layout: [R0..R15, G0..G15, B0..B15] or interleaved? Sources and imply 16 coeffs per channel. Source layout: first 3 are DC (R,G,B), next 45 are rest. This implies interleaved by channel for DC, but contiguous for rest? Actually, says "16 coefficients for Red, 16 for Green, 16 for Blue". says "first 3 elements are DC color... next 45 elements are rest". This suggests: [R0, G0, B0, R1..R15, G1..G15, B1..B15] is NOT the case. Let's look at code: c0 = sh.fixedrows::<3>(0) -> R0, G0, B0 c1 = sh.fixedview::<3,1>(3,0) -> R1, G1, B1? If c1 is indices 3, 4, 5, then the layout is interleaved by degree/order, not channel. Let's re-read code carefully. c0 is indices 0,1,2. c1 is indices 3,4,5? No, fixedview::<3,1>(3,0) usually means stride 1, starting at 3, taking 3 elements. So indices 3,4,5. c2 is indices 6,7,8. c3 is indices 9,10,11. This implies the layout is: [R0, G0, B0, R1, G1, B1, R2, G2, B2,...] Wait, says "16 coefficients for Red, 16 for Green, 16 for Blue". This is a contradiction. Let's check: "SH coefficients are stored in an array of 163 floats, in increasing order of degree and order." This usually means [R0, R1,..., R15, G0,..., G15, B0,..., B15]. However, the code in accesses R1, G1, B1 together. Let's assume the code in is the implementation truth for the "splat" repo. The code: c0 = sh[0:3] -> R0, G0, B0 c1 = sh[3:6] -> R1, G1, B1 c2 = sh[6:9] -> R2, G2, B2 c3 = sh[9:12] -> R3, G3, B3 This means the array is interleaved by coefficient index across channels. Index 0: R0, G0, B0 Index 1: R1, G1, B1... Index 15: R15, G15, B15 Let's verify with "16 coefficients for Red...". This might describe the logical set, not memory layout. Or might be wrong about layout. Given is a direct implementation reference, we follow its layout: Interleaved by coefficient index. viewdir: Tuple (x, y, z) normalized direction. Returns: Tuple (r, g, b) """ x, y, z = viewdir # Extract coefficients for all channels at once for efficiency # Layout: [R0, G0, B0, R1, G1, B1,..., R15, G15, B15] # Degree 0 r0, g0, b0 = shcoeffs[0], shcoeffs[1], shcoeffs[2] # Degree 1 r1, g1, b1 = shcoeffs[3], shcoeffs[4], shcoeffs[5] r2, g2, b2 = shcoeffs[6], shcoeffs[7], shcoeffs[8] r3, g3, b3 = shcoeffs[9], shcoeffs[10], shcoeffs[11] # Degree 2 r4, g4, b4 = shcoeffs[12], shcoeffs[13], shcoeffs[14] r5, g5, b5 = shcoeffs[15], shcoeffs[16], shcoeffs[17] r6, g6, b6 = shcoeffs[18], shcoeffs[19], shcoeffs[20] r7, g7, b7 = shcoeffs[21], shcoeffs[22], shcoeffs[23] r8, g8, b8 = shcoeffs[24], shcoeffs[25], shcoeffs[26] # Degree 3 r9, g9, b9 = shcoeffs[27], shcoeffs[28], shcoeffs[29] r10, g10, b10 = shcoeffs[30], shcoeffs[31], shcoeffs[32] r11, g11, b11 = shcoeffs[33], shcoeffs[34], shcoeffs[35] r12, g12, b12 = shcoeffs[36], shcoeffs[37], shcoeffs[38] r13, g13, b13 = shcoeffs[39], shcoeffs[40], shcoeffs[41] r14, g14, b14 = shcoeffs[42], shcoeffs[43], shcoeffs[44] r15, g15, b15 = shcoeffs[45], shcoeffs[46], shcoeffs[47] # Compute contributions # Base r = SHC0 r0 g = SHC0 g0 b = SHC0 b0 # Degree 1 r += evalshdegree1(r1, r2, r3, x, y, z) g += evalshdegree1(g1, g2, g3, x, y, z) b += evalshdegree1(b1, b2, b3, x, y, z) # Degree 2 r += evalshdegree2(r4, r5, r6, r7, r8, x, y, z) g += evalshdegree2(g4, g5, g6, g7, g8, x, y, z) b += evalshdegree2(b4, b5, b6, b7, b8, x, y, z) # Degree 3 r += evalshdegree3(r9, r10, r11, r12, r13, r14, r15, x, y, z) g += evalshdegree3(g9, g10, g11, g12, g13, g14, g15, x, y, z) b += evalshdegree3(b9, b10, b11, b12, b13, b14, b15, x, y, z) # Apply bias and ReLU r = max(0.0, r + 0.5) g = max(0.0, g + 0.5) b = max(0.0, b + 0.5) return (r, g, b) Training Schedule: Optimization begins with only the degree-0 band (base color) active. One further band is unlocked every 1,000 iterations until all four bands (degrees 0-3) are active. This ensures the diffuse base color is correct before fitting higher-order components. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The basis functions Yl^m(\mathbf{d}) are fixed polynomials and are never updated during training; only the coefficients k are learned. If the viewing direction is not normalized, the polynomial evaluation will be incorrect. High-degree SH coefficients can cause memory bandwidth pressure during rendering. Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking is an optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces memory bandwidth pressure caused by high-degree spherical harmonics (SH) by evaluating view-dependent colors over multiple frames rather than every frame. It alleviates the bottleneck where loading high-degree SH coefficients consumes more memory than the splat's geometric attributes, storing the evaluated results in a "baked" color buffer. Unlike standard per-frame SH evaluation, this method trades immediate visual fidelity for rendering performance, converging to the correct view-dependent color within a short, fixed number of frames. Spherical Beta (SB) is a specular appearance model that adds explicit specular lobes on top of a diffuse base color, used for view-dependent color in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It is distinct from Spherical Harmonics (SH) by using a parametric lobe function rather than a global basis expansion, allowing for sharper highlights with fewer parameters. It is orthogonal to SH, where SH (typically degree 0) supplies the diffuse base and SB adds the specular component. The Spherical Beta (SB) function is a directional appearance representation used to model view-dependent effects, such as specular reflections, in 3D Gaussian splatting. It replaces spherical harmonics (SH) to capture higher-frequency directional variations by using asymmetric, bounded-support lobes. Unlike SH, which uses global basis functions, SB uses localized kernels that can model skewed and sharper directional variation, offering greater flexibility at the cost of increased optimization difficulty. A representation where each point in the point cloud carries spherical harmonics parameters to model directional appearance, as opposed to directionally invariant RGB values. Using spherical harmonics yields better rendering quality than using learnable directionally invariant RGB values. On the Blender dataset, removing spherical harmonics ('w/o sh') reduces PSNR from 30.3 dB to 27.1 dB, SSIM from 0.945 to 0.932, and increases LPIPS from 0.078 to 0.155. A ray-traced variant of 3D Gaussians that treats Gaussians as volumetric primitives and ray marches them in a NeRF-like manner to achieve high quality at the cost of performance. It introduces a slab-by-slab integration scheme and augments spherical harmonics with a spherical Gaussian encoding to better capture view-dependent color. While this yields higher PSNR than 3DGS, it comes with a 6× training slowdown and approximately 25× lower frame rates. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Each Gaussian stores 48 coefficients (16 per channel × 3 channels). This is significantly more than a single RGB triplet (3 floats). Time: Evaluation is a fixed number of polynomial operations per Gaussian, described as costing "almost nothing at display time". However, loading 48 floats per Gaussian can cause memory bandwidth bottlenecks. Measured Performance: On the Average-30K dataset, using full SH (degree 3) achieves a PSNR of 26.05, whereas removing SH (No-SH) reduces PSNR to 25.35. On the Blender dataset, using SH yields a PSNR of 30.3 dB, SSIM of 0.945, and LPIPS of 0.078, compared to 27.1 dB, 0.932, and 0.155 without SH. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Captures view-dependent effects like highlights and reflections. Compact representation compared to neural networks. Limitations: High memory usage for high degrees. Can introduce artifacts if not trained properly (e.g., weird colors on poorly observed sides). When to use: When view-dependent appearance (specularities, reflections) is important for photorealism. When rendering speed is critical and neural network queries are too slow. When not to use: When memory bandwidth is the primary bottleneck and view-dependent effects are negligible. When only diffuse, view-independent color is required. Spherical harmonics were repurposed from irradiance environment maps to represent the view-dependent color of 3D Gaussians in the 3D Gaussian Splatting method. The method was introduced by Kerbl et al. in 2023. The SH expansion is analogous to a Fourier series on the sphere, where low-degree harmonics capture smooth diffuse shading and higher degrees capture sharper directional variations.
