name: Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking
head: Baked view-dependent color buffer, Progressive SH evaluation, Progressive Spherical Harmonics
body: Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking is an optimization for 3D Gaussian Splatting that reduces memory bandwidth pressure caused by high-degree spherical harmonics (SH) by evaluating view-dependent colors over multiple frames rather than every frame. It alleviates the bottleneck where loading high-degree SH coefficients consumes more memory than the splat's geometric attributes, storing the evaluated results in a "baked" color buffer. Unlike standard per-frame SH evaluation, this method trades immediate visual fidelity for rendering performance, converging to the correct view-dependent color within a short, fixed number of frames. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D Gaussian splats with stored SH coefficients (e.g., Degree 3), camera view direction, and a convergence parameter N (number of frames to fully update all visible splats). Output: A "baked" view-dependent color buffer containing the evaluated RGB color for each visible splat. Data Structures: Splat Attributes: Position, scale, orientation, base color, and flags, consuming 52 bytes per splat. SH Coefficients: For Degree 3, 45 additional floating-point values (16 coefficients times three for RGB, minus three since the base color is handled separately). Baked Color Buffer: Stores the evaluated RGB color for each splat. Size depends on the number of visible splats. For Degree 3, the SH data adds 180 bytes per splat (45 \times 4 bytes) to the staging memory load, which is more than triple the 52 bytes of geometric data. Algorithm: 1. Initialization: Create a baked color buffer for all visible splats and initialize it with the base color or the previous frame's baked color. 2. Progressive Update Loop: For each frame f (where f=1, 2, \dots, N): a. Determine the subset of splats to update, targeting a fraction of 1/N of the total visible splats per frame. b. Select a subset of splats (e.g., sequential or random) comprising 1/N of the total visible splats. c. For each selected splat i: i. Evaluate the spherical harmonics function C(\mathbf{v}i) using the splat's SH coefficients and the view direction \mathbf{v}i. ii. Write the resulting RGB color to the baked color buffer for splat i. d. For splats not selected in this frame, retain their previously baked color value. 3. VR Handling: In Virtual Reality, account for different camera directions for left and right eyes. It is sufficient to progressively bake color values for only one eye and reuse them for the other, or evaluate based on the direction to the center of both eyes. 4. Rendering: Use the baked color buffer for shading during the current frame's rasterization. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def progressiveshbaking(splats, viewdirections, numframestoconverge=10): """ splats: List of splat objects with.shcoeffs (45 floats for Degree 3) and.basecolor viewdirections: List of 3D view direction vectors numframestoconverge: N, frames to fully update all visible splats """ numsplats = len(splats) bakedcolors = [splat.basecolor for splat in splats] # Initialize with base color splatsperframe = max(1, numsplats // numframestoconverge) currentsplatidx = 0 for frame in range(numframestoconverge): for in range(splatsperframe): if currentsplatidx >= numsplats: break # Evaluate spherical harmonics: C(v) = sum{l=0}^{L} sum{m=-l}^{l} c{lm} Y{lm}(v) # Standard SH evaluation routine bakedcolors[currentsplatidx] = splats[currentsplatidx].basecolor currentsplatidx += 1 if currentsplatidx >= numsplats: break return bakedcolors Parameters: Convergence Frames (N): Number of frames to fully update all visible splats. Typical value: 10. SH Degree: Degree 3 is used, requiring 45 additional coefficients per splat (16 coefficients times three for RGB, minus three since the base color is handled separately). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: VR Eye Discrepancy: Left and right eyes have different view directions. Reusing baked colors from one eye for the other may cause slight inaccuracies, but is deemed sufficient. Motion Artifacts: Under sufficiently high frame rates, progressive updates cause little to no apparent lag even under motion. Memory Bandwidth: High-degree SH (e.g., Degree 3) adds 180 bytes per splat to staging memory, which is a significant bottleneck compared to 52 bytes of geometric data. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Storing Degree 3 SH coefficients adds 180 bytes per splat (45 \times 4 bytes) to the staging pass memory load. This is more than triple the 52 bytes used for position, scale, orientation, color, and flags. Time: Updating all harmonics per frame is expensive. On the Kinuta scene, updating all harmonics takes 1.6 ms, while updating 1/10th takes 0.6 ms and 1/30th takes 0.5 ms. On the Campus scene, updating all harmonics takes 4.4 ms, while updating 1/10th takes 1.5 ms and 1/30th takes 1.1 ms. Measured Performance: Kinuta Scene: All: 1.6 ms, 1/10th: 0.6 ms, 1/30th: 0.5 ms. Campus Scene: All: 4.4 ms, 1/10th: 1.5 ms, 1/30th: 1.1 ms. Berlin Scene: All: 0.4 ms, 1/10th: 0.2 ms, 1/30th: 0.1 ms. Garden Scene: All: 2.6 ms, 1/10th: 1.9 ms, 1/30th: 1.8 ms. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significantly reduces memory bandwidth pressure and staging time for high-degree SH. Convergence is typically fast enough (e.g., 10 frames) to cause barely noticeable artifacts. Limitations: Progressive updates introduce a temporary lag in view-dependent color updates, but under sufficiently high frame rates, this causes little to no apparent lag even under motion. Requires additional memory for the baked color buffer. When to Use: Use when rendering high-degree SH (e.g., Degree 3) and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Use in VR where per-eye evaluation is expensive. When Not to Use: Use when SH degree is low (e.g., Degree 0 or 1) and bandwidth is not a concern. Progressive View-Dependent Color Baking was introduced in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting for large models and VR rendering. It addresses the performance bottleneck caused by the large memory footprint of high-degree spherical harmonics coefficients. The technique was developed as part of the Splatshop project, which focuses on efficiently editing large Gaussian Splat models. Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Spherical Beta View-Dependent Color
head: Spherical Beta, Spherical Beta (SB) appearance model, Spherical Beta lobes
body: Spherical Beta (SB) is a specular appearance model that adds explicit specular lobes on top of a diffuse base color for view-dependent rendering in 3D Gaussian Splatting. It replaces higher SH bands with parametric lobes, achieving sharper highlights with fewer parameters while remaining orthogonal to the SH diffuse base. Inputs: Gaussian splat parameters: position, covariance (or scale/rotation), opacity, and base color. SH coefficients (optional, typically degree 0 for SB-only specular, or degree 3 for hybrid). SB lobe parameters: number of lobes, axis direction, sharpness, and color. Outputs: Final pixel color for each splat during rasterization. Each SB lobe stores 6 floats in the following order: [r, g, b, \theta, \phi, \beta]. r, g, b: Color components of the lobe. \theta, \phi: Spherical angles defining the lobe axis direction. \beta: Sharpness parameter. During preprocessing (load time), lobe parameters are converted and stored as half floats (16-bit). One 16-byte texel is stored per lobe per splat. Lobes are packed into an RGBA32F texture atlas with 2 texels per lobe, indexed by splat.index. 1. Preprocessing: At load time, convert lobe parameters (axis from spherical angles \theta, \phi, sharpness \beta, and activated color rgb) into half-floats. 2. Densification: Handle the sbnumber parameter through densification strategies (DefaultStrategy and MCMCStrategy). 3. Rendering: For each splat, compute the color contribution of each lobe. 4. Composition: Add the lobe contributions to the base color (from SH or base color). 5. Clamping: Clamp the base color to zero before adding lobe contributions to prevent negative base colors from absorbing part of the highlight. 6. Export: Export SB parameters to PLY files via additive properties named sbparams, matching the reference implementation's naming convention. Leave standard fdc / frest schema untouched. For mixed lobe counts during merge, columns are channel-major (sbparams{channel lobes + lobe}). Absent lobes are padded with a raw value that activates to zero, since softplus(0) ≈ 0.1 would add a visible specular term. The color contribution of each lobe is calculated as: C{lobe} = \text{softplus}(rgb) \cdot \max(\text{dot}(dir, axis), 0)^{4 \cdot \exp(\beta)} Where: dir: View direction vector. axis: Lobe axis direction vector derived from \theta, \phi. rgb: Color components of the lobe. \beta: Sharpness parameter. \text{softplus}(x) = \ln(1 + e^x). The final color is: C{final} = \max(C{base}, 0) + \sum{i=1}^{N{lobes}} C{lobe, i} Where C{base} is the color from SH degree 0 or base color. Number of lobes (N{lobes}): Up to 4 lobes are rendered. The trainers default to 2 lobes. shdegree: The degree of spherical harmonics used for the diffuse base. Typical value: 0 (for SB-only specular) or 3 (default in nerfstudio). sbnumber: The number of SB lobes to use. Typical values: 0 (purely diffuse), 2 (Beta Splatting setting). SBMAXLOBES: The maximum number of lobes supported, set to 2 in the implementation. It bounds the shader loop and atlas size. Negative Base Colors: The base color must be clamped to zero before adding lobe contributions. Many splats have negative base colors, which would otherwise absorb part of the highlight. Format Support: Compressed PLY, SOG, and SPZ formats currently do not support lobe data storage. Only uncompressed PLY is supported. Beta Kernel: This implementation only covers the Spherical Beta color lobes, not the Beta kernel. The Beta kernel replaces the Gaussian falloff with opacity (1 - r^2)^\beta and a hard cutoff, and requires changes to quad extent, bounds/culling, and per-splat values. Files using the kernel will not render correctly with this PR. Splat with Lobes but no SH: For splats with lobes but no SH, the color is re-evaluated as the camera moves. Rejection of Unsupported Formats: The splat and plycompressed formats reject SB lobes rather than dropping them silently. Preprocessor Guard: PlayCanvas's preprocessor treats bare #if NAME as #ifdef NAME. Therefore, #if SBLOBES > 0 is used instead of #if SBLOBES to ensure a 0-valued define is treated as false. Column Validation: If the count of sbparams columns is not a whole number of lobes or exceeds the supported count, the file is rejected with a warning to prevent misinterpreting one channel as another. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computesphericalbetacolor(splat, viewdir): """ Compute the final color for a splat using Spherical Beta lobes. Args: splat: Object containing: basecolor: Color from SH degree 0 or base color (3 floats) lobes: List of lobe parameters, each being [r, g, b, theta, phi, beta] sbnumber: Number of lobes to use viewdir: View direction vector (3 floats) Returns: Final color (3 floats) """ # Clamp base color to zero to prevent absorption of highlights basecolor = [max(c, 0.0) for c in splat.basecolor] totallobecolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] # Iterate over the specified number of lobes for i in range(splat.sbnumber): lobe = splat.lobes[i] r, g, b, theta, phi, beta = lobe # Convert spherical angles to axis vector axis = [sin(theta) cos(phi), sin(theta) sin(phi), cos(theta)] # Compute dot product dotproduct = viewdir[0] axis[0] + viewdir[1] axis[1] + viewdir[2] axis[2] # Compute lobe contribution # softplus(rgb) softplusrgb = [log(1 + exp(r)), log(1 + exp(g)), log(1 + exp(b))] # max(dot(dir, axis), 0)^(4 exp(beta)) exponent = 4.0 exp(beta) lobefactor = max(dotproduct, 0.0) exponent # Add to total lobe color totallobecolor[0] += softplusrgb[0] lobefactor totallobecolor[1] += softplusrgb[1] lobefactor totallobecolor[2] += softplusrgb[2] lobefactor # Final color finalcolor = [ basecolor[0] + totallobecolor[0], basecolor[1] + totallobecolor[1], basecolor[2] + totallobecolor[2] ] return finalcolor Note: sin, cos, log, exp, and max are standard mathematical functions. A method for baking view-dependent color into textures, differing from SB's parametric lobe approach by using baked textures for view-dependent effects. Choose when hardware supports texture sampling efficiently and when pre-baking is feasible. Time Complexity: The shader computes one pow operation per lobe. With up to 4 lobes, this is a constant number of operations per splat. Memory Complexity: Each lobe stores 6 floats. With 2 lobes, this is 12 floats per splat, compared to 45 floats for SH bands 1-3. Measured Performance: On MipNeRF-360 (7 scenes, 30k steps, RTX 4090): MCMC SH0/SB2: 29.602 dB PSNR, 104 MB PLY size, 0.91 GB Peak VRAM, 52.0 FPS, 487s train time. Default SH0/SB2: 29.465 dB PSNR, 332 MB PLY size, 2.17 GB Peak VRAM, 31.1 FPS, 616s train time. Comparison to SH3/SB0: MCMC SH0/SB2 vs MCMC SH3/SB0: +0.15 dB PSNR, -56% PLY size, -39% Peak VRAM, +19% Render speed, -5% Train time. Default SH0/SB2 vs Default SH3/SB0: +0.30 dB PSNR, -54% PLY size, -53% Peak VRAM, +5% Render speed, -16% Train time. Strengths: Higher PSNR, smaller model size (44-46% of SH3), roughly half the peak VRAM, faster render speed, and faster training time compared to SH degree 3. Limitations: Only uncompressed PLY is supported for lobe data storage. The Beta kernel is not included, which would require more extensive changes to the renderer. When to Use: When view-dependent specular highlights are important and computational efficiency is a priority. SB is a strict win over SH3 in terms of PSNR, size, VRAM, and speed. When Not to Use: When compressed PLY, SOG, or SPZ formats are required, as they do not support lobe data storage. When the Beta kernel is required, as this implementation only covers the Spherical Beta color lobes. Spherical Beta (SB) is the specular model from Deformable Beta Splatting (Liu et al., SIGGRAPH 2025). It was integrated into the PlayCanvas engine (Pull Request #9729) for WebGL2 and WebGPU, and into the nerfstudio-project/gsplat (Pull Request #1056) for training and export. The model was designed to provide higher PSNR and faster speed at half the size and memory than SH degree 3. name: Spherical Beta Function
head: SB color representation
body: The Spherical Beta (SB) function is a directional appearance representation used to model view-dependent effects, such as specular reflections, in 3D Gaussian splatting. It replaces spherical harmonics (SH) to capture higher-frequency directional variations by using asymmetric, bounded-support lobes. Unlike SH, which uses global basis functions, SB uses localized kernels that can model skewed and sharper directional variation, offering greater flexibility at the cost of increased optimization difficulty. The SB function represents the color or intensity of a Gaussian surfel as a sum of K directional lobes. Each lobe is defined by a principal direction and two shape parameters that control the asymmetry and sharpness of the lobe. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Viewing direction \omega \in \mathbb{R}^3 (unit vector), number of lobes K, set of principal directions \{sk\}{k=1}^K, and shape parameters \{\alphak, \betak\}{k=1}^K. Output: Scalar value f{SB}(\omega) representing the directional intensity or color component. Data Structures: For each Gaussian primitive, the view-dependent color is stored as: K: Integer, number of lobes (typically small, e.g., 1-4). sk: 3D vector, principal direction of the k-th lobe. Normalized to unit length. \alphak: Scalar, shape parameter > 0. Controls the "rise" side of the lobe. \betak: Scalar, shape parameter > 0. Controls the "fall" side of the lobe. Formula: The SB function is defined as: f{SB} (\omega; \alpha, \beta, s) = \sum{k=1}^{K} (1+sk \cdot \omega)^{\alphak -1} (1-sk \cdot \omega)^{\betak -1} Where: sk \cdot \omega is the dot product between the principal direction and the viewing direction. \alphak, \betak > 0. The term (1+sk \cdot \omega) is non-negative because sk \cdot \omega \in [-1, 1]. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sphericalbetafunction(omega, lobes): """ Compute the Spherical Beta function value for a given viewing direction. Args: omega: numpy array, shape (3,), unit viewing direction vector. lobes: list of dicts, each containing: 's': numpy array, shape (3,), principal direction (unit vector). 'alpha': float, shape parameter > 0. 'beta': float, shape parameter > 0. Returns: float: The SB function value. """ total = 0.0 for lobe in lobes: s = lobe['s'] alpha = lobe['alpha'] beta = lobe['beta'] # Dot product s. omega dot = np.dot(s, omega) # Compute terms # Note: (1 + dot) and (1 - dot) are always in [0, 2] term1 = (1.0 + dot) (alpha - 1.0) term2 = (1.0 - dot) (beta - 1.0) total += term1 term2 return total Parameters: K: Number of lobes. Not given in the sources. \alphak, \betak: Optimized during training. Typical values are not given, but they must be > 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioned Gradients: Extreme values of \alphak or \betak generate very sharp and flat regions, causing ill-conditioned gradients and stronger sensitivity to initialization compared to Spherical Gaussians. Overfitting: The flexibility of SB increases the risk of overfitting, as observed in DBS. Boundary Conditions: The function is well-defined for all \omega on the unit sphere since 1 \pm sk \cdot \omega \ge 0. Time Complexity: O(K) per evaluation, where K is the number of lobes. This is comparable to SH of similar order but may be more expensive if K is large. Memory Complexity: Stores K directions (3 floats each) and 2K shape parameters (2 floats each). Total 5K floats per Gaussian. Performance: In DP-GES, using SB increased FLIP error slightly compared to GES (mainly due to higher-frequency effects being captured, which FLIP interprets as warping error) but improved view-dependent appearance. Reverting to SH reduced FPS from 472 to 480 and PSNR from 28.11 to 27.72 on MipNeRF360, indicating SB is slightly more expensive but yields higher quality. Strengths: Can model skewed and sharper directional variation than SG or SH. Limitations: Harder to optimize, sensitive to initialization, prone to overfitting. The Spherical Beta function was introduced in the context of Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering to model higher-frequency view-dependent effects. It extends the concept of Spherical Gaussians (SG) by allowing asymmetric lobes. It is used in DP-GES (Depth Peeling for High-Fidelity Gaussian-Enhanced Surfel Rendering). name: Physics-based Gaussian Simulation
head: PhysGaussian, Gaussian Splashing, VR-GS, Spring-Gaus, Feature Splatting
body: Physics-based Gaussian Simulation integrates continuum mechanics or particle dynamics directly into 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), treating each Gaussian kernel as a discrete physical particle with volume. This approach creates a unified simulation-to-rendering pipeline where the geometric representation serves as the simulation mesh, enabling physically accurate dynamics, real-time interaction, and editing of high-fidelity virtual content. Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes static appearance, these methods decouple or tightly couple physical state (position, velocity, deformation) from radiometric properties to support dynamic scenes. Inputs: 1. Initial 3DGS representation: A set of N Gaussians \{Gi\}{i=1}^N, where each Gi is defined by mean position \mui, covariance matrix \Sigmai (or rotation Ri and scale Si), opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color ci. 2. Physical parameters: Mass mi, damping coefficients, and material properties (e.g., stiffness, viscosity). 3. External forces: Gravity, collisions, or user interactions. Outputs: 1. Updated Gaussian parameters: New positions \mu'i, covariances \Sigma'i, and potentially updated colors/opacities if coupled with rendering. 2. Rendered image: Computed via standard 3DGS rasterization using the updated physical state. The core data structure extends the standard 3DGS attribute list with physics-specific fields: Position (\mu): 3D vector (x, y, z). Velocity (v): 3D vector (vx, vy, vz). Mass (m): Scalar value, potentially learned from input video or assigned based on volume. Covariance (\Sigma): 3 \times 3 symmetric positive-definite matrix, often parameterized by rotation R and scale S. Physical State Flags: Boolean or integer flags indicating if a Gaussian is part of the active simulation domain (e.g., fluid vs. solid). 1. Initialization: Reconstruct initial 3DGS from input images/video using standard 3DGS optimization. Assign physical properties: Mass mi is learned from input video dynamics or estimated from Gaussian volume. Velocity vi is initialized to zero or estimated from temporal changes in position. Define material parameters (stiffness, damping) based on object type (solid, fluid). 2. Physics Simulation Step: Compute forces Fi acting on each Gaussian i: Fi = F{gravity} + F{collision} + F{interaction} + F{internal} F{gravity} = mi \cdot g. F{collision}: Derived from contact detection with other Gaussians or static meshes. F{internal}: Depends on the chosen physics model: Continuum Mechanics (PhysGaussian): Uses continuum deformation of Gaussian kernels, treating the cloud as a deformable body. Position-Based Dynamics (Gaussian Splashing): Uses Position-Based Fluids (PBD) constraints to enforce incompressibility and cohesion. Spring-Mass (Spring-Gaus): Applies spring forces between neighboring Gaussians based on a spring-mass model. Update velocity and position using a numerical integrator (e.g., Verlet or Euler): vi^{t+1} = vi^t + \frac{Fi}{mi} \Delta t \mui^{t+1} = \mui^t + vi^{t+1} \Delta t. Update covariance \Sigmai to reflect deformation: For continuum deformation, \Sigmai is transformed by the local deformation gradient. For PBD, \Sigmai may be adjusted to maintain volume consistency. 3. Rendering Step: Rasterize the updated Gaussians using standard 3DGS alpha blending. Deferred Shading: Some methods (e.g., VR-GS) use deferred shading to avoid blending artifacts from multiple shading calculations. Material Rendering: For fluids/solids, material parameters (diffusiveness, specularity, roughness, normals) are applied to each Gaussian to enhance physical appearance. Normals are aligned with surface normals to improve reflection accuracy. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def physicsbasedgaussiansimulation(gaussians, dt, externalforces): """ Simulate physics for a set of 3D Gaussians. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: (3,) position vector v: (3,) velocity vector m: float mass Sigma: (3,3) covariance matrix type: str ('solid', 'fluid', 'particle') dt: float time step externalforces: dict of force functions, e.g., {'gravity': lambda m: m 9.81} Returns: Updated list of Gaussians """ for g in gaussians: # 1. Compute Forces F = np.zeros(3) # Gravity if 'gravity' in externalforces: F += externalforces'gravity' # Internal Forces (Model-dependent) if g.type == 'solid': # Continuum mechanics or Spring-Mass # Example: Spring-Mass with neighbors for neighbor in getneighbors(g, gaussians): displacement = g.mu - neighbor.mu distance = np.linalg.norm(displacement) if distance > 0: # Hooke's Law F += -k (distance - restlength) (displacement / distance) elif g.type == 'fluid': # Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) # Compute density and pressure density = computedensity(g, gaussians) pressure = computepressure(density) # Apply pressure force F -= pressure gradientofdensity(g, gaussians) # Collision Forces for other in gaussians: if g is other: continue dist = np.linalg.norm(g.mu - other.mu) if dist < collisionradius: # Repulsive force F += repulsionforce(g, other, dist) # 2. Integrate # Verlet integration or Euler a = F / g.m g.v += a dt g.mu += g.v dt # 3. Update Covariance (Deformation) if g.type == 'solid': # Update Sigma based on deformation gradient # Simplified: Rotate and scale based on velocity gradient g.Sigma = updatecovariance(g, g.v, dt) return gaussians Time Step (\Delta t): Typically 1/60 s for real-time VR. Stiffness (k): For spring-mass models, tuned to prevent oscillation. Collision Radius: Determines interaction range between Gaussians. Mass (m): Learned from input video or estimated from volume. Precision: High-velocity simulations may require double precision to avoid numerical instability. Boundaries: Gaussians near scene boundaries may experience incorrect collision forces if not handled with boundary conditions. Degenerate Input: If initial Gaussians are poorly distributed, physics simulation may produce unrealistic artifacts (e.g., clumping). Performance: Computing neighbor interactions for large N is O(N^2) without spatial hashing. What it is: A ray-marching algorithm for distance fields. Difference: Focuses on efficient ray traversal for implicit surfaces, not physics simulation. When to choose: When rendering static or deforming distance fields without explicit particle dynamics. Link: OTS Marching Ray Marching Algorithm What it is: Technique to encode view-dependent appearance using spherical harmonics. Difference: Handles radiometric properties, not physical dynamics. When to choose: When view-dependent effects (specularity) are needed but physics is not. Link: View-dependent color with Spherical Harmonics What it is: Blending technique for smooth volume rendering. Difference: Focuses on visual blending, not physical forces. When to choose: When smooth, blobby appearance is desired without physics. Link: Weighted Blending (Fuzzy Metaballs) What it is: Optimization strategy for 3DGS. Difference: Focuses on training convergence, not runtime simulation. When to choose: When training static 3DGS models. Link: Two-Stage Optimization Pipeline Time: Physics simulation is O(N) for simple forces but O(N^2) for neighbor interactions without spatial acceleration structures. Rendering remains O(N) per pixel. Memory: Additional memory for velocity, mass, and neighbor lists. Hardware: Tested on VR headsets and GPUs. Resolution: Real-time at 1080p for moderate N. Scene: Dynamic scenes with interacting objects. Scales with number of Gaussians; spatial hashing can reduce neighbor search to O(N). Strengths: Physically accurate dynamics, real-time interaction, high-fidelity rendering. Limitations: Computationally expensive for large scenes, requires careful tuning of physical parameters. Use for dynamic, interactive scenes requiring physical realism. Do not use for static scenes or when performance is critical and physics is not needed. PhysGaussian: Integrates physics-based continuum mechanics directly within 3DGS. Gaussian Splashing: Combines 3DGS with Position-Based Dynamics (PBD) for fluids. VR-GS: Physical dynamics-aware interactive Gaussian Splatting for VR. Spring-Gaus: Applies spring-mass model to dynamic 3DGS. Developed as extensions to 3DGS to enable animation and dynamic content. Addresses the gap between generated and manually crafted 3D content in VR/AR. VR/AR environments, robotics, autonomous driving, and dynamic scene editing. From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting: Theory and Applications, https://doi.org/10.1109/sibgrapi67909.2025.11223276, fetched 2026-10-26 From Volume Rendering to 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://www.visgraf.impa.br/Data/RefBib/PSPDF/tutorial-sib2025/tutorial-sib2025.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Weighted Blending (Fuzzy Metaballs)
head: Blending intersections, Fuzzy Metaballs rendering, Hidden-surface solution for Fuzzy Metaballs, Sort-free Gaussian rendering, Weighted Blending of Intersections
body: Weighted Blending is a sort-free, image-order rendering technique for 3D Gaussians that resolves the hidden-surface problem by computing a weighted average of all ray-Gaussian intersection depths. Unlike NeRF-style methods that sort intersections and use closer Gaussians to attenuate further ones, this method blends all intersections simultaneously without sorting, extending Order Independent Transparency (OIT) principles to 3D opaque surfaces. Inputs: Ray direction \vec{v} (normalized), set of N 3D Gaussians. Outputs: Blended intersection depth tf, opacity \alpha, and optionally normal \vec{n}f or color \vec{c}f. Data Structures: Gaussian i: \mui (vector), \Sigmai^{-1} (matrix), \lambdai (scalar). Per-ray accumulators: tf (scalar), \alpha (scalar), \vec{n}f (vector), \vec{c}f (vector). Steps: 1. For each Gaussian i, compute the intersection distance ti along the ray \vec{v} using the linear approach (point of maximum likelihood): ti = \frac{\mui^T \Sigmai^{-1} \vec{v}}{\vec{v}^T \Sigmai^{-1} \vec{v}} 2. Compute the unnormalized log distance di for Gaussian i: di = -\frac{1}{2} \left[ (ti \vec{v} - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (ti \vec{v} - \mui) \right] + \log(\lambdai) 3. Compute the unnormalized Gaussian density \deltai: \deltai = \exp(di) 4. Compute the weight wi for each intersection: wi = \exp \left( \beta1 di \sigma \left( \frac{\beta3}{\eta} ti \right) - \frac{\beta2}{\eta} ti \right) where \sigma(x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-x}} is the sigmoid function. The term h(ti) = \sigma \left( \frac{\beta3}{\eta} ti \right) down-weights intersections behind the camera. 5. Compute the final blended depth tf: tf = \frac{1}{\sumi wi} \sumi wi ti 6. Compute opacity \alpha: \alpha = \sigma \left( \beta4 \sumi \deltai + \beta5 \right) 7. For other properties like normal \vec{n}i or color \vec{c}i, apply the same weighted average using wi. Parameters: \beta1, \beta2: Balance high-quality hits (high di) vs. camera proximity (low ti). \beta3: Controls sigmoid decay for behind-camera intersections. \beta4, \beta5: Control opacity scaling and offset. \eta: Rough scale of the object, used to normalize ti for scale invariance. Typical values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Intersections behind the camera (ti < 0) are down-weighted by the sigmoid term in the original model. The original formulation assumes \sum \lambdai = 1. Losing this global normalization causes minor differences in pose estimation but is negligible for shape estimation. Precision issues may arise if \lambdai is very small, causing \log(\lambdai) to underflow. Ensure \lambdai is bounded away from zero or use log-sum-exp tricks if necessary. Fuzzy Metaballs is an algebraic, implicit surface representation that defines geometry as the zero level set of a function composed of multidimensional Gaussians (ellipsoids) rather than isotropic ones. It serves as the foundational object representation for differentiable rendering pipelines, enabling robust optimization by relaxing hard thresholds to ensure smooth gradients during ray-tracing. Unlike Weighted Blending, which focuses on sort-free image-order rendering, Fuzzy Metaballs provides the underlying implicit field definition that allows for the computation of surface normals and distance-based losses. A simplified rendering model for shape reconstruction that reduces the original 5 hyperparameters to 2 (\beta1, \beta2) by removing the sigmoid term for behind-camera contributions and replacing the sigmoid alpha function with a decaying exponential. Weight: wi = \exp \left( \beta1 di - \frac{\beta2}{\eta} ti \right). Alpha: \alpha = 1 - \exp \left( - \sumi \deltai \right). Pitfall: Losing the global normalization condition (\sum \lambdai = 1) causes minor differences in pose estimation, but these are negligible for shape estimation. A hyperparameter-free rendering variant that requires sorting intersections and uses alpha compositing (transmission) to compute weights, enabling differentiable rendering without tunable parameters. Step: Sort all ray-Gaussian intersections by depth ti. Compute accumulated transmission Ti for each intersection based on earlier (closer) intersections. Transmission: Ti = \exp \left( -\sumj \deltaj 1[tj < ti] \right), where 1[\cdot] is the indicator function. Weight: wi = Ti (1 - \exp(-\deltai)). Comparison: This approach is slower than the sort-free models but performs nearly identically in quality, while requiring no hyperparameters. Time Complexity: O(N) evaluations of Gaussians for each ray, where N is the number of Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On a Quadro P2000 (CUDA), Fuzzy Metaballs forward pass takes 3.0 \pm 0.2 ms and backward pass 9.6 \pm 0.5 ms for 160x120 images. On an i5-7287U (CPU), forward pass takes 3.0 \pm 0.15 ms and backward pass 13.2 \pm 1.4 ms for 80x60 images. Strengths: Sort-free, differentiable, scale-invariant (with \eta), simple implementation (60 lines of JAX code). Limitations: The original model requires tuning 5 hyperparameters. The Zero Parameter Model is slower due to sorting. When to use: When differentiable rendering of 3D Gaussians is required without the overhead of sorting, particularly for shape reconstruction. Originated from the Fuzzy Metaballs paper and further detailed in "Flexible Techniques for Differentiable Rendering with 3D Gaussians". The method was developed to provide a sort-free solution to the hidden-surface problem for 3D Gaussian representations, extending Order Independent Transparency (OIT) to opaque surfaces. It is used in differentiable rendering pipelines for shape reconstruction from video. Flexible Techniques for Differentiable Rendering with 3D Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2308.14737, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Approximate Differentiable Rendering with Algebraic Surfaces, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-19824-335, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Fuzzy Metaballs
head: Fuzzy Metaballs representation, differentiable renderer for GMMs
body: Fuzzy Metaballs is an algebraic, implicit surface representation that defines geometry as the zero level set of a function composed of multidimensional Gaussians (ellipsoids) rather than isotropic ones. It serves as the foundational object representation for differentiable rendering pipelines, enabling robust optimization by relaxing hard thresholds to ensure smooth gradients during ray-tracing. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of multidimensional Gaussian components \{Gi\}, each defined by a center \mui, a covariance matrix \Sigmai, and a weight \lambdai. Training views \{Ij\} are used for supervision. Outputs: An implicit field function F(x,y,z) and, in optimization contexts, updated Gaussian parameters \mut, \Sigmat, \lambdat. Data Structures: Each Gaussian component Gi is represented by: \mui \in \mathbb{R}^3: The center position. \Sigmai \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: The covariance matrix, which must be positive semi-definite. \lambdai \in \mathbb{R}: The scalar weight or "mass" of the component. Method Steps: 1. Field Evaluation: For any point x = (x,y,z) in space, compute the contribution of each Gaussian component Pi(x) using the multivariate Gaussian probability density function: Pi(x) = \exp\left(-\frac{1}{2}(x - \mui)^T \Sigmai^{-1} (x - \mui)\right) 2. Implicit Surface Definition: Compute the total field value F(x) by summing the weighted contributions and subtracting a threshold T: F(x) = \sumi \lambdai Pi(x) - T The surface is defined where F(x) = 0. The threshold T is relaxed compared to hard-threshold blobby models to allow for differentiable ray intersection. 3. Ray Tracing Formulation: In a ray-tracing context, rays intersect all Gaussians. The "fuzzy" nature implies that the contribution of each Gaussian is weighted by its density along the ray, avoiding binary occlusion decisions. 4. Surface Optimization (VRP-UDF): Emit rays Vk from training views, uniformly sample query points \{qn\} to obtain unsigned distance function (UDF) values and compute rendering weights distribution \{wn\} around the surface. Select Gaussians \{Gt\} close to the ray and near the surface, interpolate rendering weights at their projected positions, and compute the direction of increasing weight. Apply a surface loss to move Gaussians along this direction. Parameters: T: The threshold for sufficient density. Not given in the sources as a fixed value. \lambdai: Component weights. Not given in the sources as a fixed value. \text{sg}(\cdot): Stop-gradient operation applied to the target position to prevent backpropagation through the UDF model during Gaussian optimization. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Singularity: If \Sigmai is not positive definite, \Sigmai^{-1} is undefined. Ensure \Sigmai is constructed from valid rotations and positive scales. Precision: For points far from \mui, Pi(x) underflows to zero. Use a cutoff distance based on the eigenvalues of \Sigmai to ignore negligible contributions for performance. Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Two-Stage Optimization Pipeline
head: Two-Stage Strategy, Two-Stage Refinement
body: The Two-Stage Optimization Pipeline is a post-processing refinement method for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that decouples geometric alignment from material/lighting optimization to improve reconstruction quality and enable relighting. It addresses the limitations of coarse geometry from initial regressors and accumulated pose errors by first correcting camera poses and refining geometry, then locking geometry to optimize material and lighting parameters using pre-computed visibility. It differs from standard 3DGS by introducing explicit normal vectors and a visibility pre-computation step, and from pose-free methods like CF3DGS by using a dedicated pose correction stage. Inputs: A set of registered images, initial camera poses (with seed image pose fixed), and an initial 3D Gaussian point cloud (optionally with normals). Outputs: Optimized camera poses, refined 3D Gaussian primitives (positions, covariances, opacities, colors/coefficients), and optimized material/lighting parameters. Data Structures: 3D Gaussian Primitive: Position \mathbf{p}, covariance matrix \Sigma (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, spherical harmonic coefficients for color/view-dependence, and an additional normal vector \mathbf{n}. Camera Pose: 6-DoF transformation matrix. Visibility Map: Per-Gaussian visibility V(\omegai) pre-computed over the hemispherical domain defined by normal \mathbf{n}. Steps: 1. Stage 1: Pose Correction and Geometry Refinement 1. Pose Optimization: Optimize all camera poses to minimize point-to-camera ray consistency loss (Eq. 8 in). The seed image pose is fixed. Previous training epoch poses serve as initial values. 2. Geometry Optimization: Optimize a vanilla 3D Gaussian point cloud augmented with normal vectors \mathbf{n}. Use normal gradient-based densification to improve geometry. 3. Densification and Pruning: Apply explicit 3D Gaussian primitives densification and pruning strategies from [28] to refine scene details beyond the coarse geometry of the initial scene regressor. 2. Pre-computation: Visibility 1. For each Gaussian i, pre-compute its visibility V(\omegai) across the hemispherical domain determined by its normal \mathbf{n} using ray tracing. 3. Stage 2: Material and Lighting Optimization 1. Lock Geometry: Fix the positions, covariances, opacities, and normals of all 3D Gaussians. 2. Optimize Material/Lighting: Optimize material and lighting parameters using the rendering equation integrated with the pre-computed visibility V(\omegai). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostageoptimization(images, initialposes, initialgaussians): # Stage 1: Pose and Geometry # Fix seed pose (index 0) fixedposeidx = 0 # Optimize poses using ray consistency loss # initialposes are used as starting values optimizedposes = optimizeposes( images=images, poses=initialposes, lossfn=rayconsistencyloss, fixedidx=fixedposeidx) # Optimize geometry with normals # Augment Gaussians with normal vectors gaussians = initialgaussians for gaussian in gaussians: gaussian.normal = computeinitialnormal(gaussian) gaussians = optimizegeometry( gaussians=gaussians, images=images, poses=optimizedposes, densificationfn=normalgradientdensification) # Refine geometry with densification/pruning from [28] gaussians = refinegeometry(gaussians, strategy=pruningdensificationfrom28) # Pre-compute visibility for gaussian in gaussians: gaussian.visibility = precomputevisibility( gaussian=gaussian, domain=hemisphericaldomain(gaussian.normal)) # Stage 2: Material and Lighting # Lock geometry lockedgaussians = lockgeometry(gaussians) # Optimize material and lighting materialparams, lightingparams = optimizemateriallighting( gaussians=lockedgaussians, images=images, poses=optimizedposes, visibility=gaussians.visibility, lossfn=renderinglosswithvisibility) return optimizedposes, gaussians, materialparams, lightingparams Parameters: Seed Image Pose: Fixed during Stage 1. Densification/Pruning Strategy: From [28] (Not given in the sources). Visibility Domain: Hemispherical domain determined by normal \mathbf{n}. Edge Cases: Accumulated Pose Errors: Addressed by Stage 1 pose optimization. Coarse Geometry: Addressed by Stage 1 densification/pruning. GPU Memory Limitations: Initial scene regressor uses low-resolution images, necessitating Stage 2 refinement. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Improves rendering quality beyond coarse geometry. Enables realistic relighting. Strengths: Corrects accumulated pose errors, refines geometry, enables relighting. Limitations: Requires two stages, increasing complexity. Initial geometry may be coarse. When to Use: When high-quality reconstruction and relighting are needed, and initial poses/geometry are available but imperfect. When Not to Use: When real-time performance is critical and two-stage optimization is too slow. Origin: Proposed in for finalizing neural scene reconstruction and in for point-based relighting. History: Developed to address limitations of incremental registration and coarse geometry in 3DGS. Usage: Used in 3DGS-based pose-free methods and point-based relighting pipelines. name: Ray Marching with Neural SDF
head: DeepSDF Rendering, Neural SDF Ray Marching
body: Ray Marching with Neural SDF is a rendering technique that approximates the Signed Distance Field (SDF) using a deep neural network and renders images by marching rays along the estimated distance field. It differs from traditional SDF rendering by replacing the analytical distance function with a learned implicit representation, allowing for the reconstruction of complex geometries from data rather than explicit modeling. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A trained neural network model (typically a Multi-Layer Perceptron) representing the SDF, camera parameters (position, orientation, field of view, resolution), and lighting configuration. Outputs: A 2D image (height \times width) representing the rendered scene. Data Structures: Camera: Defined by width (int), height (int), fov (float, default \pi/3), position (3D vector), and aspectratio (float, width/height). Ray Buffer: A tensor of shape [width height, 1] storing the current distance along each ray, initialized to zeros. Position Buffer: A tensor of shape [width height, 3] storing the 3D coordinates of the current ray sample points. Parameters: maxsteps: Maximum number of ray marching iterations. Default is 30. epsilon: Convergence threshold. If the remaining distance is less than epsilon, the ray is considered to have hit the surface. Default is 10^{-3}. maxdist: Maximum distance a ray can travel before being clipped. Default is 10.0. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Create a distance tensor distances of shape [width height, 1] initialized to zeros on the GPU. 2. Ray Setup: Calculate ray directions for each pixel based on the camera's fov, aspectratio, and position. Normalize directions. Compute initial positions as \mathbf{p}0 = \mathbf{o} + \text{distances} \cdot \mathbf{d}, which effectively sets initial positions to camera origins. 3. Marching Loop: Iterate up to maxsteps times: a. Query SDF: Evaluate the neural network f(\mathbf{p}) at all current positions \mathbf{p} to get signed distances. b. Convergence Check: If all distances are less than epsilon, break the loop. c. Step Update: Update distances by adding the sampled SDF value: \text{distances} \leftarrow \text{distances} + f(\mathbf{p}). Recalculate positions: \mathbf{p} \leftarrow \mathbf{o} + \text{distances} \cdot \mathbf{d}. d. Clipping Check: If all rays have either converged (distance < epsilon) or exceeded maxdist, break the loop. 4. Normal Estimation: At the final positions, estimate normals using central finite differences with step size e = 10^{-3}. Compute offsets: \mathbf{dx} = (e, 0, 0), \mathbf{dy} = (0, e, 0), \mathbf{dz} = (0, 0, e). Calculate normal components: nx = f(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{dx}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{dx}) ny = f(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{dy}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{dy}) nz = f(\mathbf{p} + \mathbf{dz}) - f(\mathbf{p} - \mathbf{dz}) Normalize the resulting vector \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz). 5. Shading: Calculate brightness using a single directional light. Clamp the dot product of the normal \mathbf{n} and light direction \mathbf{l} to [0, 1]: \text{brightness} = \max(0, \mathbf{n} \cdot \mathbf{l}). 6. Clipping: Set brightness to 0 for pixels where the final distance exceeds maxdist. 7. Output: Reshape brightness to height \times width, convert to numpy, scale by 255, and cast to uint8. name: RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing
head: RBF volume rendering, SPH volume rendering, Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) volume rendering
body: RBF Particle Volume Path Tracing renders volumetric data represented as a collection of particles by modeling the scene as a continuous scalar field composed of additive weighted radial basis functions (RBFs), specifically Gaussians. It solves the visual clutter and pathological performance issues associated with BVH-based ray tracing of overlapping splatted particles by treating the volume as a single unified field rather than discrete geometric proxies. Unlike splatting, which projects particles into 2D billboards, this method allows for adjustable smoothing or sharpening via kernel parameters and supports full path tracing through the integration of RBF reconstruction into a volume sampling kernel API. The method combines a Bounding Volume Hierarchy (BVH) for spatial acceleration with Delta Tracking (Woodcock tracking) for unbiased Monte Carlo integration of the Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE). Inputs: Particle dataset: N particles, each defined by position \mathbf{x}i, radius ri, and weight wi. Rendering parameters: radiusSupportFactor (\sigma, default 3), clampMaxCumulativeValue (optional threshold). Transfer functions: Color map C(\cdot) and opacity map \alpha(\cdot) mapping scalar field values to color and extinction. Ray: Origin \mathbf{o}, direction \omega. Outputs: Radiance L(0, \omega) along the ray. 1. Particle Volume: Arrays of size N: positions (\mathbb{R}^3), radii (\mathbb{R}), weights (\mathbb{R}). 2. BVH: Built using Embree. Leaf nodes: Each leaf corresponds to a single particle. Node bounds: Determined by the particle's base radius multiplied by radiusSupportFactor (\sigma ri). Value Ranges: Each node stores the minimum and maximum scalar field values \Phi achievable within its bounding volume. These are estimated during preprocessing. 1. BVH Construction: Build a BVH over the N particles. The bounding box for particle i is expanded by a factor of \sigma (default 3) to account for the Gaussian kernel's support. 2. Value Range Estimation: For each leaf node (particle i), evaluate the RBF field \Phi on a small grid (e.g., 10^3 points) within the support radius \sigma ri. Determine the local minimum and maximum values for that leaf. Propagate these ranges up the tree to update interior node ranges. Store the global minimum and maximum values for the entire dataset. Note: This step has worst-case complexity O(N) and is optional if the user can manually specify clampMaxCumulativeValue. 1. RBF Scalar Field The scalar field \Phi(\mathbf{x}) at query point \mathbf{x} is the sum of Gaussian kernels from all contributing particles i: \Phi(\mathbf{x}) = \sumi \phii(di(\mathbf{x})) where di(\mathbf{x}) = \|\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}i\| is the distance from particle center \mathbf{x}i. 2. Gaussian Kernel The kernel for particle i with weight wi and radius ri is: \phii(\mathbf{x}) = wi e^{-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{di(\mathbf{x})}{ri}\right)^2} The kernel is truncated at a support radius of \sigma ri. Outside this radius, the contribution is zero. 3. Radiative Transfer Equation (RTE) Assuming non-scattering media (\sigmas = 0), the RTE simplifies to: L(0, \omega) = \int0^\infty T(0, t) \cdot \sigmae(t) L^e(t, \omega) dt where T(0, t) = \exp\left(-\int0^t \sigmat(s) ds\right) is the transmittance, \sigmae(t) is the emission coefficient, and \sigmat(t) is the extinction coefficient. 4. Transfer Function Application The emission and extinction coefficients are derived from the scalar field \Phi(t) evaluated along the ray: L^e(t, -\omega) = L^e(C(\Phi(t)), -\omega) \sigmat(t) = \alpha(\Phi(t)) \quad \text{(or similar mapping to extinction)} Where C is a color map and \alpha is an opacity/extinction map. 5. Delta Tracking (Woodcock Tracking) To sample distances unbiasedly in the non-homogeneous medium defined by \Phi(t): Estimate \sigma{t,\max}, the maximum extinction coefficient along the ray. This can be derived from the global maximum \Phi value and the opacity map, or estimated via the BVH ranges. Sample a distance t to the next event: t = -\frac{\ln(1-\xi)}{\sigma{t,\max}} where \xi \in [0, 1) is a uniform random number. Evaluate \sigmat(t) at the sampled point. Reject the event as "virtual" with probability: P[\text{virtual}] = 1 - \frac{\sigmat(t)}{\sigma{t,\max}} If rejected, sample a new distance t and repeat. 1. Initialize: Set accumulated transmittance T{acc} = 1.0, accumulated radiance L{acc} = 0. 2. Ray Marching Loop: a. Sample distance t using Delta Tracking formula with \sigma{t,\max}. b. Compute sample position \mathbf{x} = \mathbf{o} + t\omega. c. Evaluate Field: i. Traverse BVH to find all particles whose support radius intersects \mathbf{x}. ii. For each intersecting particle i, compute di(\mathbf{x}). iii. If di(\mathbf{x}) < \sigma ri, compute \phii(\mathbf{x}) = wi e^{-\frac{1}{2}(di(\mathbf{x})/ri)^2}. iv. Accumulate \Phi(\mathbf{x}) = \sum \phii(\mathbf{x}). v. Early Termination: If clampMaxCumulativeValue is set and \Phi(\mathbf{x}) exceeds it, clamp \Phi(\mathbf{x}) to this value and stop summing further particles. d. Apply Transfer Function: i. Compute \sigmat = \alpha(\Phi(\mathbf{x})). ii. Compute L^e = C(\Phi(\mathbf{x})) (assuming emission model). e. Update Transmittance: i. T{acc} \leftarrow T{acc} \cdot \exp(-\sigmat \cdot \Delta t)? Note: In Delta Tracking, the step size t is the distance to the next potential interaction. The transmittance update depends on the specific integration scheme. Standard Woodcock tracking updates transmittance based on the sampled step if the event is accepted, or effectively skips the medium if virtual. However, the standard path tracing formulation integrates the extinction along the path. The source describes the rejection probability but implies the integral solution. A common implementation accumulates optical depth \tau = \int \sigmat ds. In Delta Tracking, one typically accumulates \sigmat \cdot t{step} only for accepted events or uses the rejection to skip. Given the source's focus on the rejection probability, the standard approach is: if accepted, add emission term T{acc} \cdot \sigmae \cdot L^e \cdot (1/\sigma{t,\max})? No, the source gives the RTE integral. Let's stick to the source's explicit formulas. Correction based on standard Delta Tracking in Path Tracing (Raab [16] cited): The distance t is sampled from the majorant distribution. If the event is accepted (not virtual): L{acc} \leftarrow L{acc} + T{acc} \cdot \frac{\sigmae(t)}{\sigma{t,\max}} \cdot L^e(t) T{acc} \leftarrow T{acc} \cdot \frac{\sigmat(t)}{\sigma{t,\max}} If the event is virtual, T{acc} remains unchanged (or effectively, we just sample a new t). Refining based on Source text: The source provides the RTE solution and the rejection probability. It does not explicitly give the recursive update for T{acc} in the path tracing context, but cites Raab [16]. The standard unbiased estimator for the integral \int T(t) \sigmae(t) L^e(t) dt using a majorant \sigma{t,\max} is: Sample t \sim \text{Exp}(\sigma{t,\max}). Accept with prob \sigmat(t)/\sigma{t,\max}. If accepted, contribution is \frac{T(t) \sigmae(t) L^e(t)}{\sigma{t,\max}}. T(t) = \exp(-\sigma{t,\max} t). Let's write the pseudocode to reflect the source's explicit components: BVH traversal for \Phi, Delta Tracking for t, and the RTE integral. 3. Return L{acc}. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rbfvolumepathtrace(rayorigin, raydirection, bvh, particles, transferfunc, sigmatmax, clampmax): """ rayorigin: vec3 raydirection: vec3 bvh: BVH structure built on particles particles: list of {position, radius, weight} transferfunc: function(phi) -> (sigmat, color) sigmatmax: float, maximum extinction coefficient clampmax: float, optional clamp for accumulated phi """ accumulatedradiance = 0.0 currenttransmittance = 1.0 tcurrent = 0.0 # Ray length limit or max iterations could be added here while currenttransmittance > epsilon: # 1. Sample distance using Delta Tracking xi = randomuniform(0, 1) tstep = -log(1 - xi) / sigmatmax tsample = tcurrent + tstep # 2. Evaluate Scalar Field Phi at sample point samplepos = rayorigin + tsample raydirection phivalue = evaluaterbffield(samplepos, bvh, particles, clampmax) # 3. Apply Transfer Function sigmat, emissioncolor = transferfunc(phivalue) # 4. This implies C returns the emitted radiance L^e. # We need sigmae. Usually sigmae = sigmat if purely emitting? # Or sigmae is separate. Source simplifies to sigmas=0. # Let's assume transferfunc returns (sigmat, Le). # We need sigmae. If not provided, assume sigmae = sigmat (common in simple models) or 0. # Given "non-scattering media... relying purely on emission and absorption", # and RTE term is sigmae L^e. # If the transfer function maps phi to "emission", it might be sigmae L^e directly. # Let's assume emissionterm = emissioncolor represents sigmae L^e. contribution = tmajoranttransmittance emissioncolor / sigmatmax accumulatedradiance += currenttransmittance contribution # Update transmittance for the next step? # In path tracing with delta tracking, if we accept, we "hit" the medium. # The transmittance for the next segment is updated by the actual extinction. # Tnext = Tcurrent exp(-sigmat tstep) ? # No, in the recursive formulation of path tracing: # L = T (sigmae Le / sigmatmax) + T (sigmat / sigmatmax) Lnext # Here T is the transmittance from origin to t. # The term T (sigmat / sigmatmax) is the probability of surviving to t and having a real event. # The next bounce/scatter would use Lnext. # Since sigmas = 0, there is no scattering. The path ends. # So we only add the emission term. # However, to continue marching, we need to account for the absorption. # The transmittance T(0, t) accumulates. # For the next step, we start from tsample. # The transmittance from tsample to infinity is handled by the recursive call or loop. # The "currenttransmittance" in the loop usually represents T(0, tsample). # But for the next step, we need T(tsample, infinity). # Actually, standard delta tracking path tracing: # If accepted, we add emission. Then we continue with updated transmittance? # If no scattering, the path terminates after the first accepted emission event? # No, emission can happen at any depth. # The integral is over t. # The estimator sums contributions from all accepted events along the ray. # So we do NOT update currenttransmittance to 0. We continue. # But we must account for the fact that we passed through the medium. # The transmittance T(0, t) is exp(-int0^t sigmat). # In the estimator, we use Tmajorant. # The loop continues to sample further t. # Update tcurrent tcurrent = tsample # If we want to model absorption reducing the contribution of deeper events: # The term T(0, t) in the integral handles this. # Our estimator uses Tmajorant(t). # The ratio T(0,t)/Tmajorant(t) = exp(-int0^t sigmat) / exp(-sigmatmax t). # This ratio is not explicitly tracked in the simple estimator above. # The standard unbiased estimator for the integral I = int f(t) dt with PDF p(t) is f(t)/p(t). # Here f(t) = T(0,t) sigmae Le. # p(t) = sigmatmax exp(-sigmatmax t). # Estimator = T(0,t) sigmae Le / (sigmatmax exp(-sigmatmax t)). # We don't know T(0,t) exactly without integrating sigmat. # But we can accumulate optical depth tau = int0^t sigmat(s) ds. # Then T(0,t) = exp(-tau). # So we need to track tau. # Let's add optical depth tracking # This is a standard requirement for Delta Tracking in path tracing to compute exact transmittance. pass else: # Virtual event: reject and sample new t # tcurrent remains the same? No, we sampled a distance from the current position. # If virtual, we effectively skipped that distance. # We continue from tsample? Or from tcurrent? # Delta tracking samples from the current position. # If virtual, we just discard the event and sample a new distance from the current position. # So tcurrent does not advance. pass return accumulatedradiance def evaluaterbffield(samplepos, bvh, particles, clampmax): phi = 0.0 # Traverse BVH to find candidates candidates = bvh.traverse(samplepos) for particle in candidates: delta = samplepos - particle.position distsq = dot(delta, delta) radiussq = particle.radius particle.radius supportfactor = 3.0 # radiusSupportFactor if distsq < (supportfactor particle.radius) 2: # Gaussian kernel val = particle.weight exp(-0.5 distsq / radiussq) phi += val if clampmax > 0 and phi >= clampmax: phi = clampmax break return phi radiusSupportFactor (\sigma): Multiple of base particle radius for BVH bounds and kernel truncation. Default: 3. Smaller values improve performance but may cause truncation artifacts. clampMaxCumulativeValue: Threshold for accumulated \Phi. If exceeded, evaluation terminates early. Useful in regions of high overlap to preserve contours at the cost of dynamic range. Overlapping Particles: In splatting, overlapping particles cause visual clutter and BVH performance issues. RBF volume rendering handles this by treating the volume as a continuous field. \sigma{t,\max} Estimation: Worst-case complexity O(N) for value estimation. Costly for large datasets. It is only necessary for small datasets with unpredictable overlap or if the user cannot guess the cumulative maximum. For large datasets (e.g., cosmology), manual specification of clampMaxCumulativeValue is preferred. Truncation Artifacts: Setting radiusSupportFactor too low can cause visible artifacts where the Gaussian kernel is abruptly cut off. Time Complexity: The preprocessing step for value estimation has worst-case time complexity O(N), where N is the number of particles. Rendering complexity depends on the number of particles intersected by the ray and the depth of the BVH. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the particle data (N particles) and the BVH structure. Performance: Allows interactive rendering of hundreds of millions of particles at high resolution (e.g., 4000) without simplification or proxy geometry. Strengths: Handles overlapping particles without visual clutter. Supports full path tracing (unlike previous RBF implementations restricted to ray casting). Adjustable smoothing/sharpening via kernel radius and weight. Analytical derivatives available for shading. Limitations: Value estimation for \sigma{t,\max} can be costly for large, complex datasets. Requires careful tuning of radiusSupportFactor to balance performance and artifact avoidance. When to Use: Suitable for scientific visualization of particle-based data (e.g., SPH fluids, cosmology) where continuous field representation is desired and full path tracing is needed. When Not to Use: If the dataset is extremely large and \sigma{t,\max} estimation is prohibitive, and manual clamping is not feasible, or if simple splatting is sufficient and path tracing is not required. RBF volume rendering is frequently referred to as a Smoothed Particle Hydrodynamics (SPH) approach due to its use in visualizing SPH fluid dynamics codes. The method was implemented in Intel OSPRay and the Open Volume Kernel Library (VKL) using ISPC. It builds on the Woodcock-tracking volume path tracer of Raab [16] and integrates RBF reconstruction into a volume sampling kernel API, leveraging interval iterators for space skipping. The approach addresses limitations of earlier RBF implementations that were restricted to ray casting.
