name: Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture
head: Multi-core time-sliced pipeline, Time-slicing
body: The Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture is a hardware design methodology for volume rendering that achieves real-time performance by overlapping distinct pipeline stages through time-slicing. It solves sequential processing bottlenecks by allowing multiple tasks to run simultaneously on shared or replicated functional blocks, enabling continuous hardware-software communication and interactive frame rates. The architecture decomposes the volume rendering pipeline into independent functional blocks that are configured or replicated as sub-cores based on processing requirements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volumetric data (voxels), transformation matrices (Model-View-Projection), and rendering parameters (opacity, shading models). Output: Final rendered image frame. Data Structures: Context Memory: A shared RAM structure used for inter-component communication. It stores intermediate results (e.g., dot products) for several clock cycles so they can be accessed by other components. Normal Mode Registers: Provide a common interface for components to access context memory. Context Address Snooping Mechanism: Allows components to monitor and access stored information in the context memory. Sub-cores: Basic functional blocks (multipliers, adders, inner product processors) that are physically considered as sub-cores. They are configured or replicated to execute specific operations. Numbered Steps: 1. Pipeline Decomposition: Divide the rendering pipeline into functional blocks: classifier, gradient calculator, shearing-warping block, shader, and composer. 2. Component Implementation: Implement these blocks as independent, reusable components/sub-cores. The gradient calculator, shearer-composer, shading processor, and matrix multiplication processor are composed from basic functional blocks like multipliers, adders, or inner product processors. 3. Configuration/Replication: Based on the processing required by the calling module, the embedded sub-core is configured or replicated to execute a specific operation. 4. Time-Sliced Execution: Use time-slicing to overlap execution stages. This allows the simultaneous processing of several tasks, such as calculating a dot product for a voxel in the classifier and using that same value in the shader and composer within the same time frame. 5. Inter-Component Communication: Components communicate via the common interface provided by context RAM, normal mode registers, and the context address snooping mechanism. Calculated values (e.g., dot products) are stored in corresponding RAM cells to be called up by another component. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class TimeSlicedPipeline: def init(self): self.contextmemory = {} self.stagestages = ['classifier', 'gradientcalculator', 'shearwarp', 'shader', 'composer'] self.pipelinebuffer = [None] len(self.stagestages) def processvoxel(self, voxeldata): # Stage 1: Classifier self.pipelinebuffer[0] = self.executeblock('classifier', voxeldata) # Stage 2: Gradient Calculator self.pipelinebuffer[1] = self.executeblock('gradientcalculator', voxeldata) # Stage 3: Shear-Warp self.pipelinebuffer[2] = self.executeblock('shearwarp', voxeldata) # Stage 4: Shader (reads gradient from context memory) gradient = self.pipelinebuffer[1] dotproduct = self.dotproduct(self.pipelinebuffer[2], gradient) self.contextmemory['dotproduct'] = dotproduct self.pipelinebuffer[3] = self.executeblock('shader', self.pipelinebuffer[2], dotproduct) # Stage 5: Composer (reads dotproduct from context memory) self.pipelinebuffer[4] = self.executeblock('composer', self.pipelinebuffer[3], self.contextmemory['dotproduct']) return self.pipelinebuffer[4] def executeblock(self, blockname, args): # Hardware mapping: functional blocks are composed of sub-cores # (multipliers, adders, inner product processors) configured per operation # Exact sub-core configuration logic is not specified in the sources return args[0] if args else None def dotproduct(self, vec1, vec2): return sum(a b for a, b in zip(vec1, vec2)) def starttimeslicing(self, voxelstream): # In hardware, time-slicing overlaps stages so multiple voxels are processed concurrently # while stage N processes voxel i, stage N+1 processes voxel i-1 results = [] for voxel in voxelstream: results.append(self.processvoxel(voxel)) return results Parameters: Time-Slice Duration: Not given in the sources. Number of Sub-cores: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Not given in the sources. Boundaries: Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: Not given in the sources. The Vg500 Parallel Pipeline Architecture is a highly parallel, template-based ray-casting hardware implementation designed for real-time volume rendering. It solves the bandwidth and computation bottlenecks of single-pipeline ray casters by employing four identical rendering pipelines that process adjacent voxel values in the x-direction simultaneously. Unlike general-purpose GPU approaches or the larger VIRIM architecture, the Vg500 integrates the entire ray-casting pipeline (interpolation, gradient estimation, shading, classification, and compositing) into a single ASIC, enabling the rendering of 256^3 volumes at 30 fps on a standard PCI card. Time Complexity: Enables real-time rendering by overlapping execution stages. Memory Complexity: Uses context memory for inter-component communication, storing intermediate results for several clock cycles. Measured Performance: Provides real-time frame rates for volumetric datasets through time-sliced multi-core execution. Scaling: Component reusability and multi-core layout allow users to choose required functions, simplifying layout and enabling scalability. Strengths: Real-time performance, continuous hardware-software communication, interactive user interface, simplified layout through component reusability. Limitations: Specific limitations are not detailed in the sources. When to Use: When real-time rendering of volumetric datasets is required, and hardware integration is feasible. When Not to Use: When software-only solutions are preferred, or when the overhead of hardware design is prohibitive. The Time-Sliced Pipelined Architecture was developed as part of the Shear-warp factorization volume rendering visualization system (SWE). It was designed to provide real-time rendering capabilities by implementing a multi-core structure compliant with the rendering pipeline. The architecture emphasizes component reusability and hierarchical design to simplify layout and improve efficiency. It is used in systems like the VolumePro, where the Vg500 ASIC implements a similar pipelined approach. name: Vg500 Parallel Pipeline Architecture
head: Cube-4, EM-Cube, VolumePro / vg500 ASIC
body: The Vg500 Parallel Pipeline Architecture is a highly parallel, template-based ray-casting hardware implementation designed for real-time volume rendering. It solves the bandwidth and computation bottlenecks of single-pipeline ray casters by employing four identical rendering pipelines that process adjacent voxel values in the x-direction simultaneously. Unlike general-purpose GPU approaches or the larger VIRIM architecture, the Vg500 integrates the entire ray-casting pipeline (interpolation, gradient estimation, shading, classification, and compositing) into a single ASIC, enabling the rendering of 256^3 volumes at 30 fps on a standard PCI card. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 3D volume data stored in off-chip Voxel Memory (SDRAM), camera/view parameters, and transfer function lookup tables. Output: Final rendered image pixels written to an off-chip Pixel Memory. Data Structures: Voxel Memory: Consists of 16-bit wide SDRAM modules. Data is organized into 2 \times 2 \times 2 neighboring voxels called miniblocks, which are stored linearly and read/written in bursts of eight voxels. Miniblock Addressing: A miniblock at position [x, y, z] in the volume is assigned to memory module k using the formula: k = \left(\lfloor x/2 \rfloor + \lfloor y/2 \rfloor + \lfloor z/2 \rfloor\right) \mod 4 This linear skewing guarantees that rendering pipelines always have access to four adjacent miniblocks in any of the three slice orientations. Pipeline State: Each pipeline maintains internal shift registers to hold intermediate values (such as interpolated samples and gradients) for communication with neighboring pipelines. Algorithm Steps: The architecture implements template-based ray-casting. Rays are projected from each pixel on a base plane, which is co-planar to the volume face most parallel to the image plane. The resulting base-plane image is subsequently warped onto the final image plane by off-chip graphics hardware. Within the Vg500 ASIC, the processing per sample along the ray proceeds as follows: 1. Voxel Fetch: Each pipeline reads voxel data from the Voxel Memory, with each voxel read exactly once per frame. 2. Interpolation: Sample values along the ray are calculated using tri-linear interpolation of the fetched voxel data. 3. Gradient Estimation: A 3D gradient is computed using central differences between the tri-linear samples. 4. Shading: The gradient is used in the shader stage to compute sample intensity according to the Phong illumination model. 5. Classification: Lookup tables in the classification stage assign color and opacity to each sample point. 6. Compositing: Illuminated samples are accumulated into base plane pixels using front-to-back compositing. Parallelism and Data Flow: The four pipelines (Pipeline 0–3) operate in parallel, processing adjacent voxel or sample values in the x-direction. Each pipeline is connected to its immediate neighbor by shift registers in each major unit (Interpolation, Gradient, Shading, Classification, Compositing), providing values to neighbors in the same cycle. The pipelines on the far left (Pipeline 0) and far right (Pipeline 3) are connected in a wrap-around fashion. Specifically, the shift registers of the rightmost pipeline recirculate values needed in the next cycle and send them to the leftmost pipeline. An off-chip Voxel Memory supplies data to all pipelines, and all pipelines write pixel values to an off-chip Pixel Memory. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processpipeline(pipelineid, raystep): # Initialize accumulated base plane pixel (R, G, B, alpha) basepixel = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # 1. Voxel Fetch: Read 2x2x2 miniblock from Voxel Memory # Memory controller handles linear skewing and burst reads of 8 voxels voxelblock = readminiblock(pipelineid, raystep) # 2. Interpolation: Tri-linear interpolation of the 8 voxels samplevalue = trilinearinterpolate(voxelblock, raystep.t) # 3. Gradient Estimation: Central differences between tri-linear samples # Neighboring samples are provided via shift registers from adjacent pipelines gradient = centraldifferencegradient(samplevalue, pipelineid) # 4. Shading: Phong illumination model intensity = phongillumination(gradient, raystep.direction) # 5. Classification: Lookup table assignment color, opacity = lookuptableclassify(intensity) # 6. Compositing: Front-to-back accumulation cin, ain = basepixel[:3], basepixel[3] cout = tuple(cin[i] + (1.0 - ain) color[i] opacity for i in range(3)) aout = ain + (1.0 - ain) opacity basepixel = cout + (aout,) # 7. Shift Register Update: Pass values to neighbors # Pipeline 3 wraps around to Pipeline 0 shiftregisterupdate(pipelineid, samplevalue, gradient) return basepixel def readminiblock(pipelineid, raystep): # Hardware memory interface fetches 8 voxels from the 2x2x2 miniblock return [0.0] 8 def trilinearinterpolate(voxelblock, t): # Standard tri-linear interpolation using 8 voxel values and parameter t return sum(voxelblock) / 8.0 def centraldifferencegradient(samplevalue, pipelineid): # Hardware gradient unit computes 3D gradient using central differences return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) def phongillumination(gradient, direction): # Hardware shading unit computes intensity using Phong model return 1.0 def lookuptableclassify(intensity): # Hardware classification unit maps intensity to (R, G, B, alpha) via LUT return (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 0.0) def shiftregisterupdate(pipelineid, samplevalue, gradient): # Hardware shift registers pass values to adjacent pipelines pass Parameters: Clock Speed: 133 MHz. Memory Bandwidth: 533 million 16-bit voxels per second (4 \times 133 \times 10^6). Volume Memory: 32, 64, or 128 MBytes of SDRAM. Performance: Over 500 million tri-linear samples per second, sufficient to render 256^3 volumes at 30 frames per second. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Miniblock Skewing: Linear skewing of miniblocks is required to guarantee that rendering pipelines always have access to four adjacent miniblocks in any of the three slice orientations. Wrap-around Logic: The shift registers of the rightmost pipeline must correctly recirculate values to the leftmost pipeline to maintain continuity across the x-direction boundaries. A hardware architecture for real-time volume rendering using the Pixel-Planes 5 system, consisting of graphics processors and pixel processors, where pixel processors store voxel function values and gradients, and graphics processors handle ray tracing and compositing. It separates the heavy classification and shading computations from the ray traversal logic to leverage massive parallelism in the pixel processor array. Time Complexity: Real-time performance is achieved for 256^3 volumes at 30 fps. The architecture processes 4 voxels per clock cycle across 4 pipelines. Memory Complexity: Requires 32–128 MBytes of off-chip SDRAM for volume storage. The ASIC itself contains approximately 2 Mbits of on-chip SRAM. Measured Performance: Renders 256^3 datasets at 30 fps. Memory bandwidth is 533 million 16-bit voxels/second. Strengths: High throughput via parallel pipelines; single-ASIC implementation reduces physical size and cost compared to DSP-based solutions like VIRIM; efficient memory access via miniblock skewing and burst mode. Limitations: Limited to template-based ray-casting (base-plane warping required for arbitrary view angles); does not allow arbitrary intermixing of volumes and polygons. When to use: Real-time volume visualization on PC-class hardware where high frame rates for moderate-resolution volumes (256^3) are required. When not to use: Applications requiring dynamic polygon-volume interaction or arbitrary view angles without warping artifacts. The Vg500 architecture is the core of the VolumePro system, developed by Mitsubishi Electric. It is based on the Cube-4 technology, which Mitsubishi licensed and developed into the Enhanced Memory Cube-4 (EM-Cube) architecture. The VolumePro system was an improved commercial version of EM-Cube, implemented as a PCI card for Windows NT computers. The vg500 ASIC contains approximately 3.2 million random logic transistors and is fabricated in 0.35 \mum technology. It was designed to overcome the limitations of earlier architectures like VIRIM, which required 16 DSPs and achieved only 2.5 fps for similar volume sizes, while being physically larger. name: Pixel-Planes 5 Volume Rendering Architecture
head: Pixel-Planes 5 Architecture
body: A hardware architecture for real-time volume rendering using the Pixel-Planes 5 system, consisting of graphics processors and pixel processors, where pixel processors store voxel function values and gradients, and graphics processors handle ray tracing and compositing. It separates the heavy classification and shading computations from the ray traversal logic to leverage massive parallelism in the pixel processor array. Inputs and Outputs Input: A 3D voxel dataset (e.g., 256 \times 256 \times 256), classification mapping, shading parameters, and observer position. Output: A color image in the frame buffer. Data Structures Pixel Processor Backing Store: Stores function value and gradient for several voxels. In the reference implementation, each pixel processor is assigned 64 voxels. Hierarchical Enumeration: A pyramid of binary volumes installed in each graphics processor to encode coherence. Local Cache: Retains voxels received by a graphics processor for reuse. Numbered Steps 1. Voxel Storage: Pixel processors store function value and gradient for their assigned voxels in their backing store. 2. Classification and Shading: Pixel processors perform classification and shading calculations for all voxels in their backing store. 3. Ray Tracing Initiation: Graphics processors trace rays to generate an image. 4. Voxel Request: Graphics processors request sets of voxels from pixel processors as necessary. 5. Interpolation and Compositing: Graphics processors perform tri-linear interpolation and compositing operations on the requested voxels. 6. Frame Buffer Update: Graphics processors transmit resulting pixel colors to the frame buffer. Strategies for Optimization 1. Hierarchical Enumeration: Install a pyramid of binary volumes in each graphics processor to encode coherence and tell the graphics processor which voxels are interesting (non-transparent) and worth requesting. 2. Adaptive Sampling: Use an adaptive sampling scheme to reduce the number of rays required to generate an initial image. 3. Caching: Retain all voxels received by a graphics processor in a local cache. If the observer does not move, cached voxels drive successive refinement. If the observer moves, cached voxels may still be useful depending on movement distance. Formulas and Parameters Shading Time: Applying a monochrome Phong shading model at a single voxel using a pixel processor takes about 1 msec. Total Classification/Shading Time: For a 256 \times 256 \times 256 voxel dataset, with each pixel processor assigned 64 voxels, the time to classify and shade the entire dataset is about 64 msec. Pitfalls Recomputation: If the user changes the classification mapping such that the set of interesting voxels changes, the hierarchical enumeration must be recomputed, taking several seconds. Hardware Layout: 32 graphics processors (10-20 MFLOP each), 1/4 million pixel processors, 1024 x 768 pixel color frame buffer, 5 Gbit/sec ring network. Performance Estimate (Classification/Shading): For a 256 \times 256 \times 256 voxel dataset, the time to classify and shade the entire dataset is about 64 msec. Frame Rate Estimate (Observer Position Change): 10 fps for slightly coarse images, 1 fps for high-quality images. Frame Rate Estimate (Shading/Classification Change): 20 fps for coarse images, 2 fps for high-quality images, if the hierarchical enumeration is not invalidated. Strengths: High parallelism for shading/classification; potential for real-time interaction. Limitations: Recomputation of hierarchical enumeration is slow (several seconds) if classification mapping changes significantly. The Pixel-Planes 5 architecture was developed under joint funding by DARPA and the NSF, with development starting in the late summer of 1986. It was expected to become operational during the summer or fall of 1989. Although not explicitly designed for volume rendering, its flexibility made it well suited to the task. name: Screen Quad Rendering
head: FBO composition pass, Screen Render Pass, Two-pass rendering pipeline
body: Screen Quad Rendering is the final compositing stage in a two-pass splatting pipeline, where pre-rendered volumetric data stored in off-screen Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) is composited into the default framebuffer. It solves the problem of transferring intermediate rendering results (such as color and auxiliary buffers) from GPU memory to the display surface. It differs from its siblings by explicitly decoupling the volume splatting geometry pass from the final screen composition. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: colorTexture: 2D texture containing the accumulated splat color, bound to unit 0. Format: GLRGBA, type GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. positionTexture: 2D texture containing auxiliary data (e.g., world-space positions), bound to unit 3. Format: GLRGBA32F, type GLFLOAT. viewportSize: Vector2 uniform specifying the target resolution. upscale: Scalar uniform dividing the first-pass texture resolution. Default value 1. crossSection: Scalar uniform for debug overlay positioning, clamped to [0, 1]. Outputs: Default framebuffer (screen) with the composited image. Data Structures: The intermediate rendering state is stored in an FBO with two attachments: 1. GLCOLORATTACHMENT0: colorTexture (RGBA, Unsigned Byte). 2. GLCOLORATTACHMENT3: positionTexture (RGBA32F, Float). Draw buffers are configured as drawBuffers[] = {GLCOLORATTACHMENT0, GLNONE, GLNONE, GLCOLORATTACHMENT3}. Steps: 1. Pass 1 (Splatting): Render the volume primitives into the FBO described above. The texture resolution is scaled by upscale (default 1). 2. Pass 2 (Screen Render Pass): a. Bind the default framebuffer (ID 0). b. Bind colorTexture to texture unit 0 and positionTexture to texture unit 3. c. Set uniforms: viewportSize, upscale, and crossSection. d. Clear the color attachment with {r:0.0, g:0.0, b:0.0, a:1.0} and set loadOp to 'clear', storeOp to 'store'. e. Draw a full-screen triangle using the screen pass shader. f. End the render pass. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def screenquadrenderpass(colortexture, positiontexture, viewportsize, upscale, crosssection): # Clamp cross-section to [0, 1] if crosssection < 0: crosssection = 0 if crosssection > 1: crosssection = 1 # Bind default framebuffer (ID 0) bindframebuffer(0) # Bind textures to units 0 and 3 bindtexture(colortexture, unit=0) bindtexture(positiontexture, unit=3) # Set uniforms setuniform("viewportSize", viewportsize) setuniform("upscale", upscale) setuniform("crossSection", crosssection) # Begin render pass with clear value {r:0.0, g:0.0, b:0.0, a:1.0} beginrenderpass( colorattachment=colortexture, clearvalue=(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0), loadop="clear", storeop="store") # Draw full-screen triangle drawfullscreentriangle() # End render pass endrenderpass() def bindframebuffer(id): pass def bindtexture(tex, unit): pass def setuniform(name, val): pass def beginrenderpass(colorattachment, clearvalue, loadop, storeop): pass def drawfullscreentriangle(): pass def endrenderpass(): pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Wayland Compositing: On Wayland, forcing output alpha to 1.0 in the fragment shader prevents compositing artifacts. Upscale Factor: If upscale > 1, the intermediate textures are smaller than the viewport, requiring filtering during the final draw. Performs a screen-space copy with injected debug logic and alpha forcing. Uses a single oversized triangle to avoid diagonal seams and double-shading artifacts. Time Complexity: Depends only on screen resolution, not volume size. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the intermediate FBO attachments. Strengths: Decouples volume rendering from display output, enabling post-processing and debug overlays. Limitations: Requires two passes; intermediate FBOs consume VRAM. When to use: When post-processing, debug overlays, or separate auxiliary buffer handling is required. This method originates from standard OpenGL and WebGPU rendering pipelines. It is implemented in real-time volume visualization applications. It leverages hardware-accelerated rasterization for the final composition step. gabrielmuller/zazen, https://github.com/gabrielmuller/zazen, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dongeronimo/webgpuvolumerendererdemo, https://github.com/dongeronimo/webgpuvolumerendererdemo, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Screen-space blit / Resample copy
head: Fullscreen Blit with Crosshair, Resample copy, Screen-space blit, blit.wgsl
body: This method performs a screen-space copy (blit) of a source texture, typically a compute-shader output, into a target render target. It simultaneously overlays a debug crosshair and forces the output alpha to 1.0 to prevent compositing artifacts on certain windowing systems like Wayland. It differs from a standard blit by injecting pixel-level crosshair logic and alpha forcing directly in the fragment shader. Input: A source texture accessed via a Shader Resource View (SRV) bound at slot uSRVSlot. Output: A target render target view (RTV) identified by slice uSlice and mip level uMip, cleared to transparent before drawing. Parameters: pSRVSrc (source SRV handle), pShader (shader object containing vertex and pixel shaders), uSRVSlot, uSlice, and uMip. The implementation relies on Direct3D 11 API objects for state management, including render target views, depth stencil views, and viewport structures. 1. Context Acquisition: Get the immediate device context (pDXContext) from the device. 2. Save State: Retrieve the current render target view (pRTVBack) and depth stencil view (pDSVBack) using OMGetRenderTargets. 3. Set Target: Bind the target render target mvvpRTVs[uSlice][uMip] using OMSetRenderTargets. 4. Clear: Clear the target render target to transparent using ClearRenderTargetView. 5. Set Viewport: Create a viewport matching the texture dimensions (VpDepth) and set it using RSSetViewports. Save the previous viewport (VpBack) for restoration. 6. Bind Resources: Bind the source SRV (pSRVSrc) at slot uSRVSlot using PSSetShaderResources. 7. Set Topology: Set the primitive topology to D3D11PRIMITIVETOPOLOGYTRIANGLESTRIP. 8. Bind Shaders: Set the vertex shader guVSScreenQuad using VSSetShader and the pixel shader guPSResample using PSSetShader. 9. Draw: Issue a draw call for 3 vertices using Draw(3, 0). 10. Unbind: Unbind the source SRV, vertex shader, and pixel shader by setting them to nullptr (or null SRV) at their respective slots. 11. Restore State: Restore the original viewport using RSSetViewports with VpBack. 12. Restore Targets: Restore the original render and depth-stencil targets using OMSetRenderTargets. The vertex shader renders a single oversized triangle using vertex indices 0, 1, 2. Positions are (-1.0, -1.0), (3.0, -1.0), (-1.0, 3.0). UVs are (0.0, 1.0), (2.0, 1.0), (0.0, -1.0). This covers the entire screen and extends beyond to ensure full coverage. The fragment shader samples the source texture at the interpolated UV coordinate. It calculates screen dimensions and the absolute offset in pixels from the screen center (0.5, 0.5). It determines if the pixel is inside the crosshair arms: Horizontal arm checks offsetpx.x <= 12.0 AND offsetpx.y <= 2.0 (outer) or <= 1.0 (inner); Vertical arm checks offsetpx.y <= 12.0 AND offsetpx.x <= 2.0 (outer) or <= 1.0 (inner). It returns white (1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) for inner crosshair, black (0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) for outer crosshair, and the sampled color with alpha forced to 1.0 otherwise. The alpha forcing prevents alpha-compositing issues on Wayland when TAA resolve smuggles grass-blade markers in the alpha channel. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendertargetpopulate(pSRVSrc, pShader, uSRVSlot, uSlice, uMip): # 1. Get immediate device context pDXContext = getimmediatedevicecontext() # 2. Save current render targets pRTVBack = CPDXRenderTargetView() pDSVBack = CPDXDepthStencilView() pDXContext.OMGetRenderTargets(1, pRTVBack, pDSVBack) # 3. Set target render target targetrtv = mvvpRTVs[uSlice][uMip] pDXContext.OMSetRenderTargets(1, targetrtv, None) # 4. Clear target to transparent pDXContext.ClearRenderTargetView(targetrtv, Colors.Transparent) # 5. Set viewport to texture dimensions uNumViewports = 1 VpBack = D3D11VIEWPORT() pDXContext.RSGetViewports(uNumViewports, VpBack) VpDepth = CD3D11VIEWPORT(mpTexture, targetrtv) pDXContext.RSSetViewports(uNumViewports, VpDepth) # 6. Bind source SRV pDXContext.PSSetShaderResources(uSRVSlot, 1, pSRVSrc) # 7. Set primitive topology pDXContext.IASetPrimitiveTopology(D3D11PRIMITIVETOPOLOGYTRIANGLESTRIP) # 8. Bind shaders vs = pShader.GetVertexShader(guVSScreenQuad) ps = pShader.GetPixelShader(guPSResample) pDXContext.VSSetShader(vs, None, 0) pDXContext.GSSetShader(None, None, 0) pDXContext.PSSetShader(ps, None, 0) # 9. Draw 3 vertices pDXContext.Draw(3, 0) # 10. Unbind resources pNullSRV = LPDXShaderResourceView(None) pDXContext.PSSetShaderResources(uSRVSlot, 1, pNullSRV) pDXContext.VSSetShader(None, None, 0) pDXContext.PSSetShader(None, None, 0) # 11. Restore viewport pDXContext.RSSetViewports(uNumViewports, VpBack) # 12. Restore render targets pDXContext.OMSetRenderTargets(1, pRTVBack, pDSVBack) Unverified code. Viewport Mismatch: The viewport must be set to the texture dimensions, not the window dimensions, to ensure correct sampling coordinates. State Restoration: Failing to restore the original render targets and viewport can corrupt subsequent rendering passes. Time: O(1) relative to scene complexity; O(N) relative to screen resolution (N = number of pixels). The cost is dominated by the fragment shader execution over the screen area. Memory: O(1) additional memory for state storage (backups of RTV/DSV/Viewport). The source and target textures occupy their respective memory. Hardware: Tested on Direct3D 11 hardware. Resolution: Performance scales linearly with screen resolution. Scene: Independent of scene geometry or voxel count, as it operates on screen-space textures. Strengths: Efficient screen-space data transfer. Built-in debug visualization (crosshair). Avoids CPU-GPU synchronization overhead by using immediate context commands. Limitations: Specific to Direct3D 11 API in the provided implementation. Crosshair logic is hardcoded and not configurable via parameters in the base method. Alpha forcing may be undesirable for non-debug blits. Use when transferring compute shader output to a render target for display or further processing. Use when a debug crosshair is needed for screen-space alignment. Use when targeting Wayland compositors to avoid TAA-related alpha artifacts. Do not use for general-purpose texture copying where alpha preservation is critical and the Wayland TAA issue is not present. Do not use if the crosshair overlay is not desired. The method originates from the voxelG and VoxelizerX projects, which are unofficial implementations of voxel rendering techniques. The specific blit implementation with crosshair overlay is documented in the RenderTarget::Populate function of VoxelizerX and the associated shader code in voxelG. The technique is part of the rendering pipeline for screen-space blitting in voxel renderers. The crosshair overlay was added to assist with debugging screen-space coordinates and alignment. The alpha forcing was introduced to address specific artifacts observed on Wayland compositors with TAA. name: Fullscreen Triangle Rendering
head: Fullscreen Texture Blit, Post-Process Quad, Screen Quad Texture Display, gl_VertexID fullscreen quad
body: Fullscreen Triangle Rendering displays an off-screen render texture onto the entire viewport using a dedicated shader, enabling HUD overlays and screenshot captures. It differs from sibling methods by generating a single oversized triangle via glVertexID to avoid diagonal seams and double-shading artifacts inherent in standard quad strip approaches. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A source render texture and viewport dimensions (width, height). Output: The color buffer of the default framebuffer (screen). Data Structures: Explicit VBO layout: 4 vertices, each containing 3 position floats and 2 texture coordinate floats, totaling 20 floats per quad. Vertex 0: (-1, -1, 0, 0, 0) Vertex 1: (-1, 1, 0, 0, 1) Vertex 2: (1, -1, 0, 1, 0) Vertex 3: (1, 1, 0, 1, 1) glVertexID layout: No explicit VBO is required; geometry is generated procedurally in the vertex shader. Steps: 1. Bind the default framebuffer (ID 0). 2. Clear the color buffer. 3. Bind the render texture to a sampler unit. 4. Bind the dedicated shader program. 5. Set uniforms: screenWidth, screenHeight, and crosshairType. 6. Draw geometry using GLTRIANGLESTRIP with 4 vertices. Formulas: For the glVertexID approach: 1. Compute UV coordinates: uv = \text{vec2}((\text{gl\VertexID} \ll 1) \& 2, \text{gl\VertexID} \& 2) 2. Compute clip-space position: \text{gl\Position} = \text{vec4}(uv \times 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fullscreentrianglerender(sourcetexture, width, height): # State initialization activeframebuffer = 0 colorbuffer = [0.0] (width height 4) samplerunit = [None] activeshader = None # 1. Bind default framebuffer activeframebuffer = 0 # 2. Clear color buffer for i in range(len(colorbuffer)): colorbuffer[i] = 0.0 # 3. Bind source texture samplerunit[0] = sourcetexture # 4. Bind shader activeshader = fullscreentriangleshader # 5. Set uniforms activeshader.uniforms["screenWidth"] = width activeshader.uniforms["screenHeight"] = height activeshader.uniforms["crosshairType"] = 0 # Default value not specified in sources # 6. Draw using triangle strip # Issue draw call: primitive=GLTRIANGLESTRIP, first=0, count=4 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Diagonal Seams: Standard quad rendering can cause seams if the diagonal is shared incorrectly. Double-Shading: Overlapping triangles in quad strips can cause double-shading. Aspect Ratio: If the source texture does not match the viewport aspect ratio, distortion occurs. Performance: While theoretically more optimal by avoiding duplicated ray tracing along the quad edge, no measurable performance difference was observed at the granularity used. Time Complexity: O(1) relative to scene complexity; depends only on screen resolution. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory for vertex data (if using explicit VBO) or O(0) if using glVertexID. Strengths: Simple implementation, no vertex buffer management required with glVertexID, avoids diagonal seams and double-shading. Limitations: Limited to displaying a single texture; not suitable for complex geometry or multiple textures without additional passes. When to Use: Post-processing, HUD overlays, screenshot capture. When Not to Use: Complex 3D scene rendering, multi-texture blending in a single pass. The technique is used in real-time graphics for displaying textures on the screen, particularly in voxel raytracing and post-processing pipelines. The glVertexID approach generates the geometry procedurally, avoiding explicit vertex buffer overhead. name: Rendering Pipeline Architecture
body: Rendering Pipeline Architecture refers to the structural organization of hardware-accelerated splatting techniques, where volumetric or point-cloud data is decomposed into primitives (splats) and rasterized to form an image. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large-scale volumetric datasets in real-time by leveraging GPU rasterization pipelines for transformation, projection, and compositing. It differs from ray-marching methods by using screen-space accumulation (compositing along sheets) rather than per-ray sampling, and from single-pass mesh rendering by explicitly handling transparency and depth occlusion through multi-stage or specialized accumulation buffers. The splatting family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized. 1. Primitive Representation: The volume is decomposed into primitives. These may be explicit geometric shapes (cubes, cells, splats) or implicit functions sampled via texture hardware. Each primitive k is defined by its position \mathbf{p}k, density/extinction coefficient gk or \rhok, and a reconstruction kernel h (typically a Gaussian). 2. Transformation: Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., shear-warp). For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening. 3. Rasterization: The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane. This step leverages hardware-accelerated scan-conversion, depth testing, and blending. The contribution of a voxel D to a screen point (x,y) is determined by the footprint function F(x,y), which is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view direction: F(x,y) = \int h(x-xD, y-yD, z) \, dz The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density: P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D) where \text{weight}(x,y) = F(x-xD, y-yD). 4. Compositing: Contributions are accumulated to form the final image. This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly. Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time). 5. Hardware Acceleration: Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity. A fragment-processing stage that reconstructs continuous and cardinal attributes (normals, colors) into a G-Buffer using weighted blending and ternary depth tests. Choose this when accurate per-splat attribute reconstruction with transparency is required. Combines splat and mesh rendering to enable high-quality shader effects in a single pass by interpolating attributes in object space via elevation map patches. Choose this when avoiding multi-pass blending artifacts and blurring is critical. Separates depth testing, color accumulation, and normalization into distinct passes to ensure exact perspective-correct filtering without explicit sorting. Choose this when exact weight normalization and correct occlusion handling are prioritized over single-pass performance. The concept of splatting was introduced by Levoy as a method for volume visualization. The family evolved to address the limitations of early software-based rendering by leveraging GPU hardware acceleration. Subsequent developments focused on improving attribute quality [1066-splat-attributes-pass.md], reducing pass counts [1254-single-pass-splat-rendering-pipeline.md], and ensuring numerical correctness in perspective projection [2837-three-pass-gpu-point-rendering-pipeline.md]. name: Splat Attributes Pass
head: Blending Pass, G-Buffer Pass
body: The Splat Attributes Pass is the fragment processing stage in hardware-accelerated surface splatting that reconstructs continuous and cardinal attributes from overlapping splats into a reconstruction buffer (G-Buffer). It solves the problem of correctly accumulating per-fragment data (such as normals and colors) from translucent, overlapping point sprites by applying a weighted blending scheme based on radial distance and depth proximity. It differs from standard alpha blending by incorporating a depth-proximity falloff factor to prioritize splats closer to the visible surface, and it sets itself apart from sibling passes by explicitly separating the accumulation of continuous attributes (via weighted sums) from cardinal attributes (via maximum-weight selection, handled in the subsequent Attribute Accumulation and Blending pass). The pass processes each fragment generated by the rasterization of a splat (point sprite). It calculates a composite weight for the splat based on its position within the sprite and its depth relative to the scene geometry, then accumulates weighted attributes into the G-Buffer textures. Inputs: Splat Data: Per-splat attributes including center position, radius, color, and linear depth in view space. Depth Buffer: The current depth buffer containing the depth of the closest visible surface at each pixel. Viewport Size: The dimensions of the render target. Outputs: G-Buffer Textures: gnormal (vec4, location 0): Stores the accumulated weighted normal vector in the RGB channels. gcolor (vec4, location 1): Stores the accumulated weighted color in the RGB channels and the accumulated weight in the Alpha channel. The G-Buffer is implemented as two 2D textures (or render targets): 1. gnormal: Format RGBA (or RGB with unused alpha), type float. Layout: xyz = weighted normal sum, w = unused or padding. 2. gcolor: Format RGBA, type float. Layout: rgb = weighted color sum, a = weight sum. epsilon: A small constant used to normalize the depth-proximity falloff. Typical value: 0.25. 1. Fragment Position Calculation: Calculate the 2D offset of the fragment from the center of the point sprite in screen space. \mathbf{p}{offset} = \mathbf{p}{frag} - \mathbf{p}{center} where \mathbf{p}{frag} is the fragment's position in normalized device coordinates (NDC) or screen space relative to the sprite center. In the reference implementation, this is derived from glPointCoord: \mathbf{p}{offset} = \text{gl\PointCoord} - (0.5, 0.5) 2. Radius Check: Calculate the squared magnitude of the offset. If the fragment lies outside the unit circle (radius 0.5 in NDC), discard the fragment. m^2 = \mathbf{p}{offset} \cdot \mathbf{p}{offset} If m^2 > 0.25, discard. 3. World-Space Offset Conversion: Convert the screen-space offset to a world-space offset proportional to the splat's radius. \mathbf{p}{world\offset} = \mathbf{p}{offset} \times 2 \times r where r is the splat radius. 4. Depth Offset Calculation: Calculate the depth offset from the center of the splat sphere to the fragment's position on the sphere surface. d{offset} = \sqrt{r^2 - \mathbf{p}{world\offset} \cdot \mathbf{p}{world\offset}} 5. Fragment Depth in View Space: Calculate the depth of the fragment on the splat surface in view space by subtracting the depth offset from the linear depth of the splat center. z{frag} = z{linear} - d{offset} where z{linear} is the linear depth of the splat center. 6. Surface Depth Retrieval: Sample the depth buffer at the fragment's screen coordinates to get the depth of the visible surface. z{surface} = \text{LinearDepth}(\text{Texture}(\text{DepthBuffer}, \frac{\text{gl\FragCoord.xy}}{\text{ViewportSize}}).x) 7. Occlusion Test: If the splat fragment is behind the visible surface (z{frag} > z{surface}), discard the fragment. This ensures only the front-facing parts of splats contribute to the attributes. 8. Weight Calculation: Compute two falloff weights and combine them. Radial Falloff (w1): Decreases with distance from the splat center. w1 = 1 - \frac{\sqrt{m^2}}{0.5} Depth-Proximity Falloff (w2): Increases as the splat surface approaches the visible surface (smaller gap). w2 = \frac{z{surface} - z{frag}}{\epsilon} where \epsilon is the epsilon parameter (e.g., 0.25). Combined Weight (w): w = w1 \times w2 9. Normal Calculation: Compute the view-space normal at the fragment's position on the splat sphere. \mathbf{n} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{p}{world\offset}, d{offset}) Note: The reference code constructs the normal vector from the world-space offset and the depth offset component. 10. Attribute Accumulation: Accumulate the weighted attributes into the G-Buffer using additive blending (or manual accumulation in a compute shader). Normal: \mathbf{g\normal.xyz} \leftarrow \mathbf{g\normal.xyz} + w \cdot \mathbf{n} Color: \mathbf{g\color.rgb} \leftarrow \mathbf{g\color.rgb} + w \cdot \mathbf{c} where \mathbf{c} is the splat color. Weight: \mathbf{g\color.a} \leftarrow \mathbf{g\color.a} + w Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. void main() { // 1. Calculate offset from center in screen space vec2 fromcenterptspc = glPointCoord - vec2(0.5, 0.5); // 2. Calculate squared magnitude float magsq = dot(fromcenterptspc, fromcenterptspc); // 3. Discard if outside the point circle if (magsq > 0.25) { discard; } // 4. Convert screen-space offset to world-space offset // Note: Assumes orthographic-like projection scaling for the offset calculation vec2 fromcenterwldspc = fromcenterptspc 2.0 i.radius; // 5. Calculate depth offset from the sphere surface float depthoffset = sqrt(i.radius i.radius - dot(fromcenterwldspc, fromcenterwldspc)); // 6. Calculate fragment depth in view space float depth = i.linearDepth - depthoffset; // 7. Sample the depth buffer to get surface depth vec2 texcoords = glFragCoord.xy / viewportsize; float surfacedepth = linearDepth(texture(gdepth, texcoords).x); // 8. Discard if splat is behind the surface if (depth > surfacedepth) { discard; } // 9. Calculate radial falloff weight float w1 = 1.0 - (sqrt(magsq) / 0.5); // 10. Calculate depth-proximity falloff weight float w2 = (surfacedepth - depth) / epsilon; // 11. Combine weights float weight = w1 w2; // 12. Compute view-space normal from geometry // The normal is derived from the vector from the splat center to the fragment on the sphere vec3 normal = normalize(vec3(fromcenterwldspc, depthoffset)); // 13. Accumulate weighted normal // Assuming atomicAdd or render target blending is handled by the pipeline // Here we compute the value to be added vec3 normalcontrib = weight normal; // 14. Accumulate weighted color vec3 colorcontrib = weight i.color; // 15. Accumulate weight float weightcontrib = weight; // Output values to be accumulated into G-Buffer // In a real shader, this would be written to a render target with ADD blending // or accumulated in a compute shader buffer. // For the purpose of this article, we define the final G-Buffer values as sums: // gnormal.xyz = sum(wi normali) // gcolor.rgb = sum(wi colori) // gcolor.a = sum(wi) // Note: The actual writing depends on the specific rendering API setup. // If using OpenGL blending: // glFragData[0] = vec4(normalcontrib, 0.0); // For gnormal // glFragData[1] = vec4(colorcontrib, weightcontrib); // For gcolor } This configuration sets up the blending state for the Splat Attributes Pass to ensure correct accumulation of translucent splats. It involves clearing the color buffer to RGBA(0,0,0,0) to ensure zero initial alpha, disabling depth testing, and enabling blending with separate blend factors: RGB uses GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA / GLONE, and Alpha uses GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA / GLONE, with the blend equation set to GLFUNCADD for both. This setup is typically used when rendering instanced quads representing splats. A full-screen triangle pass that reads an intermediate sRGB-blended splat accumulation texture, converts it to linear space, and outputs the result for premultiplied alpha blending onto the final SceneColor buffer. It takes parameters including an intermediate texture (IntermediateTexture) and a sampler (IntermediateSampler). Time Complexity: O(N \cdot F), where N is the number of splats and F is the average number of fragments per splat (determined by the splat radius and screen resolution). The depth buffer sampling and discard operations are constant time per fragment. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H) for the G-Buffer textures, where W and H are the viewport dimensions. Performance: The pass is highly parallelizable and benefits from hardware-accelerated rasterization and blending. The depth test and discard logic can reduce the effective workload if splats are largely occluded. Strengths: Provides physically plausible attribute reconstruction (normals, colors) for surface splatting by considering depth proximity. It is efficient as it leverages standard GPU fragment processing. Limitations: The accuracy of the normal and color reconstruction depends on the density of splats and the correctness of the depth buffer. If splats are too sparse, the G-Buffer may contain gaps or inaccurate normals. The use of a fixed epsilon value may not be optimal for all scene scales. When to use: When surface splatting is required for rendering point clouds or Gaussian splats, and accurate per-pixel normals and colors are needed for lighting or further processing. When not to use: If only a simple color accumulation is needed without normal reconstruction, or if the depth buffer is not available or unreliable. The Splat Attributes Pass is part of the rendering pipeline for surface splatting, a technique used to render point clouds and Gaussian splats as smooth surfaces. The method of using depth-proximity falloff to weight attributes is described in the context of point cloud rendering using OpenGL. The broader context of splatting as a volume rendering technique involves treating volumetric data as geometric primitives rasterized onto the screen. The specific implementation details, including the G-Buffer layout and weight calculation, are derived from open-source point cloud rendering projects. arminkz/PointCloudRendering, https://github.com/arminkz/PointCloudRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, https://github.com/YuanBaoSMadLab/OpenSplat4D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Splat Depth Pass
head: Front-Face Depth Pass, Visibility Pass
body: The Splat Depth Pass computes the depth of the front surface of a point sprite (splat) for each fragment, enabling correct occlusion handling during surface splatting. It differs from standard binary depth testing by applying a small epsilon shift to the calculated depth, which prevents z-fighting and gaps between overlapping splats by ensuring consistent blending at surface boundaries. Inputs and Outputs Input: Fragment shader context including glFragCoord (window-space coordinates), glPointCoord (normalized texture coordinates within the point sprite, range [0,1]), and vertex attributes i.radius (splat radius in world space) and i.depth (or equivalent linear depth of the point center). Output: glFragDepth (window-space depth value written to the depth buffer). Data Structures No explicit data structures are required; the method operates on per-fragment state provided by the graphics API. Steps 1. Calculate offset from center: Compute the 2D vector from the center of the point sprite to the current fragment. \mathbf{v}{center} = \text{gl\PointCoord} - [0.5, 0.5] 2. Check circular boundary: Calculate the squared magnitude of \mathbf{v}{center}. If |\mathbf{v}{center}|^2 > 0.25, the fragment lies outside the unit circle and is discarded. 3. Compute world-space offset: Scale the normalized offset by the splat's radius to get the world-space 2D offset vector. \mathbf{v}{world} = \mathbf{v}{center} \times 2 \times i.radius 4. Calculate depth offset: Determine the z-offset from the center of the sphere to the front surface at the current 2D position using the Pythagorean theorem. d{offset} = \sqrt{i.radius^2 - \mathbf{v}{world} \cdot \mathbf{v}{world}} 5. Compute final depth: Subtract the depth offset from the center's linear depth and add an epsilon value to shift the depth slightly towards the camera. d{final} = \text{linearDepth}(\text{gl\FragCoord}.z) - d{offset} + \epsilon 6. Write depth: Assign d{final} to glFragDepth. Formulas Boundary Check: |\mathbf{v}{center}|^2 \le 0.25 Depth Offset: d{offset} = \sqrt{r^2 - |\mathbf{v}{world}|^2} Final Depth: z{frag} = z{center} - d{offset} + \epsilon Parameters epsilon (\epsilon): A small constant added to the depth to blend splats close to the surface. Value: 0.25 (derived from epsilonMultiplier in the source implementation). Edge Cases and Pitfalls Z-fighting and Gaps: Without the epsilon shift, overlapping splats at the same depth may cause z-fighting or visible gaps due to precision errors. The epsilon ensures splats near the surface are blended correctly. Precision: The calculation assumes linear depth. If non-linear depth is used, linearDepth() must convert window-space Z to linear eye-space Z before subtraction. Radius Zero: If i.radius is zero, the depth offset is zero, and the depth equals the center depth minus epsilon. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. vcenter = glPointCoord - vec2(0.5, 0.5) magsq = dot(vcenter, vcenter) if magsq > 0.25: discardfragment() vworld = vcenter 2.0 i.radius dotval = dot(vworld, vworld) radiussq = i.radius i.radius depthoffset = sqrt(max(radiussq - dotval, 0.0)) linearcenterdepth = linearDepth(glFragCoord.z) finaldepth = linearcenterdepth - depthoffset + epsilon glFragDepth = finaldepth A technique that maintains exactly one surface layer per pixel using a depth band to decide blending, replacing, or discarding fragments. It differs from the standard Splat Depth Pass by accommodating depth uncertainty, though it may cause occlusion artifacts in complex geometry. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment. The calculation involves basic arithmetic operations and a square root. Memory Complexity: O(1) auxiliary memory. No additional buffers are allocated; it writes directly to the depth buffer. Strengths: Simple to implement in the fragment shader; effectively handles occlusion for point-based surface rendering; prevents z-fighting via epsilon adjustment. Limitations: Relies on the assumption that splats are spherical and uniformly sized. Does not handle transparency or volume accumulation directly (handled by subsequent passes). When to use: When rendering point clouds as surfaces where correct occlusion is required before color accumulation. When not to use: For volume rendering where depth is integrated along rays, or when splats are not spherical. The method is derived from implementations of point cloud surface rendering, specifically those using spherical splats to approximate surfaces. The specific epsilon adjustment technique is documented in the PointCloudRendering repository. arminkz/PointCloudRendering, https://github.com/arminkz/PointCloudRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Single-Layer Ternary Depth Test
head: Single-layer depth test, Ternary Depth Test, Ternary Depth Test for Surface Reconstruction, Three-way z-test, Weyrich et al. depth test, Z-blend test
body: The Single-Layer Ternary Depth Test is a rasterization technique for surface splatting that maintains exactly one surface layer per pixel, using a depth band to decide whether to blend, replace, or discard incoming fragments. It solves the problem of handling overlapping splats during surface reconstruction by replacing the standard binary pass/fail depth test with a ternary logic that accommodates depth uncertainty. It differs from depth-interval grouping by maintaining only a single surface layer per pixel, which simplifies the pipeline but causes visibility and occlusion artifacts in complex geometry. Inputs and Outputs Input: A stream of splat fragments, each with a depth value d (or zd) and associated color/weight data. State: Each pixel maintains a single stored depth value d{stored} (or zs) and a running accumulated sum (e.g., EWA sum) for the single surface layer. Output: The final color and opacity for the pixel, representing the single closest surface layer. Data Structures Pixel State: A single depth value zs (or d{stored}) is stored in the depth buffer or a dedicated surface layer buffer. No multi-layer stack is maintained. Parameters \varepsilon{\Delta z}: A scaling factor for the depth extents of the splat. Typically set to 1.0. \varepsilon{bias}: A bias term accounting for numerical inaccuracies, comparable to glPolygonOffset's parameter unit. hz: The depth extent (or half-height) of the splat. Algorithm Steps 1. Compute Epsilon Band: For each incoming splat, compute the epsilon band size \varepsilon based on the splat's depth range hz: \varepsilon:= hz \cdot \varepsilon{\Delta z} + \varepsilon{bias} 2. Compare Depths: For each incoming fragment with depth d (or zd), compare it to the currently stored depth d{stored} (or zs) for that pixel. 3. Apply Ternary Test: Determine the action based on the difference between the fragment depth and the stored depth: Z-Blend: If the fragment depth falls within the \varepsilon-band of the stored value, i.e., |d - d{stored}| \le \varepsilon (or equivalently, not (zd < zs - \varepsilon) and not (zd > zs + \varepsilon)), blend the fragment into the running EWA sum. Z-Fail (Discard): If the fragment is significantly behind the stored layer (zd < zs - \varepsilon), discard the fragment. Z-Pass (Replace): If the fragment is significantly in front of the stored layer (zd > zs + \varepsilon), replace the stored layer with this new fragment (updating d{stored} and resetting/initializing the sum). Note: The sources describe the "Z-Pass" condition as replacing the stored layer. In a standard single-layer rasterization context, this implies the new fragment is considered the new "closest" surface, overwriting the previous state. 4. Normalization: After processing all fragments for a pixel, the accumulated color and weight are normalized. Because only a single surface layer is maintained and no coverage-based opacity is involved in the basic test, the normalized output is fully opaque wherever any surfel contributes, even at silhouettes with low accumulated weight. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def singlelayerternarydepthtest(fragment, pixelstate): """ fragment: object with attributes.depth (zd),.color,.weight pixelstate: object with attributes.storeddepth (zs),.accumulatedcolor,.accumulatedweight Returns: Updated pixelstate """ # 1. Compute epsilon band size # hz is the depth extent of the splat, assumed to be available from fragment or global config # epsilondeltaz is typically 1.0 # epsilonbias accounts for numerical inaccuracies epsilon = fragment.hz epsilondeltaz + epsilonbias zd = fragment.depth zs = pixelstate.storeddepth # 2. Ternary Depth Test if zd < zs - epsilon: # Z-Fail: Fragment is significantly behind the stored layer # Discard fragment, do not update pixel state return pixelstate elif zd > zs + epsilon: # Z-Pass: Fragment is significantly in front of the stored layer # Replace the stored layer pixelstate.storeddepth = zd pixelstate.accumulatedcolor = fragment.color fragment.weight pixelstate.accumulatedweight = fragment.weight return pixelstate else: # Z-Blend: Fragment is within the epsilon band # Blend into the running sum pixelstate.accumulatedcolor += fragment.color fragment.weight pixelstate.accumulatedweight += fragment.weight return pixelstate The pseudocode assumes fragment.hz is available. In practice, this is derived from the splat's geometry. The "Replace" action resets the accumulation, which is consistent with maintaining a single layer where the new front-most fragment becomes the sole contributor. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Hard Opaque Fringes: Because the normalized output is always fully opaque wherever any surfel contributes, even at silhouette pixels where only a few surfels partially cover the pixel footprint and the accumulated weight is low, the method produces hard, opaque fringes along object boundaries. This results in a "crusty" shell appearance rather than a gradual opacity falloff. Self-Occlusion Artifacts: The single-layer constraint exacerbates self-occlusion errors at concavities (e.g., inside ears or under chins). Deeper surfels that should form a second layer are incorrectly rejected by the ternary test, resulting in holes or translucent patches that reveal the background through what should be an opaque, self-occluding object. Usage Context: The ternary depth test is used only for surface reconstruction; regular depth tests are still required for triangle pipelines. Complexity: Time complexity is linear with respect to the number of splats per pixel, as each splat is processed once with constant-time depth comparisons. Memory complexity is O(1) per pixel, as only a single depth value and accumulation buffer are maintained. Performance: The method is computationally efficient due to the lack of multi-layer management and sorting overhead associated with depth-interval grouping. Strengths: Simple implementation; low memory footprint; effective for simple, convex surfaces where single-layer assumption holds. Limitations: Fails to handle complex geometry with self-occlusion or multiple surface layers per pixel. Produces aliasing and silhouette artifacts due to the lack of coverage-based opacity. When to use: Suitable for simple surface splatting where performance is critical and geometry is relatively simple (e.g., convex objects). When not to use: Unsuitable for complex scenes with concavities, self-occlusion, or where accurate silhouette rendering is required. The Single-Layer Ternary Depth Test was introduced by Weyrich et al. in 2007 as a method for surface splatting. It was designed to handle overlapping splats during surface reconstruction by providing a more robust depth test than the standard binary pass/fail test. It serves as a baseline for comparison against more advanced techniques like depth-interval grouping, which was introduced to address the limitations of the single-layer approach. 3DSS: 3D Surface Splatting for Inverse Rendering, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2605.05876, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) A hardware architecture for surface splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/1275808.1276490, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Radix Sort for Splat Depth
head: 16-bit Radix Sort for Splatting, Depth Sorting via Radix Sort, Tsplat depth sort
body: This method sorts projected 3D Gaussian splats by their depth values to establish a front-to-back rendering order, which is critical for correct alpha blending of translucent splats. It distinguishes itself from comparison-based sorts by leveraging the bit-pattern ordering of IEEE 754 floating-point numbers to achieve O(n) time complexity with small constants, resulting in performance that is consistently 2 times faster for ~100k–200k elements. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of projected splats, where each splat contains a depth field (f32). Output: The projected list sorted in ascending order of depth (front-to-back). Auxiliary: aux buffer of same size as projected; countslo, countshi histogram arrays; offsets prefix sum array. Data Structures: projected: Array of splat structs. Each struct has depth: f32. countslo, countshi: Arrays of u32 with size 65,536 (2^{16}). offsets: Array of u32 with size 65,536. aux: Array of splat structs, same size as projected. Parameters: Parallel sort threshold: 50,000 splats. If splat count < 50,000 or no thread pool is available, use sequential radix sort. Otherwise, use a parallel unstable sort on depth bit patterns. Algorithm Steps: 1. Edge Case: If the number of splats is \le 1, return immediately. 2. Histogram Initialization: Initialize countslo and countshi to zero. 3. Histogram Population: Iterate through each splat in projected: Let k be the bit pattern of splat.depth reinterpreted as a u32. Increment countslo[(k & 0xFFFF)]. Increment countshi[(k >> 16)]. 4. Pass 1 (Low 16 bits): Compute prefix sums of countslo into offsets. Scatter splats from projected to aux based on the low 16 bits of their depth bit pattern (k \& 0xFFFF). 5. Pass 2 (High 16 bits): Compute prefix sums of countshi into offsets. Scatter splats from aux back to projected based on the high 16 bits of their depth bit pattern (k >> 16). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def sortbydepth(projected: list, aux: list, countslo: list, countshi: list, offsets: list) -> None: n = len(projected) if n <= 1: return # Parallel threshold check if n >= 50000: # Use a parallel unstable sort on depth bit patterns projected.sort(key=lambda s: s.depth.tobits()) return # Reset histograms for i in range(65536): countslo[i] = 0 countshi[i] = 0 # Populate histograms for splat in projected: k = splat.depth.tobits() # Reinterpret f32 bits as u32 countslo[k & 0xFFFF] += 1 countshi[k >> 16] += 1 # Pass 1: Sort by low 16 bits # Compute exclusive prefix sums for offsets offsets[0] = 0 for i in range(1, 65536): offsets[i] = offsets[i-1] + countslo[i-1] # Scatter to aux for splat in projected: k = splat.depth.tobits() bucket = k & 0xFFFF idx = offsets[bucket] aux[idx] = splat offsets[bucket] += 1 # Pass 2: Sort by high 16 bits # Compute exclusive prefix sums for offsets offsets[0] = 0 for i in range(1, 65536): offsets[i] = offsets[i-1] + countshi[i-1] # Scatter back to projected for splat in aux: k = splat.depth.tobits() bucket = k >> 16 idx = offsets[bucket] projected[idx] = splat offsets[bucket] += 1 Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Float Bit Pattern: This method relies on positive float bit patterns preserving ordering when reinterpreted as u32. Precision: The method uses the full 32-bit float representation. No precision loss occurs during the bit reinterpretation, but sorting stability is not guaranteed unless the secondary key (e.g., original index) is included, which is not done in this basic variant. Gaussian Sorting orders 3D Gaussians by their distance from the camera to ensure correct alpha blending during rasterization. It solves the transparency accumulation problem by establishing a front-to-back draw order, which is critical because Gaussians with non-zero opacity must be rendered in depth order. It builds on Radix Sort for Splat Depth by applying the radix sort to a global index buffer of Gaussian attributes rather than just projected splat depths. Fast Splat Sorting is an optimization for volume rendering pipelines that replaces the single 48-bit combined tileID+depth radix sort with two sequential, smaller-key sorts: a 32-bit depth sort of visible splats followed by a 16-bit tileID sort of generated fragments. It sets itself apart from its parent Radix Sort for Splat Depth by decoupling depth ordering from tile assignment, and from Gaussian Sorting by relying on explicit fragment duplication rather than implicit spatial partitioning. This separation reduces computational complexity by leveraging the fact that the number of visible splats (n) is typically smaller than the number of fragments (m). Gaussian Splat Sorting sorts projected 3D Gaussian splats front-to-back within screen-space tiles to enable correct alpha blending. It differs from its parent Radix Sort for Splat Depth by operating on a per-tile basis using a combined tile-ID and depth key, and from Gaussian Sorting by relying on a simple monotonic depth proxy rather than complex geometric comparisons. Default Camera Sort is a compositing technique for oriented Gaussian ellipses (splats) that sorts them back-to-front relative to a camera viewpoint to ensure correct translucent blending. It differs from its siblings by automatically binding the sort order to the active scene camera without requiring explicit provider configuration. This method compresses the conventional 64-bit depth sorting key into 32 bits to reduce sorting traffic and the number of radix passes required for splat sorting. It differs from popular CUDA implementations that use 64-bit keys by mapping depth to a specific range where only the lower 23 mantissa bits vary, allowing tile IDs to occupy the minimum necessary higher bits. This optimization is particularly beneficial for Vulkan sorting implementations, which are often slower than CUDA's built-in sorting, while maintaining quality metrics comparable to 64-bit approaches. DistWar is a method that accelerates sorting by exploiting hardware-accelerated visibility ordering in the rasterizer to perform a fast depth test and bypass the CUDA radix sort. This method converts float16 values to uint16 such that lexicographical comparison of the uint16 representation preserves the original float16 ordering. It operates by viewing the tensor as uint16, casting to int32, XORing with the sign mask 0x8000, and casting back to uint16. The constant 0x8000 flips the sign bit to ensure correct unsigned integer sorting. Time Complexity: O(n) for the radix sort passes, where n is the number of splats. The constant factor is small due to the fixed 2-pass structure. Memory Complexity: O(n) for the auxiliary buffer aux and O(1) for the histogram arrays (fixed size 65,536). Performance: Consistently 2 times faster than comparison-based sorts for ~100k–200k elements. Strengths: Linear time complexity, predictable performance, no recursion depth issues, efficient use of cache due to sequential memory access in scatter/gather phases. Limitations: Requires positive depth values. Not stable by default. Parallelization threshold must be tuned for specific hardware. When to Use: When sorting large numbers of splats for front-to-back rendering where performance is critical and depth values are positive. When Not to Use: When stability is required without additional overhead, or when depth values include negative numbers that are not handled by bit manipulation. This method is described in the context of optimizing 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization pipelines. It is part of the broader effort to accelerate splatting by replacing slower comparison-based sorts with hardware-friendly radix sorts. The use of a 2-pass 16-bit radix sort on float bit patterns is a standard optimization for depth sorting in GPU rendering. name: Gaussian Sorting
head: Depth Sorting for Alpha Blending, Gaussian Depth Sorting
body: Gaussian Sorting orders 3D Gaussians by their distance from the camera to ensure correct alpha blending during rasterization. It solves the transparency accumulation problem by establishing a front-to-back draw order, which is critical because Gaussians with non-zero opacity must be rendered in depth order. It builds on Radix Sort for Splat Depth by applying the radix sort to a global index buffer of Gaussian attributes rather than just projected splat depths. Inputs: A list of N Gaussians, each defined by a position \mathbf{p}i, opacity \alphai, and other attributes (color, covariance, etc.). A view matrix \mathbf{V} transforming world space to camera space. A regular buffer (not sparse residency) storing Gaussian attributes. Outputs: A sorted index buffer \mathcal{I} of length N, where \mathcal{I}[k] is the index of the k-th closest Gaussian to the camera. Data Structures: Gaussian Attribute Buffer: A contiguous GPU StorageBuffer containing one entry per Gaussian. Index Buffer: An array of uint32 of size N, initialized to [0, 1, \dots, N-1]. Depth Buffer: An array of float or uint32 of size N to store computed depths for sorting. Steps: 1. Transform to Camera Space: For each Gaussian i, compute \mathbf{p}'i = \mathbf{V} \mathbf{p}i. The depth is the z-component zi = \mathbf{p}'i.z. 2. Compute Distances: Use zi as the sort key for each Gaussian. 3. Radix Sort Indices: Perform a radix sort on the index buffer \mathcal{I} based on the computed depths z{\mathcal{I}[j]} using compute shaders. 4. Render: Pass the sorted index buffer to the vertex shader to fetch attributes from the storage buffer in front-to-back order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussiansort(gaussians, viewmatrix): """ Sorts Gaussians by depth for alpha blending. Args: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: pos: (x, y, z) in world space opacity: float viewmatrix: 4x4 matrix transforming world to camera space. Returns: sortedindices: List of integers, indices into gaussians list, sorted front-to-back. """ n = len(gaussians) indices = list(range(n)) depths = [] # Step 1 & 2: Transform to camera space and extract z-depth for i in range(n): p = gaussians[i].pos # Homogeneous transformation: pcam = V [p.x, p.y, p.z, 1]^T w = viewmatrix[3][0]p[0] + viewmatrix[3][1]p[1] + viewmatrix[3][2]p[2] + viewmatrix[3][3] z = (viewmatrix[2][0]p[0] + viewmatrix[2][1]p[1] + viewmatrix[2][2]p[2] + viewmatrix[2][3]) / w depths.append(z) # Step 3: Stable radix sort indices by depths sortedindices = stablesortbykey(indices, depths) return sortedindices def stablesortbykey(keys, values): """ Stable sort that returns indices sorted by values. Python's built-in sort is stable; GPU implementations use a 2-pass radix sort on uint32 reinterpreted floats. """ return sorted(range(len(keys)), key=lambda i: values[i]) Parameters: Buffer Type: Regular buffer is used instead of sparse residency buffers. Sorting Algorithm: Radix sort. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sparse Residency Buffers: Avoid using sparse residency buffers. They require indirection texture lookups for UV coordinates in virtual texturing, adding lookup overhead. Furthermore, support is limited: less than a third of desktop GPUs and just over 10% of Android devices support sparseResidencyBuffer. MoltenVK (Apple) generally lacks this feature. Even on hardware that supports it, performance may be unsatisfactory. Precision: The depth values must be compared accurately. Using the z-coordinate in camera space is standard. Degenerate Input: If multiple Gaussians share identical depths, a stable sort or a secondary key must be used to impose a weak ordering, such as comparing original indices or base vertices. A method that introduces a temporal coherence heuristic into the tile sorting phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization, avoiding the computational cost of re-sorting Gaussians whose depth order has not changed between consecutive frames. It sets itself apart from standard per-frame sorting by leveraging the high degree of similarity between adjacent video frames to skip redundant sorting operations. An ordering technique that sorts draw calls front-to-back based on the dot product of the vector between chunk positions and the camera position, reducing z-buffer burden and increasing speed for alpha blending. It is applied by calling vertpool.order with a lambda comparing two DAICs a and b: if \text{dot}(b.\text{pos} - a.\text{pos}, \text{cam}.\text{pos}) < 0 return true; if > 0 return false; otherwise return (a.\text{baseVert} < b.\text{baseVert}) to impose a weak ordering. Sorts Gaussians in z-order at regular intervals during training to resolve cache contention in the alpha blending backward pass. It significantly slows down training when the number of Gaussians is small due to massive atomic contention and false sharing, where threads in different tiles write to the same cache line. When the per-Gaussian backward pass is enabled, omitting repeated z-ordering during densification reduces this false sharing issue. Time Complexity: O(N) for radix sort on fixed-width keys. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the index buffer and depth arrays. Performance: Using regular buffers avoids the indirection texture lookup overhead required by sparse residency buffers, leading to better performance on supported hardware. Strengths: Ensures correct alpha blending for transparent Gaussians. Works on a wide range of hardware due to the avoidance of sparse residency features. Limitations: Sorting is required for every frame to maintain correct alpha blending order. Sparse residency buffers are not recommended due to poor support and performance. When to use: When rendering 3D Gaussians with opacity that require correct alpha blending. When not to use: When Gaussians are opaque and depth sorting is not required for correctness. Gaussian Sorting originated with the introduction of 3D Gaussian Splatting by Kerbl et al., where Gaussians with opacity require alpha blending and must be sorted by distance from the camera. The method was further detailed in implementations such as "Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting", which highlighted the use of compute shaders for depth calculation and radix sorting of indices. The approach is also referenced in unofficial implementations like thomasantony/splat and adapted in voxel engine contexts for front-to-back rendering of chunks.
