name: Temporal Coherence Heuristic for Gaussian Sorting
body: A method that introduces a temporal coherence heuristic into the tile sorting phase of 3D Gaussian Splatting rasterization, avoiding the computational cost of re-sorting Gaussians whose depth order has not changed between consecutive frames. It sets itself apart from standard per-frame sorting by leveraging frame-to-frame similarity to skip redundant sorting operations. Inputs: Screen-projected 3D Gaussians with their camera-space depth z, and the sorted depth order from the previous frame. Outputs: A depth-sorted list of Gaussians per tile, ready for front-to-back alpha compositing. Gaussian List: An array of Gaussian primitives per tile, each containing screen-space position, covariance, opacity, and depth z. Tile Sort State: For each tile, a record of the sorted Gaussian indices from the previous frame. 1. Initialize: For the first frame, perform a standard depth sort of Gaussians within each tile. 2. Frame Start: For subsequent frames, iterate through all tiles. 3. Check Coherence: For each tile, compare the current depth z of the Gaussians against the depth order stored from the previous frame. 4. Skip or Re-sort: If the relative depth order of all Gaussians in the tile remains unchanged, skip sorting for that tile. If any Gaussian's depth order has changed relative to its neighbors, re-sort the tile. 5. Composite: Render all tiles using the resulting sorted Gaussian lists. SortMode: Enum defining sorting frequency (Always, SortEveryNFrames, CutoutsEveryNSorts). SortRefreshRate: Uint parameter (1-60) specifying frames between sorts when SortEveryNFrames is active. CutoutsRefreshRate: Uint parameter (1-60) specifying frames between cutout updates when CutoutsEveryNSorts is active. Not given in the sources. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def temporalcoherencesort(gaussianspertile, previoustilesorts, frameindex): currenttilesorts = [] for tileidx, gaussians in enumerate(gaussianspertile): if frameindex == 0: currenttilesorts.append(sortbydepth(gaussians)) else: prevsort = previoustilesorts[tileidx] currentsort = sortbydepth(gaussians) if isdepthorderchanged(currentsort, prevsort): currenttilesorts.append(currentsort) else: currenttilesorts.append(prevsort) return currenttilesorts def sortbydepth(gaussians): return sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.depth) def isdepthorderchanged(currentsort, previoussort): if len(currentsort) != len(previoussort): return True epsilon = 1e-6 # Tolerance for floating-point precision for curr, prev in zip(currentsort, previoussort): if abs(curr.depth - prev.depth) > epsilon: return True return False Controls how frequently the depth sorting pass executes to balance performance and visual stability. SortMode: Enum defining sorting frequency (Always, SortEveryNFrames, CutoutsEveryNSorts). SortRefreshRate: Uint parameter (1-60) specifying frames between sorts when SortEveryNFrames is active. CutoutsRefreshRate: Uint parameter (1-60) specifying frames between cutout updates when CutoutsEveryNSorts is active. Reduces sorting overhead when depth order is stable across frames. Memory overhead: stores previous frame's sort order per tile. Performance gain depends on scene dynamics; diminishes in highly dynamic scenes. Not given in the sources for exact complexity metrics or hardware-specific performance. The method was introduced in the context of large-scale and scalable formulations for 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically in the work referred to as "Gaufre". It addresses efficient Gaussian sorting in large-scale scenes, building on earlier spatial partitioning lessons from scaling NeRFs. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) wuyize25/gsplat-unity, https://github.com/wuyize25/gsplat-unity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Fast Splat Sorting
head: Depth and TileID Sorting, Split Radix Sort for Splatting, Separating Depth and Tile Sorting, Splat Sorting Dispatch
body: Fast Splat Sorting is an optimization for volume rendering pipelines that replaces the single 48-bit combined tileID+depth radix sort with two sequential, smaller-key sorts: a 32-bit depth sort of visible splats followed by a 16-bit tileID sort of generated fragments. It sets itself apart from its parent Radix Sort for Splat Depth by decoupling depth ordering from tile assignment, and from Gaussian Sorting by relying on explicit fragment duplication rather than implicit spatial partitioning. This separation reduces computational complexity by leveraging the fact that the number of visible splats (n) is typically smaller than the number of fragments (m). The method replaces the standard 48-bit radix sort (used in 3DGS) which sorts fragments by a combined key of tileID and depth. Instead, it performs two distinct sorting passes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n visible splats, each with a 32-bit depth value, plus camera parameters and sorting flags. Intermediate: A set of m fragments, where each fragment corresponds to a splat intersecting a specific tile. Each fragment carries a 16-bit tileID. Output: An ordering array of indices, sorted such that splats are ordered by depth within each tile, and tiles are processed in raster order. Data Structures: 1. Splat Data: Each visible splat i has a depth value di (stored as f32). 2. Fragment Data: Each fragment j has a tileID tj (stored as u16). 3. Ordering Array: Uint32Array of size m, storing indices to the fragment list. Steps: 1. Depth Sort (Visible Splats): Collect all n visible splats. Perform a radix sort on the 32-bit depth values. This step produces a list of splats sorted by depth. 2. Fragment Generation: For each splat in the depth-sorted list, determine which tiles it intersects. Generate a fragment for each intersected tile. Each fragment inherits the splat's depth and is assigned the tile's 16-bit ID. Note: The sources mention using tighter AABBs and approximate tile-ellipse intersection tests to reduce false-positive fragments, but the sorting logic itself assumes the fragments are already generated. 3. TileID Sort (Fragments): Perform a radix sort on the m fragments using their 16-bit tileID as the key. Because the splats were already sorted by depth in Step 1, and radix sort is stable, the resulting list is sorted primarily by tileID (raster order) and secondarily by depth (front-to-back). Formulas: The total complexity is split as follows: T{48\text{-bit}}(m) \approx T{32\text{-bit}}(n) + T{16\text{-bit}}(m) Where T{48\text{-bit}}(m) \approx 3 \times T{16\text{-bit}}(m) assuming linear scaling of radix sort runtime with the number of bits. Parameters: numsplats (u32): Total number of splats to process. camerax, cameray, cameraz (f64): Camera position coordinates. directionx, directiony, directionz (f32): Camera viewing direction vector. radial (bool): Enables radial sorting mode. fastsort (bool): Enables fast sorting mode. frontsort (bool): Selects between 16-bit front sort and 32-bit sort. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode implements the dispatch logic described in the sources. It includes validation checks and inline stable radix sort implementations to avoid external dependencies. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fastsplatsort(buffers, maxsplats, numsplats, camera, direction, radial, fastsort, frontsort, ordering): # Validate input array lengths and bounds if not (len(buffers.rangemeshids) == len(buffers.rangebases) == len(buffers.rangecounts)): raise ValueError("rangemeshids, rangebases, and rangecounts must have equal lengths") if not all(0 <= idx < buffers.rangecounts[i] for i, idx in enumerate(buffers.centerupdaterangeindices)): raise ValueError("centerupdaterangeindices out of bounds") if sum(buffers.rangecounts) 3 != len(buffers.updatecenters): raise ValueError("updatecenters length mismatch") if not all(0 <= idx < buffers.rangecounts[i] for i, idx in enumerate(buffers.matrixupdaterangeindices)): raise ValueError("matrixupdaterangeindices out of bounds") if len(buffers.updatematrices) != len(buffers.matrixupdaterangeindices) 16: raise ValueError("updatematrices length mismatch") activesplats = 0 if frontsort: activesplats = sort16centersfrontinternal(buffers, maxsplats, numsplats, camera, direction) else: activesplats = sort32centersinternal(buffers, maxsplats, numsplats, camera, direction, radial, fastsort) # Copy sorted indices to output array if activesplats > 0: ordering[0:activesplats] = buffers.ordering[0:activesplats] return activesplats def sort16centersfrontinternal(buffers, maxsplats, numsplats, camera, direction): # Performs 16-bit radix sort on fragment tileIDs return stableradixsort16(buffers.fragmenttileids, buffers.fragmentindices, numsplats) def sort32centersinternal(buffers, maxsplats, numsplats, camera, direction, radial, fastsort): # Performs 32-bit radix sort on visible splat depths return stableradixsort32(buffers.splatdepths, buffers.splatindices, numsplats) def stableradixsort16(keys, indices, n): # Standard 16-bit stable radix sort (counting sort per 8-bit digit) for digit in [0, 1]: counts = [0] 256 for i in range(n): counts[(keys[i] >> (digit 8)) & 0xFF] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] output = [0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): d = (keys[i] >> (digit 8)) & 0xFF output[counts[d] - 1] = indices[i] counts[d] -= 1 indices[:] = output return n def stableradixsort32(keys, indices, n): # Standard 32-bit stable radix sort (counting sort per 8-bit digit) for digit in [0, 1, 2, 3]: counts = [0] 256 for i in range(n): counts[(keys[i] >> (digit 8)) & 0xFF] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] output = [0] n for i in range(n - 1, -1, -1): d = (keys[i] >> (digit 8)) & 0xFF output[counts[d] - 1] = indices[i] counts[d] -= 1 indices[:] = output return n Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fragment Count: The number of fragments m can be significantly larger than n. The 16-bit sort must handle this larger dataset efficiently. False Positives: Without tight bounding boxes, the fragment generation step may create unnecessary fragments, increasing m and slowing down the 16-bit sort. The sources recommend using tight AABBs and approximate tile-ellipse intersection tests to mitigate this. Validation: The implementation must validate that range arrays and update arrays have consistent lengths and bounds to prevent out-of-bounds memory access. Sort Stability: The algorithm relies on stable radix sort to preserve the depth ordering established in Step 1 when sorting by tileID in Step 2. A variant that explicitly splits the generation of depth-sorted per-tile splat lists into two separate radix sort routines. It sets itself apart by decoupling depth ordering from tile assignment, allowing the use of smaller key sizes (32-bit and 16-bit) instead of a single large key. Time Complexity: The total sorting time is the sum of a 32-bit sort on n splats and a 16-bit sort on m fragments. Assuming linear scaling with bit-width, the 48-bit sort is approximately three times as expensive as the 16-bit sort. Measured Performance: Berlin Scene: 0.24 ms total (0.11 ms depth + 0.13 ms tileID) vs. 0.39 ms for 48-bit sort. Campus Scene: 1.00 ms total (0.38 ms depth + 0.62 ms tileID) vs. 1.86 ms for 48-bit sort. Scaling: Performance improves significantly when the majority of splats contribute to the rendered image across multiple tiles, as the depth sort operates on a smaller set of visible splats. Strengths: Reduced computational complexity and better GPU utilization by avoiding large 48-bit sorts. Limitations: Requires an additional fragment generation step. Performance depends on the ratio of fragments to splats (m/n). If m is very large, the 16-bit sort may become a bottleneck. When to Use: Use when rendering large Gaussian Splat models where the 48-bit sort is a bottleneck and the number of visible splats is significantly smaller than the number of fragments. When Not to Use: Avoid if the fragment generation step is already expensive or if the scene has a very high ratio of fragments to splats. Fast Splat Sorting was introduced in the "Splatshop" paper (2025) as part of an efficient CUDA-based splat editing system. It was developed to address the performance limitations of the original 3DGS rendering pipeline, which used a combined 48-bit tileID+depth radix sort. The method leverages the observation that sorting visible splats by depth first, and then sorting the resulting fragments by tileID, is more efficient than sorting all fragments by a combined key. name: Two-Stage Sorting
head: Schutz et al. sorting, Separate Sorting, Two-pass sorting
body: Two-Stage Sorting is a sorting optimization for volume rendering pipelines that splits the generation of depth-sorted per-tile splat lists into two separate radix sort routines to reduce VRAM usage and computational complexity. It sets itself apart from single-stage approaches by decoupling depth ordering from tile assignment, allowing the use of smaller key sizes (32-bit and 16-bit) instead of a single large key. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of n visible Gaussians, each with a depth value \hat{\mu}z and a spatial position determining its tile assignment. Output: Depth-sorted lists of splats for each tile, ready for rasterization. Data Structures: 1. Compacted Depth Buffer: Stores indices of visible Gaussians and their 32-bit depth values. 2. Intermediate Gaussian Values: Stores attributes needed for rasterization and blending. These are not compacted to avoid indirection during gradient computation. 3. Tile Index Buffer: Stores the tile index for each Gaussian. Parameters: Tile Size: 16 \times 16 pixels. Max Resolution for 16-bit Tile Indices: 2^{16} \times 256 (roughly 16 megapixels). Note that this limit is slightly lower when image dimensions are not a multiple of 16. Sorting Algorithm: Must be stable (e.g., radix sort) to maintain the order established in the first stage. Steps: 1. Pre-processing: Identify indices of all visible Gaussians and their depth \hat{\mu}z. Write these to compacted buffers using an atomic counter. 2. First Sort (Depth): Perform a radix sort using 32-bit keys to establish depth ordering of the Gaussians. 3. Second Sort (Tile): Perform a radix sort using 16-bit keys (or 32-bit for very high resolutions) to sort splats into per-tile lists. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def twostagesort(gaussians, tilesize=16, imagewidth=1920, imageheight=1080): # Step 1: Pre-processing # Identify indices of all visible Gaussians and their depth, writing them to compacted buffers using an atomic counter. # In a GPU implementation, an atomic counter manages buffer writes to avoid race conditions. visibleindices = [i for i, g in enumerate(gaussians) if g.visible] depthbuffer = [gaussians[i].depth for i in visibleindices] gaussianindices = visibleindices # Intermediate Gaussian values are kept in original order/structure and NOT compacted to avoid indirection during gradient computation. # Step 2: First Sort (Depth) # Perform a radix sort using 32-bit keys to establish depth ordering of the Gaussians. # Standard LSD radix sort for 32-bit integers. Stability is required. depthsortedperm = stableradixsort32bit(depthbuffer, gaussianindices) depthsortedindices = [gaussianindices[i] for i in depthsortedperm] # Step 3: Second Sort (Tile) # Calculate tile indices for each Gaussian. numtilesx = (imagewidth + tilesize - 1) // tilesize tileindices = [] for idx in depthsortedindices: tilex = int(gaussians[idx].pos.x) // tilesize tiley = int(gaussians[idx].pos.y) // tilesize tileidx = tiley numtilesx + tilex tileindices.append(tileidx) # Perform a radix sort using 16-bit keys (or 32-bit for very high resolutions) to sort splats into per-tile lists. # Stability preserves depth order within tiles. tilesortedperm = stableradixsort16bit(tileindices, range(len(depthsortedindices))) tilesortedindices = [depthsortedindices[i] for i in tilesortedperm] # Construct per-tile lists pertilelists = buildpertilelists(tilesortedindices, tileindices, numtilesx) return pertilelists def stableradixsort32bit(keys, values): # Standard LSD radix sort for 32-bit integers. return [v for, v in sorted(zip(keys, values), key=lambda x: x[0])] def stableradixsort16bit(keys, values): # Standard LSD radix sort for 16-bit integers. return [v for, v in sorted(zip(keys, values), key=lambda x: x[0])] def buildpertilelists(sortedindices, tileindices, numtilesx): # Constructs a flat buffer or list-of-lists mapping tile IDs to splat indices. tilemap = {} for idx in sortedindices: tidx = tileindices[idx] if tidx not in tilemap: tilemap[tidx] = [] tilemap[tidx].append(idx) return tilemap Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Resolution Limit: Tile indices must fit in 16 bits. For resolutions exceeding roughly 16 megapixels, 32-bit keys must be used for the second sort. Non-Multiples of 16: If image dimensions are not a multiple of 16, the effective max resolution for 16-bit tile indices is slightly lower. Gradient Computation: Compacting intermediate Gaussian values needed for rasterization and blending should be avoided to prevent additional indirection during the backward pass. Time and Memory Complexity: Original 3DGS: Uses a single 64-bit key sort. Assuming a 48-bit effective key size and an average of 8 tiles per Gaussian, the complexity is O(8 \cdot (16 + 32)n) = O(384n). Two-Stage Sorting: First Sort (Depth): O(32n). Second Sort (Tile): O(8 \cdot 16n) = O(128n). Combined Complexity: O(32n) + O(128n) = O(160n). VRAM Usage: Reduced because it eliminates the need for 64-bit data types to store sorting keys. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in sorting time and VRAM usage compared to single-stage sorting, with benefits increasing as the number of Gaussians increases. Limitations: Requires a stable sorting algorithm. The 16-bit tile index limit restricts maximum resolution unless 32-bit keys are used for the second stage. When to Use: Use when VRAM is constrained or when sorting performance is a bottleneck. Suitable for resolutions up to ~16 megapixels with 16-bit tile keys. When Not to Use: For very high resolutions (>16MP) where 32-bit keys for the second stage negate some VRAM benefits. If the rendering pipeline does not support stable radix sorts. Two-Stage Sorting was introduced by Schutz et al. [73] as an optimization for Gaussian Splatting rendering pipelines. It addresses the computational inefficiency of single-stage radix sorts that use large keys to encode both depth and tile information. The method is implemented in Faster-GS. name: Gaussian Splat Sorting
head: Clip-space w depth sorting, Tile-based sorting using clip-space w
body: Gaussian Splat Sorting sorts projected 3D Gaussian splats front-to-back within screen-space tiles to enable correct alpha blending. It uses clip-space w as a monotonic distance proxy to handle reverse-z projection. Inputs: clipposw: Clip-space w component of the splat position. tileid: Screen-space tile identifier. id: Unique splat identifier. Outputs: sortkeys: Array of 32-bit sort keys. sortvalues: Array of splat IDs corresponding to the keys. Data Structures: sortkeys: 32-bit integer array where the upper 16 bits store tileid and the lower 16 bits store the quantized depth. sortvalues: 32-bit integer array storing the original splat id. Steps: 1. Calculate View Depth: Extract the clip-space w component and clamp to zero. d{\text{view}} = \max(0.0, \text{clip\pos\w}) 2. Normalize Depth: Map the view depth to [0, 1] using a rational function. d{01} = \frac{d{\text{view}}}{1.0 + d{\text{view}}} 3. Quantize Depth: Convert the normalized depth to a 16-bit unsigned integer. d{16} = \lfloor d{01} \times 65535.0 \rfloor \ \& \ 0\text{xFFFF} 4. Create Sort Key: Combine the tile ID and quantized depth into a single 32-bit key. \text{key} = (\text{tile\id} \ll 16) \ | \ d{16} 5. Store Keys and Values: Write the key and the splat ID to the respective sort buffers at the current offset. \text{sort\keys}[\text{offset}] = \text{key} \text{sort\values}[\text{offset}] = \text{id} Parameters: Depth quantization bits: 16. Depth normalization constant: 1.0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Not given in the sources. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def gaussiansplatsort(clipposw: float, tileid: int, splatid: int, sortkeys: list[int], sortvalues: list[int], offset: int) -> None: # Step 1: Calculate view depth viewdepth = max(0.0, clipposw) # Step 2: Normalize depth to 0-1 range depth01 = viewdepth / (1.0 + viewdepth) # Step 3: Quantize depth to 16-bit integer depth16 = int(depth01 65535.0) & 0xFFFF # Step 4: Create sort key by combining tile ID and depth key = (tileid << 16) | depth16 # Step 5: Store key and splat ID in sort buffers sortkeys[offset] = key sortvalues[offset] = splatid Not given in the sources. The method uses clip-space w as a monotonic distance proxy to handle reverse-z projection for front-to-back sorting within tiles. name: Tile-based Gaussian Sorting with Comparison-Free Sorter
head: Comparison-free key sorter, Stage 2 Gaussian Sorting
body: This method is a hardware-oriented sorting module designed for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that outputs the current maximum depth value in a linear delay, tailored to match the one-point-at-a-time consumption of alpha-blending. It differs from pipelined heap designs [20] by emitting <tile-id, depth> keys and consuming tiles front-to-back, yielding fixed per-output latency and avoiding O(\log n) priority-queue operations. Inputs and Outputs: Input: 15-bit unsigned depth values (sign bit skipped as all numbers are positive) and associated values for Gaussian splats within a tile. Output: The address of the largest element (current maximum depth) every 2 cycles, allowing the renderer to consume the front-most splat. Data Structures: Sub-sorter Buffer: Each of the four parallel sub-sorters has a 4 KB key buffer and a 4 KB value buffer, capable of holding 256 data elements. Global Buffer: A shared 12 KB key buffer and 12 KB value buffer for excess points beyond the local 2000-point limit per tile. Bit Grouping: The 15-bit data is divided into groups of sizes (3, 4, 4, 4) bits. Parameters: Tile Size: 16×16 pixels. Sub-sorter Capacity (N): 256 data elements. This value was chosen because a capacity of 512 elements resulted in a critical path delay (N-input OR gate) that limited the frequency to below 500 MHz in a 28 nm process, failing to meet the target of 800 MHz. Processing Rate: One maximum value output every 2 cycles. Algorithm Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the 15-bit depth values into four bit groups: 3 bits, 4 bits, 4 bits, and 4 bits. 2. Clustering: Send these bit groups to the cluster stage for sorting. 3. Sequencing: Process the sorted clusters in the sequence stage to determine the address of the largest element. 4. Output: Emit the address of the maximum value every 2 cycles. 5. Buffer Management: If a tile contains more than 2000 points (exceeding the 4 KB local buffer capacity), excess points are stored in the shared global buffers (12 KB key/value) to prevent image holes caused by discarding points. N = 256 # Sub-sorter capacity BITGROUPS = [3, 4, 4, 4] # Bit group sizes for 15-bit data TARGETFREQMHZ = 800 PROCESSFREQMHZ = 800 # Assumed based on target def sortgaussiansplats(depthvalues15bit): """ Sorts 15-bit depth values using a comparison-free sorter. Returns the address of the maximum element. """ # Step 1: Divide 15-bit data into bit groups # Note: Implementation of bit extraction depends on specific hardware encoding. # Assuming standard binary representation. groups = [] currentbit = 14 for groupsize in BITGROUPS: mask = (1 << groupsize) - 1 groupval = (depthvalues15bit >> currentbit) & mask groups.append(groupval) currentbit -= groupsize # Step 2: Cluster stage sorting # The cluster stage sorts these groups. # In a comparison-free sorter, this typically involves radix-like or # permutation-based logic tailored to the bit groups. sortedgroups = clustersort(groups) # Step 3: Sequence stage to find max address # The sequence stage processes the sorted groups to identify the # address of the largest element. maxaddress = sequencestage(sortedgroups) return maxaddress def clustersort(groups): """ Placeholder for the specific hardware logic of the cluster stage. In the context of the source, this stage handles the sorting of the (3,4,4,4) bit groups. """ # The source does not provide the internal algorithm of the cluster stage, # only that it receives the groups and passes to the sequence stage. # Assuming a standard radix or permutation network for fixed-width groups. return sorted(groups, reverse=True) # Simplified logical representation def sequencestage(sortedgroups): """ Processes sorted groups to get the address of the largest element. """ # The source states this stage gets the address of the largest element. # In a comparison-free sorter, this often involves decoding the # most significant group to identify the max index. return 0 # Placeholder for hardware-specific address generation Edge Cases and Pitfalls: High Variability in Point Density: Gaussian point density per tile varies significantly (from a few hundred to 5000 points). Setting a strict upper bound on processed points per tile and discarding the rest causes image "holes". The shared global buffer mitigates this. Frequency Constraints: Increasing sub-sorter capacity to 512 elements reduces the maximum operating frequency below 500 MHz in a 28 nm process due to the critical path delay of the N-input OR gate. Time Complexity: Linear sorting delay for outputting the maximum value, avoiding the O(\log n) operations found in heap-based approaches. Memory Complexity: Each sub-sorter uses 8 KB (4 KB key + 4 KB value) for 256 elements. A global buffer of 24 KB (12 KB key + 12 KB value) is shared among four sub-sorters. Performance: The design targets 800 MHz in a 28 nm process. It outputs one maximum value every 2 cycles. Strengths: Fixed per-output latency, high sustained throughput, and reduced memory requirements for rasterization compared to heap-based methods. It aligns well with the one-point-at-a-time consumption of alpha-blending. Limitations: The critical path delay limits the sub-sorter capacity to 256 elements to maintain the target frequency. Requires shared global buffers to handle high variability in point density, adding complexity to memory management. This method was proposed in a 2026 paper by as a hardware accelerator for 3D Gaussian Splatting. It addresses the inefficiencies of previous pipelined heap designs [20] which reorder splats by tile index for cache coherence, imposing a cyclic tile scan and extra complexity. The comparison-free sorter is tailored specifically for the monotonic depth consumption of 3DGS alpha-blending. name: Default Camera Sort
head: Back-to-front sort, Splat Painter's Sort, sort splats for the scene camera by default
body: Default Camera Sort is a compositing technique for oriented Gaussian ellipses (splats) that sorts them back-to-front relative to a camera viewpoint to ensure correct translucent blending. It differs from its siblings by automatically binding the sort order to the active scene camera without requiring explicit provider configuration. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A cloud of splats managed by SplatNode, and a camera viewpoint (either the scene camera or a custom provider). Output: A compositing order of splats sorted back-to-front relative to the camera. Data Structures: The SplatNode manages the SplatCloud and triggers the sort operation on a background thread whenever the camera moves. Steps: 1. Determine Viewpoint: Check if a cameraPositionProvider is set. If null (the default), use the scene camera position. If provided, invoke the lambda to retrieve the Position object representing the custom viewpoint. 2. Calculate Depths: For each splat i, calculate the distance di from the splat's center position Pi to the camera position C: di = \| Pi - C \| 3. Sort: Sort the splats in descending order of di (back-to-front). The sort executes on a background thread to avoid blocking the main rendering loop. 4. Update Compositing Order: The node automatically applies the sorted order to the rendering pipeline. Formulas: di = \| Pi - C \|: Euclidean distance from splat center Pi to camera position C. Sort order: descending di ensures back-to-front compositing. Parameters: cameraPositionProvider: A lambda returning a Position object representing the camera's world position. If null, the scene camera is used (default). If provided, it enables the back-to-front painter's sort for that specific viewpoint. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Orbiting Artifacts: If cameraPositionProvider is explicitly set to null in older versions where it was required for sorting, or if the automatic default sort is inactive, the compositing order remains as loaded. This causes visual popping artifacts when orbiting the camera because the splat order does not update to match the new viewpoint. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def updatesortorder(splatcloud, camerapositionprovider): if splatcloud is None: return # Step 1: Determine camera position if camerapositionprovider is not None: camerapos = camerapositionprovider() else: # Default: use scene camera camerapos = scenecamera.position # Standard engine call to retrieve active camera # Step 2: Calculate depths depths = [] for i in range(splatcloud.count): splat = splatcloud.splats[i] # Euclidean distance diffx = splat.pos.x - camerapos.x diffy = splat.pos.y - camerapos.y diffz = splat.pos.z - camerapos.z depth = (diffx2 + diffy2 + diffz2)0.5 depths.append((depth, i)) # Step 3: Sort back-to-front (descending depth) # Stable sort is preferred to maintain original order for equal depths depths.sort(key=lambda x: x[0], reverse=True) # Step 4: Apply order # Reorder the splat cloud or update the index buffer sortedindices = [item[1] for item in depths] splatcloud.applyrenderorder(sortedindices) Sorts visible meshes in ascending order of squared distance to the camera position. Choose when implementing custom sort logic outside the default node behavior. See Gaussian Sorting. Optimized sorting techniques for performance-critical rendering. Choose when the default sort is too slow. See Fast Splat Sorting. Specific implementations tailored for Gaussian splat rendering pipelines. Choose for specialized Gaussian rendering workflows. See Gaussian Splat Sorting. Tile-based sorting approach that pairs tile IDs with depth values. Choose for tile-based renderers or when depth precision issues arise with standard sorting. See 32-bit Tile-Depth Pair Sorting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: The sort is executed on a background thread to prevent frame drops during camera movement. Strengths: Eliminates visual popping artifacts during camera orbiting by automatically updating the compositing order. Removes the need for manual camera position tracking in standard use cases. Limitations: Not given in the sources. When to use: Standard Gaussian splat rendering where correct translucent blending is required and the camera moves. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The Default Camera Sort was introduced as part of the SplatNode implementation in the SceneView library, specifically in commit e7e8fd4. It was developed to address visual popping artifacts that occurred when orbiting cameras in Gaussian splat visualizations, which previously relied on a static load order or required an explicit cameraPositionProvider. The change was part of a broader effort to improve the robustness of Gaussian splatting on platforms like iOS and VisionOS, removing potential AI-generated bugs associated with previous default sort sources. name: Camera Distance Sorting
head: Mesh Sorting by Camera Distance
body: Camera Distance Sorting is a method for ordering visible meshes in a scene based on their proximity to the camera. It solves the problem of correct rendering order for opaque or transparent geometry by ensuring that closer objects are processed appropriately relative to further ones. It sets itself apart from general-purpose sorting by specifically utilizing squared Euclidean distance to the camera position as the primary key, optimizing for the common case of perspective projection where depth correlates with distance. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of visible meshes (or splats), each with a known position in world space and a camera position. Output: The same list of meshes, sorted in ascending order of distance from the camera. Data Structures: Mesh: Contains a position field (e.g., glm::vec3 or float[3]) representing its center or origin. Camera: Contains a position field (e.g., glm::vec3 or float[3]). Steps: 1. For each mesh in the visible list, calculate the squared distance between the mesh's position and the camera's position. 2. Sort the list of meshes based on these calculated squared distances in ascending order (smallest distance first). Formulas: Let Pm be the position of a mesh and Pc be the position of the camera. The squared distance D^2 is calculated as: D^2 = \| Pm - Pc \|^2 = (xm - xc)^2 + (ym - yc)^2 + (zm - zc)^2 where (xm, ym, zm) and (xc, yc, zc) are the respective coordinates. Parameters: Sorting order: Ascending (nearest to furthest). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Using squared distance avoids the computational cost and potential precision issues of square roots, as the relative order remains unchanged. Identical Distances: The sort is not guaranteed to be stable unless a stable sorting algorithm is used. Ties in distance may result in arbitrary ordering among meshes at the same distance. Camera Position: The camera position must be in the same coordinate space as the mesh positions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cameradistancesort(meshes, cameraposition): """ Sorts a list of meshes by their squared distance to the camera. Args: meshes: List of objects with a 'position' attribute (vec3). cameraposition: The camera's position (vec3). Returns: List of meshes sorted by ascending distance to the camera. """ # Calculate squared distance for each mesh # Using a list of tuples (squareddistance, meshindex, mesh) to preserve original reference distancelist = [] for i, mesh in enumerate(meshes): dx = mesh.position.x - cameraposition.x dy = mesh.position.y - cameraposition.y dz = mesh.position.z - cameraposition.z squareddist = dxdx + dydy + dzdz distancelist.append((squareddist, i, mesh)) # Sort by squared distance (ascending) # Note: Python's sort is stable, so original order is preserved for ties distancelist.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) # Extract sorted meshes sortedmeshes = [item[2] for item in distancelist] return sortedmeshes Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for sorting N meshes, where each distance calculation is O(1). Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the distance values during sorting. Performance: Efficient for moderate numbers of meshes. The avoidance of square roots makes the distance calculation very fast. Strengths: Simple to implement, computationally inexpensive, effective for perspective cameras. Limitations: Does not account for occlusion or depth buffer interactions directly; assumes distance is a sufficient proxy for rendering order. Not suitable for orthographic cameras where depth is independent of distance in the same way. This method is derived from the leven project by Nick Gildea, which implements a voxel-based rendering engine. The specific step of sorting visible meshes by squared distance to the camera is documented in the project's source code and associated notes. It represents a standard optimization in real-time rendering pipelines where depth sorting is required for transparency or correct occlusion handling. nickgildea/leven, https://github.com/nickgildea/leven, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Depth Sorting for Transparency
head: Bin Sorting, Radix Sort for Depth
body: Depth sorting for transparency is a rendering technique that organizes gas (smoke) and obstacle data into bins based on their distance from the camera, then renders them in back-to-front order to ensure visually correct foreground/background interaction. It solves the problem of incorrect alpha blending in OpenGL, which requires scene elements to be drawn from furthest to nearest to correctly composite transparent layers. Unlike previous simulation methods that rendered all obstacle data before any gas information, this method renders them simultaneously by emptying bins for all element types in reverse distance order. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of scene elements (smoke particles/voxels and obstacle primitives like boxes or spheres), camera position (Cx, Cy, Cz), minimum distance D0, maximum distance D1, and total number of bins B. Outputs: A sorted rendering order where elements are drawn back-to-front. Data Structures: Depth Bins: A vector of lists. Each list (bin) represents a range of distances from the camera. Element Representation: Smoke/Gas: Stored as individual elements with position (x, y, z). Box Obstacles: Decomposed into six individual quad faces. For each quad, a representative position is calculated by averaging the coordinates of its four vertices: x{avg} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{4} xi}{4}, \quad y{avg} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{4} yi}{4}, \quad z{avg} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{4} zi}{4} Other Obstacles: Similar representative positions are calculated for other primitive types (e.g., spheres). Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialize Bins: Create separate bin vectors for smoke and each obstacle type. The number of bins is B. 2. Calculate Distance: For each element, calculate the Euclidean distance to the camera: d = \sqrt{(x - Cx)^2 + (y - Cy)^2 + (z - Cz)^2} For box quads, use (x{avg}, y{avg}, z{avg}) instead of (x, y, z). 3. Assign to Bin: Map the distance d to a bin index b using the formula: b = \left\lfloor B \frac{d - D0}{D1 - D0} \right\rfloor Clamp b to the range [0, B-1] if necessary. 4. Store Elements: Place the element's data (coordinates, color, alpha) into the list corresponding to bin b for its specific type. 5. Render: Iterate through the bins from the greatest index (B-1) to the smallest (0). For each bin index, render all elements present in that bin for all element types (smoke and obstacles) simultaneously. Parameters: B: Total number of bins. Not given in the sources. D0: Minimum distance. Not given in the sources. D1: Maximum distance. Not given in the sources. Environment Size: A cube with sides of 64 units was used in the reference implementation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def depthsortandrender(elements, camerapos, numbins, mindist, maxdist): """ elements: dict mapping elementtype to list of element objects. Each element has pos (x,y,z) and type ('smoke', 'boxface', etc.) camerapos: tuple (Cx, Cy, Cz) numbins: integer B mindist: float D0 maxdist: float D1 """ # Step 1: Initialize bins for each element type bins = {etype: [[] for in range(numbins)] for etype in elements.keys()} # Step 2 & 3: Calculate distance and assign to bin for etype, elemlist in elements.items(): for elem in elemlist: # Get representative position if etype == 'boxface': # Average of 4 vertices xavg = sum(v.x for v in elem.vertices) / 4.0 yavg = sum(v.y for v in elem.vertices) / 4.0 zavg = sum(v.z for v in elem.vertices) / 4.0 pos = (xavg, yavg, zavg) else: pos = elem.pos # Calculate Euclidean distance dx = pos[0] - camerapos[0] dy = pos[1] - camerapos[1] dz = pos[2] - camerapos[2] dist = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz) 0.5 # Map to bin # Clamp to avoid index errors if dist is outside [mindist, maxdist] if maxdist == mindist: binidx = 0 else: binidx = int(numbins (dist - mindist) / (maxdist - mindist)) binidx = max(0, min(numbins - 1, binidx)) bins[etype][binidx].append(elem) # Step 5: Render back-to-front for binidx in range(numbins - 1, -1, -1): # Render all types in the same bin simultaneously for etype in bins.keys(): for elem in bins[etype][binidx]: renderelement(elem) Complexity: The bin/radix sort algorithm used has a complexity of O(N). Performance: The method proved generally effective with no discernable errors in foreground/background interaction, despite changes in camera angle or distance. Strengths: Ensures correct alpha blending for transparent smoke; allows simultaneous rendering of obstacles and gas; efficient O(N) sorting. Limitations: Requires decomposition of complex obstacles (e.g., boxes into quads) to calculate representative positions; precision depends on bin resolution B and distance range [D0, D1]. When to use: When rendering transparent volumes (smoke, fire) interacting with opaque obstacles in a real-time OpenGL context. When not to use: When exact depth precision within a bin is critical and B is small; when obstacles cannot be easily decomposed into representative primitives. This method was developed as part of a thesis on the efficient computation and rendering of smoke animation. It was implemented to allow real-time simulation by reorganizing the scene for depth sorting, addressing the limitation that OpenGL requires back-to-front drawing order for correct transparency handling. The implementation used a 64-unit cube environment and compared favorably to previous methods that rendered obstacles before gas, which caused visual errors. name: 32-bit Tile-Depth Pair Sorting
head: 32-bit Key Sorting, Resolution-adaptive quantized depth sorting key, VkSplat 32-bit Key Sorting
body: This method compresses the conventional 64-bit depth sorting key into 32 bits to reduce sorting traffic and the number of radix passes required for splat sorting. It differs from popular CUDA implementations that use 64-bit keys by mapping depth to a specific range where only the lower 23 mantissa bits vary, allowing tile IDs to occupy the minimum necessary higher bits. This optimization is particularly beneficial for Vulkan sorting implementations, which are often slower than CUDA's built-in sorting, while maintaining quality metrics comparable to 64-bit approaches. Inputs and Outputs Input: Projected splat depth z (positive real value), tile ID (integer). Output: A 32-bit unsigned integer sorting key. Data Structures The sorting key is a 32-bit unsigned integer (u32) packed with two fields: 1. Tile ID: Occupies the most significant bits (MSBs). The number of bits is resolution-adaptive. 2. Quantized Depth: Occupies the remaining least significant bits (LSBs). This field uses at least 18 bits for standard resolutions (e.g., 1080p with 16x16 tiles). Steps 1. Map Depth: Transform the positive real depth value z into a new value z' using the mapping function: z' = \frac{2z+1}{z+1} This maps z \in (0, \infty) to z' \in (1, 2). 2. Interpret as Float: Treat z' as a standard IEEE 754 single-precision (FP32) floating-point number. Because z' \in (1, 2), the exponent bits are constant, and the ordering of z' is preserved in the bit pattern of the mantissa. 3. Ensure Mantissa Distinctness: Verify that the mapping ensures distinct depth values result in differences only in the lower 23 mantissa bits of the FP32 representation. 4. Pack Key: Extract the bit pattern of the FP32 value z'. Determine the number of bits required for the tile ID based on image resolution and tile size. For images up to 1080p with a 16x16 tile size, this is at most 14 bits. Place the tile ID in the highest bits of the 32-bit integer. Place the higher bits of the floating-point mantissa (from the mapped depth) in the lower bits of the 32-bit integer. The resulting 32-bit integer serves as the sorting key. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def packtiledepthkey(tileid: int, depth: float, imgwidth: int, imgheight: int, tilewidth: int, tileheight: int) -> int: """ Packs tile ID and quantized depth into a 32-bit sorting key. Args: tileid: The integer ID of the tile containing the splat. depth: The positive real depth value of the splat. tilewidth: Width of a tile in pixels. tileheight: Height of a tile in pixels. imgwidth: Total image width in pixels. imgheight: Total image height in pixels. Returns: A 32-bit unsigned integer sorting key. """ # Step 1: Map depth to range (1, 2) zprime = (2.0 depth + 1.0) / (depth + 1.0) # Step 2: Extract FP32 bit pattern (little-endian assumed for GPU sorting) import struct fp32bits = struct.unpack('<I', struct.pack('<f', zprime))[0] # Step 3: Determine bit allocation numtilesx = (imgwidth + tilewidth - 1) // tilewidth numtilesy = (imgheight + tileheight - 1) // tileheight totaltiles = numtilesx numtilesy tileidbits = totaltiles.bitlength() if totaltiles > 1 else 0 # Step 4: Pack key # Extract mantissa (lower 23 bits of FP32 for range 1, 2)) mantissa = fp32bits & 0x7FFFFF depthbits = 32 - tileidbits # Clamp depthbits to available mantissa bits (23), ensuring at least 18 as per typical usage depthbits = max(18, min(depthbits, 23)) # Shift mantissa to keep the most significant depthbits quantizeddepth = mantissa >> (23 - depthbits) # Tile ID in MSBs, quantized depth in LSBs return (tileid << depthbits) | quantizeddepth Parameters Key Size: 32 bits. Tile Size: 16x16 pixels is a common configuration. Resolution: Tested up to 1080p. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Precision Loss: Compressing to 32 bits reduces depth precision compared to 64-bit keys, though no difference in quality metrics was observed for resolutions up to 1080p. Endianness: The bit packing assumes a specific endianness for the float-to-int conversion; the implementation must match the hardware's endianness. Depth Range: The mapping function assumes positive real depths; negative or zero depths are not defined by the formula. Time Complexity: Reduces the number of radix passes compared to 64-bit sorting. Memory Complexity: Reduces intermediate data movement in the front end by halving the key size. Performance: On an NVIDIA RTX 4090 GPU, [RoofGS achieves 10× end-to-end acceleration. Strengths: Optimizes for Vulkan sorting performance, which is often slower than CUDA. Reduces sorting traffic. Limitations: Reduced depth precision compared to 64-bit keys, though quality impact is negligible for typical resolutions. This method was introduced in RoofGS and VkSplat as part of efforts to accelerate 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) rendering and training. It addresses the bottleneck of sorting projected splats by depth, which is a critical step in object-order splatting pipelines. The technique is specifically designed to mitigate the performance gap between Vulkan and CUDA sorting implementations. name: Tile Binning for Splatting
head: Tile Binning, Tsplat tile binning
body: Tile Binning for Splatting groups depth-sorted splats into per-tile buckets to improve cache locality during the compositing phase of Gaussian Splatting rendering. It solves the problem of scattered memory access patterns by organizing splats into coarse depth bins (typically 16x16 pixel blocks) within each tile, serving as the foundational data structure for subsequent rasterization passes. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on a count-then-scatter two-pass approach to organize splats by tile. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of projected splats, each with a bounding box in screen space and a depth value. The splats are sorted by depth prior to binning. Output: A flattened array of splat indices (bins.splatindices) ordered by tile, and an offset array (bins.offsets) indicating the start index of each tile's splats in the flattened array. Data Structures: bins.offsets: An array of size num\tiles + 1. bins.offsets[i] stores the starting index in bins.splatindices for tile i. bins.offsets[numtiles] stores the total number of splats. bins.cursor: A temporary array of size num\tiles, initialized as a copy of bins.offsets[..numtiles], used during the scatter pass to track the current write position for each tile. bins.splatindices: A pre-allocated buffer of size equal to the total number of splats, storing the indices of the splats, ordered by tile. Parameters: TILEW, TILEH: Tile dimensions in pixels. Standard value is 16x16. width, height: Render resolution in pixels. Steps: 1. Calculate Tile Grid: Compute the number of tiles in x and y directions: num\tiles\x = \lceil width / TILE\W \rceil num\tiles\y = \lceil height / TILE\H \rceil num\tiles = num\tiles\x \cdot num\tiles\y. 2. Pass 1: Count Splat-Tile Intersections: Initialize bins.offsets of size num\tiles + 1 to zero. For each splat p in the input list: Determine the tile range [tx0, tx1] \times [ty0, ty1] covered by the splat's bounding box. For each tile (tx, ty) in this range, calculate the linear tile index t = ty \cdot num\tiles\x + tx. Increment a counter for tile t (e.g., counts[t] += 1). 3. Prefix Sum: Perform an exclusive prefix sum on the counts to determine start offsets. For i from 1 to num\tiles: bins.offsets[i] += bins.offsets[i-1] After this step, bins.offsets[i] holds the start index for tile i in the output array. The total number of splats is bins.offsets[numtiles]. 4. Initialize Cursors: Copy the start offsets to the cursor array: bins.cursor[i] = bins.offsets[i] \quad \text{for } i \in [0, num\tiles-1]. 5. Pass 2: Scatter Splat Indices: For each splat index idx and splat p: Determine the tile range [tx0, tx1] \times [ty0, ty1] covered by the splat's bounding box. For each tile (tx, ty) in this range, calculate the linear tile index t = ty \cdot num\tiles\x + tx. Place the splat index idx into the output array at the current cursor position for tile t: bins.splat\indices[bins.cursor[t]] = idx Increment the cursor for tile t: bins.cursor[t] += 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def tilebinsplats(splats, width, height, TILEW=16, TILEH=16): numtilesx = (width + TILEW - 1) // TILEW numtilesy = (height + TILEH - 1) // TILEH numtiles = numtilesx numtilesy # Initialize offsets to zero offsets = [0] (numtiles + 1) cursors = [0] numtiles # Pass 1: Count for splat in splats: xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = splat.boundingbox tx0 = xmin // TILEW ty0 = ymin // TILEH tx1 = (xmax + TILEW - 1) // TILEW ty1 = (ymax + TILEH - 1) // TILEH tx0 = max(0, min(tx0, numtilesx - 1)) ty0 = max(0, min(ty0, numtilesy - 1)) tx1 = max(0, min(tx1, numtilesx - 1)) ty1 = max(0, min(ty1, numtilesy - 1)) for ty in range(ty0, ty1 + 1): for tx in range(tx0, tx1 + 1): t = ty numtilesx + tx offsets[t + 1] += 1 # Evidence uses t+1 or row+tx+1 # Prefix Sum for i in range(1, numtiles + 1): offsets[i] += offsets[i-1] # Initialize cursors for i in range(numtiles): cursors[i] = offsets[i] # Pass 2: Scatter splatindices = [0] offsets[numtiles] for idx, splat in enumerate(splats): xmin, ymin, xmax, ymax = splat.boundingbox tx0 = max(0, min((xmin // TILEW), numtilesx - 1)) ty0 = max(0, min((ymin // TILEH), numtilesy - 1)) tx1 = max(0, min(((xmax + TILEW - 1) // TILEW), numtilesx - 1)) ty1 = max(0, min(((ymax + TILEH - 1) // TILEH), numtilesy - 1)) for ty in range(ty0, ty1 + 1): for tx in range(tx0, tx1 + 1): t = ty numtilesx + tx pos = cursors[t] splatindices[pos] = idx cursors[t] += 1 return splatindices, offsets Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tile-Local Bin Construction assigns Gaussian-tile intersection entries to coarse depth bins within each tile and constructs a flattened tile-bin-major pair stream using direct atomic operations for count and scatter. It solves the problem of organizing splats for cache-efficient compositing by grouping them into depth-ordered buckets, serving as the foundational data structure for subsequent rasterization passes. It is distinguished from its siblings by its reliance on direct atomics for the count/scatter phase, which provides the default performance baseline on modern hardware. Stable Tile ID Sorting groups depth-sorted fragments into per-tile lists using a stable radix sort on tile IDs, preserving the depth order within each tile. It computes a 16-bit tile ID for each fragment and uses it as the key for a 16-bit radix sort. After sorting, it computes the first and last indices for each tile by launching a kernel with one thread per fragment, updating the previous tile's lastIndex and the current tile's firstIndex when tile IDs differ. Splat Compaction is a GPU compute shader that builds a compact list of visible splat indices to enable subsequent passes to only process visible splats. It uses input buffers SplatClusterIndexBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmap, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, and SelectedClusterBuffer (all StructuredBuffer<uint>) and outputs CompactedSplatIndices (RWStructuredBuffer<uint>) and VisibleSplatCount (RWStructuredBuffer<uint>). Parameters include TotalSplatCount, OriginalSplatCount, UseLODRendering, and THREADGROUPSIZE (256). Splat Reordering is a technique to reduce reconstruction buffer bandwidth by storing splats in a pre-rasterization cache and rasterizing all splats for a specific tile consecutively as a batch. It maintains a list of splats for each reconstruction buffer tile, selects one tile at a time, and rasterizes all splats inside that tile as a batch, processing tiles in scan-line order. It uses a modified priority queue ordering criterion for cyclic processing: i \prec j is defined as: false if i < Ic \leq j; true if j < Ic \leq i; i < j otherwise, where Ic is the currently processed tile index. The tile size is typically 8x8 pixels. A pitfall is that using N linked lists on-chip fails for large output resolutions because it cannot support more than N concurrent lists. Conventional heap insertion/removal requires O(log n) operations, but pipelined heap insertion and removal achieve constant throughput (two cycles in FPGA implementation), independent of heap size. Tile Binning for Splatting originated from the need to optimize Gaussian Splatting rendering on GPUs. The specific application to Gaussian Splatting involves adapting these techniques to handle the unique properties of Gaussian primitives, such as their bounding boxes and depth sorting. name: Tile-Local Bin Construction
head: Gaussian-tile binning with atomic count/scatter, Tile-bin-major pair stream construction
body: Tile-Local Bin Construction assigns Gaussian-tile intersection entries to coarse depth bins within each tile and constructs a flattened tile-bin-major pair stream using direct atomic operations for count and scatter. It solves the problem of organizing splats for cache-efficient compositing by grouping them into depth-ordered buckets, serving as the foundational data structure for subsequent rasterization passes. The method uses direct atomics for the count/scatter phase as its default configuration, with alternative aggregation variants producing identical bin-offset arrays and Gaussian-ID streams. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of baseline entries E. Each entry e \in E contains: t(e): Tile identifier. g(e): Gaussian flat identifier. s(e): Original baseline sort key (encoding baseline depth order). z(e): Depth value. Clipped depth range [z{min}, z{max}]. Number of bins K. numtiles: Total number of tiles to process. Output: binOffsets[t, 0...K]: Array defining the concatenated interval for all bins in tile t. The segment for bin b is [binOffsets[t,b], binOffsets[t,b+1]). P: Tile-bin-major pair stream storing tuples (s(e), g(e)). Optional sidecars: flatIds and Packed-GW geometry attributes. Data Structures count[t, b]: Integer array initialized to zero, tracking the number of entries assigned to bin b in tile t. cursor[t, b]: Write pointer initialized from binOffsets, tracking the next available write position within bin b of tile t. P: Array of pairs. The stream is ordered such that all entries for tile t, bin 0 precede entries for tile t, bin 1, etc.. Parameters K = 64: Number of depth bins (default). \epsilon = 10^{-4}: Epsilon for log-space stability. z'{min} = \max(z{min}, \epsilon). z'{max} = \max(z{max}, z'{min} + 10^{-6}). Algorithm 1. Initialize count[t, b] = 0 for all tiles t and bins b \in \{0, \dots, K-1\}. 2. For all entries e \in E in parallel: a. Compute the bin index b(e) using the log-depth bin mapping. b. Atomically increment count[t(e), b(e)]. 3. Perform an exclusive scan on the count array to compute binOffsets[t, b]. 4. Initialize cursor[t, b] to binOffsets[t, b] for all t, b. 5. For all entries e \in E in parallel: a. Retrieve bin b = b(e). b. Retrieve write position p = \text{atomic increment of cursor}[t(e), b]. c. Write P[p] = (s(e), g(e)). d. If flat-id sidecar is enabled, write flatIds[p] = g(e). e. If Packed-GW geometry sidecar is enabled, materialize selected geometry attributes at index p. Log-Depth Bin Mapping Formula The bin index b is computed as follows: u = \text{clamp}\left(\frac{\ln(\max(z, \epsilon)) - \ln(z'{\min})}{\ln(z'{\max}) - \ln(z'{\min})}, 0, 1 - 10^{-6}\right) b = \lfloor K \cdot u \rfloor b = \text{clamp}(b, 0, K-1) Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def tilelocalbinconstruction(entries, zmin, zmax, K, numtiles, enableflatids=False, enablepackedgw=False): epsilon = 1e-4 zprimemin = max(zmin, epsilon) zprimemax = max(zmax, zprimemin + 1e-6) def logdepthbin(z): zsafe = max(z, epsilon) u = (math.log(zsafe) - math.log(zprimemin)) / (math.log(zprimemax) - math.log(zprimemin)) u = max(0.0, min(u, 1.0 - 1e-6)) b = int(math.floor(K u)) return max(0, min(b, K - 1)) # 1. Initialize counts count = [[0] K for in range(numtiles)] # 2. Parallel Count Pass for e in entries: b = logdepthbin(e.z) count[e.t][b] += 1 # 3. Exclusive Scan for Offsets binOffsets = [[0] (K + 1) for in range(numtiles)] for t in range(numtiles): currentoffset = 0 for b in range(K): binOffsets[t][b] = currentoffset currentoffset += count[t][b] binOffsets[t][K] = currentoffset # 4. Initialize Cursors cursor = [row[:K] for row in binOffsets] # 5. Parallel Scatter Pass totalentries = sum(binOffsets[t][K] for t in range(numtiles)) P = [None] totalentries flatIds = [None] totalentries if enableflatids else None gwattrs = [None] totalentries if enablepackedgw else None for e in entries: b = logdepthbin(e.z) p = cursor[e.t][b] cursor[e.t][b] += 1 P[p] = (e.s, e.g) if enableflatids: flatIds[p] = e.g if enablepackedgw: gwattrs[p] = materializegeometry(e) # Standard geometry materialization return binOffsets, P, flatIds, gwattrs Edge Cases and Pitfalls Depth Range Estimation: The z{min} and z{max} are derived from percentile selection of sampled candidates using exact order statistics, not histogram approximation. Incorrect range estimation leads to bin overflow or underflow. Log-Space Stability: The use of \epsilon and clamping prevents \ln(0) and ensures numerical stability for depths near zero. Atomic Contention: Direct atomics are used for count and scatter. Order Within Bin: The atomic scatter operation does not guarantee any specific order within a bin. A post-binning sorting step that restores exact baseline depth order for specific segments of the tile-bin-major pair stream to ensure correct rasterization, while leaving other segments in their tile-local bin order. It balances correctness and speed by repairing only segments likely to cause artifacts or bottlenecks. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: On an RTX 4090, the default direct atomic implementation takes approximately 2.86811 ms. This is faster than warp-private histograms (3.32800 ms), block-local hash aggregation (2.92911 ms), and two-stage aggregation (2.85863 ms), though warp-key grouping is slightly faster at 2.85796 ms. Memory: Requires storage for count, binOffsets, cursor, and the output pair stream P. The size of P is equal to the number of entries |E|. Strengths: Simple implementation, good performance on modern GPUs with efficient atomic units, robust log-depth binning handles wide depth ranges well. Limitations: Atomic contention can become a bottleneck in highly clustered scenes. Tile-Local Bin Construction is part of the TileGS rasterization pipeline, introduced in the paper "TileGS: Tile-Local Depth Binning for Gaussian Splatting Rasterization". It builds on the concept of tile binning for splatting, which groups depth-sorted splats into tile buckets to improve cache locality during compositing [Parent]. The method uses direct atomic operations for count/scatter as the default construction strategy, chosen for its performance characteristics on contemporary hardware. name: Selective Exact Repair
body: Selective Exact Repair is a post-binning sorting step in the TileGS rasterization pipeline that restores exact baseline depth order for specific segments of the tile-bin-major pair stream to ensure correct rasterization, while leaving other segments in their tile-local bin order. It solves the problem of depth ambiguity introduced by atomic scatter operations during bin construction, which produce entries in arbitrary order within a bin. Unlike full sorting, which is prohibitively expensive for large bins, this method selectively repairs only segments that are likely to cause visible artifacts or performance bottlenecks, balancing correctness and speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The pair stream P and its sidecars (flat-id, geometry) after Tile-Local Bin Construction, along with bin offset arrays binOffsets[t, b] for tile t and bin b. Output: A repaired pair stream where selected segments are sorted by the original baseline key s(e), with sidecars aligned. Data Structures: binOffsets[t, b]: Array of integers storing the start index of bin b in tile t. Size: (T \times (K+1)), where T is number of tiles and K is number of bins per tile. P: Array of pairs (depth key, index). sidecars: Arrays aligned with P (e.g., flatid, geometry). R: List of segments to repair, each tuple (t, b, \text{begin}, \text{end}). used: Integer counter for total entries in R. Brep: Maximum number of entries allowed in R (Not given in the sources). Parameters: K: Number of bins per tile (Default: 64). l: Length of a segment (\text{end} - \text{begin}). l{\text{tile}}: Total length of all bins in a tile (\text{binOffsets}[t, K] - \text{binOffsets}[t, 0]). Thresholds (from Table 4 in): No-repair threshold: l \le 1. Local exact-repair maximum: 512 entries. Always-keep long segment cutoff: l \ge 320. Global-tail bucket: l > 512. Tile-share cutoff: l / l{\text{tile}} \ge 45\%. Local-256 share cutoff: 129 \le l \le 256 AND l / l{\text{tile}} \ge 10\%. Early bin repair: b < 2 AND l \ge 16. Steps: 1. Initialize R = \emptyset and \text{used} = 0. 2. Iterate over logical segment IDs q = t \times K + b in tile-bin order. 3. For each segment (t, b): a. Get \text{begin} = \text{binOffsets}[t, b] and \text{end} = \text{binOffsets}[t, b+1]. b. Calculate length l = \text{end} - \text{begin}. c. Calculate l{\text{tile}} = \text{binOffsets}[t, K] - \text{binOffsets}[t, 0]. d. Set \text{keep} = \text{false}. e. If 129 \le l \le 256 AND l / l{\text{tile}} \ge 0.10, set \text{keep} = \text{true}. f. If b < 2 AND l \ge 16, set \text{keep} = \text{true}. g. If \text{keep} is true AND \text{used} + l \le B{\text{rep}}, add (t, b, \text{begin}, \text{end}) to R and update \text{used} = \text{used} + l. 4. For all segments (t, b, \text{begin}, \text{end}) in R: a. Sort P[\text{begin}:\text{end}) by original baseline key s(e). b. Keep flat-id and geometry sidecars aligned with the sorted pair order. 5. Return repaired pair stream and aligned sidecars. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def selectiveexactrepair(P, sidecars, binOffsets, K, Brep): R = [] used = 0 T = len(binOffsets) for t in range(T): for b in range(K): begin = binOffsets[t][b] end = binOffsets[t][b + 1] l = end - begin if l <= 1: continue ltile = binOffsets[t][K] - binOffsets[t][0] keep = False if 129 <= l <= 256 and l / ltile >= 0.10: keep = True if b < 2 and l >= 16: keep = True if keep and used + l <= Brep: R.append((t, b, begin, end)) used += l for (t, b, begin, end) in R: segmentkeys = [P[i][0] for i in range(begin, end)] segmentindices = list(range(begin, end)) sortedpairs = sorted(zip(segmentkeys, segmentindices), key=lambda x: x[0]) for newpos, (key, oldpos) in enumerate(sortedpairs): actualpos = begin + newpos P[actualpos] = P[oldpos] for sc in sidecars: sc[actualpos] = sc[oldpos] return P, sidecars Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The depth key s(e) must be the same near-depth-shifted key used during range estimation to ensure consistency. Boundaries: B{\text{rep}} limits the total repair cost. If not given, it must be defined by the implementation. Degenerate Input: Segments with l \le 1 are skipped, avoiding unnecessary sorting overhead. Constructs the initial bin-major stream. Choose this when you need fast, approximate depth ordering. Consumes the repaired stream. Choose this for the final rendering pass. Time Complexity: Sorting is performed only on selected segments. The cost is O(\sum{s \in R} ls \log ls), where ls is the length of segment s. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the pair stream and sidecars, plus O(|R|) for the repair list. Measured Performance: The selective policy uses fixed global thresholds, not tuned per scene. The default path (No-GW, K=64) is recommended. Strengths: Avoids full sorting cost while ensuring correctness for critical segments. Limitations: May still have artifacts in un-repaired segments if they are large and unordered. Originated in the TileGS paper. It is part of the TileGS rasterization pipeline for Gaussian Splatting. TileGS: Tile-Local Depth Binning for Gaussian Splatting Rasterization, https://doi.org/10.2312/pg.20261013, fetched 2026-10-29

name: Continuous Attribute Interpolation
head: Bilinear Interpolation Attribute Sampling, Correct Interpolation Variant, Direct Interpolation Variant, Geometry and Attribute Sampling, MLS Attribute Sampling
body: Continuous Attribute Interpolation is a method for obtaining continuous reconstruction of UV coordinates for attribute interpolation on splats, specifically designed to avoid visual artifacts at splat boundaries. It solves the problem of discontinuous attribute sampling that arises when intersecting view rays with flat splat planes, which can cause large UV coordinate jumps for neighboring fragments. It sets itself apart from naive direct interpolation by using a "correct interpolation" variant that projects intersections onto a plane defined by elevated neighboring points, ensuring smooth attribute transitions. The method operates on a model represented as a set of elevation and attribute maps, where each patch corresponds to a piece of the 3D model parameterized as a height field over a planar domain. The pipeline operates in a single rendering pass, storing elevation maps in Vertex Buffer Objects (VBOs) and attribute maps in texture objects. Inputs: View ray origin and direction. Splat geometry: A set of input points defining the patch, including their 3D positions and attributes (e.g., normals, texture coordinates). Patch metadata: A 4 \times 4 transformation matrix per patch. Attribute maps: Regular grids storing resampled attributes (normals, textures). Outputs: Corrected UV coordinates for the fragment. Interpolated attribute values (normals, textures) at the fragment location. Elevation Map: A regular grid stored in a VBO. Each cell corresponds to a sample on the support plane. Attribute Map: A regular grid (texture) storing resampled attributes. Resolution is chosen independently per map. Patch Data: For each splat, the system maintains the set of input points and the associated support plane. 1. Patch Partitioning and Overlap Handling: The 3D model is partitioned into regions, each corresponding to a surface patch. To ensure continuous rendering and avoid gaps between patches, patches are made to slightly overlap. An input point is included in a region if its \epsilon-neighborhood intersects the point set of that region, where \epsilon > 0 is a small practical value. 2. Attribute Resampling (Pre-processing): Attributes (normals, textures) are resampled from the original 3D model onto the regular grids of the attribute maps. MLS Method: Normal vectors at arbitrary height field locations are computed as normal vectors of the associated Moving Least Squares (MLS) surface. Bilinear/Delaunay Method: If normal vectors are given per input point, they are resampled on a regular grid on the support plane using bilinear interpolation within a Delaunay triangulation of the projected input points on the support plane. Texture attributes are handled identically to normal vectors. 3. Ray-Splat Intersection: Intersect the view ray with the oriented splat in object space to find the intersection point. 4. UV Coordinate Determination: Two variants exist for determining the UV coordinates on the attribute map: Direct Interpolation Variant: Read off attribute parameters directly on the base plane of the splat. Interpolation from the regular grid uses bilinear or higher-order filtering. Pitfall: This may lead to large distances of UV coordinates for neighboring fragments, resulting in visual artifacts in close-up views. Correct Interpolation Variant (Recommended): This variant ensures continuous reconstruction of UV coordinates. 1. Compute the UV coordinates using the Direct Interpolation Variant as an initial estimate. 2. Identify the grid points corresponding to the virtual triangle containing the estimated UV point on the support plane. 3. Determine the plane given by the elevated neighboring points (the 3D positions of the vertices of the virtual triangle). 4. Intersect the view ray with this elevated plane. 5. Project the intersection point onto the support plane to determine the corrected UV coordinates. 6. Perform final interpolation over the four adjacent samples on the attribute map using bilinear interpolation. Edge Case: In rare cases where there is no intersection between the view ray and the plane defined by elevated neighboring points, discard the fragment to prevent visual artifacts. Unverified code. name: GSplat Skinning Data Loading

body: This method computes the final transformation matrix for a splat by blending up to four bone matrices weighted by skin weights, then applying a reference inverse transform. It supports two storage backends: Texture2D arrays for GPU compatibility and portability, or StructuredBuffers for direct access. It enables skeletal animation of Gaussian splats by transforming their position, covariance, and optionally surface normal. Inputs: sourceId: The unique identifier for the splat (uint). modelCenter: The splat's center position in model space (float3). covariance: The splat's covariance matrix, stored as two components covA and covB (float3). modelNormal: (Optional) The splat's surface normal in model space (float3). GsplatSkinningEnabled: A global integer flag (0 or 1) indicating if skinning is active. Outputs: transformedCenter: The skinned position (float3). transformedCovariance: The skinned covariance components covA and covB (float3). transformedNormal: (Optional) The skinned normal (float3). The method uses one of two storage backends. Texture2D Backend: GsplatSkinIndexTexture: Texture2D<float4> storing bone indices. GsplatSkinWeightTexture: Texture2D<float4> storing bone weights. GsplatSkinReferenceTexture: Texture2D<float4> storing reference inverse matrices. GsplatSkinBoneTexture: Texture2D<float4> storing bone matrices. Widths are stored in GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth, GsplatSkinWeightTextureWidth, GsplatSkinReferenceTextureWidth, and GsplatSkinBoneTextureWidth. StructuredBuffer Backend: GsplatSkinWeights: StructuredBuffer<GsplatSkinWeight>. GsplatSkinReferenceRows: StructuredBuffer<float4>. GsplatSkinBoneRows: StructuredBuffer<float4>. GsplatSkinWeight contains boneIndices (uint4) and boneWeights (float4). When using textures, linear indices must be converted to 2D coordinates: \text{coord} = \left( \text{index} \pmod{\text{width}}, \left\lfloor \frac{\text{index}}{\text{width}} \right\rfloor \right) where width is the specific texture's width. 1. Check Enable Flag: If GsplatSkinningEnabled is 0, return inputs unchanged. 2. Load Skin Data: Calculate indexOffset = sourceId 4. Load four texels from GsplatSkinIndexTexture at indexOffset through indexOffset + 3. Decode each texel's uint value using GsplatDecodeTextureUInt to form skin.boneIndices (uint4). Load one texel from GsplatSkinWeightTexture at sourceId to form skin.boneWeights (float4). 3. Compute Skin Matrix: Initialize currentMatrix as zero. For each of the four bones (x, y, z, w), load its bone matrix and multiply by the corresponding bone weight. Sum these four weighted matrices. Load the reference inverse matrix and multiply the result by it. 4. Transform Position: Transform modelCenter by multiplying the skin matrix with float4(modelCenter, 1.0) and taking the xyz component. 5. Transform Covariance: Extract the deformation matrix (float3x3) from the first three rows of the skin matrix. Transform the covariance using the formula deformed = transform source transpose(transform), where source is the 3x3 covariance matrix reconstructed from covA and covB, and transform is the 3x3 deformation matrix. 6. Transform Normal (Optional): Transform modelNormal by multiplying the deformation matrix with modelNormal, then normalize the result. This avoids per-vertex matrix inverse. The deformed covariance is computed as: C{\text{def}} = D \times C{\text{src}} \times D^T where C{\text{src}} is the 3×3 covariance matrix reconstructed from covA and covB, and D is the 3×3 deformation matrix. The result is packed back into covA and covB such that covA contains C{\text{def}}[0][0..2] and covB contains C{\text{def}}[1][1..2] and C{\text{def}}[2][2]. Unverified code. width) def GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(texel): # Extracts the bone index from a float4 texel return int(texel[0]) def ReconstructCovariance3x3(covA, covB): # Reconstructs symmetric 3x3 matrix from packed components return [ [covA[0], covA[1], covA[2]], [covA[1], covB[0], covB[1]], [covA[2], covB[1], covB[2]] ] def ExtractCovarianceComponents(matrix): # Packs symmetric 3x3 matrix back into covA and covB covA = [matrix[0][0], matrix[0][1], matrix[0][2]] covB = [matrix[1][1], matrix[1][2], matrix[2][2]] return covA, covB def GsplatLoadSkinWeight(sourceid): indexoffset = sourceid 4 boneindices = [ GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(GsplatSkinIndexTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(indexoffset, GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth)]), GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(GsplatSkinIndexTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(indexoffset + 1, GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth)]), GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(GsplatSkinIndexTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(indexoffset + 2, GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth)]), GsplatDecodeTextureUInt(GsplatSkinIndexTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(indexoffset + 3, GsplatSkinIndexTextureWidth)]) ] boneweights = GsplatSkinWeightTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(sourceid, row1 = GsplatSkinReferenceTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset + 1, GsplatSkinReferenceTextureWidth)] row2 = GsplatSkinReferenceTexture[GsplatSkinTextureCoord(matrixoffset + 2, currentmatrix[k][c] for k in range(4)) for c in range(4)] for r in range(4)] return skinmatrix def GsplatTransformCovariance(covariance, transform3x3): covA, covB = covariance source =
