range(3)] return ExtractCovarianceComponents(deformed) def ApplySkinning(modelcenter, covariance, modelnormal, sourceid): if GsplatSkinningEnabled == 0: return modelcenter, covariance, modelnormal skinmatrix = GsplatSkinMatrix(sourceid) # Transform Position poshomogeneous = [modelcenter[0], modelcenter[1], modelcenter[2], 1.0] transformedposhomogeneous = [sum(skinmatrix[r][c] poshomogeneous[c] for c in range(4)) for r in range(4)] transformedcenter = (transformedposhomogeneous[0], transformedposhomogeneous[1], transformedposhomogeneous[2]) # Transform Covariance deformationmatrix = [ [skinmatrix[0][0], skinmatrix[0][1], skinmatrix[0][2]], [skinmatrix[1][0], skinmatrix[1][1], skinmatrix[1][2]], [skinmatrix[2][0], skinmatrix[2][1], skinmatrix[2][2]] ] transformedcovariance = GsplatTransformCovariance(covariance, deformationmatrix) # Transform Normal transformednormal = deformationmatrix @ modelnormal # Vector-matrix multiplication transformednormal = tuple(v / ((sum(vv for v in transformednormal))0.5) for v in transformednormal) return transformedcenter, transformedcovariance, transformednormal GsplatSkinningEnabled: Integer flag (0 or 1). sourceId: Unique splat identifier. Bone weights: Typically sum to 1.0, but the algorithm sums weighted matrices regardless. Skinning Disabled: If GsplatSkinningEnabled is 0, all skinning functions return immediately without modifying inputs. Reference Matrix Construction: When using the Texture2D backend, the reference inverse matrix is stored with only 3 rows. The 4th row must be explicitly set to (0, 0, 0, 1) to form a valid 4 \times 4 matrix. Covariance Reconstruction: The source covariance matrix must be correctly reconstructed from covA and covB components before transformation. The result must be re-extracted into covA and covB. Precision: Matrix multiplications involve floating-point operations. Precision issues may arise with very small or very large bone weights, though standard float32 is implied. Time: Constant time O(1) per splat, involving a fixed number of texture/buffer loads (up to 13 texels for Texture2D backend: 4 indices, 1 weight, 4 bone rows, 3 reference rows) and matrix multiplications. Memory: Depends on the backend. Texture2D uses 4 textures where each bone index consumes 4 texels and each source consumes 1 texel for weights and 3 texels for reference inverse. StructuredBuffer allows direct indexing, potentially simpler but may have different memory layout requirements. Not given in the sources. Scales linearly with the number of splats. The cost per splat is constant regardless of scene complexity, as it depends only on the splat's local skin data. Strengths: Supports skeletal animation for Gaussian splats. Texture2D backend offers GPU portability. StructuredBuffer backend offers direct access. Limitations: Limited to 4 bones per splat. Requires pre-computed skin weights and bone matrices. Texture2D backend requires coordinate conversion. Use when skeletal animation of Gaussian splats is required. Choose Texture2D backend for maximum GPU compatibility. Choose StructuredBuffer backend for potentially simpler memory access patterns if the hardware supports it efficiently. This method is part of the UnitySplats project by ARLOOPA, specifically designed for Gaussian Splatting in Unity. It enables dynamic skinning of splats, allowing them to deform with skeletal animations. arloopa/UnitySplats, https://github.com/arloopa/UnitySplats, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Attribute Accumulation and Blending
head: Splat attribute blending, Voronoi cardinal attributes
body: Attribute Accumulation and Blending is the fragment processing stage in hardware-accelerated surface splatting that reconstructs continuous and cardinal attributes from overlapping splats into a reconstruction buffer. It builds on the Splat Attributes Pass and distinguishes itself from siblings like Splat Depth Pass and Tile Binning for Splatting by handling two distinct attribute types: continuous attributes are accumulated via weighted blending, while cardinal attributes are resolved via maximum-weight comparison, effectively assigning each screen-space pixel to the splat with the highest weight within an \varepsilon-band. This method operates in conjunction with a ternary depth test to manage z-pass, z-fail, and z-blend conditions. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Source splat fragment with screen-space depth zs, weight wf, and attributes \mathbf{a}s (continuous or cardinal). Destination reconstruction buffer state with depth zd, accumulated weight wd, and accumulated attributes \mathbf{a}d. Output: Updated reconstruction buffer state (zd, wd, \mathbf{a}d). Data Structures: The reconstruction buffer stores per-pixel: zd: Depth value (float). wd: Accumulated weight (float). \mathbf{a}d: Accumulated attributes (vector of floats, size depends on attribute type). Parameters: \varepsilon{\Delta z}: Scales depth extents. Typical value: 1.0. \varepsilon{bias}: Accounts for numerical inaccuracies, comparable to glPolygonOffset's unit parameter. \varepsilon: The blending band size, computed as \varepsilon:= hz \cdot \varepsilon{\Delta z} + \varepsilon{bias}, where hz is the splat's depth range. Steps: 1. Ternary Depth Test: Compare zd and zs using the \varepsilon band: If zd < zs - \varepsilon: z-fail. Discard fragment. If zd > zs + \varepsilon: z-pass. Proceed to attribute update. Otherwise: z-blend. Proceed to attribute blending. 2. Attribute Update (z-pass): Replace destination weight and attributes with source values: (wd, \mathbf{a}d):= (wf, \mathbf{a}s) 3. Attribute Blending (z-blend): Continuous Attributes: Blend weighted source attributes into the destination: (wd, \mathbf{a}d):= (wd + wf, \mathbf{a}d + wf \cdot \mathbf{a}s) Cardinal Attributes: Compare weights. If wd < wf, replace destination with source; otherwise keep destination: \text{if } wd < wf \text{ then } (wd, \mathbf{a}d):= (wf, \mathbf{a}s) \text{ else } (wd, \mathbf{a}d):= (wd, \mathbf{a}d) Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def accumulateattributes(zd, wd, ad, zs, wf, as, iscontinuous, epsilon): # Ternary Depth Test if zd < zs - epsilon: # z-fail: discard fragment return zd, wd, ad if zd > zs + epsilon: # z-pass: replace destination weight and attributes return zd, wf, as # z-blend: accumulate if iscontinuous: # Continuous attributes are blended newwd = wd + wf newad = ad + wf as return zd, newwd, newad else: # Cardinal attributes: maximum weight comparison if wd < wf: return zd, wf, as else: return zd, wd, ad This variant handles the post-accumulation phase where normalized attributes are fed to fragment shader units for deferred shading. After accumulation, continuous attributes are normalized by dividing accumulated attributes by accumulated weight: af = ad / wd. Surface completion is detected using higher-level signals such as glDrawElements(), glDrawArrays(), or glEnd() after rendering individual splats. A key pitfall is that accumulated splats define a surface only after all affecting splats have been processed; completion cannot be reliably deduced from individual splats or accumulated values alone. Time Complexity: O(1) per fragment per splat. The ternary test and attribute update are constant-time operations. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the reconstruction buffer, where N is the number of screen pixels. The buffer stores depth, weight, and attributes per pixel. Performance: The method avoids deep depth buffers, which were tested but found to have insufficient benefit to justify storage costs and complexity. Strengths: Efficiently handles overlapping splats via the \varepsilon-band blending. Supports both continuous and cardinal attributes. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \varepsilon parameters to avoid artifacts from near-degenerate splats or orthogonality issues. The blending band size depends on the splat's depth range hz. When to use: Hardware-accelerated surface splatting where both continuous (e.g., color, normal) and cardinal (e.g., material ID) attributes need to be reconstructed. When not to use: When exact depth ordering is required without blending (use z-pass only). When memory bandwidth is extremely limited and high overlap exists, the \varepsilon-band may cause excessive blending artifacts. The method originates from hardware architectures for surface splatting, specifically described in. It builds on the EWA screen-space filter approximation by Botsch et al. [2005] for efficient ray-splat intersection and filtering. The ternary depth test was introduced to handle the accumulation of overlapping splats without the complexity of deep depth buffers used in earlier software implementations by Pfister et al. [2000] and Räsänen [2002]. A hardware architecture for surface splatting, https://doi.org/10.1145/1275808.1276490, fetched 2026-10-28

name: Single-Pass Splat Rendering Pipeline
head: Single-Pass High-Quality Splatting
body: The Single-Pass Splat Rendering Pipeline is a real-time rendering technique that combines splat and mesh rendering components to enable high-quality shader effects (reflection, refraction) in a single rendering pass. It solves the problem of multi-pass blending artifacts and high memory/workload associated with dense point sets by reorganizing input data into elevation map patches. Unlike sibling methods that reconstruct smooth attributes by blending in screen space (requiring at least three passes and causing blurring), this method interpolates attributes at an earlier stage in object space using patch information, resulting in a single pass and improved normal/attribute quality. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D point set representing the model, optionally with per-point attributes (color, normal). Output: A final image rendered in a single pass. Data Structures: The model is decomposed into patches. Each patch is defined by: 1. Plane Parameters: A 3D point (origin), a normal vector, and a grid resolution. 2. Height Field: A rectangular array of height values (elevation map) sampled on a regular grid over the planar domain. Some grid points may be flagged with a special height value indicating no point exists above that grid location. 3. Attribute Maps: Optional texture maps (e.g., color, normal) stored as texture objects for each patch individually. 4. Transformation Matrix: One 4x4 matrix per patch. Storage: VBO (Vertex Buffer Object): Stores point positions and elevation data for each patch. Point positions on the patch plane are expressed by a single index value (combined row and column address in the sampling grid). Index Buffer: A linear list 1, 2, \dots, n, where n is the number of points in the patch. No connectivity encoding is needed. Texture Objects: Store additional attribute maps. Algorithm Steps: 1. Patch Construction (Pre-processing): Partition the input 3D point set into patches. Each patch is parameterized as an elevation map over a planar domain. Resample the surface patch on a regular grid using Moving Least Squares (MLS) surface reconstruction. Overlap Handling: To prevent gaps due to MLS limitations, patches are made to slightly overlap. An input point near a boundary is included in a patch if its \epsilon-neighborhood intersects the point set of the region, where \epsilon > 0. Resample attribute fields (normals, textures) onto the regular grid. 2. Upload to GPU: Upload VBOs (elevation data) and Texture Objects (attributes) to graphics memory. 3. Rendering Loop: Iterate over all patches. For each patch: Address the respective texture objects. Trigger the corresponding VBO for rendering using the linear index buffer. 4. Vertex Shader: Translation: Translate point positions according to their elevation values from the VBO. Rotation: Rotate the translated points using the patch's 4x4 transformation matrix to place them on the surface of the original model. Radius Calculation: Set the radius of each point (point sprite) based on the sampling step size \mu and elevation variance to prevent holes. The base radius is \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{2}\mu. Radii are increased in areas where variance between neighboring elevation values results in spatial gaps. 5. Rasterization: Rasterize the points as point sprites. 6. Fragment Shader: Splat Simulation: Transform point-sprite fragments to simulate splatting, as point sprites are screen-aligned primitives. Continuous Attribute Interpolation: Determine per-fragment UV coordinates by projecting the fragment back onto the patch plane. Interpolate attributes (normals, textures) from nearby points using the patch's regular grid structure. This replaces screen-space blending with object-space interpolation. Illumination: Compute final fragment color by summing contributions from lighting, texture mapping, reflectance mapping (e.g., environment cube maps), and refraction mapping. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def buildpatches(pointset): patches = [] # Standard spatial partitioning of point set into regions regions = [pointset[i:i+chunk] for i in range(0, len(pointset), chunk)] for region in regions: # Moving Least Squares surface reconstruction gridsize = 16 heights = [[0.0] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] # Epsilon overlap handling epsilon = 0.01 # Attribute resampling normals = [[(0.0, 1.0, 0.0)] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] colors = [[(1.0, 1.0, 1.0)] gridsize for in range(gridsize)] # Plane fitting and transform planeorigin = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) planenormal = (0.0, 1.0, 0.0) transformmatrix = [[1.0]4 for in range(4)] patches.append({ 'grid': gridsize, 'heights': heights, 'normals': normals, 'colors': colors, 'transform': transformmatrix, 'origin': planeorigin, 'normal': planenormal, 'uvec': (1.0, 0.0, 0.0), 'vvec': (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) }) return patches def renderpatches(patches): for patch in patches: # Address textures and trigger VBO indices = list(range(1, patch['grid'] patch['grid'] + 1)) # GPU draw call using linear index buffer for idx in indices: worldpos, radius = vertexshader(idx, patch) rasterizepoint(worldpos, radius) def vertexshader(index, patch): row = (index - 1) // patch['grid'] col = (index - 1) % patch['grid'] basepos = (patch['origin'][0] + row patch['uvec'][0] + col patch['vvec'][0], patch['origin'][1] + row patch['uvec'][1] + col patch['vvec'][1], patch['origin'][2] + row patch['uvec'][2] + col patch['vvec'][2]) height = patch['heights'][row][col] translatedpos = (basepos[0] + height patch['normal'][0], basepos[1] + height patch['normal'][1], basepos[2] + height patch['normal'][2]) # Apply 4x4 transform worldpos = translatedpos mu = 1.0 / patch['grid'] baseradius = 0.5 math.sqrt(2.0) mu # Variance-based radius scaling to prevent holes hcenter = height hneighbors = [patch['heights'][r][c] for r in range(max(0, row-1), min(patch['grid'], row+2)) for c in range(max(0, col-1), min(patch['grid'], col+2)) if (r, c) != (row, col)] variance = sum((h - hcenter)2 for h in hneighbors) / max(1, len(hneighbors)) radius = baseradius (1.0 + variance 0.1) return worldpos, radius def fragmentshader(worldpos, patch): # Project fragment to patch plane for UV griduv = (0.5, 0.5) # Interpolate attributes normal = patch['normals'][0][0] diffuse = patch['colors'][0][0] # Standard lighting and shader effects lightcolor = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) reflectcolor = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) refractcolor = (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) finalcolor = tuple(a + b + c for a, b, c in zip(lightcolor, reflectcolor, refractcolor)) return finalcolor Parameters: \epsilon (Epsilon): A positive value used during patch construction to include input points near a patch boundary if their \epsilon-neighborhood intersects the point set of the region, ensuring patches slightly overlap to prevent gaps. \mu (Sampling step size): Determines the base splat radius. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gaps between patches: Moving Least Squares resampling cannot guarantee no gaps. Patches must overlap slightly using \epsilon to ensure continuous error-free rendering. Holes due to elevation variance: If elevation values vary significantly between neighbors, the base radius may be insufficient. Radii must be increased in these areas. Complexity: The pipeline consists of one single rendering pass, simplifying overall rendering complexity compared to current GPU-based splatting techniques which require at least three rendering passes. Performance: Aggressively utilizes practical components of both splat and mesh rendering. Avoids performance-hungry GPU functionality such as multiple render targets and additional blending passes. Quality: Improves visual quality of reconstructed attributes (normals, texture coordinates) by interpolating in object space rather than blending in screen space. Allows for enhanced shader effects (reflection, refraction) without densely sampled models. Memory: The resampled model is stored completely on graphics hardware. Connectivity is implicit and reconstructed in the fragment shader, requiring no additional memory for connectivity structures. The Single-Pass Splat Rendering Pipeline was introduced by Tilo Ochotta, Stefan Hiller, and Dietmar Saupe in September 2006. It was published as Konstanzer Schriften in Mathematik und Informatik Nr. 219. The method builds on previous work regarding elevation map data structures for point-sampled surfaces. name: Three-Pass GPU Point Rendering Pipeline
head: Hardware Accelerated Point Splatting Pipeline
body: The Three-Pass GPU Point Rendering Pipeline is a method for hardware-accelerated point splatting that correctly handles transparency and perspective distortion by separating depth testing, color accumulation, and normalization into distinct rendering stages. It differs from single-pass approaches by explicitly accumulating filter weights to enable accurate normalization of the final color, ensuring that the contribution of each splat is weighted by its actual footprint area under perspective projection. The pipeline renders a volume represented as a set of points (splats) using standard GPU rasterization capabilities, specifically leveraging GLPOINTS primitives. Input: A set of N 3D points \mathbf{p}i, each associated with a color \mathbf{c}i and a reconstruction kernel (typically Gaussian) with variance \sigma^2. Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the normalized color value \mathbf{C}{final}(x,y). The method relies on standard GPU framebuffers: 1. Depth Buffer: Stores the depth z of the closest splat fragment. 2. Color Accumulation Buffer (Pass 2): Stores the weighted sum of colors \sum \mathbf{c}i wi. 3. Weight Accumulation Buffer (Pass 2): Stores the sum of weights \sum wi. Note: In some implementations, the color and weight buffers may be combined or handled via separate render targets. The core requirement is that the second pass accumulates both values. 1. Pass 1: Depth Offset Rendering Render the scene using GLPOINTS. The vertex shader computes the screen-space position and the depth. Crucially, the depth value written to the depth buffer is offset slightly along the viewing ray. This offset ensures that during Pass 2, the depth test correctly identifies the front-most splat without self-occlusion artifacts caused by floating-point precision limits at the exact surface. No color or weight accumulation occurs in this pass; only the depth buffer is updated. 2. Pass 2: Weighted Accumulation Render the splats again using GLPOINTS. Depth Test: Enable depth testing. Use the depth value from the splat's center (or a consistent reference point) to compare against the depth buffer populated in Pass 1. Only fragments that pass the depth test (i.e., are front-most) are processed. Fragment Shader: Compute the 2D footprint of the splat on the screen. For perspective-accurate splatting, this involves computing the variance matrix of the resampling filter in screen space, often denoted as R0 + H or approximated as Q{000}. Calculate the weight wi for the fragment based on the distance from the splat center and the kernel variance. Accumulate the weighted color: C{acc} \leftarrow C{acc} + \mathbf{c}i wi. Accumulate the weight: W{acc} \leftarrow W{acc} + wi. Blending: Use additive blending (GLADD) for both color and weight accumulators. The depth buffer is read but not written to (depth mask disabled or depth test only). 3. Pass 3: Normalization Render a full-screen quad (or use a post-processing pass). For each pixel, retrieve the accumulated color C{acc} and accumulated weight W{acc}. Compute the final color: \mathbf{C}{final} = \frac{C{acc}}{W{acc}} Handle the edge case where W{acc} \approx 0 (no splats covered the pixel) by setting \mathbf{C}{final} to a background color or zero. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def pass1depthoffset(points, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """ Renders points to update only the depth buffer with an offset. """ gl.depthmask(True) gl.colormask(False, False, False, False) gl.enable(gl.DEPTHTEST) for point in points: # Transform point to clip space clippos = projmatrix viewmatrix point.position # Compute depth offset along viewing ray # The offset is small, e.g., epsilon depth depthoffset = computeviewingrayoffset(clippos) # Write depth with offset gl.depthfunc(gl.LEQUAL) drawpoint(clippos.position.xy, depth=clippos.z + depthoffset) def pass2accumulate(points, viewmatrix, projmatrix): """ Renders points to accumulate weighted color and weights. """ gl.depthmask(False) # Do not update depth buffer gl.colormask(True, True, True, True) gl.enable(gl.BLEND) gl.blendfunc(gl.ONE, gl.ONE) # Additive blending # Separate render targets for Color Accum and Weight Accum # Or use a single texture with RGB for color, A for weight for point in points: # Compute screen-space footprint (EWA or similar) # This requires inverting the projection matrix to get kernel variance # Q000 approximation or full variance matrix R0 + H variancematrix = computescreenspacevariance(point, viewmatrix, projmatrix) # Determine if splat is visible (passed depth test from Pass 1) # The GPU depth test handles this automatically if depth buffer is intact if isvisible(point): # Compute weight w based on fragment distance and variance w = computekernelweight(fragmentuv, point.center, variancematrix) # Fragment shader accumulates: # coloraccum += point.color w # weightaccum += w drawpoint(point.position, weight=w) def pass3normalize(): """ Post-process the accumulated buffers to produce final image. """ gl.depthmask(False) gl.colormask(True, True, True, True) gl.disable(gl.BLEND) # Render a full-screen quad # Fragment shader: # Cfinal = coloraccum / weightaccum # if weightaccum < epsilon: Cfinal = backgroundcolor renderfullscreenquad(normalizefragmentshader) Depth Offset: The offset in Pass 1 must be small enough to not cause visible depth errors but large enough to prevent z-fighting in Pass 2. Typical values are a small fraction of the near plane distance. Variance Matrix Inversion: Computing the screen-space kernel variance requires inverting the projective mapping. This can be numerically ill-conditioned if the splat degenerates into a line segment (viewing direction parallel to the splat normal). Zero Weight: Division by zero in Pass 3 must be guarded against. If no splats cover a pixel, the weight is zero. This variant refers to the core assembly logic often used in simpler or CPU-based implementations, or as a baseline for GPU pipelines. It involves initializing canvases (depth, color, label, index), sorting points by depth, and iterating to write colors to pixels where the point's depth is less than the current depth at that pixel. A written mask is created to identify valid pixels, and invalid pixels are cleared. Point Cloud Rendering projects a set of 3D points into screen space and aggregates their contributions. It is distinguished by its differentiability, allowing gradients to flow from the rendered image back to the 3D point positions and attributes, which is useful for optimization tasks. This method reduces performance costs by performing expensive Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) splatting only on visible surfels. It uses a multi-pass approach similar to deferred shading, separating visibility determination from color accumulation. It employs temporal coherency to accelerate the visibility pass and a secondary visibility pass (Bi - B{i-1}) to fix artifacts caused by hidden points becoming visible. This allows expensive filtering to be skipped for hidden points. Time Complexity: O(N) for N points, assuming constant-time kernel evaluation and rasterization. The three-pass structure adds a constant overhead factor of 3 to the rendering pipeline. Memory Complexity: Requires additional framebuffers for color and weight accumulation. Typically, two additional textures (or one texture with multiple channels) are needed. Strengths: Correctly handles perspective distortion and transparency. Leverages standard GPU hardware for rasterization and depth testing. Limitations: Requires multiple passes, which can be inefficient on hardware with limited render target support or high overhead for state changes. Numerical instability in variance matrix inversion can occur for grazing angles. When to Use: When high-quality perspective-accurate point splatting is required and the GPU supports multiple render targets or efficient post-processing. When Not to Use: For simple orthographic projections where single-pass methods suffice, or on hardware with severe limitations on framebuffer operations. The three-pass approach for hardware-accelerated point splatting was developed to address the limitations of earlier methods that struggled with perspective accuracy and transparency. It builds on the principles of splatting, where volumetric data is decomposed into primitives and rasterized. The specific technique of using a depth offset pass and separate accumulation/normalization passes was introduced to ensure correct weighting under perspective projection, as described in "Perspective Accurate Splatting". name: Point Cloud Rendering
head: Depth-based sprite, Nailboard, Textured Particles, Textured Particles / Point Cloud Rendering
body: Point cloud rendering treats raw 3D point data as discrete sprites or spheres to generate 2D images. It serves as a bridge between explicit geometric representations and differentiable rendering pipelines. Unlike mesh-based rendering which relies on rasterization of triangles, or voxel-based methods which fill space with grid cells, point cloud rendering directly projects individual points, often using spatial influence functions to handle sparsity and occlusion. It is distinct from its sibling Deferred Splatting with Temporal Coherency and Bi-Bi-1 Visibility Pass by its focus on explicit point-to-pixel aggregation rather than deferred visibility buffers, and from Three-Pass GPU Point Rendering Pipeline by its specific algorithmic choices for influence calculation and occlusion handling. The method consists of three primary phases: projection, influence calculation, and aggregation. Input: A point cloud P = \{P{xyz}^{(i)}\}{i=1}^N, where each point has 3D coordinates and associated features (e.g., color Ci). Camera parameters (intrinsics K, extrinsics R, t) defining the view. Output: A 2D image I of resolution H \times W with RGB channels. Point Cloud: A list or tensor of shape (N, 3 + F), where N is the number of points and F is the number of feature channels (e.g., 3 for RGB). Camera: Defined by projection matrix M = K[R|t]. Pixel Grid: A 2D array of size H \times W. 1. Calculate Screen Space Coordinates For each 3D point P{xyz}^{(i)}, compute its screen space coordinates p{uv}^{(i)} = (ui, vi) via matrix multiplication with the camera projection matrix M. This step is differentiable with respect to P{xyz}. \begin{bmatrix} ui \\ vi \\ wi \end{bmatrix} = M \cdot \begin{bmatrix} P{xyz}^{(i)} \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Normalize by wi to get normalized device coordinates, then map to pixel indices. 2. Compute Influence Calculate the spatial influence Ii of each point P{xyz}^{(i)} on target pixels. A naive approach assumes a size of one pixel, but this leads to sparse images. To solve this, influences larger than one pixel are created using truncated Gaussian blur or distance-based influence values. Let di be the distance from the pixel center to p{uv}^{(i)}. The influence Ii is a function of di and potentially the point's depth. 3. Aggregate Points Determine the final color for each pixel by aggregating contributions based on influence Ii and z-values (depth) to handle occlusion. Several aggregation strategies exist: Weighted Sum: Compute a weighted sum of point colors based on influences Ii. The source notes this approach does take occlusion into account, though other methods explicitly address occlusion by selecting the closest point. Closest Point (Lin et al.): Select the single closest point to the camera for a given pixel. This prevents optimization of occluded points. K-Nearest (Li et al.): Select the K nearest 3D points to the camera and weigh them based on spatial influence Ii. Distance-Weighted (Wiles et al.): Weigh all 3D points according to distances from the camera in addition to spatial influence Ii. Voxelization (Insafutdinov et al.): Generate 3D voxels from the point cloud and render them using a volume rendering method. The following pseudocode implements the standard differentiable point cloud rendering pipeline using influence-based aggregation. It assumes a framework supporting automatic differentiation. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderpointcloud(points, features, cameramatrix, imagesize): """ points: List of (x, y, z) tuples. features: List of (r, g, b) tuples. cameramatrix: 3x4 list of lists representing projection matrix M. imagesize: Tuple (H, W). """ H, W = imagesize N = len(points) numchannels = len(features[0]) # Step 1: Project points to screen space projected = [] for i in range(N): x, y, z = points[i] # Homogeneous multiplication w = cameramatrix[2][0]x + cameramatrix[2][1]y + cameramatrix[2][2]z + cameramatrix[2][3] if w <= 0: continue # Behind camera u = (cameramatrix[0][0]x + cameramatrix[0][1]y + cameramatrix[0][2]z + cameramatrix[0][3]) / w v = (cameramatrix[1][0]x + cameramatrix[1][1]y + cameramatrix[1][2]z + cameramatrix[1][3]) / w if 0 <= u < W and 0 <= v < H: projected.append((u, v, w, features[i])) # Step 2 & 3: Compute influence and aggregate sigma = 1.0 # Influence size parameter image = [[0.0] numchannels for in range(H W)] influencesum = [0.0] (H W) for u, v, depth, feat in projected: for py in range(H): for px in range(W): distsq = (px - u)2 + (py - v)2 influence = math.exp(-distsq / (2 sigma2)) idx = py W + px for c in range(numchannels): image[idx][c] += influence feat[c] influencesum[idx] += influence # Normalize by sum of influences to get weighted average finalimage = [[0.0] numchannels for in range(H W)] for idx in range(H W): denom = max(influencesum[idx], 1e-6) for c in range(numchannels): finalimage[idx][c] = image[idx][c] / denom return finalimage Influence Size (\sigma): Controls the spread of the point's contribution. Large values prevent derivatives from becoming zero for distant points but reduce rendering quality. Aggregation Method: Choice between weighted sum, closest point, or K-nearest. Sparsity: Assuming point influence size is one pixel leads to very sparse images. Occlusion: The source notes that simple weighted sum approaches do take occlusion into account, though explicit closest-point selection is often preferred for optimization. Optimization Trade-off: There is a trade-off between rendering quality and optimization convergence; large influence sizes help gradient flow but blur details. Depth Precision: Using 3D textures for point clouds can cause resolution to lose precision. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Differentiable with respect to point positions and features, enabling use in neural network training. Simple to implement. Limitations: Can produce sparse images if influence is not properly sized. Occlusion handling is approximate unless specific strategies (like K-nearest) are used. When to use: When working with raw point cloud data, particularly in differentiable rendering contexts where reduced 3D supervision is used. Point cloud rendering has gained prominence with the advent of differentiable rendering and its application in scene understanding with reduced 3D supervision. It is often used in self-supervised learning of monocular depth estimation, where a color image is used to estimate depth, which is then converted to a point cloud and projected to a virtual camera view. The method is also relevant in visualizing volumetric data, where points are treated as particles or sprites. name: Deferred Splatting with Temporal Coherency and Bi-Bi-1 Visibility Pass
head: Accurate Point Selection, Deferred Point Selection, Deferred Splatting, Deferred Splatting with Temporal Coherency
body: A rendering algorithm that reduces the performance cost of high-quality point-based rendering by performing expensive Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) splatting computations only on visible surfels, using a multi-pass approach similar to deferred shading. It separates visibility determination from color accumulation, using temporal coherency to accelerate the visibility pass and a secondary visibility pass (Bi - B{i-1}) to fix artifacts caused by hidden points becoming visible. Unlike previous methods that perform low-level selection entirely by the GPU during rendering, this method performs low-level selection (visibility culling) explicitly before the expensive EWA splatting pass, allowing the expensive filtering to be skipped for hidden points. Inputs: A set of dynamic point clouds or surfels, organized by object. High-level selection results: A set of potentially visible surfels for the current frame i, determined by per-object view frustum culling, LOD selection, and simple per-object occlusion culling. The set of surfels visible in the previous frame, denoted B{i-1}. Transformation matrices for all objects at the current frame i. Outputs: The final normalized color buffer representing the rendered image. The set of visible surfels for the current frame, denoted Bi, which is stored in index buffers for use in the next frame. Surfel Index Buffer: A single video memory buffer used for all objects. Stores 2^n consecutive integers from 0 to 2^n - 1. n is the number of bits reserved for the surfel index within the 32-bit identifier. Typical value: n=20, allowing 1M surfels per object. Boolean Flags Array: An array of boolean flags used to approximate the set difference Bi - B{i-1}. Each flag is associated with a group of m consecutive surfel indices. The flag indicates if one of the surfels in the group belongs to B{i-1}. Typical group size m=64 surfels. Memory cost: Requires 8MB for storing flags in the worst case (for 2^{20} surfels). 32-bit Identifier: Used to store surfel identity in the color buffer during Pass 2. Split into n bits for the surfel index (is) and (32-n) bits for the object index (io). Typical allocation: n=20 for is, leaving 12 bits for io (allowing 4096 visible objects). For large landscapes, alternative schemes (e.g., 11/20 or 14/17) may be used, with a single bit storing the active scheme. The rendering algorithm for frame i consists of the following passes: 1. Visibility Splatting with B{i-1}: Render all surfels visible in the previous frame (B{i-1}) into the depth buffer using hardware point primitives with per-fragment depth and shape correction. This pre-computes a depth buffer without holes for the majority of the scene, accelerating the process by exploiting temporal coherency. Note: Use each object's transformation matrix at the current frame i, not the previous frame, to support dynamic scenes. 2. Render Surfel Indices: Render all input surfels declared visible by the high-level selection as a single pixel of the color buffer using the surfel index instead of color. The depth test discards hidden points. The resulting subset of visible surfels is denoted Bi. The GPU vertex program computes the 32-bit identifier on the fly using 1 instruction: identifier = (io << n) | is. The object index (io) is passed as a uniform parameter. The clear color value before this pass must be set to 0xFFFFFFFF (the last allowed surfel of the last allowed visible object) to ensure it never represents a real surfel index. 3. Compute Bi - B{i-1} Approximation: While sorting the result of Pass 2, compute a conservative approximation of the set difference Bi - B{i-1} using the Boolean Flags Array. This identifies surfels that are visible in the current frame but were hidden in the previous frame. 4. Visibility Splatting with Bi - B{i-1}: Perform visibility splatting only on surfels that are visible in the current frame but were hidden in the previous frame (Bi - B{i-1}). This handles newly visible geometry and fixes holes in the depth buffer caused by temporal coherency artifacts. 5. EWA Splatting with Bi: Render only the visible surfels (Bi) onto the color buffer using hardware point primitives with additive blending mode. The weight of each fragment is computed from a Gaussian centered at the current surfel position in screen space, using a fragment program. To avoid aliasing, use surfel mipmaps (several prefiltered texture samples per surfel). The vertex program performs linear interpolation between the two closest mipmap levels. The interpolation coefficient is computed from the Jacobian matrix, which was already computed during the resampling filter determination. 6. Normalization: Render the resulting color buffer as a full-screen textured rectangle with a simple fragment program that divides RGB components by the alpha component, which contains the sum of weights. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. NBITSSURFEL = 20 NBITSOBJECT = 32 - NBITSSURFEL CLEARIDENTIFIER = 0xFFFFFFFF GROUPSIZEM = 64 def deferredsplatting(framei, Bprev, highlevelselection, transforms): """ Renders frame i using deferred splatting with temporal coherency. Bprev: set of (objectid, surfelindex) visible in frame i-1 highlevelselection: list of (objectid, surfelindex) from frustum/occlusion culling transforms: dict mapping objectid -> transformation matrix at frame i """ # Pass 1: Visibility Splatting with B{i-1} # Render surfels from Bprev to build initial depth buffer. # Uses transforms[framei] for dynamic scenes. # GPU pass: draw points with per-fragment depth/shape correction. for oid, si in Bprev: drawpointwithdepthcorrection(oid, si, transforms[oid]) # Pass 2: Render Surfel Indices # Render high-level selected surfels as 1-pixel points. # Store 32-bit identifier in color buffer. Depth test discards hidden points. # GPU pass: vertex program computes identifier = (oid << NBITSSURFEL) | si for oid, si in highlevelselection: identifier = (oid << NBITSSURFEL) | si draw1pxpointwithidentifier(identifier) # Read color buffer and decode identifiers to build Bi and index buffers. colorbuffer = readcolorbufferfromgpu() Bcurr = [] indexbuffers = {} numgroups = (1 << NBITSSURFEL + GROUPSIZEM - 1) // GROUPSIZEM booleanflags = [False] numgroups for pixel in colorbuffer: identifier = pixel.color if identifier == CLEARIDENTIFIER: continue objectid = identifier >> NBITSSURFEL surfelindex = identifier & ((1 << NBITSSURFEL) - 1) Bcurr.append((objectid, surfelindex)) if objectid not in indexbuffers: indexbuffers[objectid] = [] indexbuffers[objectid].append(surfelindex) # Update boolean flags: mark group if surfel was in Bprev if surfelindex in Bprev: booleanflags[surfelindex // GROUPSIZEM] = True # Pass 3: Visibility Splatting with Bi - B{i-1} # Identify surfels in Bcurr not covered by Bprev flags. Bdiff = [] for objectid, surfelindex in Bcurr: if not booleanflags[surfelindex // GROUPSIZEM]: Bdiff.append((objectid, surfelindex)) # GPU pass: draw points with depth correction for newly visible geometry for oid, si in Bdiff: drawpointwithdepthcorrection(oid, si, transforms[oid]) # Pass 4: EWA Splatting with Bi # Render visible surfels with additive blending and EWA filtering. # GPU pass: fragment program computes Gaussian weight, interpolates surfel mipmaps for oid, surfelindices in indexbuffers.items(): for si in surfelindices: drawewasplat(oid, si, transforms[oid]) # Pass 5: Normalization # Divide RGB by Alpha (sum of weights). # GPU pass: full-screen quad with fragment program dividing RGB by A normalizedbuffer = normalizecolorbuffer() return normalizedbuffer, Bcurr Bi: The set of surfels visible in frame i, determined by the depth test in Pass 2. B{i-1}: The set of surfels visible in the previous frame (i-1), used to exploit temporal coherency. Identifier Bit Allocation: The 32-bit identifier is split into n bits for the surfel index (is) and (32-n) bits for the object index (io). Typical value: n=20, allowing 1M surfels per object and 4096 visible objects. Group Size (m): The size of the groups for the boolean flags array. Typical value: 64 surfels. This requires 8MB for storing flags in the worst case. It is a compromise between accuracy and memory cost. Temporal Coherency Artifacts (Holes): Occur when objects move significantly between frames, causing surfels visible in the current frame to be missed if only B{i-1} is used. This is handled by Pass 3, which processes Bi - B{i-1}. Clear Color Value: The clear color value before Pass 2 must never represent a real surfel index. It is set to 0xFFFFFFFF (the last allowed surfel of the last allowed visible object) to ensure it is the most improbable identifier. Hidden Splat Accumulation: Holes in the depth buffer cause hidden splats to be accumulated into the color buffer, creating artifacts. Pass 3 prevents this by ensuring all newly visible points are depth-corrected. Dynamic Scenes: During Pass 1 and Pass 3, use each object's transformation matrix at the current frame i, not the previous frame. This allows the algorithm to work on dynamic scenes and dynamic point clouds. Aliasing: Oversampling discards superfluous points, leading to aliasing artifacts for high-frequency textures. This is mitigated by using surfel mipmaps and linear interpolation between mipmap levels. Time Complexity: The algorithm accelerates rendering by reducing the number of surfels processed in the expensive EWA splatting pass (Pass 4) to only those visible in the current frame (Bi), rather than all surfels. The cost of the EWA pass becomes independent of scene complexity. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the Surfel Index Buffer (2^n integers) and the Boolean Flags Array (8MB for typical settings). Measured on a 2GHz AMD Athlon system with an NVIDIA GeForceFX 5900 graphic card, at 512x512 resolution: | Scene | Points | FPS Without Selection | FPS With Selection | Culled % | |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- |:--- | | Head | 285k | 34 | 39 | 70% | | Tree | 750k | 8.6 | 32 | 88% | | Forest | 6800 trees | 0.8-1.5 | 10-16 | 90-98% | Pass 1 Time: 7-11 ms (11.5-13.5M primitives/sec). Pass 2 Time: 6.6 ms (reading color buffer) + 1.7-2.2 ms (sorting indices). Total ~8.3-8.8 ms. Pass 3 Time: 0.8-1.2 ms (11.5-13.5M primitives/sec). Pass 4 Time: 9-11.5 ms (11-13M primitives/sec). Pass 5 Time: 0.7 ms. Strengths: No preprocessing required; suitable for dynamic point clouds; accurate per-primitive view frustum and occlusion culling; hardware accelerated; significant speedup on complex scenes (up to 10x). Limitations: Pass 2 (Render Indices) can become the most expensive pass for large scenes due to color buffer read-back and sorting; requires CPU involvement for sorting indices unless using SuperBuffers/PixelBufferObjects. Use for applications manipulating dynamic point clouds for editing, modelling, and implicit surface visualization via particle systems. Particularly effective when the scene has high occlusion and temporal coherency between frames. The method was introduced by G. Guennebaud, L. Barthe, and M. Paulin in the paper "Deferred Splatting". It builds on previous work such as the GPU-based EWA splatting algorithm by Guennebaud and the surfel splatting techniques by Pfister et al.. The algorithm was developed to address the performance bottleneck of high-quality point-based rendering, where expensive EWA filtering is applied to hidden points. By deferring the expensive splatting to only visible points, similar to deferred shading in rasterization, the method achieves significant performance gains. It is used in applications requiring real-time rendering of dynamic point clouds, such as implicit surface visualization and particle systems. name: Custom Pass Rendering
head: DemoRenderer pipeline, Multi-pass Octree Rendering Pipeline, NanoVolume Custom Pass Rendering, SSVDAG rendering passes
body: Custom Pass Rendering is a multi-pass, object-order rendering architecture that decouples volumetric traversal and shading from the standard graphics pipeline by executing a sequence of specialized fragment shaders as "custom passes". It solves the problem of rendering large, sparse volumetric datasets (such as VDB grids) in real-time by leveraging hardware-accelerated rasterization for post-traversal effects (SSAO, shadows, normal filtering) while using GPU-based ray traversal for the primary volume sampling. It differs from pure ray-marching methods by separating the expensive volume traversal into a dedicated pass that outputs hit positions and normals to screen-space buffers, which are then consumed by subsequent passes for lighting and compositing. Inputs: Volumetric data structure (e.g., NanoVDB octree). Camera parameters: View-Projection matrix, View matrix, Camera position, Screen resolution, Field of View (FOV). Scene bounding box and octree metadata (center, half-side, levels). Outputs: Final composited color buffer. Intermediate screen-space buffers: Depth, Hit Position, Hit Normal, Material ID, Shadow map, Ambient Occlusion (AO). The pipeline relies on a set of Frame Buffer Objects (FBOs) or Render Textures, each attached to a specific render target. All textures are sized to the screen resolution (W \times H). 1. FBO[0] (Primary Rays/Depth): Attachment 0: glTexDepth (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGBA32F, GLLINEAR filtering). 2. FBO[1] (Hit Pos/Norm): Attachment 0: glTexHitPos (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGB32F, GLNEAREST filtering). Attachment 1: glTexHitNorm (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGB32F, GLNEAREST filtering). 3. FBO[2] (Materials, optional): Attachment 0: glTexHitMaterial (GLTEXTURE2D, GLR8UI, GLNEAREST filtering). 4. FBO[3] (Normal Filtering): Attachment 0: glTexHitNormFiltered (GLTEXTURE2D, GLRGB32F, GLNEAREST filtering). 5. FBO[4] (Shadows): Attachment 0: glTexShadows (GLTEXTURE2D, GLR32F, GLNEAREST filtering). 6. FBO[5] (AO): Attachment 0: glTexAO (GLTEXTURE2D, GLR32F, GLNEAREST filtering). 7. FBO[6] (AO Blurred): Attachment 0: glTexAOBlurred (GLTEXTURE2D, GLR32F, GLNEAREST filtering). 1. Initialization: Create NUMPASSES RendererMonitor instances and start them. Load the volumetric data (e.g., NanoVDB) into GPU-accessible memory (e.g., ComputeBuffer or GLTEXTUREBUFFER). 2. Pass 1: Primary Ray Traversal (Pos/Norm Computation): Compile and link a shader (e.g., SHADERPOSNORMFILE). Set uniforms: screenRes (vec2), depth (int, TEXNUMDEPTH), projectionFactor (float). Execute a full-screen pass. For each pixel, compute the camera ray direction \mathbf{r}d from screen coordinates: \mathbf{r}d = \text{normalize}(\text{fromHomog}(\mathbf{P}^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{v}1) - \text{fromHomog}(\mathbf{P}^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{v}0)) where \mathbf{v}0, \mathbf{v}1 are clip-space rays at z=0 and z=1. Perform GPU-based ray traversal (e.g., DAG/SDAG traversal) against the volume octree to find the first hit. If a hit is found, write the hit position \mathbf{p}{hit} and normal \mathbf{n}{hit} to glTexHitPos and glTexHitNorm respectively. Calculate a "diffuseness" metric dif for normal estimation: \text{dif} = \max(0.001, \frac{2.0 \cdot (\mathbf{n}{hit} \cdot \text{projectionFactor})}{\mathbf{p}{hit}.x}) Apply clamping: if \text{dif} > 5.0, mix with 1.0 using a smoothstep over range [5.0, 20.0]. If no hit, discard or write background. 3. Pass 2: Material Lookup (Optional): If useMaterials is true, compile SHADERMATERIALFILE. Bind the material octree buffer to TEXNUMMATOCTREE. Uniforms: matOctree, screenRes, depth, matOctreehalfSide, matOctreeCenter, matOctreeLevels. For each pixel with a valid hit position, query the material ID from the octree and write to glTexHitMaterial. 4. Pass 3: Normal Filtering: Compile SHADERNORMALFILTERFILE. Uniform: inputTex (TEXNUMHITNORM). Apply a bilateral or Gaussian filter with kernel size MSIZE (default 10) and sigma sigma (default 4.0) or bsigma (default 0.4) to glTexHitNorm to produce glTexHitNormFiltered. 5. Pass 4: SSAO (Screen-Space Ambient Occlusion): Compile SHADERSSAOFILE. Uniforms: hitPosTex (TEXNUMHITPOS), hitNormTex (TEXNUMHITNORMFILTERED), depthTex (TEXNUMDEPTH), noiseTex (TEXNUMAONOISE). Generate ssaoNSamples (default 32) 3D samples in a hemisphere oriented by the surface normal. Generate a noise texture of size ssaoNoiseTexSide (default 64). For each pixel, sample the hemisphere, project samples to screen space, and compare against the depth buffer to calculate occlusion. Write visibility factor to glTexAO. 6. Pass 5: AO Blur: Compile SHADERBLURFILE. Uniform: inputTex (TEXNUMAO). Apply a blur filter to glTexAO to produce glTexAOBlurred. 7. Pass 6: Shading: Compile SHADERSHADINGFILE. Uniforms: screenRes, hitPosTex, hitNormTex, shadowsTex, aoTex, depthTex, materialTex. If materials are enabled, define USEMATERIALS and NUMMATERIALS. For each pixel: Retrieve hit position, normal, shadow factor, and AO value. Determine diffuse color: use material color if useMaterials is true, else default (e.g., 0.8, 0.8, 0.8). Compute final color using lighting model (diffuse, ambient) and apply AO. Output to final color buffer. 8. Pass 7: Volume Rendering (NanoVolume Pass): In the Unity implementation, a separate NanoVolumePass is executed. Include headers: CustomPassCommon.hlsl, PseudoRandom.hlsl, NanoVolumePass.hlsl. Setup stereo eye index if in stereo mode. Load camera depth at varyings.positionCS.xy. Get position inputs using GetPositionInput. Calculate normalized view direction. Call NanoVolumePass with camera position and negated view direction. Return color with alpha blending: float4(color.rgb, color.a). Render State: ZWrite Off, Cull Off, Blend One OneMinusSrcAlpha. The following Python-like pseudocode implements the SSAO occlusion calculation from Pass 4, based on the provided GLSL shader: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computessao(hitpos, hitnorm, depthtex, noisetex, projmat, viewmat, campos, samples, radius, sidenoisetex): occlusion = 0.0 count = 0.0 rvec = noisetex[coord % sidenoisetex] tangent = normalize(rvec - hitnorm dot(rvec, hitnorm)) bitangent = cross(hitnorm, tangent) tbn = matrix(tangent, bitangent, hitnorm) for i in range(len(samples)): samp = tbn @ samples[i] samp = hitpos + samp radius offset = vec4(samp, 1.0) offset = projmat @ viewmat @ offset offset.xyz /= offset.w offset.xyz = offset.xyz 0.5 + 0.5 sampledepth = depthtex[offset.xy] rangecheck = 1.0 if abs(depthtex[coord].x - sampledepth) < radius else 0.0 if sampledepth < length(campos - samp): occlusion += rangecheck count += 1.0 return 1.0 - occlusion / count if count > 0.0 else 1.0 Projection Factor: \text{projectionFactor} = \frac{\text{inv\2tan\half\fovy}}{\text{screen\tolerance}} where \text{inv\2tan\half\fovy} = \frac{1.0}{2.0 \cdot \tan(0.5 \cdot \text{fovy})} and \text{screen\tolerance} = \frac{1.0}{\text{screenRes}[1]}. Typical FOV is 60 degrees. Diffuseness Metric (for Normal Estimation): \text{dif} = \max(0.001, \frac{2.0 \cdot (\mathbf{n} \cdot \text{projectionFactor})}{\mathbf{p}.x}) Clamped via: \text{dif}{final} = \begin{cases} \text{dif} & \text{if } \text{dif} \le 5.0 \\ \text{mix}(\text{dif}, 1.0, \frac{\text{dif}-5.0}{15.0}) & \text{if } 5.0 < \text{dif} < 20.0 \\ 1.0 & \text{if } \text{dif} \ge 20.0 \end{cases}. SSAO Occlusion: \text{occlusion} = \sum{i=0}^{N-1} \left( \frac{\text{sampleDepth} < \|\mathbf{c}{cam} - \mathbf{s}i\|}{\|\mathbf{c}{cam} - \mathbf{s}i\|} \cdot \text{rangeCheck} \right) where \mathbf{s}i is the i-th sample in tangent space, transformed to world and then clip space, and \text{rangeCheck} is 1.0 if the sample is within radius, 0.0 otherwise. Final visibility: \text{visibility} = 1.0 - \frac{\text{occlusion}}{\text{count}}. sigma: 4.0f (Normal filtering/SSAO smoothing). bsigma: 0.4f (Bilateral filtering/SSAO smoothing). msize: 10 (Kernel size for normal filtering). ssaoRadius: Calculated as eo->getHalfSide(eo->getNLevels()) 100.0f. ssaoNSamples: 32 (Number of SSAO samples). ssaoNoiseTexSide: 64 (Noise texture side length). renderMode: 0 (Default render mode). useDif: true (Enable diffuse shading). filterNormals: true (Enable normal filtering). doSSAO: true (Enable SSAO). doShadows: true (Enable shadows). useMaterials: false (Enable material lookup). Precision: The use of GLRGBA32F for depth and position buffers ensures high precision for ray origin/normal storage, preventing z-fighting or normal artifacts in large scenes. Boundaries: The SSAO pass discards pixels where hitPos == vec3(0,0,0) (background). Degenerate Input: If the volume octree is not loaded (materialOctree is NULL), the material pass is skipped. Stereo: The Unity implementation explicitly handles stereo eye indexing via UNITYSETUPSTEREOEYEINDEXPOSTVERTEX. Time Complexity: Dominated by the GPU ray traversal pass (Pass 1) and the SSAO pass (Pass 4). SSAO is O(W \cdot H \cdot N{samples}). Memory Complexity: Requires multiple full-screen textures (Depth, Pos, Norm, Material, Shadow, AO, AO Blurred). Total memory \approx 7 \times W \times H \times \text{bytesPerPixel}. For 1080p, this is roughly 7 1920 1080 4 bytes \approx 58 MB for 32-bit floats, plus overhead. Performance: Real-time performance is achievable on modern GPUs due to hardware-accelerated rasterization for post-processing passes and efficient GPU-based traversal. Strengths: Decouples volume traversal from lighting, allowing for efficient screen-space lighting techniques (SSAO, Shadows). Supports material lookups and complex shading models. Limitations: Requires multiple render passes, increasing overhead. Screen-space techniques (SSAO) suffer from edge artifacts and require depth/normal buffers. Custom Pass Rendering originated from the SSVDAG (Sparse Sparse Volume DAG) project and was adapted for Unity via the NanoVolume renderer. It was developed to enable real-time rendering of large, sparse volumetric datasets (like those from medical imaging or scientific simulations) by leveraging the efficiency of GPU-based ray traversal combined with standard graphics pipeline features for lighting. The method is used in research and demo applications for visualizing VDB-based volumes. ajaspe/ssvdag, https://github.com/ajaspe/ssvdag, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial) andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, https://github.com/andersblomqvist/unity-nanovdb-renderer, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: DirectXSplat Renderer API
head: DirectXSplat, DirectXSplat Rendering Pipeline, directxsplat::Renderer
body: DirectXSplat is a C++/Direct3D 12 library for rendering 3D Gaussian Splats, providing a rasterization pipeline that handles scene upload, preparation, rendering, and frame submission with explicit resource management. It differs from general-purpose splatting libraries by enforcing a host-owned device/queue/command list/fence architecture, allowing integration into existing D3D12 applications while managing its own internal COM references and resource transitions. It is optimized for high performance, claiming up to 2.4x faster rendering than gsplat in matched-quality benchmarks on NVIDIA hardware. The method operates as a prepare-then-render pipeline. The host application owns the D3D12 device, command queue, and fences, while the renderer manages the Gaussian splat data structures and recording of rendering commands into the host's command list. Inputs: ID3D12Device, ID3D12CommandQueue, ID3D12Fence: Host-owned D3D12 primitives. Scene data: Loaded via LoadSceneFromFile from formats including PLY, compressed PLY, SPZ,.splat, SOG, and hierarchical LOD metadata. RenderInput: Camera matrices, view parameters, and frame index. RenderTargetBinding: Color target resource, RTV handle, format, states, viewport, and scissor. Outputs: Rendered image on the provided color target. RenderResult: Contains submission status, sync points, and potential errors. D3D12Context Stores non-owning pointers to ID3D12Device, ID3D12CommandQueue, and ID3D12Fence. Does not retain COM references. RenderFrameContext fence: ID3D12Fence (must match the one passed to D3D12Context::Initialize). completedFenceValue: uint64t (latest known completed value, typically from GetCompletedValue()). submissionFenceValue: uint64t (nonzero, unique per frame, strictly greater than all previously signaled values and completedFenceValue). frameIndex: uint32t (host frame index). RenderTargetBinding colorTarget: ID3D12Resource colorRtv: D3D12CPUDESCRIPTORHANDLE colorFormat: DXGIFORMAT colorStateBefore: D3D12RESOURCESTATES colorStateAfter: D3D12RESOURCESTATES transitionMode: ResourceTransitionMode (LibraryManaged or CallerManaged). viewport: D3D12VIEWPORT scissor: D3D12RECT RendererConfig residencyBudgetGaussians: uint64t (Default: 16 \times 1024 \times 1024). uploadBudgetGaussians: uint64t (Default: 650,000). warmUploadBudgetGaussians: uint64t (Default: 1,200,000). maxUploadsPerFrame: uint32t (Default: 16). chunkTargetSize: uint32t (Default: 65,536). lod0ScreenRadius: float (Default: 72.0f). lod1ScreenRadius: float (Default: 24.0f). cullScreenRadius: float (Default: 0.35f). residencyCacheFrames: uint32t (Default: 120). enableGpuTiming: bool (Default: true). Gaussian Primitive Fields position: Vec3 scale: Vec3 rotation: Vec4 (quaternion) opacity: float sh: array of floats (Spherical Harmonics coefficients). 1. Initialize Context: Create D3D12Context with host ID3D12Device, ID3D12CommandQueue, and ID3D12Fence. 2. Initialize Renderer: Call Renderer::Initialize(context). 3. Load Scene: Call LoadSceneFromFile(scenePath) to create a directxsplat::Scene object. The loader detects format automatically (PLY, SPZ, etc.). 4. Create Uploaded Scene: Call Renderer::CreateUploadedScene(loadedScene, sceneHandle) to transfer data to GPU memory. 5. Prepare Frame Context: Populate RenderFrameContext with the fence pointer, GetCompletedValue(), a unique submissionFenceValue, and frameIndex. 6. Prepare Scene: Call Renderer::PrepareSceneForRender(sceneHandle, input, frameContext, &preparationResult). 7. Configure Render Target: Populate RenderTargetBinding with the color target, RTV, format, states, viewport, scissor, and transition mode. 8. Render: Call Renderer::Render(commandList, targetBinding, sceneHandle, input, frameContext, &renderResult). The command list must be reset and open. If renderResult.submission.uploadSyncPoint is valid, the host must wait on the direct queue for that sync point before executing the command list. 9. Submit: Close the command list, execute it on the direct queue via ExecuteCommandLists, and signal the fence with submissionFenceValue. 10. Handle Errors: If Render returns an error with submissionRequired == true, the command list work must still be submitted/signaled or device-lost cleanup entered. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class D3D12Context: def Initialize(self, device, queue, fence): pass def Shutdown(self): pass class Renderer: def Initialize(self, context): pass def CreateUploadedScene(self, scene, handle): pass def PrepareSceneForRender(self, scene, input, framectx, prepresult): pass def Render(self, cmdlist, target, scene, input, framectx, result): pass def DestroyUploadedScene(self, handle): pass def Shutdown(self): pass class RenderFrameContext: def init(self): self.fence = None self.completedFenceValue = 0 self.submissionFenceValue = 0 self.frameIndex = 0 class RenderTargetBinding: def init(self): self.colorTarget = None self.colorRtv = None self.colorFormat = None self.colorStateBefore = 0 self.colorStateAfter = 0 self.transitionMode = 0 self.viewport = None self.scissor = None class RenderResult: def init(self): self.submission = type('obj', (object,), {'uploadSyncPoint': type('obj', (object,), {'IsValid': lambda: False, 'fence': None, 'value': 0})(), 'submissionRequired': False})() class Status: def init(self, ok=True): self.ok = ok def LoadSceneFromFile(path): return type('obj', (object,), {'ok': lambda: True, 'value': None})() context = D3D12Context() context.Initialize(device, directQueue, directFence) renderer = Renderer() renderer.Initialize(context) loadedscene = LoadSceneFromFile(scenepath) if not loadedscene.ok(): raise Error(loadedscene.status) scenehandle = renderer.CreateUploadedScene(loadedscene.value) for frameindex in range(numframes): # 1. Prepare Frame Context framecontext = RenderFrameContext() framecontext.fence = directFence framecontext.completedFenceValue = directFence.GetCompletedValue() framecontext.submissionFenceValue = nextuniquefencevalue() # Must be > all previous and > completedFenceValue framecontext.frameIndex = frameindex # 2. Prepare Scene for Render preparationresult = RenderPreparationResult() status = renderer.PrepareSceneForRender(scenehandle, renderinput, framecontext, preparationresult) if not status.ok: raise Error(status) # 3. Configure Render Target targetbinding = RenderTargetBinding() targetbinding.colorTarget = colortargetresource targetbinding.colorRtv = colorrtvhandle targetbinding.colorFormat = colorformat targetbinding.colorStateBefore = D3D12RESOURCESTATES.RENDERTARGET targetbinding.colorStateAfter = D3D12RESOURCESTATES.PRESENT targetbinding.transitionMode = ResourceTransitionMode.LibraryManaged targetbinding.viewport = viewport targetbinding.scissor = scissor # 4. Render renderresult = RenderResult() status = renderer.Render(commandlist, targetbinding, scenehandle, renderinput, framecontext, renderresult) # Error handling for submission required if not status.ok and renderresult.submission.submissionRequired: # Command list work may already be recorded; must submit or cleanup pass # 5. Handle Sync Points if renderresult.submission.uploadSyncPoint.IsValid(): directQueue.Wait(renderresult.submission.uploadSyncPoint.fence, renderresult.submission.uploadSyncPoint.value) # 6. Submit Command List commandlist.Close() directQueue.ExecuteCommandLists([commandlist]) directQueue.Signal(directFence, framecontext.submissionFenceValue) renderer.DestroyUploadedScene(scenehandle) renderer.Shutdown() context.Shutdown() lod0ScreenRadius: 72.0f. Splats larger than this in screen space use LOD0. lod1ScreenRadius: 24.0f. Splats between LOD1 and LOD0 radii use LOD1. cullScreenRadius: 0.35f. Splats smaller than this are culled. residencyBudgetGaussians: 16,777,216. Maximum Gaussians resident in GPU memory. uploadBudgetGaussians: 650,000. Maximum Gaussians uploaded per frame. Fence Values: submissionFenceValue must be nonzero, unique per frame, strictly greater than every previously signaled value on that fence, and strictly greater than completedFenceValue. Resource Formats: colorRtv must describe colorTarget, and colorFormat must match the RTV's single-sampled format. Unsupported formats fail pipeline creation. Submission Required: If Render returns an error with submissionRequired == true, command-list work may already be recorded. The host must submit/signal it or enter device-lost cleanup. Mutual Exclusion: Rendering and scene mutation are mutually exclusive for the same uploaded scene. BeginSceneMutation waits for active render encoding to finish. Device Lost: If queue execution or signaling fails after renderer work was recorded, call renderer.NotifyDeviceLost() before shutdown. Performance: Benchmarked on NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4070 SUPER, Windows 11. DirectXSplat achieves up to 2.4x faster FPS than gsplat in resident-scene benchmarks. Bicycle dataset (6.1M splats, 1237x822): 382.51 FPS (DirectXSplat) vs 165.82 FPS (gsplat). Garden dataset (5.8M splats, 1297x840): 319.14 FPS (DirectXSplat) vs 131.68 FPS (gsplat). Treehill dataset (3.8M splats, 1267x832): 491.86 FPS (DirectXSplat) vs 224.86 FPS (gsplat). Memory: Memory-conscious design with persistent uploaded scenes and configurable residency/upload budgets. Strengths: High performance, native D3D12 integration, explicit resource management, support for multiple scene formats (PLY, SPZ,.splat, SOG). Limitations: Tied to Direct3D 12; requires host to manage D3D12 primitives (device, queue, fences, command lists). DirectXSplat is a C++/Direct3D 12 library for rendering 3D Gaussian Splats, designed to render scenes captured via techniques described in "3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering". It was developed to provide a fast, embeddable renderer with host-owned resource management. pbkx/DirectXSplat, https://github.com/pbkx/DirectXSplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Ray-Centric and Hardware-Accelerated Rendering
body: Ray-centric rendering computes pixel color by tracing rays from the camera through volumetric data and accumulating density and color along the path, typically executed on the GPU for performance. It differs from splatting by processing samples per-ray rather than per-primitive, avoiding sorting overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel. It preserves internal volume information, unlike isosurface extraction methods such as Marching Cubes. The family traces rays from the camera through volumetric data to compute pixel color and opacity. Rays are marched through the volume using step-based sampling or acceleration structures, with contributions accumulated along the ray path. GPU hardware acceleration is used for parallel execution. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import math def batchifyrays(raysflat, chunk=32768, kwargs): """ Renders rays in smaller mini-batches to avoid OOM. Args: raysflat: Tensor of shape (B, 11). chunk: Size of mini-batches. kwargs: Arguments passed to renderrays. Returns: Dictionary of output tensors with shape (B,...). """ allret = {} numrays = raysflat.shape[0] # Iterate through rays in chunks for i in range(0, numrays, chunk): # Extract chunk raybatch = raysflat[i: i + chunk] # Render the chunk ret = renderrays(raybatch, kwargs) # Accumulate results for k in ret: if k not in allret: allret[k] = [] allret[k].append(ret[k]) # Concatenate results along the batch dimension (dim 0) for k in allret: allret[k] = torch.cat(allret[k], dim=0) return allret def renderrays(raybatch, networkfn, networkqueryfn, Nsamples=64, retraw=False, lindisp=False, perturb=0.0, Nimportance=0, networkfine=None, whitebkgd=False, rawnoisestd=0.0, verbose=False, pytest=False): """ Renders a single batch of rays. Args: raybatch: Tensor of shape (Nrays, 11). networkfn: Coarse network function. networkqueryfn: Function to query network with pts and viewdirs. Nsamples: Number of coarse samples. lindisp: Use disparity sampling. perturb: Noise for stratified sampling. Nimportance: Number of fine samples. networkfine: Fine network function.... other args... Returns: Dictionary with keys: rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, etc. """ Nrays = raybatch.shape[0] # Unpack ray parameters rayso = raybatch[:, 0:3] # (Nrays, 3) raysd = raybatch[:, 3:6] # (Nrays, 3) # Viewdirs are the last 3 components if present viewdirs = raybatch[:, -3:] if raybatch.shape[-1] > 8 else None # Bounds bounds = torch.reshape(raybatch[..., 6:8], [-1, 1, 2]) near = bounds[..., 0] # (Nrays, 1) far = bounds[..., 1] # (Nrays, 1) # Generate tvals tvals = torch.linspace(0., 1., steps=Nsamples, device=raybatch.device) # Compute zvals (sample depths) if not lindisp: zvals = near (1. - tvals) + far tvals else: zvals = 1. / (1./near (1. - tvals) + 1./far tvals) # Expand zvals to [Nrays, Nsamples] zvals = zvals.expand([Nrays, Nsamples]) # Stratified sampling if perturb > 0.: mids =.5 (zvals[..., 1:] + zvals[...,:-1]) upper = torch.cat([mids, zvals[..., -1:]], -1) lower = torch.cat([zvals[...,:1], mids], -1) trand = torch.rand(zvals.shape, device=raybatch.device) # Pytest override for deterministic results if pytest: torch.manualseed(0) trand = torch.rand(zvals.shape, device=raybatch.device) zvals = lower + (upper - lower) trand # Compute 3D points # pts shape: (Nrays, Nsamples, 3) pts = rayso[..., None,:] + raysd[..., None,:] zvals[...,:, None] # Query network raw = networkqueryfn(pts, viewdirs, networkfn) # Process raw output to get rgb, weights, etc. # Note: raw2outputs is a helper function defined in the NeRF source code # that implements the alpha compositing formula. rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, weights, depthmap = raw2outputs( raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd, pytest=pytest) # Hierarchical sampling if Nimportance > 0: # Store coarse outputs rgbmap0, dispmap0, accmap0 = rgbmap, dispmap, accmap # Calculate midpoints of coarse samples zvalsmid =.5 (zvals[..., 1:] + zvals[...,:-1]) # Sample fine depths based on weights # samplepdf is a helper function for inverse CDF sampling zsamples = samplepdf(zvalsmid, weights[..., 1:-1], Nimportance, det=(perturb==0.), pytest=pytest) # Detach to break gradient flow from fine to coarse zsamples = zsamples.detach() # Concatenate and sort zvals, = torch.sort(torch.cat([zvals, zsamples], -1), -1) # Recompute points pts = rayso[..., None,:] + raysd[..., None,:] zvals[...,:, None] # Query fine network runfn = networkfn if networkfine is None else networkfine raw = networkqueryfn(pts, viewdirs, runfn) # Process fine output rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, weights, depthmap = raw2outputs( raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd, whitebkgd, pytest=pytest) ret = {'rgbmap': rgbmap, 'dispmap': dispmap, 'accmap': accmap} if retraw: ret['raw'] = raw if Nimportance > 0: ret['rgbmap0'] = rgbmap0 ret['dispmap0'] = dispmap0 ret['accmap0'] = accmap0 return ret def raw2outputs(raw, zvals, raysd, rawnoisestd=0.0, whitebkgd=False, pytest=False): """ Converts raw network output (rgb, sigma) to final image components. Implements volume rendering equation. """ # raw shape: (Nrays, Nsamples, 4) -> (rgb, sigma) rgb = raw[...,:3] sigma = raw[..., 3:4] # Add noise to sigma noise = 0. if sigma.shape[-1] > 0: noise = torch.randn(sigma.shape, device=raw.device) rawnoisestd sigma = sigma + noise # Compute delta (distance between samples) deltas = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] # Approximate last delta to avoid boundary issues deltas = torch.cat([deltas, torch.oneslike(deltas[...,:1]) 1e10], dim=-1) # Compute alpha alpha = 1.0 - torch.exp(-torch.relu(sigma) deltas) # Transmittance T = torch.cumsum(1. - alpha, dim=-1) T = torch.cat([torch.oneslike(T[...,:1]), T[...,:-1]], dim=-1) # Weights weights = alpha T # Compositing rgbmap = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgb, dim=-2) accmap = torch.sum(weights, dim=-1) depthmap = torch.sum(weights zvals, dim=-1) / (accmap + 1e-10) dispmap = 1. / (depthmap + 1e-10) return rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, weights, depthmap def samplepdf(zvalsmid, weights, Nimportance, det=False, pytest=False): """ Hierarchical sampling: sample Nimportance points from the distribution defined by weights. """ # weights shape: (Nrays, Nsamples-1) # zvalsmid shape: (Nrays, Nsamples-1) # Get pdf pdf = weights / (weights.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) + 1e-10) cdf = torch.cumsum(pdf, dim=-1) cdf = torch.cat([torch.zeroslike(cdf[...,:1]), cdf], dim=-1) # Uniform samples if det: u = torch.linspace(0., 1., Nimportance, device=weights.device) u = u.expand([weights.shape[0], Nimportance]) else: u = torch.rand([weights.shape[0], Nimportance], device=weights.device) # Inverse CDF indices = torch.searchsorted(cdf, u, right=True) indices = torch.clamp(indices, 0, cdf.shape[-1] - 2) # Linear interpolation within bins z0 = zvalsmid[torch.arange(weights.shape[0]), indices] z1 = zvalsmid[torch.arange(weights.shape[0]), indices + 1] c0 = cdf[torch.arange(weights.shape[0]), indices] c1 = cdf[torch.arange(weights.shape[0]), indices + 1] # Avoid division by zero denom = c1 - c0 denom = torch.where(denom < 1e-10, torch.oneslike(denom), denom) t = (u - c0) / denom zsamples = z0 + t (z1 - z0) return zsamples Batched Ray Rendering is a memory-management strategy for object-order volume rendering that processes large batches of rays in smaller, fixed-size chunks to prevent Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors on the GPU. It builds on Ray-Centric and Hardware-Accelerated Rendering by explicitly managing the batch size relative to available VRAM, and differs from Chunked Trilinear Volume Rendering by chunking the rays (the query set) rather than the volume data (the lookup grid). See Batched Ray Rendering. A GPU-accelerated rendering technique that traces rays from the camera through each pixel into a 3D volume to compute color and opacity, implemented in a single pass using fragment shaders. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data directly on the GPU without generating intermediate polygonal meshes. It differs from isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) by preserving internal volume information, and from splatting (Splatting) by avoiding sorting and blending overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than texture-based splatting. See GPU Implementation Pipeline. A volume rendering method implemented using NVIDIA OptiX. It uses a Ray Generation shader, Miss shaders for radiance and shadow, and Hit/Any-Hit/Intersection shaders for volume traversal and shading. Initialize shaders: Set shaderraygen to raygendefault. Add miss shaders missradiance and missshadow. Configure volume object group: Set group.type = VOLUMESTRUCTUREDREGULAR. Assign hit group shaders: Closest Hit closesthitvolumeradiance and closesthitvolumeshadow, Any Hit anyhitvolumeradiance and anyhitvolumeshadow, and Intersection intersectionvolume. Shader assignments: Ray Gen: raygendefault. Miss: missradiance, missshadow. Volume Closest Hit: closesthitvolumeradiance, closesthitvolumeshadow. Volume Any Hit: anyhitvolumeradiance, anyhitvolumeshadow. Volume Intersection: intersectionvolume. A rendering pipeline that rasterizes primary rays for speed and traces secondary rays for lighting effects (reflections/refractions) within the same 3D representation. Compute all primary ray intersections with the scene. Render these primary rays using rasterization (splatting). Discard Gaussian hits that fall behind a ray's closest intersection. Compute and trace secondary rays using 3DGRT. Ray casting and marching are standard techniques for high-quality volume visualization, leveraging the parallel nature of GPU fragment shaders for per-pixel ray marching. The specific GPU implementation pipeline utilizes a slab method for AABB intersection and front-to-back compositing within a single fragment shader pass. The integration of ray tracing APIs like NVIDIA OptiX allows for more complex traversal and shading models, while recent hybrid approaches combine the speed of rasterization for primary rays with the accuracy of ray tracing for secondary effects like reflections.
