body: Batched Ray Rendering is a memory-management strategy for object-order volume rendering that processes rays in fixed-size chunks to avoid Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors. It solves the problem where the number of rays in an image exceeds the capacity of the accelerator's VRAM or when the neural network model is too large for a full-batch forward pass. It sets itself apart from its sibling, GPU Implementation Pipeline, by explicitly iterating over subsets of rays rather than evaluating the full batch at once. The method decomposes the rendering of all rays for an image into sequential mini-batches. It prepares ray data, iterates through rays in chunks, renders each chunk, and concatenates the results. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Ray origins \mathbf{rays\o}, ray directions \mathbf{rays\d}, near/far bounds, optional view directions \mathbf{viewdirs}, and rendering parameters (N{samples}, N{importance}, etc.). Output: Rendered color map \mathbf{rgb\map}, disparity map \mathbf{disp\map}, accumulated transmittance \mathbf{acc\map}, and optionally coarse outputs and raw network outputs. Data Structures: Ray Tensor: A 2D tensor of shape (B, 11) where B is the batch size. The last dimension concatenates: \mathbf{rays\o}: 3 floats (origin x, y, z) \mathbf{rays\d}: 3 floats (direction x, y, z) near: 1 float far: 1 float \mathbf{viewdirs}: 3 floats (optional, if useviewdirs is true). Accumulation Dictionary (allret): Maps output keys (e.g., rgbmap, rgb0) to lists of tensors, one list entry per chunk. Parameters: chunk: Size of mini-batches. Default is 1024 \times 32 = 32768. Nsamples: Number of samples per ray for the coarse pass. Nimportance: Number of additional samples for the fine pass. If 0, hierarchical sampling is skipped. lindisp: Boolean. If false, samples are linear in depth. If true, samples are linear in disparity (inverse depth). Default is false. perturb: Amount of noise added for stratified sampling. Default is 0. (often overridden to 1.0 during training). rawnoisestd: Standard deviation for noise added to raw sigma values. networkfn: Coarse network function. networkfine: Fine network function. If None, the coarse network is reused. Steps: 1. Preparation: Reshape \mathbf{rays\o} and \mathbf{rays\d} to [-1, 3] and float type. Broadcast scalar near and far values to match the shape of \mathbf{rays\d} (specifically \mathbf{rays\d}[...,:1]). Concatenate \mathbf{rays\o}, \mathbf{rays\d}, near, and far along the last dimension to form the base ray tensor. If useviewdirs is true, concatenate \mathbf{viewdirs} to the ray tensor. 2. Batching Loop (batchifyrays): Initialize an empty dictionary allret. Iterate through the ray tensor in chunks of size chunk. For each chunk, call renderrays. For each key in the returned dictionary, append the tensor to the corresponding list in allret. After the loop, concatenate all lists in allret along dimension 0 to form the final output tensors. 3. Rendering a Chunk (renderrays): Unpack \mathbf{rays\o}, \mathbf{rays\d}, \mathbf{viewdirs}, near, and far from the ray batch. Generate t{vals} as a linear space from 0. to 1. with N{samples} steps. Compute z{vals} (sample depths): If lindisp is false: z{vals} = near \times (1. - t{vals}) + far \times t{vals}. If lindisp is true: z{vals} = 1. / (1./near \times (1. - t{vals}) + 1./far \times t{vals}). Expand z{vals} to shape [N{rays}, N{samples}] to apply to all rays in the batch. If perturb > 0., perform stratified sampling: Calculate midpoints mids = 0.5 \times (z{vals}[..., 1:] + z{vals}[...,:-1]). Calculate upper bounds upper = \text{concat}([mids, z{vals}[...,-1:]]). Calculate lower bounds lower = \text{concat}([z{vals}[...,:1], mids]). Generate random noise t{rand} with shape [N{rays}, N{samples}]. Update z{vals} = lower + (upper - lower) \times t{rand}. Pitfall: This implementation deviates from theory because the first and last bins are half the size of others to fit N samples into [0,1], whereas theory assumes equal bin lengths. Compute point positions \mathbf{pts} = \mathbf{rays\o} + \mathbf{rays\d} \times z{vals}. Query the network using networkqueryfn(pts, viewdirs, networkfn) to get raw output (e.g., RGB and sigma). Process raw output using raw2outputs to get \mathbf{rgb\map}, \mathbf{disp\map}, \mathbf{acc\map}, weights, and depth map. Hierarchical Sampling (if N{importance} > 0): Store coarse outputs with 0 suffix (e.g., \mathbf{rgb\map\0}). Calculate midpoints of coarse samples z{vals\mid} = 0.5 \times (z{vals}[..., 1:] + z{vals}[...,:-1]). Sample fine depths z{samples} using samplepdf on z{vals\mid} and weights weights[..., 1:-1]. Detach z{samples} from the computation graph to break gradient flow from the fine pass to the coarse pass. Concatenate coarse z{vals} and fine z{samples}, then sort them to form the final z{vals}. Recompute \mathbf{pts} using the new sorted z{vals}. Query the fine network (or coarse if networkfine is None). Process the fine raw output using raw2outputs. Return results including coarse outputs if N{importance} > 0 and raw output if retraw is true. 4. Finalization: Reshape all output tensors in allret to match the original batch dimensions (excluding the last dimension which corresponds to the sample dimension). Extract \mathbf{rgb\map}, \mathbf{disp\map}, and \mathbf{acc\map} into a list, and return them along with the remaining dictionary items. Pseudocode: Unverified code. exp(-sigma deltaz) # deltaz = zvals[i] - zvals[i-1] # We assume zvals are sorted. # deltaz calculation: deltaz = zvals[..., 1:] - zvals[...,:-1] # Add a large value for the last bin or handle boundary # Standard NeRF implementation often uses: # deltaz = torch.cat([deltaz, torch.Tensor([1e10]).expand(deltaz[...,:1].shape)].to(deltaz), -1) # However, for simplicity and based on standard NeRF code: deltaz = torch.cat([deltaz, torch.zeroslike(deltaz[...,:1]) + 1e10], -1) alpha = 1. - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-2) # T[..., 0] is 1-alpha[0]. We want T[0]=1. # Actually, the standard NeRF code does: # T = torch.cumprod(1. - alpha + 1e-10, dim=-2) # And then weights = alpha T[...,:-1] ? No. # Let's stick to the explicit formula: # weights[i] = alpha[i] T[i] where T[i] = prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1-alpha[j]) # Re-calculate T correctly # T[i] = product of (1-alpha) for j < i # T[0] = 1 # T[1] = 1-alpha[0] #... # We can compute this via cumprod on shifted array ones = torch.oneslike(alpha[...,:1]) alphashifted = torch.cat([ones, alpha[...,:-1]], dim=-1) T = torch.cumprod(1. - alphashifted + 1e-10, dim=-1) weights = alpha T rgbmap = torch.sum(weights[..., None] rgb, -2) depthmap = torch.sum(weights zvals, -1) dispmap = 1. / torch.max(1e-10 torch.oneslike(depthmap), depthmap / torch.sum(weights, -1)) accmap = torch.sum(weights, -1) if whitebkgd: rgbmap = rgbmap + (1. - accmap[..., None] rgbmap) # This is approximate, usually: rgbmap + (1-acc)1 return rgbmap, dispmap, accmap, weights, depthmap def samplepdf(zvalsmid, weights, Nimportance, det=False, pytest=False): """ Hierarchical sampling. zvalsmid: (Nrays, Nsamples-1) weights: (Nrays, Nsamples-1) """ # Get bins # zvalsmid are midpoints between coarse samples # We sample from the distribution defined by weights # This is a simplified implementation. # Standard NeRF uses inverse CDF sampling. # Calculate bin edges (coarse samples) # zvalsmid is already midpoints. # We need to sample from the intervals defined by the coarse zvals. # Let's assume zvals (coarse) is available in the caller scope or passed. # For this self-contained pseudocode, we assume we have coarse zvals. # However, samplepdf usually takes zvalsmid and weights. # Reconstruct bin edges from midpoints? It prevents memory overflow by iterating over subsets of rays rather than evaluating the full batch at once. Chunked Ray Rendering is a memory-management strategy for object-order volume rendering that processes rays in fixed-size batches (chunks) rather than all at once. It solves the Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors that occur when the number of rays in an image exceeds the capacity of the accelerator's VRAM or when the neural network model is too large for a full-batch forward pass. It sets itself apart from its parent, Batched Ray Rendering, by explicitly handling the sharding of these chunks across multiple hosts and devices in distributed settings, ensuring that partial results are correctly concatenated and reshaped into the final image. This method renders volumetric datasets as a collection of overlapping 3D detailed kernels, combining GPU-accelerated splatting for coarse structure with raycasting for local detail. It solves the trade-off between the speed of splatting and the accuracy of raycasting by using a hierarchical representation where each node contains a 3D texture. Unlike pure splatting, it enhances each footprint with raycasted details along the kernel's extent, and unlike pure raycasting, it batches these operations per fragment. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of rays B and samples per ray N{samples}, i.e., O(B \cdot N{samples}). The batching introduces negligible overhead compared to the network query cost. Memory Complexity: Dominated by the chunk size. VRAM usage is proportional to chunk \times N{samples}, independent of the total image resolution. This allows rendering high-resolution images on hardware with limited VRAM. Measured Performance: Default chunk size is 1024 \times 32 = 32768 rays. Strengths: Prevents OOM errors; enables training and inference on large scenes or high-resolution images with limited GPU memory. Limitations: Sequential processing of chunks may underutilize GPU parallelism if chunks are too small; does not inherently optimize ray traversal (relies on the underlying renderrays implementation). When to use: When rendering large images or using large neural networks that exceed VRAM capacity for a full-batch forward pass. When not to use: When VRAM is sufficient for full-batch rendering, as full-batch may be faster due to reduced kernel launch overhead and better parallelism. Batched Ray Rendering is a core component of the NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) rendering pipeline. It was introduced in the original NeRF paper to enable the training of neural networks on high-resolution images by managing memory usage during the forward pass. The method is widely used in subsequent NeRF variants and neural rendering frameworks. yashbhalgat/HashNeRF-pytorch, https://github.com/yashbhalgat/HashNeRF-pytorch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) dgsmith7/nerf-mlp, https://github.com/dgsmith7/nerf-mlp, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF: A Volume Rendering Perspective | Yue Yu - GitHub Pages, https://yconquesty.github.io/blog/ml/nerf/nerfrendering.html, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Chunked Trilinear Volume Rendering
body: Chunked Trilinear Volume Rendering evaluates a neural field or trilinear volume by processing rays in fixed-size batches. It prevents memory overflow by iterating over subsets of rays rather than evaluating the full batch at once. Inputs: rays: Tensor of shape (Nraysall,...) containing ray origins and directions. chunk: Integer specifying the number of rays per processing batch. tensorf: The neural field or trilinear volume evaluation function. device: The compute device (e.g., CUDA). istrain: Boolean flag for gradient tracking mode. whitebg: Boolean flag for background color assumption. ndcray: Boolean flag for NDC coordinate transformation. Nsamples: Integer for samples per ray. Outputs: rgbs: Concatenated RGB color maps. depthmaps: Concatenated depth maps. None: Placeholder for alphas, weights, and uncertainties to maintain interface compatibility. rgbs: List of tensors, each of shape (chunk, 3) or (remainingrays, 3). depthmaps: List of tensors, each of shape (chunk, 1) or (remainingrays, 1). rayschunk: Tensor of shape (chunk,...) or (remainingrays,...). 1. Initialize empty lists for output tensors: rgbs, alphas, depthmaps, weights, uncertainties. 2. Calculate total rays: N{\text{rays\all}} = \text{rays.shape}[0]. 3. Determine the number of chunks: N{\text{chunks}} = \lfloor N{\text{rays\all}} / \text{chunk} \rfloor + \mathbb{I}(N{\text{rays\all}} \bmod \text{chunk} > 0) where \mathbb{I} is the indicator function. 4. Iterate chunkidx from 0 to N{\text{chunks}} - 1: a. Extract and move chunk to device: \text{start} = \text{chunk\idx} \times \text{chunk}, \text{end} = (\text{chunk\idx} + 1) \times \text{chunk}, \text{rays\chunk} = \text{rays}[\text{start}:\text{end}] copied to device. b. Perform the forward pass through the neural field: \text{rgb\map}, \text{depth\map} = \text{tensorf}(\text{rays\chunk}, \text{is\train}=\text{is\train}, \text{white\bg}=\text{white\bg}, \text{ndc\ray}=\text{ndc\ray}, N\samples=N\samples). c. Append results to lists: \text{rgbs}.\text{append}(\text{rgb\map}), \text{depth\maps}.\text{append}(\text{depth\map}). 5. Concatenate along ray dimension and return: \text{concatenate}(\text{rgbs}), \text{None}, \text{concatenate}(\text{depth\maps}), \text{None}, \text{None}. Nsamples: Default -1. Number of samples per ray. whitebg: Default True. Background color assumption for alpha compositing. ndcray: Default False. Enables NDC coordinate transformation. istrain: Default False. Enables gradient tracking mode. Explicitly returns None for alphas, weights, and uncertainties. Pipelines expecting full volumetric outputs will crash or produce invalid data if they unpack all five return values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def concatenate(tensors, dim=0): """Concatenates a list of tensors along the specified dimension.""" if not tensors: return None import numpy as np return np.concatenate(tensors, axis=dim) def copytodevice(tensor, device): """Copies a tensor to the specified compute device.""" return tensor.to(device) def chunkedtrilinearvolumerendering(rays, chunk, tensorf, device, istrain=False, whitebg=True, ndcray=False, Nsamples=-1): rgbs = [] alphas = [] depthmaps = [] weights = [] uncertainties = [] Nraysall = rays.shape[0] numchunks = Nraysall // chunk + int(Nraysall % chunk > 0) for chunkidx in range(numchunks): start = chunkidx chunk end = (chunkidx + 1) chunk rayschunk = copytodevice(rays[start:end], device) rgbmap, depthmap = tensorf( rayschunk, istrain=istrain, whitebg=whitebg, ndcray=ndcray, Nsamples=Nsamples) rgbs.append(rgbmap) depthmaps.append(depthmap) finalrgbs = concatenate(rgbs, dim=0) finaldepths = concatenate(depthmaps, dim=0) return finalrgbs, None, finaldepths, None, None Not given in the sources. body: Chunked Ray Rendering is a memory-management strategy for object-order volume rendering that processes rays in fixed-size batches (chunks) rather than all at once. It solves Out-Of-Memory (OOM) errors that occur when the number of rays in an image exceeds the accelerator's VRAM capacity or when the neural network model is too large for a full-batch forward pass. It sets itself apart from its parent, Batched Ray Rendering, by explicitly handling the sharding of these chunks across multiple hosts and devices in distributed settings, ensuring that partial results are correctly concatenated and reshaped into the final image. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of rays defined by origins \mathbf{o} and directions \mathbf{d}, typically shaped (H, W, 3) or flattened to (N, 3) where N = H \times W. A rendering function modelfn that accepts ray bundles and returns per-ray properties (color, depth, etc.). Configuration parameters including chunksize (or renderchunksize) and devicecount. Outputs: Rendered image tensors (e.g., RGB, depth) reshaped to (H, W, C), where C is the number of output channels. Data Structures: Ray Bundle: A dictionary or object containing tensors for ray origins, directions, and potentially other attributes (e.g., camera indices, time). Tensors are typically 2D: (N, D) where N is the number of rays and D is the feature dimension (e.g., 3 for origins). Chunk List: A list of ray bundles, each containing a subset of the total rays. Result Accumulator: A list of output tensors from each chunk, concatenated along the ray dimension (axis 0) before reshaping. Parameters: chunksize (or renderchunksize, maxraybatch): The maximum number of rays processed in a single forward pass. Typical values range from 1024 to 8192, chosen to fit within available VRAM while maximizing throughput. devicecount: The number of parallel devices (GPUs/TPUs) used for rendering. whitebkgd: Boolean flag for background compositing (default True). perturb: Boolean flag for sampling perturbation (default False for video rendering to avoid noise). defaultretkey: Optional string ('fine' or 'coarse') to select output key from modelfn. Steps: 1. Initialization: Flatten ray origins and directions to 2D tensors of shape (N, 3) where N = H \times W. Initialize empty lists for results. 2. Chunk Generation: Determine the number of chunks: N{\text{chunks}} = \lceil N / \text{chunk\size} \rceil. Generate start indices: \text{idx0s} = \text{range}(0, N, \text{chunk\size}). 3. Iteration: For each start index idx0 in idx0s: a. Slice: Extract the chunk of rays: \mathbf{o}{\text{chunk}} = \mathbf{o}[\text{idx0}: \text{idx0} + \text{chunk\size}], \mathbf{d}{\text{chunk}} = \mathbf{d}[\text{idx0}: \text{idx0} + \text{chunk\size}]. b. Padding (Distributed): If rendering across multiple devices, calculate the actual chunk size. If actualchunksize % devicecount != 0, pad the chunk with edge-mode values (e.g., repeating the last ray) to make the number of rays divisible by devicecount. Track the padding amount. c. Sharding (Distributed): Shard the chunk across hosts and devices. Calculate raysperhost = chunkrays.origins.shape[0] // jax.processcount(). Determine start and stop indices for the current host. Shard the chunk using a framework-specific utility. d. Forward Pass: Call the rendering function: resultschunk = modelfn(rayso=chunko, raysd=chunkd,...). If cudaray is enabled, staging is disabled, and the entire batch is processed at once. e. Unsharding (Distributed): Unreplicate and unshard the results from devices back to the host. Remove the previously added padding from the results to avoid corrupting image dimensions. f. Accumulate: Append the results (e.g., rgbchunk, depthchunk) to the result lists. 4. Concatenation: Concatenate all accumulated results along axis 0: \mathbf{R}{\text{total}} = \text{concat}(\mathbf{R}1, \mathbf{R}2, \dots). 5. Reshaping: Reshape the concatenated results from (N, C) back to (H, W, C). 6. Visualization Subset (Optional): If extracting a subset of rays for visualization, generate a deterministic random index set and subset the final rendering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Padding Removal: Padding must be tracked and removed during unsharding to avoid corrupting image dimensions. CUDA Raymarching: Staging is disabled when cudaray is True; the entire ray batch is processed at once, bypassing chunking. Non-Square Images: Flattening (H, W, 3) to (N, 3) requires storing H and W separately to correctly reshape results. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def chunkedrayrendering(rayso, raysd, modelfn, chunksize=4096, devicecount=1, H=None, W=None, device='cuda', whitebkgd=True, perturb=False): """ Render rays in chunks to manage memory and enable distributed sharding. Args: rayso: Tensor of ray origins, shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3). raysd: Tensor of ray directions, shape (H, W, 3) or (N, 3). modelfn: Function that takes (rayso, raysd) and returns rendered properties. chunksize: Number of rays per chunk. devicecount: Number of devices for sharding. H, W: Image dimensions. Required if rayso is 2D. device: Target device string. whitebkgd: Background compositing flag. perturb: Perturbation flag. Returns: rgb: Rendered RGB image, shape (H, W, 3). depth: Rendered depth image, shape (H, W). """ # Extract dimensions and flatten to (N, 3) if rayso.dim() == 3: Hin, Win, = rayso.shape rayso = rayso.reshape(-1, 3) raysd = raysd.reshape(-1, 3) H, W = Hin, Win else: N, = rayso.shape if H is None or W is None: raise ValueError("H and W must be provided when rayso is 2D.") N = rayso.shape[0] rgbs = [] depths = [] # Generate chunk indices idx0s = range(0, N, chunksize) for idx0 in idx0s: # Slice chunk endidx = min(idx0 + chunksize, N) chunko = rayso[idx0:endidx].clone() chunkd = raysd[idx0:endidx].clone() actualchunksize = chunko.shape[0] padding = (devicecount - (actualchunksize % devicecount)) % devicecount # Padding for distributed sharding if padding > 0: lastrayo = chunko[-1:].expand(padding, -1) lastrayd = chunkd[-1:].expand(padding, -1) chunko = torch.cat([chunko, lastrayo], dim=0) chunkd = torch.cat([chunkd, lastrayd], dim=0) # Move to device chunko = chunko.to(device) chunkd = chunkd.to(device) # Forward pass # Note: Sharding/unsharding logic is framework-specific (e.g., JAX pmap, PyTorch DDP) with torch.nograd(): out = modelfn(chunko, chunkd, whitebkgd=whitebkgd, perturb=perturb) # Extract results rgbchunk = out['rgb'] # Shape: (actualchunksize + padding, 3) depthchunk = out['depth'] # Shape: (actualchunksize + padding,) # Remove padding if padding > 0: rgbchunk = rgbchunk[:-padding] depthchunk = depthchunk[:-padding] # Accumulate rgbs.append(rgbchunk.cpu()) depths.append(depthchunk.cpu()) # Concatenate and reshape if not rgbs: return None, None rgbcat = torch.cat(rgbs, dim=0) depthcat = torch.cat(depths, dim=0) rgbimage = rgbcat.reshape(H, W, 3) depthimage = depthcat.reshape(H, W) return rgbimage, depthimage A variant that splits a huge tensor (ray bundle) into a list of minibatches to avoid out-of-memory issues. It uses a simple list comprehension to split the input tensor into chunks of size chunksize. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the total number of rays. The constant factor is slightly higher than non-chunked rendering due to the overhead of loop iterations and tensor concatenations. Memory Complexity: O(\text{chunk\size} \times D), where D is the memory footprint per ray (including intermediate activations). This allows rendering images with N \gg \text{chunk\size} on hardware with limited VRAM. Measured Performance: Typical chunksize values range from 1024 to 8192 rays, with specific implementations using 1024, 4096, or 8192. The optimal value depends on the model size and available VRAM. Larger chunks improve throughput by reducing kernel launch overhead, but risk OOM errors. Strengths: Enables rendering of high-resolution images and large scenes on consumer-grade GPUs. Supports multi-host distributed rendering by sharding chunks across devices. Limitations: Slightly slower than full-batch rendering due to overhead. Requires careful tuning of chunksize to balance memory and speed. Padding overhead is minimal but non-zero. When to use: When rendering large images or using large neural networks that exceed VRAM capacity. Essential for distributed rendering setups. When not to use: When cudaray is enabled, as staging is disabled and the entire batch is processed at once. For very small scenes where full-batch rendering fits in memory, chunking adds unnecessary overhead. Chunked Ray Rendering originated as a practical necessity in the development of Neural Radiance Fields (NeRF) and related neural rendering techniques. As NeRF models grew in complexity and image resolutions increased, the memory requirements for processing all rays in an image simultaneously exceeded the capacity of available GPUs. Early implementations in libraries like nerfies and multinerf introduced chunking to manage memory and enable distributed training and rendering. It is particularly important in distributed settings where rays are sharded across multiple hosts and devices. ziyc/L-Tracing, https://github.com/ziyc/L-Tracing, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) google-research/multinerf, https://github.com/google-research/multinerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) google/nerfies, https://github.com/google/nerfies, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Xharlie/pointnerf, https://github.com/Xharlie/pointnerf, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, https://github.com/damn8daniel/nerf-from-scratch, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, https://github.com/yashtmy/nerf-3d-vision, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) AlexSheldrick/densityboundedrayweights, https://github.com/AlexSheldrick/densityboundedrayweights, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) NeRF-Factory/IDDR-NGP, https://github.com/NeRF-Factory/IDDR-NGP, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) InanXR/FLASH, https://github.com/InanXR/FLASH, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) GitHub - apchenstu/TensoRF: [ECCV 2022] Tensorial Radiance Fields, a..., https://github.com/apchenstu/TensoRF, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Hybrid Splatting/Raycasting with Smooth Transition
head: Smooth Transition
body: This method renders volumetric datasets as a collection of overlapping 3D detailed kernels, combining GPU-accelerated splatting for coarse structure with raycasting for local detail. It solves the trade-off between the speed of splatting and the accuracy of raycasting by using a hierarchical representation where each node contains a 3D texture. Unlike pure splatting, it enhances each footprint with raycasted details along the kernel's extent, and unlike pure raycasting, it batches these operations per fragment. Inputs: A volumetric dataset represented hierarchically; a selected region (node) from the hierarchy; screen coordinates (x, y) for fragments. Outputs: Final color and opacity values for each pixel. Data Structures: 1. Hierarchical Representation: An octree structure where each node represents a coarse region of the dataset. 2. 3D Texture: Attached to each octree node, containing the necessary information (resampled data) for rendering that specific region. 3. Gaussian Kernel (Gi): A truncated radially symmetric Gaussian function associated with each sample point/node. 4. Bounding Sphere (Bi): The bounding box of the truncated Gaussian kernel, treated as a sphere centered at the original sample point. 5. 2D Lookup Table: Pre-computed via a classical pre-integrated classification scheme (Engel et al., 2001), storing color and opacity values. Parameters: Resampling Rate: Defines the density of sample points/kernels. Key control feature. 3D Texture Resolution: Defines the detail level stored in the GPU texture. Key control feature. Segment Length (l): Derived from the 3D texture resolution and the extent of the truncated kernel Gi. Steps: 1. Selection: At runtime, select a subpart of the hierarchical representation (an octree node) to render. 2. Splatting Projection: Project the Gaussian kernel Gi associated with the selected node onto the screen. This generates footprints Fi. 3. Fragment Processing: For each fragment f{i,x,y} at screen coordinates (x, y) within a footprint Fi: a. Ray Casting: Cast a ray through the fragment into the volume. b. Intersection: Determine the intersection of this ray with the bounding sphere Bi of the kernel Gi. This yields two points pa and pb. Note: In extreme cases, pa = pb. c. Segment Division: Divide the segment pa pb into n equal sections of length l. The step size l is derived from the 3D texture resolution and the kernel extent. d. Lookup: For each segment, perform a lookup into the 2D pre-integrated classification table to obtain a base color and opacity value. e. Weighting: Weight the result of the 2D lookup with the segment length l to handle varying segment sizes. This uses the approximation scheme from Roettger et al. (2000). f. Composition: Accumulate the weighted color and opacity values from all segments along the ray to enhance the appearance of the fragment. 4. Final Image: Compose the enhanced footprints to yield the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderhybridkernel(kernelnode, screenfragments): """ Renders a single kernel node using hybrid splatting/raycasting. Args: kernelnode: An octree node containing a 3D texture and Gaussian parameters. screenfragments: List of fragments (x, y) covered by the kernel's footprint. Returns: Accumulated color and opacity for each fragment. """ # Extract kernel properties G = kernelnode.gaussiankernel B = kernelnode.boundingsphere texture3d = kernelnode.texture3d lookuptable = kernelnode.preintegratedtable # Derive segment length from texture resolution and kernel extent # Not given in the sources: specific formula for deriving l from resolution/extent l = derivesegmentlength(texture3d.resolution, G.extent) results = {} for fragment in screenfragments: x, y = fragment.coords rayorigin, raydirection = fragment.getray() # Intersection with bounding sphere # Not given in the sources: specific intersection algorithm for sphere pa, pb = intersectraysphere(rayorigin, raydirection, B.center, B.radius) # Handle degenerate case if pa == pb: results[fragment] = (0.0, 0.0) # Or identity, depending on composition rules continue # Calculate segment vector segmentvector = pb - pa segmentlength = length(segmentvector) # Number of equal sections n = round(segmentlength / l) if n == 0: n = 1 stepsize = segmentlength / n accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 # Iterate over segments for i in range(n): # Start point of current segment tstart = i stepsize tend = (i + 1) stepsize # Sample points along the segment # Not given in the sources: exact sampling positions (e.g., midpoint) pstart = rayorigin + raydirection tstart pend = rayorigin + raydirection tend # Lookup in 2D table # Not given in the sources: how to map 3D positions to 2D table indices # Assuming table is indexed by distance and some other parameter (e.g., gradient) basecolor, baseopacity = lookuptable.query(pstart, pend) # Weight by segment length # Not given in the sources: exact weighting formula from Roettger et al. (2000) # Typically involves multiplying by stepsize or a normalized factor weightedcolor = basecolor stepsize weightedopacity = baseopacity stepsize # Accumulate # Not given in the sources: exact composition equation (e.g., front-to-back) accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity = composite(accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity, weightedcolor, weightedopacity) results[fragment] = (accumulatedcolor, accumulatedopacity) return results Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Varying Segment Lengths: Standard 2D table lookups assume fixed segment lengths. Since segment lengths vary with kernel size, results must be weighted by length l using the Roettger et al. (2000) approximation scheme. Degenerate Intersection: If the ray is tangent to or outside the bounding sphere, pa = pb. This case must be handled explicitly. Precision: The derivation of the sampling step l must be careful to align with the 3D texture resolution to avoid aliasing or blurring. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of fragments and the number of segments n per fragment. n is derived from the kernel extent and texture resolution. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the size of the hierarchical octree and the 3D textures attached to each node. Strengths: Combines the speed of splatting with the detail of raycasting; allows for variable resolution per region via the hierarchical structure. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of 3D textures and lookup tables; complexity in managing the hierarchical structure and segment weighting. When to Use: When rendering large volumetric datasets where some regions require high detail and others do not, and hardware acceleration for splatting is desired. When Not to Use: When uniform high resolution is required across the entire volume, or when memory bandwidth is severely constrained. The method was introduced in the paper "From Volume Splatting to Raycasting - A Smooth Transition". It builds on the idea of representing volumetric datasets as overlapping 3D detailed kernels. The hierarchical representation uses an octree, similar to approaches by Laur and Hanrahan. The pre-integrated classification scheme references Engel et al. (2001), and the segment weighting approximation references Roettger et al. (2000). name: GPU Implementation Pipeline
head: Single-pass GPU Raycasting, Volumetric Raycasting
body: The GPU Implementation Pipeline traces rays from the camera through each pixel into a 3D volume to compute color and opacity, implemented in a single pass using fragment shaders. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data directly on the GPU without generating intermediate polygonal meshes, differing from splatting (Splatting) by avoiding sorting and blending overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than texture-based splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D texture (volume) containing scalar density/intensity values; a 2D texture (jitter) for anti-aliasing; camera parameters (ViewMatrix, ModelViewProjectionMatrix, RayOrigin); rendering parameters (steplength, backgroundcolour, gamma, top, bottom, viewportsize, aspectratio, focallength). Output: A 2D color buffer with the final rendered image. Data Structures: volume: 3D texture storing scalar voxel data. jitter: 2D texture storing pre-generated random values for ray step jittering. Ray: A pair of 3D vectors containing origin and direction. AABB: Axis-Aligned Bounding Box defined by top and bottom corner vectors. Numbered Steps: 1. Initialize State: Create the volume data structure and load or generate data into the volume texture. 2. Compute Matrices: Calculate the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix using a perspective projection with field of view m{fov}, aspect ratio \frac{scaled\width}{scaled\height}, near plane 0.1, and far plane 100.0. Compute the view matrix by translating along the Z-axis: Tz = -4.0 \cdot \exp(\frac{m{distExp}}{600.0}). 3. Compute Ray Origin: Invert the view matrix and transform the world origin (0,0,0) to obtain the ray origin in world space. 4. Bind Shaders and Uniforms: Bind the fragment shader and set all uniform values including matrices, viewport dimensions, ray parameters, and texture units. 5. Clear Buffer: Clear the color buffer with backgroundcolour. 6. Fragment Shader Execution (Per Pixel): Execute the raycasting routine for the active mode (e.g., Alpha blending). Formulas: Ray Direction: \mathbf{d}{screen} = \left( 2\frac{x}{W} - 1, 2\frac{y}{H} - 1, -f \right), transformed by the View Matrix to world space \mathbf{d}. Ray-Box Intersection (Slab Method): \mathbf{d}{inv} = 1/\mathbf{d}, \mathbf{t}{top} = \mathbf{d}{inv} \cdot (\mathbf{top} - \mathbf{origin}), \mathbf{t}{bottom} = \mathbf{d}{inv} \cdot (\mathbf{bottom} - \mathbf{origin}), t0 = \max(0, \max(\min(\mathbf{t}{top}), \min(\mathbf{t}{bottom}))), t1 = \min(\max(\mathbf{t}{top}), \max(\mathbf{t}{bottom})). Ray Parameters: \mathbf{ray}{start} = (\mathbf{origin} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t0 - \mathbf{bottom}) / (\mathbf{top} - \mathbf{bottom}), \mathbf{ray}{stop} = (\mathbf{origin} + \mathbf{d} \cdot t1 - \mathbf{bottom}) / (\mathbf{top} - \mathbf{bottom}), \mathbf{r} = \mathbf{ray}{stop} - \mathbf{ray}{start}, L = \|\mathbf{r}\|, \mathbf{s} = \text{step\length} \cdot \mathbf{r} / L. Transfer Function: \alpha = \frac{e^v - 1}{e^1 - 1}, \mathbf{c} = v \cdot (1,1,1) + (1-v) \cdot (0,0,0) where v is the sampled intensity. Alpha Blending: \mathbf{C}{acc}.rgb = \alpha \mathbf{c} + (1-\alpha) \mathbf{C}{acc}.a \cdot \mathbf{C}{acc}.rgb, \mathbf{C}{acc}.a = \alpha + (1-\alpha) \mathbf{C}{acc}.a. Background Blend: \mathbf{C}{final}.rgb = \mathbf{C}{acc}.a \cdot \mathbf{C}{acc}.rgb + (1 - \mathbf{C}{acc}.a) \cdot \text{pow}(\text{background\colour}, \gamma).rgb, \mathbf{C}{final}.a = 1.0. Gamma Correction: \mathbf{C}{out}.rgb = \text{pow}(\mathbf{C}{final}.rgb, 1/\gamma). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def raycastfragment(viewmatrix, aspectratio, focallength, viewportsize, rayorigin, top, bottom, backgroundcolour, steplength, gamma, volumetex, jittertex, fragcoord): # 1. Ray direction dscreen = vec3( (2.0 fragcoord.x / viewportsize.x) - 1.0, (2.0 fragcoord.y / viewportsize.y) - 1.0, -focallength) dscreen.x = aspectratio dworld = (viewmatrix vec4(dscreen, 0.0)).xyz # 2. Ray-box intersection dinv = 1.0 / dworld ttop = dinv (top - rayorigin) tbottom = dinv (bottom - rayorigin) tmin = min(ttop, tbottom) tentry = max(max(tmin.x, tmin.y), 0.0) tmax = max(ttop, tbottom) texit = min(tmax.x, tmax.y) if tentry >= texit: return vec4(0.0) # 3. Ray parameters raystart = (rayorigin + dworld tentry - bottom) / (top - bottom) raystop = (rayorigin + dworld texit - bottom) / (top - bottom) rayvec = raystop - raystart raylength = length(rayvec) stepvec = steplength normalize(rayvec) # 4. Jitter jitterval = jittertex(fragcoord / viewportsize).r pos = raystart + stepvec jitterval # 5. Ray marching acccolor = vec4(0.0) while raylength > 0 and acccolor.a < 1.0: intensity = volumetex(pos).r alpha = (exp(intensity) - 1.0) / (exp(1.0) - 1.0) c = vec4(intensity, 0.0, 0.0, alpha) acccolor.rgb = alpha c.rgb + (1.0 - alpha) acccolor.a acccolor.rgb acccolor.a = alpha + (1.0 - alpha) acccolor.a raylength -= steplength pos += stepvec # 6. Background blend finalrgb = acccolor.a acccolor.rgb + (1.0 - acccolor.a) pow(backgroundcolour, gamma) finala = 1.0 # 7. Gamma correction outrgb = pow(finalrgb, 1.0 / gamma) return vec4(outrgb, finala) Parameters: steplength: Distance between samples. Smaller values increase accuracy but reduce performance. gamma: Gamma value for color correction. Typical value: 2.2. backgroundcolour: Color of the background. Typical value: Black (0,0,0). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Floating-point precision in texture lookups can cause artifacts if the volume is not properly normalized. Boundaries: The ray-box intersection must handle rays that do not intersect the volume (t0 > t1) by skipping the march. Empty Blocks: In multi-resolution structures, rays may pass through empty blocks. If a sample point is in an empty block, the ray should be advanced to the next non-empty block to avoid occlusion artifacts. This method performs object-order volume rendering by ray marching through a 3D texture stored in GPU memory, applying a transfer function to map scalar values to color and opacity, and compositing the result front-to-back. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data (such as medical DICOM series or synthetic density fields) directly on the GPU without generating intermediate polygonal meshes. It differs from isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) by preserving internal volume information, and from splatting (Splatting) by avoiding sorting and blending overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than texture-based splatting. The NVIDIA GeForce3 Volume Rendering Pipeline is a hardware-accelerated method for interactive volume rendering that utilizes per-fragment dependent texture reads and 4-way multi-texturing to eliminate intermediate scratch buffers. It distinguishes itself from prior scratch-buffer-dependent approaches (such as the SGI Octane2 method) by performing dynamic texture lookups based on fragment attributes, thereby avoiding expensive memory copy operations. This method implements a real-time rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting that streams Gaussian data to GPU memory on demand using a virtual memory system. It solves the memory capacity bottleneck of large scenes by mapping logical page IDs to physical GPU memory pages, replacing unused pages based on a least-recently-used (LRU) policy. Unlike software-based tile-sorting approaches (e.g., Kerbl et al.), this method performs global distance sorting of Gaussians in a GLSL compute shader before splatting them via the hardware rasterizer. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot M), where N is the number of pixels and M is the number of samples per ray. Measured Performance: On an Nvidia GeForce 8800 Ultra with 768 MB graphics texture memory, a 512^3 volume with 8.9:1 data reduction (SVR size 256^3, piecewise segment length 8 voxels) achieves global light integration (A) in 284-552 ms and first order scattering incremental refinements (B) in 62-233 ms. Strengths: Real-time interactivity; single-pass execution avoids intermediate buffers for the final compositing pass. Limitations: Computationally heavy per pixel compared to splatting; artifacts can appear if empty blocks are not handled correctly in multi-resolution structures. When to Use: When visualizing dense volumetric data with internal structure is required and real-time performance is needed. When Not to Use: When the volume is sparse and splatting would be more efficient, or when isosurface extraction is sufficient. The GPU Implementation Pipeline was introduced as a technique for interactive volume rendering using fragment shaders. It builds on the principles of ray casting and hardware acceleration. The method was developed to provide a basic skeleton for a visualizer that can be easily extended with a feature-rich GUI. body: This method performs object-order volume rendering by ray marching through a 3D texture stored in GPU memory, applying a transfer function to map scalar values to color and opacity, and compositing the result front-to-back. It solves the problem of visualizing volumetric data (such as medical DICOM series or synthetic density fields) directly on the GPU without generating intermediate polygonal meshes. It differs from isosurface extraction (e.g., Marching Cubes) by preserving internal volume information, and from splatting (Splatting) by avoiding sorting and blending overheads for dense volumes, though it is computationally heavier per pixel than texture-based splatting. Inputs: Volumetric scalar field data (e.g., 8-bit or 16-bit unsigned integers). Camera parameters: position, view matrix, projection matrix. Transfer function: a 1D texture mapping scalar values to RGBA. Optional: Surface depth map for occlusion, lighting parameters (direction, color), shadow maps. Outputs: A 2D color buffer (RGBA) representing the rendered volume. Optional: G-buffer attachments (normal, depth) for deferred rendering. 3D Volume Texture: Format: GLRED internal format with GLUNSIGNEDBYTE (8-bit) or GLUNSIGNEDSHORT (16-bit) data type. Dimensions: Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Compression: Supports r8unorm (1 byte/block), bc4-r-unorm (8 bytes/block, 4x4), or astc-12x12-unorm (16 bytes/block, 12x12) for WebGPU. Memory Layout for Compressed Upload: blocksWide = ceil(width / blockLength). blocksHigh = ceil(height / blockLength). bytesPerRow = blocksWide bytesPerBlock. Upload via queue.writeTexture with { bytesPerRow, rowsPerImage: blocksHigh }. Transfer Function Texture: Format: GLRGBA8 or GLRGBA16F. Dimensions: 256 \times 1 (mapping 0–255 input values to RGBA). Gradient Texture (Optional): Format: GLRG16F (16-bit float per component). Dimensions: Dx \times Dy \times Dz. Filters: GLLINEAR, Wrap: GLCLAMPTOBORDER. Uniforms (Vertex Shader): modelMatrix (mat4), modelViewMatrix (mat4), projectionMatrix (mat4), cameraPosition (vec3). inverseModelViewProjectionMatrix (mat4) for WebGPU ray generation. Uniforms (Fragment Shader): volumeTex (sampler3D), transferTex (sampler2D). boxSize (vec3): Physical dimensions of the volume bounding box. alphaScale, dtScale (float): Scaling factors for opacity and step size. useLighting, useSurface, useWatermark (bool). light0/1/2 (vec3), lightColor0/1/2 (vec3). surfaceDepthTex (sampler2D), surfaceColorTex (sampler2D). 1. Volume Loading and Preprocessing: Load raw scalar data from file (e.g., DICOM stack or binary). Create 3D texture. If 16-bit, use GLUNSIGNEDSHORT; if 8-bit, use GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. Compute histogram of volume data to determine normalization range (max value). Compute gradients using a compute shader (if lighting is enabled): Dispatch ceil(Dx/8) \times ceil(Dy/8) \times ceil(Dz/8) blocks. Read from volume texture, write to GLRG16F gradient texture. Apply smoothing pass by dispatching smoothGradientsCompute with the same block dimensions. 2. Ray Generation (Vertex Shader): Method A (WebGL/GLSL): Compute unnormalized ray direction: \text{rayDirUnnorm} = \text{position} - \text{cameraPosition} Normalize: \text{rayDir} = \text{normalize}(\text{rayDirUnnorm}). Apply X-axis mirroring if useVolumeMirrorX is true. Method B (WebGPU/WGSL): Generate a full-screen triangle. Calculate near and far points in object space by multiplying screen coordinates by inverseModelViewProjectionMatrix. 3. Ray-Volume Intersection (Slab Method): Define volume bounding box centered at origin with size boxSize (physical dimensions in mm, not voxel count). Intersect ray with box to get interval [t0, t1]. If useSurface is true: Sample surfaceDepthTex at fragment coordinate. Convert depth to camera distance. Clamp t1 = \min(t1, \text{surfaceDistance}). Clamp t0 = \min(t0, \text{surfaceDistance} - 0.0001) to prevent black artifacts from surface occlusion. If t0 \ge t1, discard fragment. Clamp t0 = \max(0.0, t0). 4. Step Size Calculation: Compute base step size components: dt0 = \frac{1.0}{\text{volumeTexSize} \cdot |\text{rayDir}|} dt = \min(dt0.x, \min(dt0.y, dt0.z)) \cdot dtScale If dt < 0.00001, output black and return (prevents context loss). Alternatively, calculate iterations: N = \lceil \text{maxSize} \cdot (1.0 / \text{stepScale}) \cdot 2.0 \rceil. 5. Ray Initialization: Calculate start position in real space: p = \text{cameraPosition} + t0 \cdot \text{rayDir} Apply dithering to reduce banding: \text{random} = \text{fract}(\sin(\text{gl\FragCoord.x} \cdot 12.9898 + \text{gl\FragCoord.y} \cdot 78.233) \cdot 43758.5453) \cdot 5.0 p = p + \text{random} \cdot dt \cdot \text{rayDir} Transform p and step vector dP = \text{rayDir} \cdot dt to texture space (normalized 0–1): p{\text{sized}} = \frac{p}{\text{boxSize}} + \text{vec3}(0.5) dP{\text{sized}} = \frac{\text{rayDir} \cdot dt}{\text{boxSize}} Compute alpha normalization factor to compensate for viewing angle: l = \|\text{rayDir} \cdot \text{boxSize}\| l{\min} = \min(\text{boxSize}.x, \min(\text{boxSize}.y, \text{boxSize}.z)) \text{alphaNormalization} = \frac{l{\min}}{l} \cdot \text{alphaScale}. 6. Ray Marching Loop (Fragment Shader): Initialize accumulated color C = (0,0,0,0) and transmittance T = 1.0. Loop i from t0 to t1 with step dt (or fixed number of steps, e.g., 64 or 512): 1. Sample volume: v = \text{texture}(\text{volumeTex}, p{\text{sized}}).r. 2. Get color and opacity from transfer function: c{\text{vol}} = \text{texture}(\text{transferTex}, \text{vec2}(v, 0.5)) c{\text{vol}}.a \cdot= \text{alphaNormalization} 3. Compute lighting (if enabled and c{\text{vol}}.a > 0): Sample gradient texture for normal. Compute diffuse/specular shading. Apply precomputed transmittance/shadow if available. 4. Front-to-back compositing: C = C + c{\text{vol}} \cdot T T = T \cdot (1.0 - c{\text{vol}}.a) 5. Advance position: p{\text{sized}} += dP{\text{sized}}. 6. If T < \epsilon (e.g., 0.001), break loop. 7. Post-Processing: Apply gamma correction: C{\text{final}} = C^{\frac{1}{\text{finalGamma}}} (typical gamma 6.0 for microscopy data). If useWatermark and fragment is at image center, write watermark value to blue channel. Unverified code. 1.0, position[1] 2.0 - 1.0, 0.0, 1.0]) # Ray direction is from camera to object point raydirunnorm = [objpos[i] - cameraposition[i] for i in range(3)] return objpos, raydirunnorm def fragmentmain(raydirunnorm: list, cameraposition: list, boxsize: list, volumetexsize: list, dtscale: float, alphascale: float, finalgamma: float, usesurface: bool, surfacedepthtex: dict, fragcoord: list, volumetex: dict, transfertex: dict, uselighting: bool) -> list: raydir = normalize(raydirunnorm) t0, t1 = slabintersect([0.0, 0.0, 0.0], raydir, boxsize) if t0 >= t1: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] if usesurface: depth = texturesample(surfacedepthtex, fragcoord) surfacedist = cameradistancefromdepth(depth) t1 = min(t1, surfacedist) t0 = min(t0, surfacedist - 0.0001) if t0 < 0.0: t0 = 0.0 if t0 >= t1: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Step size dt0 = [1.0 / (volumetexsize[i] abs(raydir[i])) for i in range(3)] dt = min(dt0) dtscale if dt < 0.00001: return [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0] # Dithering randomval = fract(sin(fragcoord[0] 12.9898 + fragcoord[1] 78.233) 43758.5453) 5.0 p = [cameraposition[i] + t0 raydir[i] + randomval dt raydir[i] for i in range(3)] # Transform to texture space psized = [p[i] / boxsize[i] + 0.5 for i in range(3)] dPsized = [raydir[i] dt / boxsize[i] for i in range(3)] # Alpha normalization l = length([raydir[i] boxsize[i] for i in range(3)]) lmin = min(boxsize) alphanorm = (lmin / l) alphascale acccolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] transmittance = 1.0 # Fixed steps or loop until t1 t = t0 while t < t1: v = texturesample(volumetex, psized) vcolor = texturesample(transfertex, [v, 0.5]) vcolor[3] = alphanorm if vcolor[3] > 0.0 and uselighting: # Compute lighting (diffuse, specular, shadows) #... lighting code... vcolor[0] = lightingfactor vcolor[1] = lightingfactor vcolor[2] = lightingfactor acccolor[0] += vcolor[0] transmittance acccolor[1] += vcolor[1] transmittance acccolor[2] += vcolor[2] transmittance transmittance = (1.0 - vcolor[3]) if transmittance < 0.001: break psized = [psized[i] + dPsized[i] for i in range(3)] t += dt # Gamma correction acccolor[0] = pow(acccolor[0], 1.0 / finalgamma) acccolor[1] = pow(acccolor[1], 1.0 / finalgamma) acccolor[2] = pow(acccolor[2], 1.0 / finalgamma) return [acccolor[0], acccolor[1], acccolor[2], 1.0] dtScale: Step size multiplier. Typical values depend on volume resolution and desired detail. alphaScale: Opacity scaling factor. finalGamma: Gamma correction exponent. Typical value: 6.0 for fluorescence microscopy. NumSteps: Fixed number of iterations (e.g., 64 in WebGPU sample, up to 512 in WebGL sample). threshold: Minimum opacity threshold for raycasting. mabsorption: Absorption coefficient (default 0.1). mdensityMult: Density multiplier (default 1.0). Voxel Aspect Ratio: CT slice spacing (mm) often differs from pixel spacing (<1mm). Rendering a volume as a cube flattens the anatomy. The bounding box boxSize must reflect physical dimensions in millimeters, not voxel counts. Step Size Underflow: If dt < 0.00001, the context may be lost. Output black and return. Surface Occlusion Artifacts: If a surface is between the camera and the volume, t0 must be pushed back by a small tolerance (0.0001) to prevent black artifacts. Compressed Texture Upload: Incorrect bytesPerRow and rowsPerImage calculations for compressed formats (BC4, ASTC) lead to texture corruption. Performance: High sample counts ("ridiculous number of samples") make this method expensive. Suitable for small volumes or infrequent updates. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot P), where N is the number of pixels and P is the number of ray marching steps per pixel. Performance is linear with resolution and step count. Memory Complexity: O(V) for the 3D volume texture, plus O(V) for gradients if computed. O(P) for temporary buffers if deferred rendering is used. Measured Performance: WebGL2 implementation with 512 steps per pixel can be slow on mobile devices. WebGPU implementation with 64 steps and MSAA (4x) is feasible for real-time on modern desktop GPUs. GpuHypertexture method is noted as "expensive" and suitable only for experimentation or small 3D textures. Strengths: High visual quality with accurate lighting and shadows. Supports complex transfer functions and surface occlusion. No sorting required (unlike splatting). Limitations: Computationally intensive for large volumes or high step counts. Banding artifacts if dithering is not used. Requires careful handling of aspect ratios for medical data. When to Use: Real-time visualization of moderate-sized volumes (e.g., 128³ to 256³) where lighting and transparency effects are critical. When Not to Use: Very large volumes (e.g., 1024³) without level-of-detail techniques, or when frame rates are extremely critical and lighting is not needed. Origin: Volume raycasting has been a standard technique since the 1980s. The specific implementations cited here adapt the technique to modern web APIs (WebGL2, WebGPU) and GPU architectures. Development: adapts the technique for DICOM volumes in a web application, emphasizing physical accuracy (mm vs voxels). implements a transfer function based on FluoRender for microscopy data, using Three.js and WebGL2. provides a C++/OpenGL implementation with deferred rendering and gradient computation. demonstrates WebGPU-specific features like compressed texture upload and MSAA. presents a "GpuHypertexture" approach for synthetic density fields with precomputed lighting. Usage: Medical imaging (DICOM), scientific visualization (microscopy), and synthetic effects (clouds, fire). feat(body-exposure): render a DICOM series in 3D, not a description of one, https://github.com/rizkyazhar486/Panacea/pull/1585, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) JaneliaSciComp/web-vol-viewer, https://github.com/JaneliaSciComp/web-vol-viewer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, https://github.com/jose-villegas/VolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Volume Rendering and 3D Textures | webgpu/webgpu-samples | DeepWiki, https://deepwiki.com/webgpu/webgpu-samples/6.1-volume-rendering-and-3d-textures, fetched 2026-10-27 theomission/hypertexture, https://github.com/theomission/hypertexture, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: NVIDIA GeForce3 Volume Rendering Pipeline
head: Dependent Texture Read Volume Rendering, GeForce3 Volume Rendering Pipeline, Nvidia GeForce3 Hardware Volume Rendering with Dependent Texture Reads, Register Combiner Shading
body: The NVIDIA GeForce3 Volume Rendering Pipeline is a hardware-accelerated method for interactive volume rendering that utilizes per-fragment dependent texture reads and four-way multi-texturing to eliminate the need for intermediate scratch buffers. It solves the performance bottleneck of previous hardware approaches (such as the SGI Octane2 method) by avoiding expensive memory copy operations, enabling real-time interaction with multi-dimensional transfer functions. Unlike sibling methods that rely on 3D textures and ray marching [2584-volume-rendering-with-3d-textures-and-ray-marching.md] or virtual memory management [8407-real-time-rendering-pipeline-with-virtual-memory.md], this pipeline is constrained by the GeForce3's hardware limitation of supporting only 2D dependent texture reads, forcing the 3D transfer function to be separable into a 2D component and a 1D component. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset, a 3D transfer function defined as a separable product of a 2D function (data value, gradient magnitude) and a 1D function (second derivative), and a normal map for shading. Output: A 2D image with color and alpha values computed via the transfer function and shading model. Data Structures and Layout: The pipeline utilizes four distinct textures accessed via four-way multi-texturing: 1. VGH Texture: A 3D texture (or 2D slice representation) containing Volume Gradient Histogram data or similar pre-computed statistics. 2. VG Dependent Texture: A 2D texture storing the mapping for data value and gradient magnitude. 3. H Dependent Texture: A 2D texture storing the mapping for the second derivative axis. 4. Normal Texture: A 2D texture storing quantized surface normals for shading. Numbered Steps: 1. Fragment Generation: For each fragment, compute the necessary scalar values: data value (v), gradient magnitude (g), and second derivative (h). 2. Normal Quantization: Quantize the surface normal vector \mathbf{n} = (nx, ny, nz) into 16-bit precision. Encode the first 8 bits of the normal as the Red channel and the second 8 bits as the Green channel of the Normal Texture. 3. Shading Computation: Compute lighting using either the pixel texture method (described in parent articles) or the Register Combiner extension. If using Register Combiners, the normal texture is sampled to retrieve lighting coefficients. 4. Transfer Function Evaluation (Separable): 2D Component: Sample the VG Dependent Texture using coordinates derived from v and g to obtain intermediate color and alpha values. 1D Component: Sample the H Dependent Texture using the coordinate derived from h. Composition: Multiply the alpha values from the 2D and 1D components to compose the final alpha. The color is typically not multiplied along the second derivative axis. 5. Register Combiner Processing: Use the NVIDIA Register Combiner extension to implement the second derivative axis processing and combine the results from the multi-texture stages. The central processing stage in the pipeline is the Register Combiner. 6. Final Blending: Multiply VG&H Alpha: This stage is required to combine the alpha from the 2D VG texture and the 1D H texture. Blend VG&H Color: This stage is usually not executed because color rarely varies along the second derivative axis. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragmentshader(v, g, h, normaln): """ v: scalar data value g: gradient magnitude h: second derivative normaln: 3D normal vector (normalized) """ # Step 1: Quantize and encode normal for shading texture lookup # 16-bit quantization: 8 bits for first component, 8 bits for second # Assuming standard normalization to [0, 1] before quantization nquantized = quantize16bit(normaln) normaltexcoord = encodenormalto2d(nquantized) # Step 2: Sample Shading Normal Texture # Lighting calculation depends on the specific shading model (e.g., Phong) # implemented via Register Combiners or pixel texture method shadingcoefficients = sampletexture(NORMALTEXTURE, normaltexcoord) colorshaded = computeshading(shadingcoefficients, lightdirections) # Step 3: Sample 2D Transfer Function (Value & Gradient) vgtexcoord = encodevg(v, g) vgresult = sampletexture(VGDEPENDENTTEXTURE, vgtexcoord) colorvg = vgresult.color alphavg = vgresult.alpha # Step 4: Sample 1D Transfer Function (Second Derivative) htexcoord = encodeh(h) hresult = sampletexture(HDEPENDENTTEXTURE, htexcoord) alphah = hresult.alpha # Step 5: Compose Transfer Function # Alpha is multiplied (required) finalalpha = alphavg alphah # Color is typically not blended along the second derivative axis # If color blending is required, it would be: finalcolor = colorvg hresult.color # But sources state Blend VG&H Color stage is usually not executed finalcolor = colorvg # Step 6: Apply Shading # Register combiners may blend the transfer function color with shading # The exact register combiner program is hardware-specific, but logically: finalcolor = applyshading(finalcolor, colorshaded) return finalcolor, finalalpha def quantize16bit(normal): # Encode normal into 16-bit scheme # First 8 bits as Red, second 8 bits as Green # Implementation detail for encoding 3D normal into 2D texture coordinates pass def encodevg(v, g): # Map v and g to 2D texture coordinates pass def encodeh(h): # Map h to 1D texture coordinate (x-axis of 2D texture) pass def encodenormalto2d(nquantized): # Map 16-bit quantized normal to 2D texture coordinates pass Parameters: Texture Resolution: The dependent texture along the second derivative axis utilizes 8-bit resolution. Normal Quantization: 16-bit quantization scheme. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dimensionality Constraint: The GeForce3 hardware only supports 2D dependent texture reads. This strictly constrains the 3D transfer function to be a separable product of a 2D function (data value, gradient magnitude) and a 1D function (second derivative). Non-separable 3D transfer functions cannot be directly implemented. Color Variation: Assuming color does not vary along the second derivative axis is a common optimization; if it does, the "Blend VG&H Color" stage must be enabled, but sources indicate this is rarely done. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Eliminates the need for a scratch buffer, reducing memory overhead compared to previous hardware methods. Measured Performance: Significantly improves rendering performance by avoiding expensive copy operations required by the SGI Octane2 method. Scaling: Performance is limited by the GeForce3's 4-way multi-texturing capability and the 2D dependent texture read constraint. Strengths: Real-time interaction with multi-dimensional transfer functions; no scratch buffer overhead; efficient use of 8-bit resolution for the second derivative axis. Limitations: Cannot handle non-separable 3D transfer functions; limited to GeForce3 hardware capabilities. When to use: When real-time volume rendering with multi-dimensional transfer functions is required on GeForce3 hardware and the transfer function can be approximated as separable. When not to use: When non-separable 3D transfer functions are necessary or when higher-end hardware with 3D dependent texture reads is available. The NVIDIA GeForce3 Volume Rendering Pipeline was introduced in the context of interactive volume rendering using multi-dimensional transfer functions. It was developed to address the performance limitations of earlier hardware implementations, specifically the SGI Octane2 method which relied on scratch buffers and expensive copy operations. The method leverages the NVIDIA Register Combiner extension and the GeForce3's support for per-fragment dependent texture reads and 4-way multi-texturing. It was presented in papers by Kindlmann et al. around 2001. name: Real-Time Rendering Pipeline with Virtual Memory
head: Virtual Memory Gaussian Streaming Pipeline
body: This method implements a real-time rendering pipeline for 3D Gaussian Splatting that streams Gaussian data to GPU memory on demand using a virtual memory system. It solves the memory capacity bottleneck of large scenes by mapping logical page IDs to physical GPU memory pages, replacing unused pages based on a least-recently-used (LRU) policy. Unlike software-based tile-sorting approaches (e.g., Kerbl et al.), this method performs global distance sorting of Gaussians in a GLSL compute shader before splatting them via the hardware rasterizer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene of 3D Gaussians, each assigned to a logical page ID; camera position and orientation; a proxy mesh representing the spatial distribution of these pages. Output: A final 2D image with alpha-blended Gaussians. Data Structures: 1. Page Table: A single array structure (selected over hierarchical for better memory locality). Each entry contains: pageid (logical identifier), physicalpageindex (index of the physical memory page), valid (boolean indicating valid data), LOD (detail level), lastuseframe (frame index of last access), required (boolean flag for current frame necessity), and an LOD-dependent list of contained pages. 2. Gaussian Buffer: A storage buffer containing the actual Gaussian properties (translation, rotation, scale, opacity, spherical harmonics) for all active physical pages. 3. Index Buffer: A buffer of indices, one per Gaussian, used to sort and retrieve Gaussian properties. 4. Staging Buffer: A temporary buffer used to transfer new page data before copying to the Gaussian Buffer. Numbered Steps: 1. Proxy Rendering: Render a proxy mesh where each face is marked with a pageid to generate a list of visible page IDs required for the current frame. 2. Page Table Update: a. Traverse the page table entries and mark entries as required if their pageid is in the visible list. b. Identify free physical pages (those with valid=false or whose pageid is not in the required list) and store them along with their lastuseframe. c. Remove pages from the required list that are already present in the page table at the correct LOD; the remaining required list contains only pages missing from GPU memory. 3. Data Streaming: a. Copy the data for the remaining required pages into the Staging Buffer. b. Select free physical pages from the list generated in Step 2b based on the Least-Recently-Used (LRU) order (lowest lastuseframe). c. Copy the Staging Buffer contents into the Gaussian Buffer at the selected physical page indices. d. Update the Page Table entries for these pages to mark them valid, set their physicalpageindex, and update lastuseframe to the current frame. e. Write the list of currently valid physical pages to a buffer accessible by the GPU renderer. 4. Index Generation: A compute shader converts the list of valid physical pages into a list of sortable indices and calculates the distance of each Gaussian from the camera. 5. Global Sorting: A compute shader performs a radix sort on the index buffer based on the calculated camera distances to ensure Gaussians are sorted back-to-front for correct alpha blending. 6. Rendering: a. Dispatch a vertex shader for every Gaussian in the sorted index buffer; the vertex shader retrieves Gaussian properties from the Gaussian Storage Buffer using the sorted index. b. Geometry Construction: If geometry shaders are available, use them to construct rectangular quads from the point primitives. If geometry shaders are unavailable, render point primitives as squares. c. Fragment Shader: Discard pixels outside the splatted Gaussian shape (ellipse). d. Alpha Blending: Combine the quads via alpha blending to create the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class PageTableEntry: pageid: int physicalpageindex: int valid: bool lod: int lastuseframe: int required: bool containedpages: list[int] # LOD-dependent list of contained pages class Gaussian: position: list[float] # vec3 rotation: list[float] # quat scale: list[float] # vec3 opacity: float shcoeffs: list[float] pagetable: list[PageTableEntry] gaussianbuffer: list[Gaussian] indexbuffer: list[int] cameraposition: list[float] gaussiansperpage: int = 1024 # Not given in the sources, assumed constant for layout stagingbuffer: list[Gaussian] def updatepagetable(visiblepageids: list[int], currentframe: int) -> list[int]: # Step 2a: Mark required pages for entry in pagetable: entry.required = entry.pageid in visiblepageids # Step 2b: Identify free pages and store with last use frame freepages = [] for entry in pagetable: if not entry.required: freepages.append(entry) # Sort free pages by lastuseframe (LRU order) freepages.sort(key=lambda e: e.lastuseframe) # Step 2c: Remove pages already present in the page table at the correct LOD requirednewpages = [] for pageid in visiblepageids: present = False for entry in pagetable: if entry.pageid == pageid and entry.valid and entry.required: present = True break if not present: requirednewpages.append(pageid) # Step 3: Data Streaming # Copy new required pages to a staging buffer stagingbuffer.clear() for pageid in requirednewpages: pagedata = fetchpagedatafromstaging(pageid) stagingbuffer.extend(pagedata) # Choose free physical pages based on LRU order and copy to Gaussian buffer for i, pageid in enumerate(requirednewpages): if i < len(freepages): targetentry = freepages[i] startidx = targetentry.physicalpageindex gaussiansperpage for j, g in enumerate(stagingbuffer[igaussiansperpage: (i+1)gaussiansperpage]): gaussianbuffer[startidx + j] = g # Update Page Table targetentry.valid = True targetentry.lastuseframe = currentframe targetentry.required = True return requirednewpages def fetchpagedatafromstaging(pageid: int) -> list[Gaussian]: # Simulates reading page data from CPU memory or staging area return [Gaussian() for in range(gaussiansperpage)] def renderframe(): # Step 4: Index Generation & Distance Calculation distances = [0.0] len(indexbuffer) for i, idx in enumerate(indexbuffer): g = gaussianbuffer[idx] dx = g.position[0] - cameraposition[0] dy = g.position[1] - cameraposition[1] dz = g.position[2] - cameraposition[2] distances[i] = (dxdx + dydy + dzdz) 0.5 # Step 5: Global Sorting (Radix Sort) sortedindices = radixsortindices(indexbuffer, distances) # Step 6: Rendering # Dispatch vertex shader for every Gaussian in sortedindices # Retrieve properties from gaussianbuffer # Geometry shader constructs rectangular quads (or fallback to point primitives as squares) # Fragment shader discards pixels outside splatted Gaussian shape # Alpha blending combines quads for idx in sortedindices: g = gaussianbuffer[idx] # Vertex shader computes screen-space quad vertices # Rasterizer fills fragments # Fragment shader evaluates Gaussian alpha and discards if below threshold pass def radixsortindices(indices: list[int], distances: list[float]) -> list[int]: # Standard GPU radix sort implementation # Sorts indices array in-place based on distances array combined = list(zip(distances, indices)) combined.sort(key=lambda x: x[0]) return [idx for, idx in combined] Parameters and Typical Values: Page Size: Not given in the sources. LOD Threshold: Not given in the sources, though LOD-dependent lists are mentioned. Frame Time Budget: The pipeline aims to complete within a threshold, e.g., 16 ms. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Fallback Rendering: Using point primitives instead of geometry shader quads results in square fragments. This causes a significant increase in fragment shader invocations and subsequent discards, reducing performance. Memory Locality: A hierarchical page table was considered but rejected in favor of a single array to improve memory locality. Time Complexity: Sorting is performed using a radix sort on the index buffer, which is generally O(N) for N Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is bounded by the number of physical pages loaded into GPU memory, determined by available VRAM and the LRU eviction policy. Performance: The method is designed for real-time performance, targeting frame times below 16 ms. It avoids the overhead of sparse residency indirection textures by using an index buffer. Strengths: Global sorting ensures correct alpha blending; virtual memory allows rendering scenes larger than VRAM; single-array page table improves locality. Limitations: Requires geometry shaders for optimal performance (fallback is inefficient); global sorting can be costly for extremely large numbers of Gaussians compared to tile-based approaches. This method originates from research on applying virtual memory concepts to 3D Gaussian Splatting. It contrasts with the original 3DGS implementation by Kerbl et al., which uses a CUDA-based software renderer with tile-based sorting. The approach adapts virtual texturing techniques (Barrett [30]) to the specific data structure of Gaussian splats, using a proxy mesh to determine visible pages.
