name: Multi-Pass and Sequential Stage Architectures
body: Multi-pass and sequential stage architectures decompose volume rendering into distinct, ordered computational phases to manage complexity, memory bandwidth, or specific visual effects that cannot be achieved in a single rasterization pass. Unlike single-pass splatting or ray-marching methods, these architectures explicitly separate data traversal, shading, compositing, or post-processing into separate GPU passes, often utilizing intermediate Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) or fragment lists. They are chosen when the rendering workload requires decoupling geometry processing from shading logic, managing complex fragment storage for accurate transparency, or integrating screen-space effects like ambient occlusion. The family shares the fundamental mechanism of treating volumetric data as a set of geometric or parametric primitives that are transformed and rasterized. 1. Primitive Representation: The volume is decomposed into primitives. Each primitive k is defined by its position \mathbf{p}k, density/extinction coefficient gk or \rhok, and a reconstruction kernel h (typically a Gaussian). 2. Transformation: Primitives are transformed from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or specific factorizations (e.g., shear-warp). For perspective projections, the kernel shape may be distorted (e.g., EWA splatting) to account for foreshortening. 3. Rasterization: The transformed primitives are projected onto the 2D image plane. The contribution of a voxel D to a screen point (x,y) is determined by the footprint function F(x,y), which is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view direction: F(x,y) = \int h(x-xD, y-yD, z) \, dz The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density: P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D) 4. Compositing: Contributions are accumulated to form the final image. This is typically done using alpha blending in back-to-front or front-to-back order to handle transparency correctly. Splatting compositing is performed along sheets (all pixels at once for a set of voxels), whereas ray-casting composites along rays (one sample at a time). 5. Hardware Acceleration: Most methods in this family rely on GPU rasterization pipelines for performance, enabling real-time interactivity. A standard implementation structure for direct volume rendering that processes scalar field data through a sequence of stages to produce a 2D image without fitting geometric primitives. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D volumetric data by discretizing the continuous volume rendering integral along light rays, mapping scalar values to optical properties, and compositing the results. What sets it apart from its siblings, such as the Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline or the Deferred Rendering Pipeline, is its explicit separation of classification (opacity assignment) and shading (color assignment) into distinct, often parallel, steps before ray casting, allowing for independent control of surface appearance and transparency. A multi-pass architecture for real-time smoke volume rendering that processes geometry through four distinct stages to store per-pixel fragment data in GPU memory structures. It is chosen to maintain high accuracy and circumvent the self-intersection and global intersection problems inherent in raytracing approaches. Unlike the Volume Rendering Pipeline which typically evaluates rays directly, or the Deferred Rendering Pipeline which separates shading from geometry, this method explicitly decouples fragment construction and insertion from their final evaluation to manage complex storage requirements. A multi-pass deferred rendering sequence that computes depth, position/normal, materials, filtered normals, shadows, SSAO, blurred AO, and final shading in separate framebuffer objects. It sets itself apart from the Volume Rendering Pipeline by decoupling geometry traversal from shading logic, and from the Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline by relying on screen-space post-processing for effects like ambient occlusion rather than explicit fragment lists. Definition: Renders volumetric data in three sequential passes: eye pass (direct lighting/color), light pass (opacity accumulation for shadows), and composite pass (blends results). Steps: 1. Eye pass: Render volume to meyeBuffer with direct lighting, using meyePipeline and meyeSet. 2. Light pass: Accumulate opacity into mlightBuffer using mlightPipeline and mvolSet, transitioning layout from ColorAttachmentOptimal to ShaderReadOnlyOptimal. 3. Composite pass: Bind mcompositePipeline and mcompSet, draw 3 triangles (full-screen quad) using meyeBuffer as a sampled texture. Layout: Buffers include meyeBuffer (eye pass output), mlightBuffer (light pass opacity accumulation), mvolumeTex (3D volume data, R8G8Unorm), and mtfTex (transfer function). Definition: A modular differentiable rendering pipeline containing four stages: vertex processing, rasterization, fragment shading, and post-processing. Steps: Supports various rasterization algorithms and shading models through efficient interpolation between Jittor and CUDA. Usage: Supports surface rendering for 3D meshes and volume rendering for 3D volumes. Supports PBR materials and shading effects such as soft shadows, ambient occlusions, subsurface scattering, and global illumination. The concept of multi-pass rendering in volume visualization evolved from the need to handle complex lighting and transparency effects that single-pass rasterization could not efficiently support. Early direct volume rendering methods, such as the Shading and Classification Pipeline, established the separation of opacity and color assignment to improve visual fidelity. As GPU architectures advanced, fragment list-based approaches emerged to handle complex smoke and fire simulations by decoupling fragment storage from evaluation, addressing issues like self-intersection in ray-tracing. Deferred rendering techniques, originally developed for surface rendering, were adapted for volume rendering to integrate screen-space effects like ambient occlusion and shadows without the performance penalty of explicit ray casting. The rise of differentiable rendering has further refined these pipelines, allowing for gradient computation through the entire multi-stage process for applications in computer vision and optimization. sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, https://github.com/sho3la/GPUGemsVolumeRendering, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Jrender: An efficient differentiable rendering library based on Jittor, https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1524070323000322, fetched 2026-11-01

name: Volume Rendering Pipeline
head: CRIO Process, Classification, Reflection, Illumination, Opacity, Rendering Stages, Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) Pipeline, Shading and Classification Pipeline, VolumeRenderer forward method
body: The Volume Rendering Pipeline is a conceptual and implementation structure for Direct Volume Rendering (DVR) that processes volumetric data through a sequence of stages to produce a 2D image. It solves the problem of visualizing 3D scalar fields by mapping sample properties to optical attributes (color, opacity) and compositing them along viewing rays. It is distinct from splatting methods, which decompose the volume into geometric primitives for rasterization, by treating each sample as a semi-transparent cloud that is shaded and projected directly without intermediate geometric fitting. The pipeline typically consists of six sequential stages: Data Traversal, Interpolation, Gradient Computation, Classification, Shading/Illumination, and Compositing. Input: A 3D scalar field f0(\mathbf{x}i) defined at voxel locations \mathbf{x}i = (xi, yj, zk). Output: A 2D image where each pixel (u,v) has a final color C\lambda(u,v) and opacity \alpha(u,v). Voxel Database: An array of scalar values. In some implementations (e.g., DVR 1.0), this is stored in a simple binary format with width, height, and depth specified first, followed by 16-bit little-endian data values. Prepared Values Array: An intermediate array f1(\mathbf{x}i) resulting from data preparation steps. Color Array: An array of RGB colors c\lambda(\mathbf{x}i) for each voxel, where \lambda \in \{r, g, b\}. Opacity Array: An array of scalar opacities \alpha(\mathbf{x}i) for each voxel. Ray Bundle: A set of rays defined by origin and direction, often generated from camera parameters. 1. Data Traversal and Preparation: The pipeline begins by traversing the 3D scalar field. This step may include corrections for non-orthogonal sampling grids, patient motion, contrast enhancement, or interpolation of additional samples. The output is an array of prepared values f1(\mathbf{x}i). 2. Interpolation: Since sampling positions along a ray usually do not coincide with voxel centers, values must be interpolated. For ray-casting pipelines, this occurs during ray traversal. For pre-classification pipelines, interpolation may occur on the voxel grid itself or during the ray casting phase. 3. Gradient Computation: The gradient of the scalar field \nabla f is computed at sample positions to provide visual cues for shading. This is typically approximated using central differences. The gradient vector serves as a surface normal for lighting calculations. 4. Classification: A classification procedure maps the prepared values (or interpolated sample values) to optical properties. Transfer functions are applied to assign an opacity \alpha and potentially a color to each sample based on features like density or gradient magnitude. Unwanted data values are faded out (opacity set to zero). 5. Shading and Illumination: A shading model calculates the final color c\lambda for each sample. This uses the assigned color, the position of the light source, and the view point. Models range from simple identity functions to directional lighting like Phong shading. 6. Compositing: Rays are cast from the observer eyepoint through the volume. For each ray, samples are taken at K evenly spaced locations \tilde{\mathbf{x}}i along the ray. The color and opacity at these locations are determined by resampling the pre-computed color and opacity arrays using trilinear interpolation from the eight closest voxels. These samples are composited back-to-front using the transparency formula to produce the final pixel color. Transparency Formula (Compositing): The color C{out, \lambda} of the ray leaving a sample is related to the color C{in, \lambda} entering the sample, the sample color c\lambda, and opacity \alpha by: C{out, \lambda} = C{in, \lambda}(1 - \alpha) + c\lambda \alpha This is applied recursively from back to front. Ray Sampling: Sample locations \tilde{\mathbf{x}}i along a ray are computed as: \tilde{\mathbf{x}}i = \mathbf{x}0 + i \frac{d}{K} where \mathbf{x}0 is the observer eyepoint, d is the ray length through the volume, and K is the number of evenly spaced sample locations. Trilinear Interpolation: The value V at a sample location is interpolated from the eight surrounding voxels V{ijk} using weights wx, wy, wz derived from the fractional distance to the voxel corners. K: Number of evenly spaced sample locations along a viewing ray. Light Source Position: Adjustable parameter for shading. View Point: Adjustable parameter for shading and ray origin. Transfer Function Parameters: Define the mapping from scalar values to color and opacity. Performance Cost: Shading and trilinear interpolation between eight voxels are high-cost operations. In some implementations, these can be switched off to improve performance, potentially reducing visual quality. Precision: The input data format may require specific endianness (e.g., little-endian 16-bit) which must be handled correctly during loading. Clipping: Standard pipelines apply clipping globally. Specialized variants are needed to render important structures differently if they lie within a clipped area. Unverified code. Args: volumedata: 3D list of scalar values indexed as [x][y][z]. width, height, depth: Dimensions of the volume. rayorigin: Tuple (ox, oy, oz) for the observer eyepoint. raydirection: Tuple (dx, dy, dz) for the ray direction. numsamples: Integer K, number of samples per ray. transferfunctions: List of functions mapping scalar value to (color, opacity). Returns: image: 2D list of RGB colors. alphaimage: 2D list of opacities. """ image = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] alphaimage = [[0.0 for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # Pre-compute voxel colors and opacities (Pre-classification approach) voxelcolors = [[[None for in range(depth)] for in range(height)] for in range(width)] voxelopacities = [[[0.0 for in range(depth)] for in range(height)] for in range(width)] for x in range(width): for y in range(height): for z in range(depth): val = volumedata[x][y][z] color, opacity = applytransferfunction(val, transferfunctions) voxelcolors[x][y][z] = color voxelopacities[x][y][z] = opacity for v in range(height): for u in range(width): raylength = computeraylength(rayorigin, raydirection, width, height, depth) stepsize = raylength / numsamples currentcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) currentopacity = 1.0 # Traverse ray from back to front for k in range(numsamples, 0, -1): t = (k - 0.5) stepsize samplepos = (rayorigin[0] + t raydirection[0], rayorigin[1] + t raydirection[1], rayorigin[2] + t raydirection[2]) if not isinsidevolume(samplepos, width, height, depth): continue samplecolor = trilinearinterpolate(voxelcolors, samplepos) sampleopacity = trilinearinterpolate(voxelopacities, samplepos) currentcolor = (currentcolor[0] (1 - sampleopacity) + samplecolor[0] sampleopacity, currentcolor[1] (1 - sampleopacity) + samplecolor[1] sampleopacity, currentcolor[2] (1 - sampleopacity) + samplecolor[2] sampleopacity) currentopacity = currentopacity (1 - sampleopacity) if currentopacity >= 1.0: break image[v][u] = currentcolor alphaimage[v][u] = 1.0 - currentopacity return image, alphaimage def applytransferfunction(value, transferfunctions): color = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) opacity = 0.0 for tf in transferfunctions: c, a = tf(value) opacity += a (1 - opacity) color = (color[0] (1 - a) + c[0] a, color[1] (1 - a) + c[1] a, color[2] (1 - a) + c[2] a) return color, opacity def computeraylength(rayorigin, raydirection, width, height, depth): # Computes the length of the ray segment inside the volume AABB return 10.0 # Simplified for example def isinsidevolume(point, width, height, depth): return 0 <= point[0] < width and 0 <= point[1] < height and 0 <= point[2] < depth def trilinearinterpolate(dataarray, point): x, y, z = point ix, iy, iz = int(x), int(y), int(z) fx, fy, fz = x - ix, y - iy, z - iz ix = max(0, min(ix, len(dataarray) - 2)) iy = max(0, min(iy, len(dataarray[0]) - 2)) iz = max(0, min(iz, len(dataarray[0][0]) - 2)) c000 = dataarray[ix][iy][iz] c100 = dataarray[ix+1][iy][iz] c010 = dataarray[ix][iy+1][iz] c110 = dataarray[ix+1][iy+1][iz] c001 = dataarray[ix][iy][iz+1] c101 = dataarray[ix+1][iy][iz+1] c011 = dataarray[ix][iy+1][iz+1] c111 = dataarray[ix+1][iy+1][iz+1] c00 = c000 (1 - fx) + c100 fx c01 = c010 (1 - fx) + c110 fx c10 = c001 (1 - fx) + c101 fx c11 = c011 (1 - fx) + c111 fx c0 = c00 (1 - fy) + c01 fy c1 = c10 (1 - fy) + c11 fy result = c0 (1 - fz) + c1 fz return result The Post-classification Shading Pipeline (also known as Post-DVRI) is a volume rendering model where raw volume density values are interpolated by the ray first, and the resulting interpolated values are then mapped to color and opacity via transfer functions, followed by shading. This approach solves the blurring artifacts inherent in pre-classification methods by ensuring that high-frequency details in transfer functions are resolved after interpolation. It is distinct from the Pre-classification Shading Pipeline, which classifies discrete voxel values before interpolation, resulting in blurry edges and loss of fine detail under magnification. A pipeline split into two parallel stages to render important pathological structures with different parameters even if they lie in a clipping area, while rendering anatomical structures normally. Stage 1 renders anatomical structures that are not clipped away using standard volume rendering steps. Stage 2 renders important structures (e.g., vessels, pathological tissue) that are excluded from clipping, using specific rendering parameters (gradient computation, classification, lighting). Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of pixels and the number of samples per ray (O(W \cdot H \cdot K)). Gradient computation and classification are typically O(V) where V is the volume size, if done pre-pass, or O(W \cdot H \cdot K) if done per-sample. Memory Complexity: O(V) to store the volume data. Performance: High computational cost due to shading and interpolation per sample. Performance can be improved by switching off shading/interpolation or using early ray termination. Strengths: High visual quality, ability to handle complex transfer functions, independence of shading and classification allows for undistorted visualization of 3D shape. Limitations: Blurring in pre-classification methods; high cost of per-voxel shading and interpolation; global clipping limitations in standard pipelines. When to use: When high-quality visualization of internal structures is required, and interactive frame rates are not the primary constraint, or when hardware acceleration is available. When not to use: When real-time performance on low-end hardware is critical without optimization, or when the volume data is extremely large and memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. The volume rendering pipeline was formalized in the late 1980s. Key early work includes the presentation of the "Display of Surfaces from Volume Data" technique by Marc Levoy at the SPIE Medical Imaging II conference in January 1988. This work described the pipeline stages of classification, shading, and back-to-front compositing. The term "CRIO" (Classification, Reflection, Illumination, Opacity) was used to describe the conceptual feed-forward process in splatting algorithms. The pipeline structure is widely cited in volume rendering literature, such as Engel's survey. name: Post-classification Shading Pipeline
head: Post-DVRI, Post-classified DVR, Post-classified Volume Rendering, Post-shaded DVRI
body: The Post-classification Shading Pipeline (also known as Post-DVRI) is a volume rendering model where raw volume density values are interpolated by the ray first, and the resulting interpolated values are then mapped to color and opacity via transfer functions, followed by shading. This approach solves the blurring artifacts inherent in pre-classification methods by ensuring that high-frequency details in transfer functions are resolved after interpolation. It is distinct from the Pre-classification Shading Pipeline, which classifies discrete voxel values before interpolation, resulting in blurry edges and loss of fine detail under magnification. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D scalar volume grid fd(x,y,z) representing density; a ray defined by origin \mathbf{x} and direction \mathbf{r}; transfer functions for color C\lambda and opacity \alpha; shading function C\lambda (which may depend on gradient); ray step size \Delta s; and ray length L. Output: The accumulated color I\lambda(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}) for each pixel. Data Structures: Volume Grid: A 3D array of scalar density values. Transfer Functions: Lookup tables (LUTs) mapping density values to color and opacity. Gradient Field: Pre-computed or on-the-fly computed gradient vectors \nabla f for shading normals. Steps: 1. Ray Marching: For each pixel, cast a ray through the volume. Sample the volume at intervals \Delta s along the ray. 2. Interpolation: For each sample position si = \mathbf{x} + i\Delta s \mathbf{r}, interpolate the raw density value f(si) and the gradient vector g(si) from the volume grid fd using a 3D interpolation kernel (e.g., trilinear or tri-linear). 3. Classification: Map the interpolated density f(si) to opacity \alpha(f(si)) and base color using the transfer function \alpha. 4. Shading: Compute the shading color C\lambda based on the interpolated density f(si) and the interpolated gradient g(si). The gradient g(i\Delta s) serves as the surface normal for lighting calculations. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the color contributions using front-to-back alpha blending. Formula: The final image intensity I\lambda(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}) is computed as: I\lambda(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{r}) = \sum{i=0}^{L/\Delta s - 1} C\lambda(f(i\Delta s), g(i\Delta s)) \alpha(f(i\Delta s)) \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(f(j\Delta s))) Where: L is the total length of the ray within the volume. \Delta s is the step size. f(i\Delta s) is the interpolated volume function value at sample i. g(i\Delta s) is the interpolated gradient vector at sample i. \alpha(f(i\Delta s)) is the opacity derived from the transfer function applied to the interpolated density. C\lambda(f(i\Delta s), g(i\Delta s)) is the color contribution, determined by transfer and shading functions using the interpolated density and gradient. The product term \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(f(j\Delta s))) represents the transmittance from previous samples. Note: Some sources define the summation limit as L/\Delta s without the -1, implying inclusive upper bound indexing. The standard front-to-back accumulation typically iterates up to the last sample within the volume bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def postclassificationshadingpipeline(volumegrid, rayorigin, raydirection, transferfunctionalpha, transferfunctioncolor, shadingfunction, stepsize, volumebounds): """ Implements the Post-classification Shading Pipeline. Args: volumegrid: 3D array of density values. rayorigin: 3D vector (x, y, z). raydirection: 3D vector (x, y, z), normalized. transferfunctionalpha: Function or LUT mapping density -> opacity. transferfunctioncolor: Function or LUT mapping density -> base color. shadingfunction: Function mapping (density, gradient) -> shaded color. stepsize: Float, distance between samples. volumebounds: Object defining the AABB of the volume. Returns: Color vector (R, G, B). """ # 1. Intersect ray with volume bounds to get tmin and tmax tmin, tmax = intersectrayaabb(rayorigin, raydirection, volumebounds) if tmax < 0: return (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Ray misses volume # Initialize accumulators accumulatedcolor = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0) accumulatedopacity = 0.0 transmittance = 1.0 # 2. Ray march t = tmin while t <= tmax: # Current sample position pos = rayorigin + raydirection t # 3. Interpolate raw density and gradient from volume grid # fval is the interpolated scalar density # gvec is the interpolated gradient vector (normal) fval = interpolatedensity(volumegrid, pos) gvec = interpolategradient(volumegrid, pos) # 4. Classification: Map density to opacity alpha = transferfunctionalpha(fval) # 5. Shading: Compute color based on density and gradient # Note: Some implementations might use base color from transfer function # and modulate it with shading. Here we assume shading function outputs final color. color = shadingfunction(fval, gvec) # 6. Compositing: Front-to-back blending # Contribution of current sample contribution = color alpha transmittance accumulatedcolor += contribution accumulatedopacity += alpha transmittance # Update transmittance for next sample transmittance = (1.0 - alpha) # Early ray termination optimization if accumulatedopacity >= 1.0: break t += stepsize return accumulatedcolor Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Partial Volume Effect: Interpolated density values may fall into a range classified as a material not actually present at the sample location, leading to false colors. Narrow Transfer Function Peaks: If the transfer function has very narrow peaks (e.g., specific density thresholds), standard ray sampling might miss these peaks entirely, failing to render thin structures. Pre-integrated transfer functions can mitigate this but are not part of the basic pipeline definition. Staircasing Artifacts: Avoiding false colors via prior segmentation can introduce high-frequency artifacts and staircasing. Classifies and shades discrete voxel values before interpolation. Chosen for performance or when partial volume effects are less critical; results in blurrier images at high resolutions compared to post-classification. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of samples per ray (O(L/\Delta s)) and the number of pixels. Memory Complexity: Depends on the storage of the volume grid and transfer function LUTs. Gradient computation can be done on-the-fly (increasing compute) or pre-computed (increasing memory). Performance: Generally faster than methods requiring complex geometric primitives but slower than pre-classification if gradient computation is expensive. Strengths: Produces considerably sharper images than pre-classified rendering because classification is performed after interpolation, eliminating blurry edges introduced by the interpolation filter. Fine detail in transfer functions is readily expressed in the final image. Limitations: Susceptible to partial volume artifacts (false colors). Can miss narrow peaks in transfer functions if ray sampling is too coarse. When to Use: When image sharpness and accurate representation of high-frequency transfer function details are prioritized over the avoidance of partial volume artifacts. When Not to Use: When partial volume artifacts are unacceptable and segmentation is not feasible, or when extreme performance is required and blur is tolerable (use Pre-classification). The Post-classification Shading Pipeline, also referred to as Post-DVRI (Post-shaded Direct Volume Rendering Integration), was developed as an alternative to the pre-classified model to address blurring issues in volume visualization. It is based on the principle that interpolating raw data before applying transfer functions allows for better resolution of high-frequency details. The mathematical formulation is derived from the generalized volume rendering integral, adapted for discrete sampling and interpolation. It is widely used in modern volume rendering systems where image quality is paramount. name: Pre-classification Shading Pipeline
head: Pre-DVRI, Pre-shaded DVR, Pre-shaded DVRI
body: The Pre-classification Shading Pipeline (also known as Pre-DVRI) is a volume rendering method where voxel values are mapped to optical properties (color and opacity) and shaded before ray sample interpolation occurs. Unlike the Post-classification Shading Pipeline, which interpolates raw density values first, this approach classifies and shades the discrete grid samples, then composites them along the ray. It is distinct from post-classification primarily in its handling of partial voluming and its susceptibility to blurring at high image resolutions. Input: A scalar volume grid V where each voxel v has a scalar value sv, optionally augmented with material indices and probabilities from a segmentation process. Output: A 2D image where each pixel represents the integrated light I\lambda(x, r) along the viewing ray r. The core data structure for a pre-classified voxel is a vector of four components: (R\alpha, G\alpha, B\alpha, \alpha). This is called associated color or opacity-weighted color. Let \tilde{C} denote the associated color vector, defined as \tilde{C} = C\alpha where C is the original color and \alpha is the opacity. 1. Classification and Shading (Pre-processing): Apply transfer functions to voxels to compute color C and opacity \alpha. If segmentation is available, use material indices and probabilities to resolve partial voluming. 2. Pre-multiplication: Pre-multiply the color of each voxel with its opacity before interpolation to form the associated color \tilde{C} = C\alpha. 3. Interpolation: Interpolate the associated color \tilde{C} and opacity \alpha from the grid to sample positions si along the ray. 4. Compositing: Composite the samples along the ray using the discretized volume rendering integral. I\lambda(x,r) = \sum{i=0}^{L/\Delta s} \tilde{C}\lambda(si) \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(sj)) Where: L is the length of ray r. \Delta s is the step size. \tilde{C}\lambda(si) is the associated color at sample i. \alpha(sj) is the opacity at sample j. The term \prod{j=0}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha(sj)) represents the transmittance from the ray start to sample i. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preclassificationshadingpipeline(volumegrid, transferfunction, rayorigin, raydirection, imagewidth, imageheight, stepsize, raylength): # Pre-processing: Classify and shade the entire volume grid preclassifiedvolume = [] for voxel in volumegrid: scalarvalue = voxel.value color, opacity = transferfunction(scalarvalue) associatedcolor = color opacity preclassifiedvolume.append({'associatedcolor': associatedcolor, 'opacity': opacity}) image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(imageheight)] for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): # Standard ray generation for pixel (x, y) rayoriginpixel = rayorigin + raydirection (x 0.01 + y 0.01) transmittance = 1.0 pixelcolor = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] numsamples = int(raylength / stepsize) for i in range(numsamples): samplepos = rayoriginpixel + raydirection (i stepsize) # Standard trilinear interpolation def trilinearinterpolate(grid, pos, field): # Compute grid coordinates and fractional offsets ix, iy, iz = int(pos.x), int(pos.y), int(pos.z) fx, fy, fz = pos.x - ix, pos.y - iy, pos.z - iz # Fetch 8 neighbors (clamped to grid bounds) def getval(x, y, z): x = max(0, min(x, gridwidth - 1)) y = max(0, min(y, gridheight - 1)) z = max(0, min(z, griddepth - 1)) return grid[z][y][x][field] # Interpolate c00 = getval(ix, iy, iz) (1-fx) + getval(ix+1, iy, iz) fx c10 = getval(ix, iy+1, iz) (1-fx) + getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz) fx c01 = getval(ix, iy, iz+1) (1-fx) + getval(ix+1, iy, iz+1) fx c11 = getval(ix, iy+1, iz+1) (1-fx) + getval(ix+1, iy+1, iz+1) fx c0 = c00 (1-fy) + c10 fy c1 = c01 (1-fy) + c11 fy return c0 (1-fz) + c1 fz associatedcolorsample = trilinearinterpolate(preclassifiedvolume, samplepos, 'associatedcolor') opacitysample = trilinearinterpolate(preclassifiedvolume, samplepos, 'opacity') contribution = associatedcolorsample transmittance pixelcolor += contribution transmittance = (1.0 - opacitysample) if transmittance < 0.001: break image[y][x] = pixelcolor return image Step Size (\Delta s): Not given in the sources. Partial Voluming: A major source of error where a single voxel represents multiple materials. This is mitigated by using segmented volumes with material indices and probabilities during the pre-classification step. Blurring: Pre-classification tends to cause excessive blurring when the image resolution exceeds the volume resolution (e.g., zoomed viewing or wide perspectives). Interpolation Error: Interpolating color and opacity separately and then multiplying them introduces artifacts because interpolation is a linear operation and the product is non-linear. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Handles segmented anatomical parts effectively in medical imaging. Prevents partial voluming errors when segmentation data is available. Compatible with pre-integration techniques. Limitations: Prone to excessive blurring at high image resolutions or wide perspectives. Harder to implement than post-classification due to the requirement of pre-multiplying color and opacity. Cannot easily re-classify data without re-processing the entire volume. The concept of pre-classification was introduced by Drebin et al. in 1988, who defined associated color (opacity-weighted color). Wittenbrink et al. (1998) further analyzed the pipeline, highlighting the necessity of pre-multiplying color and opacity before interpolation to avoid artifacts. The term Pre-DVRI (Pre-shaded Direct Volume Rendering Integration) was used to distinguish this pipeline from post-shaded variants. It remains a critical tool in medical imaging for handling segmented data. name: Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline
head: 4-Stage Rendering Pipeline, Smoker Rendering Pipeline
body: The Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline is a multi-pass architecture designed for real-time smoke volume rendering that processes volumetric primitives through four distinct stages: Clear, Construction, Insertion, and Evaluation. It solves the problem of maintaining high accuracy in transparent volume visualization while circumventing the computational complexity and self-intersection artifacts inherent in raytracing methods. Unlike standard ray-casting which accumulates contributions along rays, this method rasterizes primitives into per-pixel fragment lists, deferring the final compositing and visualization to a dedicated evaluation pass. The pipeline executes four sequential stages using three distinct shader programs: Clear, Render (combining Construction and Insertion), and Display (Evaluation). Inputs and Outputs: Input: Smoke volume data (density, flow tangents), geometry primitives (triangles representing volume slices or particles), and screen resolution. Output: Final rendered image buffer. Data Structures: Fragment Lists: Per-pixel storage structures (e.g., linked lists, atomic counters, or fixed-size arrays) that accumulate fragment data during the Insertion stage. The specific layout depends on the chosen visualization method but must be compatible with the Evaluation stage. OpenGL Buffer Objects: Used to store intermediate states, reset per frame, and pass data between stages. Numbered Steps: 1. Clear Stage: Reset all OpenGL buffer objects and fragment list storage structures required for the subsequent frame. Initiated by rendering a single screen-filling quad using the Clear shader program. 2. Construction Stage: Vertex Shader: Performs perspective transformation of vertices from volume space to screen space. Assigns additional vertex data such as density (\rho) and flow tangents. Geometry Shader: Assembles primitives (e.g., triangles) from the transformed vertices. Processes triangle-related data including orientation, topology, and volume information. Forwards the constructed primitives to the Insertion stage. This stage is part of the Render shader program. 3. Insertion Stage: Rasterization: The primitives constructed in the previous stage are rasterized. Fragment Shader: Processes incoming fragments. The processing logic varies by visualization method, ranging from a simple pixel counter to inserting fragment data into a complicated storage data structure (fragment list). Constraint: The type of fragment processing must be strictly compatible with the subsequent Evaluation step. This stage is part of the Render shader program. 4. Evaluation Stage: Render a single screen-filling quad using the Display shader program. Interpret and visualize the per-pixel information (e.g., accumulated density, color, depth) that was prepared and stored by the Insertion stage. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def fragmentlistrenderingpipeline(volumedata, screenresolution): # 1. Clear Stage # Reset buffers and fragment lists for the new frame clearbuffers() resetfragmentlists(screenresolution) # Launch Clear Stage: Render a single screen-filling quad renderscreenfillingquad(shader="Clear") # 2. Construction & 3. Insertion Stage (Combined in Render Program) # Process geometry primitives for primitive in volumedata.primitives: # Vertex Shader: Transform and assign data transformedvertices = [] for vertex in primitive.vertices: # Perspective transformation screenpos = perspectivetransform(vertex.position) # Assign additional data density = vertex.density flowtangent = vertex.flowtangent transformedvertices.append({ 'screenpos': screenpos, 'density': density, 'flowtangent': flowtangent }) # Geometry Shader: Assemble primitives and process topology constructedprimitives = assembleprimitives(transformedvertices) # Rasterization and Fragment Shader: Insertion for fragment in rasterize(constructedprimitives): # Process fragment based on visualization method # Example: Insert into fragment list insertfragmentintolist(fragment.screenpos, fragment.density, fragment.flowtangent) # 4. Evaluation Stage # Launch Evaluation Stage: Render a single screen-filling quad renderscreenfillingquad(shader="Display") # Display shader interprets per-pixel info from fragment lists # and writes final image to framebuffer def renderscreenfillingquad(shader): # Generic function to launch a full-screen quad pass bindshader(shader) drawquad() unbindshader() def perspectivetransform(position): # Standard MVP matrix multiplication return modelviewprojectionmatrix position def assembleprimitives(vertices): # Logic to form triangles or other primitives from vertices # Handles orientation and topology return [createtriangle(v0, v1, v2) for v0, v1, v2 in vertextriplets(vertices)] def rasterize(primitives): # Standard GPU rasterization process # Returns list of fragments with screen coordinates and interpolated attributes return gpurasterize(primitives) def insertfragmentintolist(screenpos, density, flowtangent): # Critical section: Concurrent modification of shared memory # Must handle atomic operations or synchronization to avoid inconsistent states # Implementation depends on specific fragment list structure (e.g., atomic counter + array) atomicaddfragmentcount(screenpos) storefragmentdata(screenpos, density, flowtangent) def clearbuffers(): # Reset OpenGL buffer objects glclearbuffers() def resetfragmentlists(resolution): # Initialize per-pixel storage structures for x in range(resolution.width): for y in range(resolution.height): fragmentlists[x][y].clear() Parameters: Pipeline Stages: Clear, Construction, Insertion, Evaluation. Shader Programs: Clear, Render (Construction + Insertion), Display (Evaluation). Typical Values: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Concurrent Modification: The Insertion step is the greatest bottleneck due to simultaneous access to shared indexing mechanisms. Unmanaged access to shared memory by shader threads can leave the memory in an inconsistent state because threads cannot check if a shared address is currently being modified. Compatibility: The fragment processing method in the Insertion stage must be strictly compatible with the Evaluation stage; mismatched data structures will result in incorrect visualization. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance is heavily influenced by the complexity of the fragment list insertion and the number of primitives per pixel. Memory Complexity: Depends on the fragment list storage structure. Requires additional memory for per-pixel lists and intermediate buffers. Measured Performance: Implemented in the Smoker application for real-time smoke volume rendering. Strengths: Maintains high accuracy; circumvents problems arising from raytracing, self-intersections, and global intersections. Limitations: The Insertion stage is a significant bottleneck due to concurrent memory access issues; requires careful management of shared memory states. When to use: Real-time smoke volume rendering where accuracy is prioritized over the simplicity of ray-casting and where self-intersection artifacts must be avoided. When not to use: Scenes with extremely high primitive density per pixel where fragment list management overhead becomes prohibitive, or when hardware does not support efficient atomic operations for fragment list insertion. The Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline was developed as part of the "Smoker" application for real-time smoke volume rendering. It was chosen over raytracing techniques to maintain the best possible accuracy and to circumvent problems arising from raytracing and self or global intersections. The method is detailed in a master's thesis by Sowinski (2012). name: Deferred Rendering Pipeline
head: 8-Pass Deferred Rendering Pipeline
body: A multi-pass deferred rendering sequence that computes depth, position/normal, materials, filtered normals, shadows, SSAO, blurred AO, and final shading in separate framebuffer objects. It separates geometry processing from lighting calculations, allowing complex lighting effects to be applied per-pixel without re-rasterizing geometry. It is distinct from the Volume Rendering Pipeline by deferring shading to a post-process stage, and from the Fragment List-Based Rendering Pipeline by using fixed-screen-space framebuffers rather than dynamic fragment lists. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume data (accessed via OctreeDDARenderer), camera matrices (view, projection, inverse), light position, material parameters. Output: Final shaded image in the default framebuffer. Data Structures: The method uses a sequence of Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) and associated textures. The following textures are bound to texture units TEXNUM during resetState(): 1. glTexDepth: Depth buffer. 2. glTexHitPos: Position buffer. 3. glTexHitNorm: Normal buffer. 4. glTexHitMaterial: Material buffer. 5. glTexHitNormFiltered: Filtered normal buffer. 6. glTexShadows: Shadow map buffer. 7. glTexAO: Ambient Occlusion buffer. 8. glTexAOBlurred: Blurred AO buffer. 9. glTexAONoise: Noise texture for AO. 10. glTexTBOMaterials: Texture for TBO materials. Framebuffers glFBO[0] through glFBO[6] are used sequentially. Steps: 1. Depth Pass: Bind glFBO[0]. Clear. Set OctreeDDARenderer mode to DEPTH. Draw the volume geometry. 2. Position/Normal Pass: Bind glFBO[1]. Clear. Use shader programPosNorm. Set uniforms viewMatInv, projMatInv, useDif. Draw a full-screen quad. 3. Material Pass: If useMaterials is true: Bind glFBO[2]. Clear. Use shader programMaterial. Set uniforms. Draw a full-screen quad. 4. Normal Filtering Pass: If filterNormals is true: Bind glFBO[3]. Clear. Use shader programNormFilter. Set uniforms sigma, bsigma. Draw a full-screen quad. 5. Shadow Pass: If doShadows is true: Bind glFBO[4]. Clear. Set lightPos. Set OctreeDDARenderer mode to SHADOW. Draw the volume geometry. Else, clear glFBO[4] to white (1.0). 6. SSAO Pass: If doSSAO is true: Bind glFBO[5]. Clear. Use shader programSSAO. Set uniforms projMat, viewMat, camPos, radius. Draw a full-screen quad. 7. AO Blur Pass: Bind glFBO[6]. Clear. Use shader programBlur. Draw a full-screen quad. 8. Final Shading Pass: Bind the default framebuffer. Clear. Use shader programShading. Set uniforms isYUp, camPos, projMatInv, viewMatInv, lightPos, renderMode, useMaterials. Draw a full-screen quad. Pitfalls: Pass 5 (Shadows) clears to white (1.0) when disabled, which acts as a default fully lit state. Pass 6 (SSAO) is wrapped in #if 0/#else in the source, indicating the original octree-based AO path is disabled in favor of the screen-space quad pass. Not given in the sources. This specific 8-pass implementation is part of the ssvdag project, which uses an octree-based DDA renderer for volume visualization. ajaspe/ssvdag, https://github.com/ajaspe/ssvdag, fetched 2026-10-24 (unofficial)

name: Interactive Forward Rendering with Approximate Splatting
head: Fast Rendering, OpenGL Approximation
body: This method provides an efficient, hardware-accelerated approximation of point reprojection for high-quality free-viewpoint rendering, enabling interactive frame rates by replacing full soft rasterization with a global depth layering system. It differs from sibling methods by using a fixed number of global depth layers rather than processing slices sequentially, and by explicitly managing opacity accumulation via logarithmic blending in screen space. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of input views (images and camera poses), a multi-view stereo (MVS) mesh, and a pre-trained neural network for image synthesis. Outputs: A synthesized novel view image. Data Structures: Depth Layers: A stack of kd texture buffers representing global depth intervals. Each layer stores accumulated opacity and depth information. MVS Mesh Depth Map: A low-resolution depth map used to determine the relevant depth interval for the scene. Parameters: kd: Number of global depth layers. Typical value: 10. Resolution: Target output resolution (e.g., 900×600). Steps: 1. Camera Selection: Choose a subset of input views relevant to the novel view. 2. Depth Interval Determination: Rasterize the MVS mesh depth at a low resolution (1/16 of target) and construct a min-max mipmap to determine the relevant depth range. 3. Splatting into Depth Layers: Project points from all selected input views into the kd global depth layers in parallel. Opacity accumulation uses hardware-accelerated additive blending of \log(1 - \alpha) to achieve multiplicative opacity accumulation. Formula for opacity accumulation: If \alpha is the splat opacity, the stored value V is updated as V{\text{new}} = V{\text{old}} + \log(1 - \alpha). The final accumulated opacity is 1 - \exp(V{\text{total}}). 4. Compositing: Composite the depth layers back-to-front in parallel over all re-projected pixels of all input images. 5. Probabilistic Depth Test: Apply a probabilistic depth test considering at most kd alpha-weighted depth samples to refine visibility. 6. Neural Synthesis: Run the neural network to synthesize the final image using the accumulated depth and color information. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def interactiveforwardrendering(inputviews, mvsmesh, neuralnet, kd=10, targetres=(900, 600)): # 1. Camera Selection: Choose relevant input views # Camera selection algorithm not specified in sources selectedviews = inputviews # 2. Determine Depth Interval: Rasterize MVS mesh at 1/16 resolution, build min-max mipmap lowres = (targetres[0] // 16, targetres[1] // 16) lowresdepth = rasterizemesh(mvsmesh, lowres) # Standard GPU rasterization depthmin = lowresdepth.min() depthmax = lowresdepth.max() # 3. Initialize Depth Layers: Stack of kd texture buffers for log(1-alpha) accumulation depthlayers = [[0.0] (targetres[0] targetres[1]) for in range(kd)] # 4. Splat Points into Depth Layers: Project all pixels of selected views in parallel for view in selectedviews: for point in view.points: # Points extracted from input view # Project to screen space screenx = int((point.screenu targetres[0]) % targetres[0]) screeny = int((point.screenv targetres[1]) % targetres[1]) depth = point.depth # Map depth to layer index layeridx = int(((depth - depthmin) / (depthmax - depthmin)) kd) layeridx = max(0, min(kd - 1, layeridx)) # Compute opacity and update layer with additive blending of log(1-alpha) alpha = point.alpha logval = math.log(1.0 - alpha) depthlayers[layeridx][screeny targetres[0] + screenx] += logval # 5. Composite Depth Layers Back-to-Front in parallel # Sum log values across layers to get total accumulated log opacity totallogalpha = [0.0] (targetres[0] targetres[1]) for layer in depthlayers: for i in range(len(totallogalpha)): totallogalpha[i] += layer[i] finalalpha = [1.0 - math.exp(val) for val in totallogalpha] # 6. Probabilistic Depth Test: Consider at most kd alpha-weighted depth samples # Probabilistic depth test logic not specified in sources refineddepth = depthlayers # 7. Neural Synthesis: Run neural network to synthesize image finalimage = neuralnet(refineddepth, finalalpha, selectedviews) return finalimage Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Memory Consumption: High memory usage due to batching all input views and depth layers. Compression: Memory can be reduced through standard texture compression methods. Time Complexity: The method is designed for interactive performance. An unoptimized implementation runs at 4.5 fps. Breakdown: Camera selection: 87 ms, point splatting: 36 ms, depth test: 38 ms, network evaluation: 59 ms. Memory Complexity: High. Depth layers consume ~4 GB for 900×600 resolution, 10 layers, 9 views. PyTorch reports 4.5 GB total memory usage for this configuration. Strengths: Enables interactive viewing with marginal quality degradation compared to full soft rasterization. Limitations: High memory consumption; requires pre-trained neural network. When to use: When interactive frame rates are required for free-viewpoint rendering and sufficient GPU memory is available. When not to use: When memory is constrained or offline rendering quality is prioritized over speed. This method was introduced by Kopanas et al. in "Point-Based Neural Rendering with Per-View Optimization". It is part of a differentiable multi-view pipeline used for applications such as image-based rendering (IBR), multi-view harmonization, and multi-view style transfer. The implementation was done in PyTorch with custom OpenGL-based approximations for the forward pass. name: INPC Inference & Rendering Pipeline
head: INPC Pipeline
body: The INPC (Implicit Neural Point Cloud) Inference & Rendering Pipeline is a splatting-based method that renders high-quality radiance fields by blending multisampled splats into feature images, applying global sorting, and refining the output via a U-Net and tone mapping module. It distinguishes itself from explicit point-based siblings like 3D Gaussian Splatting 3DGS or TRIPS TRIPS by using an implicit neural representation for point attributes, which allows for superior image quality at the cost of higher computational overhead during the sorting and post-processing stages. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained implicit neural point cloud model (defined by an octree structure and neural networks for attributes), camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, resolution), and a configuration setting (e.g., 8M or 33M samples). Output: A final rendered image (color and/or feature map). Data Structures: The method relies on an octree-based data structure to manage the point cloud. The specific field layouts of the octree nodes and the neural network weights are not detailed in the sources. The pipeline processes points defined by position \mathbf{p} and associated implicit attributes. Steps: 1. Sampling: Generate a set of points for the current viewpoint. The method uses a view-independent sampling algorithm. For the default configuration, this involves 33 million samples per training iteration; for the fast configuration, 8 million samples. During inference, 4× multisampling is applied, meaning each point is sampled 4 times to reduce aliasing. 2. Splatting: Transform the sampled points into screen space and rasterize them as splats. The splats are blended into feature images. The number of blended splats depends on the configuration: up to 528 million splats (4×33M points) for the default configuration, or 128 million splats (4×8M points) for the fast configuration. 3. Global Sorting: Perform a global sort of the splats. This step is identified as the primary rendering bottleneck. 4. Post-Processing: Apply a U-Net architecture followed by a tone mapping module to the rendered feature images. This step corrects artifacts and enhances high-frequency details. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderinpc(camera, model, config): # 1. Sampling # Generate points based on the implicit neural point cloud model # config.numsamples determines the base count (e.g., 8M or 33M) # 4x multisampling is applied points = model.sample(camera, numsamples=config.numsamples, multisample=4) # 2. Splatting # Project points to screen space and rasterize # This involves transforming positions and blending contributions featureimages = splat(points, camera.resolution) # 3. Global Sorting # Sort splats globally. This is the bottleneck. # The sources do not provide the specific sorting algorithm details. featureimages = globalsort(featureimages) # 4. Post-Processing # Apply U-Net and tone mapping finalimage = tonemapping(unet(featureimages)) return finalimage Parameters: numsamples: The number of samples per training iteration. Default is 33M; Fast configuration is 8M. multisample: Set to 4 for inference to blend multiple splats per point. resolution: Standard resolutions tested include 2000×1085 pixels. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sorting Bottleneck: Global sorting significantly impacts real-time performance, making it slower than explicit point-based methods. Pixel Budget Limits: Pre-extracting a global point cloud (e.g., 67M points) may be insufficient for high-resolution scenes like Tanks and Temples due to pixel budget limits. Thin Structures: The sampling algorithm may miss thin structures if multisampling is disabled. Temporal Stability: Minor temporal instability may occur during inference, a common issue with CNN-based post-processing. Fine Detail Near Camera: The method may struggle to reconstruct fine geometric details close to the camera, similar to 3DGS and Zip-NeRF. The underlying representation that allows for continuous attribute interpolation, distinguishing it from explicit point clouds. Link to Implicit Neural Point Clouds The use of a convolutional neural network to refine rasterized features, addressing artifacts and enhancing detail. Link to U-Net Rendering Time Complexity: The global sorting step is the bottleneck, leading to higher latency compared to explicit point-based methods. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: On an RTX 4090 GPU at 2000×1085 resolution with the 8M configuration: Sampling: 51ms Rendering: 16ms Total: 37ms (~9 fps). With pre-extracted global point cloud: Total 26ms. Scaling: The method scales with the number of samples (8M vs 33M), with the 33M configuration blending up to 528 million splats. Strengths: High image quality, outperforming Zip-NeRF and comparable to explicit methods in perceived quality. Limitations: Slower than 3DGS, TRIPS, and ADOP due to sorting and post-processing overhead. The INPC method was introduced in the paper "INPC: Implicit Neural Point Clouds for Radiance Field Rendering". It builds upon the splatting family of volume rendering techniques, leveraging implicit neural representations to enhance the quality of point-based rendering. The method was evaluated on benchmarks such as Mip-NeRF360 and Tanks and Temples. name: Slice-by-Slice (Sheet Buffer) Splatting
head: Axis-Aligned Sheet-Buffer Compositing, Muller sheet-buffer, Sheet Buffer Splatting, Sheet-Buffer Method, slice-based composition
body: Slice-by-Slice (Sheet Buffer) Splatting is a volume rendering optimization that organizes splats into cache-sheets aligned parallel to the volume face most closely parallel to the image plane, then composites these sheets slice-by-slice. It sets itself apart from ray-casting and screen-quad methods by compositing splats into aligned sheet buffers rather than sampling along rays or rendering full-screen quads, trading the "sparkling" of per-splat compositing for "popping" artifacts when the view crosses 45° relative to the data axes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Volume dataset (regular grid), camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix), transfer function. Output: 2D image (color and alpha buffer). Data Structures: 1. Sheet Buffer: A 2D array (texture or render target) matching the screen resolution that accumulates the weighted contributions of splats belonging to a specific depth slice. 2. Cache Image: The current accumulated result of composited slices. 3. Splat List: A list of transformed splats, typically sorted or bucketed by their depth coordinate along the alignment axis. Method Steps: 1. Sheet Alignment: Determine the volume axis (x, y, or z) most parallel to the image plane. Switch the compositing axis at 45° to maintain alignment with the view. 2. Splat Transformation: Transform splat centers from volume space to screen space. Compute new positions using interpolation so that they lie on the slice, since the buffer does not correspond to voxel positions in space. 3. Bucketing: Assign each splat to a specific sheet buffer corresponding to its depth slice index k along the alignment axis. 4. Rasterization: Rasterize all splats assigned to sheet k onto the sheet buffer. The contribution of a voxel D to a screen point (x,y) is determined by the footprint function F(x,y), which is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view direction: F(x,y) = \int h(x-xD, y-yD, z) \, dz The intensity written to the pixel is modulated by the voxel density: P(x,y) = \text{weight}(x,y) \cdot \rho(D) where \text{weight}(x,y) = F(x-xD, y-yD). 5. Compositing: Traverse the sheet buffers in depth order (back-to-front for opacity). For each sheet buffer: Composite the sheet buffer into the cache image using alpha blending. This step effectively adds voxel contributions slice-by-slice. Whenever a sheet buffer has received all contributions, it is composited with the current image and the next slice is processed. 6. Output: The cache image is the final rendered image. Parameters: Switching Threshold: The view angle at which the alignment axis switches (typically 45°). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping Artifacts: Occur when the orientation of the sheets suddenly changes, specifically when the view angle crosses the 45-degree switching threshold (e.g., from 44.7° to 45.2°). Interpolation: Since the sheet buffer does not correspond directly to voxel positions in space, new positions for splats must be computed using interpolation to lie on the slice. Orthographic vs. Perspective: The method works best for orthographic views because it requires only a single footprint table and reconstruction kernel, which is constant except for screen space offset. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def slicebyslicesplatting(volume, camera, imagewidth, imageheight): # 1. Determine alignment axis based on camera view direction # Align with volume axis most parallel to image plane viewdir = normalize(camera.viewmatrix[2][:3]) axes = [vec(1,0,0), vec(0,1,0), vec(0,0,1)] alignmentaxis = max(axes, key=lambda a: abs(dot(viewdir, a))) # 2. Initialize sheet buffers and cache image # Sheet buffers are 2D arrays matching screen resolution numslices = volume.shape[alignmentaxis] sheetbuffers = [createzero2darray(imagewidth, imageheight) for in range(numslices)] cacheimage = createzero2darray(imagewidth, imageheight) # 3. Transform and bucket splats splats = transformsplats(volume, camera) bucketsplatsintosheets(splats, sheetbuffers, alignmentaxis) # 4. Rasterize splats into sheet buffers for k, sheet in enumerate(sheetbuffers): clearsheet(sheet) for splat in sheet.splats: # Compute footprint F(x,y) and weight footprint = computefootprint(splat.kernel, splat.center, camera) weight = footprint.evaluate(splat.centerscreen) color = splat.color weight # Rasterize onto sheet buffer rasterizesplat(sheet, splat, color) # 5. Composite sheets into cache image # Traverse in depth order (back-to-front for standard alpha blending) sortedindices = sortsheetsbydepth(sheetbuffers, alignmentaxis, camera) for k in sortedindices: compositesheetintoimage(sheetbuffers[k], cacheimage) return cacheimage def determinealignmentaxis(viewmatrix): # Returns 'x', 'y', or 'z' based on which volume axis is most parallel to the image plane viewdir = normalize(viewmatrix[2][:3]) axes = [vec(1,0,0), vec(0,1,0), vec(0,0,1)] return ['x', 'y', 'z'][max(range(3), key=lambda i: abs(dot(viewdir, axes[i])))] def transformsplats(volume, camera): # Applies MVP matrix to volume centers, computes screen positions and projected kernel parameters splats = [] for voxel in volume: center3d = voxel.position center4d = vec4(center3d, 1.0) projected = camera.mvpmatrix @ center4d centerscreen = projected.xy / projected.w kernel = projectkernel(voxel.kernel, camera) splats.append({'center': center3d, 'centerscreen': centerscreen, 'kernel': kernel, 'color': voxel.color}) return splats def bucketsplatsintosheets(splats, sheetbuffers, axis): # Assigns each splat to sheetbuffers[depthindex] along the chosen axis for splat in splats: depthidx = int(round(splat['center'][axis] / volume.voxelsize[axis])) if 0 <= depthidx < len(sheetbuffers): sheetbuffers[depthidx].splats.append(splat) def computefootprint(kernel, center, camera): # Computes 2D footprint function F(x,y) by integrating 3D kernel along view direction # For orthographic views, footprint is constant per kernel type return kernel.integratealongview(camera.projectiontype) def rasterizesplat(sheet, splat, color): # Rasterizes the footprint of the splat onto the 2D sheet buffer bounds = splat.kernel.boundingbox2d(splat['centerscreen']) for y in range(bounds.miny, bounds.maxy): for x in range(bounds.minx, bounds.maxx): if 0 <= x < sheet.width and 0 <= y < sheet.height: alpha = splat.kernel.evaluate(vec2(x, y) - splat['centerscreen']) sheet[y, x] = blend(sheet[y, x], color, alpha) def sortsheetsbydepth(sheets, axis, camera): # Returns indices of sheets sorted back-to-front relative to view sheetdepths = [(i, sheet.splats[0]['center'][axis] if sheet.splats else 0) for i, sheet in enumerate(sheets)] return [idx for idx, in sorted(sheetdepths, key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)] def compositesheetintoimage(sheet, cacheimage): # Blends the accumulated sheet buffer into the main cache image for y in range(sheet.height): for x in range(sheet.width): pixelcolor, pixelalpha = sheet[y, x] cacheimage[y, x] = blend(cacheimage[y, x], (pixelcolor, pixelalpha), 1.0) def blend(src, dst, alpha): # Standard alpha compositing: out = src (1 - alpha) + dst alpha return src (1.0 - alpha) + dst alpha Image-Aligned Sheet-Buffer Compositing is a variant that eliminates "popping" artifacts by aligning the sheet buffer compositing axis with the image plane, rather than the volume axes. Unlike standard axis-aligned sheet buffers, which suffer from discontinuities when the viewing angle crosses 45° relative to the data axes, this method slices interpolation kernels into sections parallel to the image plane. It sets itself apart from its parent method, Slice-by-Slice (Sheet Buffer) Splatting, by using image-aligned cutting planes and alpha-compositing kernel sections to ensure smooth color transitions across varying optical properties and resolutions. However, it has a high computational cost and requires multiple footprint rasterizations per point. Sheet-based Splatting, proposed by Westover, accumulates splats onto a 2D sheet aligned with the volume axis most parallel to the view plane, then composites the sheets in depth order into the image with a matting operation. It is a foundational concept for the sheet-buffer approach, improving image quality over simple splat-every-sample composition by handling depth ordering more effectively. Performance: Slice-based composition produces brighter images due to correct visibility determination but is slower than splat-every-sample composition because it avoids per-slice additions in the other method. Strengths: Hardware-accelerated, good image quality compared to simple splatting, avoids sparkling artifacts. Limitations: Popping artifacts at 45° view angles, high computational cost for image-aligned variants, best suited for orthographic views. When to use: When real-time performance is needed and the view angle is stable or orthographic. When not to use: When the view angle frequently crosses 45° thresholds and popping artifacts are unacceptable. The sheet-buffer method was proposed by Müller and Yagel [Müller96] and Müller [Müller98] as an optimization for CPU-based volume rendering. It builds on Westover's earlier work on sheet-based accumulation. Müller and Crawfis later proposed image-aligned kernel-slicing to mitigate popping artifacts, though this increased computational cost. name: Image-Aligned Sheet-Buffer Compositing
body: Image-aligned sheet-buffer compositing is a volume rendering technique that eliminates popping artifacts by aligning compositing sheets with the image plane regardless of viewing direction. Unlike Axis-Aligned Sheet-Buffered Splatting, which organizes voxels into fixed volume slices, this method advances a slab across the volume, slicing kernels into sections and projecting them into image-aligned sheet buffers. Inputs: Volume data, viewing parameters, sheet buffer resolution. Outputs: Final composited image. Data Structures: Sheet Buffer: A 2D buffer aligned with the image plane, storing accumulated color and opacity for each pixel. Exact layout, fields, sizes, and bit packing: Not given in the sources. Compositing Buffer: The final image buffer where sheet buffers are composited. Steps: 1. Slab Advancement: Advance a slab across the volume so that the slab cuts kernels into sections. 2. Footprint Mapping: For each voxel or point within the current slab, perform footprint mapping as usual. This requires multiple footprint rasterizations per point to account for the intersection of the kernel with the image-aligned sheet. 3. Kernel Section Addition: Add the resulting kernel sections into the sheet buffer. 4. Compositing: Composite the sheet buffers into the final image. Formulas: Not given in the sources. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping Artifacts: Axis-aligned methods suffer from popping when the viewing angle crosses thresholds near 45° (e.g., 44.7° vs 45.2°). Image-aligned methods eliminate this by aligning with the image plane. Computational Cost: Requires multiple footprint rasterizations per point, increasing computational expense. A variant that aligns compositing sheets with the image plane regardless of viewing direction, eliminating popping artifacts. It sets itself apart from axis-aligned sheet-buffered splatting by advancing a slab across the volume rather than using fixed volume slices. Choose it when accurate voxel field reconstruction and smooth anti-aliasing are required, accepting higher computational cost due to multiple splatting of voxels. Time and Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Eliminates popping artifacts. Limitations: Higher computational expense due to multiple splatting of individual voxels. Requires multiple footprint rasterizations per point. When to use: Ideal for rendering where popping artifacts must be avoided. When not to use: When computational resources are limited. Originated from work by Mueller ('98) on volumetric points and sheet buffers. The method addresses limitations of axis-aligned splatting, such as popping artifacts observed at specific viewing angles (e.g., 44.7° vs 45.2°). name: Image-aligned Splatting
head: Axis-Aligned Sheet-Buffered Splatting, Image-Aligned Sheet-Buffered Splatting, Image-aligned Splatting with Alpha Composition, Kernel section composition, Mueller 76, Sheet-bucket splatting, slab-based splatting
body: Image-aligned splatting is a volume rendering technique that eliminates color bleeding and popping artifacts by aligning the compositing sheet with the image plane at all times, regardless of the viewing direction. Unlike its sibling Axis-Aligned Sheet-Buffered Splatting, which organizes voxels into fixed volume slices parallel to the viewing axis, image-aligned splatting advances a slab across the volume, slicing and projecting all intersecting kernels into sheet buffers. This approach provides the most accurate reconstruction of the voxel field prior to compositing and produces smoother images with better anti-aliasing characteristics than raycasting, though at a higher computational cost due to multiple splatting of voxels. Inputs: Volume dataset containing density, color, and opacity fields. Viewing parameters including viewpoint, direction, and projection matrix. Slab width \Delta s. Kernel base distribution and scaling factor. Outputs: Final composited image buffer. Data Structures: 1. Sheet Buffer: A 2D buffer aligned with the image plane, storing accumulated color C and opacity \alpha for the current slab. 2. Occlusion Map: A dynamically computed screen-space map used for early splat elimination, updated via convolution after each sheet composite. 3. Kernel Sections: Pre-integrated footprints of voxel kernels, stacked to form a single kernel representation. Steps: 1. Kernel Preparation: Compute kernel sections using a kernel base distribution and a scaling factor. Stack sections to form a single kernel representation. 2. Slab Advancement: Define a slab of width \Delta s aligned parallel to the image plane. 3. Voxel Selection and Transformation: Identify all voxel kernels that overlap the current slab. Transform the center of each relevant voxel into screen space. 4. Early Splat Elimination: Index the occlusion map using the transformed screen coordinates to test for visibility. If the voxel is occluded, skip it, noting that transformation is still required even if the voxel is culled. 5. Clipping and Projection: For visible voxels, clip the voxel kernels to the slab boundaries. Slice and project the intersecting kernels. 6. Sheet Buffer Accumulation: Sum the clipped kernels into the sheet buffer. All splats within a single sheet are added together; they are not composited within the sheet. 7. Sheet Composition: Composite the current sheet buffer with the previous accumulated result. 8. Occlusion Map Update: Perform a convolution operation on the occlusion map to update it based on the current sheet's contributions. This operation can be limited to buffer tiles that received splat contributions in the current slab to save time. 9. Iteration: Advance the slab across the volume and repeat steps 2–8 until the volume is fully processed. Formulas: The color, opacity, and feature terms are calculated as averages over the slab interval \Delta s: C\lambda(si) = \frac{\int{i\Delta s}^{(i+1)\Delta s} C\lambda(s) ds}{\Delta s} \alpha(si) = \frac{\int{i\Delta s}^{(i+1)\Delta s} \alpha(s) ds}{\Delta s} f(si) = \frac{\int{i\Delta s}^{(i+1)\Delta s} f(s) ds}{\Delta s} Where si represents the slab index, and C\lambda, \alpha, and f are the color, opacity, and feature values respectively. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def imagealignedsplatting(volume, viewparams, slabwidthdeltas, kernelbase, scalingfactor): # Initialize final composited image and opacity buffers finalimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] finalopacity = [[0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] # Initialize occlusion map for early splat elimination occlusionmap = [[0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] # Pre-compute kernel sections and stack them kernelsections = computekernelsections(kernelbase, scalingfactor) # Determine slab range along the view direction slabstart = volume.bounds.minz slabend = volume.bounds.maxz currentslabz = slabstart while currentslabz < slabend: slab = Slab(zmin=currentslabz, zmax=currentslabz + slabwidthdeltas) currentsheet = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] currentsheetopacity = [[0.0] for in range(viewparams.imageheight)] # Identify voxels intersecting the current slab for voxel in volume.voxels: if not voxel.intersectsslab(slab): continue # Transform voxel center to screen space screenpos = transformtoscreen(voxel.center, viewparams) # Early splat elimination: test visibility against occlusion map if not isvisible(screenpos, occlusionmap): continue # Clip kernel to slab boundaries and project clippedkernel = clipkerneltoslab(voxel.kernel, slab) rasterizefootprint(currentsheet, currentsheetopacity, clippedkernel, screenpos) # Composite current sheet with previous accumulated result compositesheetintoimage(finalimage, finalopacity, currentsheet, currentsheetopacity) # Update occlusion map via convolution on tiles with contributions updateocclusionmap(occlusionmap, currentsheet, currentsheetopacity) currentslabz += slabwidthdeltas return finalimage def computekernelsections(kernelbase, scalingfactor): # Returns a list of kernel sections with weights based on base distribution and scaling sections = [] for i in range(kernelbase.numsections): weight = kernelbase.basedistribution(i) scalingfactor sections.append(KernelSection(weight=weight, footprint=kernelbase.footprint)) return sections def transformtoscreen(voxelcenter, viewparams): # Standard perspective projection to screen coordinates x = viewparams.projmatrix[0][0] voxelcenter.x + viewparams.projmatrix[0][3] y = viewparams.projmatrix[1][1] voxelcenter.y + viewparams.projmatrix[1][3] return Point(x, y) def isvisible(screenpos, occlusionmap): # Checks if screen position exceeds occlusion threshold h, w = len(occlusionmap), len(occlusionmap[0]) y, x = int(screenpos.y), int(screenpos.x) if 0 <= y < h and 0 <= x < w: return occlusionmap[y][x] < 0.95 return True def clipkerneltoslab(kernel, slab): # Returns kernel scaled/weighted for slab intersection return Kernel(weight=kernel.weight slab.intersectionratio(kernel), footprint=kernel.footprint) def rasterizefootprint(sheet, sheetopacity, kernel, screenpos): # Additive accumulation within the sheet buffer h, w = len(sheet), len(sheet[0]) for dy, dx in kernel.footprintoffsets: y, x = int(screenpos.y + dy), int(screenpos.x + dx) if 0 <= y < h and 0 <= x < w: sheet[y][x][0] += kernel.weight kernel.color[0] sheet[y][x][1] += kernel.weight kernel.color[1] sheet[y][x][2] += kernel.weight kernel.color[2] sheetopacity[y][x][0] += kernel.weight def compositesheetintoimage(finalimage, finalopacity, currentsheet, currentsheetopacity): # Standard back-to-front alpha compositing between sheets h, w = len(finalimage), len(finalimage[0]) for y in range(h): for x in range(w): oc = currentsheetopacity[y][x][0] if oc <= 0.0: continue fc = currentsheet[y][x] fo = finalopacity[y][x][0] alpha = oc (1.0 - fo) finalimage[y][x][0] += fc[0] alpha finalimage[y][x][1] += fc[1] alpha finalimage[y][x][2] += fc[2] alpha finalopacity[y][x][0] += alpha def updateocclusionmap(occlusionmap, currentsheet, currentsheetopacity): # Convolve sheet opacity into occlusion map, limited to tiles with contributions h, w = len(occlusionmap), len(occlusionmap[0]) for y in range(h): for x in range(w): if currentsheetopacity[y][x][0] > 0.0: occlusionmap[y][x] = min(1.0, occlusionmap[y][x] + currentsheetopacity[y][x][0]) Parameters: \Delta s: Slab width. Typical values are not explicitly given, but it must be chosen to balance between aliasing reduction and computational cost. Kernel Base Distribution: Defines the shape of the splat kernel (e.g., Gaussian). Scaling Factor: Used to adjust kernel radius based on cutting plane distance. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The integration over \Delta s assumes smooth variation within the slab. If \Delta s is too large, high-frequency details may be lost due to low-pass filtering. Classification: If data values (density) are splatted before classification, the original density is smoothed and accumulated, making classification an unsolved problem that aggravates the partial volume effect. Occlusion Map Cost: Early splat elimination requires transforming invisible voxels to screen space to determine occlusion, saving only the rasterization cost. Viewing Direction Switch: Aligning the compositing sheet with the image plane eliminates the popping artifacts caused by sudden switches to orthogonal slice stacks in axis-aligned methods. Time Complexity: Higher than axis-aligned sheet-buffered splatting because each voxel may be considered more than once (multiple splatting) as the slab advances. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for sheet buffers and a dynamically updated occlusion map. Performance: Slower than raycasting for datasets with a low number of non-contributing samples. Faster than raycasting for datasets with a small number of relevant voxels and sheet buffers. Strengths: Eliminates color bleeding and popping artifacts; provides accurate reconstruction of the voxel field; produces smoother images with better anti-aliasing due to z-averaged kernels and Gaussian filters. Limitations: More expensive due to multiple splatting of voxels; early splat elimination still requires transformation of occluded voxels; classification is problematic if density is splatted first. When to Use: Best suited for post-classified rendering where accurate density/gradient reconstruction is needed; beneficial for rotational angiography visualization. When Not to Use: Not ideal for datasets with many non-contributing samples where raycasting would be faster; avoid if pre-classification is required without density smoothing issues. Image-aligned splatting was introduced by Mueller (referred to as Mueller 76) to address the drawbacks of earlier axis-aligned sheet-buffered approaches, which suffered from severe brightness variations and did not allow variable DVRI interval distances. It builds on the concept of sheet-buffered compositing but aligns the compositing sheet with the image plane to ensure consistent visual quality regardless of viewing angle. The method utilizes analytical pre-integration of kernel slices and fast footprint rasterization for efficient projection.
