name: Scatter Samples to Image
head: Sample Scattering to Image, ScatterSamplesToImage
body: Scatter Samples to Image is a post-processing step that scatters computed sample values from arbitrary screen-space positions into a regular image grid. It maps non-uniformly distributed samples to a standard raster image for visualization. Unlike Splatting, which uses geometric kernels to blur and accumulate contributions, this method performs a direct assignment of values to pixel coordinates without filtering. Inputs and Outputs: samplepositions: A tensor of shape 2 \times N, where N is the number of samples. samples: A tensor of shape C \times N, where C is the number of channels. imageout: A tensor of shape C \times H \times W. samplemaskout: A tensor of shape 1 \times H \times W, containing 1 where samples were taken and 0 elsewhere. defaultvalues: A vector of doubles providing default values for the 8 channels, used in the PyTorch interface ScatterSamplesToImage. Data Structures: samplepositions: 2 \times N tensor. samples: C \times N tensor. imageout: C \times H \times W tensor. samplemaskout: 1 \times H \times W tensor. Steps: 1. Initialize imageout and samplemaskout. 2. Initialize samplemaskout to all zeros. 3. For each sample index k from 0 to N-1: a. Retrieve position (xk, yk) from samplepositions[:, k]. b. Retrieve values v{k,1}, \dots, v{k,C} from samples[:, k]. c. Convert (xk, yk) to integer pixel coordinates (i, j) by flooring or rounding. d. Check if (i, j) is within the image boundaries [0, W-1] \times [0, H-1]. If outside, ignore this sample. e. For each channel c from 0 to C-1: write v{k,c} to imageout[c, j, i]. f. Set samplemaskout[0, j, i] = 1. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def scattersamplestoimage(samplepositions, samples, imageshape, defaultvalues=None): C, N = samples.shape H, W = imageshape # Initialize output tensors imageout = [[[0.0] W for in range(H)] for in range(C)] samplemaskout = [[[0.0] W for in range(H)] for in range(1)] # Apply default values if provided; otherwise pixels receiving no samples remain untouched if defaultvalues is not None: for c in range(C): for r in range(H): for col in range(W): imageout[c][r][col] = defaultvalues[c] # Scatter samples for k in range(N): x = samplepositions[0][k] y = samplepositions[1][k] col = math.floor(x) row = math.floor(y) # Check boundaries if 0 <= col < W and 0 <= row < H: for c in range(C): imageout[c][row][col] = samples[c][k] samplemaskout[0][row][col] = 1.0 return imageout, samplemaskout Parameters: defaultvalues: A vector of doubles providing default values for the 8 channels, used in the PyTorch interface ScatterSamplesToImage. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Samples located outside the image boundaries are ignored. Pixels in the output image that receive no samples are left untouched (no default value overwriting). Multiple samples may map to the same pixel; the last sample processed overwrites previous values. A variant that uses scatter-like logic to render a 2D heatmap from trace data. It initializes a canvas of width traceCount 2 and height sampleCount. It computes min and max values across the 2D array samples[traceCount][sampleCount], calculating range as max - min (defaulting to 1 if 0 to avoid division by zero). For each pixel (i, j), it calculates normalized value v = (samples[i][j] - min) / range, computes color intensity color = \lfloor v \times 255 \rfloor, and sets RGBA to (color, color, color, 255). Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of samples, as each sample is processed once. Memory Complexity: O(C \times H \times W) for the output image and mask. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Extremely fast for direct mapping; no kernel evaluation or sorting required. Limitations: No anti-aliasing or smoothing; artifacts appear if samples are sparse or misaligned with pixels. When to use: When samples are already on a grid or when a raw, unfiltered representation is desired. When not to use: When smooth visualization or blending is required; use Splatting instead. The method is described in the context of adaptive sampling and reconstruction for volume visualization. name: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting
head: Texture-Atlas Splatting
body: Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting is a learned sparse scene representation that eliminates runtime neural network inference by baking view-independent high-frequency texture into a hardware-accelerated 2D texture atlas. It represents the scene as a sparse set of oriented 2D Beta kernels, separating low-frequency view-dependent appearance (stored per-surfel) from high-frequency spatial texture (stored in the atlas). This approach achieves 7–9× faster rendering than 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) on common benchmarks by reducing overdraw via flat Beta kernels and replacing expensive ray-surfel intersection shaders with an exact rational reformulation. Inputs: A set of optimized 2D surfels (position \boldsymbol{\mu}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity oi, and view-dependent color parameters) and a trained multi-resolution hash grid E\theta with MLP decoder f\theta. Outputs: A compressed RGB texture atlas (55–320 MB for typical scenes) and the surfel attributes. The final rendered image. Data Structures: 1. Surfel Attributes: For each surfel i: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position. \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4: Rotation (quaternion). \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^2: 2D scale. oi \in \mathbb{R}: Opacity. f{SV}(\mathbf{d}): View-dependent color function parameters (stored per-surfel). 2. Texture Atlas: A 2D RGB texture where each surfel i maps to a rectangular region. The texels store the signed residual color \rho(\mathbf{x}) = f\theta(E\theta(\mathbf{x})). The atlas is allocated once after sparsification. Numbered Steps: 1. Primitive Representation: Represent the scene as a sparse set of oriented 2D surfels. Each surfel i is defined by its position, rotation, scale, and opacity. 2. Kernel Selection: Use the Deformable Beta kernel \mathcal{B}(x;b) instead of a Gaussian. The kernel shape is controlled by a parameter b \in \mathbb{R}: \mathcal{B}(x;b) = (1-x)^{\beta(b)} where x \in [0,1] is the squared radial distance from the kernel center normalized to 1 at the edge of the support, and \beta(b) = 5\sigma(b) with \sigma being the sigmoid function. Small b values produce flat, hard-edged disks to reduce overdraw; large b values produce soft, Gaussian-like profiles. The parameter b is restricted to lie between a flat disk and a soft Gaussian. 3. Appearance Decomposition: Decompose the fragment color \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) into a per-surfel view-dependent term and a view-independent residual: \mathbf{c}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{d}) = \text{ReLU}\left(\text{ReLU}(f{SV}(\mathbf{d}) + b{SV}) + f\theta(\mathbf{E}\theta(\mathbf{x}))\right) where b{SV} = 0.5 is a fixed offset providing a neutral gray baseline, f{SV} is the per-surfel view-dependent color, and f\theta(\mathbf{E}\theta(\mathbf{x})) is the residual from the hash grid E\theta and MLP decoder f\theta. 4. Training: Query the hash grid at every fragment along the surfel's surface during training to absorb fine spatial texture. Per-surfel attributes remain constant across the surfel to absorb low-frequency view-dependent appearance. Use signed texture residuals (positive and negative color offsets) to provide representational power, allowing a single surfel to reproduce color variation that positive-only textures cannot. Train jointly with the multi-view error criterion of FastGS to limit densification. Introduce a falloff prior using Beta kernels to regularize kernels toward flat, hard-edged profiles, dampening positional gradients and reducing primitive count. 5. Baking: Sample the hash-grid across the surface of each primitive during training. Bake the output of the hash-grid sampling into a compressed RGB texture atlas. Finetune the atlas texels directly against the training images to overcome hash collisions from training. 6. Rendering: Perform fast, per-fragment texture fetches from the atlas. Evaluate the ray-surfel intersection using an exact rational reformulation of the intersection test. Composite the surfels in front-to-back order using alpha blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def sigmoid(x): return 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-x)) def betakernel(x, b): """Compute the Deformable Beta kernel value.""" beta = 5.0 sigmoid(b) x = max(0.0, min(1.0, x)) return (1.0 - x) beta def dot(v1, v2): return v1[0]v2[0] + v1[1]v2[1] + v1[2]v2[2] def normalize(v): length = math.sqrt(dot(v, v)) return [v[0]/length, v[1]/length, v[2]/length] def projectscreenbounds(surfel, camera): # Standard projection of surfel bounding box to screen coordinates # Returns object with xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax pass def intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydir, surfel): # Exact rational reformulation of ray-surfel intersection # Returns t, u, v parameters pass def transformtolocal(surfel, worldpos): # Transforms world position to surfel's local 2D coordinate system pass def renderscene(surfels, camera, textureatlas): # Initialize output image with zeros image = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(camera.height camera.width)] # Sort surfels front-to-back by depth along view direction sortedsurfels = sorted(surfels, key=lambda s: dot(s.position, camera.viewdirection)) for surfel in sortedsurfels: screenbounds = projectscreenbounds(surfel, camera) for y in range(screenbounds.ymin, screenbounds.ymax): for x in range(screenbounds.xmin, screenbounds.xmax): # Exact rational ray-surfel intersection test rayorigin = camera.center raydir = normalize(camera.screentoray(x, y) - rayorigin) t, u, v = intersectrayplane(rayorigin, raydir, surfel) if t > 0 and 0.0 <= u <= 1.0 and 0.0 <= v <= 1.0: # Compute normalized squared distance from surfel center localpos = transformtolocal(surfel, rayorigin + t raydir) distsq = dot(localpos, localpos) kernelval = betakernel(distsq, surfel.bparam) alpha = surfel.opacity kernelval if alpha > 0.0: # Sample baked texture atlas at local UV coordinates residual = textureatlas.sample(u, v) # Compute view-dependent color fsv = surfel.computeviewdependentcolor(raydir) bsv = 0.5 basecolor = max(0.0, fsv + bsv) finalcolor = max(0.0, basecolor + residual) # Front-to-back alpha compositing idx = y camera.width + x c = image[idx] image[idx] = [ c[0] + (1.0 - c[0]) finalcolor[0] alpha, c[1] + (1.0 - c[1]) finalcolor[1] alpha, c[2] + (1.0 - c[2]) finalcolor[2] alpha ] return image Parameters: b{SV} = 0.5: Fixed offset inside the inner ReLU activation. Texture atlas size: 55–320 MB for typical scenes. \beta(b) = 5\sigma(b): Shape parameter scaling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Hash Collisions: Hash collisions from training can degrade quality. Finetuning the atlas texels directly against training images mitigates this. Overdraw: Soft Gaussian tails cause redundant overlaps. Using flat Beta kernels (small b) reduces overdraw and primitive count. Sparsity: Pipelines using per-primitive textures start from a converged dense model with densification frozen, capping sparsity. This method allocates the atlas once after sparsification, allowing higher sparsity. A kernel family defined by \mathcal{B}(x;b) = (1-x)^{\beta(b)} that interpolates between flat disks and soft Gaussians via the parameter b. Chosen to reduce overdraw compared to standard Gaussians. The process of converting view-independent neural queries (hash grid + MLP) into a static 2D texture map. Enables hardware-accelerated sampling without runtime neural inference. When a block requiring rendering is encountered, the UE4 submodule supplies the block and level index information, while the inference submodule provides corresponding regional meshes and feature maps. If feature maps are not ready, inference is carried out to generate them. Uses dynamic inference instead of storing all texture maps to reduce storage overhead for large-scale scenes. Time Complexity: Rendering is dominated by texture fetches and simple arithmetic, avoiding neural network evaluations. The rational intersection test is computationally cheaper than standard ray-surfel shaders. Memory Complexity: Requires a texture atlas of 55–320 MB for typical scenes, which is larger than memory-optimized 3DGS representations but fits on low-to-mid-range GPUs. Performance: Renders 7.1–9.1× faster than 3DGS and 1.2–1.8× faster than FastGS and Speedy-Splat on common benchmarks. Strengths: High rendering speed due to elimination of runtime neural inference; reduced overdraw via flat kernels; high sparsity. Limitations: Larger memory footprint than some compressed 3DGS variants; requires training to bake the atlas; signed residuals require careful handling of negative values in texture formats. When to Use: Real-time rendering of high-fidelity scenes where GPU compute is limited by neural network inference overhead. When Not to Use: When memory is extremely constrained and smaller scene representations are prioritized over rendering speed. Ultrafast Spatial Texture-Atlas Splatting was introduced by Petkov and Klaus from Siemens Healthineers in 2026. It builds on 2D Gaussian Splatting (2DGS) and FastGS, aiming to solve the rendering overhead caused by runtime neural network evaluations in neural radiance representations. The method leverages the observation that view-independent high-frequency texture can be baked into a texture atlas, while view-dependent low-frequency appearance remains per-surfel. name: Lighting and Material Interaction
body: This family defines how photometric properties and illumination are computed for splatted primitives, addressing the gap between raw geometric density and visually plausible appearance. It differs from sibling methods by injecting per-primitive shading calculations or baked lighting data into the rendering pipeline, allowing for dynamic lighting interactions, baked global illumination, or direct user editing of material properties per primitive. Photon Splatting captures direct illumination by rasterizing a light-view map and projecting photons into a sparse voxel octree structure [2832-photon-splatting.md]. It solves the problem of efficiently storing incoming radiance as a direction distribution and energy proportional to the subtended solid angle of the light source [2832-photon-splatting.md]. It differs from Per-Splat Relighting by baking lighting information directly into the voxel data structure during a pre-computation phase, rather than computing shading dynamically per splat during rendering [2832-photon-splatting.md, 3371-per-splat-relighting.md]. Choose this method when pre-computing direct illumination into a sparse voxel octree is preferred for static lighting or radiance storage [2832-photon-splatting.md]. Per-Splat Relighting computes a dynamic lighting multiplier for each Gaussian splat based on its world position, normal, ambient occlusion, and confidence, enabling real-time dynamic illumination [3371-per-splat-relighting.md]. It differs from pre-shading by deferring photometric calculations to the rendering pass, allowing interactive light changes while avoiding the complexity of full path tracing by treating each splat as an independent shading unit [3371-per-splat-relighting.md]. Choose this method when dynamic, real-time lighting changes are required without full path tracing overhead [3371-per-splat-relighting.md]. Definition: Recolorization or shadow additions by checking if a splat center intersects with a spherical brush and adjusting its color value. Parameters: Color channels are stored in 16-bit format to support brushes with smooth falloff and low opacity. Pitfalls: Splat models often do not lend themselves well to painting detailed features (text, lines, symbols) because they represent sparse geometry; models from images use few splats on clean surfaces, preventing detailed color changes. Color leaks may occur into differently colored parts of a surface if state-of-the-art Gaussian splat reconstructions rarely feature clean and opaque surfaces. Choose this method when artistic recolorization or shadow additions are needed directly on sparse geometry. The techniques described herein originate from the practical requirements of editing and rendering large-scale Gaussian Splat models, specifically detailed in the development of "Splatshop". Splatshop: Efficiently Editing Large Gaussian Splat Models, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70214, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Photon Splatting
head: Capturing Direct Illumination (Photon Splatting)
body: Photon Splatting captures direct illumination by projecting photons from light sources onto scene geometry and storing them in a sparse voxel octree. It solves the problem of efficiently accumulating incoming radiance for subsequent indirect illumination calculations by treating light-view map pixels as photons. It differs from Per-Splat Relighting by focusing on the initial capture and storage of direct light energy into the voxel structure rather than per-surface lighting updates. Inputs: Light-view map: A world position map rendered from the light's perspective, where each pixel represents a photon. Sparse Voxel Octree: A hierarchical data structure representing the scene, where leaf nodes store photon data. Outputs: Updated Octree: Leaf nodes contain direction distributions and energy values proportional to the subtended solid angle of the light-view map pixel. Data Structures: Light-View Map: Stores world positions and depth. Octree Leaf Node: Stores photon data. Brick Structure: Voxels are repeated at brick boundaries to enable hardware filtering. Atomic Operations: Hardware atomic adds are limited to integer textures. Empty Voxels: Photons are stored at the surface, and empty voxels are collapsed. Steps: 1. Render Light-View Map: Render the scene from the light's view using standard rasterization to generate a world position map. 2. Splat Photons: Launch a fragment shader with one thread per light-view-map pixel. For each pixel, determine the corresponding leaf node in the octree based on the world position. Calculate the photon's energy, which is proportional to the subtended solid angle of the pixel as seen from the light. Store the photon as a direction distribution and energy in the leaf node. 3. Handle Atomic Operations: Since atomic add operations are only available for integer textures, use a 16-bit normalized texture format for storage. Denormalize the values when accessing them later. 4. Resolve Brick Boundary Inconsistencies: Because voxels are repeated for adjacent bricks, direct copying causes thread collisions and bandwidth issues. Use the "Value Transfer to Neighboring Bricks" method to ensure coherence. Formulas: E \propto \Omega, where E is the stored photon energy and \Omega is the subtended solid angle of the light-view map pixel as seen from the light. Parameters: Light-View Map Resolution: Typically higher than the lowest level of the voxel grid to avoid gaps. Texture Format: 16-bit normalized (e.g., RG16F) to support atomic adds. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Atomic Operations: Hardware atomic adds are limited to integer textures, requiring 16-bit normalized formats and careful denormalization. Thread Collisions: Copying photons directly to all required locations in adjacent bricks leads to significant performance degradation due to parallel random scattering and bandwidth issues. Empty Voxels: Photons are stored at the surface, and empty voxels are collapsed, ensuring photons are always placed at the finest level of the voxel structure. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splatphotons(lightviewmap, octreeleaves): # One thread per pixel in lightviewmap for pixel in lightviewmap: worldpos = pixel.worldposition solidangle = pixel.subtendedsolidangle # Find leaf node in octree based on world position leaf = octreeleaves.findleaf(worldpos) # Photon data: direction and energy proportional to solid angle energy = solidangle direction = normalize(lightposition - worldpos) # Atomic add required for concurrent updates on 16-bit normalized buffer leaf.buffer.atomicadd(energy, direction) def transfertoneighbors(octreeleaves): # Six passes, two for each axis (x, y, z) for axis in ['x', 'y', 'z']: # Pass 1: Add current node's data to the neighbor in positive direction for leaf in octreeleaves: neighbor = leaf.getneighbor(axis, direction=+1) neighbor.buffer += leaf.buffer # Pass 2: Copy summed data from neighbor back to current node for leaf in octreeleaves: neighbor = leaf.getneighbor(axis, direction=+1) leaf.buffer = neighbor.buffer This method addresses the inconsistency of duplicated voxels at brick boundaries. It uses six passes (two per axis: x, y, z) to propagate data. In the first pass of an axis, each thread adds its voxel data to the neighbor in the positive direction. In the second pass, it copies the summed data from the neighbor back. This ensures coherence along each axis without atomic operations or thread collisions, leveraging neighbor pointers for efficient access. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: Efficient for scenes with high-resolution light-view maps. Strengths: Avoids atomic operations in the transfer step and prevents thread collisions. Limitations: Requires a complete octree assumption for the simplified explanation of value transfer. Photon Splatting was introduced in Interactive Indirect Illumination Using Voxel Cone Tracing (2011). It builds on the idea of using light-view maps to capture direct illumination for subsequent indirect illumination calculations. The method was developed to address the challenges of storing photons in a sparse voxel octree while maintaining performance and accuracy. name: Per-Splat Relighting
body: Per-Splat Relighting computes a lighting multiplier for a splat based on lights, normal, ambient occlusion, and confidence. It differs from Photon Splatting by calculating lighting analytically per-splat rather than accumulating photon densities, allowing real-time updates when light positions or intensities change without re-radiating photons. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: splatlighting buffer (packed lighting records), lightrig buffer (light definitions), worldposition of the splat center, unlitlevel (base color), ambient color, gain scalar. Output: Relit color value. Data Structures: The splatlighting buffer stores per-splat metadata packed into a 4-component vector where rg is an octahedral normal, b is ambient occlusion, and a is confidence. The lightrig buffer is an array where each light occupies 4 consecutive elements: i4+0 is a vec3 representing light position or direction, i4+1 contains a vec3 tint and a float alpha for the light type, i4+2 holds setup parameters (r for inverse range, g for decay, b for spot cone cosine threshold, a for spot exponent), and i4+3 is a vec3 spot direction vector. Numbered Steps: 1. Unpack Lighting Record: Retrieve the lighting record for the current splat index from splatlighting and extract the octahedral normal (rg), AO (b), and confidence (a). 2. Normalize Normal: Convert the octahedral normal to a 3D vector, calculate its length, and normalize it if the length is greater than zero; otherwise, default the normal to (0, 0, 1). 3. Initialize Direct Light: Set direct illumination to zero. 4. Loop Over Lights: For each light i in the lightrig: extract tint from lightrig[i4+1], setup from lightrig[i4+2], and determine type by rounding tint.a to the nearest integer; initialize tolight from lightrig[i4+0].xyz and attenuation to 1.0; if type is not 0, calculate relative as lightrig[i4+0].xyz - worldposition, compute dist, skip if dist < 1e-6, normalize tolight to relative / dist, and compute attenuation using the omniattenuation formula with dist, setup.r, and setup.g; if type equals 2, calculate conecosine as max(dot(-tolight, lightrig[i4+3].xyz), setup.b), compute rim as (1.0 - conecosine) / max(1e-4, 1.0 - setup.b), and update attenuation by multiplying it by 1.0 - pow(clamp(rim, 0, 1), setup.a); finally, accumulate direct by adding tint.rgb attenuation max(dot(worldnormal, tolight), 0). 5. Compute Irradiance: Calculate irradiance as ambient ao + direct confidence. 6. Return Result: Return unlitlevel + gain irradiance. Formulas: Omni Attenuation: \text{omni\attenuation}(dist, inv\range, decay) = \max(1.0 - (dist \cdot inv\range)^4, 0)^2 \cdot dist^{-decay} Where dist is the distance from splat to light, inv\range is the inverse range of the light (setup.r), and decay is the decay exponent (setup.g). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def decodeoctnormal(oct): v = vec3(oct.x, oct.y, 1.0 - abs(oct.x) - abs(oct.y)) if v.z < 0: v.xy = 1.0 - abs(v.yx) vec2(sign(v.x), sign(v.y)) return normalize(v) def persplatrelight(splatindex, worldposition, unlitlevel, ambient, gain, splatlighting, lightrig): record = splatlighting[splatindex] octnormal = record.rg ao = record.b confidence = record.a decodednormal = decodeoctnormal(octnormal) normallength = length(decodednormal) worldnormal = decodednormal / normallength if normallength > 0 else vec3(0, 0, 1) direct = vec3(0, 0, 0) numlights = len(lightrig) // 4 for i in range(numlights): baseidx = i 4 tint = lightrig[baseidx + 1] setup = lightrig[baseidx + 2] lightdata = lightrig[baseidx + 0] lighttype = int(tint.a + 0.5) tolight = lightdata.xyz attenuation = 1.0 if lighttype != 0: relative = lightdata.xyz - worldposition dist = length(relative) if dist < 1e-6: continue tolight = relative / dist invrange = setup.r decay = setup.g term = max(1.0 - (dist invrange)4, 0.0) attenuation = (term 2) (dist -decay) if lighttype == 2: spotdir = lightrig[baseidx + 3].xyz conecosine = max(dot(-tolight, spotdir), setup.b) rim = (1.0 - conecosine) / max(1e-4, 1.0 - setup.b) attenuation = 1.0 - pow(clamp(rim, 0.0, 1.0), setup.a) diff = max(dot(worldnormal, tolight), 0.0) direct += tint.rgb attenuation diff irradiance = ambient ao + direct confidence return unlitlevel + gain irradiance Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Normal: If the decoded normal has zero length, it defaults to (0,0,1), which can cause incorrect shading for flat surfaces or degenerate splats. Division by Zero: The spot light rim calculation uses max(1e-4, 1.0 - setup.b) to prevent division by zero when the cone angle is very narrow (setup.b close to 1.0). Near-Zero Distance: Lights at the exact splat position are skipped (dist < 1e-6) to avoid NaNs or infinite attenuation. Time Complexity: O(L) per splat, where L is the number of lights, executed per fragment during splat rendering. Memory Complexity: O(1) additional memory per splat for the lighting record packed in splatlighting. Strengths: Real-time capable; supports dynamic light movement and intensity changes without precomputation. Limitations: Only handles direct lighting and simple AO; no indirect bounces; performance scales linearly with light count. When to use: Real-time applications with dynamic lighting. When not to use: Offline rendering requiring global illumination or very high light counts where performance is critical. Per-Splat Relighting is a technique used in real-time Gaussian Splatting renderers, such as the one implemented in the godot-gaussian-splatting repository, which adapts traditional lighting concepts to the splat-based rendering pipeline by storing lighting metadata within the splat data structure. name: Particle Splatting for Density Field Construction
head: 3D Density Field Construction via Splatting, CPU splatting, wax density field
body: This method constructs a volumetric density field on the CPU by rasterizing interpolated particles into a 3D grid, enabling subsequent ray-marching of complex surfaces like wax. It differs from its parent Splatting by explicitly targeting CPU-side grid construction for density-based rendering rather than direct image-space compositing, and from its child Image-Space Particle Splatting for Density Field Construction by operating in object space with a fixed uniform grid, which avoids the resolution limits of image-space buffers but requires managing 3D memory allocation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N particles with positions \mathbf{p}i interpolated between fixed time steps, and associated scalar attributes such as temperature. Output: A 3D texture (density field) stored in GPU memory, containing density and coupled attributes per voxel. Data Structures: Grid: A 3D voxel grid aligned with the container boundaries. Dimensions: 48 \times 94 \times 48 voxels. Layout: Two channels per voxel: (1) density \rho, (2) temperature \times density T \cdot \rho. Format: Data3DTexture with RG channel layout. Internal format is RG32F (float32) or RG16F if 32-bit float filtering is unsupported. Occupancy Grid: A 4^3 block occupancy grid used to skip empty regions during ray-marching, reducing texture reads by a factor of 3. Parameters: Kernel: Separable kernel defined as h(u) = (1 - u^2)^3. Temporal Smoothing Time Constant: \tau = 0.04 seconds. Normalization: Density is normalized to approximately 1.0 at the core of the wax. Steps: 1. Interpolation: Interpolate particle positions between two fixed time steps to ensure temporal consistency. 2. Splatting: For each particle i at position \mathbf{p}i: determine the bounding box of the kernel footprint within the 3D grid; for each voxel v within the footprint, calculate the normalized distance u from the voxel center to \mathbf{p}i, compute the kernel weight w = (1 - u^2)^3, add w to the density channel of voxel v, and add w \cdot Ti to the temperature-density channel of voxel v. 3. Normalization: Normalize the density values such that the core density is \approx 1. 4. Temporal Smoothing: Apply in-place temporal smoothing to the density field to reduce flickering using the update rule \rho{new} = \rho{old} \cdot e^{-dt/\tau}, where dt is the frame time delta and \tau = 0.04 s. 5. Upload: Upload the resulting 3D grid to the GPU as a Data3DTexture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def constructdensityfield(particles, gridshape, tau, dt): """ Constructs a 3D density field by splatting particles into a grid. Args: particles: List of dicts with 'pos' (vec3), 'temp' (float). gridshape: Tuple (W, H, D) defining grid size. tau: Temporal smoothing constant (0.04). dt: Time delta in seconds. Returns: grid: 3D list of shape (W, H, D, 2). Channel 0: Density. Channel 1: Temperature Density. """ W, H, D = gridshape # Initialize grid with zeros grid = [[[0.0, 0.0] for in range(D)] for in range(H)] for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): grid[x][y][z] = [0.0, 0.0] # 1. Temporal smoothing (in-place decay) keep = math.exp(-dt / tau) for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): grid[x][y][z][0] = keep grid[x][y][z][1] = keep # 2. Splat particles kernelradius = 1.0 for p in particles: px, py, pz = p['pos'] temp = p['temp'] # Determine voxel bounds (inclusive) minx = max(0, math.floor(px - kernelradius)) maxx = min(W - 1, math.ceil(px + kernelradius)) miny = max(0, math.floor(py - kernelradius)) maxy = min(H - 1, math.ceil(py + kernelradius)) minz = max(0, math.floor(pz - kernelradius)) maxz = min(D - 1, math.ceil(pz + kernelradius)) for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): dx = x - px dy = y - py dz = z - pz usq = dxdx + dydy + dzdz if usq < 1.0: u = math.sqrt(usq) weight = (1.0 - uu)3 grid[x][y][z][0] += weight grid[x][y][z][1] += weight temp # 3. Normalize density to ~1 at core (standard scaling implementation) maxdensity = 0.0 for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): if grid[x][y][z][0] > maxdensity: maxdensity = grid[x][y][z][0] if maxdensity > 0: scale = 1.0 / maxdensity for x in range(W): for y in range(H): for z in range(D): grid[x][y][z][0] = scale grid[x][y][z][1] = scale return grid Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Use RG32F if possible; fall back to RG16F only if 32-bit float filtering is unsupported, which may introduce quantization artifacts. Temporal Stability: The smoothing constant \tau=0.04 s ensures temporal coherence, with measurements showing 0.00% of surface voxels cross the rendering threshold even at 60 Hz with ±30% frame-time jitter. Occupancy Optimization: A 4^3 block occupancy grid skips empty regions during ray-marching, reducing texture reads by a factor of 3. Evaluates density directly in the image buffer using multiple render targets, avoiding 3D grid memory limits and preserving sharp features, but at the cost of image-space resolution constraints. Time Complexity: O(N \cdot R^3) per frame, where N is the number of particles and R is the kernel radius in voxels. Measured performance on a Xeon 2.1 GHz processor shows CPU splatting takes 1.1 to 1.25 ms median, and 1.3 to 1.9 ms p95. Memory Complexity: O(W \cdot H \cdot D) for the 3D grid. For a 48 \times 94 \times 48 grid with 2 channels of float32, this requires approximately 48 \cdot 94 \cdot 48 \cdot 8 bytes \approx 1.7 MB. Strengths: Low CPU overhead; simple implementation; effective for wax-like surfaces with temporal coherence; occupancy grid reduces ray-marcher texture reads by 3x. Limitations: Fixed resolution grid limits detail; memory usage scales with volume size. When to Use: Small to medium-sized volumetric simulations (e.g., wax lamps) where CPU-side density construction is preferred for simplicity and compatibility with software rendering pipelines. This method was implemented in the "lava-lamp" project by Nathan Drll, featuring a wax surface constructed via CPU splatting and ray-marched in a glass container. name: Image-Space Particle Splatting for Density Field Construction
head: Image-Space Volume Visualization for Dynamic Particle Simulations, Image-space approach, Perspectively correct glyph raycasting
body: This method visualizes dynamic particle simulations by reconstructing a density field in image space using perspectively correct splatting and ray casting, avoiding the resolution limits and geometric smoothing artifacts of object-space uniform grids. It differs from its parent Particle Splatting for Density Field Construction by evaluating the density volume directly in the image buffer via multiple render targets rather than constructing a 3D grid on the CPU, thereby preserving sharp geometric features and reducing memory usage for high-resolution views. Inputs: Particle positions pj and masses mj stored in a GPU vertex buffer. Camera parameters (eye position e, viewing direction v) and bounding box of the particle system. Kernel support radius h. Outputs: Final composited image of the frame. Feedback data (number of active rays) for adaptive sub-pass control. 1. Ray Parameter Textures: Floating point textures (32-bit precision) storing ray direction, length, and current sampling position for each pixel. Dimensions equal the viewport resolution. 2. Density Slice Textures: Floating point textures (16-bit precision) storing density values. Multiple render targets (MRT) are used to store several density slices simultaneously. 3. Particle Vertex Buffer: Stores pj and mj for all particles, updated once per frame. 4. Depth Buffer: Used to terminate rays that step behind the bounding box or exceed opacity thresholds. h: Support radius of the kernel function. \lambda{min}: Start parameter of the ray (front face of bounding box). \lambda{max}: End parameter of the ray (back face of bounding box). \Delta\lambda: Distance between density slices. s{max}(f): Maximum number of sub-passes for frame f. Typical values: Viewport 512 \times 512, \Delta\lambda = 1/256. 1. Initialization (Frame f=0): Calculate the maximum required sub-passes to sample the entire bounding box: s{max}(0) = \max{\forall \text{rays}} \left\lceil \frac{-\lambda{min}}{\Delta \lambda} \right\rceil. 2. Particle Sorting (Optional Optimization): Sort particle indices according to their image-space depth using a Radix Sort on the GPU (CUDA). This allows determining the range of particles contributing to each density slice in O(n) time on the CPU, or via parallel reduction in O(m \log(n)) for m slices. 3. Culling: Move particles that do not contribute to the current density slice outside the viewing frustum. This requires uniform depth spacing between slices. 4. Sub-pass Loop (for s = 0 to s{max}(f)-1): 4.1. Position Update: Update the sampling position p for each active ray: \lambda = \lambda{min} + s \times \Delta\lambda p = e + \lambda v. If the new p lies inside the bounding box, mark the ray as active. If the ray has stepped behind the bounding box, terminate it. The depth test kills fragments for inactive rays. 4.2. Splatting (Density Evaluation): Splat perspectively correct footprints of the particle kernel functions into the density slice textures (Multiple Render Targets). The image space size of the point-sprite is determined by h. Use the method of perspectively correct glyph raycasting. Compute density \bar{\rho}(p) at the sampling position p using additive blending: \bar{\rho}(p) = \sum{j} mj W(|p - pj|, h) where W is a symmetric polynomial density kernel (e.g., smooth step function) with support radius h. The first slice is placed at \lambda, and subsequent slices are \Delta\lambda apart. 4.3. Occlusion Query (Adaptive Control): Issue hardware occlusion queries to count active rays. To minimize overhead, issue six queries during the last few sub-passes of the current frame at sub-pass indices: s{max}(f) - \{50, 20, 5, 2, 1, 0\}. 5. Volume Ray Casting and Compositing: Perform direct volume rendering using ray casting on the reconstructed density slices. Interpolation: Interpolate between density slices within a stack for a continuous iso-surface. Reuse one slice from the previous sub-pass to interpolate between stacks. Gradient Computation: Compute gradients for illumination. For a single particle, the gradient is the vector from pj to p. The overall gradient is the summation of weighted gradients via additive blending. Termination: Accumulate opacity along active rays. Terminate rays if accumulated opacity exceeds a threshold or if the depth buffer indicates the ray is behind the bounding box. Composite the result with previous sub-passes to generate the final image. 6. Display and Feedback Adjustment: Display the image of frame f. Exploit frame-to-frame coherence by postponing the evaluation of occlusion query results until the frame is finished. Collect query results in order. Determine s{max}(f+1) for the next frame: Set s{max}(f+1) to the sub-pass of the first query with too few active rays. If all queries show too few active rays, reduce: s{max}(f+1) = s{max}(f) / 2. If no query has few enough active rays, increase: s{max}(f+1) = s{max}(f) + 25, limited by s{max}(0). Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def initializeframe(f, lambdamin, deltalambda): if f == 0: return math.ceil(-lambdamin / deltalambda) return None def updateraypositions(rays, s, lambdamin, deltalambda, boundingbox): lambdaval = lambdamin + s deltalambda for ray in rays: ray.p = ray.e + lambdaval ray.v if ray.p in boundingbox: ray.active = True elif ray.p isbehindboundingbox(ray): ray.active = False return rays def splatparticles(particles, rays, densitytextures, h, kernelfunc, lambdamin, deltalambda): for sliceidx, texture in enumerate(densitytextures): texture.clear() lambdaval = lambdamin + sliceidx deltalambda activerays = [r for r in rays if r.active and r.p in boundingbox] for ray in activerays: density = 0.0 for particle in particles: dist = math.sqrt(sum((ray.p[k] - particle.p[k])2 for k in range(3))) if dist < h: density += particle.mass kernelfunc(dist, h) texture.write(ray.pixelcoord, density) def computegradients(particles, rays, gradienttextures, h): for sliceidx, texture in enumerate(gradienttextures): texture.clear() for ray in rays: if ray.active: grad = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for particle in particles: dist = math.sqrt(sum((ray.p[k] - particle.p[k])2 for k in range(3))) if dist < h: vec = [ray.p[k] - particle.p[k] for k in range(3)] grad = [grad[k] + vec[k] particle.mass for k in range(3)] texture.write(ray.pixelcoord, grad) def raycastandcomposite(densitytextures, gradienttextures, rays, threshold): finalimage = {} for ray in rays: if not ray.active: continue accumulatedopacity = 0.0 color = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for sliceidx, densitytexture in enumerate(densitytextures): density = densitytexture.read(ray.pixelcoord) gradient = gradienttextures[sliceidx].read(ray.pixelcoord) opacitycontribution = 1.0 - math.exp(-density) colorcontribution = computelighting(gradient, opacitycontribution) color = [color[k] + colorcontribution[k] (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) for k in range(3)] accumulatedopacity += opacitycontribution (1.0 - accumulatedopacity) if accumulatedopacity > threshold: break finalimage[ray.pixelcoord] = color return finalimage def adjustsubpasses(queryresults, currentmaxsubpasses, initialmaxsubpasses): threshold = 10 for subpassidx, count in queryresults: if count < threshold: return subpassidx if all(count < threshold for, count in queryresults): return max(1, currentmaxsubpasses // 2) return min(currentmaxsubpasses + 25, initialmaxsubpasses) Perspective Correction: Splatting must be perspectively correct to avoid distorted or cube-like appearances of the filter kernel in image space. Non-Uniform Depth Slices: Culling efficiency is nullified if density slices do not have uniform depth values, as determining contributing particles becomes computationally expensive. Latency: Hardware occlusion queries introduce latency. Results are not immediately available; frame-to-frame coherence is exploited to hide this latency by adjusting s{max} for the next frame. Precision: Ray parameters use 32-bit floats, density values use 16-bit floats. Insufficient precision may affect accuracy. Time Complexity: Sorting particles: O(n) with Radix Sort on GPU (CUDA) for all slices, or O(m \log(n)) for m slices using parallel reduction. Splatting: Proportional to the number of active particles and pixels. Ray Casting: Proportional to the number of active rays and slices. Memory Complexity: Ray parameters: 8 \text{ MB} for a 512 \times 512 window. Density slices: 12 \text{ MB} for 8 slices in a 512 \times 512 window. Total: \approx 20 \text{ MB}, compared to 256 \text{ MB} for a full 512^3 object-space volume. Performance: Tested on Intel Core2 2.4 GHz, NVIDIA GeForce 280 GTX. Laser ablation dataset (742,141 particles) rendered at 1500 \times 450 at 0.7 \text{ fps}. Strengths: Avoids resolution limits of uniform grids; conveys all geometric features without smoothing sharp corners. Lower memory footprint for high-resolution views. Adaptive sub-pass count reduces computation for sparse scenes. Limitations: Requires GPU hardware for occlusion queries and MRTs. Sorting overhead may not be beneficial for small datasets. Non-uniform depth slicing negates culling benefits. The method was developed by M. Falk, S. Grottel, and T. Ertl. It is used for visualizing signal transduction in cells, protein surfaces (SES/MSS approximation), and laser ablation molecular dynamics simulations. It builds on the concept of metaballs for density field definition and uses perspectively correct glyph raycasting presented by Klein et al. [KE04]. Interactive Image-Space Volume Visualization for Dynamic Particle Simulations, https://openalex.org/W2284871597, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Multi-View Splatting Pipeline with Fill-Rate Filtering
head: Multi-View Splatting Pipeline
body: This method generates multi-view 2D images from a 3D point cloud by rasterizing points as splats, then filters the resulting views based on pixel coverage density. It distinguishes itself from standard splatting by explicitly discarding views with insufficient fill rate, ensuring structured output quality for downstream tasks like dataset generation. Inputs: Point cloud data: tuple (\mathbf{xyz}, \mathbf{rgb}, \mathbf{label}) loaded from a.pt file. Camera configuration: trajectory parameters and intrinsic/extrinsic matrices. Parameters: splatradius (default 2, covering a 5 \times 5 disk), minfillrate (default 0.30), viewport width W, height H. Outputs: For each kept view: camera pose, color image (JPEG), label image (16-bit PNG), color-mapped label (PNG), and index map (.npy). Intrinsics from the first kept view saved to intrinsic.txt. Data Structures: CameraPose: Dataclass containing extrinsics (Tensor [4,4]), intrinsics (Tensor [4]), position (tuple), target (tuple), pitchdeg (float). SplattingRenderer: Holds the point cloud and rendering state. Steps: 1. Load Data: Load point cloud (\mathbf{xyz}, \mathbf{rgb}, \mathbf{label}) using torch.load. 2. Generate Poses: Compute camera poses using generatetrajectory(xyz, config, device). 3. Batch Poses: Extract intrinsics and extrinsics into batches via posestobatch(poses). 4. Initialize Renderer: Create SplattingRenderer with cambatch, splatradius, and device. 5. Load Point Cloud: Pass (\mathbf{xyz}, \mathbf{rgb}, \mathbf{label}) to renderer.loadpointcloud(). 6. Render Views: Call renderer.renderall(intrbatch, extrbatch, W, H) to get colorlist, labellist, indexlist. 7. Compute Fill Rates: For each view i, calculate fill rate fi = \frac{1}{H \cdot W} \sum{x,y} \mathbb{I}(\text{index}i[x,y] \ge 0). 8. Filter Views: Keep indices i where fi \ge \text{min\fill\rate}. 9. Save Outputs: For each kept view, save pose, color, label, mapped label, and index map. If no views meet the threshold, print a warning and skip saving. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np from typing import List, Tuple, Dict, Any def generatetrajectory(xyz: torch.Tensor, config: Dict[str, Any], device: torch.device) -> List[Dict[str, torch.Tensor]]: """Generate camera poses from point cloud center and config.""" poses = [] numviews = config.get("numviews", 10) radius = config.get("radius", 10.0) for i in range(numviews): angle = 2 np.pi i / numviews pos = torch.tensor([radius np.cos(angle), radius np.sin(angle), 0.0], device=device) extr = torch.eye(4, device=device) extr[:3, 3] = pos intr = torch.tensor([config.get("focal", 500.0), config.get("width", 512), config.get("height", 512), 0.0], device=device) poses.append({"extr": extr, "intr": intr}) return poses def posestobatch(poses: List[Dict[str, torch.Tensor]]) -> Tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]: """Extract intrinsics and extrinsics into batched tensors.""" intrbatch = torch.stack([p["intr"] for p in poses]) extrbatch = torch.stack([p["extr"] for p in poses]) return intrbatch, extrbatch class SplattingRenderer: def init(self, cambatch: int, splatradius: int, device: str): self.cambatch = cambatch self.splatradius = splatradius self.device = torch.device(device) self.xyz = self.rgb = self.label = None def loadpointcloud(self, xyz: torch.Tensor, rgb: torch.Tensor, label: torch.Tensor): self.xyz = xyz.to(self.device) self.rgb = rgb.to(self.device) self.label = label.to(self.device) def renderall(self, intrbatch: torch.Tensor, extrbatch: torch.Tensor, W: int, H: int) -> Tuple[List[np.ndarray], List[np.ndarray], List[np.ndarray]]: colorlist, labellist, indexlist = [], [], [] M = intrbatch.shape[0] pointids = torch.arange(self.xyz.shape[0], device=self.device, dtype=torch.int32) for start in range(0, M, self.cambatch): end = min(start + self.cambatch, M) subintr = intrbatch[start:end] subextr = extrbatch[start:end] uv, depths, visible = self.projectbatch(subintr, subextr, W, H) for j in range(end - start): c, l, idx = self.assembleview(uv[:,:, j], depths[:,:, j], visible[:,:, j], W, H, pointids) colorlist.append(c) labellist.append(l) indexlist.append(idx) return colorlist, labellist, indexlist def projectbatch(self, intr: torch.Tensor, extr: torch.Tensor, W: int, H: int): N = self.xyz.shape[0] xyzh = torch.cat([self.xyz, torch.ones(N, 1, device=self.device)], dim=1) camxyz = torch.matmul(xyzh, extr.transpose(0, 1)) uv = torch.matmul(camxyz[:,:2, None], intr[:,:2, None].transpose(1, 2)).squeeze(-1) / camxyz[:, 2,:, None] depths = camxyz[:, 2,:] visible = (depths > 0).float() return uv, depths.unsqueeze(1), visible.unsqueeze(1) def assembleview(self, uv: torch.Tensor, depths: torch.Tensor, visible: torch.Tensor, W: int, H: int, pointids: torch.Tensor): # Rasterization with splatradius and deterministic depth handling # Uses CUDA sort-unique: sort by (pixelidx, depthasc), keep first per pixel # Returns numpy arrays matching expected output shapes colorimg = np.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=np.uint8) labelimg = np.zeros((H, W), dtype=np.uint8) indexmap = np.full((H, W), -1, dtype=np.int32) return colorimg, labelimg, indexmap def multiviewsplattingpipeline( pointcloudpath: str, config: Dict[str, Any], W: int, H: int, splatradius: int = 2, minfillrate: float = 0.30, device: str = "cpu") -> None: # 1. Load point cloud data = torch.load(pointcloudpath) xyz, rgb, label = data['xyz'], data['rgb'], data['label'] # 2. Generate camera poses poses = generatetrajectory(xyz, config, device=torch.device(device)) # 3. Extract intrinsics and extrinsics intrbatch, extrbatch = posestobatch(poses) # 4. Initialize renderer renderer = SplattingRenderer(cambatch=1, splatradius=splatradius, device=device) # 5. Load point cloud into renderer renderer.loadpointcloud(xyz, rgb, label) # 6. Render all views colorlist, labellist, indexlist = renderer.renderall(intrbatch, extrbatch, W, H) # 7. Compute fill rates fillrates = [(idxm >= 0).mean() for idxm in indexlist] # 8. Filter views keptindices = [i for i, f in enumerate(fillrates) if f >= minfillrate] if not keptindices: print("Warning: No views meet the minimum fill rate threshold.") return # 9. Save outputs firstkept = keptindices[0] np.savetxt("intrinsic.txt", intrbatch[firstkept].cpu().numpy()) for i in keptindices: np.savetxt(f"pose{i}.txt", poses[i]["extr"].cpu().numpy()) # Save color as JPEG, label as 16-bit PNG, mapped label as PNG, index as.npy # Standard image I/O (e.g., imageio, PIL) handles format conversion np.save(f"index{i}.npy", indexlist[i]) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If all views fall below minfillrate, no output is saved and a warning is printed. Precision issues in depth sorting may affect which point wins in overlapping splats; the implementation uses a sort-unique strategy on CUDA to ensure deterministic results. A method to generate multi-view 2D images from a plenoptic point cloud when original captured images are unavailable, using a renderer (e.g., MPEG PccAppRenderer) that interpolates view-dependent colors based on camera alignment. The colour of point j as seen from viewpoint i is computed as a weighted average: Colourj = \frac{\sumi wi \cdot Colouri}{\sumi wi}, where n (default 10) controls the sharpness of the weight scaling function. Nc denotes the number of camera viewpoints used to capture the 3D object or scene, determining the size of the plenoptic color vector. Time Complexity: Dominated by rasterization (O(N) for standard splatting, O(N \log N + N \cdot k) for EWA due to kNN covariance estimation) and view assembly (O(W \cdot H) per view). Memory Complexity: O(N) for point cloud storage, O(W \cdot H) for intermediate buffers per view. Performance: EWA splatting is significantly more expensive than standard splatting due to covariance estimation. Strengths: Ensures high-quality, dense coverage in output views by filtering sparse ones. Limitations: Computationally intensive for EWA; may discard useful views if minfillrate is set too high. This pipeline is used in the DALA-CitywallV3 dataset generation process. It leverages PyTorch and CUDA for efficient point cloud processing and rendering. name: BCC Grid Rendering
head: BCC vs CC Grid Rendering, Body-Centered Cartesian Grid
body: BCC Grid Rendering is a volume rendering technique that utilizes a Body-Centered Cartesian (BCC) lattice for spatial sampling instead of the standard Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid. It solves the problem of excessive memory and computational cost in point-based volume rendering by reducing the required number of sample points to 70.3% of a CC grid while maintaining lossless compression for spherically bandlimited signals. It is distinct from CC rendering by its higher packing efficiency for isotropic signals. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volumetric dataset defined on a BCC lattice, camera parameters (view and projection matrices), and a rendering kernel. Output: A 2D raster image. Data Structures: The data is stored in a BCC lattice structure. A BCC lattice can be viewed as two interleaved simple cubic lattices, or as a cubic lattice with an additional point at the center of each cube. Lattice Points: Defined by integer coordinates (i, j, k) and a parity bit or offset indicating whether the point belongs to the primary cubic sublattice or the body-centered sublattice. Attributes: Each lattice point stores density/extinction coefficient \rho and potentially other scalar/vector fields. Steps: 1. Lattice Generation: Construct the BCC grid from the input data. If the input is on a CC grid, resample or interpolate onto the BCC lattice. Not given in the sources. 2. Transformation: Transform the BCC lattice points from world space to clip space using the standard Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix, identical to CC rendering. 3. Slicing/Sorting: Sort the transformed points by depth (Z-buffer) to ensure correct front-to-back or back-to-front compositing. 4. Rasterization (Splatting): For each point, project its 3D footprint onto the 2D image plane. Shift: When rendering BCC grids, slices must be shifted by 1/2 relative to the CC grid alignment to account for the body-centered offset. Footprint: Compute the 2D footprint F(x,y) for each point. The evidence states that BCC grids assume spherically bandlimited signals, under which assumption compression is lossless. Weighting: Calculate the weight based on the distance from the pixel center to the point's projected center, modulated by the point's density \rho. 5. Compositing: Accumulate the splatted contributions into the frame buffer using alpha blending. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderbccgrid(points, camera, width, height, kernelradius=3.0): """ points: List of dicts with keys 'pos' (x,y,z), 'density', 'type' ('primary'/'center') camera: Object with 'mvp' (4x4 matrix), 'shiftoffset' (0.5) width, height: int kernelradius: float, radius of the splat footprint """ # Initialize frame buffer (RGBA) fb = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] # 1. Transform to clip space clippoints = [] for p in points: # MVP transform clipw = (p['pos'][0] camera.mvp[0][3] + p['pos'][1] camera.mvp[1][3] + p['pos'][2] camera.mvp[2][3] + camera.mvp[3][3]) if clipw <= 0.0: continue clippoints.append({ 'x': (p['pos'][0] camera.mvp[0][0] + p['pos'][1] camera.mvp[1][0] + p['pos'][2] camera.mvp[2][0] + camera.mvp[3][0]) / clipw, 'y': (p['pos'][0] camera.mvp[0][1] + p['pos'][1] camera.mvp[1][1] + p['pos'][2] camera.mvp[2][1] + camera.mvp[3][1]) / clipw, 'z': (p['pos'][0] camera.mvp[0][2] + p['pos'][1] camera.mvp[1][2] + p['pos'][2] camera.mvp[2][2] + camera.mvp[3][2]) / clipw, 'density': p['density'] }) # 2. Sort back-to-front for standard alpha blending clippoints.sort(key=lambda p: p['z']) # 3. Rasterize (Splat) for p in clippoints: # NDC to screen coordinates sx = (p['x'] + 1.0) 0.5 width sy = (1.0 - (p['y'] + 1.0) 0.5) height # Apply BCC slice shift by 1/2 sx += camera.shiftoffset width sy += camera.shiftoffset height # Splat footprint for dy in range(-kernelradius, kernelradius + 1): for dx in range(-kernelradius, kernelradius + 1): px, py = int(sx + dx), int(sy + dy) if 0 <= px < width and 0 <= py < height: distsq = dxdx + dydy # Gaussian/quadratic kernel weight weight = max(0.0, 1.0 - distsq / (kernelradius kernelradius)) alpha = weight p['density'] if alpha <= 0.0: continue # Front-to-back alpha blending oldrgba = fb[py][px] newa = alpha + oldrgba[3] (1.0 - alpha) if newa > 0.0: # Monochromatic density visualization fb[py][px] = ( (p['density'] alpha + oldrgba[0] oldrgba[3] (1.0 - alpha)) / newa, (p['density'] alpha + oldrgba[1] oldrgba[3] (1.0 - alpha)) / newa, (p['density'] alpha + oldrgba[2] oldrgba[3] (1.0 - alpha)) / newa, newa) return fb Parameters: Shift Offset: 0.5 in normalized screen coordinates or lattice units. Kernel: Spherical/Gaussian, optimized for isotropic signals. Edge Cases: Non-Spherical Signals: If the signal is not spherically bandlimited, the BCC grid may not provide lossless compression, and artifacts may appear. Boundary Conditions: Not given in the sources. BCC Grid Sampling uses a Body-Centered Cartesian (BCC) lattice to store volume data, requiring fewer sample points than a standard Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid while maintaining lossless compression for spherically bandlimited signals. It is distinct from CC sampling by its higher packing efficiency for isotropic signals. The BCC grid reduces required point samples to 70.3% of a cubic grid, while a 4D BCC grid requires only 50% of the equivalent 4D cubic grid samples. In practice, BCC grid rendering took 70% of the time of CC grid rendering for the Foot dataset, although renderings were almost identical. For the Turbulent Jet 4D example, BCC rendering took 1.01s (71% of CC time) with 138 time steps, compared to 1.23s for CC with 99 time steps. Time Complexity: Rendering time is proportional to the number of sample points. Since BCC reduces the number of required points to 70.3% of a CC grid, the theoretical rendering time is reduced by a similar factor, assuming constant cost per point. Memory Complexity: Memory usage is reduced by approximately 29.7% compared to CC grids for the same spatial resolution and signal fidelity. Measured Performance: In the Turbulent Jet 4D example, BCC rendering took 1.01s (71% of CC time) with 138 time steps, compared to 1.23s for CC with 99 time steps. The BCC grid had 87M total points vs 168M for CC, but only 7.4M relevant voxels vs 9.4M for CC. For the Foot dataset, BCC rendering took 70% of the time of CC rendering, although renderings were almost identical. Strengths: Significant reduction in memory and computation for isotropic, spherically bandlimited signals. Lossless compression under the spherical bandlimit assumption. Limitations: Only optimal for spherically bandlimited signals. Requires careful handling of the 1/2 shift during rasterization. When to Use: Point-based volume rendering of isotropic data where memory and performance are critical. When Not to Use: Non-isotropic signals, or when compatibility with standard CC-based tools is required. The BCC grid was introduced as an alternative to the Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid for volumetric data representation. The concept is based on the work of Theussl ('01) and Neophytou ('02). The BCC lattice is known in mathematics and signal processing for its optimal packing density for spheres, which translates to fewer sample points needed for reconstruction of bandlimited signals. It has been applied to time-varying datasets such as turbulent jets and flows. name: BCC Grid Sampling
head: BCC Lattice Sampling, Body Centered Cartesian
body: BCC Grid Sampling is a 3D sampling method that uses a Body-Centered Cartesian (BCC) lattice to store volume data, requiring fewer sample points than a standard Cubic Cartesian (CC) grid while maintaining lossless compression for spherically bandlimited signals. It is distinguished from its sibling FCC Lattice Sampling by its optimality conditions: BCC is optimal for band-limited and isotropic signals, whereas FCC is optimal when the signal spectrum is spherical or when sampling rates are depressed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A continuous volumetric signal f(\mathbf{x}) assumed to be bandlimited with a spherical frequency spectrum. Output: A discrete set of sample values located at the nodes of a BCC lattice. Data Structures: The BCC lattice is defined as the dual of the Face-Centered Cartesian (FCC) lattice in the frequency domain. In the spatial domain, this structure gives rise to two interleaved CC grids. Lattice Definition: The BCC lattice can be viewed as a simple cubic lattice with an additional point at the center of each cube. Interleaving: The lattice consists of two interpenetrating simple cubic sublattices. If the primary grid has spacing d, the two sublattices are offset by (d/2, d/2, d/2) relative to each other. Sampling Interval: The sources describe the sampling interval of the interleaved grids as being related by a factor involving \sqrt{2} and 1/\sqrt{2}, specifically noting the interval separation as 1/\sqrt{2} apart in the context of the reciprocal relationship. Note: The source text contains garbled mathematical notation ("1 ⁄ ( 2)", ".and apart"), but explicitly states the resulting sample count reduction. Number of Samples: A volume sampled into a BCC grid requires approximately 71% of the samples of a usual cubic Cartesian (CC) grid. This is derived from the density ratio of the BCC lattice to the CC lattice. Formula: N{BCC} \approx \frac{\sqrt{2}}{2} N{CC} \approx 0.707 N{CC}. 4D Extension: For a time-varying (4D) volume, a 4D BCC lattice requires only 50% of the samples of a 4D CC grid. Reconstruction and Filtering: Optimal Filter: To preserve the spherical shape of the BCC grid-sampled volume's frequency spectrum, point-based object-order methods must use spherical (radially symmetric) filters. Pitfall (Aliasing): Reconstruction of a BCC grid with trilinear filters leads to aliasing. This occurs because the trilinear filter's frequency response is not radially symmetric, causing it to include higher spectra during interpolation. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode illustrates the generation of BCC sample coordinates from a bounding box, assuming a target sample density relative to a CC grid. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def generatebccsamples(xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax, ccspacing): """ Generates sample points for a BCC lattice within a bounding box. The BCC lattice is constructed as two interleaved CC grids. The effective spacing for the BCC lattice is adjusted to achieve the ~71% sample reduction compared to a standard CC grid with the same physical resolution, or equivalently, the same resolution with fewer points. Note: Exact implementation of 'ccspacing' adjustment depends on whether the goal is fixed physical resolution or fixed point count. Here we assume we want to cover the volume with BCC points such that the density is sqrt(2)/2 of a CC grid with spacing 'ccspacing'. """ samples = [] # Calculate the effective spacing for the BCC sublattices. # To maintain equivalent resolution, the BCC lattice points are # denser than a sparse CC grid but sparser than a dense CC grid. # The source states BCC requires 71% of CC samples. # We generate two interleaved grids. # Sublattice 1: Simple cubic grid with spacing 'ccspacing' # Sublattice 2: Simple cubic grid with spacing 'ccspacing', # offset by (ccspacing/2, ccspacing/2, ccspacing/2) # However, to achieve the 71% reduction, the 'ccspacing' used for # the BCC construction must be larger than the target CC spacing, # or we simply select points from a finer grid. # The source implies the BCC lattice itself has the lower density. # A BCC lattice with nearest-neighbor distance 'd' has density # 2/d^3. A CC lattice with nearest-neighbor distance 'd' has density 1/d^3. # To compare fairly, we usually align the unit cells. # The source says: "requires 2/sqrt(2) = 71%". This implies the # BCC lattice with the same unit cell volume as a CC lattice # has half the points? No, BCC has 2 points per cell, CC has 1. # The 71% figure comes from the ratio of densities for equivalent # Nyquist limits. # Implementation strategy: # 1. Define the bounding box. # 2. Determine the step size for the interleaved grids. # Let the target CC grid have spacing S. # The BCC lattice that provides equivalent spherical bandlimiting # has a lattice constant such that its density is sqrt(2)/2 of the CC. # For simplicity in generation, we iterate over a grid that covers # the volume and select points belonging to the BCC pattern. # Let's use a base spacing 'step' for the interleaved grids. # The offset is step/2. step = ccspacing # Generate Sublattice 1 x = xmin while x <= xmax: y = ymin while y <= ymax: z = zmin while z <= zmax: samples.append((x, y, z)) z += step y += step x += step # Generate Sublattice 2 (Offset) x = xmin + step / 2 while x <= xmax: y = ymin + step / 2 while y <= ymax: z = zmin + step / 2 while z <= zmax: samples.append((x, y, z)) z += step y += step x += step return samples def reconstructbcc(samples, querypoint, filterfunc): """ Reconstructs the value at querypoint using BCC samples. WARNING: Using a non-spherical filter (like trilinear) causes aliasing. """ value = 0.0 for samplepos, sampleval in samples: dist = math.sqrt( (querypoint[0] - samplepos[0])2 + (querypoint[1] - samplepos[1])2 + (querypoint[2] - samplepos[2])2) # Must use a radially symmetric filter (e.g., sinc or Gaussian) weight = filterfunc(dist) value += sampleval weight return value BCC Lattice Storage refers to the specific data organization of the BCC grid, which arises as the dual of the FCC lattice in the spatial domain. It consists of two interleaved CC grids with a sampling interval separation of 1/\sqrt{2} (as per source notation). This structure requires 71% of the samples of a usual cubic Cartesian (CC) grid. For 4D volumes (time-varying), a 4D BCC storage requires only 50% of the 4D CC samples. It is best used in conjunction with point-based object-order methods using spherical (radially symmetric) filters to preserve the spherical shape of the frequency spectrum. Reconstruction with trilinear filters leads to aliasing due to the lack of radial symmetry in the filter's frequency response. Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: BCC sampling requires approximately 71% of the memory of a CC grid for the same volume resolution. In 4D, it requires 50%. Time: BCC rendering took 70% of the time of CC rendering for the Foot dataset. Measured Performance: On the Foot dataset, BCC rendering achieved 70% of the time required by CC rendering. The UltraVis system, which optimizes cache performance, can render a 256^3 volume at 10 frames/s. While not exclusively BCC, the system highlights that cache management is key to fast volume rendering due to massive data sizes. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Significant reduction in sample count (and thus memory and potentially computation) for spherically bandlimited signals. Limitations: Trilinear interpolation causes aliasing because the filter is not radially symmetric. It is less common than CC grids. When to Use: Use BCC grids with point-based object-order methods that employ spherical (radially symmetric) filters. Do not use with trilinear filters if aliasing is a concern. The BCC lattice is the dual of the Face-Centered Cartesian (FCC) lattice in the spatial domain. The spacing of samples in the BCC lattice is the reciprocal of that in the frequency domain, according to the Fourier scaling theorem. The concept extends to higher dimensions, such as 4D volumes. The efficiency of BCC grids is particularly relevant for signals with spherical frequency spectra, which are common in volume generation due to the sampling kernels used. name: FCC Lattice Sampling
head: FCC Lattice Storage, FCC dataset lattice, FCC lattice, Face Centered Cubic (FCC) Lattice, Face-centered cartesian lattice
body: FCC Lattice Sampling is a 3D sampling method that defines a volume grid as a subset of the Cartesian lattice, offering superior sampling efficiency and optimality for signals sampled at a depressed rate compared to standard Cubic Cartesian (CC) grids. It is distinguished from its sibling BCC Grid Sampling by its optimality conditions: while BCC is optimal for band-limited and isotropic signals, FCC is optimal when the signal spectrum is spherical or when sampling rates are depressed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D signal (volume data) defined over space. Output: A set of sample points located on the FCC lattice, and the corresponding scalar values at those points. Data Structures: The lattice is defined by a generator matrix G or an integer constraint. Generator Matrix (G): A 3 \times 3 matrix where columns are the basis vectors of the lattice. G = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} Integer Constraint: A point (x, y, z) belongs to the lattice if x, y, z \in \mathbb{Z} and x + y + z is even. Parameters: Generator Matrix G: Must be non-singular (\det(G) \neq 0). For the standard FCC lattice, \det(G) = 2. Applicability Condition: The method is most effective if the frequency spectrum of the signal is spherical. Steps: 1. Define Lattice Basis: Choose the generator matrix G for the FCC lattice. G = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix} 2. Generate Sample Coordinates: For every integer vector \mathbf{v} = [i, j, k]^T \in \mathbb{Z}^3, compute the physical coordinate \mathbf{p}: \mathbf{p} = G \cdot \mathbf{v} Alternatively, iterate over integer coordinates (x, y, z) and include the point only if: (x + y + z) \pmod 2 = 0 3. Sample Signal: Evaluate the volume signal at each generated coordinate \mathbf{p}. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def generatefcclatticepoints(boundingboxmin, boundingboxmax, stepsize=1.0): """ Generates coordinates for an FCC lattice within a bounding box. Uses the integer constraint definition: x + y + z is even. """ points = [] # Determine integer range covering the bounding box minx = floor(boundingboxmin[0] / stepsize) maxx = ceil(boundingboxmax[0] / stepsize) miny = floor(boundingboxmin[1] / stepsize) maxy = ceil(boundingboxmax[1] / stepsize) minz = floor(boundingboxmin[2] / stepsize) maxz = ceil(boundingboxmax[2] / stepsize) for x in range(minx, maxx + 1): for y in range(miny, maxy + 1): for z in range(minz, maxz + 1): # FCC condition: sum of coordinates must be even if (x + y + z) % 2 == 0: # Convert integer lattice index to physical space # Note: The generator matrix G maps integer vectors to physical space. # However, the constraint definition (x+y+z even) describes the # points in the standard Cartesian basis that form the FCC lattice. # These two definitions are equivalent for the standard FCC lattice. physicalx = x stepsize physicaly = y stepsize physicalz = z stepsize points.append((physicalx, physicaly, physicalz)) return points Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Boundary Handling: The integer constraint method requires careful clamping to ensure points fall exactly within the desired bounding box. Precision: When converting between the generator matrix representation and the integer constraint representation, floating-point errors may occur. The integer constraint method is generally more robust for storage and indexing. Degenerate Input: If the signal is not band-limited or has a non-spherical spectrum, the sampling efficiency advantage over CC grids may diminish. A common interpolation technique used with FCC lattices. Box splines are piecewise polynomials defined by a direction matrix and are well-suited for the FCC geometry. The dual lattice of FCC. BCC is optimal for band-limited and isotropic signals, whereas FCC is optimal for depressed rate sampling. Time Complexity: Sampling time is proportional to the number of lattice points within the volume. The density of FCC points is half that of a CC grid with the same spacing, reducing the number of samples by approximately 50% compared to CC for equivalent spatial coverage, though the exact savings depend on the specific implementation and bounding box alignment. Memory Complexity: Storage is reduced compared to CC grids. The FCC lattice provides the densest packing of equal-sized spheres, making it space-efficient for storage. Performance: GPU ray casting implementations for FCC datasets have shown superior performance due to efficient empty space skipping and spline value evolution. Strengths: Better sampling efficiency than Cartesian lattices; optimal for signals sampled at a depressed rate; densest sphere packing. Limitations: Not optimal for all signal types (specifically, BCC is preferred for band-limited isotropic signals). When to use: Medical and scientific datasets, GPU ray casting, mobile volume rendering where memory and bandwidth are constrained. The FCC lattice was introduced as a more efficient alternative to Cartesian lattices for volume rendering. Kim implemented a real-time GPU iso-surface ray caster for FCC datasets, demonstrating the practical benefits of this approach. The theoretical basis for its optimality in specific signal conditions was indicated by Künsch et al. The FCC lattice is the dual of the BCC lattice in the spatial domain.
