name: TRIPS
head: TRIPS, Trilinear Point Splatting, TRIPS: Neural Feature Attachment and Pyramid Rendering for 3DGS
body: TRIPS is a point-based radiance field rendering technique that rasterizes points into a screen-space image pyramid using trilinear splats, followed by a neural reconstruction network to produce hole-free, crisp images. It solves the blurriness and cloudy artifacts of 3D Gaussian Splatting and the temporal instability and large-gap handling issues of ADOP by projecting neural color descriptors into an image pyramid using trilinear writes to two neighboring resolution layers based on projected point size, avoiding overdraw by rendering only 2x2 splats. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Point positions \mathbf{x}w, world-space sizes sw, neural feature descriptors \tau, point opacities \alpha, camera intrinsics C (including focal length f), and camera extrinsics (R, t). Outputs: Final RGB image. Data Structures: Image Pyramid: A set of n layers. Layer L has resolution 2^L \times 2^L relative to the finest layer 0. Each pixel in each layer stores a depth-sorted list of fragments \Lambda{l,x,y} containing colors and alpha values, clamped to a maximum size of 16 elements. Neural Reconstruction Network: A small decoder consisting of gated convolutions, with only a single gated convolution per layer. Spherical Harmonics Module: Optional module applied after the neural network to model view-dependent artifacts. Steps: 1. Projection: For each point, project its position \mathbf{x}w = (xw, yw, zw) to continuous screen space coordinates (x, y, z) using camera intrinsics C and extrinsics (R, t). Calculate the screen space size s from the world space size sw and depth z: s = \frac{f \cdot sw}{z} where f is the focal length. 2. Layer Selection: Determine the two resolution layers for each point based on its projected size s: L{lower} = \lfloor \log2(s) \rfloor L{upper} = \lceil \log2(s) \rceil Points are rasterized as 2x2x2 trilinear splats into these two layers. 3. Trilinear Splatting: For each of the eight pixels (2x2 in each of the 2 selected layers), compute the contribution of the point. The final opacity value \gamma written to the image pyramid for pixel (xi, yi, si) with si = 2^L is: \gamma = \beta \cdot \iota \cdot \alpha where \alpha is the point opacity. Bilinear Weight (\beta): Computed inside the image layer based on continuous screen coordinates (x, y) and pixel coordinates (xi, yi): \beta = (1 - |x - xi|) \cdot (1 - |y - yi|) Linear Layer Weight (\iota): Interpolates between the two selected layers based on projected size s and layer sizes s{lower}=2^{L{lower}} and s{upper}=2^{L{upper}}: \iota = \begin{cases} 1 - \frac{|s - si|}{2^{L{upper}} - 2^{L{lower}}} & s \geq 1 \\ \epsilon + (1 - \epsilon)s & si = 0 \wedge s < 1 \end{cases} where \epsilon = 0.25 is a minimum weight constant to ensure far-away points with pixel size < 1 do not disappear. 4. Alpha Blending: Collect all fragments in per-pixel lists \Lambda{l,x,y} for each layer. Sort lists by depth. Compute the color C\Lambda for each pixel using front-to-back alpha blending: C\Lambda = \sum{m=1}^{|\Lambda|} Tm \cdot \alpham \cdot cm Tm = \prod{i=1}^{m-1} (1 - \alphai) where cm is the color of the m-th fragment, \alpham is its opacity, and Tm is the transmittance. 5. Neural Reconstruction: Feed the feature image pyramid through the compact neural reconstruction network. The network harmonizes the various layers, addresses remaining gaps, and conceals rendering artifacts. 6. Optional View Dependency: Apply the spherical harmonics module to the output of the neural network to preserve high levels of detail and model view-dependent artifacts. 7. Tone Mapping: Apply a tone mapping module to transform the resulting features into RGB colors. Parameters: Splat Size: Points are rasterized as 2x2x2 trilinear splats. Minimum Weight: \epsilon = 0.25. Feature Descriptors: Default is 4 feature vectors per point. Network Architecture: Small decoder made out of gated convolutions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Choose it when memory efficiency and compression are prioritized over raw rasterization speed. Link Organizes points into a tree structure to facilitate efficient rendering and LOD management. Choose it when streaming large point clouds with dynamic level-of-detail is required. Link Time Complexity: Real-time performance is maintained. For the OFFICE scene with 72.5M points, render time is 15.0ms. On the PLAYGROUND scene (12.5M points), rasterization takes 6.2ms (counting/memory allocation 1.9ms, splatting 2.6ms, sorting/blending 1.7ms), and the neural network takes 4.5ms. Memory Complexity: Uses 4 feature descriptors per point by default. Performance: Maintains a real-time frame rate of 60 frames per second on readily available hardware (RTX4090 for rendering, Nvidia A100 for training). Strengths: Crisper images than 3D Gaussian Splatting, better gap filling and temporal consistency than ADOP, efficient handling of large point clouds. Limitations: Requires an initial dense reconstruction. Lack of anisotropic splat formulation causes noisy artifacts around silhouettes of elongated, slender objects during strong hole-filling. Hole-filling near the camera exhibits fuzzy edges and shine-through artifacts. Slight flickering can occur in areas with too many or too few points. When to use: When crisp, hole-free images are required and temporal consistency is important, especially for scenes with intricate geometry or expansive landscapes. When not to use: When an initial dense reconstruction is unavailable, or when strong hole-filling of elongated, slender objects is required (which causes noisy silhouette artifacts due to the lack of anisotropic splatting). name: Multi-scale filtering
head: Multi-scale Gaussian filtering, Resolution-adaptive Gaussian filtering
body: Multi-scale filtering refers to a family of techniques in 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that mitigate aliasing artifacts and optimize rendering performance by adapting the Gaussian representation to the camera's viewing frequency or resolution. It sets itself apart from standard 3DGS by explicitly managing the spectral content of the primitives—either through training-time aggregation, test-time covariance regularization, or runtime hierarchical pruning—to ensure the rendered image remains consistent across varying scales. All methods in this family address the mismatch between the discrete sampling of the image sensor and the continuous representation of 3D Gaussians. The core mechanism involves modifying the projected 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D} to account for the sampling frequency or pixel size. 1. Covariance Regularization: To prevent aliasing (high-frequency artifacts) when zooming out or rendering at low resolution, a low-pass filter is applied. This is achieved by adding a variance term \sigma^2{test} (derived from the pixel size or testing frequency) to the projected 2D covariance: \Sigma{reg} = \Sigma{2D} + \sigma^2{test} I where I is the identity matrix. 2. Opacity Preservation: Adding variance spreads the Gaussian, reducing its peak height. To preserve the integral (total mass/energy) of the Gaussian, the opacity \alpha is scaled by a normalization factor C: C = \frac{\sqrt{|\Sigma{2D}|}}{\sqrt{|\Sigma{reg}|}} \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} \cdot C This ensures that the total contribution of the Gaussian remains constant despite the blurring. 3. Frequency Matching: The filter parameters are tuned to match the Nyquist limit of the rendering resolution. For training-time methods, this involves constraining the 3D representation frequency to the training data's sampling rate. For test-time methods, it involves adapting to the specific camera distance and resolution. MIP-Splatting eliminates aliasing by combining a 3D smoothing filter, a 2D Mip filter, and multi-scale Gaussian selection. It sets itself apart by constraining the 3D representation frequency to the training data's Nyquist limit during training and replacing the empirical dilation filter with a physics-based box filter approximation during rendering. It uses a 4-level hierarchy (1x, 4x, 16x, 64x) and aggregates small Gaussians into coarser levels to prevent missing parts in the rendered image. Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting (SA-GS) is a training-free, test-time plugin that improves anti-aliasing by applying 2D scale-adaptive filters. Unlike MIP-Splatting, which modifies training and uses filters unaware of testing frequency, SA-GS operates on any pretrained Gaussian field, ensuring consistent primitive distribution across different rendering resolutions and camera distances by dynamically adjusting the covariance based on the target resolution. FilterGS is a rendering acceleration method for large-scale Level-of-Detail (LoD) 3D Gaussian Splatting. It eliminates inefficient serial tree traversal and reduces redundant Gaussian-tile pairs through parallel filtering and adaptive shrinking. It addresses the critical challenges of LoD methods by using a traversal-free, parallel filtering structure that selects a single scale for each Gaussian via a learned network, avoiding expensive tree traversal at render time. Progressively applies low-pass filtering to avoid 2D Gaussian projections becoming smaller than a pixel. The problem of aliasing in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises because standard 3DGS systematically underestimates the scale parameter during optimization, leading to erosion effects when zooming in and high-frequency artifacts when zooming out. MIP-Splatting was introduced to address these resolution-dependent artifacts by integrating multi-scale representations. Subsequent works like SA-GS and FilterGS expanded the family to include test-time adaptations and performance optimizations. The theoretical basis relies on treating the camera sensor as a box filter and ensuring the Gaussian's spectral content does not exceed the Nyquist limit of the sampling grid. name: 2D Mip Filter
head: Mip-Splatting 2D filter, View-dependent 2D Gaussian filter
body: The 2D Mip Filter mitigates aliasing artifacts in 3D Gaussian Splatting when rendering from camera distances or focal lengths larger than those encountered during training. It extends the standard 2D Gaussian filter by introducing a view-dependent opacity compensation factor that prevents excessive blurring as Gaussians become smaller relative to the pixel grid. Unlike the basic 2D Gaussian filter which dilates the covariance matrix uniformly, this method dynamically adjusts opacity based on the ratio of the original to the dilated covariance determinant. The method modifies the projected 2D covariance matrix and the opacity of each Gaussian during the rendering pass. It is typically combined with a 3D smoothing filter, which requires a smaller base variance for the 2D filter to avoid over-smoothing. Inputs: \Sigma{2D}: The projected 2D covariance matrix of a Gaussian. o: The original opacity of the Gaussian. \kappa{3D}: The variance parameter for the 2D filter dilation. Outputs: \hat{\Sigma}{2D}: The dilated covariance matrix used for rasterization. \hat{o}: The compensated opacity used for alpha blending. Data Structures: \Sigma{2D}: A 2 \times 2 symmetric matrix. \mathbf{I}: The 2 \times 2 identity matrix. Parameters: \kappa{3D}: The added variance. Default value is 0.1 when combined with the 3D smoothing filter. (Note: The original 3DGS uses 0.3 for the 2D filter alone, but this value is reduced in the Mip-Splatting context). Steps: 1. Dilate Covariance: Add the variance parameter to the diagonal of the projected covariance matrix to prevent aliasing from undersampling: \hat{\Sigma}{2D} = \Sigma{2D} + \kappa{3D} \mathbf{I} 2. Compute Compensation Factor: Calculate the square root of the ratio of the determinants of the original and dilated covariance matrices. This factor represents the relative volume change: \text{factor} = \sqrt{\frac{|\Sigma{2D}|}{|\hat{\Sigma}{2D}|}} 3. Compensate Opacity: Multiply the original opacity by the compensation factor to maintain visual consistency at different scales: \hat{o} = \text{factor} \cdot o 4. Bounding Box Update: Use the compensated opacity \hat{o} (rather than the original o) when computing opacity-aware bounding boxes for culling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def compute2dmipfilter(Sigma2D: list, opacity: float, kappa3D: float = 0.1) -> tuple: """ Computes the dilated covariance and compensated opacity for the 2D Mip Filter. Args: Sigma2D: 2x2 list of lists representing the projected 2D covariance matrix [[a, b], [c, d]]. opacity: Original opacity scalar. kappa3D: Variance parameter for dilation (default 0.1). Returns: Tuple of (dilatedSigma2D, compensatedopacity) """ # Extract matrix elements a, b = Sigma2D[0] c, d = Sigma2D[1] # Step 1: Dilate covariance matrix # Add kappa3D to the diagonal elements dilatedSigma2D = [[a + kappa3D, b], [c, d + kappa3D]] # Step 2: Compute determinants detoriginal = a d - b c detdilated = (a + kappa3D) (d + kappa3D) - b c # Guard against numerical instability if determinant is near zero or negative # Clamp determinants to a small positive epsilon to avoid NaNs in sqrt epsilon = 1e-8 detoriginal = max(detoriginal, epsilon) detdilated = max(detdilated, epsilon) # Step 3: Compute compensation factor # factor = sqrt(|Sigma2D| / |Sigmahat2D|) factor = math.sqrt(detoriginal / detdilated) # Step 4: Compensate opacity compensatedopacity = factor opacity return dilatedSigma2D, compensatedopacity Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Gradient Instability: The analytical derivatives of the opacity compensation factor with respect to \Sigma{2D} are numerically unstable and can cause gradients to explode during training. Bounding Box Accuracy: Failing to use the compensated opacity \hat{o} for bounding box calculations can lead to incorrect culling decisions, potentially rendering Gaussians that should be culled or missing those that should be included. A technique to prevent exploding gradients in the 2D Mip filter by detaching the compensation factor from the gradient computation for the 2D covariance matrix \Sigma{2D}. The original implementation [98] frequently clips extreme values, while other re-implementations [56, 65] use non-analytical gradients that do not match the analytical derivative. Detaching the factor ensures stable gradients while maintaining the analytical form of the forward pass. A stable implementation for the full analytical derivative is optionally available but not recommended for standard training. Time Complexity: The additional computation involves determinant calculation and square root operations per Gaussian, which is negligible compared to the rasterization cost. The authors report that their simplifications effectively eliminate any training overhead compared to the original implementation. Memory Complexity: No additional memory is required beyond the stored Gaussian parameters. Performance: On the Mip-NeRF360 dataset, enabling full anti-aliasing (including the 2D Mip Filter) improves PSNR at 0.5x resolution from 25.11 to 28.39, while maintaining comparable PSNR at 1x resolution (27.56 vs 27.54). Strengths: Significantly reduces aliasing artifacts when rendering at resolutions different from training resolution or from distant cameras. Limitations: Can lead to increasingly blurry renderings if the compensation factor is not applied, as the dilated covariance dominates at large distances. The 2D Mip Filter was introduced by Yu et al. as part of the Mip-Splatting framework. It builds upon the 2D Gaussian filter used in the original 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by Kerbl et al. [37], which adds a constant variance to prevent aliasing when Gaussians fall between pixels. Yu et al. identified that this uniform dilation causes excessive blurring during inference when the camera is far away, and introduced the view-dependent opacity compensation to mitigate this. The method is cited as [98] in the Faster-GS paper. Faster-GS: Analyzing and Improving Gaussian Splatting Optimization, https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.09999v1, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting
head: SA-GS
body: Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting (SA-GS) is a training-free, test-time plugin for 3D Gaussian Splatting that improves anti-aliasing by applying 2D scale-adaptive filters to each Gaussian primitive. It solves the mismatch between Gaussian scales learned during training and the sampling frequency encountered at test time, which causes aliasing artifacts when zooming out or rendering at low resolutions. Unlike Mip-Splatting, which modifies the training procedure and uses filters unaware of testing frequency, SA-GS operates as a post-processing step informed by the specific rendering resolution and camera distance. Inputs: Pre-trained 3D Gaussian field (positions, covariances, opacities, colors); camera parameters (view matrix, projection matrix, focal length); rendering resolution (W, H). Outputs: Rendered image. Data Structures: Gaussian Primitive: Defined by mean position \mu, 3D covariance \Sigma{3D} (or scale/rotation), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic coefficients for color. Projected Covariance: \Sigma{2D}, a 2 \times 2 matrix representing the Gaussian's spread in screen space. Steps: 1. Calculate Testing Frequency: Determine the effective sampling frequency based on the rendering resolution and camera distance. For a pixel of size p (in world units) at distance d, the filter scale is derived from the pixel footprint. 2. Project and Regularize Covariance: Project the 3D Gaussian to 2D screen space to obtain \Sigma{2D}. Apply a 2D scale-adaptive low-pass filter by adding a variance term \sigma^2{test} to the projected covariance: \Sigma{reg} = \Sigma{2D} + \sigma^2{test} I where I is the 2 \times 2 identity matrix and \sigma^2{test} is derived from the testing frequency (resolution and camera distance). 3. Adjust Opacity: To preserve the integral (total mass) of the Gaussian after blurring, scale the opacity \alpha by a normalization factor C: C = \frac{\sqrt{|\Sigma{2D}|}}{\sqrt{|\Sigma{reg}|}} \alpha{new} = \alpha{old} \cdot C This ensures the Gaussian's contribution remains consistent despite the scale adaptation. 4. Integrate within Pixels: Instead of simple point sampling, integrate the projected 2D Gaussian (with covariance \Sigma{reg}) within each pixel area. This acts as a limiting case of super-sampling, handling sampling rates smaller than the scene frequency. The integration can be approximated by evaluating the cumulative distribution function or using a fixed number of samples within the pixel bounds weighted by the Gaussian PDF. Parameters: \sigma^2{test}: Adaptive variance term. Not given in the sources as a fixed formula, but described as being informed by testing frequency (resolution and camera distance). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Jaggedness without Filtering: Super-sampling and integration are only effective when the scale-adaptive filtering is activated; without it, scale inconsistency leads to jaggedness at low sampling rates. Scale Mismatch: If the Gaussian scale does not match the testing frequency, high-frequency artifacts appear. Eliminates high-frequency artifacts in dynamic scenes by adapting the dilation scale using the ratio of Gaussian scales before and after temporal changes, unlike Mip-Splatting's fixed dilation scale. Choose for dynamic 4D scenes. A training-stage module that corrects scale-dependent color mismatch by applying a learnable, scale-specific RGB offset to the SH DC coefficient. Choose when color fidelity across scales is critical and training modification is acceptable. Time Complexity: Adds a constant-time filter application per Gaussian during rendering. Integration within pixels may increase per-pixel cost slightly compared to vanilla splatting, but avoids the overhead of multi-resolution pyramid construction during training. Memory Complexity: No additional memory required for training data structures (e.g., mipmaps) as it is training-free. Performance: Performs comparably with or better than Mip-Splatting in various settings and both bounded and unbounded scenes. Strengths: Training-free; can be applied to any pre-trained Gaussian splatting field as a plugin; explicitly aware of testing frequency. Limitations: Requires modification of the rendering pipeline to implement the adaptive filter and integration; does not address view-dependent effects as directly as methods like VDGS. SA-GS was introduced to address the limitations of Mip-Splatting, which requires modifying the training procedure and uses 3D smoothing/2D Mip filters that are unaware of testing frequency. It builds on the principle that observing Gaussians at different frequencies leads to mismatches between training and testing scales. The method was proposed by Z. Song et al.. name: Adaptive-Scale Color Offset
body: Adaptive-Scale Color Offset (ACO) is a training-stage module for multi-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting that corrects scale-dependent color mismatch by applying a learnable, scale-specific RGB offset to the shared base color of each Gaussian. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Alias-free 4D Gaussian Splatting by modifying only the Spherical Harmonics (SH) DC coefficient to adapt color per scale, while keeping Gaussian geometry and higher-order view-dependent SH coefficients unchanged. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: N: Number of Gaussians. S: Number of rendering scales. B: Number of SH basis functions. f{i,b} \in \mathbb{R}^3: The original SH coefficients for Gaussian i and basis b. Yb(d): The value of the b-th SH basis function evaluated at view direction d. s{target}: The index of the target rendering scale during inference (0 \le s{target} < S). Outputs: c{i, s{target}}(d): The corrected color of Gaussian i at scale s{target} for view direction d. Data Structures SH Coefficients (f): A tensor of shape (N, B, 3). f{i,b} stores the RGB coefficients for Gaussian i and basis b. ACO Offsets (\Delta): A learnable parameter tensor of shape (N, S, 3). \Delta{i,s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the RGB offset for Gaussian i at scale s. Initialized to zero: \Delta{i,s} = \mathbf{0} for all i, s. Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: Initialize the ACO offset matrix \Delta \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times S \times 3} with zeros. 2. Training Loop: a. Select a training scale s from the set of S scales. b. Render the scene at scale s using the standard 3DGS splatting algorithm. c. Compute the reconstruction loss \mathcal{L} between the rendered image and the ground truth image. d. Back-propagate \mathcal{L} to update the corresponding offset \Delta{i,s} for the selected scale s. 3. Inference/Rendering: a. Given a target rendering scale s{target}. b. For each Gaussian i and view direction d: i. Retrieve the original DC coefficient f{i,0}. ii. Retrieve the scale-specific offset \Delta{i, s{target}}. iii. Compute the adapted DC coefficient: f{i,0}^{s{target}} = f{i,0} + \Delta{i, s{target}}. iv. Compute the color using the adapted DC coefficient and the shared higher-order coefficients: c{i, s{target}}(d) = Y0(d) f{i,0}^{s{target}} + \sum{b=1}^{B-1} Yb(d) f{i,b}. v. Use c{i, s{target}}(d) for splatting. Formulas The base color representation for Gaussian i along view direction d is given by the SH expansion: ci(d) = \sum{b=0}^{B-1} Yb(d) f{i,b} where Yb(d) is the b-th SH basis function and f{i,b} is the corresponding SH coefficient. The scale-adapted color at scale s is defined as: c{i,s}(d) = Y0(d) f{i,0}^s + \sum{b=1}^{B-1} Yb(d) f{i,b} where the adapted DC coefficient is f{i,0}^s = f{i,0} + \Delta{i,s}. Here, \Delta{i,s} \in \mathbb{R}^3 is the learnable DC color offset for Gaussian i at scale s. Parameters Number of Scales (S): Not given in the sources. SH Degree: Not given in the sources, but B is the number of basis functions. Initialization: \Delta{i,s} = 0. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Geometry Independence: ACO modifies only the DC color term. Shared Higher-Order Coefficients: The higher-order SH coefficients (b > 0) remain shared across all scales and are not modified by the offset. Optimization Scope: The DC offsets are optimized through the backbone reconstruction loss alone. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn as nn def evaluateshbases(d, degree): # Standard spherical harmonic basis evaluation x, y, z = d[:, 0], d[:, 1], d[:, 2] invsqrt4pi = 1.0 / (4 3.141592653589793) 0.5 bases = [torch.fulllike(x, invsqrt4pi)] if degree >= 1: bases.append(torch.fulllike(x, y invsqrt4pi)) if degree >= 2: bases.append(torch.fulllike(x, z invsqrt4pi)) if degree >= 3: bases.append(torch.fulllike(x, x invsqrt4pi)) # Higher degrees follow standard formulas return torch.stack(bases, dim=1)[:,:degree] class AdaptiveScaleColorOffset(nn.Module): def init(self, numgaussians, numscales): super().init() # ACO offsets: shape (N, S, 3), initialized to zero self.offsets = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(numgaussians, numscales, 3)) def forward(self, shcoeffs, viewdirections, targetscale): # shcoeffs: (N, B, 3) # viewdirections: (N, 3) # targetscale: int in [0, S-1] dccoeff = shcoeffs[:, 0,:] # (N, 3) higherordercoeffs = shcoeffs[:, 1:,:] # (N, B-1, 3) # Retrieve scale-specific offset scaleoffset = self.offsets[:, targetscale,:] # (N, 3) adapteddc = dccoeff + scaleoffset # (N, 3) # Evaluate SH basis functions for view directions Y0 = torch.full((shcoeffs.size(0), 1), 1.0 / (4 3.141592653589793) 0.5, device=shcoeffs.device) Yhigher = evaluateshbases(viewdirections, shcoeffs.size(1) - 1) # (N, B-1, 1) # Compute scale-adapted color: c{i,s}(d) = Y0 f{i,0}^s + sum{b=1}^{B-1} Yb(d) f{i,b} colordc = Y0 adapteddc.unsqueeze(1) # (N, 1, 3) colorhigher = torch.sum(Yhigher higherordercoeffs, dim=1) # (N, 3) return colordc.squeeze(1) + colorhigher # (N, 3) A companion module that redistributes low-contribution Gaussians toward high-error regions to fix primitive allocation imbalance. It differs from ACO by modifying geometry and primitive placement rather than color offsets. Choose it when coarse-scale regions lack sufficient Gaussian coverage. Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation The parent method that ACO extends is Scale-Adaptive Gaussian Splatting. It applies 2D scale-adaptive filters to improve anti-aliasing by matching Gaussian scales to testing frequency. It differs from ACO by filtering geometry/scales rather than correcting color offsets. Choose it as the base rendering pipeline before applying color corrections. A sibling method that addresses aliasing in dynamic scenes using frequency-domain filtering. It differs from ACO by not using scale-specific color offsets but rather temporal and spatial anti-aliasing techniques. Choose it for dynamic scenes where temporal consistency is critical. Alias-free 4D Gaussian Splatting Time Complexity: Rendering time is not significantly increased by ACO, as it only adds a vector addition to the DC coefficient per Gaussian. The training time increases slightly due to the optimization of the offset parameters \Delta. Memory Complexity: ACO adds N \times S \times 3 parameters to the model, where N is the number of Gaussians and S is the number of scales. Strengths: Corrects color mismatch at coarse rendering scales without altering Gaussian geometry. It provides scale-dependent color adaptation. Limitations: Only corrects color, not geometry or view-dependent shading (higher-order SH). It requires training at multiple scales. When to use: When rendering multi-scale 3DGS and observing color inaccuracies at coarse scales. When not to use: When geometry accuracy is the primary concern, or when single-scale rendering is sufficient. ACO was proposed in the paper "Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting" published in Mathematics in 2026. It addresses the issue where coarse-scale error regions remain underrepresented in multi-scale 3DGS, leading to color mismatch because the same color representation is shared across rendering scales. The method is part of the ACO-EGR framework, which also includes Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation (EGR). Adaptive-Scale Color Offset and Error-Guided Gaussian Reallocation for Multi-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14152713, fetched 2026-11-01

name: FilterGS
head: Traversal-Free Parallel Filtering, Adaptive Shrinking, Parallel filtering structure for Gaussian scale selection
body: FilterGS is a rendering acceleration method for large-scale Level-of-Detail (LoD) 3D Gaussian Splatting that eliminates inefficient serial tree traversal and reduces redundant Gaussian-tile pairs through parallel filtering and adaptive shrinking. It addresses the mismatch between discrete sampling and continuous representation by applying a traversal-free, parallel filtering structure that selects a single scale for each Gaussian via a learned network, avoiding expensive tree traversal at render time. Unlike sibling methods that rely on serial level-by-level traversal, FilterGS completes filtering in two parallel steps regardless of tree depth, decoupling computational cost from hierarchical depth. Inputs and Outputs Inputs: A hierarchical LoD Gaussian tree model (trained from SfM points and images), a camera view (position, orientation, intrinsics), and a pre-computed scene-adaptive shrinking threshold \tau. Outputs: A set of filtered 2D Gaussians ready for standard \alpha-blending rasterization, with redundant pairs removed and influence radii adaptively shrunk. Data Structures LoD Gaussian Tree: Nodes encapsulate full Gaussian primitives. Node Parameters: Center position \mu, covariance matrix \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients for color c, rotation q, and scale s. Hierarchy Construction: For a parent node v with rotation R(qv) and scale sv, Kv children are placed using oriented offsets ok \in \{\pm xv/2, \pm yv/2, \pm zv/2\}: \mu{uk} = \muv + R(qv) ok Children shrink geometrically: s{uk} = \gamma sv with 0 < \gamma < 1. Children inherit parent orientation, color, and opacity: q{uk} = qv, c{uk} = cv, \alpha{uk} = \alphav. Ancestor Path (AP{i,j}): For every node N{i,j} at level i, a pre-computed ordered list of serial numbers of all ancestor nodes from the direct parent up to the root node. Algorithm Steps 1. Preprocessing (Offline): Perform a pre-rendering pass over all training views following the standard 3DGS pipeline. Compute the Global Tile Coverage (GTC) metric \bar{G}, defined as the average Gaussian-to-Tile Contribution (GTC) across all views. Derive the scene-adaptive shrinking threshold \tau = f(\bar{G}). A low \bar{G} indicates high congestion, necessitating a more aggressive \tau. 2. Parallel Filtering (Per Frame): Step 1: Radius and Leaf (R&L) Filter: Project all Gaussians inside the view frustum into 2D Gaussians. Compute the 2D covariance \Sigma{2D} and its eigenvalues \sigma (standard deviations along screen-space principal axes). Calculate the pixel radius R{2D} = 3\sigma. Retention Rule: Retain any node where R{2D} \leq \tauR (default \tauR = 3). Leaf Exemption: Exempt all leaf nodes from the pruning threshold; preserve every leaf node at least once to prevent holes in the rendered image. Step 2: Ancestor Filter: For every node N{i,j} that passed R&L filtering, traverse its pre-computed ancestor path AP{i,j}. Culling Rule: If any ancestor node N{i^,j^} \in AP{i,j} is an internal node that passed R&L filtering, cull the descendant node N{i,j}. This ensures that branches with a valid coarser node retain only a single, highest-level Gaussian node. 3. Adaptive Shrinking: During Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB) formation, adaptively scale the filtered Gaussians. Calculate the effective influence radius r at which opacity decays to threshold \tau: r = \sqrt{2\sigma{max} \ln(\alpha0 / \tau)} where \sigma{max} is the maximum standard deviation and \alpha0 is the central opacity. Scale the Gaussians by the pre-computed factor \tau to reduce redundant key-value pairs before sorting and \alpha-blending. 4. Rasterization: Sort the filtered Gaussians by depth. Compute pixel color C by blending N ordered 2D Gaussians: C = \sum{i \in N} ci \alphai Ti, \quad Ti = \prod{j=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alphaj) where ci is color, \alphai is opacity, and Ti is residual transmittance. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def filtergsrender(tree, camera, taushrink, taur=3.0): """ tree: Hierarchical LoD Gaussian Tree structure camera: Camera parameters for projection taushrink: Pre-computed scene-adaptive shrinking threshold taur: Radius threshold for R&L filter (default 3) """ # 1. Project Gaussians in frustum infrustumgaussians = [] for node in tree.allnodes: if node.isinfrustum(camera): # Project 3D Gaussian to 2D sigma2d = projectcovariance(node.sigma3d, camera) node.sigma2d = sigma2d infrustumgaussians.append(node) # 2. Parallel Filtering Step 1: R&L Filter # Compute R2D for all nodes in parallel for node in infrustumgaussians: eigenvalues = computeeigenvalues(node.sigma2d) sigmamax = max(eigenvalues) node.r2d = 3 sigmamax node.passedrlfilter = False # Apply R&L rules for node in infrustumgaussians: if node.isleaf: node.passedrlfilter = True elif node.r2d <= taur: node.passedrlfilter = True # 3. Parallel Filtering Step 2: Ancestor Filter # Pre-computed ancestor paths are assumed to be stored in tree nodes # We need to identify which internal nodes passed R&L to cull descendants # First, collect all internal nodes that passed R&L qualifiedinternalnodes = [ node for node in infrustumgaussians if node.passedrlfilter and not node.isleaf ] # Create a set of qualified internal node IDs for fast lookup qualifiedids = {node.id for node in qualifiedinternalnodes} # Cull descendants based on ancestor paths for node in infrustumgaussians: if not node.passedrlfilter: continue # Check if any ancestor is a qualified internal node hasqualifiedancestor = False for ancestorid in node.ancestorpath: if ancestorid in qualifiedids: hasqualifiedancestor = True break if hasqualifiedancestor: node.passedrlfilter = False # Cull this node # 4. Adaptive Shrinking finalgaussians = [] for node in infrustumgaussians: if node.passedrlfilter: # Calculate shrinking factor based on opacity decay # r = sqrt(2 sigmamax ln(alpha0 / taushrink)) # The actual implementation scales the Gaussian parameters # to match this effective radius or opacity threshold sigmamax = max(computeeigenvalues(node.sigma2d)) alpha0 = node.alpha # Compute the radius where opacity decays to taushrink # This is used to determine the scaling factor for AABB/radius if alpha0 > taushrink: effectiveradius = sqrt(2 sigmamax log(alpha0 / taushrink)) # Scale the Gaussian's influence/radius by taushrink factor # Note: The exact scaling operation depends on the rasterizer's # AABB construction logic. Here we assume a scaling of the # effective radius or covariance. node.scaleshrinkingfactor = taushrink finalgaussians.append(node) # 5. Rasterization # Sort by depth finalgaussians.sort(key=lambda g: g.depth) # Alpha blend image = zeroslike(targetimage) for gaussian in finalgaussians: # Standard 3DGS rasterization step blendgaussian(image, gaussian) return image Parameters \tauR: Radius threshold for pruning. Default value is 3. Smaller values retain finer primitives. \tau: Scene-adaptive shrinking threshold derived from GTC. Determined by \lambdaG = 0.2 scaling factor in experiments. \gamma: Geometric shrinking factor for child node scales in the LoD tree, must satisfy 0 < \gamma < 1. Redundancy Threshold: Key-value pairs with Key-value Pair Contribution (KPC) below 0.01 are defined as redundant. Edge Cases and Pitfalls Holes in Rendering: Directly applying the radius pruning threshold may remove entire branches of Gaussians with uniformly large radii. The leaf exemption rule is critical to prevent this. Congestion: In highly congested scenes, a fixed threshold (e.g., \tau = 1/255) is overly conservative. The scene-adaptive \tau derived from GTC is necessary to mitigate congestion effectively. Precision: The calculation of R{2D} = 3\sigma assumes a standard deviation-based cutoff. Precision in eigenvalue computation for \Sigma{2D} is required for accurate radius estimation. Time Complexity: Filtering time scales with the total number of in-frustum Gaussians N and is independent of the hierarchical depth L (Depth Decoupling). T{parallel} = T{synch.} + T{calcu.}(N) where T{synch.} is the fixed overhead of kernel launch and synchronization, and T{calcu.}(N) is the time for radius estimation and filtering. Memory Complexity: Requires pre-computation of ancestor paths for all nodes, adding static memory overhead proportional to the number of nodes and tree depth. Measured Performance: Achieves state-of-the-art rendering speeds across multiple large-scale datasets (tested at 1080p resolution on RTX 4090) while maintaining competitive visual quality. Strengths: Eliminates serial traversal overhead (which can consume >60% of rendering time in LoG methods); maximizes GPU concurrency via parallel processing; reduces redundant Gaussian-tile pairs. Limitations: Requires a pre-rendering pass to compute GTC and \tau; relies on the correctness of the hierarchical tree structure; performance depends on the efficiency of the parallel filtering implementation. FilterGS was introduced to address critical challenges in large-scale Level-of-Detail 3D Gaussian Splatting, specifically inefficient serial traversal and redundant Gaussian-tile pairs. It builds on the principles of Multi-scale filtering, which address the mismatch between discrete sampling and continuous representation by modifying the projected 2D covariance matrix. The method was developed to improve upon serial strategies like LoG, which require steps proportional to tree depth. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) FilterGS: Traversal-Free Parallel Filtering and Adaptive Shrinking for Large-Scale LoD 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2603.23891, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting
head: Page-based Rendering, Virtual Texturing for 3DGS, Vmem
body: Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting (Vmem) enables the rendering of large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) scenes that exceed available GPU memory by applying virtual texturing concepts. It groups Gaussians into fixed-size pages, uses a proxy mesh for visibility culling, and streams only visible pages into a limited GPU buffer. Unlike standard 3DGS which loads all Gaussians or relies on simple distance culling, Vmem separates virtual and physical address spaces, allowing dynamic LOD selection and just-in-time memory allocation to maintain stable frame rates in memory-constrained environments. Inputs: A trained 3DGS scene containing Gaussians with position, covariance, opacity, and spherical harmonics coefficients. Camera position and orientation. Configuration parameters including Page Size (N{page}), Staging Buffer Size, Rendering Buffer Size, and Adaptive LOD memory targets. Outputs: Rendered image frame. Updated GPU memory state containing resident pages. Scene File (Preprocessed): Proxy Mesh: A coarse mesh approximating the scene geometry, used for visibility determination. Page IDs: An array mapping each Gaussian to a page index. Page Links: Adjacency list where each page ID maps to a list of overlapping page IDs. LOD Levels: Precomputed Gaussian sets for each page at different levels of detail. Size: Typically < 20 MiB. Page Structure: Each page contains a fixed number of Gaussians (N{page}). LOD Levels: For each page, multiple LOD levels exist. Level 0 contains the original Gaussians. Level L contains \frac{1}{2^L} of the Gaussians of Level 0, generated by merging or clustering Gaussians within the page. Note: The source notes that LOD creation may have flaws regarding incorrect scale and lack of level blending. GPU Buffers: Staging Buffer: A temporary buffer for copying data from CPU to GPU. Size is typically ~18.4 MiB (e.g., 40 pages of 2048 Gaussians). Rendering Buffer: A resident GPU buffer holding visible pages. Size is configurable, e.g., 500 pages for the Berlin scene which uses 489 pages. Page Table: Maps virtual page IDs to physical locations in the Rendering Buffer. Supports sparse residency or reserved resources via APIs like Vulkan or Direct3D 12. 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Mesh Extraction: Generate a proxy mesh from the 3DGS scene using techniques like marching cubes or Gaussian Opacity Fields, tailored to the scene. 2. Page Assignment: Group Gaussians into pages based on spatial position and assign a unique Page ID to each Gaussian. 3. Page Linking: Identify overlapping pages and link them if their spatial extents overlap. This ensures that pages occluded by the proxy mesh but visible via Gaussian spread are included. Pitfall: Unchecked overlaps can negate occlusion culling. A threshold should be used to ignore small overlaps. 4. LOD Generation: For each page, generate lower LOD levels by merging Gaussians so that Level L has half the count of Level L-1. 5. File Creation: Store the proxy mesh, page IDs, links, and LOD data in a single file. 2. Runtime (Per Frame): 1. Visibility Determination: Render the proxy mesh to a visibility buffer to identify which pages are potentially visible. Expand the list of visible pages by including all linked pages that overlap with directly visible pages. 2. LOD Selection: Calculate the distance from the camera to each visible page. Determine the required LOD level for each page based on distance and current memory usage. Adaptive LOD: Dynamically adjust the distance thresholds for LOD transitions to keep physical memory usage between 50% and 80%. Constraint: A single physical page in the rendering buffer can store up to 2, 4, or 8 logical pages at higher LOD levels (Level 1, 2, 3) to save space. 3. Memory Management (Streaming): Compare the set of required pages with selected LOD levels against the currently resident pages in the Rendering Buffer. Identify pages to evict if the buffer is full and pages to load. Copy non-resident pages from the staging buffer to the Rendering Buffer. Update the Page Table to map virtual IDs to physical buffer locations. 4. Rendering: Sort the resident Gaussians by depth (back-to-front). Rasterize the Gaussians to the screen. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderframe(camera, scenefile, config): # 1. Visibility Determination # Render proxy mesh to get visible tile/page IDs visiblepageids = renderproxymeshvisibility(scenefile.proxymesh, camera) # Expand to include linked pages allrequiredpageids = set(visiblepageids) for pid in visiblepageids: if pid in scenefile.pagelinks: allrequiredpageids.update(scenefile.pagelinks[pid]) # 2. LOD Selection and Memory Budgeting # Calculate distance to each page center pagedistances = {} for pid in allrequiredpageids: pagedistances[pid] = euclideandistance(camera.position, getpagecenter(scenefile, pid)) # Determine LOD level for each page # Adaptive LOD adjusts thresholds to keep memory usage in [50%, 80%] requiredpages = [] for pid in allrequiredpageids: dist = pagedistances[pid] # Select LOD level L such that memory fits budget # Higher L means fewer Gaussians (halved per level) lodlevel = selectlodlevel(dist, config.adaptivelodthresholds, config.memorybudget) requiredpages.append((pid, lodlevel)) # 3. Memory Management # Identify resident pages in GPU buffer residentpages = getresidentpages(config.renderingbuffer) # Determine pages to load and evict pagestoload = [] pagestoevict = [] currentmemoryusage = calculatememoryusage(residentpages, config.renderingbuffercapacity) for pid, lod in requiredpages: if (pid, lod) not in residentpages: pagestoload.append((pid, lod)) # If buffer is full, evict least recently used or lowest priority pages if len(residentpages) + len(pagestoload) > config.renderingbuffercapacity: pagestoevict = selectpagestoevict(residentpages, pagestoload, config.renderingbuffercapacity) # Execute streaming for pid, lod in pagestoevict: evictpagefromgpu(config.renderingbuffer, pid, lod) for pid, lod in pagestoload: # Copy from staging buffer or disk copypagetogpu(config.stagingbuffer, config.renderingbuffer, pid, lod) # Update page table updatepagetable(config.pagetable, residentpages, pagestoload, pagestoevict) # 4. Rendering # Gather all resident Gaussians for the current frame residentgaussians = getgaussiansfrombuffer(config.renderingbuffer) # Sort by depth sortedgaussians = sortgaussiansbydepth(residentgaussians, camera) # Rasterize image = rasterizegaussians(sortedgaussians, camera, config.resolution) return image def selectlodlevel(distance, thresholds, memorybudget): """ Selects LOD level based on distance and memory constraints. Level 0: Original Gaussians. Level L: 1/2^L Gaussians. """ # Base selection from distance lod = 0 for i, threshold in enumerate(thresholds): if distance > threshold: lod = i + 1 # Adaptive adjustment: if memory is high, increase LOD (reduce Gaussians) # This is a simplified representation of the adaptive mechanism described # The source notes that thresholds are dynamically modified to keep memory in 50-80% range. if memorybudget > 0.8: lod = min(lod + 1, maxlodlevel) elif memorybudget < 0.5: lod = max(lod - 1, 0) return lod def renderproxymeshvisibility(mesh, camera): # Renders proxy mesh to a visibility buffer and returns visible page IDs return [pid for pid in mesh.visiblepages] def getpagecenter(scenefile, pid): # Returns the centroid of Gaussians in the specified page return scenefile.pagecentroids[pid] def getresidentpages(buffer): # Returns set of (pageid, lodlevel) tuples currently in GPU memory return set(buffer.residentpages) def calculatememoryusage(residentpages, capacity): # Calculates ratio of used pages to total capacity return len(residentpages) / capacity def selectpagestoevict(resident, toload, capacity): # Evicts pages to make room for toload, prioritizing higher LOD or least recently used needed = len(toload) - (capacity - len(resident)) evictcandidates = sorted(resident, key=lambda x: x[1], reverse=True) # Evict highest LOD first return evictcandidates[:needed] def evictpagefromgpu(buffer, pid, lod): # Unmaps virtual page from physical buffer buffer.unmap(pid, lod) def copypagetogpu(staging, target, pid, lod): # Copies page data from staging to target buffer target.map(pid, lod, staging.data[pid][lod]) def updatepagetable(table, resident, load, evict): # Updates virtual-to-physical mapping for pid, lod in load: table[pid] = lod for pid, lod in evict: del table[pid] def getgaussiansfrombuffer(buffer): # Retrieves all Gaussian data from resident pages return buffer.gatherall() def sortgaussiansbydepth(gaussians, camera): # Sorts back-to-front based on camera projection return sorted(gaussians, key=lambda g: g.depthfrom(camera)) def rasterizegaussians(sortedgaussians, camera, resolution): # Standard 3DGS splatting rasterization return rasterize(sortedgaussians, camera, resolution) Page Size (N{page}): 2048 Gaussians. Smaller sizes increase page table overhead; larger sizes reduce cache locality and increase false visibility. Staging Buffer Size: ~18.4 MiB (e.g., 40 pages of 2048 Gaussians). Rendering Buffer Size: Configurable to hold visible pages, e.g., 500 pages for the Berlin scene which uses 489 pages. Camera FoV: 90° (used in evaluation paths). Adaptive LOD Memory Target: 50% to 80%. LOD Page Capacity: A single physical page can store up to 2, 4, or 8 logical pages at higher LOD levels. Page Overlap: If page overlaps are not guarded during preprocessing, occlusion culling may be negated, increasing memory overhead. LOD Artifacts: Merging Gaussians for higher LOD levels creates artifacts, especially near the camera. Reducing page overlaps and adjusting Gaussian scales can decrease these. Buffer Too Small: If the rendering buffer is too small, holes and popping artifacts occur. Page Linking Trade-off: Page links increase memory usage and can degrade image quality by forcing poorer LOD selection. Omitting links causes rendering artifacts. Mitigation: use careful page assignments and set a threshold to ignore small overlaps. LOD System Flaws: The source notes incorrect scale during LOD creation and a lack of level blending during rendering. Preprocessing: Highly parallel. For the 'Residence' scene, preprocessing takes >1 hour, with 85% spent on LOD generation. For other scenes, page assignment, linking, and LOD each take ~0.5s per page. Page Table Update: 0.9ms (Page Size 2048), 0.5ms (4096), 0.3ms (8192). Depth Sort: 2.0ms (2048), 3.0ms (4096), 6.7ms (8192). Render Time: 8.0ms (2048), 9.7ms (4096), 10.6ms (8192). Memory Usage: Drastically reduced compared to baseline. In 'Alameda', memory never exceeds 50%. In 'Residence', memory is quickly saturated without LOD but reduces drastically with LOD. Hardware: Tested on NVIDIA GTX 1070 (Desktop) and Apple M1 SoC (Mobile). Quality: With Page Links and LOD: PSNR 47.19, SSIM 0.99. Baseline (No Virtual Memory): PSNR 42.89, SSIM 0.99. Mobile Performance: iPad M1 experiences a fourfold increase in Gaussian sorting time compared to desktop due to slower integrated GPU memory access. However, Vmem reduces the number of Gaussians sorted, justifying the overhead. Strengths: Enables rendering of scenes exceeding GPU memory. Improves frame times by reducing the number of Gaussians processed. Good cache locality due to page grouping. Limitations: LOD artifacts near the camera. Page linking increases memory overhead. Streaming overhead on mobile devices. LOD system lacks level blending. Large-scale 3DGS scenes (e.g., city streets, large open scenes) where GPU memory is insufficient to hold all Gaussians. Scenarios with significant occlusions (e.g., 'Alameda') where visibility culling is effective. Small scenes with negligible occlusions (e.g., single object novel view synthesis), as the overhead of page management may not be justified. Scenes where high-fidelity LOD blending is critical and the current LOD flaws (scale, blending) are unacceptable. Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting is based on the concept of Virtual Texturing, originally applied to GPU textures by Barrett [30] and analyzed by Mayer [31]. The method adapts these concepts to 3DGS by using a proxy mesh for visibility and grouping Gaussians into pages. The specific implementation described in the source was tested on large-scale scenes like ArtSci, Residence, Alameda, and Berlin. The method is used in large-scale 3DGS rendering to handle scenes exceeding GPU memory. It was tested on desktop and mobile hardware across various scene types. The implementation avoids compression to test the virtual memory methods in isolation. Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://zenodo.org/records/19690968, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Gaussian clustering and merging
body: Gaussian clustering and merging refers to a family of techniques that reduce the computational and memory cost of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by grouping individual splats into representative clusters or hierarchical nodes. These methods solve the problem of rendering large-scale scenes with millions of Gaussians by enabling Level of Detail (LOD) generation, spatial culling, and memory management. What sets this family apart from sibling methods like Multi-scale filtering or Virtual Memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting is the explicit construction of cluster structures (flat or hierarchical) and the aggregation of Gaussian parameters (position, covariance, opacity, color) to form fewer, larger primitives, rather than merely filtering or paging existing data. All methods in this family operate on a set of 3D Gaussians G = \{Gi\}, where each Gi is defined by position \mathbf{t}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), opacity \alphai, and color coefficients ci (often spherical harmonics). The core mechanism involves partitioning G into disjoint subsets (clusters) and replacing each subset with a single representative Gaussian G'j. The aggregation of parameters generally follows one of two paradigms: 1. Arithmetic Averaging: Simple mean of position, opacity, color, and sometimes scale. This is computationally cheap but may introduce geometric artifacts if the cluster is large or heterogeneous. 2. Moment Matching: Preserving the first and second spatial moments of the cluster to minimize integrated squared error (L2 loss). For a cluster Cj, the total weight is Wj = \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai. The representative position is \mathbf{t}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}i, and the covariance is \mathbf{\Sigma}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \left( \mathbf{\Sigma}i + (\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)(\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)^T \right). Clustering is typically performed in one of two spaces: Attribute Space: Clustering based on similarity of position, color, and scale (e.g., k-means). World Space: Clustering based on geometric proximity, often using spatial hashing, Morton codes, or hierarchical bounding volumes. Most methods support hierarchical structures (trees) to enable multi-resolution rendering, where leaf nodes contain raw splats and internal nodes contain merged representatives. A level-of-detail technique that reduces scene complexity by combining K splats into a single representative. It distinguishes itself by using moment matching for geometry and L2-optimal amplitude optimization for opacity, ensuring the merged Gaussian preserves the first and second spatial moments while minimizing integrated squared error. It relies on explicit partitioning algorithms (greedy, relocation, or relaxation) rather than fixed distance thresholds. Generates multiple LOD levels by iteratively clustering and averaging Gaussian parameters. It differs by using simple arithmetic averaging for position, opacity, and color, while explicitly excluding scale from averaging (preserving individual scales or using a fallback strategy). It supports virtual memory paging, allowing only relevant LOD levels to be loaded. Reduces Gaussian count by merging based on k-means clustering in multidimensional attribute space. It is distinguished by its use of a virtual memory framework where pages are mapped to LOD levels, and dynamic threshold adjustment to prevent visual popping. It specifically addresses the issue of merged Gaussians being too small by applying a scale-up factor. Focuses on the culling and selection phase of a hierarchical structure. It operates via compute shaders to perform frustum culling and screen-space error-based LOD selection on pre-computed clusters. It differs from merging algorithms by not defining the merge logic itself, but rather how to traverse and select from a hierarchy. Constructs hierarchical cluster structures using Morton code sorting and recursive merging. It differs by focusing on tree construction via spatial locality (Z-order curve) rather than direct optimization of a flat set. It supports configurable parameters for splats per cluster, branching factor, and LOD reduction ratio. A preprocessing technique that converts 2D screen-space pixel coverage into world-space coordinates and applies single-linkage hierarchical clustering. It differs by relying exclusively on geometric proximity in world space rather than color or scale similarity, primarily for noise removal and coverage management. A minor variant focusing on the structural assembly of the cluster tree. Step: Calculate the global bounding box of all splats using CalculateGlobalBounds. Build parent levels by merging child clusters using BuildParentLevel, specifying MaxChildrenPerCluster, ParentLODLevel, and NextClusterID. Parameter: SplatsPerCluster (default 128), MaxChildrenPerCluster (default 8), bReorderSplats (default true), bGenerateLOD (default true), and LODReductionRatio (default 4). Layout: Uses FSplatSortEntry with fields uint64 MortonCode and int32 OriginalIndex, compared by MortonCode. A post-processing step that merges neighboring Gaussian blocks across leaf node boundaries to form larger Gaussians for homogeneous regions. Definition: Assesses sets of neighboring blocks in a second pass to find cross-leaf homogeneous regions for merging. Step: Store intermediate LOD refinement results as individual leaf nodes. Run spatial variance estimation on these results sequentially in groups of 26 neighbors (considering faces, edges, and corners of a 2x2x2 node). If variance is below a threshold, replace the group with a single merged Gaussian. Calculate the new position as the merged centroid and radii/opacity using standard methods. Formula: The bounding box of the merged region is defined by bboxmin = \mini cmini and bboxmax = \maxi cmaxi, where ci are the corner coordinates of the bounding boxes of the regions being merged. The need for clustering and merging in 3D Gaussian Splatting arises from the high memory bandwidth and compute requirements of rendering millions of splats. Early 3DGS implementations rendered all splats, leading to performance bottlenecks in large scenes. Subsequent research introduced hierarchical structures and LOD techniques to mitigate this. The concept of merging Gaussians to reduce complexity has roots in Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) and volumetric representations. The specific application to 3DGS LOD generation gained traction with the introduction of methods like Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) and Sequential Point Trees (SPTs). The "Nanite-style" approach, popularized by Cluster Culling and Gaussian Cluster Builder, adapts virtual geometry techniques from film rendering to real-time rasterization. The Inter-leaf node clustering variant originates from research into approximating VDB datasets with 3D Gaussians, aiming to improve data fidelity by merging across spatial boundaries. The K-wise moment-matched merging approach emphasizes mathematical optimality in the merging process, ensuring minimal visual error compared to simple averaging. name: K-wise moment-matched merging with L2-optimal amplitude
head: cost-aware merging, substitutive LOD merging
body: K-wise moment-matched merging with L2-optimal amplitude is a level-of-detail technique that reduces the complexity of a 3D Gaussian Splatting scene by partitioning K splats into a single representative splat. It solves the substitutive-LOD problem by preserving the first and second spatial moments of the cluster to minimize geometric distortion, while explicitly optimizing the amplitude (opacity) of the merged splat to minimize the L2 integrated squared error. It distinguishes itself from simple arithmetic averaging by providing a closed-form geometric interpretation of merging error and from culling methods by retaining all visual information in a compressed form. Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians G = \{Gi\}, where each Gi is defined by position \mathbf{t}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i, opacity \alphai, and color coefficients ci. A target cluster size K. Outputs: A reduced set of N/K representative Gaussians G' = \{G'j\}. Data Structures: Cluster: A list of indices \{i1, i2,..., iK\} mapping to the original splats. Representative Gaussian G'j: \mathbf{t}'j: Position (float32). \mathbf{\Sigma}'j: Covariance matrix (float32, 3x3 symmetric). \alpha'j: Amplitude/Opacity (float32, optimized). c'j: Color coefficients (float32, weighted average). Algorithm Steps: 1. Partitioning: Partition the set of splats G into disjoint clusters Cj of size K. The source specifies three partitioning algorithms: Greedy hierarchical (à la Runnalls). Cost-increment relocation. Joint relaxation. Note: Cost-increment relocation matches greedy merging performance within 5.5% at compression factors of four and above. 2. Moment Matching (Position and Covariance): For each cluster Cj, compute the total weight Wj and the representative position \mathbf{t}'j and covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}'j using the standard moment-matching formulas: Wj = \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}i \mathbf{\Sigma}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \left( \mathbf{\Sigma}i + (\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)(\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)^T \right) 3. L2-Optimal Amplitude: Optimize the amplitude \alpha'j of the representative splat to minimize the L2 integrated squared error between the original cluster and the merged splat. The source identifies L2 as the primary cost metric for this method. The optimal amplitude is derived analytically to minimize \int \| \sum{i \in Cj} Gi(\mathbf{x}) - G'j(\mathbf{x}) \|^2 d\mathbf{x}. Implementation Note: The exact closed-form scalar equation for \alpha'j is not explicitly provided in the source text, but it is described as "L2-optimal". It relies on the analytical merging framework of Analytical Merging of Gaussian Splats which provides the geometric interpretation of relative merging error. 4. Color Aggregation: Compute the color c'j as the weighted average of the cluster colors: c'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai ci Pseudocode: Unverified code. name: Analytical Merging of Gaussian Splats
head: Amplitude-optimised moment-matched template merging, Closed-form L2 integrated squared-error merging
body: Analytical merging of Gaussian splats is a closed-form framework for merging two Gaussian splats by minimizing the L2 integrated squared-error between the original pair and the merged representative. It provides a geometric interpretation of the relative merging error, specifically relating it to the angle between the splats' parameters. This method serves as the core merging primitive for the parent technique, K-wise moment-matched merging with L2-optimal amplitude, enabling efficient level-of-detail reduction and fitting optimization. The method computes a single representative Gaussian splat from two input splats such that the L2 error between the sum of the two original splats and the single merged splat is minimized. The solution is derived analytically, ensuring the merged splat matches the first and second moments of the input pair while optimizing the amplitude (opacity/scale factor) to minimize the residual error. Inputs: Two Gaussian splats, G1 and G2. Each splat is defined by: Mean position \mu \in \mathbb{R}^3. Covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (symmetric positive definite). Amplitude (opacity/scale) a \in \mathbb{R}. Color/Feature vector c \in \mathbb{R}^k. Outputs: A single merged Gaussian splat G{merged} with parameters \mu', \Sigma', a', c'. Data Structures: The implementation requires storing the mean, covariance, amplitude, and color for each splat. The covariance is typically stored in a symmetric 3 \times 3 matrix or its 6 unique elements. Steps: 1. Compute Merged Mean and Covariance: The merged mean \mu' and covariance \Sigma' are calculated as the moment-matched average of the two input splats. This ensures the spatial distribution of the merged splat approximates the combined distribution of G1 and G2. \mu' = \frac{a1 \mu1 + a2 \mu2}{a1 + a2} [G: Standard weighted average for moment matching]. \Sigma' = \frac{a1 (\Sigma1 + (\mu1 - \mu')(\mu1 - \mu')^T) + a2 (\Sigma2 + (\mu2 - \mu')(\mu2 - \mu')^T)}{a1 + a2} [G: Parallel axis theorem application for covariance merging]. 2. Compute Merged Amplitude: The amplitude a' is optimized to minimize the L2 error. The optimal amplitude is the sum of the input amplitudes, adjusted by the geometric relationship between the splats. a' = a1 + a2 [G: Base amplitude before error correction]. The relative merging error \epsilon is given by \epsilon = \sin^2 \alpha, where \alpha is the geometric angle parameter derived from the covariance matrices and means. The optimal amplitude is a' = (a1 + a2) \sqrt{1 - \epsilon} [G: Derived from minimizing L2 error with respect to amplitude]. 3. Compute Merged Color/Feature: The color c' is a weighted average of the input colors, weighted by their amplitudes. c' = \frac{a1 c1 + a2 c2}{a1 + a2} [G: Standard weighted average]. Formulas: Relative Merging Error: \epsilon = \sin^2 \alpha. Geometric Angle \alpha: The angle \alpha is determined by the relative orientation and scale of the covariance matrices \Sigma1 and \Sigma2 and the distance between means \mu1 and \mu2. The exact formula for \alpha is not explicitly provided in the sources, but it is described as a geometric parameter in the error derivation. Optimal Amplitude: a' = (a1 + a2) \sqrt{1 - \sin^2 \alpha} = (a1 + a2) |\cos \alpha| [G: Simplified from \epsilon = \sin^2 \alpha]. Parameters: No free parameters are required for the core merging algorithm. The method is closed-form and deterministic. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Covariance: If either \Sigma1 or \Sigma2 is singular or near-singular, the geometric angle \alpha may be ill-defined. Regularization of the covariance matrices (e.g., adding a small identity matrix) may be required. Zero Amplitude: If both a1 and a2 are zero, the merged splat is undefined. This case should be handled by skipping the merge or returning a null splat. Precision: The calculation of \sin^2 \alpha requires careful handling of floating-point precision, especially when the splats are very similar (\alpha \approx 0) or very different (\alpha \approx \pi/2). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def mergegaussians(g1, g2): """ Merges two Gaussian splats using closed-form L2 optimal amplitude. Args: g1: Tuple (mu1, Sigma1, a1, c1) g2: Tuple (mu2, Sigma2, a2, c2) Returns: Tuple (mu', Sigma', a', c') """ mu1, Sigma1, a1, c1 = g1 mu2, Sigma2, a2, c2 = g2 # Step 1: Compute merged mean totalamplitude = a1 + a2 if totalamplitude == 0: return (mu1, Sigma1, 0.0, c1) # Handle degenerate case muprime = (a1 mu1 + a2 mu2) / totalamplitude # Step 2: Compute merged covariance # Using parallel axis theorem Sigmaprime = (a1 (Sigma1 + np.outer(mu1 - muprime, mu1 - muprime)) + a2 (Sigma2 + np.outer(mu2 - muprime, mu2 - muprime))) / totalamplitude # Step 3: Compute geometric angle alpha and error epsilon # Note: The exact formula for alpha is not provided in the sources. # This is a placeholder for the geometric computation described in. alpha = computegeometricangle(mu1, Sigma1, mu2, Sigma2) epsilon = np.sin(alpha)2 # Step 4: Compute optimal amplitude aprime = totalamplitude np.sqrt(1 - epsilon) # Step 5: Compute merged color cprime = (a1 c1 + a2 c2) / totalamplitude return (muprime, Sigmaprime, aprime, cprime) def computegeometricangle(mu1, Sigma1, mu2, Sigma2): """ Placeholder for the geometric angle computation. The exact formula is not provided in the sources. """ # Not given in the sources. return 0.0 A technique to progressively refine Gaussian representations by partitioning candidate Gaussians into groups and merging them using geometry-conditioned soft weights, exposing only coarse representations at early training stages. It partitions 16 candidates for a token into G = 2^s groups, where each group has size bs = 16 / G. For each group g, normalized gate weights are calculated as w{p,g,i} = \exp(\ell{p,g,i}/\tau) / \sum{j=1}^{bs} \exp(\ell{p,g,j}/\tau), where \ell{p,g,i} is the gate logit and \tau is a temperature parameter. The merged output for an attribute z is \bar{\mathbf{z}}{p,g} = \sum{i=1}^{bs} w{p,g,i} \mathbf{z}{p,g,i}. To avoid abrupt transitions, linear interpolation is used: \mathbf{z}^{(s)} = (1-\lambda) \mathbf{z}^{(s-1)} + \lambda \bar{\mathbf{z}}^{(s)}, where \lambda \in [0, 1] is the transition coefficient. This method does not introduce new candidates but progressively relaxes the merging applied to the same underlying set of predictions. Time Complexity: The merging of two splats is O(1) if the geometric angle \alpha is precomputed or approximated. The computation of \alpha itself depends on the eigenvalue decomposition of the covariance matrices, which is O(1) for fixed dimensionality (3D). Memory Complexity: O(1) per merge operation, as it only requires storing the parameters of the two input splats and the one output splat. Measured Performance: Implemented in Luxar for merging Gaussian splats during fitting or LOD reduction. The method provides a systematic rate-distortion analysis across benchmark volumes, showing effective resolution analysis and noise floor estimation. Strengths: Closed-form solution ensures deterministic and fast merging. The geometric interpretation of the error provides insight into the quality of the merge. Limitations: The exact formula for the geometric angle \alpha is not provided, which may hinder implementation. The method is limited to merging two splats at a time; merging more than two requires iterative application. When to use: When efficient LOD reduction or fitting optimization is required for Gaussian splatting representations. When not to use: When the geometric angle \alpha cannot be reliably computed or when merging more than two splats simultaneously is required without iterative application. The method was introduced in the context of Luxar, a tool for Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualisation of multidimensional scientific data. The supplementary materials provide a closed-form L2 integrated squared-error framework for merging two Gaussian splats, with a geometric interpretation of the relative merging error. The method is part of a broader effort to improve the efficiency and scalability of Gaussian splatting techniques. name: Stage-dependent merging
head: Grouped merging, Soft-weighted merging
body: Stage-dependent merging is a technique for progressively refining Gaussian representations by partitioning candidate Gaussians into groups and merging them using geometry-conditioned soft weights, exposing only coarse representations at early training stages. It sets itself apart from its sibling Analytical Merging of Gaussian Splats by using a learned, soft-weighted aggregation rather than a closed-form L2-optimal geometric merge, allowing for a smooth transition from coarse to fine detail during training. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 16 candidate Gaussians per token, partitioned into groups. Each candidate i has attributes \mathbf{z}{p,g,i} (e.g., position, covariance, SH coefficients) and a gate logit \ell{p,g,i}. Outputs: A merged set of Gaussians \bar{\mathbf{z}}{p,g} for each group, which are then interpolated to form the final representation for the current stage. Data Structures: Candidates are stored in groups of size bs. Gate logits \ell{p,g,i} are scalar values per candidate. Attributes \mathbf{z} are vectors/matrices depending on the specific Gaussian property. Steps: 1. Partitioning: At stage s, partition the 16 candidates into G = 2^s groups, where each group has size bs = 16 / G. 2. Gate Weight Calculation: For each group g, calculate normalized gate weights using a softmax function conditioned on the gate logits and a temperature parameter \tau: w{p,g,i} = \frac {\exp (\ell {p,g,i}/\tau)} {\sum {j=1}^{bs}\exp (\ell {p,g,j}/\tau)} where \ell{p,g,i} is the gate logit for the i-th candidate in group g, and \tau is the temperature parameter. 3. Merging: Compute the merged output for attribute \mathbf{z} in group g by taking the weighted sum of the candidates' attributes: \bar {\mathbf {z}}{p,g} = \sum {i=1}^{bs} w{p,g,i}\,\mathbf {z}{p,g,i} 4. Smooth Stage Transition: To avoid abrupt transitions between stages, linearly interpolate between the previous coarser representation \mathbf{z}^{(s-1)} and the current less-merged representation \bar{\mathbf{z}}^{(s)} using a transition coefficient \lambda \in [0, 1]: \mathbf {z}^{(s)} = (1-\lambda)\,\mathbf {z}^{(s-1)} + \lambda \,\bar {\mathbf {z}}^{(s)} This procedure does not introduce new candidates but progressively relaxes the merging applied to the same underlying set of predictions. Parameters: \tau: Temperature parameter for the softmax gate. \lambda: Transition coefficient for stage interpolation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def stagedependentmerge(candidates, gatelogits, stages, tau, lambdaval, prevstagerepr): """ candidates: List of 16 Gaussian objects, each with attributes z (vector/matrix) gatelogits: List of 16 floats (lp,g,i) stages: Integer, current training stage tau: Float, temperature parameter lambdaval: Float, transition coefficient [0, 1] prevstagerepr: List of merged Gaussian objects from stage s-1 """ numcandidates = 16 numgroups = 2 stages groupsize = numcandidates // numgroups currentstagerepr = [] for g in range(numgroups): groupcandidates = candidates[g groupsize: (g + 1) groupsize] grouplogits = gatelogits[g groupsize: (g + 1) groupsize] # Calculate softmax weights explogits = [math.exp(l / tau) for l in grouplogits] sumexp = sum(explogits) weights = [e / sumexp for e in explogits] # Merge attributes mergedz = None for i, z in enumerate(groupcandidates): if mergedz is None: mergedz = z.copy() mergedz.attributes = {} for attrname, attrval in z.attributes.items(): if attrname not in mergedz.attributes: mergedz.attributes[attrname] = 0.0 mergedz.attributes[attrname] += weights[i] attrval currentstagerepr.append(mergedz) # Smooth stage transition finalrepr = [] for i, mergedz in enumerate(currentstagerepr): if prevstagerepr and i < len(prevstagerepr): prevz = prevstagerepr[i] # Interpolate attributes interpolatedz = mergedz.copy() interpolatedz.attributes = {} for attrname in mergedz.attributes: valcurr = mergedz.attributes[attrname] valprev = prevz.attributes.get(attrname, 0.0) interpolatedz.attributes[attrname] = (1 - lambdaval) valprev + lambdaval valcurr finalrepr.append(interpolatedz) else: finalrepr.append(mergedz) return finalrepr A variant used in large-scale reconstruction where cells are optimized independently and then merged. After optimization, 3D Gaussians outside the original region (before boundary expansion) are deleted for each cell to prevent floaters in other cells. The non-overlapping cells are then merged. The merged scene is seamless in appearance and geometry without obvious border artifacts because some training views are common between adjacent cells, eliminating the need for further appearance adjustment. Complexity: The merging operation is linear with respect to the number of candidates per group (bs) and the number of groups (G). Since bs \times G = 16, the complexity per token is constant O(1) with respect to the total number of candidates, but depends on the dimensionality of the attributes \mathbf{z}. Performance: Exposes only coarse representations at early stages, potentially reducing computational load during initial training phases. Strengths: Allows for progressive refinement and smooth transitions between levels of detail. Limitations: Requires learning gate logits and managing stage transitions. Stage-dependent merging was introduced in GlobalSplat: Efficient Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting via Global Scene Tokens. It is designed to enable efficient feed-forward rendering by managing the complexity of Gaussian representations through a staged merging process. name: Hierarchical Gaussian Merging
head: Gaussian Merging for LOD, LOD Generation via Merging, LOD Level Generation, Unified LOD Approach
body: Hierarchical Gaussian Merging generates multi-resolution representations of 3D Gaussian Splatting scenes by iteratively reducing the Gaussian count through averaging-based merging. It solves the problem of rendering large Gaussian sets at varying distances by creating a hierarchy of simplified LOD levels, where each level contains half the Gaussians of the previous one. Unlike moment-matching approaches that preserve spatial covariance structure, this method uses simple arithmetic averaging for most properties, prioritizing computational simplicity and unified buffer formats over geometric fidelity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians G^{(0)} at Level 0, and a target maximum page size N{max} for spatial grouping. Output: A sequence of Gaussian sets G^{(0)}, G^{(1)}, \dots, G^{(L)}, where |G^{(l+1)}| \approx \frac{1}{2}|G^{(l)}|. Data Structures: Gaussians are grouped into "pages" to manage memory and visibility checks. Page: A container holding up to N{max} Gaussians. Gaussian: Defined by position \mathbf{t}, scale \mathbf{s}, rotation \mathbf{q}, opacity \alpha, and color coefficients c. Unified Buffer: LOD splats use the same memory format as original splats to facilitate efficient rendering. Steps: 1. Page Assignment: Initially, assign each mesh face a separate page. Assign each Gaussian to the page of the nearest mesh face. If a page exceeds N{max}, subdivide the corresponding mesh face (e.g., by adding a vertex at an edge midpoint) and reassign Gaussians. Repeat subdivision until all pages are within capacity. To prevent thin triangles, rotate the vertex order and choose different edges for subsequent subdivisions. 2. LOD Generation (Merging): For each level l from 0 to L-1: Group Gaussians from G^{(l)} into clusters (typically one cluster per page or spatial unit). For each cluster, compute the representative Gaussian G'{new} for G^{(l+1)} by averaging properties: Position: \mathbf{t}' = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{t}i Opacity: \alpha' = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \alphai Color: c' = \frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} ci Rotation: \mathbf{q}' = \text{Normalize}\left(\frac{1}{N} \sum{i=1}^{N} \mathbf{q}i\right) (Standard quaternion averaging for unit quaternions) Scale: Not averaged. The source explicitly states merging is done with an average for all properties but their scale. The specific handling of scale is not given in the sources. (Typically, scale might be averaged or kept from the largest child, but this is unspecified). Parameters: N{max}: Maximum Gaussians per page. Not given in the sources. L: Number of LOD levels. Determined by the halving process until a minimum count is reached. Edge Cases: Scale Ambiguity: The method explicitly excludes scale from averaging. The implementation must define how scale is derived (e.g., max, mean, or inherited). Page Subdivision: Repeated subdivision can create degenerate thin triangles. The algorithm must manage vertex rotation and edge selection to maintain mesh quality. Time Complexity: LOD generation is linear with respect to the number of Gaussians for the averaging step, plus the cost of mesh subdivision for page balancing. Memory Complexity: Requires storing L levels of Gaussians. Since each level halves the count, total memory is roughly 2 \times |G^{(0)}|. Strengths: Simple implementation; unified buffer format allows efficient GPU memory management; fast generation. Limitations: Arithmetic averaging of position and rotation can introduce geometric artifacts and blurring, especially for large clusters or heterogeneous regions. Scale handling is undefined, potentially leading to visual inconsistencies. When to use: When rendering performance and memory bandwidth are critical, and visual fidelity of merged splats is secondary to simplicity. This method is described in the context of "Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting," which introduces page-based memory management for 3DGS. It is also referenced in the OpenSplat4D project.
