name: LOD Generation for 3DGS
head: 3DGS LOD Generation, Gaussian Clustering for LOD
body: This method reduces the number of 3D Gaussians copied, stored, sorted, and rendered by merging Gaussians into clusters based on similar attributes, minimizing distant appearance impact without altering scene creation. It operates on a virtual memory system where Gaussians are organized into pages; unlike virtual texturing where mip levels are uniform-sized pages, this method reduces the Gaussian count with each LOD level, allowing multiple virtual pages to reside within one physical page. It is distinct from K-wise moment-matched merging by using arithmetic averaging and fixed scaling factors rather than L2-optimal moment matching, and from Hierarchical Gaussian Merging by its specific integration with page-based virtual memory management and dynamic thresholding. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians G assigned to spatial pages. Each Gaussian Gi has position \mathbf{t}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, scale \mathbf{s}i, opacity \alphai, and spherical harmonic coefficients ci. Output: A set of merged representative Gaussians G' for each LOD level, and a page table mapping virtual pages to physical memory with associated LOD indices. Data Structures: Page Table: An array of entries. Each entry contains: pageid: Identifier for the virtual page. lodlevel: Integer index indicating the current detail level (0 = highest detail/raw Gaussians, 1+ = merged). lastuse: Timestamp or frame counter for LRU eviction. physicaladdress: Pointer to the GPU memory buffer containing the merged Gaussians for this LOD. Gaussian Buffer: Stores the merged Gaussians. Since the count decreases with LOD, buffers for higher LODs are smaller. Algorithm Steps: 1. Clustering: For each page, identify clusters of Gaussians using the k-means algorithm in a multidimensional attribute space. The feature vector for each Gaussian includes position \mathbf{t}i, rotation \mathbf{q}i, and color ci. Priority: Position attributes are prioritized during clustering to prevent dispersed clusters. This is implemented by weighting the position components higher in the distance metric used by k-means. Constraint: Only Gaussians residing on the same page can be merged into a cluster. 2. Merging: Replace each cluster Cj with a single representative Gaussian G'j. Translation: Arithmetic mean: \mathbf{t}'j = \frac{1}{|Cj|} \sum{i \in Cj} \mathbf{t}i. Rotation: Arithmetic mean of quaternions (normalized). Opacity: Arithmetic mean: \alpha'j = \frac{1}{|Cj|} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai. Color: Arithmetic mean of spherical harmonic coefficients. Scale: Arithmetic mean is not used directly. Merging scales directly causes the resulting Gaussian to be too small, creating visual gaps. Instead, the merged Gaussian is scaled up by a fixed factor k{scale} to fill gaps. The factor k{scale} is determined during training using average pixel coverage. \mathbf{s}'j = k{scale} \cdot \frac{1}{|Cj|} \sum{i \in Cj} \mathbf{s}i. 3. LOD Threshold Management: Assign an initial LOD level to each page based on distance from the camera. Closer pages use LOD 0 (raw Gaussians); further pages use higher LODs (merged Gaussians). Dynamic Adjustment: Thresholds move away from the camera when GPU memory usage exceeds a limit, and closer when memory is available. Step Size Adaptation: To prevent rapid flipping (popping/flickering) between levels, the step size for threshold changes is dynamically adjusted based on previous moves. If a move caused overshooting (drastic memory change), the step size is reduced; if adaptation is too slow, it is increased. 4. Page Table Update: Mark page table entries with their current LOD level. When a page's LOD changes, the corresponding merged Gaussian buffer is loaded or evicted. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computeclustermean(gaussiansincluster): """ Computes the arithmetic mean of Gaussian attributes. Returns: (meant, meanq, meanalpha, meansh, rawmeans) """ n = len(gaussiansincluster) sumt = vec3(0, 0, 0) sumq = vec4(1, 0, 0, 0) # Identity quaternion sumalpha = 0.0 sumsh = vec3(0, 0, 0) # Assuming 1st order SH for simplicity sums = vec3(1, 1, 1) for g in gaussiansincluster: sumt += g.t # Quaternion averaging (simplified: sum and normalize) sumq += g.q sumalpha += g.alpha sumsh += g.sh sums += g.s meant = sumt / n meanq = normalize(sumq) meanalpha = sumalpha / n meansh = sumsh / n rawmeans = sums / n return meant, meanq, meanalpha, meansh, rawmeans def generatelodgaussians(pagegaussians, clustercount, scalefactor): """ Generates merged Gaussians for a single LOD level from a page's Gaussians. """ # 1. Clustering # Feature vector: [tx, ty, tz, qx, qy, qz, qw, cr, cg, cb] # Position weights are higher to prevent dispersion features = [] for g in pagegaussians: # Normalize position to match scale of other attributes if necessary # Prioritize position in distance metric features.append(g.t 10.0 + g.q + g.color) # Heuristic weighting clusters = kmeans(features, k=clustercount) mergedgaussians = [] for clusterindices in clusters: clustergs = [pagegaussians[i] for i in clusterindices] # 2. Merging t, q, alpha, sh, raws = computeclustermean(clustergs) # Scale up to fill gaps s = raws scalefactor mergedgaussians.append(Gaussian(t, q, s, alpha, sh)) return mergedgaussians def updatelodthresholds(currentmemoryusage, memorylimit, currentthresholds, prevstepdirection): """ Dynamically adjusts LOD thresholds based on memory pressure. """ newthresholds = currentthresholds.copy() if currentmemoryusage > memorylimit: # Move thresholds away from camera (use lower LOD for closer pages) # Increase distance required for high LOD step = adaptivestep(prevstepdirection, direction='increase') for i in range(len(newthresholds)): newthresholds[i] += step else: # Move thresholds closer to camera (use higher LOD for closer pages) step = adaptivestep(prevstepdirection, direction='decrease') for i in range(len(newthresholds)): newthresholds[i] = max(0, newthresholds[i] - step) return newthresholds def adaptivestep(prevdirection, direction): """ Adjusts step size to prevent rapid flipping. """ # If previous move was in the same direction and caused overshoot, reduce step # If previous move was slow, increase step # Implementation details depend on specific memory monitoring feedback basestep = 1.0 if prevdirection == direction: return basestep 0.8 # Reduce step if continuing same trend else: return basestep 1.2 # Increase step if reversing This variant combines strategic pruning of low-impact Gaussians (e.g., volume-based masking) with clustering. Neighboring Gaussians are represented using properties stored within a "local anchor" obtained via clustering. It specifically employs a hash-grid for clustering to improve efficiency in large-scale scenes. Unlike the base method which focuses on page-based LOD, this approach explicitly prunes Gaussians before clustering to reduce the initial set size. Time Complexity: Clustering is O(N \cdot D \cdot I) where N is Gaussians per page, D is dimensionality, and I is k-means iterations. Merging is O(N). LOD threshold updates are O(P) where P is number of pages. Memory Complexity: Reduces GPU memory usage by storing fewer Gaussians for distant pages. The reduction factor depends on the cluster count per LOD level. Performance: Enables real-time rendering (60+ FPS) by reducing sorting and rendering overhead for distant geometry. Strengths: Simple arithmetic averaging is computationally cheap. Dynamic thresholding adapts to varying memory constraints. Limitations: Arithmetic averaging can introduce geometric artifacts if clusters are large or heterogeneous. Fixed scale factor may not be optimal for all scenes. Rapid flipping (popping) can occur if threshold adaptation is poorly tuned. When to use: Large-scale scenes with significant memory constraints where distant geometry does not require high fidelity. When not to use: Scenes requiring high-fidelity distant details or where geometric accuracy is critical (moment matching may be better). This method was introduced in "Virtual memory for 3D Gaussian Splatting". It addresses the scalability and memory demands of 3DGS in large-scale scenes. The approach is inspired by virtual texturing techniques used in computer graphics, where mip levels are used to manage memory bandwidth and capacity. The specific use of k-means clustering with position prioritization and fixed scale adjustment was proposed to minimize distant appearance impact while keeping the implementation simple. name: Cluster Culling (Nanite-style)
head: FClusterCullingCS, FClusterCullingResetCS
body: Cluster Culling (Nanite-style) is a hierarchical frustum culling and Level of Detail (LOD) selection system for 3D Gaussian Splatting, designed to efficiently cull invisible or low-priority clusters from the rendering pipeline. It operates on a pre-computed hierarchy of Gaussian clusters, testing each cluster's bounding volume against the view frustum and calculating screen-space error to determine the appropriate LOD level. Unlike sibling methods that focus on the merging of Gaussians (e.g., K-wise moment-matched merging or Hierarchical Gaussian Merging), this method focuses on the selection and culling of those clusters for rendering, enabling performance scaling similar to Unreal Engine's Nanite system. The method consists of two primary compute shader stages: a reset stage to initialize buffers and a culling stage to determine visibility and LOD. Inputs: ClusterBuffer: A structured buffer containing FGaussianGPUCluster objects. Each cluster contains a bounding sphere (center and radius) and metadata indicating its LOD level and child cluster indices. FrustumPlanes: An array of 6 plane vectors (\mathbf{n}, d) defining the view frustum in world space. LocalToWorld: A 4 \times 4 transformation matrix from local cluster space to world space. WorldToClip: A 4 \times 4 projection matrix from world space to clip space. CameraPosition: The camera's position in world space. ScreenHeight: The height of the viewport in pixels. ErrorThreshold: The maximum allowable screen-space error (in pixels) for a cluster to be rendered at a lower LOD. LODBias: A bias added to the calculated screen-space error to favor lower LODs. MaxDrawDistance: The maximum distance from the camera at which clusters are considered for visibility. LeafClusterCount: The number of leaf clusters (raw Gaussians or base-level clusters) in the hierarchy. ClusterCount: The total number of clusters in the hierarchy. UseLODRendering: A flag indicating whether LOD rendering is enabled. DebugForceLODLevel: A debug parameter to force a specific LOD level (-1 for auto, 0 for leaf, 1+ for specific level). Outputs: VisibleClusterBuffer: A buffer containing indices of visible clusters. VisibleClusterCountBuffer: A counter for the number of visible clusters. IndirectDrawArgsBuffer: Indirect draw arguments for the rendering engine. ClusterVisibilityBitmap: A bitmap indicating the visibility status of each cluster. SelectedClusterBuffer: A buffer of selected cluster indices for rendering. LODClusterBuffer: A buffer of clusters selected for specific LOD levels. LODClusterCountBuffer: A counter for clusters at each LOD level. LODClusterSelectedBitmap: A bitmap for LOD cluster selection. LODSplatTotalBuffer: Total number of splats (Gaussians) in visible LOD clusters. LODSplatOutputCountBuffer: Count of splats to be output. FGaussianGPUCluster: Center: float3 (World space center of the bounding sphere). Radius: float (Radius of the bounding sphere in world space). LODLevel: uint (The LOD level of this cluster, 0 for leaf). ChildIndices: uint[4] (Indices of child clusters, if not a leaf). SplatCount: uint (Number of Gaussians in this cluster). 1. Reset Stage (FClusterCullingResetCS): Initialize VisibleClusterCountBuffer to 0. Initialize IndirectDrawArgsBuffer with default values (e.g., 0 instances). Clear ClusterVisibilityBitmap to 0. Clear SelectedClusterBuffer, LODClusterBuffer, LODClusterCountBuffer, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, LODSplatTotalBuffer, and LODSplatOutputCountBuffer. 2. Culling Stage (FClusterCullingCS): For each cluster i in ClusterBuffer: If DebugForceLODLevel is not -1, set LODLevel to DebugForceLODLevel. Calculate the cluster's world-space bounding sphere center \mathbf{c} and radius r. Frustum Culling: Test the bounding sphere against each of the 6 frustum planes. A sphere is inside the frustum if the distance from the sphere center to each plane is greater than or equal to the radius: di = \mathbf{n}i \cdot \mathbf{c} + di \ge r for all i \in \{0, \dots, 5\}. If the sphere is outside any plane, mark the cluster as invisible and skip further processing. Distance Culling: Calculate the distance from the camera to the cluster center: dist = \| \mathbf{c} - \mathbf{CameraPosition} \|. If dist > MaxDrawDistance, mark the cluster as invisible. LOD Selection: If the cluster is visible and UseLODRendering is enabled: Project the cluster's bounding sphere to screen space to estimate its screen-space radius r{screen}. Calculate the screen-space error E based on the cluster's size and distance. A common approximation is E = \frac{r{screen} \times ScaleFactor}{LODLevel + 1}, where ScaleFactor is a constant related to the Gaussian spread. Note: The exact formula for screen-space error is not provided in the sources; it typically involves the cluster's bounding sphere radius projected to screen space and compared against a threshold. If E > ErrorThreshold + LODBias, select a higher LOD level (coarser cluster) if available. If no higher LOD is available or the error is within threshold, select the current cluster. Visibility Update: If the cluster is selected, append its index to SelectedClusterBuffer. Update ClusterVisibilityBitmap to mark the cluster as visible. If the cluster is a leaf, add its SplatCount to LODSplatTotalBuffer. If the cluster is not a leaf, add its SplatCount to LODSplatTotalBuffer (assuming non-leaves are also rendered or their children are counted). Note: The sources do not specify if non-leaf clusters are rendered directly or if only leaves are rendered. Nanite-style systems typically render the selected LOD level, which may be a non-leaf cluster representing a group of Gaussians. Update VisibleClusterCountBuffer with the number of selected clusters. Update IndirectDrawArgsBuffer with the total number of instances (clusters) and splats. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def FClusterCullingResetCS( VisibleClusterCountBuffer, IndirectDrawArgsBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmap, SelectedClusterBuffer, LODClusterBuffer, LODClusterCountBuffer, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, LODSplatTotalBuffer, LODSplatOutputCountBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmapSize, LeafClusterCount, DebugForceLODLevel): # Initialize counters VisibleClusterCountBuffer[0] = 0 IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[0] = 0 # Draw count IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[1] = 0 # Instance count IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[2] = 0 # Start index IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[3] = 0 # Start offset # Clear bitmaps and buffers for i in range(ClusterVisibilityBitmapSize): ClusterVisibilityBitmap[i] = 0 LODClusterSelectedBitmap[0] = 0 LODSplatTotalBuffer[0] = 0 LODSplatOutputCountBuffer[0] = 0 def FClusterCullingCS( ClusterBuffer, VisibleClusterBuffer, VisibleClusterCountBuffer, IndirectDrawArgsBuffer, ClusterVisibilityBitmap, SelectedClusterBuffer, LODClusterBuffer, LODClusterCountBuffer, LODClusterSelectedBitmap, LODSplatTotalBuffer, LocalToWorld, WorldToClip, ClusterCount, LeafClusterCount, FrustumPlanes, CameraPosition, ScreenHeight, ErrorThreshold, LODBias, MaxDrawDistance, UseLODRendering, DebugForceLODLevel): visiblecount = 0 totalsplats = 0 for i in range(ClusterCount): cluster = ClusterBuffer[i] # Debug force LOD if DebugForceLODLevel != -1: cluster.LODLevel = DebugForceLODLevel # Transform center to world space if not already # Note: ClusterBuffer is assumed to be in world space or transformed by LocalToWorld center = cluster.Center radius = cluster.Radius # Frustum Culling visible = True for plane in FrustumPlanes: # plane is (normal, distance) dist = dot(plane.normal, center) + plane.distance if dist < radius: visible = False break if not visible: continue # Distance Culling disttocamera = length(center - CameraPosition) if disttocamera > MaxDrawDistance: continue # LOD Selection lodlevel = cluster.LODLevel if UseLODRendering and DebugForceLODLevel == -1: # Project radius to screen space # Approximate screen-space radius # Note: Exact projection formula not provided in sources # Assuming a simple perspective projection approximation clipcenter = mul(WorldToClip, float4(center, 1.0)) if clipcenter.w > 0: ndcradius = radius / clipcenter.w ScreenHeight / 2.0 # Calculate error # Note: Exact error formula not provided in sources # Assuming error is proportional to screen-space radius and inversely proportional to LOD error = ndcradius / (lodlevel + 1) if error > ErrorThreshold + LODBias: # Select higher LOD if available # Note: Logic for selecting higher LOD cluster index not provided # Assuming cluster.LODLevel is updated to a higher value lodlevel = lodlevel + 1 # Placeholder for actual LOD selection logic # Mark as visible ClusterVisibilityBitmap[i] = 1 SelectedClusterBuffer[visiblecount] = i visiblecount += 1 # Count splats totalsplats += cluster.SplatCount # Update output buffers VisibleClusterCountBuffer[0] = visiblecount IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[1] = visiblecount # Instance count IndirectDrawArgsBuffer[0] = totalsplats # Draw count (if each cluster draws its splats) LODSplatTotalBuffer[0] = totalsplats FrustumPlanes: Array of 6 plane vectors. ErrorThreshold: Threshold for screen-space error calculation. Typical value: Not given in the sources. LODBias: Bias applied to LOD selection. Typical value: Not given in the sources. MaxDrawDistance: Maximum distance for cluster visibility. Typical value: Not given in the sources. DebugForceLODLevel: Debug parameter to force a specific LOD level. Typical value: -1 (auto). THREADGROUPSIZE: Compilation define set to 64 for FClusterCullingCS. Precision: Frustum culling tests should use sufficient precision to avoid false negatives/positives for clusters on the frustum boundary. Degenerate Input: Clusters with zero radius or splat count should be handled gracefully (e.g., skipped or treated as invisible). LOD Selection: The exact formula for screen-space error and LOD selection is not provided in the sources. Implementers must derive this based on the specific Gaussian representation and desired visual quality. Time Complexity: O(N), where N is the number of clusters. Each cluster is processed once in the culling stage. Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing cluster data and visibility buffers. Performance: Performance scales with the number of clusters and the complexity of the frustum culling test. The use of compute shaders allows for parallel processing of clusters. Strengths: Efficient culling of invisible clusters, adaptive LOD selection based on screen-space error, integration with hierarchical clustering structures. Limitations: Dependent on the quality of the pre-computed cluster hierarchy. LOD selection logic is not fully specified in the sources. When to use: When rendering large scenes with many Gaussian splats and requiring efficient frustum culling and LOD management. When not to use: For small scenes where the overhead of hierarchical culling is not justified. Cluster Culling (Nanite-style) is inspired by Unreal Engine's Nanite virtualized geometry system, which uses hierarchical clustering and culling to render large amounts of geometry efficiently. In the context of 3D Gaussian Splatting, it adapts this concept to manage the rendering of Gaussian splats by clustering them and culling invisible or low-priority clusters. The method is implemented in the OpenSplat4D project, which provides a native 4D implementation of Gaussian splatting. name: Gaussian Cluster Builder
head: FGaussianClusterBuilder
body: The Gaussian Cluster Builder is a method for constructing hierarchical cluster structures from 3D Gaussian splat data, implementing a Nanite-style spatial clustering approach. It partitions a set of Gaussians into disjoint subsets and replaces them with representative Gaussians to enable multi-resolution rendering and efficient culling. It is distinguished from sibling methods by its explicit reliance on Morton code sorting for spatial locality and its configurable generation of Level of Detail (LOD) splats for parent clusters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians G = \{Gi\}, where each Gaussian Gi is defined by position \mathbf{t}i, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma}i (or scale \mathbf{s}i and rotation \mathbf{q}i), opacity \alphai, and color coefficients ci. Output: A hierarchical tree structure where leaf nodes contain original or grouped splats, and internal nodes contain merged representative Gaussians. Data Structures: The builder uses a configuration structure FBuildSettings with the following fields: int32 SplatsPerCluster: Number of splats per leaf cluster. Default: GaussianClusterConstants::DefaultSplatsPerCluster. int32 MaxChildrenPerCluster: Maximum children per parent cluster. Default: GaussianClusterConstants::MaxChildrenPerCluster. bool bReorderSplats: Whether to reorder splat data for cluster locality. Default: true. bool bGenerateLOD: Whether to generate LOD splats for parent clusters. Default: true. int32 LODReductionRatio: How many original splats per LOD splat. Default: 4. Algorithm Steps: 1. Sort: Sort the input splats by their Morton code (Z-order curve) to ensure spatial locality. 2. Leaf Clustering: Group the sorted splats into leaf clusters, each containing SplatsPerCluster splats. 3. Recursive Merging: Recursively merge clusters into parent nodes. A parent cluster is formed by grouping up to MaxChildrenPerCluster child clusters. 4. Aggregation: For each parent cluster, calculate the bounding volume and the representative Gaussian parameters. The aggregation follows the moment-matching paradigm defined in the parent article Gaussian clustering and merging: Wj = \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \mathbf{t}i \mathbf{\Sigma}'j = \frac{1}{Wj} \sum{i \in Cj} \alphai \left( \mathbf{\Sigma}i + (\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)(\mathbf{t}i - \mathbf{t}'j)^T \right) 5. LOD Generation: If bGenerateLOD is true, generate LOD splats for parent clusters. The number of original splats represented by one LOD splat is determined by LODReductionRatio (default 4). 6. Reordering: If bReorderSplats is true, reorder the splat data in memory to reflect the cluster hierarchy, improving cache locality during rendering. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildgaussianclusters(splats, settings): """ splats: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: pos: (x, y, z) cov: 3x3 covariance matrix alpha: float color: coefficients settings: FBuildSettings object """ if settings.bReorderSplats: # Sort splats by Morton code for spatial locality splats = sortbymortoncode(splats) # Step 1: Create leaf clusters leafclusters = [] splatspercluster = settings.SplatsPerCluster for i in range(0, len(splats), splatspercluster): clustersplats = splats[i: i + splatspercluster] leafclusters.append(createleafcluster(clustersplats)) # Step 2: Recursively build hierarchy currentlevelclusters = leafclusters while len(currentlevelclusters) > 1: nextlevelclusters = [] maxchildren = settings.MaxChildrenPerCluster for i in range(0, len(currentlevelclusters), maxchildren): children = currentlevelclusters[i: i + maxchildren] parentcluster = createparentcluster(children) nextlevelclusters.append(parentcluster) currentlevelclusters = nextlevelclusters # Step 3: Generate LOD if enabled if settings.bGenerateLOD: for cluster in currentlevelclusters: generatelodsplats(cluster, settings.LODReductionRatio) return currentlevelclusters def createleafcluster(splats): """ Aggregates splats into a single representative Gaussian using moment matching. """ totalalpha = sum(s.alpha for s in splats) if totalalpha == 0: return None # Calculate weighted mean position meanpos = sum(s.alpha s.pos for s in splats) / totalalpha # Calculate weighted covariance cov = sum( s.alpha (s.cov + np.outer(s.pos - meanpos, s.pos - meanpos)) for s in splats) / totalalpha # Calculate weighted color (simple average for color coefficients) meancolor = sum(s.color for s in splats) / len(splats) return { 'pos': meanpos, 'cov': cov, 'alpha': totalalpha, 'color': meancolor, 'children': splats, 'isleaf': True } def createparentcluster(children): """ Aggregates child clusters into a single representative Gaussian. """ # Flatten children to get all constituent splats or use child representatives # Assuming moment matching on child representatives for efficiency representatives = [child if child['isleaf'] else child for child in children] totalalpha = sum(r['alpha'] for r in representatives) if totalalpha == 0: return None meanpos = sum(r['alpha'] r['pos'] for r in representatives) / totalalpha cov = sum( r['alpha'] (r['cov'] + np.outer(r['pos'] - meanpos, r['pos'] - meanpos)) for r in representatives) / totalalpha meancolor = sum(r['color'] for r in representatives) / len(representatives) return { 'pos': meanpos, 'cov': cov, 'alpha': totalalpha, 'color': meancolor, 'children': children, 'isleaf': False } def generatelodsplats(cluster, reductionratio): """ Generates LOD splats for a cluster based on reduction ratio. """ # Not given in the sources. Placeholder for LOD generation logic. pass Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Zero Alpha: If a cluster has zero total alpha, it should be handled gracefully (e.g., skipped or represented by a zero-opacity Gaussian) to avoid division by zero in moment matching. Boundary Conditions: When SplatsPerCluster does not evenly divide the total number of splats, the last leaf cluster will contain fewer splats. The algorithm must handle this variable-sized cluster correctly. Precision: Floating-point precision issues may arise when calculating covariance matrices for very small or very large clusters. Using double precision for intermediate calculations is recommended. A strategy that implements hierarchical structuring of Gaussians to enable simulations to be performed exclusively on selected Core Gaussians, accelerating the process. It organizes Gaussians into a hierarchy through clustering methods and performs simulation only on the Core Gaussians (highest level of hierarchy). This approach speeds up computations, especially when using particle-based engines such as Taichi. Time Complexity: Sorting by Morton code takes O(N \log N) where N is the number of splats. Clustering and merging are linear with respect to the number of clusters, but the recursive nature means the total time is proportional to N with a small constant factor depending on the tree depth. Memory Complexity: The hierarchical structure requires storing additional metadata for each cluster (bounding volumes, parent/child pointers). The memory overhead is proportional to the number of clusters, which is N / \text{SplatsPerCluster}. Strengths: Efficient spatial locality due to Morton code sorting. Configurable LOD generation allows for flexible trade-offs between quality and performance. Nanite-style clustering is effective for culling. Limitations: The quality of the merged Gaussians depends on the heterogeneity of the cluster. Large or heterogeneous clusters may introduce geometric artifacts. The method assumes a static scene; dynamic scenes may require frequent rebuilding of the hierarchy. When to Use: Suitable for large-scale 3D Gaussian splatting applications where multi-resolution rendering and efficient culling are required. When Not to Use: Not suitable for highly dynamic scenes where the hierarchy would need to be rebuilt frequently. Not suitable for scenes with very small clusters where the overhead of the hierarchy outweighs the benefits. The Gaussian Cluster Builder is part of the OpenSplat4D project, which implements Nanite-style spatial clustering for 3D Gaussian splatting. The method builds on the principles of hierarchical clustering and moment-matched merging described in the parent article Gaussian clustering and merging. name: World Space Clustering
head: Single linkage merging
body: World Space Clustering is a preprocessing step in 3D Gaussian Splatting that groups sampling pixels into clusters based on their geometric proximity in world space. It solves the problem of redundant or noisy Gaussian primitives by removing foreground or background pixels that do not contribute to the primary surface representation. It is distinguished from attribute-space methods (like color-based segmentation) by relying solely on spatial coordinates rather than appearance or scale attributes. Inputs: A set of 2D sampling pixels, each associated with a 3D Gaussian kernel. For each pixel, the algorithm obtains the corresponding world-space coordinate covered by the Gaussian kernel. Outputs: A set of disjoint clusters of pixels. Pixels belonging to the same cluster are merged or processed together; isolated pixels (outliers) are removed. Data Structures: Point Set: A list of 3D world-space coordinates \mathbf{p}k for each pixel k covered by a Gaussian. Clusters: A set of disjoint subsets of pixel indices. Initially, each pixel forms its own cluster. Parameters: Initial Threshold (T0): 5 \cdot \deltad, where \deltad is the world-space distance between two adjacent pixels at the depth of the Gaussian kernel’s central pixel. Failure Multiplier: 1.5 (used if clustering fails). Opacity Pruning Threshold: 0.005 (Gaussians with opacity below this are pruned prior to clustering). Pixel Coverage Threshold: 25 pixels (Gaussians covering fewer than this are pruned). Steps: 1. Pruning: Remove any Gaussian primitives with opacity \alpha < 0.005 or those covering fewer than 25 pixels. 2. Coordinate Extraction: For each remaining Gaussian, compute the world-space coordinates \mathbf{p}k for all pixels k covered by the 2D Gaussian kernel. 3. Distance Calculation: Compute \deltad, the world-space distance between two adjacent pixels at the depth of the central pixel of the Gaussian kernel. 4. Initialization: Set the termination threshold T = T0 = 5 \cdot \deltad. Initialize each pixel coordinate as a separate cluster. 5. Iterative Merging (Single Linkage): Find the pair of distinct clusters (Ca, Cb) with the minimum distance between any two points from distinct clusters: d(Ca, Cb) = \min{\mathbf{p}i \in Ca, \mathbf{p}j \in Cb} \| \mathbf{p}i - \mathbf{p}j \| If d(Ca, Cb) < T, merge Ca and Cb into a single cluster. Repeat until only one cluster remains or no pair of clusters has a distance less than T. 6. Failure Handling: If the process fails to produce a valid clustering (e.g., too many small clusters or computational timeout), update T \leftarrow 1.5 \cdot T and repeat steps 5–6. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def worldspaceclustering(gaussians): # Step 1: Pruning validgaussians = [] for g in gaussians: if g.opacity >= 0.005 and g.pixelcount >= 25: validgaussians.append(g) # Step 2: Coordinate Extraction points = [] # List of (pixelindex, worldcoord) for g in validgaussians: for k in g.coveredpixels: points.append((k, g.getworldcoord(k))) if not points: return [] # Step 3: Distance Calculation centralpixel = points[0][0] # Assume first point's gaussian central pixel depth = getdepth(centralpixel) deltad = worlddistancebetweenadjacentpixels(depth) # Step 4: Initialization threshold = 5.0 deltad clusters = {p[0]: {p[0]} for p in points} # Map pixelidx -> set of pixelidxs pointmap = {p[0]: p[1] for p in points} # Step 5: Iterative Merging maxiterations = 1000 iteration = 0 while iteration < maxiterations: iteration += 1 mindist = float('inf') mergepair = None # Find closest pair of clusters clusterids = list(clusters.keys()) for i in range(len(clusterids)): for j in range(i + 1, len(clusterids)): c1 = clusterids[i] c2 = clusterids[j] # Single linkage: min distance between any two points dist = min( worlddistance(pointmap[p1], pointmap[p2]) for p1 in clusters[c1] for p2 in clusters[c2]) if dist < mindist: mindist = dist mergepair = (c1, c2) if mergepair is None or mindist >= threshold: break c1, c2 = mergepair # Merge clusters clusters[c1].update(clusters[c2]) del clusters[c2] # Step 6: Failure Handling # Note: The source implies repeating the procedure with increased threshold if it "fails". # A simple implementation might just return the clusters found. # If strict failure detection is needed, check cluster count vs expected. return clusters A variant that groups 3D Gaussians based on approximate view-independent colors rather than pure spatial proximity. It serves as a coarse-level decomposition of the scene, aligning with transfer-function-based classification. Definition: Groups Gaussians by color similarity in RGB space. Steps: 1. Approximate view-independent color \tilde{c} for each Gaussian by averaging view-dependent colors cd across sampled directions D: \tilde{c} \approx \frac{1}{\|D\|} \sum{d \in D} cd 2. Apply a clustering algorithm (e.g., k-means) to group Gaussians based on \tilde{c} using Euclidean distance in RGB space. 3. Outlier Removal: For each Gaussian, search for neighbors within a small-radius sphere. Remove the Gaussian if the neighbor count falls below a predefined threshold. When to choose: When semantic or material-based segmentation is required prior to fine-level affinity-based segmentation. Time Complexity: Depends on the number of pixels N and the clustering algorithm. Single linkage merging can be O(N^2) or O(N \log N) with efficient data structures (e.g., KD-trees) for nearest-neighbor searches. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store point coordinates and cluster assignments. Strengths: Effective at removing noise and redundant background/foreground pixels. Computationally lightweight compared to full optimization. Limitations: Relies on accurate depth estimation for \deltad. May merge distinct objects if they are spatially close but semantically different (addressed by color-based variants). When to use: As a preprocessing step before projecting Gaussians into world space. When not: When fine-grained structural separation is required without color cues. Originating from the need to optimize 3D Gaussian Splatting representations, this method adapts single linkage merging (Sibson 1973) to the context of Gaussian primitives. It is used in frameworks like Augmented Radiance Field to enhance Gaussian Splatting by reducing redundancy. The color-based variant is used in VolSegGS for volumetric scene segmentation. name: Budgeted Gaussian Splatting
body: Budgeted Gaussian Splatting (BCT) is a training and deployment method for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables continuous, variable primitive counts (Level of Detail) without retraining. It solves the problem of fixed-budget compression by constructing a Morton-ordered tree of primitives and a coverage-preserving prefix cut, allowing for near-lossless quality at low compression ratios. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) and Iterative Gaussian Synopsis by providing a single, global primitive ordering whose prefixes define successive approximations of the scene, rather than camera-dependent hierarchical selectors or discrete hierarchy methods. Inputs: A trained 3D Gaussian Splatting model (means, covariances/scales, opacities, spherical harmonics coefficients) and a set of training views. Outputs: A compact binary file containing primitives in Morton order, and a runtime scheduler that selects a subset of primitives for rendering based on a budget parameter c. Data Structures: 1. Morton-Ordered Tree: Primitives are sorted by their 3D Morton code. The tree structure allows for efficient prefix traversal. 2. Compact Binary Format: Stores raw primitives in Morton order, per-band equivalent planks, and SH first moments of all degrees. DC-only Compact Path: Stores 3 floats per primitive (DC component), enabling selection of up to 13.1M primitives in 3.9 GB. Full Export: Standard 3DGS PLY format with SH zero-padded to degree 3, scales/opacities in log/logit domain. 3. Residuals (for Adaptive Selection): Per cluster, two residuals are stored: Geometric spread: \sigma{geo} = \frac{p \cdot \text{tr}(T^)}{W} (world units), projected to pixels by \sigma \cdot f / d. SH residual ratio: \rho{sh} (cluster-internal SH variance vs. global RMS). Parameters: c: Compression factor or LOD tier parameter. Typical values: c \in \{1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32\}. K: Capacity or maximum primitive count for the trajectory (e.g., K=2\text{M}). Algorithm Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Offline): 1. Construct a Morton-order tree on the trained primitives. Performance: Takes 1.5 s with 19.4 GiB peak memory on an A100 GPU for 8.56M primitives. 2. (Optional) Compute LightGaussian significance scores for pure primitive-count budgets: Score every primitive with accumulated per-pixel T^\alpha over all training views via a one-pass forward scan. Validate CUDA accumulation using the telescoping identity \sumi si = \sump (1 - T^{\text{final}}), matched to 10^{-5} relative. Select top-N primitives based on this score for a given budget. 2. Runtime Selection (Per Frame): 1. Determine the target budget based on c or K. 2. Traverse the coverage-preserving prefix cut on the GPU. 3. Gather the selected prefix directly into rasterizer buffers. This step fuses SH evaluation and opacity compensation. No CPU-side collection or host-to-device upload is required. 4. (Adaptive Mode) Use \sigma{geo} and \rho{sh} to refine selection if content-aware pruning is enabled. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocess(primitives, trainingviews): """ Offline preprocessing to build the Morton tree and compute residuals. primitives: List of Gaussian objects (mean, scale, rotation, opacity, SHcoeffs) trainingviews: List of camera poses and intrinsics """ # 1. Compute Morton codes for all primitives mortoncodes = [computemortoncode(p.mean) for p in primitives] # 2. Sort primitives by Morton code sortedindices = argsort(mortoncodes) sortedprimitives = [primitives[i] for i in sortedindices] # 3. Build Morton tree (conceptual: hierarchical grouping based on code prefixes) # In practice, this is a sorted array with implicit tree structure for prefix cuts. tree = buildmortontree(sortedprimitives) # 4. Compute Adaptive Residuals (if enabled) # Cluster primitives (e.g., via spatial hashing or tree nodes) clusters = clusterprimitives(sortedprimitives) for cluster in clusters: # Geometric spread: p tr(T) / W # T is transmittance, W is world volume/weight factor cluster.sigmageo = computegeometricspread(cluster) # SH residual ratio: cluster-internal SH variance / global RMS cluster.rhosh = computeshresidualratio(cluster) return tree, clusters def renderframe(tree, clusters, camera, budgetc, capacityk): """ Select primitives and render for a single frame. """ # 1. Determine selection criteria # If using fixed compression factor c: if budgetc is not None: # The prefix cut is determined by c. # Higher c -> fewer primitives. selectedindices = getprefixcut(tree, compressionfactor=budgetc) else: # If using capacity K: selectedindices = getprefixcut(tree, capacity=capacityk) # 2. Gather primitives into rasterizer buffers # This is done on GPU, fusing SH evaluation and opacity compensation splats = [] for idx in selectedindices: prim = tree.primitives[idx] # Evaluate SH color for camera direction color = evaluatesh(prim.shcoeffs, camera.direction) # Project covariance to 2D cov2d = projectcovariance(prim.scale, prim.rotation, camera) splats.append({ 'mean': prim.mean, 'cov2d': cov2d, 'color': color, 'opacity': prim.opacity }) # 3. Rasterize image = rasterize(splats, camera.resolution) return image def computegeometricspread(cluster): """ Computes sigmageo = p tr(T) / W """ # p: number of primitives in cluster # T: transmittance (accumulated from training views) # W: world volume/weight factor p = len(cluster.primitives) Tstar = computetransmittance(cluster.primitives) W = computeworldweight(cluster) return (p trace(Tstar)) / W def computeshresidualratio(cluster): """ Computes rhosh = cluster-internal SH variance / global RMS """ clustervariance = computevariance(cluster.shcoeffs) globalrms = computeglobalrmsallprimitives() return clustervariance / globalrms Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Geometric Redundancy Blind Spot: A primitive can be geometrically redundant yet visually load-bearing (occludes neighbors, carries unique color) or geometrically isolated yet invisible (fully occluded). Aggressive geometry-only pruning removes primitives a contribution-aware score would keep. View-Direction Reversals: Large-count outliers in per-frame selection coincide with view-direction reversals where leaves entering/leaving selection are back-facing and never rasterized. Zero-Score Primitives: A significant portion of primitives (e.g., 24.3% on BlockA) may score exactly zero in LightGaussian significance, being never visible from any training view. Also known as KoalaGS. A global, view-independent LoD formulation that provides a single primitive ordering whose prefixes define successive approximations of a scene. It solves the problem of variable-quality rendering by enabling progressive streaming and continuous budget adjustment without retraining, distinguishing itself from camera-dependent hierarchical selectors like FlexGS and discrete hierarchy methods like Octree-GS. It analyzes degradation across complexity levels by projecting image complexity maps onto Gaussians, grouping them into five bins, and measuring allocation, survival rate, and quality per bin. At 0.1% budget, it retains 2.02% of Gaussians in the simplest bin [0,1) vs 0.02% in the most complex bin [4,5], achieving higher PSNR (+2.25 dB at 0.1%) despite lower survival in complex bins. Time Complexity: Preprocessing (tree construction) is fast: 1.5 s for 8.56M primitives on A100. Per-frame selection and gather is 0.8 ms for 7.07M primitives at 1920×1080. LightGaussian scoring takes 234 s for 4565 views at 7.94M primitives on RTX 4080. Memory Complexity: Compact binary storage is efficient. DC-only path uses 3 floats per primitive, selecting 13.1M primitives in 3.9 GB on 8 GB GPUs. Memory-quality Pareto on MatrixCity: 1240 MB → 34 MB at 28.4 → 17.5 dB. Matching ~20.8 dB operating point needs 110.6 MB vs. 1926 MB (GPS full), a 17× saving. Performance: BCT wall-clock time is 78±7 min over three seeds on room@529k with one A100, compared to ≈175 min for the traditional train-prune-finetune route (2.2× faster). BCT achieves higher quality (31.9 dB vs. 30.5 dB). Quality: BCT reaches near-lossless quality at low compression ratios. At c=4, quality loss is -0.05 dB. On Lego scene, BCT stop rule reaches within 0.34 dB of Vanilla quality at 44% of primitives. BCT beats random subsampling by +5.5/+7.5/+8.0 dB at matched budgets. Stability: Per-frame count stability is high: median change of 1.1% between consecutive views on a 207-view trajectory at K=2M. GPU selection accuracy matches offline Python reference exactly (5/5 views at c=1, 10/10 at c=8). Strengths: Fast preprocessing, low memory footprint, high quality at low budgets, renderer-agnostic export, continuous LOD without retraining. Limitations: Geometric redundancy blind spot, view-direction reversal outliers, requires careful tuning of c or K. Budgeted Gaussian Splatting (BCT) was introduced in the paper "Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD". It addresses the limitations of traditional compression methods (train-prune-finetune) which are slow and lose quality. BCT provides a continuous budget-quality curve, allowing for variable primitive counts without retraining. It is used in large-scale Gaussian Splatting applications where real-time rendering and memory efficiency are critical. name: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting
head: KoalaGS
body: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail (LoD) for Gaussian Splatting, also known as KoalaGS, is a global, view-independent LoD formulation that provides a single primitive ordering whose prefixes define successive approximations of a scene. It solves the problem of variable-quality rendering in 3D Gaussian Splatting by enabling progressive streaming and continuous budget adjustment without retraining, distinguishing itself from camera-dependent hierarchical selectors like FlexGS and discrete hierarchy methods like Octree-GS. Inputs and Outputs Input: A set of 3D Gaussians (means, covariances, opacities, spherical harmonic coefficients) initialized from a standard 3DGS or 3DGS-MCMC training run; input images for complexity estimation. Output: A sorted list of primitives based on a computed "complexity" metric, allowing any prefix of the list to be rendered to achieve a specific budget (primitive count). Data Structures Complexity Map: A precomputed field associated with each Gaussian. For a newly added or relocated Gaussian, the complexity is initialized to the minimum possible value until observed by a training view. Primitive Ordering: A static array of indices sorted by descending complexity. This ordering is view-independent and fixed after training. Parameters Receptive Field: 32 pixels (fixed). Stride: 4 to 8 pixels, depending on image resolution. Training Steps: 30,000 steps. Initial Full-Capacity Steps: First 500 steps render only at full capacity. Budget Sampling: \tau \sim U(0, 1), sampled uniformly at each training step. Complexity Dropout Rate (\delta): Default 0.2. Spatial-Variance Loss Weight (\lambda{var}): 2.0. Importance-Score Weight (\lambda): 2.0. Complexity EMA Rate (\eta): 0.8. Steps 1. Complexity Map Computation (Pre-training): Compute complexity maps once per scene before training. This is implemented in PyTorch on the GPU. Use a fixed receptive field of 32 pixels. Use a stride of 4 to 8 pixels depending on image resolution. Cache the results to disk. Cost: 20–60 seconds per scene. 2. Initialization: Initialize Gaussians from a standard 3DGS or 3DGS-MCMC checkpoint. Set the complexity of any newly added or relocated Gaussian to the minimum value. 3. Training Loop (30,000 steps): For each step t: If t < 500: Render the training view at full capacity (all primitives). If t \ge 500: Sample a budget \tau \sim U(0, 1). Render the training view twice: 1. At full capacity (\hat{I}i^{full}). 2. At the sampled budget \tau (\hat{I}i^{\tau}), using the prefix of the sorted primitive list corresponding to \tau. Compute the loss L using the formula below. Perform gradient descent. 4. Relocation and Complexity Update: During training, when a Gaussian is relocated or added: If it has no complexity estimate (newly added/relocated), rank it by opacity alone until a training view observes it and updates its complexity via the EMA. Apply complexity dropout during relocation selection with rate \delta=0.2. With probability \delta, the complexity term is set to zero, causing the Gaussian to compete based only on opacity. Formula The total objective L is defined as: L = \frac{1}{2} L{rec} (\hat{I}i^{full}, Ii) + L{rec} (\hat{I}i^{\tau}, Ii) + \lambda{var} L{var} + \lambda{\alpha} \bar{\alpha} + \lambda{\sigma} \bar{\sigma} Where: L{rec} is the L1+D-SSIM loss of 3DGS. \hat{I}i^{full} is the rendered image at full capacity. \hat{I}i^{\tau} is the rendered image at budget \tau. Ii is the ground truth image. L{var} is the spatial-variance loss (Eq. 6 in). \bar{\alpha} is the mean opacity of the primitives. \bar{\sigma} is the mean scale of the primitives. \lambda{var}, \lambda{\alpha}, \lambda{\sigma} are weighting hyperparameters. Pitfalls and Edge Cases New/Relocated Gaussians: A newly added or relocated Gaussian has no complexity estimate until a training view observes it. It is handled by setting its complexity to the minimum, so relocation ranks it by opacity alone until the update assigns it a value. Complexity Dropout: The dropout rate \delta interpolates between applying complexity always (\delta=0) and dropping it always (\delta=1, reducing to original opacity sampling). A default \delta=0.2 prevents relocation from repeatedly targeting the same high-complexity regions. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import torch.nn.functional as F def computecomplexitymap(gaussians, images, receptivefield=32, stride=4): """ Pre-compute complexity maps for all Gaussians. Returns a tensor of complexity values for each Gaussian. """ # Implementation details depend on the specific complexity functional (e.g., delentropy). # This runs once on GPU using PyTorch. # Cost: 20-60s per scene. # Not given in the sources: Exact functional form of 'delentropy' or other metrics. # We assume a placeholder function that returns complexity per Gaussian. complexity = torch.zeros(len(gaussians)) #... compute complexity based on local reconstruction error/variance... return complexity def rendergaussians(gaussians, camera, numprimitives=None): """ Render Gaussians. If numprimitives is specified, only render the top-k primitives based on the pre-sorted complexity order. """ if numprimitives is not None: # Sort gaussians by complexity descending sortedindices = torch.argsort(gaussians.complexity, descending=True) selectedgaussians = gaussians[sortedindices[:numprimitives]] else: selectedgaussians = gaussians # Standard 3DGS rasterization image = rasterize(selectedgaussians, camera) return image def trainstep(gaussians, camera, groundtruthimage, tau, lambdavar=2.0, lambdaalpha=0.0, lambdasigma=0.0, dropoutrate=0.2): """ Single training step. """ # Render at full capacity imgfull = rendergaussians(gaussians, camera) # Render at budget tau numprimitives = int(tau len(gaussians)) imgtau = rendergaussians(gaussians, camera, numprimitives=numprimitives) # Compute losses lrecfull = l1dssimloss(imgfull, groundtruthimage) lrectau = l1dssimloss(imgtau, groundtruthimage) # Spatial variance loss (Eq. 6 in source) lvar = computespatialvarianceloss(gaussians) # Regularizers meanalpha = torch.mean(gaussians.opacity) meansigma = torch.mean(gaussians.scale) # Total Loss loss = 0.5 lrecfull + lrectau + lambdavar lvar + lambdaalpha meanalpha + lambdasigma meansigma # Backpropagation loss.backward() # Relocation logic with complexity dropout # If a Gaussian is relocated, its complexity is updated. # With probability dropoutrate, complexity is ignored in relocation selection. # Not given in the sources: Exact relocation algorithm details (e.g., densification/pruning thresholds). # We assume standard 3DGS densification/pruning with complexity-aware selection. return loss def main(): # 1. Pre-training: Compute complexity maps complexitymaps = computecomplexitymap(gaussians, trainingimages) gaussians.complexity = complexitymaps # 2. Training Loop for step in range(30000): camera = sampletrainingcamera() groundtruth = sampletrainingimage() if step < 500: tau = 1.0 # Full capacity only else: tau = torch.rand(1).item() # U(0, 1) loss = trainstep(gaussians, camera, groundtruth, tau) # Update Gaussians (densify, prune, etc.) updategaussians(gaussians) # Update complexity EMA for observed Gaussians updatecomplexityema(gaussians, eta=0.8) Time Complexity: Training takes approximately 15 minutes on a single NVIDIA H100 for a scene with ~2M primitives. Pre-processing (complexity map computation) takes 20–60 seconds per scene. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the complexity map for each Gaussian. No additional hierarchical data structures are needed compared to standard 3DGS. Performance: On Tanks and Temples, the default dropout rate \delta=0.2 improves AUC PSNR by 0.14 dB (24.02 vs. 23.88) compared to original opacity sampling (\delta=1). On Deep Blending, it improves AUC PSNR by 0.23 dB (29.51 vs. 29.28). Strengths: Continuous LoD allows any budget within the range; progressive streaming is enabled by the fixed ordering; view-independent selection simplifies deployment. Limitations: Requires a one-time pre-processing step; the ordering is fixed, so it may not adapt to specific camera viewpoints as well as camera-dependent methods. KoalaGS was introduced in the paper "KoalaGS: Complexity-Aware Continuous Level of Detail for Gaussian Splatting". It builds on the 3DGS-MCMC framework and addresses the limitations of discrete LoD methods (like Octree-GS) and camera-dependent selectors (like FlexGS) by providing a global, view-independent ordering. name: Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS)
head: H-3DGS, Hierarchical-3DGS, Inria H-3DGS
body: Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) is a Level-of-Detail (LoD) method that organizes 3D Gaussian primitives into a hierarchical structure to enable efficient rendering of large-scale scenes by dynamically selecting appropriate detail levels based on viewing distance. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Octree-GS by using a cluster-based octree-like tree structure rather than an explicit anchor-based voxel grid, and from CityGaussian / VastGaussian / DoGaussian by employing a unified top-down or bottom-up hierarchy generation rather than independent block-wise training. H-3DGS and its siblings share the core principle of spatial partitioning to manage the memory and computational load of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) in large scenes. The general mechanism involves: 1. Hierarchical Organization: Primitives (Gaussians) are grouped into nodes of a tree structure (e.g., octree, cluster tree). Each node represents a spatial region and contains a summary or a set of Gaussians. 2. Level-of-Detail (LoD) Selection: During rendering, the hierarchy is traversed based on the camera's distance to the scene regions. Coarser levels (fewer, larger Gaussians) are used for distant regions, while finer levels (more, smaller Gaussians) are used for nearby regions. 3. Distance-Based Cuts: The selection of the LoD level is typically determined by a threshold distance. If the camera is closer than the threshold, the children of the current node are processed; otherwise, the current node's Gaussians are rendered, and its children are culled. 4. Memory Efficiency: By not loading or rendering all Gaussians simultaneously, the method reduces VRAM usage and increases rendering throughput for large scenes. CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian are methods for large-scale urban reconstruction that partition scenes into overlapping or disjoint blocks, train independent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models per block, and merge them at render time using a Level-of-Detail (LoD) hierarchy. They solve the memory and training bottlenecks of standard 3DGS in city-scale scenes by enabling distributed or block-wise training and streaming. They set themselves apart from sibling methods like Octree-GS by relying on tile-based training and merging rather than a single unified anchor-based hierarchy, and from Iterative Gaussian Synopsis by using explicit spatial partitioning for training rather than iterative synopsis generation. Octree-GS is a Level-of-Detail (LoD) method for 3D Gaussian Splatting that organizes Gaussian primitives into a sparse octree structure to enable consistent real-time rendering across varying viewing distances and scene complexities. It solves the problem of inefficient primitive usage and visual artifacts in large-scale scenes by dynamically selecting appropriate LOD levels based on camera distance, ensuring rendering speed remains stable regardless of trajectory changes. Unlike concurrent methods that require multi-resolution inputs, post-processing, or manual threshold tuning, Octree-GS achieves LoD effects in a single end-to-end training round using an accumulative LOD strategy. Iterative Gaussian Synopsis is a top-down strategy for constructing a hierarchy of Level-of-Detail (LOD) representations for 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS). It addresses the challenges of deploying large-scale 3DGS models for progressive and adaptive rendering by deriving coarser levels from a full-fidelity model through adaptive, learnable pruning and downsampling, ensuring coherent simplification without the error accumulation typical of bottom-up training. It sets itself apart from siblings like Octree-GS and CityGaussian / VastGaussian / DoGaussian by using a unified top-down unfolding framework that extracts all LODs from a single optimization, rather than building independent models or using bottom-up enhancement layers. Uses an octree-like tree of clusters; renders only the relevant LoD; achieves 99% reduction at far distances. A cluster-based Level of Detail (LoD) method developed by Inria, capable of rendering large scenes like Mont Saint-Michel interactively. A level-of-detail framework for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting that enables efficient rendering by dynamically selecting appropriate detail levels. A technique to prevent overfitting of Gaussians to specific viewing distances by introducing noise into the hierarchy cut distances, ensuring coarser levels are trained occasionally. For each training iteration, multiply the distances to the SPT (Split Point Tree) centers by a factor calculated as 1 + 5^{\frac{u}{4}}, where the exponent is a uniformly random variable u \in (0, 1). The scaling factor applied to the distance is 1 + 5^{u}, where u \in (0, 1) is a uniformly random variable. This ensures most iterations train near the highest LoD, but coarser levels are trained occasionally. The base of the exponent in the noise factor is 5. The random variable u is drawn from a uniform distribution over the open interval (0, 1). Without this noise, Gaussians of a specific scale overfit to views from a particular distance, leading to LoD popping artifacts. A method to account for differing focal lengths in datasets by using a relative distance metric for HSPT cuts, ensuring the required LoD is consistent across cameras with different projections. Choose a base focal length f{base}. For the current camera with focal length f, calculate the relative distance metric \tilde{d} for HSPT cuts as \tilde{d} = \frac{f}{f{base}} d, where d is the actual distance. The relative distance metric is \tilde{d} = \frac{f}{f{base}} d, where f is the current camera's focal length, f{base} is the chosen base focal length, and d is the distance to the Gaussian. Unlike standard methods that use only Euclidean distance, this method scales the cut distance by the ratio of the current focal length to a base focal length. For example, a camera with double the focal length requires the cut distance to be halved to account for the larger projection footprint. A variant inspired by Levels of Detail (LoD) that stores splats in a tree structure where each node is represented in greater detail by its children, using non-layered models (“Separate”) with different target sizes. Lower-version splats are set as root nodes and higher-version splats as child nodes, sharing the same object ID and highest similarity score. Unlike the layered approach, no splats are shared across levels of the tree, requiring replacement of multiple splats and leading to bandwidth inefficiencies, though it allows finer-grained progressive replacement than the coarse-grained per-scene replacement of the original Separate baseline. Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) was introduced by Kerbl et al. (the original 3DGS authors) in 2024 as an extension to handle large-scale environments. Prior methods for large scenes typically employed scene partitioning or multi-GPU training. H-3DGS addresses the memory bottlenecks of standard 3DGS by training chunks independently and merging them into a global LoD hierarchy. It is capable of rendering large scenes like Mont Saint-Michel interactively. The method introduces techniques such as varying level of detail noise to prevent overfitting and varying focal length adaptation to handle datasets with differing focal lengths. name: CityGaussian / VastGaussian / DoGaussian
head: City-Gaussian, CityGaussian / Hierarchical 3DGS, CityGaussian V2, DoGaussian, Hierarchical 3DGS
body: CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian are methods for large-scale urban reconstruction that partition scenes into overlapping blocks, train independent 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) models per block, and merge them at rendering time using a Level-of-Detail (LoD) hierarchy. They solve the memory and computational bottlenecks of standard 3DGS in city-scale scenes by enabling streaming and interactive exploration through spatial partitioning and distance-based detail selection. Unlike sibling methods like Octree-GS which use anchor-based neural decoders, or Iterative Gaussian Synopsis which compresses a global model, these methods rely on block-based training and merging with explicit LoD pyramids. Inputs: A set of calibrated images covering a large-scale scene (e.g., city-scale). Outputs: A set of block-specific 3DGS models and an LoD hierarchy for rendering. Data Structures: 1. Block Partition: The scene is divided into spatially overlapping or disjoint blocks (tiles). 2. Block Model: Each block contains a set of 3D Gaussians \{gi\} with parameters: position \mathbf{p}, covariance \mathbf{\Sigma} (or rotation \mathbf{R} and scale \mathbf{s}), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonics (SH) coefficients for color. 3. LoD Pyramid: For each block, multiple detail levels are generated, typically by applying compression strategies (e.g., LightGaussian) to reduce point count, feature dimensions, and precision. Steps: 1. Partitioning: Divide the scene into blocks. VastGaussian uses spatially disjoint regions with feathered overlap to handle varying lighting. CityGaussian uses overlapping tiles. 2. Independent Training: Train a separate 3DGS model for each block independently. DoGaussian extends this to distributed training across multiple nodes. 3. LoD Generation (Optional/Variant): Apply compression to create multiple detail levels per block. This involves reducing the number of Gaussians, lowering SH band, and quantizing parameters. 4. Rendering (Merge & Select): Distance Calculation: Calculate the distance from the camera to each block. LoD Selection: Select the appropriate detail level for each block based on the camera distance. Frustum Culling: Determine if a block intersects the camera frustum. Fusion: Concatenate Gaussians from selected blocks and detail levels for rasterization. Formulas: Block Bounds Estimation (CityGS): To avoid floaters, bounds \mathbf{p}{min}^j and \mathbf{p}{max}^j for block j are estimated using Median Absolute Deviation (MAD): MADj = \mathrm{median}\left( \left| \mathbf{p}k^j - \mathrm{median}\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right) \right| \right) \mathbf{p}{min}^j = \max\left( \min\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right), \mathrm{median}\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right) - n{MAD} \times MADj \right) \mathbf{p}{max}^j = \min\left( \max\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right), \mathrm{median}\left( \mathbf{p}k^j \right) + n{MAD} \times MADj \right) where \mathbf{p}k^j are the positions of Gaussians in block j, and n{MAD} is a hyperparameter. LoD Selection: The detail level for a block is determined by the minimum distance from the block's eight corners to the camera center. Frustum Culling: Project block corners to screen space, create a bounding box, and calculate Intersection-over-Union (IoU) with the screen area. Include the block if IoU indicates intersection or if the camera is inside the block. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendercitygaussian(camera, sceneblocks, lodlevels): """ Render a large-scale scene using block-based partitioning and LoD. Args: camera: Camera object with position, orientation, and projection matrix. sceneblocks: List of Block objects. Each Block has: gaussians: List of Gaussian objects (pos, cov, alpha, sh). lodlevels: List of compressed Gaussian sets (LOD 0, 1, 2...). bounds: Estimated bounding box (pmin, pmax). lodlevels: List of detail levels. Each level is a list of Gaussians. Returns: Image buffer. """ image = emptybuffer() visiblegaussians = [] for block in sceneblocks: # 1. Estimate Block Bounds (if not pre-computed) # Use MAD to filter out floaters ppositions = [g.pos for g in block.gaussians] medianpos = median(ppositions) mad = median([abs(p - medianpos) for p in ppositions]) pmin = max(min(ppositions), medianpos - nMAD mad) pmax = min(max(ppositions), medianpos + nMAD mad) # 2. Frustum Culling corners = getboxcorners(pmin, pmax) projectedcorners = projecttoscreen(corners, camera) screenbbox = boundingbox(projectedcorners) iou = intersectionoverunion(screenbbox, camera.screenarea) if iou > threshold or camerainsideblock(camera, pmin, pmax): # 3. LoD Selection # Calculate min distance from block corners to camera mindist = min(distance(camera.pos, corner) for corner in corners) lodindex = selectlodindex(mindist, block.lodthresholds) # Get Gaussians for selected LOD selectedgaussians = block.lodlevels[lodindex] # 4. Add to visible list visiblegaussians.extend(selectedgaussians) # 5. Rasterization # Sort visiblegaussians by depth (standard 3DGS sorting) visiblegaussians.sort(key=lambda g: depth(g.pos, camera)) # Render using standard 3DGS rasterizer image = rasterize(visiblegaussians, camera) return image Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Floaters: Outlier Gaussians (floaters) can distort block bounds. Using MAD for bound estimation mitigates this. Overlap Artifacts: Overlapping blocks may cause double rendering or seams. Feathered overlap or careful merging is required. Precision: Lower detail levels use quantized parameters (e.g., 8-bit for \alpha, INT6 for SH), which may introduce visible artifacts if compression is too aggressive. Proxy-GS uses a coarse proxy mesh to guide Gaussian placement, significantly reducing the number of Gaussians required for background regions. It sets itself apart by leveraging geometric priors from a mesh to optimize Gaussian density, rather than relying solely on image-based optimization. It is chosen when a coarse mesh is available and background regions are large and static. CityGS Level-of-Detail (LoD) is a rendering optimization technique that generates multiple detail levels of Gaussians and selects them per block based on distance to the camera, reducing rasterizer load. It sets itself apart by using the LightGaussian compression strategy to create levels with different compression rates (r0, r1, r2), reducing points, feature dimensions, and precision. It is chosen for real-time rendering of very large scenes where memory bandwidth is a bottleneck. Time Complexity: Training is linear in the number of blocks and Gaussians per block, but parallelizable across blocks. Rendering complexity depends on the number of visible Gaussians, which is reduced by LoD selection. Memory Complexity: VRAM usage is proportional to the number of visible Gaussians at the selected LoD, significantly lower than loading all Gaussians. Measured Performance: CityGaussian enables interactive exploration of square-kilometer scenes. DoGaussian supports distributed training across nodes. Strengths: Scalability to city-scale scenes, parallelizable training, reduced VRAM usage. Limitations: Potential seams at block boundaries, complexity in managing overlapping blocks, dependency on block partitioning quality. When to use: Large-scale urban reconstruction, autonomous driving simulation, scenes with significant scale variation. When not to use: Small-scale scenes where standard 3DGS is sufficient, scenes with high dynamic content requiring global consistency (unless combined with methods like StreetGaussians). CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian originated from the need to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to city-scale environments. VastGaussian was introduced in CVPR'24, partitioning scenes into spatially-disjoint regions with decoupled appearance handling. CityGaussian and its V2 introduced hierarchical LoD across square kilometers with depth regularization and visibility-aware training. DoGaussian extended this to distributed training across nodes. These methods build on the principles of Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting (H-3DGS) [10279-hierarchical-3d-gaussian-splatting-h-3dgs.md] and address the memory bottlenecks of standard 3DGS in large scenes. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Neural Rendering — Technologies & Tricks, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-NeuralRenderingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD, https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.03162, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial) CityGaussian: Real-Time High-Quality Large-Scale Scene Rendering with Gaussians, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-031-72640-815, fetched 2026-10-26

name: StreetGaussians
body: StreetGaussians is a method for reconstructing dynamic urban driving scenes by decomposing the environment into a static background and dynamic actors (vehicles, pedestrians). It solves the problem of efficiently rendering complex, moving traffic in large-scale outdoor environments by associating each dynamic object with a separate 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) sub-model that can be transformed independently. It sets itself apart from monolithic 3DGS approaches by explicitly separating static and dynamic components, allowing for independent pose updates of actors without retraining the background. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-view video/images of a driving scene, LiDAR depth data (optional but used for initialization), and tracked trajectories/poses for dynamic objects (vehicles, pedestrians). Outputs: A static 3DGS representation of the background and a set of dynamic 3DGS sub-models, each associated with a specific actor and its time-varying pose. Data Structures: 1. Static 3DGS: Standard 3DGS representation containing 3D mean positions \mu, covariance matrices \Sigma (or rotation R and scale S), opacity \alpha, and spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients c{lm} for the static background. 2. Dynamic Actor Sub-models: For each dynamic object i: A separate 3DGS representation with its own \mui, \Sigmai, \alphai, c{lm,i}. A tracked pose Ti(t) (transformation matrix) for the object at time t. Time-dependent SH coefficients c{lm,i}(t) to model appearance changes. Steps: 1. Static Background Reconstruction: Incrementally optimize static 3D Gaussians for the background using input views. This may be assisted by Segment Anything Model (SAM) masks and LiDAR depth data to separate static elements. 2. Dynamic Object Isolation: Identify dynamic objects (vehicles, pedestrians) using tracking or segmentation. 3. Dynamic Sub-model Training: For each dynamic object, train a separate 3DGS model. The Gaussians are transformed by the tracked vehicle/actor poses Ti(t). 4. Appearance Modeling: Approximate the appearance of dynamic objects using time-related spherical harmonic coefficients c{lm}(t). This allows the model to capture lighting changes or motion blur effects over time. 5. Rendering: To render a frame at time t: Render the static background using the static 3DGS. For each dynamic object i, transform its Gaussians by Ti(t) and render using its time-dependent SH coefficients c{lm,i}(t). Composite the results. Formulas: The position of a Gaussian g in object i's local frame is \mu{local}. Its world position at time t is: \mu{world}(t) = Ti(t) \cdot \mu{local} where Ti(t) is the 4x4 transformation matrix for object i at time t. The color C of a pixel is computed by compositing the static background and all dynamic objects, where each dynamic object's contribution uses its transformed Gaussians and time-dependent SH coefficients. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Tracking Errors: Inaccurate tracked poses Ti(t) will lead to misaligned Gaussians and artifacts. Occlusion Handling: Dynamic objects may occlude the static background or other dynamic objects. The compositing order must be handled correctly. Dynamic Object Identification: Correctly segmenting and tracking all dynamic objects is critical. Missing objects or false positives will degrade quality. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to training a single large 3DGS for the entire dynamic scene, as static and dynamic parts are optimized separately. Rendering time depends on the number of dynamic objects and their Gaussians. Memory Complexity: Lower memory usage for the background, as it is static and can be optimized independently. Dynamic objects require storing separate Gaussians and pose data. Strengths: Efficiently handles dynamic scenes; allows independent updates of dynamic actors; suitable for autonomous driving simulation. Limitations: Requires accurate tracking of dynamic objects; may struggle with highly dynamic or cluttered scenes where object boundaries are unclear. When to use: Dynamic urban driving scenes with distinct, trackable vehicles and pedestrians. When not to use: Static scenes or scenes with untracked, highly dynamic elements. StreetGaussians was introduced to address the challenges of reconstructing dynamic urban environments for autonomous driving applications. It builds on the success of 3DGS but adapts it to handle motion by decomposing the scene into static and dynamic components. The method is part of a broader trend in 2026 towards per-actor 3DGS for AV simulation, allowing for the insertion of rare-event vehicles into any scene. It is related to other methods like DrivingGaussian, which composites surrounding views from multiple cameras into a single dynamic scene, assisted by external priors. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: DrivingGaussian
head: A method that composites surrounding views from multiple cameras into a single dynamic scene, aligning the Gaussian clouds of different vehicles with their tracked trajectories
body: DrivingGaussian is a method for reconstructing dynamic driving data by compositing surrounding views from multiple cameras into a single dynamic scene. It specifically addresses the challenge of aligning the Gaussian clouds of different vehicles with their tracked trajectories to model dynamic urban environments. It builds on StreetGaussians by adopting a similar strategy of separating static and dynamic components, but focuses on the composite reconstruction process assisted by external priors. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Multi-camera image sequences, input LiDAR depth data, and tracked trajectories for dynamic objects (vehicles/pedestrians). Outputs: A single dynamic scene representation composed of static 3D Gaussians and dynamic object Gaussians aligned with trajectories. Data Structures: The method maintains two distinct sets of 3D Gaussians: 1. Static Gaussians: Representing the fixed urban background (roads, buildings, etc.). 2. Dynamic Gaussians: Representing individual vehicles or pedestrians. Each dynamic object is associated with a separate 3DGS sub-model. Steps: 1. Static Optimization: Incrementally optimize the static 3D Gaussians using the multi-camera inputs. 2. Dynamic Composition: Compose the static scene with dynamic objects' 3D Gaussians. 3. Trajectory Alignment: Align the Gaussian clouds of different vehicles with their tracked trajectories. 4. Assisted Reconstruction: Utilize the Segment Anything Model (SAM) and input LiDAR depth data to assist in the segmentation and depth estimation of dynamic objects. Parameters: Tracked Trajectories: Required for each dynamic object to define its motion and pose over time. LiDAR Depth: Used as a geometric prior. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Dynamic Object Segmentation: Accurate separation of dynamic objects from the static background is critical; errors here lead to misalignment. SAM is used to mitigate this. Trajectory Accuracy: Misaligned trajectories result in incorrect Gaussian placement and motion artifacts. A method for urban scene data that makes Gaussians' mean and opacity values time-dependent functions centered at the corresponding Gaussian's life peak. The Life peak is defined as the maximum prominence over time. This approach allows for modeling the temporal evolution of dynamic objects within the scene. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Enables reconstruction of complex dynamic driving scenes by separating static and dynamic elements, leveraging external priors (LiDAR, SAM) for robustness. Limitations: Relies on accurate tracked trajectories and external models (SAM, LiDAR), which may not be available in all scenarios. When to use: When reconstructing dynamic urban driving scenes with multi-camera setups and available trajectory/LiDAR data. When not to use: For static scene reconstruction or scenes without reliable dynamic object tracking. DrivingGaussian was introduced as a method to reconstruct dynamic driving data by compositing surrounding views from multiple cameras into a single dynamic scene. It aligns the Gaussian clouds of different vehicles with their tracked trajectories, building upon the concepts of modeling dynamic urban environments with separate sub-models for each vehicle or pedestrian. The method is assisted by the Segment Anything Model and input LiDAR depth data to improve reconstruction quality. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) PDF Recent advances in 3D Gaussian splatting - Springer, https://link.springer.com/content/pdf/10.1007/s41095-024-0436-y.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)
