name: Momentum-GS
head: Momentum Self-Distillation for 3DGS, Block-wise Momentum-GS
body: Momentum-GS is a block-wise training method for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a momentum-updated teacher model to provide global self-distillation guidance to local block students. It solves the geometric inaccuracies and "floaters" caused by independent block training in methods like CityGaussian by decoupling the block count from the GPU count and restoring cross-block spatial consistency. Unlike CityGaussian, which relies on a static coarse prior and spatial contraction, Momentum-GS dynamically updates the teacher via exponential moving average (EMA) of student parameters. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A large-scale scene dataset (images, poses), a block partitioning strategy (e.g., grid-based tiling), and hyperparameters for momentum decay (\beta), learning rate (\eta), and block weighting. Output: A set of 3D Gaussians optimized for the entire scene, with improved geometric consistency and reduced artifacts compared to independent block training. Data Structures: 1. Student Gaussians (Gs): The set of Gaussian parameters (mean \mu, covariance \Sigma, opacity \alpha, spherical harmonics coefficients C) for the current block being trained. 2. Teacher Gaussians (Gt): A global set of Gaussian parameters, initialized from a coarse prior or previous iteration, updated via EMA. 3. Block Weights (wb): A scalar value per block, calculated based on reconstruction accuracy. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the Teacher Gaussians Gt using a coarse global prior or a single-pass training on a downsampled scene. Initialize Student Gaussians Gs for each block. 2. Block Partitioning: Divide the scene into non-overlapping or overlapping blocks. 3. Training Loop (per block b): a. Forward Pass: Render the current block's Student Gaussians Gs^b to generate images. b. Distillation Loss: Compute a distillation loss between the rendered output of Gs^b and the rendered output of the global Teacher Gaussians Gt. This guides the student to maintain global consistency. c. Reconstruction Loss: Compute the standard photometric reconstruction loss between rendered images and ground truth images. d. Total Loss: Combine losses: \mathcal{L}{total} = \mathcal{L}{rec} + \lambda \mathcal{L}{distill}, where \lambda is a weighting factor. e. Optimization: Update Gs^b using gradient descent. f. Block Weighting: Calculate the reconstruction accuracy for block b and update its weight wb. 4. Teacher Update (EMA): After each optimization step or epoch, update the Teacher Gaussians Gt using the exponential moving average of the Student Gaussians Gs: Gt \leftarrow \beta Gt + (1 - \beta) Gs where \beta is the momentum coefficient (typically close to 1, e.g., 0.99). 5. Iteration: Repeat steps 3-4 for all blocks until convergence. Parameters: Momentum Coefficient (\beta): Controls the decay rate of the EMA. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but standard EMA values in self-distillation are used. Distillation Weight (\lambda): Balances reconstruction and distillation losses. Not given in the sources. Block Size: Determines the granularity of the partitioning. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: EMA updates can suffer from numerical instability if \beta is too close to 1 or if gradients are noisy. Boundaries: Block boundaries may still exhibit artifacts if the distillation guidance is not strong enough. Degenerate Input: If the coarse prior is poor, the teacher may guide students to incorrect geometries. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. Gt = initializecoarseprior(scenedata) Gsblocks = initializestudentblocks(scenedata) beta = 0.99 # Momentum coefficient lambdadistill = 0.1 # Distillation loss weight learningrate = 0.01 for epoch in range(numepochs): for blockid, blockdata in enumerate(sceneblocks): # Forward pass for student renderedstudent = render(Gsblocks[blockid], blockdata.cameras) # Forward pass for teacher (global consistency) renderedteacher = render(Gt, blockdata.cameras) # Compute reconstruction loss lossrec = photometricloss(renderedstudent, blockdata.gtimages) # Compute distillation loss lossdistill = distillationloss(renderedstudent, renderedteacher) # Total loss loss = lossrec + lambdadistill lossdistill # Update student parameters Gsblocks[blockid] = optimize(Gsblocks[blockid], loss, learningrate) # Update block weight based on reconstruction accuracy blockaccuracy = computeaccuracy(renderedstudent, blockdata.gtimages) blockweights[blockid] = blockaccuracy # Update Teacher Gaussians using EMA for blockid in range(numblocks): Gt = beta Gt + (1 - beta) Gsblocks[blockid] CityGS is a divide-and-conquer training method for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a coarse global prior to enable parallel block-wise finetuning and a Level-of-Detail (LoD) strategy for real-time rendering. It solves the geometric inaccuracies and floaters caused by independent block training by initializing each block with a globally consistent Gaussian set, ensuring seamless fusion without complex alignment. Unlike Momentum-GS, which uses a momentum-updated teacher for self-distillation, CityGS relies on a static coarse prior and spatial contraction for data assignment. Gaussian-JEPA is a self-supervised pretraining method for 3D Gaussian assets that predicts latent features of masked target blocks from shared context, using joint-embedding predictive learning to avoid raw-attribute reconstruction. It sets itself apart from Gaussian-MAE by predicting latent representations instead of reconstructing Gaussian parameters, and from contrastive methods by explicitly supervising missing spatial content through latent prediction of held-out blocks. It builds on Momentum-GS by providing a robust, object-level feature representation that is consistent across stochastic resampling, which serves as a foundation for downstream tasks like shape completion and segmentation. Reconstructing large-scale scenes following a distributed learning approach. Time Complexity: Training time is reduced compared to full-scene optimization due to block-wise parallelization, but the EMA update adds overhead. Memory Complexity: Requires storing both student and teacher Gaussian sets, increasing memory usage. Measured Performance: Reports ~18.7% LPIPS improvement over CityGaussian with far fewer blocks. Scaling: Decouples block count from GPU count, allowing for scalable training on large scenes. Strengths: Restores cross-block spatial consistency, reduces floaters, and improves convergence quality. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of momentum and distillation weights; may be sensitive to the quality of the initial coarse prior. When to Use: Large-scale scene reconstruction where geometric consistency is critical. When Not to Use: Small scenes where full-scene optimization is feasible and faster. Momentum-GS was marked as a 2026 SOTA update. It leverages momentum self-distillation, where a teacher model (an exponential moving average of the parameters) guides the optimization of the student, improving convergence quality for large scenes. It addresses the challenges of distributed learning and Level of Detail (LoD) techniques in large-scale scene reconstruction, where geometry accuracy and reconstruction time remain bottlenecks. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Gaussian Splatting — All Variants Cheat Sheet, https://www.chengjianglong.com/ml/3D-GaussianSplattingSOTAUpdated.html, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Recent Advances and Trends in Learning‐Based 3D Representations, https://doi.org/10.1111/cgf.70530, fetched 2026-10-26

name: CityGS Training Pipeline
head: Block-wise Parallel Training with Global Prior, CityGaussian, CityGaussian Training
body: CityGS is a divide-and-conquer training method for large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) that uses a coarse global prior to enable parallel block-wise finetuning and a Level-of-Detail (LoD) strategy for real-time rendering. It solves the geometric inaccuracies and floaters caused by independent block training by initializing each block with a globally consistent Gaussian set, ensuring seamless fusion without complex alignment. Unlike Momentum-GS, which uses a momentum-updated teacher for self-distillation, CityGS relies on a static coarse prior and spatial contraction for data assignment. Inputs: A set of input images with known intrinsics \kappa and poses \taui. Initial sparse point cloud (e.g., from COLMAP). Hyperparameters: global training iterations (N{global}=30,000), SSIM threshold \epsilon, block bounds [b{j,min}, b{j,max}], and LoD compression rates r0, r1, r2. Outputs: A fused set of 3D Gaussians G{final} organized into detail levels for rendering. Data Structures: Each Gaussian Gk contains: Position pk \in \mathbb{R}^3. Opacity \alphak \in [0, 1]. Covariance defined by scaling and rotation. Spherical Harmonics (SH) features f^k \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 16} for view-dependent color ck \in \mathbb{R}^3. Steps: 1. Generate Global Prior: Train the initial COLMAP points using all input images for 30,000 iterations with standard 3DGS densification/pruning to produce a coarse global Gaussian set GK = \{Gk | k = 1,..., K\}. 2. Contract Global Prior: Normalize the positions of GK to [-1, 1] using the min/max corners p{min}, p{max} of the scene bounds to get \hat{p}k. Apply non-linear contraction to handle positions with infinity norm > 1: \text{contract}(\hat{p}k) = \begin{cases} \hat{p}k & \text{if } \|\hat{p}k\|\infty \le 1 \\ \left(2 - \frac{1}{\|\hat{p}k\|\infty}\right) \frac{\hat{p}k}{\|\hat{p}k\|\infty} & \text{if } \|\hat{p}k\|\infty > 1 \end{cases} where \|\cdot\|\infty is the infinity norm. 3. Partition Space: Divide the contracted cubic space evenly into blocks. For each block j, identify the subset of Gaussians G{Kj} contained within the block bounds [b{j,min}, b{j,max}] in the contracted space. 4. Handle Empty Blocks: If a block j has too few Gaussians (Kj below a threshold), enlarge its bounds b{j,min} and b{j,max} until the threshold is met. This adjustment is used only for data assignment to ensure sufficient training data, not for filtering final Gaussians. 5. Assign Training Data: For each block j and image pose \taui, determine if the image should be used for training block j using two criteria combined via logical OR (sum): Visibility Criterion (B1): Calculate the SSIM loss between the image rendered by the global prior I{GK}(\taui) and the image rendered by the block's contribution I{GK \setminus G{Kj}}(\taui). If L{SSIM}(I{GK}(\taui), I{GK \setminus G{Kj}}(\taui)) > \epsilon, then B1(\taui, G{Kj}) = 1, else 0. Spatial Criterion (B2): Check if the camera pose position \hat{p}{\taui} (in world coordinates, contracted) falls within the block bounds: B2(\taui, G{Kj}) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } b{j,min} \le \text{contract}(\hat{p}{\taui}) < b{j,max} \\ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}. Final Assignment: B(\taui, G{Kj}) = B1(\taui, G{Kj}) + B2(\taui, G{Kj}). If B > 0, the image is assigned to block j. 6. Parallel Finetuning: Train each block j in parallel. Initialize the block's Gaussians with the corresponding subset G{Kj} from the global prior. Train in the original uncontracted space using the assigned images. The loss is the weighted sum of L1 and SSIM losses. 7. Post-processing: After training, filter the finetuned Gaussians of block j to keep only those physically located within the block's original spatial bounds (in uncontracted space). Concatenate all filtered blocks to form the final dense model. 8. Level-of-Detail (LoD) Generation: Compress the fused Gaussians into multiple detail levels using compression rates r0, r1, r2. 9. Rendering: For a given view, dynamically select the appropriate LoD level based on camera distance or resolution requirements. Splat the selected Gaussians to screen space, sort by depth, and render via alpha blending: ci(\mathbf{x}) = \sum{k=1}^K \alphak \mathbf{c}k Gk^{2D}(\mathbf{x}) \prod{t=1}^{k-1} (1 - \alphat Gt^{2D}(\mathbf{x})) where Gk^{2D} = \text{proj}(Gk, \kappa, \taui) is the projected 2D Gaussian distribution. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def citygstrainingpipeline(images, poses, initialpoints): # Step 1: Generate Global Prior # Train for 30,000 iterations using all images globalgaussians = train3dgs(initialpoints, images, poses, iterations=30000) # Step 2: Contract Global Prior pmin, pmax = getscenebounds(globalgaussians.positions) contractedgaussians = [] for g in globalgaussians: phat = normalize(g.position, pmin, pmax) if np.linalg.norm(phat, ord=np.inf) <= 1: contractedpos = phat else: contractedpos = (2 - 1/np.linalg.norm(phat, ord=np.inf)) (phat / np.linalg.norm(phat, ord=np.inf)) contractedgaussians.append(Gaussian(position=contractedpos, attributes=g.attributes)) # Step 3: Partition Space blocks = createevenpartitions(contractedgaussians) # Step 4 & 5: Assign Data and Handle Empty Blocks blockdataassignments = {} for j, block in enumerate(blocks): # Identify Gaussians in block bounds gkj = [g for g in contractedgaussians if isinbounds(g.position, block.min, block.max)] # Handle empty blocks by enlarging bounds if necessary if len(gkj) < threshold: block.min, block.max = enlargebounds(block.min, block.max, gkj, threshold) gkj = [g for g in contractedgaussians if isinbounds(g.position, block.min, block.max)] assignedimages = [] for i, (img, pose) in enumerate(zip(images, poses)): # B1: Visibility check # Render global prior and block contribution imgglobal = render(globalgaussians, pose) imgblockcontrib = render(gkj, pose) # Simplified: render difference ssimloss = computessim(imgglobal, imgblockcontrib) b1 = 1 if ssimloss > epsilon else 0 # B2: Spatial check poseposcontracted = contract(pose.position, pmin, pmax) b2 = 1 if isinbounds(poseposcontracted, block.min, block.max) else 0 if b1 + b2 > 0: assignedimages.append(img) blockdataassignments[j] = (gkj, assignedimages) # Step 6: Parallel Finetuning finetunedblocks = [] for j, (gkj, assignedimages) in blockdataassignments.items(): # Initialize with global prior subset blockgaussians = copy(gkj) # Train in original uncontracted space blockgaussians = finetune(blockgaussians, assignedimages, loss='l1+ssim') # Step 7: Post-processing # Filter to keep only Gaussians within original spatial bounds (uncontracted) # Note: block bounds were defined in contracted space, need to map back or use original bounds # The source says "filter out the finetuned Gaussians contained within its spatial bound" # Assuming spatial bound refers to the block's region in world space filteredgaussians = [g for g in blockgaussians if isinworldbounds(g.position, block.worldmin, block.worldmax)] finetunedblocks.append(filteredgaussians) # Concatenate blocks finalgaussians = concatenate(finetunedblocks) # Step 8: LoD Generation lodlevels = generatelod(finalgaussians, rates=[r0, r1, r2]) return lodlevels def contract(phat, pmin, pmax): # Normalize pnorm = (phat - pmin) / (pmax - pmin) 2 - 1 # Map to [-1, 1] # This matches the description: "normalize positions to [-1, 1]" # Then apply contraction norminf = np.linalg.norm(pnorm, ord=np.inf) if norminf <= 1: return pnorm else: return (2 - 1/norminf) (pnorm / norminf) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Empty Blocks: Extremely uneven Gaussian distributions may result in blocks with no Gaussians. The algorithm explicitly enlarges block bounds to ensure a minimum number of Gaussians, preventing overfitting due to lack of training data. Contraction Boundary: The contraction function is continuous but non-linear. Positions with infinity norm exactly 1 are unaffected. SSIM Threshold: The choice of \epsilon affects data assignment. Too high, and blocks may lack training data; too low, and blocks may train on irrelevant views. Time Complexity: Training is parallelized across blocks, reducing wall-clock time compared to single-process global training. The global prior generation takes 30,000 iterations. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the global prior and all block data. The contraction step is memory-efficient as it operates on positions. Performance: Achieves real-time rendering on large-scale scenes using LoD. Strengths: Eliminates floaters and geometric inaccuracies at block boundaries; enables parallel training; simple fusion via concatenation. Limitations: Requires a high-quality global prior; performance depends on the effectiveness of the contraction and partitioning. CityGaussian (CityGS) was introduced to address the challenges of training and rendering large-scale 3DGS in real-time. It builds on the 3DGS method and introduces a divide-and-conquer strategy with a global prior and LoD. name: Gaussian-JEPA Pretraining
head: Gaussian Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture, Gaussian-JEPA, Joint-Embedding Predictive Learning for 3D Gaussian Splats
body: Gaussian-JEPA is a self-supervised pretraining method for 3D Gaussian assets that predicts latent features of masked target blocks from shared context, using joint-embedding predictive learning to avoid raw-attribute reconstruction. It sets itself apart from Gaussian-MAE by predicting latent representations instead of reconstructing Gaussian parameters, and from contrastive methods by explicitly supervising missing spatial content through latent prediction of held-out blocks. It builds on Momentum-GS by providing a robust, object-level feature representation that is consistent across stochastic resampling, which serves as a foundation for downstream tasks like shape completion and segmentation. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D Gaussian asset X represented as a set of anisotropic primitives with 14 parameters each: centroids C (3), opacity O (1), scales S (3), rotation quaternions R (4), and DC spherical-harmonic coefficients SH (3). Output: Frozen feature representations of Gaussian tokens that capture geometric and appearance information, optimized via a joint-embedding predictive objective. Data Structures and Layout: 1. Gaussian Primitive Vector: 14-dimensional vector per primitive. 2. Token Group: A set of k=32 primitives centered around a FPS-selected centroid. Each group is processed into a single token ti \in \mathbb{R}^{384}. 3. Token Sequence: T \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times 384}, where n=64 is the number of token groups. 4. Context: TC \in \mathbb{R}^{(n-nt) \times 384}, the tokens not in any target block. 5. Target Blocks: \{Bm\}{m=1}^M, non-overlapping sets of token indices. Preprocessing: 1. Sample p=1,024 distinct primitives from an 8,192-entry buffer with replacement. 2. Center centroids and divide by maximum radius to fit in a unit sphere. 3. Map opacity logits through sigmoid to [-1, 1]. 4. Exponentiate log-scales, center, and normalize in 3D attribute space. 5. Normalize rotation quaternions to unit length and sign-canonicalize by the first component. 6. Multiply DC coefficients by spherical-harmonic constant, clip to [-0.5, 0.5], and scale by \sqrt{2/3}. Tokenization: 1. Compute centroids C' of the sampled primitives. 2. Select n=64 centers U using Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) on C'. 3. For each center ui, gather k=32 neighbors Ii using hard KNN based on centroid distance. 4. Express neighborhood centroids relative to the group center ui. 5. Apply tokenizer \psi: Pointwise MLP: 14 \to 128 \to 256 with BatchNorm and ReLU. Max pooling over the k primitives to get a group descriptor. Concatenate descriptor with each local feature. Pointwise MLP: 512 \to 512 \to 384 with BatchNorm and ReLU. Max pooling to produce one 384-D token ti per group. 6. Assemble T = [t1, \dots, tn]. 7. Embed centers U using MLP \rho (3 \to 128 \to 384) for positional embeddings. Multi-Scale Target Sampling: 1. Define schedule s = [s1, \dots, sM] with s1 \ge \dots \ge sM and total budget nt = \sum sm. Default: M=4, s=[11, 9, 7, 5]. 2. Initialize available indices A0 = \{1, \dots, n\}. 3. For m = 1 to M: Select anchor am uniformly from A{m-1}. Select sm nearest available centers Bm to am. Update Am = A{m-1} \setminus Bm. 4. Context indices C = AM. Note: Non-overlap applies to token-center indices. Context and target tokens may share underlying Gaussian primitives due to independent KNN neighborhoods. Training Loop: 1. Online Encoder: Process context TC with online encoder f\theta to get ZC = f\theta(TC, \rho(UC)) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times (n-nt) \times 384}. 2. EMA Encoder: For each block m, process full token field T with EMA encoder f\xi to get Hm^\xi = f\xi(T, \rho(U)) \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times n \times 384}. 3. Target Selection: Select target features Zm^\xi = Hm^\xi[Bm] \in \mathbb{R}^{B \times sm \times 384}. 4. Context Projection: Map ZC to predictor width Dp=192: ZC' = Wp ZC. 5. Prediction: Create query q \in \mathbb{R}^{192}, repeat sm times: Qm = \mathbf{1}{sm} q^T. Concatenate context and queries: [ZC'; Qm]. Embed positions: \Pim = [\rho\phi(UC); \rho\phi(U{Bm})] where \rho\phi is 3 \to 128 \to 192 MLP. Pass through 4-layer Transformer predictor h\phi (width 192, 6 heads). Retain final sm query outputs Vm \in \mathbb{R}^{sm \times 192}. Apply linear heads rb (192 \to 384) for b \in \{\text{geo, app}\} to get predictions \hat{Z}m^b \in \mathbb{R}^{sm \times 384}. 6. Target Projections: For each Zm^\xi, apply two independent MLP projectors gb (384 \to 384 \to 384, GELU) to get Ym^b. Detach and normalize: Zm^b = \text{LN}(\text{sg}(Ym^b)). 7. Loss Computation: Prediction Loss: L{\text{pred}} = \frac{1}{M} \sum{m=1}^M \sum{b \in \{\text{geo, app}\}} \text{SmoothL1}(\hat{Z}m^b, Zm^b). Grounding Loss: Concatenate all Y^b across batch and blocks to Y^b \in \mathbb{R}^{Lt \times D}. Compute regularization R{\text{vis}}(Y^b): Centering: R{\text{center}} = \frac{1}{D} \|\mub\|^2, where \mub = \frac{1}{Lt} \sumi Yi^b. name: CityGS-X
head: Anchor-Based Octree 3D Gaussian Splatting (Baseline), CityGS-X backbone, UrbanGS
body: CityGS-X is a large-scale urban reconstruction method that extends block-based partitioning with a geometry-aware architecture, refining block boundaries according to building footprints to achieve high accuracy. It targets urban scenes by combining semantic segmentation to allocate Gaussians specifically on building facades and road surfaces, avoiding unnecessary density in empty space. Unlike its siblings which may use fixed grids or proxy meshes, CityGS-X uses an anchor-based octree where visible anchors generate "Neural Gaussians" via shared MLPs, decoupling spatial hierarchy from feature optimization to improve memory efficiency and rendering speed. Inputs: Sparse point cloud from Structure-from-Motion (SfM); semantic segmentation maps (for urban context); camera poses and intrinsics. Outputs: Rasterized image; optimized anchor features and Gaussian parameters. Data Structures: 1. Octree: Branching factor b. Levels l \in \{0, 1, \dots, L{max}\}, where l=0 is the coarsest. Voxel side length at level l is vl = v0 / b^l, where v0 is determined by scene scale. 2. Anchors: Each non-empty voxel instantiates one anchor. Total anchors N. Layout per anchor ai: fi \in \mathbb{R}^d: Learnable feature vector. pi \in \mathbb{R}^3: Position at voxel center. li: Level index. \{\delta^ki\}{k=1}^K: Set of K learnable offset vectors. Per-anchor scaling, rotation, and opacity parameters (base attributes). Note: The sources state that existing methods optimize fi independently across levels, but CityGS-X (as the baseline for TopoGS) retains this structure for the definition of the anchor generation. Algorithm Steps: 1. Octree Construction: Build an octree with branching factor b over the scene bounding volume using the SfM sparse point cloud. 2. Anchor Instantiation: For every non-empty voxel at every level l, instantiate an anchor at the voxel center. This yields N anchors organized into L{max} + 1 levels. 3. Visibility Filtering (Per Camera): Level-of-Detail (LoD) Filtering: For a training camera c, retain anchor ai at level li only if li \leq \hat{l}(pi, c). The threshold \hat{l} depends on the anchor-to-camera distance and a scene-dependent reference distance. View-Frustum Culling: Remove anchors outside the camera frustum. Let V be the resulting visible anchor set. Let mv \in \{0, 1\}^N be the Boolean mask selecting visible anchors. 4. Neural Gaussian Generation: For each visible anchor ai \in V: Compute viewing direction di and camera-relative distance. Decode attributes for K Neural Gaussians using three shared Multi-Layer Perceptrons (MLPs): MLP{op}: Decodes opacity. MLP{cov}: Decodes covariance (scaling/rotation). MLP{col}: Decodes color. Inputs to MLPs: Anchor feature fi, viewing direction di, and camera-relative distance. The offsets \{\delta^ki\} likely modulate these base attributes to create the K variants. 5. Rasterization: Rasterize the generated Gaussians via differentiable tile-based splatting to produce the final image. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def citygsxrender(anchors, camera, mlpop, mlpcov, mlpcol): """ anchors: List of Anchor objects. camera: Camera object with pose and intrinsics. mlpop, mlpcov, mlpcol: Shared MLPs. """ visibleanchors = [] # Step 3: Visibility Filtering for anchor in anchors: # LoD Filter # lhat depends on distance(anchor.pos, camera.pos) and scenerefdist if anchor.level > computelodthreshold(anchor.pos, camera, scenerefdist): continue # Frustum Cull if not isinfrustum(anchor.pos, camera): continue visibleanchors.append(anchor) gaussians = [] # Step 4: Neural Gaussian Generation for anchor in visibleanchors: # Compute view direction and relative distance viewdir = normalize(anchor.pos - camera.pos) reldist = distance(anchor.pos, camera.pos) # Decode base attributes from shared MLPs # Note: The exact input concatenation to MLPs is not fully specified, # but typically involves fi, viewdir, and reldist. baseopacity = mlpop(anchor.feature, viewdir, reldist) basecov = mlpcov(anchor.feature, viewdir, reldist) basecolor = mlpcol(anchor.feature, viewdir, reldist) # Generate K Neural Gaussians using offsets for k in range(anchor.numoffsets): offset = anchor.offsets[k] # Apply offset to base attributes # Specific combination of offset with base cov/opacity is not detailed in sources. # Assuming additive or multiplicative modulation. finalcov = applyoffset(basecov, offset) finalopacity = applyoffset(baseopacity, offset) finalcolor = applyoffset(basecolor, offset) gaussians.append(Gaussian( pos=anchor.pos, cov=finalcov, opacity=finalopacity, color=finalcolor)) # Step 5: Rasterization image = tilebasedsplatting(gaussians, camera) return image Parameters: b: Octree branching factor. Not given in the sources. L{max}: Maximum octree depth. Not given in the sources. v0: Initial voxel side length. Determined by scene scale. K: Number of Neural Gaussians per anchor. Not given in the sources. d: Dimension of anchor feature vector fi. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases: Empty Voxels: Anchors are only instantiated in non-empty voxels, reducing memory overhead. Far-away Anchors: LoD filtering prevents rendering sub-pixel Gaussians for distant anchors, improving performance. Time Complexity: Rendering time depends on the number of visible anchors |V| and the number of Neural Gaussians K per anchor. O(|V| \cdot K). LoD filtering reduces |V| significantly for distant views. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the total number of anchors N and the feature dimension d. O(N \cdot d). The octree structure allows sparse storage. Strengths: High accuracy in urban reconstruction due to geometry-aware block refinement and semantic allocation. Efficient rendering via LoD and frustum culling. Decoupled feature optimization allows for hierarchical management. Limitations: Relies on SfM sparse point cloud for initialization, which may be sparse in textureless urban areas. Independent optimization of features across levels may lead to inconsistencies (a problem TopoGS aims to solve). When to use: Large-scale urban scenes with distinct building facades and road surfaces. When high geometric accuracy is required for urban planning or autonomous driving simulations. When not to use: Indoor scenes or scenes with complex dynamic objects not covered by semantic segmentation (use StreetGaussians or Momentum-GS instead). CityGS-X originates from the need to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to city-scale environments. It builds on block-based partitioning methods like VastGaussian and CityGaussian, which divide scenes into overlapping tiles. CityGS-X extends this by incorporating geometry-aware architecture and semantic segmentation to refine block boundaries and allocate Gaussians only on relevant surfaces (facades, roads). It serves as the baseline for "Anchor-Based Octree 3D Gaussian Splatting" methods, where anchors in an octree tree generate Gaussians via neural networks. 3D Gaussian Splatting Rasterization: A Survey, https://doi.org/10.20944/preprints202607.0776.v2, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) TopoGS: Topology-Aware Anchor Feature Aggregation for Large-Scale 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.27868, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial)

name: Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representations
head: Gaussian Pyramid, Multi-resolution Gaussian Pyramid
body: Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representations render very large datasets in real time by storing a multi-resolution pyramid of Gaussians. This method addresses the memory and bandwidth bottlenecks inherent in flat 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) by organizing primitives into a spatial hierarchy, allowing the renderer to adaptively select detail levels based on view distance and available resources. It sets itself apart from flat splatting by introducing spatial locality and from sibling methods like Budgeted-GS by relying on strict tree-based cut conditions rather than global budget optimization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of 3D Gaussians \{Gi\} representing the scene, typically derived from a trained 3DGS model. Output: A hierarchical data structure (e.g., octree or pyramid) where each node contains aggregated Gaussian parameters, enabling real-time rendering of large-scale scenes. Data Structures: The method constructs a multi-resolution pyramid or tree structure. Each node in the hierarchy summarizes the radiance and opacity of its children, effectively merging Gaussians in occupied regions. The exact bit-packing and field layouts for the aggregated Gaussians are not specified in the provided sources. Steps: 1. Hierarchy Construction: Build a spatial hierarchy (such as an octree) over the scene geometry. Each node is associated with a merged Gaussian that summarizes the radiance and opacity of its children. 2. Aggregation: For each node, aggregate the properties of its child Gaussians. This creates a coarser representation at higher levels of the pyramid. 3. Traversal and Selection: During rendering, traverse the hierarchy to select the appropriate level of detail (LoD) for each view. The selection is view-adaptive, allowing the renderer to choose a sparse subset of nodes that approximate the scene geometry at varying distances. 4. Splatting: Render the selected Gaussians using standard 3DGS splatting techniques. Gaussians are only stored in occupied regions, which naturally adapts to view distance and improves memory efficiency. Parameters: Hierarchy Depth: Determines the number of resolution levels. Not given in the sources. Aggregation Method: How child Gaussians are merged into parent nodes. Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Aggregating Gaussians may introduce approximation errors. The sources do not specify error bounds. Boundaries: The method handles boundaries by only storing Gaussians in occupied regions. It uses a "capacity floor" derived from optimal transport. Enables real-time rendering of ultra-large-scale datasets by organizing Gaussians into a recursive tree structure. It differs from flat splatting by introducing spatial hierarchy and from Budgeted-GS by relying on a strict tree-based cut condition. Time Complexity: Real-time rendering is achieved through adaptive level selection and efficient GPU execution. The exact complexity is not specified. Memory Complexity: Memory efficiency is improved by storing Gaussians only in occupied regions and using a multi-resolution pyramid. Strengths: Real-time performance on large datasets; adaptive detail selection; memory efficiency. Limitations: The specific implementation details (e.g., exact aggregation formulas, traversal algorithms) are not provided in the sources. When to use: When rendering very large datasets in real time is required. When not to use: When high-fidelity, non-hierarchical rendering is needed without memory constraints. It builds on CityGaussian / VastGaussian / DoGaussian, which divides the city into tiles and uses a LoD pyramid for streaming. name: Budgeted-GS
head: Factoring LOD
body: Budgeted-GS is a post-hoc method that converts any trained 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) model into a multi-resolution hierarchy of moment-matched aggregates, enabling real-time rendering of city-scale scenes on consumer GPUs by selecting the level of detail that fits the target device's memory. It solves the problem of excessive memory consumption in large-scale 3DGS by introducing a "capacity floor" derived from optimal transport in phase space, which determines the minimum number of primitives required for a given error budget, allowing the same model to serve GPUs with widely different memory capacities. Unlike standard 3DGS which optimizes a fixed set of primitives, Budgeted-GS separates the representation into a hierarchy where a single quality parameter selects the appropriate level of detail per view, ensuring that redundant primitives are merged or dropped based on a pixel-footprint scheduler. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A trained 3DGS model consisting of a flat set of raw planks (Gaussian primitives) defined by their spatial cells, opacity weights, and value models. Output: A rendered image stream emitted to any standard splatting rasterizer, where the stream consists of selected primitives from the factoring tree based on the current view and memory budget. Data Structures: The core data structure is the Factoring Tree, an octree of scale bands. Nodes: Each node corresponds to a leaf in the spatial octree and a specific scale band. Content: Nodes contain "moment-matched equivalent planks," which are pre-computed aggregates of raw planks that preserve the first and second moments (mean and covariance) of the original primitives within that spatial and scale region. Layout: The tree is structured as leaf × scale-band. Raw planks are stored at the finest scale bands, while coarser bands store aggregated planks. Steps: 1. Construction: Convert the trained model (flat set of raw planks) into the factoring tree of leaf × scale-band nodes containing moment-matched equivalent planks. This construction pass takes a few seconds. 2. Scheduling: For each view, determine the level of detail using a one-parameter pixel-footprint scheduler. 3. Selection: Select raw, fine, or aggregate content based on the threshold t. If the pixel footprint of a primitive is smaller than t, use aggregated content; otherwise, use raw or fine content. 4. Rendering: Emit the selected stream of primitives to a standard splatting rasterizer. Formulas: The selection threshold t is calculated as: t = c \cdot \frac{d}{f} Where: t: The pixel-footprint threshold. c: A constant parameter. d: Distance from the camera to the primitive. f: Focal length of the camera. The capacity floor, which dictates the minimum number of primitives N^ per tile j, is given by: N^j \propto \frac{Kj sj}{dj} Where: Kj: A constant related to the tile. sj: Scale of the primitives in tile j. dj: Distance to tile j. Parameters: c: Constant in the pixel-footprint threshold formula. Typical value not given in the sources. t: Threshold for LOD selection. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method relies on moment-matching, which may introduce approximation errors when aggregating primitives. The sources mention "bounded volumetric loss" but do not specify the error bounds. Boundaries: The octree structure handles spatial boundaries, but the scale bands must be carefully defined to ensure smooth transitions between LOD levels. Not given in the sources. Degenerate Input: The method assumes a trained 3DGS model. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def distance(p1, p2): """Euclidean distance between two 3D points.""" return math.sqrt(sum((a - b) 2 for a, b in zip(p1, p2))) def computefootprint(plank, cameraposition, camerafocallength): """Compute pixel footprint by projecting Gaussian covariance to screen space.""" # Standard implementation: transform covariance to camera space, # project to 2D Jacobian, compute bounding box area in pixels. # For this article, we assume the primitive provides its projected radius. return plank.getscreenradius() 2.0 def budgetedgsselectprimitives(cameraposition, camerafocallength, tree, constantc): """ Selects primitives from the factoring tree based on the pixel-footprint threshold. Args: cameraposition: 3D coordinates of the camera. camerafocallength: Focal length f. tree: List of nodes, each containing 'center', 'scaleband', 'rawplanks', 'aggregateplanks'. constantc: Constant c for threshold calculation. Returns: List of selected primitive objects to be passed to a rasterizer. """ selected = [] for node in tree: d = distance(cameraposition, node.center) t = constantc (d / camerafocallength) # Select raw/fine or aggregate based on footprint threshold for plank in node.rawplanks: footprint = computefootprint(plank, cameraposition, camerafocallength) if footprint < t: # Use aggregate if available, else raw if node.aggregateplanks: selected.extend(node.aggregateplanks) else: selected.append(plank) else: selected.append(plank) # Add aggregate planks for regions where they are selected if node.aggregateplanks: for aggplank in node.aggregateplanks: footprint = computefootprint(aggplank, cameraposition, camerafocallength) if footprint < t: selected.append(aggplank) return selected def rendersplats(primitives, camera): """Standard splatting rasterization step.""" # Implementation details for rasterizing Gaussian splats are standard and external to this method. # This function accumulates screen-space contributions per pixel. return [] A quality modeling approach that classifies 3DGS videos into four tiers of models with varying qualities using a binary Gaussian mask based on significance distribution, considering both opacity and ellipsoid size to filter out less significant primitives. It identifies and filters out Gaussian primitives with lower transparency and smaller ellipsoid sizes, as they have minimal impact on rendering quality. Three distinct masking thresholds are established to classify the 3DGS videos within each Group of Frames (GoF) into four tiers of models with varying qualities. Thresholds are determined by referencing previously obtained saliency distribution maps and adjusting thresholds based on saliency weights within different tiles; for high-saliency regions, as many Gaussian primitives as possible are retained, while for less visually significant regions, thresholds are increased to exclude unnecessary primitives. All tiles of different quality levels are encoded to facilitate subsequent delivery from server to client. Time Complexity: The construction pass takes a few seconds. Rendering time depends on the number of selected primitives, which is dynamically adjusted by the scheduler. Memory Complexity: The method reduces memory usage by aggregating primitives, allowing city-scale scenes to fit on consumer GPUs. The exact memory savings depend on the scene and the chosen quality parameter. Measured Performance: Validated on 13 public scenes under a preregistered protocol, demonstrating real-time rendering of city-scale scenes. Scaling: The method scales to large scenes by using a multi-resolution hierarchy. The capacity floor provides a theoretical limit on the number of primitives needed. Strengths: Enables real-time rendering of large-scale scenes on consumer hardware; flexible quality adjustment via a single parameter; avoids wasted optimization effort in training. Limitations: Requires a post-hoc construction pass; relies on the accuracy of the moment-matching approximation; performance depends on the scene's complexity and the chosen quality parameter. When to use: When rendering large-scale, city-scale scenes on hardware with limited memory. When not to use: For small-scale scenes where standard 3DGS fits in memory; when training time is a critical constraint and budget-centered training is not used. Budgeted-GS was introduced in the paper "Budgeted-GS: Real-Time Large-Scale Gaussian Splatting via Factoring LOD". It is grounded in a measurable capacity floor derived from optimal transport in phase space, which answers how many primitives a scene actually needs and how many can safely be given up. The method builds on the principles of 3D Gaussian Splatting Parent but extends it to handle large-scale scenes by introducing a multi-resolution hierarchy and a budget-centered training approach. name: Gaussian Hierarchies
head: H-3DGS hierarchy
body: Gaussian Hierarchies enable real-time rendering of ultra-large-scale 3D Gaussian Splatting datasets by organizing Gaussians into a recursive tree structure. It solves the memory and bandwidth bottlenecks of flat Gaussian representations by providing a view-adaptive Level of Detail (LoD) mechanism, allowing the renderer to select a sparse subset of nodes that approximate the scene geometry at varying distances. It differs from flat splatting by introducing spatial hierarchy and from sibling methods like Budgeted-GS by relying on a strict tree-based cut condition rather than global budget optimization. Inputs: A set of original 3D Gaussians (leaves), camera position \mathbf{p}{\text{cam}}, and a global LoD threshold T. Outputs: A cut set of nodes to render. Data Structures: The structure is a tree where: Leaves: Correspond to the original optimized Gaussians. Non-leaf nodes: Approximate their children. Each node i has a mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i and a scale metric si^j. Tree Layout: Implicit or explicit parent-child pointers. Algorithm: 1. Initialize an empty cut set \mathcal{C}. 2. Perform a Breadth-First Search (BFS) starting from the root node. 3. For each node i visited: a. Evaluate the cut condition c{\text{hier}}(i, \text{cam}). b. If c{\text{hier}}(i, \text{cam}) is true: i. Add node i to \mathcal{C}. ii. Skip processing all children of node i. c. If false, continue BFS to process children of node i. 4. Return \mathcal{C}. Formulas: The cut condition is defined as: c{\text{hier}}(i, \text{cam}) = \left\| \boldsymbol{\mu}i - \mathbf{p}{\text{cam}} \right\|2 \geq md(i) where: \boldsymbol{\mu}i is the mean position of node i. \mathbf{p}{\text{cam}} is the camera position. md(i) is the distance threshold for node i, calculated as: md(i) = \frac{T}{\maxj si^j} T is a global LoD threshold parameter. si^j represents the scale components of node i. Parameters: T: Global LoD threshold. Typical values are not explicitly given in the sources, but it controls the granularity of the hierarchy. Edge Cases: Precision: Distance calculations must handle floating-point precision near the threshold boundary. Boundaries: The cut set must be proper, meaning no parent or child of an included node is also included. Degenerate Input: If a node has no children (leaf), the condition is evaluated against the leaf's properties. This strategy determines how nearby Gaussians are merged into non-leaf nodes. The sources indicate that non-leaf nodes approximate their children, but the specific grouping algorithm (e.g., clustering, spatial hashing) is not detailed in the provided excerpts. It is a prerequisite for building the hierarchy tree. Time Complexity: The BFS traversal is linear with respect to the number of nodes in the hierarchy. The cut condition evaluation is constant time per node. Memory Complexity: The hierarchy structure adds overhead for parent-child pointers and aggregated node properties, but allows for significant reduction in the number of Gaussians rendered per frame by skipping distant subtrees. Performance: Limits typical training to roughly 500,000 Gaussians per GB of GPU memory, imposing strict constraints on detail and extent without hierarchy. With hierarchy, ultra-large scale reconstructions become feasible. Strengths: View-adaptive LoD, efficient memory usage for large scenes. Limitations: Requires hierarchical construction; performance depends on the quality of the cut condition and tree balance. Gaussian Hierarchies were introduced in H-3DGS by Kerbl et al. in 2024. The method addresses the memory limitations of standard 3D Gaussian Splatting, which typically supports only ~500,000 Gaussians per GB of GPU memory. It enables real-time rendering of ultra-large-scale reconstructions by leveraging external memory and hierarchical culling. A LoD of Gaussians: Unified Training and Rendering for Ultra-Large Scale Reconstruction with External Memory, https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2507.01110, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Gaussian Merging and Retrieval
head: Adaptive Merging, Screen-size based Merging
body: Adaptive Gaussian Merging and Retrieval is a dynamic memory management and Level of Detail (LoD) strategy for 3D Gaussian Splatting that maintains a hierarchical structure based on primitive screen size to handle large scenes with limited GPU memory. It solves the problem of VRAM exhaustion during online optimization by merging sub-pixel Gaussians into coarser parents and offloading them to CPU RAM, while retrieving finer details when the camera zooms in. Unlike static hierarchies, this method is view-adaptive, triggering merges and retrievals based on the current viewpoint's projection of the Gaussians. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives Gi organized in a hierarchy; the current camera viewpoint (projection matrix and intrinsics); a merging threshold \taul; a retrieval threshold \tauh. Outputs: An updated active set of Gaussian primitives (leaves and intermediate nodes) optimized for rendering; updated parent-child links in the hierarchy. The hierarchy consists of nodes. Each node stores: 1. Gaussian Parameters: Position \mathbf{p}, opacity \alpha, rotation \mathbf{q} (quaternion), scale \mathbf{s}, and Spherical Harmonics (SH) coefficients. 2. Topology: IDs of parent node(s) and child node(s). 3. Status: Flags indicating if the node is currently in the active set (on GPU) or offloaded (on CPU). \taul = 0.5 pixels: The screen size threshold below which a Gaussian is considered sub-pixel and eligible for merging. \tauh = 1 pixel: The screen size threshold above which a merged node triggers retrieval of its finer children. Merge Trigger Threshold: Merging is only triggered if more than 20% of the Gaussians satisfy Si < \taul. 1. Compute Screen Sizes: For every Gaussian Gi in the current active set, compute its screen size Si from the current viewpoint. This involves projecting the Gaussian's covariance ellipse onto the image plane and measuring its extent in pixels. 2. Check Merge Condition: Count the number of Gaussians where Si < \taul. If this count exceeds 20% of the total active Gaussians, proceed to merge; otherwise, skip merging for this frame. 3. Select Candidates: Identify the set of Gaussians C{merge} = \{Gi \mid Si < \taul\}. 4. Grouping via KNN: For each candidate Gi \in C{merge}, find the 4 closest Gaussians using a fast K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) search. 5. Deduplication: Remove duplicate entries in the grouping list to ensure a Gaussian primitive does not have multiple parents in the same merge operation. 6. Merge Operation: Perform merging on groups of 4 Gaussians using KL-divergence based merging. This creates a new parent Gaussian G{parent} that approximates the children. 7. Update Hierarchy: Remove the sub-pixel children from the active set. Add G{parent} to the active set. Establish child-parent links between G{parent} and its children. Optimization: If a Gaussian already has a parent, check if all its children are being merged. If so, "pull" the existing parent from the hierarchy (promote it to active) instead of creating a new node. 8. Offloading: Move small footprint leaf Gaussian primitives that are not in the active set to CPU RAM to free VRAM. 9. Retrieval (Navigation): When navigating, for any merged node G{parent} in the active set, compute its screen size S{parent}. If S{parent} > \tauh: Reload the finer child Gaussians from CPU RAM to GPU. Update the coarse parent nodes with the new children's parameters. Remove G{parent} from the active set. Add the children to the active set. 10. Loop Closure Handling: When loop closure is detected, move all Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction of Unordered Input with Global Consistency nodes (hierarchy nodes following the transform of the keyframe most used to spawn its children) asynchronously to avoid latency. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def adaptivemergeandretrieve(activegaussians, cameraview, taul=0.5, tauh=1.0, mergethreshold=0.2): """ activegaussians: List of Gaussian objects with fields: id, params, parentid, childrenids, isoffloaded cameraview: Object with project() method to compute screen size """ # Step 1: Compute screen sizes for g in activegaussians: g.screensize = computescreensize(g.params, cameraview) # Step 2: Check merge condition subpixelgaussians = [g for g in activegaussians if g.screensize < taul] if len(subpixelgaussians) <= len(activegaussians) mergethreshold: # Not enough sub-pixel Gaussians to trigger merge return activegaussians # Step 3 & 4: Grouping via KNN # Note: KNN search is performed on the spatial coordinates of subpixelgaussians mergegroups = [] for g in subpixelgaussians: neighbors = fastknnsearch(g, subpixelgaussians, k=4) mergegroups.append([g] + neighbors) # Step 5: Deduplication # Ensure no Gaussian has multiple parents in the same batch uniquegroups = removeduplicates(mergegroups) # Step 6 & 7: Merge and Update Hierarchy newactiveset = [] nodestoremove = set() nodestoadd = [] for group in uniquegroups: # Step 6: Merge using KL-divergence parentgaussian = kldivergencemerge(group) # Step 7: Update links for child in group: nodestoremove.add(child.id) child.parentid = parentgaussian.id if parentgaussian.id not in [n.id for n in nodestoadd]: nodestoadd.append(parentgaussian) # Optimization: Check if existing parent should be pulled # If a Gaussian already has a parent and all its children are in nodestoremove, # promote the existing parent instead of adding a new one. # (Implementation detail: Check existing parents of children in group) # Update active set for g in activegaussians: if g.id not in nodestoremove: newactiveset.append(g) newactiveset.extend(nodestoadd) # Step 8: Offloading # Gaussians not in newactiveset and marked as leaf/small are offloaded to CPU for g in activegaussians: if g.id not in [ng.id for ng in newactiveset]: g.isoffloaded = True return newactiveset def retrieveifzoomed(activegaussians, cameraview, tauh=1.0): """ Called during navigation to retrieve finer details if zoomed in. """ newactiveset = [] nodestoreload = [] for g in activegaussians: if g.screensize > tauh and g.haschildren(): # Step 9: Retrieve children = loadchildrenfromcpu(g.childrenids) nodestoreload.extend(children) # Remove parent from active set pass else: newactiveset.append(g) newactiveset.extend(nodestoreload) return newactiveset Time Complexity: The merge operation involves a KNN search, which is typically O(N \log N) or O(N) with approximate methods, where N is the number of sub-pixel Gaussians. The merge itself is constant time per group of 4. Retrieval is proportional to the number of nodes exceeding \tauh. Memory Complexity: Reduces GPU VRAM usage by offloading sub-pixel Gaussians to CPU RAM. The hierarchy structure adds minimal overhead (parent/child IDs). Performance: Enables handling of large scenes with limited GPU memory. The 20% trigger threshold prevents frequent merging overhead. Double buffering is used to avoid stutter during retrieval. Strengths: Dynamic adaptation to view; efficient memory usage; fast hierarchy updates compared to static methods. Limitations: Requires careful tuning of \taul and \tauh. KNN search can be costly if not optimized. Asynchronous updates for loop closure are necessary to avoid latency. Origin: Proposed in "Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction of Unordered Input with Global Consistency" (2024). Context: Part of the broader effort to scale 3D Gaussian Splatting to large-scale scenes (e.g., cities) where memory constraints are a bottleneck. It builds on the concept of hierarchical 3D Gaussian representations. Usage: Used in online/progressive reconstruction systems where keyframes are added incrementally. Immediate 3D Gaussian Splat Reconstruction of Unordered Input with Global Consistency, https://doi.org/10.1145/3799902.3811167, fetched 2026-10-26

name: Hierarchical LOD for 3D Gaussian Splitting
head: 3DGS Hierarchy
body: Hierarchical LOD for 3D Gaussian Splitting enables real-time rendering of very large scenes by organizing 3D Gaussian primitives into a tree-based hierarchy with interior and leaf nodes. It solves the resource limitation problem where optimizing and rendering every primitive in a massive scene is infeasible. Unlike sibling methods that may rely on static tiling or specific street-level constraints, this method constructs a dynamic Level-of-Detail (LOD) cut based on projected screen size, allowing for smooth transitions between detail levels [S1, 6143-citygaussian-vastgaussian-dogaussian.md]. Inputs: A set of 3D Gaussian primitives \{gi\}, each defined by mean \mui, covariance \Sigmai, spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and opacity oi. Outputs: A hierarchy tree where every node (leaf or interior) is associated with a 3D Gaussian, and a rendering cut for a given view V. Data Structures: Node: Contains attributes \mu, \Sigma, SH, \text{falloff} (opacity for interior nodes), and an Axis-Aligned Bounding Box (AABB). Hierarchy: A binary tree structure. Leaf nodes correspond to original optimized Gaussians. Interior nodes correspond to merged Gaussians derived from their children. Steps: 1. Build BVH: Create an initial AABB enclosing all primitives. The extent is calculated as 3\times the stored size of the primitives (using the cutoff from the original 3DGS paper). This AABB is the root node. Recursively perform a binary median split on the current node to create child nodes. To split, project the means of all Gaussians in the group onto the longest axis of their bounding box. Partition the group by assigning each primitive to a child based on the position of its projected mean relative to the median of all projections. 2. Merge Interior Nodes (Bottom-Up): Starting from the leaves, recursively merge children to compute attributes for interior nodes. Compute normalized weights wi for each child i: wi = \frac{w'i}{\sum{i'} w'{i'}} where w'i are unnormalized merging weights. Calculate unnormalized merging weights w'i based on the projected contribution of the child Gaussian. Assuming isotropic Gaussians with little overlap: w'i = oi Si where Si is the surface of the ellipsoid, proportional to \sqrt{|\Sigma'i|} (the square root of the determinant of the 2D covariance). In practice, Si is computed directly as the projected surface area. Compute the merged mean \mu^{(l+1)}: \mu^{(l+1)} = \sum{i}^{N} wi \mui^{(l)} Compute the merged covariance \Sigma^{(l+1)} using the parallel axis theorem: \Sigma^{(l+1)} = \sum{i}^{N} wi \left( \Sigmai^{(l)} + (\mui^{(l)} - \mu^{(l+1)})(\mui^{(l)} - \mu^{(l+1)})^T \right) Compute the merged SH coefficients: SH^{(l+1)} = \sum{i}^{N} SHi^{(l)} wi Compute the merged falloff (opacity for interior nodes): \text{falloff}^{(l+1)} = \sum{i}^{N} oi^{(l)} wi Note: This value can exceed 1. It is called "falloff" because it behaves as opacity during rendering, but resulting alpha values are clamped to 1. 3. Hierarchy Cut Selection: For a given view V, define the granularity \epsilon(n) of a node n as the projected screen size of its bounding box over leaf Gaussians. Specifically, use the largest dimension of the bounding box. Select a cut by including nodes n whose projected AABB axis lengths \epsilon(n) are smaller than a target granularity \tau\epsilon (e.g., 1 pixel). The cut is found in linear time (or constant time per node in parallel settings) because a parent's AABB is never smaller than its children's. 4. Smooth Transition: The cut may contain nodes that over-fulfill the granularity criterion. To ensure smooth transitions, interpolate between a node n and its parent p. Calculate interpolation weight tn based on \epsilon(n) and \epsilon(p). Pitfall Handling: Direct interpolation of rotation axes can cause undesired rotations. Instead, render the two children using the same parameters as the parent, and progressively interpolate towards their separate values. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def buildhierarchy(primitives): """ primitives: List of Gaussian objects with attributes: mu: (3,) mean position Sigma: (3,3) covariance matrix SH: Spherical Harmonic coefficients o: opacity size: stored size for AABB expansion """ # Step 1: Build BVH rootaabb = computeinitialaabb(primitives) # 3x stored size root = Node(aabb=rootaabb, children=[], isleaf=False) queue = [root] while queue: node = queue.pop(0) if node.isleaf: continue # Leaf nodes are original primitives # Project means onto longest axis of node's AABB longestaxis = getlongestaxis(node.aabb) projections = [dot(p.mu, longestaxis) for p in node.children] medianproj = median(projections) leftchildren = [] rightchildren = [] for i, p in enumerate(node.children): if projections[i] < medianproj: leftchildren.append(p) else: rightchildren.append(p) # Create child nodes leftnode = createnode(leftchildren) rightnode = createnode(rightchildren) node.children = [leftnode, rightnode] queue.append(leftnode) queue.append(rightnode) return root def mergenode(node): """ Recursively merge children to compute interior node attributes. Called bottom-up. """ if node.isleaf: return node # Leaf attributes are already optimized left = mergenode(node.children[0]) right = mergenode(node.children[1]) # Compute unnormalized weights based on projected surface # Si is proportional to sqrt(det(Sigma'i)) wprimeleft = left.o left.Si wprimeright = right.o right.Si wsum = wprimeleft + wprimeright wleft = wprimeleft / wsum wright = wprimeright / wsum # Merge Mean node.mu = wleft left.mu + wright right.mu # Merge Covariance (Parallel Axis Theorem) diffleft = left.mu - node.mu diffright = right.mu - node.mu node.Sigma = (wleft (left.Sigma + outerproduct(diffleft, diffleft)) + wright (right.Sigma + outerproduct(diffright, diffright))) # Merge SH node.SH = wleft left.SH + wright right.SH # Merge Falloff (Opacity) node.falloff = wleft left.o + wright right.o # Update AABB node.aabb = unionaabb(left.aabb, right.aabb) return node def selectcut(root, viewmatrix, resolution, tauepsilon=1.0): """ Select nodes for rendering based on projected granularity. Returns list of (node, interpolationweight) tuples. """ cut = [] def traverse(node, parentnode): # Project AABB to screen space projectedbbox = projectaabb(node.aabb, viewmatrix, resolution) # Granularity is the largest dimension of the projected bbox epsilonn = max(projectedbbox.width, projectedbbox.height) # If node is smaller than threshold, include it if epsilonn <= tauepsilon: # Check if parent is also in cut or needs interpolation if parentnode is not None: projectedbboxp = projectaabb(parentnode.aabb, viewmatrix, resolution) epsilonp = max(projectedbboxp.width, projectedbboxp.height) # Interpolation weight calculation # tn determines how much to blend between parent and child # If epsilonn is much smaller than epsilonp, tn approaches 1 (use child) # If epsilonn is close to epsilonp, tn approaches 0 (use parent) # Implementation detail: exact formula for tn not fully specified in sources, # but relies on comparing epsilon(n) and epsilon(p). tn = computeinterpolationweight(epsilonn, epsilonp) cut.append((node, tn, parentnode)) else: cut.append((node, 1.0, None)) else: # If node is too large, do not include it or its children return for child in node.children: traverse(child, node) traverse(root, None) return cut def rendercut(cut, viewmatrix): """ Render the selected cut with smooth transitions. """ for node, tn, parentnode in cut: if parentnode is not None: # Render child with parent's parameters, interpolating to child's rendergaussianwithinterpolation(parentnode, node, tn, viewmatrix) else: rendergaussian(node, viewmatrix) Time Complexity: Hierarchy construction is linear with respect to the number of primitives for the BVH build and merging. Cut selection is linear time (or constant time per node in parallel settings). Memory Complexity: Requires storing the hierarchy tree. Interior nodes add memory overhead but allow for significant reduction in the number of primitives rendered at a distance. Performance: Enables real-time rendering of very large datasets by reducing the number of rasterized Gaussians for distant content. Strengths: Maintains the fast rasterization routine of leaf nodes for interior nodes; provides a good tradeoff between quality and speed. Limitations: Merging strategy assumes isotropic Gaussians with little overlap for weight calculation; violations of this assumption may reduce quality at higher LOD levels. Ambiguity in rotation axes requires special handling during interpolation. This method was introduced in the paper "A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets". It addresses the problem of limited available resources for optimization when dealing with data that is much sparser than traditional radiance field captures. The method subdivides the scene into chunks, optimizes them independently, and builds a hierarchy for each chunk to enable LOD-based real-time rendering. A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets, https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p-mb2TzVJZk, fetched 2026-10-31

name: Hierarchy Cut Selection and Level Switching
head: Granularity-based Cut Selection, Smooth Level Switching
body: This method selects a specific cut through a hierarchical tree of 3D Gaussians to maximize rendering performance while maintaining visual quality, based on the projected screen size of nodes. It enables smooth transitions between hierarchy levels by interpolating Gaussian attributes (position, color, covariance) rather than abruptly swapping nodes, ensuring visual continuity during level-of-detail changes. It differs from sibling methods by using a granularity-based threshold on the largest dimension of the projected bounding box to determine the cut, and by explicitly handling orientation mismatches during hierarchy generation to prevent interpolation artifacts. Inputs: A hierarchical tree of 3D Gaussians, where each node n contains a set of leaf Gaussians and stores the axis-aligned bounding box (AABB) of its contained leaf Gaussians. A camera view V. A target granularity parameter \tau\epsilon (e.g., 1 pixel). Outputs: A set of nodes forming the "cut" through the hierarchy to be rendered. Interpolation weights tn for nodes undergoing transition. Node Structure: Each node n in the hierarchy stores: children: List of child nodes. parent: Reference to parent node. leafgaussians: List of 3D Gaussian primitives contained directly in this node (if it is a leaf in the hierarchy, or the base primitives if it is an internal node aggregating leaves). aabb: Axis-aligned bounding box encompassing all leaf Gaussians contained within the subtree of n. This is pre-computed during hierarchy generation. granularity: The projected screen size \epsilon(n), computed once per view. 1. Compute Granularity: For each node n in the hierarchy, compute its granularity \epsilon(n) for the current view V. Retrieve the AABB of node n. Identify the largest dimension of this bounding box, denoted as L{max}(n). Project L{max}(n) onto the screen plane using the camera projection matrix for view V. Let the resulting screen-space length be \epsilon(n). 2. Select Cut: Identify the nodes to include in the rendering cut. Iterate through all nodes n in the hierarchy. A node n is included in the cut if: 1. \epsilon(n) < \tau\epsilon (the node's projected size is smaller than the target granularity). 2. \epsilon(parent(n)) \ge \tau\epsilon (the parent's projected size is not smaller than the target granularity). This logic ensures that for any branch, either all children are selected (if the parent is too large) or the parent is selected (if all children are small enough), but never a mix that violates the hierarchy structure. Note: Due to the hierarchy generation properties, the AABB of a parent can never appear smaller than one of its children in screen space, guaranteeing a valid cut. 3. Calculate Interpolation Weights: For nodes n that are in a transition state (i.e., they are candidates for inclusion but their parent is also being considered or they are blending with their parent), calculate the interpolation weight tn. If node n is in the cut and its parent p is not (or vice versa, depending on the transition direction), compute: tn = \frac{\tau\epsilon - \epsilon(n)}{\epsilon(p) - \epsilon(n)} Clamp tn to [0, 1]. If tn = 0, use the parent's attributes. If tn = 1, use the child's attributes. Intermediate values blend the attributes. 4. Interpolate Gaussian Attributes: For each Gaussian in the cut (or blending between parent and child), interpolate its properties. Position, Color, Spherical Harmonics: Interpolate linearly using tn. Covariance: Do not interpolate the covariance matrix directly. Instead: 1. Decompose the covariance into scale and rotation components for both parent and child. 2. Interpolate the scale linearly. 3. Interpolate the rotation linearly (not using slerp). 4. Reconstruct the covariance from the interpolated scale and rotation. Opacity (\alpha): Interpolate opacity carefully to maintain color consistency. At the start of the transition (when blending parent to children), the children share the parent's attributes initially. To ensure the blended color of the children equals the parent's color at the start of the transition, modify the child's opacity \alpha' using the parent's opacity \alphap. For two children, solve for \alpha' in the equation: \alphap cp = \alpha' cp + (1 - \alpha') \alpha' cp This yields: \alpha' = \frac{1}{1 - (1 - \alphap) \frac{1}{2}} Use this \alpha' to blend \alpha from the parent to the children using the same linear interpolation scheme as other attributes. 5. Orientation Matching (Pre-computation): During hierarchy generation (not per-frame), perform orientation matching to prevent interpolation artifacts. Starting from the root, recursively reinterpret the axes of orientation for each child Gaussian. The goal is to minimize the relative rotation between the child node and its parent. This is done via exhaustive search over possible axis permutations/rotations. This step prevents undesired rotations when interpolating Gaussians with the same shape (covariance) but different rotation/scaling orientations. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def computegranularity(node, cameraview): """ Computes the projected screen size of the largest dimension of the node's AABB. """ aabb = node.aabb # Get the largest dimension of the AABB maxdim = max(aabb.max - aabb.min) # Project this length onto the screen using the camera view # This involves projecting the AABB corners or simply the diagonal length # into screen space and taking the max extent. # For simplicity, assume a function that projects a 3D length to screen pixels projectedsize = projectlengthtoscreen(maxdim, cameraview) return projectedsize def selectcut(hierarchyroot, targetgranularity, cameraview): """ Selects the cut through the hierarchy based on granularity. Returns a list of nodes to render and their interpolation weights. """ cutnodes = [] transitionnodes = [] # Nodes that need blending with parent # Pre-compute granularity for all nodes # In practice, this can be done in a single pass or cached for node in hierarchyroot.traverseall(): node.granularity = computegranularity(node, cameraview) # Find the cut for node in hierarchyroot.traverseall(): if node.parent is None: continue parent = node.parent childgran = node.granularity parentgran = parent.granularity # Condition: Child is smaller than threshold, Parent is not if childgran < targetgranularity and parentgran >= targetgranularity: cutnodes.append(node) # This node is transitioning from parent to child # Calculate interpolation weight # tn = (tau - epsilon(n)) / (epsilon(p) - epsilon(n)) denominator = parentgran - childgran if denominator == 0: tn = 1.0 # Avoid division by zero, though logically parent >= child else: tn = (targetgranularity - childgran) / denominator tn = clamp(tn, 0.0, 1.0) transitionnodes.append((node, parent, tn)) return cutnodes, transitionnodes def interpolategaussianattributes(parentgauss, childgauss, t, alphap): """ Interpolates Gaussian attributes between parent and child. """ result = Gaussian() # Position, Color, SH: Linear interpolation result.position = lerp(parentgauss.position, childgauss.position, t) result.color = lerp(parentgauss.color, childgauss.color, t) result.shcoeffs = lerp(parentgauss.shcoeffs, childgauss.shcoeffs, t) # Covariance: Interpolate scale and rotation separately parentscale, parentrot = decomposecovariance(parentgauss.covariance) childscale, childrot = decomposecovariance(childgauss.covariance) interpscale = lerp(parentscale, childscale, t) # Linear interpolation for rotation, not slerp interprot = lerprotation(parentrot, childrot, t) result.covariance = composecovariance(interpscale, interprot) # Opacity: Special handling for transition start # Calculate alpha' for children # alpha' = 1 / (1 - (1 - alphap) 0.5) for two children # Note: This formula assumes 2 children. For N children, the factor might differ. # The source specifies this for "two children". alphaprime = 1.0 / (1.0 - (1.0 - alphap) 0.5) # Blend opacity # The source says "use this alpha' weight to blend alpha from the parent to the children" # It implies the child's effective opacity during transition is alphaprime, # and we blend between parent alpha and child alphaprime? # Or does it mean the child's alpha is set to alphaprime initially? # The equation alphap cp = alpha' cp + (1-alpha') alpha' cp suggests # that the rendered color of the blended children equals the parent color. # Let's assume we blend the opacity using t, but the child's base opacity is adjusted. # Re-reading: "This alpha' weight is used to blend alpha from the parent to the children" # This likely means: result.alpha = lerp(alphap, alphaprime, t) ? # Or does it mean the child's alpha is alphaprime, and we blend alphap and alphaprime? # Given the context of "start of transition", t=0 should yield parent. # If t=0, result.alpha = alphap. # If t=1, result.alpha = childgauss.alpha (original). # The formula for alpha' is derived to ensure color consistency at the start. # Let's assume the child's opacity is modified to alphaprime for the blending calculation. result.alpha = lerp(alphap, alphaprime, t) return result def decomposecovariance(cov): """ Decomposes covariance matrix into scale and rotation. """ # Eigen decomposition or Cholesky decomposition # Returns scale (vector) and rotation (matrix/quaternion) pass def composecovariance(scale, rot): """ Recomposes covariance matrix from scale and rotation. """ # Cov = R S S^T R^T pass def lerprotation(rot1, rot2, t): """ Linear interpolation of rotation (e.g., quaternion components). Not slerp. """ # Simple component-wise lerp for quaternions, handling sign ambiguity if needed pass \tau\epsilon: Target granularity. Typical value: 1 pixel. \alphap: Parent opacity. Direct Covariance Interpolation: Interpolating the covariance matrix directly causes undesired rotation artifacts when Gaussians have the same shape but different rotation/scaling orientations. This is mitigated by interpolating scale and rotation separately. Orientation Mismatch: Without orientation matching during hierarchy generation, interpolating Gaussians with the same covariance but different axes leads to visual disturbances. Exhaustive search is used to minimize relative rotation between parent and child axes. Opacity Blending: Incorrect opacity blending can cause color inconsistencies during transitions. The specific formula for \alpha' ensures that the blended color of the children matches the parent's color at the start of the transition. Division by Zero: If \epsilon(p) = \epsilon(n), the interpolation weight calculation involves division by zero. This should be handled by clamping or defaulting to 1.0. Time Complexity: The cut can be found in linear time O(N) with respect to the number of nodes, or in constant time per node in a massively parallel setting. Memory Complexity: Requires storing the hierarchy tree and pre-computed AABBs and granularities. The memory overhead is proportional to the number of nodes in the hierarchy. Performance: Maximizes rendering performance by selecting the coarsest possible nodes that still meet the visual quality threshold (granularity). Visual Quality: Maintains visual quality by ensuring smooth transitions between levels of detail through attribute interpolation. Strengths: Linear time cut selection, smooth transitions, handles orientation mismatches. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of orientation matching during hierarchy generation. Linear interpolation of rotations may not be as accurate as slerp, but is faster and deemed sufficient. Origin: This method is described in the paper "A Hierarchical 3D Gaussian Representation for Real-Time Rendering of Very Large Datasets" by Bernhard Kerbl, Andreas Meuleman, Georgios Kopanas, Michael Wimmer, Alexandre Lanvin, and George Drettakis. History: The method is part of the broader development of hierarchical 3D Gaussian Splatting techniques for real-time rendering of large-scale scenes. Usage: Used in CityGaussian, VastGaussian, and DoGaussian for streaming and rendering large-scale 3D Gaussian representations.
