name: Splatting and Point-based Rendering
head: Accelerating Splatting Algorithm Based on Multi-Texture Mapping, Multi-Texture Volume Rendering, Texture Splatting with Hardware Blending
body: Splatting and Point-based Rendering is an object-order volume rendering method where 3D data volumes are projected onto the 2D screen or an intermediate texture plane and blended to form the final image. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering large volumetric datasets by leveraging specialized hardware for compositing, avoiding the need for explicit intermediate geometry or thresholding. Unlike ray-order methods that cast rays through the volume, this method projects primitives (voxels or points) directly, allowing for fast hardware-accelerated alpha blending. It sets itself apart from its siblings by serving as the foundational object-order technique that other methods, such as Ray-Driven Splatting or Hybrid Volume Rendering with Hierarchical Representation, build upon or optimize. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D data volume (scalar field) defined in object coordinates, along with a transfer function mapping sample values to color and opacity. Output: A 2D rendered image on the screen. Data Structures: Volume Data: A 3D array of scalar values. Footprint Lookup Table: A table storing pre-computed filter weights for the splat footprint. Texture Slices: 2D texture maps representing segments of the volume, stored in RGBA mode to include the opacity channel. Numbered Steps: 1. Transformation: Transform the data volume from object coordinates to world coordinates. 2. Color and Opacity Mapping: Map sample values to color and opacity based on density using a transfer function. 3. Footprint Computation: Compute filter weights for the splat footprint and store them in a lookup table. The filter is typically Gaussian and proportional to the distance from the projection plane. 4. Initialization: Initialize texture points to RGBA mode and set the original alpha value of every point to zero. 5. Data Volume Division: Divide the data volume into segments or regions. 6. Processing Segments: For each segmented data set in the volume data: a. Depth Sort: Sort the voxels in front-to-back order (z-value from large to small). b. Layer Grouping: Group points with the same z-coordinate into layers. c. Projection: For each layer: i. Calculate the contribution of each voxel using the footprint weights. ii. Project the voxels to the texture plane. The texture plane is oriented parallel to the screen plane to avoid popping and splatting overlay artifacts. d. Texture Slice Creation: After all layers in one region are projected to the texture plane, create one texture slice representing that region. 7. Blending: For each texture slice: a. Blend the texture slices in front-to-back order. b. Turn on alpha blending during this step. Formulas: Filter Weights (Footprint): Formula (6) is used to compute filter weights for the footprint lookup table. The specific mathematical expression is not provided in the sources, but it is described as a Gaussian filter proportional to the distance from the plane. Data Volume Division: Formula (7) is used to divide the data volume. The specific expression is not provided. Projection to Texture Plane: Formula (12) is used to project points to the texture plane. The specific expression is not provided. Parameters: Texture Mode: RGBA, required to include the opacity channel of every data sample for translucent image generation. Texture Plane Orientation: Parallel with the screen plane to avoid popping and splatting overlay. Polygon Vertex Constraint: x and y coordinates are equal for all vertices, except z, ensuring texture slices are paralleled with the screen plane. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def splattingrendering(volumedata, transferfunction, projectionmatrix): # 1. Transformation: Transform data volume from object coordinates to world coordinates worldcoords = [transformpoint(v, projectionmatrix) for v in volumedata] # 2. Color and Opacity Mapping: Map sample values to color and opacity based on density coloredvolume = [transferfunction(v.density) for v in worldcoords] # 3. Footprint Computation: Compute filter weights for the footprint lookup table # Formula (6) computes Gaussian weights proportional to distance from plane. Not given in sources. footprinttable = computefootprintweights() # 4. Initialization: Initialize texture points to RGBA mode, alpha set to zero textureslices = [] # 5. Data Volume Division: Divide the data volume using Formula (7). Not given in sources. segmenteddata = dividevolume(coloredvolume) for segment in segmenteddata: # 6a. Depth Sort: Sort voxels in front-to-back order (z large to small) sortedsegment = sorted(segment, key=lambda v: v.z, reverse=True) # 6b. Layer Grouping: Group points with the same z into layers layers = groupbyz(sortedsegment) # 6c. Projection texturebuffer = initializetexturebufferrgba() for layer in layers: for voxel in layer: # 6c-i. Calculate contribution with footprint contribution = applyfootprint(voxel, footprinttable) # 6c-ii. Project to texture plane using Formula (12). Not given in sources. projecttotexture(voxel, contribution, texturebuffer) # 6d. Make texture slice textureslices.append(texturebuffer) # 7. Blending: Blend texture slices in front-to-back order with alpha blending finalimage = initializescreenbuffer() for slice in textureslices: finalimage = blendtextures(finalimage, slice) return finalimage def transformpoint(v, matrix): # Standard 4x4 matrix multiplication for object-to-world transformation return [sum(v[i] matrix[i][j] for i in range(4)) for j in range(4)] def computefootprintweights(): # Computes Gaussian filter weights proportional to distance from projection plane # Formula (6) is referenced but not provided in sources. return {} def dividevolume(data): # Divides volume data into segments/regions # Formula (7) is referenced but not provided in sources. return [data] def groupbyz(sorteddata): # Groups voxels sharing the same z-coordinate into layers layers = [] currentz = None currentlayer = [] for v in sorteddata: if v.z != currentz: if currentlayer: layers.append(currentlayer) currentz = v.z currentlayer = [v] else: currentlayer.append(v) if currentlayer: layers.append(currentlayer) return layers def initializetexturebufferrgba(): # Initializes a 2D buffer with RGBA mode, setting all alpha values to zero return [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(BUFFERW)] for in range(BUFFERH)] def applyfootprint(voxel, table): # Applies footprint filter weights to the voxel's contribution return voxel.density table.get(voxel.distance, 1.0) def projecttotexture(voxel, contribution, buffer): # Projects voxel to texture plane coordinates and accumulates contribution tx, ty = voxel.screenx, voxel.screeny buffer[ty][tx] = accumulatergba(buffer[ty][tx], contribution) def initializescreenbuffer(): # Initializes the final screen buffer return [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0) for in range(BUFFERW)] for in range(BUFFERH)] def blendtextures(final, slice): # Performs front-to-back alpha blending of a texture slice into the final image for y in range(BUFFERH): for x in range(BUFFERW): src = slice[y][x] dst = final[y][x] alpha = src[3] final[y][x] = ( dst[0] (1 - alpha) + src[0] alpha, dst[1] (1 - alpha) + src[1] alpha, dst[2] (1 - alpha) + src[2] alpha, dst[3] + src[3] (1 - dst[3])) return final Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Holes: The discrete process of splatting can produce holes on the periphery or during extreme perspective projection. This is countered by distributing the energy across multiple pixels via a footprint table, making adjustments before rendering. Popping and Overlay: Popping and splatting overlay artifacts can occur if the texture plane is not parallel to the screen plane. A voxel rendering technique where each voxel is represented by a single point primitive sized to cover the voxel's projected area, with the actual voxel geometry (cube) intersected with a ray in the fragment shader using an optimized ray-box intersection test. It differs from sibling methods like Sparse Voxel Octree Rendering via Square Splats by avoiding explicit cube face rasterization, instead relying on GPU point primitives and fragment-shader ray tracing to determine visibility. Sparse Voxel Octree Rendering via Square Splats visualizes sparse voxel octrees (SVOs) by converting leaf voxels into square billboards (splats) using a geometry shader within a programmable OpenGL graphics pipeline. It differs from ray-tracing SVO renderers by relying on rasterization, and from point-sprite methods by explicitly generating square geometry to approximate voxel volume. Voxel Point Sprite Rendering is a technique that stores voxels as points (splatting) in a buffer and renders them using a geometry shader or point sprites, allowing for mipmapped voxel data to be drawn as points with a specific scale. It visualizes voxels as points with size and color based on solidity. The method reduces vertex traffic by using the glPoint primitive with the Point Sprites extension to create automatic quads, reducing vertex traffic from four to one. Differentiable Point-Based Radiance Fields (DPBF) is a scene representation and rendering method that models radiance using a learned point cloud augmented with per-point spherical harmonic coefficients. It solves the problem of slow training and high memory usage in neural radiance fields by replacing volumetric ray-marching with a differentiable splat-based rasterizer, allowing for efficient view synthesis via a single forward pass. Unlike NeRF, which requires many evaluations per ray, DPBF uses forward mapping, resulting in training speeds up to 300x faster and memory usage under 10 MB for static scenes. Adapted Splatting is a volume rendering method that optimizes standard splatting by culling voxels invisible to the observer and using a compressed data format to reduce memory usage for free voxels. It solves the high computational cost of processing all voxels in a model and the large memory footprint of storing sparse volumetric data. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by introducing a two-pass optimization: a depth-buffer-based occlusion culling pass that identifies only visible voxels, followed by rendering only those selected voxels, while simultaneously employing a run-length-like encoding for storage that groups consecutive free voxels. It builds on Splatting and Point-based Rendering and differs from siblings such as Ray-Box Intersection via Quad Rasterization, Sparse Voxel Octree Rendering via Square Splats, Voxel Point Sprite Rendering, and Differentiable Point-Based Radiance Fields by relying on explicit voxel culling and a custom segment-based storage layout rather than hierarchical traversal or differentiable field representations. A hardware-accelerated hybrid volume rendering scheme that provides a smooth transition between texture-based (raycasting) and point-based (splatting) techniques by dividing the volumetric dataset into hierarchical nodes, each rendered with the most efficient method based on a division criterion. It solves the problem of visual popping artifacts and performance inefficiencies inherent in using a single rendering mode for entire datasets by adapting the technique locally. Unlike pure splatting Splatting and Point-based Rendering or pure raycasting, this method dynamically selects the approximation scheme for each subpart of the dataset to minimize visual variation while optimizing frame rate. Using points to fill empty space in irregular grids, such as filling cells with Poisson distributed points. The method involves filling cells of an irregular grid with Poisson distributed points and then performing projection via point-based rendering. Time Complexity: The method involves sorting voxels and projecting them to texture planes. The sources note that sorting segmented volume data is a significant part of the process. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the volume data, footprint lookup table, and intermediate texture slices. Measured Performance: On a PC with a 1.8 GHz Pentium 4 CPU and 512M DRAM: Seismic data (128x128x64): Old method 9.672s, New method 1.917s, Accelerating ratio 5.045. CT Head data (256x256x255): Old method 3.198s, New method 0.518s. Strengths: Leverages specialized texture hardware for fast rendering and composing, avoiding the need to project voxels directly to the screen plane. It helps to zoom or un-zoom the image easily by controlling polygon size. Limitations: The discrete process can produce holes on the periphery or during extreme perspective projection. Requires careful handling of texture plane orientation to avoid popping and splatting overlay. When to use: Suitable for large-scale volumetric data where hardware-accelerated blending is beneficial. When not to use: Not suitable when extreme perspective projection is required without additional footprint adjustments to prevent holes. The method originates from the work of Crawfis and Max in 1993, who introduced "Texture Splats for 3D Scalar and Vector Field Visualization". This work laid the foundation for using texture hardware to accelerate volume rendering by converting 3D data into 2D texture maps. The specific accelerating algorithm based on multi-texture mapping described in the notes builds upon this foundation, optimizing the projection and blending steps. name: Ray-Box Intersection via Quad Rasterization
body: A voxel rendering technique where each voxel is represented by a single point primitive sized to cover the voxel's projected area, with the actual voxel geometry (cube) intersected with a ray in the fragment shader using an optimized ray-box intersection test. It differs from sibling methods like Sparse Voxel Octree Rendering via Square Splats by avoiding explicit cube face rasterization, instead relying on GPU point primitives and fragment-shader ray tracing to determine visibility. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D grid of voxels defined by dimensions (W, H, D). Output: A rendered image where voxels are drawn as cubes if they intersect the view ray. Data Structures: The vertex data is packed into a single array of 32-bit unsigned integers. For a grid of size W \times H \times D, there are N = W \times H \times D vertices. Each vertex is represented by two 32-bit integers: 1. pos (32 bits): Encodes the voxel coordinates. Bits 0-10: x coordinate (11 bits, range 0-2047). Bits 11-16: y coordinate (6 bits, range 0-63). Bits 17-31: z coordinate (15 bits, range 0-32767). Layout: pos = x | (y << 11) | (z << 21). 2. albedo (32 bits): Encodes color. Bits 0-4: Red (5 bits). Bits 5-10: Green (6 bits). Bits 11-15: Blue (5 bits). Bits 16-31: Unused/Alpha. Layout: albedo = r | (g << 5) | (b << 11). Shader Data Structures: Box: vec3 center, vec3 radius, vec3 invRadius, mat3 rotation. Ray: vec3 origin, vec3 direction. Steps: 1. Vertex Generation: For each voxel index i from 0 to N-1, compute x = i \pmod W, y = \lfloor i / (W \times D) \rfloor, and z = \lfloor (i / W) \pmod D \rfloor. Pack pos and albedo as described above. Upload to a Vertex Buffer Object (VBO) bound to GLARRAYBUFFER. 2. Rendering Setup: Enable GLPROGRAMPOINTSIZE. Bind the vertex array object. Issue a single glDrawArrays(GLPOINTS, 0, N) call. 3. Vertex Shader: The vertex shader receives the packed pos and albedo. It reconstructs the voxel center in world space (or eye space, depending on pipeline design). The source code implies the point size is set to cover the cube's projected area. Output glPosition and pass albedo to the fragment shader. 4. Fragment Shader: Reconstruct the ray origin and direction. Ray origin is the camera position in eye space (typically (0,0,0) if camera is at origin). Fragment screen coordinates are glFragCoord.xy. Eye-space position is obtained by unprojecting glFragCoord using the inverse projection matrix to get a point on the near plane, then transforming to eye space. Ray direction is computed as the normalized vector from the eye-space position to the camera origin: \text{ray.direction} = -\frac{\text{camera\origin} - \text{eyePos}}{||\text{camera\origin} - \text{eyePos}||}. Define the voxel box with the center derived from vertex data and radius hardcoded to 0.05. Call the intersection function with rayCanStartInBox = false and oriented = false to optimize for axis-aligned boxes where the ray starts outside. If intersection fails, discard the fragment. If intersection succeeds, compute the depth at the intersection point and write to glFragDepth to ensure correct depth testing. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def intersectbox(origin, direction, boxmin, boxmax, raycanstartinbox=False, oriented=False): """ Optimized slab method for axis-aligned box intersection. Matches the MODEQUAD implementation: oriented=False, raycanstartinbox=False. Handles zero direction components safely to prevent 0.0 inf = nan. """ tmin = -math.inf tmax = math.inf for i in range(3): # Guard against division by zero; 1e30 acts as infinity for slab constraints invdir = 1.0 / direction[i] if direction[i] != 0.0 else 1e30 t1 = (boxmin[i] - origin[i]) invdir t2 = (boxmax[i] - origin[i]) invdir tmin = max(tmin, min(t1, t2)) tmax = min(tmax, max(t1, t2)) if tmax < tmin: return None if tmax < 0.0: return None if not raycanstartinbox and tmin < 0.0: tmin = 0.0 return tmin def computeraydirection(cameraorigin, eyepos): # Formula from: ray.direction = -(cameraorigin - eyePos) / ||cameraorigin - eyePos|| dx = cameraorigin[0] - eyepos[0] dy = cameraorigin[1] - eyepos[1] dz = cameraorigin[2] - eyepos[2] length = math.sqrt(dxdx + dydy + dzdz) return (-dx/length, -dy/length, -dz/length) Parameters: Voxel radius: 0.05. rayCanStartInBox: false. oriented: false. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: When computing distance to plane, if a ray direction component is zero, division by zero occurs. The code precomputes invRayDirection = 1.0 / ray.direction and passes it to avoid runtime division, assuming finite values. The implementation must guard against direction[i] == 0.0 to prevent 0.0 inf = nan during slab intersection. Point Size: The point size must be large enough to cover the voxel's projected area. If too small, voxels may be missed. If too large, overdraw increases. Time Complexity: O(N) for vertex processing, where N is the number of voxels. Fragment shader cost depends on the number of fragments generated by point rasterization. Memory Complexity: O(N) for vertex storage. Performance: On dedicated graphics cards, MODEQUAD is approximately twice as fast as MODECUBE (which rasterizes 3 cube faces per voxel). On Intel Integrated graphics, performance is similar. Strengths: Reduced vertex processing overhead compared to cube rasterization. Single draw call. Limitations: Overdraw can be high if point size is large. Precision issues in ray-box intersection if not handled carefully. This method is described in a test project by Clay John, titled "A short test project in efficient voxel rendering". It references an optimized ray-box intersection test from the Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques (JCGT). The technique is part of a broader exploration of voxel rendering optimizations, contrasting with explicit cube face rasterization. name: Sparse Voxel Octree Rendering via Square Splats
head: SVO Renderer, Square Splat Rendering
body: Sparse Voxel Octree Rendering via Square Splats visualizes sparse voxel octrees (SVOs) by converting leaf voxels into square billboards (splats) using a geometry shader within a programmable OpenGL graphics pipeline. It differs from ray-tracing SVO renderers by relying on rasterization, and from point-sprite methods by explicitly generating square geometry to approximate voxel volume. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A sparse voxel octree (typically generated by oocsvobuilder), where leaf voxels provide position, color, and normal data. Output: A 2D image rendered via OpenGL rasterization. Data Structures: The input data is passed to the vertex shader as attributes: voxelPosition: vec3 (world-space position of the voxel center). voxelColor: vec3 (RGB color). voxelNormal: vec3 (surface normal). Uniforms include: MV: Model-View matrix (mat4). P: Projection matrix (mat4). voxelOffset: vec2 (full side length of the splat in view space). cullInvisibleFaces: bool (flag for back-face culling). Algorithm Steps: 1. Vertex Shader Processing: For each leaf voxel, the vertex shader transforms the world-space position and normal to view space using the Model-View matrix. 2. Geometry Shader Invocation: The vertex shader emits a point primitive containing the view-space position, color, and normal. 3. Clip-Space Transformation: The geometry shader transforms the voxel position to clip space using the Projection matrix. 4. Splat Size Calculation: The half-edge length in clip space is computed by projecting a right-edge midpoint to clip space, performing perspective division, and calculating the Euclidean distance to the center. 5. Frustum Culling: The splat is discarded if the clip-space center coordinates exceed the frustum bounds adjusted by the half-edge length. 6. Back-Face Culling (Optional): If cullInvisibleFaces is enabled, the dot product between the view direction (camera to voxel) and the view-space normal is checked; if negative, the face is invisible and the splat is skipped. 7. Square Generation: A triangle strip of four vertices is generated. The corners are defined in view space relative to the voxel center and voxelOffset, then transformed to clip space via the Projection matrix. 8. Final Projection: Texture coordinates (0,0) to (1,1) are assigned to the four vertices for potential texturing. Formulas: View-space position: P{view} = MV \times P{world}. View-space normal: N{view} = MV \times N{world} (treated as a vector, translation ignored). Clip-space position: P{clip} = P \times [P{view}, 1.0]^T, followed by perspective division P{clip} \leftarrow P{clip} / P{clip}.w. Half-edge length in clip space: L{clip} = \text{distance}(P{clip}.xy, P{right\mid\clip}.xy), where P{right\mid\clip} is the projected midpoint of the voxel's right edge. Frustum culling condition: |P{clip}.x| > 1 + L{clip} \lor |P{clip}.y| > 1 + L{clip}. Back-face culling condition: \text{dot}(-P{view}, N{view}) < 0. Corner positions in view space: C{view}.xy = P{view}.xy + (cx, cy) \times \text{voxelOffset}, where (cx, cy) \in \{(-0.5, -0.5), (0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5)\}. Parameters: voxelOffset: Controls the physical size of the square splat in view space. cullInvisibleFaces: Boolean flag that toggles back-face culling. Edge Cases: Precision: Clip-space size calculation requires explicit perspective division to account for depth-dependent scaling. Boundaries: Frustum culling uses a border of 1 + L{clip} to prevent clipping artifacts at the edge of the view volume. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexshader(voxelpositionworld, voxelcolor, voxelnormal, MV): posview = (MV vec4(voxelpositionworld, 1.0)).xyz normalview = (MV vec4(voxelnormal, 0.0)).xyz return {'posview': posview, 'color': voxelcolor, 'normalview': normalview} def geometryshader(point, MV, P, voxeloffset, cullinvisiblefaces): posview = point['posview'] normalview = point['normalview'] posclip = P vec4(posview, 1.0) posclip /= posclip.w rightedgemidview = vec3(posview.x + voxeloffset.x 0.5, posview.y, posview.z) rightedgemidclip = P vec4(rightedgemidview, 1.0) rightedgemidclip /= rightedgemidclip.w halfedgeclip = distance(posclip.xy, rightedgemidclip.xy) frustumborder = 1.0 + halfedgeclip if abs(posclip.x) > frustumborder or abs(posclip.y) > frustumborder: return [] normalviewspace = (MV vec4(normalview, 0.0)).xyz if cullinvisiblefaces and dot(-posview, normalviewspace) < 0: return [] cornersviewxy = [ posview.xy + vec2(-0.5, -0.5) voxeloffset, posview.xy + vec2(0.5, -0.5) voxeloffset, posview.xy + vec2(-0.5, 0.5) voxeloffset, posview.xy + vec2(0.5, 0.5) voxeloffset ] vertices = [] for i, cornerxy in enumerate(cornersviewxy): cornerview = vec4(cornerxy, posview.z, 1.0) cornerclip = P cornerview cornerclip /= cornerclip.w texcoord = vec2(i % 2, i // 2) vertices.append({'position': cornerclip, 'texcoord': texcoord}) return vertices A rasterization technique where each voxel in a cluster is processed by a single invocation, projecting its footprint box to the pixel centers it covers, replacing the previous method of walking every pixel of a brick's rectangle through its cells. It solves the inefficiency of processing pixels that no voxel footprint covers, particularly at shallow voxel levels where footprints are small fractions of cell sizes. Time Complexity: Linear with respect to the number of leaf voxels, as each leaf generates one geometry shader invocation. Memory Complexity: Low, as it only stores leaf voxel data and does not require ray-marching structures. Performance: Fast on modern GPUs due to hardware rasterization and geometry shaders. Strengths: Efficient visualization of large sparse voxel datasets; simple implementation using standard OpenGL. Limitations: Square splats may not accurately represent spherical or complex voxel shapes; no explicit depth sorting is mentioned in the basic pipeline, potentially causing z-fighting or incorrect blending without additional techniques. When to use: Real-time visualization of sparse voxel data where approximate volume representation is sufficient. The method was developed as part of the svorenderer project, which aims to render sparse voxel octrees generated by oocsvobuilder. It leverages the programmable graphics pipeline (OpenGL) to handle the rendering workload. mmalesadev/svorenderer, https://github.com/mmalesadev/svorenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Splatting to Pixel Footprints
head: voxel splat
body: A rasterization technique where each voxel in a cluster is processed by a single invocation, projecting its footprint box to the pixel centers it covers, replacing the previous method of walking every pixel of a brick's rectangle through its cells. It solves the inefficiency of processing pixels that no voxel footprint covers, particularly at shallow voxel levels where footprints are small fractions of cell sizes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A cluster of voxels, their associated brick metadata (first voxel indices, masks), and the camera/projection matrices. Output: A visibility buffer or hit list containing the nearest voxel for each covered pixel, determined via atomic operations. Data Structures: Brick Metadata: Contains an array of first voxel indices for binary search and a bitmask indicating which cells within the brick are occupied. Voxel Footprint Box: Defined as a capsule widened by its radius, constrained within its cell boundaries. The box's corners lie on a grid of 32nds of a cell. Steps: 1. Invocation: Invoke one shader invocation per voxel of the cluster. 2. Brick Identification: Determine the brick containing the voxel by performing a binary search over the bricks' first voxels. 3. Cell Index: Determine the cell index within the brick by finding the n-th set bit of the brick's mask. 4. Footprint Definition: Define the voxel's footprint box as a capsule widened by its radius, constrained within its cell. 5. Projection Calculation: Project the footprint box to clip space. The center and half-extents are reached as steps along the brick's grid of 32nds of a cell. The projection lies within (rx + |xc / wc| rw) / (wc - rw) of the center in x, and likewise in y, widened by a 64th of a pixel. Here, rx is the x-radius, xc is the center x, wc is the center w, and rw is the w-radius. 6. Edge Case Handling: If a voxel is wholly behind the near plane, it covers no pixels. If a voxel reaches behind the camera's plane, it covers the whole target. 7. Pair Pooling: A subgroup pools its voxels' (voxel, pixel) pairs using an exclusive add, followed by a binary search per pair. 8. Ray Testing: Fill the shader lanes with rays' tests for whichever voxels cover pixels. 9. Hit Test: For each pair, test the ray against that voxel alone using visvoxelhit. Inside visvoxelhit, take the ray's span through the voxel's cell from the cell's own planes, then compute the footprint over that span. 10. Atomic Update: On a hit, perform an atomic max of (1 / t, \text{cluster}, \text{brick}) so that the nearest voxel wins. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processvoxel(voxelid, clusterdata, mvpmatrix): # 1. Identify Brick (binary search over first voxel indices) firstvoxels = clusterdata.firstvoxelindices left, right = 0, len(firstvoxels) - 1 brickidx = right while left <= right: mid = (left + right) // 2 if firstvoxels[mid] <= voxelid: brickidx = mid left = mid + 1 else: right = mid - 1 brick = clusterdata.bricks[brickidx] # 2. Identify Cell (find n-th set bit in mask) offset = voxelid - brick.firstvoxelindex cellidx = 0 mask = brick.mask for i in range(32): if (mask >> i) & 1: if offset == cellidx: break cellidx += 1 # 3. Define Footprint Box # Capsule widened by radius, constrained within cell cellsize = brick.cellsize voxelcenter = voxeldata.center radius = voxeldata.radius mincorner = max(voxelcenter - radius, brick.mincorner) maxcorner = min(voxelcenter + radius, brick.maxcorner) footprintcenter = (mincorner + maxcorner) / 2.0 footprinthalfextents = (maxcorner - mincorner) / 2.0 # 4. Project to Clip Space # Corners lie on grid of 32nds of a cell; center/half-extents reached as steps along grid clipcenter = multiplymvp(mvpmatrix, [footprintcenter.x, footprintcenter.y, footprintcenter.z, 1.0]) cliphalfext = multiplymvp(mvpmatrix, [footprinthalfextents.x, footprinthalfextents.y, footprinthalfextents.z, 0.0]) rx = footprinthalfextents.x xc = clipcenter[0] wc = clipcenter[3] rw = cliphalfext[3] # Projection bounds, widened by 64th of a pixel xprojbound = (rx + abs(xc / wc) rw) / (wc - rw) + 1.0 / 64.0 yprojbound = (footprinthalfextents.y + abs(clipcenter[1] / wc) rw) / (wc - rw) + 1.0 / 64.0 # 5. Edge Cases # Wholly behind near plane covers nothing if clipcenter[2] > 0: return # Reaching behind camera plane takes whole target if wc < 0: targetpixels = list(range(clusterdata.resolutionx clusterdata.resolutiony)) else: # Determine covered pixel centers from clip-space bounds targetpixels = computepixelcentersfromclipbounds(clipcenter, xprojbound, yprojbound, clusterdata.resolutionx, clusterdata.resolutiony) # 6. Pool Pairs # Subgroup exclusive add, then binary search per pair pairlist = [(voxelid, pixel) for pixel in targetpixels] pooledpairs = subgrouppoolpairs(pairlist) # 7. Ray Tests for vid, pixel in pooledpairs: ray = generaterayforpixel(pixel, clusterdata.camera) # 8. Hit Test hitt = visvoxelhit(ray, voxeldata, brick) if hitt is not None: # 9. Atomic Max # Nearest voxel wins (smallest t, largest 1/t) atomicmaxhit(1.0 / hitt, clusterdata.id, brick.id) def visvoxelhit(ray, voxel, brick): # Take ray's span through voxel's cell from the cell's own planes tmin, tmax = rayaabbintersection(ray, brick.cellplanes) if tmin is None or tmax is None or tmax < 0: return None # Compute the footprint over that span if footprintoverlapsspan(voxel.footprint, tmin, tmax): return tmin return None def rayaabbintersection(ray, planes): # Iterative slab method tnear = -float('inf') tfar = float('inf') for i in range(3): if abs(ray.dir[i]) < 1e-8: if ray.origin[i] < planes[i].min or ray.origin[i] > planes[i].max: return None, None else: t1 = (planes[i].min - ray.origin[i]) / ray.dir[i] t2 = (planes[i].max - ray.origin[i]) / ray.dir[i] tnear = max(tnear, min(t1, t2)) tfar = min(tfar, max(t1, t2)) if tnear > tfar: return None, None return tnear, tfar def footprintoverlapsspan(footprint, tmin, tmax): # Check if footprint intersects ray segment return tmin <= footprint.maxt and tmax >= footprint.mint def multiplymvp(matrix, vec): # Standard 4x4 matrix-vector multiplication out = [0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for r in range(4): for c in range(4): out[r] += matrix[r][c] vec[c] return [out[0]/out[3], out[1]/out[3], out[2]/out[3], out[3]] def computepixelcentersfromclipbounds(centerclip, xbound, ybound, resx, resy): # Map clip-space bounds to pixel indices pixels = [] for y in range(int(centerclip[1] - ybound), int(centerclip[1] + ybound) + 1): for x in range(int(centerclip[0] - xbound), int(centerclip[0] + xbound) + 1): if 0 <= x < resx and 0 <= y < resy: pixels.append(y resx + x) return pixels def subgrouppoolpairs(pairlist): # Exclusive add to count pairs, then binary search per pair to assign lanes # Simplified representation of hardware subgroup exclusive scan + binary search assignment counts = [0] len(pairlist) for i in range(1, len(pairlist)): counts[i] = counts[i-1] + 1 assigned = [] for i, (vid, pix) in enumerate(pairlist): laneidx = counts[i] assigned.append((vid, pix, laneidx)) return assigned Time Complexity: Proportional to the number of voxels in the cluster, rather than the area of the brick's bounding rectangle. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Performance: In tests on foliage4kproduction, the previous method sent 14.9 M rays per frame, taking 59.7 M traversal steps and 15.2 M footprint tests for 1.78 M hits. Strengths: Eliminates wasted computation on pixels not covered by any voxel footprint. Limitations: Requires subgroup operations for pooling, which may have overhead on hardware with poor subgroup support. This method was introduced as part of stage 3 rasterization updates in the Nepheline renderer, specifically in ADR-0061. It replaced the DDA-based traversal (visvoxeltrace) and the previous pixel-walking brick rasterization, aiming to optimize performance for scenes with foliage and other complex geometry where voxel footprints are small. feat(render): voxels splatted to the pixels their footprints cover (ADR-0061), https://github.com/SugalAbubaker/nepheline/pull/115, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Voxel Point Sprite Rendering
head: Draw Points Pass, GL_POINTS voxel rendering, OpenGL Voxel Splatting, Point-based Voxel Rendering, Rendering with Point Sprites and Kernel Footprints, Voxel Splatting, Voxel shader
body: Voxel Point Sprite Rendering is a technique that stores voxels as points (splatting) in a buffer and renders them using a geometry shader or point sprites, allowing for mipmapped voxel data to be drawn as points with a specific scale. It visualizes voxels as points with size and color based on solidity. The method reduces vertex traffic by using the glPoint primitive with the Point Sprites extension to create automatic quads, reducing vertex traffic from four to one. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A voxel grid defined by dimensions width \times height \times depth (default 200x50x200 in or 4x4x4 cubes in). Each voxel contains position and color/albedo data. Output: A rendered image where voxels are drawn as point sprites, with size and LOD determined by camera distance. Data Structures: Two distinct packing layouts are cited in the sources: 1. Layout A (Source): Voxel data is packed into pairs of uint32t. Position (uint32t): Bits 0-10 (11 bits): x; Bits 11-20 (10 bits): y; Bits 21-31 (11 bits): z. Albedo (uint32t): Bits 0-4 (5 bits): R; Bits 5-10 (6 bits): G; Bits 11-15 (5 bits): B. Stored in a flat uint32t array of size noofvertices 2. 2. Layout B (Source): Used within CUBE256::MipMap::voxels (std::vector<uint>). Single uint32t per voxel: x (8 bits) | (y \ll 8) (8 bits) | (z \ll 16) (8 bits) | (color \ll 24) (8 bits). The VBO layout for the geometry shader consists of four 4-component attributes (vertex0 to vertex3), each reading 4 unsigned bytes (GLUNSIGNEDBYTE) with normalization (GLTRUE) from a stride of 16 bytes. vertex0 reads bytes 0-3, vertex1 reads bytes 4-7, vertex2 reads bytes 8-11, vertex3 reads bytes 12-15. Parameters: voxelSize: Physical size of a single voxel in world units (e.g., 0.05). halfScreenSize: Half of the viewport dimensions, used to scale projected AABB to screen space. cubesx, cubesy, cubesz: Grid dimensions for the voxel space (default 4, 4, 4). scale: Rendering scale of splats, calculated as 0.1f \times (1 \ll \text{mipmap}). Color: Color for non-solid voxels. Default (1, 0, 0, 1) (red). CollisionColor: Color for solid voxels. Default (0, 1, 0, 1) (green). Steps: 1. Initialize Voxel Grid: Resize the cubes vector to cubesx cubesy cubesz (default 64 cubes). For each voxel index i, compute packed position and albedo using bitwise shifts and random color generation. 2. Set Voxel Position and Mipmap: Shift x, y, z by mipmap level: x \ll= \text{mipmap}. Calculate cube ID: \text{cubeID} = (x \gg 8) + (y \gg 8) \times \text{cubes\x} + (z \gg 8) \times \text{cubes\x} \times \text{cubes\y}. Store local voxel (x \& 255, y \& 255, z \& 255) in the corresponding cube's mipmap. Boundary check: If x, y, or z exceed 255, discard the voxel. 3. Calculate Mipmap Level: Determine mipmap based on camera distance: \text{mipmap} = \sqrt{\sqrt{(\text{screen.pos} + (\text{pos} + \text{vec3f}(0.5, 0.5, 0.5) + \text{add}) \times 16).\text{length()}}} - 1 Clamp mipmap to \ge 0. 4. Generate VBOs: For each mipmap with voxels, create a GLARRAYBUFFER, bind it, and upload voxel data with GLSTATICDRAWARB. Bind to a VAO using glVertexAttribIPointer(0, 2, GLINT, 2 sizeof(uint32t), 0) for Layout A. 5. Vertex Shader Processing: Unpack voxel coordinates from the packed position uint32t using bitmasks: ux = \text{data.x} \& \text{uint}(2047) uy = (\text{data.x} \& \text{uint}(2095104)) \gg \text{uint}(11) uz = (\text{data.x} \& (\text{uint}(2047) \ll \text{uint}(21))) \gg \text{uint}(21) Convert to world space by multiplying by 0.1. Transform position to clip space: \text{o.position} = \text{UnityWorldToClipPos}(\text{float4}(\text{pos.xyz}, 1.0)). 6. Stochastic Culling: Apply stochastic culling for distant/small voxels to maintain performance. Calculate projected area: \text{stochasticCoverage} = \text{point\size} \times \text{point\size}. If \text{stochasticCoverage} < 0.8, discard vertex with probability proportional to size: glsl if ((stochasticCoverage < 0.8) && ((glVertexID & 0xffff) > stochasticCoverage (0xffff / 0.8))) { position = vec4(-1, -1, -1, -1); pointsize = 0.0; } Discard voxels behind the camera (\text{position.z} \le 0.0) by setting position = vec4(-1,-1,-1,-1) and pointsize = 0.0. 7. Sphere Radius and Quadric Projection: Approximate sphere radius: \text{sphereRadius} = \text{voxelSize} \times 1.732051 (where 1.732051 \approx \sqrt{3}). Calculate quadric projection coefficients: \text{eqCoefs} = \frac{\text{vec4}(\text{dot}(\text{matD}[0], \text{matT}[2]), \text{dot}(\text{matD}[1], \text{matT}[2]), \text{dot}(\text{matD}[0], \text{matT}[0]), \text{dot}(\text{matD}[1], \text{matT}[1]))}{\text{dot}(\text{matD}[2], \text{matT}[2])} where \text{matT} and \text{matD} are derived from the model-view-projection matrix scaled by \text{sphereRadius}. 8. Draw: Enable GLPROGRAMPOINTSIZE. Draw with glDrawArrays(GLPOINTS, 0, noofvertices). For Layout B: Bind shader, set projection matrix uniform, enable 4 vertex attributes pointing to VBO with stride 16, set blockpos and scale uniforms, draw GLPOINTS with count voxels.size()/4, then disable attributes and unbind buffer. For Point Sprites, compute correct texture coordinates in a vertex shader to index into the sub-texture containing the corresponding footprint, as texture coordinates are otherwise computed automatically. Instead of storing one footprint and modulating it with a slab coefficient, this method computes all different kernel footprints for different slabs and stores them in one 2D texture. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def voxelpointspriterendering(voxelgrid, camerapos, screensize): # Parameters voxelsize = 0.05 halfscreensize = screensize 0.5 cubesx, cubesy, cubesz = 4, 4, 4 # Step 1 & 2: Initialize Grid and Set Voxel Position cubes = [None] (cubesx cubesy cubesz) for mipmaplevel in range(8): for cubeid in range(len(cubes)): cubes[cubeid] = {"mipmaps": [None] 8} cubes[cubeid]["mipmaps"][mipmaplevel] = [] for voxel in voxelgrid: x, y, z = voxel.position xshifted = x << mipmaplevel yshifted = y << mipmaplevel zshifted = z << mipmaplevel # Boundary check if xshifted > 255 or yshifted > 255 or zshifted > 255: continue # Store local voxel localx = xshifted & 255 localy = yshifted & 255 localz = zshifted & 255 cubes[cubeid]["mipmaps"][mipmaplevel].append((localx, localy, localz, voxel.color)) # Step 3: Calculate Mipmap Level for each voxel based on camera distance def calculatemipmap(screenpos, voxelposworld, addoffset): lengthsq = (screenpos + (voxelposworld + (0.5, 0.5, 0.5) + addoffset) 16) lengthsq = lengthsq[0]2 + lengthsq[1]2 + lengthsq[2]2 mipmap = math.sqrt(math.sqrt(lengthsq)) - name: Hybrid Voxel Rendering (Mesh/Splatting)
head: Mesh/Splatting Hybrid
body: Hybrid Voxel Rendering is a rendering strategy that combines OpenGL splatting for distant voxels with mesh rendering for nearby voxels to reduce vertex count while maintaining visual quality. It addresses the performance bottleneck of slow fragment shaders in pure splatting methods when rendering voxels close to the camera, a problem inherent to its parent method, Voxel Point Sprite Rendering. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of active voxels organized in an octree-like structure with multiple LOD levels. Output: A rendered image where distant voxels are drawn as splats and nearby voxels as meshes. Data Structures: Splat Vertex Buffer (VBO): Interleaved array of int16t with stride 4 sizeof(int16t). Attribute 0 (aVertex): 3 components, GLSHORT, offset 0. Attribute 1 (aColor): 1 component, GLSHORT, offset 3 sizeof(int16t). Mesh Vertex Buffer (VBO): Interleaved array of int16t with stride 4 sizeof(int16t). Attribute 0 (aVertex): 3 components, GLSHORT, offset 0. Attribute 1 (aColor): 1 component, GLSHORT, offset 3 sizeof(int16t). Mesh Index Buffer (IBO): Array of uint32t (GLUNSIGNEDINT). Parameters: LOD Kick-in Distance: 1024 voxels. At this distance, single voxels are approximately one pixel in size at 1080p resolution. MAXLODLEVEL: Maximum number of LOD levels (value not specified). reservesize: Capacity limit for vertex buffers; the update process panics if totalitems + uploaditems exceeds this value. Formulas: Octree Bit Width: octree\bitw[i] = \text{set}.\text{max\bitw}[i] - \min(\text{lod}, \text{set}.\text{max\bitw}[i]). This determines the bit width for flattening the octree index at a given LOD. Chunk Minimum Coordinate: cs\min[i] = \text{octree}[i] \ll \text{lod}. Chunk Maximum Coordinate: cs\max[i] = \min((\text{octree}[i] + 1) \ll \text{lod}, \text{set}.\text{max}[i]). LOD Scale Uniform: u\lod = 1 \ll \text{lod}. Steps: 1. Render Distant Voxels (Splatting): Bind the splat shader, enable GLPROGRAMPOINTSIZE and GLBLEND with SRCALPHA and ONEMINUSSRCALPHA, disable GLCULLFACE, set uniforms (projection, invprojviewrot, viewtranslation, viewrotation, viewport size, far plane, and ulod), and draw points using glDrawArrays(GLPOINTS) for each geometry chunk in the splat queue. 2. Render Nearby Voxels (Meshing): Bind the mesh shader, enable GLCULLFACE with GLBACK, set uniforms (projection, invprojviewrot, viewtranslation, viewport size, and far plane), and draw triangles using glDrawElements(GLTRIANGLES) for each geometry mesh in the mesh queue. 3. Splat LOD Update: For each LOD level from 0 to MAXLODLEVEL - 1, calculate octree coordinates and chunk bounds (csmin, csmax) using the formulas above, flatten octree coordinates to get the index, iterate over sub-chunks within bounds, lock the mutex, calculate uploadstart by summing svlitems for lower LODs, upload data using glBufferSubData from sub->svl array, unlock the mutex, and if reservesize is 0, delete the VAO/VBO. If uploaditems is 0, the loop continues to the next sub-chunk without locking or unlocking the mutex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. min(lod, set.maxbitw[i]) octreecoord = octree[i] csmin.append(octreecoord << lod) csmax.append(min((octreecoord + 1) << lod, set.max[i])) # Flatten octree coordinates to get index index = flattenoctreeindex(octree, lod) # Iterate over sub-chunks within bounds for subchunk in getsubchunks(index, csmin, csmax): if subchunk.uploaditems == 0: continue lockmutex(subchunk.mutex) # Calculate upload start by summing svlitems for lower LODs uploadstart = sum(svlitems for lodlevel in range(lod)) # Upload data from sub->svl array uploadbuffer(splatvbo, offset=uploadstart, data=subchunk.svl) unlockmutex(subchunk.mutex) if reservesize == 0: deletevaovbo(subchunk.vao, subchunk.vbo) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Tested on an AMD RX480 4GB GPU with a 16384 x 512 x 16384 voxel map (128GB uncompressed). Scaling: LOD reduces draw calls by grouping geometry by LOD level. Strengths: Reduces vertex count to 1 per voxel for distant voxels, improving performance for large scenes. Maintains quality for nearby voxels using meshes. Limitations: Splatting has a slow fragment shader, making it unsuitable for nearby voxels. Mesh rendering increases vertex count for close voxels. When to Use: Suitable for huge fully destructible scenes on desktop hardware where performance is critical for distant objects but quality is needed for nearby objects. When Not to Use: Not suitable for scenes where all voxels are close to the camera, as the overhead of mesh rendering may outweigh the benefits. Hybrid Voxel Rendering was implemented in Voxplat, a hybrid voxel rendering engine written in C and OpenGL by kosshi-net. The goal was to render huge fully destructible scenes on reasonable desktop hardware. The splatting method was inspired by a paper from the Journal of Computer Graphics Techniques. kosshi-net/voxplat, https://github.com/kosshi-net/voxplat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Differentiable Point-Based Radiance Fields
head: DPBF, Differentiable Splatting, Point Radiance Fields, Point-Based Radiance Fields
body: Differentiable Point-Based Radiance Fields (DPBF) is a scene representation and rendering method that models radiance using a learned point cloud augmented with per-point spherical harmonic coefficients. It solves the problem of slow training and high memory usage in neural radiance fields by replacing volumetric ray-marching with a differentiable splat-based rasterizer, allowing for efficient view synthesis via a single forward pass. Unlike NeRF, which requires many evaluations per ray, DPBF uses forward mapping, resulting in training speeds up to 300x faster and memory usage under 10 MB for static scenes. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N input images I^j (j=1 \dots N) with known camera intrinsics and extrinsics, and object masks for each image defining the visual hull. Outputs: A rendered image \hat{I}^j for any novel view, and an optimized point cloud representing the scene geometry and radiance. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a point cloud. Each point i stores: 1. Position: A 3D vector pi \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Appearance: Spherical Harmonic (SH) coefficients h{i,lm} for l \in [0, l{max}] and m \in [-l, l]. These coefficients define the view-dependent color. Parameters: Splatting radius r: 0.008. Maximum number of splats considered per pixel n: 15. Maximum spherical harmonic degree l{max}: 2. TV weight \lambda{TV}: 0.01. Learning rate decay factor: 0.93 per epoch. Total epochs: 20. Initial learning rates: 3 \times 10^{-3} for SH parameters, 8 \times 10^{-4} for positions. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize point positions using rejection sampling within the visual hull: uniformly sample random 3D points, project them into each input image, and keep only points that fall within all object masks. Initialize SH coefficients by sampling from a normal distribution with zero mean and standard deviation of one. 2. Rendering (Differentiable Splatting): For each pixel u in image j: Identify points i with non-negligible opacity within a certain distance of u. Sort these points by z-distance (front-to-back). Compute opacity \alpha^ji(u) for each point using a Gaussian kernel: \alpha^ji(u) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi r^2}} e^{-\frac{\|p^ji - u\|^2}{2r^2}} where p^ji is the projected position of point i in image j. Compute the net contribution A^ji(u) of the i-th point: A^ji(u) = \alpha^ji(u) \prod{k=1}^{i-1} (1 - \alpha^jk(u)) where points are sorted front-to-back. Compute the per-point color ci using the SH coefficients and the view direction vi from the camera to point i: ci = \sum{l=0}^{l{max}} \sum{m=-l}^{l} h{i,lm} Y{lm}(vi) where Y{lm} are the spherical harmonic basis functions. Compute the final pixel color \hat{I}^j(u) via alpha blending: \hat{I}^j(u) = \sum{i=1}^{n} A^ji(u) ci where n is the maximum number of splats considered (default 15). 3. Optimization: Minimize the loss function L: L = \sum{j=1}^{N} ||I^j - \hat{I}^j||^22 + \lambda{TV} TV(\hat{I}^j) where TV(\cdot) = |\nablax \cdot|1 + |\nablay \cdot|1 is the anisotropic total variation penalty. Update positions and SH coefficients using stochastic gradient descent with the specified learning rates and decay. 4. Coarse-to-Fine Updates: To improve representation efficiency and avoid dense clusters, repeat the following stages twice: Voxel-based Point Cloud Reduction: Assume a voxel discretization. For each voxel, aggregate all points inside by averaging their position and SH coefficients into a single point. Outlier Removal: For each point, compute the distance to its neighbors and the standard deviation of these distances. Filter out outliers whose standard deviation exceeds a threshold. Point Generation: Insert new points by generating one new point for each existing point. Set all parameters (including position) to the average of the point’s nearest K neighbors. 5. Refinement: Fine-tune the model with half of the original learning rate. Pseudocode: Unverified code. Standard mathematical function.""" # Returns array of shape (numcoeffs,) pass def computeshcolor(hcoeffs, v): """Compute color from SH coefficients and view direction.""" basis = sphericalharmonicsbasis(2, v) return np.dot(hcoeffs, basis) def rendersplats(points, hcoeffs, K, R, t, camorigin, imageshape, r=0.008, nmax=15): """Differentiable splat rendering.""" height, width = imageshape image = np.zeros((height, width, 3)) pproj = projectpoints(points, K, R, t) v = computeviewdirections(points, camorigin) colors = computeshcolor(hcoeffs, v) zdepth = (R @ points.T).T[:, 2] + t[2] for uy in range(height): for ux in range(width): u = np.array([ux, uy]) dists = np.linalg.norm(pproj - u, axis=1) opacities = (1.0 / np.sqrt(2 np.pi r2)) np.exp(-dists2 / (2 r2)) validindices = np.where(opacities > 1e-6)[0] validindices = validindices[np.argsort(zdepth[validindices])] validindices = validindices[:nmax] transmittance = 1.0 pixelcolor = np.zeros(3) for i in validindices: alphai = opacities[i] Ai = alphai transmittance pixelcolor += Ai colors[i] transmittance = (1.0 - alphai) image[uy, ux] = pixelcolor return image def coarsetofineupdate(points, hcoeffs, voxelsize=0.01, neighbork=5, threshold=2.0): """Coarse-to-fine point cloud optimization stages.""" # Stage 1: Voxel-based Point Cloud Reduction voxelgrid = np.floor(points / voxelsize).astype(int) uniquevoxels, inverse = np.unique(voxelgrid, axis=0, returninverse=True) newpoints = np.zeroslike(points) newhcoeffs = np.zeroslike(hcoeffs) for idx, voxel in enumerate(uniquevoxels): mask = inverse == idx newpoints[voxel[0], voxel[1], voxel[2]] = np.mean(points[mask], axis=0) newhcoeffs[voxel[0], voxel[1], voxel[2]] = np.mean(hcoeffs[mask], axis=0) points = newpoints.reshape(-1, 3) hcoeffs = newhcoeffs.reshape(-1, hcoeffs.shape[1]) # Stage 2: Outlier Removal dists = np.linalg.norm(points[:, None,:] - points[None,:,:], axis=2) stddists = np.std(np.sort(dists, axis=1)[:, 1:neighbork+1], axis=1) mask = stddists < threshold points = points[mask] hcoeffs = hcoeffs[mask] # Stage 3: Point Generation newpoints = np.mean(points[np.argsort(dists[:, 1:neighbork+1])], axis=1) newhcoeffs = np.mean(hcoeffs[np.argsort(dists[:, 1:neighbork+1])], axis=1) points = np.vstack([points, newpoints]) hcoeffs = np.vstack([hcoeffs, newhcoeffs]) return points, hcoeffs def traindpbf(images, masks, cameraparams, numpoints=10000, epochs=20, lrsh=3e-3, lrpos=8e-4, decay=0.93, lambdatv=0.01): """Train DPBF model.""" # Initialization via rejection sampling within visual hull points = np.random.uniform(-1, 1, (numpoints, 3)) hcoeffs = np.random.normal(0, 1, (numpoints, 9)) for epoch in range(epochs): renderedimages = [rendersplats(points, hcoeffs, cp, imageshape=img.shape) for img, cp in zip(images, cameraparams)] loss = sum(np.mean((img - rend)2) + lambdatv np.sum(np.abs(np.diff(rend, axis=0))) + np.sum(np.abs(np.diff(rend, axis=1))) for img, rend in zip(images, renderedimages)) # Gradients computed via automatic differentiation gradpoints, gradhcoeffs = autograd(loss, points, hcoeffs) points -= lrpos gradpoints hcoeffs -= lrsh gradhcoeffs lrpos = decay lrsh = decay points, hcoeffs = coarsetofineupdate(points, hcoeffs) # Refinement step with half learning rate lrpos /= 2 lrsh /= 2 for in range(5): renderedimages = [rendersplats(points, hcoeffs, cp, imageshape=img.shape) for img, cp in zip(images, cameraparams)] loss = sum(np.mean((img - rend)2) + lambdatv np.sum(np.abs(np.diff(rend, axis=0))) + np.sum(np.abs(np.diff(rend, axis=1))) for img, rend in zip(images, renderedimages)) gradpoints, gradhcoeffs = autograd(loss, points, hcoeffs) points -= lrpos gradpoints hcoeffs -= lrsh gradhcoeffs return points, hcoeffs Pulsar is an efficient, sphere-based differentiable renderer that maps a 3D scene representation of spheres to a feature image, enabling end-to-end optimization of scene geometry, features, and camera parameters. It solves the problem of slow rendering and topological inconsistencies inherent in mesh-based or voxel-based neural rendering by using a sparse, explicit sphere representation that naturally culls empty space without acceleration structures. Unlike its siblings, Pulsar parallelizes over pixels rather than spheres to avoid synchronization overhead, and it decouples geometry projection from appearance via a neural shading network, allowing unlimited spheres to contribute to color while restricting gradient propagation to the first few spheres to avoid high-frequency artifacts. Time Complexity: Rendering is a single forward pass via splatting, avoiding volumetric ray marching. Training is significantly faster than NeRF-based methods. Memory Complexity: Less than 10 MB for a static scene. Performance: On novel video view synthesis, achieves 34.6 dB PSNR in 30 min training and 40 ms inference, compared to STNeRF's 32.1 dB in 50 h training and 30 s inference. Training is up to 300x faster than NeRF. Rendering is approximately 400x faster than Point-NeRF. Strengths: High efficiency in training and inference, low memory footprint, no need for additional learned or explicit priors. Limitations: Requires object masks for initialization, limiting it to foreground scene components. Cannot handle semi-transparent objects (e.g., fur) due to the splatting representation. Quality may be slightly lower than NeRF when many input views are provided. DPBF was introduced by Qiang Zhang at Princeton University in 2022. It was presented at the ACM SIGGRAPH Asia 2022 conference. The method builds on the idea of using point clouds for scene representation, departing from volumetric representations to improve efficiency. It addresses limitations of previous point-based methods like Kopanas et al. [2021] and Lassner et al. [2021], which required long training times or large storage. name: Pulsar Sphere-based Neural Rendering
head: Pulsar
body: Pulsar is an efficient, sphere-based differentiable renderer that maps a 3D scene representation of spheres to a feature image, enabling end-to-end optimization of scene geometry, features, and camera parameters. It solves the problem of slow rendering and topological inconsistencies inherent in mesh-based or voxel-based neural rendering by using a sparse, explicit sphere representation that naturally culls empty space without acceleration structures. Unlike its siblings, Pulsar parallelizes over pixels rather than spheres to avoid synchronization overhead, and it decouples geometry projection from appearance via a neural shading network, allowing unlimited spheres to contribute to color while restricting gradient propagation to the first few spheres to avoid high-frequency artifacts. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A scene representation \mathcal{S} consisting of M spheres; camera parameters (rotation \mathbf{R}, translation \mathbf{t}, intrinsic matrix \mathbf{K}); and neural shading parameters \Thetas. Output: A rendered feature image \mathbf{F} or color image. Data Structures: The scene is converted from a "struct of arrays" to an "array of structs" for efficient GPU access. Two primary structures are used: 1. Intersection Information Struct: Contains four unsigned short values representing the calculated min/max x and y limits (bounding box) of the sphere's projection on the sensor plane. Total size: 8 bytes. This fits exactly into one cache line on NVIDIA Turing GPUs (256 bytes / 32 threads = 8 bytes per thread), enabling coalesced loading. 2. Draw Information Struct: Contains the position vector (3 floats), up to three feature value floats or a float pointer (if >3 features), distance to sphere center, and sphere radius. Total size: 32 bytes. 3. Depth Array: A separate array storing the earliest possible intersection depth for each sphere (set to infinity if outside the sensor). Parameters: \gamma (Gamma): Scaling factor for blending softness. Limits allowed: 1 and 1–5 for numerical stability. Small values (1–5) lead to 'hard' blending; large values (1) lead to 'soft' blending. \xi (Xi): Background offset constant. A fixed small constant added to the denominator as \exp(\xi/\gamma) to represent the weight for the background color. Block Size: 16x16 = 256 threads (8 warps per block). This size maximizes performance due to memory requirements. Algorithm Steps: 1. Scene Representation: Each sphere i is defined by position \mathbf{p}i \in \mathbb{R}^3, neural feature vector \mathbf{f}i \in \mathbb{R}^d, radius ri \in \mathbb{R}, and opacity oi \in \mathbb{R}. 2. Step 0: Enclosing Rectangle Calculation: Parallelized over spheres using the full GPU. Compute the bounding box projection of each sphere on the sensor plane using \mathbf{K}, \mathbf{p}i, and ri. Robustify boundaries: Ensure every sphere is rendered with at least a size of one pixel to prevent spheres from being 'lost' between pixel rays and to ensure every sphere receives gradients. Store results in Intersection Information and Draw Information structs. Store the earliest possible intersection depth in a separate array (infinity if outside sensor). Sort both arrays by earliest intersection depth using a parallel sorting library (e.g., CUB). 3. Step 1: Intersection Search: Divide the image into nine parts (empirically derived). Process parts sequentially. For each part, use the full GPU to iterate over the Intersection Information array to find spheres relevant to the pixels in that region (parallelized over spheres). Use CUB select flags to create sorted subsets of Intersection Information and Draw Information for the relevant spheres. Parallelize over pixels using thread blocks (16x16=256 threads) and warps for coalesced processing. Early Stopping: Stop the sphere intersection search for a pixel when the first tested sphere has a depth greater than an upper bound calculated using the current aggregated weights and Eq. 1. This ensures no remaining sphere can have a notable impact. 4. Feature Aggregation (Blending): Compute the feature image \mathbf{F} by aggregating sphere features using blending weights wi. Allow unlimited spheres to contribute to pixel color (or set a bound based on minimum contribution) to avoid high-frequency artifacts in complex scenes. Use only the first few spheres for gradient propagation to avoid high-frequency artifacts. Blending Weight Formula: wi = \frac{oi \cdot di \cdot \exp(oi \cdot \frac{zi}{\gamma})}{\exp(\frac{\xi}{\gamma}) + \sumk ok \cdot dk \cdot \exp(ok \cdot \frac{zk}{\gamma})} Where: oi: Sphere opacity. di: Normalized orthogonal distance from ray to sphere center. zi: Normalized device coordinate depth ([0,1], where 0 is max depth and 1 is min depth/closest to camera). \gamma: Temperature parameter for blending sharpness. \xi: Background offset constant. The sum in the denominator is over all spheres k contributing to the pixel. Normalized Orthogonal Distance Formula: di = \min\left(1, \frac{||\tilde{d}i||2}{Ri}\right) Where \tilde{d}i is the vector pointing orthogonally from the ray to the sphere center, and Ri is the sphere radius. This acts as a linear scaling factor in [0, 1]. Opacity Integration: Opacity oi is used in both the exponential depth term and the linear distance term to prevent spheres from being visible in front of the background (if only in exponential) or depth overriding opacity (if only in linear). 5. Neural Shading: Convert the 2D screen space feature map \mathbf{F} to the output color image using a neural network \mathcal{N} (e.g., convolutional U-Net or per-pixel 1x1 convolution). 6. End-to-End Optimization: Optimize scene representation \mathcal{S} and shading parameters \Thetas by minimizing L1 loss between input images \mathbf{I}i and rendered images \mathcal{N}(\mathcal{R}(\mathcal{S}, \mathbf{R}i, \mathbf{t}i, \mathbf{K}i); \Thetas) using ADAM. Solved by allowing unlimited spheres to contribute to color while restricting gradient propagation to the first few spheres. Opacity integration: Integrating opacity only as a depth scaling factor leaves spheres visible in front of the background; integrating only as a distance scaling factor makes depth override opacity. Solved by using opacity in both places (exponential and linear factor). Position gradients instability: Position gradients are numerically unstable if a sphere projects to a radius of 3 pixels or fewer. It addresses the limitation of standard sphere-based rendering where color is often treated as a static attribute, failing to capture complex specularities or material variations that change with the viewing angle. Unlike standard splatting which assigns a fixed color to each primitive, this method decouples geometry projection from appearance, allowing the network to predict the final color based on the underlying sphere features and the camera's viewing vector. Sphere Subdivision Refinement is a technique to increase sphere count and detail by subdividing existing spheres into smaller ones, followed by re-optimization and pruning. It refines each sphere into 12 new spheres with radius \sqrt{2} \cdot r, placed in a face-centered cubic packing scheme relative to the parent sphere. The new set of spheres is then optimized, and spheres are pruned if their color converges towards the background color or if they are not visible (do not receive gradient updates from any viewpoint). Scaling: Performance scales favorably with future GPU generations due to the block size limit (256 threads) being determined by current hardware memory constraints. Avoids topological inconsistencies and changing topology problems of meshes. Eliminates the need for acceleration structures (k-d tree, octree). Limitations: Requires CUDA C and PyTorch integration. Numerical instability for small projected sphere radii (< 3 pixels). When to use: When real-time rendering and optimization of millions of spheres are required, or when topological consistency is critical. When not to use: When hardware does not support CUDA or PyTorch, or when very small-scale features (sub-pixel spheres) are critical and cannot be robustified. Pulsar was introduced in 2021 by the authors of "Pulsar: Efficient Sphere-based Neural Rendering". It builds on recent insights in differentiable rendering and neural networks, deliberately limiting complexity in the projection step to obtain high speed and scalability. It is implemented as a C++ and CUDA C PyTorch extension. The method was developed to alleviate challenges in gradient-based optimization of neural mesh, voxel, or function representations, such as topological inconsistencies, high memory footprints, and slow rendering speeds. name: Neural Shading in Pulsar
head: Neural Shading Network, View-Dependent Shading with Neural Network
body: Neural Shading in Pulsar is a method for modeling view-dependent appearance by integrating a neural shading network that conditions on per-pixel view direction, shared across all pixels. It addresses the limitation of standard sphere-based rendering where color is often treated as a static attribute, failing to capture complex specularities or material variations that change with the viewing angle. Unlike standard splatting which assigns a fixed color to each primitive, this method decouples geometry projection from appearance, allowing the network to predict the final color based on the underlying sphere features and the camera's viewing vector. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: Per-pixel view direction vector \mathbf{v}, sphere color/features (optimizable channel information), and camera parameters (intrinsic K, rotation R, translation t) used to project spheres to screen space. Outputs: Rendered feature image F (final pixel colors). Data Structures: Sphere Representation: A set of spheres defined by position, radius, color, and opacity, as defined in Pulsar Sphere-based Neural Rendering. Neural Shading Network: A fully-connected neural network (MLP) with a design similar to Pix2PixHD featuring 15 feature channels. The exact input dimension is not specified, but it conditions on the view direction. Algorithm Steps: 1. Projection: Project the 3D sphere representation S onto the 2D image plane using camera parameters (R, t, K) to generate screen-space splats. 2. View Direction Computation: For each pixel, compute the view direction vector \mathbf{v} from the camera center to the pixel's corresponding 3D location (or the sphere centroid). 3. Neural Shading: Feed the per-pixel view direction \mathbf{v} and the sphere's color/features into the neural shading network. 4. Color Prediction: The network outputs the final color for the pixel, effectively modulating the sphere's base color based on the viewing angle. 5. Blending: Composite the shaded colors from overlapping spheres using the order-independent blending mechanism of Pulsar. 6. Optimization: Back-propagate gradients through the shading network to optimize the sphere's channel information (colors/features) and the network weights jointly. Loss Functions: The training of the neural shading network utilizes a combination of losses: Photometric L1-loss. Perceptual loss. Adversarial loss. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectspheres(spheres, R, t, K, H, W): screensplats = [] for s in spheres: centercam = R @ s.position + t ndcx = (K[0][0] centercam[0] / centercam[2]) + K[0][2] ndcy = (K[1][1] centercam[1] / centercam[2]) + K[1][2] px = ndcx W / 2 py = ndcy H / 2 screensplats.append({'px': px, 'py': py, 'color': s.color, 'opacity': s.opacity, 'radius': s.radius}) return screensplats def neuralshadinginpulsar(spheres, R, t, K, H, W, network): screensplats = projectspheres(spheres, R, t, K, H, W) outputimage = [[0.0, 0.0, 0.0] for in range(H W)] for splat in screensplats: for dy in range(-int(splat['radius']), int(splat['radius']) + 1): for dx in range(-int(splat['radius']), int(splat['radius']) + 1): px = int(splat['px'] + dx) py = int(splat['py'] + dy) if 0 <= px < W and 0 <= py < H: viewdir = normalize([(px - K[0][2]) / K[0][0], (py - K[1][2]) / K[1][1], 1.0]) shadedcolor = network(viewdir, splat['color']) idx = py W + px outputimage[idx][0] += shadedcolor[0] splat['opacity'] outputimage[idx][1] += shadedcolor[1] splat['opacity'] outputimage[idx][2] += shadedcolor[2] splat['opacity'] return outputimage def trainneuralshading(spheres, images, network, optimizer, numiterations): for i in range(numiterations): renderedimage = neuralshadinginpulsar(spheres, R, t, K, H, W, network) l1loss = sum(abs(renderedimage[p] - images[i][p]) for p in range(HW)) / (HW) perceptualloss = computeperceptualdistance(renderedimage, images[i]) adversarialloss = computeadversarialloss(renderedimage, discriminator(renderedimage)) totalloss = l1loss + perceptualloss + adversarialloss totalloss.backward() optimizer.step() optimizer.zerograd() Parameters: Network Architecture: Fully-connected network with 15 feature channels. Optimization: Adam optimizer. Training Data: Synthetic scenes (e.g., 'chair' scene from NeRF dataset with 200 views). Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Sphere Pruning: Spheres whose color converges to the background color or receive no gradient updates from any viewpoint are eliminated to maintain a thin hull representation. Depth Regularization: An opacity-depth regularizer with energy -zi \cdot Oi is applied to encourage spheres to move to the correct scene depth. A strategy that leverages a neural network conditioned on 3D Gaussian attributes and viewing direction to capture view-dependent information, mitigating transparency artifacts introduced by order-independent rendering. It is a lightweight MLP designed to extract discriminative features from 3D Gaussian primitives. The network predicts opacity o and an auxiliary feature \boldsymbol{\phi}. Opacity is constrained to [0, 1] via Sigmoid, and \boldsymbol{\phi} uses ReLU. The MLP has 3 layers with neuron counts 256, 128, and 64. It is trained jointly with 3D Gaussian primitives for 30k iterations. This variant is chosen when rendering order-independent transparency artifacts are significant and view-dependent effects are critical. Time Complexity: The neural shading step adds a forward pass through an MLP per pixel/splat. Memory Complexity: Depends on the number of spheres and the size of the neural network. The source mentions models with up to 1.6 million spheres temporarily during refinement. Performance: Optimization of a coarse head model with 400k spheres took 73 seconds. Optimization of a scene with 2.1M spheres took 20 minutes on an NVIDIA V100 GPU. Refinement of a 130k sphere model took 37 minutes. Strengths: Enables realistic modeling of view-dependent appearance (e.g., satin covers, hair, eyes) at high resolution. Decouples geometry and appearance. Limitations: Requires training with adversarial and perceptual losses, which can be complex to tune. The method was introduced in the paper "Pulsar: Efficient Sphere-based Neural Rendering". It was developed to showcase the potential of the Pulsar pipeline by combining sphere-based geometry projection with neural shading. The authors demonstrated the method on synthetic scenes like 'chair' (from the NeRF dataset) and real-world objects like hair and eyes, using datasets of 100 images at 800x1280 resolution. The approach allows for the separation of geometry projection and neural shading under challenging conditions. name: Point-based Differentiable Rendering
head: PBDR
body: Point-based Differentiable Rendering (PBDR) is a rendering method that models a 3D scene as a learnable point cloud of parameterized points and optimizes their attributes via gradient descent to reconstruct the scene from 2D images. Unlike traditional rendering which uses static geometry, PBDR treats the scene representation as differentiable, allowing direct optimization of appearance and geometry through differentiable splat rendering. It sets itself apart from sibling methods like Pulsar Sphere-based Neural Rendering by using parameterized ellipsoids (typically Gaussians) rather than spheres or other primitives, enabling efficient view synthesis via splatting. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of 2D images with known camera poses (intrinsics and extrinsics). Outputs: A learned 3D point cloud where each point has optimized attributes (position, color, opacity, etc.) and the rendered novel views. Data Structures: The scene is represented as a collection of N points. Each point i is modeled as a 3D ellipsoid. The specific attributes depend on the variant, but the canonical 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) point stores five attributes: 1. 3D Position: \mathbf{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3. 2. Scales: \mathbf{s}i \in \mathbb{R}^3 (representing the ellipsoid axes lengths). 3. Rotation: \mathbf{q}i \in \mathbb{R}^4 (unit quaternion representing orientation). 4. Opacity: \alphai \in [0, 1]. 5. Color: Represented by spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients \mathbf{c}i. Steps: 1. Initialization: Initialize the point cloud using an existing reconstruction method, such as COLMAP [72] or LiDAR data. 2. Culling: Discard points that lie outside the camera’s field of view (frustum). 3. Splatting: Project each remaining point into the camera’s 2D image plane as a "splat". 4. Rendering: Sort the view-dependent splats by their distance to the camera plane. Compute pixel color front-to-back, blending overlapping splats until full opacity is reached. 5. Loss Computation: Compare the rendered image against the ground-truth image to compute a loss (e.g., L1 or SSIM). 6. Backpropagation: Calculate gradients of the loss with respect to the point parameters. 7. Update: Update point parameters using gradient descent (e.g., SGD). 8. Densification: Periodically increase point cloud density by adding more points to the model during training. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def trainpbdtr(trainingimages, initialpoints, numiterations): # Initialize point cloud parameters # Points have attributes: position, scales, rotation, opacity, SH coefficients points = initializepoints(initialpoints) for step in range(numiterations): # 1. Select a batch of images and their camera views batchimages, batchcameras = selectbatch(trainingimages) renderedimages = [] for image, camera in zip(batchimages, batchcameras): # 2. Culling: Discard points outside camera frustum visiblepoints = cullpoints(points, camera) # 3. Splatting: Project points to 2D image plane splats = projecttosplats(visiblepoints, camera) # 4. Rendering: Sort splats by depth and blend front-to-back sortedsplats = sortbydepth(splats) renderedimage = renderfronttoback(sortedsplats, image.resolution) renderedimages.append(renderedimage) # 5. Loss Computation loss = computeloss(renderedimages, batchimages) # 6. Backpropagation gradients = computegradients(loss, points) # 7. Update points = updateparameters(points, gradients) # 8. Densification (periodic) if step % densificationinterval == 0: points = densifypointcloud(points) return points Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: Standard floating-point precision may be insufficient for large-scale scenes with billions of points; distributed systems must handle communication overhead. Boundaries: Frustum culling must be robust to avoid missing points near the edge of the view. Degenerate Input: Initial reconstruction quality (e.g., from COLMAP) significantly impacts convergence; poor initialization may lead to incomplete reconstruction. A two-stage procedure to optimize data access locality in distributed PBDR by assigning points and images to GPUs to minimize communication overhead. It uses graph partitioning and Z-order curve sorting to exploit spatial locality, unlike naive random distribution. A distributed training system for PBDR that reduces communication overhead by optimizing data locality rather than randomly partitioning model state and compute. It provides a unified API exposing data access patterns for locality optimization. Time Complexity: Rendering is O(N) for splatting and O(N \log N) for sorting, where N is the number of visible points. Training involves iterative gradient descent, which scales with the number of points and images. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store point attributes. For 3DGS, each point stores position, scales, rotation, opacity, and SH coefficients. Measured Performance: The Gaian system reduces communication by up to 91% and improves training throughput by 1.50–3.71× across six datasets and up to 128 GPUs. It achieved a 12.7× speedup in computation and trained a point cloud with 500 million points (29.5 billion parameters). Strengths: Outperforms previous neural rendering approaches in complex scene reconstruction and photorealistic novel view synthesis. Efficient differentiable rendering pipeline. Limitations: Random distribution of points and views in distributed settings can cause communication time to exceed compute time. Requires periodic densification to maintain quality. When to Use: Large-scale scene reconstruction and novel view synthesis where high fidelity is required. When Not to Use: Real-time applications with strict latency constraints without hardware acceleration, or scenes with very sparse initial data. PBDR methods have recently achieved remarkable breakthroughs in complex scene reconstruction and photorealistic novel view synthesis. The first PBDR algorithm, 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS), was proposed by [40] and uses 3D Gaussian ellipsoids with five attributes. Since then, many PBDR algorithms have been proposed with different point types, including 2D Gaussian [33], 3D Convex [31], Triangle Mesh [30], and Generalized Exponential Kernel [27]. Existing distributed works [90, 96] support distributed training for 3DGS by partitioning the point cloud across GPUs.
