name: Sorting Algorithms
body: Sorting Algorithms in volume rendering splatting reorder volumetric primitives (typically 3D Gaussian splats) by depth to ensure correct front-to-back alpha blending. This solves the order-dependent transparency problem inherent in splatting, where incorrect draw order leads to visual artifacts. Unlike siblings that may use partial ordering or hardware-specific tricks, this family focuses on generating a strict depth-sorted index buffer for the rasterizer. Builds on the splatting family's shared mechanism of treating volumetric data as transformed primitives rasterized onto the image plane Parent. Reorders 3D Gaussian splats by depth on the CPU to enable correct front-to-back alpha blending. Offloads sorting from the GPU to avoid compute stalls, making it suitable when GPU compute shaders are unavailable or underutilized. Merges pre-sorted splat lists from multiple independent renderers into a single globally depth-sorted order buffer using a cascaded binary merge tree. Chosen for unified multi-scene rendering to prevent incorrect depth ordering and excessive overdraw. Sorts particles along a view-dependent half-angle axis using an odd-even merge sort, then renders them in slices. Sets itself apart by decoupling the sorting axis from the view direction to allow efficient accumulation of opacity from the light's perspective for volumetric shadows. A data-independent network sorting algorithm used on the GPU to achieve exact depth ordering of splatted voxels per frame. Chosen over partial-ordering methods because volume rendering requires strict front-to-back or back-to-front ordering for correct transparency compositing. Produces a permutation of indices rather than reordering data values, maintaining data association during sorting. Chosen when voxel attributes (density, color) must remain linked to their spatial keys without packing keys and indices into a single register. A compositing technique for splats (oriented ellipses) that sorts them back-to-front relative to a camera viewpoint to ensure correct translucent blending. When cameraPositionProvider is null, the SplatNode automatically sorts its splats for the scene camera's current position. If cameraPositionProvider is provided, the node sorts splats for the viewpoint returned by that provider instead of the scene camera. The sorting is performed on a background thread whenever the camera moves. Without a cameraPositionProvider (and thus without sorting), the compositing order remains as loaded, causing visual popping artifacts when orbiting the camera. A sorting method that shuffles full records (data) rather than just indices, used to increase cache coherency with frequently-accessed sorted data. It generates a simple spatial index for each input value, performs index sorting on the key-index pair array, and then performs the full shuffling step for record sorting if needed. Record sizes tested are 32, 64, and 128 bits, breaking a regular array of records into a structure of arrays with typical length types. The final shuffle step involves accessing data in arbitrary-like order from the original array while outputting sorted data sequentially, leading to non-coalesced reading which is a major bottleneck. Using texture fetching provides a factor of three improvement in shuffling performance over typical mapping using global memory for uniformly distributed inputs. Originating from the need to resolve order-dependent transparency in splat-based volume rendering, these algorithms evolved alongside 3D Gaussian Splatting. Early implementations relied on CPU sorting due to GPU limitations, while modern approaches leverage GPU subgroups and merge networks for real-time global sorting. feat(sceneview): sort splats for the scene camera by default and add …, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/commit/5f2a4dd1f683ddb444669be54b78ce7913b55b70, fetched 2026-10-30 (unofficial) Fast 4-way parallel radix sorting on GPUs, https://www.sci.utah.edu/~csilva/papers/cgf.pdf, fetched 2026-10-29 (unofficial)

name: CPU-Based Splat Sorting
head: Splat Sort, WebGL-based Rendering Framework with Decoupled Sorting, WebWorker Splat Sort
body: CPU-Based Splat Sorting is a method for reordering volumetric primitives (specifically 3D Gaussian splats) by depth on the central processing unit to enable correct front-to-back alpha blending. It solves the problem of order-dependent transparency in splatting by ensuring that splats are drawn from nearest to farthest relative to the camera. Unlike GPU-based sorting methods such as Bitonic Sort, which require significant compute resources and can stall the rendering pipeline, this method offloads the sorting task to the CPU, often using asynchronous workers (e.g., WebWorkers) to allow the GPU to focus exclusively on rasterization. This separation of concerns trades sorting latency for rendering stability, making it suitable for environments where GPU compute shaders are unavailable or where the CPU is underutilized during the render loop. The method transforms 3D splat positions into view space, extracts a depth metric, and sorts the splats based on this metric to produce an index buffer for rendering. Inputs: viewProj: A 4 \times 4 Model-View-Projection matrix. positions: An array of N 3D positions, typically interleaved as (x, y, z) floats. vertexCount (N): The number of splats to sort. Outputs: depthIndex: A vector of N unsigned integers representing the original indices of the splats, sorted by depth from front (smallest depth) to back (largest depth). Splat Pair: A structure or tuple containing: depth: A floating-point value representing the splat's distance from the camera along the view axis. originalindex: An integer index identifying the splat's position in the original positions array. 1. Project Positions: For each splat i from 0 to N-1: Let \mathbf{p}i = (xi, yi, zi) be the 3D position. Compute the homogeneous clip-space coordinate: \mathbf{v}i = \text{viewProj} \cdot \begin{bmatrix} xi \\ yi \\ zi \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} Extract the depth value di by perspective division: di = \frac{v{i,z}}{v{i,w}} where v{i,z} and v{i,w} are the z and w components of \mathbf{v}i. 2. Create Pairs: Construct a list of pairs L = [ (d0, 0), (d1, 1), \dots, (d{N-1}, N-1) ]. 3. Sort: Sort the list L in ascending order based on the depth value d. Comparator: For pairs A and B, A precedes B if A.\text{depth} < B.\text{depth}. 4. Extract Indices: Create the output depthIndex vector by extracting the originalindex from each pair in the sorted list L. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cpusplatsort(viewprojmatrix, positions, vertexcount): """ Sorts splats by depth on the CPU. Args: viewprojmatrix: 4x4 matrix (list of lists or array) positions: List of (x, y, z) tuples vertexcount: Integer number of splats Returns: depthindex: List of integers representing sorted indices """ # Step 1 & 2: Project and create pairs splatpairs = [] for i in range(vertexcount): x, y, z = positions[i] # Transform position with MVP matrix # Assuming viewprojmatrix is a 4x4 structure accessible as [row][col] # Homogeneous coordinate calculation w = (viewprojmatrix[3][0] x + viewprojmatrix[3][1] y + viewprojmatrix[3][2] z + viewprojmatrix[3][3]) zclip = (viewprojmatrix[2][0] x + viewprojmatrix[2][1] y + viewprojmatrix[2][2] z + viewprojmatrix[2][3]) # Perspective divide to get depth if w == 0: depth = float('inf') # Guard against division by zero else: depth = zclip / w splatpairs.append((depth, i)) # Step 3: Sort by depth (ascending: front to back) splatpairs.sort(key=lambda pair: pair[0]) # Step 4: Extract sorted indices depthindex = [pair[1] for pair in splatpairs] return depthindex Sorting Algorithm: Standard comparison-based sorts (e.g., Quicksort, Mergesort) are used on the CPU. Precision: Floating-point depth calculation is standard, though integer-based approximations may be used for performance in specific implementations (see Subtopics). Asynchrony: In web environments, this function is typically executed in a background thread (WebWorker) to prevent blocking the main render loop. Camera Jumps: Rapid camera movement, such as jumping between opposite sides of the scene, causes momentary visual artifacts because the Z-order does not update fast enough relative to the render loop. The sorting latency creates a mismatch between the camera position and the sorted splat order. Large Dimensions: Scenes with very large spatial dimensions may cause "Index out of bounds" errors during sorting, particularly if integer-based sorting is used with insufficient precision. Performance Bottleneck: Sorting ~1 million splats on a CPU takes approximately 150ms, resulting in a sorting throughput of ~4fps, whereas the main render loop targets 60fps. This disparity means the sorting is often asynchronous and may lag behind real-time camera movement. This variant calculates a scalar key for each 3D Gaussian splat to determine rendering order, combining projected size and opacity to prioritize "important" splats (large and opaque) for front-to-back alpha blending. It differs from simple depth sorting by incorporating splat importance metrics, ensuring that visually significant splats are composited correctly even if their geometric depth is slightly ambiguous. Choose this when opacity and size vary significantly across splats and simple depth sorting results in incorrect transparency accumulation. The CPU Fallback Sort Path is a rendering strategy that executes splat sorting on the CPU when GPU compute sorting is disabled or unavailable, such as on platforms like the Android Filament Java API which lack compute shader support. It differs from GPU-based methods by relying on CPU-side sorting algorithms to produce a sorted order buffer, which is then uploaded to a shader-readable structured buffer instead of using GPU append or UAV buffers. Choose this when GPU compute capabilities are restricted or when implementing a fallback for mobile/embedded devices. This variant implements CPU-based splat sorting in C++ using WebAssembly (WASM) SIMD instructions to accelerate the sorting process, or uses transform feedback for partial GPU acceleration. It differs from standard CPU sorting by leveraging vectorized instructions to improve throughput. Key parameters include integerBasedSort (forces slower floating-point sort if false, used for large scenes where integer sort fails) and splatSortDistanceMapPrecision (adjusts precision to alleviate artifacts). Choose this for web-based viewers requiring optimized performance on modern CPUs. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) for standard comparison-based sorting algorithms on the CPU. Memory Complexity: O(N) to store the depth-index pairs and the output index buffer. Measured Performance: Sorting approximately 1 million splats takes ~150ms on a typical desktop CPU, yielding a sorting rate of ~4fps compared to a 60fps render loop. Strengths: Avoids GPU compute overhead and synchronization stalls associated with GPU sorting. Works on hardware without compute shader support (e.g., certain mobile APIs). Allows the GPU to dedicate all resources to rasterization. Limitations: High latency relative to frame time can cause visual artifacts during rapid camera movement. Sorting performance is significantly slower than GPU-based parallel sorts for very large N. May cause "Index out of bounds" crashes in scenes with very large dimensions if precision settings are not adjusted. When to Use: When GPU compute is unavailable or when implementing a robust fallback path for cross-platform compatibility. When Not to Use: In real-time applications requiring strict synchronization between camera movement and splat order, or when sorting millions of splats per frame with low latency requirements. CPU-based splat sorting originated as a pragmatic solution for web-based 3D Gaussian Splatting viewers, where GPU compute shaders were either unavailable or inefficient for sorting tasks compared to rendering. The approach was popularized by implementations like antimatter15/splat, which utilized WebWorkers to perform sorting asynchronously, allowing for smooth rendering despite the slow sorting speed. It serves as a fallback for platforms like Android Filament, which lack compute shader support, and is often optimized with SIMD instructions in WASM environments for better performance. antimatter15/splat, https://github.com/antimatter15/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, https://github.com/liaozhangsheng/gsplat-opengl, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) Monte Carlo Energy Aggregation for Mobile 3D Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-37167-617, fetched 2026-10-29 mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, https://github.com/mkkellogg/GaussianSplats3D, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Splat Sorting Key Calculation
head: Importance Sorting, Splat ordering metric, Splat sort key
body: This method calculates a scalar key for each 3D Gaussian splat to determine the rendering order, typically for front-to-back alpha blending. It combines the splat's projected size and opacity to prioritize "important" splats (large and opaque) to be drawn first, ensuring correct accumulation of color and alpha. Inputs: A list of N splats. For each splat i: Scale components: s{0,i}, s{1,i}, s{2,i} (log-space scales). Opacity: \alphai (logit-space opacity). Position and rotation are not used in the key calculation itself but are required for subsequent rendering steps. Outputs: An array of indices sortedindices of length N, such that splats are ordered from highest key to lowest key. Data Structures: sizeList: Float32Array of length N. Stores the calculated key for each splat. sizeIndex: Uint32Array of length N. Stores the original index of each splat. Formula: The key Ki for splat i is defined as: Ki = \frac{\exp(s{0,i} + s{1,i} + s{2,i})}{1 + \exp(-\alphai)} Where: \exp(s{0,i} + s{1,i} + s{2,i}) represents the volume or area metric derived from the log-scales. 1 + \exp(-\alphai) is the sigmoid denominator, converting logit opacity to probability space. Steps: 1. Initialize sizeList as a Float32Array of length N and sizeIndex as a Uint32Array of length N. 2. For each splat index i from 0 to N-1: a. Read s{0,i}, s{1,i}, s{2,i} and \alphai. b. Calculate the numerator: Vi = \exp(s{0,i} + s{1,i} + s{2,i}). c. Calculate the denominator: Oi = 1 + \exp(-\alphai). d. Compute key: Ki = Vi / Oi. e. Set sizeList[i] = Ki. f. Set sizeIndex[i] = i. 3. Sort sizeIndex in descending order based on the values in sizeList. Specifically, if Ka > Kb, then index a should precede index b in the sorted array. 4. Return sizeIndex. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def calculatesplatsortkey(splats): """ splats: list of dicts or objects with keys 'scale0', 'scale1', 'scale2', 'opacity' Returns: list of indices sorted by importance (descending) """ import math n = len(splats) if n == 0: return [] # Arrays to store keys and original indices sizelist = [0.0] n sizeindex = list(range(n)) for i in range(n): # Read raw vertex properties s0 = splats[i].get('scale0') s1 = splats[i].get('scale1') s2 = splats[i].get('scale2') alpha = splats[i].get('opacity') # If scale0 does not exist, key remains 0 (or default) if s0 is None: sizelist[i] = 0.0 sizeindex[i] = i continue # Calculate volume metric from log-scales volume = math.exp(s0 + s1 + s2) # Calculate opacity from logit opacity = 1.0 / (1.0 + math.exp(-alpha)) # Key is volume opacity key = volume opacity sizelist[i] = key sizeindex[i] = i # Sort indices based on sizelist in descending order sizeindex.sort(key=lambda idx: sizelist[idx], reverse=True) return sizeindex Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Missing Scales: If scale components are missing, the key defaults to 0 or a minimal value. Precision: Using exp() on large scale values can cause overflow. In practice, scales are usually small, but clamping or using log-sum-exp tricks may be necessary for extreme cases. Degenerate Input: If all splats have identical keys, the sort order is arbitrary. This is acceptable as long as the rendering is consistent. Time Complexity: O(N \log N) due to the sorting step. The key calculation is O(N). Memory Complexity: O(N) for storing sizeList and sizeIndex. Performance: Sorting on the CPU (e.g., in a WebWorker) offloads the GPU, allowing it to focus on rendering. Strengths: Allows progressive loading by sorting only loaded splats. Limitations: Does not account for view-dependent effects like spherical harmonics in the key calculation. The key is static per splat and does not update with camera movement, so it is most effective when the camera is relatively stable or when splats are sorted per frame if performance allows. This method is used in 3D Gaussian Splatting renderers, particularly in web-based implementations where CPU-based sorting is preferred for simplicity and compatibility. The approach prioritizes visual importance over geometric depth, which is crucial for Gaussian splats where the "size" of a splat can vary dramatically. antimatter15/splat, https://github.com/antimatter15/splat, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, https://github.com/akbartus/Gaussian-Splatting-WebViewers, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: CPU Fallback Sort Path
head: CPU-only cutout path, Portable CPU-sort path
body: The CPU Fallback Sort Path is a rendering strategy that performs splat sorting on the CPU when GPU-based compute sorting is disabled, unavailable, or unsupported by the target API. It serves as a portable alternative to GPU sorting algorithms (such as bitonic sort) by offloading the O(n \log n) sorting work to a background thread, allowing the GPU to focus exclusively on rasterization and composition. It is distinct from the standard GPU sort path by utilizing shader-readable structured buffers (or texture uploads) rather than append/unordered access views (UAVs) for data transfer. The method determines the active sorting path based on a configuration flag and allocates specific buffer types to facilitate CPU-to-GPU data transfer. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A list of splats (typically represented as 3D Gaussians with position, scale, rotation, opacity, and color) requiring back-to-front sorting for correct alpha blending. Output: A sorted sequence of splat indices or data ready for GPU consumption. Data Structures: The implementation relies on GraphicsBuffer types (specifically in Unity-style APIs) or equivalent texture buffers in other engines: 1. OrderBuffer: A buffer storing the sorted order of splats. If CpuFallbackEnabled is true: GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured. If CpuFallbackEnabled is false: GraphicsBuffer.Target.Append. 2. OrderSizeBuffer: (Only allocated if fallback is disabled) An IndirectArguments buffer of size 1, used to store the count of sorted items for indirect draw calls. 3. BoundsBuffer: (Only allocated if fallback is disabled) A Structured buffer of size 6, likely storing bounding box coordinates or related metadata. Parameters: CpuFallbackEnabled (Boolean): Determines the active path. When true, the system uses the CPU fallback path. Algorithm Steps: 1. Check the value of CpuFallbackEnabled. 2. If CpuFallbackEnabled is true: a. Create OrderBuffer with target type Structured. b. Perform the sorting operation on the CPU (details depend on the specific variant, e.g., Radix Sort or Painter's Sort). c. Upload the sorted data to the OrderBuffer. 3. If CpuFallbackEnabled is false: a. Create OrderBuffer with target type Append. b. Allocate OrderSizeBuffer (IndirectArguments, size 1). c. Allocate BoundsBuffer (Structured, size 6). d. Proceed with GPU-based sorting (not detailed in this article). Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def initializesortpath(cpufallbackenabled: bool): """ Initializes the buffer structures for the sorting pipeline. """ if cpufallbackenabled: # CPU fallback path: use structured buffer for shader reading orderbuffer = creategraphicsbuffer(target=GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured) # Sorting logic is handled by the specific CPU variant (e.g., Radix or Painter's) # which writes directly to or uploads to orderbuffer else: # GPU compute path: use append buffer orderbuffer = creategraphicsbuffer(target=GraphicsBuffer.Target.Append) # Additional buffers required for GPU append logic ordersizebuffer = creategraphicsbuffer(target=GraphicsBuffer.Target.IndirectArguments, size=1) boundsbuffer = creategraphicsbuffer(target=GraphicsBuffer.Target.Structured, size=6) return orderbuffer, ordersizebuffer, boundsbuffer Edge Cases and Pitfalls: API Limitations: On platforms like Android with Filament's Java API, compute shaders are unavailable, necessitating this CPU path. Data Transfer Overhead: Re-uploading sorted data to the GPU after every sort can dominate performance, particularly on mobile hardware. An out-of-place sorting algorithm used on the CPU to sort face centroids for volume rendering splatting. It achieves linear time complexity O(n) at the expense of auxiliary memory. It differs from Logarithmic Distance Bucket Sort by using exact integer comparison rather than distance-based bucketing, making it suitable for general-purpose sorting where precise ordering is required without depth-peeling assumptions. A sorting algorithm executed on the CPU to order splats back-to-front for correct alpha blending, necessitated by the lack of compute shader support in the Android Filament Java API. Steps: Perform an O(n \log n) sort on a LongArray using SplatBuffers.sortBackToFront on a background thread. Re-upload the sorted data to the texture buffers after every re-sort. Parameters: The CPU sort is considered acceptable up to approximately 300,000–500,000 splats. Beyond this, Level of Detail (LOD) or pruning is required. Pitfalls: Performance bottleneck at high splat counts. At 233k splats, a single re-sort transfers approximately 5.6 MB of data, which dominates performance on mid-range phones due to fill rate and overdraw. Complexity: Time complexity is O(n \log n) per re-sort. Memory bandwidth usage is approximately 16 bytes per splat re-uploaded (24 bytes if a third texture is used). Time Complexity: O(n \log n) for standard CPU sorts (e.g., Painter's Sort). Linear time O(n) is possible with Radix Sort variants. Memory Complexity: Depends on the algorithm. Radix sort requires auxiliary memory. Painter's sort requires storage for the sorted array and texture buffers. Performance: On mid-range mobile devices, the CPU sort and subsequent data upload (approx. 16–24 bytes/splat) can become the dominant bottleneck. At 233k splats, the transfer size is ~5.6 MB per sort. Strengths: Portable across platforms lacking compute shader support (e.g., Android Filament Java API). Allows the GPU to focus on rendering. Limitations: Not scalable to very high splat counts (>500k) without LOD/pruning. CPU-GPU data transfer overhead is significant. When to use: When GPU compute sorting is unavailable or disabled, or on mobile devices where CPU sorting is acceptable for the target splat count. When not to use: When rendering millions of splats on hardware with efficient GPU sorting capabilities. The CPU Fallback Sort Path emerged as a necessary adaptation for rendering Gaussian Splats on platforms with limited graphics API support, specifically Android using the Filament engine, which lacks compute shader support in its Java API. It allows the sceneview/sceneview project to support Gaussian Splatting on mobile web and Android by offloading sorting to the CPU. The UnitySplats project also implements a CPU fallback path to handle cases where GPU sorting is disabled, providing a robust fallback for Unity-based applications. arloopa/UnitySplats, https://github.com/arloopa/UnitySplats, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial) Explore: Gaussian splatting, OpenUSD, AI world generation, volumetric video — study, https://github.com/sceneview/sceneview/issues/4023, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: CPU Radix Sort for Face Centroids
head: Floating Point Radix Sort, LSD Radix Sort
body: An out-of-place sorting algorithm used on the CPU to sort face centroids for volume rendering splatting, achieving linear time complexity at the expense of auxiliary memory. It differs from its sibling Logarithmic Distance Bucket Sort by using exact integer comparison rather than distance-based bucketing, making it suitable for general-purpose sorting where precise ordering is required without depth-peeling assumptions. Inputs: Array of N face centroids (floating-point values, typically distances). Outputs: Array of N sorted face centroids (ascending order). Auxiliary Data: An auxiliary array of size N and a count array of size 256. Data Structures: 1. input: Array of N 32-bit IEEE 754 floating-point numbers. 2. output: Array of N 32-bit unsigned integers (sorted keys). 3. counts: Array of 256 unsigned integers (histogram for counting sort). Steps: 1. Transformation: Convert each floating-point number in input to a 32-bit unsigned integer representation that preserves numerical order. This handles the sign bit inversion required for negative numbers in IEEE 754. 2. Pass 1 (LSD): Perform a counting sort on bits 0–7 of the transformed integers. Initialize counts to zero. Iterate through input, extract the lower 8 bits of each transformed value, and increment the corresponding index in counts. Compute prefix sums (cumulative counts) in counts to determine output positions. Distribute elements from input to output based on the computed positions. 3. Pass 2: Perform a counting sort on bits 8–15. Use output from Pass 1 as input and write to input (or a second auxiliary buffer, swapping roles). 4. Pass 3: Perform a counting sort on bits 16–23. 5. Pass 4: Perform a counting sort on bits 24–31 (MSD). 6. Final Output: The result is in the array written by Pass 4. Formulas: Float to Int Transformation: f{int} = f \oplus ((-(f \gg 31)) \mid 0x80000000) Where f is the bit-cast of the 32-bit float to an unsigned integer. This transformation ensures that negative floats sort before positive floats and maintain relative order. Bit Extraction: For block k (where k \in \{0, 1, 2, 3\}), the key for counting sort is: key = (f{int} \gg (8 \times k)) \ \& \ 0xFF Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def floattouint32(fbits): """Convert IEEE 754 float bits to signed-magnitude-like uint32 for sorting.""" # fbits is the raw 32-bit integer representation of the float signmask = -(fbits >> 31) # 0xFFFFFFFF if negative, 0x00000000 if positive return fbits ^ (signmask | 0x80000000) def cpuradixsortfacecentroids(centroidsfloat): """ Sorts an array of floating-point face centroids using LSD Radix Sort. centroidsfloat: List of floats. Returns: List of sorted floats. """ n = len(centroidsfloat) if n == 0: return [] # Step 1: Convert floats to sortable integers ints = [floattouint32(floattobits(c)) for c in centroidsfloat] # Auxiliary arrays output = [0] n counts = [0] 256 # Current data source and destination src = ints dst = output # Step 2-5: Four passes for 8-bit blocks for k in range(4): # Reset counts for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 # Count occurrences for i in range(n): key = (src[i] >> (8 k)) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 # Compute prefix sums (cumulative counts) # counts[i] will store the starting index for key i in the output total = 0 for i in range(256): temp = counts[i] counts[i] = total total += temp # Distribute elements to dst for i in range(n): key = (src[i] >> (8 k)) & 0xFF pos = counts[key] dst[pos] = src[i] counts[key] += 1 # Swap src and dst for next pass src, dst = dst, src # Convert back to floats sortedfloats = [bitstofloat(d) for d in src] return sortedfloats def floattobits(f): import struct return struct.unpack('I', struct.pack('f', f))[0] def bitstofloat(i): import struct return struct.unpack('f', struct.pack('I', i))[0] Parameters: Block size: 8 bits (4 passes total). Count array size: 256. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: NaN Values: The transformation assumes standard IEEE 754 numbers excluding NaNs. NaNs may not sort correctly or consistently. Precision: The transformation relies on the specific bit layout of IEEE 754. Non-compliant floating-point representations will fail. Memory: The algorithm is out-of-place, requiring O(N) auxiliary memory. LSD Block Sorting is a CPU-based radix sort algorithm that sorts 32-bit integers by processing them in 8-bit blocks from least significant to most significant. It solves the problem of ordering face centroids for volume rendering splatting by achieving linear time complexity through five sequential counting sort passes. It differs from its sibling Logarithmic Distance Bucket Sort by using exact integer comparison rather than distance-based bucketing, making it suitable for general-purpose sorting where precise ordering is required without depth-peeling assumptions. Time Complexity: Linear O(N), where N is the number of faces. The constant factor is small due to the fixed number of passes (4) and small radix (256). Memory Complexity: O(N) auxiliary space for the output array and O(1) for the count array (size 256). Performance: Sorts upwards of 15 million faces per second on the tested hardware. Comparison: Significantly faster than shellsort (584 ms), heapsort (507 ms), and quicksort (281 ms) for sorting one million floating-point numbers (radixsort took 64 ms). Strengths: Predictable performance independent of data distribution; much faster than comparison-based sorts for large N. Limitations: Requires auxiliary memory; not in-place; assumes IEEE 754 format. When to use: When sorting large numbers of face centroids on the CPU where GPU sorting is unavailable or disabled. When not to use: When memory is extremely constrained (due to auxiliary array requirement) or when the data is already nearly sorted and a specialized adaptive sort might be preferred (though the source notes that re-sorting is generally more efficient than adaptive sorts for this use case due to viewing direction changes). Originated in the context of the K-Buffer and its applications to volume rendering. The method was selected over other common sorting algorithms (shellsort, heapsort, quicksort, mergesort) because re-sorting face centroids with a fast sort is more efficient in practice than using an algorithm optimized for re-sorting previously sorted sequences, as the ordering can change significantly from frame to frame due to viewing direction changes. The specific float-to-int transformation is based on established techniques for sorting IEEE 754 floats as integers. THE K-BUFFER AND ITS APPLICATIONS TO VOLUME RENDERING, https://ctsilva.github.io/thesis/steve-callahan-ms-thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: LSD Block Sorting (Radix Sort)
head: LSD counting sort
body: LSD Block Sorting is a CPU-based radix sort that orders 32-bit integers by processing them in 8-bit blocks from least to most significant. It solves the depth-ordering requirement for volume rendering splatting by achieving linear time complexity through sequential counting sort passes, differing from distance-based bucketing methods by relying on exact integer comparison. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of N 32-bit unsigned integers representing face centroids or keys. Output: The array sorted in ascending order. Auxiliary: An auxiliary array of size N used to store intermediate results. Data Structures: input: Array of N 32-bit integers. output: Array of N 32-bit integers. counts: Array of 256 integers to store frequency for each 8-bit block value (0–255). Steps: 1. Count Pass: Traverse the input array once to count occurrences of all four 8-bit blocks (bits 0–7, 8–15, 16–23, 24–31) for every element. 2. Sort Pass 1 (Bits 0–7): Perform a stable counting sort on bits 0–7 of the input array, writing the results to the auxiliary array. 3. Sort Pass 2 (Bits 8–15): Perform a stable counting sort on bits 8–15 of the auxiliary array (input), writing the results back to the original input array. 4. Sort Pass 3 (Bits 16–23): Perform a stable counting sort on bits 16–23 of the input array, writing the results to the auxiliary array. 5. Sort Pass 4 (Bits 24–31): Perform a stable counting sort on bits 24–31 of the auxiliary array (input), writing the final sorted results back to the original input array. Counting Sort Logic (per pass): For each pass, extract the relevant 8-bit block from each number using bitwise operations: key = (value >> shift) & 0xFF. Use these values as indices to accumulate frequencies in counts. Compute cumulative sums over counts to determine final positions in the target array. Place elements into the target array in reverse order to maintain stability. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def lsdblocksort(inputarray, n): outputarray = [0] n counts = [0] 256 # Pass 1: Count occurrences for all 4 blocks for i in range(n): val = inputarray[i] counts[(val >> 0) & 0xFF] += 1 counts[(val >> 8) & 0xFF] += 1 counts[(val >> 16) & 0xFF] += 1 counts[(val >> 24) & 0xFF] += 1 # Pass 2: Sort bits 0-7, write to outputarray for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 for i in range(n): key = (inputarray[i] >> 0) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): key = (inputarray[i] >> 0) & 0xFF outputarray[counts[key]-1] = inputarray[i] counts[key] -= 1 # Pass 3: Sort bits 8-15, write to inputarray for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 for i in range(n): key = (outputarray[i] >> 8) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): key = (outputarray[i] >> 8) & 0xFF inputarray[counts[key]-1] = outputarray[i] counts[key] -= 1 # Pass 4: Sort bits 16-23, write to outputarray for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 for i in range(n): key = (inputarray[i] >> 16) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): key = (inputarray[i] >> 16) & 0xFF outputarray[counts[key]-1] = inputarray[i] counts[key] -= 1 # Pass 5: Sort bits 24-31, write to inputarray for i in range(256): counts[i] = 0 for i in range(n): key = (outputarray[i] >> 24) & 0xFF counts[key] += 1 for i in range(1, 256): counts[i] += counts[i-1] for i in range(n-1, -1, -1): key = (outputarray[i] >> 24) & 0xFF inputarray[counts[key]-1] = outputarray[i] counts[key] -= 1 return inputarray Parameters: Block size: 8 bits. Number of passes: 5 total (1 counting pass + 4 sorting passes). Bit shifts: 0, 8, 16, 24. Edge Cases: Empty array (N=0): Return immediately. Precision: Uses 32-bit unsigned integers, avoiding floating-point precision issues. Degenerate input: Handles duplicate keys correctly due to stable counting sort implementation. A CPU-based sorting algorithm for volume rendering voxels that orders them back-to-front relative to the camera position. It solves the depth-sorting requirement for alpha blending or depth peeling by mapping voxel distances into fixed logarithmic buckets. It differs from Morton-order-based splat sorting (e.g., SVRaster) by relying solely on radial distance rather than ray-direction-dependent spatial locality, making it robust for arbitrary camera orientations but potentially less cache-friendly for static scenes. Time Complexity: Linear O(N), established by the constant five passes through the array. Memory Complexity: O(N) for the auxiliary array. Performance: A C++ implementation sorts upwards of 15 million faces per second. Strengths: Linear time complexity, simple implementation without machine-level optimizations, deterministic ordering. Limitations: Requires auxiliary memory, not in-place, performance can be improved with hardware-specific optimizations. The algorithm is described in Steve Callahan's MS thesis, "THE K-BUFFER AND ITS APPLICATIONS TO VOLUME RENDERING". It serves as a CPU fallback sort path for ordering face centroids in volume rendering applications, specifically within the k-buffer algorithm framework. THE K-BUFFER AND ITS APPLICATIONS TO VOLUME RENDERING, https://ctsilva.github.io/thesis/steve-callahan-ms-thesis.pdf, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Logarithmic Distance Bucket Sort
head: Back-to-Front Voxel Sorting, DistanceSorter
body: Logarithmic Distance Bucket Sort is a CPU-based sorting algorithm for volume rendering voxels that orders them back-to-front relative to the camera position. It solves the depth-sorting requirement for alpha blending or depth peeling by mapping voxel distances into fixed logarithmic buckets. It differs from Morton-order-based splat sorting (e.g., SVRaster) by relying solely on radial distance rather than ray-direction-dependent spatial locality. Inputs: positions: Float32Array of voxel centers, interleaved as [x1, y1, z1, x2, y2, z2,...]. cameraPosition: [number, number, number] representing the camera origin. outIndices: Optional pre-allocated Uint32Array for output. Outputs: Uint32Array of indices into positions, sorted such that voxels with larger distances from the camera appear first (back-to-front). Data Structures: The implementation maintains static state to avoid reallocation between frames: counts: Uint32Array of size BUCKETCOUNT (65536). Stores bucket occupancy during the first pass. starts: Uint32Array of size BUCKETCOUNT. Allocated for potential reuse, though the algorithm computes bucket positions in a local array during execution. lastCameraPosition: [number, number, number] or null. Stores the previous camera position for early-exit optimization. Parameters: BUCKETCOUNT: 65536 (256 \times 256). Formulas: Logarithmic distance: Li = \log(d^2), where d^2 = (x - cx)^2 + (y - cy)^2 + (z - cz)^2. Inverse scale factor: S = \frac{\text{BUCKET\COUNT} - 1}{\text{logRange} \parallel 1}, where \text{logRange} = \max(L) - \min(L). Bucket index: bi = \min(\text{BUCKET\COUNT} - 1, \lfloor (Li - \min(L)) \times S \rfloor). Algorithm Steps: 1. Early Exit Check: If lastCameraPosition exists, outIndices is provided, and outIndices.length equals numVoxels, calculate the dot product of lastCameraPosition and cameraPosition, compute their squared lengths, and evaluate \cos \theta = \frac{\mathbf{c}{last} \cdot \mathbf{c}{curr}}{\|\mathbf{c}{last}\| \|\mathbf{c}{curr}\|}. If | \cos \theta - 1 | < 0.01, return outIndices immediately. 2. Initialization: Determine numVoxels as positions.length / 3. Allocate or reuse indices array of size numVoxels. If counts or starts are null or have incorrect length, allocate them as Uint32Array of size BUCKETCOUNT; otherwise, clear counts by filling with zeros. 3. Log Distance Calculation: Initialize minDist to \infty and maxDist to -\infty. For each voxel i, extract coordinates (x, y, z), compute squared Euclidean distance d^2, compute logarithmic distance Li = \log(d^2), store it in a temporary logDistances array, and update minDist and maxDist. 4. Bucket Scaling: Calculate logRange = maxDist - minDist. Compute inverse scale factor S using the formula above. 5. First Pass (Counting): For each voxel i, calculate bucket index bi and increment counts[bi]. 6. Calculate Bucket Starts: Initialize position = 0. Iterate j from BUCKETCOUNT - 1 down to 0: set bucketStarts[j] = position and update position += counts[j]. This ensures back-to-front ordering. 7. Reset Counts: Clear counts array by filling with zeros. 8. Second Pass (Distribution): For each voxel i, calculate bucket index bi using the same formula as Step 5. Calculate output position p = \text{bucketStarts}[bi] + \text{counts}[bi], set indices[p] = i, and increment counts[bi]. 9. State Update: Store cameraPosition in lastCameraPosition for the next frame. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If logRange is 0 (all voxels at the same distance), the denominator in the scale factor defaults to 1 to prevent division by zero, effectively mapping all voxels to bucket 0. The early-exit condition assumes sort order remains valid if the camera direction has not changed significantly, but does not account for camera translation. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math BUCKETCOUNT = 65536 counts = None starts = None lastcameraposition = None def sortvoxels(positions, cameraposition, outindices=None): global counts, starts, lastcameraposition numvoxels = len(positions) // 3 # Early exit optimization if (lastcameraposition is not None and outindices is not None and len(outindices) == numvoxels): lx, ly, lz = lastcameraposition cx, cy, cz = cameraposition dot = lx cx + ly cy + lz cz lensq1 = lx lx + ly ly + lz lz lensq2 = cx cx + cy cy + cz cz costheta = dot / math.sqrt(lensq1 lensq2) if abs(costheta - 1.0) < 0.01: return outindices # Initialize output if outindices is not None and len(outindices) == numvoxels: indices = outindices else: indices = [0] numvoxels # Represents Uint32Array # Initialize static arrays if counts is None or starts is None or len(counts) != BUCKETCOUNT: counts = [0] BUCKETCOUNT starts = [0] BUCKETCOUNT else: for i in range(BUCKETCOUNT): counts[i] = 0 # Calculate log distances logdistances = [0.0] numvoxels mindist = float('inf') maxdist = float('-inf') cx, cy, cz = cameraposition for i in range(numvoxels): x = positions[i 3] y = positions[i 3 + 1] z = positions[i 3 + 2] dx = x - cx dy = y - cy dz = z - cz distsq = dx dx + dy dy + dz dz logdist = math.log(distsq) logdistances[i] = logdist if logdist < mindist: mindist = logdist if logdist > maxdist: maxdist = logdist # Calculate scaling logrange = maxdist - mindist if logrange == 0: logrange = 1 distinv = (BUCKETCOUNT - 1) / logrange # First pass: Count for i in range(numvoxels): bucketidx = math.floor((logdistances[i] - mindist) distinv) if bucketidx >= BUCKETCOUNT: bucketidx = BUCKETCOUNT - 1 counts[bucketidx] += 1 # Calculate bucket starts (back-to-front) position = 0 bucketstarts = [0] BUCKETCOUNT for i in range(BUCKETCOUNT - 1, -1, -1): bucketstarts[i] = position position += counts[i] # Reset counts for second pass for i in range(BUCKETCOUNT): counts[i] = 0 # Second pass: Distribute for i in range(numvoxels): bucketidx = math.floor((logdistances[i] - mindist) distinv) if bucketidx >= BUCKETCOUNT: bucketidx = BUCKETCOUNT - 1 pos = bucketstarts[bucketidx] + counts[bucketidx] indices[pos] = i counts[bucketidx] += 1 # Update last camera position lastcameraposition = [cx, cy, cz] return indices Time Complexity: O(N + B), where N is the number of voxels and B is BUCKETCOUNT (65536). Memory Complexity: O(N + B). Performance: The use of logarithmic distance mapping compresses the dynamic range of distances, allowing a fixed number of buckets to provide reasonable depth resolution across varying scene scales. The early-exit optimization significantly reduces cost when the camera is static or moving very slightly. Strengths: Simple implementation, low memory overhead compared to full radix sorts, effective early-exit for static scenes. Limitations: Does not account for spatial locality (unlike Morton/Z-order sorting), which may result in poorer cache performance during the subsequent splatting/composition phase compared to spatially coherent sorts. Sorting is strictly based on distance, so voxels at the same distance are not ordered relative to each other. This method is implemented in the unofficial WebGL port of Nvidia's SVRaster paper, specifically in the DistanceSorter class. It is designed as a CPU fallback or primary sorter for 3D Gaussian Splatting rendering in WebGL contexts where GPU-based sorting might be complex or unavailable. It contrasts with the SVRaster paper's primary suggestion of using ray direction-dependent Morton ordering. Gaussian Splatting Alternative: WebGL Implementation of Nvidia's SVRaster, https://github.com/samuelm2/svraster-webgl, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Cascaded 2-way Merge for Global Splat Sorting
body: Cascaded 2-way Merge is a GPU-based algorithm that merges pre-sorted splat lists from multiple independent renderers into a single globally depth-sorted order buffer using a cascaded binary merge tree. It solves the problem of incorrect depth ordering and excessive overdraw when rendering multiple active Gaussian Splat scenes in a unified viewport. Unlike per-renderer rendering, where each renderer handles its own depth sorting and draw calls independently, this method delegates sorting execution to a global sorter and rendering to a global renderer. The method operates on K active renderers, each providing a list of splats sorted by depth. The goal is to produce a single list of N = \sum{k=0}^{K-1} \text{cnt}k splats sorted by depth. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: K renderers. Renderer k has RemainingCount (\text{cnt}k) splats. Outputs: mglobalOrderBuffer containing the final sorted global order indices. Data Structures: The algorithm uses four scratch buffers and one global output buffer, all of size mtotalSplatCount: 1. mpackScratchOrders: GraphicsBuffer of type uint, name 'Gsplat.PackScratchOrders'. 2. mpackScratchDepths: GraphicsBuffer of type float, name 'Gsplat.PackScratchDepths'. 3. mmergeScratchOrders: GraphicsBuffer of type uint, name 'Gsplat.MergeScratchOrders'. 4. mmergeScratchDepths: GraphicsBuffer of type float, name 'Gsplat.MergeScratchDepths'. 5. mglobalOrderBuffer: GraphicsBuffer holding the final sorted global order, bound via kglobalOrderBuffer property. Parameters: krendererIdx: Index of the current renderer being packed. ksrcCount: Number of splats in the current renderer's range. kdstOffset: Offset in the destination scratch buffer for the current renderer's packed data. koffsetA: Offset of Source A (merged result) in the destination buffer. koffsetB: Offset of Source B (current renderer) in the destination buffer. kcountA: Number of elements in Source A. kcountB: Number of elements in Source B. Algorithm Steps: 1. Packing Phase: For each renderer k from 0 to K-1, if \text{cnt}k > 0, dispatch mkernelPackOrders with parameters krendererIdx = k, ksrcCount = cntk, kdstOffset = offk. The kernel reads raw orders/depths from res.OrderBuffer/res.InputKeys and writes to mpackScratchOrders/mpackScratchDepths at offset offk. 2. Initialization: Set mergedCount = activeGsplats[0].RemainingCount, mergedOffset = 0, mergedInPack = true. 3. Cascaded Merge Loop: Iterate k from 1 to K-1. Calculate total = mergedCount + cntk. Select Source A: if mergedInPack is true, use mpackScratchOrders/Depths; otherwise use mmergeScratchOrders/Depths. Select Source B: always mpackScratchOrders/Depths at offset offk. Select Destination: if k == K-1 (final pass), use mglobalOrderBuffer with dstDepths = null; otherwise use the buffer not currently holding the merged result. Dispatch merge kernel: use mkernelMergeTwo if final, otherwise mkernelMergeTwoWithDepth. Set parameters koffsetA = mergedOffset, koffsetB = offk, kcountA = mergedCount, kcountB = cntk, koutputOffset = 0. Bind sources and destination. Dispatch with thread count \lceil \text{total} / 256 \rceil. 4. Finalization: After the loop, set mtotalRemainingCount = mergedCount. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cascaded2waymerge(activegsplats, mtotalsplatcount, mglobalorderbuffer): K = len(activegsplats) if K < 2 or mglobalorderbuffer is None: return # Scratch buffers packorders = [0] mtotalsplatcount packdepths = [0.0] mtotalsplatcount mergeorders = [0] mtotalsplatcount mergedepths = [0.0] mtotalsplatcount # Step 1: Packing Phase offset = 0 for k in range(K): cntk = activegsplats[k].RemainingCount if cntk == 0: continue # Dispatch mkernelPackOrders: reads raw orders/depths from res.OrderBuffer/res.InputKeys # writes to mpackScratchOrders/mpackScratchDepths at offset off for i in range(cntk): packorders[offset + i] = activegsplats[k].OrderBuffer[i] packdepths[offset + i] = activegsplats[k].InputKeys[i] offset += cntk # Step 2: Initialization mergedcount = activegsplats[0].RemainingCount mergedoffset = 0 mergedinpack = True # Step 3: Cascaded Merge Loop for k in range(1, K): cntk = activegsplats[k].RemainingCount if cntk == 0: continue total = mergedcount + cntk isfinal = (k == K - 1) # Select Source A (current merged result) if mergedinpack: srcaorders, srcadepths = packorders, packdepths else: srcaorders, srcadepths = mergeorders, mergedepths # Select Source B (renderer k's data) srcboffset = offset - cntk srcborders, srcbdepths = packorders, packdepths # Select Destination if isfinal: dstorders = mglobalorderbuffer dstdepths = None else: if mergedinpack: dstorders, dstdepths = mergeorders, mergedepths else: dstorders, dstdepths = packorders, packdepths # Dispatch merge kernel koffseta = mergedoffset koffsetb = srcboffset kcounta = mergedcount kcountb = cntk koutputoffset = 0 threadcount = (total + 255) // 256 if isfinal: # Dispatch mkernelMergeTwo (final pass, no depth output) pass # Sources do not provide kernel internals else: # Dispatch mkernelMergeTwoWithDepth (intermediate passes, outputs depths) pass # Sources do not provide kernel internals # Update State mergedcount = total mergedoffset = 0 mergedinpack = not mergedinpack # Step 4: Finalization mtotalremainingcount = mergedcount Edge Cases and Pitfalls: If K < 2 or mglobalOrderBuffer is null, the merge process returns immediately without performing any merges. If a renderer's count is 0, it is skipped during the packing phase. The algorithm requires GPU subgroups/wave operations, which are only available in D3D12, Metal, or Vulkan graphics APIs. WebGPU supports subgroups but Unity has not implemented it for this feature. Global sort is all-or-nothing: presence of any uncompressed renderer forces fallback to per-renderer sorting. Global Splat Merge and Rendering is a technique that merges multiple independent Gaussian Splat renderers into a single global draw call by packing their splat data, spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and depth/order information into shared global buffers, then performing a cascaded merge of depth-sorted orders. It merges two or more active Gaussian splat renderers into a single globally depth-sorted draw call to reduce overdraw and improve sorting accuracy across scenes. Unlike per-renderer rendering, where each renderer handles its own depth sorting and draw calls independently, this method delegates sorting execution to a global sorter and rendering to a global renderer, triggered when camera movement exceeds thresholds or refresh rate dictates. Global Depth Sorting for 3DGS sorts Gaussians across multiple renderers globally using GPU subgroups/waves to maintain correct depth ordering in a unified scene. It is activated by the EnableGlobalSort boolean setting, which requires all active renderers to use compressed assets. A key pitfall is that global sort is all-or-nothing: the presence of any uncompressed renderer forces a fallback to per-renderer sorting. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Performance depends on the GPU's subgroup/wave support. Scaling: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Reduces overdraw, improves sorting accuracy across scenes, enables unified rendering of multiple scenes. Limitations: Requires compressed assets for all renderers, limited to specific graphics APIs, all-or-nothing activation. When to use: When rendering multiple Gaussian Splat scenes in a single viewport with overlapping depth ranges. When not to use: When renderers use uncompressed assets, or when the target platform does not support GPU subgroups (e.g., older APIs, WebGPU in Unity). The method originates from the wuyize25/gsplat-unity project. It builds on the b0nes164/GPUSorting library for GPU-based sorting primitives. The technique was developed to address the limitations of per-renderer sorting in multi-scene environments, providing a more efficient and accurate way to composite multiple Gaussian Splat scenes. wuyize25/gsplat-unity, https://github.com/wuyize25/gsplat-unity, fetched 2026-10-27 (unofficial)

name: Global Splat Merge and Rendering
head: Global Splat Sort & Merge, GsplatGlobalRenderer, Merged Draw
body: Global Splat Merge and Rendering is a technique that merges multiple independent Gaussian Splat renderers into a single global draw call by packing their splat data, spherical harmonic (SH) coefficients, and depth/order information into shared global buffers, then performing a cascaded merge of depth-sorted orders. It merges two or more active Gaussian splat renderers into a single globally depth-sorted draw call to reduce overdraw and improve sorting accuracy across scenes. Unlike per-renderer rendering, where each renderer handles its own depth sorting and draw calls independently, this method delegates sorting execution to a global sorter and rendering to a global renderer, triggered when camera movement exceeds thresholds or refresh rate dictates. Inputs: A set of active Gaussian Splat renderers, each providing packed splat data, SH coefficients, and local depth-sorted order buffers. Camera state (translation and rotation) to determine if sorting needs refresh. Configuration parameters: EnableGlobalSort, MaxRenderOrder, CameraTranslationRefreshTreshold, CameraRotationRefreshTreshold. Outputs: A single globally depth-sorted order buffer. A single draw call rendering all active splats with correct depth ordering. The method relies on several global buffers allocated based on the total number of splats and the maximum SH bands among all active renderers. RendererParams struct (16-byte stride per renderer): Brightness: float (4 bytes) ScaleFactor: float (4 bytes) GammaToLinear: uint (4 bytes) SHDegree: uint (4 bytes). Global Buffers: mglobalPackedBuffer: uint[4] per splat. Stores packed splat data (center xyz, scale, rgba, quaternion). mglobalOrderBuffer: uint per splat. Stores the global render order. mrendererOffsetsBuffer: uint per active renderer. Stores the starting index in the global buffers for each renderer. mrendererTransformsBuffer: float[16] per renderer. Stores the 4x4 transformation matrix for each renderer. mrendererParamsBuffer: 16 bytes per renderer. Stores RendererParams. mglobalSH1Buffer: uint[2] per splat (if mglobalSHBands >= 1). mglobalSH2Buffer: uint[4] per splat (if mglobalSHBands >= 2). mglobalSH3Buffer: uint[4] per splat (if mglobalSHBands >= 3). mglobalSH4Buffer: uint[4] per splat (if mglobalSHBands >= 4). Scratch Buffers: mpackScratchOrders: Used during order packing. mpackScratchDepths: Used during depth packing. mmergeScratchOrders: Used during cascaded merge. mmergeScratchDepths: Used during cascaded merge. 1. Initialize Kernels: Find kernel indices for PackRendererOrders, MergeTwo, MergeTwoWithDepth in MergeShader, and CopyUint4, CopyUint2 in CopyBufferShader. 2. Check Dirty State: If mglobalBuffersDirty is true or ActiveSplatCountsChanged is true, proceed to rebuild global buffers. 3. Calculate Totals: Compute mtotalSplatCount as the sum of splat counts from all active renderers. Compute mrendererOffsets for each active renderer k as the cumulative sum of splat counts of previous renderers. Determine mglobalSHBands as the maximum SH bands among all active splats. 4. Allocate Global Buffers: Create GraphicsBuffers for mglobalPackedBuffer, mglobalOrderBuffer, mrendererOffsetsBuffer, mrendererTransformsBuffer, mrendererParamsBuffer, and SH buffers (mglobalSH1Buffer to mglobalSH4Buffer) based on mglobalSHBands. Set mrendererOffsetsBuffer data. 5. Copy Per-Renderer Data: For each active renderer k, copy its packed splat data, SH coefficients, and order data into the global buffer sub-ranges starting at mrendererOffsets[k]. 6. Dispatch Merge Passes: Use PackRendererOrders to pack orders/depths, then MergeTwo or MergeTwoWithDepth for cascaded merging of orders across renderers using scratch buffers (mpackScratchOrders, mpackScratchDepths, mmergeScratchOrders, mmergeScratchDepths). 7. Render: Delegate rendering to GsplatGlobalRenderer using the globally sorted order buffer. EnableGlobalSort: Boolean flag that activates the global merge pipeline. MaxRenderOrder: Maximum depth sorting layers allowed; range 1 to 20. CameraTranslationRefreshTreshold: Distance threshold in world units that forces recomputation of sorting and cutouts regardless of refresh rate; range 0.05 to 1.0, default 0.2. CameraRotationRefreshTreshold: Rotation threshold in degrees that forces recomputation of sorting and cutouts regardless of refresh rate; range 0.2 to 30.0, default 10. kmergePassName: String constant "Gsplat.MergeKWay" used for GPU profiling samples. Growth: If a renderer uses AsyncUpload and its SplatCount grows frame-to-frame, the global buffers must be rebuilt when the count changes. Otherwise, the global sub-ranges only contain splats present at the first build, leaving the merge to read stale/under-sized buffers. Uncompressed Assets: If any active renderer uses an uncompressed asset, the whole scene falls back to per-renderer rendering, even if EnableGlobalSort is true. Time Complexity: Dominated by the cascaded merge pass, which is O(N \log K) where N is the total number of splats and K is the number of active renderers. The merge is performed on the GPU using compute shaders. Memory Complexity: O(N) for global buffers, where N is the total number of splats. Additional memory for scratch buffers during merge is required. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales with the number of active renderers and total splat count. The cascaded merge tree depth increases logarithmically with the number of renderers. Strengths: Reduces overdraw by globally sorting splats across multiple renderers. Improves sorting accuracy across scenes. Limitations: Requires all active renderers to use compressed assets. Rebuilding global buffers can be expensive if splat counts change frequently. When to Use: When rendering multiple Gaussian Splat scenes in a single frame and global depth sorting is desired. When Not to Use: When renderers use uncompressed assets, or when the number of active renderers is small and per-renderer sorting is sufficient. The method is part of the Gsplat-Unity project, an unofficial implementation of 3D Gaussian Splatting for Unity. It builds on Cascaded 2-way Merge for Global Splat Sorting to handle cross-renderer depth ordering. name: Half-Angle Slicing with Odd-Even Merge Sort
head: Half angle slicing technique
body: Half-angle slicing is a GPU-based volume rendering technique for particle systems that sorts particles along a view-dependent axis (the half-angle between the light and view directions) using an odd-even merge sort, then renders them in slices to handle transparency and shadows correctly. It sets itself apart from standard front-to-back splatting by decoupling the sorting axis from the view direction, allowing for efficient accumulation of opacity from the light's perspective to compute accurate volumetric shadows in a single pass. Unlike Bitonic Sort which sorts strictly by depth, this method sorts by a projected coordinate that aligns with the light transport, enabling the "slicing" strategy where particles are rendered in batches to build a light-space opacity texture. The method operates in three main phases: simulation, GPU-based sorting, and slice-based rendering with opacity accumulation. Inputs: Particle positions, velocities, lifetimes, and spawn data; camera view/projection matrices; light view/projection matrices; time delta. Outputs: Final composited image with volumetric shadows; opacity texture for light-space accumulation. The implementation relies on specific Framebuffer Objects (FBOs) and textures, typically stored in a grid layout for efficient GPU access. 1. Simulation FBOs (Ping-Pong): Two FBOs, mSimulationFbo[0] and mSimulationFbo[1]. Size: PARTICLES x PARTICLES (e.g., 256x256). Internal Format: GLRGBA32F. Data Type: GLFLOAT. Purpose: Store particle state (position, velocity, etc.) for simulation updates. No depth buffer. 2. Particle Data Texture: Size: PARTICLES x PARTICLES (e.g., 256x256). Format: GLRGBA32F. Layout: Each texel vec4 contains position.x, position.y, position.z, and lifetime (or spawn data). 3. Opacity FBO: One FBO. Size: OPACITYTEXTURERESOLUTION x OPACITYTEXTURERESOLUTION (e.g., 1024x1024). Internal Format: GLRGBA. Data Type: GLUNSIGNEDBYTE. Purpose: Accumulate opacity from the light's perspective. No depth buffer. PARTICLES: Square root of total particle count. Default: 256. mMaxParticleCount: Total particles = PARTICLES PARTICLES. Default: 65536. SLICES: Number of depth slices for rendering. Default: 128. OPACITYTEXTURERESOLUTION: Resolution of the light-space opacity texture. Default: 1024. 1. Calculate Half-Vector for Sorting: Determine the sorting axis based on the angle between the view direction (\mathbf{v}) and the light direction (\mathbf{l}). If \mathbf{v} \cdot \mathbf{l} > 0.0: \mathbf{halfVector} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} + \mathbf{v}) mFlipped = \text{false} Else: \mathbf{halfVector} = \text{normalize}(\mathbf{l} - \mathbf{v}) mFlipped = \text{true} 2. Simulate Particle Movement: Bind the previous frame's position texture (mSimulationFbo[1 - mCurrent]) to texture unit 0. Bind the spawn data texture to texture unit 1. Execute the simulation shader for 1 frame (or BASELIFETIME / PRESIMULATIONDELTATIME frames on the first frame to initialize). Update mCurrent to swap ping-pong buffers. 3. Execute Odd-Even Merge Sort: Sort the particles based on their projection onto the \mathbf{halfVector}. Calculate total sort steps: mTotalSortSteps = \frac{\log2(mMaxParticleCount) \cdot (\log2(mMaxParticleCount) + 1)}{2} Loop mTotalSortSteps times: Swap read/write FBOs: mCurrent = 1 - mCurrent. Decrement mSortPass. If mSortPass < 0: Increment mSortStage. Set mSortPass = mSortStage. Bind source texture to unit 0. Pass uniforms to sort shader: uPass = float(1 << mSortPass) uStage = float(1 << mSortStage) Decrement mSortStepsLeft. If it reaches 0, reset counters (mSortPass, mSortStage, mSortStepsLeft). 4. Render Slices (View Pass): Loop i from 0 to SLICES - 1. Determine particle range: startIndex = i (mMaxParticleCount / SLICES) count = mMaxParticleCount / SLICES Set camera matrices to view space. Bind opacity texture to unit 1. Set blend mode: If mFlipped is true: GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA, GLONE Else: GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA Draw the current slice of particles using point sprites. 5. Opacity Pass (Light View): Bind the opacity FBO. Set matrices to light camera (light view/projection). Draw the same particle slice with blend mode GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA to accumulate opacity into the opacity texture. 6. Final Composite: Draw the floor (or scene geometry) and a fullscreen quad. Bind the accumulated opacity texture (from step 5) to unit 2. Use the light view projection matrix to sample the opacity texture for shadow calculation. Blend mode: GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA, GLONE. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. PARTICLES = 256 MAXPARTICLES = PARTICLES PARTICLES SLICES = 128 OPACITYRES = 1024 def halfangleslicing(viewdir, lightdir, dt, time): # 1. Calculate Half-Vector dotval = dot(normalize(viewdir), normalize(lightdir)) if dotval > 0.0: halfvec = normalize(lightdir + viewdir) flipped = False else: halfvec = normalize(lightdir - viewdir) flipped = True # 2. Simulation # Bind simfbo[1-current] to unit 0, spawn data to unit 1 # Run simulation shader (1 frame or init frames) # Swap current buffer current = 1 - current # 3. Odd-Even Merge Sort totalsteps = (log2(MAXPARTICLES) (log2(MAXPARTICLES) + 1)) / 2 sortpass = 0 sortstage = 0 sortstepsleft = totalsteps for step in range(totalsteps): # Swap buffers current = 1 - current sortpass -= 1 if sortpass < 0: sortstage += 1 sortpass = sortstage # Bind source texture (simfbo[current]) to unit 0 # Pass uPass = 1 << sortpass, uStage = 1 << sortstage # Run sort shader sortstepsleft -= 1 if sortstepsleft == 0: sortpass = 0 sortstage = 0 sortstepsleft = totalsteps # 4. Render Slices & 5. Opacity Accumulation for i in range(SLICES): startidx = i (MAXPARTICLES / SLICES) count = MAXPARTICLES / SLICES # View Pass setcameramatrices(viewmatrix, projmatrix) bindtexture(opacitytex, unit=1) if flipped: setblend(GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA, GLONE) else: setblend(GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA) drawparticles(startidx, count) # Light View Pass (Opacity Accumulation) bindframebuffer(opacityfbo) setcameramatrices(lightviewmatrix, lightprojmatrix) setblend(GLONE, GLONEMINUSSRCALPHA) drawparticles(startidx, count) bindframebuffer(defaultfbo) # 6. Final Composite setcameramatrices(viewmatrix, projmatrix) bindtexture(opacitytex, unit=2) # From light view setblend(GLONEMINUSDSTALPHA, GLONE) drawfloorandquad() Precision: The sorting relies on floating-point comparisons. Ensure the half-vector calculation is normalized to avoid bias. Boundaries: When sampling the opacity texture in the final composite, check for coordinates outside [0, 1] to avoid wrapping artifacts. Degenerate Input: If particles are exactly on the sorting plane, the sort stability depends on the implementation of the odd-even merge sort shader. This variant extends the half-angle slicing technique to handle the gradual angular spreading of light during multiple scattering events, which is essential for capturing fine angularly dependent effects with large forward-scattering particles. It models the angular dispersion of light experiencing its first few scattering events for efficient single-pass rendering on programmable graphics hardware. A key pitfall in this approximation is the presence of the light term L\lambda on both sides of the governing equation (Equation 7 in the source), requiring separation of intensity and distribution to solve iteratively or approximately. Time Complexity: The sorting phase uses odd-even merge sort, which has a time complexity of O(\log^2 N) steps for N particles, where each step is a parallel comparison-exchange operation. The rendering phase is O(S \cdot N) where S is the number of slices, but each slice is processed in parallel. Memory Complexity: Requires O(N) storage for particle data and O(R^2) for the opacity texture, where R is the opacity texture resolution. Performance: The method is designed for GPU acceleration, leveraging parallel sorting and rasterization. The use of ping-pong FBOs and texture-based particle storage allows for efficient data access on the GPU. Strengths: Handles volumetric shadows efficiently; works well with particle systems; leverages hardware rasterization. Limitations: Sorting is view-dependent and must be recomputed if the camera or light moves significantly; the odd-even merge sort can be complex to implement efficiently on all GPU architectures; limited to particle-based volumes. The half-angle slicing technique was originally described by Kniss et al. [KPHE02] for rendering volumetric effects. The specific implementation using GPU-based odd-even merge sort and ping-pong FBOs for particle shadows is based on a webGL implementation by David Li, which in turn was ported from a NVIDIA article on smoke particles. The technique is used in real-time volume rendering, particularly for atmospheric phenomena and particle systems where shadows are required. name: Bitonic Sort
head: ABisort, Bitonic Sort for GPGPU, Govindaraju et al. Bitonic Sort, Particle Sorting (Bitonic Sort)
body: Bitonic Sort is a data-independent network sorting algorithm used on the GPU to achieve exact depth ordering of splatted voxels for every frame. It is chosen over partial-ordering methods like Odd-Even Merge Sort because the application requires exact ordering at each frame, making sort-while-drawing inconvenient. It is preferred over Adaptive Bitonic Sort (ABisort) in some implementations due to library accessibility and ease of adaptation, despite ABisort having potentially better theoretical complexity. Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of view-transformed voxels already resident in GPU memory, typically stored in a texture (View Transformed Voxels Texture). Each voxel is represented as a <key, value> pair, where the key is the depth value b and the value is the voxel index. Output: A sorted array of voxels stored in a texture (Depth-Sorted Voxels Texture), ordered by depth. Data Structures: The algorithm uses the Multiple Render Target (MRT) extension to store keys and values in separate render targets. A one-to-one correspondence exists between the key texture and the value texture. This correspondence allows keeping four <key, value> instances in a single RGBA texel. Parameters: uPass: Current pass number in the sort algorithm. uStage: Current stage number within the pass. uHalfVector: The half-angle vector used for sorting particles. N: Total number of particles/voxels to sort. Algorithm Steps: 1. Initialization: Reset pass and stage counters if the sorting direction needs to be reversed. 2. Ping-Pong Buffering: Use two framebuffers to swap read/write roles between passes. 3. Index Computation: Compute the particle index i from texture coordinates. 4. Direction Determination: Determine the comparison direction compare based on the current pass, stage, and index i. 5. Partner Calculation: Calculate the partner address using adr = i + compare uPass and fetch partner data. 6. Comparison: Sort based on the dot product with the half vector: output self if selfProjectedLength compare < partnerProjectedLength compare, else output partner. 7. Write: Write the sorted result to the appropriate render target. 8. Finalization: After all passes, a fragment shader fills the Depth-Sorted Voxels Texture from the sorted render targets. Pseudocode: The following pseudocode describes the fragment shader logic for a single comparison step in the Bitonic Sort network. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def bitonicsortstep(i, uPass, uStage, prevpositions, currentpositions): # Standard bitonic sort direction logic based on stage and index compare = 1 if (i >> uStage) & 1 else -1 # Calculate partner address adr = i + compare uPass # Fetch data from previous render target selfdata = prevpositions.sample(i) partnerdata = prevpositions.sample(adr) selfkey = selfdata.key # Depth value b selfval = selfdata.value # Voxel index partnerkey = partnerdata.key partnerval = partnerdata.value # Perform comparison using direction multiplier lhs = selfkey compare rhs = partnerkey compare if lhs < rhs: currentpositions.write(i, selfkey, selfval) currentpositions.write(adr, partnerkey, partnerval) else: currentpositions.write(i, partnerkey, partnerval) currentpositions.write(adr, selfkey, selfval) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Data Independence: Unlike Quicksort, Bitonic Sort does not branch on data values, making it suitable for GPU SIMD/SIMT architectures but potentially slower for small datasets due to fixed work. Exact Ordering: Requires all passes to complete for exact ordering; partial results are insufficient for correct compositing. Fixed Operations: The algorithm performs a predetermined number of comparisons regardless of data distribution, which can be inefficient for partially sorted or small datasets. Time Complexity: O(N \log^2 N) comparisons and swaps. Adaptive Bitonic Sort (ABisort) claims O((N \log N)/P) complexity, where P is the number of stream processors. Performance: On an NVIDIA GeForce 7800, Govindaraju's Bitonic Sort was approximately twice as fast as the best CPU QuickSort implementation at the time of the source. Strengths: Provides exact ordering every frame; highly parallelizable; cache-efficient memory access patterns in optimized implementations. Limitations: Fixed number of operations regardless of data distribution; not suitable for dynamic datasets where partial ordering is acceptable (Odd-Even Merge Sort is preferred there). When to Use: When exact depth sorting is required for every frame in volume splatting. When Not to Use: When partial ordering is sufficient (e.g., particle systems spread over multiple frames) or when adaptive sorting performance is critical and library access permits. Bitonic Sort was originally developed as a network sorting algorithm. In the context of GPU volume rendering, Govindaraju et al. [GRHM05] improved early implementations [KW05] by introducing cache-efficient memory accesses, leading to high performance on GPUs like the NVIDIA GeForce 7800. Gress and Zachmann [GZ06] later designed Adaptive Bitonic Sort (ABisort) with optimal complexity. In the specific implementation described in the sources, Govindaraju's method was chosen over ABisort due to the accessibility and adaptability of the library. name: Index Sorting
head: Key-index pair sorting
body: Index sorting is a sorting variant that produces a permutation of indices rather than reordering data values, allowing related information to be traced back to the original array. It solves the problem of determining related information from the sorted index, which is required because sorting values alone is insufficient for real applications. Unlike methods that pack keys and indices into a single register to save memory, index sorting keeps key counting independent from index values, preserving full precision and index range (up to 4 billion pairs on 32-bit hardware). Inputs and Outputs: Input: An array of keys K of size n, and an initial index array I of size n. Output: A sorted permutation array P (indices). Data Structures: K: Array of keys, typically 32-bit integers or floats. I: Array of indices, initialized as I[i] = i for 0 \le i < n. P: Permutation array, same size as K, storing the sorted indices. Steps: 1. Initialize Index Array: Generate a companion index array I where I[i] = i. This indicates the original position of each value in K. 2. Perform Key Sorting: Execute a radix sort algorithm on the key array K to generate a permutation array P. The sorting logic operates independently on the keys; the indices in I are not involved in the comparison or counting phases. 3. Shuffle Indices: Apply the permutation P to the index array I to produce the final sorted index array. This step rearranges the indices according to the sorted order of the keys. Formula: I{sorted}[j] = I[P[j]] for 0 \le j < n. 4. Access Data: To retrieve the original data associated with the j-th sorted element, use the value I{sorted}[j] as an offset into the original data arrays. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def indexsort(keys, n): # Step 1: Initialize index array indices = [i for i in range(n)] # Step 2: Sort keys to get permutation # Standard radix sort permutation generation. # The sources do not provide the internal kernel, so this step is marked as a standard operation. # In a full implementation, this would use counting sort passes to compute # prefix sums and place indices into the permutation array based on key digits. permutation = [0] n #... radix sort logic to fill permutation... # Step 3: Shuffle indices with the permutation sortedindices = [0] n for j in range(n): sortedindices[j] = indices[permutation[j]] return sortedindices Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Cache Misses: Index sorting exacerbates cache misses compared to value sorting because the shuffling step involves non-coalesced memory access patterns when applying the permutation to the indices. Memory Bandwidth: The additional shuffle step increases memory bandwidth requirements. Precision: Combining keys and indices into a single register reduces precision and index range. Index sorting avoids this by keeping them separate, allowing full 32-bit index ranges. Distance-aware index sorting optimizes sorting by computing distance data once and using an auxiliary structure to avoid redundant calculations during comparison. It computes the distance squared from the origin and the index for all blocks, sorts the auxiliary structure, and maps the sorted indices back to the original blocks. The auxiliary structure is a DistanceIndexPair containing a float mdistanceSquaredFromOrigin and an int mindex. Radix sort is asymptotically faster and not comparison-based, potentially replacing a custom BlockDistanceComparator. Time Complexity: Typically 1.5 to 1.8 times slower than value sorting due to non-coalesced shuffling. Optimization: Using a coalesced radix index sorting scheme reduces the performance penalty to a negligible factor of about 1.1. Memory: Requires storage for both the key array and the index array, doubling the memory footprint compared to sorting keys alone if the original data is not needed in place. Strengths: Preserves full precision and index range; simple to implement on top of existing radix sort kernels. Limitations: Higher memory bandwidth usage; potential for cache thrashing during the shuffle phase if not optimized. Index sorting was discussed in the context of GPU-based parallel sorting, specifically highlighting its application in scenarios where data association is crucial. The method was analyzed on NVIDIA GTX 280 hardware, demonstrating that while naive index sorting suffers from performance penalties, optimized coalesced approaches mitigate these issues.
