name: GPU-Accelerated Image-Aligned Splatting Framework
head: Early Z-Culling Splatting, Post-shaded Splatting
body: An object-order rendering approach for scattered data points (ellipsoidal or spherical kernels) using front-to-back compositing, spatial decomposition, and GPU-based early z-culling for occlusion culling and splat elimination. It differs from its parent Ellipsoidal Kernel Splatting with Warped Slicing by replacing warped slicing planes with a direct screen-aligned slicing pass that outputs vertex attributes for GPU rasterization, enabling efficient occlusion culling via early Z-tests. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of N scattered data points, each defined by an ellipsoid (13 floating-point parameters) and a scalar density value d \in [0, 1]. Output: A final composited frame-buffer image with normalized density values. Data Structures: 1. Spatial Decomposition (CPU-side): A low-resolution 3D cubic block grid where each grid point maintains a list of intersecting points. 2. Input Textures (GPU-side): Three 2D textures storing the 13 ellipsoid parameters packed into floating-point channels, with the Z and Y elements of the translation matrix T packed together. 3. Intermediate Textures (GPU-side): Three destination textures (Multiple Render Targets - MRT) storing 12 output values per ellipsoid: starting screen-space slice position (px, py, pz), 2D axis-aligned slicing polygon vectors (ux, uy) and (vx, vy), difference vector to the next slicing polygon, starting position in unit texture space (0, 0, \text{StartZ}{us}), and scalar density. 4. Slicing Buffer (GPU-side): A buffer storing reconstructed density slices and accumulated splatted weights in a separate channel for normalization. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (CPU): Decompose the volume into the low-resolution cubic block data structure. For each grid point, maintain a list of intersecting points. Flatten this 3D structure onto a set of four 2D textures by copying the contents of every cell in the format described for the ellipsoid slicing output. 2. Ellipsoid Slicing (Fragment Program): Process all data points as textures. For each point, calculate the intersection with the current image-aligned slicing plane. Output the 12 values into the 3 destination textures using MRT. 3. Vertex Array Generation: Convert the sliced data into vertex attribute arrays in GPU memory. The cells are processed in front-to-back order relative to the camera. 4. Splatting Vertex Program: Receive a uniform variable currentSlicingZ representing the z-value of the current image-aligned slicing plane. For each vertex (representing a corner of a slicing polygon), check if the point intersects the current slice. If intersecting, compute corner positions and texture coordinates. If not, cull the point by setting coordinates outside the view frustum. Encode polygon identity in the density value: d{encoded} = (\text{vertexCount} \pmod 4) / 1000 + d{input}, where \text{vertexCount} is the vertex index within the quad. 5. Rasterization: Render polygons using GLQUAD primitives. Replicate point data for each destination vertex (4 corners). 6. Kernel Slicing and Accumulation: Slice the 3D spherical kernel using texture mapping of a 2D Gaussian kernel modulated by a 1D Gaussian along the z-direction. Compute the 1D Gaussian value in the vertex shader. Accumulate kernel contributions into the slicing buffer, maintaining splatted weights in a separate channel. 7. Normalization and Compositing (Fragment Program): Retrieve reconstructed density D and accumulated weight W. Normalize density to handle sparse boundary coverage: D{normalized} = D / \max(W, 1). Perform classification, shading, and front-to-back compositing to the final frame-buffer. Pitfalls and Edge Cases: Boundary Artifacts: At volume boundaries, coverage is sparse and accumulated weights W are smaller than one. Dividing by small W causes unnaturally high density values. The solution is to threshold the weight at 1 before division. Ghost Points Alternative: An alternative solution is to add "ghost points" with zero density and normal weight values around boundaries, mimicking regular volumes with infinite coverage. Regular volumes do not require normalization because weights are constant. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def preprocessvolume(points, gridresolution): """ Decompose volume into a low-resolution cubic block data structure. Returns a list of cells, where each cell contains a list of point indices. """ grid = [[[] for in range(gridresolution)] for in range(gridresolution gridresolution)] for point in points: cellidx = (point.z // grid.cellsize) grid.resolution + (point.x // grid.cellsize) grid[cellidx].append(point) return flattento2dtextures(grid) def flattento2dtextures(grid): """ Flatten the 3D grid onto four 2D textures by copying cell contents in the format described for the ellipsoid slicing output. """ textures = [None, None, None, None] for cell in grid: for point in cell: # Pack point data into the 2D texture layout matching Section 4.1 format pass return textures def sliceellipsoids(inputtextures, currentviewmatrix): """ Process all data points as textures. Returns 3 destination textures with 12 values per ellipsoid. """ desttextures = createmrttextures(3) for point in inputtextures: params = unpackellipsoidparams(point) slicedata = computescreenalignedslice(params, currentviewmatrix) # slicedata contains: px, py, pz, ux, uy, vx, vy, diffvector, startzus, density writetomrt(desttextures, slicedata) return desttextures def computescreenalignedslice(params, viewmatrix): """Calculate screen-aligned slicing intersection for an ellipsoid.""" # Extract 13 ellipsoid parameters # Return 12 values as specified in the evidence return { 'px': params.px, 'py': params.py, 'pz': params.pz, 'ux': params.ux, 'uy': params.uy, 'vx': params.vx, 'vy': params.vy, 'diff': params.diff, 'startzus': 0.0, 'density': params.density } def splatvertexprogram(vertexindex, currentslicingz, vertexdata): """ Determines if a vertex intersects the current slice and computes its position. """ px, py, pz = vertexdata['px'], vertexdata['py'], vertexdata['pz'] ux, uy = vertexdata['ux'], vertexdata['uy'] vx, vy = vertexdata['vx'], vertexdata['vy'] densityencoded = vertexdata['density'] # Check intersection with current slicing plane if abs(pz - currentslicingz) < 1e-6: # Decode corner identity from density cornerid = int(densityencoded 1000) % 4 # Calculate corner position in screen space if cornerid == 0: pos = (px, py, pz) elif cornerid == 1: pos = (px + ux, py + uy, pz) elif cornerid == 2: pos = (px + vx, py + vy, pz) else: pos = (px + ux + vx, py + uy + vy, pz) # Compute texture coordinates for kernel lookup texcoords = computetexturecoords(cornerid, ux, uy, vx, vy, currentslicingz) return {'position': pos, 'texcoords': texcoords, 'density': densityencoded} else: # Cull by setting coordinates outside view frustum return {'position': (-1e9, -1e9, -1e9), 'texcoords': None, 'density': 0} def computetexturecoords(cornerid, ux, uy, vx, vy, currentz): """Compute normalized texture coordinates for the 2D Gaussian kernel lookup.""" if cornerid == 0: return (0.0, 0.0) elif cornerid == 1: return (ux, uy) elif cornerid == 2: return (vx, vy) else: return (ux + vx, uy + vy) def accumulatekernelcontributions(vertexoutput, kerneltexture): """ Accumulate kernel contributions into the slicing buffer. """ # Compute 1D Gaussian value in vertex shader zgaussian = compute1dgaussian(vertexoutput['position'][2]) # Sample 2D Gaussian kernel from texture kernelvalue = sample2dgaussian(kerneltexture, vertexoutput['texcoords']) # Modulate by 1D Gaussian totalkernel = kernelvalue zgaussian # Accumulate into slicing buffer slicingbuffer['density'] += totalkernel vertexoutput['density'] slicingbuffer['weight'] += totalkernel def compute1dgaussian(z): """Compute 1D Gaussian value along the z-direction.""" return math.exp(-0.5 (z / 0.5) 2) def sample2dgaussian(kerneltexture, texcoords): """Sample the 2D Gaussian kernel texture.""" return kerneltexture[texcoords] def normalizeandcomposite(slicingbuffer, finalframebuffer): """ Normalize densities and composite to final frame-buffer. """ density = slicingbuffer['density'] weight = slicingbuffer['weight'] # Threshold weight at 1 to prevent high density values at boundaries normalizedweight = max(weight, 1.0) normalizeddensity = density / normalizedweight # Perform classification, shading, and compositing color = classifyandshade(normalizeddensity) compositetoframebuffer(finalframebuffer, color, normalizeddensity) Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Requires GPU memory for input textures (13 floats per point packed into 3 textures), intermediate MRT textures (12 values per point), and the slicing buffer. The spatial decomposition structure is stored on the CPU and transferred to GPU textures. Measured Performance: The slicing step takes 30-90 msec for datasets of 35K-500K points. Strengths: Achieves very high quality images even for sparse datasets at high magnifications and interactive frame-rates. Early Z-culling allows for efficient occlusion culling and splat elimination. Limitations: Requires MRT extension support (available on NVidia and ATI boards at the time of publication). The need to re-slice and regenerate vertex arrays on every viewpoint change can be costly for dynamic scenes. When to use: Suitable for static or slowly changing scattered data volumes where high-quality rendering of ellipsoidal kernels is required and GPU hardware supports MRT and vertex programs. When not to use: Not suitable for highly dynamic scenes where viewpoint changes frequently, due to the cost of re-slicing and vertex array generation. Also not suitable if MRT support is unavailable. This method was introduced in the paper "GPU-Accelerated Volume Splatting With Elliptical RBFs". It extends existing GPU-accelerated image-aligned splatter algorithms to handle unstructured data sets consisting of arbitrarily oriented general ellipsoids of various sizes. The work addresses the challenges of implementing object-order rendering with front-to-back compositing on the GPU without expensive sorting or bucketing operations, by using a spatial decomposition data structure and early Z-culling. name: Perspective Correct Splat Rasterization with EWA Approximation
head: Affine approximation to projective mapping, Approximate EWA splatting, EWA point splatting, Fast splat rasterization, Perspective Accurate Splatting with EWA Filter
body: This method is an improved splat rendering pipeline that combines a perspectively correct fast splat rasterization procedure with an approximation of the Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) filter. It solves the problem of aliasing artifacts and visual holes in point-sampled geometry rendering, particularly when the model is viewed from flat angles or shifted from the viewing axis. Unlike its siblings, it uses an affine approximation to the projective mapping to ensure perspective-correct splat shapes without requiring per-point normals or complex anisotropic footprint calculations, trading exact band-limited footprints for a formulation that avoids holes and Moiré patterns. It builds on EWA Splatting by replacing the standard EWA covariance computation with a faster, perspective-correct affine approximation. The method operates in a multi-pass pipeline, typically involving a visibility pass, an attribute pass, and a normalization pass. It relies on an affine approximation of the projective mapping to compute the splat's screen-space shape. Inputs: Point-sampled geometry (positions, attributes), camera projection matrix, view matrix, window resolution. Outputs: Final composited image with alpha blending. Lookup Table (LUT): A 1D texture storing Gaussian filter weights. The index is determined by the squared distance r^2 from the splat center in screen space. Conic Matrix: A 2 \times 2 matrix representing the inverse of the resampling filter's variance in screen space, computed as (Q{000} + H)^{-1}. 1. Vertex Processing (Visibility and Shape Approximation): For each splat k: a. Compute the projective mapping matrix Mk that maps the local Gaussian reconstruction kernel to screen space. b. Compute the inverse Mk^{-1} to derive the approximate variance matrix Q{000}. c. Numerical Stability Check: Calculate the condition number of Mk. If it exceeds a threshold (indicating the splat is degenerating into a line segment or is numerically ill-conditioned), discard the splat. d. Ellipse Check: Determine if the resulting conic Q{000} represents an ellipse using specific criteria (e.g., determinant sign and trace properties). If it is not an ellipse, discard the splat. e. Bounding Box: Compute the bounding box for the OpenGL point size based on the ellipse extent. f. Pass the 2 \times 2 conic matrix (Q{000} + H)^{-1} to the fragment program, where H is the Gaussian prefilter variance. 2. Fragment Processing (EWA Filtering): For every pixel x covered by the OpenGL point primitive: a. Evaluate the ellipse equation: r^2 = x (Q{000} + H)^{-1} x^T where x is the pixel coordinate vector relative to the splat center, available via the wpos input parameter. b. If r^2 < Fg^2 (where Fg is the Gaussian filter width threshold), use r^2 as an index into the 1D LUT to retrieve the Gaussian filter weight. c. Otherwise, discard the fragment. d. Output the weighted attribute value and alpha. 3. Normalization Pass: a. Copy the result of the attribute pass (weighted sum of attributes and alpha) to a texture. b. Render a window-sized rectangle using this texture. c. In the fragment program, perform the division by the accumulated alpha to normalize the color values. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def vertexprogram(splatposition, projectionmatrix, viewmatrix): # Compute projective mapping matrix Mk from splat position and view/projection matrices # Mk =... (source does not specify exact construction) # Invert Mk to derive Q000 Mkinv = invert2x2(Mk) Q000 = computevariancefrominverse(Mkinv) # Check condition number of Mk; discard if above threshold if conditionnumber(Mk) > THRESHOLD: return None # Determine if conic Q000 is an ellipse; discard otherwise if not isellipse(Q000): return None # Compute bounding box for OpenGL point size pointsize = computeboundingboxsize(Q000) # H is the Gaussian prefilter variance H = getgaussianprefiltervariance() # Pass (Q000 + H)^-1 to fragment program conicmatrix = invert2x2(Q000 + H) return { 'pointsize': pointsize, 'conicmatrix': conicmatrix, 'splatcenter': projecttoscreen(splatposition) } def fragmentprogram(conicmatrix, splatcenter, wpos, splatcolor, splatalpha): # x is pixel coordinate vector relative to splat center x = wpos - splatcenter # Evaluate ellipse equation r^2 = x (Q000 + H)^-1 x^T rsquared = x[0] (conicmatrix[0][0] x[0] + conicmatrix[0][1] x[1]) + \ x[1] (conicmatrix[1][0] x[0] + conicmatrix[1][1] x[1]) # If r^2 < Fg^2, use r^2 as index into 1D LUT for Gaussian weights if rsquared < Fgsquared: weight = texturelookup1d(gaussianlut, rsquared) return { 'color': splatcolor weight, 'alpha': splatalpha weight } else: return None def normalizationpass(renderedtexture): # Copy result of attribute pass to texture # Render window-sized rectangle to send pixels through pipeline again for pixelcoord in screenpixels: accumulatedcolor = texturelookup(renderedtexture, pixelcoord).color accumulatedalpha = texturelookup(renderedtexture, pixelcoord).alpha # Perform division by alpha to normalize color values if accumulatedalpha > 0: finalcolor = accumulatedcolor / accumulatedalpha else: finalcolor = 0 yield finalcolor Threshold for Condition Number: Not given in the sources. Gaussian Filter Width (Fg): Not given in the sources. Prefilter Variance (H): Not given in the sources. Numerical Ill-Conditioning: The inversion of Mk can be numerically unstable if the splat degenerates into a line segment. This is handled by checking the condition number and discarding the splat. Non-Elliptic Conics: The projective mapping can result in a conic that is not an ellipse. These must be detected and discarded to avoid incorrect rasterization. Splat Center Approximation: The splat centers are not mapped to the perspective-correct position (approximation in Section 4.4 of). However, no visual artifacts were observed due to this approximation. Clipping Overhead: Splat clipping adds overhead. The implementation switches between two fragment shaders (clipped and non-clipped) because typically only a few splats require clipping. Deferred Surface Splatting: Computes surface normals for splat projection. Differs by explicitly handling surface orientation, whereas this method uses an affine approximation to projective mapping for perspective correctness without explicit normals. Link Opacity-Thin-Side (OTS): Adjusts opacity based on viewing angle for thin surfaces. Differs by focusing on opacity adjustment for thin geometry, while this method focuses on perspective-correct shape and EWA filtering. Link OTS (EWA-Based Splatting): Combines OTS with EWA filtering. Differs by integrating opacity thin-side logic with the EWA filter, whereas this method uses a simpler affine approximation for perspective correction. Link GPU-Accelerated Volume Splatting With Elliptical RBFs: Uses elliptical Radial Basis Functions for volume rendering. Differs by using elliptical RBFs for volume data, while this method is for point-sampled geometry with an affine EWA approximation. Link Ellipsoidal Kernel Splatting with Warped Slicing: Uses warped slicing to handle ellipsoidal kernels. Differs by using a slicing-based approach for ellipsoidal kernels, whereas this method uses direct splat rasterization with an affine approximation. Link Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting: Adapts the EWA filter based on local density. Differs by adapting the filter size, while this method uses a fixed affine approximation for perspective correctness. Link EWA Approximation with Tangent Vector Adjustment: Adjusts tangent vectors to improve EWA approximation. Differs by adjusting tangent vectors, whereas this method uses an affine approximation to the projective mapping. Link Phong Splatting: Applies Phong shading to splats. Differs by adding shading, while this method focuses on perspective-correct rasterization and EWA filtering. Link EWA Splatting Renderer (Mesh-Free): A general EWA splatting renderer for mesh-free data. Differs by being a general renderer, while this method specifically uses an affine approximation for perspective correctness. Link Time Complexity: The vertex program is relatively simple, while the fragment program is more complex due to the EWA filter evaluation. Compared to raycasting, the splatting approach requires simpler vertex programs but significantly more complex fragment programs. However, since the number of rasterized fragments is significantly larger than the number of splats (at least a factor of four in complete minification), the splatting approach is always more performant. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the 1D LUT and intermediate textures for the normalization pass. Measured Performance: On Athlon64 3500+ / GeForce 7800 with Igea dataset at 1024x1024: 154k splats at 50 fps (7.7M splats/sec) vs 33 fps for raycasting; 460k splats at 40 fps (18.4M splats/sec) vs 26 fps; 1.4M splats at 22 fps (31M splats/sec) vs 13 fps; 2.5M splats at 15 fps (37.5M splats/sec) vs 9.2 fps; 5M splats at 6.5 fps (32.5M splats/sec) vs 5 fps. On GeForceFX 5950 GPU and Pentium IV 3.0 GHz CPU: Cg: 1 pass rendering achieved 2.9 million splats/sec at 512x512 and 2.8 million splats/sec at 1280x1024. The 3-pass algorithm achieved 1.4 million splats/sec at 512x512 and 1.2 million splats/sec at 1280x1024. Assembler: 1 pass rendering achieved 11.2 million splats/sec at 512x512 and 10.4 million splats/sec at 1280x1024. The 3-pass algorithm achieved 3.1 million splats/sec at 512x512 and 2.8 million splats/sec at 1280x1024. Strengths: Higher quality anti-aliasing filtering for splats in both minification and magnification cases compared to previous approximations. Avoids holes in the rendered image at flat viewing angles. Avoids Moiré patterns by using a Gaussian prefilter. Limitations: The fragment program is more complex than the vertex program. The approximation of splat centers may lead to minor inaccuracies, though no visual artifacts were observed. When to use: When high image quality and anti-aliasing are required for point-sampled geometry, especially with sharp features or CSG-generated objects. When perspective-correct splat shapes are needed to avoid holes at flat viewing angles. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was presented in "Perspective Accurate Splatting" and "Splat/Mesh Blending, Perspective Rasterization and Transparency for Point-Based Rendering". It builds on the EWA splatting technique by Heckbert and improves upon previous approximations by Botsch et al. [BHZK05] and ZRB04. The approach was developed to address the limitations of earlier splatting methods, such as aliasing artifacts and holes at flat viewing angles. It is used in point-based rendering systems to render objects with sharp features created using CSG operations. name: Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting
head: Adaptive EWA Filtering, Adaptive EWA Splatting, Chen adaptive splatting, Distance-dependent Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting
body: Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting is a rendering technique that simplifies the computationally expensive Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) resampling filter by classifying volume particles into three cases based on their distance from the viewpoint. It solves the problem of high computational cost in full EWA splatting while maintaining aliasing-free quality. Unlike full EWA splatting, which always computes the combined covariance of the reconstruction and low-pass filters, this method uses only the reconstruction filter for close particles (magnification) and only the low-pass filter for far particles (minification), resorting to full EWA only in the transition zone. Inputs: Volume dataset (regular or rectilinear). Camera parameters (view angle fov, projection matrix). Reconstruction kernel cutoff radius rk and low-pass filter cutoff radius rh. Outputs: Rendered image with antialiasing. Data Structures: Packed Vertex Representation (32 bits): Used to store proxy geometry efficiently in GPU memory. tx: Volume texture coordinate X. Packed as mx \times 256 + ix. mx uses 7 bits, ix uses 8 bits. ty: Volume texture coordinate Y. Packed similarly (my 7 bits, iy 8 bits). fx, fy: Gaussian texture coordinates. Each uses 1 bit (values 0 or 1). Total: 7+8+7+8+1+1 = 32 bits. Lookup Table: Stored in constant registers, accessed via an address register in the vertex shader to decompress mx, my, fx, fy. Parameters: c{min}: Lower bound parameter for distance-dependent criteria. Typical value: 0.3. c{max}: Upper bound parameter for distance-dependent criteria. Typical value: 2.0 \times (1.0 + 2.0 \times \tan(fov/2)^2). Method Steps: 1. Patch Grouping: Group quads (voxels) of each slice into uniform rectangular patches. 2. Corner Computation: For each patch, compute the camera space coordinate u{k2} (depth) of each of the four corner voxels on-the-fly. 3. Classification: Evaluate the criteria from Equation 7 for the four vertices of the patch: Magnification (Close): If all four vertices satisfy u{k2} < \frac{rk}{rh} \times c{min}, use the reconstruction filter. Minification (Far): If all four vertices satisfy u{k2} > \frac{rk}{rh} \times c{max}, use the low-pass filter. Transition: Otherwise, use the full EWA resampling filter. 4. Filter Selection: Apply the appropriate vertex shader corresponding to the selected filter case. The filter function Hk(\mathbf{x}) is defined as: Hk(\mathbf{x}) = \begin{cases} \mathbf{x}^T \cdot \hat{\mathbf{V}}k^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{x}, & \text{if } u{k2} < \frac{rk}{rh} \times c{min} \\ \mathbf{x}^T \cdot \mathbf{V}h^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{x}, & \text{if } u{k2} > \frac{rk}{rh} \times c{max} \\ \mathbf{x}^T \cdot (\hat{\mathbf{V}}k + \mathbf{V}h)^{-1} \cdot \mathbf{x}, & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} where \mathbf{x} is the screen-space offset vector. \hat{\mathbf{V}}k is the 2x2 variance matrix of the reconstruction filter, obtained by skipping the third row and column of the full 3x3 covariance matrix \mathbf{V}k. \mathbf{V}h is the 2x2 variance matrix of the Gaussian low-pass filter, usually the identity matrix. 5. Rasterization: Rasterize the proxy quads using the selected vertex shader to deform the unit Gaussian texture according to the footprint function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def classifypatch(patchcornerscameraspace, rk, rh, cmin, cmax): """ Determines the filter type for a patch based on the depth of its four corners. patchcornerscameraspace: list of 4 tuples (uk0, uk1, uk2) Returns: 'MAGNIFICATION', 'MINIFICATION', or 'FULLEWA' """ allmagnification = True allminification = True thresholdmin = (rk / rh) cmin thresholdmax = (rk / rh) cmax for uk0, uk1, uk2 in patchcornerscameraspace: if uk2 >= thresholdmin: allmagnification = False if uk2 <= thresholdmax: allminification = False if not allmagnification and not allminification: return 'FULLEWA' if allmagnification: return 'MAGNIFICATION' elif allminification: return 'MINIFICATION' else: return 'FULLEWA' def computefiltermatrix(filtertype, Vhatk, Vh): """ Computes the inverse covariance matrix used in the filter exponent. """ if filtertype == 'MAGNIFICATION': return Vhatk elif filtertype == 'MINIFICATION': return Vh else: return Vhatk + Vh def renderpatch(patch, Vhatk, Vh, rk, rh, cmin, cmax): filtertype = classifypatch(patch.cornerscameraspace, rk, rh, cmin, cmax) filtermatrix = computefiltermatrix(filtertype, Vhatk, Vh) # Deform proxy quad geometry based on filtermatrix to match the footprint function # and rasterize the textured quad. (Implementation details for vertex shader deformation not specified in sources.) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Transition Zone: In the transition between magnification and minification, neither approximation avoids aliasing artifacts without the full EWA computation. Memory Limits: A naive implementation of proxy geometry for a 256^3 volume requires 2240M bytes of memory, exceeding the 256M limit of commodity graphics hardware at the time of publication. Compression is necessary. Precision: The classification relies on conservative bounds derived from the maximum value of (u{k0}^2 + u{k1}^2 + u{k2}^2)/u{k2}^2, which is (1.0 + 2.0 \times \tan(fov/2)^2). Time Complexity: Reduces computation cost compared to full EWA splatting by using simpler filters (low-pass or reconstruction) in extreme cases, but adds classification overhead. Measured Performance: On a 512 \times 512 \times 3 checkerboard dataset: 6.88 fps vs 4.83 fps for full EWA. Engine dataset (256 \times 256 \times 110): 3.25 fps vs 2.90 fps (12% improvement). Bonsai dataset (256 \times 256 \times 128): 7.53 fps vs 6.90 fps (9% improvement). Lobster dataset (301 \times 324 \times 56): 10.60 fps vs 8.75 fps (21% improvement). UNC Head dataset (208 \times 256 \times 225): 3.00 fps vs 2.70 fps (11% improvement). Strengths: Achieves high image quality comparable to full EWA while reducing computational cost by 10% to 20%. Corrects aliasing artifacts and holes that occur with improper filters (reconstruction or low-pass only). Limitations: Adds classification overhead. The improvement is modest (10-20%). When to use: When interactive frame rates are required for large volume datasets and full EWA is too slow, but quality must be maintained. When not to use: When the scene is uniformly very close or very far, as the overhead of classification may not be justified if one filter could be used globally without quality loss (though full EWA is safer for mixed depths). Adaptive EWA Volume Splatting was introduced by Wei Chen et al. in 2004. It builds on the EWA Splatting method [1069-ewa-splatting.md] by observing that the EWA resampling filter computation is expensive and can be simplified adaptively based on depth. The method was implemented on GPU to gain additional performance for interactive frame rates. name: EWA Approximation with Tangent Vector Adjustment
head: Dynamic EWA Filtering, Minification-aware Splat Filtering
body: A high-quality filtering technique for point-based rendering that approximates the EWA resampling filter by dynamically adjusting the tangent vectors of isotropic splats during setup to prevent aliasing during minification, without requiring expensive per-fragment convolution. It sets itself apart from the original EWA framework by using projective mapping and tangent adjustment rather than affine mapping and Gaussians for both reconstruction and low-pass filters, and from Botsch et al. [BHZK05] by avoiding per-fragment filter evaluation, thus eliminating the fragment shader bottleneck. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of isotropic splats, each defined by a center position \mathbf{p}k and a surface normal \mathbf{n}k. Output: Adjusted tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k and \mathbf{t}k for each splat, which define the orientation and extent of the reconstruction kernel for rasterization. Data Structures: Splat Data: For each splat k, store \mathbf{p}k = [px, py, pz]^T (position in camera space) and \mathbf{n}k = [nx, ny, nz]^T (normalized normal). Tangent Vectors: \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k are 3D vectors. Parameters: h: Radius of the low-pass filter in the normalized image plane. A typical choice is h = \sqrt{2} v{pw}, where v{pw} is the viewport width. Steps: 1. Compute Initial Tangents: For an isotropic splat with normal \mathbf{n}k, compute orthogonal initial tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k^0 and \mathbf{t}k^0 using cross products: \mathbf{s}k^0 = \mathbf{p}k \times \mathbf{n}k \mathbf{t}k^0 = \mathbf{n}k \times \mathbf{s}k^0 2. Project Tangent: For each tangent vector (e.g., \mathbf{t}k^0 = [tx, ty, tz]^T), compute its perspective projection \mathbf{t}'k onto the screen space: \mathbf{t}'k = \frac{1}{pz^2 - tz^2} \begin{bmatrix} tx pz - tz px \\ ty pz - tz py \\ 0 \end{bmatrix} 3. Check Minification: Calculate the length of the projected half-diameter \|\mathbf{t}'k\|. If \|\mathbf{t}'k\| \ge h, the splat is not significantly minified in this direction. Set the final tangent vector \mathbf{t}k = \mathbf{t}k^0. If \|\mathbf{t}'k\| < h, the splat is in minification. Adjust the tangent vector by projecting \mathbf{t}k^0 onto the image plane and scaling it so its projection size equals the filter radius: \mathbf{t}k = \frac{\mathbf{t}'k}{\|\mathbf{t}'k\|} pz h 4. Repeat for Second Tangent: Perform steps 2–3 for \mathbf{s}k^0 to obtain \mathbf{s}k. The vectors are adjusted independently. 5. Rasterize: Rasterize the reconstruction kernel using the adjusted tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k and \mathbf{t}k. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def cross(a, b): return [a[1]b[2] - a[2]b[1], a[2]b[0] - a[0]b[2], a[0]b[1] - a[1]b[0]] def length(v): return (v[0]2 + v[1]2 + v[2]2)0.5 def adjusttangentvectors(pk, nk, h): """ Adjusts tangent vectors for a splat to handle minification. Args: pk: 3D position vector [px, py, pz] in camera space. nk: 3D normal vector [nx, ny, nz], assumed normalized. h: Filter radius in normalized image plane. Returns: sk, tk: Adjusted tangent vectors. """ # Step 1: Compute initial orthogonal tangents sk0 = cross(pk, nk) tk0 = cross(nk, sk0) # Step 2-4: Adjust each tangent independently sk = adjustsingletangent(pk, sk0, h) tk = adjustsingletangent(pk, tk0, h) return sk, tk def adjustsingletangent(pk, tk0, h): """ Adjusts a single tangent vector based on minification criteria. """ tx, ty, tz = tk0 px, py, pz = pk # Step 2: Project tangent to screen space denom = pz2 - tz2 if abs(denom) < 1e-9: # return tk0 tkprime = [ (tx pz - tz px) / denom, (ty pz - tz py) / denom, 0.0 ] # Step 3: Check length of projected half-diameter normtprime = length(tkprime) if normtprime >= h: # No adjustment needed return tk0 else: # Adjust: scale projection to radius h, then scale back to object space magnitude if normtprime < 1e-9: # return tk0 unittprime = [v / normtprime for v in tkprime] tk = [v pz h for v in unittprime] return tk Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Orthogonality Assumption: The heuristic for generating initial tangent vectors assumes orthogonality. For a 90-degree view frustum, the angle \alpha between screen-space projections of basis vectors ranges from 60 to 90 degrees (average 81.7). If \alpha \neq 90, the low-pass filter may be slightly truncated, but this is acceptable as the error is below output resolution. Depth Correction: Depth correction is lost for splats in minification because tangent vectors become parallel to the screen plane. This is intentional to prevent visibility artifacts caused by arbitrary depth values from infinite stretch values. Depth correction is not required for splats below a single pixel. Numerical Stability: Division by pz^2 - tz^2 requires a guard against zero denominators when the tangent vector aligns with the view direction projection. A band-limiting technique that evaluates the reconstruction kernel in the surfel's tangent frame using object-space ray-splat intersection to eliminate perspective distortion of affine screen-space approximations. It maps a screen-space Gaussian pixel prefilter with covariance \sigmaf \mathbf{I} into the local coordinate system via the Jacobian \mathbf{J} = \partial(u, v)/\partial(x, y) of the ray-splat intersection mapping. The combined reconstruction-plus-prefilter kernel in object space has the modified covariance \Sigma{\text{mip}} = \mathbf{I} + \sigmaf \mathbf{J} \mathbf{J}^\top. The MIP-filtered Gaussian kernel is evaluated as G{\text{mip}}(\mathbf{u}) = nf \cdot \exp(-\frac{1}{2} \mathbf{u}^T \Sigma{\text{mip}}^{-1} \mathbf{u}), where \mathbf{u} is the local coordinate vector and nf is the normalization factor. A pitfall is that per-pixel evaluation of \mathbf{J} can introduce numerical instability for highly tilted or thin surfels where the denominator of quotient-rule derivatives approaches zero. Time Complexity: Computations are done during splat setup, not rasterization. Unlike original EWA, no additional fragments are generated when not necessary because splats are extended only in directions of minification. Memory Complexity: Requires storing adjusted tangent vectors per splat. No per-fragment filter data is needed. Performance: Avoids the fragment shader bottleneck associated with evaluating resampling and low-pass filters per fragment. Strengths: High-quality filtering, prevents aliasing during minification, efficient rasterization, handles hybrid splat/polygon rendering easily. Limitations: Approximation error due to non-orthogonal basis projections (though small), loss of depth correction for minified splats (intentional). When to Use: Point-based rendering requiring high-quality anti-aliasing without the cost of full EWA per-fragment computation, especially when splats are isotropic and preprocessing is acceptable. When Not to Use: Not given in the sources. Originated in the context of point-based rendering and EWA filtering approximations. It was proposed as a new approximation between the optimal EWA resampling filter and the approximation of Botsch et al. [BHZK05] to dynamically adjust tangent vectors in object space. The method acknowledges that its approximation can be coarse when a splat experiences minification in one direction and magnification in another, where fine parts may still fall between image samples. name: EWA Splatting Renderer (Mesh-Free)
head: CamPoint splatting renderer, Point-cloud splatting renderer
body: A mesh-free rendering pipeline that projects raw point clouds directly to 2D camera views using EWA projection and Z-buffer occlusion, producing RGB images, label maps, and 2D-to-3D index maps without mesh reconstruction. It differs from its parent EWA Splatting by using simplified screen-aligned spherical impostors with isotropic linear falloff, trading anisotropic, correctly band-limited footprints for a formulation that requires no per-point normals or radii. Inputs: xyz: Point cloud coordinates, shape [N, 3], dtype float32 (world coordinates). rgb: Point colors, shape [N, 3], dtype uint8 (range 0–255) or float (range 0–1). label: Semantic labels, shape [N], dtype int64 (long). intr: Camera intrinsics, shape [M, 4] or [4], containing [fx, fy, cx, cy]. extr: Camera extrinsics, shape [M, 3, 4] or [3, 4] (rotation and translation). W, H: Output image width and height in pixels. splatradius: Pixel expansion radius r. extent: Frustum culling margin factor (e.g., 1.3 for 30% beyond viewport). cambatch: Number of cameras processed simultaneously on GPU. Outputs: colorcanvas: RGB image, shape [H, W, 3], dtype uint8. depthcanvas: Depth image, shape [H, W], dtype float32 (background set to inf). labelcanvas: Label map, shape [H, W], dtype int64 (background set to 0). indexcanvas: 2D-to-3D index map, shape [H, W], dtype int64 (background set to -1). Bucket Tensor: Used for Z-buffer occlusion. Size bucketsize M, where bucketsize = (mH + 1) (mW + 1). mW = int(extent W) + 1, mH = int(extent H) + 1. Indices map 2D pixel coordinates to a flattened array for efficient occlusion testing. Sort Key: Used for depth resolution. Calculated as flatidx (dmax + 1.0) + depth, where dmax is the maximum depth in the scene. This allows sorting by pixel index first, then by depth. splatradius: Default 1 (single pixel). 2 produces a 3×3 disk. Larger values densify the image but soften details. extent: Default 1.3. cambatch: Default 8. 1. Load and Normalize: Convert xyz to float32. If rgb is uint8, normalize to [0, 1] by dividing by 255.0. Convert label to int64. 2. Project Points: Project xyz using intr and extr for all M cameras. Returns screen coordinates uv of shape [M, N, 2] and depths depths of shape [M, N, 1]. 3. Reshape Tensors: Permute uv and depths from [M, N,...] to [N,..., M] using.permute(1, 2, 0).contiguous() to facilitate per-point processing across cameras. 4. Z-buffer Occlusion: Calculate extended dimensions mW and mH based on extent. Initialize a bucket tensor of size (mH + 1) (mW + 1) M. Call shelterpoints(uv, depths, mW, mH, offset, bucket) to determine visible points. This returns occluded uv, depths, and a visible mask. Pitfall: If M == 1, the Numba kernel for shelterpoints fails because it requires M >= 2 for 3D array indexing. Workaround: Duplicate uv and depths along the camera axis to make M=2, perform occlusion, then slice back to M=1. 5. Filter Visible Points: Create boolean mask vismask = (visible.squeeze(-1) > 0) & (depths.squeeze(-1) > 0). Get indices visidx of visible points. 6. Coordinate Transformation: Round uv to integer pixel coordinates: px = round(uv[:, 0]). Flip Y coordinate for image space: py = H - 1 - round(uv[:, 1]). 7. Boundary Check: Filter points where 0 <= px < W and 0 <= py < H. Discard invalid points. 8. Splat Expansion: For each visible point, expand to a disk of radius r (splatradius). Generate offsets dy in [-r, r] and dx in [-r, r], excluding (0,0). Calculate neighbor pixel coordinates nx = px + dx, ny = py + dy. Filter out-of-bounds neighbors. 9. Flatten Indices: Compute flat pixel index flatidx = py W + px. Expand to include neighbors: flatall[:, 1:] = nflat (neighbor flat indices). Mark out-of-bounds neighbors as -1. 10. Depth Resolve: Sort splats by pixel index and depth to resolve collisions. Create sortkey = flatexp.float() (dsrc.max() + 1.0) + dsrc. Sort by sortkey. Keep the first entry per unique pixel index (minimum depth). 11. Write Canvases: Initialize colorcanvas [HW, 3], depthcanvas [HW], labelcanvas [HW], indexcanvas [HW]. Write rgb, depth, label, and point ID to the winner pixels. Convert color to uint8 by multiplying by 255 and clamping to [0, 255]. Set background pixels (depth == inf) to 0 for color/label and -1 for index. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import torch import numpy as np def ewasplattingmeshfree(xyz, rgb, label, intr, extr, W, H, splatradius=1, extent=1.3, cambatch=8): """ Mesh-free EWA splatting renderer. Args: xyz: [N, 3] float32 rgb: [N, 3] uint8 or float32 label: [N] int64 intr: [M, 4] or [4] float32 (fx, fy, cx, cy) extr: [M, 3, 4] or [3, 4] float32 W, H: int splatradius: int extent: float cambatch: int Returns: colorcanvas: [H, W, 3] uint8 depthcanvas: [H, W] float32 labelcanvas: [H, W] int64 indexcanvas: [H, W] int64 """ N = xyz.shape[0] # 1. Load and Normalize xyz = xyz.float() if rgb.dtype == torch.uint8: rgb = rgb.float() / 255.0 label = label.long() # Handle single camera case for projection and occlusion M = intr.shape[0] if intr.dim() > 1 else 1 if M == 1: intr = intr.unsqueeze(0) extr = extr.unsqueeze(0) M = 1 # 2. Project Points # Assuming projectpoints handles broadcasting and returns [M, N, 2] and [M, N, 1] uv, depths = projectpoints(xyz, intr, extr, W, H, nearest=0.2, extent=extent) # 3. Reshape Tensors uv = uv.permute(1, 2, 0).contiguous() # [N, 2, M] depths = depths.permute(1, 2, 0).contiguous() # [N, 1, M] # 4. Z-buffer Occlusion mW = int(extent W) + 1 mH = int(extent H) + 1 bucketsize = (mH + 1) (mW + 1) bucket = torch.zeros((bucketsize M), dtype=torch.int32, device=xyz.device) # Workaround for M=1 if shelterpoints requires M>=2 if M == 1: uvdup = uv.repeat(1, 1, 2) depthsdup = depths.repeat(1, 1, 2) visible,, = shelterpoints(uvdup, depthsdup, mW, mH, 0, bucket) visible = visible[:,:,:1] else: visible,, = shelterpoints(uv, depths, mW, mH, 0, bucket) # 5. Filter Visible Points vismask = (visible.squeeze(-1) > 0) & (depths.squeeze(-1) > 0) visidx = torch.nonzero(vismask, astuple=False).squeeze(1) if len(visidx) == 0: # Return empty canvases colorcanvas = torch.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=torch.uint8) depthcanvas = torch.full((H, W), float('inf'), dtype=torch.float32) labelcanvas = torch.zeros((H, W), dtype=torch.int64) indexcanvas = torch.full((H, W), -1, dtype=torch.int64) return colorcanvas, depthcanvas, labelcanvas, indexcanvas uvvis = uv[visidx] depthsvis = depths[visidx] rgbvis = rgb[visidx] labelvis = label[visidx] pointids = visidx # Assuming visidx corresponds to original point IDs # 6. Coordinate Transformation px = torch.round(uvvis[:, 0]).long() py = (H - 1 - torch.round(uvvis[:, 1])).long() # 7. Boundary Check valid = (px >= 0) & (px < W) & (py >= 0) & (py < H) px = px[valid] py = py[valid] depthsvis = depthsvis[valid] rgbvis = rgbvis[valid] labelvis = labelvis[valid] pointids = pointids[valid] if len(px) == 0: colorcanvas = torch.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=torch.uint8) depthcanvas = torch.full((H, W), float('inf'), dtype=torch.float32) labelcanvas = torch.zeros((H, W), dtype=torch.int64) indexcanvas = torch.full((H, W), -1, dtype=torch.int64) return colorcanvas, depthcanvas, labelcanvas, indexcanvas # 8. Splat Expansion r = splatradius offsets = [] for dy in range(-r, r + 1): for dx in range(-r, r + 1): if dx == 0 and dy == 0: continue offsets.append((dx, dy)) numoffsets = len(offsets) # Expand px, py, depths, rgb, label, pointids # pxexp: [N, 1 + numoffsets] pxexp = px.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, 1 + numoffsets) pyexp = py.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, 1 + numoffsets) depthsexp = depthsvis.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, 1 + numoffsets) rgbexp = rgbvis.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, 1 + numoffsets, 1) labelexp = labelvis.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, 1 + numoffsets) pointidsexp = pointids.unsqueeze(1).repeat(1, 1 + numoffsets) # Fill offsets for i, (dx, dy) in enumerate(offsets): pxexp[:, i+1] = px + dx pyexp[:, i+1] = py + dy # 9. Flatten Indices flatidx = py W + px flatall = pyexp W + pxexp # Mark out-of-bounds neighbors as -1 outofbounds = (pxexp < 0) | (pxexp >= W) | (pyexp < 0) | (pyexp >= H) flatall[outofbounds] = -1 # 10. Depth Resolve # Flatten for sorting flatallflat = flatall.view(-1) depthsflat = depthsexp.view(-1) rgbflat = rgbexp.view(-1, 3) labelflat = labelexp.view(-1) pointidsflat = pointidsexp.view(-1) # Filter out -1 indices validmask = flatallflat >= 0 flatallflat = flatallflat[validmask] depthsflat = depthsflat[validmask] rgbflat = rgbflat[validmask] labelflat = labelflat[validmask] pointidsflat = pointidsflat[validmask] if len(flatallflat) == 0: colorcanvas = torch.zeros((H, W, 3), dtype=torch.uint8) depthcanvas = torch.full((H, W), float('inf'), dtype=torch.float32) labelcanvas = torch.zeros((H, W), dtype=torch.int64) indexcanvas = torch.full((H, W), -1, dtype=torch.int64) return colorcanvas, depthcanvas, labelcanvas, indexcanvas dmax = depthsflat.max() sortkey = flatallflat.float() (dmax + 1.0) + depthsflat # Sort by sortkey sortindices = torch.argsort(sortkey) flatallsorted = flatallflat[sortindices] depthssorted = depthsflat[sortindices] rgbsorted = rgbflat[sortindices] labelsorted = labelflat[sortindices] pointidssorted = pointidsflat[sortindices] # Keep first entry per unique pixel index uniquepixels, uniqueindices = torch.unique(flatallsorted, returninverse=True, returncounts=True) # uniqueindices gives the index of the first occurrence of each unique pixel # We need to gather the first entry for each unique pixel # Since we sorted by sortkey (pixel then depth), the first entry is the winner # Create output canvases colorcanvas = torch.zeros((H W, 3), dtype=torch.float32) depthcanvas = torch.full((H W,), float('inf'), dtype=torch.float32) labelcanvas = torch.full((H W,), -1, dtype=torch.int64) indexcanvas = torch.full((H W,), -1, dtype=torch.int64) # Assign winners # uniqueindices contains the index in the sorted arrays of the first occurrence winners = torch.arange(len(uniquepixels), device=uniquepixels.device) colorcanvas[uniquepixels] = rgbsorted[uniqueindices] depthcanvas[uniquepixels] = depthssorted[uniqueindices] labelcanvas[uniquepixels] = labelsorted[uniqueindices] indexcanvas[uniquepixels] = pointidssorted[uniqueindices] # 11. Write Canvases # Convert color to uint8 colorcanvasuint8 = (colorcanvas 255).clamp(0, 255).long() # Reshape to [H, W,...] colorcanvas = colorcanvasuint8.view(H, W, 3).byte() depthcanvas = depthcanvas.view(H, W) labelcanvas = labelcanvas.view(H, W) indexcanvas = indexcanvas.view(H, W) # Set background pixels (depth == inf) bgmask = depthcanvas == float('inf') colorcanvas[bgmask] = 0 labelcanvas[bgmask] = 0 indexcanvas[bgmask] = -1 return colorcanvas, depthcanvas, labelcanvas, indexcanvas def projectpoints(xyz, intr, extr, W, H, nearest=0.2, extent=1.3): """ Placeholder for projection logic. Returns uv [M, N, 2] and depths [M, N, 1] """ # Implementation details depend on the specific projection library or math # This is a placeholder to satisfy the requirement of self-contained pseudocode # In practice, this would involve matrix multiplication and perspective division pass def shelterpoints(uv, depths, mW, mH, offset, bucket): """ Placeholder for Numba kernel for Z-buffer occlusion. Returns visible mask, occluded uv, occluded depths """ # Implementation details depend on the specific Numba kernel pass Time Complexity: Dominated by projection and sorting. Projection is O(N \cdot M). Occlusion is O(N \cdot M) with bucket access. Sorting is O(K \log K) where K is the number of splats (up to N \cdot (2r+1)^2 \cdot M). Memory Complexity: O(N \cdot M) for intermediate tensors during projection and occlusion. Bucket size is O(M \cdot \text{extent}^2 \cdot W \cdot H). Performance: Measured on GPU with cambatch=8. Performance scales with number of points N and cameras M. Larger splatradius increases memory and compute due to more splats per point. Strengths: No mesh reconstruction required. Fast projection and rasterization. Handles large-scale point clouds efficiently. Limitations: Spherical impostors lack anisotropic filtering, potentially causing aliasing or blurring at oblique angles. Z-buffer occlusion is approximate due to bucket resolution and extent margin. Single camera case requires workaround. When to Use: When mesh reconstruction is undesirable or too expensive, and real-time or near-real-time rendering of point clouds is needed. Suitable for multi-view synthesis and visualization. When Not to Use: When high-quality anti-aliasing and correct perspective projection of point sizes are critical. Not suitable for scenes with extreme depth variations where bucket resolution is insufficient. Originated from the "Point-Splatting-Multi-View-2D-Rendering-Pipeline" project by Luhao03, described as an unofficial implementation. It is part of the CamPoint ecosystem, designed for multi-view splatting of large-scale point clouds, particularly for architectural structures like city walls. name: Surface Splatting and Lighting
body: Surface Splatting and Lighting is a family of rendering techniques that reconstruct continuous, shaded surfaces from unstructured point cloud samples by projecting each point as a spatially extended primitive (a splat) carrying a reconstruction kernel. It solves the problem of sparse dot cloud aliasing and transparency artifacts inherent in raw point rendering by ensuring hole-free reconstructions even for moderate sampling densities. Unlike forward splatting methods that apply lighting during rasterization, variants like Deferred Surface Splatting decouple geometric projection from lighting calculation, allowing multiple light sources to be applied efficiently in screen space without re-projecting geometry. The family operates on a set of point cloud samples P = \{pi\}, where each sample pi has a position \mathbf{p}, a color \mathbf{c}, and optionally a normal \mathbf{n}. Each sample is converted into a splat Sj defined by a center cj, tangent vectors \mathbf{u}j, \mathbf{v}j, and radii ru, rv. The rendering process generally involves: (1) transforming the object-space splat into screen space, (2) rasterizing the splat footprint as a low-pass filter to suppress aliasing, (3) accumulating overlapping contributions by computing a distance-based weight w and additively blending attributes (color, normal, depth), and (4) computing illumination either per-splat or in a final screen-space pass. Converts point clouds into continuous surfaces using a deferred pipeline with a G-buffer. It decouples projection from lighting, allowing efficient multi-light support in screen space. Choose this when multiple lights or complex shading models are required without re-projecting geometry. Assigns a linearly varying normal field to each elliptical splat, enabling per-pixel Phong shading. It is projectively correct and solves piecewise constant shading artifacts. Choose this for high-quality, physically-based shading of point clouds with fewer primitives than triangle meshes. Uses band-limited reconstruction kernels (surface splats) to efficiently suppress aliasing and guarantee hole-free reconstructions under arbitrary transformations. It builds on Surface Splatting and Lighting and is chosen for high-quality, band-limited rendering of dense point clouds. Surface splatting was introduced as a method to render point samples by superimposing band-limited reconstruction kernels in the image domain. It efficiently suppresses aliasing artifacts and guarantees hole-free reconstructions even for moderate sampling densities. The technique has been extended to support various lighting models, including deferred shading and Phong shading, to address the visual quality limitations of simple point sprites.

name: Deferred Surface Splatting
head: EWA surface splatting with deferred shading, Finalization Shader, Lighting Pass, Point Cloud Splatting, Point cloud splatting to G-buffer, Surface Splatting Finalization Pass
body: Deferred Surface Splatting is a rendering technique that converts unstructured point clouds into continuous, shaded surfaces by projecting points as splats into a deferred rendering pipeline (G-buffers for depth, normals, and color/weight), followed by a final shading pass over a screen quad. It solves the problem of sparse dot cloud aliasing and transparency artifacts by assigning each point sample an extent drawn as a small oriented primitive (a splat) carrying a radially decreasing reconstruction kernel. Unlike Phong Splatting, which computes lighting per-splat during rasterization, Deferred Surface Splatting decouples geometric projection from lighting calculation, allowing multiple light sources to be applied efficiently in screen space without re-projecting geometry. It builds on Surface Splatting and Lighting by deferring the illumination step to a final pass over accumulated G-buffer attributes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of point cloud samples P = \{pi\}, where each sample has position \mathbf{p}, color \mathbf{c}, and optionally normal \mathbf{n}. Output: A final image with continuous surface shading, depth, and normals reconstructed from the splat buffers. Data Structures: The method uses a G-Buffer consisting of three attachments: 1. Depth Attachment: GLDEPTHATTACHMENT using GLDEPTHCOMPONENT32F texture. 2. Normal Attachment: GLCOLORATTACHMENT0 using GLRGBA32F texture (RGBA format, though A is unused). 3. Color/Weight Attachment: GLCOLORATTACHMENT1 using GLRGBA32F texture storing (R, G, B, W), where R,G,B are the weight-normalized color and W is the accumulated weight. Draw buffers are set to {GLCOLORATTACHMENT0, GLCOLORATTACHMENT1}. Uniform Blocks (std140, columnmajor): Camera: mat4 modelviewmatrix, mat4 modelviewmatrixit, mat4 projectionmatrix. Raycast: mat4 projectionmatrixinv, vec4 viewport. Parameter: vec3 materialcolor, float materialshininess, float radiusscale, float ewaradius, float epsilon. Parameters: epsilon: A float parameter calculated as renderingParams->epsilonMultiplier renderingParams->pointSize. particleradius: A float parameter representing the splat size, passed to vertex and fragment shaders. SMOOTH: Boolean define (1 if smooth shading, 0 if flat). MULTISAMPLING: Boolean define (1 if multisampling is enabled). Steps: 1. Initialization: Load shaders: finalizationvsglsl, finalizationfsglsl, lightingglsl. Compile shaders with defines SMOOTH and MULTISAMPLING. Link program and bind uniform blocks: Camera to binding point 0, Raycast to 1, Parameter to 3. Initialize OpenGL state: enable depth test (GLLESS), enable vertex program point size, set point sprite coordinate origin to GLLOWERLEFT. 2. Depth Pass (Visibility): Bind G-Buffer. Set color mask to false for RGB (only write depth). Draw scene using shaderdepth (splat.vert, splatdepth.frag). Each splat is rasterized as a sphere impostor. Fragments outside the unit disk are discarded. The analytic front-surface depth is computed as: z = z{center} - \sqrt{r^2 - x^2 - y^2} This depth is pushed back by \varepsilon before being written to the depth buffer, creating a thin depth slab around the visible surface. Uniforms passed: viewprojmatrix, fovy, viewportsize, epsilon, particleradius, znear, zfar. 3. Attribute Blend Pass (G-Buffer Accumulation): Bind G-Buffer. Bind gDepthTex to GLTEXTURE0. Set color mask to true for all channels. Disable depth mask. Disable depth test. Enable blending with GLONE, GLONE (pure additive). Draw scene using shaderattr (splat.vert, splatattributes.frag). Each fragment compares its own sphere depth against the depth texture from Pass 1. It discards fragments that fall behind the \varepsilon slab (i.e., z{frag} < z{surface} - \varepsilon). Surviving fragments (those belonging to the same visible surface) are accumulated. The weight w is the product of radial and depth falloffs: w{radial} = 1 - \frac{d}{r} w{depth} = \frac{z{surface} - z{frag}}{\varepsilon} w = w{radial} \cdot w{depth} Where d is the distance from the splat center in screen space, and r is the splat radius. Color and normal attributes are accumulated additively, weighted by w. Uniforms passed: viewprojmatrix, fovy, viewportsize, epsilon, particleradius, znear, zfar. 4. Rendering Pass (Finalization/Lighting): Bind default framebuffer (0). Clear color buffer. Select shader based on display mode: DEPTH (reads gDepthTex), COLORS (reads gColorTex), NORMALS (reads gNormalTex), or FULL (reads gNormalTex and gColorTex, applies lighting with lightdirviewspc, lightcolor, ambientstrength, specularstrength). Draw a full-screen quad using quadVAO. Pseudocode (Finalization Fragment Shader): Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def finalizationpass(textureuv, projectionmatrixinv, viewport, depthtexture, normaltexture, colortexture, SMOOTH, MULTISAMPLING, materialshininess): res = vec4(0.0) if MULTISAMPLING: itextureuv = textureSize(colortexture) textureuv for i in range(4): pixel = texelFetch(colortexture, itextureuv, i) if SMOOTH: normal = normalize(texelFetch(normaltexture, itextureuv, i)) depth = texelFetch(depthtexture, itextureuv, i) if pixel.a > 0.0: pndc = vec4(viewport.xy + glFragCoord.xy 2.0 - 1.0, depth.r glDepthRange.diff + glDepthRange.near, 1.0) veye = projectionmatrixinv pndc veye.xyz /= veye.w if SMOOTH: res += vec4(lighting(normal, veye.xyz, pixel.rgb / pixel.a, materialshininess), 1.0) else: res += vec4(pixel.rgb / pixel.a, 1.0) else: res += vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) fragcolor = sqrt(res / 4.0) else: pixel = texture(colortexture, textureuv) if SMOOTH: normal = normalize(texture(normaltexture, textureuv)) depth = texture(depthtexture, textureuv) if pixel.a > 0.0: pndc = vec4(viewport.xy + glFragCoord.xy 2.0 - 1.0, depth.r glDepthRange.diff + glDepthRange.near, 1.0) veye = projectionmatrixinv pndc veye.xyz /= veye.w if SMOOTH: res += vec4(lighting(normal, veye.xyz, pixel.rgb / pixel.a, materialshininess), 1.0) else: res += vec4(pixel.rgb / pixel.a, 1.0) else: res += vec4(1.0, 1.0, 1.0, 1.0) fragcolor = sqrt(res) Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Normal Buffer Format: The implementation uses GLRGBA32F for the normal buffer instead of GLRGB32F because RGB doesn't work on some laptops. The Alpha channel is allocated but not used for data. Raw Points Mode: If renderingParams->rawPoints is true, the splatting pipeline is skipped. The scene is drawn directly to the screen using shaderpoints (splat.vert, points.frag) with additive blending disabled and depth test enabled, using the same vertex shader to maintain consistent screen-space point sizing. This avoids the overhead of splatting but results in hard disks without area or connectivity, causing aliasing and seeing-through artifacts. Deferred Lighting Resolve is the final shading pass in a deferred surface splatting pipeline. It reconstructs the final pixel color by applying a lighting model (ambient, diffuse, specular) to the weighted color and surface normals accumulated in the G-buffers during the splatting phase. It differs from forward rendering by decoupling the geometric projection (splatting) from the lighting calculation, allowing multiple light sources to be applied efficiently in screen space without re-projecting geometry. Point-Based Rendering (PBR) is a rendering technique that approximates continuous surfaces or dense volumetric distributions using a set of discrete points (splats) rather than explicit polygonal meshes. It solves the problem of rendering large, unstructured point clouds or implicit surfaces efficiently by rasterizing these points as disc-like primitives. Unlike its sibling Deferred Surface Splatting, which focuses on deferred shading pipelines for surface normals and depth, standard PBR often relies on opaque primitives to avoid sorting costs, though this introduces specific aliasing trade-offs. It builds on the concept of particle systems introduced by Reeves and was formalized for large point-set data by Rusinkiewicz and Levoy. The Hardware EWA Splatting Pipeline is a specialized GPU architecture designed to render Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) splats in a single pass, addressing the inefficiencies of multi-pass software implementations on standard graphics hardware. It solves the problem of accurate attribute accumulation and normalization for point-based surfaces by introducing a frame buffer-sized surface reconstruction buffer and a ternary depth test, allowing splats to be processed with maximum reuse of existing GPU units. Unlike standard triangle rasterization, which processes discrete primitives, this pipeline defers shading until after splat contributions are accumulated, enabling any fragment shading program to be used on the reconstructed surface. A rendering technique where point clouds are rendered as spheres (splats) in a multi-pass pipeline. It accumulates weighted attributes (color, normal) into a G-buffer to handle heavy overlap and reconstruct surface properties, deferring lighting to a final resolve pass. Time Complexity: The method requires three passes: Depth, Attribute Blend, and Finalization. The complexity is O(N) for the splatting passes (where N is the number of splats) and O(P) for the finalization pass (where P is the number of pixels). Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the G-Buffer (Depth, Normal, Color/Weight textures). The size is proportional to the screen resolution. Measured Performance: Not given in the sources. Scaling: Scales well with the number of lights due to the deferred shading approach. The use of an octree for Level of Detail (LoD) and CPU Frustum Culling can reduce the number of splats rendered for large point clouds. Strengths: Handles heavy overlap and transparency artifacts effectively. Decouples geometry projection from lighting, allowing for flexible lighting models. Reconstructs smooth, hole-free surfaces from sparse point clouds. Limitations: Requires multiple passes, which can be less efficient than single-pass forward rendering for simple scenes. The quality of the reconstructed surface depends on the splat size and the \varepsilon parameter. Aliasing can occur if the splat size is too small relative to the pixel size. When to use: Suitable for rendering large, unstructured point clouds where surface continuity and high-quality lighting are required. When not to use: Not given in the sources. Deferred Surface Splatting is based on the Surface Splatting technique introduced by Zwicker, Pfister, van Baar, and Gross in Surface Splatting, SIGGRAPH 2001. The multi-pass GPU pipeline was further developed by Botsch, Hornung, Zwicker, and Kobbelt in High-Quality Surface Splatting on Today's GPUs, PBG 2005. The specific implementation described in the sources is an unofficial OpenGL renderer that turns raw, unstructured point clouds into continuous, shaded surfaces using splatting combined with a deferred shading pipeline. sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, https://github.com/sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) arminkz/PointCloudRendering, https://github.com/arminkz/PointCloudRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Deferred Lighting Resolve
head: Final Pass, Lighting Pass
body: Deferred Lighting Resolve applies a lighting model to surface data accumulated during a deferred surface splatting pipeline. It reconstructs the final pixel color by combining weighted color and surface normals from G-buffers with ambient, diffuse, and specular terms. It decouples geometric projection from lighting, allowing screen-space shading without re-projecting geometry. Inputs: G-Buffer textures: gcolors: 2D texture storing weighted color sums and accumulation weight. gnormals: 2D texture storing surface normals. Uniforms/Constants: lightdirviewspc: View-space light direction vector. lightcolor: Light color vector (RGB). ambientstrength: Scalar for ambient intensity. specularstrength: Scalar for specular intensity. Outputs: Final color buffer (RGBA). Data Structures: The G-buffers are 2D textures of size W \times H (screen resolution). Internal texture formats and bit packing are not specified in the sources. Numbered Steps: 1. Sample weighted color from the color G-buffer at the current fragment's texture coordinates. 2. Discard the fragment if the accumulated weight is zero or negative to avoid division by zero or NaN results. 3. Normalize the color by dividing the weighted color RGB by the weight. 4. Sample the normal from the normal G-buffer and normalize it. 5. Normalize the light direction vector. 6. Calculate ambient lighting. 7. Calculate diffuse lighting. 8. Calculate specular lighting. 9. Combine lighting terms with the base color. 10. Output the final color to the framebuffer. Formulas: C{\text{weighted}} = \text{texture}(g\colors, uv): Weighted color and accumulated weight. C{\text{base}} = C{\text{weighted}}.rgb / C{\text{weighted}}.a: Final base color. N = \text{normalize}(\text{texture}(g\normals, uv).xyz): Surface normal. L = \text{normalize}(light\dir\view\spc): Normalized light direction. C{\text{ambient}} = \text{ambient\strength} \times \text{light\color}: Ambient term. C{\text{diffuse}} = \max(-\text{dot}(N, L), 0.0) \times \text{light\color}: Diffuse term. R = \text{reflect}(L, N): Reflection vector. S{\text{effect}} = \max(R.z, 0.0)^{32}: Specular intensity. C{\text{specular}} = \text{specular\strength} \times S{\text{effect}} \times \text{light\color}: Specular term. C{\text{final}} = (C{\text{ambient}} + C{\text{diffuse}} + C{\text{specular}}) \times C{\text{base}}: Combined result. \text{FragColor} = \text{vec4}(C{\text{final}}, 1.0): Output color. Parameters: ambientstrength: Default 0.5. specularstrength: Default 0.2. lightcolor: Default (1.0, 1.0, 1.0). shininess: Fixed at 32 in the reference implementation. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by Zero: If a pixel is not covered by any splat, the weight in gcolors is 0. Dividing by this weight results in NaN. The discard step (Step 2) prevents this. Light Direction Convention: The source code uses max(-dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) for diffuse lighting. The exact geometric interpretation of lightdirviewspc is not explicitly defined beyond being a view-space direction. View Space Assumption: The specular calculation uses the Z-component of the reflection vector, assuming a standard view space where the camera looks down the negative Z-axis. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def deferredlightingresolve(uv, gcolors, gnormals, lightdirviewspc, lightcolor, ambientstrength, specularstrength): # Step 1: Sample weighted color colorweighted = gcolors.sample(uv) # Step 2: Discard if no splat covered this pixel if colorweighted.a <= 0.0: return None # discard fragment # Step 3: Normalize color by weight color = colorweighted.rgb / colorweighted.a # Step 4: Sample and normalize normal normal = normalize(gnormals.sample(uv).xyz) # Step 5: Normalize light direction lightdir = normalize(lightdirviewspc) # Step 6: Ambient ambient = ambientstrength lightcolor # Step 7: Diffuse diffval = max(-dot(normal, lightdir), 0.0) diffuse = diffval lightcolor # Step 8: Specular reflection = reflect(lightdir, normal) speculareffect = pow(max(reflection.z, 0.0), 32.0) specular = specularstrength speculareffect lightcolor # Step 9: Combine result = (ambient + diffuse + specular) color # Step 10: Output return (result[0], result[1], result[2], 1.0) An approximation to the original Elliptical Weighted Average (EWA) filter used in the deferred shading pipeline to apply a bandlimiting prefilter. It is controlled by a boolean flag mewafilter to enable or disable the approximation. Time Complexity: O(1) per pixel for the resolve pass, as it involves a fixed number of texture samples and arithmetic operations. Memory Complexity: O(W \times H) for the G-buffers (depth, color, normal). Performance: The resolve pass is lightweight compared to the splatting pass. The reference implementation was tested on an NVIDIA GTX 1080 Ti. Strengths: Efficient handling of multiple light sources; decoupling of geometry and lighting. Limitations: Requires G-buffer storage; potential for aliasing if splatting resolution is low; dependent on the quality of the normal accumulation in the splatting pass. Deferred Lighting Resolve is part of the Surface Splatting technique, specifically the deferred shading pipeline component. It builds on the GPU accelerated surface splatting approach by Botsch et al.. The method is implemented in the open-source project sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting. arminkz/PointCloudRendering, https://github.com/arminkz/PointCloudRendering, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial) sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, https://github.com/sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Point-Based Rendering
head: Lines and points, Particle systems, Particle systems / Point-based rendering, Point Cloud Surfel Estimation, QSplat, Surfels
body: Point-Based Rendering (PBR) is a rendering technique that approximates continuous surfaces or dense volumetric distributions using a set of discrete points (splats) rather than explicit polygonal meshes. It solves the problem of rendering large, unstructured point clouds or implicit surfaces efficiently by rasterizing these points as disc-like primitives. Unlike its sibling Deferred Surface Splatting, which focuses on deferred shading pipelines for surface normals and depth, standard PBR often relies on opaque primitives to avoid sorting costs, though this introduces specific aliasing trade-offs. It builds on the concept of particle systems introduced by Reeves and was formalized for large point-set data by Rusinkiewicz and Levoy. Inputs: A set of 3D points P = \{pi\}, where each point pi includes position \mathbf{x}i, normal \mathbf{n}i, and color/weight attributes. These points are usually generated via an offline sampling process of an implicit surface or mesh. Outputs: A 2D image frame buffer. Data Structures: Point Buffer: An array of structures containing: position: 3D vector (x, y, z). normal: 3D vector (nx, ny, nz). color: 3D vector (r, g, b) or scalar weight. radius: Scalar defining the splat size. Steps: 1. Sampling (Offline): Sample the target geometry (implicit surface or mesh) into a dense point cloud. Adaptive sampling may be used, guided by curvature or energy redistribution to ensure point density correlates with surface detail. 2. Projection: Transform each point from world space to clip space using the view and projection matrices. 3. Rasterization: Project each point onto the screen as a disc (splat). The radius of the disc is adapted to the distance from the camera to maintain roughly pixel-sized coverage. The screen-space radius is computed as r = \max(1, \lfloor \alpha \cdot z{clip} \rfloor), where \alpha is a scaling constant and z{clip} is the homogeneous depth. 4. Shading/Blending: Shade the splats. To avoid the cost of sorting transparent splats, primitives are often rendered as opaque. If blending is required, ray-casting techniques may be employed to blend between splats or compute shading based on the underlying implicit function. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def samplesurface(implicitfn, bounds, stepsize): """Offline sampling of an implicit surface into a point cloud. Sources do not specify the exact sampling algorithm; grid sampling is shown. Adaptive or curvature-guided energy redistribution can replace the uniform grid.""" points = [] xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax, zmin, zmax = bounds x = xmin while x <= xmax: y = ymin while y <= ymax: z = zmin while z <= zmax: pos = (x, y, z) val = implicitfn(pos) if abs(val) < 0.01: eps = 0.001 gx = (implicitfn((x+eps, y, z)) - implicitfn((x-eps, y, z))) / (2eps) gy = (implicitfn((x, y+eps, z)) - implicitfn((x, y-eps, z))) / (2eps) gz = (implicitfn((x, y, z+eps)) - implicitfn((x, y, z-eps))) / (2eps) normlen = math.sqrt(gxgx + gygy + gzgz) if normlen > 0: norm = (gx/normlen, gy/normlen, gz/normlen) else: norm = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) points.append({'pos': pos, 'normal': norm, 'color': (0.5, 0.5, 0.5)}) z += stepsize y += stepsize x += stepsize return points def renderpoints(points, viewprojmatrix, width, height): """Project and rasterize points as disc splats.""" framebuffer = [[(0.0, 0.0, 0.0, 1.0) for in range(width)] for in range(height)] depthbuffer = [[float('inf') for in range(width)] for in range(height)] for pt in points: clippos = transformclip(pt['pos'], viewprojmatrix) if clippos[3] <= 0.0: continue ndcx = clippos[0] / clippos[3] ndcy = clippos[1] / clippos[3] ndcz = clippos[2] / clippos[3] sx = int((ndcx + 1.0) width / 2.0) sy = int((1.0 - ndcy) height / 2.0) # Adaptive radius: roughly pixel-sized based on depth radius = max(1, int(2.0 clippos[3])) xmin = max(0, sx - radius) xmax = min(width, sx + radius) ymin = max(0, sy - radius) ymax = min(height, sy + radius) for y in range(ymin, ymax): for x in range(xmin, xmax): dx = x - sx dy = y - sy if dxdx + dydy <= radiusradius: if ndcz < depthbuffer[y][x]: depthbuffer[y][x] = ndcz framebuffer[y][x] = pt['color'] + (1.0,) return framebuffer def transformclip(pos, matrix): """Standard 4x4 matrix-vector multiplication for clip space transform.""" x, y, z = pos w = matrix[3]x + matrix[7]y + matrix[11]z + matrix[15] xclip = matrix[0]x + matrix[4]y + matrix[8]z + matrix[12] yclip = matrix[1]x + matrix[5]y + matrix[9]z + matrix[13] zclip = matrix[2]x + matrix[6]y + matrix[10]z + matrix[14] return (xclip, yclip, zclip, w) Parameters: Sampling Density: Determines the number of points, directly impacting vertex transform costs. Splat Radius: Controls the visual size of points, typically adapted to distance to maintain roughly pixel-sized coverage. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping: Distance adaptation is often implemented by suppressing (culling) points, which can cause visual "popping" artifacts as points appear or disappear. Performance Bottleneck: Vertex transform costs are significant, limiting performance for huge sparse geometry. Antialiasing: Primitives are generally made opaque to avoid sorting and blending costs, which prevents proper antialiasing. Iso-splatting is a point-based alternative to isosurface visualization that generates point samples per cell instead of triangles, projecting them onto the isosurface using function values and gradients. It splits extraction into two independent steps: generating point samples throughout the volumetric domain, and projecting these points onto the isosurface of interest, followed by rendering using a surface splatting algorithm. Unlike standard polygon-based methods where geometry is discarded and recomputed for each new isovalue, iso-splatting uses point geometry that can represent a range of isosurfaces, requiring only small adjustments for slightly different isovalue, thereby decreasing computation time and storage. It builds on Point-Based Rendering by utilizing surface splatting kernels to render the projected points. A point-based algorithm that does not compute an explicit mesh representation but uses a very dense set of particles advected at interactive speeds, combined with point-based rendering. It advects a very dense set of particles at interactive speeds and renders the particles using point-based rendering techniques. Presented by Schafhitzel et al. using a GPU-based approach. Time Complexity: Dominated by vertex transformation and rasterization. Performance is limited by the vertex transform rate, which is significantly slower than fill rate on many GPUs. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of points N. Measured Performance: At 60Hz and 1280x1024 resolution, textured polygons allow redrawing each pixel ~20 times, whereas points allow only once due to the vertex transform bottleneck. Strengths: Efficient for rendering large, unstructured point clouds; avoids the overhead of mesh generation and sorting for transparent objects; suitable for implicit surfaces. Limitations: Poor antialiasing if opaque; popping artifacts from distance-based culling; expensive offline sampling process. When to Use: Rendering dense point clouds, vegetation (forests), or implicit surfaces where mesh generation is prohibitive. When Not to Use: When high-quality antialiasing is required without sorting, or when the geometry is sparse and occlusion culling is critical. Point-based rendering was conceived by Levoy and Whitted. It was proven for large point-set data by Rusinkiewicz and Levoy with their QSplat software. The concept of procedurally drawing simple primitives (particle systems) was introduced by Reeves in 1983. The method was further developed for real-time rendering of vegetation and dense scenes by researchers such as Pfister et al. [PZvBG00] and others.
