name: Particle Sprite Rendering
head: Billboard Rendering, Particle System Renderer, Point Sprite Rendering, particle system
body: Particle Sprite Rendering displays 3D data points as members of a particle system without surface fitting or interpolation, using animation for depth cues. It differs from surface rendering by not mapping data points onto a surface, avoiding surface fitting overhead and interpolation bias. Inputs and Outputs Input: Radar Cross Section (RCS) data points (phi, theta, rad, strength, polarity). Output: A sequence of frames (images) stored in Utah Raster Toolkit (RLE) format. Data Structures Particle List: A dynamic linked list storing particles and their respective centroid. Centroid: Defined by user-specified origin in world coordinates and shape (e.g., spherical). View Volume: Defined by Viewer Position (PRP), Camera Looking Direction (CW), View Plane Normal (VPN), and View Up Vector (VUP). Numbered Steps 1. Initialization: All particles start at the same time. The starting position is determined by the centroid shape and coordinate system (spherical or cartesian). For RCS data, particles start at a sphere around the centroid with radius zero. 2. Time Step Loop: 1. Check for Spawning: Iterate through the particle list for new particles. If spawning, generate the new system and add to the linked list. 2. Check for Death: If a particle is dead, mark it and ignore it in subsequent steps. 3. Move Particle: Update particle position based on velocity. Velocity is determined by the strength of the RCS return. 4. Render Particles: Render the current state of the particle system. 5. Increment Time Step: Advance the simulation time. Formulas Particle Position: Derived from RCS data phi and theta, with radial distance starting at zero. Particle Alpha: \alpha = \text{clamp}(1.0 - \text{distanceFromCenter} \times 2.0, 0.0, 1.0) \times uParticleAlpha Where distanceFromCenter is the distance from the center of the point sprite. Particle Color (Modulated by Shadow Opacity): \text{color} = (1.0 - vOpacity \times 0.75) \times uParticleColor Where vOpacity is the shadow opacity and uParticleColor is the base color. Output Premultiplied Alpha Color: \text{FragColor} = \text{vec4}(\text{color} \times \alpha, \alpha) Parameters Centroid Shape: Spherical (chosen for RCS to represent the center of a spherical coordinate system). Coordinate System: Spherical or Cartesian. Clipping: World limits including front and back. Memory Requirement: At least 16 megabytes. Filtering (Polarity Specific): W Polarity: Low pass filter at 20 dBsm, High pass filter at 65 dBsm. Particle color: Red. HH Polarity: High pass and low pass filter limits set to 0. Particle color: Blue. HV and VH Polarity: High pass and low pass filter limits set to 0. Particle color: Green. Multi-Polarity: Low pass filter set to 0, High pass filter set to 70. Pseudocode Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. class Particle: position: Vector3 velocity: float color: Color isdead: bool spawntime: float lifetime: float class ParticleSystem: particles: List[Particle] centroid: Centroid timestep: float currenttime: float def renderparticlesystem(system: ParticleSystem, viewparams: ViewParams): """ Renders the particle system for a single frame. """ system.currenttime += system.timestep # 1. Check for spawning newparticles = generatenewparticles(system.centroid, system.currenttime) for p in newparticles: system.particles.append(p) # 2. Check for death and move aliveparticles = [] for p in system.particles: if p.isdead: continue # Check if particle has exceeded lifetime if system.currenttime - p.spawntime > p.lifetime: p.isdead = True continue # Move particle # Velocity is determined by strength of RCS return p.position += p.velocity system.timestep aliveparticles.append(p) system.particles = aliveparticles # 3. Render particles # Use Z-Buffer and Wu antialiased lines for rendering for p in aliveparticles: renderparticle(p, viewparams) def renderparticle(p: Particle, viewparams: ViewParams): """ Renders a single particle as a sprite. """ # Project particle to screen space screenpos = project(p.position, viewparams) # Determine size based on perspective (handled by vertex shader in modern pipelines) # or fixed size for legacy Wu line rendering size = calculatespritesize(p.position, viewparams) # Draw sprite # Legacy: Wu antialiased lines drawn by incrementing one pixel at a time # along the major axis. For each increment, two pixels are drawn bracketing the axis. # Intensity determined by distance from actual line. drawwulinesprite(screenpos, size, p.color) # Modern Fragment Shader approach (if using point sprites): # if (distanceFromCenter > 0.5) discard # alpha = clamp(1.0 - distanceFromCenter 2.0, 0.0, 1.0) uParticleAlpha # color = (1.0 - vOpacity 0.75) uParticleColor # FragColor = vec4(color alpha, alpha) def generatenewparticles(centroid: Centroid, time: float) -> List[Particle]: """ Generates new particles based on centroid and time. All particles start at the same time. """ # For RCS data, particles start at a sphere around the centroid with radius zero # Coordinates derived from phi and theta of RCS data particles = [] for datapoint in centroid.data: p = Particle() p.position = sphericaltocartesian(datapoint.phi, datapoint.theta, 0.0, centroid.origin) p.velocity = datapoint.strength # Velocity determined by strength p.color = getcolorbypolarity(datapoint.polarity) p.spawntime = time p.lifetime = calculatelifetime(datapoint.strength) p.isdead = False particles.append(p) return particles def getcolorbypolarity(polarity: str) -> Color: if polarity == 'W': return Color(1.0, 0.0, 0.0) # Red elif polarity == 'HH': return Color(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) # Blue elif polarity in ['HV', 'VH']: return Color(0.0, 1.0, 0.0) # Green else: return Color(1.0, 1.0, 1.0) # Default White Edge Cases and Pitfalls Random Placement: Random particle placement is not used for RCS data because data is mapped to specific locations. Static Images: Static images lack sufficient cues for the volumetric nature of the data. This is addressed by animating the development over time and allowing view rotation while growing. Resolution Loss: Significant loss of resolution occurs when transferring images to tape and displaying on NTSC monitors, causing blurring. Lack of standard aspect ratios in NTSC monitors alters the look of data, potentially hiding areas or falsely indicating large returns. Time Complexity: Not explicitly defined in sources. Rendering time was approximately 95 seconds per frame for the final data set. Memory Complexity: At least 16 megabytes of memory required. Measured Performance: Rendering a final data set required 10 minutes to load data files. The final video tape lasted 3 minutes, took 1900 separate images, and required 6 hours to record. Strengths: Minimal filtering and data manipulation; no surface fitting overhead; no interpolation bias; animation provides additional 3D cues. Limitations: Not designed for interactive display; significant resolution loss on NTSC monitors; aspect ratio sensitivity. When to Use: When displaying robust, vectorized data sets (like RCS) where volumetric nature needs to be conveyed through animation and minimal data manipulation is desired. When Not to Use: When interactive display is required; when high resolution on standard monitors is critical without post-processing. Origin: Based on the description by Reeves [Ree 83]. History: The code was written in AT&T C++ version 2.1. The system was designed with portability and flexibility as primary considerations. It was used for viewing Radar Cross Section (RCS) data in three dimensions. Usage: Used for generating frame-by-frame depictions of environments for video recording and playback, providing additional 3D cues for data analysis. name: Footprint Evaluation
head: Footprint Mapping, Westover 1990, Westover Splatting, Splatting (Westover), Westover's Splatting, Westover's Footprint Evaluation
body: Footprint Evaluation is an object-order direct volume rendering algorithm that projects each voxel from the volume grid onto the 2D image plane as a "splat" (footprint) and accumulates these contributions to form the final image. It solves the problem of efficiently rendering volumetric data by distributing each sample's energy across a region on the screen using a pre-integrated reconstruction kernel, rather than casting rays per pixel. It sets itself apart from its siblings and nearest alternatives by using a forward-mapping scheme where the footprint is the integral of the 3D kernel along the view ray, allowing for pre-computation and fast rasterization, whereas Perspective-Correct Point Splatting Vertex Shader and Centralized Conics Approach focus on geometric projection accuracy, and Exact Half-Space Clipping focuses on boundary handling. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volume grid of voxels with values f(vk), a viewing direction (orthographic or perspective), a reconstruction kernel w, and a compositing order (front-to-back or back-to-front). Output: A 2D image where each pixel contains the accumulated color and opacity from all overlapping splats. Data Structures: 1. Volume Grid: Array of voxels. Each voxel has a position (i,j,k) and a value f(vk) (density/color). 2. Footprint Table: A 2D lookup table storing the pre-integrated values of the reconstruction kernel. It represents the integration of the 3D spherically symmetric kernel along one axis (typically the view ray). Layout: A 2D array of floating-point values. The center of the table corresponds to the projected voxel center. The size of the table determines the support of the footprint. Generic vs. View-Transformed: For orthographic projection with uniform grid spacing and symmetric kernels, a single generic footprint table is used for all voxels. For perspective projection or non-uniform spacing, a view-transformed table is computed per view (or per voxel) to account for elliptical distortion. 3. Compositing Buffer: The final image buffer storing accumulated color and opacity. 4. Sheet Buffer (Optional): In the sheet-buffer method, splats are accumulated in intermediate buffers aligned with the volume face most parallel to the image plane before being composited into the final buffer. Numbered Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Footprint Table Generation): Select a 3D reconstruction kernel w(x,y,z), typically a Gaussian. Compute the 2D footprint function F(x,y) by integrating the 3D kernel along the view ray (z-axis): F(x,y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} w(x,y,z) \, dz Sample F(x,y) on a 2D grid to create the Footprint Table. The resolution of this table should be high enough to avoid aliasing but low enough to fit in memory. For perspective projection, compute the orientation and scale of the elliptical footprint for the current view. 2. Voxel Traversal and Projection: Determine the traversal order of voxels. This is typically done by sorting voxels based on their depth along the view ray. Common strategies include: Back-to-front: Guarantees correct visibility but is slower. Front-to-back: Faster because compositing can stop when pixels are fully opaque. Sheet-based: Group voxels into slabs parallel to the image plane to optimize cache usage and compositing. For each voxel vk at position (xk, yk, zk) with value f(vk): Project the voxel center to the image plane coordinates (xs, ys) using the view and projection matrices. Determine the screen-space extent of the footprint. For orthographic projection, this is a circle (if the kernel is isotropic). For perspective projection, it is an ellipse. If using a view-transformed table, map the elliptical extent to the generic circular table extent using a transformation T^{-1}. 3. Rasterization (Splatting): Identify all pixels (x,y) that lie within the footprint's extent. For each pixel in the extent: Calculate the displacement (dx, dy) = (x - xs, y - ys) from the projected voxel center. Look up the weight w(x,y)s from the Footprint Table. If the footprint is elliptical, interpolate from the view-transformed table or map the coordinates to the generic table. Compute the contribution: C = f(vk) \times w(x,y)s. Composite this contribution into the Compositing Buffer (and/or Sheet Buffer) using the chosen compositing operator (e.g., front-to-back alpha blending). 4. Final Compositing (if using Sheet Buffer): If the sheet-buffer method is used, composite the accumulated sheet buffers into the final Compositing Buffer in front-to-back order. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def footprintevaluation(volume, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, kernelwidth, footprinttablesize): """ Renders a volume using Footprint Evaluation (Splatting). Args: volume: 3D array of voxel values. viewmatrix: 4x4 view matrix. projectionmatrix: 4x4 projection matrix. kernelwidth: Radius of the reconstruction kernel. footprinttablesize: Size of the 2D footprint lookup table. Returns: image: 2D array of pixel colors. """ # 1. Preprocessing: Generate Footprint Table # Assume a 3D Gaussian kernel w(x,y,z) = exp(-(x^2+y^2+z^2)/sigma^2) # Integrate along z to get 2D footprint F(x,y) footprinttable = generatefootprinttable(kernelwidth, footprinttablesize) # Initialize Compositing Buffer (Color and Opacity) # Using front-to-back compositing: Cout = Cin + Csplat (1 - Ain) # Aout = Ain + Asplat (1 - Ain) # For simplicity, assume alpha compositing is handled by the hardware or a specific function compositingbuffer = initializebuffer(volume.shape[0], volume.shape[1]) # 2. Determine Traversal Order # Sort voxels by depth along the view ray voxels = getvoxels(volume) sortedvoxels = sortbydepth(voxels, viewmatrix) # 3. Project and Splat for voxel in sortedvoxels: # Project voxel center to screen space screenpos = project(voxel.position, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix) xs, ys = screenpos.x, screenpos.y # Determine footprint extent in screen space # For orthographic, extent is circular. For perspective, it's elliptical. # Here we assume a simplified circular extent for the generic table extentradius = getfootprintradius(voxel, projectionmatrix) # Iterate over pixels in the footprint extent for dy in range(-extentradius, extentradius + 1): for dx in range(-extentradius, extentradius + 1): x = int(xs + dx) y = int(ys + dy) # Check if pixel is within image bounds if not isinbounds(x, y, compositingbuffer): continue # Calculate weight from footprint table # Normalize dx, dy to table coordinates tablex = normalize(dx, extentradius, footprinttablesize) tabley = normalize(dy, extentradius, footprinttablesize) weight = lookupfootprint(footprinttable, tablex, tabley) # Compute contribution contribution = voxel.value weight # Composite into buffer compositepixel(compositingbuffer, x, y, contribution) return compositingbuffer def generatefootprinttable(kernelwidth, tablesize): """ Generates a 2D footprint table by integrating a 3D Gaussian kernel along the z-axis. """ table = zeros(tablesize, tablesize) sigma = kernelwidth / 2.0 # Approximate sigma for Gaussian center = tablesize // 2 for i in range(tablesize): for j in range(tablesize): x = (i - center) / tablesize y = (j - center) / tablesize # Integrate 3D Gaussian along z: integral of exp(-(x^2+y^2+z^2)/sigma^2) dz # This results in a 2D Gaussian: exp(-(x^2+y^2)/sigma^2) sqrt(pi)sigma # For simplicity, we store the normalized 2D Gaussian profile value = exp(-(x2 + y2) / (2 sigma2)) table[i][j] = value return table def compositepixel(buffer, x, y, contribution): """ Adds the contribution to the pixel in the buffer. Assumes simple additive accumulation for density/color. For proper alpha compositing, use front-to-back or back-to-front formulas. """ buffer[x][y] += contribution Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Aliasing: Standard splatting suffers from aliasing when the volume sampling rate is higher than the image sampling rate (e.g., high-resolution volumes or perspective views). This is caused by the discrete evaluation of the splatting equation. Solutions include Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment [1288-antialiased-splatting-with-footprint-alignment.md] or EWA filters. Overlapping Splats: When splats overlap, the compositing order affects the result. Front-to-back compositing is faster but may produce incorrect results if the traversal order is not perfectly sorted. Back-to-front guarantees correctness but is slower. Perspective Projection: The footprint becomes elliptical, requiring additional computation for orientation and scaling. Sheet Buffer Popping: In the sheet-buffer method, sudden changes in the orientation of the compositing sheets can cause popping artifacts. Kernel Size: Large footprints increase blurring; small footprints generate gaps. The footprint size must be tuned for the pixel-to-voxel ratio. Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment is a forward-mapping volume rendering technique that prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views by dynamically scaling splat sizes and attenuating splat energy for voxels beyond a critical distance. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by varying the kernel size and energy as a function of depth to match the diverging integration grid rays, ensuring the integration grid sampling frequency remains above twice the maximum volume raster frequency. The Separable Footprint (SF) projector is a forward mapping algorithm for X-ray Computed Tomography (XCT) that calculates line integrals through a voxelized volume by explicitly modeling the finite width of both detector pixels and volume voxels. Unlike Siddon or Joseph methods, which treat voxels and pixels as infinitesimal lines, SF provides higher quantitative accuracy and avoids specific artifacts, at the cost of increased computational complexity. The Footprint Function Mechanism implements 3D spherically symmetric splatting kernels in volume rendering by reducing computational dimensionality from 3D to 2D. It projects volumetric data onto a 2D image plane by pre-computing the integration of the 3D kernel along one axis and storing the result as a 2D lookup table. This approach avoids per-pixel 3D kernel evaluations by relying on 2D table lookups and interpolation, as detailed in Footprint Evaluation. Time Complexity: O(k^2 n^3), where n^3 is the number of voxels and k is the kernel size (footprint radius). This is faster than ray-casting's O(k^3 n^3) because the convolution is precomputed and each voxel is splatted exactly once. Memory Complexity: Depends on the footprint table size and the number of voxels. The footprint table is small (2D), but the volume data is large (3D). Measured Performance: Splatting is inherently faster than ray-casting for moderate screen sizes and specific datasets, but good quality results may require as much CPU time as ray-casting. It is efficient for real-time rendering on older hardware due to its simplicity and parallelizability. Strengths: Fast due to pre-integrated kernels and object-order processing. Simple static parallel decomposition. Easy to implement and parallelize. Supports scattered data (e.g., SPH) with sorting. Limitations: Poor quality without anti-aliasing techniques (aliasing artifacts). Blurry images for zoomed views due to Gaussian kernel properties. High fill-rate for zoomed splats. Incorrect compositing when splats overlap, especially with changing traversal orders. Not well-suited for perspective projection without additional transformations. When to Use: Real-time volume rendering where speed is prioritized over perfect accuracy, or for orthographic projections of moderate-resolution volumes. When Not to Use: High-quality offline rendering, perspective views with high dynamic range, or when strict anti-aliasing is required without additional techniques. Footprint Evaluation, also known as Westover Splatting, was first described by L. Westover in 1990 in the paper "Footprint evaluation for volume rendering". It was introduced as a forward mapping algorithm for rendering regular grids on a CPU. The method was developed to address the computational cost of ray-casting by pre-computing the integration of the reconstruction kernel. It has since been extended to support perspective projection, anti-aliasing, and hardware acceleration. name: Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment
head: Antialiased splatting method, Perspective Anti-Aliased Splatting
body: Antialiased Splatting with Footprint Alignment is a forward-mapping volume rendering technique that prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views by dynamically scaling splat sizes and attenuating splat energy for voxels beyond a critical distance. It sets itself apart from standard splatting by varying the kernel size and energy as a function of depth to match the diverging integration grid rays, ensuring the integration grid sampling frequency remains above twice the maximum volume raster frequency. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A volume dataset (typically stored as a subset of extracted voxels), camera parameters (eye position, view plane distance z{img}, pixel extent p, viewing frustum half-angle \phic), and a transfer function. Output: A 2D image with anti-aliased volume rendering. Data Structures: The volume subset is stored as a 2D array of splat rows. Each row is an array of voxels. Each voxel stores its location (x, y, z) in eye space, a normal vector, and a pre-computed transfer function value (e.g., color, opacity). Voxels in a row are not necessarily contiguous. The splat kernel is pre-computed and stored in a 256 \times 256 table, which is texture-mapped onto the polygon representing the splat. Critical Distance (zk or k): The distance zk along the z-axis where the volume raster sampling frequency p equals the integration grid sampling frequency \phi(z) divides eye space into two regions: Region 1 (z < zk): No aliasing; standard splatting is sufficient. Region 2 (z > zk): Aliasing possible; low-pass filtering (scaling/attenuation) is required. The critical distance is calculated from similar triangles: zk = \frac{p \cdot z{img}}{p - 1} where p is the extent of a pixel and z{img} is the distance from the eye point to the view plane. Note: uses k for this distance. Algorithm Steps: 1. Traverse the volume: Iterate through the voxels in back-to-front or front-to-back order. 2. Determine Distance: For each voxel, compute its distance zv (or d) from the eye point along the viewing axis. 3. Check Region: If zv < zk (or d < k): Draw the splat with its standard size in eye space. The polygon can be aligned parallel to the x-y plane or perpendicular to the ray. If zv \ge zk (or d \ge k): Scale Radius: Scale the splat footprint radius to match the diverging rays. Using similar triangles: r2 = r1 \cdot \frac{zv}{zk} where r1 is the radius at zk and r2 is the radius at zv. expresses this as r2 = (k/d) \cdot r1 where r1 is the radius at distance k (this implies r1 in S1 is the scaled radius at k, effectively the base unit for scaling beyond k). The geometric intent is identical: radius grows linearly with distance beyond zk. Attenuate Energy: Attenuate the splat's energy (e.g., alpha channel) to preserve total projected energy and avoid brightness artifacts. The total attenuation factor is (zk / zv)^2. states E2 = (k^2 / d^2) \cdot E1. explicitly states: "We attenuate the alpha channel of the polygon according to the value of (zk/zv)". This implies the alpha is scaled by the square root of the energy attenuation factor, or that the energy attenuation is defined differently in their compositing model. Footprint Alignment: Rotate the splat polygon so it is perpendicular to the ray passing from the eye point through the voxel position. Two alignment strategies exist: 1. Grid-aligned: Align stretched footprint with the y-axis of the grid. 2. Ray-perpendicular: Rotate stretched footprint to be perpendicular to the ray. Ray-perpendicular is more accurate near zk, while grid-aligned is better far from zk. 4. Render: Texture map the pre-computed kernel onto the polygon and composite into the screen buffer. Voxel Interpolation (Tri-Linear): For trilinear interpolation, the value is distributed to 8 surrounding voxels: 1. Offset voxel-space position by -0.5 to align with voxel centers: p = (x-0.5, y-0.5, z-0.5). 2. Find lower-left corner: corner = (\lfloor px \rfloor, \lfloor py \rfloor, \lfloor pz \rfloor). 3. Calculate fraction vector: f = (1.0, 1.0, 1.0) - (\lfloor p \rfloor + 1 - p). 4. Loop over i, j, k \in \{0, 1\}: Invert fraction component for each axis at start of loop. Weight w = fx \cdot fy \cdot fz. Add value \cdot w to voxel at corner + (i, j, k) if in bounds. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def renderantialiasedsplats(volumesubset, camera, kerneltable): """ volumesubset: List of rows, each row is a list of Voxel objects. camera: Object with eyepos, zimg, pixelextent p, frustumangle phic. kerneltable: 256x256 texture map of the splat kernel. """ # Calculate critical distance zk zk = (camera.p camera.zimg) / (camera.p - 1) for row in volumesubset: for voxel in row: # 1. Calculate distance from eye zv = voxel.pos.z # 2. Alignment Errors: Footprint polygon not aligned perpendicularly with the sight ray causes errors in projected polygon extent, largest at the viewing frustum boundary. Sight rays from pixels other than the center traverse the footprint at an oblique angle. There is no known efficient solution outside of ray-driven splatting. Pre-integration: Pre-integrating a distorted kernel for one z-location and scaling it for another does not yield the correct footprint because relative kernel distortion varies with z. Grid Alignment: Aligning footprints with the grid causes indexed ray integrals to differ significantly from true ray integrals for rays maintaining a large angle with the viewing axis. Time Complexity: O(N) where N is the number of voxels in the subset. Per-voxel cost involves distance calculation, scaling factor computation, and polygon setup/compositing. Memory Complexity: Depends on the volume subset size. Storing a 2D array of splat rows with non-contiguous voxels requires storing location and normal for each voxel. Kernel table is 256 \times 256. Performance: Achieved real-time performance on Silicon Graphics hardware for datasets like 512 \times 512 \times 103 (386K splats). Strengths: Prevents sample-rate aliasing in perspective views. Efficient compared to ray-driven splatting or computing unique footprints for every voxel with diverging rays. Can be implemented using standard rendering hardware (texture-mapped polygons). Limitations: Approximation errors in footprint alignment and projection. Grid-aligned alignment is less accurate for rays at large angles. Ray-perpendicular alignment is more accurate but requires rotation per voxel. Does not address aliasing from non-ideal reconstruction filters, only sample-rate aliasing. When to Use: Perspective volume rendering where aliasing artifacts are visible due to diverging rays or high volume resolution relative to image resolution. When Not to Use: Orthographic views with low resolution (aliasing is uniform and less severe, or handled by standard filtering). Origin: The method was introduced in the late 1990s. references "Perspective Splatting" (DTIC ADA363073) and "Splatting Errors and Antialiasing" (DTIC ADA606764, IEEE TVCG 1998). Development: Standard splatting (Westover) was designed for orthographic views. Perspective splatting introduced aliasing issues due to non-uniform sampling. This method extends splatting to perspective by scaling kernels and attenuating energy. Usage: Used in the "Tenderer" implementation on Silicon Graphics hardware. Applied to terrain datasets from satellite photographs and microtubule studies from confocal microscopy. name: Separable Footprint (SF) Projector
head: SF method, Separable Footprint (SF) Method
body: The Separable Footprint (SF) projector is a forward mapping algorithm for X-ray Computed Tomography (XCT) that calculates line integrals through a voxelized volume by explicitly modeling the finite width of both detector pixels and volume voxels. Unlike Siddon or Joseph methods, which treat voxels and pixels as infinitesimal lines, SF provides higher quantitative accuracy and avoids specific artifacts, at the cost of increased computational complexity. The SF method computes the projection of a 3D volume onto a 2D detector plane. It is characterized by its separability, allowing the 3D integration to be decomposed into independent 1D operations along the grid axes, which ensures that numerical values scale appropriately with changes in voxel or detector sizes. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D volumetric grid V with dimensions (Nx, Ny, Nz) and voxel spacings (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z). A set of ray paths defined by source and detector positions/orientations. Output: A 2D projection image P representing the line integrals (attenuation) measured by the detector pixels. Data Structures: The volume is stored as a regular grid. Detector geometry is defined by pixel dimensions (\Delta u, \Delta v) and the transformation from world space to detector space. Algorithm Steps: 1. Ray Tracing: For each detector pixel, determine the corresponding ray path through the volume. This involves calculating the intersection of the ray with the volume bounding box. 2. Footprint Calculation: For each voxel intersected by the ray, calculate the "footprint" or overlap volume between the voxel and the effective detector pixel area projected back into the volume space. The SF method assumes the detector response and voxel shape are separable along the principal axes. 3. Weight Computation: Compute the weight w{ijk} for each voxel (i,j,k) based on the geometric overlap. The separability implies that the 3D overlap integral can be computed as the product of 1D integrals along the x, y, and z axes. 4. Accumulation: Accumulate the weighted voxel values into the detector pixel: P = \sum{i,j,k} w{ijk} V{ijk} where V{ijk} is the value of the voxel at (i,j,k). Parameters: Voxel sizes (\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z): Must be provided for accurate scaling. Detector pixel sizes (\Delta u, \Delta v): Must be provided for accurate scaling. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The method is quantitatively accurate, but requires careful handling of floating-point precision when calculating small overlaps. Boundaries: Rays grazing the volume boundary must be handled to avoid missing contributions or double-counting. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def forwardproject(volume, voxelspacing, detectorgeometry): """ Performs forward projection using the Separable Footprint method. Args: volume: 3D array of voxel values. voxelspacing: Tuple (dx, dy, dz) of voxel dimensions. detectorgeometry: Object containing source positions, detector positions, and detector pixel dimensions (du, dv). Returns: projection: 2D array of projected values. """ # Initialize output projection buffer projection = zeros(detectorgeometry.shape) # Iterate over each detector pixel for u, v in detectorgeometry.pixels: # Determine ray direction and origin for this pixel rayorigin, raydirection = detectorgeometry.getray(u, v) # Calculate intersection with volume bounding box tmin, tmax = intersectbox(rayorigin, raydirection, volume.bounds) if tmax <= tmin: continue # Calculate the footprint weights for intersected voxels # The SF method separates the 3D integration into 1D components # along the grid axes. weights = computeseparablefootprintweights( rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, voxelspacing, detectorgeometry.pixelsize) # Accumulate weighted voxel values for voxelindex, weight in weights.items(): projection[u, v] += volume[voxelindex] weight return projection def computeseparablefootprintweights(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, voxelspacing, detectorpixelsize): """ Computes the separable footprint weights for a ray passing through the volume. This function calculates the overlap integral assuming separability along axes. """ # Implementation detail: Calculate the intersection intervals along x, y, z axes # for the ray segment within the volume. # Then, convolve these intervals with the detector pixel response function # projected into the volume space. # The weight for a voxel is the product of the 1D overlaps along each axis. # Note: Exact formula depends on the specific separable kernel used (e.g., box, triangle). # Standard SF uses a box kernel for both voxel and detector. weights = {} # Iterate over voxels intersected by the ray # This requires efficient traversal (e.g., 3D DDA) voxels = traversevoxels(rayorigin, raydirection, tmin, tmax, voxelspacing) for voxel in voxels: # Calculate 1D overlap along x, y, z overlapx = calculate1doverlap(rayorigin.x, raydirection.x, voxel.xmin, voxel.xmax, detectorpixelsize.x) overlapy = calculate1doverlap(rayorigin.y, raydirection.y, voxel.ymin, voxel.ymax, detectorpixelsize.y) overlapz = calculate1doverlap(rayorigin.z, raydirection.z, voxel.zmin, voxel.zmax, detectorpixelsize.z) # Weight is the product of overlaps normalized by voxel volume weight = (overlapx overlapy overlapz) / (voxelspacing.x voxelspacing.y voxelspacing.z) weights[voxel.index] = weight return weights Accuracy: Quantitatively accurate; numerical values scale appropriately with changes in voxel and detector sizes. More accurate than Siddon or Joseph methods, which do not model finite widths. Computational Cost: More computationally expensive than Siddon or Joseph methods due to the complexity of calculating finite footprints. Artifacts: Avoids artifacts produced by Siddon/Joseph methods in cases where finite width effects are significant. Implementation: Implemented in CPU (C/C++) and GPU (CUDA) environments. The SF method was introduced by Long et al. in 2010 as one of the most popular and effective models for calculating XCT line integrals through a voxelized volume. It is part of a class of methods (along with Distance Driven) that explicitly model the finite width of detector pixels and volume voxels, contrasting with earlier methods like Siddon (1985) and Joseph (1982). It is used in software packages such as LEAP for both forward and back projections, particularly in optimization-based reconstruction algorithms that require the adjoint (transpose) of the X-ray Transform. name: Footprint Function Mechanism
head: 2D reconstruction kernel, Footprint Function, Splatting Dimension Reduction (Footprint), footprint table
body: The Footprint Function Mechanism implements 3D spherically symmetric splatting kernels in volume rendering by reducing computational dimensionality from 3D to 2D. It projects volumetric data onto a 2D image plane by pre-computing the integration of the 3D kernel along one axis and storing the result as a 2D lookup table. This approach avoids per-pixel 3D kernel evaluations by relying on 2D table lookups and interpolation, as detailed in Footprint Evaluation. Inputs: A 3D spherically symmetric splat kernel function h(x, y, z). A regular volumetric grid with spacing parameters. Camera projection parameters (orthographic or perspective). Outputs: A 2D lookup table representing the footprint function. A rendered image where each pixel contains the accumulated contribution of all splats. Data Structures: Footprint Table: A 2D array of floating-point values. The dimensions correspond to the spatial extent of the kernel in the image plane. The table is indexed by integer offsets (i, j) from the center, representing discrete samples of the continuous function. Voxel Data: Standard volumetric grid values (density/scalar) and positions. Formulas: The footprint function F(x, y) is defined as the integral of the 3D kernel h along one dimension (typically w or z), assuming spherical symmetry: F(x, y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x, y, w) \, dw where (x, y) is the displacement from the projected sample point on the image plane. The contribution to a pixel at projected coordinates (xD, yD) with density \rho is: \text{Contribution}(x, y) = \rho \cdot F(x - xD, y - yD). Steps: 1. Pre-compute the Footprint Table: Numerically integrate h(x, y, w) along the w axis for a grid of (x, y) values covering the 2D extent, and store the results in a finely sampled 2D lookup table. If the volume grid spacing is regular, the view projection is orthographic, and the splat kernel is radially symmetric, this table is computed once and reused. Otherwise, it must be recomputed per view (for non-symmetric kernels) or per voxel (for perspective projections). 2. Project Voxels: For each voxel in the volume, calculate its projected center (xD, yD) on the image plane using the current camera projection matrix. 3. Determine Extent: Identify the bounding box of the footprint table that overlaps with the image plane region influenced by the voxel. 4. Sample and Composite: For each pixel (xp, yp) within the footprint's extent: calculate the displacement vector (dx, dy) = (xp - xD, yp - yD); map (dx, dy) to the indices of the pre-computed 2D footprint table; interpolate the value from the footprint table; retrieve the voxel's density \rho; compute the weighted contribution \rho \cdot \text{interpolated\footprint}(dx, dy); composite this value into the pixel's existing buffer. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def precomputefootprint(kernelfunc, extent, resolution): """Pre-compute 2D footprint table by integrating 3D kernel along w-axis.""" tablesize = 2 resolution + 1 footprinttable = [[0.0] tablesize for in range(tablesize)] center = resolution dw = 2 extent / resolution for i in range(tablesize): for j in range(tablesize): x = (i - center) (extent / resolution) y = (j - center) (extent / resolution) integral = 0.0 for k in range(resolution): w = -extent + (k + 0.5) dw integral += kernelfunc(x, y, w) dw footprinttable[i][j] = integral return footprinttable, extent, resolution def bilinearinterpolate(table, idxx, idxy, resolution): """Bilinear interpolation for the footprint table.""" tablesize = 2 resolution + 1 fx = idxx - int(idxx) fy = idxy - int(idxy) ix = int(idxx) iy = int(idxy) x0, x1 = max(0, ix), min(tablesize - 1, ix + 1) y0, y1 = max(0, iy), min(tablesize - 1, iy + 1) val = (table[y0][x0] (1 - fx) (1 - fy) + table[y0][x1] fx (1 - fy) + table[y1][x0] (1 - fx) fy + table[y1][x1] fx fy) return val def renderwithfootprint(volumedata, footprinttable, extent, resolution, imagewidth, imageheight): """Render volume using pre-computed footprint table.""" image = [[0.0] imagewidth for in range(imageheight)] tablesize = 2 resolution + 1 center = resolution for voxel in volumedata: # Project 3D voxel position to 2D image plane coordinates using the camera matrix px, py = voxel.position.x 1.0, voxel.position.y 1.0 minx = max(0, int(px - extent)) maxx = min(imagewidth, int(px + extent)) miny = max(0, int(py - extent)) maxy = min(imageheight, int(py + extent)) for y in range(miny, maxy): for x in range(minx, maxx): dx = x - px dy = y - py idxx = center + dx (resolution / extent) idxy = center + dy (resolution / extent) if 0 <= idxx < tablesize and 0 <= idxy < tablesize: footval = bilinearinterpolate(footprinttable, idxx, idxy, resolution) contribution = voxel.density footval image[y][x] += contribution return image Parameters: Footprint Table Resolution: Not given in the sources. Integration Steps: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Perspective Projection: The footprint shape changes with depth. The table cannot be reused across the entire volume; it must be recomputed per voxel or approximated. Non-Symmetric Kernels: If the kernel is not radially symmetric, the integration axis matters, and the table must be recomputed for each view orientation. Precision: Numerical integration errors in pre-computation can lead to bias. Interpolation errors in the 2D table can cause blurring or artifacts. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: Significant speedup over direct 3D kernel evaluation per pixel. Simple to implement with standard 2D interpolation routines. Limitations: Requires pre-computation. Less flexible for non-symmetric or anisotropic kernels without significant overhead. Perspective projections require per-voxel table generation or approximation, which can negate performance gains. When to use: Orthographic projections, regular grids, and symmetric kernels. When not to use: Perspective projections with high accuracy requirements, or non-symmetric kernels, unless the per-voxel recomputation cost is acceptable. The concept was introduced by Westover in the context of volume rendering, specifically to improve the efficiency of splatting algorithms. The original splatting algorithm considered the splat as a 3D spherically symmetric reconstruction kernel. Westover observed that since the splat is reconstructed into a 2D image raster, it can be implemented as a 2D reconstruction kernel by integrating the 3D kernel along one dimension. This technique is often referred to as "footprint function" or "2D reconstruction kernel". Later work by Westover also introduced accumulating splats onto a 2D sheet aligned with the volume axis most parallel to the view plane to further improve quality. name: Centralized Conics Approach
head: Botsch et al. Splat Extent Approximation, Botsch et al.'s approximation, Zwicker et al. Centralized Conics Approach
body: The Centralized Conics Approach is an efficient approximation method for computing the screen-space position and extents of a splat in point-based rendering. It approximates the projected Gaussian kernel's footprint by utilizing the inverse of a 2D-to-2D projective mapping from the splat's parameter space to screen space. Unlike methods that prioritize geometric exactness or robustness under extreme perspective, this approach trades precision for computational speed. Inputs and Outputs: Input: The splat's center position, the two vectors spanning its elliptical shape in local space, and the camera projection matrix. Output: The screen-space center and the approximate extents of the splat. Data Structures: The method relies on a 2D-to-2D projective mapping matrix M. Steps: 1. Construct the 2D-to-2D projective mapping matrix M that maps coordinates from the splat's local parameter space to screen space. 2. Compute the inverse of this mapping matrix, M^{-1}. 3. Apply M^{-1} to screen-space coordinates to approximate the splat's position and extents. Formulas: Let M be the projective mapping matrix. The screen-space position \mathbf{p}{screen} relates to the local parameter space position \mathbf{p}{local} by \mathbf{p}{screen} \sim M \mathbf{p}{local}. The approach computes the extents by inverting this relationship: \mathbf{p}{local} \sim M^{-1} \mathbf{p}{screen}. Parameters: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: The method is numerically unstable when the projection of the splat approaches a line. In such cases, the condition number of the mapping matrix increases rapidly, leading to large roundoff errors during inversion. This instability can cause the screen-space extents to be underestimated, resulting in rendering artifacts. A rasterization technique that uses the inverse of a projective mapping matrix to transform screen coordinates back to object space for kernel evaluation, while simultaneously computing window-space depth values via linear interpolation of homogeneous coordinates. It sets itself apart from standard perspective splatting by avoiding explicit matrix inversion through the use of adjoint matrices and optimizing depth computation by embedding the window-space depth formula directly into the homogeneous interpolation weights. This method computes perspective-correct splat shapes for point-based rendering by approximating the projective mapping of Gaussian reconstruction kernels from their local tangent planes to image space using affine mappings derived from conic isocontours. Unlike previous methods that used affine approximations exact only at the kernel center, this approach ensures accuracy at the kernel cutoff boundary, preventing artifacts such as holes and incorrect elongation under extreme perspective projections. It solves the problem where previous projections integrated kernels along the z-axis rather than the oblique ray from the camera, causing particles to be too faint by \cos(\theta) and insufficiently elongated radially. The Centralized Conics Approach is computationally efficient, making it suitable for real-time rendering on hardware such as NVIDIA GPUs. Its primary limitation is numerical instability under extreme perspective projections where the splat projects to a near-line. This instability can lead to underestimation of extents and visual artifacts. It is best used when performance is critical and extreme perspective distortions are rare or acceptable to approximate. The method is attributed to Zwicker et al. for the centralized conics approach, while the efficient approximation formulas are credited to Botsch et al.. It was noted in the context of GPU-based raycasting of quadric surfaces by Sigg et al. as an efficient but potentially unstable solution compared to methods that avoid matrix inversion. sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, https://github.com/sebastianlipponer/surfacesplatting, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Projective Splat Rasterization with Depth Optimization
head: Adjoint Matrix Splat Rasterization, Inverse Projective Mapping for Splatting
body: A rasterization technique for point-based rendering that uses the inverse of a projective mapping matrix to transform screen coordinates back to object space for kernel evaluation, while simultaneously computing window-space depth values via linear interpolation of homogeneous coordinates. It sets itself apart from standard perspective splatting by avoiding explicit matrix inversion through the use of adjoint matrices and optimizing depth computation by embedding the window-space depth formula directly into the homogeneous interpolation weights. Inputs and Outputs: Input: Splat center \mathbf{p}k, tangent vectors \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k, view frustum near/far constants a, b, and screen coordinates (x, y) of the fragment. Output: Object-space coordinates (u, v) for kernel evaluation and window-space depth d(x) for z-buffering. Data Structures: \mathbf{M}k: A 3 \times 3 matrix representing the forward projective mapping from parameter space (u, v) to screen space. \mathbf{N}k: A 4 \times 3 matrix representing the scaled inverse mapping with the depth optimization row. Steps: 1. Compute Forward Mapping Matrix \mathbf{M}k: Construct the matrix from the splat's screen-space center and tangent vectors: \mathbf{M}k = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{s}k & \mathbf{t}k & \mathbf{p}k \end{bmatrix} where \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k, \mathbf{p}k are column vectors forming the 3 \times 3 matrix acting on \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. The forward mapping is defined as: \begin{bmatrix} xz \\ yz \\ z \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{M}k \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. 2. Compute Adjoint Matrix: Calculate the adjoint of \mathbf{M}k using three cross products to avoid explicit matrix inversion: \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k) = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}k \times \mathbf{p}k \\ \mathbf{p}k \times \mathbf{s}k \\ \mathbf{s}k \times \mathbf{t}k \end{bmatrix}. Let \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 denote the third row of this matrix. 3. Compute Scaling Factor: Calculate the scalar \alpha to normalize the homogeneous coefficient w such that it relates to the view-space depth pz (the z-component of \mathbf{p}k) and the window-space depth constant b: \alpha = \frac{b}{\text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 \cdot \mathbf{p}k}. Note that \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 \cdot \mathbf{p}k is the dot product of the third row of the adjoint matrix and the center vector \mathbf{p}k. 4. Construct Inverse Mapping Matrix \mathbf{N}k: Scale the adjoint matrix by \alpha to form the first three rows of \mathbf{N}k. To optimize depth computation, extend \mathbf{N}k to a 4 \times 3 matrix by adding a fourth row (\mathbf{N}k)4: (\mathbf{N}k)4 = \alpha \cdot \text{adj}(\mathbf{M}k)3 + \begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 0 \\ a \end{bmatrix}. This construction ensures that the homogeneous weight w in the inverse mapping equals b/pz, allowing the fourth component to directly yield the window-space depth d(x) = a + b/z via linear interpolation. 5. Rasterize and Interpolate: Rasterize the triangle covering the splat's bounding box. For each pixel (x, y), compute the homogeneous coordinates by multiplying the inverse matrix \mathbf{N}k with the screen coordinate vector \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}: \begin{bmatrix} uw \\ vw \\ w \\ d \end{bmatrix} = \mathbf{N}k \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}. The values uw, vw, w (and d if using the 4 \times 3 matrix) are linearly interpolated across the primitive. The object-space coordinates are recovered by perspective division: u = \frac{uw}{w}, \quad v = \frac{vw}{w}. The window-space depth is directly available as the fourth component d when the 4 \times 3 matrix is used, or computed as a + b/z if only the 3 \times 3 matrix is used. 6. Kernel Evaluation: Use the recovered (u, v) to evaluate the splat's reconstruction kernel. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def projectivesplatrasterization(pk, sk, tk, a, b, x, y): # Forward mapping matrix Mk = [sk, tk, pk] Mk = columnstack([sk, tk, pk]) # Adjoint matrix rows are cross products adjM = rowstack([cross(tk, pk), cross(pk, sk), cross(sk, tk)]) # Scaling factor alpha ensures w = b/pz at the center denom = dot(adjM[2], pk) alpha = b / denom # Construct 4x3 inverse mapping matrix Nk Nk = zeros((4, 3)) Nk[:3,:] = alpha adjM Nk[3,:] = alpha adjM[2] + array([0.0, 0.0, a]) # Compute homogeneous coordinates for screen point (x, y) coords = Nk @ array([x, y, 1.0]) uw, vw, w, d = coords # Recover object-space coordinates u = uw / w v = vw / w return u, v, d Parameters: a, b: Constants derived from the near and far planes of the view frustum, mapping 1/z to the window space depth range [0, 1]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Matrix Inversion Cost: Explicitly inverting \mathbf{M}k is computationally expensive, which the method avoids by using the adjoint matrix. Degenerate Splats: If \mathbf{p}k, \mathbf{s}k, \mathbf{t}k are collinear or \mathbf{p}k is at the origin, the adjoint matrix may be singular or the scaling factor undefined. In practice, check for near-zero denominators and skip rasterization or fall back to a safe default. Precision: Linear interpolation of homogeneous coordinates is valid for projective mappings. However, ensure that w does not become zero or negative during interpolation, which would cause division by zero or incorrect depth ordering. Clip fragments where w \le 0. Time and memory complexity are Not given in the sources. Measured performance with specific hardware, resolution, and scene data is Not given in the sources. Scaling behavior is Not given in the sources. Strengths include perspective accuracy, avoidance of expensive matrix inversion, and seamless integration with standard z-buffering via window-space depth interpolation. Limitations include the requirement for careful handling of homogeneous weights to avoid division by zero. Performance may degrade if splats are very large or numerous, requiring efficient culling. Originated in the context of point-based rendering, specifically for perspective-accurate splatting. The method is described in "Splat/Mesh Blending, Perspective Rasterization and Transparency for Point-Based Rendering". It addresses the need for efficient, perspective-correct rasterization of splats without the overhead of full 3D-to-2D projection inversion per pixel. name: Perspective Accurate Splatting via Projective Conic Mapping
head: Affine Approximation of Projective Conics, Homogeneous Coordinate Splatting, Perspective Accurate Splatting, Perspective Correct Splatting, Projective Conic Splatting, SPH Perspective Rendering Fix
body: This method computes perspective-correct splat shapes for point-based rendering by approximating the projective mapping of Gaussian reconstruction kernels from their local tangent planes to image space using affine mappings derived from conic isocontours. Unlike previous EWA splatting methods that used affine approximations exact only at the kernel center, this approach ensures accuracy at the kernel cutoff boundary, preventing holes and artifacts under extreme perspective projections. It builds on the Centralized Conics Approach by providing the specific mechanism for deriving the correct variance matrix in screen space. Inputs: A set of point samples pk with associated colors fk and local tangent frames defined by tangent vectors \mathbf{t}u, \mathbf{t}v. A Gaussian reconstruction kernel g with a user-specified cutoff value Fg (typically 1 < Fg < 2). Camera projection parameters. Outputs: Screen-space splat accumulation (color and weight) for each pixel. Data Structures: Tangent Frame Matrix (\mathbf{M}k): A 3 \times 3 matrix mapping local 2D coordinates (u, v) to 3D world space, defined as \mathbf{M}k = \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{t}u \\ \mathbf{t}v \\ \mathbf{p}k \end{bmatrix}. Points \mathbf{p} on the tangent plane are expressed as \mathbf{p} = (u, v, 1) \mathbf{M}k. Conic Matrix (Qh): A 3 \times 3 symmetric matrix representing the implicit form of a conic \phi(x, y) = Ax^2 + 2Bxy + Cy^2 + 2Dx + 2Ey - F = 0 in homogeneous coordinates: Qh = \begin{bmatrix} A & B & D \\ B & C & E \\ D & E & -F \end{bmatrix}. The equation is \mathbf{x} Qh \mathbf{x}^T = 0 where \mathbf{x} = [x, y, 1]. Variance Matrix (Rk): The 2 \times 2 covariance matrix of the Gaussian kernel in the local tangent frame. Mapped Variance Matrix (Q'''): The 2 \times 2 variance matrix of the reconstruction kernel in image space, derived from the projective mapping. Steps: 1. Define Local Kernel Isocontour: The Gaussian kernel is truncated at an isocontour defined by Fg. In the local tangent frame, this isocontour is a central conic expressed in homogeneous coordinates: \begin{bmatrix} u & v & 1 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}k & 0 \\ 0 & -Fg^2 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} u \\ v \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = 0 Let Q{local} be the 3 \times 3 matrix \begin{bmatrix} \mathbf{R}k & 0 \\ 0 & -Fg^2 \end{bmatrix}. 2. Compute Projective Mapping: Determine the mapping from the local tangent plane to the image plane by inverting the tangent frame matrix \mathbf{M}k^{-1} and applying the camera projection. 3. Derive Mapped Conic (Q'''): Apply the projective transformation to the local conic Q{local} to obtain the conic in image space. The resulting matrix Q''' represents the variance matrix of the reconstruction kernel in screen space. 4. Check Numerical Stability: Invert \mathbf{M}k to compute the mapping. Check the condition number of \mathbf{M}k. If the condition number exceeds a threshold (indicating the splat is degenerating into a line segment), discard the splat. 5. Validate Conic Type: Determine if the mapped conic is an ellipse. Calculate the discriminant \Delta = AC - B^2 from the upper-left 2 \times 2 submatrix of the mapped conic matrix. If \Delta \le 0 (parabola or hyperbola), discard the splat. 6. Compute Screen-Space Variance: The effective variance matrix for the splat in screen space is Q''' + H, where H is the resampling filter matrix. The inverse (Q''' + H)^{-1} is passed to the fragment shader. 7. Rasterize Splat: Compute the bounding box of the projected conic to determine the OpenGL point size or fragment shader execution region. For each pixel \mathbf{x} in the bounding box, evaluate the ellipse equation: r^2 = \mathbf{x} (Q''' + H)^{-1} \mathbf{x}^T If r^2 < 1, the pixel is inside the splat. Accumulate color weighted by the Gaussian value and accumulate weight. 8. Normalize: In a final pass, divide accumulated color by accumulated weight to normalize. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import numpy as np def perspectiveaccuratesplatting(points, cameramatrix, Fg=1.5, condthreshold=1e6): """ Render points using perspective accurate splatting via projective conic mapping. """ imageheight, imagewidth = 1024, 1024 coloraccum = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth, 3)) weightaccum = np.zeros((imageheight, imagewidth)) for pt in points: pk = np.array(pt['p']) tu = np.array(pt['tu']) tv = np.array(pt['tv']) color = np.array(pt['color']) # 1. Construct Tangent Frame Matrix Mk Mk = np.vstack([tu, tv, pk]) # 2. Check Condition Number of Mk if np.linalg.cond(Mk) > condthreshold: continue # 3. Invert Mk try: Mkinv = np.linalg.inv(Mk) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue # 4. Define Local Conic Matrix Qlocal Rk = np.eye(2) # Assumed isotropic variance for simplicity Qlocal = np.zeros((3, 3)) Qlocal[:2,:2] = Rk Qlocal[2, 2] = -Fg2 # 5. Compute Homography from tangent plane to image plane # Hproj maps homogeneous (u,v,1) to homogeneous (x,y,1) in screen space Hproj = np.zeros((3, 3)) for i in range(3): for j in range(3): Hproj[i, j] = cameramatrix[i, j] Mkinv[j, 0] + cameramatrix[i, j+1] Mkinv[j, 1] + cameramatrix[i, j+2] Mkinv[j, 2] Hproj /= Hproj[2, 2] # 6. Project Conic to Image Space Qimage = Hproj.T @ Qlocal @ Hproj Qprime = Qimage[:2,:2] # 7. Check if Conic is Ellipse A, B, C = Qprime[0, 0], Qprime[0, 1], Qprime[1, 1] Delta = A C - B2 if Delta <= 0: continue # 8. Compute Resampling Filter Variance Hfilter = np.eye(2) # Identity resampling filter Variance = Qprime + Hfilter # 9. Invert Variance for Fragment Shader try: Varianceinv = np.linalg.inv(Variance) except np.linalg.LinAlgError: continue # 10. Compute Bounding Box eigenvalues, = np.linalg.eigh(Varianceinv) a = 1.0 / np.sqrt(eigenvalues[0]) b = 1.0 / np.sqrt(eigenvalues[1]) width, height = 2 a, 2 b cx, cy = Qimage[0, 2] / Qimage[2, 2], Qimage[1, 2] / Qimage[2, 2] ymin, ymax = int(cy - height), int(cy + height) xmin, xmax = int(cx - width), int(cx + width) # 11. Rasterize for y in range(max(0, ymin), min(imageheight, ymax)): for x in range(max(0, xmin), min(imagewidth, xmax)): offset = np.array([x - cx, y - cy]) rsq = offset @ Varianceinv @ offset if rsq < 1.0: weight = np.exp(-0.5 rsq) coloraccum[y, x] += color weight weightaccum[y, x] += weight # Pass 3: Normalization for y in range(imageheight): for x in range(imagewidth): if weightaccum[y, x] > 1e-6: coloraccum[y, x] /= weightaccum[y, x] return coloraccum Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Ill-conditioned Mapping: If the splat degenerates into a line segment, \mathbf{M}k becomes ill-conditioned. Check the condition number and discard if too high. Non-Elliptical Conics: Projective mapping can result in hyperbolas or parabolas. Check the discriminant \Delta and discard if \Delta \le 0. Precision: Perspective geometry should be computed in double precision to improve accuracy. SPH Specifics: For SPH particles, the kernel is evaluated at the impact parameter (perpendicular to the ray) rather than the offset in the particle plane. Pixels are placed at the depth of the slicing plane, not the particle depth. A texture mapping technique for point cloud color data that maintains uniform sample density across the unit sphere, addressing distortion and sampling efficiency issues in color atlases. It complements the geometric accuracy of this splatting method by ensuring high-quality attribute rendering. Time Complexity: Dominated by the vertex shader computation for each point (matrix inversions, conic mapping) and the fragment shader evaluation for each pixel in the bounding box. The bounding box size depends on the perspective distortion and kernel cutoff. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of points and pixels covered by splats. Requires storage for depth buffer, color buffer, and weight buffer. Performance: Implemented on modern GPUs using vertex and fragment programs. The three-pass approach (depth, accumulation, normalization) is efficient. The method avoids holes and artifacts, improving visual quality at the cost of slightly more complex vertex shader computations compared to affine approximations. Strengths: Perspective-correct splat shapes, no holes under extreme perspective, high image quality with anisotropic filtering. Limitations: More complex than affine methods, requires careful handling of degenerate cases and numerical stability. This method was introduced by Jussi Räsanen, Mario Botsch, Carsten Dachsbacher, and Mark Pauly. It addresses the limitations of previous EWA splatting methods by Heckbert and Zwicker, which used affine approximations exact only at the kernel center. The method was implemented in a point rendering algorithm using GPU vertex and fragment programs. It is also referenced in the context of SPH particle rendering fixes in the pynbody library. Opt-in exact AMR rendering, new pynbody.imaging package, and SPH perspective fixes, https://github.com/pynbody/pynbody/pull/1048, fetched 2026-10-26 Perspective Accurate Splatting, http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/149345, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Stretch-invariant polar capped color map
head: Stretch-invariant polar capped map, plane-chart cylindrical projection with azimuthal equidistant polar caps, polar capped color map, polar capped map, spherical representation P
body: The stretch-invariant polar capped color map is a texture mapping technique that encodes point cloud color data onto a 2D image while maintaining uniform sample density across the unit sphere, solving the non-uniform density flaw of standard cylindrical plane-chart projections. It generates one texture map per scan location to store color information for textured splats while preserving occlusion equivalence with the original point cloud. The method maps texture coordinates (s, t) to a 3D direction vector (x, y, z) on the unit sphere using a hybrid projection: a plane-chart cylindrical projection for the equatorial band and azimuthal equidistant projections for the polar caps. Texture coordinates (s, t) are assumed to lie in [0, 1]. The geometry (point positions) is stored separately as regular (x, y, z) data to avoid precision loss from encoding depth in image formats like PNG, while the texture map stores only color data. Inputs: Forward: Texture coordinates (s, t). Inverse: Normalized direction vector (\bar{x}, \bar{y}, \bar{z}) from scan location sk to point p. Outputs: Forward: Unit direction vector (x, y, z). Inverse: Texture coordinates (s, t). Formulas and Steps: The sphere is divided into three regions based on the latitude angle \psi. 1. Bottom Cap (\psi \in -\pi/2, -\pi/4)): Corresponds to texture coordinate s \le 1/6. [Forward Mapping (Texel to Direction): Let ub = 6s - 0.5, vb = t - 0.5, and rb = ub^2 + vb^2. \begin{aligned} x &= \frac{ub}{rb} \sin\left(\frac{\pi rb}{2}\right) \\ y &= \frac{vb}{rb} \sin\left(\frac{\pi rb}{2}\right) \\ z &= -\cos\left(\frac{\pi rb}{2}\right) \end{aligned} Inverse Mapping (Direction to Texel): Let r = 2\pi \arccos(\bar{z}). \begin{aligned} s &= \frac{\frac{\bar{x} r}{\sin(\pi r / 2)} + 0.5}{6} \\ t &= \frac{\frac{\bar{y} r}{\sin(\pi r / 2)} + 0.5}{6} \end{aligned} 2. Top Cap (\psi \in (\pi/4, \pi/2]): Corresponds to texture coordinate 1/6 < s \le 2/6. Forward Mapping (Texel to Direction): Let ut = 6s - 1.5, vt = t - 0.5, and rt = \sqrt{ut^2 + vt^2}. \begin{aligned} x &= \frac{ut}{rt} \sin\left(\frac{\pi rt}{2}\right) \\ y &= \frac{vt}{rt} \sin\left(\frac{\pi rt}{2}\right) \\ z &= \cos\left(\frac{\pi rt}{2}\right) \end{aligned} Inverse Mapping (Direction to Texel): Let r = 2\pi \arccos(\bar{z}). \begin{aligned} s &= \frac{\frac{\bar{x} r}{\sin(\pi r / 2)} + 1.5}{6} \\ t &= \frac{\frac{\bar{y} r}{\sin(\pi r / 2)} + 0.5}{6} \end{aligned} 3. Equatorial Band (\psi \in [-\pi/4, \pi/4]): Corresponds to texture coordinate s > 2/6. Forward Mapping (Texel to Direction): Let \psi = t \frac{\pi}{2} - \frac{\pi}{4} and \theta = (1.5s - 0.5)2\pi. \begin{aligned} x &= \cos(\psi) \cos(\theta) \\ y &= \cos(\psi) \sin(\theta) \\ z &= \sin(\psi) \end{aligned} Inverse Mapping (Direction to Texel): Let \psi = \arcsin(\bar{z}) and \theta = \operatorname{atan2}(\bar{y}, \bar{x}). \begin{aligned} s &= \frac{\frac{\theta}{2\pi} + 0.5}{1.5} \\ t &= \frac{\psi + \frac{\pi}{4}}{2\pi} \end{aligned} Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def forwardmap(s: float, t: float) -> tuple: """Maps texture coordinates (s, t) to a 3D direction vector (x, y, z).""" if s <= 1.0 / 6.0: # Bottom Cap ub = 6.0 s - 0.5 vb = t - 0.5 rb = ub ub + vb vb # Guard against division by zero at exact pole center if rb == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, -1.0) sinval = math.sin(math.pi rb / 2.0) x = (ub / rb) sinval y = (vb / rb) sinval z = -math.cos(math.pi rb / 2.0) return (x, y, z) elif s <= 2.0 / 6.0: # Top Cap ut = 6.0 s - 1.5 vt = t - 0.5 rt = math.sqrt(ut ut + vt vt) # Guard against division by zero at exact pole center if rt == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0, 1.0) sinval = math.sin(math.pi rt / 2.0) x = (ut / rt) sinval y = (vt / rt) sinval z = math.cos(math.pi rt / 2.0) return (x, y, z) else: # Equatorial Band psi = t (math.pi / 2.0) - (math.pi / 4.0) theta = (1.5 s - 0.5) 2.0 math.pi x = math.cos(psi) math.cos(theta) y = math.cos(psi) math.sin(theta) z = math.sin(psi) return (x, y, z) def inversemap(xbar: float, ybar: float, zbar: float) -> tuple: """Maps a normalized direction vector (xbar, ybar, zbar) to texture coordinates (s, t).""" # Normalize input to handle unnormalized vectors length = math.sqrt(xbar2 + ybar2 + zbar2) if length == 0.0: return (0.0, 0.0) xbar /= length ybar /= length zbar /= length psi = math.asin(zbar) if psi <= -math.pi / 4.0: # Bottom Cap r = 2.0 math.pi math.acos(zbar) sinval = math.sin(math.pi r / 2.0) # Guard against division by zero at exact poles if sinval == 0.0: return (0.5 / 6.0, 0.5 / 6.0) s = ((xbar r / sinval) + 0.5) / 6.0 t = ((ybar r / sinval) + 0.5) / 6.0 return (s, t) elif psi > math.pi / 4.0: # Top Cap r = 2.0 math.pi math.acos(zbar) sinval = math.sin(math.pi r / 2.0) if sinval == 0.0: return (1.5 / 6.0, 0.5 / 6.0) s = ((xbar r / sinval) + 1.5) / 6.0 t = ((ybar r / sinval) + 0.5) / 6.0 return (s, t) else: # Equatorial Band theta = math.atan2(ybar, xbar) s = (theta / (2.0 math.pi) + 0.5) / 1.5 t = (psi + math.pi / 4.0) / (2.0 math.pi) return (s, t) Parameters: s, t: Texture coordinates, typically in [0, 1]. \psi: Latitude angle, range [-\pi/2, \pi/2]. \theta: Longitude angle, range [-\pi, \pi]. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Division by zero occurs in the cap formulas when rb=0 or rt=0 (exact pole centers) or when \sin(\pi r / 2) = 0 (poles). The pseudocode handles these centers explicitly. Precision loss is avoided by storing geometry as (x,y,z) rather than encoding depth in the texture, as noted in the source. The equatorial band formula for s involves division by 1.5; numerical error may push s slightly outside [2/6, 1], requiring standard clamping or wrapping in practice. Time Complexity: The mapping operations are O(1) per point/texel, involving basic trigonometric functions and arithmetic. Memory Complexity: Requires one texture map per scan location sk. Using texture maps for color data greatly reduces disk memory footprint compared to storing all color data in point structures, and allows for lossy image compression. Strengths: Minimizes distortion across every region of the unit sphere and achieves more uniform sample density compared to standard cylindrical plane-chart projections. Maintains occlusion equivalence with the original point cloud. When to use: When rendering point clouds with textured splats and uniform sampling density across the sphere is critical for visual quality or algorithmic consistency. When not to use: Not given in the sources. The method was proposed by M. Comino, A. Chica, and C. Andujar in 2019. It addresses a flaw in the cylindrical plane-chart projection used by Comino et al. in 2017, which resulted in non-uniform sample density across the unit sphere. The approach follows Snyder et al. for the mathematical formulation of the stretch-invariant projection. It is used in the context of view-dependent hierarchical rendering of massive point clouds through textured splats. View-dependent Hierarchical Rendering of Massive Point Clouds through Textured Splats, https://doi.org/10.2312/ceig.20191203, fetched 2026-10-26
