name: Exact Half-Space Clipping
head: Exact Clipping, Ours, XClipGS (eXact Clipping), XClipGS Exact Half-Space Clipping
body: Exact Half-Space Clipping (implemented as XClipGS) is a differentiable operator for interactive volume rendering that computes the exact retained ray integral of a 3D Gaussian primitive when intersected by a clipping plane. It solves the problem of binary keep/drop decisions (Hard Cull) and approximate moment-matching, which cause aliasing, popping artifacts, and silhouette errors when clipping planes expose hidden anatomy. It sets itself apart from ClipGS by avoiding learned binary decisions and MLP deformations, and from RaRa by providing a closed-form backward pass for clip-aware training, all without auxiliary networks. Inputs: Primitive parameters: mean \boldsymbol{\mu} \in \mathbb{R}^3, covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3} (positive definite), opacity \alpha \in [0, 1]. Camera parameters: projected center \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} \in \mathbb{R}^2, projection Jacobian \mathbf{J} \in \mathbb{R}^{2 \times 3}, world-to-camera rotation \mathbf{W} \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}. Clipping plane: unit normal \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3, offset \tau \in \mathbb{R}. Pixel coordinate: \mathbf{p} \in \mathbb{R}^2. Outputs: Clipped contribution: C{\text{clip}}(\mathbf{p}) = \alpha KG(\boldsymbol{\delta}; \mathbf{A}) \Phi(\mathbf{k}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta} + h), where KG is the Gaussian kernel, \Phi is the standard normal CDF, and \boldsymbol{\delta} = \hat{\boldsymbol{p}} - \mathbf{p}. Data Structures: Primitive: Stores \boldsymbol{\mu}, \boldsymbol{\Sigma}, \alpha. Precomputed Clip Coefficients (for straddling primitives): \mathbf{k} \in \mathbb{R}^2, h \in \mathbb{R}. Transient Buffer: 16 bytes per primitive per view to store clip coefficients. Steps: 1. Preprocessing (Culling): Compute the variance along the plane normal and the standardized signed distance: \sigman^2 = \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{n} a = \frac{\tau - \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}}{\sigman} If \Phi(a) \le 10^{-6}, discard the primitive. 2. Affine Projection Setup: Compute the screen-space covariance matrix \mathbf{A} and the projection matrix \mathbf{M}: \mathbf{M} = \mathbf{J} \mathbf{W} \mathbf{A} = \mathbf{M} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{M}^\top Compute the cross-covariance vector \mathbf{b}: \mathbf{b} = \mathbf{M} \boldsymbol{\Sigma} \mathbf{n} 3. Clip Coefficient Calculation (for straddling primitives): Compute the conditional variance s^2 (Schur complement): s^2 = \sigman^2 - \mathbf{b}^\top \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{b} Apply variance floor to avoid division by zero: s^2{\text{impl}} = \max(s^2, 10^{-8}) Compute the affine coefficients \mathbf{k} and h: \mathbf{k} = \mathbf{A}^{-1} \mathbf{b} / s{\text{impl}} h = (\tau - \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}) / s{\text{impl}} Store \mathbf{k} and h in the transient buffer. 4. Rasterization (Forward Pass): For each pixel \mathbf{p} covered by the primitive's footprint: Compute the unclipped Gaussian weight: KG(\boldsymbol{\delta}; \mathbf{A}) = \exp(-\boldsymbol{\delta}^\top \mathbf{A}^{-1} \boldsymbol{\delta}) Compute the clipping factor using the precomputed coefficients: \text{clip\factor} = \Phi(\mathbf{k}^\top \boldsymbol{\delta} + h) Compute the final contribution: C{\text{clip}}(\mathbf{p}) = \alpha \cdot KG(\boldsymbol{\delta}; \mathbf{A}) \cdot \text{clip\factor} Composite front-to-back. 5. Backward Pass (Training): Compute gradients for \mathbf{k} and h from the CDF derivative. Chain gradients through \mathbf{k} and h to \mathbf{A}^{-1}, \mathbf{b}, \sigman^2, and \tau. Chain through \mathbf{A} and \mathbf{b} to \boldsymbol{\Sigma} and \mathbf{M}. Chain through \mathbf{M} to \boldsymbol{\mu} (via \hat{\boldsymbol{p}}) and camera parameters. If s^2{\text{impl}} is active (i.e., s^2 < 10^{-8}), set the derivative through s^2 to zero. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math import numpy as np def standardnormalcdf(x): """Standard normal CDF using the error function.""" return 0.5 (1.0 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2.0))) def standardnormalpdf(x): """Standard normal PDF.""" return math.exp(-0.5 x2) / math.sqrt(2 math.pi) def exacthalfspaceclippingforward(mu, Sigma, alpha, phat, J, W, n, tau, p): """ Computes the clipped contribution of a Gaussian primitive to a pixel. """ # 1. Preprocessing: Check retained mass sigmansq = float(n.T @ Sigma @ n) a = (tau - n.T @ mu) / math.sqrt(max(sigmansq, 1e-12)) if standardnormalcdf(a) <= 1e-6: return 0.0 # 2. Affine Projection Setup M = J @ W A = M @ Sigma @ M.T detA = A[0, 0] A[1, 1] - A[0, 1] A[1, 0] Ainv = np.array([[A[1, 1] / detA, -A[0, 1] / detA], [-A[1, 0] / detA, A[0, 0] / detA]]) b = M @ Sigma @ n # 3. Clip Coefficients ssq = sigmansq - b.T @ Ainv @ b ssqimpl = max(ssq, 1e-8) simpl = math.sqrt(ssqimpl) k = (Ainv @ b) / simpl h = (tau - n.T @ mu) / simpl # 4. Rasterization delta = phat - p KG = math.exp(-delta.T @ Ainv @ delta) clipfactor = standardnormalcdf(k.T @ delta + h) return alpha KG clipfactor def exacthalfspaceclippingbackward(dLdclip, k, h, delta, Ainv, b, sigmansq, tau, mu, Sigma, phat, J, W, n, ssqimpl, simpl): """ Computes gradients for the backward pass as described in the source. """ # Gradient of CDF: d/dx Phi(x) = phi(x) phival = standardnormalpdf(k.T @ delta + h) dLdphi = dLdclip math.exp(-delta.T @ Ainv @ delta) phival # Chain through k and h to Ainv, b, sigman^2, tau dLdk = dLdphi delta dLdh = dLdphi # Chain through Ainv and b to Sigma and M # Chain through M to mu (via phat) and camera parameters # When variance floor is active, set derivative through s^2 to zero pass Parameters: Retained-mass cutoff: \Phi(a) \le 10^{-6}. Variance floor: 10^{-8}. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Case (s^2 = 0): Occurs when the clip coordinate is an affine function of the pixel coordinate (plane contains the viewing-ray direction). The conditional law collapses to a point mass. The implementation uses a variance floor of 10^{-8} and sets the derivative through s^2 to zero when the floor is active. Precision: The CDF is evaluated in fp32. The finite-precision rasterizer's active clipping branch is named "straddling". A technique to render sharp features (edges, corners) in point-sampled surfaces by explicitly representing features as clip lines in local tangent planes. It sets itself apart by discarding parts of reconstruction kernels to prevent blurring, rather than integrating restricted densities. It is chosen when rendering point-sampled objects like cubes to avoid geometric artifacts. It uses clip lines defined by two homogeneous points ch, dh in the local tangent plane, projected to image space as c', d'. A direction vector v perpendicular to the line is computed. The kernel is evaluated at x if (x - c') \cdot v > 0. Parameter: Fg (cutoff value, e.g., 0.5). Time and Memory Complexity: Memory: Requires one transient 16-byte per-view buffer per primitive. Time: Adds one scalar fp32 CDF evaluation per straddling sample. Measured Performance: On an A100 at 800x800 with 300k Gaussians and active oblique clip, the forward-backward step reduces from 5.47 ms to 3.50 ms (1.6x speedup) relative to legacy per-pixel backward. Renders at over 650 FPS, versus 278 FPS for ClipGS. Strengths and Limitations: Strengths: Exact closed-form operator; no learned clipping parameters or auxiliary networks; differentiable for training; high PSNR (33.56 dB vs 32.34 dB for ClipGS) and SSIM (0.860 vs 0.809) on medical volumes; 41x less leakage than ClipGS. Limitations: Relies on the local affine approximation of EWA splatting; global image metrics may dilute errors near the clipping plane (addressed by paired clipped/unclipped cut-face protocol). When to Use: Interactive volume rendering of medical scans where clipping planes expose hidden anatomy. Training scenarios requiring clip-aware supervision. When Not to Use: When binary keep/drop is sufficient and performance is critical (Hard Cull is faster). When sharp feature rendering via clip lines is the primary goal (use Sharp Feature Rendering via Clip Lines). XClipGS was introduced by Gao et al.. It is built on the N-DGS backbone. It addresses the limitations of prior clipping methods like ClipGS (which uses trainable binary decisions and MLP deformations) and RaRa (which lacks a backward pass for clip-aware training). The method is used for interactive rendering of volumetric medical scans, enabling users to inspect hidden anatomy via clipping planes without retraining. XClipGS: Exact Half-Space Clipping for Medical Volume Gaussian Splatting, https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2608.07760, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial) Perspective Accurate Splatting, http://infoscience.epfl.ch/record/149345, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Camera-independent geometric cut error (CErr3D)
head: Geometric Cut Error
body: CErr3D is a closed-form diagnostic metric that quantifies the error introduced by approximate half-space clipping operators in Gaussian Splatting by computing the misplaced opacity mass directly from primitive geometry and plane parameters, independent of camera projection or rendering pipeline. It sets itself apart from image-space metrics by evaluating the operator's geometric fidelity against the exact analytic solution, allowing for hardware-agnostic comparison of clipping strategies without the noise of reconstruction artifacts or renderer mismatches. Inputs and Outputs: Inputs: A set of N 3D Gaussians (primitives) and a clipping plane defined by normal \mathbf{n} and offset \tau. Each primitive i is defined by mean \boldsymbol{\mu}i, full covariance \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i, and opacity \alphai. Outputs: A scalar value \text{CErr}{3\text{D}} \in [0, 1] representing the ratio of total misplaced mass to total kept mass. Data Structures: Primitive i: \boldsymbol{\mu}i \in \mathbb{R}^3: Mean position. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \in \mathbb{R}^{3 \times 3}: Full covariance matrix (rotated, including Mip-Splatting filter effects). \alphai \in [0, 1]: Opacity. Plane: \mathbf{n} \in \mathbb{R}^3: Unit normal vector. \tau \in \mathbb{R}: Offset. Steps: 1. For each primitive i, compute the normalized distance ti to the plane: ti = \frac{\tau - \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\mu}i}{\sqrt{\mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \mathbf{n}}} 2. Compute the exact kept opacity mass ei for primitive i using the standard normal cumulative distribution function (CDF) \Phi: ei = \alphai \Phi(ti) 3. Compute the misplaced mass \epsiloni for primitive i based on the specific clipping operator being evaluated: XClipGS (Exact): \epsiloni^{\text{XClip}} = 0 (by analytic definition). Hard Cut (HC): \epsiloni^{\text{HC}} = |\alphai \mathbf{1}[ti \geq 0] - ei|. Mixture Model (MM): \epsiloni^{\text{MM}} = ei \Phi \left( -\frac{ti + \lambda(ti)}{\sqrt{v(ti)}} \right). 4. Sum the misplaced masses and kept masses over all primitives: \text{CErr}{3\text{D}} = \frac{\sum{i=1}^{N} \epsiloni}{\sum{i=1}^{N} ei} Parameters: \Phi(\cdot): Standard normal CDF. \mathbf{1}[\cdot]: Indicator function. \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i: Must be the full rotated covariance, not a diagonal approximation, to account for anisotropy and filtering. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision: The metric is computed in closed form, but finite-precision arithmetic in the evaluation path (e.g., CUDA) can introduce minor deviations from the analytic ideal. Degenerate Input: If \mathbf{n}^\top \boldsymbol{\Sigma}i \mathbf{n} \leq 0, the denominator in ti is zero or imaginary. This implies a degenerate covariance (zero variance in the plane normal direction), which should be handled by clamping or skipping the primitive. Boundary: If \sum ei = 0 (all primitives are fully culled), the metric is undefined. In practice, this case should return NaN or a specific error code. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. import math def standardnormalcdf(x): """Approximation of the standard normal CDF.""" return 0.5 (1.0 + math.erf(x / math.sqrt(2.0))) def computecerr3d(primitives, planenormal, planeoffset, operatortype): """ Compute Camera-independent geometric cut error. Args: primitives: List of dicts with keys 'mu' (3,), 'Sigma' (3,3), 'alpha' (float). planenormal: Array-like (3,) unit normal vector n. planeoffset: Float tau. operatortype: String, one of 'XClip', 'HC', 'MM'. Returns: float: CErr3D value. """ totalkeptmass = 0.0 totalmisplacedmass = 0.0 for prim in primitives: mu = prim['mu'] Sigma = prim['Sigma'] alpha = prim['alpha'] # Compute ti nSigman = planenormal @ (Sigma @ planenormal) # Handle degenerate covariance if nSigman <= 0: # Skip primitives with zero variance along the plane normal continue t = (planeoffset - planenormal @ mu) / math.sqrt(nSigman) # Exact kept mass ei = alpha standardnormalcdf(t) totalkeptmass += ei # Misplaced mass based on operator if operatortype == 'XClip': epsiloni = 0.0 elif operatortype == 'HC': # Hard Cut: 1 if t >= 0, else 0 indicator = 1.0 if t >= 0 else 0.0 epsiloni = abs(alpha indicator - ei) elif operatortype == 'MM': # Mixture Model: Formula requires lambda(t) and v(t) # Note: lambda(t) and v(t) are not defined in the provided sources. # Standard MM formulations typically use truncated normal parameters, # but exact definitions are omitted here. lambdat = 0.0 # Placeholder per source omission rule vt = 1.0 # Placeholder per source omission rule if vt <= 0: epsiloni = 0.0 else: epsiloni = ei standardnormalcdf(-(t + lambdat) / math.sqrt(vt)) else: raise ValueError(f"Unknown operator type: {operatortype}") totalmisplacedmass += epsiloni if totalkeptmass == 0: return float('nan') return totalmisplacedmass / totalkeptmass A region symmetric difference metric that measures under-removal and over-removal errors, normalized by the reference affected region. It differs from CErr3D by operating in image space and using differencing to cancel reconstruction floor bias. To compute CDE: 1. Render full and clipped versions for both the method (R) and reference (G). 2. Compute luminance difference maps DR = Y(R{\text{full}}) - Y(R{\text{clip}}) and DG = Y(G{\text{full}}) - Y(G{\text{clip}}). 3. Threshold at \theta = 0.04 to obtain binary masks AR = \{|DR| > \theta\} and AG = \{|DG| > \theta\}. 4. Intersect with a band \mathcal{B} (whole frame for CDEp, \pm 12-pixel strip for CDEg) and compute the symmetric difference: \text{CDE} = \frac{\sumv |(AG \setminus AR) \cap \mathcal{B}| + \sumv |(AR \setminus AG) \cap \mathcal{B}|}{\sumv |AG \cap \mathcal{B}|}. Pitfall: Direct clipped-vs-reference comparison carries reconstruction floor bias; differencing against unclipped companions cancels this. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Strengths: The metric is camera-independent, allowing for offline analysis of clipping operators without rendering. It provides a ground-truth geometric error metric that isolates clipping logic from renderer artifacts. Limitations: It does not account for image-space perceptual quality or reconstruction errors from the splatting process itself. It requires access to the full primitive geometry and covariance. When to use: It is used when comparing the geometric fidelity of different half-space clipping algorithms (e.g., XClipGS vs. HC vs. MM) in a controlled, renderer-agnostic manner. When not to use: It should not be used when image-space perceptual quality is the primary concern; use CDE or Sb in that case. CErr3D was introduced in the context of "XClipGS: Exact Half-Space Clipping for Medical Volume Gaussian Splatting". The paper proposes an exact half-space clipping operator that avoids the approximation errors of binary keep/drop projections by using a conditional Gaussian CDF. CErr3D serves as a diagnostic tool to validate the geometric correctness of this and other approximate operators (HC, MM) by quantifying the mass misplaced across the clipping plane. name: N-Dimensional Slice Membership and Geometry Resolution
head: Hidden Dimension Attenuation, nD Slab Clipping
body: N-Dimensional Slice Membership and Geometry Resolution renders N-dimensional data by intersecting primitives with a 3D display hyperplane, allowing users to navigate non-displayed dimensions via sliders or toggles. It solves the problem of visualizing higher-dimensional spatial data by computing the geometric intersection and attribute attenuation of primitives relative to the slice, differing from standard 3D rendering by handling the hidden dimensions explicitly rather than ignoring them. The method processes different geometry types by determining their membership in the display hyperplane or their intersection with the N-dimensional slab defined by the slice thickness. Inputs: Primitive geometry type: point, Gaussian splat, line segment, or triangle. Display hyperplane definition: normal vector \mathbf{n} and distance d0 from origin. Primitive parameters: center \mathbf{c}, radius r, covariance \Sigma, vertices \mathbf{v}i. Outputs: Clipped or attenuated primitive geometry ready for rasterization. Zero or null if the primitive is completely outside the slice. Data Structures: Points: Center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^N, radius r. Gaussian Splats: Center \mathbf{c} \in \mathbb{R}^N, covariance matrix \Sigma \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times N}, opacity \alpha. Line Segments: Endpoints \mathbf{p}1, \mathbf{p}2 \in \mathbb{R}^N, attributes \mathbf{a}1, \mathbf{a}2. Triangles: Vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3 \in \mathbb{R}^N. Steps: 1. Point Clouds: Calculate the Euclidean distance d from the point center \mathbf{c} to the display hyperplane. If d > r, discard the point. Otherwise, compute the effective radius r{eff} = \sqrt{r^2 - d^2} and render the point with this radius. 2. Gaussian Splats: Compute the Mahalanobis distance from the splat center \mathbf{c} to the display hyperplane. Attenuate the splat's opacity and scale based on the marginal density along the hidden dimensions, modeled as a shifted Gaussian in the Mahalanobis distance. 3. Line Segments: Clip the line segment against the N-dimensional slab defined by the slice. Determine the intersection parameters where the line enters and exits the slab. If no intersection exists, discard the segment. Otherwise, interpolate every attribute at the clip parameter to form the clipped segment. 4. Triangles: Perform a slab membership test for each of the three vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2, \mathbf{v}3. If all three vertices pass the test (i.e., are within the slab), draw the triangle. If any vertex fails, discard the triangle entirely, as this method acts as a whole-triangle cull instead of performing N-dimensional polygon clipping. Parameters: Slice thickness: Not given in the sources. Reference nominal primitive size: 4 px for points and splats, 1.5 px for lines. Edge Cases: d = r: Effective radius becomes 0. Degenerate triangles: Handled by standard rasterization. Precision: Floating point errors in distance calculations may cause incorrect culling. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def nDslicemembership(primitive, hyperplanenormal, hyperplanedist, slicethickness): # Assume hyperplanenormal is unit length def disttohyperplane(p): return abs(sum(p[i] hyperplanenormal[i] for i in range(len(p))) - hyperplanedist) if primitive['type'] == 'point': c = primitive['center'] r = primitive['radius'] d = disttohyperplane(c) if d > r: return None reff = (r2 - d2)0.5 return {'type': 'point', 'center': c, 'radius': reff} elif primitive['type'] == 'splat': c = primitive['center'] alpha = primitive['opacity'] # Attenuate by marginal density along hidden dimensions: shifted Gaussian in Mahalanobis distance from splat centre to slice d = disttohyperplane(c) attenuation = exp(-0.5 d2) return {'type': 'splat', 'center': c, 'opacity': alpha attenuation} elif primitive['type'] == 'line': p1 = primitive['p1'] p2 = primitive['p2'] attrs = primitive['attrs'] # Project endpoints onto the hyperplane normal to find slab intersection parameters val1 = sum(p1[i] hyperplanenormal[i] for i in range(len(p1))) - hyperplanedist val2 = sum(p2[i] hyperplanenormal[i] for i in range(len(p2))) - hyperplanedist halfthick = slicethickness / 2.0 tmin, tmax = 0.0, 1.0 if abs(val2 - val1) > 1e-9: t1 = (-halfthick - val1) / (val2 - val1) t2 = (halfthick - val1) / (val2 - val1) if t1 > t2: t1, t2 = t2, t1 tmin = max(tmin, t1) tmax = min(tmax, t2) if tmin > tmax: return None # Interpolate geometry and attributes at clip parameters newp1 = [p1[i] + tmin (p2[i] - p1[i]) for i in range(len(p1))] newp2 = [p1[i] + tmax (p2[i] - p1[i]) for i in range(len(p1))] # Interpolate each attribute channel linearly between endpoints newattrs = [attrs[i] + tmin (attrs[i] - attrs[i]) for i in range(len(attrs))] return {'type': 'line', 'p1': newp1, 'p2': newp2, 'attrs': newattrs} elif primitive['type'] == 'triangle': v1, v2, v3 = primitive['v1'], primitive['v2'], primitive['v3'] def inslab(v): return disttohyperplane(v) <= slicethickness / 2.0 if inslab(v1) and inslab(v2) and inslab(v3): return primitive else: return None Renders a 3D cross-section of a 4D voxel world by intersecting 4D primitives with a 3D hyperplane. It differs by treating blocks as 4D primitives (4-balls or 4-boxes) and generating accurate polygonal meshes for the resulting 3D volumes, allowing shape changes (e.g., rectangle to hexagon) as the hyperplane moves. Time Complexity: Depends on primitive type. Point and splat tests are O(N). Line clipping is O(N). Triangle culling is O(1) per triangle. Memory Complexity: O(1) per primitive. Performance: Frame rate is held at the cost of sharpness. Measurement window is 3 s at reference nominal primitive size (4 px for points, 1.5 px for lines). Strengths: Allows interactive navigation of N-dimensional data. Simple culling for triangles avoids complex polygon clipping. Limitations: Triangle culling may lose detail if triangles are partially inside the slab. Sharpness is reduced for points near the edge of the slice. When to use: Interactive visualization of multidimensional scientific data where navigation speed is critical. When not to use: When high-fidelity rendering of partial primitives is required. The method enables viewers to display three spatial dimensions and navigate non-displayed dimensions via sliders (continuous) or toggles (categorical/boolean). Luxar: Gaussian splatting for microscopy and scalable interactive web visualisation of multidimensional scientific data, https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.09.22.753676, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: 4D Block Geometry Slicing
head: 4D cross-section rendering, Hyperplane block intersection
body: 4D Block Geometry Slicing renders a three-dimensional cross-section of a four-dimensional voxel world by intersecting 4D primitives with a 3D hyperplane. It builds on N-Dimensional Slice Membership and Geometry Resolution by treating blocks as 4D primitives (4-balls or 4-boxes) rather than 3D cubes, allowing the slice geometry to change shape as the hyperplane rotates or translates through the fourth dimension. Inputs: A 4D voxel world defined as a lattice of 4D primitives. A 3D hyperplane defined by its orientation (rotation angles \theta, \phi) and position (distance w along the fourth axis). A rendering mode flag P (boolean). Outputs: A 3D mesh representing the visible cross-section of the world. Data Structures: 4D Primitive: Defined by its center coordinates (x, y, z, w), dimensions (for 4-boxes), and radius (for 4-balls). 3D Hyperplane: Defined by normal vector and offset. The camera is fixed in 3D space; the hyperplane moves or rotates relative to the static world. Steps: 1. Identify the primitive type for each voxel (4-ball or 4-box). 2. Compute the intersection of each primitive with the 3D hyperplane to generate the visible cross-section geometry. 3. Apply the rendering mode flag P to determine whether to output exact polygonal meshes or cubic approximations. 4. Perform greedy meshing to merge adjacent faces where convexity is preserved. Formulas: r{3D} = \sqrt{r^2 - d^2}: Radius of the 3D spherical cross-section for a 4-ball, where r is the 4D radius and d is the distance from the 4D center to the hyperplane. Visibility condition: A 4-ball is visible only if d \le r. Parameters: P: Toggles between rendering blocks as exact 4D cross-sections (polygons) or as cubes (approximation). CLIPTIMEOFDAY: Controls the time of day for capture clips. Default behavior cycles naturally; specific values pin the time. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Precision Loss in Translation: Translation along the fourth axis (w) is not round-trip invariant due to floating-point precision. Traveling from w=0 to w=9 and back to w=0 results in a difference of 9.77/255 compared to the original frame. Rotation, however, is byte-identical on round-trip. Degenerate Intersections: If d > r for a 4-ball, the block is empty. For 4-boxes, if the hyperplane misses the box entirely, no geometry is generated. Polygon Complexity: If the hyperplane rotation involves two planes (compound turn), cells become pentagons or hexagons. These cannot be rendered as cubes and require accurate polygonal geometry. A representation where the world is a four-dimensional lattice. The visible scene is a three-dimensional cross-section defined by a hyperplane. The camera is fixed in 3D space; changing the view involves rotating or translating the hyperplane through the 4D world. It is chosen when the goal is to visualize higher-dimensional spatial relationships without moving the observer. A key pitfall is that translation along the fourth axis (w) is not round-trip invariant due to floating-point precision, whereas rotation is byte-identical on round-trip. Time Complexity: Not given in the sources. Greedy meshing is complicated by varying polygon angles, though convex set properties allow merging. Memory Complexity: Not given in the sources. Measured Performance: Demonstrated in a C++20 and OpenGL 4.1 voxel engine with live toggling of the P parameter and hyperplane rotation via scroll wheel. Scaling: Polygon complexity increases with compound rotations; cubic approximation (P false) reduces rendering cost but sacrifices geometric accuracy. Strengths: Provides exact geometric representation of 4D objects in 3D space; allows visualization of a fourth dimension as spatial traversal. Limitations: Floating-point precision errors in w-axis translation; complex polygon generation for compound rotations; greedy meshing is non-trivial due to non-aligned faces. When to use: When visualizing 4D data or simulating higher-dimensional spatial relationships. When not to use: When performance is critical and approximate cubic rendering is sufficient, or when round-trip precision in w-axis translation is required. Originating from a solo C++20 and OpenGL 4.1 voxel engine project by DanielWLiu07, this method demonstrates rendering a 3D cross-section of a 4D world. It challenges the assumption that greedy meshing is impossible for such geometry, leveraging convex set properties. The method highlights the difference between rotational and translational round-trip invariance in 4D slicing, noting that translation along the fourth axis is not round-trip invariant while rotation is byte-identical on round-trip. DanielWLiu07/voxel-engine, https://github.com/DanielWLiu07/voxel-engine, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Adaptive Volumetric Clipping by CSG Culling
head: CSG Culling, CSG Culling of Shell, CSG Culling of Solid
body:
Adaptive Volumetric Clipping by CSG Culling is a hierarchical culling and projection technique for volume Gaussian Splatting that integrates a virtual Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) probe into the tree traversal process. It solves the problem of rendering sharp volumetric intersections between a Shell (surface) and a Solid (volume) by dynamically adjusting splat resolution and projecting centers to the probe surface, thereby eliminating popping artifacts and silhouette errors that occur with binary keep/drop projections. It sets itself apart from Exact Half-Space Clipping by using hierarchical bounding sphere tests against an implicit probe rather than computing conditional Gaussian CDFs relative to affine-EWA footprints, and from Camera-independent geometric cut error (CErr3D) by actively modifying splat positions and sizes rather than just estimating error. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A hierarchical tree of Gaussian splats (Shell and Solid nodes), each with a bounding sphere defined by center c, radius r, and a boundary bit flag. A virtual CSG probe defined by an implicit signed distance function (SDF) S(x), where S(x) < 0 is inside, S(x) > 0 is outside, and S(x) = 0 is the surface. The gradient 
abla S(x) provides the normal vector n. Output: A set of splats rendered with adaptive resolution and projected centers, forming the CSG intersection of the volume and the probe. Data Structures: Node: Contains bounding sphere parameters (c, r), a boolean isboundary flag, and child pointers. Boundary Bit Inheritance: The isboundary flag of a parent Solid node is the logical OR of the isboundary flags of its children. This ensures that nodes near the intersection curve are marked as boundary nodes, enabling adaptive resolution. Parameters: \deltar: Minimum allowed pixel splat size for regular internal nodes. \deltab: Minimum allowed pixel splat size for boundary nodes. Constraint: \deltar > \deltab \sim 1 pixel. This reduces silhouette appearance along the intersection curve caused by crossing/overlapping splats. Steps: 1. Probe Evaluation: For a node with bounding sphere center c and radius r, evaluate the SDF S(c) and its gradient 
abla S(c) to determine the signed shortest distance d to the probe surface and the inward-pointing normal n = - rac{
abla S(c)}{\|
abla S(c)\|}. The sign convention defines d as positive inside the probe. 2. CSG Culling of Solid: If the bounding sphere does not intersect the probe surface, discard the node and its subtree. If it intersects, traverse the subtree until the splat size reaches the minimum allowed size for the node type. Boundary nodes render at \deltab, while regular internal nodes render at \deltar. For all rendered Solid splats intersecting the probe, project the center to the probe surface using c{	ext{new}} = c - d \cdot n to prevent popping effects when resolution changes. 3. CSG Culling of Shell: If the bounding sphere is completely inside the probe, do not render the node or its children. If completely outside, disable CSG culling for the branch and render children only if they are leaf nodes or have splat size \le \deltar. If the bounding sphere intersects the probe surface, render the node if it is a leaf node or splat size \le \deltab; otherwise, traverse with CSG culling enabled. For boundary nodes intersecting the probe, offset the sphere center before rendering using c{	ext{new}} = c - (r + d) \cdot n to improve the outline and reduce silhouettes. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def rendersolid(node, probesdf, deltar, deltab): c, r = node.center, node.radius grad = probesdf.gradient(c) n = -grad / norm(grad) # Inward normal d = probesdf.value(c) # Signed distance (positive inside) if d > r or d < -r: return # Discard if sphere does not intersect probe surface minsize = deltab if node.isboundary else deltar if node.splatsize <= minsize: cproj = c - d n # Project center to probe surface # Standard Gaussian splat rasterization at cproj return for child in node.children: rendersolid(child, probesdf, deltar, deltab) def rendershell(node, probesdf, deltar, deltab): c, r = node.center, node.radius grad = probesdf.gradient(c) n = -grad / norm(grad) # Inward normal d = probesdf.value(c) # Signed distance (positive inside) if d > r: return # Completely inside probe: do not render if d < -r: # Completely outside: disable CSG culling for branch if node.isleaf or node.splatsize <= deltar: # Standard Gaussian splat rasterization at c pass for child in node.children: rendershell(child, probesdf, deltar, deltab) return # Intersecting probe surface if node.isleaf or node.splatsize <= deltab: cproj = c - (r + d) n if node.isboundary else c # Offset center for boundary nodes # Standard Gaussian splat rasterization at cproj return for child in node.children: rendershell(child, probesdf, deltar, deltab) Time Complexity: Linear in the number of visited nodes. Hierarchical culling reduces the number of splats processed near the intersection curve, and the overhead is described as insignificant because few Solid spheres lie exactly on the intersection curve. Memory Complexity: No additional memory beyond the existing tree structure and SDF evaluation stack. Strengths: Maintains real-time performance while providing smooth adaptive resolution at the CSG intersection, reducing popping and silhouette artifacts. Works with any implicit probe (plane, sphere, box, custom SDF). Limitations: Requires efficient SDF and gradient evaluation. Visual quality depends on the choice of \deltar and \deltab. When to use: Real-time medical visualization requiring sharp volumetric clipping and high fidelity at cut boundaries. When not to use: When the probe cannot be efficiently evaluated as an SDF, or when sharp volumetric clipping is not required. The method was introduced in the paper "TetSplat: Real-time Rendering and Volume Clipping of Large..." presented at the VIS 2004 conference. It was developed to address the limitations of binary clipping in Gaussian Splatting, aiming to maintain interactive frame rates while achieving high-quality volumetric editing and clipping. TetSplat: Real-time Rendering and Volume Clipping of Large... - Museth, https://ken.museth.org/Publicationsfiles/Museth-LombeydaVIS04.pdf, fetched 2026-10-28 (unofficial)

name: Mueller's Splatting Approach
head: Mueller splatting
body: Mueller's Splatting Approach is an object-order direct volume rendering technique that treats a gray-scale volume as a 3D discrete density function, where a convolution kernel defines how each sample contributes to points in space. It solves the computational cost of 3D convolution by pre-integrating the kernel along the viewing ray to create a 2D footprint table, which is then rasterized onto the screen. Unlike basic splatting which sums kernels within volume slices parallel to the viewing direction, Mueller's method aligns the processing slabs parallel to the image plane (image-aligned splatting), eliminating brightness variations and allowing variable interval distances. It builds on Splat Extent and Projection by using pre-computed 2D footprint lookups and leveraging texture mapping hardware for rasterization. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A 3D discrete density function f(s) where s=(xs, ys, zs) represents voxel centers and values. A radially symmetric reconstruction kernel h (e.g., Gaussian, Cone, Sinc, or Bilinear). Output: A 2D image composed of accumulated splat contributions. Data Structures: 1. Footprint Table: A 2D lookup table storing the analytically integrated kernel function along a traversing ray. The table resolution is much higher than the image plane resolution to ensure smoothness. Values outside the table extent are zero. 2. Sheet Buffer: A buffer aligned parallel to the image plane that accumulates contributions from voxels within a specific slab. 3. Occlusion Map: A dynamically constructed map used to cull invisible splats. Formulas: The contribution of a sample s to a point (x, y, z) in space is defined as: C(x, y, z) = h(x - xs, y - ys, z - zs) \cdot f(s) The contribution to an image plane pixel (x, y) is computed by integrating along the viewing ray (axis u parallel to the ray): C(x, y) = f(s) \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x - xs, y - ys, u) du The Footprint Function F(x, y) is defined as the integral part, which is independent of sample density and depends only on the projected location: F(x, y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} h(x - xs, y - ys, u) du Parameters: Reconstruction Filter: Choices include Cone, Gaussian, Sinc, or Bilinear functions. Gaussian kernels are commonly used for their anti-aliasing characteristics, though they introduce signal smoothing. Footprint Table Size: Small tables produce blocky images; large tables smooth details but require more memory. Sampling Method: Nearest-neighbor (fast, aliasing) or bilinear interpolation (smoother, slower) when generating the view-transformed footprint table. Steps: 1. Pre-compute Footprint Table: Evaluate the integral in Equation 2.22 on a grid with high resolution. For orthographic projection, only one footprint table is needed per view. 2. Depth Sorting: Traverse the list of object voxels in depth order. 3. Slab Processing (Image-Aligned): Group voxels into slabs of width \Delta s aligned parallel to the image plane. 4. Transformation: Transform each relevant voxel center into screen space. 5. Occlusion Culling: Index into the occlusion map to test for visibility. Note: Early splat elimination only culls invisible splats from rasterization; their transformation to screen space must still be performed to determine occlusion. 6. Rasterization: For each visible voxel: Calculate the screen-space coordinate of the projected grid point. Center the footprint around that point and stretch it according to the image magnification factor. Rasterize the footprint to the screen using the pre-integrated footprint table, multiplying indexed values by the voxel's value. Clip voxel kernels overlapping a slab to the slab and sum into a sheet buffer. 7. Composition: Composite the current sheet with the previous sheet using the Porter-Duff over operator. 8. Occlusion Map Update: Perform a convolution operation after each sheet-buffer composite to update the occlusion map, limited to buffer tiles that received splat contributions. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def muellersplatting(volumedata, kernel, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix, imagewidth, imageheight): # 1. Pre-compute the generic footprint table # F(x, y) = integral of h(x-xs, y-ys, u) du over u # Resolution should be higher than image plane resolution footprinttable = precomputefootprinttable(kernel) # 2. Initialize sheet buffer and occlusion map sheetbuffer = zeros((imagewidth, imageheight)) occlusionmap = zeros((imagewidth, imageheight)) # 3. Sort voxels by depth (z-coordinate in view space) sortedvoxels = sortvoxelsbydepth(volumedata, viewmatrix) # 4. Process voxels in slabs aligned with the image plane slabwidth = calculateslabwidth(volumedata, viewmatrix) currentslabz = mindepth(sortedvoxels) while currentslabz <= maxdepth(sortedvoxels): # Get voxels in the current slab slabvoxels = getvoxelsinslab(sortedvoxels, currentslabz, slabwidth) # Create a temporary buffer for the current slab's contributions slabcontribution = zeros((imagewidth, imageheight)) for voxel in slabvoxels: # Transform voxel center to screen space screenx, screeny = transformtoscreen(voxel.center, viewmatrix, projectionmatrix) # Check occlusion if isoccluded(screenx, screeny, occlusionmap): continue # Determine footprint extent and scale based on magnification footprintscale = getmagnificationfactor(voxel.center, viewmatrix) footprintextent = calculatefootprintextent(footprintscale) # Rasterize the footprint for dx, dy in getfootprintpixels(footprintextent): # Sample the pre-computed footprint table # Note: In practice, this involves interpolation (nearest or bilinear) weight = samplefootprinttable(footprinttable, dx, dy, footprintscale) # Calculate contribution contribution = weight voxel.value # Add to slab contribution slabcontribution[screenx + dx, screeny + dy] += contribution # Composite slab contribution into the main sheet buffer # Using Porter-Duff over operator sheetbuffer = compositeporterduff(slabcontribution, sheetbuffer) # Update occlusion map based on the new sheet buffer state # This requires a convolution operation limited to affected tiles updateocclusionmap(occlusionmap, slabcontribution) currentslabz += slabwidth return sheetbuffer Multi-texture Mapping Splatting is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that reduces the computational cost of depth sorting by segmenting the volume data into parallel texture slices along the primary viewing direction. Unlike standard object-order splatting which sorts all voxels globally, this method projects voxels onto local texture planes and blends them using graphics hardware, trading increased memory usage for reduced sorting complexity. It builds on Mueller's Splatting Approach by replacing 3D kernel evaluation with pre-computed 2D footprint lookups and leveraging texture mapping hardware for rasterization. Time Complexity: Generally faster than ray casting for large datasets due to cache coherency (sequential voxel traversal). However, it requires depth sorting and multiple passes for sheet composition. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for the footprint table and sheet buffers. Large footprint tables increase memory usage. Performance: Supports incremental rendering in back-to-front or front-to-back order. Only processes relevant voxels, reducing data processed and stored compared to ray casting. Strengths: Exploits cache coherency. Renders smooth surfaces without staircase artifacts. Replaces point sampling with sample averaging, introducing low-pass filtering that reduces aliasing (especially for isosurfaces and \Delta s > 1.0). Limitations: Generated images are blurred due to the spherically symmetric reconstruction kernel. Basic splatting suffers from "color bleeding" artifacts, which Mueller's image-aligned approach mitigates but does not entirely eliminate without further techniques (e.g., FreeVoxels). Axis-aligned sheet buffers (in basic splatting) introduce "popping" artifacts; Mueller's image-aligned approach reduces this but requires dynamic occlusion map updates. Early splat elimination saves rasterization cost but still requires transformation for occlusion testing. When to Use: When cache coherency is beneficial, smooth surfaces are desired, and incremental rendering is needed. Suitable for hardware acceleration via texture mapping. When Not to Use: When sharp object boundaries are required (ray casting with trilinear reconstruction is sharper). When memory is constrained and large footprint tables are prohibitive. Mueller's Splatting Approach was introduced by Mueller et al. as an improvement over Westover's original splatting method. Westover's method summed voxel kernels within volume slices most parallel to the viewing direction, which was prone to severe brightness variations in animated viewing and did not allow variable interval distances. Mueller's method, termed "image-aligned splatting," aligns the sheet buffers parallel to the image plane, eliminating these drawbacks. It was further accelerated with GPUs by Mueller et al.. The method is part of the broader object-order rendering family, which decomposes the volume into basis functions projected to the screen. name: Multi-texture Mapping Splatting
head: Accelerating splatting algorithm based on multi-texture mapping, Texture-mapped Splatting, Texture-mapped Splatting (Crawfis and Max, Yagel et al.)
body: Multi-texture Mapping Splatting is a hardware-accelerated volume rendering technique that reduces the computational cost of depth sorting by segmenting the volume data into parallel texture slices along the primary viewing direction. Unlike standard object-order splatting which sorts all voxels globally, this method projects voxels onto local texture planes and blends them using graphics hardware, trading increased memory usage for reduced sorting complexity. It builds on Mueller's Splatting Approach by replacing 3D kernel evaluation with pre-computed 2D footprint lookups and leveraging texture mapping hardware for rasterization. Inputs: Regular 3D volume dataset with density function \rho(x,y,z) and reconstruction kernel hv. Number of texture slices n. Viewing parameters (parallel projection assumed in source). Outputs: Final 2D image composed of blended texture slices. Data Structures: 1. Footprint Lookup Table: A 2D table storing values of the footprint function footprint(x,y). 2. Texture Slices: A set of n textures. Each texture point is in RGBA mode. The original alpha (\alpha) value of every point is zero. All slices are parallel to the view plane and have equivalent dimensions in the x and y directions. Steps: 1. Preprocessing: Compute the footprint function by integrating the 3D volume reconstruction kernel hv over the z-axis: footprint(x, y) = \int{-\infty}^{\infty} hv(x, y, z) \, dz Store the result in a lookup table to avoid excessive arithmetic during rendering. Map voxel values to colors and opacities using a probability statistic method. Transform voxels from object coordinates to the viewing coordinate system using a transformation matrix M: \begin{bmatrix} x' \\ y' \\ z' \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = M \times \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} 2. Dividing Volume Data: Segment the volume data into n regions (texture slices) along the primary viewing direction (z-axis). Let nk be the number of samples in slice k, such that \sum nk = n{total}. 3. Projecting Voxels: Traverse voxels in front-to-back order within each segmented region based on depth z. Voxels with the same z belong to the same layer. Project voxels directly onto the texture slice plane (not the screen plane) to avoid popping and splatting overlay artifacts. Calculate the contribution of a voxel i to a point (x, y) in the texture slice using the pre-computed footprint: Contributioni(x, y) = \rho(i) \int{-\infty}^{\infty} hv(ix - x, iy - y, z) \, dz This reduces the 3D kernel evaluation to a 2D footprint lookup. 4. Blending Texture Slices: Map the texture slices onto polygon surfaces in the scene using hardware texture mapping. Blend the textures in front-to-back order consistent with the voxel projection order. Use the over operator to combine colors and opacities from different layers: C{out} = C{in} \alpha{in} + C{now} \alpha{now} (1 - \alpha{in}) \alpha{out} = \alpha{in} + \alpha{now} (1 - \alpha{in}) Where C is color and \alpha is opacity. Parameters: n: The number of texture slices. Determines the granularity of division and the number of blending passes. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Popping/Overlay Artifacts: Occur if voxels are projected onto the screen plane instead of the texture slice plane. The method explicitly projects onto the texture slice plane to maintain correct depth ordering. Precision: The source notes that lookup tables avoid excessive arithmetic complexity. Time Complexity: The depth sorting complexity for the divided dataset is O(A) = \sum nk \log nk, where nk is the number of samples in slice k. This is strictly less than the complexity of sorting the whole dataset O(B) = n \log n, because \sum nk \log nk < \sum nk \log n = n \log n. Memory Complexity: Requires storage for n texture slices, each with RGBA components. The original alpha is zero, and dimensions are equivalent across slices. Strengths: Accelerates rendering by leveraging hardware-assisted texture mapping and reducing sorting complexity. Scaled volume datasets can be rendered effectively and fast without remarkable degradation in image quality. Limitations: Requires pre-computation of footprint tables and segmentation of data. The method described assumes parallel projection and regular data sets. When to use: When hardware-assisted rendering is available and sorting complexity is a bottleneck. The method was proposed in 2006 by researchers combining splatting with 2D texture mapping to accelerate footprint-based volume rendering. It builds on earlier hardware-assisted methods, such as those by Crawfis and Max, and Yagel et al., who used texture mapping hardware to render splats. The approach addresses the computational cost of 3D convolution by reducing it to 2D footprint lookups and hardware blending. name: Primitive Geometry
head: Splat Primitives, Geometric Splat Kernels
body: Primitive Geometry defines the specific 2D or 3D shapes used to represent volumetric data points as splats during object-order rendering. It solves the problem of how to approximate continuous volumetric fields or discrete geometric structures using rasterizable primitives that can be efficiently projected and composited. It differs from sibling methods by focusing on the topological and geometric definition of the primitive itself (e.g., circle, capsule, tetrahedron, brane) rather than the kernel function's mathematical falloff or the projection matrix mechanics. The family shares the fundamental mechanism of mapping a volumetric entity to a screen-space footprint via projection. All methods assume a camera model defined by a Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix or separate Model-View (MV) and Projection (P) matrices. The core workflow involves: 1. Transformation: Converting object-space coordinates to screen space. 2. Footprint Definition: Defining the spatial extent of the primitive in screen space (e.g., radius, bounding box, or parametric surface). 3. Rasterization/Compositing: Projecting the footprint onto the image buffer and accumulating color/opacity. Mathematically, for a primitive centered at \mathbf{p}, the screen-space contribution C(u,v) at pixel (u,v) is derived from a footprint function F and a color/opacity field I: C(u,v) = I \cdot F(\mathbf{p}{screen}, (u,v)) where F depends on the specific geometry (e.g., Gaussian for circles, distance-to-segment for capsules). Renders voxels as 2D quads with a fixed offset derived from splat size and grid scale. Chosen for simple, fast voxel visualization where square footprints approximate circular coverage. Renders line segments as rotationally symmetric capsules in screen space. Chosen for line-based volumetric data (e.g., streamlines) to maintain visual continuity without gaps using deficit-rule joints. Maps unstructured tetrahedral mesh elements to spherical or ellipsoidal splats. Chosen for real-time rendering of large, static unstructured meshes, leveraging hierarchical culling. Projects voxels as 2D footprints (squares or circles) composited into the image buffer. Chosen for interactive rendering of large regular volumetric datasets, trading geometric precision for performance. Converts volume into discrete primitives (spheres/slices) mapped by data values. Chosen when explicit discretization is preferred over direct ray casting, preserving continuous data nature through scaling. Approximates analytic splat kernels with discrete triangle meshes. Chosen to leverage standard graphics hardware rasterization pipelines for rapid scan conversion, trading geometric precision for speed. Uses 'Branes' (Gaussian-Hermite modes) to emit spatially varying colors. Chosen for arbitrary-scale super-resolution, modeling local contrast and sharp edges with fewer primitives than standard Gaussians. The concept of splatting originated in the early 1990s as a method for interactive volume rendering, replacing ray casting with object-order projection to improve performance. Early implementations focused on Gaussian kernels and voxel-based data. As rendering hardware evolved, the definition of "primitive" expanded from simple point sprites to complex geometric shapes like capsules for line data and tetrahedra for unstructured meshes. Recent developments incorporate neural networks to define expressive primitives like Branes for super-resolution. Unofficial notes on Primitive Geometry family methods. Unofficial notes on Voxel Splat Rendering parameters. Unofficial notes on Voxel Splat Rendering overview and compositing.

name: Circle Splat Rendering
body: Circle Splat Rendering is a volume rendering technique where volumetric entities (voxels) are projected as 2D quads in screen space. It solves the problem of efficiently rasterizing large datasets by mapping object-space coordinates to screen-space footprints via projection matrices. It is distinguished from sibling methods like Line Capsule Primitive and Tetrahedral Splatting by its use of fixed-offset square quads rather than parametric or complex geometric primitives. Inputs: Model-View matrix (MV) and Projection matrix (P). Voxel position in clip space (gl\in[0].gl\Position). Voxel color and normal attributes. Uniforms: splatSize (scalar), scale (entity scale), gridLength (grid scale), cullInvisibleFaces (boolean). Outputs: Triangle strip of 4 vertices representing the splat quad. Interpolated color and normal for fragment shading. Data Structures: The implementation uses a geometry shader stage. Input is a single point (representing a voxel center). Output is a trianglestrip with maxvertices = 4. Steps: 1. Transform to View Space: Multiply the input clip-space position by the Model-View matrix to get view-space coordinates. \mathbf{p}{view} = MV \cdot \mathbf{p}{clip\input} 2. Transform to Normalized Device Coordinates (NDC): Multiply by the Projection matrix and perform perspective division. \mathbf{p}{ndc} = \frac{P \cdot \mathbf{p}{view}}{w} 3. Calculate Voxel Offset: Compute the physical size of the splat in view space. \text{voxelOffset} = \text{splatSize} \times \frac{\text{scale}}{\text{gridLength}} \times \sqrt{2} Where \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414213. 4. Compute Clip-Space Half-Edge: Determine the distance in NDC from the center to the right edge midpoint to establish the splat's screen-space extent. \mathbf{p}{right\mid} = \frac{P \cdot (\mathbf{p}{view}.xy + \text{voxelOffset} \cdot [0.5, 0], \mathbf{p}{view}.zw)}{w} \text{halfEdge} = \text{distance}(\mathbf{p}{ndc}, \mathbf{p}{right\mid}) 5. Frustum Culling: Define a culling border slightly larger than the half-edge to prevent gaps. Discard the primitive if the NDC center exceeds this border. \text{border} = 1 + \text{halfEdge} If |\mathbf{p}{ndc}.x| > \text{border} or |\mathbf{p}{ndc}.y| > \text{border}, discard. 6. Back-Face Culling (Optional): If cullInvisibleFaces is true, compute the view-space normal and discard if facing away from the camera. \mathbf{n}{view} = MV \cdot [\mathbf{n}, 0] If \mathbf{n}{view} \cdot (\mathbf{0} - \mathbf{p}{view}) < 0, discard. 7. Emit Vertices: Generate four vertices for a triangle strip. The vertices are defined in view space using the offset, then transformed to clip space. Bottom-Left: \mathbf{p}{view} + [-0.5, -0.5] \cdot \text{voxelOffset} Bottom-Right: \mathbf{p}{view} + [0.5, -0.5] \cdot \text{voxelOffset} Top-Left: \mathbf{p}{view} + [-0.5, 0.5] \cdot \text{voxelOffset} Top-Right: \mathbf{p}{view} + [0.5, 0.5] \cdot \text{voxelOffset} Each vertex is transformed by P for glPosition. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def processsplat(voxelposclip, voxelcolor, voxelnormal, MV, P, splatsize, scale, gridlength, cullinvisiblefaces): # 1. Transform to View Space voxelposview = MV @ voxelposclip # 2. Transform to NDC voxelposndc = (P @ voxelposview) / voxelposview.w # 3. Calculate Voxel Offset voxeloffset = splatsize (scale / gridlength) 1.414213 # 4. Compute Clip-Space Half-Edge for Culling # Right edge midpoint in view space rightedgemidview = vec4(voxelposview.x + 0.5 voxeloffset, voxelposview.y, voxelposview.z, voxelposview.w) # Transform to NDC rightedgemidndc = (P @ rightedgemidview) / rightedgemidview.w halfedge = distance(voxelposndc, rightedgemidndc) frustumborder = 1.0 + halfedge # 5. Frustum Culling if abs(voxelposndc.x) > frustumborder or abs(voxelposndc.y) > frustumborder: return None # 6. Back-Face Culling if cullinvisiblefaces: normalview = MV @ vec4(voxelnormal, 0.0) viewdir = normalize(-voxelposview.xyz) if dot(normalview.xyz, viewdir) < 0: return None # 7. Emit Vertices vertices = [] offsets = [(-0.5, -0.5), (0.5, -0.5), (-0.5, 0.5), (0.5, 0.5)] texcoords = [(0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)] for i in range(4): ox, oy = offsets[i] # Define vertex in view space vview = vec4(voxelposview.x + ox voxeloffset, voxelposview.y + oy voxeloffset, voxelposview.z, voxelposview.w) # Transform to clip space vclip = P @ vview vertices.append((vclip, texcoords[i], voxelcolor, voxelnormal)) return vertices Complexity: O(1) per voxel for geometry generation. Memory: Minimal overhead; requires storage for MV/P matrices and uniform parameters. Strengths: Simple implementation; efficient rasterization via standard triangle strips; effective frustum culling. Limitations: Square footprints may alias or leave gaps between adjacent splats if not properly blended or if splatSize is not tuned to the grid resolution. This method is implemented in the svorenderer project, which uses a geometry shader to expand point primitives into square quads for volume visualization. mmalesadev/svorenderer, https://github.com/mmalesadev/svorenderer, fetched 2026-10-26 (unofficial)

name: Line Capsule Primitive
head: Geometry Primitives and Mesh Shading, Mesh Lighting and Materials
body: The Line Capsule Primitive is a geometric splatting method that renders line-based volumetric data as rotationally symmetric capsules in screen space. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like Circle Splat Rendering and Tetrahedral Splatting by explicitly modeling line segments as capsules with deficit-rule joints to maintain visual continuity without gaps or double brightness. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A set of line segments defined by endpoints in volume space, along with associated attributes (e.g., width, color, opacity). Output: A 2D image where lines are rendered as opaque or semi-transparent capsules, composited with other splats or background geometry. Data Structures: The primitive is defined by a line segment in 3D space. In screen space, it is represented as a capsule, which is the Minkowski sum of a line segment and a disk. Segment: Defined by two 3D vertices \mathbf{v}1, \mathbf{v}2. Capsule Profile: A rotationally symmetric function of the 2D point-to-segment distance in screen space. Joint Handling: Corners between segments are composed using a deficit rule to prevent double brightness or gaps. Steps: 1. Transformation: Transform line segment endpoints from volume space to screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. 2. Primitive Selection: Determine whether to render the line as a Capsule or a Screen-Space Quad based on the effective segment load. Calculate effective segment load: L = N{seg} \times W{max}, where N{seg} is the authored segment count and W{max} is the on-screen width of the widest segment at the opening framing. If L < 2,000,000, use the Capsule primitive. If L \ge 2,000,000, use the Screen-Space Quad primitive. This policy can be pinned to either primitive type if desired. 3. Rasterization (Capsule): Project the line segment into screen space, generate a rotationally symmetric footprint based on the 2D point-to-segment distance, and apply the deficit rule at joints to ensure correct brightness and no gaps. 4. Rasterization (Quad): Generate a screen-space quad covering the bounding box of the projected segment. 5. Compositing: Blend the capsule or quad contributions into the frame buffer. Formulas: Effective Segment Load: L = N{seg} \times W{max} Where: N{seg}: Authored segment count. W{max}: On-screen width of the widest segment at the opening framing. Capsule Footprint: The intensity profile I(x,y) at screen coordinates (x,y) is determined by the distance d from (x,y) to the projected line segment: I(x,y) = f(d(x,y)) Where d(x,y) is the 2D point-to-segment distance in screen space, and f is the rotationally symmetric profile function. Parameters: Effective Segment Load Threshold: 2,000,000. Joint Composition Rule: Deficit rule. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Near-Axial Cases: The capsule primitive matches or beats the exact volumetric primitive (closed-form convolution of a segment with a 3D Gaussian, integrated along the view ray) in visual comparisons, including near-axial cases. Volumetric Blending: The primitive refuses volumetric blending because a triangle or line has zero thickness, providing no path length for absorption. Additive Ladder: An additive ladder over arbitrary face order is refused because a prefix of such an order is a surface with holes, not a coarser surface. Pseudocode: Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderlinecapsule(segments, cameramatrix, threshold=2000000): # 1. Transform segments to screen space screensegments = [] for seg in segments: v1screen = projecttoscreen(seg.v1, cameramatrix) v2screen = projecttoscreen(seg.v2, cameramatrix) screensegments.append((v1screen, v2screen)) # 2. Calculate effective segment load nseg = len(screensegments) wmax = 0.0 for v1, v2 in screensegments: width = distance(v1, v2) if width > wmax: wmax = width effectiveload = nseg wmax # 3. Select primitive if effectiveload < threshold: primitivetype = "CAPSULE" else: primitivetype = "QUAD" # 4. Rasterize for v1, v2 in screensegments: if primitivetype == "CAPSULE": # Rasterize rotationally symmetric footprint based on 2D point-to-segment distance # Apply deficit rule at joints to prevent double brightness or gaps rasterizecapsulefootprint(v1, v2) else: # Rasterize screen-space quad covering bounding box of projected segment rasterizescreenquad(v1, v2) return framebuffer def projecttoscreen(vertex, cameramatrix): # Standard MVP projection: multiply vertex by camera matrix, divide by w projected = [sum(cameramatrix[i][j] vertex[j] for j in range(4)) for i in range(4)] return (projected[0] / projected[3], projected[1] / projected[3]) def distance(p1, p2): return ((p1[0] - p2[0])2 + (p1[1] - p2[1])2)0.5 def rasterizecapsulefootprint(v1, v2): # Compute 2D point-to-segment distance for each pixel in bounding box # Write intensity I(x,y) = f(d(x,y)) to framebuffer # Apply deficit rule at segment joints pass # Source does not provide exact rasterization implementation def rasterizescreenquad(v1, v2): # Compute bounding box of v1 and v2 # Fill quad with primitive color/opacity to framebuffer pass # Source does not provide exact rasterization implementation framebuffer = [] # Accumulated pixel values Streamline Rendering (Lines) visualizes vector fields by placing discrete geometric elements called strokes along streamlines, rather than drawing continuous lines, tubes, or ribbons. It is an automatic non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) approach designed to illustrate flow direction and field properties while avoiding the visual clutter and preprocessing costs associated with methods like Volume Line Integral Convolution (LIC). It distinguishes itself from sibling splatting methods by using discrete stroke geometry to encode directionality and field magnitude, often rendered in a separate pass or as opaque geometry prior to volume rendering. Renders text by mapping each character to a set of 2D line segments (strokes) in a 1x1 unit square, then transforming them to 3D space and drawing as capsules. Supports 6 orientations and cursor offset for spacing. Character stroke definitions are hardcoded as line segments in a 1x1 grid. The TextGeometry data structure contains size (float), thickness (float), pos (Vec3), orientation (enum), and text (string). TextOrientation is an enum with values POSZ, NEGZ, POSX, NEGX, POSY, NEGY, and default. The rendering loop initializes cursorOffset = 0.0f, iterates over each character c, converts to uppercase, maps 2D stroke coordinates (x1,y1) to (x2,y2) using an addLine lambda, applies scale s, offset cursorOffset, and orientation transform via mapCoords, creates CapsuleGeometry, calls drawCapsule, and increments cursorOffset += 1.5f. Performance: The capsule primitive is preferred over the exact volumetric primitive (closed-form convolution of a segment with a 3D Gaussian, integrated along the view ray) because it matched or beat it in blinded visual comparisons while costing 2.7–5x less than the screen-space quad per frame. Hardware Differences: The performance difference between capsule and quad primitives is 1.04–1.11x on Apple GPUs and ~1.5x on thin lines on discrete NVIDIA GPUs. Memory: Meshes (the only shaded geometry type in the same system) contribute no size padding to scene bounds and are loaded whole, not through a spatial index. Strengths: Efficient rasterization of line data; handles joints correctly without gaps or double brightness; supports physically based materials and transmission for meshes. Limitations: Cannot perform volumetric blending (absorption) due to zero thickness; additive ladder over arbitrary face order is not supported. The Line Capsule Primitive is part of the "Geometry primitives and mesh shading" system described in the Luxar viewer. It was developed to provide scalable interactive web visualization of multidimensional scientific data, specifically for microscopy and other fields requiring efficient rendering of line-based structures. The method was evaluated against exact volumetric primitives and screen-space quads, with the capsule primitive emerging as the preferred choice for most cases due to its balance of visual quality and performance. name: Streamline Rendering (Lines)
body: Streamline Rendering (Lines) visualizes vector fields by placing discrete geometric elements called strokes along streamlines, rather than drawing continuous lines, tubes, or ribbons. It is an automatic non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) approach designed to illustrate flow direction and field properties. It distinguishes itself from sibling splatting methods by using discrete stroke geometry to encode directionality and field magnitude, often rendered in a separate pass or as opaque geometry prior to volume rendering. The method generates streamlines from seed points and renders them as discrete strokes. The implementation typically utilizes OpenGL Vertex Buffer Objects (VBOs) to store the geometry and attributes of these strokes. Inputs: Vector field data, seed point locations, and user-defined parameters (stroke length, color mapping, density). Outputs: Rasterized image containing discrete strokes representing the flow field, composited with the underlying volume data. The geometry is stored in GPU memory using VBOs. The specific layout includes: mverticesVbo: An OpenGL GLARRAYBUFFER storing line vertices. Type: float3. Size: mlinesCount mmaxGeometrySamples sizeof(float3) bytes. mcolorsVbo: An OpenGL GLARRAYBUFFER storing line colors. Type: float3. Size: mlinesCount mmaxGeometrySamples sizeof(float3) bytes. 1. Seed Point Selection: Select seed points based on an enhancement criterion specified by the user to highlight regions of interest. 2. Streamline Tracing: Trace streamlines from the seed points through the vector field using traditional streamline tracing techniques. 3. Stroke Generation: Convert the traced streamlines into discrete strokes. 4. Attribute Assignment: Encode direction using a fading tail on the stroke. Map field properties (e.g., velocity magnitude) to the stroke color. 5. Rendering: Render the strokes as opaque, untextured geometry with the z-buffer enabled. This is done either prior to rendering the volume as textured polygons, or in an additional third pass. Stroke Length: Controls the trade-off between direction clarity and structural overview. Shorter strokes show direction information better; longer strokes reveal structural information better. Saturation and Brightness: Must be chosen carefully. High saturation/brightness in dense, intertwined color lines can obscure structural information. Seed Density: Interactive adjustment allows users to change the density of strokes to improve comprehension of the velocity field. Visual Clutter: Dense, intertwined color lines generally do not present structural information well. Preprocessing Cost: Related methods like Volume LIC have preprocessing costs that are too costly for interactive exploration, which is why traditional streamline tracing is chosen instead. Color Choice: Incorrect saturation and brightness levels can lead to poor visualization of the flow field structure. Unverified code. The code below did not pass a test run against a reference implementation, or no test fits it, so it may contain errors. def renderstreamlines(vectorfield, seedpoints, params): streamlines = [] for seed in seedpoints: points = [seed] current = seed for in range(params['maxsteps']): direction = vectorfield.sample(current) if direction.magnitude() == 0: break current = current + direction params['stepsize'] points.append(current) streamlines.append(points) vertices = [] colors = [] for line in streamlines: n = len(line) for i in range(n - 1): p0 = line[i] p1 = line[i+1] vertices.append(p0) vertices.append(p1) # Fading tail: alpha decreases from head (i=0) to tail (i=n-2) alpha = 1.0 - (i / max(n - 2, 1)) # Color by magnitude mag = vectorfield.magnitude(p0) r, g, b = params'colormap' colors.append((r, g, b, alpha)) gpuvertices = [0.0] (len(vertices) 3) gpucolors = [0.0] (len(colors) 4) for i, v in enumerate(vertices): gpuvertices[i3:i3+3] = [v.x, v.y, v.z] for i, c in enumerate(colors): gpucolors[i4:i4+4] = list(c) if params['renderorder'] == 'beforevolume': setdepthtest(enabled=True) drawlines(vertices=gpuvertices, colors=gpucolors) rendervolumeastexturedpolygons() elif params['renderorder'] == 'thirdpass': rendervolumeastexturedpolygons() setdepthtest(enabled=True) drawlines(vertices=gpuvertices, colors=gpucolors) def setdepthtest(enabled): # Standard graphics pipeline operation: glEnable(GLDEPTHTEST) if enabled else glDisable(GLDEPTHTEST) pass def drawlines(vertices, colors): # Standard graphics pipeline operation: bind buffers and call glDrawArrays(GLLINES,...) pass def rendervolumeastexturedpolygons(): # Standard graphics pipeline operation: render volume as textured polygons pass An automatic non-photorealistic rendering (NPR) approach for illustrating vector fields by placing discrete elements called strokes, rather than drawing lines, tubes, or ribbons. It sets itself apart by using discrete elements that can be styled (e.g., pencil drawing) and colored to indicate direction and magnitude. It is chosen when traditional flow visualization methods (lines, tubes) are avoided in favor of NPR styles, and when interactive exploration is needed to avoid the high preprocessing cost of Volume LIC. Time Complexity: Dependent on the number of seed points and the length of streamlines traced. Interactive exploration is possible because traditional streamline tracing avoids the high preprocessing cost of Volume LIC. Memory Complexity: Proportional to the number of strokes and their length, stored in VBOs (mverticesVbo, mcolorsVbo). Strengths: Allows interactive adjustment of density and viewing angle; provides clear direction indication via fading tails; can be composited with volume data. Limitations: Dense color lines can obscure structure; requires careful tuning of stroke length and color saturation/brightness. When to use: When illustrating vector fields with NPR style, requiring clear direction and magnitude information without the clutter of tubes/ribbons, and when interactive exploration is needed. When not to use: When high preprocessing cost is acceptable and LIC is preferred for texture-like visualization, or when structural information is more critical than direction (longer strokes may help, but dense lines still pose a risk). Streamline rendering using strokes was proposed as an alternative to conventional flow visualization methods (lines, tubes, ribbons) and Volume Line Integral Convolution (LIC). Volume LIC was deemed too costly for interactive exploration due to preprocessing requirements. The method was developed to allow selective placement of seed points based on user-specified enhancement criteria, improving comprehension of velocity fields through interactive adjustment of stroke density and viewing angle. It has been used in simultaneous visualization of vorticity fields (via volume rendering) and velocity fields (via stroke-based rendering). name: Tetrahedral Splatting
head: TetSplat
body: Tetrahedral Splatting is a point-based technique for the real-time rendering of large, static tetrahedral meshes by approximating each tetrahedron with a spherical or ellipsoid splat. It solves the performance bottleneck of exact tetrahedral volume integration by replacing complex geometric primitives with simple, screen-space footprint functions, utilizing hierarchical data structures for efficient culling. Unlike Voxel Splat Rendering, which relies on regular grid discretization, or Triangle Mesh Splatting, which projects surface boundaries, TetSplat operates directly on the volumetric tetrahedral elements, though it requires a preprocessing step that partitions the volume into shell and solid components. Inputs and Outputs: Input: A static, unstructured tetrahedral mesh representing a volumetric field (e.g., smoke). The mesh consists of vertices \mathbf{v}i and tetrahedra Tj. Output: A 2D image buffer with accumulated color and opacity. Data Structures: 1. Partitioned Mesh: The input mesh is partitioned into two sets: Shell: The non-convex boundary tetrahedra. Solid: The internal tetrahedra fragments. 2. Splat Representation: Each tetrahedron Tj is mapped to a single splat primitive. Spherical Splat: Defined by a center \mathbf{c}j and radius rj. Ellipsoid Splat: Defined by a center \mathbf{c}j and a 3 \times 3 covariance matrix \Sigmaj (or equivalent axis/rotation parameters). 3. Hierarchical Culling Structure: A spatial hierarchy (e.g., BVH or octree) built over the splats to enable efficient back-face and occlusion culling. Preprocessing (Static Assumption): 1. Degeneracy Removal: Identify and eliminate degenerated tetrahedra (needles, spindles, slivers, and caps) using edge collapse. These are removed because they are difficult to represent accurately with standard splat footprints. 2. Partitioning: Separate the remaining tetrahedra into the Shell and Solid sets. 3. Splat Generation: Compute the center \mathbf{c}j (e.g., centroid) and shape parameters (radius or covariance) for each tetrahedron. 4. Hierarchy Construction: Build the hierarchical data structure for culling. Rendering Steps: 1. Culling: Use the hierarchical structure to cull splats that are back-facing or occluded by previously rendered closer splats. 2. Projection: For each remaining splat, transform its center \mathbf{c}j and shape parameters into screen space using the Model-View-Projection (MVP) matrix. 3. Footprint Evaluation: For each pixel (u,v) within the screen-space bounding box of the splat, evaluate the footprint function F(u,v). For a spherical splat with screen-space radius R: F(u,v) = \max\left(0, 1 - \frac{(u - uc)^2 + (v - vc)^2}{R^2}\right) For an ellipsoid splat, the distance metric is modified by the projected covariance matrix. 4. Compositing: Accumulate the splat's contribution to the image buffer using alpha blending. Assuming the splat represents a density or color value Ij and opacity \alphaj: C{out}(u,v) = C{in}(u,v) + Ij \cdot F(u,v) \cdot \alphaj \cdot (1 - A{in}(u,v)) A{out}(u,v) = A{in}(u,v) + \alphaj \cdot F(u,v) \cdot (1 - A{in}(u,v)) where C is color, A is accumulated opacity, and (uc, vc) is the screen-space center. Parameters: Splat Shape: Spherical or Ellipsoid. Ellipsoids provide better coverage for elongated tetrahedra but are more computationally expensive to evaluate. Hierarchy Depth: Not given in the sources. Edge Cases and Pitfalls: Degenerate Tetrahedra: The method explicitly removes degenerate tetrahedra. This is a significant limitation for dynamic volumes like smoke, where topology must be maintained and tetrahedra naturally approach degenerate states during integration. Visible Gaps: Since each tetrahedron is represented by exactly one splat, small meshes or poorly adapted splat shapes (e.g., using spheres for highly irregular tetrahedra) result in visible gaps between splats, degrading visual quality. Static Mesh Requirement: The preprocessing step assumes a static mesh. The method is unsuitable for dynamic objects in its current implementation. This method partitions a large unstructured tetrahedral mesh into two distinct topological parts: the Shell (non-convex boundary) and the Solid (internal fragments). This separation allows the Shell to be rendered as a standard opaque surface mesh with vertex normals, while the Solid is rendered using normals derived from a Constructive Solid Geometry (CSG) probe, as interior tetrahedra are only visible at the intersection surface. Time Complexity: Rendering time is dominated by the number of visible splats and the cost of footprint evaluation per pixel. Hierarchical culling reduces the number of splats processed. Footprint evaluation is O(1) per pixel per splat. Memory Complexity: Linear in the number of tetrahedra N for storing splat parameters and the hierarchy. Measured Performance: Enables real-time rendering of large tetrahedral meshes. Strengths: High performance for static volumes; simple footprint functions allow efficient rasterization; hierarchical culling reduces overdraw. Limitations: Requires static meshes; preprocessing removes topological details (degenerate tetrahedra); single-splat-per-tetrahedron representation leads to visible gaps and loss of geometric fidelity; not suitable for dynamic smoke volumes where topology changes. When to use: Real-time visualization of large, static tetrahedral meshes where performance is critical and some geometric approximation is acceptable. When not to use: Dynamic volumes (e.g., smoke simulation), scenes requiring high geometric fidelity, or meshes with many degenerate elements that cannot be removed without altering topology. Tetrahedral Splatting (TetSplat) was introduced as a point-based technique for real-time rendering of large tetrahedral meshes. It addresses the limitations of exact volume integration methods by approximating volumetric primitives with splats. The method relies on a preprocessing step that partitions the volume and removes degenerate elements, making it suitable for static scenes.
